484295.title: Evaluating Stricter Radar-Based Criteria to Reduce False Alarms and Tornado Warnings in the U.S.
484295.authors: Tyson Smith, Gary K. Herberger Young Scholars Academy, Scottsdale, AZ
484295.abstract: In the United States, the tornado warning system has faced a 70% false alarm rate for decades. This creates false alarm fatigue in residents who live in tornado-prone areas, resulting in lower shelter rates as well as a lack of trust in the National Weather Service. Lowering the false alarm rate can save lives by bringing less fatigue, and improving shelter rates. My research question is if it's possible to lower the false alarm rate efficiently, while still stabilizing the missed event count at a low level. I hypothesize that if I tighten the criteria for tornado warnings, I could keep the amount of missed events low, because a majority of harmful tornadic storms are visible on radar. Instead of using the traditional warning method of issuing an alert whenever there are signs of possible rotation, I chose to focus on only warning when there is distinct and direct rotation visible on radar. After looking at 8 communities and 133 tornado warnings in communities devastated by tornadoes that killed 10+ people, my results showed that the average false alarm rate dropped by 49%, or to about 30% of its original value. For each additional missed event, there were 8.7 less false alarms. My research found that missed events are more statistically insignificant than previously realized. This is because a majority of missed events happen further away from weather radar because of the curvature of the earth. And since these radars are naturally placed in areas of higher population, those missed events happen further away large communities, impacting less people and causing less harm. These results have shown that it is possible to minimize the false alarm rate, while keeping missed events low, meaning that making the criteria stricter would be a significant benefit to millions of Americans. Deploying this system can save countless lives and billions of dollars in the long term, by sheltering less and using less resources on non-tornadic storms.

484388.title: An Atmospheric Scientist Dips His Foot in the Ocean, a Mentoring Experience in Oceanic Kelvin Waves
484388.authors: Paul E. Roundy, Univ. at Albany, Albany, NY
484388.abstract: The western and central Pacific creates an interface between atmospheric equatorial waves altered through their interactions with moisture and the mean flow that can favor the development of westerly wind bursts and subseasonal oceanic Kelvin waves during the initial stages of El Niño. George provided an ideal working situation together with a young scientist to dig in to understand how these events behave. We extracted the mooring data to identify the oceanic Kelvin wave signals and used approaches George had previously advanced for working with atmospheric waves. Finding the mooring data insufficient, we used the observed associations of these data with long historical records of sea level gauge data to reconstruct the oceanic Kelvin wave signals farther back in time. The results provide interesting contrast between how these Kelvin waves behave between different El Niño events. After a look at 1982, I will give a review of the same approaches comparing the present developing El Niño event to that of 1997.

484405.title: From Flood to Flow: HydroShield Panels for Urban Flood Resilience
484405.authors: Gonzalo Aranda, Southern Utah University, Cedar City, UT; Southern Utah University, Cedar City, UT; Southern Utah University, Cedar City, UT; and A. Tafur
484405.abstract: Flooding has become one of the fastest-growing natural hazards worldwide, affecting an estimated 1.47 billion people and causing billions of dollars in annual damage. Climate change, rapid urbanization, and inadequate infrastructure have increased both the frequency and severity of flood events, exposing vulnerable communities to recurring cycles of destruction and recovery. While most flood mitigation strategies focus on forecasting, drainage systems, levees, and emergency response, far less attention has been given to the resilience of the structures that directly experience floodwaters. This research investigates how hydrological principles can inform the development of flood-adaptive housing systems that reduce structural failure and long-term socioeconomic losses in high-risk regions. The study examines the interaction between flood dynamics and residential construction materials through an interdisciplinary review of hydrology, hydraulic engineering, materials science, and disaster resilience literature. Case studies from Peru, Brazil, India, Bangladesh, and the southern United States were analyzed to identify common patterns of housing damage associated with hydrostatic pressure, hydrodynamic loading, prolonged submersion, sediment transport, and debris impacts. Findings indicate that many conventional residential materials, including concrete, brick, drywall, untreated wood, and steel-reinforced systems, undergo significant degradation when exposed to sustained flooding, leading to recurring reconstruction costs and increased vulnerability. To address this challenge, the research proposes the conceptual development of the HydroShield System, a flood-resilient wall assembly designed using hydrologically informed performance criteria. Rather than focusing solely on structural strength, the design prioritizes resistance to key flood-related stressors identified in hydraulic modeling studies. The proposed system incorporates a fiberglass composite core, waterproof epoxy bonding agents, a flexible silicone membrane, and a hydrophobic exterior coating. Together, these components are intended to reduce water infiltration, resist corrosion, maintain structural integrity during extended submersion, and absorb impact forces generated by debris-laden floodwaters. Hydrological analysis played a central role in defining system requirements. Floodwaters exert both hydrostatic and hydrodynamic forces that increase with water depth and flow velocity. Studies indicate that even one meter of water can impose more than 1,000 pounds of lateral force on a wall surface, while sediment-rich flows can transform transported debris into repetitive impact hazards. The HydroShield concept was therefore evaluated through theoretical performance modeling under scenarios involving prolonged inundation, high-velocity surface flows, repeated debris impacts, and freshwater-to-saltwater exposure transitions. Results suggest that composite-based systems may provide superior resistance to water-induced deterioration compared with traditional materials while maintaining performance across diverse flood environments. Beyond structural performance, the research evaluates the economic and social implications of resilient housing adaptation. Preliminary modeling suggests that flood-resistant construction systems could significantly reduce reconstruction frequency, lower long-term maintenance costs, and increase housing lifespan in vulnerable communities. The modular design framework further supports implementation through local manufacturing, scalable production, simplified transportation, and community-based installation programs. These characteristics are particularly relevant for low-income regions where repeated flood losses create persistent barriers to economic recovery and development. The study also recognizes that resilience extends beyond physical infrastructure. Housing loss is associated with displacement, psychological stress, educational disruption, and long-term reductions in community stability. Consequently, improving flood resilience at the household level may generate benefits that extend beyond engineering metrics alone, contributing to greater social and economic sustainability in flood-prone regions. Although the HydroShield System remains a conceptual model requiring experimental validation, prototype testing, and computational fluid dynamics simulations, this research demonstrates the value of integrating hydrological risk assessment with material innovation. The findings support a broader shift in flood management philosophy from rebuilding after disaster toward designing infrastructure capable of enduring increasingly severe hydrological events. As global flood risk continues to rise, adaptation strategies must evolve accordingly. By combining hydrological understanding with resilient construction design, communities may be able to move beyond repetitive recovery cycles and toward a future where homes remain standing even when waters rise. This research proposes that effective flood resilience begins not after the flood has passed, but before the first drop of water arrives.

484407.title: A Comparison of the April 25 through 28, 2011 Super Tornado Outbreak, the February 5 and 6, 2008 Super Tuesday Tornado Outbreak, and the March 17 through 18, 1925 Tri-State Tornado Outbreak
484407.authors: Caitlin J. Lawrence, USA Weather, Inc, Carmichaels, PA
484407.abstract: This research will compare the April 25 through 28, 2011 Super Tornado Outbreak, the February 5 and 6, 2008 Super Tuesday Tornado Outbreak, and the March 17 through 18, 1925 Tri-State Tornado Outbreak to gain A better understanding of the meteorological factors that led to the varying numbers of tornadoes that occurred over time, the tornado longevities, and the strengthening and weakening of the tornadoes during their lifecycles throughout these outbreaks to examine similarities and differences between the outbreaks to discover the favored atmospheric scenarios that contributed the most and least to these events to increase severe forecasting skills among meteorologists that will help lead to understanding key weather features that lead to these events ahead of time to help meteorologists keep the public safe and informed

484417.title: George's Special Sauce: Seeing the Right Scale for Wave-Convection Interactions
484417.authors: Brian E. Mapes, RSMAS, Miami, FL
484417.abstract: Internal waves and convection are distinct: for instance, vertical heat flux [w'T'] is zero for waves, yet a defining raison d'etre for convection. But buried in those deceptively simple primes and brackets is the problem of scale. The assigning of parcels vs environments, in its simplest form. The attribution of "convection" to measureables, not theoretical concepts like "parcels", in practical form. George was a model of grace and honour in crediting Yukari Takayabu with finding the firm ground of a robustly measurable phenomenology, which he carried to new heights with Matt Wheeler. Scale separation was the key: seeking synoptic-scale waves, so much larger than the convection that the interaction is tractable to study. I myself was lost in the weeds of the mesoscales, which are both wave-mediated and convecting in and of themselves. Thanks to George's pathbreaking and then sustained drumbeat of research and dissemination, the question of wave-convection interactions has been transformed from a speculative-seeming dynamical obscurity to a pillar of tropical meteorology, a textbook topic for the next generations to keep advancing. This history seems ripe for a celebration at the Kiladis Symposium, with enough facets that several speakers could usefully illuminate them in a coordinated way.

484426.title: Leading to Lift Up Others: Lessons Learned from Leading NOAA During Turbulent Times
484426.authors: Timothy C Gallaudet, Former NOAA Administrator, Annapolis, MD
484426.abstract: After serving for three decades as an oceanographer in the US Navy, Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet was appointed to lead the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) during the first Trump administration. While serving with NOAA, Gallaudet developed a signature leadership philosophy that was focused on empowering federal employees, supporting their development, and lifting them up. He describes this approach in his memoir Holding Fast in Heavy Seas: Leadership for Turbulent Times, which was published by Koehler Books in July. Finding himself caught up in the "Sharpiegate" incident and other frustrating events caused Gallaudet to wonder if remaining in office was worth the effort, but his decision to hold fast and lead with empathy and humility kept NOAA on an even keel despite the often stormy environment. He applied the lessons from his life and military service to provide positive servant leadership to NOAA, defying the odds and boosting morale and employee satisfaction to record levels. Drawing from both career accomplishment and personal tragedy, Gallaudet’s leadership philosophy enabled him to connect with employees at every level, making them feel valued and respected. Holding Fast in Heavy Seas provides an inspiring playbook for people of any calling who aspire to improve in their ability to positively influence others and cultivate a talented and engaged workforce across sectors, career stages, and experiences.

484522.title: The Recipe Matters More Than the Kitchen:Mathematical Foundations of the AI Weather Prediction Pipeline
484522.authors: Piyush Garg, RWE Trading Americas Inc., Bellevue, WA; and D. R. Gergel, A. E. Shao, and G. Yacalis
484522.abstract: Architecturally diverse artificial intelligence (AI) weather models now achieve broadly comparable medium-range forecast skill. Spherical Fourier Neural Operators, graph neural networks, vision transformers, and latent diffusion transformers all produce competitive forecasts when properly trained, despite fundamentally different mathematical properties: spectral versus spatial representations, global versus local receptive fields, and deterministic versus generative inference. This convergence poses a direct challenge to how the community tests, scores, and compares these models. Standard verification with root-mean-square error (RMSE) and the anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC) ranks models that are statistically near-indistinguishable, rewards physically unrealistic smoothing, and offers no diagnosis of why a model succeeds or fails. This work addresses the session's central question, what metrics and validation frameworks are appropriate for AI-based numerical weather prediction, by presenting both a holistic evaluation framework and a mathematical theory that explains what that framework measures. We evaluate ten state-of-the-art AI weather models (AIFS, AIFS-ENS, Atlas, Aurora, FourCastNet 3, FengWu, FuXi, GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and SFNO) spanning five architecture families and four loss-function categories. All models are run under a unified inference protocol using NVIDIA Earth2Studio and verified against ERA5 across thirty seasonally diverse initialization dates, adopting WeatherBench2's verification standard and latitude-weighting conventions. Rather than re-establishing AI-versus-NWP comparisons documented elsewhere, we deliberately construct an AI-only intercomparison designed to isolate the contribution of the learning pipeline, the combination of loss function, training strategy, and data distribution, from that of the model architecture. The framework scores each model across six diagnostic dimensions that go well beyond single-number verification. Spectral fidelity measures the retention of high-wavenumber energy relative to ERA5, capturing the blurring that RMSE actively rewards. Physical consistency evaluates whether forecasts respect geostrophic balance, non-divergence, thermal-wind, and hydrostatic relationships. Error growth and predictability-horizon diagnostics characterize the lead-time evolution of skill and its doubling time. Extreme-event skill quantifies forecast bias during record-breaking conditions. Inter-model consensus, through a new Error Consensus Ratio, separates error that is shared across all architectures from error that is model-specific. These dimensions are synthesized into a single Holistic Model Assessment Score (HMAS), and we show how established physics-based verification metrics can be adapted into rigorous, AI-relevant diagnostics rather than discarded. Underpinning the diagnostics is a unified mathematical framework with three results that make the evaluation predictive rather than merely descriptive. First, a Loss-Induced Spectral Bias theorem proves, in spherical-harmonic coordinates, that any MSE-trained model must converge toward the conditional mean and therefore systematically lose high-wavenumber spectral energy, with a deficit equal to the conditionally unpredictable variance at each scale. Empirically, all seven MSE-trained models in our set exhibit exactly this universal high-wavenumber spectral collapse, while non-MSE models (trained with CRPS or score-matching objectives) are immune, a clean confirmation that the dominant spectral defect is a property of the loss, not the architecture. Second, a Pipeline Error Decomposition separates forecast error into architecture (approximation) and loss, data, and training (estimation) contributions, and shows that estimation error dominates at current operational grid scales. Third, an Out-of-Distribution Bound predicts linear growth of forecast bias with the margin by which an event exceeds the training-data record; we observe this linear bias–exceedance relationship empirically, with cold extremes attenuated more strongly than warm extremes. These theoretical and empirical results converge on a single conclusion with direct implications for testing and validation: the learning pipeline, not the architecture, dominates the determination of forecast skill. Three independent lines of evidence support this. The universal spectral collapse is predicted to be loss-induced and observed only in MSE-trained models. The Error Consensus Ratio rises from approximately 0.50 at day 1 to above 0.60 by day 8, demonstrating that most error variance is shared across architecturally distinct models and reflects the atmosphere's intrinsic predictability limit rather than architecture-specific failure. And intra-family variation in extreme-event attenuation spans the full inter-model range, meaning two models sharing an architecture can differ as much as models from different families, with the difference traceable to pipeline choices. For a testing-and-validation audience, the practical consequence is that architecture-leaderboard rankings measure largely shared, predictability-limited error and obscure the pipeline factors that actually separate models; evaluation protocols must be designed accordingly. Finally, we extend Pareto-optimal model hierarchies into a prescriptive Pipeline Pareto Surface, accompanied by a Spectral Feasibility Score that bounds achievable forecast quality from training-data climatology before a model is trained. This reframes evaluation as a tool not only for ranking finished models but for screening proposed pipelines in advance, identifying when a loss function or data strategy imposes a ceiling on attainable skill regardless of architecture or compute. The complete six-dimensional framework is released as an open-source benchmarking package built on Earth2Studio, providing reproducible, physically grounded diagnostics that any modeling center can apply to its own systems. We present this work as a contribution to testing frameworks, evaluation metrics, and validation techniques for AI-driven weather prediction. Its core message for the AI4NWP community is that rigorous evaluation of these models requires diagnostics tied to atmospheric physics and predictability theory, not pixel-wise error alone, and that such diagnostics can be both mathematically principled and operationally practical. By coupling a holistic scoring framework to a theory that predicts what each metric will reveal, the work offers a path toward standardized, interpretable, and forward-looking validation standards for the rapidly expanding ecosystem of operational AI weather models.

484532.title: Cyclone Ditwah (2025): Moderate Winds, Exceptional Rainfall, Extreme Impacts
484532.authors: Sai Kulkarni, Loughborough University, Department of Geography and Environment, Loughborough, LEC, United kingdom; and J. Hillier
484532.abstract: Cyclone Ditwah made landfall in Sri Lanka in 2025, as a moderate-intensity tropical cyclone, with peak sustained winds of approximately 65-75 km h⁻¹. Despite its relatively weak wind field, the system produced extreme and prolonged rainfall, resulting in record flooding and landslides across Sri Lanka and southern India. The combined impacts were severe, with total economic losses estimated at ~USD 4.1 billion and substantial human and infrastructure disruption. The present study integrates best-track data (IBTrACS), ERA5 reanalysis, and satellite-derived rainfall (CHIRPS) to examine the relationship between cyclone intensity, rainfall distribution, and impacts across the North Indian Ocean (2022–2025). Results show that peak wind speed is a poor predictor of cumulative rainfall (R² = 0.02, p > 0.05), highlighting the decoupling between wind intensity and hydrological hazard. Ditwah produced disproportionately high rainfall relative to other higher-intensity cyclones, driven by slow translational speed, sustained moisture convergence, and orographic enhancement over southern India and Sri Lanka. Comparison with recent regional events further demonstrates that moderate cyclones can generate the highest societal losses when rainfall-driven hazards dominate. The event underscores the importance of compound hazard interactions, particularly flooding and landslides, in controlling cyclone impacts. Despite advances in forecasting and warning dissemination, current systems remain largely wind-centric and do not fully integrate cascading multi-hazard risk. These findings highlight the need for impact-based, multi-hazard early warning frameworks that explicitly incorporate rainfall, translational speed, and secondary hazards to better represent cyclone risk in South Asia.

484601.title: Evaluating Meteorological and Radar Conditions of High-Impact Flash Flooding in the Southwest U.S.
484601.authors: Jenny Arredondo, NWS, Tempe, AZ; University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. Trampp, I. Smith, and J. Estupinan
484601.abstract: Flash flooding is among the most lethal weather hazards in the Southwest U.S., where rugged terrain and impermeable surfaces convert intense rainfall into rapid, life-threatening runoff. During the North American Monsoon (NAM), rapid runoff frequently inundates low-water crossings and developed areas, causing significant to catastrophic impacts to life and property. A major operational challenge for forecasters is distinguishing among base, considerable, or catastrophic flood-impact categories during rapidly evolving events. This classification is often hindered by sparse surface observations and the rapid nature of desert hydrologic responses in many parts of the NOAA/NWS Phoenix Weather Forecast Office’s (PSR) County Warning Area (CWA). This project evaluates the synoptic and mesoscale meteorological conditions associated with PSR’s most significant flood events, with an emphasis on considerable and catastrophic impacts. Additionally, the study analyzes storm-scale radar characteristics, specifically the spatial and temporal evolution of cellular convection, and their relationship to downstream flood impacts. Radar-derived quantitative precipitation estimates (QPE) are overlaid on Flash Flood Monitoring and Prediction (FFMP) basin boundaries to characterize rainfall accumulation, peak rate, duration, coverage, and placement over affected basins. The scope includes monsoon events and transitional or tropical systems extending into October. Radar-derived rainfall characteristics are compared across historical events of varying impact severity using exploratory statistical and machine-learning methods. The goal is to provide forecasters with enhanced diagnostic patterns and empirical rainfall signals to improve decision-making, increase lead times, and better communicate the severity of high-impact flash flood events.

484655.title: Earth Intelligence From Space: A Physics-Aware AI Framework for Satellite Remote Sensing
484655.authors: Jonathan H. Jiang, Jet Propulsion Laboratory (Retired); University of California, Los Angeles, Pasadena, CA
484655.abstract: Satellite remote sensing has evolved from spaceborne imaging into a quantitative observing system for the coupled Earth system. This study synthesizes advances in physical remote sensing, climate-process observations, model evaluation, scientific machine learning, and emerging digital-twin infrastructure. I argue that the next era should be defined not by more pixels alone, but by Earth-system intelligence: information that is physically interpretable, uncertainty-aware, comparable with models, and useful for understanding and decision-making. The study develops a radiance-to-decision framework linking spectral physics, forward models, optimal-estimation retrieval, cloud and radiation diagnostics, observation operators, physics-aware artificial intelligence (AI), and adaptive observing. Recent missions such as PACE, EarthCARE, and NISAR, together with open data systems, satellite simulators, foundation models, and digital-twin initiatives, show that many components of this vision already exist. The challenge is to connect them without losing calibration traceability, process understanding, or uncertainty. The core recommendation is that AI for satellite remote sensing should be trained and evaluated not only on data fit, but also on physical consistency, uncertainty calibration, domain robustness, and model comparability. Such a framework can help transform satellite observations from products into trustworthy climate evidence and, ultimately, actionable Earth-system intelligence.

484664.title: Future Projection of the East Asian Summertime Subtropical Intraseasonal Oscillations Under Global Warming
484664.authors: Ken-Chung Ko, National Kaohsiung Normal Univ., Kaohsiung, Taiwan
484664.abstract: The future and present simulations of the High Resolution Atmospheric Model (HiRAM) has been adopted to examine future changes of the summertime intraseasonal oscillation (ISO) in the East Asian monsoon region during July-September from 1979 to 2008. The NCEP re-analyses have been used to compared with the model simulations. The ISO is successfully simulated in the HiRAM present run. In the future simulation, the ISO weakens and TCs also decrease. However, more TCs with higher-intensity can be expected in the westerly ISO of the future simulation. It is therefore suspected that the future ISO, though less active, will create favorable conditions for higher-intensity TCs to form in the westerly phase. These insights can be useful for evaluating how the ISO changes under global warming.

484665.title: Statistical Quantification of the Orientation and Cross-Roll Wavelength of Horizontal Convective Rolls
484665.authors: Garett R.T Warner, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and Y. Pan and D. J. Stensrud
484665.abstract: Horizontal convective rolls (HCRs) are elongated, counter-rotating circulations in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL). Accurately quantifying their orientation and cross-roll wavelength is essential for evaluating simulations against observations, testing theoretical models, and improving ABL parameterizations. To quantify these HCR properties in an evolving environment, we evaluate, refine, and combine statistical methods that analyze large-eddy simulation (LES) snapshots or radar scans. Three methods are considered: i) the primary mode of two-dimensional (2D) Fourier analysis, ii) the volume flux ratio (VFR), a simplified version of the mass flux ratio (MFR), and iii) autocorrelation fields, with a newly developed automated algorithm to eliminate visual inspection. Statistical results are evaluated against two LES cases: i) updraft bands with known orientation and wavelength enforced by heterogeneous surface heating, and ii) narrow-mode HCRs over a homogeneous surface. The primary Fourier mode captures overall roll orientation well but can misidentify cross-roll wavelength, showing that the primary spectral mode does not always match the quasi-linear structure of interest. VFR provides satisfactory estimates of overall roll orientation. The major axes of center autocorrelation contours provide satisfactory estimates of overall roll orientation, but only when these axes span sufficient along-roll distance. Given a satisfactory orientation estimate, an automated algorithm that analyzes the autocorrelation field successfully reproduces expected cross-roll wavelengths. An advantage of analyzing autocorrelation fields is the applicability to operational radar scans of scalar fields at fixed elevation angles. An example operational radar scan is analyzed to show the importance of noise-reduction strategies for obtaining the expected roll orientation and cross-roll wavelength. Being an automated algorithm, this method can be easily applied to a subdomain of LES results or radar scans to investigate localized or spatially evolving HCRs and may also be used to quantify the orientation and wavelength of other quasi-linear structures like surface-layer streaks, nighttime canopy waves, and Langmuir cells in water bodies.

484669.title: Improving Seasonal Precipitation Forecast Skill by Combining WR-GMM and Numerical Weather Prediction
484669.authors: Jihun Ryu, Utah State University, Logan, UT; and C. Ratterman, B. Vernon, D. C. Collins, M. Rosencrans, and W. Zhang
484669.abstract: Improving the skill of seasonal precipitation forecasts remains a critical challenge. To address this challenge, we develop an extended Weather Regime–Gaussian Mixture Model (exWR-GMM) framework that combines large-scale circulation information with operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts. The exWR-GMM framework characterizes dominant atmospheric circulation regimes by applying Gaussian Mixture Models to 500-hPa geopotential height fields. Regime-specific precipitation patterns are then reconstructed and integrated with the original NWP precipitation forecasts through a skill-based blending procedure. This approach is designed to leverage both the dynamical forecast information in NWP systems and the observed statistical relationships between circulation regimes and precipitation variability. We apply the framework to four operational seasonal forecasting systems, including CFSv2, ECMWF, ECCC, and JMA, and evaluated forecast performance over the Contiguous United States. Both deterministic metrics and probabilistic tercile-based verification measures are used to assess forecast performance across lead times from one to four months. Results indicate that exWR-GMM consistently enhances precipitation forecast skill relative to the original model forecasts. Improvements are evident in both deterministic and probabilistic verification metrics and generally become larger with increasing lead time. The consistent performance across multiple forecasting systems demonstrates the robustness and transferability of the framework. These results suggest that circulation-informed statistical–dynamical blending offers a practical pathway for improving operational seasonal precipitation prediction. A web-based platform is currently under development to provide public access to exWR-GMM forecast products.

484761.title: Automation of Tropospheric Doppler Radar Wind Profiler (TDRWP) Data Quality Control Utilizing a Neural Network Software
484761.authors: Corey Dale Walker, Amentum Space Exploration Division, Huntsville, AL
484761.abstract: Aerospace vehicles transiting the 6–17 km region of the atmosphere experience maximum aerodynamic stress and loads. In this altitude band, the combination of vehicle velocity and atmospheric density contributes to a region of maximum dynamic pressure, posing significant structural risks during vehicle ascent. To mitigate these wind load risks for space vehicles launching from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA’s) Kennedy Space Center (KSC) collocated on the United States Space Force’s (USSF’s) Eastern Range (ER) at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center Natural Environments (MSFC NE) Branch utilizes the Tropospheric Doppler Radar Wind Profiler (TDRWP) during simulated and actual days of launch to assess the winds and provide safety assessments for GO / NO GO decision making. Additionally, MSFC NE provides databases including from the TDRWP to engineering teams for aerodynamic modeling. These databases have been screened using a manual quality control (MQC) process as part of generating archives for downstream vehicle analyses. However, this legacy MQC process has historically presented limitations based on the required time and labor input. This presentation outlines the MQC process, identifies its primary deficiencies, and details the development of an improved automation. The software utilizes server scripts ran daily to pull TDRWP data from KSC servers, processes the data using a neural network, and then pushes the outputs to a shared drive at MSFC NE to be utilized by analysts on demand. By modernizing the data evaluation process to reduce labor-intensive steps, the software resolves previous man-power issues and enables the continuous, reliable archival of QC-processed TDRWP data, ultimately enhancing launch vehicle safety assessments and atmospheric analyses by providing input databases in less time.

484769.title: Understanding and Predicting El Niño: Tony Busalacchi’s Legacy to Climate Science
484769.authors: Michael J. McPhaden, PMEL, Seattle, WA
484769.abstract: Many seasonal climate forecast models predict that an El Niño rivaling some of the strongest on record will develop in 2026. If it materializes, it will be accompanied by far-reaching climate impacts, increasing the probability of severe droughts, heavy rainfall, damaging floods, persistent heatwaves, and extreme weather worldwide. Today, skillful El Niño forecasts provide a the opportunity to prepare for and mitigate these harmful consequences on society, the environment, and the biosphere. Research and development efforts over the past half century that have greatly advanced our ability to observe, understand, and predict El Niño and its widespread impacts on human and natural systems. As an enterprising oceanography graduate student at Florida State University in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Tony Busalacchi led pioneering studies of wind-forced ocean circulation related to El Niño. These foundational studies—and his subsequent modeling and observational work focused on spaceborne measurements at NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center and the University of Maryland—laid the groundwork for community-wide progress in understanding the key processes driving the development and predictability of El Niño/Southern Oscillation (ENSO) variations. These accomplishments represent just one chapter of Tony’s storied career, which encompasses wide-ranging research in global climate and an extraordinary record of scientific leadership. This presentation will describe the development and impacts of the 2026–27 El Niño, using it as a framework to highlight Tony’s groundbreaking research on ENSO and his enduring contributions to the scientific community.

484842.title: Flood Detection and Mapping in a Caribbean Small Island State: A Comparison of COSMO-SkyMed and Sentinel-1 SAR
484842.authors: Deanesh Ramsewak, The University of Trinidad and Tobago, CARENAGE, Chaguaramas, Trinidad and Tobago; and J. Takami, B. Edwards, and M. Codling
484842.abstract: Extreme rainfall events are becoming increasingly frequent and intense across the Caribbean, posing significant challenges for flood monitoring and disaster response in Small Island Developing States (SIDS). Conventional optical satellite imagery is often unsuitable for rapid flood assessment because persistent cloud cover commonly accompanies major storm events. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), with its ability to acquire imagery independent of daylight and weather conditions, provides an effective alternative for operational flood mapping. While the freely available Sentinel-1 mission has become the global standard for satellite-based flood monitoring, higher-resolution commercial SAR systems such as COSMO-SkyMed may offer additional benefits for mapping inundation in complex tropical landscapes and densely developed urban environments. However, comparative assessments of these sensors within Caribbean SIDS remain limited. This study looks at the performance of Sentinel-1 and COSMO-SkyMed SAR imagery for mapping the widespread flooding that affected the island of Trinidad in the south eastern Caribbean following an extreme rainfall event in October 2018. The event resulted in extensive inundation of communities, transportation infrastructure, and agricultural lands, particularly within the low-lying Caroni River floodplain. The primary objectives were to (1) delineate flood extent using each SAR dataset, (2) compare the spatial characteristics of the resulting flood maps, and (3) assess the relative advantages of each sensor for operational flood mapping within a Caribbean SIDS context. All image processing and analysis were conducted using Google Earth Engine, providing a cloud-based environment capable of supporting rapid and reproducible SAR workflows. Standard SAR pre-processing procedures, including radiometric calibration and image enhancement, were applied prior to flood extraction. Water bodies were identified using radar backscatter characteristics associated with inundated surfaces, and flood extent maps were generated for each sensor. OpenStreetMap building data and ancillary spatial information were incorporated to support visual interpretation of inundated developed areas and facilitate comparison between the two datasets. Both Sentinel-1 and COSMO-SkyMed successfully identified the principal flood-affected areas associated with the October 2018 event, including extensive inundation throughout the Caroni River basin and surrounding floodplain. The comparison demonstrates that although both sensors effectively captured the overall spatial distribution of flooding, notable differences were observed in the level of detail and mapped flood extent. The higher spatial resolution of COSMO-SkyMed enabled improved delineation of flood boundaries and greater representation of localized inundation, particularly within heterogeneous urban and peri-urban environments. In contrast, Sentinel-1 produced smoother and more generalized flood polygons, reflecting its coarser spatial resolution. Additionally, the difference in acquisition timing relative to flood evolution meant that the COSMO-SkyMed image captured more of the peak flood coverage than the Sentinel-1 image. Despite these differences, Sentinel-1 provides reliable regional-scale flood mapping while offering the significant advantages of open access, regular revisit frequency, and global coverage. The findings highlight the complementary nature of commercial high-resolution SAR and freely available Sentinel-1 observations for flood monitoring. COSMO-SkyMed offers considerable value where detailed mapping of urban flooding, infrastructure impacts, or post-disaster damage assessment is required, whereas Sentinel-1 remains highly suitable for routine operational monitoring and regional disaster response because of its accessibility and acquisition frequency. Integrating multiple SAR platforms within cloud computing environments such as Google Earth Engine has the potential to significantly strengthen national flood mapping capabilities, particularly in data-limited Caribbean SIDS where timely situational awareness is essential for emergency management. This research demonstrates the applicability of operational SAR-based flood mapping workflows for tropical island environments and contributes to the growing use of Earth observation technologies in support of hydrological hazard assessment, disaster risk reduction, and climate resilience. The methodology is readily transferable to other Caribbean islands and provides a foundation for developing near-real-time flood monitoring systems that support evidence-based decision-making before, during, and after extreme hydrometeorological events. Keywords: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR); Flood Mapping; Small Island Developing States (SIDS), Trinidad

484850.title: When Disaster Doesn't Follow the Script: Lessons Learned from an Electrical Fire
484850.authors: Maureen McCann, Spectrum News 13, Orlando, FL; and Z. Covey and B. Karrick
484850.abstract: In Florida, we spend countless hours preparing for hurricanes, but real-world disasters don’t always arrive as expected. This presentation explores how an annual hurricane preparedness exercise unexpectedly became the foundation for responding to a power outage and subsequent electrical fire that forced the evacuation of our workplace just days before Christmas. With employees suddenly displaced to a back-up location two hours away, our team relied on the planning, communication, continuity, and adaptability skills developed through years of hurricane drills. Attendees will learn how preparedness principles can translate across hazards, the challenges of maintaining operations during a prolonged displacement, and key lessons in resilience when the crisis isn’t the one you planned for.

484916.title: Thermodynamic Influences on Tropical Convective Updraft Intensity
484916.authors: Brandon Oliver Wolding, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and S. Seidel, A. E. Sebok, C. J. Schumacher, H. Jimenez-Gonzalez, and R. Rios-Berrios
484916.abstract: Our goal is to characterize how and why lower tropospheric thermodynamic variability influences tropical convective updraft intensity. Convective mass flux data from five global storm-resolving models and convective updraft velocity data from the Green Ocean Amazon field campaign are examined. Two metrics of thermodynamic variability are considered, the first related to the buoyancy of air undergoing undiluted ascent, the second a measure of lower free tropospheric (LFT) subsaturation. While both increased ``undiluted'' instability and decreased LFT subsaturation support increased convective mass flux and precipitation, these thermodynamic changes have opposing impacts on mean updraft buoyancy and vertical velocity in the mid-troposphere. A hierarchy of simple models suggests these opposing impacts can be understood by considering how thermodynamic variability impacts ``lucky'' parcels experiencing little entrainment differently than ``unlucky'' parcels experiencing heavy entrainment. Increased LFT humidity benefits heavily entraining parcels the most, promotes the survival of marginally buoyant convective air, and decreases mean updraft intensity. In contrast, increased ``undiluted'' instability is most beneficial to the least entraining parcels, promotes further intensification of the most buoyant air, and increases mean updraft intensity.

484935.title: Probabilistic Precipitation Forecast Products: How Visual Displays and Accessibility Can Yield Significantly Different Perceptions of Usefulness for Similar Information
484935.authors: Kathryn Semmens, Nurture Nature Center, Easton, PA; and R. A. H. Carr, B. Montz, K. Maxfield, and P. Painter
484935.abstract: Communicating risk often requires understanding and sharing probabilistic information – information that can provide worst case scenarios and help guide effective decision-making. However, probabilistic information is often challenging for even professional stakeholders to use, let alone share with more general audiences. While the information itself may be useful to support stakeholder decision-making, how it is designed, accessed, and shared may create considerable barriers to its effective use. Best practices for risk communication can address these needs and challenges related to the information itself and its presentation, design, and accessibility. The Nurture Nature Center (NNC) is a non-profit organization that has conducted social science research related to flood forecast products, working closely with the U.S. National Weather Service through collaborative, iterative research processes to improve the design and dissemination of flood information. Recently, NNC has worked with the Weather Prediction Center (WPC) to conduct a multi-phase research project to gather user feedback about WPC’s hydrometeorological and precipitation forecast products. As part of this project, NNC held scenario-based focus groups across the country in a variety of settings (e.g. urban, rural, coastal, mountains) to inform user-tested recommendations related to design improvements for probabilistic and deterministic rainfall products, including the Quantitative Precipitation Forecast (QPF), the Probabilistic QPF (PQPF) and the Probabilistic Precipitation Portal (PPP), among others. Through focus group discussions and surveys, NNC engaged professional stakeholders, including water resource professionals, emergency managers, stormwater managers, and transportation and health officials, to identify needs and gather feedback on the forecast products. Analysis of the feedback from 59 participants over 10 focus groups provides insights about the utility of the products and how design changes can increase products’ usefulness for communication and decision-making. Of particular interest, the findings show stark differences between participants’ perceptions of usefulness of the PQPF products (often shared as static images) and the PPP (an interactive platform with customization options), with the latter being much more positively received and understood. While the probabilistic precipitation products provide similar information, the design and accessibility differences highlight the importance of the visual display and interactivity embedded in products. This presentation will detail the social science research study and share the findings related to the varying perceptions of usefulness for probabilistic precipitation products. Additionally, we will share lessons learned for best practices in forecast product design, dissemination, and communication to support more effective risk communication related to flooding and other extreme weather events.

484974.title: Insights into PM10 in Oklahoma: Sensor Deployment and Calibration
484974.authors: Dastin Tain Scott, University of Oklahom, Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and S. M. Loria-Salazar, C. J. Flynn, K. Ardon-Dryer, H. Moosmuller, E. West, and H. M. Webb
484974.abstract: Among the many components of the troposphere, mineral dust plays a critical role in Earth’s radiative forcing and human and ecosystem health. Due to its central location within the U.S. Southern Great Plains, Oklahoma experiences relatively high concentrations of particulate matter (PM) from a combination of natural and anthropogenic sources, including wind erosion, drought, agricultural activities, unpaved roads, wildfires, and prescribed burns. While fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅; particles with aerodynamic diameter ≤ 2.5 µm) has been extensively studied for its chemical composition and well-documented impacts on air quality and human health, less attention has been paid to coarse particulate matter. PM₁₀ (particles with aerodynamic diameter ≤ 10 µm), which is often dominated by mineral dust, remains comparatively understudied despite its importance for regional air quality, climate interactions, and respiratory health. Dust has historically been a major environmental challenge across the Great Plains, from the Dust Bowl of the 1930s to more recent dust storms and wildfire-related events, including those observed in March 2025. These extreme events underscore the need to better understand the sources, transport, and variability of PM10 across the region. Improved monitoring and more accurate source attribution of PM10 are important for better understanding and mitigating its impacts on air quality across Oklahoma and the Great Plains. Low-cost PM sensors have demonstrated greater uncertainty in measuring PM₁₀ concentrations than in measuring PM₂.₅, highlighting the need for careful calibration and validation. This study presents results from multiple QuantAQ sensors, including calibration efforts aimed at improving measurement accuracy. The analysis focuses on characterizing the dust size distributions in Lubbock, TX, and Norman, OK, and identifying potential sources and transport pathways. By addressing these gaps, this study aims to improve measurement and understanding of PM10 dynamics and implications for air quality across the Great Plains.

485048.title: Who Feels the Heat? Uncovering Spatially Varying Drivers of Socio-Environmental Heat Inequality in Miami-Dade County Using Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression.
485048.authors: SEGUN ADEWALE OJO, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and S. Fotheringham
485048.abstract: Due to increased urbanization and the urban heat island effect, metropolitan areas experience disproportionately higher temperatures, making extreme heat one of the deadliest climate-related dangers. Although land cover, socioeconomic status, and urban heat have all been linked in earlier research, many of these findings are based on global statistical models that presume these associations remain constant everywhere. These presumptions hinder policymakers' capacity to develop focused, site-specific heat-reduction policies by overlooking the geographic diversity of urban environments. To provide a more nuanced understanding of urban heat inequality than traditional regression approaches, this study specifically addresses this limitation by examining how environmental and urban characteristics affect land surface temperature at the census tract level and identifying where these relationships are strongest by explicitly accounting for spatial stationarity. The research period was 2024, and the mean warm-season (June–September 2024) land surface temperature was calculated using Landsat 8 images. The normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), impervious surface, population density, elevation, wind direction and speed, and proximity to a large body of water are other variables. 565 census tracts were included in the final study following data preparation and quality verification. In contrast to conventional OLS or GWR, Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR) allows each explanatory variable to function at its own ideal specific bandwidths rather than estimating fewer coefficients, improving localized process estimates while taking multiscale spatial variation into account. The results demonstrate that MGWR substantially reduces residual spatial autocorrelation from Moran's I = 0.509 in the OLS model to 0.142 and significantly improves model performance, with R² of 0.821 (adjusted R² = 0.788). Local NDVI varies, but impermeable surfaces consistently show higher LST across the tracts. The LST values decrease with increasing wind speed. Owing to vertical shadowing, densely populated coastal high-rise corridors also have lower LST; the distance to water indicates that the increase in LST values is more gradual the farther a tract is from water. Goodness-of-fit statistics and residual spatial autocorrelation were used to assess the model's performance. The result that MDC's LSTs are dynamic and extremely heterogeneous spatially is further supported by the Monte Carlo spatial variability test, which reveals that all microclimatic predictors aside from wind speed and distance to water have significant non-stationarity. These findings imply that localized environmental factors, rather than consistent county-wide interactions, control heat exposure. Expanding urban vegetation, maintaining natural cooling corridors, and boosting tree canopy in highly populated areas are examples of geographically specialized measures that reflect neighborhood-specific characteristics and should replace generalist interventions in heat mitigation strategies. Beyond these empirical results, this study shows how important multiscale spatial modeling is for capturing local variability in urban heat exposure, offering a solid framework to support equitable heat adaptation measures and evidence-based climate resilience planning. Keywords: Heat Inequality, Urban Heat Exposure, Land Surface Temperature, Climate Policy, Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR)

485068.title: Tracking Pyrocumulonimbus Microphysical Aerosol Process with Single-Particle Black Carbon Observations (Invited Presentation)
485068.authors: Joshua P. Schwarz, NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and A. E. Perring, A. Thames, and G. Michailoudi
485068.abstract: Pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) events eject wildfire smoke above “normal” emissions, and even significant amounts directly into the stratosphere. Due to their dependence both on fire occurrence and local meteorology, it is possible that pyroCb will become a dominant source of smoke to the stratosphere in a future climate. Hence, characterizing their emissions and untangling the various chemical and physical processes that determine the properties and impacts of their emissions is a research priority. Here we will present the limited information currently available about pyroCb from examination of single-particle black carbon microphysical observations, and connect it to deductions about processes occurring during and after pyroCb smoke transport. This presentation will touch upon recent observations from the NASA INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE) and NOAA Stratospheric Aerosol processes, Budget, and Radiative Effects (SABRE) campaigns, with early implications for understanding of pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) dynamics."

485100.title: Regional Contribution of Anthropogenic Carbon Monoxide in the Asian Summer Monsoon Upper Troposphere and Lower Stratosphere
485100.authors: Yutian Wu, LDEO, Palisades, NY; and X. Wang, PhD, J. Zhang, L. L. Pan, W. Randel, and J. Lee
485100.abstract: We study the regional contribution of anthropogenic carbon monoxide (CO) to the Asian summer monsoon upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS) by using a tagged CO, specified dynamics, model experiment. We find that in climatological mean, surface emission from South Asia (SAS) makes the largest contribution to the UTLS anthropogenic CO, followed by East Asia (EAS), with smaller contributions from other regions. Furthermore, for the UTLS CO that is emitted from EAS and SAS, the year‐to‐year variability is large, and there are years in which the contributions from EAS and SAS are comparable. Composite analysis is performed to understand the dynamical mechanism. For the transport of EAS CO, we find that enhanced convection over the western Pacific plays an important role in leading to more UTLS CO via reduced westerly and advection to the Pacific Ocean in the midtroposphere as well as intensified northeasterly and confinement in the UTLS.

485104.title: Developing an Improved Equivalent Roughness Length Model for Boundary Layer Flow over Heterogenous Roughness Patches.
485104.authors: Isaac Joseph Medina, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and C. Meneveau
485104.abstract: Current parametrization of the surface roughness length scale (z0) in numerical weather prediction and global climate models is currently limited to look up tables, or ad-hoc techniques that rely on area weighting methods that cannot account for dynamics associated with subgrid-scale developing internal boundary layers. To address this challenge, we develop a general model for z0 that can be applied to cases of arbitrary heterogenous roughness patches. The method is based on the fundamental theory of internal boundary layer development by Elliot (1958). This analytical approach predicts the development of the internal boundary layer following a change in roughness. It can also predict the downstream evolution of the friction velocity over a roughness patch and based on this approach, we find a new closed form solution for the patch integrated drag force. For perpendicular patches we equate the total drag force of two patches to that of an equivalent patch spanning the combined area, extending the methodology telescopically the streamwise length of the domain. For parallel patches, we equate the equivalent patch to the sum of all parallel patches, assuming no interaction in the spanwise direction between patches. Combining these methods allows for a full grid cell parameterization of z0 which is only a function of patch roughness, area, and relative position and orientation with the incoming wind velocity. Model predictions are compared to Large Eddy Simulation data available in literature and new simulation results, demonstrating improved capabilities compared to existing ad-hoc roughness averaging methods. Predictions yield lower errors for the equivalent roughness estimations, and unlike traditional models, exhibit patch order dependency and friction velocity modeling capabilities.

485135.title: Development of Operational AI Weather Prediction Models at JMA
485135.authors: Futo Tomizawa, JMA, Tsukuba, Ibaraki, Japan; and H. Yonehara, H. Kawada, T. Yoshida, N. Fujikane, J. Tanoshita, S. Yamashita, K. Ogasawara, and S. Hirasedo
485135.abstract: AI-based weather forecasting has demonstrated high predictive skill in medium-range forecasting and has already been introduced into operational workflows at several meteorological centers. In such a context, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) has formulated a strategy for the operational implementation of AI-based weather prediction models and initiated the development of its in-house models in 2026. This presentation provides an overview of the status of these models and plans for their further development. Our initial development focuses on a global deterministic forecasting model. As the first stage of this effort, we established baseline models by fine-tuning existing AI weather models, such as AIFS, GraphCast, and Aurora, using GSM analysis, the operational global analysis data of JMA. Since these models were originally pretrained on ERA5, they tend to exhibit degraded forecast skill when initialized from GSM analysis. However, fine-tuning substantially improved forecast accuracy. The resulting models outperformed JMA’s operational global forecast (GSM forecast) in terms of both statistical scores for the upper-air fields and tropical cyclone track prediction. As the second stage, we are developing our in-house models, using the fine-tuned models as performance baselines. The model is based on the 3D Swin Transformer architecture, with modifications to account for spherical geometry. Trained on ERA5 and GSM analysis using a customized loss function, we have confirmed that this model achieves forecast skills comparable to the baseline models. We are continuing development, with a particular focus on improving tropical cyclone track forecast accuracy, while developing and comparing alternative model architectures. We are also developing a unified global–regional forecasting model to provide high-resolution forecasts over Japan. Our prototype employs a stretched-grid approach implemented using ECMWF’s Anemoi framework. The prototype has been evaluated against JMA’s operational global and regional models, and further development is underway to improve its forecast accuracy.

485216.title: A Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts Framework Approach for County-Level Wildfire Susceptibility Forecasting
485216.authors: Siddharth Damodharan, University of Colorado Colorado Springs, Colorado Springs, CO; and J. Kalita
485216.abstract: Wildfire activity has increased significantly across the western United States, creating significant ecological, social, and economic impacts. Thus, it remains important to forecast wildfire patterns to properly mitigate, prevent, and allocate resources in the event of a wildfire. However, even with the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, forecasting wildfires remains difficult, particularly due to the highly imbalanced nature of wildfire data, strong geographic priors, and the multiscale temporal dynamics of environmental drivers, such as vegetation dryness, precipitation deficits, and atmospheric variability. Traditional machine learning approaches include Random Forest and gradient-boosted decision trees, which have demonstrated strong performance, especially in wildfire susceptibility forecasting. Yet, many existing methods still struggle to model and predict temporal specialization, particularly across heterogeneous environmental processes. In this work, we propose a semantically grounded hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts Framework for county-level wildfire susceptibility forecasting. To evaluate this framework, we assess the model's performance in forecasting wildfire susceptibility across Colorado between 2020 and 2024. Our proposed architecture decomposes wildfire dynamics into three semantic expert groups representing fuel conditions, ignition/spread conditions, and terrain-climate structure. Each expert then contains temporal sub-experts designed to model high-, medium-, and low-frequency environmental behavior. We then use a lightweight routing network that dynamically combines expert predictions in response to evolving environmental conditions. We then benchmark the proposed framework against XGBoost as a baseline and county-level climatology priors, using temporally held-out 2020-2024 wildfire data. Experimental results indicate that grounded expert decomposition substantially improves performance relative to frequency-only MoE architectures, which exhibit expert collapse toward persistent low-frequency dynamics. The final hierarchical MoE achieved a mean PR-AUC of approximately 0.28 with a mean F1 score of 0.372, compared to XGBoost’s mean F1 score of 0.2434 and a mean PR-AUC of 0.2307. Ablation studies further reveal that semantically meaningful decomposition stabilizes expert specialization and improves the interpretability of wildfire susceptibility modeling. These findings thus suggest that semantically structured temporal expert architectures may provide a more promising direction for interpretable environmental forecasting systems, operating under highly imbalanced and geographically structured conditions.

485243.title: Stationarity and Ergodicity In the Extratropical Response to an Equatorial Heat Source
485243.authors: Nicholas Hall, University of Toulouse, Toulouse, France
485243.abstract: Over the last decade there has been increasing interest in ENSO diversity and its potential remote effects. Nonlinearity in atmospheric physics can lead to multiple pathways to a diverse set of extratropical responses, complicating interpretation and raising questions about the sample size needed to draw robust conclusions. Specifically: 1) There is a variety of El Nino events, and asymmetry between El Nino and La Nina SST anomalies; 2) The convective response to SST anomalies is nonlinear, favouring further asymmetry in the Rossby wave source; 3) Transient eddies modify the Rossby wave response in a nonlinear manner. In this study we concentrate exclusively on the third factor: nonlinear atmospheric dynamics. We use an empirically forced dynamical model that is capable of reproducing a realistic atmospheric mean state and variability. This allows for long integrations and large ensembles not normally accessible with fully specified GCMs. Equal and opposite deep tropospheric heat sources are placed in the equatorial Pacific with a range of amplitudes and positions, and the Pacific-North American response is examined. For each experiment the model is run for 3600 months (~300 years) in perpetual DJF. The experiments are repeated for 12-month runs with an ensemble of 1440 initial conditions, so in principle each month is equivalent to a 120-year run. In the long runs the Pacific-North American response displays amplitude-saturation nonlinearity, and considerable asymmetry between positive and negative sources. The response is only weakly dependent on the position of the source, especially for strong heating. Further experiments with heat sources derived from ENSO-composite precipitation show quite realistic extratropical signals. The ensemble runs develop a 1440-member ensemble mean that develops to closely resemble the mean of the long run at month 12. But 120-member sub-ensembles show considerable variety, at least as great as the sensitivity to position and amplitude. The day by day trajectory of the ensemble mean response shows progressive group propagation, but sub-ensemble means show a fascinating recharge-discharge behaviour between North America and the North Atlantic.

485248.title: Southern Ocean Trends In Aerosol and Clear-Sky Shortwave Reflection (Invited Presentation)
485248.authors: Clare E. Singer, NOAA GFDL, New York, NY; and R. Pincus
485248.abstract: Observations reveal significant negative trends in reflected shortwave radiation over the 21st century primarily driven by clouds. In the clear-sky, the Northern Hemisphere is dimming, while the Southern Hemisphere exhibits an unexpected widespread atmospheric clear-sky brightening, particularly over the remote Southern Ocean (SO). We ascribe this brightening to an increase in aerosol optical depth (AOD). Based on observed correlations between monthly-mean wind speed and AOD over the SO, we conclude the trends in AOD come from enhanced wind-driven sea spray aerosol emissions driven by increasing near-surface winds. I will first show these observational results and then examine how these clear-sky reflection and AOD trends are represented in climate models. Using the CERESMIP extended-forcing simulations in free-running configurations and nudged to reanalysis winds, I will quantify how each linkage in this chain of causality -- from wind stress to aerosol emissions to clear-sky albedo -- is represented by the models. I will conclude with discussion of the relevance of these clear-sky albedo trends for the maintenance of a hemispheric albedo symmetry and the model skill in simulating this phenomenon.

485253.title: Historical and Future Changes in Snow Depth across New England using Downscaled CMIP6 Projections
485253.authors: Amber R Stokes, University of Maine, Orono, ME; and K. M. Schild and S. Birkel
485253.abstract: New England is one of the fastest warming regions in North America, which is significantly impacted by anthropogenic contributions, causing a shift in the seasonal timing of snowpack. Seasonal snow cover is a critical part of the hydrologic and climate systems in New England, as snowmelt in high elevation regions brings water supply to many residents of New England, including indigenous communities. The shifting of the spring snow season will have drastic impacts on many economic industries, including wild blueberry harvests in Maine. How quickly this shift in spring snow is expected to happen in the future is still unknown, as New England is a region that is lacking important downscaled model synthesis with observational data for understanding its snowpack evolution. Here we use a combined in situ measurement and computer modeling approach to show how spring snow across New England has evolved historically and how it may change in the future under a warming climate. This study utilizes statistically downscaled snow depth results from a suite of model runs pulled from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6). Statistical analyses are performed to study the spatiotemporal variation of spring snowpack in New England, which are then compared to NOAA National Weather Service (NWS) NOWData for weather stations across New England. In addition, methods such as the Mann-Kendall mutation test and the Taylor skill score are used to evaluate statistical variables and detect trends. Results from this study will help us better constrain how snow trends are changing in New England, and which models are most aligned with observational data. Additionally, the methods presented here can be expanded to other snowy environments to analyze the accuracy of regional model prediction. In better predicting the amount, frequency, and timing of spring snow in New England, we will have a more informed idea of downstream impacts of the changing snow season, including water security, soil health, flood forecasting, and drought awareness.

485255.title: Historical and Future Variations in Snow Depth across New England using Downscaled CMIP6 Projections
485255.authors: Amber R Stokes, University of Maine, Orono, ME; and K. M. Schild and S. Birkel
485255.abstract: New England is one of the fastest warming regions in North America, which is significantly impacted by anthropogenic contributions, causing a shift in the seasonal timing of snowpack.
