485275.title: Global and Diurnal Variations of Tropospheric Ammonia Observed from the FengYun Satellite Constellation
485275.authors: Zhao-Cheng Zeng, Peking University, Beijing, China; and M. Sheng, J. Hua, and R. Zhou
485275.abstract: Satellite observations play a crucial role in quantifying ammonia sources by capturing large-scale variations of atmospheric NH3 concentrations. As the world's first geostationary hyperspectral infrared sounder, the Geostationary Interferometric Infrared Sounder (GIIRS) on board China's FengYun-4 satellite series provides a unique opportunity to monitor the diurnal cycle of NH3. Using NH3 retrievals from July 2022 to date, this study investigates the spatio-temporal variability of NH3 columns over East Asia, with a focus on daytime variations (07:00–19:00 LT – local time) in major agricultural regions. Inter-comparison with polar-orbiting IASI and CrIS data shows that GIIRS NH3 retrievals are consistent in capturing spatial patterns and temporal dynamics. This talk will highlight the valuable capability of FY-4B/GIIRS in identifying and tracking daytime dynamics of NH3 sources over East Asia, offering new insights beyond current low-Earth orbit (LEO) instruments. At global scale, however, the diurnal cycle of NH3 remains under-constrained in regions lacking geostationary satellite observations, which poses a challenge to accurate emission quantification. To address this gap, we construct an integrated constellation to achieve quasi-geostationary-like global monitoring coverage, comprising China's FengYun-3 (FY-3) series satellites and the Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS). FY-3E operates in a dawn-dusk orbit with an equatorial overpass time of 05:30/17:30 (Local Solar Time, LST), while FY-3F operates in a mid-morning orbit with an overpass time of 10:00/22:00 LST. Both satellites are equipped with the second-generation High Spectral Infrared Atmospheric Sounder (HIRAS-II). CrIS, with an overpass time of 01:30/13:30 LST, provides supplementary observations in an afternoon orbit. In this study, hyperspectral infrared observations from the constellation are utilized to retrieve global NH3 columns based on the optimal estimation method. Six global NH3 maps are retrieved per day at approximately 4 h intervals. The constellation reasonably captures the diurnal (every 4-hour) and seasonal cycles of NH3 columns, effectively mitigating the constraints in regions without geostationary observations. Consistency of the retrievals among different satellites is demonstrated by comparing with geostationary observations from GIIRS.This study demonstrates the capability of an integrated constellation comprising FY-3E/HIRAS-II in a dawn-dusk orbit, FY-3F/HIRAS-II in a mid-morning orbit, and CrIS in an afternoon orbit to monitor global NH3 distributions and diurnal variability at an unprecedented six local times per day. This approach highlights the potential of polar-orbiting meteorological satellites to enhance the global climate monitoring. FengYun GIIRS and HIRAS-II NH3 retrieval datasets are publicly available on Zenodo with links and future updates provided on the project website (https://fengyunair.github.io/). FengYun satellite Level 1 data are publicly available from the FengYun Satellite Data Center at http://satellite.nsmc.org.cn/portalsite/default.aspx.

485282.title: A 2% Tax on Global Earnings, 4x Worse in the Tail: Pricing Physical Climate Risk Across the World's 2700+ Largest Public Companies
485282.authors: Wahib Ghazni, Jupiter Intelligence, San Mateo, CA
485282.abstract: Climate impact analyses are often expressed in degrees of warming and return periods. Financial decisions are made in earnings, cash flow and valuation. Most climate risk information fails in the gap between the two: it describes the hazard but not what the hazard costs the companies that investors, lenders, and insurers actually hold. This paper closes that gap at market scale. Using Jupiter Intelligence's entity-level climate risk model (JEM), I mapped more than 2,700 public companies spanning the S&P 500, Russell 1000, and MSCI ACWI indexes to over 2.1 million geolocated physical assets spanning 250+ location types. Each footprint is modeled for flood, wind, wildfire, and heat under SSP2-4.5 in the present day and under SSP5-8.5 at 2030, 2050, and 2070. Hazard-driven damage and downtime are propagated through asset-type-specific interruption economics into company-level EBITDA impact and cash-flow value-at-risk at the 99.5th percentile. The first finding concerns the present, not the future. Under today's climate, in an ordinary year, physical hazards already impose an expected burden of roughly $153 billion in EBITDA impact, near 2% of aggregate corporate earnings. This is an unpriced tax already being paid, mostly through business interruption rather than property damage. The 1-in-200-year outcome is more than four times larger, at roughly $660 billion; for dozens of companies, a single tail year exceeds a full year of earnings. Second, sector rankings of this risk are metric-dependent. Defensible financial lenses produce materially different orderings, and the choice of exposure base alone moves a major global sector from first place to ninth. Measured against complete exposure, the intensity leaders match hazard fundamentals: energy, materials, and utilities. Third, geography is robust where sectors are not. Asia-Pacific and Latin American intensities run two to three times North American levels under every metric applied. However, that stability is horizon-dependent. Under high emissions the map converges, and the regions that look safest today erode fastest. Consumer discretionary overtakes energy as the most exposed sector by 2070, Europe develops the highest tail-risk rate of any region, and regional diversification loses effectiveness on precisely the pathway where it is most needed. These results carry a design lesson for catastrophe analytics. Climate intelligence is decision-useful only when it is built from asset-level exposure, explicit interruption economics, and a full stack of financial metrics across horizons: building blocks, not compressed scores.

485283.title: Progress and Vision of the Multi-University Consortium for Advanced Data Assimilation Research and Education (CADRE)
485283.authors: Xuguang Wang, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
485283.abstract: Data assimilation is the science of fusing information from numerical model forecasts with information from observations. It is the backbone of Earth system prediction. DA faces significant scientific and technical challenges associated with the next-generation high-resolution, multiscale, and coupled Earth system modeling and with the large amount of complex and diverse observations. An important question is how machine learning (ML), and especially deep learning, fits into this picture. DA is transdisciplinary in nature and a serious gap in the DA workforce was identified worldwide. A university-led Consortium for Advanced Data Assimilation Research and Education (CADRE), an initiative funded by NOAA beginning in 2024, was created in response to the problems described above. This talk will first discuss progress made by CADRE in the past two years, including (1) innovative research, (2) workforce development and community building, and (3) acceleration of DA research into operations. Vision of CADRE will also be discussed.

485289.title: Tailored Weather Support at the U.S. Air Force's 16th Weather Squadron
485289.authors: Samuel J. Childs, 16th Weather Squadron | USAF, West Lafayette, IN; and B. T. Gallo, E. L. Kuchera, C. Hoover, G. R. Brooks, C. J. Melick, PhD, S. Rentschler, W. T. Sedlacek, and M. Steiner
485289.abstract: Air Force Weather operations provide timely, accurate, and relevant weather information to support conventional and special operations of the Department of the Air Force and Army - globally, around-the-clock, 365 days a year. The Product Applications and Tailoring Flight of the 16th Weather Squadron (16 WS/WXP) is charged with rapidly innovating, exploiting, and operating cutting-edge NWP models to generate timely, relevant, and actionable environmental and information warfare (IW) insights to achieve decision-superiority in support of our national interests. As part of executing our mission, 16 WS/WXP has developed ensemble-based weather threat assessment products in service of warfighter operations. These forecast products are essential for mission and training support that directly enables the protection of our primary asset (people) and over $18 billion in Air Force inventory. We will highlight some of our latest weather-based threat assessment products that directly support aircraft and balloon launches as well as an upgrade of our ensemble forecasting and verification capabilities.

485293.title: Assessing the Performance of the Teledyne Model T640/X Alignment Factor in Climate-Distinct Regions Across the United States
485293.authors: Keelie N. Steiner, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and B. A. Nault and P. F. DeCarlo
485293.abstract: Continuous measurements from Federal Equivalent Method (FEM) instruments are increasingly used to characterize fine particulate matter (PM2.5) variability and support regulatory air quality assessments. However, differences between FEM and Federal Reference Method (FRM) measurements can introduce uncertainty into the interpretation of regulatory PM2.5 mass concentrations across diverse climate regions. In 2024, Teledyne adopted an alignment factor for its designated FEM Advanced Pollution Instrument Model T640 (hereafter T640/X) to correct systematic differences between the T640/X and FRM mass concentrations. The alignment factor uses ambient temperature and PM2.5 mass concentration to adjust estimated PM2.5 concentrations, adding an empirical layer to the initial proprietary correction employed by the T640/X instruments. Due to variability in aerosol physicochemical properties and meteorology across the United States, the universal applicability of the alignment factor for federally regulated PM2.5 mass concentration is uncertain. To evaluate the alignment factor’s performance, data from the T640/X and collocated FRMs were analyzed at six climatically distinct U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) air monitoring sites from 2017-2022. These results were compared with EPA FRM-FEM equivalency criteria. While the alignment factor does improve agreement, in some cases, between the T640/X and FRM, most site-years fail to meet EPA criteria. Performance noticeably varies by site, and these discrepancies were investigated in terms of regulatory design values (DVs) and local meteorological conditions. Based on the failures to meet EPA equivalency criteria and site-specific differences in temperature-relative humidity regimes, these results suggest that the alignment factor is not consistent across differing climates. Due to the observed differences with the FRM, the FEM status should be reevaluated.

485294.title: Working Towards Rapid-Refresh Regional Modeling using MPAS-JEDI at the U.S. Air Force's 16th Weather Squadron
485294.authors: Samantha I Baker, U.S. Air Force, 557th Weather Wing, Offutt AFB, NE; and R. Strickler, M. T. Vaughan, A. J. Elliott, M. Searls, B. T. Gallo, J. Martinelli, and E. L. Kuchera
485294.abstract: The 16th Weather Squadron Science Team is tasked with developing cutting-edge scientific practices to provide their customers with the most accurate weather forecasts possible. The 16th is currently working on implementing a global non-closed loop data assimilation system using JEDI and MPAS. Although it has been challenging at times, we have successfully gotten a developmental workflow up and running, delivering simulated satellite imagery on the Science and Services test webpage. This presentation will cover our endeavors over the past year, which has been primarily battling various workarounds on how to get JEDI sustainably implemented on a high-performance computer without an outside internet connection.

485299.title: Evaluating the Network-Wide Transition from Silicon Photodiodes to ISO 9060:2018 Class C Thermopile Pyranometers in Meteorological Mesonets
485299.authors: Victor A. Cassella, Kipp Zonen, Sterling, VA
485299.abstract: Meteorological mesonets have traditionally deployed silicon photodiode pyranometers to achieve high spatial observation density within constrained equipment budgets. However, the limited spectral response of silicon sensors (approximately 360–1120 nm) introduces measurement biases that can approach 15% under certain atmospheric conditions, including diffuse illumination, heavy cloud cover, and rapidly changing sky conditions. This study evaluates the operational, technical, and scientific impacts of upgrading a mesoscale weather network from legacy silicon pyranometers to modern ISO 9060:2018 Class C thermopile pyranometers. With a spectrally flat broadband response spanning approximately 285–3000 nm, Class C thermopile pyranometers eliminate the spectral selectivity inherent to silicon sensors and provide more accurate measurements of broadband global solar irradiance across a wide range of atmospheric conditions. Comparative results from parallel field deployments of silicon and thermopile sensors are presented to quantify reductions in both spatial and temporal measurement uncertainty following the network-wide upgrade. The study also examines the engineering considerations associated with transitioning an operational mesonet to thermopile technology, including sensor integration, data logger compatibility, calibration procedures, power requirements, and station metadata management necessary to preserve continuity within long-term climate records. Practical deployment strategies are discussed that enable modernization with minimal changes to existing station infrastructure. Results demonstrate that replacing legacy silicon pyranometers with ISO 9060:2018 Class C thermopile instruments significantly improves the accuracy of surface energy balance calculations, satellite product validation, solar resource assessment, and photovoltaic forecasting. In addition to improved measurement quality, thermopile sensors exhibit greater long-term stability, lower calibration drift, extended recalibration intervals, and reduced sensor replacement frequency, resulting in lower total life-cycle costs despite higher initial acquisition costs. These findings provide practical guidance for meteorological networks considering network-wide sensor modernization while balancing measurement quality, operational requirements, infrastructure compatibility, and long-term maintenance costs.

485306.title: The In-Situ Sensing Facility: Agile Observation Networks for Field Campaign Success
485306.authors: Jacquelyn C. Witte, NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and W. O. J. Brown, H. Voemel, C. Roden, S. W. Hoch, and T. Hock
485306.abstract: The National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), funded by the US National Science Foundation, has been supporting field deployments for atmospheric research since the 1960s, with its Earth Observing Laboratory (EOL) coordinating large-scale programs. EOL’s In-situ Sensing Facility (ISF) was forged out of decades of instrument development, advances in technology and software, and an evolution of services and support in response to the changing landscape of research. Today, ISF has evolved into three measurement systems: (1) Airborne Vertical Atmospheric Profiling System - dropsonde technology, (2) Integrated Sounding System - combined in-situ and remote ground-based profiling instruments, and (3) Integrated Surface Flux System - suite of mesonet, turbulence and energy balance sensors mounted on scalable towers. These requestable observing systems are designed for scalability and flexibility, emphasizing sensor development and integration, data management, and robust deployments to remote or challenging locations. Observations from ISF's measurement systems have guided regional model and forecast development, supported boundary layer meteorology and turbulence studies, and enhanced our understanding of severe weather and convective processes. When configured together ISF forms the foundation of LOTOS (Lower Troposphere Observing System) - a proposed sensor network to sample fundamental state parameters vertically through the boundary layer and horizontally across the surrounding landscape to provide a wealth of data to advance process studies and model algorithm development. We present an overview of our facilities' instrument capabilities and the LOTOS concept.

485318.title: Building Design Modifications to Minimize the Impact of Climatic Extreme Wildfires in Canada
485318.authors: Abhishek Gaur, National Research Council Canada, Ottawa, ON, Canada; and N. Benichou and M. Riahinezhad
485318.abstract: 1. Introduction Wildfires are an increasingly important climate-related hazard affecting communities located within the Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI), where human development intersects with fire-prone vegetation. In recent years, Canada has experienced several catastrophic WUI fires, including those affecting Fort McMurray (2016), Lytton (2021), and Jasper (2024), resulting in extensive losses of homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods. Climate change is expected to further increase wildfire activity through warmer temperatures, prolonged droughts, and more frequent periods of extreme fire weather (Wotton et al. 2017). Consequently, buildings constructed today may experience substantially different wildfire conditions over their service life than those reflected in current building design guidance. 2. Objective This study assesses how projected future changes in wildfire hazard may influence building design requirements across Canada. Using the National Guide for Wildland-Urban Interface Fires (WUI Guide; Bénichou et al. 2021) as the assessment framework, the study evaluates wildfire resiliency related construction requirements at 393 National Building Code of Canada (NBC) reference locations. In addition, the study investigates the extent to which vegetation management around the properties can offset projected changes in construction requirements, providing insight into complementary adaptation strategies for future building codes and community resilience planning. 3. Methodology The analysis covered 393 climatic reference locations listed in Table C-2 of the National Building Code of Canada. Baseline wildfire hazard at these locations was derived from national Burn-P3 simulations for 1970–2017, which combine stochastic ignitions, fire-weather sequences, fuel types, and topography to estimate burn probability and head fire intensity (HFI) at 250m spatial resolution across Canada (Erni et al. 2024). For each NBC location, the prevailing hazard class was represented by the modal grid-cell value within a 15-km radius. Future fire weather was derived from the 50-member CanLEADv1 ensemble (Van Vliet et al. 2024) prepared using bias-adjusted projections of temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, and wind speed from the Canadian Regional Climate Model v4 (CanRCM4). Historical conditions for 1986-2016 were compared with projections for 2054-2084, corresponding approximately to 2.5°C of global mean warming under RCP8.5 (corresponding to a 50-year future building design horizon). Daily weather variables were used to calculate the Fine Fuel Moisture Code, Initial Spread Index, and Buildup Index, which were then combined with wind speed, slope, and Canadian Forest Fire Behavior Prediction System (FBP) fuel types to generate gridded HFI estimates. A location-specific Climate Change Factor was calculated as the ratio of future to historical 31-year mean HFI. These factors were interpolated to the 250-m fuel-grid resolution and applied to baseline Burn-P3 HFI to obtain climate-adjusted fire intensity, while burn probability was held constant to isolate the effect of changing fire weather. Climate-adjusted HFI and baseline burn probability were then combined using the hazard-classification procedure in the WUI Guide. Baseline and future hazard classes were translated into building Construction Classes, from CC3 to CC1, including the additional fire-resistance levels CC1[FR1] and CC1[FR2]. Construction requirements were evaluated under ember-only or low, moderate, and high exposure assumptions and for five fuel-management configurations extending from no mitigation to treatment of Priority Zones 1A-3, or approximately 100 m around the building, following the WUI Guide. 4. Results Wildfire hazard is projected to increase across 366 out of the 393 locations analyzed, as shown in Figure 1. This translates into shifts in the design hazard class with as many as 53 locations falling into a “High” hazard class in future as compared to a baseline value of 28. These shifts in design wildfire hazard class have direct implications for exposure classification and construction class (CC) requirements under the Guide for WUI Fires. In many communities, maintaining current levels of fire resilience may require upgrading to more stringent CCs. For example, under high exposure with priority zone mitigation in 1A and 1, the number of locations requiring CC1 rises from 142 to 159, reflecting a tangible shift in construction requirements that would trigger additional fire-resistant design measures such as non-combustible cladding, enhanced ventilation protection, and tempered glazing. The influence of property level fuel management can’t be overstated. Results show that the both, the current and future projected hazard can be completely offset if effective fuel management is performed up to 100m from the property. Therefore, a strong recommendation from this work is to focus wildfire mitigation efforts on this particular strategy which is both, cost-effective and environmentally friendly. 5. Conclusions This Canada-wide assessment demonstrates that buildings constructed today are likely to face substantially greater wildfire hazards over their expected service life. Under a 2.5°C global warming scenario, 366 of the 393 NBC reference locations assessed are projected to experience an increase in wildfire hazard, while the number of locations classified as “High” wildfire hazard, according to the WUI Guide, rises from 28 to 53. These changes lead to higher exposure classifications and more stringent wildfire-resistant construction requirements in many communities. Under limited priority-zone fuel management, for example, the number of locations requiring the highest level of wildfire-resistant construction, Construction Class 1, increases from 142 to 159. The results also show that fuel management extending to approximately 100 m around buildings can substantially reduce wildfire exposure, allowing most locations to retain their current construction class despite worsening future fire weather. Maintaining wildfire resilience under a changing climate will therefore require an integrated approach combining climate-informed building design with effective vegetation management. References Bénichou, N. et al.: National guide for wildland-urban-interface fires: guidance on hazard and exposure assessment, property protection, community resilience and emergency planning to minimize the impact of wildland-urban interface fires, National Research Council of Canada (2021). Erni, S. et al.: Mapping wildfire hazard, vulnerability, and risk to Canadian com-munities. Int. Jour. of Disaster Risk Reduction 101, 104221 (2024). Van Vliet, L., et al.: Developing user-informed fire weather projections for Cana-da. Climate Services 35, 100505 (2024). Wotton, B. M. et al.: Potential climate change impacts on fire intensity and key wildfire suppression thresholds in Canada. Environ. Res. Lett. 12, 9, 095003 (2017).

485319.title: Beyond the Forecast: Making Weather Information Useful for Decision-Makers
485319.authors: Bridget Smith, Arlington, VA; and M. Strobin
485319.abstract: Weather forecasts, outlooks, and probabilistic information derive their value by helping users make timely, informed decisions. For many users—such as emergency managers, airport managers, transportation officials, school administrators, utility operators, and other weather-sensitive decision-makers—the central question is not simply “What will the weather be?” but “What should I do, when should I do it, and how confident should I be?” This presentation will explore how weather information is decision support, with a focus on practical communication strategies that help non-meteorologists interpret risk, uncertainty, timing, and potential impacts. Effective decision support begins with recognizing that many users of weather information are not scientists and may not have formal meteorological training. They are often operating under time pressure, balancing competing priorities, and making decisions that carry safety, operational, financial, or public-confidence implications. In these contexts, technically accurate information is necessary but not sufficient. Forecasts must be communicated in ways that are clear, actionable, and aligned with the user’s decision points. A forecast that is meteorologically precise but difficult to interpret may fail to support the very decisions it is intended to inform. The presentation will discuss several communication challenges that commonly arise in decision support; including how to convey probability, uncertainty, timing, thresholds, confidence, and impact severity. These challenges are especially important when users must decide whether to activate emergency operations, delay or cancel transportation activities, adjust staffing, issue public messaging, or take protective actions. For example, an emergency manager may need to know whether a low-probability, high- impact event warrants early coordination, while an airport manager may need to understand how forecast confidence affects de-icing plans, runway operations, staffing, or passenger communications. In each case, the usefulness of the forecast depends on whether the information is translated into the user’s operational context. This presentation will include a practitioner-focused case study examining poor examples of weather communication and decision support. Using AIWind, the discrepancies between forecasts and social media posts, and snowfall predictions, we will examine why communication was ineffective and how it could have been improved to support the end user’s needs. Possible issues may include overreliance on technical terminology, unclear probability language, insufficient discussion of impacts, lack of user-specific thresholds, inconsistent confidence messaging, or failure to distinguish between forecast information and recommended decision-relevant considerations. The presentation will then reframe these examples through a decision-support lens. Rather than asking whether the forecast was “right” or “wrong,” the discussion will ask whether the communication helped the user understand the decision environment: Is the outcome possible? When could it occur? How likely is it? What impacts matter most? What decisions need to be made now versus later? What information may change? Focusing on these questions, meteorologists can better connect forecast information to user needs without overstating certainty or making decisions on behalf of the user. Participants will leave with practical considerations for improving weather decision support for external audiences, including the importance of understanding user decisions in advance, communicating impacts alongside probabilities, using plain language, identifying decision thresholds, and creating space for two-way dialogue. Ultimately, effective decision support is not simply the delivery of forecast information; it is the translation of weather risk into usable insight for people who must act under time constraints and uncertainty. By examining both ineffective and effective communication practices, this presentation will highlight opportunities to make weather information more understandable, more relevant, and more actionable for the communities and operations that depend on it.

485335.title: Evaluation of MTG-IRS Hyperspectral Infrared Observations Using the NOAA CrIS Observation and AI-Derived Geophysical Information
485335.authors: Flavio Iturbide-Sanchez, NOAA, College Park, MD; and P. Beierle, E. S. Maddy, K. Zhang, W. Mccullough, and S. Li
485335.abstract: The Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS), flown onboard the NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 satellites, is a hyperspectral infrared sounder providing high-accuracy radiance measurements in the infrared spectral range from 650 to 2550 cm-1. CrIS observations underpin operational numerical weather prediction, atmospheric composition monitoring, and climate applications, and their demonstrated radiometric accuracy and long-term stability make them a well-established on-orbit radiometric reference for the evaluation of hyperspectral infrared sounders on newly launched satellite platforms. The InfraRed Sounder (IRS) onboard the Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) satellite represents a transformative capability for geostationary hyperspectral infrared sounding. MTG-IRS provides high-spectral-resolution infrared radiance measurements across the longwave and midwave with rapid temporal refresh, enabling continuous monitoring of the three-dimensional thermodynamic structure of the atmosphere. This unique combination of hyperspectral resolution and high temporal sampling offers new opportunities for observing rapidly evolving weather systems, including pre-convective environments and the life cycle of deep convection, with direct relevance to nowcasting and rapid-refresh numerical weather prediction. In this study, the radiometric performance of MTG-IRS is evaluated through detailed radiometric intercomparison with collocated CrIS observations in support of ongoing efforts to assess the quality of MTG-IRS calibrated observations for weather applications. Space–time matched MTG-IRS and CrIS radiances are identified, accounting for differences in viewing geometry, atmospheric path length, and sampling characteristics inherent to geostationary and polar-orbiting platforms. MTG-IRS spectra are convolved to the CrIS spectral response functions to enable consistent hyperspectral radiance comparisons. Following rigorous quality control, statistical analyses are performed across key infrared absorption bands sensitive to atmospheric temperature, water vapor, surface properties, and cloud characteristics, allowing assessment of radiometric consistency and spectral stability. To further interpret observed radiance differences and reduce scene-dependent effects, simulated observations are employed using atmospheric state information representative of the collocated observations. Beyond radiometric evaluation, the geophysical information content of MTG-IRS observations is assessed using the Multi-Instrument Inversion and Data Assimilation Preprocessing System–Artificial Intelligence (MIIDAPS-AI). MIIDAPS-AI is a mature system developed at NOAA that applies deep neural networks to retrieve atmospheric temperature and water vapor profiles, as well as surface and atmospheric stability parameters, from hyperspectral infrared radiances. This work demonstrates the application of the MIIDAPS-AI system to MTG-IRS observations, with the goal of producing thermodynamic profiles and atmospheric stability indices in near real time. The high temporal sampling of MTG-IRS enables evaluation of rapidly evolving thermodynamic structures associated with convective initiation and development, highlighting the potential of MTG-IRS retrievals to support rapid-update NWP systems and advanced nowcasting applications. Together, these results support the readiness of MTG-IRS hyperspectral infrared observations for operational exploitation at NOAA and their potential impact on high-frequency atmospheric monitoring from geostationary orbit.

485354.title: Updating Climatic Design Data in the National Building Code of Canada 2025 for Climate Change
485354.authors: Abhishek Gaur, National Research Council Canada, Ottawa, ON, Canada; and A. Attar and M. Armstrong
485354.abstract: 1. Introduction Climatic data are fundamental to building design. In Canada, these data are provided for 680 locations in Table C-2 of Appendix C of the National Building Code of Canada (NBC) and are used to establish design requirements for environmental loads affecting the structural performance of the primary structural system, the building envelope and its moisture protection and drainage performance, as well as the building’s energy performance including design of HVAC systems. Historically, these values were derived from climate observations based on the assumption that climatic conditions were stationary and that past climate would remain representative of future conditions. However, increasing evidence of climate change across Canada challenges this assumption and raises concerns that buildings designed solely using historical observations may be exposed to climatic conditions that exceed those considered during design. To address this issue, the National Research Council Canada (NRC), Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC), the Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium (PCIC), with support from Codes Committees including representation from industry, academia, and municipal, federal, provincial and territorial governments, incorporated projected future climatic conditions into climate design elements in the 2025 edition of the NBC. 2. Objective The objective of this work was to update climatic design data in the 2020 NBC to account for future climate change impacts across Canada and ensure that future building designs reflect anticipated climatic conditions. 3. Methodology Future values of climatic design parameters were developed through targeted climate-modelling for the locations listed in Table C-2 of the NBC. Climate projections were generated for average global warming levels ranging from 0.5°C to 3.5°C relative to the 1986-2016 baseline period. For this work, climatic changes corresponding to an average global warming level of 2.5°C were selected to represent conditions over a 50-year design horizon under RCP8.5 scenario. A Minimax Method was used to identify the recommended design values considering climate change impacts. Under this approach, where projected climate change results in more extreme exposure conditions for buildings, the future projected value is selected; where the projected conditions become less extreme, the current updated value is retained. For example, future global warming is expected to reduce heating demand while increasing cooling demand. Accordingly, 2020 NBC January design temperatures and heating degree-days remain the recommended design values, whereas projected future July dry- and wet-bulb temperatures are recommended for design. 4. Results The assessment demonstrates that projected climate change affects climatic design variables differently across regions of Canada. January 1% and 2.5% design temperatures are projected to increase by approximately 5°C on average across the locations listed in Table C-2. Because colder conditions govern heating system design, no future adjustment is applied and the updated historical values are retained as the conservative design basis. Heating degree-days below 18°C are projected to decrease by approximately 1,100°C-days on average, and current values are similarly retained as the conservative design basis. In contrast, July design temperatures are projected to increase at all locations. The average projected increase is approximately 4.1°C for the July 2.5% dry-bulb temperature and 3.4°C for the corresponding wet-bulb temperature. These future increases are directly applied to the updated historical values, with implications for cooling capacity, dehumidification requirements, overheating risk, building occupants health, glazing selection, solar shading, and building-envelope design. Precipitation-related parameters exhibit substantial increases under projected future climate conditions. Annual total precipitation is projected to increase at all locations8 listed in Table C-2 by approximately 12% on average, while annual maximum rainfall is projected to increase by approximately 22%. The projected average increases in both the 15-minute rainfall used for roof-drainage design and the one-day rainfall used to assess roof ponding are approximately 29%, with increases occurring at all locations listed in Table C-2. These results indicate the need for increased roof-drainage capacity, appropriately sized drains and scuppers, and enhanced consideration of rainwater accumulation and structural roof loading. Building-envelope moisture exposure is also projected to increase in many regions. Future Moisture Index values are adopted where projected moisture loading is higher, representing approximately two-thirds of the locations listed in Table C-2, while current values are retained at the remaining one-third. These changes may influence requirements for drainage cavities, cladding assemblies, moisture protection, and durability of wood-based components. Driving rain wind pressure (DRWP) is projected to increase at all locations by approximately 9% on average, indicating greater moisture exposure for wall assemblies, windows, flashings, and other building-envelope interfaces. Projected wind changes are incorporated through regional climate-change factors. A factor of approximately 1.05 is applied across most of Canada, while a factor of 1.10 applies in Ontario, the Atlantic provinces, and portions of British Columbia west of 120°W. Snow loads show a markedly different response. For the ten provinces, projected future ground snow and rain-on-snow loads are generally lower, therefore, current values remain the governing design cases under the Minimax Method. In Yukon, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut, a climate-change factor of 1.05 is applied. 5. Conclusions This work presents the updated climatic design parameters incorporated into the 2025 edition of the NBC to account for the impacts of projected climate change on building design. Table 1 summarizes the recommended climatic design values, which either retain the 2020 NBC values or adopt projected future values, depending on the climatic parameter and its engineering application. Table 1. Summary of recommended design values at NBC Table C-2 locations. 485360.title: Weather Regimes Distinguish Renewable Power Supply Droughts from Transmission Bottlenecks In the ERCOT Power Grid
485360.authors: Puja Das, MIT, Cambrige, MA; and Z. Wei, R. Khorramfar, S. Amin, L. Qiu, and M. F. Howland
485360.abstract: Resource-adequacy (RA) risks are increasingly governed by weather as wind and solar penetration grows and demand is electrified. Therefore, it is critical for grid planning to recognize which meteorological conditions drive RA risks and how the risky meteorological conditions change with decarbonization level. Prior research focused on a large portion of the Western United States found that 43-100% of cumulative risk in grids with up to 60% renewable penetration are driven by high-pressure blocking that simultaneously raises demand and suppresses power supply. Since each grid region has distinct geophysical and power grid contexts, it is useful to elucidate whether this characteristic of a single, dominant meteorological driver of RA risk holds in other rapidly decarbonizing regions. Here, we investigate ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas), which has a distinct climatology from the Western United States and has a higher penetration of wind power. We further extend the analysis to consider a transmission network model, rather the commonly used copperplate (lossless) grid modeling, which allows us to distinguish between power supply and transmission-driven RA risk. To reveal the driving mechanisms of the risk, we combine regional climatology with the spatially detailed power-system modeling. We classify daily circulation using self-organizing maps trained on summer 500-hPa height anomalies, and composite their surface conditions against modeled failures. To identify each failure's cause, we re-solve dispatch with unconstrained transmission, which isolates supply shortfalls from transmission network bottlenecks. We first verify the model against historical observations by matching fleets to ERCOT's installed 2019 and 2025 capacity and testing on out-of-sample weather, and find the model sheds energy at similar times the grid strained. In the observed record we find events are either purely temperature-driven, raising demand without a meaningful supply deficit, or compound, combining temperature-driven demand with some supply stress. We then apply the model to a fully decarbonized ERCOT grid. At 100% renewable penetration, wind-supply droughts become the leading cause of failure arising through two different circulation patterns that both suppress the southerly Great Plains low-level jet, one through subsidence under a ridge and the other by reversing the jet under an eastern trough. In contrast, failures due to transmission-limitation, occur under different weather regimes and are mostly driven by demand spikes. Finally, we model various renewable penetrations from 20% to 100%, and we find power supply shortfalls account for most shed energy at penetration level. These ERCOT simulations suggest that decarbonization level changes how severe a risky meteorological event is, rather than producing fundamentally new risky meteorological conditions.

485373.title: Evaluation of Mixed Precipitation Forecasts at NWS Gray
485373.authors: Jacob Denault, Ohio University, Ernest F. Hollings Undergraduate Scholar, Kettering, OH
485373.abstract: This research project investigates forecasting discrepancies during significant winter weather events involving mixed precipitation, which includes sleet and freezing rain. This work provides critical knowledge on persistent biases in mixed precipitation forecasting and demonstrates how to modify forecasts to more accurately predict winter precipitation types. These insights will help Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) within the National Weather Service (NWS) refine their mixed precipitation forecasts to better serve the public. To complete this analysis, we catalog winter weather headlines issued from 2016 to 2025 by the NWS Gray, Maine office using the Iowa Environmental Mesonet’s Valid Time Extent Code (VTEC) Browser. This catalog included Winter Weather Advisory and Winter Storm Warning headlines at five different zones across NWS Gray’s County Warning Area (CWA) that forecasted sleet and/or freezing rain. We then verify these headlines against Meteorological Aerodrome Report (METAR) observations at locations within the five zones to check for forecast accuracy. From there, we decipher trends regarding whether NWS Gray consistently under- or overforecasted sleet and freezing rain for each zone. Our results indicate that combined across all five zones, NWS Gray was most likely to underforecast sleet and overforecast freezing rain, although the sleet signal was weaker. This occurred especially across the inland and mountainous zones where NWS Gray issued the bulk of the winter weather headlines. For the coastal zones, both sleet and freezing rain were most likely to be overforecast, albeit only slightly so. These findings suggest that inland and mountainous areas see more sleet and less freezing rain than expected during winter weather events, while coastal areas observe somewhat less freezing rain and sleet than previously thought.

485399.title: Enhancing Tropical Cyclone Forecasts with TROPICS Microwave Data Assimilation in HAFS
485399.authors: Isaac Moradi, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and S. Kalluri, V. S. Tallapragada, and W. J. Blackwell
485399.abstract: This study evaluates the impact of assimilating observations from the Time-Resolved Observations of Precipitation Structure and Storm Intensity with a Constellation of Smallsats (TROPICS) mission into NOAA's Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS). HAFS uses the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) data assimilation system, with Variational Bias Correction (VarBC) coefficients estimated from the NOAA global model. Assimilation experiments were conducted for Hurricanes Franklin, Idalia, Lee, and Nigel, and Typhoon Lan. Results show that assimilating TROPICS Millimeter-wave Sounder (TMS) observations generally improves tropical cyclone track and intensity forecasts, with the largest benefits at longer forecast lead times and during periods of rapid storm evolution. The high temporal sampling provided by the TROPICS constellation complements conventional polar-orbiting microwave sensors by reducing observational gaps over the tropics, demonstrating the value of high-revisit microwave observations for improving tropical cyclone analyses and forecasts in HAFS.

485401.title: Assimilation of Spaceborne Radar Observations in the NASA GEOS framework
485401.authors: Isaac Moradi, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and Y. Zhu, R. Todling, and S. Pawson
485401.abstract: Spaceborne precipitation radars provide unique observations of the vertical structure of precipitation, offering valuable information for improving weather analyses and forecasts. We present recent developments toward assimilating spaceborne radar observations within the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework for NASA's Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS). The new capability includes a radar forward operator and associated variational data assimilation components and is demonstrated using observations from the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar (DPR). Experiments during August 2023–January 2024 show good agreement between simulated and observed reflectivities, with mean differences generally below 2 dB, enabling the successful assimilation of a large number of DPR observations. Assimilation of DPR observations improves the analyzed distribution of precipitation and hydrometeors and produces beneficial adjustments to atmospheric variables, including wind, temperature, pressure, and water vapor, particularly for tropical cyclone cases. These results demonstrate the potential of spaceborne radar observations to improve the representation of precipitating systems in GEOS and provide an important step toward the operational use of spaceborne radar observations in global Earth system prediction.

485408.title: Breaking Down the Current State of Academic Freedom and Scientific Research
485408.authors: Chris Marchesano, Climate Science Legal Defense Fund, New York City, NY
485408.abstract: Over the last year, the scientific community has rallied against unprecedented attacks on academic freedom, including government suppression and censorship in university classrooms, and the upending of America’s vaunted merit-based grantmaking process. For many public scholars and researchers, it is difficult to navigate the current legal landscape around these issues. In this session, the Climate Science Legal Defense Fund will dissect the status of academic freedom in America — the various legislative and administrative attacks happening across the country, the current realities surrounding the public funding of science, and the relevant litigation primed to reach the Supreme Court. We will also provide a primer on your First Amendment rights, so that you can engage in the scientific endeavor with minimal personal and professional risk.

485409.title: When Sampling Mismatches Take Over: Machine-Learning Approach to Find Weather Regimes that Drive Large Scatterometer and Buoy Wind Differences.
485409.authors: Shikhar Rai, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, MA; and S. E. Wijffels, H. Seo, J. T. Farrar, T. Lee, and R. A. Weller
485409.abstract: Satellite scatterometers and moored buoys provide complementary observations of near-surface ocean winds. However, direct comparisons reveal that approximately 20% of collocated matchups in the tropical Pacific exhibit differences exceeding 2 m/s in wind speed and 25 degrees in direction, which exceeds the expected accuracy limitations of these observing methods. In this study, we develop a multivariate, data-driven approach to identify environmental regimes associated with high and low satellite--buoy consistency, which links satellite--buoy discrepancies to concurrent buoy measurements and oceanic and wave reanalysis fields. Using collocated observations from QuikSCAT and ASCAT scatterometers and Tropical Atmosphere Ocean (TAO) buoys in the tropical Pacific, we first partition the matchup dataset into low- and high-discrepancy regimes, and then train a Random Forest classifier to predict matchup quality as a function of environmental conditions. The model demonstrates strong skill in identifying low-discrepancy matchups and generalizes well across both QuikSCAT and ASCAT, indicating that the underlying weather regimes associated with the level of satellite--buoy agreement are robust. Key predictors include wind speed magnitude, air-sea temperature difference, relative humidity, wind-wave significant height, Stokes drift, and short-timescale variability in wind speed, direction, air temperature, and relative humidity. These results show that, rather than arising from instrumental errors, satellite--buoy wind differences are systematically linked to environmental conditions and different sampling resolutions of these two observing technologies. This approach provides a physically interpretable basis for identifying when high-confidence matchups are possible and offers potential applications in satellite validation, data assimilation, and the development of blended wind products in the tropical oceans.

485462.title: A Multi-Band Radar Simulation Framework for S/Ku-Band Uniform/Staggered/NPRT Waveform Evaluation
485462.authors: Luyao Sun, Sun Yat-sen University Shenzhen Campus, Guangming District, Shenzhen City, Guang, 44, China
485462.abstract: To address the range-velocity ambiguity dilemma and precipitation attenuation discrepancy across radar frequency bands, a two-dimensional simulation framework spanning S-band (3 GHz) to Ku-band (13.6 GHz) is constructed in this study, which supplies diverse simulation datasets for ground-based Ku-band radar validation and supports uniform PRT, staggered PRT and non-uniform pulse repetition time (NPRT) waveforms. Comparative simulations are carried out based on distinct attenuation characteristics of two bands, quantitatively revealing severe signal attenuation of Ku-band radar under heavy precipitation and obvious echo discrepancies relative to S-band. Taking NEXRAD Level-II observations as ground truth containing full polarimetric spectral moments (\(Z_H\), \(V_r\), \(S_W\), \(Z_{DR}\), \(\rho_{hv}\), \(\Phi_{DP}\)), the simulator generates raw radar I/Q signals. A waveform-adapted spectral moment estimation algorithm is implemented to retrieve polarimetric parameters, followed by quantitative error analysis between estimated values and NEXRAD truth data. Three typical precipitation regimes (severe convection, stratiform rain and light precipitation) are selected for grouped experiments to comprehensively discuss the merits and limitations of the NPRT scheme under varied meteorological conditions. The proposed unified simulation platform enables integrated performance evaluation of multi-frequency and multi-PRT strategies, offering theoretical reference for waveform design, attenuation correction and velocity dealiasing of ground-based Ku-band dual-polarization weather radars.

485465.title: 30 Years of application of the Wheeler-Kiladis Diagram and Convectively Coupled Equatorial Waves
485465.authors: Matthew C. Wheeler, BoM, Melbourne, VIC, Australia
485465.abstract: Nearly three decades after the development of what has become known as the Wheeler-Kiladis diagram, the wavenumber-frequency analysis of tropical cloudiness and rainfall has become and remains one of the most recognisable diagnostics in tropical meteorology. Originally motivated as a means to understand the propagating features seen in satellite cloud imagery during TOGA-COARE, the diagram provided a compact and physically interpretable view of the organisation of tropical convection across scale, propagation direction, frequency, and equatorial symmetry. It also helped reveal and establish convectively coupled equatorial waves as observable, dynamically meaningful, and practically important features of the tropical atmosphere. In this talk for the George Kiladis Symposium, I will reflect on the origins, interpretation, and subsequent use of the Wheeler-Kiladis diagram, with particular emphasis on its role in shaping our understanding of convectively coupled Kelvin waves, equatorial Rossby waves, mixed Rossby-gravity waves, inertio-gravity waves, tropical depression-type disturbances, the Madden-Julian oscillation, and the broader spectrum of tropical variability. I will discuss how the diagram and related framework of tropical wave analysis have been applied in observations, model evaluation, operational monitoring, and subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction, and how it has influenced thinking about the interactions among equatorial waves, the Madden-Julian Oscillation, tropical cyclogenesis, extreme rainfall, and the global circulation. I will consider why the Wheeler-Kiladis diagram has endured, what it has clarified, where it has sometimes been over-interpreted, and how new observations, reanalyses, high-resolution models, machine learning methods, and prediction systems may extend its value in the years ahead. The presentation will also celebrate George’s broader contributions to the field of tropical meteorology and climate: his ability to combine careful observational analysis, dynamical insight, and intuitive meteorological perspective, but also his ability to garner collaboration through his friendly disposition, allowing significant scientific advancements in multiple areas. Looking back over our 33 years of collaboration, the talk will honour both the legacy of George's work and the continuing challenge of understanding and applying spectral analysis and convectively coupled equatorial waves for improved atmospheric prediction and meteorological services.

485468.title: Characterizing Overpredicted Tropical Cyclone Intensity in NHC's Official and Numerical Model Forecasts
485468.authors: Yunji Zhang, Pennsylvania State Univ., University Park, PA
485468.abstract: Rapid intensifications in tropical cyclones (TCs) have been highlighted by operational and research communities for decades due to their significant impacts on coastal regions and our limited capabilities in accurately forecasting these events. However, a brief examination of NHC's 24-hour official forecasts of North Atlantic (AL) and Eastern Pacific (EP) TCs from 2001 to 2025 suggests that the occurrence of overpredicted TC intensity by at least 15 kt (1393) is even slightly higher than the occurrence of underpredicted intensity by at least 15 kt (1366), although overprediction by 30 kt happens less frequent (134) than underprediction by 30 kt (268). Nonetheless, the frequent occurrence of overpredicted TC intensity by the NHC official forecasts indicates our limited understanding of TC intensity changes, and this study aims to document these events. These intensity overprediction events (by at least 15 kt) are distributed over the major AL and EP areas where TCs are frequently observed, although events with overprediction of at least 30 kt tend to occur more frequently in EP (98) than AL (32), and furthermore, than the Caribbean (3) and the Gulf (1). All 1393 events are categorized based on their observed 24-hour intensity change: intensifying (47), maintaining (334), peaking (24), weakening (633), and rapid weakening (355). The 30-kt overprediction mostly happens in weakening (52) and rapid weakening (77) events. The official forecasts generally intensify the TCs in the maintaining and peaking events (the peaking events could be associated with the onset of the eyewall replacement cycles) and intensify too fast in the intensifying events. On the other hand, for the weakening events, the official forecasts generally predicted a flat or slightly more intense evolution, while for the rapid weakening events, the forecasts were weakening too slowly. Among the cases with more than 30 kt of intensity forecast error, the official forecasts tend to intensify the TC in weakening events and maintain the intensity in rapid weakening events. In general, intensity overprediction often happens when the TC intensification rate changes, and this is true for both the NHC's official forecasts (OFCL) as well as numerical models such as the HWRF model (HWFI).

485471.title: Turning of Wind Stress Direction by Shoaling Waves
485471.authors: Henry Potter, Texas A&M Univ., College Station, TX
485471.abstract: Momentum fluxes at the air-sea interface transfer energy from the wind into the ocean. This energy exchange propels surface currents, forms and grows waves, and causes the ocean to mix, which affects the local environment and drives ocean circulation. The ocean's response to momentum exchange is sensitive to the direction of the surface stress, which is usually taken to align with the wind. However, the actual orientation of wind stress can deviate from the wind direction for reasons that are not well understood. This is a problem because it leads to errors in ocean models that require accurate representation of atmospheric forcing. Quantifying the stress direction near shore is especially difficult because wave shoaling and breaking, fluctuating wind-swell angles, coastal currents, and rapid bathymetric changes create an amalgam of dynamic forces that can alter the stress. Using a year of coastal flux measurements recorded in Duck, North Carolina, as part of the DUring Nearshore Events eXperiement (DUNEX), we tackle this complex issue. Our results show that stress steering is dominated by waves with little impact from currents. Converting the stress vector from an x-y reference frame to a wind-wave reference frame reveals that the stress follows the wind but is turned either towards or away from the wave direction. The turning depends upon the wave age and the wind-wave angle. We present our results from this study and discuss their implications.

485480.title: From Science to Security: CU Boulder Builds a Unified Approach to VLEO
485480.authors: Katelynn R. Greer, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and E. Thiemann and A. B. Crews
485480.abstract: In April of 2026, CU-Boulder hosted the VELO Frontiers workshop. Jointly presented by LASP (Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics) and NSI (Center for National Security Initiatives), this was an opportunity to understand the needs of government and industry and how CU can provide the needed research. The issues identified in VLEO included atmospheric drag & environment forecasting, sensors, propulsion & power, the atomic oxygen environment, materials, real-time data, human factors, and programmatic & business aspects. In this presentation, we present the workshop findings, a way forward, and an example re-entry experiment.

485487.title: Evaluating the Latest Space-based v11.2 OCO-2 / v11 OCO-3 XCO2 Data Against Ground-based GGG2020.1 TCCON, v2.4 COCCON, and Airborne ATom Measurements
485487.authors: Saswati Das, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and M. K. Sha, S. Kulawik, M. Kiel, J. Laughner, G. Osterman, V. H. Payne, and J. St. Clair
485487.abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is naturally present in Earth’s carbon cycle but is also emitted into the atmosphere in large amounts due to anthropogenic activities. Such activities strongly influence and alter the carbon cycle by impacting the ability of natural sinks to reduce atmospheric CO2, necessitating precise, accurate, and long-term measurements. Operating for over a decade and five years, respectively, the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2) and -3 (OCO-3) missions (hereafter collectively termed OCO) provide space-based retrievals of the column-averaged dry-air mole fraction of CO2 (XCO2). The OCO missions aim to provide sufficiently precise XCO2 measurements to aid in the quantification of carbon cycle fluxes at regional scales and to better understand their seasonal and interannual variability. Given the long-standing data record of the OCO missions, continual validation efforts are essential to ensure the scientific robustness of OCO XCO2 data products. In this study, we compare the latest OCO data versions (v11.2 OCO-2 and v11 OCO-3) against ground-based measurements from the COllaborative Carbon Column Observing Network (COCCON). COCCON utilizes portable Fourier-Transform InfraRed (FTIR) spectrometers (EM27/SUN) to provide precise column-averaged measurements of XCO2 and is highly advantageous in locations that the Total Carbon Column Observing Network (TCCON)—OCO’s primary validation source—does not cover. Global comparisons against GGG2020.1 TCCON suggest bias values close to 0 ppm in the Land Nadir/Glint and Target modes for OCO-2, and in the Land Nadir/Glint and Ocean Glint modes for OCO-3 with standard deviation values less than or equal to 0.94 ppm. We provide the first global analysis of OCO XCO2 datasets against the latest v2.4 COCCON dataset across all OCO observation modes. Comparisons over selected sites suggest a significant reduction in global biases compared to earlier COCCON versions, with Land Nadir/Glint biases of approximately 0.25 ppm for OCO-2 and 0.46 ppm for OCO-3, and standard deviation values equal to 0.94 ppm and 0.89 ppm, respectively. As all COCCON data are gradually reprocessed to the latest version (v2.4), improved biases across all OCO observation modes are expected. Expanding the OCO validation effort, we also analyze OCO-2 XCO2 retrievals against the airborne Atmospheric Tomography Mission (ATom), which consists of around-the-world flights conducted across four seasons between 2016 and 2018. The results suggest average bias and standard deviation values of 0.01 ppm and 1.26 ppm, respectively. The aircraft profiles were extended using model data from CarbonTracker and CAMS. We provide the latest validation analysis for the OCO missions and the most up-to-date information on biases and uncertainty, establishing the datasets' robustness for use by the scientific community.

485499.title: A Research-Informed Framework for Building Undergraduate STEM Identity, Climate Literacy, and the Future Earth System Science Workforce Through AI/ML-Enabled Earth System Science Education and Research Communication
485499.authors: Muhammad Shehzore Hashmi, Montana State University, Bozeman, MT; and G. Garcia, Z. Gobena, O. Badaki, and C. Lang
485499.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming Earth system science by improving climate models, analyzing satellite observations, and reducing uncertainty in climate prediction. However, audience analysis conducted with undergraduate STEM students shows that many remain unaware of how AI is used in Earth system science and often perceive climate science as a discipline limited to environmental scientists while associating AI primarily with generative tools such as ChatGPT. These misconceptions create barriers to climate literacy, interdisciplinary participation, and awareness of career pathways in Earth system science. This project presents a research-informed science communication framework designed to engage undergraduate STEM students with contemporary AI/ML-enabled Earth system science through multimedia educational resources and digital storytelling. Developed as part of the NSF Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics (LEAP) Summer Momentum Fellowship at Columbia University, the framework was informed by audience analysis, interviews with climate scientists and science communication experts, and iterative communication design. The framework integrates multiple complementary communication products, including an educational podcast featuring climate scientists, an animated explainer video, an opinion article, interactive web-based simulations, and online educational resources. Together, these resources translate complex concepts, including climate models, uncertainty, satellite observations, cloud processes, and machine learning, into accessible, engaging narratives for undergraduate audiences. Rather than presenting AI as a replacement for scientists, the framework emphasizes how AI can support scientific discovery while physics and human expertise remain central to Earth system science. A central objective of the framework is to strengthen undergraduate STEM identity by demonstrating that Earth system science is inherently interdisciplinary and depends on contributions from engineering, computer science, mathematics, physics, biology, chemistry, data science, and related disciplines. The communication strategy validates students' concerns about climate change, artificial intelligence, and future careers before introducing authentic examples of AI-enabled climate research and practical pathways into undergraduate research, internships, REUs, graduate education, and Earth system science careers. To evaluate the framework, embedded pre- and post-engagement surveys will assess changes in participants' climate literacy, AI literacy, perceptions of Earth system science, and STEM identity after interacting with the communication products. These assessments will inform future refinement of the framework and provide evidence for its effectiveness in supporting undergraduate engagement with Earth system science. By combining evidence-based science communication, multimedia learning, digital storytelling, and authentic climate research, this project presents a scalable framework for broadening participation in Earth system science and addressing issues of AI literacy and workforce development for undergraduate STEM students.

485574.title: Optimization of Quantitative Precipitation Estimation Algorithms Using Dual-Polarization Radar Data
485574.authors: Karol Dzwonkowski, Military University of Technology, Warsaw, MZ, Poland; and M. J. Mierzwiak, I. Winnicki, S. Pietrek, and K. Kroszczyński
485574.abstract: Climate change and rising atmospheric temperatures are leading to the intensification of precipitation due to the atmosphere's increased water vapor holding capacity. Prolonged and intense rainfall poses new challenges for radar meteorology and quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE). Operational algorithms based on empirical relationships typically utilize radar reflectivity (Z) to estimate rainfall intensity (R). This study aims to optimize numerical parameters for both classic Z–R relationships and advanced polarimetric dependencies, incorporating differential reflectivity (ZDR) and specific differential phase (KDP). The study evaluates several R-estimation models, including the Marshall-Palmer (M–P) relation operationally used in Poland, as well as R(Z), R(Z, ZDR), R(Z, KDP), and R(KDP). A least-squares method is employed to determine numerical parameters and perform local calibration, enabling the minimization of estimation errors and precise tuning of empirical models to actual precipitation conditions. Data from four C-band weather radars located in Poland were utilized to analyze three cases of intense rainfall associated with cold fronts. All radar observations (Z, ZDR, KDP) and rain gauge precipitation data (R) underwent rigorous quality control procedures, including dedicated filtering to ensure the removal of non-meteorological echoes and data outliers. Radar-derived precipitation totals were assessed against measurements from a network of 625 rain gauges. Furthermore, the paper presents a methodology for integrating area-based radar data with point-source rain gauge measurements. Radar data were extracted from a 25 km² area (5×5 pixels) to mitigate spatial displacement effects between radar and gauge observations. A critical aspect of the study was the temporal alignment of 5-minute radar data with 10-minute rain gauge accumulations. To assess the impact of thermodynamic factors on precipitation structure, the performance of the developed algorithms was evaluated at fixed altitudes of 1 km and 2 km above sea level. Validation results demonstrate that the use of polarimetric parameters significantly improves QPE accuracy and reduces estimation errors compared to standard reflectivity-based relationships. At an altitude of 1 km, the R(Z, KDP) relationship yielded an approximately 67% lower RMSE (0.65 vs. 1.98 mm/10min) and 68% lower MAE (0.39 vs. 1.23 mm/10min) compared to the operational M–P relation, and an approximately 7% lower RMSE and 3% lower MAE compared to the calibrated standard R(Z) relationship. Notably, R(Z, KDP) also showed the lowest residual bias (median residual of 0.01 mm/10min, versus 0.04 mm/10min for R(Z) and 0.70 mm/10min for M–P), indicating minimal systematic error. Beyond the specific results, this study offers a methodological contribution to evaluating QPE reliability, an aspect of growing importance as accurate precipitation data become critical for flood forecasting and the country's hydrometeorological safety. Assessing algorithm performance across multiple altitudes provides novel insight into how the vertical precipitation profile affects retrieval accuracy — a factor often overlooked in operational QPE assessments. As cold fronts are a major, recurring source of intense precipitation expected to intensify under climate change, this methodology offers a practical basis for improving QPE under such conditions. These findings can be integrated into operational hydrometeorological support systems, enhancing decision-making in crisis management during severe weather events. Future research will focus on determining universal numerical values for empirical and polarimetric parameters recommended for various synoptic conditions. Keywords: quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE), weather radars, polarimetric parameters, rain gauge validation.

485586.title: Effects of WRF Parameterization Schemes and Boundary Conditions on Urban Boundary Layer Variables for Tracer Inversions
485586.authors: Kevin Joseph Fletcher, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and Z. Barkley and K. J. Davis
485586.abstract: Tracer inversions (e.g., greenhouse gases, pollutants, and other trace gases) require accurate Eulerian transport fields in conjunction with Lagrangian particle models to estimate surface tracer fluxes. The Weather Research and Forecasting model (WRF) is often used for inversions because it is highly flexible in its domain, grid spacing, parameterization schemes, and boundary conditions. However, these parameterization schemes and boundary conditions can introduce biases. The most relevant variables to tracer inversions are boundary layer height and boundary layer winds. Also relevant are the surface heat and momentum fluxes that drive boundary layer growth. The Indianapolis Flux Experiment (INFLUX) collected flux data through a network of towers in Indianapolis, IN, and the surrounding countryside, and wind and boundary-layer height measurements from a Doppler lidar located northeast of the city, allowing a comprehensive evaluation of relevant modeled meteorological variables. We run a thirty-member ensemble varying the boundary layer scheme, land cover, land surface model, and lateral boundary conditions for 2018. We evaluate each member for biases in boundary layer height, boundary layer averaged wind speed, wind direction, sensible and latent heat flux, and friction velocity. We evaluate these biases on a seasonal cycle to determine how the parameterization schemes affect biases throughout the year. By comparing these models, we can better select models to use for inverse modeling in an urban environment.

485587.title: Quality Control of Convective Boundary Layer Depth Observations from WSR-88D Radars Using Machine Learning
485587.authors: Robin Erick Kirchner Jr., The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and D. J. Stensrud, B. Stouffer, and Y. Zhang
485587.abstract: Quality Control of Convective Boundary Layer Depth Observations from WSR-88D Radars Using Machine Learning Erick Kirchner, David J. Stensrud, Braedon C. Stouffer, and Yunji Zhang Department of Meteorology and Atmospheric Science The Pennsylvania State University Results over the past decade have shown that quasi-vertical profiles (QVPs) of differential reflectivity (ZDR) from WSR-88D radars can be used to determine convective boundary layer (CBL) depth (h) by tracking a “channel” of reduced ZDR with height and time within a daytime QVP (Banghoff et al. 2018). These results are improved by multiplying ZDR by a measure of its azimuthal variance, creating a new variable called DVar, which allows for the determination not only of h but also the entrainment zone depth (Δh) as shown in Stouffer et al. (2024). The ability to routinely measure h and Δh across the U.S. using the operational WSR-88D network opens exciting new avenues for CBL research. The DVar QVP channels are unclear for almost half of the days, however, owing to the impacts of rainfall and other environmental conditions that influence the ZDR measurement from Bragg scatterers. Thus, researchers have had to perform manual quality control of DVar QVPs at a significant time expense. Of great importance for future CBL research and data assimilation using DVar QVPs would be the development of an automated quality control (QC) algorithm. Using machine learning, a computer can be provided the DVar QVPs and automatically QC each one as “Good” (DVar channel present) or “Bad” (DVar channel not present) at a fraction of the time required by a human. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was selected, since CNNs specialize in image data by using a “convolution kernel” (image filter) that passes over all parts of the image and extracts the most important information for making a prediction. A 60-20-20 train-validation-testing split across 50 radar sites for one calendar year (2022, yielding a total data set of 17,916 QVPs) was used to train, validate, and test the model. During the training step, raw QVPs were interpolated onto a 28 x 28 grid and provided to the CNN along with the true QC label. For better generalization, no effort was made to constrain what the model saw in its training dataset, i.e. the CNN was provided DVar QVPs across different radar sites and all days of year - including precipitation cases, bad DVar channels, good DVar channels, and ambiguous channels. After training, the model was optimized on the validation dataset using an automated hyperparameter search algorithm called Optuna. The hyperparameters yielding the highest Receiving Operative Characteristic (ROC) Area Under The Curve (AUC) score were chosen. Since False Alarms (bad QVPs classified as good QVPs) are costly to research and data assimilation, a classification threshold that yielded a median Probability of False Detection (POFD) closest to 10% on the validation dataset was chosen. Finally, the model was tested, yielding a median Probability of Detection (POD), POFD, Peirce Skill Score, ROC AUC, balanced accuracy, and standard accuracy of 71.26%, 10.24%, 61.54%, 91.15%, 80.77%, and 82.72%, respectively at the chosen classification threshold (56.70%). While this CNN will greatly improve processing time for future research involving DVar QVPs, it requires the full QVP image to perform accurate quality control. Ideally, to maximize the use of DVar QVP observations a machine learning algorithm designed to quality control DVar QVPs scans as they arrive from the radar would be needed. A Recurrent Neural Network, which has the capability to process timeseries data and predict the quality control status of the next incoming data point, will be explored and initial results discussed. Figure caption: 2022 testing dataset ROC curves across 50 random initializations of the QVP CNN model. Purple line is the median POD along a common interpolated grid of POFD values. Shading along the median curve indicates the minimum and maximum interpolated POD values at each POFD. Contours represent the Peirce Skill Score. Dash-dotted line indicates a user-set maximum allowed POFD threshold with the star indicating the highest Peirce Skill Score at that threshold. Grey dashed line is the ROC Line of No Skill (PSS = 0). Figure code (used as a baseline) provided by Lagerquist and Gagne II (2019). References: Banghoff, J. R., D. J. Stensrud, and M. R. Kumjian, 2018: Convective boundary layer depth estimation from S-band dual-polarization radar. J. Atmos. Oceanic Technol., 35, 1723-1733, https://doi.org/10.1175/JTECH-D-17-0210.1 Stouffer, B. C., D. J. Stensrud, C. L. Comer, Y. Zhang, and M. R. Kumjian, 2024: An investigation of convective boundary layer depth and entrainment zone properties using dual-polarization radar and balloon-borne observations. J. Atmos. Oceanic. Technol., 41, 1213-1228, https://doi.org/10.1175/JTECH-D-23-0165.1. Lagerquist, R., and D.J. Gagne II, 2019: "Interpretation of deep learning for predicting thunderstorm rotation: Python tutorial". https://github.com/djgagne/ams-ml-python-course/blob/master/module_4/ML_Short_Course_Module_4_Interpretation.ipynb.

485588.title: Diurnal Variability of Clouds and Precipitation under Synoptic, Thermodynamic, and Mesoscale Forcing during TRACER IOP
485588.authors: Min Deng, DOE, Upton, NY; Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY; and M. P. Jensen, S. Giangrande, K. Johnson, A. Zhou, and M. Wang
485588.abstract: Cloud and precipitation over the Houston metropolitan region are influenced by atmospheric processes operating across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. However, the extent to which synoptic weather regimes, monthly thermodynamic evolution, and mesoscale boundaries shape their diurnal variability remains insufficiently characterized. Using observations collected by the U.S. Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement facility during the June–August 2022 Tracking Aerosol Convection Interactions Experiment, we examine the diurnal evolution of cloud occurrence and precipitation under contrasting environmental conditions. Vertically resolved cloud occurrence is derived from the Active Remote Sensing of Clouds product, while spatial cloud fraction is estimated from merged six-azimuth, dual-wavelength scanning radar observations. Surface precipitation and scanning-radar-derived precipitation statistics are used to characterize the corresponding precipitation response. The vertically pointing and scanning radar measurements reveal broadly consistent diurnal variations in cloudiness, despite representing different sampling volumes. Cloud and precipitation occurrence vary substantially among synoptic weather regimes identified using a self-organizing map classification. Within the dominant anticyclonic regime, additional variability is associated with monthly changes in the thermodynamic environment and with mesoscale forcing by bay-breeze circulations, cold-pool outflows, and their interactions. Bay-breeze-only periods exhibit relatively weak cloud development, whereas interactions between the bay breeze and cold-pool outflows delay and prolong the afternoon cloud maximum and enhance the coupling between cloud development and precipitation. These results show that the observed diurnal cycle cannot be explained by a single forcing mechanism.
