Instead, cloud and precipitation variability during TRACER reflects the combined influence of synoptic-scale circulation, evolving thermodynamic conditions, and mesoscale boundary interactions.

485607.title: Thirty-Five Years Using NCAR Resources to Further Understanding of Cloud Properties and Processes
485607.authors: Greg M. McFarquhar, CIWRO/SOM, Norman, OK
485607.abstract: NCAR observatory facilities and programs have had a big impact on the career development and scientific output of the presenter. This presentation will review how NCAR programs and facilities have impacted the presenters career, starting from participation in the 1992 Advanced Study Program (ASP) graduate student colloquium, including collaborative scientific visits in many years, work as an NCAR Associate/Project scientist from 1994 to 2001, teaching in subsequent ASP summer colloquium, and sponsorship from NCAR during a sabbatical in 2015-2016, and involvement in many field campaigns using NCAR resources such as the 1993 Central Equatorial Pacific Experiment (CEPEX), the 1999 Indian Ocean Experiment (INDOEX), the 2003 Bow Echo and Mesoscale Convective Vortex Experiment (BAMEX), the 2004 Alliance Icing Research Study, the 2009/2010 Profiling of Winter Storms (PLOWS) experiment, the 2011/2013 Instrument Development and Education in the Atmospheric Sciences (IDEAS), the 2015 Plains Elevated Convection Study (PECAN), the 2018 Southern Ocean Cloud Radiation Aerosol Transport Experimental Study (SOCRATES), the 2023 Experiment of Sea Breeze Convection, Aerosols, Precipitation and Environment (ESCAPE) and the 2024 Cold Air Outbreak Experiment in the Sub-Arctic Region (CAESAR). The critical role of NCAR resources in advancing scientific discoveries from these campaigns will be discussed. Finally, it will be shown that pressing scientific questions necessitate the continued involvement of the NCAR observational platforms to evaluate scientific hypotheses as relates to aerosol invigoration (field campaigns needed along the Gulf Coast of the United States), characterization of high latitude cirrus (campaigns over Alaska and the Rocky Mountains), and the impact of Southern Ocean clouds on Earth System models (campaigns needed over Australia and out of Antarctic). A continued role of NCAR facilities over the next 35 years will permit continued scientific discoveries.

485612.title: NOAA-NASA Joint Archive (NNJA): Publicly Accessible, Curated Observations
485612.authors: Jessica Knezha, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and S. Frolov, A. El Akkraoui, J. M. Souza, J. S. Whitaker, S. Fredrick, A. Schneider, J. Woollen, S. Cohen, D. A. Rothenberg, and H. Mohrmann
485612.abstract: The NOAA-NASA Joint Archive (NNJA pronounced like the word “ninja”) is a publicly accessible, curated collection of Earth system observations spanning 1979 to present, created to accelerate reanalysis production, support development of artificial intelligence (AI) applications, and enable access to the observational records underlying modern reanalyses. A major highlight of the archive is the full range of Earth system observations in one accessible location. The archive encompasses atmospheric satellite radiances and conventional measurements, in-situ ocean profiles, ocean satellite retrievals, sea ice concentrations and freeboard retrievals, and land surface observations from over 60 sensors provided by NOAA, NASA, and their partners. The dataset extends into near-real time through continuous archival of the NOAA operational data. NNJA observations are distributed through Amazon Web Services in formats compatible with established data assimilation systems and are accompanied by channel-level black and white lists that capture the quality history of the satellite record. Data integrity is verified through a three-tier process: file-level metadata checks, cross-validation against existing black and white lists from prior NOAA and NASA reanalyses, and a comparison of assimilation statistics with reference reanalysis and operational products. To lower barriers for the machine learning community, a companion dataset (NNJA-AI) transforms NNJA observations from legacy formats to column-oriented Apache Parquet, enabling sufficient large-scale queries and direct integration with AI training workflows. While the atmospheric portion of the dataset is mature from years of atmospheric data assimilation, the oceanic portion is a new feature representing the shift to coupled data assimilation and the need for a full range of data inputs. The data archive is growing and improving through usage in the ongoing reanalysis production at NOAA. Beyond the use in the next generation of reanalysis, we expect NNJA to be useful to the broader community as a comprehensive source of observational data.

485614.title: Unresolved Convection, Resolved Consequences: Tropical Cyclones, Upscale Error Growth, and Extratropical Predictability in Physical and AI Models
485614.authors: Gan Zhang, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL
485614.abstract: Whether AI weather models learn multi-scale chaotic dynamics or merely interpolate within training distributions remains an open question, partly for lack of stringent, physically grounded tests. Tropical cyclone (TC)–extratropical interactions offer such a probe: the upscale growth of forecast error from tropical convection to the midlatitude waveguide is canonically multi-scale and chaotic. We test whether the lack of explicitly resolved convection matters for upscale error growth with the AI-hybrid NeuralGCM, a physical dynamical core whose subgrid parameterizations are learned from ERA5, with no structural representation of the convective processes involved. Across 108 out-of-sample cases initialized at TC genesis (2020–2022), NeuralGCM ensembles reproduce the extratropical error-growth patterns and Week-2 Z500 skill of the physics-based ECMWF-IFS. Wave activity flux diagnostics show the NeuralGCM propagating Rossby wave energy along physically consistent pathways in complex cases. Even though convection is left unresolved, the learned parameterizations transmit sufficient bulk upscale forcing to drive the correct midlatitude wave response. Exploiting emulator efficiency, we then run 359 genesis-initialized reforecasts spanning 12 objectively clustered track archetypes, compared against a 360-day genesis-free baseline. Leveraging the sample size inaccessible to physics-based ensembles, we show that week-2 impacts on US and European predictability are strongly track-, time-, and metric-dependent, including unexpected significant effects from westward-moving, non-recurving TCs. The results also expose that training objectives — CRPS-trained stochastic versus deterministic parameterizations — shape which aspects of chaotic dynamics a model learns.

485616.title: Near-Surface Extreme Wind Events and Their Responses to Climate Forcings In a Hierarchy of Global Climate Models
485616.authors: Gan Zhang, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and M. Rao, I. Simpson, K. Reed, B. P. Medeiros, H. H. Chou, and T. A. Shaw
485616.abstract: Near-surface extreme winds profoundly affect human society, yet process-based understanding of their changes under climate forcings remains limited. This study systematically investigates the responses of high (HWE) and low (LWE) wind extremes (10-meter) to climate forcings using a hierarchy of climate model experiments from multiple general circulation models that participated in the Cloud Feedback Model Intercomparison Project. We analyze idealized atmosphere-only aquaplanet (Aqua) simulations and more realistic land-atmosphere (AMIP) simulations to identify robust responses to climate forcings and trace the sources of structural uncertainty. In Aqua simulations, tropical LWE changes exhibit large inter-model spread, which can be partly traced to model-dependent responses of low-pressure systems. In contrast, extratropical HWE intensify robustly with surface warming, linked to the strengthening of high-latitude extratropical cyclones. The AMIP simulations confirm the robust intensification of extratropical HWE. The more realistic boundary conditions in AMIP simulations act as a constraint, reducing inter-model spread in tropical zonal means compared to Aqua simulations. A comparison of uniform and patterned 4-K warming experiments suggests that the global magnitude of warming, rather than the specific warming pattern, dominates the large-scale responses of wind extremes. However, regional projections of extreme wind changes, especially over land, remain highly uncertain due to divergences in model formulations. Case studies reveal that major disagreements in HWE changes can stem from fundamental differences in representing the type and seasonality of extreme-producing weather systems. Our results underscore that reducing uncertainty in regional wind projections requires constraining the physical representation of weather systems in climate models.

485620.title: Global Lightning Fatalities
485620.authors: Ronald L. Holle, Holle Meteorology & Photography, Oro Valley, AZ
485620.abstract: An average of 3,691 lightning deaths occur globally per year based on recently-published data; many more are not documented. This total is summarized from all published national studies of fatalities that include several years or longer during time spans ending in 1979 and later. This summary includes national-scale fatality data from 60 nations. Global estimates published in the last decade are 6,000 and 24,000 lightning fatalities per year. As a result of the known total being 3,691, it is possible that the estimate of 6,000 annual global lightning death may be verified. Whether the total reaches the estimate of 24,000 needs data from locations in Africa and Southeast Asia. At present, the largest documented national total is 2,234 from India. Specific numbers for each country will be provided in an extended abstract to be submitted for the AMS MALD conference website. In general, lightning fatality rates increase toward the tropics. Unfortunately, many developing countries tend to be in tropical and subtropical areas with higher lightning flash densities than temperate areas. The lowest lightning fatality rates are in developed countries of North America, Western Europe, Japan, and Australia due to the availability of more substantial housing, metal-topped vehicles, lightning safety education, and lower lightning density in some of these regions. Many of the fatality studies are from Europe death rates are low. In contrast, the two highest rates are from Africa, where fatality rates for 51 other African nations are not yet summarized in any publication. The number of annual lightning fatalities in the United States decreased from around 400 deaths early in the 20th century to as low as 11 deaths in 2021. This trend occurred along with a decrease from a 60% rural population in 1900 to 20% at present. Also in this period, there was increased quality of dwellings, workplaces, schools, and other public and private buildings. Also important was a huge increase in the ready availability of fully enclosed, metal-topped vehicles. Additionally, a significant lightning safety education and awareness campaign has been sustained across the U.S. for over twenty five years. On average, for every U.S. lightning death, 10 lightning-related injuries are estimated. However, the ratio may be greater in developing countries where lightning affects large numbers of people working in labor-intensive subsistence agriculture. In additional lightning-vulnerable situations, people in developing countries are at risk inside lightning-unsafe schools and other structures where children and others are concentrated and large casualty counts occur. The number of lightning fatalities and injuries in developing countries is largely unknown due to a number of factors. An issue is that many events that involve only one person may not be reported or considered newsworthy. There are also language and literacy barriers to knowing lightning casualties in remote regions of developing nations. The global population in developing countries is increasing in absolute number, but the trend toward a reduced percentage of the population in rural areas has not occurred in many developing countries. As a result, it is likely that one cannot expect any significant change in the lightning fatality rates in developing countries when the population is mostly rural, working in labor-intensive agriculture, living and working in lightning-unsafe homes and workplaces, and having very limited lightning risk avoidance awareness or high quality medical treatment available.

485646.title: An Explanation for the Unique Rainfall Regime of the Congo Basin
485646.authors: Sharon E. Nicholson, FSU, Tallahassee, FL; and A. H. Fink
485646.abstract: The Congo Basin is unique in many ways. For one, it is the site of the world's most intense thunderstorms. Some 70 to 90% of the rainfall is produced by Mesoscale Convective Systems (MCSs), but these represent only 2 to 3% of the rain-bearing systems affecting the region. There are few teleconnections to other regions or to large-scale forcings. A related peculiarity is the very small spatial coherence of rainfall variability on monthly time scales. This contrasts sharply with other areas of Africa. This paper examines this lack of spatial coherence and explore possible causes of this unique characteristic. The methodology is linear correlation between and within regions of Africa and spatial correlation as a function of distance within regions. An analysis was carried out on 90 regional sectors that covered all of Africa. For nearly all regions precipitation showed strong and significant correlations with precipitation in numerous other regions. The correlations among regions were particularly strong in subtropical areas, with broad expanses of the continent experiencing drought or wetter conditions in the same years. This was especially the case for regions within the Sahel, within eastern Africa, and within Southern Africa. However, the four regions covering the Congo Basin showed no correlation with any other region, not even with each other. The lack of spatial teleconnections within the Congo Basin was in an analysis based on five large geographical sectors of the continent. Within each sector the rainfall climatology is similar. The annual rainfall for each region within the sector was correlated with the sector average. For most regions the correlation with the geographical sector ranged from .6 to greater than .8. A glaring exception was the four regions of the Congo Basin. The correlation ranges from 0 to .4. Nowhere else was the correlation this low. An additional analysis calculated rainfall correlations as a function of distance. Initial correlations at a distance up to 25 km generally exceeded .8 and correlations were still .4 to .5 at 500 km distance. For the Sahel the initial correlation is roughly .7 and remains at .35 500 km away. East Africa also shows high correlations, particularly in the ON season, where the correlation exceeds .4 at 500 km. The correlations for the Congo Basin are very different. They drop very rapidly within 100 km and from 300 to 500 km they hover around .05 to .1. Clearly, the spatial coherence of precipitation is weak in the Congo Basin. We examined factors associated with two wet periods in the Congo Basin. The main factors producing the wet conditions were CAPE and total column water vapor, which influences CAPE. Over the central basin the mean total column water vapor in 2016–2020 was anomalously high compared to the mean for 1979–2014 and was much higher than during the dry period 2000–2014. CAPE was also higher in the earlier wet period than in the 2000–2014 dry period. CAPE was markedly below the LTM during 2000–2014. An examination of both CAPE and CIN for four seasons similarly underscored the importance of CAPE and CIN in this region. During each CAPE was considerably higher than CIN and the difference was much greater than for other regions of Africa. These results illustrate extreme thermodynamic instability over the Congo Basin throughout the year. Clearly CAPE plays a major role in the interannual variability of Congo rainfall. It stands to reason that, in a high CAPE environment, small local perturbations can produce a storm, in the absence of external, largescale forcing. This could potentially explain the very local rainfall signal within the Congo Basin and the near absence of large-scale forcing. It can also provide a means to project climate changes in the region.

485648.title: Evaluation of Satellite Estimates of Precipitation in Equatorial Africa
485648.authors: Sharon E. Nicholson, FSU, Tallahassee, FL
485648.abstract: This presentation examines the reliability of satellite estimates of precipitation in the Congo Basin and over Lake Victoria and its catchment. Nine satellite products are considered. They are assessed by way of inter-comparison and by comparison with observational data sets. The three locations considered include a region with little observational gauge data (the Congo Basin), a region with extensive gauge data (Lake Victoria catchment) and an inland water body (Lake Victoria). Several important results emerge. For one, the diversity of estimates is generally very large, except for the Lake Victoria catchment. Most of the products either over-estimate or underestimate rainfall over the lake. The problem over over-lake rainfall is particularly severe for IMERG-F. Estimates by IMERG-F are roughly 36% higher than those from TRM 3B43. Estimates are also very problematic for the Congo Basin. Four sets of data were evaluated: the western region with high station gauge density, the eastern region with few stations, a time period (1983-94) when station gauge density was relatively high, and a time period (1998-2010) with few gauges available. The results confirm the importance of gauge data in producing reliable satellite estimates. The three different analyses performed (for the Congo Basin, for Lake Victoria, and for Victoria’s catchment) are in good agreement with respect to the most reliable satellite products. The more reliable satellite products for monthly and annual rainfall include IMERG-F, TRMM 4B43, GPCP 2.3, CHIRPS2, and PERSIANN-CDR. RMSE for the various estimates by the various satellites range from 20 mm/mo to 60 mm/mo. The diversity of estimates makes it difficult to assess the factors governing the interannual variability of rainfall in these regions. This is shown by way of correlation with sea- surface temperatures, with the Niño 3.4 temperatures, and with the Dipole Mode Index over the Indian Ocean. Some guidance is given as to the best products to utilize. Overall, any user must establish that the product in reliable in the region studied

485656.title: A Long-Duration Balloon Constellation As an Assimilation-Ready In-Situobserving System: Continuous Surface-to-Lower-Stratosphere Profiling And Multi-Reference Validation
485656.authors: Xiaoxu Tian, Independent, Clarksville, MD; and A. Tindle
485656.abstract: The upper-air observing system rests on three pillars, each with a structural gap. Radiosondes give high-resolution in-situ profiles but are launched from land roughly twice a day. Aircraft reports are plentiful yet confined to flight corridors and cruise altitudes. Satellites cover the globe, but their boundary-layer information is indirect and vertically coarse. The marine boundary layer and the data-sparse ocean basins are therefore poorly sampled in the quantity assimilation systems value most: direct, vertically resolved, in-situ profiles — a shortfall that helped motivate the most recent Earth-observation decadal survey to name the planetary boundary layer a priority observable. Sorcerer long-duration superpressure balloons address this gap with an unusual measurement property: because wind is the balloon's own GPS-tracked motion, the platform returns full-vector winds — not a single line-of-sight component — at every sampled altitude, unaffected by cloud and available over open ocean. We report six months of such profiles from the Sorcerer fleet. A balloon holds its buoyancy ceiling for weeks to months, drifts across the globe multiple times while profiling the troposphere and lower stratosphere, and descends toward the surface, sampling to a float ceiling near 14 km at roughly 50 m median vertical spacing. Float, sounding, and boundary-layer labels partition one continuous profile rather than three instruments; merging them recovers the full column. We validated 100 flights and 406,023 observations against two independent in-situ references — radiosondes and aircraft — together with the 137-level ECMWF operational analysis, treated as a consistency reference rather than independent truth because it assimilates observations of both kinds. Against radiosondes matched within 100 km, bias-corrected temperature agrees to 1.1 K and winds to 2.9 and 3.3 m s⁻¹ across 83 mid-latitude land profiles. Aircraft winds agree to a trimmed 2.5 and 2.9 m s⁻¹. Agreement with the operational analysis is consistent with both. The boundary-layer mode reaches an observation type no fixed network provides. Of 503 segments collocated within 50 km of an analysis column, 58 % lie over open ocean, with temperature agreeing to 1.09 K and winds to 1.9 and 2.3 m s⁻¹. Over the ocean the analysis is itself weakly observation-constrained and the bias model is land-radiosonde-trained, so this is mutual consistency rather than independent validation — but it characterizes in-situ marine boundary-layer measurements the radiosonde network cannot supply at all. Resolving the radiosonde-temperature and aircraft-wind errors against collocation separation bounds the instrument contribution at roughly 1 K and, in the eastward component, 2.1 m s⁻¹ — order-of-magnitude estimates that constrain the instrument term of an observation-error budget without by themselves specifying one. The products are encoded in IODA and BUFR, the latter delivered to the U.S. National Weather Service for ingest into operational forecasting workflows, and have been exercised end to end in a JEDI-based configuration. This contribution characterizes the measurement and its uncertainty; forecast-impact assessment is a separate, ongoing effort. Several limits condition how these data should be used. All validation collocations are Northern-Hemisphere, and no dedicated Southern-Hemisphere deployment has yet been made. Deep boundary-layer descents are commanded, and so occasional rather than routine. A daytime radiative warm bias at float altitude has been identified, flagged, and excluded from the validated products, with a hardware revision in development. Within those bounds, the platform delivers characterized, full-vector, cloud-independent in-situ profiles through a column that the existing network samples least well.

485668.title: A Physics-Based Parameterization for the Nearshore Drag Coefficient Based on Machine Learning
485668.authors: Beibei E, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and H. Potter and S. Zhang
485668.abstract: The drag coefficient (CD) is essential for estimating momentum flux across the air-sea interface, yet nearshore it remains difficult to represent using open-ocean parameterizations. Although recent observational studies have identified the dominant physical controls on nearshore CD, their nonlinear and interacting effects remain difficult to incorporate into practical bulk parameterizations. Here, we combine eddy covariance observations and machine learning (ML) to identify the dominant controls on nearshore CD and develop a physics-based parameterization. Measurements were collected at the U.S. Army Corps Field Research Facility (FRF) in Duck, North Carolina, as part of DUNEX (DUring Nearshore Events eXperiment) from November 2021 to January 2023. Four sonic anemometers mounted at 14-26 m on a beach tower sampled momentum fluxes associated with different footprints across the surf, shoaling, and inner shelf zones. These observations were combined with concurrent wave, current, bathymetric, tidal, and meteorological measurements from the FRF network. ML models explained up to 83% of the observed CD variability and identified wind direction, water depth, and wind speed as the dominant predictors. Interaction analysis further suggested that directional effects, characterized by CD decreasing as winds shift from shore-normal to alongshore, and depth-induced effects, reflected by CD decreasing with depth, are strongly coupled. Wind speed controls the overall magnitude of CD, with comparatively limited influence on its directional and depth dependence. Guided by these relationships, we developed a parameterization using wind speed as the baseline with explicit direction, depth, and interaction corrections. The resulting parameterization explains approximately 66% of the observed CD variability and substantially outperforms the Coupled Ocean-Atmosphere Response Experiment (COARE) 3.6 algorithm. These results demonstrate a framework for translating ML into physically interpretable nearshore CD parameterizations and provide a practical pathway for representing coastal heterogeneity in bulk air-sea flux algorithms.

485679.title: Hierarchical Large-Eddy Simulations of the Boundary Layer over Heterogeneous Terrain and Canopy at Bankhead National Forest Using the Energy Research and Forecasting (ERF) Model
485679.authors: Aaron Wang, PNNL, Richland, WA; and C. Kaul, Y. Liu, J. D. Fast, H. Liu, Z. Yang, Y. Qian, L. K. Berg, A. Lattanzi, A. Almgren, and H. Gopalan
485679.abstract: Forest canopies in the atmospheric boundary layer modulate turbulent fluxes, yet canopy heterogeneity is usually underrepresented in coarse-grid atmospheric models. This work uses idealized large-eddy simulations performed with the Energy Research and Forecasting (ERF) model and informed by observational data from Bankhead National Forest to examine a model hierarchy: from a homogeneous canopy to a realistically heterogeneous canopy, and finally to a realistic canopy with terrain. Neutral and stable conditions are tested, with the stable cases based on the radiosonde sounding. The results show that the temporally and horizontally averaged wind profiles are very similar between the runs with homogeneous and heterogeneous canopies, but the local turbulence structures are sensitive to the local canopy properties. The clearing around the main measurement site exhibits substantially higher wind speed and TKE, accompanied by flow descent into the canopy. The TKE and heat flux in the stable case agree reasonably well with the observations when the observational analysis window is shortened to reduce transient-state effects. Lagrangian particles in the realistic-canopy case are transported away from the canopy more efficiently than those in the homogeneous-canopy cases, owing to the vertical velocity induced by canopy heterogeneity. In summary, we show that canopy heterogeneity can affect local turbulence structures and the mean vertical transport of passive particles. This implies that caution is needed when comparing local observations with coarse-grid atmospheric models, and that moisture and aerosol fluxes originating from the surface may be underestimated if canopy heterogeneity is not accounted for.

485701.title: Effects of Heterogeneous Surfaces on Carbon Dioxide Transport in Stable Boundary Layers
485701.authors: Shenghao Zhang, KU Leuven, Leuven, Flemish-Brabant, Belgium; and J. Meyers
485701.abstract: Introduction: Surface heterogeneity can significantly affect the exchange of momentum, heat, and scalars between the atmosphere and the surface. In the nocturnal stable boundary layer, spatial heterogeneity arising from differences in surface may generate steady secondary motions, thereby preventing locally measured turbulent CO₂ fluxes from corresponding directly to surface sources and sinks. Large-eddy simulations (LES) are particularly well suited to investigating CO₂ flux non-closure because they provide full-field velocity and scalar information, allowing the contribution of non-propagating steady motions to be captured. This study uses a series of idealized LES to analyze the effects of surface-temperature and CO₂-flux heterogeneity on the CO₂ flux balance in the stable boundary layer. All cases are subjected to identical inflow conditions generated by a background simulation. The background flow is characterized by fixed surface Rossby and buoyancy numbers, with the potential temperature and CO₂ concentration fields reaching a statistically steady state in the presence of subsidence. A square patch is placed at the center of the computational domain. Zhang and Meyers (2026) have investigated cases in which its surface temperature or CO₂ emission flux are higher than that of the surrounding area, representing spatial variations caused by different vegetation types and surface thermal properties. The new simulations complete the set of heterogeneous cases with lower surface temperatures or CO₂ emission fluxes. A schematic is shown in Figure 1 and a case list is shown in Table 1. The simulations are performed using the SP-Wind solver, which solves the filtered incompressible Navier–Stokes equations together with the transport equations for potential temperature and CO₂ concentration. Results: When the surface temperature remains homogeneous while the CO₂ flux within the patch differs from that of the surrounding area, a shallow CO₂ internal boundary layer (IBL) forms above the patch. Within this IBL, the CO₂ flux shows a decoupling between the flux near the surface and the flux aloft. The results of Zhang and Meyers (2026) show that a higher patch temperature causes the near-surface IBL to become locally unstable, thereby enhancing the vertical turbulent transport of CO₂. Even when the surface CO₂ flux is completely homogeneous in the horizontal directions, the vertical turbulent CO₂ flux can increase by approximately 50% when the patch is only 1.65 K warmer than the surroundings, and the magnitude of this enhancement increases with increasing horizontal temperature difference. However, In the latest results, when the patch temperature is 1.65 K lower than that of the surroundings, the stable stratification within the IBL is strengthened, turbulent mixing is further suppressed, and the vertical development of the internal boundary layer is also restricted. Even when the surface CO₂ source flux remains homogeneous, the vertical turbulent CO₂ flux is reduced by nearly 30%, as shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3. In contrast to a warmer patch, which enhances mixing and smooths the flux profile, a colder patch produces a shallower IBL and further strengthens the decoupling between the surface flux and the overlying stable boundary layer. The results from the warmer-patch and newly added colder-patch cases reveal opposite relationship with CO₂ flux heterogeneity. Zhang and Meyers (2026) concluded that a competitive relationship exists between a higher patch temperature and CO₂ flux heterogeneity: greater heterogeneity in the patch CO₂ flux produces more significant flux decoupling, whereas a higher temperature smooths the profile by enhancing mixing. By contrast, with lower patch-temperature this competitive relationship does not exists due to the fact that vertical turbulent transport is further suppressed. Although spanwise heterogeneity also lead to strong secondary motions, its effects are primarily confined to the vicinity of the patch edges. A detailed CO₂ budget analysis near the center of the patch further supports the conclusions of Zhang and Meyers (2026). Under temperature heterogeneity, the pronounced changes in streamwise mean advection, vertical mean advection, and vertical turbulent flux together establish a new CO₂ budget balance, with the difference that the signs of these contributions reverse when the sign of the temperature difference is reversed. On the other hand, CO₂ flux heterogeneity primarily modifies the budget-partitioning between the vertical turbulent flux and streamwise mean advection. Ongoing and future work: Building on these findings, our ongoing work aims to examine more closely the mechanisms governing IBL growth. To separate streamwise IBL development from the secondary motions generated at the spanwise patch edges, we simplify the configuration to one-dimensional step changes in surface temperature and CO₂ flux along the streamwise direction. We are also developing a simple LES-free numerical model, which uses Monin–Obukhov similarity theory, including stability corrections to construct profiles of velocity and scalar quantities given the upstream and downstream surface conditions. The IBL height can be then predicted by imposing a matching condition between the two equilibrium profiles, analogous to classical equilibrium models for step changes in surface roughness (Elliott, 1958). LES data are used to validate the predicted IBL growth and, potentially, to fit the parameters of a blending model. References: Zhang, S., & Meyers, J. (2026). Carbon Dioxide Transport in the Stable Boundary Layer over Heterogeneous Surfaces: An Idealized Large-Eddy Simulation Study. Boundary-Layer Meteorology, 192(7), 36. Elliott, W. P. (1958). The growth of the atmospheric internal boundary layer. Eos, Transactions American Geophysical Union, 39(6), 1048-1054.

485704.title: Low-Level Storm-Relative Flow in Tornadic and Nontornadic Supercells: Using Great Plains Environments to Model Impacts on Supercell Behavior
485704.authors: Luke Anderson, Valparaiso University, Valparaiso, IN; and M. D. Flournoy and R. A. Saba
485704.abstract: A few recent studies have used high-resolution deterministic- and ensemble-based approaches to model supercell behavior in composite VORTEX2 environments in the Great Plains. These are derived from the Parker (2014) VORTEX2 tornadic and nontornadic profiles. A key difference between these two wind profiles is the degree of streamwiseness in the lowest few-hundred m AGL, which has subsequent impacts on low-level mesocyclone organization and steadiness; simulated tornadic storms feature stronger and steadier low-level dynamic lift than nontornadic ones. In a more comprehensive study of Great Plains supercell environments, Coniglio and Parker (2020, CP20) noted less differences in low-level streamwiseness but instead greater differences in storm-relative flow. This suggests that different storm-scale processes may drive storm-environment relationships in the CP20 dataset. This study uses high-resolution idealized modeling experiments, created using the CP20 profiles as the homogeneous base state, to examine these storm-scale processes. The resulting analyses showed some similarities, but also some fairly different storm scale processes from the modeled supercells initialized using the composite VORTEX2 environments. Rather than primarily crosswise low-level horizontal vorticity, the forward flank outflow is the primary reason for a weaker low-level updraft in the nontornadic environment. This study also sheds light on a more generalizable tornadogenesis failure mode in Great Plains supercells.

485705.title: JEDI Variational Bias Correction for Global Forecast System Satellite Data Assimilation: a Convergence and Spin-Up Stability Analysis
485705.authors: Diana Sophia Suralik, NWS, Riverdale Park, MD; RSMAS, Coral Gables, FL
485705.abstract: Variational Bias Correction (VarBC) is a critical component of modern numerical weather prediction systems, enabling adaptive correction of systematic observation biases within variational data assimilation frameworks. VarBC has been extensively tested and operationally applied within the NOAA Global Forecast System (GFS) using the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) system, where it has demonstrated substantial benefits for satellite radiance assimilation. As NOAA transitions toward the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework, an evaluation of VarBC performance within JEDI is needed to determine the behavior and advantages achieved. VarBC performance in JEDI has not yet been extensively evaluated and variations in software architecture and observation handling may impact its effectiveness. This project establishes two JEDI assimilation experiments using identical satellite radiance datasets to evaluate VarBC stability and spin-up dynamics, with one utilizing standard operational bias coefficient initialization and a second initialized from zero. VarBC performance is evaluated across both configurations through bias predictor coefficient evolution, observation-minus-background (O - B) and normalized standard deviation diagnostics. The evaluation assesses adaptation rates, channel-to-channel consistency throughout assimilation cycles, and the system's capacity to reduce mean bias and variance from different starting states. Ultimately, this work provides a critical account of VarBC behavior and convergence characteristics within JEDI, identifies strengths and limitations of the current implementation, and provides actionable recommendations to aid in the transition to operations.

485718.title: From Cold Fronts to Cold Season: Building Meteorologists' Capacity to Deliver Health Messaging
485718.authors: Sarah Gillani, Center for Outbreak Response Innovation, Baltimore, MD
485718.abstract: Climate-sensitive infectious diseases — from seasonal respiratory illness to vector-borne threats like West Nile virus and Eastern equine encephalitis — demand communication channels that reach the public routinely, locally, and through trusted messengers. Broadcast meteorologists are uniquely positioned to fill this role: they already translate complex environmental science into actionable guidance, and they reach large local audiences daily. The Johns Hopkins Center for Outbreak Response Innovation (CORI) operates on the hypothesis that if the public routinely receives disease information, they will respond more effectively when urgent communication is needed during outbreaks. Market research conducted by CORI at the 2026 AMS Annual Meeting (N=271) demonstrates readiness on both sides of the screen. Among surveyed meteorologists who currently provide information to the public (n=49), 95.9% believe they should have a role in communicating health information beyond weather-related risks. Among general public respondents, 92.1% (n=215) said it would be helpful for meteorologists to provide health information such as flu forecasts, and 87.4% (n=222) indicated they would watch a recurring local health forecast. Yet only about two-thirds of meteorologists reported feeling comfortable delivering brief health updates on-air, and the most commonly cited barrier was a lack of training and access to credible, ready-to-use health information. This presentation introduces a training developed in direct response to that need. Drawing on CORI's partnerships with nine TV stations across English- and Spanish-language markets covering respiratory illness and many other public health threats, the training equips meteorologists to identify credible surveillance data, translate it into accurate 30–60 second broadcast segments, and time messaging to seasonal disease patterns — building a sustainable, trusted channel for infectious disease communication before, during, and after outbreaks.

485728.title: Reconciling Cloud-Droplet Nucleating, Residual, and Scavenged Particles with Cloud Supersaturations during the Eastern Pacific Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment (EPCAPE) (Invited Presentation)
485728.authors: Lynn M Russell, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, LA JOLLA, CA; and A. S. Williams, V. Berta, C. Pelayo, D. Lubin, J. L. Dedrick, R. Farley, A. C. Aiken, PhD, E. Ravichandran, M. D. Petters, L. Robinson, R. Y. W. Chang, M. Wheeler, J. Wentzell, J. Liggio, and M. A. Miller
485728.abstract: The DOE ARM Eastern Pacific Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment (EPCAPE) provided an unprecedented characterization of aerosol-cloud interactions by sampling hundreds of hours of cloud-droplet nucleating, residual, and cloud-scavenged particles with simultaneous measurements of very consistent bulk cloud properties. The consistency of the typically northwesterly air masses arriving at the two EPCAPE sites of Scripps Pier and Mt. Soledad after roughly following the southern California coast for the prior two days meant that the mixture of urban and marine emissions had limited variability. This consistency in both the aerosol sources and cloud structure meant that the cloud, aerosol, and precipitation measurements from February 2023 to February 2024 provide a sufficiently large data set for statistical analyses of aerosol-cloud interactions through correlations of paired variables as well as multilinear regressions. These analyses provide multiple overlapping perspectives, which can be reconciled provide complementary lines of evidence to improve quantification of aerosol-cloud interactions. Particles on which cloud droplets nucleate were measured outside of clouds as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) at supersaturations from 0.1 to 1.0%, and comparing measured cloud concentrations and diameters provides estimates of the effective cloud supersaturation. For example, CCN concentrations are similar to cloud droplet number concentrations at supersaturations near 0.1%. This correspondence suggests that the effective supersaturation of the cloud was typically 0.1%, with a range of values likely representing variability in updrafts. This value is consistent with satellite-retrieved droplet number concentrations coinciding with in situ CCN concentrations. A third line of evidence is provided by a “bottom-up” calculation of the critical diameter based on measured composition that matches the Hoppel minimum diameter and indicates a maximum cloud supersaturation of 0.2%, reflecting the ensemble of updraft velocities that contributed to growing the accumulation mode in the preceding cloud cycles. These multiple retrievals of cloud supersaturation show subtle differences in complementary methods, as well as overall consistency that constrains the uncertainty. Size-resolved and single-particle measurements sampled below and in cloud also provide new constraints on particle activation and droplet growth. For example, single-particle composition measurements support calculating the fraction of droplets that are activated at the effective cloud supersaturation in both haze and cloud conditions. Quantifying upwind and on-site cloudiness provides clear associations to aqueous cloud oxidation reactions of sulfate, nitrate, and organic components. Hygroscopic properties show sensitivity to sulfur and nitrogen-containing organic compounds. Together these results show aerosol-cloud and cloud-aerosol effects for a variety of aerosol sources and cloud conditions, providing important constraints for modeling aerosol indirect effects.

485744.title: An Exploration of Heat Warning Threshold in North Carolina and Potential Implications for Localizing Extreme Heat Warning Standards
485744.authors: McKenzie Rose Peters, North Carolina State Climate Office, Raleigh, NC; and T. Glotfelty
485744.abstract: Heat stress is commonly communicated using heat index (HI), whereas wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) provides a more comprehensive measure of heat stress, that considers exposure to sun and wind. As extreme heat becomes a growing concern, we explore whether current National Weather Service (NWS) heat index thresholds adequately represent hazardous heat conditions by comparing NWS heat advisories (HI ≥105°F) and extreme heat warnings (HI ≥110°F) with WBGT threat levels across North Carolina. We analyze 30-minute observations from the North Carolina Environment and Climate Observing Network (ECONet) during the 2020–2025 heat seasons (May 1 – September 30). Daily maximum WBGT threat levels are determined by requiring conditions to persist for at least two consecutive hours to match NWS heat index criteria. Results show that High and Extreme WBGT conditions occur more frequently than NWS heat advisories and warnings based on current HI thresholds, indicating that hazardous heat is potentially under-warned. Lowering the heat advisory threshold to 98°F across the NC Piedmont and Coastal Plain captured all Extreme WBGT conditions and approximately 75% of High WBGT conditions while placing heat advisories on only 16% of all days in the study period. An 88°F threshold in the western Mountains similarly captured all High and Extreme WBGT conditions and 80% of Moderate WBGT conditions, reflecting the region’s cooler climatology. The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services derived heat index thresholds that coincide with an increase in emergency room visits due to heat-related illness for use in their Heat Health Alert System. In comparison to their work, we found that our thresholds align nicely, especially their early season thresholds. These findings suggest that region-specific reductions in HI thresholds would better align public heat messaging with hazardous heat, improving preparedness and response to extreme heat.

485746.title: Regional Meteorological/Chemical Data Assimilation and Top-Down Emissions Esitmation with DART as Modified for Atmospheric Composition Assimilation (Chem-DART): Developments and Applications
485746.authors: Arthur P. Mizzi, ARC, Moffett Field, MA; and M. S. Johnson, C. H. Hsu, Y. Cui, D. K. Henze, B. C. McDonald, R. Kumar, K. Miyazaki, J. Benik, A. Raman, D. J. Posselt, and L. Wu
485746.abstract: We will present a summary of the latest developments for and applications of WRF-Chem/Chem-DART - the NSF NCAR Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF; Skamrock et al., 2019) model with online atmospheric chemistry (WRF-Chem; Grell et al., 2005) interfaced with the NSF NCAR Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART; Anderson et al., 2009) as modified to include regional atmospheric composition assimilation and "top-down" emission estimation using the "state-augmentation method." (Chem-DART; Mizzi et al., 2016; 2018). This is the 10th year anniversary of WRF-Chem/Chem-DART. It is being used for atmospheric composition data assimilation and emissions estimation research throughout North America, East Asia, and Western Europe. It assimilates a broad suite of meteorological and chemical in-situ, profiler, and satellite observations that include NOAA PrepBufr observations and carbon monoxide (CO), carbon dioxide (CO2), ozone (O3), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur dioxide (SO2), particulate matter (PM), aerosol optical depth (AOD), formaldehyde (HCHO), and methane (CH4) retrievals from TEMPO, TROPOMI, OMI, MOPITT, IASI, MODIS, GOME, SCIAMACHY, MLS, TES, CrIS, and OCO-2). WRF-Chem/Chem-DART recent developments include: A modular real-time scripting system that manages all forecasting/assimilation/emissions estimation cycling tasks: (a) downscaling large-scale meteorological and chemical input data to the WRF-Chem domains for initial and/or boundary conditions (ICs/BCs); (b) generating the anthropogenic, biomass burning, and biogenic emissions; (c) generating the meteorological/chemical IC/BC and emissions ensemble members; (d) collecting and preprocessing the observations; and (e) managing the assimilation, dynamic emissions estimation, and forecasting steps. Refactoring of the atmospheric composition and emissions ensemble generation algorithm to: (a) use unique perturbation patterns for each atmospheric composition and emissions state variable; (b) use parallel coding for optimization of the perturbation algorithms; and (c) generate greater and more reasonable spread about the ensemble mean spread. Optimize the real-time scripting system code. We will present results from four WRF-Chem/Chem-DART applications: TEMPO/TROPOMI NO2 and HCHO observing system (Hsu et al., 2024), real data independent (Hsu et al., 2026a), and real data joint (Hsu et al., 20206b) assimilation/emissions estimation/forecast experiments. Generally, these experiments show that the increased temporal resolution of the TEMPO observations improves analysis/forecast/emission estimation skill relative to TROPOMI. Additionally, they show that jointly constraining nitrogen oxide (NOx) and non-methane volatile organic compound (NMVOC) emissions significantly improves the analysis/forecast skill for ozone (O3). TROPOMI CH4 real data assimilation/emissions estimation/forecast experiments (Cui et al., 20206). The goal of this application is to explicitly quantify regional methane emissions for California. The optimized emissions (based on constraining CH4 concentration and emissions) in conjunction with improved atmospheric transport (based on constraining the meteorology) shows improved agreement with independent tower measurements. Tropospheric Regional Atmospheric Composition and Emissions Reanalysis 2005-2023 (TRACER-I) preliminary results. TRACER-I will begin/began its production runs near the end of 2026 Q3. We will present an overview of the TRACER-I regional reanalysis system and preliminary results (concentrations, emissions, and uncertainties) from the April reanalyses for all years. Very-High-Resolution (≤ 3 km horizontal grid resolution) real data assimilation/emissions estimation/forecast experiments preliminary results. This is very much a work-in-progress. The goal is to explore and improve very-high-resolution meteorological and/or atmospheric composition forecasting/assimilation/emissions estimation. We will present results comparing five experiments: (i) CNTL Exp - control experiments that assimilate meteorology only at 5 km and at 2.5 km horizontal grid resolutions; (ii) CHEM DA Exp - experiments that are similar to the CNTL Exps except we also assimilate atmospheric chemistry observations without emissions estimation; and (iii) EMISS DA Exp - experiments that are similar to CHEM DA Exps except we also impose dynamic emissions estimation. We will conclude our presentation with a summary of expected future work and research directions for regional atmospheric composition forecasting/assimilation/emissions estimation.

485754.title: An Interactive GIS-Based 3D Flood Simulation Tool to Support Resilient Community Design
485754.authors: Dan Pisut, ESRI, Palm Springs, CA
485754.abstract: Flood events pose threats to human life and property. To effectively mitigate these disasters there is a need for a range of flood simulation tools. These range from engineering tools based on highly detailed physics models for hydraulic and civil engineering professionals to more rapid and approximate simulation tools for a wider audience looking for initial insight. In this paper we describe a new rapid flood simulation tool that is integrated into GIS software and runs on off-the-shelf GPU-based hardware. This flood simulation tool is designed to support rapid simulation and initial exploration but does not handle all the conditions and flow regimes that can occur in the real world. However, it does allow for custom DEMs, rain rate, infiltration, roughness, sinks, buildings/barriers, etc. It can be used by GIS users to obtain previews of water flows for the supported subset of conditions, for initial geo-design and exploration of design alternatives, and as a useful way to explore and validate data quality. The simulation results are integrated into the GIS, meaning that attributes of the flood (both spatial and temporal) can be joined and analyzed with other features, such as buildings, roads, or other map features. We will demonstrate how this tool can be used to iterate mitigation options, including engineered and nature-based solutions, and effectively communicate plans during stakeholder engagement.

485784.title: The NESDIS Product Requirement Change Management (PRCM) Process: Bridging User Needs to Operational Earth Science Capabilities
485784.authors: Xiaofang "Bonnie" Zhu, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; NESDIS, Silver Spring, MD; and D. Achuthavarier and W. W. Wolf
485784.abstract: Translating evolving multi-agency operational requirements into sustained satellite product capabilities requires a structured, transparent governance framework. The NOAA NESDIS Product Requirement Change Management (PRCM) process—governed by the NESDIS Product and Service Governance team—serves as the centralized enterprise entry point for all Level-2 and higher product change requests. Operating under official NESDIS procedural guidelines (NESDIS-PLN-1316.1), PRCM bridges user needs from NOAA Line Offices and interagency partners directly into the NESDIS science investment and operational transition pipelines. This presentation outlines PRCM’s end-to-end architecture and multi-stage evaluation workflow. Submitted requests undergo initial screening, technical review by a multi-office PRCM Board, and Impact Assessment Team evaluations to determine technical feasibility, architecture impacts, and operational readiness. From 2021 through 2026, PRCM processed 63 requests, funding 40 for operational transition—including the RAVE fire weather product and the machine-learning-based LightningCast model. Modernized via automated Smartsheet tracking and a PRCM portal, PRCM provides a transparent, one-stop framework to systematically bridge targeted user needs with next-generation operational capabilities.

485786.title: Frameworks for Public-Private Partnerships in the Weather Enterprise
485786.authors: Michael C. Kruk, NOAA, Gulfport, MS
485786.abstract: The NOAA Technology Partnerships Office (TPO) is responsible for technology transfer and commercialization across NOAA, and offers a unique and critical perspective on the collaborative frameworks essential for advancing the weather and water enterprise. Our participation brings a grounded, practical viewpoint on how to bridge the gap between federal innovation and private sector application, a core theme of this vital symposium, and how to foster public-private partnerships. The presentation will share insights and case studies from our extensive experience managing Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs), patent licensing agreements, and other collaborative vehicles. Our discussion will focus on how these tools are actively used to transition cutting-edge technologies, from advanced observational platforms to novel AI/ML algorithms, from NOAA's research labs into the hands of private industry, ultimately enhancing the nation's predictive capabilities and creating economic value. In addition, the presentation will feature key discussion points from the perspective of a federal technology transfer office, including strategies for overcoming barriers to technology transition, best practices for structuring effective data sharing agreements, and the role of federal partnerships in de-risking new technologies for commercial adoption. Finally, the discussion will provide actionable strategies for building the robust public-private partnerships necessary to empower a thriving and resilient enterprise.

485791.title: Bridging Data Silos in NOAA NESDIS: The CAPTURE Process for Enterprise Data Governance and Decision Support
485791.authors: Xiaofang "Bonnie" Zhu, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and O. Miskala-Dinc, MS, R. Romero, W. W. Wolf, D. Achuthavarier, I. Guch, and K. Ferede
485791.abstract: Effective science data stewardship relies on bridging discipline-oriented silos, establishing robust metadata governance, and connecting observational infrastructure with user-driven operational needs. Within NOAA’s National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS), a wealth of product and portfolio information has been maintained across separate, unlinked catalogs—including the Integrated Product List (IPL), Five-Year Product Plan (FYPP), Enterprise Algorithm Project Plans (EPP), and Environmental Observing Requirements Option System (EORES). This fragmented architecture introduced data inconsistencies, complicated decision support, and necessitated costly annual data calls. To establish a dynamic, connected database, the NESDIS Product and Service Governance team developed the CAPTURE (Centralized Analytics & Product Tracking for Unified REporting) hub. Built in Jira Assets with front-end eazyBI dashboards, CAPTURE consolidates, leverages, and cross-validates disparate sources into an object-oriented relational database. By connecting satellite sensors, algorithms, product attributes, office ownership, and user priorities, CAPTURE delivers end-to-end data traceability and auto-generated data documents. The platform provides actionable business intelligence to answer critical questions at the click of a button—such as instantly identifying downstream product and user impacts when a sensor experiences degradation. This presentation details CAPTURE’s architecture, prototype dashboards (e.g., sensor impact, algorithm flyout charts), and backend dataset reconciliation. Furthermore, as NESDIS transitions to Jira Cloud, we share progress on testing Atlassian Analytics to enhance dashboard capabilities, alongside the implementation roadmap for stakeholder roadshows. CAPTURE demonstrates how collaborative stewardship and unified analytics empower scientists, product owners, and leadership across the enterprise.

485807.title: The Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS): New Sensors, Algorithm Enhancements, Artificial Intelligence, and Operational Applications
485807.authors: Shuyan Liu, Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies, College Park, MD; and Y. K. Lee, X. Liang, J. X. Yang, W. Wang, and H. Meng
485807.abstract: The Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS) is NOAA’s operational one-dimensional variational (1DVAR) retrieval system for retrieving atmospheric temperature and water vapor profiles, hydrometeor parameters, surface emissivity, skin temperature, precipitation, and cryospheric parameters from passive microwave radiance observations. Based on physically based radiative transfer modeling and one-dimensional variational optimization, MiRS provides a unified retrieval framework applicable across a broad range of passive microwave sounders and imagers, providing consistent environmental data records (EDRs) for weather forecasting, and other Earth System applications. Recent developments have substantially expanded MiRS capabilities through support for both next-generation and commercial microwave observing systems, including Metop-SG A1 MWS, the Arctic Weather Satellite (AWS), Tomorrow.io microwave sounders, QuickSounder, and TROPICS. Weather Stream’s Global Environmental Monitoring System (GEMS2) and Spire’s Hyperspectral Microwave Sounder (HyMS) will be included in MiRS soon. Long-term sustainment efforts have also strengthened calibration, validation, quality monitoring, and operational reliability for legacy and current operational sensors, including SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, Metop-B, Metop-C, and GPM. Significant algorithm enhancements have further improved MiRS retrieval performance. A novel Level-1B brightness temperature denoising technique was applied to Tomorrow.io’s microwave sounders and effectively removes striping and other structured instrument artifacts while preserving geophysical signals, improving radiometric quality and downstream retrieval performance across multiple microwave sensors. Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an integral component of the evolving MiRS framework. Machine learning based precipitation enhancement has been integrated into MiRS, substantially improving rain rate estimation while maintaining the physical consistency of the underlying 1DVAR retrieval. The newly developed MiRS-AI framework employs deep neural networks to retrieve atmospheric temperature and water vapor profiles directly from satellite brightness temperatures, providing improved retrieval accuracy together with significantly enhanced computational efficiency. A regression-based method has been applied to derive Level-1B brightness temperature limb-correction coefficients, providing an efficient, data-driven alternative to conventional limb-correction approaches, which will be updated with an AI approach. Additional AI applications include sea surface temperatures retrievals, surface emissivity retrievals, and microwave imagery enhancement. Recent operational evaluations and validation demonstrate the maturity and operational readiness of the MiRS framework across an expanding constellation of microwave sensors. These advances further establish MiRS as NOAA’s unified operational microwave retrieval system, enabling the integration of new sensors, algorithm innovations, and AI technologies into operational environmental satellite products. Future work includes support for JPSS-3/4, expanded commercial satellite missions, and additional AI-enhanced retrieval capabilities.

485824.title: An Interactive Visualization System to Replay NOAA Hurricane Reconnaissance Data
485824.authors: Diego Xiao Barbero, NOAA/OMAO Aircraft Operations Center, Lakeland, FL; and J. Zawislak, J. J. Murdock, and R. T. Knapp
485824.abstract: The sheer volume of disparate data collected on each hurricane reconnaissance mission by NOAA/OMAO’s Aircraft Operations Center (AOC) presents an ongoing challenge to synthesizing that data cohesively. The data collected by the WP-3D and G-IV aircraft holds extensive operational and research value, but previous in-house tools relied on standalone, user-input-dependent Python scripts that produced little spatial or radar context. This problem motivated the objective of this project, which is the development of the AOC Mission Visualizer, a browser-based tool that combines retrieval, visualization, and synchronization of mission data within a single client-side environment that requires no installation and can run entirely offline if mission data is cached locally. The tool visualizes missions in two- and three-dimensional maps with configurable time-series plots of any recorded variable, and can time-synchronize flight-level data with precipitation radar recordings. If there is an internet connection, a storm archive browser will help the user automatically retrieve full-resolution mission data based on year, storm, and flight ID, removing the need to manually upload files, and offering the option to overlay corresponding GOES imagery and best track information for the storm. The outcome of the project is that the visualization tool supports mission debriefs, aircrew training, and meteorological research. For example, AOC Flight Directors already use the Visualizer to replay historical missions for interesting in-flight encounters with extreme turbulence, eyewall passes, and rapid intensification events. As AOC’s Science Branch fully integrates this tool into its processes, the tool promises to modernize AOC’s ability to better train aircrews to safely fly hurricanes, improve data quality control within a meteorological context, and understand hurricane behavior, all of which allow AOC to accomplish NOAA’s broader mission to improve hurricane forecasting and prepare the public for hazards that storms bring to their communities.

485825.title: Evaluating Temporal Resolution Effects on Optical Flow-based Satellite Cloud Nowcasting
485825.authors: Matthew P. King, Air Force Institute of Technology, Wright-Patterson AFB, OH; and S. Aho, C. L. Zoellick, PhD, and C. Pasillas, PhD
485825.abstract: Short-term cloud forecasting (0–3 hours) remains highly relevant to both military and commercial applications. Given the high-temporal-resolution scanning cadences of modern operational geostationary satellites, optical flow-based cloud nowcasting has emerged as a compelling option for providing timely predictions of 3D cloud locations. These predictions have demonstrated accuracy metrics that rival those of high-resolution mesoscale models in short prediction scales and offer low computational costs for first guess inputs to machine learning-based models. While some imagers provide data at 5-minute or even 1-minute cadences, the impact of such high-temporal-resolution imagery on the accuracy of optical flow-based nowcasting remains an open question. In this study, we investigate the effects of varying the temporal resolution input to the recently published I-NOW algorithm (King et al., 2026). Through a series of experiments, we determine whether increased temporal resolution imparts greater accuracy to brightness temperature and cloud field nowcasts. King, M. P., J. M. Apke, S. D. Miller, K. Haynes, Y. Noh, and J. M. Haynes, 2026: Nowcasting 3D Cloud Fields Using Forward Warping Optical Flow. J. Atmos. Oceanic Technol., 43, 213–237, https://doi.org/10.1175/JTECH-D-24-0140.1.

485830.title: Evaluation of Three Ice Accumulation Models for use in the Freezing Rain Accumulation National Analysis (FRANA)
485830.authors: Bryce Vining, NOAA Ernest F. Hollings Scholarship Program, Norman, OK; and D. D. Tripp, J. J. Gourley, and A. A. Rosenow
485830.abstract: Freezing rain is a highly impactful winter weather phenomena which can pose great risks to public safety and infrastructure. Recently, a new product called the Freezing Rain Accumulation National Analysis (FRANA) was developed to offer a real-time analysis of ice storms for nowcasting and post-event verification. However, its core ice accretion model, the Freezing Rain Accumulation Model (FRAM) has been shown to have a high bias in estimating ice accretion. This project aims to evaluate the performance of two alternative ice accretion models developed by the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory (CRREL) and a newly developed random forest (RF) regression model and benchmark against the FRAM. The FRAM, CRREL, and RF models are evaluated against a 12 year archive of Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) ice accretion data. Findings reveal a consistent high bias in the CRREL simple model with potential for bias correction. A bias-correction scheme was developed and applied resulting in the model becoming competitive with FRAM. The more complex CRREL model incorporating calculations for several heat fluxes was evaluated but does not outperform FRAM. The newly developed RF model was evaluated to have a modest increase in predictive skill in comparison to the FRAM model. Additionally, the RF mitigates the high bias of FRAM. This model could potentially provide more accurate analyses of high magnitude ice storms in FRANA. This study quantifies the performance and behavior of three ice accumulation models for the National Weather Service to make an informed decision regarding potential updates to FRANA.

485833.title: Conditions Facilitating Resuspension of Volcanic Ash at Mt. St. Helens
485833.authors: Peyton Braun, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and C. Neuman
485833.abstract: More than 45 years later, the impacts of the 1980 Mt. St. Helens volcanic eruption persist as strong winds periodically pick up deposited ash and loft it into the atmosphere. Though smaller ash resuspension events are often confined within the crater, larger events can send ash above 10,000 feet and over 50 miles away, creating an aviation and public health hazard. To determine the meteorological conditions facilitating ash resuspension, 34 events, spanning 2002 to 2026, were identified through media reports, timelapse videos, and pilot reports. Satellite imagery, webcam imagery, reanalysis data, and surface observations were examined to develop criteria for defining each event’s severity. Results indicate small-scale resuspension is relatively common in dry summer conditions while larger resuspension events impacting aviation and public health occur infrequently. The synoptic pattern often features a 500mb ridge offshore of the Pacific Northwest, promoting broad near-surface easterly flow across the region which warms and dries as it descends over the Cascades. Strong westerly winds have also been observed to facilitate resuspension, though this is a far less common phenomenon. This study provides an operational framework for meteorologists to identify conditions conducive to ash resuspension while laying the groundwork for a tool which, after further refinement, will send an email notification when it detects upcoming conditions suitable for resuspension. The combination of a heightened understanding of resuspension and an alerting system for potential event days will enable more accurate forecasting with longer lead times, strengthen hazard messaging, improve aviation safety and route planning, and reduce the likelihood of harmful ash encounters in the Mt. St. Helens area.

485840.title: Developing a Marine Wind and Wave Height Climatology for ENSO Phases in the Pacific Northwest
485840.authors: Zoe Crow, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; University of Maine, Orono, ME; and C. Neuman
485840.abstract: Strong winds and large seas routinely impact the Pacific Northwest (PNW) coastal waters by creating life-threatening conditions for mariners, halting bar crossings, and disrupting regional economic activity. To support operational forecasting, a marine wind and wave height climatology was developed for offshore PNW buoys utilizing historical hourly observations from National Data Buoy Center buoys 46015, 46029, 46041, 46050, and 46089. Periods of record vary by buoy, collectively spanning 1984–2025. Wind and wave observations were classified according to Portland National Weather Service marine hazard criteria, providing forecasters with a climatological framework for identifying anomalous seasonal conditions and communicating associated risks to mariners. Seasonal influence of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) on regional wind and wave hazards was also investigated by comparing the total hours and days of hazardous sea conditions across ENSO phases. During the cool season (October–March), hazardous seas and gale force wind gusts occurred more frequently during moderate to strong La Niña winters at buoys 46029, 46041, and 46050. On average, these winters experienced 20–30 more days of hazardous seas and 10–15 more days of gale force wind gusts compared with weak La Niña or neutral winters. In contrast, no discernible relationship between hazardous conditions and ENSO phases was found during the warm season (April–September). These results are consistent with the typical northward displacement of the polar jet stream during La Nina winters, which brings more frequent storms to the PNW. These findings provide forecasters and mariners with seasonal guidance on the likelihood of hazardous wind and wave conditions based on ENSO phase forecasts.

485874.title: Conditions Facilitating the Resuspension of Volcanic Ash at Mt. St. Helens
485874.authors: Peyton Braun, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and C. Neuman
485874.abstract: More than 45 years later, the impacts of the 1980 Mt. St. Helens volcanic eruption persist as strong winds periodically pick up deposited ash and loft it into the atmosphere.
