485875.title: Southern vs. Arctic Ocean Low-Level Cloud Radiative Effects and Implications for Mixed-Phase Cloud Thinning
485875.authors: Lauren M. Zamora, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and J. F. Kok, A. T. Evan, A. Kuwano, K. Moore, and X. Li
485875.abstract: Mixed-phase cloud thinning (MCT) is a proposed polar climate intervention in which added ice-nucleating particles (INPs) may glaciate low mixed-phase clouds, enhance longwave cooling, and reduce polar warming during polar night. However, observational constraints on this mechanism remain limited and polar cloud simulations are subject to high uncertainties. Here, we use satellite and reanalysis products to conduct a natural experiment with conditions analogous to the presence and lack of MCT. Using CloudSat/CALIPSO cloud observations and ECMWF and MERRA-2 meteorology, we compare meteorologically matched shallow, single-layer, mixed-phase clouds over the Southern Ocean with those over the Arctic Ocean, where INP concentrations are higher. Since dust is an effective INP source below -15 °C, differences between the Southern and Arctic oceans may be driven by greater dust abundance in the Arctic. At temperatures below -15 °C, Southern Ocean low-level clouds are less glaciated, are optically thicker, and produce larger longwave cloud radiative effects at the surface directly below clouds than Arctic clouds under matched meteorological conditions. Also, over open ocean, Southern Ocean clouds are more prevalent. These contrasts are consistent with the sign of the response expected from MCT. The largest differences occur at the surface over sea ice, where longwave cloud forcing directly underneath clouds differs by about 7.6 to 8 W m-2, while differences are on the order of 0.8 to 1.6 W m-2 at the top of the atmosphere over the warmer open ocean. Cloud responses in higher, thicker, or multilayer clouds remain uncertain. Overall, our results suggest that INP seeding of low-level polar clouds could reduce surface warming under favorable conditions, although impacts are not large enough to substitute for greenhouse gas emissions reductions.

485904.title: Sensitivity of Heavy Precipitation Forecasts to Wind and Moisture Errors Under Strong Large-Scale Moisture Flux Environments
485904.authors: Hsu-Feng Teng, National Taiwan University, Taipei, Taiwan
485904.abstract: This study assesses the impact of wind and moisture error characteristics on forecasting strong large-scale moisture flux systems over the western North Pacific, and quantifies the relative importance of specific error reductions for heavy precipitation forecast improvements in Taiwan. Twenty-five extreme rainfall events characterized by strong moisture flux and significant operational forecast errors in the Global Forecast System were selected. On average, these events produced a maximum accumulated rainfall of 942 mm in southern Taiwan, associated with a moisture flux of 603 kg m-1 s-1. Due to wind and moisture biases, total rainfall was underestimated by an average of 313 mm. Through additional data assimilation processes, each individual improvement in zonal wind, meridional wind, or moisture reduced moisture flux forecast errors, thereby mitigating precipitation errors by 54%. Results from sensitivity experiments indicate that the precipitation forecast improvements were more sensitive to moisture enhancements than to wind adjustments. Specifically, the contributions of moisture at mid-levels and within the cyclonic circulation to increased precipitation were more significant than those at low-levels and within the southwesterly monsoon flow. In summary, this study demonstrates the error characteristics of moisture flux toward Taiwan and highlights the key factors for mitigating the underestimation in heavy precipitation forecasts.

485918.title: AI - Structure-Level Risk Model for 2025 Eaton and Palisades Fires
485918.authors: Nate Joseph Dailey, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC
485918.abstract: This research builds structure-level models for the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires to better understand the factors that caused these events to be so destructive. For each building in the respective fire footprint, variables representing structure density, presence of vegetation, slope, wind alignment, and structure age are included. These variables were inputted into logistic regression and XGBoost models to predict whether residential-scale structures burned or survived, using models trained and tested within each fire area as well as across fires. Within-area models achieved accuracies of 0.67–0.73, with XGBoost producing more balanced performance across classes (F1: 0.75–0.79 burned, 0.52–0.63 unburned) than logistic regression (F1: 0.80 burned, 0.44–0.52 unburned). Cross-area models retained reasonable predictive performance (accuracies of 0.64–0.70), demonstrating that the models generalize across distinct fire events. Density of surrounding structures and the presence of vegetation were the most impactful predictors, but slope, structure age, wind alignment, and structure area were also significant factors. These findings are consistent with prior research identifying built-environment characteristics as key drivers of structural loss during urban conflagrations. Because the models rely solely on pre-fire data, they are transferable to other fire-prone urban areas. Given the scale of destruction and long-term social and economic impacts caused by the Eaton and Palisades fires, structure-level risk models such as this can support mitigation, defensible-space strategies, and city planning aimed at reducing future wildfire losses.

485938.title: NEXRAD Weather Radar Capability Improvements - 2027
485938.authors: Michael J. Istok, Washington, DC; and C. Fay and S. D. Smith
485938.abstract: The Next Generation Weather Radar (NEXRAD) program tri-agencies (Department of Commerce, National Weather Service (NWS); the Department of War (DOW), United States Air Force (USAF); the Department of Transportation, Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)) plan to support a long-term activity to steadily improve the science and technology of the Weather Surveillance Radar - 1988 Doppler (WSR-88D) until the Radar Next technical solution is deployed. Research and development (R&D) is focused on improving the bias, variance, and coverage of the base data; the performance of clutter filtering; and enhancing the radar meteorological algorithms. The NEXRAD program relies on research partners to conduct R&D and follows a methodological process to integrate new capabilities into the operational baseline. The NEXRAD Radar Operations Center releases WSR-88D software builds containing the approved research to operations improvements. These include new scan strategies, radar products, improvements to base data quality, and scientific enhancements to the suite of radar-meteorological algorithms. Simultaneously, the NWS is preparing for the next generation of weather radars (Radar Next) and undergoing a major transformational shift in technology and operations. By the end of 2027, all radar data and products are planned to be sent to the Centralized Integrated Real-Time Repository for Unified Service (CIRRUS) in the NWS Enterprise Cloud (NEC) for dissemination to the weather enterprise, and the on-premises Advanced Weather Interactive Processing System (AWIPS) will be replaced by the cloud-based Hydrometeorological Interactive Virtual Environment (HIVE). The priorities of the radar research-to-operations program will change to meet the needs of the current NEXRAD network and Radar Next. New capabilities to mitigate data quality impacts, use of dual polarization data, and leveraging modern data solutions (e.g., Cloud, remote access, etc.) should be incorporated to support the NEXRAD agencies and the broader weather enterprise. This paper outlines recent enhancements to the WSR-88D network, while offering insights into the future with migrating NEXRAD data to the Cloud to support the NWS’ vision.

485939.title: Updates from the NOAA Earth's Radiation Budget (ERB) Program
485939.authors: Victoria Breeze, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and G. Frost
485939.abstract: The NOAA Earth's Radiation Budget (ERB) Program conducts and funds Congressionally-mandated research to understand natural and human activities that might alter the reflectivity and radiative balance of the atmosphere. ERB projects provide baseline information about atmospheric composition and how it is changing; improve the representation of aerosols in existing Earth System models; model how wildfire emissions, volcanic eruptions, space debris, and hypothetical climate interventions could affect atmospheric composition and chemistry; and, investigate the fundamentals of cloud-aerosol interactions in the marine boundary layer. This presentation will provide an update to the AMS community on ERB program priorities, recent research highlights, and potential funding opportunities and/or areas of collaboration. Special focus will be given to the recent Stratospheric Aerosol processes, Budget and Radiative Effects high-altitude aircraft mission (SABRE Tropics) and ongoing Balloon Baseline Stratospheric Aerosol Profiles (B2SAP) observations and subsequent data available to the AMS community.

485940.title: Verification and Analysis of Spring Snowmelt Flood Outlooks for the Red River Valley of the North (2004-2025)
485940.authors: Hailey Morse, Valparaiso University, Corning, NY; and T. Grafenauer and A. Lee
485940.abstract: The Red River Valley is a unique river system shared by North Dakota, Minnesota, and Canada characterized by its vast flatness, making it susceptible to flooding. This was proven in 1997, when wet antecedent conditions, record snowfall, and a delayed fast snowmelt caused widespread flooding throughout the region, which is the motivation for improving forecasting of river flooding. In 2004, River Forecast Centers began issuing spring flood outlooks to help emergency management proactively plan for spring snowmelt flooding. Spring flood outlooks are probabilistic 90-day forecasts, issued roughly once a month between the end of January and April. The purpose of this study is to verify the accuracy of these outlooks focusing on the spring snow melt floods and understand what environmental factors can affect the accuracy of the outlooks. The verification process consisted of running python code to determine whether systemic biases existed by producing several plots using 3 month ensemble streamflow prediction (ESP) outlooks from the North Central River Forecast Center (NCRFC) and stream level data from the United States Geological Survey (USGS). Then, environmental factors that affect the magnitude and rate of snowmelt runoff were investigated and utilized in determining trends within outlooks with under-forecasting or over-forecasting biases. This presentation will discuss the results of the verification process and how these results can improve messaging of potential spring snowmelt floods across the Red River Valley. Additionally, the environmental conditions associated with outlook biases will be discussed to understand how to potentially advance long-term river flood forecasting.

485953.title: An Evaluation of VLEO Constellation Architectures for In Situ Joule Heating Observations
485953.authors: Joshua Sendgikoski, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and K. R. Greer
485953.abstract: With an expanding infrastructure at Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) altitudes, constraining the effects and interactions of ionospheric plasma has become a critical area of study. Joule heating, the result of collisional friction between plasma and neutral molecules, is a primary driver of energy and momentum exchange in the coupled ionosphere-thermosphere (I-T) that significantly influences our ability to monitor and track satellites in VLEO. However, due to a lack of observational data at altitudes where it is zoned most intensely, the spatial and temporal scales of Joule heating are largely unknown. While advances in satellite engineering have made dedicated VLEO constellations for atmospheric observation feasible in the near future, there is a lack of study on the optimal orbital architectures required for such missions. We present an Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) to evaluate high-latitude VLEO in situ Joule heating observations at 250 km altitude. Using the Coupled Thermosphere Ionosphere Plasmasphere Electrodynamics (CTIPe) model as a synthetic "ground-truth", and NASA's Community Coordinated Modeling Center's (CCMC) Kamodo software to simulate satellite flythroughs, we analyze two distinct architectures across a range of scales: a linear "string-of-pearls" train and a 2D triangular formation. Our results demonstrate that logarithmically-spaced formations effectively capture multi-scale structures, while triangular formations capture 2D horizontal gradients yet exhibit a strict resolution threshold with increasing circumradii. Ultimately, our results indicate the critical importance of constellation geometries in achieving effective resolutions able to capture dynamic plasma structures in VLEO, and highlight the distinct sensitivity of the I-T.

485961.title: Improved Wave-Spectral Estimation of Friction Velocity Under Tropical Cyclone and Storm Conditions Using Hybrid Adaptive Equilibrium Range Detection
485961.authors: Benjamin Henkel, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and H. Potter and C. O. Collins III
485961.abstract: Accurate estimation of air-sea momentum flux at high wind speeds remains a persistent source of uncertainty in tropical cyclone (TC) intensity prediction. Wave-spectral approaches offer an alternative to wind-based bulk formulas for estimating friction velocity, but their reliability depends on correctly identifying the spectral equilibrium range (ER), the frequency band exhibiting the canonical f⁻⁴ slope. Existing ER detection methods, relying on fixed frequency bands, sliding-window slope stability, or curvature transitions, frequently fail to converge or degrade under the mixed sea states and evolving spectral peaks typical of TC wave fields. To address this problem, we developed the Hybrid Adaptive Equilibrium Range Method (HAERM). HAERM is an automated, physically constrained algorithm that searches a peak-relative frequency domain for contiguous log-log windows near f⁻⁴. It uses explicit linearity (R²) and slope-proximity criteria, then selects the optimal window via a joint quality-extent objective function. When applied to measurements made during the 2010 Impact of Typhoons on the Ocean in the Pacific campaign, HAERM detected a valid ER in 99.7% of the 4092 observed spectra. This is comparable to the best existing method and far exceeding sliding-window/transition-based approaches by valid ER detection rates. Validated against direct-covariance friction velocity measurements, HAERM achieved the smallest bias of the four methods tested (−0.006 m s⁻¹, compared with +0.016 to −0.034 m s⁻¹ for the others), and remained essentially unbiased as wind stress increased, where the other high-coverage methods drifted systematically low. At Ocean Weather Station Papa (OWS-P), HAERM was applied to wave spectra measured by the Datawell Waverider buoy from 2018–2025. Friction velocity was estimated from the wave spectra and used to estimate 10-m neutral equivalent wind speeds following Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory. These were then compared to winds independently measured at OWS-P. Relative to the independently measured winds, HAERM achieved the lowest RMSE and the smallest bias in gale-force and severe-storm wind regimes (≥15 m s⁻¹), where competing wave-based methods diverged substantially. HAERM also produced the smallest fraction of physically implausible implied drag coefficients, although all methods underestimate the drag coefficient below roughly 5 m s⁻¹, where much of the momentum flux is not carried by the wave field. These results indicate that HAERM’s advantage is not confined to a single campaign but extends to long-term storm-force observations at a reference ocean station, within the wind range sampled (≤26 m s⁻¹).

485974.title: Communicating Weather Impacts Effectively in a Climate of Increased Tornado Warnings & Severe Thunderstorm Warnings
485974.authors: Drew Anderson, FOX 29 Philadelphia & Penn State, West Chester, PA
485974.abstract: There has been a stark increase in the number of tornado warnings and severe thunderstorm warnings in the Philadelphia area over the last decade, compared to the three decades prior. If this trend continues, are local risks being communicated effectively to residents? Guided by viewer feedback and research, we will walk through best practices for communicating severe weather impacts. Viewers want specifics on how severe thunderstorms and tornadoes will affect them, so localize the risk. For example, the average peak wind speed of a tornado in Southeastern Pennsylvania, Southern New Jersey, and Delaware is now 100 mph—up from 90 mph in previous decades. When alerting the public about tornado or microburst potential, explain what 100 mph winds can do to a home. Additionally, data shows that social media posts detailing severe weather impacts consistently outperform posts that have a radar image or a map of a warning. While the National Weather Service does an excellent job sharing impacts in the text of their warnings, local media, emergency management, and community officials have a growing opportunity in a changing climate: the opportunity to elaborate on local risks when communicating severe weather threats. Driven by case study data, we will detail how to share severe thunderstorm and tornado risks more effectively, focusing on best practices for social media, broadcast, person-to-person communication, and email communication.

485984.title: Using a Scenario-Based Approach to Gather Stakeholder Feedback on NWS Products and Services
485984.authors: Valerie Were, CIRA, Silver Spring, MD; CIRA, Silver Spring, MD; and J. Loerzel, M.Sc., M.P.A., L. Williams, B. G. López, and H. Murphy
485984.abstract: The mission of the National Weather Service (NWS) is to “provide weather, water and climate data, forecasts, warnings, and impact-based decision support services for the protection of life and property and enhancement of the national economy.” To support that mission, the Mission Evaluation and Performance Division began evaluating NWS products and services by using scenarios as a method for gathering feedback from stakeholders. Scenarios are a narrated sequence of possible future events and actions, and are useful for exploring how decision-making unfolds as a scenario progresses. They are also useful for understanding what end users need from NWS products and services. This talk will discuss the lessons learned from applying a scenario-based approach to evaluations of NWS products and services in several weather contexts, including winter weather. Overall, scenarios are proving useful for understanding stakeholder decision making as weather conditions change and will enable the construction of a repository of how decision-making shifts as NWS products and services evolve.

485985.title: NASA’s Convection-Allowing Model (GEOS-CAM): Performance Improvement Over the Last Four Years
485985.authors: Michelle E. Frazer, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and G. Partyka, W. Putman, and S. Rabenhorst
485985.abstract: NASA has contributed its experimental GEOS-CAM to NOAA’s annual Spring Forecasting Experiment (SFE) since 2023, allowing forecasts for days 1-3 to be evaluated alongside other experimental and operational deterministic convection-allowing models (CAMs). GEOS-CAM employs a Finite-Volume Cubed-Sphere (FV3) dynamical core and is run on a global c2160 stretched grid with 2-km resolution over CONUS. As NASA does not have an operational mandate, GEOS-CAM is uniquely useful as a flexible testbed of continuous development working towards resolving various convective regimes. Subjective and objective evaluations show that GEOS-CAM’s performance at the SFE compared to its peers has improved steadily from 2023 to 2026. Its relative performance also improves with increasing lead time. Underperformance at early lead hours can be traced to GEOS-CAM not assimilating radar data as the other flagship models do. Among the deterministic CAMs evaluated at the 2026 SFE, for occurrences of reflectivity >=40 dBZ (indicating convective precipitation), GEOS-CAM’s forecast skill is ranked lowest (out of five) for day 1, but highest (out of four) for day 3. In analyzing Roebber performance diagrams and metric evolution by reflectivity threshold and lead time, we note that the Probability of Detection (percentage of observed events correctly forecasted) does not descend monotonically with increasing lead time. Rather, there is a clear 24-hr cycle with localized peaks present for GEOS-CAM around 19 UTC (2PM CDT) but a few hours later (and of lower magnitude) for most of the other models (see Figure 1). These peaks demonstrate GEOS-CAM’s significant skill at predicting the character and timing of convective initiation and largely explain its elevated performance at longer lead times. --- Figure 1: Results from the 2026 SFE evaluation of flagship deterministic CAMs for >=40 dBZ composite radar reflectivity verified against MRMS radar data. Stats were calculated for the full CONUS domain on the HRRR nominal 3km grid for the SFE period of 27-Apr-2026 to 29-May-2026. Considering only days where all models ran forecasts, there are 31 daily forecasts analyzed for the 00z initialization (left column) and 30 for the 12z initialization (right column). Note some models only produced runs out to 48 hours for one or both initialization times. To produce these categorical statistics, hits, misses, and false alarms were calculated considering a 13-gridbox-wide (nearly 40km diameter) circular neighborhood. The top row shows Critical Success Index [hits/(hits + misses + false alarms)], second row Success Ratio [hits/(hits + false alarms)], third row Probability of Detection [hits/(hits + misses)], and bottom row Frequency Bias [(hits + false alarms)/(hits + misses + false alarms)] by forecast lead hour. MRMS average daily events for each lead hour are shown by gray shading and the secondary y-axis.

485988.title: Investigating Hailstone Fall Speed Variability in the June 16, 2025, Wellfleet, NE Hailstorm with the NSSL HailCam System
485988.authors: Caden Schmear, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and S. M. Waugh and J. Segall
485988.abstract: Even as hail causes billions of dollars of property damage in the United States each year, accurate forecasting of hail and its impacts remains a challenge. Much of the current understanding of hailstone fall speed variability is based on theoretical calculations, idealized experiments, or post-event analysis, all of which suffer from a number of limitations. To provide more direct observations of real hail fall speeds, NSSL's Hail Camera provides high-speed imaging of hailstones in freefall via in-situ deployments. This study investigates one 10-minute HailCam deployment during the June 16, 2025, Wellfleet, NE hailstorm, using a combination of image processing techniques and manual filtering to identify over 1700 individual falling hailstones ranging from just under 0.5 to just over 3 inches in diameter. For each stone, its size, shape, and three-dimensional velocity are calculated. Various factors potentially influencing near-surface hailstone fall characteristics during this particular event are examined, including hailstone size, eccentricity, and irregularity, ambient environmental winds, storm-relative placement, and storm characteristics. These results are evaluated against previous research, surface observations, and operational products to examine the applicability of our current research and operational knowledge base to a real-world hail event. Results highlight the localized variability in hailstone fall characteristics observable via the Hail Camera imaging. Hailstones from this event tended to fall more slowly than predicted by multiple previous studies. Hailstone sphericity significantly impacted fall speed, with more non-spherical stones exhibiting greatly reduced fall speeds. Hailstone fall speeds and 3-dimensional velocity vectors noticeably changed from event start to finish as environmental characteristics, storm characteristics, and stone properties changed. Hailstones falling closer to a downburst core displayed increased fall speeds. Larger hailstones displayed faster horizontal velocities than smaller hailstones, frequently exceeding the observed surface wind velocities, potentially indicating that their velocity was more influenced by above-surface winds.

485989.title: Evaluation of GOES-19 Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) Hourly and Daily Shortwave Radiation Budget Products.
485989.authors: Adeleke Segun Ademakinwa, STC at NOAA/NESDIS/STAR, Riverdale Park, MD; and H. Y. Kim, L. E. Flynn, and H. Liu
485989.abstract: The hourly and daily Shortwave Radiation Budget (SRB) products generated at 0.25° x 0.25° spatial resolution from the GOES-19 Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) SRB 10-minute products are examined in this study. These hourly and daily products for one year (Jul 2025 – Jun 2026) are evaluated against a reference -- the Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System (CERES) Synoptic Radiative Fluxes and Clouds products (SYN1deg). Evaluated fluxes include the Reflected Shortwave (SW) Radiation at top of the atmosphere (RSR), the Downward SW Radiation at the Surface (DSR), and the Photosynthetically Active Radiation at the surface (PAR). The hourly and daily SRB fluxes are remapped from the ABI’s 0.25° x 0.25° spatial resolution to the CERES grid (1° x 1°) before evaluation. Initial findings from the month of January 2026 demonstrate robust agreement between the ABI and CERES SYN1deg radiative flux products (specifically RSR, DSR, and PAR). Analysis of both hourly and daily products reveals correlation coefficients (r) exceeding 0.9. Systematic biases remain within 17.5 Wm-2 for daily observations and below 30.6 Wm-2 for hourly datasets, with the PAR product exhibiting the largest relative bias. The one-year-long analyses of the datasets is utilized to examine the seasonal and diurnal variations in ABI’s SRB product performance, and to evaluate flux uncertainties based on cloud amount, surface type and albedo, as well as the effects of different data quality filtering strategies. Furthermore, potential systematic biases between the ABI and CERES SRB measurements are highlighted and quantified, to establish the reliability of ABI GOES-19 SRB products for broader science applications such as seasonal atmospheric modeling applications and localized environmental impacts studies.

485996.title: Challenges and Alternatives for EOFs In Earth System Data: A Guide
485996.authors: Christine A. Shields, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO
485996.abstract: Modes of variability (MOVs) are important sources of predictability across timescales. A common approach to diagnosing MOVs is the application of Empirical Orthogonal Functions (EOFs). However, many challenges exist such that EOFs must be used with awareness and intention, especially when applied to large ensembles. Mode swapping, center of action variability, and sign flipping are common examples of EOF pitfalls that complicate physical interpretation. Utilizing data from two different Earth system modelling large ensemble frameworks, the Community Earth System Model (CESM) and the Energy Exoscale Earth System Model (E3SM), as well as reanalysis data, we coalesce the most common challenges found in large ensembles and discuss solutions, alternatives, as well as interpretability of these methods. EOFs are powerful tools, however their limitations need to be acknowledged when applied to climate variability problems.

486022.title: Real-Case LES of Stable Boundary Layer Flow over a Forested Complex Terrain: A Triple-Decomposition Approach
486022.authors: Joran Dartevelle, von Kãrmãn Institute for fluid dynamics (VKI), 1640 Sint-Genesius-Rode, Belgium; BioDynE, University of Liege, Gembloux, Belgium; and S. Stipa, F. Lebeau, and W. Munters
486022.abstract: Eddy covariance (EC) is the most commonly used method for measuring gas and energy exchanges between the Earth’s ecosystems and the atmosphere. However, the estimated fluxes are based on assumptions of stationarity and horizontal homogeneity (Foken, 2008), which are generally called into question at night and over inhomogeneous terrain geometry (Aubinet, 2008). Although these monitoring stations are well-equipped, a significant portion of the nighttime data collected is discarded due to low-level, intermittent turbulence, drainage flows, low-level jets (LLJs), and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities (KHIs) at the top of the stable boundary layer (SBL). The generated sub-mesoscale motions and internal gravity waves cannot be distinguished from turbulent transport using simple Reynolds decomposition and averaging, and they violate the EC assumptions. At the Integrated Carbon Observation System (ICOS) eddy covariance site in Vielsalm (a mixed forest in the Belgian Ardennes), the energy balance closure is comparable to or slightly greater than that of a similar canopy ecosystem. However, nighttime periods are systematically excluded from valid data. This motivates a reassessment grounded in fundamental principles and based on large eddy simulation (LES) of how mesoscale forcings, wave motions and turbulence coexist and interact above and within a forest canopy under stable stratification conditions. It also considers how their combined effects distort estimates of fluxes measured by the tower. We present a modeling framework based on a nested, unidirectional CERRA to Weather Research and Forcasting (WRF) model to FastEddy pipeline, focusing on nighttime periods over Vielsalm (Fig. 1a). The CERRA reanalysis initializes and laterally forces a two-domain WRF configuration (mesh sizes ranging from 3 km to 1 km, consistently using the MYNN boundary layer scheme to avoid conflicts with the innermost gray-zone domain). This domain drives FastEddy v5.0.0 (Sauer and Muñoz-Esparza, 2020), a GPU-native LES, running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell workstation (96 GB of VRAM) at a horizontal resolution of 5.5 m over a domain of approximately 9 × 9 km² with a cubically stretched vertical grid (surface spacing ≈ 4 m). This grid spacing allows for the resolution of the upper stable boundary layer (SBL) depth from 60 to 110 m and the leading edge of the overlying LLJ. The mixed coniferous and deciduous canopy (25-30 m) is modeled using FastEddy’s two-equation canopy drag closure model (Shaw and Schumann 1992; Shaw and Patton 2003), and the base-state stability profile is anchored to a representative sounding from Vielsalm rather than to idealized default values. Two-hour integrations (one hour of setup using the time-varying cellular perturbation method, one hour of analysis) are designed to capture the formation and dissipation of KHI waves at the inversion layer, as well as the underlying turbulence regime of the canopy. The central scientific contribution is a triple decomposition designed specifically for LES fields that are themselves forced by a time-varying numerical weather prediction (NWP) boundary state, a configuration in which the classical Reynolds decomposition is not well-posed: the non-stationary mesoscale trend injected through the boundaries contaminates any fixed-window averaging operator. We decompose each simulated state variable into (i) a mesoscale component extracted as the coarsest-scale approximation of a discrete wavelet transform (DWT) using the Daubechies 4 wavelet family, removing the non-stationary trend without imposing a fixed averaging time; (ii) a submesoscale/wave component obtained from a joint Hilbert Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (HPOD) of the DWT residuals with the three components of the velocity and the potential temperature, exploiting phase coherence across velocity and scalar fields to isolate coherent wave structures like KHI billows and gravity waves; and (iii) a residual turbulent component (Fig. 1b). We establish the orthogonality properties linking the three subspaces analytically, so that variance and flux budgets computed from the decomposition remain exactly conservative. The LES is validated against a flux tower dataset located at the center of the domain, which revealed the same shear layer instability billows in the data in terms of reduced (dimensionless) frequency. A slight difference in the average velocity causes a subtle difference in frequency between the LES and the data. Submesoscale structures are also compared against the classic theoretical model of the Taylor-Goldstein equation. The roles of each component (mesoscale, submesoscale and turbulence) are examined in terms of turbulent fluxes and analysed in relation to the eddy covariance methodology, in order to gain insight and improve it. Additionally, we demonstrate the presence of streamwise vortices caused by the shear layer and topography. These result in significant spatial variability in the surface flow around the tower in the spanwise direction, which could be related to Görtler instabilities. In conclusion, we successfully produced a high-resolution simulation of the wind flow in and above a canopy over complex terrain in a real setting, using a nested approach with the Cell Perturbation Method. This enables us to present a triple decomposition, which separates the mesoscale contribution from the submesoscale and the turbulence. This data-driven decomposition, based on the HPOD, facilitates examination of transport at and around the tower location and identification of instability structures. References 1. Aubinet, M., 2008. EDDY COVARIANCE CO2 FLUX MEASUREMENTS IN NOCTURNAL CONDITIONS: AN ANALYSIS OF THE PROBLEM. Ecological Applications. https://doi.org/10.1890/06-1336. 2. Foken, T., 2008. The Energy Balance Closure Problem: An Overview. Ecological Applications 18, 1351–1367. https://doi.org/10.1890/06-0922.1 3. Sauer, J.A., Muñoz-Esparza, D., 2020. The FastEddy® Resident-GPU Accelerated Large-Eddy Simulation Framework: Model Formulation, Dynamical-Core Validation and Performance Benchmarks. Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems 12, e2020MS002100. https://doi.org/10.1029/2020MS002100 4. Shaw, R.H., Patton, E.G., 2003. Canopy element influences on resolved- and subgrid-scale energy within a large-eddy simulation. Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, A tribute to George W. Thurtell’s contributions in micrometeorology 115, 5–17. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0168-1923(02)00165-X 5. Shaw, R.H., Schumann, U., 1992. (b) Triple decomposition of the vertical velocity the 1st may 2023 around 1 AM. Top figure : trend part, Middle figure : submesoscale part bottom figure : turbulence part.

486058.title: AERIS S2S Forecasts for A-LEAF Grid Probabilistic Reliability Assessment: A Prototype Workflow
486058.authors: W. Neal Mann, ANL, Lemont, IL; and R. Kotamarthi and D. K. Fytanidis
486058.abstract: Season-ahead resource adequacy studies are carried out by grid balancing authorities and others to quantify system outage risks, sometimes leading to corrective action. These studies usually use recent historical weather instead of sub-seasonal weather forecasts due to the low skill of physics-based NWP models at these timescales. However, new AI/ML weather forecasting models are emerging with enough skill to be usable for S2S forecasting, which could improve grid emergency preparedness. To this end, we have created a prototype workflow to couple the Argonne Earth System Model for Reliable and Skillful Predictions (AERIS) weather foundation model with the Argonne Large-scale Electricity Analysis Framework (A-LEAF) power system model for season-ahead grid reliability assessments. AERIS is a generative Swin diffusion transformer model trained on global ERA5 reanalysis data, 1960–2018, including temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and u- and v-component wind velocity at 13 pressure levels. The model architecture was chosen to create skillful forecast ensembles of at least 90 steps ahead. A-LEAF is a suite of power system simulation models for short-term operations/dispatch, medium-term reliability and resource adequacy assessment, and long-term capacity investment and retirement planning. The A-LEAF probabilistic reliability assessment (RA) model samples random outage draws from temperature-dependent outage probability curves for thermal power plants. A county-level model of the 2021 ERCOT (Texas) grid was chosen for the demonstration. A single AERIS forecast initialization (2020-06-27T18:00:00Z) was chosen with a 50-member ensemble of forecast dry bulb temperature at 2 m. Each forecast member produced a single daily temperature value for 91 days (13 weeks) ahead, and this was temporally downscaled to hourly values via a simple cubic splines interpolation. Each county in ERCOT was assigned a single AERIS grid point by calculating the minimum distance from the county centroid. The temperature time series from all ensemble members were fed into the A-LEAF RA model, and 100 random outage draws were created for each time step, nearly 11 million total. The A-LEAF RA model then simulated outage-aware dispatch under all 50 AERIS temperature scenarios. The result was 50 hourly time series of expected unserved energy for the 91-day-ahead period. Nine days of elevated expected unserved energy were identified: five consecutive days in July, and two sets of two consecutive days in August. Lower but still significant risks were seen in another 30 of the 91 days. This shows that it is technically feasible to use a skillful S2S weather forecasting model for season-ahead grid reliability and resource adequacy assessments. Future work could include AERIS enhancements including additional weather variables, A-LEAF enhancements including more location-specific outage models, applications in other balancing authority areas, and the integration with the GridFM platform (GridFM.org).

486062.title: East Pacific Easterly Waves in the CESM2 Large Ensemble: Current Climate Characteristics and Projected Changes Under Future Warming
486062.authors: Yihao Zhou, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and E. D. Maloney
486062.abstract: This study investigates the characteristics of east Pacific (EPAC) easterly waves (EWs) in 10 ensemble members of the Community Earth System Model version 2 Large Ensemble (CESM2-LENS) under the current climate and their projected changes under future warming by the end of the 21st century under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 3–7.0 (SSP370) warming scenario. Under the current climate, the CESM2 ensemble mean produces realistic mean precipitation, horizontal winds, and EW-filtered vorticity variability over the EPAC, although the EW-filtered precipitation amplitude is underestimated relative to observations. CESM2 generally reproduces the distribution of EW tracks identified using 700-hPa curvature vorticity in the Caribbean and EPAC, along with the horizontal structure, amplitude, and propagation of EW disturbances. However, CESM2 EWs exhibit a more top-heavy vertical profile and a more pronounced eastward-tilted vertical velocity structure relative to ERA5, suggesting biases in convective vertical structure and diabatic heating processes. Under the future warming scenario, mean precipitation over the EPAC strengthens and shifts southward, while the increase in EW-filtered precipitation variability is modest. EW track density and anomalous vorticity amplitude decrease along the Central American coast but increase within the southwestern ITCZ region. Increased static stability with warming and weaker upper-level vertical velocity per unit precipitation largely explain the weakened midlevel vorticity in EWs. The weakened dynamical signal of the EWs may limit convective activity, thus resulting in only modest changes in EW precipitation amplitude, which should be treated with caution given the CESM2 biases in simulating diabatic heating processes that control the evolution of EW moisture.

486064.title: NOAA’s Experimental High Resolution Monthly High Tide Flooding Outlook: Leveraging the Coastal Ocean Reanalysis (CORA) to Achieve Spatially-Continuous Flood Guidance
486064.authors: Matthew P Conlin, National Ocean Service, Barrington, NH
486064.abstract: High Tide Flooding (HTF) is an escalating hazard for U.S. coastal communities, yet prediction of HTF is complicated by the need for integrated models that account for numerous processes - each with varying levels of predictability - as well as information about the local environment. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) delivers monthly HTF outlooks at U.S. tide gauges, which provide probabilistic estimates of daily HTF likelihood out to a year in the future using a statistical model that combines tides, sea level trends, recent sea level anomalies, and non-tidal residual climatologies evaluated against local flood thresholds. However, many coastal communities lie relatively far from a tide gauge and have therefore lacked localized HTF guidance. NOAA is developing a new experimental, high-resolution monthly HTF outlook, which leverages the Coastal Ocean Reanalysis (CORA) to expand NOAA’s existing monthly HTF outlooks to a spatially continuous 400-500 m resolution along the U.S. Gulf and East coasts. We show that using CORA to derive daily HTF predictions at water level gauges is comparable to using water level observations, with multiple metrics indicating reduction in average HTF model skill of less than or equal to 5%. Furthermore, we assess potential accuracy in low-energy inland environments by comparing with observations from coastal community-supported water level stations in estuarine and back-barrier locations. Results indicate that, while the resolution of CORA may be too coarse to capture some small hydrologic features, CORA often reliably represents local water levels and flood potential (daily maxima RMSE = 0.07 m), providing confidence in CORA-derived HTF predictions in these environments. These advances will empower users to better visualize community-level HTF likelihood across space, time, and flood thresholds.

486065.title: Impact of El Niño on Terrestrial Hydrology: Streamflow and Soil Moisture
486065.authors: Venkataraman Lakshmi, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and B. Fang, Z. Zhu, T. Piechota, and G. Tootle
486065.abstract: The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) impacts terrestrial hydrology through changes in precipitation and air temperature, which in turn affect evapotranspiration, runoff, streamflow, and soil moisture. The ongoing 2026-2027 ENSO event is expected to be a strong to very strong El Niño and provides timely opportunity to examine terrestrial hydrologic responses in comparison with previous major events. In this work, we use ENSO indices together with streamflow from gauge observations, air temperature and evapotranspiration from ERA5, evapotranspiration from MODIS, and soil moisture from ERA5 and SMAP. By combining in-situ measurements, Earth observations, and standard model outputs, we construct a robust global dataset for assessing ENSO-related hydrologic anomalies. A specific focus of this work is to examine the progression of streamflow and soil moisture, including both surface and deeper root-zone soil moisture, during the current El Niño and compare it with the 2015-2016 and 2023-2024 El Niño events, the most recent major El Niño within the SMAP record. Using SMAP surface and root-zone soil moisture, including downscaled products at 400 m and 1 km resolution, we investigate whether soil moisture responses are consistent across depth or differ between shallow and deeper layers. Studying soil moisture in un-impaired watersheds worldwide, together with precipitation, evapotranspiration, and streamflow, will improve our understanding of how ENSO-driven atmospheric anomalies are linked to terrestrial hydrologic system.

486068.title: HEAT28: A NASA Urban Extreme-Heat Risk Analysis Pathfinder Digital Twin for Stakeholder-Driven Resilience
486068.authors: Duane E. Waliser, JPL, Pasadena, CA; and R. Basilio, S. Chien, G. Hulley, U. Rebbapragada, H. Hua, D. J. Posselt, L. Mandrake, C. Miller, R. McGranaghan, D. Niyogi, B. Smith, S. T. (Pitter) Combley, and L. Rogers
486068.abstract: Extreme heat is an increasingly consequential urban risk, affecting public health, outdoor work, mobility, energy demand, infrastructure operations, and major public events. HEAT28 is a NASA/JPL-led urban heat intelligence pathfinder designed to advance stakeholder-driven risk information for resilience planning and operations. The effort uses the Los Angeles Basin and the lead-up to the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games as a testbed for developing decision-ready heat products that can support local needs while informing transferable NASA resilience capabilities. HEAT28 is being formulated as a campaign-level NASA Earth Science and Technology Office and Earth Action activity that integrates spaceborne, airborne, drone, and ground observations with urban weather modeling, land-surface information, data fusion, AI/ML, uncertainty characterization, and stakeholder engagement. The objective is not simply to generate heat maps, but to develop a repeatable risk-analysis workflow that connects user decisions to required variables, spatial and temporal scales, thresholds, uncertainty, latency, and product formats. Candidate products include neighborhood- to venue-scale heat exposure analyses, gap-filled hindcasts, nowcasts, day-ahead heat guidance, shaded-route and cooling-intervention assessments, and post-event evaluation products. The effort aligns strongly with NASA RASI objectives: translating NASA science into timely, usable risk information for state, local, and institutional stakeholders. HEAT28 can complement RASI extreme heat, energy infrastructure, air quality, and disaster-risk products by demonstrating how NASA observations, models, digital-twin concepts, and system engineering can support compound-risk questions involving heat, health, mobility, power demand, air quality, and emergency preparedness. We will describe the HEAT28 concept, stakeholder-engagement strategy, anticipated product architecture, and relevance as a transferable framework for NASA-enabled urban resilience decision support.

486083.title: Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Flood Warnings
486083.authors: Omid Emamjomehzadeh, New York University, Brooklyn, NY; and M. Xu and O. Wani
486083.abstract: Flood-warning decisions depend on hydrologic forecasts that are subject to model error and input errors. These uncertainties are particularly consequential in small catchments, where short response times and the asymmetric costs of missed floods and false alarms complicate operational decision-making. We develop a Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization framework for converting hourly streamflow forecasts into flood-warning decisions. The framework estimates forecast residuals from historical data, constructs an ambiguity set around their empirical distribution using Wasserstein distance, and identifies warning rules that minimize worst-case expected decision loss across plausible out-of-sample error distributions. The framework is evaluated in more than 200 CAMELSH catchments with drainage areas smaller than 50 km². Hourly streamflow is predicted using a regional long short-term memory network informed by static catchment attributes and four dynamic meteorological variables: hourly total precipitation, 2-m air temperature, downward shortwave radiation at the surface, and 2-m specific humidity. The model is trained using data from October 2005 through September 2020, validated from October 2000 through September 2005, and tested from October 2020 through September 2024. During the test period, High-Resolution Rapid Refresh forecasts with lead times from 1 to 18 hours provide the meteorological inputs. Performance is assessed across catchments, forecast lead times, and levels of hydrologic prediction skill. The proposed framework is compared with deterministic threshold-based warnings and probabilistic warnings generated by resampling historical forecast errors. Evaluation considers event detection, false alarms, missed floods, and decision loss. This study provides a transferable framework for environmental warning decisions when limited historical errors may not adequately represent operational forecast uncertainty.

486089.title: Indigenous Oral Histories and Climate Modeling Yield New Perspectives on the Oklahoma Dust Bowl
486089.authors: Vannak Koiy, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and M. Mose, F. King, M. Loria-Salazar, Z. Ke, and H. Moosmuller
486089.abstract: Histories of the Oklahoma Dust Bowl have been dominated by white‑centered narratives that emphasize agricultural failure, drought severity, and large‑scale displacement. Yet these accounts overlook the experiences, ecological knowledge, and cultural memory of the Tribal Nations who lived through the same environmental crisis. This study integrates Indigenous oral histories with climate modeling to develop a more inclusive and scientifically grounded understanding of the Dust Bowl. We compile archival documents, interviews, and traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) from Native communities in Oklahoma and compare these accounts with mainstream historical narratives. Using reconstructed climate fields, including wind intensity, drought indices, soil moisture, and dust flux, we evaluate the extent to which atmospheric conditions align with reported experiences across communities. Indigenous narratives highlight distinct themes, including culturally informed land‑stewardship practices, differing perceptions of dust severity, and disproportionate impacts on health, mobility, and cultural lifeways. By combining lived experience with modeled climatological conditions, our analysis reveals both points of convergence and meaningful divergences between settler and Indigenous accounts. More broadly, this integrated framework demonstrates the value of TEK in reconstructing historical climate events and emphasizes the need for more inclusive environmental histories. Our findings offer new perspectives on the Dust Bowl while informing contemporary discussions of dust, drought, and climate resilience across the Southern Plains.

486091.title: Long-Window 4DVar for Reanalysis Using Differentiable Models (invited)
486091.authors: Jeffrey S. Whitaker, UCAR Cooperative Programs for the Advancement of Earth System Science (CPAESS), Boulder, CO; and G. J. Hakim, B. Huang, and S. Frolov
486091.abstract: For reanalysis, unlike operational NWP, the data assimilation system can make use of observations that lie in the future with respect to the analysis time. One approach is to use 4DVar with the analysis time set at the beginning of a time window long enough to include all future observations that could impact the analysis. Long windows have the additional benefit of reducing the dependence of the solution on the background term, which is notoriously difficult to specify accurately. Implementing long-window 4DVar has proven difficult, due to limitations of the usual incremental update procedure using a tangent linear approximation to the full nonlinear forecast model combined with inner/outer loop iteration and linear optimization. Here we examine the feasibility of long-window 4DVar using a differentiable model combined with libraries developed for machine learning applications to manage gradient descent and back-progagation of gradients of a loss function. The model we use is NeuralGCM, and we assimilate real surface pressure observations. Using a fairly coarse horizontal resolution (2.8 degrees) we demonstrate stable cycling with no background term in the loss function and a window length of 4 days. Even without accounting for model error, the resulting 500 hPa geopotential height errors (relative to ERA5) are up to 50% smaller than was obtained using an ensemble Kalman filter for the 20th Century Reanalysis project, at much less computational cost. We hypothesize that the key to success in this approach is that a long trajectory effectively eliminates the need for a background term, significantly reducing the search space for the optimization algorithm while allowing the model dynamics to faithfully represent un-observed variables. Using Python/JAX in both the model and the data assimilation algorithm drastically simplifies the code, since nearly all of the complexity is encapsulated in the JAX/XLA libraries for auto-differentiation, JIT compilation and optimization.

486100.title: Advise You Have the Weather: Monitoring the Real-Time Status of Automated Surface Weather Stations
486100.authors: Joel Siegel, FAA, Oklahoma City, OK; and R. Moradi
486100.abstract: The National Airspace System (NAS) relies on a network of over 2,300 Automated Surface Observing Systems (ASOS) and Automated Weather Observing Systems (AWOS) to keep operations running safely and efficiently. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has even built regulatory requirements around these systems, particularly for airlines, specifying their use for critical phases of flight. Even though ASOS and AWOS networks are generally reliable, unexpected outages and technical glitches still happen, occasionally cutting off the crucial weather data that flight operations depend on. The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 placed a requirement on the FAA to display these outages and disruptions to the public via a dashboard. This new strategic decision-making tool, hosted on the FAA's Weather Cameras website, provides near real-time status updates for every ASOS and AWOS across the NAS, including an estimated repair time, if available. Beyond giving pilots and operators clear visibility, the dashboard enables users to report outages directly to the FAA for investigation, while also offering an open Application Programming Interface (API) so third-party developers can pull the data into their own tools. We will provide a summary of the capabilities, potential use cases, and how the FAA will use the information submitted by users to improve the safety of the NAS.

486106.title: Skillful Subseasonal Precipitation Forecasts Integrating Climate Simulations with Numerical Weather Predictions
486106.authors: Cheng Zheng, Stony Brook Univ., Stony Brook, NY; Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY; and E. K. M. Chang
486106.abstract: Skillful subseasonal predictions provide advanced notice of weather events and benefit society across sectors such as disaster preparedness, agriculture, water management, and energy production. Traditionally, dynamical models generate subseasonal forecasts through extended-range simulations. Recently, data-driven models, some trained with climate model simulations, have shown potential for making skillful subseasonal predictions. However, both approaches still exhibit relatively low skill at the subseasonal timescale. Here, we present a hybrid method that combines dynamical and climate models with a data-driven tool, demonstrating superior skill in predicting subseasonal precipitation and precipitation extremes compared with the state-of-the-art ensemble dynamical forecast system from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). We trained a data-driven tool to learn how tropical and extratropical large-scale conditions influence precipitation in thousands of years of climate model simulations, without using observational data. This tool is then applied in a hybrid mode, using recently observed and ECMWF-predicted tropical and extratropical large-scale conditions as inputs to predict observed precipitation. In reforecasts, the hybrid model consistently outperforms the ECMWF dynamical forecast. We also participate in AI Weather Quest, a real-time subseasonal forecasting competition, by running the hybrid model in real time, where it also outperforms the operational ECMWF dynamical forecast for subseasonal precipitation. As this model uses only a small number of predictors and relatively simple methods, there are many ways to further improve its performance, and it provides a foundation for future development of hybrid subseasonal prediction tools that integrate information from dynamical predictions into data-driven tools trained with climate model outputs.

486107.title: Diagnosing Diabatic Forcing of Seasonal Progression of the Northern Hemisphere Winter Storm Tracks
486107.authors: Cheng Zheng, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY; and E. K. M. Chang, S. Lee, and A. Mewhinney
486107.abstract: The climatological seasonality of boreal winter storm tracks, featuring a midwinter minimum over the North Pacific, can be reproduced by general circulation models (GCMs). However, the diabatic forcings that drive this seasonality are not well understood. Using an idealized GCM framework, we show that the observed winter seasonality of storm tracks can be reproduced by imposing time-evolving diabatic forcings derived from reanalysis data. Model results indicate that both surface forcing and atmospheric moist heating (MH) are important drivers. By systematically removing individual forcings, we find that extratropical MH plays a dominant role from a diagnostic perspective. This result reveals a strong self-feedback process: the seasonality of extratropical MH drives the seasonality of storm tracks, while storm tracks, through associated precipitation processes, shape seasonality of extratropical MH. We hypothesize that surface forcing and tropical MH act as the fundamental external drivers of winter storm track seasonality. In addition to their direct effects, they exert indirect influences through modulation of the feedback between storm tracks and extratropical MH. To represent this feedback, we develop an iterative modeling framework that constructs extratropical MH associated with simulated storm track seasonality. When this feedback is included, the model successfully reproduces storm track seasonality using only surface forcing and tropical MH, without requiring reanalysis information for the seasonality of extratropical MH. These results indicate that, although extratropical MH appears dominant diagnostically, surface forcing and tropical MH are the fundamental drivers of winter storm track seasonality, with both direct and indirect influences.

486128.title: Tropical Upper-Tropospheric Potential Vorticity Intrusions during Sudden Stratospheric Warmings
486128.authors: John R. Albers, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and T. Birner and J. Dias
486128.abstract: Foundational research by Dr. George Kiladis helped establish that extratropical Rossby waves propagating into tropical "westerly ducts" during boreal winter are a vital component of the atmospheric momentum balance, driving the intrusion of high potential vorticity (PV) air into the tropical upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS) and modulating equatorial convection. Building upon this framework of extratropical-tropical wave propagation, this study examines how UTLS PV intrusions are influenced by extreme perturbations to the large-scale background flow: sudden stratospheric warmings (SSWs). While climatological PV intrusions are primarily driven by synoptic-scale wave breaking within the classical Pacific and Atlantic ducts, our analysis reveals that in the period surrounding a SSW, PV intrusion activity includes synoptic to planetary-scale wave breaking that is significantly stronger, penetrates further into the deep tropics, and exhibits distinct geographic distributions. We show that these anomalous intrusions are governed by planetary-scale wave disturbances that deform the extratropical meridional PV gradient equatorward. As these material PV deformations unfold, planetary-scale wave breaking along the edge of the polar vortex extends downward into the subtropical UTLS. At the same time, the planetary-scale deformation directly reorganizes the geographic structure of the UTLS waveguide, altering the preferred pathways for synoptic-scale wave breaking. Together, these combined scale interactions provide a robust explanation for why different wavenumber stratospheric wave events produce unique tropical intrusion patterns. Planetary wavenumber one (displacement) SSWs intensify the classic PV intrusion maximum over the Pacific Ocean, while wavenumber two (split) SSWs reorganize the tropical wind field to create dual intrusion maxima over both the Pacific and Indian Oceans. By bridging the synoptic-scale westerly duct dynamics pioneered by Dr. Kiladis with stratospheric planetary-scale wave breaking, this work highlights a direct, instantaneous dynamical link between the polar stratosphere and the tropical troposphere.

486134.title: Identifying Meteorological Drivers of Weather Induced Power Outages
486134.authors: Aliza Abraham, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Arvada, CO; and S. Letizia, A. S. Wise, N. Hamilton, and P. Moriarty
486134.abstract: Severe weather events are one of the primary causes of power outages in the United States. To improve power system resilience, we aim to better understand which weather events are most likely to cause outages. With this information, utilities can better prepare for these events and respond more quickly to outages when they occur. Furthermore, understanding which weather events are most impactful helps atmospheric scientists identify case studies that can be used to improve weather forecasting and modeling. In this investigation, we combine meteorological observations with historical power outage records. The observations were collected as part of the American Wake Experiment (AWAKEN) experiment, a three-year measurement campaign conducted in northern Oklahoma (Moriarty et al., 2024). In the current study, we use data from seven surface meteorological stations deployed at AWAKEN. County-level power outage records are obtained from Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Environment for Analysis of Geo-Located Energy Information (EAGLE-I) dataset (Brelsford et al., 2024). Following the procedure outlined in Lee et al. (2024), outage events that coincide with National Weather Service warnings and advisories are considered to be weather-driven. We first manually inspected the meteorological time series alongside the time series of outage data. Many of the largest outage events coincide with consistent meteorological features: a sharp increase in wind speed, a sudden change in wind direction, a temperature drop, an increase in relative humidity, and pressure fluctuations (Fig. 1a). These features are indicative of mesoscale convective systems, known to be frequent and severe in Oklahoma. Next, we implemented two machine learning techniques to determine the likelihood of a power outage at any given time and to identify the meteorological drivers of these outages. A random forest classifier was trained to output the probability of a significant outage based on meteorological data, then Shapley values (Lundberg & Lee, 2017) were used to rank the contributions of each meteorological feature to the outage probability. Consistent with the results of the manual inspection, wind speed peaks, pressure fluctuations, and wind variability (the combination of the standard deviations of wind speed and direction) were found to be the dominant drivers of the most significant power outages (Fig. 1b). The machine learning analysis described above was then used to compile an interface that atmospheric scientists can use to identify interesting case studies for further investigation, entitled the Automated Logging of Extremes (ALEX) Outage Event Library dashboard. This dashboard allows the user to select and inspect events of interest based on the predicted outage likelihood, the properties of the outage, and the dominant drivers of the event. For each event, time series of meteorological variables (including comparisons with HRRR outputs), Shapely values, data availability from the AWAKEN experiment, and NEXRAD radar reflectivity data are displayed. These features facilitate the validation of numerical weather prediction models and in-depth analysis of the physical phenomena occurring during severe weather events. Figure 1. (a) Meteorological parameters from the AWAKEN met station plotted alongside number of customers out of power for the event on May 7, 2024. The gray shaded area indicates the period of severe weather warnings issued by the National Weather Service. (b) Shapley values indicating the strength of the meteorological drivers contributing to the probability of an outage on May 7, 2024. Positive values (pink) indicate that the feature increases the likelihood of an outage, while negative values (blue) decrease the likelihood. References Brelsford, Christa, Sarah Tennille, Aaron Myers, et al. “A Dataset of Recorded Electricity Outages by United States County 2014–2022.” Scientific Data 11, no. 1 (2024): 271. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-024-03095-5. Lee, Sangkeun Matthew, Supriya Chinthavali, Narayan Bhusal, Nils Stenvig, Anika Tabassum, and Teja Kuruganti. “Quantifying the Power System Resilience of the US Power Grid Through Weather and Power Outage Data Mapping.” IEEE Access 12 (2024): 5237–55. https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2023.3347129. Lundberg, Scott M., and Su-In Lee. "A unified approach to interpreting model predictions." Advances in neural information processing systems 30 (2017). Moriarty, Patrick, Nicola Bodini, Stefano Letizia, et al. “Overview of Preparation for the American WAKE ExperimeNt (AWAKEN).” Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy 16, no. 5 (2024): 053306. https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0141683.

486167.title: Strengthened Walker Circulation Linking to Weakened East Asian Winter Monsoon in Recent Decades
486167.authors: Renhe Zhang, Fudan University, Shanghai, Shanghai, China
486167.abstract: The Walker Circulation (WC) is a crucial atmospheric circulation system over the tropical Pacific. While current climate models show WC weakening in recent decades, observations exhibit an intensification instead. The discrepancy indicates critical gaps in understanding the interdecadal variability of the tropical atmospheric circulation. The East Asian winter monsoon (EAWM), one of the most active atmospheric circulation systems in the extratropical regions, can significantly influence tropical climates. Using reanalysis data during 1948–2020, this study reveals that the interdecadal weakening of the EAWM may enhance the WC since the mid-1980s. During 1948–1986, the northerly wind anomalies associated with strong EAWM extended southward into the western tropical Pacific (WTP), cooling the local sea surface temperature (SST) and intensifying the low-level westerlies over the WTP in the wintertime. In the following summer and winter the westerly anomalies caused pronounced SST warming in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, and thus weakened WC appeared in this period. However, during 1987–2020, the interdecadal weakening of EAWM decoupled with the tropical westerly anomalies, thereby displaying negligible impacts on the SST warming. Both the weakened westerly anomalies and SST warming were favorable for the strengthening of WC in the following summer and winter. Therefore, an intensified WC appeared. Our findings reveal the importance of the extratropical origin from EAWM for the strengthening of the WC in the recent decades.

486191.title: MPAS-GOCART2G-JEDI for Atmosphere–Aerosol Coupled Data Assimilation
486191.authors: Soyoung Ha, NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and S. W. Wei
486191.abstract: NSF NCAR has recently developed a next-generation, online-coupled atmosphere–aerosol data assimilation and forecasting system based on the atmospheric Model for Prediction Across Scales coupled with the 2nd-generation Goddard Chemistry Aerosol Radiation and Transport model and interfaced with the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration system (MPAS-GOCART2G-JEDI). The system provides a unified framework for assimilating and evaluating satellite observations to support both air quality and weather prediction. This talk will summarize our recent efforts in developing coupled atmosphere–aerosol data assimilation within MPAS-GOCART2G-JEDI. Using a wildfire smoke case study, we will demonstrate the impact of satellite observations on air quality and weather forecasts through cycling experiments. The results highlight the potential of MPAS-GOCART2G-JEDI as a community framework for advancing coupled Earth system data assimilation and improving atmospheric composition and weather prediction.

486192.title: MPAS-DART for Advanced Atmospheric Data Assimilation
486192.abstract: The atmospheric Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS-A), the NSF NCAR’s next-generation numerical weather prediction model, is interfaced with DART directly on the model’s native horizontal and vertical coordinates to compute nonhydrostatic analysis increments, minimizing artificial errors associated with variable and vertical-coordinate transformations. The system has recently been extended to support storm-scale ensemble data assimilation, including rapid regional cycling at sub-hourly intervals, with a particular focus on radar data assimilation. This presentation will summarize recent updates to MPAS-DART as a unified framework for global and regional ensemble analysis and forecasting in numerical weather prediction. A real case study will demonstrate the potential of a non-Gaussian ensemble analysis method within MPAS-DART to improve severe-storm prediction by more effectively constraining noisy ensemble analyses. The talk will also introduce the MPAS-DART online tutorial as a practical resource and provide information on accessing the source code.

486194.title: An Approach to Polarimetric Phased Array Bias Correction
486194.authors: David Ringheiser, RTX Collins Aerospace, Marlborough, MA; and D. Pepyne
486194.abstract: Compared to weather radar employing mechanically scanned parabolic reflectors, polarimetric phased array radar (PPAR) offer many benefits, including faster volume scans, dynamic, adaptive weather tracking and diagnosis with near instantaneous "inertia-less" beam steering and software defined beamshaping and waveform diversity. For meteorological applications continuous alignment of the horizontal and vertical (H/V) beams relative to the earth's horizon and sustained high cross-polarization isolation between the beams is a necessity. In addition to the element level amplitude and phase alignment required of all phased-arrays, the differential changes to the beam shapes and cross-polarization coupling that occurs as the beam of a PPAR is steered must be corrected to mitigate errors in the recovered polarimetric weather products. This paper presents an approach developed for the RTX Skyler flat-panel PPAR. Based on the PPAR projection matrix concept of Zhang et al, the approach applies an aimpoint dependent correction matrix to the H/V IQ timeseries as it is ingested, pulse-by-pulse from the receiver to adjust their amplitudes and phases to correct for the various sources of H/V bias. These include geometry such as physical tilt-back of the panel, the electrical behavior of the array's dipole elements, calibration determined gain and phase center changes with beam-steering, transmitter amplitude and phase differences, and so on. In addition to IQ correction, the system H and V noise powers are adjusted to account for the mathematical change in effective noise power due to the application of the correction matrix. Once corrected, IQ signal processing proceeds as if the IQ were coming from a mechanical dish radar. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach using realistic simulated Skyler IQ derived from archived WSR-88D storm cases.

486196.title: Effect of Surface Wave Shoaling on Air-Sea Momentum Exchange
486196.authors: Joshua Port, University of Rhode Island, Narragansett, RI; and F. Addona, T. Hara, F. Veron, and P. P. Sullivan
486196.abstract: In order to accurately model storm surge and near shore wind fields, it is important to understand the efficiency with which momentum is transferred between atmosphere and ocean in shallow coastal waters. While there is observational evidence that shoaling surface waves may increase the drag coefficient both inside and outside the surf zone, the physical mechanism of drag increase by shoaling waves is not well understood. Thus, laboratory observations and large-eddy simulations (LESs) are combined to examine the extent to which shoaling wind-forced waves modify the drag coefficient and the wind turbulence field above them, and to clarify the physical reason for the drag coefficient enhancement by shoaling waves. The LESs are run with different combinations of incoming wave steepness and water depth in alignment with the observational wave tank data obtained using particle image velocimetry (PIV). The test cases span from deep water non-breaking waves to shoaling pre- and post-breaking waves. Incoming wave age is set to be typical of dominant surface waves under tropical cyclones. Both observational and LES data clearly show that the drag coefficient increases with wave shoaling even after wave amplitude significantly decreases by depth-induced breaking. The LES study shows that the primary reason for the drag increase is enhanced background roughness. Changing wave shape and speed due to shoaling may also contribute to the drag increase while enhancing airflow separation and the wave form drag.

486203.title: High-Temporal-Resolution Water Vapor and Temperature Profiling by Raman Lidar Using Kalman Filtering and Validation Against Radiosonde Observations
486203.authors: Michihiro Teshiba, EKO Instruments Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan; and K. Matsuki, M. yabuki, and T. Hasegawa
486203.abstract: Raman lidar is a powerful tool for continuous profiling of atmospheric water vapor (WV) and temperature, but retrievals based on short integration times suffer from significant noise arising from both photon-counting statistics and analog detection. To address this, we apply a Kalman filter-based approach to derive 5-minute profiles from Raman lidar observations at two coastal sites in southwestern Japan — Fukue Island and Shimokoshiki Island. Raw lidar data are output at 5-minute intervals. WV mixing ratio profiles are derived using a 15-minute moving average, while temperature profiles require a 60-minute moving average due to the weaker Raman backscatter signal from nitrogen. A Kalman filter is then applied along the time dimension to these averaged profiles to further reduce residual noise while preserving genuine atmospheric variability. The filter uses altitude-dependent observation noise derived from measurement uncertainty, enabling adaptive smoothing that is stronger where signal-to-noise ratio is low. Both forward-only (causal) and RTS smoother (non-causal) implementations are evaluated, addressing the trade-off between real-time applicability and optimal smoothing performance. To validate the resulting profiles, we compare lidar retrievals before and after Kalman filtering against collocated radiosonde observations. The Kalman filter consistently reduces profile-to-profile noise and improves RMSE against radiosonde, while preserving physically meaningful atmospheric structures such as moisture gradients and temperature inversions. These results demonstrate the potential of this processing framework to deliver high-quality, high-temporal-resolution boundary layer profiles suitable for process studies, model validation, and future data assimilation applications.

486205.title: Assessing the Performance of a New Wind Gust Prediction Method Using Observations and a Numerical Model
486205.authors: Kelsey Lavon Grimme, Ernest F. Hollings Scholarship Program, Boulder, CO; and D. D. Turner and S. Murdzek
486205.abstract: Wind gusts near the surface have important applications in fire weather, aviation, and logistics. However, there lacks a consistent method for wind gust prediction. Typically, wind gusts are predicted by applying a multiplier to the 10 m wind speed, but that multiplier varies by region, terrain, and stability. In numerical models, wind gusts are represented as wind gust potential, a predicted upper bound for the 10 m wind gust. In this work, the 10 m wind speed and wind gust potential were leveraged to create a Gaussian distribution, from which a new estimate of wind gust was diagnosed. Preliminary testing on data from an uncrewed aircraft system in Grand Forks, ND, indicates that the new wind gust prediction method does have predictive power. Compared to results from the previously used multiplier method, the new wind gust prediction method saw a 9.4% decrease in standard deviation of error and a 53.8% decrease in mean error on the data assessed. In order to assess how robust the method is to factors such as time of day, season, and terrain, this study uses vertical profiles of the boundary layer to test the performance of the new method across a range of environments. Additionally, performance of the method on co-located High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) columns is also assessed to determine whether the physical processes reflected in the wind gust prediction are adequately represented in the model. Results will indicate whether the new wind gust prediction method is a robust improvement upon the previously used multiplier method.

486210.title: Enabling the Future of Impact-Based Decision Support at the National Hurricane Center
486210.authors: Micaela Maywald, University at Albany, Albany, NY; and L. Kelly, J. J. Alland, and J. R. Rhome
486210.abstract: Hurricane risk communication currently relies heavily on meteorological hazards, such as wind, rainfall, and storm surge. These variables alone fail to capture the real-world impacts of hurricane hazards, making it challenging for the public, especially vulnerable communities, to anticipate the conditions they may face and make informed decisions. To bridge the gap, this project presents an Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS) Toolkit. This internal, interactive viewer integrates a wide range of datasets into a single GIS environment. The toolkit enables rapid exposure and vulnerability analyses by combining forecast hazards with infrastructure, population, and community datasets. This provides a more comprehensive assessment of populations and assets at risk. Overall, this effort represents an important step toward the future of integrated IDSS at the National Hurricane Center.

486219.title: Forecasting Aerosols in a Stretched Grid Configuration of the Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS)
486219.authors: Allison Collow, Univ. of Maryland Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and W. Putman, C. Mogno, and C. A. Turner
486219.abstract: Initially developed to predict hazardous weather across the United States in a global model, the Goddard Earth Observing System Convection Allowing Model (GEOS-CAM) has potential to be used for other applications such as air quality and flight planning for suborbital field campaigns related to atmospheric composition however no evaluation against aerosol observations has been conducted before.
