A key feature of GEOS-CAM is a stretched grid such that the spatial resolution is roughly 2 km over the United States but coarsens to roughly 12 km on the opposite side of the world allowing for such fine resolution to be modeled daily in a computationally efficient manner. After a short spin-up with a meteorological replay to the quasi-operational GEOS system, GEOS-FP, forecasts are initialized in GEOS-CAM twice daily with 72-hour forecasts at 0z and 48-hour forecasts at 12z. This presentation will introduce the underlying configuration used for aerosols in GEOS-CAM, detailing considerations that need to be taken for fine resolution and stretched grid modelling. Forecasts of aerosol optical depth (AOD) and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in GEOS-CAM will then be evaluated against GEOS-FP and observations from surface networks including AERONET and IMPROVE as well as satellite retrievals. Although initial findings reveal that forecast skill in GEOS-CAM lags behind GEOS-FP, recommendations will be given for improving future versions of the system including the assimilation of AOD.

486220.title: Flooded with Frames: Public Perceptions of Green Infrastructure Mitigation Strategies in Urban Spaces
486220.authors: Zoey Rosen, Fordham University, Norman, OK; and A. Alexander and C. B. Voter
486220.abstract: The impacts of flooding is an increasing hydrometeorological concern globally, especially in urban spaces. Cities, in response, design mitigation strategies in order to combat the consequences of excess water. These flood mitigation strategies also simultaneously reduce the impacts of excessive heat, which are also exacerbated in urban areas. Despite the mutual benefits, these measures are framed under different names (Green Infrastructure or Low Impact Development) and discussed only around one of the impacts (flooding, instead of flooding and heat). Through a national survey of the United States and a document analysis of the extent of recent investments and future ambitions related to green stormwater infrastructure (GSI), this work aims to contextualize the public perceptions of Green Infrastructure and their support to pay for these implementations through grants or loans at a local or municipal level. Though this data is scoped to look at changes in perception based on location (urban, suburban, and rural) and where that city is located (US climate zones), we anticipate that these findings can be extended to other international areas with similar mitigation foci. Especially as the impacts of flooding and excessive heat in urban areas are becoming more pressing with the changing climate, it is important to understand how we communicate about mitigation, which will benefit meteorologists and practitioners worldwide.

486221.title: GPU Performance of Earth System Models.
486221.authors: Mark A Taylor, Sandia National Lab, Albuquerque, NM
486221.abstract: I'll give an overview of the work done by the Interagency Council for Advancing Meteorological Services (ICAMS) High Performance Computing Implementation Team (HPC-IT). In the past year we have been hosting presentations on algorithms, programming models and related technologies for efficiently running Earth System Models on GPU HPC systems. I'll then present some recent result from the E3SM project, including performance results on the US DOE's exascale and petascale platforms. I'll show the performance of E3SM's cloud resolving atmosphere model running at 3 km on both DOE Exascale systems, as well as E3SM's high resolution (12 km) fully coupled model which exploits the modern HBC hybrid node-architecture by running non-GPU enabled components concurrently on the CPUs left idle by the GPU-enabled components.

486226.title: Cross-Evaluation of Arctic Multi-Year Sea Ice Datasets (2022–2024): Spatial Hotspots, Phenomenological Timelines, and Retrieval Limitations
486226.abstract: Accurate quantification of Arctic Multi-Year Ice (MYI) is critical for understanding polar weather processes and marine navigation safety. However, widely used satellite-derived sea ice products rely on fundamentally distinct observational paradigms: pure passive microwave retrievals (AMSR2 NT2), combined active/passive Bayesian classification (EUMETSAT OSI SAF), kinematic Lagrangian tracking (NSIDC Sea Ice Age), and operational human-in-the-loop charting (U.S. National Ice Center; NIC). In this study, we remapped these four datasets across 2022–2024 onto a unified 12.5 km EASE-Grid 2.0 to evaluate daily categorical agreement (Open Water, First-Year Ice, and MYI) using 3X3 confusion matrices, spatial cross-correlations, and morphological boundary metrics. Spatial and statistical analyses reveal distinct seasonal disagreement regimes across the Arctic domain. In winter with all four datasets available, they show generally good agreement based on the confusion matrices, while spatial disagreements are non-random and tightly clustered along dynamic advection and physical deformation zones, particularly along the Beaufort Gyre boundary. During the summer melt period with NSIDC’s and NIC’s products available, a distinct divergence emerges between NSIDC's and NIC's sea ice type products. Daily tracking of Cohen's Kappa and False Alarm Ratios demonstrates that standalone passive microwave algorithms (AMSR2) experience performance degradation in early spring, whereas active scatterometer-supplemented approaches (OSI SAF) perform better. The primary physical drivers behind AMSR2's misclassification can be attributed to thermodynamic surface melting and atmospheric liquid-phase cloud contamination. This work establishes a baseline for evaluating these four distinct products in their current versions and provides direction for future algorithmic enhancements.

486228.title: Evaluating WRF Freezing-Rain Prediction and Ice-Accretion Estimates in Connecticut
486228.authors: Sloane Elizabeth Poppei, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; and M. Astitha and D. Cerrai
486228.abstract: Snow and ice accretion on electric power infrastructure can increase conductor loading and contribute to power outages during winter storms. However, these impacts remain difficult to predict because freezing rain depends on the vertical temperature structure of the atmosphere, the presence of supercooled liquid precipitation, and the timing of transitions between rain, freezing rain, sleet, and snow. This study is part of the NSF CAREER APEX-STORM project, which aims to improve the prediction of snow and ice accretion on power and transportation infrastructure to support winter-storm outage and restoration forecasting. The purpose of this work is to evaluate freezing-rain prediction in the Weather Research and Forecasting model and examine how model errors affect estimates of ice accretion. The WRF simulations use Global Forecast System initial and boundary conditions and the Thompson microphysics scheme. Four winter storms affecting Connecticut are examined: 3–5 February 2022, 15–17 January 2024, 8–9 February 2025, and 15–17 February 2025. These events were selected because freezing rain occurred near the NASA Global Precipitation Measurement Ground Validation site at the University of Connecticut and because they overlap with the broader observational campaign. Available meteorological, precipitation-gauge, disdrometer, imaging, and radar observations are used to examine precipitation type, amount, timing, and vertical precipitation structure. Surface observations from Integrated Surface Database stations, including Automated Surface Observing System sites, are also used to evaluate model performance. Freezing-rain occurrence is evaluated using several precipitation-type approaches, including diagnostic algorithms from the Unified Post Processor, the Air Force Weather Agency method, and model-derived approaches based on temperature and hydrometeor fields. Model performance is evaluated using categorical verification metrics that describe detection, false alarms, and overall skill, along with comparisons of event timing. Errors are also examined using 2-meter temperature, vertical temperature profiles, and modeled rain, snow, graupel, cloud water, and cloud ice mixing ratios. Modeled freezing rain is then converted into flat and radial ice-accretion estimates to examine how precipitation-type and temperature errors affect estimates of conductor loading. Preliminary results show that freezing-rain prediction varies across diagnostic methods and events, with performance especially sensitive to small near-surface temperature errors and the timing of precipitation-type transitions near 0°C. Finally, preliminary observations from a non-energized experimental power-line span at the UConn Depot Campus will be discussed as part of the broader APEX-STORM effort to understand how winter weather affects conductor tension and sag. Together, this work supports the development of improved icing estimates for winter outage prediction and electric-utility storm preparedness.

486231.title: Linking Deep Convection and Dynamical Variabilities in the UTLS
486231.authors: Rei Ueyama, NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, CA; and M. Park
486231.abstract: Deep convection has an impact on the thermodynamics and chemical composition of the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). To investigate the role of convection on the UTLS thermodynamics and composition, we first analyze the thermal variability in the tropical and midlatitude UTLS using dense, high vertical resolution radio occultation (RO) based temperature retrievals from the Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) from 2002 to 2025. We then examine the UTLS thermal variability in relation to convective activity derived from the satellite-derived global convective cloud top altitude fields. Deep convection and tropopause properties exhibit large interannual variability as well as shorter-term variabilities, which challenges the interpretation of possible long-term trends. However, preliminary analyses suggest that deep convection has become more intense and frequent in recent decades, likely attributed to warmer surface temperatures. Tropical cold-point tropopause (CPT) temperatures exhibit a slight warming trend, accompanied by decreasing lapse-rate tropopause altitude. The warming trend in the CPT temperatures also has an impact on the entry value of water vapor near the tropical tropopause layer region. We explore the long-term variability in convective activities in the tropics and its link to variabilities in the tropical tropopause, large-scale transport, and water vapor.

486232.title: From Forecast to Action: Integrating Meteorology, Flood Intelligence, and Emergency Management into Operational Decision Making.
486232.authors: Bryce Houlton, Guadalupe County Emergency Management, Seguin, TX
486232.abstract: As weather events become increasingly complex and impactful, emergency managers and meteorologists must move beyond simply sharing forecasts to building a unified, operational decision making process that protects lives and property. This presentation explores how Guadalupe County, Texas, developed a hazard specific response framework that directly links National Weather Service forecast products, hydrologic data, automated flood sensors, and outdoor warning systems to emergency management operations. Participants will examine a standardized operational matrix that establishes predefined actions for severe weather, tornadoes, flooding, and winter weather based on forecast confidence and anticipated impacts. The presentation demonstrates how meteorological information including Storm Prediction Center outlooks, National Weather Service watches and warnings, river forecasts, and real-time flood sensor data is translated into actionable emergency management decisions such as Emergency Operations Center activation, public warning issuance, resource deployment, and interagency coordination. The session also highlights the integration of automated outdoor warning sirens, polygon based warning activation, GBRA river monitoring, and impact based decision support into a comprehensive county warning strategy. Through practical examples, attendees will learn how emergency managers and meteorologists can establish common operating procedures, improve communication, and provide consistent, timely protective actions for their communities. Designed for emergency managers, National Weather Service meteorologists, hydrologists, public safety officials, and emergency communications professionals, this presentation provides a scalable framework that jurisdictions of any size can adapt to strengthen preparedness, improve operational coordination, and enhance public warning capabilities before, during, and after hazardous weather events.

486240.title: Creating a Culture of Communication: Training NSF NCAR and UCAR Staff How to Translate Earth System Science for the General Public
486240.authors: Daniel W. Zietlow, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. A. Aquino, T. Barnes, P. Montaño, MS, MA, A. Rhinehart, T. M. Weckwerth, and K. Wolfson
486240.abstract: To build trust with the public and highlight the societal relevance of Earth system science research, it is important to empower staff at scientific institutions with evidence-based communication strategies. To foster these skills, the U.S. National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) Center for Excellence in Education, Engagement & Early-Career Development (EdEC) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research’s (UCAR) Center for Science Education (SciEd) have partnered to develop an interactive training workshop for NSF NCAR and UCAR staff. Open to anyone at the organization interested in science communication training, including engineers, technicians, and researchers to educators, administrators, and technicians, these workshops train staff to craft compelling narratives for non-technical audiences. During this presentation, we will discuss evaluation results highlighting best practices for designing impactful science communication training and discuss our efforts to cultivate a lasting cohort of alumni. Finally, we will lead a short, interactive demo of our training content to illustrate how we help staff turn complex science into clear, accessible stories that spark curiosity and connection.

486241.title: Beyond Prediction: Transforming Earth System Predictability into Actionable Decision Support
486241.authors: Xin-Zhong Liang, University of Maryland College Park, College Park, MD
486241.abstract: The grand challenge facing Earth system science is no longer simply improving predictive skill, but transforming advances in Earth system predictability into actionable intelligence that improves human decisions and societal resilience. Although substantial progress has enhanced our ability to predict climate variability and extremes across subseasonal, seasonal, and interannual timescales, converting predictive capability into effective decisions remains a fundamental scientific and operational challenge. Addressing this challenge requires integrating advances in regional Earth system modeling, hydroclimate and impact prediction, artificial intelligence, uncertainty quantification, and stakeholder-centered system design into a unified scientific framework. This presentation introduces an integrated framework for transforming Earth system predictability into actionable decision support through regional Earth system modeling, hydroclimate and impact prediction, and interactive decision-support systems. The framework combines regional dynamical downscaling, optimized multi-physics and multi-model ensembles, improved land-surface initialization, hybrid physics–AI modeling, and probabilistic prediction to generate credible forecasts of hydroclimate variability and associated impacts, including extreme precipitation, water availability, crop productivity, and other climate-sensitive systems. These predictions are translated into actionable intelligence through impact models and interactive decision-support platforms developed through stakeholder engagement and coproduction, enabling users to evaluate management alternatives while explicitly accounting for uncertainty and risk. The USDA-funded Dashboard for Agricultural Water use and Nutrient management (DAWN) serves as an operational example demonstrating how advances in Earth system prediction can be transformed into practical climate services for agricultural decision-making. Although agriculture provides the primary application, the underlying framework is broadly applicable to water resources, ecosystem management, disaster resilience, energy systems, public health, and other sectors where climate information must support risk-informed decisions. The presentation concludes by discussing future directions toward integrated human–Earth system prediction, in which advances in regional Earth system modeling, impact prediction, artificial intelligence, and interactive decision support collectively extend Earth system predictability beyond scientific forecasting to actionable intelligence that strengthens climate resilience across diverse societal sectors.

486265.title: Attributing 2013–2024 Drivers of Global Ammonia Emissions Using IASI Observations: Implications for Future Climate Change
486265.authors: Drew C. Pendergrass, Oberlin College, Oberlin, OH; and D. Shindell, L. Clarisse, M. Van Damme, M. Beaudor, J. Jiang, and S. Zhai
486265.abstract: Improved agricultural productivity has been accompanied by increasing emissions of ammonia (NH3). Because of its nonlinear impact on fine particulate matter (PM2.5), NH3 controls have been identified as cost-effective means of improving air quality. However, policy assessment is hampered by large uncertainties in NH3 emissions and trends. Here, we perform a daily ensemble Kalman filter inversion of 2013–24 IASI NH3 observations at 4°×5° resolution to estimate NH3 emissions and trends. We find global NH3 emissions total 85 Tg a-1 on average, similar to levels estimated by emissions inventories but reallocated regionally. We then use a machine-learning approach to diagnose drivers of NH3 emissions trends. We find a significant 1.09 Tg a-2 NH3 increasing trend in global emissions over the 2014–23 period. While peatland fires, correlated with El Niño events, are major drivers of global interannual variability, the increasing NH3 trend is largely driven by agricultural activity, especially livestock. We find an observable climate-driven increasing trend of 0.13 Tg a-2, which in China is substantial enough to offset 48% of NH3 reductions due to controls on fertilizer use. We project the climate penalty to 2100 using Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) output and estimate a global climate NH3 emissions penalty of between 3.5 Tg a-1 (4.5 W m-2 forcing) and 6.6 Tg a-1 (7.0 W m-2) by the end of the century, in line with estimates from process-based models.

486267.title: A SCHISM-Explainable AI Framework for Attributing Compound Flood Drivers during Hurricane Matthew (2016) in Winyah Bay
486267.authors: Huan Wang, Coastal Carolina University, Conway, SC; Coastal Carolina University, Conway, SC; and S. Bao
486267.abstract: Coastal compound flooding is driven by interactions among oceanic, fluvial, and pluvial processes. Quantitatively attributing the contributions of these drivers remains challenging because of their nonlinear interactions and the high computational cost of conventional numerical sensitivity experiments. This study develops a hybrid SCHISM–AI–SHAP framework that integrates the Semi-implicit Cross-scale Hydroscience Integrated System Model (SCHISM), a surrogate artificial intelligence model, and the explainable AI method SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to identify the dominant drivers of compound flooding in Winyah Bay, South Carolina, during Hurricane Matthew (2016). SCHISM reproduced water elevations and velocities across the coupled ocean–estuary–river system and generated dynamically consistent training data for the surrogate model. The trained surrogate model demonstrated high predictive skill, enabling efficient and physically interpretable attribution using SHAP. The results indicate that flooding during Hurricane Matthew was governed by a coupled surge–river–tide system characterized by two distinct phases: phase 1, dominated by storm surge, and phase 2, dominated by upstream river inputs. The SCHISM–AI–SHAP framework provides a computationally efficient and physically consistent approach for attributing compound-flood drivers in complex coastal systems.

486280.title: NOAA’s Low Earth Orbit Observations Strategy: Current Status and Future Plans
486280.abstract: NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) Program will develop the next generation of Low Earth orbit (LEO) environmental and weather satellites designed to succeed the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) series. Because LEO satellites provide over 80% of the data used in 3 to 7 day numerical weather prediction models, NEON plays a critical role in maintaining continuous global atmospheric monitoring. To build a more agile and resilient system, NEON will transition from large, multi-instrument satellites to a disaggregated architecture of smaller, single-instrument spacecraft launched on flexible timelines. This shift is exemplified by its QuickSounder pathfinder mission and the upcoming NEON Series-1, which will carry advanced microwave sounders. Leveraging commercial partnerships and agile procurement strategies to lower costs and rapidly field updated weather technologies is also a core part of the NEON strategy. The JPSS mission remains robust, with the primary NOAA21 satellite and secondary NOAA20 satellite operating nominally, while JPSS4 is on schedule to launch in 2027. Program science activities include observing system experiments for the formulation of NEON, value assessments of LEO satellites, and innovations to exploit mission data for critical applications. LEO data have been used extensively to track poor air quality during recent wildfires and to support response efforts during severe weather events. Furthermore, data from new LEO missions such as JAXA’s AMSR3 and the U.S. Space Force’s Weather System Follow-on Microwave (WSF-M) are providing unique and critical microwave imager observations to weather forecasters. Observing system impact studies and value assessments of LEO data demonstrate the importance of these observations for high impact weather applications. This abstract presents the current status of the NEON and JPSS missions alongside the latest scientific applications of their observations.

486286.title: An Observational Analysis Evaluating Drivers of Severe Weather Production in Supercell Thunderstorms Near Surface Boundaries
486286.authors: Jasen Greco, UNC Charlotte, Charlotte, NC; and C. E. Davenport and C. Nixon
486286.abstract: Supercell thunderstorms are characterized by a deep, persistently rotating mesocyclone, and are well-known for their production of severe weather, including large hail, gusty winds, and/or tornadoes. The structure, intensity, severe weather production, and longevity of a supercell thunderstorm is heavily influenced by its surrounding environment. Notably, synoptic-scale frontal boundaries are synonymous with strongly heterogeneous environments, and have been demonstrated to augment severe weather production as a result of supercell-boundary interactions. Prior studies have characterized the distance and intensity of severe weather production near boundaries, but have yet to fully elucidate when supercell-boundary interactions favor different types of severe weather (i.e., only tornadoes, only hail, or some combination). One study recently suggested that supercells with only hail production were located on the more stable side of a boundary, associated with a higher lifting condensation level and weaker low-level storm-relative helicity compared to supercells that produced tornadoes. Given that tornado production is also known to be enhanced near boundaries, it would be worthwhile to identify the conditions that would support a single type of severe weather, such as only hail or only tornadoes, or conditions that may support a combination of severe weather reports, such as tornadoes and hail. Thus, the goal of this study is to explore the sensitivity of the type of supercell severe weather production near frontal boundaries. A large observed dataset of 106 discrete supercells interacting with warm or stationary boundaries drawn from both previous work (Magee and Davenport 2020; Nixon et al. 2024) and more recent cases was leveraged. The pre-existing Magee and Davenport (2020) dataset contained 34 discrete supercell cases near boundaries, while the Nixon et al. (2024) dataset contained 18 discrete supercells near boundaries. The additional dataset gathered for this study added 54 more cases of discrete supercells near boundaries. Severe hazard production type varied notably depending on boundary type: tornado-only production occurred more frequently near warm fronts, which were also associated with more severe tornadoes with higher average EF-scale ratings compared to tornadoes produced near stationary fronts. Conversely, hail-only production was more prevalent near stationary fronts, which yielded higher overall hail intensity and larger mean hail diameters compared to hail produced near warm fronts. In supercell-boundary interactions associated with both hail and tornado production, hail formation typically preceded tornado development. However, cases in which tornadoes occurred first featured higher average EF-scale ratings and a wider distribution of tornado intensities, whereas hail-first cases yielded significantly larger hailstones on average. These patterns in severe weather intensity and sequencing will be explained using near-storm environmental information as well as mesoscale gradients in quantities such as low-level storm-relative helicity, CAPE, CIN, and LCL heights. Ultimately, these results and ongoing efforts will provide operational meteorologists with actionable insights to better anticipate specific hazard types as discrete supercells interact with surface boundaries.

486287.title: Long-Lasting Impacts of George’s Research and Mentorship on Examining Global Atmospheric Energy Oscillations Associated with the Madden-Julian Oscillation
486287.authors: Naoko Sakaeda, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
486287.abstract: This presentation summarizes my recent work that was supposed to be done while I was a postdoc under George’s mentorship. After many years away from George’s direct mentorship, I rediscovered the lasting impacts of George’s research and mentorship that guided me to finally complete the project. Here I present my findings, which build upon his prior work, and how I applied the important principles of research he taught me. I will present the robust evidence of global moist static energy anomalies that evolve with the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) beyond the tropics, based on three reanalyses. I find that the MJO alters the direction of cross-equatorial energy and mass transport as it propagates eastward, leading to hemispheric oscillations in global moist static energy. This global energy oscillation is connected to how the MJO modulates the ITCZ and Hadley circulation. When the MJO intensifies the Hadley circulation, energy is also anomalously transported poleward away from the tropics, offsetting the tropics-wide increase in energy gain via anomalous radiation and surface latent heat flux. The poleward energy transport away from the tropics is stronger in the Northern than in the Southern Hemisphere due to a hemispheric asymmetry in the Hadley cell structure, likely driven by differences in landmass distribution. The preferential energy transport in the Northern Hemisphere accumulates energy and mass in the northern midlatitudes, partly explaining the strong MJO teleconnections observed there. The documented global atmospheric energy of the MJO builds upon George’s prior studies on MJO structure and its connection to the extratropics by providing a new perspective on the dynamical connections between the MJO, a tropics-wide intraseasonal oscillation, and teleconnections.

486288.title: NOAA’s HAFS Multistorm Hurricane Model - New “HAFS-B” Operational Candidate
486288.authors: Lewis James Gramer, University of Miami, Cutler Bay, FL; and A. Hazelton, X. Lu, W. Ramstrom, S. Gopalakrishnan, G. J. Alaka Jr., Z. Zhang, B. Liu, C. K. Wang, J. Shin, J. Peng, and Y. Weng
486288.abstract: For over a decade, NOAA’s Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Lab (AOML) Hurricane Research Division (HRD) has worked with partners at NOAA’s Office of Modeling and Development (formerly, EMC) to provide major advances in hurricane prediction. During the past five years, HRD has implemented and tested a configuration of the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) that is capable of simultaneously simulating several tropical cyclones - HAFS Multistorm or “Multi”. Multi allows up to five high-resolution, storm-following nests in a single basin-scale outer domain. Over the past three years, HRD has spearheaded the push to operationalize Multi by testing it in real time as part of the Hurricane Forecast Improvement Project’s (HFIP) Real-Time Experimental (HREX) effort; HRD has also supported NOAAs Office of Model Development (OMD) in testing a simplified version of Multi in HREX. The 4x-daily real-time tests of Multi provided critical insight into model behavior, data assimilation and initialization, cyclogenesis, and improved physical parameterizations, thus highlighting the transformative potential of multi-storm, moving-nest technology for operational hurricane forecasting. Details of these advancements will be briefly reviewed. OMD and HRD intend to work together to implement a version of Multi for operational forecasting beginning with the 2028 Atlantic season. In addition, Multi is already being used as a basis for experiments to implement telescoping nests (including an inner domain at ~600 m horizontal resolution), improve physics parameterizations, and to improve model initialization (including adoption of the JEDI platform, incremental analysis update, and novel satellite and ocean data assimilation techniques). The goal of this work is both to continue advancing Multi for operational forecast improvements in the next few years, and to ensure forecast spread in the suite of operational hurricane forecasts for NOAA consensus modeling going forward. We will present recent results from the above developments including track, intensity, structure, ocean state, and rapid intensification, along with a summary of past performance for comparison.

486297.title: Layer-Dependent Diurnal Moist Static Energy Biases in the Unified Forecast System During the MJO Preconditioning Stage: A DYNAMO Case Study
486297.authors: Weiwei Li, NCAR, Erie, CO; and S. Sun, L. Bengtsson, M. Zhang, J. Dudhia, E. Grell, J. M. Simonson, PhD, T. J. Hertneky, and L. B. Nance
486297.abstract: Accurate simulation of the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) requires realistic diurnal evolution and vertical distribution of moist static energy (MSE). While prior studies documented MSE bias in simulations, vertically dependent physical processes responsible for these biases remain insufficiently understood. This study applies a hierarchical modeling and evaluation approach, combining fully-coupled Unified Forecast System (UFS) forecasts with observation-constrained single-column model (SCM) experiments, to enable vertically and diurnally resolved assessment of MSE during two MJO events from the DYNAMO field campaign. Results reveal a diurnal loop of layer-dependent biases: daytime errors precondition nighttime residual energy, which in turn influences MSE and convection on the following day. These biases are associated with deficiencies in the convective parameterization, in which convective latent heating is concentrated in the upper troposphere while the transition layer receives insufficient energy input, reflecting a missing shallow-to-deep convective transition. The convective parameterization also converts cloud condensate, especially ice, too efficiently, reinforcing an overly top-heavy energy structure. This residual energy aloft persists overnight, suppressing the re-establishment of low-level instability and limiting convective development the following day. This hierarchical, vertically resolved analysis provides a process-based pathway for diagnosing issues in tropical energetics on the diurnal timescale during the MJO preconditioning stage, with potential implications to improve MJO prediction in the UFS and related forecast systems.

486303.title: Removing Aircraft Motion from Scanning Doppler Wind Lidar
486303.authors: Nathan Malarich, CIRES, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and W. A. Brewer, M. Zucker, R. Alvarez II, S. Baidar, B. J. Carroll, M. W. Holloway, S. Sandberg, A. S. Makowiecki, and C. Warneke
486303.abstract: Doppler lidars provide horizontal wind profiles and mixing heights, which are useful for calculating chemical fluxes. An airborne lidar with a scanning arm out the side window can measure both above and below the aircraft, providing mixing heights from within the boundary layer alongside in situ chemical instruments. However, the moving parts of the side-scanner must be well-characterized to know the precise lidar beam pointing, otherwise aircraft motion can contaminate the 3D wind measurements. We use the ground-reflection data to determine offsets in the lidar beam pointing. A least-squares fit routine fits a single offset for each of the two motor rotation angles, as well as a heading-offset between the scanner arm and an inertial navigation unit. The ground-reflection data also provides clues to scanner bearing degradation or loose screws. We use this data to inform maintenance schedules and post-processing corrections. With this hard-target calibration, our side-scanning lidar has 1 m/s agreement with in situ winds for each profile measurement, and 0.75 m/s agreement for profiles averaged across a flight leg.

486307.title: Airborne Mass Balance of Marcellus Shale
486307.authors: Nathan Malarich, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and S. Baidar, W. A. Brewer, S. S. Brown, X. Ren, M. W. Holloway, M. Zucker, R. Marchbanks, S. Sandberg, I. B. Pollack, R. Alvarez II, B. J. Carroll, C. Warneke, B. J. McCarty, P. Kelley, P. Stratton, J. Lau, and S. Renton
486307.abstract: Natural gas production from Marcellus shale has doubled in the past decade, while unconventional drilling and emissions monitoring technologies have matured, making overall emissions uncertain. To help constrain the basin-wide emissions estimates, the NOAA Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR) conducted airborne mass balance measurements during summer 2025. The NOAA Twin Otter aircraft flew repeated closed-loop patterns around the predominant unconventional drilling regions. The 7 flight days in southwest Marcellus and 5 days in northeast Marcellus enables statistics to capture uncertainty in transport as well as true time-variability in emissions, while the repeated two-box pattern was able to resolve transient emissions across a single flight day. The aircraft payload included in situ measurements of CH4, C2H6, CO2, CO, and NOy. Additionally, the aircraft had a scanning Doppler lidar to provide wind profiles and mixing heights throughout the flights. We estimate total CH4 and C2H6 emissions during these flights, and compare them against inventories and previous measurements.

486348.title: Convective-Scale Land-Atmosphere Strongly Coupled DA with “Group Filter” Treatment of Cross-Component Sampling Error
486348.authors: Xuguang Wang, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; Consortium for Advanced Data assimilation Research and Education (CADRE), Norman, OK; and A. T. Johnson
486348.abstract: Convection Initiation (CI) along the Great Plains dryline is a common occurrence in the spring and early summer, can affect the evolution of high impact severe weather events, and is sensitive to interactions with the land surface. Cases of dryline CI are therefore expected to particularly benefit from strongly coupled data assimilation (SCDA) in convection-permitting forecast systems such as RRFS. However, the sampling error associated with ensemble-based estimates of the cross-component background error covariance can be more complex than the within-component sampling error and doesn’t necessarily increase as a function of horizontal distance from an assimilated observation. Since distance-based covariance localization implicitly assumes sampling error to increase roughly isotropically with distance from the observation, alternative treatments of the cross-component sampling error are necessary to optimize ensemble-based land-atmosphere SCDA at convective scales. In this study, the ensemble “group filter” is adopted together with distance-based localization to further dampen ensemble-based cross-component covariances where there is high variability among sub-ensemble estimates of the covariance. The performance of SCDA analyses and forecasts with the CADRE-MPAS-JEDI DA system on a dryline CI case study will be presented and the impact of adopting the group filter treatment of sampling error will be demonstrated with both single-observation tests and cycled DA experiments.

486354.title: My Research Journey Influenced By David Randall: From PBL to Land-Atmosphere Interaction and to the General Circulation (Invited Presentation)
486354.authors: Xubin Zeng, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ
486354.abstract: I have had the privilege of interacting with Prof. David Randall for more than three decades, during which his mentorship has profoundly shaped my career. In this brief overview, I highlight some of my group’s recent research in data analysis, model development, suborbital mission measurements, and spaceborne mission concept development across three key areas. Our work on the planetary boundary layer (PBL) has been influenced by Prof. Randall’s perspective of the PBL as a global phenomenon—closely linked to clouds and the free troposphere—rather than a local micrometeorological process. Our studies on land–atmosphere interactions have benefited from his insights into land data development, dynamic vegetation, and the global coupling between land and atmosphere. Finally, our research on the global atmosphere has been inspired by his teaching, his vision for understanding organized convection–general circulation interactions, and his leadership in the GEWEX Cloud Systems Study.

486381.title: An Additive Inflation Algorithm for CMA-GFS En4DVar
486381.authors: junjie deng, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China; and R. Wang, L. Zhang, J. Gong, L. Lei, and Z. M. Tan
486381.abstract: One strategy to mitigate sampling errors and model errors for ensemble-based data assimilation methods is covariance inflation. An additive inflation method is proposed to the current China Meteorological Administration (CMA) operational global data assimilation (DA) system. It uses an ensemble four-dimensional variational (En4DVar) system that incorporates flow-dependent background error covariances from short-term ensemble forecasts, and a static multiplicative inflation method to increase ensemble spread. Compared to the traditionally applied static multiplicative inflation, the proposed additive inflation has dynamical error growth and can better consider the impact of model errors on flow-dependent background error covariances. Single-point observation experiments indicate that additive inflation retains flow-dependent characteristics of the analysis increments, and produces smaller magnitudes of analysis increments but more accurate analyses than multiplicative inflation. Cycling assimilation experiments demonstrate that compared to multiplicative inflation, additive inflation improves the analyses of geopotential height and temperature than multiplicative inflation, and the advantages of additive inflation over multiplicative inflation are mainly contributed from small wavenumbers. Forecasts launched from analyses indicate that additive inflation produces significantly improved forecasts than multiplicative inflation for all state variables from surface to 10 hPa both over the northern and southern hemispheres, although the significant improvements over the southern hemisphere have smaller magnitudes and shorter lead times than over the northern hemisphere.

486391.title: Recommendations for Scale Separation and Localization Strategies for GFS based on Scale-Dependent Variability in Ocean and Sea Ice Ensembles
486391.authors: Emma Dufresne, NOAA, College Park, MD; and A. Shlyaeva and G. Vernieres
486391.abstract: The most recent update to the Global Forecast System (GFS) includes updating the physical model to the Unified Forecast System (UFS), which couples the atmosphere/land, ocean, sea ice, and wave components. At the same time, the GFS data assimilation (DA) is being upgraded to a weakly coupled approach, implementing three-dimensional variational data assimilation (3DVar) for the ocean and sea ice components of the control member which initializes the long-range forecast. Future updates to GFS will include an ensemble DA system for ocean and sea ice. Due to the promising results of including ensembles in forecast prediction, this research focuses on how to improve the ocean and sea ice background error covariance matrix and localization using the ensembles. Ensemble background error covariances are localized to remove spurious long-distance correlations. The effectiveness of this localization depends on accurately representing the spatial scales of forecast errors; this motivates efforts to improve the characterization of these lengthscales. Therefore, spatial error correlations in coupled ocean and sea ice ensembles are explored to determine dependencies on geographical region, season, and model variables. Based on ensemble variability, meaningful horizontal lengthscales are presented and compared to those currently assumed in the static background-error covariances used in the ocean and sea ice 3DVar. Preliminary results indicate that short-range ensemble-based horizontal lengthscales for sea surface temperature are influenced by synoptic variability rather than the Rossby radius of deformation. Furthermore, cross correlations of ocean and sea ice variables are presented to provide insight into the importance of coupling between earth systems.

486403.title: The 2026 AMS Early Career Leadership Academy
486403.authors: Liz Baugher Gilden, AMS ECLA Chair, Reston, VA; and A. M. Morrison
486403.abstract: The AMS Early Career Leadership Academy (ECLA) aims to build and sustain a network of early career leaders in the weather, water, and climate (WWC) sciences.. ECLA provides an opportunity for participants to connect with colleagues across sectors, learn and grow as leaders, support one another as collaborators and peer mentors, all with the intent to one day take on leadership roles within their respective workplaces and AMS. ECLA is a unique AMS program in that it is a cross-commission endeavor. Oversight of the program and selection of the ECLA participants is the responsibility of an Advisory Committee that is chaired by the AMS Commissioner of Education and Engagement and the AMS Commissioner of Professional Affairs. ECLA participants are selected from a pool of early-career applicants as defined by AMS and work in the WWC enterprise. The ECLA Planning Committee organizes most ECLA activities and is composed of previous ECLA class members, as well as members of the AMS Board on Representation, Accessibility, Inclusion, and Diversity (BRAID) and the AMS Board for Early Career Professionals (BECP). The Early Career Leadership Academy offers an Orientation Webinar, four online Leadership Webinars, peer mentoring sessions and culminates with a two and a half day in-person meeting. New this year, ECLA was co-located with the AMS Madison Summit which provided additional networking opportunities for participants. To meet the specific leadership needs of participants, most topics for webinars and meeting sessions were derived from participant’s applications. Some topics of 2026 ECLA program focused on individual leadership style, difficult conversations, mentoring and career growth, and resiliency while facing difficult challenges and uncertainty. In this presentation, we describe the goals of the AMS ECLA program, discuss specific activities carried out by the ECLA 2026 class and how these enhance leadership skills, and provide an overview of future ECLA plans. Application submissions for the 2027 ECLA program will begin to be accepted in early 2027 on the AMS website.

486404.title: Withdrawn: Beyond the Degree: Empowering Atmospheric and Geoscience Students to Build Purposeful Career Pathways
486404.authors: Liz Baugher Gilden, AMS ECLA Chair, Reston, VA; and P. Asher
486404.abstract: Atmospheric and geoscience training equips students and researchers with highly transferable skills, yet many students and early career professionals struggle to translate their academic experience into purposeful career trajectories. The National Association of Colleges and Employers (NACE) defines career readiness as the foundation for a successful career trajectory, or simply as "the new career currency" (NACE, 2026). According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, geoscience employment is projected to grow nearly 4% between 2024 and 2034, with opportunities spanning the private sector, federal and state government, academia, consulting, and nonprofit organizations. Despite this pressure, students and postdoctoral researchers frequently lack exposure to and understanding of the full breadth of these pathways. Drawing on direct advising experience with undergraduate and graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, we examine common career-readiness gaps and the sector-specific knowledge students need to navigate them successfully. Key themes include understanding where atmospheric and geoscience professionals work and why, translating field and research experience into workforce-ready skills valued across sectors, and making informed decisions about career transitions. We offer actionable strategies for students and early career professionals seeking to move from academic training into purposeful, sector-aligned careers, and invite participants to share their own experiences and pathways.

486406.title: Surface-Layer Similarity Relationships over Complex Terrain: Insights from the Marshall Testbed
486406.authors: Temple R. Lee, NOAA, Oak Ridge, TN; and T. P. Meyers, D. D. Turner, and J. Kochendorfer
486406.abstract: Accurate representations of surface-layer (SL) exchanges of momentum, heat, and moisture are of vital importance for the land-surface and atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) parameterizations used within numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. Many of these use an approach referred to as Monin-Obukov Similarity Theory (MOST) that was developed decades ago using observations obtained from flat terrain. However, questions oftentimes arise regarding the applicability of MOST-derived relationships to areas of complex, inhomogeneous terrain. In this study, we investigate the applicability of MOST relationships for fluxes of momentum, heat, and moisture at a site located near Marshall, Colorado, using nine months of observations obtained from a 10-m tower outfitted with a suite of micrometeorological and flux measurements. These tower observations are complemented by those from multiple ABL profilers. These profilers include a Vaisala WindCube which uses targeted sampling of the wind and turbulence fields of the lowest 300 m of the atmosphere, observations from the Collaborative Lower Atmospheric Mobile Profiling System (CLAMPS) which has an onboard Atmospheric Sounder Spectrometer by Infrared Spectral Technology (ASSIST) to obtain high-temporal resolution vertical profiles of temperature and water vapor, and a Doppler wind lidar for inferring wind and turbulence fields over the full ABL depth. We find that the robustness of the MOST relationships significantly varies as a function of wind direction. When winds are from the east and the upwind footprint is relatively homogenous, MOST much better represents the momentum, heat, and moisture fluxes than when winds are from the west and the site samples descending flows off the Rocky Mountains. These findings highlight some of the underlying limitations with MOST and suggest the need to consider modifications to the current suite of SL parameterizations in NWP models.

486413.title: Storm-Organization-Aware Evaluation of Probabilistic Generative Precipitation Nowcasting Models
486413.authors: Diyali Goswami, Sustainability and Data Sciences Lab, Boston, MA; Northeastern University, Boston, MA; and A. R. Ganguly
486413.abstract: Machine learning models for precipitation nowcasting have advanced rapidly in recent years. Probabilistic generative approaches such as PreDiff (Gao et al., 2023), DiffCast (Yu et al., 2024), CasCast (Gong et al., 2024), FlowCast (Ribeiro and Faganeli Pucer, 2026), and FREUD (Schusterbauer et al., 2026) report substantial gains over deterministic baselines on the Storm Event Imagery (SEVIR) benchmark (Veillette et al., 2020), which has become a widely used standard for evaluating precipitation nowcasting models. Standard practice on this benchmark reports the Critical Success Index, Heidke Skill Score, Fractions Skill Score, and Continuous Ranked Probability Score as aggregate scalars averaged across events, lead times, and intensity thresholds. Model comparisons therefore reduce performance to a small number of global scores, potentially obscuring systematic differences in when and why particular models succeed or fail. Object-based verification methods such as the Contiguous Rain Area decomposition attribute forecast errors within individual events to distinct pattern, volume, and displacement components (Ebert and McBride, 2000; Das et al., 2024), but whether model skill varies systematically across storm-organization types remains largely unexplored. Operational meteorology has long described storms using organizational categories such as isolated cells, cell clusters, squall lines, training convection, back-building systems, and convective systems with trailing, leading, or parallel stratiform precipitation (Parker and Johnson, 2000; Gallus et al., 2008; sensu Schumacher and Johnson, 2005). This vocabulary encodes physically meaningful differences in spatial scale, motion, coherence, persistence, and predictability (Houze, 2004). Isolated convective cells may initiate, intensify, and dissipate within tens of minutes; squall lines and training convection translate or repeatedly pass over organized corridors; back-building systems regenerate upstream and may remain nearly stationary; and stratiform precipitation can extend across broad areas surrounding organized convection. Forecast error may consequently vary across storm-organization types. Moreover, high-impact events with substantial public-safety consequences, including flash floods produced by slow-moving, training, and repeatedly regenerating convection, arise from specific organization modes that current benchmark reporting does not isolate (Doswell et al., 1996; Schumacher and Johnson, 2005). Two machine learning nowcasters with identical mean CSI may succeed and fail on entirely different storms. Aggregate skill alone does not reveal which storm organizations a model handles well or why. This work therefore asks a simple question: do machine learning nowcasting models fail on the same storms, or on systematically different ones? To answer it, we extend the widely used SEVIR nowcasting benchmark with a storm-organization decomposition layer that reports canonical skill scores for meteorologically interpretable regimes. We characterize each event in SEVIR VIL using seven physically motivated storm-organization axes computed from the input radar sequence: spatial scale, linearity, fragmentation, persistence, mobility, structural stability, and regeneration. The axes are calculated for every event and percentile-normalized across the test set to ensure comparability. Gaussian mixture clustering is then applied to the seven-dimensional feature vectors to obtain a soft partition into interpretable storm regimes spanning isolated convective cells, organized linear systems, and larger mesoscale systems. This probabilistic partition reflects the physical reality that storm organization exists along a continuum rather than within rigid categories, while providing an interpretable, machine-usable representation linked to established operational storm-mode terminology. The probabilistic nowcasting models are evaluated on the extended benchmark using standard skill-scoring conventions, producing event-level measurements for each canonical metric. Aggregate scores are reported alongside regime-specific breakdowns of the same metrics, enabling direct identification of the storm regimes each model handles well and those on which it systematically underperforms. Preliminary results reveal substantial regime-specific variation that aggregate reporting conceals. Per-cluster CSI at the one-pixel scale spans a factor of two across the identified regimes, while per-cluster CSI at the extreme intensity threshold of 219 spans more than a factor of four. Different architectures exhibit distinct regime-specific strengths and weaknesses, and no single model dominates across all storm types. Full model-by-regime breakdowns will be presented at the conference, together with a discussion of what these patterns imply for comparing, selecting, and combining machine learning nowcasting systems in operational practice. The organization axes, cluster assignments, and regime-specific evaluation outputs will be released as a community resource, enabling future nowcasting models to be evaluated directly on the extended benchmark.

486415.title: Evidence for Enhanced Dynamical Efficiency of Organized Maritime Shallow Convection in Large-Domain LES
486415.authors: Mikael Kurt Witte, NPS, Monterey, CA
486415.abstract: Converging lines of modeling and observational evidence indicate that cloud-scale dynamics are modulated by mesoscale organization of shallow convection. Large-eddy simulations have demonstrated that moisture aggregation and cloud clustering are emergent properties of shallow convection fundamentally linked to mesoscale variability (Seifert and Heus, 2013, hereafter SH13; Bretherton and Blossey, 2017, hereafter BB17; Janssens et al., 2023a, hereafter J23a). Observational studies corroborate this picture: subcloud layer dynamics are more vigorous in more organized cloud fields (McCoy et al., 2025), and clustered shallow cumuli are optically thicker than their unclustered counterparts (Alinaghi et al., 2024). Together, these results imply that cloud clusters exhibit stronger in-cloud updrafts, at least in part due to reduced entrainment rates relative to disorganized clouds. Yet most shallow convection parameterizations in global atmospheric models prescribe a constant fractional entrainment rate as a function of convective mode (e.g., "shallow," "congestus," "deep") with no mechanism to modulate entrainment as a function of moisture aggregation. Even as kilometer-scale global models continue to mature, parameterizations of subgrid-scale vertical motions—including shallow convection—will remain necessary for the foreseeable future, and these schemes must account for the dependence of cloud-scale dynamics on the mesoscale environment to accurately reproduce patterns of cloud cover. This study bridges the fundamental task of identifying convective aggregation and the applied task of deriving closure relationships between resolved kilometer-scale prognostic variables and subgrid parameters such as fractional entrainment rate in a mass flux scheme. We use large-domain (L ≫ 10 km), high-resolution (dx < 50 m) simulations of subtropical maritime precipitating shallow convection to advance mechanistic understanding of correlations between mesoscale moisture aggregation and shallow convective cloud properties. The simulations employ two free-tropospheric moisture profiles (following SH13) and two horizontal domain sizes (approximately 40 and 80 km). We address two central questions: (1) What are the macrophysical characteristics (cloud object number density, geometric thickness, areal coverage) of cloud clusters formed in mesoscale moist patches? (2) Without directly quantifying entrainment and detrainment rates, what evidence do the simulations provide for greater dynamical efficiency in cloud clusters—e.g., greater buoyancy perturbations, stronger updrafts, deeper cloud tops? High-frequency (10 s) two-dimensional outputs are analyzed using the block decomposition approach of BB17: the domain is subdivided into mesoscale blocks of horizontal scale O(10 km), and blocks are sorted by total water path (TWP) to identify the moistest and driest quartiles. Our principal findings are as follows. Macrophysical differences between "moist" and "dry" free-tropospheric profile simulations are larger than previously reported, with the moist-profile runs producing higher liquid water path, rain water path, and cloud fraction; however, domain-mean statistics show relatively little sensitivity to domain size. Moisture aggregation, quantified by the interquartile TWP difference, is more pronounced in the moist-profile runs and develops more slowly than in BB17 or J23a—consistent with the known sensitivity of aggregation timescales to model numerics (Janssens et al., 2023b). Clouds in the moistest quartile are geometrically thicker and exhibit substantially higher liquid and rain water paths than their driest-quartile counterparts. The clearest evidence for invigorated dynamics appears in the moist–dry contrast of in-cloud buoyancy perturbation, which grows over time in the moist-profile simulations. Finally, although the largest interquartile vertical velocity differences occur in the moist-profile 80 km domain simulation, the absolute magnitudes of mean updraft and downdraft speeds are comparable across all runs—reflecting the nuanced feedbacks among mesoscale aggregation, precipitation, subcloud layer stability, and cloud-layer dynamics.

486428.title: Convectively Coupled Equatorial Waves
486428.authors: Zeljka Stone, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM
486428.abstract: The analytical research on equatorially trapped waves in adiabatic atmosphere goes back to Matsuno, 1966, who looked at the shallow water equations on an equatorial beta plane. Matsuno modeled four types of waves, the Kelvin wave for the meridional mode n =− 1 or meridional wind speed v = 0, the mixed Rossby-gravity wave for n = 0, equatorial Rossby wave for n = 1,2 and inertio-gravity waves for n = 0,1,2,3. The meridional mode n comes from the y dependence of the solution to Matsuno's model that has the Hermite function meridional structure. It tells us if the wave is symmetric around the equator (odd n) or antisymmetric (even n). Those waves can propagate eastward or westward; the Kelvin wave propagates eastward, the Rossby wave westward, and mixed Rossby-gravity wave and inertio-gravity waves can propagate either eastward or westward. Today we know that the observed convectively coupled equatorial waves (except the MJO) have their equivalent in the Matsuno's modes. The seminal work of George Kiladis and Matthew Wheeler that resulted in wave number-frequency power spectrum plots of outgoing longwave radiation, 1999 inspired many theoreticians to study convectively coupled equatorial waves. How adiabatic waves couple with convection, how their characteristics are altered, why and how the phase speeds change and what is the mechanism by which the modes grow or decay in time? In this talk I will address some of those questions while giving an overview of convectively coupled equatorial waves as we understand them today.

486430.title: Enhancing Energy & Infrastructure Decisions Using NASA Capabilities
486430.authors: Shanna T. (Pitter) Combley, NASA, Washington DC, DC; NASA, Washington DC, DC; and A. G. Kashdan
486430.abstract: NASA’s Energy & Infrastructure (E&I) Program within the Earth Science Division empowers stakeholders and scientists to use NASA Earth data to co-develop novel solutions that aid in decision-making and meet user needs. E&I researchers work with stakeholders like cities and states, Tribal communities, energy companies, other federal agencies, and universities to use NASA Earth observations, data, and tools to make informed decisions around energy and infrastructure applications. E&I projects are cross-cutting in NASA Earth Science, with applications such as: energy and power systems analysis; resilient infrastructure at NASA Centers and adjacent communities; digital twin assessments for urban heat mitigation and decision-making; health and short-term weather decision support and analysis; and capacity building. The E&I Program is also planning and implementing expansions in its Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) and Risk Analysis and Solutions Innovators (RASI) projects. These efforts will enhance and develop new capabilities including: enabling weather analysis at additional timescales; Serving new users such as asset management, utility, and other private sector companies to leverage NASA energy and infrastructure data; supporting hydroelectric and data center operations to integrate additional energy and water relevant datasets into their monitoring systems; and collaborating with Los Angeles to plan for heat resilience during the 2028 Olympics.

486431.title: Asymmetric Upper-Ocean Response to Hurricane Erin (2025)
486431.authors: Isaiah Sutberry, Texas A&M Univ., College Station, TX; and H. Potter
486431.abstract: As part of the Office of Naval Research–funded Study on Air–Sea Coupling with WAves, Turbulence, and Clouds at High Winds (SASCWATCH), a plentiful amount of ocean-observing instruments were deployed ahead of Hurricane Erin in 2025. These included 24 surface drifters, three ElectroMagnetic Autonomous Profiling EXplorers (EM-APEX), and four Air-Launched Autonomous Micro Observers (ALAMO). These measurements provide an unusually detailed view of the upper ocean before, during, and after the passage of Hurricane Erin. This study examines Hurricane Erin’s cold-wake by exploring the temporal and spatial variations in temperature, density, heat content, and horizontal currents to characterize changes in upper-ocean stratification and identify the mechanisms contributing to vertical mixing and heat redistribution. The observations reveal an asymmetry across the storm track in multiple upper-ocean properties, with greater cooling generally occurring to the right of the storm. The maximum rate of cooling occurred approximately six hours after storm passage. The observations of this study also identify a localized area that experienced substantially less cooling. Sea surface height anomalies, satellite observations, and in situ current measurements indicate that this reduced response was associated with the preexisting geostrophic circulation and spatial variability in upper-ocean structure. These results demonstrate that the cold wake of Hurricane Erin was controlled not only by storm-induced mixing but also by the ocean conditions encountered along the storm track. By resolving the spatial structure and timing of the upper-ocean response, this study provides observational constraints for improving coupled hurricane–ocean models and forecasts of hurricane intensity.

486443.title: What Could Hurricane Season Mean for Us? Translating Seasonal Hurricane Information into Place-Based Exposure Guidance Across Counties, CWAs, and Marine Zones
486443.authors: Anthony Luis Corrales, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and D. S. Harnos and M. Rosencrans
486443.abstract: Seasonal tropical cyclone outlooks describe how active the hurricane season may be, but decision-makers also need to understand what a season could mean where people live and work. Basin activity and landfall counts do not fully describe geographic exposure because the reach of impacts, in this case tropical-storm-force winds, also depends on storm track, size, structure, and evolution before and after landfall. A single season can create concurrent planning demands across coastal, inland, and marine jurisdictions. This project develops a reproducible framework for translating historical storm records and preseason climate information into place-based hurricane exposure products. Using HURDAT2 storm tracks and reconstructed 34-kt wind radii, historical wind footprints from 1950–2025 are intersected with counties, National Weather Service County Warning Areas, marine zones, and regions. The resulting record provides localized climatologies, identifies recurring storm pathways, and supports comparisons between local exposure, basin activity, and landfall metrics. Results show that exposure can extend beyond landfall and that basin activity and local exposure are related but not interchangeable. Large-scale climate conditions organize exposure indirectly through changes in storm formation and pathways, with ENSO providing the clearest climate-to-exposure relationship. Retrospective forecast testing found the strongest seasonal signal for aggregate county-exposure categories, while more geographically and physically specific targets were less consistent. Local maps are therefore presented as climatological and scenario context rather than as independent forecasts. An interactive research website brings these components together through historical climatologies, climate-state analogs, storm tracks, reconstructed wind swaths, and an experimental aggregate seasonal outlook. The platform separates forecast information from geographic context so users can explore what is known without implying unsupported local predictability. This framework provides a foundation for incorporating S2S hurricane information into multi-jurisdictional planning and future stakeholder evaluation.

486449.title: Evaluation of the National Blend of Models (NBM) Probabilistic Guidance for Heat Forecasting
486449.authors: Tamille Starr Hutson, William M. Lapenta Student Internship Program, Sunrise, FL; and M. Anderson
486449.abstract: Florida is among the most vulnerable states for heat-related illness due to its warm climate, high humidity, and growing exposure to extreme heat events. The National Weather Service plays an essential role in addressing these trends, providing meteorological research and operational tools critical for evaluating and communicating heat-related risks. As extreme heat events become more frequent, the need for reliable and calibrated forecast guidance has become fundamental. This project focuses on evaluating the National Blend of Models (NBM) probabilistic guidance for heat forecasting, specifically assessing the calibration and reliability of the model outputs during the 2026 summer season across the west coast of Florida. Probabilistic apparent and high temperature data are provided within the NBM suite of products providing a comprehensive way to evaluate and communicate heat events. Traditional heat forecasting has historically relied upon deterministic, single value outputs. While these provide a result they often do not capture the uncertainty in atmospheric modeling, particularly during extreme heat events. The methodology used in this study utilizes a handcrafted, comprehensive probabilistic dataset derived from daily NBM guidance and climatological records compared against observational data from eight distinct locations within the WFO Tampa Bay forecast area. Statistical verification is used to evaluate the NBM outputs against observed temperatures and NWS tools including Heat Index, HeatRisk, and Wet Bulb Globe Temperature. This research also correlates NBM probabilistic thresholds with heat-related illness data to support more consistent and impact-based messaging tactics.

486450.title: ENSO Teleconnections in a Warming Climate
486450.authors: Ian Gifford, University of Miami, Miami, FL; and E. J. Becker and B. Kirtman
486450.abstract: The extratropical response from conditions in the equatorial Pacific, known as teleconnections, are remote drivers of local climate from the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Changes in the Walker Circulation modify upper-level divergence patterns with the background flow, acting to shift sources of Rossby Waves, manipulating jet stream meander amplitudes and locations. How a warming background state, especially one undergoing recent acceleration, influences this teleconnection mechanism remains an open question. The winters of 2008 and 2024 featured weak La Niña’s of similar amplitude, as measured by the Nino-3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly. However, the 2008 La Niña occurred in cooler global conditions than the 2024 La Niña. Would a warmer background state enhance La Niña teleconnections by increasing the apparent sea surface temperature anomaly, i.e. was the 2024 event inherently stronger? Observed conditions and long lead time European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts Seasonal Forecasting System 5 model runs are applied to a dry atmosphere general circulation model to study this. Specifically, the consequences of winter North American teleconnections under a cooler average 1998-2007 background state and a modern warmer average 2014-2023 background state are investigated. The Pacific North American (PNA) Oscillation demonstrates that the warmer background state strengthens the expected La Niña associated (negative) PNA phase as compared to the cooler background state. The North America subtropical jet is enhanced in the warmer background state as compared to the cooler background state. The jet core increases in area from 3.5 million square kilometers to 5.5 million square kilometers and the jet center shifts east and north.

486458.title: Urban Formaldehyde and NO2 Photochemical Aging Under Varying Atmospheric Conditions
486458.authors: Heejoo Kang, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and S. Yun, E. Mattson, J. L. Jimenez, and J. de Gouw
486458.abstract: Formaldehyde (HCHO) has been widely studied to improve our understanding of regional air quality, based on its role as a radical precursor and its strong secondary production from the oxidation of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Since HCHO is one of the most common VOC oxidation products with global satellite observations available, several diagnostic metrics, such as formaldehyde-to-NO2 ratio (HCHO/NO2; FNR), have been developed to characterize photochemical regimes and O3 production sensitivities. Satellites have been widely used as a primary tool for air quality assessment due to their broad spatial coverage ranging from nationwide to global, thus playing an important role in filling gaps in regions without extensive air quality monitoring. However, satellite-based remote sensing can suffer from a clear-sky bias, due to the limited sensitivity of the optical sensors in the presence of clouds. As a result, satellites may not capture the suppressed photochemical activity, which controls the photolysis rate and secondary HCHO production. Therefore, ground-based observations are essential to understand how the chemical evolution of HCHO and NO2 differs under various photochemical conditions. This project investigates HCHO and NO2 chemistry in the context of photochemical aging of air masses, by analyzing an in-situ measurement dataset collected at the La Casa Site in Denver, Colorado. A Cavity Ring-Down Spectrometer (Picarro G2307) has been deployed at the site since June 2026 to continuously measure HCHO, CH4, and H2O. Solar radiation and basic meteorological parameters have been collected by the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE) as part of the National Core (NCore) Network, along with key atmospheric species, including O3, CO, NO, NO2, NOy, and particulate matter. PM2.5 chemical composition data from the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry mEasurement NeTwork (ASCENT) were used in the analysis to understand the air mass characteristics. The surface chemistry of HCHO and NO2 across varying sky conditions has been evaluated by comparing observed and modeled solar radiation. Despite a variety of local emission sources and transported wildfire smoke, HCHO generally showed positive correlations with photochemical age calculated from NOx/NOy ratio, while NO2 showed negative correlations. The resulting HCHO/NO2 strongly correlates with chemical age, highlighting the role of photochemical evolution in driving HCHO and NO2 variability. These findings will provide valuable insight into a more accurate interpretation of HCHO as a photochemical metric, as well as suggest observational constraints to better address clear-sky bias in the satellite-based dataset.

486460.title: Explaining the Extreme Pattern Effect in Climate Sensitivity Parameter in Marine Cloud Brightening Patch Experiments
486460.authors: Michael S. Diamond, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and E. O'Meara and H. Hirasawa
486460.abstract: Marine cloud brightening (MCB), in which sea salt would be deliberately emitted into the marine boundary layer to reflect sunlight directly or indirectly by brightening clouds, has the potential to offset some climate impacts but its efficacy is uncertain. Part of this uncertainty is due to the strong regional heterogeneity of how MCB would affect top-of-atmosphere energy balance and global temperatures. Recent "patch" experiments in which MCB is applied one region at a time have shown a dizzying span of effective climate feedback parameters for MCB, ranging from barely negative in the Arctic to -9 W m-2 in the tropical southeast Atlantic. We show that this pattern effect is driven largely, but not entirely, by differences in effects on the Walker circulation. For the southeast Atlantic, the MCB pattern effect suggests that a full reversal of the tropical Pacific sea surface temperature gradient would accompany any substantial global cooling using just that region. Radiative kernels are used to decompose the pattern effect into feedback components related to Plank, water vapor and the lapse rate, surface albedo, and longwave and shortwave cloud radiative feedbacks.

486474.title: Process-Oriented Evaluation of African Easterly Waves In the Unified Forecast System
486474.authors: Weiwei Li, NCAR, Erie, CO; and Z. Wang, S. Sun, and M. B. Ek
486474.abstract: African easterly waves (AEWs) are a prominent weather system over Africa. They modulate mesoscale convective systems and extreme precipitation over West Africa and can lead to tropical cyclone formation over the tropical North Atlantic. Accurate representation of AEWs is thus crucial for reliable projections of the regional climate and extremes in those regions. In this study, we evaluate the Unified Forecast System (UFS), configured using its prototype high-resolution version 4 (HR4), for forecast lead times up to seven weeks over a 27-year period (1994-2020). Evaluation reveals that the model realistically reproduces the horizontal spatial structure and dominant energy pathways of AEWs. However, the UFS produces overly active AEWs, overestimating AEW variance from Week 1. Energetics analysis for AEWs demonstrates that all diagnosed energy conversion terms are overestimated, which is consistent with a positive eddy kinetic energy (EKE) bias and excessive AEW variance. An EOF-based AEW activity index indicates that useful predictive skill is only up to Week 3. The large-scale environment only partially explains these forecast errors. The analysis reveals systematic southward displacements of the AEW activity, the African easterly jet (AEJ), and the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) moisture distribution with increasing forecast lead time. Further analysis shows a warm bias across the domain that amplifies with lead time. Meanwhile, the model exhibits a weakening of the 850-hPa meridional temperature gradient compared to ERA5, suggesting a less favorable background baroclinic environment, which however appears inconsistent with the enhanced baroclinic energy conversion diagnosed in the model. This discrepancy implies that other factors (such as eddy-scale thermal anomalies and vertical motions) may compensate for or outweigh the mean-state effect. Lastly, the ITCZ moisture bias, combined with the excessive generation of eddy available potential energy due to diabatic processes, pinpoints model deficiencies in the organization and coupling of diabatic heating with AEWs.

486477.title: Dependence of Atmospheric Ozone and PM2.5 on Wildfire Emissions in Australia and North America
486477.authors: Evelyn Keefe, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and R. R. Buchholz, D. M. Leung, L. K. Emmons, R. Roy Chowdhury, K. Shores, and A. Lowery
486477.abstract: Wildfires present a significant threat to human health and air quality, largely through the emission of aerosols and trace gases. Tropospheric ozone (O3) and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) are harmful pollutants produced from biomass-burning fire emissions that cause problems for human health. Despite health concerns, the full scope of wildfire emissions on global pollutant concentrations remains uncertain. This study examines how global surface concentrations of O3 and PM2.5 change depending on wildfires in Australia, boreal North America, or temperate North America. We utilize the Community Earth System Model version 2.2 (CESM2.2) to run five-year sensitivity simulations. We compare model simulations with and without fire emissions in the region of interest to determine the impact on pollutant concentrations. We additionally experiment with different dust emission schemes to determine which scheme aligns closest to reality and should be used in sensitivity studies going forward. Our results show that fires in Australia, boreal North America, and temperate North America contributed 0.599%, 0.364%, and 0.086%, respectively, to surface ozone concentrations and 0.141%, 0.221%, and 0.064%, respectively, to PM2.5 concentrations. This work supports the larger Hemispheric Transport of Air Pollution Phase 3 (HTAP3) Fires model intercomparison project. Quantifying these regional contributions may support a deeper understanding of global health and air quality, as well as improve forecasting and decision-making related to wildfire events in different parts of the world.

486488.title: WoFSCast Performance in the 2026 HWT Spring Forecasting Experiment
486488.authors: Corey K. Potvin, NSSL, Norman, OK; and J. Martin, M. Silcott, J. A. Duarte, A. J. Clark, B. C. Matilla, and P. C. Burke
486488.abstract: The last few years have seen an explosion of data-driven models forecasting out to days ahead, but few current AI models focus on the “watch-to-warning” timeframe (e.g., 0–6 h) targeted by NSSL’s Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS). WoFSCast addresses this gap, providing high-quality ensemble 3-km forecasts at one tenth the cost and wall clock time required to generate traditional physics-based WoFS ensemble forecasts. WoFSCast is based upon Google Deepmind’s Graphcast neural network architecture, adapted for training and inference on WoFS’ daily-relocated limited-area domain.
