WoFSCast was successfully run in real-time during the 2026 Hazardous Weather Testbed Spring Forecasting Experiment (SFE; 27 Apr – 29 May). Encouragingly, WoFS and WoFSCast forecasts of composite reflectivity were rated very similarly by SFE participants. Participants often noted that the smaller number of storms in WoFSCast forecasts favorably compensated for the overproduction of storms in the WoFS. Objective verification confirms these impressions, with WoFSCast exhibiting a much lower (closer to one) storm frequency bias and false alarm ratio than WoFS, albeit at the expense of slightly reduced probability of detection. The subjective and objective SFE evaluations of WoFSCast will comprise the first part of our presentation. The second part of the presentation will overview the latest WoFSCast developments. A new version of WoFSCast trained with a probabilistic loss function exhibits even sharper forecasts than the MSE-trained WoFSCast. Inspired by the performance of NVIDIA’s Stormscope model, we are also incorporating radar observations into WoFSCast, beginning with Multi-Radar / Multi-Sensor composite reflectivity. We have also begun incorporating storm attributes and environmental fields (e.g., maximum hail diameter, ML CAPE) into WoFSCast. Preliminary results of both lines of work are encouraging. Finally, we will present the latest on our nascent efforts to develop a 1-km version of WoFSCast, which promises to enable real-time thunderstorm forecasting guidance at unprecedented resolution.

486496.title: Multi-Scale Variabilities and Interactions In the Global Monsoon
486496.authors: Tim Li, University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, HI
486496.abstract: A long-standing question in atmospheric science concerns how, and to what extent, climate variabilities across different timescales interact to shape global weather and climate extremes. Here we address this issue through a quantitative framework that integrates both larger-scale control and upscale feedback processes over the global monsoon (GM) domain. Land precipitation on the interannual timescale exhibits a coherent in-phase relationship across all the sub-monsoon systems, largely governed by El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Meanwhile, Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) accounts for about 30–65% of total intraseasonal precipitation variability across the sub-monsoon regions. Significant positive correlations are found between the interannual variability (IAV) and the intensity of the intraseasonal oscillation (ISO) and between the ISO and the intensity of synoptic-scale variability (SSV) across the GM domain, indicating a large-scale control of lower-frequency modes to higher-frequency variabilities. It is further demonstrated that higher-frequency variabilities (e.g., SSV and ISO) exert marked upscale feedback to lower-frequency modes through nonlinear rectification of condensational heating. About 90% of extreme precipitation days occur during the active phase of the ISO across the GM domain, laying a foundation for sub-seasonal prediction of weather and climate extremes weeks and even months ahead.

486498.title: Competing Effects of Tropical Cyclone Frequency and Intensity on Future Storm Surge Risk
486498.authors: Jackson Parker, SUNY, Stony Brook, NY; and B. O. Blanton, J. McManus, K. A. Reed, and B. A. Colle
486498.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) are responsible for some of the most damaging coastal flood events, and projections of future TC hazards depend on climatological quantities that have considerable uncertainty in the future. TC intensity theoretically scales with warming sea surface temperatures, but TC frequency is influenced by large-scale dynamical factors that are simulated inconsistently in global climate models. Frequency perturbations alter which storms compose the extreme tail of the storm surge distribution, while intensity perturbations shift the conditional severity of each event. We introduce a factorial decomposition framework for partitioning surge hazard uncertainty among these climatological drivers, and demonstrate it for two regions. Using a synthetic TC model (TCWiSE) we simulate a nine 10,000-year synthetic TC ensemble spanning three frequency multipliers (×0.72, ×1.0, ×1.22) and three intensity multipliers (×1.0, ×1.05, ×1.10), bracketing the projected spread in global TC frequency and intensity increase range identified in synthesis studies at ~3°C of warming. TCWiSE tracks and modeled wind fields force the ADvanced CIRCulation model (ADCIRC) which produces storm surge values for several stations along the United States (U.S.) Atlantic and Gulf Coasts. Results show that the nine-scenario envelope at the 100-year return level (the 1% annual exceedance probability water level) spans −0.11 m to +0.52 m on the Atlantic Coast and −0.19 m to +0.40 m on the Gulf Coast. The scenario combining a 28% frequency reduction with a 10% intensity increase produces a station-mean change of only +0.10 m (Atlantic) and +0.03 m (Gulf), with lower storm frequencies nearly canceling the intensity driven increases. A two-way ANOVA reveals that frequency uncertainty dominates scenario variance at the 100-year return period on both coasts, explaining 60.5% (Atlantic) and 63.3% (Gulf) of the total variance. Intensity overtakes frequency only beyond a region-dependent crossover (143 years on the Atlantic Coast and 370 years on the Gulf Coast). Additionally, this presentation will discuss the signal to noise ratio (SNR) for different simulation lengths (100-10,000 years) and discuss the required simulation lengths necessary to detect climate signals at various return periods. The framework demonstrated here provides a replicable template for quantifying competing sources of TC climatology uncertainty, directly transferable to other regions and variables of interest.

486516.title: Where Hemispheres Collide, an Equatorial Atmospheric Tomography Mission to Identify Origins of Chemical Reactivity in the Tropics
486516.authors: Michael Prather, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA
486516.abstract: The tropics are the powerhouse of atmospheric chemistry. The sunlight is most intense and temperatures greatest, and thus chemical reactions like OH + CH4 are at their peak. The tropical oceans contain the intertropical convergence zones where the hemispheres collide and mix and then separate again. We know the southern hemisphere is much less polluted, less influenced by continental sources, and sustains much lower levels of tropospheric O3 than the more industrially polluted northern hemisphere. The differences between the chemical reactivity of the northern and southern hemispheres are a critical element in understanding the budgets and quantifying the anthropogenic emissions of greenhouse gases and other global pollutants. The best place to observe the collision of hemispheric chemistries is over the ocean basins where the convergence zones allow us to characterize the chemistries of each hemisphere before and after they mix. We need to collect a four-season set of chemical profiling along and on either side of the convergence zones of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans. We need to characterize the chemical heterogeneity for those species that drive the major reactivity of the region. Given the scales of heterogeneity found in ATom profiling for the few species measured at 1 Hz in ATom (H2O, O3), it is essential to have 1 Hz measurements for all species occurring at abundances large enough to influence photochemical reactivity (e.g., lightning NOx). We re-examine the ATom cross-equator flights here to identify the types and origins of air masses driving tropical chemistry.

486523.title: Leadership and Transformation: Antonio Busalacchi’s Legacy at the University of Maryland (2000–2016)
486523.authors: James A. Carton, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD; and L. W. Uccellini
486523.abstract: During his 16-year tenure at the University of Maryland (UMD, 2000–2016) following a distinguished career at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Antonio "Tony" Busalacchi transformed Earth system science research and federal-academic collaboration. This presentation examines his transformative impact on the university and interagency research and operational communities. By the 1990s, the University of Maryland had established diverse environmental research and teaching programs spanning biological, chemical, and physical sciences, as well as public health and policy. However, interdisciplinary connections across campus remained fragmented. Recognizing the immense potential of cross-institutional synergy, university leadership sought to establish an interdisciplinary center outside of traditional academic departmental structures. Building on initial efforts by NASA’s Franco Einaudi and UMD’s Bob Hudson, this initiative culminated in the creation of the Earth System Science Interdisciplinary Center (ESSIC) and the appointment of Tony Busalacchi as its founding director. Under Busalacchi's leadership, ESSIC initially connected UMD’s Atmospheric and Oceanic Science, Geology, and Geographical Sciences departments with NASA Goddard. The center quickly expanded to house a major NOAA cooperative institute linking NESDIS and the National Weather Service, now known as the Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies (CISESS). This framework provided federal agencies direct access to academic research and student talent while broadening and elevating UMD’s research profile. Between 2002 and 2012, this partnership expanded dramatically through leadership support from UMD Dean Stephen Halperin, UMD President C. Daniel Mote, NCEP Director Louis W. Uccellini, and NOAA Chief of Staff Scott Rayder. This effort culminated in the co-location of the new ESSIC facility in UMD’s Discovery District, situated directly across from the NOAA Center for Weather and Climate Prediction (NCWCP). Alongside Pacific Northwest National Laboratory’s (PNNL) Joint Global Change Research Institute, this hub established a critical mass of researchers in remote sensing and Earth system dynamics. Crucially, it accelerated research-to-operations (R2O) pathways across the five NOAA/NWS centers, NOAA/OAR, and NESDIS divisions housed at NCWCP. Busalacchi further broadened this impact by establishing a university-wide Council on the Environment to bridge the natural and social sciences, pioneering today’s emphasis on "science to action". While maintaining his international scientific leadership activities—highlighted by his election to the National Academy of Engineering in 2016—he helped guide the Department of Atmospheric and Oceanic Science from traditional meteorology toward an integrated Earth system approach. His legacy established a nationally recognized model for federal-academic integration that continues to shape environmental science leadership today.

486527.title: Do Grid-Patterned Cities Struggle to Cool during the Day?
486527.authors: Abdul Mateen Syed, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA; Monash University, Melbourne, VIC, Australia; Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India; and M. Parlange, B. Biswal, and M. G. Giometto
486527.abstract: In convective boundary layers (CBLs), the interplay between thermal forcing and mechanical shear organizes turbulence into large-scale coherent structures that dictate global momentum and heat transport. However, the extent to which urban geometries modulate the organization of these structures remains less understood. Recent simulations of staggered arrays show that roughness displaces large-scale horizontal rolls above the canopy, yet it remains unknown whether aligned geometries produce a comparable or opposite effect, and whether any such reorganization alters heat transport. Here, direct numerical simulations resolve the flow within the roughness sublayer of a CBL over an aligned array of cubical obstacles, spanning forced, mixed, and free convection at a roughness Reynolds number Re=1200. We find that the aligned morphology geometrically locks the thermal updrafts, confining them along the canyon axes below a breakdown height of 0.6h. Beyond this height, the channeling of the array suppresses radial expansion into open cells, and the plumes instead merge anisotropically in the streamwise direction. Counterintuitively, and in contrast to canonical CBLs that self-organize to maximize heat transfer, this geometric confinement imposes an energetic penalty, with the net heat transport efficiency decreasing monotonically with increasing unstable stratification. These findings demonstrate that aligned urban morphology physically inhibits convective heat transfer, limiting the ability of grid-patterned cities to cool during the day and highlighting the need for geometry-aware surface flux parameterizations in mesoscale models.

486529.title: The Intersection of HFIP and AOML’s Hurricane Research Division: Improving the Hurricane Value Chain
486529.authors: Ghassan J. Alaka Jr., AOML, Miami, FL; and S. Gopalakrishnan, J. A. Sippel, A. Poyer, and W. Komaromi
486529.abstract: The Hurricane Research Division (HRD) at NOAA’s Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory (AOML) serves as a core engine of the Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program (HFIP) community. Together, HRD and HFIP drive transformative advances across the hurricane forecasting value chain, specifically in numerical modeling, data assimilation, and the operational integration of reconnaissance observations from NOAA’s Hurricane Field Program. This sustained partnership delivers a high return on investment through the rapid development and enhancement of operational systems, transitioning from the foundational Hurricane Weather Research and Forecasting (HWRF) model to the next-generation Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS). To meet HFIP’s 5- and 10-year strategic targets, HRD is advancing multi-basin moving nest capabilities, expanding regional ensembles, and optimizing reconnaissance data impacts using high-resolution physics parameterizations and next-generation data assimilation. Aligning with HFIP’s vision for artificial intelligence, HRD is integrating AI-driven frameworks to advance computationally-efficient hurricane modeling and produce robust probabilistic guidance. HRD is also focused on improving TC hazard prediction, including wind gusts, extreme rainfall, and associated severe weather risks. These efforts strengthen the connection between research and operations to directly support NWS and OAR strategic goals.

486534.title: Central Atlantic Origin of the Increasing Trend In U.S. Gulf Coast Hurricane Landfalls Since 1975
486534.abstract: During the past 50 years, hurricane landfalls have increased along the eastern U.S. Gulf Coast, from an average of 0.2 per year during 1975-1985 to 0.9 per year during 2014-2024 (p=0.01 for the 1975-2024 linear trend). In contrast, the number of hurricane landfalls has remained steady along the U.S. Atlantic Coast (p=0.42 for the 50-year trend). To investigate these trends, a statistical-dynamical hurricane track and intensity model is used to generate 10,000 synthetic tropical cyclones (TCs) for (1) a control run using 1975 background conditions with no linear trends in steering flow or TC intensity applied, and experiments with added 1975-2024 trends in (2) TC steering flow (300-850 hPa winds), (3) TC intensity (through changing environmental conditions), and (4) both steering flow and intensity. It is found that changes in steering flow are required to explain the larger observed increase in Gulf Coast hurricane landfalls compared to Atlantic Coast landfalls. Compared to the control run, Gulf Coast landfalls increase 56% in the experiment that includes trends in TC intensity and 141% when trends in steering flow are also included. In contrast, Atlantic Coast landfalls increase 87% in the experiment with trends in TC intensity, but only 38% when changes in steering flow are also included. The changes in steering flow are linked to warming of tropical and subtropical North Atlantic sea surface temperature, which has generated a trend toward lower atmospheric pressure and weaker anticyclonic winds. The result is a trend toward more northerly winds in the western Atlantic and Caribbean, steering TCs farther south and increasing the likelihood of Gulf Coast hurricane landfalls.

486535.title: From First Guess to Continuous Tracking: Evaluating PHI Recommenders and Threats-in-Motion for Severe Weather Warnings in the Hazardous Weather Testbed
486535.authors: Kristin M. Calhoun, NOAA/OAR/NSSL, NORMAN, OK; and K. L. Manross, P. A. Campbell, R. B. Steeves, M. Krocak, K. L. Berry, J. Cintineo, T. Sandmael, J. W. Monroe, J. G. Madden, A. W. Lyza, A. V. Bates, and G. J. Stumpf
486535.abstract: As the National Weather Service (NWS) shifts toward an expanded Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS) approach, automated "first-guess" severe weather warning tools show significant promise in enhancing warning consistency and balancing task priorities. This study details findings from a Spring 2026 virtual Hazardous Weather Testbed (HWT) evaluation involving 18 NWS forecasters testing severe weather warning recommenders derived from Probabilistic Hazard Information (PHI) alongside Threats-in-Motion (TIM) within Hazard Services-Convective. Using both live operations and controlled archive cases, the experiment evaluated how automated baseline geometry and continuous tracking alter warning workflows, inter-office consistency, and cognitive workload. Results demonstrate that the warning recommenders proved exceptionally valuable as a triage starting point, particularly for less-experienced forecasters or during rapid storm initiation and short-staffed shifts. However, individual forecaster warning consistency gains were lower than anticipated due to deeply ingrained local office philosophies and differing decision points. In general, forecasters expressed overwhelming readiness for TIM, emphasizing that allowing continuous, dynamic updates to active warning polygons fundamentally lightens cognitive load compared to managing static, overlapping boxes. The primary operational concern for TIM centered on political boundaries and partner dissemination, specifically regarding how automated moving polygons interact with county-based emergency notification systems and local sirens. Overall, this framework supports a more continuous and consistent flow of hazard information that starts with the forecaster and yields the guidance necessary to extend effective lead time for partners and the public. This presentation highlights forecaster feedback across diverse convective regimes, providing actionable Research-to-Operations (R2O) insights on balancing human factors, automation, forecaster expertise, and communication for future warning systems.

486555.title: From Forecast to Windshield: Delivering Hyper-Local Weather Hazard Alerts Using Connected Vehicle Infrastructure
486555.authors: Mike Vickich, Texas A&M Transportation Institute, Houston, TX; Texas A&M Transportation Institute, Houston, TX
486555.abstract: Current weather alerting for drivers is largely limited to pre-trip planning tools and coarse, regionally-scoped watches and warnings that may not reach travelers in real time or at the spatial resolution needed for actionable decision-making on the roadway. This presentation, developed as part of an effort funded by a U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) grant as a part of the V2X (Vehicle-To-Everything) Accelerator Program, describes a use case deployment for delivering hyper-local, real-time weather alerts—including flash flooding, slick pavement from rain or ice, high-wind hazards on bridges and overpasses, and reduced visibility—directly to vehicles using Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything (C-V2X) communications. The system integrates data from the National Weather Service, a comprehensive roadway flood warning system, and roadside environmental sensors into a cloud-based aggregation engine that standardizes hazard information into geospatial formats such as GeoJSON and SAE J2735 Traveler Information Messages (TIMs). These messages are disseminated through two complementary pathways: (1) cloud-based APIs feeding third-party mobile navigation applications for the broader driving population, and (2) direct broadcast from roadside units (RSUs) to C-V2X-equipped on-board units (OBUs) for vehicles with direct connectivity, enabling lower-latency, infrastructure-based delivery where available. This work, supported by USDOT funding, highlights the potential for connected vehicle infrastructure to bridge the gap between traditional weather dissemination and real-time, location-specific roadway safety applications, with implications for both meteorological data providers and transportation agencies seeking to operationalize weather intelligence at the point of need.

486560.title: The Impact of Boundary-Layer Turbulence on Tornado Potential in Simulated Supercells in Southeast U.S. Environments
486560.abstract: Few simulations have analyzed high-resolution evolution of high-shear, low-CAPE (HSLC) supercells and their tornado-like vortex (TLV) production. Recent simulations of HSLC supercells using composite environments from the Southeast U.S. left key research questions unanswered. In particular, the lack of TLV production was evident across an ensemble of simulations in these environments. These results have posed the question of whether the tornadogenesis process and sources of vorticity for simulated TLVs are similar to previous simulated efforts of supercells in Great Plains environments. Concurrently, recent simulated efforts have included turbulent boundary layers rather than the typical laminar boundary layer. The impacts of this inclusion have yet to be thoroughly analyzed, although previous observational and simulated studies have hypothesized that the vorticity parameterized in the turbulent boundary layers may be influential in the tornadogenesis process (Markowski 2024, Gebauer et al. 2026). This study aims to conduct a suite of simulations that builds directly from the initial ensemble suite. These simulations will generate turbulent boundary layers, introducing additional sources of vorticity that may influence TLV production. A horizontal grid spacing of 125 m will be used to simulate the turbulent structures while maintaining computational efficiency to run a suite of simulations. A stretched vertical grid as fine as 20 m in the lowest portions of the profile to 280 m aloft will further allow for a comprehensive low-level analysis. Based on these results, we can determine if the tornadogenesis process in HSLC environments differs from storms initiating in other environments. These findings will clarify whether a turbulent boundary layer and its associated near-surface vorticity streaks influence tornadogenesis in Southeast environments. Regardless of the outcome, it will be a novel and impactful result for understanding tornado processes, HSLC supercell dynamics, and forecasting Southeast supercells and tornadoes using environmental parameters.

486562.title: The Value of Weather Forecasts to the US Public: Factors Influencing Willingness to Pay
486562.authors: Jeffrey K. K. Lazo, Jeffrey K. Lazo Consulting LLC, Gunnison, CO
486562.abstract: The primary objective of this study is to estimate the value of current weather information and forecasts to the general public of the United States. This work in progress builds on prior work on the sources, perceptions, uses and value of current weather forecasts to the US public (Lazo 2024; Lazo and Chestnut 2000; Lazo and Chestnut 2002; Lazo et al. 2009). The current effort is designed to improve value estimates derived in the 2022 survey (Lazo 2024). That work generated a US national benefit estimate of over 102 Billion US Dollars to the US public of current weather information. To improve the 2022 survey effort (partially in response to substantive reviewers’ comments), a December 2025 survey with 255 respondents used mainly open-ended questions to elicit information on what “use forecasts” meant to respondents, their sources of information, and additional questions to help develop closed-ended questions on vulnerability to weather, prior impacts of weather, and perceptions of weather information quality. Current work is focused on improving the valuation scenario and methods using a dichotomous choice contingent valuation framework (CVM) (Champ et al. 2003). CVM has been a primary method for valuing weather information that is generally considered a public good and thus there is little market based information on its value (Anaman and Lellyett 1996; Head et al. 2024; Nguyen et al. 2013; Wehde et al. 2021). Additional work will develop exploratory and then confirmatory factor analysis of several latent structures that, while highly interesting in their own right, are assessed for their influence on respondent’s Willingness to Pay for weather information. These latent variables include (1) Cultural Risk Theory (Lazo et al. 2015), (2) Weather Salience (Stewart et al. 2012), and newly developing scales on (3) Personal Weather Impact (Lazo 2024), (4) perceptions of weather information quality (e.g., trust, confidence, satisfaction (Henderson et al. 2023)), and (5) vulnerability to weather (Birkmann 2006). Online expert focus groups with meteorologists (to be) implemented in August 2026 developed the characteristics and levels for describing current forecasts and information and the counterfactual of “degraded or no weather information from the US Weather Enterprise.” In-person cognitive interviews with members of the general public are used to evaluate the survey instrument prior to a second round of pre-testing in September 2026. Full implementation of a final survey instrument is planned for late 2026 to a sample of approximately 2,400 respondents (including about 10% Spanish speakers). This presentation will focus on the initial modeling of the five “latent” factors and their influence on Willingness-to-Pay. This moves beyond standard non-market valuation economic theory by incorporating attitudes, perceptions, experience, and “non-economic” measures into the valuation estimation. This approach is similar to Hybrid Choice Modeling (Ben-Akiva et al. 2002; King 2023). Estimates will be aggregated to national values and the policy implications briefly discussed. 486565.title: The Value of Weather Forecasts to the US Public: An Initial Estimate
486565.authors: Jeffrey K. K. Lazo, Jeffrey K. Lazo Consulting LLC, Gunnison, CO

486574.title: METGOAT: A Tool for Expert Human Analysis and Annotation of Meteorological Features
486574.authors: Ezekiel Caldon, Ohio University, Athens, OH; and A. Drager
486574.abstract: The Meteorological and Environmental Tool for Graphical Object Annotation and Tracking (METGOAT) is a modular, open-source web application that empowers researchers to easily draw, manipulate, and tag analyzed meteorological features on maps and imagery for a variety of research applications. METGOAT started as a tool allowing researchers to label and track cold pool outflow boundaries, sea-breeze fronts, and convective cells in multivariate observational data or simulation outputs associated with the DOE ARM TRacking Aerosol Convection Interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER) campaign. However, the app remains under active development, and it can be used across a variety of applications requiring human labeling of meteorological features from time-evolving maps of one or more variable. METGOAT is also being expanded so that it can be used in conjunction with machine learning (ML) frameworks to create training and testing datasets for new tracking algorithms, as well as be used to edit machine-generated labels and tracks by hand. One example of a future use case for the tool is refining outputs from the tobac Python module to better characterize storm cell merger and splitting events. The main component of the tool is a web user interface that allows users to import sets of map images and data, draw and manipulate contours on a canvas, and export these contours into usable data formats such as KML, GeoJSON, and CSV. The intuitive interface empowers the user to precisely plot, modify, and track objects: users can zoom and pan, toggle between plotted variables, forward and backward through time, and display overlays to help track features’ evolution. The implementation as a simple, open-source web application allows for interoperability, ease of use, and the development of companion modules across the scientific and development communities. Roadmaps for an attendant Python module, application programming interface (API), and database framework are also identified to allow METGOAT to be used as a collaborative and connective tool within scientific workflows. The METGOAT-Python module would be a conduit for users to directly port data to and from the web interface, such as human and ML-made feature contours and meteorological images and data. The associated database and API framework would enable persistent storage of annotation data on a remote server and collaborative use of the application in a self-hosted environment. This modular approach to the tool’s development maintains the accessibility and interoperability of METGOAT across scientific applications, while building its capabilities as a powerful analysis tool. This presentation will include a live demonstration of the user interface, as well as a description of the architecture and development of the application. Finally, we would like to enthusiastically invite interested developers to learn about and contribute to the web interface, Python module, and/or database code stack for METGOAT. The GitHub repository for the project can be accessed at https://github.com/METGOAT, released under the Apache 2.0 license.

486575.title: Large-Eddy Simulation of Observed Signals of Nighttime Canopy Waves
486575.authors: Da-Kai Peng, Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA; and Y. Pan
486575.abstract: Understanding internal gravity waves excited by turbulent motions is essential for improving the understanding of the stable boundary layer (SBL). Stably stratified canopy flows provide a natural laboratory for studying such wave-turbulence interactions. During the Canopy Horizontal Array Turbulence Study (CHATS), signals of nighttime canopy waves were observed using both an aerosol backscatter scanning lidar and sonic anemometers, but during different episodes. Specifically, the signals observed using sonic anemometers are identified from autocorrelation functions at spanwise separation distances greater than the canopy height, requiring a wide array of sonic anemometers at canopy top as well as statistically stationary mean flows. Periods meeting those requirements, unfortunately, do not overlap with the operation of the scanning lidar. The lack of overlapping wave episodes raises a question: Do signals observed using the scanning lidar and sonic anemometers coexist in the same stably stratified canopy flow? The objective of this work is to examine the potential coexistence of those nighttime canopy wave signals using numerical experiments. Canopy-resolving large-eddy simulation (LES) runs are performed to reproduce observed periods of stably stratified, statistically stationary mean flows during CHATS. The simulated flow fields are analyzed to detect wave signals in autocorrelation functions (as suggested by sonic-anemometer measurements) and horizontal snapshots of flow variables (as suggested by scanning-lidar observations). Results before reaching quasi-steady state have already suggested the presence of wave signals in horizontal snapshots of vertical velocity and potential temperature fields. The investigation of autocorrelation functions awaits quasi-steady-state results. Further analyses of the LES results focus on the formation mechanisms of nighttime canopy waves.

486591.title: Securing the Spectrum with Engineering, Science, and Policy: Protecting Environmental Remote Sensing Despite Congested Radio Frequencies
486591.authors: Jordan J. Gerth, NESDIS, Silver Spring, MD; and L. Zhou
486591.abstract: Radio frequency (RF) spectrum is an indispensable, finite resource supporting Earth observations and associated operations in the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS). For passive microwave remote sensing of atmospheric thermodynamics, satellite command and telemetry, and real-time data dissemination, protected spectrum access enables life-saving weather services for the American public. However, the rapid expansion of commercial broadband wireless, 5G/6G deployments, and dense low-Earth-orbit satellite constellations has created unprecedented spectral congestion, raising the risk of radio frequency interference (RFI) in critical Earth observation channels. This presentation outlines the operational, regulatory, and technological framework that safeguards spectrum allocations that NOAA and NESDIS use in meeting its mission. We examine strategies for monitoring and protecting passive scientific sensing bands—where non-substitutable physical properties govern natural microwave emissions (e.g., 23.8 GHz and 183 GHz for water vapor, 50–60 GHz for temperature profiling).These bands are sensed with the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS), part of the backbone Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS), as well as other current and future operational microwave sensors. There are also direct downlinks and data distribution channels involving weather satellites that require spectrum allocations. Key interagency and international advocacy mechanisms are presented, highlighting NOAA’s coordination with the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), as well as active technical initiatives. Preserving spectrum integrity is fundamental to maintaining numerical weather prediction accuracy and early weather warning capabilities while boosting American innovation in the development and deployment of advanced telecommunications.

486592.title: Accelerating Innovation to Operations: An Update on the NOAA Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Program
486592.authors: Alexander Bukvich, NOAA, Gulfport, MS; and M. C. Kruk
486592.abstract: The NOAA SBIR Program continues to be a critical engine for advancing NOAA's science and technology enterprise by harnessing the ingenuity of the nation's small businesses. This presentation will provide an update on the program's recent progress and future directions, highlighting how targeted investments are accelerating the transition of innovative research into operational applications and commercial products. Over the past few years, the NOAA SBIR program has funded a diverse portfolio of projects addressing key NOAA mission priorities. Significant advancements have been made in areas such as uncrewed systems (UxS), the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to Earth observation, and the development of novel 'omics-based sensors for ecosystem monitoring. We will showcase recent success stories where SBIR-funded technologies are now providing actionable data for coastal resilience, improving numerical weather prediction models, and supporting the New Blue Economy. We will discuss upcoming funding opportunities and the program's strategic alignment with NOAA priorities. This session invites collaboration with the broader scientific community to identify emerging needs and opportunities, ensuring the NOAA SBIR program remains at the forefront of environmental science and technology innovation, ultimately fostering a more resilient and informed society.

486594.title: ACTRIS CiGas Topical Centre: Harmonised European Observations of Reactive Trace Gases Advancing VOC Source Apportionment and Ozone Formation Studies
486594.authors: Thérèse Salameh, IMT Nord-Europe, Institut Mines-Télécom, Univ. Lille, Centre for Energy and Environment, Lille, Nord, France; and W. Aas, M. Dufresne, F. Moreau, R. Djaghloul, S. Sauvage, A. Font, T. Leonardis, N. Locoge, D. Durant, A. Novelli, H. Fuchs, M. Claflin, V. Pospisilova, S. Jorga, S. Reimann, Z. Le Bras, R. Tillmann, A. Claude, R. Holla, R. Wegener, M. G. Adam, N. Sarnela, S. Hame, and K. Seemeyer
486594.abstract: Reducing gas emissions and addressing climate change impact, require sustainable, long-term monitoring of atmospheric composition from local to global scales. However, atmospheric observations often suffer from limited metrological traceability to the International System of Units (SI), and measurement uncertainties are not always sufficiently quantified. Robust metrological frameworks are therefore essential to ensure data accuracy, comparability across monitoring techniques, and long-term consistency. High-quality atmospheric observations are critical for providing reliable scientific evidence to support environmental policies and decision-making. Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) play a central role in atmospheric chemistry by influencing the oxidizing capacity of the atmosphere and acting as key precursors of tropospheric ozone and secondary organic aerosols, both of which affect air quality and the Earth's radiative balance. Within the European Research Infrastructure ACTRIS (Aerosol, Cloud and Trace Gases Research InfraStructure: https://www.actris.eu/), the Topical Centre for Reactive Trace Gases in-situ Measurements (CiGas: https://actris.eu/topical-centre/cigas) provides the operational harmonisation and quality assurance framework for reactive trace gas observations, including VOCs, condensable vapours and nitrogen oxides (NOx). CiGas brings together six units located across Europe (IMT Nord Europe - France, EMPA - Switzerland, UHEL - Finland, DWD - Germany, and Forschungszentrum Jülich FZJ for VOC and NOx - Germany). The key-mission of CiGas is to offer current state-of-the-art operational support to ACTRIS National Facilities (NFs), observational and exploratory platforms, which are operating instrumentation for continuous long-term measurements of VOCs, condensable vapours and NOx in the atmosphere. This support includes the development of harmonised methodologies, quality assurance procedures, calibration strategies, and innovative measurement approaches to ensure high-quality, comparable datasets while addressing emerging scientific and societal needs. CiGas also delivers tailored services to external users, including the WMO Global Atmosphere Watch (GAW) programme, other atmospheric observation networks, academia, industry, and public authorities, notably in support of the implementation of the New European Ambient Air Quality Directive (EU) 2024/2881. This contribution presents an overview of CiGas activities and highlights recent collaborative research initiatives, including the ACTRIS/EMEP Intensive Measurement Period (IMP) campaign conducted in 2022 (Aas et al. 2026), and the ACTRIS/EMEP/RI-URBANS EUROVOC pan-European campaign carried out in September 2024 (https://www.actris.eu/news-events/news/eurovoc-2024-pan-european-campaign-launched-investigate-volatile-organic-compound). We will present recent results on VOC source apportionment across contrasting urban and rural environments, with particular emphasis on the contribution of emerging sources such as Volatile Chemical Products (VCPs). We will also investigate the factors controlling ozone formation across Europe by combining long-term observations, intensive field campaign datasets, and machine-learning approaches. We will provide insights into the respective contributions of meteorological conditions, long-range transport, and ozone precursors (including methane, carbon monoxide, VOCs, and nitrogen oxides) to observed temporal trends in tropospheric ozone. These analyses improve our ability to predict tropospheric ozone levels across Europe and to quantify the relative influence of these drivers in background, rural, and urban environments. These results demonstrate the value of harmonised European atmospheric observation infrastructures in improving our understanding of reactive atmospheric processes and in providing robust scientific evidence to support air quality and climate research. 486595.title: Closing the Information Gap: Using User Research to Redesign Volcanic Ash Advisory Engagement
486595.authors: Amber Hill, SAE, Silver Spring, MD; and I. Wahagheghe and A. Luong
486595.abstract: When a volcano erupts, NOAA’s National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) Satellite Analysis Branch (SAB) utilizes a multi-channel distribution network to disseminate Volcanic Ash Advisories (VAAs) to users via internal systems like AWIPS and their public-facing website. Following the December 6, 2025 Kilauea eruption, a critical question on user interaction with SAB surfaced: when an eruption occurs, why do some users reach out via phone for clarification, while the vast majority of their National Weather Service (NWS) colleagues and external partners remain silent? To understand the operational habits driving these behaviors, the User Engagement and Needs Assessment Branch launched a mixed-methods study, combining targeted user interviews, spanning NWS forecasters and external partners, with an analysis of website traffic. While we initially set out to understand why some users preferred phone calls over our online volcanic ash products, our research evolved to uncover broader insights. We discovered that communication logistics are critical to user success, particularly the increasing reliance on Slack for real-time updates. Join us as we share the behavioral patterns we found and discuss how these insights are reshaping our engagement strategy for the next eruption.

486596.title: Right Research, Right Time: A Lifecycle Framework for Strategic Usability Testing in Scientific Product Development
486596.authors: Amber Hill, SAE, Silver Spring, MD; and I. Wahagheghe and A. Luong
486596.abstract: Do you want to make your products more user-friendly but you are not sure which research method to use or when to use them? Integrating user research into the fast-paced development of scientific products is often easier said than done. This presentation introduces a practical 'Product Usability Lifecycle Framework' designed to help you navigate this process. We will guide you through the specific testing methods best suited for each stage—Discover, Define, Develop, and Deliver—so you know exactly which test to use and when to use them. We’ll also cover best practices for recruiting the right participants, ensuring your research is both relevant and impactful. You will leave with a ready-to-use matrix for mapping research methods to project milestones, helping you avoid common pitfalls like testing too late or using the wrong tools. Join us to learn how to prioritize the most effective research activities for NOAA’s National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) products and services, ensuring they meet the high standards of operational reliability and scientific accuracy from concept to final deployment.

486599.title: International Space Weather Coordination Activities for Research and Operations
486599.authors: James F. Spann Jr., NOAA, Lanham, MD; and I. Azeem, E. M. Lynch, Y. Collado-Vega, D. Vassiliadis, M. A. Garcia, C. Naylor, C. Wallace, J. P. Luntama, M. Ishii, J. Andries, J. Costa, C. De Nardin, G. Molina, N. Gopalswamy, K. Korreck, K. Hammond, D. Scipion, and M. Bisi
486599.abstract: The growing vulnerability of global infrastructure to space weather necessitates robust international coordination across both scientific and operational domains. This presentation provides a comprehensive overview of the current global collaborative landscape that drives cooperative space weather research and services. By mapping the efforts of key international coordinating bodies, we will highlight existing organizational and operational gaps. Furthermore, we will identify critical areas where enhanced international partnerships can significantly advance our fundamental understanding of space weather, improve data exchange and access, and enhance worldwide operational resilience.

486602.title: Incorporating User Feedback into NESDIS Commercial Data Pilot Evaluations and Transition to Operations
486602.authors: Alison M. Agather, Science and Technology Corp., Silver Spring, MD; and G. Peltzer, A. Lomax, H. Patel, N. Laudier, C. Smith, J. K. Zajic, L. Byerle, T. Vo, and R. I. Lana
486602.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) Commercial Data Program (CDP) acquires satellite data to supplement gaps in NOAA’s observing system. In 2024 and 2025 CDP conducted a pilot study to assess commercially-acquired global navigation satellite system reflectometry (GNSS-R) data for ocean surface winds (OSW) to demonstrate their quality and impact on NOAA’s forecasts, products, and numerical models. Prior to the transition into operations, CDP sought user feedback from operational partners about the GNSS-R OSW data. This presentation summarizes user feedback in evaluation of OSW data and lessons learned during the user engagement process. This presentation also identifies process improvements for future data pilots, transition-to-operation activities, and data purchases.

486612.title: Assessing Changes in Built-Environment Exposure to Hail using the Hail Impact Monte Carlo Model Version 2
486612.authors: Stephen M. Strader, Villanova Univ., Villanova, PA; and L. Bundy and W. S. Ashley
486612.abstract: Global insurance payouts due to convective storm perils (i.e., wind, hail, and tornadoes) have recently surpassed combined annual losses from flooding, drought, and earthquakes. These changes point to the need for better tools to assess potential convective storm hazard impacts on society. One such tool that we have developed is the Hail Impact Monte Carlo (HailMC) model. The HailMC is a spatially explicit model that simulates hail events across a user-defined region to assess potential impacts on underlying exposure landscapes. Recently, we have improved the HailMC modeling workflow and data inputs (i.e., hail swath morphology, hail size estimation, climatological inputs, etc.), which has led to version 2 of the HailMC. HailMC v2 provides more accurate and precise estimates of potential hail impacts on society for past, present, and potential future time periods. This presentation will provide an overview of the HailMC v2 methods, updates, and applications. As an illustration of the model’s utility, we simulate 5,000 years of severe hail (≥0.5 inch) swaths for historical (1990-current), current (2025), and future (2025-2055) time periods across the Midwest United States, including the Chicago, IL metropolitan area. We match each hail swath simulation epoch with the underlying built-environment exposure data (i.e., housing units) from the same period to determine potential hail impact frequency and magnitude changes within the region. Findings from this work underscore the importance of tools such as the HailMC v2 for assisting researchers and stakeholders to understand how evolving climatic and societal factors shape hail disasters and how their influence may change in the future. This improved knowledge, in turn, may be used to inform mitigation strategies to build resilience in the face of continued climatological and societal change.

486613.title: Future Changes in Winter Lightning Activity around Hokkaido, Japan, Simulated with a Bulk Lightning Model
486613.authors: Takumi Tomioka, The University of Osaka, Suita, Japan; and Y. Sato and S. Asai
486613.abstract: This study examines future changes in winter lightning activity around Hokkaido, northern Japan, using a bulk lightning model (BLM), which explicitly predicts hydrometeor charging through non-inductive riming electrification and diagnoses lightning initiation from the electric field. Winter lightning along the coast of the Sea of Japan is a serious hazard for wind turbines and other infrastructure, and offshore wind power development is being promoted around Hokkaido. However, projections based on empirical lightning flash parameterizations (LFPs) strongly depend on the choice of proxy, and how winter lightning in this region will respond to a warmer climate remains unclear. Here, we performed a pseudo-global warming experiment (PGWE) using BLM and compared the results of a present-day experiment (PD experiment) and future experiment by the PGWE. The PD experiment reproduced the observed precipitation and the main lightning areas. In the future experiment, the simulated lightning frequency accumulated over the winter (DJF) became about five times higher than that in the PD experiment, and the increase was concentrated on particular days and regions, in contrast to the broader increase in precipitation. Cloud water and graupel increased in the 0° to −20°C mixed-phase layer, and graupel charge separation amount increased by about a factor of three, and clouds occurred more frequently under conditions favorable for positive graupel charging. The regional lightning response was not uniquely determined by charge separation alone, highlighting the value of process-based diagnostics that include electric-field formation for assessing future cold-season lightning risk. Acknowledgments: This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI (Grant Numbers 24H00257 and 24H00269) and by the SECOM Science and Technology Foundation. This study was conducted as part of a collaborative research project with the Central Research Institute of Electric Power Industry (CRIEPI). The MANL data were provided by JMA through the “Meteorological Research Consortium,” a framework for research cooperation between JMA and the Meteorological Society of Japan (MSJ).

486621.title: Bias Correction of the NOAA Climate Forecast System to Improve Net Basin Supply Forecasts for the Laurentian Great Lake
486621.authors: Noah Barnes, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI
486621.abstract: Fluctuations of the Laurentian Great Lakes water levels can disrupt shipping and navigation and contribute to flooding and erosion in the region, resulting in significant consequences for people, property, and ecosystems. Water level fluctuations result from changes in net basin supply (NBS), the total available water in each lake's basin. Historically, the NBS of each lake has been calculated as the residual of the difference between the lakes' water levels and the inflows and outflows of their connecting channels and diversions. An alternative to the residual method is component net basin supply (CNBS). CNBS estimates NBS by assigning precipitation and runoff into the basin as supply gains, and evaporation from the basin as a supply loss.To create better forecasts that help prepare communities for changes in water levels, a predictive model for Great Lakes component net basin supply, NBS-Predictor, was developed by the Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory (GLERL) and the Cooperative Institute for Great Lakes Research (CIGLR). The purpose of this study was to determine if Great Lakes water supply forecasts produced by NBS-Predictor could be improved by bias correcting model-input climate forecasts from the Climate Forecast System (CFS) with the observationally constrained Climate Forecast System Reanalysis (CFSR). Bias correction of CFS data was tested using the following quantile mapping methods: linear scaling, empirical quantile mapping with replacement, and quantile delta mapping. Machine learning techniques, consisting of linear regression and random forest trees, were explored as alternative methods of bias correction. The impact of bias correction on NBS-Predictor skill was evaluated by generating water supply forecasts for the 2011-2022 time period after using each bias correction method, and by comparing the forecast skill to a baseline forecast using raw CFS output. Skill improvement ranged from modest to detrimental across all bias correction methods, suggesting that the CNBS model may already accomplish bias correction in its forecasts by removing the baseline climatology within its source code. Future work for this project could explore edits to source code manipulations of input climate data, and the use of quantile-mapped climate data as feature inputs to a machine learning model to synthesize all available data when performing bias correction.

486626.title: Closing the Gap: Improving the Quality Assurance of NOAA PSL's California Soil Moisture Monitoring Network
486626.authors: Jonah Robert Hurley, OAR, University Park, PA; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and L. Bariteau and K. Counts
486626.abstract: Soil moisture data provides crucial information for farmers, firefighters, researchers, hydrologists, and many other professionals around the country. As a result, it is important that soil moisture datasets are as accurate as possible in order to provide the most representative data to decision makers and researchers. NOAA’s Physical Sciences Laboratory has a network of observation sites across California, with many of them providing soil moisture observations at multiple levels. Data from these stations has gone largely uncontrolled since at least 2019, and some have not been assessed since installation (most installed 2005 - 2014). Combined with infrequent maintenance since 2020, this has led to numerous data problems or unnoticed instrument failures. To combat this, this project aims to create a method for automated QA of soil moisture in order to better alert scientists when instruments fail or when data is unreliable. In addition, more in-depth analysis was done of several stations to improve these error-detection algorithms and document common problems that occur with soil moisture sensors. The first stage of this project involved collecting metadata about the stations in the observation network, including location and soil composition. After this was complete, data was inspected manually station by station, beginning with the whole period and zooming into a yearly, monthly, daily, and hourly scale as needed. Maintenance logbooks and the PSL website were also used to note any known outages or instrument failures. Along the way, improved QA procedures were developed to automatically catch more erroneous values and ease data inspection. Since the soil moisture sensors are measuring the period of an electric oscillation, and these oscillations are partially dependent on temperature as well as moisture, accurate soil temperature measurements are also required to calculate accurate soil moisture values. This further complicates the QA process and can lead to even larger periods of missing or inaccurate data. Some common issues that were encountered include instrument failure, ponding, near/frozen soil, crossed wires, disturbed sensors, low voltage/broken communication lines, and clogged rain gauges (impacting data interpretation). Infrequent maintenance since 2020 has led to some of these issues lasting months or even years. However, an improved QA process has led to much cleaner datasets. Some statistical tools used involve checking for sudden, large changes in value, large standard deviations, and values outside of acceptable ranges. Combined with manual data removal for harder to detect issues (such as crossed wires), the stations that have been inspected have much more accurate data. While not all of the stations in PSL’s observation network were able to be inspected, the tools created and knowledge gained from this project should make the QA process for both past and future data much less strenuous going forward.

486632.title: Training on the Use of GOES Data In Tandem with Other Datasets for Short-Fuse Warnings In the National Weather Service
486632.authors: Daniel E. Bikos, CIRA, Ft. Collins, CO; and J. G. LaDue, D. D. Nietfeld, and K. Christian
486632.abstract: The GOES-R era introduced the use of GOES data in National Weather Service (NWS) short-fuse warnings that had been previously not possible or very limited. Improvements in latency in AWIPS (about 1.5 minutes), spatial and temporal data resolution and new bands which led to new RGB and derived products allowed for this development. A collaboration between the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere (CIRA) and the National Weather Service (NWS) Operations Training Unit (OTU) has developed training for short-term forecast and warning operations with the target audience being NWS forecasters. Data fusion techniques are applied with an emphasis on short-fuse warning types. Data fusion in our context refers to applying more than one type of weather information to address a forecast or warning problem. Examples of types of weather information include satellite, radar, lightning, environmental data, videos, and pictures. Learning how to combine multiple data sources via data fusion techniques is the primary theme of the training. This includes challenges such as variable priorities in data types during an event due to data type limitations or even missing a particular data type. Training has been developed on various short-fuse warning phenomena such as dust storm warnings, flash flood warnings, severe thunderstorm / tornado warnings, and special marine warnings. Fire detection has also been a focus with multiple training sessions introducing the topic along with a challenging partial cloud cover case. The training is made available on the NOAA Commerce Learning Center (CLC) and CIRA web-pages. This presentation will cover recently developed data fusion training along with plans for future training.

486638.title: Evolving Geography of Magnetic Storm Impacts on North American Telegraph Systems: 1851-1921
486638.authors: Jeffrey J. Love, USGS, Denver, CO
486638.abstract: Telegraph systems were North America's first continent-scale electrical infrastructure and were the earliest widespread technology impacted by geomagnetically induced currents. We compiled 43 geographically specific reports of magnetic storm impacts to telegraph systems between 1851 and 1921. These reports were found within newspapers, trade journals, and historical publications, and they document impacts such as fires, sparks, burned components, and communication failures. We compare these reports with contemporaneous distributions of telegraph stations, census-based population centers, and modern estimates of surface impedance derived from the United States Magnetotelluric Array (Kelbert et al. 2026). The geographic distribution of impacts evolved in parallel with the westward expansion of telegraph infrastructure: first developed in the northeastern United States during the 1850s and progressing to a continent-scale footprint by the early twentieth century. This demonstrates that technological exposure to space weather hazards increased as communication networks expanded across North America. However, even after telegraph systems had become widespread, impacts remained concentrated in particular regions. This indicates that infrastructure alone cannot explain the observed pattern. Instead, the historical record reflects the combined influence of geomagnetic storm forcing, telegraph network geometry, and regional geoelectric response associated with variations in Earth’s electrical conductivity. These results show that historical telegraph reports provide more than anecdotal accounts of magnetic storms: they constitute a long-term empirical record of evolving technological vulnerability. The analysis illustrates how changes in infrastructure can substantially modify the societal consequences of comparable geomagnetic disturbances, a relevant parallel to our increasingly electric-dependent society. This study provides historical perspective for assessing the vulnerability of modern electrically interconnected systems.

486643.title: Evaluating Tropical Eastern Pacific Sea Surface Temperature Variability as a Source of Subseasonal Precipitation Predictability in Peru and Ecuador
486643.authors: Gabrielle R. H. Brown, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and K. Pegion
486643.abstract: Recent extreme precipitation events in coastal Peru and Ecuador highlight the need to better understand sources of subseasonal predictability in the tropical eastern Pacific. Our previous work examined the 2017 and 2023 flooding events associated with two extreme Coastal El Niño episodes, using reanalysis, observations, and initialized subseasonal forecasts and experiments from the National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research Community Earth System Model version 2 (CESM2). That comparative analysis showed that oceanic initial conditions were the primary contributor to subseasonal forecast skill, and that model performance improved in 2023 compared to 2017 with useful precipitation guidance available up to 3 – 4 weeks in advance. However, it also revealed two important takeaways: (1) Events that appear similar at the surface do not guarantee similar predictability and (2) Coastal El Niño events and their related precipitation impacts are not well understood. Motivated by this finding, the present study investigates tropical Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) variability outside of canonical El Niño-Southern Oscillation patterns to identify the characteristics of Coastal El Niño and assess its impacts on precipitation in coastal Peru and Ecuador. Using the NOAA Optimum Interpolation SST Version 2 High-Resolution dataset and Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data, we examine how the location, magnitude, and evolution of coastal SST warming relate to precipitation for this region. These relationships are then used to develop a definition of Coastal El Niño, which is compared with the existing definition based on the Niño 1+2 region. We hypothesize that Coastal El Niño represents an important and under-recognized source of subseasonal precipitation predictability and that the existing Coastal El Niño definition does not fully capture the characteristics of Coastal El Niño events.

486653.title: Development of the Storm Induced Erosion Risk Neural Network to Predict Coastal Morphologic Change
486653.authors: Rangley C Mickey, USGS, St. Petersburg, FL; and M. L. Palmsten, R. McCall, A. de Bakker, P. Athanasiou, D. Passeri, J. Gorski, J. Thomas, M. Verdoes, and A. Poisson
486653.abstract: Sandy coastline environments experience high waves and water levels during storms which can disrupt ecosystem services, damage infrastructure, and reshape morphology over hours to days. Operational forecasts of coastal change are needed to provide scientific data to coastal managers and emergency responders for decision-making. This study develops a prototype machine learning model, specifically an artificial neural network (ANN), to predict magnitudes of dune erosion on the U.S. Gulf of America (Gulf of Mexico) and Atlantic sandy coasts. The model herein called Storm Induced Erosion Risk Neural Network (SIERNN; pronounced siren), was trained from ~30,000 numerically modeled, one-dimensional (1D) depth-averaged hydrodynamic and sediment transport simulations (Mickey et al., in review). The training set included ~2000 beach profiles with simulated evolution from 15 synthetic tropical cyclones. The input profile characteristics, the synthetic tropical cyclone hydrodynamics, and simulated post-storm profile characteristics served as the training database for development of the machine learning model. A two-step meta-model approach using a classification ANN (to predict erosion occurrence) and a regression ANN (to predict change of foredune crest elevation and foredune volume) was developed and tested through various sensitivity assessment to determine best setup practices for the ANN. ANN architectural sensitivity tests provided insight into which combination of hidden layers (ANN depth; 1 – 10 layers tested) and nodes (ANN width; 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) perform best for this type of prediction. ANN were trained and tested on a case study for Hurricane Florence that made landfall on the U.S. south Atlantic coast in 2018. Training and testing indicated SIERNN’s best performance was achieved from ANNs with architectures of 3+ hidden layers and 32-64 nodes. In hindcast testing, averaged SIERNN prediction ensemble results have similar root-mean square error (RMSE) and bias (1.34 m and -0.66 m for dune crest elevation, respectively; 13.17 m3 and -3.21 m3 for eroded dune volume, respectively) magnitudes as contemporary deterministic and machine learning model studies. Additionally, SIERNN had similar testing performance when using ANNs trained with only half of the original databank, indicating SIERNN improvements could be made with less morphological training data. Comparison of SIERNN ensemble test predictions to a 1D XBeach (Roelvink et al., 2009) deterministic hindcast simulation (using same model and methods as training data models) illustrated that the ANN performed better than the simplified 1D model (ANN dune volume change bias: -3.61 m3, RMSE: 12.15 m3; 1D model dune volume change bias: 9.51 m3, RMSE: 18.35 m3). SIERNN development highlighted training data generation methods, optimal hyper-parameters, training data size, and training data variables for application in predicting dune volume and dune crest elevation change. The conclusions from this investigation into ANN development and sensitivity suggest improving training data generation as the next focus of development. References Mickey, R.C., McCall, R., Palmsten, M., de Bakker, A., Athanasiou, P., Passeri, D.L., Gorski, J., Thomas, J., Verdoes, M., Poisson, A. in review. Development of the storm induced erosion risk neural network for sub-national scale prediction of coastal morphologic change. Roelvink, D., Reniers, A., Van Dongeren, A.P., De Vries, J.V.T., McCall, R., Lescinski, J., 2009. Modelling storm impacts on beaches, dunes and barrier islands. Coastal engineering, 56(11-12), pp.1133-1152.

486654.title: 3-D Wind Profiles on the Move: Applying Truck-Based Doppler Lidar to Air Quality, Emissions, and Wildfires
486654.authors: Maxwell Wittman Holloway, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and B. J. Carroll, S. Baidar, N. Malarich, M. Zucker, S. Sandberg, R. Marchbanks, and W. A. Brewer
486654.abstract: Boundary layer wind profiling from moving ground-based platforms is a measurement capability that can advance weather and air quality studies, by providing spatial and temporal coverage that goes beyond what airborne systems or fixed ground sites currently offer. A Doppler lidar integrated with a truck has been developed and deployed by the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory to provide boundary layer wind profiles while moving. The lidar has two channels to measure simultaneous vertical winds (w) and horizontal wind vector profiles, i.e., 3-D wind profiles above the truck. To keep the lidar beams pointing vertically, a motion stabilization cradle has been constructed to house the lidar head and stabilize it against any pitch or roll of the truck in real-time. To account for the remaining platform motion, inertial navigation units are used to track the lidar beam orientation and any large platform velocities are removed onboard in real-time with digital demodulation. The lidar architecture and platform integration have also been field-hardened to increase instrument reliability and capability for measuring from city highways to mountainous dirt roads. In this presentation, the lidar architecture and truck platform integration will be presented alongside highlights of recent field deployment applications. This mobile wind profiler provides localized wind profiles with high accuracy, even in complex terrain such as canyons or major cities. The 3-D winds can also be used to assess turbulence and boundary layer height. This system has been used in air quality studies to better understand flows and boundary layer heights over polluted cities, in wildfire studies to monitor ambient conditions and smoke-filled valleys, and in emissions studies to calculate trace gas fluxes.

486655.title: Public Awareness and Preferences for a More Unified Fire Warning System
486655.authors: Makenzie Krocak, NOAA, Norman, OK; and J. T. Ripberger, K. Gupta, D. Hogg, A. C. Wanless, E. F. Meister, A. Fox, M. O. Mattox, and P. Skinner
486655.abstract: While research in the fire weather space has increased dramatically over the past few years, critical gaps limit our understanding of how individuals and communities perceive, interpret, and respond to wildfire risk, especially on warning scales. Fire warnings in the United States differ fundamentally from other weather alerting systems, primarily because they are issued at the request of local- or state-level agencies (like local emergency management agencies, forestry services, or other emergency service agencies). As interest grows in developing a more unified fire warning system, researchers and practitioners need to understand whether the public is aware of how the current system operates and what characteristics they believe a future system should have. This work introduces the first wave of the Wildfire and Society survey, an online survey administered by the University of Oklahoma Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis through an online platform. The sample was collected with Verasight, a survey sampling company that recruits participants through numerous mediums (e.g., random digit dialing, online ads, email solicitation, etc.), with a final target sample of 1,500 nationally representative respondents and a 1,000 respondent oversample in elevated fire risk areas (i.e., the Wildland-Urban Interface). The approximately 20-minute survey was designed to characterize how the public perceives wildfire risk, their experience and understanding of current wildfire alert practices, and their preferences for a future, more unified fire warning system. Respondents were shown a vignette describing the current system and possible alternative systems, followed by questions that elicit their support for those systems. Results provide one of the first assessments of how the American public believes fire warnings should be issued and communicated, offering guidance for researchers and practitioners working to modernize the fire warning system.

486656.title: Cloud-Optimized Data Formats for Commercial Microwave Sounder Data
486656.authors: Teagan King, Tomorrow.io, Boston, MA; and S. J. J. Munchak, E. L. Nelson, and A. Siefkas
486656.abstract: As Tomorrow.io's microwave sounder (TMS) constellation grows, operational data systems must deliver increasing data volumes while supporting both low-latency production workflows and downstream scientific analysis. Traditional data formats can present challenges for scalable cloud processing and efficient access, particularly as downstream products and users increasingly rely on distributed computing environments and cloud-native analysis tools. To address these challenges, Tomorrow.io integrated operational generation of Zarr data format satellite products within its commercial microwave sounder processing pipeline. While Zarr has become a common choice for large gridded geoscience datasets, applying it to TMS products introduces unique considerations due to scan-spot observation geometry, redundancies in the L0 data packets downlinked from the satellites, and the need to support production workflows. This presentation describes the design and implementation of a cloud-native processing workflow, including lessons learned integrating Zarr generation into an operational production environment. We discuss considerations for performance, interoperability, scalable reprocessing, and resilient pipeline design. We also highlight how cloud-optimized data products have streamlined access for downstream science teams while supporting reliable customer data delivery. By sharing practical experience operationalizing cloud-native data products for commercial microwave sounder observations, this work illustrates how modern data formats and cloud-native processing pipelines can help bridge the gap between satellite observations and both operational and research applications, providing a scalable foundation for end users.

486662.title: Best Practices for Promoting Undergraduate Development through Summer REU Programs at UW/CICOES
486662.authors: Muyin Wang, PMEL, Seattle,, WA; Univ. of Washington, Seattle, WA; and J. Selmont
486662.abstract: The University of Washington’s (UW) Cooperative Institute for Climate, Ocean, and Ecosystem Studies (CICOES) has welcomed undergraduate students to participate in a nine-week summer internship that opens doors to hands-on research and scientific discovery since 2008. Our program has grown from one student at the beginning to a maximum of 15 students per year with support from NOAA, the UW College of the Environment, and NSF. Students conduct independent research under the supervision of mentors, who provide individualized guidance throughout all stages of the research process, from project design and data collection to analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of results. A unique feature of our program is the wide range of disciplines that comprise the CICOES research environment. The combination of affiliated academic units and our federal partners provides an intellectual panorama that exposes our interns to a broad and deep portfolio, resulting in a wide variety of projects. This program design requires management across a diffuse ecosystem of multiple partners from different academic units and external organizations. It also creates the need for additional cohort-building and shared experiences among the interns separate from and in addition to their research projects. In presentation, we will show how we have accomplished running the program smoothly through several programmatic activities, from pre-program online activities, through the end-of-program symposium.

486669.title: Connecting Data and Tools to Improve Air Quality Monitoring and Health Surveillance
486669.authors: John A. Haynes, NASA, Alexandria, VA; and H. J. Chapman and L. Judd
486669.abstract: Technological advances and increasing global connectivity have transformed how emerging health threats are identified, creating novel opportunities for data-driven decision-making. Although data gaps and disciplinary silos remain, integrating diverse expertise offers a pathway toward a more comprehensive framework for understanding complex environmental challenges and developing tangible solutions. Earth science applications tender powerful tools for improving environmental health research by integrating remote sensing and geospatial data into risk assessments for air quality and disease risk. Examples include assessing exposure to air pollution, monitoring ecological landscapes favorable for pathogen emergence, and identifying geographic hotspots for disease vectors and transmission. One noteworthy endeavor is the NASA Health and Air Quality Applied Sciences Team (HAQAST), launched in 2011, which connects NASA data and tools with environmental health and air quality researchers and stakeholders. This presentation will describe how NASA’s Health and Air Quality Applications portfolio is uniquely positioned to incorporate satellite- and ground-based observations to better understand emission trends, vector landscapes that influence habitat suitability, and inform public health decisions. Audience members will be encouraged to acquire knowledge and skills through the Applied Remote Sensing Training Program (ARSET) courses, expand networking in the GEO Health Community of Practice, and access data resources and visualization tools through the interagency-supported Earth Information Center.

486671.title: Developing a Paleofire and Paleotempest Record for the Western Gulf Coast
486671.authors: Nicholas Bostedt, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and J. A. Solomon, Q. Yao, S. Shepherd, M. Waters, and R. Vachula
486671.abstract: Wildfires and hurricanes have both been documented to be increasing in frequency with anthropogenic climate change. Wildfires can disrupt local ecology in areas that are not fire-adapted by burning native wildlife, and hurricanes have caused significant impacts on coastal environments through wind, storm surge, and excessive rainfall. Charcoal analysis is a crucial part in constructing paleofire data, however, current information for the Gulf Coast region is extremely sparse. Most coastal paleofire datasets are located in Southeast Australia or Southern Patagonia, however tropical cyclones have not had a notable historical presence in these areas. We present an in-depth paleofire record dating back ~2100 cal yr BP from a core taken from Texas Point National Wildlife Refuge. The core was analyzed for charcoal fragments, loss on ignition (LOI), and x-ray fluorescence (XRF) to examine potential connections between wildfire and hurricanes. Although the area has been impacted by many notable hurricanes in both recent history and as seen through LOI data from the core, there is little correspondence with the charcoal accumulation rates (CHAR). Despite there being no long-term relationship, there is an upward trend in CHAR data since the late 17th century due to anthropogenic influences. There is also a correspondence between carbonate percentages within the LOI data and the peak of the Little Ice Age, when the environment switched between a saltwater and freshwater system due to sea level fluctuations. These trends are indicative of how coastal ecosystems have changed during the late Holocene, as some marine elements have risen in concentration with increased warming. These elements, such as chlorine, can be lethal to coastal animal species, and an association with sea level rise may lead to enhanced terrestrial biodiversity impacts.

486692.title: Multidecadal Downscaling of Sea Surface Height for the U.S. Northeast, Southeast, and Gulf Coasts for High Tide Flooding Prediction
486692.authors: Laura McGee, University of Colorado/CIRES and NOAA/Physical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and M. Newman, S. Shin, J. R. Albers, P. Hovenga, J. A. Callahan, M. P. Conlin, S. Moghimi, F. Cassalho, and Y. J. Zhang
486692.abstract: High tide flooding affects communities across the United States, but the current NOAA High Tide Flooding Outlook predicts flooding only at tide gauge locations. A downscaled dynamical model forced with forecast model output could instead predict subseasonal-to-seasonal high tide flooding along the coast at much finer spatial scales. This study evaluates the feasibility of a depth-averaged SCHISM 2D model for predicting high tide flooding events over the period 1993-2018, using reanalysis data as “perfect” boundary conditions in place of the imperfect forcing an operational climate forecast would supply. Results from three small regional domains with nearshore boundaries (Northeast, Southeast, and Gulf) are compared to observations and two basin-scale models: ADCIRC+SWAN and one year of a 3D SCHISM simulation. For daily maximum water levels, the SCHISM 2D model performs as well as ADCIRC+SWAN in all three domains and as well as a 3D SCHISM model in the Northeast and Southeast.
