Extreme water level events, defined as the 95th percentile of detrended daily maximum water levels, are captured more accurately by SCHISM 2D than ADCIRC+SWAN along the Southeast and Gulf coasts, with mixed results in the Northeast. Testing whether tides and non-tidal residuals are linearly separable shows that adding the modeled tides in post-processing underpredicts daily maximum water level variance by up to 10%, yet this has little impact on predicting extreme water levels. Sensitivity tests further show that the choice of tidal representation matters more for extreme prediction than whether tides are added in boundary conditions or in post-processing.

486695.title: From Data to Decisions: Retailers Co-Developing NOAA Environmental Tools for Resilience
486695.authors: Jenny Dissen, North Carolina Institute for Climate Studies, Asheville, NC
486695.abstract: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Industry Partnerships program—led by National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) in partnership with the Retail Industry Leaders Association (RILA)—connects the retail sector with actionable weather and climate products to build economic and environmental resilience. As the largest private-sector employer in the U.S. economy, retail operations rely heavily on stable logistics, physical assets, and workforce continuity. Since 2021, NOAA and RILA have engaged directly with retail planners and operators to identify critical data needs across the end-to-end supply chain, spanning site selection, seasonal inventory management, asset protection, and safety. This co-development process has driven the refinement of a targeted suite of NOAA tools designed to help commercial actors anticipate extreme weather disruptions and long-term climate variability. Featured applications include the Storm Events Database, the U.S. Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database, the U.S. Climate Atlas, tropical cyclone tools (IBTrACS and ADT-HURSAT), the emerging Event Footprint Catalog, and specialized precipitation and wind climatologies. This presentation highlights select use cases as part of the Partnerships program describing retailers experience with weather and climate data, such as how weather and climate data supports seasonal stock positioning; how historical storm and footprint data aids in supply chain; or how storm history and flooding data is used for site selection. These practical data-to-decision in the retail industry context also showcases how sustained public-private collaboration bolsters NOAA’s partnerships programs and how environmental data is key to safeguarding national supply chains and strengthening broader economic resilience.

486706.title: Case Study of the Record Flash Rate Thunderstorm in Northern Florida/Southern Georgia
486706.authors: Chloe June Knight, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and M. J. Peterson
486706.abstract: Continental Mesoscale Convective Systems (MCSs) have been long recognized as the highest flash rate thunderstorms on Earth due to their vast size, complex structure, and favorability for intense convection. However, at the scale of individual convective cells, maritime thunderstorms produce the most lightning activity detected by space-based lightning imagers. We asses these “Lightning-Dense Thunderstorms” (LDTs) using continuous lightning measurements from the Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) for the first time, enabling novel analysis across their life cycle. Our case study focuses on the top LDT thunderstorm that we have identified over land. This case was a relatively small MCS thunderstorm that occurred on March 19th, 2018, and reached its peak intensity over Tallahassee FL, expanding into Thomasville and Valdosta Georgia as it interacted with a warm front present along the Florida Panhandle. As this case occurred in an onshore location with radar coverage, it provides new insights into the environmental conditions and convective cloud processes that drive exceptionally high flash rates and improves our understanding of LDTs, specifically in the costal environments that are frequently impacted by severe weather.

486721.title: Social Science in the Tornado Space: A look at VORTEX Program Projects
486721.authors: Kodi L. Berry, NOAA/OAR/NSSL, Norman, OK
486721.abstract: For the past ten years, the Verification of the Origins of Rotation in Tornadoes EXperiment-Southeast (VORTEX-SE) and VORTEX-USA projects have supported the integration of physical and social science disciplines to improve tornado understanding, prediction, preparedness, and public response. Key findings from social science research highlight critical challenges in the tornado warning framework. These include the unique risks faced by mobile and manufactured home residents, the difficulties inherent in nocturnal events, and the complexities of managing overlapping hazards. Furthermore, research supported by VORTEX-USA challenges the common misconception of public complacency during severe weather events. This presentation will provide an overview of the key insights and research outcomes generated through VORTEX funding over the last decade.

486722.title: A Visualization and Training Tool Developed for NOAA Hurricane Hunters to More Safely Fly Hazardous Weather
486722.authors: Diego Xiao Barbero, NOAA/OMAO Aircraft Operations Center, Lakeland, FL; and J. Zawislak, J. J. Murdock, and R. T. Knapp
486722.abstract: The sheer volume of disparate data collected on each hurricane reconnaissance mission by NOAA/OMAO’s Aircraft Operations Center (AOC) presents an ongoing challenge to synthesizing that data cohesively. The data collected by the WP-3D and G-IV aircraft holds extensive operational and research value, but previous in-house tools relied on standalone, user-input-dependent Python scripts that produced little spatial or radar context. This problem motivated the objective of this project, which is the development of the AOC Mission Visualizer, a browser-based tool that combines retrieval, visualization, and synchronization of mission data within a single client-side environment that requires no installation and can run entirely offline if mission data is cached locally. The tool visualizes missions in two- and three-dimensional maps with configurable time-series plots of any recorded variable, and can time-synchronize flight-level data with precipitation radar recordings. If there is an internet connection, a storm archive browser will help the user automatically retrieve full-resolution mission data based on year, storm, and flight ID, removing the need to manually upload files, and offering the option to overlay corresponding GOES imagery and best track information for the storm. The outcome of the project is that the visualization tool supports mission debriefs, aircrew training, and meteorological research. For example, AOC Flight Directors already use the Visualizer to replay historical missions for interesting in-flight encounters with extreme turbulence, eyewall passes, and rapid intensification events. As AOC’s Science Branch fully integrates this tool into its processes, the tool promises to modernize AOC’s ability to better train aircrews to safely fly hurricanes, improve data quality control within a meteorological context, and understand hurricane behavior, all of which allow AOC to accomplish NOAA’s broader mission to improve hurricane forecasting and prepare the public for hazards that storms bring to their communities.

486724.title: Diagnosing Tropical Cyclone Predictability and Forecast Sensitivity Using a Deep Learning Weather Prediction Model
486724.authors: James D. Doyle, NRL, Monterey, CA; and D. J. Lloveras
486724.abstract: Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) models have emerged as highly accurate forecasting systems, but their utility as diagnostic tools for tropical cyclone (TC) predictability remains largely unexplored. This study leverages GraphCast, a state-of-the-art DLWP model trained on ERA5. We utilize a modified loss function to mitigate "double penalty" errors, allowing for highly realistic forecasts. Using backpropagation, we compute analytical sensitivity maps analogous to traditional adjoint models. This approach circumvents steep development costs and extends lead times beyond the typical 48-hour limit to 5+ days. We apply this framework to diagnose track and intensity predictability across multiple historically challenging TC cases. For Hurricane Teddy (2020), we reveal that forecast sensitivity (5-7 day) depends heavily on the lifecycle stage: during initial intensification, Teddy's track is sensitive to local, near-storm initial conditions, whereas during its extratropical transition, the forecast is surprisingly most sensitive to a distant storm (Tropical Storm Beta) that altered the large-scale steering flow. To establish the generality of this approach, we expand our analysis to other tropical cyclones such as Typhoon Hagibis (2019) and Hurricane Eta (2020). We use these diagnosed sensitivity gradients to compute optimal, small initial-state perturbations that dramatically correct 5-day forecast errors. Our results demonstrate that DLWP backpropagation is a computationally efficient framework for identifying critical atmospheric features governing TC predictability and targeting observational resources, representing a significant advancement in understanding what influences TC track and intensity.

486725.title: Diagnosing High-Impact Weather Predictability Using Deep Learning Forecast Sensitivity
486725.authors: James D. Doyle, NRL, Monterey, CA; and D. J. Lloveras
486725.abstract: Predicting high-impact weather (HIW) events remains a major challenge in geosciences due to complex nonlinear atmospheric dynamics and sensitive dependence on initial conditions. While traditional adjoint sensitivity analysis is a powerful tool to identify where initial-state changes most strongly affect forecasts, it is hindered by computational cost, complex software, and limitations to short integration times. To address these limitations, we present a novel, highly efficient framework utilizing a fully differentiable machine learning (ML) weather prediction model, GraphCast, to compute forecast sensitivities via backpropagation. By leveraging analytical gradients, this approach calculates forecast sensitivities and optimal perturbations much faster than traditional physics adjoints, enabling dynamically consistent sensitivity analysis at long lead times (5+ days). We validate the physical realism of the ML-derived sensitivities against the traditional adjoint of COAMPS for severe atmospheric river and flooding events, demonstrating close agreement in identifying cohesive mesoscale features and upstream vertical tilts. We apply this framework to the severe Western European storm, Storm Pedro (Feb. 2026), to diagnose the upstream dynamical seeds of downstream forecast errors. Sensitivity and optimal perturbation analyses reveal that small initial errors associated with upstream shortwave troughs, atmospheric rivers, and tropopause polar vortices grow rapidly. Wave activity flux and perturbation energy budget analyses indicate that these perturbations extract energy from the background flow through mid-level baroclinic production and propagate along the jet waveguide, ultimately driving large downstream forecast errors. This ML-based sensitivity framework provides an agile, powerful tool for diagnosing predictability barriers, advancing physical understanding of HIW dynamics, and guiding targeted observation strategies.

486727.title: Cloudbusting: Lifting the Fog on Extended Aviation Weather Information
486727.authors: Brady Allen Nickols, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL; and N. E. Starzec, L. M. Kanofsky, B. Wills, A. Viken, and W. Adkins
486727.abstract: General aviators are highly vulnerable to weather-related aviation accidents and need clear, consistent, and accessible weather decision support, especially during high-impact and high-visibility national events. However, there is limited publicly accessible information regarding aviation weather or aviation hazards beyond Day 1. This project explored the National Weather Service (NWS) Aviation Weather Center’s (AWC) graphical aviation weather outlooks for Day 2 and Day 3 over a 30 day period during summer 2026. These products, which were designed to address that information gap, were issued as part of AWC’s suite of event-driven decision support services (DSS) during the 2026 World Cup. AWC issued over 130 DSS graphics between June 15 and July 12, 2026. Five core graphics were issued daily, and supplemental graphics were issued as needed. These graphics were analyzed to explore the distribution of issued aviation hazard types, impact categories, and forecast trends as Day 3 became Day 2. The most common aviation hazards listed on the graphics during this time period were thunderstorms and low ceilings; while hazards like turbulence and icing were rarely mentioned. We also identified a couple of challenges related to the categorical scales which may have contributed to both inconsistent forecasts as well as a limited ability to portray high-end scenarios in the DSS graphics. Finally, a number of different forecast trends were observed in this dataset, possible reasons for which will be discussed. Our recommendations for future graphical outlooks for aviation were based on hands-on experience exploring potential solutions to these challenges and feedback from potential users.

486728.title: Combining Lagged, Postprocessed HRRR and Weather Company GRAF Hourly Probabilistic Precipitation Forecasts
486728.authors: Thomas M. Hamill, The Weather Company, Boulder, CO
486728.abstract: At the 2026 AMS WAF/NWP meeting in Madison WI, I discussed the separate calibration of 3-km NOAA High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and 4-km Weather Company Global and Regional Atmospheric Forecast (GRAF) precipitation forecasts using MRMS data as the target. Each calibration generates probabilistic precipitation distributions each hour on the model-native grid using a point mass of zero precipitation and a weighted mixture of Gamma distributions. These are produced through a deep learning approach called an “attention residual U-Net.” The probabilistic forecasts were shown to be highly skillful and reliable. Through the incorporation of terrain information, they also exhibit realistic spatial variability in the western US related to mountain ranges. In this proposed talk, I will explore the potential benefit from the combination of probability distributions. Can we generate improved forecasts by combining probabilistic data derived from the HRRR and GRAF systems? Will inclusion of lagged-forecast information further improve the forecasts? Results will be presented at the conference.

486749.title: The NOAA Atlas 15 Data Repository for Present-Day Estimates of the Next-Generation Precipitation Frequency Standard
486749.authors: Lynne C Trabachino, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; RTI International, Fort Collins, CO; and K. Sanchez, M. P. St. Laurent Jr., and S. Perica
486749.abstract: The nation’s new authoritative precipitation design atlas, NOAA Atlas 15, is currently under development by the National Weather Service Office of Water Prediction. Atlas 15 aims to deliver seamless estimates across the contiguous United States (CONUS) and outside CONUS (OCONUS), including Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico/U.S. Virgin Island and select affiliated Pacific islands. To support Atlas 15 development, we have developed the longest and most comprehensive collection of station-based precipitation observations. The collection contains precipitation observations compiled from over 100 source datasets drawing from national, state, and local networks, including over 130,000 station records, distributed throughout CONUS and OCONUS, with record lengths up to 180 years between 1805 and 2026. This presentation focuses on the development and implementation of automated and manual workflows for processing disparate sources of daily, hourly, and sub-hourly, precipitation observations to produce time series of annual maximum precipitation amounts for durations between 5 minutes and 60 days for application in the NOAA Atlas 15 Volume 1. The discussion highlights efforts made to address the challenges associated with the design and development of a sustainable codebase that supports reproducible production of outputs.

486750.title: Quantifying Controls on North American Convective Events
486750.authors: PJ Tuckman, University Corporation of Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and K. A. Emanuel
486750.abstract: Severe convection and its associated hailstorms, tornadoes, and severe winds are generally preceded by large amounts of Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE). Recent studies have shown the importance of local surface fluxes and moisture gradients in the buildup of CAPE, but this work has generally been qualitative. Here, we quantify how convective energy and initiation respond to changes in the environment by altering inputs to a boundary layer energy budget derived from CONUS404 reanalysis data. We find that a 20% higher Bowen ratio leads to about 7% more convective events, with this effect being stronger at low Bowen ratios, and that a warmer capping inversion leads to about 13% fewer events per degree, but also stronger convection when events do occur. Quantifying these sensitivities is essential to understanding how land-use change and other climate forcings will impact severe convection.

486765.title: Bridging Weather Extremes and Urban Transport with Knowledge-Integrated Artificial Intelligence Systems
486765.authors: Auroop R. Ganguly, Northeastern University, Boston, MA
486765.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), integrated with and grounded in physical and technological principles, holds transformative potential for meteorological science and transportation engineering. However, recent literature and state-of-practice suggest gaps in pure data-driven approaches, including reduced performance for extreme weather events, poor out-of-distribution generalization for climate downscaling, and inaccurate modeling of urban flood extent and depth, along with downstream impacts on transit systems and accessibility to critical facilities. This presentation discusses these challenges and points to foundational advances within these topical areas at their interfaces. Furthermore, it details translational frameworks designed to integrate these methods into actionable tools for urban transportation planning and real-time operations under compound pluvial, fluvial, and coastal flooding hazards. Through case studies drawn from ongoing academic research and translational ventures, the presentation discusses distinct advantages and potential pitfalls of AI, network science, hybrid physics-AI, and knowledge-guided data mining at the important nexus of extreme weather and urban mobility. The presentation concludes with specific examples to highlight how foundational and translational research advances in these areas can lead to entrepreneurial activities from the scale of communities to the planet.

486774.title: Diversity In the Strength and Timing of the Dengue Response to the El Niño-Southern Oscillation across the Indonesian Archipelago
486774.authors: Kristopher B. Karnauskas, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and Q. Adams, J. Ibiebele, G. Lombard, D. Hamer, G. Wellenius, and K. Shioda
486774.abstract: Indonesia, an equatorial nation of 288 million spanning over 13% of Earth’s circumference between the Indian and Pacific Oceans, is an ideal natural laboratory for studying how climate variability such as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) shapes vector-borne disease transmission. Dengue fever, transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti mosquitos, is sensitive to changes in temperature and precipitation, which can be driven by ENSO. Using dengue surveillance and climate data spanning 18 years (2007-2024), we find pronounced diversity in both the strength and timing of the dengue response to ENSO across the archipelago. Peak correlations between ENSO and island-averaged monthly dengue case anomalies range from 0.50 (Sumatra) to 0.75 (Borneo), at lags ranging from near-zero (Borneo) to five months (Java). This lag reflects two steps: (1) from ENSO to local temperature and precipitation anomalies, set by climate dynamics, and (2) from those anomalies to cases, set by epidemiological factors—with temperature dominating the spread in association strength and precipitation the spread in timing across a latitudinal gradient in monsoon onset. There is thus no one-size-fits-all model for forecasting dengue across such an expansive nation; yet, this heterogeneity presents a leverageable opportunity, since ENSO is predictable months ahead and each region’s characteristic lag converts that skill into spatially resolved early warning. Combining islandwide regressions with the ensemble of mid-2026 ENSO forecasts, we expect elevated dengue incidence across all four major islands (~48,000 excess cases, ~61% above normal, July 2026 through March 2027), with uncertainty dominated by epidemiological factors rather than ENSO forecast spread.

486775.title: An Investigation into the Controlling Factors of Persistent, Near-Surface Temperature Inversions
486775.authors: Benjamin Marosites, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC; and A. L. Hiscox, S. Bhimireddy, D. A. R. Kristovich, J. Sun, and J. Wang
486775.abstract: Near-surface temperature inversions are relevant for air quality, spray drift, and frost risk. While most studies focus on nocturnal stable boundary layers that follow the standard diurnal cycle, far less is understood about multi-day, shallow inversions in weak terrain, especially the synoptic and local conditions that allow them to persist through daytime heating. Here, we define persistent inversions as lasting longer than 24 hours and examine the atmospheric setup, site conditions, and surface controls associated with their development and maintenance. This descriptive analysis incorporates observations from the 2018 SAVANT Campaign. The field site was a mix of corn and soy and featured shallow topographic terrain, common to the Great Plains region. Four towers were deployed in a gully system spanning approximately 0.5 km2. Each tower was instrumented with meteorological observations at several heights up to 20 m. A previous investigation into inversions at this field site explored the climatological frequency, duration, timing, and wind influences of near-surface temperature inversions during a harvest season in the Great Plains region of the US. That study was unique because it documented the amount of variability at the local scale and highlighted the importance of local terrain, flow structure, and vegetation in governing inversion behavior. However, several persistent events were outliers to the typical pattern. Initial investigations indicated that persistent events were more common in a single location (UCONV) prior to harvest and possibly driven by directional wind shear patterns. Building on those findings, the data for this analysis focus on five persistent inversion episodes recorded at a single tower site prior to harvest. By combining synoptic weather analyses, radiosondes, all-sky imagery, and wind profiles from sodar and radar, we show the connection between synoptic scale forcings, terrain influence, and local scale inversions. Initial evaluations focus on quantifying the relative contributions of wind shear and cloud cover. This analysis documents the connections between land-atmosphere interaction across scales. Documenting these persistence mechanisms provides critical insights into improving localized boundary layer predictions and interpreting surface flux measurements in shallow, agricultural terrain.

486779.title: Deep Learning Reveals a Divergent Future for Global Wildfires under Shifting Climate Zones
486779.authors: Jinil Bae, Pukyong National University, Busan, Nam-gu, South korea; and R. Son, D. B. Lee, and J. S. Kug
486779.abstract: Wildfires are expected to intensify under climate change, yet fire modules in Earth system models rely on empirically fixed fuel-moisture-ignition relationships, leaving unclear whether they capture how these shift as climate changes. Here we present K-FireNet, a deep neural network that learns climate-fire relationships directly from observations across 30 Köppen climate classes, projecting global fire activity under a high-emission scenario and comparing results against a conventional Earth system model. K-FireNet reproduces the spatial distribution, seasonal cycle, and interannual variability of observed burned area from GFED5 with high fidelity (spatial r = 0.92, temporal r = 0.89). Applied to future projections, this validated model diverges sharply from process-based CESM2.1: while CESM2.1 simulates a continued rise in global burned area tracking atmospheric CO2, K-FireNet shows no discernible trend, as AMOC weakening and a southward-shifting ITCZ increase precipitation across Africa and Australia, suppressing fire there and offsetting rising activity at high northern latitudes. The two models also diverge in seasonality, with K-FireNet revealing shifts in fire-season timing and duration that CESM2.1's fixed seasonal cycle cannot capture. Building on these projections, we further estimate the resulting fire-carbon emissions. Despite projecting smaller burned area, K-FireNet points to a much larger rise in emissions—poorly captured in frameworks such as the Paris Agreement—rising about 60% by 2100, nearly double CESM2.1's 30%, driven by the spatial overlap between intensifying fire activity and expanding vegetation biomass. Evaluating the socioeconomic damage caused by these emissions using a Social Cost of Carbon framework reveals a further contrast: absolute damage concentrates among major emitters such as Russia and China, but once normalized by GDP, low-income African countries impose the largest relative damage, showing that wildfire climate damage can fall disproportionately on the most vulnerable nations rather than the largest emitters. This work was funded by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Korea government (MSIT) (RS-2024-00343921).

486783.title: The NWP Moonshot Initiative: A New Vision of Community-Based Modeling for NOAA
486783.authors: John E. Ten Hoeve III, OAR, Silver Spring, MD; and D. T. Kleist, K. Garrett, and C. R. Alexander
486783.abstract: Over the last few decades, the quiet revolution in numerical weather prediction (NWP) has resulted in gradual improvements, a trend which is now accelerating due to new supercomputing capabilities that have enabled global cloud-resolving models and new AI/ML modeling approaches. These new technologies and capabilities create a unique opportunity to transform NOAA’s modeling suite in partnership with the U.S. modeling community. At the same time, the Unified Forecast System (UFS) is about a decade old. We have learned a great deal through the first five years of the Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC), a function charged with transforming the UFS into a community-based modeling system. This presentation will focus on how the experience gained over the last 5-10 years will inform the next 5-10 years to support a more integrated U.S. NWP community of developers and users across government, academia, industry, and non profits. This transformation will be accelerated through a NWP Moonshot Initiative, led by the NOAA Administrator Dr. Neil Jacobs. In close partnership with the community, NOAA will consolidate and modernize its operational modeling suite and production schedule through refactorization of the UFS for advanced software and HPC architectures, expansion of hybrid AI and physics-based ensemble prediction systems, and the adoption of the NSF NCAR Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) as the future dynamical core of the UFS. By adopting MPAS, a flagship community-based NWP model, NOAA will gain a larger community of potential contributors, as well as a dynamical core that provides improved skill at convective scales. The future 5-10 year vision is a hybrid AI and physics-based, km-scale, coupled, global ensemble system that will replace current global and regional systems. It will be driven by a JEDI-based hourly or sub-hourly data assimilation (DA) system, resulting in a near real-time global analysis of the Earth system state at convection-resolving scales. This technological moonshot is predicated on the success of a parallel organizational moonshot, which requires a new way of working across NWS, OAR, and partner organizations such as NCAR and JCSDA. As part of this moonshot, Agile, cross-organizational teams are being established with co-ownership between OAR and NWS. Technical leads will be empowered as product owners to make incremental decisions that move NOAA towards the ultimate vision. This presentation will discuss this new approach, how external partners can contribute to these teams, and how NOAA plans to stay coordinated over the long term with organizations such as NCAR and JCSDA, on which we depend for continued development of MPAS and JEDI, respectively.

486789.title: Assessing Snowpack Impact on S2S Predictions of Precipitation and Drought within NOAA’s SFS Forecast Framework
486789.authors: Cenlin He, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and W. Li, S. Sun, M. J. Barlage, R. Abolafia-Rosenzweig, Z. Zhang, and T. S. Lin
486789.abstract: Winter and spring snowpack anomaly could affect summer precipitation and drought conditions in many global regions through land memory and feedback among snow, soil moisture, and precipitation. In this study, we assess the global UFS/NoahMP simulations of summer precipitation and drought conditions affected by an improved treatment of winter and spring snowpack physics in Noah-MP land surface model within the NOAA SFS forecast framework. The improved snowpack physics have been recently developed by our team to better capture the observed snow density and snow cover fraction in western U.S. mountains as well as reduce surface temperature bias. Here, we aim to quantify the impact of these new snowpack parameterizations on S2S prediction of precipitation and drought, using the western US as a testbed, to evaluate if the prediction is improved via the snowpack-soil-atmosphere feedback. We aim to assess this across several representative years (El Niño, La Niña, ENSO-neutral) with different initialized seasons (winter vs. spring).

486791.title: Single-Patch Heterogeneity and the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
486791.authors: Harunari Soeda, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and E. Bou-Zeid
486791.abstract: Surface heterogeneity consisting of an isolated patch in relatively homogeneous surroundings appears in many forms — urban heat islands, lakes, solar farms, deforested clearings, polar polynyas — yet its impact on the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) remains poorly understood. Such patches are too large for turbulence to quickly homogenize yet too small for the atmosphere to equilibrate locally with the surface. Using idealized large-eddy simulations with the PALM model, we systematically investigate how isolated hot patches interact with the ABL under neutral, unstable, and stable background stratification. A dimensional analysis yields three governing parameters: a heterogeneity Richardson number (Ri), a Rossby number (Ro), and a patch-to-boundary-layer length-scale ratio (Rs). Under neutral conditions, the patch generates a coherent buoyant plume whose inclination angle scales linearly with Ri Rs, giving a compact predictive framework for plume structure. Unstable surroundings suppress distinct plume formation, since background convection dominates the localized forcing. Stable surroundings confine the thermal anomaly to a shallow layer regardless of heat-flux magnitude, demonstrating that stratification fundamentally limits vertical transport even from a much warmer patch. Patch geometry exerts a strong control on dispersive — but not turbulent — heat fluxes: patches of finite cross-stream width drive lateral convergence that amplifies upward transport, while semi-infinite patches suppress this mechanism and instead show near-surface divergence. Locally, dispersive fluxes downstream of finite patches can reach roughly 20% of the turbulent flux under neutral conditions. This contribution, which is routinely missed by eddy-covariance towers, is thus directly relevant to the long-standing surface energy-imbalance problem in heterogeneous terrain. We further show that this dispersive contribution is highly sensitive to the horizontal averaging scale used to compute it, with implications for how patch-scale heterogeneity should be treated in grid-averaged NWP and regional climate models. Together, these results indicate that finite-patch geometry must be explicitly represented in boundary-layer schemes and observational strategies in order to accurately capture the full physics of heat and mass transport.

486802.title: Validation and Verification of GNSS RO Space Weather Products Using Geospatial Analysis
486802.authors: Solana Yuewen Huang, NESDIS/STAR, College Park, MD; and C. Cao and X. Shao
486802.abstract: Global Navigational Satellite Systems (GNSS) Radio Occultation (RO) provides vital high vertical resolution measurements of the neutral atmosphere as well as ionosphere for space weather models such as NOAA’s GLOTEC. COSMIC-2 and PlanetiQ are two missions currently supplying GNSS RO Space Weather data for operational and research needs. One challenge of using varied GNSS RO data sources, however, is data quality assurance. Although GNSS signals can be degraded by radio frequency interference (RFI) and ionospheric irregularities such as equatorial plasma bubbles, these different degradation sources can have similar signal patterns. This complication makes validation and verification of products generated by different processing centers critical. This project establishes a quality assurance framework for space weather products by creating a central geospatial database in QGIS. It integrates CDAAC and STAR Space Weather Products such as PlanetiQ Total Electron Content (TEC), and COSMIC-2 ionospheric scintillation data and bubble maps. This geospatial analytical framework allows for a direct occultation event based evaluation of the differences between the products generated by different producers. Preliminary assessments successfully quantified STAR and CDAAC PlanetiQ TEC data discrepancies, such as anomalous and invalid TEC values, for algorithmic refinements. We are also assessing the feasibility of incorporating a novel deep learning model into this existing quality assurance workflow to detect RFI. We architected a supervised classification model using a Liquid Neural Network (LNN) model to process COSMIC-2 data. This model was trained using RFI index, S4 scintillation index, and elevation angle thresholds as class delineating features with the goal of distinguishing RFI contamination and ionospheric scintillation from clean signals. Model-derived RFI and scintillation probability outputs are currently being geospatially compared with CDAAC COSMIC-2 scintillation classifications to identify disagreement between occultation tracks. We envision that this LNN model will significantly accelerate data processing once it is fully developed in the near future.

486805.title: CMI - An Overview of the NWP Index at the NOAA/NWS Office of Modeling and Development
486805.authors: Shannon R Shields, SAIC, Riverdale Park, MD; and A. M. Bentley, J. J. Levit, A. Benjamin, M. P. Row, Q. Shi, and S. Banihashemi
486805.abstract: The NWP Index generated by the enhanced Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) is based on the NWP Index as described in Appendix A of Rawlins et al. (2007): “The [NWP] index, N, is a measure of the forecasting skill of the global NWP model over persistence for up to five days ahead.” The METplus NWP Index included in the NOAA/NWS Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) Evaluation and Verification System (EVS) is a measure of the statistical skill of an operational global deterministic model against the model’s own persistence forecast. Global deterministic models verified in EVS include the NWS Global Forecast System and Climate Forecast System, as well as the global deterministic models from the Canadian Meteorological Centre, Fleet Numerical Meteorology and Oceanography Center, European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, and Met Office. Currently, the NWP Index evaluates four synoptic variables across the Northern Hemisphere, Southern Hemisphere, and tropics: mean sea level pressure, 500-hPa geopotential height, and wind speeds at both 250-hPa and 850-hPa. The METplus StatAnalysis tool is used in EVS to generate the NWP Index statistical files for 00Z and 12Z cycles, separately, over a combined lead time of Days 1–5. For each term in Table A1 of Rawlins et al. (2007) (i.e., Northern Hemisphere 500-hPa geopotential height at Day 1), all matching partial sums (SL1L2) are aggregated separately for the forecast and reference (persistence) models. The Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) is then derived from the SL1L2 output. For each term, a skill score is calculated from the aggregated forecast and persistence RMSE. Ultimately, the NWP Index is computed from the weighted average of all the skill scores for each term. An NWP Index value greater than 1 indicates that the forecast outperformed persistence, while a value less than 1 indicates that persistence outperformed the forecast. NWP Index time series plots are generated in EVS using Python to compare the various global deterministic models.

486810.title: Correlative Studies of Fall Speed and Particle Spacing Show How Raindrops Interact
486810.authors: Darrel G. Baumgardner, Droplet Measurement Technologies, Longmont, CO; and M. Thurai, PhD, W. Bang, and G. Lee
486810.abstract: The Meteorological Particle Spectrometer (MPS) is an optical array probe that captures the images of liquid and solid hydrometeors with a resolution of 50 µm, measures their fall speeds with a precision greater than one cm s-1 and derives the distance between sequential particles down to separations less than a millimeter. This fine-scale information, complemented with 100 hz sonic anemometer measurements, provides an in-depth look at how water droplet fall speeds are not necessarily independent of one another, nor are they randomly separated in time or space. In this study, several years of summertime MPS measurements, made in Inchon, Korea, were analyzed to assess size-dependent correlations between sequential rain drops that passed through the MPS sample volume. In particular, the measured fall speeds were compared with nominal, laboratory-derived fall speeds to link fall speed anomalies with the presence of nearby drops and small-scale turbulent eddies. The measurement of the elapsed time between raindrops arriving in the laser beam, at a temporal resolution of one nanosecond, allowed the derivation of drop separation distances. It is generally assumed that cloud droplets are randomly located in space, unless some process like entrainment and mixing alters this spatial pattern. Likewise, precipitation particles most likely are randomly separated in space unless some process like turbulence intervenes to alter this randomness. In this presentation we will present observations that suggest that there are underlying factors that lead to non-random separation between raindrops, factors that are related to the relative size and fall speeds of adjacent raindrops, as well as influenced by the intensity of small-scale turbulent eddies. In the figure below, the fall velocities of sequential raindrops are shown with the first raindrops velocity on the ordinate and the second raindrops velocity on the abscissa. Each data point is colored according to the size of the first drop. There are clear, size-related groupings of drops whose fall velocities are correlated depending on the first drops size. These dependencies will be discussed in terms of the physical processes that can lead to types of correlations.

486811.title: Evaluating the Hurricane Analysis and Forecasting System (HAFS) Rainfall Forecast Skill for Hurricane Helene: A Comparison of HAFS-A, HAFS-B, and HAFS-M
486811.authors: Suchit Srisai Basineni, AOML, Miami, FL
486811.abstract: Hurricane Helene produced catastrophic inland flooding up to 31” after its landfall in the Florida Big Bend. Helene officially caused $78.7 billion in damage according to the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), but estimates now range from $225 to $250 billion. Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models like the Hurricane Analysis and Forecasting System (HAFS) exist to forecast precipitation outputs, but skill-based analysis studies have been limited. This Project analyzes quantitative precipitation forecasts (QPF) from three HAFS configurations: HAFS-A, HAFS-B, and HAFS-Multistorm (HAFS-M). Instead of evaluating forecasts individually, every model initialization had a common rainfall window compared to hourly Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) Quantitative Precipitation Estimation (QPE). Forecast skill was quantified using the Equitable Threat Score (ETS), Fraction Skill Score (FSS), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), bias, and swath-based metrics of size and centroid position. A significant factor in error in landfalling tropical cyclones (TCs) is track error, so each forecast is re-scored by shifting its track to the best-track line. HAFS-M was shown to have lower track error from 60 to 30 hours before landfall compared to HAFS-A and HAFS-B, but did not exhibit better ETS skill, though it did perform better in higher rainfall thresholds. As expected, all models exhibited better skill scores as lead time reduced. A deeper analysis of local land interactions is a future step in this project. This case is also a prototype for a verification framework for analyzing numerous past TCs, and potentially for future TC rainfall skill analysis.

486812.title: Eurasian–North American Hot Extremes: Intercontinental Covariability and Associated Physical Mechanisms
486812.authors: Bin Yu, EC, Toronto, ON, Canada; and H. Lin and D. Cao
486812.abstract: This study examines the intercontinental covariability of summer heatwave-related hot extremes between Eurasia and North America using 66 years (1959–2024) of ERA5 reanalysis and observational data. Hot extremes are characterized by the warm extreme index (TX90), and maximum covariance analysis identifies three leading modes explaining nearly 80% of the squared covariance between the two continents. These modes exhibit coherent circumglobal teleconnection patterns linking major hot-extreme regions across Eurasia and North America. Dynamical analyses show that the covariability is associated with quasi-stationary zonal wavenumber-5 Rossby wave trains maintained by synoptic eddy forcing and barotropic interactions along the midlatitude jet, providing an efficient pathway for intercontinental teleconnections. Thermodynamically, TX90 variability is governed primarily by surface radiative processes: downward shortwave radiation is regulated by cloud cover, whereas downward longwave radiation is enhanced by lower-tropospheric warming and increased water vapor. Near-surface air temperature anomalies reinforce extreme heat, while cloud-radiative effects partly offset warming; surface turbulent heat fluxes play a secondary role. Sea surface temperature anomalies contribute weakly, suggesting that atmospheric circulation dominates the covariability, with tropical Pacific cooling providing only a secondary influence. These results demonstrate that Northern Hemisphere summer hot extremes are coordinated by large-scale atmospheric dynamics, while local radiative feedbacks amplify and sustain regional extremes.

486822.title: Advancing Extended-Range Severe Weather Prediction in the NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed
486822.authors: Thomas Galarneau, NSSL, Norman, OK; and K. A. Hoogewind, I. L. Jirak, M. J. Hosek, and A. J. Clark
486822.abstract: The Severe Weather Extended-range Forecasting and Verification Experiment (SWERVE) is a virtual activity hosted in the NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed from February through April. Over the past two years, SWERVE has provided a collaborative testbed for more than 30 participants—including operational forecasters, researchers from multiple NOAA laboratories and cooperative institutes, and academic partners—to assess the capability and skill of extended-range severe weather prediction. Participants use and evaluate a mix of operational and experimental guidance to generate and verify extended-range severe weather forecasts for the contiguous United States. During weekly virtual meetings, participants issue real-time severe weather outlooks for Days 8–10 and Weeks 2 and 3 using operational model guidance, experimental AI/ML-based tools, and climatological benchmarks. Days 8–10 forecasts follow the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) Days 4–8 probabilistic outlook format, supplemented with lower probability thresholds (5%, 15%, 30%), and include a 3-day window outlook spanning Days 8–10. Weeks 2 and 3 forecasts assess the likelihood of above-, near-, or below-normal severe weather activity based on the number of “enhanced-level” severe weather days. In 2025, enhanced days were defined using SPC enhanced-outlook practically perfect hindcast (PPH) thresholds for tornadoes (PPH ≥ 10%) and hail (PPH ≥ 30%). In 2026, the definition was refined to include areal coverage thresholds and require at least one significant severe report (EF2+ tornado or ≥2-inch hail). SWERVE also includes structured subjective evaluations of group forecasts and guidance products, including operational ML-based guidance at SPC and experimental ML tools developed by NSSL, the University of Oklahoma, and NCAR; and extended-range products from CPC and AOML. Results from SWERVE Year 1 (2025) indicate that Week 2–3 forecasts often added value beyond climatology, especially during regimes influenced by favorable large-scale teleconnections [e.g., strong Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) activity and a retracted North Pacific jet in mid-March 2025]. Forecasts were more challenging during periods of midlatitude blocking and low-predictability wave-breaking events (e.g., late March 2025). SWERVE Year 2 (2026) showed somewhat similar results and also highlighted the potential value of post-processed forecast products derived from AI emulators such as GraphCast, PanguWx, FourCastNet, and the Weather Next 2 ensembles. A more difficult aspect of extended-range forecasting in SWERVE Year 2 was the lack of a coherent MJO signal, including a somewhat disorganized wavenumber 2 structure in the tropics that muted the ability to identify midlatitude impacts and forecasts of opportunity. This presentation will summarize the SWERVE concept, design, and execution, and highlight key results from the forecast and verification exercises across the first two years. Outcomes from SWERVE are informing the development of new AI/ML-driven severe weather forecast guidance designed for evaluation in a pseudo-operational testbed setting.

486828.title: Radar Data Quality Improvements across the San Francisco Bay Area from the Advanced Quantitative Precipitation Information (AQPI) Program
486828.authors: Jonathan Rutz, Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E), La Jolla, CA; and R. B. Vilela, M. Steen, and J. Shates
486828.abstract: The San Francisco Bay Area is a densely-populated and economically-productive region of the U.S. West Coast, embedded within complex terrain, and vulnerable to heavy precipitation from landfalling atmospheric rivers (ARs). The Advanced Quantitative Precipitation Information (AQPI) program now operates a network of 6 scanning radars, 5 X-band and 1 C-band, across the Bay Area. These radars are strategically located to complement the existing Next-Generation Radar (NEXRAD) network and improve Bay Area radar data quality in three key ways: 1) reduction of near-surface coverage gaps, 2) increased spatial resolution, and 3) increased temporal resolution. This presentation will summarize and provide examples of these improvements. In addition, this presentation will highlight promising results from AQPI radar mosaic precipitation estimates during a storm on 11-12 Apr, 2026. This is the first event for which the C-band radar was operational and integrated into the mosaic. For simplicity, this preliminary analysis will focus on areas not previously observed by AQPI radars, such that the large majority of mosaic skill is obtained through the newly integrated C-band observations.

486832.title: Defining a Mars L1 Space Weather Capability from Exploration Decisions to Measurements
486832.authors: Michael Kirk, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and D. da Silva, C. Bard, G. A. DiBraccio, G. Cataldo, C. O. Lee, P. Chamberlin, A. Pulkkinen, R. Gowrishetti, and M. Weih Engel Jeveaux
486832.abstract: Future Mars exploration will require space-weather information that is not only scientifically accurate, but timely, actionable, and directly connected to operational decisions. We are developing an end-user-driven framework to define the measurements and data products needed for a future Mars–Sun L1 space-weather capability. The approach begins with exploration use cases and traces these needs to forecast quantities, acceptable uncertainties, data latency and cadence, and ultimately candidate observations. Existing heliophysics and planetary datasets, physics-based and data-driven models, and uncertainty-quantification methods are then used to determine where current Sun-to-Mars predictions fail and which additional measurements most improve decision-relevant forecast skill. Quantitative trade studies evaluate both measurement value and the extent to which information can be inferred from other heliospheric assets rather than measured locally. These results are incorporated into an operational traceability framework linking exploration hazards and decisions to forecast products and Mars L1 measurement requirements. The goal is to define a focused Mars space-weather capability around the information end-users require, providing a defensible bridge between heliophysics observations and the operational architecture needed for increasingly Earth-independent human and robotic exploration.

486833.title: The Climate TRACE Platform: Providing Open and Transparent Greenhouse Gas Emissions Estimates Using Remote Sensing, AI Models, and Collective Data
486833.authors: Aaron Davitt, WattTime, Denver, CO; Climate TRACE, Denver, CO; and K. Raniga, D. Moore, Z. Doctor, I. Saraswat, A. Piscopo, T. So, A. Russo, A. Kouch, L. Betz, L. Sridhar, P. Thomas, A. Watt, C. Lewis, and G. McCormick
486833.abstract: Global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions estimates are essential for monitoring emissions and planning mitigation. Existing GHG inventories provide a strong foundation for understanding emissions across sectors, countries, and time. Building on these inventories, the Climate TRACE coalition formed to improve the usefulness of GHG emissions data by expanding asset (source)-level coverage, increasing spatial and temporal resolution, and reducing reporting delays. Climate TRACE developed an open-access emissions framework and dataset, available at climatetrace.org, to improve the accuracy, coverage, and resolution of global GHG estimates. The framework integrates existing emissions data and fills remaining gaps using sector-specific methods that leverage AI, GeoAI, and statistical models combined with remote sensing and collective data. The resulting dataset is one of the first to provide global, asset-level emissions estimates (e.g., individual power plants and dairy farms) across most anthropogenic sectors. It includes monthly emissions from January 2021 to the present with a two-month reporting lag, and provides subnational estimates worldwide from 2015 onward. By combining asset-level detail, existing emissions data, frequent updates, and broad sector coverage, Climate TRACE provides critical infrastructure for emissions monitoring and mitigation planning. First, it brings together fragmented datasets into a consistent, global framework across regions, time periods, and sectors, while expanding coverage to improve the usefulness of emissions data, particularly in data-scarce but high-emitting regions (e.g., Iran, Algeria, and Qatar). Second, the asset-level emissions estimates have also shown potential to improve top-down (inversion-modeled) methane estimates compared with coarser prior datasets, helping narrow differences between top-down and bottom-up estimates and improve methane tracking. Third, Climate TRACE has also expanded its framework and dataset to include PM2.5 emissions from major emitting sources, supporting assessments of local air quality impacts. Our goals are to make GHG and non-GHG emissions visible to deliver information that is relevant to all parties working to achieve net-zero global emissions. The emissions data is free and open to the public via our UI and API at climatetrace.org, which can be used to search emissions by owner, source/asset, and by different administrative boundaries. Climate TRACE is an open coalition, and we invite groups and individuals to inquire about collaborating with us to provide accessible emissions data.

486836.title: A Generalized Calibration/Validation (Cal/Val) Framework for the NESDIS Commercial Data Program
486836.authors: Lin Lin, NOAA NESDIS/SAE, Silver Spring, MD; and N. Laudier, C. Pan, F. Iturbide-Sanchez, C. Cao, L. Zhou, S. Iacovazzi, G. Peltzer, and H. Patel
486836.abstract: Commercial satellite capabilities are rapidly expanding across a wide range of remote sensing modalities, offering new opportunities to augment NOAA’s operational observing capabilities. To fully realize these opportunities, NOAA/NESDIS’s Commercial Data Program (CDP) is advancing a generalized Calibration and Validation (Cal/Val) framework designed to evaluate the diverse architectures and data products of commercial satellite systems. This presentation introduces a standardized instrument-agnostic methodology for evaluating commercial satellite technology, focusing on data quality, traceability, scientific integrity, and operational readiness. Navigating commercial constellations requires overcoming unique challenges, including rapid iteration cycles, heterogeneous instrument designs, and non-standardized product specifications. To address these challenges, the generalized CDP framework establishes objective, evidence-based performance criteria evaluating data accuracy, noise characterization, and spatial/spectral alignment to ensure commercial measurements meet scientific standards for operational applications. Central to this approach is leveraging subject matter expert domain knowledge to tailor performance metrics and evaluation protocols to specify functional areas. As a representative application, this presentation highlights commercial microwave sounder radiances—critical observations for numerical weather prediction (NWP). Using the Commercial Microwave Sounder Pilot, we show how CDP Cal/Val evaluations progress from initial data characterization and feasibility assessments to continuous validation. Ultimately, this robust Cal/Val framework establishes the scientific foundation required to inform future transition-to-operations (T2O) pathways while maintaining the integrity and reliability of NOAA’s operational baseline.

486838.title: Cloud-Adaptive Multivariate Additive Inflation for Improved Assimilation of All-Sky Infrared Radiance
486838.authors: Andrew S. Shearer, OU Meteorology, Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and A. T. Johnson and X. Wang
486838.abstract: Infrared (IR) Brightness Temperature (BT) data assimilation (DA) has been shown to improve convective-scale forecasts. However, ensemble-based DA is widely used at the convective scale but has well-known drawbacks that lead to suboptimal assimilation of IR BTs, including insufficient model spread. Insufficient model spread may cause the ensemble forecast to misrepresent the vertical and cross-variable structure of the background error covariance. For example, this may occur when all ensemble members forecast clear skies at a location where deep convection has initiated. Reducing this limitation is expected to benefit all-sky IR radiance assimilation. Within radar DA, multivariate additive inflation was used to improve the model's spread, particularly when all ensemble members missed an observed storm. Assimilation of all-sky IR BTs is more complex than assimilation of radar reflectivity, as Shearer et al. (2026) found that the vertical and cross-variable structure of systematic covariances with BT depend on the presence and type of cloud. If such a method were to be used for IR BT DA, coherent covariance structures of different cloud types would be needed, as covariance structures of deep convection would not be sufficient for all-sky IR BTs. This study further extends the multivariate additive inflation for all-sky IR BT assimilation by introducing a cloud-adaptive methodology based on the results of Shearer et al. (2026). Single-observation tests will be presented to qualitatively demonstrate the advantages of the cloud-adaptive additive inflation, followed by its impact on the performance of the convective-scale CADRE-MPAS-JEDI cycled DA system.

486841.title: Diagnosing the Electrical Evolution of a Tornado Outbreak During Hurricane Beryl
486841.authors: Brooke Anne Fegley, Texas A&M University, Shreveport, LA; Texas A&M Univ., College Station, TX; and T. Logan and K. Calindi
486841.abstract: Periods of increased lightning activity in tropical cyclones can indicate changes in storm intensity. Due to hurricanes being warm core systems, they are typically much less electrified than a typical supercell thunderstorm. However in 2024, Hurricane Beryl produced large amounts of lightning prior to landfall near Matagorda, Texas. Not only was this electrification unusual, but Beryl also produced a significant tornado outbreak throughout Texas and Louisiana. This study examines the electrified versus non-electrified tornadic cells within Beryl and the areas of greatest lightning activity relative to the locations of the tornadoes. Lightning observations from the Houston Lightning Mapping Array (HLMA) and the Earth Networks Total Lightning Network (ENTLN), NEXRAD Radar and Multiradar Multisensor (MRMS) products, GOES satellite radiances, and storm reports were used to identify and track the dynamical and electrodynamical behavior of Beryl relative to the tornado outbreak. A lightning burst metric was employed to look at the total lightning in the entire Beryl domain to analyze areas of increased electrical activity as well as compare/contrast tornadic cells with and without lightning activity. The Tracking Algorithm for Mesoscale Convective Systems (TAMS) was also utilized to help pinpoint areas of colder cloud tops and their timing relative to lightning activity and hurricane-induced tornadoes. Initial analysis indicated that periods of decreased electrical activity (e.g., lightning “dives”) occurred in cells that produced tornadoes which suggests electrification could be a potential tool for decision making processes. This study aims to provide more insight into highly electrified hurricanes and establish the value of lightning observations as a possible indicator of tornadogenesis within hurricane-induced tornado outbreaks.

486844.title: Operational Earth Observations for a Changing Earth System
486844.authors: Paolo Ruti, EUMETSAT, Darmstadt, HE, Germany; and B. R. Bojkov, J. Saalmueller, E. Obligis, F. Kaspar, J. Rourke, C. Accadia, and R. Chalex
486844.abstract: In 2026, EUMETSAT celebrated 40 years of designing, developing and delivering critical Earth-observation data. While EUMETSAT continues to launch its new generation of operational satellites, it is also working towards contributing to the WMO Integrated Global Observing System vision for 2050. In this presentation, we would like to highlight the most recent advances in EUMETSAT’s new fleet of instruments and their applications across different Earth-system domains, from continued support to global and regional weather prediction to weather-chemistry interactions, hydrology and environmental monitoring. Looking ahead, the presentation will also outline how EUMETSAT is preparing for the longer-term evolution of operational Earth observation through its foresight initiatives towards 2050. These activities aim to anticipate emerging user needs across the weather, climate and environmental value chain, and to translate them into future observational scenarios. In this context, EUMETSAT is strengthening its international collaboration with partner agencies and the broader user community to ensure that future observing systems remain robust, agile and responsive to a changing Earth system.

486847.title: Creating Engaging Educational Videos for the National Weather Service's School Outreach Program
486847.authors: Alyssandra Bella Lanese, OAR, Boulder, CO
486847.abstract: The National Weather Service has a National School Outreach Program, in which meteorologists take time out of their busy schedules to give Zoom presentations to students in kindergarten through twelfth grade. The program has been receiving over 900 requests for presentations each year, well beyond program capacity. As a member of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s 2026 William M. Lapenta internship program, I created video versions of three of these presentations to support the program’s outreach efforts: “Learning about the Water Cycle,” “Weather Basics,” and “All about Space Weather.” These videos will be shared to schools by the program’s members in the case that they were unable to present to them virtually and are expected to be played at hundreds of schools across the United States. The process of creating these videos included drafting scripts based on the program’s archived slidedecks, sending these scripts for approval, filming the content, and editing the footage in Canva and Premiere Pro. Collaboration with a National Weather Service Multimedia Specialist was key to ensuring the videos were produced to a high standard. The program’s target audience is elementary students between third and fifth grade, the most requested age group for talks. With this audience in mind, the overall goal was to create interactive video presentations, and this was achieved by filming experiment demonstrations and including question and answer sections in the videos. In this presentation, I will provide an overview of the production process and content of these videos and some suggested future video productions. The project’s objective was to expand upon NOAA’s mission of service by providing educators with accurate, concise, and accessible science lessons. By having these presentations in a video format with a permanent online location, the National Weather Service is expected to expand their outreach efforts to thousands of students.

486850.title: Creating Innovative and Engaging Education Videos
486850.authors: Alyssandra Bella Lanese, OAR, Boulder, CO
