486859.title: Advancing NOAA NESDIS Commercial Data Program: From Microwave Sounder Pilot Toward Operational Use
486859.authors: Chunhui Pan, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; NOAA NESDIS/SAE, Silver Spring, MD; NOAA/NESDIS (STC), Silver Spring, MD; and N. Laudier, L. Lin, F. Iturbide-Sanchez, H. Meng, D. C. Herndon, G. Chirokova, B. C. Ruston, I. Banos, and X. Zhang
486859.abstract: The NOAA NESDIS Commercial Data Program (CDP) is evaluating commercial microwave sounding (MWS) observations to complement government satellite capabilities and strengthen NOAA's operational observing system. Through pilot studies and the ongoing MWS Data Buy project, NOAA is assessing the scientific value and operational readiness of commercial MWS observations for numerical weather prediction (NWP) and environmental monitoring. This presentation summarizes lessons learned from NOAA's commercial MWS pilot projects, including data quality assessment, user applications, and numerical weather prediction (NWP) modeling. These end-to-end evaluations have provided valuable insights into the scientific, technical, and operational challenges and opportunities associated with transitioning commercial microwave sounding observations from pilot demonstrations to sustained operational use. Results are discussed in the context of NOAA's science and operational requirements, highlighting current commercial capabilities, remaining gaps, and opportunities for future improvements. The presentation will also discuss ongoing MWS data acquisition through the MWS Data Buy project and NOAA's efforts to establish a sustainable framework for incorporating commercial MWS observations into its operational observing system. These activities support NOAA's broader strategy of leveraging public-private partnerships to develop a hybrid Earth observing architecture that integrates commercial and government satellite observations to improve weather forecasting and environmental prediction.

486861.title: Modulation of Direct Continental US Tropical Cyclone Fatalities by ENSO and the Atlantic Meridional Mode
486861.authors: Philip J. Klotzbach, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. M. Bell, S. G. Bowen, E. Bercos-Hickey, D. Chavas, S. Girimurugan, M. Hemmati, M. R. Lowry, J. Muller, C. M. Patricola-DiRosario, C. J. Schreck III, L. G. Silvers, and K. M. Wood
486861.abstract: Over 2600 fatalities have been directly attributed to tropical cyclones (TCs) impacting the continental US from 1963–2025, with Hurricane Katrina (2005) alone causing 520 direct fatalities, predominately in Louisiana and Mississippi. Direct fatalities are those attributed to the physical characteristics of the storm, with ~80% of direct fatalities being caused by freshwater flooding, storm surge, and wind. More recently, Hurricane Helene (2004) resulted in 176 direct fatalities in the southeast US. Because prior work has demonstrated that basinwide North Atlantic TC activity favors increased direct continental US fatalities, here we investigate the relationship between El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Atlantic Meridional Mode (AMM), and direct continental US fatalities, while acknowledging that socioeconomic factors also play a critical role. La Niña, characterized by an anomalously cold eastern/central tropical Pacific Ocean (negative ENSO phase), favors increased direct continental US fatalities relative to El Niño (positive ENSO phase with an anomalously warm eastern/central tropical Pacific Ocean), likely due to more conducive tropical Atlantic and Caribbean vertical wind shear conditions in La Niña events as well as an increased probability of TCs making landfall. When the AMM is positive, characterized by a warm northern tropical Atlantic relative to southern tropical Atlantic, it also favors increased direct continental US fatalities, likely due to both lower shear and warmer waters across the tropical Atlantic and Caribbean facilitating higher TC activity. We find even stronger direct continental US fatality differences when combining La Niña and a positive phase of the AMM relative to El Niño combined with a negative phase of the AMM. Given relatively skillful seasonal forecasts for ENSO, the AMM, and basinwide North Atlantic TC activity by the start of the North Atlantic hurricane season, these findings may help anticipate an increased or decreased probability of significant continental US direct fatality-causing events.

486865.title: Conceptual and Measured Aircraft Icing in Convective Clouds
486865.authors: Wayne R. Sand, Big Sky Weather Consulting, Essex, MT
486865.abstract: The National Hail Research Experiment (NHRE), conducted in the early 1970s, aimed to understand the potential for hail suppression by cloud seeding. As part of this experiment, the author piloted the armor-plated T-28 aircraft through large multicell convective clouds with radar reflectivity levels reaching up to 55 dBZ. Hail growth requires supercooled liquid water, which is also the fuel for aircraft icing. Even though aircraft icing was not a part of NHRE, icing was encountered during every cloud penetration. The author analyzed the data collected from the T-28 flights and combined it with data from a state-of-the-art 10-cm weather radar. The analysis included a record of where icing was encountered. Both his master’s thesis and PhD dissertation were based on these analyses and included a record of icing encounter areas. Over the years, he completed hundreds of additional convective cloud penetrations of various cloud sizes while operating instrumented aircraft for the University of Wyoming. He later investigated numerous in-flight icing encounters and accidents as a Certified Consulting Meteorologist (CCM). This paper integrates aircraft and radar data with the author's extensive flying and consulting experience to present a conceptual and measured overview of aircraft icing in convective clouds.

486870.title: Evaluating and Understanding Seasonal Forecasts of Snowpack and Snow Drought in the Western U.S.
486870.authors: Michael John Miller, University at Albany, Albany, NY; and H. Wang and A. M. DeAngelis
486870.abstract: Snowpack serves as a critical water resource in the Western U.S., making its monitoring and prediction - especially the assessment of snow drought - essential for effective water management. Peak spring Snow Water Equivalent (SWE) anomalies are typically shaped by meteorological drivers in preceding and concurrent months and subsequently influence late-spring and summer soil moisture and runoff. Given the importance of snowpack for water resources, there is a need to assess our current predictive capabilities. This study evaluates monthly SWE forecasts produced at NOAA’s Weather Prediction Center-Extended Prediction Division, generated by driving a VIC land surface model offline with bias-corrected NMME meteorological forecasts. These forecasts are verified against an existing VIC land analysis driven by observed meteorological forcings. A comprehensive statistical forecast skill assessment was used to determine how predictive accuracy varies based on geographic region, forecast target month, and lead time. A core component of the analysis involves investigating the underlying factors contributing to model skill. One such factor that was looked into was the persistence of snowpack throughout the winter season. Results show that NMME-driven forecasts derive their skill from a combination of snowpack persistence, which accounts for much of the predictive skill near the timing of peak spring SWE at short forecast lead times, and the forecast skill in precipitation and temperature at longer lead times. It was also found that spring SWE forecasts can be statistically skillful at lead times of four months across most major mountain ranges. Finally, case studies were conducted for extreme snow drought events, specifically focusing on the historic water years of 2015 and 2026. These case studies showed that SWE forecasts at shorter lead times have the skill to predict SWE anomalies, however the magnitude of these forecasted ensemble medians are less than what was actually observed. By linking large-scale statistical assessments with specific case studies, this work highlights both the current capabilities and limitations of seasonal snowpack forecasting, providing insights which can be used to improve seasonal snowpack and snow drought prediction in the future.

486872.title: A Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Efficient Water-Level Forecasting on Sugar Creek in Charlotte, North Carolina
486872.authors: Lydia Tolman, NOAA, Tuscaloosa, AL; and F. L. Ogden
486872.abstract: ADHydro, a physics-based hydrology model, simulates rainfall-runoff response, producing a time series of overland (pluvial) and riverine (fluvial) flooding maps with high accuracy. However, the computational cost of ADHydro and similar models makes them impractical for the rapid and repeated forecasting that flash flood warning requires. This project develops a graph neural network (GNN) as a deep learning surrogate that learns to approximate ADHydro’s behavior at a fraction of the computation cost of the physics model itself. This allows for faster, real-time prediction necessary for flash flood warning. This study focused on Sugar Creek in Charlotte, North Carolina, with the GNN operating on a 7,286 element channel network to capture both downstream and upstream interaction. Using recent conditions and forecasted rainfall, the model predicts water depth 10, 30, and 60 minutes forward. Trained on one summer of ADHydro simulation output, the model is evaluated using a variety of metrics as well as its performance against a persistence baseline. Training and test data are split by storm events rather than moments in time to avoid data leakage, with the largest storm held out for testing. This project provides promising results for the future of flash flood prediction, demonstrating that a lightweight, learned model can recover meaningful hydrologic physics without the governing equations.

486874.title: Real-Time Wind Assimilation for Low-Altitude Autonomous Aviation Using Aircraft, Surface, and Numerical-Model Data
486874.authors: John James Celenza, Zipline International, South San Francisco, CA; and R. Rahimi
486874.abstract: Low-altitude autonomous aircraft operate within a wind environment that is incompletely represented by conventional observing networks and rapidly updating numerical guidance. Zipline has developed a minute-scale wind analysis system that combines aircraft-derived wind estimates, surface observations, and numerical model background fields to support weather-aware flight operations. For operations in the contiguous United States, the system assimilates wind estimates derived from Zipline aircraft, together with METAR observations, into High-Resolution Rapid Refresh background winds. Observation-minus-background innovations are distributed using spatial, temporal, source-quality, and observation-density weighting. Spatial influence can expand where neighboring innovations demonstrate directional consensus, while scalar speed innovations are treated separately from vector direction to reduce artificial high-wind features caused by directional disagreement. The system also incorporates safeguards intended for operational decision support, including observation-freshness filtering, spatially varying data-recency requirements, temporal smoothing, threshold hysteresis, and a degraded mode when surface-network coverage becomes insufficient. Testing conducted in our commercial operating regions compared background and assimilated winds with independent future observations, examined reliability and operational downtime across hazard thresholds, and evaluated whether candidate thresholds increased exposure to weather-related vehicle dangers. The presentation will describe the assimilation method, lessons learned from integrating aircraft observations with conventional meteorological data, and the challenges of balancing responsiveness, spatial representativeness, stability, and conservatism in operational low-altitude aviation.

486880.title: Microphysical Processes and Thermodynamics during Maritime Fog Events on Sable Island
486880.authors: Jesus Ruiz-Plancarte, Naval Postgraduate School, Monterey, CA; and R. Yamaguchi, E. Pardyjak, S. W. Hoch, K. Y. Huang, I. Gultepe, D. G. Ortiz-Suslow, J. Kalogiros, H. J. S. Fernando, and Q. Wang
486880.abstract: Marine fog remains a significant hazard to transportation and coastal operations, yet the physical processes governing its formation and dissipation are not fully understood. As part of the Fog and Turbulence Interactions in the Marine Atmosphere (FATIMA) project, comprehensive observations collected on Sable Island, Canada, during July 2022 were used to investigate the evolution of maritime fog. Eddy-covariance turbulence measurements, fog microphysical observations, radiosonde soundings, and surface meteorological data were analyzed for two contrasting fog events (15 and 30 July) to examine the coupled influences of boundary-layer structure, turbulence, and droplet evolution during the formation and dissipation stages. Although both events satisfied conventional fog criteria, they evolved under markedly different environmental conditions. The 15 July event developed within a more turbulent and weakly unstable surface layer, promoting rapid droplet growth, broader droplet size distributions, and a deeper fog layer. In contrast, the 30 July event formed under stronger near-surface stability with suppressed turbulence, resulting in smaller droplets, narrower spectra, and a shallower fog layer. Differences in the temporal evolution of stability, turbulent kinetic energy, and droplet size indicate that boundary-layer stability regulates both turbulent transport and condensational growth throughout the fog life cycle. These results emphasize that maritime fog evolution is governed by the interaction of thermodynamic structure, turbulence, and microphysical processes rather than by any single controlling mechanism, providing observational insight for improving fog representation in numerical weather prediction and boundary-layer parameterizations.

486888.title: Whole Atmosphere Modeling at NASA GSFC: GEOS-MLT
486888.authors: Fabrizio Sassi, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and R. Todling, J. Yue, G. Liu, J. pettit, A. Lee, S. Pawson, and D. Janches
486888.abstract: We present initial results from a new high altitude atmospheric global model based on the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) framework extended to the lower thermosphere (~210 km). This model is the result of a newly established partnership between the Earth sciences and Heliophysics science communities at GSFC with the goal to integrate tools and methods used in terrestrial weather with observations and physical properties of the thermosphere. We refer to this model as GEOS-MLT (mesosphere and lower thermosphere). This is the first step towards a goal of providing NASA with a whole atmosphere predictive capability that integrates holistically terrestrial and space weather, supporting at the same time research and operational uses. A description of the salient features of the model will be followed by an illustration of the current capabilities, as well limitations. We will conclude with an illustration of the vision path in the future to achieve these goals.

486894.title: Multistatic Radar Retrievals from Idealized Prescribed Fire Simulations
486894.authors: Emma Mae Miller, Advanced Radar Research Center, Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. Schvartzman, S. Emmerson, D. S. Zrnic, and M. Williams
486894.abstract: The transport of smoke and embers originating from wildland fires can impact decision making for wildland firefighters, land management agencies, emergency managers, and the public. Remote sensing provides unique means for monitoring aspects of the plume as well as the environment. Previous work with polarimetric weather radars has shown that wildland fire pyrometeors can be detected using dual-polarization variables. Beyond physical characteristics of pyrometeors and the plume structure, the full three-dimensional wind field is important for improving smoke transport models. The application of passive radar technology to wildland fire allows for the characterization of all three wind components as well as other derived fields, like vorticity. This work targets an idealized simulation using a collected vertical profile from a prescribed fire using a 3D non-hydrostatic, non-linear, time-dependent numerical modeling system called Cloud Model 1 (CM1). CM1 was modified from its typical case-use of severe weather to set a user-specified surface heat flux which induces a buoyant updraft. Multiple fire locations can be added to the same domain, allowing for more realistic simulations. Beyond the simulations, a multistatic radar system emulator is used to retrieve u,v, and w- wind components within the plume. This allows for further analysis for smaller scales of motions seen along the edges and near the convective updraft. Future work with observations from prescribed fires in the Southeastern United States will help to verify and provide an intercomparison between the simulation world and that of the real world.

486896.title: Determining the Drag Coefficient and Near-Surface Momentum Flux in Tropical Cyclones from a Small Uncrewed Aircraft System
486896.authors: Joshua B. Wadler, Embry Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; and C. De Loach, J. J. Cione, PhD, J. A. Zhang, D. H. Richter, M. Z. Stachura, and J. Elston
486896.abstract: Direct measurements of momentum flux in the tropical cyclone surface layer remain extremely limited, resulting in substantial uncertainty in the drag coefficient (CDN) used by operational hurricane models. Here we use 34 Black Swift Technologies S0 small Uncrewed Aerial Systems (sUASs), deployed from the NOAA WP-3D (P-3) hurricane hunter aircraft during the 2024–2025 hurricane seasons, to directly estimate momentum flux and drag coefficient over a wider range of wind speeds than previously available aircraft-based measurements. Measurements were transmitted from the sUAS at 3.25-3.5 Hz. Overall, measurements indicate no constant flux layer between ~20 m and 60 m altitude, regardless of whether the sUAS is nearly stationary flying into the wind or flying downwind. Multiple profiles indicate a peak in momentum flux between 20 and 60 m altitude. Thus, measurements of momentum flux are highly sensitive to sampling altitude. Between 200 and 500 m altitude, the composite dataset indicates that there is no statistically significant linear decrease in average momentum flux with height, but that may be due to sampling biases. Combined, the sUAS dataset extends previous aircraft-based computations of CDN from binned means of 27.5 m s-1 to 50 m s-1 with reasonable agreement on the overlapping wind speeds. In the current study, bin-averaged CDN peaks at 2.18 x 10-3 at 25 m s-1 with decreases to 45 m s-1. This study demonstrates the viability of the new sUAS platform for turbulence-quality measurements in hurricane conditions.

486898.title: Probabilistic AI Nowcasting of Severe Convective Weather
486898.authors: John L. Cintineo, NOAA / OAR / National Severe Storms Laboratory, Madison, WI; and K. M. Calhoun, T. Sandmael, R. B. Steeves, and P. A. Campbell
486898.abstract: Predicting the timing, location, and intensity of severe convective hazards in the near-term remains a difficult task. Given the chaotic nature of convection and limited observations, providing calibrated probabilistic guidance can aid numerous users in decision making. This research blends remotely sensed observations (e.g., radar, satellite, lightning), with short-term NWP analyses and forecasts to probabilistically predict convective hazards such as hail, wind, and tornadoes in the 0-6 hour time frame across the contiguous U.S. While probabilities are a natural result of NWP or AIWP ensembles, we present a more frugal approach using purely convolutional methods. We detail our data sampling strategy, AI model architecture and experiments, and evaluation of the model across all lead times using the NCEI Storm Event Database.

486901.title: Quantifying the Impact of Floods on the Financial Performance of Commercial Properties
486901.authors: Kieran Patrick Fitzmason, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; and H. Zeff, M. Hino, A. Sebastian, J. S. Sagi, and G. W. Characklis
486901.abstract: As physical assets that cannot be relocated, real estate is uniquely exposed to weather- and climate-related risks. Most research has focused on the effects of extreme weather on sales and valuation of single-family residential properties. There is comparatively little literature on weather-related risks to commercial properties in the United States despite the prevalence and economic importance of this asset class. While a handful of studies have documented negative impacts of major disasters (e.g., Hurricanes Sandy and Harvey) on commercial real estate sales and loan performance, the underlying mechanisms linking extreme weather to property-level financial conditions are not well understood. These mechanisms may include not only direct physical damage, but also indirect effects such as localized declines in economic activity, business interruption, rising insurance costs, and post-event shifts in market risk perceptions. The relative importance of these indirect channels for different types of properties is unknown. In this research, we estimate the effect of flood events on the financial performance of commercial properties in the United States over the 1998-2025 period. We draw on longitudinal data on the annual income and expenses of 96,753 properties included in commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) conduit deals. We combine these records with tract-level data on National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) claims and structure-level damage assessment data to respectively quantify neighborhood- and property-level exposure to flooding. Using a difference-in-differences design, we estimate the dynamic effects of these flood exposure measures on property-level financial outcomes while allowing for heterogenous treatment effects by property type (e.g., multifamily, retail, office). We examine short- and long-term effects on revenues, operating expenses, net operating income, occupancy, and mortgage delinquency. By evaluating the impacts of floods on different components of property cashflow, this study seeks to illuminate the underlying channels through which weather-related shocks affect the financial stability of commercial properties.

486905.title: Evaluating East Pacific Warming as a Solution to the Southwest Pliocene Precipitation Gap under Regional Refinement
486905.authors: Andrew Feder, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO
486905.abstract: Modeling of the Pliocene epoch in the southwest United States has failed to produce precipitation consistent with the regional proxy record. In this project, we implement a number of model forcing changes in CESM-MPAS to test whether they close this proxy-model precipitation gap. Regional refinement is also deployed to improve representation of orography-precipitation effects, as well as Eulerian moisture tracking to see changes in regional moisture sourcing. In the literature, two main hypotheses have been advanced to explain the wet Pliocene southwest; permanent El Niño, and intense California margin warming. By itself, we find that even very strong California margin warming added to a Pliocene-type climate is insufficient to bring southwest precipitation in line with what we would expect based on the proxy record. But, paired with changes in the distribution of plant types suggested by the paleobotanical record, enhanced evapotranspiration and land recycling help to very nearly close the gap. We conclude that, given the stronger oceanic proxy evidence for California margin warming than for permanent El Niño, and that it can quite nearly account for land precipitation proxy evidence in our modeling, it represents the much stronger candidate for resolving the gap.

486910.title: The Importance of Mesoscale Vortices in Organizing Convection During the Texas Hill Country Flash Floods of July 2025 and 2026
486910.authors: Thomas Galarneau, NSSL, Norman, OK; and J. J. Gourley
486910.abstract: Destructive flash floods are a recurring hazard across the Texas Hill Country, a region encompassing the Edwards Plateau and bounded to the east by the Balcones Escarpment just west of Interstate-35 in south-central Texas. During 4–6 July 2025, intense thunderstorms produced three-day rainfall totals of 16–18 inches across portions of the region. The resulting flash floods caused 137 fatalities, making the event the deadliest U.S. flash flood since the 1976 Big Thompson Canyon, Colorado, flash flood. The most catastrophic impacts occurred in Kerr County during the early morning of 4 July, when a nearly stationary supercell produced more than 10 inches of rain in approximately 3 h over the headwaters of the Guadalupe River basin. Resulting flood waves along the South Fork of the Guadalupe River and Cypress Creek inundated downstream communities, including the Camp Mystic for Girls Summer Camp. One year later, during 14–18 July 2026, another prolonged flash-flood episode affected the Hill Country through the repeated development of nearly stationary mesoscale convective systems. The heaviest rains, exceeding 15 inches, fell along the Balcones Escarpment north and northwest of Uvalde, Texas, during 14–16 July, with localized totals approaching 30 inches, while a separate rainfall maximum exceeding 12 inches developed over the Guadalupe River headwaters in Kerr County. Although the 2026 episode produced greater rainfall amounts over a broader area and longer period, two flash flood-related fatalities were reported as of the writing of this abstract, far fewer than during the 2025 disaster. Both events featured slow-moving convection in conjunction with mesoscale convective vortices (MCVs), but developed within distinctly different synoptic-scale flow regimes. This presentation examines how MCVs organized and sustained extreme-rain-producing convection within contrasting synoptic-scale flow regimes by modulating the key ingredients for extreme rainfall (lift, instability, moisture, and vertical wind shear) and focusing repeated convection over vulnerable Texas Hill Country watersheds. Furthermore, the hydrologic responses to the events are compared and contrasted given the differing durations over which extreme rainfall occurred. The two events illustrate contrasting pathways through which MCVs can organize extreme-rain-producing convection. During July 2025, a positively tilted 500-hPa ridge extended from northern Mexico into the Midwest, with an upstream trough over the southwest U.S. and southwesterly flow of approximately 20 kt extending from Mexico into central Texas. This flow steered a single, long-lived MCV from west of the Sierra Madre on 2 July into the Texas Hill Country by 4 July. Within an environment of near-record total-column water vapor, the MCV established a focused corridor of ascent and enhanced vertical wind shear that supported the organization of both an MCS and a nearly stationary supercell. The July 2026 event occurred beneath a more amplified trough–ridge pattern, with anomalously strong ridging over the Plains and Midwest. Anticyclonic wave breaking during 13–14 July fractured the southern portion of the downstream trough, producing a cutoff low that moved slowly westward on the southern flank of the ridge from southeast Texas on 14 July to southwest Texas by 17 July. This cutoff low provided a broad, persistent envelope of lift, instability, and vertical shear within which repeated MCSs and at least three MCVs developed. Thus, whereas the 2025 flood was strongly linked to a single, long-lived MCV originating in Mexico, the 2026 event featured multiple MCVs embedded within a slowly evolving synoptic-scale cutoff-low circulation. These cases motivate an updated MCV climatology that quantifies their frequency across the southern United States, the number occurring within individual multiday events, and the fraction originating over Mexico. Moreover, the prominent roles of mesoscale vortices in both flood events have important implications for predictability across medium- to short-range lead times. Results from both the MCV climatology, together with an evaluation of rainfall forecasts from operational global ensembles and the convection-allowing Warn-on-Forecast System, will also be presented.

486912.title: Potential Benefits of Assimilating Phased Array Radar Data for Convective-Scale Analysis and Prediction of Supercell Storms: A Proof-of-Concept OSSE Study
486912.abstract: This study investigates the impact of Phased Array Radar (PAR) scanning strategies on short-term convective-scale analyses and forecasts through an Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) framework. The WRF model, coupled with the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) ensemble adjustment Kalman filter, is used to assimilate synthetic radar observations from PAR and WSR-88D scanning strategies across three idealized supercell cases: slow-moving, fast-moving, and fast-moving/fast-growing storms. For the slow-moving storm, PAR and WSR-88D experiments produce comparable analyses and forecasts, with only marginal improvement from PAR. In contrast, for fast-moving and fast-growing storms, the 5-minute WSR-88D scan introduces substantial temporal errors associated with storm advection and evolution, resulting in distorted storm structure. The rapid 1-minute update capability of PAR significantly reduces these errors, producing superior analyses and forecasts. These findings suggest that the implementation of a future US national PAR network would substantially enhance the accuracy of short-term severe weather forecasts.

486916.title: Training to Support Effective Application of Evolving Satellite Products in Environmental Monitoring and Forecasting
486916.authors: Patrick N. Dills, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. Stevermer, B. Guarente, A. Hirsch, E. Houlihan, A. M. Smith, and V. Vincente
486916.abstract: Meteorologists, hydrologists, and other environmental experts have an ongoing need for training that supports the effective application of satellite products in monitoring and forecasting of various weather phenomena and potentially hazardous environmental conditions. To keep up with new and evolving products and to understand their benefits, limitations, and best uses, users need easy access to learning resources and hands-on practice. A full suite of courses and curricula (collections of courses on specific topic areas), accessible on the newly updated MetEd learning platform (meted.ucar.edu), contains information about these products and how to use them to evaluate and monitor evolving weather situations and hazards. Freely available online case exercises incorporate real-world scenarios to provide forecasters and other users practice integrating the strengths and capabilities of both geostationary (GEO) and low Earth orbiting (LEO) satellite products. Recently published training focuses on multiple newer products including RGB imagery for atmospheric and surface features including smoke, cloud cover, and high-latitude applications; and microwave and scatterometer products covering both high latitude and tropical regions. Additional topics include assessing potential pyroCb development in wildfire environments, fog and low cloud detection, day and nighttime cloud characterization, blowing snow, monitoring snow cover melt, sea ice characterization, and products for monitoring river ice and flooding. The goal of the training materials shared in this presentation is to help demonstrate relevance and advance day-to-day operational use of the latest GEO and LEO environmental satellite products. Learners accessing the courses are given the opportunity to work through an event’s timeline and interact with and analyze products to be able to make decisions and answer questions supporting the selection, understanding, and interpretation of appropriate satellite products for a given task. The available courses help forecasters and other users integrate and apply the latest advances in environmental remote sensing products to their operations.

486919.title: County-Level Wildfire Susceptibility Forecasting Using a Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts Artificial Intelligence Framework
486919.authors: Siddharth Damodharan, University of Colorado Colorado Springs, Colorado Springs, CO; and J. Kalita
486919.abstract: Wildfire activity has increased significantly across the western United States, creating significant ecological, social, and economic impacts. Thus, it remains important to forecast wildfire patterns to properly mitigate, prevent, and allocate resources in the event of a wildfire. However, even with the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, forecasting wildfires remains difficult, particularly due to the highly imbalanced nature of wildfire data, strong geographic priors, and the multiscale temporal dynamics of environmental drivers, such as vegetation dryness, precipitation deficits, and atmospheric variability. Traditional machine learning approaches include Random Forest and gradient-boosted decision trees, which have demonstrated strong performance, especially in wildfire susceptibility forecasting. Yet, many existing methods still struggle to model and predict temporal specialization, particularly across heterogeneous environmental processes. In this work, we propose a semantically grounded hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts Framework for county-level wildfire susceptibility forecasting. To evaluate this framework, we assess the model's performance in forecasting wildfire susceptibility across Colorado between 2020 and 2024. Our proposed architecture decomposes wildfire dynamics into three semantic expert groups representing fuel conditions, ignition/spread conditions, and terrain-climate structure. Each expert then contains temporal sub-experts designed to model high-, medium-, and low-frequency environmental behavior. We then use a lightweight routing network that dynamically combines expert predictions in response to evolving environmental conditions. We then benchmark the proposed framework against XGBoost as a baseline and county-level climatology priors, using temporally held-out 2020-2024 wildfire data. Experimental results indicate that grounded expert decomposition substantially improves performance relative to frequency-only MoE architectures, which exhibit expert collapse toward persistent low-frequency dynamics. The final hierarchical MoE achieved a mean PR-AUC of approximately 0.28 with a mean F1 score of 0.372, compared to XGBoost’s mean F1 score of 0.2434 and a mean PR-AUC of 0.2307. Ablation studies further reveal that semantically meaningful decomposition stabilizes expert specialization and improves the interpretability of wildfire susceptibility modeling. These findings thus suggest that semantically structured temporal expert architectures may provide a more promising direction for interpretable environmental forecasting systems, operating under highly imbalanced and geographically structured conditions.

486921.title: Turbulent Length Scales and Anisotropy In the Atmospheric Boundary Layer: Effects of Thermal Stability
486921.authors: Elliott James Walker, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and W. Zhang and C. D. Markfort
486921.abstract: The nature of turbulence in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) is strongly affected by thermal stratification. The resulting stability regime dictates the spatial organization of the flow by generating or suppressing turbulent structures of specific scales and geometries. Different structures in turbulent flow exhibit varying levels and types of anisotropy across scales, which can be characterized using the stress anisotropy tensor, the trace-free part of the Reynolds stress tensor. Isotropic turbulence is a common “textbook” assumption used to simplify models, but does not hold in the lower levels of the ABL. Discarding this assumption and accounting for anisotropy, e.g. by including invariants of the stress anisotropy tensor as additional scaling parameters, has been shown to significantly improve scaling relations and closure models. While modeling this second-order phenomenon adds complexity to closure formulations, its strong dependence on thermal stability presents a distinct pathway for empirical parameterization. Currently, there is a relative lack of observational field data for developing and validating such models, especially at altitudes greater than ~60 meters. Furthermore, the vertical transition of turbulence towards isotropy with increasing height has not yet been well characterized. To address this, we analyze a one-year, high-resolution meteorological dataset collected from the 200-meter tower at Texas Tech University (TTU), featuring 50 Hz sonic anemometer measurements across ten vertical levels. Because field-based turbulence characterizations are highly sensitive to methodological choices, we implement a data processing pipeline that accounts for instrument errors, tower shadowing, and non-stationarity of the turbulent boundary-layer flow. In addition, as the spectral gap separating turbulent and larger-scale (e.g. sub-mesoscale) motions varies between different stability conditions, we utilize stability-dependent averaging time periods. By visualizing the anisotropy tensor in a barycentric map and categorizing its states into not only the limiting cases of one-component/linear, two-component/planar, and three-component/isotropic but also intermediate transitional states, we characterize both the stability and height dependence of ABL turbulence anisotropy. We also investigate the ratios of different components of the turbulence intensity and the turbulence length scales, which exhibit marked variation with both altitude and stratification conditions. This work provides the empirical grounding needed to advance anisotropic modeling, yielding more physically accurate representations of the atmospheric boundary layer.

486928.title: Reconstructing and Time-Advancing Coherent Turbulent Wind Fields In Tropical Cyclones Using Diffusion Super-Resolution
486928.authors: Miguel Sanchez Gomez, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO; and R. King, A. Glaws, and O. Sallam
486928.abstract: Tropical cyclones threaten coastal and offshore infrastructure through intense, rapidly varying turbulent winds. The engineering wind models used in infrastructure design are based on simplified boundary layer theory (Kaimal et al., 1972; Mann, 1994) and therefore neglect the complex turbulent and mean wind field characteristics of the hurricane boundary layer. Numerical models offer a path to improve these engineering models for tropical cyclone conditions. Regional-scale models capture the large-scale structure of intense storms but often misrepresent the near-surface wind field (Sanchez Gomez et al., 2025a). Large-eddy simulations (LES) resolve the smaller-scale turbulent structures in the tropical cyclone boundary layer (Li et al., 2021; Sanchez Gomez et al., 2025b) and can inform structural load assessments and design standards (Worsnop et al., 2017). However, LES remains too costly for the large ensembles that design and hazard assessment require. We present a diffusion-based super-resolution (SR) framework that reconstructs and time-advances coherent turbulent wind fields in tropical cyclones from coarse numerical weather prediction output. We build on the work from Sallam et al. (2025), where a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) super-resolves planar hurricane wind fields from a horizontal grid spacing dx = 1.5 km to dx = 66 m. To improve the turbulence reconstruction of the flow, we condition the reverse diffusion process on the large-scale flow quantities that govern shear and buoyancy production of turbulence. To reconstruct three-dimensional turbulence in the hurricane boundary layer, each height is autoregressively conditioned on the super-resolved field immediately below through a spatially adaptive modulation layer. For time advancement, we propose a coupled neural operator—DDPM framework. The U-Net neural operator deterministically predicts velocity tendencies that are integrated with a forward Euler scheme, while the DDPM stochastically refines each provisional state before it is fed back. We train and evaluate the framework using mesoscale–microscale coupled simulations of five historical storms spanning three intensity levels. The large-scale structure and intensification of each storm is captured in a precursor two-domain, vortex-following simulation with grid spacings of 4.5 km and 1.5 km, respectively, using the Weather Research and Forecasting model (Skamarock et al., 2019). An offline coupling framework is used to simulate the hurricanes in the microscale at , as explained in Sanchez Gomez et al. (2025b). Hurricanes Nate, Harvey, Delta, Michael, and Laura are simulated, spanning intensities from Category 2—4 in the Saffir-Simpson wind scale (NHC NOAA, 2021). Although we capture the intensification of each storm over multiple days in the mesoscale, we simulate the storms in the LES over a 1-hour long period. We simulate Hurricane Nate and Harvey in the microscale as Category 2 storms, Hurricane Delta and Michael as Category 3 storms, and Hurricane Laura and Michael as Category 4 storms. Note that we simulate Michael at two stages of intensification. The LES storm dataset is split in half for training and testing the super-resolution framework: Hurricanes Nate, Michael (Category 3), and Laura are used for training; Harvey, Delta, and Michael (Category 4) are reserved for model validation. The SR framework generates coherent planar turbulent wind fields and three-dimensional turbulent structures consistent with the LES (Figure 1). The super-resolved planar wind fields capture the large-scale structure of the mesoscale simulation, including eyewall asymmetries, together with the fine turbulent features from the LES (Figure 1 top). Small turbulent structures are reconstructed inside the storm’s eye, while larger and more intense turbulent features develop in the eyewall region, consistent with the LES. By using autoregressive conditioning, the planar turbulent reconstructions also develop vertical coherence (Figure 1 bottom). As in the LES, turbulent structures are smaller near the surface than farther aloft, and vortical structures form preferentially near the surface. The coupled neural operator—SR framework produces physically consistent turbulence evolution (Figure 2). The coupled framework is initialized with the LES solution and time-advanced over a 300-second rollout with a 2-second integration time step. After the rollout period, the super-resolved wind fields retain a large-scale structure that is consistent with the mesoscale solution, and the turbulent flow resembles the LES solution. In both the LES and SR, the fastest and most turbulent winds occur in the eastern storm quadrant, while turbulence is reduced in the western quadrant and nearly quiescent inside the eye. The final reconstructed wind field also exhibits elongated turbulent structures aligned with the predominant wind direction, as in the LES. Overall, the enhanced SR model reproduces the turbulence statistics of the LES while retaining the large-scale storm structure of the mesoscale, and coupling a neural operator to the DDPM effectively time-advances tropical cyclone turbulence into realistic storm realizations. Future work will extend the framework to time-advance three-dimensional turbulence, offering a direct and cheaper alternative to LES for infrastructure design and hazard assessment. 486929.title: Methane Emissions Quantification in the San Joaquin Valley: Integrating High-Precision In Situ Monitoring with WRF-STILT
486929.authors: Jennifer Wu, University of Colorado, Boulder, Boulder, CO; and J. E. Kim, B. Farris, E. Emerson, A. Vijayan, and D. K. Henze
486929.abstract: Recent top-down atmospheric observations in U.S. oil and gas basins reveal methane emissions up to 60% higher than EPA inventory estimates. Improved source attribution and quantification methods are thus urgently needed to target this key driver of near-term warming. In the San Joaquin Valley of California—a major industrial and agricultural region—accurately separating methane contributions from petroleum production, natural gas infrastructure, dairies, and agriculture remains a critical challenge for regional mitigation strategies. Here, we leverage a network of high-precision ground-based spectrometers (Aeris MIRA Ultra LDS) to collect continuous methane data from September 2024 through July 2025 across five monitoring sites: Arvin, Oildale, Sandrini, Buena Vista, and CSU Bakersfield. Atmospheric transport is simulated using the Stochastic Time-Inverted Lagrangian Transport (STILT) model driven by high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) meteorological fields. To identify periods of elevated methane while eliminating nocturnal boundary layer bias, we calculate hourly z-scores across the continuous record to isolate significant anomaly events. Using 48-hour 2500-particle hourly backward trajectories to construct the transport model, we optimize spatial emission scaling factors relative to gridded EPA Greenhouse Gas Inventory baselines within a Bayesian inverse framework. We test and validate our inversion framework using observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs) before applying it to real-world ground-based observations to present preliminary basin-wide methane emissions estimates during targeted high z-score observation periods.

486933.title: Mesoscale Observational Overview of the 24 March 2023 Rolling Fork-Winona-Amory, Mississippi Tornado Event
486933.authors: Anthony W. Lyza, NOAA/OAR/NSSL, Norman, OK; and R. L. Miller, M. D. Flournoy, T. J. Galarneau, A. A. Alford, M. C. Coniglio, and T. A. Murphy
486933.abstract: A pair of long-lived supercell thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes across northern and central Mississippi during the evening hours of 24 March 2023 before growing upscale into a quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) and producing additional tornadoes in northern Alabama. The southern supercell was particularly destructive, producing a trio of destructive EF3–EF4 tornadoes across central Mississippi, impacting the communities of Rolling Fork, Winona, and Amory and causing 21 fatalities. This supercell passed through a dense mesoscale observational array deployed as part of the Propagation, Evolution, and Rotation in Linear Storms (PERiLS) field campaign. These observational platforms included NEXRAD Doppler radars, the NOAA X-Pol (NOXP) mobile Doppler radar, 915-MHz Doppler wind profilers from the NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory (PSL), Doppler wind lidars from the NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) and University of Louisiana at Monroe (ULM), and multiple radiosonde platforms and surface observing stations. In this presentation, we document the evolution of the mesoscale environment during the 24 March event from initial development of the supercells through upscale growth into a tornadic QLCS. Our analysis includes evaluation of the Doppler wind profiler and lidar platforms as well as wind profiles derived from NOXP and the nearby NEXRAD radars using the extended velocity azimuth display (EVAD) technique, with additional environmental data and validation provided by the PERiLS radiosondes and surface observational analysis. Preliminary analyses illustrate a rapid evolution in the environment ahead of the primary supercell, including a substantial increase in low-level wind shear and coincident convective destabilization, particularly within about 2 h of supercell arrival.

486934.title: Overview of the FY2026 NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed Activities
486934.authors: Anthony W. Lyza, NOAA/OAR/NSSL, Norman, OK; and K. M. Calhoun, P. A. Campbell, A. J. Clark, S. R. Ernst, T. J. Galarneau, I. L. Jirak, C. M. Kuster, K. C. Thiel, J. E. Trujillo-Falcón, J. W. Monroe, J. G. Madden, and M. Fox
486934.abstract: The NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed (HWT) is a joint collaboration between NOAA’s National Severe Storms Laboratory, Storm Prediction Center (SPC), and National Weather Service (NWS) Norman Weather Forecast Office (WFO). The HWT serves as both a physical space and a conceptual framework for testing and evaluating emerging technologies and findings in a collaborative environment, engaging both researchers and operational end-users. The HWT evaluates products and technologies for forecasting and warning severe convective threats within a timescale of minutes to a few weeks. HWT topics span the purview of WFOs and their partners, including local emergency managers and broadcast meteorologists, to national centers, particularly SPC. During the FY2026 HWT season, seven experiments/activities were conducted over 32 experiment weeks. These activities engaged 299 total participants, including 115 NWS forecasters, 128 research and academic partners, 25 emergency managers, 14 international forecasters, nine broadcast meteorologists, and eight private sector partners. 2026 HWT activities included the Visualizing Uncertainty in Severe Weather Forecast Graphics activity, the Phased Array Radar (PAR) activity, the Severe Weather Extended-Range forecasting and Verification Experiment (SWERVE), the Hazard Services-Probabilistic Hazard Information (HS-PHI) Recommender Experiment, the Spring Forecasting Experiment (SFE), the Satellite Proving Ground (SPG) experiment, and the Validating Operational Multilingual Communication and Effective Service Experiment.

486939.title: Diurnal Variation of Dust Aerosol First Indirect Effects in Marine Low-Level Clouds over the Tropical North Atlantic
486939.authors: Ebenezer Boakye Yiadom, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte, NC; and I. Chang, A. A. Adebiyi, and S. K. Pandey
486939.abstract: Mineral dust is a major natural aerosol over the tropical North Atlantic, yet its influence on marine warm-cloud microphysics and aerosol indirect effects remains poorly constrained. Previous work has shown that Saharan dust can suppress the aerosol first indirect effect by increasing cloud droplet effective radius in thin, low-liquid-water-path clouds, likely through a combination of coarse dust acting as giant cloud condensation nuclei and dust-induced warming that modifies supersaturation and droplet evaporation. However, the extent to which this dust–cloud microphysical response varies across the diurnal cycle remains unclear. This study investigates the diurnal modulation of dust aerosol first indirect effects over marine low-level clouds in the tropical North Atlantic. We focus on single-layer warm clouds and examine how the relationships among aerosol loading, cloud condensation nuclei, cloud droplet number concentration, and cloud droplet effective radius vary under low- and high-dust conditions as a function of liquid water path and local time. The analysis will combine satellite observations and reanalysis products to examine how dust loading and vertical placement influence cloud microphysical responses under different cloud and meteorological conditions. The first indirect effect will be quantified using the sensitivity of cloud droplet effective radius and cloud droplet number concentration to aerosol loading and cloud condensation nuclei-related variability at fixed liquid water path. By separating the analysis into daytime, nighttime, morning, and afternoon conditions, this work will test whether dust-driven changes in cloud droplet size and droplet number are amplified or weakened during specific parts of the diurnal cycle. Particular attention will be given to thin, low-liquid-water-path clouds, where dust is expected to exert the strongest microphysical influence. The results will provide new insight into whether the sign and magnitude of dust aerosol indirect effects depend on local time and whether diurnal sampling differences contribute to uncertainty in satellite-based estimates of dust–cloud interactions. This work will improve understanding of how Saharan dust modifies marine warm-cloud microphysics, and the associated radiative effects over the tropical North Atlantic.

486945.title: Mountain and Lake Dynamics Coupled to Urban Air Quality: Novel Airborne Doppler Lidar Measurements over Salt Lake City
486945.authors: Brian J. Carroll, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and S. Baidar, N. Malarich, C. Womack, X. Ren, C. Warneke, and S. S. Brown
486945.abstract: The mountainous Salt Lake City region of Utah is a densely populated region subject to summer air quality issues, regularly exceeding the National Ambient Air Quality Standard for ozone. Air quality in the region is heavily influenced by the local meteorology of the complex terrain and lakes, and improving understanding of these influences requires measurements with high spatial and temporal resolution in challenging terrain. State-of-the-art airborne Doppler lidar wind and turbulence profiles from the NOAA Twin Otter research aircraft provided unprecedented spatial and temporal information about the atmospheric boundary layer dynamics in the region during the 2024 Utah Summer Ozone Study (USOS). Meteorological drivers in the region were repeatedly sampled, including canyon flows and lake breezes. The airborne measurements and the multitude of ground-based mobile and stationary measurements present in the area that summer were used to investigate the role of these local atmospheric boundary layer dynamics on summertime ozone. Model comparisons will also be shown between the operational HRRR model and lidar wind profiles over the Great Salt Lake and throughout the area to assess model performance in this complex terrain.

486946.title: D-CFLOS: A Generalized Framework for Deterministic Cloud-Free Line-of-Sight Analysis on Three-Dimensional Cloud Datasets
486946.authors: Hungjui Yu, CIRA, FORT COLLINS, CO; and J. M. Haynes, Y. J. Noh, R. DeMaria, and S. D. Miller
486946.abstract: Cloud-Free Line of Sight (CFLOS) is an important quantity for applications including aviation, optical sensing, and atmospheric observations. Accurate CFLOS estimation requires detailed three-dimensional (3D) cloud structure, yet operational methods are often limited by probabilistic cloud representations or computational constraints. We present the Deterministic-CFLOS (D-CFLOS), a generalized framework for estimating cloud obstruction, cloud-free distance, and line-of-sight transmissivity directly from the high-resolution 3D cloud analyses. The approach converts user-defined observation geometries to ray paths and performs efficient ray tracing through volumetric cloud fields. To support a broad range of applications, the framework includes multiple analysis modules for linear, areal, and total-sky CFLOS estimations. The current D-CFLOS framework supports analysis using multi-satellite-based near-real-time global 3D cloud products developed at the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere (CIRA). Examples demonstrate the capability of D-CFLOS to quantify cloud obstruction and atmospheric transmission under diverse viewing geometries in near-real-time. The framework is also designed for flexible adaptation to many different kinds of 3D atmospheric/geographical datasets while maintaining computational efficiency for large analyses. The D-CFLOS framework provides actionable line-of-sight information that complement traditional cloud products and may support applications in atmospheric science, aviation, remote sensing, satellite missions, renewable energy, and other disciplines requiring efficient visibility and propagation analyses through 3D atmospheric environments. This presentation will highlight current developments and case applications, including ongoing improvements in cloud visibility computation using machine-learning based cloud water content profile data.

486947.title: Internal Boundary Layer Development during Hurricane Landfall and Impacts on Near-Surface Wind Fields (Invited Presentation)
486947.authors: Miguel Sanchez Gomez, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO; and M. J. Churchfield and J. Jonkman
486947.abstract: Tropical cyclones threaten coastal infrastructure through intense, rapidly varying turbulent winds. The engineering wind models used in infrastructure design are based on simplified boundary layer theory (Kaimal et al., 1972; Mann, 1994; Von Kármán, 1948) and therefore neglect the complex turbulent and mean wind field characteristics of the hurricane boundary layer. These conditions grow even more complex at landfall, where abrupt changes in the surface exchange of momentum, moisture, and heat reshape the near-surface winds and generate internal boundary layers (IBLs) within the three-dimensional storm structure. Numerical models offer a path to improve these engineering models for landfalling tropical cyclone conditions. Regional-scale models capture the large-scale structure of intense storms but often misrepresent the near-surface wind field (Ren et al., 2020; Sanchez Gomez et al., 2025a). Large-eddy simulations (LES) resolve the smaller-scale turbulent structures in the tropical cyclone boundary layer (Li et al., 2021; Sanchez Gomez et al., 2025b) and can inform structural load assessments and design standards (Sanchez Gomez et al., 2023; Worsnop et al., 2017). We conduct an ensemble of mesoscale-microscale coupled simulations of Hurricane Delta to investigate the development of the IBL during landfall and its influence on the spatiotemporal evolution of the mean wind and turbulence. The large-scale structure and intensification of Delta are captured in a precursor two-domain, vortex-following simulation with grid spacings 4.5 km and 1.5 km, respectively, using the Weather Research and Forecasting model (Skamarock et al., 2019). An offline coupling framework is used to simulate the hurricane in the microscale at dx = 33.33 m (Sanchez Gomez et al., 2025b). We simulate 20 realizations of the storm in the LES, enabling ensemble-averaged statistics that isolate the evolution of the mean wind and turbulence during landfall. Delta is simulated as a Category 3 storm in the Saffir-Simpson wind scale (NHC NOAA, 2021). Although we capture the intensification of the storm over multiple days in the mesoscale, each LES realization spans a 70-minute period, of which the first 30 minutes are discarded for turbulence spin-up. We define the mean wind as the ensemble average across the 20 LES realizations and characterize turbulence through the ensemble-mean turbulent kinetic energy (TKE). We sample mean wind and TKE profiles at multiple offshore and inland locations within the eyewall (colored circles in Figure 1a) to characterize the growth of the IBL and its influence on the vertical structure of the hurricane boundary layer. Figure 1b–d shows the sampled profiles, with solid lines denoting offshore conditions and dashed lines onshore locations. An IBL develops immediately after landfall (Figure 1b—d). As offshore hurricane winds encounter the rougher land surface, enhanced drag produces large near-surface wind shear that initiates an IBL and modifies the vertical structure of the hurricane boundary layer. Inland profiles exhibit increased near-surface wind shear relative to offshore conditions (Figure 1b,c). Although the largest changes in the mean wind profile occur below 100 m, the influence of the growing IBL extends throughout the lowest kilometer of the boundary layer, including the development of a super-geostrophic wind maximum near 500 m. The enhanced shear also increases TKE, first near the surface and then progressively upward as the IBL deepens (Figure 1d). Note that part of the offshore-onshore contrast in Figure 1 may also reflect azimuthal variability in the mean wind and turbulence of the storm (Sanchez Gomez et al., 2025b). Our results show the development of an IBL associated with the adjustment of hurricane winds and turbulence following landfall at a single analysis time. We will extend this analysis to characterize the spatiotemporal evolution of the IBL as the hurricane eyewall moves inland from the open ocean. These high-fidelity simulations provide a framework for improving engineering wind models and evaluating American Society of Civil Engineers design standards for civil and energy infrastructure (ASCE, 2021) under landfalling hurricane conditions. 486948.title: Testing Simplified Approaches for Deriving high-Resolution Climate Projections of Wind and Solar Energy Generation
486948.authors: Stephen Po-Chedley, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, CA; and R. Arthur, J. Zhang, M. Monteagudo, M. Signorotti, and J. C. Golaz
486948.abstract: Earth system models (ESMs) are typically run at coarse (~100km) horizontal resolution and public archives typically contain output at daily or monthly resolution. This data is incredibly useful for studying changes in climate over large spatial scales, but may not capture important spatial and temporal details. For example, standard monthly output cannot be used to study changes in the diurnal cycle, changes in the distribution of daily extremes, or to accurately represent the current or future local climate in regions of sharp climatological gradients. However, realistic climate scenarios at high spatiotemporal resolution are critical for stress testing planned infrastructure investments. For this reason, climate projection data is frequently bias corrected and dynamically or statistically downscaled to obtain realistic geophysical information with the necessary spatiotemporal resolution for the given application. Unfortunately, such techniques can be complex to implement and computationally expensive. Simpler techniques include adding monthly mean changes (derived from coarse ESM projections) to observational data. Such techniques can be implemented relatively easily, can make use of existing stores of climate output, and sidestep the need for bias correction by leveraging present-day, high-resolution gridded or in-situ observations. Here we undertake a “perfect model” test to understand the validity of simpler approaches to producing high spatiotemporal resolution climate projection data, with a focus on wind and solar energy generation estimates. Such estimates are essential for long-term energy infrastructure planning studies, especially capacity expansion plans. We treat hourly, km-scale, dynamically downscaled simulations of the current and future climate from the Western United States Dynamically Downscaled Dataset (WUS-D3) as truth and test two simplified approaches to estimate plausible high-resolution future climate states. We use present-day data from the dynamically-downscaled simulation as a proxy for the observed state and shift this state to the future using coarse-resolution climate simulation data. We compute and apply shifts using a) changes in the monthly average geophysical data (ignoring changes in the diurnal cycle and sub-monthly variability) and b) changes in geophysical quantiles derived from daily data (known as quantile delta mapping). Since wind and solar energy generation is sensitive to the representation of diurnal and sub-monthly geophysical variability, we compute time series of future wind and solar capacity factors at representative sites, using both the perfect model “truth” data and estimates derived from both simplified methods. Finally, we quantify the accuracy of the resulting projections of future wind and solar energy potential with respect to the perfect model data. We close by discussing the implications of our findings in the context of energy infrastructure planning.

486965.title: Using Large-Eddy Simulations with Realistic Environmental Flow to Understand Tornado-Scale Vortices and Extreme Near-Surface Wind Gusts in Tropical Cyclones
486965.authors: Daniel P. Stern, NRL, Monterey, CA; and G. H. Bryan, D. H. Richter, and J. A. Zhang
486965.abstract: Sub-kilometer scale vortices—sometimes termed tornado-scale vortices (TSVs)—are known to be responsible for producing extreme near-surface wind gusts within the eyewall of tropical cyclones (TCs). Our previous studies have used large-eddy simulations (LES) of idealized TCs in a quiescent environment to show that although individual vortices are transient (with lifetimes on the order of a few minutes), these TSVs are ubiquitous, and so the likelihood of a given location experiencing such a feature is substantial. While progress has been made in understanding eyewall vortices, much remains unknown, and there is currently no consensus regarding the fundamental physical mechanisms by which TSVs form. In addition, a key limitation of our prior simulations was the absence of environmental flow, which is known from observations to strongly constrain the spatial distribution of near-surface extreme wind gusts. In our ongoing work, we are conducting new large-eddy simulations that incorporate mean flow and environmental vertical wind shear, and we are using these simulations to gain insight into the origin mechanisms of TSVs, their dynamics and relationship to extreme near-surface wind gusts, and their modulation by shear. We will also analyze simulated dropsondes and sUAS data for comparison to real observations. Preliminary results show that the vortices are preferentially found in the left-of-shear semicircle, consistent with dropsonde observations of extreme wind gusts. Through sensitivity tests where various physical processes are artificially suppressed, we find preliminary evidence that the vortices may form as a result of a boundary layer instability, from the local vertical shear of the radial flow.

486966.title: Advances in the Use of Global Navigation Satellite System Polarimetric Radio Occultation Measurements for NWP and Weather Applications
486966.authors: Estel Cardellach, Council of Scientific Research of Spain, Cerdanyola del Valles, B, Spain; and C. Marquardt, F. J. Turk, R. Padullés, E. R. Kursinski, J. Brandmeyer, M. Talpe, V. Nguyen, and Y. Cheng
486966.abstract: Conventional radio occultations (RO) track the phase delay induced by water vapor and air density gradients in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals as they propagate through the Earth’s atmosphere. Standard RO products such as bending angle profiles from the Constellation Observing System for Meteorology, Ionosphere and Climate (COSMIC-2), the EUMETSAT Metop satellites and numerous other publicly and commercially available RO products are routinely assimilated into operational Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) forecast models. The positive impact to forecasts of temperature and winds when RO data are included in the suite of observations ingested into data assimilation (DA) systems is well documented. Polarimetric RO (PRO) enhances standard RO by receiving the GNSS signals with a dual-polarization RO receiver. In addition to the capabilities of the conventional RO, PRO can provide an indication of precipitation at each vertical level, offering a potential to advance the assimilation of satellite data in precipitating conditions. PRO observations provide unique diagnostics and observations for investigating the thermodynamic environment in and near precipitation, and assumptions underlying parameterizations used by operational NWP forecast models. In this presentation, highlights and recommendations from the 3rd GNSS Polarimetric Radio Occultation Workshop are presented. The workshop took place 10-12 November 2025, hosted by EUMETSAT in Darmstadt, Germany. It represented a forum for addressing multiple uses and applications that have been studied in the seven years that PRO data have been available. Over 70 people participated, representing government agencies, research centers, universities and the commercial space sector. Presentations were given regarding the status of PRO-capable satellite data, processing techniques and applications being developed from current and future observations, with a focus on its use for NWP modeling. Recommendations were prepared for meteorological, space and research organizations including Coordination Group for Meteorological Satellites (CGMS) member agencies, the EUMETSAT Radio Occultation Meteorology Satellite Application Facility (ROM SAF), and satellite data providers.

486981.title: Environmental Impacts of Upper-Tropospheric Trough on the Development of Heavy-Rain-Producing Systems during the East Asian Monsoon
486981.authors: Shusaku Ueno, Kyoto University, Uji, 26, Japan; and T. Takemi
486981.abstract: In the East Asia region including Japan, a monsoon rainy season lasts typically from June to early August, which is called “Baiu” in Japanese. During this period, a zonally elongated stationary front, i.e., a Baiu front, exists around the Japanese islands and brings long-lasting rainfalls. In recent years, mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) frequently occurred and in some cases brought torrential rainfall and flash floods. Although various factors contribute to the development of heavy-rain-producing MCSs along the Baiu front, recent case studies indicated that upper-tropospheric troughs can play important roles. For example, the troughs make the atmospheric stability unstable, form the dynamically induced large-scale upward motion, and intensify lower-level disturbances. In this study, we investigate the roles of the trough in MCSs formation by conducting numerical experiments. The experiments consisted of a control run (CTRL) in which precipitation was reproduced under an atmospheric environment containing an upper-level trough and sensitivity experiments in which the strength of the trough was reduced to 50% and 0% of that in CTRL, hereafter referred to as PV50 and PV00, respectively. Quasi-geostrophic potential vorticity (QGPV) piecewise inversion was used to modify the strength of the trough. This technique calculates dynamically balanced streamfunction and geopotential fields associated with the given PV field. From these fields, the corresponding temperature and wind fields can also be derived. Using this technique, the upper-level trough was identified as a PV anomaly, and the atmospheric fields associated with the anomaly were superimposed on a background field. This procedure produced modified atmospheric environments in which the trough strength was artificially reduced. These modified environments were used as the initial and boundary conditions for the sensitivity experiments. After conducting experiments, the results were compared to examine the effects of the trough on the location, strength, and temporal evolution of MCSs and rainfall. The experiments were applied to the heavy rainfall event occurred over western Japan in July 2018. The results showed that the accumulated rainfalls were reduced by 12% in PV50 and by 25% in PV00 from CTRL. The area size with strong rainfall intensity also decreased as the trough was weakened. Furthermore, the MCSs developed around the Baiu front were shifted northward from CTRL to PV50 and PV00. The Baiu front is typically located along the southern flank of the upper-tropospheric jet stream. In all simulations, the lower-level Baiu front was formed along the upper-level jet stream. However, in PV00, meanders of the jet stream were weakened by eliminating the trough, which resulted in northward displacement of the jet stream and the Baiu front. In addition, environmental parameters favorable for MCS and rainfall, including moisture flux convergence, convective available potential energy (CAPE), and the depth of the moist absolute unstable layer (MAUL), were all smaller in PV00 than in CTRL. These changes were generated by the trough, and contributed to the reductions in rainfall amount and intensity in PV50 and PV00.

486982.title: Cloud-Top Height Estimation Based on IR Sounders — Towards the Use of the Geostationary Himawari Sounder.
486982.authors: Yurika Yamada, JMA, Kiyose-Shi, Tokyo, Japan
486982.abstract: The Japan meteorological agency plans to launch Himawari-10 in JFY 2030, which will be equipped with an infrared (IR) hyperspectral sounder — the Geostationary HiMawari Sounder (GHMS). It is undoubtable that IR sounders provide indispensable observation data to enhance the performance of numerical weather prediction models through data assimilation. In addition, geostationary IR sounders, with high spatial and temporal resolutions, are expected to be used for weather monitoring and nowcasting. For example, cloud properties like cloud-top height (CTH) derived from IR observations are used to monitor severe weather phenomena by meteorological officers and optimize flight routes in the aviation industry, particularly in the areas where ground observations are limited or not available. However, while IR observations are sensitive to radiative impact from clouds, existing CTH estimation methods by IR observations sometimes underestimate cloud altitude of thin and high clouds due to their little radiative signatures. This implies that existing methods may not be the best approach for users who are interested in actual cloud altitudes. Synergetic use of both radar/lidar and IR observations based on artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques (AI/ML) can be a promising alternative. Cloud vertical distributions observed by Cloud Profiling Radar (CPR) and Atmospheric Lidar (ATLID) onboard the Earth Cloud Aerosol and Radiation Explorer (EarthCARE) can be valuable reference data, while IR sounders, like GHMS and Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS), possess information on vertical distributions of atmospheric temperature and humidity which can improve the performance of the estimation on cloud altitudes. AI/ML can integrate these observations. In this study, the applicability of ML techniques for CTH estimation was investigated using CrIS observations as proxy data of the GHMS. The use of CrIS observations for CTH estimation will be demonstrated in the presentation.

486985.title: LES-Quality Urban Wind Field Emulation by Combining Adaptive Fourier Neural Operator with Flow Matching
486985.authors: Yunhyeong Lee, Pukyong National University, Busan, South korea; and J. Shin and R. Son
486985.abstract: Accurately reproducing city-scale turbulence and abrupt wind shifts is essential for the safe operation of urban air mobility, yet remains computationally expensive for real-time applications. Here, we propose AFNO+FM, which combines an Adaptive Fourier Neural Operator (AFNO) with a Flow Matching-based generative module to emulate WRF-based large-eddy simulations (LES) by super-resolving atmospheric wind fields from 1.5-km to 0.1-km resolution. Compared with interpolation and convolution neural network (CNN)-based baselines, AFNO reduces pixel-wise errors by approximately 8.2% than the CNN-based model, achieving wind-speed RMSE of 1.84 m/s and an R2 of 0.83. Beyond these conventional metrics, AFNO+FM substantially improves the physical realism of the reconstructed flow fields, most closely reproducing WRF-LES in terms of high-wavenumber power-spectra, the non-Gaussian heavy-tailed distribution of vorticity, the spatial correlation decay of the vertical velocity perturbation (w′), the mass-conservation residuals, and vortex-stretching alignment. These results demonstrate that superior point-wise accuracy alone does not guarantee physical reliable flow reconstruction and that integrating generative modeling with deterministic neural operators provides an effective pathway toward real-time LES-quality urban wind prediction. This work was funded by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Korea government (MSIT) (RS-2024-00343921).

486988.title: Deep Learning Enables Adaptive Multi-Model Ensemble for Terrestrial GPP
486988.authors: Hyeontae Noh, Pukyong National University, Busan, South korea; and J. S. Kim and R. Son
486988.abstract: Multi-model ensembles are widely used to reduce uncertainties in climate projections, yet conventional equal-weight averaging cannot account for regional differences in model skill arising from structural and parameter uncertainties. Here, we present a deep-learning-based multi-model ensemble (DL-MME) that learns adaptive spatiotemporal weights for individual Earth system models. We demonstrate the framework for terrestrial gross primary production (GPP), a fundamental carbon flux linking the atmosphere and biosphere whose accurate estimation essential for understanding the global carbon cycle. Compared with a conventional equal-weight ensemble (base-MME), DL-MME reduces the root mean square error by approximately 20% and improves the coefficient of determination (R2) by 22% against FLUXNET observations. The learned weighting patterns exhibit strong climate dependence, closely aligning with Köppen-Geiger climate zones and revealing systematic relationships between model contributions and process representations, including nutrient cycling and vegetation phenology. Appling DL-MME to future climate projections yields significantly higher GPP, suggesting greater potential for sustained ecosystem productivity and carbon uptake under future climate change. This work was funded by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Korea government (MSIT) (RS-2024-00343921).

486991.title: Future Trends in Upper-Atmospheric Shear Instability from Climate Change
486991.authors: Joana Sousa Negrao de Medeiros, University of Reading, Reading, RDG, United kingdom; University of Reading, Reading, Reading, United Kingdom; and P. D. Williams
486991.abstract: Understanding how jet streams respond to a warming climate is crucial for anticipating changes in atmospheric circulation and their broader impacts. Previous studies have highlighted the influence of anthropogenic warming on the meridional temperature gradient, which directly affects jet stream dynamics and variability. This study investigates projected trends in upper-level jet stream shear instability under future climate change scenarios using CMIP6 multi-model simulations. Building on previous findings linking anthropogenic warming to strengthened meridional temperature gradients, we analyse annual means of zonal wind speed, vertical wind shear, and stratification profiles from 2015 to 2100 globally. Results show strengthened multi-model annual-mean vertical shear at 250 hPa, particularly in high-emission scenarios, with trends ranging from 0.04 to 0.11 m s⁻¹ (100 hPa)⁻¹ decade⁻¹ depending on the scenario and region, equivalent to a total relative increase of 16-27% over 86 years. Decreasing trends are observed in the annual-mean Brunt-Väisälä frequency (N²) at 250 hPa, with multi-model ensemble mean values across regions ranging from -0.018 to -0.040 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻² decade⁻¹ for lower and higher emissions scenarios, respectively, equating to a total relative decrease of 10-20%. Similarly, the annual-mean Richardson number (Ri) shows decreasing trends of -0.014 to -0.050 decade⁻¹ across emissions scenarios and regions, which is a total relative decrease of 38-47%.
