These findings suggest more favourable conditions for the generation of Clear-Air Turbulence (CAT), posing critical challenges for aviation safety and operations in a warming climate.

486993.title: Synoptic Climatology of Fastest Jet Stream Winds Over the North Atlantic: Dynamical Properties and Climate Change Projections
486993.authors: Joana Sousa Negrao de Medeiros, University of Reading, Reading, RDG, United kingdom; and J. A. Knox and P. D. Williams
486993.abstract: Clear-air turbulence (CAT) is most frequently encountered near intense upper-tropospheric jet streams, yet the large-scale flow regimes hosting the most hazardous environments remain incompletely characterised. We present a synoptic climatology of the strongest jet stream winds (top 100 events) at 250 hPa using ERA5 reanalysis (1979–2024) and Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) simulations spanning historical (1979–2015) and late-century (2070–2100) periods under intermediate (SSP2-4.5) and high-emission (SSP5-8.5) Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. Extreme wind events regularly exceed 100 m s−1 and are overwhelmingly anticyclonic in ERA5 (94%), consistent with strongly curved and dynamically imbalanced jet regimes known to favour enhanced shear, inertial instability, and gravity-wave generation conducive to CAT. A pronounced climatological maximum is identified over the western North Atlantic, a region of sustained aviation exposure. Both emission scenarios produce intensification of anticyclonic extremes under future forcing, but through fundamentally different dynamical mechanisms. Under high emissions, the anticyclonic expansion is dominated by shear vorticity, reflecting intensified baroclinic shear driven by enhanced meridional temperature gradients, accompanied by increases in jet sinuosity and significant wind speed intensification (0.4 m s−1 decade−1, 𝑝 < 10−7). Under intermediate emissions, the response is curvature-dominated, with sharper, more localised extremes in jet streak regions dynamically predisposed to anticyclonic Rossby wave breaking, tropopause folding, and persistent blocking. These contrasting dynamical pathways indicate distinct mechanisms of upper-level hazard amplification along major North Atlantic flight corridors, with implications for regime-aware turbulence risk assessment across different emissions trajectories.

486997.title: David Randall’s Vision for Bridging Climate Modeling and Observations with Cloud-system Resolving and Single-Column Models (Invited Presentation)
486997.abstract: In the late 1980s, global climate models (GCMs) were beginning to incorporate increasingly sophisticated cloud parameterizations. The U.S. Department of Energy launched the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program in 1989 to improve understanding of atmospheric radiation and cloud processes through long-term observations. As debates over cloud absorption and cloud-radiation interactions emerged during the early 1990s, Dave Randall recognized a much broader opportunity. He envisioned these sites as natural laboratories for testing and improving cloud parameterizations in climate models. That vision was articulated in his seminal 1996 Journal of Climate paper, "Single-column models and cloud ensemble models as links between observations and climate models." Richard Somerville and Sam Iacobellis contributed single-column model (SCM) results, while I contributed cloud-system resolving model (CRM) simulations. Dave's insight was to articulate a practical modeling hierarchy in which observations, CRMs, SCMs, and GCMs each played complementary roles in parameterization development and evaluation. This framework not only transformed how cloud parameterizations were evaluated but also provided an enduring scientific rationale for the long-term operation of the ARM observational sites. This modeling hierarchy continues to underpin the evaluation and development of cloud parameterizations from conventional GCMs to today's Earth system models. My own journey with Dave began in late 1989. After he gave a seminar at UCLA, I drove him to Los Angeles International Airport, and during that drive he offered me a Research Associate position at Colorado State University (CSU). A few months later, shortly after defending my Ph.D., I moved to CSU—despite the reservations of both Dave and my Ph.D. advisor, the late Professor Akio Arakawa, about the timing. Looking back, it was one of the best decisions of my career. Dave had the foresight to recruit me to help develop CRM research to support his ARM project, and I spent the next ten years at CSU enjoying the most scientifically productive period of my career. His vision consistently opened new research directions and created opportunities for those around him and the broad communities. Dave's leadership also shaped the ARM Cloud Parameterization Working Group, which he led during its formative years. Under his guidance, the working group developed large-scale forcing datasets for SCM and CRM simulations and organized a series of influential model intercomparison projects. One particularly important project used summertime continental ARM observations—datasets comparable to those that had previously been available primarily for tropical oceanic field campaigns. These comparisons led to new understanding of cloud processes over land, including the roles of convective inhibition, condensate advection, and the diurnal cycle in shaping model behavior. Dave also had an extraordinary talent for turning simple ideas into influential parameterizations. One day, he sketched a remarkably simple equation relating cloud fraction directly to cloud condensate mixing ratio on a piece of paper. Using CRM simulations, I determined several empirical coefficients, including the dependence of the slope on relative humidity. The resulting formulation became widely known as the Xu-Randall cloud fraction parameterization and has been implemented in many GCMs. In truth, however, the key insight was Dave's. I have often felt it would be more appropriately called the Randall parameterization. His scientific vision extended well beyond cloud parameterizations. Dave advocated probability density function (PDF) approaches for planetary boundary layer (PBL) parameterization before they became widely adopted. He introduced me to Vince Larson when Vince was a postdoctoral researcher at CSU, hoping that we would begin a collaboration. Although that collaboration did not develop immediately, Dave's instinct proved correct. Years later, our work converged through the IPHOC higher-order turbulence scheme, developed by his former student, Dr. Anning Cheng, who joined my group at NASA. IPHOC also benefited from collaborations fostered by Dave's NSF Center for Multiscale Modeling of Atmospheric Processes (CMMAP), illustrating once again how his scientific vision connected people and ideas across institutions and decades. Reflecting on these experiences, what stands out most is not only Dave's remarkable scientific creativity, but also his ability to see connections long before others did. He recognized the importance of linking observations, CRMs, SCMs, and GCMs into a unified framework that continues to guide atmospheric science today. For those of us fortunate enough to work with him, his greatest legacy is not only the ideas he created, but also the generations of scientists he inspired to pursue them.

486998.title: Tracking FY25 Transitions of NOAA’s Innovative Research and Development into Use
486998.authors: Fiona M. Horsfall, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and K. Geddes and A. Bukvich
486998.abstract: NOAA is focused on ensuring the transition of its research and development (R&D) into use for the benefit of the American public. Annual reporting helps NOAA track its investment in cutting edge science and technology to ensure effective use of federal funding. The NOAA Line Office Transition Managers Committee (LOTMC) is comprised of senior leaders from across NOAA and is focused on the transition of R&D into use to achieve the NOAA mission and benefit society. The LOTMC reports to the NOAA Science Council on the transition of NOAA R&D into operations (R2O), commercialization (R2C), applications (R2A), and other uses (R2X). The LOTMC is responsible for developing NOAA’s Annual Transition Report that describes R&D projects across NOAA that have successfully transitioned to their intended end use. This presentation offers an overview of the Fiscal Year (FY) 2025 Annual Transition Report, including an analysis of R&D transitions across the agency and highlights of select projects that demonstrate the successful transition of research. The report details 253 unique R&D transitions from across NOAA’s line offices, showcasing how scientific discoveries and technological innovations are put into use to improve forecasts, provide information on drought conditions, monitor endangered species, enhance emergency preparedness, and much more. The report also features key success stories that demonstrate the real-world impact of these transitions. Examples include NOAA’s First AI-Powered Regional Forecast Model - HRRR-Cast, the Aleutian Islands Pacific cod stock assessment, the compact coronagraph-1 (CCOR-1) solar imager on the GOES-19 satellite, and advancements in Rice’s whale monitoring. These initiatives underscore NOAA's commitment to maximizing the impact of its research investments in order to complete its mission, protect tax payer investment in research dollars, and benefit the American public.

486999.title: Integrating User and Product Intelligence to Improve User Support and NESDIS Decision-Making.Customer Relationship Management (CRM) and Enterprise Knowledge Base
486999.authors: Thanh Vo, NOAA/NESDIS/SAE Affiliate and STC, Inc., Silver Spring, MD; and R. I. Lana, J. Jankot, J. D. Taylor, and M. Yapur
486999.abstract: How can every customer interaction become actionable intelligence? How can user support requests, feedback, and evolving needs be connected with product knowledge to improve customer support, product awareness, and future product development? As NESDIS serves diverse users and stakeholders through real-time operational support, it must also continuously improve its products and services while making the most effective use of limited resources. Achieving both goals requires systematically capturing user interactions, needs, and feedback, transforming them into enterprise knowledge that informs customer support, product improvements, communication strategies, and management decisions. To address this challenge, NESDIS is piloting an enterprise Customer Relationship Management (CRM) platform integrated with an enterprise knowledge base that connects user interactions, support history, customer needs, and product information within a single operational environment. By synchronizing user intelligence with product intelligence, the platform enables faster, more consistent customer support, improves product discovery and user awareness, identifies unmet needs, and transforms user interactions into actionable knowledge for product and service improvements, resource planning, and evidence-based decision-making across NESDIS. This presentation describes the pilot architecture and lessons learned in synchronizing user intelligence with product intelligence to support customer service, AI-assisted knowledge retrieval, product communication, service improvement, and evidence-based management decisions. The pilot demonstrates how CRM and an enterprise knowledge base can evolve from operational support tools into strategic capabilities that continuously connect users, products, and organizational decision-making.

487015.title: Developing Scientific Literacy through Meteorology: Integrating Statistical and Probabilistic Thinking
487015.authors: Yukimasa Tsubota, J. F. Oberlin University, Machida-shi, Tokyo, Japan
487015.abstract: Earth system science (ESS), originally advanced by NASA in the 1980s, has evolved into an interdisciplinary framework integrating global observations, numerical modeling, and interactions among the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, geosphere, and human activities. As scientific understanding has advanced, the emphasis has expanded from describing individual phenomena to understanding complex systems, uncertainty, and future projections. These developments require students not only to understand scientific mechanisms but also to interpret data, models, probability, and uncertainty. Meteorology has undergone a similar transformation. Weather forecasting has progressed from deterministic prediction based on individual numerical weather prediction models toward probabilistic forecasting using ensemble prediction systems. Climate research likewise relies increasingly on ensembles and probability distributions to evaluate possible future conditions and extreme events. Modern meteorology therefore provides an especially appropriate context for developing both statistical and probabilistic thinking. Despite these scientific advances, weather and climate are still frequently taught using conventional instructional approaches. Students learn physical mechanisms and scientific facts but have fewer opportunities to examine how uncertainty arises, evaluate probability distributions, compare multiple predictions, or use probabilistic information in decision making. As society increasingly depends on forecasts of weather, climate, and natural hazards, these abilities are becoming essential components of scientific literacy. For more than four decades, we have continuously developed meteorology-based learning modules in response to advances in meteorological science and educational technology. The curriculum initially emphasized weather observations, data analysis, and simple hands-on experiments using everyday materials. It subsequently expanded to include numerical weather prediction, climate change, Earth system science, computational modeling, statistical analysis, and AI-supported learning environments. Throughout these developments, however, the central educational objective has remained unchanged: enabling students to think scientifically by interpreting evidence, constructing and evaluating models, and recognizing the limitations of scientific information rather than simply memorizing conclusions. Recent learning modules explicitly connect statistical analysis with probabilistic reasoning in both Earth system science and meteorology. In one Earth system science laboratory, measurements of radioactive decay introduce stochastic processes in which individual events cannot be predicted, while repeated observations under controlled experimental conditions reveal statistically stable probability distributions. Meteorological observations provide a complementary and more complex example in which the underlying probability distribution itself may change over time. Using long-term daily temperature records from Yokohama, Japan (1901–2025), students construct relative-frequency distributions of summer daily minimum, mean, and maximum temperatures using 30-year moving windows at 10-year intervals (1901–1930, 1911–1940, ..., 1991–2020). The 30-year windows provide climatological reference periods while allowing students to examine how the distributions themselves change through time. The analysis shows a clear shift toward higher temperatures, whereas the standard deviations remain comparatively stable. Students can then compare observed distributions with theoretical probability models, calculate threshold-exceedance probabilities, and examine whether a probability model derived from one climatic period remains applicable to another. This progression introduces an important concept often hidden in elementary applications of probability: the probability distribution itself need not be stationary. A stochastic process such as radioactive decay can be investigated under approximately stationary experimental conditions, whereas meteorological observations occur within a changing climate system. Thus, students move beyond simply fitting a probability distribution to data and begin asking whether the assumptions underlying that distribution are physically and temporally appropriate. Extreme temperatures, heavy rainfall, and other weather hazards further provide opportunities to examine return periods, exceedance probabilities, and the limitations of extrapolating simple statistical models to rare events. Weather forecasting activities extend probabilistic thinking from observations to prediction. Students compare forecasts produced by different numerical weather prediction models and operational forecasting agencies, quantitatively evaluate forecast performance, and discuss why forecasts differ. Rather than searching for a single “correct” forecast, they learn to interpret multiple possible outcomes and evaluate the reliability of predictions. Climate projections extend the same reasoning to longer time scales through ensemble simulations and uncertainty in future climate conditions. These learning experiences suggest a distinction between two complementary perspectives in science education. Statistical thinking enables students to organize observations, identify patterns, characterize variability, and understand past and present conditions. Probabilistic thinking enables them to reason from distributions, evaluate uncertainty, assess the likelihood of future events, and make informed decisions under uncertainty. Meteorology integrates these perspectives particularly well because it is simultaneously an observational, experimental, modeling, and predictive science. We therefore propose that meteorology provides an ideal context for developing probabilistic thinking as a core component of scientific literacy in Earth system science education. In an era in which artificial intelligence can instantly generate forecasts, climate information, statistical analyses, and scientific explanations, scientific literacy requires more than obtaining answers. Students must be able to evaluate assumptions, interpret uncertainty, recognize the limitations of models, compare multiple sources of evidence, and make rational decisions based on probabilistic scientific information.

487024.title: Tropical Cyclone Compound Hazard Modeling for Building-Level Economic Losses in Coastal North Carolina
487024.authors: Jiahang He, Boston University, Boston, MA; and J. Parker, B. O. Blanton, C. Szpilka, D. Liu, K. M. Dresback, R. L. Kolar, B. A. Colle, L. Nozick, and I. S. Wing
487024.abstract: Tropical cyclones threaten coastal regions through multiple co-occurring hazards; however, risk assessments typically model these hazards individually and do not include building-level losses. To better prepare populations at risk and develop appropriate mitigation strategies, accurate estimation of regional hazard exposure is essential. Our approach generates a statistically robust dataset of TC hazards for North Carolina (NC) by integrating statistical and numerical models to simulate 1,000 years of combined wind, rainfall-induced fluvial flooding, and coastal storm surge at 250-m grid spacing, with outputs translated directly to building damage estimates for 575,453 single-family homes ($443 billion in value). Our hazard modeling framework uses synthetic TC tracks from the Tropical Cyclone Wind and Impact Simulation Environment (TCWiSE) and wind fields computed by the Generalized Asymmetric Holland Model (GAHM). TC track parameters are used by the Precipitation-Climatology and Persistence (P-CLIPER) rainfall model to generate spatial rainfall distributions that drive the Ensemble Framework for Flash Flood Forecasting (EF5). Finally, storm surge and waves are simulated with the ADvanced CIRCulation (ADCIRC) and Simulating WAves Nearshore (SWAN) models, forced by GAHM wind fields and boundary conditions from EF5. The integrated framework yields wind, rainfall, fluvial inundation, and surge footprints for each of 604 synthetic events across the 1,000-year record, resolved on a 3.84-million-cell grid spanning Eastern NC. The results of our simulations span and exceed the historical range, reaching 89 m/s peak 10-m open-terrain wind and 784 mm accumulated precipitation across the 604-event catalog. By decomposing each hazard's footprint from its severity at the building-storm level, the framework reveals that wind reaches 62.9% of homes but is mild per event (5.1% mean loss ratio), while compound wind-surge-flood events are rare in the ensemble record (0.19% of building-storm pairs) yet considerably more severe, contributing 9.4% of total losses. Results and challenges from the development of this framework will be presented as well as implications for regional insurance portfolios.

487025.title: Actionable Aviation Radiation Information During Space Weather Events: A Data-Driven Model
487025.authors: Janet Green, TDL, Golden, CO; and K. Lee, T. P. O'Brien III, A. J. Boyd, H. M. Bain, and S. J. Watson
487025.abstract: The goal of this work is to more accurately define radiation hazards to aviation caused by space weather and create an application that delivers actionable information to airline industry users. We achieve this by incorporating real-time measurements from the Responsive Environmental Assessment Commercial Hosting (REACH) system, a network of radiation-monitoring dosimeters deployed on a low-altitude satellite constellation. By combining measurements from multiple satellites, we generate global maps showing high radiation regions during space weather events. While Earth's atmosphere absorbs most of this radiation (reducing it to negligible levels at ground level), it remains a potential health risk at airline cruising altitudes. Flight crews and frequent flyers may be exposed to multiple events over time, accumulating significant radiation doses. To address this hazard, the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) - guided by the FAA's CARI-7 model— issues advisories specifying the intensity and geographic regions where radiation levels are expected to be elevated. Airlines use this information to divert flights to lower altitudes or latitudes, reducing passenger and crew exposure. Currently, the predicted radiation hazard zones are based on a statistical compilation of historical measurements. This statistical model does not always capture actual event variations which can lead to unnecessary flight diversions or unnecessary radiation exposure. We present our progress toward developing a method and application that defines high-radiation regions based on real-time REACH data rather than maps derived from historical statistics. Our new data-driven model shows improved accuracy and reduces the uncertainty in the location of high-radiation regions by a factor of two. We compare accumulated radiation dose along common flight paths to identify the routes most affected. The comparison demonstrates that small errors in radiation locations can significantly alter accumulated dose on certain routes, highlighting the need for improved accuracy. Finally, we describe our efforts to advance this application to a higher Technology Readiness Level and collaborate with users to meet their operational needs.

487027.title: Aircraft-Based Evaluation and Emission Optimization for NOAA Air Quality Forecasting Systems
487027.authors: Youhua Tang, George Mason Univ., College Park, MD; and P. C. Campbell, W. Li, X. Ren, B. D. Baker II, F. Yang, K. Wang, J. Huang, E. Waxman, A. Rollins, M. M. Coggon, K. Bates, C. Warneke, L. Xu, K. Zuraski, W. S. Chace, S. S. Brown, C. Womack, G. Novak, P. R. Veres, C. Stockwell, J. He, R. H. Schwantes, B. C. McDonald, and Y. Jung
487027.abstract: We used aircraft-based atmospheric composition observations from recent field campaigns, including FIREX-AQ, AEROMMA, and MAGEQ, to evaluate and improve chemical transport models (CTMs). The spatial and temporal resolutions of current global and regional CTMs are often insufficient to resolve fine-scale atmospheric features, particularly over urban areas. This limitation can affect the representation of atmospheric chemistry, leading to systematic biases such as underestimation of the NOₓ lifetime and overestimation of the conversion of NOₓ to NOz. Another major source of uncertainty is the meteorological forecast used to drive the CTM, which strongly influences simulated pollutant transport patterns, especially for narrow plumes transported over long distances. Despite these limitations, comparisons between CTM simulations and aircraft observations remain highly valuable because aircraft measurements provide comprehensive four-dimensional (three-dimensional space plus time) observations using some of the most reliable atmospheric composition measurements available. These datasets also serve as benchmark observations for a variety of applications, including satellite retrieval calibration and validation, model evaluation, and emission estimation using mass balance methods. Based on comparisons with aircraft observations, we derived regional emission adjustment factors for primary emitted species across the contiguous United States (CONUS), including CO and hydrocarbons. Applying these emission adjustments improved the agreement between CTM simulations and both aircraft observations and surface Air Quality System (AQS) measurements, demonstrating the value of aircraft observations for constraining emission inventories and enhancing regional air quality simulations.

487035.title: Creation and Analysis of a Comprehensive Tornado Duration Dataset
487035.authors: Matthew D. Flournoy, NSSL, Norman, OK; and A. W. Lyza, C. Nixon, T. Sandmael, and E. Bentley
487035.abstract: Numerous studies have used the U.S. tornado record to better understand the meteorological and societal threats posed by tornadoes. Of the various recorded tornado characteristics, many studies focus on damage-based intensity and path length. These are the most societally relevant characteristics, as tornadoes that are stronger and cover more area pose a greater threat to life and property. Between path length and tornado duration, the latter is the more meteorologically relevant characteristic, as duration is only a function of the atmospheric processes supporting prolonged vortex maintenance (while path length is also influenced by storm motion). Fewer studies have focused on duration, and those used a small subset of the tornado record rather than a comprehensive timeframe. This work carries tornado segment start and end times from the NCEI Storm Events Database through a workflow involving automated segment splicing (Storm Prediction Center’s “OneTor” process) and manual quality control. The result is a comprehensive U.S. tornado dataset from 1995–2024 that includes the duration of each tornado, expanding upon a recent OneTor update in spring 2026 that includes tornado end times from 2007 onwards. We present aspects of a U.S. tornado duration climatology, including diurnal, seasonal, and regional patterns. We also examine general environmental characteristics of shorter- vs. longer-duration tornadoes to parse any meaningful differences that could be relevant for forecasting or mesoscale process understanding.

487036.title: Observing and Modeling Cloud Microphysics in Tropical Cyclone Stratiform Regions
487036.authors: Xuejin Zhang, AOML, Miami, FL; and X. Yang, P. Tan, J. A. Zhang, Z. Zhang, R. Sun, and L. M. Harris
487036.abstract: Microphysical processes are critical drivers of tropical cyclone intensity change through their associated latent heating/cooling effects and precipitation processes. These processes play an important role in the interactions between dynamics and physics in weather prediction models. However, accurately modeling complex microphysics processes remains a significant challenge in numerical weather prediction models. Currently, two primary approaches exist in modeling microphysical processes. Spectral bin microphysics schemes that directly compute concentration numbers and particle size distributions (PSDs) of hydrometeors based on explicit microphysical equations are typically employed for studying individual microphysical processes in research models. Bulk microphysics schemes represent the collective effects of microphysical processes using fixed PSDs and predicted hydrometeor quantities and are widely used in operational models. While spectral bin schemes provide a detailed representation of individual microphysical processes, they are computationally intensive. Conversely, bulk schemes are more computationally efficient and represent the aggregate thermodynamic effects of microphysical processes and associated precipitation, and are therefore preferred for operational models. In this study, we focus on bulk microphysics used in operational hurricane prediction models. We first characterize cloud microphysical properties in hurricane environments using observations from NOAA's Hurricane Field Program and other recent airborne cloud field campaigns. We then simulate tropical cyclone evolution and precipitation using the GFDL bulk microphysics scheme version 3 (GFDL MP v3) within the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS). Sensitivity tests are also conducted by varying particle size distribution parameters across multiple hydrometeor categories, guided by in-situ observations. We demonstrate how observation-informed adjustments derived from these sensitivity tests improve the simulation of heating/cooling profiles and precipitation in HAFS. Finally, we propose modifications to the GFDL MP v3 scheme based on robust evaluation and validation metrics, with the goal of improving forecasts of tropical cyclone rapid intensification and precipitation. The results also highlight the importance of accurately representing stratiform cloud microphysics and associated diabatic heating and cooling in simulations of tropical cyclone structure and intensity evolution.

487048.title: Practical Strategies for Initialization of the Seasonal Forecast System
487048.authors: Philip Pegion, NOAA, BOULDER, CO; NOAA/PSL, Boulder, CO; and S. Sun, N. Barton, W. Wang, and F. Yang
487048.abstract: Due to model errors and small signals at timescales beyond weather, a set of retrospective forecasts (re-forecasts) are necessary to bias-correct and calibrate the raw model output in order to make forecasts useful. Due to model errors and small signals at timescales beyond weather, a set of retrospective forecasts (re-forecasts) are necessary to bias-correct and calibrate the raw model output in order to make forecasts usefulHowever, producing a 30-to-40-year reanalysis is time-consuming (at least a year) and often requires reduced resolution compared to the operational system. Some existing systems, like CFSv2 and SEAS5, address this by extending the reanalysis in real time, although CFSv2’s realtime initialization is not identical to the re-forecast period. NOAA, however, is transitioning to a single, high-resolution operational analysis for initializing all global applications, from medium-range to seasonal. This change, coupled with an accelerated implementation schedule for a new Seasonal Forecast System (SFS) that needs to become operational before the required reanalysis is complete, necessitates alternative initialization strategies. We are currently evaluating options such as using existing reanalyses and employing "replay" where the forecast model is nudged toward an existing reanalysis to emulate it, which improves consistency between the initial state and the forecast model. Our work will compare these methods' impact on skill assessment and systematic bias estimation for forecasts initialized with the high-resolution, operational GFS analysis. Additionally, we will investigate replaying the SFS model to the high-resolution analysis as a means to reduce initialization shock and minimize the discrepancy between re-forecasts and real-time forecasts.

487049.title: NOAA’s Next-generation Prediction System for Daily High Tide Flooding Risks on Subseasonal to Annual Timescales
487049.authors: John R. Albers, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and M. Newman, P. Hovenga, T. Xu, W. Sweet, J. A. Callahan, and K. Kavanaugh
487049.abstract: Currently, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s National Ocean Service (NOAA/NOS) makes extended range predictions of the daily risks of high tide flooding (HTF), for forecast leads of up to one year, monthly at 98 tide gauge locations along the US coastline. NOAA/NOS predicts the daily probability of exceedance of hourly water levels above a specified flood threshold by combining the tide prediction with the (extrapolated) linear trend of mean sea level and a probabilistic prediction of the anomalous hourly non-tidal residual (NTR). While these forecasts leverage our ability to predict tides, they do not take advantage of state-of-the-art seasonal climate forecast models, which are becoming more skillful in predicting sea level anomalies in some regions and for some seasons, and assume Gaussian water level distributions. In this presentation, we introduce an updated version of the NOAA/NOS HTF prediction system developed for operational use, which for the first time includes prediction of both the tide and the climate anomaly. It has three key improvements: (1) the monthly mean NTR anomaly is taken from operational seasonal climate forecast models (the North American Multi-Model Ensemble; NMME), with prediction uncertainty represented by the forecast ensemble spread; (2) the PDF of hourly NTR anomalies is non-Gaussian and determined separately for each month from past observations using a “stochastically-generated skewed” (SGS) distribution, which captures the observed seasonal evolution of the skewed and heavy-tailed NTR distributions; and (3) the determination of daily risk of exceeding high tide flooding threshold is computed directly, rather than approximated, from large ensembles of predicted hourly still water level anomalies. Skill of the updated version is compared to the original version at all tide gauge locations, using out-of-sample (cross-validated) probabilistic metrics appropriate for extreme values, and the impact of each of the improvements on skill is diagnosed.

487054.title: Cloud and Convective Characterization of Optical Lightning Measurements from the 2017 GOES-R Post Launch Test Field Campaign
487054.authors: Sarah M. Stough, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and K. R. Wheeler, T. D. Walker, and M. Quick
487054.abstract: Lightning information has shown utility as a diagnostic of thunderstorm intensity due to the intrinsic connections between thunderstorm kinematics, microphysics, and electrification. Many of these relationships were identified over decades of insights gained from Lightning Mapping Array (LMA) research, from which correspondence between updraft intensification and increases in lightning flash frequency as well as decreases in lightning flash size has been shown. Ground-based LMA networks detect total lightning radio emission and enable high-fidelity lightning flash reconstruction within an approximate 100-km range. Satellite-borne optical lightning instruments enable more widespread lightning detection, but capture different elements of the flash process and at different temporal and spatial sampling resolutions. These differences limit direct application of lightning-convection relationships learned using ground-based lightning radio emissions to spaceborne optical lightning measurements. In 2017, the GOES-R Post Launch Test field campaign was conducted to validate the recent launch of the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) and Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM). During the campaign, a rich collection of airborne lightning and cloud measurements was collected from the high-altitude ER-2 aircraft in concert with complementary ground-based lightning and Doppler radar observations from a variety of regions and convective modes. The airborne Fly’s Eye GLM Simulator (FEGS), designed to calibrate and validate the GLM, offers uniquely detailed multispectral optical measurements of lightning. During the campaign, six flights captured coincident lightning measurements from the FEGS and regional Lightning Mapping Arrays (LMAs) over a range of convective modes. FEGS optical lightning data from these flights are characterized using information from matched lightning flashes detected by LMAs, enabling links between optical energy and LMA-inferred attributes such as lightning flash size and altitude. They are then further contextualized using cloud depth inferred from the airborne Cloud Physics Lidar as well as precipitation type and ice water content retrieved from ground-based polarimetric Doppler radars. These data are used to inform how optical measurements of lightning vary with cloud and convective context to improve the use of optical lightning data for the diagnosis of deep convection.

487057.title: The Evolution of NSF NCAR Dropsonde Technology in the GPS Era
487057.authors: Terry Hock, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and H. Vömel and M. Goodstein
487057.abstract: The NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) Earth Observing Laboratory (EOL) has developed dropsonde technology for nearly six decades, serving as a key leader in advancing airborne atmospheric profiling across an ever-changing landscape of research aircraft and balloon platforms. This presentation focuses on the most significant transformation in that history: the introduction of GPS technology for high-precision wind measurement in the mid-1990s, and the multiple generations of GPS dropsondes that have evolved since. The Airborne Vertical Atmospheric Profiling System (AVAPS), first fielded in 1996, established the foundation for modern dropsonde observations, delivering high-resolution vertical profiles of pressure, temperature, humidity, and winds from release altitude to the surface. Alongside the sondes themselves, EOL has developed launch systems spanning a wide range of complexity — from simple manual launchers to fully automated, high-capacity systems — deployed on a broad variety of platforms, including uncrewed aircraft. These capabilities support fundamental research across the U.S. and international atmospheric science communities, with AVAPS systems operating on NSF NCAR, NOAA, USAF, NASA, University of Wyoming, DLR, and other research aircraft worldwide. Dropsonde observations also play a key operational role in NOAA and U.S. Air Force Reserve hurricane reconnaissance, where soundings from reconnaissance flights significantly improve hurricane track and landfall forecasts, and in atmospheric river reconnaissance supporting West Coast precipitation forecasting. This presentation will review the evolution of dropsonde and launcher technology, the expansion of system capabilities, and the broad range of national and international research and operational programs supported over the past 30 years.

487058.title: When "Minor" Isn't Minor: Reassessing Coastal Flood Thresholds Using Exposure Metrics
487058.authors: Faezeh Maghsoodifar, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and H. Moftakhari, R. Atkins, J. A. Callahan, J. Carter, C. Zuzak, G. Dusek, D. Marcy, T. Meckley, B. W. Parker, H. Stiller, W. Sweet, and C. Weaver
487058.abstract: Coastal flood thresholds aid hazard communication, preparedness, and adaptation planning. However, a “minor” flood threshold may not represent the same level of probabilistic risk across different coastal environments. This study evaluates minor coastal flood thresholds along the U.S. Gulf and Atlantic coasts across 19 coastal states. Probabilistic flood risk is quantified by integrating coastal water-level probability distributions with exposure-based consequence functions derived from building inventory, population, and depth-damage information. The national analysis compares the exceedance probability of current minor flood thresholds and the share of modeled probabilistic risk occurring below those thresholds. An uncertainty-propagation analysis characterizes the influence of uncertainty in water-level distributions, exposure estimates, depth-damage relationships, and threshold definitions on these risk estimates. Detailed analyses are conducted for six selected coastal urban areas representing contrasting hydrodynamic and exposure settings. Spatial analyses are used to identify statistically significant clusters of elevated risk and locations where a substantial share of modeled risk occurs below the current minor flood threshold. These patterns reveal areas where existing thresholds may not adequately represent local impacts. For case-study areas with suitable historical impact records, candidate threshold adjustments are evaluated using skill-based metrics to determine whether recalibration improves the identification of damaging flood conditions. By linking water-level probability, consequences, uncertainty, spatial patterns, and targeted threshold adjustments, this study evaluates where current minor flood thresholds align with local risk and where they may overlook meaningful consequences for preparedness and coastal resilience planning.

487061.title: On the Use of Millimeter-Wave Radiometry to Study Thunderstorm Electrification
487061.authors: Timothy J. Lang, MSFC, Huntsville, AL
487061.abstract: In the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) era (1997-2015), most spaceborne and airborne passive microwave-based research on thunderstorms focused on W-band and lower frequencies (i.e., < 100 GHz), especially the window channels near 85 GHz and 37 GHz, plus 19 GHz and below if the science target was hailstorms. Meanwhile, higher frequencies like ~183 GHz generally have been used to profile water vapor in the atmosphere rather than to study thunderstorms. However, recent observations have demonstrated that G-band frequencies, even those highly sensitive to water vapor like 183 GHz, provide useful information about thunderstorm electrification, including lightning production, strength of electric fields, and the presence of gamma-ray glows. This presentation will show observations from the Airborne Lightning Observatory for Fly’s Eye Geostationary Lightning Mapper Simulator and Terrestrial Gamma-ray Flashes (ALOFT) campaign, as well as comparisons between the International Space Station Lightning Imaging Sensor (ISS LIS) and spaceborne millimeter-wave radiometers like Temporal Experiment for Storms and Tropical Systems (TEMPEST) and Microwave Humidity Sounder (MHS). The observations show that G-band channels offer advantages over lower frequencies when viewing thunderstorms, including finer spatial resolution, reduced sensitivity to surface emissivity, and excellent response to scattering by millimeter-sized graupel, particularly in the upper levels of the thundercloud. Notably, G-band channels consistently show greater importance compared to lower frequencies in machine-learning algorithms (e.g., random forest) that seek to predict the likelihood of lightning, retrieve electric field strength, or detect gamma-ray glows. The results suggest that future radiometer missions, many of which will lack low-frequency channels, nonetheless will provide scientifically valuable datasets for thunderstorm research.

487070.title: Characterization of Liquid Water Content in Performance Testing of Nephos, a Convection-Cloud Chamber
487070.authors: Thea Elizabeth Spigrelli, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT; and A. Sedlacek, F. Yang, and D. Hillman Girod
487070.abstract: The Environmental Science and Technologies department at Brookhaven National Laboratory has recently built a one cubic meter convection cloud chamber, referred to as Nephos. The chamber creates a repeatable “cloud-in-a-box” that can be used to isolate and investigate key cloud microphysical properties and processes governing cloud optical and precipitation properties under well-controlled laboratory environments. Liquid water content (LWC), which is the mass of cloud droplets per volume of air, is a crucial parameter for determining the potential for precipitation, the radiative properties of a cloud, and its lifetime. One important but still not fully understood question is how LWC responds to increasing aerosol concentration under different environmental conditions. Using Nephos, we ran several experiments to characterize the dependence of LWC on the aerosol injection rate and the sidewall temperature forcings. Aerosol injection rates ranging from approximately 0.2 to 7 particles cm−3 s−1 were explored, while temperatures of the chamber’s six panels were independently controlled between -4 ◦C and 30 ◦C with three panels being heated, and three being cooled. Cloud droplet size distributions were measured using a white light source optical particle counter (Promo 2000; Welas), and aerosol number concentration measurements were obtained using a condensation particle counter (CPC; TSI Inc.). All collected data were analyzed using the Igor Pro analysis program (Wavemetrics) and data from the Welas and CPC were converted into compatible formats. Results show that the cloud chamber produced steady-state clouds over a broad range of LWCs, from approximately 0.05 g/m3 to greater than 1 g/m3. Further, we were able to show that LWC changes with both the aerosol injection rate and side-wall temperature forcing.

487071.title: The NSSL Multimoment Bulk Cloud Microphysics Scheme: What's New?
487071.authors: Edward Mansell, NSSL, Norman, OK; NOAA/National Severe Storms Laboratory, Norman, OK
487071.abstract: The National Severe Storms Lab bulk cloud microphysics scheme (NSSL-MP) is a research-oriented code geared toward deep (and severe) convection but with sufficient computational efficiency to be feasible for real-time applications (e.g., Warn-on-Forecast System). It can currently be run fully two-moment (2M), or partially three-moment (3M) mode. 3M adds the reflectivity moment for rain, graupel, and hail, which allows prediction of the size distribution function shape parameter and improved size sorting. Key features include a (large) hail species and pseudo-3-moment treatment of 2M sedimentation that adaptively prevents excessive size sorting. Bulk particle densities of graupel and hail are also predicted, allowing the graupel category to represent initiation by freezing drops (high density) or rimed ice (low density), as well as evolve over time through dry and wet growth or melting. The hail category is not defined by density but rather is initiated by conversion of large graupel in wet growth, enabling substantial hail shaft radar reflectivities and appreciable surface hail accumulations that are difficult to achieve with a single rimed species. This presentation will give an overview of key features and recent updates. The hail conversion uses a new option to convert the tail of the graupel distribution in more robust manner and avoid spurious generation of reflectivity. Similar reflectivity conservation is also applied to freezing of large rain drops. Wet and dry growth can be allowed to occur simultaneously over the large/small ranges of the graupel and hail size distributions (delineated by the wet growth diameter), leading generally to more ice mass and potential hail accumulation. Three-moment rain has a new diameter-independent active breakup scheme based on spectral bin results, which helps correct a warm bias in cold pools in 3M simulations. Other work includes tracking the depletion of ice nuclei and an option to include a separate dust ice nuclei category. The CR-SIM dual-polarimetric radar emulator now includes support for NSSL 2M/3M for WRF and CM1.

487079.title: All-Sky Assimilation of GOES ABI Infrared Water Vapor Channels in MPAS-JEDI and Its Impact on Numerical Simulations of Hurricanes
487079.authors: Chengfeng Feng, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and Z. Pu
487079.abstract: Our previous studies (Feng and Pu 2022, 2025) investigated the all-sky assimilation of GOES-16 infrared water vapor channels using WRF with the WSM6 microphysics scheme and the NCEP GSI-based 3D ensemble-variational hybrid data assimilation (DA) system. We found nonlinear conditional biases in the all-sky scaled observation-minus-background (OmB) departures with respect to the symmetric cloud proxy variable, along with increased interchannel correlations under cloudy-sky conditions. We alleviated the nonlinear conditional biases by adding a quartic polynomial of cloud predictors to the variational bias correction (VarBC) and reduced the interchannel correlations through channel selection. This study revisits the characteristics of these cloud-dependent nonlinear biases and interchannel correlations when assimilating all-sky brightness temperatures (BTs) from GOES ABI infrared water vapor channels within the MPAS-JEDI framework. MPAS-A, the atmospheric forecast model, employs the "convection_permitting" physics suite with the Thompson microphysics scheme, and the forecast domain is transformed and trimmed from the 15–3 km global mesh to enable convection-permitting simulation. The JEDI 4DEnVar system uses a purely flow-dependent background error covariance derived from 60-member ensemble forecasts. Hurricane Milton (2024) serves as the test case. Based on newly characterized nonlinear biases and interchannel correlations, we apply and further develop our previous methods to address these problems in MPAS-JEDI. The impact of all-sky GOES ABI DA on numerical simulations of Hurricane Milton (2024) is evaluated. Further developments include the implementation of machine learning–based bias correction methods and a reevaluation of channel selection strategies. Additional case studies are also being conducted using GOES-U observations.

487084.title: How Has Phased-Array Radar Advanced Our Understanding of Storm-Scale Meteorology?
487084.authors: A. Addison Alford, NOAA/OAR/NSSL, Norman, OK; and C. M. Kuster, K. Tuftedal, E. Blumenauer, W. M. Phipps, E. Morrow, M. Marker, A. E. Reinhart, T. J. Schuur, J. C. Snyder, J. T. Carlin, B. Smith, C. G. Berry, Student, and J. B. Boettcher
487084.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration National Severe Storms Laboratory (NOAA NSSL) has been a leader in the development of phased-array radar (PAR) technology for weather applications. A primary tool NSSL has employed in the past decade has been the Advanced Technology Demonstrator (ATD) PAR, which is a full-scale, S-band, dual-polarization system. The advances in PAR technology and applications afforded by the ATD include progress in dual-polarization calibration of a planar PAR, advancements in beamforming techniques, and the development of flexible and adaptive scanning concepts. These technical achievements have resulted in more than 500 hours of meteorological data collected by the ATD to date. Using these data, the NSSL PAR Program has explored both operational and basic research concepts. This presentation focuses on the latter by reviewing key efforts to leverage ATD datasets to advance storm-scale science with an emphasis on potential research-to-knowledge transition pathways. To focus this presentation, we will overview recent progress in using rapid-update polarimetric information to observe mid- and upper-level precursors to surface hazards including tornadoes, severe winds, and extreme precipitation. In particular, we will show that precipitation loading, melting, and evaporation processes are likely attendant to local downdrafts that influence the near-surface kinematic fields in the vicinity of and prior to surface hazards. Across different storm modes and hazard types, the relative importance of the aforementioned precipitation processes will be discussed. Finally, we will briefly discuss how the results of this PAR-based study may be applied to concepts of operations afforded by both current and potential future radar systems.

487086.title: Integrating a Multilayer Perceptron into Variational Bias Correction for Data Assimilation
487086.authors: Chengfeng Feng, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and Z. Pu
487086.abstract: Biased observations can lead to inaccurate outcomes in both data-driven weather forecasting models and data assimilation (DA). A critical pillar of satellite DA is variational bias correction (VarBC), which adaptively corrects systematic observation biases through a linear combination of bias-correction (BC) coefficients and predictors embedded within a variational DA system. However, this linear formulation may be inadequate for the more complex biases associated with clouds, precipitation, and surface characteristics that arise across different time scales in all-sky, all-surface satellite DA. One promising way to advance VarBC is to incorporate a neural network (NN). This study first establishes the feasibility of such an approach by theoretically proving the equivalence between the offline version of VarBC and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with L2 regularization. We then describe how to implement an MLP into VarBC (VarBC-MLP), addressing how to initialize the BC coefficients, update their error covariance, and compute the MLP Jacobian. Finally, we compare the performance of traditional VarBC and VarBC-MLP in correcting (1) polynomial position biases under an identity forward model, and (2) scan-angle and air-mass biases under an idealized radiative transfer model mimicking the GOES water vapor channels. The Lorenz-96 model, 3DVAR, and an ensemble of DA are employed for these experiments. Success of this method would imply that neural networks and data assimilation can be unified within a single gradient-descent framework, enabling more flexible neural networks to handle the complicated observation biases encountered in all-sky, all-surface satellite DA.

487088.title: Retrieving the Maximum Winds in Tornadoes from Weather Radar
487088.authors: A. Addison Alford, NOAA/OAR/NSSL, Norman, OK; and A. W. Lyza, M. D. Flournoy, and J. C. Snyder
487088.abstract: Using mobile and fixed weather radars to observe the wind fields in tornadoes remains a challenge. Poor road networks and local terrain make siting a radar near a tornado difficult, which can preclude low level wind field measurements. When a radar is located favorably near a tornado, the measurements obtained are often complicated by the tornado translation relative to the radar viewing angle and the size of the radar gate relative to the vortex. Notwithstanding other uncertainties in radar measurements, tornado translation and radar gate size may be accounted for via several potential historical methods. This presentation reviews the existing methods to account for 1) tornado translation relative to the radar viewing angle and ultimately retrieve an estimate of the maximum, ground-relative wind and 2) methods to correct for the averaging effects related to the radar beam size across a tornadic vortex. We will present a new, comprehensive methodology by which the maximum winds in tornadoes may be retrieved from radar measurements, accounting for translation relative to the radar viewing angle and radar gate size relative to the vortex. We will also review how the methodology may be related to other damage-based and engineering-based techniques of post-event tornado surveys, including a way to standardize retrieved radar-based wind measurements.

487091.title: Evaluation of GFDL and Thompson Bulk Microphysics Schemes in HAFS Tropical Cyclone Forecasts
487091.authors: Peisen Tan, Mississippi State University, MIAMI, FL; and X. Zhang and A. E. Mercer
487091.abstract: Cloud microphysics parameterizations strongly influence precipitation processes, latent heating, and storm structure in numerical weather prediction models. Although operational bulk microphysics schemes have demonstrated differing forecast performance in tropical cyclone prediction, the physical mechanisms responsible for these differences remain poorly understood. In particular, it is unclear how differences in the representation of hydrometeor populations and microphysical process rates propagate to storm structure, precipitation evolution, and forecast skill. Improving this process-level understanding is essential for advancing operational hurricane prediction while maintaining the computational efficiency required for real-time forecasting. In this study, we investigate the physical differences between the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL) and Thompson bulk microphysics parameterizations implemented within NOAA's Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) using retrospective simulations of multiple Atlantic tropical cyclones. The objective is not only to quantify differences in forecast performance, but also to identify the microphysical processes responsible for those differences. The two schemes are evaluated with respect to tropical cyclone track and intensity forecasts, precipitation structure, and the three-dimensional evolution of hydrometeor fields, including rainwater, cloud water, snow, graupel, and cloud ice. Differences in the spatial organization and temporal evolution of these hydrometeors are analyzed to diagnose how each parameterization modifies precipitation production, latent heating, eyewall structure, rainband evolution, and overall storm organization throughout the forecast. Model simulations are evaluated against available operational analyses and satellite- and radar-based observations where applicable. To further investigate the physical drivers of forecast differences, machine learning techniques are employed to identify the relative importance of microphysical variables associated with variations in storm intensity, precipitation distribution, and forecast skill. Feature-importance analyses provide a quantitative framework for linking parameterized microphysical processes to model performance and identifying which hydrometeor characteristics contribute most strongly to differences between the two schemes. Our preliminary results reveal systematic differences in the representation and evolution of tropical cyclone microphysics between the GFDL and Thompson parameterizations, leading to distinct storm structures and forecast behavior. By connecting forecast performance to the underlying physical processes represented within each scheme, this study provides new insight into why operational bulk microphysics parameterizations produce different tropical cyclone forecasts. The results contribute to improving cloud microphysics representation in HAFS and demonstrate how data-driven diagnostics can complement traditional model evaluation to guide future development of tropical cyclone microphysics parameterizations.

487093.title: The NSSL Hailcam: How Do Direct Observations of Falling Hail Compare Against Post-Impact Observations?
487093.authors: Sean M. Waugh, NOAA, Norman, OK; and J. Segall
487093.abstract: The NSSL HailCam system has been deployed in two field seasons thus far, collecting unprecedented observations of falling hail across a variety of storms, ranging in severity, storm mode, and geographical region. To date, over 8.2 TB of image data have been collected, with 9.6 million images covering 8.1 hrs of hail fall. With this data, direct in-situ observations of falling hail size, shape, and velocity have been collected. Broad results from these deployments will be explored, comparing observed hailstone size and distributions against reported observations to document and highlight limitations of traditional observing methods. Unique hailstones will be presented to illuminate the natural variability of real hailstones against the often assumed spherical shape. Finally, comparisons against radar observations concurrent with these deployments will be made to highlight potential limitations in current radar based hail detections.

487094.title: Near-Surface Turbulence Regime Evaluation over the Arctic Tundra
487094.authors: Benjamin Parker Harrison, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and Y. Pan and J. D. Fuentes
487094.abstract: Recent observations indicate that the Arctic has warmed about four times faster than the global average over recent decades. This accelerated warming highlights the need for a better understanding of air-surface interactions that regulate the exchange of momentum, heat, moisture, and trace gases between the surface and the atmosphere. Previous studies have shown that near-surface turbulence in the stable Arctic boundary layer can be classified into three regimes: fully turbulent, transitional, and intermittent. The objective of this study is to examine previously proposed turbulence regimes and the associated classification metrics using a new flux-tower dataset collected during March–April 2022 in Utqiagvik, Alaska. The dataset includes 50-Hz sonic-anemometer measurements at five heights, 1-Hz air temperature and relative humidity measurements at seven heights, and 1-Hz radiative fluxes at one height. After data quality checking, we use an advanced stationarity analysis technique to limit subsequent turbulence-regime classification to periods with statistically stationary mean flows across all measurement heights. For each stationary period, two previously proposed classification metrics are examined: one describing the intensity of weak turbulent motions and the other quantifying the temporal variability of turbulent activity. Results suggest that the turbulence-intensity metric does not consistently distinguish among the visually identified turbulence regimes, implying that it may not be a robust indicator of turbulence state under Arctic stable conditions. In contrast, the metric describing the temporal variability of turbulent activity behaves reasonably, but by itself, does not uniquely identify the different regimes. Modifying or replacing the turbulence-intensity metric will allow for improved regime classification, and thus better representation of turbulent transport and air-surface exchanges in Arctic weather and climate models.

487099.title: Near-Surface Turbulence Regimes over the Arctic Tundra
487099.authors: Benjamin Parker Harrison, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and Y. Pan and J. D. Fuentes
487099.abstract: Recent observations indicate the Arctic has warmed about four times faster than the global average over recent decades. This accelerated warming highlights the need for a better understanding of air-surface interactions that regulate the exchange of momentum, heat, moisture, and trace gases between the surface and the atmosphere. Such exchanges strongly influence the structure and evolution of the atmospheric boundary layer, and consequently, weather, climate, and air chemistry. Previous studies have shown that near-surface turbulence in the stable Arctic boundary layer can be classified into three regimes: fully turbulent, transitional, and intermittent. Reliable identification of these regimes is essential for developing and evaluating parameterizations used in numerical weather prediction and climate projection models. The objective of this study is to evaluate previously proposed turbulence-regime classifications and their associated metrics using data collected during March–April 2022 in Utqiagvik, Alaska. We use an advanced technique to obtain periods of statistically stationary mean winds. For each stationary period, two previously proposed classification metrics are examined: one describing the intensity of weak turbulent motions and the other quantifying the temporal variability of turbulent activity. Results suggest that the turbulence-intensity metric does not consistently distinguish among the visually identified turbulence regimes, implying that it may not be a robust indicator of turbulence state under Arctic stable conditions. In contrast, the metric describing the temporal variability of turbulent activity behaves reasonably, but by itself, does not uniquely identify the different regimes. Modifying or replacing the turbulence-intensity metric will allow for improved regime classification, and thus better representation of turbulent transport and air-surface exchanges in Arctic weather and climate models.

487100.title: The Missing Length Scale In the Surface-Layer Similarity Theory for Near-Neutral Atmospheric Flows
487100.authors: Ying Pan, ; and J. P. Horne, D. K. Peng, and K. J. Davis
487100.abstract: Surface-layer similarity theories are an indispensable component of atmospheric models. Recent flux-tower data collected over urban canopies suggest that the Monin-Obukhov similarity theory (MOST) with a roughness-sublayer correction tends to underpredict the eddy viscosity regardless of the static stability conditions. For stable or near-neutral conditions, the same similarity theory either well- or under-predicts the integral time scale. Knowing that eddy viscosity is a product of integral length and velocity scales, while the integral time scale is the ratio of integral length and velocity scales, we detect a potential underestimation of the integral length scale for stable and near-neutral conditions. Such static stability conditions do not support the development of convective circulations, implying that some other unknown mechanisms are responsible for the underestimated integral length scale. The objective of this work is to examine whether such underestimated integral length scale is unique for urban environments or not. Because the roughness-sublayer correction to MOST originates from vegetation canopy studies, we utilize the Canopy Horizontal Array Turbulence Study (CHATS) data collected in a walnut orchard field. The investigation uses pre-determined near-neutral periods with statistically stationary mean winds. Preliminary results suggest that the vertical momentum flux may vary by 25% between the canopy top and the roughness-sublayer top, much larger than a variation within 10% expected for near-surface flows above a canopy. In addition, the temperature measurements involve large temporal-scale variations that are absent from velocity measurements, implying potential passage of airmass of distinct temperatures. Further analyses focus on the causes of the vertical variation of momentum flux and the large temporal-scale variations in temperature, as well as their connections to potentially missing length scales in existing surface-layer similarity theories.

487107.title: From Daytime Shading to Nighttime Trapping: A Mechanism Decomposition of Urban-Tree Thermal Comfort
487107.authors: Sohei Yamada, New York University, Brooklyn, NY; and M. Ghandehari
487107.abstract: That thermal comfort indices such as the Physiologically Equivalent Temperature (PET) and the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) describe human heat load better than air temperature does is well established. The open question is mechanistic: a tree changes radiation, humidity, and wind at once, so which mechanisms actually drive its comfort effect, and how does their balance shift between day and night? Answering this is what turns "trees cool" into guidance on where and when a tree most effectively relieves human heat stress. We decompose the comfort effect of a consolidated 0.5-hectare urban forest in Brooklyn, New York, from a measurement-validated, coupled computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation, attributing it to five additive mechanisms: shortwave shading, longwave trapping, advective air-temperature cooling, the humidity penalty from transpiration, and canopy wind attenuation. From one internally consistent counterfactual—trees present versus all tree effects removed—we reconstruct the mean radiant temperature and compute PET and UTCI on the pedestrian plane (1 m above ground), and track how much each mechanism contributes. At midday, the comfort effect is governed almost entirely by shortwave shading. At the canopy center, UTCI falls by about 3.4 K and mean radiant temperature by about 11.5 K, while air temperature drops only about 0.5 K, so the benefit is large but tightly localized: it decays within roughly 40 to 60 m, whereas the weaker air-temperature cooling extends farther downwind. The humidity added by transpiration slightly offsets the advective cooling. Daytime comfort, in short, is a radiation-and-shading phenomenon, not an air-temperature one, and an assessment based on air temperature alone would overstate the spatial reach of a tree's daytime health benefit. The novel and decision-relevant part is what happens after sunset, and it is exactly what this decomposition is built to resolve. Shortwave shading vanishes at night, leaving longwave trapping and canopy wind attenuation as the active mechanisms, and both can raise, rather than lower, the heat load beneath a canopy. Whether the comfort effect stays cooling, weakens, or reverses at night—and over what radius—is the question we quantify mechanism by mechanism and hour by hour. Because each mechanism is reported separately, the study is informative whichever way the nighttime balance falls, and it shows which lever—shade by day, ventilation at night—a planner should pull at each time. For the heat-and-health community, this yields a physically grounded, street-scale, time-resolved account of when, and by what mechanism, urban trees reduce or fail to reduce human heat stress, moving tree-siting guidance beyond a single daytime cooling number and toward the mechanism that matters at each hour.

487110.title: Storylines of Near-Term Global Tropical Cyclone Activity under Uncertain Radiatively-forced Trend and Decadal Variability
487110.authors: Yi Xia, Columbia university, New York, NY; LDEO, New York, NY; and C. Y. Lee, A. H. Sobel, S. J. Camargo, R. Seager, and K. Reed
487110.abstract: Global Tropical Cyclone (TC) activity is largely modulated by sea surface temperature (SST) variations, which arise from both external radiative forcings and internal variability of the climate system. The future evolution of both drivers, however, remains uncertain, leaving near-term projections of TC activity poorly constrained. The radiatively-forced response of the climate system is inconsistent between observations and climate model simulations, most notably over the eastern equatorial Pacific and the Southern Ocean: observations exhibit cooling trends in both regions, whereas the majority of models in the fifth and sixth Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP5 and CMIP6) simulate warming. In addition, our simulation skill for decadal climate variability remains limited, including for the leading modes of global SST variability—the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation (IPO) and the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO). To address these two sources of uncertainty, we explore storylines for near-term TC activity through 2050 by conducting a set of atmosphere-only global climate model simulations using the Community Atmosphere Model (CAM) at horizontal resolutions of approximately 0.25° and 2°. As each storyline is characterized by a well-defined combination of radiatively-forced trend and decadal climate variability, they provide a physically interpretable framework for assessing future climate risks, including scenarios that may fall outside the spread of current CMIP-type ensembles due to systematic biases in the model's radiatively radiatively-forced response and uncertainty in decadal climate variability. TC activity across storylines is compared using density maps of simulated genesis, track, and Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE), from both global and basin-specific perspectives. Preliminary results show that the model-simulated trend yields more active TC activity along the Northeastern Pacific coast compared to the observationally-extrapolated trend, suggesting that CMIP-type projections may overestimate TC risk in this region if the models are biased in their radiatively-forced trend. Further superimposing these trends with a positive IPO anomaly leads to even more active TCs in this region. To understand what is driving the diverging activity patterns across storylines, the large-scale environmental conditions relevant to TC activity, such as potential intensity and shear, are also examined. Differences in TC-induced precipitation across storylines are further assessed for each ocean basin to characterize potential impacts on adjacent continental regions. Specifically, the best- and worst-case storylines for TC-related risk are identified.

487115.title: Scientific Decisions Underlying Future Projections of Intensity-Duration-Frequency Precipitation Values in NOAA Atlas-15
487115.authors: Kenneth E. Kunkel, North Carolina State Univ., Asheville, NC; and X. Sun, J. Anheuser, D. R. Easterling, L. Sun, and P. Katlana
487115.abstract: NOAA Atlas 15 (NA15), the new precipitation frequency (PF) standard for the nation, is currently under development.. Volume 2 of NA15 will consist of future projections of precipitation Intensity-Duration-Frequency (IDF) values under several scenarios and Global Temperature Index levels. Durations to be included range from 5 minutes to 60 days. Frequencies range from 50% Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP) to 0.1% AEP. The meteorological conditions that cause extreme precipitation events is a function of duration. Short-duration precipitation extremes will be governed primarily by convective cells while long-duration extremes may be determined by persistent long-wave patterns in the atmospheric circulation. We rely on climate models to provide information for future conditions. The spatial resolution, physical representation, and temporal coverage of currently-available climate model datasets varies widely, because of the tradeoff between very computationally-intensive, high spatial resolution models (which limits the number of model years) and lower resolution models, which are often available in large ensembles. We have analyzed a large number of model output sets, including high spatial (convection-permitting) resolution dynamically-downscaled models (CONUS404, Northern Illinois University, NA-CORDEX, EDDEv2), regional statistically-downscaled models (LOCA2, STAR, UWPD, GARD-LENS), and global models of varying resolution (MESACLIP, NOAA SPEAR, NCAR LENS2). We will describe the similarities and differences in these model output sets and their use for making NA15 projections of future precipitation frequency estimates.

487123.title: The Nighttime Heat-Exposure Fallacy: Fixed-Time Satellites Distort Exposure Far More Than Intensity
487123.authors: Sohei Yamada, New York University, Brooklyn, NY; and M. Ghandehari
487123.abstract: Nighttime heat has emerged as a health threat distinct from daytime heat. When temperatures fail to fall at night, the cardiovascular and thermoregulatory systems are denied their recovery, and large epidemiological studies link nighttime warmth to excess mortality even after adjustment for daytime maxima. The physical quantity that best captures this risk is not an instantaneous temperature but a cumulative one, the overnight temperature excess integrated through the night (degree-hours). Assessing this exposure where people actually live requires land surface temperature (LST) at neighborhood scale, but the high-resolution thermal-infrared sensors used for heat-risk mapping—Landsat today, and sun-synchronous missions to come—observe at a fixed, usually mid-morning, time and do not sample the hours that make up the nighttime integral. How badly this fixed-time sampling distorts cumulative nighttime exposure has not been fully quantified; the sampling question has been examined mainly for heat-island intensity, a fundamentally different, instantaneous metric. For six US cities spanning three Köppen climate zones, we build a continuous, 30 m LST reference (oracle) by additively fusing the spatial detail of Landsat with the temporal continuity of geostationary GOES-16, and we validate it against independent ECOSTRESS observations that were held out from training. The oracle agrees with ECOSTRESS to a debiased RMSE of about 1.9 K by day and 1.8 K by night; the near-equality of day and night accuracy confirms that the nighttime diurnal cycle is captured and that the validation is not circular. We then sample this single validated oracle at each satellite's overpass time and, holding everything else fixed, measure how overpass-time sampling distorts two classes of metric: exposure (nighttime degree-hours, an absolute integral tied to health) and intensity (the 95th-minus-5th-percentile spatial contrast, a relative measure of the heat island). The two diverge in kind. The relative error in exposure reaches several hundred percent while the error in intensity stays near 6 percent—a divergence of roughly 13- to 630-fold across cities that persists under the most sophisticated diurnal-cycle reconstruction and across intensity definitions and thresholds. The mechanism is an asymmetry of recovery: a single daytime image preserves the spatial rank of hot and cool pixels, so intensity survives, but it misses the nighttime absolute level by 3 to 5 K, so the exposure integral does not, because nighttime cooling is governed by thermal inertia, humidity, and wind that a daytime image does not carry. This yields a concrete observation-design rule: measuring health-relevant nighttime exposure requires a sample from late afternoon through the deep night, and in none of the six cities studied is the mid-morning overpass optimal. Current high-resolution, morning-overpass sensors such as Landsat and Terra/Aqua overestimate nighttime exposure more than threefold, and this time-sampling error is a mechanism separate from spatial aggregation that higher spatial resolution alone does not fix. Using an established exposure-measurement-error simulation, we further show how the sampling error attenuates the estimated heat-mortality association, turning an observation-design choice into a bias in epidemiological inference. The message for the heat-and-health community is a caution: high-resolution heat-vulnerability assessments built on a single daytime overpass systematically misrepresent the nighttime heat that most endangers health, and next-generation fixed-overpass thermal missions should include a nighttime observation if they are to serve public health.

487132.title: Exploring the Ability of Machine Learning to Infer Subgrid-scale Convective Cloud Fraction from Coarse-Resolution Environmental Conditions
487132.authors: Hungjui Yu, CIRA, FORT COLLINS, CO; and L. Ver Hoef, K. L. Rasmussen, Ph.D., and I. Ebert-Uphoff
487132.abstract: Global climate models (GCMs) typically run at resolutions of ~100 km, capturing large-scale environmental conditions but unable to explicitly resolve convection and cloud processes. While convection-permitting models provide kilometer-scale simulations, their high computational cost limits their application. This study explores machine learning (ML) as a computationally efficient framework for bridging large-scale environmental conditions and subgrid-scale convective proxy. We first train a simple pixel-based multilayer perceptron (MLP) to predict convective cloud fractions from environmental variables derived from convection-permitting simulations. Without explicit spatial or temporal contexts, the model successfully reproduces convective cloud fraction with structural similarity index measure (SSIM) values exceeding 0.8 and capturing realistic diurnal cycles and orographic convection.
