Sensitivity and ablation experiments show that model performance depends on both the diversity of environmental conditions and nonlinear interactions among physical variables, highlighting the importance of multivariate environmental controls on convection. To further investigate these relationships, we apply interpretable machine learning approaches, e.g. Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM), to identify and quantify the important large-scale environmental factors for subgrid-scale cloud proxy. These ML approaches provide complementary capabilities for prediction and physical interpretation. Unlike convolutional neural networks, the proposed pixel-based framework performs value-to-value mapping independently at each grid point, making it largely independent of spatial resolution and grid configuration. These approaches are well suited for diagnosing GCM and reanalysis datasets, enabling cross-model applications and offering a scalable pathway for studying convection across diverse environmental regimes and future climate scenarios.

487137.title: The NOAA NESDIS Commercial Data Program Wildfire Pilot
487137.authors: Gerard Peltzer, NOAA NESDIS, Silver Spring, MD; Science and Technology Corporation, Columbia, MD; and N. Laudier, M. Pavolonis, I. A. Csiszar, and W. Schroeder
487137.abstract: Wildfires pose a significant threat to communities across the United States, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) supports wildfire response efforts by providing crucial fire observations for early fire detection and monitoring of fire intensity and progression. NOAA is seeking to augment its remote sensing fire detection and monitoring capabilities with commercial space-based multispectral capabilities. The NOAA National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) is conducting a Commercial Data Program pilot study to assess the quality and impact of available commercial multispectral imagery, including infrared capabilities, to aid in wildfire detection, monitoring, and mapping. In this presentation, we will discuss the current Wildfire Pilot and provide data assessment and evaluation results to-date, including key findings and lessons learned. We will discuss future plans and the transition to operations path toward commercial data purchases to provide measurements to support NOAA’s current and anticipated operational wildfire mission needs.

487154.title: NOAA's National Ocean Service Core Model Evaluation Plan
487154.authors: Patrick Bernard Burke, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; NOAA, Silver Spring,, MD; and S. Moghimi, E. Myers, J. Xu, A. Zhang, K. E. Bailey, L. bloemendaa, S. B. Smith, J. Peth, H. Spencer, and W. Tyburczy
487154.abstract: NOAA's National Ocean Service (NOS) currently employs a diverse suite of community-supported physical oceanographic models, including ADCIRC, SCHISM, FVCOM, and ROMS. While this diversity enables NOS to meet a wide range of mission requirements, it also fragments resources by requiring support for multiple modeling frameworks. To address this, NOS will conduct a formal evaluation to identify an optimal set of core model codes capable of meeting its operational and statutory needs while positioning the program to adopt emerging advances in computing, data integration, and predictive methodologies. Physical oceanographic models are foundational to NOS operations, particularly for marine navigation and ecological forecasting, and integration with NOAA’s Unified Forecasting System (UFS). They also underpin numerous downstream applications across NOS and other NOAA line offices. Accordingly, this evaluation will focus on these models and their underlying core codes. NOS user and statutory mission requirements will guide the assessment, which will include standardized comparisons using objective performance metrics such as accuracy, forecast skill, resolution, and computational efficiency. In parallel, market research will document other qualitative information, such as projected community support and sustainability over the next 5-10 years. The evaluation will also examine each model’s capacity to leverage advances in high-performance and cloud computing, GPU and emerging hardware architectures, machine learning and hybrid modeling approaches, automated data assimilation, and ensemble forecasting. The outcome will guide strategic investment in a streamlined, future-ready modeling portfolio for NOS. Transparent communication and feedback from the modeling community is critical to ensure the success of this evaluation.

487156.title: Assessing the Impacts of NOAA STAR-generated COSMIC-2 and Commercial GNSS RO Bending Angles on GFS Forecasts
487156.authors: William J. S. Miller, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; NOAA, College Park, MD; and Y. Chen, X. Shao, and C. Cao
487156.abstract: In collaboration with the University of Maryland, NOAA’s Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR) has developed algorithms for processing Level-0 Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) radio occultation (RO) signals and satellite orbital data from the COSMIC-2, PlanetiQ, and Spire missions to bending angles. Currently, STAR provides this processed data in real-time for assimilation into numerical weather prediction models. This presentation reports on a series of Observing System Experiments (OSEs) conducted over May and June 2026 to evaluate the impact of these data on the Global Forecast System (GFS). Our offline GFS system resembles the operational configuration except that it is run at half-resolution (~26 km) on the horizontal spectral grid and it uses 40 rather than 80 ensemble members for background error estimation. RO bending angles are assimilated using the one-dimensional NCEP Bending Angle Model (NBAM) forward operator with default settings for observation error estimates and quality control parameters. We assess the individual and combined impacts of STAR-processed COSMIC-2, PlanetiQ, and Spire data against baseline experiments that withhold these datasets. Results show that assimilating RO data from all three platforms generally improved medium-range forecasts, reducing mean bias and root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) in temperature and geopotential height against the ECMWF analysis for most layers in the tropics, northern hemisphere and southern hemisphere. Additionally, COSMIC-2 and commercial RO data assimilation reduces short-to-medium range forecast water vapor errors in the tropical lower-to-middle troposphere when measured against radiosondes. Some instances of relatively minor forecast degradations from assimilating commercial RO data have been identified, and preliminary investigation of the causes will be presented. These results confirm that NOAA STAR can provide high-quality, real-time GNSS RO bending angle retrievals that positively impact forecast skill.

487160.title: Analysis of HAFS Forecasts Using the Scale-Aware Tiedtke Convective Scheme
487160.authors: Andrew T. Hazelton, Univ. of Miami CIMAS, Miami, FL; and S. Gopalakrishnan, J. Shin, M. Rather, L. J. Gramer, and G. J. Alaka Jr.
487160.abstract: The Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System is NOAA’s flagship Hurricane Model, and has been in operations since 2023. Work is ongoing to improve HAFS forecasts of TC track, intensity, structure, and impacts. One avenue of research that we are exploring is improvement to the convective physics in HAFS, to improve both the model’s skill as well as the diversity between HAFS-A and HAFS-B. Specifically, we are testing and improving the scale-aware Tiedtke scheme in HAFS. The track biases are notably different from those in the default Scale-Aware SAS scheme, with generally stronger ridging in most cases. However, there is a weak bias in intensity when using the default version of the scale-aware Tiedtke scheme. We test modifications to the entrainment and scale-awareness calculations in order to improve these intensity biases. Tests of the original and modified versions are performed on an idealized version of HAFS to explore details of how the physics differences alter TC inner-core structure. In addition, we have performed tests with real-storm versions of the model, including real-time experiments from 2024 and 2025 as well as retrospective tests for the 2022-2026 hurricane seasons. We explore how the Tiedtke scheme results in different inner-core structures in extreme hurricanes such as Melissa (2025) and also results in ridging and track differences for cases like Hurricane Ian (2022). The goal of this project is ultimately to develop a version of the scheme that helps to consistently improves overall skill in HAFS and provides useful forecast spread between HAFS-A and HAFS-B.

487162.title: Building Community, Building Careers: A Cross-Institutional Model for Student Conferences
487162.authors: Marissa Anne Vara, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. M. Cyccone, V. Do, M. Schaberg, A. Christensen, G. Forbes, M. Payne, and K. C. L. Gordillo
487162.abstract: The NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR), University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR), UCAR Community Programs (UCP), and Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES) Summer Student Conference gives interns structured practice in skills research careers demand beyond technical training: a lightning talk session and early career panel, presenting work to a mixed audience, translating research for peers outside their subfield, fielding questions in real time, and building professional networks beyond their home institution. For many students, this is their first chance to practice these skills in a low-stakes setting and to learn that communication, networking, and collaboration are skills to be developed, not innate talents. As a cross-institutional gathering, the conference builds a wider professional network than any single internship program could offer alone. Each year, 10-15 internship programs from across the NSF NCAR, UCAR, UCP, and CIRES communities participate, bringing together 70-90 students conducting research across the Earth system sciences (ESS). For many first-time researchers and students from institutions with limited research infrastructure, the conference offers a unique opportunity to engage with a broader scientific community, explore new career pathways, and build professional networks that extend well beyond their summer experience. This presentation shares lessons learned from designing and running a multi-institutional student conference as a professional development and workforce initiative. It explores: 1) how structured presentation opportunities help students develop scientific communication, networking, and collaboration skills, particularly for those with limited prior research experience; 2) how cross-program exposure broadens students' awareness of ESS career pathways while fostering interdisciplinary connections and lasting professional networks; and 3) practical strategies for scaling a collaborative student conference across multiple institutions and programs. Attendees will leave with a transferable framework for creating high-impact student conferences that strengthen research communication, build community, and prepare the next generation of Earth system scientists.

487167.title: Comparing Various Methods for Assimilating Ceilometer Cloud Cover Observations Using a Perfect-Model OSSE with DART
487167.authors: Shawn Murdzek, CIRES, CU Boulder, and NOAA/OAR/Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and J. Anderson, D. Dowell, and S. Ha
487167.abstract: Low-level cloud cover has a large impact on the surface energy budget, aviation safety, and the energy sector. One of the best sources of low-level cloud information comes from ceilometers, which are part of the Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) suite. Given the widespread nature of ceilometers, assimilating these observations has the potential to improve model forecasts of low-level clouds. Currently, ceilometer observations are assimilated into NOAA’s rapidly updating NWP systems using the stratiform cloud-hydrometeor data-assimilation (SCHDA) technique (Benjamin et al. 2021). While the SCHDA improves cloud ceiling forecast skill, it is somewhat ad hoc, not based on data assimilation theory, and is not intended for ensemble forecast systems. In our previous work, we demonstrated that using an ensemble square root filter may be a viable alternative for assimilating ceilometers into a rapidly updating NWP system. In this talk, we expand upon those results by using the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) with the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) to assimilate ceilometer observations. Using a perfect-model observing system simulation experiment, we will compare the performance of the SCHDA to two algorithms in DART: the ensemble adjustment Kalman filter and the quantile-conserving ensemble filter framework (QCEFF). Given the non-Gaussian nature of cloud cover from ceilometers (e.g., discrete and doubly bounded), the QCEFF may be a good candidate for assimilating these observations. Benjamin, S. G., and Coauthors, 2021: Stratiform Cloud-Hydrometeor Assimilation for HRRR and RAP Model Short-Range Weather Prediction. Mon. Wea. Rev., 149, 2673–2694, https://doi.org/10.1175/MWR-D-20-0319.1.

487179.title: Evaluating Aerosol-Induced Convective Invigoration in Isolated, Developing Storms (Invited Presentation)
487179.authors: Adele Igel, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA; and H. E. Pimperl
487179.abstract: We have used a combination of geostationary satellite data, meteorological data, and ground-based aerosol data from the Southern Great Plains (SGP) to assess the impact of aerosol concentration on the rate of storm development. We tracked 225 isolated, developing, deep-convective storms in the vicinity of SGP. From the time series of each tracked storm, we derived the rise rate of the storm top. Up to about 60% of the variance in rise rates can be explained by the meteorological environment, with a larger percentage of the variance explained for more strict isolation criteria. After controlling for meteorology, the data suggests that invigoration occurs with an increase in the concentration of aerosol particles smaller than 65 nm whereas enervation occurs with an increase in concentration of particles larger than 100 nm. These relationships strengthen for certain subsets of the data. The results suggest that future research should focus on identifying the conditions under which each response is expected.

487180.title: The NOAA NESDIS GNSS-R Ocean Surface Winds Pilot Project and Transition to Operations
487180.authors: Gerard Peltzer, NOAA NESDIS, Silver Spring, MD; Science and Technology Corporation, Columbia, MD; and N. Laudier, A. Lomax, A. M. Agather, P. Chang, Z. Jelenak, B. C. Ruston, and F. Said
487180.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Services’ (NESDIS) Commercial Data Program (CDP) has conducted a Commercial Weather Data Program pilot study on Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R) data for determining ocean surface winds (OSW). As part of the pilot, NOAA has utilized commercially provided GNSS-R data to develop a NOAA GNSS-R ocean wind product. In this presentation, we will discuss the recently completed GNSS-R pilot and provide data assessment and evaluation results to-date, including key findings and lessons learned. We will discuss future plans and the NESDIS transition to operations path toward commercial GNSS-R data purchases to provide OSW measurements that support NOAA’s current and anticipated operational mission needs.

487181.title: Following the Learning Curve: Training Dynamics for Climate Emulator Explainability
487181.authors: Jacob Landsberg, Boston University, Boston, MA; and N. Saphra, K. Rucker, A. Wikner, and E. A. Barnes
487181.abstract: AI climate emulators have emerged as promising alternatives to dynamical climate models, offering competitive S2D skill at a fraction of the computational cost. However, as these emulators are designed as “black-box” models, studying the physical mechanisms underpinning their outputs remains challenging. Better understanding why an emulator makes its prediction is crucial for both assessing its viability in a changing climate and improving its skill. In this work, we investigate the training dynamics of ACE2, a fully data-driven, atmosphere-only climate model. We interrogate the model over the full course of its training, analyzing 480 model checkpoints (120 epochs over 4 random initial seeds). With this approach, we better diagnose when, and the mechanisms by which, the model learns complex climate modes like the MJO, ENSO teleconnections and spatial spectra. Preliminary results indicate that proper expression of spatial variance competes between different wavenumbers, possibly limiting the models’ ability to fully portray an accurate zonal energy spectrum. Further evaluation of climate modes indicates that at the beginning of training, ACE2 improves climatological mean skill in tandem with improving representation of ENSO and the MJO, yet this connection weakens by the end of training. Through these analyses we demonstrate that a model's training trajectory, and not just its final state, offers a valuable window into what an emulator has learned and why.

487182.title: Microphysical Processes Controlling the Spatial Structure of Stratocumulus Cloud Water and Precipitation
487182.authors: Adele L. Igel, ; and L. Hornung, M. K. Witte, K. Loftus, K. K. Chandrakar, M. van Lier-Walqui, and H. Morrison
487182.abstract: Models at all scales still struggle to simulate warm stratocumulus clouds. In large eddy simulations, models may be able to reproduce the domain-mean cloud water and rain water structure, but often cannot reproduce the spatial structure of these fields, particularly for rain water. This problem seems to be mitigated by using a Lagrangian particle scheme rather than a bin or bulk microphysics scheme. This study aims to identify the microphysical processes that control the spatial structure of precipitation through the use of a suite of mechanism-denial Lagrangian particle simulations. The results should be able to provide guidance on ways to improve bulk microphysics schemes for simulating these clouds.

487186.title: On the Large-Scale Vertical Velocity Intermittency of Turbulent Wall Flows (Invited Presentation)
487186.authors: Gabriel G. Katul, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and C. Manes, E. Buono, M. Heisel, E. Bou-Zeid, D. Poggi, C. Peruzzi, and T. Banerjee
487186.abstract: Large-scale intermittency (LSI) in the turbulent vertical velocity (w') component of wall-bounded high Reynolds number flows is necessary to describe transport across the wall-normal direction by energy-containing eddies. LSI is of significance to vertical momentum and heat exchanges with surfaces, pollutant dispersion, sediment movement and suspension, among others. These processes depend disproportionately on rare but intense wall-normal velocity events. The rarity of such events is usually measured by the flatness factor (FF) of w'. Extremes in w' bursts are commonly compared to their Gaussian tail expectations using deviations of FF from 3. The FF measuring LSI is presumed to be a property of production-range outer eddies and differs from the much studied fine-scale intermittency that is a property of the inertial and dissipation range eddies. At fine or Kolmogorov micro-scales, increases in intermittency are attributed to the role of viscosity in damping less energetic velocity increments and allowing only the most energized events to survive a viscosity censoring mechanism. On the other hand, energy-containing eddies in w' encode key signatures of the flow boundary conditions, coherent structures, up-drafts/down-draft events, or bursts in an otherwise less active or quiescent state. LSI has received significant attention in studies of coherent structures and their detection using data-driven approaches. Such approaches utilize the local topology of the flow to detect LSI and remain diagnostic - not prognostic - by design. In canonical wall-bounded turbulent flows at very high Reynolds number, it may be conjectured that the dynamics of the most energetic eddies, and hence of FF, are controlled by inertial and pressure forces instead of viscous forces. Yet, a theory that predicts the origin of LSI from the Navier-Stokes equations, or some approximated version of them, at very high Reynolds numbers is yet to be achieved even for the most idealized flow conditions. It is this gap in LSI that motivates the work here. The talk proposes such a theory for a neutrally stratified wall-bounded turbulent flow based on a dominant balance between inertial and pressure forces. This balance can be represented by two terms that capture the observed weak dependence of FF on wall-normal distance and flow configuration (see Figure), highlighting the dominant role of large-scale energy anisotropy and turbulent velocity variances. The theory also explains why measured FF has a local minimum at the transition from the inertial to the outer layer. These findings clarify the physical origin of large-scale intermittency, explain why conventional gradient-diffusion models fail to reproduce FF, and offer improved formulations for applications where intermittent vertical transport plays a role. The theory has no 'tunable' parameters and demonstrates why FF cannot be described using down-gradient closure approximations employed in large-scale meteorological and climate models. At very high Reynolds number, it predicts that FF = (Aw)-4+(Au2+Av2)/(2 Aw2), where Aw, Au, and Av are the root-mean squared velocity terms normalized by the friction velocity for the vertical velocity (w'), the longitudinal velocity (u'), and the lateral velocity (v') components. Figure legend: Variation of FF against the normalized distance from the wall in inner units approximating a local Reynolds number Re across a wide corpus of laboratory experiments (Open channel: OC and Wind Tunnel: WT). MN stands for the OC experiments in Manes et al. (2011), HL stands for the WT experiments in Heisel et al. (2020), PR stands for the OC experiments in Peruzzi et al. (2020), PG stands for the OC experiments in Poggi et al. (2002), and S, R, and P stand for smooth, rough and porous bed types and the numbers denote different experimental runs.

487187.title: Influences of Asian Emissions and Stratospheric Transport on Background Ozone over the Western US, 1980–2026
487187.authors: Yifan Li, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and M. Lin
487187.abstract: Surface ozone levels in the U.S. Intermountain West have undergone substantial changes over the past several decades. In particular, ozone design values in nonattainment areas have become increasingly decoupled from continued reductions in local anthropogenic precursor emissions over the past decade. Quantifying the sources of background ozone variability from daily to multi-decadal timescales is therefore essential for interpreting these recent trends. Here, we investigate changes in springtime background ozone over the Intermountain West since 1980, with a particular focus on the drivers of variability during 2012–2026. We combine long-term ozone and meteorological observations with a suite of GFDL-AM4V chemistry–climate model simulations designed to isolate the effects of anthropogenic emission trends and meteorological variability. We identify three distinct periods of springtime ozone evolution. During 1980–2012, ozone increased substantially, with nearly half of the high-elevation sites examined, including Great Basin National Park, exhibiting trends of 0.2–0.5 ppbv yr⁻¹. Model simulations attribute much of this increase to rising anthropogenic emissions in Asia and their influence on background ozone over the western United States. During 2012–2022, ozone declined, with observed trends of approximately −0.3 to −0.4 ppbv yr⁻¹, although these trends were not statistically significant. The model simulations capture this decline and indicate that reductions in Asian anthropogenic emissions were the dominant driver. The pronounced negative ozone anomaly of approximately 3–7 ppbv during spring 2020–2021 was further influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic-related reductions in global emissions. Since 2023, springtime ozone has rebounded, reaching elevated levels through 2026 despite continued reductions in local anthropogenic precursor emissions. This recent increase coincided with enhanced subsidence associated with upper-level troughing and appears to have been strongly influenced by more frequent stratospheric ozone intrusions. The number of days with maximum daily 8-hour average (MDA8) ozone exceeding 60 and 70 ppbv increased during 2023–2026, and most days exceeding 70 ppbv were associated with stratospheric intrusions. At nonattainment sites in the Denver area, excluding days influenced by stratospheric intrusions reduced the fourth-highest springtime MDA8 ozone by approximately 1–4 ppbv during these years. These findings demonstrate that long-term, emission-driven changes in background ozone are superimposed on substantial interannual variability associated with stratospheric influence. The increasing importance of stratospheric ozone intrusions in recent years helps explain why surface ozone in the Intermountain West has become less responsive to continued reductions in local anthropogenic precursor emissions and highlights the need to account for both hemispheric emission changes and stratosphere–troposphere exchange when interpreting ozone trends and evaluating future air-quality strategies.

487192.title: The RAPTOR Mobile Radar Suite at NSSL
487192.authors: Pamela Heinselman, NSSL, Norman, OK; and J. C. Snyder, D. Wasielewski, J. J. Gourley, G. Kunkle, Z. Barney, A. A. Alford, V. C. Chmielewski, M. Coniglio, M. D. Flournoy, A. Lyza, A. E. Reinhart, and J. Zhang
487192.abstract: Weather radars, particularly mobile configurations, serve as vital instruments for monitoring atmospheric processes across a broad spectrum of scales. These range from synoptic-scale features—such as atmospheric rivers, frontal rain bands, and tropical or extratropical cyclones—to mesoscale phenomena like quasi-linear convective systems, and down to convective storm- and substorm-scale structures, including supercells, multicells, mesocyclones, tornadoes, landspouts, and gust fronts. Beyond traditional meteorological phenomena, these observational capabilities extend to fire weather research, encompassing the tracking of active wildfire evolution and smoke behavior, fire-induced convection, and post-fire hazards like debris flows and burn scar flooding. Building upon the National Severe Storms Laboratory’s (NSSL) extensive legacy of utilizing weather radar to investigate severe storms and hazards, the acquisition of the new RAPTOR (Rapid-deployable Agile Polarimetric Transportable Observational Radar) mobile radar suite marks a significant advancement. This suite features two new mobile X-band radars and one new mobile C-band radar, all of which are solid-state, dual-polarization, parabolic-dish systems capable of agile local operations or long-term remote deployment. Each system is integrated into a medium-duty truck equipped with a self-leveling mechanism, an independent generator for off-grid use, and a mechanical lift that elevates the antenna above the cab. This design ensures an unobstructed 360-degree scanning capability and mitigates the clutter contamination that often compromises mobile radar observations and limits deployment options. Complementing the mobile radar fleet is a series of low-cost, highly transportable, vertically pointing radars (PodRads), which are currently being designed and developed to capture vertical velocities inside tornadoes and other hazardous environments. This presentation will detail these innovative radar assets and outline plans for future research initiatives leveraging these tools to study severe convective storms, fire weather, and other high-impact meteorological events.

487195.title: Assimilation of CYGNSS Winds in HAFS: Comparing Level-2 Fully Developed Seas and Level-3 Merged Storm Wind Products and Their Impacts on Hurricane Forecast
487195.authors: Chengfeng Feng, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and J. Stoddard, Z. Pu, C. S. Ruf, Z. Zhang, and V. S. Tallapragada
487195.abstract: Forecasts of tropical cyclones (TCs), particularly their rapid intensification (RI), remain a major challenge, largely because of scarce observations within TC inner cores over the ocean. Frequent ocean surface wind speeds across TC inner cores and their surroundings can be provided by the NASA Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS). This study assimilates the CYGNSS Level-2 (L2) Fully Developed Seas (FDS) wind speeds and the Level-3 (L3) Storm-Centric Gridded (SCG)-related wind speeds carried by the L3 Merged Storm (MRG) product into the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) using the GSI-based hybrid four-dimensional ensemble-variational data assimilation (DA) system, and compares their DA statistics and forecast impacts for Hurricanes Ida (2021) and Ian (2022). Forecasts are verified against HURDAT2 best-track data and MRMS radar observations. Results suggest that the L2 normalized innovations are approximately Gaussian with negative conditional biases at high wind speeds, and assimilating L2 FDS winds consistently improves track, minimum sea level pressure, and inner-core structure forecasts, even during RI periods, whereas L3 normalized innovations are broader and more biased, and assimilating the L3 SCG-related winds yields more mixed and generally weaker results, largely because the influence of ignoring representation error is amplified by smaller wind speed uncertainties of L3 blended FDS–SCG winds, although the pure L3 SCG winds can reduce negative biases where they dominate. Overall, the CYGNSS L2 FDS winds currently provide more dependable TC forecasts than the L3 SCG-related winds within the HAFS DA framework; however, the potential of assimilating L3 MRG product can be unleashed through proper treatment of their observation errors.

487199.title: Coupled Land–Atmosphere Data Assimilation for the DOE E3SM Earth System Model Using DART
487199.authors: Zhaoxia Pu, ; and S. Zhang, D. Xu, B. Raczka, L. R. Leung, and J. Anderson
487199.abstract: Coupled data assimilation (DA) provides a promising pathway toward dynamically balanced Earth system initialization and improved subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction. This presentation describes ongoing efforts to develop a strongly coupled land–atmosphere DA framework for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) using the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART). Ensemble DA capabilities have been developed within DART for both the atmospheric and land components of E3SM. Recent E3SM–DART atmospheric assimilation experiments demonstrate performance consistent with established CAM6–DART capabilities and indicate the potential to reduce model spin-up and improve atmospheric initialization for S2S prediction. In parallel, E3SM Land Model (ELM)–DART experiments have been conducted through the assimilation of global Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) soil moisture observations. The impacts of these experiments on land initialization, land–atmosphere interactions, and S2S prediction are currently being evaluated. Current development focuses on integrating the atmospheric and land DA capabilities into a unified framework that permits observations assimilated in one component to influence both atmospheric and land states through ensemble-estimated cross-component covariances. This presentation highlights recent progress in E3SM–DART atmospheric and land DA, discusses key scientific and technical challenges associated with strongly coupled assimilation, and outlines future directions toward an integrated land–atmosphere initialization system for S2S prediction.

487206.title: (Invited Presentation) Forecasting and Data Assimilation for Stable Boundary Layers over Complex Terrain: Progress, Challenges, and Lessons from Field Programs
487206.authors: Zhaoxia Pu, Univ. of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT
487206.abstract: Stable boundary layers (SBLs) over complex terrain remain among the most challenging atmospheric regimes for numerical weather prediction and data assimilation (DA). Weak and intermittent turbulence, strong stratification, terrain-induced flows, cold-air pooling, and pronounced spatial and temporal variability can produce large forecast errors that are difficult to correct through conventional assimilation approaches. These challenges become increasingly important as numerical weather prediction systems move toward kilometer and sub-kilometer resolutions, where terrain-driven circulations and boundary layer heterogeneity are more explicitly represented. Over the past decade, intensive field programs, including MATERHORN and CFACT, have provided comprehensive observations of stable boundary layers and terrain-induced circulations across complex-terrain environments. These observations have advanced our understanding of drainage flows, cold-air pools, boundary layer transitions, turbulence, and multiscale interactions, while also revealing persistent deficiencies in numerical simulations. Data assimilation studies using these observations have further demonstrated both the potential and limitations of current DA systems for improving analyses and forecasts in strongly heterogeneous terrain. This presentation reviews recent progress and continuing challenges in forecasting and data assimilation of stable boundary layers over complex terrain, drawing on lessons learned from MATERHORN, CFACT, and related modeling and DA studies. Emphasis will be placed on what field observations have revealed about key sources of forecast error, how advances in modeling and data assimilation have improved the representation and prediction of terrain-driven boundary layer processes, and where significant challenges remain. These lessons provide guidance for improving high-resolution prediction systems and for developing future observing and data assimilation strategies for complex terrain.

487216.title: Learning to Fly.....All Types of Weather
487216.authors: Richard B. DiMaio, Oakton College, Des Plaines, IL
487216.abstract: As an instructor of Aviation Weather at a 4 year university as well as two 2 year colleges, it is important to attempt to bridge the gap for students who desire to transfer to a higher level of academics. This presentation will focus on how to educate students using daily aviation weather briefing at a 2 year college so that they could more seemlessly transfer into a 4 year program. Given a classroom of 22 students, 11 groups consisting of a major US city will be assigned. Each week, additional elements of atmospheric phenomena that is taught through the normal syllabus will be applied using aviation-related components such as wind direction and speed both surface and aloft, cloud heights and bases, visibility, icing, turbulence, precipitation type, severe weather, mid-latitude cyclones and tropica weather. All of these will applied week by week so that students can present a weather briefing. The students will be assigned an airport and an airline. They will be building their weather briefings as we go through the course of the semster and presenting them weekly to the class.

487217.title: The Daily Aviation Weather Briefing: A Four Pronged Approach to Understanding and Operating In All Types of Aviation Weather.
487217.authors: Richard B. DiMaio, Lewis University, Romeoville, IL
487217.abstract: As an instructor of Aviation Weather at a 4 year university it is important to attempt to educate studetns of all aviation discipline: Aviation Administration, Flight Management, Air Traffic Control and Flight Dispatch using the Daily Weather Briefing.Given a classroom of 30 students, 15 groups, each consisting of a regional Air Traffic Control Center and associated Center Weather Service Unit will be assigned. Each week, additional elements of atmospheric phenomena that is taught through the normal syllabus will be applied using aviation-related components such as wind direction and speed both surface and aloft, cloud heights and bases, visibility, icing, turbulence, precipitation type, severe weather, mid-latitude cyclones and tropica weather. All of these will applied week by week so that students can present a weather briefing.

487222.title: Improving Spheroidal Backscattering of Geometric Optics using a Deep Neural Network
487222.authors: Neil Harris Cutting, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; Texas A&M Univ., College Station, TX; and P. Yang and S. Wang
487222.abstract: Accurately modeling light scattering by non-spherical particles across a broad range of size parameters remains a major challenge. Exact methods are preferred at small and intermediate size parameters, whereas geometric optics approximations are generally required for much larger particles because of their substantially lower computational cost. For spheroidal particles, the Improved Geometric Optics Method (IGOM) provides an efficient means of computing optical properties but tends to underestimate phase function backscattering, particularly at relatively small size parameters. IGOM does not consider coherent backscatter enhancement (CBE), resulting in an underestimated phase function in the backscattering region. Recently, the Separation of Variables and T-matrix Method (SV-TM) has extended exact light scattering calculations for homogeneous and two-layer spheroids to size parameters approaching 2000. However, its computational cost increases rapidly with particle size, making database generation impractical when the size parameter exceeds approximately 1000. In this study, we propose a physics-informed Deep Neural Network (DNN) to improve the backscattering behavior of IGOM using SV-TM solutions for spheroids as training references over 160° to 180°. Training data will be generated with SV-TM over the size parameters spanning from 100 to 1000 for a range of particle aspect ratios and refractive indices. After training and validation within this range, the DNN will be extrapolated to larger size parameters to evaluate whether the learned correction applied by the DNN remains physically consistent beyond the training domain. An angular taper will smoothly confine the correction to the backscattering region while preserving the original IGOM solution at smaller scattering angles. The proposed framework aims to combine the backscattering accuracy of SV-TM with the computational efficiency of IGOM and provide an efficient approach for modeling spheroidal particles in the large-size-parameter regime.

487234.title: Impacts of Greenness Vegetation Fraction Parameter Perturbations on Cycled DA Performance
487234.authors: Brett Castro, OU School of Meteorology with CADRE, Norman, OK
487234.abstract: Accurately predicting the timing and location of dryline convection initiation (CI) requires accurate representation of the initial conditions of both the land and atmosphere because of the role of land-atmosphere interactions in dryline CI. Land-atmosphere strongly coupled data assimilation (SCDA) therefore has the potential to improve convective-scale prediction in dryline CI cases. However, the design of ensemble perturbations used in data assimilation (DA) typically neglects the uncertainty related to land surface parameters such as greenness vegetation fraction (GVF). Experiments involving a chosen case study aimed at isolating and comparing the contributions to forecast uncertainty from GVF perturbations to the contributions from soil state perturbations show that uncertainty in GVF has a measurable impact on the pre-convective environment. For example, when observing the magnitude of forecast variance from GVF perturbations, it is found to be approximately half of that seen from soil state perturbations for relevant land-surface and atmosphere variables. Meanwhile, the spatial scale of coupled covariance structures associated with GVF perturbations are shown to be larger than for soil state perturbations. Based on these encouraging impacts from GVF perturbations on a convective-scale forecast, these GVF perturbations were included in the CADRE-MPAS-JEDI cycled SCDA system. The impact of these newly implemented GVF perturbations will be evaluated using an experiment that assimilates conventional observations hourly over a 4-day period that includes the chosen dryline CI event.

487242.title: Contrasting Responses of Extratropical and Tropical North Atlantic Upper-Ocean Temperature to AMOC Multidecadal Variability under Global Warming in CESM1-LE
487242.authors: Jun-Chao Yang, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, Shandong, China; and Q. Yu, C. Zhu, Y. Zhang, and X. Lin
487242.abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation multidecadal variability (AMOC-MV) is a primary driver of North Atlantic upper-ocean temperature variations, yet its influence undergoes significant regional reorganization under global warming. Using the Community Earth System Model version 1 Large Ensemble (CESM1-LE), we demonstrate that while AMOC-MV-driven upper-ocean temperature variability weakens substantially in the extratropical North Atlantic under the Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5 scenario, its modulation on subsurface temperature variability remains robust in the tropical North Atlantic. The extratropical weakening is attributed to reduced ocean heat convergence and associated circulation changes, whereas the sustained tropical linkage results from a southward shift of the subsurface temperature dome. These findings reveal a complex AMOC-MV thermal fingerprint under global warming: a progressive decoupling in the extratropics that challenges existing decadal prediction frameworks, alongside a persistent tropical connection that offers a reliable monitor for future AMOC-MV changes.

487249.title: WX Forge: Generating NWS Textual Forecast Products using AI
487249.authors: Rayette Toles-Abdullah, Amazon Web Services, Upper Marlboro, MD
487249.abstract: NWS forecasters spend 15–30 minutes per shift drafting routine text products that follow predictable formats. During high-impact weather, that time competes with situational awareness and decision support. WX Forge generates first drafts of four NWS product types (AFD, ZFP, HWO, PNS) in under 10 seconds. The system decodes FM-12 SYNOP observations from BUFR files in the WMO WIS 2.0 Global Cache on S3, computes synoptic interpretation (pressure gradients, moisture axes, frontal positions), and passes structured prompts to Amazon Nova Pro on Bedrock. Output matches official NWS formatting — WMO headers, section structure, standard abbreviations. No fine-tuning is required. The prompt addresses the model as a WFO Science and Operations Officer, provides computed meteorological context, and enforces strict format rules. This mirrors the UK Met Office approach that achieved 83% gale warning accuracy in Shipping Forecast automation using the same model family. No generated text reaches the public without forecaster review. WX Forge shifts time from drafting to analysis. We discuss failure modes: hallucinated conditions under sparse data, missing NWP model guidance, and plausible-sounding errors that require expert detection.

487251.title: Seasonal Prediction and Predictability of Winter Energy Demand Extremes over North America
487251.abstract: Winter temperature variability places acute strain on North American energy infrastructure, driving peak electricity demand, accelerating natural gas depletion, and increasing grid volatility. While seasonal climate forecasts routinely focus on standard mean temperature anomalies, direct seasonal predictions of energy-tailored demand metrics—both seasonal mean Heating Degree Days (HDD-M) and tail-risk demand extremes (HDD-X)—remain unexplored. In this study, we provide a novel evaluation of the seasonal prediction skill of NOAA/GFDL’s Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (SPEAR) ensemble for extended winter (JFM) energy demand (HDD-M and HDD-X, defined by the 90th percentile threshold) across North America for the 1993–2023 period against ERA5 reanalysis across initializations multiple months in advance. To isolate true year-to-year predictive capability from long-term trend signals, we compute both raw and detrended correlation skill. Our results demonstrate that SPEAR exhibits robust, statistically significant skills for both HDD-M and HDD-X concentrated over key energy-demand regions, particularly Northeastern North America, Eastern Canada, and Alaska. While HDD-M displays slightly broader spatial coverage in the central continent, HDD-X retains high, statistically significant skill in Northeastern North America and Alaska out to multiple months in advance. This high spatial coherence indicates that dynamical initializations capture large-scale atmospheric-oceanic teleconnections beyond long-term climate trends. These findings establish the actionable utility of dynamical seasonal forecasts for informing mid-to-long-range load forecasting, and grid risk management during peak winter demand.

487269.title: Intraseasonal Variability of Precipitation in Northwestern Peru and its Connection with the Madden-Julian Oscillation and Eastern Pacific El Niño
487269.authors: Juan C. Sulca Sr., UNIVERSIDAD NACIONAL DE INGENIERIA, LIMA, LIMA, Peru; and V. C. Mayta and K. Takahashi Guevara
487269.abstract: Northwestern Peru (NWP) exhibits strong precipitation variability with major societal impacts, yet the mechanisms governing its intraseasonal variability remain poorly understood. This study investigates intraseasonal precipitation variability during the January–April rainy season over 1981–2018 and its links to large-scale atmospheric circulation. The first three empirical orthogonal function (EOF) modes of band-pass-filtered station precipitation account for 45% of the total variance. EOF1 (32%) is characterized by a monopolar pattern, whereas EOF2 (8%) and EOF3 (6%) display dipolar structures with opposite anomalies between the northern coast and the Andean–Amazonian regions. All modes are associated with enhanced low-level westerly moisture transport from the eastern Pacific toward the Andes, but their large-scale circulation signatures differ. EOF1 is largely independent of El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and is primarily forced by anomalous upper-level divergence over NWP associated with the initial intrusion of Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) convection into South America, mainly during RMM phase 8. In contrast, EOF2 and EOF3 are strongly amplified by warm eastern Pacific sea surface temperature anomalies, particularly during the 1983, 1998, and 2017 coastal El Niño events. Positive EOF2 and EOF3 events are linked to anomalous low-level westerlies and enhanced moisture transport from the far-eastern Pacific, occurring mainly during MJO phases 8 and 1, respectively, under eastern Pacific El Niño conditions. In general, global MJO indices are less strongly related to precipitation variability than regional intraseasonal upper-level divergence and low-level zonal wind indices, suggesting that global indices do not necessarily capture the MJO features relevant to specific applications.

487272.title: A Temperature-Dependent Single-Scattering Database for Ice and Mixed-Phase Particles at Microwave and Submillimeter Channels
487272.authors: Dongchen Li, Texas A&M University, College station, TX; Texas A&M University, College station, TX; and P. Yang
487272.abstract: Accurate single-scattering properties of atmospheric ice and mixed-phase particles are essential for interpreting observations at microwave and submillimeter channels from current and upcoming satellite missions, including the Polarized Submillimeter Ice-cloud Radiometer (PolSIR) and the INvestigation of Convective Updrafts (INCUS). A temperature-dependent single-scattering database is developed to cover the frequency channels of PolSIR, INCUS, and other existing and planned satellite sensors. Electromagnetic-scattering computations are performed using the state-of-the-art separation-of-variables and T-matrix (SV–TM) combined method, which provides rigorous solutions for homogeneous and two-layer spheroids while substantially reducing the computational cost associated with repeated orientation computations. Spheroidal geometries have two degrees of freedom, namely particle size and aspect ratio, and can be used as first-order surrogates for complex ice particles in practice. A wide range of particle geometries is represented by prolate and oblate spheroids with aspect ratios from 0.1 to 10. With the shell thickness as an additional morphological parameter, two-layer spheroids are also included to represent partially frozen and mixed-phase particles containing both liquid water and ice. The temperature dependence of the refractive indices of ice and water is explicitly incorporated because it can substantially affect absorption, scattering, and polarization at microwave and submillimeter wavelengths. The single-scattering properties are computed for both randomly oriented particles and particles with specific orientations to account for aligned ice crystals and supercooled droplets in the atmosphere. The database provides full phase matrices and associated optical properties for radiative-transfer simulations, satellite retrieval development, and uncertainty assessment, supporting the interpretation of ice-cloud and convective observations from current and future satellite missions. Furthermore, vector radiative-transfer simulations are performed to demonstrate the applicability of the database.

487273.title: Towards Constraining Soil NOx Fluxes and the Responses to Soil Moisture from TEMPO
487273.authors: Dien Wu, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Laughner, S. Ogle, Z. Wang, A. Chen, and O. M. Griffith
487273.abstract: Soil microbial NOx emissions contribute to ~15% of the global nitrogen budget but can contribute substantially larger and more variable amounts at cropland scales. Their responses to soil moisture remain uncertain because direct flux observations from soil chambers and Eddy Covariance remain sparse. Atmospheric satellite observations have increasingly been used to detect soil NOx pulses, while most focus on the midwestern US and the California Central Valley and agricultural management practices are not clearly considered. Here we present soil NOx fluxes from both a bottom-up process-based biogeochemical model (DayCent) and a top-down modeling framework. DayCent simulates carbon and nitrogen dynamics in plant-soil systems, providing NOx emissions at a daily time step. Soil temperature, pH, and carbon availability directly regulate nitrification and denitrification processes, while tillage, fertilization, and soil moisture further affect NOx production and emission by altering organic matter decomposition, ammonium supply, and gas diffusion through the soil profile. The simulations are informed by daily weather data from Daymet, local soil characteristics and agricultural management data from multiple USDA sources and the Operational Tillage Information System. In parallel, we leverage hourly TEMPO tropospheric NO2 columns and develop a top-down framework that accounts for NOx chemical lifetime, NO2/NOₓ partitioning, and boundary-layer mixing using the STILT-NOx chemical dispersion model, while reducing canopy and anthropogenic influences using LAI, TROPOMI SIF, CO, and CrIS NH₃. Preliminary results reveal substantial differences in the soil moisture response across six croplands. The southmost irrigated cropland, Yaqui Valley, exhibits a nonlinear relationship between NO2 and soil moisture. Other selected US croplands show variable behaviors, suggesting stronger influence from seasonally varying boundary layer mixing, chemistry, and agricultural management. This observation-based framework represents a step toward constraining soil NOx fluxes over agricultural ecosystems with satellite data incorporating their responses to weather, management and soil conditions.

487276.title: A Generalized Approach for Evaluation of Microphysics Parameterizations Derived from In-Situ Snowfall Observations
487276.authors: Brian Filipiak, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; Eversource Energy Center, Storrs, CT; and S. Lang, A. Loftus, D. Cerrai, and M. Astitha
487276.abstract: Assumptions surrounding microphysical processes play an important role in the accuracy of how numerical weather simulations represent precipitation and clouds, which can impact radiative properties. While development of microphysics schemes rely on state-of-the-art cloud physics knowledge from observations and theoretical experiments, improvements of schemes often are done through a tuning process, in which process rates or specific parameterizations may be adjusted. These changes are then tested in simulations and compared to an observed field, such as accumulated precipitation or reflectivity. However, improvements in tuning do not also correspond to physically accurate representations of the adjusted processes, and they are often examined using a specific test case or over one particularly region. We present an approach to utilize ground and airborne in-situ observations to evaluate assumptions in microphysical parameterizations systematically, and it can be applied throughout the microphysics scheme. This technique does not rely on model simulations and is purely driven by observational datasets. Discussion around the assumptions, strengths, and limitations of the technique are included, as well as how different hydrometeor species present distinct challenges to identify and evaluate. As proof of concept, sample calculations for snow hydrometeors in the Thompson and NASA Goddard Microphysics will be shown. This approach has promise to be applied across multiple observational platforms and be used in systematic evaluation of microphysics schemes. Additionally, processing observations with this approach could become a precursor to data driven applications, such as machine learning or parameter uncertainty analysis.

487279.title: Improving the Prediction of Microphysical and Radiative Processes during Winter Storms in the United States Leveraging In-Situ Observations
487279.authors: Brian Filipiak, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; Eversource Energy Center, Storrs, CT; and S. Lang, A. Loftus, D. Cerrai, and M. Astitha
487279.abstract: Microphysical processes can have significant impacts on different components of winter storm prediction including precipitation and the optical properties of clouds, which can modify radiative feedback interactions. During winter in the mid-latitudes, ice-phase hydrometeors like snow and graupel reach the surface, which does not happen in the tropics or during convective storms. Here, we showcase the results from a systematic evaluation of the parameterized relationships for snow in the NASA Goddard microphysics scheme, using in-situ ground and aircraft NASA observations from around the globe. The evaluation focuses on the mapping function for snow intercept, density, and characteristic size, as well as bulk fields like effective radii and simulated reflectivity. The results of the observation-based evaluation are utilized to refine and improve the impact of snow hydrometeors in the resulting precipitation and radiative fields. Case studies of both lake-effect and synoptic scale snowstorms are included to show the impact of these refinements. These results can be used to understand where snow parameterizations have limitations and show how this technique could be expanded to other hydrometeor species or microphysics schemes.

487280.title: Turbulence Kinetic Energy: an Overlooked Signature of Extreme, Tree-Felling Wind Events
487280.authors: Isabella Osetinsky-Tzidaki, ICCLIPP - Israeli Consulting in Climatological Projects and Practices, Bat Yam, M, Israel; and E. Fredj
487280.abstract: Abrupt, tree-felling wind events pose a hazard to life and property that conventional extreme wind warnings routinely miss, because peak gust and mean wind speed alone do not capture the destructive potential of a rapidly fluctuating wind field. This gap is illustrated here by a forensic case as follows. One of the co-authors, in the course of her consulting practice had been requested to provide an expert opinion on the wind speed during a serious traffic accident of the rollover of a passenger car traveling at normal speed on a central-city road when a tree snapped and fell across its path. Video footage shows a tree being ripped from a roadside green space like a match from a box and, in a split second, thrown horizontally onto the road, causing a car to crash into it, fly into the air, flip several times and overturn. According to the local weather station (AWS), wind speeds at the time were high, but not unusually high for the area, so it cannot be definitively determined as the cause. A review of the falling-trees-related literature led to the conclusion that it is possible to solve this riddle using turbulent kinetic energy (TKE). In this way, three AWS wind speed channels - gust, one-minute wind speed maximum (WS1m), and ten-minute mean wind speed (WS) – were used, first, for establishing a set of the data quality-control rules (with a help of precipitation data) specific for the site. Then, the turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) was calculated as a function of WS and the turbulence intensity, which is a function of the gust factor GF=WS1/WS. It was found that the moment a tree flew from the green area onto the road coincided precisely with a sharp, transient spike in TKE. This TKE value turned out to be not just a seasonal maximum, but the highest one for this site over the entire observational period from 2006 to 2026. The above incident took place in a big city on the southeastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea (southern Levant). Extending the diagnostic analysis to the entire twenty-year period showed that each annual TKE maximum coincides with one of two distinct, highly dynamic synoptic systems over the Levant: the Northern Cyprus Low moving northeast of Cyprus, or the smaller, fast-moving Southern Cyprus Low rapidly passing eastward between Cyprus and Egypt. Both synoptic systems briefly align dense sea-level pressure isobars perpendicular to the southeastern meridional coastline of the Mediterranean Sea, generating the sharp wind shear that drives extreme TKE. Because these patterns can be identified in operational forecasting models based solely on sea-level pressure data, they establish a physically grounded early-warning criterion: when either of these synoptic patterns is present in the forecast, city officials can be alerted to inspect exposed trees before, rather than after, they fall - turning an overlooked statistical extreme into an actionable warning.

487284.title: A Climatological Analysis of Projected Tropical Cyclone Exposure on Second-Level Administrative Divisions in the Western North Pacific
487284.authors: Edward Buntain Robison, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN; and J. A. Ocegueda Sanchez and D. Chavas
487284.abstract: Tropical Cyclones (TCs) occur globally every year and have major impacts upon the lives of others, particularly those living in tropical regions. Previous research has looked at typhoons affecting individual countries or entire regions, but there is less precedent for basin-wide analyses of historical TC impacts at a higher spatial resolution. In this study, we determine which regions in the Western North Pacific have been most affected by TCs with gale-force winds (above 34 knots), and analyze how that may change with projected warming due to increasing global atmospheric CO2 levels. We analyze the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS) dataset from 1980-2024, and run wind models to reconstruct wind profiles of historical TCs. We create average TC tracks and administrative regional density maps of historical TCs by reproducing their wind swaths with a statistical model. Overall, the Northern Philippines, Taiwan, and Southern Japan are found to be affected by gale-force TC winds most often. By comparing the current record in early (1980-2000) and late (2001-2024) periods, we find there has been a slight southward shift in the distribution of administrative regions affected by gale-force TC winds. We are currently performing the same framework on TC tracks detected using Tempest Extremes on the high resolution data of MESACLIP simulations, to analyze the projected impacts by 2100 under different RCP projections. At the same time, we are conducting a socio-economic analysis of estimated population distribution and economic costs associated with damages from TCs. We aim to provide scientists and policymakers a better understanding of where adaptation to severe TCs is most critical for communities facing ongoing changes of Earth’s warming climate.

487285.title: Detecting Local Surface Heat Islands and Vegetation Losses Due to Global Data Centers (Invited Presentation)
487285.abstract: The rapid expansion of cloud computing and artificial intelligence has led to a global proliferation of data centers. While the immense energy and water demands of these facilities are heavily discussed, their localized microclimatic consequences remain largely unquantified. In this study, we utilize satellite-derived observations of land surface temperature and surface greenness to isolate the environmental footprint of nearly 10,000 data centers worldwide. Our analysis reveals the emergence of a distinct "data center surface heat island effect," characterized by a mean summer surface warming of 1.44°C. This localized surface warming is closely accompanied, and primarily modulated, by significant reductions in local vegetation cover at data center sites. However, at these scales, we do not find robust evidence that data centers are uniquely warmer than similar impervious structures, despite hypotheses that high anthropogenic heat rejection during operation would further elevate their temperatures. Given the limitations of current tools to test this hypothesis, we outline appropriate experimental designs to isolate operational heat emissions and their downstream impacts. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that data centers can act as prominent drivers of local environmental modification, underscoring the critical need for integrated spatial planning and targeted mitigation strategies to protect adjacent communities.

487292.title: Towards Incorporating Data-Assimilation In HRRRCast: A Score-Based Approach
487292.authors: Daniel Shawol Abdi, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and I. Jankov, C. J. Lewellyn, N. Silverman, N. Krall, C. Miller, and E. White
487292.abstract: HRRRCast v3 is a convection-permitting, AI-based weather prediction system trained on multi-year HRRR and GFS datasets, with improvements in resolution (3 km), variable coverage, and treatment of extreme events. However, with the operational phase-out of HRRR anticipated, HRRRCast’s current reliance on HRRR analyses as training targets and implicit background states present a structural limitation. This transition motivates the need for a self-consistent data assimilation (DA) capability that can ingest observations directly and reduce dependence on external analysis products. While prior developments in HRRRCast have improved forecast fidelity–particularly for convective-scale features–the absence of an internal DA framework now represents a primary bottleneck for operational viability. To address this, we investigate score-based data assimilation (SDA), formulating DA as a Bayesian inference problem in which a learned generative prior (from HRRR analysis) is combined with observation-driven likelihoods. Our implementation reuses the diffusion-based architecture and employs analytic, primarily linear observation operators (e.g., interpolation and neighborhood-based mappings), enabling efficient evaluation of both operators and their adjoints. Results indicate that SDA can recover physically consistent multivariate relationships, even when only a subset of variables is directly assimilated, and can flexibly incorporate varying observation densities. At the same time, performance depends sensitively on operator design and observation coverage. We will share our experience applying SDA within HRRRCast, including practical challenges, mixed outcomes, and comparisons with traditional approaches.

487306.title: Lagrangian Perspective on East Asian Summer Atmospheric Rivers: Origin, Pathway and Impacts
487306.authors: Seohyun Chung, Seoul National University, Seoul, 41, South korea; and Y. Kwon and S. W. Son
487306.abstract: East Asian summer atmospheric rivers (ARs) have been examined primarily through detection-based snapshots, limiting insight into their pathways and evolution. Given their diverse shapes, this study proposes an AR tracking algorithm connecting the AR centroids weighted by moisture transport and applies it to 26 summers. By genesis location, ARs are clustered into midlatitude ARs from inland China and subtropical ARs from the lower-latitude oceans. While the two groups produce comparable precipitation intensities upon landfall, midlatitude ARs pass over the East Asian populated regions more frequently and extensively, dominating the climatological AR-related precipitation. These midlatitude ARs form within migratory cyclones and intensify as they encounter the western flank of the North Pacific subtropical high. Our findings suggest that AR genesis over inland China can serve as an early signal for East Asian summer precipitation, and that a Lagrangian perspective can extend our understanding of ARs to their entire life cycle.

487309.title: Making Warn-on-Forecast a Reality: 1–3 Hour Effective Lead Time for Multiple Hazards
487309.authors: Patrick C. Burke, NSSL, Norman, OK; and C. M. Gravelle, K. Garrett, Y. Jung, M. Friedlein, M. Fox, T. Lindley, D. Church, M. Silcott, M. Krocak, R. Bowers, K. Sherburn, R. A. Graham, NWS, J. M. Laflin, J. Stoppkotte, P. Ayd, K. Magee, R. Martin, and A. M. Ward
487309.abstract: The experimental Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS) from NOAA’s National Severe Storms Laboratory was developed to give forecasters a means to resolve uncertainty associated with individual thunderstorms, beyond the narrow time horizon imposed by using radar signatures and conceptual models in watch and warning operations. WoFS is a 3-km grid-spacing ensemble that achieves a rapid pace for data assimilation and product delivery, and all forecasts are updated every 30 minutes. Its on-demand, regional domain(s) usually coincide with high probability severe weather, flash flood, and fire weather areas in national outlook products. Numerous testbed activities since 2021 have noted that probabilistic WoFS guidance enables greater forecaster confidence in both primary hazard type and the likely locations of severe thunderstorms, at 1-plus hour lead time. This, in turn, enables pre warning messaging that is more specific in space and time than broader scale convective or flash flood watches, and/or enables local adjustments to watch timing and coverage. Pre-warning messaging can be crucial for many end users like hospitals, schools, and outdoor venues, who need extended lead time to move people to safety. When the National Weather Service communicates a pre-warning message to public safety officials or to the public via official products and services, this can prompt pre-positioning of emergency resources, cessation of outdoor activities, and a host of other decisions that may result in a more effective response to the eventual warning. Although a definition for effective lead time is elusive, NSSL has used a stringent criteria to document 101 instances of 1-plus hour effective lead time directly attributable to WoFS since 2019. In these cases the affected NWS office messaged the specific hazard or impact that later occurred, with narrow spatial focus on the order of a few counties or less. These cases have been categorized as follows: tornado; hail; wind; flash flood; fire weather, aviation, decision support (often involving lightning). Trends show the number of instances rose sharply in 2021–2022 when WoFS use expanded nationally, especially in real-time mesoanalysis chat rooms. Another rise occurred in 2025–2026 during an ongoing NWS WoFS demonstration that has increased the frequency of domain availability. This work will examine the 101 documented cases of 1-plus hour lead time to describe the breadth of potential WoFS applications and identify go-to WoFS products and common practices for delivering WoFS informed messaging. Figure: A slide summarizing the first week when the NWS-led VLAB-WoFS came online in summer 2025. Local NWS Offices used WoFS that week for long lead-time messaging of multiple hazards, including significant severe winds in the Midwest and deadly flash flooding in Maryland. The Western U.S. also used WoFS runs for fire weather that same week.

487315.title: Evaluation of AI-Generated Ensembles Through Case Studies and Ensemble Sensitivity Analysis
487315.authors: Laura Dailey, The Pennsylvania State Univ., State College, PA; and S. J. Greybush, H. Singh, M. Adrian, and R. Maulik
487315.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as an increasingly valuable tool for numerical weather prediction (NWP), providing skillful forecasts at a fraction of the computational cost of physics-based models. These predictions are initialized from data assimilation systems that require computationally expensive ensembles to estimate background error covariances. A newly developed diffusion-model ensemble system generates a suite of global ensemble forecasts from NASA's GEOS-IT data assimilation analyses, producing six-hour ensemble forecast members from a deterministic analysis with substantially reduced computational cost. A system like this can generate a large number of ensembles, and thus more robust statistics, in a computationally efficient manner. This study evaluates the meteorological performance of the AI-generated ensemble through several case studies of extreme weather events, including a mid-latitude cyclone, a hurricane, and a major snowstorm. Cases from 2023, the period used for model validation, are first examined to analyze forecast performance, followed by similar events from 2024 to assess the model's ability to generalize beyond its validation dataset. Ensemble mean and ensemble spread are evaluated for predicted variables from the model output (e.g. surface pressure, virtual temperature, specific humidity, ozone mixing ratio, and the zonal and meridional winds) over a domain centered around each storm. To investigate the intervariable relationships represented by the AI ensemble (which are critical for data assimilation), ensemble sensitivity analysis is applied to quantify how uncertainty in one atmospheric variable is related to subsequent uncertainty in another. For example, sensitivities between the mass and wind field are examined to determine whether the AI-generated ensemble reproduces physically realistic relationships found in traditional physics-based models (e.g. GEOS-IT) and potentially other AI ensembles. Spatial correlation maps are used to identify differences in the atmospheric features that contribute most strongly to forecast uncertainty and allow us to understand if the model would develop a reasonable suite of ensembles even during more extreme events. This work provides one of the first meteorological evaluations of this AI ensemble prediction system, assessing both its forecast skill and its representation of physically consistent intervariable relationships. The goal is to learn about the model’s errors and biases in the 2023 case studies, provide guidance for developing this model to be more accurate, and to re-evaluate model performance during similar events in the 2024 case studies to quantify improvements.

487321.title: Gender Differences in Weather Knowledge, Preparedness, and Hazard Perception Among Students, Faculty, and Staff at Iowa State University
487321.authors: Bryce Charles Bruggeman, Iowa State University, Ames, IA; and S. Adams and L. C. Maudlin
487321.abstract: Many aspects of meteorology are generally misunderstood by the public. Misunderstandings involving severe weather, often shaped by a lack of basic knowledge of and experiences with severe weather, can alter perceptions of the hazards and dangers associated with severe weather events. Two surveys were administered, one in October 2024 and one in September 2025, to students, faculty, and staff at Iowa State University and assessed participants’ basic knowledge of severe weather (tornadoes, hurricanes, and wildfires), noted their previous experiences with those types of events, and evaluated their perceptions of the associated hazards. This study focuses on the differences observed between groups based on self-reported gender identity using a suite of statistical tests. While some small differences exist between groups in the overall basic knowledge of tornadoes, hurricanes, and wildfires, larger differences exist in their emotions related to, levels of preparedness for, and safety actions taken during these events, as well as how they receive weather information and alerts. Results from this study can inform professional meteorologists about the demographic differences in their audiences and the factors to consider when working to improve severe weather communication and to mitigate the number of annual weather-related fatalities.

487322.title: Compound Heat and Drought Severity Across Monsoon Regions During the 2023 Warm Season
487322.authors: Abby Alem, Pomona College, Claremont, CA; and R. Cheng
487322.abstract: Heatwaves (HWs)—periods of anomalously high temperature persisting for multiple consecutive days—are becoming more frequent, longer in duration, and more severe worldwide. When HWs co-occur with drought conditions, the resulting "hot drought," or compound drought-heatwave (CDHW) event, can trigger ecological and socioeconomic impacts far exceeding either hazard alone. Monsoon regions are uniquely vulnerable to these compound events: a weak or delayed monsoon season suppresses precipitation while solar heating continues, driving conditions favorable for simultaneous heat and moisture deficits. Across densely populated, monsoon-dependent regions of the world, CDHW events carry profound social costs (heat-related illness and mortality), agricultural costs (crop failure and livestock stress), and economic costs (strained energy and water systems). This research characterizes recent and historical CDHW severity across major global monsoon regions using the Climate Prediction Center's daily gridded temperature and precipitation dataset (1980–2023). Following an established detection framework, daytime and nighttime HWs are defined as periods of three or more consecutive days exceeding the calendar-day 80th percentile of maximum and minimum temperature, respectively, with severity quantified as the total accumulation above this threshold. Droughts are identified using the 12-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI12): a drought is classified as a period of two or more consecutive weeks where SPI12 values fall below or equal to a threshold of -0.5. Drought severity is quantified as the cumulative sum of SPI12 values across the event duration. CDHW events are defined as weeks in which a HW and drought are simultaneously active. We compute the percent change in 2023 CDHW severity relative to the 1980–2023 historical baseline to contextualize the anomalous nature of the 2023 warm season across these regions. Here, we present the preliminary analysis of CDHW vulnerabilities in global monsoon regions.

487323.title: HYDRO - A Framework for Localized Analysis of Sudden Hydroclimatic Shifts (FLASH): Climatology, Trends, and ENSO Influence across the CONUS
487323.authors: Yafang Zhong, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and J. A. Otkin, PhD, D. M. Anande, T. Gerken, P. C. Stoy, and T. W. Ford
487323.abstract: Rapid subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) hydroclimatic transitions, driven by severe fluctuations in atmospheric evaporative demand and precipitation, pose growing risks to agriculture and water resource management. This study introduces the Framework for Localized Analysis of Sudden Hydroclimatic Shifts (FLASH), a unified approach designed to systematically track four rapid-transition phenomena: flash drought (FD; rapid shift toward moisture deficit), flash pluvial (FP; rapid shift toward moisture surplus), flash recovery (FR; rapid drought termination), and flash drying (FDR; rapid removal of pluvial conditions). Utilizing soil moisture from a 1980–2022 reanalysis dataset, we quantify the climatology, long-term trends, and teleconnection influences across the contiguous U.S. (CONUS). Climatological analyses show season-dependent hot spots, with eastern regions maintaining a balanced frequency across all four event types, while the western and central U.S. skew toward wet extremes (FP and FDR). Spectral assessments demonstrate a west-to-east geographic gradient in characteristic frequencies, shifting from decadal regimes in the West to higher-frequency variations in the East. Long-term trend analyses reveal a systemic shift in FLASH metrics from 1980–2022, driven by a sharp seasonal divergence between the strengthening of rapid drying (FD, FDR) and the dampening of rapid wetting (FP, FR) in the western U.S., Midwest, and central Great Plains. Finally, teleconnection analyses show that ENSO primarily modulates the intensity of FLASH events rather than altering their occurrence frequency.

487328.title: Evaluation of Aerodynamic Resistance for Surface-Air Exchange Using National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) Observations
487328.authors: Xinhao Li, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA; and D. Pan
487328.abstract: Surface-air exchange is pivotal in regulating land-atmosphere interactions, surface energy balance, and the dry deposition of trace constituents such as reactive nitrogen (NH3, NOx) and ozone. Central to this exchange, aerodynamic resistance (Ra) serves as a foundational parameter in land surface models (LSMs) and chemical transport models (CTMs) to quantify turbulent fluxes. However, Ra has not been systematically evaluated across diverse ecosystems using observations because collocated multi-scalar vertical profile and flux observations have been historically scarce. Moreover, existing resistance schemes generally assume scalar-independent Ra based on Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory (MOST), although this assumption has rarely been evaluated using multi-scalar observations. In this study, we present a comprehensive, observation-based assessment of flux-gradient-inferred effective Ra using eddy covariance and multi-layer profile measurements from 47 terrestrial sites across the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) from 2017 to 2024.
