Incorporating vertical profiles of multiple scalars, including temperature (T), water vapor (H2O), and carbon dioxide (CO2), together with corresponding flux measurements yields observationally constrained effective Ra estimates for evaluating parameterization schemes used in LSMs and CTMs. Our results reveal pronounced biases in existing Ra schemes, characterized by systematic overestimation during daytime and underestimation at night. Modeled Ra deviates markedly from observation-derived estimates across different land-cover types, including forests, grasslands, and croplands. Furthermore, the effective Ra inferred from temperature differs substantially from those inferred from H2O and CO2, particularly over tall canopies, suggesting that conventional scalar-independent Ra does not fully capture canopy-scale turbulent transport with different vertical source or sink distributions and roughness sublayer processes. Our multi-scalar observational Ra evaluation provides practical constraints for improving resistance schemes in LSMs and CTMs. These findings underscore the necessity of refining Ra parameterizations, establishing a robust foundation for simulating boundary-layer turbulent fluxes and atmospheric emission and deposition processes over natural ecosystems.

487330.title: Does Climate Science Divide Us? New Approaches to Climate Change Framing and Motivation
487330.authors: Robert Winthrop, University of Maryland, College Park, MD
487330.abstract: Most scientists and politicians have treated climate change as a massive yet conventional environmental problem, caused by greenhouse gases rather than toxic chemicals. This approach made climate change a technical challenge for experts to define and solve, limiting the citizen's role to compliance. Sound climate science is essential for progress on climate change mitigation and adaptation. Unfortunately, ac­curate information and a logical argument alone do little to motivate useful climate action. Affect needs to be part of the strategy. Climate science must inform policy but science alone can neither frame the problem nor define the goals of policy in ways that are politically effective. This poses a serious challenge for meteorologists and other atmospheric science professionals, who have a central role in communicating to the public both the facts of climate change and the opportunities for constructive action. The dominant science-centric approach to climate policy and communication has several drawbacks. First, it emphasizes highly technical objectives (such as a goal of “net zero” greenhouse gas emis­sions) that lack cultural salience and fail to build public consensus. Second, mainstream policy is anti-motivational, demanding individual sacrifice through major economic change now in return for the promised benefits of a more moderate climate trajectory decades in the future. Third, by framing global warming almost exclusively around technical objectives remote from everyday human experience, the politics of climate action has been doomed to a duel over abstractions, ask­ing: do you believe in climate change? This fosters a lack of trust between climate advocates and the skeptics they target for persuasion. Anthropogenic climate change is actually the reflection of a coupled human – natural system: it is fundamentally a social problem with enormous environmental consequences. Some key implications of this distinction for climate communication and mitigation strategies are explored. A more effective strategy for fostering climate-positive action requires shifting from a psychological to a socially grounded approach, from in­dividual to collective agency, and from thin reason to a more comprehensive view of knowledge and motivation. Effective motivation for climate mitigation is more likely to emerge when framed as a co-benefit of other objectives (from cleaner air to self-reliance or maintaining a valued way of life) that evoke deeper public support. Rather than limiting climate communication to the transmission of scientific data and arguments, a better approach involves the interaction of climate professionals with other citizens by exploring opportunities for more satisfactory ways of living under a changing climate regime. Rather than compliance, solutions require citizen engagement, innovation, and mobilization in dialog with disciplinary expertise, an expression of post-normal science.

487331.title: Weather Intelligence for Road Transportation and Electric Vehicle Decisions: Applications from the CLEETS Global Center
487331.authors: Ashish Sharma, Discovery Partners Institute, University of Illinois Urbana Champaign, Chicago, IL; and S. Wu, A. Wadhwa, P. Li, O. Rana, N. Hamed, L. Cipcigan, M. Albano, R. Gjomemo, A. Satish Kumar, Y. Xu, F. Yao, and K. Vohra
487331.abstract: Extreme weather increasingly affects transportation systems, electric vehicle (EV) performance, energy demand, infrastructure resilience, and community well-being. The NSF–UKRI Global Center for Clean Energy and Equitable Transportation Solutions (CLEETS) is developing integrated decision-support tools that combine high-resolution weather intelligence, artificial intelligence, Earth observations, and transportation analytics to improve the resilience of our mobility systems. This study highlights operational applications being developed at the CLEETS data science cross-cutting thrust with examples across the US and UK. Some of these applications include: (i) a geospatial tool for identifying flood-resilient locations for alternative-fuel and EV infrastructure across Illinois (FuelPlanner); (ii) a high-resolution weather intelligence platform for real-time transportation impact assessment and weather-aware route optimization (AerisIQ); (iii) an agent-based modeling framework for evaluating travel behavior, journey optimization, EV battery performance, and charging demand across the US and UK (CLEETS-ABM); and (iv) a near-real-time flood-informed routing system for South Wales and the West Midlands (CLEETS-SMART). Together, these applications demonstrate how weather intelligence can improve traveler safety, increase EV reliability, support resilient infrastructure investments, and promote equitable access to clean transportation. The work illustrates CLEETS' interdisciplinary approach to integrating atmospheric science, transportation engineering, artificial intelligence, and community-centered planning to accelerate the transition toward cleaner, more resilient, and more equitable transportation systems.

487349.title: Comparing Quantile Conserving and Gaussian Ensemble Filters for Boundary Layer Data Assimilation.
487349.authors: Stephen Asare, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and H. G. Chipilski and J. Kay
487349.abstract: As convective-scale data assimilation (DA) pushes the limits of traditional Gaussian-based algorithms, non-Gaussian methods are increasingly necessary to accurately represent complex, non linear boundary layer processes. This study investigates the impacts of non-Gaussian DA through a series of highly controlled, Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs), systematically comparing Quantile Conserving Ensemble Filters (QCEF) against the standard Ensemble Adjustment Kalman Filter (EAKF). Focusing on single-profiler DA experiments, we quantify the impacts of thermodynamic and kinematic variables on the analysis. To rigorously evaluate the behavior of each filter, we first quantify the spatial non-Gaussianity of the prior ensembles to identify regions where traditional assumptions degrade. Filter performance is then assessed by comparing observation-space prior and posterior distributions, root-mean-square error (RMSE), and ensemble spread. Furthermore, we evaluate how different ensemble filters update unobserved state variables, which depends both on the observation-space update and type of regression in QCEF. By examining the analysis increments, this study provides the first comparison between QCEF and EAKF in their effectiveness to assimilate boundary layer profilers.

487350.title: Impact of Skin Temperature Parameterization on MJO Simulations
487350.authors: Shan Sun, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and W. Li
487350.abstract: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) remains a major source of global predictability on subseasonal-to-seasonal timescales, yet state-of-the-art global weather and climate models frequently struggle to simulate its initiation and propagation. A key source of model uncertainty is from the representation of upper-ocean diurnal variability, particularly the amplitude of diurnal skin sea surface temperature, which modulates surface energy fluxes. In this study, we utilize coupled Unified Forecast System (UFS) simulations to investigate MJO events observed during the CINDY/DYNAMO field campaign. We compare two distinct parameterization schemes for skin temperature: NSST and Skinsst and examine how variations in diurnal amplitude of skin sea surface temperature alter the diurnal cycle of surface latent heat flux and quantify its downstream impacts on MJO intraseasonal variability. Using a budget analysis of atmospheric moist static energy, we track the diurnal evolution and vertical distribution of heat and moisture within the column in the latest UFS with the inclusion of large‐scale moisture‐flux convergence. Our results demonstrate how accumulated diurnal flux biases influence deep convection. By pinpointing these systematic errors within the daily cycle, this work provides a process-based roadmap for refining air-sea coupling, improving tropical energy representations, and enhancing MJO forecasting skill in the UFS.

487363.title: An Ensemble-Based Framework for Inverse Design of Weather Interventions
487363.authors: Kenta Kurosawa, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD
487363.abstract: Forecast uncertainty poses a major challenge for designing effective weather interventions. We present an ensemble-based model predictive control framework that directly exploits ensemble forecasts to optimize intervention strategies without requiring tangent linear or adjoint models. The framework combines data assimilation with ensemble prediction to sequentially estimate flow-dependent control inputs. We demonstrate the approach using a convection-permitting numerical weather prediction model for the August 2021 extreme rainfall event over Japan. Idealized offshore drag forcing is optimized to reduce downstream precipitation. Across five independent experiments with different observation-noise realizations, the proposed framework consistently reduces accumulated precipitation over the target region by approximately 23%, while producing reproducible intervention locations and spatially robust precipitation reductions. These results demonstrate that forecast uncertainty can be utilized as a resource for robust weather intervention design in realistic atmospheric systems.

487369.title: Tropical Cyclone Clustering Probability Based on Environmental Conditions
487369.authors: Adam C. Burnett, New York University, New York, NY; and E. P. Gerber
487369.abstract: Do tropical cyclones (TCs) tend to cluster together or spread apart? We investigate whether the presence of a TC makes other TCs more or less likely to form nearby. Some mechanisms of TC genesis, such as the rolling-up of the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ), can give rise to several TCs at once in the same region. On the other hand, as a TC passes, it leaves in its wake a drier atmosphere and cooler sea surface temperatures (SSTs), which are unfavorable conditions for additional TCs. By analyzing best-track data, we find that TC genesis is significantly more likely given the presence of another TC track in the vicinity. This result naively suggests that TCs tend to cluster, but neglects the fact that the presence of TC tracks is correlated with large-scale environmental conditions, such as SST, vertical wind shear, and absolute vorticity, that are favorable for TC formation. To control for these correlations, we model TC genesis probability using a variety of environmental fields and genesis potential indices (GPIs) based on reanalysis and observational data. We first explore the simplest possible version of a GPI. Using linear regression, we find that SST and precipitation explain much of the variance in TC frequency. Because TCs are discrete rare events, Poisson regression is better suited to this problem and provides an improved fit. The inclusion of additional environmental fields, however, provides only a small improvement. More complex regression methods, such as zero-inflated Poisson regression, random forests, and multi-layer perceptrons, also provide only small improvements over Poisson regression. Exploring a range of GPI models of varying complexity, we consistently find that TCs tend to cluster, even after controlling for the influence of environmental conditions. Our findings suggest that there exist additional environmental conditions correlated with TC activity that are not captured in the GPIs, which may include a dynamical tendency toward clustering of TC genesis. In addition, these relatively simple probability models are physically motivated and provide a benchmark for TC genesis probability as a function of environmental conditions.

487378.title: Changing Dynamics of Monsoon Depression–Induced Extreme Rainfall and Its Impact over the Indian Region
487378.authors: Riti Shrivastava, IITM, Pashan, Pune, Maharashtra, India
487378.abstract: Monsoon depressions (MDs) and Deep Depressions (DDs), whose windspeeds are between 17-27 knots and 28-33 knots, is one of the most important rainfall induced phenomena in India that can cause great damage. They are among the primary synoptic systems that are responsible for moisture transport in the Indian Summer Monsoon Rainfall. A decline of approximately 15% in the strong MDs have been highlighted in current research, although catastrophic rainfall events connected to these systems have heightened due to westward track shifts and enhanced atmospheric moisture availability. Extreme rainfall events linked to monsoon depressions have repeatedly led to devastating floods, crop losses, displacement, and widespread economic disruption across eastern and central India. These patterns highlight the urgent need to examine both the climatic drivers and the socioeconomic consequences of such events, especially as future warming is expected to intensify these risks. Despite the importance, the rainfall and spatial trend around the track of the storm is less studied. This study develops a storm centred detailed study of rainfall in and around each storm point. The main research question of this study is how are the intensity, frequency, and spatial dynamics of monsoon depression–induced extreme rainfall events changing under historical and future climate forcing, and how might these shifts affect the socioeconomic conditions of vulnerable regions across India? This study tracks MDs and DDs, each year in June, July, August and September months (JJAS) from 2001-2025 (25 years) and studies their relationship with rainfall patterns in and around each storm point (every 24 hours). The storm tracking is through the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) Best Track dataset. High-resolution Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) gridded rainfall data are combined with best tracks to characterize rainfall within a fixed 2 degree-radius footprint surrounding the evolving storm center. A suite of diagnostics is employed to quantify storm rainfall characteristics, including core-versus-periphery rainfall distribution, maximum rainfall and its displacement from the storm center, quadrant-wise rainfall asymmetry, total storm rainfall volume, and intensity-based metrics such as the 95th and 99th percentile rainfall. Track-based rainfall footprints are used to examine how precipitation evolves throughout the storm lifecycle and to identify regions where extreme rainfall preferentially occurs. In addition, annual and seasonal variations in storm-associated rainfall characteristics are analyzed to investigate changes in the contribution of monsoon depressions to extreme precipitation over India. The preliminary analysis of the eight Bay of Bengal-origin monsoon depressions during the 2025 monsoon season reveals substantial event-to-event variability in rainfall intensity, accumulation, and spatial distribution. While some systems produced exceptionally high accumulated rainfall and rainfall volumes, others generated localized but intense precipitation, demonstrating that storm severity cannot be captured by a single metric. The results suggest that storm evolution, propagation, and persistence strongly influence the magnitude and spatial extent of extreme rainfall. These findings highlight the importance of a multi-metric framework—including rainfall intensity, spatial coverage, rainfall volume, and extreme percentile statistics—to comprehensively characterize monsoon depression impacts. The quantified rainfall footprints also provide a foundation for future assessments linking evolving monsoon depression behavior with flood exposure, agricultural losses, and socioeconomic vulnerability across India.

487379.title: Aerosol–Boundary Layer Interactions under Urban Expansion Intensify Storms and Flood Risk in the Texas Triangle (Invited Presentation)
487379.authors: Paola Crippa, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN; Univ. of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN; and G. Moraglia and M. Aboelnour
487379.abstract: Rapid urban expansion across the Texas Triangle is expected to modify atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) structure, aerosol loading, and regional hydro-meteorological hazards, yet the coupled interactions among ABL dynamics, atmospheric chemistry, convection, and runoff remain insufficiently constrained. This study investigates how projected end-of-century urban growth influences extreme precipitation and flood susceptibility using the Weather Research and Forecasting model with chemistry (WRF-Chem) coupled to a stochastic flood-risk framework. Two high-impact storms, a cold-season frontal system and a prolonged warm-season convective event, are simulated under present-day and future urban-expansion scenarios, with identical meteorological boundary conditions to isolate urban induced effects. Results show that urbanization-driven aerosol perturbations, through their interaction with the evolving urban boundary layer, rather than land-surface changes alone, dominate precipitation responses. In the cold-season event, expanded urban emissions enhance activation of accumulation-mode cloud condensation nuclei, within the mixed layer, increasing latent heat flux and strengthening convective updrafts, leading to statistically significant precipitation increases over San Antonio and Austin. In contrast, the warm-season storm exhibits a heterogeneous response over Dallas–Fort Worth, with early aerosol-driven enhancement of western precipitation followed by reduced buoyancy and suppressed rainfall to the east as storm evolution progresses over the enlarged urban footprint. Coupled hydrological analysis indicates that these precipitation changes mediated by ABL–chemistry interactions translate into a systematic expansion of high-runoff and flood-prone areas. Both WRF-Chem diagnostics and a stochastic SCS-CN framework identify amplification of existing flood-risk hotspots and emergence of new vulnerable zones. Importantly, the simulated aerosol-induced convective invigoration likely represents a conservative lower bound due to unresolved supersaturation at subgrid scales. While limited to two storms, this work demonstrates a scalable, process-based framework linking urban growth, ABL evolution, atmospheric chemistry, aerosol–cloud interactions, and flood risk. The results highlight increasing hydro-meteorological vulnerability in rapidly urbanizing regions and underscore the need for explicit representation of ABL–chemistry coupling in integrated modeling approaches to assess future extremes under combined urbanization and climate change.

487382.title: The Antarctic Boundary Layer from the High Plateau to the Coast - Insights from Recent Field Measurements and Parameterization Developments in a Climate Model (Invited Presentation)
487382.authors: Étienne Vignon, CNRS - LMD, Paris, France
487382.abstract: The Antarctic Boundary Layer from the High Plateau to the Coast — Insights from Recent Field Measurements and Parameterization Developments in a Climate Model Étienne Vignon, Valentin Wiener, Justine Charrel, Pierre Tiengou, Alexis Berne and Christophe Genthon Although the Antarctic ice sheet is a very homogeneous ice and snow desert, the atmospheric boundary layer is highly contrasted between the High Plateau, the escarpment slopes, and the coastal margins. While the boundary layer over the flat, pristine High Plateau is extremely stable—with probably the strongest near-surface temperature inversions on Earth—very strong near-surface katabatic winds flow down the ice sheet slopes, eroding the snow surface and transporting large quantities of blowing snow. The katabatic boundary layer then undergoes a sharp and highly turbulent transition at the coast, a so-called ‘katabatic jump’, when the continental outflow meets the marine boundary layer. Conducting meteorological and turbulence measurements in this extreme boundary layer is particularly challenging due to the harsh climate conditions, especially during the cold polar night and in remote locations far from the few scientific bases. Despite its importance for both polar and global climate, the Antarctic boundary layer remains particularly difficult to simulate in climate models, as it pushes physical parameterizations to their limits. In this presentation, we will present recent results obtained from the analysis of valuable and original observations collected by autonomous measurement platforms deployed along a coast-to-Plateau transect in Adélie Land, East Antarctica, as part of the AWACA project (awaca.ipsl.fr/en/). After meticulously processing sonic anemometer data, the properties of turbulence in the surface layer at four contrasting sites have been investigated and reveal similar spectral behaviors, despite very different stability conditions and anisotropy regimes. We will also present recent developments that have been performed to improve the representation the boundary-layer dynamics in the LMDZ general circulation model after a careful evaluation with in situ observations. These developments range from improvements to the turbulent diffusion parameterization—to capture the very stable regime on the Plateau and avoid numerical oscillations in katabatic flows—to the introduction of a blowing snow parameterization. We will then propose recommendations for simulating the katabatic boundary layer, addressing model resolution, parameterization calibration, and choices. Finally, we will suggest avenues for further development, particularly to improve the abrupt coastal transition of the boundary layer.

487390.title: Subsidized Crop Insurance
487390.authors: Homa Taheri, Indiana University Bloomington, Chicago, IL
487390.abstract: Subsidized crop insurance is a central tool for managing weather-related production risk in U.S. agriculture, yet its effects on production, climate vulnerability, and public spending remain uncertain. I study how crop insurance enrollment affects agricultural production and determine the subsidy rate that maximizes social welfare. Using a county-crop-year panel of corn and soybeans in the U.S. Midwest from 1996 to 2025, I find that higher enrollment increases mean yield, with an estimated elasticity of approximately 0.08. At the average insured share, a 0.10 increase in enrollment raises yield by about 1 percent. Enrollment also increases borrowing through the Commodity Credit Corporation, consistent with insurance relaxing farmers’ credit and liquidity constraints. Despite these production effects, I find no evidence that greater insurance participation increases yield sensitivity to extreme heat, yield variance, or downside risk. Estimates for the intensive margin of insurance coverage are small and unstable and do not become more adverse under extreme heat. These findings provide little evidence that subsidized insurance encourages climate-related production moral hazard. I then use a sufficient statistics framework to evaluate alternative subsidy rates. A benchmark that considers farmers’ risk-protection benefits alone implies an optimal subsidy of zero. Accounting for reductions in government disaster-relief payments raises the optimal subsidy to 39 percent, compared with an observed average buy-up subsidy rate of approximately 57 percent. When the credit-related production benefits of insurance are also included, the optimal subsidy can exceed the observed rate. The results show how the design of crop-insurance subsidies depends on whether policymakers account for interactions among climate risk, agricultural credit, production, and disaster assistance.

487391.title: Predictability of Interannual Variations in East Asian Summer Rainfall under the Combined Influence of Active Monsoon and Landfalling Tropical Cyclones
487391.authors: Fei Zhang, Fudan University, Shanghai, 31, China; and Z. Wu
487391.abstract: East Asian summer rainfall (EASR) exhibits substantial spatial and temporal diversity. One of its prominent and impactful forms is monsoon–TC landfall (MS-LTC) rainfall, which occurs when the East Asian summer monsoon (EASM) coincides with landfalling tropical cyclones (TCs) and typically leads to extreme rainfall and flooding over China. However, the physical mechanisms governing MS-LTC rainfall and its seasonal predictability remain poorly understood. Observations from 1983 to 2023 show that the leading mode of MS-LTC rainfall is dominated by interannual variability, featuring two anomaly centers located over the Western North Pacific (WNP) and North China, and associated with a meridional dipole circulation over East Asia (EA), comprising a low-latitude cyclone and a mid-latitude anticyclone. Two independent and physically meaningful precursors have been identified: Arctic sea ice concentration (SIC) anomalies over the Greenland and Barents Seas, and cold sea surface temperature anomalies (SSTAs) in the far eastern equatorial Pacific (Niño1+2 region). The Arctic SIC anomalies can persist from the preceding winter through summer, primarily maintained by the sea ice–albedo feedback and the ocean memory effect over the Greenland and Barents Seas, respectively. Both observations and numerical experiments demonstrate that these anomalies excite a downstream Rossby wave train, facilitating the development of the meridional dipole pattern over EA. Concurrently, La Niña–like SST cooling induces a baroclinic response over EA that exhibits a circulation structure opposite to the Pacific–East Asia (PEA) teleconnection, thereby sustaining the dipole pattern. A physics-based empirical prediction (P-E) model that combines MAM SIC and JFM Niño1+2 indices achieves the highest skill in predicting MS-LTC PC1 during the hindcast period. This P-E model provides a physically grounded and operationally feasible tool for the seasonal prediction of MS-LTC rainfall.

487394.title: Present and Future Spatio-Temporal Characteristics of European Supercells in 2.2-km grid Simulations
487394.authors: Abdullah Kahraman, Newcastle University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NBL, United kingdom; and H. J. Fowler, C. Short, E. J. Kendon, and K. Halladay
487394.abstract: Supercells occasionally bring very large hail, tornadoes, severe wind gusts, heavy rain and excessive lightning in Europe, yet not much is known about them compared to the US supercells, largely owing to the absence of a pan-European radial-velocity product and convection-permitting simulations with supercell-relevant diagnostics configured within the climate framework. The Met Office has conducted a new set of 2.2-km grid simulations over a pan-European domain, covering 30 years in total. New diagnostics calculated at every time step enable investigation of the comparatively understudied characteristics of European supercells. We use updraft-helicity tracks to examine storms’ spatio-temporal evolution throughout their lifetimes for the first time, alongside changes in environmental conditions and hazard-related metrics. The study will compare the general characteristics and associated hazards of supercells in the present climate and a high-emissions future, thereby improving understanding of European supercell climatology, its response to global warming, and the links between supercell outbreaks and large-scale atmospheric circulation.

487395.title: Advancing Assimilation of Data From Uncrewed Systems to Improve Tropical Cyclone Forecasts
487395.authors: Jason A. Sippel, NOAA, College Park, MD; AOML, Miami, FL; and H. S. Kim, Z. Zhang, A. Aksoy, D. Wu, S. Ditchek, K. Sellwood, and H. kang
487395.abstract: This presentation will review efforts at NOAA to improve tropical cyclone forecasts by assimilating data from uncrewed systems (UxS). From 2022-2025, NOAA successfully released nearly 50 small uncrewed aircraft systems (sUAS) during P-3 reconnaissance missions into a total of 10 tropical cyclones. The sUAS missions typically gather observations low in the hurricane planetary boundary layer (PBL), where crewed missions cannot safely fly. Retrospective testing in both experimental and operational hurricane models has revealed that assimilating sUAS observations significantly modifies the tropical cyclone (TC) inner-core structure and positively impacts track and intensity forecasts. The data will be assimilated operationally into NOAA’s Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) for the first time in 2026. Preliminary testing with other UxS, including uncrewed surface vehicles (USVs) has also demonstrated positive impacts on TC forecasts. Meanwhile, several recent case studies have also shown that assimilating glider data positively impacts ocean analyses, though their impacts on TC atmospheric forecasts have been mixed. The presentation will conclude with a vision for a coupled version of NOAA’s HAFS model, where atmospheric and subsurface UxS are expected to jointly improve TC forecasts.

487397.title: Hybridizing Ensemble Score and Kalman Filters for Improved Assimilation of Partially Observed Systems
487397.authors: Hristo G. Chipilski, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and Z. Xiong, F. Bao, S. Liang, J. Tang, and G. Zhang
487397.abstract: Training-free, diffusion-based ensemble data assimilation (DA) methods like the Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) have recently shown promising results for estimating nonlinear dynamical systems. However, observation networks characterized by extreme spatial sparsity remain challenging because unobserved state variables are not directly constrained by the available observations. To address this limitation, we introduce the Ensemble Score Filter with Linear Regression (EnSF-LR). At each analysis time, EnSF-LR first applies the standard EnSF to update observed state components. Similar to other two-step ensemble filters, it then uses linear regression based on the empirical prior covariance matrix to update the remaining unobserved variables. This presentation will demonstrate the benefits of the resulting hybrid DA algorithm through idealized experiments with Lorenz models. Comparisons against standard ensemble Kalman filters (EnKFs) will focus on the large-ensemble limit, allowing approximation accuracy to be distinguished from the effects of sampling error.

487398.title: Instability-Aware Atmospheric River Intervention using Differentiable AI Weather Foundation Models
487398.authors: Moyan Liu, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ; and Q. Huang and U. lall
487398.abstract: Deep learning weather foundation models provide a new opportunity to investigate the controllability of complex atmospheric systems. By learning high-dimensional spatiotemporal dynamics directly from Earth system data, these models not only achieve state-of-the-art weather prediction but also provide differentiable representations that enable gradient-based analysis and control. Atmospheric rivers (ARs), whose evolution is sensitive to upstream conditions, provide an ideal testbed for exploring targeted intervention strategies. We develop an instability-aware framework for atmospheric river (AR) intervention using Aurora, a differentiable AI weather foundation model. The framework incorporates two complementary approaches for exploring atmospheric sensitivity. First, finite-time Lyapunov exponent (FTLE) analysis identifies dynamically unstable upstream regions where small perturbations are naturally amplified along atmospheric transport pathways. Second, we employ the model adjoint to quantify the sensitivity of downstream AR impacts to localized perturbations, capturing the coupled dynamical and thermodynamic processes governing atmospheric evolution. Together, these complementary sensitivity analyses provide the foundation for developing a sparsity-promoting optimization framework that identifies a minimal set of intervention locations and nudging strengths to achieve targeted attenuation of AR impacts with low intervention energy. We demonstrate the framework on a California atmospheric river event. FTLE and adjoint analyses provide complementary perspectives on atmospheric sensitivity: FTLE highlights regions of intrinsic instability, while the adjoint quantifies objective-specific sensitivities associated with downstream impacts. These insights inform the design of sparse, multi-site intervention strategies that efficiently reduce AR impacts. This work establishes a general framework for exploring atmospheric controllability using differentiable AI weather foundation models, with potential applications in extreme weather mitigation, hazard reduction, and future climate intervention research.

487399.title: Comparison of GNSS-Derived and ERA5 Precipitable Water over Poland
487399.authors: Michał Jerzy Mierzwiak, Military University of Technology, Warsaw, MZ, Poland; Military University of Technology, Warsaw, MZ, Poland; and A. Araszkiewicz, K. Dzwonkowski, and J. Siewert
487399.abstract: GNSS-derived precipitable water (PW) products are widely used in weather monitoring and atmospheric research, while their relevance to climate studies continues to increase as progressively longer and more homogeneous GNSS time series become available. However, the quality of GNSS-derived PW depends on the adopted observation models, processing strategy, and the accuracy of the meteorological parameters used to convert zenith wet delay into precipitable water. The objective of this study was to assess the agreement between precipitable water (PW) derived from ground-based GNSS observations and ERA5 reanalysis data over Poland from January 2025 onward. GNSS observations from approximately 100 stations of the Polish ASG-EUPOS network were processed using the GAMIT/GLOBK software. The applied geophysical modelling included the FES2014b ocean tide model and atmospheric loading based on ECMWF data. Tropospheric delays were modelled using the Vienna Mapping Functions 1 (VMF1). Zenith tropospheric delays estimated from GNSS observations were converted into PW using surface pressure and temperature data from ERA5. The resulting GNSS-derived PW series were compared with ERA5 total column water vapour values at individual stations and across the entire network. The analysis included temporal agreement, systematic differences, correlation, and the spatial distribution of discrepancies between the two datasets. The preliminary results demonstrate the ability of a dense GNSS network to reproduce the temporal and spatial variability of atmospheric water vapour under unusual conditions. They also provide an initial assessment of the consistency between independently derived GNSS and ERA5 PW products and reveal regional and temporal patterns in their differences. These findings constitute a basis for extending the analysis to longer time periods, with particular emphasis on the stability of GNSS-derived PW series, the consistency of long-term PW changes observed by GNSS and ERA5, and the identification of regional trends potentially associated with climate variability and climate change. The study therefore contributes to evaluating the suitability of GNSS-derived PW not only for high-resolution atmospheric monitoring and validation of numerical weather and reanalysis products, but also for future climate-oriented analyses over Poland.

487401.title: A Citizen Science Co-Learning Framework to FIll Critical Data Gaps in Remote High-Altitude Regions
487401.authors: Michael P Crowe, Meteorological Service of Canada, Ottawa, ON, Canada; and L. Bharati, D. Kayastha, S. Mandahar, D. Pradhananga, R. Rajkarnikar, R. Roberge, and J. Smith
487401.abstract: High-altitude environmental monitoring is critically needed as climate change and extreme weather disasters increasingly threaten water security, food security, biodiversity, and mountain communities. Previous efforts to establish Automated Weather Stations (AWS) in these remote regions have often proved unsustainable due to the challenges of maintaining and servicing equipment. The High-altitude Monasteries for Data Acquisition, Tracking and Awareness (HiM-DATA) initiative proposes an innovative citizen science and co-learning approach in Nepal that leverages the strategic location of Himalayan monasteries as sites for AWS installations. Many monasteries are situated in remote, high-altitude areas, are occupied year-round, and provide secure, accessible locations for long-term environmental monitoring. As trusted community hubs, they also provide an ideal setting for reciprocal learning, bringing together scientists, monks, nuns, teachers, students, and local communities to exchange knowledge about the changing mountain environment. This collaboration creates opportunities to integrate scientific observations with generations of traditional Indigenous and local environmental knowledge, enriching the interpretation of climate trends and strengthening community awareness and adaptation through the monastic tradition of education and knowledge sharing. By training monks, nuns, teachers, and students to operate and maintain AWS equipment, interpret environmental data, and contribute local observations, HiM-DATA aims to establish a sustainable monitoring network while overcoming many of the logistical and administrative barriers that have limited previous initiatives, including site access and permitting challenges within protected areas. While Himalayan monasteries in Nepal are the initial implementation sites, the HiM-DATA model is designed as a transferable framework that can be adapted to other trusted community institutions—including schools, health posts, ranger stations, municipalities, research stations, clubs, and community centres—in remote mountain regions worldwide. By fostering enduring local partnerships, HiM-DATA will fill critical environmental data gaps, improve understanding of high-altitude weather and climate processes, and strengthen mountain weather forecasting and multi-hazard early warning systems, benefiting both scientific research and mountain communities.

487402.title: Exascale Generative Data Assimilation for Global and Regional Weather Prediction
487402.authors: Hristo G. Chipilski, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and G. Zhang, X. Wang, Z. Zhang, I. Lyngaas, H. J. Yoon, J. Y. Choi, S. Liang, J. Wang, A. M. Aji, F. Bao, P. J. van Leeuwen, and D. Lu
487402.abstract: We present a generative data assimilation (DA) approach in which the analysis is obtained by drawing samples from the atmospheric state distribution conditioned on available observations and historical states. This formulation treats DA as a single conditional inference problem rather than as a sequence of separate forecast and analysis steps. The method is built around STORM, a spatiotemporal transformer designed to efficiently represent multiscale atmospheric dependencies. A linear-scaling global attention mechanism enables information exchange over large spatial domains without the quadratic computational cost of conventional attention. The implementation scales to 32,768 GPUs on the Frontier supercomputer and sustains 1.6 exaFLOP/s. Experiments using ERA5 and HRRR demonstrate that the resulting system produces probabilistic state estimates that are both accurate and stable over time. The results show encouraging performance for hurricane track and intensity prediction, as well as for regional forecasts of near-surface temperature at kilometer-scale resolution.

487410.title: Global Crowd-Sourced, Resolution-Flexible Urban Parameters for Earth System Modeling with Local Climate Zone Representation
487410.authors: Yuan Sun, The University of Manchester, Manchester, United kingdom; and Y. Cheng, K. Oleson, L. Zhao, M. Demuzere, G. Mills, C. He, D. O. Topping, C. Jay, S. Lindley, and Z. Zheng
487410.abstract: Urban climate adaptation is an increasingly critical need for cities worldwide. However, accurately estimating the global extent of urban areas and characterizing their physical properties remains challenging. The local climate zone (LCZ) framework has emerged as a powerful bridge between the climate science community and broader adaptation actors, facilitating a shared understanding of urban climate and supporting adaptation through standardized land-surface characteristics. Current implementations of LCZ-based urban land-cover representation in physical-process-based numerical simulations primarily adopt a look-up table approach, in which each built LCZ class is assigned a single set of urban parameter values. This simplification neglects the variability within LCZs across cities and regions, thereby limiting their representativeness of local urban heterogeneity for large-scale urban climate simulations. This study develops a global LCZ-based two-dimensional urban parameter dataset, LCZ-PARAM2D, for simulating urban climate in Earth system models with relatively coarse grid spacing. Being crowdsourced rather than generated from scratch, LCZ-PARAM2D offers a cost-efficient approach to secondary development based on established high-resolution global LCZ maps and urban parameter datasets. This LCZ-based urban parameter dataset reveals variability across 3,598 global urban areas and 401 socio-climatic background regions. The standard dataset is resolved by a standard grid spacing of 0.05° (～5 km), while remaining flexible for user customization. It is intended to contribute not only to improving the scientific basis of urban climate modeling but also to supporting interdisciplinary collaboration and climate adaptation planning at scales ranging from global to local.

487414.title: Validation of Temperature, Water Vapor and Carbon Trace Gas Profile Retrievals from the NOAA Unique Combined Atmospheric Processing System (NUCAPS)
487414.authors: Jeff T. Szkodzinski, STAR, Glen Burnie, MD; and M. G. Divakarla, T. Zhu, M. Kulko, T. Wang, and K. L. Pryor
487414.abstract: This study provides an overview of the validation of operational retrievals of atmospheric temperature, water vapor, and carbon trace gases, namely carbon monoxide (CO), methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2), from the NOAA Unique Combined Atmospheric Processing System (NUCAPS). It utilizes data from the Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS), and the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) onboard the NOAA operational low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites, including the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (SNPP) and Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) series with NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. The CrIS sensor is an infrared Fourier transform spectrometer that measures Earth radiance spectra. These observations are processed by NUCAPS to retrieve three-dimensional atmospheric profiles of temperature, water vapor, and trace gases under non-precipitating (clear to partly cloudy) conditions. The NUCAPS atmospheric vertical temperature profile (AVTP) and atmospheric vertical moisture profile (AVMP) EDRs are validated against well-established independent truth datasets, primarily radiosonde data obtained from the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS) Reference Upper-Air Network (GRUAN) and the U.S. Department of Energy’s Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility. NUCAPS CO, CH4 and CO2 profile EDRs are compared to total column data from ground-based Total Carbon Column Observing Network (TCCON) sites. This research provides an overview of the statistical analyses and metrics used to validate NUCAPS sounding retrievals against ground truth datasets. The current work that is underway is an integral component of validating the robustness of the NUCAPS algorithm against global JPSS performance requirements. Various agencies, NWS forecasters, stakeholders, field campaigns and the broader user community who utilize hyperspectral datasets rely heavily on the availability of high quality atmospheric profiles for operational and research purposes.

487417.title: Advancing the Next Generation of Hurricane Prediction: The Role of the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS)
487417.authors: Sundararaman Gopalakrishnan, AOML, Miami, FL; NOAA/AOML/HRD, Miami, FL; AOML, Miami, MA; and W. Ramstrom, L. J. Gramer, A. Hazelton, W. Komaromi, A. Poyer, and G. J. Alaka Jr.
487417.abstract: Advancing the Next Generation of Hurricane Prediction: The Role of the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) Presenter: Sundararaman Gopalakrishnan Co-Authors: William Ramstrom, Lew Gramer, Andrew Hazelton, William Komaromi and Aaron Poyer Since its launch in 2009, NOAA’s Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program (HFIP) has reduced hurricane track and intensity forecast errors by over 50%, including similar reductions during rapidly intensifying storms. While key forecast metrics—track, intensity, and size—remain vital, there is growing demand from emergency managers and the public for more actionable guidance on hazards associated with landfalling storms. Damaging impacts—wind gusts, flash flooding, and tornadoes—often occur not in the eyewall but in the rainbands. As development of the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) accelerates, a key question is emerging: Can HAFS provide reliable guidance for severe weather hazards associated with tropical cyclones? To answer this, it’s essential to evaluate not only the inner-core structure but also the model’s ability to represent rainbands, including precipitation. At HRD, an advanced experimental version of HAFS is being tested in real time under HFIP during the 2024, 2025, and 2026 hurricane seasons. This multi-storm configuration, unlike the operational storm-centered HAFS, uses a fixed parent domain within the basin and moving nests to track any number of hurricanes simultaneously at 2 km resolution. It has already shown significant track and intensity improvements, particularly from storm-storm interactions, and may be especially well-suited for capturing land-storm interactions and severe tropical weather over land. The basin-scale HAFS at 2 km shows potential for operations by 2028. More recently, the modeling group at HRD created telescopic nests that enable sub-km-scale HAFS, setting up convection-resolving HAFS predictions possible for the first time. We will discuss the T&E results of the basin-scale HAFS at 2 km and beyond. Furthermore, we will examine how sub-km-scale HAFS can enhance predictions for hazards such as rainfall, wind gusts, and tornadic events associated with landfalling storms (e.g., Hurricanes Beryl, Milton, Helene).

487419.title: Bayesian Estimation of Microphysical Parameter Uncertainty with Ensemble Conjugate Transform Inversion (ECTI)
487419.authors: Hristo G. Chipilski, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and D. J. Posselt
487419.abstract: One of the major challenges in cloud and precipitation modeling is the presence of bounded quantities. For example, precipitation amounts are inherently non-negative and often exhibit highly skewed distributions near their lower bounds. Similar constraints apply to cloud microphysical parameters, which govern the evolution of cloud processes in Earth system models. As a result, parameter estimation methods based on linear/Gaussian assumptions frequently struggle to accurately calibrate these microphysical parameters from cloud-sensitive observations. In this talk, we investigate the feasibility of a newly developed inversion algorithm — the Ensemble Conjugate Transform Inversion (ECTI) — for estimating microphysical parameters within a single-column cloud model. ECTI builds on a recent generalization of Kalman filter theory to non-Gaussian distributions (Chipilski 2025) and leverages generative AI methods. We highlight the advantages of ECTI implementations that incorporate different normalizing flows and compare their performance against the benchmark Ensemble Kalman Inversion (EKI) as well as other nonlinear generalizations.

487420.title: Meteotsunami Three Ways: Dissecting the May 2025 Lake Michigan Event Using SWOT, in-situ Observations, and Hydrodynamic Modeling
487420.authors: Alexa Yeo, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO
487420.abstract: On May 15th, 2025, a bowed squall moved east over Lake Michigan, causing a series of high frequency water level fluctuations throughout the lake, consistent with meteotsunami waves. Here, we employ three data sources to study the generation, growth, and dissipation of the waves, which includes in situ observations from Spotter buoys and nearshore NOAA NWLON stations, satellite remote sensing from NASA SWOT, and hydrodynamic modeling of the event using FVCOM. Coastal water level observations are continuous in time but limited in space, while satellite-derived elevations provide a more spatially continuous view of the lake surface but are limited in time. Hydrodynamic modeling provides both spatial and temporal information but is only as accurate as the atmospheric input. By combining these data sources, we are able to confirm the generation of a meteotsunami and evaluate the capability of existing operational products to resolve the event. We’ve shown that an operational configuration of the hydrodynamic model is able to capture the meteotsunami event when forced by operational weather forcing from the HRRR but the skill at any one location varies in timing and amplitude. This work demonstrates the capability of operational models as a tool for forecasting and predicting meteotsunami hazards as well as provides the first capture of a meteotsunami by SWOT.

487428.title: Estimating Climate Change Damages & Adaptation Costs for Illinois
487428.authors: Trent Ford, Univ. of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL; and S. Dall'Erba, A. Hultgren, R. Sriver, and C. Proistosescu
487428.abstract: State and local governments are already facing extensive costs due to climate change, including direct costs from extreme weather and costs of necessary adaptation. Accurate assessments of costs of future adaptation, residual costs after adaptation, and the potential costs of inaction on climate change are critical to inform state and local decisions now and into the future. To this end, our team has undertaken the first-ever climate change damage and adaptation cost assessment for the state of Illinois. The assessment objective is to estimate the future costs of inaction on climate change, the costs of future adaptation, and the residual costs after adaptation, in a manner that is rigorous, transparent, and directly usable for policy design. This first phase of the assessment focuses on health, transportation, buildings, agriculture, and ecosystems, and on the hazards of extreme heat, heavy rain and pluvial flooding, drought, and changing temperature seasonality. The cost estimates are summarized for near-term (2030-2059), mid-term (2045 - 2074), and long-term (2060 - 2089) periods relative to the historical period of 1995 - 2026, based on downscaled CMIP6 climate projections and state-of-the-art economic damage analysis.

487429.title: Expanding a Sector-Specific Framework for Drought Early Warning: Insights from Lessons Learned and User Feedback
487429.authors: Amanda M. Sheffield, Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences | University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and A. J. Hoell, V. Deheza, M. L. Anderson, E. Hasenbeck, M. Hurwitz, J. F. Kalansky, and R. Worsnop
487429.abstract: Since August 2024, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA's) National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS) and Physical Sciences Laboratory have been partnering with the California Department of Water Resources, NOAA National Weather Service, and others to deliver a user-oriented and evidence-based approach to drought early warning for sectors of our Nation’s economy susceptible to the hazards of too much and too little water. For two water years, this effort has piloted delivery of sector-specific drought scenarios based on integrated information products, services, and experimental applications that include observations, forecasts, and deep knowledge of local-to-regional-scale drought behavior for Southern California. Focused on three sectors (agriculture, water utilities, and public health), these scenarios enable users to make proactive decisions ahead of drought by providing forward-looking outlooks of the most likely drought outcomes up to one year into the future. This water year (October 2026 - Sept 2027), the pilot will be expanding to all of California and Nevada. California-Nevada has diverse and variable weather and climate and a complex water supply system (including a shared Sierra Nevada mountain range) that depends on environmental conditions across the entire Southwest United States. Because of this, drought and its impacts vary depending on a user’s location, sector, water supply and demand, and time in extended dry conditions. Building on lessons learned and partner enthusiasm, the expansion into California and Nevada highlights the critical need for tailored decision support, given the diverse drought adaptation strategies, planning capacity, and climate profiles of each state. Barriers and challenges to delivery of this kind of information are different across California and very different from Nevada. The pilot continues to provide opportunities to evaluate and incorporate new monitoring and forecast information in a user-centric approach for the public health, agriculture, and water utilities sectors. Past outlooks and more information about the Pilot can be found at https://www.drought.gov/drought-in-action/drought-early-warning-modern-sector-specific-approach. This presentation will highlight key lessons learned in Southern California and through the expansion to all of California-Nevada, including components of this user-centric drought early warning approach such as drought assessment, analyzing risk, communicating risk, and supporting our partners drought response and preparedness. For example, the public health sector emerged as one of the most engaged user groups, providing valuable input to shape these outlooks to better inform public health planning and decisions. The California Department of Public Health is fully supporting the expansion and views it as a joint effort. Their specific emphasis is on air quality due to wildfire smoke, airborne particulates due to blowing dust and dry soils, and heat. We also have undertaken a causal mapping analysis examining the physical and human drivers of the January 2025 wildfires in the Los Angeles area, their effects on human health, and antecedent drought development in Southern California. The causal mapping analysis identified both strategies to better prepare for the next dry season and research opportunities to explore the roles of Earth system variability related to the El Nino-Southern Oscillation and the urban-wildland interface in predicting drought and fire in this region.

487430.title: Fledgling Veery, a Cubesat Scatterometer Pathfinder: Pre-launch Update and Expected Performance
487430.authors: M. Patrick Walton, Care Weather Technologies, Inc., Springville, UT; and A. R. Laraway, C. R. Paul, K. L. Ward, T. A. Whiting, T. Waites, B. Skinner, A. Gupta, Q. C. Earnest, P. Veals, and D. G. Long
487430.abstract: The refresh rate of global ocean surface vector wind monitoring has long been constrained by the large size and corresponding high cost of satellite observing systems. To lay the groundwork for major improvements in refresh rates, Care Weather is developing Veery, a small scatterometer re-designed from the ground up for mass production. Others have demonstrated that a high flight rate and iterative development program can reduce the size and cost of aerospace systems. This approach provides tolerance for quickly demonstrating new, high-risk, high-reward technologies on orbit. During the next 12-24 months, Care Weather is launching an iterative series of four “Fledgling” Veeries, CubeSat pathfinder scatterometers intended to demonstrate end-to-end rotating fan-beam scatterometry on orbit. Fledgling Veery is expected to perform on par with alternative scatterometers, albeit with lower spatial resolution and uptime. More importantly, Fledgling paves the way for the more advanced Veery scatterometer, expected to match the state of the art in scatterometry from a platform that is mass-producible for hourly refresh of global ocean surface vector winds.

487438.title: Toward Effective Assimilation of Cloud Observations Using Machine Learning: Thermodynamic Analyses in a 1D Idealized Framework
487438.authors: Bing-Xue Zhuang, McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada; ECCC, Dorval, QC, Canada; and F. Fabry and D. Jacques
487438.abstract: Satellites and radars provide broad coverage of cloud and precipitation observations at high spatiotemporal resolution, offering valuable information for improving short- and medium-range forecasts. However, linear and Gaussian assumptions underlying many conventional data assimilation (DA) schemes often inadequately represent the complex and highly nonlinear relationships between hydrometeors and other model variables, leading to inappropriate adjustments to environmental conditions associated with the corrections to hydrometeor fields. As a result, the analyzed clouds or precipitation systems tend to dissipate rapidly in the subsequent forecast since the environment is essentially not favorable for their presence. To address this challenge, the present study uses a 1D idealized DA framework with existing global ensemble forecasts from Environment and Climate Change Canada. By viewing millions of vertical profiles, ML models are trained to generate thermodynamic increments corresponding to the cloud discrepancy between two arbitrary ensemble members. Compared with an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF), which generates increments via background error covariances estimated from ensemble forecasts, the ML increments generally produce temperature and moisture analyses with smaller errors throughout the troposphere. The ML and EnKF increments of temperature and moisture are then used to generate new forecasts to evaluate their impacts on subsequent forecasts. The results show that ML increments better sustain the inserted clouds and suppress the spurious clouds, resulting in improved forecast skill scores of clouds for up to 9 hours. Moreover, the temperature and moisture forecasts with ML increments present lower root-mean-square errors for the entire 18-hour forecast period. This idealized DA experiment demonstrates that ML models have the capability to better describe the relationships between clouds and thermodynamic fields, resulting in more accurate analyses and notably enhanced forecasts, especially for cloud evolution.

487439.title: SASCWATCH: Study on Air-Sea Coupling with WAves, Turbulence, and Clouds at High winds
487439.authors: David H. Richter, University of Notre Dame, South Bend, IN; University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN; and M. M. Bell, B. Villas Boas, S. R. Jayne, H. Potter, J. E. Rudzin, E. Sanabia, M. Schonau, J. A. Zhang, and J. B. Wadler
487439.abstract: Air-sea fluxes at high winds have long been highly uncertain due to the complex processes involved and the difficulties in making observations in hazardous conditions, yet their characterization is crucial for understanding and forecasting extreme weather events such as tropical cyclones (TCs). Despite decades of dedicated research, roadblocks in two key areas continue to plague efforts in reducing uncertainty in the high-wind air-sea flux coefficients needed for accurate model forecasts: surface waves and boundary layer turbulence. Within TCs, neither the surface wave spectral properties nor near-surface turbulence statistics have been directly characterized in a comprehensive way, and many efforts to estimate fluxes rely on inferences or untested assumptions. The next frontier in understanding the complex ocean-wave-atmosphere coupled system requires a detailed investigation of turbulence and waves within TCs, using a suite of observational and simulation tools. These include ocean drifters with wave measurement capabilities, uncrewed aerial drones for measuring direct fluxes in the boundary layer, coupled wind-atmosphere-ocean mesoscale modeling, reduced-order TC models and data assimilation, and turbulence- and spray-resolving simulations. In 2025, complex and highly-coordinated deployments into Hurricanes Erin and Imelda were successfully completed, providing unprecedented insight into air-sea coupling in extreme conditions. In 2026, plans exist for targeting two storms in similar ways. This presentation will provide an overview of the ONR-sponsored SASCWATCH project, including the motivations for such a study, summary of the 2025 and 2026 field campaigns, and future plans.

487440.title: A Final Overview of Deep-Learning Techniques to Create Probabilistic Forecasts of Fire Weather Elements for the National Blend of Models
487440.authors: Allison Layne, CIRA and NWS/OSTI/MDL, Silver Spring, MD; and J. Crockett, R. Lagerquist, K. McGrath, P. J. Roebber, and G. Wagner
487440.abstract: The National Blend of Models (NBM) is a nationally consistent and skillful suite of calibrated forecast guidance based on a blend of both National Weather Service (NWS) and non-NWS numerical weather prediction model data and post-processed model guidance. Improvements have been made to the NBM to transform its deterministic fire weather guidance into calibrated probabilistic guidance in version 5.0, implemented May 5, 2026. Our project’s purpose is to use artificial intelligence techniques, specifically machine-learned uncertainty quantification, to further improve these forecasts. For this research, we use the U-net++ (Zhou et al. 2019) deep-learning architecture with time-series components (Chiu et al. 2020). We tailored this model specifically to our meteorological application in other ways such as using residual prediction, a custom dual-weighted mean squared error loss function, and a patchwise training approach (Lagerquist et al. 2021). Similar to the NBM, we leverage weather variables from a variety of models. While the NBM uses more inputs from global models and ensemble systems, we restricted our model to using five high-resolution models and post-processed model guidance, along with a simple average of those five models. Other sources of information provided to the training included lagged observations and time-constant fields. Our model is trained against the Unrestricted Real-time Mesoscale Analysis as truth to predict 2-m temperature, 2-m dewpoint, 10-m zonal wind, 10-m meridional wind, and 10-m wind gust. Currently, we have focused our research efforts on predicting the short-range period, specifically the 36-hour lead time. However, we plan to predict hourly lead times out to 48 hours. We evaluated the deterministic performance of our model against the NBM version 5.0 over a 10-month period. For the thermodynamic elements, our model produced forecasts with overall slightly higher mean absolute error and bias when compared to the NBM, with the exception of bias for 2-m dewpoint. However, our model made significant improvements to most evaluation metrics for wind gust forecasts. One area for improvement in our forecasts remains at the most extreme ends of the distributions, especially for wind gusts. Multiple experiments using various combinations of recent model bias have already been completed to address this, with the final configuration set. These results, along with the remaining work to create well-calibrated ensembles, will be presented, as this project is expected to end later in 2027. Chiu, H., E. Adeli, and J. 487449.title: On-Demand Interactive Computing for the NOS Coastal Cloud Sandbox
487449.authors: Micah J Wengren, NOAA, Santa Cruz, CA; and M. Lalime, T. C. Vance, B. Vanderplow, P. Tripp, J. A. Ducker, Z. Wills, M. Alvis, K. Powell, A. Stephens, M. Austin, and K. Knee
487449.abstract: The NOS Coastal Cloud Sandbox project aims to expedite NOAA and NOAA partners’ ability to co-develop a suite of core physics-based numerical ocean models and deploy them to specific coastal domains and associated stakeholder-driven scientific and societal applications. To achieve this objective, and to overcome IT and policy barriers that have traditionally prevented such collaboration within a shared environment, the US IOOS Office, in partnership with Tetra Tech, Lynker Technologies, and the NOAA OCIO, developed and deployed the Cloud Sandbox in 2024 on NOAA’s Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud computing environment. Throughout 2024 - 2026, iterative improvements were made to the Cloud Sandbox, including: The ability to authenticate and provision user accounts for non-NOAA collaborators via the Okta identity management platform Dedicated, isolated computing environments for modeling teams, with individual and group permission controls, on Sandbox ‘head nodes’, allowing users full control over sharing and managing permissions for the data, workflows, and model outputs Support for the full suite of operational NOS core ocean models and frameworks, such as: ROMS, FVCOM, SCHISM, ADCIRC, UFS, and others Enabling these capabilities matured the Sandbox into a robust, powerful platform for ocean model development. However, shortcomings were still evident in the overall platform including the lack of: Enhanced accessibility, such as a secured, web-based user interface and NOAA ICAM integration for authentication of NOAA users Interactive, dynamic computing options for post-processing, validation, and analysis of model outputs Integrated development environment capability for in-place editing of associated software and scripts and collaboration with external version control systems (e.g. GitHub) Provisioning of user-configured and managed Python environments with full isolation Flexible support for post-processing workflows enabled by the Scientific Python (SciPy) library ecosystem, coupled with the scalability of Dask and Dask Gateway clusters Support for GPU and AI-based workflows and analysis of model outputs and development of derived products To address these shortcomings, the Sandbox team deployed Nebari (https://nebari.dev), an open source JupyterHub-based computing platform that compliments the core Sandbox system and provides all of the above capabilities and more. Nebari is now the ‘front door’ for the Sandbox, allowing users web-based access to the platform and enabling a range of workflows not previously possible. The NOS Cloud Sandbox is available at: https://coastalsandbox.nos.noaa.gov/. This presentation will give an overview of the Sandbox Nebari platform and highlight a few of the workflows and use-cases it has supported for Sandbox model development and for NOS’ modeling-adjacent and AI workflows.

487454.title: Development and Transition of Tropical Cyclone Forecast Products for Improved Impact-Based Decision Support Services
487454.authors: John Kaplan, AOML, Miami, FL; and M. DeMaria, W. Hogsett, P. Santos, J. A. Zhang, A. Brammer, G. S. Manikin, D. E. Rudack, K. Schwartz, J. Martinez, K. Asmar, D. A. Zelinsky, M. Onderlinde, P. P. Papin, S. M. Camposano, and K. Y. Wong
487454.abstract: Reviewer's Abstract: 17th Conference on Transition of Research to Operations [17R2O] A proposal to develop, refine, and transition several tropical cyclone forecast guidance aids into National Weather Service operations is currently being funded by the NOAA Joint Technology Transfer Initiative (JTTI) program . The proposal comprises 6 sub-projects that provide a variety of guidance aids that can be utilized to improve the impact-based decision support services (IDSS) value chain that begins with data collection and ends with the delivery of risk communication products and services for end-user decision making. The individual sub-projects are as follows: (1) A Probabilistic Genesis Model guidance project that seeks to transition both the Florida State University developed Tropical Cyclone Logistic Guidance for Genesis model (TCLOGG) and the Colorado State/CIRA statistical-dynamical genesis model (EGGI) into operations at the National Center for Environmental Prediction (NCEP); (2) A Wind Gust Algorithm sub-project whose goal is develop and implement a wind gust parameterization for use in predicting tropical cyclone wind gusts into the operational HAFS Hurricane model; (3) The Wind Speed Probability (WSP) Model 2.0 Topography project that seeks to include statistically-based wind gust algorithms that are functions of sustained wind magnitude, location, surface roughness, and terrain height into the National Hurricane Center (NHC) Tropical Cyclone Wind Speed Model; (4) The National Blend of Models (NBM) Integration sub-project for which the goal is to integrate the wind speed and gust forecasts from the WSP2.0 into the probabilistic NBM wind products; (5) The Ensemble and AI-based uncertainty sub-project that seeks to incorporate new AI-based methods for estimating track and intensity uncertainty into NHC’s WSP2.0 hazard products; and (6) WSP2.0 Calibration and Validation sub-project whose goal is develop and refine new probabilistic methods for recommending tropical cyclone wind watches and warnings based upon the updated NHC Wind Speed 2.0 model forecasts. Results from the above sub-projects will be presented at the meeting and future plans will also be discussed. Disclaimer: The views, opinions, and findings contained in this report are those of the authors and should not be construed as an official National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration or U.S. government position, policy, or decision

487457.title: A Coastal Advection Roughness Length Parameterization for Numerical Weather Prediction Modeling of the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
487457.authors: James Anthony Hlywiak, NRL, Monterey, CA; and S. Gaberšek, F. Turney, J. Ruiz-Plancarte, D. G. Ortiz-Suslow, R. Yamaguchi, Q. Wang, J. M. Schmidt, J. Singh, L. Shen, B. M. Salazar, and D. Flagg
487457.abstract: Accurately diagnosing the vertical turbulent fluxes of momentum, temperature, and moisture within the atmospheric surface layer (ASL) is a critical function of bulk-layer turbulent flux closure schemes within Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) and Large Eddy Simulation (LES) models. State-of-the-science bulk-layer closure schemes are predicated on the assumption of a constant flux layer between the lowest resolved model layer and the surface. Although recognized to be invalid near heterogeneous surfaces, to date, no suitable alternatives have been developed for ASL parameterization near coastal environments, where strong thermal and roughness gradients induce complex multiscale turbulent structures within the ASL, such as internal boundary layers and low-level jets. Here, we discuss a recently developed parameterization which addresses the invalidity of the bulk-flux formulae using a modified, flow-dependent, localized aerodynamic roughness length for onshore flow conditions, named the Coastal Advection Roughness Length (COARL) parameterization. We begin by describing results from a recently published manuscript, which presents the theoretical basis for COARL supported by meteorological flux tower observations collected at a coastal site within central California as part of the Office of Naval Research sponsored Coastal Land-Air-Sea Interaction (CLASI) project. The measurements reveal that departures in the estimated from the expected homogeneous values are sensitive to the residence time of the flow, which is approximated using the local wind speeds and distance from the coast. This relationship permits a simple, semi-empirical parameterization for neutral buoyancy ASLs. In the second half of this presentation, we discuss implementation of COARL within a version of the Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) single column model (SCM). Output from SCM simulations forced with time-varying wind, temperature, and moisture profiles from a regional model are compared with LIDAR and surface meteorological tower measurements at the Naval Research Laboratory Coastal Environmental Observation Station (CEOBS), revealing the potential of COARL to improve simulations of coastal atmospheric boundary layers within LES and NWP models alike.

487460.title: A Machine Learning-Based Sub-seasonal Prediction Model for North American Heat Waves
487460.authors: Hosmay Lopez, NOAA/AOML, Miami, FL; NOAA/AOML, Miami, FL; and R. West, D. Kim, B. Zavadoff, E. J. Becker, S. K. Lee, and B. Kirtman
487460.abstract: Extreme high-temperature events are a leading weather-related cause of mortality and economic disruption, yet forecasting them beyond the 7–10 day synoptic scale remains a persistent challenge for current dynamical models. Although state-of-the-art numerical models—such as those from the Subseasonal Consortium (SubC)—provide valuable guidance, they frequently underestimate the magnitude and persistence of localized heat waves at 2- to 4-week lead times due to misrepresentations of chaotic atmospheric noise and land-atmosphere feedbacks. To bridge this sub-seasonal predictability gap, this study introduces a hybrid machine learning framework centered on a Random Forest (RF) classifier trained on the SubC multi-model ensemble (MME) hindcasts. Using ERA5 reanalysis data, we identified nine dominant quasi-stationary heat wave clusters across the contiguous United States. The RF model integrates a physically grounded set of predictors, including local land-surface metrics (e.g., soil moisture and heat fluxes), remote forcing indices (i.e., the Madden-Julian Oscillation, El Niño Southern Oscillation, and tropical Atlantic SSTs), and principal components of large-scale atmospheric circulation. The results demonstrate that the RF model significantly extends the predictability horizon for U.S. heat waves, consistently outperforming the dynamical SubC MME at 2- to 4-week leads. By Week 4, the RF classifier maintains a robust Area Under the Curve of 0.72 compared to the MME’s 0.62, effectively offering a two-week extension in predictability while minimizing false negatives. Case studies of recent high-impact extremes—including the 2021 and 2024 Pacific Northwest, 2023 Southwest, and 2024 Northeast heat waves—highlight the framework's capability to provide reliable, highly accurate early warnings. Furthermore, utilizing SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and permutation feature importance, we verify that the RF model achieves this enhanced skill by isolating the climate system's "slow manifold" rather than overfitting to synoptic noise. Explainability analyses reveal distinct geographic predictability regimes: Pacific Northwest heat waves are heavily influenced by remote teleconnections and localized atmospheric configurations, whereas Southwest and Northeast events are overwhelmingly preconditioned by land-surface memory, particularly deep soil moisture deficits. Ultimately, this machine learning approach successfully leverages key boundary conditions to provide earlier, physically consistent, and more accurate sub-seasonal warnings of extreme thermal events.

487467.title: Atmospheric Normal Modes in SABER Temperature Data
487467.authors: Rolando R. Garcia, NCAR, Boulder, CO
487467.abstract: Atmospheric normal modes are theoretical eigensolutions of the governing equations on the sphere linearized about a basic state at rest. Remarkably, many of these modes are realized in the atmosphere and can be readily detected in surface pressure data. The global structure in latitude and altitude of some of the modes, in particular the 5-day wave, has been documented in recent work by Kiladis and Madden by regressing reanalysis fields at various pressure levels on the sea-level pressure EOFs that describe the oscillation. Here we present the directly observed temperature structure of two atmospheric normal modes, the k=1, 5-day wave and the k=3, 2-day wave throughout the middle atmosphere, from about 100 hPa to 10-4 hPa (~15 – 105 km), using a 23-year record of temperature data from the SABER infrared radiometer onboard NASA’s TIMED satellite. We show that the structure of the 5-day wave resembles closely the theoretical normal mode, with little phase variation up to the upper mesosphere, and is present throughout the year. On the other hand, the 2-day wave shows very strong seasonal variability with large amplitudes seen only at the solstices and considerable phase tilt. The phase behavior is consistent with forcing by instability of the summer jets in both hemispheres, supporting previous theoretical interpretations of the excitation mechanism for this mode.

487470.title: Ground Based Demonstration of an Airborne High Spectral Resolution Temperature Profiling Lidar
487470.authors: Madison Hetlage, NASA, Hampton, VA; and J. W. Hair, T. Shingler, A. R. Nehrir, and D. B. Harper
487470.abstract: Despite a strong desire for airborne thermodynamic gradient profiling within the planetary boundary layer (PBL), current airborne temperature profilers are limited to passive sounding techniques which lack the spatiotemporal resolution desired by the PBL community and often fail to capture strong inversions due to their reliance on a-priori constraints. Although active temperature profiling lidars using rotational Raman scattering and differential oxygen absorption exist for ground-based use, these techniques are not well suited for moving, airborne platforms. This work looks to demonstrate the effectiveness of the temperature high spectral resolution lidar (HSRL) technique for this application. This technique exploits the thermally sensitive Doppler broadened linewidth of the Rayleigh scattering signal. In this approach, two distinct spectral notch filters are used to create two molecular-only scattering channels. The ratio of these channels enables an observation dependent on the molecular scattering spectral lineshape and independent of aerosol scattering. This takes advantage of the strong signal strength of elastic scattering and allows for the use of commonly flown Nd:YAG and Nd:YVO4 lasers. To demonstrate this technique, a second molecular channel has been added to the NASA LaRC first generation airborne aerosol profiling instrument, HSRL-1. This effort leverages the current HSRL-1 instrument and data acquisition infrastructure, particularly the flight-tested Nd:YVO4 laser, receiver, and detectors.
