This presentation will cover the temperature HSRL retrieval technique, its theoretical optimization, and the critical aspects to its successful implementation in a real system. Results from the reconfigured HSRL-1 system operating in a ground-based zenith-pointing configuration will also be presented in detail alongside co-located radiosonde measurements. Finally, considerations for the airborne application of this measurement will be discussed.

487472.title: Nocturnal Transient Warmings In an Urban Environment
487472.authors: Darryn W. Waugh, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and L. Hersh, J. K. Lundquist, N. E. Prince, S. Murphy, Y. Pan, and K. J. Davis
487472.abstract: Nocturnal transient warming (NTW) events are defined as periods of warming that occur during the night, and interrupt the usual nocturnal cooling. There is rapid warming to initiate the event, and rapid cooling at the end. While previous studies have documented NTWs, there have been few studies of their occurrence within cities. Here we examine the occurrence and cause of NTW events within Baltimore City using observations from the Baltimore Social Environmental Collaborative (BSEC) integrated urban field laboratory and the ARM Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE) field campaign. Analysis of the BSEC surface weather station network shows that NTWs occur within the city, but their occurrence varies with location and wind conditions. Specifically, NTWs occur more often in open, vegetated sites and less often in areas with impervious surfaces. They occur on clear nights with initially calm winds that are interrupted by a transient increase in wind speeds, which is often connected with a low-level jet. BSEC and CoURAGE data will be used to test the hypothesis that the increased wind speeds are associated with vertical mixing that transports warm air aloft down to the surface, yielding a NTW event. Following this period of mixing, winds calm and rapid cooling continues. We will also test that this does not occur at non-vegetated sites because impervious surfaces retain heat so there is less radiative cooling at night, resulting in weak vertical temperature gradients. Hence, even if vertical mixing does occur, the impact on near-surface temperatures is negligible These NTW events may also impact local air quality, and their occurrence indicates that predictions of intra-urban temperature variability will need to take into account the combination of land cover in addition to mesoscale atmospheric dynamics.

487477.title: Tropical Cyclone Precipitation Forecast Evaluation using the Hurricane Analysis and Forecasting System (HAFS) and the Warn-on Forecast System (WoFS): New Comparison Tools and Initial Results
487477.authors: Ethan Murray, CIMAS- University of Miami Cooperative Institute for Marine & Atmospheric Studies, Miami, FL; NOAA / AOML / HRD, Miami, FL; and J. A. Zhang, S. Gopalakrishnan, G. J. Alaka Jr., A. Hazelton, and S. S. Basineni
487477.abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) precipitation forecasts within leading numerical weather prediction (NWP) models lack systematic evaluation. To fill this gap, precipitation forecasts from the Hurricane Analysis and Forecasting System (HAFS) and the Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS) are analyzed, since both models have shown previous skill in forecasting TC precipitation across a limited number of cases. To unite HAFS and WoFS under a common precipitation evaluation framework, all forecasts from 2022 to 2025 are compared to observations and precipitation analyses including MRMS and Stage IV. Case studies of particularly successful and challenging forecasts are presented. Model assessment across all cases relies upon traditional skill-based, object-based, and probabilistic metrics. The analysis is stratified across storm properties like intensity, size, translation speed, and TC life stage (coastal versus inland, tropical versus extratropical transition). Cases are also compared across environmental characteristics such as wind shear, moisture, orography and atmospheric stability. Future work aims to implement this flexible precipitation evaluation framework into the real-time HAFS product suite for the 2027 Atlantic Hurricane Season and to make it easily accessible for validating TC precipitation in other models.

487480.title: Assessing Oceanic Drivers of Decadal Hydroclimatic Stress Predictability Using Earth System Large Ensembles
487480.authors: Samar Minallah, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. G. Yeager, G. A. Meehl, N. Rosenbloom, and I. R. Simpson
487480.abstract: On interannual to decadal timescales, internal climate variability often dominates over the externally forced response, particularly at regional scales where signal-to-noise ratios are low, limiting actionable climate prediction. Here, we use the CESM2 and E3SMv2 Large Ensembles to investigate how major modes of internal ocean variability across the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans influence terrestrial climate stress, focusing on vapor pressure deficit (VPD), the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), and the Keetch–Byram Drought Index (KBDI). We establish the strength, spatial extent, and robustness of ocean–land relationships to identify regions where low-frequency ocean variability consistently influences climate stress, and evaluate their potential for decadal prediction by reconstructing the climate stress response from oceanic predictors. The reconstructed signal is then used to quantify explained variance, identify regions with high signal-to-noise ratios, and assess how residual variability limits prediction. This work identifies where and under what conditions internal ocean variability provides a meaningful source of decadal climate predictability, providing a framework for evaluating regional hydroclimatic stress predictability across Earth system large ensembles.

487485.title: Obs4Extremes: A WCRP ESMO Initiative for Compound and Cascading Climate Extremes
487485.authors: Samar Minallah, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. Doherty, Y. Rao, M. Schröder, G. Schrier van der, H. Abraha, and C. Macintosh
487485.abstract: The WCRP Earth System Modelling and Observations (ESMO) Working Group on Observations for Researching Climate (WGORC) is proposing a new Task Team on Observations for Compound and Cascading Climate Extremes. While observational frameworks for single-variable extremes are well established, compound and cascading extremes require coordinated multi-variable observations. However, advancing their characterization is constrained by several challenges: the lack of consistent multi-variable observational datasets, limited understanding of how observational uncertainties propagate into compound-event analysis, insufficient guidance on defining and quantifying compound events, and weak integration of observations into Earth system model evaluation and operational applications. The proposed Task Team will address these gaps by assessing the observational foundations needed to classify, quantify, monitor, and evaluate compound and cascading climate extremes. The Task Team will focus on identifying observational requirements for representative classes of compound events, evaluating the strengths, limitations, uncertainties, and gaps of existing datasets, developing guidance on indices and metrics, and identifying priorities for future observing systems and observational products. This presentation will introduce the motivation, scope, and objectives of the proposed Task Team and invites community feedback on its priorities, activities, deliverables, and opportunities for collaboration.

487489.title: Evolution and Scaling of Water-Side Dynamics in Developing Wind-Wave Fields: Phase-Dependent Stresses, Production, and Dissipation
487489.authors: Shelby Lynne Metoyer, NRL, Stennis Space Center, MS; NRL, Stennis Space Center, MS; and S. Matt, D. Wang, and I. Savelyev
487489.abstract: The transfer of momentum and energy across the air-sea interface dictates upper-ocean dynamics, yet the mechanistic links between wave evolution and subsurface turbulence remain notoriously difficult to quantify. Using laboratory-based high-resolution Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) measurements, we investigate the evolution, scaling, and phase-dependence of the water-side stresses, turbulence production, and dissipation beneath developing wind-waves. As the sea state develops, the near-surface flow transitions from a shear-dominated to a wave-dominated regime, culminating in a distinct phase dependence of the measured physical parameters as waves exhibit more pronounced nonlinearity. Airflow separation, nonlinear wave effects, and microbreaking drive persistent counter-gradient momentum fluxes that result in negative turbulence production on the leeward face of wave crests, while enhancing turbulence production and Reynolds stress on the windward slope of the crests. This leads to a distinct and stable asymmetric bimodal phase-dependent distribution of Reynolds stress, turbulence production and dissipation. Remarkably, despite this phase-dependent disruption of local turbulent equilibrium, the presence of counter-gradient momentum fluxes, development of highly nonlinear waves, airflow separation, and microbreaking, the turbulent kinetic energy dissipation rate (ε) maintains a classical 1/z decay with depth. Furthermore, ε demonstrates excellent law-of-the-wall scaling, correlating robustly with both increases in the water-side friction velocity (u_*) and the bulk wind speed (U_0.65) in excellent agreement with field observations. These results demonstrate that while wave development fundamentally reorganizes subsurface momentum transport into stable, bimodal states, macroscopic parameterizations of turbulent dissipation remain highly resilient.

487495.title: HYSPLIT Application Upgrades in Support of the FIFA World Cup 2026TM
487495.authors: Sonny Zinn, NOAA, College Park, MD; and B. Berhane, F. Shen, R. Jiang, and A. Crawford
487495.abstract: The HYSPLIT model developed and maintained by NOAA’s Air Resources Laboratory (ARL) is one of the most widely used atmospheric transport and dispersion models. It is also a critical software tool that the National Weather Service (NWS) operationally employs to make dispersion forecasts for emergency responders and planners. ARL collaborated closely with the NWS from December 2025 to July 2026 to support the FIFA World Cup 2026TM, improving how automated HYSPLIT dispersion simulations are configured and performed and how the NWS accesses simulation results through automated scripts. Over a six-month period, we employed an agile software development approach: we regularly met with the NWS to collect requirements, implemented and tested incremental changes, and refined the system based on their feedback. This development cycle was repeated to ensure the implementation met NWS needs and this proved to be a successful development approach.

487496.title: Combined Diode-Laser-Based Direct-Detection Doppler Wind Lidar and High Spectral Resolution Lidar: Initial Results
487496.authors: Luke Colberg, Montana State University-Bozeman, Bozeman, MT; and D. J. Maxwell and K. S. Repasky
487496.abstract: This poster presents the design and initial results of a combined direct-detection Doppler wind lidar (DWL) and high spectral resolution lidar (HSRL). The primary advancement of this work is that the instrument design enables radial wind speed measurements insensitive to the aerosol loading. The instrument architecture uses diode lasers, which makes the design eye-safe, robust, scalable, and compatible with eventual development into a low-cost and field-deployable instrument. Previous demonstrations of this technique were conducted with two separate lidars, one being the DWL and the second being the HSRL, and this work builds on that demonstration by combining the two lidars into a single instrument. The DWL uses a double-edge etalon configuration, and the HSRL is a rubidium vapor absorption cell design. These systems operate on the rubidium D2 transition at 780 nm. The DWL incorporates the backscatter ratio measurements from the HSRL directly in the wind speed retrieval, which makes the double-edge etalon design capable of simultaneously measuring radial wind speeds in varying aerosol conditions, such as those in the aerosol-dense planetary boundary layer and the aerosol-sparse free troposphere. A laboratory prototype has been constructed, and validation tests in comparison with a sonic anemometer are ongoing. The prototype demonstrates radial wind speed measurements using this instrument concept. This poster will provide an overview of the instrument design and present the capabilities based on the initial laboratory measurements.

487501.title: Operational Product Updates, Advanced Monitoring, and AI Innovations
487501.authors: Zhaohui Cheng, NOAA, College Park, MD
487501.abstract: Real-time satellite product operations deliver automated Level 2 and higher environmental products from both geostationary and polar-orbiting satellite systems to support critical weather, water, climate, and oceanographic applications. This presentation highlights recent operational product deployments, enhancements to product quality monitoring, emerging AI-driven monitoring capabilities, and the operational impacts of newly deployed satellite products on forecasters and other end users. Recent operational updates include the operational deployment of the OceanSAT-3 Ocean Surface Winds product suite, which provides 12.5-km resolution Level 2A and Level 2B products in NetCDF and BUFR formats, as well as 12.5-km AWIPS Ocean Surface Winds and AWIPS Ambiguity Ocean Surface Winds (solutions 1–4). By providing additional sampling times and broad swath coverage, OceanSAT-3 reduces observation gaps in the tropics and supplies valuable wind observations that improve NCEP numerical weather prediction models and enhance tropical storm monitoring and forecasting. This presentation also highlights the NHC AWIPS Converter, a cloud-native application operating within the NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF) that transforms multiple operational satellite products into AWIPS-compatible products. The converter delivers multi-sensor microwave imagery and derived wind products directly to the National Hurricane Center, improving tropical cyclone monitoring and analysis. In addition, NESDIS has recently expanded its operational oceanographic product portfolio through the nationwide integration of High-Frequency Radar Network (HFRNet) ocean surface current and wave products, providing critical data to support Search and Rescue (SAR) operations, coastal hazard monitoring, and ocean model verification. To ensure operational reliability and high data quality, NESDIS continues to modernize its monitoring capabilities by leveraging cloud-native technologies and artificial intelligence. This presentation will also highlight two AI pilot projects. The first uses the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) to automate Mesoscale Domain Sector (MDS) notification workflows, reducing manual effort and improving operational efficiency. The second demonstrates an AI-driven, real-time anomaly detection capability that continuously monitors satellite products, automatically identifies potential anomalies, and enables faster response to operational issues. Together, these advancements demonstrate how cloud computing and AI are transforming satellite product operations through increased automation, enhanced monitoring, and the timely delivery of high-quality environmental information to operational users.

487503.title: Guiding Future GNSS-RO Constellation Design via OSSE Frameworks
487503.authors: Lidia Cucurull, NOAA/NESDIS, Boulder, CO; and S. P. F. Casey, A. Vidal, and A. Lim
487503.abstract: As the space sector looks toward the next 25 years, defining the optimal scale and configuration of future satellite constellations is critical for cost-benefit viability. This presentation details an advanced Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) framework developed at NOAA to quantify the impact of scaling Radio Occultation (RO) soundings within a representative 2035 observing system. Our research addresses the evolution of needs by evaluating a range of daily RO soundings, from a modest 6,000 to an ambitious 100,000 profiles. Results demonstrate that 6,000 daily profiles provide a vital "anchor" for data assimilation systems, significantly reducing stratospheric model bias and improving the bias correction of satellite radiances. While forecast skill continues to improve with increased data density, our study identifies a point of diminishing returns between 50,000 and 100,000 daily profiles. Furthermore, we explore technology trends related to orbital deployment by analyzing sounding distributions. While uniform spatial and temporal distributions yield incremental forecast improvements over polar-concentrated sampling, the primary driver of skill remains the sheer volume of RO data relative to a baseline without such observations. By utilizing significantly higher horizontal and vertical model resolutions than previous studies, this work provides a definitive quantification of future mission needs. We will conclude by demonstrating the continued high value of RO observations and offering evidence-based guidance for optimizing the global distribution and density of future RO constellations.

487504.title: Enabling LLM-based Analysis of Probabilistic Weather Forecasts
487504.authors: Nikhil Manakkal, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and D. Strom and T. Wixtrom
487504.abstract: National Weather Service (NWS) meteorologists routinely analyze a vast quantity of numerical model data in order to understand the forecast scenario. This consumes valuable time and risks burying subtle but critical details. Public and partner audiences have many different needs and require a wide variety of Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS). There is a need for a system that could summarize forecast information in a manner that is easily understandable and readily accessible. To better address these operational needs, the NWS Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) is developing a family of Model Context Protocol (MCP) services that will allow forecasters to request and synthesize forecast data using natural language. The MCP standard allows Large Language Models (LLMs) to connect with authoritative large-scale datasets. Written once and applied broadly, these tools can fetch data in a manner that is consistent, scalable, and activated using natural language. Recent advancements in LLM technology allow data from multiple tool calls to be stitched together and communicate only what is relevant to the user’s request. In this project, we demonstrate the capabilities of MCP tools for distilling forecast guidance from multidimensional probabilistic weather models into a single textual narrative. We approach this problem from two angles: 1) point analysis and 2) spatial analysis. This allows forecasters to assess weather conditions over a variety of spatial scales and forecasting scenarios. We will present a demo of our chat application showcasing the ability to respond to plain language data queries and spatially highlight gridded data on a map. We will consider the prompt consistency of our MCP tools with different LLM models and prompt wording, and discuss guardrails to reduce and catch hallucinations.

487507.title: Toward AI-Ready NCAR Data: Streaming and Discovery of Radar and Aircraft Datasets through GDEX
487507.authors: Chia-Wei Hsu, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. Conroy, H. Hampapura, D. C. Schuster, A. del Moral Méndez, Ph.D, B. Javornik, T. Y. Cha, and J. A. Aquino
487507.abstract: Radar and aircraft data collected through the National Science Foundation (NSF) National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) have traditionally been stored in the Earth Observing Laboratory (EOL) NCAR Field Data Archive, where users request and download the data to a local machine before processing it. However, high-resolution weather data generates massive datasets, creating severe transfer bottlenecks for radar data exploration. To advance data accessibility, the NSF NCAR Geoscience Data Exchange (GDEX) is exploring a complementary pathway: porting radar data to a streamable format built on Computational and Information System Laboratory’s (CISL’s) new data infrastructure. GDEX utilizes 'Boreas', an on-premises S3-compatible object storage system, to store radar datasets. This gives users the flexibility to stream data on demand from anywhere with an internet connection, accelerating quick exploration alongside traditional downloads while enabling data-proximate computing on the NSF NCAR High Performance Computing (HPC) systems (Casper and Derecho). As a pilot study, we transformed the 2022 NSF-funded PRECIP field campaign EOL S-Pol radar dataset into Zarr, an Analysis-Ready, Cloud-Optimized (ARCO) data format. We converted the data from its original NetCDF/CfRadial1 format into Zarr/CfRadial2 format, using open-source tools including Xarray, Zarr, Xradar, and Py-ART. This enables fast data discovery and streaming, and offers researchers another way to work with the data tailored to their needs. Beyond enabling human users to stream and explore the data more easily, this improved accessibility also opens the door for AI agents to directly access and interact with the data. With the data made “AI-ready”, meaning it is more discoverable, readily accessible, and ensuring high interoperability across different data repositories through this cloud-native infrastructure, AI-driven tools could assist with tasks such as data discovery, search, and preliminary exploration, pointing toward new AI-assisted workflows for working with NSF NCAR's data holdings. We also piloted this approach with aircraft data, porting flight data from Research Aviation Facility (RAF) into GDEX, to demonstrate that this streaming infrastructure can extend beyond radar to serve field data more broadly, complementing NSF NCAR's existing data access options.

487512.title: CESM’s Sulfate Bias During the Asian Summer Monsoon: Investigating Observationally Constrained SO2 Loss and Mechanisms During Convection
487512.authors: Trisha Tambe, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA; UCAR, Boulder, CO; and W. Smith, B. Gaubert, S. Tilmes, M. C. Barth, L. K. Emmons, R. S. Hornbrook, E. C. Apel, S. R. Hall, A. Franchin, R. Ueyama, L. G. Huey, A. Rollins, E. Waxman, O. Eppers, and F. Köllner
487512.abstract: Sulfate aerosols in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS) influence radiative balance, stratospheric chemistry, and air quality far downwind of their source. Asian summer monsoon (ASM) deep convection is a principal pathway delivering sulfur to the UTLS, where long lifetimes and broad horizontal transport allow a regional emission signal to become a global one. Recent work has shown that the Community Atmosphere Model version 6 Chemistry (CAM6-chem) represents observed sulfur dioxide (SO2) in the ASM UTLS during the ACCLIP (2022) airborne campaign but considerably overestimates sulfate (SO42-) by up to a factor of five in fresh convective outflow. Given this specific model configuration is commonly used to predict long-term changes in the Earth system, SO42- overestimation is a significant issue worthy of investigation. Here we show that the SO42- high bias originates during convective transport itself, not from chemistry outside of convection: CESM2.2 delivers SO42- to the UTLS already formed, while observations follow a scavenge-then-rebuild pattern. In this work we present an empirical estimate of the multiphase sulfur chemistry in East Asia utilizing methods that can also be used to evaluate other models. Our first objective was to find an observationally-constrained SO2 oxidation rate in the UTLS. This involved a multi-step analysis combining backward trajectories from NSF NCAR Gulfstream V observations, satellite observations identifying convective events, and Lagrangian parcel analysis. An SO2 chemical lifetime of 6.2 [5.1-7.9, 95% CI] days was determined from observations at altitudes between 12 and 15 km, a result insensitive to extending the analysis through the free troposphere. We then asked whether the SO2 gas-phase oxidation by OH accounts for any portion of the model SO42- high bias. While the simulated SO2 chemical lifetime was shorter than observed, scaling the model reaction rate improved model SO42- by just 5% while degrading SO2 agreement. Given this result, we investigated whether gas-phase chemistry represents the full picture by finding a theoretical SO2 lifetime. Using standard JPL kinetics values and a simplified box model for OH, we demonstrated a near-closure of the observed UTLS sulfur budget through gas-phase chemistry, ruling out a significant influence of multiphase chemistry on the observed SO2 loss. Combining these results, we conclude that chemistry after convective transport does not significantly contribute to the SO42- high bias. We next examine convective processes, starting with an evaluation of model bias at different points along the convective outflow pathway. Model-to-observation SO42- ratios rose from 1.89 in cloud-free inflow to 5.19 in fresh outflow, while the corresponding CO ratio fell from 0.86 to 0.63. The fact that these ratios vary in opposite directions illustrates how the model transports too little air into the outflow region while simultaneously delivering too much SO42-, thus attributing a majority of the issue to convective processes. Given this narrower target, we evaluate CESM2.2 / CAM6-chem SO42- deposition against surface acid deposition network measurements across Asia, assess observation-model agreement with other soluble aerosols such as organic aerosols, and determine the contribution of boundary layer emissions to the smaller pre-convective bias calculated in the inflow. By performing these analyses, we not only work towards a targetable deficiency in the representation of convective sulfur processing, but we also demonstrate a partitioning bias. For a week following convective outflow, observed CO-normalized SO42- increased by a factor of 20 while modeled values increased minimally. Because the excess sulfur arrives as aerosol mass rather than a gas-phase intermediate, it persists as particle surface area, affecting the heterogeneous chemistry that takes place on that surface; this can have consequences on the model’s nitrogen and halogen partitioning that governs stratospheric ozone loss. This also affects the model’s radiative properties; since the ASM lofts air that is transported globally, we identified a source of bias that can affect widely-used predictions of Earth system variability.

487515.title: Enhancing NASA GEOS Simulations of Dust Mineralogy and Trace Metal Elements with a Soil Mineralogy Atlas Retrieved from EMIT Mission
487515.authors: Hongbin Yu, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD; and D. Kim, M. Chin, P. R. Colarco, J. Zheng, H. Bian, Z. Zhang, and A. Lyapustin
487515.abstract: The mineral dust cycle has emerged as a core theme of Earth system science, by virtue of its strong coupling with the system’s energy, water, and carbon cycles. Dust also affects the health of human beings and ecosystems. All the interactions of dust particles with other components of the Earth /environment system depend strongly on dust mineralogical and chemical compositions. Most of dust transport models treat dust as particles with a globally uniform mineralogy and chemical composition. In this study, we have developed a new modeling capability in the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) model to characterize the heterogeneity of dust mineralogical and chemical compositions through integrating the soil mineralogy atlas (SMA) acquired from the Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT) with a surface-based SMA. A total of 14 minerals is simulated in the model. We will discuss in the presentation: (a) an approach of integrating the EMIT and surface-based SMAs in GEOS to simulate dust mineralogy, (b) evaluations of GEOS simulations of dust mineralogy and trace metal elements with a climatology of in situ observations and the retrievals of aerosol composition (e.g., dust, hematite, goethite, iron oxide) from POLDER-3/PARASOL and EPIC/DSCOVR, and (c) spatial and seasonal variations of dust mineralogy, trace metal elements, and implications of using the simulated trace metal ratios for identifying origins of dust plumes. This new GEOS dust modeling capability can be used to improve the representation of dust-cloud-radiation interactions and enable interdisciplinary studies of dust impacts on biogeochemical cycles.

487521.title: Extreme Precipitation Events and NOAA Atlas 15
487521.authors: Debbie Martin, RTI International, Broomfield, CO; and M. P. St. Laurent Jr., C. Trypaluk, A. Jordan, and J. Hanrahan
487521.abstract: The Office of Water Prediction (OWP) within NOAA’s National Weather Service is developing NOAA Atlas 15 to serve as the nation's new, authoritative precipitation frequency (PF) standard. The methodology developed for Atlas 15 considers historical nonstationarity captured via gauge observations. The PF analysis uses annual maximum series. In some cases, known significant events occurred that were not captured in the observational data for various reasons such as improper digitization or gauge failure. Observer forms, post-event storm surveys and other available resources allowed infilling of missing extreme rainfall observations. This presentation will provide insights into extreme events that have been added to the analysis, the techniques used to identify and collect those data, and the resulting impacts on the statistics. The discussion will also highlight the data quality control and statistical framework developed for reproducible precipitation frequency analysis and applied in the Atlas 15 effort.

487530.title: Verifying WPC’s Day 3-7 Hazard Outlooks for Extreme Heat
487530.authors: Lily Thuy Lai, NWS, College Park, MD
487530.abstract: Extreme heat is one of the leading weather-related causes of death in the United States. In support of the NWS mission to protect life and property by providing forecasts, warnings, and impact-based decision support services, the NWS Weather Prediction Center’s (WPC) Day 3-7 Hazards Outlook communicates the potential for impactful heat during the medium range portion of the seven day forecast. This study evaluates the spatial accuracy of the heat component of the Hazard Outlook and its capacity to support public risk communication through the issuance of reliable Watch/Warning/Advisory (WWA) products. Daily issued outlooks were cross-checked with ERA5-Land reanalysis temperature data and heat alerts issued by local NWS Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) across the contiguous United States (CONUS) from 2020 through 2026. Hit rates, false alarms, misses, Critical Success Index (CSI) scores, and spatial accuracy were evaluated at varying lead times preceding extreme heat events. Gridded analysis reveals an overly conservative forecasting bias across southwestern regions, as well as increased heat volatility and lower predictability across the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains. Analysis was also performed against the NWS/CDC HeatRisk tool to assess its utility as input guidance. Verification of hazard predictability ultimately contributes towards improving forecasting accuracy and refining the current criteria that triggers emergency responses to hazardous heat. Identification of meteorological patterns and localized forecast limitations improves lead-time and preparation measures, ensuring optimal public readiness and mitigation during extreme heat events.

487531.title: Observations of Near-Surface Shear Across Convective Environments
487531.authors: Melanie Jones, NSSL, Norman, OK; and E. N. Smith and J. Gebauer
487531.abstract: Wind shear in the lowest few kilometers of the atmosphere has proven to discriminate between tornadic and nontornadic environments. Furthermore, a recent study by Markowski (2024) revealed a new potential pathway for tornadogenesis driven by streaks of vertical vorticity that are generated by the wind shear in the lowest few meters of the atmosphere. Gathering information on this near surface layer, traditionally done through radiosonde launches, is key for forecasting severe weather and understanding this newfound theory. Radiosonde profiles, however, tend to be unreliable at the near-surface due to large spatial and temporal data gaps between launches and the rapid ascent sondes often experience through this layer. Instead of using radiosondes for near-surface information, this project utilizes a robust, 15+ year dataset from over 102 fixed Oklahoma Mesonet stations. The Oklahoma Mesonet is a vast network of meteorological observation stations that collect information on near-surface variables at high temporal resolutions. Wind speed is recorded at both 2 meters and 10 meters above ground level, with the latter being accompanied by wind direction. Composite analyses of average bulk wind shear, calculated from the Mesonet stations, were conducted among differing convective regimes, specifically focusing on tornadic versus nontornadic environments. Additional case studies of notable severe storm setups were evaluated to assess whether near-surface bulk wind shear values from the Mesonet are reliable discriminators between tornadic and nontornadic environments.

487534.title: From Climate Information to Institutional Decision-Making: Creating Economic Value Through the U.S, Weather Enterprise
487534.authors: Robert F. Brammer, Brammer Technology, LLC, Woburn, MA; Brammer Technology, Andover, MA
487534.abstract: From Climate Information to Institutional Decision-Making: Creating Economic Value Through the U.S. Weather Enterprise[i] Robert F. Brammer, Ph.D. Weather, water, and climate information is becoming increasingly important to consequential financial, engineering, regulatory, and public policy decisions throughout the United States. Property and casualty insurance, construction, and electric power illustrate how weather and climate information increasingly shapes underwriting, infrastructure design, and long-term investment decisions. Similar challenges are emerging across many sectors of the economy as weather extremes, long-lived infrastructure, and growing societal exposure increase the consequences of decision-making under uncertainty. Much of the Weather Enterprise has traditionally focused on improving observations, numerical prediction, climate modeling, forecast dissemination, and decision support. The Weather Information Value Chain developed by the World Meteorological Organization, the American Meteorological Society, and other researchers provides a useful description of how scientific information ultimately creates economic value through improved decisions. This presentation extends the Weather Information Value Chain by introducing an Institutional Decision Framework that explains how scientific advances become engineering practice, legal and regulatory decisions, corporate governance, and ultimately financial and economic value. The presentation builds upon longstanding Weather Enterprise initiatives promoting collaboration among government, academia, and the private sector, including the National Weather Service's “Weather-Ready Nation” initiative. Those efforts have significantly strengthened production, communication, and application of weather information. This presentation extends that perspective by emphasizing collaboration between the Weather Enterprise and the institutions that ultimately make consequential economic, engineering, financial, regulatory, and governance decisions. The objective is not only to improve weather and climate information, but to improve the institutional decisions through which that information creates societal and economic value. The presentation introduces an “Institutional Decision Framework” defined as the engineering standards, professional practice, legislation, judicial decisions, administrative regulations, and corporate governance structures through which weather and climate information is translated into institutional decisions. Although scientific advances have substantially improved weather and climate information, comparatively less attention has been devoted to understanding the institutional processes through which that information becomes engineering practice, financial decisions, regulatory action, and public policy. Although advances in science create opportunities for better decisions, institutions ultimately determine whether those opportunities are realized. Building codes must be revised before improved hurricane projections reduce future losses. Flood hazard information must be incorporated into floodplain management, insurance pricing, and infrastructure investment before societal benefits are achieved. Legislative bodies establish statutory authority for many adaptation measures, while courts increasingly evaluate whether government agencies, regulated industries, and private organizations have reasonably incorporated evolving scientific knowledge into their decisions. Climate scenarios must become part of stress testing, capital allocation, and enterprise risk management before they influence financial resilience. Three representative industries, comprising about 10% of the $30T U.S. GDP, illustrate how the framework operates in practice. Property and casualty insurance, construction, and electric power were selected because they are among the nation's most weather- and climate-sensitive industries, involve large capital investments with long planning horizons, operate within well-developed engineering and regulatory institutions, and face increasingly significant climate-related financial exposures. Although the institutional details differ substantially, each industry demonstrates a distinct pathway through which improved scientific information creates measurable financial and economic value. Property and casualty insurance demonstrates how weather and climate information supports underwriting, pricing, reinsurance, reserving, capital management, and regulatory compliance. Construction illustrates the integration of climate information into engineering design, project planning, material selection, building codes, and long-lived infrastructure investment. Electric power demonstrates applications involving reliability, transmission expansion, generation portfolios, renewable energy integration, wildfire mitigation, and grid resilience. The presentation also examines the continuing evolution of climate stress testing as an important mechanism for translating scientific advances into institutional decision-making. Originally developed within financial supervision, climate stress testing is expanding into broader applications involving infrastructure planning, insurance, corporate governance, engineering resilience, and enterprise risk management. Improved climate scenarios, closer integration of physical and financial risk analysis, and more transparent treatment of uncertainty have the potential to strengthen institutional decision-making while improving the credibility and defensibility of adaptation and investment strategies. Looking ahead over the next five to ten years, several developments may significantly increase the economic value created by the U.S. Weather Enterprise. These include improved environmental observing systems, enhanced characterization and communication of uncertainty, integrated environmental information networks, advanced computational capabilities, hybrid artificial intelligence and physics-based modeling, and expanded decision-support systems. Equally important, emerging generative and agentic AI technologies may accelerate collaboration by translating scientific advances into institution-specific decision support, identifying emerging information needs, supporting climate stress testing, and facilitating continuous feedback between research and practice. These technologies are not intended to replace scientific discovery or human judgment; rather, they may improve the speed, transparency, and effectiveness with which scientific advances become institutional decisions. This presentation argues that the future Weather Enterprise should increasingly be viewed not only as a producer of scientific information, but also as the scientific foundation of an AI-enabled institutional decision-support ecosystem. In this broader role, advances in climate science create greater value by continuously informing the engineering, financial, legal, and governance institutions responsible for society's most consequential long-term decisions. The central conclusion is that future economic value from the Weather Enterprise will depend not only on continued scientific and technological advances but also on strengthening the institutional processes that convert improved weather and climate information into better engineering, regulatory, legal, financial, and governance decisions. By extending the traditional Weather Information Value Chain to include the Institutional Decision Framework, this presentation offers a broader perspective on how the Weather Enterprise can contribute to financial performance, economic resilience, and more effective public policy in an increasingly weather- and climate-sensitive economy. The greatest future economic value of the Weather Enterprise may come not only from producing better scientific information, but from enabling better institutional decisions. [i] The U.S. Weather Enterprise is the collaborative partnership among federal, state, and local government agencies, private-sector organizations, universities, professional societies, and nonprofit organizations that develop, communicate, and apply weather, water, and climate information to support public safety, economic activity, and environmental decision-making

487544.title: Characterizing 1–5 Day Stratospheric Waves Using Balloon Observations from the Strateole-2 Campaigns and ERA5 Reanalysis
487544.authors: Lan Luan, NorthWest Research Associates, Boulder, CO; and M. J. Alexander and M. Bramberger
487544.abstract: Tropical waves drive the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (QBO), and waves with all scales and frequencies contribute. Long duration superpressure balloon observations have revealed that waves with a period of 1–5 days and short vertical wavelengths significantly influence the variability in the tropical lower stratosphere. Drifting passively with the wind on a constant density surface for months, these quasi-Lagrangian balloon observations uniquely measure wave intrinsic frequency. The intrinsic frequency is the frequency embodied in wave dispersion relations that relates frequencies and horizontal and vertical wavenumbers for different wave types. Previous work with super-pressure balloon data has identified waves in this period range as inertia-gravity waves with extreme aspect ratios: Vertical wavelengths only O~1km but horizontal wavelengths O~1000km. A likely source for these waves is tropical mesoscale convective systems. However, the representation of waves within this intrinsic frequency band (periods of 1-5 days) remains uncertain, and these waves may be an under-represented class of waves in models simulating the QBO. In this study, we analyze temperature and wind observations from the past Strateole-2 campaigns in 2019–2020 and 2021–2022 as well as the campaign beginning in fall 2026 to characterize wave activities with periods of 1–5 days, and we evaluate their representation in the ERA5 reanalysis. The Lagrangian balloon observations provide continuous measurements in the tropical lower stratosphere at around 18–20 km. We interpolate ERA5 temperature and wind fields along balloon trajectories and use an S-transform method to extract 1–5 day wave signals from both the observations and ERA5 reanalysis fields. Analysis of wave total energy shows that ERA5 exhibits weaker and less frequent wave signals compared to the observations. The difference is likely due to limitations in vertical resolution and representation of tropical mesoscale convective systems in ERA5. This study provides new insights into wave dynamics in the tropical lower stratosphere and informs efforts to improve their representation in atmospheric reanalyses and models.

487546.title: The MANTAS Tool: Leveraging AI to Enhance the FAIR-ness of Environmental Data Collected by Uncrewed Systems
487546.authors: Andrew Evans, PhD, NESDIS, Stennis Space Center, MS; and C. Cayson, P. Panday, and J. Weick
487546.abstract: Environmental data collected by uncrewed systems—such as gliders, sail drones, and remotely operated vehicles—represents a significant technological asset for organizations like NOAA. However, the current data ecosystem is hindered by fragmented, field specific management practices characterized by isolated tools, manual data handling, and inadequate metadata standards. This disorganized structure is an antiquated approach which prevents scientists from easily discovering and utilizing environmental datasets, essentially creating "data silos" where research data becomes trapped on inaccessible, unsearchable local servers. To overcome these operational barriers and achieve FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles, a unified, cloud-native architecture is required to replace legacy, manual workflows with a streamlined cloud ingestion engine, an automated pipeline, standardized ISO-compliant templates, and AI-enhanced metadata tagging. FAIR data will become a necessity as the adoption of uncrewed systems continues to increase the amount of data accessible, and for full utilization of that data for the ocean economy and maritime safety and security. We have developed a unified, cloud-native architecture designed to solve the operational barriers of fragmented management and achieve FAIR data principles. This solution prevents environmental data collected by uncrewed systems from becoming trapped in isolated data silos on inaccessible local servers. The system is built upon three critical pillars: a standardized ISO compliant template, AI-enhanced metadata tagging, and a streamlined cloud ingestion engine. To bridge the operational gap between secure on-premise networks and commercial cloud environments, the MANTAS toolkit leverages advanced tools like an AI-powered "pre-flight cockpit" for metadata creation and validation. MANTAS allows users to save profiles so that metadata fields from previous expeditions can be prepopulated with vital information such as ORCIDs, RORs for agency identification and tagging, and platform and sensor payload information. Additionally, MANTAS systematically addresses the science-wide issue of disparate keyword dictionaries by utilizing vocabulary crosswalks and Gemini-powered AI to automatically generate contextually relevant keywords. This allows researchers to uniformly tag data using SKOS semantic crosswalks to link relevant keywords across disparate dictionaries such as GCMD and NERCs or others. MANTAS utilizes the APIs of these dictionaries to tag data with both the keyword for discoverability, and the UUID of those keywords so that updates and edits are maintained by the dictionary owners and not reliant on users or the archive for updates. Furthermore, its "Orphan Hunter" functionality proactively ensures long-term data integrity by preventing files from becoming disconnected from their source project or cruise level identifiers. Finally, MANTAS is fully integrable to NCEI’s Open Information Stewardship Service (OISS). This allows for future applications to replace legacy, manual workflows with a fully automated, cloud-native pipeline to the NCEI archive for long term data preservation. Replacing fragmented, manual processes with this cohesive, automated pipeline, the architecture transforms how ocean data is processed, secured, and shared. This systematic approach to FAIR data not only secures environmental data across agency boundaries but also leverages AI to ensure that vast archives of environmental data are instantly discoverable and can be fully leveraged.

487547.title: Next-Generation Precipitation Frequency Standard for Present-Day Estimates: Development of the NOAA Atlas 15 Volume 1 Framework
487547.authors: Janel Hanrahan, RTI International, Research Triangle Park, NC; and S. Perica, D. Martin, and M. Lago
487547.abstract: The Office of Water Prediction (OWP) within NOAA’s National Weather Service is developing NOAA Atlas 15 to serve as the nation's precipitation frequency (PF) standard. This updated framework will deliver seamless estimates across both the contiguous United States (CONUS) and domains outside CONUS (oCONUS), including Alaska, Hawaii, and select U.S. territories. To account for the nonstationarity, NOAA Atlas 15 is structured into two distinct volumes: Volume 1 establishes a present-day snapshot of PF estimates by incorporating historical nonstationarity captured via gauge observations, while Volume 2 utilizes climate model projections to deliver future estimates tied to potential changes in global temperature. While NOAA Atlas 15 encompasses both volumes, this presentation focuses on the technical development and refinement of the Volume 1 framework as it progresses toward stakeholder and public review. The discussion highlights improved regionalization techniques implemented across both the Mean Annual Maximum (MAM) and PF frameworks, including the spatial delineation and statistical weighting of gauge stations, as well as the methods used to derive confidence intervals. Furthermore, unique modeling challenges specific to data-sparse oCONUS regions will be addressed, alongside forthcoming supplementary products, including seasonality analyses of precipitation exceedances and the development of localized rainfall-only frequency estimates.

487549.title: The Influence of Turbulence Kinetic Energy and Static Stability on Stratosphere–Troposphere Exchange in an Idealized Tropical Cyclone
487549.authors: John Mark Mayhall, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Haleyville, AL; and P. Duran and X. Chen
487549.abstract: Stratosphere–troposphere exchange (STE) is the irreversible exchange of air across the tropopause, which transports water vapor and ice into the stratosphere while transporting ozone into the upper troposphere. This exchange can affect air quality in the troposphere and increase water vapor in the lower stratosphere, which subsequently alters stratospheric radiation absorption and temperature. As synoptic-scale systems, tropical cyclones (TCs) regulate STE. The outflow and overshooting convective towers can transport tropospheric air, water vapor, and ice into the stratosphere, while TC-driven subsidence can draw stratospheric air and ozone into the troposphere. Despite the prevalence of STE induced (or enhanced) by TCs, turbulent processes in the outflow layer that drive TC-induced STE remain poorly understood. Using an idealized Cloud Model 1 (CM1) simulation of a TC, this study analyzes a turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) budget to characterize the relationship among TKE budget terms, TC intensity, and STE. The diurnal cycle of TKE and water species, as well as the TKE budget terms, is analyzed in a tropopause-centered reference frame. Preliminary results show that TKE is enhanced at night, can extend up to 2 km above the tropopause, and is correlated with water vapor and ice near the tropopause. TKE shear production, in particular, is enhanced at night due to a stronger TC outflow and is partially countered by increases in TKE dissipation and negative buoyancy. The net increase in TKE production overnight leads to stronger vertical transport of TKE. This can enhance STE overnight and, subsequently, warm the lower stratosphere through increased radiation absorption.

487554.title: Phase 2 of the AMS Weather Enterprise Study
487554.authors: Keith L. Seitter, American Meteorological Society, Boston, MA
487554.abstract: The American Meteorological Society launched a special study on the weather enterprise in 2023, two decades after the release of the influential National Academies study: Fair Weather: Effective Partnerships in Weather and Climate Services. Phase 1 of the AMS Weather Enterprise Study produced a report that described the state of the weather enterprise as of January 2025. This report chronicled the development of a robust and balanced enterprise in which each sector of the enterprise — private, government, academic, and NGO — focused on what it did best in cooperation and collaboration with the other sectors in order to provide the best possible weather products and services to the nation’s people and its economy. Over the past two years, there have been major changes in resource allocations for the federal agencies engaged in weather and climate activities, as well as a significant expansion of private sector capabilities. As the restructuring of the federal agencies continues amid evolving policy frameworks in energy, technology, transportation, workforce, education, and other sectors, it is clear that the entire weather enterprise is evolving as well. Phase 2 of this study intends to support having that evolution be intentional — based on deliberative discussion among stakeholders — toward a Weather Enterprise that best serves the public good. This paper will present the current status of that Phase 2 effort, and discuss ways for a broader cross section of the community to be involved in it.

487556.title: Development of the Configurable Atmospheric Chemistry (CATChem) Component within NOAA's Unified Forecast System
487556.authors: Wei Li, NOAA/ARL, College Park, MD; George Mason Univ., Fairfax, VA; and B. D. Baker II, M. Bruckner, R. H. Schwantes, Z. Moon, B. Koziol, Y. Tang, P. C. Campbell, J. He, Q. Z. Rasool, L. Zhang, B. C. McDonald, and D. Tong
487556.abstract: The Configurable Atmospheric Chemistry (CATChem) component is being developed to unify all chemistry-related code within a single, flexible framework in NOAA's Unified Forecast System (UFS). CATChem features a modular core architecture in which a Process Manager orchestrates gas chemistry, aerosol, emission, and deposition components through centralized state management. A column virtualization approach transforms 3D atmospheric fields into independent 1D columns, reducing memory pressure and enabling efficient OpenMP/MPI parallelization with improved cache performance. To accelerate the addition of new scientific processes, a Python-based Process Generator uses YAML configuration and Jinja2 templating to automatically produce standardized Fortran code, test suites, and documentation, reducing the typical development cycle from weeks to days while eliminating common errors in field access and memory management. CATChem couples to the UFS through a NUOPC (National Unified Operational Prediction Capability) cap that handles multi-phase initialization, field advertisement, and bidirectional state transformation between NUOPC and CATChem data structures. Major GOCART-2G aerosol components — including dust, sea salt, organic and black carbon, and sulfate — have been implemented and tested within the UFS framework. All model behavior is controlled through a hierarchy of YAML configuration files covering simulation settings, species properties, emission mappings, and NUOPC field mappings. Preliminary comparisons with the Global Chemistry and Aerosol Forecast System (GCAFS) show comparable results across all implemented aerosol species, demonstrating that the newly built framework faithfully reproduces established operational performance. CATChem is designed to serve as the unified atmospheric chemistry component for NOAA's next-generation forecasting systems, providing a configurable and extensible foundation for applications ranging from global aerosol forecasting to regional air quality prediction.

487558.title: The Influence of Clouds on the Interpretation of TEMPO Observations: STAQS Validation Results and a View Toward HAMAQ
487558.authors: Laura Judd, NASA, Newport News, VA; and S. Janz, J. Park, J. Crawford, B. C. McDonald, C. R. Nowlan, G. Gonzalez Abad, H. Wang, and X. Liu
487558.abstract: One of the largest challenges in validating air quality retrievals from new hourly observations from geostationary instrumentation is interpreting the time-of-day influence on assumptions made within the algorithm. For example, TEMPO trace gas retrievals are reliant on cloud information to estimate the vertical sensitivity of the observations to the atmosphere. Errors in cloud information can lead to unintended biases and cloud-scenes as well as the temporal patterns in cloud coverage may skew temporal averages in data. This presentation will present up-to-date validation results on TEMPO’s L2 trace gas products during the Synergistic TEMPO Air Quality Science field study in August 2023 with an airborne spectrometer. A particular focus will be given on the impact of cloud inputs on the validation results in two algorithm versions, V3 and V4, using the TEMPO cloud algorithm input as well as independent information at cloud characteristics from the airborne spectrometer and the GOES ABI Cloud Mask product. Finally, looking toward future field campaigns, this presentation will discuss the typical timing of clouds over the two deployment locations of the Hemispheric Airborne Measurements of Air Quality (HAMAQ) mission in 2028: Mexico City and Atlanta. These discussions will frame the timing of the deployment as it relates to cloud coverage and air quality, and expectations for science quality measurements in each domain.

487572.title: Investigating AI-based Forecasts of PM2.5 from the Aurora Foundational Model Using NCEP Aerosol Initial Conditions
487572.authors: Ellie Hojeily, NOAA Center for Atmospheric Sciences and Meteorology (NCAS-M II), Washington, DC; University at Albany, Atmospheric Sciences Research Center, Albany, NY; and J. Wang, L. Cui, and C. H. Lu
487572.abstract: There has been increasing interest in AI-based air pollution forecasting systems since predicting air quality is traditionally expensive and prone to uncertainty (i.e., emissions) that may be well-resolved through data-driven approaches. Microsoft’s AI-based foundational model, Aurora, was fine-tuned for air quality using ECMWF's global atmospheric composition model, the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS). The present study seeks to quantify Aurora skill at predicting surface PM2.5 relative to NOAA's global aerosol model, GEFS-Aerosols, during a wildfire (June 6-10, 2023) and winter (January 18-24, 2025) case. The ability of Aurora to generalize to new initial conditions is evaluated by initializing with aerosol and meteorological information from GEFS analyses. Aurora and GEFS-Aerosols performance is evaluated by comparison with surface PM2.5 observations from AirNow. Results indicate that, for the wildfire case, Aurora forecasts tended to underestimate the severity of the wildfire episode in comparison to GEFS-Aerosols which overestimated severity. Despite this, GEFS-Aerosols produces higher critical success index scores than the Aurora forecasts. Aurora was compatible with GEFS initial conditions, producing a more severe and accurate prediction of the wildfire episode using aerosol and meteorological information from GEFS. Regardless of initial conditions, Aurora forecasts exhibited unrealistic plume behavior characterized by the model failing to sustain wildfires as a point source. As a result, forecasts became unreliable for wildfires past forecast hour 48. The winter case better demonstrated Aurora’s capabilities as a PM2.5 forecasting model, with it outperforming GEFS-Aerosols over CONUS out to forecast hour 120. However, forecasts initialized with CAMS or GEFS initial conditions became increasingly similar with lead-time, appearing to converge to a common solution. This study served as an introduction to AI-based PM2.5 forecasting from a pre-trained foundational model. Events like the winter case that are dependent on meteorological conditions and anthropogenic behaviors are well captured by the model since they can be explained by the surface and static variables in Aurora’s architecture. Conversely, Aurora struggles to capture and maintain the severity of wildfires since Aurora has no way of knowing that a wildfire is occurring beyond seeing a PM2.5 hotspot during initialization. Future development of AI-based PM2.5 forecasting capabilities should consider explicit representation of wildfire emissions and fine-tuning on multiple sources of atmospheric composition data, such as CAMS, GEFS-Aerosols or NASA's MERRA-2 and GEOS-CF.

487576.title: Animal-Level Measurement and Mitigation of Beef Cattle Enteric Methane Emissions
487576.authors: Sara Place, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Vargas, E. M. Paula, L. Sitorski, K. Stackhouse-Lawson, P. H. V. Carvalho, E. Burke, M. Werner, C. Wharton, M. Swenson, A. Schilling-Hazlett, I. Reis, M. Souza, C. Velasquez, A. Jannat, L. Thomas, E. J. Raynor, A. Shadbolt, and L. Campos
487576.abstract: Methane emissions from cattle can arise from enteric fermentation processes within the animal’s gastrointestinal tract. Enteric methane is primarily emitted from cattle through their nostrils and mouth and represents 26.5% of US methane emissions. Our research group has measured over 2,200 individual animals in 17 experiments with an automated head chamber system (GreenFeed, C-Lock Inc., Rapid City, SD, USA). Key findings from our research can be categorized in three areas: animal-to-animal variation, dietary influences on enteric methane emissions, and evaluation of extant empirical prediction models of enteric methane emissions from beef cattle. Animal-to-animal variation of methane emissions from cattle fed the same diet can vary by 30% from highest to lowest emitting animals when corrected for body size and feed intake. This variation highlights opportunities for discovery and mitigation in the areas of the rumen microbiome and genetic selection for reduced methane emissions. Additionally, we have demonstrated that as cattle progress through their production cycle (i.e., from grazing pasture to feedlot finishing), their methane emissions rank (high to low emitting) can change within their cohort of cattle. Production system and diet specific assessment of methane emissions are key for evaluating bottom-up estimates of emissions from cattle sources. Our findings have confirmed that as cattle move from grass-based diets when grazing to grain-based diets in confinement feedlots, their methane emissions decrease, especially when expressed per unit of feed consumed and per unit of body weight gained. Additionally, we have evaluated different dietary ingredients, including the inclusion of supplemental fat sources in feedlot cattle diets. Adding fat can lower methane emissions by over 20% per animal per day; however, the effect is dependent both on fat type and dose in the diet. Finally, we have evaluated published empirical models for methane emissions of cattle both fed in confinement and in grazing conditions. For cattle fed in confinement, all 72 retrieved equations from the literature had low accuracy and precision when evaluated against an independent dataset. For grazing cattle, four retrieved models performed excellent with regard to accuracy and precision when evaluated against an independent dataset; however, all four required knowledge of forage intake, which is difficult to assess in both research and commercial conditions. Our work evaluating prediction models points to the need for further improvements or alternative approaches (e.g., combining modeled estimates) in cattle fed in confinement, and the need for technological advancements in grazing cattle to assess forage consumption. In summary, measurement of cattle with technology such as the automate head chamber system can lead to discoveries regarding the control of animal-to-animal variation and mitigation of methane emissions. Additionally, this technology can improve estimates of bottom-up inventories of enteric methane emissions from beef cattle production systems.

487577.title: The FireHouse: Breaking Down Silos in Fire Weather Social Science to Unify End-User Insights
487577.authors: Stephanie M. Hoekstra, CIRA/GSL, Los Angeles, CA; and E. Wells
487577.abstract: As fire weather social science research grows, valuable end-user insights often remain siloed within individual projects, obscuring systemic operational challenges. To turn these isolated findings into clear, high-priority action items, our team at the Cooperative Institute for Research of the Atmosphere (CIRA) and NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) developed the FireHouse 1.0 Report. Our primary motivation is to overcome these research silos by synthesizing end-user needs and recommendations across the entire wildland fire lifecycle. To achieve this, we utilized a systematic, four-stage qualitative analysis to evaluate data from nine distinct projects completed between 2024 and early 2026, representing 634 diverse participants. Participants included meteorologists, land and fire agency personnel, emergency managers, and Tribal environmental professionals who evaluated a wide range of operational systems and tools, including the Next Generation Fire Detection system, high-resolution smoke models, and standard NWS watches and warnings, to name a few. This cross-project synthesis revealed core patterns across four main themes: observations and monitoring, forecasts and modeling, warnings and immediate response, and strategic adaptation and institutional governance. This report was just the initial spark; we will continuously iterate on this analysis, publishing subsequent versions (e.g. FireHouse 2.0 and 3.0) as new projects are completed and their findings are integrated into our framework. As our immediate next step, we transitioned these field-validated findings into the FireHouse online portal—a public, interactive, and "living" website. We now invite the broader research community to contribute their own social science findings and end-user needs to this active portal. By collectively breaking down traditional research silos, we can scale this portal into the premier centralized hub for all unified fire weather insights–providing a powerful, shared evidence base to inform critical policy decisions, strengthen future research and grant proposals, and guide strategic adaptation across the fire cycle.

487583.title: Igniting Impact: Advancing Fire Weather Decision Support Services
487583.authors: Stephanie M. Hoekstra, CIRA/GSL, Los Angeles, CA
487583.abstract: As fire environments grow more complex, fire management professionals are seeking deeper operational integration with NWS meteorologists. Based on 19 focus groups and a national survey of 475 fire professionals, this poster explores how to evolve Fire Weather Decision Support Services (DSS) to better align with end-user timelines and tactical realities. Although National Weather Service (NWS) local office products are highly valued—serving as the primary information source for 84.2% of fire partners and achieving a perfect 7/7 median utility score—the research identifies critical opportunities to modernize communication. This poster will highlight key operational shifts drawn from the study's 10 recommendations. Core examples include the need for 72-hour trend forecasting to align with partner resource cycles, the implementation of "Particularly Dangerous Situation" (PDS) headers for extreme events, the strategic issuance of “marginal” Red Flag Warnings during near-criteria conditions to provide partners with necessary administrative cover, and a growing demand for high-touch, two-way communication. While these recommendations are primarily designed for NWS operational forecasters, the underlying data offers insights to others who may benefit from having a better understanding of end-user fire weather needs for the strategic development of future fire weather tools and products.

487589.title: Bridging Data Silos with the NESDIS Storefront: A Unified AI-Powered Access Point via the INDUS Embedding Model
487589.authors: Adam Behnke, Tactis, Washington, DC; and T. Schubarth, T. Scourby, A. Mangini, R. I. Lana, J. Su, B. Chell, I. Wahagheghe, and T. Vo
487589.abstract: NOAA’s National Environmental Satellite Data and Information Service (NESDIS) manages vast environmental data holdings essential for emergency response and government operations. However, public accessibility is hindered by a fragmented ecosystem of over 30 unconsolidated websites and 25 disparate APIs, making NESDIS data access inefficient and imposing a high cognitive load on stakeholders. To address these barriers, we present the Next Generation Public Data Delivery Portal, or the Storefront, a pilot portal that utilizes an AWS-hosted multi-tier Medallion pipeline to transition NESDIS from a traditional file provider to an outcome-oriented provider. The system processes data from over 60 NOAA endpoints through fixed Bronze, schema-validated Silver, and AI-optimized Gold layers, powering a high performance, single federated entry point for cross-domain queries across atmospheric, oceanic, and terrestrial datasets. Additionally, the AI Query Orchestrator, composed of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Claude 3.5 Haiku, interpret the queries to fetch and synthesize relevant data into human-readable summaries. The system also integrates the INDUS scientific embedding system to provide domain-specific context for Earth science terminology that general-purpose models often fail to contextualize. By combining federated scalability with the precision of INDUS-driven embeddings, the Storefront establishes a blueprint for federal data transparency. Future work includes expanding the platform with geohash-based spatial indexing and cross-agency federation with USGS, EPA, and FEMA data sources.

487590.title: Incorporating Sub-Seasonal to Seasonal (S2S) Ensemble Precipitation Forecasts to Improve S2S Streamflow Predictions In the United States
487590.abstract: In the United States, ensemble streamflow forecasts are generated from the Hydrologic Ensemble Forecast Service (HEFS), operated by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Weather Service. On sub-seasonal to seasonal (S2S) timescales (i.e., weeks 3 - 4), HEFS is often driven by randomly resampled climatology, rather than a forecast. However, recent advances in ensemble weather prediction, including meteorological preprocessing techniques, present an opportunity to improve S2S streamflow predictions. Here, we present work that leverages two approaches developed at NOAA’s Physical Sciences Laboratory (PSL) that have been shown to improve S2S precipitation forecasts: (i) the parametric Censored Shifted Gamma Distribution method and (ii) the neural-network-based ResUnet, FiLM, and Climatological-Offramp. The improved weeks 3-4 probabilistic accumulated precipitation forecasts are used in a hydrological weighting (postprocessing) scheme, whereby the streamflow traces are resampled so as to reflect the precipitation forecast. As such, the streamflow postprocessing approach can incorporate the forecast, but in a way that can work seamlessly with existing operational workflows. The approach is demonstrated by applying the techniques to the Global Ensemble Forecast System v12 (GEFSv12) precipitation forecasts, but is general and could be applied to other S2S products. Applications will be discussed for case studies relevant to societal applications that would benefit from better S2S streamflow predictions, including Forecast Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO).

487611.title: Architecture, Design, and Performance of the Next Generation Landsat Imager (LandIS)
487611.authors: Julie Montoya, Raytheon, HAWTHORNE, CA; RTX, El Segundo, CA
487611.abstract: The Landsat Instrument Suite (LandIS) program was awarded in 2024 by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the United States Geological Survey (USGS) and development on this revolutionary new sensor progresses at a rapid pace ensuring program readiness and protecting data continuity that spans 50 years of observations. LandIS is a low earth orbit (LEO) instrument set to fly at an altitude of 653 kilometers (km) and providing improved spatial resolution by up to a factor of three. This along with new spectral bands (from 400 nanometers (nm) to 12 microns) is expected to uncover new insights into patterns that may have been missed on prior missions and enables the creation of new science data records as well. This presentation will review the architecture, design choices, and sourcing philosophy which enabled the increased capabilities, provide status on the current build and test process completed to date, and review the new scientific and meteorological advancements that LandIS will hopefully uncover.

487618.title: Refining Machine Learning to Create Wind Wave and Swell Wave Height and Period Values for Ocean Observation and Input into Numerical Wave Model Forecasts
487618.authors: Lance E. Steele, Weathernews, Norman, OK
487618.abstract: Harnessing over two decades of National Data Buoy Center (NDBC) ocean observations, Machine Learning (ML) was applied to the data in order to create algorithms to separate the overall observed significant wave height into wind wave (sea) height and swell wave height. ML algorithms were also created to estimate sea and swell wave periods once the waves were separated. After a year of research, the resulting algorithms have been put into use to create observations used by our marine forecasting sector, and eventually this data will go into model initialization and verification. The 2025 NDBC data have also been added to the ML training data set, and 2026 data is being used to verify the results. Previous work focused on two "white box" algorithms, a decision tree to separate seas/swells and linear regression algorithms to calculate the height of the resulting sea/swell. This was to make it easier to hard code the algorithm into the program. Now that the operational framework is running in Python, the focus has shifted to a "black box" random forest regressor algorithm that shows lower error when calculating wave heights. The resulting accuracy and thought process behind the change in focus will be presented.

487630.title: An Evaluation of Aerosol Optical Depth in GEOS-CAM During the Summer of 2026
487630.authors: Carson Alexander Turner, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and A. Collow
487630.abstract: Accurately forecasting aerosols is essential for predicting air quality and its impacts on human health. Weather prediction models that couple aerosols to the meteorology, such as the Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) Forward Processing (GEOS-FP), provide a wealth of information that can be used to further our understanding of air quality prediction. Recent advancements in the use of a stretched grid to allow for high spatial resolution over the United States have allowed for the GEOS Convection Allowing Model (GEOS-CAM) to generate forecasts of meteorological and aerosol diagnostics at a resolution as fine as ~2.5 km. While aerosols in GEOS-FP have been thoroughly evaluated in a research framework, validation of aerosols within GEOS-CAM has been limited up until this point. By performing a more in-depth assessment of aerosols within GEOS-CAM, recommendations can be made for applications of these forecasts and areas of improvement within GEOS-CAM. To evaluate GEOS-CAM, AOD forecasts were compared with the GEOS-FP prediction system and ground-based observations of AOD values from the Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET). While GEOS-CAM accurately forecasted daily AOD variability, it struggled to capture AOD increases associated with an extreme smoke event. Forecasts of AOD from GEOS-FP showed high correlations with observations, accurately capturing this event with a lead time out to 18 hours. While both systems are subject to biases related to smoke emission, transport, and optical properties, it is hypothesized that the discrepancy between GEOS-CAM and GEOS-FP is largely caused by the lack of AOD data assimilation in GEOS-CAM. Further evaluation is required to assess seasonal performance and GEOS-CAM’s ability to capture large-scale events, such as Saharan dust plumes reaching the southeast United States before guidance can be provided on the use of GEOS-CAM output for air quality applications. To further understand how well aerosols are represented by GEOS-CAM, future work will include identifying the influence of AOD assimilation on aerosol forecasts in GEOS-FP, expanding the analysis to fine particulate matter (PM2.5), and evaluating aerosol composition within GEOS-CAM.

487631.title: Quantifying the Relative Contributions of Marine Air Penetration and Agricultural Irrigation to Planetary Boundary Layer Development in California’s Central Valley
487631.authors: KUAN-YUN WANG, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA; and S. H. Chen, C. Schmitt, Y. Yu, K. Suvočarev, I. McDonald, X. M. Chen, P. Di, Y. C. Liu, Y. Hsu, R. Thiruvenkatachari, and J. Avise
487631.abstract: Summertime planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) across California’s Central Valley (CV) is modulated by several processes, including agricultural irrigation and marine air penetration (MAP). Previous studies have examined the effects of irrigation and MAP separately, using numerical models for the former and observational or reanalysis data for the latter. This study uses numerical modeling to quantify the relative contribution of irrigation and MAP to PBLH changes across the CV during 21-26 July 2022 and to investigate the underlying mechanisms. Four experiments are conducted in combinations of with (WIR) and without (WoIR) agricultural irrigation, and with and without MAP. The MAP effect is removed by filling up mountain gaps (FM) to a minimum of 700 meters along the coastal range. Compared with WoIR, the cooler surface temperature (i.e., lower sensible heat flux) due to stronger evapotranspiration in WIR weakens dry convection, resulting in a decrease of PBLH in the northern (southern) CV by 0.5-1.5 km (0.5-1 km) where the irrigation rate is high. In contrast, the MAP effect stabilizes the lower atmosphere by advecting cold air to the lower atmosphere and lowers PBLH across the CV roughly by 0.5-1 km. The stabilization layer in the northern CV is shallower than that in the southern CV. Overall, between the two effects, irrigation contributes to >50% of the total PBLH reduction in the northern and southern CV, whereas MAP contributes to ~100% of the total PBLH reduction in the central CV, with the contribution decaying away from the MAP sources.

487641.title: A Cloud-to-Ground Lightning Time Series and Climatology Dataset for the Contiguous United States
487641.authors: Daniel J. Cecil, NASA MSFC, Huntsville, AL; and K. L. Cummins and M. J. Murphy
487641.abstract: A gridded dataset has been developed to characterize lightning and thunderstorm activity in the contiguous United States for the period 2003-2025. A re-processed version of the cloud-to-ground (CG) portion of Vaisala’s XWeather National Lightning Detection Network (NLDN) flash archive forms the basis of this dataset, to be published in support of scientific research and reproducibility.
