Whereas NLDN network and processing capabilities have improved over the years, leading to detection of weaker discharges and improved discrimination of intracloud from CG lightning, this dataset prioritizes temporal consistency. Therefore, a single flash typing algorithm is applied to all data, using NLDN’s legacy algorithm from prior to 13 Aug 2015. Counts of positive and negative CG flashes are stored, with separate counts of low amplitude positive and negative CG flashes also stored so users have the option of filtering out the low amplitude flashes that are more readily detected in recent years than in prior years. The resulting dataset has a set of 23 yearly files, with the values for each year separated by month, hour of local solar time, and latitude and longitude. Separate parameters for positive and negative CG flashes (all, low peak current, high peak current, and single-stroke) include: flash counts sum of multiplicity (to compute means) sum of peak currents (to compute means) For counting storm frequency or intensity, parameters are not separated by time of day: Duty cycle (total 5-minute intervals with flashes) Mean and 95th percentile 5-minute flash rate Thunderstorm count (with at least 60 minute gap between flashes in a grid cell) Hours with at least 1, 10, 20, or 50 flashes in grid cell We will present spatial maps and time-series plots of selected parameters that demonstrate the 23-year time-evolution of CG lightning behavior over the conterminous Unites States (CONUS), demonstrating a downward trend in CG activity over most of region, with a steady increase in the percentage and mean peak current for positive flashes.

487654.title: Applications of Potential Intensity Theory to Operational Tropical Cyclone Intensity Forecasting
487654.authors: Mark DeMaria, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Kaplan, G. Chirokova, G. Foltz, K. Schwartz, and K. Musgrave
487654.abstract: Having an accurate upper bound estimate of tropical cyclone (TC) maximum wind is of great utility for operational intensity forecasting. The operational Statistical Hurricane Intensity Prediction Scheme (SHIPS) model was first implemented for the Atlantic basin in 1991, for the eastern North Pacific in 1996, followed by the Rapid Intensification Index (RII) in 2003 for both basins. Using the framework described by Emanuel (1988), the potential intensity (PI) minus the current intensity was tested as input to SHIPS and was found to be the leading predictor at almost every forecast period, and similarly for the RII. The statistical-dynamical Logistic Growth Equation Model (LGEM) was implemented operationally in 2006, which relaxed some of the assumptions in SHIPS and made greater use of PI by incorporating it directly into the differential equation used to predict intensity changes. The utility of PI in NHC’s suite of statistical-dynamical intensity models for 1991-present will be reviewed. PI theory indicates that the maximum intensity is a function of the sea surface temperature (SST) and the atmospheric thermodynamic structure. However, in NHC’s statistical-dynamical intensity models, an empirical PI formation has been used that is only a function of the SST, the storm translational speed, and the TC basin. Additional predictors to account for upper-level temperature and ocean cooling effects are included in NHC’s statistical intensity models, but separately from the PI estimate. A new PI formulation is being developed as a generalization of the theoretical PI formulation by Bister and Emanuel (1998) that directly includes input from the atmospheric temperature and moisture profiles and ocean cooling effects through a mixing parameterization. The new version also includes vertical shear effects on PI through an atmospheric entrainment parameter. The updated PI formulation and its impact on NHC’s statistical-dynamical models will be described.

487661.title: Smoke, Dust, and Resilience: Unraveling the March 2025 Oklahoma Compound Hazards
487661.authors: S. Marcela Loria-Salazar, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and C. J. Flynn, C. R. Homeyer, H. M. Webb, S. M. Hitchcock, and D. Schvartzman
487661.abstract: On March 14, 2025, an intense low-pressure system over the Southwest U.S. collided with humid air masses, triggering a severe weather outbreak across multiple states. Texas and Oklahoma were hit particularly hard, experiencing destructive winds up to 85 mph, widespread dust storms, and rapidly advancing wildfires. Satellite imagery captured extensive dust plumes and smoke emissions, especially near wildfire zones in Oklahoma. The extreme conditions led to over 170,000 acres burned, more than 400 structures damaged or destroyed, widespread power outages, and multiple fatalities, prompting a state of emergency. This study examines the intricate relationships between meteorological drivers and aerosol behavior during this multi-hazard event. Leveraging a suite of satellite and ground-based remote sensing tools, in situ observations, back trajectory analyses, and meteorological reanalysis data, we assess how aerosol physical, optical, and chemical properties evolved throughout the event. We also examine the atmospheric conditions that facilitated long-range dust transport and the ignition of wildfires. Our findings provide critical insights into the growing threat of compound hazards in the Southern Great Plains and underscore the importance of integrated observational strategies for enhancing regional resilience and air quality management

487669.title: The Hemispheric Airborne Zonal Investigation (HAZI)
487669.authors: Katherine Travis, NASA Langley Research Center, Williamsburg, VA; and J. Crawford, W. Tang, and J. Laughner
487669.abstract: Transport of chemical and meteorological tracers is an essential component of any Earth System model. Errors in transport are a limiting factor in many areas of understanding atmospheric composition, from calculating emission fluxes to determining impacts on downwind receptor locations. The Atmospheric Tomography Mission (ATom) provided an excellent dataset to probe the remote environment over all four seasons. However, ATom did not probe how pollution evolves from source to sink. The Hemispheric Airborne Zonal Investigation (HAZI) proposes to use the new NASA B777, which has the capability to fly up to 18 hours continuously, to measure continuous vertical profiles of the troposphere in a similar manner to ATom, but zonally in the Northern Hemisphere during spring, when long-range transport is most pronounced. The international constellation of geostationary satellites currently in place in the Northern hemisphere provides strong constraints on the magnitude and variability of pollution in source regions that can be connected by HAZI flights. The HAZI science objectives are as follows: Observe the processes the govern intercontinental transport between Asia and North America, and North America and Europe. Assess the performance of model emission inventories at source regions and the impact of transport uncertainties on calculating long-range impacts. Determine the factors governing chemical transformation of gas-phase and aerosol pollutions during transport. The B777 would provide in situ profiles throughout the troposphere on the outbound leg of each flight. On the return flight, either profiling or high-altitude remote sensing would be possible. Given the size of the B777, there are many opportunities for cross-disciplinary science. Examples include providing the greenhouse gas community with profiles of difficult to retrieve species such as carbonyl sulfide (OCS) that can provide constraints on the biosphere uptake of CO2 and providing the stratospheric community measurements of very short-lived substances (VSLS) in the upper troposphere that deplete stratospheric ozone and are currently unregulated. The development of the HAZI concept seeks to maximize these opportunities and welcomes further ideas and collaborations.

487672.title: Assessing Model Simulations of Surface PM2.5 during the ASIA-AQ Field Campaign using Airborne High Spectral Resolution Lidar Measurements
487672.authors: Amy J. Scarino, Coherent Applications, Inc. - Psionic, LLC, Hampton, VA; and R. A. Ferrare, J. W. Hair, T. Shingler, M. Fenn, M. Clayton, S. Burton, P. Saide, M. Mohanty, P. Castellanos, J. Crawford, and K. Travis
487672.abstract: Near-surface aerosol retrievals from four NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) airborne High Spectral Resolution Lidars (HSRLs) have been used to develop machine learning (ML) regression models to infer surface and aloft particulate matter with aerodynamic diameters less than 2.5 µm (PM2.5) and 10 µm (PM10). These ML models are trained on airborne HSRL data collected since 2011 over major urban regions in the United States and Asia, matched with coincident hourly surface PM observations from the EPA Air Quality System and international air quality monitoring networks. Surface PM2.5 derived from airborne HSRL-2 measurements over the Philippines, South Korea, Taiwan, and Thailand using these models are used to evaluate PM simulations from the Weather Research and Forecasting Model coupled with Chemistry (WRF-Chem) and the Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2) models during the Airborne and Satellite Investigation of Asian Air Quality (ASIA-AQ) field campaign. This evaluation will highlight regional model performance and advance our understanding of surface and vertical PM distributions across complex Asian urban environments and impacted by various aerosol types.

487673.title: DataStreme: Meteorology for Educators MOOC
487673.authors: Erin Smoak, M.S. and M.Ed., American Meteorological Society, Savannah, GA; and C. M. Kauffman
487673.abstract: Established in the mid-1990s, the AMS DataStreme Program has served as a premier professional development initiative for K-12 educators. Throughout its history, the program has transitioned from local, in-person meetings to hybrid and online graduate-level courses, and most recently, to an open online course format. These courses are currently accessible to the general public at no cost and without a formal application process, although the primary focus remains on K-12 education. Educators who successfully complete the open online course are eligible to apply for an intensive in-person residency. The pilot for DataStreme: Meteorology for Educators was conducted online from June through August 2026. This online component addressed fundamental meteorological concepts, such as weather mapping, mid-latitude systems, cloud formation, precipitation, radar technology, and severe weather phenomena. Participants also engaged in Project Atmosphere, a one-week residency at the NWS Training Center during July, which provided more advanced theoretical knowledge, hands-on experiences, and pedagogical skill building. Participants developed and presented standards-aligned lessons or activities based on course content for immediate classroom implementation. Furthermore, they curated additional resources and reflected on integrating atmospheric science into their teaching practices. The inaugural cohort provided comprehensive feedback regarding both the virtual and residential components of the course. We will report on these evaluation results, along with lessons learned from the pilots of our ocean sciences and climate science MOOCs held in Fall 2026. All courses are scheduled to launch publicly in early 2027.

487680.title: Evaluating Community-Scale Exposure to Hazardous Air Pollutants in the U.S. Gulf Coast Using Advanced Mobile Monitoring Coupled with Machine Learning
487680.authors: Alana Jane Dodero, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and Y. Zhang, P. G. Lewis, L. Padilla, D. Peters, A. Adame, M. Olin, K. McCary, R. Mammadov, and L. Hildebrandt Ruiz
487680.abstract: The United States Gulf Coast represents one of the largest clusters of petrochemical, refining, and industrial manufacturing facilities globally, with the Houston Ship Channel and Port Arthur industrial complexes being key components. Emissions from these facilities contribute substantially to ambient concentrations of hazardous air pollutants (HAPs), including carcinogenic volatile organic compounds (VOCs), posing potentially significant health risks to surrounding communities. To estimate ambient air toxics concentrations and lifetime cancer risks at the census tract level, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) AirToxScreen assessment is often used as the primary national screening tool for such evaluations. However, AirToxScreen relies heavily on bottom-up emissions inventories and regional-scale chemical transport models, where neighborhood-scale spatial variability, unquantified fugitive releases, and micro-scale meteorological influences are often difficult to represent. Such discrepancy may lead to uncertainties in evaluating air toxin exposure and health risks in heavily industrialized urban regions. To address this gap and characterize community-scale VOC exposure, four seasonal mobile monitoring campaigns were conducted across Greater Houston and Port Arthur using the Texas A&M University Rapid Onsite Atmospheric Measurement Van (ROAM-V). Measurements were collected over a broad range of meteorological conditions, providing repeated daytime observations representative of multiple seasons and allowing spatial variability to be distinguished from transient pollution events. High-frequency measurements of 14 hazardous VOCs were aggregated to 300-m grid cells and subsequently used to estimate census tract-level concentrations and lifetime cancer risks using U.S. EPA inhalation unit risk values. To further investigate whether these differences reflect limitations in the spatial and temporal coverage of mobile monitoring or systematic biases in AirToxScreen, an observationally constrained Random Forest machine learning model was developed to predict VOC concentrations throughout the Houston and Port Arthur regions. The model integrates mobile observations and spatial predictors describing proximity to industrial facilities, major roadways, and other land-use characteristics to estimate concentrations across locations and conditions where direct measurements were not available. In addition to extending observational coverage, the model is used to identify the relative importance of meteorological and land-use factors controlling VOC variability and to evaluate whether the elevated risks observed from mobile monitoring are representative of broader community exposure. Measurement data coupled with machine learning-derived cancer risk estimates were compared with corresponding AirToxScreen predictions to evaluate the performance of the national assessment. Across the study domain, AirToxScreen substantially underestimated cancer risk relative to observations, with measurement-based estimates averaging approximately five times greater than modeled values. The largest discrepancies occurred in census tracts adjacent to major industrial facilities, suggesting that emissions-based national assessments may not adequately capture localized concentration enhancements associated with complex industrial emission sources and meteorological influences. This work demonstrates that repeated seasonal mobile monitoring combined with machine learning can provide high-resolution assessments of hazardous air pollutant exposure that complement traditional monitoring networks and emissions-based modeling frameworks. By evaluating the spatial patterns and potential sources of disagreement between observations and AirToxScreen, this study provides insight into the limitations of current national-scale exposure assessments and offers a framework for improving community-scale estimates of air toxics concentrations and associated health risks in industrialized urban environments.

487684.title: Training for Tomorrow: New York State Weather Risk Communication Center’s Role in Exercise Development
487684.authors: Allison L Finch, New York State Weather Risk Communication Center, Albany, NY
487684.abstract: The New York State Weather Risk Communication Center (NYSWRCC) develops customized weather-based exercise materials to support emergency preparedness and response across New York State. These resources simulate high-impact weather events and are designed for a wide range of training environments, from discussion-based tabletop exercises to complex, statewide full-scale exercises. Each scenario incorporates realistic meteorological information and forecast products that emergency managers would have during a real-world event. From the drawing board to the exercise table, this presentation will follow how the NYSWRCC plays a vital role in supporting the preparedness and readiness efforts throughout the state.

487686.title: The Role, Workflow, and Information Needs of Utility Meteorologists in Public Safety Power Shutoff Decision Support
487686.authors: Emily Wells, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and B. J. Hatchett
487686.abstract: Utility-ignited wildfires rank among the costliest disasters in the United States. Proactive de-energization of electrical infrastructure, commonly called Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS), is an emergency response tactic used by utility companies during critical fire weather conditions to reduce utility-caused ignitions. PSPS has emerged as an effective but disruptive mitigation that utilities consider to be a “last resort”, acknowledging the disruptions de-energization poses to customers. While weather and fuel conditions trigger PSPS events, a critical gap exists in understanding how utility meteorologists use, produce, and communicate evolving fire weather information into operational decision support for utility leadership. Further, meteorological decision support processes driving PSPS decisions likely vary widely between utilities. While some large investor-owned utilities have invested in proprietary tools and observational networks to develop and inform PSPS processes, many other utilities—from large IOUs to rural co-ops—currently lack this capacity. Thus, we conducted interviews to create the first cross-utility synthesis of how meteorological decision support feeds into utility PSPS decisions. Based on 19 semi-structured interviews with utility meteorologists from 17 distinct utilities across the U.S., we synthesize and deepen knowledge regarding the use and communication of meteorological information leading up to, during, and following PSPS de-energizations. This decision timeline approach was used to capture how utility meteorologists’ roles evolve over the weeks to seconds leading up to a potential PSPS–and how their role shapes and is shaped by the information they use and communicate along the way. We will illustrate the PSPS decision timeline, mapping the types of meteorological information used, generated, and communicated by utility meteorologists to utility leadership towards risk-informed PSPS decisions. We also highlight the critical fire weather patterns leading up to PSPS events and identify key unmet needs and recommendations concerning the integration of meteorological information in PSPS decision making. Ultimately, this work identifies and contextualizes ways in which the broader fire weather research and operational communities can support utilities that currently make, or plan to make, PSPS decisions.

487687.title: Hydrology Copilot: A Cloud-Native AI System for Hydrological Data Analysis
487687.authors: Mahya Hashemi, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and S. V. Kumar, J. Hartwig, J. C. Lopeze, C. R. Hain, D. M. Mocko, J. L. Case, and J. Bolten
487687.abstract: Petabyte-scale Earth observation archives are increasingly open, yet meaningful access remains gated by technical expertise. Discovering, subsetting, and analyzing datasets such as NASA's North American Land Data Assimilation System-version 3 (NLDAS-3) still demands specialized tooling, local computing infrastructure, and fluency in geospatial programming. For most potential users (i.e., water managers, operational forecasters, students, and interdisciplinary researchers), this expertise barrier rather than data availability, is now the primary obstacle. Lowering this barrier requires interfaces that are not only friendlier at the point of discovery but trustworthy through the entire access-to-analysis workflow, including the ability to trace and reproduce results after the fact. We present Hydrology Copilot: a cloud-native, multi-agent AI framework that makes petabyte-scale Earth observation data directly usable through natural language. Rather than a conversational wrapper over a language model, the system coordinates specialized agents that parse a user's request, validate it against dataset boundaries, generate executable Python code, run that code against cloud-hosted archives, and return both results and the underlying code for inspection. To demonstrate operational capability at scale, we implement the system on NLDAS-3, which provides surface meteorological forcing and land-surface model output across North and Central America at 1-km resolution, and derive drought diagnostics as a representative analytical workflow. The framework integrates five contributions, each addressing a distinct stage of the data-access pipeline. First, scalable data virtualization using Kerchunk-based cloud-optimized access achieves a 1.5 to 4.6 times improvement in I/O latency across benchmark queries, ranging from a 4.6 times speedup for regional single-day extractions to 1.5 times for continental monthly aggregations, enabling interactive analysis without local data duplication. Second, transparent code generation through Microsoft Azure AI Foundry agents exposes every executable Python workflow, so that analyses are verifiable, reproducible, and traceable after access rather than opaque. Third, persistent conversational memory enables multi-turn analytical discourse across sessions, allowing users to build complex analyses incrementally without re-specifying parameters. Fourth, intelligent query validation enforces dataset boundaries and resolves ambiguous requests before any code executes, reducing silent errors. Fifth, a multi-agent architecture coordinates query parsing, code generation, and visualization, distributing responsibilities in a way that improves traceability and constrains the reasoning failures common to monolithic LLM applications. We evaluate the system through drought-monitoring workflows of increasing complexity, from basic precipitation mapping to flash-drought detection and multi-year standardized-index trend analysis. Across these tasks, Hydrology Copilot produces reliable code, generates results validated against reference drought products and the operational U.S. Drought Monitor, and maintains efficient performance as analytical complexity increases. The generated visualizations show consistent, domain-appropriate encoding following minimal domain-specific guidance. While demonstrated here for hydrology and drought, the architecture is domain-agnostic: the virtualization layer, code-generation agents, and validation logic are independent of the specific dataset, and the framework is designed to extend to other Earth observation collections and application areas. By coupling natural-language interaction with transparent, reproducible computation over cloud-native archives, Hydrology Copilot advances beyond proof-of-concept demonstrations toward a deployable framework that removes expertise gatekeepers while preserving the scientific rigor required for operational use.

487689.title: Influence of Subtropical Westerlies on the Equatorial Wave Spectrum: Implications for Future Changes In Kelvin Wave Variance
487689.authors: Chaim I. Garfinkel, Hebrew Univ. of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel
487689.abstract: Models from phase 6 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) simulate an intensification of equatorial Kelvin Waves (KW) with global warming. In contrast, the power spectrum is projected to weaken for most other wavenumber-frequency combinations, including higher wavenumber Equatorial Rossby waves (ER). These changes are attributed to the greenhouse gas forcing, while aerosols partially mitigate this effect. The qualitatively different projected responses of KW and ER suggest that dynamical forcings play an important role in the physical mechanism of the changes. This hypothesis is tested using targeted simulations of the Model of an Idealized Moist Atmosphere in which we impose perturbations to upper-tropospheric zonal winds that mimic projected end-of-century changes. These simulations demonstrate that future changes in KW depend on changes in the Southern Hemisphere subtropical jet. A similar dependence is also evident in CMIP6 models. These results have implications for future projections of KW activity in models with biased subtropical westerlies. Bartana, H., Garfinkel, C.I., Schwartz, C. et al. Influence of subtropical westerlies on the equatorial wave spectrum: implications for future changes in Kelvin wave variance. Clim Dyn 64, 321 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00382-026-08275-0

487690.title: UPv4: Rapid Operational AI Precipitation Nowcasting
487690.authors: David Aaron Evans, Tomorrow.io, Golden, CO; and R. Chase, F. Cannon, A. Chawla, B. Taylor, M. Huguet, M. Pope, M. E. Green, and A. E. Payne
487690.abstract: For rapidly evolving, high-impact precipitation systems, reducing forecast latency supports timely operational decisions. We introduce Tomorrow.io’s Unified-Precipitation-Nowcast, version 4 (UPv4), an AI weather prediction system that uses latent conditional flow matching. UPv4 produces updated forecasts with approximately four minutes of latency at each radar volume update, enabling users to continuously reassess precipitation evolution across the contiguous United States (CONUS) at 0.01° spatial resolution, two-minute temporal resolution, and lead times of up to 40 minutes. UPv4 combines Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) data with Tomorrow.io’s proprietary satellite observations to produce a more complete and robust representation of precipitation than radar-only systems can provide. This multisensor approach improves coverage in regions where radar availability or data quality remains limited. We evaluate UPv4 using aggregate metrics, including probability of detection (POD), critical success index (CSI), Heidke skill score (HSS), and false alarm ratio (FAR). Across these metrics, the system outperforms conventional nowcasting approaches, including optical flow and persistence. We also conduct point-based evaluations using precipitation observations from Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) stations. These evaluations show that UPv4 more accurately predicts precipitation onset and cessation, which directly supports aviation and other operational stakeholders that depend on rapidly updated, location-specific guidance. Overall, these results demonstrate that AI weather prediction can strengthen operational nowcasting by improving short-term precipitation guidance and more accurately representing the propagation of precipitation systems during the first forecast hour.

487695.title: Towards Constraining Cloud Adiabaticity with BEACONS Data to Improve Aerosol–Cloud Radiative Forcing Estimates
487695.authors: Matthew Christensen, PNNL, Washougal, WA; and D. D. Turner and R. Krishnamurthy
487695.abstract: Cloud adiabaticity provides a critical diagnostic of how low-level clouds are modified by entrainment, precipitation, and boundary-layer mixing. Because adiabaticity is often assumed to be constant in satellite retrievals and affects liquid water path and droplet concentration, understanding its variability is essential for reducing uncertainty in aerosol indirect forcing estimates. Using ship-based observations from the Marine ARM GPCI Investigation of Clouds (MAGIC) campaign, together with data from several Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) fixed sites, we compute adiabatic liquid water path (LWPAD) and compare it with Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and ground-based microwave radiometer retrievals of LWP to obtain the adiabatic fraction (fad). LWPAD is highly sensitive to cloud geometric thickness. Based on nearly 100 MAGIC cases, errors in satellite-retrieved cloud geometric thickness, particularly uncertainties in cloud-base height, can produce order-of-magnitude overestimates of LWPAD relative to estimates constrained by ceilometer, W-band radar, and interpolated sonde measurements. Furthermore, in classical non-raining closed-cellular clouds, satellite-derived fad is approximately 2–3 times larger than that calculated from ground-based microwave radiometer retrievals, primarily because the satellite retrieval places cloud top substantially higher in the atmosphere than indicated by W-band radar, leading to the overestimation of cloud thickness. This cloud-top bias appears especially important in strongly stratified boundary layers, where closed-cell clouds are commonly found. MAGIC cases also show strong diurnal variability, with fad near 0.55 during the day and 0.81 at night, as well as significant differences between closed- and open-cell cloud regimes. We will extend this analysis to future Boundary Layer Exploration of Aerosols and Clouds ON Ships (BEACONS) observations by applying a machine-learning model to identify key drivers, predict fad, and determine its role in aerosol indirect radiative forcing.

487696.title: Underestimated Role of Ozone Depletion and Recovery for SH Surface Climate Changes
487696.authors: Chaim I. Garfinkel, Hebrew Univ. of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel
487696.abstract: The role of the stratosphere for surface climate in the Southern Hemisphere since 1980 is isolated using two sets of simulations in four different coupled ocean-atmosphere climate models. In the first set, the stratosphere is nudged to observations (NUDGED) while allowing for the rest of the atmosphere to evolve freely, while in the second set the ocean-atmosphere system is free-running (FREE) with CMIP6 forcing files that include ozone depletion. Surface climate trends in NUDGED are double or more those in FREE, implying a systematic underestimation of trends by the ozone forcing used for CMIP6. This underestimate is evident over SH continents including Australia, and is evident in temperature, precipitation, and sea level pressure. The sea ice trends also differ between the two sets of simulations. These results have implications for attempts to attribute surface climate changes to ozone depletion, and indicate that ozone had an even stronger impact than has been previously thought.

487714.title: Present-Day and Future Urban-Rural PM2.5-Attributable Mortality in the United States and China Under Different Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
487714.authors: Claire Yu, Duke University, Durham, NC; and D. Shindell and Q. Zhang
487714.abstract: Ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is one of the largest environmental risk factors for premature mortality globally. The concentrations and health burdens of PM2.5 are not distributed evenly across settlements. Urban populations are generally exposed to higher concentrations because of their close proximity to anthropogenic emission sources, while rural populations may face different forms of exposure as natural sources such as mineral dust become increasingly relevant. How these across-settlement patterns change over the coming century and how they compare between countries at different stages of the air quality transition has received less attention than national or global overall burden estimates. We explore the following questions: (1) how PM2.5 concentrations, attributable mortality, and their urban-suburban-rural distributions evolve under a strongly mitigated pathway relative to a high emissions pathway; (2) to what extent settlement-level gaps or disparities in PM2.5-attributable mortality rates would narrow, persist, or widen in the future; (3) what factors drive changes in settlement-level mortality burdens; and (4) what role natural aerosols such as dust play in residual exposure and urban-rural differences as anthropogenic emissions decline. We examine these questions for the contiguous United States and for China from the years 2015 to 2100 using an ensemble of six Earth system models from Phase 6 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) driven by two distinct Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) with different warming targets (i.e. SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0). We estimate PM2.5-attributable all-cause mortality with the Global Exposure Mortality Model (GEMM) age-specific response functions at 0.5-degree gridded resolution. Urban, suburban, and rural settlements are categorized based on grid-level population density using fixed population shares for each country. Our analysis of the six-model ensemble shows that population-weighted PM2.5 compliance against the WHO guideline of 5 μg/m3 is 20% and 30% in 2015 for urban and rural settlements respectively in the United States. Corresponding compliance in China is substantially lower (0% and 4% respectively). Under SSP1-2.6, by the end of the century, urban and rural compliance in the United States would increase to 80% and 85% respectively, while urban and rural compliance in China would only increase to 4% and 10%. Strong mitigation thus expands the population share meeting the WHO PM2.5 guideline; however, the gains are markedly uneven across countries and settlement types. China could achieve substantial reductions in concentrations and health gains, but would remain far from the WHO’s stringent health-protective standard. For SSP3-7.0, compliance at the end of the century is about 55% for urban and 70% for rural regions in the United States, as well as less than 5% for both urban and rural areas in China. 2015 urban-rural mortality rate differences under SSP1-2.6 start at roughly 28 and 71 deaths per 100,000 people in the United States and China, respectively, but by 2100, settlement classes in the United States converge to a gap of about 2, while in China the difference narrows but the settlement classes remain separated at a gap of around 35. With aggressive mitigation, both countries may see at least partial reductions in unevenly distributed settlement class health burdens, yet China’s urban-rural gap is unable to close completely, likely due to a combination of influences beyond just emissions. A logarithmic mean divisia index decomposition indicates that declining exposure is the largest factor reducing mortality in each country and pathway, age structure is consistently adding to mortality and considerably larger in China, and baseline mortality can act as a "swing factor" sufficient to move China from decreasing to increasing mortality under SSP3-7.0. We also investigate how dust-sourced PM2.5 in the future may contribute to the urban-rural mortality rate gaps across scenarios and countries over time. Taken together, these results imply that burdens remaining late in the century are shaped increasingly by age structure, baseline health, and natural aerosol sources rather than by anthropogenic emissions alone, which suggests that emissions policy by itself may not be sufficient to close health disparities within or between countries.

487725.title: Systematic Biases in the Simulation of Eastern Mediterranean Heatwaves by CMIP Models: implications for projections
487725.authors: Chaim I. Garfinkel, Hebrew Univ. of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel
487725.abstract: Heatwaves over the Eastern Mediterranean are projected to intensify substantially during the twenty-first century, yet considerable uncertainty remains regarding the extent to which individual climate models are fit for purpose in projecting these future changes. Here, we investigate whether historical process-based model evaluation can provide a physically meaningful constraint on future heatwave projections using 11 CMIP6 models. Future heatwaves exhibit substantially larger absolute temperature anomalies owing to a warmer background climate, whereas their evolution relative to the climatology of each climate state remains remarkably similar to that of historical events. Individual CMIP6 models preserve highly consistent temporal heatwave signatures across climate states, indicating that future warming primarily amplifies heatwave intensity rather than fundamentally altering the underlying dynamical evolution. However, there are systematic biases: heatwaves onset too suddenly and persist for too long in all models. The spread in the ability of models to capture the dynamical processes leading to heatwaves is used to weight the models, and the resulting weighted ensemble substantially improves the representation of lower-tropospheric circulation anomalies. The duration of heatwaves in the weighted ensemble tends to increase in the future, while in the poorer performing models heatwaves tend to shorten in a warmer climate. These results demonstrate that physically informed model weighting can provide meaningful constraints on future projections of the processes governing Eastern Mediterranean heatwaves, and provide a potential methodology for other regions.

487786.title: Energy Poverty Classifications and Forecasts Using Various Machine Learning Techniques for Regions within LAC
487786.authors: Sarah Sharlene Balkissoon, Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology, Valsayn, Trinidad and tobago; and D. Farrell, D. Lowe, S. E. Haupt, and N. I. Fox
487786.abstract: Energy poverty evaluation and predictability assessment using machine learning techniques of random forest (RF) and extreme gradient boosting (XBG) were conducted for three Caribbean countries and two Latin American countries for the periods of 1999, 2005 and 2016, 2017 respectively. It was determined that the percentage of the sampled populations who were not at risk of energy poverty were approximately 73%, 51%, 12% for St. Kitts and Nevis, St. Lucia, and Antigua and Barbuda respectively as well as an estimated 91%, 67% for Suriname and Brazil correspondingly. For all the countries, the most used fuel for lighting and cooking were public electricity and LPG/Gas/Cooking Gas. It was noted as well from the Brazilian analysis that those households which utilized alternative sources of electricity other than the main grid or both main and other sources, such as wind and solar generated, incurred less susceptibility to energy poverty. The accuracies improved when using XGB compared to RF for most cases. The greatest and least overall accuracies came from the countries with least and most class variability. These were Suriname and St. Lucia in that order. For all the models, as expected, income was the most important feature; however, it was noted that other important features by permutation importance included demographic and housing-related features to varying extents for the countries in this study. Another finding is that for Suriname and Brazil respectively, access to amenities and the subjective features of residents' opinions concerning their standards of living were important features for these South American countries. A comparison of the spatial distribution of energy poverty for countries in the Caribbean and South America is done as well as a temporal analysis of the energy poverty class distribution for Brazil based on its Federal Units. Future Implications of energy poverty in this region are also explored in this study.

487798.title: Rapid Refresh Forecast System Assimilation Development Including CADRE Contributions (Invited)
487798.authors: Therese Thompson Ladwig, NOAA Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and M. Hu, C. Zhou, D. Dowell, G. Ge, J. Hu, S. Pan, H. Wang, R. Li, S. Murdzek, L. Lin, H. Luo, K. C. Eure, E. P. James, A. Back, H. Lin, J. Beck, A. Burke, S. Liu, D. Holdaway, and X. Wang
487798.abstract: A new era of community assimilation and modeling at convection-allowing scales has begun. This era is enabled with the community adoption of the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI), the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS), along with the unified post-processer (UPP). NOAA regional modeling research and development is using these components to develop new versions of the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS). This presentation will share research results from the first experimental real-time RRFS prototype built with MPAS and JEDI, named RRFSv2X. The RRFSv2X began running in real-time in early 2026 and received favorable feedback from the Spring Forecast Experiment (SFE) and the Flash Flood and Intense Rainfall Experiment (FFaIR). It includes hourly data assimilation cycling using both JEDI 3DEnVar and GETKF with 1-hour 30 ensemble member MPAS forecasts and subsequent deterministic forecasts out to 48 hours. Current development includes efforts to increase the observation types being assimilated toward matching all observations assimilated by RRFSv1. Improving observation processing including thinning, quality control, and error settings are being investigated in the MPAS + JEDI framework. The cycling strategy is evolving from cold start and partial cycling towards more continuous cycling with blending. The assimilation methodology is being advanced and optimized to improve accuracy and computational performance. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations of RRFSv2X will be shared in this presentation. MPAS forecasts initialized from RRFSv1 and MPAS forecasts initialized from HRRR will be compared to evaluate the initial conditions provided by the JEDI cycling. The operational HRRR and RRFSv1 will also be used as benchmarks for comparisons with RRFSv2X forecasts including reflectivity statistics and case study evaluations for several 2026 hazardous weather events. Initial comparisons show promising results and are helping identify areas for further development. This presentation will also highlight examples of the Consortium for Advanced Data Assimilation Research and Education (CADRE) contributions to RRFS. CADRE is accelerating university research contributions to NOAA through the joint use of JEDI and MPAS. CADRE advances in radar reflectivity assimilation, coupled land-atmospheric assimilation, and boundary layer observations have shown promise for improving RRFS and results will be included in this presentation.

487830.title: The Boundary Is Alive: Towards an Ecological Perspective on Land-Atmosphere Boundary Layer Dynamics (Invited Presentation)
487830.authors: Ankur R. Desai, University of Wisconsin-Madison, State College, PA
487830.abstract: Land-atmosphere dynamics involves the exchange and feedbacks of momentum, heat, water, and trace gases between Earth's terrestrial surface and the overlying atmospheric boundary-layer (ABL). Much of the history of advances in ABL science tends to define the surface as a relatively passive system whose exchanges are primarily represented by the physics of fluid transport through porous media, often in simplified spatial arrangements. However, every surface of that Earth is full of living organisms whose evolutionary adaptations to the physical limits of the setting impart significant modulation of those exchanges. In this talk, I'll present some of the ways that, in the words of my colleague Dennis Baldocchi, "physics wins, biology is how it's done", or to quote another colleague "If physics is the law, then biology is a bunch of lawyers" (looking to exploit every loophole). Over the past decades, my lab has looked specifically at the role of how ecosystems shape spatial heterogeneity that impacts the evolution of the ABL and can feed back into behavior of organisms in their processes to grow, reproduce, and establish a new generation. Further, this perspective lends some insight into how we efforts to enhance biodiversity or conserve ecosystems can be broadened to consider ABL impacts, and expand our perspective on ecosystem services.

487834.title: NOAA's Hurricane Field Program: Improving Observations, Understanding, and Forecasts of Tropical Cyclones
487834.authors: Heather M. Holbach, UCAR, Boulder, CO; AOML, Miami, FL; and J. A. Sippel, A. Hazelton, G. J. Alaka Jr., and C. Slocum
487834.abstract: NOAA's Hurricane Field Program (HFP), which supports the "Advancing the Prediction of Hurricanes Experiment", has been gathering observations of tropical cyclones (TCs) for over 40 years. The program is led by scientists from the Hurricane Research Division at NOAA’s Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory in collaboration with the Cooperative Institute For Marine And Atmospheric Studies, University Corporation for Atmospheric Research, and Northern Gulf Institute. They partner with NOAA’s Aircraft Operations Center, who maintain and operate the WP-3D and Gulfstream IV-SP (G-IV) Hurricane Hunter aircraft, and NCEP’s National Hurricane Center and Office of Modeling and Development, who task airborne missions to gather data used by forecasters for analysis and forecasting and for ingest into operational numerical weather prediction models. They also partner with NOAA’s National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service for instrument development and evaluation. The goal of the HFP is to improve TC forecasts using an integrated approach of analyzing observations from aircraft, initializing and evaluating forecast models with those observations, and developing new airborne instrumentation and observing strategies targeted at filling observing gaps and maximizing the data’s impact in model forecasts. This talk highlights recent HFP contributions toward improved TC understanding and prediction. In particular, it describes how the HFP addresses high-priority forecast challenges, summarizes recent collaborations, describes advancements in observing systems monitoring structure and intensity, as well as in assimilation of aircraft data into operational models, and emphasizes key advances in understanding of TC processes, particularly those that lead to rapid intensification. The talk concludes with a discussion of ongoing R2O efforts within HFP, addressing both challenges and successes.

487842.title: Methodology of Generating Water Depth Estimates for Vehicle Pad Abort Landing Assessments
487842.authors: Robert E. Barbre, Jr., MSFC, Huntsville, AL
487842.abstract: The Marshall Space Flight Center Natural Environments Branch’s (MSFC NE) has developed a robust methodology to generate and disseminate geospatial contours of specified water depths, known as waterlines, to support space vehicle programs in assessing the risks associated with landing in shallow water following a pad abort. Leveraging bathymetry databases that provide measured depths and quantified uncertainties, MSFC NE delivers tailored waterlines to inform operational decisions. Recent advancements include integrating water depth data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Office of the Coast Survey’s National Bathymetric Source, which utilizes diverse surveys and standardized modeling techniques. Waterlines are produced by interpolating depth data at required probability levels, treating each measurement’s reported depth and uncertainty as a mean and standard deviation, respectively. Custom tools enable the generation of waterlines at any desired depth and probability, accounting for the inherent uncertainties in water depth measurements. This paper describes the process to develop and distribute waterlines and discusses the rationale for selecting probability levels to guide the development and evaluation of vehicle flight rules.

487845.title: Earth Global Reference Atmospheric Model (Earth-GRAM Improvement of Boundary Layer Horizontal Winds
487845.authors: Patrick W. White, NASA, Huntsville, AL; and D. Menk
487845.abstract: The Earth Global Reference Atmospheric Model (Earth-GRAM) is a reference atmosphere used for design and mission planning of various aerospace systems. Earth-GRAM was originally developed in response to the need for a design reference atmosphere that provides complete global geographical variability, altitude coverage (surface to orbital altitudes), and seasonal and monthly variability of thermodynamic variables and wind components. Another feature of Earth-GRAM is that, in addition to providing the geographical, height, and monthly variation of the mean atmospheric state, it includes the ability to simulate spatial and temporal perturbations in these atmospheric parameters. Upcoming upgrades to Earth-GRAM contain improvements to the boundary layer model including approximations for horizontal winds. These boundary layer improvements were achieved by applying Monin-Obukhov Stability theory and a Penman-Montieth latent heat flux scheme to improve horizontal winds. The boundary layer horizontal wind approximations were then compared to similar measurements at Kennedy Space Center, FL to validate the model improvements. The forthcoming boundary layer upgrades within Earth-GRAM will improve the characterization of horizontal winds, which is particularly important for predicting spacecraft landing dynamics under parachutes.

487847.title: Verification of WPC’s Day 3-7 Hazard Outlooks for Extreme Heat
487847.authors: Lily Lai, NWS, College Park, MD
487847.abstract: Extreme heat is one of the leading weather-related causes of death in the United States. In support of the NWS mission to protect life and property by providing forecasts, warnings, and impact-based decision support services, the NWS Weather Prediction Center’s (WPC) Day 3-7 Hazards Outlook communicates the potential for impactful heat during the medium range portion of the seven day forecast. This study evaluates the spatial accuracy of the heat component of the Hazard Outlook and its capacity to support public risk communication through the issuance of reliable Watch/Warning/Advisory (WWA) products. Daily issued outlooks were cross-checked with ERA5-Land reanalysis temperature data and heat alerts issued by local NWS Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) across the contiguous United States (CONUS) from 2020 through 2026. Hit rates, false alarms, misses, Critical Success Index (CSI) scores, and spatial accuracy were evaluated at varying lead times preceding extreme heat events. Gridded analysis reveals an overly conservative forecasting bias across southwestern regions, as well as increased heat volatility and lower predictability across the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains. Analysis was also performed against the NWS/CDC HeatRisk tool to assess its utility as input guidance. Verification of hazard predictability ultimately contributes towards improving forecasting accuracy and refining the current criteria that triggers emergency responses to hazardous heat. Identification of meteorological patterns and localized forecast limitations improves lead-time and preparation measures, ensuring optimal public readiness and mitigation during extreme heat events.

487851.title: Development of CRTM AI Emulators with Uncertainty Prediction for OMPS Nadir Instruments to Enable Rapid Multi-JPSS SDR Quality Evaluation
487851.authors: Xin Jin, NOAA, Canton, MI; ERT Inc, Greenbelt, MD; NOAA, College Park, MD; and B. Yan
487851.abstract: The Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) provides an effective framework for simulating Ozone Mapping and Profiler Suite (OMPS) radiances, enabling instrument anomaly detection, radiance product quality assessment, and cross-satellite performance evaluation for OMPS sensors aboard Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and future missions. However, the high computational cost of CRTM limits its operational utility for near-real-time monitoring. In addition, uncertainties in surface reflectance databases for the OMPS Nadir Mapper (NM) and Nadir Profiler (NP) reduce the consistency of forward radiance simulations. To address these challenges, we will develop a deep neural network (DNN) -based OMPS radiance emulators with uncertainty prediction for OMPS NM and NP across multi-missions, such as SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and JPSS-4. Using NOAA-21 OMPS NM as a demonstration case, its training dataset includes one year of CRTM simulations using NOAA-21 OMPS observations acquired every five days throughout 2025 under clear-sky conditions. It also includes effective surface reflectance, satellite and solar viewing geometry, ECMWF forecast products such as atmospheric temperature, humidity, and ozone profiles, as well as surface pressure and temperature. Additionally, pre-processing and proper quality-control procedures will be developed to produce standardized OMPS-observed radiance in the dataset, including Earth-sun-distance correction, normalization of OMPS Earth radiance by solar flux, removal of cloud-contaminated data, collocation with ECMWF products. Moreover, DNN will be applied to the dataset to train model coefficients for the CRTM radiance simulation AI emulator. To determine the AI emulator prediction uncertainty, Deep Ensembles will be utilized to train a separate AI uncertainty model. Furthermore, to detect optimal input features to the CRTM AI emulators, we will apply SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to the DNN AI emulator to quantify the contribution of each input variable (e.g., ozone profile, temperature profile, solar zenith angle, viewing geometry, surface properties) to the predicted radiance. Similarly, we will apply the same approach to the rest of the OMPS NM and NP instruments across SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and JPSS-04. The performance of the CRTM AI emulators will be assessed against CRTM simulators using data beyond the training data set. It is expected that these new AI emulators can reproduce CRTM simulations with high accuracy and substantially reduced computational efficiency, thus enabling rapid operational quality monitoring, instrument anomaly detection, and cross-platform calibration assessment for current, historical, and future OMPS missions. A companion study will explore potentials of these AI emulators in detecting two types of inter-sensor radiometric calibration errors in Yan et al. (2026). Disclaimer: the presentation contents are solely the opinions of the authors and do not constitute a statement of policy, decision, or position on behalf of NOAA or the U. S. Government.

487857.title: NASA Artemis II Day-of-Launch Atmospheric Winds for Ascent
487857.authors: Karen M. Altino, NASA, Huntsville, AL; and N. L. Curtis and K. Welch
487857.abstract: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Artemis program requires a Day-of-Launch Initialization-Load (I-Load) Update (DOLILU) process to maximize launch availability and ensure that vehicle structural loads and trajectory parameters are acceptable during ascent. This process is executed in the hours prior to launch. Wind and atmosphere data are incorporated into the vehicle steering commands uploaded onto vehicle flight computers on day-of-launch. The Marshall Space Flight Center Natural Environments Branch (MSFC NE) provides engineering design support for Artemis for DOLILU as part of the Natural Environments and Mission Analysis (NEMA) team. MSFC NE members process wind data from multiple sources at the Eastern Range including low-resolution rawinsonde and Tropospheric Doppler Radar Wind Profiler (TDRWP) data in combination with monthly climatological mean wind and atmosphere data from the Earth Global Reference Atmosphere Model (Earth-GRAM) to generate a vertically complete profile of the atmosphere from the surface up to 600,000 feet. That data is utilized in independent verification and validation (IV&V) of trajectory and loads analyses for the vehicle, which provides a go/no-go for launch as well as the I-Load steering commands. For the Artemis II launch on 1 April 2026, MSFC NE successfully supported the launch on a day characterized by benign winds. However, the team encountered unique challenges with TDRWP profile features influenced by weather conditions, aircraft activity, and instrumentation – making it challenging to find a valid TDRWP profile throughout the day. This presentation will describe and provide analysis regarding the wind features seen throughout the launch countdown.

487858.title: Beyond Surface Fluxes: Observing and Modeling the Forest Canopy–Atmospheric Boundary-Layer Continuum (Invited Presentation)
487858.authors: Heping Liu, Washington State University, PULLMAN, WA; and Y. Ma, Z. Lan, Q. Zhang, L. Zhang, T. W. Juliano, P. Hawbecker, and J. A. Sauer
487858.abstract: Forest canopies mediate exchanges of momentum, heat, water vapor, and other scalars between the land and atmosphere, yet many land surface models represent these exchanges using a single big-leaf canopy module. Such representations do not explicitly resolve the vertically distributed and spatially heterogeneous processes through which canopy-scale motions connect with processes in the overlying atmospheric boundary layer. This presentation integrates multilevel observations and multiscale modeling to examine turbulent exchange across the forest canopy–atmospheric boundary-layer continuum. Observations at the U.S. Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Bankhead National Forest site include eddy-covariance measurements at seven levels within and above the forest canopy, complemented by Doppler lidar, radar wind profiler, Raman lidar, ceilometer, and radiosonde measurements of boundary-layer structure and evolution. These observations are integrated with the WRF-LES–MCANOPY modeling system, which couples large-eddy simulation with a vertically resolved, multilayer canopy representation. Together, the observations and simulations are used to examine how canopy structure, spatial heterogeneity, and terrain shape turbulent exchange and coherent motions and how these processes connect with the evolving atmospheric boundary layer during the morning-to-afternoon transition. This integrated framework will help identify when bulk canopy representations are adequate and when vertically resolved observations and models are needed.

487861.title: Data Quality Analysis of NSSL’s RAPTOR Mobile Radars
487861.authors: Jonathan J. Gourley, NOAA/National Severe Storms Laboratory, Norman, OK; and D. Wasielewski, G. Kunkle, J. C. Snyder, A. V. Ryzhkov, and P. Heinselman
487861.abstract: In early 2026, NSSL acquired one C-band and two X-band mobile weather radars, representing a significant upgrade to the suite of mobile observing facilities. The Rapid-deployable Agile Polarimetric Transportable Observational Radars (RAPTORs) are built on the backbone of reliable, commercial, solid-state radars that are used widely in operational, fixed-tower contexts. Each radar features a powered lift system to raise the antenna, reducing beam blockage and ground clutter. They come equipped with a spacious operator cab with six large monitors, ample storage space, onboard generators, and security cameras. When connected to commercial power, the new facilities provide the capability for remote, unsupervised operation, enabling longer-term deployments at fixed locations. Throughout the year, several datasets of opportunity have been collected in Oklahoma. These datasets are utilized to assess several characteristics of the radar variables. By using rainfall observations at vertical incidence, the calibration of differential reflectivity is assessed and quantified. After the differential reflectivity has been bias-adjusted, it is combined with specific differential phase measurements to estimate the theoretical horizontal reflectivity in rain using the polarimetric self-consistency principle. These comparisons enable us to quantify the calibration of horizontal reflectivity. Following the data quality analysis and bias-adjustment procedures, the variables are used to estimate precipitation rates via different polarimetric relations proposed in the literature.

487864.title: Developing an Airborne Multi-Sensor System for Coastal Sea Spray Production Observations
487864.authors: Magdalena D. Anguelova, NRL, Washington, DC; and J. D. Ouellette, D. J. Dowgiallo, S. P. Menk, M. S. Vermillion, and C. G. Merrick
487864.abstract: Sea spray droplets form from bursting bubbles within whitecaps, which are the visual expression of waves breaking with air entrainment. Once produced, these droplets evolve into sea spray aerosols that affect marine visibility by promoting marine clouds and fog. Sea spray also regulates electro-optical transmission in the marine boundary layer through scattering and absorption. Sea spray provides an additional pathway for air-sea interactions quantified by surface fluxes. For example, sea spray mediates the enthalpy flux (sensible + latent heat), contributing to tropical cyclone intensification. Because such interactions feedback to weather and climate, surface fluxes serve as boundary conditions in numerical weather prediction and general circulation models. Sea spray production is modeled using a size-dependent source function, S(r). Because S(r) cannot be measured directly, it is typically derived from vertical profiles of droplet concentration size distribution n(r, z), scaled with a forcing factor such as wind speed U, whitecap fraction W, or wave energy dissipation. Many open-ocean formulations of S(r) exist, but they do not apply well in coastal zones where bottom topography and land–sea breeze systems modify wave steepness and breaking behavior. These limitations arise from data scarcity. In-situ coastal measurements are insufficient to parameterize sea spray production. Satellite remote sensing is also limited because microwave retrievals of U and W in coastal regions are compromised by land contamination due to coarse retrieval resolutions (≈ 25 × 35 km). The lack of data for wave breaking and sea spray production in coastal zones restricts validation of surface emissivity models used in radiative transfer, remote sensing, and data assimilation systems. To address these knowledge gaps, we have initiated a new project developing an airborne system to collect high-resolution coastal data on sea spray production. To obtain S(r), we need measurements of both forcing factor W and the droplet size distribution n(r) from profiles n(r, z). For W, we have improved open-ocean scaling of using W parameterizations based on W WindSat retrievals from brightness temperature TB. Whitecap remote sensing leverages the high, blackbody-like emissivity of sea foam at microwave frequencies up to 37 GHz. The relative transparency of the atmosphere at these microwave frequencies is a major advantage over visible or infrared systems. However, extending such observations to coastal zones requires higher spatial resolution. A recent feasibility study demonstrated that millimeter-wave frequencies (up to 150 GHz) can capture surface processes associated with wave breaking at fine spatial scales when sensors operate at low altitudes (below 1 km). For n(r, z), optical particle counters deployed from various platforms have been the conventional measurement method. More recently, a W-band (75–110 GHz) Doppler radar—commonly used for cloud and precipitation studies—has been adapted for sea spray observations. Following this approach, we are developing a 94 GHz Doppler radar system to measure sea spray profiles n(r, z). Specifically, it is assumed that the droplet size distribution n(r) at a given height z can be represented by a log-normal distribution with three parameters: the mode droplet radius r, the logarithmic width σ, and the total (size- and height-integrated) droplet concentration N (often given as total liquid water q instead of number of droplets). The size-resolved droplet concentration n(r) is related to the radar backscatter cross section via the Rayleigh approximation. From this relationship, one can calculate q, r, and σ from the first 3 moments of the Doppler spectrum related, respectively, to the radar reflectivity factor Z (0th moment); the mean fall velocity from the Doppler shift (the 1st moment); and the mean Doppler width (2nd moment). We will describe the physics behind these measurements and present the requirements for a system to measure the necessary variables. We will investigate the various Doppler radar systems that can be used and identify the ones that best meet the requirements for air-sea interaction observations. We will finish with a description of the system we are building and the planned deployment in upcoming field experiments.

487867.title: Updating Space Weather (SWx) Benchmarks for Critical Infrastructure Protection
487867.authors: Patrick Dandenault, APL, Gaithersburg, MD; and L. Paxton, A. Vourlidas, E. Paouris, A. Kouloumvakos, A. Ridley, C. Wu, R. Mesquita, J. Caggiano, J. E. Hicks, R. A. Vogel, B. Talbot, P. Paki, and C. Cannizzaro
487867.abstract: This presentation will provide an update on the program, “Updating Space Weather (SWx) Benchmarks for Critical Infrastructure (CI) Protection”, that supports Department of Homeland Security Science and Technology Directorate (DHS S&T) and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency National Risk Management Center (CISA NRMC). The goals of the program are to update and refine the space weather (SWx) benchmarks which were first released in 2018 by the Space Weather Operations, Research and Mitigation (SWORM) Subcommittee of the National Science and Technology Council. This effort also makes use of the 2019 Institute for Defense Analyses (IDA) report, “Next Step Space Weather Benchmarks” and addresses the needs identified in the 2019 National Space Weather Strategy and Action Plan with the goal of supporting the CI stakeholder community (operators and owners). This benchmarks R&D program is being executed at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (JHU/APL) with the goal of updating the 2018 SWx Benchmarks. The program is designed to address the following five focus areas: (1) Induced Geo-electric Fields; (2) Ionizing Radiation; (3) Ionospheric Disturbances; (4) Solar Radio Bursts; and (5) Upper Atmospheric Expansion. For each of the five focus areas, we will identify benchmark values across the following four scenarios: (1) 1-in-30-year events; (2) 1-in-100-year events; (3) 1-in-300-year events; and (4) 1-in-1000-year events. The levels of drivers and atmospheric responses will be provided in a format that is useful to real-world stakeholders, to be used with their existing system-impact tools to help them better understand and plan for vulnerabilities and risks. The purpose of the SWx benchmarks is to provide input for creating engineering standards, develop vulnerability assessments and risk estimates, establish decision points and thresholds for action, understand risk, develop effective mitigation procedures and practices, and enhance response and recovery planning. The benchmarks are designed to capture an event’s ability to affect the nation and provide clear and consistent descriptions of SWx events based on current scientific understanding and the historical record. Each benchmark specifies the physical characteristics and conditions against which a SWx event can be measured. The benchmarks describe the nature and intensity of extreme SWx events, providing a point of reference, and improve our understanding of the effects of SWx. Our R&D approach is to take into consideration the last seven-plus years of research in the five phenomena and incorporate updated results and datasets. This effort will generate initial inputs for developing vulnerability assessments and risk estimates, establish decision points and thresholds for action, improve mitigation procedures, and enhance response and recovery planning for our nation’s CI owners and operators. We are using state-of-the-art first-principles modeling and observational datasets, along with the needs and requirements gathered from CI stakeholder focus groups to recommend revisions to the existing benchmarks and where appropriate define new benchmarks. Extensive validation will be used for each scenario in which observational data are available for each phenomenon. The levels of drivers and atmospheric responses will be provided in a format that is useful to real-world stakeholders to be used with their existing system-impact tools to help them better understand and plan for vulnerabilities and risks.

487868.title: Coupling WoFS to FLASH: Case Studies and Next Steps for Real-Time Implementation
487868.authors: Jonathan J. Gourley, NOAA/National Severe Storms Laboratory, Norman, OK; and D. R. Stratman, N. Yussouf, P. C. Burke, A. J. Clark, P. Heinselman, and L. J. Wicker
487868.abstract: The FLASH system has been running operationally in the National Weather Service for a decade, providing valuable guidance to forecasters on heavy rainfall occurrence and concomitant flash flooding. At present, the FLASH system is best described as diagnostic given that it is forced by MRMS-estimated rainfall rates. There is the potential to increase lead time through the incorporation of future rainfall scenarios. The WoFS is presently designed to generate 6-h forecasts of rainfall using an 18-member ensemble. Forecasts are initialized every 30 min and the quantitative precipitation forecasts (QPFs) are output every 5 min. There is an experimental version of WoFS that runs on a grid with a 1-km mesh size. The 1-km QPFs have been used to force the FLASH system for several cases including the July 2025 Texas Hill Country flash flood disaster and two flash flooding events in the West. This presentation will summarize findings from these case studies. The next phase of the project is real-time coupling of WoFS to FLASH. Through the support of NOAA’s Precipitation Prediction Grand Challenge (PPGC) initiative, WoFS-FLASH will be configured to run in real-time. The model coupling will add new flash flooding products to the WoFS product suite, providing great potential to deliver rapidly updating information on specific areas forecast to be impacted by flash flooding with several hours of lead time. The presentation will highlight some of the challenges in real-time coupling and will propose new products, including probabilistic, impact-based ones. As the model coupling effort progresses, we invite feedback from potential users on new products, displays, and capabilities.

487875.title: Scalar-Specific Departures from the Constant-Flux-Layer Assumption Organized by Multiscale Turbulence
487875.authors: Heping Liu, Washington State University, PULLMAN, WA
487875.abstract: Sensible heat (SH) and latent heat (LH) fluxes can vary with height in the atmospheric surface layer, contrary to the constant flux layer assumption (CFLA). Using two-level eddy-covariance measurements over a heterogeneous irrigated cotton field, we quantify CFLA departures between 8.7 and 2.7 m; gradient sign indicates whether flux increases or decreases with height, and magnitude indicates departure strength. SH and LH departures differ in magnitude and sometimes direction: stronger SH height variation does not necessarily correspond to stronger LH variation. Scale-resolved analysis shows middle- and large-scale motions organize departure magnitude, while small-scale turbulence tends to favor decreasing flux with height. Category-mean budgets indicate near-zero gradients can be consistent with compensation among opposite-signed contributions. Thus, near-CFLA behavior may emerge from cross-scale compensation. Over heterogeneous landscapes, scalar-specific height variations in SH and LH can reinforce or offset in their sum, potentially contributing to variations in apparent energy-balance closure ratios.

487887.title: GREMLIN: GOES Radar Estimation via Machine Learning to Inform NWP
487887.authors: Kyle A. Hilburn, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO
487887.abstract: Imagery from the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) has been a key element of U.S. operational weather forecasting since 1975. The latest generation, the GOES-R Series, offers new capabilities to support the need for high-resolution rapidly refreshing imagery for situational awareness. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) / machine learning (ML) have enabled new approaches for using GOES observations in numerical weather prediction (NWP), and for monitoring and nowcasting convection and severe weather. One such new approach is GREMLIN, GOES Radar Estimation via Machine Learning to Inform NWP. GREMLIN is a machine learning approach to data fusion of Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) radiances and Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) flashes to produce synthetic radar reflectivity fields. This presentation will provide an update on the status of GREMLIN. It will describe new datasets that expand predictors and predictands, and broaden the seasonal and geographic coverage. New loss function approaches that improve both accuracy and spatial sharpness will be discussed. It will review new ML architecture approaches to further support spatial sharpness of predictions. Overall, the goals of GREMLIN development are to keep the number of parameters as small as possible and keep the receptive field as large as possible, to produce a model as accurate and spatially sharp as possible that generalizes across seasons and different precipitation regimes.

487888.title: From Legacy to ARCO: Virtualizing NSF NCAR's Geoscience Data Exchange to Advance FAIR Data Access
487888.authors: Harsha Hampapura, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. Conroy, C. W. Hsu, and D. C. Schuster
487888.abstract: Over the past several years, NSF NCAR has consolidated the majority of its research data (previously scattered across disparate, lab-specific repositories) into the Geoscience Data Exchange (GDEX), a single curated Data Commons. This consolidation has markedly improved findability, but the accessibility and interoperability dimensions of FAIR remain a work in progress: the bulk of GDEX holdings are still archived in legacy, file-based formats poorly suited to efficient cloud and remote access, and only a small fraction are analysis-ready and cloud-optimized (ARCO). This talk describes our effort to close that gap by making legacy GDEX datasets ARCO. We present our ARCO strategy and share best practices that helped us organize, chunk, and index data for efficient remote access. Where practical we create Zarr stores; for the large volume of legacy data we cannot economically duplicate, we build kerchunk reference stores that virtualize existing files as cloud-optimized datasets without copying the data again. The resulting real and virtual Zarr stores can be read directly with standard packages like xarray, in workflows that run on laptops, HPC, and the cloud. Making data ARCO is necessary but not sufficient, so we also report on education and outreach activities that turn availability into use: an open example-notebook repository (gdex-examples) and a GDEX Cookbook that give researchers runnable reference workflows. We further report on how LLM-assisted search-and-discovery tools, such as a GDEX Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, can drive ARCO adoption and usage. We close with lessons learned in moving the needle on ARCO adoption across our user community: what accelerates uptake, and where technical and human barriers persist.

487891.title: Land Surface Precipitation and Hydrology in the NASA MERRA-21C Reanalysis
487891.authors: Rolf H. Reichle, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and A. M. Fox, Q. Liu, L. C. Andrews, and A. El Akkraoui
487891.abstract: The NASA Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications for the early 21st Century (MERRA-21C) is a new atmospheric reanalysis product covering the period from 1998 to the present. The product provides – in addition to many atmospheric variables – 1-hourly, global estimates of land surface conditions for 1998–present at ~25-km resolution. In the tropics and midlatitudes, MERRA-21C uses observations-based precipitation to force the land surface. The precipitation product used in MERRA-21C is the NASA Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement – Final (IMERG-Final; Version 7) product, which merges observations from rain gauges and satellites. The use of the IMERG-Final satellite-gauge precipitation product in MERRA-21C constitutes a major advance over its predecessor, MERRA-2, which ingests a gauge-only precipitation product over land (except Africa). The gauge-only product used in MERRA-2 suffers from typically very sparse gauge coverage across much of the globe, and its quality has degraded considerably since ~2020. Besides the difference in the precipitation input datasets, the method for merging the observed precipitation into MERRA-21C has been refined from that of MERRA-2. Moreover, the land surface model of MERRA-21C benefits from improved parameterizations and parameter datasets relative to that of MERRA-2. This presentation evaluates MERRA-21C precipitation and land hydrology estimates, along with those of MERRA-2 and those of the fifth-generation global atmospheric reanalysis produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ERA5). MERRA-21C land surface hydrology estimates show clear improvements over those of MERRA-2, including soil moisture, snow, evaporation, and streamflow estimates, when verified against reference products and independent satellite and in situ measurements, and generally also compare favorably with ERA5 land hydrology estimates. Much of this improvement in land surface hydrology is seen in the Southern Hemisphere and can be traced back to the IMERG-Final precipitation inputs used in MERRA-21C. Compared to monthly GPCPv3 observations, the corrected MERRA-21C precipitation is better than the corrected MERRA-2 precipitation. The corrected MERRA-21C precipitation is also better than the precipitation generated by the atmospheric models within the cycling MERRA-21C and MERRA-2 systems. From October 2025, after the end of the IMERG-Final Version 7 product, the land surface in MERRA-21C is forced with the precipitation generated by the atmospheric model in the MERRA-21C system. To avoid a step change in the climatology of the MERRA-21C land surface estimates, the model-generated precipitation is rescaled to the climatology of IMERG-Final before it is applied to the land surface. Initial plans to transition MERRA-21C to using the satellite-only, near-real-time IMERG-Late precipitation product were abandoned because we found that the quality of the IMERG-Late precipitation estimates has degraded beginning in 2024, particularly over tropical land and in the Southern Hemisphere. These findings highlight both the substantial hydrological benefit of improved precipitation forcing in MERRA-21C and the practical challenges of sustaining a consistent, high-quality precipitation record for reanalysis systems operating in near-real time.

487894.title: Evolving Satellite Observing Systems and Water-Cycle Consistency in a 25-Year Multi-Sensor Land Reanalysis
487894.authors: Andrew M Fox, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and R. H. Reichle, Q. Liu, and L. Andrews
487894.abstract: Soil moisture and snow are key storages within the terrestrial water cycle, regulating runoff generation, evapotranspiration, and land–atmosphere coupling while providing memory that contributes to the predictability of hydrological variability and extremes. Retrospective land analyses combine observations and land surface modeling to provide spatially and temporally complete estimates of these water-cycle states. The observing systems used, however, are inherently nonstationary as new satellite missions become available.
