Understanding how this evolving observational constraint shapes long-term analysis behavior is essential for distinguishing hydrological variability and change from artifacts associated with changes in the observing system. We examine this question using an experimental global land reanalysis spanning June 2000 through May 2024, conducted with the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) Land Data Assimilation System. The experimental reanalysis was generated during the science development of the M21C-Land reanalysis, a supplemental, land-only data product included in the forthcoming NASA “MERRA-21C” suite of reanalysis products. The GEOS Catchment model at the heart of the land reanalysis is driven with surface meteorological data from a GEOS atmospheric reanalysis for NASA instrument teams and observation-based precipitation. The land-model physics and assimilation configuration of the land reanalysis remain fixed while land observations are progressively assimilated, including MODIS snow-cover fraction, ASCAT and CYGNSS surface soil-moisture retrievals, and SMOS and SMAP L-band brightness temperatures. A companion open-loop integration without land data assimilation, driven with identical surface meteorology and observation-based precipitation forcing, isolates the effects of the assimilated observations. The observing system evolves from predominantly snow-cover constraints in the early 2000s to dense, multi-sensor microwave coverage of surface soil moisture during the SMAP era. Correspondingly, the assimilation reduces the typical magnitude of the observation-minus-forecast residuals by approximately 3–5% during the early microwave period and by 10–15% following the introduction of SMAP, with clear step changes in analysis behavior aligned with major observing-system transitions. Independent evaluation against International Soil Moisture Network in situ measurements shows increases of approximately 0.04–0.07 in near-surface soil-moisture correlation during the later, multi-sensor period, whereas root-zone improvements are weaker and more spatially heterogeneous. Agreement with ERA5-Land similarly increases as the observing system expands, particularly for surface soil moisture. MODIS assimilation substantially improves reanalysis estimates of snow occurrence and seasonal persistence but has less influence on estimates of snow water equivalent and snow depth. Because soil-moisture observations are assimilated as bias-corrected anomalies, this component of the analysis produces little net change in long-term soil-water storage. Water-budget diagnostics show that snow-cover assimilation, in contrast, directly adds and removes snow water, with positive increments exceeding negative increments over the 25-year period. Most of this net water addition is subsequently exported as runoff, with comparatively small, persistent effects on soil-water and snow storage, evapotranspiration, and other terrestrial water-cycle components. These results demonstrate that the changing observational constraint is a major control on the consistency and behavior of long-term land reanalysis products. Variables directly sensed by the assimilated observations respond most strongly, whereas deeper or integrated water stores remain more dependent on model physics and surface meteorological forcing. These differences must be considered when using reanalysis products to characterize water-cycle variability, trends, and extremes across observing-system transitions. Finally, we will describe how lessons learned from the experimental reanalysis informed the design of M21C-Land, provide an update on the M21C-Land production status, and present initial validation diagnostics.

487897.title: Lessons Learned from Forecasting Pyrocumulonimbus Events during the 2026 Wildfire Season (Invited Presentation)
487897.authors: Derek V. Vincent Mallia, Univ. of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and I. Mocuta, C. W. Johanson, C. White, L. Wilson, and D. A. Peterson
487897.abstract: There is mounting evidence that large wildfires are lofting smoke higher in the atmosphere via intense pyroconvection. This can have significant implications for air quality modeling and forecasting applications. Larger and more intense wildfires could also increase the frequency of fire-initiated thunderstorms, i.e., pyrocumulonimbus clouds (pyroCbs). In addition to injecting smoke further up into the atmosphere, pyroCbs can create unpredictable weather underneath the cloud and expose fire management crews to dangerous fire conditions. There is a significant and largely unmet need for pyroCb forecasts to support fire management operations. A series of pyroCb forecast tools were deployed for the 2026 INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE) field campaign that included: a (1) probabilistic forecast derived from an ensemble of 1-D plume rise model simulations (PyroCON), a (2) statistical forecast algorithm (PyroCast), and an (3) equation derived from bulk models (PFT). For this presentation, we will analyze results from our pyroCb forecasts for the 2026 North American wildfire season. Preliminary results indicate that pyroCb forecast indices were valuable for identifying wildfires and regions that had the potential to trigger pyroCbs. There were several situations in which forecasting pyrocumulonimbus events proved challenging, including two wildfires in central Utah that produced pyroCbs in conditions that were not considered especially favorable for deep pyroconvection. Identifying situations where wildfires have the potential for exceptional growth periods is needed for forecasting pyroCbs with thermodynamic profiles that are not ideal for pyroconvection.

487898.title: From Simple Physics to Operational Forecasts: Developing and Integrating a Wildfire Spread Model into Energy Research and Forecasting Framework for Emergency Response
487898.authors: Ganesh Vijayakumar, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO; and A. Wise, J. D. Mirocha, A. Almgren, A. Lattanzi, and H. Gopalan
487898.abstract: Wildfire emergency managers need more than historical fire statistics and risk maps. During an active wildfire, they need predictions of where the fire will spread, how fast it will move, and how the fire will interact with local winds, terrain, and atmospheric conditions. Providing this information requires connecting two traditionally separate modeling areas: fire behavior models that simulate fire spread and numerical weather prediction (NWP) models that simulate atmospheric processes. This presentation describes a unified development framework that allows a wildfire model to be used both as a standalone fire behavior model and as a fully coupled fire–atmosphere model inside a next-generation NWP system. Traditionally, fire models and fire–weather models have been developed as separate systems, such as standalone fire spread tools and coupled weather–fire models. In this framework, the same fire model can be used for different applications without developing separate modeling systems. This provides a common exascale computing framework for wildfire prediction from rapid standalone simulations to high-fidelity two-way fire–atmosphere forecasting. The framework is based on a modular and physics-based fire behavior model. It includes established wildfire spread approaches such as Rothermel-based formulations, elliptical fire growth models, Balbi’s physical fire spread model, and Cheney–Gould grassland fire behavior relationships. Additional physical processes include fuel moisture effects, crown fire initiation, ember transport, terrain effects, and wind influence on fire propagation. The model is designed to remain simple and efficient while maintaining the important physical processes needed for realistic fire behavior prediction. A major challenge is integrating this fire model with a high-resolution atmospheric prediction system. In a fully coupled simulation, the interaction between fire and atmosphere is calculated dynamically. Heat and moisture released by the fire modify the atmospheric boundary layer, turbulence, and local wind fields. At the same time, the evolving atmospheric conditions control fire intensity, spread rate, and plume development. The unified framework provides a consistent approach to exchange information between fire and atmosphere components while maintaining numerical efficiency and scalability. The presentation will discuss the technical development needed to move from a standalone fire model to a coupled fire–weather prediction capability. This includes designing the coupling between fire physics and atmospheric processes, maintaining consistency between different model components, validating the coupled system against known fire behavior, and adapting the framework for modern high-performance computing architectures. The approach also reduces the need to maintain separate fire models and coupling systems, allowing future improvements in fire physics to directly benefit both standalone and coupled applications. The resulting framework supports scalable wildfire simulations on modern computing platforms, including GPU-based systems. Depending on the operational need, users can run fast standalone fire simulations or perform fully coupled fire–atmosphere predictions when feedback between the fire and atmosphere is important. This flexibility enables high-resolution ensemble forecasts and scenario-based predictions that can support emergency response, infrastructure protection, and wildfire risk management. Beyond wildfire applications, this work demonstrates a pathway for developing next-generation environmental prediction systems. By combining modular physics, advanced numerical methods, and exascale computing, the framework provides a unified approach for transferring research models into operational prediction capabilities.

487899.title: Changes in Global and Regional Extreme Temperatures Over Land: An Extreme Value Theory Perspective
487899.authors: Adam Michael Bauer, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL; and V. Sapkota, I. Baxter, T. A. Shaw, and B. B. Cael
487899.abstract: Abstract: Heat waves are among the most damaging consequences of climate change, yet how the distribution of extreme temperatures is changing remains unclear. Here, we show that the generalized extreme value distribution is fit-for-purpose to analyze extreme temperatures over land. We find that there is no statistically significant trend in global maximum temperatures relative to the mean in the reanalysis record. However, we do find statistically significant regional trends: about 14% of the land surface has a statistically significant positive trend relative to the mean, and about 17% of the land surface has a significant negative trend. We show that climate models struggle to reproduce the distributional characteristics of extreme temperatures found in reanalysis, other than the distributional mean. Finally, we find that biases in the variability, rather than the mean-state, of the extreme temperature distribution dominate biases in projections of extreme temperature risk over large fractions of the land surface. Plain Language Summary: Heat waves have deleterious impacts on human and natural wellbeing, and these impacts are expected to grow as the world warms. However, how and where the distribution of extreme temperatures is changing over time in response to increased greenhouse gas emissions remains unclear. In this paper, we develop a well-posed statistical framework, based on extreme value theory, to study changes in the extreme temperature distribution both at a global and regional level. Our framework allows us to make a few important insights. First, we argue that, in the reanalysis record, the global average heat wave is not growing faster than global average temperatures; however, this global perspective glosses over important regional heterogeneities, where in some locations the growth rate of the average heat wave is outpacing the growth rate of average temperatures by half a degree Celsius per decade. We then show that climate models struggle to reproduce the regional pattern of heat wave distribution characteristics outside of the distribution mean. Finally, we quantify the relative importance of variability and the mean-state in determining biases in extreme temperature risk between climate models and reanalysis. We find that, in both the historical record and when projecting extreme temperature risk into the future, bias in variability dominates the influence of bias in the mean-state over large fractions of the land surface. Thus more research is needed on understanding regional climate variability to improve and constrain projections of extreme temperature risk.

487911.title: A Physics-Informed Neural Network Surrogate for AERMOD Benzene Dispersion
487911.authors: Neev Pratap, Lawrence E. Elkins High School, Sugar Land, TX; and K. Vyas
487911.abstract: Atmospheric dispersion modeling is an essential tool for understanding pollutant transport, assessing exposure risks, and supporting regulatory compliance near industrial facilities. AERMOD, the U.S. EPA’s preferred regulatory model for many near-field dispersion applications, is widely used for these purposes but is less suited to applications requiring continuous and differentiable concentration fields. In this work, we develop a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) as a differentiable surrogate for AERMOD’s steady-state dispersion calculations, with application to petrochemical and refinery benzene dispersion across the Houston Ship Channel. The proposed model uses a regime-aware training procedure that combines supervised loss on AERMOD-labeled concentration data with a steady three-dimensional advection-diffusion residual that constrains predictions according to governing transport physics. Exact-zero AERMOD labels are treated differently under calm and near-calm wind conditions, preventing potentially artificial low-wind outputs from being enforced directly as supervised targets while retaining the physics-informed constraint. Held-out testing demonstrated strong agreement with AERMOD on supervised signal cases, achieving an RMSE of 0.051 µg m⁻³, a Spearman correlation of 0.989, and 99.7% of predictions within a factor of two of corresponding AERMOD values. An ablation study using an otherwise identical data-only neural network produced an RMSE of 0.189 µg m⁻³, allowing the contribution of the physics-informed loss to be evaluated independently of network architecture. Because the PINN represents concentration as a continuous and differentiable function of source, receptor, emissions, and meteorological conditions, it can support downstream applications such as gradient-based source inversion and rapid spatial exposure assessment that are less straightforward with receptor-based forward calculations alone. More broadly, this work demonstrates how physics-informed surrogate modeling can combine regulatory-model supervision with governing transport constraints to extend the computational capabilities of atmospheric dispersion modeling.

487920.title: Withdrawn: Future Tropical Cyclone Frequency Under Stabilised Global Warming
487920.authors: Savin Suvnesh Chand, Federation University Australia, Mount Helen, Australia
487920.abstract: Anthropogenic climate change is projected to alter tropical cyclone (TC) frequency, yet it remains unknown whether projected declines continue once global warming stabilises under low-emission pathways. Using a common-model ensemble of CMIP6 simulations (1970–2100) and an objective Okubo–Weiss–Zeta (OWZ) detection framework, we compare TC frequency across historical conditions and three future emissions scenarios (SSP1–2.6, SSP3–7.0, and SSP5–8.5). Consistent with previous studies, continued warming under SSP3–7.0 and SSP5–8.5 produces sustained declines in global TC frequency. In contrast, under SSP1–2.6, the decline weakens after mid-century and approaches a new equilibrium following the stabilisation of global temperatures. This response is strongest in the Southern Hemisphere, while the Northern Hemisphere exhibits similar patterns but with greater inter-model variability. These findings suggest that global TC frequency does not decline indefinitely but instead stabilises under climate stabilisation, highlighting the importance of stabilisation pathways for future TC projections and climate mitigation assessments.

487921.title: Extreme Rainfall Intensity versus Spatial Coverage Across Dam-Overtopping Pathways in Eastern US
487921.authors: Hodo Inyang Orok, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and C. A. Bieri and D. A. Hence
487921.abstract: Extreme rainfall is commonly described by large surface accumulations during an event, yet accumulated totals alone do not capture how precipitation is organized in space and time: where the heaviest rainfall occurs, how broadly it is distributed, and how its intensity evolves. Distinguishing likely precipitation distribution scenarios is important for understanding the related hydrologic and infrastructure impacts. This study examines the spatial and temporal evolution of heavy precipitation accumulations within identified atmospheric pathways preceding dam overtopping in the Eastern United States. Radar- and rain gauge-based precipitation observations are evaluated within northern and southern regions and over successive periods leading to overtopping. Rainfall intensity is represented by the upper portion of the daily precipitation distribution, while spatial coverage quantifies the proportion of the regional domain exceeding selected rainfall thresholds. These measures are compared across atmospheric pathways to determine whether stronger rainfall is consistently associated with a broader spatial footprint. Initial results indicate that rainfall intensity and coverage do not always evolve together. Some pathways contain concentrated areas of high rainfall with comparatively limited regional coverage, whereas others exhibit less concentrated rainfall distributed across a broader area. Their relationship may also change as overtopping approaches, reflecting differences in the timing and organization of precipitation. These findings show that rainfall magnitude and spatial extent provide complementary information and should be interpreted together when characterizing extreme precipitation. Connecting both dimensions with atmospheric pathways offers a more complete description of the rainfall environments observed before dam overtopping.

487924.title: PrecipWatch: A Low-Latency Satellite Precipitation Portal for Nowcasting and Operational Decision Support
487924.authors: Shuyan Liu, Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies, College Park, MD; and J. Dong, F. Ozpaker, Y. Hong, V. Petkovic, M. Arulraj, P. Xie, L. J. Campbell, and H. Meng
487924.abstract: Timely access to precipitation information is essential for weather forecasting, flood prediction, hazard monitoring, and operational decision support. NOAA NESDIS produces a comprehensive suite of satellite-based precipitation products from both low Earth orbit (LEO) and geostationary (GEO) observing systems. However, operational use is often limited by product latency, fragmented access pathways, and the lack of a unified platform for visualization and quality monitoring. To address these challenges, NOAA is developing PrecipWatch, a cloud-based satellite precipitation portal designed to provide centralized, low-latency access to precipitation products while supporting advanced product development and near real-time validation. PrecipWatch integrates multiple NOAA precipitation retrieval systems into a common framework, including the Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS), the Snowfall Rate (SFR) algorithm, the Enterprise Microwave Rain Rate and Type (EMRRT) retrieval, the Climate Prediction Center Morphing Technique (CMORPH2), and the STAR Enterprise Rain Rate (ERR) product. The system combines internally generated direct-broadcast (DB)-based products with an externally available web portal to provide a unified environment for processing, visualization, dissemination, and performance monitoring. Cloud-native architecture and scalable processing enable rapid product generation and improved accessibility for National Weather Service (NWS) forecasters and other operational users. In addition to improving product accessibility, PrecipWatch incorporates several scientific enhancements to advance satellite precipitation monitoring. Direct-broadcast data substantially reduces latency for internally generated MiRS, SFR, and EMRRT products. A blended radar-satellite precipitation analysis is being developed by combining Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) estimates with satellite precipitation retrievals to improve spatial coverage, particularly over radar-gap regions and complex terrain. Snowfall estimation is being enhanced through the integration of GEO infrared observations, LEO passive microwave measurements, numerical weather prediction fields, and machine learning techniques to improve detection and retrieval of shallow snowfall systems, including lake-effect snow. Near real-time validation is incorporated through the NOAA Satellite Precipitation Validation System (NPreciSe), providing continuous performance monitoring using MRMS and Stage IV reference datasets together with standard detection and estimation metrics. The PrecipWatch web portal provides interactive map-based visualization, time-loop animation, product sampling, satellite overpass forecasting, and standardized displays designed for operational forecasting. By combing multiple precipitation products, validation information, and visualization capabilities within a single interface, the system improves situational awareness and supports rapid decision making during high-impact weather events. PrecipWach represents an important step toward next-generation satellite precipitation services by integrating mature precipitation retrieval algorithms, low-latency direct broadcast data and cloud processing, scientific product enhancements, and continuous validation within a unified framework. The presentation will include a demonstration of the PrecipWatch Initial Operational Capability (IOC), showcasing integrated product visualization, validation, and low-latency data access.

487946.title: Assessing the Impact of Hyperlocal Heat Exposure Modeling on Health and Equity Outcomes In Baltimore City
487946.authors: Darryn W. Waugh, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and K. Gao, A. Eyni, I. Horst, B. Jin, B. F. Zaitchik, J. Madrigano, A. Datta, F. Curriero, and M. Lasater
487946.abstract: Characterizing neighborhood scale variations in urban air temperature is critical to quantify the impact on human health, identify vulnerable communities, and develop and assess equitable mitigation strategies. However, there are insufficient direct measurements within cities and it is necessary to rely on statistical estimates to map fine-scale temperature variations. Here we report on a multidisciplinary project to assess the uncertainties in these temperature maps for Baltimore City and the impacts of this uncertainty on health assessments and city planning. We leverage the availability of a range of in-situ air temperature data (i.e., two different fixed networks, and car-and bike-based mobile sampling) within Baltimore City to compare high-resolution maps produced using different in-situ data and distinct advanced statistical approaches. We further examine the sensitivity of health assessments for a range of heat-related health outcomes, decision support tool outcomes, and equity analyses from the developed temperature maps. Preliminary analysis shows similarity in nighttime temperatures for different data and statistical methods but larger differences for daytime temperatures. These differences include the locations of the neighborhoods experiencing the highest temperatures. We will present results on the impact of these differences on various health and city planning applications.

487963.title: Satellite Based Identification of transported Wildfire Smoke Over the Great Lakes Using PACE HARP2 Aerosol Retrievals
487963.abstract: Wildfire smoke from Canadian fires frequently degrades air quality across the Great Lakes region, emphasizing the need for reliable methods for identifying transported smoke using satellite observations. As wildfire activity continues to increase in frequency and intensity, improved characterization of smoke transport and regional variability is essential for understanding its atmospheric and environmental impacts. This study evaluates whether aerosol microphysical properties retrieved by NASA's Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) Hyper-Angular Rainbow Polarimeter-2 (HARP2) can distinguish transported wildfire smoke from background atmospheric aerosols over the Great Lakes. Smoke and background aerosol periods from May-September 2025 were identified using aerosol optical depth (AOD) thresholds and verified with true color imagery from the PACE Ocean Color Instrument (OCI). Pixel level aerosol microphysical properties, including Angstrom Exponent (AE) and Single Scattering Albedo (SSA), were analyzed to distinguish smoke from background atmospheric conditions. A supervised logistic regression classifier was developed using AE and SSA observations and later applied to HARP2 retrievals spanning May-September 2024 and 2025 to estimate daily smoke occurrence. The model identified distinct aerosol populations associated with wildfire smoke and produced a physically interpretable decision boundary that separates smoke and background aerosols. Daily smoke classifications successfully identify documented wildfire smoke transport events while predicting low smoke probabilities during background aerosol periods, demonstrating that HARP2 aerosol retrievals can resolve regional smoke variability. These results demonstrate the value of PACE HARP2 aerosol retrievals for characterizing transported wildfire smoke and regional aerosol variability, highlighting their potential to improve understanding of wildfire smoke impacts over the Great Lakes.

487974.title: A Preliminary Analysis of Extreme Rainstorm Characteristics in Mainland China
487974.authors: Chunguang Cui, Institute of Heavy Rain,CMA, Wuhan, China
487974.abstract: The interannual variation trend of the number of station-events of extraordinary rainstorms (daily precipitation exceeding 250 mm) observed at national meteorological stations in Mainland China from 1951 to the present has been compiled, and a very clear upward trend is found. A total of 15 extreme rainstorm events with daily precipitation exceeding 500 mm were identified from 1951 to 2024. For these 15 events, a preliminary analysis was conducted on the following aspects: 1. Main synoptic influencing systems; 2. Moisture transport channels; 3. Characteristics of low-level and boundary-layer jet streams; 4. Environmental factors; 5. Microphysical characteristics. It was found that half of the events were affected directly or indirectly by typhoons; among the 15 cases, 12 events featured the presence of dual low-level jet streams. Related analytical studies are still ongoing. Some preliminary conclusions have been obtained. Forecasting capability for extreme rainstorms.

487975.title: A Multiscale Analysis of the Formation Mechanisms of an Extreme Rainstorm Event over the Northeastern Tibetan Plateau
487975.authors: Hongli Li, Institute of Heavy Rain, China Meteorological Administration, Wuhan, China
487975.abstract: Using the Qinghai Analysis Data (QHA), together with surface observations, Himawari-8 satellite data, and ERA5 reanalysis data, a multi-scale comprehensive analysis was conducted for an extreme rainstorm event that occurred on 13-14 August 2022 on the northeastern side of the Tibetan Plateau. The results show that this rainstorm occurred under a favorable large-scale circulation background. Cold and warm air masses from the north and south converged on the northeastern side of the plateau, forming an upper-level divergence and lower-level convergence vertical configuration. The precipitation was distributed in a banded pattern along the Huangshui and Yellow River Valleys, exhibiting significant topographic constraints and nocturnal enhancement. A meso-β-scale convective system was the direct weather system responsible for the heavy rainfall. It underwent a complete life cycle of development, maturation, and dissipation, and its evolution corresponded well with variations in precipitation intensity, with the heaviest rainfall occurring during the mature stage of convection. The 600 hPa easterly shear line and low-level easterly flow were the key dynamic factors triggering convection. Under the forcing of the trumpet-shaped valley topography, warm and moist air continuously converged, ascended, and extended westward, triggering severe convection in the presence of deep unstable stratification and a highly humid environment. During the mature stage of convection, dynamic lifting, latent heat release, and ice-phase microphysical processes formed a positive feedback mechanism. Melting near the 0℃ level and raindrop collision-coalescence significantly enhanced precipitation efficiency. The QHA successfully captured the mesoscale structural characteristics of this rainstorm event, providing an important basis for the monitoring and early warning of heavy precipitation in the complex terrain on the northeastern side of the Tibetan Plateau.

487977.title: Study on the Characteristics and Mechanism of Sudden Heavy Rainfall in Mountainous Areas
487977.authors: Xiaofang Wang, Institute of Heavy Rain, CMA, Wuhan, Wuhan, Hubei, China
487977.abstract: Based on a 37-year long time series of sudden heavy rain samples in the Southwest Mountainous Region, identification criteria for sudden heavy rain events in the Western Mountainous Region were proposed. A sudden heavy rain event is defined as a precipitation event where 1-hour precipitation is greater than or equal to 20 mm and continuous 3-hour precipitation is greater than or equal to 50 mm. A total of 15,023 sudden heavy rain events from 468 national stations over 37 years (1981-2017) were statistically analyzed, focusing on their spatiotemporal distribution characteristics and vertical structure features. Three high-frequency zones were identified: the Sichuan Basin, southern Guizhou-northern Guangxi, and western Hunan. The daily variation exhibits both unimodal and multimodal structures with a high nocturnal occurrence. In higher terrain areas, such events mostly occur from afternoon to evening, while in lower terrain areas like basins, they tend to occur at midnight. 90% of the events last less than 24 hours, with the highest frequency of sudden heavy rain events lasting 6-12 hours. The accumulated precipitation of sudden heavy rain is closely related to duration but has little relation to rainfall intensity. Favorable environmental conditions for sudden heavy rain: 1) Abnormal cyclonic circulation in the high-frequency area enhances low-level atmospheric convergence and the transport of warm and moist air; 2) Abnormal convergence of meridional disturbance circulation, columnar water vapor flux, stronger warm and moist airflow in the lower layer, and stronger vertical wind shear in the lower troposphere caused thereby; 3) Cyclonic circulation or shear in the convective lower layer wind field, convergence of wind speed, large local precipitable water, convective instability, high CAPE values, and low CIN values.

487985.title: A Novel Submesoscale Parameterization and Its Application In Ocean and Coupled Models
487985.authors: Zhiwei Zhang, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, Shandong, China
487985.abstract: Submesoscale processes (submesoscales) are oceanic motions with spatial scales of O(1–10) km. They play an important role in vertical material and tracer transport in the upper ocean and significantly modulate large‑scale ocean dynamics, air-sea interactions, and biogeochemical cycles, making them a frontier topic in oceanography. Since prevailing global ocean and climate models cannot resolve submesoscale processes, their vertical transport effects must be parameterized in models. Developing submesoscale parameterization schemes is thus an urgent need to improve model performance. In recent years, the presenter and collaborators have conducted large‑scale coordinated observational experiments on submesoscales, yielding new insights into submesoscale dynamics. We have proposed a new generation theory for submesoscale generation and subsequently developed a new submesoscale parameterization scheme—the Zhang23 scheme—which has been implemented and tested in several ocean and coupled models, such as MOM6, LICOM, ROMS, and COAWST. This scheme helps reduce model biases, such as in sea surface temperature and mixed‑layer depth simulations. This presentation will systematically introduce the development and application of this new submesoscale parameterization scheme.

487996.title: The Eye from Above: Tracking Three Decades of Eastern U.S. Deep Convection Using GOES-East
487996.authors: Patrick Jeremiah Newman, University of Massachusetts Lowell, Woburn, MA
487996.abstract: Leveraging the GOES Fundamental Climate Data Record (GOES-FCDR) provides a nearly continuous dataset for calculating climatological trends. This project presents a climatological analysis of mid-latitude continental deep convective systems utilizing 4km, 11 µm infrared channel data from successive generations of operational GOES-East satellites over the Eastern CONUS, focusing on the meteorological spring and summer months (March-August) from 1995 to 2024. With many earlier studies focused on the evolution of tornadic trends, this study isolates large-scale continental deep convective systems, such as Mesoscale Convective Systems (MCSs). By employing the Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds (tobac) Python package alongside custom spatial filtering, we successfully detect localized cold-core cloud features, their surrounding structural cloud shields, and linked storm trajectories. Tracking parameters and thresholds include ≤215 K for identifying convective brightness temperature cold core features, as well as an areal extent of at least 960 km2 for broader storm characteristics. These parameters allow us to track the most mature and intense phases of convective activity, thereby allowing for an evaluation of monthly climatological metrics, including track location densities, maximum areal footprint, domain coverage, track persistence and track geographic length. To evaluate long-term spatial variations, filtered storm trajectories are aggregated into multi-year spatial plots. These distributions, alongside temporal time series of system counts and structural behavior, highlight changes to the convective season. Ultimately, this tracking framework establishes a baseline for understanding how large-scale continental deep convective storm structure and frequency has fluctuated across the Eastern United States over a 30-year climate record.

487997.title: Urban heat island dynamics: Assessing planetary boundary layer height using airborne Doppler lidar
487997.authors: Ken Husty Tungpalan, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and B. J. Carroll, S. Baidar, and C. Warneke
487997.abstract: The planetary boundary layer (PBL) is the lowest layer of the atmosphere and has been heavily studied due to its impact on human health as it mixes pollutants and drives chemical reactions like tropospheric ozone formation. The Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect significantly influences the PBL, characteristically elevating the boundary layer height (BLH) while altering local weather and amplifying pollutant mixing. As urbanization and climate change intensify, understanding this UHI-PBL interaction becomes critical. This study utilizes a master oscillator power amplifier microjoule-class pulsed coherent Doppler lidar system deployed aboard a NOAA WP-3D aircraft during the 2026 Texas Air Quality Study (TexAQS). The lidar provides full wind profiles above and below the aircraft every 1 km along the flight path. By analyzing measurements of mean horizontal wind and BLH, this research identifies and quantifies the signature of the UHI effect within the cities of Texas. To achieve this, we utilize a fuzzy logic framework integrating wind variance, wind speed, wind shear, and aerosol backscatter to determine a unified measurement of the BLH. This approach enables the spatiotemporal visualization and quantification of atmospheric dynamics over complex terrain. This research will show results of the BLH over the urban regions contrasted with nearby rural areas to reveal any UHI effect, along with an analysis of other boundary layer dynamical factors contributing to the observed variations. Ultimately, these insights will advance our understanding of urban atmospheric dynamics, providing a critical foundation for improving local air quality forecasts and urban mesoscale models, safeguarding public health in rapidly urbanizing regions.

487998.title: Can Rubberized Road Material Reduce the Urban Heat Island Effect?
487998.authors: Jessica Ann Muniz, University of Georgia, Dahlonega, GA
487998.abstract: Many cities across the United States experience a meteorological phenomenon called the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect. UHI is the experience of significantly higher temperatures in urban areas compared to rural areas, due to the presence of more buildings and paved roads, among other factors. Elevated temperatures can pose health hazards, particularly during the daytime. We hypothesized that increasing rubber concentrations in road materials would lower surface temperatures, thereby reducing the Urban Heat Island effect in Atlanta, Georgia. For the experiment, we placed two samples in an outdoor area with direct sunlight exposure: one sample of rubberized road material and another of asphalt road material. Infrared sensors recorded the surface temperatures of both samples for five days. After analyzing recorded surface temperatures, we observed that at noon, the surface over the rubberized material is on average 5°C (9°F) hotter than over the asphalt. At midnight, the surface over the rubberized material is 0.85°C (1.5 °F) cooler than over the asphalt. Though preliminary findings suggest that rubber materials may not be optimal for daytime temperature mitigation, UHI-related health outcomes are more prevalent overnight. Our findings suggest that further analysis is warranted on road segments and under different experimental designs at and above the surface.

488002.title: Tornado and Thunderstorm-Wind-Gust Monitoring, Forecasting, and Nowcasting Technologies in National Meteorological Centre of China
488002.authors: Yongguang Zheng, National Meteorological Centre of China Meteorological Administrattion, Beijing, China; and B. Yang, K. Zhou, M. Chen, and L. Han
488002.abstract: Severe convective weather forecasting is one of the challenging tasks in operational forecasting, with tornado monitoring and forecasting being particularly difficult within this field. This presentation introduces the advances in tornado and thunderstorm-wind-gust monitoring and forecasting technologies at the National Meteorological Centre (NMC) of China. The NMC has developed: 1) 0-3 day tornado and thunderstorm-wind-gust forecasting techniques based on global numerical weather prediction (NWP) model forecasts; 2) 0-6 hour short-term forecasting techniques for tornadoes and thunderstorm wind gusts combining high resolution NWP model forecasts, updraft helicity, and AI forecasting methods; 3) 0-2 hour monitoring and warning techniques integrating convective-storm structural characteristics, AI-based identification methods, and the “Fenglei” AI large model for nowcasting; along with a tornado and thunderstorm-wind-gust disaster field survey system. Based on the favorable environmental conditions and physical mechanisms, NMC has developed over 50 severe convective physical parameters including the significant tornado parameter (STP) and supercell parameter (SCP), where STP and maximum updraft helicity (UH) prove effective for short-range (0-72 hour) and short-term (0-6 hour) forecasting tornado respectively. Tornado and thunderstorm-wind-gust monitoring relies on tornado vortex signatures and dual-polarization parameter evolution observed by dual-polarization Doppler weather radars, leading to the development of a multi-task deep learning tornado identification model based on radar data and a deep learning thunderstorm wind gust identification model. These technologies have been integrated into the SWAN3.0 system - the operational short-term forecasting and nowcasting platform for severe convective weather of China Meteorological Administration. The work is funded by the China National Natural Science Foundation project (Granted No. U2342204).

488003.title: The Influence of Coastal Soil Moisture on the Sea Breeze Circulation and the Marine Atmospheric Boundary Layer in Idealized Simulations
488003.authors: Peter M Finocchio, NRL, Monterey, CA; and K. Biernat, J. D. Doyle, and C. A. Reynolds
488003.abstract: Coastal circulations like the sea breeze are key drivers of variability within the marine atmospheric boundary layer (MABL) near the coast. We conducted a set of 36 idealized, mesoscale simulations designed to better understand how coastal soil moisture influences the MABL through the sea breeze circulation. We find that decreasing coastal soil moisture increases the strength, extent, and depth of the sea breeze circulation over the ocean. The onshore flow associated with the sea breeze in the simulations with the driest soil moisture extends over 200 km seaward from the coast and has near-surface wind speeds exceeding 8 m/s. The stronger onshore flow in the drier soil conditions increases humidity within the MABL by enhancing surface latent heat fluxes near the coast. Statistical analysis of all 36 simulations with different soil moisture, SST, and cloud settings reveals that the sea breeze characteristics over the ocean have the strongest relationship to the depth of the mixed layer over land and the weakest relationship to the lower-tropospheric static stability over the ocean. Afternoon clouds and convection limit the diurnal growth of the mixed layer over land by reducing surface heat fluxes and stabilizing the lower troposphere. As a result, the simulations with clouds have weaker, shallower, and more coastally confined sea breezes over the ocean than corresponding cloud-free simulations. These findings suggest that accurate representation of coastal soil moisture and cloud processes in numerical weather prediction models is crucial for forecasting basic characteristics of the MABL more than 200 km offshore.

488005.title: Lowering the Barrier to Observational Fieldwork with the Met Instruments Project
488005.authors: Quinton Kirsch, Met Instruments Project, Saint Louis, MO; and L. E. Llewellyn
488005.abstract: The Met Instruments Project (MIP) is an independent atmospheric observing initiative focused on the development and operation of flexible observing systems for field research and environmental monitoring. The project seeks to reduce logistical barriers associated with specialized atmospheric observations by developing platforms that emphasize rapid deployment, modularity, maintainability, standardized documentation, and scientifically useful data collection. Central to this effort is the Quickly Deployable Automated Weather Station (QDAWS), a portable fixed-site observing platform developed through iterative engineering and operational field experience. Since its initial deployment, QDAWS has supported numerous field operations under a range of environmental conditions, including radiosonde operations, winter weather, and severe convection. Lessons from these deployments have informed improvements in instrumentation, telemetry, power systems, deployment procedures, and environmental adaptability while establishing a foundation for future platform development. This presentation provides an overview of the Met Instruments Project, the operational philosophy guiding its observing systems, and the development of QDAWS as the project’s flagship platform. Current and planned capabilities, including mobile mesonets, modular QDAWS configurations, and expanded performance characterization, are discussed in the context of developing a scalable independent atmospheric observing program. This presentation highlights how iterative system development, field experience, and standardized operational practices can support increasingly capable observing systems for future research applications and scientific collaborations.

488006.title: Evaluating an MPAS-Based Warn-on-Forecast System in NOAA Testbeds
488006.authors: Nusrat Yussouf, CIWRO, Norman, OK; and C. Schwartz, Y. Wang, J. Martin, B. C. Matilla, M. Silcott, P. C. Burke, H. Obermeier, P. Skinner, K. H. Knopfmeier, S. M. Trojniak, J. Correia Jr., L. J. Wicker, E. Mansell, A. J. Clark, C. Liu, S. Ha, C. A. Kerr, D. R. Stratman, I. L. Jirak, and J. A. Nelson Jr.
488006.abstract: To advance watch-to-warning scale probabilistic guidance for severe convective hazards and extreme precipitation, NOAA’s Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS) is transitioning from its legacy Weather Research and Forecasting model with GSI-based ensemble Kalman filter data assimilation (WoFSv1) to a Model for Prediction Across Scales–based framework (WoFSv2). A 3-km MPAS–Data Assimilation Research Testbed ensemble system was developed and run on cloud-based high-performance computing resources. WoFSv2 was demonstrated and evaluated during the 2026 Hazardous Weather Testbed Spring Forecasting Experiment (HWT-SFE), where its performance was compared with WoFSv1 for probabilistic guidance of severe weather hazards, including tornadoes, large hail, and damaging winds. Evaluations were also conducted during a stand-alone Hydrometeorology Testbed Flash Flood and Intense Rainfall Experiment (HMT-FFaIR) to examine the system’s ability to predict extreme rainfall rates and flash-flood threats. Results from these testbed evaluations, including objective and subjective comparisons with the WRF-based WoFSv1 baseline, will be presented. Preliminary findings demonstrate promising performance for probabilistic severe-weather and heavy-rainfall guidance while also identifying areas requiring further development. Lessons learned from these evaluations are informing the continued transition of WoFSv2 to the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration framework (JEDI) using the Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter.

488009.title: 25 Years of Documenting Pediatric Vehicular Heatstroke
488009.authors: Jan Null, San Jose State University Dept. of Meteorology & Climate Sciences, Half Moon Bay, CA
488009.abstract: 25 Years of Documenting Pediatric Vehicular Heatstroke Author: Jan Null, CCM NoHeatstroke.org San Jose State University Since 1998, at least 1060 children in the United States have died inside hot vehicles due to Pediatric Vehicular Heatstroke (PVH). When these incidents occur, meteorologists in the public, private, and academic sectors are often asked questions like “how hot might it have gotten inside that vehicle?” That single question changed the course of the next 25 years of my life. Unable to find reliable research, I began conducting my own studies of how quickly vehicles heat across a range of temperatures. What started as scientific curiosity soon became a long-term commitment to understanding—and preventing—Pediatric Vehicular Heatstroke (PVH). Along the way, I collaborated with child safety organizations and researchers, including colleagues at Stanford University, resulting in a 2005 paper in Pediatrics that remains one of the most frequently cited studies on vehicle heating and children. This presentation also addresses the epidemiology of PVH, which has literally reached epidemic proportions. Both the temporal and geographic distribution of incidents are tracked, as are the types of circumstances under which they occur. Additionally, how these cases fit into the overall gathering of “heat” related deaths nationwide and how these cases may (or may not) be prosecuted is examined. Ultimately, there should be two “take-aways” for the meteorological community. First, they will have accurate and timely information to provide to their audiences. And secondly, they will have safety recommendations that will help prevent future tragedies.

488016.title: Measurements of Ångström Exponent of Aerosol By Ozone Lidar with Four Wavelengths
488016.authors: Cao Nianwen, Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology, Nanjing City , 32, China
488016.abstract: Ozone lidar measurements were conducted at four wavelengths—276 nm, 287 nm, 299 nm, and 396 nm—to determine the aerosol Ångström exponent k. These wavelengths are generated by Raman scattering of CO₂, H₂/D₂, and CH₄, pumped by 266 nm and 355 nm lasers. We presented the simulation of the Ångström exponent k of aerosols from synthetic ozone lidar signals at three wavelengths and the measurements of the Ångström exponent k of aerosols from an ozone lidar at four wavelengths. Ozone lidar signals were simulated at three wavelengths: 276 nm, 287 nm, and 299 nm. From these simulated signals, the Ångström exponent k was calculated to be 0.85, while the ideal value is 1. The aerosol extinction coefficient was calculated to be 0.825×10−3 km−1 in the altitude range from 400 m to 520 m using the measured ozone lidar signal at the 396 - nm wavelength. We utilized the measured ozone signals at 276 nm, 287 nm, and 299 nm, along with an aerosol extinction coefficient of 0.825×10−3 km−1, to calculate the Ångström exponent K in the range of 1.6 - 1.98.

488019.title: Operational Application of Machine Learning Weather Prediction at Weathernews: From Tropical Cyclone Ensembles to Regional Nowcasting and Downscaling
488019.authors: Fuki Kudo, Weathernews Inc., Chiba, 12, Japan
488019.abstract: With the rapid advancements in Machine Learning Weather Prediction (MLWP) models, Weathernews Inc. is actively advancing the operational deployment and integration of MLWP across a diverse range of Business-to-Business(BtoB) and Business-to-Consumer(BtoC) applications. This presentation highlights both the technology behind MLWP-based forecast generation and its practical integration into real-world services for end-users, featuring selected use cases spanning global to regional scales. For global applications, we present an operational approach to tropical cyclone (TC) forecasting. In our TC forecasting pipeline, we operate a multi-model ensemble system that integrates conventional numerical weather prediction (NWP) physics models with MLWP, based on comprehensive case evaluations. By leveraging the distinct strengths of models such as Google DeepMind's in predicting both TC tracks and intensity, we have achieved improvements in overall forecast accuracy. In this presentation, we share these verification results along with concrete examples of how this capability is applied to our BtoB solutions, including marine weather services. Similarly, in the domains of regional short-range forecasting and spatial downscaling, we pursue dual approaches that link model generation with service integration. We present practical examples of applying these forecast technologies to actual content, including "AI Nowcast"—which combines our proprietary analysis data with open-source frameworks such as Anemoi to improve location-specific forecast accuracy—and downscaling approaches that utilize Diffusion Models to capture fine spatial patterns, aimed at enhancing the quality of precipitation content in our mobile applications. Through these examples, we share our concrete initiatives and future perspectives on transitioning state-of-the-art MLWP technologies into operational, real-world business services (R2O) from a private sector viewpoint.

488021.title: Morphology-Conditioned Susceptibility of Marine Stratocumulus Clouds Suggests Weak Marine Cloud Brightening Potential
488021.authors: Tom Goren, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel; and G. Choudhury and G. Feingold
488021.abstract: Marine low-level clouds span a continuum of morphologies but are often classified into discrete morphological regimes. In this talk, we present a new ternary framework that represents cloud morphology as a continuum within a triangular space whose vertices are defined by three cloud optical depth bins. This framework provides a new way to quantify aerosol-cloud interactions continuously across the full spectrum of marine cloud organization. We find that the morphology-dependent susceptibilities of liquid water path and cloud albedo to cloud droplet number concentration can offset one another across the most frequently observed morphologies, resulting in little or even negative net in-cloud albedo response. These findings suggest that marine cloud brightening may be weak for many marine low-level clouds, or even produce the opposite effect to that intended.

488022.title: Water Vapor DIAL to Improve Forecasting Skills for Stationary Linear Mesoscale Convective Systems: Development and Field Observations
488022.authors: Masahide Nishihashi, MRI, Tsukuba, Japan; and E. Oikawa, T. Nagai, T. Sakai, O. Uchino, S. Yoshida, and M. Abo
488022.abstract: We have been developing a compact diode-laser-based differential absorption lidar (DIAL) to measure the vertical distributions of water vapor up to an altitude of 3-4 km both day and night to improve the forecasting skills for localized heavy rainfall related to stationary linear mesoscale convective systems (SLMCSs), which are called "Senjo-Kousuitai" in Japan. We have focused on improving the transmittance of the receiving spectrometer, increasing and stabilizing the transmitted laser power, optimizing observational parameters, and improving the adjustment processes of the DIAL for field deployment. After experimental observations at the Meteorological Research Institute, a field observation campaign was conducted in Nagasaki, located on the western coast of Kyushu, Southwest Japan, from July to October 2025. Nagasaki is an optimal location for the observation of the vertical distributions of water vapor inflowing from the East China Sea, which has the potential to trigger SLMCS. For approximately three months during the summer, the DIAL operated almost stably. While multiple SLMCSs occurred in Kyushu from August to September 2025, high concentrations of water vapor exceeding 20 g/m³ were observed at an altitude of around 500 m. However, the maximum observed altitude was generally limited to about 1 to 1.5 km. While the presence of low-level clouds was one factor contributing to this, functional issues with the DIAL were also suspected; therefore, efforts were made to improve DIAL’s functionality following the field observations. After replacing the photomultiplier tube with a new model in 2026, the photon count increased significantly by 3 to 4 orders of magnitude, and the maximum observation altitude increased to approximately 4 to 5 km during the night. The vertical distributions of water vapor concentration observed with the DIAL were generally consistent with radiosonde observations and the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) Meso-scale Analysis values. However, the maximum observation altitude was limited to about 1 km during the day due to insufficient removal of the solar background light. Therefore, we are working to reduce the solar background light by adding an etalon to the receiving spectrometer and doubling the interference filters. We are conducting field observations in Nagasaki from June through October 2026. We will also present the results of these observations.

488032.title: Adding Variables to Aila AI Model with Multi-Decoder Learning
488032.authors: Leila Hieta, Finnish Meteorological Institute, Helsinki, Uusimaa, Finland; and M. Partio, M. Laine, O. Räty, M. Paasiniemi, T. Himanka, E. Nevala, A. Hakola, and O. Laine
488032.abstract: Advances in data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) are fundamentally transforming how national meteorological services produce weather forecasts. Rather than relying solely on physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems, neural networks can be trained directly on historical weather analyses to produce forecasts with skill comparable to state-of-the-art NWP models while shifting the main computational cost from daily forecast production to large-scale model training. The Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI) has trained Aila, a regional limited-area AI weather model, as part of the ECMWF Machine Learning Project — a collaborative initiative between ECMWF and its member states to advance machine learning in numerical weather prediction. Aila is built using Anemoi, an open and modular framework for integrating modern machine learning methods into operational meteorology. Aila adopts a graph neural network architecture with an encoder–processor–decoder structure, employing a stretched-grid approach that has higher spatial resolution over the Northern Europe while retaining broader atmospheric context. The model has been trained on approximately 40 years of ECMWF ERA5 global reanalysis data complemented by several years of high-resolution regional Harmonie-AROME analyses, utilizing the large-scale GPU resources of the LUMI supercomputer. While the base model demonstrates strong performance, expanding established architectures to predict parameters excluded from the initial training dataset typically requires prohibitively expensive retraining. This study presents the development of a multi-decoder (MD) extension to the Aila architecture to address this limitation. The MD approach enables the training of additional variables beyond the base model's original variable set with significantly reduced computational overhead. By freezing the weights of the pre-trained base model and attaching a separate, independently optimised decoder module, the system learns to predict new target variables without modifying the underlying graph-based latent representations or disrupting the atmospheric dynamics encoded during base model training. The results demonstrate that the multi-decoder extension achieves convergence at a fraction of the computational cost required for full-model retraining, while effectively leveraging the spatial resolution and atmospheric state representation of the frozen base model. The MD framework establishes a scalable pathway for iterative model development, enabling efficient expansion of Aila's variable set and facilitating impact forecasting by mapping the model's latent atmospheric state directly to downstream meteorological and societal applications.

488036.title: On the Physics of the Diurnal Cycle of Moist Convection (Invited Presentation)
488036.authors: Kerry A. Emanuel, MIT, New Harbor, ME; and I. Baxter, T. Y. Lee, F. Solari, J. Tang, and L. Yao
488036.abstract: Observations of rainfall and lightning clearly show that the strong diurnal cycle of convection over land peaks well after the daily maximum in both solar radiation and surface enthalpy flux, while over the oceans there is a broad peak late at night into early morning. Historically, convection in both climate models and single-column models peaks too early over land, while cloud-permitting models show systematically later peaks. We show that a single-column model with advanced radiation and convection schemes is in good agreement with observed diurnal cycles over both land and sea when the weak temperature gradient approximation (WTG) is enforced, and we interpret the results with the help of a simple analytic model based on boundary layer quasi-equilibrium and WTG.

488037.title: An Overview of Potential Intensity (Invited Presentation)
488037.authors: Kerry A. Emanuel, MIT, New Harbor, ME
488037.abstract: The basic idea of potential intensity has its roots in the work of Kleinschmidt, Riehl, Malkus and Lilly. Subsequent work developed and refined an energy cycle approach that complements the derivation based on balanced dynamics. In this talk I will review the history of the potential intensity theory and argue that the comparison of reanalysis-derived potential intensity with both observed lifetime maximum intensities probably provides the most robust current estimates of the ratio of the surface enthalpy exchange to drag coefficients at hurricane-force wind speeds.

488052.title: Analyzing Spatial Biases in Weather Prediction Center Excessive Rainfall Outlook Forecasts Separated by Region, Season, and Event Type
488052.authors: Adam Joseph Thompson, NOAA, College Park, MD; and E. Bower, M. Klein, and M. Chenard
488052.abstract: Historically, flash flooding/excessive rainfall has proven to be one of the costliest forms of meteorological disasters in terms of life and property in the United States. Moreover, recent studies have determined that the frequency of intense precipitation has increased in recent years with the advent of climate change. Therefore, accurate and accessible forecasting of these events is more paramount than ever. The Excessive Rainfall Outlook (ERO), produced and released by the Weather Prediction Center, is a probabilistic forecast product providing spatial visualization of flash flood risk in the contiguous United States. This product is widely accessible; however, recent studies have questioned the accuracy of these forecasts, showing a significant number of flash flood events falling outside of an ERO risk category. The goal of this study is to assist ERO forecast operations by providing a visualization of spatial ERO forecast biases through comparing past forecasts to verified flood data. The Day 1-3 ERO products, issued at 0900 UTC each day, are verified in this study. These EROs are verified against the Unified Flood Verification System (UFVS) observations and proxies for flash flood events, which have served as the verification for numerous other studies at the WPC. This dataset combines several excessive rainfall proxies, including Stage IV rainfall exceeding 1-, 2-, 5-, and 10-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI), Stage IV rainfall exceeding Flash Flood Guidance (FFG), NWS-verified local storm reports, and USGS stream gauge reports of “Flood Stage”. The Method for Object-based Diagnostic Evaluation (MODE) tool from the Model Evaluation Tools (MET) is used to perform object-based verification of the EROs against their corresponding UFVS observation objects. MODE computes various object statistics, including interest, contingency table statistics, object centroids, and more. The ERO forecast centroids are first sorted by region and event type, then the magnitude/direction of the displacement between the forecast centroid and its corresponding observation centroid are calculated for each matched object pair, providing a metric for spatial forecast accuracy. Interestingly, with mean centroid displacement magnitude as a metric for accuracy, there appears to be little to no connection between risk level and forecast accuracy. Moreover, the average forecast accuracy shows negligible improvement from day 3 to day 2, but shows a significant improvement from day 2 to day 1. When examining specific regional and event classifications, the “West Coast” region and “Atmospheric River" events exhibit very similar centroid displacement patterns; the ERO forecasts are consistently biased to the south and west of the verification. The similarity between these displacement patterns is consistent with the fact that Atmospheric River events are primarily confined to the West Coast of the US. The analysis performed in this study will shed light on the historical forecast biases associated with each event type/region at each risk level, enabling ERO forecasters to analyze and account for these biases when creating their forecast within a specific region or for a particular event type. This will hopefully improve the overall accuracy of these forecasts and thereby support NOAA’s mission of protecting life and property in the United States.

488058.title: Advancing Satellite Data Assimilation: Deep Learning Architecture and Scalable Cloud Processing for Environmental Intelligence
488058.authors: Sudhir Raj Shrestha, NESDIS, Riverdale Park, MD; NOAA, College Park, MD; and Y. Chen
488058.abstract: The NOAA Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR) is strategically leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) to transform the generation and delivery of high-quality environmental intelligence. This effort represents a paradigm shift from computationally intensive, physics-based solvers toward AI-native frameworks capable of emulating complex radiative transfer and inversion processes. By deploying deep learning architectures across the satellite data value chain—from sensor calibration and retrievals to data assimilation and real-time forecasting—STAR has achieved orders-of-magnitude gains in processing speed while preserving the physical fidelity of legacy systems. This transformation is exemplified through the modernization of foundational enterprise systems such as the Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS-AI) and the Multi-Instrument Inversion and Data Assimilation Preprocessing System (MIIDAPS-AI), as well as the CRTM AI-Emulator for near realtime Observation minus background (O-B) bias monitoring and the AI-CRTM for AI-based forward modeling and Jacobian computations to support NWP data assimilation and inversion retrieval systems. Furthermore, STAR is advancing Global Navigation Satellite System Radio Occultation (GNSS-RO) processing by developing an AI/ML-based bending angle reference model that bypasses computationally intensive forward modeling, enabling rapid, scalable O-B evaluation for high-volume commercial RO data. STAR is also advancing AI/ML-based classification frameworks to detect Radio Frequency Interference (RFI), improving the accuracy of ionospheric scintillation products. These next-generation systems now enable near-instantaneous processing of massive global data volumes from advanced sensors including ATMS and CrIS,while preserving physically realistic vertical profiles of atmospheric state variables and the spectral integrity of traditional one-dimensional variational (1DVAR) approaches by enforcing physical consistency between radiometric observations and geophysical retrievals.. To support a shift toward “science-on-demand,” STAR is working on architecting scalable cloud-native ecosystems centered on Analysis-Ready, Cloud-Optimized (ARCO) data. A key milestone in this effort is the deployment of an enterprise, end-to-end multi-mission RO processing system on the NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF). As satellite observing systems, including high-density commercial SmallSat RO constellations like Spire and PlanetiQ, deliver data at increasingly fine spatial and temporal resolutions, STAR is addressing challenges in data volume, storage, and accessibility through cloud-optimized formats such as Zarr. These formats enable efficient data chunking, rich metadata management, and rapid subsetting, allowing users to request precisely targeted data via standardized Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) APIs. This infrastructure—built on Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) and Infrastructure as Code (IaC)—enables data-proximate computing, scalable analytics, and the systematic preparation of AI-ready datasets. By integrating AI-native processing with ARCO data aligned to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, NESDIS STAR delivers low-latency, high-fidelity environmental intelligence to the National Weather Service (NWS), the Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC), and the global community. These capabilities are critical for modern disaster response, fire weather monitoring, and life-saving decision support. This presentation will focus on the convergence of AI-native observations and ARCO-enabled cloud infrastructure that delivers substantial operational and societal value to the National Weather Service and emergency management partners enabling an accelerated data-to-decision pipelines, enhanced data equity and access, operational resilience to hazard and disaster response such as Fire weather, severe storms, space weather anomalies, and tropical cyclones ultimately supporting gold standard open science.

488059.title: Maximizing the Forecast Value of the GeoXO Hyperspectral Infrared Sounder: A Research-to-Operations Roadmap
488059.authors: Philip E. Ardanuy, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and J. J. Gerth and J. G. Yoe
488059.abstract: By the early 2030s, the convergence of geostationary hyperspectral infrared sounding, hybrid and cloud-native exascale numerical weather prediction, advanced 4D variational and ensemble data assimilation, and AI-assisted quality control will create unprecedented opportunities to improve high-impact weather forecasting. This presentation proposes a phased research-to-operations (R2O) roadmap that matures the GeoXO Hyperspectral Infrared Sounder (GXS) from an emerging observing capability into an operational component of NOAA's forecast enterprise. A distinguishing feature of the roadmap is a paired precursor strategy that combines actual MTG-S1/IRS observations with simulated GXS observations throughout algorithm development, data assimilation, and operational demonstrations. Actual MTG-S1/IRS data provide operational experience with calibration, cloud effects, latency, and quality control, while simulated GXS observations reproduce planned Western Hemisphere viewing geometries, instrument characteristics, and NOAA priority weather regimes. Together they support complementary observing system experiments (OSEs) and observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs), reducing implementation risk while maximizing operational readiness before launch. This approach is informed through lessons learned in a previous NOAA and Cooperative Institute best practice that generated high-quality simulated Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) radiances and derived products in real time over the contiguous United States, helping to ensure enterprise readiness for the GOES-R series prior to launch and commissioning. The roadmap leverages NOAA testbeds, proving grounds, UFS/EPIC, and JCSDA to mature direct radiance assimilation, principal-component methods, AI-assisted quality control, all-sky assimilation, and forecaster decision-support products. It also investigates a future GXS-enabled 4D wind-analysis capability, in which repeated hyperspectral observations improve dynamically consistent wind analyses through feature tracking and advanced data assimilation rather than direct wind measurement. The strategy calls for three NOAA high-impact operational transition case demonstrations: earlier detection and improved prediction of atmospheric rivers affecting the U.S. West Coast, improved Caribbean hurricane track and rapid-intensification forecasts through enhanced depiction of storm environment evolution, and more skillful Warn-on-Forecast prediction of severe Midwest convection by continuously monitoring pre-convective instability, moisture transport, and mesoscale boundaries. The roadmap defines measurable scientific, computational, and organizational readiness milestones, including testbeds, proving grounds, and operational rehearsals, that establish a credible, low-risk pathway for transitioning GeoXO into sustained NOAA operations through a continuous Operations-to-Research-to-Operations (O2R2O) cycle.

488069.title: Advancing Satellite Instrument Calibration/Validation to Support NWP Data Assimilation
488069.authors: Changyong Cao, NOAA, College Park, MD
488069.abstract: Satellite observations are a cornerstone of modern numerical weather prediction (NWP), providing critical information on atmospheric temperature, moisture, clouds, and surface conditions across the globe. With increasing dependence on satellite radiances in operational data assimilation systems, the accuracy, stability, and consistency of satellite measurements are essential for improving forecast skill and advancing Earth system prediction. Accurate satellite radiance calibration and validation (cal/val) are fundamental to maximizing the impact of satellite observations in NWP and quantifiable through Observing System Experiments (OSEs). The quality of assimilated radiances directly affects observation-minus-background (O–B) departures, which serve as key diagnostics for monitoring observation quality, identifying systematic biases, evaluating forecast model performance, and improving data assimilation strategies. Therefore, continued advances in satellite cal/val are required to ensure high-quality observations and to fully realize their potential through NWP assimilation. This presentation will highlight emerging approaches for advancing satellite radiance cal/val through artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). Recent developments in advanced AI architectures, such as liquid neural network (LNN)-based models, provide new opportunities for automated calibration monitoring, radiance bias characterization, anomaly detection, and atmospheric layer Jacobian. This could enable more comprehensive assessments of observation quality, instrument performance, and forecast impact. By integrating AI capabilities with physical understanding and established calibration frameworks, these efforts aim to enhance the accuracy, efficiency, and scalability of satellite instrument cal/val and strengthen the role of satellite observations in next-generation NWP data assimilation.

488073.title: The Fire Management Survey: Developing a Nationwide Panel of Fire Managers
488073.authors: Vanessa Dunham, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; OU Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis (IPPRA), Norman, OK; and E. F. Meister, M. Krocak, J. T. Ripberger, D. Hogg, A. C. Wanless, A. Fox, K. Gupta, M. O. Mattox, and P. Skinner
488073.abstract: Wildfire frequency and impacts continue to increase across the US, particularly within the wildland-urban interface. However, unlike other hazards such as tornadoes or severe thunderstorms, the US lacks a unified warning system specifically designed for wildfires. Developing this system requires a clear understanding of the use of the current fire alerting system, including how fire managers (FMs) receive, interpret, and act on forecast information. However, little is known about the national FM population, including how they translate this forecast information into operational decisions. The Fire Management Survey (FM Survey) aims to fill this knowledge gap by building a nationwide panel of wildfire management professionals working at local, state, regional, and federal levels. The FM Survey will field routine surveys focused on interagency coordination under the current fire alerting system and the preferences for the design and implementation of a new, unified fire warning system. The panel was built by creating a database with contact information from FMs across the country, and distributing an initial recruitment survey that explains the purpose of the project, requests informed consent, and collects baseline information aligned with the survey’s primary goals. This presentation will share preliminary results from the panel development and recruitment survey, and discuss plans for future FM Survey waves.

488082.title: Utilizing Planetary Boundary Layer Height Data from Multiple Observing Systems in the NASA GEOS SystemUtilizing Planetary Boundary Layer Height Data from Multiple Observing Systems in the NASA GEOS System
488082.authors: Eun-Gyeong Yang, GMAO, Greenbelt, MD; University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; and Y. Zhu, N. Arnold, M. Ganeshan, P. Selmer, E. McGrath-Spangler, J. R. Lewis, V. Buchard, H. Salmun, S. P. Palm, D. L. Wu, J. E. Yorks, I. Adams, N. Roldan-Henao, and A. Cresanti
488082.abstract: The Planetary Boundary Layer (PBL), which mediates energy and moisture exchanges between the Earth’s surface and atmosphere, remains challenging to accurately simulate and observe. In this study, a strategic framework is developed to build a global Planetary Boundary Layer Height (PBLH) analysis and monitoring capability in the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) data assimilation (DA) system, leveraging multiple observing systems including radiosonde, GNSS-RO, spaceborne lidars (CALIPSO, CATS, ICESat-2), ground-based lidar (NASA MPLNET), and ground-based radar wind profilers. As PBLH data can be sensitive to potentially disparate observables and retrieval algorithms, new model PBLH definitions consistent with each observation type are added to the forecast model for the calculation of first guess departures from observations (OmF). Moreover, to better capture capping inversions, a novel method is developed to improve background error covariance using PBLH data, benefiting PBL thermodynamic analysis. In addition, a comprehensive assessment of PBLH data from multiple observing systems is performed using either consistent or inconsistent PBLH definitions in the GEOS. The results underscore the importance of using physically and instrumentally consistent model PBLH definitions and robust quality control and thinning procedures tailored to each observation type. Notable discrepancies among lidar-based PBLH datasets, particularly over the ocean, highlight the need for corresponding lidar-based model definitions and advanced retrieval algorithms. The developed framework enables a robust evaluation of current and future PBLH datasets and serves as a foundation for an effective assimilation strategy. Furthermore, the study develops the advanced data assimilation techniques tailored to PBL and investigates observation impacts on PBL thermodynamic structure.

488088.title: Utilizing Emerging Technologies to Advance Scientific Understanding and the Predictability of High Impact Weather
488088.authors: Joseph J Cione, PhD, AOML, Miami, FL; and J. B. Wadler, J. A. Zhang, A. Hollingshead, N. Pawlenko, M. DeMaria, and A. Brammer
488088.abstract: Over the past 60 years, routine analyses of pressure, temperature, moisture, and wind near the hurricane surface and at very high altitudes have been rare. Safety concerns and other logistical and platform viability constraints have made in-situ data collection within these diverse regions of the Tropical Cyclone (TC) prohibitive. In addition to state variables, accurate assessments of momentum, heat, and mass exchanges within these critical regions of the storm are needed in order to consistently predict changes in TC structure, intensity and track. This presentation will discuss the development and use of various uncrewed observing systems and other advanced technologies used in recent years (and under development) that have pushed/will push the limits of our understanding within difficult to observe regions of TCs. Outcomes and lessons learned from these past and present concepts of operations along with ongoing and future development of promising technologies designed to advance our understanding and ability to better predict these dynamic and dangerous systems will be presented.

488089.title: A Systematic Evaluation of the MRMS v12.3 Operational QPEs
488089.authors: Jian Zhang, NOAA/OAR/NSSL, Norman, OK; and R. A. Clark III, L. Tang, S. Cocks, S. Martinaitis, A. P. Osborne, A. Arthur, and C. Langston
