488089.abstract: The Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system, developed by the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) and the Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), represents a sophisticated integration of the WSR-88D and Canadian weather radar networks with diverse environmental data sources, including automated surface stations, satellites and numerical weather prediction model data. As an essential operational tool for the National Weather Service (NWS) since October 2014, MRMS facilitates hazardous weather situational awareness by generating high-resolution (1-km), rapid update (2-min) and low-latency (< 2-min) gridded 3D and 2D products. Among these products are a suite of high-accuracy quantitative precipitation estimations (QPEs), which are vital for flash flood warnings, drought monitoring and water resource management. The operational MRMS system was updated to version 12.3 on August 5, 2025, which included several enhancements to the QPE products. This study provides a comprehensive performance assessment of the updated products, including one radar-based and two multi-sensor QPEs, over the subsequent one-year period. The analysis is systematically structured around different seasons, geographical areas, rainfall intensities, and the quality of radar network coverage. Detailed findings from this evaluation, along with perspectives on future research developments, will be presented at the conference.

488101.title: NCAR's High Altitude Observatory: From Wartime Innovation to the Future of Space Weather Prediction
488101.authors: Thomas E. Berger, NCAR, Boulder, CO
488101.abstract: Walter Orr Roberts installed North America's first solar coronagraph at the Climax Molybdenum Mine near Leadville, Colorado in 1940. By 1941, his then-secret observations of solar eruptions for the U.S. Army Air Force demonstrated a critical link between coronal activity and radio disruption—enabling advance warning to operators in the European and Pacific Theaters. This pioneering work established a foundational principle: observing the solar corona is essential to understanding and predicting solar eruptions. In 1946, the Climax program evolved into the High Altitude Observatory, a joint University of Colorado–Harvard enterprise that became NCAR's leading center for space weather research. In 1965, HAO relocated its coronagraph operations to the NOAA Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii, where it remains one of the few near-real-time coronagraph operations. HAO is a world leader in coronagraph design, spectropolarimetry, and magnetic field remote sensing—the techniques key to measuring magnetic fields in the solar atmosphere, holding the promise of finally revealing the triggers of solar eruptions. HAO continues innovating through advanced filter designs, computational inversion methods, and now the Coronal Solar Magnetism Observatory (COSMO)—the world's largest coronagraph upon completion. COSMO will deliver unprecedented observations of the full coronal magnetic field, enabling key research into the prediction of Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs)—the primary drivers of severe space weather. This effort will be complemented by CORONET, a global network of smaller coronagraphs providing 24/7 real-time CME observations to operational forecasting centers, enabling timely warnings of solar energetic particles and geomagnetic storms. From wartime necessity to operational forecasting, HAO exemplifies how sustained scientific leadership transforms basic research into societal benefit.

488104.title: Commercial GNSS-RO and GNSS-R Data at Spire: Operational Status and Emerging Capabilities
488104.authors: Vu Nguyen, Spire Global, Arvada, CO; and P. Jales, M. Talpe, J. C. Cartwright, G. Savastano, and S. Vetra-Carvalho
488104.abstract: Spire Global operates one of the world's largest commercial GNSS radio occultation (RO) constellations, delivering profiles in near-real-time to NOAA and EUMETSAT under operational agreements since 2020, with demonstrated positive impact on global forecast skill. Dual-frequency GNSS measurements from the same constellation also support space weather applications, with total electron content (TEC) products operationally ready and scintillation products advancing toward a future evaluation pilot. Building on this operational foundation, Spire is advancing several capabilities toward government evaluation. Newly deployed polarimetric RO (PRO) payloads measure horizontal and vertical polarization signals; differential phase shifts between them correlate well with precipitation events (validated against IMERG), and the reconstructed RHCP bending angle profiles are suitable for direct NWP assimilation. These PRO data have recently been evaluated by ESA EDAP, but not yet by NOAA, and Spire is ready to support such an evaluation. Separately, two GNSS-R satellites generate delay-Doppler maps for soil moisture and ocean wind speed (OSW) retrievals. The first NOAA Data Pilot (2023–2024) established a positive impact of the Spire OSW product in JEDI assimilation, and data delivered under Ocean Surface Winds Data Pilot Round 2 is being evaluated for future operational use. Grazing-angle GNSS reflections from the RO constellation additionally support surface characterization (such as inland water body delineation and sea ice characterization) and altimetry, both areas of active interest for agency evaluation. Looking ahead, satellites launched in 2026 into 14:00 and 17:00 LTAN orbital planes diversify coverage and improve temporal sampling, a key lever for maximizing RO impact in data assimilation. Spire is also positioned to help address the low-latitude RO coverage gap left by the loss of COSMIC-2, and seeks to work with government partners on launching additional lower-inclination satellites to fill this gap. This talk will summarize Spire's current operational status, share lessons from operational integration with NOAA and EUMETSAT, and outline capabilities ready for government evaluation, including PRO and low-latitude coverage sustainment beyond COSMIC-2.

488105.title: Organization and Evolution of Boundary-Layer Energy During Tropical Cyclone Intensification
488105.authors: Jun A. Zhang, NOAA / AOML / HRD, Miami, FL; and P. Zhu, Y. Dai, and X. Zhang
488105.abstract: The tropical cyclone boundary layer serves as the primary energy reservoir supporting storm intensification, yet how this energy is organized and evolves remains poorly understood. This study investigates the three-dimensional evolution of boundary-layer energy during tropical cyclone intensification using high-resolution Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) simulations. Boundary-layer moist static energy is used as a diagnostic of the energy reservoir to characterize its spatial organization and temporal evolution and to examine its relationship to storm structure, environmental vertical wind shear, and tropical cyclone intensity change. This presentation introduces an energy-based perspective for understanding tropical cyclone boundary-layer evolution and discusses its implications for air–sea interaction, storm intensification, and the development of physically based diagnostics for next-generation hurricane forecast systems.

488108.title: Evaluating The Role of Agricultural Biophysical Function in the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
488108.authors: James F Cross, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and D. Drewry
488108.abstract: Understanding land-atmosphere coupling in agricultural landscapes is critical for improving predictions of regional climate and boundary-layer dynamics. Although biophysical processes strongly influence surface energy partitioning, current land surface models employed to study land-atmosphere coupling often lack the fidelity to accurately represent differing crop species, limiting understanding of how agricultural landscapes interact with and influence the ABL. Agricultural systems present unique challenges due to rapid changes in canopy structure and phenology, which alter albedo, roughness, and evapotranspiration rates throughout the growing season, while multi-crop landscapes add further challenges associated with spatial heterogeneity. To address these complexities, we employ large-eddy simulations (LES) using the PArallellized Large eddy siMulation (PALM) model system. Eddy-covariance towers at Iowa State University’s Sustainable Advanced Bioeconomy Research (SABR) farm provide energy flux and environmental observations over four unique agricultural systems under identical climatic conditions, including both annual and perennial systems. Here we use these observations to drive the development of physics‑constrained machine-learning emulators for three of these agricultural systems (corn, soybean, and miscanthus) designed to reproduce surface energy fluxes under early‑season conditions based on crop phenology and surface climate. Initial simulations reveal that biophysical differences between annual and perennial crops produce a prolonged period of differential surface heating early in the season when evaluated at daily scales. As canopies mature, contrasts in ABL development become more muted but persist. Ongoing work extends this framework to assess how cumulative effects from varying planting configurations shape surface microclimate and boundary‑layer evolution across the early growing season. These efforts aim to integrate crop‑specific biophysical behavior into a coherent modeling framework, ultimately advancing a more holistic understanding of how planting decisions shape land-atmosphere feedback across agricultural landscapes.

488110.title: Numerical Investigation of Fog Mitigation through Salt Injection
488110.authors: Erika Roesler, Sandia National Laboratories, ALBUQUERQUE, NM
488110.abstract: Fog can impact critical infrastructure, such as roadways and airports, and increase the potential for travel delays and risks to life and property. For nearly 80 years these challenges have motivating research investigating salt aerosol dispersal as a means to improve visibility during fog conditions. In this study, we report the prevalence of fog in one narrow valley in Elmira, New York in 1968 where NASA conducted 31 fog seeding experiments at the Chemung County Airport. This campaign included experimentation with the two fog dispersal mechanisms: 25 ground-based and 6 aerial seeding events. Here, we present the results of Large Eddy Simulations (LES) that aim to mimic the 1968 experiments. The LES is evaluated by comparing model results of unmodified and mitigated fog against observations made during the 1968 campaign. The LES performance is further parametrically tested with a variety of microphysical routines to determine how numerical simulations can be used to understand fog dispersal under these conditions without the large-scale outdoor test environment. A new warm microphysical box model is also presented and compared to the LES and historical experiments. Simulations are also compared to the reanalysis data from ERA5. These results are presented with information about fog prevalence the region today and how might this information can be used to derisk airport and aviation activity. SNL is managed and operated by NTESS under DOE NNSA contract DE-NA0003525. SAND2026-24829A

488112.title: Machine Learning Emulators for Ensemble Data Assimilation: A Lorenz-63 Case Study
488112.authors: Jorge Velasco Zavala, Florida State Univeristy, Tallahassee, FL; and O. Zavala-Romero, H. G. Chipilski, M. Nikolaitchik, and J. Poterjoy
488112.abstract: We studied the performance of different machine learning (ML) emulators of the Lorenz-63 system in the context of ensemble data assimilation (DA): dense, LSTM, and recurrent neural networks, each evaluated in a plain and a residual variant. Our goal is to determine whether standalone surrogate quality — how faithfully an emulator reproduces a chaotic system's dynamics — actually predicts how well that emulator performs once embedded in a DA workflow. We first assess each emulator as a surrogate in isolation, comparing energy distance, k-step RMSE, Lyapunov exponents, and invariant distributions, and their Tangent Linear Model (TLM) approximation against the true system. All emulators reproduce Lyapunov spectra close to the true L63 system. However, energy distance and k-step RMSE expose clear architectural differences: recurrent architectures outperform non-recurrent ones, residual connections improve performance across the board, and giving non-recurrent architectures a short window of past time steps as input sequences closes most of the gap with the recurrent models. We then embed each emulator as the forward model in a Deterministic Ensemble Kalman Filter (DEnKF) and compare the resulting posteriors, via energy distance (ED), against a Particle Filter (PF) posterior computed with the true Lorenz-63 dynamics as a proxy for the true state. Despite the substantial architectural differences seen in the standalone surrogate tests, all emulators perform similarly in the DA cycle archiving a similar ED to the PF posterior and RMSE to the ground truth.

488116.title: JPSS-4 and QuickSounder Product Operations Plan
488116.authors: Shuang Qiu, NESDIS, College Park, MD; NESDIS, College Park, MD
488116.abstract: The Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) continues to modernize its polar-orbiting satellite constellation with the transition of the JPSS-4 satellite, renamed NOAA-22 post-launch in Fall 2027. This Product Operations Plan outlines the comprehensive strategy for processing and distributing NOAA-22 data products during the critical Launch, Early Orbit & Activation (LEO&A) phase and subsequent nominal operations. Key objectives include maintaining data continuity for critical Key Performance Parameter (KPP) products, managing the JPSS constellation configuration (including NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and NOAA-22), and ensuring readiness among operational users such as the National Weather Service (NWS) and international partners. The Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) Program, a critical component of NOAA’s National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS), is scheduled to launch its inaugural QuickSounder mission in Spring 2027. QuickSounder serves as a pathfinder mission to support essential weather forecasting, disaster management, and climate monitoring. This presentation outlines the comprehensive Product Operations Plan designed to manage QuickSounder’s end-to-end data lifecycle, from LEO&A through nominal operations. This plan provides a framework for sustaining reliable, near-real-time global observations while establishing a roadmap for future NEON-series satellite operations.

488117.title: Modeling Historic and Future Compound Flood Inundation on the Kennebec River Using Pattern-Specific Climate Signals
488117.authors: Lindsay Lawrence, Northeastern University, Swampscott, MA
488117.abstract: Riverine flooding in New England is costly and difficult to predict, and its impacts are ultimately felt at the local scale. Connecting large-scale climate change to flooding in a single community, however, remains a challenge. This study bridges that gap for the Kennebec River at Gardiner, Maine, a flood-vulnerable waterfront community. Prior work used self-organizing maps (SOMs) to identify several distinct synoptic and land surface patterns tied to New England riverine peak flow events. Continued work also quantified how these patterns evolve in the Community Earth System Model (CESM) V2 Large Ensemble (LENS2). Here, those results are used to build percent-change rasters collectively and for each SOM pattern. The rasters perturb high-resolution meteorological forcing variables to represent how each flood-generating setup evolves in the near, mid, and far future. The perturbed forcing drives a two-step HEC-RAS model. A one-dimensional model first estimates discharge from widely available river-stage records, and a two-dimensional model then simulates inundation depth and extent. HEC-FIA is used to convert the modeled flooding into structure-level damage estimates. Comparing historic events to future scenarios reveals how flood inundation and expected damage may change over time. The goal is to preserve the distinct character of each flood mechanism and deliver physically grounded projections that support flood mitigation and adaptation planning in New England.

488118.title: Impact of Vertical Localization in JEDI-SOCA LETKF for Regional High-Resolution Ocean Data Assimilation
488118.authors: Pubali Mukherjee, Mercator Ocean International, Toulouse, France; and H. S. Kim, H. kang, and G. Foltz
488118.abstract: Covariance localization is critical in ensemble-based ocean data assimilation (DA) to eliminate spurious long-range correlations arising from limited ensemble sizes. Although horizontal localization is commonly implemented in operations, vertical localization remains underutilized despite sharp vertical gradients and stratification in the ocean. To address this, the present study utilizes the Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (LETKF) within the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration – Sea ice and Ocean Data Assimilation (JEDI-SOCA) system to assess how vertical localization affects analysis quality in a high-resolution, 1/12-degree eddy-resolving MOM6 regional setup. The experimental framework employed a 24-hour cycling window for September 2022, incorporating 20-member GEFS atmospheric forcing perturbations, covariance inflation of 0.5 for both the Relaxatio-to-Prior Spread (RTPS) and Relaxation-to-Prior Perturbations (RTPP), alongside a depth-based Gaspari-Cohn vertical localization function instead of traditional layer-based approaches. Two 24-hour cycling experiments were performed, both assimilating thinned sea surface salinity (SSS), absolute dynamic topography (ADT), sea surface temperature (SST), and in-situ T/S profiles. These experiments differed only in the vertical localization using an 18 model-level length scale. The results indicate that incorporating vertical localization markedly enhances forecast performance and successfully constrains the upper-layer stratification and subsurface salinity maxima. Hence, these outcomes validate the ongoing development of vertical localization techniques within JEDI-SOCA to support high-resolution ocean analysis.

488119.title: Snoqualmie Drought Resilience: An Indigenous Perspective on Drought From the Pacific Northwest
488119.authors: Matt Baerwalde, Snoqualmie Tribe, Snoqualmie, WA
488119.abstract: In 2024, the Snoqualmie Tribe initiated the Snoqualmie DROUT (Drought Resilience for Our Tribe) Project with support from a NOAA NIDIS grant along with a Washington State Department of Ecology drought planning grant. The project centers Snoqualmie Indigenous Knowledge (IK) and is intended to convene and collaborate with the basin’s key water users and managers, identify current and future drought impacts on the ecological function of the Snoqualmie River basin and the Tribe’s water supply, and identify mitigation opportunities with potential to offset some of the effects of droughts. This talk will give an overview of Indigenous Knowledge and its importance to applied scientific investigations and assessments, and it will describe how IK was sourced and applied in the Snoqualmie DROUT Project. With IK as a guiding framework, the Snoqualmie Valley in Washington State will be described along with the Tribe’s approach to drought resiliency: convening and collaborating with other locals to understand current and future water needs, fostering the concept of reciprocity when making environmental management decisions, and our DROUT Project results, which include comparisons of consumptive use impacts of various sectors with the impacts from snow drought, along with comparisons of potential mitigation options such as aquifer storage and recovery (ASR), managed aquifer recharge (MAR), floodplain reconnection, and headwater storage. These comparisons can now be used by the Snoqualmie Tribe and partners to prioritize further feasibility and implementation efforts.

488126.title: The Value of Weather Information and Emergency Decision Support at the University of North Carolina - Asheville
488126.authors: Lexi Dooley, University of Miami, Coral Gables, FL; University of North Carolina Asheville, Asheville, NC, Asheville, NC; NOAA, Asheville, NC; and L. Cox
488126.abstract: This presentation emphasizes the importance of forecasting in college athletics and the pathway to revising emergency procedures for severe weather events on campus, with a focus on lightning. Through an unusual collaboration among NCEI, NCICS, NEMAC, NCSU, and UNCA, research was conducted at the intersection of atmospheric science education and collegiate outdoor sporting events. Decision-making authorities in companies and organizations have become more aware of the benefits of weather forecasting over the past 10 years. As meteorology has become more accurate and instrumentation has improved, forecasts can prevent significant human impacts and financial losses for outdoor events. Additionally, the recent increase in the availability of weather information through non-standardized mobile applications and other public forecast sources has led many institutions to rely on unverified, generalized forecasts without appropriate meteorological interpretation, potentially weakening weather-related safety protocols. The University of North Carolina Asheville is a small Division I university with an on-campus Department of Atmospheric Sciences (ATMS). In conjunction with the ATMS department, the Athletics Forecasting Program (AFP) was created to help the Department of Athletics prepare for severe weather that could affect outdoor sporting events and to help athletics staff become more weather-aware. According to an economic analysis of potential postponements and cancellations, $20,000 per year can be saved across game day operations, staffing, and revenue. During research on forecasting and athletics at the university, the weather safety and preparedness protocol was also examined. Neighboring institutions' procedures were used as examples of how the university can improve its weather preparedness on campus, across athletics, and throughout the entire school. This scalable and replicable approach can lead to lasting improvements in university emergency management standard operating procedures. This presentation will tell the story of how AFP was created and how it led to a university-wide stakeholder engagement to implement improved emergency procedures on campus.

488137.title: Learning Forced Spectral Change in Storm Tracks from Heterogeneous Climate Sources with Unequal Replication
488137.authors: David M. Straus, Center for Ocean-Land-Atmosphere Studies, Fairfax, VA; George Mason University, Fairfax, VA; and S. A. Bruce and P. Bagchi
488137.abstract: Extra-tropical storm tracks organize much of the day-to-day weather of the mid-latitudes, particularly during the cold season. They also transport heat and momentum towards the poles and thus strongly influence the general circulation of the atmosphere. Although individual atmospheric disturbances (storms) have time scales of two to ten days, the configuration and strength of their tracks show significant variability on a very wide range of time scales, from intra-seasonal to inter-annual to inter-decadal and longer. The storm track variability within a season is due to the fundamental non-linear dynamics of the atmosphere and the transient response to short-term changes in tropical heating. Large inter-annual variations of the storm tracks are known to occur in association with the SST anomalies of the El-Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO). On time scales of more than ten years, the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and the Atlantic Multi-Decadal Oscillation (PDO and AMO respectively) of the mid-latitude oceanic SSTs influence the configuration and strength of the storm tracks. Underlying the longer time scale storm track variability is the non-stationary evolution of the entire climate system due to changes in the composition of the atmosphere, primarily carbon dioxide and aerosols. Understanding this latter variability is the subject of this research. We seek to better understand the signature of the external forcing of the climate system on the strength, position, and seasonal cycle of the storm tracks, extracting this signal from the internal variations due to the atmosphere and ocean with which it is highly entangled. Our data sources are the large (100 member) LENS2 ensemble of climate model simulations as well as Reanalyses. The LENS2 large ensemble of NCAR utilizes the CESM2 climate model, with simulations run from 1880 to 2015 utilizing observed atmospheric composition and solar forcing. We utilize two Reanalysis data sets, termed ERA5 and JRA-3Q, that run from 1950-2024. We approach this problem through the joint second-order structure of three sets of coupled two-dimensional fields, each resolved by frequency, by time within the cold season, and by year. Focus on frequencies corresponding to 1-10 day cycles isolates propagating mid-latitude cyclones and anti-cyclones. Each set of coupled fields co-vary in a systematic manner due to the structure of mid-latitude storms. The lower-tropospheric temperature (moisture) and meridional wind couple to transport heat (moisture) poleward. The upper-tropospheric zonal and meridional wind covariance transport momentum. For each pair, both the individual spectra and the complex co-spectra are utilized. The fundamental statistical difficulty is that our best estimate of the past history of the atmospheric circulation (given by Reanalyis), being a single realization, combines forced signals and internal variability. Atmospheric model simulations, on the other hand, provide multiple realizations of the history of this circulation, from which in principle the forced and internal components may be separated. An ensemble provides many model realizations under a shared forcing history, subject to structural model discrepancy. Replication reduces stochastic uncertainty within a source. It does not remove systematic discrepancy between sources. We use ensemble replication to characterize internal variability and the model-implied forced response. We use reanalysis to anchor conclusions to the realized climate. Results include: An uncertainty-quantified evolutionary cross-spectral product of each pair of coupled variables, for ERA5, JRA-3Q, and LENS2, resolved by synoptic frequency, within-winter time, and location. A discrepancy-aware estimate of each model-implied forced coupled field spectral trajectory, split into its mean-mediated ENSO part and its residual. Model-fidelity diagnostics: maps of the climatology and ENSO-teleconnection discrepancy, flagging where the ensemble misrepresents observed structure. An envelope-bounded assessment of forced storm-track displacement, with Pacific and Atlantic intensity and latitudinal displacement, as well as longitudinal shift and width. A test of the Pacific mid-winter minimum, and of whether its depth and timing change under forcing and with ENSO phase. A statement of whether observed changes exceed internal variability under historical forcing, robust to bounded model discrepancy up to a stated magnitude, phrased as separation of forced and internal components rather than formal detection and attribution. An assessment of whether changes are broadband amplitude changes or frequency-selective redistributions, including shifts in the dominant eddy timescale where the spectral peak is identifiable.

488152.title: Ice Nucleation Pathways in Fresh pyroCumulonimbus Smoke: Preliminary Lidar Retrievals from the 2026 NASA INSPYRE Campaign
488152.authors: Sabrina Maria Vlk, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA
488152.abstract: Pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) storms are extreme wildfire-induced convective events capable of injecting smoke directly into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). Once in the UTLS, injected smoke can influence the formation of persistent, radiatively significant cirrus anvils that exhibit unique behavior compared to typical cirrus clouds, including extended lifetimes and anomalous radiative forcing. Studying the microphysical pathway that produces these anvils is therefore integral to understanding their climate impact. Two competing ice-formation mechanisms are possible: heterogeneous nucleation, in which smoke particles act directly as ice-nucleating particles (INPs) at relatively low ice supersaturation, and homogeneous freezing, in which ice forms from aqueous solution droplets at a higher ice supersaturation threshold. Which pathway dominates has direct consequences for ice crystal number concentration (ICNC), size distribution, optical depth, and ultimately the persistence of the anvil and its radiative forcing. Existing observational and modeling work has focused almost exclusively on aged, transported smoke sampled days to months after injection, typically using ground-based lidar remote sensing. However, fresh smoke that is sampled within the first few hours after a pyroCb event is known to differ substantially from aged smoke in terms of composition, mixing state, and by extension in ice nucleating efficiency. In situ measurements of fresh smoke from the 2019 Williams Flats Fire, for example, show black carbon to organic carbon ratios distinct from those measured in aged pyroCb plumes, suggesting that conclusions drawn from aged smoke studies may not transfer directly to fresh smoke. The question motivating this study then becomes: in the hours immediately following a pyroCb injection event, which ice nucleation pathway controls ice crystal formation in the anvil, and how does that pathway shape the anvil's microphysical properties, persistence, and immediate radiative impact? We address this question using data from the NASA INSPYRE campaign, which deployed the ER-2 and NSF/NCAR GV aircraft. Preliminary results will be shown from applying an existing lidar-based aerosol retrieval framework, which had previously only been developed and validated for aged, transported smoke, to CPL curtains from fresh smoke ER-2 overflights collected during the 2026 INSPYRE deployment period. Retrieved vertical profiles of smoke mass, surface area, and number concentration within hours of injection will be presented, along with resulting estimates of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and INP concentration in the context of the fresh smoke microphysical environment. This retrieval, together with coincident in situ aerosol and microphysical measurements from the GV, will provide the foundation for a planned follow up analysis in which fresh smoke INP retrievals drive an established heterogeneous versus homogeneous nucleation competition framework, directly testing which pathway controls ice formation in early pyroCb anvils. Prior applications of this framework have relied solely on simulation or ground-based remote sensing paired with aged smoke. By identifying which nucleation pathway dominates in fresh pyroCb smoke and directly contrasting these results with established aged smoke behavior, this study will help resolve a key point of uncertainty in how quickly and by what mechanism pyroCb anvils evolve. Additionally, this will provide observational grounding for how nucleation pathways relate to anvil persistence and radiative forcing.

488156.title: Network Control Facility - AWIPS Support & Collaboration
488156.authors: Robert Lehmann, RTX, College Park, MD
488156.abstract: Network Control Facility The Network Control Facility (NCF) serves as the central operational backbone and technical support for the National Weather Service IT infrastructure. Managed under the NWS Office of Central Processing (OCP), the NCF provides 24/7/365 system monitoring, central communications management, and technical support across more than 130 NWS operational sites. This includes Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs), River Forecast Centers (RFCs), National Centers (NCs), and Central Weather Service Units (CWSUs). Remedy to Redmine Transition The NCF’s migration from BMC Remedy to Redmine has recently been completed. This transition allows for an improved agile project tracking and better integration of NCF workflows with cross-team activities. Operational Cadence (12-Hour Shift Structure) The NCF maintains a 24/7/365 operational model through a structured 12-hour shift system. Day shifts run from 6:30 AM to 6:30 PM, and night shifts run from 6:30 PM to 6:30 AM. The team utilizes a 4-on/4-off rotational schedule to ensure sustained coverage and high team performance. Incident Escalation Procedures Front-Line Operations serves as the primary Tier 1 defense, handling initial troubleshooting and ticket creation. Issues that require specialized technical analysis are formally escalated to Tier 2 support, including Systems Integration and Support (SI&S) or Application Software Maintenance (ASM) teams. This pathway ensures clear communication, accountability, and adherence to resolution timelines.

488157.title: Withdrawn: In-Line Adaptive NWP Postprocessing: Cutting out the Manual Training Time-Sink
488157.authors: Paul J. Roebber, CIRA, Whitefish Bay, WI; and M. S. Antolik
488157.abstract: Operational weather forecast services have used numerical weather prediction (NWP) model statistical postprocessors such as Model Output Statistics (MOS) to improve predictions for decades. When numerical models are updated, however, the time and effort required to collect and retrain postprocessor equations with the newer model data can lead to delays in their implementation. For example, the Global Forecast System (GFS) was upgraded from versions 14 through 16 between 2019 and 2021 yet no updates to the MOS equations occurred during that time. In this talk, we show that an adaptive postprocessor, based on a multilayer perceptron neural network consisting of 16 input variables chosen for physical relevance, a single hidden layer with 48 nodes, and 4 output nodes, can produce solutions competitive with the then latest generation of MOS for 2-meter temperature and dewpoint and 10-meter wind speed. These results are obtained for a range of station locations in the CONUS and Alaska, which together demonstrate the applicability of the technique to substantially different climatological and geographical conditions. The period of study is 1 February 2015 through 30 September 2023, where three successive years of 91-day moving windows are used for training and validation and the next independent time step beyond this time is used for prediction. The fitness function is based on an evenly weighted mean squared error (MSE), where the error for each of the outputs is measured relative to the GFS MSE for that variable on the same sample. Stochastic gradient descent is used, with early stopping and node dropout to prevent overfitting. A learning rate schedule is applied that begins at 0.075 and decreases linearly to 0.005 over 30 epochs and oscillates between 0.005 and 0.0005 thereafter. Cases that exhibit larger error with respect to the raw GFS are repeated in the next sample. The network provides predictions out to 240 hours, but the system is trained without reference to lead time so that the same network will produce a prediction for all variables for any lead time, thus avoiding “windshield-wiper” effects. Only the first 72 hours of GFS forecast values are used as inputs in the training. A single set of predictions for all available lead times and variables runs in a median time of 12.9 seconds on a MacBook Pro with an Apple M1 chip. It is notable that the MOS equations, despite no updates during the test period in which the GFS model underwent substantial changes, did not exhibit degradation. The relative advantage of the adaptive system, then, is that if it is implemented, no further changes are required, regardless of model updates or retirements, or site selections, or additional model inputs.

488159.title: 'Investigating Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences (SBES) Data Documentation Gaps and Surfacing User Needs Through Data Review and Pilot Implementation of SBES Metadata Schema'
488159.authors: Anna Long, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and K. R. Metta
488159.abstract: Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences (SBES) extreme weather research investigates how people perceive and respond to significant events, forecasts, and warnings. This field of research is valuable for directing weather and risk communication strategy to optimize protection of life and property. Presently, SBES data discoverability and reusability is hampered, creating redundancy and inefficiency in research progress as dataset linkages cannot be as effectively established. Documentation inconsistencies are thought to complicate data reuse in this research domain. In an attempt to ground the SBES data documentation process, the Social Science Program (SSP) team in NOAA’s Weather Program Office (WPO) has developed a metadata schema as part of their Societal Data Insights Initiative. The Integrated Societal-data Platform for Interdisciplinary Research and Evaluation (InSPIRE) schema was designed for the SBES community based on best practices in data documentation. The current project focused on a data review and pilot implementation of the InSPIRE schema. The InSPIRE schema’s coverage and capability was tested on SBES datasets uploaded to a generalist and a specialty repository, allowing for the comparison of different schema structures and requirements. A small set of exploratory interviews and hands-on testing of repository upload workflows informed understanding of the documentation experience and surfaced early feedback on the InSPIRE schema. The data review revealed moderate overlap in the InSPIRE schema and existing schemas’ capabilities as well as an overall underutilization of SBES-specific metadata fields. Initial takeaways from the pilot implementation and user experience exploration suggest that schema advertisement/accessibility and less intuitive documentation workflows may offer some justification for inconsistent usage of specialty schemas/fields. This work developed greater context for data documentation gaps in SBES research and provided useful insights to refine the InSPIRE schema. These preliminary findings reaffirm the value in a documentation tool with streamlined, flexible, and technically clear procedures. Additionally, providing active and continual support to users throughout the InSPIRE schema’s onboarding process is integral to its bandwidth and success in standardizing SBES data documentation and advancing data connectivity and research progress.

488162.title: Building a Layered Live Fuels Index for Large Wildfire Occurrence
488162.authors: Jayden G Vogler, Cornell University, Rochester, NY; and R. Barnes, N. J. Nauslar, M. S. Elliott, and A. D. Werkema
488162.abstract: Storm Prediction Center forecasters use several fire danger indices, including Energy Release Component (ERC) and Spread Component (SC) percentiles, to evaluate fuel receptiveness to burning in conjunction with fire intensity and spread. This project develops a new index that considers live fuel characteristics, particularly in the grass and shrub rangelands of the western CONUS. Python scripts amalgamated seven annual raster fuel and fire environment layers, upscaled the data to a 2.5 km NDFD spatial resolution, then applied fire risk thresholds developed by Dr. Matthew Reeves. These layers were then summed as Boolean rasters into a meaningful index ranging from 0 to 7. The input layers include shrub, invasive grass, and standing dead percent coverage, Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) drought severity values, and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) peak greenness data. Live fuels contribute to fuel loading and become combustible as moisture content declines after peak greenup. Invasive grasses, such as cheatgrass, medusahead, and field brome, cure earlier than many native species and fill in bare spots in rangelands, creating continuous fine fuels that allow for faster fire spread. This index also includes wildfire history to account for previous fire occurrence and future burn potential. To verify the effectiveness of this index, observed non-prescribed fire perimeters from 2020 and 2026 were overlaid on their respective annual index maps. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Level II Ecoregions 9.3, 9.4, 10.1, 10.2, and 11.1 were then evaluated using Cliff’s Delta and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves to assess the index’s ability to distinguish burned from unburned pixels and assign higher risk levels to areas that burn. Positive effect sizes, high AUC values, and qualitative analyses support this index as a complementary operational tool for SPC forecasters and emergency managers.

488169.title: Automated Product and Tool Development at the New York State Weather Risk Communication Center
488169.authors: Alexander A. Jacques, University at Albany, SUNY, Albany, NY; and D. Van Hoesen, M. Michaud, A. Denaroso, and N. P. Bassill
488169.abstract: The New York State Weather Risk Communication Center (NYSWRCC) started in late 2023 as a partnership between the University at Albany and New York State to provide weather risk and impact information to state agencies, emergency managers, and other critical stakeholders. Today, the Center consists of operational meteorologists as well as specialist positions focused on social science, product research and development, and technical operations. Significant new technical development at NYSWRCC has taken place over the past year. The Center operates a redundant high-performance computing system that serves as the core hardware infrastructure. Routine Python ingest procedures collect numerous observational data resources, National Weather Service outlook and alert products, numerical weather prediction output, air quality information, and other available data to generate tailored products specific to New York State. These data resources are often merged with non-meteorological datasets (e.g., population GIS layers) and crafted specifically using criteria and thresholds provided by NYSWRCC stakeholders. The resultant products are made available for Center meteorologists to incorporate into briefings disseminated to NYSWRCC partners and on website displays for direct access with minimal latency. Developed interactive web tools allow partners to consume and explore relevant weather information in real time for situational awareness. This presentation will highlight the various methods used to develop this software and provide examples of internal and external products from major cold and warm season weather events across New York State over the previous year.

488171.title: Withdrawn: An Adaptive Postprocessor for a Deep Learning Fire Weather Version of the National Blend of Models
488171.authors: Paul J. Roebber, CIRA, Whitefish Bay, WI
488171.abstract: The overarching goal of this research is to devise and test an approach that will allow the Deep Learning based National Blend of Models (NBM) to seamlessly adapt to model changes over time, without the need to retrain the complex network. An important aspect of this is to reduce the dimensionality of the problem without sacrificing performance, since the NBM grid contains almost 4 million points for 100 forecast ranges (out to 264 hours), and the network will produce 100-member ensembles of 5 variables for each of those locations and times. In pursuit of this goal, FORTRAN code is developed that reads in gridded ensemble data and fits Weibull distributions (shape and scale) to wind speed and wind gust factor, von Mises distributions (mu and kappa) for wind direction, and mixed Normal distributions (mean, standard deviation, and mixing parameter) for temperature and dewpoint temperature. A series of subroutines perform the necessary maximum likelihood estimations and Nelder-Mead optimizations. Another subroutine uses the distribution parameters to create empirical ensembles (of user-selected size) for each of the 5 target variables. We use the original ensemble data to empirically estimate the 5-variable correlation structure. For the purpose of determining performance, another subroutine calculates deterministic and probabilistic error at each grid point using URMA values for verification and compares the results for the original ensemble and the generated ensemble. These tests show that the approach works, that is, that the generated ensembles perform as well as the original ensemble. This allows the development of a process that modifies the distribution parameters in an adaptive manner, based on day-to-day as well as long term performance measures. This approach involves a simple neural network design based on a single-hidden layer multilayer perceptron to adapt the distribution parameters. Further details will be provided at the meeting.

488172.title: PyroCAST (the PyroCumulonimbus Atmospheric aSsessment Tool) Based on Thermodynamic Profiles from NUCAPS
488172.authors: Lance Wilson, DeVine Consulting, Inc, Monterey, CA; and D. A. Peterson, T. M. McHardy, L. Porter, J. A. Otkin, S. Batzli, D. Parker, M. Pavolonis, L. Choos, R. B. Pierce, J. Sieglaff, C. Camacho, M. Surratt, and J. R. Campbell
488172.abstract: Results and updates are presented from the demonstration of a prototype pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) early-warning forecasting application. PyroCbs are a dangerous type of fire weather that produce immediate hazards to firefighters and aircraft, and longer-term impacts on the climate system due to high-altitude smoke injection. Forecasts of pyroCb events are driven by a machine learning algorithm that uses thermodynamic profiles from the NOAA Unique Combined Atmospheric Processing System (NUCAPS) to provide probabilistic guidance for pyroCb development near wildfires identified using Next Generation Fire System (NGFS) data, which currently uses GOES data as its primary input, and is available over the contiguous United States, Alaska, and western Canada. This algorithm fills an immediate community need as a “nowcasting tool” to identify the probability of pyroCb development over specific fire events with lead times of 0-12 hours, which is similar to guidance for conditions related to other types of rapidly-evolving severe convective weather (e.g., tornadoes, large hail, flash flooding, etc.). It can be used in all fire-prone regions worldwide, which is especially important for stakeholders in data sparse regions, such as portions of Alaska and Canada. All input data are currently processed using the Geolocated Information Processing System (GeoIPS®), which is the U.S. Navy’s modular, Python-based meteorological data processing software. A near real-time demonstration of this product was conducted throughout the 2026 Northern Hemisphere fire season in conjunction with the INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE). The product was made available as a layer within the RealEarth™ NGFS collection and as a data fusion image product on an NRL-hosted website.

488178.title: Very Short-Term Streamflow Modelling for Small Creeks and Streams In Missouri Using Radar Nowcasts and the National Water Model
488178.authors: Evan James Travis, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO; EWR Radar Sytems, Kirkwood, MO; and M. Templeton and N. I. Fox
488178.abstract: A method for improving NOAA’s National Water Model (NWM) for temporal scales on the order of ≤ 6 hours is presented. Presently, the short-range configuration of the operational NWM cycles hourly and uses meteorological forcing from the Rapid Refresh (RAP) and High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) numerical weather models to produce a deterministic, 18-h forecast. The deficiencies of numerical weather models and the superiority of extrapolating observations in the near term have been well studied. We demonstrate the advantages of a novel, “very short range”, rapidly cycling configuration of the NWM which replaces precipitation forcing from the RAP and HRRR with extrapolation nowcasts of instantaneous precipitation rate from the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor system (MRMS). We assert that such a configuration has utility in predicting streamflow for small catchments that are prone to flash flooding. Additionally, using the hydrological evaluation metrics relative volume error (RVE), relative peak error (RPE), peak timing error (PTE), and Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE), it is shown that simulated streamflow for these streams, which often lack stream gauges, largely do not see the same magnitudes of degradation in skill that arise from a lack of streamflow data assimilation compared to larger rivers—a well-known shortcoming of the NWM. We qualitatively assess hydrographs produced from the very short-range, nowcast configuration and the operational short-range NWM with respect to observations for certain flash flood events. It is shown, unsurprisingly, that errors in the MRMS extrapolation nowcasts propagate down to the hydrological simulations, but that the timing of the hydrographs’ rises can be well captured.

488180.title: Low-Frequency Covariability between North Pacific Sea Surface Temperatures and U.S. Hazardous Convective Weather Environments
488180.authors: Ivy Elizabeth Glade, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO
488180.abstract: Hazardous convective weather (HCW)—severe storms producing tornadoes, hail, or damaging winds—threatens life and property across the United States (U.S.) east of the Rocky Mountains. While intraseasonal and interannual variability, including the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), is known to influence U.S. HCW, the potential role of low-frequency climate variability remains uncertain. We identify an ENSO-independent, low-frequency mode of covariability between North Pacific sea surface temperatures (SSTs) and springtime U.S. HCW environments using maximum covariance analysis (MCA). The MCA-derived SST pattern is found to be associated with reduced HCW environmental favorability. The associated atmospheric circulation anomalies physically connect variability in North Pacific SSTs to HCW environmental conditions over the central and eastern U.S. through modification of moisture transport and vertical wind shear. Analysis of tornado and hail days shows a weaker but generally consistent relationship, suggesting the environmental signal extends to the observed storm report record. These results identify a potentially predictable source of low-frequency variability in U.S. HCW environments, with implications for seasonal-to-decadal prediction and the interpretation of long-term changes in HCW risk.

488185.title: A New Accurate and Generalizable ML Modal Aerosol Activation Parameterization
488185.authors: Andrew V. Geiss, PNNL, Richland, WA; and P. L. Ma
488185.abstract: We present a novel machine learning approach to parameterizing aerosol activation, the process by which atmospheric aerosols become hydrated and form cloud droplets, in Earth system models. The parameterization is designed for use with modal representations of aerosols with variable aerosol mode specification including size, hygroscopicity, and number of modes. We demonstrate how neural network attention mechanisms can be used to achieve a flexible parameterization that allows a single neural network to work alongside multiple aerosol model configurations. Offline testing demonstrates that our approach results in a more accurate parameterization than training bespoke feed-forward neural networks for each modal aerosol configuration, and that the ML model is capable of generalization to configurations that were not seen during training. The new ML model has been implemented online in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) with 4 aerosol modes and we demonstrate that the online performance mirrors the accuracy of the offline high-fidelity parcel model simulations the neural network was trained on.

488201.title: Assimilating Boundary Layer Depths Observed by WSR-88Ds to Improve the Prediction of a Derecho
488201.authors: Braedon Stouffer, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA; and D. J. Stensrud and Y. Zhang
488201.abstract: Recent work has shown that dual-polarization WSR-88D radars can be used to accurately estimate the height of the planetary boundary layer (PBLH). While assimilation of these observations is relatively novel, it has been shown to improve model representation of moisture in the lower troposphere which is a key component for severe thunderstorm prediction. We expand on this previous work by developing techniques to assimilate WSR-88D PBLH observations using the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) system. Forecasts are generated using a configuration of the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) that is similar to the Rapid Refresh Forecast System version 2 (RRFSv2) which is currently under development as part of NOAA’s Unified Forecast System. We choose the derecho that occurred in North Dakota on 20-21 June 2025 as a case study to evaluate the impacts of the data assimilation on the predicted evolution of the significant severe thunderstorm event. Results show that assimilating the radar-derived PBLH modifies the pre-convective environment such that it is more supportive of convective maintenance and organization. Skill scores using the Practically Perfect Hindcast are improved relative to the experiments without PBLH assimilation, especially when the assimilation of radar reflectivity is included. Differences in the environments that lead to improved forecasts will be examined and recommendations for further research and operational implementation will be provided.

488203.title: Convectively Coupled Equatorial Waves: George's Contributions from Discovery to Predictions
488203.abstract: Over the past four decades, tropical meteorology has evolved from using satellite observations to discover convectively coupled equatorial waves (CCEWs) to exploiting their predictability for extended forecasts of high-impact weather around the globe. George Kiladis has been at the center of this transformation, helping translate fundamental discoveries, from early observational studies to modern forecast systems that represent and predict CCEWs. In this talk, we will trace this scientific journey and reflect on the ingredients behind its success. We will highlight George's ingenuity, curiosity, and physical insight into tropical dynamics and moist convection, together with his ability to bridge observations, theory, numerical modeling, and forecasting. Through these efforts, George and his collaborators established tropical synoptic variability as a cornerstone of subseasonal prediction, demonstrating that accurately representing CCEWs is essential for skillful extended-range forecasts and their global impacts.

488206.title: Theoretical Understanding of Historical Declines In Land Surface Relative Humidity
488206.authors: Wenyu Zhou, PNNL, Richland, WA; and L. R. Leung, B. Harrop, Z. Chen, and C. C. Chang
488206.abstract: Understanding how land relative humidity (RH) has changed and how well earth system models reproduce those changes is critical, yet progress has been hindered by limited observational coverage, biases in global reanalyses, and the complex coupling within the land–atmosphere system. Here, we show that the spatiotemporal variability of land RH, as well as its distinct drying trends among observations, reanalyses, and models, can be theoretically understood from the ratio of precipitation (P) to a modified potential evapotranspiration PET^o (PETo). Unlike conventional PET, which explicitly depends on RH and therefore cannot be used to explain RH itself, PETo is formulated by prescribing a fixed high RH under the assumed well-watered conditions. This formulation, motivated by the asymptotic behavior of RH at high soil moisture, allows a simple representation of the soil-moisture feedback on RH and avoids the circular argument by using the conventional PET to understand RH. Over 1973–2024, land RH decreased substantially because the intrinsic increase in PET^oPETo with temperature—a direct consequence of the Clausius–Clapeyron relation—outpaced the modest increase in land precipitation. The ERA5 reanalysis overestimates the observed RH decline, consistent with its excessive surface warming and underestimated precipitation. The P-PETo framework reproduces these coherent biases and enables a physically based calibration of reanalysis RH using observed temperature and precipitation. Climate models simulate a wide range of historical land RH trends, yet nearly all runs underestimate the observed drying. The P-PETo framework successfully reproduces both the intermodel spread and the discrepancy between models and observations, attributing them to contributions from precipitation and PETo. The weaker historical drying simulated by earth system models primarily results from underestimated subtropical precipitation declines associated with insufficient intensification of subtropical highs and biases in subtropical climatology. Overall, the P-PETo framework provides a theoretical but quantitative framework for understanding land RH changes and a physical calibration of biased land RH in reanalyses. Zhou et al., PNAS 123(10), e2512645123. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2512645123.

488210.title: Verifying Satellite-Based Quantitative Precipitation Estimates Against Stage IV for Landfalling Tropical Cyclones in the Contiguous United States
488210.authors: Erica Bower, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and J. A. Nelson Jr.
488210.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) are known to produce extreme rainfall, which can lead to flooding and other hazards when near land areas. As TCs approach land, their rainfall distribution and structure can be monitored in real time using satellite-based quantitative precipitation estimates (QPE). However, these products have limitations in the representation of heavy rainfall, some of which are related to the collection of microwave data. This study assesses the performance of four satellite-based QPE products (CMORPH v1.0, CMORPH2, IMERG Final Run, and IMERG Late Run) in cases of landfalling TCs in the contiguous United States (CONUS) using the radar-based Stage IV QPE as ground truth. In general, the satellite products tend to perform better over the coastal ocean areas where minimal radar coverage is still available as opposed to over land areas. All four products fail to represent rainfall totals exceeding 10 inches per day over land areas despite greater detection of heavy rainfall over ocean areas. Of the four products studied, the CMORPH v1.0 and IMERG Late Run products typically had the highest skill at greater rainfall totals. The displacement of precipitation objects at various rainfall thresholds tended to be lower for these products compared to the CMORPH2 and IMERG Final Run products. Further research is required to determine the exact causes of these biases in the satellite QPE and ways to address these discrepancies in future iterations of the products.

488211.title: The Weather Prediction Center’s Urban Rain Rate Dashboard and Future Developments
488211.authors: Erica Bower, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and A. T. King, D. Bright, and J. A. Nelson Jr.
488211.abstract: The Urban Rain Rate Dashboard (URRD) is a tool produced at the NWS Weather Prediction Center (WPC) to offer guidance for city resource managers in determining the threat for flood-inducing heavy rainfall over the next 7 days. The dashboard compares quantitative precipitation forecasts (QPF) from numerical weather prediction ensembles to NOAA Atlas 14 Average Recurrence Intervals (ARIs). This identifies areas where rainfall may exceed various thresholds critical to urban environments. The probability of a 2-year ARI exceedance is displayed on the national map that greets users when they first visit the site. Users may then choose from the 101 cities included on the dashboard to find more specific information about their city. Clicking on the city of interest leads the user to a page that provides details about the timing, magnitude, and spatial distribution of potential rainfall scenarios for that particular urban area. The page includes short-term guidance at hourly temporal resolution and daily risk outlooks for days 4 through 7. Further development on the URRD has included many new features that will soon be publicly available. First, an “archive mode” will be released, allowing users to look back at the URRD from previous dates or events in their specific city. The exact dashboard that was available at the time will be displayed, with the addition of check marks indicating time frames when flood observations or proxies were found. Second, a “gridded mode” of the URRD will be made available. This will provide users with total location availability for the tool. A user can choose any location in the contiguous United States along with a radius for generating a circular “neighborhood” around the point of choice. The URRD information will then be displayed for the user’s custom location and neighborhood of interest. In addition to these new features, there have been several updates to the user interface, making it more user friendly and providing the users with more resources for the map tools. Finally, the URRD will integrate planned NOAA updates, including the transition from the High-Resolution Ensemble Forecast System to the RRFS Ensemble Forecast System and the incorporation of Atlas 15 ARIs for the contiguous United States upon the release of the dataset.

488212.title: An Energy System Relevant ACE2 Weather Ensemble for the Past and Future
488212.authors: Andrew V. Geiss, PNNL, Richland, WA; and M. Fernandez, C. Tebaldi, A. Gettelman, E. A. Barnes, S. Taraphdar, H. Tran, and P. L. Ma
488212.abstract: The FORESIGHT (Framework for Optimizing Reliable Energy Systems and Infrastructure Given High-uncertainty Trajectories) project has developed a 100-member global weather ensemble using the Ai2 Climate Emulator v2 (ACE2) as part of an effort to assess the range of potential weather impacts on the US energy grid over the next two decades. Here, we describe and evaluate the ensemble, which is the first component of a framework that involves global weather emulation, AI downscaling over the conterminous United States (CONUS), hydrology modeling, and energy systems modeling. The ensemble consists of 10 historical members from 1980-2025, driven by past observed SSTs, and 100 future members from 2025-2045, driven by a range of SST trajectories that have been sampled from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project v6 (CMIP6) ensemble. We assess the ensemble’s ability to reproduce historical weather variability over CONUS, suitable responses to major modes of global weather variability, and capture a reasonable range of variability for several key variables for energy production and grid operation. The low computational cost of the AI emulator allows the production of an additional 100-member hindcast ensemble that treats 2005-2025 as the predictive period, enabling validation that would not typically be possible with conventional global weather model ensembles, and showing the utility of the ensemble for decadal predictability experiments.

488223.title: Using Artificial Intelligence Weather Prediction with Satellite Observations in Tropical Cyclone Analyses and Forecasts
488223.authors: Christopher Slocum, NESDIS, Fort Collins, CO; and M. N. Razin and J. Martinez
488223.abstract: The recent wave of data-driven Artificial Intelligence Weather Prediction (AIWP) models can generate forecast fields within minutes rather than hours like with traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models. Initial studies suggest that the AIWP models—initialized using the operational global NWP analyses—produce skillful track forecasts competitive with the operational global NWP. More recent work has begun using regionalized AIWP with initial conditions from operational tropical cyclone NWP models. Both instances lack several hours of additional observations around tropical cyclones. This work explores the potential of using NESDIS satellite-derived products to augment existing initial conditions between model analyses for use by AIWP models. Specifically, this work uses tropical-cyclone-centric, satellite-derived temperature, moisture, and wind products to create the new, storm-centric initial conditions. This work will provide quantitative assessment of the impact of these initial conditions by evaluating the environmental diagnostic quantities and track forecasts for the 2025 and 2026 Northern Hemisphere tropical cyclone seasons, discuss various strategies for updating the model fields, and assess the potential for operationalizing the satellite-driven AIWP for tropical cyclone applications. Disclaimer: The scientific results and conclusions, as well as any views or opinions expressed herein, are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect those of NOAA or the Department of Commerce.

488224.title: From the South Pole to the Arctic Ocean: In-Situ Observations of Polar Boundary Layer Stability (Invited Presentation)
488224.authors: John J. Cassano, University of Colorado-Boulder, Boulder, CO; and G. Jozef Hamilton and M. Dice
488224.abstract: Often the polar boundary layer is described in terms of persistent, strong temperature inversions and strong static stability but some studies have highlighted locations where weaker stability can occur frequently, even during the polar night. Here we analyze radiosonde observations from the yearlong MOSAiC expedition in the central Arctic Ocean and multiple years of observations from five Antarctic locations. We use the artificial neural network approach of self-organizing maps to classify boundary layer potential temperature profiles at each site and based on this SOM analysis we identify polar boundary layer stability regimes based on near-surface stability and stability just above the boundary layer. The stability regimes allow for comparison across a variety of polar environments from sea ice over the central Arctic Ocean to coastal Antarctic locations to sites on the high Antarctic plateau. We find that near neutral boundary layer stability occurs frequently over Arctic sea ice and at Antarctic coastal sites while exceptionally strong inversions were common over the Antarctic plateau. Near surface wind speed, serving as a proxy for mechanical mixing, and downwelling longwave radiation were assessed for each stability regime across the six sites with radiative forcing being strongly correlated with boundary layer stability while wind speed exhibited a less clear relationship with stability.

488226.title: A JPSS VIIRS Perspective of the Aspen Acres Fire in southern Colorado
488226.authors: Jorel Torres, CIRA, FORT COLLINS, CO
488226.abstract: The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument is on board three Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) polar-orbiting satellites that are orbiting the globe and producing datasets for users to access online. The JPSS constellation currently consists of the Suomi-National Polar-orbiting Partnership (SNPP), NOAA-20 and the NOAA-21 satellites, where JPSS-4 and JPSS-3 are expected to be added to the constellation within the next decade. The VIIRS instrument comprises of 22 spectral bands that consist of 5 Imagery Bands (I-Bands), 16 Moderate Bands (M-Bands) and one Day/Night Band (DNB) that provides unique visible imagery at night. All VIIRS bands exhibit high spatial resolutions of 375 (i.e., I-Bands) and 750 meters (i.e., M-Bands and DNB). VIIRS also has an extensive list of products, where applications can range from detecting and characterizing the properties of water and ice clouds, snow, sea surface temperatures, sea/lake/river ice, fog, fires, severe and tropical weather, vegetation health and aerosols. This presentation showcases a suite of fire related VIIRS product and imagery observations of the Aspen Acres Fire, that erupted across southern Colorado and burned ~100,000 acres during summer of 2026. A mix of VIIRS individual bands, multi-spectral imagery (e.g., GeoColor), RGBs, and derived products will be highlighted to help users learn how to identify fire hotspots, smoke, burn scars and interpret fire intensities throughout the evolution of the Aspen Acres Fire. Satellite training materials (e.g., two-page product reference documents, teletraining sessions, foundational courses, satellite blogs) will be provided to assist users in the interpretation of the products and help users know when they can expect the data across their domain. Additionally, the presentation will describe how users can access the near-real-time VIIRS data via online webpages, such as the JPSS Sectors on CIRA SLIDER, RealEarth, and JSTAR Mapper.

488227.title: A Calibration/Validation Framework for the NOAA NEON Program Era
488227.authors: Siena Iacovazzi, Global Science and Technology, Inc., Lanham, MD; and L. Zhou, I. Guch, Z. Jelenak, P. S. Chang, M. Seybold, S. Kalluri, L. Lin, J. J. Gerth, C. Cao, A. Heidinger, C. Pan, F. Iturbide-Sanchez, L. Neely, K. Yienger, N. Laudier, and M. Sammons
488227.abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) observations have been critical for weather forecasting, environmental observation, and public safety. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) Office of LEO Observations manages NOAA’s current Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS). This system provides global LEO observations that serve as the backbone of both short- and long-term forecasts, including those that help predict and prepare for severe weather events. The Office of LEO Observations also manages the Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) Program. The NEON Program will supplement and eventually replace JPSS and lay the groundwork for the next generation of LEO satellites to continue, improve, and extend NESDIS’ global observations for weather forecasting and environmental monitoring. The NEON Program architecture has a “buy and partner where we can, build what we must” philosophy. It also embraces the approach of establishing an observing system constellation that consists of multiple small- to medium-sized spacecraft missions that each manifest a single instrument from the necessary observing system suite. This departs from the current and legacy satellites that consist of the full instrument suite integrated onto a single large spacecraft for each mission. Results of early NEON formulation activities have determined its success will require leveraging innovative advances in commercial space (e.g., New Space) and better understanding of how commercial industry can provide spacecraft, launch services, and ground services. A goal is to reduce Government involvement in NEON projects where possible. Since the NEON Program departs significantly from JPSS by having much more flexibility to choose from available options to obtain necessary satellite observations – i.e., satellite acquisitions that rely more on commercial space, commercial data buys, and partnerships – it becomes necessary to have an adaptable NEON science data product calibration/validation (cal/val) plan architecture. NEON cal/val analyses and assessments will communicate data product quality to all stakeholders. They will also be integral to program decision making processes about data releasability and usability. In addition, they are needed to identify and be used to mitigate anomalies and biases in data products that may prevent them from being implemented to their full potential. Thus, the NEON science data product cal/val framework must have the ability to define cal/val activity scope and implementation milestones and link these milestones to the data product decisions they support, in a manner that is tailorable to the intent of each NEON project. This can reduce the time needed for certain data product declaration events, which is important since NEON missions are expected to be shorter-lived than their JPSS counterparts. This will be discussed in detail in this presentation.

488232.title: Safety at Sea: An Evaluation of Wind and Wave Warning Polygons for the Digital Transformation of Marine Forecasts
488232.abstract: The World Meteorological Organization’s S-412 specifications convert text-based marine weather warnings into digital polygons on electronic charts, improving warning interface and accuracy to protect life and property at sea. The National Weather Service’s Ocean Prediction Center (OPC) began producing forecaster-edited full-basin northern Atlantic and Pacific grids for the National Digital Forecast Database (NDFD) in January 2026 to prepare for the production of these 24-hour warning polygons. Yet the expected performance enhancement of polygons generated from forecaster-edited grids vs deterministic model output has yet to be quantified. This study develops an area-based, native-grid method to evaluate NDFD and Global Forecast System (GFS) 24-hour wind warning polygons via an experimental, near-global dataset: the Multi-Sensor Worldwide Ocean Winds (MWOW). The 24-hour ocean wave warning polygon accuracy is quantified via a separate hit/miss approach using satellite altimetry data. In both the North Atlantic and North Pacific events studied, polygons from NDFD forecaster grids slightly increase the probability of detecting hazardous wind and wave conditions compared to GFS model polygons, with the largest improvement occurring at high hazard levels. The overall performance of NDFD and GFS polygons suggests deterministic model polygons may suffice for countries lacking operational ocean forecast grids, but an improvement is needed at high hazard levels. These results and methods will help guide the direction of S-412 development to provide accurate warning polygons on mariner’s electronic charting and display systems (ECDIS) and support safe global navigation in the years to come.

488235.title: Decadal Predictability of Very Heavy Precipitation over the Southeast US Linked to Pacific Modes of Variability
488235.authors: Mari R. Tye, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. G. Yeager, C. A. Shields, R. R. McCrary, and G. A. Meehl
488235.abstract: Very heavy winter precipitation over the southeastern United States can contribute up to 30% of the seasonal total precipitation and can be very disruptive; yet the drivers of their multi-year variability remain understudied. This research evaluates the decadal predictability of very heavy winter precipitation over the southeastern United States and its relationship with Pacific Modes of Variability (MOV). The capability of the Community Earth System v2 Large Ensemble to reproduce historical intensity, variability and spatial patterns of very heavy precipitation is assessed compared to ERA5. Very heavy winter precipitation over the southeastern United States is highly correlated with all Pacific MOVs; positive phases correlate with increased event frequency and intensity. While El Niño characterizes precipitation processes at the subseasonal scale, the Interdecadal Pacific Variation dominates decadal precipitation processes. Analysis of the different CESM2 ensemble members indicates that the strongest model correlations exist for members with moderate MOV intensity and phase persistence, similar to the phase intensity and persistence presented in ERA5. Furthermore, there is a systematic spatial bias in the location of very heavy precipitation. When evaluating the relationship between Pacific MOVs and very heavy winter precipitation over land, 5 members have a very strong positive correlation (>0.75); the number of members with a strong positive correlation increases substantially when the slight eastward offset in precipitation is incorporated in analyses.

488239.title: Examining the Long-Term Tropical Cyclone Wind Radii Record and Comparison to Observation
488239.authors: Lisa Bucci, AOML, Weston, FL; Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory, Miami, FL; and J. P. Cangialosi, B. J. Reinhart, P. Collado, MA, and J. L. Colón Pérez
488239.abstract: The impacts of tropical cyclones (TCs) are driven by a storm’s track and maximum sustained winds, but are also significantly influenced by its horizontal scale. Despite its importance, storm size has often been an underappreciated aspect of tropical cyclone hazard messaging, as both research and media coverage have traditionally focused more on forecast track and intensity. Accurate assessments of wind radii—specifically the maximum radial extent of 34-, 50-, and 64-kt surface winds, along with the radius of maximum winds—are critical for storm surge modeling, maritime routing, and the issuance of timely warnings. This study analyzes TC wind radii climatology across the North Atlantic, eastern Pacific, and central Pacific basins to improve the characterization and communication of tropical cyclone structure. Wind radii estimates from the HURDAT2 "best track" dataset (2004–2025) were used to produce climatologies of azimuthally and quadrant-averaged storms based on intensity, latitude, geographic location, and forward speed. Best track estimates were compared against Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations. While 50-kt wind radii showed the highest correlations across all basins, 64-kt (hurricane-force) wind radii in the SAR data were often larger than best track estimates. Finally, an interactive website was developed to provide National Hurricane Center forecasters with climatological norms and real-time comparisons of ongoing events to the historical record.

488244.title: Poleward Migration of Tropical Cyclones over 1980–2024 Is Dominated By Pacific Variability
488244.authors: Wenyu Zhou, PNNL, Richland, WA; and L. R. Leung, C. C. Chang, M. Zhao, H. H. Hsu, H. C. Liang, C. Y. Tu, K. Balaguru, and J. Lu
488244.abstract: Since 1980, occurrences of tropical cyclones (TCs) have migrated poleward, bringing TC-related hazards to higher latitudes. Whether this poleward migration reflects long-term climate change or temporary climate variability remains unclear. Here, we present analyses and modelling evidence showing that TC latitudes are strongly modulated by a tripolar SST pattern of Pacific variability (TPI) whose temporary, multi-decadal trend largely drove the observed poleward migration. Interannually, TPI alters the TC-favorable environment and shifts TC latitudes more effectively than El Niño-Southern Oscillation or Hadley cell. With such interannual modulation, multi-decadal trends in TPI result in corresponding TC migrations. When the effect of TPI is removed from observations or when evaluated over periods with insignificant or negative TPI trends in long-historical TC-permitting simulations, TC migration becomes insignificant or even equatorward. As TPI exhibits alternating positive and negative trends over similar 45-year periods but shows no significant trends since 1970 or 1950, the TPI trend over 1980-2024 — and its associated poleward TC migration – is unlikely to persist under long-term climate change. Indeed, future TC changes projected by global TC-permitting models differ markedly from the observed trends, aligning with their distinct warming patterns and circulation changes. Despite the projected Hadley expansion, future TC changes do not feature poleward migration but an overall reduction, and global high‑latitude TCs are projected to decrease rather than increase.
