Our results highlight that climate variability plays a larger role than previously recognized in the observed poleward migration, and that response of TC distribution to long-term climate change can be distinct from past multi-decadal trends. Zhou et al., Nat. Geosci. 19, 42–51 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-025-01866-2.

488250.title: Evaluating Different Storm Types Responsible for Flooding In Southeast Michigan Using a Convection-Permitting WRF Ensemble
488250.authors: Kevin Thomas Gray, University of Illinois, Urbana, IL; and F. Dominguez, B. Jewett, and D. M. Putri
488250.abstract: The United States Fifth National Climate Assessment indicates that the Great Lakes region has already experienced a 45% increase in the most intense 1% of rainfall and the increasing trend is expected to continue into the future. With the increase in heavy precipitation, flooding has also increased, especially in urban areas. The study presented herein is part of an effort with the United States Department of Defense (DoD) to increase preparedness for heavy rainfall and flooding events. As a case study, we focus on southeastern Michigan, where the United States Army Garrison Detroit Arsenal is located. Detroit is built upon relatively low and flat land, making the area susceptible to flooding. Flooding near the Detroit Arsenal in the past has led to damages costing millions of dollars. A Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) ensemble is used to produce forecasts for heavy precipitation events in the last 20 years which led to flooding in Detroit. The 24-member ensemble uses convection-permitting grid spacing of 3 km to better capture convective cores that may be responsible for heavy precipitation. The high-resolution output is also necessary to force a hydrological model, which provides inundation information at the building scale for the Detroit Arsenal and surrounding area. The historical precipitation events investigated are categorized by the dynamic forcing mechanism associated with the heavy precipitation: extratropical cyclone, cold front, warm front, stationary front, and tropical cyclone remnants. Flooding is strongly influenced by precipitation intensity, duration, and spatial coverage, all of which tend to vary between the different storm types. While previous studies focus on evaluating convection-permitting ensembles for a specific storm type, few consider a range of storm types. By evaluating the ensemble performance for different storm types presented herein, the DoD can be provided with information about confidence in a forecast for a certain storm type. Since different flooding scenarios may be expected for different storm types, this information is useful for making critical decisions leading up to a heavy rain event. Preliminary results indicate that the WRF ensemble performs best when simulating tropical cyclone remnants and extratropical cyclones. Stationary fronts appear to be the most difficult storm type for the ensemble to capture. Despite this, the WRF ensemble generally exhibits greater skill than deterministic forecasts from the Global Forecast System (GFS) and North American Mesoscale (NAM) models for all storm types. Comparisons against forecasts from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model are underway. In the future, we plan to run the ensemble in real-time at lead times greater than publicly available convection-allowing models so that decision-makers can begin using the ensemble output.

488253.title: The NOAA NESDIS Commercial Data Program Overview and Status
488253.authors: Natalie Laudier, NOAA/NESDIS, Silver Spring, MD; and M. R. Gasbarro, G. Peltzer, C. Pan, H. Patel, L. Lin, A. Lomax, R. Deinlein, C. Ritchie, P. J. Powers, and A. M. Agather
488253.abstract: Leveraging the expanding commercial space industry, the NOAA National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) Commercial Data Program (CDP) is crucial for acquiring vital satellite data to meet NOAA’s operational needs in weather forecasting and space weather applications. The NESDIS CDP pursues two key efforts: Commercial Data Pilot projects, which evaluate the quality and impact of commercial data for environmental applications; and Commercial Data Purchases, which procure essential data services for daily operational use. This presentation will provide comprehensive updates on the current status and future trajectory of these pilot projects and continuous operational data acquisitions. We will briefly discuss the evaluation results from the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-Reflectometry for Ocean Surface Winds Pilot and the Microwave Sounder Pilot, outlining future plans for transitioning this data into NOAA’s operations. We will also discuss future plans for piloting and acquiring additional data types as well as the future of commercial procurement of GNSS Radio Occultation measurements.

488260.title: The Impact of Sub-Sampling UAS Observations on Data Accuracy and Turbulence Metrics
488260.authors: Lauren Amarys Baez Sepulveda, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; and J. B. Wadler, J. J. Cione, J. A. Zhang, M. Z. Stachura, and J. Elston
488260.abstract: The Black Swift Technologies S0 is a small uncrewed aerial system (sUAS) that is routinely deployed from National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA’s) WP-3D Hurricane Hunter aircraft. Beginning with the 2026 hurricane season, the S0 data will be operationally assimilated into the NOAA Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) model. The sUAS is equipped with instrumentation that acquires and transmits atmospheric measurements such as temperature, pressure, and relative humidity. In addition, the S0 carries a custom five-hole pressure probe capable of estimating wind speed and wind direction at frequencies up to 75 Hz. The standard atmospheric sensors sample at rates up to 5 Hz, while the pressure probe can acquire data as high as 75 Hz. Currently, all measurements transmit near 5 Hz since real-time UAS telemetry from the S0 balances aircraft flight information, system health, and meteorological data within its limited communication bandwidth. The air-deployed sUAS was recovered for the first time following a mission on April 9, 2026. Thus, the complete 5 Hz environmental data, and 75 Hz winds from the pressure probe were fully recovered. This study investigates what is lost from the high-frequency reference dataset when only a subset of the data is transmitted. Measurements were also evaluated alongside observations from dropsondes and the NOAA P-3 flight-level data to verify their integrity. By testing the fidelity of the reports, we can ensure efficient use of communication bandwidth while preserving measurement accuracy. This study evaluates how different transmission frequencies preserve atmospheric information required to accurately represent dynamic and rapidly evolving turbulence fluctuations.

488271.title: Application of NOSIA to Inform Future NEON Architecture Investments
488271.authors: Louis E. Cantrell Jr., Profitable Weather, LLC, Laurel, MD
488271.abstract: Space-based microwave (MW) sounders provide critical atmospheric profiles essential for numerical weather prediction and decision support. Without MW sounder data, service uncertainty increases across critical societal areas: Electric Power (+2.07%), Hurricane (+1.70%), Extreme Heat (+1.67%), Extreme Cold (+1.19%), and Flood (+1.08%). To inform NOAA’s Near-Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellite investments (2034–2044), this study evaluates transitioning from the Joint Polar Satellite System’s (JPSS) Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) to the next-generation Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA). We integrated physical sensor capabilities, NOAA Earth Observation Requirements Evaluation System (EORES) requirements, Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) forecast impact data, and the NOAA Observing System Integrated Analysis (NOSIA-2-2) value tree (~35,000 nodes). Relative Gap Assessments (RGA) revealed that SMBA delivers significant performance gains over ATMS, including a 30-minute reduction in data latency, a 30% increase in vertical resolution, and a 30% improvement in measurement accuracy. Evaluating multi-period deployment strategies across the 1330 and 1730 orbit planes demonstrates that all proposed configurations maintain JPSS baseline continuity through 2041. Post-2041, performance diverges: a single-orbit strategy provides baseline operational continuity with modest gains, whereas a dual-orbit SMBA strategy (1330 and 1730 planes) maximizes socio-economic benefits and uncertainty reduction across all mission areas. Hurricane and Electric Power services show the highest sensitivity to these enhancements. A dual-orbit SMBA constellation is recommended to optimize future NEON investments and maintain long-term observational continuity.

488273.title: Remote Sensing of Precipitation from Space - Perspectives from GPM and the International Precipitation Working Group (Invited)
488273.authors: Sarah E. Ringerud, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and G. Panegrossi and G. J. Huffman
488273.abstract: The Global Precipitation Measurement Mission (GPM) has surpassed 10 years in operation, building a legacy of unprecedented advances in understanding the global distribution and characteristics of rain and snow. Its predecessor, the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) operated a similar mission in the Tropics from 1997-2015. During this timeframe global precipitation products derived from satellite observations have become a crucial component of a diverse set of international applications. This is demonstrated through thousands of attributions in the scientific literature, public outreach and education, and real-time use by forecasters, decision makers, and commercial enterprises. In 2001 the International Precipitation Working Group (IPWG) was established as a permanent Working Group of the Coordination Group for Meteorological Satellites (CGMS). The IPWG is co-sponsored by CGMS and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and focuses the scientific community on operational and research satellite-based quantitative precipitation measurement issues and challenges. IPWG currently has more than 500 registered members from around the globe organized in a set of Working Groups with specific deliverables related to product creation, validation, machine learning and incorporating CubseSats and SmallSats into the constellation, as well as Focus Groups charged with coordinating discussions around topics of mutual interest. This presentation will focus on the evolution of the way we measure and validate precipitation from space and perspectives on these topics from a recent meeting of the IPWG. Discussion will also include continuing challenges along with the outlook for the post-GPM era.

488275.title: Improving Forecasts of Hurricane Beryl (2024) Genesis through Assimilation of All-Sky Infrared Radiances in HAFS-JEDI
488275.authors: Chandler Michael Pruett, Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA; and X. Chen and F. Hsiao
488275.abstract: Predicting tropical cyclogenesis remains a major challenge because it often occurs over data-sparse oceans and is controlled by complex multiscale interactions among tropical convection, precursor disturbances, and the large-scale environment. This study examines the impact of assimilating all-sky infrared (IR) brightness temperatures from geostationary satellites on forecasts of the genesis of Hurricane Beryl (2024), a particularly challenging case for operational prediction. Notably, all-sky IR radiances are not currently assimilated in operational hurricane forecasting systems. To evaluate their potential value, we employ NOAA’s latest hurricane data assimilation-forecast framework, the Hurricane Analysis and Forecasting System with Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (HAFS-JEDI). Results demonstrate that assimilating all-sky IR radiances, in addition to conventional observations, improves forecasts of Hurricane Beryl’s genesis in HAFS-JEDI. The inclusion of IR radiance observations substantially modifies the initial moisture field and circulation structure of the precursor easterly wave. These adjustments promote a more realistic coupling between deep convection and the parent disturbance, resulting in a more accurate prediction of tropical cyclogenesis and the subsequent rapid intensification of Beryl. We will further examine the dynamical mechanisms through which all-sky IR DA enhances forecast skill using a series of sensitivity experiments, and discuss pathways for further improving the performance of all-sky IR DA within the HAFS-JEDI framework.

488278.title: Antonio Busalacchi: Earth System Science Leadership
488278.authors: Susan K. Avery, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO
488278.abstract: Antonio Busalacchi: Earth system science leadership Antonio (Tony) Busalacchi has been a remarkable change leader - pushing and supporting the evolution of atmospheric science to its key important role in earth system science. His work at NCAR/UCAR illustrates that leadership in not only the development of the structural change to accomplish interdisciplinary science but also the cultural, organizational, and community leadership to enable that change. And as a result, our science has grown tremendously in embracing new understandings of our planet and its relationship with human society. In this presentation I will try to present what I have seen in the growth of our understanding through earth system science - and how that was enabled by Tony's leadership.

488294.title: Clustering vs. Areal Coverage: Modes and Mechanisms of Convective Organization During ORCESTRA/PICCOLO
488294.authors: Allison A. Wing, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and S. A. Kennison, W. T. Hsiao, M. M. Bell, and J. H. Ruppert Jr.
488294.abstract: Tropical convection organizes across a wide range of scales with contributions from a variety of different mechanisms. Here we leverage ship-borne radar observations from a 40-day deployment of the Colorado State University SEA-POL radar on the German RV Meteor to investigate the characteristics and mechanisms of mesoscale organization of convection within the Atlantic Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). First we investigate statistical relationships between the spatial morphology of convection, the area-mean rain rate, and rain intensity. The area-mean rain rate observed by the radar is related most strongly to metrics of organization that reflect large raining area, as expected, but is surprisingly anti-correlated with metrics that measure the spatial clustering of rain cells. However for a fixed area-mean rain rate, the rain intensity increases with increased spatial clustering. We explore possible reasons for this behavior, by considering the relationship between the large-scale environment and spatial clustering of convection and using the radar data to evaluate theories of convection. Next we consider mechanisms driving the observed mesoscale organization. Using large eddy simulations of observed rain events combined with observational estimates, we find that cloud-radiative feedbacks only contribute significantly to supporting convective organization at scales greater than ~3 days and ~700 km. This scale dependence is explained by a simple framework that considers the generation of longwave cloud-radiative effect by anvil clouds as the long-term memory of precipitation.

488304.title: Turbulence Anisotropy as an Organizing Principle for Urban Roughness Sublayer Parameterization (Invited Presentation)
488304.authors: Khaled Ghannam, Northeastern University, Chelsea, MA; Northeastern University, Boston, MA
488304.abstract: Turbulence in the urban roughness sublayer (RSL) systematically deviates from canonical surface layer similarity assumptions, a departure driven by an imbalance between the production and dissipation of turbulent kinetic energy, height-dependent fluxes, strong flow heterogeneity, and the injection of turbulent energy from building-scale wakes. These complexities make RSL flows difficult to parameterize in weather and climate models, which predominantly rely on Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory (MOST). To improve these parameterizations, this presentation combines eddy-covariance measurements from an urban RSL tower in Boston with theoretical development to characterize the unique aspects of RSL turbulence through the lens of Reynolds stress anisotropy, its implications for flux-variance relations, and closure schemes that utilize a Rotta-type relaxation timescale. The analysis uses multiresolution decomposition of the velocity and scalar fields to characterize the scalewise turbulence anisotropy through the barycentric map representation of the Reynolds stress tensor, allowing for a mapping of trajectories toward isotropy as a function of scale. The scale decomposition demonstrates that large-scale motions commensurate with Townsend's attached-eddy range exhibit marked anisotropy and poor agreement with MOST, despite contributing substantially to the total variances. Conversely, small-scale inertial motions display higher isotropy and an improved agreement with theoretical similarity relationships. These findings suggest that departures from MOST within the urban RSL are inherently a scale-dependent phenomenon tied to the anisotropy of the flow. Because MOST is a local similarity theory where turbulence scales directly with surface fluxes, the presence of large-scale anisotropic motions that are inefficient at transporting fluxes contaminates this scaling. The presentation concludes by providing new similarity arguments utilizing turbulence anisotropy as an organizing principle, offering a physical framework for parameterizing urban RSL turbulence in low-resolution models

488312.title: Investigation of the Influence of MJO and ENSO on Severe Weather Potential in the United States
488312.authors: Wesley Taylor, Millersville Univ., Thomasville, PA
488312.abstract: Multiple peer-reviewed studies show that ENSO and MJO influence severe weather in the USA during the springtime months, including subseasonal favorability for hail and tornado presence. In this study, we quantify severe weather potential in the USA using North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR) CAPE data. Because a large portion of the severe weather occurs in the spring and early summer in the United States, we study the variability of severe weather potential during the springtime months of March through May relative to variability in MJO phase and ENSO state. In order to assess how MJO progression dynamically affects, we evaluate the time-lagged response of CAPE to antecedent MJO phase and ENSO state to better understand when and where CAPE anomalies in the USA are linked to these teleconnections. Specifically, we evaluate time-lags ranging from 0 to 28 days. Preliminary results suggest that different MJO-ENSO confluences are statistically better linked to anomalous CAPE downstream in time. In our presentation, we quantify the role of MJO-ENSO teleconnections on the spatial patterns and the timing of anomalies in severe weather potential in the USA, and discuss how MJO-ENSO combinant states could be used for high lead time (>7 days) regional mesoscale forecasting purposes.

488314.title: Machine Learning for Observation Simulation In Numerical Weather Prediction OSSEs
488314.authors: Nikki C Privé, Morgan State University, Greenbelt, MD
488314.abstract: Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) require the simulation of the entire global observing network with a much realism as possible. Two different applications of machine learning techniques to the development of an OSSE framework are described. In the first application, a decision tree with XGBoost is used to simulate different types of atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) from a Nature Run including visible and water vapor AMVs. In the second application, mixture density networks are used to predict the bias and standard deviation of observation innovations for radiance observations. The predicted observation innovations are used to develop an observation error simulator that takes the atmospheric state into account. For both applications, MERRA21C hourly reanalysis and the associated real world observations are used to train the machine learning framework, and the trained model is then transferred to take Nature Run inputs on the same grid from a fraternal twin model for prediction in an OSSE framework. Performance of the machine learning methods are compared to traditional OSSE simulation methods using the same Nature Run. The potential of using machine learning methods to reduce the computational resources needed for Nature Runs is discussed.

488316.title: Toward a Resilience Ecosystem Roadmap: Connecting Education, Workforce Development, and Community Resilience
488316.authors: Frank Niepold III, NOAA Climate Program Office, Silver Spring, MD; and N. Gardiner, K. Rainer, J. Kretser, C. McDougall, and S. Schoedinger
488316.abstract: Communities become more resilient when they build collective capacity through education, strong social networks, workforce development, and civic participation that enable people to understand risks, make informed decisions, and implement local resilience solutions. NOAA's 2020 Community Resilience Education Theory of Change demonstrated how education strengthens community resilience by developing environmental literacy, fostering civic engagement, and supporting informed local decision-making. Building on this foundation—and informed by the implementation needs of NOAA's Climate-Ready Workforce initiative — a new coalition is expanding the theory of change to explicitly incorporate workforce development alongside resilience planning, infrastructure, and finance. This evolution recognizes that resilient communities require both climate-literate residents and a climate-ready workforce capable of planning, designing, implementing, and sustaining resilience solutions. The coalition is developing a Resilience Ecosystem Roadmap that connects formal and informal education with workforce and professional development and articulates how those systems support other four systems essential to climate resilience, i.e., climate and social science, resilience planning and policy, physical infrastructure, and funding and finance. Together, these systems create the human and organizational capacity needed to strengthen community resilience and support implementation of NOAA's Climate-Ready Workforce initiative, as well as complementary local, state, Tribal, and national resilience efforts. Through a series of facilitated, collaborative processes, educators, researchers, workforce leaders, community organizations, Tribal partners, government agencies, practitioners, and funders are co-developing a shared theory of change, i.e., the roadmap, that enables organizations to work independently while contributing to common national outcomes. The resulting roadmap is intended to help align investments, strengthen cross-sector collaboration, integrate education and workforce development into resilience planning and implementation of community climate actions, and identify scalable approaches that support implementation of community resilience strategies. Conference attendees will learn how an integrated education-workforce development approach better prepares people and communities to understand climate risks and design, finance, build, maintain, and lead resilience solutions. The presentation will share the coalition’s emerging theory of change, collaborative design process, and opportunities to integrate and strengthen existing education and workforce efforts to advance NOAA's Climate-Ready Workforce initiative while accelerating resilience in communities nationwide.

488322.title: Investigating Marine Stratocumulus Processes in the Eastern North Atlantic Using Explainable Machine Learning Techniques
488322.authors: Ezekiel Caldon, Ohio University, Athens, OH; Ohio University, Athens, OH; and V. P. Ghate
488322.abstract: Turbulence and microphysical processes are tightly coupled in marine stratocumulus topped boundary layers, influencing cloud structure, precipitation, and radiative properties across a range of spatial and temporal scales. However, the multiscale nature of these interactions presents significant challenges for their accurate representation in a range of atmospheric models. In this study, we analyze these processes using data from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Eastern North Atlantic (ENA) site. 29 cases of stratocumulus cloud conditions spanning 676 hours were identified from 7 years of data. The cloud and drizzle macro- and microphysical properties were retrieved by combining data from vertically pointing cloud radar, lidars and radiometers. Profiles of radiative fluxes were calculated by using radiosonde reported thermodynamic profiles and cloud properties as an input to the Rapid Radiative Transfer Model (RRTM). On average the cloud top height was 1.3 km with clouds 361 m thick and cloud base rain rate of 2.62 mm day-1. The radiative cooling at the cloud top was –65.22 W m-2 yielding updraft velocity at closest level to cloud base of 0.40 m s-1. The average cloud optical depth was 14.57 and cloud droplet number concentrations of 85 cm-3. We specifically focus on understanding the factors modulating boundary layer coupling, cloud base rain rate, and liquid water path through the extreme gradient-boosted (XGBoost) machine learning (ML) model framework. The models were developed using hourly and minute data to capture the adjustment timescales. The SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis revealed cloud top height (CTH), updraft velocity closest to cloud base, and liquid water path (LWP) largely determined the decoupling at hour resolution, while at minute resolution decoupling was determined by LWP, CTH, and latent heat flux. Similarly for cloud base rain rate, concentrations of cloud particles, cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and droplets had the greatest effect at hourly timescales while cloud-top radiational cooling, lifting condensation level (LCL), and CTH had the greatest effect at minute resolution. These results are useful for scale-aware cloud parameterizations aimed at simulating aerosol-cloud-precipitation-turbulence processes at a range of model resolutions. Caption for attached figure: (top) KAZR reflectivity (shades) and ceilometer cloud base height (black dots) from 20161115 to 20161117, (middle) visible satellite imagery, and (bottom) satellite LWP. The satellite snapshots are for 20161115 10 UTC, 20161115 15 UTC, 20161116 10 UTC, and 20161116 15 UTC. The local time is 2 hours behind UTC. ENA ARM site shown as red star.

488327.title: Where and When Would Mixed-Phase Cloud Thinning Most Effectively Preserve Arctic Sea Ice?
488327.authors: Lili Manzo, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA; and X. Li, I. Eisenman, Y. Dong, and J. F. Kok
488327.abstract: How can we counter Arctic sea ice loss? One potential climate intervention is mixed-phase cloud thinning (MCT). However, the conditions under which MCT would have the strongest effects remain uncertain. Here, we simulate MCT over various Arctic subregions and seasonal windows and quantify the resulting sea ice response to determine the optimal time and location for cloud-seeding. In practice, MCT would be achieved by seeding wintertime mixed-phase clouds (MPCs, containing both water droplets and ice crystals) with ice-nucleating particles (INPs). Higher INP concentrations encourage glaciation, which reduces cloud optical depth and, consequently, atmospheric heat trapping. Known limitations in representing aerosol-cloud interactions in large-scale models complicate our ability to accurately simulate MCT. As a proxy for the effects of cloud seeding, we instead make Arctic MPCs transparent to LW radiation in the Community Earth System Model (CESM). This allows us to bypass the impact of potential errors from poorly represented cloud microphysical processes. The magnitude of the resulting reduction in cloud LW radiation is grounded by observationally based constraints on the warming effects of polar MPCs. The results of these simulations help quantify the potential of MCT to slow Arctic sea-ice loss and identify the optimal conditions for its future implementation.

488328.title: A Rotation-Convection Instability Framework For African Easterly Waves (Invited Presentation)
488328.authors: Ángel Francisco Adames Corraliza, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI
488328.abstract: African easterly waves (AEWs) are among the most studied tropical weather systems. Yet the processes governing their structure and growth are not fully understood. While it is often assumed that AEWs grow from dry barotropic-baroclinic instability, many studies have underscored the importance of deep convection. In this study, we examine the structure and moist thermodynamics of AEWs in ERA5 data. As in other tropical weather systems, it is found that AEWs exhibit a vertical tilt in their vorticity that is opposite to what is expected from baroclinic growth. They also exhibit convection that is shifted towards the vortex center and roughly collocated with enhanced free tropospheric moisture and cool anomalies. A linear model is presented to capture this behavior. Deep convection is assumed to obey weak temperature gradient balance while the shallow circulations that respond to the mean mid-level easterly jet are assumed to be quasi-geostrophic (QG). Unstable wave solutions are found when convection responds to lower tropospheric moisture and temperature anomalies. This instability is stronger than baroclinic instability and vanishes when convection responds to QG forcing rather than the thermodynamic environment. The unstable waves exhibit the tilt towards the shear that is found in reanalysis. Convection is also shifted towards the circulation center, leading to growth from vortex stretching. It is proposed that this instability is part of a paradigm of “rotation-convection instabilities” that can adequately explain the growth of slow, convectively coupled tropical waves.

488329.title: How Deep Convection Drives Rapid Intensification in Hurricanes: Combining Airborne Radar Observations and WRF Simulations
488329.authors: Joshua B. Wadler, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; and M. S. Fischer and D. S. Nolan
488329.abstract: It is widely known that hurricane intensity change is related to the spatial organization of precipitation within the storm, yet the physical mechanisms linking convective structure to intensification are not completely understood. This study draws on the TC-RADAR database which contains airborne tail Doppler radar observations from NOAA's P-3 aircraft, spanning 1997 to 2024, to explore this relationship. Earlier work classified radar observations into four precipitation regimes (stratiform rain, shallow convection, moderate convection, and deep convection) and found that deep convection showed the strongest azimuthal asymmetry (concentrated downshear-left in weakening storms, but more evenly distributed in intensification storms). In the current study we quantify how deep convection kinematically modifies the background vortex by constructing vorticity and angular momentum budgets, with the goal of clarifying its contribution to rapid intensification. We find that deep convection located in the upshear-left quadrant produces the largest mid-level relative vorticity of any precipitation type. When environmental conditions favor upshear-side propagation, this convectively generated vorticity appears capable of driving vortex growth upward from that quadrant. To corroborate these kinematic findings, we conduct a parallel analysis using a high-resolution, idealized hurricane simulations in the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. These simulations allow us to contrast the thermodynamic contributions of deep convection against those of the other precipitation modes. Together, the observational and modeling results unite multiple theories for hurricane intensity change and offer new insight into how different precipitation structures, along with radial and downdraft ventilation, govern the evolution of hurricane intensity.

488330.title: Reproducing, Interpreting, and Extending the Aerosol-Cloud-Turbulence Interaction in the Convection-Cloud Chambers Using Large-Eddy Simulations and Bin Microphysics (Invited Presentation)
488330.authors: Aaron Wang, PNNL, Richland, WA; PNNL, Richland, WA; and F. Yang, M. Ovchinnikov, S. K. Krueger, and R. A. Shaw
488330.abstract: Cloud–aerosol–turbulence interactions are important yet under-resolved and underrepresented processes in atmospheric models. These interactions have been studied in laboratory convection-cloud chambers, such as the Pi Chamber at Michigan Technological University, which generates turbulent clouds through mixing driven by a warm, moist bottom surface and a cold, moist top surface. Large-eddy simulation and bin microphysics are valuable tools for reproducing, interpreting, and extending these laboratory experiments. One application is the design of a new tall chamber and associated experiments for the Aerosol-Cloud-Drizzle Convection Chamber (ACDC2) project. In addition to enabling studies of drizzle initiation, the proposed tall convection-cloud chamber provides detailed control of sidewall temperatures, offering a unique opportunity to investigate cloud-top entrainment under controlled laboratory conditions. This talk will focus on the chamber design that can produce a cloud top resembling the entrainment interfacial layer of a stratocumulus cloud. A statistically steady cloud is generated by cooling the lower portions of the sidewalls while warming the bottom surface. A temperature inversion is established at the cloud top by maintaining the upper sidewalls and top surface at temperatures warmer than the bottom surface. The resulting turbulent kinetic energy profile and budget resemble those of a convective boundary layer, and inhomogeneous mixing is observed near the cloud top. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed chamber for controlled studies of cloud-top entrainment.

488333.title: Building Climate-Ready Communities Through Workforce Learning: Lessons From NOAA’s Climate-Ready Workforce Initiative
488333.authors: Frank Niepold III, NOAA Climate Program Office, Silver Spring, MD; and N. Gardiner, K. Rainer, and A. McDuell
488333.abstract: As communities increasingly develop climate adaptation and resilience plans, their success depends on people with the knowledge, skills, and abilities needed to implement them. Building this human infrastructure requires developing learning ecosystems that bridge employers, education and training providers, community-based organizations, municipalities, and community members. NOAA’s $60 million Climate-Ready Workforce (CRW) initiative supports eight regional partnerships that integrate climate-focused workforce development with climate-based adaptation needs across coastal and Great Lakes communities. These partnerships bring diverse organizations together to co-develop learning ecosystems that prepare workers for careers addressing climate risks while expanding equitable access to high-quality employment. This presentation explores how each Climate-Ready Workforce initiative has uniquely created career pathways that utilize a variety of work-based learning strategies (e.g., technical skill development, externships, internships, apprenticeships, on-the-job training). This presentation will also highlight the support mechanisms needed for this work including: wrap-around services, cross-sector partnerships, and locally relevant learning experiences. Identifying key partners and supportive wraparound services have been both integral and a learning gap for this Initiative overall. Additionally, it will share an emerging Climate-Ready Workforce specific theory of change, implementation strategies, and current lessons learned. The session will conclude with recommendations for integrating climate-ready workforce development into broader resilience learning efforts and discuss how training and education systems can serve as foundational infrastructure for implementing climate adaptation at community and regional scales.

488334.title: Convective and Moist Thermodynamic Quasi-Equilibria In The Tropical Lower Troposphere
488334.authors: Ángel Francisco Adames Corraliza, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI
488334.abstract: The lower tropospheric thermodynamics of a tropical convecting region are examined. Following recent studies, a zero-buoyancy plume model in which the bulk area-averaged entrainment is an inverse function of the saturation deficit is used to examine how lower tropospheric quasi-equilibrium impacts large-scale motions. As in other forms of quasi-equilibrium, the saturation moist static energy (MSE) of the lower free troposphee (LFT) covaries with the boundary layer MSE. However, assuming that parcels entrain and detrain in the LFT yields four additional consequences: (1) convection responds quickly to MSE sources and sinks, adjusting the LFT saturation deficit towards steady state within the order of a day, (2) Increasing entrainment in the LFT as humidity increases causes large-scale mass fluxes to become more top heavy, (3) precipitation abruptly increases once a critical humidity value is exceeded, and (4) there is a near cancellation of column processes in slow tropical systems, causing the local moisture tendencies to be primarily driven by horizontal advection. These results indicate that moist thermodynamic processes in the tropical lower troposphere tend to be in equilibrium, restricting the behavior of tropical weather systems.

488337.title: Future Impacts of Next-Generation Meteorological Satellites in Observing System Simulation Experiments
488337.authors: Erica McGrath-Spangler, Goddard Earth Sciences Technology and Research II (GESTAR II), Baltimore, MD; GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; Morgan State Univ., Baltimore, MD; and N. Prive, B. Karpowicz, A. Heidinger, A. Gambacorta, and S. Kalluri
488337.abstract: NOAA and NASA are developing the next-generation satellite series and the associated instruments and applications. The Geostationary Extended Observations (GeoXO) and the Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) will provide valuable new observations that will enable improvements in weather forecasting and nowcasting through innovative technologies. The GeoXO mission is a geosynchronous orbit mission with a planned hyperspectral infrared sounder (GXS) that will provide high temporal resolution soundings of the atmosphere focused over the Western Hemisphere for the first time. NEON will provide low-Earth Orbit observations using an agile architecture, initially focused on microwave instruments before expanding to other critical instrument types necessary for the future. Each series is planned for launch in the 2030s and require an estimate of impact in a future observing system scenario. The NASA Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) framework can evaluate the expected NWP impact in this future scenario using several metrics, including forecasts and the forecast sensitivity to observation impact (FSOI), and provide essential context for decision-makers.

488350.title: A Machine Learning Approach to Flight-Level to 10 Meter Surface Reductions
488350.authors: William Bouza, AOML, Miami, FL; University of Miami CIMAS, Miami, FL; and M. S. Fischer and J. A. Sippel
488350.abstract: Reliable estimates of 10-m winds within tropical cyclones are difficult to obtain consistently, yet they are essential for intensity estimation, forecasting and hazard assessment. Current operational practice estimates surface winds by applying pressure-altitude-dependent reduction factors to reconnaissance flight-level observations. While dropsondes provide direct measurements of the near-surface wind profile, their spatial and temporal sampling is limited, and do not measure sustained 1-minute wind. Airborne Tail Doppler Radar (TDR) provides substantially greater coverage, but observations are limited in height to a minimum of 500-m heights above the surface. To address these observational limitations, we developed the Surface Estimation from Aircraft Reductions (SEAR) model to estimate tropical cyclone 10-m surface winds from flight-level aircraft reconnaissance observations. SEAR is a two-stage gradient-boosting machine learning model in which the first stage estimates 500-m winds from flight-level observations and the second stage estimates the mean wind within the lowest 150-m (WL150) from the predicted 500-m winds from stage one. WL150 is then converted to a 10-m wind estimate using derived reduction factors. The model incorporates flight-level observations together with storm-relative and environmental predictors and is trained using airborne Doppler radar analyses from the Tropical Cyclone Radar Archive of Doppler Analyses with Recentering (TC-RADAR) and high-resolution dropsonde observations collected by NOAA’s Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory Hurricane Research Division. SEAR was developed using North Atlantic aircraft reconnaissance observations and is intended to provide consistent estimates of tropical cyclone 10-m surface winds from real-time reconnaissance data. We evaluate SEAR using tropical cyclones from the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, which were excluded entirely from model development and therefore provide the first fully independent validation dataset for the model. Model performance will be evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE), root-mean-square error (RMSE), bias, and additional validation statistics. This evaluation will quantify the performance of SEAR on an independent hurricane season and assess its potential to improve operational estimates of tropical cyclone 10-m surface winds.

488359.title: Advancing GNSS-R Derived Ocean Surface Heat Fluxes Using Machine Learning
488359.authors: Juan A. Crespo, UCLA, Los Angeles, CA; JPL, Pasadena, CA; and S. Asharaf and M. A. Bourassa
488359.abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R) uses GPS signals reflected from the ocean surface, enabling observations under various weather conditions. This study introduces a novel methodology for deriving NASA’s Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS) Level-2 ocean surface turbulent heat-flux products. Leveraging CYGNSS satellite measurements, we implemented a hybrid approach that uses machine learning to estimate friction velocity, which then serves as input to a modified aerodynamic bulk-flux algorithm for computing turbulent heat fluxes. Preliminary results indicate that the method improves the accuracy of CYGNSS-derived latent and sensible heat-flux estimates, with substantial reductions in bias and error relative to buoy-based bulk-flux estimates. The broader objective is to reduce the nonlinear propagation of uncertainty inherent in conventional wind-based bulk-flux products and to establish a physically consistent, transferable retrieval architecture for GNSS-R observations. Beginning with CYGNSS, the framework is intended for application to current and future GNSS-R missions. This presentation will describe the methodology, summarize the preliminary results, and discuss the remaining challenges.

488365.title: Predicting Cloud Condensation Nuclei Abundance from Measured Aerosol Physicochemical Properties Using a Machine Learning Algorithm
488365.authors: Ajinkya Subhash Desai, LLNL, Livermore, CA; and A. Chakraborty, B. Marosites, W. Zhai, M. A. Zawadowicz, J. R. O'Brien, S. Collis, J. E. Shilling, C. J. Flynn, G. Kulkarni, J. Uin, O. Y. Enekwizu, M. Levin, J. Kyrouac, M. Tuftedal, E. Andrews, and J. Howie
488365.abstract: Regional weather predictions are hindered by uncertainties in aerosol-induced changes in cloud properties and radiative forcing. A crucial role in these aerosol-cloud interactions is played by cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), i.e., seeds for cloud droplet formation, which suffer from an observational deficit. This deficit can be overcome by estimating the number concentration of CCN (NCCN), from other measurable aerosol physicochemical properties using Machine Learning (ML) models. In this study, we explore the utility of an XGBoost tree-based ML model at predicting NCCN, with a parsimonious use of measured aerosol variables and observations. We aim to maximize model accuracy while ensuring alignment with established aerosol activation physics. We use observations collected from the Aerosol Observation System (AOS) at the US Department of Energy’s Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Observatory in the Southern Great Plains (SGP) of Oklahoma to train and test the model. At this facility, the mean NCCN is estimated using a commercial cloud condensation nucleus counter operating at a water vapor supersaturation of 0.4%. CCN dependencies on a suite of relevant aerosol variables representing chemical composition, optical properties, and particle number size distribution, selected based on physics-based constraints such as aerosol size and hygroscopicity, are explored. We include winter observations due to the increased hygroscopicity of chemical species in that season. We assessed multicollinearity using a pairwise Pearson Correlation matrix and excluded variables with an absolute correlation coefficient greater than 0.7 with their paired predictors to reduce feature redundancy. Our model demonstrates that NCCN has the highest sensitivity to size-normalized medium-sized particle number concentrations (mobility diameter ranging from 80-200 nm). This is explained by the fact that medium-sized particles activate at lower supersaturations than finer particles (mobility diameter < 80 nm), due to their lower surface curvature reducing the activation barrier. Moreover, supersaturation levels dictate the critical diameter at which activation occurs; at the intermediate supersaturation level selected here, the activation of medium-sized particles is more likely to be sensitive to chemical composition changes. Next, NCCN is found to have additional sensitivity to both light-scattering and absorption coefficients for green wavelengths. This initially appears physically counterintuitive, given the weak hygroscopicity of Black Carbon aerosols, which strongly absorb light across the broad spectrum. However, aged light-absorbing aerosols (e.g., Black Carbon) are typically coated with sulfates and nitrates, which are strongly hygroscopic chemical species, thereby increasing their capacity to be activated as CCN. Our model highlights the most economical set of aerosol variables for predicting NCCN, with high computational efficiency, while giving physically consistent results. It further establishes a foundation for exploring CCN predictions based on seasonality and paves pathways for comparison with more complex ML models such as neural networks and probabilistic and/or distributional models.

488372.title: A Broadband Radiative Closure Study Over the Arctic Using NASA ARCSIX Airborne Observations and Radiative Transfer Modeling
488372.authors: Erica Kay Dolinar, NRL, Monterey, CA; and A. Bucholtz, T. McHone, N. B. Melton, Y. W. Chen, and K. S. Schmidt
488372.abstract: This study performs a broadband radiative closure analysis by comparing airborne broadband radiation (BBR) measurements taken onboard the NASA P-3 aircraft during the Arctic Radiation-Cloud-Aerosol-Surface Interaction Experiment (ARCSIX) field campaign with a set of 1-D radiative transfer modeling experiments. Upward and downward broadband solar (0.2 – 3.6 µm) and infrared (4.5 – 42 µm) irradiances were measured over the Arctic during two deployment periods in 2024, strategically capturing the critical transitions of the Arctic boundary layer before and after the onset of sea ice melt. To evaluate the radiative consistency of the observed atmospheric, cloud, and surface states, radiative transfer simulations are performed using the 1-D Fu-Liou-Gu (FLG) broadband radiative transfer model. The modeling experiments are constrained with either meteorological reanalyses (e.g., MERRA-2) or the comprehensive set of in-situ thermodynamic, cloud microphysical, and surface properties measured in support of the overarching ARCSIX science goals. A set of sensitivity experiments are designed to quantify the response of computed radiative fluxes to key input parameters, including spectrally-variable versus spectrally-flat surface albedos, cloud optical property assumptions (including ice crystal habit and mixed-phase cloud water path), and associated meteorological profiles. These experiments shed light on the physical and optical assumptions made in radiative transfer models. The Arctic environment is changing rapidly, driven by complex, coupled feedbacks among sea ice, clouds, aerosols, and the regional radiative energy budget. Accurately representing these high-latitude processes in global Earth System and numerical weather prediction (NWP) models remains a major challenge due to persistent parameterization uncertainties.

488379.title: Advancing Coastal Wind Gust Prediction in Landfalling Hurricanes Using Large-Eddy Simulations
488379.authors: Xiaomin Chen, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and C. M. Rozoff and E. A. Hendricks
488379.abstract: The incapability of mesoscale numerical models to resolve small-scale gusts remains a major obstacle to advancing forecasts of damaging gusts that reach the height of coastal infrastructure during hurricane landfall. Leveraging a semi-idealized large-eddy simulation (LES) framework, this study examines the gust transition across a range of land surfaces during onshore hurricane-force winds. Compared to shorter averaging intervals, 10-min sustained wind speeds are much less affected by wind perturbations associated with boundary layer streaks and better represent the near-surface reference mean wind. Frictional deceleration of gusts over land is strongest below 200 m, a layer much shallower than the vertical extent of the mean-flow adjustment. Gust factors (GFs) decrease with height over both water and land. Near the surface, GFs increase from ~1.3 over the ocean to 1.6–2.0 over land, depending on surface roughness. GFs generally decrease linearly with increasing sustained wind speed at multiple heights. Localized EF-1/EF-2-equivalent gusts remain prevalent beyond the near-coast zone. Above 100 m, gust intensities rapidly increase to EF-3/EF-4, primarily due to the strong increase in sustained wind speed with height. Along-trajectory momentum budget analysis indicates that extreme near-surface gusts are driven primarily by downward transport of high momentum associated with boundary layer streaks. These findings will advance the prediction and assessment of wind hazards associated with landfalling hurricanes.

488384.title: Estimating Current and Future Dust Exposure from the Shrinking Salton Sea
488384.authors: Xuan Liu, University of California San Diego, San Diego, CA; and W. C. Porter, S. H. Chen, J. F. Kok, G. Okin, A. A. Adebiyi, L. Xu, and A. T. Evan
488384.abstract: Dust is a major contributor to airborne particulate matter (PM) in arid and semi-arid regions, where expanding dry lakebeds and disturbed soils can be important emission sources. The ongoing shrinkage of California's Salton Sea is expanding exposed playa, creating a growing regional dust source that may be enriched with contaminants from historical agricultural and industrial activities. However, it remains unclear how much dust emitted from the Salton Sea playa contributes to regional PM10 exposure, and how this contribution will change as the playa expands. To address these questions, we apply the Air Force Weather Agency (AFWA) dust emission scheme within the Weather Research and Forecasting Model with Chemistry (WRF-Chem) to simulate dust emissions across the Salton Basin. We improve model inputs using high-resolution surface and meteorological datasets and optimize model configuration using a 3 km–1 km nested domain and meteorological nudging. We further improve the dust emission parameterization by replacing the sandblasting efficiency equation and incorporating dynamic bare soil fraction and vegetation drag partitioning derived from high-resolution satellite products. Model performance is evaluated against meteorological and aerosol observations, with emphasis on hourly wind and PM10 concentrations during four synoptic and convective dust events. We implement a source-tagging approach to quantify contributions from individual dust source regions, particularly the Salton Sea playa. Initial results indicate that communities southeast of the Salton Sea experience the highest population-weighted daily PM10 exposure from playa dust, which is estimated to increase by ~70% under the 2029 equilibrium playa extent scenario. These source-specific exposure estimates support assessments of dust-related health impacts and help inform air quality strategies in the Salton Basin.

488391.title: Process-Based Evaluation of Stratosphere-Troposphere Coupling In CMIP6 and AMIP6 Models
488391.authors: Amy H. Butler, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and D. Elsbury, Z. Lawrence, and E. M. Bednarz
488391.abstract: Motivated by evidence that differences between modeled and real-world ocean boundary conditions correlate with differences in remote parts of the large-scale circulation, even the stratosphere, this study evaluates stratosphere-troposphere coupling (STC) in reanalysis and pairs of climate models running with either prescribed 1979-2014 ocean boundary conditions (AMIP6) or with a fully coupled ocean (CMIP6, historical). Relative to AMIP6, CMIP6 models produce colder sea surface temperatures (SSTs) over the tropical-subtropical Pacific and Arctic, but warmer SSTs over the tropical East Pacific, East Atlantic, and Southern Ocean. These regional SST biases correlate with more equatorward-shifted subtropical jets and accelerated polar vortices in CMIP6 relative to AMIP6. The too-strong and too-cold CMIP6 polar vortices relative to AMIP6 and ERA5 reanalysis are further linked to overly weak climatological stationary waves in both hemispheres and issues simulating upward wave-mean flow interactions in the Southern Hemisphere spring. Both AMIP6 and CMIP6 produce early season planetary waves that are too weak in either hemisphere compared to ERA5, but then become too strong later in the season, paralleling delayed sudden stratospheric warming timing and biases in annular mode persistence seasonality. AMIP6 better captures El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) teleconnections to the North and South Pacific; however both AMIP6 and CMIP6 still struggle to simulate ENSO-polar vortex interactions, suggesting that the source of these model biases is not solely due to poorly simulated SSTs. Similarly, the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (QBO) morphology is comparable in AMIP6 and CMIP6.

488392.title: Hurricane Helene and the 2024 Flash Drought: Evidence for a Coupled Hydrological Whiplash Event
488392.authors: Kalena Charlotte Riemer, Washington University in St. Louis (WUSTL), St. Louis, MO; and P. C. Stoy, Y. Zhong, S. Ranjbar, S. Hoffman, T. Gerken, A. R. Desai, D. S. Henderson, and J. A. Otkin, PhD
488392.abstract: Understanding hydrological whiplashes – rapid transitions from dry to wet periods or vice versa – is increasingly important for water resource prediction and management. A unique hydrological whiplash occurred in the southeastern United States (SEUS) in autumn 2024, when historic flooding from Hurricane Helene was followed by rapid-onset flash drought. Hundreds of gauges across the eastern U.S. recorded no measurable precipitation in October 2024 following the hurricane in late September. This series of events highlights a gap in current drought monitoring systems, which do not accurately anticipate dryness after extreme wet conditions. Soil moisture generally hinders convective precipitation in the eastern U.S., where evapotranspiration (ET) and surface-atmosphere feedbacks are often energy-limited, suggesting that the hurricane itself may have contributed to the onset and propagation of flash drought. To understand potential connections between extreme wet and dry events at regional scales, we characterize changes in regional climate, soil moisture, evapotranspiration (ET), convective likelihood, and surface-atmosphere feedback strength before and after Hurricane Helene, and compare these against typical autumn conditions across the SEUS. We do so by integrating reanalysis, satellite‑derived fluxes, land surface modeling, and drought object tracking to diagnose mechanisms of flash drought onset, along with evaluating surface energy partitioning of how the Bowen ratio shifted after Hurricane Helene. Convective precipitation for September and October comprises some ⅔ and ½ of total precipitation, respectively, over the 30-year climatology, suggesting that its suppression will play an important role in regional hydroclimatology. A persistent subtropical ridge was present upwind of the study region through October, suppressing frontal systems. An analysis of drought ‘objects’ using the Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds (TOBAC) algorithm demonstrated that a drought object from the north and west re-entered the SEUS in October 2024 and contributed to record drought extent – nearly 80% of the CONUS – as determined by the U.S. Drought Monitor. Median convective triggering potential (CTP) at five inland sounding stations in October was not different from the long-term median, but the atmospheric humidity index (HiLow) was elevated at all stations; some 50% of days or more in October 2024 had HiLow values for which convection is unlikely, versus ⅓ in normal years. In addition to blocking from a persistent subtropical ridge, wet soils after the hurricane contributed to the autumn 2024 flash drought in the SEUS, which suggests that extreme wet events may precede drought. This case study underscores the need to add land-atmosphere feedbacks into drought monitoring and prediction frameworks.

488393.title: AI-RTMA: High Resolution AI Data Assimilation for the Realtime Mesoscale Analysis
488393.authors: Alexander Schein, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; NOAA/OAR/GSL, Boulder, CO; and M. Craine, G. Ge, T. T. Ladwig, and L. Lin
488393.abstract: The Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis (RTMA) (De Pondeca et al 2011) is an hourly, high-resolution (2.5 km) meteorological analysis produced for operational use, particularly for nowcasting and aviation (Morris et al 2020). RTMA uses a 2D-Var system to perform data assimilation, a computationally expensive step that takes several minutes to perform. Recent developments in machine learning for data assimilation (ML DA) have shown promise to reduce this time to a matter of seconds, drastically increasing the speed of analysis updates. One ML DA system, A Data Assimilation Framework (ADAF) (Xiang et al 2024) has shown encouraging results. Based on a Swin vision transformer architecture, ADAF trains on RTMA data, using HRRR for its background fields and ground station plus satellite observations to develop its final analysis. However, ADAF has only been trained and tested on a custom 0.05 x 0.05 degree grid - much coarser than the 2.5 km RTMA grid - and its station and satellite data involve products not currently used by RTMA. This new work extends the ADAF model to the RTMA grid, and uses surface observation data from the Mesonet and METAR station networks, similar to what is assimilated by RTMA. The model architecture is also modified to allow for longer-distance spatial context in the attention step, greatly improving data assimilation performance on the high-resolution grid. The model takes approximately 350 seconds per epoch to train on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, completes training within 24-36 hours, and can generate a complete analysis in less than 4 seconds on a single H100. Preliminary testing against non-assimilated METAR station observations shows the model’s RMSE for 2-meter temperature and specific humidity are within 5-15% of RTMA, and are effectively identical for 10-meter winds. Further development and testing is ongoing, especially on station data quality control as well as adding satellite observation data, with the goal of replicating the current 2D-RTMA and eventually transitioning to a three-dimensional analysis in line with the next generation of NOAA operational products. References: De Pondeca, M. S. F. V., and Coauthors, 2011: The Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis at NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Prediction: Current Status and Development. Wea. Forecasting, 26, 593–612, https://doi.org/10.1175/WAF-D-10-05037.1. Morris, M. T., J. R. Carley, E. Colón, A. Gibbs, M. S. F. V. De Pondeca, and S. Levine, 2020: A Quality Assessment of the Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis (RTMA) for Aviation. Wea. Forecasting, 35, 977–996, https://doi.org/10.1175/WAF-D-19-0201.1. Xiang, Y., Jin, W., Dong, H., Weyn, J., Bai, M., Fang, Z., et al. (2025). ADAF: An artificial intelligence data assimilation framework for weather forecasting. Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems, 17, e2024MS004839. https://doi.org/10.1029/2024MS004839

488400.title: Advancing the Readiness Level: Deployment and Use of a Ground-based Infrared Spectrometer for Thermodynamic Profiling at a NWS Weather Forecast Office
488400.authors: David D. Turner, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and B. LaSorsa, D. Brewer, S. Belak, L. Rosenthal, B. Adler, L. Bianco, K. Counts, and A. Dumont
488400.abstract: Uncertainties in the vertical structure of temperature and moisture in the boundary layer are one of the primary challenges associated with both situational awareness and forecasting for many meteorological phenomena. Ground-based infrared spectrometers (IRS) have demonstrated the ability to provide accurate high-temporal resolution profiles of temperature and water vapor in the atmospheric boundary layer in a range of different field campaigns, which have been used in numerous process studies, model evaluation efforts, data assimilation tests, and more over the last decade. As part of the CRADA with the vendor, we deployed an IRS, the Atmospheric Sounder Spectrometer by Infrared Spectral Technology (ASSIST), at the National Weather Service facility at Sterling, VA, in March 2026. Thermodynamic profiles were retrieved in real-time from the IRS’s observed radiance spectra using the TROPoe thermodynamic retrieval, and retrieved profiles and images showing both time-height cross-sections and skew-T plots were made available to NWS staff. These data were compared to radiosonde data launched at the Sterling site, and evaluated using colocated surface met observations. The IRS data were also used in real time by NWS forecasters to gain a better understanding of the state of the boundary layer for a range of applications ranging from frontal passages, preconvective-to-convective evolution, estimation of daytime convective temperatures, wind events, and more. Forecasters found the thermodynamic profiles from the IRS to be “confidence boosters” for multiple different challenging forecast situations. In this presentation, we will summarize the deployment, presenting interesting events where the IRS provided useful additional information and cases where it did not.

488408.title: Towards Continuous Data Assimilation at NOAA
488408.authors: Laura Slivinski, NOAA/OAR/PSL, Boulder, CO; and D. Holdaway and J. E. Ten Hoeve III
488408.abstract: NOAA has recently developed a moonshot vision for global leadership in weather prediction. One of the goals under this vision is to develop a continuous global data assimilation (DA) system with MPAS and JEDI to produce ‘on-demand’ initializations for physical and AI-based forecast models. NOAA Research, the National Weather Service, and the Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation have initiated a collaboration to make progress towards this goal over the next two years. Aspects of this project will include the development and tuning of a prototype global, hourly-cycling MPAS-JEDI system; development and evaluation of an AI DA system that can frequently initialize AI forecasts; development of a generic in-core DA capability within JEDI; and restructuring of observation preprocessing to support hourly DA. An overview of the plans for these activities will be presented.

488415.title: Non-Isotropic, Intermittent Mixing at the Top of the Convective Boundary Layer
488415.authors: David D. Turner, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and N. N. Karle, G. N. Raghunathan, T. Heus, and D. Rosenberg
488415.abstract: Turbulence in the convective boundary layer (CBL) plays a critical role in the vertical transport of heat and moisture. Characterizing it using higher-order statistics and scaling behavior is a major observational challenge. High-resolution Raman Lidar observations over a 3-day consecutive period in May 2018 from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement Southern Great Plains site were analyzed. The MicroHH large eddy simulation model was used to create simulated Raman lidar observations for these days also, and was analyzed using identical methods. These observations and simulated observations data show that in the well-mixed layer, the decay exponent derived using the classical autocovariance approach displays good agreement with the theoretical 2/3 value. However, in the vicinity of the CBL top, the exponent is larger than 2/3, indicating departure from Kolmogorov scaling. Using an optimal estimation framework, the Degrees of Freedom for Signal was derived, demonstrating that the lidar does have information on this exponent, lending confidence to the results. This is hypothesized to be associated with non-isotropic turbulent mixing. The skewness and excess kurtosis profiles were also derived from the same dataset. These data demonstrate that, around the top of the CBL, the turbulent mixing cannot be described as a gaussian process. The negative excess kurtosis demonstrates that the mixing is intermittent and caused by non-local mixing associated with larger eddies.

488425.title: Recognizing Storm Signatures: Machine Learning for High-Impact Extreme Precipitation in Bay Area Watersheds
488425.authors: Victoria Ford, Eagle Rock Analytics, Sacramento, CA; and J. Espinoza, H. Inda Diaz, B. McClenny, N. Schroeder, O. Doherty, J. Xu, D. Baral, T. Downs V, and A. Riggi
488425.abstract: Accurately identifying the atmospheric conditions that drive impactful hydrological events is essential for water utilities responsible for managing water supply, flood risk, and infrastructure resilience. In California, precipitation-producing storms represent both critical water resources and significant hazards, particularly when atmospheric rivers (ARs) and extratropical cyclones (ETCs) generate extreme rainfall across vulnerable watersheds. While advances in machine learning (ML) have improved weather prediction capabilities, many approaches prioritize predictive performance without providing the physical understanding needed for operational decision-making. We present an explainable machine learning framework designed to balance model predictions with physically interpretable atmospheric characteristics, enabling water managers to identify, understand, and anticipate impactful storms. We utilize a two-stage Boosted Decision Tree (BDT) machine learning framework to identify heavy precipitation producing atmospheric conditions for a water utility in Santa Clara County, California. The ML model is trained on historical atmospheric reanalysis data (ERA5) from 1994 to 2024 spanning the northeastern Pacific Ocean and western North America with observed precipitation records across the San Francisco Bay Area. Atmospheric predictors include variables commonly used by operational meteorologists, such as moisture transport, pressure fields, geopotential heights, and large-scale circulation patterns. To efficiently characterize complex atmospheric states, empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis is applied to reduce dimensionality while retaining the dominant modes of variability associated with storm evolution. Model interpretation is achieved using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis to quantify the contribution and importance of individual atmospheric features driving precipitation occurrence, combining both predictive capability and meteorological insight. We identify six dominant atmospheric patterns associated with impactful precipitation events in the San Francisco Bay Area. Two patterns represent atmospheric river configurations distinguished by the orientation and location of the core moisture plume, influencing precipitation distribution and duration. Two patterns represent atmospheric blocking regimes characterized by the positioning and evolution of upper-level troughs and ridges that control storm persistence and track. One pattern represents rapidly intensifying bomb cyclones associated with compact, fast-moving low-pressure systems capable of producing intense precipitation over short time periods. The final pattern represents a broader synoptic-scale low-pressure regime associated with the position and strength of the Aleutian Low and large-scale Pacific circulation. We will share hydrologically relevant metrics per pattern, including total precipitation, median storm duration, seasonal occurrence, and pattern sequencing. These analyses establish a historical event framework that allows past impactful storms to be grouped according to shared atmospheric drivers rather than individual event characteristics. This provides water managers with a structured reference for understanding storm behavior and evaluating potential impacts from future weather systems. By combining dimensionality reduction, interpretable ML, and meteorological analysis, this approach creates a balance between computational performance and operational understanding. The methodology is designed to be transferable and can be replicated for other watersheds and regions seeking to identify locally relevant precipitation patterns and improve hydrologic decision support. Ultimately, this work provides a scalable foundation for transforming complex atmospheric data into actionable information for water resource management and climate resilience. Key Takeaways: Learn about correlations and patterns between high precipitation storm patterns and resulting hydrological insights in the San Francisco Bay Area. Gain insights into developing workflows and decision-support tools that translate identified storm patterns into actionable information for water resource planning and operational preparedness. Learn more about a replicable framework for applying storm pattern recognition methods to other watersheds and communities across the San Francisco Bay Area and beyond.

488429.title: Developing a Three-Credit Professional Meteorology Course for Undergraduate and Graduate Students
488429.authors: Jacob Carstens, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and D. Margolin, A. P. Praino, K. Savoie, and C. A. Finley
488429.abstract: In the past two years, the domestic job market for weather and climate professionals has been particularly volatile. Additionally, reliance on various private entities for weather and climate data and services has expanded significantly. The need to prepare undergraduate and graduate atmospheric science students for careers in private industry has thus never been stronger. This presentation reviews the development, updates, and execution of "Introduction to Professional Meteorology" at the University of North Dakota in Fall 2026. It is a three-credit elective course open to both undergraduate and graduate students, taught previously by a faculty member with significant career experience in the renewable energy sector. The three-credit nature of the course permits more experiential, data-driven activities and assessments relative to one-credit courses that are often limited to providing surveys of different career pathways. These include the development of business plans, participation in mock forensic meteorology exercises, building private sector partnerships into academic grant writing, and energy load forecasting. Several aspects of the course development are reviewed, including designing materials in tandem with professionals across the weather, water, and climate community, building students' professional networks through the course, and incorporating written, verbal, and visual communication skills. Additional challenges and lessons learned are discussed for future offerings of the course, including working with a student body that includes graduate students, upper-division undergraduate majors, and one atmospheric sciences minor without a full math, physics, and computer programming background.

488430.title: Tropical Cyclone Climatology and Change in the MESACLIP Ensemble
488430.authors: Jacob Carstens, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and C. J. Hunter, J. M. Done, A. C. Didlake Jr., C. M. Zarzycki, and D. Fu
488430.abstract: The MESACLIP (MESoscale Atmosphere-ocean interactions in seasonal-to-decadal CLImate Prediction) project has produced an extensive ensemble of coupled climate simulations, with tropical cyclone (TC)-permitting (0.25° atmosphere) and ocean mesoscale eddy-resolving (0.1°) grid spacing. This allows a range of investigations at the intersection of TCs and climate risk, with both an extensive sample of TCs and no reliance on parametric models for TC wind and precipitation hazards. This study overviews TC climatology and change across the MESACLIP historical and future forcing scenarios. TCs are objectively tracked from modeled pressure and geopotential thickness fields using TempestExtremes. The algorithm is first applied to a 10-member ensemble with historical forcing spanning 1920-2005. Global patterns of TC genesis, track, intensity, and size are evaluated against satellite-era best track observations. Additionally, the environments unique to TCs are investigated in unprecedented detail for climate studies, with particular attention on environmental vertical wind shear and periods of rapid TC intensity change. Four Representative Concentration Pathways are used in MESACLIP to simulate tiers of future warming from 2006-2100, each of which are investigated here in the context of TC climatology and change. The more aggressive RCP8.5 and RCP6.0 tiers each have 10-member ensembles where TCs are tracked, and one simulation is also available for each of the less aggressive RCP4.5 and RCP2.6 tiers. Changes in TC behavior over time are tracked using distinct 30-year climatological periods within the broader 1920-2100 period covered by MESACLIP, motivating upcoming work on future changes in TC structure, hazard distribution, and interaction with the surrounding environment.

488434.title: Impact of Weak Atmospheric Rivers on Orographic Precipitation Gradient in Northern California.
488434.authors: Sam Morgan, University of Massachusetts Lowell, Boulder, CO; and M. R. Abel and L. M. Swenson
488434.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) contribute the majority of cool-season precipitation to California’s Sierra Nevada. Prior research suggests a potential future decrease in high elevation Sierra Nevada cool season precipitation, due to a reduction in the influence of orographic precipitation enhancement with climatological warming. This motivates an untested hypothesis: weak ARs produce larger orographic precipitation gradients (OPGs) than strong ARs, due to their tendency to have very little precipitation at low elevations. To test this hypothesis, we construct a catalog of ARs making landfall on the northern California coast (1980-2024) using the Guan and Waliser tARget v4 algorithm applied to ERA5. We classify ARs into “strong” and “weak” by their northern California Integrated water Vapor Transport (IVT) magnitude tercile and compute OPGs from precipitation from the 4 km gridded CONUS 404 dataset. We examine mechanistic controls on OPG variability using composites of IVT direction, magnitude, landfall location, and two different OPG calculation methods. Preliminary results show that weak ARs landfalling in northern California have a broader IVT direction distribution than strong ARs, and have a more westerly mean direction, significantly different from the mean southwesterly direction of strong ARs (p < 0.05). Past work has linked OPG to AR direction, indicating direction may be a critical distinction in the OPG differences between weak and strong ARs. OPGs calculated through a method of linear regression show larger OPGs (p < 0.05) in strong ARs than weak ARs. However, calculating OPG as a ratio of high to low elevation precipitation amounts shows that weak ARs have larger OPGs than strong ARs, which results from the very small low elevation precipitation amounts during weak ARs. Investigating composite distributions of precipitation for the weak and strong ARs reveals a more linear orographic enhancement during weak ARs, and a more regime-like orographic enhancement during strong ARs, suggestive of additional factors controlling the orographic precipitation response such as Sierra Barrier Jets. These factors are discussed to contextualize and understand the results.

488445.title: Impact of Weak Atmospheric Rivers on Orographic Precipitation Gradients in Northern California from 1980-2024.
488445.authors: Sam Morgan, University of Massachusetts Lowell, Boulder, CO; and M. R. Abel and L. M. Swenson

488461.title: Boundary Layer Influences on Cloud Dissipation Over Monterey Bay Using AWP and HALO
488461.authors: Devynn G Bishop, NASA, lexington, KY; and K. Lord, M. A. Demetillo, and K. M. Bedka
488461.abstract: Marine fog affects coastal visibility, marine transportation, and helps regulate coastal temperatures. It is a persistent forecasting challenge along the California coast because it is governed by complex, multi-scale interactions between the upper ocean and the marine boundary layer. While previous studies have shown that air-sea temperature differences and boundary layer inversions influence the fog lifecycle, the localized mechanisms responsible for fog dissipation remain uncertain. To investigate the atmospheric conditions associated with marine fog dissipation, observations collected during an airborne field campaign over Monterey Bay were analyzed. These observations were obtained during the Active and Passive Profiling EXperiment (APEX), conducted in conjunction with the NASA-NOAA West Coast and Heartland Hyperspectral Microwave Sensor Intensive Experiment (WHyMSIE). High-resolution observations of relative humidity, aerosol backscatter, and water vapor mixing ratio from the High Altitude Lidar Observatory (HALO), along with three-dimensional wind observations from the Aerosol Wind Profiler (AWP), were collected on November 9, 2024. These observations were analyzed alongside NOAA sea surface temperature (SST) products to characterize the atmospheric and oceanic conditions associated with the fog. In Monterey Bay, sea surface temperatures remained cooler than the near-surface air, providing favorable conditions for marine fog. However, as the fog was transported southward, the atmosphere became progressively drier. Wind speed and wind direction also varied with height within the marine boundary layer, indicating the presence of vertical wind shear.
