Results show that, over the analyzed time period, the northern portion of the flight exhibited a 32.7% higher water vapor mixing ratio than the southern portion. Additionally, when comparing the 0–125 m and 300–500 m layers, horizontal wind speeds increased by 63.5%, consistent with enhanced vertical wind shear and vertical mixing. These observations suggest that enhanced vertical wind shear and the transport and mixing of drier air within the marine boundary layer contributed to the observed fog dissipation over Monterey Bay.

488466.title: In-Situ Measurements of Black Carbon In a Periglacial Environment of Interior Alaska
488466.authors: Abhishek Singh, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and S. Aggarwal
488466.abstract: Black carbon (BC) is an important short-lived climate forcer that accelerates snow and ice melt through atmospheric absorption and deposition. Despite its climatic importance, in-situ atmospheric BC measurements in glacierized regions of interior Alaska remain scarce. During the summer of 2026, continuous BC and PM observations were conducted at the Gulkana Glacier region using an AE43 Aethalometer and low-cost PM sensors over multiple two-day campaigns in June, July, and August. Concurrent meteorological observations from the nearby USGS station were used to characterize atmospheric conditions during sampling. Preliminary results indicate predominantly low BC concentrations characteristic of a remote glacier environment, punctuated by episodic concentration enhancements that may reflect regional transport events. Ongoing analysis will examine relationships among BC, PM, and meteorological variables to characterize summertime aerosol variability in the Gulkana Glacier region. These measurements provide one of the first observational datasets describing atmospheric BC in this periglacial environment and contribute baseline information for future investigations of aerosol transport and cryosphere-atmosphere interactions.

488468.title: A Graph Neural Network for Global Daily Fire Radiative Power Prediction at Medium-Range Lead Times
488468.authors: Li Zhang, University of Colorado Boulder/CIRES & NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; and J. Wang, I. Jankov, Y. Liu, H. Chen, R. Ahmadov, L. Bernardet, and S. Kondragunta
488468.abstract: Skillful prediction of biomass-burning activity several days in advance is essential for air-quality forecasting, smoke management, and aerosol–weather coupling in Earth system models. A specific operational constraint motivates this work: the GBBEPx daily satellite fire radiative power (FRP) product used to initialize NOAA's GEFS-Aerosols global aerosol prediction system is available with an operational latency of approximately 1.5 days. The latest observed fire emissions are therefore unavailable at forecast initialization, requiring the system to use the most recently available daily emissions and implicitly assuming that fire activity remains representative throughout the latency period and the subsequent forecast. A predictive FRP capability would replace that assumption with an explicit forecast. This study presents a data-driven model for predicting global daily FRP at lead times of one to seven days. The model adapts a spatiotemporal graph neural network to the fire-prediction problem, driven by reanalysis meteorology, static land-cover and vegetation-state information, and recent fire history, with satellite-derived GBBEPx FRP as the training target. The approach accounts for the regionally distinct characteristics of global fire regimes through appropriate constraints. Trained in 2020–2022 and verified against fully independent observations for two holdout years bracketing the training period, 2019 and 2023, the model reproduces the global seasonal cycle of daily FRP, including the boreal-summer maximum. Skill is closely reproduced across both years, indicating that performance does not depend on temporal proximity to the training window. At the 1° scale relevant to aerosol forecasting, the critical success index spans approximately 0.32 to 0.55 across month and lead-day combinations, and Kling–Gupta efficiency is positive in the large majority of them, with skill degrading only gradually out to seven days. These results indicate that regional-scale fire activity is predictable several days in advance, with intensity calibration identified as the principal remaining challenge before predicted FRP can be converted to biomass-burning emissions for aerosol forecasting.

488469.title: Tracking Wildfire Chemistry across Diverse Spatial Scales
488469.authors: Lu Xu, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, MO; Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, MO
488469.abstract: Wildfires pose imminent threats to air quality and significantly impact global atmospheric composition. Understanding the effects of wildfire emissions on the atmospheric composition requires addressing two questions. First, what drives the variability in plume composition during near-field evolution? Second, how does the plume composition evolve during long-range transport? To answer these questions, we analyze data from recent laboratory experiments and field campaigns focused on characterizing wildfire emissions and their evolution. Our analysis sheds light on the near-field variability and chemical evolution across vast distances downwind for key species (e.g., organic aerosol, ozone, brown carbon, volatile organic compounds, NOy species). The outcomes of this research will enhance our ability to assess air quality in regions near wildfire sources, quantify wildfire contributions to regional ozone levels, and inform air quality policies to mitigate pollution during wildfire events in populated areas.

488471.title: Compressed Sensing Surrogates for Efficient Bayesian Quantification of Parameter Uncertainty: Experiments with an Idealized Cloud Model
488471.authors: Shifur Rahman Shakil, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and H. G. Chipilski, N. Dexter, and D. J. Posselt
488471.abstract: Earth system models often use column-based parameterization schemes with uncertain parameters. Nevertheless, a fully Bayesian characterization of this uncertainty from observations remains computationally intractable. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are commonly used as data-driven surrogates because of their expressiveness in high-dimensional problems. However, their high training costs and limited interpretability motivate the evaluation of alternative approximation methods. In this paper, we evaluate compressed sensing (CS) as a polynomial-based surrogate constructed by solving a weighted square-root LASSO problem. An idealized single-column cloud model (SCCM) is used as a testbed for estimating uncertain microphysical parameters, with both surrogates coupled to a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm for Bayesian inference. We find that the DNN- and CS-based MCMC posteriors agree quantitatively and qualitatively, with the remaining discrepancies associated with enhanced sensitivity to a small number of microphysical parameters. However, the CS surrogate is substantially less expensive: its training cost remains nearly constant as the training dataset grows, whereas the DNN training cost increases approximately linearly. During inference, the CS surrogate reduces the MCMC wall-clock time by roughly a factor of two. Given its comparable posterior accuracy, the computationally efficient CS approach provides a viable alternative for estimating uncertain parameters and opens new possibilities for calibrating column-based parameterization schemes in Earth system models.

488481.title: Observational Analysis of Large-Scale Atmospheric Controls on Regional Surface Mass Balance of Greenland Using the SUMup Database
488481.authors: Casey Lauren Reynolds, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and C. Strong and S. Rupper
488481.abstract: The Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) is a significant contributor to global sea level rise, yet uncertainty persists about surface mass loss driven by large-scale atmospheric circulation. The Surface Mass Balance and Snow on Sea Ice Working Group (SUMup) dataset provides an in situ record of surface mass balance (SMB) variability across the GrIS. Using SUMup SMB data and ERA-20C reanalysis (1900-2000), we identified large-scale atmospheric patterns associated with GrIS SMB variability. SMB observations were objectively clustered into three geographic regions (Northeast (NE), Southeast (SE), and West (W)), and monthly climatology, seasonal regression, synoptic composite, and empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analyses were used to characterize atmospheric controls on regional SMB variability. SMB trends accounted for less than 2% of total variance, so all data were detrended to isolate interannual variability. Results showed distinct circulation mechanisms in each region. NE SMB in June-August (JJA) was associated with patterns resembling the positive North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and negative Pacific North American (PNA) pattern, with La Niña-like sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies, suggesting a tropical teleconnection. SE SMB in December-February (DJF) was associated with a propagating wavenumber-3 (wave-3) circulation pattern, identified via Hilbert EOF analysis. W SMB was affected by a recurring downstream blocking ridge in DJF and September-November (SON), with a tropical Rossby wave source in SON. These signals were consistent across multiple reanalysis datasets and century sub-periods, reinforcing confidence in the findings and positioning SUMup as an observational benchmark for future general circulation model experiments examining anthropogenic impacts on GrIS SMB. These observationally derived circulation-SMB relationships are now being evaluated in a 10,000-year Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL) simulation with anthropogenic forcing held fixed at 1990 levels, isolating internal atmospheric variability from forced climate change. This allows assessment of whether the identified NAO/PNA, wave-3, and blocking mechanisms appear on multi-centennial and millennial timescales, and examination of inter-century differences. Analysis across the full simulation period will determine whether these teleconnections represent robust, persistent modes of GrIS SMB variability or are contingent on the specific climate state captured by the 20th century.

488486.title: Towards Operational Field-Scale Evapotranspiration Forecasting: A Multi-Landscape Evaluation of Deep Learning Models
488486.authors: Apoorva Jha, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA; and N. E. Bambach, V. Singh, M. C. Anderson, W. Kustas, A. McElrone, M. Swintek, A. Petrosian, M. Earles, and K. R. Knipper
488486.abstract: OpenET has established field-scale operational evapotranspiration (ET) mapping as a key driver of sustainable water management. OpenET is built on an ensemble of models that utilize satellite- and meteorological-based input datasets to estimate actual ET at the daily timestep. Included in that ensemble is the ALEXI/DisALEXI framework that was the focus of this study. A natural next step to the current suite of OpenET capabilities is to extend the retrospective products into forecasting systems capable of predicting ET several days in advance such that it aids processes like irrigation scheduling, water allocation, and heat wave response. While deep learning has shown considerable promise for spatiotemporal forecasting, operational deployment requires models that generalize across heterogeneous landscapes, remain computationally practical at scale, and maintain reliable performance beyond the environments in which they were developed. Understanding this gap is critical before ET forecasting can transition from research demonstrations to operational systems. We present a systematic multi-site benchmark for field-scale ET forecasting using a multi-year, satellite-derived ET record spanning California landscapes selected to capture broad contrasts in climate, land cover, and spatial extent—from relatively homogeneous single-crop parcels to large, heterogeneous regions containing mixed agriculture and natural vegetation. Forecasting architectures representing recurrent, video-prediction, and transformer-based model families are evaluated alongside non-learned reference forecasts under a common experimental protocol, ensuring that performance differences reflect the forecasting methods rather than differences in evaluation. The benchmark is explicitly designed to mirror the challenges encountered in operational deployment. We evaluate whether forecasting skill is maintained as landscapes become larger and more heterogeneous, whether models trained on some sites transfer successfully to previously unseen locations, and whether joint multi-site training improves generalization relative to site-specific models. Recognizing that operational suitability depends not only on predictive skill but also on computational feasibility, every model is additionally evaluated in terms of inference cost and training time, allowing forecast quality and computational efficiency to be assessed together rather than independently. The goal of this study is to provide an operational-readiness assessment of deep learning for field-scale ET forecasting. Initial results indicate that across the full site-by-architecture matrix, the most accurate architecture, a convolutional recurrent network, reaches a mean absolute error of 0.44 mm/day but trails on spatial and temporal fidelity. A simpler recurrent architecture achieves the strongest spatial fidelity and the highest temporal coherence (𝛾² of 0.93, versus 0.72 for the most accurate model), at the cost of roughly 18% higher forecast error. A third architecture, a convolutional encoder-decoder, trains in well under half the compute of either alternative, but has the weakest temporal coherence of the three (𝛾² of 0.58). We will present emerging results with an open benchmarking framework designed to support evidence-based architecture selection and accelerate the transition of ET forecasting from research prototypes toward scalable operational systems.

488487.title: Leveraging Satellite Data for Wildfire Monitoring and Public Health Impact Assessment
488487.authors: Hazem Mahmoud, NASA LaRC ASDC ADNET, Yorktown, VA; and S. Scott and G. Mojica
488487.abstract: Wildfires represent a critical environmental challenge in North America, directly threatening air quality, ecosystems, and human health. NASAs Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) mission provides unprecedented hourly observations of formaldehyde (HCHO), cloud properties, and tropospheric composition across North America, enabling transformative wildfire monitoring and impact analysis. This example demonstrates TEMPO's operational utility for wildfire science through three applications: (1) rapid fire detection using HCHO anomalies and NO2 retrievals; (2) real-time air quality forecasting through HCHO measurements correlated with smoke plume dynamics; and (3) public health impact assessment by integrating TEMPO data with health records and surface monitors. Case studies from the June 2024 Excelsior Fire event in Los Angeles showcase TEMPO's ability to detect formaldehyde enhancements, distinguish pyrocumulus clouds from background atmospheres, and track pollution transport across multiple states. Integration of TEMPO data through NASA tools (Worldview, Earthdata Search, GIS services) enables emergency responders, public health officials, and researchers to make rapid, data-driven decisions. Our work demonstrates how advanced satellite remote sensing, coupled with strategic data infrastructure, accelerates the transition from research observations to operational Earth Action solutions for climate resilience and public health protection.

488490.title: A Hybrid Dynamical-Machine Learning Tool Based on ENSO and the MJO for Operational Realtime Subseasonal Precipitation Forecasting
488490.authors: Cheng Zheng, SUNY, Stony Brook, NY; and E. LaJoie, W. M. Thiaw, W. Wang, H. Kim, and E. K. M. Chang
488490.abstract: Precipitation over North America is strongly modulated by the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO). Statistical forecast tools that leverage the observed states of these two predictors can provide skillful subseasonal precipitation predictions and are currently used to support operational subseasonal outlooks. Here, we develop a hybrid dynamical–machine learning (ML) tool, that combines observed ENSO and MJO conditions with MJO forecasts from dynamical forecast systems as predictors, to support subseasonal (weeks 3-4) precipitation forecasting at NOAA's NWS Weather Prediction Center's Extended Prediction Division (WPD-EPD). The hybrid framework offers two key advantages. First, its ML component is trained using large-ensemble climate model simulations rather than the relatively limited observational record. The substantially larger training dataset from climate models enables the ML component to learn more robust relationships between ENSO and the MJO with precipitation, resulting in improved predictive skill compared with statistical models trained solely on observations. Second, incorporating dynamical MJO forecasts, which are skillful on subseasonal time scales, enables the hybrid model to yield higher forecast skill than conventional statistical approaches that rely only on past observed conditions of ENSO and MJO. When the tool is tested using ECMWF and GEFS hindcasts, the hybrid tool outperforms the dynamical-only forecasts during fall and early winter, and exhibits comparable skill during winter and early spring. When the hybrid model forecast is optimally combined with the dynamical forecasts, the resulting product outperforms the dynamical-only forecasts over all seasons. The forecast tool, developed at Stony Brook University, has been delivered to the EPD and is currently supporting operational real time forecasting. The performance of this tool will be discussed and compared with current operational tools.

488491.title: Joint NOx and NMVOC Emission Inversions Using TEMPO and TROPOMI Data and the Downstream Impacts on Long-Lived Trace Gases
488491.authors: Chia-Hua Hsu, National Institute for Environmental Studies, Japan, Tsukuba, Japan; National Institute for Environmental Studies, Tsukuba, Japan, Japan; and D. K. Henze, A. P. Mizzi, C. Lyu, R. H. Schwantes, C. Harkins, O. R. Cooper, J. He, M. Li, D. B. Millet, K. Wells, J. Kaiser, S. Kondragunta, S. Kondragunta, K. Bates, R. B. Pierce, C. B. Francoeur, S. Wang, S. Wang, C. R. Nowlan, X. Liu, B. C. McDonald, and G. Gonzalez Abad
488491.abstract: Nitrogen oxides (NOx) and non-methane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs) are major air pollutants and primary precursors to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and ozone (O3). We aim to constrain summertime anthropogenic and biogenic NOx and NMVOC emissions by assimilating TEMPO and TROPOMI NO2 and formaldehyde (HCHO) observations using WRF-Chem/Chem-DART. TEMPO and TROPOMI NO2 data show good consistency, whereas TROPOMI HCHO is systematically lower than TEMPO HCHO by 30–40% over the southeastern US. A simple bias correction was applied to TROPOMI HCHO prior to data assimilation. Top-down NOx emissions derived from TEMPO and TROPOMI data exhibit similar magnitudes, yielding emissions 5–20% lower than prior estimates. For biogenic isoprene, posterior emissions are substantially reduced by 50–60%, indicating a significant overestimation in prior biogenic NMVOC emissions. Top-down anthropogenic NMVOC emissions derived from both satellites are also 20–30% lower in urban areas. We evaluated the model simulations against several independent datasets to assess emission inversion performance. TEMPO-derived biogenic isoprene emissions show better spatiotemporal representation compared to TROPOMI, as evidenced by good agreement with CrIS isoprene retrievals and ground-based HCHO observations. While overall top-down NOx emissions appear to be underestimated, TEMPO-derived emissions demonstrate better performance when evaluated against surface AQS and AEROMMA aircraft observations, particularly in the Los Angeles Basin. Updating anthropogenic NMVOCs effectively mitigates the overprediction of HCHO and other NMVOC species in urban areas—as illustrated by DC-8 aircraft measurements—with TEMPO providing better constraints on NMVOC emissions. Joint NOx and NMVOC inversions yielded the best O3 simulations compared to NMVOCs-only inversions. We also discovered that NMVOCs emission estimates are sensitive to NOx updates, resulting in a 10% difference in posterior emissions due to complex NOx–OH–HCHO chemical feedbacks. Finally, updating NOx and NMVOC emissions had a marked impact on atmospheric oxidation capacity, altering OH levels by up to 20–40%. These shifts in OH levels directly affect the lifetimes of long-lived species such as CO and CH4, changing their regional instantaneous lifetimes by ~25%, which significantly impacts the quantification of their sources and sinks. Our work highlights the crucial role of future multi-species joint emission inversions in accounting for complex chemical feedbacks to yield more accurate top-down emission estimates.

488492.title: MAGGIE: Marine Assimilation with Generative Graphs in E3SM
488492.authors: Luke P. Van Roekel, LANL, Berthoud, CO; LANL, Los Alamos, NM; and A. Roberts, P. M. Caldwell, O. J. Ikuyajolu, A. E. Shao, I. Grooms, T. Hillebrand, and E. K. de Jong
488492.abstract: Accurate ocean and sea-ice initialization is essential for accurate coupled prediction from subseasonal to interannual timescales, but sparse observations, the cost of conventional data assimilation (DA), and the inability to strongly couple DA components limit the production of balanced initial conditions. Direct insertion of reanalysis fields can also introduce initialization shock and model drift. We present Marine Assimilation with Generative Graphs in E3SM (MAGGIE), a DOE Genesis Mission project to develop a generative data assimilation framework, for constructing observation-constrained ensembles of coupled ocean–sea-ice initial states directly on the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) native unstructured mesh. MAGGIE learns a prior distribution of multivariate ocean and sea-ice time series states from E3SM simulations and uses observations to guide sampling toward physically plausible states consistent with available measurements. MAGGIE combines latent score-based diffusion models with graph neural networks (GNNs). Performing diffusion in a compressed latent space reduces computational cost, while the GNN represents native-mesh connectivity, preserves multivariate relationships, and avoids information loss from interpolation to regular grids. Unlike conventional ensemble-based DA, MAGGIE learns spatial and multivariate structure from E3SM simulations without finite-ensemble covariance estimates or conventional localization. Separating the generative prior from observation conditioning enables multimodal observations to be incorporated without retraining the model. The E3SMv3 coupled ocean–sea-ice configuration serves as the test bed, with observations from SWOT, Argo floats, Ice-Tethered Profilers, and ICESat-2. Generated ensembles will be compared with existing E3SM initial conditions using observational consistency, physical balance, ensemble uncertainty, initialization drift, and coupled forecast skill. Early results from the implementation and evaluation of MAGGIE will be presented.

488494.title: Asymmetry of El Niño and La Niña Precipitation Diversity
488494.authors: Sunyong Kim, APEC Climate Center, Busan, Korea, Republic of (South); and J. S. Kug
488494.abstract: El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) precipitation diversity exhibits pronounced phase-dependent asymmetry over the tropical Pacific. Observations indicate enhanced precipitation diversity over the western North Pacific during La Niña and over the equatorial central Pacific during El Niño. This asymmetry is associated with the positively skewed distribution and intensified extremes of tropical precipitation, implying that diversity tends to increase during ENSO phases with enhanced mean precipitation. Atmosphere-only simulations reasonably reproduce the observed asymmetric features of ENSO-related precipitation diversity, whereas fully coupled simulations underestimate its amplitude and shift the center westward. Inter-model comparisons further demonstrate weak consistency between the two simulations, with atmosphere-only experiments generally reproducing stronger precipitation diversity, suggesting an important role of SST forcing in determining the asymmetric ENSO precipitation diversity across tropical Pacific regions.

488497.title: DMS Uplift By Tropical Cyclones As a Source of SO2 In the Upper Troposphere
488497.authors: Sijia Lou, Nanjing University, Nanjing, 32, China
488497.abstract: Airborne observations from ACCLIP on 2 August 2022, combined with Lagrangian particle dispersion model (LPDM) back trajectories, reveal that SO2 mixing ratios at 14-16 km were enhanced by a factor of 4-6 in regions influenced by tropical cyclones (TCs). These enhancements are linked to rapid lofting of marine dimethyl sulfide (DMS) into the upper troposphere (UT). GEOS-Chem simulations indicated that on 31 July 2022, TC-scale circulation injected DMS into the UT within hours, with a mean flux of 9.4 kg h-1 across 0.5-12 km and 8.4% of emissions penetrating above 12 km, consistent with observations of elevated DMS at the same altitudes. Because of its low solubility and longer UT lifetime (59.2 h vs. 5.7 h at the surface), DMS sustains SO2 production that is largely resistant to wet scavenging. This TC-driven pathway provides a significant natural SO2 source in the UT, with implications for aerosol–cloud–climate interactions.

488500.title: SO2... What’s Next?: Automating the Detection of SO2 Interference in Ozonesonde Profiles in Volcanic Regions
488500.authors: Anna Grace Hagberg, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and G. A. Morris and Z. D. Griffith
488500.abstract: Balloon-borne measurements provide a high-quality, in-situ record of ozone profiles in the atmosphere via ozonesonde instruments. Ozonesondes utilize a redox reaction involving ozone bubbled into a potassium iodide solution. However, sulphur dioxide (SO2) in the sample air interferes with the ozone measurement as it causes a flow of electrons opposite to the ozone reaction. This SO2 reaction creates sharp drops–referred to as notches–in the measured ozone signal that do not reflect actual atmospheric ozone variability. These artificial notches in ozone profiles complicate the interpretation of individual profiles and can affect long-term trend analyses in volcanic and highly polluted regions susceptible to SO2-rich plumes. The current approach to this problem relies on characterization of these notches through performing visual inspection of individual profiles. This process is time-intensive and can only be verified through the use of a dual-sonde payload. However, these dual-sonde flights are resource intensive and the reliability of their data is variable and not yet fully characterized. The Ticosonde project launched dual-sonde payloads intermittently from 2012-2020 in San Jose, Costa Rica, providing a ground-truth database for ozone and SO2 in the troposphere and lower stratosphere. This work leverages the Ticosonde database to develop a machine learning algorithm to automate the identification of SO2 interference in the standard, unfiltered ozonesonde data. The machine learning architectures selected for evaluation are a Gaussian Mixture Model and a Convolutional Neural Network. Insights from this investigation are designed for implementation, characterizing SO2 interference in long-term records at baseline observatories as well as short-term campaigns. Preliminary results are promising, with the two different models agreeing with each other on 96% of the Costa Rica notches, and agreeing with visual inspection on 86% of the notches.

488504.title: Calibration and Validation of the SOLAR-1 Magnetometer
488504.authors: Konstantinos Horaites, CIRES, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and N. Howard, F. Inceoglu, J. V. Rodriguez, B. Short, D. Vassiliadis, M. Grotenhuis, J. Kronenwetter, M. Argall, B. Vasquez, I. Dors, C. Smith, and R. Torbert
488504.abstract: The Space Weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness - 1 (SOLAR-1, formerly SWFO-L1) NOAA mission was launched in September 2025, as a successor to the DSCOVR mission. The satellite observes incoming solar wind particles and fields before they reach Earth, and in particular the in situ magnetic field serves as a "key parameter" for operational prediction of space weather events. Our magnetometer team began the process of in-flight instrument commissioning as the spacecraft journeyed to the L1 Lagrange point, and we project the data will be fully validated by early 2027. This presentation reviews our post-launch calibration-validation efforts: the determination of instrumental zero-level offsets, characterization of noise signals originating from the spacecraft, and cross-comparison of the magnetometer measurements with other L1 satellites. Notably, the proximity of the SOLAR-1 and IMAP satellites, which were launched together in a rideshare configuration, has enabled an unprecedented level of cross-calibration between the two satellites' fluxgate magnetometers. We discuss the state and quality of the magnetometer measurements, which will be of great value to the operational and scientific communities.

488514.title: Tomorrow.io Satellite Microwave Sounder Data Evaluations in the IFS System
488514.authors: Zaizhong Ma, UMD/CISESS, College Park, MD; University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and N. Bormann, D. Duncan, K. Lean, E. Turner, S. Panditharatne, M. Crepulja, M. Dahoui, and S. Kalluri
488514.abstract: This study presents the first comprehensive evaluation and all-sky assimilation of observations from the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) CubeSat constellation within the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Integrated Forecasting System (IFS). Observations from three sun-synchronous satellites (TMS-02, TMS-05, and TMS-06) collected during September–November 2025 are processed and assimilated in IFS Cycle 50r1 with a 12-hour 4D-Var configuration at TCo399 (~27 km) resolution. Each TMS instrument carries a 12-channel microwave radiometer with temperature sounding channels near 118 GHz, humidity sounding channels near 183 GHz, and window channels near 91 and 204 GHz. The objective is to assess the quality and numerical weather prediction (NWP) impact of commercial CubeSat microwave sounding observations and provide guidance for future miniaturized satellite observing systems. Data quality is assessed using observation-minus-background (O-B) statistics from the ECMWF system, with emphasis on channel-dependent behaviour, orbital and scan-dependent biases and temporal stability. Results are compared with those from heritage microwave sounders (i.e., MHS and MWHS-2) to place the CubeSat observations in an operational context. While global mean biases and noise performance for these early TMS instruments are in line with expectations, there are significant orbital biases and other anomalies present, particularly for TMS-05 and -06. The findings indicate remaining issues with calibration and instrument characterisation, and these will need to be improved for the data quality to become comparable to that of operational heritage sensors. Observing System Experiments (OSEs) are then conducted over a selected three-month period to evaluate the forecast impact of assimilating TMS observations into ECMWF’s global data assimilation system. Only channels demonstrating sufficient data quality are included. Orbital biases are addressed through a tailored bias correction and ad-hoc quality control. With these instrument-specific treatments in place, the three TMS satellites achieve overall a mostly neutral impact when added to the full operational observing system.

488515.title: From NetCDF to Cloud-Native: Operationalizing Zarr for Historical Forecast Access at Scale
488515.authors: Lorenzo Riches, Solcast, a DNV Company, North Sydney, NSW, Australia; and H. Jack
488515.abstract: At Solcast, a DNV company, we are heavy consumers of NWP data to support our PV and Wind production forecasting products. The distribution wall described by this session is not hypothetical for operational forecast providers—it is a daily constraint on what products we can build. We have completed a full migration of our operational NWP (Numerical Weather Prediction) data stores from NetCDF to cloud-optimized Zarr (v3). We are currently serving over 200 fields across 7 models (and growing), with historical issues extending more than 2 years into the past, in total comprising over 800TB of data (when uncompressed at 32-bit precision). Critically, this was not a format modernization for its own sake: it was driven by concrete product requirements that were effectively impossible under sequential-access formats, while remaining a 1:1 functional replacement for existing gridded-extraction use cases. This submission presents the architecture, the design trade-offs, measured performance, the operational difficulties we encountered, and a set of open questions we believe the community must resolve for cloud-native distribution to become a durable standard rather than a fragmented collection of bespoke implementations. The core requirement: historical forecasts at arbitrary lead time NWP forecast data is a critical input to many of our products. The central motivation for the migration was supporting historical forecast access—the ability to reconstruct the full NWP forecast as it was available at a point in the past. The primary use-cases for this data are back-testing, forecast skill evaluation by customers and training data generation. Data storage is a significant portion of the operational costs, especially when persisting all issues and lead times, so having both single point and grid optimized optimised store is prohibitive. Critically, the data access pattern here is often a single location or small region covering a long period of time but often needs to scale to entire continents or the globe. For example, a real use case we had was extracting 11 GFS (Global Forecast System, NOAA) parameter fields for 6-hourly issues over 2 years of history, in total 11 * 4 * 365 * 2 = ~32,000 individual files each comprising 90 hourly steps. Our new Zarr archive enables this retrieval in 25 minutes on a single CPU core; putting what before was a multi-day extract job onto the level of a small batch job. Our pre-existing NetCDF based archive (single file per issue time) could not serve this use case without prohibitively large amounts of compute: extracting a single location involved an approximately million-fold overhead of download I/O and decompression by pulling the whole grid then extracting the single point. During this session we will be presenting results showing the performance of the store, the operational trade-offs and discuss the additional complexity. Design Decisions We will discuss our design decisions around: Chunking: how we struck a balance between single-location-many-issues and whole-grid-single-issue queries without duplicating data; and our use of the relatively obscure Zarr “shards” feature to mitigate the performance characteristics of S3 as a storage backend particularly around listing and copying large numbers of objects. Single Zarr archive per-model: this provides excellent discoverability of available models and their parameters, without requiring bespoke in-house libraries. Standardised parameter naming, units, and level: this enforces consistency for consumers, and provides a framework for new models being added to the store. Single centralised writer: how we ensure data integrity but also keep writes performant enough to populate years’ worth of history in hours. Pain points We will highlight the pain points with using Zarr for this purpose and how we mitigate against them. Writing: concurrent writes can subtly (and not-so-subtly) corrupt data; partial writes can corrupt data; the “append” dimension (issue time in our case) cannot be re-ordered or have subsets of values deleted; getting an archive into a corrupt state at best means a lot of time deleting data and in the worst case means you can’t trust anything in your archive. Reading: The default fill value means that the reader in unable to differentiate between “this value is NaN” and “this data was never initialised”; reading the archive while it is being updated can cause errors with the standard interfaces; although large-region-single-issue queries are servable they require fine-tuning and cannot be naively served by using defaults; and finally many of our data scientists need to be retrained as to be able to use the stores requires understanding of concepts like chunking and careful planning of compute graphs. We also encountered the tooling-maturity gap between the specification and robust, production-grade implementations that led us to a native re-write rather than using virtualization and available tooling. Questions to the community Should the community converge on chunking and layout conventions, so datasets are genuinely interoperable rather than technically-Zarr-but-practically-bespoke? What is the maturity and experience in the community using virtualization/reference-based access to legacy archives and native rewrites (i.e. Icechunk) how we build the trust in the tools and datasets so that we can stop duplication, praising initiative like Dynamical.org but seeing what happened to HRRRZARR and the Planetary Computer makes them a hard sell. It is encouraging to see a focus on improving the distribution, however how do we ensure historical NWP forecasts are available to distribute in the first place?

488523.title: Toward Impact-Based Forecasting for Aviation: Integrating PIREPs, METAR/SPECI, and Number of Flight
488523.authors: Mochammad Donny Anggoro, Newcastle University, newcastle upon tyne, United kingdom; and H. J. Fowler, A. Kahraman, and P. Davies
488523.abstract: Despite Indonesia’s extensive and geographically dispersed aviation network, few studies have quantified operational exposure to meteorological hazards at individual airports. The purpose of this study is to evaluate Indonesian airport vulnerability, describe the seasonal and daily incidence of aviation risks, and assist in the creation of Impact-Based Forecasting (IBF) thresholds tailored to individual airports. Pilot reports and average hourly arrival, departure, and local-flight movements were integrated with METAR/SPECI. Traffic-weighted exposure was assessed by multiplying each hazard's hourly frequency by traffic during the corresponding hour. Records were harmonised at airport-hour resolution and temporal climatologies. Tailwinds and inclement weather/rain events dominated pilot reports. Initial airport-level assessments ranked convective systems as the leading hazard, followed by heavy rain and tailwinds; convective-system influence scores ranged from 70 to 100, while heavy-rain scores ranged from approximately 43 to 61. Exposure was concentrated in Java and Sulawesi. Soekarno–Hatta International Airport consistently recorded the highest traffic intensity and traffic-weighted exposure, followed by Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport and Juanda International Airport. Across Indonesia’s time zones, rainfall exposure peaked at approximately 17:00–19:00 LT, whereas convective exposure peaked at approximately 15:00–17:00 LT. Monthly exposure was lowest in August and highest in April, November, and December, reflecting suppressed rainfall during the peak dry season and enhanced convective activity during the transitional and early wet-season periods. Future work will integrate runway, approach, and fleet characteristics with delay, go-around, and air-traffic-flow-management impact labels to develop and validate an airport–hour model classifying impacts as low, medium, or high.

488526.title: JMA's Development Plans for Machine Learning Weather Prediction and AI-Enhanced Forecast Guidance Systems
488526.authors: Yohei Shirayama, JMA, Minato-ku, 13, Japan; and M. Kazumori, Y. Tanaka, Y. Ota, and S. Hagiya
488526.abstract: This presentation provides an overview of the Japan Meteorological Agency’s (JMA) plans for the development of machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models and AI-enhanced forecast guidance systems. In June 2026, JMA released an enhanced version of its Numerical Weather Prediction Strategic Plan Toward 2030. The plan is based on the 2025 revision of the policy document “Meteorological Operations Focusing on Science and Technology Toward 2030”, which identifies the utilization of advanced AI technologies as a key measure for enhancing meteorological services. Based on this plan, JMA is advancing the parallel development of conventional physics-based weather prediction models and forecasting technology using AI, with the aim of improving meteorological information for disaster prevention and mitigation. For MLWP models, JMA plans to begin with the development of a global forecasting model, followed by enhancing its resolution in and around Japan, and introducing ensemble prediction capabilities. For AI-enhanced forecast guidance, JMA plans to develop DNN-based technologies for the seamless blending of multiple forecast outputs, as well as multi-model forecast guidance derived from the blended forecasts.

488530.title: Development of Ship-Based Water Vapor and Wind Lidar for Monitoring Moisture Inflow Causing Heavy Rain In Japan: Preliminary Result
488530.authors: Tetsu Sakai, MRI, Tsukuba, 08, Japan; MRI, Tsukuba, Ibaraki, Japan; and T. Nagai, S. Yoshida, M. Nishihashi, E. Oikawa, T. Nagao, H. Seko, and T. Hasegawa
488530.abstract: The frequency of occurrences of torrential rainfall has been increasing in Japan over the last fifty years. To understand the mechanism of torrential rainfall and predict it accurately and at an earlier stage, it is desirable to monitor moist air flowing from the ocean to the land that cause the rainfall. To meet this requirement, we have deployed a coherent differential absorption lidar (DIAL) that simultaneously measures the vertical distributions of water vapor and wind in the lower troposphere on board the Japan Meteorological Agency research vessel Keifu Maru since 2026 (Fig. 1). The dimensions of the lidar are 1.0 m in width, 1.0 m in length, and 1.1 m in height, and the weight is 250 kg, making it installable in the limited space on the vessel's deck. It transmits laser pulses at wavelengths around 1.53 µm with a pulse energy of 14 µJ and a repetition rate of 16 kHz at a zenith angle of 11.2° in azimuth-angle intervals of 90° every 1 seconds. The backscatter signal from the atmosphere is heterodyne detected by a balanced receiver and converted to an electrical signal. The temporal and vertical resolutions of the measurement are 10 minutes and 100 m, respectively. To account for the vessel’s motion on lidar measurement, an inertial navigation system is used to measure the vessel’s position, attitude, and motion. The lidar allows continuous unattended measurement during the month-long voyage. Figure 2 shows the preliminary results of the time-height cross sections of water vapor density, horizontal wind direction, and horizontal wind speed measured with the lidar on the Keifu Maru at berth in Daiba on 22 April 2026. In this presentation, we will present the details of the lidar system and the preliminary results of the measurements taken over the ocean in the summer of 2026.

488534.title: Observations From LIDAR-derived Visibility Distribution Around Hong Kong International Airport Under Haze and Thin Mist
488534.authors: Man Lok Chong, Hong Kong Observatory, Hong Kong, China
488534.abstract: Doppler LIDAR systems, originally deployed at the Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA) for wind shear and turbulence detection, offer a secondary capability for deriving visibility. As the LIDARs operate at wavelengths near the visible spectrum, they receive backscatter from atmospheric aerosols via Mie scattering. The visibility can be derived from the range-corrected received power at each LIDAR range gate, with real-time adjustments based on measurements from neighbouring forward scatterometers. Hence, a continuous distribution of aerosols can be derived from plan position indicator (PPI) scans and range height indicator (RHI) scans, providing early indication of visibility deterioration caused by advection. The method is particularly effective for dry aerosols like haze, but would also be able to detect low visibility resulting from thin mist. However, LIDAR signals attenuate rapidly in the presence of fog or low clouds. A few cases with haze and mist detected by the LIDAR would be presented. The visibility trend derived from LIDAR generally aligns with independent visibility meter readings.

488536.title: Data-Driven Characterization of North Atlantic Tropical Cyclone-Linked Atmospheric Rivers Affecting Western Europe
488536.authors: Sachit Parekh, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA; and M. N. Malasala, K. Wu, X. Wu, and V. S. Tallapragada
488536.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are long, narrow channels of atmospheric water vapor that are responsible for significant impacts across the subtropical regions, subjecting areas to heavy rains and strong winds. During the Atlantic hurricane season, moisture associated with an active tropical cyclone (TC) can become incorporated into a water vapor transport feature akin to that of an AR. Such an AR can further impact western Europe, leading to periods of intense rainfall. This research defines this phenomenon as a tropical cyclone-linked atmospheric river (TCLAR) and aims to characterize the synoptic structure of TCLARs that form over the North Atlantic and affect western Europe. Prior events in the Western Pacific and North Atlantic were previously analyzed by Cordeira et al. (2013) and Doiteau et al. (2021), and this research aims to contextualize this phenomenon in the North Atlantic as a whole. AR catalogs developed by Rutz et al. (2014) and Guan and Waliser (2015) are used in conjunction with HURDAT2 to visually identify TCLAR events from the 2000-2015 hurricane seasons. Multivariate ERA5 data is then used to analyze their synoptic-scale atmospheric environments. A total of 28 TCLAR events lasting at least 24 hours are identified among 241 named tropical cyclones during the 15-year period. Preliminary observations suggest that TCLAR formation in the North Atlantic is the result of the influences of lower- and upper-level jets and an extratropical cyclone centered over northern Europe. The analysis also suggests that the subtropical high during a TCLAR event is shifted to the southeast. Composite analyses of the synoptic-scale atmospheric setup throughout the evolution of the 28 observed events are conducted, with particular emphasis being placed on the TC-jet stream interaction at the onset of each event. Additional analyses examine relationships between the TC’s water vapor content, the intensity of the European extratropical cyclone, and the strength and orientation of the resulting AR. TCLAR events are further compared based on the post-event status of the associated TC.

488539.title: Incorporating Ocean Coupling, Vertical Wind Shear, and Ventilation in Potential Intensity for Category ‘6’ Tropical Cyclone Hot Spots
488539.authors: I-I Lin, National Taiwan Univ., Taipei, Taiwan; and C. C. Lien, Y. C. Liao, Y. Chang, C. C. Wu, Y. Wang, and H. C. Huang
488539.abstract: With the occurrence of super-typhoon Haiyan (2013, 170kts) of intensity far exceeded the regular category-5 Tropical Cyclones (TCs) and its catastrophic damage, more than 10 years ago, Lin et al. 2014 proposed the need of adding Category ‘6’ to the Saffir-Simpson TC scale. Since then, there has been more and more such extreme Category ‘6’ TCs (here defined as > 160kts in 1-min maximum sustained wind speed) occurring globally (Lin et al. 2021). It is about time to ask whether these Category ‘6’ TCs are indeed different from the traditionally-known Category 5 TCs (here defined as 137 to <160kts). If so, are the environmental conditions between Category ‘6’ vs. Category 5 TCs differentiable? Here we conduct systematic exploration comparing all Category ‘6’ vs. Category 5 cases in the past 4 decades (1982 -2024). Among the various environmental factors examined, the useful distinguishable factors are upper ocean heat content (OHC), sea surface temperature (SST), and vertical wind shear (VWS). In view of the importance of these factors, we explore the possibility to incorporate VWS, and perhaps the Ventilation index in the Ocean Coupling Potential Intensity (OCPI, Lin et al. 2013) for Category ‘6’ hot spot prediction.

488540.title: Impact of Precipitation on Wildland Fire Emissions and Combustion Phase: Need for a Geostationary CO Capability over North America for Fire Phase Monitoring
488540.authors: Aishwarya Raman, ARC, Moffett Field, CA; and J. M. Ryoo, J. Avise, M. S. Johnson, I. G. Brosnan, T. S. Park, J. Bruening, S. Houweling, F. Boersma, S. Lama, F. Li, P. Saide, S. Kondragunta, J. Wang, and M. Zhou
488540.abstract: Fire emission inventories assign a fixed NO₂-to-CO ratio to each vegetation class, making combustion efficiency the balance between flaming (NOₓ-rich) and smoldering (CO-rich) phases a function of land cover alone. Fuel moisture strongly controls this balance, and in regions like California, where Atmospheric Rivers drive wet winters, wildfire emissions carry a memory of the preceding winter’s precipitation. In fires following a wet winter, energy that would drive high-temperature flaming is instead consumed evaporating fuel moisture, lowering combustion efficiency and releasing more incompletely combusted CO and soot. We investigate whether combustion efficiency is controlled by antecedent precipitation in California by comparing vegetation-specific emission ratios from the FINNv2.5 and RAVE inventories with co-located TROPOMI CO and NO₂ columns over California wildfires from 2019 to 2023, sampled within 25 km of MODIS active-fire detections and paired with winter precipitation and summer 1000-hour dead fuel moisture. We assess whether the satellite DNO₂/DCO enhancement ratio, across California ecoregions and in mature and old-growth forests, matches the patterns the inventories predict. Satellite-observed and inventory-predicted combustion efficiency agree in dry years but diverge sharply after wet winters. In 2020 the spatial correlation between the FINNv2.5 NO₂/CO ratio and the TROPOMI enhancement ratio is weakly positive (r = 0.3–0.5), whereas after the extreme atmospheric-river winter of 2023 the correlation between the emission inventory and satellite-observed ratios over California collapse to r= −0.03. The DNO₂/DCO ratio declines after strong AR winters and varies strongly within a single ecoregion, tracking the memory of fuel moisture and the resulting smoldering emissions, whereas FINNv2.5 and RAVE, moisture-independent by construction, do not show this strong spatial and temporal variability in emission factor ratios. Tracking each fire while its DCO persists reveals a longer smoldering tail after wet winters, a phase missed in emission inventories. These results show that static inventories fail to predict fire chemistry after extreme wet events. Constraining this bias is critical for the fire emission inputs to NASA GEOS-CF and chemical data assimilation. The Fire Light Detection Algorithm 2 (FILDA-2) provides fire-level modified combustion efficiency retrievals that characterize variability in the flaming-smoldering combustion balance, enabling combustion-state-dependent constraints on CO and NOX emission factors and potentially linking the combustion ratios to static land-cover-based inventories. Because our method needs co-located CO and NO₂, and TEMPO measures NO₂ but not CO, it underscores the need for a geostationary CO capability over North America.

488549.title: From Forecasts to Preparedness: An Agentic AI Workflow for Early Warning Services in Djibouti
488549.authors: Yang You, Shanghai Meteorological Service, Shanghai, Shanghai, China; and H. Liu
488549.abstract: As the United Nations Early Warnings for All initiative advances, many priority countries now have reliable access to global satellite observations and numerical weather forecasts. Yet relatively limited staffing and technical capacity still hinder national meteorological services from rapidly translating complex forecasts into localized, actionable warnings and preparedness actions. Using Djibouti as the focal case, this feasibility study assesses whether an agentic AI workflow intended for national meteorological services in priority countries can organize multi-source monitoring and forecast data, local warning rules, and preparedness knowledge to shorten the path from forecast assessment to warning preparation and preparedness action under staffing and technical constraints. The approach neither replaces forecasters nor automatically makes warning decisions or issues official warnings. Instead, it helps national meteorological services use existing data and expertise, while operational staff retain final authority. To this end, we developed an agentic AI workflow for generating preparedness reports. Guided by local operational rules, the agentic AI workflow organizes tasks by location, hazard, and time range. As it carries out these tasks, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is used to call satellite monitoring and numerical forecast analysis tools and retrieve warning rules and preparedness knowledge from local repositories as needed. The resulting inputs are then passed to a locally deployed large language model (LLM), which serves as the reasoning engine. The localized LLM synthesizes these inputs and drafts structured, source-traceable reports for operational staff to edit and approve. The agentic AI workflow was applied to a rainfall event in Djibouti on 27 March 2026. In this application, it first invoked satellite monitoring tools to detect and track developing cloud systems and precipitation signals in Fengyun-4B observations. Next, it used CMA-GFS, NOAA GFS, and ECMWF forecasts to assess the event's evolution, main impact period, potentially affected areas, and model agreement. Using this multi-source assessment, the local LLM integrated the forecast evidence with Djibouti's warning thresholds and pre-event preparedness guidance from the local knowledge base. It then generated a localized preparedness report covering the weather situation, priority impact areas, main impact period, and the resulting preparedness guidance. The process took less than 15 minutes, indicating its potential to support local warning decisions and preparedness actions. Finally, a qualitative post-event comparison with the official rainfall warning issued by the Djibouti National Meteorological Agency found broad agreement on rainfall risk, affected areas, and timing. The novelty lies not in a new weather forecasting model or automated warning system, but in organizing multi-source monitoring and forecast data, local warning rules, and preparedness knowledge into an executable agentic AI workflow. Rather than replacing forecasters, it supports operational staff in national meteorological services by processing information and drafting preparedness reports. Next, we will compare the agentic AI workflow with the existing manual process in terms of report preparation time, factual consistency, source traceability, and transferability across hazards and countries.

488553.title: Agricultural Exposure Changes to Hail using MESH and the Hail Impact Monte Carlo Model Version 2
488553.authors: Logan R. Bundy, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL; and S. M. Strader, W. S. Ashley, and V. A. Gensini
488553.abstract: Hail is a recurring billion-dollar threat to U.S. agriculture, yet its impacts remain difficult to characterize because conventional storm reports can be spatially biased, insurance records capture only a subset of losses, and the radar record is relatively short. This study uses two complementary approaches to quantify agricultural hail exposure and potential impacts. First, quality-controlled daily Maximum Estimated Size of Hail (MESH) data from NOAA’s Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor system are used to develop a 1-km climatology (2008–2025) of agricultural hail exposure across the Midwest United States. Second, to extend the analysis beyond the observational record both in the past and in the future, MESH-derived distributions of hail frequency, seasonality, size, and swath morphology are incorporated into the Hail Impact Monte Carlo model version 2 (HailMCv2). As an illustration of the model’s utility, we simulate 5,000 years of hail swaths with maximum hail sizes of at least 0.5 in. for historical (1990–present), current, and future (through 2055) conditions across the Midwest. Simulated swaths are intersected with temporally consistent historical, current, and projected cropland surfaces to estimate annual exceedance probabilities, return periods, and potential agricultural impacts across the three epochs. The resulting framework evaluates the potential emergence of a concentrating agricultural bull’s-eye, whereby a shrinking cropland footprint and greater overlap between hail occurrence and critical crop growth stages may intensify regional losses despite a smaller exposed landscape. By linking radar observations with HailMCv2 simulations, this work moves agricultural hail assessment beyond the short observational record and toward a probabilistic risk framework that can support producers, insurers, and risk managers under current and future conditions.

488554.title: Regulation and Routing Models for Operations: Current Upper and Middle Great Lakes Model Development Efforts to Facilitate Water Management
488554.authors: Patricia Bye, US Army Corps of Engineers, Detroit, MI; and A. Abedelmdoust, N. Gervasi, C. Bayer, M. DeBues, D. Fielder, J. Jury, S. Redondo, I. Tariq, and J. Ward
488554.abstract: The Laurentian Great Lakes’ water levels and between lake channel flows are coordinated between the United States and Canada to support bi-national water management under the International Joint Commission (IJC). Therefore, these levels and flows are simulated through coordinated regulation and routing models (RRMs). In the case of the Great Lakes system, RRMs are used by government agencies and researchers from the US and Canada for water level forecasting, outflow regulation, decision-support, adaptive management and academic research purposes. The Coordinated Great Lakes Regulation and Routing Model (CGLRRM) is the current operationalized RRM for Great Lakes water management on Lake Superior. This model was developed over the course of years and was last updated in the early 2000s. Since then, CLGRRM users have recognized its need to be modernized to improve functionality and flexibility. First, CGLRRM was developed using Fortran, which has since become a less prevalent coding language in scientific and operational communities. CGLRRM was the source of many difficulties during the International Upper Great Lakes Study (IUGLS) because the regulation plan had been hardcoded in a way that did not allow easy testing of modifications or deviations. To improve adaptability, maintainability, and future development, the decision was made to translate the model into Python, an open-source programming language. The Python-based version of the model is named the Great Lakes Regulation and Routing Model (GLRRM). The Lake Ontario module of GLRRM (GLRRM-Ontario) was developed first and was successfully applied during the Plan 2014 expedited review, demonstrating the benefits of a modern, flexible, and open-source modeling framework. The successful implementation of GLRRM-Ontario increased confidence among Great Lakes water management agencies regarding the value of investing in the modernization of RRMs for the Upper Great Lakes. This experience also highlighted the opportunity to integrate the Lake Ontario and Upper Great Lakes components into a unified GLRRM framework. Building on this foundation, GLRRM has undergone continued major development for the Upper Lakes, including a complete rework of the legacy Lake Superior and Middle Lakes (Lakes Michigan-Huron, St. Clair, and Erie) modules into Python. The unified GLRRM model now incorporate the flexibility to simulation the operational flow deviations, water payback methods, and experimental water supply and regulation sequences to better evaluate regulation strategies on present and future hydroclimate conditions across all lake modules. This presentation will describe GLRRM improvements, specifically for the Upper Lakes modules, and how these updates support operations and future plan reviews, including plan 2012 review through enhanced flexibility, deviation frameworks, and modern open-source programming.

488555.title: Translating Weather to Agricultural Risk using Global Yield Modeling Strategies
488555.authors: Logan R. Bundy, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL; and J. B. Davis, M. S. Russo, and E. Adamchick
488555.abstract: The growing season of 2026 highlighted a persistent challenge for global commodities: obtaining timely, reliable information about production conditions and translating those signals into yield risk. We present results from a phenology-aware, process-based crop yield model that integrates weather and hydroclimatic variables with crop calendars and stage-specific sensitivities to estimate evolving conditions across major production regions. Rather than treating all weather anomalies equally, the framework evaluates stress according to its timing within the crop life cycle and produces standardized weekly condition indices relative to historical conditions. We demonstrate how the framework was used operationally during 2026 to monitor agricultural commodities ranging from corn, soybeans, and cotton to dairy production. Current yield trajectories are compared with historical records to evaluate model performance and estimate probabilities of below trend, near trend, and above trend outcomes. These probabilities are updated as new observations become available, allowing persistent and yield relevant stress to be distinguished from short-lived weather anomalies. Further, we compare the yield signals with other available condition data and vegetation health indices to evaluate how effectively the framework identified departures from expectations before harvesting. Commodity market stakeholders and supply chain users can use this approach for an interpretable connection between weather, crop development, and production uncertainty. Overall, this framework supports earlier recognition of changing yield expectations and geographically concentrated supply disruptions while explicitly communicating uncertainty. The 2026 case study illustrates how phenology aware monitoring can move beyond generic weather anomaly maps toward scalable, commodity intelligence for sourcing, market assessment, and risk management.

488558.title: Advances in Ocean Surface Wind Applications for the National Weather Service (NWS) Ocean Tsunami Center (OTC)
488558.authors: Christopher Lee Smith, Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies, University of Maryland, College Park, MD
488558.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) Ocean Tsunami Center (OTC) is responsible for issuing marine wind warnings over much of the North Pacific and North Atlantic. From June 2025 to May 2026, there were 66 hurricane-force extratropical cyclones analyzed in OTC’s Atlantic waters and 40 in the Pacific. In a domain with limited in-situ observations, satellite observations are critical to verify warnings and protect the life and property of mariners at sea. Over the past year, the availability of the OceanSat-3 (OSCAT-3) scatterometer and ocean surface winds derived from multiple Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite missions has revolutionized the observation of powerful extratropical cyclones. The OTC can task-order SAR overpasses from the RADARSAT-2 and RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) satellites up to three days before an event, capturing high-resolution ocean surface winds and identifying the features that drive them. This presentation will provide an overview of OTC applications leveraging these newly available technologies.

488561.title: Accelerating OMPS Sensor Data Record Data R2O Transition: Feasibility of Inter-Sensor Radiometric Calibration Bias Analysis across OMPS Nadir Instruments Using CRTM AI Emulators
488561.authors: Banghua Yan, NOAA, College Park, MD
488561.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) currently operates three Ozone Mapping and Profiler Suites (OMPS) nadir instruments aboard the Suomi NPP (SNPP), NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 satellites to maintain long-term records of ultraviolet (UV) satellite radiance observations. The fourth OMPS instrument will be scheduled to launch aboard the JPSS-04 satellite next year or later. The OMPS nadir instrument includes two ultraviolet imaging spectrometers: Nadir Profiler (NP) and Nadir Mapper (NM). The OMPS NP collects data between 250 nm and 310 nm, offering vertical ozone profile information, while the OMPS NM focuses on wavelengths from 300 nm to 380 nm, providing data on total column ozone. The total column amount and vertical distribution of atmospheric ozone derived from the OMPS NM and NP Sensor Data Record (SDR) data are assimilated to the NOAA satellite data assimilation system. Therefore, accelerating the research-to-operations (R2O) transition for OMPS SDR data through advanced calibration and validation algorithms is critical to enabling the assimilation of ozone products derived into the NWS data assimilation system, particularly given the planned launch of JPSS-04. One important activity in SDR calibration and validation process is to characterize latitude-dependency of inter-sensor radiometric calibration biases across multi-mission OMPS instruments. This is especially critical, as both OMPS NM and NP can show certain latitude-dependent calibration biases caused by factors such as solar intrusion, wavelength shift, and residual instrument-oriented stray light impacts. In the past few years, the NOAA Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) has played an important role in assessing these inter-sensor radiometric calibration biases. However, the CRTM for the UV radiative transfer process—even under clear skies—is computationally heavy, partially due to the extra computation required for Rayleigh (molecular) scattering, aerosol scattering and polarization, unlike microwave and infrared radiation which are dominated by emissions and absorptions. To address this issue, in a separate study [1], we are adapting ML techniques to develop CRTM radiance simulation AI emulators for each of the SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and JPSS-04 OMPS NM and NP instruments. The wavelengths for the first three OMPS instruments cover the range from 250 nm to 380 nm, while those for the JPSS-04 OMPS nadir instrument cover the range from 250 nm to 439 nm. The AI model coefficients for each OMPS instrument will be derived using a training dataset consisting of CRTM simulated radiance at OMPS wavelengths and EUMETSAT Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) forecast products regarding atmospheric profiles and surface properties. Due to the lack of sufficient surface reflectance information covering the OMPS wavelength range, the CRTM simulations for each instrument will utilize the NOAA-21 OMPS-derived surface effective reflectance dataset. This study will focus on investigating the feasibility of inter-sensor radiometric calibration bias estimation across OMPS instruments using the newly developed CRTM AI emulators for multi-mission OMPS nadir instruments. This investigation also includes identifying following two distinct inter-sensor radiometric calibration biases: Biases due solely to various instrument-specific calibration errors, by applying each instrument's specific AI emulator coefficients to the corresponding OMPS instrument. Biases due to both the independent instrument-specific calibration error and the instrument bandpass difference-caused bias, by applying the same instrument-based AI emulator coefficients (such as the NOAA-21 AI emulator coefficients) to each of the multi-mission OMPS instruments. This approach will allow us to accurately distinguish the contributions of instrument-specific calibration errors, such as regional solar intrusion on NP short wavelength observations at high solar zenith angles over the Northern Hemisphere, from the overall inter-sensor calibration errors. The findings will help us improve the OMPS SDR calibration algorithms to produce quality-consistent OMPS SDR data across regions. Furthermore, we will compare the computation accuracy and speeds between the traditional CRTM tool and the AI emulator. It is expected that the use of various CRTM AI emulators for multi-mission OMPS nadir instruments will largely accelerate our calibration and validation process of upcoming JPSS-4 OMPS SDR data, thus speeding up the R2O transition of JPSS-04 OMPS SDR data. Disclaimer: the presentation contents are solely the opinions of the authors and do not constitute a statement of policy, decision, or position on behalf of NOAA or the U. S. Government.

488563.title: Effects of Kinetic-Thermal Energy Interactions on Turbulence Cascade and Energy Dissipation Estimation in the Stratified Atmospheric Surface Layer
488563.authors: Jielun Sun, Northwest Research Associates, Boulder, CO
488563.abstract: Effects of Kinetic-Thermal Energy Interactions on Turbulence Cascade and Energy Dissipation Estimation in the Stratified Atmospheric Surface Layer Jielun Sun1,Gary Granger2, Steven Oncley2, Chris Roden2, Sebastian Hoch2, Chenning Tong3,Larry Mahrt1 1 NorthWest Research Associates, Boulder, CO 2 National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO 3 Clemson University, Clemson, SC Collocated hot-films and sonic anemometers were deployed at heights ranging from 0.5 to 4 m above the ground surface in the field campaign, M2HATS/SHINE. Analysis shows that hot-film voltages respond not only to turbulent motions but also to turbulent air temperature fluctuations, reflecting the coupling between kinetic and thermal energy in stratified atmospheric flows governed by kinetic and total energy conservation. Hot-film power spectra exhibit a well-developed inertial subrange under weakly-stable conditions associated with strong nighttime winds and unstable conditions driven by positive buoyancy, whereas a bottleneck phenomenon occurs under moderately to strongly stable conditions. This stability dependence is attributed to variations in kinetic-thermal energy exchange, which contribute differently to turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) across stability regimes in addition to the continual TKE loss through energy dissipation in the turbulence cascade. These results indicate that Kolmogorov's hypothesis remains valid under both neutral and convective conditions but breaks down under stable condition, where TKE is consumed by downward heat transfer. Consequently, intermittent transitions between stable and weakly stable conditions, driven by fluctuations in wind speed, lead to intermittent development of the inertial subrange. Energy dissipation derived from hot-film and sonic-anemometer measurements is compared with its analytical formulation. The close agreement between energy dissipation rates measured at four heights and the airflow deformation derived from bulk wind shear demonstrates that air viscosity is independent of airflow deformation.

488573.title: Weakening Snow Pattern Consistency across the Northern Hemisphere
488573.authors: Sujay V. Kumar, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD; and J. M. Pflug, C. Vuyovich, M. Wrzesien, J. Tarricone, A. Getirana, and K. Yang
488573.abstract: Snow patterns have historically provided predictable seasonal cycles that underpin global water security, ecosystem function, and climate regulation, with over one billion people depending on snowmelt for freshwater supply. However, the reliability of these patterns and their spatial variability remain poorly quantified at global scales. Here, we present the first comprehensive assessment of snow pattern repeatability across the Northern Hemisphere using 24 years of satellite observations, revealing profound spatiotemporal heterogeneity that challenges fundamental assumptions underlying snow-based water resource planning. While tundra regions maintain the highest pattern repeatability, ephemeral snow zones exhibit minimal predictability, establishing a clear hierarchy of snow reliability. Peak winter months show the strongest pattern consistency, but shoulder seasons demonstrate rapidly declining stability during critical snowmelt periods. Most critically, we document systematic weakening of snow pattern persistence across the Northern Hemisphere, indicating widespread breakdown of historically reliable snow cycles. This degradation spans diverse mountain systems from the Himalayas to North American ranges, representing fundamental shifts in global snow dynamics. Our findings reveal that seasonal snow patterns are becoming systematically unreliable across vast Northern Hemisphere regions, necessitating urgent adaptation of water management strategies and highlighting the critical importance of sustained global snow monitoring for resilience planning.

488581.title: NOAA NWS NDBC AWS 2.0
488581.abstract: NDBC AWS 2.0 is a cloud modernization initiative between NOAA's National Data Buoy Center and Amazon Web Services, refactoring NDBC's legacy buoy data ingestion and processing infrastructure onto AWS. The project leverages a serverless, event-driven architecture—utilizing AWS IoT Core, Lambda, Step Functions, and Amazon Bedrock—to ingest, quality-control, and derive AI-powered insights from oceanographic and meteorological observations across NDBC's national buoy fleet. This presentation will overview the end-to-end solution design, highlight how generative AI is being applied to automated data quality assessment and operational decision support, and share lessons learned from the ongoing Proof-of-Concept delivery. The session is led by the AWS Account Team in coordination with NDBC.

488585.title: Talking to Air: An AI Agent Empowering End Users to Access Earth Observations
488585.authors: Xiaomeng Jin, School of Environment and Biological Sciences, New Brunswick, NJ; and T. Patel
488585.abstract: Earth observations provide extensive information on air pollution and its environmental and public health impacts, but accessing, processing, and interpreting these complex datasets often requires specialized technical expertise. We present Talking to Air, an artificial intelligence agent that provides conversational access to satellite and ground-based air quality observations. Built with the Model Context Protocol and LangGraph, the platform uses a modular multi-agent architecture to automate dataset discovery, retrieval, processing, visualization, and interpretation. It connects with NASA services including the Common Metadata Repository API, Harmony, and AppEEARS. The platform supports NO2, HCHO, aerosol optical depth, and ozone observations from multiple geostationary and polar-orbiting instruments and integrates them with EPA AQS measurements. Its objectives are to simplify access to air quality data, automate analysis workflows, generate interactive visualizations and summaries, and enable scalable, reproducible environmental analysis. Users can submit requests such as “Show today’s NO2 map over New Jersey” or “Compare the change of NO2 in 2005 vs. 2020,” and the system generates corresponding maps, time series, and AI-generated summaries. By lowering technical barriers, Talking to Air broadens the use of Earth observations for research, education, stakeholder engagement, air quality management, and public health decision-making.

488588.title: Subseasonal Predictability of Extreme Ocean Wave Events in the North Pacific
488588.authors: Cameron Raymond Paquette, NRL, Monterey, CA; NRL, Monterey, CA; and M. A. Janiga, W. Crawford, and E. Rogers
488588.abstract: Predicting ocean waves on subseasonal timescales is a growing field of study due to the advances in coupled global Earth system models with direct benefits for commercial shipping and coastal communities. Previous work indicates that the state of tropical teleconnections such as the Madden Julian Oscillation (MJO) and El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) can both influence sea states and offer predictive insights on subseasonal time scales. However, many questions still remain about the predictability of extreme ocean waves. We establish the predictive capability of extreme ocean waves through two unique perspectives. First, we identify the leading modes of variability in significant wave height anomalies (SWH) in the North Pacific basin through empirical orthogonal functions (EOFs) using ERA5 data from 1991-2020. The first two modes of SWH variability are described as a basin-wide oscillation in positive and negative significant wave height anomalies, and a dipole in SWH anomalies across the North Pacific, together describing about 24% of the variability. By using the leading SWH EOFs as a diagnostic for determining extreme states, we assess the predictive skill of North Pacific SWH within GEFSv12 reforecast dataset during extreme SWH EOF conditions. We also identify relationships between the states of the MJO and ENSO to the forecast skill of extreme SWH anomalies. Second, we quantify GEFS forecast skill during individual high-amplitude cases by using an object-based tracker to identify spatiotemporal objects of elevated SWH. By using the object-based tracker, differences between the track characteristics of wave objects detected by ERA5 reanalysis and GEFS reforecasts can be quantified, which includes track location, phase speed, wave direction and frequency, and others.

488593.title: The NOAA Unique Combined Atmospheric Processing System (NUCAPS): Status, Augmentations, and Future Hyperspectral Sounding Capabilities
488593.authors: Murty G. Divakarla, Science and Technology Corporation, Columbia, MD; STC @NOAA/NESDIS/STAR, College Park, MD; and T. Zhu, T. Wang, M. Kulko, J. T. Szkodzinski, M. Pettey, M. Wilson, and K. L. Pryor
488593.abstract: As the official operational hyperspectral enterprise sounding product system, the NOAA Unique Combined Atmospheric Processing System (NUCAPS) continues to evolve to support the generation of an array of NOAA unique hyperspectral sounding products from the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) sensor aboard NOAA-20/21 and the Infrared Atmospheric Sounder Interferometer (IASI) on MetOp-C. The algorithm is implemented as an enterprise solution within the Hyperspectral Enterprise Algorithm Package (HEAP) to produce vertical profiles of temperature, water vapor, ozone, various trace gases (e.g., CO, CH4, and CO2), and the Outgoing Longwave Radiation (OLR).
