The algorithm, built on the heritage of the Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS) science team algorithm, starts with a microwave-only (MW) retrieval, utilizing concurrent microwave sounder observations such as the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) on JPSS and the Advanced Microwave Sounding Unit (AMSU) on MetOp-C. Subsequent retrieval steps involve a cloud-clearing procedure and fast eigenvector regression to produce an initial solution for the final infrared plus microwave (IR+MW) physical retrieval. All the NUCAPS operational products from the current JPSS and MetOp satellites have attained validated maturity meeting the JPSS product requirements. Products are available worldwide through the NOAA Comprehensive Large Array-data Stewardship System (CLASS). The NUCAPS algorithm is a part of the Community Satellite Processing Package (CSPP) to disseminate products through Direct Broadcast (DB) services. A variety of NUCAPS sounding products are also ingested into the Advanced Weather Interactive Processing System (AWIPS-2) for use by many U.S. National Weather Service Forecast Offices (NWSFOs). The NUCAPS algorithm is being augmented for the JPSS-4 CrIS and the EUMETSAT Second Generation (EUMETSAT-SG) IASI Next Generation (IASI-NG) hyperspectral sounder. To leverage Machine Learning (ML) techniques for algorithm improvements, the NUCAPS team has initiated efforts to enhance various system sub-components while maintaining the integrity of the physical retrieval algorithm. Primary focus areas include optimizing first-guess cloudy and clear regression, refining bias-tuning methodologies, improving surface emissivity calculations using the Combined ASTER and MODIS Emissivity over Land (CAMEL) database, and reducing boundary layer retrieval biases. Simultaneously, the team has migrated the latest NUCAPS algorithm to the AWS cloud platform to support the generation of consistent, long-term products from the JPSS satellite series. A pilot validation of reprocessed time-series products from S-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21—using matched truth measurements for temperature, water vapor, and trace gases—is currently underway, with initial results demonstrating high consistency and compliance with JPSS requirements. This paper provides an overview of these developments, as well as algorithm augmentations for upcoming hyperspectral sounders, including JPSS-4 CrIS and EUMETSAT-SG IASI-NG. Future plans, such as incorporating additional viable products like Ammonia (NH3), ongoing collaborations with user agencies, and future campaigns of opportunities for sounding product applications and validation, will also be discussed.

488607.title: Modelling Emissions of Ammonia and Methane from Animal Feeding Operations in the Northern Colorado Basin
488607.authors: Matthew Davis, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and E. R. Lill, R. Rhoades, I. B. Pollack, K. Cossel, and E. V. Fischer
488607.abstract: Ammonia (NH3) is an important environmental pollutant that both negatively contributes to human health through the formation of fine particulates and harms vulnerable ecosystems through acidification, eutrophication, and nutrient overload. Methane (CH4) is a powerful greenhouse gas, and in the United States, agricultural production is the largest source of CH4 emissions. In the CORNCOB (Characterizing Oil, gas & agRicultural emissions in the Northern COlorado Basin) field study, high time-resolution measurements of NH3, CH4 and ethane (C2H6) were made in the northern Colorado Front Range (part of the Denver-Julesburg Basin) from a mobile lab between March 8 – April 9, 2025. This region contains a mix of agricultural and oil & gas CH4 emission sources and is situated near nitrogen-limited mountain ecosystems as well as near urban areas. Here, NH3 and C2H6 were used as tracers to attribute observations of CH4 to agriculture or oil & gas (O&G) respectively. By applying a Gaussian plume dispersion model and Bayesian inversion approach, we characterize NH3 and CH4 surface fluxes from a set of six well-studied Animal Feeding Operations (AFOs). We estimate emission fluxes from these AFOs of 820 ± 600 g CH4 ha-1 h-1 and 883 ± 500 g NH3 ha-1 h-1. We further estimated an NH3 surface emission potential of 2,600,000 mol mol-1 [90% confidence interval : 590,000 mol mol-1 – 6,000,000 mol mol-1], an order of magnitude larger than crops fertilized with 250 kg N ha-1. Finally we observe rapid surface deposition, with an estimate a near-surface lifetime against deposition as 6.6 minutes [95% confidence interval: 3.4 – 11.4 min], and contextualize those results in terms of inadvertent fertilization to nearby surfaces.

488609.title: The Early Afternoon Reversal of the Sensible Heat Flux In a Deep Alpine Valley
488609.authors: Manuela Lehner, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Tirol, Austria; and J. Gallet, H. C. Ward, N. Wildmann, and I. Stiperski
488609.abstract: The surface-energy budget during undisturbed, clear-sky conditions is typically strongly driven by incoming solar radiation, with the diurnal cycles of turbulent sensible and latent heat fluxes following the diurnal cycle of net radiation. Multi-year observations from an eddy-covariance station at the floor of the Austrian Inn Valley have, however, shown the frequent occurrence of an early reversal of the sensible heat flux during undisturbed conditions, with its maximum before solar noon and a transition to negative fluxes already in the early afternoon up to several hours before local sunset. Negative sensible heat fluxes after the sign reversal reach magnitudes similar to the positive fluxes in the morning as they coincide with the thermally driven up-valley flow in the afternoon and thus the typically strongest wind speeds of the day. During the summer Extended Observational Period (sEOP) of the TEAMx Observational Campaign, a network of seven eddy-covariance stations was deployed on the floor of the Inn Valley for a six-week period in June/July 2025. The stations were aligned along and across the valley axis with distances of about 200 m, covering an area of about 900 x 400 m2. Measurements at the center station were conducted at five vertical levels, up to 17 m above ground. Additional profiling instrumentation provided information on the stratification and flow in the valley atmosphere. The diurnal cycle of the sensible heat flux shows links to the evolution of the thermal valley-wind circulation extending beyond the near-surface wind field. Observations from the station network, however, also highlight the variability across the network, with the time of heat flux reversal differing by up to a few hours, thus suggesting additional local influences. Here we combine data from the different measurement platforms, including sensible-heat flux budgets determined from the station network, to explore mechanisms contributing to the observed early flux reversal.

488614.title: An Assessment of WRF Model Forecast Improvements Brought by the Assimilation of TAC-Thermo AI-Enhanced Thermodynamic Soundings.
488614.authors: Tana Ann Gobble, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and J. R. Mecikalski and S. S. Harkema
488614.abstract: This presentation will overview recent efforts to assimilate soundings generated by the Total Atmospheric Characterization–Thermodynamics (TAC-Thermo; Harkema et al. 2026) artificial intelligence (AI)-based algorithm into the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) community model to assess forecast improvements. Developed from 2023-2025, TAC-Thermo is a global AI–data fusion system designed to improve satellite-retrieved thermodynamic profiles, with specifically a focus on data sparse regions (e.g., oceans, polar regions, mountainous areas). TAC-Thermo uses available satellite retrieval soundings (e.g., those from CrIS, IASI, IASI-NG, and MTG-IRS in the near future) and numerical weather prediction model output fields to generate thermodynamic soundings that are more accurate than any individual input sounding, when comparisons to radiosondes are made. The TAC-Thermo algorithm upscales satellite-retrieved temperature and moisture profiles to capture thermodynamic features (up to ~12 km) on sigma vertical coordinate levels. Since TAC-Thermo data are of high quality, the hypothesis is that the assimilation of them into the initial conditions of the WRF model should help demonstrate: (a) how well they improve the subsequent forecasts over synoptic scale regions; and (b) how much value these soundings have in date denied situations (e.g., when a prior forecast analysis is very old) or in data sparce regions. The presentation will highlight recent progress in terms of our WRF model and WRF data assimilation set-up, the caveats we have discovered when processing TAC-Thermo data, how the error statistics compare to other satellite-based soundings, and how the subsequent WRF model forecasts are altered and improved. Other project details will be given as related to our overall experimental design.

488616.title: Bridging Atmospheric Pathways and Watershed-Scale Precipitation Observations for Dam Overtopping Analysis Across Spatial Scales
488616.authors: Hodo Inyang Orok, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and D. A. Hence
488616.abstract: This study develops an integrated framework linking atmospheric pathways with watershed-scale precipitation observations preceding dam overtopping in the Eastern United States. Atmospheric and hydrologic datasets describe extreme events at different spatial scales. Large atmospheric domains capture broad circulation patterns, while precipitation observations and watershed boundaries provide more localized information. Connecting these scales remains challenging, particularly for uncommon events such as dam overtopping, where similar outcomes may occur under different atmospheric and rainfall conditions. Atmospheric reanalysis, precipitation observations, watershed boundaries, and documented overtopping events are examined across nested spatial domains, ranging from the broader Eastern United States to regional subdivisions. Data-driven classification and composite analysis are used to identify recurring atmospheric environments and to link them to observed differences in rainfall intensity, coverage, and spatial organization. The analysis evaluates whether changes in the spatial domain alter the emphasized atmospheric features and the rainfall patterns associated with the resulting pathways. Initial applications indicate that broad and regional analysis domains provide related but different perspectives on the conditions preceding overtopping. Larger domains emphasize extensive circulation features, whereas regional analyses provide greater detail on localized moisture, vertical motion, and rainfall organization. The results demonstrate the importance of considering spatial scale when connecting atmospheric forcing with watershed precipitation observations. This framework helps bridge meteorological and hydrologic information without assuming that one spatial representation or atmospheric pattern explains every overtopping event. It also provides a reproducible basis for examining how large-scale weather conditions are expressed through rainfall at watershed-relevant scales.

488617.title: Characterizing Fugitive Emissions of Methane from Oil & Gas Infrastructure in the Northern Colorado Basin
488617.authors: Matthew Davis, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and E. R. Lill, R. Rhoades, I. B. Pollack, K. Cossel, and E. V. Fischer
488617.abstract: Methane (CH4) is a powerful greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change. In the United States, agriculture is the largest source of methane emissions (37%) while the second largest source is fugitive emissions from oil and natural gas extraction (31%). To curb emissions in line with climate change goals, it is important to distinguish between the emissions from agricultural sources versus fossil fuel extraction where they are co-located. This issue is particularly pronounced in Northeastern Colorado where oil and gas facilities are intermingled with large numbers of animal feeding operations (AFOs). In the CORNCOB (Characterizing Oil, gas & agRicultural emissions in the Northern COlorado Basin) field study, high time-resolution measurements of NH3, CH4 and ethane (C2H6) were made in the Denver-Julesburg Basin from a mobile lab between March 8 – April 9, 2025. NH3 and C2H6 were used as tracers to attribute observations of CH4 to agriculture or oil & gas (O&G) respectively. By applying a Gaussian plume dispersion model and Bayesian inversion approach, we estimated CH4 emissions from a set of facilities in the Colorado Department of Public Health and the Environment (CDPHE) ONGAEIR emission inventory to evaluate whether our observations were in line with the existing inventory.

488618.title: Investigating Land-Surface Heterogeneity Impacts on Convective Initiation and Storm Development Across the Southeastern U.S.
488618.authors: David S Henderson, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and M. Eppley-Ishida, J. A. Otkin, PhD, and J. R. Mecikalski
488618.abstract: Convective initiation (CI) and subsequent storm evolution across the southeastern United States are strongly influenced by spatial heterogeneity in land-surface conditions and the resulting land-atmosphere interactions and evolution of the planetary boundary layer (PBL). Identifying the environmental and land-surface conditions associated with the timing and location of deep convection remains challenging. This study investigates the timing, location, and characteristics of the first occurrence of intense thunderstorms across the southeastern United States using collocated satellite and ground-based remote sensing observations, with a focus on cases observed during the DOE ARM AMF3 field campaign in the Bankhead National Forest. The satellite and ground-based observations are combined with high-resolution WRF model simulations to investigate the lower-atmospheric processes associated with observed initiation locations and to assess how changes in land-surface heterogeneity affect convective evolution and the timing of the most intense rainfall. Geostationary satellite observations from the GOES-19 ABI and ground-based radar are analyzed using the Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds (TOBAC) framework to identify regions of rapid cloud growth and the timing and location of the first observed CI for case studies during the summer 2025. This provides the opportunity to investigate land-atmosphere interactions before the deep convection and outflow boundaries modify the local environment. We examine how spatial heterogeneity in land characteristics influences the location, timing of initial CI events, and the intensity of subsequent rainfall. Complementary high-resolution WRF model simulations and ground observations from the DOE ARM AMF3 field campaign are used to investigate the role of lower-atmospheric processes, including surface energy imbalances and low-level circulation patterns. We examine how variability in observed land-surface conditions influences CI using WRF sensitivity experiments to assess how associated land-atmosphere processes affect the timing and intensity of precipitation. Together, the multi-platform observations and simulations provide an observationally constrained framework for connecting land-surface heterogeneity and lower-atmospheric processes to the downstream convective evolution.

488626.title: Satellite Observations of Blowing Dust Initiation Across the Southwestern United States
488626.authors: William Line, NESDIS, Fort Collins, CO; and J. D. Turner, D. Hillger, and M. Bleiweiss
488626.abstract: Blowing dust is a significant hazard across the southwestern United States, where it can rapidly reduce visibility, degrade air quality, and disrupt transportation. Long-term observations of where and when dust begins are limited. To address this gap, NOAA satellite imagery was used to develop a 20-year record of blowing dust initiation and source locations from 2001 through 2020. The dataset includes 3,492 initiation points identified on 1,066 days across the region from 25° to 43°N and 124° to 97°W. The completed record shows clear spatial, seasonal, annual, and diurnal patterns. Events occur most frequently during spring and generally begin from late morning through early afternoon, with substantial year-to-year variability related to drought and regional weather patterns. Frequently active source regions include portions of the southern and central High Plains, the Chihuahuan Desert, and the Great Basin. Follow-on work is using the record to examine the conditions that influence dust-source activation. Dust locations are being compared with surface wind speed, soil moisture, soil texture and order, land cover, and vegetation. Results show that frequently active dust-source regions do not necessarily correspond to areas with the greatest exposure to strong winds, indicating that dust susceptibility depends on a combination of surface conditions. Additional work is examining the broader meteorological environments associated with dust initiation across different source regions. This presentation will summarize the completed observational record, highlight key spatial and temporal patterns, and show how it is being used to better understand the surface and meteorological controls on blowing dust initiation.

488629.title: SamudrACE - UFS: A Seasonal-to-Decadal Coupled Atmosphere-Ocean Model Trained on Observation-Based Reanalysis
488629.authors: Troy Arcomano, Allen Institute for AI (Ai2), SEATTLE, WA; and J. Duncan, E. Wu, S. Clark, C. Bretherton, and O. Watt-Meyer
488629.abstract: Recently, there have been several machine learning-based emulators of coupled, numerical climate models (e.g., SamudrACE for CM4 and E3SM). Given their ability to successfully reproduce the dynamics of these coupled climate models, and the existence of observation-based products that include the full ocean state, albeit over a short period of time, the question remains whether a similar coupled emulator can successfully emulate observation-based reanalysis products. Here, we present SamudrACE-UFS, a coupled emulator that can simulate the full-depth ocean, sea ice, and atmosphere trained on observation-based products. Samudra predicts the ocean and sea ice based on training data from the NOAA UFS replay dataset, where MOM6 is nudged to ORAS5. The atmosphere model is the newly developed stochastic ACE trained on ERA5 (ACE2S-ERA5). Both models are first trained separately and then trained jointly during the final stage to account for small systematic differences between the ERA5 and UFS datasets. SamudrACE-UFS can successfully reproduce the observed warming of the atmosphere and ocean over the last 30 years and serves as a reasonable coupled forecast system, demonstrating moderate skill at seasonal prediction for out-of-sample forecasts. This work represents the first steps toward a fully coupled climate emulator trained on observation-based products, while also outlining the challenges of training such a system with limited datasets and non-closed energy budgets.

488636.title: Connecting Satellite Capabilities to NWS Operations Through Event-Based Case Studies
488636.authors: William Line, NESDIS, Fort Collins, CO
488636.abstract: The Satellite Liaison Blog documents operational uses of satellite imagery and products during impactful weather events. Posts are developed through satellite analysis, references in National Weather Service forecast products, and direct interactions with forecasters. This approach provides timely examples of how satellite information is being used in operations while also identifying opportunities for additional use, training, and product improvement. Selected events from 2026 will include convection, blowing dust, wildfires, winter weather, low clouds and fog, and marine hazards. Animations of GOES and JPSS imagery and products will be used to show how satellite information supported situational awareness, hazard identification, and monitoring of rapidly changing conditions. The examples will also show how forecasters access and display satellite information in AWIPS and web-based tools, along with some of the limitations that can affect operational use. The blog gives NESDIS scientists insight into which products and techniques are proving useful and how they fit into forecast workflows. It also gives forecasters practical examples of how other offices are applying satellite information during real events. Event-based case studies can help connect satellite science and product development with operational needs, spread effective applications across the NWS, and guide future training and transition activities.

488638.title: Air Toxics and Methane Emissions and Downwind Impacts from Oil and Gas Well Blowout In Galeton, CO
488638.authors: Lena Low, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. Davis, K. Cossel, W. Zhang, D. Pan, J. Stickney, I. T. Ku, Y. Zhou, J. L. Collett Jr., and E. V. Fischer
488638.abstract: Recent studies have provided new insight into emissions of air toxics and other volatile organic compounds (VOCs) during development of new oil and gas (O&G) wells. However, less is known about the potential for much higher emission rates and downwind exposures resulting from well-site accidents. Providing an opportunity to study uncontrolled O&G emissions, an O&G well blowout near a small rural Colorado town in April 2025 resulted in >4 days of uncontrolled liquid flow, totaling an estimated 3.8 million liters. Representing Colorado’s largest recorded spill, the blowout manifested as an artificial geyser that reached heights above 25 m. Within the first few hours of the incident, local officials issued a voluntary exclusion zone within 0.8 km of the well pad; some individuals did not return to their residences for several months. Government officials also closed the local elementary school for two weeks. During the blowout, our team drove two mobile platforms to intercept and characterize plume concentration, composition, and evolution. We surveyed 10 cross-sections of the plume at ~1.5-4 km downwind of the well. The maximum real-time methane (CH4) mixing ratio was 40 ppmv at the plume center and 1.5 km downwind. Near the edge of the same plume transect, we collected a whole air canister with 36 ppbv of benzene. Leveraging real-time and canister measurements, we extrapolate >50 VOC mixing ratios including several air toxics at the plume center; the estimated maximum benzene was ~116 ppbv. Using dispersion modeling (AERMOD) we invert downwind observations to constrain CH4 emission rates and evaluate potential hourly exposure of air toxics within the community. While these results are specific to this particular incident, they provide important estimates of emissions and downwind exposure relevant to considering impacts of potential accidents in other O&G development locations, including those in more densely populated regions.

488644.title: An Overview of Current UAS Capabilities for Measuring Turbulence within the Atmospheric Boundary Layer (Invited Presentation)
488644.authors: Sean C.C. Bailey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY; and N. Gustenyov, T. M. Bell, G. Britto Hupsel de Azevedo, and J. O. Pinto, Phd
488644.abstract: Weather-sensing uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS) offer a cost-effective solution to bridge observational gaps for in-situ atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) measurements. Over recent decades, these platforms have undergone continuous development, demonstrating marked success in investigating complex ABL phenomena, including convection initiation, air-sea interaction, complex terrain flows, and urban-canopy interactions. From an operational perspective, UAS have also proven valuable for improving numerical weather prediction through the data assimilation of high-resolution thermodynamic and kinematic boundary layer profiles. Integrating highly diverse platforms with varied sensor configurations requires cross-calibration and intercomparison to establish baseline accuracies. Multi-platform flight campaigns organized by the International Society for Atmospheric Research using Remotely piloted Aircraft (ISARRA), including a recent intercomparison evaluating approximately 40 UAS from 15 operators, have compared these aircraft measurements to those provided by Doppler lidar, radiosondes, and surface masts. The result demonstrate that while the accuracy of the measurements remains system-dependent, UAS are capable of routine profiling activities with fidelity comparable to contemporary in-situ measurement systems. For boundary-layer turbulence measurements, UAS offer distinct physical advantages in achieving statistical convergence. By traversing the flow spatially on timescales faster than the decorrelation times of coherent structures, these platforms capture a near-instantaneous snapshot of turbulence structure along the flight path. Furthermore, their lower cruising speeds (between 10 m s⁻¹ and 30 m s⁻¹) relative to crewed aircraft (between 50 m s⁻¹ and 200 m s⁻¹) enable significantly higher spatial resolution at equivalent sensor sampling rates. Observations collected during the ISARRA Small-UAS Coordination for Atmospheric Low-Level Environmental Sampling (SCALES) flight week campaign highlight this capability. Measurements of turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) and dissipation rate from multiple turbulence-sensing UAS flown north and south of downtown Tulsa, Oklahoma, were utilized to evaluate the NSF NCAR FastEddy© GPU-accelerated Large-Eddy Simulation (LES) model operating at a building-resolving grid spacing of 5 m. The observed UAS data demonstrated that the model and aircraft produced closely matching turbulence intensities within urban building wakes. Beyond urban microclimates, UAS flights are uniquely suited for conducting targeted diagnostics of large-scale coherent turbulent structures and complex terrain dynamics. During flight investigations over complex terrain along a 6 km transect, horizontal wind magnitude measurements exhibited strong signatures of horizontal convective rolls. Conditionally averaging velocity fluctuations based on their relative position within these roll architectures revealed that vertical velocity TKE and turbulence anisotropy depend directly on location within the roll structure. These findings provide preliminary support for the modification of small-scale turbulence by larger-scale roll dynamics. Finally, UAS platforms are demonstrating the capability to resolve fine-scale inertial turbulence statistics and spectral energy transfer. High-frequency hot-wire velocity sensor measurements were collected via UAS to examine energy spectrum scaling, specifically evaluating the value of the Kolmogorov constant and spectral bottleneck behavior at high wavenumbers. Classical Kolmogorov-Obukhov phenomenology predicts a three-dimensional velocity spectrum following power-law scaling within the inertial subrange governed by the Kolmogorov constant (CK). While Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) allow direct evaluation of the 3D spectrum, high-Reynolds-number laboratory experiments typically measure the one-dimensional longitudinal spectrum, which exhibits identical scaling governed by C1. Low Reynolds number laboratory assessments widely report C1=0.5 (CK = 1.5). In contrast, measurements in high-Reynolds-number atmospheric flows often yield C1=0.62 (CK=2.5), values that remain debated due to concerns over measurement non-stationarity and surface proximity. The high-resolution UAS measurements validate these higher atmospheric Kolmogorov constants while providing some physical insight into the discrepancies observed between lower-Reynolds-number laboratory settings and atmospheric boundary layer flows.

488645.title: A Tell of Two Seasons – The Importance of Long-Term, Detailed Air Quality Observations for an Urban Environment
488645.authors: Benjamin A. Nault, Johns Hopkins University, BALTIMORE, MD; Johns Hopkins Univ. and Aerodyne Research Inc, Nottingham, MD; and L. Aiyer, D. Blomdahl, N. Ferdousi-Rokib, K. Koehler, S. Milletich, M. Miles, O. Oladeji, A. Pettijohn, M. Tehrani, K. N. Steiner, A. Yassine, T. P. Canty, A. M. Ring, J. Hunter, B. F. Zaitchik, and P. F. DeCarlo
488645.abstract: Many highly instrumented field studies investigating the factors influencing urban air quality (AQ) typically last for 1 – 2 months, maximum, providing highly detailed information during that specific period/season. However, those factors may not be representative of other seasons. Furthermore, a combination of changing emissions and emission standards, as well as the influence of episodic events (e.g., transported pollution, heat waves) may be missed during these studies. Baltimore, Maryland provides a test case investigating the factors impacting ozone (O3) and particulate matter (PM) AQ for an urban area, as the region has multiple highly instrumented AQ monitoring sites and was one of the urban areas investigated through the Department of Energy Urban Integrated Field Laboratory studies. In this study, we use observations from these AQ monitoring sites from the last ~2 decades in tandem with the observations collected during the Baltimore Social Environmental Collaborative (BSEC) to investigate the trends and factors impacting AQ in the greater Baltimore region. For O3, we find that both the extreme (90th percentile) and mean summer mixing ratios have been decreasing across the region (~ 0.4 – 1.1 ppbv yr-1 decrease); however, winter “baseline” O3 has been increasing by ~0.4 ppbv yr-1. We find that a combination of lowered nitrogen oxides emissions and mixing ratios (titration) as well as influence from changing volatile organic compounds (VOC) emissions and reactivity (production) influence this increase in baseline O3. This in turn has led to a longer season when people are exposed to O3 mixing ratios above the World Health Organization recommendations. The spatial distribution of these VOCs is explored with different mobile experiments conducted during the BSEC time frame. For PM, we find that, after decreasing until ~2018, mass concentration has since remained relatively constant for the last ~7 years. Furthermore, we find that the winter and summer seasons both have consistently high PM mass concentrations during this time period, influenced by different sources (residential wood heating and traffic in winter) and PM production (nitrate in winter and secondary organic aerosol in summer) – observations that would not have been easily discernable without the added measurements from BSEC combined with the AQ monitoring sites’ data. Due to these two seasonal maxima and differing sources, the results highlight the importance of understanding sources of PM as AQ standards are lowered to ensure improved population health.

488650.title: From Hazard to Decisions: A Panel on Severe Convective Storm Risk for Risk Management & Insurance Applications
488650.abstract: Severe convective storms (SCS), including hail, tornadoes, and straight-line winds, are a persistent and increasingly important source of insured losses in the United States. Their high frequency, localized impacts, and spatially dispersed nature create distinct challenges for hazard characterization, catastrophe modeling, underwriting, portfolio management, and financial risk management. This panel will bring together perspectives from academia, catastrophe modeling, insurance, reinsurance, and risk analytics to discuss how SCS risk is being measured, modeled, and incorporated into operational and strategic decision-making. The discussion will focus on the gap between physical representations of severe weather and the information required by insurers, reinsurers, and other financial decision-makers. Topics will include advances in radar- and satellite-based hazard characterization, event and loss attribution, model calibration and validation, changing exposure and vulnerability, and the use of emerging datasets and analytical approaches to support underwriting and portfolio decisions. Panelists will also discuss current limitations in SCS modeling, areas where academic and industry perspectives diverge, and priorities for improving the transparency and usability of risk information.

488653.title: Using Established Partnerships to Communicate Localized Daily Heat Threats in South Carolina
488653.authors: Madison Sydney Nordberg, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC; and A. L. Hiscox, B. W. Robertson, G. J. Carbone, and J. Salinas
488653.abstract: As heat-related illnesses cause more fatalities each year, a communication gap exists in how individuals and organizations receive vital information about decision making especially on local scales. To address a pre-established need for clearer heat information, a daily email communication was sent to key partners of the regional weather forecast office, who were individuals and groups across the study area who are impacted by heat in their operations. This featured heat index, wet bulb globe temperature, and HeatRisk forecasts at a local scale. Forecasts were analyzed for accuracy depending on category and heat measure to understand how often forecasts provided reliable risk levels, showing that only utilizing forecasts may miss the worst of the impacts, and observed weather can support further understanding. The findings and methods from the 2025 study period guided the continuation of the email for 2026 and could help future communication about heat risk and could eventually be expanded to other metropolitan areas in the weather forecast region.

488655.title: Exploring the Limits of Stratospheric Aerosol Injection Detectability
488655.authors: Sergio Ibarra Espinosa, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; NOAA, College Park, MD; and A. Crawford
488655.abstract: Natural or engineered Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) poses a detection challenge. Volcanic eruptions have been detected with balloons or satellites, but smaller SAI can be difficult to detect and properly attribute. We used the Baseline Balloon Stratospheric Aerosol Profiles (B2SAP) network, to track air parcels impacting observations between 2019 and 2025. B2SAP is equipped with POPS instruments, provides a potential monitoring capability, but its detection probability for SAI events has not been quantified. We used the HYSPLIT model to develop a transfer coefficient matrix (TCM) for each B2SAP observation. After that, we calculated the probability of detection injection events, with categories, bigger like Hunga Tonga 2022, medium with Raikoke 2019 eruption and then small for values close to background. To close the loop, we also calculated the injection amount with a smooth kalman filter. Finally, we evaluated reversibility of air parcels from and back source-receptor, MERRA2 v/s ERA5 and point versus line release.

488659.title: Tony: The Early Years
488659.authors: Mark A. Cane, Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory of Columbia Unversity, Palisades, NY
488659.abstract: I discuss three of Tony’s earliest papers: Busalacchi and O’Brien, 1981, which is, for me, the most important numerical ocean model simulation of all time; Busalacchi and Cane, 1985, a hindcast of the 1982-83 El Niño sea level; Busalacchi and Cane, 1988, a study of equatorial wave propagation in zonally varying stratification. The first paper was part of Tony’s thesis; the others were done during his postdoc with me. Busalacchi and O’Brien 1981 convincingly demonstrated a causal connection on interannual timescales from wind stress variations to sea level in the tropical Pacific, confirming Wyrtki’s analysis. It went beyond that by showing that the connection could be found in the sparse, problematic wind data available pre-satellite, pre-TOGA-TAO, and that the connection could be made with a model with only simple shallow water equation (SWE) physics. It was one of the earliest if not the earliest numerical ocean model calculations to actually teach us something about the physics of the real ocean. Busalacchi and Cane 1985 was a straightforward calculation within the multimode SWE framework of sea level response to winds. It showed that the first two vertical modes are needed to capture sea level variations with a reasonably correct amplitude and phase. It is a “classic” SWE calculation in that the mean stratification is taken to be constant in space and time, whereas it is obvious that the climatological stratification varies considerably in the equatorial Pacific. We treated this in the 1988 paper, borrowing an approach used for radiative transfer, which allowed us to consider the effect of abrupt changes in stratification rather than the slowly varying stratification required by the well-known WKBJ method. It turned out that waves propagate through stratification changes with minimal loss of energy due to internal reflections. Consequently, amplitude increases when wave speed slows.

488660.title: The Role of Wood Burning for Heating on Urban Air Quality
488660.authors: Benjamin A. Nault, Johns Hopkins University, NOTTINGHAM, MA; and N. Ferdousi-Rokib, S. Milletich, A. Pettijohn, K. N. Steiner, K. Koehler, B. F. Zaitchik, and P. F. DeCarlo
488660.abstract: Current U.S. regulations for annual PM2.5 is 9 µg m-3 while W.H.O. recommends that annual PM2.5 should not exceed 5 µg m-3. As increasing temperatures and influence of wildfires are increasing PM2.5 mass concentrations during summer periods, identifying and reducing other sources of PM2.5 concentrations to reduce annual concentrations is imperative. One of these other sources is wood burning for heating. Here, we use a combination of long-term regulator observations, a low-cost monitoring network, and an air quality monitoring supersite that is part of the DOE Baltimore Social-Environmental Collaborative, to investigate the role of wood burning heating in the Baltimore region and its impact towards the area’s annual PM2.5 mass concentration and optical properties as well as human health. We find that between late fall to early spring (~November - ~March), there is a comparable amount of total PM2.5 mass concentration as there is during summer. However, unlike summer, where the majority of the PM2.5 originates from the photochemical production of secondary organic aerosol, organic aerosol only composes ~50% of the total PM2.5 during these colder periods. Furthermore, most of the organic aerosol is primary, originating from biomass burning, as identified with positive matrix factorization with an aerosol chemical speciation monitor (ACSM) and also confirmed with results collected from an aethalometer. The composition of this OA is further explored with the ACSM, highlighting the increased exposure towards different polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), a class of hazardous air pollutants that may lead to poor health outcomes. The optical properties of this wood burning OA are evaluated with the aethalometer, looking at the impact towards aerosol absorption. Spatially, the impact of this wood burning is explored with the low-cost sensors, demonstrating mixed results in the impact of this wood burning aerosol that is highly dependent on meteorological conditions. We will explore the potential impact in best case scenario eliminating wood burning both at the urban level and neighborhood level. The results will be placed into the context of monthly PM2.5 trends observed in other cool-to-cold climate urban areas in the U.S. to provide potential context in what other urban areas can do to reduce PM2.5.

488661.title: Building an AI/ML-Ready Earth System Science Workforce: Lessons from the NSF NCAR Machine Learning Bootcamp
488661.authors: Mariana Goodall Cains, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and P. Montaño, MS, MA, A. Rhinehart, G. Leguy, C. Hannay, K. J. Mayer, K. Dagon, D. Howard, D. J. Gagne II, C. Becker, B. Guarente, N. Sobhani, and J. Amaya
488661.abstract: The Earth system science (ESS) community and workforce must be literate in AI/ML fundamentals and skilled in ESS applications to harness technological innovations, advance research, and prepare for the future. To that end, the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) anticipates workforce needs by bringing together domain knowledge, AI/ML proficiency, and pedagogical expertise. The presented study showcases the learning impact of NSF NCAR’s Introduction to Machine Learning for Earth System Scientists bootcamp, a cross-organizational training bootcamp that builds institutional and community literacy in AI/ML leading to enhanced weather modeling and forecasting. Nearly 150 NSF NCAR and UCAR Community Programs (UCP) staff have benefited from the hybrid, synchronous AI/ML bootcamp courses running in 2023 and 2025. The bootcamp was purposefully designed with ESS domain-specific applications to increase AI/ML comprehension and use of AI/ML in ESS research. Through tangible ESS applications, the bootcamp trains the current workforce on theoretical foundations of AI/ML, AI/ML techniques and models, and evaluation and critique of AI/ML. The training provides expert-vetted ESS applications of supervised machine learning artificial neural networks (ANN), convolutional neural networks (CNN), decision trees, and explainable AI (XAI). Results from the pre-bootcamp and post-bootcamp evaluations show measured improvement in bootcamp participants' confidence identifying and applying foundational AI/ML concepts, as well as tractable knowledge for taking the new steps in their AI/ML education. Additionally, in collaboration with UCP, the synchronous NSF NCAR machine learning bootcamp training material is being converted into online, asynchronous modules on the MetEd platform, which has served 800,000+ registrants globally over 20 years. These asynchronous modules transform our training reach from hundreds of NSF NCAR and UCP staff to tens of thousands of ESS students and community members to strengthen the community’s understanding of when conventional or AI/ML approaches are most appropriate for a given scientific challenge.

488662.title: Best Practices for Mesonets Measuring and Reporting Reference Evapotranspiration
488662.authors: Kendall DeJonge, ARS, Fort Collins, CO
488662.abstract: Data collected and reported by mesonets can be useful for a variety of purposes, including weather forecasting, drought and flood monitoring, and hydrologic modeling. A primary use of mesonets in agricultural regions is for calculating reference evapotranspiration, a standardized measurement resulting from temperature, relative humidity, solar radiation, and wind, and sited on a well-watered grass or tall crop reference surface. Here we will discuss some of the nuances and best practices for station siting and maintenance, data quality, and reporting of reference evapotranspiration data.

488663.title: CMIP6-Projected Changes in Northern Hemisphere Extratropical Cyclones and their Relations to Common Climate Modes
488663.authors: Matthew Solomon Lynne, University at Albany - State University of New York, Albany, NY; and A. Dai
488663.abstract: Much effort has been made to elucidate how climate change will impact extratropical cyclone (ETC) characteristics and their variations over the coming decades. Driven by interactions between ETCs and the background environment, the two leading modes of daily variability over the dominant Northern Hemisphere (NH) storm tracks are the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and the Pacific-North American Pattern (PNA). Thus, background warming may alter the impacts of these two climate modes on ETCs. While many studies have argued that midlatitude storm tracks will likely shift poleward on a hemispheric scale, it is less clear how their associated impacts and connections to common climate modes may vary. Using 11 models from the CMIP6 ensemble, an impact-based ETC tracking algorithm is applied to sea level pressure fields from historical and SSP2-4.5 experiments. ETC characteristics and their relations to the NAO and PNA seen in reanalysis data are well replicated by the CMIP6 historical simulations, making this ensemble suitable for future change analyses. Defining ETC frequency as the percent of time a location is within an ETC’s outermost isobar, we analyze ETC characteristic changes between the present and future simulations and their relations with NAO and PNA. This reveals how the NAO and PNA’s impact on ETCs may be modulated by global warming. Long-term trends in dynamically relevant variables such as baroclinic and barotropic energy conversion aid in identifying the physical mechanisms responsible for such changes. This work provides further understanding of how daily ETC variations related to common climate modes may be modified by continued warming.

488664.title: Using Seasonal Activity Metrics to Develop a Spatial Climatology of Eastern and Central Pacific Tropical Cyclones
488664.authors: Nicholas S. Grondin, University of Tampa, Tampa, FL; and M. E. Fibbi
488664.abstract: In this study, we develop spatial climatology of tropical cyclone (TC) activity in the eastern and central North Pacific basins using seasonal activity metrics. We subdivide the region (10–32.5°N, 86–176°W) into 31 7.5°x7.5° quadrants. For each quadrant, we calculate count (number of named storms, hurricanes, and major hurricanes), day (e.g., named storm days, etc.), and integrated (e.g., Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE)) metrics for each year from 1971 to 2024. We analyze average and extreme levels of activity of each metric and compute the ratio of basin’s activity that occurred within each quadrant. We perform a trend analysis of activity in the coastal quadrants along the American Pacific Coast and the quadrant inclusive of the main Hawaiian Islands. Lastly, we also compare quadrant-level activity between phases of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation. We identify that activity is most concentrated in quadrants east of 125°W, including those along the Pacific Coast of Mexico. Most notably, some of the highest levels of activity across all metrics include the quadrant encompassing southern Baja California Sur (Cabo San Lucas). Trends in activity were varied, with the most notable finding being a general increasing trend in activity for the quadrant encompassing the major resort cities of Puerto Vallarta and Manzanillo. Consistent with previous research, we also identify the eastern quadrants of the basin frequently have increased values for the ACE and the day metrics during most La Niña years, while during El Niño years the spatial pattern in metrics is less consistent. Results of this project will have applicability in improving the seasonal forecasts for the region, which is particularly important given the unique geography TC impacts in the basin.

488665.title: Effect of Building Configuration and Release Location on the Sensitivity of Urban Canopy Air Temperature to Anthropogenic Heat Flux
488665.authors: Sean Robert O'Brien, Boston University, Boston, MA; and D. Li
488665.abstract: Anthropogenic heat flux (Qa) is a known driver of the urban heat island effect, and affects the urban climate through changing flow fields and scalar transport. When quantifying the warming effect of anthropogenic heat flux using a sensitivity concept Sa=ΔTa/ΔQa where ΔTa refers to the response of urban air temperature to an anthropogenic heat flux forcing (ΔQa), past studies have found a wide range of values spanning more than an order of magnitude. In this study, we seek to understand the effect of building configuration and release location on, defined using the volume-averaged air temperature within the urban canopy. We perform large eddy simulations over an idealized two-dimensional urban canyon and employ a forcing-response-feedback framework to interpret the simulation results. We found that the dependence of Sa on building configuration and release location arises from the coupling between urban canopy air and the overlying atmosphere above the urban canyon, which is modulated by both the background wind speed and anthropogenic heating. Through an analysis of the various physical processes and feedbacks contributing to Sa, our results improve the understanding of urban air temperature sensitivity to anthropogenic heat flux and provide guidance on how to reduce the effects of anthropogenic heat release.

488692.title: Identifying and Characterizing Consecutive MCS Events Across the Central and Eastern United States
488692.authors: Kelsey Kressler, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and S. M. Hitchcock
488692.abstract: When two or more MCSs occur over a short temporal window (< 12 hours) in the same geographic area, their impacts can be greatly amplified and forecasting challenges increase due to uncertainty in environmental recovery timing. Despite their compounding effects, consecutive MCS events are less studied than their individual event counterparts. This study investigates consecutive MCS events using GridRad V4.2 composite radar reflectivity data over the central and eastern US east of the Rocky Mountains by creating MCS storm objects and applying two methods to identify spatial recurrence. The first method identifies days when two simultaneous MCSs have centroids separated by distances less than 250 km and persist across 3 or more successive hours. The second approach uses gridded MCS object mask overlaps to identify MCSs within 3-, 6-, and 12-hour time windows. Preliminary results suggest that there are a total of 14 consecutive MCS days in June 2019 with 11 simultaneous MCSs and 10 identified in a 6-hour rolling window with 7 days overlapping between both methods. This will be expanded to warm seasons between 2016 and 2021. This work will provide a characterization of consecutive MCS events across the central and eastern United States, with the goal of identifying environmental conditions and storm dynamics that favor consecutive MCS events.

488705.title: Studying Aerosol-Cloud Interactions Using Remote Sensing Observations Constrained by Machine Learning-Derived Cloud Condensation Nuclei (CCN) Concentrations (Invited Presentation)
488705.authors: Lan Gao, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and J. Redemann, E. D. Lenhardt, R. A. Ferrare, J. W. Hair, A. R. Nehrir, C. Hostetler, T. Shingler, B. Cairns, A. Sorooshian, and I. Chang
488705.abstract: A substantial portion of the uncertainty in anthropogenic climate forcing arises from our limited understanding of the instantaneous effect of aerosols on cloud albedo, commonly referred to as the radiative forcing from aerosol-cloud interactions (RFaci). The magnitude of RFaci can be constrained through observed relationships between aerosol properties and cloud droplet number concentration (Nd) or effective radius (Re). For large-scale assessments, these relationships have traditionally been derived from satellite observations using column-integrated proxies for cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), such as aerosol optical depth (AOD) or aerosol index (AI). However, these proxies may be inadequate for constraining RFaci because aerosol activation primarily occurs near cloud base rather than throughout the atmospheric column. In addition, aerosol optical properties depend not only on particle concentration but also on particle size distribution and composition. Since CCN represents only a subset of the aerosol population, its relationship with aerosol optical properties is often weak or variable, introducing substantial uncertainty into satellite-based estimates of RFaci. In this study, we utilize a novel, vertically resolved CCN product derived using a machine learning algorithm applied to observations from NASA's airborne High Spectral Resolution Lidar Generation-2 (HSRL-2) collected over the western Atlantic. Using this product, we investigate the relationships between various aerosol proxies and cloud properties retrieved by the Research Scanning Polarimeter (RSP) during coordinated HSRL-2/RSP flights. Joint histograms of aerosol proxies and cloud parameters demonstrate that the vertically resolved CCN product provides a more robust constraint on aerosol-Nd and aerosol-Re relationships across a broad range of cloud liquid water paths than conventional aerosol optical property proxies. To extend this framework to satellite observations, we apply a similar methodology using Cloud-Aerosol Lidar with Orthogonal Polarization (CALIOP) and Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) measurements over the same study region. We then compare aerosol-cloud interaction relationships derived from the airborne and satellite observations to assess the consistency of spaceborne estimates and identify the limitations introduced by conventional satellite aerosol proxies.

488710.title: GPU-Accelerated Microclimate Modeling for Urban Heat Mitigation Planning: A Place Based Case Study in Austin, Texas
488710.authors: Trevor Brooks, Univ. of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX; and N. Sudharsan, H. Kamath, P. Bixler, and D. Niyogi
488710.abstract: Increasing global temperatures, in conjunction with the intensification of the urban heat island (UHI) effect pose growing risks to public health, energy demand, and outdoor comfortability, especially in fast growing cities in the southern United States. In partnership with the City of Austin, Texas, this project develops a high-resolution micrometeorological modeling framework that aims to quantify the thermal comfort benefits of proposed urban heat mitigation interventions prior to implementation. The goal is to provide the city with a defensible and spatially explicit evidence base to guide design decisions across candidate mitigation sites. The framework is built around the Universal Climate Index (UTCI), which is a physiological based outdoor thermal comfort metric that integrates air temperature, mean radiant temperature (MRT), wind speeds, and humidity into a single index that is expressed in terms of equivalent temperature. UTCI is more ideal from a city standpoint (as opposed to simpler metrics like air temperature) because it can capture variables such as radiative effects, and therefore better estimate the thermal exposure that pedestrians actually experience at street level. Importantly, these radiative effects are the dimensions that are most directly altered by common intervention methods such as shading infrastructure and surface material changes (e.g. reflective pavements). UTCI calculations are done via SOLWEIG-GPU, a validated thermal comfort model. Beyond traditional before/after comparisons, this study aims to show effects of interventions along a temporal trajectory and with different strategies per site. This framing is intended to allow for more nuanced planning decisions, for example a phased implementation strategy that a singular end-end comparison would obscure. Importantly, for ease of translation to decision makers, model outputs integrated into a 3D, browser-accessible visualization using Cesium, with the longer goal of developing digital twins of these mitigation sites. This layer is indented to translate quantitative model results into accessible formats for City staff, planners, and public stakeholders in a way that supports both technical evaluation and community communication. This work contributes a reproducible and scalable workflow for evaluating urban heat mitigation strategies that pairs an open-source, physically based microclimate modeling pipeline with high-performance computing to make city-scale, multi-scenario thermal comfort assessment accessible. By coupling this pipeline with an emerging visualization platform, the project aims to demonstrate a practical bridge between academic microclimate research and applied municipal decision-making, offering a transferable methodology for other cities pursuing evidence-based urban heat mitigation planning.

488717.title: Green Infrastructure Governance, Goals, and Gaps In U.S. and German Cities [INVITED]
488717.authors: Sara Meerow, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO
488717.abstract: Cities worldwide are increasingly investing in urban forestry, green infrastructure, and nature-based solutions to enhance sustainability and resilience. Green infrastructure spatial planning, or the decision-making processes for determining which functions are prioritized and where different types of urban vegetation get implemented within cities, is not well understood. This is an important knowledge gap because research shows that there are tradeoffs between functions, landscape designs, and locations, but these remain under-examined. Research suggests that cities need more clearly defined green infrastructure goals, decision-making processes aligned with those aims, and strategic, multifunctional planning to overcome persistent barriers. This study examines these aspects of green infrastructure spatial planning practices in diverse cities across two front-runner countries, the United States and Germany. We compare the results of surveys of local officials engaged in green infrastructure and urban forestry in a stratified random sample of over 100 cities across both countries. Qualitative and quantitative analyses reveal that cities are implementing a wide range of green infrastructure types to gain multiple benefits. While there are significant differences between the countries, strategic spatial planning processes for multifunctionality, equity, and future climate change are still uncommon, and cities perceive many barriers to expanding green infrastructure.

488719.title: Climatological Features of Additional Sea-Level Gradient Tools Pertinent to the Los Angeles International Airport Station ("LAX")
488719.authors: Charles J. Fisk, Individual, Newbury Park, CA
488719.abstract: In a recent study (Fisk, 2021) the climatological aspects of the LAX to Daggett (“LAX-DAG”) sea-level pressure gradient statistic, that which quantifies (“offshore” and “onshore” flow tendencies between the two stations were surveyed over a range of time scales (hourly, monthly, and daily) covering the 1949-2021 period, excluding a data gap for the years 1965-1972. A list was also provided identifying four additional stations relative to LAX whose gradient statistics can aid in characterizing the regional sea-level pressure gradient “landscape”. The present study incorporates one of these, LAX to Bakersfield (“LAX-BFL”) plus the LAX-San Francisco Airport gradient (“LAX-SFO”), previously unlisted. More recently, the missing Daggett Sea-Level Pressure observations for 1965-72, have since been found online, enlarging the LAX-DAG hourly history to a virtually complete 77-years, 1949-2025. Like the LAX-DAG statistic, the LAX-BFL and LAX-SFO’s primary uses are that of a forecasting tool for high-wind events, especially Santa Ana episodes for LAX-DAG. In addition to the forecasting of strong North to North-Westerly flow episodes that occasionally occur over Southern California during the Winter, Spring, and Fall, the LAX-SFO gradient can also help specify the anticipated character of upslope flow events on the south-facing Transverse Mountain Ranges of the Ventura County vicinity during major Pacific Storm events, improving estimates of the possible heavy rainfall levels that will result. In this presentation a series of tables, time-series graphs, hour-by-month climograms, and other graphics are provided highlighting the various features of the three tools.

488720.title: Accelerating Community Model Development Through Process-Oriented Diagnostics and Machine Learning
488720.authors: Augustin Vintzileos, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA; Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD; and B. A. Cash and J. L. Kinter
488720.abstract: The calibration of physical parameterizations remains one of the most challenging and time-consuming aspects of community Earth system model development. Improvements in one performance metric (e.g., CONUS surface temperature or 500-hPa height forecast skill) often degrade others because a single set of parameter values is expected to represent multiple physical regimes governed by different processes. Examples include transitions in air–sea turbulent exchange from interfacial turbulence to wave-mediated processes under high winds, as well as regime changes in convection, cloud microphysics, and boundary-layer turbulence. These challenges motivate a process-oriented model development strategy in which physically distinct regimes are identified and evaluated separately. We present PROMETHEUS (PROcess-oriented Model dEvelopment Through dEcision tRee HeUristic System), a framework that usesw interpretable machine learning for process-oriented diagnostics to objectively partition atmospheric columns into Column States. Column States are defined as groups of atmospheric columns exhibiting statistically distinct behavior in a target variable or model error, providing an objective representation of different physical regimes. Rather than calibrating parameterizations globally, PROMETHEUS enables targeted investigation and optimization within individual Column States using Single Column Models or other reduced-complexity modeling systems, transforming a single global tuning problem into a collection of process-specific development problems. As an initial demonstration, we use the tendency of outgoing longwave radiation as a proxy for tropical convective evolution. The resulting decision tree identifies physically interpretable combinations of moisture structure, vertical motion, thermodynamic profiles, and surface conditions associated with distinct convective regimes. For example, the widely recognized oceanic skin-temperature threshold near 28°C emerges only after the atmosphere has been preconditioned by large-scale moisture convergence and upper-level ascent, illustrating how decision trees can expose conditional process dependencies that are obscured in traditional diagnostics. We discuss how PROMETHEUS can support the Unified Forecast System (UFS) community by providing objective process-level diagnostics, guiding targeted parameterization development, enabling conditional bias correction, and accelerating model development cycles through systematic identification of process-specific deficiencies.

488724.title: Improved Quantification and Modeling of Agricultural Volatile Organic Compound Emissions and Their Impacts on Ozone Non-Attainment in California’s Central Valley
488724.authors: Sean Youn, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and Q. Z. Rasool, R. H. Schwantes, I. B. Pollack, C. Harkins, M. M. Coggon, J. Gilman, M. A. Robinson, C. Stockwell, C. Warneke, E. Y. Pfannerstill, Q. Zhu, S. W. Kim, C. Arata, A. Bucholtz, A. H. Goldstein, D. K. Henze, and B. C. McDonald
488724.abstract: California’s Central Valley suffers from some of the most severe ozone pollution in the nation, with surface concentration levels regularly exceeding federal and state regulatory standards. This is due in part to significant emissions of ozone precursors, including volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and nitrogen oxides (NOx), from agricultural sources in the Central Valley. Accurately quantifying these precursor emissions, which have traditionally been underrepresented in inventories, is essential for understanding, and eventually mitigating, ozone exceedences. Towards this goal, we update agricultural VOC emissions in a national emissions inventory (GRA2PES) using emissions fluxes derived from an aircraft campaign (RECAP-CA) over the San Joaquin Valley, as well as ground-based agricultural VOC emissions relative to ammonia observed in the 2015 NOAA SONGNEX campaign. These updates show an increase in agricultural VOCs compared to existing inventories, including approximately doubling the emissions of alcohols. The updated VOC emissions, in conjunction with updates to agricultural NOx, are incorporated into high-resolution WRF-Chem simulations which yield increased ozone concentrations more consistent with observations (AEROMMA and AQS). Sensitivity analyses are also performed to identify potential policy solutions to target ozone pollution reduction in the region.

488725.title: Parameterization of Topographic Effects on the Wind Speeds in the Gridded Tropical Cyclone Model (GTCM)
488725.authors: Katherine Sinclair Maclay Schwartz, CIRA, Cottage Grove, OR; and M. DeMaria, J. Kaplan, and R. DeMaria
488725.abstract: Topographic effects can produce localized maxima in the surface wind fields of landfalling tropical cyclones (TCs) which can have significant impacts on the damages produced by these storms. Thus, proper modeling of topographic features is vitally important. This study makes use of the idealized topography types as defined by Tan and Fang (2018) as well as the topography elevation data in 30 arc-second resolution from the ETOPO Global Relief Model (Amante and Eakins, 2009) to develop a topographical parameterization for the National Hurricane Center (NHC) operational Gridded Tropical Cyclone advisory Message (GTCM). The GTCM provides a 2-dimensional wind field from NHC’s official text forecast using a parametric vortex and a land-surface model. The GTCM accounts for variations in land surface type, but not elevation. The training data for the parametrization was obtained for sixteen landfalling cases from the Caribbean, East and West Pacific from the modeling study of Done et al (2020), which simulated the low level winds of landfalling tropical cyclones including terrain effects with a high-resolution boundary layer model. The topography types will be used to provide statistical adjustments to the 10 m wind differences between the GTCM (without terrain) and the Done model forecasts (with terrain), where both use parametric wind models above the surface layer. Preliminary results of the GTCM terrain model and examples from recent tropical cyclones will be presented.

488756.title: Diurnal and Seasonal Wind Variabilities of Sixteen Stations in Colorado Utilizing Hour-by-Month Climograms
488756.authors: Charles J. Fisk, Individual, Newbury Park, CA
488756.abstract: Climatological surface wind analyses, taking into account winds’ two-dimensional nature and large variabilities across differing time scales ( sub-hourly, hourly, diurnal, and annual) can be performed utilizing a variety of graphical or tabular formats and detail levels. Although full every-hour climatologies are desirable, they require synthesizing 288 hour‑by‑month data points per station, a volume that typically leads researchers to adopt simplified sampling schemes such as seasonal groupings, day–night partitions, or every‑third‑hour statistics. A methodology developed and refined over several prior studies enables complete hour‑by‑month wind visualization on concise, single‑page graphical layouts. These graphics complement traditional tabular summaries and wind roses, and their compact format makes them especially effective for multi‑station comparisons in operational and research settings. Three previous studies along these lines investigated the various diurnal and seasonal wind characteristics for 33 different California stations (Fisk, 2008,2009) and four for Arizona (Fisk, 2018). Three types of charts for each California station were constructed, depicting: 1.) Mean Vector Wind Directions, Speeds, and Constancies for each of the 288 hour by month data points, 2.) Mean Sixteen Point Compass Prevailing Wind Directions, Speeds, and Percent Climatological Frequencies for each, and also 3.) Mean Scalar Wind Speeds and Percent Climatological Frequencies for each. For the Arizona stations, the Prevailing Wind Direction chart was an eight-point compass one, and there was a fourth chart depicting upper-99th percentile wind speeds irrespective of direction. The present analysis evaluates the histories of sixteen wind-recording stations over Colorado with appreciable periods of records (~ 25 years or greater), thru early 2026. The number of charts per station is reduced to two, the previous “Prevailing Winds” category dropped. The current selection for the Colorado stations includes 1.) Mean Vector Wind Directions (“Resultants”) and Constancies, and 2.) Mean Scalar Wind Speeds and Percent climatological frequencies of the mean speeds. The Mean Vector Wind Directions (1), in unit-length orientation at each point, are designated as the “Mean (or “Average”) Wind Directions”; in reality, weighted Mean Directions, as mean vector wind direction orientations are influenced by the individual observations’ comparative north-south and east-west component magnitudes. Higher component magnitudes slant the mean statistic in their direction. The “Constancy” statistic (values between 0 and 100) describes the composite steadiness of the individual wind observations’ relative to their particular overall resultant direction. It’s calculated by the ratio of the mean vector wind speed to the mean scalar wind times 100. Low values can be interpreted as periods with light and variable winds or adjacent hourly transition periods subject to land-breeze to sea-breeze changeovers, mountain breezes, valley winds, or frontal passages.

488760.title: Extreme Heat and Poor Air Quality In Community Health Centers: Perspectives from Staff and Patients
488760.authors: Karen Albright, OCHIN, Portland, OR; and K. H. GEORGE, R. Gold, M. Pisciotta, A. Steeves-Reece, B. McGrath, H. Estiri, and R. Gunn
488760.abstract: Background. Extreme heat and poor air quality events are increasing in frequency and severity and pose significant health risks. Patients served by community health centers (CHCs) experience these weather exposures disproportionately due to adverse contextual drivers of health. CHCs have a crucial role in alleviating the health impacts of extreme heat and air quality events but lack evidence of effective interventions to implement. Objective. To explore how extreme heat and poor air quality impact CHC staff and patients and to describe current CHC and community responses. Methods. Qualitative study using semi‑structured interviews, patient focus groups, and direct observation, analyzed thematically. Setting. CHCs in a multi‑state U.S. collaborative sharing a common electronic health record system. Population Studied. CHC providers, staff, and patients. Intervention/Instrument. Observation of CHC operations; interviews with CHC providers and staff; focus group with CHC patients. Outcome Measures. Thematic outcomes characterized patient experiences, CHC responses, and care processes related to extreme heat and poor air quality. Results. Patients reported health impacts from extreme heat and poor air quality, most commonly asthma exacerbations and diabetes management challenges. Many clinic staff had limited experience addressing weather‑related health impacts directly, though those working with highly affected populations—such as patients with asthma or those experiencing homelessness—reported greater involvement. CHCs lacked formal weather‑specific programs but provided indirect support through contextual needs screening and resource navigation and targeted support for high‑risk patients, including education and medication adjustments. Partnerships primarily involved community‑based organizations addressing contextual drivers and local coalitions focused on emergency preparedness and weather exposure planning. Conclusions. Findings will be integrated with advisory committee input, stakeholder interviews, and quantitative analyses of extreme heat, poor air quality, and EHR data to identify promising CHC‑led interventions. This evidence will inform intervention selection, design, and prioritization in future primary care–based efforts to alleviate the impacts of extreme weather.

488768.title: Spatial Sensitivity of Irrigated Agricultural Extent to Snowmelt Across the Western United States
488768.authors: James Larson, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and N. D. Mueller and J. W. Hurrell
488768.abstract: Irrigated agriculture across the western United States is sustained in large part by mountain snowpack, which stores winter precipitation and releases it as spring and summer runoff to downstream agricultural valleys. Declining snowpack volume and earlier melt timing are well documented across the region. Far less is known about how strongly interannual variability in upstream water supply propagates into the spatial extent of irrigated land, and how that sensitivity varies geographically. We develop a gridded statistical framework linking satellite-derived irrigated extent (IrrMapper) to upstream water availability and local atmospheric conditions (TerraClimate). For each grid cell at ~10 km resolution we delineate the contributing upstream watershed, then fit per-cell regressions of irrigated fraction on upstream runoff, local potential evapotranspiration and precipitation, and a linear time trend. The resulting coefficient fields constitute a map of spatial sensitivity across the western US. They identify where irrigated extent is tightly coupled to upstream supply versus buffered by externalities such as storage, groundwater access, or water-rights structure, and they separate the supply signal from local atmospheric demand and secular land-use trends. We examine the hydrologic and institutional structure of this spatial pattern, and apply the fitted relationships to project irrigated extent under perturbed future runoff scenarios.

488769.title: Enhancing Aviation Safety through Display of Rapidly Updating C&V Guidance at the NWS Aviation Weather Center
488769.authors: Robert M. Hepper, NOAA/NWS/AWC, Kansas City, MO; and N. E. Starzec, A. E. Cross, A. P. Korner, J. Lind, S. J. Avey, S. Alvidrez, and J. Colavito
488769.abstract: Accurate and timely ceiling and visibility (C&V) forecast information is crucial for safe and efficient aviation operations. To enhance decision support and better communicate risks associated with low ceilings and visibility at the Core 30 airports, The National Weather Service (NWS) Aviation Weather Center (AWC) deployed a rapidly updating C&V Dashboard on AviationWeather.gov. The development of the C&V Dashboard was done in close collaboration with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Aviation Weather Research Program (AWRP), a key partner in ensuring safety of the National Airspace System (NAS). The dashboard provides a user friendly display of forecast output from the Localized Aviation MOS Program (LAMP) with fifteen minute time resolution, and updated forecast information every fifteen minutes. The combination of rapid updates and high temporal resolution enhances NWS Impact Decision Support Service (IDSS) capabilities and facilitates direct user monitoring of C&V short term forecasts during rapidly changing weather conditions, such as fog formation or clearing at airports with high sensitivity to visibility restrictions. Additionally, the dashboard uses LAMP probabilistic data to show the likelihood of C&V conditions falling below critical thresholds, providing decision-makers with more actionable information. This presentation will detail the development of the dashboard and its capabilities, the results of a user assessment conducted collaboratively between the AWC Aviation Weather Testbed (AWT) and the FAA Aviation Weather Demonstration and Evaluation Services, and provide use case examples in which the dashboard could be leveraged to enhance the safety and efficiency of aviation of air traffic flow management. *This research is in response to requirements and funding by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

488772.title: Potential Vorticity Perspective of Medium-Range Forecast Errors of Atmospheric Rivers
488772.authors: Jian-Wen Bao, NOAA, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and S. A. Michelson and E. Grell
488772.abstract: We will present a case study to demonstrate the power of the diabatic potential vorticity (PV) perspective in diagnosing error sources in UFS medium-range forecasts of wintertime atmospheric rivers (ARs). We will show that the ‘‘forecast minus analysis’’ PV pattern on a cross-tropopause isentropic surface in the extratropics can reveal characteristic features of PV forecast errors and how these features relate to the forecast model’s uncertainties in simulating the complex sequence of multiscale interactions between the dynamics of Rossby waves at the tropopause and latent heating in the ARs associated with warm conveyor belts. The case study focuses on using both GFS and ERA5 analyses to diagnose PV errors in forecasts from the Atmospheric River Analysis and Forecast System (AR-AFS), a newly developed UFS application, for a wintertime heavy precipitation event along the US West Coast. We will use the results from the case study to illustrate that the challenge in medium-range AR-related weather forecasts lies in probabilistically predicting Rossby wave dynamics while accounting for stochastic feedback from diabatic effects at smaller scales. It will be shown that the diabatic PV perspective provides a conceptually robust and practically useful method of diagnosing and understanding the multiscale error dynamics of medium-range AR forecasts from NWP models.

488783.title: Investigating the Correlation between SO2 Gas in the Marine Boundary Layer and Surface Chl-a Levels off the California Coast using AEROMMA and Satellite Data
488783.authors: Abby Buschkoetter, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and T. W. Bell and P. J. Lee
488783.abstract: In the ocean-atmosphere sulfur cycle, phytoplankton release dimethyl sulfide (DMS), a volatile organic compound, as a byproduct in their growth. This byproduct can diffuse across the air-sea interface to further react in the marine atmosphere. Once in the atmosphere, the reaction pathway of DMS yields a series of products including sulfur dioxide (SO2). SO2 further oxidizes in the atmosphere, contributing to aerosol formation and cloud condensation nuclei, thus impacting Earth’s radiative forcing and climate. There is a known link between phytoplankton production of DMS and biogenically sourced SO2 in the marine boundary layer (MBL). This study examines if there is any observable correlation between surface chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) and boundary layer SO2—specifically by examining the relationship between SO2 levels in the MBL from the 2023 West Coast Marine AEROMMA flight missions and surface Chl-a levels from a gap-filled satellite product. To maintain focus on only marine-sourced SO2, the sample area was restricted to exclude data over land; a positive, linear correlation was found overall between surface Chl-a and SO2. Correlation was shown to vary based on parameters such as aerial wind speed and distance to the coast. Higher correlation was observed for altitudes below 200 m, at distances farther from the coast, and when wind speed was considered. This strong positive correlation between the two variables off the coast of California raises the question of what the appropriate spatial resolution is to observe the strongest correlation between the two variables.

488798.title: NOAA NESDIS’s Strategic Investments, Connecting Testbeds to Operations
488798.authors: E. Claire McCaskill, NESDIS, Alexandria, VA; and J. Kent, J. M. Garcia-Rivera, C. Nazmi, and R. Esmaili
