488798.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data and Information Service (NESDIS) uses a product portfolio management approach for satellite derived operational products that promotes dynamic responsiveness to the evolving NOAA mission needs. The approach aims are three-pronged: being responsive to NOAA’s mission objectives, ensuring robust operations, and promoting quality scientific innovation to operations. A close collaboration between the NESDIS Chief Scientist, the Satellite Program Office Senior Scientists, and NOAA Line Offices (National Weather Service, National Marine Fisheries Service, Office of Atmospheric Research, National Ocean Service, and Office of Marine and Aviation Operations) ensures the success of this process, enabling NESDIS investments to best serve the user community. The process works closely with NOAA’s Testbeds and Proving Grounds, ensuring that emerging science innovation has a clear path to operations. This presentation will describe the NESDIS product portfolio management approach and detail how recent testbed projects are being transitioned to operations. These topics will be demonstrated through various NESDIS product examples in geophysical categories such as wildland fires and precipitation.

488800.title: Land-Atmosphere Interactions Across Seasons and Space in the Western U.S. (Invited)
488800.authors: Lucas Vargas Zeppetello, UC Berkeley Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management, Oakland, CA; and L. Zhang, D. Battisti, and M. M. Lague
488800.abstract: Interannual fluctuations in average summertime temperatures across the western United States are captured by a leading empirical orthogonal function that explains over 50% of the total observed variance. These summertime variations are empirically associated with winter and springtime soil moisture anomalies in one particular region, the American Southwest. We use a combination of remote sensing and in-situ observations to quantify the influence of this causal chain and find that soil moisture deficits in the southwest explain roughly one third of the overall summertime temperature variance in the western US. Further, our results indicate that 40% of the observed warming trend across the western United States since 1981 has been driven by wintertime precipitation trends in the US southwest. Despite these results, the specific causal pathway connecting winter and springtime soil moisture anomalies in the southwest to pan-western summertime temperature anomalies is not clear. Using novel experiments with the CESM2 general circulation model that impose soil moisture anomalies in the southwest on March 1 of each simulation year, we demonstrate that a global-scale atmospheric anomaly associated with soil moisture deficits in the southwestern US has substantial memory and influences temperature throughout the following season. However, the anomaly associated with these experiments is substantially smaller than the observed temperature variations driven by observed soil moisture anomalies that are typically weaker than those we apply in the climate model. Since we are using a climate model that does not include coupling between the atmosphere and ocean, this curious result prompts the question; are coupled land-ocean-atmosphere interactions important for seasonal temperature anomalies in the western US? If so, this implies that studies of land-atmosphere interaction must quantify the land’s influence on the ocean, and consider multiple co-interacting timescales associated with this coupling. Overall, our results suggest that studies of land-atmosphere interaction must move beyond spatially and temporally coincident anomalies and consider coupling that is distal in both space and time.

488803.title: Extreme Marine Heatwaves in The Global Oceans During The Past Decade
488803.abstract: This study assesses the sensitivity of marine heatwave (MHW) intensity to different MHW thresholds, and examines the contributions of linear sea surface temperature (SST) warming and record-breaking SSTs to extreme MHWs (xMHW) over 2012‒2024. The xMHW is defined by the high threshold of the 97.5th percentile and is compared to the super MHWs (sMHW) and MHWs due to the SST warming trend (wMHW). The sMHW is identified when and where the daily SST exceeds the highest historic value during the previous years on a given calendar day. The wMHW is approximated as the difference between xMHW and dMHW. The dMHW is defined using detrended SSTs at the threshold of the 97.5th percentile. Averaged over 2012‒2024, sMHW and wMHW account for approximately 52% and 43% of xMHW, indicating a more important role of record-breaking SST than that of SST warming trend. Spatially, sMHW dominates over wMHW in high-latitude oceans and during the period of 2012‒2018; in contrast, wMHW dominates over sMHW mostly in the tropical oceans and during the period of 2019‒2024. On global average, sMHW and wMHW increase with time at a rate of 1.1, and 3.3 degree-days per year. However, their relative contributions to xMHWs diverge: the sMHW ratio decreases at -3% per year, but the wMHW ratio increases at 3.6% per year, indicating a growing role of long-term warming in xMHW events.

488806.title: NOAA AI and PEOPLE: Enabling World Class Science to World-Class Operations
488806.authors: Rob Redmon, NOAA, Nederland, CO; and D. Rao, C. Slocum, H. McCullough, B. Meyer, S. W. Bieda III, PhD, M. Jones, M. Youngman, A. Anderson, and J. Chen
488806.abstract: NOAA's science and service delivery are rapidly evolving to better serve the public, driven by convergence of advanced Artificial Intelligence, data-driven modeling and deeper connections between humans and information services. Since the 1980s, NOAA has been using machine learning to post-process weather forecasts, to retrieve geophysical parameters using satellite data, and to detect and monitor ocean biology. The recent increase in volume and complexity of environmental observations and curated training data along with flexible specialized high performance computing environments, and cross domain fusion (e.g. merging natural hazards, economics, supply chain resilience) has led to a new AI revolution for Earth system modeling, predictive capabilities, and seamless human-AI collaboration. The NOAA Center for Artificial Intelligence (NCAI) is actively engaged in a coordinated effort to advance AI research and application across NOAA. As part of this initiative, NCAI is committed to fostering a strong community of practice and accelerating the integration of trustworthy and responsible AI into NOAA’s core mission areas. We recognize the transformative potential of AI to enhance forecast performance, improve efficiencies, and innovate how NOAA's data assets are used. This presentation will showcase NOAA’s AI governance strategy, our future plans, and NCAI’s implementation activities with a focus on empowering the broad weather, water, and climate enterprise through collaboration and knowledge sharing. We’ll detail the formation of NCAI’s Community of Practice, highlighting available AI-ready resources, including data standards and workforce training resources. We invite the audience to raise critical questions and discussion that would aid NOAA and NCAI in advancing NOAA’s forecasting capabilities and strengthening our shared weather, water, climate enterprise for the benefit of an empowered society.

488810.title: An Observation-Based Benchmark of Instantaneous Radiative Forcing from Changing CO2 Concentrations
488810.authors: Aleksandra Strzałka, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and T. S. L'Ecuyer and D. S. Henderson
488810.abstract: The increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide since preindustrial times has altered Earth’s radiative balance and remains a major driver of climate change. The radiative effects of higher CO₂ concentrations are commonly investigated using climate-model simulations. In this study, we take a different approach by examining the radiative forcing from CO₂ in radiative transfer calculations initialized with cloud and atmospheric aerosol profiles derived from A-Train observations. A full year of active sensor observations from CloudSat and CALIPSO are used to constrain present day atmospheric conditions in radiative transfer calculations with preindustrial, present day, doubled, and quadrupled CO₂ concentrations. Longwave radiative fluxes and atmospheric heating rates from the resulting perturbations to CloudSat 2B-FLXHR-LIDAR product are used to evaluate the spatial distribution of instantaneous CO₂ radiative forcing in the absence of feedbacks. Comparisons between cloudy and cloud-free conditions demonstrate how clouds modulate local radiative responses to increasing CO₂. The analysis quantifies the relative influence of high and low clouds on changes in upwelling and downwelling longwave fluxes and atmospheric radiative cooling under each scenario. By incorporating observed cloud and aerosol distributions, this study provides an observation-guided complement to climate-model simulations, contributing to a better understanding of how clouds shape the spatial pattern of radiative effects from rising atmospheric CO₂.

488825.title: Withdrawn: Driving User-Centric Innovation: Enhancing NCEI Data Access Through Targeted UX Research and Continuous Feedback
488825.authors: Jeremy Hall, NESDIS, Asheville, NC; and J. E. Myer
488825.abstract: To ensure data access services directly align with evolving user requirements, NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) has established a rapid feedback loop driven by active stakeholder engagement and continuous user input. This presentation highlights how NCEI leverages customer experience (CX) and user experience (UX) insights to optimize workflows, improve data accessibility, and deliver a modern, intuitive User Interface (UI) and API. By leveraging NOAA-supported feedback tools such as UserZoom and Touchpoints, NCEI captures targeted user insights and applies them iteratively throughout software development—both before and after public release. Attendees will gain insight into the end-to-end UX strategy behind NCEI’s new Search, Discovery, and Data Access UI/API, demonstrating NESDIS’s commitment to customer-centric design, robust data service delivery, and continuous operational improvement.

488826.title: Atmospheric Controls on Solar Irradiance Variability and Photovoltaic Deployment Across New York State
488826.authors: Aisha Mohammed, SUNY, Albany, NY; and J. M. Freedman
488826.abstract: Atmospheric Controls on Solar Irradiance Variability and Photovoltaic Deployment Across New York State Aisha M. Mohammed, Jeffrey M. Freedman State University of New York, Albany, New York, (USA) The Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA) in New York State (NYS) is setting an ambitious goal for solar photovoltaic (PV) capacity, but the reliability of this resource depends on more than the long-term average irradiance. Aerosols, clouds, short-term irradiance ramps, multi-day low solar periods, and atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) processes can modify the amount of solar irradiance reaching the surface. In turn, this influences the availability of available solar energy, the magnitude of the variation in that resource, and where PV deployment is most efficient. In this study, we investigate the effects of atmospheric processes and atmospheric variability (e.g., clouds) on the spatial suitability and expected performance of PV deployment across NYS. To address this, we use NYS Mesonet observational data to characterize the spatial and temporal structure of surface solar irradiance (SSI), primarily global horizontal irradiance (GHI), temperature, humidity, and soil-related variables, together with New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) county-level PV deployment data across NYS. For preliminary results, daytime hours were classified into mostly clear, partly cloudy, and overcast/strongly attenuated conditions using a clear sky index-based cloud proxy. We show that although summer has the highest fraction of mostly clear hours, it also includes many variably cloudy periods (e.g., the presence of BL cumulus clouds) that can cause rapid changes in the PV output. To examine how the existing PV capacity relates to seasonal solar resource and ramp frequency, NYS Mesonet observations are first used to calculate station-level solar metrics. These station metrics are then aggregated by county and compared with NYSERDA county-level PV deployment data. The results show that counties with stronger solar resources in most seasons generally have more installed PV capacity, but this relationship is weaker in summer. This indicates that the solar resource alone does not explain current PV deployment patterns. Instead, PV deployment appears to reflect a combination of atmospheric conditions and practical factors such as population, policy, land availability and restrictions, and grid access. These irradiance-based regimes will be linked to BL and Land Surface (LS) variables such as planetary boundary layer height, lifting condensation level, humidity, wind, soil moisture, and surface fluxes. Irradiance is converted to estimated PV power output using an irradiance-based power model, and we quantify solar ramp rates, daily energy yield, capacity factor, and the frequency, duration, and magnitude of low solar periods for each regime. A spatial correlation of irradiance anomalies between stations and counties is used to show to what extent geographically dispersed PV siting reduces variability across the grid. After that, the metrics based on the regime variability are applied to compare PV deployment strategies including high irradiance siting, geographically disperse siting, low variability siting, and PV overbuilding paired with limited battery storage and curtailment. The goal is to identify which strategies are most efficient in reducing the ramping and low solar risk, providing a variability-informed complement to the existing capacity-based solar resource assessments for NYS. This study is expected to show that cloud regime and BL structure explain a substantial share of the spatial differences in PV ramping and low solar risk across NYS, and that the geographic dispersion and overbuilding can meaningfully reduce storage requirements relative to single-site deployment. Results of this study will offer practical guidance for utilities and state energy planners on siting and storage decisions as NYS scales up the solar PV under the CLCPA targets.

488829.title: Large-Eddy Simulations of a Stable Boundary Layer on Collocated Grids: Sensitivity to Lower Boundary Conditions
488829.authors: Antonia Englberger, DLR, Wessling, BY, Germany; and A. Dörnbrack, P. K. Smolarkiewicz, and A. A. Wyszogrodzki
488829.abstract: This study investigates two distinct approaches for parameterizing surface-atmosphere momentum and heat exchange at the lower boundary in large-eddy simulations (LES) of the stably-stratified boundary layer (SBL). The conventional indirect approach determines the drag coefficient and surface heat flux dynamically via Monin-Obukhov similarity theory (MOST), whereas a direct approach prescribes these quantities as empirical constants. Simulations of the GABLS1 benchmark are conducted with the Eulerian/semi-Lagrangian solver EULAG, which employs a collocated grid. While both boundary-condition formulations yield quantitatively equivalent first-order statistics of horizontal mean wind speed, potential temperature, and Reynolds stress profiles, they fundamentally differ in their representation of turbulence organization. Higher-order statistical analysis reveals that the indirect MOST-based approach triggers coherent turbulent events characterized by elevated skewness and kurtosis, a broader probability density function of vertical velocity, and distinct quadrant-metric signatures. In contrast, the direct approach produces a more uniformly distributed turbulence field with suppressed coherent structures and reduced higher-order moments. To achieve mean-profile agreement with the indirect approach and GABLS1 benchmarks, the direct method requires an empirically elevated drag coefficient, consistent with established findings that climate models necessitate enhanced mixing relative to MOST predictions. Additionally, increasing the subgrid-scale backscatter coefficient yields a low-level jet height and SBL depth in closer quantitative agreement with reference simulations. The results demonstrate that while lower-boundary parameterization has minimal impact on bulk flow properties in idealized LES setups, it shapes the dynamical organization of resolved turbulence. This distinction carries direct implications for numerical weather prediction models when LES models are utilized as dynamical core. Future studies could leverage the collocated-grid formulation as a robust framework for simulating complex terrain and non-canonical flows. In particular, the integration of explicit mixing enhancements—such as adjusted drag coefficients, increased backscatter, or tailored numerical schemes—alongside direct boundary prescriptions represents a promising direction for further investigations.

488832.title: Smoke Toxicity Index
488832.authors: Shobha Kondragunta, NOAA/NESDIS/STAR, College Park, MD; and F. Li, M. Kopacz, and M. Proud
488832.abstract: OAA's operational air quality forecasting is designed to provide hazardous air quality guidance for surface ozone and fine particulate matter, two of the six criteria pollutants. Only emissions of precursors that lead to secondary ozone and fine particle formation for anthropogenic, biogenic, and biomass burning sources are included in the inventories that drive the air quality forecast models. However, biomass burning smoke plumes contain many hazardous air pollutants (HAPs, e.g., polyaromatic hydrocarbons) that are very toxic to human health. First responders and NOAA National Weather Service incident meteorologists responding to fire emergencies on the ground have no information on the toxicity of smoke plumes. As fires happen more often in the wildland urban interface, the toxicity of plumes is no longer dictated solely by burning vegetation. Contributions of built environment to smoke plume toxicity is unknown yet significant for human exposure. NOAA is conceptualizing a new project to develop a smoke plume toxicity index in near real time so first responders can take needed precautions to minimize exposure. The algorithm will be consistent with the currently operational emissions algorithm that uses satellite fire detections and fire radiative power to estimate emissions of trace gases and fine particles for air quality forecast models. For smoke plume toxicity index, we will adapt emissions factors for various HAPs from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) database and derive emissions to calculate smoke toxicity index. In this presentation, we will present the concept and design of the algorithm being carried out under the newly formed Smoke Exposure working group within NOAA's Fire Observations Research and Services Team (FOReST).

488834.title: Exploring the Roles of SST Lateral Boundary Conditions in Florida Wet-Season Onset
488834.authors: Rachel Gaal, University of Miami, Miami, FL
488834.abstract: The onset of the South Florida wet season exhibits substantial interannual variability, yet the mechanisms controlling these year-to-year fluctuations remain poorly understood. Previous studies suggest that variability in regional sea-surface temperatures (SSTs), particularly within the Loop Current and Florida Current system, may influence seasonal rainfall behavior, but the pathways linking ocean variability to wet-season onset remain uncertain. To test this linkage using a modeling framework, we use the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to investigate whether alternate spatial and temporal resolutions of SST lateral boundary conditions (LBCs) contribute to wet-season onset variability through changes in atmospheric moisture availability and moisture-flux convergence. Three experiments are conducted using SST fields derived from ERA5, NOAA Daily Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature (DOISST; 0.25°), and GHRSST OSTIA (GHRSST; 0.05°), with simulations covering 18 wet seasons (March - September) using a nested WRF configuration with 12-km and 4-km domains. The 4km inner domain is used to diagnose wet-season onset characteristics, while the outer 12km domain is used to assess associated synoptic conditions during pre-onset (March-April) and onset (May-June) timeframes. This study aims to evaluate the sensitivity of regional climate simulations to SST boundary choices and investigates whether regional SST variability represents a meaningful source of predictability for Florida wet-season onset and seasonal precipitation.

488839.title: Assessing the Performance of high-Resolution Climate Models at Simulating Southern Florida Wet Season Rainfall
488839.authors: Rachel Gaal, University of Miami, Miami, FL; and B. Kirtman, E. J. Becker, and A. C. Clement
488839.abstract: Southern Florida (SoFL) wet-season rainfall is shaped by coastal geometry, land–sea interactions, and large-scale moisture convergence, making it a challenging target for climate models and downscaled products. This study evaluates SoFL wet-season precipitation in HighResMIP coupled and uncoupled simulations, the MESACLIP CESM-HR ensemble, and three statistically downscaled CMIP6 products—BCCAQ, LOCA2, and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6—against PRISM and ERA5 during historical (1981–2005) and recent SSP5-8.5 (2015–2024) periods. Statistically downscaled products best reproduce the observed annual cycle and wet-season rainfall magnitude, although some methods show reduced daily variability and frequency–intensity tradeoffs. HighResMIP coupled simulations capture wet-season onset but underestimate rainfall amplitude and intensity, while uncoupled simulations produce broader rainfall variability and a more realistic wet-season demise but retain coastal dry biases. MESACLIP shows the largest errors, including weak seasonal amplitude, delayed transitions, and excessive low-intensity rainfall. Across GCM-based categories, rainfall occurs too frequently but with insufficient intensity, especially in high-rainfall coastal regions. These results indicate that nominal 25-km resolution alone is insufficient for representing SoFL wet-season precipitation, highlighting the need for improved convection, air–sea coupling, and mesoscale land–sea interaction processes.

488845.title: Soil Moisture and SST Controls on Sea-Breeze Convection over South Florida
488845.authors: Rachel Gaal, University of Miami, Miami, FL
488845.abstract: Sea-breeze convection produces a substantial fraction of warm-season rainfall across South Florida, yet the extent to which land-surface and oceanic boundary conditions influence convective development and organization remains unclear. We address this question using a suite of convection-permitting WRF sensitivity experiments in which antecedent soil moisture and coastal sea-surface temperatures (SSTs) are systematically perturbed. These simulations are designed to disentangle the individual and combined effects of terrestrial and oceanic forcing across a set of representative South Florida sea-breeze events. For selected case studies, analyses focus on changes in precipitation timing, intensity, and spatial organization to quantify the relative contributions of soil-moisture and SST variability to convective development. The primary objective is to identify the dominant environmental controls on Florida sea-breeze convection and quantify the relative roles of land-surface and oceanic forcing in shaping warm-season precipitation variability.

488851.title: Progress and Updates on NOAA's Low Earth Orbit (LEO) Earth Observation Programs
488851.authors: James M. Valenti, NESDIS, Lanham, MD
488851.abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites provide critical observations of Earth’s land, oceans, cryosphere, and atmosphere that are essential for numerical weather prediction, disaster response, environmental monitoring, and maintaining climate data record continuity. Since the launch of the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (Suomi-NPP) in 2011, the NOAA/NASA Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) has delivered consistent, high-quality global observations through a planned series of five polar-orbiting satellites. NOAA-21, launched as JPSS-2 in 2022, is currently the primary operational satellite in the constellation, while NOAA-20 serves as the secondary, on-orbit backup. Each satellite provides global coverage twice daily, and the two are positioned 50 minutes apart in the afternoon orbit, enabling timely, actionable insights that are vital for protecting lives and property and supporting the U.S. economy. NOAA will end delivery of all remaining Suomi-NPP science products on November 1, 2026, after the satellite provided data for more than three times its five-year operational lifetime. JPSS-4 will be the next satellite in the series to launch on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in 2027. The satellite moved ahead of JPSS-3 in the launch sequence to carry Libera, a new NASA-designed instrument that measures solar radiation. Libera was integrated onto JPSS-4 in early 2026, while JPSS-3 was placed into storage with a planned launch in 2032. The four baseline instruments on the JPSS satellites include the hyperspectral Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) and the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS), which provide atmospheric temperature and moisture profiles for weather forecasting; the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), a highly sensitive visible and infrared imager that monitors environmental conditions such as snow and ice cover, volcanic ash, wildfires, drought, surface temperature, harmful algal blooms, and air quality, even in low-light settings; and the Ozone Mapping and Profiler Suite (OMPS), which monitors global ozone and provides data used in weather and climate models. The JPSS-3 and JPSS-4 satellites will extend these capabilities into the 2030s. Building on the success of JPSS, NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) program is a next-generation initiative for managing future polar-orbiting and other LEO observation systems as loosely associated projects. The program is designed to complement existing programs of record, reduce observational gaps and risks, and ensure the continuity of global LEO observations. NEON strengthens NOAA’s vital relationships with national and international partners such as NASA, the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (EUMETSAT), and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), while also expanding collaboration with other international, commercial, and domestic partners to broaden capabilities and reach. To support these efforts, LEO is working on a Polar EUMETSAT/NEON Ground station Upgrade - Implementation Network, referred to as PENGUIN. The first NEON mission, QuickSounder, is planned for launch in 2027. As a pathfinder mission, QuickSounder aims to demonstrate the feasibility of launching a small, commercial off-the-shelf satellite bus on a compressed schedule. This approach is designed to support more frequent and rapid satellite launches, enhancing weather forecasting by accelerating the deployment of current technology. The QuickSounder satellite has been integrated with the same type of ATMS instrument flying on JPSS satellites. Insights gained from QuickSounder are shaping the concepts for the first operational NEON mission, known as Series 1. Series-1 will carry NEON’s first new operational instrument, the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA), which will serve as the backbone of microwave sounding observations. LEO is currently reviewing responses to the SMBA request for proposal. The NEON program will also explore new ways to leverage commercial partnerships to advance technology as part of the Temperature and Moisture Advanced Technology Evolution (TMATE) project. Through the NEON program, NOAA is advancing the future of environmental monitoring by embracing cutting-edge technologies and strengthening collaboration with commercial partners. This forward-looking initiative reflects NOAA’s ongoing commitment to ensuring the continuity of critical Earth observations while strengthening weather forecasting capabilities to better protect lives, property, and the U.S. economy.

488853.title: Estimating Flash Flood Risk across the Colorado Plateau
488853.authors: Sherlyn C Hilton, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and J. D. Horel
488853.abstract: Flash flood reports and National Weather Service flash flood warnings across the Colorado Plateau of the southwestern United States are examined during five summer seasons (June-September 2021-2025) to identify watershed characteristics associated with flash flooding. Landform, weather, and recreation-related variables derived from datasets with spatial resolutions ranging from 10 to 1000 m are aggregated within United States Geological Survey Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC) watersheds. Across the region, 6% of over 320,000 stream segments and 25% of nearly 15,000 unpaved road-stream crossings are classified as hazardous. Since flash floods are known to be underreported, flash flood warnings are used as a proxy for likely hazard occurrence. A random forest model is then used to assess the relative importance of terrain, weather, and human factors influencing the distribution of flash flood warnings at the HUC-10 watershed level. The fractions of hazardous stream segments, high-runoff soils, lightning frequency, and watershed area had the greatest relative importance for explaining the distribution of flash flood warnings within the watershed. These findings may help inform risk communication and warning strategies across the Colorado Plateau.

488854.title: David Randall and the Evolution of Cloud-Top Entrainment Instability (Invited Presentation)
488854.abstract: David Randall's Ph.D. research established the first theoretical framework identifying the thermodynamic conditions under which entrainment-induced evaporative cooling produces negative buoyancy at cloud top. He described this mechanism as Conditional Instability of the First Kind Upside-down (CIFKU), a concept that later became widely known in the literature as cloud-top entrainment instability (CTEI). Building on Doug Lilly's hypothesis that cloud-top entrainment could destabilize marine stratocumulus, and motivated by the development of a boundary-layer parameterization for the UCLA GCM, Randall's work placed the idea on a firm theoretical foundation. In this talk, I revisit the early development of this work, drawing on conversations with Dave about the motivation behind the research, the origins of CIFKU, and the influence of Professor Akio Arakawa during his graduate years. I then trace how the idea evolved through its application in atmospheric models and subsequent observational, theoretical, and numerical studies. I briefly discuss our 2008 large-eddy simulation study, which revisited the original hypothesis, and conclude by discussing the continuing debate over the relevance of the stability criterion to the stratocumulus transition, reflecting on Dave's enduring contributions to boundary-layer meteorology and atmospheric modeling.

488856.title: Advancing Operational Water Prediction Through Development of the National Water Model (INVITED)
488856.authors: Brian Cosgrove, NWS Office of Water Prediction, Silver Spring, MD; and F. L. Ogden and F. Salas
488856.abstract: The National Water Model (NWM) is nearing a transformational upgrade with wide-reaching operational impacts. First implemented in 2016, the NWM provides forecast guidance for 3.6 million miles of waterways across the continental United States, south-central Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Since its initial implementation, the Office of Water Prediction (OWP) has operationally deployed eight updates, with the most recent (version 3.1) entering into operations in 2026. The NWM provides 24x7 guidance for streamflow and other hydrologic states and fluxes used by NWS River Forecast Centers, the Federal Emergency Management Agency and other government entities, along with academic and commercial sectors, and the public. Version 3.1 was the last version of the model to utilize the WRF-Hydro modeling system, with future updates using the Next Generation Water Resources Modeling Framework (NextGen). Under development by OWP in collaboration with its federal and academic partners, NextGen is a model-agnostic, standards-based, open-source, water resources model interoperability software framework, designed to harness the best available water prediction capabilities for use in research and operations. It is being purpose-built with a design that supports execution of a wide range of model formulations and process modules (e.g. SAC-SMA, differentiable HBV, LSTM, Noah-OWP-modular, Snow17, a Conceptual Functional Equivalent (CFE) to the WRF-Hydro based NWM, and others), standardized connection points for community-authored modules, a low overhead for model developers, and an architecture that facilitates execution on platforms from laptops to supercomputers. It will enable domain scientists to utilize the modeling approach that best fits their application and support the creation of forcing- and physics-based ensembles. NextGen will accelerate improvements in model skill and responsiveness to the needs of government, private and academic end users. Use of the NextGen framework to support the NWM in NWS operations is targeted for 2028, with the release of NWM version 4.0. This presentation will focus on the recent implementation of NWM v3.1 into operations along with an update on progress towards development of the NextGen-based NWM v4.0. It will detail how major foundational elements of NextGen are coming together to form a robust, performant, operations-oriented configuration. Overall benefits to NWM operations will be discussed as will entry points for community contribution and a timeline for continued development and implementation.

488858.title: Impacts of Wind Farms on Shallow Cumulus Convection: a Large-Eddy Simulation Study
488858.authors: Zane Reid Frey, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and S. K. Krueger and M. Calaf
488858.abstract: Shallow cumulus clouds are widespread over the tropical and subtropical oceans, where their formation, evolution, and organization are governed by coupled turbulent transport of momentum, heat, and moisture within the trade-wind boundary layer. These environments also contain substantial offshore wind resources, yet studies of wind farm dynamics have largely emphasized neutral, stable, or dry convective boundary layers. As modern offshore turbines occupy an increasing fraction of the subcloud layer, the potential for turbine-scale and farm-scale wakes to interact with moist convective transport remains poorly understood. Conversely, cloud-driven circulations may alter the vertical momentum transport and wake recovery that sustain wind farm performance in these environments. In this study, we use large-eddy simulations to investigate this two-way coupling across a hierarchy of shallow cumulus and wind farm configurations. First, we perform idealized simulations examining nonprecipitating shallow cumulus over a fully developed, horizontally periodic wind turbine array. Varying turbine packing density allows us to isolate the microscale response of the subcloud and cloud layers to wind farm forcing while removing farm entrance, exit, and edge effects. We then extend the analysis to finite wind farms embedded within much larger domains that enable wind farm wake recovery and mesoscale cloud organization. Both nonprecipitating and precipitating shallow cumulus regimes are considered to investigate how wind farm wakes interact with convective organization, entrainment, precipitation, and cold-pool dynamics. Preliminary results indicate that wind farm loading modifies the vertical structure and spatial organization of shallow cumulus without necessarily reducing cloud fractions. Finite-farm simulations further suggest that wake recovery and the associated entrainment of drier air can produce a local decrease in clouds, but the effects on the cloud layer outside of the farm-wake region are still being investigated. Ultimately, these simulations can provide a framework for understanding coupled wind farm–cloud dynamics in trade-wind boundary layers and how these dynamics may affect future development of offshore wind in tropical environments.

488874.title: Project EXCEED for PMP: Downscaling reanalysis for extreme precipitation
488874.authors: Laura Slivinski, NOAA/OAR/PSL, Boulder, CO; and K. M. Mahoney, S. Frolov, B. M. Basarab, G. P. Compo, I. Ebert-Uphoff, P. N. Schumacher, A. Libardoni, K. A. Hilburn, H. Chen, Y. Liu, S. Lee, S. Khajehei, and M. Pritchard
488874.abstract: To support NOAA’s effort to modernize probable maximum precipitation (PMP) estimates to support, e.g., infrastructure investments, Project EXCEED (EXtreme preCipitation Estimates from Enhanced Downscaling) aims to improve the historical record of extreme precipitation by developing and evaluating physical and machine learning-based methods for super-resolving global reanalyses over the US. To achieve this, a collaborative team from NOAA OAR, CU CIRES, CSU/CIRA, and NVIDIA is developing an efficient and statistically reliable AI downscaling framework, including a common pipeline to evaluate different methods’ abilities to represent several historical case studies of extreme precipitation. The project will evaluate existing machine learning architectures as well as develop new models to take global reanalyses as input and high-resolution, radar-based precipitation datasets as targets. Ultimately, the project aims to apply these validated AI models to the 80-member, 200-year 20th Century Reanalysis (20CRv3) dataset. If successful, this would produce a multi-decadal, high-resolution probabilistic precipitation record over the U.S. that properly characterizes extreme event uncertainties. A successful outcome of this project will also include gaining a better understanding of the strengths and limitations of these downscaling models for reconstructing different types of extreme precipitation events. The emphasis of this presentation is to provide an overview of the entire project, including the evaluation framework.

488894.title: Commercial and COSMIC-2 GNSS-RO Near-real-time Product Processing and Generation at NOAA/STAR and Performance Assessment
488894.authors: Yong Chen, STAR, Riverdale Park, MD; NOAA, College Park, MD; and X. Shao, T. C. Liu, X. Zhou, X. Jing, M. Chen, J. Zhou, B. Zhang, W. Miller, C. Cao, and S. R. Shrestha
488894.abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) radio occultation (RO) provides high-vertical-resolution, all-weather observations critical for numerical weather prediction (NWP). The rapid expansion of commercial SmallSat RO constellations (e.g., Spire, PlanetiQ), complemented by the COSMIC-2 mission, has significantly increased global sampling density and improved forecasts for high-impact weather. However, integrating these heterogeneous multi-mission datasets introduces operational and quality challenges, particularly concerning LEO precise orbit determination (POD) uncertainties and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) variability. To address these challenges, NOAA/STAR has implemented an enterprise-level, end-to-end GNSS RO processing system within the NOAA NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF). This system enables real-time, low-latency ingestion, automated workflows, and robust data product generation. For neutral atmosphere (NA) processing, it transforms Level 0/1A observations into LEO POD, clock biases, excess phase, full spectrum inversion (FSI) bending angles, and refractivity profiles, which are subsequently formatted into BUFR products for operational NWP assimilation. For space weather (SWx) processing, the system derives absolute total electron content (aTEC) and electron density profiles (EDP). Rigorous calibration and validation (Cal/Val) remain central to the framework: NA products undergo observation-minus-background (O–B) diagnostics against GFS and ECMWF models, while SWx products are cross-validated against external CDAAC/vendor datasets and the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) model. Ultimately, this scalable STAR framework will improve the accuracy and availability of multi-mission GNSS-RO data, significantly enhancing NWP forecast skill and strengthening space weather monitoring.

488900.title: Modernizing Local Storm Reports and Storm Data Collection through Open Source Intelligence and Agentic AI
488900.authors: Eric A. Allen, NWS, Bohemia, NY; and L. Batty, C. M. Gravelle, R. Walsh, M. Youngman, and G. Selig
488900.abstract: Traditional weather verification methodologies within the National Weather Service (NWS) have historically prioritized validating meteorological parameters and phenomena against observed conditions, focusing on “what the weather was” through public and partner reports and physical observations. Although essential for warning verification, this framework leaves a critical operational gap because many weather-related impacts are not consistently documented in the Storm Events Database. This limits the ability to systematically capture and analyze the full scope of real-world societal consequences, or “what the weather did,” in relation to issued forecasts, warnings, and Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS). To close this gap and transition toward comprehensive outcome-oriented validation, the NWS needs a repeatable, scalable mechanism to discover and organize hyper-local ground truth regarding cascading infrastructure, economic, and public safety impacts. To address this operational need, NOAA and Zignal Labs established a 12-month Cooperative Research and Development Agreement to demonstrate the direct utility of open-source intelligence for enhancing real-time situational awareness and improving the collection of Storm Events Data. This presentation details how a high-volume data stream spanning social media, broadcast media and news reports, online forums, and other digital sources was analyzed using an Agentic AI framework to modernize and enhance Local Storm Reports (LSRs) and the Storm Events Database. Moving beyond legacy keyword filtering, this effort demonstrates how interconnected AI agents use natural language processing and geospatial enrichment to identify local narratives of structural damage, utility failures, and life-safety hazards. While at the same time integrating automated bot detection, deepfake identification, and source credibility metrics to reduce noise and flag potentially unreliable information. Attendees will learn how the system transforms complex public-source data into structured messages and timelines, providing NWS meteorologists and hydrologists with timely situational awareness during active weather and detailed impact information that can improve both time-sensitive Impact-Based Warnings and post-storm reporting. This capability could serve as a foundational input for a complementary generative AI system prototyped with Amazon Web Services (AWS) and deployed in the VLab Cloud. By seamlessly feeding structured open-source data into the AWS tool to automatically draft preliminary LSRs and validate them against meteorological data, this end-to-end workflow would allow operational meteorologists and hydrologists to efficiently review, edit, and submit more comprehensive storm impact reports. This approach could standardize post-storm data collection and establish a foundation for evaluating the societal value of IDSS.

488909.title: Evaluating Wildfire Smoke Impact on Ozone Production in the Denver Region Using In Situ Measurements Coupled with a Generalized Additive Model
488909.authors: Audrey Lyp, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and B. Dix, L. D. Anderson, D. Blauth, E. Mattson, S. Yun, D. Day, J. L. Jimenez, and J. de Gouw
488909.abstract: Wildfire smoke emits and transports ozone (O3) precursors, volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and nitrogen oxides (NOx = NO + NO2), which influences O3 production in the Denver area. During 2024, Denver experienced over 40 O3 exceedance days, several of which corresponded with enhanced wildfire smoke. However, it remains unclear whether elevated O3 levels in Denver during smoke events are mainly due to transported O3 within the smoke plume or local formation from the reaction between transported biomass burning VOCs and nearby NOx emissions. To better understand wildfire impact on O3 production in the Denver region, we couple in situ VOC measurements collected by our group in Summer 2024 at the La Casa site in Denver with a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) designed to assess wildfire smoke influence on air quality across the United States. Model results can be used to attribute increases in observed O3 due to wildfire smoke. Enhancements in observed VOCs are used as a biomass burning tracer to evaluate model performance in identifying smoke days. Smoke impacts from both long-range transport (Canadian wildfires) and short-range transport (local Colorado wildfires) are observed in the Summer 2024 VOC data set and are used to assess smoke plume age influence on measured VOC concentrations and resulting implications for O3 production in Denver.

488911.title: Predicting MODIS-derived Cloud Regimes from NOAA20CR Synoptic-Scale Characteristics using Neural Networks to Relate Meteorological Conditions to Cloud Spatiotemporal Variability
488911.authors: Cassidy Johnson, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere, Fort Collins, CO; and C. White, L. Ver Hoef, I. Ebert-Uphoff, Y. J. Noh, and J. M. Haynes
488911.abstract: Cloud properties, frequencies, and spatial distributions are most accurately observed by satellite records, but the satellite era is relatively short when compared to climatology timescales. There are also the issues of spatiotemporal gaps, intersensor calibration difficulties, and orbital drift complications that affect satellite records of clouds. Reanalysis datasets provide some cloud information on much longer timescales, but the cloud properties in these datasets are not as accurate as those provided by satellite measurements. In this study, we will investigate how we can take advantage of the long record of spatial and temporal environmental variables in the NOAA20CR reanalysis dataset and use those variables to predict MODIS-derived cloud regimes using a simple neural network, namely a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) model, with plans to eventually transition to a convolutional neural network (CNN). The ultimate goal is to use the trained MLP (or CNN) model to perform a hindcast (with the possibility of hindcasting as far back as 1806) and perform an exploratory data analysis of predicted cloud regimes in the pre-satellite era using the most representative and historically accurate NOAA20CR variables for prediction. The purposes of this study are to investigate how synoptic-scale weather facilitates or inhibits the formation of certain cloud regimes, utilize these relationships to predict cloud spatiotemporal variability on a climatological scale, and provide environmental context for observed long-term trends in cloud regimes. The first step of this project is to gather reanalysis fields from NOAA20CR and evaluate which variables make the most sense for MODIS cloud regime predictions. The way this is done is by training a simple 2-layer, 32-unit MLP model and utilizing ablation studies and permutation importance to identify how various combinations of input variables affect the performance of the model. Accuracy scores, F1 scores, and general classification reports are used to analyze the input variables’ impact on the model’s overall performance. The next step is analyzing which cloud regimes are best and worst predicted, which is done by analyzing F1 scores for each individual regime, as well as creating confusion matrices to visualize which regimes tend to have the most true positive and true negative predictions and which have the least. This study is done on the full globe as well as several smaller regions to evaluate regional performance. By leveraging the relationship between synoptic-scale meteorological conditions and MODIS-derived cloud regimes, this study provides a way for us to extend cloud regime records prior to the satellite era while simultaneously improving our understanding of the large-scale processes that govern cloud variability. Links to datasets: Twentieth Century Reanalysis (NOAA20CR) dataset: https://psl.noaa.gov/data/20thC_Rean/ MODIS dataset: https://measures.gesdisc.eosdis.nasa.gov/data/CloudRegimes/MODIS_CR_Equal_Area_3h.1.0/

488921.title: AskNWS: Transforming Weather Communications with Generative AI
488921.authors: Eric A. Allen, NWS, Bohemia, NY; and C. M. Gravelle, M. Youngman, J. W. Rogers, and A. Anderson
488921.abstract: National Weather Service (NWS) forecasters dedicate a significant level of effort to synthesizing complex weather hazards, hydrological forecasts, and historical weather information into actionable, plain language messages tailored to individual communities and individual people. A single, generalized forecast message is rarely sufficient to address the public's diverse needs, as individuals and communities face distinct vulnerabilities, risks, and interests that require uniquely customized weather context, which often exceeds available forecaster time and resources. To streamline this operational workflow and enhance public safety communications, the Next Generation Weather Communications Project, in partnership with Esri, developed AskNWS, a Generative AI-powered chatbot built on the authoritative data and information of the NWS. Intended initially for an audience of internal NWS forecasters and core decision-support partners, this tool will allow them to quickly address the specific questions of individuals and communities by easily generating and validating customized responses. Furthermore, it leverages the success of the Lilt Language Translation project to provide seamless multi-lingual translations that reach broader populations. Developed through an iterative Agile framework, the Minimum Viable Product (MVP) leverages Amazon Bedrock to route queries across high-performing Large Language Models. A foundational technical achievement of the project is the deployment of scalable Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, which standardize real-time AI access to the NWS API for active alerts and forecasts, the NWPS API for river gauge observations and forecasts, and the xmACIS API for climatological context. By pairing these data streams with interactive map display capabilities and direct source citations, the platform ensures complete transparency and situational awareness for the user. Initial testing by NWS stakeholders demonstrated that AskNWS provides significant immediate value. Key takeaways include enabling forecasters to rapidly query multiple data sources to generate localized weather, water, and climate responses, adjust technical depth on demand, and produce safety messaging in multiple languages. It significantly enhances the information provided by legacy Point-and-Click forecasts by synthesizing them with active Watches, Warnings, and Advisories and other forecast products, providing critical context that does not exist in standard Point-and-Click pages. Furthermore, automating the retrieval of historical weather data via xmACIS addresses a top NWS operational request, with the potential to save an estimated 20-25+ hours per day across Weather Forecast Offices. Future development phases will focus on resolving LLM output inconsistency through strict parameter optimization, enhancing platform stability to minimize API retrieval errors, and broadening the integration of NWS API and other data, ultimately paving the way for AskNWS to evolve into an internal forecaster decision-support tool and potentially into a direct, public-facing service. This presentation demonstrates a practical roadmap for operationalizing Generative AI and standardizing meteorological API access in safety-critical environments.

488922.title: Updating the Request Process for GOES-R Mesoscale Domain Sectors (MDS)
488922.authors: Joshua C. Jankot, NESDIS, College Park, MD; and S. Superczynski, J. C. Jankot, R. R. Handel, J. D. Taylor, J. Shallcross, and E. Smail
488922.abstract: Currently led by GOES-19 (GOES-East) and GOES-18 (GOES-West), the GOES-R satellite series features the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) as a landmark technological advancement in environmental remote sensing. The ABI provides high-frequency mesoscale scans at 30- or 60-second intervals, delivering critical rapid-scan support for the primary forecast and warning mandates of the National Weather Service (NWS) and NOAA’s core weather mission. These capabilities also offer significant advantages to the Department of Defense (DoD), international allies, and numerous research projects across the global scientific community. By capturing severe weather events in near real-time, the instrument enables unprecedented temporal resolution that significantly improves the monitoring of rapidly evolving meteorological threats. This presentation analyzes the structured workflow for submitting Mesoscale Domain Sector (MDS) requests, highlighting how NOAA assesses and balances live operational priorities against the varied demands of international and research stakeholders. Through a selection of operational and research case studies, we demonstrate the direct influence of 30-second and 1-minute rapid scanning, outline the environmental phenomena under review, and illustrate the tangible advantages gained by forecasters and scientists. These real-world examples emphasize how data translates into increased lead time for warnings and more accurate situational awareness. Finally, the session explores recent updates to NOAA’s domestic, research, and international MDS request framework, focusing on the transition of specific responsibilities from the NESDIS Satellite Analysis Branch to NWS Central Operations (NCO) and Senior Duty Meteorologists to optimize operational efficiency and responsiveness.

488934.title: Surface Controls on Storm Development for the 04 July 2025 Extreme Storms in Central Texas
488934.authors: Edward K. Vizy, The University of Texas at Austin, AUSTIN, TX; and K. H. Cook
488934.abstract: The 04 July 2025 Central Texas extreme rainfall event produced catastrophic flash flooding in the Texas Hill Country and resulted in over 135 deaths. The storm is estimated to have caused $18 to $22 billion in economic losses, including approximately $1.1 billion in direct damage to residential structures. While weather forecasters recognized this storm as a potential threat well in advance, overnight the storm underwent greater-than-anticipated intensification, contributing to the severity of its impacts. The processes responsible for such storm intensification and the production of extreme rainfall over short time scales are not yet well understood. This study seeks to improve our understanding of these processes by investigating the influence of land and ocean surface conditions on the evolution of the storm. Utilizing high resolution, convection-permitting model simulations, we evaluate the role of Gulf of Mexico sea surface temperature anomalies (SSTAs) and antecedent soil moisture distributions in the storm’s development. Our analysis indicates that regional Gulf of Mexico SSTs influenced the intensity of this rainfall event by affecting the intensity and persistence of the Great Plains low-level jet. Replacing the observed warm coastal and central Gulf of Mexico SSTs with contemporary climatological (time mean) SSTs strengthened the low-level jet, enhancing moisture transport into Central Texas, increasing convective instability and moisture convergence, and producing greater rainfall accumulations. Although Central Texas experienced moderate to exceptional drought conditions at the beginning of July 2025, soil moisture in Central Texas immediately before storm development was anomalously wet due to regional convective activity prior to this event. When soil moisture was initialized to drier climatological conditions, the low-level jet responded in a way that reduced low-level moisture availability, convective instability, and moisture convergence, leading to lower rainfall totals. When both surface forcings were evaluated simultaneously, Gulf of Mexico SSTs exerted the dominant control on storm evolution and precipitation, indicating that SST forcing outweighed the influence of antecedent soil moisture in the combined response for this event. This study highlights the importance of advancing our understanding of how surface conditions influence extreme storm development to improve our ability to predict their evolution and assess their impacts at regional scales. These insights support the development of more physically realistic hazard models, with applications to flood risk assessment, catastrophe modeling, and climate risk management.

488935.title: Partnering to Provide Environmental Information Services at the National, Regional, and State Levels
488935.authors: Tamara G. Houston, NESDIS, Asheville, NC; and M. J. Brewer
488935.abstract: To better support its users, NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) uses a three-tiered approach for environmental information services that leverages the expertise and capabilities of partners at the national, regional and state levels. In particular, NCEI’s partnership with NOAA’s Regional Weather Records Centers and the American Association of State Climatologists provides regional and state level context to NCEI’s national suite of products. Also as part of the partnership, the Regional Weather Records Centers and State Climate Offices utilize data and information from NCEI as an input for many of the value-added products and services they provide to their users. This presentation will highlight recent regional and state engagements and products developed to meet specific stakeholder needs.

488937.title: Using MOSAiC Observations to Evaluate the Rapid Refresh (RAP) Weather Model over Arctic Sea Ice.
488937.authors: Noah Aaron Schneiderman, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. D. Turner and C. J. Cox
488937.abstract: Weather forecasts in the Arctic have become more essential in recent years as human activity expands in the region. A key tool in making these forecasts is the Rapid Refresh (RAP), a weather model whose domain encompasses the North American and central regions of the Arctic. The RAP has a 13-kilometer horizontal resolution and provides 21-hour forecasts initialized hourly and 51-hour forecasts initialized every 6 hours, and is the only American model with hourly initializations that covers the Arctic. In spite of this, however, few efforts have been made to evaluate the RAP's performance in the unique Arctic environment, particularly over sea ice. Considering the dearth of in-situ observations collected over the open Arctic ocean, the high-quality data obtained by the 2019-2020 Multidisciplinary Drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate (MOSAiC) field campaign offers an exceptional opportunity to fill this gap in verification efforts. In this study, we compare forecasts made by the RAP (version 5, which is currently run operationally by the National Weather Service) to MOSAiC observations taken during the polar night, focusing especially on the RAP's lower-tropospheric temperature, humidity, and wind speed errors and why these arise. We devote special attention to the RAP's ability to accurately predict both the presence and characteristics of Arctic clouds, as incorrectly modeled clouds lead to further errors in the RAP's near-surface forecasts. Preliminary results show that the RAP tends to overpredict the occurrence of clouds over Arctic sea ice, showing a cloudy bias at initialization that worsens as forecast progress. When the RAP correctly forecasts cloudy or clear skies, it also tends to initialize too cold and cool further over time; this cold bias is especially severe around 100-250m above ground level, and appears related to the model's tendency to underrepresent the strength of surface-based inversions, which occur frequently in the Arctic. The RAP's tendency to overpredict clouds is tied to this cold bias, but the underlying cause may be more complex; one additional area of interest is the model's concentration of aerosols, particularly ice nuclei.

488943.title: Exploring Genesis Pathway Prediction for Atlantic Tropical Cyclones Using Machine Learning
488943.authors: Sean Tyler Barnier, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and R. E. Hart, D. J. Halperin, and R. McTaggart-Cowan
488943.abstract: While tropical cyclone (TC) prediction has historically focused on track and intensity, reliable genesis prediction is also essential to long-range forecasting. One way to view the genesis problem is using genesis “pathways”. McTaggart-Cowan et al. (2008; 2013) developed a classification scheme based on the magnitudes of quasi-geostrophic synoptic-scale forcing and lower-level baroclinicity in the TC environment. Five pathways were recognized: non-baroclinic, low-level baroclinic, trough induced, weak tropical transition, and strong tropical transition. However, current genesis forecasts from operational tools, such as TC Logistic Guidance for Genesis (TCLOGG; Halperin et al. 2017), do not inherently take these differences between genesis events into account. This project aims to classify and predict the pathways of genesis events using machine learning in such a fashion that could be implemented using real-time operational model output. Best track data from the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS; Knapp et al. 2010), high-resolution gridded data from the ECMWF Reanalysis v5 (ERA5; Hersbach et al. 2020), and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) pathway classifications from McTaggart-Cowan et al. (2013) were used for all Atlantic TCs during 1979 – 2011. Composite means of TC pre-genesis environments for each pathway showed important hallmarks of their representative pathways, and statistically significant differences from each other. Experiments with machine learning classifiers were conducted, aiming to replicate the LDA classifications. Future plans for this project include using machine learning classifications as a diagnostic for TCLOGG forecast successes and failures, which may also provide grounds for incorporating genesis pathway predictions into TCLOGG forecasts. References Halperin, D. J., R. E. Hart, H. E. Fuelberg, and J. H. Cossuth, 2017: The Development and Evaluation of a Statistical–Dynamical Tropical Cyclone Genesis Guidance Tool. Wea. Forecasting, 32, 27–46, https://doi.org/10.1175/WAF-D-16-0072.1. Hersbach, H., and Coauthors, 2020: The ERA5 global reanalysis. Quart. J. Roy. Meteor. Soc., 146, 1999–2049, https://doi.org/10.1002/qj.3803. Knapp, K. R., M. C. Kruk, D. H. Levinson, H. J. Diamond, and C. J. Neumann, 2010: The International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS): Unifying tropical cyclone best track data. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 91, 363-376. doi:10.1175/2009BAMS2755.1 McTaggart-Cowan, R., G. D. Deane, L. F. Bosart, C. A. Davis, and T. J. Galarneau Jr., 2008: Climatology of tropical cyclogenesis in the North Atlantic (1948– 2004). Mon. Wea. Rev., 136, 1284–1304. McTaggart-Cowan, R., T. J. Galarneau, L. F. Bosart, R. W. Moore, and O. Martius, 2013: A Global Climatology of Baroclinically Influenced Tropical Cyclogenesis. Mon. Wea. Rev., 141, 1963–1989, https://doi.org/10.1175/MWR-D-12-00186.1.

488945.title: D3 (Drought Data Dashboard): An Open, Multi-Scale Platform for Drought Monitoring and Local Partnerships
488945.authors: Zachary H. Hoylman, University of Montana, Missoula, MT; University of Montana, Missoula, MT; and K. Bocinsky and K. Jencso
488945.abstract: Drought monitoring increasingly draws on a wide range of gridded, station-based, and model-derived datasets. The challenge is turning this growing volume of information into assessments that are timely, transparent, and useful for decision-making. The Drought Data Dashboard (D3), developed by the Montana Climate Office in collaboration with state agencies, federal partners, and university researchers, provides an open platform for exploring and integrating drought information from national to local scales. D3 brings together a range of drought indicators across 11 analysis timescales and multiple reference periods, allowing users to compare 30-year, contemporary drought conditions against period-of-record baselines and view gridded products alongside station observations. A local-to-regional plugin architecture lets partners integrate their own monitoring networks, such as the Montana Mesonet, directly into the same interface, extending the platform's coverage without centralizing its data. The dashboard also supports interactive convergence-of-evidence analysis, allowing users to combine indicators and timescales into custom composite maps. Results can be shared through persistent links or exported as geospatial data, making the assessment process easier to communicate and reproduce. The platform pairs precomputed cloud-based products with client-side analysis, allowing national-scale datasets to remain responsive while supporting calculations tailored to individual users. Emerging knowledge-guided machine-learning products further extend the system by providing soil moisture estimates and modeled streamflow percentiles for ungaged basins. This presentation will demonstrate D3 and discuss how flexible baselines, transparent methods, and local partnerships can support a more adaptable drought-monitoring enterprise. https://d3drought.org/

488948.title: The Evolution of Decomposing Atmospheric Rivers into their Thermodynamic and Dynamic Components into the Mid-21st Century.
488948.authors: Timothy D. Corrie III, Univ. of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and S. Rahimi and A. Rhoades
488948.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are filamentary bands of water vapor that transport more water daily than the Amazon River to coastal regions such as the western United States (WUS). We present an AR moisture budget decomposition framework to contextualize historical and future AR-flood potential, which separates the thermodynamic and dynamic components of cold-season ARs. This decomposition framework contains two parts: A column-integrated water vapor (IWV) vs 850-mb wind analysis (w850), and a total moisture budget analysis employed on two high-resolution modeling datasets, the WUS Dynamically Downscaled Dataset (WUS-D3) and the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM). The IWV vs w850 analysis showcases a simplified framework, while the total moisture budget analysis presents decision-relevant moisture changes across multiple WUS subregions. We perform the simplified IWV vs w850 framework on the WUS-D3 and E3SM as a baseline measurement. The total moisture budget will be performed on the WUS-D3 only because of limitations with the E3SM dataset. Nevertheless, there is still added value on comparing the simplified and total moisture budgets in terms of AR-flood potential. These moisture budget analyses have been performed in the context of cold season extreme precipitation events, but less has been studied from an AR perspective, particularly using kilometer-scale datasets. We quantify the uncertainty in both frameworks, considering internal variability, structural uncertainty, and AR Detection Tool choice. We show that hydrometeorological shifts in intense (weak) ARs could be primarily thermodynamically (dynamically) driven. We also show that the total uncertainty of the dynamic component of ARs is greater than that of the thermodynamic component. Nevertheless, we show that the relative uncertainty in thermodynamical and dynamical responses are dominated by internal variability and structural uncertainty (i.e. inter-model variability). Using California as an example, we then analyze how these thermodynamical and dynamical responses shape decision-relevant hydrometeorological variables that shape flood risk and water supply planning, such as precipitation, temperature, snowpack, surface runoff, and evaporation.

488949.title: Analytic Theory for Surface Cloud Radiative Effect In the Arctic: Implications for Optimizing Climate Interventions Seasonally/Regionally
488949.authors: Clare E. Singer, NOAA GFDL, New York, NY
488949.abstract: The Arctic climate is dominated by the seasonal cycle of insolation, resulting in large seasonal variations of cloud radiative effect (CRE), primarily in the shortwave, at the surface and top-of-atmosphere. Furthermore, the surface properties vary substantially across land, ice, snow, and open-water. In this work I focus on the surface CRE, and develop analytical models to explain the spatial and seasonal patterns of SWCRE and LWCRE. I evaluate the accuracy through comparison with control simulations from CESM2. I use these models to interpret changes in surface CRE in CESM2 climate intervention experiments of deliberate perturbation to Arctic clouds. In the shortwave, I account for multiple scattering and aerosol cloud interactions, and find that variations in surface albedo, not cloud properties, are most important for explaining the SWCRE. I explain the simulated seasonal spring/summer dipole of surface SWCRE change under this intervention scenario as a compensation between the instantaneous Twomey adjustment and a lagged sea ice response. This analytic understanding of seasonal surface CRE has implications for optimizing the timing of cloud interventions in the Arctic environment.

488950.title: Bridging the R2O2R Gap with Training at the Community Coordinated Modeling Center
488950.authors: Elana Resnick, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; ASRC Federal, Beltsville, MD; and L. Mays, Y. Zheng, J. Yue, C. Corti, M. Y. Chou, J. Wang, and A. Lundkvist
488950.abstract: The Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center supports the space weather community by helping bridge the gap between research models and operational deployment. R2O2R is integrated into CCMC space weather and space science simulation services, including Runs-on-Request, Instant Run, and Continuous Runs (real-time). CCMC serves near real-time model outputs and data products via its Continuous Runs system and public facing web apps, such as the Integrated Space Weather Analysis system (ISWA) and Scoreboards. As an important element of bridging the gap in the R2O2R process, CCMC also focuses on hands-on training with CCMC models and tools, empowering researchers and operators to effectively execute, evaluate, and apply CCMC tools for space weather research and space weather situational awareness. Examples of this include targeted tutorials at annual and biannual workshops (CEDAR, GEM, IRI), the 2026 Space Weather Workshop, Heliophysics Summer Schools, and international courses with the European Space Weather and Space Climate Association (E-SWAN) prior to European Space Weather Week in 2025 and 2026. Participants are trained to configure, run, visualize, and evaluate state-of-the-art models hosted at CCMC. They also learn the research and operational uses of CCMC platforms such as the ISWA system, Scoreboards and the Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information (DONKI). At CEDAR and IRI workshops participants also gained practical, on-site experience compiling specific models, building input files, executing the runs, and visualizing the output. Enabling and training users in model execution, model-data comparison, and performance metrics creates a direct O2R feedback loop: use experiences, edge cases, and tool improvements and usability insights flow directly back to CCMC developers to improve model capabilities. Through this targeted framework of CCMC tool training, model evaluation, and interactive visualization, CCMC actively sustains a robust, functioning R2O2R ecosystem across heliophysics and planetary domains.

488951.title: Validity of Space-for-Time Substitution for Quantifying the Impact of Local Land Use on Surface Climate (Invited Presentation)
488951.authors: Xuhui Lee, Yale University, New Haven, CT; Yale University, New Haven, CT
488951.abstract: In space-for-time substitution, spatial differences in surface climate between two contrasting land types are equivalent to temporal changes in the climate caused by replacement of one type with the other. For example, the surface temperature difference observed at a pair of sites in a cropland and an adjacent forest is interpreted as a climate signal of local deforestation. Two assumptions are implicit in this substitution framework. Assumption I: the spatial contrast in surface climate between land types remains constant despite changes in the large-scale background climate. Assumption II: local land use changes do not influence the overlaying atmospheric boundary layer (that is, no land-atmosphere feedback). This study aims to evaluate these two assumptions using sub-grid data generated by the land component of earth system models, under historical, current and future climates. Three types of land use contrast – urban land versus rural land, crop versus forest, and lake versus land – are examined across latitudes and across climate zones. In this analysis, the total climate effect of land use change consists of a direct effect due to changes in surface biophysical properties (albedo, Bowen ratio and surface roughness) and an indirect effect arising from land-atmosphere feedback. Results are interpreted via a surface energy decomposition scheme. There are four key findings: (1) Assumption I is valid for urban versus rural and crop versus forest. The space-for-time substitution method gives accurate prediction of the direct climate effect of urban land expansion. (2) Assumption I does not hold for land-lake thermal contrast. A regime shifts occurs in the SSP5-8.5 scenario: the global land is cooler now but becomes warmer than global lakes at the end of the century. The primary causes of this trend are reduction in the lake Bowen ratio and increase in the downward longwave radiation from the atmosphere to the surface. (3) Assumption II does not hold in historical deforestation. The indirect effect is much larger than the direct biophysical effect of historical cropland expansion. (4) In regions projected to undergo moderate urban land expansion in the future, the indirect effect (via reduction in low cloud) is much stronger than the direct biophysical effect of land replacement.

488954.title: 2D, or Not 2D...? Advancing our Multidimensional Perspective on Global Clouds with OVERCAST, a Near Real-Time Satellite/Model-Fusion Analysis
488954.authors: Steven D. Miller, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and J. M. Haynes, Y. J. Noh, C. White, B. J. Daub, J. E. Solbrig, J. Apke, E. Rose, K. Haynes, M. P. King, K. A. Hilburn, I. Ebert-Uphoff, L. Ver Hoef, C. Seaman, N. Tourville, C. Johnson, G. Uttmark, J. D. Turner, S. M. Ortland, J. M. Forsythe, M. J. Foster, C. Phillips, and S. Wanzong
488954.abstract: Since the inception of satellite-based meteorological observations, imaging radiometers measuring reflected sunlight and emitted thermal infrared radiation from the Earth scene have effectively mapped the locations and basic properties (e.g., cloud top height, phase, effective particle size, and the vertically-integrated water content) worldwide. Whereas these observations have revolutionized our understanding of global cloudiness and their role in the Earth system, their limited, two-dimensional (2D) perspective misses critical details of relevance to scientific research and operational users alike. These limitations are compounded by diurnal effects, with the loss of sunlight precluding all but the most rudimentary characterization of cloud location and top-height. These details bear relevance to a host of applications, including cloud radiative impacts (e.g., downwelling longwave which influence Earth’s radiation budget and nighttime surface temperatures), aviation-relevant parameters impacting visibility (layers, ceilings) and airframe icing (supercooled liquid water), and slant-range transmittance (for search and rescue, renewable energy, and laser propagation applications). Despite the myriad benefits of capturing three dimensional (3D) cloud structure, doing so practically from the space platform has remained elusive; relegated to a small collection of active sensors capable of probing the clouds along limited “curtains” of the sky. However, advances in observation technology, together with the inference capabilities of machine learning, have begun to break down the traditionally understood 2D/3D barriers. In coordination with Office of Naval Research (ONR) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere (CIRA; Colorado State University) and the Cooperative Institute for Meteorological Satellite Studies (CIMSS; University of Wisconsin-Madison) have developed and demonstrated a global, high space/time resolution, 24-hr near real-time analysis of 3D cloud fields which validate favorably against active sensor observations. The “Optical Variability Evaluation of Regional Cloud Asymmetries in Space and Time” (OVERCAST) analysis is based on the composite of the international constellation of geostationary satellites (the “GeoRing”) and polar-orbiting satellites to fill in the high-latitudes, blends conventional physical retrievals, statistical algorithms, and machine learning techniques to render novel 3D cloud profile information, including vertical extent, liquid/ice/mixed phase, and water content both day and night. This presentation updates the community on the OVERCAST methodology, satellite blending techniques, algorithm advances, verification efforts, and selected applications enabled by the 3D cloud field. New methods of data gridding, conforming to the broader science community, and efforts to produce a multi-year analysis, aim to position OVERCAST as a generalized resource for a broad community of researchers, users, and stakeholders.

488960.title: Multi-Instrument Satellite Characterization of Arctic Cloud Thermodynamic Phase: NASA PACE and EarthCARE ATLID
488960.authors: Eleni Konstantelos, San Jose State University, San Jose, CA; and M. Diao, X. Xu, and B. van Diedenhoven
488960.abstract: Satellite-based cloud observations spanning both the spatial and temporal domains, as well as the vertical dimension, remain a key gap for constraining cloud thermodynamic phase in Earth system models, particularly in the Arctic, where liquid-containing cloud tops critically modulate the surface energy budget.
