This study demonstrates a multi-instrument characterization approach by combining retrievals from NASA's Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, Ecosystem (PACE) mission, the hyperspectral Ocean Color Instrument (OCI) and polarimeters SPEXone and HARP2, with lidar profiles from EarthCARE's Atmospheric Lidar (ATLID), to characterize cloud thermodynamic phase across the pan-Arctic domain (60–90°N). While PACE's three instruments provide broad spatial and temporal coverage of cloud-top phase and microphysical properties, ATLID adds full-column vertical phase structure along coincident orbital tracks, illustrating the added value of combining active and passive satellite observations for 3D cloud characterization. Daily cloud-top phase and cloud type are examined across latitudinal and longitudinal bands, along with sensitivity tests for the treatment of unknown-phase pixels and aerosol-cloud interaction patterns across geographic regions and cloud types. Results show that cloud-top liquid frequency increases with colder temperatures, higher latitudes, and colder seasons, consistent with reduced ice-nucleating particle availability in clean polar air allowing supercooled liquid to persist at cloud top. We further compare these satellite-derived patterns against ground-based and shipborne observations from the Cold-Air Outbreaks in the Marine Boundary Layer Experiment (COMBLE) and the Multidisciplinary drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate (MOSAiC), assessing how well multi-instrument satellite characterization captures cloud phase behavior documented by field campaigns in the Arctic.

488963.title: Environmental Conditions that Support Different Modes of Diurnal Convection over Southwest Sumatra
488963.authors: Emily M. Riley Dellaripa, Colorado State University, Ft. Collins, CO; and E. D. Maloney and C. A. DeMott
488963.abstract: Diurnal convection is the “heartbeat” of the tropics - consistently occurring each day over land driven primarily by surface solar heating. Near coastal zones, late afternoon diurnal convection frequently propagates offshore overnight leading to local maxima in rainfall offshore of many Maritime Continent islands including off the southwest coast of Sumatra. The robustness of offshore propagating convection over southwest Sumatra makes the offshore propagation feature present in the long-term mean diurnal cycle of convection. However, this feature is not present every day. This work aims to describe the different modes of diurnal convection over southwest Sumatra and what environmental conditions support each mode. Unique to this study is the use of CYGNSS wind speed and surface flux estimates to examine how air-sea feedbacks support the different modes of diurnal convection over southwest Sumatra. The different modes of diurnal convection are determined by empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis of IMERG version 7 precipitation from August 2018 - July 2024 near the southwest coast of Sumatra. Each day is identified as having either offshore propagating, landlocked, shoreward, marine, or weak diurnal convection. Similarities and differences will be discussed regarding the evolution of diurnal convection during offshore propagating, landlocked, and marine days, as well as their distinguishing environmental conditions. The mode of diurnal convection depends upon the availability of column moisture, the direction of free-troposphere low-level wind, and the sign of anomalous surface latent heat fluxes (LHFLXs). For example, offshore propagating days have enhanced total column water vapor, surface LHFLXs, and offshore winds at 850 hPa compared to the landlocked days. Further details will be given in the presentation.

488970.title: Interannual and Interseasonal Variabilities of Ice Nucleating Particles In the Arctic: Insights from Measurements and Model Simulations from Ny-Ålesund
488970.authors: Yang Shi, PNNL, Richland , WA; and X. Liu, E. K. Wilbourn, M. Mazzola, R. Traversi, and N. Hiranuma
488970.abstract: Ice nucleating particles (INPs) influence the formation of Arctic mixed-phase clouds through initiating heterogeneous ice nucleation and thus are critical for regional climate. However, global climate models struggle to represent INP concentrations in the Arctic. In this study, we conducted a systematic comparison between simulations from the Department of Energy’s Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 1 (E3SMv1) and long-term meteorological, aerosol, and INP measurements collected intermittently in 2018 and 2019 at Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard. We found that the simulated aerosol properties (aerosol number concentrations and dust and sea salt mass concentrations) are mostly within one order of magnitude difference from observations, with the biases attributed to the model’s misrepresentations of wet scavenging, secondary formation and transport of aerosols, as well as emission of the local high latitude dust (HLD). We developed a new ice nucleation parameterization for Svalbard-emitted HLD based on local sediment samples, which shows a hump at around -10 °C, indicating the presence of organic matters. With this new parameterization along with other ice nucleation schemes for HLD, low latitude dust, and sea spray aerosols, our model reproduces observed INP concentrations and seasonality within the uncertainty range of aerosol properties. Our model results highlight the important contribution from locally emitted HLD to the INP population at Ny-Ålesund. Future studies integrating long-term observations across diverse locations and vertical levels in the Arctic with improved model representation of HLD are needed to further advance our understanding of Arctic INP properties, sources, and their role in aerosol-cloud interactions.

488971.title: The Role of Land Cover Type In the Evolution of Flash Drought: Simulating In WRF/MPAS Model and Sensitivity
488971.authors: Yibo Chen, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. I. Christian
488971.abstract: In the realm of sub-seasonal to seasonal weather and climate extremes, a complex and relatively newer topic is Flash Drought (FD). In short, FD is a drought that has unusually quick onset, often has limited warning, and can be highly impactful. The 2012 central United States flash drought caused in excess of $30 billion damage. FDs are typically driven by a combination of enhanced evaporative demand below average precipitation, but other mechanisms such as land cover type add to the complexity of understanding FD development. This study uses the WRF and MPAS model with Noah-MP to simulate the significant 2012 flash drought and analyze how land cover will impact the development of rapid drought intensification. Limited studies have analyzed FD from a modeling perspective. Therefore, this study aims to close this gap by quantifying the role of land cover type in the evolution using coupled model simulations. Several WRF and MPAS simulations with different parametrizations were run and verified to the NLDAS-2 dataset. Early results showed WRF and MPAS capable of recreating flash drought when compared to NLDAS-2 Soil Moisture. Model outputs also demonstrated different land covers in proximity impact the land diagnosis, such as soil moisture, evapotranspiration and potential evapotranspiration. WRF and/or MPAS simulations with modified land cover will be generated based on the performance of existing model runs. The results from the modified land cover group will be compared to the existing group of simulations to explore the dynamical evolution of FD development with respect to land cover type.

488974.title: Student Experiences and Persistence in Atmospheric Science Programs: Findings from a National Mixed-Methods Study
488974.authors: Dawn Marie Kopacz, Univ. of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and R. H. Humphrey, H. Cashwell, A. Drager, and H. N. Mikulak
488974.abstract: While previous research has explored factors influencing retention and attrition in geosciences, relatively little has focused specifically on undergraduates pursuing atmospheric science degrees. This ongoing mixed-methods study seeks to better understand the experiences of atmospheric science and related majors and identify factors that support or hinder their persistence in their academic program. An initial survey was administered in Fall 2024, yielding more than 125 responses from students enrolled in atmospheric science programs across the United States. A second round of data collection conducted in Spring 2026 produced an additional 64 responses. The survey examined students’ use of academic advising and support resources, participation in co-curricular activities, motivations for selecting their institution and major, and intentions to remain in their atmospheric science program. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in Spring 2026 with seven survey participants to further examine themes related to belonging, peer and faculty connections, perceived challenges, and factors influencing decisions to remain in or leave the major. This presentation will highlight themes from survey and interview analyses related to student success, belonging, support systems, and persistence, and discuss implications for departmental practices aimed at supporting undergraduate students within the discipline.

488977.title: Satellite-Derived Wildfire Intelligence from the Next Generation Fire System (NGFS)
488977.abstract: The Next Generation Fire System (NGFS), developed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR) and the Cooperative Institute for Meteorological Satellite Studies (CIMSS), is a satellite-based tool for wildfire operators. The NGFS is designed to fully exploit operational environmental satellite systems by emulating human expert analysis of satellite imagery, frequently resulting in early detection of new fires and near-continuous monitoring of established fires. The NGFS can be applied to geostationary satellites such as the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES), or low-Earth-orbit sensors such as the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS). Following successful demonstrations in the NOAA Fire Weather Testbed, the NGFS has been adopted by a growing number of users, including the National Weather Service, land managers, dispatchers, firefighters, and emergency managers. While the early adoption of the NGFS was via an experimental system, the NGFS is being transitioned to full operations. While the core capabilities of the NGFS are ready for operations, the system continues to evolve to address unmet user needs, including unifying active fire detection and characterization across a broad range of operational environmental satellite systems, with the goal of further addressing the data overload challenge facing operators. In addition, a Wildland Fire Data Portal, which provides access to NGFS products and satellite imagery via machine and human interfaces, continues to be developed to improve data access and interoperability. This presentation will introduce the NGFS, provide an update on the operational transition, highlight real-world impacts from the past couple of US fire seasons, and describe ongoing improvements and new features.

488986.title: NOAA NCEI Climate Monitoring: Recent Enhancements to Products and Services
488986.authors: Andrew P. Ballinger, NOAA/NCEI, Asheville, NC; and S. Applequist, J. Blunden, J. Enloe, C. Fenimore, K. Gleason, A. Sanchez-Lugo, and R. Vose
488986.abstract: NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) provides environmental data, products and services to drive resilience, prosperity and equity for current and future generations. NCEI’s Monitoring Team develops and maintains a diverse range of products and services, including data exploration tools, web applications and monthly reports, to provide authoritative summaries of observed climate conditions across multiple spatial scales, from global analyses down to county and city levels across the United States. Monthly and annual climate summaries are primarily derived from NOAA's observational datasets: NOAA GlobalTemp (version 6.1.0; 1850–present) for global analyses and NOAA's nClimGrid-monthly for the CONUS (1895–present) and Alaska (1925–present). These datasets undergo rigorous testing, development and maintenance, providing consistent climate records spanning more than a century and enabling recent weather events to be placed into long-term historical context. Initially developed more than 25 years ago and continuously updated to incorporate additional features and interactive visualizations, Climate at a Glance has become a widely used NOAA web application for exploring monthly temperature and precipitation data. It provides interactive maps and time series at global, national, statewide, climate division and county scales. Users can evaluate conditions relative to selected baseline periods or rank months from coolest to warmest (or driest to wettest) on record. Recent development efforts have focused on modernizing the suite of monitoring products through expanded data coverage, improved visualization and enhanced operational efficiency. Examples include expanding data coverage through incorporation of Hawaiʻi into monthly temperature and precipitation analyses, modernizing legacy mapping workflows through Python-based automation, standardizing map design and color palettes, accessibility improvements, adding new climatological categories and streamlining production pipelines. Collectively, these enhancements improve the accessibility, consistency, efficiency, and long-term sustainability of NOAA's operational climate monitoring products while strengthening the delivery of historical and contemporary climate information to the public, decision-makers and other stakeholders.

488996.title: Evaluating the Representation of Fires in Georgia, USA, in the FINN Biomass Burning Emissions Inventory
488996.authors: Sophia Louise Patrin, UCAR, Boulder, CO
488996.abstract: Biomass burning emissions inventories transform observational data into inputs for chemical transport and Earth system models, but uncertainty remains in their representation of fire activity in regions where prescribed and agricultural burning are common. This study evaluates the Fire INventory from NCAR (FINN) v2.5 in Georgia, USA, during June 2022 by comparing FINN detections and PM₂.₅ emissions with U.S. EPA fire records. Georgia provides a useful case study because prescribed burns accounted for approximately 70% of reported fire activity statewide in 2022. Fire detection performance, spatial agreement, PM₂.₅ emissions, and burned-area representation were assessed using point-to-grid and grid-to-grid approaches. FINN represented fewer than 10% of EPA-reported fires under exact matching criteria, and the mean daily spatial correlation between inventories was approximately -0.03. Burned area was the strongest predictor of detection; a tenfold increase approximately doubled the odds of detection. Although FINN more frequently represented larger fires, approximately 68% of EPA-reported PM₂.₅ emissions and approximately 72% of reported burned area were associated with fires not represented by FINN under the exact-matching framework. June accounted for 3.5% of annual EPA-reported fire activity and occurred near the annual minimum in FINN detection performance (F1 score = 0.12), indicating that it was not representative of year-round conditions. These results suggest that, in Georgia, FINN more effectively represents larger fires than smaller events, and that inventory differences may influence modeled PM₂.₅ concentrations, smoke exposure estimates, and air-quality assessments.

488998.title: Bridging Data and Decisions: User Engagement, System Upgrades, and Service Delivery at NOAA NCEI
488998.authors: Glenn Kerr, NOAA, Asheville, NC; NOAA, Asheville, NC; and M. J. Brewer
488998.abstract: NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) provides environmental data, products and services to drive resilience and prosperity in a rapidly changing world. NCEI’s User Engagement Team interacts with users across all economic sectors in order to better understand their needs for past weather and climate information and connect them with data and products to facilitate effective, data-driven decisions. This presentation provides an overview of the support services and engagement activities conducted by NCEI’s User Engagement Section, spanning expert consultation, order fulfillment, and formal data certification. It discusses how user interaction data are collected and leveraged to improve NCEI’s products, access platforms, and service delivery. Additionally, the presentation showcases examples of unique user requests. An update will also be provided on recent enhancements to NCEI’s Search, Discovery, and Data Access system and GIS map services as well as changes to several foundational datasets.

489006.title: Microphysical Buffering Makes Water-Vapor Supersaturation Aloft Insensitive to Cloud Updraft Speed (Invited Presentation)
489006.authors: Daniel Rosenfeld, The Hebrew Univ. of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, JM, Israel; and C. Fan
489006.abstract: Cloud-base supersaturation provides the initial link between aerosol loading and droplet activation. Well above cloud base, however, supersaturation emerges jointly with the cloud’s dynamical and microphysical evolution, while updraft velocity is itself an outcome of the coupled interactions among thermodynamic forcing, condensation, condensate loading, precipitation formation, and drag. Supersaturation is depleted by condensation onto the integrated surface area of cloud droplets. As collision–coalescence advances, many small droplets merge into fewer large drops, reducing the total droplet surface area for a given liquid-water content. Precipitation formation and unloading further reduce that area. The condensational sink therefore weakens, allowing relatively high supersaturation to develop. We examine this behavior with a 2000-bin spectral-bin microphysics parcel model in which the updraft evolves prognostically. Eight thermodynamic environments spanning weakly negative to strongly positive net buoyancy are combined with four CCN concentrations and three parcel depths. The prescribed cloud-base temperature is 23 °C, placing the freezing level well above cloud base and providing a deep warm-cloud layer in which collision–coalescence can continue to develop to approximately 6 km. Thermodynamic instability determines whether a cloud can grow and sets its initial ascent pathway. Once cloud growth is sustained, a stronger updraft provides less time for collision–coalescence to develop and keeps more small droplets suspended. Their large integrated surface area enhances condensation and reduces supersaturation. Conversely, a weaker updraft allows more time for coalescence and precipitation unloading, leaving fewer, larger drops and a smaller integrated surface area. The resulting weaker condensational sink can offset the weaker cooling rate and permit higher supersaturation. These opposing pathways buffer supersaturation at an aerosol-dependent level. Among the sustained trajectories, supersaturation near 5–6 km clusters at approximately 15–20% for CCN = 25 cm⁻³, 18–22% for 100 cm⁻³, and 12–16% for 500 cm⁻³, and diminishes when coalescence is suppressed at CCN = 2000 cm⁻³, despite large differences in thermodynamic forcing and updraft speed. Thus, once instability is sufficient for the cloud to grow, it has little additional influence on supersaturation; aerosol loading largely determines the buffered value. The weakest-forcing cases that stall or undergo late redevelopment are exceptions to this convergence. The simulations contain neither ultrafine aerosol particles available for secondary activation aloft nor entrainment and mixing that could introduce additional aerosol into the rising parcel. In real clouds, newly entrained or initially present ultrafine particles could activate as supersaturation rises, increasing droplet surface area and strengthening the condensational sink. These omissions may affect the absolute supersaturation values, but they do not diminish the buffering mechanism reported here: supersaturation aloft remains regulated by the coupled adjustment of droplet surface area, coalescence, precipitation unloading, buoyancy and vertical motion.

489007.title: Withdrawn: Investigating the Influence of Cloud Microphysical Processes on ECS in the ClimaAtmos RCEMIPII CRM Setting
489007.authors: Olivia Alcabes, Caltech, Pasadena, CA; California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA; and A. Jaruga and T. Schneider
489007.abstract: Accurate climate models are crucial for predicting the future of the Earth system, with cloud feedbacks being a major source of inter-model differences. Processes occurring in clouds are at too small of a scale to fully resolve in climate models, so they must be parameterized. These parameterizations can have a strong influence on the equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) of a model. We implement a thermodynamic non-equilibrium parameterization for cloud condensates in the CliMA climate model that specifies different condensation and deposition rates, coupled to a 1M bulk cloud microphysics model. We test the influence of different cloud microphysical processes on ECS using the radiative-convective equilibrium (RCEMIPII) cloud resolving model (CRM) setting. We find that many different cloud microphysical parameters can have a strong control on the ECS in the RCEMIPII setup, and that the influence of different parameters on ECS is dependent on the initial state. This study provides insight into which cloud microphysical parameterizations exert strong controls on climate sensitivity. Future work will investigate the potential of using observations to constrain the most important cloud microphysical processes.

489009.title: Quantification of the Heatwave – Wildfire Feedback In the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) with an Interactive Fire Module
489009.authors: Li Xu, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA; and Q. Zhu, W. J. Riley, Q. Tang, Y. Chen, M. J. Prather, and J. T. Randerson
489009.abstract: Fire-chemistry-climate interactions play a critical role in shaping atmospheric composition and regional climate, yet their representation in Earth system models remains a challenge. Here we explore heatwave-wildfire interactions using the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) version 3, , in which we developed and implemented interactive fire emission coupling module. This module enables direct interaction between burned area, wildfire emissions, aerosols, chemistry and climate, providing a robust framework for investigating fire-chemistry-climate interactions. Model-predicted burned area and fire carbon emissions show reasonable agreement with the observation-based Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED5), demonstrating that the coupled system captures the primary spatial and temporal characteristics of global wildfire dynamics. Moreover, interactive fire emissions coupled with the prognostic chemistry module well reproduce key atmospheric chemistry constituents, confirming the reliability of the fire-chemistry coupling. Analysis of daily surface meteorological variables from fully coupled and uncoupled fire emission simulations reveals that wildfires decrease surface air temperatures during periods of high fire emissions, reducing the duration and intensity of heatwaves. At the same time, fire-emitted aerosols increase surface relative humidity. These changes, in turn, reduce fire activity during periods of extreme heat in high-wildfire regions, reflecting a negative feedback loop from the coupled fire-aerosol-radiation interactions. While this feedback may help dampen fire activity during periods of extreme fire weather, the coupling between heatwaves and fire-emitted particulate matter poses a dual threat to human health.

489011.title: Integrated Predication of Precipitation and Hydrology for Early Action (InPRHA): A Transdisciplinary Approach to Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems
489011.authors: Margaret Orr Hoeflich, NOAA, Cherry Hill, NJ
489011.abstract: Hydrometeorological extremes present escalating risks to communities globally. Preparing, warning, and responding to these events requires seamless integration across meteorological forecasting, hydrological modeling, and social science. The Integrated Predication of Precipitation and Hydrology for Early Action (InPRHA) Project is a global collaboration under the World Meteorological Organization’s (WMO) World Weather Research Programme (WWRP). InPRHA aims to bridge the gap between physical science predictions and actionable disaster risk reduction. This presentation provides an overview of InPRHA's organizational structure, current priorities and activities, and ongoing projects. It will also highlight key coordination efforts, including task team focus areas, community webinars, and strategic international partnerships, designed to integrate physical and social sciences to advance muti-hazard early action systems globally.

489016.title: Evolution and Modernization of the Snow Cover Extent (Northern Hemisphere) Climate Data Record
489016.authors: Brooke Adams, NCEI- National Centers for Environmental Information, Asheville, NC; and C. Hutchins
489016.abstract: The Snow Cover Extent (Northern Hemisphere) Climate Data Record (CDR) version two product bundle forms a coherent suite that spans six decades of satellite-era snow monitoring. The CDR consists of a suite of two products; the weekly 190 kilometer (1966-present) and the daily 24 kilometer (1988-present). This foundational dataset was originally developed by David Robinson at Rutgers University and was competitively selected by the NOAA's Climate Data Record Program in 2012. This version two release reflects multiple years of collaboration between NOAA and Rutgers transitioning the CDR into the NCEI production environment. The version two CDR provides both weekly 190 kilometer and daily 24 kilometer binary (snow/no snow) snow cover data over the Northern Hemisphere in netCDF format featuring updated and harmonized Climate and Forecast (CF) metadata. The daily product complements the weekly series with a more detailed spatial representation of SCE. Both CDRs are suitable for synoptic, hydrologic, and model-evaluation applications. A comprehensive view of the snow cover extent CDR bundle will be presented, along with future plans for its continued evolution and analysis. We aim to strengthen engagement with the polar meteorology community, aligning product development with user requirements to enhance the CDRs value for research and monitoring.

489030.title: Communicating Wind Hazards: Toward Tornado-Level Messaging for Derechos and Other high-End Wind Events
489030.authors: Jay J. Trobec, KELO-TV, Sioux Falls, SD
489030.abstract: Television weather broadcasters are widely viewed as trusted sources of weather information, especially during periods of severe weather. It is routine for broadcasters to interrupt regularly scheduled programming to provide continuous coverage of hurricanes and tornadoes. It is much less common to see programming interrupted for convective wind events such as derechos, bow echoes, rear-inflow jets, or straight-line winds. This disparity exists even though these severe wind events can generate wind speeds comparable to tornadoes, resulting in structural or infrastructural damage to property, or injuries to people. We propose that broadcast meteorologists operationally respond to wind-driven storms as they do tornadoes due to potential damaging wind impacts, societal disruption, and threats to personal safety. Even though wind events are classified as severe thunderstorms – often considered a lower level of hazard than tornadoes – we propose broadcasters manage significant wind events with the same level of urgency as with tornadoes, conceivably including continuous live coverage. Such coverage would improve viewer awareness, risk perception, and protective decision-making before and during destructive convective wind events.

489036.title: Low-level Temperature Inversions at the South Alabama Mesonet
489036.authors: Sytske K Kimball, University of South Alabama, Mobile, AL; and A. G. Clark and C. C. Clark
489036.abstract: Low-level temperature inversions occur, typically at night, when solar radiation ceases and the earth’s surface cools due to the emission of long-wave (or infrared) radiation. As a result, temperatures decrease with increasing height in an atmospheric layer extending from the earth’s surface up to heights of several hundred meters. Low winds and clear skies provide optimal conditions for inversions to form by minimizing atmospheric mixing and maximizing longwave radiation loss to space. While low-level temperature inversions are a fascinating physical phenomenon in themselves, they also have significant economic and health and safety implication. Inversions facilitate the drift of fine drops of pesticides and fertilizers as well as pesticide vapor, causing potentially harmful substances to reach residential areas or non-target agricultural interests. As such, state and federal regulations prohibit pesticide application during inversions. Knowing whether an inversion has developed, however, can be arduous and ambiguous without air temperature measurements at two or more heights. Fog often accompanies temperature inversions due to the cooling of the air as the surface cools, causing hazardous driving conditions. In winter time, the accelerated cooling during an inversion in otherwise above freezing ambient conditions can cause frost to form near the surface, potentially damaging crops and vegetation. For the above reasons, many Mesonets report inversion formation using warning tools on their websites. The South Alabama Mesonet has recently upgraded its inversion monitoring capability to temperature and relative humidity measurements at 4 levels above the surface (0.6m, 2m, 5m, and 10m) using consistent instrumentation at each level. The instruments are Campbell Scientific HygroVUE5 sensors housed in Campbell Scientific RAD06 radiation shields. The RAD06 shields have 6 layers of louvers with a double-louver system of internal baffles to block ground reflections and to provide enhanced intrusion protection. Given the multiple pairs of sensors that can be defined using 4 measurement levels, this configuration allows for multiple definitions of temperature inversions and sub inversions. Therefore, one of the challenges of this work has been to produce an accurate inversion definition that is meaningful for the required applications. To properly define an inversion, temperature sensor accuracy must be taken into account. The temperature difference between a higher- and a lower-level temperature is, therefore, required to be 0.8℃ or more; at least twice the HygroVUE sensor accuracy (±0.4℃); The minimum duration of this difference is required to be an hour. Multiple definitions were tested and will be discussed during the conference presentation. Temperature inversion intensity (or strength) can be defined in two ways: 1) the largest observed temperature difference during the inversion’s existence, and 2) the integrated temperature difference over the time the inversion exists. Inversion duration is defined as the number of consecutive minutes (the South Alabama Mesonet measures at 1-min time intervals) that inversion conditions exist. Preliminary results for two months (March and April 2026) of data from the South Alabama Mesonet station at the University of South Alabama Campus, show that using a 3-level inversion definition, 36 inversions occurred during the 2-month period with an average strength of 1.59°C and a maximum strength of 4.30°C. The average duration of the 3-level inversions was 12.7 hours and the maximum duration was 14.5 hours. In some cases, the inversions were observed to set in prior to the occurrence of sunset. When extending the definition to 4 levels, 43 events were identified, with an average and maximum strength of 1.73°C and 5.32°C, respectively. The average and maximum duration was 11.6 and 14.4 hours, respectively. At the conference, inversion statistics based on several inversion definitions will be presented. The number of months of data and the number of Mesonet stations will be increased. The latter will allow an investigation of the spatial distribution of inversion properties and the effects of site characteristics like terrain slope and obstructions (trees and buildings). The characteristics of sub-inversions will be discussed and the sensitivity to various meteorological parameters, including wind speed and dew-point temperatures, will be explored.

489038.title: Data-Driven Modal Analysis of Coherent Structures in Large-Eddy Simulations of Atmospheric Boundary Layers
489038.authors: Martin A. Beshara, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and M. Sanchez-Gomez, D. Munoz-Esparza, B. Kosović, and J. K. Lundquist
489038.abstract: Flow in convective atmospheric boundary layers organizes into coherent turbulent structures that govern the production, transfer, and redistribution of energy. In complex atmospheric flows, these structures can evolve, merge and translate, so changes in a measured signal may reflect either physical evolution or simple advection through the analysis domain. This challenge is particularly relevant to hurricane boundary layers, where organized features such as mesovortices can alter local momentum and energy pathways. Figure 1a shows the x-y 100-m wind-speed field from Hurricane Harvey (2017), a case study in which observations have documented mesovortical structure. We study coherent structures in convective boundary layers (CBLs) using large-eddy simulations (LESs) and modal methods. LES resolves the energetic turbulent eddies in these flows and provides time-resolved, three-dimensional flow fields suitable for diagnosing their organization. The wide range of scales present in a well-resolved LES make it in some cases difficult to infer dominant, evolving structures from pointwise inspection or conventional statistics alone. However, data-driven modal methods provide a compact representation that identifies spatial patterns directly from the flow data and quantifies their temporal behavior. Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) provides an energetically optimal basis, identifying the structures that account for the largest fraction of resolved variance. Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) complements POD by associating modes with characteristic frequencies and growth or decay rates. Together, these complementary approaches identify dominant structures and their temporal evolution, providing a basis for distinguishing physical change from apparent changes associated with translation. To demonstrate this framework in a controlled setting, we first apply POD to LES of an idealized dry CBL over flat terrain generated with the GPU-accelerated FastEddy framework. The simulation uses 20-m square horizontal grid cells on a 512x1026x250 grid, with the lowest model level at 10 m and 20-m vertical spacing through the boundary layer. Periodic lateral boundaries are used. The flow is driven by a constant surface sensible heat flux of 0.12 K m s-1 and geostrophic wind (ug,vg)=(10,0) m s-1. The model time step is 0.04 s, and three-dimensional fields are saved every minute for three hours. This resolution explicitly resolves the energy-containing CBL scales and helps limit numerical contamination of higher-order POD modes. POD yields spatial modes ordered by their contribution to time-averaged variance and associated temporal coefficients. For example, reconstruction of the vertical-velocity field using only the first two modes retains over 70% of the total resolved variance while recovering the dominant coherent structure in an x-z plane (Fig. 1b). Consistent with this reconstruction, the singular-value spectrum shows that the leading modes contain most of the resolved variance (Fig. 1c). This controlled CBL case provides a benchmark before applying POD and DMD to cold-air outbreaks and tropical cyclones, including Hurricane Harvey, to quantify how coherent structures shape energy pathways in realistic, non-stationary boundary-layer flows.

489039.title: When the Benchmark is Uncertain: Impacts of Energy Balance Closure Corrections on Evaluation of Remote Sensing Evapotranspiration Products
489039.authors: Pushpendra Raghav, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and Y. Kim, B. C. D. Andrade, M. Kumar, J. Huntington, and J. M. Volk
489039.abstract: Eddy covariance (EC) observations provide the primary benchmark for evaluating satellite- and model-based evapotranspiration (ET) products and underpin their transition into operational applications. Yet EC measurements are themselves subject to well-known uncertainties arising from incomplete energy balance closure. These factors can substantially influence reported model performance, contributing to inconsistent conclusions across validation studies and reducing confidence in operational ET assessments. We present a global analysis quantifying how benchmark uncertainty affects the evaluation of leading ET products. Using a global network of EC sites spanning diverse climates and vegetation types, we evaluate product performance under multiple energy balance closure correction strategies ranging from traditional forced-closure to recently developed physiological-based corrections. We quantify how product rankings, error statistics, and apparent model skill change across alternative validation assumptions and identify the hydroclimatic conditions where these effects are most pronounced. Our results demonstrate that conclusions regarding ET product performance can depend strongly on the choice of benchmark correction methodology, with some products exhibiting substantially different relative skill under alternative assumptions. We provide practical guidance on selecting appropriate energy balance closure correction methods for ET product evaluation. The findings establish best practices for more consistent and reliable validation of ET products used in operational water-resource management, drought monitoring, and hydrologic applications.

489042.title: CME Prediction in STEREO at NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center
489042.authors: Mark Miesch, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and E. Adamson, C. Martinkus, G. Millward, and R. A. Steenburgh
489042.abstract: Providing our first sustained stereoscopic view of the Sun, NASA's Solar TErrestrial RElations Observatory (STEREO) is one of the most innovative solar physics missions of the space age. Launched in 2006, STEREO consisted of two nearly identical observatories, A and B, that orbited the Sun at slightly different distances and thus speeds—one trailing the Earth in its orbit and the other leading. The science goals emphasized coronal mass ejections (CMEs) in particular, leveraging the dual perspective to seek fundamental insights into their initiation and propagation through the heliosphere. STEREO-B was lost in 2014 but STEREO-A continues to operate, providing unique coronagraph imagery off the Sun-Earth line. It was realized early on that STEREO's unique perspective could be exploited to benefit space weather forecasting. A team of scientists at SWPC and CIRES set to work on creating an operational forecasting pipeline that ingested multi-perspective coronagraph imagery from STEREO and SOHO/LASCO into a new application called the CME Analysis Tool (CAT). The purpose of CAT was to allow SWPC forecasters to use this imagery to interactively determine the 3D properties of observed CMEs, including their speed, direction, and angular width. The idealized Cone representation of a CME from this fitting exercise was then introduced into an MHD simulation, based on the WSA-Enlil coupled model, to follow the CME's propagation from the Sun to the Earth. This was not only the first use of stereoscopic imagery for CME prediction, it was also the first use of high performance computing for operational space weather forecasting. The CAT-WSA-Enlil pipeline became operational in 2013 and is still relied upon today for CME arrival time prediction at SWPC. In this presentation, I will overview the pipeline and assess its impact on forecast skill. I will also consider how STEREO has inspired future CME prediction at SWPC, including a redesigned, browser-based version of CAT called pyCAT, and a look ahead to the Vigil mission.

489044.title: Towards Improved Understanding of Processes Controlling Convective Storm Lifecycle via Feature Tracking Analysis
489044.authors: Zhe Feng, PNNL, Richland, WA; and A. Varble, PhD, M. W. Stanford, J. Marquis, E. Jo, W. I. Gustafson Jr., H. Xiao, J. D. Fast, S. Glienke, Z. Zhang, and J. Hardin
489044.abstract: Earth-system and weather-forecast models are transitioning toward global storm-resolving, kilometer-scale configurations that promise more realistic simulations of deep convective clouds and their associated extreme weather, but their fidelity is limited by incomplete understanding of the processes controlling convective storm initiation, growth, and vertical development. We leverage Lagrangian feature tracking with the open-source PyFLEXTRKR framework applied to coordinated radar, satellite, and sounding observations and to realistic high-resolution simulations to diagnose how environmental conditions and internal storm dynamics govern convective cell evolution. A convective cell tracking database combining scanning polarimetric radar, geostationary satellite cloud property retrievals, and sounding-derived environmental conditions shows that wider cells grow deeper and produce more intense precipitation. Further, cell width and depth are jointly controlled by mid-tropospheric relative humidity (RH) and vertical wind shear, with narrow cells most sensitive to RH and wide cells more strongly constrained by convective available potential energy (CAPE). Large-eddy simulations indicate that the probability of congestus clouds transitioning to deep convection is dominated by mid-tropospheric RH, with secondary contributions from lower-level CAPE, cloud-base updraft width, and fractional entrainment, highlighting the combined roles of environmental moisture, buoyancy, and mixing in storm deepening. An ensemble of LASSO simulations spanning 2.5-km, 500-m, and 100-m grid spacings shows that km-scale models retain the bulk relationship between cloud-base updraft width and storm depth, and reproduce the contrasting importance of mid-level humidity versus CAPE for narrow and wide cells. However, they underestimate the sensitivity of narrow-cell depth to mid-level dryness and the associated entrainment-driven buoyancy dilution. Simulations of all resolutions produce significantly more tracked shallow cells than is observed. Additional analysis reveals that simulated congestus-depth clouds precipitate too frequently (by up to a factor of 2.5) due to erroneous warm-phase precipitation onset. These structural microphysical biases lead to an overproduction in the number of simulated cells and persist across model resolutions. Together, these results demonstrate that cell-tracking diagnostics applied to realistic high-resolution simulations and evaluated against observations provide a powerful process-based framework for assessing model fidelity and improving understanding of entrainment mixing, microphysics parameterizations, and environmental controls on convective cloud evolution, helping to guide development of next-generation km-scale Earth system and weather-forecast models.

489048.title: Seasonal Precipitation Predictability Based on Sea Surface Temperature Forecasts from a Cyclostationary Linear Inverse Model
489048.authors: Melissa Breeden, OAR, Boulder, CO; and A. J. Hoell, D. J. Vimont, K. Toride, W. Anderson, and J. Verdin
489048.abstract: Generating skillful seasonal precipitation forecasts remains a key challenge over many areas of the world, including several that are relevant to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network, a leading organization in acute food insecurity monitoring and forecasting. In this study, we test how much seasonal precipitation forecast skill can be produced using sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts from a cyclostationary linear inverse model (CSLIM) trained on observed estimates. To generate precipitation forecasts up to one year in advance, we use a novel method that learns lead- and season-specific relationships between CSLIM SST forecasts and observed precipitation empirical orthogonal functions. Furthermore, we attribute precipitation forecast skill to different SST modes of variability, including the El Niño / Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and a long-term warming trend. The skill of precipitation forecasts derived from CSLIM SSTs is significant for many key rainy seasons worldwide, in several cases 6-12 months in advance. A single ENSO mode, which captures most but not all ENSO variability, is the leading source of precipitation skill for several seasons such as the short rains in East Africa, the main Southern Africa rainy season, and winter precipitation over the southeast and southwest United States. Conversely, a long-term trend accounts for most of the skill over the Sahel. West Pacific SST variability distinct from the ENSO mode, with some resemblance to the Pacific Meridional Mode, contributes modestly to skill in some cases such as the long rains in East Africa and the Middle East / Southwest Asia region. Some precipitation seasons, such as warm season southeast US precipitation, are not skillful from CSLIM SST forecasts, suggesting a limited or nonlinear relationship between SSTs and precipitation, and/or one that is hindered by seasonally unpredictable dynamics.

489050.title: Enhancing Prediction of the 10 August 2020 Midwest Derecho and Associated Surface Gusts with All-Sky Satellite Radiance Data Assimilation
489050.authors: Yunji Zhang, ; and X. Chen, D. J. Stensrud, and E. E. Clothiaux
489050.abstract: The 10 August 2020 Midwest derecho is the costliest severe thunderstorm event in the United States, and many operational systems and research studies struggled to faithfully reproduce the derecho and associated surface gusts. In this study, we assimilated microwave (MW) all-sky radiances from sensors of the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) project and infrared (IR) all-sky radiances from the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) onboard the GOES-16 satellite and examined their impact on the analyses and forecasts of surface gusts associated with the derecho. Compared with the baseline that assimilated conventional surface and upper-air observations and IR all-sky radiances from geostationary satellites, the addition of MW all-sky radiances improved the analyzed and forecasted convection-stratiform structures of the derecho. Results show that MW all-sky radiances provided additional information, compared with IR radiances, on hydrometeors within the storm, leading to improved forecasts out to 2 hr with quantitatively more accurate surface gusts. Ensemble forecasts from several analysis times also show a large number of ensemble members being able to produce faithful surface gust swaths of the derecho. This is the first study to assimilate MW all-sky radiances for a severe weather event using a convection-permitting numerical weather prediction model (our model resembles NOAA's High-Resolution Rapid Refresh), and the results suggest promising avenues for improving severe weather forecasts worldwide in the future.

489051.title: OMEGA: The Ocean Model for E3SM Global Applications: A High Performance Computing Code for Exascale Architectures
489051.authors: Mark R. Petersen, LANL, Los Alamos, NM; LANL, Berthoud, CO; and X. Asay-Davis, A. Barthel, C. B. Begeman, S. R. Brus, P. W. Jones, H. G. Kang, Y. Kim, A. Nolan, B. O'Neill, J. Overfelt, K. Smith, L. P. Van Roekel, and M. Waruszewski
489051.abstract: Omega is the next-generation ocean component of the U.S. Department of Energy's Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM). It is an unstructured-mesh ocean model based on the TRiSK family of numerical methods. Omega adopts the algorithms of the current ocean component, MPAS-Ocean, but reimplements them in C++ using the Kokkos performance portability library to enable efficient execution across diverse computing architectures. Spatial operators are implemented as Kokkos kernels, providing high performance on both CPUs and GPUs. The initial shallow-water configuration (Omega-V0) was completed in 2025. Over the past year, the primitive-equation model has been added using a non-Boussinesq formulation that conserves mass and accurately represents thermal expansion and associated sea-level. The Omega framework provides scalable support for unstructured-mesh partitioning, halo exchanges, parallel I/O, and Kokkos-based infrastructure. The ocean model includes a TEOS-10 equation of state, a high-order pressure-gradient formulation, and flux-corrected transport. Omega is currently being integrated into E3SM to exchange heat and freshwater with the atmosphere, sea-ice, and river components. Development has been supported by a comprehensive suite of verification and regression tests. We will present performance results on emerging GPU architectures, together with comparisons against MPAS-Ocean in both idealized test cases and realistic global simulations.

489058.title: Can Aerosols Modulate the “Pre-Convective” Meteorology of Deep Convection?
489058.authors: Daniel Rosenfeld, The Hebrew Univ. of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, JM, Israel; and Y. Zou
489058.abstract: Recent critiques of aerosol convective invigoration argue that many reported aerosol–convection relationships can be explained by covariance with the “pre-convective” meteorological environment. This interpretation treats thermodynamic instability, humidity, and vertical motion as independent controls that affect both aerosol loading and convective development. However, pre-convective does not necessarily mean independent of previous convection. In the tropics, repeated convective cycles continually adjust the atmospheric lapse rate toward a moist-adiabatic structure, giving the thermodynamic profile a memory that extends beyond the lifetime of individual clouds. Aerosols can modify this memory by changing cloud microphysics and the vertical distribution of latent heating. Radiative–convective-equilibrium simulations show that increased aerosol loading suppresses warm rain, transports more condensate upward, and shifts latent heating toward the upper troposphere. The resulting warming stabilizes the atmosphere and reduces CAPE over an adjustment time of several days (Dagan, 2026). Thus, a sounding classified as pre-convective may already represent an atmosphere adjusted by previous aerosol-modified convective cycles, rather than an external meteorological state that independently caused the aerosol–convection relationship. We test this interpretation using long-term tropical soundings together with boundary-layer sulfate-aerosol concentrations over the western Pacific. The soundings are stratified by aerosol loading, and their thermodynamic structure is evaluated using CAPE and the temperature difference between the observed environmental profile and a moist adiabat. Increasing aerosol loading is associated with a warmer free troposphere aloft, a more stable temperature profile, and reduced CAPE across several sounding locations. These observations support the simulated causal pathway by showing the expected thermodynamic fingerprints of aerosol-modified convection in subsequently sampled pre-convective environments. The inferred pathway is: increased aerosol → suppressed warm rain and upward-shifted latent heating → warming of the free troposphere aloft → reduced CAPE in subsequent “pre-convective” soundings. Consequently, statistical analyses that treat the thermodynamic and dynamical environment as independent meteorological confounders may remove part or all of the aerosol-induced response. Temperature, humidity, instability, vertical motion, circulation, and cloud organization can all be shaped by earlier aerosol-modified convection. Meteorology should therefore be considered both a driver of current convection and an evolving outcome of the accumulated aerosol–cloud interaction. Reference Dagan, G. (2026). Opposing transient and equilibrium effective radiative forcing from aerosol–cloud interactions. Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72896-6

489072.title: Meeting End-User Needs to Inform Research to Operations for NOAA's Subseasonal to Seasonal Applications: Lessons from Past Efforts
489072.authors: Andrea J. Ray, NOAA/Earth System Research Lab, Boulder, CO; and H. Yocum and M. Rosencrans
489072.abstract: Meeting end-user needs is of course the goal of the UFS Subseasonal to Seasonal (S2S) community, however, we still know a lot more about S2S user needs than we have been able to serve. This presentation will discuss insights from prior and ongoing work to foster enhanced collaboration with forecast and information providers and users and those who study and testbed forecasts with stakeholders to advance use of NOAA’s evolving S2S applications. The S2S time scale is a particularly rich opportunity for mitigating risks, but has some differences with weather time scale in terms of who provides information to what kinds of users and how used, in which a risk management framework and ready-set-go mindset stretching from months to days is especially important. Lead times from week2 and beyond give opportunities for making adjustments and planning in a variety of sectors including water supply, transportation, fire, agriculture, tourism, and energy. At this time scale, actions and decisions to mitigate risk are often taken by practitioners to use the probabilistic information to mitigate risks for others, vs individual actions. Many of these actions are somewhat abstract, such as decisions about future actions that may be revised as updated information is available including hedging, or about resource allocation plans (vs actual outlays), or insurance. Furthermore, there is a rich history of NOAA engagement with practitioners in this time scale, including ongoing efforts to understand user needs and experiment with information provision. These include activities at some labs and national centers, River Forecast Centers, NIDIS, and partners at the NDMC and NOAA-funded Regional Integrated Science and Assessments programs. There is a rich literature on needs in the published literature as well as reports and assessments. Some insights from existing user needs research indicates that to develop commonly needed products, UFS/S2S science needs to consider how people think about probability/skill, how that may differ for S2S vs weather, and that key end users in the S2S outlook space are practitioners who take actions to protect individuals. While this has parallels to emergency managers and media use of weather watches and warnings, often the practitioners at S2S scales are taking actions and making decisions less in view of the public. These practitioners (often making plans and adjustments for S2S water supply, transportation, fire, agricultural, tourism) are often getting their information from NOAA and external networks who more directly engage with them. This presentation will also discuss what the UFS/S2S community might do to advance use of evolving S2S applications by engaging this rich history and network climate information providers, given that their role in the 2-way R2O pipeline is research and modeling, not providing services, but what they should consider to support development of the services. UFS S2S community may not get involved with practitioners at this level, but needs to be informed by it and support getting funding and other resources in order for their work to be relevant, useful and used. This presentation will discuss some insights from across a variety of efforts of the authors and others. These include: Potential for working with NOAA social science and engagement partners, including CIs, and other ‘Boundary organizations’ or intermediaries, climate information providers, and the benefits of collecting and incorporating feedback at various stages in the R&D process. Funding needed to understand user needs, engage, and this needs to be available at various stages in the process Testbed activities for forecasters’ and others to assess and give feedback on models and prototype products. UFS has benefitted from esp the Hazardous Weather Testbed (HWT), Hydrometeorological Testbed ((HMT), Climate Testbed (CTB), and Aviation Weather Testbed (AWT) in evaluations that are relevant for those phenomenon, forecasters, and user communities - need to think ahead to how these functions will be done for S2S, feeding back O2R and R2O Need for prototypes routinely products for practitioners to give feedback. For example, in a recent operationalization of the EDDI, feedback had been collected in several stages over several years, even before the final NWS 10-102 process, leading to refinements.

489078.title: Development and Validation of a Machine Learning Model for Daily 1 km Near-Surface Air Temperature in Data-Sparse Hyper-Arid Regions
489078.authors: Hamid Norouzi, New York City College of Technology-CUNY, Brooklyn, NY; and S. AlKhaled, K. Nielsen, R. Blake, and S. Alsharrah
489078.abstract: Near-surface air temperature at sub-kilometer scales is a primary input to heat-health warning, thermal comfort planning, and infrastructure design, yet it remains poorly resolved in exactly the regions where extreme heat is most severe. Hyper-arid countries typically have sparse station networks and no dense observational baseline against which a model can be validated, which excludes them from the validation strategies most near-surface temperature models rely on. We present the development and validation of a machine learning framework that predicts daily 1 km air temperature from satellite land surface temperature (LST) in this setting. Model design is grounded in a preceding 25-year characterization of the LST-air temperature relationship across eleven stations, which showed that the surface-air difference reverses sign between day and night, scales with land cover, and is strongly non-stationary, with monthly regression slopes falling from roughly 0.7 in winter to 0.2 in summer. These findings motivate an explicitly per-overpass architecture: four independent gradient boosting regressors, one per MODIS overpass, each trained on radiative, geographic, land-cover, and temporal predictors rather than a single pooled model. Validation uses leave-one-station-out cross-validation, withholding each station entirely from training and predicting it from the remaining network. This is a stringent test of spatial generalization and is feasible where dense-network validation is not. Three of four overpasses achieve R-squared of 0.92 to 0.96 and RMSE of 2.08 to 2.42 degrees C with near-zero bias, approaching the noise floor of the LST retrieval itself. The fourth cannot be cross-validated because only one station reports at that overpass time. Spatial fields are benchmarked against ERA5-Land and MERRA-2 using centered RMSE decomposition, and resolve a daytime urban cool island and nighttime warm island that reanalysis at 11 to 55 km cannot represent.

489095.title: Snowpack Non-Stationarity and Ski Resort Vulnerability in the Western US
489095.authors: Xinxin Sui, The Univ. of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX
489095.abstract: Snow is a critical water resource in the dry, mountainous regions of the western United States. A wide range of modeling strategies has been developed to represent snow accumulation and melt, ranging from conceptual temperature-index (TI) schemes to physically explicit energy balance models and, more recently, AI-based approaches. Here we present a 74-year daily complete snow water equivalent (SWE) dataset (1950-2023) for 754 SNOTEL station locations across the western US derived using a calibrated two-parameter TI model. Despite its simplicity, the model effectively reproduces observed SWE dynamics and snow–rainfall partitioning with high skill scores across most sites, yielding a dataset that can serve as a standardized benchmark for evaluating more complex modelling approaches. The calibrated temperature threshold and degree-day factor compensate for radiative and other physical processes that the TI model does not explicitly represent. The optimal TI parameters are non-stationary, however, with the temperature threshold increasing in the recent four decades (1980–2020), which may reflect warming effects, and the neglect of parameter non-stationarity may further propagate into overestimating the decreasing trend in long-term snow estimations. Applying this long-term snow record to 160 ski resorts across the western US, we found that ski visitation generally tracks snowpack changes. Resorts in Oregon and California experience the most rapid snowpack decline, and the significant delay of snow onset date encroaches on the historically snow-reliant winter holiday period that often anchors resort revenue. This presentation discusses the new dataset, trend analyses, and implications for the ski industry.

489096.title: Observational Uncertainty and Future Directions in Assessing Urban Precipitation Effects
489096.authors: Xinxin Sui, The Univ. of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX
489096.abstract: The "La Porte anomaly", an observed precipitation change downwind of Chicago, was reported more than half a century ago in an observational study, suggesting that urbanization may enhance precipitation downwind of cities. These early works leaned mostly on rain gauges, since radar and satellite measurements were still in their early stages. In recent decades, advances in observational techniques have allowed researchers to revisit this topic using radar and satellite datasets, expanding the scope from isolated case studies to regional and global scales. However, studies using different observational datasets across diverse urban environments have yielded inconsistent results regarding urbanization’s effects on precipitation. Here, we provide an overview of how observational uncertainty and methodological differences may contribute to these discrepancies. Specifically, we summarize and quantify variations across precipitation measurement platforms (gauge, radar, and satellite), differences between successive generations of Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) satellite datasets, and scale mismatches between urbanization metrics and precipitation data. By synthesizing existing methodologies and perspectives from urban hydroclimatologists and precipitation dataset developers, we (1) examine the spatiotemporal scales and coverage of different observational data sources, (2) identify sources of uncertainty and bias across observational datasets, and (3) discuss priorities and opportunities for future urban precipitation research.

489102.title: Cropland Soils versus Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations: Airborne Flux Constraints on Distinct Sources of Agricultural NOx in California
489102.authors: Quazi Rasool, CIRES CU Boulder/NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and H. Zhang, J. Bash, Q. Zhu, M. Li, S. Youn, E. Waxman, I. B. Pollack, A. Rollins, R. H. Schwantes, C. Harkins, C. Lyu, C. H. Hsu, E. Y. Pfannerstill, B. Place, R. Cohen, A. Bucholtz, A. H. Goldstein, C. Schmitt, S. H. Chen, C. Warneke, J. Wang, and B. C. McDonald
489102.abstract: Agricultural nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions shape ozone and particle formation, yet remain among the least constrained terms in air quality models. Manure handled at animal facilities is rarely resolved separately from fertilized soil, if at all represented. We constrain a process-based Berkeley-Dalhousie-Iowa Soil NOx Parameterization (BDISNP) in WRF-Chem using airborne eddy-covariance NOx fluxes measured during RECAP-CA (June 2021) over California's San Joaquin Valley (SJV), the southern Central Valley, and an extreme ozone nonattainment region with intensive agricultural production. We replace BDISNP default climatological nitrogen (N) inputs with year-specific FEST-C synthetic fertilizer and a facility-resolved manure N field developed for 2021-2023. We correct modeled surface-layer soil temperature and moisture biases diagnosed against CIMIS stations and SMAP retrievals, then fit the emission factors to surface-scaled, footprint-weighted RECAP-CA fluxes. Because these factors scale processes rather than regional totals, they can be applied wherever the scheme uses resolved agricultural inputs. California cropland receives both synthetic fertilizer and livestock manure; we therefore separate soil emissions driven by synthetic fertilizer from all livestock-derived N, whether emitted at the facility or applied to fields. Airborne fluxes over predominantly dairy facilities with little or no cropland influence are comparable to those over fertilized fields and cannot be explained by soil N cycling alone. The fitted SJV facility emission factor indicates that approximately 3.4% of N from livestock-excreted manure is released as NO. We apply the SJV-constrained factors across the full Central Valley and evaluate them against independent 2023 SARP and AEROMMA aircraft measurements and TROPOMI and TEMPO NO2 columns, supported by meteorological assessment of the evaluation days, including CARB ceilometer PBL-height observations. Synthetically fertilized cropland soils are the largest source of Central Valley NOx at 45-55% across the simulated periods, exceeding combustion at 20-33%, and livestock manure N contributes a near-invariant 16% concentrated along the dairy-heavy SJV.

489103.title: Geomagnetic Storms Impact Terrestrial Weather
489103.authors: Joachim Raeder, University of New Hampshire, Durham, NH
489103.abstract: It has long been a mystery why small Total Solar Irradiation (TSI) changes have significant effects on Earth’s climate. Solar cycle correlation studies abound but cannot conclusively point to a viable physical mechanism. Here, I show that geomagnetic storms have a profound terrestrial weather impact. Using 67 years of hourly Disturbance storm time (Dst) index and ERA5 atmosphere data over North America, I find geomagnetic storm impacts up to two orders of magnitude larger than the long-term global mean surface temperature impact attributed to solar activity. The effects vary depending on region and season. Comparing with solar cycle studies shows that the solar cycle variations are more likely caused by storm-time solar activity bursts as opposed to slow continuous variations, such as the solar cycle scale TSI variations. As for the physical mechanisms, particle precipitation effects such as from cosmic rays, solar energetic particles, or magnetospheric electrons are least consistent with my results. In particular, the cosmic ray – cloudiness hypothesis is falsified. A top-down mechanism operating directly through the ionosphere or through stratospheric chemistry and the polar vortex appears to be more likely. (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2025GL121097 https://eos.org/research-spotlights/solar-storms-can-affect-earths-weather-a-new-study-examines-how)

489113.title: Non-Conservative Wave Effects on Inner-Shelf Circulation at Submesoscale and Smaller Scales
489113.authors: Delphine Hypolite, UCLA, Los Angeles, CA; Univ. of California, Los Angeles, CA; UCLA, Los Angeles, CA; and M. Ho, J. C. McWilliams, and L. Romero
489113.abstract: Surface gravity waves shape coastal circulation through wave breaking, bottom streaming, and wave-enhanced bottom drag, yet how these non-conservative effects propagate from the surfzone onto the inner shelf and interact with regional submesoscale currents has remained largely unexplored at realistic scales. We address this gap using a 30 m resolution simulation of the Pt. Arguello, California coast, using ROMS-NCWEC, an updated implementation of non-conservative wave effects in the Regional Ocean Modeling System one-way coupled to WaveWatchIII. Two dynamically distinct regimes emerge. Offshore, waves amplify the turbulent thermal wind balance and enhance submesoscale cyclonic vorticity, consistent with wave-modulated frontogenesis. Nearshore, breaking becomes the dominant momentum source, producing order-20× vorticity enhancement relative to a no-wave control and reorganizing the momentum balance from wind-versus-drag to breaking-plus-wind-versus-drag. Between these regimes, on the inner shelf (between the 10 m and 70 m isobaths), wave streaming competes with bottom drag; where streaming meets the wave-driven undertow, near-bed convergence drives upwelling that closes a wave-forced overturning cell and generates strongly sheared alongshore jets at the surface. These results identify the inner shelf as a dynamically active bridge between the surfzone and the outer shelf, where wave-driven momentum reorganizes circulation across scales.

489116.title: A Dynamic Agricultural NOx Emissions Capability in the Community Emissions Computing Engine (CECE) for Global and Regional Applications
489116.authors: Quazi Rasool, CIRES CU Boulder/NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and P. C. Campbell, B. D. Baker II, Z. Moon, C. Harkins, B. Koziol, M. Li, R. H. Schwantes, W. Li, J. He, M. Bruckner, L. Zhang, R. Ahmadov, J. Schnell, Y. Tang, F. Yang, B. C. McDonald, and L. Bernardet
489116.abstract: Agricultural nitrogen oxides (NOx) are among the largest and least-constrained terms in the reactive nitrogen (N) budget, with global soil estimates alone spanning 3–17 Tg N per year. Fertilized cropland soils and livestock operations emit via distinct N sources and sensitivities, yet livestock is frequently aggregated into the soil term. Both respond nonlinearly to temperature, moisture, and N availability, with soils pulsing after rewetting, so the sector must be computed online from evolving model state rather than prescribed. We present an agricultural NOx emissions capability based on the Berkeley–Dalhousie soil NOx parameterization, developed in Canopy-App, a standalone global canopy physics framework, and implemented in the Community Emissions Computing Engine (CECE) within Configurable Atmospheric Chemistry (CATChem) for the Unified Forecast System (UFS). Switchable soil-temperature response functions and canopy-reduction options enable runtime intercomparison of process assumptions without modifying the host model. A central emphasis is N input fidelity, which bounds achievable skill: resolving fertilizer and manure N as distinct pools with separate emission factors and temperature sensitivities, adding seasonality consistent with application timing, and characterizing biases in the driving soil fields. Structured around N pools, environmental response functions, and surface exchange rather than a single species, the framework is designed to extend to ammonia, nitrous oxide, and nitrous acid once organic and inorganic soil N pools are represented explicitly. Using the soil NOx module, we quantify the spread introduced by temperature response, canopy treatment, and N input choices, and identify the architectural requirements imposed on CECE: persistent, restart-safe state for N reservoirs and antecedent dry-spell history. These requirements generalize to other dynamic emission sectors; supporting them shortens the Research-to-Operations (R2O) pathway for process-based emissions parameterizations in the UFS. Keywords: Agricultural Emissions, Soil NOx, Livestock, Reactive Nitrogen, CECE, CATChem, UFS, Air Quality

489118.title: BEACON: A Decision-Centered Framework for Benchmarking AI, Hybrid, andPhysics-Based Forecast Systems for High-Impact Weather
489118.authors: Scott Swerdlin, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. Kumar, J. H. Richter, M. A. Morrison, P. A. Jimenez, S. Meech, T. M. Hopson, V. Weeks, S. Alessandrini, K. M. Newman, and J. C. Knievel
489118.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) weather models are advancing rapidly, but operational adoption requires evaluation frameworks that extend beyond traditional forecast skill metrics. NSF NCAR is developing the Benchmark Evaluations for AI and CONventional prediction systems (BEACON), an open, community-driven framework for comparing AI, hybrid AI–physics, and conventional numerical weather prediction systems using both scientific and decision-based performance metrics. Built on the METplus verification infrastructure, BEACON integrates standard verification methods with application-specific measures that quantify forecast value for real-world decisions. Rather than asking only which model is most accurate, BEACON evaluates which forecast best supports specific operational actions across hazards such as extreme heat, severe convection, flooding, wildfire, and winter weather. Initial demonstrations include heat stress forecasting using both AI and physics-based guidance, with additional applications examining cold-air arrival and severe weather. The framework is designed to accommodate deterministic, ensemble, and probabilistic forecasts while supporting rapid evaluation of emerging AI models alongside established operational systems. BEACON seeks to establish an open benchmark ecosystem that accelerates model improvement, enables reproducible intercomparisons, and provides scientifically rigorous, decision-relevant evidence for transitioning next-generation forecasting capabilities into operations.

489129.title: Inherited Biases and Usable Skill: An Energy-Focused Validation of Google’s WeatherNext 2 Against HRRR, ERA5, and DOE Field Observations
489129.authors: Nicola Bodini, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO; and M. Thomas, R. Krishnamurthy, G. Xia, and P. Moriarty
489129.abstract: AI-based weather prediction models promise operational forecast skill at a fraction of the computational cost of numerical weather prediction, but their adoption by the energy sector requires understanding not just how much they err, but where, why, and under which conditions. We present an end-to-end validation of Google's WeatherNext 2 (WN2) - a 64-member ensemble system with 0.25° resolution, 6-hourly output, and a 15-day horizon - focused on variables central to energy applications: 10-m and 100-m wind speed and 2-m temperature. WN2 forecasts spanning 2022-2025 are evaluated over the contiguous United States against the National Laboratory of the Rockies' HRRR Meteorology, Energy and Transmission (MET) Toolkit, an energy-ready, 2-km reformulation of NOAA's HRRR archive, with ERA5 (WN2's training dataset) evaluated in parallel as a control that separates errors inherited from training from those added by the AI model. Model-based findings are then tested against independent wind-profile observations from two U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) field campaigns: the American WAKE experimeNt (AWAKEN, onshore site in Oklahoma) and the Third Wind Forecast Improvement Project (WFIP3, coastal New England). At day 1, WN2 is effectively "analysis-equivalent": its distance from the HRRR MET Toolkit matches that of ERA5 itself, and the WN2−ERA5 residual is the smallest of any dataset pair. WN2 essentially reproduces ERA5, departing from it only modestly, mainly over complex terrain. The systematic errors are set at this short range: in our analysis, WN2’s mean bias remains essentially unchanged from day 1 to day 15, and skill loss at longer lead times is driven by decorrelation, not by growing bias. The signature error is a persistent negative 100-m wind-speed bias over land, present in every season, inherited from ERA5, and confirmed as real against onshore observations: at the AWAKEN sites, WN2's 0-24 h 100-m wind speed bias reaches −0.9 to −1.5 m s⁻¹, several times larger than the HRRR MET Toolkit's. At the coastal WFIP3 sites, in contrast, the bias is site-dependent, spanning −0.3 to +1.3 m s⁻¹. The errors are also uneven across the wind distribution itself: the upper tail carries a disproportionate share of the total, with WN2's ensemble mean clipping the strongest winds, especially over land. The vertical structure suffers as well: WN2 misses the observed nocturnal low-level jets at both AWAKEN and WFIP3, as its mean profiles lack the jet-nose maximum onshore and are nearly uniform with height offshore. Finally, we translate the results into operational guidance: for all three variables, RMSE against the HRRR MET Toolkit grows smoothly with lead time (roughly 50% larger by day 7 than at day 1), and initializing WN2 forecasts once daily rather than four times daily increases operational RMSE by no more than 0.6%. Overall, WN2 is usable for smooth-terrain, mean-flow, short-to-medium-range energy applications, but should not yet be relied upon for extreme winds, low-level jets, or sharp coastal gradients.

489132.title: Grid Spacing Impacts on Forecasted Tornadic Supercell Evolution in the Warn-On Forecast System
489132.authors: Austin W Dixon, CIWRO - Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK
489132.abstract: In recent years, the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) has been developing the Warn-On-Forecast System (WoFS), an ensemble of convection-allowing models developed specifically for the prediction of individual thunderstorms and their hazards. Typically, WoFS is run at 3-km horizontal grid spacing and is generally insufficient for discriminating between tornadic and nontornadic supercells. Recent studies have shown that running idealized simulations of supercells at finer grid spacings results in more accurate predictions of mesocyclone characteristics and intensity. Additional work has shown similar results within the WoFS framework. EnKF analyses of the full life cycle of the May 23, 2022 Morton, TX tornadic supercell were conducted to create control run datasets for comparing against WoFS ensemble forecasts for the same event. A suite of ensemble analyses were conducted to investigate the effects of grid spacing on WoFS ability to accurately forecast the retrieved intensity and complex evolution of the Morton supercell, which included cyclic tornadogenesis and multiple storm mergers. In particular, comparisons of low and mid-level updraft helicity as well as vertical velocity and vertical vorticity were investigated between grid spacings. Finer grid spacings were found to have greater magnitudes of all variables listed above and to more closely reflect the tornadic evolution of the observed storm. In recent years, the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) has been developing the Warn-On-Forecast System (WoFS), an ensemble of convection-allowing models developed specifically for the prediction of individual thunderstorms and their hazards. Typically, WoFS is run at 3-km horizontal grid spacing and is generally insufficient for discriminating between tornadic and nontornadic supercells. Recent studies have shown that running idealized simulations of supercells at finer grid spacings results in more accurate predictions of mesocyclone characteristics and intensity. Additional work has shown similar results within the WoFS framework. EnKF analyses of the full life cycle of the May 23, 2022 Morton, TX tornadic supercell were conducted to create control run datasets for comparing against WoFS ensemble forecasts for the same event.
