A suite of ensemble analyses were conducted to investigate the effects of grid spacing on WoFS ability to accurately forecast the retrieved intensity and complex evolution of the Morton supercell, which included cyclic tornadogenesis and multiple storm mergers. In particular, comparisons of low and mid-level updraft helicity as well as vertical velocity and vertical vorticity were investigated between grid spacings. Finer grid spacings were found to have greater magnitudes of all variables listed above and to more closely reflect the tornadic evolution of the observed storm.

489135.title: Closing the Gaps: Advancing Mars Space Weather Observations and Forecasts for Future Exploration
489135.authors: Gina A DiBraccio, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD
489135.abstract: As we prepare for future robotic and human exploration at Mars, space weather has become an increasingly important factor when considering mission risk. Solar storms, energetic particle events, and disturbances in the Martian ionosphere can affect operations, communications, navigation, radiation exposure, and other aspects of orbital and surface activities. Yet the current Mars fleet provides only intermittent and incomplete coverage of the solar and planetary conditions needed to characterize space weather hazards and support reliable operational forecasts. We provide an overview of the observational gaps that currently limit Mars space-weather understanding and prediction, including discontinuous temporal coverage, sparse spatial sampling, and the absence of continuous upstream monitoring. By assessing the current state of Mars space weather observations, we present a strategically integrated solution to fill current gaps by combining existing Mars, Earth-based, and heliospheric observations with new measurement capabilities and advanced physics-based and data-driven models. This integrated strategy shifts from the currently discrete, event-specific knowledge toward a coordinated observing architecture capable of supporting both scientific understanding and space-weather applications for future robotic and human missions.

489136.title: TEMPO Trace Gas Observations: Algorithm Status and Highlights
489136.authors: Gonzalo Gonzalez Abad, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, Cambridge, MA; and C. R. Nowlan, K. Chance, X. Liu, H. Chong, D. E. Flittner, M. Ghahremanloo, B. Henderson, W. Hou, J. Houck, L. Judd, J. Szykman, M. Tao, L. C. Valin, H. Wang, and Q. Zhu
489136.abstract: Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) is observing air quality and atmospheric composition over North America from a geostationary orbit since its operations started in August 2023. TEMPO observes the continent every 40 to 60 minutes at a spatial resolution on the order of ~ 2 × 4.5 km2. Together with the Geostationary Environment Monitoring Spectrometer (GEMS, launch 2020) monitoring Asia and the Sentinel-4/UVN (launch 2025) monitoring Europe, TEMPO is part of the current global constellation of geostationary sensors devoted to the observation of air quality. Like GEMS and Sentinel-4/UVN, TEMPO uses backscattered ultraviolet and visible solar radiation to retrieve atmospheric amounts of key trace gases and aerosols associated with air quality and atmospheric chemistry. Among the species retrieved from TEMPO, observations of nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and formaldehyde (HCHO) are important to understand emission sources and atmospheric chemistry, including the formation and destruction of tropospheric ozone. After multiple version updates over the first years of the mission, the TEMPO Level 2 CLDO4, NO2 and HCHO products have undergone significant enhancements to improve the performance and accuracy of the slant column retrievals, air mass factor calculations and post-processing corrections including destriping for CLDO4, NO2 and background for HCHO. We illustrate the performance of the retrievals (version 4), evaluating their fitting uncertainty and showing comparisons with independent correlative measurements from other satellite products, showcasing small noise levels and high accuracy with well quantified biases. We continue by illustrating the capacity of TEMPO products focusing on different case studies showing TEMPO’s high temporal and spatial resolution. We finalize discussing aspects of the retrieval subject to improvement and our plans to address them.

489138.title: Stress-Testing Observational Constraints on Aerosol-Cloud Interactions Using a Differentiable Model Hierarchy (Invited Presentation)
489138.authors: Duncan Watson-Parris, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA; University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and G. Nicolaou
489138.abstract: Observational constraints on aerosol-cloud interactions have advanced rapidly, with cloud-controlling factor regressions now yielding estimates of effective radiative forcing (ERFaci) considerably narrower than traditionally assessed ranges. Yet these methods rest on assumptions that are frustratingly hard to test against observations alone: (local) linearity, an absence of unobserved confounders, and an assumption of aerosol exogeneity despite known physical feedbacks like wet removal and aqueous-phase production. I will present work approaching these assumptions from two directions. First, by applying machine learning feature importance and causal discovery (LPCMCI) to satellite and reanalysis records, we allow the conditioning structure to be inferred directly from the data rather than specified in advance. I will share how estimates of aerosol effects on precipitation susceptibility and cloud radiative properties depend critically on this inferred structure. Second, I will introduce a framework where the true forcing is explicitly known. JAM is a new modal global aerosol model written entirely in JAX inside the differentiable JAX-GCM (JCM). Built in months rather than years by pairing domain scientists with agentic coding tools, JAM carries the full aerosol lifecycle from interactive emissions through modal microphysics and activation. By sampling the running model along real satellite orbits at native timestep resolution, we can apply the exact same estimators to pseudo-observations and compare them against JAM's directly diagnosed forcing. Crucially, to ensure we aren't just testing statistical methods against parameterized answers, we extend this hierarchy down to a JAX-based Large Eddy Simulation (LES) sharing the same physics and gradient machinery. By resolving cloud adjustments explicitly, we generate pseudo-observations from a system that doesn't assume the answer. Combined with end-to-end differentiability which allows us to calibrate the model directly against the observations that survive the test, I will argue this offers a genuinely new route to falsifiable observational constraints on ERFaci.

489139.title: Revisiting the Resolution Dependence of Dust Emissions: Insights from a Storm-resolving Model
489139.authors: Tong Ying, SIO, San Diego, CA; and A. T. Evan, D. M. Leung, and F. Judt
489139.abstract: Typical global climate models struggle to accurately simulate dust emissions, partly because their coarse horizontal resolution cannot represent important processes controlling surface winds. We combine global simulations from the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS), spanning grid spacings from 240 to 3.75 km, with a process-based offline dust emission scheme to investigate how dust emissions change as horizontal resolution increases from conventional climate-model scales to storm-resolving scales. Spatial-averaging experiments further separate the effects of changes in coarse-scale meteorological conditions from those of spatial variability resolved at finer resolution. Increasing resolution from 240 to 30 km approximately doubles global dust emission. Further refinement from 30 to 3.75 km produces little additional change in the global total but substantially redistributes emission among major dust-source regions. These regional shifts are especially pronounced in the southern Sahara and Sahel, where the kilometer-scale simulation explicitly represents most convective precipitation. A complementary comparison of the 3.75 and 120 km simulations shows that the Sahelian contribution to global dust emission during the monsoon season increases from 6.1% to 12.3%. Comparison of simulations with resolved and parameterized convection attributes much of this increase to improved representation of mesoscale convective systems associated with African Easterly Waves and their strong, intermittent surface winds. The spatial-averaging experiments show that fine-scale spatial variability, rather than changes in coarse-scale mean conditions alone, primarily controls the resolution dependence of dust emission. Spatial variability in friction velocity accounts for most of this effect, while the combined variability in friction velocity and soil moisture contributes approximately 38% of global dust emission in the 3.75 km simulation. These results show that increasing resolution does not simply amplify dust emission: reaching storm-resolving scales changes both the processes and source regions represented in the simulated global dust cycle.

489147.title: A Comparison of Hurricane Intensity and Structure Algorithm (HISA) Intensity and Wind Structure Estimates with Input from Physically-Based and Machine Learning Thermodynamic Retrievals
489147.authors: Galina Chirokova, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and M. DeMaria, A. Tomar, J. Knaff, J. M. Garcia-Rivera, M. D. Goldberg, S. Kalluri, X. Liang, Y. K. Lee, S. Liu, and H. Meng
489147.abstract: Hurricane Intensity and Structure Algorithm (HISA) is operational at NOAA/NESDIS and provides global estimates of tropical cyclone intensity, wind structure, and 2D winds at pressure levels for all global tropical cyclones. Accurate estimates of tropical cyclone intensity and structure are critical for forecasting changes in storm intensity and structure. For example, incorrect initial intensity estimates could result in rapid intensification being underforecast or completely missed. Operational tropical cyclone intensity estimates still rely strongly on the subjective Dvorak technique; however, a growing number of new instruments and methods sometimes produce significantly different intensity and structure estimates. These differences make it increasingly important to provide methods that make maximum use of the information content of satellite observing systems for tropical cyclone analysis. Many existing intensity estimation methods also tend to have a low bias, and there is a very limited number of satellite-based structure estimates. Operational HISA uses the Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS) retrievals as input. We found that the new machine-learning retrievals (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6876995) and MIRS experimental TC-specific retrievals produce more physically consistent temperature fields in the tropical cyclone environment. Replacing the current MiRS inputs with these machine-learning or MiRS-specific retrievals can significantly improve HISA performance. The presentation will discuss the HISA performance using different physically-based and machine-learning thermodynamic retrievals as input. In addition, we will discuss several new tropical cyclone products that use new microwave temperature and moisture retrievals as input and could contribute to improved tropical cyclone intensity and structure forecasts as standalone applications or as input to machine learning intensity and structure forecast models. Disclaimer: The scientific results and conclusions, as well as any views or opinions expressed herein, are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect those of NOAA or the Department of Commerce.

489149.title: Contrasting Atmospheric and Boundary-Layer Processes During Dry and Moist Heatwaves over Delhi
489149.authors: Priyanka Sharma, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and A. Wadhwa, P. Li, S. Wu, R. Kumar, and A. Sharma
489149.abstract: Delhi experiences frequent and increasingly intense heatwaves that threaten public health, energy systems, and urban sustainability. Heatwaves over northwestern India occur under both dry and humid conditions, producing distinct thermal and physiological heat stress, yet the physical mechanisms governing these two heatwave types remain poorly understood. This study combines observations, reanalysis, and the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model with an urban canopy parameterization to investigate the evolution of dry and moist heatwaves over Delhi. More detailed and accurate Local Climate Zone (LCZ)-based land classification is incorporated to better represent the city's heterogeneous urban landscape. Three two-way nested domains are configured, with the innermost domain at 1-km horizontal resolution. Simulations focus on representative dry and moist heatwave events during June 2024 and May 2025. We examine differences in boundary-layer evolution, heat and moisture transport, and large-scale atmospheric circulation through analyses of near-surface temperature, humidity, wind fields, planetary boundary-layer height, and vertical atmospheric structure. Model performance is evaluated against surface meteorological observations across Delhi. Early results provide insights into the distinct physical drivers of dry and moist heatwaves and demonstrate the value of high-resolution urban modeling for understanding neighborhood-scale heat exposure. The findings will support improved heat-risk assessments and inform urban planning and climate adaptation strategies for rapidly growing megacities.

489153.title: A Hybrid Physics-Machine Learning Framework for Improving Simulations of Urban Air-Conditioning Electricity Consumption
489153.authors: Xiangwen Deng, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ; and J. Cohen, J. Rodriguez, B. Svoma, C. Gonzales, and M. Georgescu
489153.abstract: Accurate simulation of urban air-conditioning (AC) electricity consumption is critical for reliable energy system planning under intensifying heat extremes. However, physics-based urban climate-energy models are rarely evaluated against spatially resolved electricity observations and often exhibit systematic, morphology-related biases. Here, we developed a hybrid physics–machine learning framework that leverages neighborhood-scale utility electricity data to diagnose and correct structural biases in urban climate-energy simulations. Using hourly grid-cell electricity consumption data from a Phoenix (AZ)-area utility company, we applied a random forest-based bias correction approach to 2-km AC consumption simulations for the extreme summer of 2023 produced by the Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled with a building energy model and multilayer building-effect parameterization (WRF-BEP/BEM).Within the utility service territory, where electricity consumption data are available, the framework reduced mean grid-cell summertime RMSE by 62% (from 2.1 MWh to 0.8 MWh) and standard deviation by 63%. Comparable improvements were achieved using independent summer 2022 data, with reductions of 39% in RMSE and 51% in error standard deviation, demonstrating that the framework captured persistent bias structures rather than summer-specific meteorological conditions. The framework mitigated systematic underestimation in grid cells with small building volumes (<2,000,000 m³), strengthening the approximately linear relationship between AC consumption and building volume. Decomposition of RMSE reduction revealed that scaling-based correction dominated in low-volume grid cells, whereas morphology-related contributions became increasingly important in larger-volume groups characterized by greater urban heterogeneity. The framework also improved the representation of monthly AC temperature sensitivity patterns and supported spatial cross-validation within the utility service territory, providing a basis for statewide extrapolation of bias-corrected AC electricity consumption. These results demonstrate that hybrid physics–machine learning approaches can provide an effective pathway for evaluating and improving regional climate model-based urban climate-energy simulations. Incorporating observation-constrained corrections and morphology-informed parameterizations may enhance the physical consistency of simulated intra-urban energy variability and support more reliable regional energy planning under future urban growth and climate change.

489155.title: Using LEO Satellite Data for TC Analysis and Forecasting
489155.authors: Galina Chirokova, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and K. Schwartz, J. Franklin, M. DeMaria, J. Darlow, A. Tomar, and S. J. J. Munchak
489155.abstract: Low-Earth-orbiting (LEO) satellites provide unique data that are not available from other sources. Examples include microwave imagery, scatterometer data, and unique day-night-band (DNB) visible-like nighttime imagery. Operational tropical cyclone forecasters routinely use microwave imagery for analysing tropical cyclone structure and intensity, and scatterometer winds to analyze tropical cyclone surface winds. DNB can provide information about low level circulation centers not visible in the IR channels. Historically, a serious limitation of LEO satellites has been a large latency and coarse temporal resolution - sun-synchronous LEO satellite data is only available twice per day for a given tropical cyclone. However, with the new generation of smallsats, such as tomorrow.io, these limitations are being reduced as the large number of LEO satellites combined with an increasing number of ground stations can now provide temporal coverage and latency comparable to those from geostationary satellites. We developed a collocation database for multiple LEO satellite data and tropical cyclones, which includes legacy satellites carrying microwave imagers and sounders and scatterometers, as well as for smallsats such as TROPICS and tomorrow.io constellations. This presentation will discuss the statistics of satellite overpasses over tropical cyclones for the legacy and smallsats satellites, and possible uses of that database for tropical cyclone analysis and forecasting. Specific examples include the intercomparison of the legacy low-frequency (91 GHz) and high frequency (183 and 204 GHz) microwave imagery for operational tropical cyclone analysis, and improving existing and developing new algorithms for diagnosing tropical cyclone intensity and structure from microwave satellite imagery and retrievals.

489159.title: IGNITE: Investigating Gradients in Near-Storm Instability and Thermodynamic Environments
489159.authors: Rebecca Weinstein, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA; and K. Schiro, J. M. Corner, S. W. Freeman, and P. T. Pangle
489159.abstract: To better understand how deep convection initiates and organizes with respect to environmental conditions, we performed a small field campaign in July-August 2026 near the Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) mobile facility (AMF3) in the Southeast US at Bankhead National Forest (BNF) and surrounding areas of northern Alabama, called IGNITE: Investigating Gradients of Near-storm Instability and Thermodynamic Environments. During IGNITE, a “storm-chasing” approach was taken to deploy small, portable windsondes (Sparv Embedded) to examine the evolution of thermodynamic gradients in the pre-storm and near-storm environments and their relationships to convection initiation and organization. Measurements were coordinated with the NASA Investigation of Convective Updrafts (INCUS) science team’s Testing of INCUS Measurements Experiment - Suborbital preLaunch Investigation of Convective Evolution - Alabama (TIME-SLICE-AL) radar deployments and the University of Alabama Huntsville (UAH) mobile laboratories. In this presentation, we will present key insights and lessons learned across a range of observed convective cases. Data from coordinated in situ meteorological instrumentation, radiometers, and radars will also be analyzed. We will discuss the role of moisture, cold pool properties, and dynamical influences on initiation and organization of convection in the Southeast US from the perspective of our field experiment and frame our results within the context of complementary statistical analyses.

489166.title: OCELOT: Direct Atmospheric Forecasting from Heterogeneous Earth Observations Using a Graph–Transformer Hybrid Model (Invited)
489166.authors: Azadeh Gholoubi, Axiom @ NOAA/NWS/OMD, Riverdale Park, MD; EMC, College Park, MD; and R. McLaren, M. C. Ko, X. C. Jin, N. Esposito, A. Collard, C. R. Martin, D. Holdaway, and D. T. Kleist
489166.abstract: Most recent AI weather prediction systems are trained on gridded analysis or reanalysis fields, which makes them dependent on numerical weather prediction and data-assimilation systems used to generate those states. This work presents OCELOT, an observation-space machine-learning forecasting prototype developed to predict future atmospheric observations directly from heterogeneous Earth observations without using gridded reanalysis fields as training targets. OCELOT ingests satellite radiances, scatterometer observations, radiosondes, aircraft reports, and surface observations in their native sampling geometries and measurement spaces. The model uses instrument-specific graph-attention encoders to project observations onto a shared spherical icosahedral latent mesh, a hybrid sliding-window Transformer and spatial graph neural network processor to evolve the latent state, and metadata-conditioned decoders to forecast future observations at their native locations, times, channels, and pressure levels. OCELOT is trained on global observations from 2015–2023, validated on 2024, and evaluated out of sample on 2025 observations. Forecasts are produced at +3, +6, +9, and +12 h lead times and verified directly in observation space. Results show that OCELOT produces spatially coherent short-range forecasts across independent observing systems. Microwave temperature-sounding channels achieve +12 h RMSE values of approximately 1.2–1.9 K, while more surface- and cloud-sensitive infrared window channels show larger but physically interpretable errors. Conventional observations also exhibit coherent vertical temperature structure for radiosonde and aircraft profiles. For surface variables, OCELOT remains less accurate than the operational GFS, as expected, but substantially outperforms a same-location persistence baseline at longer lead times for 2-m temperature and 10-m wind components. These results demonstrate that heterogeneous operational observations can support globally coherent, reanalysis-independent short-range AI forecasting. OCELOT provides a scalable research pathway toward observation-native machine-learning forecast systems that preserve instrument-specific sampling and enable direct cross-instrument verification.

489167.title: Disentangling Storm-Type and Precondition Controls on Hydrological Response in Flash Flood Alley: A Study Using Observation and WRF-Hydro Simulations
489167.authors: Deffi Munadiyat Putri, University of Illinois, Urbana, IL; University of Illinois, URBANA, IL; and F. Dominguez, B. Jewett, and K. T. Gray
489167.abstract: Flash floods remain the leading cause of weather-related fatalities in the United States, with Flash Flood Alley being a region particularly prone to this hazard. Storm type and antecedent soil moisture influence the rainfall-runoff response, and only a few studies have investigated their interactions using simulation-based approaches. The objective of this study is to understand the rainfall-runoff response by studying historical high quickflow events, at streamgages within the Lower Colorado–San Bernard Coastal watershed from 1996–2023. We objectively classify the identified high quickflow-producing events based on their associated storm type, including frontal lines, Mesoscale Convective System (MCS), Extratropical Cyclone (ETC), and Tropical Cyclone (TC). Our preliminary results show that cold and stationary fronts are the primary drivers of high quickflow generation at most streamgages within the catchment. To build on this finding, we use the Weather Research and Forecasting Hydrological modeling system (WRF-Hydro) to run simulations that isolate the pure storm-type signal from the effects of antecedent soil moisture on hydrograph shape, response time, and runoff coefficient. Results are expected to provide a framework for coupling storm typology with antecedent-state information in flash flood warning.

489180.title: Regional Weather Forecasting with gSAM
489180.authors: Marat Khairoutdinov, SUNY, Stony Brook, NY; Stony Brook University, Coram, NY
489180.abstract: The global System for Atmospheric Modeling (gSAM) has recently been extended to support limited-area weather forecasting using initial and lateral boundary conditions from operational numerical weather prediction systems. The forecasting system is fully automated and is capable of generating kilometer-scale forecasts over arbitrary regions of the world using GFS or IFS forecasts for real-time prediction, or ERA5 for retrospective simulations. The current implementation has been applied to daily 3.5-km forecasts over the contiguous United States (CONUS). The complete workflow, including data acquisition, preprocessing, model initialization, execution, and postprocessing, is performed automatically. On the NCAR Derecho supercomputer, a 24-hour CONUS forecast requires approximately 15 minutes using 2,048 CPU cores, allowing rapid experimentation with model physics and forecast configuration. Forecast quality is evaluated using objective verification against HRRR, MRMS, URMA, and Stage IV analyses. The results demonstrate that gSAM produces realistic forecasts of near-surface temperature, precipitation, and convective systems while identifying several systematic biases that are guiding ongoing model development. Selected case studies, including severe convective events and heavy precipitation episodes, illustrate the capabilities of the forecasting system and highlight areas requiring further improvement.

489190.title: Development and Evaluation of an Interactive Aerosol Module in the Korean Climate Model (K-CM)
489190.authors: Rokjin Park, Seoul National University, Seoul, 41, South korea
489190.abstract: The Korean Climate Model (K-CM) has represented aerosol radiative effects using a fixed monthly climatology. To improve this representation, we are developing an interactive aerosol module for K-CM by implementing the GEOS-Chem aerosol schemes. The module calculates emissions, chemical production and loss, dry and wet deposition, and transport of sulfate, nitrate, ammonium, carbonaceous aerosols, mineral dust, and sea salt. The simulated aerosol optical depth is passed to the K-CM radiation scheme, allowing the aerosols simulated online to affect the model’s radiation budget. We will introduce the module design and the current status of its development, and present results from an initial multi-year simulation. The simulated aerosol distributions will be evaluated against satellite and ground-based observations, including MODIS aerosol optical depth, AERONET measurements, and surface aerosol composition measurements, as well as against the parent GEOS-Chem model. For East Asia, we will also compare the results with a coupled aerosol–chemistry–climate simulation performed using the MIRAE Earth System Model (MIRAE-ESM). In addition, we will discuss how clouds, precipitation, and boundary-layer meteorology in the host model affect the simulated aerosol distributions. Preliminary estimates of the aerosol direct radiative effect in K-CM will also be presented based on companion experiments in which the interactive aerosols are replaced with the default aerosol climatology. We will conclude by discussing the remaining steps toward aerosol–radiation–cloud coupling in K-CM.

489198.title: Met Office Global Convective Nowcast Development in Support of HWIS
489198.authors: Graeme David Anderson, UKMO, Exeter, DEV, United kingdom; and A. Lanyon and A. Creswick
489198.abstract: Aviation operations require timely and consistent information on hazardous weather. The aim of the HWIS (Hazardous Weather Information Service) workstream of the Met Panel of the ICAO (International Civil Aviation Organisation) is to develop globally consistent forecasts of hazards to aviation on nowcast timescales by 2033. To support this aim, the Met Office is exploring new approaches to aviation hazard nowcasting. This work has included the initial development of a global gridded convective nowcast, which can be used as the basis of HWIS hazard object creation. This nowcast will use a combination of extrapolation into the future from observations and NWP (numerical weather prediction) forecasts. Initial work has focussed on identifying and developing suitable observational and NWP data sources for this processing. The extrapolation of future timesteps from observations has been tested using the well-established pySTEPS framework. Verification has been carried out on the data produced by the initial proof-of-concept nowcast system to assess its accuracy. Computational performance and runtime are also being assessed, as timely production of any nowcast product is fundamental to its usability and value. This work provides an initial assessment of the feasibility of producing operational global aviation hazard nowcasts to support future HWIS services.

489199.title: Machine Learning Calibration of Low-Cost Gas Sensors under Controlled Environmental Conditions
489199.authors: Olivier Le Pavec, IMT Atlantique, Nantes cedex 3, 44, France; and A. Bouhanguel, F. Lorant, F. Theron, A. Joubert, and A. Durrmann
489199.abstract: The rapid deployment of low-cost air quality monitoring networks provides new opportunities for high-resolution observation of atmospheric pollutants in urban and indoor environments. However, the reliability of these networks remains limited by sensor-to-sensor variability, environmental sensitivity, and measurement biases affecting low-cost sensing technologies. Ensuring observation quality requires robust calibration and quality control methods capable of improving data reliability and assessing sensor performance. This study investigates a machine learning-based approach for improving the reliability of low-cost electrochemical NO₂ sensors through calibration against a reference-grade analyzer. Seven identical low-cost electrochemical NO₂ sensors integrated into a Nexelec® air quality monitoring station were evaluated under controlled laboratory conditions using a dedicated 100-litre gas exposure chamber equipped with independent temperature and relative humidity regulation. The reported NO₂ concentration reflects the complete measurement chain, including sensor response, electronic signal conditioning, and onboard processing. The chamber enabled controlled exposure of sensors to NO₂ concentrations ranging from background levels up to approximately 2 ppm, while varying ambient conditions to characterize the influence of temperature and humidity on sensor response. Measurements from the low-cost sensors were compared against a Teledyne T Series T200P reference NO–NO₂ analyzer to quantify sensor variability and develop correction models. The calibration dataset consisted of the NO₂ concentration reported by each low-cost sensor together with temperature and relative humidity measurements as input variables. These ambient parameters were intentionally included because temperature and humidity variations are known to influence electrochemical sensor responses and can introduce additional measurement biases during operation. The reference analyzer NO₂ concentration was used as the target variable to train machine learning models capable of compensating for sensor-specific biases under varying environmental conditions. The objective was to develop a real-time correction model capable of independently correcting each new sensor observation from the sensor-reported NO₂ concentration and the associated environmental conditions, without relying on previous measurements. These parameters were selected to represent the information available during real-world deployment and support the development of correction strategies applicable to operational sensor networks. Individual machine learning models were initially developed for each sensor to characterize inter-sensor variability and evaluate the potential of machine learning-based correction approaches. This individual calibration step provides insight into differences in sensor response characteristics and establishes a reference for the future development of transferable models capable of correcting multiple sensor units within heterogeneous networks. Random Forest regression models were selected due to their ability to capture nonlinear relationships between sensor-reported concentrations and environmental parameters. Hyperparameter optimization was performed using Bayesian optimization using Python library Hyperopt, minimizing the mean absolute error on the optimization dataset. As the objective was real-time sensor correction rather than temporal forecasting, measurements were randomly separated into training and testing datasets. The optimized Random Forest models demonstrated high correction capability for sensor-reported NO₂ concentrations against reference analyzer measurements. Across the evaluated sensors, coefficients of determination ranged from 0.84 to 0.96, demonstrating the effectiveness of the optimized Random Forest models in improving individual sensor measurements. The corresponding mean absolute errors ranged from 68 to 92 ppb depending on the sensor. This variability in correction performance highlights the potential of machine learning-based calibration approaches for improving the reliability of heterogeneous sensor networks, providing a basis for identifying underperforming units and prioritizing maintenance or recalibration efforts. Moreover, the differences in correction performance reflect intrinsic sensor response variability, highlighting the importance of considering sensor variability when developing correction strategies for heterogeneous deployments. These results indicate that machine learning-based calibration can improve the quality of observations provided by low-cost electrochemical gas sensors by compensating for sensor-specific biases and environmental dependencies. By combining controlled laboratory characterization with machine learning-based correction, the proposed approach provides a framework for the future development of reliable and scalable low-cost air quality observing networks through transferable calibration strategies. Future work will extend this approach to additional gaseous pollutants, including ozone, sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen sulfide, and investigate automated methods for transferable sensor calibration, and long-term performance assessment under field deployment conditions.

489205.title: NSF-NOAA's GONG: A Global Ground-Based Network for Continuous Solar Observations
489205.authors: Alexei A. Pevtsov, National Solar Observatory, Boulder, CO; and L. Bertello, S. Bounds, D. Branston, J. Britanik, O. Burtseva, G. Card, M. Creelman, S. Gusain, A. Hamada, B. J. Harker, A. L. H. Hughes, K. Jain, S. Kholikov, R. Komm, B. Lekshmi, S. Nguyen, N. Oien, G. Petrie, T. Purdy, K. Shuman, S. C. Tripathy, and T. M. Wentzel
489205.abstract: The US National Science Foundation's (NSF) Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG) is a network of 6 robotic telescopes around the globe to provide continuous observations of the Sun. GONG delivers full-disk observations of Doppler measurements, line-of-sight magnetograms, white light and H-alpha images at a cadence of one minute, achieving a median duty cycle of about 0.9 (90% of a 24-hour day) for fully calibrated data or 0.95 for quick reduced (space weather operations) data. The data are transmitted in near-real time to NOAA/SWPC and NSO/NISP Data Centers and made available for operational space-weather forecasting and for the broader research community. GONG has been in operation since 1995. This poster presents a high-level overview of the project and introduces its three major components: network operations, data processing, and science support. Each of these components is described in more detail in coordinated posters. We also discuss current plans for maintaining GONG operations, and its future replacement – the next-generation GONG (ngGONG).

489206.title: An Efficient Numerical Approach for Implementing Spatially Correlated Observation Errors In Operational Data Assimilation
489206.authors: Rishabh Bhatt, University of Reading, Reading, RDG, United kingdom; and M. Bonavita, N. Bormann, M. Chrust, S. L. Dance, A. Fowler, E. Holm, S. Newman, N. Nichols, I. Pasmans, and J. Scott
489206.abstract: Global operational forecasting centres, including ECMWF and the UK Met Office, generally do not account for spatial observation-error correlations within their data assimilation (DA) systems. To reduce the impact of neglected correlations, a common strategy is to thin the observations and use a diagonal observation-error covariance matrix (R) with inflated observation-error variances. However, this strategy discards a large proportion of potentially valuable observations and may lead to a suboptimal analysis compared with a system that explicitly accounts for these correlations. Although recent developments have enabled robust estimation of observation-error correlations for several satellite instruments, their incorporation into operational DA systems remains a significant computational challenge. Treating observation-error correlations requires applying the inverse of R (the precision matrix) during each iteration of the minimisation procedure used to solve the variational DA problem. Since operational DA cycles assimilate millions of observations, explicitly constructing or applying a dense precision matrix is computationally prohibitive and introduces substantial communication overhead between processors. We propose a practical approach for implementing spatially correlated observation errors that substantially reduces the computational cost without explicitly forming the precision matrix. We focus on spatial observation-error correlations for AMSU-A observations from the all-sky assimilation system at ECMWF and the UK Met Office. Recently derived estimates reveal that AMSU-A correlations exhibit a sparse banded structure. Accordingly, our approach exploits large-scale sparse direct solvers, to efficiently perform the required matrix operations in parallel. The approach is evaluated within an idealised incremental 3D-Var framework using AMSU-A observations from ECMWF’s operational system at a higher observation density than in the operational configuration. We evaluate the method against two baselines. First, we compare the proposed method with an implementation that explicitly forms and applies the precision matrix in terms of the computational time and the number of minimisation iterations. Second, we compare the assimilation experiment that accounts for the full correlation structure of R with experiments using i) a diagonal error-covariance matrix without variance inflation, and ii) a diagonal covariance matrix with variance inflation in terms of the spatial length scales represented in the analysis increment. Furthermore, we investigate the sensitivity of the proposed method to matrix reordering techniques and address practical implementation challenges associated with observation distribution across multiple processors. The results will provide insight into the feasibility of a future implementation of spatially correlated observation errors within OOPS, the DA framework used at ECMWF.

489209.title: Simplifying Severe Weather Messaging as Probabilistic and Intensity Forecasts Improve
489209.abstract: Advancements in severe weather science have led to continual improvement in severe weather forecasts through time. These improvements in understanding and forecast guidance now allow for more specific and precise forecasts of severe weather coverage and intensity. Recently, the NOAA/NWS Storm Prediction Center has leveraged these advancements to add multi-tier conditional intensities to their convective outlooks for Days 1 to 3. However, messaging these threats can be increasingly challenging due to added complexity of the forecast and increased public vulnerability to the threats from these storms. This presentation will discuss verification of these conditional intensities, the techniques that the SPC has utilized to forecast them, and how collaboration from the broader weather community has helped to simplify and unify the message ahead of impactful severe weather events.

489211.title: Operationalizing Co-Production: Lessons Learned from Engaging Industry in Climate Services
489211.authors: Allison Crimmins, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and B. Smith and M. Coates
489211.abstract: Drawing on engagement best practices and applied research, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)’s Industry Partnerships leadership details outcomes from implementing a systematic framework for co-creating climate tools and services with industry end-users. We illustrate the utility of this framework through case studies in architecture, insurance, and retail, demonstrating how aligning engagement strategies with specific industry needs and organizational cultures can significantly enhance the usability and uptake of climate data. The demand for climate information in the private sector is outpacing current engagement models. As businesses across various industries—from architecture and engineering to insurance and retail—seek to quantify their physical climate risk, there is a critical need for climate service providers to evolve their methodologies. Traditional “outreach-driven” models often fail to translate complex environmental data into the business-relevant metrics required for actionable decision-making. We share key lessons learned from implementing NOAA’s service delivery framework, highlighting the importance of iterative feedback loops, stakeholder-driven priority setting, and the proactive translation of complex climate projections into business-aligned decision frameworks. We also address common challenges in co-production, such as balancing scientific rigor with rapid industry timelines and the scalability of these partnerships. By shifting the paradigm from service delivery to sustained co-creation, practitioners can more effectively support industries in building long-term resilience. This work provides a realistic blueprint for federal and private-sector providers aiming to broaden their impact and bridge the gap between climate science and societal application.

489212.title: Highlighting How Major U.S. Industries Use Weather and Climate Data to Strengthen Community Resilience
489212.authors: Allison Crimmins, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and B. Smith, M. D. Coates, S. Luce, C. Schrems, and J. Dissen
489212.abstract: According to major reinsurers, the five-year average loss for insurers from natural catastrophes has grown to $155 billion. The insurance sector faces increasing costs from large-scale disasters that complicate risk pricing, impacting the home and business owners they serve. At the same time, recent research from the National Retail Federation shows that an estimated 3.4% of retail sales are directly affected by weather, and that weather influences about $1 trillion in annual global retail sales. For retailers, hazardous weather conditions can disrupt supply chains and business operations, leading to financial loss. For decades, climate and weather data has been central to operational decision making in these sectors. As the risk of weather and climate impacts increase, these data are playing an increasingly important role as tools used in building and strengthening community resilience during extreme weather. This talk will focus on what the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has learned from these sectors about how they use weather and climate data to strengthen community resilience across the country. We will begin by highlighting innovative insurance solutions in the American south, showcasing the synergistic role between engineers and insurers in their effort to harden homes against damage from tropical storms and bolster insurability using NOAA data. Then, we will highlight the retail sectors’ role in supporting communities in disaster mitigation and response, investigating how they are using NOAA data to bolster community resilience and strengthen supply chains. By engaging across multiple industry sectors, NOAA has both uncovered valuable user applications that shape weather and climate data development and begun to reveal how their ability to utilize this data plays a key role in each other's resilience—further shaping the resilience of the communities they serve. While extreme weather poses negative impacts to insurers, their retail customers, and the consumers, there is also incredible opportunity for cross-sector collaboration that minimizes impacts, recovery times, and financial losses. Central to this opportunity is ensuring these sectors have the ability to find, understand, and use weather and climate data for their roles in strengthening community resilience.

489214.title: Best Practices for Developing Impactful Narratives to Communicate Atmospheric Science
489214.authors: Allison Crimmins, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and S. Luce, B. Smith, and M. D. Coates
489214.abstract: “Sometimes reality is too complex. Stories give it form.” – Jean Luc Goddard Storytelling offers a unique opportunity to synthesize scientific ideas and concepts into a format that resonates with audiences, facilitating deeper comprehension of the material. ESRI ArcGIS StoryMaps serves as a dynamic platform for translating atmospheric science information into immersive experiences; by integrating geospatial data, multimedia assets, and descriptive text, authors can craft compelling narratives that breathe life into datasets and complex topic areas. When executed with precision, these digital stories function as robust instruments for education and engagement. This presentation will detail the approach employed to produce 13 distinct StoryMaps developed under a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) initiative focused on accelerating the industry adoption of weather and climate data. We will examine the comprehensive lifecycle of StoryMap development—spanning initial conceptualization and design through to final dissemination—while offering best practices for ensuring narratives remain impactful and accessible. Finally, we will showcase specific project outcomes, including a StoryMap series that explores the climatological evolution and future outlooks for three Alaskan communities.

489215.title: Advancing NOAA Earth Science and Data with the Open Information Stewardship Service (OISS) and the Large Language Model for OISS (LOISS)
489215.authors: Kenneth S. Casey, NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Silver Spring, MD; and R. Berkheimer, N. A. Ritchey, J. Hung, and K. Roberts
489215.abstract: To support users’ Earth science data analysis and AI workflows, and to ensure NOAA meets its legislated mandates for long-term preservation and independent understandability of its environmental data in a cost effective manner, the National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS), has implemented a new enterprise cloud archive and data stewardship service known as the Open Information Stewardship Service (OISS). This new cloud archive is a core enterprise component of the NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF). OISS leverages a semantically-enabled knowledge graph which stores not just the outputs of each step of a workflow, but the workflows themselves as well, ensuring full provenance, scientific reproducibility, and adherence to the principles of gold standard science. By exposing this rigorously-curated knowledge graph to modern large language models (LLMs) and AI tools, OISS ensures AI interactions are grounded in NOAA’s data and provenance and supports modern, open science workflows. The presentation will provide an update on OISS and its associated chat interface, the LLM for OISS (LOISS). Through OISS and LOISS, data stewards, earth data scientists, and other users will be able to connect their workflows more seamlessly to NOAA’s vast archive of environmental data and information.

489224.title: Lessons Learned in Service Delivery, User Engagement, and Product Lifecycle from NOAA’s Industry Proving Grounds
489224.authors: Michael J. Brewer, NOAA, Asheville, NC; and A. Crimmins, B. Smith, M. Coates, A. Formby-Fernandez, C. Schrems, J. Dissen, R. Vose, and S. Ansari
489224.abstract: NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) ran the Industry Proving Grounds Program (IPG) from 2022-2026. The goal of the program was to radically improve the uptake and use of weather and climate data in the Reinsurance & Finance, Retail, and Architecture & Engineering sectors. New and expanded datasets, new delivery tools, and new data formats were implemented to both shorten the time required to uptake data into industry models and tools, and to simplify understanding of data holdings and applicability. Repeatedly, industry highlighted that they were not atmospheric scientists and requested NOAA provide data so that non-scientists could use it for business and to enhance the U.S. economy. While IPG covered a range of activities, this talk will focus on lessons learned and successes in continuous engagement with focused user communities, building a product development apparatus to address their needs, and ensuring information delivered was of value and met needs and expectations. We will also focus on some of the successful products and services that came from IPG and the value of those tools.

489226.title: From Cloud Structure to Cloud Dynamics: Doppler Measurements from the EarthCARE Cloud Profiling Radar
489226.authors: Pavlos Kollias, Stony Brook Univ., Stony Brook, NY
489226.abstract: The joint ESA–JAXA Earth Cloud, Aerosol and Radiation Explorer (EarthCARE) satellite was launched on 28 May 2024. EarthCARE carries the first Doppler cloud profiling radar in space, providing a new capability for studying clouds from orbit. Previous spaceborne cloud radars focused primarily on cloud occurrence, vertical structure, and precipitation. With the addition of Doppler velocity measurements, EarthCARE now provides direct observations of cloud dynamics and the atmospheric motions that shape cloud evolution. This presentation will provide an overview of what we have learned during the first two years of the mission. Examples will include the global climatology of deep convective cores, gravity waves, and organized updrafts and downdrafts in shallow clouds. These observations also provide new insight into hydrometeor sedimentation, turbulence, and the coupling between cloud dynamics and cloud microphysical processes. The presentation will conclude with a discussion of the opportunities and current limitations of Doppler observations from space. EarthCARE marks the beginning of a new generation of spaceborne Doppler radar missions, including JAXA's PMM, NASA's FALCON radar mission, and ESA's WIVERN mission. Building on the EarthCARE observational record, these missions will progressively improve our ability to observe cloud dynamics across a broad range of spatial scales, from shallow clouds and gravity waves to deep convection and mesoscale organization, moving toward routine global observations of atmospheric dynamics from space.

489228.title: C3DIR: A Deep Learning 3-Dimensional Cloud Property Retrieval for Passive Satellite Imagers
489228.authors: Charles White, NOAA/NESDIS, Madison, WI; and Y. J. Noh, J. M. Haynes, and I. Ebert-Uphoff
489228.abstract: Operational cloud products derived from satellite imaging instruments often struggle to accurately identify and characterize multiple distinct, vertically overlapping cloud layers due to limitations of passive visible, near-infrared, and infrared observations. We develop the Cloud 3-Dimensional Imager Retrieval (C3DIR), a deep learning model trained using observations from the Earth, Cloud, Aerosol, and Radiation Explorer (EarthCARE) to estimate vertically resolved cloud properties from multiple geostationary imagers. C3DIR is aimed at pushing 3-D cloud algorithms closer towards operational use. The model predicts the occurrence and water content of ice, liquid and rain at predefined altitudes along the imager line of sight and uses a voxel-level collocation approach. This representation enables the model output to be flexibly sampled from different viewing geometries and facilitates comparisons with other observing systems. We evaluate C3DIR using both EarthCARE and ground-based remote sensing observations focusing on different aspects of its estimated 3-D volumes. Qualitative comparisons show that C3DIR is able to depict multiple distinct, overlapping cloud layers in strong agreement with the EarthCARE ACM-CAP product. Quantitative comparisons with the EarthCARE ACM-CAP product illustrate that C3DIR can reliably characterize ice water content, but larger uncertainties remain for the water content of liquid-phase clouds and rain. Intercomparisons with algorithms that underpin the NOAA operational cloud products show several areas where C3DIR may offer significant improvement including cloud-top height, cloud-base height, and cloud detection. Overall, we show that several aspects of C3DIR’s design improve the accuracy and flexibility of cloud properties derived from satellite imaging instruments.

489230.title: Developing Drought Alerts to Serve Communities with Early Warning
489230.abstract: Drought is a pervasive, complex hazard with far-reaching economic, environmental, and societal impacts. With annual losses nearing $10 billion in the United States, drought is linked directly and indirectly to severe agricultural losses, reduced energy production, diminished water quality and availability, and an increase in wildfires and human health issues. Because drought typically has a gradual onset, communities and local officials often struggle to recognize when conditions are actively deteriorating until severe impacts are already underway. This operational gap underscores the critical need for proactive early warning systems that can alert decision-makers to worsening conditions before they cascade into catastrophic losses. To address this need, this study leverages a multi-indicator approach—integrating spatial data from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) alongside the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI)—to develop a suite of new early warning products designed to trigger actionable alerts for local communities. By building comprehensive historical records for every U.S. county using these datasets, we generated localized year-to-date accumulations, historical drought ranks, and rate-of-intensity-change metrics. These integrated indices evaluate not just the current severity of a dry period, but its historical context, compounding deficits, and the velocity at which conditions are degrading. By translating these accumulating deficits and rapid-onset trajectories into timely, geographic-specific alerts, these new products equip water managers, agricultural stakeholders, and emergency planners with the actionable, localized data required to implement early mitigation strategies and protect vulnerable populations.

489233.title: Illinois' Record Breaking Tornado Year
489233.authors: Trent Ford, Univ. of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL
489233.abstract: The state of Illinois recorded over 180 tornadoes in the first 6 months of 2026, smashing the previous annual record of 142 tornadoes set in 2024. This incredible tornado year in the Land of Lincoln extends a streak of 4 consecutive years with at least 100 tornadoes in the state, well above the 1991-2020 annual average of 60 tornadoes. The seeming step change in recent Illinois tornado frequency comes amid reports of "tornado alley shifting east"; however, disregarding the long history of tornado frequency in the southern Midwest and Mid-South US that rivals that of the Great Plains. All of these issues have been challenging for science communication and planning for emergency management, hazard mitigation, and public concern of severe weather and climate change. We will review the wild 2026 tornado year in Illinois in the context of recent upticks in tornado activity and longer-term trends in severe weather in the Midwest region. We will also provide some lessons learned and perspectives on real-time science communication to diverse stakeholder groups concerned/impacted by severe weather, including (1) separating weather and climate variability, (2) articulating (un)certainty in climate change connections to severe weather, and (3) solutions to reduce tornado vulnerability irrespective of weather variability and climate trends.

489236.title: Regional and Seasonal Evaluations of WRF-CMAQ Aerosol Extinction from EQUATES using CALIOP and Airborne High Spectral Resolution Lidar (HSRL) Datasets
489236.authors: Travis D. Toth, NASA Langley Research Center, Hampton, VA; and A. J. Scarino, M. Clayton, R. Mathur, B. Henderson, J. Szykman, M. B. Follette-Cook, and C. Turner
489236.abstract: The Weather Research and Forecasting-Community Multiscale Air Quality (WRF-CMAQ) modeling system is commonly applied to study and predict air quality (AQ), including surface concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), across both the contiguous United States (CONUS) region and broader Northern Hemisphere. Past studies concerning validation of aerosol optical properties from CMAQ have largely focused on column aerosol optical depth, and aerosol extinction validation in particular has been limited to case studies from field campaigns. Long-term validation (e.g., from routine satellite measurements) is critical however, as CMAQ aerosol extinction impacts the radiative processes in the model, which subsequently impacts the AQ (including PM2.5) model component. NASA’s Cloud-Aerosol Lidar with Orthogonal Polarization (CALIOP), which flew aboard the Cloud-Aerosol Lidar and Infrared Pathfinder Satellite Observations (CALIPSO) satellite, provided a 17-year record (2006-2023) of atmospheric profiles of aerosol extinction retrievals. Such an extensive data record allows for regional and seasonal evaluations, and trend analyses, of surface layer aerosol extinction from CMAQ over large spatial domains like CONUS. To supplement these assessments, NASA’s airborne High Spectral Resolution Lidar (HSRL) underflights of CALIPSO are leveraged where/when available, as they provide invaluable information (i.e., direct measurements rather than retrievals) of aerosol optical properties and aerosol type classification near the surface. In this work, WRF-CMAQ surface layer aerosol extinction (Angstrom interpolated to 532 nm) simulated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Air QUAlity TimE Series (EQUATES) Project is spatially and temporally collocated with Version 5 CALIPSO aerosol extinction retrievals and airborne HSRL measurements from various field campaigns, both at 532 nm. These CMAQ/lidar comparisons are performed for all available collocations and partitioned by surface type, lidar-based aerosol classification, region, and season. Overall, near-surface CMAQ aerosol extinction is shown to exhibit a consistent low bias relative to CALIOP observations over CONUS. CMAQ agrees better with CALIOP over water than over land in general, and the strongest agreement is found for the CALIOP “marine” aerosol classification. For the subset of cases for which we have airborne HSRL underflights of CALIPSO, HSRL near-surface aerosol extinction is generally smaller than that of CALIOP and thus CMAQ agrees well with HSRL (within ~0.01-0.02 km-1 on average). This study is part of NASA’s Health and Air Quality Applied Sciences Team (HAQAST) Program. Accordingly, an overview of HAQAST is provided, along with an explanation of how these lidar-based assessments of WRF-CMAQ align with the objectives of NASA Earth Action.

489243.title: Modernizing National Weather Service Operations with NWS HIVE
489243.authors: Nicholas Hampshire, NWS, New Braunfels, TX; and R. Henry-Reeves, S. T. Jacobs, and A. Just
489243.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) is fundamentally transforming its operational forecasting paradigm by transitioning from legacy, physically restricted infrastructure to NWS HIVE, a centralized, cloud-based application environment. Designed to replace the legacy Advanced Weather Interactive Processing System (AWIPS), NWS HIVE will serve as a unified collaborative hub built on a modern microservices architecture with a human-centric user interface. By decoupling forecasters from fixed physical office locations, NWS HIVE will unlock unprecedented operational portability. This allows meteorologists to deliver life-saving forecasts, warnings, and impact-based decision support directly from emergency management centers, wildfire front lines, or any remote location. NWS HIVE integrates modern DevSecOps pipelines to drastically accelerate software deployment, leverages cloud elasticity to scale computational power instantly during severe weather events, and facilitates seamless, real-time collaboration and office backup across the entire enterprise. NWS officially launched active development of the NWS HIVE environment in mid-2026. Current and upcoming milestones focus on the development of Phase 1 Initial Operating Capability (IOC) services including data management, visualization, and hazard generation. Through late 2026 and early 2027, NWS will finalize a cloud-native design, execute a Proof of Concept, and initiate operational testing. This roadmap sets the stage for the completion of Phase 1 by the end of 2027, with full Phase 2 capability with dissemination near the end of 2028. Ultimately, this presentation will outline how NWS HIVE will culminate in the total decommissioning of legacy on-premises AWIPS infrastructure by the end of 2028, establishing a highly agile, resilient forecasting ecosystem built for the future.

489244.title: Mesoterps: Advancing a University Micronet for Environmental Monitoring and Campus Community Awareness
489244.authors: Allison Fenley, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and R. Sanford
489244.abstract: Mesoterps: Advancing a University Micronet for Environmental Monitoring and Campus Community Awareness The University of Maryland (UMD) is expanding its campus-wide micronet, originally deployed to monitor microclimate variability and enhance campus safety. The network comprises low-cost automated weather stations powered by Raspberry Pi units running WeeWX software, strategically sited to capture high-resolution observations of temperature, dew point, atmospheric pressure, wind speed and direction, rainfall rate and heat stress indicators. To facilitate replication and community access, data is streamed continuously and made publicly available at weather.umd.edu. As of May 2026, the network includes ten weather stations, one CO2 sensor, and one Black Bulb Globe thermometer. At least three additional stations are planned for deployment by December 2026, increasing spatial coverage and improving data granularity across campus. Additionally, three particulate matter sensors are planned for deployment, providing measurements for PM1, PM2.5, and PM10. Future network expansion includes storm drain monitoring, a lightning sensor network, and the addition of solar radiation and UV sensors. This added instrumentation will extend the network’s utility for UMD Emergency Management, supporting flood and extreme weather risk assessment alongside the network’s existing environmental monitoring capabilities. Parallel efforts are underway to improve the website’s data visualization tools, offering more intuitive, actionable representations of current and historical conditions for the UMD community. Together, these developments expand the local environmental monitoring capacity and position the UMD micronet as a model for replication by other universities.

489245.title: Studying the Spatial and Temporal Variations In Surface PM2.5 Concentrations In Virginia Using Lidar, Model, and In Situ Datasets
489245.authors: Travis D. Toth, NASA Langley Research Center, Hampton, VA; and A. Plowman
489245.abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is harmful to human health and estimates of PM2.5 using space-based measurements help to characterize ground-level air quality (AQ). This is especially true in rural or remote regions where ground-based monitoring networks are often sparse. This study employs satellite-based active remote sensing from the NASA Cloud-Aerosol Lidar with Orthogonal Polarization (CALIOP) instrument, on the Cloud-Aerosol Lidar and Infrared Pathfinder Satellite Observations (CALIPSO) satellite, to derive near-surface PM2.5 concentrations across Virginia for 2006 to 2019. This study then evaluates the performance of these retrievals against collocated in situ measurements operated by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and outputs from the EPA’s Community Multiscale Air Quality (CMAQ) model during the Air QUAlity TimE Series (EQUATES) Project. Overall, the agreement between CALIOP and in situ PM2.5 is weak (R ~0.2, slope ~0.6), with daytime performance (R ~0.25, slope ~0.6) better than that during nighttime conditions (R ~0.15, slope ~0.4). Despite this relationship, the CALIOP-derived PM2.5 spatial distributions across Virginia compare well with in situ and model PM2.5 patterns, with consistent hotspots in regions like Roanoke, the Richmond-Washington corridor, and Hampton Roads. The long-term trends in PM2.5 also generally agree between all three datasets, with annual mean PM2.5 exhibiting a clear decline for the 2006 to 2019 period. Additionally, CALIOP achieves greater than ~90% agreement in identifying PM2.5 values ≤ 35 µg m-3 when in situ values are also ≤ 35 µg m-3, demonstrating reliability in detecting low PM2.5 levels even when the overall correlation is weak. Ultimately, CALIOP provides an additional source of AQ information for those areas in Virginia for which there are few or no ground monitors as well as a foundation for further development and comparisons with other satellite and airborne lidar systems. Additional future work may involve sensitivity studies of the various parameters in the lidar-based PM2.5 derivation equation, estimating PM2.5 as a function of lidar aerosol type classification, case studies, and expanding to a larger area (e.g., the southeastern U.S. or entire contiguous U.S.). Finally, this study contributes to NASA’s Health and Air Quality Applied Sciences Team (HAQAST) Program. As such, we present a brief overview of HAQAST and illustrate how our lidar‑based PM2.5 analyses advance NASA Earth Action priorities.

489249.title: Rethinking Atmospheric Boundary Layer Observations in the AI Era
489249.authors: Katia Lamer, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY
489249.abstract: Many of the atmospheric phenomena society seeks to predict—from severe weather to water availability—depend on processes occurring within the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL). Yet the ABL remains one of the most challenging parts of the atmosphere to observe, shaped by interactions among the land surface, human activity, aerosols, turbulence, and clouds across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. Over the years, advances in sensor technology, observing platforms, and experimental design techniques have transformed our ability to observe this complexity. However, none of these advances in isolation can fully capture the multidimensional nature of the atmospheric boundary layer. At the same time, atmospheric science is entering a new era in which artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important tool for prediction. Much of the recent AI developments have relied on datasets generated by physics-based models because they provide regularly gridded, multi-parameter representations of the atmosphere, while observations remain sparse and carry uncertainty. In this keynote, I argue that observations must remain central to atmospheric boundary layer science in the AI era; achieving this will require a shift in how we collect, curate and analyze observation. First, we must continue to expand our observational reach through integrated, multi-sensor experiments that sample the atmosphere across scales, regions, and conditions. Second, we must characterize and integrate the observations already available, including those from operational networks, field campaigns, the private sector, and the public. Achieving this will require innovative cross-calibration techniques and a culture of crediting data provenance. Third, we must develop analysis approaches, including AI methods, that are designed to learn directly from heterogeneous observations rather than relying primarily on the convenience of model-generated data. As AI reshapes atmospheric science, observations must remain more than validation data. They are the empirical foundation of scientific discovery and the benchmark that allows us to determine how much complexity our predictive systems truly need.

489253.title: Knowledge Meshes and Natural Language Processing for Earth System Operations: A Reference Architecture for Trusted Decision Support
489253.authors: Ryan Berkheimer, NOAA, Mars Hill, NC; and B. Backus, R. Rangachar, H. Patel, S. L. Bunin, R. Redmon, and J. A. B. Webster PhD, PhD
489253.abstract: As planetary-scale Earth observation and environmental modeling datasets continue to expand in volume and complexity, transitioning advanced research into trusted operational decision support requires innovative informatics frameworks. Traditional static data repositories often struggle to provide real-time, context-aware insights to the diverse spectrum of end users, ranging from research scientists and operational forecasters to policymakers and the public. This presentation details an operational reference architecture that integrates Knowledge Meshes with Natural Language Processing (NLP) to transform raw, heterogeneous data streams into process-threaded, semantically contextualized facts. By leveraging NLP-driven user "personas," the Knowledge Mesh dynamically tailors search, analysis, and visualization interfaces to match a user’s background, intent, and specific operational goals. The architecture accepts both investigative queries (e.g., "what if" scenario modeling) and decisional instructions ("what now" and "what next") through a unified, multi-modal access interface. Built upon cloud-native, event-driven pipelines and modular interfaces, this framework embeds FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and TRUST (Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, Technology) principles directly into low-latency operational workflows. We present an overview, current status, and actionable recommendations evaluating the feasibility of KM/NLP in maintaining factual grounding, communicating process-coupled uncertainty via federated methodologies, and enhancing interoperability with global digital twin capabilities. Demonstrating reproducible workflows across coastal, ocean, terrestrial, atmospheric, and space domains, this work illustrates how combining Knowledge Meshes and NLP accelerates the transition of AI/ML research into sustained, resilient operational practice (R2O). We finally discuss future opportunities for the work in terms of new enablements in cognitive-AI, networking and communication patterns, and geophysical operations support.

489261.title: Evaluating Increasingly NWP-Derived Feature Sets for Deep Learning Forecasts of Warm Season Rainfall
489261.authors: Andrew E. Mercer, Mississippi State Univ., Mississippi State, MS
489261.abstract: The Southeastern United States (SEUS) contains several major agricultural regions that depend on abundant warm-season (June-August) precipitation during peak growing periods. However, predictability of daily rainfall in the SEUS remains relatively low during the warm season due to limitations in convective representation in numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems like the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. Despite advancements in convection-allowing models, these processes remain difficult to characterize owing to observational limitations and uncertainties in model physics. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have demonstrated promise for improving post-processing of NWP output for complex weather forecasting problems such as warm season SEUS rainfall. However, many AI applications rely on predictor variables that originate from increasingly processed representations of the atmosphere, ranging from prognostic state variables to derived environmental diagnostics and direct storm-scale forecast products. As AI models incorporate predictors that are more closely tied to the parent NWP system, they may become increasingly dependent on model-specific assumptions and precipitation depictions rather than learning independent atmospheric relationships. This, in turn, could result in AI forecasts that increasingly mirror the parent NWP system, potentially limiting the added value of the AI system. This study evaluates the sensitivity of AI-based warm-season precipitation forecasts to predictor selection using a spatiotemporal deep learning framework combining a convolutional neural network and gated recurrent unit architecture. Models will be trained using a six-year (2015-2020) database of WRF-simulated warm-season rainfall events across the SEUS. The study will explore multiple feature sets representing increasing levels of derivation from the parent model, including atmospheric base-state variables, derived thermodynamic and kinematic diagnostics, and direct storm-scale forecast proxies. Combinations of these feature sets will also be explored to determine the extent to which increasingly derived predictors influence AI precipitation forecasts. Daily rainfall occurrence from the Multisensor Precipitation Estimates dataset will serve as the prediction target. Results will quantify how forecast skill and similarity to the parent WRF precipitation forecast evolve as progressively derived predictor information is introduced into the AI framework.

489263.title: Frequent Surface-Rotor Stability Decoupling Limits the Representativeness of Surface-Based Offshore Observations
489263.authors: Valerie Vasquez-Barros, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, CO; and N. Bodini, S. Zippel, A. Kirincich, and J. K. Lundquist
489263.abstract: Understanding atmospheric stability throughout the wind turbine rotor layer is critical for predicting wake evolution, power production, wake steering performance, and structural loading. Measurements within the rotor region are often unavailable, and so measurements from near the surface or at an offshore wind turbine transition piece (20 m above the surface) are often assumed to be representative of the rotor layer. Here, we use sonic anemometer, profiling lidar, and thermodynamic profiler observations collected from an instrumented barge deployed during June-September 2024 as part of the Third Wind Forecast Improvement Project (WFIP3) campaign off the U.S. northeast coast to evaluate how well near-surface measurements represent atmospheric stability at wind turbine hub height. Surface stability is based on the Obukhov Length from sonic anemometers. Rotor-region stability is defined by the bulk Richardson number using profiling lidar and thermodynamic profiler measurements. Surface-based and rotor-layer stability classifications disagree more than 30% of the time (see Figure), with the dominant decoupling regime characterized by unstable surface conditions beneath a stably stratified rotor layer (purple data points in Figure). This significant disagreement persists regardless of whether a 6m or 24m sonic anemometer is used to characterize surface stability. The frequency of these decoupling events increases through late summer into fall as hub-height stratification strengthens, while individual events become shorter-lived, indicating frequent transitions between coupled and decoupled states. Decoupling events are characterized by slower wind speeds consistent with weaker turbulent mixing through the marine boundary layer. Surface observations often fail to represent the atmospheric stability experienced by offshore wind turbines during summer marine conditions. Consequently, relying solely on near-surface measurements may underestimate the occurrence of stable rotor-layer conditions that influence wake behavior, offshore wind farm power performance, and estimates of structural loads.

489271.title: “It’s Not the Same Mountain it Was 20 Years Ago”: Ski Areas and Resorts’ Vulnerability and Adaptation to Shrinking Winter Seasons
489271.authors: Zachary Paganini, City University of New York, New York, NY; and A. Crimmins
489271.abstract: This paper reports on a series of engagements with ski areas and resorts as a component of the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI)’s Industry Partnerships Program. Ski areas and resorts are a crucial sub-sector in the U.S. tourism industry and are often key economic drivers in the rural and often remote areas where they are located. The changing climate is leading to warmer temperatures, shorter seasons, and declining snowfall totals to many regions of the U.S. These trends threaten the economic resilience of the sub-sector by shrinking the ski season, which in turn reduces ski area revenues. Solutions such as artificial snowmaking and new snow storage technologies are increasingly important for filling gaps in snow coverage, yet these solutions carry new constraints and challenges- such as the need to understand and anticipate ideal snowmaking conditions. Crucially, there are differences between large and small ski areas’ financial and technical capacity to respond to these challenges to their business model, suggesting that integration of environmental information into planning and operations is emerging as a competitive advantage within the sub-sector. Drawing on 12 interviews and two surveys with ski area and resort operators, owners, and weather service providers, this paper discusses how environmental data supports ski areas and resorts’ sustainability and economic resilience, and what gaps ski areas have identifying in their approach to environmental data integration.

489273.title: Stratocumulus drizzle readily, cumulus drizzle selectively: Evidence from ground-based observations across four oceanic regions
489273.authors: Katia Lamer, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY; and P. Kollias, J. Kim, Z. Zhu, F. Yang, A. Battaglia, and E. Luke
489273.abstract: Despite years of research, the processes controlling warm-rain formation remain uncertain. Leveraging multiple years of ground-based radar, lidar and radiometer observations collected across four oceanic regions, we systematically reassess the properties of precipitation just beneath cloud base.
