The observations show that warm-rain characteristics are remarkably similar within the same cloud regime even across different oceanic basins. By contrast, they vary substantially between stratocumulus and cumulus regimes. These results indicate that cloud-regime properties exert a stronger influence on warm precipitation than regional environmental variability. Precipitation is observed beneath marine stratocumulus in over 56% of cloudy columns with liquid water path (LWP) < 130 g m⁻², rising to more than 84% in columns with LWP beyond 130 g m⁻². This indicates that marine stratocumulus routinely support warm-rain formation and suggests that barriers to precipitation onset in this regime are weaker than commonly assumed. For the same LWP, oceanic cumulus precipitate less frequently than stratocumulus but on average produce two times larger and one to two orders of magnitude fewer precipitation drops. This contrast is consistent with cumulus presenting two times stronger updrafts and lower adiabaticity than stratocumulus, both of which can affect drop growth histories. Whereas the precipitation characteristics of stratocumulus are generally consistent with growth by collision–coalescence during gravitational free fall in low LWP clouds, those of cumulus cannot be explained without invoking additional processes. Together, these findings suggest that warm-precipitation parameterizations should more explicitly account for the influence of small-scale dynamical processes on precipitation growth. The apparent importance of drop growth histories further motivates continued exploration of Lagrangian particle-tracking approaches in both models and observations.

489275.title: Mesoterps: Advancing a University Micronet for Enhanced Environmental Monitoring and Emergency Management
489275.authors: Allison Fenley, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and R. Sanford
489275.abstract: Mesoterps: Advancing a University Micronet for Enhanced Environmental Monitoring and Emergency Management The University of Maryland (UMD) is expanding its campus-wide micronet, originally deployed to monitor microclimate variability and enhance campus safety. The network comprises low-cost automated weather stations powered by Raspberry Pi units running WeeWX software, strategically sited to capture high-resolution observations of temperature, dew point, atmospheric pressure, wind speed and direction, rainfall rate, and heat stress indicators. Data is streamed continuously and made publicly available at weather.umd.edu. As of May 2026, the network includes ten weather stations, one CO2 sensor, and one Black Bulb Globe thermometer. At least three additional stations are planned for deployment by December 2026, increasing spatial coverage and improving data granularity across campus. Additionally, two Davis AirLink sensors are planned for deployment, providing particulate matter measurements for PM1, PM2.5, and PM10. Future network expansion includes storm drain monitoring, a lightning sensor network, and the addition of solar radiation and UV sensors. This added instrumentation will extend the network’s utility for UMD Emergency Management, supporting flood and extreme weather risk assessment alongside the network’s existing environmental monitoring capabilities. Parallel efforts are underway to improve the website’s data visualization tools, offering more intuitive, actionable representations of current and historical conditions for the UMD community. Together, these developments position Mesoterps as a model for university-based environmental monitoring and campus emergency preparedness.

489276.title: Constraining the Spatially and Temporally Resolved Trends and Variability of the Tropospheric Hydroxyl Radical
489276.authors: Daniel Craig Anderson, University of Maryland Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; NASA/GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; University of Maryland Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; and B. N. Duncan, J. Liu, PhD, and A. H. Souri
489276.abstract: The hydroxyl radical (OH) is the dominant tropospheric oxidant, affecting local air quality, the production of background ozone, and the lifetime of methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Despite its central role in atmospheric chemistry, there are few observational constraints on the abundance, trends, and spatiotemporal variability of OH. In addition, global chemistry models often disagree on these values, even when constrained with the same emissions. We present here updates to a satellite-constrained tropospheric column OH product developed with a combination of machine learning and observations from multiple NASA instruments, demonstrating the feasibility of this approach over multiple photochemical regimes from 60 N to 60 S. We highlight the relative importance and impacts of uncertainty sources, including clouds, retrieval errors, and the accuracy of chemical mechanisms on the OH product. We also show the spatially resolved trends in OH during different seasons and global regions, determining the underlying processes driving those trends and comparing them to other observationally constrained OH products. Finally, we make recommendations for improvements to the current satellite observation system that could increase our ability to constrain the global oxidative capacity.

489283.title: Independent Validation of Storm Precipitation Analyses Using Convection-Permitting WRF Reconstructions of Pre-Radar Extreme Rainfall Events
489283.authors: Moniki Ferreira, Applied Weather Associates, LLC, Monument, CO; and B. Kappel and D. Hultstrand
489283.abstract: Probable maximum precipitation (PMP) studies depend on storm depth-area-duration (DAD) analyses derived from the Storm Precipitation Analysis System (SPAS), a proprietary objective-analysis methodology developed by Applied Weather Associates that interpolates gauge and, where available, radar observations into gridded storm-total and duration-specific depth fields. For extreme events that predate weather radar, these analyses rest almost entirely on gauge networks that were often sparse, supplemented in some cases by informal post-event measurements. The July 1974 Saskatchewan storm examined here is an extreme case: its analyzed peak depth traces to a single informal post-event measurement, with no radar coverage and roughly twenty interview-based observation points. Such values are difficult to corroborate, because any observational check tends to draw on the same measurements that produced the analysis. This study asks whether convection-permitting numerical reconstruction can provide an independent, physics-based check on these analyses, one that does not depend on the original observations. We reconstructed two pre-radar extreme rainfall events using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model at 3 km convection-permitting resolution (cumulus parameterization disabled on the inner domain), forced by ERA5 reanalysis boundary conditions: the July 1954 Saxony, Germany storm (SPAS 2015) and the July 1974 Saskatchewan, Canada storm (SPAS 1744). Both events fall within flat, non-orographic terrain, so the simulated convective environment is governed by the synoptic forcing rather than by fixed topographic anchoring. Control simulations captured 94 percent (16.14 versus 17.23 in.) and 66 percent (8.09 versus 12.32 in.) of the SPAS-analyzed peak depth for the 1954 and 1974 events, respectively. For the 1974 storm, we then constructed a four-member start-time ensemble, perturbing only the initialization time (spin-up of 23, 35, 47, and 59 hours) while holding physics, domain, and boundary source fixed, so that ensemble spread isolates sensitivity to initialization rather than to model configuration. Peak capture across members ranged from 40 to 85 percent, with the strongest member (59-hour spin-up) reaching 10.51 in. against the analyzed 12.32 in. All four members displaced the storm core 194 to 367 km to the northeast of the observed location; none reproduced significant depth within 50 km of the analyzed center. Because the region lacks orographic forcing, a displaced member represents the same storm realized along a different track rather than a fundamentally different event, and its internal structure remains diagnostically useful. The DAD comparison was evaluated in a position-independent framework, comparing the most intense core each realization produced against the analyzed core regardless of location. In this framework the modeled and analyzed storms agree closely in structure. At the point scale, the strongest member matches or exceeds the SPAS one-hour intensity (105 percent of the analyzed value), confirming that the simulated convection attains the correct instantaneous rate. The agreement then diverges systematically with duration: the member reaches 67 percent of the SPAS depth at six hours and 84 percent at twenty-four hours. This signature, correct short-duration intensity with a shortfall at intermediate durations, is consistent across all four members and reflects the known tendency of convection-permitting simulations to underrepresent the sustained stationarity required to accumulate the observed multi-hour totals. Critically, the areal-decay structure of the modeled DAD, how rapidly depth falls off as averaging area increases, tracks the SPAS analysis in shape while diverging in magnitude. The simulated storm decays more rapidly with area than the analysis, with the ratio of analyzed to modeled area-reduction factor increasing to roughly 1.3 near 10,000 mi-squared. This is precisely the area range in which the analyzed storm produces anomalously high volume relative to other storms in the regional suite, and in which the resulting generalized transposition factors have been difficult to justify. These results support a specific application: using the physically consistent WRF field as an independent spatial basemap for a SPAS re-analysis, with the observed peak retained as the magnitude anchor. In this configuration the model supplies the areal structure, which it reproduces well, while the station observations continue to control magnitude and location through the isopercental interpolation, preserving the observed point depth where gauge coverage is strongest. A preliminary area-reduction adjustment, derived from the four-member ensemble median and applied to the observed six-hour peak, reduces the integrated storm volume by approximately 19 percent, concentrated in the mid-to-large area sizes that drive the high transposition factors, while leaving the point depth unchanged. Results from the full SPAS re-analysis driven by the WRF basemap, and from densification of the start-time ensemble to place the area-reduction adjustment on a percentile rather than a four-member basis, will be presented. Taken together, the reconstructions demonstrate that convection-permitting modeling can serve as an independent, physics-based validation of pre-radar storm analyses, corroborating analyzed storm shape and areal structure even where it cannot reproduce the observed magnitude, and providing an objective basis for refining depth-area relationships whose original observational support is thin.

489292.title: Resolving Uncertainty with Uncertainty: Developing a Probabilistic Outlook Graphic in the Watch-to-Warning Timeframe for the NWS in Bismarck
489292.authors: Cyrus Delconte, NOAA Hollings Scholar, Silver Spring, MD; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; OU Institute for Public Policy, Research, and Analysis, Norman, OK; and C. Schultz, S. R. Ernst, and M. Jones
489292.abstract: Many members of the public, communicators, and emergency responders require notice that extends beyond a typical severe thunderstorm or tornado warning in order to make crucial decisions and take necessary protective actions. The 30 minutes to 4 hours before warning issuance, often called the ‘watch-to-warning’ timeframe, begets considerable uncertainty both from a meteorological and communications standpoint. Because of the critical nature of this time frame, NWS forecasters aim to give these populations as much pertinent information and advanced lead time as possible for the protection of life and property. Previous literature on probabilistic communication has not specifically focused on this watch-to-warning timeframe; thus, a primary objective of the present work was to evaluate communication styles and strategies in this critical time period. This thought process led to the development of a product that will more effectively communicate storm risk areas and timelines for the watch-to-warning timeframe. Based on the operational needs of NWS meteorologists, previous research on the best visual and probabilistic communication methods, and input from emergency managers within the state, such a graphical product can be created and assessed when compared to currently operational products for social media and communications use. In order to create the first edition of prototypes for this product, literature review, survey work with emergency managers, and forecaster input were used. The survey, assessing a varied population of emergency managers in North Dakota, sought to understand their perceived level of risk for their jurisdiction, what actions they would be taking during the watch-to-warning timeframe, and what probabilistic thresholds they would need to take these actions for different hazards and severity levels. It also addressed the current NWS Bismarck watch-to-warning graphic. Upon acquiring results, the prototypes were made. These graphical prototypes aimed to discriminate in preferences between probabilistic information display, hazard display, and color, along with usefulness to North Dakota emergency managers. Focus groups with said emergency managers were the primary mechanism used to assess the efficacy of these prototypes. Focus group results agreed with both the literature and the survey results, with emergency managers preferring to use numerical probability information in the watch-to-warning timeframe. Despite this, there were many questions and uncertainties with the method of display of these numerical probabilities, which is an avenue that could be pursued by future research. Additionally, emergency managers preferred the red-orange-yellow, or ‘stoplight’, color palette for its urgency, with an interesting tendency to prefer different opacities based on forecaster confidence and closeness to the warning timeframe. Overall, participants preferred to have more information, not less, from the NWS. In fact, emergency managers indicated that almost all of the prototype graphics presented could serve some sort of use to them (with some graphics and findings preferred for communication outside of the severe convective space, as well). Through the synthesis of all gathered and researched information, revised graphical prototypes and other key communication recommendations were given to NWS Bismarck staff with the intention of operational implementation over time. Ultimately, the combined results of this project will allow for stronger communication from the NWS to critical and vulnerable audiences during severe convective events and will create a more weather-ready nation.

489293.title: A Retrospective of AWIPS Common AWIPS Visualization Environment (CAVE) and Environmental Data EXchange (EDEX)
489293.authors: James Edward Calkins, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and S. T. Jacobs, A. Just, and R. Henry-Reeves
489293.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) plans to end the use of its long-time forecasting system, AWIPS, within the next year. As AWIPS has been a major part of NWS operations for over 20 years, this is a perfect opportunity to review how NWS field offices have ingested, decoded, and displayed data during the AWIPS era. The presentation will describe how CAVE and EDEX have been used by NWS forecasters, as well as the benefits and drawbacks of these components as technology has evolved over the past several decades. Lastly, comparisons to how NWS forecasters will interact with data in the post-AWIPS era will be shown.

489294.title: Human-Caused Sea Level Rise Added Three In Four U.S. High-Tide Flood Days Observed Since 2000
489294.authors: Daniel M. Gilford, Climate Central, Princeton, NJ; and Y. Lin, K. Dahl, A. Pershing, M. B. Martin, R. Kopp, and B. Strauss
489294.abstract: Sea levels along the U.S. coasts continue to rise largely due to human-caused climate change, driving incremental increases in coastal flood risks. But the anthropogenic contributions to these changing risks have not been systematically analyzed nationwide. Understanding the human contribution to sea level impacts is critical for local decision-making, loss and damage determinations, legal proceedings, and climate risk communication. We quantify human-caused climate change's contributions to sea level rise and coastal flood days (NWS minor threshold exceedances) at 71 tide gauge locations across the United States and its territories. Using two published complementary approaches—a literature- and observation-based sea level budget and an updated semi-empirical model constrained by historical temperature and sea level records—we estimate attributable sea level rise since 1900. These methods agree that human-caused sea level rise has raised local water levels at 97% of U.S. sites where the local sea level budget closes; the exceptions are in southeast Alaska, where near-field glacial mass losses produce a negative human-caused local signal. Across U.S. locations, attributable sea level rise added 77% of the total observed flood days over 2000–2025 (site-to-site range: 53–95%). Between 1970–1989 and 2006–2025 attributable flood days increased roughly 8×; this increase is accelerating, approximately doubling every 12 years since 1970. Our findings show a clear, widespread, and intensifying fingerprint of climate change on the country’s coastal flood hazards and risks. The multi-method attribution framework developed here enables us to place attribution estimates on both historical and real-time flooding events. We demonstrate web tools that make these results accessible to media and the public using Climate Central's Coastal Risk Finder.

489298.title: Future Trends in Extreme Snowfall Over Mountain Regions
489298.authors: Robert Nazarian, Fairfield University, Fairfield, CT; Fairfield University, Fairfield, CT; and E. Chow, A. McClure, B. Matijevic, A. A. Akinsanola, and J. Broccolo
489298.abstract: Mountain regions and their foothills are home over a quarter of the global population and supply freshwater to nearly half the world’s population, making climate-driven changes in their extreme precipitation a critical societal concern. Extreme snowfall in these regions presents distinct hazards, including severe flooding, hazardous transit conditions, and altered freshwater runoff rates. In this study, we evaluate historical trends in mountain extreme snowfall using the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) ensemble alongside observational and reanalysis datasets, analyzed future trends through the end of the century using the CMIP6 ensemble, and investigates the underlying physical mechanisms. The CMIP6 ensemble demonstrates strong agreement with climatology, confirming the models' skill in simulating high-elevation extreme snow events. Projections indicate an increase in both mean and extreme snowfall poleward of 70°N, contrasted with widespread declines across mid- to low-latitude mountain ranges. Applying a diagnostic scaling framework to decompose these trends reveals that dynamic changes are the primary driver of the projected shifts. These dynamic changes are principally driven by a poleward shift of the low-level jet and corresponding poleward shift of the storm tracks. Understanding these mechanisms bridges the gap between global climate models and local extreme weather, providing essential insights for managing downstream water resources, predicting snowmelt timing, and planning regional watershed resilience.

489301.title: The Regional Flood Index: Combining Physical and Economic Products to Build an Archive of Flooding Events.
489301.authors: Jared J. Rennie, NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Asheville, NC
489301.abstract: Floods are one of the most common weather disasters in the US, totaling billions of dollars in damage and multiple deaths each year. Strides have been made to predict floods, however, little has been done to analyze these events in a spatial and climatological context. NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) provides historical analysis on weather events such as heat, drought and wildfires, but little on flooding. Work has been done to leverage publicly available flood information, as well as utilize AI and cloud innovations, to create a database of current and historical flooding events to better understand personal and economic risks. Following the footsteps of the Regional Snowfall Index (RSI), the Regional Flooding Index (RFI) ranks flooding impacts on a scale from 1 to 5, similar to the Fujita/Enhanced Fujita scale for tornadoes or the Saffir-Simpson scale for hurricanes. The index utilizes three different data sources: river gauges provided by USGS, precipitation estimates from the multi-radar multi-sensor (MRMS) product, and VIIRS flood composites the SNPP and NOAA-20 polar orbiting satellites. RFI is based on the spatial extent of the event, the amount of flooding, and the juxtaposition of these elements with storm reports from the National Weather Service and economic products provided by the Department of Commerce. The end goal is a cloud-ready dataset displaying these events alongside other relevant information to support forecasting and emergency management operations. This presentation will go into more detail about the methodology in building the RFI, and provide case studies of relevant events, including Helene and the Texas Hill Country.

489302.title: Exploring the Influence of Atmospheric Stability and Temperature Advection on Coastal Low-level Jets During WFIP-3
489302.authors: Akarshna Krishnarjun Iyer, Hampton University, Lakeville, MN; and R. Delgado, D. D. Turner, and T. Myers
489302.abstract: The marine atmospheric boundary layer (MABL) is the lowest portion of the atmosphere directly influenced by the ocean surface. It can exhibit fluctuations in atmospheric stability due to wind direction, changes in air-sea temperature differences, latent heating, and overall synoptic conditions. These changes in stability can strongly influence wind speeds and vertical structure, directly affecting coastal operations like marine navigation, aviation, and offshore wind energy generation. To advance wind forecasting in the MABL, the third Wind Forecast Improvement Project (WFIP-3) sponsored by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the Department of Energy (DOE), and other organizations, began collecting observations off the coast of New England in February 2024. This study utilizes High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model data extracted at three WFIP-3 locations: Block Island, Nantucket, and a barge site (deployed about 50 kilometers South of Martha’s Vineyard). An important phenomenon that takes place in the MABL is the low-level jet (LLJ), which is a concentrated stream of fast-moving air found in the lower troposphere. This work investigates the coastal LLJ and its impacts on atmospheric stability and weather conditions offshore. Three years of HRRR data (2023-2025) were used to derive stability metrics, temperature advection, and vertical wind profiles. LLJs were identified using criteria that consider height, wind speed, and quantified shear above the jet nose. Then, their frequency, intensity, and direction were evaluated under different stability and advection regimes. Results indicate that overall LLJ flow direction plays an important role in determining LLJ characteristics. Coastal LLJs are most frequently associated with southerly or northerly flow. Southerly jets seem more correlated with warm air advection and stable atmospheric conditions, while northerly jets seem more correlated with cold air advection and reduced stability. The influence of marine or continental regions can also modify these temperature tendencies. At lower altitudes, southerly jets are more common than northerly jets and the strongest LLJs typically occur at higher altitudes. These findings improve the understanding of what physical mechanisms govern coastal LLJ formation.

489304.title: I, For One, Welcome Our AI Overlords
489304.authors: Jared J. Rennie, NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Asheville, NC
489304.abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning have shifted from emerging concepts to essential drivers of the weather, water, and climate enterprise. However, many professionals are now tasked with integrating these technologies without a clear roadmap for their mission-specific application. While adoption concerns persist, AI offers unprecedented potential to streamline workflows and translate complex atmospheric equations into actionable insights. Leveraging vast datasets from NOAA and other repositories, our field is uniquely positioned for AI-driven innovation. This presentation examines the current landscape—highlighting successes like the use of Artificial Intelligence Global Forecasting System (AIGFS) in day to day operations, Large Language Models (LLMs) to tap into APIs from NCEI, IEM, and Copernicus, and generative AI tools to help with the small tasks – like Gemini building and reviewing this abstract. Positive impacts will be shown, while addressing the challenges and ethical frameworks necessary for responsible evolution in the enterprise.

489309.title: Artificial Intelligence for Ocean and Coupled Earth System Forecasting
489309.authors: Niraj Agarwal, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and J. DaRosa and S. Frolov
489309.abstract: Machine Learning emulators have shown extraordinary skill in replicating atmospheric states and their application to emulate ocean and coupled Earth systems offers similar promise. We have developed a 3D global ocean-only emulator for medium- to extended-range predictions, trained on NOAA’s UFS-Replay dataset using ECMWF’s Anemoi ecosystem. Available at 6-hour and 24-hour time steps, the emulator provides stable and skillful forecasts for key ocean quantities from surface to 500m depth on lead times up to several months. We coupled this independently developed ocean-only emulator with an atmosphere-only emulator (also trained on UFS-Replay using Anemoi) by exchanging the states of the coupled variables at an appropriate interval during the inference. Using a comprehensive suite of baselines to isolate the impact of coupling, we have shown that the two-way coupling significantly impacts the forecast of key surface ocean quantities (such as SST and SSH) and surface fluxes at 10–15-day lead times. The atmospheric variables however show a relatively lower impact on standard error metrics at these time scales, but this is under active investigation using longer lead times and process-level diagnostics. The framework is also set for further advancement using a more optimized set of coupled variables (including sea ice), increased spatial resolution, and refined ocean-only and atmosphere-only components using iterative fine tuning. The most up-to-date results will be presented from all the experiments, along with the lessons learned and future directions.

489311.title: Calibration and Validation of FireTIRS for Ground and Airborne Thermal-Infrared Fire Observations
489311.authors: Suvan Anthony Cabraal, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX; and J. F. Smekens, D. Julio, and J. Thompson
489311.abstract: FireTIRS, the Fire Thermal InfraRed Spectrometer, is a compact (17 × 17 × 5 cm), lightweight (<0.6 kg), and power-efficient (<20 W) multispectral infrared imager designed for ground and airborne deployments. The system was developed to improve observations of rapidly changing active fires at spatial and temporal scales that are difficult to capture with conventional satellite measurements alone. FireTIRS combines seven radiometric microbolometers with a visible camera, GPS-based timing, and environmental sensors for coordinated ground-based and airborne measurements. As wildfires increasingly threaten ecosystems and communities, particularly in the wildland–urban interface, there is a growing need for field-based observations capable of resolving fire behavior at the spatial, temporal, and spectral scales that govern these processes. Our goal is to combine and coordinate these multispectral measurements to provide a consistent view of fire-front position, thermal structure, fire radiative power, emissions-related behavior, and rate of spread across multiple spatial scales. This work focuses on the calibration and validation required to make FireTIRS measurements scientifically impactful. We process raw multisensor observations into Level-1C (calibrated, geolocated, and atmospheric corrected radiance) and Level-2 (derived surface temperature and emissivity) products. The primary challenges are aligning sensors with different spatial resolutions and fields of view, correcting thermal measurements for changes in instrument and ambient temperature, synchronizing multiple image streams, accounting for atmospheric effects, and converting imagery into georeferenced fire products while preserving small-scale variability across the fire front. We describe procedures for geometric calibration, sensor alignment, radiometric harmonization, environmental correction, image-to-map georeferencing, and atmospheric correction for both stationary and airborne observations. Geometric calibration is used to estimate camera intrinsics, lens distortion, and the relative position and orientation of each sensor, enabling spatially registered and geolocated measurements. Environmental calibration uses controlled chamber temperatures, a stable blackbody source, internal environmental measurements, and lens-temperature sensors to quantify and correct for changes in the measured thermal signal under varying deployment conditions. Together, these procedures produce Level-1C calibrated, temporally synchronized, geolocated, and atmospherically corrected radiance products, which are subsequently used to derive Level-2 surface temperature and emissivity products. The complete workflow is evaluated using prescribed-fire observations collected in Central Texas. Validation focuses on inter-sensor registration, thermal consistency, mapped fire-front position, fire radiative power, and estimates of fire progression and rate of spread. This work demonstrates that compact multi-sensor systems can provide scientifically relevant measurements of fire behavior when calibration, environmental correction, synchronization, georeferencing, and atmospheric correction are treated as integral components of the observation system.

489316.title: Bridging the Gaps: Advancing Public Health via a Multi-Tiered Karenia brevis Respiratory Irritation Forecast for Southwest Florida Beaches
489316.authors: Katie M. Collins, CSS-Inc, under contract to NOAA, Fairfax, VA; and A. Hounshell, J. Papas, K. St.Laurent, M. Tomlinson, and R. Stumpf
489316.abstract: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) occur when potentially toxic phytoplankton grow to concentrations that can lead to ecological or human health risks. Toxins produced by some HABs can become airborne, leading to acute respiratory irritation and other symptoms when exposed. For example, Karenia brevis (red tide) which blooms along the US Gulf Coast, produces a suite of brevetoxins that can become aerosolized and may cause acute respiratory conditions such as coughing, runny nose, and/or watery eyes for most people and are a severe health risk to those with asthma or other underlying respiratory conditions. Previous work has found that the exposure and impact risk of aerosolized toxins depends on bloom intensity at the beach and the duration and strength of onshore winds. To provide advanced warning of potential respiratory K. brevis impacts, NOAA’s National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science (NCCOS) developed the Gulf Coast Red Tide respiratory irritation forecast to provide beach-goers with a category-based risk of respiratory irritation (‘very low’, ‘low’, ‘moderate’, or ‘high’) at individual beaches. The forecast combines K. brevis cell concentrations collected at individual beaches from a variety of sources (state and county agencies, local community scientists) with high resolution 2.5km wind forecasts provided by NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS), National Digital Forecast Database (NDFD). The forecast is displayed via a publicly available ArcGIS interface that allows forecast users to monitor beaches across the Texas and Florida coast for respiratory irritation risk every 3 hours over the next 30 hours. Forecasts are used by beach-goers to make informed decisions based on the forecasted respiratory risk. Following a rigorous model analysis and working with local Florida public health officials, resource managers, and key red tide scientists and communicators, we have identified several next steps for improvements to expand the utility of the developed public health risk forecast. This involves a transition from a purely observational model to a scaled, multi-tiered risk communication framework: 1) Tier 1 (Environmental): a forecast layer evaluating persistence of offshore wind conditions to develop a standard ‘low risk’ forecast even when cell counts are unavailable; 2) Tier 2 (Satellite): a future capability that integrates satellite data into the respiratory irritation risk for nearshore beach locations where cell concentrations are unavailable and for offshore areas (for boaters); and 3) Tier 3 (Observational): the existing high-confidence, cell-concentration-driven forecast, which has been operational since August 2021. Here, we will present the utility of HAB risk forecasting for protecting public health and discuss ongoing efforts to update and refine respiratory irritation forecast visualization and accuracy to assure the products meet stakeholder needs. Target: 25th Symposium on the Coastal Environment - 15th Symposium on the Weather, Water, and Climate Enterprise Backup: 18th Conference on Environment and Health In-Person Oral Presentation

489327.title: Convectively Coupled Equatorial Waves: Applications of George's Research in Weather Forecasting
489327.abstract: For many decades, George Kiladis has served as a leading figure in tropical meteorology, specifically through his contributions to the study of convectively coupled equatorial waves (CCEWs). Improving how numerical weather prediction models simulate large-scale tropical features like CCEWs is crucial for advancing synoptic- to planetary-scale convection modeling. Such advancements hold the potential to decrease forecast errors within the tropics and mitigate the propagation of errors into the midlatitudes. Drawing upon George's pioneering observational analyses of how tropical precipitation couples with atmospheric circulation, this presentation highlights the application of his research to weather prediction systems (both machine learning and traditional). We examine the varying degrees of success and difficulty these systems encounter when simulating the diverse spatial scales of tropical phenomena. We introduce applications and diagnostic tools established from George's observational research to demonstrate how they assess vertical and horizontal CCEW structures, providing valuable perspectives on the interplay between moist convection and wave profiles in forecast models. Major highlights from these applications include evaluating moisture and temperature variability within CCEW coupling, testing the influence of the Global Forecast System's convection scheme on convective coupling, and illustrating the impact of tropical processes on the accuracy of extratropical forecasts.

489330.title: Power-Transformed Mixing Ratios and Number Concentrations for Direct Assimilation of Polarimetric Radar Data: Fraternal Twin OSSEs
489330.authors: Peng Liu, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and J. Gao, G. Zhang, and J. T. Carlin
489330.abstract: Polarimetric radar data (PRD) contain rich information on cloud and precipitation microphysics, but assimilating PRD within a double-moment microphysics scheme requires that both hydrometeor mixing ratios (q) and number concentrations (Nt) be updated simultaneously to exploit the radar information fully. Because of the large dynamic range of hydrometeor Nt and the significant disparity of magnitude and range between q, Nt, and the other analysis variables, updating Nt directly poses challenges for the minimization process in variational DA systems. In this study, we apply Box-Cox power transformations to q and Nt for all six hydrometeor species to alleviate challenges in minimizing the cost function. Our newly developed parameterized forward operators (Zhang et al. 2021) incorporating the continuous melting model of Liu et al. (2024) are employed to directly assimilate reflectivity (ZH), differential reflectivity (ZDR), and specific differential phase (KDP). Experiments are performed with a convective-scale 3DVAR system in a fraternal twin observing system simulation experiment (OSSE) for an idealized supercell. Different versions of WRF are used for the truth simulation and for the assimilation and forecast model. Cycled analyses are performed at 5-min intervals over 90 min, with the exponent for mixing ratios fixed at 0.4 and exponents of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 tested for number concentrations. Results from sensitivity experiments show that jointly updating q and Nt with an exponent of 0.1 reduces the analysis errors of radar variables and improves the analysis of polarimetric radar signatures. Updating Nt benefits ZDR assimilation the most, consistent with the sensitivity of ZDR to particle size at a given water content. The additional assimilation of KDP yields smaller analysis errors for reflectivity and mixing ratios of water vapor and rainwater compared to ZDR assimilation alone. Sensitivity tests further show that overly small PRD observation errors improve the fit to radar observations but degrade the analyses of model state. Among the threshold values tested for reflectivity and polarimetric variables, assimilating polarimetric variables at grids where reflectivity exceeds 15 dBZ provides the best overall analysis. Ongoing work extends this framework to hybrid ensemble–variational assimilation and to real WSR-88D observations.

489331.title: NOAA Testbeds & Proving Grounds: Advancing Probabilistic Hazards Forecasting for Decision Support
489331.authors: Jordan Dale, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and J. A. Nelson Jr., A. J. Ray, P. T. Marsh, J. J. Brost, S. J. Avey, J. W. Scheck, J. Correia Jr., A. Pratt, P. Santos, D. A. Zelinsky, D. Lindsey, A. Lyza, L. B. Nance, E. M. Petrescu, M. Rosencrans, W. M. Sellers, J. A. Sippel, P. J. Stone, and K. Fenton
489331.abstract: NOAA's thirteen Testbeds (TBs) and Proving Grounds (PGs) facilitate the transition of research into operations, ultimately benefiting society. They advance probabilistic hazards forecasting through four key methods: Testing and refining innovations: TBPGs evaluate new forecasting and communication techniques, including probabilistic guidance. Examples include the Hazardous Weather Testbed (HWT) and Hydrometeorology Testbed (HMT) evaluating Convective-Allowing Model (CAM) runs and the Unified Forecast System (UFS), and the Climate Testbed (CTB) extending NOAA's Unified Forecast System (UFS) prototypes for probabilistic forecasting. Product design and development: They help developers create products that communicate risk and translate hazards into impacts, optimizing watches/warnings and facilitating social science studies. Examples include HMT's work on a probabilistic Winter Storm Severity Index and the Aviation Weather Testbed (AWT) evaluating probabilistic ensemble RRFS convective and cloud forecasts. Forecaster and user engagement: TBPGs introduce new products to NOAA forecasters and users (e.g., emergency managers, broadcast meteorologists) for feedback, involving over 500 individuals annually. This socializes emerging product types within the Weather Forecast Office network. Feedback to research: TBPGs provide operational and testing feedback to research communities, influencing research priorities and leading to solutions for identified issues. The Developmental Testbed Center (DTC) and NWS Operations PG (OPG) are key in this, with the OPG also evaluating training needs. TBPGs support the Research-to-Operations (R2O) process through collaborative developmental testing in quasi-operational frameworks, involving researchers, operational scientists, and partners. These iterative, two-way interactions between developers and end-users facilitate both R2O and Operations-to-Research (O2R). Some of the R2X contributions across TBPGs include: Probabilistic Hazards Forecasting - Implementing an iterative process in developing new product lines, including testing and evaluation of the Warn on Forecast System (WoFS), WoFSCast, and using social science to understand how best to communicate these products; Contributions to NOAA's Precipitation Prediction Grand Challenge; and Contributions to NOAA's Unified Forecast System (including RRFS, HAFS, and SFS). This presentation will also provide an overview of the TBPG network, its operations, recent accomplishments, and upcoming challenges.

489337.title: Profiling the Mountain Boundary Layer: Structure and Variability from Aircraft Observations
489337.authors: Sarah Paratoni, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria; and C. Probst, N. Sandt, I. Stiperski, A. Gohm, P. Gasch, and M. Lehner
489337.abstract: The mountain boundary layer (MoBL) is shaped by complex interactions between terrain, surface heating, valley circulations, and synoptic forcing, producing high spatial and temporal variability that remains challenging to observe and forecast. This study uses dual-aircraft observations, radiosondes, and ground-based instrumentation to examine the vertical structure, variability, and evolution of the MoBL within an Alpine valley. Airborne observations were collected in the Austrian Inn Valley during the winter and summer Extended Observational Periods of the 2025 TEAMx Observational Campaign with two research aircraft: the German Aerospace Center (DLR) Cessna 208B Grand Caravan equipped with an in-situ turbulence probe (flying both in the winter and summer campaign) and the Technische Universität Braunschweig Cessna F406 equipped with both in-situ turbulence sensors and the five beam Dopper lidar system AIRflows (flying in the summer campaign only). These measurements are analyzed to identify characteristic vertical structures in wind speed, direction and turbulence metrics identifying the different regions of the MoBL under a range of meteorological conditions to assess spatial variability, morning-to-afternoon boundary layer evolution, and contrasts between winter and summer conditions. Radiosonde profiles provide thermodynamic context, including information on stability and moisture variability. The two-aircraft approach during the summer campaign additionally enables a comparison between in-situ wind measurements and wind profiles retrieved from the airborne Doppler lidar AIRflows. Thanks to its high horizontal resolution of up to about 100 m, AIRflows provides new observational capabilities for examining fine-scale wind structure in mountain valleys. Initial comparisons are used to characterize thermally driven flows in winter and summer and to investigate how differences in stratification contribute to the observed variability in MoBL structure. Together, these measurements provide a detailed view of MoBL structure across spatial, diurnal, and seasonal scales and help identify key features important for weather prediction models over complex terrain.

489345.title: Broadening Perspectives and Building Interdisciplinary Expertise Through the Research Experiences and Mentorship in Urban Systems (REMUS) Program
489345.authors: Casey Davenport, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte, NC; and S. Clinton
489345.abstract: Over half (56%) of the global population currently lives in urban areas, with that proportion expected to increase up to 68% by 2050. In the United States, an even larger share of the population lives in cities (83%), which is also expected to grow to 89% by 2050. This growth in urban populations, combined with the multisystem and multiscale effects of climate change, is anticipated to significantly stress urban areas through pressures on resources such as food, energy, housing, and water. Interdisciplinary groups of researchers are needed to advance our understanding of urban science, provide solutions to the many complex and interacting problems, as well as to develop and maintain sustainable cities of the future. Undergraduate students in the geosciences and environmentally related disciplines are particularly well-positioned to contribute to the growth of urban science and develop innovative solutions. The Research Experiences and Mentorship in Urban Systems (REMUS) program is an innovative undergraduate summer research experience designed to build interdisciplinary capacity in urban science. Hosted at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, the program immerses students in the study of urban systems within a rapidly growing metropolitan region in the southeastern United States. REMUS engages diverse student cohorts in mentor‑guided research projects that examine urban environments from multiple disciplinary perspectives. Faculty mentors represent urban ecology, environmental engineering, earth and atmospheric sciences, Geographic Information Science, and environmental justice, and are drawn from several departments and colleges. Through REMUS, the program: 1) enables students to better comprehend interdisciplinary interactions in a dynamic social-ecological-technological system; 2) immerses students in complex, real-world sustainability and environmental justice issues; 3) allows students to gain proficiency in data collection, management, and analysis; and 4) facilitates a peer mentoring and networking community within and across participant cohorts. This presentation will provide an overview of the REMUS program, including how it is uniquely positioned as an NSF REU site, the disciplinary make-up of the cohorts and faculty mentors, recent research projects, as well as the range of professional development activities including incorporation of multiple Python coding workshops emphasizing data exploration and analysis of a real-world urban dataset.

489347.title: Large Eddy Simulation of Atmospheric Boundary Layers at High Winds Using Measured Wave Spectra
489347.authors: Peter Sullivan, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. H. Richter, E. Sanabia, S. R. Jayne, J. Davis, B. Villas Boas, M. Schonau, and L. Centurioni
489347.abstract: The impact of large surface waves on the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) under high wind conditions is relatively un-explored. To investigate this regime a suite of large-eddy simulations (LES) of high wind ABLs over a spectrum of resolved waves are performed. The instantaneous wave fields h(x,y,t) are built using measured frequency wave spectra collected in the ONR multi-university research initiative (MURI) SASCWATCH. The maximum frequency of the buoy measurements is f_p \sim 0.5 Hz. In the LES, the wave fields are assumed to propagate with initially random amplitudes and phases with U_10 wind speeds varying from 17 to 30 m s^{-1}; the wave age C_p/U_10 \sim \cal{O}(1) and the significant wave height is up to 8 m. LES experiments with both aligned winds and waves and also with swell are considered. The results show a signature of the wave fields on the streamwise wind and a significant correlation between the wave heights and the surface pressure field. Surprisingly, there is no intermittent separation over the dominant waves. An analysis of the momentum flux in the ABL surface layer shows a resolved pressure (form) stress that depends on wind speed and proximity to the wave surface which is potentially of importance in surface layer measurements at high winds. Finally, the total drag coefficient from the LES agrees with wind-wave tank observations where the wave age based on friction velocity C_p/u_* \sim 0.1. To examine the sensitivity of the LES results to grid resolution, an idealized boundary layer flow is simulated with horizontal and vertical mesh spacings less than 1\% of the peak wavelength in the wave spectrum.

489348.title: Reconciling Observed and Modeled Estimates of Urban Terpenoid Emissions
489348.authors: Yingnan Zhang, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA; and K. Wu, H. Wang, E. Y. Pfannerstill, S. Nagalingam, M. M. Coggon, C. Stockwell, V. M. Ruiz, C. Ho, Y. Yu, J. Novelly, C. Pawlak, S. Kim, C. Warneke, A. H. Goldstein, and A. B. Guenther
489348.abstract: Extensive observations highlight the significance of terpenoids in urban air quality. However, emission frameworks fail to capture their magnitude and spatial variability, limiting air quality management and atmospheric modeling. Here we reconcile observed and modeled urban terpenoid emissions and uncover intense, underrepresented anthropogenic sources in Greater Los Angeles by combining improved emission inventories, airborne flux measurements, and ground-based mobile measurements. We demonstrate that an enhanced biogenic inventory significantly reduces the discrepancy between modeled and observed isoprene fluxes, and the remaining gap in monoterpenoids is explained predominantly by anthropogenic sectors. We identify that these emissions originate from previously overlooked food industry and commercial businesses, which exhibit a biogenic-like temperature dependence. These anthropogenic sources account for 44% of the top 10% observed monoterpenoid flux hotspots and contribute 17% of the total flux. Given their ubiquity in urban and industrialized regions worldwide, these poorly characterized sources may influence air quality beyond Los Angeles.

489356.title: Optimizing Coronagraph Imagery Through Background Subtraction
489356.authors: Donald J Schmit, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and G. Dima
489356.abstract: Coronagraphs provide a unique diagnostic capability for detecting ejected solar plasma and inferring the trajectory. Raw coronagraph images are a mixture of instrumentally scattered or diffracted light and heliospheric light focussed on the detector. The ability to detect coronal mass ejections relies on the ability to isolate evolution in the coronal scene. We discuss different data reduction and visualization techniques that can be applied to NOAA's CCOR-1 and CCOR-2 data to help highlight CME structure. For CCOR-1, background generation is complicated by the rotation of the coronal image due to spacecraft processes. For CCOR-2, background generation is complicated by a variable component of instrumental straylight. We discuss various strategies for improving the fidelity of background subtracted images.

489357.title: Multi-Satellite Constraints In a Perturbed Parameter Ensemble Reduce Uncertainty In Modeled Aerosol Forcing
489357.authors: Yusuf Bhatti, SRON Space Research Organisation Netherlands, Leiden, South Holland, Netherlands; and H. Jia, L. Regayre, D. Watson-Parris, N. Schutgens, A. Nenes, U. Im, B. van Diedenhoven, A. Arifi, X. Wang, C. Svenhag, G. Jan van Zadelhoff, and O. Hasekamp
489357.abstract: Aerosol interactions with radiation and clouds remain a dominant source of uncertainty in estimates of human influence on climate, limiting confidence in historical climate attribution and future projections. A challenge in attempts to reduce this uncertainty with observations is to match multiple aerosols and clouds at different locations and times simultaneously. Here, we use observations from the recently launched PACE and EarthCARE satellites of aerosol amount, size, absorption, and vertical distribution, together with Cloud Droplet Number Concentration, to constrain the Aerosol Effective Radiative Forcing (ERF) in aerosol-climate model simulations using a perturbed parameter ensemble. We show that the combined use of the observations constrains natural and anthropogenic emissions, physical aerosol properties, and processes, resulting in a reduction of ERF parametric uncertainty by 34%. ERFari and ERFaci uncertainty credible interval ranges are reduced by 66% and 32%, respectively. We find an observation-consistent ERF of -1.52 [-2 to -1.1] W m2, which suggests stronger aerosol cooling than the current IPCC estimate of -1.3 [-2.0 to -0.6] W m-2. We further introduce the Aerocom Multi-Model Perturbed Parameter Ensemble (MM-PPE), which applies a set of aerosol and cloud process perturbations across multiple climate models, separating model parametric and structural uncertainties, to evaluate the robustness of these observational constraints across different model structures.

489358.title: How Urgent Changes Were Handled in AWIPS and How We Can Do Better in NWS Hydrometeorological Interactive Virtual Environment (NWS HIVE)
489358.authors: James Edward Calkins, NWS, Elkridge, MD; and S. T. Jacobs, A. Just, and R. Henry-Reeves
489358.abstract: Throughout the AWIPS Era, the National Weather Service (NWS) has often been forced to scramble to make urgent changes to the AWIPS baseline in order to comply with new NWS Directives, data format changes, and other Federal Government orders. These changes often required a rapid turnaround, required a “turnkey” approach in operations, and/or the NWS had limited to no ability to properly test the changes in advance. Since AWIPS is a highly configurable system, changes to the baseline often had to be integrated into local configurations at field sites in ways that could not be properly evaluated in advance. The presentation will explain the complications and pitfalls observed with these urgent changes in AWIPS, and how the process will be improved upon as the National Weather Service moves to NWS HIVE and NWS CIRRUS.

489363.title: The Evolution of Hazard Generation in AWIPS and How It Informs The Future Of Hazard Operations in NWS Hydrometeorological Interactive Virtual Environment (NWS HIVE)
489363.authors: Mark Armstrong, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and S. T. Jacobs, A. Just, R. Henry-Reeves, and D. Hood
489363.abstract: Creating and disseminating critical weather hazard alerts is one of the most critical aspects of National Weather Service (NWS) operations. It has evolved from simple hand-typed text bulletins and non-graphical software that preceded AWIPS to a capable and complex suite of products and software. It has seen the establishment of the machine-readable Valid Time Event Coding (VTEC) paradigm and the development of new software to produce it. The WarnGen and Graphical Hazard Generator (GHG) software was designed to allow forecasters to quickly produce hazards in standard formats that leaned heavily on pre-defined templates. The final iteration of hazard generation in AWIPS is the Hazard Services software that combines the features of GHG, WarnGen and RiverPro. This presentation will summarize the development of hazard products and software in AWIPS and discuss the lessons learned throughout the AWIPS era. Finally, it will describe how the AWIPS program plans to continue to evolve the software and hazard products in HIVE.

489365.title: ADT-HURSAT as an Updated, Consistent Record of Historical Tropical Cyclone Intensity as Compared to IBTrACS
489365.abstract: Understanding long-term trends in tropical cyclone activity is complicated by inconsistencies in tropical cyclone best tracks due to changes in agency best tracking practice over time. The Advanced Dvorak Technique Hurricane Satellite (ADT-HURSAT) dataset was created as a joint effort between the National Centers for Environmental Information and the University of Wisconsin-CIMSS using Advanced Dvorak Technique on Hurricane Satellite (HURSAT) data to create data consistent over the period of record. ADT-HURSAT has been updated to span from 1978-2024 and was recently publicly released from NCEI for the first time, including a data access notebook to make analysis on the dataset more accessible to users. Insights into the data may be gained in a comparison to the best track data provided in the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS). Average biases in intensity in the dataset are dependent on the scene type identified by the ADT as well as the intensity of the storm. These biases project onto latitudinal dependence given latitudinal distributions of storm characteristics. Results confirm ADT-HURSAT should not be used for intensity measurement for a particular storm, however ADT-HURSAT is unique in its consistency allowing for climate quality analysis.

489378.title: Assessing MPAS-GOCART2G on a Variable Resolution Mesh for Regional Modeling of Atmospheric Aerosols and Wildfire Smoke Impacts
489378.authors: Katherine Wilson, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and M. C. Barth, F. Lacey, and R. Kumar
489378.abstract: The Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS)-GOCART2G is a soon-to-be-released version of MPAS that incorporates chemistry using the GOCART2G aerosol scheme. This model performs as expected on a 60 km quasi-uniform global mesh, and the integration of the GOCART2G scheme is ideal for long-term global aerosol modeling. Here we evaluate the MPAS-GOCART2G aerosol and meteorology results using variable resolution (60-3 km) to test how the model performs at resolutions needed to capture the effects of aerosols on mesoscale convective systems. The MPAS-GOCART2G 60-3 km grid mesh is centered over the southeast U.S. for the April 27, 2011 super-outbreak storm case. During this event, biomass burning aerosol emissions were high due to wildfires in Mexico and Central America, allowing for analysis of black, organic, and brown carbon, as well as dust and sea salt emissions. This event additionally includes severe weather over the Southeastern United States, so that the model’s ability to capture convection can also be assessed. MPAS-GOCART2G output is compared to ASOS surface stations, MODIS aerosol optical depth, accumulated precipitation measurements, and other observations to validate its accuracy with a variable resolution mesh. MPAS-GOCART2G will then be compared to MPAS-A output of the same case that does not include aerosols to determine how the presence of wildfire smoke affected the outbreak. This comparison will include preliminary results on how severe storm parameters and precipitation intensity were altered by the aerosols.

489380.title: Progress Toward Surface Cycling and Soil Analysis in the RRFS MPAS-JEDI Prototype
489380.authors: Liaofan Lin, CIRA, Boulder, CO; CIRA/CSU and NOAA/OAR/GSL, Boulder, CO; and A. Back, M. Hu, C. Zhou, S. Benjamin, and T. T. Ladwig
489380.abstract: Accurate representation of land surface conditions is essential for convection-allowing numerical weather prediction (NWP). In NOAA's operational High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and Rapid Refresh Forecast System version 1 (RRFSv1), atmospheric analyses are periodically reset while land and soil states are continuously cycled to maintain realistic land-atmosphere interactions. As development transitions to the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) with the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI)-based RRFS prototype, equivalent capabilities for land surface initialization and cycling are being developed within the new modeling and data assimilation framework. Building upon retrospective studies demonstrating the benefits of continuous surface cycling and soil nudging for improving near-surface forecast skill, these capabilities have now been implemented in NOAA Global Systems Laboratory's real-time RRFSv2x MPAS-JEDI experiments. Recent developments also include refinements to the soil nudging algorithm, particularly over snow-covered regions, to improve the physical consistency of soil state updates. This presentation summarizes recent progress in the implementation and evaluation of surface cycling and soil nudging within RRFSv2x. Retrospective experiments at both 12-km and convection-allowing 3-km CONUS resolutions are conducted to evaluate the impacts of continuous surface cycling and the updated soil nudging scheme on near-surface forecasts and local-scale weather prediction. Results will be presented to evaluate improvements in near-surface forecast skill and land-atmosphere coupling. The presentation will also discuss lessons learned from implementing these capabilities in real-time RRFSv2x experiments and outline ongoing efforts toward a future soil analysis capability within the MPAS-JEDI framework.

489386.title: What Lies Within the "Valley of Death"? Sharing Human-Centered Lessons Learned for Strengthening Collaboration and Moving Innovation into Real-World Use
489386.authors: Isha M. Renta López, Semilla Cultural, Fredericksburg, VA; and C. Williamsberg and A. Arnold
489386.abstract: In 2000, a National Research Council report framed the challenge of moving research into operations as “crossing the Valley of Death.” More than 25 years later, the phrase remains familiar shorthand across the Weather, Water, and Climate Enterprise. Considerable effort has gone toward building bridges across the valley, but far less toward understanding what makes the valley so difficult to cross in the first place. Bridges may help individual efforts reach the other side, but they do not address the deeper conditions that repeatedly hinder the movement of research into practice. Lasting improvement requires us to look beneath the surface and examine the institutional, procedural, and human factors that shape the transition process. To better understand these barriers, NOAA’s Weather Program Office (WPO) conducted a human-centered evaluation of the weather-related research transition pipeline between the Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR) and the National Weather Service (NWS). Drawing on interviews with staff across both line offices, participants described substantial improvements in communication and coordination in recent years, and highlighted past successes and best practices that enabled effective transitions. However, they also emphasized that significant gaps remain and identified opportunities to strengthen the process moving forward. Since completing the evaluation, WPO has continued engaging NOAA partners to share these findings as the research transition landscape continues to evolve. Yet the movement of research into the real-world is not unique to NOAA and extends across the Weather, Water, and Climate Enterprise. Therefore, this presentation translates the evaluation’s findings into practical takeaways for professionals across the enterprise. By looking beneath the surface of research transitions, attendees will gain insight into the often-hidden factors that determine whether research advances or stalls, including the roles of people and relationships, requirements, governance, and organizational culture. Participants will also leave with a human-centered approach they can apply to diagnose barriers within their own processes for moving innovation into real-world use and identify opportunities to make those processes more coordinated, responsive, and effective.

489392.title: Ice-Nucleating Properties of Modern Cloud-Seeding Materials Across Field and Laboratory Experiments
489392.authors: Amie Dobracki, Rainmaker Technologies, El Segundo, CA; and K. Suski, A. G. Hallar, N. Hiranuma, S. China, M. A. Garcia, I. B. McCubbin, M. Ostlie, A. Garcia, G. Carrillo-Cardenas, J. Bail, J. Jennings, K. Kaushal, D. Sapkota, and E. Farkash
489392.abstract: Cloud seeding has long been used to enhance precipitation in water-limited regions, with glaciogenic seeding of wintertime orographic clouds remaining a primary strategy in the western United States. Silver iodide (AgI), commonly dispersed using pyrotechnic flares, is the principal seeding material because of its structural similarity to ice and effectiveness as a heterogeneous ice-nucleating particle (INP). Despite its widespread use, the ice-nucleating properties of AgI-based materials have largely been characterized using older flare formulations and limited particle-resolved instrumentation. Here, we characterize the microphysical, morphological, chemical, and ice-nucleating properties of aerosols generated from modern cloud-seeding materials using complementary field and laboratory experiments. Field experiments conducted at Powder Mountain, Utah (41.43°N, −111.74°W), included sequential releases of AgI-based flares, powdered AgI, ground-generator emissions, and aerosolized Snomax and fungal protein suspensions under similar meteorological conditions. Materials were dispersed from an unmanned aerial vehicle or ground-based sources and sampled through a 10 m turbulent inlet. Aerosol size distributions were measured using a Scanning Mobility Particle Sizer (SMPS). Temperature-dependent INP concentrations were evaluated using the Portable Ice Nucleation Experiment (PINE) chamber. Offline droplet-freezing assays were used to complement the PINE measurements and characterize INP concentrations at warmer freezing temperatures (> −15 °C). Aerosol particles were also collected on filters for offline scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis of particle morphology and composition. Particle size distributions varied strongly with material and dispersal methods. Ground-generator and biological aerosols exhibited modes near 40 nm, flare emissions were dominated by particles near 100 nm, and powdered AgI exhibited a substantially coarser mode between approximately 3 and 5 µm. Initial PINE measurements indicate variability in ice-nucleating activity among the tested materials and dispersal methods, consistent with observed differences in aerosol size distributions and particle morphology. Complementary laboratory experiments used a Continuous Flow Diffusion Chamber (CFDC) to investigate the ice activation of flare-derived particles and prospective biogenic seeding agents at −10 °C and −15 °C and nominal supersaturations of −5 %, 0 %, 5 %, and 10%. Particle size distributions and number concentrations were measured concurrently using an Electrical Low Pressure Impactor (ELPI). These initial experiments used polydisperse aerosol populations, with size-selected activation measurements planned for future work. Preliminary CFDC results indicate activated fractions of up to 15 % for flare-derived particles and approximately 5 % for biogenic particles. Although the biogenic particles exhibited lower activated fractions under the conditions tested, their measurable ice-nucleating activity demonstrates promise as alternative cloud-seeding agents. Together, these measurements link the properties of modern seeding materials with their ice-nucleating behavior, helping us understand how different materials may perform under varying cloud conditions and how they can be used more effectively in cloud-seeding operations.

489393.title: Rapid Weakening of Intense Tropical Cyclones in Moderate Vertical Wind Shear (Invited Presentation)
489393.authors: Peter M Finocchio, NRL, Monterey, CA; and D. P. Stern, R. Rios-Berrios, and A. J. DesRosiers
489393.abstract: We use idealized simulations to understand the relative roles of tropical cyclone (TC) size and the structure of vertical wind shear in the rapid weakening (RW) of intense TCs. The first set of simulations exposes a small and intense vortex to wind profiles with moderate shear concentrated in an upper layer, a middle layer, or a deep layer of the troposphere. Both the vortex and the environmental shear imposed in the simulations are designed to emulate Hurricane Delta (2020), a small Category-4 hurricane that rapidly weakened in moderate vertical wind shear. RW occurs in the simulations with each of the imposed wind profiles and is due to shear enhancing storm-relative inflow in the middle and upper troposphere. This inflow causes deep downdrafts to form on the upshear side of the eyewall and to the left of tilt. Backward trajectories reveal that the increasing shear causes a nearly five-fold increase in the number of air parcels radially transported from the surrounding middle troposphere into the inner core. This radial ventilation cools the eyewall and likely contributes to the formation of downdrafts upshear. Both the downdrafts and ventilation signatures in the eyewall are evident one hour before the onset of RW and while the vortex tilt magnitude is still small (< 5 km). In simulations with upper-level shear, the vortex tilt increases more gradually than in the other shear simulations, but an eyewall replacement cycle consistently occurs shortly after the onset of RW. Increasing the size of the vortex exposed to moderate shear reduces the amount and duration of weakening. The larger vortices resist moderate shear more effectively than the smaller vortices by maintaining more coherent eyewall convection, driven by higher surface enthalpy fluxes in the inner core.

489394.title: Towards a Continuously Cycled AI Weather Prediction Model: Expanding an LETKF-Based Data Assimilation System for HRRRCast
489394.authors: Vanderlei Vargas Jr., CSU/CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; DTC, Boulder, CO; and D. S. Abdi, I. Jankov, and J. Jacobson
489394.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) approaches to Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) have advanced rapidly, and convection-allowing ML models such as HRRRCast can now generate ensemble forecasts at a small fraction of the computational cost of traditional physics-based systems. In its current form, however, HRRRCast depends on analyses from the operational High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model for its initial conditions. This dependency presents two practical limitations. First, the HRRR is scheduled to be retired, which means the analysis product that currently initializes HRRRCast will no longer be available, and a sustainable alternative source of initial conditions will be required. Second, the HRRR analysis is not available immediately; the time needed to produce it delays when downstream HRRRCast forecasts can be generated. A self-contained cycled ensemble Data Assimilation (DA) capability, one in which HRRRCast uses its own forecast background to initialize the next cycle, would address both issues. Such a system would remove the reliance on an external analysis and, by avoiding the wait for the HRRR analysis, could reduce forecast latency and accelerate the delivery of forecasts. It may also, secondarily, improve forecast quality; however, improved skill is not the primary objective of this work. The central motivation is to establish an independent, timely, and sustainable initialization pathway for an ML-based forecast system, and to understand the behavior, benefits, and limitations of coupling an ML forecast model with its own ensemble DA. We present the development and initial evaluation of a prototype ensemble DA system built around HRRRCast. The system employs a Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (LETKF) to assimilate surface observations into the HRRRCast ensemble within a cycled framework, generating flow-dependent analysis increments that update the ML forecast state and provide initial conditions for subsequent forecasts. In its initial configuration the system assimilates 2-m temperature (T2M), which serves as a controlled starting point for characterizing the coupled ML-DA cycle. We examine the system’s behavior through its analysis increments, the fit of the background and analysis ensembles to observations, and the resulting short-range forecast evolution. The verification framework combines deterministic evaluation of T2M against surface observations with probabilistic evaluation of composite reflectivity against Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor (MRMS) observations, using reliability diagrams, Relative Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves, and neighborhood Fractions Skill Score (FSS) computed across multiple intensity thresholds and spatial scales. Together these diagnostics establish a baseline for assessing observation impact, ensemble spread and reliability, and forecast skill in an ML-based cycling context, and they provide the infrastructure needed to evaluate subsequent extensions on a consistent footing. These initial experiments are intended to demonstrate feasibility and to expose the practical behavior of ensemble DA when the forecast model is a machine learning emulator rather than a physics-based model. Building on this prototype, we are exploring several directions aimed at expanding the system’s capability and probing its limits. A first set of questions concerns the scope of assimilation: extending beyond T2M to additional surface variables such as winds, humidity, and pressure and, more generally, incorporating additional observation sources to enrich the analysis. A second set concerns the cadence and durability of cycling, including the potential move toward higher-frequency, rapid-refresh updates (for example, hourly rather than six-hourly cycles) and continuous cycling well beyond the initial set of DA cycles to assess the longer-term stability of the coupled ML-DA system. A third set concerns the configuration of the LETKF itself, where the sensitivity of the analysis to key parameters, localization radius, ensemble inflation, and the specification of observation-error covariances, warrants systematic examination. Finally, we intend to broaden verification along two axes: evaluating the downstream impact of assimilation on a wider range of forecast fields, potentially including precipitation, wind, and composite reflectivity, and extending the assessment to longer forecast horizons, on the order of 48 to 72 hours. The relative benefit, feasibility, computational cost, and mutual interactions among these directions remain open questions, and the work of the coming period will help determine which prove most valuable. Taken together, this effort represents an early step toward a self-contained, continuously cycled ensemble DA capability for a machine learning convection-allowing forecast model; one motivated primarily by the need for an independent and low-latency initialization pathway as the HRRR is phased out. In this presentation, we will describe the current system design and cycling framework, present preliminary results, and outline the verification methodology used across variables, thresholds, and scales. We will also discuss the principal challenges encountered and the open questions that motivate the next phase of work, with the broader aim of understanding both the potential and the limitations of coupling machine learning forecast models with their own ensemble data assimilation.

489396.title: Building the Foundation for Cloud-Native NWS Operations: The NWS Enterprise Cloud (NEC) Build-out In AWS
489396.authors: Carissa Klemmer, NWS, College Park, MD; and J. Bowmar, J. Fiscus, K. L. Sheets, J. Callaway, R. Henry-Reeves, and D. Hood
489396.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) is undergoing a major technological transformation, modernizing systems to support a nimble atmosphere. At the heart of this modernization is the NWS Enterprise Cloud (NEC), a centralized cloud computing and data platform, designed to be scalable and agile to adapt to new and emerging technologies. This presentation details the technical architectural design, security, current status, and future vision.

489398.title: Enhancing the POWER Web Platform to Expand Societal Impact to Larger Groups of Users in Energy, Infrastructure and Agricultural Systems
489398.authors: Paul W. Stackhouse Jr., NASA Langley Research Center, Hampton, VA
489398.abstract: The global community in the societal sectors of energy, infrastructure and agriculture continue to grow in their ability and thus need to access and utilize data for their various decision processes that optimize energy production, energy savings, building system and agricultural planning. To address the needs for consistent environmental near-surface conditions within these sectors, the NASA Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resource (POWER) project facilitates the use of NASA Earth Science data on a global scale from the early 1980s through to near-real time. This is accomplished by devising a suite of web services including a complete API service, an interactive user tool called the Data Access Viewer (DAV), image services and various methods of direct download to provide key weather and energy parameters needed in each sector. Available data products are comprised of radiative fluxes, including solar, from several NASA projects (i.e., LaRC Surface Radiation Budget and CERES) and consistent meteorological data from NASA assimilation models (i.e., MERRA-2) and other NASA missions (i.e., GPM IMERG) have been reformatted and disseminated to the public via a user friendly web GIS-enabled based data portal (https://power.larc.nasa.gov) at the native resolution of each data product. Parameters and units are customized relative to needs of the various supported communities after engaging with representatives of those communities in a number of ways. Thus, user selected data formats are available making the data parameter immediately amenable to key industry wide decision support tools in our areas of focus. Enabling such data access has resulted in sustained growth in the usage of about 30% per year with a 2026 monthly average usage by 119 thousand unique users making over 28 million requests. Nevertheless, despite this growth there are many needs for data and information that can be better addressed through innovative solutions allowing to scale up to different levels of users in those sectors. This talk reviews the current tools and our user interaction strategy including various user stories in different sectors. We then show how new capabilities such as our customized “regional” information tool and our developing Chatbox-like interface will enable larger numbers of users in those sectors obtain the information needed for their various decisions. Additionally, we describe the POWER teams efforts to improve existing data products and add new products through various satellite based observations and data products to further meet the needs within the various communities. We will lastly highlight our efforts to provide long-term risk information from CMIP6 future projections utilizing the NEX GDDP downscaled data products as an effort to support the RASI project and those users in these sectors looking for simpler ways to digest potential future meteorological conditions.

489400.title: Aerosol–Cloud Interactions Under a Spectrum of Realistic Meteorological Conditions Using a Comprehensive Library of Large-Eddy Simulations
489400.authors: Ehsan Erfani, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV; and R. Wood, P. Blossey, L. A. McMichael, S. Doherty, and R. M. Eastman
489400.abstract: Subtropical warm clouds strongly affect Earth's radiation budget, yet large uncertainties exist in quantifying their response to aerosol perturbations within global climate models (GCMs). This is due to GCMs’ coarse spatial resolution that limits their ability to represent the complex processes governing warm clouds.
