Large-eddy simulation (LES), by explicitly resolving turbulent and entrainment processes, provides a more physically based approach for quantifying these clouds. The response of warm clouds to aerosols depends strongly on ambient environmental conditions, yet most LES studies have focused on a limited set of scenarios or an idealized setup. To address this limitation, we have developed a comprehensive library of LES simulations using the University of Washington System for Atmospheric Modeling (UW-SAM). The UW-SAM is coupled with a prognostic aerosol scheme that accounts for important aerosol budget tendencies, including entrainment from the free troposphere, surface sources, collision-coalescence, interstitial scavenging, and sedimentation. More than 2,200 forward Lagrangian trajectories were generated within the Northeast Pacific stratocumulus region during the summers of 2018–2021, and satellite and reanalysis datasets were compiled along each trajectory. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was applied to eight cloud-controlling factors to identify 54 representative cases encompassing the observed range of meteorological, aerosol, and cloud phase space. These selected trajectories form the basis for a library of “unperturbed” 48-hour, large-domain, high-resolution simulations that realistically capture the evolution of warm clouds under a spectrum of environmental conditions. In addition, an LES library of “perturbed” aerosol experiments has also been completed, in which early-morning, domain-wide injections of aerosols (dry radius ~30 nm) are applied for one hour. Together, the paired unperturbed and perturbed simulations provide a unique tool for testing hypotheses related to warm cloud processes and for isolating aerosol effects across a broad range of meteorological conditions. Results show that the aerosol-induced change in cloud radiative effect varies with the background aerosol concentration, liquid water path, and precipitation. In addition, aerosol perturbation affects mesoscale cell size and the diurnal cycle of liquid water path. The injection strategy mirrors those used in GCM studies and therefore allows for process-level validation of global-scale assumptions under high-resolution, realistic conditions.

489412.title: Summary of the 2026 Atlantic and Eastern/Central North Pacific Hurricane Seasons
489412.authors: Michael J. Brennan, National Hurricane Center, Miami, FL; and C. Brenchley
489412.abstract: Highlights and impacts of tropical cyclones that occurred during the 2026 Atlantic and Eastern North Pacific hurricane seasons will be provided. A summary of forecast verification and operational successes and challenges during the season will also be included, with a focus on high-impact events.

489416.title: Evaluating the Potential of Geospatial Foundation Models for Field-Scale Evapotranspiration Mapping: Accuracy, Transferability, and Applications
489416.authors: Junhua Chen, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and J. L. Huntington and Y. Xie
489416.abstract: Operational, high-resolution estimates of evapotranspiration (ET) are essential for agricultural water use accounting and management, yet conventional ET mapping approaches (e.g., empirical, surface energy balance models, and resistance-based models) can be computationally complex and/or constrained by data availability (e.g., thermal and meteorological data), spatial resolution, accuracy, and spatiotemporal transferability. Geospatial foundation models (GFMs), pretrained on large-scale, multisource Earth observation data, offer a potential cost-effective and scalable alternative for generating ET estimates across broad regions and over time. Here, we introduce a preliminary version of physics-informed GFM and evaluate its potential for field-scale ET mapping across the western United States. The model is pretrained using multisource satellite and climate observations to learn and reconstruct irrigation-sensitive dynamic patterns in vegetation greenness, surface wetness, and land surface temperature. The pretrained model is then fine-tuned using monthly ensemble ET estimates from OpenET for 2020 over randomly selected training regions and applied to generate monthly ET estimates across seventeen western U.S. states. Our preliminary result shows a strong agreement between FM-derived and the OpenET ensemble mean estimates with an RMSE of 15.27 mm month⁻¹ and an R² of 0.92. The model also shows a strong temporal transferability by applying the 2020 fine-tuned model directly to 2019 (RMSE = 17.53 mm month⁻¹; R² = 0.87). In contrast, zero-shot geographic transfer is challenging. For example, applying the model trained from eleven western states to the six High Plans states (Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, South Dakota, and North Dakota) shows a limited performance with an RMSE of 24.95–26.69 mm month⁻¹. However, geographic transferability can be substantially improved (RMSE 15.74 mm month⁻¹) with only 50 target-region training plots (each covering 128 × 128 30-m pixels). Although a more comprehensive assessment is needed, these results suggest that the developed FM could provide acceptable field-scale ET estimates with strong temporal transferability and efficient adaptation to new geographic regions using limited local training data. While purely experimental, this capability provides a promising pathway for complementing computationally intensive approaches toward operational ET mapping and applications.

489417.title: Evolving Environmental Data Discovery: The NCEI Access Service User Interface
489417.abstract: The National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) stewards one of the largest and most heterogeneous collections of environmental datasets globally, serving a diverse domestic and international user base across research, weather forecasting, commerce, and public safety sectors. Efficient discovery and retrieval across such vast, multi-domain holdings present significant data management challenges. To meet the needs of these diverse holdings and users, NCEI developed a composable Search, Discovery, and Data Access system, culminating in the public release of an enhanced user interface (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/search/) designed to streamline spatial and programmatic data retrieval. This system integrates multi-faceted search capabilities with spatial and temporal filtering, significantly improving metadata indexing and data accessibility across disparate environmental domains. By prioritizing developer experience (DevEx), NCEI creates a rapid feedback loop driven by stakeholder and user input; continuous enhancements are implemented to streamline workflows and maximize data accessibility. This presentation details the architectural enhancements of the system and its UI, demonstrates its multi-faceted search workflows, and discusses its broader impact on enabling open science and data interoperability.

489425.title: Assessing the Need for High-Resolution Air Temperature Modeling in the Built Environment Using Machine Learning and Observations
489425.authors: Zackary Mages, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY; and K. Lamer and D. J. Sailor
489425.abstract: Air temperature influences numerous societal sectors like energy demand and human health, especially during extreme heat events in densely populated cities. Accurately forecasting these events is crucial, and mesoscale weather models, although improving in their spatial resolution, are limited by the theoretical constraints of model parameterizations. Higher-resolution urban micrometeorological models present an alternative, but they are computationally expensive and difficult to initialize, which limits their widespread use. Determining when high-resolution modeling is necessary and when mesoscale predictions are sufficient can help guide future investments in forecasting capabilities. Phoenix, AZ, a rapidly growing city with some of the most extreme temperatures in the United States, serves as an ideal testbed to assess these types of decisions. This study quantifies fine-scale air temperature variability using a machine-learning framework and an extensive observational dataset consisting of mobile (vehicle-based) and fixed weather station measurements combined with satellite-derived land surface properties. For summertime conditions across an approximately 100 km × 100 km domain in the Phoenix metropolitan area, a gradient boosting regression model reconstructs near-surface air temperature at 100-m spatial and 30-min temporal resolution with high accuracy (R² = 0.96, RMSE = 1.01°C). The resulting temperature fields are used to characterize subgrid-scale variability within areas comparable to the grid spacing of typical mesoscale weather models. Results show that air temperature variability within a single mesoscale grid cell frequently exceeds 4°C during extreme heat events, indicating that mesoscale predictions may not adequately represent thermal conditions relevant to building-scale decision making and heat-risk assessment. Relationships between air temperature variability and land-surface characteristics are further examined to identify the factors that drive fine-scale thermal heterogeneity. These findings provide a quantitative framework for identifying where mesoscale model predictions are sufficient and where higher-resolution simulations are needed, helping to prioritize future advances in urban weather forecasting.

489431.title: From Kilometers to Meters: Downscaling Near-Surface Weather with High-Resolution Earth Observations
489431.abstract: Near-surface atmospheric conditions can change over tens to hundreds of meters due to land cover and topography, yet this variability is absent from current weather analyses and forecasts. It is unclear whether such meter-scale variability reflects irreducibly chaotic dynamics or contains a component predictable from surface characteristics and large-scale atmospheric forcing. In this work, we show that a substantial, physically coherent component of meter-scale near-surface weather is statistically recoverable from existing observations. By conditioning coarse atmospheric state on sparse surface station measurements and high-resolution Earth observation data, we infer spatially continuous fields of near-surface wind, temperature, and humidity at 10 m resolution across the contiguous United States. Relative to ERA5, the inferred fields reduce error by over 30% for 2 m temperature and dewpoint and 10 m wind, while explaining substantially more spatial variance at fixed time steps. They also exhibit physically interpretable structure, including urban heat islands, evapotranspiration-driven humidity contrasts, and wind speed differences across land cover types. Our findings expand the frontier of weather modeling by demonstrating a computationally feasible approach to continental-scale meter-resolution inference.

489432.title: The Importance of Orographic Representation for Simulating Rainfall over the Coastal Tropical Eastern Pacific
489432.authors: Jingyi Hu, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and X. Chen
489432.abstract: One of the rainiest regions on Earth lies in the coastal eastern tropical Pacific (ETP), where precipitation is concentrated along the coastline and extends westward over the open ocean along the Intertropical Convergence Zone. Rainfall over this region also exhibits a pronounced diurnal cycle, characterized by long-distance offshore propagation from the coast during the local early morning through afternoon. Despite the climatic importance of rainfall over this region, global models exhibit substantial and systematic precipitation biases over the ETP. Previous studies have identified several processes that may contribute to convection development and rainfall over the region, including diurnal gravity waves generated by the Andes, surface gap winds from Central America, and cross-equatorial southerly trade winds. Because these processes are all strongly influenced by the complex topography of Central and South America, we hypothesize that rainfall biases in global models are at least partly attributable to errors in representing orography at coarse resolution. This study investigates this hypothesis from both high-resolution modeling and theoretical perspectives. We first conduct semi-idealized, high-resolution regional simulations designed to isolate the impacts of orographic representation on ETP rainfall. Control simulations using realistic high-resolution topography and diurnally repeating boundary conditions reproduce the observed spatiotemporal characteristics of rainfall, including its offshore diurnal propagation. The simulated rainfall propagation is generally consistent with the cold phase of gravity waves generated by the Andes. In contrast, when the orography is coarsened to a resolution representative of global models, the coastal rainfall maximum shifts southward, while the offshore propagation of both gravity waves and rainfall becomes substantially slower. The southward displacement of the coastal rainfall maximum closely resembles a systematic bias found in many global models. Using a novel idealized theoretical model that can be forced by realistic vertical profiles of background wind and buoyancy frequency, we further show that the changes in rainfall distribution and offshore propagation are consistent with linear theory. Coarse-resolution topography fails to represent small-scale heating maxima associated with individual mountain peaks, thereby altering the characteristics of the generated gravity waves and contributing to the simulated rainfall biases. Based on these results, we propose a simple approach for improving rainfall simulations over regions such as the ETP in coarse-resolution models by accounting for subgrid-scale orographic variance. We demonstrate that incorporating this information leads to substantial improvements in the simulated rainfall distribution and diurnal offshore propagation, even when coarse-resolution topography is used.

489435.title: Experimental Testing and Evaluation of the Warn-on-Forecast System on NOAA High-Performance Computing and Cloud Platforms to Support WoFSv2 Development
489435.authors: Jianping Huang, NOAA, Riverdale Park, MD; and F. Yang, K. Garrett, Y. Jung, H. Wang, A. Rabassa, C. M. Gravelle, K. S. SPEROW, P. C. Burke, A. J. Clark, L. J. Wicker, N. Yussouf, J. Martin, K. H. Knopfmeier, Y. Wang, and T. A. Jones
489435.abstract: The Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS), developed by NOAA's National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL), provides rapidly updating, convection-allowing probabilistic guidance for severe weather forecasting and warning decision support. While a recent National Weather Service (NWS) demonstration of cloud-based WoFS runs has yielded robust documentation of WoFS application to NWS operations, continued development requires a resilient computing environment for systematic testing, evaluation, and improvement of the forecasting system. To support this effort, the NWS Office of Modeling and Development (OMD), in collaboration with NSSL, is porting the Weather Research and Forecasting Model–Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation data assimilation system (WRF-GSI)-based WoFS Version 1 to NOAA's Research and Development High Performance Computing (RDHPC) systems, including Ursa, the Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System 2 (WCOSS2), and NOAA's Integrated Modeling Backbone for Unified Supercomputing (NIMBUS). This porting adapts the research workflow to NOAA HPC and cloud environments through workflow automation, software portability, fault tolerance, exception handling, and system integration, providing a reproducible framework for large-scale testing and evaluation. In parallel, OMD is evaluating an enhanced initialization strategy that uses the Rapid Refresh Forecast System Version 1 Data Assimilation System (RRFSv1-DAS) ensemble to initialize WoFS while leveraging deterministic RRFS forecasts with Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS)-derived perturbations for lateral boundary conditions. This approach takes advantage of the improved RRFS analysis while maintaining compatibility with the existing boundary perturbation methodology, providing a pathway toward improved forecast accuracy and practical upgrade to the current WoFS configuration. The NOAA HPC effort also provides a controlled platform for reproducing and diagnosing failures encountered during real-time cloud-based forecast demonstrations , while enabling systematic evaluation of system stability, computational performance, and forecast sensitivity. The resulting engineering experience and scientific evaluation will help guide future system development while improving the reliability, scalability, and maintainability of the WoFS research framework. This presentation will summarize the current status of the NOAA HPC testing and evaluation of WoFS v1, progress in integrating RRFSv1-DAS ensemble initialization, and representative use cases that illustrate best practices and lessons learned from adapting a research forecasting system to NOAA HPC computing and cloud environments. This presentation will also discuss how these efforts contribute to the development of the Model for Prediction Across Scales – Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (MPAS-JEDI) based WoFS Version 2 for future NWS operations on the NIMBUS cloud platform.

489438.title: Improving Historical Reanalysis of Tropical Cyclone Waves, Water Levels and Coastal Inundation
489438.authors: Philip Orton, Stevens Institute of Technology, new york, NY; and R. Luettich, R. Marsooli, N. Nwogwu, and M. Temimi
489438.abstract: Hurricanes, and more broadly tropical cyclones (TCs), play an outsized role in our nation’s coastal and inland flood hazards, and a key to building our nation’s resilience is to better understand historical extreme events. However, our ability to replicate their coastal hazards in detail with models is limited by our incomplete observations and often biased models of atmospheric conditions during these extreme storms. For example, the ERA5 atmospheric reanalysis has coarse resolution (28 km) relative to the small spatial scales of powerful or small TCs, and as a result in some cases it underestimates wind extremes near the core of the storm. Parametric TC vortex models can help resolve the extreme winds and their variations near the storm vortex, but often poorly replicate winds further from the storm center. The Generalized Asymmetric Holland Model (GAHM) enables inclusion of asymmetry due to both the large-scale wind field and azimuthal variation in the storm size, which can be particularly important for capturing storms undergoing extratropical transition. By blending ERA5 and GAHM into one storm wind and pressure field, we hypothesize that more accurate simulations can be made for water levels and waves, particularly for transitioning storms. In this presentation, we will present an evaluation of this improved approach for estimating historical hurricane winds and pressure. Three different meteorological forcing approaches are tested on a large set of historical TCs, simulating water levels and waves using the ADCIRC+SWAN coupled model. The resulting improved methods will help deepen our societal knowledge of the probability of extreme, rare events and thus, this project will help improve public safety and emergency management nationwide.

489442.title: Benchmarking HRRRCast: A Comprehensive Verification of a Convection Allowing AI Model
489442.authors: Vanderlei Vargas Jr., CSU/CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; DTC, Boulder, CO; and G. Ketefian, K. Newman, C. P. Kalb, J. H. Gotway, M. A. Harrold, D. S. Abdi, I. Jankov, and J. Jacobson
489442.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence Weather Prediction (AIWP) models begin to generate convection allowing ensemble forecasts, the question of how to verify them thoroughly, at scale, and in ways that expose behavior specific to data-driven models has become pressing. AIWP models frequently exhibit tendencies that are difficult to detect from summary scores or short evaluation windows: spatial smoothing of fine-scale structure, damping of high-intensity extremes, and ensemble spread that may be poorly calibrated relative to forecast error. For convection allowing applications, where users care about the location, intensity, and probability of high-impact features such as strong reflectivity, these behaviors carry direct consequences and demand a verification approach that is comprehensive in variable, metric, intensity threshold, and spatial scale, and that is applied over a period long enough to yield statistically robust conclusions. We present a comprehensive, long-period benchmarking verification of the HRRRCast convection allowing AIWP ensemble over the Contiguous United States (CONUS). HRRRCast ensemble forecasts are generated over an extended evaluation period spanning multiple months and verified against surface observations and Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor (MRMS) analyses. By aggregating a large sample of forecast/observation pairs across many initializations and meteorological regimes, the study aims to establish a robust, reproducible benchmark of HRRRCast performance; one that characterizes systematic behavior rather than performance on individual events, and that can serve as a reference against which future model versions, alternative configurations, and other convection allowing systems can be compared on a consistent footing. The verification is designed to probe the specific strengths and weaknesses of a data-driven forecast rather than to reduce performance to a single number. Multiple forecast fields are assessed against independent observations using a combination of deterministic, ensemble-probabilistic, and neighborhood-based approaches, chosen so that complementary aspects of forecast quality, accuracy, calibration, discrimination, and spatial skill are examined together rather than in isolation. Because the value of a convection allowing forecast depends strongly on spatial scale and event intensity, performance is evaluated across a range of scales and intensity thresholds and as a function of forecast lead time, so that skill can be traced from broad, common conditions to rarer, higher-impact events. Particular attention is paid to the ensemble’s dispersion and to the joint behavior of sharpness and reliability, which together indicate whether the ensemble is appropriately calibrated and whether apparent skill reflects genuine predictive information rather than the spatial smoothing that can artificially inflate certain measures. The specific fields, observational references, and diagnostics will be finalized as the study develops, with the aim of assembling a broad and complementary set rather than relying on any single measure. Applied uniformly and at scale, the framework produces more than a set of summary numbers: it yields a detailed, scale and threshold resolved picture of where a convection allowing AIWP ensemble is trustworthy and where it is not. The resulting statistics form a reproducible benchmark and a diagnostic baseline for the continued development of HRRRCast, and the methodology is designed to transfer directly to other AIWP convection allowing systems, enabling consistent, like-for-like comparison as the field grows. In this presentation we will describe the long-period forecast dataset and verification design, present results characterizing the forecast quality of the HRRRCast ensemble across variables, spatial scales, intensity thresholds, and lead times, and highlight the behaviors, both favorable and unfavorable, that emerge only under large-sample evaluation. We will discuss the particular challenges of verifying a data-driven convection allowing ensemble, including the treatment of smoothing, extremes, and ensemble calibration, and reflect on what a comprehensive benchmark of this kind reveals about the readiness of AIWP for convection allowing applications.

489443.title: Evaluation of Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) Data in NOAA's Next-Generation GFSv17 Data Assimilation System
489443.authors: Xiaoyan Zhang, SAIC@NOAA/NWS/OMD, College Park, MD; and Y. Wang, A. Collard, H. Liu, J. Jin, D. Holdaway, and E. Liu
489443.abstract: As commercial small satellite constellations continue to expand, evaluating their data quality and developing pathways for operational use in numerical weather prediction (NWP) have become increasingly important. This study presents NOAA's Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) pilot effort to evaluate Level-1B radiances from the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) constellation (S02, S05, and S06) within the next-generation Global Forecast System (GFSv17). A complete end-to-end processing and data assimilation workflow was developed using the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) system. The workflow includes BUFR data ingestion, radiative transfer modeling with the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM), quality control (QC), observation error model development, variational bias correction (VarBC), and cycled data assimilation experiments in the coupled GFSv17 system. The quality of the TMS observations was evaluated by comparing cross-sensor Observation-minus-Background (O–B) diagnostics with the operational Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) as a reference. The identified systematic biases from TMS observation were substantially reduced using a matched-scene variational bias correction (VarBC) scheme. Three GFSv17 cycling experiments were conducted to evaluate the forecast impact of assimilating all-sky TMS radiances from (1) window and water vapor channels, (2) 118 GHz temperature sounding channels, and (3) all available TMS channels. These experiments are designed to quantify the contribution of each channel group, with particular emphasis on assessing the value of the new 118 GHz temperature sounding channels in an operational global data assimilation system. Forecast verification results and the relative impacts of the different channel groups will be presented.

489448.title: tcpyPIv2.0: Tropical Cyclone Potential Intensity in Python version 2
489448.authors: Daniel M. Gilford, Climate Central, Princeton, NJ; and B. Mares
489448.abstract: tcpyPI is a freely available, validated, and documented Python implementation of the tropical cyclone (TC) potential intensity (PI) algorithm. Downloaded more than 40,000 times and developed openly on GitHub, tcpyPI is widely used across the tropical meteorology community, including for investigating individual storm properties, evaluating PI climatology, enabling tropical cyclone downscaling, and performing climate detection and attribution studies. Other environmental indices similarly-designed to analyze TC climatologies have been developed, but have not yet been brought together with PI into a single consistent and easy-to-deploy software implementation. tcpyPI v2.0 closes this gap by adding the ventilation index, a midlevel moist-entropy deficit calculation, genesis potential indices in multiple forms, and the power dissipation index to the software package. By analyzing each of these with additive log-space decompositions, the user can separate each into their individual environmental contributions across temporal and spatial scales. PI and each derived index are applied to gridded datasets through a fast, vectorized xarray interface. Version 2 also resolves a discontinuity inherited from the original PI implementation: defining the level of neutral buoyancy as the topmost positively buoyant level made Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE) values jump, affecting PI by up to 8 m/s in ~2% of profiles (as shown from a 2024 ERA5 sample). Through the implementation of a maximum-work CAPE definition we remove the algorithm’s jump: PI now responds continuously to its inputs, and spurious discontinuities in gridded PI fields and across sensitivity experiments are eliminated (legacy behavior remains reproducible via an algorithm option). tcpyPI v2.0 is available via PyPI and conda-forge. A newly developed Model Context Protocol (MCP) server improves tool accessibility, demonstrated here in agentic workflows such as Claude Code. We illustrate the improvements above by analyzing the seasonal cycles of PI and the genesis potential index over the North Atlantic using ERA5 data, with each separated into its seasonal environmental contributions via log decomposition.

489453.title: Using AI to Identify 25 Years of Rain Events Based on 1-Minute Rain Rates from a Weighing-Bucket Rain Gauge at Ground Level
489453.authors: Claude E. Duchon, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and A. P. Duchon, J. Castro, E. J. Becker, B. G. Illston, C. M. Luttrell, D. Grimsley, and C. A. Fiebrich
489453.abstract: Year 2027 will mark the 25th consecutive year of measuring 1-minute rain accumulation from a weighing-bucket rain gauge (3 vibrating wires Geonor T-200B) mounted in a pit such that its orifice is at ground level and surrounded by filter pads to prevent splash-in. The observation site is in a large level field in Norman, OK with negligible obstructions. The goal of this long-term observation program is to develop a climatology of the structure of rain events in central Oklahoma that also may be applicable to much of the southern plains. We are interested in potential trends in the time series of five variables: (1) rain event accumulation, (2) rain event duration, (3) time of day during which a rain event occurs, (4) maximum rain rate and time of occurrence during a rain event, and (5) the time interval between successive events. The first step toward the long-term goal is to identify the start and end times of a rain event defined by the following procedure. A possible rain event begins during the minute the rain rate is >/=0.5 mm/h (~0.02 in/h) or >/=0.0083 mm/min. As the accumulation of rain from successive rain rates >/=0.5 mm/h continues and exceeds 2.54 mm (0.1 in), a rain event has occurred, but with the end of the rain event yet to be determined. Eventually, a rain rate <0.5 mm/h will occur. Its occurrence could signal the last minute of the rain event, or it may be just an isolated rain rate <0.5 mm/h or the beginning of a sequence of rain rates <0.5 mm/h. In the isolated case, the accumulation of rain continues; in the sequence case, the length of the sequence and the magnitude of rain rates (are they close to 0.0 mm/h or slightly less than 0.5 mm/h?) are important in determining whether to end the rain event at the beginning of the sequence or continue accumulation after the sequence. If rain accumulation continues, eventually it will become apparent the rain has ended because all or nearly all rain rates are <0.5 mm/h for a period of around 25 minutes and longer. The criterion >/=0.5 mm/h was selected because it accounts for the vast majority of rainfall and simultaneously limits the time length of rain events. Once the 25-year record of rain event start and end times is available, the second step is to apply a computer program that has been written to calculate the five variables listed above. The third step is to analyze these climate variables for various statistical properties including trends. This presentation deals with the first step, identifying start and end times, as described in the following. Currently, analysts have manually determined start and end times for more than 700 rain events occurring from 2003 through 2015 employing the criteria discussed above. This tedious exercise has yet to be done for the start and end times for rain events occurring from 2016 through 2026. However, recent advances in large language models (LLMs) for software such as Claude Code by Anthropic can be applied to our data to: (1) create user interfaces to optimize analyst work (speed and effort) of the latter period, (2) highlight inconsistencies over the 13 years of manual coding of rain events with a fully traceable system back to raw data; and (3) quickly develop and compare multiple machine learning models to make estimates of rain event start and end times for unncoded data. The first part of the presentation will show, through a number of examples, how this application has been developed with the support of AI. The outcome of this effort as applied to identifying rain events during the 2016-2026-time frame will comprise the second part our presentation and its success will be crucial for future rain event identification because 1-minute rain rate measurements at the Norman site and their analysis will continue indefinitely.

489461.title: Modeling Admitted Private Flood Insurance Performance in North Carolina
489461.authors: Austin McCarthy Lord, UNC Chapel Hill, Institute for Risk Management and Insurance Innovation (IRMII), Chapel Hill, NC; and K. Fitzmaurice, A. Sebastian, and G. W. Characklis
489461.abstract: In the United States, substantial portions of flood damage occur among uninsured homes. This is, in part, because flood insurance is only required for homeowners within the FEMA-designated floodplain. Homeowners outside the floodplain still face risk from large events but may lack the knowledge or appetite to pay for a standard policy offered through the National Flood Insurance Program. Private flood insurance may be able to help cover this gap in insurance through marketing to preexisting clients, tailoring coverage to reduce premiums, and competition. The goal of this research is to model the performance of private flood insurance in North Carolina, one of the few states with an admitted flood insurance program which allows insight into regulator-approved pricing. We use a combination of premium prices provided by the North Carolina Rate Bureau, flood modeling, and address-level flood damage data to model the performance of policies at varying levels of coverage. Preliminary findings indicate that homeowners may obtain much of the benefit of flood insurance at a decreased cost through adjusting the terms of their policies. These findings may be used by regulators and legislators to encourage investment in admitted residential flood insurance policies by private insurers.

489462.title: Scaling Language Access: Engineering Reliable AI and Expanding Translation Services for World Cup 2026 and Beyond
489462.authors: Monica L Bozeman, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and H. Gorski, S. T. Halvorson, C. Martin, J. Schulz, J. Petr, C. Rohrbach, J. E. Calkins, and I. Blaylock
489462.abstract: The 2026 FIFA World Cup served as a pivotal opportunity for the National Weather Service (NWS) AI Translation Program to accelerate the maturation of its multilingual support capabilities for a high-visibility, international event. To mitigate the language barrier for life-saving weather information for international visitors, the NWS AI Language Translation Program quickly deployed four new language models—Arabic, German, Russian, and Portuguese—integrating them into the weather.gov/translate site and providing location-specific multilingual support across 12 NWS Weather Forecast Offices. Additionally, the Program implemented an automated translation capability within the NWS Decision Support Services (DSS) Builder tool, which empowered forecasters to instantly translate partner briefings, delivering life-saving multilingual weather information to emergency managers during match events. Beyond just releasing these additional languages to expand services, the Program desired reliable AI quality by subjecting the new and existing translation models to continuous performance monitoring and targeted training. Therefore, we built upon rigorous linguistic methodologies established in our previous work, and implemented and made the verification process more efficient to critically evaluate the performance of the language models. This presentation discusses the design of this verification process, detailing how automated skill scores and targeted model corrections allow forecasters to confidently deliver multilingual weather information to the public. In addition, we dive into findings from both our ongoing verification analysis and web traffic analytics during the events of the FIFA World Cup. Lessons learned from this exercise informed the future of NWS translation practices, including how to scale this framework for future initiatives and languages.

489463.title: Evaluating Global Forecast System (GFS) v17 Performance Using the NOAA/NWS office of Modeling and Development (OMD) Evaluation and Verification System (EVS) v2.0
489463.authors: Qi Shi, Lynker at NOAA/NWS/OMD, Madison, AL; and A. M. Bentley, S. R. Shields, L. Stefanova, T. R. Hultquist, M. P. Row, J. J. Levit, J. Meixner, C. A. Thomas, R. Sun, and S. Banihashemi
489463.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) plans to implement version 17 (v17) of the Global Forecast System (GFS). GFSv17 represents a significant advancement in operational global numerical weather prediction by introducing a fully coupled Earth-system modeling framework that integrates atmosphere, land, ocean, sea ice, and wave components. Model performance has been evaluated using the NOAA/NWS Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) Evaluation and Verification System (EVS) v2.0, which provides a comprehensive suite of statistical metrics and graphical products generated via the enhanced Model Evaluation Toolkit (METplus). Verification results are available on the GFSv17 official evaluation website to support both retrospective and real-time intercomparison between GFSv17 and GFSv16. Improvements in multiple areas are evident in the official evaluation. Results demonstrate that GFSv17 achieved statistically significant improvements over GFSv16 in anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC) for geopotential height during the retrospective period (3/1/2024–2/28/2026). Additionally, GFSv17 demonstrated statistically significantly higher CONUS 24-h QPF Equitable Threat Scores (ETS) across the majority of QPF thresholds, and lower Central Plains 2-m temperature RMSE at 00Z for Days 1–5 compared to GFSv16. The evaluation also identifies concerns for further development. For example, a comparison of CONUS-averaged surface-based CAPE values during the retrospective period reveals that while GFSv17 increased mean CAPE by approximately 20% relative to GFSv16, the mean values remain lower than observations. Overall, the evaluation indicates that GFSv17 provides improved forecast performance relative to GFSv16 across multiple verification metrics while identifying areas for continued model development.

489470.title: Identifying and Characterizing Dust Events Across the Columbia River Basin using Surface Meteorological Observation Data
489470.authors: Felicia Dogbey, Texas Tech University, LUBBOCK, TX; and K. Ardon-Dryer
489470.abstract: The Columbia River Basin includes many dry and semiarid areas where strong winds can produce dust events. Previous studies in this region have mostly focused on individual dust storms, wind erosion from agricultural land, or specific locations such as the Columbia Plateau. However, there is still limited information on the distribution, frequency, seasonality, duration, sources, and weather conditions of dust events across the wider Columbia River Basin. This study aims to develop a long-term dust event database for the Columbia River Basin using observations from 55 Automated Surface Observing System and Automated Weather Observing System stations across five states within the Columbia River Basin, with 17 stations each in Washington, Idaho, and Oregon, three stations in Montana, and one station in Wyoming.. Potential dust events were identified using reduced visibility below 10 km, wind speeds above 6 m s⁻¹, strong wind gusts, and reported weather codes, including DU for widespread dust, BLDU for blowing dust, HZ for haze, and DS for dust storm. A preliminary analysis was completed for the 17 stations in Washington State between 2000 and 2022. A total of 584 potential dust events were identified. Blowing dust was the most commonly reported dust-related weather code. Most events occurred during spring and summer, while fewer events were recorded during fall. Pasco recorded the highest number of dust events, with 107 events, followed by Walla Walla with 65 events and Spokane with 62 events. These preliminary results provide a starting point for extending the study to other parts of the Columbia River Basin. The completed database will help identify long-term changes, regional dust hotspots, possible dust-source areas, event duration, and the weather conditions linked to dust generation and transport.

489471.title: Resolving Uncertainty with Uncertainty: Developing a Probabilistic Outlook Graphic in the Watch-to-Warning Timeframe for NWS Bismarck
489471.authors: Cyrus Delconte, NOAA Hollings Scholar, Silver Spring, MD; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; OU Institute for Public Policy, Research, and Analysis, Norman, OK; and C. Schultz, S. R. Ernst, and M. Jones
489471.abstract: Many members of the public, communicators, and emergency responders require notice that extends beyond a typical severe thunderstorm or tornado warning in order to make crucial decisions and take necessary protective actions. The 30 minutes to 4 hours before warning issuance, often called the ‘watch-to-warning’ timeframe, begets considerable uncertainty both from a meteorological and communications standpoint. Because of the critical nature of this time frame, NWS forecasters aim to give these populations as much pertinent information and advanced lead time as possible for the protection of life and property. Previous literature on probabilistic communication has not specifically focused on this watch-to-warning timeframe; thus, a primary objective of the present work was to evaluate communication styles and strategies in this critical time period. This thought process led to the development of a product that will more effectively communicate storm risk areas and timelines for the watch-to-warning timeframe. Based on the operational needs of NWS meteorologists, previous research on the best visual and probabilistic communication methods, and input from emergency managers within the state, such a graphical product can be created and assessed when compared to currently operational products for social media and communications use. In order to create the first edition of prototypes for this product, literature review, survey work with emergency managers, and forecaster input were used. The survey, assessing a varied population of emergency managers in North Dakota, sought to understand their perceived level of risk for their jurisdiction, what actions they would be taking during the watch-to-warning timeframe, and what probabilistic thresholds they would need to take these actions for different hazards and severity levels. It also addressed the current NWS Bismarck watch-to-warning graphic. Upon acquiring results, the prototypes were made. These graphical prototypes aimed to discriminate in preferences between probabilistic information display, hazard display, and color, along with usefulness to North Dakota emergency managers. Focus groups with said emergency managers were the primary mechanism used to assess the efficacy of these prototypes. Focus group results agreed with both the literature and the survey results, with emergency managers preferring to use numerical probability information in the watch-to-warning timeframe. Despite this, there were many questions and uncertainties with the method of display of these numerical probabilities, which is an avenue that could be pursued by future research. Additionally, emergency managers preferred the red-orange-yellow, or ‘stoplight’, color palette for its urgency, with an interesting tendency to prefer different opacities based on forecaster confidence and closeness to the warning timeframe. Overall, participants preferred to have more information, not less, from the NWS. In fact, emergency managers indicated that almost all of the prototype graphics presented could serve some sort of use to them (with some graphics and findings preferred for communication outside of the severe convective space, as well). Through the synthesis of all gathered and researched information, revised graphical prototypes and other key communication recommendations were given to NWS Bismarck staff with the intention of operational implementation over time. Ultimately, the combined results of this project will allow for stronger communication from the NWS to critical and vulnerable audiences during severe convective events and will create a more weather-ready nation.

489472.title: From Points to Continuous Domains: Extending Physics-Informed AI to Improve CMORPH2 Orographic Precipitation Estimates
489472.authors: Yaping Li, Entarian, Greenbelt, MD; NOAA, College Park, MD; and P. Xie, S. Wu, and V. Kim
489472.abstract: Accurately monitoring precipitation over complex terrain remains a major challenge for satellite-based precipitation products. The second-generation Climate Prediction Center Morphing technique (CMORPH2) combines passive microwave precipitation retrievals from multiple low-Earth-orbiting satellites to provide precipitation estimates with high spatial and temporal resolution. Although CMORPH2 generally captures broad precipitation patterns, it often underestimates localized orographic enhancement and extreme precipitation over mountainous regions. We are developing a physics-informed artificial intelligence framework to improve CMORPH2 orographic precipitation estimates. Our earlier work began with a single-point model and was then extended to multiple locations across the western United States. These experiments demonstrated that atmospheric and terrain-related predictors provide important information that is not fully represented in satellite precipitation retrievals. The present study extends this approach from isolated points to a continuous regional domain over the western United States. The regional framework integrates CMORPH2 precipitation estimates, satellite infrared brightness temperatures, environmental fields from numerical models, and high-resolution terrain information derived from a digital elevation model. The model uses atmospheric and terrain variables that directly influence orographic precipitation, including low-level winds, moisture transport, terrain slopes, and the upslope movement of moist air. Time-lagged moisture-flux predictors are also included to capture the movement of upstream moisture toward mountainous regions before precipitation enhancement occurs. Initial point-based experiments show that adding atmospheric and terrain information improves precipitation timing and magnitude compared with using only CMORPH2 precipitation and infrared observations. Including information about moisture transport during the hours before an event further improves the estimates. Tests on independent events show that the model reduces CMORPH2 dry bias and improves event-total precipitation, although it still underestimates some localized extreme precipitation peaks. The regional model is designed to improve CMORPH2 orographic precipitation estimates across the western United States by learning the relationships among satellite observations, atmospheric conditions, terrain characteristics, and precipitation. The model will be trained and tested using separate winter seasons and atmospheric-river events. Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor precipitation estimates will be used as reference data where available. Model performance will be measured using correlation, bias, mean absolute error, root-mean-square error, accumulated precipitation, and statistics for different precipitation intensities. Permutation importance and other interpretation methods will be used to evaluate the contributions of individual atmospheric and terrain predictors. This study represents an important step toward developing a regional AI framework that can be applied operationally to improve CMORPH2 precipitation estimates over complex terrain.

489474.title: Capturing Spatiotemporal and Subgrid Variability in Global Snow Albedo Parameterization
489474.authors: Akarsh Ralhan, University of Maryland (UMD), College Park, MD; and X. Z. Liang
489474.abstract: Snow albedo is a fundamental control on the surface energy balance of snow-covered regions and strongly influences surface temperature, snowmelt timing, runoff, and land-atmosphere interactions. Through the snow albedo feedback, changes in snow surface reflectivity can substantially alter the absorption of solar radiation and propagate through the cryosphere, hydrological cycle, and climate system. Accurate representation of snow albedo is therefore essential for land surface and climate models, particularly during periods of snow accumulation, metamorphism, and seasonal melt. However, existing snow albedo parameterizations commonly rely on simplified empirical formulations that do not fully represent the coupled effects of snow grain evolution, snow depth, snow water equivalent, snow cover fraction, and vegetation masking. These limitations can lead to systematic biases in surface energy fluxes and the timing and magnitude of snowmelt. Here, we develop a physics-informed machine learning (ML) snow albedo parameterization using 19 years (2003 to 2021) of MODIS BRDF observations to predict direct and diffuse albedo in the visible and near-infrared spectral bands across diverse land cover categories (LCCs). The framework leverages cryospheric and biogeophysical predictors: solar geometry, snow cover fraction, snow water equivalent, canopy height, leaf area index, topography, and background climate as predictors. It consists of two components: a dynamic component (SNADC) that represents spatiotemporal variations in snow-covered surface reflectance and a static Snow Albedo Localization Factor (SNALF) that corrects persistent local biases associated with subgrid heterogeneity and snow-vegetation interactions. The combined parameterization reproduces MODIS snow albedo across LCCs and albedo components with an overall R2 of 0.81, MAPE of 4.9%, and RMSE of 0.023. SNALF consistently improves model performance, increasing R2 by 0.14 on average, reducing MAPE by approximately 2.1 percentage points, and decreasing RMSE by 0.01, with the largest improvements occurring for diffuse visible albedo. Feature importance analysis indicates that the dominant controls vary systematically among LCCs, with snow cover fraction and solar zenith angle emerging as the most influential predictors and vegetation characteristics, including canopy gap fraction, leaf area index, and canopy height, becoming particularly important in forested regions. Sensitivity and SHAP analyses further demonstrate physically coherent and LCC-dependent responses, including increasing albedo with snow cover fraction, canopy gap fraction, and solar zenith angle; decreasing albedo with leaf area index; and saturation with increasing snow water equivalent and snow depth. Interactive predictors such as snow depth relative to canopy height and snow depth multiplied by canopy gap fraction allow the framework to represent conditional processes such as snow burial and canopy masking that are difficult to capture with conventional single-variable empirical formulations. The parameterization is being integrated as a modular replacement for existing snow albedo schemes in the coupled regional climate model CWRF and is designed for straightforward implementation in other land surface modeling systems, including CLM, Noah-MP, and JULES.

489481.title: Sensitivity of Extreme Winter Warmth to Temperature Distribution Statistical Parameter Shifts
489481.authors: Alexander Friedman, Rutgers University, Morristown, NJ; and A. J. Broccoli
489481.abstract: Extreme wintertime warmth has distinct ecological, environmental and societal impacts. However, heat event studies in North America have been limited to the warm season, leaving a gap in the literature. Our research has determined that extreme wintertime warmth in North America, represented by exceedances above a warm tail threshold, has increased since 1950, with strong spatial variability existing in the magnitude of the trends. Using maximum daily temperature anomalies derived from the Berkeley Earth gridded dataset and ERA5 Land-Only reanalysis, we aim to quantify the impact of shifts in the statistical parameters of temperature distributions on the rate of change for these events. The shift in the central tendency, shape and spread will be examined, allowing us to better understand the differences between the original and new temperature distributions. A simple statistical model will be used to determine the contribution of central tendency, shape and spread to changes in the warm tail exceedance rate. We also aim to determine how shifts in large-scale meteorological patterns correlated with wintertime heat events influence their rate of occurrence and magnitude. Amplification and strengthening over time of geopotential height, sea level pressure and wind anomalies correlated with heat extremes may increase variability within the distribution.

489484.title: Forced Warming and Internal Variability in Idealized Quasi-Linear Convective System Organization
489484.authors: Megan E. Franke, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and K. L. Rasmussen and J. W. Hurrell
489484.abstract: Quasi-linear convective systems (QLCSs) produce much of the warm-season precipitation across the central United States while also generating hazards including hail, damaging winds, and flash flooding. Here, we use idealized simulations from the Cloud Model 1 (CM1) of a QLCS to evaluate how storm structure, behavior, and lifecycle may evolve due to climate change, and how those changes can be modulated by internal climate variability. To compare to an average climate change response, a control simulation (CTRL) is compared to a simulation perturbed with end-of-century temperature and moisture changes derived from the Community Earth System Model version 2 Large Ensemble (LENS2) 100-member mean, and to a third simulation (constant relative humidity; CRH) that applies the same temperature perturbation while holding relative humidity fixed at CTRL. Despite greater convective available potential energy, the LENS2 system fails to sustain convective initiation along the gust front and is slower to organize into a coherent line. The weaker convective organization results primarily from reduced relative humidity, which enhances entrainment of dry air and limits parcel buoyancy despite large CAPE. To assess how internal variability modulates this response, we force the CTRL sounding with the climate change signal from each individual LENS2 member, producing an ensemble of over 100 idealized squall-line simulations each representing a single plausible realization of the mid-century climate. The resulting spread in convective organization and precipitation is used to determine whether the moisture-limited response identified above is robust across plausible futures or whether some members diverge from it. These simulations isolate the roles of forced warming and internal variability in controlling future QLCS organization, precipitation, and associated hazards.

489485.title: NOAA/NESDIS Portfolio of LEO Precipitation Products and Future Plans
489485.authors: Huan Meng, NESDIS, College Park, MD
489485.abstract: NOAA/NESDIS operationally generates a set of satellite precipitation products that use observations from Low Earth Orbit (LEO) missions. These include the Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MIRS) Rain Rate, the Enterprise Microwave Rain Rate and Type (EMRRT), and the Snowfall Rate (SFR) products. MIRS RR is based on a 1DVAR physical inversion algorithm. EMRRT is derived from a Bayesian algorithm (GPROF), and SFR combines a 1DVAR-based algorithm with machine learning (ML) models. Each product is produced from multiple satellites operated by NOAA and/or its domestic and international partner agencies. These Level-2 products, whether used directly or as inputs to downstream Level-3 products, support a wide range of weather and hydrological applications. NESDIS continues algorithm development to ensure its precipitation algorithms remain scientifically robust and operationally viable. Ongoing research develops AI/ML-based algorithms and integrates AI/ML with physics-based retrieval methods to improve precipitation detection, retrieval accuracy, and computational efficiency. NESDIS is also expanding its algorithms to support new and future satellite missions and sensors, such as JPSS-4 ATMS, Metop-SG A1 MWS, and Metop-SG B1 MWI, enabling a seamless transition as the observing system evolves. In parallel, NESDIS is evaluating the use of commercial satellite observations to complement NOAA's backbone operational missions. Together, these efforts ensure the continuity and resilience of NESDIS's operational precipitation products while providing reliable, state-of-the-art information to support weather forecasting, hydrological applications, and other environmental decision-making. Besides its emphasis on scientific development, NESDIS is also working to enhance its user services. One example is the development of a centralized satellite precipitation product portal, PrecipWatch. The portal will generate and display all NESDIS precipitation products to support NWS precipitation nowcasting. To achieve the low latency required for NWS operations, the system will rely on direct broadcast data and operate in the cloud to ensure reliability and ease of access. Services such as PrecipWatch will enhance the application of NOAA’s satellite products and maximize their societal benefits. This presentation will introduce NESDIS's precipitation portfolio, summarize ongoing efforts including algorithm development for JPSS-4 and Metop-SG A1 and B1, and outline future development plans aligned with upcoming missions at NOAA, its partner agencies, and commercial entities.

489488.title: Why are Observed Droplet Spectra Wide in Adiabatic Volumes of Natural Clouds?
489488.authors: Wojciech W. Grabowski, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and K. K. Chandrakar and H. Morrison
489488.abstract: The observed widths of droplet spectra in adiabatic volumes of natural clouds have been a cloud physics conundrum from the early days of in-situ cloud observations. Observed spectral widths are often in the range of 1 to 2 µm, whereas adiabatic parcel calculations suggest widths up to only a few tenths of 1 µm. Part of the problem comes from artificial spectral broadening by at least some airborne measuring devices, but recent observations (e.g., from HOLODEC) show spectra wider than predicted by adiabatic parcel ascent. Turbulence has long been considered a possible mechanism for spectral broadening, with the mechanism referred to as stochastic condensation or eddy hopping. The key idea is that, in a turbulent environment, droplets follow different trajectories and this leads to different droplet activation and growth histories. To study droplet spectra observed at a given location within an adiabatic volume of a natural cloud one needs to consider droplet trajectories arriving at that location. We use results from simulations applying a 3D dynamic cloud model, a 1D updraft model (for cumulus), and 2D overturning eddy model (for stratocumulus) to study droplet formation and growth in adiabatic volumes of natural clouds. All these models feature Lagrangian particle–based microphysics (the superdroplet method; Shima et al. QJ 2009) that by design allow following individual droplet trajectories. 1D and 2D models either exclude or include the effects of turbulence. The overall conclusion is that turbulence can explain larger adiabatic spectral widths in simulated clouds. The turbulence impact is moderate for polluted clouds, but spectral widths in pristine conditions are up to several times larger than those without turbulence. The difference comes from a larger magnitude of supersaturation fluctuations for the same vertical velocity fluctuations because of larger phase relaxation times in pristine conditions. These results suggest the following question: Is the concept of an “adiabatic parcel” still useful when turbulence is present? The answer is “maybe” from the thermodynamics point of view, but clearly “no” when cloud microphysics is the focus.

489491.title: Preparing for ENSO: Communicating Risks and Impacts to the Ski and Retail Sector
489491.authors: Sydney Luce, The Cadmus Group, Silver Spring, MD; and A. Zycherman, H. Campbell, A. Crimmins, and Z. Paganini
489491.abstract: Extreme weather and climate events can be disruptive to industries, disrupting logistics chains, shifting operational days, and affecting bottom lines. NOAA is working to improve service delivery to industry partners to support economic resilience in response to a variety of hazards. Through a collaboration between NOAA’s Adaptation Sciences Program in the Climate Program Office and the Industry Partnerships program, we developed innovative resources to communicate immediate and future risks of El Niño and the Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events, including this year’s predictions. We explore potential impacts on two key sectors likely to be affected, the ski industry and the retail sector. ENSO events can lead to a variety of hazards and risks, including drought, heat, heavy precipitation, wildfires, flooding, and landslides. These hazards can cause major damage to the ski and retail sectors, particularly in the U.S. West, and impacts can shift over time. Building on a series of engagements and co-development of data resources with these industries, this work continues to support risk informed decision making in ways that meet those sectors' needs. This presentation will discuss the ongoing work with these two sectors, past engagements that have shaped how knowledge is disseminated, and how this information is used to inform decision making amongst practitioners. We will also discuss how timely ENSO-related information can be used to support preparedness and build economic resilience among the sectors and why risk and impact-oriented communication can be effective tools to support adaptive work.

489494.title: Closing Observation Gaps: Assimilating Deep Learning–Infilled Streamflow Records for CONUS-Scale Streamflow Prediction
489494.authors: Ganesh R Ghimire, ORNL, Oak Ridge, TN; and S. C. Kao and S. Gangrade
489494.abstract: Stream gauges provide the most reliable observations of streamflow. Continuous, long-term streamflow records are essential for a wide range of applications, including water resources planning and management, flood risk management, hydrologic modeling and forecasting, data assimilation, resilience planning, and large-scale resource assessments. However, many regions, including large portions of the conterminous United States (CONUS), remain sparsely monitored or lack continuous streamflow records because of topographic complexity, limited resources, and gauge maintenance challenges. To address these observational gaps, we implement a deep learning framework that leverages catchment memory—represented by streamflow persistence, river network connectivity, and meteorological forcings—to reconstruct missing streamflow records at U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) gauge locations. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks are trained and evaluated using "pseudo-gauge" experiments, in which complete streamflow records are artificially truncated to assess predictive skill. Three LSTM configurations are examined: (1) an individual basin model trained using upstream–downstream gauge pairs, (2) a large-sample hydrology model using conventional static basin attributes, and (3) a large-sample hydrology model using AlphaEarth Embeddings. Daily precipitation and air temperature from Daymet are used as dynamic forcing variables for all model configurations. Predictive performance is evaluated across more than 10,000 stream gauge pairs throughout the CONUS. Results demonstrate a strong dependence of predictive skill on the monitored area fraction (the ratio of upstream to downstream drainage areas), with median Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) values exceeding 0.8 when the monitored area fraction is greater than 0.4. The two large-sample LSTM models exhibit strong generalizability and perform well in previously unseen basins. Applying the best-performing approach, we reconstruct complete streamflow records for more than 700 additional USGS gauges with at least 50% data availability, increasing the number of complete daily streamflow records from approximately 3,000 to more than 3,700 for the 1980–2024 period. Incorporating these infilled records into the Dayflow streamflow reanalysis provides additional data assimilation constraints and improves streamflow prediction across the CONUS. This study demonstrates that deep learning can effectively bridge observational gaps while enhancing continental-scale streamflow predictability, providing a valuable foundation for hydrologic modeling, water resources management, and robust long-term water and energy resource planning.

489495.title: The GOES XRS Solar Flare Report: 30+ Years of Historical Solar Flare Data
489495.authors: Elysia Salvo Lucas, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and J. Machol, A. M. Mahon, and J. Mothersbaugh III
489495.abstract: The NOAA NCEI Solar and Terrestrial Physics (STP) Group has published a new composite solar flare report data product. Since the 1970s, X-ray Sensor (XRS) instruments on GOES satellites have monitored two bands of soft X-rays. They provide the operational measurements that define solar flare class, and are used for forecasting space weather events. The flare report is an aggregation of unique flares from multiple GOES satellites. It includes flare timing, magnitudes, and locations on the solar disk determined from science-quality reprocessed GOES XRS data, as well as flare locations from ground-based observatories and active region numbers (from the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center). The flare report covers 1995 to present (GOES 8-19), and is available in both NetCDF and CSV formats. GOES 1-7 data will be added early next year, adding coverage between 1975 and 1995.

489498.title: Aerosol Data Assimilation at GMAO: Latest Developments and the Transition to a JEDI System.
489498.authors: Virginie Buchard, GMAO, Greenbelt, MD; UMBC, Baltimore, MD; NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and R. Todling, P. Castellanos, M. Abdioskouei, A. S. Darmenov, and A. da Silva
489498.abstract: At NASA’s Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO), continuous advancements are being made to the aerosol data assimilation (DA) capabilities within the Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) model. As part of this ongoing evolution, the aerosol observing system has recently been expanded to include Neural Network Retrieval (NNR) Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) at 550 nm from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS). In addition, the GMAO aerosol DA framework is currently undergoing a major structural transition from the legacy Physical-space Statistical Analysis System (PSAS) to the JCSDA Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) system. This presentation highlights the technical developments and impacts of transitioning to the JEDI framework. A central focus of this upgrade is the shift from a two-dimensional PSAS analysis to a three-dimensional ensemble-variational (3D-EnVar) approach in JEDI. To support this, the input NNR AOD observations have been adapted into the Interface for Observation Data Access (IODA) format. Additionally, a Unified Forward Operator (UFO) has been developed utilizing extinction profiles as the control variable. Because AOD is a 2D column-integrated observation, transitioning to a 3D-EnVar solver allows the system to leverage 3D model background covariances and flow-dependent correlations derived from the GEOS meteorological ensemble. This effectively projects the 2D observation increments into a more realistic vertical distribution within the model background. Initially, the JEDI system will assimilate AOD at 550 nm to provide a direct benchmark and comparison against the operational PSAS system. This baseline evaluation paves the way for a planned transition to a multi-wavelength aerosol assimilation system. We will examine how this new 3D-EnVar assimilation influences global aerosol distributions and overall system performance. The impact will be demonstrated through innovation statistics and verification against independent ground-based datasets, including AERONET observations.

489499.title: Updates on the the Science Data Products Calibration and Validation for the NOAA LEO Missions
489499.authors: Lihang Zhou, ; and S. Iacovazzi, I. C. Paluch, and J. A. Weinrich
489499.abstract: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) observations are essential for advancing weather forecasting, environmental monitoring, and public safety. The paper provides a comprehensive update on the science data products Calibration and Validation (Cal/Val) activities for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)’s Low Earth Orbit (LEO) missions, managed by the NESDIS Office of LEO Observations. A primary focus of the LEO missions are currently the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS)-4 (to be renamed NOAA-22 in orbit), which is scheduled for launch in 2027; and the QuickSounder mission to be launched in mid-2027. We will present the mission's comprehensive Cal/Val strategy, covering pre-launch algorithm readiness and testing, as well as the detailed post-launch science Cal/Val plans and product timeline. Furthermore, we will highlight the Cal/Val progress achieved for recently launched partnership missions, such as the Weather System Follow-on Microwave (WSF-M), GOSAT-GW/AMSR3, and Arctic Weather Satellite (AWS). Finally, we discuss the strategic development of NOAA’s next generation Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) science Cal/Val framework, ensuring the integrity and quality of data products from both current and upcoming LEO platforms.

489501.title: Evaluation of Model Precipitation for Point-Based Locations
489501.authors: Alex Zielinski, University of Illinois of at Urbana/Champaign, River Forest, IL; and A. Tokay, C. N. Helms, S. D. Nicholls, D. B. Wolff, J. L. Pippitt, and B. Filipiak
489501.abstract: Precipitation forecasting has fundamental importance on daily activities. Public demand a response to two-to-three sequential questions: Is it going to rain and how much? In winter, a third question will be the precipitation phase. The weather forecasting models, which depend on data assimilation, model physics, initialization, and spatial and temporal resolution, are the source of precipitation forecasting. Public is aware of highly spatiotemporal variable nature of precipitation, but still seeks amount of precipitation falling in at a given location. Given the fact that more than a dozen forecasting models are available, it is imperative to evaluate the performance of these models against a ground reference, a main objective of this study. The NASA’s Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission Ground Validation (GPM-GV) program has been deploying Platforms for In-Situ Estimation Rainfall Systems (PIERS) at various locations across the US since late 2023. This study uses nine (9) PIERS+ sites, which include a PARSIVEL distrometer and dual tipping bucket gauges, for the calendar year of 2024. The sites are primarily in the Mid Atlantic, with two sites in Texas and one in Colorado at higher elevation. The PARSIVEL disdrometer was the reference for the event definitions as well as event duration, and rainfall intensity, while one of the tipping bucket gauges served as the reference for rainfall amount. While previous validation studies were based on fixed time scale (e.g. hour, day, month), this study investigates the event rainfall, a novel aspect of this study. As a caveat, the findings of this study are limited to the PIERS+ sites and study period. This study evaluates on the performance of four models: the High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model, the North American Mesoscale (NAM) model, the National Severe Storms Laboratory Model for Prediction Across Scales (NSSL-MPAS) model, and the National Severe Storms Laboratory Weather Research and Forecast (NSSL-WRF) model. These models provide hourly forecasts at 3km resolution, but their initialization frequency ranges from once every hour (HRRR) to every six hours (NAM), to every 12 hours (MAPS, WRF). It should be noted that PIERS+ is not part of any operational algorithm and therefore provides independent evaluation. This study follows a farmer’s approach, meaning that it does not invest the model production stage. Overall, the HRRR outperformed the other three models, but missed 25% of the rain event, and had a 29% dry bias, 53% error, and 0.76 correlation. The remaining three models missed about 40% of the events, resulting substantial differences in biases when missed rain events included or excluded from the statistics. The mean absolute errors were about 20% higher and correlations were about 15% lower in these three models. It is concluded that the initialization played a key role on model performances. All four models performed better for higher accumulation, longer duration, moderate rain intensity in contrast to lower accumulations, shorter durations, and light and heavy rain intensities. These sub-categorical performances are important for evaluating the models in flash and river flooding. The research project was conducted under NASA Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission, George Huffman, Project Scientist, Will McCarty, Program Scientist. The leading author was sponsored by the National Science Foundation, grant number 2349543, project title: REU Site: EXPeriments in Earth and Atmospheric Science: Learning Opportunities and Research Experience (EXPLORE).

489505.title: Architecting a NWS Data Lakehouse for Unified Meteorological Services
489505.authors: Kari L. Sheets, NWS, Bohemia, NY; and P. Kirkwood, J. Callaway, and R. Henry-Reeves
489505.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) is executing a paradigm shift in its operational infrastructure to support an increasingly agile, untethered workforce and a rapidly growing weather enterprise. Historically, meteorological, hydrological, satellite, and radar data feeds have been processed through fragmented, localized architectures resulting in severe data-duplication overhead, limited remote forecaster portability, and latencies in critical decision support. The NWS is architecting NWS CIRRUS as the foundational cloud-based data lakehouse engineered to establish a "One-NWS" framework: storing multi-dimensional environmental data once and utilizing it infinitely across a diverse ecosystem of downstream applications and application programming interfaces (APIs). Architecturally, CIRRUS converges the massive storage capacity of data lakes with the transactional integrity and query optimization of data warehouses. By implementing advanced cloud-native data-versioning layers, CIRRUS guarantees strict high availability and continuous data consistency under intense, time-sensitive operational workloads. CIRRUS democratizes public and commercial access to gold-standard weather data utilizing FAIR data principles (i.e., Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) while also accelerating the research-to-operations (R2O) cycle and facilitating the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML). Ultimately, NWS CIRRUS represents the modern core of a resilient, scalable, and highly collaborative federal weather infrastructure designed to protect lives and property in an era of accelerating environmental extremes.

489509.title: Lightning-NOx Production As Determined Using 10-Minute Temporal Resolution Scans from TEMPO
489509.authors: Dale J. Allen, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and E. Bucsela, K. E. Pickering, and J. Lapierre
489509.abstract: Lightning produces nitrogen oxides (NOx) as the extreme temperatures within lightning channels break apart molecular nitrogen (N2) and oxygen (O2). NOx produced by lightning (LNOx) plays an important role in determining mid- and upper-tropospheric concentrations of the hydroxyl radical (OH), methane (CH4), and ozone (O3). In this study, the moles of LNOx produced per lightning flash/group (production efficiency, PE) and its uncertainty will be estimated using 10-minute temporal resolutions scans taken during July 2026 from the TEMPO instrument, flash counts from the Geostationary Lightning Mapper, and flash counts from the Earth Networks Total Lightning Network. The approach is Lagrangian and assumes that the PE is proportional to scan-to-scan changes in the vertical column density (VCD) of NOx divided by scan-to-scan changes in flashes, where the VCD of NOx is obtained by dividing the TEMPO-retrieved median change in tropospheric slant column density over deep convective grid cells by a specially prepared air mass factor.

489510.title: Eyes on the Ice: Leveraging Satellite Imagery to Support U.S. National Ice Center Partners’ Navigation of Icy Waters
489510.authors: Kevin Berberich, NWS Ocean and Tsunami Center (U.S. National Ice Center), Hillcrest Heights, MD; and W. Clark, J. Edwards-Opperman, D. Helmricks, C. Gerland, J. Voveris, S. Taylor, L. Mallory, and R. Sale
489510.abstract: During the 2025–26 Northern Hemisphere winter season, the U.S. National Ice Center (USNIC) generated more than 3,400 operational ice products in support of the U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), National Weather Service (NWS) Forecast Offices, and emergency management personnel across the Great Lakes and Mid-Atlantic regions. A prolonged, cold-air outbreak and multiple winter storm events increased demand for timely ice analysis and forecasting products, resulting in the production of 712 Impact-based Decision Support Service (IDSS) products. High-resolution satellite imagery played a critical role in these efforts, allowing analysts to monitor ice formation, concentration, and extent in areas of concern and provide timely, actionable information to support operational decision-making. USNIC analysts integrated high-resolution synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery into most operational workflows to monitor rapid ice growth, improve situational awareness, and enhance decision support services during significant winter weather events this past season. Through regional examples from the 2025–26 season, this presentation demonstrates how leveraging multi-source SAR imagery enhances situational awareness, optimizes tactical maritime navigation, and establishes a new operational benchmark for mid-latitude ice charting and partner support. Future efforts will prioritize improving operational support through standardized product templates while incorporating lessons learned from a season of elevated operational activity. The presentation will also discuss challenges in acquiring and utilizing high-resolution imagery and how addressing these challenges can strengthen future ice analysis and decision support.

489516.title: Beyond Knowledge Transfer: Designing Programs for Cross-Sector Climate Resilience Education
489516.authors: Lucinda J. Shellito, University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO; and A. Virapongse, S. Bywater-Reyes, C. Romulo, and R. Gupta
