489516.abstract: Place-based climate resilience emerges through sustained collaboration among diverse groups and stakeholders, yet most climate education remains focused on knowledge transfer rather than on the infrastructure needed to make that collaboration possible. University students are future leaders in community climate resilience, but most coursework does not equip them for the realities of cross-sector work. To support workforce development, students also need experience working with diverse partners, skills for navigating the psychological and emotional toll of climate work, and a toolkit for communicating across differences in background, culture, generation, and expertise. Faculty face a parallel challenge. The potential to bring climate change education into every discipline is significant, but most educators have neither the training nor the cross-sectoral connections to act on it. Community organizations, meanwhile, often engage with universities in a temporary way, without building lasting capacity. COOLER CLImates was a pilot program designed to build that capacity, and this abstract reports on what we learned about designing and sustaining the program. COOLER (Community Collaboration and Learning for Climate Resilience) is an NSF-funded initiative at the University of Northern Colorado (NSF Award #2228170) aimed at building a local learning ecosystem for climate resilience. COOLER’s Climate Leadership Initiative (“COOLER CLImates”) was COOLER’s nine-month flagship program from September 2024 through April 2025, designed to connect university students and faculty with community organizations in northern Colorado. The pilot recruited three parallel cohorts: 10 university students, 10 faculty from a wide range of disciplines (including Anthropology, Chemistry, Math, Biology, Music, Political Science, and Nursing), and 11 community partners representing local organizations working on climate-related issues. The three cohorts met independently and together across the program year, with monthly all-cohort virtual sessions focused on professional development. Participants were encouraged to form cross-cohort project teams to address local resilience needs. Their work resulted in 11 collaborative projects aimed at supporting community climate resilience. Drawing on brown’s idea of emergent strategy, COOLER CLImates was designed such that the program structure would arise from the needs of a group, rather than imposed from above. CLImates prioritized relationship-building over prescribed outcomes and trusted that meaningful projects would emerge from connections participants formed with one another. CLImates aimed to create a sustained, trust-based collaborative space across sectors and activate participants as co-creators. The COOLER Leader Team provided facilitation, structure, and a container for that work. The direction and energy for projects came from the participants, and this is where the program’s most instructive moments emerged. A community of practice framework informed understanding of how the CLImates collaborative was learning and working together. Evaluation data, including pre- and post-surveys, formative questionnaires, and focus group interviews conducted by an external evaluator, revealed several cross-cutting themes that reflect both the promise and the practical challenges of the model used. The most significant conceptual shift observed across all three cohorts was a reframing of resilience itself. Participants entered the program thinking about resilience primarily in terms of physical infrastructure and technical solutions. By the end of the program, they consistently defined it as personal strength, emotional persistence, and the capacity to build community. A second major theme was the program’s success in reducing isolation among those interested in climate action. Faculty, students and community partners all reported that belonging to a supportive community of practice increased their motivation and provided space to process the grief and anxiety that often accompanies climate work. Over the course of the program, participants transitioned from immediate value (meeting peers and building awareness) to applied value (integrating program lessons into their professional work.) Faculty incorporated climate modules into their courses, and student leaders gained marketable skills in community activation, communication, and project management. The program also surfaced instructive limitations. Collaborative projects suffered from slow starts. Without clearly defined tasks and early milestones, some participants disengaged during the first half of the program. Communication across cohorts was persistently difficult. Students were sometimes difficult to reach via university email, creating gaps in momentum between meetings. While virtual sessions provided necessary flexibility, participants consistently reported that they were insufficient for building the depth of trust the program required, recommending more in-person interaction, particularly early in the program year. We found that while an emergent strategy approach empowers participant-driven work, more scaffolding is required to get to that point. Despite the challenges, CLImates produced tangible outcomes across all three cohorts. Participants completed projects that directly addressed local climate resilience needs, including a community workshop on health impacts of air quality, development of middle-school curricula focused on sustainable practices and waste reduction, establishment of an art supply reuse initiative, and a public education campaign addressing single-use plastics. Participant feedback highlighted the value of structured, facilitated dialogue across the different cohorts. Students reported increased confidence translating climate risks into community-relevant action. Faculty gained experience integrating climate topics into diverse disciplinary contexts. Community partners appreciated having the opportunity to establish new connections within the university and reported stronger understanding of how climate change intersects with their work. The lessons from CLImates informed the design of COOLER BLAST (Building Lasting Resilience), a one-semester student program offered in Fall 2025. BLAST incorporated the most effective CLImates professional development activities into a streamlined format requiring significantly less PI time and funding. This offered a proof of concept for how this model can be sustained beyond initial grant funding. A pilot workshop for K-12 teachers, offered in Summer 2026 with the support of the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment, extended the COOLER learning ecosystem to middle and high school teachers. Together, these programs suggest a replicable model for institutions seeking to integrate community-engaged, resilience-focused collaboration into climate education and outreach. The core insight is that emergent, participant-driven climate work is possible within academic institutions, but it requires intentional scaffolding, dedicated facilitation, and structured space for participants to develop effective collaborative relationships and process the emotional dimensions of climate work alongside the practical ones. The CLImates and BLAST programs offer tested, replicable frameworks, and a set of operational lessons for institutions ready to implement community-based climate education in the classroom.

489520.title: Fine-Tuning the Prithvi-WxC Foundation Model for NASA’s Next-Generation Downscaled Climate Product
489520.authors: Hugo Kyo Lee, JPL, Pasadena, CA; and M. S. Johnson and J. B. Roberts
489520.abstract: High-resolution regional climate information is essential for assessing climate risks and supporting adaptation and resilience planning. However, producing and updating high-resolution climate datasets through dynamical downscaling across multiple variables, regions, models, and scenarios remains computationally demanding. We present a multi-center NASA effort to develop a next-generation, machine-learning-based climate downscaling product using NASA’s Prithvi-WxC foundation model. The collaboration brings together the Regional Climate Model Evaluation System team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, the NASA Earth Exchange team at Ames Research Center, and the EarthRISE team at Marshall Space Flight Center. The initial prototype uses a selectively fine-tuned Prithvi-WxC encoder with a U-Net-style convolutional decoder to map coarse-resolution atmospheric predictors to high-resolution daily precipitation and maximum and minimum temperatures. We currently downscale North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR) data from approximately 32 km to the 800-m Parameter-elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) grid. The model was trained using data from 1996–2015 and evaluated over the independent 2016–2025 period. The resulting downscaled fields reproduce the broad coast–mountain–interior climatological patterns in precipitation and temperature. Because deterministic downscaling can retain systematic biases and suppress unresolved fine-scale variability, we are also developing a conditional stochastic refinement head that is applied to the Prithvi-UNet output. This refinement stage is designed to correct residual biases, improve the representation of spatial variability and extremes, and generate probabilistic ensembles while preserving the large-scale physical patterns captured by the foundation model. The collaboration establishes complementary roles across the three NASA centers. Together, the teams are developing a reproducible workflow for model training, evaluation, refinement, scalable production, and dissemination, providing a pathway from a research prototype to a validated and scalable NASA downscaled climate product.

489525.title: Multi-Ignition Fires Fuel Pyrocumulonimbus Storms In Canada’s Extreme Fire Seasons (Invited Presentation)
489525.authors: Rebecca C. Scholten, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA; and T. Banerjee, Y. Chen, A. Delgado, A. S. Desai, Z. Ke, T. Liu, D. Morton, D. A. Peterson, Q. Tang, S. Veraverbeke, J. Zhang, and J. Randerson
489525.abstract: Boreal wildfires are a critical and growing source of aerosols and trace gases with wide-ranging impacts on global climate and air quality. The largest impacts on ecosystems and humans are often caused by episodes of extreme fire behavior. Such extreme behavior can manifest in pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) storms, fire-induced thunderstorms that in turn fuel fires through lightning-ignited spot fires and strong wind bursts, creating hazardous and unpredictable conditions for firefighters. Yet the bottom-up fire processes, in particular fire behavior, governing pyroCb development remain poorly constrained. Current approaches largely emphasize atmospheric preconditions and treat fire radiative power as a bulk intensity proxy. Canada has experienced four consecutive record-breaking fire seasons since 2023, with a global pyroCb inventory recording 143 pyroCbs in Canada in 2023, 57 in 2024, and 74 in 2025, underscoring pyroCb activity as a persistent feature of boreal fire regimes. These consecutive extreme seasons provide a valuable opportunity to assess how multi-ignition dynamics and fire-atmosphere feedbacks shape fire activity and associated aerosol loading across the boreal domain. Using 12-hour satellite-derived fire tracking data from the Arctic-boreal Fire Atlas combined with a global pyroCb inventory, we show that fire-merging dynamics are closely linked to pyroCb development in boreal North America and Russia. Multi-ignition fires, or fire complexes, arise from multiple distinct ignition points that grow together and contribute disproportionately to large fire seasons and extreme fire behavior. We found that 67% of pyroCbs in Canada and Russia were associated with multi-ignition fires. Notably, 53% of pyroCbs over multi-ignition fires occurred within three days of a merging event, with 22% occurring on the day of merging itself. Fire line merging can thus increase the surface area with high sensible heat fluxes needed to trigger deep convection and generate rotating convective columns that drive pyroconvection. PyroCbs in turn produce high-based dry lightning that can ignite new spot fires tens of kilometers from the fire front, closing a positive feedback loop that may amplify extreme fire behavior and spread. Subdaily fire tracking data offer a promising observational tool to trace this feedback by linking merging events to subsequent pyroCb-induced ignition clusters. Understanding pyroCb development is essential for predicting extreme fire behavior and supporting the safety and efficacy of firefighting operations

489527.title: Development of a Deep Learning Precipitation Nowcasting System for CONUS
489527.authors: Thomas M. Hamill, The Weather Company, Boulder, CO; and M. Vicens-Miquel, M. L. Flora, A. McGovern, and A. J. Hill
489527.abstract: High-resolution precipitation nowcasting is essential for supporting operational decision-making across weather-sensitive sectors, including aviation, transportation, emergency management, and energy. Although numerical weather prediction (NWP) models have steadily improved, accurately forecasting rapidly evolving precipitation at fine spatial and temporal scales remains challenging because of the nonlinear evolution of precipitation systems and the computational constraints associated with real-time forecasting. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, particularly diffusion models, offer the potential to better capture small-scale precipitation structures while reducing the overly smooth forecasts commonly produced by deterministic deep learning models. This study presents the development of an operational diffusion-based precipitation nowcasting system for the contiguous United States (CONUS) through a collaboration between the University of Oklahoma's NSF AI2ES AI Institute and The Weather Company (TWC). The proposed framework generates precipitation rate forecasts every six minutes, with lead times ranging from 6 minutes to 2 hours, at 1-km spatial resolution over the entire CONUS. The model leverages recent Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) precipitation observations together with sub-hourly High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) forecasts to combine observational information with numerical weather prediction guidance. The framework investigates the contribution of additional predictor variables, including HRRR-derived fields, spatial coordinates, temporal information, and topographic features, to identify the optimal model configuration. The nowcasting system employs diffusion-based autoregressive rollouts to model the temporal evolution of precipitation, enabling high-frequency forecasts while maintaining spatial coherence at successive lead times. Model development focuses on maximizing forecast skill while satisfying the computational efficiency and reliability requirements necessary for real-time operational deployment. Performance is evaluated across the full CONUS domain using deterministic and spatial verification metrics, with particular emphasis on forecast accuracy during significant precipitation events. Preliminary evaluation indicates promising improvements in forecast skill relative to both pySTEPS and sub-hourly HRRR guidance, motivating continued model refinement and comprehensive validation prior to operational deployment. The ultimate objective and next step of this collaboration is to transition the developed nowcasting system into TWC's operational forecasting infrastructure if it demonstrates improved forecast skill and operational reliability compared with existing forecasting approaches. Beyond advancing short-term precipitation prediction, this work explores the feasibility of diffusion-based generative models for continental-scale, real-time weather forecasting and establishes a foundation for future operational AI nowcasting systems.

489533.title: Downstream Effects of Re-curving Tropical Cyclones on Large-Scale Atmospheric Circulation Under Global Warming Conditions
489533.authors: Jackie Aguilar-Delgado, Hampton University, Hampton, VA; and S. R. Guimond
489533.abstract: Over the past century, the Earth has experienced a rise in global temperatures as a result of climate change. The effects of this trend are highlighted in locations like the Arctic, where the warming in this region is increasing at a faster rate than the global average. This amplified warming, also known as Arctic amplification, could have an impact on large-scale atmospheric circulation. Previous work has concluded that Arctic amplification would lead to a reduction of the global temperature gradient that exists between the poles and the equator. The consequences of this would be weaker upper-level flow and weaker atmospheric jets in the mid-latitudes, therefore disrupting current global weather patterns. To explore this phenomenon further, this work utilizes the Model for Predication Across Scales (MPAS) to understand the impact that climate change can have on the downstream effects of a re-curving tropical cyclone as it interacts with mid-latitude flow. A “base-state” case that reflects current climate conditions is compared to a future atmosphere case that has experienced Arctic amplification in order to quantify the impact that climate change would have on these downstream effects. From preliminary results, we expect for Arctic amplification to reduce mid-latitude cyclones that are responsible for the 5-7 day weather outside of the tropics in the future as well as lessen any downstream effects that come from interactions of re-curving tropical cyclones with the mid-latitude flow. With the continued changes in climate, it becomes increasingly relevant to understand these effects so predictions can be made that could protect life and property from the implications that shifting weather patterns could have on society, politics, and the environment.

489534.title: AI Forecast Ensembles Can Achieve Positive Marginal Skill While Misrepresenting the Joint Spatial Structure
489534.authors: Lucas Howard, Boston University, Boston, MA; and E. A. Barnes
489534.abstract: Weather forecasting has increasingly moved towards expanded use of efficient and skillful MLWP models which, among other things, allow for large forecast ensembles and high fidelity uncertainty quantification. Whether AI forecast ensembles do this correctly in a joint rather than just marginal sense remains largely untested, however. In several examples covering both a small regional test as well as idealized system experiments, we show that AI emulators may endemically fail to correctly reproduce the full multivariate uncertainty structure. Using a diffusion model for probabilistic subseasonal sea level forecasts we find that marginal and joint forecast quality decouple: positive skill at every station and lead time marginally, while joint spatial structure is worse than random climatological draws. A shuffle-based permutation decomposition reveals this failure is invisible to the energy score but detected by the variogram score. Lorenz-96 experiments across 0.7-170 equivalent years show the gap persists regardless of training volume and is reproduced by a linear baseline, indicating structural inadequacy of the learned distribution. A dynamical ensemble does not replicate the failure while a deterministic emulator does, suggesting it is specific to learned emulators rather than ensemble forecasting generally. Our results suggest that even as MLWP systems continue to improve on standard skill metrics, their full joint structures should be examined and advances in training methodology explored to address this potential failure mode.

489535.title: Enhancing the PCMDI Metrics Package (PMP) for Community-Driven Evaluation of Earth System Models
489535.authors: Jiwoo Lee, LLNL, Livermore, CA; Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, CA; and K. Chang, J. Goodnight, P. Gleckler, P. A. Ullrich, S. Zhang, Y. Planton, A. Jonko, M. Velez Pardo, W. Weijer, Y. Lee, J. Caron, I. Hur, C. Yoo, J. Choi, G. Pallotta, and C. Bonfils
489535.abstract: Earth System Models (ESMs) are essential for understanding the physical climate system and informing policy decisions, and their systematic evaluation depends on shared, community-accessible infrastructure. This presentation focuses on the PCMDI Metrics Package (PMP), an open-source, Python-based framework designed for objective "quick-look" comparisons and benchmarking of ESMs against observations. The PMP has been used to evaluate thousands of simulations from successive phases of Coupled Model Intercomparison Projects (CMIPs), covering regional-to-global climatology, tropical and extra-tropical modes of variability, ENSO, MJO, regional monsoons, and sea-ice and ocean states. Over the past year, PMP has undergone substantial infrastructure modernization to strengthen its role as community-shared evaluation infrastructure. The package completed its transition away from the legacy CDAT library to a fully xarray/xCDAT-based analysis stack, alongside migration to modern Python packaging (pyproject.toml) and support for Python 3.11 and higher, improving long-term maintainability and interoperability with other community tools. PMP has also been expanding its standard Python API, improving usability and flexibility for users integrating the package into their own analysis workflows. New capabilities introduced during this period include a PMP Viewer API for interactive exploration of results, automated EOF-based classification with sign-inversion detection for teleconnection pattern analysis, two additional extratropical modes of variability including East Atlantic (EA), Scandinavian (SCA) and Pacific-South America (PSA) patterns, and new sea-ice edge evaluation metrics. Building on this foundation, PMP is contributing diagnostic capabilities to the CMIP Rapid Evaluation Framework (REF), supporting routine, standardized benchmarking of CMIP7 submissions as they become available. We have also extended PMP's evaluation framework to AI-based atmosphere and Earth system models, including recent application to output from the AI Model Intercomparison Project (AIMIP), an emerging coordinated testbed for assessing this new generation of models. Looking ahead, ongoing work aims to extend PMP's capabilities to support modeling groups throughout their development cycles, including expanded extreme diagnostics and large-scale circulation metrics such as Hadley cell expansion. Building on PMP's existing sea-ice diagnostics, we are also exploring an extension of high-latitude and Arctic region metrics in collaboration with the U.S. DOE’s HiLAT Project, alongside a broader extension of PMP's scope to decadal predictability, an area where systematic, community-standardized evaluation tools remain limited. This presentation will highlight the value of routine, community-based model evaluation, introduce these recent PMP advancements, and discuss opportunities for community engagement and collaboration. We invite feedback and suggestions from the community to further enhance our tools and methodologies.

489543.title: Developing and Evaluating an Interdisciplinary Coastal Resilience Curriculum
489543.authors: Jase E. Bernhardt, Hofstra University, Hempstead, NY; and A. Perrone and M. J. McCarthy
489543.abstract: As of March 2026, the New York State Education Department requires climate education across the K–12 curriculum, a shift welcomed by instructors and environmental stewards working toward resilient communities. In response, a team of university researchers and K-12 instructors developed an interdisciplinary coastal science unit for middle and high school students focused on community resilience. These important topics are currently not explicitly covered in required NYS science courses, despite a documented need for increased coastal science education. The new curriculum, therefore, was designed to align with NYS Science Learning Standards, addressing core climate change knowledge including human impacts on the environment and ways to enhance resilience to those changes. Lessons in the unit include hands-on investigations modeling green and gray infrastructure, and real-world examples of how Traditional Ecological Knowledge is being applied locally. The new unit culminates in a capstone project where student groups combine green (natural) and gray (engineered) elements to protect local communities from coastal hazards such as flooding, erosion, and storm surge. The emphasis of project-based learning and locally focused examples resonated strongly with students and teachers. This presentation will include an overview of the unit and capstone project, along with examples of outstanding student projects. Additionally, results from student pre- and post- surveys evaluating the unit, and interviews with instructors about their experience teaching the unit, will be covered. The approach used to develop this novel curriculum can be followed by researchers and teachers in other locations, especially those vulnerable to environmental change.

489549.title: Can AI Forecast Models Produce Reanalysis Quality Products from Only Sparse Observations?
489549.authors: Robert C. Jackson, ANL, Chicago, IL; and R. Kotamarthi, J. Wang, V. P. Ghate, S. Collis, Y. Feng, J. Stock, PhD, M. Olsen, C. Evans, D. D. Turner, S. Frolov, I. Jankov, S. W. Bieda III, PhD, and R. Redmon
489549.abstract: AI-based weather forecast models such as STORMER, AERIS, GraphCast and Pangu-Weather, trained on ERA5 reanalysis, have outperformed numerical weather prediction models with significantly reduced computational cost. Obtaining training datasets has been a challenge and this has led to the use of reanalysis datasets as the observational data equivalent for building data-based AI models. The appropriateness of using reanalysis as the proxy for observational data is disputed but this remains the best means of obtaining the training datasets; and the AI models developed using these datasets are performing well compared to the training data as well as numerical weather prediction models. However, generating the high quality reanalysis datasets remains challenging. Using all or most available data from all types of measurement platforms and measurement techniques (in situ vs remote sensing) is evolving, limited by both science challenges and computational limitations. It is also necessary when building these reanalysis datasets that we account for measurement uncertainties and produce ensembles rather than one reanalysis product. This therefore brings an interesting question to light: can we use AI models to produce “reanalysis quality” outputs by ingesting datasets that are used in the reanalysis generation models to produce ensembles of short-term ‘integrated’ reanalysis datasets to fill the observational gaps in space, time and variables? A recently developed model, AIFS-DOP, trained only on long-term sparse observational datasets using AIFS’ graph neural network-based architecture, generated these datasets with skill competitive with ERA-Interim and ERA5. However, whether this approach generalizes to other model architectures, such as diffusion and consistency-based architectures that can potentially better resolve mesoscale phenomena, is an open question. To that regard, we therefore examine generating reanalysis-quality outputs using generative AI forecast models by retraining the Swift model on the AIFS-DOP input dataset and running short term (1 time step) ensemble forecasts for the WFIP3 observation period of 2023 to 2025. We then compare the forecast temperature and winds against ERA5 reanalysis and surface and wind profiler observations obtained during WFIP3. These will demonstrate the feasibility of using AI forecast models for generating ensembles of “reanalysis quality” datasets and the spatial and temporal scales for which such an approach is suitable.

489551.title: Ground and Aircraft-based Measurements of Black Carbon and Carbon Monoxide in the New York City Metropolitan Area: Comparison to Emissions Inventories
489551.authors: Tiberias Nyapanga Okanga Mr, University of Maryland, Lanham, MD; and C. Grimes, P. Stratton, D. Felton, B. C. McDonald, X. Ren, R. R. Dickerson, and A. Asa-Awuku
489551.abstract: Black carbon (BC), an important short-lived aerosol, has a large positive radiative forcing and poses a serious public health concern, but it is difficult to measure accurately, and its emission estimates are highly uncertain. On the other hand, carbon monoxide (CO) can be measured with great accuracy and has better quantified emissions. There are common or collocated sources for BC and CO in the urban environment. Evaluating the relationship of BC and CO can help assess BC emission inventories and thus the radiative forcing effects of this light-absorbing aerosol. In this work, we first successfully evaluated an Aethalometer using a well-characterized BC surrogate. We size-selected BC surrogate particles of 200 and 300 nm in aerodynamic diameter using an Aerodynamic Aerosol Classifier (AAC), determined their mass, mp, and used a condensation particle counter (CPC) as a reference technique for measurement of number density, Np. A scatter plot of the BC mass concentrations determined by the reference technique vs. the Aethalometer has a slope within 1% of unity and a total 1σ uncertainty of 13%. The same Aethalometer model was used at a Queens roadside monitor and onboard an aircraft during a summer 2018, 2019, and 2021flight campaign in the New York City (NYC) region to determine BC mass concentrations. CO mixing ratios were also measured to define the BC-CO relationship in the NYC plume. All ground-based and flight data exhibited a positive correlation between BC and CO. Higher DBC/DCO ratios were observed on weekdays versus weekends, likely due to the greater number of diesel trucks on the road on weekdays. We estimate the emissions of BC (EBC) from the metropolitan region by using the DBC/DCO ratios from ground and flight measurements and the emission value of CO (ECO) from two emissions inventories (FIVE and NEI). We compared the EBC and the EBC:ECO ratio from ambient observations to inventories of CO and BC. Using the average value for ECO from the NEI and FIVE model inventories, and the average DBC/DCO ratio from the flights and near-road site, we estimated EBC for the NYC region to be 3.42 ± 1.33 Gg yr-1 (~25% higher than the EBC of inventories: the NEI, 2.75; and FIVE (all hours), 2.74 Gg yr-1). The greatest contributions to the uncertainty of this number are the uncertainty in ECO inventory estimates, and the variability in observed DBC/DCO ratios, as well as the seasonality of EBC– future work should explore other seasons. Our study shows that observed BC and CO combined with a CO emission inventory can be used to estimate BC emissions in urban environments.

489552.title: Early Results from the Robust Evaluation of Atmospheric Lidar (REAL) Experiment at the DOE ARM Southern Great Plains Observatory
489552.authors: Adam Theisen, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, IL; and S. Collis, I. Silber, P. Muradyan, C. J. Flynn, D. Zhang, J. M. Comstock, R. Bambha, J. Garcia, I. Razenkov, R. Holz, R. C. Jackson, R. Newsom, R. Krishnamurthy, D. Chand, S. Gupta, P. Wu, J. R. O'Brien, M. Spychala, A. Sockol, N. L. Hickmon, J. Schatz, and C. Martin
489552.abstract: The U.S. Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility recently completed the Robust Evaluation of Atmospheric Lidar (REAL) experiment, a comprehensive intercomparison designed to evaluate the performance, consistency, and scientific utility of a diverse suite of operational and research lidar systems. Conducted at ARM's Southern Great Plains (SGP) observatory from December 2025 through August 2026, REAL combined continuous observations with targeted intensive observational periods (REAL-IOPs) to characterize instrument performance across a broad range of atmospheric conditions. The experiment included operational ceilometers (CL31 and CL61), micropulse lidars (MPL and miniMPL), Doppler lidar, Raman lidar, High Spectral Resolution Lidar, and guest instruments. Enhanced radiosonde launches were coordinated during selected boundary layer regimes and EarthCARE satellite overpasses to provide additional reference observations for instrument evaluation. REAL represents one of the most comprehensive operational lidar intercomparisons conducted within ARM, bringing together instrument mentors, engineers, measurement scientists, and data users to evaluate instrument performance from both scientific and operational perspectives. Measurements spanning clear-sky conditions, cloud-topped mixed layers, recovering post-convective and frontal boundary layers, and suppressed boundary layers were used to examine consistency in cloud-base detection, boundary layer height retrievals, aerosol backscatter structure, calibration stability, overlap correction performance, and overall operational reliability. This presentation will provide an overview of the experimental design, summarize the observational dataset collected during the campaign, and present early intercomparison results highlighting areas of agreement, systematic differences, and lessons learned across the participating lidar systems. Initial findings demonstrate the value of coordinated, multi-instrument observations for identifying operational strengths and retrieval limitations while establishing a foundation for future algorithm development and standardized evaluation approaches. The REAL dataset is expected to serve as a community resource supporting future instrument assessments, satellite validation activities, and the continued evolution of ARM's lidar observing strategy.

489553.title: Automating Aviation Weather Workflows from Squadron to AOC with Agentic AI
489553.authors: Drew Arlen Burrier, RAFT, Honolulu, HI; and I. Lorenz
489553.abstract: Aviation operations across the theater require highly accurate and timely weather data to ensure flight safety and mission success. However, the manual generation of routine mission weather products creates a significant data entry bottleneck. From squadron level dispatch up to the Air Operations Center (AOC) and Headquarters, planners and meteorologists process high volumes of manual weather requests daily. This repetitive extraction and formatting of data from the Air Force Weather API diverts highly trained Airmen from complex meteorological analysis and high value threat assessment. To address this enterprise challenge, a cross functional team comprising the 17th Operational Weather Squadron (OWS), A9D, and Raft executed a rapid capability sprint to develop and deploy an Agentic AI solution within a secure Impact Level 6 (IL6) environment. The project pioneered the concept of an "Agentic Hub." This architecture utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to natively interpret natural language queries, translate them into real time Air Force Weather Cloud API calls, and automatically synthesize the data into structured aviation decision support products with utility spanning the 17th OWS floor, AOC planning cells, and Headquarters staff. As a foundational first step, the proof of concept successfully automated 85% of standard fields for the DD Form 175-1 flight weather briefing and 90% of regional Area Weather Reports. The AI agent dynamically translates flight routes into geospatial coordinates, retrieves relevant hazard data, and plots the flight path on a native map visualizer. The system also mirrors theater wide operational workflows by allowing aircrews to interactively update and regenerate briefings mid route via a conversational interface, which is a vital capability for 8 to 12 hour long haul flights when forecast models rerun. Furthermore, the system successfully demonstrated automated geospatial lookups for nearest airfields and water bodies to support immediate response rescue operations. This presentation will detail the architecture of the Agentic Hub, and the operational impact of deploying LLMs for aviation weather support. It will also outline the strategic roadmap for scaling this capability far beyond initial flight briefings. By integrating this Agentic AI directly with Air Tasking Order (ATO) and Airspace Control Order (ACO) data pipelines already in the system, the Hub is positioned to achieve "zero touch" weather workflows, proactively pairing scheduled missions with automated, AI driven weather reasoning across the entire enterprise.

489559.title: Historical Analysis of Space Weather Impacts on High Frequency Communications for Polar and Sub-Polar Commercial Flights
489559.authors: Tristan Tormey, Analytical Mechanics Associates, Hampton, VA; Analytical Mechanics Associates, Hampton, VA; NASA, Hampton, VA; and L. Strickland-Nunez, P. Mahlin, and E. Segal
489559.abstract: High frequency (HF) radio communication is used over oceanic and polar regions where very high frequency and satellite communication coverage is widely unavailable due to line-of-sight coverage. However, space weather (SWx) events, such as solar flares, coronal mass ejections, and solar energetic particles, intensify ionospheric absorption which can cause HF blackouts, disrupting pilot communications with air traffic control. During HF blackouts, the Federal Aviation Administration requires pilots to reroute or divert prior to entering the North Polar Area to ensure constant communication while in flight, increasing time and costs. The team partnered with the Allied Pilots Association to co-develop informational animations on areas of widespread HF degradation. These animations help to demonstrate the risks of SWx on in-flight communications to the aviation community. The D-Region Absorption Prediction (D-RAP) operational model hosted by NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center provides historical data for the highest affected frequency (HAF) by 1 dB of absorption. Using D-RAP to analyze the September 10th, 2017, solar flare, the team applied an empirical frequency-absorption equation (Sauer, 2008) to visualize the absorption and approximate lowest usable frequency (LUF) across the 3-30 MHz HF range, used by commercial flights. Additionally, the team created educational visuals of HF disruption over north polar flights for distribution to the aviation community. Throughout this co-development process, the team identified a need for ionospheric absorption prediction with 6-, 12-, and 24-hour lead time to assist flight dispatchers in planning safe polar flight paths before takeoff. Additionally, incorporating maximum usable frequency from other ionosphere models alongside the D-RAP HAF can help identify the most reliable frequency range to support constant HF communication.

489564.title: A Deep Dive into the Potential Uses of the Urban Rain Rate Dashboard for Emergency Managers
489564.authors: Kaylie Marie Bonifer, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and K. Semmens, R. A. H. Carr, P. Painter, K. Maxfield, and B. Montz
489564.abstract: Flooding events and their impacts continue to be significant hazards for emergency managers, with urban flooding events being a unique preparation challenge for these end-users. The Weather Prediction Center has developed the Urban Rain Rate Dashboard (URRD) to address the needs of end-users during urban flooding events and has partnered with the Nurture Nature Center to conduct social science research through focus groups, surveys, and interviews with stakeholders. Previous focus groups, conducted with stakeholders from diverse professional backgrounds, helped identify what elements of the dashboard would be most useful to a broad range of end-users. Findings from these sessions sparked interest in investigating the decision-making processes of specific stakeholders, such as emergency managers. To address this, we conducted a focus group with emergency managers representing the Chicago area to better understand how they could integrate the URRD into their operations and what recommendations participants had for the URRD. Emergency managers described their decision-making process and the usefulness of the URRD through surveys and a virtual focus group. We analyzed the qualitative data using a thematic analysis, where we provide new recommendations for the URRD and provide a deeper understanding of how emergency managers might use the URRD during single day and multi-day urban flooding events.

489565.title: The Signature of Tropical Atlantic Variability in West African Malaria Prevalence: Implications for Control Efforts
489565.authors: Sabrina Cohen, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and D. W. J. Thompson and J. W. Hurrell
489565.abstract: Malaria gives rise to high levels of infection and death among children in sub-Saharan Africa. Fluctuations in transmission arise from numerous factors, including natural climate variability and societal control measures. However, in highly-endemic West Africa, the relative climatic and societal impacts on malaria transmission have proven difficult to quantify, largely due to the paucity of observations of malaria prevalence. By utilizing the strong relationship between malaria and fever prevalence in children under age five, we demonstrate novel, robust linkages between variability in tropical South Atlantic sea surface temperatures (SST) and malaria transmission over the West African nations of Ghana, Togo, and Benin. We find that SST variability in the tropical South Atlantic, by strongly affecting wet-season precipitation along the Guinea Coast, explains 40% (interquartile range: 28%-51%) of the interannual variance in fever across the three countries. Removing the linear contribution of SSTs to fever prevalence reveals notable decreases in fever following initiation of major international aid efforts. Our results indicate the potential to guide public health strategies for malaria in the Guinea Coast region, provide insights into the possible effects of future tropical Atlantic warming on malaria transmission, and clarify the efficacy of recent international interventions.

489569.title: NOAA Phased Array Radar R&D Activities - Next Steps
489569.authors: Wayne M MacKenzie Jr Jr, Weather Program Office, Baltimore, MD; and A. E. Reinhart and R. Mendoza
489569.abstract: As the National Weather Service (NWS) legacy NEXRAD network approaches the end of its operational lifespan, the NOAA Phased Array Radar (PAR) program is strategically aligning its efforts with the broader NWS Radar Next initiative. Under this realigned direction, PAR serves as a key on-ramped technology within the Radar Next framework, bridging scientific research directly with NWS's long-term operational strategy. The primary goal of the updated program is to advance the overall maturity of phased array radar technology for weather applications while actively driving down production and deployment costs. These activities would aim to lower acquisition risks, ensure a seamless transition for the next-generation observing system, and ultimately deliver enhanced severe weather monitoring capabilities nationwide.

489570.title: Bridging the Gap in Flash Flood Communication through the Weather Prediction Center’s Excessive Rainfall Outlook Service Improvements
489570.authors: Amanda Kay Reinhart, NWS, Riverdale Park, MD; and M. Chenard, J. Lee, D. Nagele, B. Veenhuis, E. M. Guillot, M. Muccilli, and M. Klein
489570.abstract: The Excessive Rainfall Outlook (ERO) is a graphical outlook map issued by the National Weather Service (NWS) Weather Prediction Center (WPC) that forecasts the probability that rainfall will exceed flash flood guidance (FFG) within 25 miles of a point across the contiguous United States (CONUS) from Day 1 through Day 5. To estimate these risks, forecasters analyze environmental factors, advanced numerical models, and soil saturation thresholds synthesized from twelve River Forecast Centers to identify 1-, 3-, and 6-hour rainfall thresholds likely to cause high-impact flash flooding. The WPC is proposing operational updates to the ERO, transitioning the risk tier scale from four levels to five along with integrated numeric tier indexing (Levels 1 through 5) for all of the daily outlooks. The new risk category "Enhanced" (Level 3) will use a threshold of 25 percent and is situated between the existing risk categories of "Slight" (Level 2) with a threshold of 15 percent and "Moderate" (Level 4) with a threshold of 40 percent. By refining the operational framework, the WPC aims to bridge a critical decision-support gap while aligning product structure with the Storm Prediction Center’s (SPC) convective weather outlooks. WPC worked with NWS social scientists who conducted seven focus groups with 33 core partners to help address users’ communication needs and decision thresholds. This presentation will highlight WPC internal testing and verification, the NWS social science findings to guide changes to the ERO, and the feedback received during the public comment period. It will also showcase how WPC partners, such as local NWS Forecast Offices (WFOs) and emergency managers, can utilize these updates. For WFOs, the intermediate tier enables more granular threat messaging and localized probabilistic trigger points for Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS). For emergency managers and broadcast media, the Enhanced category provides a crucial intermediate action trigger, optimizing resource staging, staffing escalation, and public messaging prior to high-impact rainfall events.

489572.title: Leveraging Far-Infrared Data from the PREFIRE Mission to Develop a Novel Convective Identification Technique
489572.authors: Carolyn Bean, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and T. S. L'Ecuyer
489572.abstract: The Polar Radiant Energy in the Far-Infrared Experiment (PREFIRE) is the first modern satellite campaign to collect global observations in the far-infrared. This unique dataset affords exciting new opportunities for the study of tropical and mid-latitude deep convection in the far-infrared (FIR). Here, we use PREFIRE radiances to identify deep convection using the significant additional information content provided by FIR wavelengths. Prior work has found that relationships between brightness temperatures in the FIR “dirty window” and those near the carbon dioxide absorption band, the mid-infrared “clean” window, and the FIR water vapor rotation band hold promise for detecting and characterizing deep convection. The coldest regions of strongly convective storms display the smallest difference in brightness temperatures between the classic longwave IR window and the FIR dirty window; when high convective clouds reach far enough into the upper troposphere/tropopause, the brightness temperatures recorded in the FIR dirty window are remarkably similar to those observed in the “clean” atmospheric window, without any lower atmosphere water vapor signal. We leverage this relationship, as well as the sensitivity of longer FIR wavelengths to upper tropospheric and lower stratospheric humidity, to develop brightness temperature difference (BTD) thresholds representative of convective storms. The resulting algorithm has the potential to be more independent of location than current mid-IR methods, whose fixed window-channel brightness temperature thresholds can be susceptible to regional variations in tropopause height. We then use this algorithm to document the global distribution of convection as observed by both PREFIRE CubeSats and to present an initial survey of the full spectral emission characteristics of deep convection, further supplementing the body of work on far-infrared cloud characteristics with global satellite data.

489575.title: The Holy Grail of Integration: Measuring Intellectual Brokerage Across Weather–Society Research Communities
489575.authors: Kyle Richard Metta, NOAA, Okemos, MI; and A. Krepp, C. Williamsberg, and J. Mote
489575.abstract: Interdisciplinary research is often evaluated through publication counts, disciplinary affiliations, or collaboration networks, yet these approaches reveal little about whether distinct research communities are actually integrating knowledge. We present a bibliometric framework for measuring intellectual brokerage, defined here as the contribution of publications to connecting otherwise distinct research communities through shared intellectual foundations. Expanding on a 2025 bibliographic-coupling map of weather–society research, we examine how interdisciplinary integration has evolved over time and demonstrate complementary approaches for identifying boundary-spanning scholarship. We analyze 2,677 Web of Science publications retrieved through a broad, U.S.-affiliation-restricted search at the extreme weather–society interface. We built a network of the publications where connections are made when publications share at least three cited references. We analyze this network’s growth, topical and venue diversity, and within- versus between-community coupling through time. We evaluate intellectual brokerage using three complementary measures to understand key boundary spanning articles across intellectual silos: absolute shared-reference volume, bibliography-length-normalized coupling strength, and balanced integration of multiple communities’ literatures. Our results show that the literature expanded and diversified substantially over the study period, while intellectual integration increased much more slowly. The brokerage framework further demonstrates that interdisciplinary integration is multidimensional rather than a single measurable property. Different brokerage measures consistently identified different forms of boundary-spanning scholarship, indicating that intellectual integration is multidimensional rather than a single measurable property. Together, these findings suggest that evaluating interdisciplinarity requires multiple complementary perspectives rather than a single indicator of influence or impact. Scientific communities do not become interdisciplinary simply because they grow or collaborate. They become interdisciplinary when research increasingly draws on shared intellectual foundations across community boundaries. Beyond weather–society research, the framework provides funding agencies,and research organizations with a practical means of evaluating whether investments intended to foster interdisciplinarity are reflected in the evolving intellectual structure of a field and where future efforts may be most effectively directed.

489577.title: Inter-Comparison of JPSS VIIRS and MetOp-SG METimage Level 1B Products
489577.authors: Wenhui Wang, NOAA, Rockville, MD; and C. Cao, X. Shao, and Y. Bai
489577.abstract: The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) is a key NOAA instrument that provides early afternoon (1:30 pm local time) global observations for numerical weather predictions and environmental monitoring applications. VIIRS has 22 spectral bands, covering a spectral range from 0.41 to 12 μm. The on-orbit calibration of VIIRS is complex. It is critical to evaluate the on-orbit calibration performance to ensure high-quality VIIRS Sensor Data Records (SDR, or level 1b product). Global observation from the MetOp-SG Meteorological Imager (METimage, launched in August 2025) become available to NOAA for evaluation on July 21, 2026. Complementary to VIIRS, METimage will provide state-of-the-art mid-monitoring (9:30 am local time) observations with enhanced radiometric accuracy, broader spectral coverage, higher spatial resolution, and expanded dynamic range compared to the legacy AVHRR instruments. With a similar spectral coverage to VIIRS, METimage has 9 solar bands and 5 thermal bands that match those of VIIRS. VIIRS and METimage level 1b products need to be inter-compared to better support downstream data users. The purpose of this study is to inter-compare NOAA-21/NOAA-20 VIIRS and MetOp-SG METimage level 1b products. Previously, we have developed a comprehensive suite of vicarious calibration methods for evaluating VIIRS SDR calibration performance, such as calibration stability, bias, consistency, striping, and saturation radiance (Wang et al. 2022;2025;2026). In this study, we adapted the VIIRS Deep Convective Cloud (DCC) method to METimage. The stability and striping of METimage solar bands will be assessed over DCCs; VIIRS and METimage matched solar bands will be inter-calibrated after correcting for BRDF effect and spectral response differences. Moreover, we will also use ray-matching method (with GOES ABI as transfer radiometer) to reduce the uncertainty of inter-calibration due to different local equator crossing time. The on-orbit saturation radiances of VIIRS thermal bands were evaluated in-depth previously. The saturation radiances (or brightness temperatures) of METimage thermal bands are being assessed in this study. Initial results suggest that METimage fire bands (vii_3740, vii_3959, and vii_4050) can observe higher radiances (up to ~415 K so far) than VIIRS single gain fire bands (I4/M12, up to ~360 K), while VIIRS M13 (dual gain fire band) has a much higher maximum radiance specification (643 K). Other differences between VIIRS SDR and METimage level 1b products, such as imagery quality, geolocation schemes, quality flags, and daily data volumes, will also be analyzed and reported. Results from this study will provide valuable information to improve the quality of VIIRS SDRs and to benefit numerical weather predictions and environmental monitoring applications using both products.

489586.title: LARS: LLM-Assisted Radar Scene Classification
489586.authors: Robert C. Jackson, ANL, Chicago, IL; and B. Raut, L. Chen, J. R. O'Brien, Z. Sherman, J. Tian, S. Collis, A. Theisen, S. Gupta, and N. L. Hickmon
489586.abstract: The U.S. Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility hosts several petabytes of data for research spanning three decades. However, the sheer volume of data makes it difficult for users to identify features of interest. To address this, ARM provides labeled time periods of interest, known as “epochs,” to guide data selection. These epochs typically cover only a few weeks of a deployment, leaving a large amount of data uncategorized. One dataset that is particularly challenging to explore due to its size involves radar data from the C-band Scanning ARM Precipitation Radar (CSAPR), whose volume spans terabytes. However, most users are interested in data with specific weather phenomena occurring such as mesoscale convective systems that significantly contribute to precipitation over the globe and would like to download only this subset of the data. Therefore, having scene classifications that summarize the weather detected by the CSAPR and other weather radars increases the data’s accessibility to end users. Multimodal large language models (mLLMs), which can process images and audio in addition to text, have shown promise in interpreting atmospheric data visualizations. Therefore, in this study, we showcase LLM-Assisted Radar Scenes (LARS), a workflow that uses mLLMs to label 1,208 radar 0.5° plan position indicator (PPI) scans from the CSAPR at the ARM Bankhead National Forest (BNF) site. LARS provides a detailed codebook to the mLLM to guide classification. This codebook defines label categories, decision rules, required inputs, representative examples, and reliability criteria, ensuring consistency across annotators. It is then used as a shared rubric for both two human annotators and mLLMs for classification. Our analysis demonstrates that reflectivity images, using a National Weather Service Reflectivity colormap, along with criteria that factor in the reflectivity coverage statistics from the 0.5° PPI scans and the previous mLLM-assigned label provide the highest Cohen’s kappa scores. In particular, the GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.8, and llama4-scout models, using these criteria, label these radar scenes with a Cohen’s kappa score of 0.7 to 0.9, depending on which labeller is used as ground truth. In addition, two human labellers selected in this study, following the codebook, agree with a Cohen’s kappa score of 0.71 with the largest disagreement being with classifications of mesoscale convective systems compared to stratiform. The results suggest that the open source llama4-scout model performs as well as frontier models at radar image classification using the LARS workflow considering the uncertainty in the human-described labels.

489587.title: Using Augmented Reality to Investigate Willingness to Pay for Coastal Inundation
489587.authors: Francisco Gabriel Martinez, Fairfield University, Fairfield, CT; and R. Nazarian, M. Speretta, W. Vasquez, and J. Trudeau
489587.abstract: Translating detailed climate projections into clear, intuitive visuals to inform the public about future risks, and then using their perceptions of these risks to inform policy and coastal planning is essential as communities grapple with the myriad impacts of climate change. Towards this end, we conduct an interdisciplinary project to evaluate public willingness to pay for coastal flooding adaptation and mitigation for extreme weather events and sea level rise (SLR), aiming to bridge the gap between climate science and decision-making by elucidating long term environmental impacts for local communities. To convey SLR to study participants, we have developed a novel augmented reality (AR) experience to illustrate model projections of coastal inundation through the end of the century. As coastal areas face growing sea level and inundation threats, these immersive AR experience are crucial to translating, and superimposing, complex risk data directly onto the actual environment. We demonstrate this through an AR simulation set along four different beaches across the Long Island Sound in Connecticut: Silver Sands, Sherwood Island, Hammonasset, and Rocky Neck. Built in Unity, the simulation shows projected sea levels and annual flood levels for three key benchmark years, 2030, 2050, and 2100. To ensure realistic visuals during outdoor field deployment, we developed an algorithm for the system to superimpose virtual water and sand textures that match the real-world lighting and colors of the physical shoreline. With this AR application now developed, we are currently deploying it at the four beaches, along with an economic survey, to assess the willingness to pay for SLR adaptation and mitigation by the community. Our initial results indicate the impact that immersive visual simulations have in informing public risk perception. We will present both the AR algorithm and results from our willingness-to-pay survey and the implications that this has for developing policies that align with both projections of coastal risks to SLR as well as community members perceptions of these risks.

489591.title: A Multiscale Study of Atmospheric River Formation and Moisture Origins
489591.authors: Sierra Whiteman, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and S. D. Miller, J. M. Forsythe, and T. H. VonderHaar
489591.abstract: Atmospheric Rivers (ARs) are defined as long, narrow filaments of significant water vapor that contribute largely to global precipitation, poleward energy transport, and coastal to inland flooding events. While previous studies have placed an emphasis on particularly large scale ARs due to their potential of extensive damage, it is useful to understand the atmospheric processes associated with multiple AR scales whose impacts range from localized to widespread, and beneficial to catastrophic. ARs in this study are identified using the Global Atmospheric Rivers Database developed by Guan and Waliser (2024) with the Tracking Atmospheric Rivers Globally as Elongated Targets (tARget) algorithm. Identified rivers are classified by scale based on metrics of length, width, and depth. Length categories range from 3,000 km to 8,000 km, based upon the average length throughout their lifetime, and width categories similarly range from 400 km to 1,200 km. Differences in AR scale are explored by analyzing moisture sources and the atmospheric processes influencing their formation using ECMWF Reanalysis v5 (ERA5) and satellite remote sensing (blended passive microwave retrievals of TPW and layered precipitable water [LPW]) data. Preliminary findings show a possible influence of tropical moisture exports affecting the scale and duration of atmospheric rivers. The aim of this study is to identify key differences in the formation and structure of ARs occurring on different spatial scales, toward improving our understanding of the key scale-dependent processes that govern moisture sources, convergence, transport, and predictability.

489594.title: Further Opposite CCN Modality Effects on Droplets and Drizzle in Stratus and Cumuli
489594.authors: James G. Hudson, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV; and S. Noble and F. Emin
489594.abstract: Two stratus cloud field experiments (MASE and POST) found bimodal CCN associated with smaller droplets and less drizzle than stratus clouds associated with unimodal CCN (Hudson et al. 2018; Hudson & Noble 2024). Two cumulus field studies (ICE-T and RICO) found bimodal CCN spectra associated with larger droplets and greater drizzle than cumuli associated with unimodal CCN (Hudson & Noble 2019 & 2022). Now a third stratus and a third cumulus study corroborate these results. Moreover, since this third cumulus study occurred in significantly higher CCN concentrations (NCCN ~700 cm-3) off the Florida coast than those two published cumulus studies (NCCN < 400 cm-3) and the third stratus project was in cleaner Southern Ocean (SO) air than the published stratus studies the difference in cloud type rather than NCCN differences is now confirmed as the reason for these opposite effects on droplets and drizzle in cumuli and stratus. Figure panels A, D & G demonstrate more small droplets in coastal Florida small cumuli associated with unimodal CCN (pink, orange and especially red) while there are more large droplets (B, E & H) and greater drizzle (C, F & I) in these cumuli associated with bimodal CCN (cyan, blue and especially black). Darker colors represent droplet and drizzle spectra in clouds associated with bimodal CCN, which is due to the effects of cloud processing; that is gas to particle chemical transformations, coalescence scavenging and Brownian capture of cloud interstitial material (Hoppel et al. 1986). Reddish colors represent droplet and drizzle spectra in clouds associated with CCN less affected by cloud processing, which tend toward unimodality. Black represents clouds associated with the very most bimodal CCN, while blue includes clouds associated with CCN that are somewhat less bimodal while cyan represents the entire half of the considered clouds that trend toward bimodality. On the other hand, red represents clouds associated with the most unimodal CCN (least cloud-processed), orange is somewhat less unimodal (unprocessed) while pink represents the half of the considered clouds that tend toward unimodality. Figure panels D-I most clearly reveal the cumulus properties that were displayed in RICO and ICE-T low altitude cumuli. Panels A-C less distinctly display cumulus characteristics. This is due to major NCCN differences between cleaner onshore winds (G-I, NCCN < 700 cm-3) and polluted offshore winds (D-F, NCCN > 700 cm-3). These concentration differences lead to subsequent variations of the CCN-droplet and CCN-drizzle relationships between D-F and G-I. These differences interfere with each when both wind directions are considered in panels A-C to thus obscure the cumulus characteristics displayed in the separate Florida air masses and in RICO and ICE-T. This is most clearly exhibited in panel B by the lower large droplet concentrations in clouds associated with the most bimodal CCN black than large droplets in clouds associated with unimodal CCN (pink and orange). Panels E & H contrarily show the most large droplets in clouds associated with the most bimodal CCN black and lower large droplet concentrations in all clouds associated with unimodal CCN (reddish) as well as less bimodal CCN (blue and cyan). Panel C also shows that the most bimodal CCN are not always associated with the greatest drizzle whereas panels F & I consistently show clouds associated with the most bimodal black CCN with the most drizzle. Small droplet panel D shows unimodal/bimodal separations superior to those of panels A & G. This is probably because the least drizzle in these polluted clouds (panel F) causes less droplet coalescence, which could distort droplet spectral relationships with CCN modality. This seems to be so in panel G due to greater drizzle (panel I) in lower droplet concentration clouds. Panel D thus best agrees with ICE-T droplet results. Notably larger amounts of drizzle in cleaner RICO clouds also distorted droplet spectral-CCN modality relationships (Hudson & Noble 2022). Panels J & M demonstrate opposite greater small droplet concentrations in stratus associated with bimodal CCN (dark) than unimodal CCN (reddish) in SO. Then panels K, L, N & O demonstrate fewer large droplets and less small drizzle in stratus associated with bimodal CCN (dark) than unimodal CCN (reddish). However, panel L demonstrates a further twist in cleaner SO air where there is a bimodal/unimodal crossover within the drizzle range. This crossover is analogous to the bimodal/unimodal crossover universally observed within droplet size ranges of A-B, D-E, G-H, J-K & M-N. This is the fundamental cloud physics principle that more small droplets inhibit large droplets and drizzle while fewer small droplets foster large droplets and drizzle. Moreover, this second bimodal/unimodal crossover within the drizzle size range suggests that fewer large droplets (K) and small drizzle (left side of L) seem to enhance larger drizzle (right side of L). This last finding counterintuitively suggests that in very clean air higher concentrations of small droplets may lead to more rather than fewer large drizzle drops. The findings of the four publications noted above, and the relationships presented here indicate that the cloud processing that makes bimodal CCN spectra may have important effects on droplet and drizzle spectra that are important for indirect aerosol effects and thus for global climate. Hoppel, W.A., Frick, G.M. & Larsen, R.E., 1986. Effects of nonprecipitating clouds on the aerosol size distribution in the marine boundary layer. 489597.title: Evaluating Precipitation Differences Between Traditional and Machine Learning-Based Convective Schemes in CAM7
489597.authors: Kara Lynn Rydberg, Univ. of Florida, Port Charlotte, FL
489597.abstract: Deep convection remains one of the largest sources of uncertainty in Earth System Models because it must be parameterized rather than explicitly resolved. The operational deep convection scheme in the Community Atmospheric Model v. 7 (CAM7), the Zhang-McFarlane (ZM) parameterization, exhibits known biases in the timing and intensity of precipitation, motivating the development of machine learning (ML)-based alternatives. The Yuval and O’Gorman 2020 Scheme (YOG20), a machine-learning scheme trained on cloud-resolving model output, offers a data-driven alternative that may avoid these triggering biases and provide a more computationally inexpensive option for CAM7. However, YOG20 has not yet been evaluated within CAM7. We seek to fill this research gap by asking: How does the YOG20 ML-based convection parameterization affect simulated precipitation relative to the ZM convection scheme in CAM7? We compared both convection schemes using 3-hourly CAM7 outputs over 3 months and monthly outputs over 3 years. We then compared the outputs from these schemes with observational data from IMERG, ERA5, and MODIS to assess each scheme’s accuracy. We found that, in zonal average precipitation, the ZM scheme performs better than YOG20; however, when looking specifically at the drizzle rate, YOG20 performs significantly better than the operational ZM scheme. Furthermore, YOG20 improves the depiction of the diurnal cycle of precipitation, vertical profile of relative humidity, and cloud cover. However, biases remain in zonal precipitation and temperature. To assess the physical basis of YOG20's behavior, we applied SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis to the trained network, finding that its predictions are driven primarily by surface temperature and humidity. Future work will decompose precipitation into large-scale and convective components to identify scheme-specific differences and apply perturbed parameter estimation to reduce the remaining biases. Results of this analysis can inform future model development to improve the accuracy and physical realism of Earth System Models.

489600.title: Moisture Sensitivity Experiments of African Mesoscale Convective Systems in Convection-Permitting Resolution
489600.authors: Stephanie Marie Ortiz Rosario, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and K. M. Núñez Ocasio and Z. Moon
489600.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) are known to produce life-threatening rainfall conditions over Africa. The associated convection can also impact the Caribbean and North America, as African MCSs have been found to aid African Easterly Waves (AEWs) into tropical cyclone genesis (TCG). Moreover, changes in available environmental moisture due to changes in climate may impact the development of MCSs. Therefore, the aim of this study is to examine African MCSs via high-resolution modeling in changing moisture environments. To accomplish this goal, regional West African and East Atlantic convection-permitting experiments from the Model for Prediction Across Scales-Atmosphere (MPAS-A) are run for 5 days in September 2006, when the TCG of Helene was occurring, and the relative humidity at all pressure levels is altered to add and remove moisture (20% and 50%, respectively). MCSs in the output environments (CTRL, MOIST, and DRY) are tracked and identified using the Tracking Algorithm for Mesoscale Convective Systems (TAMS) with a cloud top temperature threshold of 228K and ITCZ filtering. Focusing on the CTRL vs MOIST results, through outgoing longwave radiation and mean zonal wind analysis, it can be shown that MCSs in the vicinity of AEW Helene’s center have more instances of being positioned in the northerlies of the AEW and experience more easterly shear in CTRL compared to MOIST, which has been studied to be a setup favorable for TCG. In addition, mean vertical velocity and diabatic heating profiles show MCSs with a bimodal bottom- and top-heavy setting in CTRL, in contrast with MOIST MCSs, which show a dominating top-heavy profile, suggesting that energy and moisture tend to be transported out of AEW instead of contributing to its TCG. Along with stronger cold pools over land in CTRL compared to MOIST, these findings may explain why CTRL underwent faster TCG than MOIST, as concluded in a previous study. Future work seeks to validate CTRL with observations and examine the entire African MCS population during the case study time and across experiments.

489601.title: From Surface to Satellite: Co-developing a Participatory Blowing Snow Validation Campaign
489601.authors: Christina Buffington, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and W. Line, C. Dierking, S. Babb, H. Mair, M. Colon Robles, J. Taylor, H. Kohl, K. Weaver, Q. McHenry, R. Boger, and J. Delamere
489601.abstract: Blowing snow, defined as loose snow lofted and transported tens to hundreds of meters high by strong winds, is a significant hazard that reduces visibility for ground and air transportation. Detecting blowing snow is a challenge for forecasters because it can be difficult to distinguish from clouds and other atmospheric features in satellite imagery. To provide forecasters with reliable blowing snow detections, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) developed a Blowing Snow satellite product from VIIRS and ABI instruments on JPSS and GOES-R, respectively. Participatory engagement in validation of the NESDIS Blowing Snow product is an opportunity to expand spatially limited ground observations from transportation webcams. In December 2025 to March 2026, we co-developed a participatory Blowing Snow pilot project using the existing blowing snow “button” in the Cloud tool of NASA’s Global Learning and Observations to Benefit the Environment (GLOBE) Observer application. Rather than designing the effort solely from a scientific perspective, project partners worked across Federal Agency (NOAA and NASA), academic research, and aviation weather communities to create observation protocols, training materials, participation guidance, and a public-facing tracking dashboard that enabled contributors and scientists to see and follow project activity. For example, instructions for observing during high winds included safety protocols developed by the Civil Air Patrol (CAP), the civilian auxiliary of the United States Air Force. Using the GLOBE Observer app, participants from twelve countries plus Antarctica contributed approximately 500 ground observations, which included photos of sky conditions, feature photos across the horizon, tags as blowing snow, and field notes. The future direction of Blowing Snow participatory research continues to be co-designed with CAP. Together, we’ve identified the need to extend training resources, make calls for observations during and after active winter weather events, expand partnerships with National Weather Service Weather Forecast Offices, community snow observers and decision makers, distinguish blowing snow from drifting snow, and expand geographic coverage in snow-prone regions.

489609.title: Capturing the Weather Events of 2026 From Satellite Imagery and Their Uses in the Media
489609.authors: Joshua Reiter, CIRA, Loveland, CO; and K. Erickson
489609.abstract: During 2026, many impactful weather events occurred across the Earth. From blizzards to wildfire outbreaks, to tropical cyclones and even dust storms, weather satellites were always in orbit above to observe a wide range of extreme meteorological phenomenon. Utilizing geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites, the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere (CIRA) has created satellite imagery to document these events, as well as archiving them on the CIRA Satellite Library. This presentation will highlight profound satellite animations and stills taken of weather events in 2026, as well as showcasing how CIRA imagery has been employed by major media outlets to tell a weather story.

489610.title: Expanding Core Partner Support for Extreme Fire Weather Events: Coordinating Particularly Dangerous Situations
489610.authors: Gregory T. Heavener, NWS, Boulder, CO; and P. T. Schlatter and J. Stark
489610.abstract: During the fall of 2025, National Weather Service Forecast Office Boulder provided over 40 hours of specialized windstorm training to new Xcel Energy meteorologists. Unfortunately due to a historic warm and dry December, and much of the winter in Colorado, several high impact wind storms occurred along the northern Front Range posing a very high wildfire threat. Coordination and collaboration with Xcel and their team of meteorologists occurred numerous times throughout the winter, helping to mitigate fire starts from downed power lines. One very high impact event led to WFO Boulder issuing the states’ first ever Particularly Dangerous Situation (PDS) Red Flag Warning for December 19, 2025. This PDS designation was a "game-changer" for local stakeholders, leading to the deployment of the first-ever PDS Strike Team by the Colorado Department of Public Safety. This presentation highlights how integrated forecasting, specialized training, and enhanced warning communication through PDS RFWs significantly advance the public safety mission during extreme fire events.

489622.title: Will the Supercell Take the Bait? Interactions and Environmental Controls of Radar Inferred Vertical Vorticity Worms
489622.authors: Josiah John Melke, Texas Tech Univ., Lubbock, TX; and C. C. Weiss
489622.abstract: Substantial research has established the importance of baroclinically generated near-surface vertical vorticity in supercell thunderstorms. More recently, numerical simulations have identified an additional potential pathway to tornadogenesis through small-scale, streamwise-aligned structures, colloquially termed vorticity worms, embedded within the surface-layer environmental inflow. As numerical models continue to improve, observational verification of these features has become increasingly important, particularly given longstanding uncertainty regarding the representation of frictional processes near the model lower boundary. To investigate these structures observationally, an objective identification algorithm was developed to detect vorticity worms in Texas Tech University Ka-band (TTUKa) mobile Doppler radar plan position indicator (PPI) scans collected during the Targeted Observation by Radars and UAS of Supercells (TORUS) and Low-level Internal Flow of Tornadoes (LIFT) field campaigns. Across 28 radar deployments spanning 15 intensive observing periods, identified vorticity worms exhibit characteristic wavelengths of approximately 500–800 m, with a composite mean spacing of ~550 m and associated vertical vorticity magnitudes averaging ~0.026 s⁻¹. Beyond documenting their occurrence, this study examines the environmental factors governing the development and persistence of vorticity worms. Preliminary results indicate that both the frequency of occurrence and vertical vorticity magnitude increase with stronger horizontal inflow winds, while both decrease with increasing surface friction, represented by spatially averaged aerodynamic roughness length derived from surrounding land-cover characteristics. Additional analyses investigate the influence of near-surface static stability using virtual potential temperature deficits estimated from mobile and stationary mesonet observations. Finally, the presentation explores interactions between vorticity worms and storm-scale features, including rear-flank gust fronts. Preliminary observations suggest that these interactions locally enhance vertical vorticity, supporting the hypothesis that vorticity worms may provide pre-existing vertical vorticity that can be amplified along boundaries and contribute to tornadogenesis. The vertical vorticity associated with these interactions is compared with that observed elsewhere along the boundary and within the surrounding inflow environment.

489624.title: Developing a Radar Climatology of Skillful Prognostic Signals to Enhance Tropical Cyclone Tornado Warning Lead Time across North Carolina
489624.authors: Brandon Wegmann, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and D. Leins and A. Swiggett
489624.abstract: Tropical cyclone tornadoes (TCTORs) often exhibit radar characteristics that differ from those of traditional Great Plains supercells, making it challenging to issue a tornado warning with positive lead time. Between 2015 and 2025, 18 named tropical cyclones produced a total of 115 TCTORs across North Carolina. The majority of tornado warning lead times fell below the National Weather Service lead time goal of 13 minutes, with almost a third of TCTORs being either unwarned or having no warning lead time at all.
