A radar climatology of key radar signatures was developed to identify combinations of prognostic and diagnostic tools that may improve tornado warning lead times. Radar signatures evaluated include VROT (Rotational Velocity), NROT (Normalized Rotation), Left Flank Velocity Enhancement (LFVE), Velocity Enhancement Signature (VES), Maximum Spectrum Width, and the angular separation between the Specific Differential Phase (KDP) and Differential Reflectivity (ZDR) centroids. The climatology encompasses North Carolina TCTORs spanning Hurricane Delta (2020) through Tropical Storm Chantal (2025) and characterizes the frequency, percentile distributions, and temporal evolution of these radar signatures in the minutes leading up to tornadogenesis. Using GR2Analyst, a sample of 35 TCTORs was analyzed for the aforementioned radar features. Given the inherent subjectivity of radar interrogation, specific guidelines were developed to ensure the study is reproducible. Results indicate that specific combinations of prognostic and diagnostic tools provide the greatest tornado warning lead times. Combinations of LFVE+KDP/ZDR Separation (2 prognostic tools), KDP/ZDR Separation+VROT (1 prognostic + 1 diagnostic tool), and LFVE+NROT+VROT (1 prognostic + 2 diagnostic tools) outperformed the remaining 54 combinations of radar signatures in terms of average tornado warning lead time. These results establish a radar climatology that quantifies the frequency and temporal evolution of key radar signatures preceding tropical cyclone tornadogenesis and identifies combinations of prognostic and diagnostic tools associated with the greatest average tornado warning lead times.

489625.title: Leveraging Geostationary HCHO Retrievals from TEMPO as a High-Resolution Diagnostic for Surface Ozone and PM2.5 Hotspots
489625.authors: Prajjwal Rawat, Hampton University, Hampton, VA; and J. Crawford, K. Travis, L. Judd, M. A. Demetillo, T. Lee, J. Szykman, R. Delgado, E. Baumann, T. F. Hanisco, and G. Gonzalez Abad
489625.abstract: Formaldehyde (HCHO) is a key intermediate in the atmospheric oxidation of volatile organic compounds and a valuable indicator of photochemical activity, with documented correlations to surface ozone and organic aerosol variability. Satellite trace-gas retrievals have transformed our ability to observe pollutant emissions and transport, however, translating column observations into a useful information about surface air quality remains challenging because uncertainties in column-to-surface coupling and dependencies on atmospheric models. This challenge is particularly important for ozone and PM2.5, whose variability is strongly influenced by secondary formation and photochemical intensity. Building on airborne field studies of HCHO–ozone dynamics, this work leverages high-precision HCHO column density (ΩHCHO) measurements from the geostationary Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) instrument to evaluate satellite-based, approaches for surface air quality assessment. TEMPO ΩHCHO observations exhibit robust correlation with co-located ground-based Pandora spectrometer observations and are compared with surface ozone and PM2.5 measurements across five major U.S. cities. TEMPO ΩHCHO are shown to effectively capture the spatial variability of ozone and PM2.5 at monitoring locations. Among the cities evaluated, Houston exhibits the most prominent hotspot beyond the spatial reach of the surface-monitoring network, while other metropolitan areas contain populated locations with elevated ΩHCHO that may benefit from expanded monitoring. These findings demonstrate the potential of TEMPO's fine spatial and temporal resolution to transform HCHO from a sparsely measured surface species into a high-resolution diagnostic of photochemical air quality conditions. TEMPO observations can therefore complement existing monitoring networks by supporting assessment of unmonitored areas and identifying pollution hotspots that may not be adequately represented by current network configurations. Because column-to-surface coupling is strongly modulated by planetary boundary layer (PBL) dynamics, we further examine how continuous ceilometer-derived PBL height influences the strength and stability of the ΩHCHO–surface air quality relationship. Together, these results establish a scalable, boundary-layer-informed framework for leveraging geostationary ΩHCHO observations to identify photochemical hotspots and advance air quality management and regulatory decision-making.

489628.title: Public Understanding of Uncertainty with Hurricane Forecast Graphics
489628.authors: Aaron Price, Ph.D., American Meteorological Society, Chicago, IL; American Meteorological Society, boston, MA; and H. S. Lee
489628.abstract: Cone graphics and spaghetti plots are two of the most common formats for communicating hurricane forecasts to the public. Although both are intended to convey a range of possible outcomes, each embeds complex constructs associated with three distinct types of uncertainty. Initialization uncertainty reflects what is and is not known about environmental variables at the start of the forecast. Ensemble uncertainty reflects differences among the computer models that contribute to the forecast graphic. Temporal uncertainty reflects change between successive model runs. In collaboration with subject matter experts and pilot testers, we developed a survey instrument to measure public understanding of the uncertainty represented in cone graphics and spaghetti plots. The survey was administered to more than 350 adults during the summer of 2026. Data were analyzed using the general linear model and the Rasch Rating Scale Model to identify associations and differences across participant groups and forecast graphic type. Preliminary results indicate that participants with higher prior knowledge of hurricanes, though not necessarily direct experience with hurricanes, performed better when interpreting spaghetti plots. These findings will inform the development of an interactive online hurricane forecast simulation designed to educate the general public about the uncertainty inherent in hurricane forecasting.

489629.title: Observing Long-Term Water Level Changes Across the Earth From the Joint Polar Satellite System
489629.authors: Joshua Reiter, CIRA, Loveland, CO; and K. Erickson
489629.abstract: Over the past decade and a half, the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) program has had continuous observance across the globe, documenting weather events and changes to the Earth’s surface during that time. The changing water levels of hydrological bodies, a slow process that takes sometimes months or years to reveal their effects, can be perceived through the JPSS satellite imagery. Utilizing the VIIRS instrument, these changes, influenced through either natural or manmade actions, will be showcased through satellite imagery products and animations. Each presented case will be supplemented by data to contextualize the demonstrated satellite imagery. Ultimately this presentation will aim to highlight how satellite imagery can be used in this unique way and emphasize its importance in observing long-term surface changes across the globe.

489630.title: Investigating the Influence of Snowfall on Land-Atmosphere Interactions and the Surface Albedo Feedback
489630.authors: Ethan Chow, Fairfield University, Fairfield, CT; and R. Nazarian
489630.abstract: In a warming climate, both global snow coverage and planetary surface albedo are projected to decrease. Despite the surface albedo feedback (SAF) being weaker than water vapor and cloud feedbacks, the SAF is crucial for regional climate change and can have significant impacts on arctic amplification, sea ice loss, and the timing and magnitude of spring snowmelt, making it a vital area of research to advance snow hydrology science. Previous work shows Global Climate Models (GCMs) project a bimodal pattern of mean and extreme snowfall magnitudes with end-of-century high latitude increases and mid-latitude decreases in a warming climate, which suggests decreases in snow cover and consequently surface albedo. Large-scale circulation, rather than thermodynamics, was found to be the primary driver of this robust pattern. This naturally leads to an open area of snow hydrology research in how land-atmosphere interactions influence the GCM’s SAF projections. In 2004 Hall showed that coupled ocean–atmosphere simulations with and without surface albedo feedback under CO2-doubling forcing indicate that SAF accounts for roughly half of the high-latitude response to the forcing, underscoring its outsized role in influencing moisture circulation and distribution at high latitudes relative to its modest contribution to the global-mean energy budget. Additionally, in the current generation of GCMs, SAF is a crucial uncertainty and diagnosing the underlying mechanisms which change GCM surface albedo, including changes in both mean and extreme snowfall, and is an important gap that needs to be addressed to advance snow hydrology modeling. We study the impact of changing snowfall in a warming climate on surface albedo and SAF by conducting a novel analysis of data from the Couple Model Intercomparison Project phase 6 (CMIP6). Specifically, we apply a multivariate linear regression to daily changes in surface albedo and variables that can drive snowfall-related changes in surface albedo, such as temperature, snowflux, and the frequency of rain-on-snow events. Preliminary results from the historical experiments suggest that snowfall flux is the primary driver of GCM surface albedo increases, with a raw regression coefficient magnitude five times stronger than rain-on-snow events, which is the strongest driver of surface albedo decreases. Likewise, in end-of-century projections using both ssp245 and ssp585 scenarios, models suggest that the change in the snowfall flux coefficient (projected minus historical) has a bimodal signal, with decreases in the high latitudes and increases in the mid latitudes. This suggests that snowflux’s influence on SAF is projected to vary by latitude. The opposite trend is observed for the surface temperature coefficient, albeit one order of magnitude smaller, suggesting the critical importance of high-latitude surface temperature fluctuations. We then consider land-atmosphere interactions in a changing climate by closing the surface energy budget, which allows us to separate the direct and indirect influences that atmospheric drivers have on sensible and latent heat. Completing this budget will help us understand the surface moisture distribution, highlighting essential model physics for capturing snow albedo feedback, ultimately strengthening GCMs to better predict coupled snowfall and hydrological responses.

489633.title: GNSS RO Observation-Space Benchmarking of GEFSv12 Reforecasts: Diagnosing UTLS Temperature Error Growth and Tropospheric Water Vapor Forecast Drift
489633.authors: Shu-Peng Ho, STAR, Riverdale Park, MD; and H. Guan
489633.abstract: Global ensemble reforecasts provide valuable records for diagnosing numerical weather prediction errors across lead times, seasons, and atmospheric regimes. However, conventional forecast-minus-analysis verification does not isolate model error because the verifying analysis contains model dependence, data-assimilation assumptions, and vertically varying uncertainty. These limitations are particularly consequential in the upper troposphere–lower stratosphere (UTLS), where sharp vertical gradients complicate temperature verification, and in the troposphere, where water vapor drift reflects interacting errors in initialization and moist physical processes. This study develops a Global Navigation Satellite System radio occultation (GNSS RO) observation-space framework for benchmarking NOAA Global Ensemble Forecast System version 12 (GEFSv12) reforecasts. Multi-mission RO profiles are collocated with GEFSv12 forecasts by time, location, vertical coordinate, and forecast lead time. Model atmospheric states are projected into RO-relevant quantities, including refractivity and, where appropriate, bending angle, allowing forecast departures to be evaluated closer to the measurement space. Diagnostics are stratified by altitude, latitude, season, lead time, and selected atmospheric regimes. In the UTLS, we used RO-derived dry-temperature, tropopause, and vertical-gradient diagnostics to characterize the structure and growth of temperature errors. In the troposphere, refractivity and moisture-sensitive diagnostics are used to assess water vapor forecast drift, with appropriate caution regarding super-refraction, horizontal gradients, and the background dependence of humidity retrievals. Examining the lead-time evolution of these departures helps distinguish errors present near initialization from errors that emerge or amplify during model integration. This work highlights the added value of STAR GNSS RO data for reforecast validation in three areas: (1) providing a stable observational anchor for cross-cycle and long-term reforecast assessment; (2) enabling vertically resolved diagnosis of model physics and forecast drift; and (3) supporting objective evaluation of forecast quality in dynamically important regions, including the tropics, midlatitude storm tracks, and polar environments. Results from this framework will help establish STAR GNSS RO as a powerful diagnostic tool for NOAA NCEP GEFSv12 reforecast evaluation, improve understanding of model strengths and weaknesses, and provide guidance for future forecast system development, calibration, and climate-quality reforecast applications.

489635.title: Effects of Risk-based Pricing Reform on Flood Insurance Uptake
489635.authors: Jesse Gourevitch, Resources for the Future, Washington, DC
489635.abstract: Insurance is critical for financial recovery following climate-related disasters, particularly for low-income households. As premiums increase in response to the growing cost of climate impacts, there are concerns that coverage may become unaffordable for many households, leading to a decline in insurance uptake. In 2021 and 2022, the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) began a major pricing reform, known as Risk Rating 2.0, to better align premiums with property-level flood risks and to improve the solvency of the program. We aim to understand the impacts of this reform on flood insurance demand by estimating the effects of NFIP premium changes on the number of policies-in-force. Using difference-in-differences models with dynamic treatment effects, we find that Risk Rating 2.0 has caused an 11 – 39% decline in new policies and a 5 – 13% decline in existing policies, depending on the amount premiums have increased. These effects are larger in zip codes with lower median household income, whereas differences across flood zones are not statistically significant. Despite the potential benefits of risk-based pricing reform, our results highlight the need for policy interventions that help low-income households maintain their insurance coverage.

489636.title: Enhanced Typhoon Remote Sensing for Japan Using GXS‑Class Hyperspectral Sounding on Himawari‑11
489636.authors: Jaevyn Faulk, BAE Systems - Aerospace & Mission Systems, Boulder, CO; and M. Shogrin and M. Vercauteren
489636.abstract: The Geostationary Extended Observation Sounder (GXS) provides high‑temporal, high‑fidelity atmospheric measurements from geostationary orbit, completing full‑disk soundings every 30 minutes and targeted 1000 km × 1000 km scans in under 2 minutes. The ability to perform meso‑scale soundings with reduced spatial and spectral pixel binning allows trading spectral and radiometric performance for finer spatial resolution and clearer views of localized thermodynamic features. A GXS‑like instrument on Himawari‑11 would improve temperature and humidity retrievals around typhoons, especially in clear and partially cloudy regions where rapid environmental changes influence storm evolution. Frequent hyperspectral sampling enhances characterization of key atmospheric features associated with typhoon development and intensification. These capabilities strengthen monitoring of typhoon behavior and severe weather across Japan and expand the scientific value of geostationary atmospheric remote sensing.

489637.title: How Do Environmental Conditions Regulate the Boundary Layer Cloud Properties and Radiative Effects: Insights from CAPE-k, COMBLE, and MARCUS
489637.authors: Zeqian(Hazel) Xia, University of Oklahoma, NORMAN, OK; and Y. Huang and G. M. McFarquhar
489637.abstract: How synoptic dynamics, cloud-scale dynamics, latent heating, aerosols, precipitation, and radiative transfer jointly control the response of cloud properties to environmental conditions remains poorly understood. Earth system models correspondingly struggle to represent mixed-phase clouds at high latitudes, leaving large uncertainties in the latitudinal gradients of cloud radiative effects (CRE) and cloud feedbacks. We address these gaps using three recent U.S. Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) field campaigns spanning both hemispheres: the Cloud and Precipitation Experiment at kennaook (CAPE-k) at kennaook/Cape Grim, Tasmania, Australia (40.7°S); the Cold-Air Outbreaks in the Marine Boundary Layer Experiment (COMBLE), with its main site at Andenes, Norway (69°N); and the Measurements of Aerosols, Radiation, and Clouds over the Southern Ocean (MARCUS), collected aboard an icebreaker transiting between Hobart, Tasmania, and the Australian Antarctic stations of Casey, Mawson, and Davis, as well as Macquarie Island. MARCUS extends this comparison across 43–68°S, spanning the latitude band where the modeled shortwave radiation bias peaks, and provides the meridional gradient linking the fixed-site observations to the region of largest model error. For each campaign we derive a common suite of environmental parameters, including cold-air outbreak (CAO) intensity (M), lower-tropospheric stability (LTS), estimated inversion strength (EIS), convective available potential energy (CAPE), sea surface temperature, boundary layer (BL) depth, wind shear, surface heat fluxes, vertical velocity and relative humidity at 700-hPa, and precipitation occurrence, together with BL cloud macrophysical properties (cloud top and base heights, temperature, and cloud fraction) and microphysical properties (phase, effective radius, and liquid/ice water content). A statistical analysis is performed to determine how the cloud properties varied with environmental conditions for the three campaigns across seasonal cycles. Even under comparable local-spring conditions and similar synoptic regimes (matched M, LTS, and EIS), cloud properties differ among sites. CAPE-k recorded higher wind speeds within the BL compared to the other two campaigns, while also exhibiting less moisture than COMBLE. CAPE-k and MARCUS showed smaller averaged cloud top heights and a broader spectral width, which is consistent with higher turbulence or the presence of liquid and ice phases simultaneously, compared to the other two sites. Thus, even in the same season and under similar synoptic conditions, BL cloud properties vary across different locations. We further applied the ARM Cloud Type Classification (cldtype) value-added product to CAPE-k and COMBLE, supplementing its seven categories with categories for multi-layer cloud and clear sky. Combining this classification with surface radiometer observations yields estimates of how hourly LW and SW CRE vary by cloud type. Low clouds were the dominant control on surface radiative input at COMBLE during local spring. Deep, optically thick clouds were far less frequent but produced the strongest SW cooling at both sites. This highlights the significance of cloud type and occurrence frequency in shaping the surface radiation balance. Because the liquid fraction within a cloud largely governs its radiative effect, the THERMOCLDPHASE product is used to classify cloud phase and compute hourly LW and SW CRE by cloud phase, testing whether phase partitioning accounts for the CRE contrast between sites. Ongoing work leverages Ka-band zenith radar Doppler spectra and radiosondes to identify rimed particles, drizzle droplets, and signatures of secondary ice particles (SIP), and to hypothesize the surface radiative impacts of SIP in mixed-phase clouds. These results provide new observational constraints on cloud-radiation interactions in contrasting high-latitude environments and offer benchmarks for evaluating model performance.

489653.title: Seasonal, Geographic, and Temperature and Pressure Dependent Variability in Stratospheric Sulfuric Acid Particle Composition
489653.authors: Elizabeth Asher, NCAR, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and A. Baron, A. Fritz, G. A. Morris, M. Martinsen, R. Querel, P. Smale, A. Bourassa, D. Zawada, and E. Hall
489653.abstract: Particle composition, including the sulfuric acid (H2SO4) weight fraction, influences the chemical, microphysical, optical, and radiative properties of stratospheric aerosols. Balloon soundings from 2004 to 2026 at three geographically distributed, long-term NOAA frost point hygrometer (FPH) sites show that the stratospheric H2SO4 weight fraction varied with pressure, season, and location from 0.45 to over 0.80. These data can be used to validate and inform state-of-the-art Earth system prediction models and satellite retrievals that often assume a fixed value for the entire atmospheric column. We found that deviations in the H2SO4 weight fraction from climatology were largely explained and predicted by variations in temperature and pressure level. Finally, Aura Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS) v6 retrievals of water vapor and temperature were used to provide global distributions of H2SO4 weight fraction from 2004 to 2026 at corresponding pressure levels. These satellite-derived distributions reveal a similar dependence on season and temperature variations, as well as on pressure level over the tropics and midlatitudes, providing a vital prognostic framework when direct water vapor measurements are unavailable. Future work will explore alternative formulations for H2SO4 weight fraction, based on ACE-FTS retrievals, particularly related to polar regimes.

489654.title: Perception vs Plan: Assessing Kentucky Disaster Climatology for Improved Hazard Mitigation
489654.authors: Harmony Lillian Guercio, Western Kentucky University, Knoxville, TN; and I. Pfeiffer, J. D. Durkee, B. C. Lampton, and S. Gunter
489654.abstract: This study uses the NOAA Storm Events Database to offer a 30-year disaster climatology for all 120 counties in Kentucky from 1996 to 2025. In order to assess hazard dominance, cumulative impacts, frequency trends, population-based reporting bias, teleconnection affects, and composite risk, recorded occurrences were divided into six hazard categories. In approximately 100 of the 120 counties, wind was the leading hazard, while flood led in much of eastern Kentucky and extreme temperatures led in portions of the west. Statistically significant increasing trends (p < 0.05) in total hazard frequency were found for over 40 counties using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression of annual event counts. These trends were mostly driven by wind events and were focused in western and south-central Kentucky. The majority of hazard occurrences in rural Kentucky never make it into the official record, with rural counties reporting an estimated 27-31% of true event occurrence, according to a population density-based reporting bias correction. In eastern Kentucky, negative Arctic Oscillation (AO) and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) phases produced winter weather frequencies two to three times higher than positive phases, whereas El Niño years reduced wind and flood activity and La Niña years increased flooding. Western Kentucky was shown to be the state’s highest-risk area by a composite risk assessment that combined event frequency (40%), property damage (35%), and casualties (25%). These results show that rural hazard exposure is underestimated by raw event databases, and that observed trends reflect both reporting infrastructure and climate variability. These findings have significant implications for resource allocation and hazard mitigation planning in Kentucky.

489661.title: Tropical Cyclones and Extreme Statistics in an AI Emulator of the 3 km X-SHiELD Global Storm-Resolving Model
489661.authors: Troy Arcomano, test4, College Station, TX; and A. Kwa, W. A. Perkins, J. McGibbon, S. Clark, O. Watt-Meyer, C. Bretherton, and L. M. Harris
489661.abstract: We present the latest iteration of HiRO-ACE, a two-stage framework for AI emulation of the 3 km resolution X-SHiELD global storm-resolving model (GSRM), and highlight its ability to generate large ensembles of data for studying the characteristics of tropical cyclones in high-resolution simulations at an inference computational cost over 2000 times lower than that of traditional numerical GSRMs. Fine-resolution predictions are generated by running an autoregressive emulator of coarsened X-SHiELD at 100 km, whose precipitation, 10m winds, and sea level pressure outputs are regionally downscaled to 3km resolution via a separately trained diffusion model. Particular importance is placed on capturing the statistics of extreme events; we describe several updates to the diffusion model training and inference over the previous iteration, which improve its ability to match the tails of distributions and generate realistic-looking extreme events. The model closely matches the reference distributions of precipitation and near-surface winds out to their 99.9999th percentile values, and broadly tracks the reference distribution of tropical cyclone intensities across different basins. As part of our goal to expand the accessibility of these tools for downstream users studying local risks and climate impacts, the HiRO-ACE training code and inference software are fully open, and tutorials for running the workflow are provided.

489663.title: Forward Modeling of Radar Reflectivity, Polarimetric Variables, and Doppler Spectra for Wildfire Smoke
489663.authors: Angela Wang, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and S. T. Peters, C. R. Williams, D. E. Kingsmill, and M. E. Frediani
489663.abstract: Wildfire smoke is an increasingly important hazard to monitor as wildfire-prone regions expand and fire seasons lengthen, degrading air quality, reducing aviation visibility, and impacting public health and ecosystems. However, significant observational gaps remain in characterizing plume microphysics and dynamics. Weather radars provide continuous, long-range, three-dimensional observations that can help fill these observational gaps. These observations can improve the evaluation of active fire and emission processes in fire behavior models through improved characterization of particle transport for fire spotting, plume formation and injection height for pyroconvection, and plume structure for boundary layer processes. A fundamental challenge in the operational use of weather radars for wildfire smoke retrievals and plume monitoring is that the relationships between particle microphysical properties and radar observables remain poorly constrained. The objective of this work is to establish a forward-modeling framework that links in situ wildfire smoke microphysics to weather radar observations. The framework combines in situ optical array probe observations collected during the NSF RaDFIRE field campaign with particle property measurements reported in the literature. Particle size distributions and shape measurements derived from the in situ measurements are used to constrain T-matrix scattering calculations that simulate radar reflectivity, dual-polarization variables, and Doppler spectra for S-, C-, X-, and W-band frequencies. The resulting scattering cross sections are incorporated into a forward radar model to simulate radar reflectivity, dual-polarization variables, and Doppler spectra. Atmospheric attenuation and particle fall-speed parameterizations are incorporated to investigate the influence of atmospheric conditions and particle dynamics on simulated radar observables. Preliminary results demonstrate the sensitivity of simulated radar observables to assumptions regarding particle sizes, shape, density and dielectric properties. The results provide insight into which particle properties most strongly influence radar returns and identify the dominant sources of uncertainty in forward modeling. Comparisons with the co-located airborne W-band Wyoming Cloud Radar and the nearby ground-based S-band NEXRAD KCBX radar observations are being used to evaluate model performance and assess the detectability of wildfire ash across multiple radar frequencies. By establishing a framework that links wildfire smoke microphysics to radar observations, this work provides a foundation for interpreting weather radar observations of wildfire smoke, developing future quantitative retrieval algorithms, multi-frequency radar analysis, and operational radar-based wildfire monitoring.

489666.title: Skillful Extended Range Forecast of the August 2016 Extreme Arctic Cyclone with 4DEnVar Assimilation Using MPAS-JEDI
489666.authors: Qian Xie, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and D. H. Bromwich
489666.abstract: Accurate prediction of Arctic cyclones remains a major challenge in numerical weather prediction due to sparse observations and complex high-latitude dynamics. This study employs the advanced Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) interfaced with the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) with a regional variable-resolution mesh of 46–12 km to investigate the predictability of an extreme Arctic cyclone in August 2016 (AC16), evaluating three assimilation experiments: three-dimensional variational (3DVar), three-dimensional ensemble–variational (3DEnVar), and four-dimensional ensemble–variational (4DEnVar). Following cycling assimilation, 7-day forecasts are performed to evaluate the forecast skill. The 4DEnVar experiment shows the best overall performance, producing analyses closest to the observations with pronounced increments. At forecast day 5, it accurately captures the peak intensity of AC16, reducing the position error by 63.2% relative to 3DVar, with a 54.4% sea surface level root-mean-square error (RMSE) reduction confirmed by buoy observations. It also shows improvements in zonal wind, temperature, and relative humidity at middle to lower levels beyond the 3-day forecast. These improvements are attributed to a better representation of key dynamical processes, including cyclone merging, baroclinic instability, and jet stream forcing, as well as the vertical coupling between the upper-level vortices and the surface cyclones. Forecasts with extended cycling assimilations confirm these improvements, though results remain sensitive to cycling length. This study highlights the strong potential of regional MPAS-JEDI 4DEnVar to improve high-latitude numerical weather prediction through its flow-dependent ensemble covariances, providing a valuable approach for forecasting extreme cyclones over the data-sparse region like the Arctic.

489678.title: Unlocking Operational Agility: Integrating NWS HIVE and NWS CIRRUS into the NWS Forecasting Ecosystem
489678.authors: Ronla Henry-Reeves, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and J. M. Coyne, T. C. Oram, J. Sieveking, N. L. Hampshire, K. L. Sheets, and D. Hood
489678.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) is entering a transformative era of operations, shifting from site-specific constraints to a truly enterprise-wide, cloud-native forecasting paradigm powered by the integration of NWS HIVE and CIRRUS. By uniting HIVE’s collaborative, microservices-based application environment with the scalable, high-performance computing capabilities of CIRRUS, the NWS will achieve unprecedented operational flexibility and resilience. This presentation will detail the strategic implementation of this integrated ecosystem, emphasizing the transition to a unified, location-independent workforce capable of deploying mission-critical services anywhere. Attendees will gain insight into the NWS roadmap for operationalizing these platforms, from the integration of real-time data ingestion and cloud-based processing to the deployment of dynamic, elastic resources during high-impact weather events. Ultimately, we demonstrate how this synergy not only modernizes our technical infrastructure but fundamentally redefines the NWS’s ability to deliver life-saving intelligence, ensuring the agency remains agile and responsive in an increasingly complex environmental landscape.

489692.title: Performance or Parsimony? Modeling Conditional Radar Rainfall Errors with Machine Learning
489692.authors: Levi Harris, Northeastern University, Boston, MA
489692.abstract: For several decades, ground radars have provided high-resolution, low-latency estimates of rainfall across much of the United States. But despite their broad success, several sources of uncertainty continue to cloud the relationship between radar returns aloft and rain rates at the surface—motivating the development of statistical models of radar rainfall (RR) error. Traditionally, error models have aimed for parsimony (e.g., Ciach and Krajewski 1999). By honing in on one or two key predictors, previous uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods in radar meteorology have achieved both computational efficiency and explainability. In contrast, this work explores multivariate models of RR error implemented using machine learning (ML). Using a multi-source dataset of ~220,000 independent hourly gauge observations aligned with 50+ auxiliary environmental variables in southern Nevada, we validated a UQ approach for the MRMS Radar Only QPE during 2021-2025 (inclusive). Here, sacrificing parsimony proves worthwhile. We find that a small neural network trained to predict the parameters of a double-exponential distribution (Ciach and Gebremichael 2020) produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates and meaningful reductions in wet biases (89.9%) and MAE (26.4%). We also propose scenario modeling maps: a visualization technique that allows users to explore simulated changes in the QPE error structure under different environmental conditions. Our results underscore an important ongoing debate within the meteorological community. Namely, do inscrutable yet skillful models (e.g., neural networks) belong in an operational setting?

489696.title: Impacts of Coastal Wind Profiler and Weather Tower Observations on High-resolution Numerical Weather Prediction Model Forecasts
489696.authors: Blake Sorenson, National Research Council, Monterey, CA; and D. P. Tyndall, S. Chen, J. M. Schmidt, C. Amerault, N. Gapp, T. Corrigan Jr., and A. Luo
489696.abstract: Rocket launching operations at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) are very sensitive to weather conditions, with strict limits on wind gusts, precipitation intensity, and lightning. A network of wind profilers and multi-level weather towers around KSC monitors the weather for launches, but these data are not assimilated operationally into any NWP models. In this project, we determine the impacts of coastal wind profiler and weather tower data assimilation on high-resolution forecasts from a research version of the Coupled Ocean Atmosphere Mesoscale Prediction System (COAMPS). Observation impacts are quantified using observing system experiments and adjointbased forecast sensitivity to observation impact (FSOI) analyzed over one month of cycled model runs in June 2023. From the FSOI results, we found that both the wind profiler and tower datasets are beneficial to the model forecasts, with the tower humidity observations providing the most beneficial impact. The towers are more beneficial than the profilers overall, though the profiler winds are more beneficial than the tower winds. The magnitude of the beneficial impact from the KSC datasets is tied closely to the synoptic-scale flow; more beneficial impact was observed during generally zonal flow conditions with notable sea breeze signatures in near-surface wind fields, while less beneficial impact was observed during meridional flow conditions with weaker or non-existent sea breeze circulations. From the data denial experiments, we found notable reductions in 2-m air temperature root mean squared error (RMSE) in the afternoon hours from 00Z and 06Z forecasts due to the assimilation of the profiler and tower data. Statistically significant reductions in 2-m dew point RMSE were found in 06Z forecasts in short forecast times, with other notable reductions in 2-m dew point RMSE that were not statistically significant at other cycles.

489697.title: Honoring the Backbone of Modern Forecasting: Celebrating the Legacy and Impact of AWIPS
489697.authors: Ronla Henry-Reeves, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and J. Glenn, S. T. Jacobs, and D. Hood
489697.abstract: For over three decades, the Advanced Weather Interactive Processing System (AWIPS) has served as the technological cornerstone of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) National Weather Service (NWS). First deployed in the 1990s across 170 facilities, AWIPS revolutionized meteorological science by integrating complex data streams into a single, cohesive workstation. As the primary tool used daily by agency forecasters, it fundamentally transformed how the nation predicts the weather, empowering meteorologists to process, display, and communicate vital data with unprecedented speed. AWIPS’s true legacy lies in its lifesaving impact; for a generation, it was the engine behind the rapid dissemination of critical warnings and advisories that protected countless communities. As the NWS prepares to transition to a next-generation system to meet future technological demands, this presentation celebrates the historic achievements, operational resilience, and profound triumphs of AWIPS. We honor a system that not only defined modern forecasting but also set the gold standard for operational meteorology and public safety.

489699.title: A Multi-Method Probabilistic System for Predicting U.S. Climate Hazards on Decadal Timescales
489699.authors: Sean C. Emmons, Climate Central, Princeton, NJ; and Z. M. Labe, PhD, K. Dahl, and A. Pershing
489699.abstract: Interannual to decadal timescales represent key planning horizons for businesses and communities assessing risk and making climate-informed decisions, yet predicting how hazards may change over this period remains difficult. Developing usable, decision-ready metrics is equally challenging, especially when physical climate risks reflect both anthropogenic climate change and internal variability. In this work, we present the ongoing development of a new multi-method probabilistic system to predict climate hazards across the contiguous United States in the 1-10 year timeframe. This framework applies four complementary prediction methods: (1) shifting the observed record forward in time to a target global mean temperature; (2) constraining a collection of initial-condition climate model large ensembles by selecting analogs whose ocean state resembles present conditions; (3) retaining the full spread across all large ensemble members; and (4) a climatological benchmark built from extrapolating the long-term trend while still considering historical variability. To account for regional differences in potential predictability, the four prediction methods are combined through a weighted blend based on each method’s skill for a given climate variable, location, and lead time, as evaluated using a historical hindcast. Here, we present early results for temperature- and precipitation-derived metrics that are selected to directly inform decisions in climate-exposed sectors. This includes probability distributions for metrics such as heating and cooling degree days for energy demand, growing degree days and freeze frequency for agriculture, and heavy precipitation for agriculture and insurance. Reliable climate information at these lead times is increasingly important as communities adapt infrastructure, plan for conditions no longer represented by historical baselines, and make decisions in sectors where sudden shifts in temperature and precipitation have significant consequences.

489713.title: Evaluating the Impact of Assimilating AR Recon Drifting-Buoy Observations over the Northeastern Pacific on GFS Forecast Skill
489713.authors: Murali Nageswararao Malasala, NOAA, Riverdale Park, MD; UCAR, Boulder, CO; and X. Wu, S. Akella, M. Aristizabal Vargas, B. Zhou, K. Wu, and V. S. Tallapragada
489713.abstract: Oceanic observations are important for constraining initial conditions in numerical weather prediction, particularly over data-sparse regions such as the North Pacific. This study evaluates the influence of assimilating drifting-buoy observations on Global Forecast System (GFS) during atmospheric river (AR) events in winter 2025–2026. Two experimental configurations are compared: a control experiment (CTL), which assimilates the full observing network, and a remove-drifter-buoy experiment (RMDB), in which all drifting-buoy observations over the northeastern Pacific are withheld from the data assimilation system. Forecast cycles from December 2025 through March 2026 are examined. Atmospheric variables, including mean sea-level pressure, 500-hPa geopotential height, integrated vapor transport, integrated water vapor, and surface temperature, are evaluated against GDAS analyses. Mean sea-level pressure is also verified directly against observed pressure at drifter locations. Downstream precipitation forecasts over the U.S. West Coast are evaluated separately against Stage-IV observations using continuous and categorical verification metrics. Results indicate that the impact of drifting-buoy assimilation is generally marginal in global-scale and pooled verification statistics. Slightly more discernible impacts are found at regional and location-specific scales, particularly over the northeastern Pacific and near the assimilated observation locations. The most consistent differences occur in surface pressure and mid-tropospheric circulation, suggesting a modest contribution from drifting-buoy observations to the representation of cyclone-scale features and regional large-scale flow. Impacts on integrated vapor transport, integrated water vapor, and surface temperature are generally smaller and vary with forecast lead time, spatial domain, and event characteristics. Effects on downstream precipitation are also lead- and threshold-dependent, with improvements in the CTL experiment occurring for some AR cases and precipitation intensities but not uniformly across all forecast periods. The influence of drifting-buoy observations is more apparent when individual AR events and specific forecast cycles are examined. Overall, the results demonstrate that drifting-buoy observations provide greater forecast value at regional, location-specific, and event-specific scales than is indicated by global or fully pooled verification statistics.

489714.title: Observations of Terrain-Induced Coherent Structures in the Atmospheric Surface Layer
489714.authors: Aliza Abraham, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Arvada, CO; and S. Yellapantula
489714.abstract: Numerical weather prediction (NWP) models struggle to capture flow over complex terrain that falls in the “terra incognita” between the spatial resolution of microscale (< 100 m) and mesoscale (> 1 km) simulations. In this regime, properties of turbulence and coherent flow structures are determined by the complex interactions between the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) and terrain features. In the current study, we use Doppler lidar data collected in a basin between ~1 km tall ridges in the Nevada desert (Fig. 1a) to investigate these interactions, particularly the effects of atmospheric stability. Wind speed measurements were recorded by a scanning Doppler wind lidar located in the center of a field of heliostats belonging to a concentrating solar thermal plant. The lidar was programmed to alternate between plan position indicator (PPI) and range height indicator (RHI) scans. Both scans center on the north-northwesterly predominant wind direction at the site, with the PPI scans covering a horizontal sector and the RHI scans measuring a vertical plane. The range of the lidar is such that the scans reach the edge of the heliostat field and extend 2100 m beyond, capturing both the flow over the heliostats and the freestream flow. Using these lidar scans and capitalizing on the strong diurnal cycle of the Nevada desert, we characterize the structure of the surface layer under different atmospheric stabilities. Under stable nighttime conditions, strong stratification is observed, including the occasional appearance of gravity waves shed from the surrounding ridges (Fig. 1b). Under convective daytime conditions, the flow is characterized by turbulent streaks generated by plumes from the heated ground surface stretched by the wind (Fig 1c). These observations can be used to inform NWP model development but providing validation datasets and insights into the physics driving the interactions between terrain and the ABL at the terra incognita scale. Figure 1. (a) Terrain surrounding the experimental site, indicated by a red dot. (b) Sample RHI (top) and PPI (bottom) scans during stable atmospheric conditions, showing signatures of stratification and gravity waves. (c) Sample scans during convective conditions showing elongated streaky structures.

489717.title: Uncertainties in Recent Tropical Stratospheric and Tropospheric Ozone Changes Limit The Use of Observational Constraints for Assessing Future Ozone Change
489717.authors: Sean M. Davis, NOAA, Boulder, CO
489717.abstract: A variety of chemical and dynamical processes in the troposphere and stratosphere affect tropical total column ozone (TCO), the net effect of which may cause changes in surface UV radiation and impact human and ecosystem health. We use dynamical linear modeling to estimate changes in tropical TCO and partial column ozone (PCO) in the troposphere and three stratospheric layers to assess agreement between satellite composites and chemistry-climate model simulations from two multi-model experiments (CCMI-1 and CCMI-2022). While both model experiments show tropical TCO increases over 2000–2021, multimodel-mean CCMI-2022 changes (+2.5 DU) agree slightly better with observations than CCMI-1 (+1.6 DU). However, this overall agreement obscures multiple systematic differences in PCO changes between the models and observations across atmospheric layers. For example, since 2000 tropical tropospheric PCO increased significantly in CCMI-2022 (+1.5 DU) but not in CCMI-1 (+0.3 DU), largely explaining the difference in TCO changes. Also, despite nearly identical stratospheric PCO changes, CCMI-2022 changes are slightly more negative than CCMI-1 in the lower stratosphere (by ~0.5 DU) and more positive in the middle/upper stratosphere. Crucially, substantial differences exist between observational PCO changes, particularly in the troposphere and middle/upper stratosphere, and these disagreements limit the ability to evaluate CCM fidelity for past changes. Furthermore, while the inter-model correlation between late and early 21st century trends is suggestive of a potential emergent constraint on future ozone trends, the spread in observational trends precludes its observational implementation.

489730.title: Zooming in on Urban Heat with the NASA-IBM Prithvi-EO-2.0 Foundation Model
489730.authors: Jonathan David Starfeldt, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; and M. J. Molina, A. Kerr, A. Yang, T. R. H. Holmes, C. R. Hain, S. E. Haupt, and A. Sayed
489730.abstract: Heat is amplified in urban areas due to impermeable surfaces and complex human-modified environments. While urban heat is well understood, the extent to which variations occur on hyper-local scales (i.e., street-level) is less studied. With over eighty percent of the United States’ population living in urban areas, it is critically important to advance our understanding and observational capabilities of urban environments. Current satellite and ground-based observing systems do not consistently provide the spatial density and revisit frequency required to resolve neighborhood-scale heat gradients and characterize their diurnal evolution. Recent advances in artificial intelligence provide methods to deal with such resolution limitations. Urban Heat MiniCubes is an AI-Ready dataset consisting of satellite data in two complementary modalities for monitoring urban heat: (i) 30 m-resolution, 8-day observations from polar-orbiting Landsat/Sentinel-1 satellites, and (ii) 2 km-resolution, 10-minute observations from geostationary GOES-R series satellites and passive microwave radiometers. These modalities individually provide high-resolution or high-frequency monitoring, but not both. Super-resolution is a machine learning technique that sharpens low-resolution images using high-resolution targets, enabling the fusion of complementary modalities in Urban Heat MiniCubes to produce high-frequency, high-resolution outputs. To enable this large increase in spatiotemporal resolution (from 2 km to 30 m and from 8-day to 10-minute intervals), we use NASA-IBM’s Prithvi-EO-2.0 foundation model, which provides compressed, common-dimension latent representations of each data modality. We demonstrate that Prithvi-EO-2.0 can generalize beyond its training domain; it achieves high reconstruction skill on Landsat land surface temperatures and GOES brightness temperatures, despite being trained on Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) surface reflectances. Generative AI-based mapping from low-resolution GOES latents to high-resolution Landsat latents enables the creation of high-resolution GOES imagery representations. Initial results from this super-resolution methodology are presented.

489733.title: Long-Term Contribution of Ozone to Health Impacts In the US (2008-2025)
489733.authors: Olivia Sablan, University of Washington Bothell, Bothell, WA; and H. Lee, J. Huang, M. Tao, A. M. Fiore, S. Magzamen, and D. A. Jaffe
489733.abstract: Ozone (O3) is a secondary air pollutant formed through photochemical reactions of nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds. As wildfires increase in frequency and intensity with a warming climate, understanding the contribution to surface O3 pollution and the health impacts from exposure to smoke O3 is becoming increasingly important. We estimated the contributions of smoke, anthropogenic, and background O3 to observed surface O3 concentrations and associated health impacts across the contiguous United States. We evaluated three sources of O3: 1) U.S. anthropogenic, 2) background (e.g., biogenic, soil, lightning emissions, transported emissions), and 3) landscape fire smoke. We calculated maximum daily 8-hour average (MDA8) smoke O3 concentrations across the contiguous United States for April - October 2008-2025 by combining EPA Air Quality System (AQS) O3 and PM2.5 measurements, NOAA Hazard Mapping System smoke plumes, satellite observations, and meteorological data in a generalized additive model (GAM). This model indicated that smoke O3 reached up to 9.7 ppb (99th percentile of EPA AQS site averages) during the study period. Background O3 was modeled with the Multiscale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols version 0 (MUSICAv0) by removing anthropogenic and biomass burning emissions. Monthly mean background estimates were applied throughout the study period as a representative background O3 contribution. Anthropogenic O3 was then estimated as the remaining observed O3 after accounting for smoke O3 and background O3. We used a health impact assessment to investigate long-term trends in mortality and asthma emergency department visits resulting from O3 exposure. Preliminary results indicate that anthropogenic and naturally occurring background O3 contribute the majority of ozone-attributable mortality and asthma emergency department visits. Smoke O3 contributes a smaller overall health burden than the other O3 sources, but its contribution has increased in recent years with increasing wildfire activity. These findings highlight the importance of continued reductions in anthropogenic O3 while improving our understanding of the health impacts of smoke O3 in a warming climate.

489738.title: Examining and Exploiting Fine-Scale Features In Clouds Using Ultra-High-Resolution Lidar
489738.authors: Grant Kirchhoff, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and M. Hayman, J. Thayer, and B. Garby
489738.abstract: Despite their importance as feedback mechanisms in weather and climate, cloud processes remain poorly understood, with insufficient observations identified as a key contributing factor. Lidars help address this observational gap by providing high-resolution measurements of cloud optical properties – such as backscatter, extinction, cloud boundary height, and thermodynamic phase. However, lidar sensing in clouds can be susceptible to nonideal sampling conditions, which can degrade measurement fidelity. In atmospheric lidar, the sampled particle field is generally assumed to be statistically homogeneous and high-occupancy over the sample volume, as well as stationary throughout integration. Using an ultra-high-resolution lidar (0.11 m in range x 70 µs in time), we show observations of fine-scale features that violate the idealized sampling assumption – like heterogeneity, rapid cloud evolution, and hydrometeor sparsity. We examine how these fine-scale features can degrade accuracy and pass undetected at conventional lidar resolutions. In doing so, we demonstrate the instrument’s potential as a probe for interrogating subresolution structure within conventional-lidar sample volumes and evaluating the assumptions underlying cloud-lidar retrievals. Lastly, we will show how ultra-high-resolution lidar can be used to not only reveal sparse sampling conditions but exploit them to enable new measurements. The instrument can track the vertical displacement of individual precipitation droplets as a function of time, thus enabling direct measurements of their vertical velocities and avoiding the dependence on inferring these quantities from bulk measurements. This capability demonstrates a regime shift in remote sensing, where hydrometeor measurements can be treated as particle resolved instead of volume averaged.

489740.title: Understanding Current Feedback-Induced Modification of the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
489740.authors: Kamran Alexander Chowdhury, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; COAPS, Tallahassee, FL; and M. A. Bourassa, M. Larrañaga, J. Zhou, X. Chen, and J. C. May
489740.abstract: There are two forms of ocean-atmosphere coupling that impact the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) over the ocean surface. One is thermal feedback (TFB) coupling, where sea surface temperatures (SSTs) and their gradients can affect wind through adjustments in pressure gradients and stability, among other mechanisms. The other is current feedback (CFB) coupling, where ocean currents alter the shear between the ocean and atmosphere, resulting in direct changes in wind stress and winds. The goal of this research is to better understand the mesoscale effects of current feedback onto the ABL, and ‘disentangle’ its effects from thermal feedback. To do this, two model simulations were run. The first one represents a full CFB-TFB-coupled ocean-atmosphere system, where currents were allowed to impact wind stress. The second one represents a no-CFB, TFB-only ocean-atmosphere system, through a new technique: the ocean from the first simulation is used to re-run the atmosphere only as an SST boundary condition. This novel method enables a clearer comparison of ABL processes, between those of an atmosphere that is affected by CFB and those of an atmosphere that is not, over the exact same oceanic features (SSTs). From the model data, when sampling atmospheric transects over the Gulf Stream in quiet synoptic regimes, TFB evidently modifies the ABL in the vicinity of SST changes. CFB appears to then further modify the ABL in two major ways. The first is as a boundary condition forcing of the surface winds by ocean currents, which can be visualized as an adjustment of wind vorticity towards ocean vorticity that is strongest near the surface. The second is as a modulator of TFB processes, such as through modifying surface heat fluxes, altering the TFB-induced adjustment of the ABL: for instance, TFB allows a gradual deepening of the ABL downwind of the Gulf Stream when the wind vector blows to the right of the current vector, and a rapid cutoff/shallowing of the ABL when the wind blows the other direction. Early results suggest that CFB may help enhance ABL changes in both cases, but more the former than the latter. TFB and CFB responses additionally exhibit a wind speed and atmospheric stability dependence, as demonstrated for wind speed with evidence of enhanced non-local/downstream TFB- and CFB- induced surface wind divergence and vorticity changes (respectively) with higher wind speeds. The location, extent, and magnitude of different CFB (and TFB) responses depending on prevailing wind direction relative to the current, wind speed, and atmospheric stability, serves as a reminder of the Gulf Stream’s asymmetric structure; and more importantly, it lends credence that different air-sea coupling mechanisms and processes dominate in different atmospheric conditions. By examining through modeling how the atmospheric boundary layer responds to current feedback – in the context of thermal feedback – this study is anticipated to advance our theoretical understanding of the coupled ocean-atmosphere system, and enable future improvements in observations and modeling of the atmosphere over the ocean.

489748.title: Observations of Aerosols and Clouds from a Commercial Vessel: BEACONS Pilot Study
489748.authors: Raghavendra Krishnamurthy, PNNL, Richland, WA; and M. Christensen, A. Wang, L. Goldberger, D. Coffman, H. Best, T. Bates, H. J. S. Fernando, B. Nagare, V. Berta, L. M. Russell, A. Macdonald, R. Hudak, and A. C. Subramanian
489748.abstract: The Boundary layer Exploration of Aerosols and Clouds ON Ships (BEACONS) project was motivated by the fundamental need for long‑term, high‑quality observations in the marine boundary layer, where clouds and aerosols remain among the largest sources of uncertainty in Earth system prediction. Ship‑based observations are especially valuable because they provide continuous sampling of remote marine environments where process‑level cloud and aerosol measurements are scarce. By enabling routine, autonomous data collection from commercial vessel routes, BEACONS will fill a major observational gap and directly support DOE’s mission to improve the representation of aerosol-cloud interactions in atmospheric models. Over the past year, the team has designed, built, and deployed modular systems on the PASHA Marjorie C commercial vessel. These systems operate with minimal crew involvement, drawing on more than ten decades of collective expertise to implement real‑time, decision‑based automation for reliable long‑duration deployments. Two instrument platforms were deployed (see Figure), one dedicated to meteorological and cloud observations, and the other to aerosol microphysics. In this presentation, we plan to present preliminary results of the marine boundary layer structure over the central-to-east Pacific Ocean, high-resolution modeling of the region for a stratocumulus to cumulus transition case, comparisons of cloud adiabaticity estimate from observations and satellite retrievals, and comparison between aerosol size distributions of pre-IMO (International Maritime Organization) - 2020 regulation shipping impacts using DOE Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Marine ARM GPCI Investigation of Clouds (MAGIC) campaign observations from 2012 to post-IMO 2020 observed during BEACONS. Future plans for the project will also be discussed.

489750.title: Add-DA: Optimizing initial Conditions to Produce a Better Forecast
489750.authors: Sergey Frolov, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and L. Slivinski, C. C. Tong, C. Miller, J. DaRosa, N. Silverman, M. Alam, and N. D. Brenowitz
489750.abstract: AI weather forecast models can now be reliably initialized from observations using emerging AI data assimilation (AIDA) approaches. However, can AIDA help us find initial conditions that are superior to those of the traditional data assimilation systems? To answer this question, we formulate the Add-DA algorithm where AIDA initial condition is optimized to produce the best forecast using the AI weather forecast model. The combined model consists of an Anemoi-based global forecast model and a custom initialization operator conditioned on a combination of the model prior and observations. This presentation will shows and discuss updated results towards this goal.

489752.title: Assessing Evolving Tropical Cyclone Hazards and Risk through 2050 Using a Multi-Model Framework
489752.authors: Sydney M Kramer, LDEO, Palisades, NY; and C. Y. Lee, A. H. Sobel, S. J. Camargo, PhD, J. D. Doyle, D. P. Stern, K. Prince, J. R. Moskaitis, and M. Hemmati
489752.abstract: Understanding how tropical cyclone (TC) characteristics evolve in the future is essential for proactive planning and enhancing coastal resilience. This project examines changes in TC intensity, frequency, track behavior, and associated hazards through 2050 using complementary modeling approaches that combine observations, Columbia HAZard model (CHAZ)-downscaled CMIP6 synthetic TCs, directly simulated HighResMIP TCs, and high-resolution COAMPS-TC simulations. The objective is to assess evolving TC hazards and risk across multiple TC basins and support scenario-based risk assessments for vulnerable coastal infrastructure. Using the CMIP6 and HighResMIP ensembles, we quantify changes in storm intensity, frequency, and landfall occurrence near selected coastal locations to identify signals of rare but plausible high-intensity track events. We then examine how these changes translate into hazard distributions at two levels under present-day and mid-century climate conditions: the first at the storm level, by estimating the probability of exceedance of landfall storm intensity; and the second at the hazard level, by estimating the probability of exceedance of the extreme winds, rainfall, and storm surge produced by these storms. Together, these analyses provide an integrated framework for assessing how TC hazards and risks may evolve through the mid-21st century.

489753.title: Evaluating the Fire Weather Matrix and PDS Decision Making in the Inland Northwest
489753.authors: Serena Klarich, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; NWS Spokane, Spokane, WA; and D. J. Butler, S. Bodnar, K. M. Butler, and E. R. Nielsen
489753.abstract: In fire prone areas of the Inland Northwest, accurate forecasting of critical fire weather is vital to protecting lives, property, and supporting the national economy. The 2027 AMS Annual Meeting theme, PEOPLE: People Educated On Planet Live Empowered, focuses on using research and data to benefit society, directly connecting to this evaluation of a fire weather decision tool. Back in 2025, the National Weather Service (NWS) Weather Forecast Office (WFO) in Spokane, WA, implemented a localized fire weather matrix. The Red Flag Warning Decision Matrix guides forecasters by balancing wind and relative humidity thresholds; stronger winds can support a warning at higher humidity, while very low humidity can support one at weaker wind speeds. This study applies the matrix to historical observations to determine how often Red Flag Warning (RFW) and Particularly Dangerous Situation (PDS) thresholds were met and identify regional differences. To assess the matrix’s historical performance, wind and relative humidity (RH) data were analyzed from 9 Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) stations (2002–2026) and 26 Remote Automated Weather Stations (RAWS) (2000–2022) across eastern Washington and northern Idaho from June through September. Station specific matrices counted the days meeting RFW or PDS level meteorological thresholds. Potential PDS days were cross referenced with NWS verification records to compare threshold exceedances with archived warnings. This comparison highlights the complexity of fire weather forecasting because an issued RFW depends on critical weather conditions and critical fuel dryness. Information from land management partners adds context to warning decisions that meteorological criteria alone cannot capture. Results show that RFW level conditions occurred across the forecast area, while sustained PDS level conditions were rare and concentrated mostly in the Columbia Basin and Central Washington. Some potential PDS days met matrix thresholds without a corresponding warning. Since this analysis applies meteorological thresholds without accounting for fuel conditions, these cases cannot be classified as missed warnings without fuel, data quality, and operational information. Historical RFW and PDS level threshold exceedances were mapped to fire zones to establish a local climatology. These findings raise an important question that will guide the continued research: when meteorological thresholds are met, how do fuel conditions and other operational factors influence whether a warning is issued?

489755.title: Probabilistic Storm Surge Ensemble Forecasting with Unstructured Hydrodynamic Modeling and Machine Learning Framework
489755.authors: Fariborz Daneshvar, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and S. Mani, W. J. Pringle, P. Velissariou, Z. Yang, G. Seroka, E. Myers, and S. Moghimi
489755.abstract: Reliable and rapid storm surge forecasting is vital for protecting coastal populations from the threats posed by tropical cyclones. Traditional probabilistic models often struggle with the heavy computational demands of processing large ensemble sets. We present UPSurgeML (short for Unstructured Probabilistic Surge with Machine Learning), an open-source, Python-based workflow designed for high-performance computing (HPC) environments like NOAA’s operational environment, which ensures NOAA operations standard compliance. By integrating an unstructured mesh (SCHISM), UPSurgeML enables seamless hydrodynamic modeling across scales, from inland waterways to the deep ocean. The core innovation lies in its machine learning surrogate modeling approach (using Karhunen–Loève Polynomial Chaos), which substantially decreases the necessary hydrodynamic ensemble size from about 1000 members down to roughly 40. The system processes Automated Tropical Cyclone Forecasting (ATCF)-formatted track data using a parametric wind model (PaHM) to deliver both deterministic and probabilistic surge guidance. This study showcases UPSurgeML skill for some retrospective storms across the Atlantic region, confirming the model's efficacy. UPSurgeML provides a computationally efficient solution for generating high-resolution probability fields and exceedance metrics, offering a robust tool for coastal hazard assessment during the Atlantic hurricane seasons.

489763.title: The Megaflash: A Short History of Our Planet's Longest Lightning Flash
489763.authors: Walter A. Lyons, FMA Research, Fort Collins, CO; and M. J. Peterson
489763.abstract: On 22 October 2017, a continuous lightning discharge snaked across an 829 km expanse of the stratiform region of a quasi-linear convective system impacting the southern U.S. According to the World Meteorological Organization, this event holds the current record for the longest distance spanned by a megaflash. The term “megaflash,” a relatively recent addition to the Glossary of Meteorology, is defined as “...a continuous mesoscale lightning flash with a horizontal path length of approximately 100 km or greater.” The deployment of the Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) on recent GOES satellite missions, along with improved data post-processing methodologies, now permits routine documentation of these massive atmospheric electrical events which have long been suspected, but for many decades were unable to be verified. Moreover, the megaflash’s discovery was a direct outgrowth of research into transient luminous events, especially sprites, which early on were discovered to be commonly induced by positive polarity cloud-to-ground strokes (+CG) possessing large charge moment changes that often occurred within MCS trailing stratiform regions. The pioneering work of the 1940s Thunderstorm Project (focused on air mass storms) formulated our initial conceptual models of deep convection (and thus electrified regions) occurring on the spatial scale of ~ 10 km. Yet the notion that spatially continuous discharges could propagate for tens of km or more through certain convective regimes can be found as early as the 1950s from radar studies by Ligda and later L-band radar observations in Oklahoma. The satellite era lead to the identification of the mesoscale convective complex (MCC) and other mesoscale convective system (MCS) configurations which expanded our conceptions of the scale of convection and electrification by more than an order of magnitude. Multiple radar and balloon-based investigations during the 1980s began resolving the complex dynamical and electrical structure of MCSs, not only within the active cores, but also their massive associated stratiform regions. Concurrently, visual and low-light video monitoring from the Space Shuttle’s Mesoscale Lightning Experiment revealed lightning could illuminate cloudy regions spanning well over 50 km. By the late 1990s, ground-based video observations of “dancing sprites” above MCS stratiform regions strongly hinted at contiguous discharges approaching 200 km in length. By the early 2000s, 3-D lightning mapping arrays (LMAs) had conclusively mapped such mesoscale stratiform lightning events - many of which spawned multiple sprite-parent +CGs as if to announce their presence. The initial 321 km WMO lightning distance record emerged from an investigation of a 2007 MCS sprite-producing megaflash within the Oklahoma LMA. A typical LMA configuration, however, given its line-of-site detection limitations, would be unable to track even longer megaflashes (which tend to propagate mostly under 3000 m AGL). The advent of the GLM, starting on GOES 16, has provided the observational capability to detect a megaflash of any length anywhere within its nearly hemispheric-coverage area, from which an increasingly refined megaflash climatology continues to emerge. A megaflash can produce dozens of CG strikes along its path, which often are very far removed from the MCS’s electrically active convective cores. Some of these CGs have extremely large charge moment changes and/or peak currents which can induce sprites, elves, and/or lightning-triggered upward lightning discharges (LTULs) from tall structures. In addition, we will briefly discuss the emerging implications for lightning safety guidance, facilities protection, forensic investigations and spacecraft launch commit criteria.

489772.title: Canopy Turbulence in Complex Terrain: Disentangling the Effects of Topography and Stability in Observations from the Amazon Forest (Invited Presentation)
489772.authors: Marcelo Chamecki, 520 Portola Plaza, 7127, Los Angeles, CA; and N. Dias, L. S. Freire, and J. D. Fuentes
489772.abstract: In dense forests such as the Amazon, strong canopy drag limits the penetration of turbulence into the vegetation. This effectively separates the canopy layer into two dynamically distinct sub-layers: (i) an upper layer that is constantly flushed by sweeps and ejections and (ii) a lower layer characterized by weak mean flow and turbulence. While the upper layer remains strongly coupled to the flow above and supports rapid gas exchange, the lower canopy is largely decoupled from the overlying atmosphere. The penetration of the turbulence into the forest is therefore critical for understanding the exchange of water vapor, carbon dioxide, biogenic volatile organic compounds, methane, spores, pollens, and other constituents across the forest-atmosphere interface. We analyze profiles of turbulence measured inside and above the forest during the GoAmazon field campaign at the K34 tower in central Amazonia. The surrounding landscape is characterized by gently varying, complex topography, with the tower situated on a small hill. Using wind direction as an indicator of differences in upwind terrain, we investigate the joint influences of atmospheric stability and topography on turbulence within and above the canopy. The analysis focuses on key properties that characterize turbulence penetration and vertical transport, including momentum flux and the variance and skewness of vertical velocity fluctuations. When statistics are normalized using velocity and temperature scales defined at the canopy top, we find that (1) turbulence statistics above the canopy depend strongly on atmospheric stability but show little dependence on wind direction; (2) turbulence statistics in the upper canopy are strongly influenced by both stability and wind direction; and (3) turbulence statistics in the lower canopy are nearly independent of stability and wind direction. These results suggest that above- canopy turbulence over gentle topography is consistent with the local equilibrium hypothesis: although the terrain influences the flow, its effects are captured by the local scaling variables defined at the canopy top. Within the canopy, however, topography exerts an additional influence on turbulent penetration that is not described by these scaling variables. We hypothesize that even gentle topography can substantially regulate the penetration of turbulence into dense forest canopies, with important consequences for the transport of gases and biological particles. Numerical simulations are needed to confirm some of these results.

489773.title: A Storm-Following Regional Deep Learning Framework for Tropical Cyclone Intensity Prediction
489773.authors: Chanh Q Kieu, Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, IN
489773.abstract: In this study, we present a regional deep learning (DL) framework that follows tropical cyclones (TCs) and predicts their full spatiotemporal evolution, using dynamically updated lateral boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the treatment of the lateral boundary conditions plays a critical role in accurately representing TC structure and intensity. Without appropriate boundary updates, the model exhibits substantial degradation in its ability to capture both the TC intensity and structural evolution. The proposed framework has been implemented in an experimental real-time forecasting system over the past two TC seasons in three major ocean basins including North Atlantic, Western Pacific, and Easten Pacific. Results show that it consistently outperforms super-resolution or traditional statistical downscaling approaches, thus providing more accurate predictions of TC intensity and storm structure. However, its overall performance remains below that of state-of-the-art physics-based numerical weather prediction models, highlighting the continued importance of explicitly representing the physical processes governing TC development and evolution. These findings suggest that, while deep learning provides a powerful tool for regional downscaling, accurate TC prediction still requires a combination of data-driven learning and physically consistent dynamical constraints.

489782.title: Unraveling the Diurnal Cycle of the Hadley Cell Width Using a Multi-Satellite Ocean Vector Wind Data Record
489782.authors: Federica Polverari, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA; and S. Hristova-Veleva and F. J. Turk
489782.abstract: Ocean surface vector winds derived from satellite scatterometer observations provide an accurate depiction of the large-scale atmospheric and oceanic circulation, offering a unique capability to study the evolution of the Hadley cell through its surface branch. Long-term satellite wind records are critical for analyzing climate variability and detecting true multi-decadal trends. The spatial extent of the Hadley cell can be effectively defined by the subtropical zero-crossing of the zonally averaged zonal wind component (U). When applying this methodology to the NASA MEaSUREs-funded Ocean Surface Winds Climate Data Record—which homogenizes retrievals across four scatterometer missions by removing inconsistencies in geometry, frequency, and inversion techniques—the results emphasize the crucial impact of unresolved diurnal variability. Specifically, the Hadley cell expands and contracts throughout the day in response to diurnal solar forcing. Despite its importance, the diurnal cycle of the Hadley cell width remains poorly understood due to the temporal sampling limitations of satellite observing systems. Sun-synchronous satellites observe at only two fixed local times per day, leaving an incomplete picture of the diurnal cycle. While ISS-RapidScat’s non-sun-synchronous orbit enabled complete diurnal sampling across local times of day, its brief mission duration was insufficient to fully characterize the diurnal signal. To overcome these sampling constraints, we present a novel approach to estimate the diurnal variability of the Hadley cell width using an expanded multi-satellite record. We utilize a methodology that integrates ocean surface wind observations from both sun-synchronous and asynchronous platforms, combining vector-capable instruments with speed-only instruments. Crucially, a refined methodology is implemented to assign wind directions to instruments providing only speed measurements, creating a multi-year, multi-satellite ocean wind vector dataset with enhanced diurnal temporal coverage. Using this high-temporal-resolution data record, we map the continuous evolution of the joint (Northern and Southern Hemisphere) Hadley cell width as a function of the Local Time of Day. Understanding this diurnal structure is essential for disentangling true geophysical changes from artificial discontinuities that occur simply because successive satellite missions observe the Earth system at different local times. The work described in this abstract is carried out at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology under a contract with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. © 2026. All rights reserved.

489784.title: New Severe Storm Motion Estimation Methodologies for Improved Confidence in Automated Detection and Guidance
489784.authors: Patrick Adrian Campbell, OU/CIWRO, Norman, OK; and J. Cintineo, K. M. Calhoun, and K. L. Berry
489784.abstract: Storm motion estimation has extensive application within meteorological research and operations, often serving as an initial component on which other results and products are based. At the National Severe Storm Laboratory (NSSL), some examples of storm motion calculation are found in the object-based K-Means clustering "segmotion" algorithm within the Multi-Radar-Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system, and in the Tornado Prediction Algorithm (TORP), which tracks detections over time to establish tornado motion.
