These in turn are used within products such as ProbSevere, ProbLighting, and Probabilistic Hazard Information (PHI) to quickly convey severe weather hazard location, direction, timing, and likelihood to decision makers. Existing methods of automated storm motion estimation have long provided results that are intuitive and actionable in many situations. However, they also often provide motion estimates that clearly do not agree with human interpretation of radar data, and these inaccuracies can have an outsized impact in derived statistics and methodologies by reducing confidence in automated storm information as a whole. This was found to be especially true in a 2026 Hazardous Weather Testbed (HWT) experiment evaluating automated warning recommenders based on PHI. In this experiment, inaccurate storm motion could cause forecaster participants to a) lose confidence in all automated warning guidance, and b) find it tedious to correct. Many errors in automated motion estimation are known to be primarily due to rapid changes in size and shape of underlying object detections, which are then tracked to result in highly variable motion estimates. Considerable work has been done to implement quality control algorithms that stabilize these changes, greatly increasing the usability of motion data. However, the quality control problem has been found to be ill-posed as many scenarios remain where motions are inaccurate and adjusting methods to improve one scenario often worsens outcomes in another. While further progress may be possible in correcting existing motion data through quality control, it is also worth pursuing new methods of motion estimation that do not rely on current object detection-based techniques. Standard computer vision optical flow techniques have become established across several fields and offer a promising approach to accurate storm motion estimation. This presentation will cover investigative work into the application of optical flow and other potential techniques to motion estimation from radar imagery in severe convective storm environments. The feasibility of new motion estimation techniques will be discussed regarding how effectively they provide a) accurate motion that agrees with human storm interpretation, b) compatible data for other algorithms and products, and c) efficient operation for practical use with existing real-time data and potential dense data streams such as Phased Array Radar.

489786.title: Structural Changes of Typhoons Goni (2020) and Yagi (2024) during Rapid Intensification
489786.authors: Juliane Schwendike, ; and Y. Deng, A. N. Ross, and R. W. Jones
489786.abstract: The mechanisms responsible for the contrasting structural evolution of rapidly intensifying storms remain incompletely understood. This study investigates why some tropical cyclones undergo structural and intensity vacillation during rapid intensification (RI), whereas others intensify steadily. Typhoon Goni (2020) and Typhoon Yagi (2024), two rapidly intensifying western North Pacific typhoons that evolved under similar environmental conditions but exhibited contrasting structural evolution, are examined using convection-permitting ensemble simulations with the Met Office Unified Model.During RI, Goni undergoes repeated transitions between ring-like and monopolar inner-core structures, accompanied by alternating strengthening and weakening phases, whereas Yagi maintains a persistent ring-like structure and intensifies steadily. Tangential momentum budget analyses show that the symmetric mean flow dominates during the strengthening phases of both storms. In Goni, however, enhancement of localised wind shear promotes increasing eyewall asymmetry, which is accompanied by increased eddy kinetic energy and stronger eddy forcing, opposing the symmetric spin-up of the vortex and leading to transitions to a monopolar structure and subsequent weakening. In contrast, Yagi exhibits little variation in localised wind shear, limiting the development of eyewall asymmetry, eddy kinetic energy, and eddy forcing, thereby allowing the symmetric spin-up of the vortex to remain dominant throughout RI. Comparison with previous studies suggests that, although different processes may initiate eyewall asymmetry, its subsequent evolution follows a common pathway in which enhanced asymmetric dynamics regulate structural vacillation. These results highlight the importance of inner-core asymmetry in influencing contrasting pathways of RI and provide a conceptual framework for interpreting vacillation cycles in TCs.

489787.title: Does WRF Downscaling Add Value beyond HRRR for Offshore Low-Level Jets? An Event-Based Evaluation during WFIP3
489787.authors: Muna Hafsah, University of Delaware, Newark, DE; and N. Bodini, J. K. Lundquist, and D. E. Veron, PhD
489787.abstract: Offshore low-level jets (LLJs) are important for wind energy because the jet nose and associated wind shear can occur within the rotor layer of modern offshore wind turbines. LLJs can also change rapidly with time. Therefore, a model may simulate the average wind profile correctly but still miss when the LLJ forms, how long it remains, and when it disappears. In our previous study of one offshore LLJ event, some Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model configurations predicted the mean LLJ structure reasonably well but did not reproduce its temporal evolution. These timing errors relative to observations also affected rotor-equivalent wind speed (REWS). However, it is not clear whether this pattern was specific to one event or occurs across different offshore LLJ cases. This study asks whether running WRF with High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) initial and boundary conditions adds useful information beyond native HRRR output. The main question is whether utilizing WRF with HRRR improves hourly LLJ occurrence, LLJ structure, LLJ temporal evolution, and rotor-scale wind speed. We further examine whether the model performance differs when employing the Mellor-Yamada-Nakanishi-Niino (MYNN) or the three-dimensional planetary boundary-layer (3DPBL) schemes, with a focus on island and far-offshore measurements, with the latter more typical of wind-energy deployment. Seventeen LLJ cases during July 2024 are selected from the Third Wind Forecast Improvement Project (WFIP3) event log. The event log provides information on LLJ occurrence and descriptions of the associated synoptic and mesoscale conditions (Bodini et al. 2026a). July is selected because it contains a relatively large number of LLJ cases, the WFIP3 barge observations are available throughout the month, and summer is an important period for regional electricity demand. Each case will be simulated with WRF at 1 km horizontal resolution using HRRR initial and boundary conditions and the MYNN and 3DPBL schemes. The simulations will be compared with native HRRR and profiling lidar and scanning lidar observations from Block Island and the WFIP3 offshore barge. The main comparison will therefore be among native HRRR, HRRR-WRF-MYNN, and HRRR-WRF-3DPBL. All datasets will be evaluated at common hourly times, and model profiles will be limited to the height range available from the observations. The offshore barge LLJ occurrence, nose height, and nose wind speed in the observations and native HRRR will be obtained from the hourly climatology of Bodini et al. (2026b), which uses the profile-based LLJ detection method developed by Quint et al. (2025). The same method will be applied to the Block Island data and the HRRR-WRF-MYNN and HRRR-WRF-3DPBL simulations at the corresponding times and locations. For each event, the fraction of observed LLJ hours detected by each model will provide an event-level detection score. During matched LLJ hours, normalized absolute errors in nose height and nose wind speed will be averaged over the event. These scores will show whether WRF downscaling improves LLJ detection and structure relative to native HRRR. Detection and structural errors will be evaluated separately. A model may reproduce nose height and nose wind speed accurately during matched hours but detect the LLJ during only a small part of the observed event. In that case, the model represents the jet structure reasonably well when the LLJ is present but does not reproduce its full observed duration. Wind-energy implications will be evaluated using REWS for a 12 MW GE Haliade turbine with a 138 m hub height and a 215 m rotor diameter, following Rosencrans et al. (2025) and Beiter et al. (2020). Observed and modeled REWS will be compared over the common rotor layer to determine whether improvements in LLJ detection and structure also improve rotor-scale wind representation. The analysis will quantify whether HRRR-driven WRF simulations improve in LLJ occurrence, nose height, nose wind speed, and REWS relative to native HRRR. It will also identify whether the added value differs between MYNN and 3DPBL, between island and far-offshore measurements, and under the synoptic conditions identified in the WFIP3 event log. The results will show when dynamical downscaling provides useful improvement for offshore LLJs and when WRF retains errors already present in HRRR

489795.title: Dynamics and Thermodynamics of Fast and Slow Madden-Julian Oscillation
489795.authors: Victor C. Mayta, University of Wisconsin, Madison, Madison, WI; and Á. F. Adames-Corraliza, K. M. Holube, and Q. J. Lin
489795.abstract: The structure and governing processes associated with fast and slow Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) propagation speed are examined. On the basis of spectral analysis and three-dimensional normal decomposition, we find that slow MJO exhibit a shorter zonal scale relative to faster MJO, in agreement with previous work. Thermodynamic differences between the two MJO are then considered by evaluating four criteria that so-called moisture modes should satisfy, and by examining their column-integrated moist static energy (MSE) budget. It is found that slow MJO satisfy all four moisture mode criteria throughout the extent of the Indo-Pacific warm pool, while fast MJO satisfy all four criteria only over the Indian Ocean. These results imply that moisture governs the thermodynamics of slow MJO, while temperature and moisture play comparable roles in fast MJO thermodynamics. When examining the column MSE budget, we find that the slow MJO MSE anomalies propagate eastward primarily via horizontal MSE advection, with zonal moisture advection accounting for up to 50% of the total MSE tendency over the Indo-Pacific warm pool. In contrast, vertical MSE advection plays a larger role in fast MJO, especially east of the Maritime Continent. Lastly, we compare the vorticity budget of fast and slow MJO. The vorticity anomalies in both fast and slow MJO propagate eastward via vortex stretching. However, advection of planetary vorticity opposes the vortex stretching and this process is stronger in slow MJO. Collectively, these findings indicate the MJO's governing processes vary with propagation speed and region.

489797.title: AI Enhanced Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts from Hybrid High-Resolution Rapid Refresh and LEO and GEO Satellite Data
489797.authors: Yongzhen Fan, CISESS/ESSIC UMD, College Park, MD; and H. Meng, R. Pernak, E. S. Maddy, and K. Garrett
489797.abstract: The impacts of extreme precipitation are deadly, damaging, and increasing. NOAA Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPF) are critical for communicating potential impacts from extreme precipitation events to the public, emergency responders, and a variety of other stakeholders. Numerical weather prediction (NWP) models continue to improve resolving convection at fine spatial and temporal scales, and at a higher cadence. This has helped to improve the performance and confidence in QPF products. However, even at short lead times, uncertainty remains in QPF in terms of timing, location, intensity, and duration of extreme rainfall events, including those associated with atmospheric rivers, tropical cyclones, and mesoscale convective systems. In this presentation, we will introduce an AI enhanced QPF from a hybrid dataset including model analyses from High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and LEO and GEO satellite remote sensing data. The satellite observations have demonstrated their value in improving HRRR QPF, especially for extreme precipitation. An ensemble model consisting of various Swin-Unet members was developed in this project to predict up to 3-hour QPF and the probability of precipitation. We will present the development of the ensemble model and the preliminary results compared with NOAA Unrestricted Mesoscale Analysis (URMA).

489807.title: Advancing Probabilistic Subseasonal-to-Seasonal Drought Forecasting Capabilities at NOAA Weather Prediction Center
489807.authors: Hailan Wang, NOAA Weather Prediction Center, Extended Prediction Division, College Park, MD; and J. Gottschalck, M. Park, L. Xu, A. DeAngelis, J. Leung, B. Pugh, A. M. Sheffield, and V. Deheza
489807.abstract: Skillful and reliable subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) drought forecasts are essential for mitigating drought-related impacts and costs. The NOAA Climate Prediction Center, now Weather Prediction Center (WPC)’s Extended Prediction Division (EPD), routinely produces and issues NOAA’s official Subseasonal-to-Seasonal (S2S) drought outlooks, to support stakeholders in drought preparedness and impact mitigation. While these products are currently deterministic, WPC/EPD has conducted extensive research and development in recent years to develop and produce new objective, probabilistic S2S drought outlooks for the U.S. This presentation will introduce our recently developed experimental, objective, probabilistic Seasonal Drought Outlook. It will present the product development framework, underlying methodology, and forecast skill based on both hindcast and real-time evaluations. This product marks EPD’s first objective forecast of drought as an integrated, multivariate, and multifaceted phenomenon, while importantly providing probabilistic information. New objective drought blends were developed to objectively integrate forecasts for drought indices of meteorological, agricultural and hydrological drought types and timescales from 1 to 60 months, while accounting for their physical characteristics and S2S forecast skill. A comprehensive skill assessment of the probabilistic product indicates that it performs reasonably well, with its most probable forecast demonstrating comparable statistical skill relative to NOAA’s current official deterministic Seasonal Drought Outlook. By providing probabilistic forecast guidance for drought (development, persistence, worsening, improvement, removal), the new product is expected to serve as the “first guess” for NOAA’s future operational probabilistic Seasonal Drought Outlook, strengthening NOAA National Weather Service (NWS) drought forecasting capabilities and enhancing its probabilistic Impact-based Decision Support Services (IDSS) for drought preparedness and response.

489808.title: Lessons Learned from Large-Eddy Simulations for the Perdigão Field Campaign (Invited Presentation)
489808.authors: Adam S. Wise, LLNL, Livermore, CA; University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA; and F. K. Chow
489808.abstract: Microscale, terrain-induced flow features remain a challenging aspect of modeling in complex terrain. The 2017 Perdigão field campaign in Portugal, characterized by flow over two parallel ridges, was rigorously instrumented with 47 meteorological towers, multiple scanning and profiling lidars, a tethered lifting system, and numerous additional instruments providing an extensive observational network to validate atmospheric models. In the 9 years since Perdigão took place, we have conducted a number of both idealized and realistic, multiscale large-eddy simulation (LES) studies that have provided insight into the complex, terrain-induced turbulent phenomena that are also influenced by thermal stratification. Because a wind turbine is located on top of one of the ridges, a major goal was to understand how the wind turbine wake interacts with these flow phenomena. Here, we present results from simulations of two distinct flow regimes, one characterized by typical unstable atmospheric conditions and the other by stable stratification and a mountain wave. The wind turbine wake interacts with the recirculation zone and mountain wave in distinct ways, with the wake deflecting upwards above the recirculation zone in unstable conditions, and the wake deflecting downwards following the terrain in stable conditions. Another goal of the field campaign was to understand the structure of turbulence dissipation rate in complex terrain during stable conditions. We compare simulations using the TKE-1.5 closure, which is a purely dissipative eddy-viscosity model, and the dynamic reconstruction model (DRM), which uses explicit filtering and velocity reconstruction combined with a dynamic eddy viscosity model. The DRM can represent backscatter of energy from sub-filter scales to resolved scales. During stable conditions, there is persistent backscatter near the tops of ridges, which we verify using meteorological tower data. The velocity deficit associated with the wind turbine wake persists over 4 km downwind within the mountain wave. The turbulence dissipation rate remains elevated much further downwind for the DRM closure compared to the TKE-1.5 closure. The Perdigão field campaign demonstrates how a broad network of instruments can be used in conjunction with LES to validate models and also to improve the representation of both small-scale turbulence and terrain-induced turbulent phenomena.

489812.title: Machine Learning Enhanced Snowfall Rate Retrievals from Passive Microwave Sensors
489812.authors: Yongzhen Fan, CISESS/ESSIC UMD, College Park, MD; and Y. Hong, J. Dong, H. Meng, O. Jiang, C. Kongoli, Y. You, and R. Ferraro
489812.abstract: Snowfall accounts for a large fraction of winter precipitation in mid- and high latitudes. The NOAA/NESDIS snowfall rate (SFR) dataset is a global, liquid equivalent snowfall rate estimation. It is derived from observations taken by passive microwave radiometers, including ATMS, MHS, GMI and SSMIS sensors, aboard nine polar-orbiting satellites. The SFR algorithm consists of two main components: snowfall detection (SD) and rate estimation. Recently, the SD component has been updated to machine learning (ML) models, which was trained against a large collection of in-situ observations. The XGBoost ML model shows the best performance, hence it’s implemented in the SFR operational retrieval system. The core of the second component, rate estimation, is a 1DVAR-based inversion model. It has been improved by using ML-based initial conditions. Lastly, the retrieved SFR values are further biased-corrected with a neural network (NN) model. The ML SD and SFR algorithms have been successfully applied to cross-scan instruments, such as ATMS and MHS sensors, and conical scanning instruments, such as GMI and SSMIS sensors. In this presentation, we will present the development of the ML SD and SFR algorithm for several recent satellite missions including the Microwave Radiometer (MWR) onboard the Arctic Weather Satellite (AWS), the Micro-Wave Sounder (MWS) and Micro-Wave Imager (MWI) onboard the Metop-SG A1/B1 satellite and the AMSR3 sensor onboard the GOSAT-GW satellite. We will also present our recent development to implement multiple non-spherical ice particle models to improve the accuracy of snowfall rate retrieval and the development of a ML image-based snowfall rate algorithm to improve spatial distribution of the NOAA SFR product.

489831.title: An Implicit Algorithm for Spherical Harmonic Transforms Using Fourier Transforms of Associated Legendre Functions
489831.authors: Suzune Nomura, Graduate School of Science, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Kyoto, Japan; and T. Enomoto
489831.abstract: This study proposes a novel method to conduct the vector spherical harmonic spectral transform method that avoids explicitly computation of associated Legendre functions, making it an implicit approach using the spherical Fourier transform. For scalar fields, an implicit spherical harmonic transform using the spherical Fourier transform has been well established. This method relies on the Fourier transform of associated Legendre functions Pnm(cosθ) (n is degree, m is order, θ∈[0, π] is co-latitude), which constitutes spherical harmonics Ynm(θ, λ) (λ∈[0, 2π) is longitude). Since their Fourier coefficients can be derived analytically via recurrence relations, this approach avoids the Legendre transform, thereby preventing rounding errors at high degrees typically caused by conventional explicit evaluations. In this study, we extend this implicit scalar framework to vector fields. Unlike in the scalar case, the spherical harmonic expansion of vector fields involves two basis functions formed by differentiating spherical harmonics with respect to co-latitude and longitude, respectively. Consequently, replacing the Legendre transform with a Fourier transform requires applying the transform to both the co-latitudinal derivative of the associated Legendre function (dPnm/dθ) and the term involving the order and the sine of the colatitude (mPnm/sinθ). By leveraging recurrence relations specific to these basis functions, both terms can be expressed as linear combinations of associated Legendre functions with shifted degrees n and orders m, without explicit derivatives or trigonometric products. As a result, the Fourier coefficients for the vector transform can be constructed directly from those already evaluated in the scalar transform. Furthermore, the Fourier transform of these basis functions needs to be precomputed only once, and the transformation process can be executed independently for each order m, providing excellent parallelization efficiency. Therefore, the proposed method is highly promising for implementing accurate and fast spectral methods in high-resolution atmospheric general circulation models.

489836.title: Teaching a Senior Meteorology Capstone Sequence as a Learning Community
489836.authors: John M. Lanicci, University Of South Alabama, Mobile, AL; and J. E. Wiley and J. T. McLeod
489836.abstract: The Synoptic Meteorology I and II courses are a 12-credit undergraduate capstone sequence for meteorology majors at the University of South Alabama (USA). The Capstone sequence is usually taken in senior year, after students have completed Introduction to Meteorology and Lab, General Meteorology and Lab, the two-semester Dynamics sequence, and Physical Meteorology. Synoptic Meteorology I and II are taught in a lecture/lab format that totals nearly 9 contact hours a week (2½ h lecture and 6¼ h lab). Such a large number of contact hours allows us to structure the course as a combination of two to three courses that are normally taught separately in most other programs around the country: Synoptic-Dynamic Meteorology, Weather Analysis and Forecasting, and Current Weather Discussion. The Synoptic I/II sequence is normally taught by two instructors: a tenured/tenure-track faculty member who is the primary instructor responsible for all aspects of the course, and an instructor who primarily acts as a co-instructor for the lab portion. During the 2024–2025 and 2025–2026 academic years, a window of opportunity arose to have a third faculty member assigned to this course for training and as a backup instructor. The authors took advantage of this opportunity to institute a Learning Community (LC) approach to Synoptic I/II, following that of Gabelnick et al. (1990), who describe a learning community as “...any one of a variety of curricular structures that link together several existing courses or actually restructure the curricular material entirely – so that students have opportunities for deeper understanding and integration of the material they are learning, and more interaction with one another and their teachers as fellow participants in the learning enterprise.” (p.19) Following this approach, one of the first tasks we undertook was a topic realignment to each of our areas of expertise within the LC, which also reassigned responsibility for the lectures and labs within our expertise areas. Second was the development and refinement of a three-tiered curriculum model for both Synoptic I and II to better align lecture topics and their application in the course. An illustration is shown in the figure below, taken from Lanicci et al. (2026). (insert Figure 1 here) Figure 1 shows that the course is divided into a lecture (leftmost column), a traditional lab (middle column), and lab practicum (right column). We introduce the theory in lecture, followed by an initial exploration of the theory through a case study/idealized example(s) in lab. This is followed by a practicum lab phase that lasts through the rest of the semester, where students attempt to apply the theory using ‘real-world’ examples in the semester-long City Forecast contest and real-time student-led Current Weather Discussions. An example of this approach is the introduction of Quasi-geostrophic (QG) theory during the sixth week of the fall semester. Several introductory labs allow the students to practice applying QG theory to some idealized case studies (we will provide an illustrative example in our presentation). We then emphasize the application of QG theory throughout the rest of the course in the practicum portion by severely restricting the use of NWP products to only selected 850- and 500-hPa products (treated as perfect progs, simply an extension of the 0000 and 1200 UTC analyses). No textual forecast products are allowed in Synoptic I; students use a combination of QG principles and fusion of multiple observational data sources for analysis and short-range (12–24h) prediction in both the City Forecasts and Current Weather Discussions. To ensure students are properly applying theory and observations in this phase of the course, they go through four rounds of Current Weather Discussions, which are graded like mini oral exams. This approach allows us to get ‘snapshots’ of student progress and comprehension throughout the semester. We allow full use of all real-time NWP products as well as NWS and other textual forecast products in Synoptic Meteorology II. However, we follow a similar analysis and forecast philosophy (monitored through another four rounds of Current Weather Discussions), to ensure that students use NWP models to confirm the diagnosis they have already made through extensive analysis of the current conditions. The three-tiered curriculum model helps ensure that students develop analysis and forecast skills based primarily on observation-based continuity analysis, conceptual models, and application of theory as opposed to simply “going right to the models.” While this curriculum model has more-or-less existed throughout the history of the course, the application of the LC allowed us to refine it and apply appropriate ‘checks and balances’ throughout the two years we employed it. While we have been pleased with the LC approach and student feedback has been very positive, this approach is not necessarily sustainable for any extended period, especially in a small undergraduate-only program such as ours. To the best of our knowledge, this is the only application of an LC to a senior capstone course within a single discipline, as most LCs are conducted as multidisciplinary course combinations for first-year courses. Within the meteorology/atmospheric science community, we only found two programs that employ a LC approach: 1) Rutgers WeatherWatcher broadcast meteorology thematic community (https://ruoncampus.rutgers.edu/unique-living-options/communities/weatherwatcher); and Iowa State’s Earth, Wind, & Fire Geoscience LC, which includes Meteorology (https://lc.iastate.edu/communities/earth-wind-and-fire). References Gabelnick, F., J. MacGregor, R. S. Matthews, and B. L. Smith, eds., 1990: Learning Communities: Creating Connections Among Students, Faculty, and Disciplines. New Directions for Teaching and Learning, #41. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass. Lanicci, J. M., J. T. McLeod, and J. Wiley, 2026: Performance of NCEP operational model products as “contestants” in a university weather forecasting contest. J. Operational Meteor., 14 (10), 145−166, DOI: https://doi.org/10.15191/nwajom.2026.1410. 5/27/2026

489840.title: Real-Time Tropical Cyclone Forecasts using the Model for Prediction Across Scales during the 2026 Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program Real-Time Experiment
489840.authors: Clark Evans, NOAA/OAR/Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and S. Trahan, C. R. Holt, B. W. Green, and L. Bernardet
489840.abstract: During the 2024 and 2025 Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program (HFIP) Real-Time Experiments, NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) conducted real-time forecasts of Atlantic tropical cyclones (TCs) using 3-km regional and 15-3 km variable-resolution global configurations of the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS). These forecasts used the GSL-led physics parameterizations from NOAA’s Rapid Refresh Forecast System. Across these two Atlantic TC seasons, these forecasts generally provided skillful and reliable predictions of TC track and intensity to five-day leads, albeit with somewhat reduced intensity skill for particularly intense TCs. Building on these successes, GSL again conducted real-time forecasts of Atlantic basin TCs using MPAS during the 2026 HFIP Real-Time Experiment. Major changes relative to 2025 included (1) the use of an Atlantic basin 3-km regional domain with no deep cumulus parameterization to reduce computational expense relative to 2025’s global variable-resolution configuration and (2) tuning of the surface momentum, thermal, and moisture roughness lengths in the MYNN surface-layer parameterization to mitigate a low wind-speed bias for particularly intense TCs that was particularly evident during the 2025 HFIP Real-Time Experiment. As in 2025, forecasts were initialized using a blend of NOAA’s Global Forecast System (GFS) and Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System-A (HAFS-A) analyses, except here updated to the pre-operational GFSv17 and prototype HAFS-A forecasts which used the Joint Effort for Data-assimilation Integration (JEDI) package to create their initial conditions. The presentation will provide full details of the real-time model configuration and forecast performance during the 2026 HFIP Real-Time Experiment. Case studies of selected TCs will be conducted to illustrate forecast strengths and weaknesses. Future research directions, including cross-NOAA collaborations with MPAS and JEDI to inform potential future HAFS operational configurations, will also be discussed.

489841.title: Advancing Methane Emissions Transparency and MRV through Satellite-Based Tip-and-Cue Monitoring
489841.authors: Yohei Toyohara, Mitsubishi Electric Corporation, Kamakura, Kanagawa, Japan; and D. Sango, N. Katsura, Y. Fujii, K. Kurihara, K. Kumeno, A. Naseem, T. Hashizume, T. Kuwano, K. Tanigawa, M. Shimouchi, and Y. Suzuki
489841.abstract: Satellite observations can provide spatially consistent evidence of methane emissions across geographically distributed energy assets, but their societal and operational value depends on whether observations can be translated into traceable, decision-ready information for end users. This study presents an applied multi-satellite Earth observation framework being implemented in Japan to support methane-related environmental, regulatory, and economic risk management in natural gas and liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply chains. The framework combines regional-scale observations from the Greenhouse Gases and Water Cycle Observation Satellite (GOSAT-GW) with targeted, higher-resolution observations to connect initial screening with facility-scale verification and follow-up action. GOSAT-GW entered nominal operations in October 2025, and Level 1B products from TANSO-3, the imaging spectrometer onboard GOSAT-GW, became available to general users in July 2026. TANSO-3 observes carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrogen dioxide using a wide mode with an approximately 911 km swath and 10 km spatial resolution, and a focus mode with an approximately 90 km swath and 1–3 km spatial resolution. Because Level 1B products contain calibrated spectral radiance rather than methane concentration maps or emission estimates, the framework first acquires TANSO-3 Level 1B products, applies retrieval processing to convert the calibrated radiance spectra into methane concentration maps, and then analyzes these maps to screen candidate regions or groups of assets for further investigation. The workflow follows a tip-and-cue approach, in which candidate locations or regions identified through TANSO-3-based methane analysis serve as tips. These tips are prioritized using meteorological fields, facility inventories, prior observations, and other contextual information to assess whether a coherent plume is likely to be observable. Higher-priority tips are then used to cue targeted observations by a high-resolution satellite constellation. The resulting plume imagery and emission estimates are integrated with facility-level information and, where available, operator logs, ground measurements, or other independent observations. The service output is designed to provide a traceable evidence package for methane-management teams at natural gas and LNG facilities, LNG buyers, public-sector agencies, and organizations responsible for measurement-based reporting. The package includes the basis for escalation, uncertainty characterization, recommended options for follow-up action, and decision rules for non-detections and uncertain results. By explicitly linking satellite-derived information to operational response pathways, the framework aims to help these users prioritize limited verification resources, identify unusual emission events, and support credible measurement-based methane reporting and mitigation decisions. A JOGMEC-supported verification project in fiscal year 2026 is assessing the framework under field conditions. The evaluation covers detection and quantification performance, observation-to-information delivery time, criteria for escalation from regional screening to targeted observation, and usability of the resulting information for operational decision-making. The project also examines applicability to measurement-based methane reporting, including the Oil & Gas Methane Partnership 2.0, and opportunities for demonstrations at natural gas and LNG production facilities. This study positions GOSAT-GW as a scalable screening layer and targeted satellites and field information as complementary verification layers within an end-user-oriented Earth observation application. The framework is intended to convert multi-scale satellite observations into actionable methane information while clearly communicating limitations associated with cloud cover, surface reflectance, wind conditions, observation timing, and event size and duration. The study summarizes the initial implementation status, verification design, and operational requirements for delivering satellite-enabled methane information that supports stakeholder decision-making and societal benefit.

489843.title: Impacts of Shortwave Trough-Atmospheric River (AR) Interactions on AR Forecasts over the U.S. West Coast
489843.authors: Wen-Shu Lin, Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and Z. Zhang, M. Zheng, X. Zou, J. Cordeira, L. Delle Monache, and F. M. Ralph
489843.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are long and narrow corridors of intense water vapor transport in the lower troposphere and are a major source of moisture for precipitation, particularly over the western United States. While landfalling ARs can provide important water supply, they can also cause hazardous flooding, making accurate prediction essential. ARs are often dynamically linked to short-wave troughs (SWTs) on their northwestern flank, which enhance upward motion and strengthen low-level winds, thereby promoting condensation and precipitation and modulating AR intensity and evolution. This study uses an AR event that made landfall over California on 9 January 2023 as the primary case to investigate the impacts of SWT-AR interactions on AR forecasts. Forecasts from 31 ensemble members of the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) are evaluated against the ERA5 reanalysis to quantify forecast errors. At a 48-hour lead time, GEFS underpredicts integrated water vapor transport (IVT) near the California coast by approximately 200 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ during the early stage of AR landfall, with larger errors in the meridional component than in the zonal component. The weaker SWT in GEFS leads to underestimated low-level winds and, together with weaker integrated water vapor (IWV), contributes to the IVT forecast errors.The GEFS ensemble exhibits a large spread in vertical velocity and precipitation, resulting in substantial uncertainty in latent heat release, which plays an important role in AR development. As the forecast evolves, GEFS delays the arrival of the peak AR IVT at the California coast by approximately 6 hours relative to ERA5 and also underestimates its magnitude. A corresponding delay and underestimation are also found in the precipitation over northern California. These results demonstrate that SWT-AR interactions can introduce significant forecast uncertainties not only in AR intensity but also in landfall timing. Two additional SWT-AR cases are further analyzed to characterize the substantial variability in forecast errors associated with SWT intensity and location, and to assess their influence on AR intensity and landfall location.

489850.title: To The Stars: Global Kilometer-Scale Experiments toward NOAA’s NWP Moonshot using the Model for Prediction Across Scales
489850.authors: Clark Evans, NOAA/OAR/Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and M. Oehler, F. Judt, C. Schwartz, and R. Rios-Berrios
489850.abstract: NOAA’s NWP Moonshot seeks to develop and implement a global, kilometer-scale, fully coupled Earth system model using the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) atmospheric dynamical core. Scientific motivation for the NWP Moonshot is provided by robust demonstrations of MPAS’s performance for regional storm-scale applications over the United States and tropical North Atlantic by the NOAA Global Systems Laboratory and initial demonstrations of real-time global kilometer-scale MPAS forecasts by the NSF NCAR Mesoscale and Microscale Meteorology laboratory. However, there remain many scientific and technological challenges that must be addressed to achieve the NWP Moonshot vision. One such scientific challenge is addressing whether global kilometer-scale forecasts can consistently increase forecast skill through explicitly (or nearly explicitly) resolving thunderstorms and their associated latent heating. To begin addressing this question, we conduct global 3.75-km atmosphere-only MPAS forecasts out to ten-day lead times using NOAA’s regional modeling physics suite. We use these forecasts to test the hypothesis that global kilometer-scale MPAS forecasts will better predict the evolution of tropical to midlatitude hemispheric-scale circulations at medium-range lead times as compared to comparably configured, coarser-resolution global MPAS forecasts. We believe that this will result from the explicit representation (rather than parameterization) of latent heat release associated with deep, moist convection that exerts a significant control on hemispheric-scale circulations. In this early-stage work, we focus on testing this hypothesis for diabatically driven meteorological phenomena and events that are known to be associated with lower predictability, such as tropical cyclone interactions with the midlatitude circulation during extratropical transition and convectively active phases of the Madden-Julian Oscillation. Preliminary results, the associated computational requirements, and the implications of each toward NOAA’s NWP Moonshot will be presented.

489851.title: NOAA/GSL Model Development and Forecasting Activities using MPAS for Future NOAA Operational Modeling Systems
489851.authors: Clark Evans, NOAA/OAR/Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and C. R. Alexander, L. Bernardet, T. T. Ladwig, M. Hu, D. Dowell, R. Ahmadov, and G. Ge
489851.abstract: NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) seeks to improve Earth-system prediction across all weather-related hazards including severe convective storms, intense rainfall, winter storms, tropical systems, and phenomena such as wildfire smoke, dust, and pollen. GSL has a rich legacy in developing modeling systems for NOAA operations, including the Rapid Refresh (RAP) and High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR), and in contributing to the development of Unified Forecast System (UFS) applications such as the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) and Global Forecast System (GFS). There is increasing stakeholder need for high-resolution modeling systems that can explicitly resolve precipitating phenomena, fire-weather behavior, aerosol radiative and cloud feedbacks, and urbanization influences to improve forecast skill and serve end-user predictive needs. These considerations inform NOAA’s Modeling Moonshot goal to develop a global, storm-scale, coupled atmosphere-ocean ensemble forecast system using the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS). For over two years, GSL has been using MPAS to develop prototypes for future NOAA operational modeling systems to address these needs. This presentation will provide an overview of MPAS development and forecasting activities led by GSL. These include high-resolution regional MPAS development toward RRFSv2, including the new RRFSv2x cycled MPAS+JEDI prototype system, and purpose-built MPAS-based high-resolution forecast systems for atmospheric rivers, aerosols, fire weather, and tropical cyclones. Forecast performance from real-time and NOAA Testbeds evaluations will be presented. The presentation will also discuss supporting developments and applications at GSL, including traditional and stochastic physics development, the integration of the MPAS dynamical core in the UFS, and work toward building the next-generation regional ensemble forecast system.

489854.title: Indoor Thermal Conditions, Wearable Physiological Responses, and Heat-Related Symptoms Under Free-Living Conditions
489854.authors: Yoshiaki Tai, Nara Medical University, Kashihara, 29, Japan; and K. Saeki
489854.abstract: Background: Although heat-related illnesses often occur in residential settings, few studies have evaluated indoor heat indices together with wearable physiological indicators for detecting early heat strain and heat-related symptoms in daily life. Objective: In this short-term longitudinal study, we examined the associations of indoor thermal indicators and wearable-measured physiological responses with pulse rate increases and self-reported heat-related symptoms among community-dwelling middle-aged and older adults. Methods: We collected repeated 1-min measurements of heat indicators, including wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT), over 3,061 person-days among adults aged ≥40 years in Nara Prefecture, Japan, from June–September in 2024 and 2025. Generalized additive models examined associations between the preceding 10-min moving averages of thermal indicators and within-individual pulse rate changes, adjusting for physical activity, hour of day, and absolute humidity for non-WBGT models. Thresholds were estimated using three-segment, piecewise linear models. A case–crossover design with conditional logistic regression was used to examine the short-term associations of ambient temperature, skin temperature, and pulse rate with symptom onset, adjusting for physical activity, indoor/outdoor setting, weekday/weekend, and asleep/awake status. Results: Overall, 4,110,392 pulse rate measurements were analyzed, and self-reported heat-related symptoms occurred on 101 person-days. Indoor WBGT and skin temperature showed threshold-like associations with pulse rate increases, with thresholds preceding a steeper rise at 30.4°C (95% confidence interval [CI] 28.6–30.8) for WBGT and 33.5°C (95% CI 31.6–35.4) for skin temperature. In the case–crossover analysis, the adjusted odds ratios for symptom onset were 1.06 (95% CI 0.83–1.34; p=0.653) for ambient temperature, 1.48 (95% CI 1.08–2.03; p=0.014) for skin temperature, and 1.71 (95% CI 1.13–2.61; p=0.012) for pulse rate. Significance: Indoor WBGT may capture residential heat-related physiological strain more clearly than air temperature alone, whereas wearable skin temperature and pulse rate may provide individualized early warning indicators during daily life.

489856.title: Characterizing Depolarization Streaks in Mesoscale Convective Systems: RaXPol Observations During the PECAN Field Campaign
489856.authors: Lauren Grose, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN; and D. J. Bodine and R. Tanamachi
489856.abstract: Depolarization streaks are distinct dual-polarimetric radar signatures that are frequently observed in the differential reflectivity (ZDR) and differential phase shift (ΦDP) fields. Physically, depolarization streaks represent areas of similarly-aligned ice crystals above the storm’s melting layer. They can be visually identified as alternating rays of relatively high and low ZDR that extend radially outward from the radar’s position. These streaks can serve as direct indicators of localized electric field strength and act as short-term precursors to lightning. In this study, we analyze depolarization streaks in a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) observed on 26 June 2015 during the Plains Elevated Convection at Night (PECAN) field campaign. The Rapid X-band Polarimetric radar (RaXPol) collected Range Height Indicator (RHI) scans approximately every 18 s. We quantify depolarization streak characteristics, such as intensity (ZDR magnitude) and spatial width (RHI-relative), and determine their relationships to storm evolution, e.g. differences between convective and stratiform regions. To achieve this, debiasing, empirically-determined thresholding, and layer averaging are applied to isolate the streaks, allowing their attributes to be objectively calculated from the processed data. We will present preliminary results showing a visual correlation between vertical velocities (fall-speed corrected Doppler velocities measured at zenith) and depolarization streak properties. Furthermore, an inverse relationship between ZDR and specific differential phase (KDP) is frequently observed, though this is subject to variability, and therefore warrants additional investigation. Subsequent analysis may provide greater insight into these characteristics and how they ultimately relate to overall storm processes.

489858.title: Investigating Discrepancies between Observed and Modeled Atmospheric Humidity Trends over Arid and Semi-Arid Regions.
489858.authors: Isla R. Simpson, NCAR, Boulder, CO
489858.abstract: As the planet warms, atmospheric humidity is expected to increase at approximately the Clausius-Clapeyron rate, assuming there is sufficient water available to satisfy the increasing atmospheric demand. While observations show this behavior over most regions, atmospheric humidity has remained approximately constant since 1980 in arid and semi-arid regions on average. This contrasts sharply with Earth System Models (ESMs), which simulate humidity increases close to Clausius-Clapeyron scaling even over these moisture-limited locations. Understanding and resolving this discrepancy is critical for improved hydroclimate projections for arid and semi-arid regions. We investigate three possible explanations for this discrepancy. First, we assess whether observational inhomogeneities could explain the lack of humidity rise in observational datasets. Second, we assess whether ESMs realistically represent climatological water availability through comparisons of simulated and observed daily variability at Ameriflux sites. Third, we explore the role of plant biogeophysical responses in enabling the atmospheric humidity rise in ESMs. These three complementary investigations evaluate three of the leading hypotheses for the origins of this discrepancy between observed and modeled atmospheric humidity trends over arid and semi-arid regions.

489861.title: Translation Speed's Influence on Tornado Wind Speed Profiles from Close-Range WSR-88D Observations.
489861.authors: Grace Skye McCoy, University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, HI; and A. W. Lyza and G. Torri
489861.abstract: Tornado vertical wind speed profiles are critical to understanding near-ground tornado dynamics. Because existing profiles are primarily based on mobile-radar observations of slow-moving supercellular tornadoes, the applicability to rapidly translating tornadoes remains uncertain. Using close-range WSR-88D observations of 105 tornadoes across 141 radar volumes from 2011 to 2023, this study investigates how translation speed influences the vertical wind speed profile of tornadoes up to 500 m above ground level (AGL). Supercellular tornadoes were predominantly slow-moving but showed a secondary maximum of faster cases separated by a local minimum near 20 m/s. Fast-moving supercellular tornadoes exhibited profiles more similar to QLCS tornadoes than to their slower-moving counterparts, with mean normalized profile differences of 4.2% and 19.4%, respectively. Thus, fast-supercells differed from slow-supercells by 4.6 times more than they differed from QLCS profiles. This similarity was not explained by differences in damage indicators or housing density, indicating that storm mode alone does not account for the observed near-ground variability. The mobile-radar supercellular profile of Kosiba et al. (2023) closely matched our slow-moving supercell profile but not the faster-translating ones, consistent with the slower translation speeds in their dataset. Below 100 m AGL, the ASCE 7-22 profile produced a mean underestimate of observed wind speeds of approximately 10% for fast-moving supercellular tornadoes and 12% for QLCS tornadoes; EF-based estimates similarly underestimated observed winds by 7% and 10%, respectively. Because ASCE 7-22 is applied as a national building standard, this bias falls hardest on regions where fast-translating tornadoes are most common, highlighting the need for further investigation into the impact of translation speed on the tornado wind speed profile.

489863.title: Sensitivity of Optical-Flow-Retrieved Wind Speed and Cloud-Top Divergence of Convective Phenomena to Temporal Input Conditions
489863.authors: Theodore M. McHardy, NRL, Monterey, CA; and D. A. Peterson, J. Apke, E. J. Hyer, and J. Campbell
489863.abstract: Optical flow techniques have recently been used to retrieve detailed cloud-top motion around convective updrafts using imagery from passive remote sensing platforms like the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI). This study quantifies the differences in retrieved cloud-top velocities when using varied input time intervals that simulate the different scan frequencies of the ABI (1-minute Mesoscale, 5-minute CONUS, and 10-minute Full Disk). These methods are applied to multiple convective phenomena, including a supercell thunderstorm and two pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) events, which were selected to cover a range of ambient wind speeds. A state-of-the-art optical flow algorithm is used to derive wind vectors and trajectories. A bulk analysis compares retrieved wind speeds across the different scan frequencies, while a detailed trajectory analysis examines where performance degrades with respect to specific dynamical structures, such as the convective core and anvil regions. Results suggest that the performance of wind speed retrievals systematically breaks down as scan frequency decreases, and this degradation is more severe in environments with higher ambient wind speeds. For all cases, motions retrieved using 5- and 10-minute scans were least accurate near the rapidly evolving convective cores. Characterizing the conditions under which these techniques can and cannot be reliably applied is critical for their advancement and for maximizing their scientific and operational utility, especially for future applications that may rely on scans with larger spatial coverage but lower temporal frequency.

489866.title: Impact of Wave-Current Interaction on Ocean Waves During Hurricanes Ian and Idalia
489866.authors: Cuong Sieu San, University of South Florida, St. Petersburg, FL; and Y. Liu, R. H. Weisberg, H. Xu, S. John, S. A. Murawski, S. Gilbert, G. T. Mitchum, T. K. Frazer, and S. Pe'eri
489866.abstract: Two-way wave–current interaction (WCI) plays a fundamental role in modulating hurricane-generated wave fields over broad continental shelves, yet its quantitative impacts remain insufficiently constrained by observations. Here, we investigate the WCI during Hurricanes Ian (2022) and Idalia (2023) over the West Florida Shelf using both a fully coupled FVCOM–SWAVE modeling system and a wave-only configuration to isolate current feedback effects. Model performance is evaluated against an extensive observational dataset, including the surface wave data from moored buoys and multiple types of free-drifting directional wave buoys spanning deep (>80 m), intermediate (20–60 m), and shallow (<20 m) waters. Both configurations reproduce the overall evolution of significant wave height (Hs), peak period (Tp), and spectral structure. Inclusion of WCI systematically improves representation of peak wave height, spectral peak magnitude, and directional spreading, particularly in regions where storm-driven currents oppose wave propagation. Maximum Hs modulation reaches ~0.7 m offshore and exceeds 0.5 m nearshore, corresponding to relative changes of ~9 % in deeper waters and up to ~20 % in shallow coastal regions, respectively. Spectral analyses demonstrate that the coupling reduces peak wave height overestimation and mitigates low-frequency shifts in high-energy conditions. These results highlight the dynamically significant role of current-induced wave modulation over wide continental shelves and underscore the importance of two-way coupling for accurate simulation of hurricane wave fields.

489872.title: Community Coordinated Modeling Center Activities Enabling Space Weather R2O2R
489872.authors: M. Leila Mays, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and Y. Zheng, A. Lundkvist, C. Wiegand, C. Didigu, C. Corti, D. De Zeeuw, E. Resnick, G. Toth, J. Topper, J. Wang, J. Yue, J. Huba, J. Jones, K. Scheiber, L. Rastaetter, M. Petrenko, M. Reiss, M. Lesko, M. Y. Chou, P. MacNeice, P. Poole, P. Manessis, R. Mullinix, S. Kumar, T. Tsui, and T. Schiewe
489872.abstract: The Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) at NASA was established in 2000 as a US multi-agency strategic investment into the national space weather program to facilitate space science and space weather research and model development, and to support the transition of advances in research models to space weather operations. CCMC’s multi-decade experience in Space Weather R2O2R is woven into its space weather and space science simulation services, including Runs-on-Request, Instant Run, and Continuous Runs (real-time). Products from CCMC’s Continuous Runs service are used to create space weather dashboards, scoreboards, and validation platforms, which display real-time models together with input and contextual data. The cornerstone of R2O2R at CCMC is serving as a proving grounds and showroom for demonstrating the operational potential of near real-time model outputs and data products via its Continuous Runs system and public facing web apps, such as the Integrated Space Weather Analysis system (ISWA) and Scoreboards. CCMC’s ISWA is a flexible user-configurable system for space weather monitoring, forecasting, anomaly analysis, event analysis, and system science. CCMC’s space weather Scoreboards collect, standardize and display multi-model predictions from the community providing situational awareness, ensemble forecast uncertainties, and a showroom for advancements, with the end-goal of validating models in a quasi-operational environment. Together with the community, CCMC builds validation studies, libraries and platforms for the Scoreboards, based on experience in facilitating and/or leading numerous post-event community modeling “Validation Challenges”. Promising models may transition to the Architecture for Collaborative Evaluations (ACE), a joint CCMC-SWPC proving ground involving cloud-based infrastructure, standardized metrics, and validation protocols to ensure research-grade code meets the requirements of national space weather operations. R2O2R is embodied throughout the model onboarding process to CCMC simulation services, proving grounds, and collaborations with the community NOAA SWPC Space Weather Prediction Testbed. The R2O2R process reflected within CCMC-provided services for the community involves a complex set of subject matter expertise, interfacing with forecasters and users, software frameworks, and infrastructure working together.

489878.title: Status of Himawari-8/9 and Their Follow-on Satellite Himawari-10
489878.authors: Kenichi KATSUYAMA, JMA, Minato City, Tokyo, Japan; and K. KATAYAMA, N. KAWANO, K. KODERA, H. ONO, T. TABATA, M. TAKAHASHI, T. TANDAI, S. Watanabe, Y. Yamada, M. YAMAMOTO, K. YASUI, and K. BESSHO
489878.abstract: The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) has been operating the Himawari-9 geostationary meteorological satellite since 13 December 2022. The unit performs an actively operational role, with the Himawari-8 satellite ready to begin backup in the event of a critical Himawari-9 malfunction. Both satellites are in geostationary orbit at 140.7°E, providing observation and data collection services for East Asia and the Western Pacific. These satellites will support JMA’s stable provision of continuous satellite observation data until Japanese Fiscal Year (JFY) 2030.Operational information regarding Himawari-8/9 is provided on JMA’s Meteorological Satellite Center (MSC) website. In January 2018, JMA launched an international service “HimawariRequest”, in collaboration with the Australian Bureau of Meteorology (BoM). The service allows National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHS) users in Himawari-8/9 coverage area to request the Target Area observation covering a 1,000 km x 1,000 km area every 2.5 minutes. As of 1 August 2026, there have been 22 registered NMHSs, and 342 international requests have been accepted since the commencement of the service. The targets of requests are tropical cyclones in the South Pacific, bush fires in Australia, volcanos in Indonesia and Tonga, and so on. In March 2023, JMA contracted Himawari-10 as the follow-on satellite to Himawari-8/9, and manufacturing began. Himawari-10 will carry the visible/infrared imager (Geostationary HiMawari Imager: GHMI) and the infrared sounder (Geostationary HiMawari Sounder: GHMS) to help enhance JMA’s services in extreme weather monitoring, nowcasting and numerical weather prediction. Furthermore, the Radiation Monitors for Space weather (RMS) developed by the National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT) will also be mounted on the satellite as hosted payload. The Himawari series of satellites have been widely used in East Asia and the Western Pacific, representing an indispensable part of this international infrastructure. At this conference, an update on the Himawari-10 program will be given, including GHMI and GHMS data specifications such as resolution, spectral channels and data volume/format.

489879.title: Democratization of Environmental Data In the Cloud and AI Weather Forecasting Using the Web-Based Tool iCHARM
489879.authors: Samuel S. Shen, San Diego State University, San Diego, CA
489879.abstract: Democratization of environmental data in the cloud and AI weather forecasting aligns with the core NOAA mission to understand and predict environmental changes, ensuring open and equitable access to vital information across public and private sectors. NOAA's Open Data Dissemination (NODD) program has made available over 40 petabytes of environmental data in the cloud. Although this brings data ever closer to users, netCDF data files and other data formats still require users to write computer code to read, analyze, and visualize the data. Yet, many users, such as schoolchildren, grandparents, and many businesspeople and governmental employees, have no computer coding skills beyond Excel, MS Word, and PowerPoint, and do not have the skills to write computer code to read these valuable data in the cloud. Would it be nice to have an easy-to-use tool that connects the data in the cloud to users? iCHARM (Cyber Hub for Analytics, Research and Monitoring) (https://icharm.app) is the tool. iCHARM can put massive observational and model weather datasets at the fingertips of all users ranging from businesspeople to engineers, from college students to scientists, and from school children to seniors. iCHARM can not only visualize maps, time series, atmospheric and oceanic flows, but also perform statistical data analysis, such as computing anomalies, standard deviations, quantiles, seasonality, regional data statistics (max, min, and average), and spectral analysis for time series (trend, histograms, periodograms, spectrograms, and autocorrelation functions) without the need for computer coding. Thus, iCHARM is like “gas stations” for environmental data. The environmental data in the cloud is like the gas stored in the fuel terminals. Gas stations distribute the gas from the terminals to drivers. iCHARM distributes the NODD data in the cloud to users’ computers, smartphones, and tablets. iCHARM’s interface is like that of a video game: intuitive, zero learning curve, and fast. Thus, users can visualize NOAA data and perform statistical analyses without writing a single line of computer code. iCHARM even allows users to make animations. In the talk, we will show concrete examples, such as using iCHARM to visualize, analyze, and interpret various kinds of weather and climate scenarios, e.g., severe storms and floods from microwave remote sensing data, large-scale droughts, hurricanes and typhoons, polar vortex currents, and El Niño Southern Oscillation. You can use iCHARM to see climate patterns or scenarios of your interest, such as the precipitation distribution of December 2025 over the Southern Pacific Convergence Zone (SPCZ), the winter weather conditions when the Nazi forces reached the suburb of Moscow on 1 December 1941, and the sea surface temperature evolution during the onset of the 2026 El Niño. iCHARM can also display weather forecasting results. Its agents automate several AI weather forecasting models, both global and regional, and produce customized forecasts for iCHARM users, again without the need for computer programming. Our demo will show that iCHARM can deliver NOAA data to the user groups who previously could not access the data, such as the teachers of history and literature. In this sense, iCHARM will help increase the number of NOAA data users and hence can promote the democratization of environmental data and weather forecasting.

489880.title: Nonlinear and Asymmetric Response of the Miocene ENSO to Increasing CO2 Forcing
489880.authors: Yiwen Li, China University of Geosciences (Beijing), Beijing, 11, China
489880.abstract: The characteristics of the Miocene El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and its response to varying atmospheric CO2levels are investigated by using the fully coupled atmosphere–ocean general circulation model FGOALS-g3. Four sensitivity experiments are conducted with prescribed CO2 concentrations of 280 ppmv (Mio_1x), 560 ppmv (Mio_2x), 840 ppmv (Mio_3x), and 1120 ppmv (Mio_4x), and include a pre-industrial simulation under modern boundary conditions to benchmark Miocene–modern differences. Sea surface temperature (SST) analyses reveal that Miocene ENSO events are weaker in amplitude than the present day, with the SST anomaly (SSTA) center extending westward and confined mainly between 150° and 100°W. ENSO’s seasonal phase-locking peaks earlier, occurring around September. The amplitude of ENSO responds nonlinearly to increasing CO2 forcing: the strongest El Niño events occur under the Mio_3x scenario, whereas ENSO variability is markedly damped under the Mio_4x case. In addition, the mean event duration and the zonal structure of SSTAs differ substantially among the CO2 scenarios. These findings highlight the complex and nonlinear behavior of ENSO under Miocene climate conditions, providing insight into its potential response in future high-CO2 climates.

489882.title: Towards A High-Resolution Machine Learning Dataset for Global Near-Real-Time Precipitation Estimation
489882.authors: Guy Shalev, Google DeepMind, Tel Aviv, N/A, Israel; and S. Rasp, B. Babenko, F. Zyda, M. Alewi Hassen, A. Sanchez-Gonzalez, and P. Battaglia
489882.abstract: Accurate precipitation data is critical for many important use-cases, such as hydrological modeling, disaster mitigation, agriculture, and more. Several such datasets exist, but usually trade-off several desirable traits - skill, latency, geographical coverage, temporal coverage, and high temporal and spatial resolutions. We present a machine learning approach for the estimation of global near-real-time precipitation, utilizing the latest WeatherNext models and recent advancements in AI weather research. The resulting dataset strikes a good balance on the above tradeoffs. We validate the approach across multiple metrics and several ground truths to assess its generalizability and applicability for extreme precipitation and operational flood forecasting.

489886.title: Relationship Between Odd-Hydrogen Radical Budgets and Ozone Production Sensitivity over South Korea
489886.authors: Hyeongjun Yoon, Seoul National University, Seoul, Seoul, Korea, Republic of (South); and D. S. Jo
489886.abstract: Tropospheric ozone production sensitivity to nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) depends not only on precursor abundance but also on the formation, interconversion, and removal of odd-hydrogen radicals (OH + HO2 + RO2). Classical radical-budget frameworks relate the transition between NOx- and VOC-sensitive chemistry to the partitioning of radical loss between peroxide-forming radical-radical reactions and radical-NOx termination reactions. These processes also provide a mechanistic basis for several photochemical indicators, including oxidation product ratios, radical loss fractions, and OH reactivity metrics. However, these classical relationships often rely on simplified chemical mechanisms that ignore or lump minor reaction pathways. We investigate how pathways represented in a near-explicit Master Chemical Mechanism (MCM) affect the relationship between detailed odd-hydrogen loss partitioning and instantaneous ozone production sensitivity, as well as the interpretation of photochemical indicators. We use 2016 Korea-United States Air Quality (KORUS-AQ) DC-8 observations to constrain the Framework for 0-D Atmospheric Modeling (F0AM) with the MCM v3.3.1. Primary and oxygenated VOCs, O3, NO, and available measurements of major peroxide and nitrate species are used as model constraints. Rapid interconversions involving alkoxy radicals are treated as internal radical cycling rather than as net odd-hydrogen production or loss. The production-loss budget is therefore constructed from net transfers into and out of the odd-hydrogen radical family. Most modeled OH and HO2 concentrations agree with observations within a factor of two, modeled NO2 closely follows the measurements, and total odd-hydrogen production and loss are approximately balanced across individual observation points. With this constrained baseline, we perturb NO and VOC concentrations to quantify the response of the instantaneous ozone production rate to changes in NOx and VOCs. Preliminary analysis shows that when the NOx-related radical loss, LN, is represented by HNO3 formation alone, the transition in ozone production sensitivity occurs at a lower LN/Q value than predicted by the classical radical-budget relationship, where Q is the total radical production rate. Expanding LN to include alkyl nitrate and peroxy nitrate formation shifts the diagnosed transition toward the value predicted by the classical relationship. This behavior suggests that incomplete representation of nitrate-forming radical loss may contribute to deviations from the classical radical-budget relationship. Ongoing analysis will quantify the contributions of individual loss pathways and examine how detailed odd-hydrogen loss partitioning affects the interpretation of concentration- and reaction-rate-based photochemical indicators. This work aims to identify the conditions under which classical radical-budget relationships remain useful and where more detailed chemical treatment is required to diagnose ozone production sensitivity over South Korea.

489887.title: A Component-Informed Transformer Framework for Multi-Parameter Aerosol Retrieval from Multi-Angle Polarimetric Observations
489887.authors: Meng Fan, Aerospace Information Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Sciences, BEIJING, 11, China
489887.abstract: Multi-angle polarimetric (MAP) observations provide valuable sensitivity to aerosol loading, absorption, and particle-size characteristics, but the retrieval of a high-dimensional aerosol state vector from satellite measurements remains strongly ill posed. This study develops AeroTransMP, a component-informed multi-angle Transformer framework for retrieving aerosol optical and microphysical properties from Directional Polarimetric Camera-2 (DPC-2) observations onboard GaoFen-5(02). The AeroTransMP framework is designed around three key components. First, three-dimensional aerosol species from MERRA-2 are converted into wavelength-dependent optical and microphysical labels, including spectral aerosol optical depth (AOD), fine-mode and CoarseAOD, absorption aerosol optical depth (AAOD), complex refractive indices, and particle-size parameters, providing physically coherent supervision beyond AOD-only labels. Second, a dual-stream Transformer encodes DPC-2 intensity and polarization angular sequences separately to exploit their complementary sensitivity to aerosol scattering and absorption. Third, an AERONET-constrained multi-task transfer-learning strategy is used to reduce the discrepancy between component-derived labels and real satellite measurements. Independent station-based spatial cross-validation against AERONET shows robust retrieval performance. The retrieved AOD at 443nm achieves a correlation coefficient (R) = 0.902, while FineAOD reach R = 0.906. The framework also retrieves aerosol absorption properties with AAOD (R = 0.640, RMSE = 0.033) and successfully estimates complex refractive indices and particle size parameters with good agreement against AERONET inversion products and physically consistent spatial distributions. The proposed framework provides an effective solution for generating multi-parameter aerosol products from DPC-2 observations and demonstrates the potential of component -informed deep learning for multi-angle polarimetric aerosol remote sensing.

489889.title: Toward Uncompromised High-Rank Data Assimilation with Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
489889.authors: Takemasa Miyoshi, RIKEN Center for Computational Science, Kobe, Japan
489889.abstract: Data assimilation (DA) optimally fuses model forecasts with observations, where the background error covariance matrix B plays a fundamental role. Ideally B should evolve with the flow and retain long-range cross-variable correlations without truncation. However, with state dimensions N of 108 to 109 in weather models, storing B requires O(N2) memory and inverting it O(N3) operations, beyond classical computing. DA with an uncompromised high-rank B has long been deemed impossible; research has instead focused on approximations: variational methods parameterize B statically, and ensemble methods impose localization, both sacrificing genuine correlations. Future fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) may overturn this long-held belief: quantum algorithms can encode the N-dimensional state on only about log2 N qubits and solve the underlying matrix equations in O(κ polylog N) operations, where κ is the condition number, making the uncompromised DA problem directly solvable. Realizing this, however, requires overcoming two difficulties: (i) an input problem of preparing B inside the quantum computer, and (ii) downstream mathematical barriers of matrix inversion and nonlocal observations. Assuming future AI surrogate models resolve (i), this study resolves (ii). A direct translation of the standard DA equations onto quantum hardware inflates the computational overhead quadratically under dense nonlocal observations such as satellite radiances, largely degrading the quantum advantage. We propose a simple remedy: recasting the analysis as a single expanded system that couples the state and observation spaces. This quantum-ready formulation never inverts B, avoids the ill-conditioning problem, and keeps the overhead linear. We verify the formulation numerically with the 40-variable Lorenz-96 model. The essential remaining barrier is the input problem (i): bridging deep-learning covariance modeling to quantum state preparation is the key challenge for our community in the FTQC era.

489891.title: A Review of Visibility Parameterizations: Focus on Arctic Low Visibility
489891.authors: Ismail Gultepe, Ontario Technical University, Oshawa, ON, Canada
489891.abstract: The objective of this work is to evaluate visibility (Vis) parameterizations and emphasize cold fog issues for low visibilities. Vis parameterizations developed earlier were based on relative humidity with respect to water (RHw), dew point depression, Ddep=Ta-Td (air temperature-dewpoint temperature), and microphysical (MP) parameters such as liquid water content (LWC), droplet number concentration (Nd), and effective diameter (Deff). RHw is obtained from Ta and Td. Therefore, to obtain Vis we should be able to use either RHw or Ddep but not both. Clearly, increasing Ddep means less RHw, leading to higher Vis conditions and lower extinction coefficient (βext). βext is obtained from a measured DSD with known efficiency factor (Qeff) which is function of visible light wavelength (λ) and particle size (r). If βext cannot be obtained directly from a numerical weather prediction (NWP) simulation, it is possible to be estimated using bulk LWC and Nd that are usually prognostically available from a NWP model. Some work uses Deff replacing Nd that can lead to higher Vis values. Therefore, when Vis is related to fog particles, it is better to use Nd because small droplets’ concentration is always greater than large droplets’ concentrations, and it is available from the simulation. If we apply a similar analysis for colder climates such as in Arctic, above-mentioned parameterizations should be modified for freezing fog (FFG) and ice fog (IFG) conditions. This work will explain why we face lower Vis estimations over the Arctic conditions. In the analysis, Vis and MP measurements from FATIMA (Fog and Turbulence in Marine Atmosphere) field campaigns representing marine atmosphere and Arctic conditions will be evaluated and Arctic low Vis conditions will be explained.

489892.title: Ensemble‐Based Assimilation of Sounding Observations With AI Weather Models
489892.authors: Huifeng Huang, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China; and L. Lei and Z. M. Tan
489892.abstract: The artificial intelligence (AI)-based weather models have shown great promise for weather forecasts. But they rely on the initial conditions provided by traditional paradigm of numerical weather prediction, which has a cycled data assimilation (DA) to combine short-term forecasts and observations. This study demonstrates the ability of state-of-the-art AI weather models within the framework of cycling DA, achieving a successful and stable cycling DA with assimilation of real-time sounding observations. For FengWu, assimilation of wind observations can better constrain the atmospheric state than assimilation of temperature observations, and both produce more accurate analyses and 6-h forecasts than assimilation of specific humidity observations. But when Pangu-Weather is applied, assimilating wind observations cannot constrain the state variables of temperature and specific humidity as well as that with FengWu. This indicates that the influences of observation types on cycling DA with AI weather models are model-dependent, associated with the intrinsic error characteristics.

489893.title: Requirements and Design of China's TanSat-2 Mission
489893.authors: Liangfu Chen, Aerospace Information Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Sciences, BEIJING, China; and M. Fan
489893.abstract: Global climate change has become a major challenge facing human society, with greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions being one of its primary driving factors. To effectively assess the progress of global GHG reduction efforts, the Paris Agreement established the Global Stocktake (GST) mechanism, which requires verification of national greenhouse gas emission inventories. Currently, developed countries such as Europe, the United States, and Japan have begun to deploy next-generation carbon monitoring satellite missions. Against this backdrop, China has also initiated the satellite technology program for the next-generation global carbon monitoring scientific experimental satellite (TanSat-2), aimed at providing scientific input for subsequent satellite development and system construction. The satellite technology program is a key phase in the design of the satellite and payload system, as well as in the development of the data reception and processing system. Its core lies in assessing the feasibility and performance indicators of the satellite design using scientific methods. Compared to traditional observational system experiments (OSE), observational system simulation experiments (OSSE) employ high-precision numerical models and virtual observation scenarios to simulate and compare satellite observation results with "true values" derived from model inversions. This enables the analysis and identification of potential error sources during the design phase, optimizing the technical specifications of the satellite platform and payload, and avoiding subsequent modification costs and time delays. This study summarizes the TanSat-2 satellite program's technical verification for global carbon stocktaking. It primarily outlines the next-generation carbon satellite design and development requirements targeting high temporal-frequency, high-precision, multi-element, and multi-scale observations. Based on the OSSE framework, the TanSat-2 satellite system design and key technical solutions are verified, offering theoretical and technical support for the design of China's next-generation anthropogenic carbon emission monitoring satellite.

489894.title: A Quantile-Conserving Ensemble Filter for Strongly Coupled Atmosphere-Ocean Assimilation
489894.authors: Kecheng Fu, Nanjing University, Nanjing, 32, China; and L. Lei
