489894.abstract: Strongly coupled data assimilation can allow atmospheric observations to constrain the upper ocean, but its relevance to tropical-cyclone prediction remains unclear at convection-permitting scales. This issue is examined through an idealized observing-system simulation experiment for Typhoon Mangkhut using a coupled WRF–3DPWP ensemble. AMSU-A channel-4 radiances are assimilated with EAKF and QCEFF-based QCF_RHF under strongly and weakly coupled configurations. Strong coupling produces a coherent ocean analysis increment that is transferred to WRF skin temperature and subsequently modifies surface sensible and latent heat fluxes, 2-m thermodynamic variables, and the lowest atmospheric model levels. QCF_RHF generates stronger ocean and near-surface atmospheric responses than EAKF. However, these signals remain confined mainly to the lower boundary layer and do not translate into robust improvements in precipitation, track, or intensity. The results identify a physically consistent ocean-to-atmosphere adjustment pathway and suggest that limited ocean ensemble spread and weak coupled cross-component covariance may constrain the atmospheric impact of strongly coupled tropical-cyclone data assimilation.

489924.title: Impact of Anthropogenic Heat and Cool Roof Interactions on the Atmospheric Environment in Seoul, South Korea
489924.authors: HyeonMin Son, Inha University, Incheon, South korea
489924.abstract: This study investigated effects of anthropogenic heat (AH), cool roof, and their synergy on the atmospheric environment in Seoul, South Korea, from July 20 to August 21, 2018, with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. Four simulations with different combinations of AH and cool roof applications were conducted to quantify the individual effects of AH and cool roof and their synergy. The results showed that the AH effect was pronounced primarily during nighttime and morning hours. Under low planetary boundary layer height conditions, AH had a relatively greater influence on sensible heat flux, leading to increased 2-m temperature and enhanced urban breeze. The pure cool roof effect was most prominent during daytime periods, resulting in reduced sensible heat flux and 2-m temperature, accompanied by weakened urban circulation. The synergy effect was enhanced during midday hours, particularly between 11:00 and 13:00 LST, when reduced AH contribution led to a decrease in sensible heat flux. The daily mean changes in 2-m temperature due to the AH effect, pure cool roof effect, and synergy effect were approximately 0.5°C, −0.8°C, and 0.04°C. The effects of AH, cool roof, and their synergy on surface temperature and wind conditions could be applicable to understanding air pollutant behavior in plastic manufacturing and recycling facilities. "This research was supported by Plastic-free Specialized Graduate Program through the Korea Environmental Industry & Technology Institute(KEITI) funded by the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment(MCEE)”

489927.title: Increasing Contribution of Landscape Fire to Primary Carbonaceous Aerosol Emission under Air-Pollutant Control Scenarios
489927.authors: Jaein Jeong, Seoul National University, Seoul, South korea; and R. Park, S. W. yeh, and S. Lee
489927.abstract: Fire-weather seasons have lengthened in recent decades, and fire weather is projected to worsen further under every emission pathway, including the most ambitious. Air-pollutant control, in contrast, removes anthropogenic aerosol but not the weather that drives landscape fire, so the fire share of aerosol emission must rise. How far this shift reaches across aerosol species and precursors, however, remains poorly quantified. This study investigates when fire emission overtakes anthropogenic emission, species by species, under strong air-pollutant control. We calibrate the Canadian Fire Weather Index against GFED4 fire emissions for each burning type over 1997–2021, and apply the calibrated sensitivity to CMIP6 projections. Projected emissions are speciated with GFED4 emission factors and compared with the anthropogenic trajectories the same scenarios prescribe. Preliminary results indicate that climate-driven fire emissions rise under future warming while anthropogenic emissions decline, so that the two cross. Globally, the crossover is confined to primary carbonaceous aerosol: fire organic and black carbon overtake their anthropogenic counterparts, whereas the inorganic precursors (SO2, NOx, and NH3) do not. These results suggest that, as anthropogenic emissions fall, landscape fire becomes the main constraint on further reductions in carbonaceous aerosol emissions, with implications for air quality planning.

489934.title: Improving Cybersecurity for Radiosonde Observations
489934.authors: Matti Lehmuskero, Vaisala Inc, Helsinki, Finland
489934.abstract: In today’s world, meteorological agencies face significant hybrid and cyber threats, such as GPS interference and cyberattacks, which can lead to inaccurate weather forecasts. These threats are increasingly sophisticated, targeting the vulnerabilities in meteorological systems. Radiosondes rely heavily on GNSS signals for determining wind, position, geopotential height, and derived atmospheric pressure. Disruptions and hybrid threats can degrade data quality or lead to premature termination of soundings. This poster presents recent advancements in Vaisala radiosondes and sounding systems in improving the resilience and cybersecurity of radiosonde observations through two complementary technologies: multi-GNSS positioning and radiosonde message authentication. Multi-GNSS operation enables RS41 radiosondes to utilize multiple satellite constellations, including GPS, Galileo, and BeiDou, increasing satellite availability and reducing reliance on any single system. Test campaigns conducted under interfered conditions demonstrate that multi-GNSS significantly improves the probability of reaching target burst altitudes and maintains measurement accuracy during periods of GPS interference. In addition, the poster introduces RS41 radiosonde message authentication as a new cybersecurity measure for upper-air observations. While radiosonde data transmissions are traditionally unencrypted and vulnerable to manipulation, message authentication allows receivers to verify the integrity and authenticity of received data. Together, multi-GNSS resilience and message authentication strengthen the reliability, availability, and trustworthiness of upper-air observations, supporting meteorological operations in an increasingly contested and cyber-aware operating environment.

489935.title: A Convective-Scale Reanalysis for the 'Swabian MOSES 2023' Field Campaign
489935.authors: Julia Thomas, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Baden-Württemberg, Germany; and H. Reich, T. Steinert, G. Geppert, K. Stephan, A. Erdmann, P. Gasch, M. Hervo, J. Keller, A. Carrassi, P. Knippertz, and A. Oertel
489935.abstract: A reanalysis can be considered the most complete representation of the atmospheric state given all available observations as well as the model background. Via data assimilation, a reanalysis allows assessing the non-local influence of observations on the time evolution of the modeled state, while aiming to maintain the physical consistency of the model state. Here, we present the pioneering, 3-month convective-scale campaign reanalysis of the 'Swabian MOSES 2023' campaign, consisting of a control (CTRL) dataset without and a campaign (CMPG) dataset with additional field campaign observations from the mobile atmospheric measurement platform KITcube during June, July and August 2023. Both are computed at hourly resolution on a 2.2 km grid centered over Germany with the quasi-operational data assimilation framework by Deutscher Wetterdienst which is based on a Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter. CMPG incorporates additional ground-based remote-sensing and in situ observations from the southwest German mountain ranges of the Black Forest and Swabian Jura, a region with moderately complex terrain. The unprecedentedly dense network of 12 Doppler wind lidars, one X-band precipitation radar, two additional radiosounding sites, Global Navigation Satellite Systems receivers, and meteorological masts increases the number of observations in the approximately 105 km2 campaign area by 45% compared to the operational measurement network. As expected, the assimilation reduces the difference between observations and model fields. Specifically, the standard deviation of the observation-to-model difference across all additional observations is reduced by 10% to 35% after assimilation. Updates of the model background are predominantly introduced in the lower troposphere and in the campaign region itself, but differences between CMPG and CTRL extend all over Germany, eastern France, and northern Italy. Mean absolute differences in the campaign region reach up to the order of 1.5 m s−1 in wind speed, 0.4K in temperature, and 0.7 g kg−1 in humidity. This pioneering campaign reanalysis can be employed to quantify the influence of individual observations and different observation types and to diagnose potential model deficiencies in complex terrain. It further serves as a high-resolution reference for detailed case studies targeting high-impact weather and provides a basis for re-forecast experiments to quantify observation impact on forecasts.

489936.title: Short-Term PQPF Without an Ensemble: Regional U-Nets Applied to Deterministic HRRR Output
489936.authors: Timothy Thielke, CIRES, College Park, MD; and J. A. Nelson Jr.
489936.abstract: Probabilistic quantitative precipitation forecasts (PQPF) at short lead times are conventionally derived from ensembles, which are expensive to run and maintain at convection-allowing resolution. Under the Disaster Supplemental Relief Act, the Weather Prediction Center (WPC) was tasked with developing short-term PQPF guidance. We show that a convolutional neural network can generate hourly precipitation exceedance probabilities across the contiguous United States (CONUS) from a single deterministic High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) run without high-performance computing. The system uses a U-Net architecture to map 27 HRRR fields to Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) hourly quantitative precipitation estimates, generating probabilities of exceeding nine thresholds from 0.01 to 5 inches over 13 geographically unique regions. Each region has a dedicated algorithm that learns the local precipitation regime and HRRR biases. Overlapping outputs are merged into a seamless national field using a windowed overlap-add method. The product was verified against MRMS for all twelve months of 2024 and has proved to be skillful by outperforming annual climatology at the 0.01-inch threshold each month. Even at higher thresholds, it showed strong skill during the cool season, though it struggled with warm-season convection. High probability of detection scores at the four lowest thresholds indicate the model’s ability to accurately place PQPF features, but increased frequency bias at the higher thresholds suggests that it will overestimate the area of peak PQPF. Reliability curve trends indicate that forecast ranking remains useful even when the model is overconfident. This insight informs the interpretation guidance now provided to forecasters. The product currently runs hourly in real time, delivers imagery and GeoJSON to a public web display, and is being refined based on feedback from WPC operational forecasters.

489938.title: Evaluation of Mid-Morning Fire Observing Capabilities as Part of an Integrated Fire Monitoring Constellation
489938.authors: Ivan A. Csiszar, NOAA NESDIS Center for Satellite Applications and Research, Riverdale Park, MD; and Y. Gu, M. Tsidulko, and W. Guo
489938.abstract: Polar orbiting satellite assets have been key components of global fire monitoring constellations. For over two decades, Terra MODIS fire observations served as critical source of mid-morning fire information. With the decommissioning of Terra, data from the Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR) on the Sentinel-3 series, and more recently, the MetOp-Second Generation METImage sensor provide continuity of fire observations from the mid-morning polar orbit. In recent years, the SLSTR fire product from the 10:00 am/pm orbit, has been evaluated for its potential to replace Terra MODIS data in NOAA’s emission modeling framework. The availability of in-orbit METImage data from the 9:30 am/pm orbit provides the opportunity for a similar assessment, including the establishment of the available dynamic range of critical midwave-infrared (MWIR) measurements and the refinement of approaches to enable the retrieval of fire radiative power (FRP) for saturated MWIR conditions. The mid-morning orbits also allow for the direct comparison against higher resolution Landsat-class fire observations. In this presentation we will discuss latest results, based on available in-orbit data, from the analysis of METImage observations against SLSTR measurements for fire hot spots from select large fire events. The analysis also includes an assessment of the relative merits and complementarity of fire data from the Sentinel-3 and MetOp-SG missions.

489942.title: The Integrated Atmospheric Observation System KITcube
489942.authors: Peter Knippertz, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Baden-Württemberg, Germany; and A. Wieser, J. Handwerker, P. Gasch, A. Oertel, A. Erdmann, and M. Kohler
489942.abstract: The KITcube integrated atmospheric observation system of the Institute for Meteorology and Climate Research – Tropospheric Research (IMKTRO) at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) is one of the most comprehensive such systems in the world. It enables the cross-scale study of atmospheric processes from the micro- to the mesoscale. By combining state-of-the-art lidar and radar remote sensing systems with traditional in-situ instruments, a unique measurement network for a worldwide deployment is created, enabling high-resolution observations both at a central main station and at distributed meso-stations. The presentation will give an overview of the system architecture, measurement strategies, and potential applications of KITcube, illustrating these for the most recent field campaigns Swabian MOSES in southwestern Germany, TEAMx in the Alps, and NAWDIC in Brittany (France). Particular emphasis is placed on the process chain from measurement through retrieval methods to data assimilation into the ICON model of the German Weather Service (DWD). As examples, Doppler retrievals from radar and lidar data will be presented, which enable the determination of mesoscale wind fields and embedded convergence zones over complex terrain and impressively demonstrate the system’s scientific value. Within KITcube, the AtmoProKIT system provides quality-assured wind profiles for model validation and assimilation. Airborne measurements, using the newly developed high-resolution AIRflows Doppler lidar and the KITsonde, complement ground-based observations and fill important gaps in the spatial coverage of atmospheric structures.

489945.title: Incorporation of AI Techniques into Operations at the National Hurricane Center
489945.authors: Aidan D. Mahoney, National Hurricane Center, Miami, FL; and D. A. Zelinsky, J. P. Cangialosi, M. J. Brennan, P. Santos, K. Musgrave, M. DeMaria, and G. Chirokova
489945.abstract: The National Hurricane Center (NHC) has recently increased its operational use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques and tools. These efforts include the evaluation of multiple AI numerical models for tropical cyclone genesis, track, and intensity forecasts, the inclusion of AI models into NHC consensus forecast aids, and the use of AI satellite based tools for tropical cyclone intensity analysis. Among the AI weather prediction models incorporated are the ECMWF AIFS, AIGFS, AIGEFS, and Google DeepMind. Other AI models and AI satellite based tools are being evaluated and/or developed including GOES-based synthetic passive microwave imagery, wind structure estimation models, and a neural-network version of the SHIPS intensity model. New real-time genesis guidance developed at NHC and based on the 1000-member Google DeepMind ensemble will be discussed as an example of successful and rapid integration of AI forecast guidance into operations. This guidance uses tracker output produced by the ensemble to generate two- and seven-day genesis probabilities and formation areas. Initial verification of the genesis guidance indicates it is remarkably well-calibrated and as skillful or more skillful than all other probabilistic genesis guidance operationally available to NHC forecasters. Results shared in this presentation will include other comprehensive verification and comparison to traditional numerical weather model output, demonstrate examples highlighting the successes and challenges of using these tools, and their benefit to and impact on the NHC mission.

489949.title: The Heterogeneous Impact of Vehicle Electrification on Thermal Environment and Ozone Pollution: A Case Study In Shanghai
489949.authors: Ning Zhang, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China
489949.abstract: The urban thermal stress and ozone pollution are main threats to human health. Vehicle electrification is a combined strategy that reduces traffic-related anthropogenic heat ( ) and pollution emission, which is promising for improving urban living environment. However, the impact of vehicle electrification on ozone pollution involves complex interactions between microclimate change and emission reduction, the combined effect of which is not clear. The heterogeneous efficiency of vehicle electrification in mitigating thermal environment and ozone pollution is important for optimizing its implementation, yet remains underexplored. In this study, the WRF-chem simulations coupled with high-resolution anthropogenic heat, land use and pollution emission dataset are used to analyze an eight-day ozone pollution episode in Shanghai. The results indicate that after vehicle electrification, urban canyon air temperature decreases 0.2 °C on average, reaching up to 1.1 °C, with the highest cooling efficiency in compact high-rise urban canyon. Although average ozone concentration increases by 0.5 ppb after reduction due to the weakened urban heat island circulation, the positive effect from the pollution emission reduction is more dominant, leading to a net ozone concentration decrease by 5.3 ppb after vehicle electrification. Ozone mitigation efficiency is higher in regions with high ratio of VOC to NOx emission intensity. This study proves the environmental benefit of vehicle electrification strategy and highlight the importance of urban morphological and emission heterogeneity to improve the strategy's efficiency.

489952.title: Satellite-Trained Latent Spaces for Evaluating km-Scale Atmospheric Simulations
489952.authors: Dwaipayan Chatterjee, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Baden-Württemberg, Germany; and P. Knippertz, N. Raabe, S. Crewell, B. Vannière, and P. DUEBEN
489952.abstract: As km-scale models produce detailed cloud fields, evaluation must test whether simulated surface--cloud radiative scenes reproduce observed structures and evolutions. We introduce a novel observation-centered framework for evaluating two km-scale weather models over central Europe within a latent space learned from geostationary satellite observations. A self-supervised encoder trained on Meteosat Second Generation (MSG) 10.8μm brightness-temperature imagery yields embeddings partitioned into eight radiative-scene regimes reflecting cloud organization, cloud-top temperature, and near-surface thermal information. MSG-equivalent fields from the Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) and ICOsahedral Non-hydrostatic model over Europe (ICON-EU) are projected into this fixed observational space and evaluated using regime occurrence, persistence, transitions, scene-by-scene correspondence, and a continuous thermal-scene evolution index. Both models reproduce key aspects of the observed diurnal evolution, including warm daytime development and transitions from surface-dominated broken clouds to cloud-dominated states, but their dominant errors differ. Both under-represent daytime shallow low clouds and pass through them too rapidly, with larger deficits in ICON-EU despite its low-cloud maximum occurring near the observed midday phase. ICON-EU often maps observed low-cloud scenes to the warm-transition regime, which it occupies too broadly and retains too long. IFS also routes departures from daytime low cloud too strongly toward this regime, while distributing corresponding observed scenes among warmer and cooler states. Beyond daytime low clouds, IFS over-retains homogeneous and cloudier nighttime regimes and under-represents widespread deep cloud toward evening, whereas ICON-EU broadens scattered deep-convective occurrence. By revealing coherent biases in scene identity and evolution, the framework provides pathway-specific targets for model evaluation and improvement.

489958.title: The Impact of Aeolus Observations on Wind and Rainfall Predictions
489958.authors: Maurus Borne, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Baden-Württemberg, Germany; and P. Knippertz, M. Rennie, and M. Weissmann
489958.abstract: Previous studies showed substantial improvements in upper-level wind and mass field forecasts from assimilating Aeolus wind observations. This study extends those analyses using the improved reprocessed Aeolus dataset (version B16) in experiments with the global ECMWF forecasting system spanning more than three years. Results show that zonal wind forecasts improve through most of the troposphere during the first forecast week, with smaller gains in Northern Hemisphere midlatitudes. The impact extends into the stratosphere, reducing Root Mean Square Errors by about 0.5%, up to 1.5% in the tropical upper troposphere. These improvements lead to more accurate rainfall forecasts in some regions and seasons, as measured by the Fraction Skill Score (FSS) and the Stable Equitable Error in Probability Space (SEEPS). They are largest during the winter half-year in the extratropics, particularly in the Southern Hemisphere, and appear primarily at the grid scale. The largest FSS improvements, reaching several percent, occur for 5–10 day leads and heavy rainfall categories, while SEEPS indicates modest but consistent gains in categorical precipitation skill. These results show co-occurring improvements in wind and precipitation, particularly in winter, which may reflect an influence of Aeolus winds on the large-scale circulation that governs the organization of cyclones, fronts, and heavy rainfall.

489959.title: Radar Next: Building the Gold Standard in Integrated Weather Intelligence
489959.authors: Jessica Schultz, NWS, Norman, OK; and M. Grow, R. Silver, and A. Mehta
489959.abstract: As the National Weather Service (NWS)’s current radar fleet is projected to experience declining availability by the early 2030s, Radar Next is focused on ensuring continuity of critical weather observations while building the world class data integration platform to meet future mission needs. The future weather radar network will consist of federally owned radars and commercial data. This includes the 3-Dimensional fusion of X-, C-, and S-band weather radar and other observations into the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)’s Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system, leveraging agile development, Artificial Intelligence, and Machine Learning. The end state will deliver the best quality radar data at any moment in time to the forecaster. The Radar Next Concept of Operations supports NWS's transition to the future cloud architecture, including the role of centralized command and control capabilities to optimize network operations, maintenance, and service delivery. The program is also exploring innovative approaches to improve network resilience, including transportable radar capabilities to mitigate extended outages and support localized decision support services during high-impact events. Continuous engagement and strategic market research with industry, academia, and other stakeholders is informing the development of a cost-effective, scalable, and sustainable radar architecture. This presentation will provide an update on the Radar Next Program and its progress during the past year, including upcoming milestones and opportunities for continued engagement as NWS advances toward the next generation of weather radar capabilities.

489960.title: Enhanced Nitrogen and Sulfur Deposition from Forest Fire Emissions across Canada and the United States
489960.authors: Irene Cheng, Environment and Climate Change Canada, Toronto, ON, Canada; and A. Cole, J. Feng, H. Cathcart, A. Robichaud, J. Chen, N. Pentcheva, and M. Bulat
489960.abstract: Ecologically sensitive regions are negatively impacted by atmospheric deposition of nitrogen, sulfur, and ozone. Deposited nitrogen and sulfur can cause acidification of surface waters and soil, which affect aquatic wildlife, vegetation, and forests. Excess nitrogen inputs can lead to eutrophication, which creates toxic conditions in aquatic ecosystems. Ozone deposition is harmful to vegetation and alters water and nutrient cycling. These detrimental effects are exacerbated by increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires, since wildfire smoke contains a mixture of pollutants including fine particulate matter, toxic metals, volatile organic compounds, nitrogen and sulfur compounds, and ozone. Research is needed to better characterize and quantify the contributions of wildfires to atmospheric deposition of contaminants. In this study, the air quality reforecast data produced by Environment and Climate Change Canada Canadian Centre for Meteorological and Environmental Predictions were used to examine the impacts on nitrogen, sulfur, and ozone deposition from wildfires. The reforecast output is generated from the Global Environmental Multiscale Modelling Air quality and CHemistry (GEM-MACH) model and consists of versions with or without emissions from forest fires. By examining the difference between the two reforecast outputs, wildfire impacts on pollutant deposition across Canada and the U.S. can be quantified. In 2019, there were four regions where deposition was significantly affected by wildfires. They include areas in Alaska, USA and Yukon Territory, northern Alberta, and northwestern Ontario, Canada. We overlaid wildfire perimeter data on the deposition rasters and found the areas with wildfire emissions correspond to greater deposition impacts. For total (dry and wet) sulfur deposition, the fluxes due to wildfires were 2-4 times higher in Alaska, 2 times higher in Yukon Territory and northern Alberta, and within a factor of 2 in northwestern Ontario. The contributions of wildfires to total nitrogen deposition were even greater. Total nitrogen deposition over burned areas was 3-6 times higher in Alaska, 3-4 times higher in Yukon Territory, and 2-3 times higher in northern Alberta, which was mostly driven by enhancements in total reduced nitrogen deposition. The increased nitrogen and sulfur deposition in Alaska and Yukon Territory are particularly significant because these regions normally have low levels of deposition in the absence of wildfires. The transport of wildfire emissions also increased deposition in downwind areas when regional statistics of wildfire contributions are examined. This analysis will be extended across multiple years to assess the variability in the deposition contributions from wildfires. The preliminary results above demonstrate the potential utility of chemical transport models for linking atmospheric deposition impacts to changes in emissions. Considering the increasing occurrence of wildfires, the production of model outputs with and without wildfire emissions is essential for assessing the effects of wildfires on atmospheric deposition and ecosystem health. Furthermore, research is needed to improve model simulations of contaminants in wildfire emissions and chemical processing in smoke plumes.

489961.title: From Community Expertise to Ontology: A Participatory Methodology for Trustworthy AI in the Weather Enterprise
489961.authors: Jonathon Mote, Fedwriters support to NOAA WPO, Hyattsville, MD
489961.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into the weather enterprise, questions of transparency, explainability, and scientific validity have taken on renewed importance. In this presentation, we argue that community-developed ontologies provide an important foundation for trustworthy AI. An ontology is a shared conceptual model that defines the key entities in a real-world domain, the relationships among them, and the vocabulary used to describe them. It provides the semantic structure that organizes a knowledge graph, allowing data from diverse sources to be connected through explicitly defined concepts and relationships rather than through data alone. Much current work on knowledge graphs begins with existing datasets and asks how they can be linked to support machine reasoning. However, this data-centric approach often leaves the underlying conceptual structure implicit, limiting the transparency of any resulting AI applications. We explore an alternative methodology that begins not with data, but with the expert communities that produce and use scientific knowledge. In partnership with the Natural Hazards Center, NOAA's Weather Program Office convened an interdisciplinary workshop bringing together researchers and practitioners from meteorology, hydrology, emergency management, infrastructure, and the social sciences. Through a structured participatory process, participants collaboratively identified the concepts, entities, and relationships that characterize flooding as a coupled physical and social system. Rather than constructing an ontology from existing databases, the workshop participants developed a shared conceptual model grounded in the collective expertise of the community. This process positioned domain experts as co-developers of the semantic framework that would ultimately support AI applications. Following the workshop, the conceptual model was translated into a formal ontology and used to construct a flood knowledge graph integrating four heterogeneous datasets spanning hazard events, weather warnings, disaster declarations, socioeconomic characteristics, and geospatial information. The resulting semantic infrastructure was implemented in a natural-language query interface that demonstrates how large language models can answer interdisciplinary questions by reasoning over explicitly defined concepts and relationships rather than disconnected datasets. With the interface, users can explore questions spanning physical hazards, social vulnerability, emergency management, and infrastructure through conversational queries while the underlying knowledge graph provides a transparent and inspectable representation of the community's understanding of the domain. The operational prototype demonstrates that participatory ontology development can be translated into an AI-enabled decision-support capability rather than remaining a conceptual exercise. By beginning with participatory conceptual modeling rather than data integration, the resulting ontology makes explicit the vocabulary, assumptions, and conceptual relationships that underlie subsequent AI applications. Because these structures are community-developed, they remain open to review, revision, and extension as scientific understanding evolves, providing an interpretable semantic foundation for integrating physical and social science information. We suggest that community-developed ontologies, coupled with knowledge graphs and natural-language interfaces, provide a scalable methodology for building AI-ready scientific infrastructure that supports more transparent, interoperable, and ultimately more trustworthy decision-support systems across the weather enterprise.

489962.title: Sensitivity of Global and Regional Weather Forecasts to Observational Density and Quality
489962.authors: Cédric Froidevaux, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Baden-Württemberg, Germany; and P. Knippertz and J. Wilhelm-Degenhardt
489962.abstract: Observations are crucial for accurate numerical weather prediction (NWP), yet coverage is uneven worldwide, contributing to regional differences in forecast skill. This study quantifies the sensitivity of weather forecasts to observational density and quality in a controlled framework, highlighting differences between the extratropics and the tropics, with a special focus on tropical Africa, one of the most sparsely observed regions. Radiosonde-like pseudo-observations (PSOs) are generated from the ERA5 reanalysis, and experiments are conducted with the ICOsahedral Nonhydrostatic (ICON) model, systematically varying PSO density and quality. Forecasts up to seven days are evaluated against ERA5 for standard meteorological variables (e.g. temperature and pressure) and against Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation (MSWEP) for precipitation. Increasing PSO density consistently improves forecast skill, particularly at short lead times, but the magnitude and persistence of these improvements differ markedly between the tropics and extratropics. In the tropics, forecast gains decrease approximately exponentially with lead time and show rapidly diminishing returns as PSO density increases, with little additional benefit beyond lead times of about four days. In contrast, forecast improvements in the extratropics decline more linearly and continue to benefit from higher PSO densities at longer lead times. Across all experiments, PSO density exerts the strongest influence on forecast skill, followed by PSO quality, whereas model resolution has a comparatively small impact. As expected, forecast improvements are smaller for precipitation than for standard meteorological variables, especially in tropical Africa, reflecting challenges associated with predicting the often organised convective systems in this part of the world. These results provide a systematic, quantitative guidance for the design of observational networks, confirming that dense local observing systems are only valuable for improving short-term forecasts, while a homogeneous global coverage is beneficial for enhancing medium-range forecast skill, calling for a more effective allocation of observational resources in regions with limited data availability.

489963.title: Connected Science: Co-Development and Convergence for Enhancing Flood Resilience
489963.authors: Jonathon Mote, Fedwriters support to NOAA WPO, Hyattsville, MD
489963.abstract: Scientific and policy problems increasingly require integrating information across disciplinary, organizational, and technical boundaries to ensure its usability. Further, growing interest in applying artificial intelligence (AI) to scientific data has highlighted the importance of making those data easier to discover, connect, interpret, and validate. Knowledge graphs offer one promising approach by organizing data around their meaning rather than around the structure of individual datasets. For example, a hydrologist's 'flood stage,' an emergency manager's 'flood warning,' and a social scientist's 'flood exposure' carry distinct meanings; a knowledge graph makes the relationships among them explicit, so data framed one way can be correctly interpreted in another While considerable attention has been devoted to the technical development of knowledge graphs, much less attention has been given to how the underlying meaning is developed in the first place. This presentation describes recent efforts to use knowledge graphs in the flood research domain. Specifically, presenters will detail the co-development and implementation of a collaborative workshop conducted with more than 50 domain specialists from across the flood enterprise that culminated in a shared conceptual model of flood risk and resilience. Rather than beginning with datasets or technical data models, the workshop began with harnessing the collective knowledge of the participants themselves. Through a series of formal educational presentations and structured collaborative activities, participants identified the vocabulary, concepts, and relationships they use to understand flood systems. Those shared concepts were then synthesized into an ontology—a common conceptual framework—that subsequently served as the foundation for building a knowledge graph capable of connecting diverse physical and social science datasets. The contribution of this work is not the flood knowledge graph itself–which is still in its developmental stages–but the broader implications of the workshop process. The case suggests a replicable approach for co-developing semantic infrastructure with communities of practice, one that begins with creating shared meaning rather than interrogating data structures and treats domain experts as collaborators in defining the conceptual foundations that make data integration possible. In this view, knowledge graphs become not merely technical artifacts but representations of a scientific community's shared understanding of a problem domain, providing a foundation for developing novel research questions, integrating data, and supporting emerging AI applications. Although exploratory, the workshop demonstrates how participatory ontology development can provide a practical foundation for integrating heterogeneous data while preserving the conceptual relationships identified by the communities who use those data. More broadly, we argue that the challenge of connecting data is as much strategic engagement and organizational prowess as it is technical ability, and collaborative approaches to developing shared conceptual frameworks may provide an important pathway for building connected scientific infrastructure. As scientific data are increasingly expected to support both human inquiry and AI-assisted discovery, beginning with the knowledge of the communities who create and use those data is an essential component of future data stewardship.

489966.title: Dynamic Vs. Diabatic Controls on Atmospheric Variability and Predictability In a Tropical Aquachannel
489966.authors: Hyunju Jung, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Baden-Württemberg, Germany; and P. Knippertz
489966.abstract: Synoptic‐ to planetary‐scale atmospheric variability in the tropics is a potential source of predictability worldwide. However, current weather prediction models struggle to fully capture this variability. Here, we conduct tropical aquachannel simulations using the ICOsahedral Nonhydrostatic model with horizontal grid spacings of 13 and 5 km, and different representations of deep and shallow convection. The channel is confined between 30°N and 30°S with zonally symmetric sea surface temperatures prescribed. All aquachannel runs exhibit prominent Kelvin wave (KW) activity. The 13‐km run with parameterized deep and shallow convection is characterized by KWs with propagation speeds varying between 15 and 27 m s−1. Only this run, the background flow of which markedly differs from the others, produces a slowly eastward‐propagating disturbance (SED) that resembles the Madden‐Julian Oscillation with off‐equatorial Rossby gyres. The other aquachannel runs exhibit wavenumber‐one KWs with an almost constant propagation speed of 24 m s−1 superposed on quasi‐standing or slowly drifting waves with much higher zonal wavenumbers. In runs with explicit deep convection, these quasi‐standing waves are primarily controlled by the vertical advection of moist static energy, while in the 5‐km run with parameterized deep and shallow convection, cloud‐radiative effects play a bigger role. The latter are also key to maintaining the SED in the 13‐km run with parameterized deep and shallow convection. This work demonstrates that subtle changes in model configuration can shift the large‐scale atmospheric variability in the tropics between standing and propagating types of waves, which would greatly influence possible interactions with the extratropics. In addition, we use data assimilation experiments based on an ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) to demonstrate that by assimilating wind observations alone, we can reduce the errors in the representation of the Kelvin waves sufficiently to provide accurate precipitation forecasts up to several weeks. Even the SED is captured well by such an forecast ensemble.

489968.title: A New Physics-Driven Algorithm to Investigate the Impact of Binary Tropical Cyclone (TC) Interaction on the Track and Intensity Evolution of TCs in Western North Pacific and North Atlantic Basins
489968.authors: Zheng-Qin Shen, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China
489968.abstract: Accurately forecasting binary tropical cyclone (TC) interactions remains a critical challenge in operational numerical weather prediction. A major limitation is that existing identification criteria rely on empirical distance thresholds which are susceptible to large-scale environmental steering. To overcome this limitation, we propose 3D-VISCOUS, a physically constrained and objective criterion rooted in the three-dimensional baroclinic structure of TCs. Under this framework, a Dominant TC (DTC) must generate sufficient vertical wind shear (VWS) to induce a wavenumber-1 convective asymmetry in the Affected TC (ATC). Based on criterion above, the movement and intensity characteristics of identified interacting TC samples in the western North Pacific (WNP) and North Atlantic (NA) during 1981–2020 were analyzed. Attributed to the distance-dependent reversal of the net steering effect from vertical structure of DTC, the interacting TCs exhibit tendency to cyclonically approach each other within critical distance (1500-1800 km) but to anticyclonically escape beyond this distance. The critical distance was naturally highlighted without any subjective distance threshold input. DTC also suppressing rapid intensity changes of intense ATCs in both basins. In the WNP, DTC modulates the thermodynamic environment surrounding the ATC. It thereby weakens the relationship between ATC intensification and vertical wind shear (VWS) by reducing intensification under weak VWS condition. Critically, evaluations of global numerical weather prediction model forecasts show that the rotation rates of interacting TCs are systematically underestimated, highlighting the need for improved depictions of three-dimensional TC interactions. These results establish 3D-VISCOUS as a powerful diagnostic for understanding binary TC dynamics and identifying deficiencies in current tropical cyclone forecast systems.

489969.title: Redesigning for the Now: Modernizing the National Centers for Environmental Information Legacy Data Processing Software via the Industry Proving Grounds Program
489969.authors: Christina Maurin, NESDIS, Asheville, NC; and M. J. Brewer, M. J. Menne, K. Fischer, L. McBride, and J. Gahtan
489969.abstract: The demand for reliable, accessible, and actionable environmental data has become paramount for risk management and decision-making. To meet this need, NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), through the Industry Proving Grounds (IPG) program, has spent the past two years modernizing critical legacy data infrastructure and software suites. These efforts have been focused on key datasets identified by industry stakeholders as vital to their operations and decision-making. The IPG program collaborates closely with the insurance/reinsurance, retail, and architecture and engineering sectors to understand the requirements necessary to leverage NOAA’s vast archives into practical, real-time data solutions. This presentation focuses on the effort through IPG to modernize several software suites underlying foundational datasets at NCEI; including the Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) observations, Global Summary of the Month/Year (GSOM/GSOY), and the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS). A core focus of this overhaul included refactoring into modern languages, leveraging relational databases, improving long-term maintainability, and creating software that can exploit cloud tools. Examples of improvements include transitioning to Python, incorporating CI/CD deployment practices, and removing reliance on outdated file formats. The full development process will be discussed, including the identification of projects from stakeholders, right-sizing modernization for each project, the QA/QC process, and future plans for continuous cloud readiness.

489974.title: Lake-Effect Cloud Detection over the Great Lakes Using Deep Learning.
489974.authors: Jongjin Seo, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI; CIMSS, Madison, WI; and M. J. Foster and A. H. Young
489974.abstract: Lake-effect clouds (LECs) are mesoscale cloud systems that develop when cold air flows over relatively warm lake surfaces, frequently producing heavy snowfall and hazardous winter weather in the Great Lakes region. Although geostationary satellites provide continuous observations of these events, automated detection remains challenging because LECs exhibit diverse spatial morphologies and often coexist with synoptic-scale cloud systems. In this study, we develop a deep learning framework for the automated detection of lake-effect clouds using multispectral observations from the GOES-16 Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) and atmospheric variables from the ERA5 reanalysis during the 2017/18–2024/25 cold seasons. The model is trained using cloud properties, infrared brightness temperatures, visible and near-infrared radiometric observations, viewing geometry, surface-type information derived from CLAVR-x products, and atmospheric variables from ERA5. A convolutional neural network based on the ResNet architecture is designed to detect lake-effect cloud occurrence over each of the five Great Lakes. The training dataset consists of manually labeled LEC and non-LEC scenes collected during multiple cold seasons and encompasses a wide range of environmental and lake surface conditions and cloud morphologies. The proposed framework establishes a foundation for objective, automated, and scalable detection of lake-effect clouds, enabling future applications in snowfall estimation, climatological analyses, and operational hazard monitoring.

489977.title: Leveraging a Probabilistic Approach with the NWS-CDC HeatRisk Framework: Early Successes from the 2026 Heat Season
489977.authors: Paul Iniguez, Lynker @ NOAA/NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and A. Vaidyanathan, J. Lee, C. Kahler, and A. K. Reinhart
489977.abstract: HeatRisk is a tiered framework and messaging service jointly developed by the NOAA National Weather Service (NWS) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to support the mitigation of heat impacts across the contiguous United States (CONUS). As a core component of NWS Impact-based Decision Support Services, HeatRisk dynamically evaluates 7-day temperature forecasts against location-specific health-based thresholds, accounting for acclimation, duration, and humidity considerations, to assess potential local heat-health impacts. Recognizing that emergency managers, health officials, industry partners, and meteorologists require nuanced, non-binary data for complex decision-making, the NWS has made probabilistic information a central focus of its messaging. The NWS Weather Prediction Center (WPC) introduced probabilistic HeatRisk for Summer 2026. This leverages 10-day ensemble temperature forecasts to provide advanced, probability-driven insights that allow decision-makers to better anticipate and communicate varying levels of heat severity. This presentation will detail the expanding uses and recent successes of HeatRisk, highlighting two key events: the early-season heat across the Southwest CONUS in March 2026, and the severe heat wave across the eastern CONUS in late June and early July 2026. Furthermore, the presentation will summarize the probabilistic HeatRisk tool's performance during its inaugural heat season, ongoing validation efforts, and potential next steps for establishing HeatRisk as the premier heat messaging tool for situational awareness and emergency preparedness. Disclaimer: The findings and conclusions in this abstract have not been formally disseminated by NOAA/the National Weather Service or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and should not be construed to represent any agency determination or policy.

489985.title: Call It What It Is: How AccuWeather's Tropical Rainstorm Classification Supports a Weather-Ready Nation by Better Communicating Impacts from Tropical Systems
489985.authors: Daniel DePodwin, AccuWeather, Inc., State College, PA
489985.abstract: Tropical storms and hurricanes cause billions of dollars in damage and create devastating impacts not only near the point of landfall but hundreds of miles inland. Building a Weather-Ready Nation requires that every link in the forecast and warning chain — from forecast to communication to public response — functions without gaps. Standard naming conventions such as tropical depression, tropical storm and hurricane have served the meteorological community for many years, but in some cases leave critical communication gaps, particularly for systems that have lost wind intensity but remain capable of causing catastrophic flooding and other significant impacts. Closing those gaps is essential to keeping communities prepared and resilient. For decades, AccuWeather has refined the science and art of communicating weather to people in ways that drive action and build community resilience. This includes developing revolutionary techniques, tools and classifications — among them the AccuWeather RealImpact™ Scale for Hurricanes and the Tropical Rainstorm (and its companion Tropical Wind and Rainstorm) designation. Together, these tools support the Weather-Ready Nation mission by ensuring that life-safety messaging remains continuous, clear, and impact-focused throughout a storm's entire lifecycle. The Tropical Rainstorm designation is an impact-focused term that better describes systems that do not meet other naming criteria such as tropical storm, yet still pose serious threats to lives and property. AccuWeather applies the designation across scenarios where a trackable tropical entity can bring heavy rain and flooding risk (or Tropical Wind and Rainstorm when significant wind gusts are also a threat). It applies to certain tropical waves that may cause impacts, National Hurricane Center (NHC)-designated "invests," Potential Tropical Cyclones, and post-landfall situations where a storm still poses significant risks but is no longer officially a tropical storm or tropical depression. This proactive approach enables earlier, more actionable communication well in advance of any official designation. A defining strength of the Tropical Rainstorm framework is its commitment to tracking systems as long as they remain a hazardous, trackable feature over land — even deep into the interior of the continent. Inland flooding is among the leading causes of weather-related fatalities in the United States, and sustained, recognizable communication of that threat is central to community preparedness. The case of Hurricane Ida illustrates this principle powerfully. After making landfall in Louisiana on August 29, 2021, Ida continued to be tracked and communicated by AccuWeather as a Tropical Rainstorm as it moved through the mid-Atlantic states three days later. Instead of referring to the system as "remnants of Ida" — language that can inadvertently signal reduced risk — AccuWeather's more specific and actionable Tropical Rainstorm label and associated messaging conveying "life-threatening flooding" appropriately communicated the risk to lives and property. The storm caused the most severe flash flooding in New York City's modern history and spawned numerous EF-1 and EF-2 tornadoes. Without a persistent, recognizable designation to anchor public and client communication, this inland surge of tropical moisture might have been significantly underestimated or prematurely dismissed. This presentation will examine the Tropical Rainstorm designation as a model for impacts-based communication. By anchoring communication around what a storm will do — rather than using terms that may understate the ongoing hazard — AccuWeather's approach provides a continuous, understandable, and actionable narrative that supports better decision-making, greater public preparedness, and ultimately, the preservation of life and property. Strengthening the connection between forecast science and community-level readiness is the shared mission of our broader meteorological community, and the Tropical Rainstorm framework represents a meaningful step in that direction.

489988.title: Measuring Vertical Profile of Sea Spray Aerosol Plumes and Dry Deposition Using a Controlled Wave Pool
489988.authors: Alexander J Johnson, Precise Systems, Lexington Park, MD; NRL, Washington D.C., DC; and R. J. Santucci, I. Savelyev, and M. C. Brinckerhoff
489988.abstract: Breaking of waves, bubble bursting, and interactions between the land-sea interface are some of the major pathways that emit sea spray aerosol. Major chemical constituents in sea spray aerosol such as chloride are important for climate processes and biogeochemical cycling. Sea-spray aerosol will also travel from the shore and deposit to surfaces by dry deposition. These aerosols are corrosive and will degrade materials over time. Investigations of the dry deposition of sea spray aerosol are limited, and therefore an improved understanding of dry deposition of sea spray aerosol could aid in predicting corrosion. The height at which sea spray aerosols deposit could influence corrosion but also other environmental processes. Additionally, there is not much work done to measure the height of a sea spray aerosol plume. Therefore, the goal of this work was to characterize dry deposition, airborne concentration, and particle mass size ranges of sea spray aerosol with height in a controlled setting that mimics the land-sea interface. Experiments were conducted at the Naval Research Laboratory’s littoral bay located in the Laboratory for Autonomous Systems Research. The littoral bay was equipped with wave actuators for controlled wave crashing to generate sea spray. The pool was filled with instant ocean to simulate the composition of ocean water near or at full strength. A scaffolding structure was used to mount equipment for 4-to-5-day exposures. Symmetric airfoils were used for measuring dry deposition of aerosols at three heights, and a filter pack assembly was used to measure respective airborne concentrations. PurpleAir sensors were used to measure particulate matter concentrations for three size ranges at each height. These data were used to estimate dry deposition velocities of aerosols at the three heights to characterize the height of the aerosol plume.

489995.title: Turbulence-Resolving LES to Contextualize Small UAS Observations of Hurricane Boundary Layer
489995.authors: Christopher John-Mark De Loach, University of Notre Dame, South Bend, IN; and J. B. Wadler, J. J. Cione, PhD, J. A. Zhang, J. Elston, M. Z. Stachura, D. P. Stern, G. H. Bryan, and D. H. Richter
489995.abstract: Air-sea exchanges of momentum, heat, and moisture within the marine boundary layer play a critical role in regulating tropical cyclone intensity. However, direct measurements near the ocean surface remain difficult due to hazardous conditions and logistical challenges associated with traditional observing platforms. Recent efforts by NOAA’s Emerging Technologies Group to deploy small uncrewed aircraft systems (sUAS) specifically the Black Swift Technologies S0 have led to high-resolution turbulence measurements in these environments. While the measurements are novel, they are 1 dimensional and need to be contextualized. For this work we use a turbulence-resolving simulation of an intense Category 5 tropical cyclone to evaluate the diagnosis of the air-sea momentum exchange coefficient (CD) using the direct covariance method. “Virtual” sUAS sample within the simulated boundary layer, allowing the investigation of how flight location, sampling strategy, and turbulence variability influence the estimation of momentum fluxes at hurricane-force winds. Further exploration of the two main assumptions of Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory: (1) a constant flux layer; and (2) winds follow a logarithmic profile in the boundary layer. These simulated results then are used to contextualize the sUAS observations from recent hurricane seasons. This work aims to improve interpretation of current sUAS datasets and inform future observational strategies for quantifying air-sea coupling and advance the use of sUAS technology in intense hazardous marine environments.

490001.title: ATCHEM - Seasonal and Diurnal Variations of Total VOC, SO2, NOX, and BC Concentrations Along with Non-Targeted Chemical Analysis of Total Suspended Particulate Matter at a Heavy Traffic Road Intersections in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia
490001.authors: Solomon Bililign, North Carolina A&T State University, Greensboro, NC; and H. Royer, M. Fiddler, J. Surratt, A. Ayele, and T. Mamo
490001.abstract: Air pollution is the second leading environmental risk factor for premature death worldwide and is linked to multiple negative health outcomes. Addis Ababa is one of the three most polluted cities in sub-Saharan Africa. This is likely to get worse with fast urbanization and population growth. Major traffic intersections in Addis Ababa are hot spots where significant emissions are recorded, which are due to congested and slow traffic coupled with an old car fleet, busses, and trucks. This study investigated the spatiotemporal variability of equivalent black carbon (eBC), nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and total volatile organic compounds (VOC) concentrations, along with the molecular composition of organic species in total suspended particulate matter (TSPM) collected in urban Addis Ababa. The level of total VOC, SO2, NOX and eBC were monitored at major traffic intersections from January 2024 to December 2025. eBC concentrations were measured using portable MicroAeth AE51, and VOCs were measured using TSI OmniTrak smart station with VOC ppb module. NOX and SO2 were measured using the Aeroqual series 500 instrument. TSPM samples were collected on Teflon filters using a Leland Legacy sampler and analyzed by reversed-phase liquid chromatography coupled to electrospray ionization interfaced to quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (RPLC/ESI-QTOFMS) operated in the negative ion mode. We will present diurnal and seasonal variations of eBC, total VOC, NOX, and SO2. Non-targeted chemical composition of filter samples suggests a mixture of traffic and biomass burning as TSPM sources, depending on the sampling site.

490013.title: NHC Transformational Activities: Service and Products Evolution in Support of Impact Decision Support Services
490013.authors: Michael J. Brennan, National Hurricane Center, Miami, FL; and D. M. Brown, R. Berg, J. R. Rhome, and P. Santos
490013.abstract: The National Hurricane Center (NHC) is executing a comprehensive strategic transformation aligned with the National Weather Service’s (NWS) broader modernization goals. This evolution focuses on three key pillars: advancing warning frameworks, expanding probabilistic tropical cyclone Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS), and integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into core forecast and warning tools. To operationalize these goals, the NHC recently underwent a major structural reorganization. The Office of the Director now includes a Service Integration Team to support the tropical service program. The former Hurricane Specialist Unit has transitioned into a modernized Operations Division, consisting of three specialized units: the Tropical Cyclone Analysis Team (Metwatch), Tropical Cyclone Ops with forecasters in both Miami and Honolulu, and Storm Surge Ops. The expanded division allows for a dedicated IDSS desk. Concurrently, the Technology and Science Branch (TSB) has evolved into the Science and Mission Integration Division (SMID), which leads operational tool development and support, Research-to-Operations (R2O) initiatives, and IT infrastructure support. This restructuring has successfully enabled the merger of the former Central Pacific Hurricane Center (CPHC) in Honolulu with the NHC. This consolidation has driven immediate efficiencies, resulting in a unified Eastern and Central Pacific Tropical Weather Outlook, operational forecast graphics for the Guam and American Samoa Areas of Responsibility, and centralized technical support. Additionally, core tropical functions from the former Tropical Analysis and Forecast Branch (TAFB)—including the tropical weather discussion, tropical wave tracking, and expanded Dvorak classifications—have been absorbed into the Metwatch team. Furthermore, the new IDSS desk significantly expands the NHC’s capabilities across social media, FEMA and state briefings, international partnerships, and support for deployed Weather Forecast Office (WFO) Emergency Response Specialists (ERS). Looking ahead, the NHC is actively executing several transformative initiatives to meet future demands: -Product Bin Expansion: Expanding the product bin from 5 to 10 to accommodate hyperactive seasons and finalize the CPHC/NHC merger by combining the Central and Eastern Pacific basin products into a single list. -AI Model Adoption: Operationalizing advanced AI and machine learning consensus models (including NOAA's AIGFS/AIGEFS, ECMWF's AIFS, and Google DeepMind among others) and other tools (satellite based, analyses, etc), building on major operational successes from the 2025 season. -Extended Forecasts: Expanding official tropical cyclone forecasts out to 7 days, complete with accompanying text and graphical products. -Next-Generation Wind Speed Probabilities (WSP 2.0): Introducing a 1,000-member, 5-km resolution model incorporating land-surface and elevation adjustments and real time dynamical and machine learning models input to enhance probabilistic IDSS. A public experiment is slated for 2027 ahead of operational implementation currently planned for 2028. -Dissemination: Leveraging AI to introduce multi-language NHC products and exploring a new Common Alerting Protocol (CAP)-based, geocentric watch/warning dissemination paradigm. This presentation will detail these organizational shifts and provide operational examples of how the NHC is evolving to meet the challenges of modern tropical forecasting.

490019.title: Demonstrating the Unification of the Central Pacific Hurricane Center and National Hurricane Center Operations
490019.authors: Michael J. Brennan, National Hurricane Center, Miami, FL; and D. Brown
490019.abstract: A summary of a 2-year demonstration of unifying the operations of the Central Pacific Hurricane Center (CPHC) and the National Hurricane Center (NHC) will be presented. Benefits include an increase in organizational effectiveness, including a blended staff of NHC forecasters working seamlessly from Miami and Honolulu to forecast tropical cyclones across the North Atlantic and the eastern and central North Pacific basins regardless of where the system is located, increasing staff availability for high workload situations. This demonstration has resulted in a significant increase in forecaster experience, more specialized/dedicated technical support to meet the workload and decreased long-term technical complexity, service enhancements including a combined eastern and central Pacific Tropical Weather Outlook, the implementation of a storm surge watch/warning for the Hawaiian Islands, and the provision of tropical cyclone forecast graphics by NHC for WFOs Guam and American Samoa.

490021.title: Super-Resolution AMSR3 Imagery for Analyzing and Forecasting Arctic Sea Ice
490021.authors: Thomas Joseph Greenwald, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and R. Ferreira
490021.abstract: For the past 4 years, enhanced resolution (3.125 km) Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer-2 (AMSR2) 36 GHz imagery has played a crucial role in daily operations at the Alaska Sea Ice Program (ASIP) and the US National Ice Center (USNIC). It has helped fill gaps in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and visible imagery, provide decision support, and track ice movements under nearly any weather condition. USNIC users, for example, have found the enhanced imagery to be the “most consistent source of sea ice information compared to other SAR and visible sources with data outages.” This research seeks to build on this success by developing even higher resolution AMSR3 imagery (the follow-on to the AMSR2) based on deep learning (DL) models, namely SwinIR and SwinIR+ESRGAN, trained to convert original 10 km resolution AMSR2 imagery into proxy higher-resolution imagery. An essential component of producing super-resolution (1-2 km) AMSR3 imagery is high-resolution (1 km) proxy 36 GHz brightness temperature datasets for training, validating, and testing the DL models. These datasets are constructed from high-resolution (30 m) Landsat imagery in the Arctic for 2020-2022, estimates of sea ice emissivity derived from AMSR2 observations, reanalysis data, and a radiative transfer model. Comparisons of the super-resolution AMSR3 imagery to high-resolution visible and SAR imagery will be presented.

490022.title: Light Curve Complexity in Ordinary and Superbolt Lightning with Continuing Current Observed from Space
490022.authors: Michael Peterson, Georgia Tech Research Institute, Smyrna, GA
490022.abstract: Optical emissions detected by space-based sensors including NOAA’s Geostationary Lightning Mappers (GLMs) and EUMETSAT’s Lightning Imager (LI) are created by currents traversing the lightning channels that extend through electrified thunderclouds. The light curves produced by lightning are ultimately driven by the thunderstorm charge structure, including the availability of charge to the flash as it propagates through the surrounding clouds. Cloud-to-Ground (CG) strokes with Continuing Current (CC) are observed by these sensors as sustained optical emissions following and co-located with the CG stroke, which include notable contributions from in-cloud currents during the long-lasting discharge. Particularly large and complex flashes – including megaflashes spanning hundreds of kilometers – produce long and often growing spans of illuminated channel during the CC phase. Channels extending into new pools of charge introduces complex behavior into the light curves from CC lightning that amplifies the background drop in channel luminosity. The full GLM record and recent LI observations are leveraged to quantify the diversity of CC waveforms and to identify where, when, how often, and in what contexts optical pulses embedded in CC arise. Particular attention is placed on variations in light curve behavior as a function of optical intensity up to the superbolt scale. Supported by the LDRD Program at Sandia National Laboratories. Sandia is managed and operated by NTESS under DOE NNSA contract DE-NA0003525

490043.title: High Resolution Hurricane Forecasts with Moving Telescoping Nest for the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS)
490043.authors: William D. Ramstrom, U Miami CIMAS, Miami, FL; AOML, Miami, FL; Univ. of Miami, Miami, FL; and L. J. Gramer, A. T. Hazelton, and S. Gopalakrishnan
490043.abstract: High resolution for hurricane modeling is critical to intensity forecasting and accurately capturing storm structure. Storm-following nesting allows us to achieve the necessary resolution to adequately capture important dynamics and structures in hurricanes, while also maintaining computational efficiency with coarser resolution for the large-scale steering flow. The Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) model has been running for several years with configurations based on storm-following nests at 1.8 - 2 km resolution. We are implementing moving telescoping nests in HAFS to allow two or more levels of storm-following nests. This will provide the capability for operational and research configurations at a variety of resolutions. Researchers will have the opportunity to run forecasts with sub-km scale inner nests. Operational configurations will be flexible to align with the compute availability and elapsed time requirements. The use of scale-aware physics schemes allows the flexibility to run forecasts at a range of resolutions. We will demonstrate cases with sub-km resolution on the inner nest for intense landfalling hurricanes, using the inner nest to examine fine-scale features in the eye, eyewall, and rainbands. In addition, we will examine the forecasts of hazards at landfall from the high resolution nests.

490049.title: Absorbing Aerosol Modifies the Diurnal Cycles of Convection and Cloud Albedo on a Global Scale (Invited Presentation)
490049.authors: Ross Herbert, Institute for Climate and Atmospheric Science, Leeds, United kingdom; University of leeds, Leeds, UK, United kingdom; Univ. of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom; and P. Stier
490049.abstract: Absorbing aerosols primarily impact the Earth system by influencing the flux of radiation into and out of the atmosphere. Although the impact to large-scale environmental conditions may be resolved by current models, the subsequent modification to clouds and precipitation processes remains largely unresolved and unquantified at the global scale. In a series of cloud-resolving simulations and observational studies (ending with a global convection-resolved simulation), we have isolated the role of aerosol-radiation interactions (ARI) on convective clouds in key regions influenced by wildfire smoke and dust. In all regions, the absorbing aerosol consistently modifies the diurnal cycles of convection by suppressing the onset of convection. However, the overall regional impact is sensitive to environmental conditions and the simultaneous role of aerosol-cloud interactions (ACI), with non-linear behaviour suggesting both ARI and ACI processes need to be accounted for to fully quantify the role of aerosols in the Earth system. In this presentation, we will highlight our key findings from our studies and the steps required to answer the remaining questions.

490053.title: IMERG V08: Key Changes and Early Results
490053.authors: Eric J. Nelkin, STC and NASA/GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; Science and Technology Corp, Hampton, VA; and J. Tan, G. J. Huffman, R. Joyce, and D. T. Bolvin
490053.abstract: The Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) product from the NASA–JAXA Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission provides global satellite precipitation estimates for diverse scientific research and societal applications. An international constellation of low-Earth orbit and geosynchronous orbit satellites enables IMERG to achieve a high resolution of 0.1° every half-hour globally, with three Runs at different latencies to support varied research and application needs. With IMERG V08 expected in the fall of 2026, this presentation describes key algorithm changes and provides a preview of early results. Major changes to the IMERG V08 algorithm include: (i) the use of the Goddard Profiling (GPROF) V08 product, which adopts a machine learning approach and demonstrates substantial improvement over the previous version; (ii) the adoption of a new IR precipitation algorithm; (iii) better representation of cold season precipitation to address prior underestimation; (iv) a refined calibration procedure, especially across discontinuities in the constellation record such as the GPM orbit boost; and (v) enhanced handling of different sensors to flexibly accommodate their anticipated levels of quality. Collectively, these advances are expected to improve the skill of IMERG estimates, address several known deficiencies in V07, ensure greater consistency across the entire data record, and expand IMERG’s capability to use shorter-lived small satellites. As IMERG V08 is currently planned to be the final major upgrade before the end of the GPM mission, these improvements position IMERG to continue delivering high-quality precipitation estimates to the scientific community for research and application endeavors.

490054.title: A Radar-Only Machine Learning Algorithm for Polarimetric Tornado Detection and Path Generation
490054.abstract: The accurate detection of tornadoes, especially weaker tornadoes with more ambiguous radar signatures, is important to both National Weather Service (NWS) warning operations and post-event damage assessment. We present a novel radar-only machine learning polarimetric tornado detection algorithm that integrates radar-based tornado detections into coherent tornado-path estimates with strength estimates trained against NWS damage surveys. This algorithm is designed to estimate the probability of a tornado on any given scan and estimate its strength using only radar-derived inputs. Models are trained against polarimetric WSR-88D radar data, and strength estimates are trained against high-quality NWS damage surveys for tornadoes ranging from EF0 to EF5. Independent validation of the object-based detection yields F1 scores, intersection-over-union values, and recall all exceeding 0.75. In addition to the machine learning algorithm, biases due to storm tilt and radar range are addressed through a separate correction, improving the consistency of the derived path location at the surface. This approach has been tested in real-time workflows and demonstrated potential as a post-event tool to guide damage surveys, especially in areas with limited access or incomplete ground verification. This work highlights the value of radar-only machine-learning methods for tornado probability estimation, path generation, and future survey-support applications.

490055.title: AIGEA: An AI-Enabled Global Ionospheric Forecasting and GNSS Risk Assessment Platform
490055.authors: Jakir Hossen, Earthwise System Solutions, LLC, Columbia, MD
490055.abstract: Accurate forecasting of ionospheric disturbances is essential for improving the resilience of Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-dependent applications, including positioning, navigation, timing, aviation, precision agriculture, and autonomous systems. Earthwise System Solutions has developed the Artificial Intelligence for GNSS Environmental Awareness (AIGEA) platform to generate 2–24-hour forecasts of global ionospheric conditions and corresponding GNSS operational risk. The AIGEA platform integrates global gridded Vertical Total Electron Content (VTEC) observations with selected geomagnetic and solar-wind measurements using an internally developed spatiotemporal AI framework. This integrated approach characterizes evolving ionospheric conditions and their external forcing while supporting consistent global forecasting. The internally developed framework generates 2–24-hour forecasts while representing the spatial and temporal evolution of ionospheric disturbances. Forecast performance is assessed using withheld observations and independent quiet- and disturbed-period cases, with standard verification metrics and baseline comparisons used to quantify forecast skill. In addition to forecasting ionospheric conditions, AIGEA translates its outputs into global GNSS operational risk maps using a proprietary risk-assessment methodology. These products identify regions where disturbed ionospheric conditions may degrade GNSS positioning, navigation, and timing performance, providing actionable situational awareness for operational users. Preliminary evaluation on an independent test dataset indicates promising forecast performance during both quiet and disturbed conditions. The derived GNSS risk products further demonstrate the potential of AI-enabled forecasting to support operational decision-making during both quiet and disturbed space weather conditions. Ongoing work is focused on evaluating additional observation sources to improve forecast accuracy, robustness, and operational utility.

490057.title: NCAR’s Integrated Surface Flux System (ISFS): A 40+ Year History of Advancing Observational Boundary Layer Research.
490057.authors: Chris Roden, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. W. Hoch, S. Oncley, J. C. Witte, A. Edwards, G. Granger, I. Suhr, M. Sears, T. Hock, and J. Hicks
490057.abstract: NCAR’s Integrated Surface Flux System (ISFS) has been conducting atmospheric boundary layer research for over 40 years. This research spans a wide spectrum of disciplines, from fundamental turbulence to surface energy balance to basic meteorology. ISFS has been deployed across numerous countries, and has participated in over 40 field campaigns. These campaign datasets remain accessible today for deep data dives and further study. In this presentation, we outline the scope and breadth of our historical research, highlight our current capabilities, and review the extensive datasets available in our field project archive. We will demonstrate how these existing data can be leveraged to better understand boundary layer phenomena and provide foundational context for new field projects. Lastly, we will provide an overview of the ISFS sensor suite, measurement capabilities, and data systems, while highlighting upcoming technical improvements and strategic directions for the facility.

490062.title: Beyond One-Size-Fits-All: Understanding Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Experiences with Weather Warning Communications in the Southeastern U.S.
490062.authors: Chongming Wang, Jacksonville State University, Jacksonville, AL
490062.abstract: People who are deaf and/or hard-of-hearing (D/HOH) require specific adaptations for emergency communications to be effective, understandable, and actionable. Despite an extensive body of research on public alert and warning, knowledge of how to best communicate with and plan for this population during weather-related emergencies remains largely lacking. The growing number of individuals with access and functional needs combined with the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events has heightened the need to reassess one-size-fits-all warning and messaging standards, and to explore how national warning frameworks can be more responsive to the lived realities of the D/HOH community. This study draws on a multi-stage mixed-methods design and directly engages D/HOH individuals at risk from tornadoes and hurricanes in the Southeastern U.S. to examine their lived experiences with accessing and understanding weather warnings and safety information, while inviting perspectives from core warning partners in weather services and emergency management to identify key progress, challenges, and opportunities for sharing critical information with this community during weather-related emergencies. Both qualitative and quantitative findings illuminate how current standardized warning practices have insufficiently addressed the communication and cultural contexts of the D/HOH population, leaving them at a distinct disadvantage during life-threatening situations.
