This research not only adds to a sparse body of literature on D/HOH emergency communication access and weather readiness by revealing the scope and magnitude of gaps in current warning practices with this group, but also surfaces strategies and pathways toward more tailored messaging that better aligns with D/HOH communication needs and preferences. Achieving the vision of a Weather-Ready Nation requires deliberate efforts to promote accessible and effective emergency communications for this underrepresented and underserved group. The D/HOH population deserves the same opportunity as everyone else to respond to weather-related emergencies and to embrace a safer future.

490063.title: Multiscale WRF-TEB Modeling for Urban Microclimates and Infrastructure Resilience: Application to Nashville, TN
490063.authors: Shamik NMN Bhattacharya, The Bredesen Center for Interdisciplinary Research and Graduate Education and ORNL, Knoxville, TN; and M. Pan and M. O. Rodgers
490063.abstract: Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models and emerging AI-driven weather models present distinct trade-offs in computational efficiency and physical detail when evaluating hazards affecting critical infrastructure. This study establishes a comparative framework between traditional physics-based NWP and deep-learning-based forecasting systems over the urban Nashville domain, with a focus on key transportation hazards, including icing, hail, severe storms, and wildfire. The framework incorporates two core components: the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to represent high-resolution, physics-based dynamics, and NVIDIA’s Earth2Studio Python library to evaluate GPU-accelerated, AI-driven global forecasts. WRF provides the high-resolution regional physics necessary to directly resolve severe weather and icing mechanisms, supplemented by HAILCAST for diagnostic hail sizing and WRF-SFIRE for coupled fire-atmosphere interactions. To accurately capture urban microclimatic influences within the target region, WRF is further coupled with the Town Energy Balance (TEB) urban canopy model, accounting for building geometry, reduced street-canyon solar access, and anthropogenic heat flux from transportation and building operations. In contrast, Earth2Studio utilizes pre-trained deep learning models initialized with ERA5 hourly reanalysis data or GFS data to generate rapid global forecasts without direct numerical integration, thereby establishing a baseline for benchmarking computational speed against physical accuracy. This work presents the design, initial implementation, and preliminary performance evaluation of this comparative framework over the Nashville urban corridor, highlighting key trade-offs between physical fidelity and computational efficiency. Ultimately, this framework supports broader project goals to evaluate electric grid resilience by simulating a 2-day extreme winter storm and localized wildfire impacts on substations, thereby assessing cascading power disruptions and socioeconomic losses.

490073.title: The GOES FCDR: Production, Analysis and Availability of the GOES 8-15 Imager Fundamental Climate Data Record
490073.authors: Kenneth R. Knapp, Knapp WeatherSat Services LLC, Asheville, NC; and A. Malik, J. L. Matthews, Y. Rao, A. Heidinger, J. Robaidek, D. Santek, and V. John
490073.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is developing a Fundamental Climate Data Record (FCDR) from the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) series, covering GOES 8 through 15 (spanning 1994-2020). The product will provide well calibrated radiances, pixel-level quality flags, and improved navigation in a standard format that is consistent with ABI data products and useful to satellite data users. Each of those improvements comes from a separate line of work, described here in turn. Imager data have been quality checked using the GEO-Ring Image Anomaly Detection (GIAD), a tool from the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (EUMETSAT) that provides quality information for every pixel. Calibration is handled separately by channel. The visible calibration is complete and consistent for the period of record. The infrared calibration will use the operational calibration in beta releases, while the final release will use climate calibration adjustments derived by EUMETSAT, who are cross comparing the geostationary infrared channels against a polar orbiting infrared sounder CDR as a reference. Image navigation is analyzed using the AUTONAV algorithm from the Space Science and Engineering Center (SSEC), which derives orbit and attitude adjustments from landmarks providing more accurate position data. Lastly, the irregular satellite scan schedule is regularized by stitching scans together every 30 minutes. This produces a mostly global image from different scans at regular, predictable times. Access to the record has been simplified as much as the data themselves. The entire dataset is stored in Network Common Data Form (netCDF) files, a much easier form than the raw data. It is also available as one data store in the cloud (using icechunk and zarr python packages), which further simplifies access to the record by providing one access point per channel. The netCDF structure matches that of GOES-R Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) Level 1b data, making the record consistent with modern observations. A beta version is available now, with a link to be provided in Denver. Final data will be available within the year. Future work will expand the GOES FCDR back to GOES 1-7 and possibly the Synchronous Meteorological Satellites (SMS-1 and SMS-2).

490077.title: The Northeast Coast Operational Forecast System (NECOFS): Modeling System Upgrade and Skill Assessment for Transition to the National Ocean Service
490077.authors: Wei Wu, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and L. Wang, S. Li, Q. Xu, J. Xu, L. Wang, S. Mani, E. Myers, A. Zhang, L. bloemendaa, and C. Chen
490077.abstract: The National Ocean Service (NOS) has been collaborating with the University of Massachusetts-Dartmouth on transitioning the Northeast Coast Operational Forecast System (NECOFS) to operations at NOAA. The NECOFS is a coastal ocean operational forecast system (OFS) which covers the entire US Northeast coastal ocean region, for providing the routine operational forecasts on water elevation, water currents, water temperature and salinity. The core hydrodynamic model of the NECOFS is the widely used, three-dimensional, unstructured grid Finite Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM). The NECOFS is planned to consolidate and replace the four existing NOS coastal ocean OFSs in this region: 1) the Gulf of Maine Operational Forecast System (GoMOFS), 2) the New York and New Jersey Operational Forecast System (NYOFS), 3) the Chesapeake Bay Operational Forecast System (CBOFS), and 4) the Delaware Bay Operational Forecast System (DBOFS). This presentation will provide an overview of the modeling system upgrade and skill assessment for the NECOFS transition to the NOS, highlighting: a) the model grid enhancement (model domain expansion, horizontal resolution refinement, and bathymetry and shoreline upgrade), b) the tidal model validation, and c) the hindcast model skill assessment.

490078.title: Uncertainty in Copula Methods for Hydrometeorological Processes
490078.authors: Avital Breverman, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Davis, CA; and N. Van, G. S. Karlovits, and W. Lehman
490078.abstract: Compound flooding, driven by the simultaneous occurrence of multiple flood drivers such as storm surge, heavy rainfall, and river discharge, requires multivariate frequency analysis to accurately characterize risk. Historically, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has relied on the total probability method (coincident frequency analysis) to evaluate compound flood risk. However, coincident frequency analysis has several significant limitations. First, the method requires the selection of a dominant variable, which is often ambiguous in compound flooding applications where multiple drivers contribute comparably to flood impacts. Second, the method relies on simulating numerous combinations of values from the marginal distributions, but those combinations are not generated to satisfy a specified joint exceedance probability and therefore may not represent the desired design event. Third, coincident frequency procedures do not provide a framework for quantifying uncertainty. Copula-based methods have emerged as a fundamental tool for characterizing the dependence structure between hydrometeorological variables, offering significant advantages over traditional coincident frequency analysis by explicitly modeling joint distributions through the separation of marginal behavior and dependence structure. In hydrometeorological applications, copulas enable the computation of bivariate or multivariate return periods for extreme events such as flood peaks and volumes, storm surges, and precipitation-runoff relationships. However, the application of copulas to hydrometeorological processes introduces two critical sources of uncertainty: 1) parametric uncertainty in the fitted copula parameters, which propagates from the parameter estimation process and affects the reliability of joint exceedance probability calculations and (2) sampling (Monte Carlo) uncertainty in the estimated design points, which arises from finite sample sizes and reflects the inherent variability in observed hydrometeorological data. This presentation will discuss a framework for quantification of parametric and Monte Carlo uncertainty.

490088.title: Impact of Low-Level Jets and Boundary-Layer Processes on Intra-Urban Variability of Heat and Energy Consumption
490088.authors: Julie K. Lundquist, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and D. W. Waugh, M. Sanchez-Gomez, K. J. Davis, A. LaPorte, and N. E. Prince
490088.abstract: Extreme electricity demand often occurs during persistent heat and cold events when the atmospheric boundary layer is strongly stratified. Low-level jets (LLJs), which frequently develop within the nocturnal boundary layer, can introduce strong wind shear. During summertime heat waves, such shear can generate turbulence and maintain vertical coupling at night, injecting warm air towards the surface, preventing nocturnal cooling and increasing electricity demand. In contrast, during wintertime cold air outbreaks, LLJs can coexist with a shallow, strongly stratified layer that remains dynamically decoupled from the atmosphere above promoting colder surface temperatures and increasing electricity demand. Distinguishing turbulent and decoupled LLJ regimes can improve understanding of meteorological conditions associated with extreme electricity demand and supply–demand stress. We combine Doppler lidar wind and turbulence observations from the ARM Coast–Urban–Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE) with surface meteorology and regional electricity-demand data to characterize how LLJ occurrence, wind shear and veer, and vertical velocity variance across urban, rural, and coastal environments and are related with electricity demand. We identify LLJs using the approach of Quint et al. (2025) and Bodini et al. (2026), and quantify the vertical mixing coincident with LLJ events, as seen in Figure 1 for June and July LLJs. Similar analysis will be carried out for specific major heat- and cold-wave case studies, assessing whether shear-generated turbulence penetrates from the LLJ toward the surface and whether this coupling modifies the evolution of nighttime temperature and humidity. LLJ and non-LLJ periods will be stratified by atmospheric stability, jet height, shear, directional veer, and turbulence to identify regimes in which strong winds aloft produce enhanced vertical mixing versus persistent surface decoupling. We also evaluate whether these boundary-layer regimes correspond to systematic differences in the timing and magnitude of regional electricity demand. By connecting vertically resolved boundary-layer dynamics to energy-system observations, this work will test whether LLJ occurrence and turbulent coupling provide information about extreme demand beyond conventional surface-temperature metrics. The results could identify atmospheric precursors to high-impact energy events and provide physically interpretable predictors for weather-informed load.

490089.title: VIIRS I-Band LST: Algorithm Development, Validation Update and Applications
490089.authors: Yuling Liu, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and P. Yu and H. Wang
490089.abstract: The VIIRS Sensor onboard the JPSS satellites (SNPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21), provides I-band observations at a spatial resolution of 375 m, offering superior spatial detail compared to the 750 m resolution of M-band observations. This enhanced spatial resolution enables more detailed analysis and improved characterization of temperature variations at the surface level, which is critical for studying surface processes, urban heat dynamics, and extreme weather phenomena. This study proposes a two-step method for I-band Land Surface Temperature (LST) retrieval. This approach involves a single-channel LST retrieval using the brightness temperature from the VIIRS I-5 band, followed by an LST correction based on M-band split-window LST. A comprehensive simulation database was generated to support regression algorithm development, and theoretical studies were conducted to evaluate the performance of the single-channel algorithm. Results indicate suboptimal performance in moist conditions and longer paths, with precipitable water vapor over 3 cm due to insufficient compensation for atmospheric effects. The incorporation of M-band LST for correction leverages its superior ability to account for atmospheric absorption, significantly improving retrieval accuracy. The proposed algorithm was tested and compared with M-band VIIRS LST products. Preliminary validation was performed using ground observations from multiple radiation networks, including the Surface Radiation Budget Network (SURFRAD), the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM), the Baseline Surface Radiation Network (BSRN), and the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON). Validation results demonstrate strong agreement with ground measurements, with an overall bias of -0.14 K and RMSE of 1.60 K for SURFRAD; a bias of -0.26 K and RMSE of 1.68 K for ARM; a bias of 0.48 K and RMSE of 2.19 K for BSRN; and a bias of -0.98 K and RMSE of 1.91 K for NEON. The high resolution I-band LST was applied to monitor urban heat dynamics across seven UrbanNet stations (including DCNet sites), using data spanning June 1 to October 22, 2024. Time-series analysis across these stations successfully captured intense heatwaves during mid-June, mid-July, and early August 2024. These findings demonstrate the capability of I-band LST to resolve extreme heat events with high spatial fidelity, underscoring its potential to advance the understanding of urban heat dynamics and inform urban heat mitigation strategies.

490090.title: Risk Perception and Public Response to Winter Storm Forecasts in the New York City Metropolitan Region: A Social Media Analysis of Four 2025-2026 Storm Events
490090.authors: Rian e Murphy, SUNY, Bellport, NY
490090.abstract: Winter storms are one of the most hazardous weather phenomena impacting the Northeastern United States, yet comparatively little is known about how the public interprets and interacts with winter storm forecasts, as well as their perceptions of the risks. While previous studies have examined the role of social media in risk communication and perception, little research has focused on winter weather in the region. Using a content analysis of Reddit and Instagram, this study examines (1) whether prior experience with a high-impact snowstorm impacts perceived risk and/or preparedness messaging on social media during a subsequent winter storm and (2) how different forecast framing strategies influence public engagement and interpretation of risk and public engagement during high impact winter storms.Social media sites such as Reddit and Instagram offer insight into how the public is responding and preparing for winter storms. Reddit allows for anonymity and community discussion amongst users, allowing for candid conversation that informs the first research question. Instagram is focused on image and visual formatting that can give insight into the emphasis placed on graphics and framing strategies, giving way to the second research question. A human content analysis is conducted using Reddit discussions and Instagram posts collected through Infegy, a social listening and consumer intelligence platform for four winter storms affecting the New York tri-state region during the 2025-2026 winter season. Search queries to obtain the posts incorporated geographic location mentioning, hashtags, and weather related keywords, and storm names. Following collection, datasets were then analyzed and manually cleaned to remove unrelated content and ensure only posts related to the certain winter storm were retained. Reddit comments are coded for themes including but not limited to perceived risk, preparedness actions, trust in forecasts, and references to previous storms. Instagram posts are categorized by communication strategy (e.g. maps, graphics, videos, or text) and compared using engagement metrics such as likes, comments, and shares.Preliminary observations from Reddit suggest that discussions were less focused on snowfall totals than on impacts to daily schedules, such as work and school closures. Many users sought information on whether their children would have the day off from school, whether they would have to drive in the snow conditions, and discussed the need to go shopping and have supplies. As the storms approached there were varying levels of confidence in the forecast, particularly for the December and January storms. Given that the New York City region had not experienced significant snowfall in many years prior to this season, there was a level of skepticism on if the forecast was correct. Early observations suggest that users frequently compared forecasts to previous storms, both in years prior and in this winter season when evaluating potential impacts. Ongoing analysis will look to compare risk perceptions to each storm that occurred, as well as whether repeated exposure to winter storms alters perceptions of risk or increases references to such previous events.

490093.title: Tropical Pacific Drifter Forecast Impacts: Identifying Conditions of Maximum Benefit
490093.authors: Carolyn A. Reynolds, NRL, Monterey, CA; and R. Stone, J. D. Doyle, and M. G. Fearon
490093.abstract: In situ surface pressure observations from drifting buoys (drifters) fill critical observing gaps over the data-sparse Pacific Ocean, where satellite information is often limited by cloud cover and precipitation. We quantify the impact of tropical Pacific drifter observations on global 24-hour forecast error using the Forecast Sensitivity Observation Impact (FSOI) diagnostic within the U.S. Navy's NAVGEM global hybrid 4DVAR system from January through March 2024. Computed with a moist total energy metric, FSOI shows that tropical drifters reduce forecast error more effectively than extratropical drifters on average, although there is substantial case-to-case variability. To understand the physical drivers of these high-impact observations, we analyze two case studies in which the tropical drifters were highly beneficial in reducing global forecast error: The East-Asian Cold Surge: During a surge of cold air originating over East Asia, highly beneficial drifters were clustered northeast of the Philippines, situated at the boundary between cold, dry continental air and warm, moist maritime air. Trajectory analysis shows air parcels initiated in this area traveled southwestward toward the equator as part of the Northeast Monsoon. The MJO–Rossby Wave Interaction: Observation impacts from drifters near the equator (around 165°E) peaked as a strong Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) transitioned from the Maritime Continent to the western Pacific, interacting with a westward-propagating equatorial Rossby wave. The highly impactful drifters were located between the low-level MJO westerlies and ambient easterlies. Both cases demonstrate that observations in "dynamically active" tropical regions—defined by sharp thermodynamic or dynamic boundaries—can be very effective in reducing short-range forecast errors. These findings underscore the value of tropical Western Pacific in situ observations and support future drifter deployments to improve the Tropical Pacific Observing System (TPOS).

490095.title: Iterating to Better: Using Commercial and Partner Data to Meet NOAA Low Earth Orbit (LEO) Observation Requirements
490095.abstract: NOAA’s Low Earth Orbit (LEO) environmental satellite data are foundational to weather forecasting, enhancing our nation’s numerical weather prediction, disaster response, and environmental monitoring capabilities. In addition to NOAA satellite data, our forecasting models incorporate trusted, high-quality data and observations from national and international partners. Leveraging partner data to help meet observational requirements is strategically efficient, allowing NOAA to prioritize available resources while maintaining continuity of critical global LEO observations. Looking to the future, NOAA’s Office of LEO Observations is exploring new opportunities to take advantage of emerging and existing external capabilities, including exploring strategic partnerships with the commercial industry and using non-traditional acquisition authorities to expedite space acquisitions. This strategy shifts towards a “Buy and Partner Where We Can, Build What We Must” framework, drawing on knowledge from legacy satellite systems like the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) to architect a resilient, next-generation constellation of LEO weather satellites delivering observations not otherwise available through data buys or data sharing agreements. Through its Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) program, NOAA is testing different elements of this model using demonstration projects - such as the QuickSounder satellite mission - that will inform the NEON program’s objective to launch small- to medium-sized satellites with Earth-observing instruments more frequently. Using lessons learned from pilot projects and partner missions, the NEON program will incorporate new technologies, instruments, and processes to improve NOAA’s data products and services. Achieving these mission objectives requires an iterative, evidence-based approach centered on robust user engagements. Ultimately, the “buy, partner, build” model will make NOAA better at what it does best: producing reliable, accurate forecasts and models that can save lives and protect key economic sectors.

490096.title: Future Projections of Michigan Lake-Land Temperature Contrasts and their Role in Moisture Convergence in the Great Lakes Region
490096.authors: Abby Lynn Hutson, Cooperative Institute for Great Lakes Research (CIGLR), South Lyon, MI; and A. Bartlett, A. Raudzens Bailey, and J. M. Keeler
490096.abstract: In the Great Lakes Region, the lake-land-atmosphere interactions are unique and complex and can play a substantial role in precipitation processes. Contrasting lake-land temperatures modulate local atmospheric stability depending on the season. In the cold season, relatively warm lake temperatures enhance precipitation over the lake, which then travels inland. Conversely in the warm season, relatively cool lake temperatures can suppress large-scale precipitation over the lakes, but they can enhance over-land precipitation through the lake-breeze circulation or moistening of the boundary layer. While the Great Lakes do provide a large source of moisture for the region, the moisture that contributes to large-scale precipitation processes in the Great Lakes Region mainly originates from far-away locations. However, the future of regional lake-land temperature contrasts may be changing, and regional moisture sources might begin to play a new and important role in the future Great Lakes climate. In this study, we investigate whether lake-land temperature contrasts are projected to change, and if those changes play a role in moisture availability for precipitation in the Great Lakes Region. To do this, we use historical and future projections from the Great Lakes Weather Research and Forecasting model (GL-WRF), which models the regional climate at a 10 km resolution forced by a pseudo-global-warming dataset. The GL-WRF uses a 1-dimensional lake model to predict lake-surface temperatures, therefore accounting for lake dynamics when projecting future temperature contrasts. We use the model to characterize future climate trends in local moisture fluxes (including evaporation from the lakes and land surfaces), trends in moisture fluxes from remote upstream sources, and whether the temperature differences between over-land air and over-lake air will change with the climate trends.

490097.title: Quantifying Hurricane Turbulence Using IWRAP and NOAA TDR Radar Data
490097.authors: Aaliyah Nicole Perez, Hampton University, Woodbridge, VA; Hampton University, Hampton, VA; and S. R. Guimond
490097.abstract: Turbulence plays a crucial role in hurricane boundary layer (HBL) dynamics as it regulates the transfer of momentum, moisture, and heat that ultimately affect the evolution of winds in the eyewall and intensify the storm system. Research on the role of organized turbulent structures in the HBL remains insufficient due to the lack of high-resolution observations and dynamic nature of the hurricane’s lowest levels at 0 – 2 km. This project aims to quantify and understand coherent turbulent structures in the HBL by comparing legacy, coarse resolution NOAA Tail Doppler Radar (TDR) data (sampling of 1500 m) with the novel, high resolution Imaging Wind and Rain Airborne Profiler (IWRAP) data (sampling of 125 m) for Hurricane Teddy and Hurricane Laura (2020) in mature and intensifying stages. Additionally, the work aims to provide valuable research results on extreme winds in the HBL to operational disciplines across sectors. This presentation will highlight comparisons of the velocity components calculated from each radar at nadir to characterize regions of coherent turbulent structures identified in the IWRAP data, and their connection to the larger-scale structure observed by the TDR. Supplemental comparisons such as the capabilities of the radars will be visually shown with the plotted velocity components to highlight their respective strengths and limitations as well. Once the comparisons are made, statistics will be presented and analyzed to assess their value for operational and scientific contexts in past and future hurricane seasons. These statistics will include maximum wind speed differences, location of the maximum winds, inflow depth, and difference in energy spectra, among other computations.

490108.title: Impact of Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder Data Assimilation on Tropical Cyclone Prediction in Regional MPAS-JEDI
490108.authors: Hsiao-Chun Lin, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and Z. Liu, I. Hernandez Banos, T. G. Lopes, D. A. Ahijevych, J. A. Mantovani Jr., J. J. Braun, and J. P. Weiss
490108.abstract: This study evaluates the forecast impact of assimilating clear-sky and all-sky brightness temperature observations from the Tomorrow.io microwave sounder (TMS) constellation within a regional numerical weather prediction model. These efforts are part of the evaluations supported by NOAA NESDIS Commercial Data Program Microwave Sounder Data Pilot. We employ a regional dual-resolution (4km-12km) hybrid 3D-Ensemble-Variational (hybrid-3DEnVar) data assimilation (DA) system based on the Model for Prediction Across Scales-Atmosphere (MPAS-A), coupled with the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework (MPAS-JEDI). Three DA experiments are conducted: a benchmark experiment, a TMS-Clear experiment that assimilates the clear-sky TMS observations, and a TMS-All experiment that assimilates all-sky TMS observations. Using Hurricane Melissa (2025) and Typhoon Bavi (2026) as case studies, this investigation assesses the assimilation of TMS data in tropical cyclone prediction. The goals of this research are twofold: first, to determine the specific forecast impact of incorporating both clear-sky and all-sky TMS radiance measurements; and second, to analyze their subsequent effects on the accuracy of tropical cyclone track and intensity forecasts.

490109.title: Value of Early Satellite- Based Fire Detection
490109.authors: Shelby Weder Loya, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and L. Batty, T. T. Lindley, M. Fox, A. Anderson, S. Curl, D. Speheger, D. Daily, and C. Mask
490109.abstract: This paper builds on a joint NWS-Oklahoma Forestry Services (OFS) pilot project aimed to estimate the efficacy of rapid satellite-based fire detection and response in which AI- assisted detections from the Next Generation Fire System (NGFS) and raw GOES data from NWS meteorologists were analyzed for several 2025 fires. Initial analysis showed that 83% of NGFS detections were identified within one minute of manual notifications issued by meteorologists, although 32% of fires identified by meteorologists were not reported by NGFS. Whether initially identified via human or NGFS, hot spot notifications detailing the geocoordinates and proximity weather conditions for emerging wildfires informed real-time OFS-generated fire spread modeling. For fires detected via satellite prior to local dispatch, post-containment fire perimeters were compared to the model projections of unsuppressed fire spread. Post-suppression burn areas averaged 61% smaller than model projections for the evaluated wildfires. Within these perimeters are structures and land used for crops and cattle grazing. Building on work previously done by the Norman, OK weather forecast office, we create a fire suppression timing model to estimate the number of at-risk structures that were not burned due to early warning, the value of those structures, and acres saved, including crop and grazing area. We then use this model to estimate the value of early satellite-based fire detection for specified historical fires.

490113.title: Applying Graph Theoretic Observation Thinning for MW and IR Satellite Radiances
490113.authors: William F. Campbell, NRL, Monterey, CA
490113.abstract: The Earth observing system is rapidly changing, with an ever increasing volume of satellite data, which can be problematic for a real-time NWP system. Most global NWP centers average (superob) observations and/or discard (thin) a large percentage of them. Although data volume is a concern, the primary reason for drastic thinning is to compensate for undiagnosed spatially correlated error, which is very difficult to account for properly. We want to ensure that two profiles from the same satellite and instrument have a certain minimum horizontal spacing to mitigate the effect of that error. An adaptable methodology using graph theory is presented to address all of these concerns in a timely fashion, and show experiments comparing the performance of traditional data thinning versus the new approach on a set of infrared and microwave satellite data typically ingested by a research version of the Navy’s global NWP model NAVGEM. This method is not restricted to satellite radiances, and is equally applicable to past, current, and future instruments. Note also that the approach is model-agnostic, equally applicable to models from other centers as well as future Navy models. We plan to present results from global cycling data assimilation runs for both microwave (MW) and infrared (IR) satellite radiances using standard thinning at baseline resolution, graph thinning at that same (uniform) resolution, and graph thinning at higher average resolution.

490123.title: A GOES-R Era Probabilistic Framework for Characterizing Dust Emission Thresholds Across Ecologically Distinct Source Regions of the Contiguous United States
490123.authors: Connor H Welch, University of Alabama in Huntsville / NASA SPoRT, Huntsville, AL; and E. B. Berndt
490123.abstract: Windblown dust is an underappreciated yet increasingly consequential atmospheric hazard across the contiguous United States (CONUS), with dust storm frequency rising in recent decades due to agricultural expansion, land degradation, and climate-driven drying. Despite this growing threat, the critical surface state and atmospheric conditions governing dust emission onset have never been systematically characterized from real-world observations at the continental scale. Current dust emission schemes rely on threshold friction velocity formulations derived from a combination of wind tunnel experiments, theoretical derivations, and empirical formulations, yet the degree to which these relationships accurately represent synoptic-scale emission events across the ecologically diverse land surfaces of the CONUS remains largely untested against real-world continental-scale observations. This ongoing work addresses this gap through an integrated observational framework applied to GOES-R era imagery spanning 2018–2026. Dust storm events are detected continuously across the full CONUS domain using DustTracker-AI, a Random Forest classifier achieving an area under the ROC curve of 0.97, providing reliable dust identification across the full diurnal cycle. Detected dust features are tracked using the TOBAC object-based framework, and emission source regions are attributed via HYSPLIT back-trajectory analysis forced with High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) archive fields. Collocated surface state and atmospheric variables — including friction velocity, soil moisture, vegetation cover, low-level lapse rate, and soil texture — are extracted from the HRRR archive at each identified source point and analyzed using a probabilistic threshold framework stratified by EPA ecoregion. The resulting probability-of-emission curves are used to derive observationally grounded effective emission thresholds, which are compared against threshold friction velocity formulations from operational dust emission schemes to assess where current implementations agree with or systematically depart from real-world emission behavior across ecologically distinct CONUS source regions. Early results from the detection and tracking workflow, dataset, and initial thresholding analysis will be presented. This work provides a foundation for the first ecoregion-stratified, observationally grounded dust emission threshold dataset for the CONUS, with direct implications for improving operational dust storm forecasting.

490128.title: Withdrawn: Regional and Point Source Methane Emissions from HALO and MethaneAIR in the Marcellus and DC/Baltimore Regions from the APMAC Campaign
490128.authors: Rory A. Barton-Grimley, NASA Langley Research Center, Hampton, VA; and A. Yerasi, J. Collins, A. R. Nehrir, J. Pittman, M. Sargent, J. Franklin, J. Bushey, and S. Wofsy
490128.abstract: Routine observations of methane over a range of spatial and temporal scales have been identified as important to constrain emissions and their drivers. Remote sensing provides a path to provide large area regional coverage with the sensitivity to separate background methane from point sources. To provide these data sets the NASA Langley High-Altitude Lidar Observatory (HALO), a combined methane integrated path differential absorption lidar and aerosol/cloud high spectral resolution lidar, and the MethaneAIR imaging spectrometer were flown on the NASA GIII research aircraft during the summer of 2025 for the Appalachian Active Passive Methane Airborne Constraints (APMAC) campaign. APMAC was flown in conjunction with the broader MAGEQ campaign to allow for the interpretation of remotely sensed XCH4 to discrete measurements in key source regions within the planetary boundary layer (PBL). As HALO and MethaneAIR have similar measurement sensitives, APMAC served as a first opportunity to evaluate and demonstrate the synergy of active/passive XCH4 retrievals and to observe XCH4 diurnally over different geographic regions. Repeat flights over the Northeast Marcellus, Southwest Marcellus, and the DC/Baltimore regions provided a comprehensive evaluation of the point source and regional emissions. For each region, several datasets were collected during repeated raster patterns, morning-afternoon-night, which were then repeated on the next day. Both instruments observed similar point source emission rates and broader changes in background methane over the surveyed domains. The diurnal changes were evaluated with both instruments collecting measurements during the daytime and HALO providing the nighttime measurements. We will discuss findings from these multi-hour/multi-day flights for point source and regional background estimation, the impact of methane estimation error due to meteorological variable uncertainty, specifically wind direction and PBL height, and the limitations that arise from differences in the weighting functions, sampling, and emission estimation methods between instruments.

490129.title: The Vigil Compact Coronagraph (CCOR-3)
490129.authors: Damien Chua, NRL, Washington, DC; and A. Thernisien, M. Carter, M. Noya, N. Rich, T. Babich, C. Crippa, J. Verzosa, D. Boyer, R. Hagood, S. Brown, M. Newman, and G. Wiggins
490129.abstract: The Compact Coronagraph (CCOR) is a novel white-light solar coronal imager built by the US Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) on behalf of the National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to provide operational space weather observations. The first CCOR launched on the GOES-East spacecraft to geosynchronous orbit on June 25, 2024. The second CCOR (CCOR-2) launched on the Space Weather Follow-On Lagrange 1 (SWFO-L1) spacecraft on September 24, 2025. In this paper, we describe the design and operations concept of the third CCOR instrument, CCOR-3. CCOR-3 is one of the remote sensing payloads on the European Space Agency (ESA) Vigil space weather monitoring mission. The Vigil spacecraft will operate at the fifth Sun-Earth Lagrange point, L5, and will allow CCOR-3 to observe the emergence of solar eruptions such as coronal mass ejections (CMEs) from a unique vantage point off the Sun-Earth line. CCOR-3 images will be used by ESA and NOAA space weather forecasters to estimate CME speed, trajectory and mass. These parameters are inputs to physics-based, heliospheric forecast models used by space weather forecasters to predict the arrival of coronal mass ejections at earth and the onset of the resulting geomagnetic storms. The CCOR-3 project is sponsored by NOAA.

490147.title: The Coronal Brightness Index: CBI, CMEs, and GLEs
490147.abstract: The publication, “The Relationship Between the Kinematics of Coronal Mass Ejections and the Brightness of the Corona” demonstrated that above a certain level of coronal brightness, the likelihood of a high-velocity CME significantly decreases. This data has allowed us to consider the question of whether coronal brightness affects, or is at least related to, the eruptiveness of flaring active regions and the velocity of any resulting CMEs. Now, we are moving that analysis into the realm of SEP and GLE events. Preliminary subsequent analysis suggests that SEP and GLE events also occur below a certain brightness threshold. This presentation discusses the expansion of CBI analysis to particle events and the path to real-time analysis with other coronagraphs such as COR2A and CCOR-1 and 2. This research is supported by the Office of Naval Research.

490154.title: Quantifying Storm-Driven Sea Ice Dynamics in the Arctic Marginal Ice Zone: Perspectives from a Decade of Wintertime Satellite Observations
490154.authors: Joseph Robinson, NRL, Washington, DC; and C. Selman, J. D. Ouellette, and E. M. Twarog
490154.abstract: Arctic cyclones sit at the intersection of thermodynamic and dynamic processes that shape the marginal ice zone (MIZ), with their extensive cloud cover modulating the surface energy budget and strong surface winds driving ice transport and deformation. Understanding these interactions is critical for the U.S. Navy and maritime operators navigating a complex and unpredictable Arctic. While previous studies on cyclone-ice interactions have relied heavily on numerical models, in this work we combine L-band satellite sea ice thickness from the Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity (SMOS) mission with Polar Pathfinder ice motion data to isolate and derive dynamic sea ice changes. We analyze a decade of wintertime Arctic MIZ-impacting storms (2013-2022) by compositing observations from over 1,000 daily cyclone positions. The dynamic response of the sea ice is examined by comparing conditions from the days immediately prior to and following storm passage. The SMOS composite observations reveal clear day-over-day MIZ responses, with substantial thickness reductions to the east of storm centers and corresponding thickness increases to the west. Concurrently, ERA5 reanalysis winds exhibit strong cyclonic motion, which aligns with pronounced observed ice motion. The coupled signature of observed thickness and ice motion yields significant ice volume fluxes, which peak in intensity to the east and northwest of storm centers. Synthesizing across the composite observations and derived quantities, we will isolate and present the dynamic component of the sea ice thickness change, highlighting sectors of storms and the broader Arctic where dynamics dominate the observed mass redistribution. We will also assess how the dynamic response depends on both meteorological drivers and the initial, pre-storm state of the sea ice, thereby identifying the strongest predictors of the observed MIZ response. Finally, to bridge observations and operations, we will leverage the observed physical relationships to evaluate U.S. Navy operational model skill across select storm case studies.

490158.title: Multidecadal Trends and Interannual Variability of Dust Events in the Tropical North Atlantic
490158.authors: Yingxi Rona Shi, University Maryland Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD; Univ. of Maryland Baltimore County, Silver Spring, MD; and L. Remer, H. Yu, T. Westberry, M. Behrenfeld, D. Hamilton, N. Meskhidze, E. B. Masso, M. Romm, and A. R. Satheesh
490158.abstract: Dust deposition is a major pathway for delivering nutrients to the surface ocean, but the aerosol system driving this transport is undergoing observable change and is expected to continue evolving as human activity and a warming climate alter atmospheric circulation and dust source regions. Understanding how dust loading and event frequency have shifted over the past two decades is therefore essential for characterizing the atmospheric side of ocean–atmosphere nutrient exchange. In this study, we use satellite aerosol products, validated against AERONET sites in the tropical north Atlantic, to characterize decadal-scale trends in dust activity across the region, then expand the analysis to the broader tropical north Atlantic and Caribbean Sea. We focus on the interannual variability of the largest dust events recorded over two decades of satellite observations, examining two fundamental but distinct metrics: mean dust loading and the frequency of large dust events. We find significantly increasing dust loading across a broad band of the tropical north Atlantic stretching from the African coast to the Caribbean. Event frequency also shows significant increases over the Caribbean Sea and near the northwest coast of Africa, while the mid-ocean region shows no significant trend in frequency despite the rise in loading, highlighting that these two metrics do not always evolve together. In contrast, both loading and frequency decline off the southwest coast of West Africa. We also analyzed regional meteorological patterns to explain the drivers of these spatially varying trends. These results provide a detailed characterization of how dust events are changing across the region, offering a foundation for future work examining potential links to ocean biogeochemical responses.

490163.title: Development of a Physics-Guided Deep Learning Air Quality Forecasting System Over Greater Boston
490163.authors: Yiyue Yang, Northeastern University, Boston, MA; and K. Do and Y. Zhang
490163.abstract: The availability of the state of science fine-scale (≤ 1km) air quality databases is crucial for community-level environmental alerts, air pollution exposure and health impact studies, and urban plannings in metropolitan areas. An advanced 3-D air quality model, the Weather Research and Forecasting model (WRF) coupled with Chemistry and Greenhouse Gases, WRF-Chem-GHG, has been deployed over tripled-nested domains centered in Greater Boston for multi-years and comprehensively evaluated against available meteorological and chemical observations. While the physics-based model exhibits consistent performance for forecasting ground-level ozone (O3) and fine particulate matters (PM2.5) across different years, it still faces limitations such as costly computational resources, complex atmospheric processes, and systematic biases. Our previous work showed that the model persistently overpredicts PM2.5 in winter months and underpredicts PM2.5 during summers with wildfires, which can be attributed to inaccurate inputs and uncertainties in its physio-chemical representations. Current challenges have hampered the deployment of a fast, reliable, and easy-to-perform real-time air quality forecasting (RT-AQF). To overcome these bottlenecks, a convolutional neural network based deep learning (DL) algorithm, U-Net, is trained with WRF-Chem-GHG, to develop a physics-guided machine learning air quality forecasting system to reproduce and improve the forecasting performance of WRF-Chem-GHG. This DL-based model is computationally more efficient than the physics-based WRF-Chem-GHG model because it avoids the 3-D simulation of chemical and physical processes. The initial testing of the DL-based model for RT-AQF for July 2025 demonstrates performance comparable to that of WRF-Chem-GHG over Greater Boston across 12-, 3- and 1-km grid resolutions. The evaluation at a 1-km grid resolution yields normalized mean biases of -9.6% for O3 and -17.0% for PM2.5 and normalized mean errors of 15.0% for O3 and 47.3% for PM2.5 against the observations from the Air Quality System networks. Satellite and urban morphology databases are being integrated into the model training features. Additionally, a convolutional multivariate Gaussian method is being implemented in the model for bias correction. These efforts are expected to further improve the performance and robustness of the physics-guided DL-based RT-AQF system.

490164.title: Deep Integration of Scientific Knowledge and Machine Learning Through Physically-Structured Neural Networks
490164.authors: Henry W Schneiderman, Pittsburgh Data Science LLC, Pittsburgh, PA
490164.abstract: The potential for incorporating scientific knowledge into neural networks is vast, yet remains largely unexplored. Conventional machine learning typically relies on standard architectures, such as transformers, convolutional networks, or multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), where input variables are simply concatenated into a single vector. When scientific knowledge is incorporated, it is often restricted to enforcing output constraints, such as the conservation of energy or mass. Only a small body of research investigates networks that internally incorporate mathematical equations representing physical processes. This capacity to embed equations and other forms of physical knowledge can be leveraged much more extensively, building upon decades of well-established atmospheric science. Incorporating scientific knowledge is often challenging because standard neural network architectures bear little resemblance to traditional scientific models. A key insight, however, is that we can move beyond these standard neural network architectures by creating networks that follow the computational flow of the scientific models they emulate. Specifically, we structure the network to match the decomposition of a given scientific problem into distinct, physically meaningful components, such as convection, extinction, and scattering, which may be further subdivided into elements like clouds, clear sky, direct and diffuse radiation, and spectral components. The resulting network comprises a collection of modules, each representing a specific physical component, where the variables connecting these modules retain their original physical meanings. Within each module, we can strategically embed neural network elements (e.g., MLPs, residual nets) while retaining scientifically based equations elsewhere. This hybrid model is then trained as a single end-to-end network, leveraging the power of data-driven learning within a structure constrained by known physics. This approach synthesizes the strengths of scientific modeling and machine learning. We avoid burdening the neural network with rediscovering known scientific laws, and instead focus neural network capacity on learning physical relationships that are less understood and/or whose scientific models are too computationally demanding. Embedded neural network elements represent highly specific physical relationships, significantly reducing their input dimensionality compared to the entire system. This minimization reduces the risk of learning spurious correlations and maximizes learning efficiency. Furthermore, this structure mitigates the "black-box" nature of typical machine learning. Because the internal structures and variables have an assigned physical meaning, we can inspect values for plausibility, and we can selectively modify functionality to include or exclude various physical components. We demonstrate the efficacy of these physically-structured neural networks by modeling radiative transfer and convection, achieving promising results on challenging, realistic datasets.

490165.title: Evaluating Global Model Estimates of the Vertical Transport and Lightning Flash Rate at Varying Grid Resolutions
490165.authors: Mary C. Barth, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. Kumar, F. Lacey, and K. Wilson
490165.abstract: The 2012 Deep Convective Clouds and Chemistry (DC3) field campaign provides a wealth of aircraft data on atmospheric composition in the inflow and outflow regions of thunderstorms. The DC3 dataset has been used to estimate convective transport of trace gases and aerosols as well as subsequent production of ozone and new particle formation. A critical part for producing ozone in convective outflows is lightning, which was measured during DC3 with lightning mapping arrays. In this presentation, we employ the soon-to-be-released Model for Prediction Across Scales coupled with the GOCART2G aerosol model (MPAS-GOCART2G) and evaluate its ability in representing convective transport of available GOCART2G trace gases (e.g., SO2) and aerosol mass concentrations. In addition, we calculate in MPAS-A the lightning flash rate based on current methods used in global and regional-scale models. Because MPAS-A provides global grid meshes at different grid spacing, several model simulations are performed, ranging from a ~60 km uniform grid mesh to a ~15 km uniform grid mesh to a 60-3 km variable resolution grid mesh, where the 3 km region is centered between eastern Colorado and central Oklahoma. We expect this model exercise to reveal how grid resolution affects calculations of convective transport, wet scavenging, and lightning flash rate that can then be constrained to better match observations.

490169.title: Evaluating a Tabular Foundation Model for Multi-Site Solar Irradiance Nowcasting
490169.authors: Emmanuel Kipchirchir, SUNY, Albany, NY; and S. Basu
490169.abstract: Accurate short-term forecasting of surface solar irradiance is essential for photovoltaic power forecasting, grid operations, energy storage management, and the continued integration of renewable energy into modern power systems. However, forecasting solar irradiance remains challenging because of rapidly evolving cloud fields and the strong spatial and temporal variability of atmospheric conditions. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have demonstrated considerable promise for environmental prediction; however, the application of foundation models to solar irradiance nowcasting remains largely unexplored. This study evaluates the performance of Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN), a transformer-based foundation model for tabular data, for multi-site nowcasting of global horizontal irradiance (GHI) using both ground-based observations from the New York State Mesonet (NYSM) and modeled irradiance from the National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB). The proposed framework integrates physics-informed feature engineering with meteorological variables, solar geometry, temporal predictors, and historical irradiance information to generate operational short-term forecasts across multiple lead times. Model performance is compared with conventional Persistence and Smart Persistence methods, as well as gradient boosting models, using established forecast verification metrics. Additional analyses investigate seasonal variability and evaluate the consistency of model performance across diverse climatic regions and between observational and modeled datasets. The presentation will demonstrate the potential of tabular foundation models for environmental prediction and discuss their applicability to next-generation solar forecasting systems that support reliable renewable energy integration and operational decision making

490170.title: Recent Advances In Aerosol Simulations with the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM)
490170.authors: Cheng Dang, UCAR, Boulde, CO; UCAR, Boulder, CO; and B. T. Johnson, S. W. Wei, and S. Ha
490170.abstract: Aerosol particles have significant impacts across the Earth System, yet quantifying these impacts remains challenging due to their heterogeneous and fast-varying distribution and short lifetime. Data assimilation (DA) helps improve aerosol analyses and forecasts by integrating numerical model simulations with satellite observations. Historically, operational aerosol DA has primarily focused on assimilating aerosol optical depth (AOD), for which aerosol optical properties (AOPs) are needed as a critical link between modeled aerosol mass concentrations and satellite radiances. Recent satellite missions, including NASA's Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission, now provide additional aerosol products such as spectral single-scattering albedo (SSA), Ångström exponent (AE), aerosol layer height, and fine- and coarse-mode effective radii, offering new constraints on aerosol composition and size that are not captured by AOD alone. Fully exploiting these observations, however, requires observation operators capable of consistently simulating these quantities from aerosol model states. In this work, we present recent updates to the aerosol component of the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM). CRTM is a fast, multi-layer radiative transfer model widely used for numerical weather prediction, satellite calibration and validation, and Earth system applications across federal agencies and universities. It serves as the operational observation operator for satellite radiance and AOD DA in the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) and Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) systems, and is also integrated into the NSF NCAR MPAS-GOCART2G-JEDI, an online-coupled atmosphere–chemistry analysis and forecasting system. We introduce expanded aerosol lookup tables (LUTs) and new observation operator capabilities to support advanced remote sensing products for aerosols, including spectral SSA and AE, enabling data assimilation of multi-channel aerosol retrievals from PACE and other next-generation satellite missions.

490171.title: Investigating Causes of Recent Wisconsin Climate Change Using Self-Organizing Maps
490171.authors: Noah Lang, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI
490171.abstract: Anthropogenic climate change is affecting temperatures and precipitation worldwide, but with widely varying regional impacts. The U.S. Midwest has experienced significantly warming temperatures and increased precipitation since 1950. Wisconsin, located in roughly the center of the region, is representative of these trends, as every season has become warmer and wetter. This study seeks to identify the sources of these changes in Wisconsin by disentangling global-scale warming trends from regional effects caused by atmospheric circulation regimes over all seasons, particularly focusing on winter and summer. Self-organizing maps (SOMs) were utilized for this purpose, with SOMs being trained on anomalies of 500 hPa heights (for temperature) and mean sea level pressure (for precipitation) in North America from 1950 to 2024 to create a representative pair of 16 synoptic-scale circulation patterns for each season (one SOM matrix each for 500 hPa heights and sea level pressure). Through comparisons of these composite maps between the earliest decade (1950s) and the final decade (2015-2024), it was found that most of the precipitation change in Wisconsin during the past 75 years occurred due to thermodynamic forcing (wetting within individual circulation patterns), rather than from changes in the frequency of the patterns (dynamic forcing). Regarding temperature, winter warming was also mainly thermodynamically driven, while summer warming was approximately equally influenced by thermodynamic and dynamic changes. Circulation regimes contributed to warming and drying trends in both winter and summer. Analysis for spring and autumn demonstrated an increase in spring and autumn temperatures that was primarily dynamical in nature, due to large shifts in 500 hPa height pattern frequency.

490172.title: Analysis of IC Detection by a Hybrid VLF-LF Lightning Location System vs. the US NLDN
490172.authors: Ryan Said, Vaisala, Louisville, CO; and M. J. Murphy
490172.abstract: In 2026, Vaisala Xweather introduced a hybrid Very Low Frequency (VLF; <50 kHz) and Low Frequency (LF; <500 kHz) location algorithm that geolocates lightning discharges using sensor data from LF precision networks together with sensor data from the global VLF network GLD360. The hybrid approach recovers discharges that an LF network alone would miss: those detected by only a single LF sensor, and those detected by two or more LF sensors but rejected by quality control because of a large error ellipse. VLF-only solutions are also permitted and are tagged as cloud discharges. Together, these mechanisms substantially improve the detection of low-amplitude cloud (IC) pulses relative to an LF precision network operating on its own. In this presentation, we give a brief overview of the hybrid location algorithm and document the resulting gain in IC pulse and IC flash yield over CONUS when US National Lightning Detection Network (NLDN) sensors are combined with GLD360 sensors, using NLDN-alone IC pulse and flash counts as the baseline. We examine the increase in IC pulses per flash and in total flash counts, comparing the latter to total lightning optical flash data from the Geostationary Lightning Mapper aboard GOES East and GOES West. We further examine a selection of CG flashes with multiple return strokes and multiple IC pulses to assess how the hybrid capability improves IC pulse detection during preliminary breakdown and affects interstroke intervals, and whether it adds spatial mapping capability that the NLDN cannot provide on its own.

490173.title: A Statistical Characterization of Commercial Aircraft Humidity Measurement Differences Relative to Frost Point Hygrometer Observations
490173.authors: Michelle Stasik, NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and G. A. Morris and E. Asher
490173.abstract: Accurate water vapor measurements are essential for understanding atmospheric dynamics, improving weather forecasts, and quantifying Earth's radiation budget. Observations collected through the Aircraft Meteorological Data Relay (AMDAR) program provide critical in-situ measurements of relative humidity, temperature, and wind throughout the troposphere and lower stratosphere that are extensively assimilated into numerical weather prediction systems. Beyond forecasting, AMDAR observations also support studies of cloud processes by characterizing relative humidity over ice (RHi) supersaturations, which influence the formation of cirrus clouds and persistent contrails. These clouds contribute to climate forcing and remain a major source of uncertainty in global climate models. However, despite the widespread use of AMDAR observations, the accuracy and uncertainty of humidity measurements from its Water Vapor Sensing System II (WVSS-II) remain incompletely characterized against high-quality reference observations. The NOAA Frost Point Hygrometer (FPH) provides highly accurate measurements of atmospheric water vapor and serves as a gold standard reference for validating humidity observations. In this study, coincident AMDAR and FPH observations from Boulder, Colorado, are collocated in space, altitude, and time to evaluate the accuracy and precision of AMDAR water vapor measurements. Relative differences in water vapor mixing ratio are calculated for collocated observations, and the dependence of measurement agreement based upon factors such as temperature, season, and tropopause-relative altitude is investigated. A logistic regression is also applied to consider the probability of disagreement between the two observing systems at various altitudes. By providing an independent assessment of AMDAR humidity observations, this work evaluates the conditions under which aircraft-based humidity measurements can be used with high confidence. Ongoing work is extending this analysis to evaluate relative humidity over ice (RHi) agreement between AMDAR and FPH observations. Preliminary results show that AMDAR mixing ratio agreement with the FPH degrades substantially with increasing tropopause-relative altitude, with the probability of disagreement reaching 75% at approximately 2.14 km below the tropopause. This indicates a marked reduction in measurement agreement within the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). In contrast, relative measurement differences demonstrate substantially stronger agreement throughout the middle and lower troposphere. Across all collocated observations, AMDAR exhibits an average absolute bias equivalent to approximately 5.6 times the FPH’s own measurement uncertainty, while individual observations can deviate by as much as 385 times the FPH uncertainty. These findings demonstrate that although AMDAR provides valuable humidity observations throughout much of the atmosphere, measurement accuracy deteriorates significantly within the UTLS, highlighting the need to account for altitude-dependent uncertainty when interpreting aircraft-based humidity observations.

490174.title: Analyzing Extreme Precipitation Events Using NASA IMERG-derived Average Recurrence Intervals
490174.authors: Sebastian S. Harkema, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and E. B. Berndt, A. Portier, J. Tan, and G. J. Huffman
490174.abstract: The average recurrence interval (ARI) metric, traditionally used to quantify flooding severity in terms of years (e.g., a 100-year flood), has been a longstanding tool for communicating this flooding/precipitation severity. However, accurate ARI estimates require long data records, which vary significantly by location and the quality of measurement. Therefore, this study will highlight the development and validation of ARIs derived from NASA’s Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) dataset. Specifically, this study expands on the previous methodologies that used NASA’s TRMM Multi-satellite Precipitation Analysis dataset (i.e., Zhou et al. 2015 and Demirdjian et al. 2019). A continuity analysis will be performed to determine how the NASA TRMM and GPM eras potential impact the IMERG-derived ARIs. Lastly, a graphical user interface (GUI) will be developed to easily display IMERG precipitation accumulations and derived ARIs. Feel free to stop by and learn more about how NASA precipitation datasets can be used to monitor extreme precipitation events. Or if you prefer, come by and interact with (and maybe break) the GUI to examine any extreme precipitation event that occurred somewhere globally from 1998 to 2026.

490176.title: Integrating NOAA VIIRS 3D Floodwater Depth into a Web-Based Flood Damage Assessment Tool: A Multi-Event Evaluation
490176.authors: Yun-Jae Choung, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; CIROH, Univ. of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; Univ. of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and S. J. Burian, D. R. Vallee, and S. Li
490176.abstract: Rapid and accurate flood damage assessment is critical for emergency response and recovery planning. This study presents a web-based Flood Damage Assessment Tool that integrates the NOAA VIIRS 30-m downscaled 3D floodwater depth product as a primary input layer for building-level damage estimation across the contiguous United States (CONUS). The tool combines VIIRS-derived flood depth with OpenStreetMap building footprints, FEMA HAZUS 4.0 depth-damage curves (with first-floor height correction), and U.S. Census geocoding to estimate structure and contents losses by building type. The pipeline is fully automated: upon loading a VIIRS flood depth GeoTIFF, the tool queries a local PostGIS database of approximately 78 million OSM buildings, intersects flooded footprints with depth values, applies the appropriate HAZUS damage functions, and returns itemized loss estimates within seconds. The tool was evaluated across multiple CONUS flood events spanning 2018–2025, including Hurricane Ida (2021), the Kentucky Flood (2025), and the Mississippi River Flood (April 2025), covering a range of hydrologic regimes and land cover conditions. Results demonstrate the tool's capability to deliver rapid damage estimates at the building scale using operationally available satellite-derived flood data, supporting the transition of VIIRS flood products from research to real-world applications in emergency management and flood risk assessment. This experimental application will be hosted at NOAA CoastWatch, Water Prediction Node (https://CoastWatch.NOAA.gov).

490178.title: Physics-Guided Deep-Learning Air Quality Forecasting: A Case Study over Greater Boston
490178.authors: Yiyue Yang, Northeastern University, Boston, MA; and K. Do and Y. Zhang

490181.title: Gaussian Plume Model Calculations of Point Source Emissions from Aircraft Measurements
490181.authors: Nethaneel R A Taylor, University of Texas El Paso, El Paso, TX; and N. Malarich, C. Warneke, S. S. Brown, R. M. Fitzgerald, I. B. Pollack, X. Ren, and P. Stratton
490181.abstract: The NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory conducts many aircraft measurements of the troposphere. Among these flights are isolated plumes of enhanced chemical concentration which are not always anticipated, and can even represent transient emissions. Thus the aircraft path is not always optimized to measure a fully dispersed plume. The aircraft may be too close to the point source for the plume to evenly mix throughout the boundary layer, or the aircraft may be too high above the ground for eddy covariance. Therefore, to calculate the flux of the full 2D plume and thus estimate the point source emission rate, the vertical structure of the plume must be modelled from fluid mechanics in a Gaussian plume model. We identify the largest plumes from the 2025 Baltimore Air Quality and Marcellus Surveys, and find that the Gaussian plume model does not always predict full mixing throughout the planetary boundary layer. Our calculation from the single largest plume gives a similar emission as the typical total-region emission.

490182.title: Developing a Medium-Range Severe Weather Risk Awareness Tool for Utility Operations in the Northeast U.S.A.
490182.authors: Matthew Seymour, MS, University at Albany, Watervliet, NY; University at Albany, Watervliet, NY; and R. G. Fovell
490182.abstract: The Northeastern U.S. (NEUS, here defined as much of Pennsylvania, New Jersey, New York and New England) is relatively overlooked with respect to the risks from severe thunderstorms, given that damage resulting from such events is not uncommon in the region. From 2016 to 2025, 92 events occurred in which at least 100 severe-weather related reports were submitted to the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) within the NEUS. Of particular interest are the utility and energy sectors that have infrastructure susceptible to the effects of severe storms. Early detection of oncoming events can assist utilities in planning staff and staging resources. This is especially important in the medium range, defined as lead times of 3 to 10 days. While predicting the precise timing and location of severe weather risks in the medium range is often unpractical, information regarding upcoming patterns that may be conducive to severe weather are highly valuable to users in the energy sector. In this project, machine learning is utilized to evaluate patterns in parameters (such as 500 hPa height, 850 hPa temperature, precipitable water, and Craven Brooks) associated with varying frequencies of severe weather in the NEUS. The product is based upon the machine learning and operational forecasts from global deterministic and ensemble models. Derived parameters, including the significant tornado parameter (STP) and derecho composite (DCP), will supplement the product. From this tool, a user will be able to easily understand whether a threat is looming, the degree of consistency & uncertainty among forecasts, and if a threat is increasing or decreasing in likelihood & intensity over time. It ultimately aims to increase situational awareness with respect to approaching severe weather risks and increase utilities’ efficiency of resource allocation.

490183.title: Resolving and Tracking MCS Lifecycle Characteristics with ISCCP-NextGen Capabilities
490183.authors: Leila Jean Gabrys, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and M. J. Foster, T. S. L'Ecuyer, and C. Bean
490183.abstract: Resolving and Tracking MCS Lifecycle Characteristics with ISCCP-NextGen Capabilities Leila Jean Gabrys, Michael Foster, Tristan L’Ecuyer, Carolyn Bean Observing and characterizing the lifecycle of mesoscale convective systems (MCSs), from initiation through the growth, maturity, and dissipation stages, is difficult at the spatiotemporal scales in which they develop. This study uses the Python-based tobac (Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds) algorithm applied to high-resolution geostationary satellite products, such as GOES and more recently ISCCP-NextGen (ISCCP-NG) with subgrid scale data available, to track MCS lifecycle characteristics both regionally and globally. We utilize tobac to observe known lifecycle factors such as convective anvil growth and deepening cores, as well as employing the algorithm’s merge/split capabilities to track differences in the transition from isolated to aggregated storms. To increase confidence in tracking results, we apply tobac across multiple spectral channels as part of an ensemble tracking approach. We further compare standard 30-minute sampling against sub-30-minute intervals to identify the resolution needed to adequately capture MCS lifecycle transitions. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this tracking methodology to a longer-term dataset, enabling analysis of trends in MCS frequency, duration, and other lifecycle characteristics over time for highly convective regions around the globe. Together, these results inform best practices for applying tobac to high-resolution geostationary data, and contribute toward a methodology for building a long-term MCS lifecycle catalog.

490184.title: Innovations Toward Enhanced Ensemble Streamflow Predictions In NOAA’s Hefs and Nextgen Frameworks
490184.authors: Mimi R. Abel, NOAA PSL, Boulder, CO; and E. Towler, A. D. Polasky, E. R. Sthapit, and W. R. Currier
490184.abstract: NOAA’s hydrologic forecasts support warnings of hydrologic hazards such as droughts and floods, and also support water and ecosystems managers who need hydrologic information for their management decisions. In particular, probabilistic streamflow forecasts offer the potential to quantify inherent uncertainty in predicting streamflow, thus bolstering informed decision-making, particularly for applications like Forecast Informed Reservoir Operations. This presentation will describe a project underway to support and contribute to the improvement of NOAA’s ensemble streamflow forecasting tools through the establishment of an experimental research and development framework for ensemble streamflow prediction that crosswalks NOAA’s operational Hydrologic Ensemble Forecast System (HEFS) and its NextGen National Water Model. The framework provides the ability to test end-to-end potential improvements for ensemble streamflow prediction, spanning improvements in meteorological forcings to streamflow post-processing techniques. We will first demonstrate improvements in ensemble streamflow prediction from statistically post-processing meteorological forcings in a distributed hydrologic model ensemble. We then will describe ongoing efforts to apply these meteorological post-processing techniques, including techniques exploring downscaling individual ensemble members, to priority watersheds using both a physically motivated hydrological model similar to that in HEFS and a Long Short-Term Memory streamflow model. Furthermore, we will show results from novel ensemble streamflow post-processing techniques. Experiments from the framework will be compared to the HEFS benchmark post-processed meteorological and streamflow reforecasts, lending operational relevance to our results.

490186.title: Development and Analysis of a Thundersnow Climatology using Geostationary Lightning Mapper Data
490186.authors: Sebastian S. Harkema, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL
490186.abstract: In 2017, the first Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) became operational. As a result, the GLM instruments have provided nearly a decade of space-based lightning observations. While one of primary focuses of GLM was to observe lightning within severe convective weather, several studies (e.g., Harkema et al. 2019) have demonstrated GLM can efficiently detect lightning within snowfall (i.e., thundersnow). Previous climatologies demonstrated that thundersnow is more likely to occur in the Intermountain West, Great Lakes, and Great Plains regions. However, those climatologies tended to use instruments that do not detect the exact location of lightning. Therefore, the GLM is an ideal instrument to develop an updated thundersnow climatology as it provides insights into spatial characteristics of thundersnow. Ground-based lightning flash characteristics will also be examined in this climatology. Specifically, this study will examine lightning flashes identified as thundersnow from 2018 to 2026 and develop a first-of-its-kind climatology using space- and ground-based lightning observations.

490187.title: NOAA’s Publicly Available Space Weather Products
490187.authors: Laurel Anne Rachmeler, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and W. Rowland, J. Riley, K. Hallock, J. V. Rodriguez, J. Machol, D. J. Schmit, B. Kress, and Q. Schiller
490187.abstract: NOAA has an extensive archive of Space Weather relevant observations, data, and products. Our digitized holdings reach back into the 1970s, though we have analog records dating back to the 1800s. Data sources include ground based sensors, satellite instruments, models, and NWS created text forecast products. We present an overview of the archival products and describe current and evolving access mechanisms. Additionally we will discuss NOAA’s latest products from SOLAR-1 and expected future products.

490188.title: The No-Analog Winter: The Evolution of Monitoring, Coordination, and Lessons Learned from the 2026 Western Snow Drought
490188.authors: Jason Gerlich, NOAA; and D. McEvoy and M. Woloszyn
490188.abstract: The record-shattering conditions of the 2026 Water Year have established a new low benchmark for snowpack for much of the West. For many states, Water Year 2026 will be characterized by historic snowpack deficits that have little or no historical analogs. At the same time, total precipitation in some regions approached historical averages and for some historic lows, while exceptionally warm temperatures led to a higher amount of rain than snow and an early start to the melt from an exceptional March heat wave event. This unprecedented season has resulted in a significant increase in the demand for enhanced snow drought monitoring, assessment, communication, and cross-government coordination. The National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS) has been developing Snow Drought Updates since 2018 with partners across every state in the Western United States, including but not limited to state climate offices, water resource departments, the USDA-Natural Resource Conservation Service, and academic partners. These updates have become a primary source for snow drought information. In this presentation we will summarize some of the data-driven and logistical hurdles faced during the 2026 season, and how the approach might be refined in the future to improve monitoring and communication. Preparing for the next extreme winter requires a cohesive West-wide coordinated effort that transcends regional boundaries and acknowledges the far-reaching national social, economic, and environmental consequences of mountain snowpack variability. This presentation will help lay the foundation for a more cohesive snow drought coordination effort.

490189.title: Initial Results from the EarthWorks DYAMOND1 Global Storm-Resolving Simulation (Invited Presentation)
490189.authors: Jim Wilson Hurrell, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and L. Sun and J. W. Hurrell
490189.abstract: EarthWorks is a global storm-resolving modeling system developed through a collaboration among Colorado State University, NCAR, and other partners to advance weather and climate research. Here we present initial results from the first EarthWorks simulation at 3.75-km horizontal grid spacing, conducted following the Phase 1 DYnamics of the Atmospheric general circulation Modeled On Non-hydrostatic Domains (DYAMOND1) intercomparison protocol. The simulation is compared with a corresponding 120-km configuration to assess the influence of horizontal resolution on the simulated climate. Preliminary analyses demonstrate several advantages of kilometer-scale global modeling. Relative to the 120-km simulation, the 3.75-km configuration provides a more realistic representation of equatorial precipitation and improves near-surface temperature and atmospheric circulation over regions of complex topography. Additional analyses are underway to evaluate precipitation extremes, weather-system structure, the physical processes responsible for these improvements, and their implications for weather and climate prediction.
