These initial results highlight the potential of global storm-resolving models to improve the representation of key atmospheric processes across weather and climate timescales. They also provide an early demonstration of the EarthWorks modeling system, advancing David Randall's long-standing vision of global cloud- and storm-resolving climate models.

490193.title: Strategic Alignment and Technical Innovation: Positioning the Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program (HFIP) for the Future
490193.authors: William A. Komaromi, IMSG, Ellicott City, MD; and A. J. Poyer, S. Gopalakrishnan, F. Yang, V. S. Tallapragada, Z. Zhang, B. Liu, G. J. Alaka Jr., J. Peng, J. A. Sippel, J. R. Rhome, D. Brown, P. Santos, W. Hogsett, J. S. Lee, and K. Garrett
490193.abstract: The Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program (HFIP) is currently advancing a pivotal phase of its innovative agenda, shifting focus toward next-generation modeling and data assimilation frameworks. This presentation outlines ongoing developmental work, including recent upgrades and physics advancements to the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS), a transition to JEDI-based Data Assimilation and improved vortex initialization (VI), multiple storm-following moving nests with a basin-scale parent domain configuration, an experimental 2-km HAFS ensemble in the Atlantic, and the training and development of AI-driven prediction models designed to augment operational forecast skill. We will also address the longer-term evolving pivot toward NOAA’s "moonshot" vision: the adoption of a unified MPAS core across all spatial scales. This ambitious multi-scale strategy demands intensive, collaborative problem-solving across the entire HFIP research and operational community. Simultaneously, we detail the program's revised governance framework and the realignment of responsibilities necessitated by NOAA’s recent organizational restructuring. By aligning stakeholder efforts across research institutions and operational centers, these strategic and structural enhancements will accelerate the transition of scientific breakthroughs into reliable, impactful hurricane forecasts for the nation.

490196.title: Lessons Learned From Fifteen Years of Probabilistic Wildfire Prediction
490196.authors: T. Todd Lindley, NWS, Norman, OK; and S. Curl, A. M. Ward, G. Murdoch, D. Daily, L. Kanclerz, and R. Hluchan
490196.abstract: In February 2011, two National Weather Service (NWS) meteorologists and a Texas Forest Service fire analyst published a novel probabilistic outlook forecasting a >60% chance of a dangerous wildfire outbreak in west Texas. The forecast was delivered to then Texas Governor Rick Perry and triggered Texas’ statewide mutual aid system which surged firefighting resources toward the risk area. Forty-eight hours later, those resources assisted local jurisdictions in fighting 40 wildfires that burned 285,000 acres and destroyed 200 structures from Amarillo to Abilene. Since then, the Southern Great Plains Wildfire Outbreak Working Group (SGPWO WG) has grown to include 300 NWS personnel and governmental fire experts across Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas. Through rigorous research-to-operations activities that translate emerging science to operational decision making, the group has collaborated hundreds of probabilistic significant wildfire outlooks, including successful predictions for some of the fastest spreading and largest wildfire incidents to impact the United States in modern times. Unlike conventional outlooks produced by any one agency that communicate critical weather and fuel dryness independently, this probabilistic guidance leverages multidisciplinary expertise toward explicit predictions of wildfire occurrence to inform pre-fire resource planning and mobilization. An economic impact study attributed mitigating actions influenced by the group's 2022-2024 forecasts to more than $800 million in saved homes and businesses. Lessons learned by the SGPWO WG are particularly relevant today as the NWS becomes a more nimble and mobile organization embedded within partnering government agencies where critical weather-dependent decisions are made. In addition, their specialized expertise is also becoming more vital as the NWS modernizes forecast processes. These lessons highlight that calibrated probabilistic messaging of the predicted holistic fire environment is possible, can accurately foretell the potential for new wildfire ignitions and the evolution of fire threats, and significantly enhance critical preparatory actions across interagency disciplines. Further, experiences demonstrate the value of nominal group techniques that leverage diverse expertise across an integration of multi-disciplinary and multi-jurisdictional operations in response to complex natural phenomena. This approach has increased trust among collaborating agencies and led to tactical satellite-based alerting and warning capabilities, which further enhance effectiveness of support provided by the probabilistic outlooks through rapid routing of pre-deployed resources to emerging incidents for initial attack and, when appropriate, advising the public of imminently dangerous wildfires. This presentation will summarize sociotechnical experiences and lessons learned from 15 years of this high-stakes multidisciplinary integration in science-based decision support.

490201.title: Inter-Model Comparison of Simulating Low-Level Jet Events Using ERF and WRF
490201.authors: Geng Xia, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO; and N. Bodini, M. Sanchez Gomez, H. Gopalan, A. Abraham, M. J. Churchfield, P. Moriarty, B. Adler, and R. Krishnamurthy
490201.abstract: Low-level jets (LLJs) are a fundamental feature of the lower troposphere and atmospheric boundary layer, characterized by a local wind-speed maximum within the lowest few hundred meters above the surface. Extensive observational, theoretical, and modeling studies have shown that LLJs are dynamically important because they regulate vertical shear, turbulence production, momentum transport, and thermodynamic exchange. Despite their importance, LLJs remain difficult to represent accurately in numerical weather prediction models. Previous modeling studies often overestimate nose height and underestimate nose wind speed. Motivated by these challenges, this study conducts an inter-model comparison of LLJ simulations using the GPU enabled Energy Research and Forecasting model (ERF) and the Weather Research and Forecasting model (WRF). Our objective is to evaluate how consistently the two models reproduce LLJ structure and evolution across a range of atmospheric environments, with particular emphasis on jet timing, intensity, and spatial structure. Through this comparison, the study aims to improve understanding of model behavior and provide guidance for future model development. To evaluate model performance across diverse LLJ regimes, three representative cases from different regions of the United States are selected. The first case is a coastal LLJ observed on 15 January 2021 from lidar profile measurements at Morro Bay along the California coastline. The second case occurred on 24 August 2023 during the AWAKEN field campaign in northern Oklahoma, and the third case was observed on 3 June 2024 during the WFIP3 field campaign along the U.S. Northeast coast. Together, these cases span a range of locations, forcing mechanisms, and jet intensities, providing a useful framework for testing model skill under differing LLJ conditions. The High-Resolution Rapid Refresh data is used to provide the initial and boundary conditions for the model simulations. For ERF, each case is initialized with the same WRF input and boundary files to ensure consistent domain configuration and forcing. This strategy is intended to support a meaningful inter-model comparison by reducing differences associated with experimental setup. Model performance is evaluated by comparing the simulated LLJ structure, temporal evolution, and intensity against available observations. Preliminary results from the AWAKEN case study (Figure) indicate that both models capture the overall evolution of the nocturnal low-level jet. ERF more closely reproduces the observed peak wind speed but simulates a vertically deeper jet, whereas WRF produces a weaker and more diffuse jet structure. Both models underestimate the subsequent upward shift of the wind-speed maximum and the development of a secondary jet. In the presentation, we will extend the analysis to examine sensitivities to turbulence, boundary-layer, and surface parameterizations and evaluate the other two cases.

490206.title: Determining the Importance of Environmental Thermodynamics on Sub-Severe Hailfall in the Southeast US
490206.authors: Sophia Alegrias, The University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH), Huntsville, AL; and S. W. Freeman, S. D. Bang, P. T. Pangle, R. S. Schumacher, N. Newman, S. Hilberg, D. Talmadge, J. Turner, R. Adams-Selin, H. C. Vagasky, J. Mascio, and C. Calkins
490206.abstract: Predicting hail size remains one of the most difficult challenges to hail forecasting, as diverse geospatial differences in storm-scale dynamics, moisture availability, terrain, and many other factors create unique and complex hail environments across the globe. Most research has focused on characterizing favorable environments for severe (≥2.5 cm) hail growth, yet sub-severe hail (<2.5 cm) events occur more frequently in some regions (such as the Southeast US) and are alarmingly under-researched. It is crucial we work toward mitigating this bias as both hail melting and growth processes must be considered for more accurate predictions of hail size. Warm, humid environments, such as those experienced in the Southeast US, are particularly favorable for enhanced melting and can lead to large overestimations of hail size at the surface if potential melting is not accounted for. Research has shown that melting rates of low density graupel are highly sensitive to lapse rates and relative humidity profiles, among initial graupel size and density. Furthermore, a recent study found that low-level relative humidity, melting layer height, and convective instability were the strongest discriminators between hail and no hail events in tropical maritime environments. Given melting processes appear to have a strong influence on final hail size, the objective of this study is to determine if environmental thermodynamics are the prevailing difference between thunderstorms that produce sub-severe and no hail at the surface. We constructed a large database of predominantly sub-severe hailstorms in the Southeast US by matching 2022-2025 citizen science hail observations from the Community Collaborative Rain, Hail and Snow (CoCoRaHS) network that were within 1 hour of a satellite overpass from the Global Precipitation Measurement Mission (GPM). Potential null hailstorm cases were limited to urban areas to mitigate population bias and were determined when neither CoCoRaHS or crowd-sourced hail reports from Meteorological Phenomena Identification Near the Ground (mPING) existed for the duration of the storm lifecycle. Representative pre-storm environmental profiles for each hail report were constructed utilizing ERA5 reanalysis data and close proximity (<50 km) radiosondes when appropriate. Results will show the influence of environmental thermodynamics on modulating sub-severe or no hail occurrence in the Southeast US. Environmental comparisons between hail-producing storms that were and were not detected by satellite remote sensing algorithms will additionally be shown. Future work will focus on analyzing radar-detected ZDR and KDP columns, overshooting top characteristics, and lightning activity of null, sub-severe, and severe hailstorms to determine if they can discriminate against hail size or occurrence.

490207.title: Transitioning NOAA’s Compact Coronagraph (CCOR-1) on the GOES-19 satellite to Operations for Space Weather Forecasting
490207.authors: Laurel Anne Rachmeler, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and D. Vassiliadis, C. Wallace, W. Rowland, J. Johnson, N. Miles, G. Millward, R. Redmon, D. J. Schmit, G. Dima, and V. Salinas
490207.abstract: Space weather events driven by coronal mass ejections (CMEs), solar flares, and solar wind pose significant risks to Earth's power grids, satellite operations, radio communications, and navigation infrastructure. The Compact Coronagraph-1 (CCOR-1) on NOAA’s GOES-19 satellite became operational on April 7, 2025; it is NOAA’s first operational space-based coronagraph. Built to measure the size, speed, and trajectory of CMEs near the sun, CCOR-1 has transitioned coronal monitoring from legacy research assets to a dedicated, operational NOAA capability. This presentation highlights the successful research-to-operations (R2O) transition of CCOR-1 and its products in FY25, detailing the inter-agency operational architecture established between the NESDIS Office of Space Weather Observations (SWO), the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), the Office of Satellite and Product Operations (OSPO), the Office of Common Services (OCS), and the National Weather Service (NWS) Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC). CCOR-1 generates high-quality total-solar-eclipse-like images every 15 minutes and delivers data within approximately 22 minutes of acquisition (less than the 30-min requirement)—a drastic improvement over legacy research instruments, which often experienced delays of up to eight hours. By delivering low-latency imagery, CCOR-1 enables SWPC forecasters to issue actionable geomagnetic storm warnings more than 24 hours in advance (https://www.spaceweather.gov/). Additionally, long-term calibration and public archival via the new Space Weather Data Portal (SPOT, https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cloud-access/space-weather-portal/) ensure that CCOR-1 data supports ongoing scientific research to better understand the physics of these solar phenomena and protect critical national infrastructure.

490208.title: Every New Beginning Is Some Other Beginning's End: Evaluating Ceiling and Visibility Forecasts from an Event-Based Perspective
490208.authors: Lindsay R. Blank, CIRA at NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; and L. D. Melling, J. Kenyon, D. M. Uden, A. Hewett, K. Y. Wong, and M. S. Wandishin
490208.abstract: The vast majority of evaluations by the Quality Assessment Product Development Team for the FAA’s Aviation Weather Research Program involve matching observations to a gridded, model-based forecast product. While the forecast projects forward over multiple time steps, the evaluation is performed, separately, over the grid for each forecast lead time. In 2026, the team completed an evaluation of forecasts of changes in flight categories (i.e., due to changes in ceiling or visibility) made by the Local Area MOS Program (LAMP)v2.7 product. The forecasts being compared used different definitions of forecast state (e.g., instantaneous vs. worst conditions over a set time period) and had different forecast lengths. Even the observations brought unforeseen challenges. This presentation will focus on the challenges of the evaluation and the steps taken to address them.

490209.title: Developing a Radar Climatology of Skillful Prognostic and Diagnostic Signals to Enhance Tropical Cyclone Tornado Warning Lead Time across North Carolina
490209.authors: Brandon Wegmann, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and D. Leins and A. Swiggett
490209.abstract: Tropical cyclone tornadoes (TCTORs) often exhibit radar characteristics that differ from those of traditional Great Plains supercells, making it challenging to issue a tornado warning with positive lead time. Between 2015 and 2025, 18 named tropical cyclones produced a total of 115 TCTORs across North Carolina. The majority of tornado warning lead times fell below the National Weather Service lead time goal of 13 minutes, with almost a third of TCTORs being either unwarned or having no warning lead time at all. A radar climatology of key radar signatures was developed to identify combinations of prognostic and diagnostic tools that may improve tornado warning lead times. Radar signatures evaluated include VROT (Rotational Velocity), NROT (Normalized Rotation), Left Flank Velocity Enhancement (LFVE), Velocity Enhancement Signature (VES), Maximum Spectrum Width, and the angular separation between the Specific Differential Phase (KDP) and Differential Reflectivity (ZDR) centroids. The climatology encompasses North Carolina TCTORs spanning Hurricane Delta (2020) through Tropical Storm Chantal (2025) and characterizes the frequency, percentile distributions, and temporal evolution of these radar signatures in the minutes leading up to tornadogenesis. Using GR2Analyst, a sample of 35 TCTORs was analyzed for the aforementioned radar features. Given the inherent subjectivity of radar interrogation, specific guidelines were developed to ensure the study is reproducible. Results indicate that specific combinations of prognostic and diagnostic tools provide the greatest tornado warning lead times. Combinations of LFVE+KDP/ZDR Separation (2 prognostic tools), KDP/ZDR Separation+VROT (1 prognostic + 1 diagnostic tool), and LFVE+NROT+VROT (1 prognostic + 2 diagnostic tools) outperformed the remaining 54 combinations of radar signatures in terms of average tornado warning lead time. These results establish a radar climatology that quantifies the frequency and temporal evolution of key radar signatures preceding tropical cyclone tornadogenesis and identifies combinations of prognostic and diagnostic tools associated with the greatest average tornado warning lead times.

490214.title: Discrete-Level Interpretability in Medium-Range Lightning Prediction: A Data-Efficient Reproduction and Extension of BoltCast
490214.authors: Somnath Luitel, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and M. Singh
490214.abstract: Medium-range lightning prediction using global numerical weather prediction (NWP) fields was recently demonstrated by BoltCast for forecast days 1–4. However, BoltCast represents several isobaric microphysical and dynamical predictors using column-maximum values, removing vertical information relevant to storm electrification. We develop an independent, BoltCast-inspired three-dimensional U-Net using one year of 0000 UTC Global Forecast System (GFS) forecasts and Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) observations—approximately 5% as many forecast initializations as BoltCast’s five-year, four-cycle dataset. The column-maximum baseline achieves a season-stratified, cross-validated precision–recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 0.614 ± 0.006. We then introduce a discrete-pressure-level formulation that retains five isobaric predictors at 250, 500, 700, and 850 hPa. The formulation matches the baseline’s predictive accuracy while enabling per-level, cross-validated permutation-importance attribution that is unavailable after column-maximum aggregation. Updraft importance peaks at 700 hPa, graupel and cloud-ice importance at 500 hPa within the mixed-phase charging region, and rainwater importance at 850 hPa, where it is the strongest individual isobaric channel. The midlevel graupel, cloud-ice, and updraft attributions are physically consistent with the non-inductive charging mechanism. Four additional physically motivated predictors—convective inhibition, 0–6-km bulk shear, midtropospheric lapse rate, and cloud water—produce no measurable improvement in predictive skill. To assess sensitivity to autocorrelation between neighboring dates, we repeat the evaluation using temporal-block cross-validation, grouping folds by calendar week and excluding dates adjacent to each test block. The model retains 96% of its season-stratified performance, with a PR-AUC of 0.589 ± 0.013. These results demonstrate that retaining discrete pressure levels can improve the physical interpretability of medium-range lightning prediction without sacrificing accuracy, although the findings remain limited to one year and a single daily initialization cycle.

490217.title: Desert-Urban SysTem IntegratEd AtmospherIc Monsoon (DUSTIEAIM): Overview, Dust Storms, and Monsoon Science from the First Summer (Invited Presentation)
490217.authors: Allison C Aiken, PhD, LANL, Los Alamos, NM
490217.abstract: The Southwest (SW) U.S. is a rapidly growing energy-rich infrastructure region that includes the Phoenix metropolitan statistical area (MSA). The Phoenix MSA is located in the Sonoran Desert, a semi-arid dryland, that experiences significant impacts to the Earth system due to dust’s role at the land-atmosphere interface and in atmospheric processes, including interactions with clouds, radiation, and precipitation. Dust aerosols play an important role in the SW U.S. desert-urban interface that is characterized by low annual precipitation, high temperatures, dry conditions, and strong winds. The conditions result in seasonally-dependent impacts to visibility and infrastructure due to dust events, including large scale ones, “haboobs”, that have particulate matter (PM) concentrations exceeding milligrams per meter cubed, an order of magnitude higher than the standard scale for PM. Specifically, during the North American Monsoon (NAM), thunderstorms around Phoenix can create haboobs at the leading edge of the storm through downdrafts and outflows that lift large quantities of dust from the land surface to create walls of dust in the atmosphere. During this presentation, we will present an overview of a new field campaign that is collecting observations within the Phoenix MSA as well as results from some of the large-scale dust storms that were sampled in summer 2026. Desert-Urban SysTem IntegratEd AtmospherIc Monsoon (DUSTIEAIM), a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility field campaign, is focused on energy and water challenges in Phoenix, Arizona. DUSTIEAIM has three interrelated science objectives focused on land-atmosphere interactions and impacts, aerosol processes and interactions with clouds and radiation, and precipitation processes and is led by an interdisciplinary science team composed of national laboratories, universities, and agencies with a broad range of subject-matter expertise. DUSTIEAIM is collecting 16 months of observations in one of America’s fastest-growing and most heat-stressed urban regions that includes approximately 50 instruments, including active and passive ground-based sensors, radars (C-band cloud precipitation radar) and lidars (doppler and micropulse), and an aerosol observing system. The AOS includes ~15 in situ instruments for measuring aerosol physicochemical properties and cloud microphysics, including water-uptake potential and optical properties that impact radiative budgets, cloud formation, atmospheric stability, and interact with convection. DUSTIEAIM observations are being collected to help redefine how we model urban-land-atmosphere interactions, monsoon storms, and aerosol-cloud-precipitation interactions, including cloud microphysics and turbulence, by collecting comprehensive observations within Phoenix from June 2026 through September 2027. DUSTIEAIM includes three intensive operational periods. The first summer NAM period occurred from July 1 – September 30, 2026. Up to six radiosondes were launched each day including standard launches and additional ones during forecasted events. Four dust storms, “haboobs”, were sampled in July and early August with particulate matter (PM10) concentrations that exceeded 1 mg/m3. Data will be shown from the in situ and profiling instruments, including the radiosondes, AOS, supermicron guest instruments, radar and lidars. We will focus on the impact of these events within the region on aerosol number and size distributions, water-uptake potential, visibility, and their distribution within the column that exceeded 1 km in altitude for most of the dust storms sampled this summer. We will also discuss their origin and movement from the S/SE across the Phoenix MSA. In summary, we will present some of the first results from DUSTIEAIM that include active and passive ground-based sensors, radars, and integrated modeling to deliver a comprehensive environmental data set at the desert-urban-agricultural interface for dust sources, sinks, and characteristics as sampled in Phoenix, Arizona to better understand dust impacts in the Southwestern U.S.

490219.title: Using Deep Learning to Locate Tropical Cyclone Centers in Satellite SAR Imagery
490219.authors: Bhavika Buddi, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and T. W. Ruff, C. Jackson, and M. Y. Murphy
490219.abstract: The Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR), within the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS), routinely processes satellite synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery to derive high-resolution ocean surface wind speeds and radial wind profiles for tropical cyclones. These products are generated in near real-time and distributed to operational forecast centers, such as the National Hurricane Center and the Joint Typhoon Warning Center. Accurate wind speed radial profiles rely on precise fixing of the storm center; however, the current center-finding algorithm suffers from significant positioning errors in over one-third of SAR scenes, requiring time-intensive manual corrections that delay product generation. This study develops a deep learning framework using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to improve automated tropical cyclone center finding in satellite SAR imagery. To determine the optimal model configuration, we systematically evaluated multiple architectures and training strategies, including single-task versus multi-task CNNs, direct coordinate regression versus heatmap regression, mean squared error versus Adaptive Wing Loss (AWL), and a range of encoder backbones. The best-performing model combined a multi-task heatmap regression approach with AWL as the loss function, and a UNet++ architecture using an EfficientNet encoder backbone. Evaluation on an independent test dataset demonstrated significant improvements in center localization accuracy, particularly for cases in which the current algorithm performs poorly. The optimal CNN model reduced the mean center-finding error from 36.40 km to 4.48 km while significantly decreasing the frequency of large localization errors (>15 km). The model also showed robust performance across a range of tropical cyclone eye structures. These results demonstrate how machine learning and artificial intelligence can enhance the operational use of satellite data by reducing manual corrections and improving the accuracy and timeliness of SAR-derived wind products for tropical cyclone forecasting and warnings.

490220.title: Assessing Future Power Demand Across U.S. Urban Regions Under SSP Climate Scenarios and Data Center Growth
490220.authors: Taylor Jean Dolan, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND
490220.abstract: Within the last six years, the electricity growth rate jumped from 0.1% to 1.7% as a result of population growth, economic development, and the rapid expansion of energy intensive infrastructure such as data centers. While previous studies have examined the interaction between climate and socioeconomic factors, few have evaluated how these factors interact with growing demand from data center development. Over the last decade, data center load growth has tripled, and is projected to either double or triple by 2028. As artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and electrification continue to expand, understanding the influence of climate and urban growth is increasingly important for long-term energy planning and grid resilience. This study utilizes the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) machine learning framework to project electricity demand across eight major U.S. cities through 2100. The historical model predicted electricity consumption using weather variables from ERA5 reanalysis along with gross domestic product (GDP) and total urban population. The resulting model was then applied to future climate projections from the Community Earth System Model Version 2 (CESM2) using the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6). Future projections utilized the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP126, SSP245, SSP370, SSP585), allowing for the changes in climate and socioeconomic conditions to be evaluated from 2017 through 2100. To examine the impact from data center expansion, projected consumption from these centers were incorporated into a separate run using long-term growth projections. The additional analysis evaluates how the expansion of computational infrastructure may impact future energy needs beyond those driven by climate and socioeconomic factors. By integrating energy projections from data centers, this allows for a more comprehensive assessment of future urban electricity demand. Preliminary results indicate increasing electricity demand across all metropolitan areas throughout the century, with magnitude and timing of growth different across SSPs and cities. The largest increase in demand without data centers occurred under SSP585, while SSP370 resulted in the smallest change by 2100. Population and GDP remained the strongest predictors of demand, with rising temperatures contributing to additional cooling demand. Differences among metropolitan areas highlight how different climate and socioeconomic conditions produce unique patterns of future electricity consumption. Incorporating data center growth substantially increases projected demand across all scenarios, exceeding demand changes projected from climate and socioeconomic factors alone. By 2100, data centers are projected to increase total electricity demand across the given cities by 270 – 641 TWh depending on the SSP. These findings demonstrate the need of integrating ongoing infrastructure growth into long-term energy planning to better assess future grid demand and resilience strategies.

490221.title: Global Impact of Assimilating Tomorrow.io Commercial Microwave Radiances in MPAS-JEDI
490221.authors: Ivette Hernandez Banos, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and Z. Liu, B. C. Ruston, H. C. Lin, T. G. Lopes, J. A. Mantovani Jr., J. J. Braun, and J. P. Weiss
490221.abstract: Denser spatial coverage and more frequent temporal sampling from commercial small-satellite constellations offer the potential to constrain analyses where operational polar-orbiting coverage is limited. However, extensive assessment of their impact on analyses and forecasts is required before these data can be adopted in operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems. This study, conducted under the NOAA NESDIS Commercial Data Program, evaluates the assimilation of brightness temperatures from the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) constellation within the Model for Prediction Across Scales–Atmosphere (MPAS-A) coupled with the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework (MPAS-JEDI). TMS provides 12 channels comprising temperature sounding near 118 GHz, water vapor sounding near 183 GHz, and a 205 GHz window channel. Using month-long global cycling experiments on a 15 km quasi-uniform mesh with a hybrid three-dimensional ensemble-variational (hybrid-3DEnVar) analysis, we assess observation impacts under clear-sky conditions, where cloud-affected observations are screened, and extend the evaluation to all-sky conditions, where they are retained and simulated. Radiative transfer is computed with the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) through the JEDI Unified Forward Operator. Clear-sky screening is based on observation minus background thresholds providing the best balance between data retention and error statistics. Clear-sky experiments demonstrate that commercial microwave observations can provide beneficial impacts on NWP analyses and forecasts. The static bias correction configuration produces the largest temperature forecast improvements but degrades water vapor and wind fields, whereas the VarBC configuration provides more balanced improvements, including enhanced temperature forecasts across the tropics and Northern Hemisphere subtropics with reduced precipitation displacement errors. In the all-sky configuration, screening is replaced by the scattering-capable CRTM solver with hydrometeor fields from the MPAS-A microphysics, and observation errors follow a symmetric error model in which the assigned error increases with a cloud predictor computed from the mean of the observed and simulated cloud signals. The all-sky evaluation comprises departure statistics stratified by cloud amount, observation counts relative to the clear-sky baseline, fits to independent observations, and forecast verification against analyses and radiosondes, with emphasis on tropical humidity and wind fields, for which the clear-sky impacts were most configuration-dependent. Together, the clear-sky and all-sky assessments quantify the impact of commercial microwave sounding data and inform key choices for operational assimilation.

490224.title: Observed Terrestrial Water Storage Drought Lifecycles and Their Systematic Underestimation In Hydrological Models
490224.authors: Meng Zhao, Univ. of Idaho, Moscow, ID
490224.abstract: Drought impacts depend not only on severity but also on how rapidly water deficits develop and how quickly they recover. These dynamics are especially important for terrestrial water storage (TWS) droughts because subsurface water stores respond more slowly than meteorological anomalies and impart strong hydrological memory. However, the timing characteristics of TWS droughts have not yet been systematically quantified at the global scale. Here, we use observations from the GRACE and GRACE Follow-On satellite missions to identify the three most severe TWS drought events at each grid cell globally and quantify key drought evolution metrics, including drought onset timing, recovery onset timing, intensification duration, recovery duration, and peak intensity. Across the three most severe drought events at each location, drought intensification (~13 months) is slightly longer than recovery (~11 months), yet the two phases are only weakly coupled (R2 = 0.04). This weak coupling reveals that drought evolution cannot be characterized by a single persistence timescale or inferred from one phase alone, but instead reflects distinct and asymmetric controls on storage depletion and replenishment. Comparison with eight ISIMIP3a global hydrological models shows that models systematically compress TWS drought lifecycles, with delayed onset, earlier recovery initiation, shorter intensification and recovery durations, and weaker peak intensity. Diagnostic analyses suggest that these biases are more closely linked to insufficient hydrological memory and limited storage buffering capacity than to the inclusion or exclusion of individual storage components, such as groundwater or surface water. We therefore argue that these biases are not simply model-specific structural errors, but reflect a broader limitation in how current land and hydrological models represent the land water storage memory processes. These findings provide the first global observational characterization of TWS drought lifecycles and offer new benchmarks for improving the representation of drought dynamics in global water models.

490225.title: How Well Do Machine Learning Emulators Reproduce Non-Gaussian Background Ensemble Statistics for Data Assimilation?
490225.authors: Diego Carrio, University of the Balearic Island, Palma, Balearic Islands, Spain; and X. Wang
490225.abstract: Ensemble-based data assimilation (DA) is often constrained by the computational cost of generating large background ensembles with physics-based numerical models. Machine-learning (ML) emulators offer a computationally efficient alternative that can enable much larger ensembles. Recent studies have evaluated the ability of ML-generated ensembles to reproduce conventional background-error statistics, including the ensemble mean, variance, and correlations (Wang and Wang 2026; Kublek et al. 2026). However, much less is known about whether ML emulators can reproduce higher-order non-Gaussian characteristics of physics-based background ensembles. This is particularly relevant for ensemble-based non-Gaussian DA methods, whose performance may be more prone to sampling errors due to the limited ensemble size. Here, we investigate how the statistical fidelity of ML-generated background ensembles changes from lower-order to higher-order and non-Gaussian properties. As an initial proof of concept, we analyze 1000-member background ensembles generated by a two-layer turbulent quasi-geostrophic (QG) model and its ML emulator. Results indicate that the ML emulator reproduces the overall Gaussian and non-Gaussian statistical behavior of the QG ensemble with reasonably good fidelity, motivating a more systematic evaluation across statistical moments. We quantify ML emulation skill as a function of statistical order, examining whether fidelity changes from the ensemble mean and variance to skewness, kurtosis, and more complex distributional characteristics such as multimodality. The analysis framework developed using the QG system will subsequently be applied to 1000-member background ensemble from the convection-allowing MPAS and its emulator, MAPCast, across multiple atmospheric variables. This study aims to determine whether computationally efficient ML ensembles can serve as statistically faithful surrogates for physics-based background ensembles beyond conventional Gaussian statistics, and ultimately support data assimilation methods that exploit non-Gaussian information.

490226.title: Modeling the Effects of Geostrophic Shear on Baroclinic Convective Boundary Layers
490226.authors: Davoud Pourabdollah, Clemson University, Clemson, SC; and C. Tong and A. H. Syed
490226.abstract: The atmospheric boundary layer is often influenced by large-scale horizontal temperature gradients and the resulting vertical variations of the geostrophic wind, i.e., baroclinicity, even under the condition of horizontal homogeneity. Baroclinicity alters the shear stress and the mean wind profiles. In this work moderately baroclinic convective boundary layers (CBL) are investigated using model equations. In such a CBL the mean shear production of the TKE in the mixed layer is still smaller than the buoyancy production; therefore, the mixed-layer scaling still applies. Yet the geostrophic shear is sufficiently strong to modify the mean momentum balance. Investigating this regime can extend standard CBL theory (Tong and Ding 2020, Tong et al. 2026) and provides a framework for representing realistic boundary layers under the influence of geostrophic shear. In this work, the mean momentum equations and an eddy viscosity model (Venkatesh and Csanady 1974) are solved in the mixed layer. The surface shear stress is used as the lower boundary conditions. The upper boundary conditions are the shear stress at the base of the inversion, which is determined by the entrainment. For a set of parameters including geostrophic wind magnitude, geostrophic shear, surface temperature flux, inversion height, roughness height, and entrainment velocity, we obtain the mixed-layer mean velocity scale and the surface shear stress. We then solve for the mean wind and shear stress profiles. Because of the moderate baroclinicity, the streamswise shear stress still approximately scales with the surface shear stress. For cold and warm convection cases, the cross-wind shear stress still scales with its value at the inversion base. However, for equivalent barotropic cases, its scaling is determined primarily by the geostrophic shear. For both equivalent barotropic and warm/cold convection cases, the mean velocity gradient induced by the geostrophic shear is a few percent of the latter. The main effect of the geostrophic shear is to alter the Reynold shear stress profiles. The results agrees broadly with those of Sorbjan (2004), and provide a basis for quantitative investigation of convective baroclinic boundary layers. Tong, C. and Ding, M., 2020. Velocity-defect laws, log law and logarithmic friction law in the convective atmospheric boundary layer. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 883, p.A36. Tong, C., Pourabdollah, D., Barskov, K. and Ding, M., 2026. Higher-order mean velocity profile in the convective atmospheric boundary layer. arXiv preprint arXiv:2602.13512. Venkatesh, S. and Csanady, G.T., 1974. A baroclinic planetary boundary-layer model, and its application to the Wangara data. Boundary-Layer Meteorology, 5(4), pp.459-473. Sorbjan, Z., 2004. Large-eddy simulations of the baroclinic mixed layer. Boundary-layer meteorology, 112(1), pp.57-80.

490227.title: The “Sleet Challenge” in Impact-Based Decision Support Services, and a Solution for the Winter Storm Severity Index
490227.authors: Dana Tobin, CU/CIRES and NOAA/NWS/WPC, Riverdale Park, MD; and K. J. Harnos, B. Veenhuis, and J. A. Nelson Jr.
490227.abstract: The 23-27 January 2026 winter storm highlighted a critical limitation in the National Weather Service (NWS) Winter Storm Severity Index (WSSI): the lack of explicit handling of ice pellets (sleet). The current WSSI’s algorithms cannot disaggregate ice pellets from snowfall accumulations in the official NWS forecast, which resulted in several artifacts during the storm, including a prominent “impact gap” between the snow and ice regions. The WSSI also overestimated impact severity in the Snow Load and Blowing Snow components. Ultimately, some NWS offices discontinued use of the WSSI suite of products in their messaging and impact-based decision support services (IDSS) for the event. To address these deficiencies, we introduce revised WSSI algorithms that integrate sleet and liquid-equivalent precipitation-type fractional forecast grids created by the NWS Weather Prediction Center (WPC). The updated WSSI algorithms effectively differentiate the distinct physical properties and associated societal impacts of ice pellets and snow, resulting in a more continuous and meteorologically accurate depiction of impacts across the transition zone. The proposed methodology maintains the current operational component structure of the WSSI to ensure continuity, while simultaneously mitigating user mistrust and enhancing product reliability. Results demonstrate that “sleet-aware” logic is essential for the future evolution of operational, impact-based winter weather forecast products to improve public safety and resilience to winter weather hazards. This work highlights a rapid O2R and R2O response cycle at WPC triggered by real-time operational feedback. When operational forecasters identified critical WSSI limitations during a major high-impact winter weather event, developers quickly responded by formulating, testing, and preparing algorithm updates to resolve these deficiencies for future operational deployment. This nimble process restores forecaster trust and enhances future IDSS delivery.

490228.title: Spatial Observations of Temperature at a New ARM Site
490228.abstract: The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility has recently established a new site at Bankhead National Forest (BNF) with various science goals. A component of the deployment at BNF is a well instrumented tower site within a forested area consisting of multiple towers, including among them measurements of energy fluxes, momentum fluxes, CO2 flux, radiation, temperature, trace gas concentration, cloud measurements, and other important variables of interest. The temperature structure of the forest is being studied with both atmospheric air temperature measurements and InfraRed Temperature sensors (IRTs), with the IRTs on the towers providing both horizontal and vertical resolution of temperature. The tallest (43 meter) tower provides temperatures at three heights from canopy top to ground level. The other two nearby shorter (10 meter) towers provide horizontally distributed sampling of the ground level temperature. In this analysis we will compare the spatial and temporal differences between the IRTs at the tower site to provide an initial look at temperature variability. In order to quantify spatial heterogeneity, the IRTs at the top level of the 43 meter tower are arranged to have one IRT viewing Evergreen tree species and another IRT viewing deciduous tree species. The long term IRT dataset, along with measurements from other site instruments, will support future studies of forest heterogeneity and land-atmosphere interactions and are freely available through the ARM Data Discovery portal.

490229.title: Building a Highly Generalizable Deep Learning Atmosphere Model by Encoding Physical Inductive Biases: From Idealized Aquaplanets to Perturbed SST Experiments
490229.authors: William Junseen Yik, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and D. R. Durran
490229.abstract: Machine learning models have revolutionized weather prediction, but the ability of these models to generalize beyond their training data remains in question. We modify the atmospheric component of DLESyM, a recent deep learning Earth system model, with a particular focus on encoding known physical inductive biases into the model so that it learns invariant atmospheric dynamics. First, we replace the standard convolutions of DLESyM with reflection equivariant convolutions motivated by the symmetry the equations of motion exhibit about the equator. Second, we use partial convolutions to couple partially defined boundary conditions like sea surface temperature and sea ice concentration to the atmosphere, preventing reliance on unphysical infilled or interpolated values. Lastly, we use soft constraints on hydrostatic balance and conservation of dry air mass to encourage physical consistency between predicted fields regardless of the initial conditions. The result is a model which is generalizable to several out of distribution test cases. To demonstrate this, we subject the model to three standardized tests ranging from highly idealized to real world. First, we test DLESyM with an aquaplanet baroclinic wave test, a typical component of the traditional dynamical core testing hierarchy. This test demands that the model both maintain an unstable equilibrium aquaplanet state but also propagate a small instability into a fully developed baroclinic wave within this environment. Here, DLESyM sets itself apart from other machine learning models which quickly show spurious continental imprinting as they revert back to the ERA5-like conditions they were trained on. Additionally, the baroclinic wave formed by DLESyM closely matches that of OpenIFS, a traditional physics based model. Second, we test DLESyM with a test which reverses the latitude of all input fields by reflecting them across the equator. Since the same equations govern the evolution of this reversed latitude atmosphere as the real world atmosphere, we expect that a model should be able to make skillful predictions in both environments. However, we show that DLESyM is unique among machine learning models in its ability to generalize to this reverse latitude world. Third, we conduct several standardized experiments from the AIMIP protocol and report on this version of DLESyM’s performance across these tests in comparison with other machine learning models and a reference physical model. Our results highlight that careful machine learning model design with a particular focus on guiding the model towards learning fundamental dynamics can produce a model which is highly generalizable beyond the historical weather data it was trained on.

490230.title: Evaluating the Predictive Skill of the Deep Learning Earth System Model (DLESyM) for High-Impact Weather Events
490230.authors: Carolyn A. Reynolds, NRL, Monterey, CA; and M. A. Janiga, J. D. Doyle, D. R. Durran, Z. I. Espinosa, and N. A. Cresswell-Clay
490230.abstract: The rapid advancement of data-driven global weather models has opened new avenues for extending the predictive skill of high-impact extratropical weather. This study evaluates the performance of the Deep Learning Earth System Model (DLESyM) in forecasting high-impact events, including atmospheric regime changes and severe cold-air outbreaks. DLESyM is one of the first AI models to explicitly couple the atmosphere to the ocean and has realistic simulations of large-scale modes of variability such as the Arctic Oscillation and blocking frequencies (Cresswell-Clay et al. 2025). We assess DLESyM’s predictive capabilities by comparing its forecast skill against the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Integrated Forecast System (IFS) and the atmosphere-only AI model GraphCast. Using ERA5 reanalysis for initial conditions and verification, we conducted daily 45-day hindcasts spanning September 2020 through August 2021. Preliminary analysis indicates that the deterministic skill of DLESyM version 1 (DLESyM v1) —measured via Anomaly Correlation Coefficient (ACC) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)—is competitive with the state-of-the-art ECMWF IFS for major teleconnection patterns, including the Arctic Oscillation (AO), Pacific-North American (PNA) pattern, and the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO). The deterministic predictive skill of DLESyM for the AO is better than the skill of a climatological forecast for lead times beyond 10 days. This demonstrates the capability of a computationally efficient deep learning model to predict large-scale atmospheric modes of variability. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between these large-scale teleconnections and regional high-impact weather events during the winter of 2020–2021, when a series of intense cold-air outbreaks over the Western Pacific and severe Nor'easters in the Western Atlantic strongly coincided with a sudden stratospheric warming event and pronounced negative phase of the Arctic Oscillation. DLESyM v1 successfully predicts the regional temperature anomalies and 500-hPa height configurations up to two weeks in advance (exhibiting comparable skill to GraphCast). Based on these results, we hypothesize that the model's predictive skill for the large-scale AO enables the accurate forecasts of extreme mid-latitude temperature anomalies. These results underscore the potential of deep learning approaches in Earth System modeling. Our next steps will include a comparison of DLESyM v1 with DLESyM v2, which includes a more sophisticated representation of the ocean, atmosphere and sea ice, and with the Earth System Prediction Capability physics-based global coupled model. We will report on the strengths and weaknesses of the different systems in forecasting these high-impact events at the AMS annual meeting. References: Cresswell-Clay, N., Liu, B., Durran, D. R., Liu, Z., Espinosa, Z. I., Moreno, R. A., & Karlbauer, M. (2025). A deep learning Earth system model for efficient simulation of the observed climate. AGU Advances, 6, e2025AV001706. https://doi.org/10.1029/2025AV001706

490232.title: Forecasting Pyrocumulonimbus across North America with a Spatio-Temporal Deep Learning Model
490232.authors: Lucas Amoudruz, Harvard, Cambridge, MA; and J. Nachamkin, E. Krell, J. Lai, J. A. Dykema, F. Keutsch, P. Koumoutsakos, and D. A. Peterson
490232.abstract: Pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) are thunderstorms triggered by intense wildfires. They are rare but consequential: they produce erratic winds and lightning that can accelerate fire spread and endanger crews on the ground, and they can propel smoke into the lower stratosphere with long-term climate impacts. Today these storms are detected after the fact rather than predicted. Satellite algorithms flag a pyroCb once deep convection is already underway, which is too late to move firefighters, warn aviation, or prepare smoke and air-quality models for a stratospheric injection. Decisions like these need hours of lead time, and with fire seasons lengthening and pyroCb activity increasing, the number of fires that must be watched on any given day is growing well beyond what forecasters can monitor by hand. Machine learning studies have shown that fire and atmospheric conditions together can separate pyroCb-producing fires from curated samples of non-pyroCb fires, so the predictive signal exists. However, operational forecasting is a more challenging task: it must screen every active fire pixel, of which only about 0.1% ever produce a pyroCb, and it must do so ahead of the event rather than diagnose conditions once convection is already underway. We present, to our knowledge, the first system that forecasts pyroCb occurrence hours in advance across the full population of active fires, along with a training and verification methodology for events that are both very rare and imprecisely located in space and time. The model combines hourly fire radiative power from the RAVE emissions product, GOES channel-13 brightness temperature fields, and GFS atmospheric variables, regridded onto common spatio-temporal grids covering 2017–2024. Labels come from the pyroCb event inventory curated by the Naval Research Laboratory, matched to the fire grid in space and time. For each active-fire pixel, a spatio-temporal patch CNN reads a few hours of history over a small surrounding window and outputs the probability that a pyroCb occurs there in the following 3-to-6-hour window. We train this model on 2017–2023, using leave-one-year-out cross-validation for model selection and threshold calibration, and evaluate multi-seed ensembles on a held-out 2024 season with 81 pyroCb events among roughly 76,000 active-fire pixels. The position and time of the detected pyroCb are uncertain. To avoid penalizing near misses, we designed a fuzzy loss that evaluates the predictions over a small spatial and temporal window around each event, with an emphasis on increasing hits over reducing false positives. On the 2024 test year, at an operating threshold calibrated on an independent validation year, the model detects about 70% of observed pyroCb events more than 3 hours ahead of time, at a false-alarm rate manageable for forecaster review. Furthermore, we show that false alarms are signatures of highly convective conditions and intense wildfires. We close with the challenges that remain on the path to operational screening of the active-fire population: interannual variability, satellite artifacts, uncertainty quantification, interpretability, and skill metrics that resist over-prediction.

490233.title: Advancing Operational Flood Monitoring: Integrating Optical and non-US Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) Assets in NOAA Operational Flood Products
490233.authors: William C. Straka III, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and S. Li, X. S. Shen, T. W. Ruff, and M. Y. Murphy
490233.abstract: Flooding remains one of the most destructive global hazards, necessitating rapid, high-resolution spatial awareness for effective forecasting and emergency response. Satellite remote sensing is essential for bridging critical observational gaps where ground-based water gauges are either absent or fail. This presentation highlights recent enhancements to NOAA’s satellite flood mapping products, driven by the synergy between NOAA optical assets and non-U.S. C-Band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) constellations, such as Sentinel-1, RCM, and RADARSAT-2. We examine operational advancements within NOAA’s Global Flood Product suite, which integrates high-temporal observations from the GOES-R ABI with high-resolution imagery from VIIRS instruments aboard JPSS platforms. A significant milestone is the VIIRS 30m Downscaled Flood Depth Product, currently transitioning into operations. By pairing VIIRS and ABI water extent retrievals with high-resolution topographic data, this technique provides continuous 3D flood depth profiles at 30-meter resolution to support localized impact modeling. To mitigate the limitations of optical sensors during cloud-heavy severe storms, we demonstrate the integration of SAR assets, including Sentinel-1, RCM, and Radarsat-2. These active microwave sensors enable all-weather, day-and-night flood mapping, filling crucial observational gaps in cloud-covered regions. Finally, we discuss how operational VIIRS products support international water management through the VIIRS Surface Water Temporal Atlas (VISTA) project. Co-led by the United Nations World Food Programme, the Food and Agriculture Organization, and the EU Joint Research Centre—supported by a Scientific Advisory Group—VISTA leverages NOAA’s 5-day VIIRS flood composite product to advance global flood monitoring, track surface water dynamics, and strengthen early warning systems worldwide.

490235.title: Remote Sensing of Mineral Dust Physical Properties and Vertical Profiles in Oklahoma, U.S.A.
490235.authors: Hayden Murphy Webb, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and S. M. Loria-Salazar, C. J. Flynn, H. Moosmuller, and M. Saito
490235.abstract: The Southern Great Plains region, particularly Oklahoma, experiences a wide range of aerosol activities influenced by both local emissions and long-range transport. Although previous studies in this region have focused on wildfire-emitted black carbon, mineral dust has received comparatively less attention. Oklahoma is frequently affected by elevated dust concentrations from local agricultural activities and transported dust from states such as Texas and New Mexico. To better understand dust’s aerosol physical properties, we study several dust plumes in Oklahoma during the spring and summer of 2023 to 2026. Specifically, aerosol optical depth (AOD), single scattering albedo (SSA), and extinction Ångström exponent (EAE) are characterized through in situ measurements at the Southern Great Plains (SGP) ARM Facility, ground-based remote sensing from NASA’s AEROENT network, and NASA satellite retrievals from DSCOVR EPIC MAIAC. These results are compared with vertical profiles derived from lidar observations (HSRL, MPL, and Raman) from the ARM SGP, as well as with modeled mineral dust properties. This study aims to reduce uncertainties in the direct radiative effect of mineral dust, which are largely attributed to variations in its composition and its evolution during transport.

490244.title: Vertical Coherence Dominates Decadal Land Water Storage Change Despite Hydroclimatic Extremes and Groundwater Pumping
490244.authors: Meng Zhao, Univ. of Idaho, Moscow, ID
490244.abstract: Whether surface and deeper water storage trends move in the same direction underpins assessments of freshwater availability. Theory predicts vertical coherence, yet it is untested globally and questioned under climate extremes and human management. Using depth-sensitive satellite observations spanning surface soil moisture (SSM) (Soil Moisture Active Passive) and total terrestrial water storage (GRACE/FO) for 2015–2025, we assess the vertical organization of multi-year land water change across ∼78 million km2 of land. We find that vertical coherence dominates, with same-sign surface and total storage trends across >70% of the analyzed area. Satellite Normalized Difference Vegetation Index reinforces this pattern, aligning with coherent trends and tracking deeper storage where surface and total trends diverge. Divergence is spatially clustered and linked to repeated hydroclimatic extremes or intensive groundwater abstraction. These results provide the first global observational test of vertical coherence in land water storage change, showing it remains dominant but can be weakened by depth-selective climatic and anthropogenic pressures.

490257.title: Quantifying Fresh Lightning NOx Production from the TEMPO and GLM Instruments
490257.authors: Zachary Thomas Watson, The University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and A. R. Naeger and K. M. Murphy
490257.abstract: Nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted from lightning are the dominant source of NOx in the upper troposphere and have significant impacts on the atmospheric composition and radiative forcing. Estimating the production efficiency (PE) of NOx emitted per lightning flash has large uncertainties and has recently been estimated using polar-orbiting satellite observations of nitrogen dioxide (NO2) over active thunderstorms, which have limited spatial and temporal coverage. Now, the Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) and Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) platforms provide continuous monitoring of NO2 and lightning, respectively, over North America throughout the day. In this work, we use a statistical approach to estimate the diurnal cycle of NOx PE over North America during the 2026 warm season (April-September). First, TEMPO observations and Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF) model simulations are used to calculate a NOx air mass factor to convert tropospheric NO2 slant column densities to NOx vertical column densities. Then, we use two different methods for calculating NOx PE: the first divides total moles of NOx from TEMPO by the GLM flash count, and the second uses a linear regression approach to relate total NOx to lightning flashes. Finally, we perform sensitivity testing for how parameters such as spatial resolution, solar zenith angle, cloud fraction, cloud pressure, and minimum flash rate thresholds affect the PE calculation and the associated uncertainties for the geostationary platform. This work will provide a first look at the diurnal cycle of NOx PE and its uncertainties from geostationary NO2 and lightning measurements.

490261.title: From Ensembles to Action: Translating AI Weather Uncertainty for Consumers and Enterprise
490261.authors: Thomas Turnbull, Google, Brooklyn, NY; and R. Galt, A. Uddin, F. Bartolić, N. Williams, and A. Bond
490261.abstract: Modern AI weather models, such as Google’s WeatherNext, can now generate massive global ensemble forecasts in seconds. Yet a fundamental challenge persists: better forecast data provides little value if it cannot be used to make a decision. Traditional approaches often overwhelm users with complex data spreads or lead them to collapse nuanced probabilities into brittle binary assumptions (“it will rain” vs. “it won’t”). In this talk, we share early insights and lessons learned from deploying uncertainty features in Weather Lab, Google’s public platform showcasing frontier AI weather and cyclone models. By providing interactive, point-based uncertainty charts for any location on the globe, Weather Lab serves as an active sandbox for exploring how users and domain specialists engage with ensemble variance. Drawing on user experience research into how people understand probabilistic information, we examine how Large Language Models (LLMs) like Gemini can serve as a translation layer. We explore prototype concepts and design patterns where natural language summaries support visual charts, helping contextualize forecast confidence, explain scenario ranges, and translate ensemble distributions into clear takeaways for everyday planning and enterprise decision making.

490262.title: Development of SynFlux Version 2, an Expanded Dataset for Ozone Dry Deposition and Model Evaluation
490262.authors: Kelly Graham, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and C. Holmes
490262.abstract: Ozone (O3) deposition to the land surface is a major loss of tropospheric ozone, an air pollutant. In vegetated regions, this deposition occurs through stomatal uptake into leaves and non-stomatal uptake to vegetation and soil surfaces. Within the leaves, ozone damages plant growth, reduces photosynthetic rates, and impairs stomatal regulation. Consequently, accurately quantifying the stomatal ozone uptake is critical for understanding air quality and biosphere impacts. The synthetic ozone flux (SynFlux) dataset provides estimates of ozone dry deposition at a network of sites by fusing data from eddy covariance flux towers and air quality monitors. This work describes SynFlux version 2 (SynFlux 2), which includes several improvements. SynFlux 2 better partitions water vapor fluxes into the evaporation and transpiration components, which improves stomatal conductance estimates, and expands the temporal and spatial coverage of the dataset to hundreds of sites worldwide. SynFlux 2 aims to improve deposition modeling through insight into the physical pathways governing gas exchange within vegetation.

490267.title: Renewable Energy Modeling over Chile Using the 3.25 km E3SM-EAMxx Regionally Refined Model
490267.authors: Jishi Zhang, UC Davis, Davis, CA; and J. C. Golaz, A. Flores-Quiroz, S. Po-Chedley, R. S. Arthur, I. Perez, M. Signorotti, M. Monteagudo, J. Wert, J. P. Watson, and E. Monier
490267.abstract: Wind and solar power generation depend on atmospheric conditions that vary over short spatial and temporal scales, making high-fidelity atmospheric simulations important for renewable resource assessment, grid planning, and operations. This need is particularly acute in regions with complex terrain and diverse climate regimes, where insufficient model resolution can lead to substantial errors in estimated generation potential. Chile provides a valuable test case because of its abundant wind and solar resources, their significant contribution to electricity generation, and its highly diverse and complex topography, which makes the region challenging to model. We conduct a long-term, present-day hindcast over Chile using the 3.25-km E3SM-SCREAM C++ (EAMxx) regionally refined model, driven by ERA5 boundary conditions, and convert simulated meteorology into wind and solar generation using the NLR-SAM model. The results are evaluated against hourly plant-level generation and curtailment records from Chile’s National Electric System. The observed generation reflects not only atmospheric resource availability but also grid constraints, plant operations, and parameters not represented in simplified generation models, complicating direct attribution of generation biases to atmospheric model errors. Despite these limitations, the observations provide rare and valuable data for evaluating the utility of high-resolution atmospheric downscaling simulations insimulating wind and solar energy generation.

490273.title: Development of an Atmospheric and Geographical Data Preprocessor Application and Data Ingest Process for the GeoFLuid Object Workbench (GeoFLOW) Framework
490273.authors: Timothy Sliwinski, CIRA, Boulder, CO; and D. Rosenberg and I. Safarik
490273.abstract: The GeoFLuid Object Workbench (GeoFLOW) is a variable-order numerical partial differential equation framework under active development at NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL). GeoFLOW aims to provide computationally efficient, high-order, low dissipation numerics that are capable of fully leveraging exascale computing resources in an effort to examine and improve the accuracy of numerical treatments of atmospheric and weather phenomena (Rosenberg, et. al. 2023). Several efforts at GSL have already utilized GeoFLOW to investigate idealized atmospheric flows similar to those of wildfire plumes and mountain-induced high-altitude internal waves. However, without the capability to ingest external information from operational models, observational datasets, or geographical datasets, none of these previous efforts used real-world boundary forcings, initial conditions, or terrain. Therefore, to advance GeoFLOW’s capabilities to examine real-world atmospheric phenomenology, the GeoFLOW PreProcessor (GPP) was developed. GPP is a new parallel Python application inspired by previous preprocessor systems such as the WRF Preprocessor System (WPS). Starting from a JSON input file describing operational model and terrain data over a specific time period and geographical region of interest, GPP generates a suitable GeoFLOW grid with or without terrain and then performs a series of geographical projections, coordinate transformations, grid interpolations, and output data formatting. The resulting output is an array of flat binary files containing information on initial and time-varying lateral boundary conditions for atmospheric state variables (currently, temperature, moisture, density, and U, V, W wind components). These outputs can then be read in by the newly updated GeoFLOW framework as boundary and initial conditions for atmospheric flow simulations. At present, this process is constrained to using only 3km horizontal resolution data from the High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) forecasting model as input for both atmospheric and terrain data. However, the framework is designed to be extensible to other operational forecasting models and geographical datasets in the future. To seamlessly hand off information to GeoFLOW, GPP was designed to transform and interpolate input data from HRRR’s simple structured rectangular discretization to GeoFLOW’s spectral element discretization, which uses a set of Lagrange interpolating polynomials whose node points define the grid points (Rosenberg, et. al. 2023). This results in an unstructured mesh of irregularly-spaced grid points that can be characterized by an average “target” grid resolution within each element. To ensure consistency between GPP and GeoFLOW, GPP uses Python wrappers around GeoFLOW’s C++ grid-generation library to build grids directly using identical JSON configuration information as would be used for a GeoFLOW simulation with or without terrain. This approach allows future updates to GeoFLOW’s grid-generation process to become available to GPP automatically, without duplicating the implementation. This presentation will highlight important elements of the architecture and development process, discuss performance and MPI parallel scalability, and present initial results of GPP-initialized GeoFLOW simulations using realistic boundary forcings and initial conditions. We will also discuss ongoing developments and plans for new capabilities, such as support for additional atmospheric variables, external terrain data sources like GMTED2010, and future NOAA operational models based on unstructured meshes (e.g RRFS based on MPAS). Works Cited: Rosenberg, D., B. Flynt, M. Govett, and I. Jankov, 2023: Geofluid Object Workbench (GeoFLOW) for Atmospheric Dynamics in the Approach to Exascale: Spectral Element Formulation and CPU Performance. Mon. Wea. Rev., 151, 2521-2540. https://doi.org/10.1175/MWR-D-22-0250.1

490277.title: Subseasonal North Pacific Ocean Wave Prediction
490277.authors: Matthew A. Janiga, NRL, Monterey, CA; and E. Rogers, S. S. Rushley, C. Paquette, and W. Crawford
490277.abstract: Hazardous ocean surface winds and waves pose a significant risk to maritime navigation, yet their prediction at extended ranges remains a complex challenge. This study investigates the modulation of wave conditions by subseasonal modes of variability and assesses their relationship with wave prediction skill in the Navy Earth System Prediction Capability (Navy ESPC), a coupled global Earth system model. We analyze overall model skill at predicting wave heights at extended-range time scales and examine linkages with the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), Pacific North American (PNA) pattern, and North Pacific Jet (NPJ). In addition, we evaluate the prediction skill of extreme swell events that are a leading cause of inundation for Kwajalein Atoll. A cluster analysis of sea level pressure anomalies over the last 20 years reveals that most extreme swell events fall under two types: (1) extreme cyclones within the climatological storm track in which most wave energy is directed westward, and (2) slightly less intense cyclones located at the southern periphery of the storm track with more southward-directed wave energy. The inundation event of January 2024 is classified as a Type 2 event. Navy ESPC simulations are able to capture the key features of this cyclone and associated wave heights at extended ranges. Finally, we explore the role of MJO and NPJ fidelity in the ability of the model to capture cyclone intensity and its unusual southward track.

490280.title: Coastal-Urban Flooding Under Future Climate Conditions: A Multi-Scale Probabilistic Modeling Framework for Community Resilience Planning
490280.authors: Peyman Taeb, Woods Hole Group, Bourne, MA; and B. Raymond and K. Bosma
490280.abstract: Coastal-urban flooding is increasingly controlled by interactions among regional storm forcing, sea-level rise, local topography, shoreline infrastructure, and the built environment. In densely developed coastal communities, flood impacts are rarely governed by a single water level alone. Instead, flooding depends on storm characteristics, tidal timing, wave effects, low-lying entry points, roadway corridors, seawalls, dunes, buildings, and subtle changes in ground elevation that determine when hydraulic connections open and how floodwater moves through neighborhoods. This presentation would describe a multi-scale coastal-urban flood modeling framework developed to support climate-informed resilience planning across Massachusetts coastal communities. The regional component uses a probabilistic coastal hazard dataset generated from a large ensemble of physically based storm simulations. Rather than relying on a single design storm, this approach represents a broad range of plausible coastal conditions, including varying storm tracks, intensities, timing, exceedance probabilities, sea-level-rise scenarios, and future climate horizons. These simulations provide the regional hazard context needed to evaluate present-day and future flood conditions. The local component translates this regional hazard information into high-resolution urban hydrodynamic analyses. Project-scale models are developed using detailed terrain, shoreline, and infrastructure data to resolve local controls on flooding, including streets, coastal gaps, seawalls, berms, redevelopment grading, buildings, and other hydraulic constrictions. These models allow water levels, flood depths, flow directions, velocities, and hydraulic connectivity to be evaluated under selected present and future conditions. Applications across multiple project sites show that similar regional coastal hazard conditions can produce very different neighborhood-scale flood responses. In some locations, flooding is controlled by a limited number of shoreline pathways where small differences in crest elevation or site grading determine whether large inland areas become connected to coastal flooding. In other locations, multiple competing pathways allow floodwater to bypass a single line of protection, making it important to understand the broader system of hydraulic connections. In redevelopment areas, proposed changes to site grading or shoreline features can modify not only flood extent, but also velocity patterns, flow redistribution toward adjacent corridors or low-lying parcels, and influence wave dynamics including runup and overtopping. The value of this framework is that it connects probabilistic coastal hazard information with physical explanations of local flood behavior. Instead of presenting future risk only as a mapped flood extent or return-period water level, the workflow helps identify dominant flood entry points, the sequence of pathway activation, areas of potential flow concentration, and locations where adaptation measures may reduce risk or unintentionally redirect flooding. This is particularly important for municipalities and project teams that must compare present-day and future conditions, prioritize limited resources, and evaluate resilience strategies in complex urban settings.

490281.title: Object-Based Climatology and Verification of the MJO
490281.authors: Matthew A. Janiga, NRL, Monterey, CA; and S. S. Rushley
490281.abstract: Traditional Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) indices project complex variability onto a simplified two-dimensional phase space, a process that often masks the significant event-to event diversity of this key climate driver. To retain this complexity, we introduce a tracking method based on wavenumber-frequency filtered precipitation that identifies MJO events as distinct, three-dimensional spatiotemporal objects. Tracking is applied to precipitation from the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) (IMERG) satellite estimates and the ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis. Applying a clustering algorithm to these objects reveals distinct types of MJO events. In both summer and winter, one cluster represents the canonical MJO—fast, long-lived, and intense—while other clusters are characterized by slower, shorter-lived, and weaker events confined to specific regions. A key finding regarding these events is a specific succession preference among winter MJO types. Events confined to the South Pacific Convergence Zone (SPCZ) frequently act as precursors to intense, long-lived events, whereas Indian Ocean events terminating at the Maritime Continent often follow them. Moreover, while individual convective anomalies propagate eastward, the locus of MJO generation shifts westward, effectively creating a stationary envelope of activity with a near-zero group velocity consistent with previous studies. Composites of extratropical teleconnections based on MJO track location possess signal-to noise ratios comparable to those from the global Realtime Multivariate MJO (RMM) index. We further find that the strength of teleconnections to the Pacific North-American (PNA) and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) modes increases with the volumetric rainfall of the MJO objects, suggesting a link between the magnitude of diabatic heating and the excitation of Rossby waves. We conclude by introducing new verification metrics that leverage the rich properties of the MJO tracks, examining how predictability varies across MJO types and discussing the implications for subseasonal prediction.

490282.title: NOAA's Experimental High Resolution Monthly High Tide Flooding Outlook: Bringing a Stakeholder Engagement Approach to State-of-the-Science Innovation
490282.authors: Karen Kavanaugh, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and C. S. Lewis and M. P. Conlin
490282.abstract: NOAA’s Monthly High Tide Flooding (HTF) Outlook provides daily likelihoods of flood threshold exceedance at a subset of NOAA tide gauges up to a year in advance using a statistical model that incorporates the astronomical tide predictions, recent sea level anomalies, and historic seasonal variation in water levels. The Monthly HTF Outlook strives to provide improved situational awareness to impacted coastal users. The development of the Monthly HTF Outlook has been part of a larger strategic framework to align corporate priorities for products and data through a replicable stakeholder engagement framework to ensure that meaningful information is provided. Key findings from virtual focus groups and informal interviews are highlighted, including ways that interagency and intraoffice collaboration has complemented this engagement approach. Examples are provided of how user input was prioritized and incorporated into recent product enhancements. For instance, initial interviews about the Monthly HTF Outlook revealed that its advanced flood risk information helped local planners allocate response staff and resources. However, flooding is a hyper-local process so it was unsurprising that stakeholders overwhelmingly expressed the need for expanding the Monthly HTF Outlook coverage to include areas between the NOAA tide gauges.
