To address this data gap, NOAA developed an experimental high resolution version of the Monthly HTF Outlook for the U.S. Gulf and East Coasts, which leveraged the Coastal Ocean Reanalysis to provide predictions at a spatially-continuous 400-500 m resolution along a large portion of the U.S. shoreline. The legacy outlook model was only run relative to the National Ocean Service minor flood threshold for NOAA tide gauges, but many users noted that this either over- or under-estimated when flood impacts actually occurred locally; the experimental product introduces 5 new flood threshold categories in 0.5ft increments above the MHHW datum to allow users to pick a vertical height that better captures when flooding actually occurs and support better scenario planning. This new experimental product was developed in consultation with stakeholders throughout the process, and engagement efforts will continue during this experimental phase to identify the design and technical requirements for future improvements to the Monthly HTF Outlook and underlying research needs for subseasonal to seasonal flood forecasts.

490295.title: Piloting a Partner-Focused Wildfire Alerting Process with Select NWS Forecast Offices
490295.authors: David Hogg, Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis, Norman, OK; and J. T. Ripberger, M. Krocak, K. Gupta, E. F. Meister, A. C. Wanless, M. O. Mattox, T. Lindley, A. Anderson, C. J. Lewellyn, K. Kryc, R. Roth, and A. Philp
490295.abstract: Researchers at the University of Oklahoma Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis, along with collaborators at the Oklahoma Mesonet and MITRE Corporation, are partnering with National Weather Service Forecast Offices (WFOs) in three distinct regions of the continental United States to conduct a year-long pilot project. This pilot aims to examine the feasibility, challenges, and required local adaptations associated with issuing short-fuse, polygon-based tactical Fire Warnings. Such warnings would provide the public early notice of an active wildfire threat ahead of locally-issued evacuation orders. Sites for the pilot project include WFOs in South Carolina, New Mexico, and Minnesota. These sites were selected across different regions of the country to represent a wide range of fire environments and fire cultures, with an intentional awareness of varied risk profiles and challenges in approaching the wildfire problem. This work involves significant partner engagement, both in aligning the new process with existing public alerting practices and in identifying realistic workflows during active fire response. Project personnel are working with local WFO staff to identify key personnel from local emergency management and fire departments, state forestry and state emergency management offices, federal land management and fire partners, and tribal nations. Each pilot project begins with a kickoff meeting and workshop, in the vein of an Integrated Warning Team meeting. The purpose of the kickoff meeting is to introduce the project, discuss pilot objectives, identify training needs, and begin exploring potential solutions to overcome local challenges and concerns around wildfire alerting. Initial impressions, lessons learned, and partner survey feedback from the pilot workshops will be shared with attendees, alongside the larger goals and inputs that are being tested through this project. The goal is to improve the National Weather Service’s capabilities to issue effective and timely wildfire alerts, thereby improving public awareness and safety.

490296.title: Characterization of Aerosols and Population Exposure over the African Continent Using Two Decades of MODIS and MERRA-2 Data
490296.authors: Zachary Thomas Watson, The University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and P. Gupta, C. Li, and S. Lee
490296.abstract: In recent decades, the African continent has been experiencing rapid population growth, but its air quality has been understudied due to a lack of ground-based measurements despite high aerosol loading. In this work, we performed the first comprehensive analysis of aerosols over the African continent by characterizing the concentrations, chemical speciation, spatiotemporal trends, and population exposure in aerosols over the African continent and its subregions from 2005-2024 from Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), Modern Era Retrospective Reanalysis Version 2 (MERRA-2), and Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET) datasets. The average aerosol optical depth (AOD) values over the African continent are 0.30 for MODIS and 0.28 for MERRA-2. Additionally, the average fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentration of 33.6 µg m-3, 6.7 times higher than the World Health Organization (WHO) Air Quality Guideline (AQG). Over Africa, AOD and PM2.5 were mainly dominated by dust and biomass burning emissions with seasonal variations driven by meteorology and fire activity. AODs from MODIS and MERRA-2 compared well with AERONET measurements, and MERRA-2 speciated AODs were consistent with aerosol optical properties from AERONET. Despite a rapid increase in population and economic productivity from 2005-2024, there were no consistent trends in AOD or PM2.5. Even with nearly constant aerosol loading, there was a substantial increase in pollution exposure. The number of people exposed to PM2.5 exceeding the highest WHO threshold (>35 µg m-3) significantly increased from 340,000,000 in 2005 to 610,000,000 in 2024, showcasing the need for improving and expanding ground-based air quality monitoring networks across the continent.

490297.title: Becoming Bigger Than Texas: Expanding the Size and Scope of AI/ML NWP Emulators at Convective Scales
490297.authors: Logan Ray Schmidtz, Texas Tech Univ., Lubbock, TX; and B. C. Ancell and C. K. Potvin
490297.abstract: Traditional numerical weather prediction (NWP) methods have been utilized in atmospheric science research with considerable success for decades. However, the use of NWP on a convective-permitting scale in a large, static domain can be very computationally expensive limiting the variability and completion in a timely manner. This cost becomes even more expensive with the use of ensemble simulations at those scales. The use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has been exponentially increasing in the last decade to aid in increasing skill, variability, and forecast lead time. There has been success in forecasting weather patterns globally by emulating ERA5 reanalysis data (e.g., Pangu-Weather, GraphCast, and FourCastNet) and some AI/ML models have shown promising results at convective scales by emulating NWP models (e.g., HRRRCast, WoFSCast). In particular, WoFSCast uses simulations from the Warn on Forecast System (WoFS), a storm-scale ensemble-based data assimilation and forecasting framework, to emulate traditional physics-based forecasts of attributes of convection such as simulated reflectivity. WoFSCast uses the graph neural network architecture developed for GraphCast, but runs on a small, dynamic domain producing a frequent storm-scale prediction in a few seconds with skill that rivals the traditional methods of WoFS. Few studies have tested the performance of AI/ML emulators against traditional models at such scales for different temporal resolutions, convective variables, and training parameters (e.g., length of training dataset). Here, a WoFSCast-based AI/ML emulator will be examined to evaluate such skill over a much larger, static domain to assess the impact of prediction interval (5–60 min) on model performance. Results will be discussed in terms of the usefulness of convective-scale emulators in ensemble prediction systems.

490298.title: Progress Updates on Community Modeling for Advancing Data Assimilation from a Program Office Perspective
490298.authors: Jan Ising, NOAA, Broomfield, CO; and M. Huang, J. Vogt, and J. E. Ten Hoeve III
490298.abstract: The Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC) under the NOAA Weather Program Office (WPO) supports community modeling data assimilation (DA) advancements for numerical weather prediction applications centered around the Unified Forecast System (UFS). These include entities across a wide range of applications such as the EPIC contract, the WPO Innovation for Next-Generation Scientists (WINGS) Ph.D dissertation fellowship, the Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA), and the Consortium for Advanced Data Assimilation Research and Education (CADRE). Broadly speaking, EPIC provides open-source code governance, cloud and on-premise hosted high-performance computing (HPC), and automated continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) test harnesses required to advance the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework. By eliminating traditional security barriers to operational codebases, EPIC enables researchers across academia, private industry, and interagency partners to co-develop, benchmark, and validate new observation operators, error covariance formulations, and artificial intelligence/machine learning-hybrid DA workflows. EPIC additionally cultivates workforce capacity through targeted partnerships, hands-on workshops, and training events. These programmatic investments democratize access to complex Earth system modeling architectures, empower early-career scientists, and sustain an efficient Research-to-Operations-to-Research (R2O2R) transition pipeline. This presentation plans to cover community DA developments from a program office perspective over the past year such as developing easy to understand DA diagnostics capabilities, building the next generation workforce, hosting community workshops, advancing the UFS DA system, supporting HPC and bringing the community together to discuss the science and workforce behind DA. Students and early career professionals are strongly encouraged to attend.

490300.title: When Data Feeds Drop: Hurricane Crosswind Exceedance Sensitivity to Satellite and In Situ Data Denial
490300.authors: Casey L Zoellick, Air Force Institute of Technology, Dayton, OH; and M. P. King and S. A. Stanton
490300.abstract: Numerical weather prediction relies on continuous observational data streams to update background states and initialize forecasts. Under standard operations, ingesting these streams requires constant system monitoring; however, technical disruptions or contested cyber environments can deliberately deny or manipulate key data feeds before reaching modeling centers. While global models degrade rapidly when satellite data are withheld, regional models forecasting localized phenomena—such as surface wind direction—depend heavily on in situ observations. Aviation forecasts are exceptionally sensitive to these fine-scale model variations, particularly within the terminal area. This study evaluates the operational consequences of intentional data denial on regional NWP forecasts during a landfalling hurricane. Two experimental simulations, withholding either satellite-based or in situ observations, are compared against a control run incorporating all available observational data. Operational impacts are assessed using the forecast onset and duration of crosswinds at increasing operational thresholds at a coastal military aerodrome. Evaluating model output through this terminal-focused lens demonstrates how specific observation degradations alter boundary-layer wind field evolution, directly influencing forecaster guidance and operational lead times.

490302.title: From Snow-Powered PIV to GAIA: Imaging the Atmospheric Boundary Layer Across Scales (Invited Presentation)
490302.authors: Jiarong Hong, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN; Particle4X, Inc., Minneapolis, MN
490302.abstract: More than a decade ago, our effort to understand flows around utility-scale wind turbines led us to ask whether natural snowfall could be used as tracer particles for field-scale particle image velocimetry. This work led to the development of snow-powered super-large-scale particle image velocimetry (SLPIV). Initial measurements visualized coherent structures in the wake of a 2.5 MW wind turbine, while companion atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) measurements validated key flow statistics through comparisons with coincident sonic anemometer measurements. Together, these studies established snow PIV as a technique for obtaining spatially and temporally resolved velocity fields across measurement domains spanning tens of meters in the real atmosphere. With the technique established, snow PIV was applied to a series of studies examining wind-turbine flows and their interactions with the ABL. Measurements of vortical coherent structures in the incoming flow showed that the size and direction of rotation of these structures influence turbine loading, power generation, and wake behavior. A complementary investigation identified turbine-operation-dependent pathways through which the wake intermittently interacts with the ground and enhances surface momentum flux. These studies linked the instantaneous spatial organization of atmospheric turbulence to turbine response and wake-induced near-surface transport. Snow PIV was then naturally extended to investigate the ABL itself. Measurements in a very-high-Reynolds-number, fully rough atmospheric surface layer revealed inclined vortical structures consistent with hairpin packets, together with uniform-momentum zones and the shear interfaces separating them. These observations linked canonical wall-turbulence concepts established through laboratory experiments and simulations to the spatial organization of turbulence in the real atmosphere. Building on these near-surface measurements, subsequent field campaigns combined snow PIV with two scanning Doppler wind lidars, expanding the observable range and enabling investigation of the interplay between large outer-flow structures and turbulence closer to the surface. This multiscale approach provided a more complete view of how atmospheric motions across different layers and spatial scales are dynamically connected. More recently, the progression toward mobile, three-dimensional atmospheric observations has continued with the development of the Grand-scale Atmospheric Imaging Apparatus (GAIA). GAIA is an autonomous drone-swarm system that combines coordinated flight, multiview imaging, and onboard particle sensing to map evolving atmospheric flows and particle transport over large spatial domains. This talk will trace the development from snow-powered PIV to multiscale ground-based measurements and, ultimately, autonomous aerial imaging, highlighting the new opportunities these techniques create for studying atmospheric flow and particle transport.

490306.title: Community Engagement through the Unified Forecast System Research to Operations (UFS-R2O) Project: Lessons learned and path forward for NOAA’s Modeling Grand Challenge Initiative
490306.authors: Vijay S. Tallapragada, NCEP, College Park, MD; NOAA, Riverdale Park, MD; and J. L. Kinter and J. S. Whitaker
490306.abstract: The Unified Forecast System Research to Operations (UFS-R2O) Project completed six years (2020-2026) of collaborative effort, significantly advancing UFS applications for operational use. Funded jointly by NOAA’s NWS Office of Science and Technology Integration (OSTI) and the Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR) Weather Program Office (WPO), the project fostered crucial partnerships between NCEP/EMC, NOAA research labs, NCAR, NRL, and various academic institutions. The project was led by three representatives (NOAA operations, NOAA research, and the academic community) and structured around three integrated applications teams: Medium Range Weather/Subseasonal to Seasonal (MRW/S2S), Short Range Weather/Convection Allowing Modeling (SRW/CAM), and Hurricane Modeling. These were supported by cross-cutting teams focused on areas including Atmospheric Composition, Data Assimilation, and Modeling Infrastructure. The leadership structure featured shared responsibility between NWS operations and community representatives for each team. UFS-R2O project achieved substantial successes, including the operational transition of several key systems along with numerous enhancements to UFS components and infrastructure including the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) and its annual upgrades, Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFSv1) for North America, a fully coupled Global Forecast System (GFSv17), a beta version of the Seasonal Forecast System (SFSv1), the Global Aerosol and Chemistry Forecast System (GCAFS), and the EMC Verification System (EVS). While successfully uniting UFS developers with a sharp focus on operational outcomes, challenges included maintaining consistent funding levels and ensuring alignment with the broader UFS team structure and community. NOAA aims to advance the skill of numerical weather prediction models by bringing academia, industry, and the U.S. government together to produce the world’s best forecast system. The new NOAA Modeling Moonshot (also known as modeling grand challenge) is aimed at modernizing the operational modeling suite through a transformation to advanced software and cloud-based HPC architectures, expansion of hybrid data-driven (AI) & physics-based ensemble prediction systems, and the adoption of the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) for a global, coupled, km-scale ensemble system driven by a continuously-operating data assimilation (DA) system. Key lessons learned and insights from the UFS-R2O project leadership will be presented, highlighting their potential application to guide the development efforts for meeting the objectives of NOAA’s Modeling Grand Challenge initiative.

490310.title: Mining with MetaGem: A Human-in-the-Loop LLM Workflow for Extracting Weather Research Portfolio Data
490310.authors: Castle A. Williamsberg, FedWriters Supporting NOAA's Weather Program Office, Athens, GA; and I. M. Renta López and A. Arnold
490310.abstract: NOAA’s Weather Program Office (WPO) manages a diverse portfolio of research and development (R&D) aimed at improving operational weather forecasts, effectively delivering life-saving weather information, and meeting the public’s growing forecast needs. In 2023, WPO consolidated project information previously maintained in separate program spreadsheets into a centralized Project Directory. This created a structured data source that can be easily queried across WPO’s entire research portfolio, reducing the administrative burden associated with agency-wide reporting and Congressional data requests. However, entering new project information into the directory remained a time-consuming and tedious process that limited staff capacity for higher-value strategic thinking. To address this challenge, WPO’s Portfolio Analysis and Research Transitions (PART) Program developed MetaGem, a human-in-the-loop workflow that uses Google’s Gemini large language model (LLM) to transform funded research proposals into structured project metadata. Rather than asking the LLM to extract everything at once, MetaGem uses a series of prompts, each designed to identify a specific type of project information, such as a project’s title, anticipated outputs, societal benefits, and relevant weather hazards. For each prompt, MetaGem provides the extracted data, shows where it found the supporting evidence in the proposal, and indicates how confident it is in the result. The project metadata is then presented in a Google Sheets-based Reviewer Tool, where WPO staff compare it with the original proposal, make any changes, and approve the information before it is automatically transferred to our Project Directory. This presentation will unpack how MetaGem turns valuable project information locked away in proposal PDFs into structured portfolio data that can be searched and analyzed for patterns and strategic insights. We will share design decisions, our iterative testing approach, and evaluation practices that helped move MetaGem from concept into a practical, human-centered workflow. Attendees will learn how breaking down a complex task into smaller prompts, linking every result to supporting evidence, making uncertainty visible through confidence assessments, protecting sensitive information, and building evaluation into the workflow from the beginning can help organizations unlock their own document collections. In doing so, MetaGem offers a practical, human-in-the-loop blueprint for transforming static scientific documents into actionable portfolio intelligence across the Weather, Water, and Climate Enterprise.

490315.title: Generation of a Whole Atmosphere Reanalysis Using WACCM-X and DART
490315.abstract: Atmosphere reanalyses are widely used in the terrestrial weather and climate communities, and have been essential in the development of AI weather models. However, the typical upper boundary of reanalyses is ~60 km, preventing their use for studying the mesosphere, thermosphere, and ionosphere. By combining the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model with thermosphere-ionosphere eXtension (WACCM-X) with the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART), we present results of a whole atmosphere reanalysis. WACCM-X extends from the surface to the upper thermosphere (~500 km), enabling assimilation of observations across an extended altitude range. Here we present results from an initial version of a WACCM-X/DART reanalysis that assimilates observations from the surface to ~100 km and covers the time period from 2005-2020. The results show that the WACCM-X/DART reanalysis is capable of capturing the dynamical and chemical variability throughout the whole atmosphere that occurs on time scales ranging from days to years.

490317.title: The Spatial Structure of Air-Sea Latent Heat Fluxes across Eastern North Pacific Atmospheric Rivers
490317.authors: Darren L. Jackson, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and G. A. Wick
490317.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are often described as narrow corridors that transport tropical moisture into the midlatitudes, yet the role of local air–sea interaction in sustaining these systems remains uncertain. While strong surface winds within ARs might be expected to enhance ocean evaporation, recent studies suggest that elevated near-surface humidity suppresses turbulent heat fluxes. This study investigates the climatological structure of air–sea turbulent heat fluxes associated with eastern North Pacific atmospheric rivers and assesses the ability of commonly used gridded flux products to represent these exchanges. Composite analyses of 149 landfalling West Coast ARs (2013–2018) using ERA5, SeaFlux, and OAFlux reveal a coherent spatial pattern in latent heat flux (LHF). Despite the strongest winds and largest integrated vapor transport (IVT), the AR core exhibits substantially reduced LHF because warm, humid boundary-layer air weakens the air–sea humidity gradient. The greatest suppression occurs near the downstream end of the AR and on the equatorward side of the AR axis, where specific humidity anomalies exceed +2.5 g kg⁻¹ and LHF is reduced by approximately 50 W m⁻² (about 50%) relative to climatology. In contrast, enhanced LHF occurs upstream and poleward of the AR core, where colder, drier air flowing over warm ocean waters produces larger air–sea temperature and humidity differences. This upstream enhancement becomes progressively stronger for extreme ARs (IVT >1000 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹), suggesting that local ocean evaporation preferentially contributes moisture before air parcels enter the AR core rather than beneath the core itself. Comparisons with three independent ship encounters confirm the observed reduction of LHF within ARs but also reveal that ERA5 and satellite-based flux products generally overestimate LHF during the most humid conditions because they underestimate near-surface specific humidity. These results demonstrate that the spatial distribution of air–sea exchange across atmospheric rivers is fundamentally controlled by near-surface thermodynamic gradients rather than wind speed alone and highlight the importance of accurately representing boundary-layer humidity when assessing local oceanic moisture contributions to AR evolution.

490318.title: A Vision for the Next Generation of the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System
490318.authors: Jason A. Sippel, AOML, Miami, FL; and S. Gopalakrishnan, Z. Zhang, A. Aksoy, D. Wu, and W. Ramstrom
490318.abstract: This presentation discusses the development of a next-generation modeling and data assimilation (DA) framework for NOAA’s Unified Forecast System (UFS) based Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS), NOAA’s current operational hurricane forecast model. HAFS has generally been successful compared to the previous generation of hurricane models, with substantial track improvements at all lead times. Despite this success, HAFS short-term intensity forecasts have not been as skillful, a problem related to shortcomings in how HAFS assimilates data from the hurricane inner core. As such, the ongoing effort leverages a multi-storm implementation of HAFS (HAFS-M) to advance HAFS data assimilation (DA) using the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) infrastructure. The HAFS-M configuration, with multiple moving nests embedded within a static parent domain, facilitates DA approaches that are not feasible in the current storm-centric version of HAFS, where the outer domain is repositioned every forecast cycle. First and foremost, this configuration allows for straightforward generation of mesoscale, flow-dependent covariances for any tropical cyclone in the basin. This more advanced system will also improve the treatment of inner-core data in HAFS with online error estimation and quality control. Recent NOAA-funded work strongly suggests that these combined improvements will further improve HAFS analyses and forecasts.

490320.title: Integrating Satellite, Model, and Ground Measurement Data through Machine Learning to Estimate Surface PMcoarse Concentrations in the United States.
490320.authors: Jennifer McGinnis, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and H. Zhu, P. Reddy, Y. Guan, and J. R. Pierce
490320.abstract: PMcoarse (particulate matter with diameters >2.5 µm and <10 µm) is a prevalent but understudied pollutant in the contiguous US (CONUS). Due to sparse observations and its high spatiotemporal variability, reliable CONUS-wide PMcoarse estimates are limited. The current ground monitoring network does not capture the full spatiotemporal variability of hourly PMcoarse, with ordinary kriging of observations resulting in an R2 of 0.2 when evaluated through leave-one-out cross validation (LOOCV). To produce better estimates of PMcoarse, we applied gradient-boosted decision trees to blend together satellite data, meteorological model output, land type, and ground observations to estimate PMcoarse concentrations away from monitors. The satellite products that we leveraged are the Ultraviolet Absorbing Aerosol Index and Aerosol Optical Depth data products from the Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of POllution (TEMPO) satellite instrument and a longwave-based dust detection algorithm from the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES). Through preliminary work, we have found that the machine learning model trained on hourly PMcoarse observations increased the R2 value to 0.50 for hourly and 0.65 for daily PMcoarse observations when evaluated through LOOCV. This work has found promising results in estimating PMcoarse across CONUS, enabling future work of the health effects and temporal trends of PMcoarse.

490321.title: When Will the Water Rise? A Look into the Factors That Control Storm Surge Timing
490321.authors: Katiria Colon Rivera, University of Puerto Rico-Mayagüez, Mayaguez, PR; and B. C. Trabing, L. P. Alaka, and A. L. Brannan
490321.abstract: Storm surge is the abnormal water level rise above the predicted tide that is caused by winds of a tropical cyclone or other strong storm. Improving storm surge forecasting is critical because storm surge, especially from tropical cyclones, continues to cause fatalities, as evident in recent events like Hurricanes Ian (2022) and Helene (2024). Providing timing information for storm surge to emergency managers is essential for timely and effective decision making; however, the National Hurricane Center does not yet have a product that directly communicates this timing information. The objective of this study is to enable storm surge timing communication by (1) improving the quality control (QC) and selection of observations used to verify the Sea, Lake and Overland Surges from Hurricanes (SLOSH) model and (2) improving our understanding of how peak water level timing varies based on tropical cyclone characteristics. Water level observations are analyzed from National Ocean Service tide stations and United States Geological Survey water level sensors for landfalling tropical cyclones along the U.S. Gulf Coast from 2008 to 2024. QC flags are objectively and manually applied to each observation, which includes identifying significant contributions from freshwater flooding input and wave runup. The QC flags ensure that data meets verification quality standards and enables a robust isolation of the storm surge signal that can directly be compared with hindcasts from the SLOSH model. The observations are found to be more consistent with the SLOSH hindcast solutions when QC'ed, especially in less recent events like Gustav (2008), Ike (2008), and Isaac (2012). The processed observations with new QC flags enable a more accurate examination of the storm surge timing. The onset time, defined as the time where water levels exceed 3 ft MHHW (Mean Higher High Water), the duration of time that water levels exceed 3 ft MHHW, and the peak water level times are all examined. The peak water level timing distribution is found to vary based on the storm’s forward speed and this presentation will discuss the other storm characteristics that affect storm surge onset, duration, and peak timing. This research is foundational for the creation of future tools to communicate storm surge timing information to emergency managers.

490323.title: Improving Operational GFS Precipitation Forecasts using Targeted AR Recon and GARRP Observations
490323.authors: Vijay S. Tallapragada, NCEP, College Park, MD; and X. Wu, B. Zhou, M. N. Malasala, K. Wu, X. Wang, M. Aristizabal Vargas, A. Wilson, and F. M. Ralph
490323.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are a primary mechanism for poleward moisture transport outside the tropics and a major source of heavy precipitation, flooding, and water resources along the U.S. West Coast. During Water Year 2026 (WY2026), the Atmospheric River Reconnaissance (AR Recon) program expanded into the Global Atmospheric Rivers Reconnaissance Program (GARRP), extending targeted observations beyond the eastern Pacific to include the western Pacific, the Gulf of America, the western Atlantic, and other ocean basins. GARRP coordinated 42 intensive observing periods (IOPs) over the Pacific and 12 over the Gulf and western Atlantic, supplemented by observations from the North American Upstream Feature-Resolving and Tropopause Uncertainty Reconnaissance Experiment (NURTURE) and the North Atlantic Waveguide, Dry Intrusion, Downstream Impact Campaign (NAWDIC). These coordinated observing efforts provided targeted dropsonde measurements in data-sparse regions critical to the evolution of ARs and downstream high-impact weather. To assess the operational value of these observations, near-real-time data denial experiments were conducted using the NCEP operational Global Forecast System version 16 (GFSv16). Forecasts with and without targeted dropsonde observations were compared to quantify their impact on analyses and subsequent forecasts. Preliminary results indicate that assimilating AR Recon and GARRP dropsonde observations improves the representation of upstream moisture transport and synoptic-scale flow, leading to more accurate forecasts of AR evolution and landfall. These improvements translate into enhanced precipitation forecast skill over the United States West Coast, especially along California and Pacific Northwest, during 24-120-hour lead times, including better prediction of precipitation intensity and spatial distribution during landfalling AR events. Positive forecast impacts are also evident for winter storms affecting the U.S. East Coast during January and February, particularly at longer forecast lead times. Ongoing analyses include examining case-to-case and regional variability in forecast sensitivity and evaluating how observation targeting strategies influence downstream forecast improvements. This work also includes the application of the new NCEP AI-based Global Ensemble Forecast System (AIGEFS) within the NCEP ensemble sensitivity framework to support more effective targeting of future observations. These results demonstrate the operational benefits of coordinated AR Recon and GARRP observations and highlight the success of targeted airborne observations in the NCEP operational forecasting. The findings provide guidance for optimizing future observing strategies and improving operational prediction of atmospheric rivers and other high-impact weather events

490340.title: Are Detailed Parameterizations of Atmospheric Physics Necessary In Earth System Models?
490340.authors: Prashant D Sardeshmukh, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and G. P. Compo and C. McColl
490340.abstract: Atmospheric models are a crucial component of earth system models. A recent study (Sardeshmukh et al J. Climate 2023) performed with the atmospheric component of NOAA’s Global Forecast System (GFS) model showed that multiplying the parameterized diabatic tendencies of every model variable at every grid point and every time step by random factors between 0 and 2 not only did not degrade the 15-day global weather forecasts but actually improved them. This study assesses how such randomizations also affect the long-term mean climate and daily weather statistics, using a newer (FV3GFS) version of the model with similar physics. Two large 40-member ensembles of global atmospheric simulations of the 1999-2018 period were generated with and without the stochastic perturbations of parameterized tendencies (SPPT). The focus was on the 20-yr means and the standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis of daily-averaged precipitable water, precipitation, mid-tropospheric vertical velocity, and near-surface air temperature. Consistent with the earlier study, the drastic randomizations did not degrade the long-term statistics of these variables beyond the uncertainty in the verifying reanalysis datasets and improved them in several instances through the noise-induced drifts and changes of variability. Overall, the results from these and several other published studies indicate that the details of atmospheric physics play a minor role in probabilistic weather predictions and in determining the long-term mean climate and weather statistics. They suggest that at the current mature stage of atmospheric modeling, what might be more fruitful than refining the deterministic physics parameterizations would be to develop better stochastic parameterizations of the chaotic physics, aided by diagnosis of short-range forecast error statistics and machine learning. Some possible ways to accomplish this will be discussed.

490350.title: Development of NOAA's AIGFS and AIGEFS Applications
490350.authors: Jun Wang, NWS, Riverdale park, MD; and L. Cui, J. Liu, B. Cui, W. Meng, X. Luo, W. Li, B. Fu, Z. Zhang, L. Zhu, J. Peng, B. Liu, A. M. Bentley, Q. Shi, S. Frolov, M. Pope, K. Blackman, and J. R. Carley
490350.abstract: Weather and climate forecasting are undergoing a revolutionary paradigm shift driven by advancing AI/ML technologies. Data-driven Machine Learning Weather Prediction (MLWP) models, utilizing state-of-the-art architectures, have achieved remarkable forecast skill combined with an unprecedented computational efficiency that traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models cannot match. In December 2025, NWS operationalized its first suite of AI/ML systems: the deterministic AIGFS, the ensemble-based AIGEFS, and the Hybrid Global Ensemble Forecast System (HGEFS). In this presentation, we provide an overview of recent developments across our global AI/ML weather forecast systems. The deterministic AIGFS v1.1 replaces its grid-point mean squared error loss with a spherical harmonic loss function featuring revised wind vector representations. Trained with extended-period datasets and an updated fine-tuning schedule, this version improved hurricane intensity and precipitation forecasts while also alleviating the smoothness issue seen at longer lead times. Furthermore, AIGFS is transitioning to the Anemoi framework to streamline data processing, training, and inference deployment, while incorporating GFS v17 datasets to support the upcoming operational GFS v17 implementation. Concurrently, the ensemble-based AIGEFS has transitioned to Anemoi utilizing the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) loss function to improve ensemble spread. New variables are integrated into the Anemoi configurations for both the AIGFS and AIGEFS models. Ensemble percentile and probability products were also recently added to both AIGEFS and HGEFS. To supplement these model-generated outputs, the Unified Post-Processor (UPP) has been updated to derive additional forecast products from the AI models to provide comprehensive forecaster guidance. Future pathways to further enhance global system performance will also be discussed.

490352.title: Exploring the Potential of Low-Cost Air Quality Sensors and Comparing HRRR Forecast vs Analysis Inputs in a High-Resolution Model for Prescribed Burn Applications
490352.authors: Emily Robin Nigro, Stanford University, Stanford, CA; UCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. Shams, M. Williams, A. Piña, B. Thigpen, K. Payne, W. Nicewonger, and H. Shin
490352.abstract: Prescribed burns are implemented by land managers to reduce wildfire risk, but the smoke they produce can pose health risks to fire personnel and nearby communities. Accurate prediction of smoke dispersion is therefore critical for planning and management decisions that minimize exposure. Here, we investigated the application of low-cost air quality sensors and a high-resolution regional weather model to improve prescribed burn smoke monitoring and forecasting. We deployed three 3D-Printed Automatic Weather Stations (3D-PAWS) in the Oconee National Forest, GA in spring 2026 to measure meteorological conditions and air quality during prescribed burns. Additionally, we used HRRR to investigate how wind conditions influenced sensor measurements and smoke transport. Finally, we analyzed WRF-LES-Chem simulations of the prescribed burn on April 9, 2026, using either HRRR analysis data or HRRR forecast data as the meteorological input. We found that 3D-PAWS air quality sensors captured smoke enhancement and smoldering when deployed adjacent to a burn unit. HRRR captured the evolving wind conditions that controlled smoke transport, and WRF-LES-Chem simulations based on HRRR analysis data reasonably reproduced the observed timing and spatial extent of smoke dispersion. Simulations based on HRRR 48-hour forecasts produced somewhat similar pollutant magnitudes but did not capture the same spatial patterns; differences between the two model experiments highlight the sensitivity of smoke projections to meteorological forecasts. This work demonstrates the potential of using low-cost sensor observations and a high-resolution regional model as complementary tools to improve understanding of prescribed fire smoke behavior and ultimately support more effective smoke management.

490354.title: Rising Heat and Drought Signals in Alaska's Fire Season: Implications for Fire Weather Operations
490354.abstract: Wildland fire activity in Alaska has grown in scale and reach over the past two decades, with large fire seasons now occurring in regions historically too cool and wet to sustain them. This poses a growing challenge for fire weather forecasters, land and fire managers, and public health agencies who depend on timely, reliable indicators of fire risk. This study evaluates long-term (1959–2025) trends in five heat and drought indicators used across the weather and fire management enterprise -- the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), vapor pressure deficit (VPD), Heat Index, and convective precipitation -- derived from ERA5 and ERA-5 Drought reanalysis data, across five Alaska Predictive Service Area (PSA) groups and the broader circumpolar north. Trends were assessed for the full fire season (April-September) and separately for its early (April-June) and late (July-September) halves using the Theil-Sen estimator and Mann-Kendall significance testing. While 6-month SPI trends are broadly positive (wetter) across Alaska, SPEI trends are drier in every PSA group, reflecting rising evaporative demand. This drying signal is strongest in April–June, when VPD and Heat Index trends are also significant across nearly all PSA groups, pointing to an earlier onset of fire-conducive conditions. This early-season signal is consistent with a broader pattern of earlier snowmelt and snow drought across Alaska, where the spring snowoff date has trended two to four days earlier per decade since 1959 -- a shift previously linked to a disproportionate share of the state's historical area burned -- suggesting earlier snow loss is an increasingly integral driver of both early-season severity and overall fire season length. Convective precipitation is increasing across Alaska as well, most notably in Southcentral (up to 6.3 mm per decade, or 3.7%, April-September) and on the North Slope (up to 7.7% in April-June) -- evidence that rising precipitation does not necessarily correspond to reduced fire or lightning-ignition risk, a distinction with direct relevance for operational fire danger rating and forecast messaging. Beyond Alaska, these trends carry implications for permafrost stability and carbon release, and the underlying warming and drying patterns are shared broadly across the circumpolar north, suggesting other high-latitude historically fire-limited regions may face a similar trajectory. These findings point to a fire season that is both intensifying and shifting earlier, with practical implications for fire weather operations, resource allocation, and public health advisories.

490358.title: Leveraging Flux Tower Measurements to Diagnose and Improve the Noah-MP Land Surface Model
490358.authors: Tzu-Shun Lin, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and R. Abolafia-Rosenzweig, C. He, Y. Cheng, A. Bennett, M. J. Barlage, and A. J. Newman
490358.abstract: Land surface models are essential for predicting land surface fluxes and states that influence weather and hydrometeorological extremes through land-atmosphere interactions. However, model predictions across spatial and temporal scales remain an outstanding challenge due to uncertainties in process-level representation, model parameters, meteorological forcing, and land-atmosphere feedback. To reduce these uncertainties, we leverage eddy-covariance observations from flux towers to diagnose and improve the Noah-Multiparameterization (Noah-MP) land surface model. Evaluation against measurements across the United States reveals a systematic overestimation of the diurnal amplitude of ground heat flux, which contributes to a nighttime surface air temperature warm bias. To address this bias, the effects of soil organic matter on soil thermal and hydraulic properties are parameterized in Noah-MP. This process-level enhancement also alters the soil moisture-latent heat flux relationship. To further quantify parameter uncertainties, a parameter sensitivity and machine learning-based optimization framework is developed and integrated into the offline Noah-MP model. To reduce equifinality, multivariate parameters are calibrated using latent heat flux, sensible heat flux, soil moisture, and soil moisture-latent heat flux coupling strength at AmeriFlux tower sites across North America and evaluated for transferability using global FLUXNET Shuttle sites. Observation-based meteorological forcing is used to minimize uncertainties associated with atmospheric forcing, enabling a more direct evaluation of model parameters. The model also incorporates canopy height data as an additional input. Sensitivity analysis shows that vegetation- and soil-related parameters exert strong controls on the soil moisture-latent heat flux coupling. Parameter attribution experiments further identify the relative contributions of soil and vegetation parameters to regulate soil moisture dynamics and latent heat flux across diverse meteorological conditions, providing potential guidance for future developments. A visualization platform is also developed to accelerate model calibration and enhancement efforts. Overall, this study demonstrates how flux tower measurements and machine learning can be combined to diagnose model structural deficiencies, constrain parameter uncertainties, improve physical processes, and enhance predictability of the land surface.

490359.title: Enhancing Coastal Flooding Resilience with Virtual Reality
490359.authors: Jase E. Bernhardt, Hofstra University, Hempstead, NY; and F. Martin
490359.abstract: Societal vulnerability to coastal hazards such as storm surge and freshwater flooding continues to increase as climate change accelerates and the built environment expands. To better convey flooding risk from storm surge and flooding, recent work has tested virtual reality (VR) simulations as a means for immersing participants in rising floodwaters. Studies have shown that VR depictions of storm surge flooding can help convince individuals take tropical cyclone threats more seriously (e.g., Bernhardt et al. 2019) and better conceptualize real world flood heights (e.g., Simpson et al. 2022). Typically, the most injuries and deaths from tropical cyclones impacting the US are due to flooding (American Meteorological Society 2023), so improved understanding of water-related hazards is imperative. To help effectively inform coastal communities about those hazards, a VR simulation of storm surge and flash flooding was developed for New York City and Long Island. To make the simulation impactful and relatable, real-world imagery was used, including an iconic view of the Brooklyn Bridge and lower Manhattan skyline. Extra water was added to the simulation to demonstrate the impacts of storm surge, sea level rise, and urban flash flooding in an immersive environment. User surveys were conducted to evaluate the efficacy of the VR simulation as an outreach tool, and also to assess its effectiveness versus traditional video of simulated coastal flooding. Survey participants rated the VR simulation strongly, finding the real-world imagery to be especially helpful in furthering their understanding of what coastal flooding will look like in a changing climate. References American Meteorological Society. (2023, August 8). Recent Trends in Tropical Cyclone Fatalities in the United States. The Front Page Blog. https://blog.ametsoc.org/2023/08/08/recent-trends-in-tropical-cyclone-fatalities-in-the-united-states/ Bernhardt, J., Snellings, J., Smiros, A., Bermejo, I., Rienzo, A., & Swan, C. (2019). Communicating hurricane risk with virtual reality: A pilot project. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 100(10), 1897-1902. Simpson, M., Padilla, L., Keller, K., & Klippel, A. (2022). Immersive storm surge flooding: Scale and risk perception in virtual reality. Journal of Environmental Psychology, 80, 101764.

490362.title: How NASA Earth Science Promotes One Health
490362.authors: Helena J. Chapman, NASA Headquarters, Washington, DC; and L. M. Judd and J. A. Haynes
490362.abstract: Emerging global health risks remain complex and require coordinated, multisectoral responses informed by the best available scientific evidence. Key frameworks, such as the NASA’s Earth Science to Action Strategy 2024-2034, the Quadripartite organizations' One Health Joint Plan of Action 2022-2026, and the UN’s Early Warnings for All Initiative, provide evidence-based guidance, statistical insights, and recommendations to help leaders prepare and mitigate community health risks. Other resources, such as the NASA Earth Observatory, Scientific Visualization Studio, and Earth Science Applications Guidebook, offer practical examples of how Earth science applications can enhance understanding of complex ecosystem interactions. By adopting the One Health approach, underpinned by the 4C’s (collaboration, communication, capacity building, coordination), researchers can build multidisciplinary collaborations, integrate diverse datasets and analytical tools, and foster meaningful dialogue on environmental risks. This presentation will showcase how three cross-cutting Earth science applications incorporate the One Health approach to evaluate environmental hazards affecting public health. Bridging diverse sectors and scientific disciplines is essential for advancing scientific knowledge, building research-stakeholder engagement, and ultimately informing health and policy decision-making.

490364.title: Predictability of Rapid Intensification in GFS, MPAS, and HAFS Forecasts During the 2026 Hurricane Season
490364.authors: Molly B. Smith, NOAA/GSL - CIRES, Boulder, CO; and C. Evans, R. Pierce, G. Padmanabhan, I. McGinnis, and J. A. Hamilton
490364.abstract: At the National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Global Systems Laboratory (GSL), model developers take part each year in the Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program (HFIP), a coordinated effort to improve the accuracy and reliability of tropical cyclone (TC) forecasts. As there are only a few months out of the year when the bulk of North Atlantic and East Pacific TCs occur, GSL’s model developers need fast, real-time verification results to show which of their model physics under development are performing the best, and what improvements need to be made and subsequently tested on the next of that year’s storms. To this end, GSL uses the Developmental Testbed Center (DTC)’s Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) to assess the skill of in-house models, and that of operational models, at predicting statistics such as rapid intensification (RI). For the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season and HFIP, GSL will run a real-time instance of the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS). These forecasts will use a regional MPAS domain with the latest versions of the physics parameterizations underpinning NOAA's operational regional modeling suite. Forecasts will be initialized twice daily at 0000 and 1200 UTC using 0.25° GFS data for initial and lateral boundary conditions. The skill of these MPAS forecasts in forecasting RI will be compared with that of the operational Global Forecast System (GFS) and NOAA's UFS Hurricane Application, HAFS. Currently two versions of the HAFS are run in operations: HAFS-A and HAFS-B. In previous years, both HAFS models have displayed superior skill in predicting RI for lead times up to 36 hours, besting both the GFS and GSL’s MPAS setups. However, HAFS has historically had a high rate of false alarms, which caused its overall forecast skill to decline. MPAS usually has a good probability of detection and no false alarms, resulting in a good skill score for later lead times. The GFS has consistently under forecasted RI at all lead times, resulting in a very low frequency bias. Although there has only been one instance of RI in the 2026 season at the time of this abstract (Hurricane Genevieve in the Eastern Pacific), model skill for this year will be examined on any further RI that does occur. The METplus verification tools, which are designed to support evidence-based decision making in model development, make it easy to verify and compare models in real time. This real-time verification allows developers to have prompt feedback on model forecasts for statistics such as RI. The METplus tools are open source, and our hope is that, as more features are added, their use continues to expand amongst the meteorological community, and to other public and private sector entities, aiding the development of new, next-generation models.

490369.title: High-Resolution Forecasting of Prescribed Fire Smoke Using Pre-Burn fire Emission Estimation
490369.authors: Shima Shams, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and H. Shin, R. Kumar, E. R. Nigro, D. Fillmore, and M. Williams
490369.abstract: Prescribed fire (Rx) is a critical land management practice used to reduce hazardous fuel loads and mitigate future wildfire risk across the US. More than 70% of Rx occurs in the southeastern U.S., with Georgia among the national leaders in Rx implementation. Rx provides ecological and wildfire mitigation benefits, but smoke emissions can affect air quality and public health. Accurate smoke forecasts are therefore critical for Rx planning and require realistic representation of fire emissions, meteorology, and atmospheric processes controlling smoke evolution. We present a polygon-based fire emission framework that estimates emissions from planned Rx perimeters to enable smoke modeling prior to ignition. These emissions are incorporated into the WRF-LES-Chem modeling system, consisting of nested 2-km and 500-m mesoscale domains with a 100-m LES inner domain to explicitly resolve fire-induced turbulence and smoke dispersion. A Rx conducted in Georgia on 9 April 2026 is used as a demonstration case. The simulations successfully reproduce the observed evolution of the smoke plume and its transport toward Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, including the timing of reduced visibility associated with the smoke event. Compared with conventional post-fire satellite-derived emission inventories, the polygon-based emission framework produces more smoke intensity. We further evaluate the sensitivity of the simulations to meteorological conditions, fire emissions, and the influence of the outer-domain planetary boundary layer parameterization on LES smoke predictions. These results demonstrate that integrating polygon-based fire emissions with high-resolution WRF-LES-Chem simulations offers a practical framework for pre-ignition Rx smoke forecasting, enabling improved Rx planning and smoke management. 490372.title: Connecting Nuclear Weapon Effects to Satellite Data Assimilation: Pipeline for Synthetic Scene Generation and CRTM Forward Modeling
490372.authors: Joshua E. Szekely, Institute for Defense Analyses, Alexandria, VA; and J. L. Bewley, PhD, S. C. Castells, A. E. Ehrenberg, N. T. Plymale, and M. R. Walker
490372.abstract: Evaluating and validating remote sensing algorithms for atmospheric nuclear detonations is severely constrained by the absolute lack of modern, high-resolution satellite observations of such events. To overcome this limitation, the Institute for Defense Analyses (IDA) is establishing a rigorous, end-to-end modeling and simulation (M&S) pipeline. This pipeline translates high-fidelity nuclear weapon effects codes into realistic synthetic atmospheric scenes, allowing the Defense Threat Reduction Agency (DTRA) to test, validate, and mature nuclear plume advisory algorithms before operational deployment. This presentation focuses on IDA’s role in orchestrating this validation ecosystem. The pipeline operates in three distinct phases: Physical Characterization: IDA ingests raw outputs from physics-based nuclear weapon effects codes—including initial fireball dynamics, thermal histories, multi-layered particle size distributions, debris mass loadings, and chemical trace gas yields (specifically nitrogen oxides, NOx). Atmospheric Environmental Coupling: These physical parameters are projected onto 3D grids representing realistic atmospheric states, capturing complex environments such as varying aerosol loadings, meteorological clouds, and vertical wind shear. CRTM Forward Modeling: Crucially, IDA couples these 3D physical grids to the JCSDA’s Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM). Operating as the forward operator, the CRTM simulates top-of-atmosphere radiances and brightness temperatures, generating synthetic observations that mimic operational sensors such as the GOES Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), Himawari Advanced Himawari Imager (AHI), and hyperspectral infrared sounders (e.g., IASI/CrIS).

490376.title: Validation of QUIC-Fire/QUIC-Smoke with LiDAR Observations of a Prescribed-Burn Smoke Plume
490376.authors: Matthew A. Nelson, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM; and C. Fronk, J. Oliveto, J. Castorena, and S. Brambilla
490376.abstract: In an effort to better understand the behavior of prescribed (Rx) burns and forest management, the Strategic Environmental Research and Development Program (SERDP) and the Environmental Security Technology Certification Program (ESTCP) organized a field experiment involving a series of Rx burns at Eglin Air Force Base (AFB) in the Florida panhandle during the month of March 2023. This experiment involved many organizations and a wide variety of measurements to characterize both the meteorological and forest parameters that drive fire behavior. We deployed a scanning LiDAR upwind of the first of the Rx burns and implemented a series of scans performed throughout the burn. Scans included a series of Doppler beam swinging (DBS), vertical fixed, and a set of range height indicator (RHI) sweeps at various azimuth angles. The series of scans allowed us to observe the temporal evolution of the upwind velocity profile, boundary layer height, and the 3D extent of the smoke plume over the course of the burn. QUIC-Fire is a fast-running, laptop compatible fire behavior model that captures the fire/atmosphere feedback. This aspect is fundamental to capture fire behavior in Rx fire applications because the aggregated behavior of multiple ignition points. QUIC-Fire includes the QUIC-URB diagnostic wind solver adapted for complex terrain and can capture plume trapping vs. penetration of the boundary layer. The fire is described through a cellular automata model that captures both wind-driven fire spread and creeping. In output, it provides temporal evolution of mass burnt, reaction rate, emissions (CO, PM2.5, water), and fire-induced winds. These quantities are passed to QUIC-SMOKE, an adaptation of the Lagrangian random-walk transport and dispersion model QUIC-PLUME for smoke transport. Through a nested grid approach, fire can be resolved at 2 m resolution and smoke transported over tens of kilometers at lower resolution. The measurements of Eglin AFB Rx burns provide the opportunity to validate several aspects of the QUIC-Fire and QUIC-SMOKE models. In our current analysis, we will compare the modeled vertical concentration slices with backscatter from LiDAR scans to assess the model’s ability to accurately simulate the fire/atmosphere interactions, smoke plume rise, and inform future model development efforts.

490377.title: Storm Surge Compounded with Extreme Temperatures in Tampa Bay
490377.authors: Emma Burke, Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH; and O. Onochie, S. Sudheer, and A. R. Enriquez
490377.abstract: Coastal communities like Tampa Bay, Florida, are exposed to multiple natural hazards, including extreme high temperatures and hurricane-related impacts such as wind, storm surge, and precipitation. The seasonality of hurricanes and high temperatures increases the chances of compound flood-heat events, which can produce greater impacts than either hazard alone. In the future, rising global temperatures and sea levels will further increase the likelihood of these compound flood-heat events. Nature-based solutions can help reduce the impact of these two hazards, as green spaces lower temperatures, increase infiltration rates, and enhance surface friction, effectively reducing flood propagation and depth. In this study, we investigate how nature-based solutions can improve the resilience of coastal communities along Tampa Bay. To do so, we simulate storm surge flooding under different what-if scenarios that include the implementation of nature-based solutions. These solutions are represented by different surface friction coefficients in a flooding model. Flood maps are overlaid with satellite-derived surface temperature data to characterize compound hazards at the local scale. The resulting maps are then used to evaluate the effectiveness of nature-based solutions in reducing risk in vulnerable communities, identified using the Socio-Vulnerability Index (SoVI). Results identify hotspots for flooding and heat risk across Tampa Bay, quantify increases in flood depth under various sea-level rise scenarios, and pinpoint optimal locations for nature-based interventions that reduce compound flood-heat risk. Findings indicate Anna Maria Island is an optimal location to implement a nature-based solution, where flood extent could be reduced by 2.9 km².

490378.title: Beyond Inflation: Backscatter Parameterizations to Address the Variability Deficit in Global Ocean Data Assimilation
490378.authors: Kate Boden, CU Boulder, Boulder, CO; and I. Grooms, D. Amrhein, J. Anderson, F. Castruccio, and M. Gharamti
490378.abstract: Ocean models are critical components for Earth System Prediction. Due to computational limitations, global ocean models are often resolved at coarse horizontal scales, on the order of 1°. At this scale, important phenomena such as mesoscale eddies are not resolved. Since mesoscale eddies account for a significant portion of ocean variability, failing to represent them and their impacts on larger-scale processes results in reduced variability in global ocean models. In ensemble-based data assimilation (DA), the lack of model variability can lead to under-dispersed ensembles that require inflation schemes. However, inflation corrections do not persist into the forecast phase, causing ensemble spread to collapse at longer lead times. This study explores an alternative approach, addressing variability directly within the model physics using a Backscatter parameterization Package “BackPack”. In total, three backscatter parameterization schemes are implemented: stochastic GM + E (Grooms et al. 2025), stochastic equation of state (Stanley et al. 2020), and deterministic Leith + E (Grooms et al. 2023). Previous studies have shown that implementing these schemes in a coarse ocean model results in significant increases in model variability (Grooms et al. 2025). We will present results from 40 ensemble member global OSSE experiments using the new ocean component of CESM, MOM6 at nominal 2/3° resolution, coupled with the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART). In total, four year-long MOM6-DART experiments were run with and without the BackPack. Results demonstrate that the BackPack substantially increases internal variability and ensemble spread, successfully lowering the amount of required inflation. While reductions in state estimation errors are modest, the BackPack significantly improves ensemble calibrations. Results from these experiments could lead to improvements in ocean reanalysis products and improved initial conditions for Earth System Prediction.

490380.title: Model Verification in Support of RRFSv2 Development at GSL
490380.authors: Jeffrey A. Hamilton, Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and M. Smith, N. Babij, R. Pierce, I. McGinnis, G. Padmanabhan, and M. S. Wandishin
490380.abstract: Verification is essential to the development and operational transition of Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) numerical weather prediction modeling (NWP) systems, historically with the Rapid Update Cycle (RUC), the Rapid Refresh (RAP), and the High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR), and presently with the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS). To support model development efforts, GSL has developed and maintained a verification system, the Model Analysis Tool Suite (MATS), with three main requirements: responsiveness, flexibility, and consistency. Various verification types are included, with slightly different methodologies, but generally metrics are produced from partial aggregated statistics derived from model-obs pairs, including both real-time and retrospective sources. The derived partially aggregated statistics are stored within a database, which is accessible from an interactive web application and ensures performant graphical representation for a variety of metrics during assessment activities. As lab-wide focus moves towards the development of the MPAS-JEDI based RRFS version 2 (RRFSv2), the MATS team at GSL have continued to upgrade the verification capabilities and accessibility of the system in support of the various priorities surrounding the new modeling frameworks' capabilities. These enhancements will facilitate improved error diagnosis and skill-benchmarking during prototype evaluation and lay the foundation for future efforts involving MPAS and JEDI as the core of NOAA NWP development. In this presentation, we will discuss the ongoing model verification efforts at GSL in support of the strategic goals of RRFSv2. We will highlight the recent enhancements addressing atmospheric composition, physical and AI-based ensembles, satellite analysis, as well as the impact of incorporating process-oriented and user-impact verification capabilities in evaluating NWP skill across the decision-making value chain during the developmental stage. Additionally, we will explore planned capabilities and uses for MATS within numerical model development at GSL and the wider community.

490381.title: Investigating a Machine-Learning Dataset for Data Corruption and Potential Impacts
490381.authors: Geoffrey Wagner, CIRA, Ft. Collins, CO; and A. Layne
490381.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) techniques, now prevalent in the atmospheric sciences and forecasting enterprise, heavily depend on sufficient amounts of quality training data. These data may be obtained from many data storage structures, including but not limited to cloud datastores, local storage drives, and even larger tape storage systems. Any such storage system is susceptible to silent data corruption, sometimes referred to as bit rot. Such corruption can occur due to natural degradation of the storage media itself or undetected internal defects in the storage circuitry, resulting in impacts as small as flipping a bit in a single value or much larger error modes that can, undetected, propagate across workloads and services (Dixit et al., 2022). While data quality control is a common practice, such quality checks may occur before data are stored and retrieved, or may fail to capture data degradation that doesn’t exceed typical data value bounds. We investigate four possible presentations of data corruption by artificially replicating them, first on synthetically generated “temperature-like” data. We then use these artificially corrupted data to devise a classification model capable of identifying whether the data are corrupt, and if so, what type of corruption is present. The trained classification model is then applied to retrieved Unrestricted Real-time Mesoscale Analysis temperature data with random artificial corruption applied, to determine if the model was capable of detecting the corruption in real meteorological data. We then use the trained model to examine our full dataset, free of artificial data corruption, to determine if and to what extent silent corruption has impacted our ML training dataset.

490382.title: Observations of Complex Flow and Dispersal Patterns in Mountainous Terrain
490382.authors: Matthew A. Nelson, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM; and R. L. Beal, S. Brambilla, and H. Boukhalfa
490382.abstract: The behavior of airborne plumes originating from complex terrain will be significantly impacted by the complicated flow structures that develop in mountainous terrain. Flow separation behind peaks and cliffs and channeling within canyons can cause plumes to deviate from prevailing wind directions producing dispersal patterns that are far more complicated than would be produced from a comparable release in flat terrain. We employed neutrally-buoyant balloons equipped with GPS trackers at New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology’s Energetic Materials Research and Testing Center (EMRTC) in 2025. The balloons serve as physical analogs to the Lagrangian tracers used by many transport and dispersion models. This method makes it possible to study how relatively small source location displacements in complex terrain can affect the plume transport over much longer distances. Failure to account for these effects can lead to errors in source attribution and strength estimation. The balloons included both high-frequency line-of-sight and low-frequency satellite-based GPS trackers to provide both highly detailed near-field and long-distance traces of the balloon movement. Some of the releases demonstrate highly complex behavior including highly localized directional shear producing trajectories that cross orthogonally from each other from different source locations. We will take advantage of the multiple examine these releases in detail.

490383.title: Measuring the Coronal Magnetic Field for Space Weather: Current Capabilities and Future Developments of Visible-IR Synoptic Coronagraphs
490383.authors: Giuliana de Toma, NCAR, BOULDER, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and T. E. Berger, S. Gibson, A. Carlile, and M. Wiltberger
490383.abstract: The UCoMP coronagraph at the Mauna Loa Solar Observatory is an imaging spectro-polarimeter with an annular field of view spanning approximately 1.05 to 2.1 solar radii and a tunable Lyot filter that enables observations between 530 nm and 1083 nm. Its flexible design allows us to infer the plasma and magnetic properties of the corona from multiple emission lines with customizable sampling and supports observing programs tailored to different science questions, including space weather. UCoMP operated routinely from July 2021 until November 2022, when a volcanic eruption cut off access to the site halting observations. Road repair is now complete and, once power is restored and observations resume, we will operate UCoMP with a combination of synoptic and CME observing programs. We describe the scientific capabilities of this class of instruments, which can routinely measure velocity, line width, density, polarization, and magnetic field (via spectro-polarimetry and coronal seismology) enabling novel space weather nowcasting and forecasting applications. The magnetic field measurements of the current UCoMP are limited to the plane-of-sky component because of its modest 20 cm aperture. A larger 1.4 m coronagraph based on UCoMP heritage has been designed as the centerpiece of the proposed Coronal Solar Magnetism Observatory (COSMO). It will allow us to infer the full coronal magnetic field (both line-of-sight and plane-of-sky components) and to monitor dynamic coronal events and plasma evolution at faster cadence and higher signal-to-noise ratio, opening new frontiers in coronal physics and advancing our understanding of space weather.

490385.title: Observational Analysis of the 5 March 2025 Bore-Driven QLCS across Northern Alabama
490385.authors: Alec Soileau, University of Alabama at Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and K. Knupp
490385.abstract: On 5 March 2025, a bore-driven Quasi-Linear Convective System (QLCS) was noted moving across much of northern Alabama. Numerous weather stations over the area have documented a 3-4 hPa pressure increase coinciding with a near 90° wind direction change along with relatively constant surface temperatures. Soundings taken from the Severe Weather Institute for Radar and Lightning Laboratories and profiling data from the NOAA Physical Science Laboratory, the UAH Mobile Integrated Profiling System, and the DOE/ARM BNF network indicate very strong low-level flow and shear oriented generally opposite of the bore’s propagation direction. Evaporative cooling due to an expansive stratiform rainband ahead of the QLCS strengthened low level stability. This in combination with the opposing low level jet led to an environment that was favorable for bore genesis and maintenance. (Haghi and Durran 2021). The QLCS exhibited substantial changes over its lifetime, many of which were captured during a 2.5 hour dual-Doppler observation period. Preliminary dual-Doppler analysis (DDA) from the ARMOR and KHTX radars retrieved strong front to rear flow along with vertical motion values greater than 20 m/s within the bore assisted convective updraft. Notably, the QLCS did not have an appreciable storm relative rear inflow jet despite producing numerous damaging wind reports across northern Alabama. The strongest convection within the DDA domain occurred at 0350 UTC coinciding with the system's proximity to Sand Mountain. It has been observed that Sand mountain’s topography can locally modify surface winds and thus QLCS characteristics. Additionally, the DDA vertical velocity fields also indicate gravity-wave like structures trailing the convection during the observation period.

490386.title: Dave Randall, My Career, and Tropical Intraseasonal Variability (Invited Presentation)
490386.authors: Eric Daniel Maloney, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO
490386.abstract: Dave Randall’s early work on tropical intraseasonal variability and tropical convection was a key inspiration for my Ph.D work in the late 1990’s on the Madden-Julian oscillation (MJO) and climate model simulations of intraseasonal variability. Our paths first crossed at NCAR atmospheric and climate modeling workshops where I presented this work. My excitement for working with Dave only grew when he invited me to apply (successfully!) for a faculty position in the Department of Atmospheric Science at Colorado State associated with his new NSF STC named the Center for Multiscale Modeling of Atmospheric Processes (CMMAP). Interactions with Dave and other scientists associated with CMMAP helped to refine my thinking on tropical convection, including novel ways of using weak temperature gradient (WTG) theory for the tropical atmosphere to understand subseasonal variability. This presentation will summarize some of the important contributions that Dave Randall has made to my career, and also discuss some new research results that have been enabled by this foundation. In particular, a WTG framework will be used to examine regional variability in the dominant moistening processes that help to maintain MJO moisture and convection anomalies. It will be shown that key feedbacks, including radiative feedbacks, are strongest in monsoon regions such as the Australian monsoon and south Asian monsoon. There, enhanced vertical shear helps to foster mesoscale organization that produces stronger cloud longwave radiative heating anomalies due to more extensive anvils. The implications of these findings for MJO dynamics and its simulation are discussed.

490387.title: Aerosol Impacts on Microphysical Processes and Cell Morphology of Deep Convective Clouds
490387.authors: Stephen M. Saleeby, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and M. Oue, S. C. Van Den Heever, and P. Kollias
490387.abstract: Over 10 years ago the Aerosol, Cloud, Precipitation and Climate initiative (ACPC) working group highlighted the need to improve our understanding of aerosol convection interactions (ACI) in deep convective clouds. The ACPC model inter-comparison project (MIP) focused on simulating ACI in isolated convection near Houston, TX. Results from this MIP demonstrated that models display reasonable agreement concerning the aerosol impacts on cloud, rain, and warm-phase cloud microphysical processes, but greater variability in the simulation of total ice mass and mixed- and cold-phase cloud processes in deep convection. These efforts from the ACPC initiative provided motivation for a Department of Energy sponsored field campaign, TRacking Aerosol Convection interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER), with an intensive operational period (IOP) that took place from June to September 2022 in the Houston, TX area. This region frequently experiences isolated convection, coastal and urban influences, and the highly variable aerosol conditions. One of the goals was to improve our understanding of aerosol influences on convective clouds in this variable coastal environment. Several convective days across the variable warm season were selected (Jun 2, Jun 17, Jun 21, Aug 7, Sept 17, Sept 18) as simulation case studies to address our goal of investigating the role played by aerosols within convective cells. Simulations were run with the Colorado State University - Regional Atmospheric Modeling System (RAMS) at convection-resolving scales (250m dx). (Compared to similar TRACER MIP simulations, this suite of simulations includes additional case days that were run at higher resolution and with a different range of aerosol initializations.) TRACER observations of the 10th and 90th percentiles of surface aerosol number concentrations were used to establish the initial aerosol conditions for respective low and high aerosol concentration sensitivity simulations. Multi-event composites of modeled variables within tobac-tracked convective clouds were generated from the simulated TRACER events to explore the range of aerosol impacts on their size, lifecycle, and precipitation microphysics. We will demonstrate how aerosol perturbations impose direct changes to the cloud droplet population in deep convective clouds, which subsequently impact key microphysical processes (such as condensation, evaporation, autoconversion, homogeneous freezing, riming, and SIP) that modify the distributions of liquid and ice in the cells as well as the overall cell morphology including the width, depth, height, and lifetime of simulated cells. In all simulated cases, an increase in aerosol loading led to an increase in ice hydrometeor mass in deep convective cells, which resulted from an increase in riming rate of liquid hydrometeors and an increase in ice crystal number due to enhanced homogeneous freezing of cloud droplets at upper levels and the Hallett-Mossop SIP process at mid-levels.

490389.title: Improving Velocity Recovery for the NEXRAD Split Cut
490389.authors: John C. Hubbert, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. Schvartzman
490389.abstract: To mitigate range–velocity ambiguities on NEXRAD, the U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) scans the lowest elevation angles twice: (1) using a long pulse repetition time (LPRT) scan to obtain unambiguous range measurements and (2) using a shorter PRT Doppler scan that provides a higher unambiguous velocity. However, the Doppler scan is susceptible to range-overlaid echoes that obscure the velocities of the weaker-trip echoes. To address this problem, the NWS employs SZ phase coding of the transmitted pulses, allowing each trip echo to have a unique phase code. Consequently, the echoes from one trip can be cohered while the non-cohered echoes from the remaining trips behave approximately as white noise. To robustly estimate the weak-trip velocity, the stronger-trip echo must first be suppressed. This is accomplished using the Legacy window-and-notch technique, in which the cohered strong-trip time series is multiplied by a von Hann window before the strong-trip echo is removed with a spectral notch filter. The weak trip is then cohered, and its velocity is estimated.
