However, this technique is not always successful, and unrecoverable velocity estimates appear as purple regions in plan-position indicator (PPI) velocity displays, commonly referred to as purple haze. This paper demonstrates that a novel regression filter can function as an arbitrary band-stop filter for suppressing the strong-trip echo without requiring an attenuating window function. As a result, more weak-trip velocity estimates can be recovered with lower standard measurement error, substantially reducing the extent of the purple-haze regions. This regression band-stop filter is referred to as the Regression Frequency Shift Filter (RFSF). Here, the RFSF technique is extended to recover Doppler velocities from three trips. The RFSF is combined with a new technique, Velocity Recovery and Dealiasing (VRAD), to further improve SZ velocity recovery. VRAD utilizes velocity estimates from the accompanying LPRT scan to fill many of the remaining purple-haze regions. This paper presents the first combined application of RFSF and VRAD for three-trip velocity recovery. Results using NEXRAD data demonstrate that the combined approach provides substantially more valid Doppler velocity estimates and lower measurement error than the Legacy NEXRAD processing technique.

490398.title: Evaluating Smallsat Impacts on Multisensor Water Vapor Products
490398.authors: John M. Forsythe, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and S. Kidder
490398.abstract: Atmospheric water vapor is the fuel which drives heavy precipitation and floods, and satellites are the only way to provide a global view. Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere (CIRA)-developed water vapor products are used by the National Weather Service track pipelines of moisture and warn of dangerous flooding conditions. Two operational NOAA products - Blended Total Precipitable Water (BTPW) and Advected Layer Precipitable Water (ALPW) are driven primarily by passive microwave retrievals from low earth orbiting sensors. These products rely on the operational NOAA and MetOp series of spacecraft, which are limited to specific orbital planes and sampling times. Smallsat data populating other orbital planes should increase the quality of these products. In the past few years, smaller low-cost orbiting passive microwave sensors have become available which might be able to make these products even better. This includes higher temporal refresh and lower latency. Initial results on the impact of smallsat data on BTPW and ALPW for heavy precipitation events will be shown, along with validation against independent sources. Recommendations for orbital planes to provide increased temporal coverage will be presented.

490413.title: pyDARTdiags: A Python Package for Manipulating, Visualizing and Understanding Earth System Observations with DART
490413.authors: Marlee Smith, NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO
490413.abstract: The Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) is an open-source software facility for ensemble data assimilation that combines information from numerical models with real world observations to enhance the value of both. This year, DART celebrates 25 years of supporting a diverse community of users and accelerating Earth system science. Real-world observations of earth-system data come from a variety of sources, including radiosondes, satellites, ships, aircraft, weather stations, and more. In DART, we strive to empower DA practitioners to use any observation in their experiments; our tools are built to make any measurement assimilation-ready. DART makes it easy to integrate new observations and already supports a tremendous variety, providing interfaces to over 40 observation sources. We also provide the functionality to use externally-computed forward operators in DART, allowing for the use of observations that have been already used in other DA systems (GSI, JEDI) to be easily transferred to the DART framework. DART users can also generate and utilize synthetic observations for OSSE experiments using the tools provided in DART. Finally, the DART framework enforces a clean separation between observations and the models they are assimilated into, making it so that observations can be used with any model able to provide the required physical values for the forward operator. With these strengths in mind, it is crucial that our users be able to effectively leverage DART’s observational capabilities. While DART excels in many aspects with regards to observations, the format and complexity of DART’s internal observation sequence files can make them challenging to manipulate and analyze outside of the DART ecosystem. Users were unable to perform custom diagnostics, integrate with Python-based workflows, or manipulate and analyze the data using open-source tools with the data in DART’s observation sequence format. To rectify these issues, we developed pyDARTdiags, a Python package for manipulating observation sequences and calculating and visualizing observation-space diagnostics for DART. It provides tools to read, manipulate, create, and analyze DART observation sequence files using familiar, modern Python libraries. pyDARTdiags improves the accessibility and user-friendliness by creating reproducible Python workflows that integrate seamlessly with the broader scientific ecosystem. This package is easily installable with pip and includes robust testing, documentation, and runnable examples that walk a user through using pyDARTdiags features and customizing for their own application. In addition to the benefits for DART users, our efforts towards pyDARTdiags have greatly contributed to the CROCODILE (CESM Regional Ocean and Carbon cOnfigurator with Data assimILation and Embedding) project, an NSF-funded collaboration between the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) to build front-ends to improve the usability of regional oceanographic modeling capabilities, using The Community Earth System Model (CESM) and CESM-DART data assimilation. This ongoing project, dedicated to creating Python interfaces for regional ocean modeling and data assimilation, utilizes pyDARTdiags’ tools and features, such as observation space diagnostics and model-to-observation comparisons in Jupyter notebook workflows. This talk will showcase the functionalities of pyDARTdiags and give concrete examples of how this package can be used to simplify and strengthen DART users’ workflows in the observation space. It will also highlight its integration into the CROCODILE project, detailing how it is being utilized and discussing future plans for the collaboration. We look forward to showcasing these new and exciting capabilities to our community.

490416.title: Analyzing the Role of Land-Atmosphere Interactions in the 2012 Central United States Flash Drought
490416.authors: Owen Rahman, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and R. Mahmood, L. Chen, M. J. Hayes, and T. Roy
490416.abstract: Land-atmosphere interactions can play a vital role in the evolution of flash droughts. This was especially true in the 2012 central United States flash drought. For this event, surface heat fluxes, soil moisture data, and atmospheric diagnostic variables were analyzed to evaluate land-atmosphere interactions using the CONUS404 hydroclimate dataset. In the 2012 flash drought, sensible heat fluxes generally dominated across the growing season. This led to severely water-limited conditions, which contributed to a general pattern of higher values of Convective Triggering Potential (CTP), higher Low-Level Humidity Index (HIlow), lower Precipitable Water (PWAT), higher Level of Free Convection (LFC) height, higher Planetary Boundary Layer Height (PBLH), higher Lifted Index (LI), and closer to 0 J kg-1 values of Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE) and Convective Inhibition (CIN). Individual rainfall events also highlight land-atmosphere interactions. For the 24-25 August 2012 rainfall event in southeastern Nebraska, the surface heat fluxes changed from sensible heat dominating to latent heat in the following days after the rain. The atmosphere reacted by decreasing CTP by nearly half, decreasing the Lifted Condensation Level (LCL) Deficit to near 0 m, increasing CAPE, making CIN more negative, decreasing PBLH by nearly half, and decreasing LI. Many of these atmospheric responses increase the convective favorability due to decreased mid-tropospheric temperatures (therefore increasing mid-tropospheric instability), and a decreased distance between the PBLH and the LCL height. Therefore, this research suggests that in 2012, land-atmosphere interactions exacerbated flash drought conditions by decreasing atmospheric convective favorability. At the same time, drought conditions can be alleviated with additional surface moisture (e.g., rainfall from synoptic systems), which can increase moisture fluxes from the surface to the atmosphere and increase atmospheric convective favorability.

490418.title: Multi-Sensor Worldwide Ocean Winds (MWOW): An SNWG Product Enabling Ocean-Atmosphere Research from Diurnal to Climate Scales
490418.authors: Svetla M. Hristova-Veleva, JPL, Pasadena, CA; Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA; and B. W. Stiles, A. Fore, F. Polverari, A. Wineteer, H. Torres Gutierrez, S. Asharaf, and D. Henze
490418.abstract: To address U.S. government agency needs identified in the 2022 Satellite Needs Working Group (SNWG) assessment cycle (Cycle 4), the Multisensor Worldwide Ocean Winds (MWOW) project at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory was established. MWOW combines wind retrievals from active and passive satellite observations, including scatterometers, radiometers, and SARs, generating globally gridded wind speed data at approximately 6-hour intervals. This represents a significant advancement over existing instrument-specific orbital datasets, providing up to 4x daily temporal sampling and near-global spatial coverage (±80° latitude). MWOW delivers a unified, instrument-agnostic set of wind estimates with harmonized retrievals from multiple instruments, precise uncertainty estimates, and unified quality indicators that provide user-transparent depiction of instrument-specific uncertainties. The resulting analysis-ready data are available from a single source, in common format and grid, eliminating the need for users to reconcile differences across heterogeneous sensors with differing spatial resolution, sensitivity to precipitation, retrieval algorithms, and non-overlapping time periods. This presentation will describe the MWOW products and briefly demonstrate their applications across multiple scientific investigations: Diurnal variability of ocean surface winds. Diurnal variability is a fundamental feature of the Earth system, with wind and sea surface temperature cycles varying geographically and across intraseasonal, seasonal, and interannual timescales (e.g., Giglio et al., 2022). Progress in understanding this variability has been limited because most satellite wind measurements come from sun-synchronous missions that sample a given location only once or twice per day. The harmonized MWOW dataset provides a new opportunity to investigate global diurnal variability of ocean surface winds and its relationship to other Earth system variables. We present preliminary results based on the MWOW v0.2 dataset showing distinct regional patterns of diurnal wind variability and their connection to atmospheric boundary layer processes. Planetary boundary layer (PBL) characterization. Ocean surface winds represent a key measurement at the air–sea interface and directly reflect interactions between the ocean and atmosphere. These winds regulate air–sea exchanges of momentum and heat, influence turbulent mixing in both the lower atmosphere and upper ocean, drive atmospheric convection through low-level convergence, and modulate ocean circulation through surface stress and stress curl. MWOW wind fields, with their enhanced temporal resolution and spatial coverage, provide critical information for understanding the horizontal and vertical variability of the PBL and for improving modeling and forecasting across a range of spatial and temporal scales. Tropical cyclone rapid intensity changes. Rapid intensity changes in tropical cyclones (TCs) remain difficult to forecast because they depend strongly on the spatial organization of precipitation and associated latent heating. Recent work introduces a precipitation-type classification based on column-integrated condensate and ocean surface wind convergence, showing that enhanced deep convection near the storm center precedes rapid intensification, while increased deep convection in outer rainbands often precedes weakening. Combining passive microwave precipitation observations with MWOW surface winds enables improved characterization of TC precipitation structure, vertical distribution of latent heating, and convective mass flux, advancing understanding of TC evolution and its role in the large-scale circulation (Jones et al., 2026). We present the framework of this approach and highlight the complementary nature with the science goals of the upcoming INCUS mission. Hadley cell variability and trends. Recent evidence suggests that the tropics have expanded over the last few decades by approximately 1° latitude per decade, considered to be an atmospheric response to the observed tropical ocean warming trend. If continued, the expansion of the tropics (the joint width of the northern and southern Hadley cells) could have substantial impacts on water resources and the ecology of the subtropics. Ocean surface vector winds, derived from scatterometer observations, provide an accurate depiction of the surface branch of the large-scale circulations, allowing direct study of Hadley cell evolution (Hristova-Veleva et al., 2015). By providing harmonized estimates of ocean winds from multiple platforms—greatly increasing spatial coverage and temporal resolution—MWOW products will significantly improve characterization of the Hadley cell and enable better understanding of its diurnal variability and long-term trends. Monitoring climate phenomena: the 2026-2027 El Niño. El Niño events have significant impacts on the entire Earth System. While most frequently presented through anomalies in tropical sea surface temperature (SST), critical signatures also appear in sea surface height (SSH) and ocean surface winds. The eastward-blowing anomalous surface winds in the Western and Central Tropical Pacific are both the precursor and the main driver of El Niño events (e.g., Hristova-Veleva et al., 2016). With its enhanced temporal and spatial coverage, MWOW provides unprecedented capability to monitor the evolution of the emerging 2026-2027 El Niño event, capturing the full diurnal cycle of wind anomalies and their teleconnections to global circulation patterns. MWOW represents a transformative tool for ocean-atmosphere research, bridging the gap between individual satellite observations and the comprehensive, analysis-ready datasets needed for advancing our understanding of Earth system processes from diurnal to climate timescales. The research was carried out at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, under a contract with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (80NM0018D0004).

490423.title: Internal Boundary Layer Development in the Coastal Regions
490423.authors: Qing Wang, Naval Postgraduate School, Monterey, CA; and J. Kalogiros, R. Yamaguchi, J. Ruiz-Plancarte, K. L. Mulreany, and A. Bucholtz
490423.abstract: An internal boundary layer develops when an air mass is advected across a surface boundary and encounters substantially different surface and thermodynamic conditions. Such development occurs frequently in coastal regions during diurnal sea-breeze circulations and synoptic disturbances. Although internal boundary layers have been investigated extensively through observations and numerical simulations, available observational datasets remain insufficient to fully characterize their large spatial variability and evolution with fetch. In this study, we employ aircraft measurements from multiple field campaigns conducted offshore of the California coast, near Duck, North Carolina, and along the Gulf of Mexico coast. We examine the evolution of boundary layer height and turbulence using in situ measurements collected by the Naval Postgraduate School Twin Otter research aircraft and its Controlled Towed Vehicle (CTV). Our analyses focus on the wind and stability conditions at the onset of offshore advection and how these external forcings influence the subsequent development of the internal boundary layer. We also present vertical profiles of optical turbulence, represented by the refractive-index structure parameter, (Cn2), derived from high-rate aircraft measurements collected during sounding profiles through the internal boundary layers.

490424.title: Real-Time Ranking of Water Vapor Amounts Derived from Satellite
490424.authors: John M. Forsythe, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Dostalek, D. Bikos, and S. J. Kusselson
490424.abstract: Water vapor is the fuel for much of what we perceive as weather, including the formation of clouds and precipitation. Since the primary source of water vapor is evaporation over the oceans, global satellite observations provide an essential measurement for forecasters. Weather forecasters routinely use two hourly multisatellite blended products, Blended Total Precipitable Water (BTPW) and four-layer Advected Layer Precipitable Water (ALPW), to track pipelines of moisture which support heavy precipitation. Each product is driven primarily by passive microwave data. As satellite and reanalysis records begin to cover more decades, it becomes possible to place the water vapor amounts into historical context and identify extreme events. Both of these NOAA operational products have been coupled to a decadal-length satellite record and a 30-year NASA MERRA-2 reanalysis record so forecasters can assess water vapor anomalies and percentile rankings in real time. These results complement traditional radiosonde records spanning many decades, and allow characterization of moisture amounts over the ocean before the systems reach land. Applications of these products for atmospheric rivers to meet the challenge of extreme precipitation event forecasting will be discussed.

490433.title: Investigating the Dynamical Drivers of Heat Waves over North America
490433.authors: Paul C. Loikith, Portland State University, Portland, OR; Portland State University, Portland, OR; and D. Singh and S. Bigalke
490433.abstract: Loikith et al. (2026) grouped daily extreme heat objects into two categories over mid-latitude North America. The first category was labeled “heat domes”, defined as an area of extreme 2-meter temperature coinciding with an upper-level anticyclone. This category included 47% of daily extreme heat objects and 69% of extreme heat objects when accounting for multi-day episodes that included a heat dome at some point. The second category included all other extreme heat objects, which were found to occur with a range of upper-level circulation patterns, most commonly, but not always, with an open ridge feature. While it is generally well established that upper-level ridging is a common feature associated with extreme heat, these results suggest that other processes and atmospheric circulation patterns play an important role. Here we further investigate these non-heat dome cases to better understand the range of synoptic patterns and physical processes that drive extreme heat over North America. A comprehensive diagnosis of the primary drivers of extreme heat is presented for a diverse set of cases, highlighting the relative contributions from advection, adiabatic warming through subsidence, land-atmosphere feedbacks, and low-level positive temperature advection. The way in which these drivers change over the course of a multi-day event and how they may contribute to event duration is also considered. Results indicate more variability in the types of circulation features associated with similarly anomalous heat over higher latitude parts of the continent, while lower latitudes primarily experience heat domes. This work ultimately aims to bridge the weather-through-climate timescales by analyzing individual events to build an understanding of the diverse drivers of extreme heat across space and time.

490441.title: Elements of a Forecast for an Extreme El Niño in the Spring of 2026
490441.authors: Nat Johnson, GFDL, Plainsboro, NJ; and L. Jia, C. McHugh, F. Zeng, A. Wittenberg, and T. L. Delworth
490441.abstract: By March of 2026, several state-of-the-art dynamical forecast models predicted a very strong El Niño for the boreal fall and early winter of 2026/27. These El Niño forecasts, which represented a substantial jump in amplitude from forecasts issued the previous month, generated considerable social and mainstream media attention despite being issued at a time of the year when predictability of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is typically quite low. Based on seasonal forecasts produced by the NOAA GFDL Seamless System for Prediction and EArth System Research (SPEAR), we discuss the unusual nature of and the factors that contributed to this early high amplitude El Niño forecast. Based on all available retrospective forecasts since 1991, the SPEAR March 2026 El Niño forecast was the second strongest on record (trailing only March 1997), and the February-March forecast jump was the second largest one-month ENSO forecast change out of more than 400 forecast changes. Using analysis fields of sea surface height, sea level pressure, and sea surface temperature, we construct regression models to diagnose the factors responsible for the high amplitude SPEAR El Niño forecast initialized in the spring of 2026. Preliminary analysis suggests that anomalously warm conditions in the subtropical eastern Pacific in March of 2026 may have contributed substantially to the unusually strong El Niño forecast.

490443.title: Considerations for Constructing Multidecadal Satellite Water Vapor Datasets
490443.authors: John M. Forsythe, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and T. H. VonderHaar, S. J. Fletcher, and S. Liu
490443.abstract: Satellite-driven multidecadal records are essential for comparison to reanalyses and for capturing processes, trends and extreme events. Water vapor is a key variable as it fuels other weather impacts such as heavy precipitation. The existing NASA Water Vapor Project - Making Earth System Data Records for Use in Research Environments (NVAP-M) dataset spans 1988-2009. It consists of daily, global total column water vapor and layer water vapor fields from a variety of satellite sensors, with a particular reliance on passive microwave sensors. The NVAP-M dataset is not currently being extended. NVAP-M was constructed from blended multisatellite observations with minimal reliance on reanalysis products. The emphasis on satellite retrievals makes it valuable for comparison and for machine learning independent of reanalysis. In creating a long-term dataset, many factors must be considered. These include biases due to preferential land or ocean sampling, excessive clear-sky sampling, and sensor calibration drift. Algorithms may be biased via the use of a Gaussian framework, while a non-Gaussian formulation can better capture extremes. These impacts will be discussed with a view towards future construction of an extended and reprocessed global water vapor dataset.

490446.title: Scaling Air Quality Health Risk to Activity Intensity and Altitude
490446.authors: Samantha J Kramer, Atmospheric Interdisciplinary Research Institute, Denver, CO; and C. D. McClure, O. Ryder, T. L. Lavezzo, and L. Chinkin
490446.abstract: Outdoor recreation is central to Colorado's economy, public health, and quality of life, yet the state's complex topography, high elevation, and diverse air quality challenges create compounded health risks for residents and visitors. While the Air Quality Index (AQI) provides general information about ambient pollutant concentrations, its categorical advisories, such as "limit outdoor exposure", are insufficiently granular to support activity-specific decision-making. Critically, current AQI recommendations do not distinguish between low-intensity activities like walking and vigorous aerobic exercise, nor do they account for demographic variability in susceptibility or the unique physiological challenges posed by high-elevation environments. This research addresses a critical methodological gap by developing a comprehensive framework for characterizing exertion-specific air quality risk applicable across diverse populations and physiological conditions. The core innovation operationalizes Metabolic Equivalents (METs), a physiologically grounded quantification of energy expenditure during different activity intensities, as the fundamental scaling mechanism linking ambient air quality to inhalation exposure risk. This approach is grounded in the principle that ventilation rate, and therefore inhaled pollutant dose, scales directly with metabolic demand: a person jogging ventilates more air than a person walking at the same location under identical ambient air quality conditions. We develop activity-specific MET classifications for Colorado's outdoor recreation landscape (hiking, trail running, skiing, cycling, water sports, recreational climbing) across demographic cohorts defined by age, health status, fitness level, and elevation acclimatization. Critically, we integrate elevation-adjusted respiratory physiology accounting for reduced oxygen availability and increased ventilation demands at high altitude and individual health vulnerability factors (asthma, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, medication use) to characterize how susceptibility to air quality impacts varies within and across populations. The scientific contributions of this work are significant: (1) A physiologically defensible framework for linking ambient air quality to activity-intensity-specific inhalation exposure and health impact; (2) Elevation-adjusted respiratory physiology applicable to high-altitude outdoor populations, with implications for occupational health, emergency response, and recreational safety; (3) Population-stratified risk characterization that moves beyond one-size-fits-all public health guidance; and (4) A methodology readily adaptable to other regions, elevation ranges, air quality challenges, and demographic profiles. The framework is designed for use by atmospheric scientists, public health professionals, occupational health specialists, emergency management agencies, schools, outdoor recreation providers, and local decision-makers.

490447.title: Preparing a Responsible AI-Ready Workforce: Supporting Students, Postdocs, and Early-Career Scientists In Effective and Ethical Use of AI for Research
490447.authors: Rebecca Haacker, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and L. Harney, M. G. Cains, J. H. Richter, M. A. Morrison, B. Guarente, and T. Ross-Lazarov
490447.abstract: We will share our approach at the U.S. National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) to embed responsible AI education across the Earth system science (ESS) research lifecycle. Our vision is an ESS workforce that understands both the opportunities and limitations of AI and can make informed decisions about when AI enhances research, when traditional approaches are more appropriate, and how to use AI ethically, transparently, and critically. By bringing together Earth system science, AI/ML expertise, and evidence-based pedagogy, NSF NCAR is building institutional and community-wide AI literacy through accessible training, resources, internships, visitor programs, and professional development. To guide this work, we hosted 12 community listening sessions in 2026 to better understand AI workforce priorities across the ESS community. We will share key findings on community-identified training needs, barriers to adoption, and opportunities for collaboration. An internal survey of NSF NCAR staff complemented this effort by assessing current AI/ML use, desired applications, confidence levels, and training needs across the organization, ensuring our strategy is grounded in both community and institutional perspectives. We will present our approach to developing AI capacity for both NSF NCAR staff and the broader research community, including partnerships with UCAR's COMET program to create and deliver AI learning opportunities. Examples include helping researchers determine where AI adds scientific value, prepare and manage data for machine learning workflows, critically evaluate AI-generated outputs, understand AI limitations and sources of bias, and apply AI in ways that support reproducibility, transparency, and scientific integrity. We will also discuss approaches that help educators leverage AI to develop instructional materials while maintaining scientific rigor and critical thinking. For example, we can share examples of implementing AI coaches in self-paced e-learning. The AI coach evaluates user-submitted text against a rubric, affirms what the learner did well, then poses guiding questions that prompt them toward their own next step instead of supplying the answer. When a learner struggles repeatedly, the coach adjusts, tailoring its feedback to the areas where they have had the most difficulty. Together, these efforts demonstrate how responsible AI education can be integrated across research, education, and professional development to build an ESS workforce capable of making informed decisions about when and how AI should, and should not, be used. By emphasizing sound scientific judgment alongside technical AI skills, we strengthen the informatics foundation needed to advance open, interoperable, trustworthy, and reproducible Earth system science.

490452.title: NWS Transformation: Championing Change for a Weather-Ready Nation through Local Community Engagement and Applied Social Science Research
490452.authors: Leticia Williams, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and T. B. Harris, C. Young, K. Negrón-Hernández, V. Were, B. G. López, R. Munroe, A. Roser, T. Hall, and J. S. Lee
490452.abstract: Weather hazards continually reshape the resilience of communities, demanding an evolution in how we deliver critical information and services—especially to those disproportionately impacted by extreme events. The National Weather Service (NWS) recognizes that access to timely, understandable, and actionable weather information is not just a goal but a necessity for building resilient communities. Supporting the NWS transformation, this coordinated, multi-level strategy for local community engagement includes aligning efforts with regional and local offices/liaisons and collaborating with key programs and partners. As we envision this shift from traditional engagement approaches to a model that is community-centric, evidence-based, and capacity-driven we know it can only be achieved through strong partnerships such as the one we have with the emergency management (EM) community. This presentation highlights an exemplary partnership: A collaborative effort between the NWS Office of Future Readiness (OFR), NWS Los Angeles/Oxnard (LOX) and San Diego (SGX), and the Los Angeles County Office of Emergency Management (OEM) to improve heat and fire hazard messaging to support protective action decision-making. Building on ongoing NWS risk communication research and coordination with LA OEM, this project seeks to capture the entire communication continuum—from pre-event awareness and confidence building, through watches, warnings, and advisories to post-event reinforcement and recovery messaging. The project is a case study of four heat and wildfire events between 2024 and 2026, and the analysis is twofold: 1) Message development analyses of NWS products and messages to organize information into more intentional subsets that align with emergency management timelines, forecast confidence, and impact thresholds; 2) A social network analysis of weather-related information seeking and sharing networks during a large-scale public event to identify key message amplifiers and hubs that connect the NWS with its critical partners and publics in that and potentially similar contexts. The project promotes a flexible, time- and confidence-based approach to communicate weather information and support resilient communities. The resulting guidance is designed to help forecasters select messages based on hazard, timing, and partner needs, while supporting stronger coordination and consistency across WFOs with partners. This presentation will share early insights, partner perspectives, and lessons learned from this interdisciplinary collaboration, offering a scalable framework for aligning hazard communication with EM needs to improve protective action outcomes. Additionally, this will provide insights into the approach of the NWS transformational strategy for local community engagement, highlight best practices for incorporating the complex human dimension of weather through social science, and discuss how emergency management professionals and other stakeholders can play a vital role in shaping its implementation.

490453.title: Advancing The Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) as an Early-Career Software Engineer
490453.abstract: The Data Assimilation Research Testbed, or DART, is an open-source, freely available software facility for ensemble data assimilation, supporting a vast and diverse community of users for over 25 years. Ensemble data assimilation is a statistical method that is used to combine information from numerical models with real world observations to enhance the value of both. Applications include generating initial conditions for forecasts and predictability studies, diagnosing model error and bias, and assessing the value of existing and planned observations. DART includes interfaces to many models and observations across all Earth system domains. DART also allows for the use of a variety of assimilation algorithms, including novel methods developed by the DAReS team that are especially effective for pollutants, sea ice concentration, and soil moisture. Our modular software design and generalized model interface routines facilitate the addition of new models, observations, and assimilation algorithms and allows for users to easily switch between the available options. Focusing on accessibility, our software is carefully engineered to run efficiently on systems ranging from laptops to top performing supercomputers. DART utilizes the power of HPC through distributed memory and parallel computation with the Message Passing Interface (MPI) to be able to run with complex, high resolution models and large numbers of observations and ensemble members. This further extends the versatility of DART by allowing users to work on more computationally demanding projects. For these reasons, DART is able to support a diverse, long-standing, and continuously growing user community. This inherent diversity in DART has also enabled me to contribute to a broad spectrum of projects, each requiring unique skills and technologies.This poster will detail the versatility of DART and its functionalities, showing how this has shaped my early-career work and development as one of two software engineers on the team. Working with DART has allowed me to engage with a wide variety of systems, environments, programming languages, assimilation algorithms, models, observations, background science, and collaborators. The poster will also describe my varied technical contributions and specifically highlight a few of my larger projects that showcase the interdisciplinary and multifaceted nature of my role in DAReS. Examples include collaborative projects with the NASA Goddard Space Flight Center and the NSF NCAR High Altitude Observatory (HAO), facilitating the use of DART data assimilation with space weather models on NASA’s Pleiades Supercomputer and the co-development of pyDARTdiags, a Python package for manipulating observation sequences and calculating observation-space diagnostics for DART.

490456.title: 1997/98 Redux? The Uniqueness of the 1997/98 El Niño North American Precipitation Signal and Its Possible Return in the Winter of 2026/27
490456.abstract: The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the dominant source of winter seasonal precipitation predictability over North America, with the canonical ENSO signal accounting for most of the predictable precipitation variance in state-of-the-art dynamical forecast models. After removing the canonical ENSO influence, however, both the North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME; 1991-present) and ECMWF CSF-20C (1901-2010) indicate that the leading pattern of predictable winter precipitation variance features enhanced precipitation on both the west and east coasts of North America. Moreover, the only previous winter since 1900 for which this pattern had a high amplitude was the winter of 1997/98, indicating that this extreme El Niño may have been unique among all previous El Niños in more than a century in terms of expected precipitation impacts over North America. Preliminary evidence indicates that its high amplitude and unusual eastward displacement were key factors for its unique expected impacts. Precipitation forecasts from the NMME initialized in the summer of 2026 bear some notable similarities to the precipitation forecasts in the summer of 1997, with enhanced precipitation over the West Coast and Southeastern U.S. relative to the canonical El Niño. These potential parallels between 1997/98 and the current El Niño suggest that the seasonally predictable precipitation response to the current El Niño may represent an unusual deviation from the canonical El Niño pattern.

490457.title: Buoyancy Influences on Seed Dispersal over Forested Hills (Invited Presentation)
490457.abstract: Due to the heterogeneity introduced by hilly terrain and the tendency for heat to ventilate from the windward side and accumulate on the leeward side of hills, investigating buoyancy's influence on turbulent flow over three-dimensional forested hills requires full coupling between the surface, the canopy, and the atmosphere. In this work, we investigate seed dispersal using large-eddy simulations of turbulent flow interacting with a coupled forest canopy over regularly repeating forested hills of ``egg-carton" (double cosine) shape and of varying steepness. The influence of source location relative to the hill and terminal velocity will be emphasized.

490458.title: Same Air, Different Story: Why Air Quality Looks Different Everywhere You Look
490458.authors: Crystal D McClure, Atmospheric Interdisciplinary Research Institute, Denver, CO; and S. J. Kramer and O. Ryder
490458.abstract: Public communication of air quality events is challenging enough without the added complexity that many countries measure their Air Quality Index (AQI) differently. Compounding this, the way the public receives air quality information at the state and local level can vary significantly depending on the source. While prior research has begun to examine the visual representation of air quality communication (e.g., dials, color bars, emojis), we conducted a systematic qualitative and quantitative analysis of the major news outlets through which the public receives this information. Using Google Puppeteer, we captured screenshots of each major news outlet simultaneously, every hour, and used this data to compare both the visual representation of AQI and the quantitative values reported by each outlet. We find that while many websites and news outlets have aligned their AQI messaging with approximately the EPA AQI scale, they do not all provide the same quantitative information. For example, two outlets can display highly variable AQI readings for the same location because they are drawing on different underlying pollutant AQI aggregates. Additionally, acute pollution events such as wildfires and urban structure fires are not well represented across platforms, with some outlets showing significantly divergent AQI values. Overall, our findings suggest that substantial work remains in unify messaging around air quality events and presenting AQI information in a coherent, standardized way.

490460.title: Forays into using the Warn-On Forecast System to Predict Freezing Rain
490460.authors: Daniel D. Tripp, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; and A. A. Rosenow, K. H. Knopfmeier, and N. Yussouf
490460.abstract: The Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS) is a convection-allowing ensemble that was designed to provide “next-hour” (0-6 hr) forecast of the path, intensity and timing of convective hazards, including tornadoes, damaging winds, hail, and flash floods. While the system comprises various components specifically optimized for convective weather, a primary driver of its performance is the rapid assimilation of radar and satellite data every 15 minutes to increase the accuracy of the initial conditions in the ensemble. This high-frequency data assimilation, paired with the ability to provide temporal output every 5 minutes, allows forecasters to view sub-hourly, storm-scale evolution which is not currently available from operational models. While previous studies have extensively outlined its performance and utility for warm-season convection, the system's ability to predict winter hazards remains unexplored. Furthermore, it is unknown which post-processing visualizations are most beneficial for end users during winter-weather events. This study utilizes the current warm-season configuration of the WoFS to explore its potential for providing decision-support to forecasters and decision makers during freezing rain events. Regardless of the modeling system employed, forecasting freezing rain is exceptionally challenging due to its high sensitivity to the thermal profile and the transient nature of this precipitation type. Freezing rain typically occurs in environments near 0°C which means even small model errors may be enough to change the surface temperature from subfreezing to above freezing -- resulting in an incorrect diagnosis of the precipitation type. Furthermore, the duration of freezing rain is highly variable; while extreme icing events can persist for over 24 hours, many high-impact scenarios last only a few minutes and may occur between the hourly output intervals of standard operational models. Even a trace accumulation during these short-lived events is sufficient to cause significant travel disruptions, making sub-hourly temporal resolution important for effective decision support. These challenges are compounded by the spatial heterogeneity of winter weather, where freezing rain frequently transitions into or mixes with other precipitation types. This lack of clear, discrete boundaries between precipitation types makes it difficult for forecasters to predict the footprint and magnitude of ice accumulation, highlighting the need for a system that can capture rapid, small-scale transitions on sub-hourly time scales. This study will provide a first look at WoFS predictions for an ice storm that occurred on January 10-11th, 2020. New freezing rain diagnostics will be shown along with new decision-support graphics. For this case study, the WoFS was able to capture the general magnitude and footprint of the ice storm. However, verification at individual ASOS stations shows that the system had a surface warm bias resulting in errors in freezing rain predictions. After sunset, the warm bias decreased and the system performed better. This presentation will overview the capabilities of the warm-season configuration of the WoFS for predicting freezing rain to provide insight for future research to design a system for winter.

490461.title: Warehouse Fires: A Mega-sized Air Quality Hazard
490461.authors: Crystal D McClure, Atmospheric Interdisciplinary Research Institute, Denver, CO; and O. Ryder, A. G. Rappold, N. Herbert, M. F. Theodori, and S. J. Kramer
490461.abstract: An increasing number of mega-warehouse facilities are located within population dense regions of the contiguous United States and are disproportionately sited near disadvantaged communities. Each mega-warehouse has an extreme fire potential, yet their fire risk remains almost entirely unstudied. Due to the immense facility size and content density, warehouse fires behave more like wildfires than typical structure fires: multi-day burning, extended heat release, significant smoke emissions, firefighting resource intensive. The contents of mega-warehouses can vary widely based on the industry but are likely to include a mixture of synthetic and natural products tightly packed, making emissions and exposure estimates obscure. In this study we investigate the localized risk of mega-warehouse fires, their potential air quality hazard, and capacity to impact population centers. We find that mega-warehouse fires have the potential to release particulate matter pollution equivalent to a 45,000-acre wildfire. We demonstrate the current regulatory and air sensor monitoring networks are unprepared to characterize these hazards, with 4 in 10 mega-warehouses having no monitoring within 5 miles and only 5.7% having hazardous air pollutant-capable instrumentation, leaving nearby residents without adequate information on their exposure during a fire. As e-commerce continues to drive warehouse expansion, this monitoring gap will only widen. Additionally, we find that mega-warehouse fires disproportionately impact communities that rank high in linguistic isolation, overall pollution impacts, and socioeconomic burden. Preparedness planning, expanded monitoring, and new research on urban emissions must be performed to effectively mitigate and communicate these hazards when an emergency strikes.

490463.title: U.S. National Ice Center's Ice Cold Forecasting
490463.authors: Sofia M. Montalvo, Naval Ice Center, Suitland, MD; and L. Sayen, B. Fajardo, I. Marcus, and F. J. Roosevelt
490463.abstract: Sea ice forecasting plays a major role in supporting safe navigation and mission success in polar and sub-polar regions. Ice conditions can directly impact ship routing, logistics, under-ice operations, and personnel safety, making accurate and timely forecasting critical for operations in the Arctic, Antarctic, and other ice-affected areas. As military, scientific, and commercial activity in these regions continues to increase, the demand for reliable ice analysis and forecasting continues to grow alongside it. While advances in satellite imagery, environmental modeling, and emerging AI/ML capabilities have improved the ability to monitor polar regions, experienced ice forecasters are still essential to interpreting changing ice conditions and providing operationally relevant guidance. Forecasters must analyze multiple data sources, understand environmental trends, recognize hazards, and determine how conditions may impact ongoing or future operations. Human analysis remains especially important in dynamic environments where rapidly changing conditions or sensor limitations can affect automated assessments. The United States National Ice Center provides continuous ice analysis and forecasting support for military, scientific, and maritime operations around the world. Support includes tailored forecasting products, iceberg analysis, route recommendations, and decision support for exercises, deployments, logistics missions, and emergency response operations. These products help commanders, vessel crews, and operational planners make informed decisions in some of the most challenging operating environments on Earth.

490465.title: Indirect Effects of Agricultural Dust Aerosols on Mixed-Phase Clouds Through Ice Nucleation
490465.authors: Tyler Richard Barone, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and X. Liu and Y. Shi
490465.abstract: Mineral dust aerosols constitute the largest fraction of atmospheric aerosol mass and play a critical role in Earth's climate system. By absorbing and scattering solar radiation, dust aerosols directly influence the Earth's radiative balance. They also indirectly modify cloud properties by serving as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and ice-nucleating particles (INPs). In addition to natural dust (ND) emitted from deserts and arid regions, anthropogenic agricultural dust (AD) aerosols are an important contributor to the global dust burden and radiative balance, particularly in the industrial era. However, AD is generally not represented in most Earth system models, leaving its effect on cloud and radiative properties poorly constrained. Following Shi et al. (2022), we implement a physically-based parameterization for AD emissions in the land component of the U.S. Department of Energy's Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 2 (E3SMv2). We explicitly simulate both ND and AD processes in the atmosphere. To evaluate the role of AD in mixed-phase clouds, state-of-the-art INP parameterizations developed for ND and AD are compared against observations from the U.S. Department of Energy's Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility. We further examine the global distribution and seasonal variability of AD impacts on mixed-phase cloud properties and the Earth's radiation budget. This work provides new constraints on the effects of agricultural dust and advances the representation of agricultural dust aerosols in Earth system models, thereby reducing uncertainties in aerosol–cloud–climate interactions.

490469.title: Development of a Probabilistic MRMS Emulator Blending Historical Sparse Observations and Reanalysis Data
490469.authors: David Ryglicki, The Demex Group, LLC, New York, NY; and J. Caramichael and N. Been
490469.abstract: Hail is among the costliest and least well characterized perils in the United States, and the observational record limits what can be resolved. The Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system provides the necessary radar-derived fields, but accessible archives extend back only to 2020 and the MYRORSS reanalysis remains incomplete. We developed a generative deep learning method that fuses freely available sparse observations with NWP reanalysis fields to produce CONUS-wide, MRMS-like probabilistic daily hail swaths from the mid-1990s forward, a roughly sixfold extension of the usable record. We report verification against withheld MRMS years and independent Storm Prediction Center and NCEI reports and describe how the architecture was constrained to make a national thirty-year reconstruction achievable at low computational cost. A record of this length supports questions the operational archive cannot address, including detection of trends and non-stationarity in hail frequency and severity, evaluation of convection-permitting climate simulations, and construction of grid-scale hail climatologies less sensitive to report density and population bias.

490476.title: Through FIRE and Clouds: Evaluating MERRA-2-Driven RTTOV Spectral Infrared Radiance Simulations with PREFIRE Observations
490476.authors: Paige Alexandria Bartels, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and M. I. Oyola-Merced, T. S. L'Ecuyer, and J. K. Shaw
490476.abstract: The Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the global mean due to positive feedback loops collectively known as Arctic amplification. At the same time, cloud processes remain one of the largest sources of uncertainty in global climate models, particularly in the far-infrared, where observational constraints historically have been limited. The NASA Polar Radiant Energy in the Far InfraRed Experiment (PREFIRE) satellites provide spectral radiance observations in the mid- and far-infrared, enabling evaluation of model representations of Arctic clouds and thermodynamic structure. This study compares PREFIRE spectral radiances in the Arctic with radiances simulated using the Radiative Transfer for TOVS (RTTOV) model driven by Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2) reanalysis. Both Arctic clear-sky and cloudy scenes are examined to evaluate systematic differences between observations and RTTOV-simulated radiances, with particular emphasis on the longer infrared wavelengths uniquely observed by PREFIRE. Scene characterization is provided using collocated ESA/JAXA EarthCARE ATLID and CPR observations together with MERRA-2 reanalysis. In addition, one-dimensional variational (1D-Var) retrievals are performed to investigate thermodynamic differences between the simulated and observed radiances and to assess their implications for atmospheric structure. Through these radiative closure studies, this work aims to assess the representation of Arctic cloud and thermodynamic structure in reanalyses, while demonstrating the value of spectral infrared observations for model evaluation.

490480.title: Machine Learning Meets Scaling Analysis: Accurate Estimation of Sensible Heat and Momentum Fluxes from Temperature Time-Series (Invited Presentation)
490480.abstract: Reliable estimates of surface turbulent fluxes (e.g., heat, moisture, momentum) at a range of scales are of significant importance in the fields of agriculture, ecology, forestry, hydrology, urban planning, weather forecasting, and numerous others. These fluxes provide the essential dynamical couplings between the land surface and its overlying atmospheric boundary layer. They modulate the local weather systems and play pivotal roles in the broader context of climate change. Several direct and indirect flux-estimating methodologies exist in the literature. Among them, the so-called eddy covariance (EC) approach is widely considered to be the gold standard. The EC approach can provide reliable flux estimates for an in-situ location with a footprint of a few hundred square meters. However, in order to estimate representative areal fluxes over heterogeneous landscapes, one needs to set up a dense network of sonic anemometers. In terms of installation, it is needless to say that such networks are cost-prohibitive and labor-intensive. Moreover, from the O&M perspective, sonic anemometers are very demanding. We have recently developed a novel machine learning-based flux estimation approach as an alternative. In our approach, only high-frequency temperature data is needed as input. From this data, we extract various statistical and dynamical traits (e.g., Higuchi dimension, permutation entropy, higher-order structure-function) and use them as input features. Via Systematic (permutation) feature importance study, we are able to identify the most relevant input features and make a connection to existing “surface renewal”-based theories.

490481.title: Virtualizing 50 Years of Satellite Observations for AI/ML Applications at UW-Madison SSEC/CIMSS
490481.authors: Clayton Suplinski, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and J. Robaidek and D. A. Santek
490481.abstract: The University of Wisconsin–Madison Space Science and Engineering Center (SSEC) maintains an extensive archive of environmental satellite observations spanning approximately 50 years and multiple generations of geostationary and other satellite instruments. These observations represent a valuable resource for climate studies and for the development and training of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) applications. However, the archive contains many generations of data formats, navigation systems, and storage conventions that can make large-scale use by modern analysis frameworks challenging. For decades, SSEC's McIDAS Abstract Data Distribution Environment (ADDE) has provided format-independent discovery, subsetting, navigation, and access to these observations while allowing the underlying data to remain in their native formats. More recently, McFETCH has provided a simplified programmatic interface for accessing these holdings. We are extending these capabilities to support modern array-based workflows, including Zarr and xarray, without requiring wholesale conversion or duplication of the multi-petabyte archive. Current development includes extending McFETCH to produce Zarr output and developing API-based access that allows users to request spatial, temporal, spectral, and other subsets of archived observations in a Zarr-compatible form. This approach combines concepts similar to VirtualiZarr with the existing capabilities of ADDE, which can interpret and transform numerous historical satellite formats at request time. In this model, the existing archive provides the authoritative source data, ADDE provides a virtualization and transformation layer, and modern interfaces present the resulting observations in forms readily usable by AI/ML and scientific analysis tools. SSEC is also developing complementary mechanisms for providing selected archive holdings to external users through its Data Exchange, including an access model in which users can directly support data-egress costs. These efforts are intended to make decades of heterogeneous satellite observations appear increasingly as a consistent, subsettable, array-oriented resource, reducing the need for researchers to understand individual historical formats while preserving the original observational record.

490482.title: Scientific Opportunities in the Tropical Western Pacific and Indian Ocean Basin
490482.authors: Ross J. Salawitch, University of Maryland, College Park, COLLEGE PARK, MD; and T. Röpke, K. Müller, I. Wohltmann, E. Z. Farago, C. Weaver, and M. Rex
490482.abstract: The Tropical Western Pacific (TWP) and Indian Ocean basin exert enormous control on Earth’s climate and the composition of stratospheric air. A strongly positive phase of the Indian Ocean Dipole has been implicated, together with an El Niño Southern Oscillation event in the Pacific, as a significant factors in the unusually warm global mean surface temperatures that occurred in 2023 and 2024. Satellite observations indicate a fundamental change in the relationship between SST and cloud albedo over broad regions of the Pacific Ocean starting around 2010, which complicates the inference of cloud feedback from historical observations. The TWP region has been sampled by prior aircraft campaigns such as CONvective TRansport of Active Species in the Tropics (CONTRAST), Coordinated Airborne Studies in the Tropics (CAST), and Airborne Tropical TRopopause EXperiment (ATTREX) in winter 2014, the Pacific Oxidants, Sulfur, Ice, Dehydration, and cONvection (POSIDON) Experiment in fall 2016, and the Stratospheric Aerosol processes, Budget and Radiative Effects (SABRE) in spring 2022 and summer 2026. The Tropical Indian Ocean (TIO) has been not extensively sampled by aircraft since the Indian Ocean Experiment (INDOEX) in winter 1999. These prior campaigns showed evidence for a strong anthropogenic imprint on airmasses with enhanced concentrations of ozone throughout the troposphere, the transport of very short-lived (VSL) halogen species into the lower stratosphere, and the influence of a so-called “atmospheric brown cloud” layer over the Indian Ocean on climate as well as air pollution. In this presentation we will discuss an analysis of ozonesonde data collected at the Palau Atmospheric Observatory (7°N, 134°E) starting in 2016, which suggests ozone-rich air masses in the upper troposphere are most prevalent in April to June, a time period not yet covered by aircraft sampling over either the TWP or the TIO. Trajectory analysis is used to relate air parcels with enhanced ozone to stratospheric in-mixing and as well as the surface emission of air pollutants from various source regions, which are predominantly connected to the Asian continent. Future airborne measurement of tracers of various emission sources would allow for the identification of specific human activities, such as biomass burning and fossil fuel combustion, that are responsible for elevated levels of ozone. Airborne measurements of aerosols and cloud structure are needed to develop a comprehensive understanding of the climatic impact of human activities and how changes in sea surface temperature alter the radiative properties of clouds. Finally, measurements of oxidants over the Indian Ocean basin and the TWP would enable chemical loss of various pollutants, such as VSL halogens, to be properly assessed as airmasses transit from the surface to the stratosphere.

490486.title: NOAA's Geostationary Earth orbit Observations (GEO) Program Status and Plans for the Future
490486.authors: Edward Grigsby, NESDIS, Silver Spring, MD
490486.abstract: The NOAA/NESDIS Geostationary Earth orbit Observations (GEO) Program was established to manage both the highly successful Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) – R Series constellation and the development of the future operational system, the Geostationary Extended Observations (GeoXO) Program. The GOES – R Series constellation is fully operational and is 10 years into its operational life with GOES-19 serving as GOES East, GOES-18 serving as GOES West, and GOES-16 and 17 in on-orbit storage. Together the GOES-R satellites watch more than half the globe – from the west coast of Africa to New Zealand, and from Antarctica to the Arctic Ocean. The GOES-R Series satellites are planned to continue operations into the 2030s. The GeoXO Program is NOAA’s next generation geostationary satellite constellation system with a first launch targeted for 2032 and three more launches in the 2030-40’s to provide constellation operations into the 2050’s. All the GeoXO satellites will have both critical imaging observational capabilities and new hyperspectral sounding instrument observations. The GeoXO satellites will operate in the same orbital locations as the GOES-R series satellites and will enable imaging continuity observations for NOAA’s NWS weather mission well into the 2050’s. Development teams have been selected for all of the GeoXO instruments and spacecraft, and the program is planning for critical design reviews in FY27 and FY28. This presentation provides a status of the GEO program elements including the GeoXO Program plans and status and roles and responsibilities in the support of NOAA’s operational organizations as well as the status of the GOES-R series constellation. Additionally, GeoXO program scope, timeline, and expected performance based on the constellation configurations and instrument complements will be discussed.

490490.title: Does a Spectrally Adjusted Loss Function Preserve Atmospheric River Structure and Dynamics in GraphCast?
490490.authors: Sean Heslin, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and W. E. Chapman and A. C. Subramanian
490490.abstract: Deterministic machine-learning weather forecasts become smoother as they are rolled forward, leading to the weakening and broadening of intense weather systems. We test whether a spectrally adjusted mean squared error (AMSE) loss reduces this smoothing in forecasts of atmospheric rivers (ARs). Forecasts from two 13-level GraphCast models trained with conventional mean squared error and AMSE are compared with the original 37-level GraphCast, ECMWF Integrated Forecasting System (IFS), and reanalysis data. In addition to bulk integrated vapor transport (IVT) verification and spectral analysis over two north Pacific AR seasons, we use straightened and normalized composites of over 1000 AR forecasts to evaluate changes between forecast days 1 and 6 in the moisture plume, frontal structure, and low-level jet. Our results demonstrate the AMSE loss function reduces overall smoothing of moisture, wind, and IVT fields, while also improving the representation of frontal temperature gradients, low-level jet ageostrophy, and moisture convergence within the AR.

490492.title: Improving Planetary Boundary Layer Thermodynamic Retrievals: Leveraging Surface-Atmosphere Interactions and Space-Based Emissivity Constraints
490492.authors: Melina Sol Yabra, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and A. Gambacorta, N. Shahroudi, S. Serbin, A. E. Kotsakis, S. D. Nicholls, and A. feldman
490492.abstract: Accurate satellite-based characterization of the Planetary Boundary Layer (PBL) is a high-priority goal outlined by the NASA Decadal Survey Incubation program. However, a major challenge in establishing a global PBL observing system is the profound influence of the Earth's surface, which both physically drives PBL evolution and radiatively complicates lower-atmospheric observations. A recent interdisciplinary community perspective established that overcoming these challenges requires tightly integrating surface states with PBL observations. This work translates that conceptual roadmap into operational practice by addressing one of the largest sources of uncertainty in space-based atmospheric sounding: surface conditions. Because the radiative signature of the surface dominates the boundary layer signal in passive retrievals, unconstrained surface heterogeneity severely limits the accuracy of temperature (T) and water vapor (q) profiles near the ground. We demonstrate the potential operational use of dynamic, space-based surface state retrievals to better estimate surface emissivity as a physical constraint. By accurately characterizing the dynamic background surface emission, this methodology aims to reduce lower-atmospheric retrieval errors and yields higher-fidelity T and q profiles within the PBL. We will discuss the performance of these improved retrievals and highlight how operationalizing surface-atmosphere coupling in retrieval algorithms provides a direct pathway to meet the stringent observational requirements necessary for predicting severe weather, hydrologic extremes, and climate variability.

490493.title: Using Kinetic Energy to Explain Seasonal MJO Teleconnections
490493.authors: Tatiana Nicole Esteva-Ingram, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and N. Sakaeda
490493.abstract: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is a tropical, convective phenomenon known to influence the extratropics through teleconnections. While studies have investigated MJO teleconnections, an incomplete understanding of the underlying mechanisms generating MJO teleconnections remains, especially outside of boreal winter. Many studies have mainly focused on the linear interactions that drive MJO teleconnections, but additional studies have also shown that non-linear, cross-scale interactions, are important to the development of MJO teleconnections in boreal winter as well. To quantify the importance of non-linear, cross-scale interactions, studies commonly use kinetic energy for their investigations. This work aims to understand the importance of cross-scale interactions to the development of the seasonal MJO teleconnections by using kinetic energy. Using reanalysis data and budget analysis, we identify favorable processes that lead to the generation of MJO-associated kinetic energy, which can facilitate MJO teleconnection development. Strong seasonality in the kinetic energy associated with the MJO is found, where the DJF MJO-associated kinetic energy extends furthest into the extratropics, consistent with previous studies. The interaction between the MJO and subtropical jet is important for MJO-associated kinetic energy generation, where the locations of generation and dissipation exhibit strong seasonality. Furthermore, there are seasonal differences in what processes are important to the generation of MJO-associated kinetic energy. Through this work, a better understanding of the importance of cross-scale interactions to the seasonal development of MJO teleconnections can help identify potential areas to improve MJO teleconnection modeling.

490495.title: Interpreting Changes In NOx As Observed By Satellite and Ground-Based Measurements during Heatwave Events
490495.authors: Deepangsu Chatterjee, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ; and X. Jin
490495.abstract: We define heatwaves as periods of at least three consecutive days when daily maximum temperature exceeds the 95th percentile threshold during May-July 2019-2023. Heatwaves modify atmospheric nitrogen dioxide (NO2) through changes in both meteorology and emissions, yet the temperature dependence of NOx emissions remains poorly constrained in chemical forecast systems. We combine Tropospheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI) NO2 columns, NASA’s GEOS-CF simulations, EPA surface NO₂ observations, and Continuous Emissions Monitoring Systems (CEMS) power-plant emissions to evaluate heatwave-driven NO2 and NOx responses across the contiguous United States. TROPOMI reveals pronounced spatial heterogeneity, with positive heatwave NO2 anomalies in most major U.S. cities, which agree with EPA ground observations. GEOS-CF simulations reproduce the broad spatial patterns but generally underestimates the magnitude of positive anomalies over urban areas. Analysis of CEMS facility emissions demonstrates that power-plant NOx emissions increase by approximately 25–30% under the warmest conditions, closely tracking comparable increases in heat input, while NOx emitted per unit heat input remains nearly constant. In contrast, GEOS-CF represents strong temperature sensitivities for natural emissions, including soil and biomass-burning NOx, but anthropogenic NOx emissions remain nearly unchanged at power-plant grid cells. Our results suggest that missing temperature-dependent power-sector activity, rather than emission-factor changes, is a primary source of model bias during heatwaves. Future studies should focus on incorporating a CEMS-derived, temperature-dependent scaling of power-sector emissions could substantially improve chemical forecasts of NO2 during extreme heat events.

490497.title: Anomaly Detection Approaches for Geospace Superstorm Investigation Using DMSP Particle Data and Machine Learning
490497.authors: Delores Jane Knipp, Univ. of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and J. Kozyra
490497.abstract: We use anomaly detection (AD) to the study of the largest space weather events, known as geospace superstorms. The rarity of these events means that most available space environment data comes from quiescent conditions or small-to-moderate storms, producing a well-defined backdrop against which unusual features that appear during extreme events can be detected. By combining the deep domain knowledge of space physicists with the technical expertise of data scientists, the project has provided new and fundamental insights into the nature of superstorms. The basic data used in the study for training and validation is ion and electron precipitation observed by Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) F13 satellite during solar cycle 23 (1997–2006). For Machine Learning purposes the data have been 'cleaned' and despiked. This study adopts an unsupervised learning approach, in which superstorms are modeled as anomalous outlier events against the well-defined backdrop of normal space weather. This model assumes that the training data contains very few anomalies, allowing it to learn the characteristics of normal conditions and thereby identify significant deviations--a process called anomaly detection. The AD model used three inputs: <1 keV ions, >1 keV electrons, and the average energy of auroral electrons—parameters linked to emergent phenomena during extreme geomagnetic activity. The model reveals a previously underappreciated pattern in the deep equatorward transport of low-energy ions. The observations are consistent with long-duration penetration electric fields (PEFs) eroding the outer plasmasphere while carrying dawnside warm ions to unusually low magnetic latitudes. The key scientific conclusion of this work is that superstorms are not merely larger versions of common storms; they are events that trigger fundamentally different physical dynamics in geospace. The study revealed two previously unappreciated "fingerprints" of these unique dynamics: (1) the deep, equatorward penetration of low-energy "warm" ions, and (2) a characteristic and unanticipated drop in the average energy of auroral electrons. The research strongly suggests that a long-duration excursion of auroral electric fields to lower latitudes acts as the critical "on-switch" that initiates these superstorm dynamics. This finding implies that AI-generated anomaly scores, which are sensitive to these physical changes, may be a more meaningful way to identify and classify hazardous events than traditional magnetic indices such as Dst or SYM-H.

490500.title: Clarifying Cloud Liquid Response to Aerosol by Accounting for Precipitation
490500.authors: August Mikkelsen, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and D. McCoy, J. M. Nugent, H. Gordon, and J. Mülmenstädt
490500.abstract: Aerosol-cloud adjustments are the largest uncertainty in predicting temperature change from human activity. Despite many Earth system models showing positive shifts in cloud liquid from enhanced aerosol, observation-based studies tend to show the opposite. Here, we use 7 years of surface remote sensing from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Eastern North Atlantic (ENA) atmospheric observatory to examine aerosol-cloud adjustments. By organizing retrievals of droplet number concentration (Nd) and liquid water path (LWP) by column maximum reflectivity (a proxy for precipitation intensity), we find adjustments change sign depending on precipitation. Positive adjustments are associated with precipitating cloud and negative adjustments with non-precipitating. Without organizing the retrievals in this way, positive adjustments are masked by a manifestation of Simpson’s paradox that otherwise implies strong negative adjustments. After performing a weighted average based on precipitation fraction, overall adjustments are found to be positive, in contrast to previous studies that inferred decreased liquid and in agreement with many Earth system models. To contextualize these results, we calculated ERFaci ranges for 3 different scenarios based on global marine precipitation fraction and the LWP-Nd susceptibilities found in this study. We then emulate future global mean surface temperature in these updated ERFaci ranges via the Finite-amplitude Impulse Response model v2.0.0 (FaIR). In all scenarios, the resulting change in the most likely range for historical aerosol cooling corresponds to intensified warming in the 21st century. Based on these results, we suggest explicitly accounting for meteorological forcings when inferring the sensitivity of LWP to enhanced Nd.

490501.title: Characterization and attribution of decadal droplet number concentration in the Azores: surface, satellite, and reanalysis
490501.authors: August Mikkelsen, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and D. McCoy, D. Zhang, T. W. Aerenson, and D. Barahona
490501.abstract: Droplet number concentration (Nd) is an essential variable of state for understanding cloud microphysics. As such, tracking long-term trends in Nd essential for understanding Earth’s future radiative balance and sensitivity to aerosol perturbations. Historically, this has been performed with satellite retrievals such as those from Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS). While spaceborne observations provide unrivalled spatiotemporal coverage, they come with many assumptions and are challenging to validate. In recent years, surface remote sensing-based retrievals of Nd have become more robust, but are relatively limited in coverage. And from both sources, it is difficult to verify the causal linkage between Nd and CCN emissions without modelling. In this work we compare 8 years of Nd derived from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Eastern North Atlantic (ENA) observatory, 24 years of MODIS Nd retrievals, and 26 years of GiOcean reanalysis data. We find that all three track seasonal and annual oscillation with reasonable skill. When examining output from GiOcean, we find that Nd is mostly dependent on SO4, black carbon (negatively), and organic carbon. Over time, aerosol and Nd change over ENA is considerably lower than continental and oceanic outflow regions. Finally, we find that the vertical distribution of aerosol species mass concentration present in GiOcean are similar (though not identical) to observations from flights in the Aerosol and Cloud Experiments in the Eastern North Atlantic (ACE-ENA) field campaign. These results offer new insight into the long-term trend of cloud microphysics at ENA and open new avenues for finer exploration of aerosol-cloud interactions in this region.

490503.title: Leveraging Probabilistic Forecast Guidance to Enhance Public-Facing NWS Products and Services
490503.authors: Danielle Nagele, NWS, Damascus, MD; and K. G. McMahon, B. Smith, D. Strom, S. R. Baxter, M. Muccilli, and E. M. Guillot
490503.abstract: To better integrate probabilistic information into public-facing products, an NWS team conducted public interviews focused on incorporating range information into the 7-day forecasts and select warnings. This agile approach used brief interviews with members of the general public to highlight potential challenges and inform design during the prototype phase of development. Findings revealed that participants generally understood range information and appreciated it especially for winter weather situations. There was a universal acceptance of weather uncertainty, but participants did prefer narrower over wider ranges. Numerically proficient users understood the charts well, while those less familiar needed written descriptions to supplement. Feedback on labeling and layout directly informed and strengthened the final prototype designs. Study results have been combined with related user experience testing, as well as relevant literature, to create more user-friendly and effective local forecast pages on the NWS homepage.

490504.title: Storm-Intensity, Seasonal, and Regional Dependence of U.S. Thunderstorm Responses to Global Warming
490504.authors: Lantao Sun, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and J. W. Hurrell, K. L. Rasmussen, Ph.D., and H. Yu
490504.abstract: How U.S. thunderstorm activity will respond to global warming remains uncertain, particularly with respect to regional, seasonal, and intensity-dependent changes. Here, we use paired 43-year, 4-km Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulations from the CONUS404 dataset to investigate changes in thunderstorm activity across the United States under global warming. Thunderstorm activity across a broad range of intensities increases during winter. In contrast, most thunderstorm activity decreases during summer, except for the most intense storms. Summer decreases are concentrated over the Northern Great Plains, the southern United States, and Florida, while severe thunderstorm activity increases over the Southern Great Plains and the Northeast. These contrasting responses arise primarily from shifts in the joint distribution of convective available potential energy (CAPE) and convective inhibition (CIN), highlighting the importance of changes in the thermodynamic environment. These results demonstrate that future changes in U.S. convective hazards depend strongly on storm intensity, season, and region.

490507.title: Analysis of Cloud-to-Ground Stroke and Flash Characteristics from a Hybrid VLF-LF LLS vs the US NLDN
490507.authors: Martin J. Murphy, Vaisala Inc., Louisville, CO; and R. Said
