490507.abstract: In 2026, Vaisala Xweather introduced a hybrid VLF-LF location algorithm that is capable of geo-locating lightning discharges using sensor data from LF precision networks together with sensor data from the GLD360. The hybrid capability allows us to improve detection efficiency in cases where a low-amplitude discharge is detected by only one LF sensor or is detected by at least two LF sensors but the geo-location fails quality control due to a large error ellipse. This capability substantially improves the detection of low-amplitude IC pulses over what an LF precision network can detect on its own. However, it may also improve detection of weak cloud-to-ground (CG) strokes. In this presentation, we analyze a selection of data from summer 2026 in the southeastern US using the US National Lightning Detection Network (NLDN) by itself, and then as part of the hybrid algorithm with the contribution of the GLD360 sensors. Both the NLDN-only and hybrid data sets are processed using the latest version of IC-CG classification algorithm. We limit this analysis to the southeast US because the majority of CG strokes are negative, and anomalously electrified storms are relatively rare, so we expect few misclassifications of weak negative IC pulses as CGs. We examine the counts and peak current distributions of events classified as CG strokes in both data sets, and we cluster these into flashes in order to examine the multiplicity distribution and analyze ground strike points with multiple strokes.

490509.title: Considering Experimental UFS Prototypes for North Atlantic Seasonal Tropical Cyclone Outlooks
490509.authors: Douglas Nedza, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA; and B. Huang and J. Zhu
490509.abstract: We analyze ensembles of April and May initialized reforecasts from experimental UFS prototypes, including Beta v1.0, P8, and HR3, to validate possible contributions to seasonal tropical cyclone (TC) outlooks in the North Atlantic (NA) basin. TC events are identified using the TempestExtremes event tracking algorithm based on characteristic features of TCs, such as a minimum local sea level pressure, warm mid-troposphere temperature, and the curl and wind speed of local surface winds. Dynamical forecasts of seasonal TC events numbers and accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) are produced by aggregating the identified TC events. We find that reforecast variations in seasonal ACE and TC event counts skillfully represent observed TC activity, validating the use of these UFS prototypes as part of operational outlooks. Biases in TC activity and their relationship to large-scale climate features, such as NA sea surface temperature and vertical-wind-shear, the Inter-Tropical Convergence and West-African Monsoon, and variations of ENSO are assessed.

490511.title: Wind Retrieval Development for the Next-Generation Geostationary Extended Observations Sounder
490511.authors: Jason Apke, ; and L. Carr, S. M. Ortland, D. Santek, T. Rink, and J. A. Otkin
490511.abstract: Tropospheric wind observations provide critical insights towards diagnosis and prediction in cloud processes, aerosol transport, energy management, weather forecast modeling, and general circulation. Such observations are typically limited to in-situ measurements (i.e., surface anemometers and rawinsondes) and localized remote sensing tools (i.e., wind profiling radars and lidars), though satellite cloud- and water-vapor-drift motions also play a key role by providing information over sparsely sampled areas of the globe such as over oceans or near the poles. The Geostationary Extended Observations (GeoXO) Sounder (GXS) will significantly expand upon that capability, providing drift motions over large domains from fine spatial and temporal resolution passive retrievals of temperature (T), moisture (q), and trace gas profiles in clear air. This presentation covers the “Passive Retrievals of 3D Optical Flows with Information Leveraged from Environmental Sounders” (PROFILES) project which aims to develop a formal winds retrieval system for GXS. PROFILES leverages state-of-the-art so-called “optical flow”-based systems which use brightness pattern tracing and image-to-image machine learning to render dense (every image pixel) 3D winds at high fidelity. The system is calibrated and trained on ancillary datasets from the Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5; NASA) Nature Run and High-Resolution Rapid Refresh numerical weather prediction model (HRRR; NOAA). This presentation will highlight challenges in model development, and early validation results from proxy-GXS datasets developed with the ECMWF Experimental Nature Run-1 km (XNR1K), which demonstrate how the winds retrieval is typically accurate to within 6 m/s with increased accuracy in the lower layers. Finally, winds readiness-level advancement will be covered, making PROFILES valuable to end-users and stakeholders at NOAA, such as needed quality control for assimilation to improve numerical weather prediction models.

490513.title: InferStudio: An Interactive Web Application for Teaching and Exploring AI Weather Prediction
490513.authors: Scott G. Pearse, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and N. Cherukuru, S. Jaroszynski, M. Rehme, J. Clyne, K. Kuzemka, and K. FitzGerald
490513.abstract: The rapid emergence of AI-based weather prediction models (e.g., Pangu-Weather, GraphCast, Aurora, AIFS) represents one of the most significant recent shifts in operational and research meteorology, yet these models remain largely inaccessible to students, educators, and even many research scientists outside a small community of specialists. Each model typically ships with its own idiosyncratic software dependencies, incompatible library versions, and command-line interfaces that assume substantial HPC and machine learning engineering experience. This creates a real barrier to entry precisely when exposing students to these tools would be most pedagogically valuable: AI weather models are reshaping the skills atmospheric science students will need for both research and private-sector careers, and hands-on engagement with them offers a uniquely current, high-interest entry point into topics ranging from numerical weather prediction fundamentals to machine learning to software engineering practice. We present InferStudio, a browser-based application built on the Python Panel framework and deployed on NSF NCAR's Casper HPC system, designed to lower this barrier by providing a single, unified interface for running and visually comparing multiple AI weather prediction models without requiring users to manage per-model software environments or write any code. InferStudio currently supports AIFS, Aurora, and Pangu (via NVIDIA's earth2studio framework) and WXFormer (via NCAR's MILES-CREDIT framework), with a modular architecture designed to accommodate additional models as the field continues to evolve. The application is organized around two primary interfaces. An "Inference" tab allows a user to select one or more AI models, specify a forecast initialization date and lead time, choose which atmospheric variables to output, and launch inference runs directly from the browser — with live status indicators and streaming console output for each model, and the option to cancel a run in progress. Behind the scenes, InferStudio manages the substantial complexity of running multiple deep learning weather models with mutually incompatible dependency stacks, insulating the user entirely from this engineering burden. A companion "Visualization" tab lets users browse completed forecast runs and interactively explore the results: a single set of variable, pressure-level, forecast-time, and colormap controls drives synchronized plots across every model included in a run, so that comparing how, for example, AIFS and Aurora each represent a developing storm system at 72 hours lead time is a matter of a few clicks rather than a scripting exercise. A verification panel computes standard forecast-skill metrics (RMSE and CRPS) against GFS analysis for the currently selected variable and level across all available lead times, letting users directly observe how forecast skill degrades with lead time — a foundational concept in numerical weather prediction that becomes considerably more concrete when a student can generate and inspect the curve themselves, for a model they just ran, rather than encountering it only in a textbook figure. InferStudio was designed from the outset with multiple audiences in mind. For instructors, it offers a ready-made platform for in-class demonstrations and assignments exploring AI weather model behavior and forecast verification against traditional NWP output, without requiring the instructor to first build or maintain the underlying software infrastructure. For students, it offers a low-barrier, exploratory environment for developing intuition about how different AI architectures behave, where they diverge from each other and from conventional forecasts, and what "forecast skill" concretely looks like — serving as a bridge between the theoretical treatment of NWP and machine learning that students typically encounter in coursework and the practical, applied familiarity with these tools increasingly expected of new graduates entering both research and private-sector forecasting roles. For researchers, the same interface supports rapid, code-free experimentation and comparison across models during early-stage investigation. This presentation will demonstrate InferStudio's current capabilities, discuss the design decisions made to balance accessibility against the genuine complexity of the underlying AI weather modeling ecosystem, and share our approach to using the tool in educational settings — including how its interface was shaped around distinct instructor, student, and researcher workflows. We will also discuss our roadmap for expanding InferStudio's model coverage and educational features, including planned support for ensemble verification metrics, case-study datasets curated for classroom use, and deeper integration of AI-versus-NWP comparison workflows designed explicitly around common atmospheric science curricula. We believe tools like InferStudio have an important role to play in ensuring that the next generation of atmospheric scientists graduates with genuine, hands-on fluency in the AI weather prediction methods rapidly becoming central to the field, rather than encountering them for the first time only after entering the workforce.

490514.title: Evaluation of Optical Flow-based Satellite Products from 5-min CONUS imagery at the 2026 Hazardous Weather Testbed
490514.authors: Jason Apke, ; and W. Line, S. D. Miller, and T. M. Juliano
490514.abstract: Emerging products which use dense (every image pixel) apparent brightness motion (or the optical flow) rendered objectively from cloud-drift motions observed by 1-min geostationary satellite imagery have demonstrated value for the National Weather Service in Convection Warning Operations via testbeds over the last four years. Such products highlight regions with sheared convection initiation, wind profile characteristics, and mature convection intensity, and can even be used to track cloud-top cooling (CTC) trends associated with the vertical growth of storms. One limiting factor of optical flow tools is their exclusive availability in mesoscale sectors, which do not provide continuous coverage of the contiguous United States (CONUS). To that end, the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere has explored expanding such products into the Advanced Baseline Imager CONUS domain, which updates once every 5-min. These products were tuned to mimic products from 1-min imagery and evaluated in front of forecasters at the 2026 hazardous weather testbed. This presentation will highlight the benefits and drawbacks to rendering optical flow at coarse temporal resolutions, how the products are blended with satellite imagery for forecaster ingestion, and where drawbacks were found to limit forecasting applications. For example, 5-min optical flow from 0.64 and 10.3 μm imagery severely limited wind related applications in active deep convection where rapid cloud morphology broke down retrieval assumptions, though the resolution was sufficient for accurate CTC tracking with some artifact correction. Such CTC can be blended with 10.3 μm infrared brightness temperatures to provide early guidance on deep convection intensity anywhere in the CONUS domain. Finally, this presentation will cover plans for additional demonstrations for CONUS products to regional centers such as the Weather Prediction Center and Ocean Prediction Center, where low-cloud winds can provide observation context on precipitation and hurricane force lows.

490515.title: From PAMIP to PAMIP2: Understanding Polar Amplification, Sea-Ice Loss, and Associated Climate Responses for CMIP7
490515.authors: Lantao Sun, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and Y. C. Liang, L. S. Graff, and G. Gastineau
490515.abstract: Polar amplification—the phenomenon whereby low-level temperatures increase more rapidly at high latitudes than at lower latitudes—has been one of the most prominent features of recent Arctic climate change. Climate models project substantial future sea-ice loss and continued amplified warming in both the Arctic and Antarctic, yet considerable uncertainties remain regarding the underlying drivers, magnitude, and evolution of these changes and their impacts on regional and global climate. The first phase of the Polar Amplification Model Intercomparison Project (PAMIP), which contributed to CMIP6, established a coordinated experimental framework for investigating the causes and consequences of polar amplification. Building on this foundation, PAMIP Phase 2 (PAMIP2), contributing to CMIP7, aims to advance process-level understanding of polar amplification through a redesigned suite of coordinated model experiments. Its primary scientific objectives are to: (1) identify the key drivers of observed Arctic amplification and leverage in-situ observations to diagnose common model biases; (2) investigate the climate response to future polar sea-ice loss and its underlying dynamical mechanisms, assess the sensitivity of these responses to model configuration, and constrain model uncertainty using observations; and (3) quantify how regional CO₂ forcing over the Arctic and Antarctic contributes to polar amplification and influences regional and global climate. These coordinated modeling efforts will bring together the climate dynamics and polar science communities to improve understanding of polar amplification and its broader implications for the global climate system.

490516.title: Why is African Convection Exceptional? Environmental Controls on Tropical Continental Storm Intensity (Invited)
490516.authors: Rick Schulte, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Pilewskie, A. J. Muehr, and S. C. van den Heever
490516.abstract: Tropical continental convection exhibits substantial regional variability despite occurring within broadly similar climatic regimes. For example, convective storms observed over central Africa tend to have greater radar reflectivities above the freezing level compared to storms over the Amazon and Maritime Continent, indicative of larger ice particles and possibly stronger updrafts. Previous studies have documented these regional differences in storm characteristics, yet the environmental factors responsible for them remain poorly understood. Here, we combine more than 25 years of precipitation features identified from the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) and Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) missions with ERA5 reanalysis data to investigate the large-scale environmental controls on tropical land-based convection. We identify eight large-scale environmental variables that are useful for distinguishing between convective storm modes, and demonstrate that principal component analysis can collapse most of the information in these variables into just two dimensions. We then examine how the depth, width, and maximum radar reflectivity of precipitating convective storms observed over these regions by spaceborne radars are related to the environments in which they were observed. Notably, the deepest and most intense convective systems are more commonly observed in warmer, drier, and more sheared environments, regardless of the region being considered. By quantifying the extent to which environmental variability explains regional differences in tropical continental convection, this study provides new insight into the physical mechanisms governing some of Earth's most intense thunderstorms. This framework will be applied to observations from the upcoming Investigation of Convective UpdraftS mission (INCUS) to better understand the links between the large scale environment and convective mass flux.

490522.title: Understanding NWS user information needs, decisions, and actions in the Day 0-7 timeframe
490522.authors: Danielle Nagele, NWS, Damascus, MD; and V. Were and L. Williams
490522.abstract: NWS social scientists leveraged NOAA-funded research to summarize and document user information needs and decisions over time. Results of this study can support academic and operational communities by aligning products and services with the needs of partners and the public, ensuring actionable information for decision makers. In particular, these insights are key to enhancing the delivery of NWS IDSS to core partners. Study findings created an actionable timeline of user needs and decisions leading up to a weather event. Beyond Day 7, users are primarily monitoring the situation and require scenario information to manage uncertainty this far out. For Days 4-7, users shift to logistical coordination requiring more detailed analysis of the forecast and critical confidence information. By Days 2-3, users begin making operational decisions like opening shelters, activating EOCs, and prepositioning resources, necessitating more specific severity and timing information with a focus on graphics. During Days 0-1, users focus on final preparations, protective measures, and response preparation requiring real-time observations and frequent updates on last-minute changes in the forecast.

490529.title: Building and Validating NHC-FLEE to Support Hurricane Evacuation Decision Research
490529.authors: Austin Reed Harris, University of Oklahoma, Oklahoma City, OK
490529.abstract: Evacuation orders are among the most consequential decisions made during hurricane events, yet evaluating alternative decision pathways remains difficult. We are developing NHC-FLEE, a hurricane evacuation modeling framework designed to support scenario-based analysis of evacuation decision making, evacuation-order strategies, and emergency-management interventions. Building on the existing Forecasting Laboratory for Exploring the Evacuation-System (FLEE), the framework transitions from a research-oriented grid structure to county- and evacuation-zone-based representations that more closely reflect operational decision environments. Current efforts focus on redevelopment of evacuation participation processes, incorporation of hazard information from multiple forecast advisories and ensemble inputs, and validation using historical evacuation observations from storms such as Irma, Ian, Dorian, and Milton. The resulting framework is intended to support future investigations of forecast uncertainty, evacuation-order issuance strategies, and their combined influence on population response and transportation impacts. Development progress, validation activities, initial proof-of-concept applications, and future directions toward hurricane evacuation decision support are presented.

490532.title: IOAS - Assimilating Polarimetric Radar Observations for PRECIP Cases in MPAS-JEDI: Impact of Power-Transformed Hydrometeor Control Variables
490532.authors: Rong Kong, NSF NCAR, Norman, OK; and Z. Liu, C. Schwartz, R. Rios-Berrios, A. Shu, T. C. Tsai, G. Zhang, P. Liu, and M. Xue
490532.abstract: This study assimilates S- and C-band polarimetric radar observations from Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA) for five convective cases that occurred during the Prediction of Rainfall Extremes Campaign in the Pacific (PRECIP) and the Taiwan-Area Heavy Rain Observation and Prediction Experiment (TAHOPE), including one tropical convection case, two mesoscale convective system (MCS) cases, and two Mei-yu cases. Specifically, the LETKF within a convective-scale MPAS-JEDI-based data assimilation system using the NSSL double-moment microphysics scheme is used to assimilate radial velocity, reflectivity (ZH), differential reflectivity (ZDR), and specific differential phase (KDP) with the Parameterized Polarimetric Radar Operator (P-PRO; Zhang et al. 2021). Two parallel experiments are performed and compared over the five cases. In the first experiment, mixing ratios and number concentrations of rain, snow, graupel, and hail are used directly as control variables. In the second experiment, the same variables are Box–Cox power transformed—introducing an exponent p that varies between 0 and 1—and used as control variables. The transform renders the skewed, non-negative hydrometeor priors more nearly Gaussian, suppressing spurious increments in precipitation-free regions. To our knowledge this is the first systematic evaluation of power-transformed hydrometeor control variables in the EnKF framework with real polarimetric observations. A sensitivity sweep over p shows that intermediate values p = 0.2–0.4 are near-optimal. Cycle-averaged ZH analysis RMSE is reduced by roughly 20–40% across the five cases relative to the untransformed update (p = 1). In the tropical convection case, the fraction of spurious weak-echo overestimation falls from 30.8% at p = 1 to 4.8% at p = 0.2. The logarithmic limit (p → 0) terminates in ensemble blowup. An analyzed ZDR overshoot grows with p, and the untransformed analysis can sometimes degrade the background in the Mei-yu case. The ZH analysis benefit persists into 1–6-h ensemble forecasts in the tropical case. Collectively, these results suggest that applying a power transform to hydrometeor control variables is beneficial for dual-polarimetric radar data assimilation.

490534.title: Long-Range Transport of Air-Sea Surface Heat Fluxes and Their Influence on Midlatitude Cloud and Precipitation
490534.authors: Juan A. Crespo, UCLA, Los Angeles, CA; JPL, Pasadena, CA; and C. M. Naud and J. F. Booth
490534.abstract: Latent and sensible heat fluxes over the oceans locally impact the genesis and evolution of synoptic and mesoscale weather systems throughout Earth’s atmosphere. However, it is still unclear how heat and moisture are further transported into the atmosphere and how initial conditions affect that transport and downstream impacts. The CYGNSS Satellite mission offers the advantage of providing detailed observations of ocean surface heat fluxes at high spatial and temporal frequencies over the lower midlatitudes in all-weather conditions. Using these observations in the Western Pacific Ocean, where a strong western boundary current in winter causes large surface heat fluxes, we explore their long-range transport. By analyzing days with the highest and lowest fluxes, coupled with forward Lagrangian trajectory models initialized in this region, we will show how stronger flux conditions tend to be generated by the development of an anticyclone, accompanied by an equatorward transport that remains within the marine boundary layer. Weaker fluxes often coincide with the arrival of an extratropical cyclone or accompanying cold front, which facilitates ascent and long-range transport to higher latitudes. On some less common occasions, high flux trajectories are ascending, and we will discuss the synoptic conditions that favor such transport. Additionally, we will show how contrasts in surface heat flux magnitude correlate with changes in cloud and precipitation structures along the downstream trajectories. Finally, we will contrast these results with those obtained in an East Pacific region where fluxes are climatologically weak.

490536.title: Enterprise Weather Solutions for Agriculture
490536.authors: Stephen Shield, Bayer, Ballwin, MO; and Q. Liu and Z. Hansen
490536.abstract: Bayer is a global leader in agriculture, with a vision of "Health for all, Hunger for none". Achieving this goal requires integrating cutting-edge biotechnology, chemistry, and digital tools to enable growers to achieve higher yield while reducing environmental impacts. Weather is a critical piece of this endeavor, as it impacts every stage of the agricultural cycle, from the timing of planting and the efficacy of fertilizer and crop protection products to the final harvest outcomes. We provide an overview of the challenges faced and how we leverage a range of weather data including historical data, short and medium range forecasts, seasonal forecasts, and climate projections to enable teams across Bayer to help growers to maximize their potential during the current growing season as well as develop the next generation of products and tools for agriculture. One key data product that enables teams across Bayer is an internally developed historical weather data product that provides higher resolution and lower data latency than other available sources. This product is machine learning based and developed via a combination of coarse/sparse weather data, topography, land use, and diurnal/seasonal information to produce a global 4km gridded historical weather dataset from 1995 to present. Performance evaluations show that in addition to offering increased data availability and resolution, it outperforms other historical data sources with lower error and bias.

490541.title: Implementation and Evaluation of JEDI-Based Ensemble Data Assimilation for the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS)
490541.authors: Samuel K. Degelia, EMC, Mesquite, TX
490541.abstract: NOAA is currently transitioning the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) to the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation (JEDI) as part of its next generation, convection-allowing regional prediction system. Ensemble data assimilation (DA) in the current RRFS configuration is performed using a Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI)-based ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF). In the JEDI-based system, ensemble DA is implemented using the gain form of the ensemble transform Kalman filter (GETKF), replacing the serial ensemble square root filter (EnSRF) currently used in GSI. To ensure a consistent transition, the JEDI-based configuration has been designed to closely emulate the operational GSI workflow, including existing observation preprocessing and quality control procedures, enabling direct comparisons between the two systems. Results from cycled and real-time parallel experiments on the 3-km North American RRFS domain will be presented to evaluate the performance of the JEDI-based EnKF relative to the existing FV3-GSI configuration. Performance is assessed through ensemble mean errors relative to both the GSI-based EnKF analyses and independent truth, evaluated across multiple observation configurations. Initial results demonstrate that the JEDI-based GETKF produces ensemble-mean analyses consistent with those from the GSI-based EnSRF across multiple observation configurations while providing a simplified workflow that allows simultaneous assimilation of multiple observation types. Given the strong agreement between the two systems, ongoing development is focused on improving the computational efficiency of the GETKF update itself, including I/O and memory usage, to support future operational implementation. The presentation will highlight both the scientific comparison between the two systems and recent progress toward reducing the computational cost of the JEDI-based GETKF within RRFS.

490543.title: Identifying Sources of Kelvin Wave Forecast Errors: A Baroclinic Mode Analysis of MPAS-A Simulations
490543.authors: Quinton Lawton, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL; and R. Rios-Berrios, F. Judt, and M. T. Chien
490543.abstract: Accurately predicting convectively coupled Kelvin waves (CCKWs) remains a major challenge for numerical models. Improving these forecasts is critical, as CCKWs strongly modulate tropical weather and trigger extreme events like tropical cyclogenesis. To investigate the root causes of CCKW forecast deficiencies, we evaluate Model for Prediction Across Scales – Atmosphere (MPAS-A) experiments at both parameterized (15–30 km) and convection-permitting (3 km) resolutions. These simulations are run with different convective schemes and initial CCKW amplitude perturbations. An object-tracking analysis reveals that parameterized MPAS-A simulations produce CCKWs that decay and propagate too quickly, echoing known biases in operational systems. Furthermore, artificially amplifying the initial CCKW yields only temporary skill improvements. These findings suggest that CCKW forecast errors stem primarily from model deficiencies in representing CCKW growth processes, rather than flawed initial conditions. To diagnose the physical drivers of under-amplified CCKW growth, we decompose the wave's vertical structure into baroclinic modes using empirical orthogonal functions (EOFs). This isolates the wave-damping impacts of deep convection (EOF1) and the growth impacts of stratiform heating (EOF2). We find that the MPAS models often produce excessively damped first modes (EOF1) and fail to fully capture the covariance between temperature and diabatic heating in the second vertical mode (EOF2). Because this second mode is essential for wave amplification, its deficiency helps explain CCKW forecast errors. Ultimately, advancing CCKW forecasts requires better representing deep convection and stratiform-driven wave growth. We also argue that data-driven forecast models and machine learning postprocessing offer promising pathways to improve CCKW predictions.

490544.title: Concerns, Blind Spots, and Recommendations for Using LLMs Effectively in the Weather Enterprise
490544.authors: Stan Rhodes, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and I. Ebert-Uphoff and D. Nietfeld
490544.abstract: With countless applications in the weather enterprise, generative AI - specifically Large Language Models (LLMs) - present many opportunities, but also risks of catastrophic failures, the erosion of trust, and other unintended consequences. AMS 2026 brought substantial feedback from the community on the opportunities and risks of LLMs. We draw from literature within and beyond the weather enterprise where varied and high-stakes fields are grappling with similar challenges. Addressing many areas of interest voiced by attendees at AMS 2026, we review coalescing guidance and key discussion points, much of which has emerged and evolved substantially in 2026. Complementing existing guidance and research findings, we assess concerns and blind spots in the use of LLMs stemming from the overlap of their properties and human proclivities, and their implications for LLM use. First, responsible use of LLMs requires conscious decisions about who is accountable for their outputs, since accountability is essential for the relational trust among people in organizations. LLMs cannot be responsible, and human responsibility does not scale, nor can it be proxied by development specifications. Second, emerging evidence suggests that LLM use may erode professionals’ skills and stunt trainees’ skill learning. Third, by its nature, LLMs may generate plausible-sounding but incorrect information when drawing from sparse data, with perilous implications for physical science professionals who may not realize how incredibly sparse some social, behavioral, and economic sciences (SBES) data actually is. Fourth, we are concerned that despite the use of LLMs in many applications that supplement or inform human decision-making, SBES experts may rarely be included in LLM application development. Solutions? A systems view–rather than focusing only on tasks and outputs–is key, recommending an approach of service design, not just tool design. Short term, LLM projects should early-on assess risks, scope knowledge domains, and design for accountable humans. When integrating LLM use, planning should include the adoption of basic tools to expose concerns and blind spots, and include SBES expertise and end users from the start through development. Long-term, responsible LLM innovation will require both building capacity for LLM-savvy SBES experts and investing in SBES research to detect, monitor, prevent, and remediate unintended consequences of LLM use in the weather enterprise.

490546.title: Past Storms, Future Confidence: Using Historical Extreme Events to Evaluate Model Fitness for Purpose in PMP Modernization
490546.authors: Kelly M. Mahoney, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and A. Back, B. M. Basarab, D. R. Jesberg, P. N. Schumacher, and A. Thompson
490546.abstract: Aligning with the 2024 National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine report on Modernizing Probable Maximum Precipitation Estimation, NOAA is advancing a model-based approach to modernize Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP) guidance. Central to this initiative are two NASEM Recommendations which call for (1) the reconstruction of historical storm events, and (2) the establishment of a Model Evaluation Project to assess model skill, evaluate strengths and limitations, and ensure datasets are "fit for purpose" for extreme precipitation estimation in current and changing climates. This talk will highlight how historical high-impact precipitation events serve as critical benchmarks for model validation. We examine a suite of historical benchmark events that cover an inclusive range of extreme precipitation-causing phenomena of interest. Event types include convective storms (e.g., Big Thompson flood of 1976), hurricanes (e.g., Harvey (2017), Helene (2024)), mesoscale convective systems (e.g., 2010 Tennessee floods), and orographic events (e.g., September 2013 Colorado Front Range Flood; West Coast atmospheric river events), through the lens of modern, state-of-the-science high-resolution model simulations. Case studies present evaluations of model runs simulating these extreme events to test physical mechanisms, spatial precipitation structures, and extreme rain rates. By analyzing where high-resolution datasets succeed or struggle in reproducing observed storm dynamics, we evaluate the degree to which these models meet "fitness for purpose" standards. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these historical model reconstructions can inform near-term storm catalogs, support extreme value analysis, and establish community confidence in long-term, ensemble-based PMP estimations.

490548.title: Madden-Julian Oscillation Dynamics in an Atmosphere Emulator Coupled to CESM
490548.authors: Natalia Jorbenadze, University of Miami, Coral Gables, FL; and W. Chapman
490548.abstract: We examine the representation and dynamics of the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) in CAMulator, a machine-learning atmosphere emulator trained on the Community Atmosphere Model version 6 (CAM6) and designed to simulate atmospheric variability on timescales ranging from days to centuries. We compare CAMulator with its parent model in two configurations: (1) an atmosphere-only, AMIP-style simulation with prescribed sea surface temperatures and no atmosphere-ocean feedback, and (2) a fully coupled simulation in which CAMulator dynamically interacts with the Parallel Ocean Program version 2 and the Community Ice CodE, the ocean and sea-ice components of the Community Earth System Model. We calculate the Wheeler-Hendon Real-time Multivariate MJO indices and construct composites of the eight MJO phases to evaluate the amplitude, spatial structure, and propagation of associated anomalies in outgoing longwave radiation, precipitation, winds, and other variables. Wheeler-Kiladis wavenumber-frequency spectra are used to assess the representation of the MJO and other major modes of tropical atmospheric variability. We further examine MJO propagation across the Maritime Continent, a longstanding challenge for CAM and many other atmosphere-only models, and evaluate the resulting extratropical teleconnections. CAMulator reproduces the principal spatial and temporal characteristics of the MJO, including its eastward propagation and associated large-scale circulation anomalies, although biases emerge in amplitude, propagation speed, spectral power, Maritime Continent crossing, and teleconnection strength. Comparing prescribed-SST and coupled configurations reveals the extent to which interactive ocean feedbacks influence these biases. These results demonstrate the potential of machine-learning atmosphere emulators to represent organized tropical variability in long climate simulations while identifying specific process-level and training targets for improving MJO fidelity.

490549.title: Scalable Bayesian Data Assimilation via Localized Sequential MCMC
490549.authors: Hamza Ruzayqat, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO
490549.abstract: Sequential Markov chain Monte Carlo (SMCMC) methods provide a provably convergent framework for Bayesian filtering in high-dimensional nonlinear and non-Gaussian state-space models while avoiding the weight degeneracy inherent in particle filters. Their computational cost, however, can become prohibitive for large-scale geophysical applications. In this talk, we present two localization strategies that substantially improve the scalability of SMCMC by exploiting the spatial locality of observations. The first approach restricts inference to a reduced observed region, enabling parallel MCMC sampling over a relatively smaller state space. The second further decomposes the localized domain into independent subdomains augmented with compact halo regions and incorporates Gaspari--Cohn tapering to smoothly account for distant observations. For linear Gaussian observational models, the resulting approximate posterior admits an explicit Gaussian mixture representation from which independent samples can be drawn exactly, whereas nonlinear or non-Gaussian observational models are handled using localized MCMC kernels. We assess the proposed methods on relatively high-dimensional filtering problems with state dimensions up to (10^5), including nonlinear multilayer shallow-water equations with both Gaussian and heavy-tailed observation noise errors. Numerical experiments with synthetic data as well as real observations from the SWOT satellite mission and NOAA ocean drifters demonstrate that the localized SMCMC methods achieve substantial computational savings while maintaining high filtering accuracy. In particular, the proposed framework naturally accommodates heavy-tailed observation noise, where ensemble Kalman methods (like Local ETKF) often exhibit degraded performance or divergence, making it a robust alternative for large-scale nonlinear Bayesian data assimilation.

490550.title: Evaluating Public Perception of Artificial Intelligence Applications in Early Warning Systems
490550.authors: Julia Adamczyk, UCAR, Boulder, CO; University of Florida, Gainesville, FL
490550.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming atmospheric sciences through advancements in forecasting, hazard detection, and environmental decision support. Recent developments in AI-based weather models and analytical tools have demonstrated the potential to improve prediction capabilities and enhance communication of hazardous weather information. However, the societal effectiveness of these technologies depends not only on technical performance but also on whether the public understands, trusts, and accepts AI-assisted warnings. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into operational meteorology and early warning systems (EWS), understanding public perceptions is essential for ensuring that these technologies support effective risk communication and decision-making. This study investigates public knowledge and perceptions of AI applications within EWS, focusing on factors influencing acceptance of AI-assisted warnings. A survey was conducted (n = 82) to examine respondents’ familiarity with AI, understanding of AI applications, perceptions of AI reliability, concerns regarding potential errors, preferences for human oversight, and willingness to act on AI-assisted hazard warnings. Relationship tests, including Spearman correlation and Chi-Square analyses, were used to evaluate associations between AI knowledge, transparency, trust, reliability perceptions, hazard scenarios, and behavioral intentions. Results indicate that greater interaction with AI does not necessarily translate into greater understanding of AI applications. While respondents generally recognized the potential of AI in meteorological contexts, familiarity with domain-specific applications such as AI-assisted EWS was more limited. These findings suggest that general exposure to AI alone may not be sufficient to improve AI literacy in meteorological-related contexts. Analysis of AI acceptance further demonstrated that trust and perceived reliability were stronger factors influencing acceptance than transparency alone. Although respondents expressed a strong desire to know when AI was used, transparency regarding AI involvement in EWS did not significantly determine willingness to act. Instead, concerns regarding AI errors were strongly associated with reduced trust and increased preference for human oversight. Respondents were not necessarily opposed to AI integration; rather, acceptance was higher when AI systems were perceived as reliable and supported by human review. These findings highlight the importance of considering societal factors alongside technological development when implementing AI in meteorological applications. Effective integration of AI into EWS will require not only accurate and reliable models but also targeted public education, clear communication strategies, and appropriate human oversight. Future work should investigate how different communication approaches, such as emphasizing AI generation, meteorologist verification, or combined human-AI decision processes, influence public trust and willingness to respond to AI-assisted warnings. Understanding public perceptions of AI provides an important foundation for developing trustworthy, accessible, and socially effective AI applications within weather forecasting and hazard communication.

490551.title: Development and Preparations for Flight Qualification of the CREWSR Electronically-Scanning Microwave Array for Sounding and Imaging Near 20-60 GHz
490551.authors: William J. Blackwell, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Lincoln Laboratory, Lexington, MA; and M. Abedin, S. Farzana, C. Kataria, S. Jeon, R. V. Leslie, A. Milstein, W. Moulder, M. Pieper, S. C. Reising, and R. Thomas
490551.abstract: We provide an update on the development and testing of a new high-performance observing system that offers high resolution and electronically scanned antenna beams at relatively low cost in a configuration that can be accommodated on a wide range of launch vehicles and hosted payload platforms. This new instrument technology leverages dynamic, data-driven sensing and provides hyperspectral microwave operation for improved profiling vertical resolution and tolerance to radio-frequency interference. Here we describe two NASA Earth Science Technology Office (ESTO) programs to improve present capabilities for high-resolution atmospheric sensing from small satellite platforms and discuss the plan for full flight qualification. The goal of the first program is to develop and test a Configurable Reflectarray Wideband Scanning Radiometer (CREWSR), a high-resolution, lightweight, low-power multiband (23, 31, and 50-58 GHz) radiometer with a scanning reflectarray. CREWSR is envisioned to be deployed on a small-satellite or flat-satellite platform. Once in orbit, the platform will accommodate a Reconfigurable Reflective Surface (RRS), as well as a multi-feed antenna cluster connected to a multiband hyperspectral microwave receiver system to provide an electronically-scanned beam for radiometric Earth observation. This new technology will enable the inclusion of relatively low frequencies on low-cost small-satellite constellations. Additionally, there is a critical need to enable development, test, and evaluation of Versatile, Intelligent, and Dynamic Earth Observation (VIDEO), and one key enabler is the recent emergence of metamaterials for use in high-performance blackbody radiometric targets. These materials are very thin (~200 microns) and lightweight (tens of grams), allowing them to be easily scaled up to realize very large targets (> 1 m^2) to subtend an entire sensor field of regard for laboratory measurements. Furthermore, the thin planar structure of the metamaterials provides a relatively small thermal mass, thereby permitting the projection of thermal features with very high spatial frequency content into the sensor field of view at the subpixel level. We have developed a 50 cm x 75 cm (20” x 30”) Radiometric Scene Generator (RSG) operating near 54 GHz with very large thermal contrast at the subpixel level for a typical spaceborne microwave radiometer. The RSG uses a scanning laser system illuminating a metamaterial surface with high microwave emissivity to project spatial features into the radiometer field of regard that can be detected and acted upon by intelligent processing algorithms. The intelligent processing algorithms utilize feature detection and machine learning techniques to recognize regions of interest in the atmospheric scene and command the sensor to react to the scene characteristics by changing the sensor response function. The first phase of laboratory testing using the RSG in conjunction with a scanning radiometer will be discussed.

490552.title: Dynamical Prediction of Western North Pacific Seasonal Accumulated Cyclone Energy with Experimental UFS Reforecasts
490552.authors: Douglas Nedza, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA; and B. Huang and J. Zhu
490552.abstract: Many agencies issue seasonal outlooks of tropical cyclone (TC) activity informing planning activities. NOAA is in the process of developing a next-generation dynamical forecast system, the Unified Forecast System (UFS). As part of this development process, ensembles of reforecasts are produced using the experimental prototypes of UFS to serve as a test-bed to evaluate seasonal forecast skill. Here, we evaluate UFS prototypes P8, HR3, and Beta v1.0 in predicting western North Pacific (WNP) seasonal TC activity in April and May initialized reforecasts. TC events are identified using the TempestExtremes event tracking algorithm based on characteristic features of TCs, such as local sea level pressure, temperature, and winds. Dynamical forecasts of seasonal TC event numbers and accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) are produced by aggregating the identified TC events. Reforecast variations in seasonal ACE are found to be highly skillful, with seasonal TC event counts demonstrating less skill. The relationship between the large-scale environment and ACE is consistent between observations and the UFS reforecasts, emphasizing the influence of ENSO variations. The UFS reforecasts exhibit a bias in the large-scale relationship with TC event numbers with a ‘too positive’ relationship with ENSO and underestimating the observed reduction (increase) of TC events in the southwest WNP during positive (negative) ENSO years.

490563.title: Investigating the Drivers of Elevated Cl2 In the Upper Troposphere and Lower Stratosphere (UTLS) during ATom-4
490563.authors: Selena Zhang, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA; and S. Solomon, K. A. Stone, D. Murphy, P. Veres, A. Rollins, and D. Jeong
490563.abstract: The chlorine radical plays an important chemical role in the atmosphere, driving ozone depletion and participating in the oxidation of volatile organic compounds such as methane and ethane. One key source of chlorine radicals is the photolysis of molecular chlorine (Cl2), a photolabile compound that is produced from numerous pathways including activation of gas-phase reservoir species (such as HCl, ClONO2, HOCl) as well as the chemical displacement of particulate chloride. During the ATom-4 campaign, elevated Cl2 was measured by the NOAA iodide chemical ionization mass spectrometer (I– CIMS) in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (8 to 12 km). In the Northern Hemisphere, elevated UTLS Cl2 was measured at relatively warm (~225 K), dry (H2O ~ 6 ppmv), and sunlit (SZA ~ 70º) conditions, while in the Southern Hemisphere UTLS Cl2 was elevated in colder (~210 K), wetter (H2O ~ 20 ppmv) and dark (SZA > 90º) conditions. We investigate these conditions for chlorine activation with a sectional aerosol model (Community Aerosol and Radiation Model for Atmospheres) coupled to the Community Earth System Model (CESM1/CARMA) nudged to meteorological reanalysis (MERRA-2). The Southern Hemisphere Cl2 is simulated in the standard version of the model, highlighting the ability of the existing kinetic parameterization to capture chlorine activation at warmer temperatures and higher pressures than typically studied. However, the model is unable to simulate Cl2 in the sunlit Northern Hemisphere given the fast photolysis sink. We propose that this is due to a missing heterogeneous chemistry source, based on concurrent ATom aerosol measurements in this region which indicate surface areas over 10 um2/cm3. To explore this, we update the chemical mechanism to include enhanced solubility of reservoir species on organic-containing surfaces, which strengthens heterogeneous chlorine activation and brings the simulated Cl2 in better agreement with measured values. These results suggest heterogeneous chlorine activation may be more prevalent in the UTLS than previously thought and highlight the importance of future in-situ measurements of Cl2 across a range of conditions to better constrain this chemistry.

490566.title: Intentional Collaboration in Extreme Precipitation: Engaging Experts and Industry Partners to Modernize NOAA’s Guidance for High-Hazard Infrastructure
490566.authors: Kelly M. Mahoney, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and B. McCormick, B. Smith, E. Mutkoski, and L. Vogelmann
490566.abstract: Modernizing Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP) guidance for design of high hazard infrastructure is essential to enhancing national resilience against extreme hydrometeorological events. Under Congressional authorization, NOAA is leading an effort to update decades-old PMP estimates using advanced modeling, extreme value statistics, and climate science. Achieving scientific rigor and broad adoption requires dedicated, intentional partner engagement embedded throughout the entire project lifecycle. Guided by co-development, transparency, and practical utility, NOAA’s PMP Modernization Project stakeholder engagement strategy builds trust across federal, state, academic, and private sector partners. Crucial next steps actively integrate partners, applied users, and external experts into the development process through technical and scientific working groups. These groups will collaborate on redefining PMP frameworks, refining statistical methods, and validating high-resolution climate and precipitation models. Simultaneously, NOAA is aligning with key industry groups to support stakeholder engagement and implementation. A prime example includes collaborating with the Association of State Dam Safety Officials (ASDSO) through their Extreme Precipitation Investigation Committee (EPIC). Through its updated charter, EPIC promotes scientific contributions, connects PMP advances with precipitation-frequency efforts, and fosters awareness across state dam safety regulators and practitioners. Together, these sustained collaborations build long-term capacity and ensure modernized PMP guidance directly enhances critical infrastructure decision-making.

490571.title: Aerosol and Earth's Climate Change: What Have We Learned from Earth Observation and What’s New Needed In the Coming Decade
490571.authors: Zhanqing Li, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD
490571.abstract: The tiny particles of aerosol play huge roles in the earth’s climate and its changes. By serving as scatters and absorbers of solar radiation, the long-term variability of aerosol loading has contributed a great deal to the fluctuations of earth’s temperature records from local to global scales. Serving as cloud condensation nuclei, aerosols modulate earth water cycle as well. The fundamental mechanisms by which aerosols influence climate—through aerosol–radiation interactions (ARI) and aerosol–cloud interactions (ACI)—have been recognized and intensively studied for decades. Yet aerosols remain the largest source of uncertainty in estimates of anthropogenic climate forcing. This uncertainty arises largely from the multifaceted nature of aerosol properties, including their size, composition, mixing state, and vertical distribution, all of which determine both the magnitude and even the sign of their climatic effects. Accurate observations of aerosol loading, physicochemical properties, and three-dimensional distributions are therefore essential for understanding and quantifying aerosol–climate interactions. Thanks to extensive observational programs from space, the surface, and aircraft, remarkable progress has been made over the past several decades, particularly during the era of NASA's Earth Observing System (EOS), the U.S. Department of Energy's Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program, and a growing suite of operational satellite and ground-based observing networks. These observations have substantially advanced our understanding of aerosol processes and their impacts on climate. Nevertheless, major gaps remain, especially in our understanding of aerosol–cloud interactions, which continue to dominate uncertainties in aerosol radiative forcing and climate feedback. Resolving this requires observation of the processes instead of just the state of the atmosphere. As the next generation of Earth Observations (EO) is being shaped through the upcoming Decadal Survey of Earth Observation from Space (DS-EOS), it is imperative to identify the measurements and observing strategies needed to address these outstanding scientific questions and reduce uncertainties in aerosol climate forcing. Such priorities will help guide future observing systems toward delivering the transformative observations required to advance climate science. As a colleague of Dr. Tony Busalacchi, who played a leading role in developing the Decadal Survey for Earth Science and Applications from Space (2018) after stepping down as the Chair of the National Academies' Board on Atmospheric Sciences and Climate, I would choose this topic as a tribute to Tony's exceptional leadership and enduring contributions to Earth observation and climate science.

490579.title: Advancing Water Resources Decision-Marking Through the Fusion of NASA Earth Observations and Land Surface Modeling
490579.authors: Jessica M. Erlingis, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and S. V. Kumar, C. R. Hain, O. Skulovich, D. M. Mocko, M. Wrzesien, K. Locke, R. A. Wade, J. M. Pflug, A. Getirana, J. Geiger, and W. Nie
490579.abstract: While in situ observations of the land surface, subsurface, vegetation canopy, and snowpack are generally sparse and representative only of the conditions at a given point or over a limited domain, Earth Observations (EOs) obtained through remote sensing techniques offer broader spatial coverage of these variables at varying temporal and spatial scales. Optimally combining EOs and physically-based land surface models through data assimilation provides physically consistent, spatially and temporally continuous hydrological information that enables decision makers in the water resources community to analyze the states and evolution of terrestrial water, energy, and vegetation conditions. NASA scientists are developing HydroGlobe, a state-of-the-art global land surface hydrology dataset. HydroGlobe covers a nearly global domain (60S-90N) with daily data at 5km spatial resolution from 2002-present. The system assimilates multiple EOs over the period of record including soil moisture, snow water equivalent, terrestrial water storage anomalies, and leaf area index. This talk showcases the current development and future applications of this dataset, which was designed in close collaboration with decision makers in the hydrological community.

490580.title: Forecast to Fireline: Advancing UFS Wind Prediction for Wildland Fire Operations
490580.authors: Samantha J Kramer, Atmospheric Interdisciplinary Research Institute, Denver, CO; and N. Perlin and B. Kirtman
490580.abstract: Wind speed prediction remains a critical shortcoming in operational fire weather forecasting, with profound implications for firefighter safety and large-fire suppression operations. Evaluation of high-resolution operational models, including Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and other national forecast systems, reveals systematic and persistent underestimation of extreme wind speeds in complex terrain. These failures are generally tied to insufficient horizontal resolution to capture topographic influences on near-surface winds, which critically modulate fire behavior, rate of spread, and operational decision-making at the fireline. This research demonstrates that short-range dynamical downscaling using the NOAA Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC) Short Range Weather Application (SRW App) produces meaningful improvements in wind representation at scales relevant to wildfire operations. The approach employs a limited-area atmospheric model with 1-km horizontal grid resolution over a 3° × 3° domain covering fire-affected regions, initialized with boundary conditions from high-resolution operational models (HRRR and RRFS v1). We conduct retrospective case studies of major fire events: the 2017 Thomas Fire (Santa Barbara/Ventura Counties, California; ~300k acres burned and the 2025 Palisades Fire (Los Angeles County, California; ~20k acres burned). Dynamical downscaling, which includes thermal and topographic physics is implemented to evaluate the representation of hour-to-hour wind speed variability, extreme values, and spatial variability tied to topographic effects. We validate these dynamical downscaling experiments against available observations from the case study fires and demonstrate that the improved wind representation is transferable across different fire scenarios and regions. While dynamical downscaling is computationally more expensive than statistical post-processing, the operational fire community has expressed genuine enthusiasm for this capability—recognizing that hour-to-hour precision in wind speed forecasts at the 1-10 km scale can be the difference between effective response and firefighter entrapment. This work establishes a pathway for transitioning high-resolution dynamical downscaling from a research tool to an operational capability that can provide actionable, life-safety-critical information to incident commanders, fire operations coordinators, and firefighting personnel. We discuss computational feasibility for real-time operational deployment, including the use of cloud computing and parallelization to reduce wall-clock forecast turnaround time. The research framework and open-source SRW-App are designed to support reproducibility and enable other researchers and operational centers to implement similar systems for their regions.

490581.title: Connecting Users to Commercial Earth Observation Data through NASA's Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) Program
490581.authors: Madi Cheyanne Clark, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and N. E. Hay, C. McEvoy, N. Jha, A. C. Blackford, V. Perekadan, K. Horn, J. Bell, D. Ostrenga, and M. Y. Martin
490581.abstract: NASA's Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) Program provides U.S. federal agencies, NASA-funded researchers, and government partners access to a growing suite of commercial Earth observation (EO) data, expanding the diversity and cadence of observations available for science and applications. Since its inception, CSDA has evaluated and onboarded providers offering high-resolution optical imagery, synthetic aperture radar, hyperspectral, and other commercial datasets, complementing NASA’s existing data products by providing additional observations. Connecting these capabilities to user needs requires sustained engagement between CSDA, data providers, and the broader research and applications community. The CSDA Data Management Team at the Office of Data Science and Informatics (ODSI) at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center supports this engagement by helping users get access to commercial EO data. The process begins with onboarding eligible U.S. Government-funded users, who can request access to commercial data through CSDA's data request forms. The program helps users identify relevant datasets, provides technical support, and resolves licensing or data-access questions. Users have applied CSDA data across disciplines including agriculture, hydrology, cryosphere, and land-cover change, generating a growing library of success stories that demonstrate the value of commercial EO data for science and decision-making. CSDA also supports time-critical needs by making commercial data available to the NASA Disasters program during major events, providing high-resolution imagery that has informed hazard assessments for storm damage, flooding, and wildfires, often within hours of tasking. Through onboarding support, a growing base of success stories, and assisting with disaster response, CSDA continues to strengthen the connection between commercial EO solutions and user needs, illustrating how public-private collaboration can expand the reach of EO investments.

490586.title: The Role of Extratropical Cyclones In a Changing Severe Convective Storm Climatology
490586.authors: Brandon Lee Weart, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL; ANL, Arlington Heights , IL; and M. LaBonte, W. S. Ashley, A. Haberlie, and V. A. Gensini
490586.abstract: Severe convective storms (SCS) cause billions of dollars in damage across the contiguous United States (CONUS) each year and are frequently associated with extratropical cyclones (ETCs), whose warm sectors provide the thermodynamic and kinematic environments favorable for deep, moist convection. Although research has examined changes in SCS environments and peril reports over time, comparatively little work has directly examined ETC and their affiliated SCS environments have changed or will change in the future. The goal of this study is to generate a climatology of ETCs across the central and eastern CONUS and, thereafter, develop an understanding of the efficiency of SCS environments affiliated with these ETCs in the production of SCS perils. Using CONUS404 and ERA5 output, an automated tracking framework for ETCs is developed to provide details on cyclone evolution, trajectory, and intensity for a historical period. Favorable SCS environments are evaluated using thermodynamic, kinematic, and composite SCS parameters, permitting ETCs to be categorized according to the magnitude and spatial extent of the SCS-favorable environment within and near their warm sectors. These implicit environmental characteristics will then be compared with explicit peril proxies from CONUS404 to examine changes in the relationship between ETC environments and SCS production over a 40-year historical period and, time and data permitting, a future climate scenario. The hypothesis is that changes in ETC characteristics contribute to observed and projected future shifts in the climatology of favorable SCS environments and their realizations. This framework will help clarify the extent to which changes in SCS climatology are linked to changes in ETC characteristics, the environments they support, and their ability to produce perils.

490587.title: Alaska’s Changing Hazard Landscape, 1959-2025: Heavier Precipitation, a Diminishing Cryosphere, and Increasing Evaporative Demand
490587.authors: Uma S. Bhatt, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; Univ. of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and J. Walsh, P. Hutton, R. Thoman, S. Vieira, C. F. Waigl, A. Bennett, P. A. Bieniek, R. Lader, and J. Littell
490587.abstract: Alaska is experiencing some of the most rapid and consequential climate changes in the United States, with cascading impacts through sea ice, hydrologic extremes, and storms. This study provides an assessment of recent changes in key weather- and climate-driven hazards using the ERA5 reanalysis and a newly developed Alaska-focused dynamical downscaled dataset spanning 1959–2025. We characterize long-term variability and trends in sea-ice seasonality, heavy precipitation events, strong wind events, storms, atmospheric rivers, snow cover and moisture deficits across Alaska and the surrounding seas. Precipitation has increased across the state, and the heaviest precipitation amounts have increased more rapidly than for the climatological mean precipitation over much of northern and central Alaska. High-wind exceedances have become more frequent over coastal waters, consistent with a loss of sea ice and warmer water temperatures, while atmospheric river events have increased over much of the region. Over land, declining snowfall fraction and shorter snow seasons have been accompanied by increased warm-season atmospheric evaporative demand. Compound hazard assessments show that increasing coastal vulnerability to flooding and erosion is attributable primarily to the reduced duration of protective sea ice, although cold-season storminess is also increasing in southwestern Alaska. An increase in wildfire burned area has coincided with a combination of reduced seasonal snow cover and an increase in the unmet surface moisture demand, particularly in Interior and Western Alaska. Together, these results depict an Alaska that is becoming wetter overall but less persistently snow- and ice-covered and increasingly exposed to heavy precipitation events, drought, wildfire and coastal hazards. The findings provide science-based information for the next National Climate Assessment and for evaluation of changes in weather- and climate-related hazards in Alaska.

490591.title: Breaking the Ambiguity Cycle: Identifying the Missing Link Between Improving Forecasts and Improved Decision-Making
490591.authors: Kathi Kaiser, KaiserUX Associates, Saint Louis, MO; Bentley University, Waltham, MA
490591.abstract: Hurricane forecasts are becoming more accurate; however, people in harm’s way do not always act in a timely manner to protect themselves. The key to motivating people to act is clear information, but when people do not accurately and confidently understand the very information intended to warn them, that information becomes a roadblock: people can get stuck in an ambiguity cycle of repetitive information-seeking that delays action. Given that forecasts are necessarily uncertain, breaking this cycle requires that people feel sufficiently confident in their knowledge of the situation to act despite its inherent ambiguity. This presentation will examine the sources and effects of the ambiguity cycle, and will illustrate how improvements to hurricane literacy in general and the design of hurricane visualizations specifically can help people avoid analysis paralysis and take timely action to stay safe. By integrating Lindell and Perry’s Protective Action Decision Model (2012) with theories of decision-making from cognitive psychology and design, I will present a revised model that highlights the critical role of two related factors – comprehension and confidence – in serving as a catalyst to break the ambiguity cycle. The revised model offers important new avenues for research and practice in the continuing effort to ensure that improving forecasts also encourage improved decision-making.

490592.title: An Introduction to NASA’s SubOrbital Archive Readiness Team (SOAR) and Efforts with Recent/Ongoing Field Campaigns
490592.authors: Stephanie M. Wingo, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; UAH / NASA Office of Data Science and Informatics (ODSI), Huntsville, AL; and S. H. Lubkin, G. T. Stano, M. Buzanowicz, M. Silverman, S. Wong, M. Thornton, H. Lethcoe, L. Li, and S. Leslie
490592.abstract: Airborne and field data collection efforts obtain targeted observations vital for advancing Earth science. NASA’s airborne and field, or suborbital, observations are archived and stewarded within the Earthdata Repository by the Earth Science Data and Information System (ESDIS) project. Previously, NASA suborbital science teams worked with individual, discipline-aligned Distributed Active Archive Centers (DAACs) for data transfer, publication, archival, documentation, workshops, and more. Today, ESDIS and Earthdata are going through a substantial organizational and technical transformation, shifting from distributed archive centers towards multi- and cross-discipline science enablement. During this evolution, the SubOrbital Archive Readiness team (SOAR) connects airborne and field data producers and science teams to the Earthdata repository. As NASA-funded airborne and field campaigns continue, science teams require continued, uninterrupted support, for and beyond what was previously provisioned by DAACs, including guidance on updated agency policy (e.g., SPD-41a), data management planning, data and metadata standards, data transfer and delivery to cloud-based infrastructure, and clarification on any necessary preservation content specification and/or documentation materials. Most importantly, science teams with recent, active, and imminent campaigns should have a consistent, reliable communication pathway amid the ESDIS transition. SOAR was established in 2026 as an integrated team of suborbital data stewardship experts with backgrounds from a variety of science disciplines and with wide ranging technical expertise. This structure allows specific expertise to be leveraged from all areas in support of individual suborbital campaigns’ needs. New and upcoming data collection producers are able to work with a SOAR point of contact to ensure clarity, accelerate pre-archival tasks, and ultimately support more timely, efficient data publication and availability. This presentation describes the SOAR team, gives an overview of SOAR’s core responsibilities, and outlines how SOAR links to other parts of the broader, evolving ESDIS structure. Roles and expectations for SOAR and data producer interactions will be discussed, including a summary of recent collaborations with NASA Earth Venture Suborbital (EVS-4) field investigation science teams. As ESDIS transforms, SOAR aims to ensure NASA airborne and field campaign observations are efficiently stewarded in alignment with FAIR and open science principles to promote data discovery and reuse.

490593.title: Ocean Surface Wind Retrieval with Spire’s Hyperspectral Microwave Radiometer
490593.authors: Yuriy Goncharenko, Spire Global Inc, Boulder, CO; and R. Whitehead, J. C. Cartwright, V. Irisov, M. K. Belal, M. Henry, K. Parow-Souchon, and J. van der Merwe
490593.abstract: This study presents the first results of ML-based ocean surface wind speed retrieval using Spire’s hyperspectral microwave radiometer. Spire’s first hyperspectral microwave radiometer, HyMS (NORAD 67394), was launched in January 2026 into a 550 km LEO orbit and became operational in late March 2026. Since May, it has supplied customers with brightness-temperature maps at a 2-hour mean latency. HyMS is a cross-track scanning radiometer operating in three sub-bands: 49.3–57.9 GHz, 89 GHz, and 183.1–191.6 GHz. The 54 GHz sub-band has 1759 channels, each with a bandwidth of 7.3 MHz and a spacing of 4.88 MHz. The 183 GHz sub-band has 877 channels, each with a bandwidth of 14.65 MHz and a spacing of 9.8 MHz. The full hyperspectral channel set is downlinked to the ground, offering reconfigurable channels. The 89 GHz band is a single 2 GHz-wide window channel. The 54 and 89 GHz bands are quasi-horizontally (QH) polarized, and the 183 GHz channels are quasi-vertically (QV) polarized. The radiometer employs the most recent advances in mm-wave technology, building on front-end receiver technology from MetOp-SG MWS, resulting in a mean per-channel NEDT of 1.74 K for the 54 GHz band, 3.9 K for the 183 GHz band, and 0.16 K for the 89 GHz window channel. When averaged to the ATMS channel center frequencies and bandwidths, HyMS shows noise performance similar to or better than on-orbit ATMS estimates. In this paper we propose a Neural-Network (NN)-based ocean wind-speed retrieval using HyMS hyperspectral radiometer data. Three ways of treating the hyperspectral data were analyzed. In the first, the 54 GHz band was split into 7 sub-channels and the 183 GHz band into 4; each sub-channel averages hundreds of HyMS channels, yielding a very low NEDT of 0.1–0.2 K. In the second, the HyMS channels were “degraded” to the 19 overlapping JPSS ATMS channels, with the aim of matching their center frequencies and bandwidths. In the third, all 2637 channels were fed into the NN. In addition to the brightness temperatures, the Earth incidence angle (EIA), polarization, and the latitude and longitude of each pixel were used as inputs. The ATMS U-Net retrieval was used as a performance baseline, and ERA5 wind speed as ground truth. HyMS data obtained from April 1 to July 22 were used for the training, validation, and test sets. Because wind fields can be highly spatially correlated, any granule used for training was excluded from the validation and test sets to avoid information leakage; the same non-overlap restriction was applied between the validation and test sets. For independent, “real-world” performance testing, only data from July 23 to August 1, together with a few older hand-picked granules, were used. Independent testing showed that the split-channel and ATMS-like datasets performed as well as the U-Net model. On all-sky data, the NN trained on the full HyMS spectrum achieved an RMSE of 1.88 m/s and a bias of 0.15 m/s, comparable to NOAA’s U-Net, whose RMSE of 1.95 m/s and bias of 0.13 m/s were estimated for clear-sky conditions only. For clear-sky conditions, Spire’s HyMS retrieval attained an RMSE of 1.64 m/s and a bias of 0.09 m/s, 19% better than U-Net. This early-results study shows that the NN trained on Spire’s hyperspectral radiometer data outperforms U-Net, which was designed for wind-speed retrieval from ATMS data, by 19% in clear-sky conditions (a direct comparison), and performs comparably in all-sky conditions, a regime for which U-Net has not been evaluated. As a further development, Spire plans to incorporate IBTrACS data, in addition to ERA5, to improve retrieval accuracy in high-wind conditions.

490595.title: Direct Measurement of the Phase of Individual Hydrometeors
490595.authors: Daniel Webster, Univ. of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and D. K. Singh, E. R. Pardyjak, and T. J. Garrett
490595.abstract: Near-surface precipitation frequently occurs as rain, snow, or mixed-phase. During near-freezing conditions, individual precipitation particles may simultaneously contain both liquid water and ice, as observed in sleet, freezing rain, and partially melted snowflakes. Although precipitation phase strongly influences winter hazards, snowpack evolution, and numerical weather prediction, direct measurements of the liquid and frozen fractions of individual hydrometeors remain extremely limited. Consequently, existing precipitation-phase observations largely rely on empirical particle classification rather than direct physical measurements. To address this gap, we present a first-principles framework for directly measuring the phase of individual hydrometeors using a Differential Emissivity Imaging Disdrometer (DEID). The approach independently determines particle mass during melting and evaporation by combining thermal imaging with particle area measurements derived from radiative temperature contrast. Because frozen particles undergo both melting and evaporation, whereas liquid particles undergo only evaporation, the two independently measured masses provide a direct means of distinguishing frozen, liquid, and mixed-phase hydrometeors. The proposed methodology also independently measures the size distributions of the frozen and liquid components throughout the melting and evaporation processes, providing particle-by-particle phase identification and phase-resolved particle-size distributions. The proposed methodology was validated using laboratory-generated ice particles in a cold-room facility operating at temperatures down to approximately −40°C. Independent measurements of particle mass and particle size distribution obtained from the DEID agreed closely with reference measurements, yielding an R^2 of 0.99 for particle masses ranging from approximately 2 to 20 mg. These results establish a foundation for real-time observations of rain, snow, and mixed-phase precipitation, with broad applications in winter weather forecasting, numerical weather prediction, hydrologic modeling, and snowpack monitoring.

490599.title: A Universal Temperature-Dependent Mass–Diameter Relationship for Frozen Hydrometeors
490599.authors: Dhiraj Kumar Singh, University of Utah, Salt lake city, UT; Univ. of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and E. R. Pardyjak and T. J. Garrett
490599.abstract: Accurate spatial estimation of frozen precipitation characteristics remains one of the major challenges in atmospheric science and hydrology because microphysical properties of snow vary substantially across space and time. Although modern remote sensing systems can measure particle size distributions over large spatial scales, accurate retrieval of snow water equivalent (SWE) and snow depth still depends on converting particle size into particle mass using empirical mass–diameter relationships. Previous studies, including the pioneering work of Locatelli and Hobbs (1974), demonstrated that the coefficients of these relationships vary with snow crystal habit. Consequently, SWE and snow depth retrieved solely from particle size distributions are subject to substantial uncertainty. To address this limitation, we propose a temperature-dependent mass–diameter formulation that enables the estimation of snowflake mass, SWE, and snow depth from measurements of particle-size distributions and air temperature (T). To establish these relationships, approximately 9 million individual snowflakes collected during the 2020–2021 winter season at Alta, Collins, Utah, were measured using the Differential Emissivity Imaging Disdrometer (DEID). Analysis of these measurements showed that the coefficients of the mass–diameter relationship, m = aD^b, are functions of air temperature, where a = f(T)and b = f(T). We further found that bulk snow density also exhibits a systematic dependence on air temperature (density = f(T)), thereby enabling snow depth to be estimated from SWE. The proposed formulation was validated using independent manual measurements of SWE and snow depth. Using these functions, estimated SWE and snow depths agree with manual observations with uncertainties of less than 11% and 13%, respectively.
