These results demonstrate that incorporating air temperature into mass–diameter relationships provides a practical, physically-based framework for improving spatial retrievals of SWE and snow depth from particle-size distributions, with broad applications in weather radar, satellite, and ground-based remote sensing, hydrologic modeling, and operational snowfall forecasting.

490600.title: Validation of Global Daily Evapotranspiration Estimates Using Remote Sensing Data and the Atmosphere–Land Exchange Inverse (ALEXI) Energy Balance Model
490600.authors: Sammy Z Akasheh, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and C. M. U. Neale, M. C. Anderson, C. R. Hain, D. Zaccaria, A. E. Suyker, D. Roberti, V. A. Souza, A. Masih, I. Z. Goncalves, R. D. C. Bispo, R. Ritzema, A. Pourghodrat, and M. Schull
490600.abstract: Evapotranspiration (ET) is a key component of the hydrologic cycle and is essential for quantifying watershed water balances, estimating irrigation water requirements, and assessing crop productivity and yield. Thermal remote sensing provides an effective means of estimating ET by exploiting the physical relationship between land surface temperature (LST), evaporative cooling, and the principles of the Two-Source Energy Balance (TSEB) model. The Atmosphere–Land Exchange Inverse (ALEXI) model is a two-source energy balance model that estimates daily ET using the difference between day and night thermal infrared-based surface temperature observations to retrieve surface energy balance components between sunrise and local noon. In this study, ALEXI was implemented using imagery from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), which provides global daily multispectral and thermal infrared observations at 375 m spatial resolution, representing a substantial improvement over existing polar orbiting and geostationary thermal sensors with spatial resolutions exceeding 1 km. When coupled with the DisALEXI disaggregation framework and Landsat imagery, the system combines the high temporal frequency of VIIRS with the high spatial resolution of Landsat to produce field-scale ET maps capable of resolving individual agricultural fields. Daily ET maps were generated on 15° × 15° global tiles using VIIRS observations for the period 2013–2026. The resulting ET products are publicly available through the Global Daily Evapo-Transpiration (GloDET) web portal (https://glodet.nebraska.edu). Model performance was evaluated using eddy covariance flux tower measurements from multiple sites across the United States and Brazil. ALEXI-derived ET estimates were extracted at the tower locations and compared with energy balance closure-corrected flux measurements for all available years between 2013 and 2026. The results showed strong agreement across a broad range of vegetation types and climatic conditions, with coefficients of determination (R²) ranging from 0.75 to 0.95. These results demonstrate the robustness and reliability of the ALEXI–VIIRS framework for estimating daily evapotranspiration over heterogeneous landscapes, highlighting its potential for regional and global applications in water resources management, agricultural monitoring, and drought assessment.

490602.title: Measuring and Reconstructing Local Wind Patterns over Complex Terrain Using Sparse Lagrangian Particle Tracking
490602.authors: Anthony Cheng, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA; and N. Wei
490602.abstract: The dynamics of turbulent air flow in the atmospheric surface layer (ASL) over complex terrain are particularly difficult to capture on the local scale–from the size of a few city blocks to a neighborhood–as wind is forced to flow through heterogeneous landscapes while subject to convective effects due to ground heating. A full description of ASL dynamics in such nonequilibrium settings requires wind velocity, pressure, and temperature data resolved both in time and three-dimensionally in space. With these data, we may characterize wind on the local scale to inform both microscale meteorological models as well as people of wind-related hazards. There has yet to be an established method to measure atmospheric pressure and temperature fluctuations in the field with high temporal and 3D spatial resolution. Recent work leverages Lagrangian Particle Tracking (LPT) to obtain flow velocity data and reconstruct pressure fields using dense particle seeding in laboratory and simulational settings. The essence of LPT is that the dynamics of a fluid may be deduced by recording the dynamics of neutrally buoyant particles seeded in the fluid. In this work, we develop a data assimilation method that uses velocity data from LPT to reconstruct pressure fields directly from the Navier-Stokes equations. Due to convection resulting from daytime ground heating, the momentum equations also include a buoyancy term in the Boussinesq limit, which provides an avenue for reconstructing temperature fields from LPT. Coupled with a field-scale 3D LPT system developed by our group, this work enables volumetric and time-resolved measurements of velocity, pressure, and temperature over complex terrain. In field-scale 3D LPT, we expect significantly sparser LPT seeding densities compared to those available in experiments and simulations, which presents difficulties for accurate 3D pressure and temperature reconstruction. In this study, we introduce a control-volume approach that achieves accurate pressure reconstruction for 2D and 3D flows from sparse LPT data. We then propose a viable path forward for accurate 3D temperature reconstruction. We begin with a theoretical validation of our method using the 2D Taylor-Green vortex, demonstrating superior pressure reconstruction accuracy compared to spectral pressure Poisson methods on sparse LPT data. We then apply our method to 3D LPT data computed from a direct numerical simulation of turbulent channel flow, which is available in the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database, and demonstrate that our method achieves similar accuracy compared to state-of-the-art pressure reconstruction methods for volumetric particle seeding densities up to an order of magnitude sparser. Finally, noting that flows in the Boussinesq limit exhibit temperature fluctuations that only drive flow in the vertical direction, we propose a method for temperature reconstruction by first reconstructing pressure in the horizontal plane, allowing temperature to be resolved vertically. To validate temperature reconstruction, we plan to compare temperature fluctuation statistics from reconstructing temperature fields in Rayleigh-Bénard convection experiments. We also plan on applying the control-volume approach to reconstructing field-scale temperature fluctuations using LPT data collected over a solar farm. Our novel work will enable the first temporally and spatially resolved volumetric pressure and temperature atmospheric flow measurements for real-world convective ASL turbulence.

490603.title: Sunsetting CASEI to Make ESDIS and Earthdata Brighter
490603.authors: Stephanie M. Wingo, UAH / NASA Office of Data Science and Informatics (ODSI), Huntsville, AL; and A. Shirey, B. Ray, T. Vo, M. Thornton, M. Silverman, S. Leslie, K. Ward, P. Przyborski, T. Stevens, W. Marcel, S. H. Lubkin, and M. Maskey
490603.abstract: An inaugural Satellite Needs Working Group (SNWG) “solution team,” NASA’s Airborne Data Management Group (ADMG) was established in 2018 to develop recommendations and guidelines to improve agency airborne and field (or suborbital) data stewardship and make non-satellite NASA Earth science data more discoverable and usable both within and beyond their initial scientific communities. A centerpiece of ADMG’s work was the development of the Catalog of Archived Suborbital Earth Science Investigations (CASEI), fully released in 2023. At the end of FY2026, the ADMG project will close out to promote the initiation and continuation of new SNWG solutions. As part of this process, the NASA Earth Science Data System (ESDS) recommended the transfer of core CASEI capacities to its Earth Science Data and Information System (ESDIS) project. This presentation gives an overview of CASEI’s history, identifies specific features transitioning to ESDIS and the Earthdata web presence, summarizes completed and ongoing transition tasks as well as next steps and an anticipated timeline for fully sunsetting the resource. What made CASEI brightest will allow the next evolution of NASA Earthdata to shine brighter for current and future users of decades worth of suborbital Earth observations. At creation, CASEI provisioned a novel single-entry-point for myriad contextual metadata necessary for appropriate data reuse, alongside smooth data access and unique graphics, for a majority of the agency’s decades of suborbital Earth science data and field campaign information. Such capabilities were previously varied across several ESDIS discipline-aligned Distributed Active Archive Centers (or DAACs); this meant that inter- and cross-disciplinary data users could face multiple starting points and often inconsistent workflows to find and access data. The CASEI web interface and programmatic API enabled intuitive exploration of field campaigns and related data products. As ESDIS evolves, transitioning from the DAAC-oriented structure towards science enablement within and across disciplines, integrating core parts of CASEI into the broader ESDIS ecosystem and the unified Earthdata web presence will further improve users’ ability to explore NASA’s suborbital Earth observations, resources, and tools to further data reuse in support of new science.

490604.title: AI - Automated Quality Assessment of Surface Meteorological Data Using Time-Series and Vision Foundation Models
490604.authors: Bhupendra Raut, ANL, Darien, IL; and R. C. Jackson, S. Pal, A. Sockol, A. Theisen, J. R. O'Brien, and S. Collis
490604.abstract: Operational data quality assessment (QA) of ground-based weather observations has traditionally relied on instrument-specific rules and threshold tests, and recently on unsupervised computer vision (CV) algorithms and supervised machine learning (ML) models developed for individual QA tasks. Recent advances in publicly available pretrained time-series and vision foundation models (FMs) introduce new capabilities for observational data analysis and QA. These models are developed for general-purpose time series and image feature detection and representation learning, and their learned representations can be innovatively repurposed to generate contextual information for downstream tasks such as data quality assessment and anomaly detection through zero-shot or few-shot inference without developing task-specific models from scratch. We explore the general-purpose time-series and vision transformer encoder-based foundation models for the following tasks. 1) Time-series analysis, by combining pretrained time-series foundation models (e.g., TimesFM and Chronos) with statistical and machine learning (ML) methods as complementary tools within a unified analysis workflow. We also used unsupervised techniques, including Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) and Matrix Profile (MP) analysis, to identify recurring patterns and anomalous behavior in time-series data, while the pretrained foundation models provide learned representations and predictions for anomaly detection and regime characterization. 2) Vision models, primarily Segment Anything Model (SAM), You Only Look Once (YOLO), Florence, and DINO (Self-DIstillation with NO labels) inference on camera imagery, can characterize environmental and operational conditions such as insects on instrument optics, precipitation, fog, dust, vehicles, and maintenance activities, which can be used to contextualize and assess the quality of other, co-located data series. The combined outputs of these diverse models contextually characterize observations along with individual measurement quality flags and provide information that is difficult to capture using conventional quality control (QC) methods alone.

490612.title: Recent Advances in MPAS-JEDI Tuning for the Next Version of the Rapid Refresh Forecast System
490612.authors: Ming Hu, NOAA/OAR/GSL, Boulder, CO; and C. Zhou, G. Ge, H. Lin, D. Dowell, J. Hu, S. Pan, H. Wang, R. Li, S. Murdzek, L. Lin, H. LUO, K. C. Eure, E. P. James, A. Back, J. Beck, A. Burke, T. T. Ladwig, S. Liu, S. K. Degelia, D. E. Lippi, X. Zhang, T. Lei, H. liu, and D. Holdaway
490612.abstract: Hourly-updating numerical weather guidance at convective-allowing scales is the foundation of severe storm forecasting. In the past two decades, NOAA has successfully developed and operated the High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR), which began an era of community-based modeling components in operations. The HRRR includes the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) for observational data assimilation, a specially configured version of the Advanced Research WRF (ARW) model, and unified post-processing (UPP). In the past 6 years, NOAA has made significant efforts to develop the new Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS). While the first version of RRFS (scheduled for summer 2026) leverages the FV3 dynamical core and GSI, a significant pivot has taken place for future versions to leverage the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) and the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI). The RRFS data assimilation (DA) team at GSL and OMD has made significant efforts to develop, implement, and tune JEDI for RRFS implementation through both real-time and retrospective experiments. A major recent milestone was the establishment of the first real-time RRFS prototype based on MPAS and JEDI, known as RRFSv2x. The system has been running continuously since the spring of 2026, providing a valuable long-term result for evaluating JEDI performance within the RRFS framework. Building on the results from these real-time experiments, the RRFS DA team has conducted additional tuning of JEDI to further enhance its positive impact on RRFS forecast performance. These efforts have been evaluated through a combination of real-time and retrospective experiments. This presentation will summarize the recent JEDI tuning efforts for RRFS, describe the methodology used, and discuss their impact on analysis and forecast performance.

490631.title: Towards Mitigation Scale: Supporting Landfill Methane Emissions Management by Connecting Spatial Scales with Satellites
490631.authors: Betsy Farris, University of Colorado, Boulder, Boulder, CO; and E. Miller, G. Cortes, M. Rutherford, E. Coffey, S. Coburn, J. de Gouw, J. Casey, G. Rieker, M. Hannigan, and D. K. Henze
490631.abstract: Landfills are the third-largest source of anthropogenic methane in the United States, and the growing constellation of methane-sensing satellites offers various methods for monitoring their emissions. We are developing tools and methods that combine open-source satellite data with ground-based measurements to monitor landfill emissions and support mitigation. In this study, we evaluate how TROPOMI, with its high precision and daily revisit, can constrain a single landfill's emissions through atmospheric inversions, and we pair this with continuous ground-based monitoring for independent validation. We use the open-access Integrated Methane Inversion (IMI) tool to test whether regional-scale inversions can support point-source, facility-level emission estimates as well as provide context about interfering sources and regional trends. At the landfill of study, we deployed low-cost point sensors and long-path laser sensors. We evaluate these data both as continuous monitoring tools and as an independent check on IMI-resolved emissions. We also examine what information plume-mapping instruments add, using Carbon Mapper detections at the same landfill to separate the facility's signal from interfering nearby sources. Our analysis spans all of 2025 to capture seasonal variability, including specific emissions events (exceedances and significant decreases). Initial results show that while the regional methane emissions are underestimated, the landfill’s local (~neighborhood) scale emissions are overestimated by the U.S. EPA inventory. We are actively investigating the cause of this disagreement. We have also identified temporal variability which is not captured by the inventories both at the landfill and regionally. To investigate these trends and specific emissions events, we pair the suite of atmospheric measurements with activity data and site conditions to begin developing an understanding of the emissions’ causes and to move towards mitigation strategies. Together, these results will inform best practices for applying open-source satellite data to landfill management and for integrating satellite and ground-based sensing into landfill emissions monitoring. We expect the same framework to extend to other sectors.

490634.title: IMAP Active Link for Real-Time (I-ALiRT) System: First Year of Observations and Potential Applications of the New Real-Time Space Weather Data Products
490634.authors: Christina O. Lee, Space Sciences Laboratory, UC Berkeley, Berkeley, CA; and E. R. Christian, L. Sandoval, D. J. McComas, M. Gkioulidou, N. Schwadron, D. Baker, M. Desai, D. Gathright, B. Heber, T. Horbury, S. Kanekal, S. Livi, J. G. Luhmann, J. G. Mitchell, J. S. Rankin, R. Skoug, D. L. Turner, and B. D. Williams
490634.abstract: The Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP) is a NASA heliophysics science mission that launched in September 2025 and provides new coordinated and comprehensive observations of the inner and outer heliosphere. Orbiting at the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point, the IMAP observatory is an ideal location for observing the space weather conditions upstream of Earth. Thus, in addition to providing new and groundbreaking heliophysics science observations, five in-situ instruments on IMAP make measurements that are critical for advancing space weather research and operational forecasting. These measurements are continuously telemetered in near real-time as part of the IMAP Active Link for Real-Time (I-ALiRT) space weather data system. I-ALiRT is based on the Real-Time Solar Wind (RTSW) data system from the NASA Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) mission and provides similar space weather data products at enhanced cadences as well as additional new data products. These new products include count rates of high-energy SEP electrons and Helium-4, solar wind charge state and elemental abundance ratios, and indication of counterstreaming solar wind electron flow. We will present the first year of I-ALiRT observations and highlight several space weather events to demonstrate how the new real-time data products from I-ALiRT can be used for monitoring and situational awareness of incoming space weather activity in the operational forecast setting. Updates on the real-time data flow architecture and public access to the I-ALiRT data will also be presented.

490635.title: Strengthening R2O Through Stakeholder Engagement and Partnership
490635.authors: Katie van Werkhoven, Research Triangle Institute, Boone, NC
490635.abstract: Successful research-to-operations (R2O) requires more than developing innovative science and technology; it requires sustained engagement with the people who will ultimately use those capabilities. This panel contribution will highlight two examples of CIROH efforts to strengthen this connection. First, the development and adaptation of the Tools for Exploratory Evaluation in Hydrologic Research (TEEHR) demonstrates how engagement with diverse end users can shape research software and services to address operational needs. Second, recent investigations of flood forecasting needs illustrate how direct engagement with emergency managers, forecasters, and other users can identify gaps and guide research priorities. Together, these efforts demonstrate the importance of treating R2O as an iterative process in which user needs inform research, operational experience drives refinement, and sustained partnerships help translate research advances into useful capabilities.

490655.title: Changing Forests and Climate in the Amazon
490655.abstract: Two anthropogenic forces act on the world's land at once: climate change and land-cover change. Both shape the atmosphere, which is in turn coupled to the surface beneath it, and together they govern the regional energy budget in ways that are challenging to disentangle. Over the Amazon, we explore how these two forces combine, using two decades of satellite observations and reanalysis resolved by forest-cover change. Our focus is on low-level clouds, whose changing patterns link the two forces: forest loss reorganizes the clouds over cleared land, while the warming, drying climate reshapes them across the region, and both leave a measurable imprint on the reflected sunlight at the top of the atmosphere. Tracing this chain from the surface, through the cloud response, to the top-of-atmosphere energy budget, we find that the response to forest loss depends on the extent of clearing and on the background climatic state, and that its imprint on the regional radiation budget operates below the resolution of current climate models and is absent from surface-only accounting. We discuss how resolving both forces together reshapes our understanding of the Amazon's changing energy budget and its trajectory under continued land-use and climate pressure.

490659.title: Understanding Sources of Precipitation Biases In Twelve Years of Rapidly Updating Numerical Weather Prediction Forecasts
490659.authors: Eric P. James, GSD, Boulder, CO; and S. Benjamin
490659.abstract: Verification of quantitative precipitation forecasts (QPF) from the NOAA High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) over the past 12 years reveals changes in QPF performance between model versions. The currently operational HRRRv4 has a reduced (improved) high bias for heavy precipitation in the eastern US; the improvement is most pronounced at short forecast lengths, highlighting the impact of data assimilation improvements. However, HRRRv4 also exhibits a low bias for light QPF. Verification of HRRRv3 and HRRRv4 against hourly gauges across the western US reveals a dry bias for light QPF in both models, but worse in short-range forecasts from HRRRv4, particularly in summer. In order to synthesize results across QPF thresholds, we present a new QPF-related metric for evaluating NWP models, termed the integrated QPF bias. HRRRv1 and HRRRv2 exhibited a high integrated QPF bias, while HRRRv3 and HRRRv4 exhibit a low bias, worsened in HRRRv4. These results are robust across several QPE datasets including hourly gauges. The integrated QPF bias is an important component of overall model moisture bias. Comparing HRRRv4 with the experimental Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS), as well as a prototype MPAS-JEDI based RRFSv2 for the past few months, reveals the relative performance of the three models. RRFSv1 exhibits a pronounced high QPF bias in summer due to excessive light precipitation (which represents a substantial portion of the net QPF bias) associated with the use of a convective parameterization. Preliminary RRFSv2 results are encouraging, with summer forecasts exhibiting a more optimal frequency bias across thresholds than either HRRR or RRFSv1, and a higher CSI for heavy QPF thresholds.

490661.title: Aerosol Population Variability Challenges the Transferability of Immersion-Freezing Parameterizations: A Multi-Campaign Aerosol-INP Closure Study
490661.authors: Yijia Sun, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY; and A. M. Fridlind, I. Silber, and D. A. Knopf
490661.abstract: In mixed-phase clouds, ice-nucleating particles (INPs) can initiate primary ice formation through immersion freezing of supercooled droplets. Whether immersion-freezing parameterizations retain quantitative predictive skill across contrasting aerosol populations remains uncertain. Closure exercises evaluate whether INP spectra predicted from independently constrained aerosol properties agree with corresponding measurements, while accounting for uncertainties. Our particle size-resolved framework combines measured aerosol size distributions, specified aerosol-source allocations, and published aerosol-aware immersion-freezing parameterizations to predict INP spectra for comparison with observations. Here, we use this framework to test parameterization transferability for contrasting aerosol populations across campaigns. We first verify the numerical implementation by reproducing a published aerosol-INP closure calculation from the October 2019 Aerosol-Ice Formation Closure (AEROICESTUDY) campaign at the Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurements User Facility (ARM) Southern Great Plains (SGP) observatory. We then apply the same framework to five cold-air-outbreak cases from the ARM Cold-air Outbreaks in the Marine Boundary Layer Experiment (COMBLE) and 52 matched aerosol–INP samples from the yearlong ARM Eastern Pacific Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment (EPCAPE) at Scripps Pier. In both marine campaigns, we evaluate two deterministic INP surface-site-density formulations and one stochastic, time-dependent nucleation-rate formulation. For COMBLE, we also evaluate two empirical formulations that are only temperature dependent. Aggregate prediction-to-observation ratios at COMBLE span more than three orders of magnitude: the empirical formulations overpredict observations by roughly two orders of magnitude, whereas the aerosol-aware formulations predict INPs in a range from an underprediction by roughly one order of magnitude to near the aggregate closure. For EPCAPE measurements, the aerosol-aware formulations span more than an order of magnitude: the rate-based formulation approaches aggregate closure with a ratio of 0.94, whereas the surface-site-density formulations underpredict by up to a factor of 17. To assess temperature-only empirical formulations performance in a contrasting continental environment, we also evaluate the temperature-only empirical formulations against a separate multiyear record of 181 SGP filter samples collected from 2020 to 2025. These formulations yield aggregate prediction-to-observation ratios of 0.52–1.57 at SGP, contrasting with their overprediction at COMBLE by roughly two orders of magnitude. Taken together, these contrasts show that transferability is conditional: quantitative agreement with INP observations for one aerosol population does not ensure comparable predictive skill for another. The cross-campaign evaluations reveal three distinct performance outcomes. The nucleation-rate formulation retains near-closure performance across both marine campaigns, whereas the surface-site-density formulations show persistent underprediction. The temperature-only empirical formulations yield aggregate prediction-to-observation ratios within a factor of two for the multiyear SGP record but overpredict COMBLE by nearly two orders of magnitude. Based on these performance evaluations, we suggest that cross-campaign aerosol-INP closure could provide a pre-implementation test for selecting INP parameterizations in cloud and Earth system models.

490662.title: Understanding Initialization Impacts on Land–Atmosphere Coupling and E3SM S2S Prediction
490662.authors: Shixuan Zhang, PNNL, Richland, WA; and L. R. Leung, Z. Pu, J. Anderson, K. Raeder, D. Xu, and B. Raczka
490662.abstract: Accurate and mutually consistent land and atmospheric initial conditions are important for subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction because soil-moisture memory, surface energy and water exchanges, and land–atmosphere feedbacks can influence forecasts for weeks to months. Inconsistencies between initialized atmospheric and land states may cause rapid model adjustment, contribute to forecast drift, and alter the subsequent evolution of coupled processes. We investigate the impacts of two initialization strategies on land–atmosphere coupling and S2S forecast evolution in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM). The first constructs initial conditions by interpolating reanalysis fields onto the E3SM model grid, whereas the second uses ensemble data assimilation through the E3SM Atmosphere Model coupled with the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (EAM–DART). We perform paired E3SM hindcasts, initialized with the two approaches, for case studies representing contrasting seasons. By comparing early forecast adjustment, near-surface atmospheric and soil conditions, surface energy and water exchanges, and land–atmosphere coupling across subseasonal lead times, we assess how differences in initialization propagate through the coupled system. The comparison provides insight into the sensitivity of the land-atmosphere coupling and the evolution of the S2S forecast to the choice of the initialization method. By tracking how differences in coupled initial conditions influence subsequent land–atmosphere evolution, this work aims to provide a framework for diagnosing initialization-related drift and guiding the design of future E3SM S2S prediction experiments.

490663.title: Comparing Machine Learning and Physics-Based Ensemble Forecasts for Realistic DA Workflows: A Case Study With MPAS-JEDI and GraphCast
490663.authors: Simon Toedtli, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. A. Ahijevych, W. Wang, and C. Snyder
490663.abstract: A major challenge in numerical weather prediction is the high computational cost of ensemble forecasts with physics-based models. The latest generation of machine learning (ML) emulators, which can match or surpass the accuracy of physics-based models across a range of lead times at a fraction of the computational cost, offer a promising path to address this issue. Recent studies have shown that classical ensemble data assimilation (DA) systems with ML-based forecasts can cycle stably and produce analyses superior to climatology when conventional observations are assimilated at multiple vertical levels. Satellite radiances, however, have not yet been assimilated in such systems. This is a significant gap, since radiances play a key role in operational settings, and their nonlinear observation operator may be difficult to evaluate with a limited set of state variables and vertical levels. It thus remains unclear whether these ML-based systems can match the performance of physics-based systems under operationally relevant conditions. This study provides a rigorous comparison, in an operationally relevant configuration, between an ensemble DA system based on an ML forecast model and one based on a physics-based forecast model. The DA system consists of a two-way coupled deterministic variational component and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF). The variational component uses covariance information from the ensemble, and the analysis ensemble is recentered on the variational analysis at each cycle. Each component assimilates a substantial subset of the global observation network, including conventional observations, radio occultation bending angle profiles, and satellite microwave radiances. Our reference system is MPAS-JEDI, a state-of-the-art global DA framework, that couples the physics-based Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) with the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework. We compare a baseline configuration, in which MPAS advances both the deterministic forecast for the variational DA and the ensemble forecasts for the EnKF, against a configuration that replaces MPAS with GraphCast for ensemble propagation. We will discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the two systems from multiple perspectives, including (1) the deterministic forecast skill, (2) time-evolution of the ensemble spread and background error covariance, and (3) the role of recentering the analysis ensemble. Overall, our results indicate that the GraphCast-based system matches or surpasses the MPAS-based system in many aspects, making such systems promising alternatives for realistic operational applications.

490668.title: Downstream Impacts of George Kiladis: Learning When, Where, and Why Subseasonal Hindcasts Are Skillful
490668.authors: Kirsten J Mayer, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and K. Dagon, J. Berner, and A. Jaye
490668.abstract: As a Hollings Scholar in 2016, I selected an intriguing summer research project about a phenomenon known as the MJO, working with the NOAA scientist George Kiladis. Though this was the first time I uttered the words “Madden-Julian Oscillation”, the summer internship with George was instrumental in my development as a research scientist and the catalyst for my continued focus on the influence of tropical phenomena on the midlatitudes. From learning about Empirical Orthogonal Functions to hiking in the Rocky Mountains, this talk will demonstrate how a few months working with George ultimately influenced the trajectory of my career, culminating today in preliminary results on how machine learning techniques can be used to predict the presence of a subseasonal forecast of opportunity and explore their underlying sources of predictability within a subseasonal forecasting system. Specifically, we use random forests to predict where and when 2m temperature hindcasts outperform a climatological reference forecast in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 2 (E3SMv2) S2S hindcasts. Pairing these classifiers with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), we identify which input features the model relied on when it correctly predicted higher skill — a step toward anticipating S2S forecasts of opportunity and diagnosing their sources.

490670.title: subE3SMulator: a E3SM-based ML Emulator for S2S Research and Prediction
490670.authors: Kirsten J Mayer, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and K. Dagon, C. Becker, D. J. Gagne II, N. Rosenbloom, and J. Schreck
490670.abstract: Situated between initial-value and boundary-condition predictability regimes, subseasonal timescales incorporate information from the coupled Earth system. Consequently, exploring subseasonal predictability requires tools that represent multiple components of the Earth system. Here we present subE3SMulator, a new machine learning (ML) emulator specifically designed for subseasonal prediction that incorporates atmospheric, land, and ocean variables. This research-oriented ML emulator is trained on the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center Perlmutter System GPUs using coupled simulations from the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 2 (E3SMv2). These simulations span more than twice the length of the satellite era and encompass both historical and projected climate variability. The ML emulator is designed to autoregressively predict the Earth system state at 6 hourly intervals, employing a WXFormer hybrid vision transformer-UNet architecture. Through generated weekly initialized subseasonal hindcasts, we explore the emulator’s performance on 2m temperature and precipitation predictions as well as the emulator’s representation of key modes of variability (e.g. Madden-Julian Oscillation). Overall, this talk will highlight key features of, results from, and planned research using subE3SMulator.

490671.title: The Greening of the CSU GCM (Invited Presentation)
490671.authors: Inez Fung, Univ. of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA
490671.abstract: “The Greening of CSU GCM” (Randall et al. J Climate, 1996) and “Comparison of Radiative and Physiological Effects of Doubled CO2” (Sellers et al. Science 1996) are pioneering studies that have highlighted the importance of biophysics, especially stomatal conductance, in climate model studies. Like cloud dynamics, biophysics is also a multi-scale problem. Between plant functional types covering hundreds of kilometers and micron-sized stomates, do models with high spatial resolution need to consider higher resolution in species functioning, microclimate? This presentation recalls the start of Randall’s pioneering studies in biophysics and climate, and explores new avenues to pursue.

490676.title: NSF NCAR’s Earth System Science Faculty Community: Supporting Program Leaders and the Next Generation of Student Researchers
490676.authors: Meghan Schaberg, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. M. Cyccone, P. Asher, P. Ahlers, and R. Haacker
490676.abstract: Managing science training programs for students (which include internships, REU’s, and course-based undergraduate research experiences) requires a unique combination of mentoring, administrative, and pedagogical expertise. To support program leaders, the Earth System Science (ESS) faculty community at the US National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research provides a space where educators and program administrators can build connections, exchange resources, engage in creative problem-solving, and support one another. The community combines two complementary components: a series of regular virtual events and an interactive digital platform. During the community’s inaugural meeting, participants identified a strong need for structured peer support and opportunities for collective troubleshooting. In response, the community offers biweekly, advisor-facilitated drop-in sessions for informal peer consultation, along with monthly meetings featuring subject matter experts, professional development, and dedicated time for community building and networking. Both these offerings are supported and complemented by a digital platform that supports networking and provides access to a curated repository of programmatic resources. In this presentation, we will highlight the community’s ongoing and upcoming activities and describe opportunities for others to participate.

490678.title: Developing Stakeholder-Informed Tools for Flash Flood Decision-Making
490678.authors: Katie van Werkhoven, Research Triangle Institute, Boone, NC
490678.abstract: Flash flood decision-making is inherently challenging because forecasters and emergency managers must interpret uncertain, rapidly evolving information and translate it into timely action. Barriers that may limit the usefulness of forecast information can be difficult to recognize from a research perspective, particularly outside the high-stress environment in which operational decisions are made. Through direct engagement with NWS forecasters and emergency managers in Western North Carolina, Vermont, and Hawaiʻi, we identified how existing forecast information supports decision-making and where users see the greatest need for improvement. A consistent need that emerged was for more user-driven ways to explore potential hydrologic impacts—both to understand the range of possible outcomes when precipitation forecasts are uncertain and to build knowledge of local hydrologic response during blue-sky periods so potential impacts can be more readily anticipated during events. In response, the project developed a scenario-based tool that allows users to explore “what-if” storm scenarios and associated watershed responses. Stakeholder feedback on the initial prototype is now guiding its evolution toward representing an envelope of plausible storms and flood impacts. This effort illustrates how engaging users early in the research process can shift R2O efforts from adapting existing products to developing new capabilities in direct response to operational needs.

490679.title: Characterizing Wave Group Effects in Submesoscale Gradients of Observed Sea States
490679.authors: Ryan Shijie Du, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and G. Marechal, B. Villas Boas, M. C. Hell, and L. Lenain, PhD
490679.abstract: Observations of surface gravity waves from in situ and remote-sensing platforms now enable characterization of the spatial variability of surface waves across the submesoscale-to-mesoscale range (1–100 km). There is evidence that wave groups produce significant wave height (SWH) variability over scales much larger than an individual wave and may dominate current-induced variability in observed submesoscale SWH gradients. Spectral wave models predict ensemble-averaged wave spectra, whereas observations sample individual stochastic realizations of the wave field. To compare model output with observations and to validate spectral wave models, we need a quantitative understanding of wave-group characteristics and the associated uncertainty in observed sea state. More broadly, wave groups represent an important source of sea-state stochasticity at scales relevant to parameterizations of air–sea interaction. Here, we quantify SWH variability due to wave-group modulation in submesoscale-resolving observations of sea surface height. We propose a definition of the two-dimensional wave envelope and quantify the spatial scales and SWH variance of wave groups based on the spectral characteristics of the directional wave spectrum. We validate this simple model using a hierarchy of observations, including two-dimensional SWH data from SWOT; two-dimensional sea surface height observations from airborne lidar; and directional wave-buoy data. In particular, the model enables the observed SWOT SWH variance to be decomposed into contributions from current-induced variability, wave-group modulation, and measurement noise.

490684.title: My Evolving Views on Human-induced Global Warming
490684.authors: John M. Wallace, University of Washington, Seattle, WA
490684.abstract: I will recount how my personal views concerning the reality and imminence of human induced global warming have evolved over the 60 years since I was a graduate student.

490700.title: From Pilot Deployment to National Infrastructure: Using a High-Density 3D-Printed Weather Station Network to Develop Rainfall Thresholds for Impact-BasedFlash Flood Warning Operations
490700.authors: Andre Brathwaite, Barbados Meteorological Services, Charnocks, Christ Church, Barbados; and M. Steinson, K. Payne, B. M. Smith, R. Zieber, W. Nicewonger, and S. L. C. Best
490700.abstract: Scaling low-cost weather networks from experimental pilot deployments to hyper-local operational systems unlocks unprecedented precision for impact-based flash flood forecasting and warning services. Since 2019, the Barbados Meteorological Services (BMS), in collaboration with the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR), has deployed a national network of more than 85 3D-Printed Automatic Weather Stations (3D-PAWS), creating an average spatial resolution of 1.5 km between observing nodes, one of the highest-density operational surface observing networks in the Caribbean. The network provides one-minute observations of rainfall and other meteorological variables, significantly increasing the spatial and temporal resolution of surface observations available to forecasters. While previous work established the network's operational value, this study leverages its data to develop objective rainfall-rate thresholds for Apparatus, the BMS’s locally developed software used to disseminate impact-based flash flood warnings. By cross-referencing one-minute 3D-PAWS rainfall observations with Doppler radar estimates, historical flood data events, and documented community impacts to identify rainfall-rate thresholds associated with increasing levels of flood severity, this study establishes objective rainfall thresholds within the BMS impact-based forecast matrix. Integrating these high-frequency observations into operational workflows accelerates warning escalations and standardizes decision-making during rapid-onset events. The results demonstrate that a dense, low-cost observing network can transcend supplementary roles to drive primary flash flood decision support, hazard monitoring, and impact-based forecasting. The resulting methodology offers a scalable, affordable early-warning framework for Small Island Developing States (SIDS) seeking to strengthen early warning capabilities through affordable, high-density meteorological observing networks.

490702.title: An Object-Based Climatology of the North Atlantic Subtropical High
490702.authors: Sarah E. Strazzo, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; and Y. Zhou
490702.abstract: The North Atlantic Subtropical High (NASH) is a prominent semi-permanent feature of the low-level atmospheric circulation that influences the summertime climate of the eastern United States through its role in modulating tropical cyclone tracks, precipitation patterns, and extreme heat. While prior research efforts have examined variability and trends in the NASH, most studies focus on a single feature, such as the position of the western ridge axis, the maximum central sea level pressure, or the Bermuda High Index. In contrast, here we introduce an object-based climatology of the NASH to (1) facilitate a more complete description of the climatological spatial features of the low-level NASH, (2) quantify the relationship between these spatial features and the climate of surrounding continental regions, and (3) explore patterns of intraseasonal and interannual variability in the NASH. We define NASH polygons (“objects”) from 850-hPa geopotential height fields in the fifth generation ECMWF reanalysis (ERA5). We specifically generate monthly and seasonal 850-hPa NASH objects using the 1560-m closed contour over the North Atlantic region. Monthly and seasonal NASH objects are generated from ERA5 850-hPa geopotential height fields for June through September during the period 1981 – 2025. Next, we employ a geographic information system to calculate spatial characteristics of the NASH objects, including the latitude and longitude bounds, major axis orientation, length-to-width ratio, area, and compactness. Climatological values of NASH spatial characteristics match expectations, with greater variance in the western (northern) boundary relative to the eastern (southern) boundary, largest spatial extent in July, and a northward shift in the minimum latitude in August and September. In general, temporal trends in the spatial metrics are not significant during the 45-year study period, with the exception of positive trends in minimum latitude during September and area during June. Additionally, apart from minimum latitude, the spatial characteristics of the NASH do not exhibit strong autocorrelation during boreal summer. Future work will apply the object-based methodology to explore predictability of the NASH in dynamical models on subseasonal-to-seasonal timescales.

490704.title: Weather or Not? A Compilation of Case Studies Involving "Go-No Go" Decisions of Commercial and Student Pilots.
490704.authors: Richard B. DiMaio, Lewis University, Romeoville, IL
490704.abstract: As an instructor of Aviation Meteorology at both a 4 year university and 2 year college, I get to experience a wide range of weather events that qualify as "go or no go". These can involve extreme cross wind, thunderstorms in the terminal area or holding area, severe turbulence or icing. It is important that students expand their weather knowledge from experiential learning. Observing flight cancellations, diversions, aborted take-offs and landings is part of a safe national air space. This oral presentation will showcase several events that can resonate with students and instructors in a manner that expands our understanding of the atmosphere and how important making the right call can be!

490705.title: Evolution of a Northeastern Pacific Tropopause Polar Vortex and Associated Downstream Forcing during the 24 January 2026 Oklahoma Winter Storm
490705.authors: Charles Durbin, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and S. Cavallo
490705.abstract: From 23 to 25 January 2026, a high-impact winter storm produced heavy snowfall, sleet, and dangerous cold conditions across the southern Great Plains (SGP). The storm developed within a strongly baroclinic environment ahead of an amplifying midlevel trough with a strong subtropical moisture source. Previous studies have shown that tropopause polar vortices (TPVs) are often associated with extreme cold air outbreaks (CAOs); however, it is less common for such CAOs to occur in conjunction with widespread precipitation. This study investigates how the evolution of a TPV and associated jet streak, as well as frontogenetic forcings, produced synoptic-and meso-scale forcings culminating in this high-impact event. European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis Version 5 (ERA5) data are employed in this study to analyze basic atmospheric conditions and to compute synoptic-and meso-scale forcings for this event. NOAA HYSPLIT backward trajectories are used to trace the airmass origin and characteristics. It is shown that a TPV interacting with both the subtropical and polar jet streams as it approached the SGP was an important feature that led to the generation of a jet streak resulting in broad synoptic-scale ascent over the region of interest due to low-level thermal advection. The presence of a high-amplitude trough with an additional TPV embedded north of the region was also important in providing ample conditions for an extreme cold air outbreak to occur in the SGP. As the trough moved eastward and southward and intersected the Gulf Coast, strong 850-hPa frontogenesis developed over a rich source of subtropical moisture to produce localized regions of heavy winter precipitation. These results establish a coherent temporal and spatial association between TPVs, its interactions with jet streams, and frontogenesis to result in an unusual and impactful winter weather event. Future studies will be needed to further isolate the exact role of each component.

490706.title: Facility-Level H2 Emissions from Refineries and Chemical Plants
490706.authors: Yuanfeng Cui, Cornell Univ., Ithaca, NY; and I. Rettig, C. Daube, N. Lariviere, C. A. Woolley Maisch, J. R. Roscioli, S. Herndon, E. M. Lunny, J. Albertson, A. Marchese, T. Röckmann, H. Wang, A. Hensen, and I. Velzeboer
490706.abstract: Hydrogen (H$_2$) is expected to play a central role in decarbonizing industrial systems due to reliance on H$_2$ as an essential feedstock chemical in refining and chemical manufacturing processes, as well as its potential use as an energy carrier in hard-to-abate sectors. However, the indirect atmospheric effects of H$_2$ emissions may offset some of the climate benefits driven by H$_2$ use. Better understanding of H$_2$ emissions is therefore important to analyze climate benefits of H$_2$ in decarbonization of industrial sectors. Current knowledge of the magnitude, variability, and drivers of H$_2$ emissions from refineries and chemical plants remains limited. Here, we combined mobile measurements with inverse modeling at 29 industrial facilities across North America and Europe to quantify H$_2$ facility-level emission rates (FLERs) from industrial infrastructure, including refineries, petrochemical, ammonia, methanol, and chlor-alkali plants. The results show that FLERs span four orders of magnitude, ranging from 0.05 to 560 kg h$^{-1}$ with strongly positive-skewed distributions. The uncertainties associated with the FLERs are of the same order of magnitude as the FLER estimates themselves. The FLERs normalized by production capacity (nFLERs) span five orders of magnitude, ranging from 0.0003 \% to 76\%. Clustering analysis of FLERs and nFLERs reveals two distinct regimes. 24 facilities consisting of refineries, ammonia, methanol, and petrochemical plants fall into the low-emission clusters (0.0003 - 0.52 \%) with averaged nFLERs consistent with the lower end of literature estimates. Five facilities consisting of refineries, ammonia, and chlor-alkali plants fall into the higher-emission regime: two refineries (3.8 - 3.3 \%), two chlor-alkali plants (43 - 76 \%), and one ammonia plant (1.6 \%). While temporal frequency of the documented high emissions remains unresolved, factors including facility type, design, and operation are considered in discussing potential contributors to high emissions. This work provides the largest empirical dataset of H$_2$ emissions for refineries and chemical plants and highlights the need for expanding future measurements for understanding temporal variability of H$_2$ emissions as well as developing better understanding around potential industrial emissions sources.

490709.title: JCSDA Support for Commercial Data
490709.authors: Benjamin C. Ruston, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and F. Vandenberghe, B. T. Johnson, C. Dang, H. Zhang, I. Banos, L. J. Hayden, and C. Sampson
490709.abstract: The Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA) is a partnership between agencies (NOAA, NASA, U.S. Air Force and Navy, NCAR, and the UK Met Office). The JCSDA leads the management of the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) project, that is used for improving and accelerating the quantitative use of research and operational satellite data in weather, ocean, environmental analysis and prediction systems. In addition, the JCSDA lead the management of the public and community driven Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM). The JEDI system provides the architecture to assimilate and evaluate new observational assets. In support of the NOAA NESDIS Commercial Data Program (CDP), JCSDA has created an end-to-end pathway to facilitate the necessary development in the JEDI components and to evaluate the impact of assimilated observations. The JCSDA has acquired NOAA CDP data and ingested, processed and evaluated both GNSS-reflectometry (GNSS-R) ocean surface wind products and Microwave sounder calibrated radiances verifying configurations within JEDI that are exchangeable between partner JEDI-enabled systems. JEDI has provided a common system, convention, and language used by vendors, evaluators, and operational centers to significantly reduce timelines and speed up the adoption of new data resources. At the JCSDA we have performed end-to-end evaluation of NOAA CDP procured observations and performed traditional forecast model scoring, as well as diagnosed the impact on the other observing systems. We have extensively used the NSF/NCAR MPAS model within JEDI and initialized with both NOAA GFS and ERA-5 initial conditions. Coordination with other NOAA CDP teams, such as Office of Modeling and Development (OMD), and the NCAR Mesoscale and Microscale Meteorology (MMM) is used to cover a wide range of scenarios such as different data denials, differing bias predictors, and assimilation settings such as observation error models or quality filtering. We will show the impact of GNSS-R and Microwave sounder observations on our systems, and some of the configuration settings and some of the general developments that have improved the JEDI capabilities for these data.

490715.title: Impact of Satellite-Derived Anthropogenic Heat on Urban Precipitation Simulated by WRF
490715.authors: Huanhuan Wang, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and Y. Cui and J. Albertson
490715.abstract: Urban anthropogenic heat (AH) plays an important role in modifying the urban energy balance, boundary layer evolution, and precipitation, yet most Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulations prescribe AH using simplified diurnal cycles. In this study, a satellite derived hourly AH dataset is developed using a Kalman Filter Surface Energy Balance (KF-SEB) framework and incorporated into the single layer Urban Canopy Model within WRF. Simulations are conducted for a summertime precipitation event over the Atlanta metropolitan area and evaluated against observations of air temperature, wind speed, and IMERG precipitation. The results show that realistic spatially and temporally varying AH alters urban surface heating, boundary layer development, and precipitation patterns, leading to improved agreement with observations compared with the default AH parameterization. This study demonstrates the value of integrating satellite-derived AH into WRF for improving urban weather and precipitation simulations and provides a practical framework for future urban forecasting applications.

490722.title: JCSDA Skylab: End-to-End Observation Workflows in JEDI
490722.authors: Benjamin C. Ruston, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and F. Vandenberghe, B. T. Johnson, L. J. Hayden, C. Dang, C. Sampson, and H. Zhang
490722.abstract: The Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA) is a partnership between agencies (NOAA, NASA, U.S. Air Force and Navy, NCAR and the UK Met Office). The two primary projects within the JCSDA are the Joint effort for data assimilation integration (JEDI), and the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM). The JEDI project has developed an abstracted data assimilation system that has been interfaced to various prediction systems and been applied to regimes such as the atmosphere, land, marine, composition and space weather applications. This flexible abstraction connects diverse observations with an ever-expanding list of numerical models, both traditional and AI-driven. Similarly, JEDI provides a consistent framework to apply diverse forward operators—such as CRTM and AI-trained RTMs—across multiple environmental domains. As JEDI and the observing system evolve, the JCSDA leverages the Skylab workflow across laptops, traditional HPCs, and cloud environments to build, verify, and evaluate observation impacts. Close collaboration with agency partners directly guides and informs the JCSDA's research-to-operations (R2O) efforts. We present JEDI capabilities that enable straightforward control of operator settings, error modeling, and dynamic observation filtering through simple configurations. Using the JCSDA Skylab framework centered on the MPAS model, we demonstrate retrospective and near-real-time atmospheric data assimilation, initialized and verified with NOAA GFS or ERA5. Recent examples include extending capabilities in JEDI for visible reflectances and reconstructed radiances in the hyperspectral infrared. JCSDA Skylab provides end-to-end evaluation of observation capabilities within a fully cycling framework. Shared YAML configurations foster broad partner collaboration across research, vendor, and operational communities by establishing a common platform within the JEDI architecture. Ultimately, Skylab’s portability and simplicity lower the barrier to entry, enabling users to readily engage with the system.

490723.title: GOES ABI Imagery Quality and Detector Performance Characterization
490723.authors: Fangfang Yu, Entarian, Greenbelt, MD; and X. Wu, Dr., H. Qian, D. Goldberg, B. Basnet, and H. Xu
490723.abstract: GOES Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) provides high-quality imagery for accurate weather forecasting and environmental monitoring throughout its mission. Detector performance changes can introduce image artifacts that degrade Level 1b (L1b) imagery and, if left unmitigated, may affect the interpretation of subtle geophysical features and propagate into downstream environmental products. Sustaining this high level of performance therefore requires comprehensive characterization of detector behavior, continuous performance monitoring, and close collaboration between calibration and operational teams to enable timely identify detector performance changes and appropriate mitigation. This study summarizes detector performance monitoring results and presents the operational framework developed for GOES ABI instruments. Detector performance for each spectral channel was examined at various temporal scales across the focal plane modules. While the vast majority of ABI detectors remain stable throughout the mission, a very small fraction experience performance changes that may result in image artifacts such as horizontal striping. The abnormal ABI detectors can be classified into four categories: shifted-response, unstable, noisy, and failed detectors, each exhibiting distinct characteristics and requiring different operational mitigation strategies. Vertical artifacts such as the barcode artifact observed in GOES-18 Band 7 imagery are also continuously monitored and characterized with long-term detector calibration data and ancillary data. To sustain the high-quality of GOES ABI L1b imagery, a science-based operational framework has been established through close collaboration between calibration and operational teams. The framework integrates automated detector performance monitoring and alert generation, scientific anomaly assessment, root cause investigation, quantitative performance evaluation, mitigation recommendation, operational implementation, and user feedback.

490728.title: Pre-Operational Evaluation of JPSS-4 Ready Science Algorithms Using Proxy Datasets
490728.authors: Murty G. Divakarla, STC@STAR, Riverdale Park, MD; Science and Technology Corporation, Columbia, MD; and I. Guch, S. Blonski, X. Shao, T. Beck, N. Sun, P. Beierle, K. Zhang, M. Hunter, E. Chomko, S. Iacovazzi, L. Zhou, and J. A. Weinrich
490728.abstract: In preparation for the JPSS-4 (J4) launch, the JPSS Program at the Center for Satellite Applications and Research (JSTAR) has developed infrastructure to route J4 science algorithms into operations. The J4 satellite will host a suite of sophisticated instruments—including the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), the Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS), the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS), and the Ozone Mapping and Profiler Suite (OMPS) to maintain continuity in environmental monitoring. Building on the foundation of the current S-NPP and NOAA-20/21 series, J4 sensors have upgrades that necessitate rigorous pre-operational evaluation of its science algorithms. This paper details the development of J4 proxy datasets designed to facilitate this evaluation, ensuring robust verification of algorithm readiness prior to launch. To support end-to-end processing and sensor characterization, JSTAR science teams have utilized data from the JPSS Joint Compatibility Tests (JCT-2) and are incorporating upcoming JCT-3B/3-A ambient and TVAC measurements. While these tests provide critical pre-launch characterization of Sensor Data Records (SDRs), they lack the comprehensive earth-view scenes necessary to fully verify J4-Ready Environmental Data Records (EDRs). Consequently, the JSTAR team identified a need for J4 proxy SDRs that incorporate realistic earth-view data. The objective is to generate proxy data for ATMS, CrIS, OMPS, and VIIRS, utilizing matched granules from the same day and orbits. The methodology involves using NOAA-21 RDRs and SDRs as a baseline, applying necessary modifications to headers, filenames, and Look-Up Tables to simulate J4 data, while addressing specific instrument changes, such as the OMPS spectral range extension and VIIRS scan rate adjustments. This paper summarizes a collaborative effort between the JSTAR science teams, the ground project team, and the Test Data Working Group (TDWG) to formalize these J4 proxy datasets. By leveraging NOAA-21 on-orbit observations from May 1, 2026, the proxy suite generated for all four instruments complements JCT measurements with real earth-view scenes (e.g., featuring realistic cloud and aerosol distributions). This creates a robust test bed for the EDR product teams, the Integrated Calibration and Validation System (ICVS), and the Algorithm Science Software Integration and System Transition Team (ASSISTT) for end-to-end testing. Through close coordination with SDR and EDR teams, this evaluation framework verifies J4-Ready algorithms; the presentation will highlight key validation outcomes, lessons learned, and the broader utility of proxy datasets for future pre-launch readiness.

490733.title: Toward Operational Groundwater Pumping Estimation with OpenET: Validation and Intercomparison across the Southwestern United States
490733.authors: Sayantan "Monty" Majumdar, DRI, Reno, NV; and P. ReVelle, B. A. Minor, D. Ketchum, T. Ott, M. Bromley, J. L. Atkin, C. Pearson, and J. L. Huntington
490733.abstract: Accurate groundwater pumping estimates are essential for sustainable water management, groundwater modeling, and water budget development, yet flowmeter records are sparse or unavailable for many irrigation systems, and existing meters are often faulty or poorly calibrated. Approaches that leverage satellite-derived, field-scale actual evapotranspiration (ETa) products, such as OpenET, offer a scalable alternative, but transitioning these research-grade products into sustained operational and regulatory use requires rigorous validation, intercomparison, and a transparent, reproducible workflow. Here, we develop and evaluate an OpenET-based framework for estimating groundwater pumping across Nevada, Arizona, and New Mexico, integrating the ensemble mean ETa product, field boundaries, irrigation status (IrrMapper, LANID), water-source type, water right place of use (POU), hydroclimate data, and in situ meter records. Irrigation consumptive use or Net ET is estimated as Net ET = ETa − ETgw − Peff, where ETgw is the portion of ETa sourced from shallow water tables (≤ ~15 ft) via crop root-zone uptake, and Peff is the effective precipitation (portion of ETa sourced from precipitation). ETgw is modeled using water table depth data, soil texture, and crop-specific extinction depths, and Peff is estimated using a simplified soil-water balance model (OTTER: Open Tool for Tracking Effective pRecipitation). Field-scale groundwater pumping is then estimated as Net ET divided by the irrigation efficiency. We validate the groundwater pumping estimates against state agency-reported pumpage and in situ meter records using bootstrapped regressions and five-fold cross-validation. Results show near-unity regression slopes that explain ~50–80% of the variance in groundwater pumping depths and ~90% in pumping volumes, with computed irrigation efficiencies (80–90%) consistent with known irrigation systems. Basin-scale intercomparisons indicate that remaining discrepancies are driven primarily by irrigated-area detection thresholds, the partitioning of groundwater and surface water supplies on mixed water right fields, and assumed irrigation efficiencies. This work provides a transparent, scalable framework for operational groundwater accounting across the southwestern U.S. and demonstrates a practical research-to-operations pathway for field-scale ET applications. A key lesson for this transition is that OpenET ETa alone is insufficient. Accurate groundwater pumping estimation requires ancillary datasets (field boundaries, irrigation status, water-source attribution, POU information, per-field irrigation efficiency) combined with estimates of effective precipitation and shallow groundwater contributions, all integrated within a single, reproducible workflow.

490734.title: Comparing Atmospheric Soundings in Forecast Models to Observations near Complex Terrain During SNOWSCAPE Campaign
490734.authors: Hailee Davis, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD; REALM REU, Salt Lake City, UT; and A. Stansfield
490734.abstract: Utah’s northern Wasatch Mountains provide a unique mountainous climate to study due to their steep topography, frequent winter storms, and proximity to the Great Salt Lake. The Seeded and Natural Orographic Winter Storms and Catchment Processes Evaluation (SNOWSCAPE) field campaign took place from January through March 2026 with the goal of improving understanding of winter storm processes and evaluating the efficiency of cloud seeding using ground generators. An assessment of how the model forecasts compared to the observed conditions throughout the campaign can highlight common model biases and lead to model improvements in complex terrain. This study focuses on identifying what biases the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and Global Forecast System (GFS) models have in the northern Wasatch Range, specifically focusing on atmospheric vertical profiles. Observations are from weather balloon data collected approximately every 3 hours during SNOWSCAPE Intensive Observing Periods (IOPs) at a site in Syracuse, Utah. Temperature, dewpoint temperature, and wind profiles were compared between the observations and vertical profiles from the closest HRRR and GFS points. Results indicate that neither the HRRR nor GFS models outperformed each other for any variable, and that temperature errors were smaller than dewpoint temperature errors. These findings show that while the HRRR has a higher resolution, it does not have a significant difference in its forecasting capabilities for vertical profiles when compared to the GFS.

490740.title: Multi-Year Analysis of Electrified Storm Cells near ARM-BNF in North Alabama
490740.authors: Bee Mia Lamsma, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and B. A. Raut, S. Gupta, and E. C. Bruning
490740.abstract: Multi-year analyses of thunderstorms and lightning flashes have been performed separately to identify characteristics and effects of these specific phenomena, however few studies have performed a combined Lagrangian analysis to understand the unique interactions present between cloud micro-physics, convective evolution, and lightning characteristics. Multi-day studies have been conducted for severe events across the world, but the ability to analyze long-term data can provide a more generalizable idea of how storms and lightning co-vary within a specific region. This study tracked radar-observed storm cells between 2019 and 2026 near the US Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility in Bankhead National Forest for a more thorough understanding of the relationship between storm characteristics such as volume, differential reflectivity (ZDR), and reflectivity alongside lightning density and area. This project used Adapt, an orchestrated storm tracking and quantification framework, alongside xlma-python, a program for analyzing Lightning Mapping Array data. Analysis of 153 events identified over 65000 storm tracks with 1.2 million lightning flashes, including a unique case displaying little lightning when reflectivity and ZDR would typically indicate otherwise. Patterns in the data were observed relating increases in lightning area and flash rate (with ZDR between 0-2 dB) to maximum reflectivity values around 40 dBz and 50 dBz, respectively. When averaging across all tracks, lightning activity increased rapidly within the first 3 radar scans following storm identification before remaining constant until the end of the cell life cycle, even when average vertical reflectivity regions did not indicate strengthening. The results of this study agree with other studies regarding the relationships between ZDR, reflectivity, lightning flash area, and flash rates, while proving that this kind of analysis is possible with large datasets and would be valuable to apply to other regions. Further developing Adapt into a thorough analysis tool allowing for association of measurements by different instruments with storm cells will continue to make larger analysis worthwhile in identifying the unique interactions present between storm characteristics, lightning, and any other measurable variable.

490746.title: Withdrawn: Aerosol-Cloud Interactions Enhance Pyrocumulonimbus Smoke Injection into the Upper Troposphere
490746.authors: Yangfan Liu, Stanford University, Stanford, CA; and Y. Wang, Y. zhang, Q. Tang, J. Li, S. Tolstoff, D. A. Peterson, and J. Fan
490746.abstract: Pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) can efficiently inject wildfire emissions into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere, where smoke can persist longer, spread farther, and potentially exert substantial climate impacts. Yet whether biomass-burning aerosols (BBA) appreciably modify pyroCb smoke injection through aerosol–cloud interactions (ACI) remains uncertain. We investigate the 2020 Creek Fire pyroCb using coupled fire–atmosphere–aerosol simulations that vary BBA emissions while keeping fire-emitted carbon monoxide (CO) emissions identical as a smoke tracer. We implement more physically based treatments of aerosol activation, ice nucleation, supersaturation prediction, and other key cloud microphysical processes. The modified model reasonably reproduces key observed characteristics of pyroCb evolution and structure, including pyroCb onset timing, maximum cloud-top height, and cloud-top temperature patterns during peak pyroCb intensity. Simulated aerosol and hydrometeor number concentrations and size distributions are also broadly consistent with available wildfire and pyroCb observations. Relative to a tenfold-reduced aerosol-emission scenario, the default-emission case produces 28.6% more fire-emitted CO above 10 km by the end of the pyroCb period, with progressively larger relative enhancements at higher altitudes where transport is dominated by intermittent strong convective pulses. The original model configuration produces substantially weaker aerosol sensitivity. In the modified configuration, higher CCN concentrations enhance condensational growth and latent heating, increasing buoyancy and strengthening the most intense portions of updraft cores. The associated enhancement of ascent and outflow expands both the updraft cores and the pyroCb convective region horizontally. Meanwhile, aerosol-induced shifts toward greater frozen hydrometeor mass and lower liquid hydrometeor mass reduce latent cooling between cloud base and ~11 km in downdraft cores adjacent to the updraft cores, weakening downward CO transport. These microphysical, dynamical, and transport responses remain qualitatively robust across sensitivity experiments varying the timing of fire thermal forcing. A tenfold reduction in the ice-nucleating activity of BBA produces little change in the CO enhancement, indicating that CCN-related processes dominate over INP-related processes for the perturbations examined. Our results demonstrate that aerosol–cloud interactions can appreciably influence pyroCb dynamics, smoke injection, and potentially climate impacts. Improved observations of wildfire aerosols and pyroCb cloud microphysics, together with model representations that retain key aerosol–cloud interaction processes, are needed to better quantify pyroCb smoke injection and its climate implications in a warming climate increasingly conducive to pyroCb formation and intensification.

490748.title: DeepAQM: A FNO-Based Deep Learning Extension of Air Quality Forecasting Models
490748.authors: Wei-Ting Hung, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA; and J. Xing, Y. Tang, B. D. Baker II, and P. C. Campbell
490748.abstract: Air quality forecasting (AQF) is important for foreseeing and protecting the public from potential hazardous air pollutants from nature and/or anthropogenic sources such as wildfires and industries. To accurately predict air quality, AQF models simulate various atmospheric physical and chemical processes, including but not limited to the transport and dispersion of air pollutants as well as the chemical reactions among air compositions. Explicit simulations often require substantial time and computational resources, which limit the capabilities of AQF models for near-real-time applications. Hence a deep learning AQF model, DeepAQM, is developed to emulate the atmospheric physical and chemical processes described in operational air quality models. Under the DeepAQM framework, we tested the novel Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) algorithm as the alternative to the existing ConvLSTM. FNO resolves parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) retrieved from input fields and shows strengths in simulating the spatial variability of atmospheric compositions across scales. FNO structure also enables cross-scale predictions without training multiple deep learning models. Current DeepAQM is developed to emulate the behaviors in the NOAA Unified Forecast System Air Quality Model (UFS-AQM), providing hourly surface PM2.5 and ozone (O3) predictions up to 72 h. DeepAQM uses the similar inputs as UFS-AQM, including its meteorological fields, geographic features, emissions, and initial and boundary conditions. Preliminary results show that DeepAQM can successfully reproduce UFS-AQM’s O3 predictions but show reduced skills for PM2.5 that are affected by various emission sources and complex chemical transformation. The high computational efficiency of DeepAQM enables large ensemble forecasts by serving as ensemble members in the existing operational AQF framework. Coupling with other techniques, such as data fusion and emission inversions, an advanced deep learning tool can be made to further improve the accuracy of air quality prediction.

490753.title: A Climatology of Supercells in the United States Using Dynamically Downscaled Simulation Output
490753.authors: Kelvin T. Hawthorne Jr., Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL; and W. S. Ashley, V. A. Gensini, and A. Haberlie
490753.abstract: Supercells produce a majority of the significant tornadoes and hail in the United States and account for a disproportionate share of severe convective storm losses. Existing supercell climatologies and future projections are generally based on 10–15-year periods, limiting the ability to distinguish long-term trends from interannual and interdecadal variability. This study develops a supercell census spanning more than four decades using the CONUS404 dataset. Simulated supercells are identified using 2–5-km AGL updraft helicity and tracked hourly across the eastern contiguous United States, producing a catalog sufficient to resolve variability across annual to multidecadal timescales. The historical climatology reproduces established spatial patterns in U.S. supercell occurrence while revealing notable regional differences in storm frequency, intensity, size, and longevity. Supercell occurrence increases by a net 19.4% between 1980-2024, although substantial interannual and interdecadal variability complicates the long-term signal. The Great Plains exhibit the historical maximum in simulated supercell activity, with a mean annual occurrence of approximately 314.3 supercells. Seasonally, the Southern Plains and Southeast exhibit peaks in simulated supercell activity during MAM, while the Midwest and Northern Plains peak during JJA. Diurnal variability is also evident, with supercell initiation peaking between 23Z and 02Z across most regions. The Northeast is the primary exception, with initiation peaking near 21Z.

490759.title: When Does a Wildfire Change the Wind That Drives It? - Evidence from Coupled ERF-LSFIRE Simulations of the Palisades and Cram Fires
490759.authors: Ye Liu, PNNL, Richland, WA; and H. Huang, T. Saltiel, S. Feng, A. M. Coleman, and A. Almgren
490759.abstract: Accurate wildfire risk assessment requires models that can represent not only how weather drives fire spread, but also when fire-generated heat and moisture begin to modify the local atmosphere and influence subsequent fire behavior. These interactions are especially important in complex terrain and rapidly evolving wind conditions, where localized feedbacks may alter the direction, rate, and extent of fire growth, and they can be particularly consequential under weaker or more variable winds, where fire-atmosphere feedbacks—rather than the ambient flow alone—can govern spread. Capturing these processes with sufficient precision has historically been computationally prohibitive, motivating modeling frameworks that leverage modern performance-portable libraries such as AMReX to deliver high-resolution coupled fire-atmosphere simulations at substantially reduced computational cost. We present ERF–LSFIRE v1.0, a coupled fire–atmosphere modeling framework that links a C++/AMReX level-set surface-fire spread model, LSFIRE, with the Energy Research and Forecasting model, ERF.
