LSFIRE can operate as a standalone model with prescribed winds or in one-way and two-way coupled configurations with ERF. In the two-way configuration, fire-generated sensible heat and moisture are returned to the atmosphere, allowing the model to represent feedbacks between fire behavior, atmospheric stability, and near-surface winds. We first verify the level-set implementation using analytical fire-spread tests over flat and uniformly sloping terrain. LSFIRE closely reproduces the analytical Rothermel–Richards elliptical spread solutions. We then apply the coupled framework to simulations of the Palisades and Cram fires to examine when fire–atmosphere feedbacks become important for localized hazard evolution. In the strongly wind-driven Palisades case, two-way coupling generates localized atmospheric perturbations but produces only modest changes in perimeter-scale fire spread. In contrast, the Cram case is characterized by weaker and more variable background winds. Under these conditions, fire feedback produces larger near-fire wind and stability perturbations and substantially alters burned-area evolution relative to the one-way coupled simulation. The comparison indicates that the importance of two-way coupling depends strongly on the balance between ambient wind forcing and fire-generated atmospheric perturbations. These results demonstrate how coupled fire–atmosphere modeling can improve understanding of localized wildfire risk by identifying the meteorological conditions under which fire feedbacks materially affect spread. ERF–LSFIRE provides a flexible, high-resolution framework for testing fire-spread formulations, examining fire–weather interactions, and evaluating the added value of two-way coupling for wildfire prediction. With further development, the framework could support operational risk assessment by helping emergency managers and utility stakeholders determine when simplified wind-driven spread models are sufficient and when fully coupled simulations are needed for more reliable decision support.

490760.title: Air Quality Monitoring Over North America with TEMPO: Mission Status and Highlights
490760.authors: Xiong Liu, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, Cambridge, MA; and G. Gonzalez Abad, C. R. Nowlan, K. Chance, R. M. Suleiman, J. Houck, J. E. Davis, H. Wang, H. Chong, W. Hou, J. Park, J. Fitzmaurice, A. Oppenheimer, M. Ghahremanloo, Z. Ayazpour, M. Tao, Q. Zhu, K. J. Daugherty, D. E. Flittner, L. M. Judd, E. L. Judd, J. Carr, J. Szykman, B. Henderson, L. C. Valin, N. A. Krotkov, O. Torres, C. Li, J. Joiner, S. Janz, T. F. Hanisco, K. E. Knowland, V. Shah, M. J. Newchurch, A. R. Naeger, R. Cohen, D. Edwards, J. Fishman, J. R. Herman, D. J. Jacob, R. B. Pierce, R. J. Spurr, and J. Wang
490760.abstract: We present a status overview of the TEMPO mission including its operation, baseline, Near-Real-Time (NRT), enhanced and research data products, upcoming algorithm improvements, and validation studies. We also highlight a wide variety of innovative science advancements and applications. TEMPO is the North America component of the geostationary (GEO) air quality constellation along with GEMS over Asia and Sentinel-4 over Europe. It is the first spaceborne instrument providing hourly daytime air pollution over North America at neighborhood scale (~10 km2 at boresight). It uses UV/visible spectroscopy to measure key elements of tropospheric air pollution chemistry including O3, NO2, HCHO and aerosols, and capture the inherent high variability in the diurnal cycle of emissions and chemistry. At night, TEMPO can observe city lights, gas flaring, maritime lights, clouds and snow in the moonlight, lightning, aurorae, and nightglow without interfering with its primary daytime air quality mission. After the successful launch of TEMPO on board IS-40E into the GEO orbit at 91°W in April 2023, it conducted its first light observations in early Aug. 2023 and started its nominal operation in Oct. 2023, kicking off a new era of air quality monitoring from space over North America. It finished its 20-month of baseline Phase E in June 2025. The baseline mission has been extended to Sep. 2026, with further extension via a NASA senior review conducted in April 2026. Baseline V3 data products were released to the public in May 2024 from NASA’s ASDC. A significantly improved V4 data products were released to the public in early Sep. 2025, including the first public release of the ozone profile product. TEMPO NRT data products with data latency of 2-3 hours and other science quality data products were funded by NASA Satellite Needs Working Group (SNWG) to assist in air quality forecasting and modeling efforts and develop better pollution control strategies. NRT products (V2, based on baseline V4) were also released to the public for the first time in early Sep. 2025. Many other research data products have been produced by the science community and TEMPO data products have been widely used by the user community including about 650 early adopters.

490762.title: Problem-Driven Ensemble Compression for Weather-Informed Energy Planning
490762.authors: Rounak Meyur, PNNL, Richland, WA; and N. Isenberg, S. Feng, and L. K. Berg
490762.abstract: Operational weather ensemble systems generate many scenarios during each forecast cycle, providing rich probabilistic information about weather-related uncertainty and the impact on energy systems. However, models across the energy-planning workflow—from day-ahead scheduling and capacity expansion to resource adequacy planning—are often computationally limited to using only a small subset of available ensemble members. Conventional distribution-based methods, such as Wasserstein clustering, preserve statistical similarity, but statistical fidelity does not necessarily ensure decision relevance. Methods optimized for average representativeness may underweight tail scenarios and therefore discard the forecast information most consequential for planning decisions. This project develops an accelerated, problem-driven scenario-compression framework and demonstrates its application to stochastic unit commitment under wind-power uncertainty. Problem-driven compression measures scenario importance based on its effects on downstream optimization decisions and objective values. Existing approaches, however, require construction of a problem-space matrix whose entries quantify the cost of applying the optimal decision from one scenario to another. This process scales quadratically with ensemble size and requires numerous auxiliary optimization solves. To reduce this computational burden, we combine low-rank matrix approximation with sparse assignment formulations. We evaluate the framework against full-ensemble stochastic unit commitment, random sampling, distribution-based reduction using Wasserstein clustering, and existing problem-driven scenario-reduction methods. Performance is assessed using objective-value degradation, wall-clock time, number of solver calls, matrix-construction time, and the incremental cost of updating the compressed ensemble when scenarios are added or removed. The proposed approach is designed to retain decision-relevant uncertainty, including high-impact tail scenarios, while reducing the computational cost of weather-informed energy planning.

490765.title: The Impact of Model Resolution and Physics on Fixing the Central U.S. Dry Bias
490765.authors: Jaelyn Longino, GFDL, Owens Crossroads, AL; and V. T. Narinesingh, M. Zhao, and H. Guo
490765.abstract: Precipitation is notoriously difficult to accurately represent in Global Climate Models (GCMs). In particular, summertime precipitation over the central United States, much of which is associated with severe convective storms, has long been underestimated. To better understand and address the central United States dry bias, we examine the impact of atmospheric model resolution and cloud microphysics using various configurations of NOAA Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory’s (GFDL) AM4 model forced by observed sea surface temperatures. Preliminary results show that increasing atmospheric resolution from 100 to 50 to 25 km monotonically reduces mean precipitation biases over the central United States. However, introducing a two-moment cloud microphysics scheme did not necessarily yield better results, though further tuning experiments are required. Furthermore, we examine how probability density functions of precipitation intensity and the diurnal cycle over the central United States respond to increased resolution. We find that these metrics also improve, primarily due to more accurate representation of mesoscale convective systems which contribute a substantial portion of summer rainfall over the central United States.

490769.title: How Do Cold Pools within Arctic Cold-Air Outbreaks Influence Cloud Mesoscale Organization?
490769.authors: Paquita Zuidema, Rosenstial School, Miami, FL; and S. Ephraim, Z. Wang, and G. R. Lorenzo Pearson
490769.abstract: Cold pools within mesoscale convection are critical for supporting the vertical velocities needed to support cloud development. Their behavior within regions containing strong surface fluxes, such as within cold-air outbreaks over the sub-Arctic oceans, or over the western boundary currents, has been less explored to date. Such cold-air outbreaks typically occur in winter months when ice production within mixed-phase clouds is also active. While cold pools are identified with the transition from closed- to open-cells in these regions, the structural relationship of the cold pools (dynamical and thermodynamic) to the cloud development and cloud lifecycle has not been well-defined to date from observations. Here we draw on two aircraft campaigns: the NASA ACTIVATE aircraft campaign off of the eastern North American seaboard, and NSF cold-air outbreak experiment in the sub-Arctic region (CAESAR) aircraft campaign, held during March, 2024. Both sampled clouds composed of mostly super-cooled liquid water organized into rolls, closed- and open-cells, precipitating ice. The CAESAR sub-cloud thermodynamic structure is documented using a downward-pointing Raman lidar while an upward-pointing microwave radiometer and radar simultaneously characterize the variability in super-cooled liquid water paths and ice vertical structure. Flight-level vertical winds suggest that, within these cold-air outbreaks, convection is initiated by wind convergence at the upwind edge of cold pools, leading to the development of mostly super-cooled liquid clouds at temperatures < -15 C. Cold pools develop up to 10 km downwind of the new convection. Mesoscale variability in surface turbulent fluxes does not seem to impact where the new convection occurs, with the strong buoyant surface fluxes also not allowing ice sublimation to stabilize the sub-cloud layer. In both campaigns, the overcast cloud regions appear more as closely-packed convective cells than as top-down radiatively-driven stratiform structures. The interplay with strong surface fluxes may explain why the cold pools are consistently smaller and weaker than are cold pools observed within the trade-wind regions. Space-based observations, will also be used to provide further context for processes unearthed through the aircraft observations.

490771.title: Torque Contributions to Atmospheric Angular Momentum Tendency During the Madden-Julian Oscillation
490771.authors: Caitlin M Roufa, Northern Illinois University, Dekalb, IL; and V. A. Gensini
490771.abstract: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is associated with intraseasonal variability of atmospheric angular momentum (AAM), a global measure of large-scale circulation variability; however, the evolution of AAM and the contributions of torques across the MJO life cycle have not yet been quantified. Global relative AAM tendency is calculated from ERA5 (1940–2025) to produce phase aware lag-lead composites, allowing for characterization of relationships between MJO phase evolution, AAM tendency, and friction, mountain, gravity wave drag, and Coriolis torques. We find coherent phase lag structure within approximately 10 days of MJO phase occurrence and opposing MJO phases associated with opposite signed AAM tendency anomalies. Friction and mountain torques represent the largest contributors to the composite torque signal with their relative contributions varying across MJO phase and lag. There is robust seasonal variation in the strength and coherence of AAM, torque, and MJO relationships, with larger signals during boreal spring and summer. This work quantifies the close association between global momentum exchange and MJO evolution, identifying the torque pathways associated with intraseasonal AAM variability. Ongoing analysis examines the spatial circulation and torque structures underlying these relationships as well as implications for tropical-extratropical interaction on subseasonal timescales.

490772.title: The Evolution of Fire-Meteorology-Cloud Interactions over the Southern African Biomass Burning Season
490772.authors: Paquita Zuidema, Rosenstial School, Miami, FL; and T. Tatro
490772.abstract: Each year, agricultural fires in southern continental Africa emit approximately one third of the world’s biomass burning aerosol. To their west, the stratocumulus cloud interactions with the shortwave-absorbing aerosols remain one of the least understood aerosol influences on climate. The highest stratocumulus cloud droplet number concentrations over the southeast Atlantic occur in July, when agricultural fires coincide with the southern hemisphere winter in Angola. Dry convection fills a shallow continental boundary layer with smoke, and a nighttime (local solar time 2-9) land breeze transports the aerosol into the marine boundary layer. Offshore aerosol transport is strengthened by low-level easterlies when the continental pressure high southeast of Angola is more pronounced. Simultaneously, the south Atlantic subtropical high is weaker, allowing extensive dispersal of aerosol offshore into the boundary layer. Meteorological co-variation at synoptic scales ultimately compensates for cloud brightening by the smoke, as the stratocumulus cloud fraction is larger when the south Atlantic subtropical high is stronger. The impact of shipping emissions on the stratocumulus deck is also more clear when the background aerosol is lower, suggesting a sampling bias can influence monthly-mean radiative estimates of marine cloud brightening from shipping emissions. In later months, more small fires are occurring in the middle of the biomass burning season (August-September) in the past decade and the overall season is shorter, as deduced from satellite-derived burned area datasets (GFEDv5 primarily) corroborated by reanalysis carbon monoxide fields. Free tropospheric winds, also known as the Southern African easterly jet, have strengthened and shifted southward, transporting smoke aerosol further southwest over the southeast Atlantic. The advection is coupled with a southern shift in the south Atlantic subtropical high and an increase in the low cloud fraction on the southern edge of the stratocumulus cloud deck. While smoke emissions sources have not changed significantly, changes in the smoke transport pathway, attributed to increasing surface temperatures in southern Africa and tropical expansion, combined with an altered low cloud distribution, explain how the all-sky shortwave top-of- atmosphere direct aerosol radiative effect has become more positive - a climate warming - in recent decades.

490777.title: Vertical Velocity Structure of Steady-state Axisymmetric Hurricanes
490777.authors: Yuyang Rao, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY
490777.abstract: Vertical velocity is an important dynamic component in understanding tropical cyclone precipitation hazards. Extant steady state axisymmetric hurricane theory suggests a near linear increase in vertical velocity at the top of the boundary layer with radius up to a maximum at the outer edge of the inner core ascent regions of tropical cyclones. This work attempts to verify this radial profile of vertical velocity through idealized high resolution numerical modelling. Multiple runs of Cloud Model 1 (CM1) in its axisymmetric hurricane configuration were generated under different environment conditions and compared to the steady state axisymmetric theory. It was found that the profile of vertical velocity generated by CM1 differs significantly from that of the theory, with ascent maximizing near the radius of maximum wind, well within the inner core region. The inner core ascent in CM1 was also much stronger in magnitude than the theory. The sources of these discrepancies were identified to be the angular momentum budget assumed in the theory not closing in the model and differing parametrizations for surface friction between the two. These discrepancies imply existing theory on steady state axisymmetric tropical cyclones needs to be further refined to accurately represent the behavior of observed tropical cyclones, particularly at the transition between the inner core and outer circulation.

490783.title: Quantifying the Indoor-to-Outdoor Flux of SOA Precursors: Results in US and China
490783.authors: Rebecca Mesburis, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and S. Yun, D. Day, P. Campuzano-Jost, M. Morris, M. Shulman, A. V. Handschy, S. Schwink, R. Robertson, A. Schaum, S. Liu, F. Xie, Z. Xu, S. Huang, R. Ou, H. Zhang, B. Yuan, Z. Peng, W. Hu, K. Bates, M. Vance, J. de Gouw, and J. L. Jimenez
490783.abstract: Atmospheric particle pollution is a severe threat to human health, increasing cardiovascular and respiratory disease and mortality worldwide. While traditional air quality research focuses heavily on transportation and industrial emissions, the role of indoor volatile organic compounds (VOCs) as an important source of regional outdoor air pollution remains underappreciated. The indoor environment is highly complex and dynamic, shaped by human activities including cooking, using cleaning and disinfection products, and operating air cleaners. In the spring of 2025, we made the first measurements of secondary organic aerosol formation potential (SOA-FP) in a real, lived-in house during the CLEAN (Consumer products, Lights, Environmental Air cleaning in Normal conditions) Home campaign in Boulder, Colorado. Using an oxidation flow reactor to expose indoor kitchen air to hydroxyl radical (OH) or ozone photochemical aging (ranging from days to weeks of equivalent outdoor photochemical aging), we quantified the SOA-FP produced by these activities and by unperturbed baseline house conditions. The total indoor SOA-FP was an order of magnitude higher than what has been measured in urban outdoor environments. Spring 2026 measurements taken in a newly built laboratory at Jinan University in Guangzhou, China reveal an even higher indoor SOA-FP, demonstrating the ubiquity of this high potential across different indoor environments. Enhanced ventilation temporarily suppressed this potential, but indoor SOA-FP rapidly recovered within hours once limited ventilation was restored, indicating that indoor surface reservoirs continuously and quickly replenish reactive precursors. Conductive polymer inlet experiments revealed that approximately 80% of the observed OH-generated SOA-FP was driven by high-volatility VOC precursors and 20% by semi and intermediate volatility precursors (S/IVOCs). Importantly, comparison to model results for SOA-FP suggest significant missing indoor precursors in current chemical mechanisms and/or in proton-transfer-reaction VOC measurements. We estimate the continuous source of SOA-FP to the outdoor atmosphere through air exchange. These results underscore a critical need to integrate indoor emissions into regional outdoor air quality models.

490802.title: Balancing Pathogen Control and Air Pollution: Byproducts of GUV222 Lamps and Their Long-Term Mitigation using a Catalyst
490802.authors: Rebecca Mesburis, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and M. Rutherford, A. V. Handschy, D. Day, M. Morris, A. C. Ziola, O. Jenks, M. Shulman, H. Stark, Z. Peng, J. de Gouw, and J. L. Jimenez
490802.abstract: Interest in germicidal ultraviolet lamps emitting at 222 nm (GUV222) has grown rapidly as a tool for reducing airborne pathogen transmission indoors. Because 222 nm light is largely absorbed before reaching living cells in skin and eyes, these devices are considered safe for continuous use in occupied spaces, offering a pathway to whole-room disinfection that does not rely on ventilation or filtration alone. However, GUV222 operation also produces ozone (O3), and in typical indoor air, rich in volatile organic compounds (VOCs) such as monoterpenes, this O3 drives gas-phase chemistry that can lead to secondary organic aerosol (SOA) formation. SOA is itself a pollutant of concern, as fine particles are efficient at reaching the lower respiratory tract. This talk presents two connected lines of work conducted in a real, unoccupied office space. First, we characterize O3-driven SOA formation triggered by GUV222 operation, focusing on the reaction with limonene, a common indoor VOC. We show that this chemistry readily produces substantial concentrations of sub-300 nm particles, a size range that is both physiologically penetrating and difficult to capture with low-cost particle sensors. We further show that a chemical kinetic model reproduces the observed SOA mass concentrations, providing a tool to simulate this trade-off in other indoor environments. Second, we evaluate a catalyst designed to remove O3 from the air. Deploying the catalyst in the same office, we observed fast, substantial reductions in O3, NOx, formaldehyde, and other oxidized VOCs, accompanied by increases in reduced VOCs. Under continuous operation, the catalyst maintained effective O3 removal, with clean air delivery rate declining only gradually (~20% over the first 6 months), consistent with an estimated minimum 1–2 year usable lifetime. We will present updated performance data from approximately 2 years of continuous, real-world aging. The catalyst was effective against O3 from two different sources – GUV222 lamps and an electrostatic precipitator – holding steady-state O3 near 5 ppb and 3 ppb, respectively, during active air disinfection in the unoccupied office. Together, these results quantify a negative effect of far-UVC disinfection and demonstrate a practical, durable mitigation strategy, underscoring the value of pairing air-cleaning technologies with complementary pollutant controls to achieve both pathogen reduction and improved indoor air quality in real-world settings.

490814.title: Mechanisms for the Unprecedented Summer Heatwave over Japan in 2025
490814.authors: Hisashi Nakamura, University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan; and K. Takemura and F. Sezaki
490814.abstract: In 2025 Japan underwent unprecedented summer-mean temperature that exceeded the preceding outstanding records set in 2023 and 2024. The prolonged heat in 2025 summer was attributable to a persistent poleward shift of the subtropical jet (STJ) over the Asian continent and around Japan, in association with the early onset and persistent enhancement of Asian monsoonal convection. The unprecedentedly early termination of the Baiu rainy period caused extremely dry condition nationwide in late June through July. During the same period, profoundly enhanced cumulus convection around the Philippines, where several typhoons sequentially formed, contributed to the marked northwestward extension of the North Pacific Subtropical High (NPSH) toward Japan and the poleward STJ shift through the Pacific-Japan (P-J) teleconnection, forming a deep warm anticyclonic anomaly over Japan. Sub-monthly events of Rossby-wave propagation along the STJ, known as the Silk Road t(or circum-global) teleconnection, occasionally amplified the anticyclonic anomaly. In addition to global warming, persistent anomalous descent and increased insolation under the NPSH contributed to the record-high surface air temperatures. Extremely high sea-surface temperatures around Japan were another contributor to the record atmospheric heatwave through positive air-sea radiative feedbacks.

490815.title: A Deep Learning Model for the Prediction of Real-Time Tropical Cyclone Landfall Location
490815.authors: Mairukh Wardi, Institute of Water and Flood Management, Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology, Dhaka, Dhaka, Bangladesh; and A. Haque
490815.abstract: Landfall is technically defined as the precise moment the center of a tropical cyclone's eye crosses the coastline, rather than its location just prior at sea. However, this study is based on the practical premise that coastal impacts driven by maximum sustained winds begin when the storm reaches its terminal maritime position immediately before landfall, after which the system typically weakens. Tropical cyclones impacting Bangladesh cause severe coastal damage driven by maximum sustained winds just before and during landfall. To improve real-time landfall location predictions in the North Indian Ocean (NIO) region, this study implements a Deep Learning algorithm - Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network integrated with Monte Carlo dropout. Using 181 years (1842-2023) of 3-hourly storm track and intensity data from the IBTrACS dataset (V04r01), missing maximum sustained winds (3-minute average) were supplemented via the DS824 dataset, with residual gaps handled through linear interpolation or median filling. Central pressure were derived using empirical wind-pressure relationships. Rather than training a generalized model across the entire basin, customized BiLSTM models wre developed for 17 target cyclones affecting the Bangladesh coast (Cyclone 1991, Akash, Sidr, Rashmi, Bijli, Aila, Mahasen, Roanu, Mora, Bulbul, Amphan, Yaas, Sitrang, Mocha, hamoon, Midhili and Remal). Each model is trained exclusively on a target's specific analogue historical storms defined by spatial proximity in formation and landfall coordinates using a fixed 80/20 train-test split. Landfall location predictions were evaluated at 24-hour, 48-hour, 72-hour, and final pre-landfall lead times. Utilizing this localized analogue-driven framework, five representative target cyclones - Rashmi (2008), Aila (2009), Yaas (2021), Yaas (2021), Sitrang (2022), and Midhili (2023) are evaluated across various input timesteps to assess the model's predictive precision.

490818.title: Rethinking Tropical Energetics: Beyond Deep Circulations
490818.authors: Oishi Chakraborty, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Mumbai, MH, India; and V. Dixit and G. Bellon
490818.abstract: For decades, the deep overturning circulation driving precipitation within the convergence zones has been assumed to be energetically direct, meaning that the same troposphere-deep ascent which causes net import of moisture in the lower pressure levels, leading to precipitation, also exports Moist Static Energy (MSE) out of the same atmospheric column in the upper-levels. Conversely, deep descent has been associated with energy import, moisture export, and arid regions. However, later studies have shown that this may not necessarily be true everywhere within the convergence zones and caveats and exceptions to this principle have been documented, to the point that a re-examination appears warranted. To investigate this, we perform Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) decomposition on vertical velocity (omega) and examine how its vertical profile influences energy and moisture transports. Our results show that most of the variability of the vertical velocity can be decomposed into a first, troposphere-deep mode and a second mode which changes sign mid-troposphere. Examination of moisture and MSE transports associated with these modes show that within the convergence zones, moisture transport, and hence, rainfall is dominated by the first mode, while energy transport is dominated by the second mode. Further inspection of the vertical profiles of the two leading modes show that the first mode imports energy in the lower-troposphere and exports energy in the upper-troposphere such that the two balance each other, making the net transport of MSE negligible. The energy transport by the second mode, on the other hand, is dominantly influenced by their transport in the upper and the lower levels where MSE values are high while the mid-tropospheric compensating mass-transport coincides with lower MSE values. These results suggest that MSE and moisture transport are more weakly coupled within convergence zones than previously thought, offering new insight into the implications of tying atmospheric energetics to the hydrological cycle. Furthermore, we apply k-means clustering algorithm to the MSE budget terms and identify five energetic regimes over the tropical oceans: a cold-ocean upwelling regime, subtropical stratocumulus regime, tropical-extratropical transition regime and finally two regimes within the precipitating tropical regions: one importing MSE, prominently highlighting the thin convergence zones and one exporting MSE, covering regions of deep convection. The clustering analysis while segregating the tropics based on dominant energy balances, highlights the strong link between energetics and convective regime amidst its weak coupling with the hydrological cycle.

490819.title: Advanced Thermodynamic Profiling using a Prototype MicroPulse DIAL: Field Validation and Precision Enhancement
490819.authors: Yuichi Uchiho, EKO Instruments Co., Ltd., Shibuya-ku, Tokyo, Japan; and K. Matsuki, T. Hasegawa, M. Yabuki, R. A. Stillwell, and S. M. Spuler
490819.abstract: In recent years, the increasing frequency of extreme weather events, such as localized heavy rainfall and severe flooding, has heightened the need for precise and continuous thermodynamic profiling of the lower atmosphere. This creates a need for ground-based, network-deployable sensors capable of thermodynamic profiling available at a commercial scale. To address this need, EKO Instruments, in collaboration with the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF-NCAR), has developed a prototype diode-laser-based MicroPulse Differential Absorption Lidar (MPD) intended for commercial production. The system employs a shared-telescope architecture capable of simultaneously capturing atmospheric water vapor (WV DIAL) and temperature profiles using an oxygen-based DIAL and High Spectral Resolution Lidar (HSRL) with a potassium vapor cell. To validate system performance, a field observation campaign was conducted on Fukue Island, Japan, with a co-located Raman lidar and radiosondes. During challenging observational conditions involving bright daytime backgrounds and cloud cover, the MPD successfully retrieved water vapor and temperature profiles up to 3 km using direct retrievals. While the initial hardware validation was promising, statistical variance for water vapor at higher altitudes and for temperature remained an issue for high-precision applications. As an additional optimization step, we applied the Poisson Total Variation (PTV) processing method to the water vapor differential absorption signals. Reprocessing the Fukue Island dataset with PTV reduced the statistical variance, resulting in a lower root-mean-square error (RMSE) compared to the data processed with the standard method. Building on these water vapor results, our future work will focus on applying the PTV method to temperature retrievals to achieve similar variance suppression and further enhance overall system performance.

490824.title: AI-Agent-Assisted Verification and Validation of Near-Wall Models (Invited Presentation)
490824.authors: Xiaohan Hu, Penn State University, University Park, PA; and M. Whitmore, T. Guimarães, S. Salavati, M. Abkar, and X. Yang
490824.abstract: Wall-stress closure remains a central modeling choice in large-eddy simulations of turbulent boundary layers. The growing availability of data-driven closures raises a practical question: which model is appropriate for a given flow, input-data regime, and quantity of interest? We address this question through a controlled a priori comparison enabled by a human-supervised, AI-agent-assisted workflow. The workflow translates published formulations into traceable implementations, constructs synthetic and single-case verification tests, and audits large parameter sweeps, while scientific decisions and acceptance criteria remain under human control. In turbulent channel flows at friction Reynolds numbers 180, 400, and 1000, we compare eight wall-stress closures, comprising four physics-based and four data-driven models, across six matching heights and four filter-width ratios. Using off-wall velocity to predict consistently filtered direct numerical simulation wall shear, we assess performance through relative root-mean-square error, conditioned means, probability density functions, and premultiplied spectra. Near the wall, convolutional architectures that use spatial patches of the off-wall velocity plane reconstruct instantaneous wall-stress fields more accurately than pointwise closures. As the matching plane moves outward and the input becomes less informative, differences among the models diminish, and the equilibrium wall model becomes competitive while preserving wall-stress spectra better than the convolutional models. These findings identify observability at the matching plane as a key control on closure performance: learned models are most useful when informative spatial inputs and instantaneous accuracy justify their complexity, whereas equilibrium closures remain attractive in less-observable regimes because they are robust, inexpensive, and training-free. The study also demonstrates how AI agents can scale reproducible verification and validation without replacing physical judgment.

490828.title: The ENIAC Forecast Model as an Educational Tool
490828.authors: Robert W. Grumbine, Private Citizen, Lanham, MD
490828.abstract: The ENIAC numerical weather prediction model was a foundational step in NWP. Thanks to notes from George Platzman, who was involved in that effort, I have produced modern language programs implementing that model as faithfully as possible without rebuilding the hardware. This, and historical support material, is in an open github repository https://github.com/grumbiner/ENIAC/ The languages it is already implemented in are Fortran-77, Fortran-90, and C. It is small, making it a good starting point for students to translate, whether themselves or via AI tools, to any other target language such as Python. This is 'challenge1' Challenge 2 is to improve on a full forecast model suite. Much of an operational center's code is care and feeding of the model -- acquiring data, constructing initial conditions, running the model, producing guidance output, and evaluating the model performance. All are present in challenge 2. But each is present in a simple form, ready to be improved upon by students. As challenge 2 is a complete suite, it can also be used by student forecasters. Components: * Initial data are acquired from GDAS runs, at 0.25 degrees * Initial conditions are developed by nearest neighbor interpolation * The model is the original. But a minor modification should improve it (Lynch, 2008). * More generally, as students have ca. 1e8 times as much computing power available on one CPU as the ENIAC did, they have much room to acquire or develop and then implement a more complex model -- and evaluate its performance. How much better is a model that takes 10 seconds instead of the 10 ms/day of the original? 100 seconds? * Conversely, they could leave the model core alone, but improve the resolution, numerics, and boundary conditions (the original boundary conditions are unconditionally unstable). Which changes give the most improvement? Which are most costly? * The output graphics are, again, very simple (sample shown below) * Model evaluation is by the S1 score only. There are many others which could be implemented. In all, the aim here is to provide a framework which students can experiment and improve upon. In so doing, they can develop and practice skills which are used in the large weather prediction systems -- software version control (github), workflow, collaborative work, and determining whether something is an improvement and if so, whether it is worth the added computational cost. While advanced models are available, an advantage of this is that students can make many mistakes, an important part of learning!, at nearly zero expense. And get rapid feedback on their success.

490829.title: Assessing Precipitation and Streamflow Uncertainty on Water Cycle Components in NextGen Hydrologic Modeling
490829.authors: Xia Feng, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and F. L. Ogden
490829.abstract: Hydrologic models are essential tools for operational flood and drought forecasting, water resource planning, and assessing future water availability. Because these models approximate complex hydrologic processes through mathematical simplification and conceptualization, they inevitably carry uncertainty arising from measurement errors, structural limitations, and parameter estimation approaches. Understanding how such uncertainties propagate through water cycle components is critical for improving model accuracy and reliability. This study evaluates the impacts of uncertainty in precipitation forcing and calibration streamflow on simulated water cycle states and fluxes using the Conceptual Functional Equivalence (CFE) rainfall-partitioning model coupled with the Noah-OWP-Modular (NOM) land-surface model and the tree-based channel routing (T-Route) model within the Next Generation Water Resources Framework (NextGen) framework. NextGen provides a modular, standards-based architecture that enables flexible coupling of diverse hydrologic models and process-specific modules across heterogeneous hydroclimatic regions. Atmospheric forcing is derived from the Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC), a multi-decadal, high-resolution meteorological dataset used in National Water Model calibration and retrospective simulations. We identify periods and regions exhibiting substantial dry and wet precipitation biases and perform calibration and validation of the coupled CFE−NOM−T-Route system using these biased forcings across selected basins. Systematic precipitation bias is then incrementally reduced to assess its influence on parameter estimates and simulated streamflow, evapotranspiration, soil moisture, and baseflow during recalibration. Additional experiments introduce systematic bias into streamflow observations to evaluate the joint effects of precipitation and streamflow uncertainty on simulated water cycle components. Seasonal and hydroclimatic characteristics are analyzed to determine the conditions under which data uncertainty exerts the greatest influence. This work advances understanding of hydrologic model sensitivity to uncertainties in forcing and calibration data, provides insight into model structural performance, and informs more effective bias‑correction strategies for hydrologic modeling.

490832.title: Let's Get Real: Courage and Authenticity In Climate Communications
490832.authors: John R. Toohey-Morales, ClimaData, Huntersville, NC
490832.abstract: The effective communication of science currently faces unprecedented challenges. As we enter a post-truth era, the dismantling of institutions and the politicization of science continue to degrade public trust in scientific expertise. Drowned out by a cacophony of competing bullhorns, clear voices struggle to break through the noise. Even broadcast meteorologists—historically polled as highly trusted scientific voices—are losing ground to audience fragmentation as viewers abandon traditional media. How, then, can climate communication navigate this landscape? Courage and authenticity offer a path forward. This presentation argues that the contemporary environment demands unprecedented professional bravery—a resoluteness expressed through sincerity, transparency, and intellectual vulnerability. Finally, this session examines a series of on-air and online case studies that, while open to debate as definitive best practices, successfully pierced the fog of the modern war on science.

490838.title: NEUS-D3: A High-Resolution Northeastern United States Dynamically Downscaled Dataset
490838.authors: Sandeep Chinta, MIT, Cambridge, MA; and C. A. Schlosser
490838.abstract: NEUS-D3 is a new high-resolution dynamically downscaled climate dataset for the Northeastern United States designed to support regional climate research and infrastructure resilience applications. The dataset is generated using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model on nested 27-, 9-, and 3-km domains over the northeastern United States. The initial release focuses on simulations driven by one selected CMIP6 global climate model and one future emissions scenario, with planned expansion to additional CMIP6 models, scenarios, and historical simulations. NEUS-D3 is designed to provide high-resolution meteorological fields, including near-surface temperature, precipitation, wind, humidity, snow, and land-surface variables that support analyses of climate extremes and regional hazards. Planned applications include assessments of winter storms, freezing rain and icing, heavy precipitation, extreme winds, snow, and other weather hazards relevant to infrastructure resilience, electric power systems, and regional climate adaptation. We introduce the NEUS-D3 domain configuration, dataset characteristics, and the first dynamically downscaled simulations. We also summarize the validation approach for the initial release and discuss planned expansion toward a multi-model, multi-scenario regional climate dataset for the northeastern United States.

490839.title: Regional Variability In Energy Conversion Processes Associated with Easterly Wave Intensification
490839.authors: Carrie Lewis-Merritt, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS; and J. P. Stachnik
490839.abstract: Across the tropics, tropical easterly waves (TEWs) make large impacts at regional and global scales through contributions to monsoons or seasonal rainfall and often serve as precursors to tropical cyclones. However, most TEW studies focus on one domain, which limits the ability to make regional comparisons. In addition, the unique regional background states of TEWs can result in differences for processes related to wave amplification and decay. In this work, we examine the interaction between thermodynamic and dynamic mechanisms related to wave intensity change in four active TEW regions. Using regional thresholds for fractional changes in curvature vorticity, we first identify rapidly amplifying and decaying instances of waves. Previous work by the authors identified a broad region of positive eddy kinetic energy (EKE) tendency concentrated at low-levels surrounding the wave center for amplifying waves across all subdomains. The EKE analysis provided insight into the differences in wave classes that might not be prognosticated from moist static energy (MSE) tendencies alone. For instance, spatial composites of column-integrated MSE tendencies showed that west Pacific TEWs still amplified despite the presence of negative tendency anomalies at the wave center. However, the column-integrated EKE tendencies were sufficiently strong at the center for the same waves, and the vertically-resolved EKE tendencies were strongly positive over low-levels. To better understand the source of these positive EKE tendencies, we first calculate the barotropic production of EKE via the horizontal and vertical shear of the zonal winds and the baroclinic conversion of energy. TEWs in all subdomains show strongly dominant baroclinic energy conversions with maximum values that exceeded more than an order of magnitude than the corresponding barotropic terms. Differences between amplifying and decaying waves are also largest for the baroclinic term with broad statistical significance near the wave center, suggesting the intensification of individual waves are particularly sensitive to these processes. In addition, we also identify striking differences in the regional structures and overall strength for both barotropic and baroclinic energy conversions, suggesting that energy conversion processes in TEWs are highly sensitive to their environment. To help identify sources of variability, we compare MSE gradients to the energy conversion terms at key vertical levels. We expect to find stronger baroclinic energy conversions in the presence of larger horizontal MSE gradients, with possibly weaker relationships to the barotropic conversion terms. Time permitting, we also subset individual TEW occurrences by MJO phase and amplitude to identify possible large-scale influences on the production of EKE via changes in environmental wind shear and/or contributions to MSE.

490842.title: The Anemoi Framework - A Status Report
490842.authors: Baudouin Raoult, ECMWF, Reading, United kingdom
490842.abstract: Anemoi is an open-source framework for the development of data-driven forecasting systems. It is developed by ECMWF and its Member and Cooperating States, with contributions from other organisations. The framework is used by models such as AIFS (ECMWF), AICON (DWD), Bris (MET Norway), Varda (MeteoSwiss), FastNet (UKMO), Meteo-France IA (Météo-France), and Aila (FMI). We present the developments since the last AMS meeting. These include support for observations to enable direct observation forecasting, new generative modelling approaches, improved scalability for larger models, and a web-based asset management service. They also include enhanced testing capabilities, support for spatial and temporal downscaling, and the first steps towards agentic development. Together, these developments mark an important step towards more capable, scalable, and operationally relevant AI forecasting systems.

490845.title: All-Sky Diurnal Dust–Cloud Interactions and Their Radiative Effects
490845.authors: Ian Chang, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte, NC
490845.abstract: Mineral dust aerosols from Africa account for approximately half of the global dust aerosol emissions and three quarters of global atmospheric aerosol mass. It remains unclear whether the increase in dust since the pre-industrial era has enhanced or partially offset anthropogenic warming. Tighter observational constraints of aerosol radiative properties are required to improve model predictions of future climate. A major limitation in most observation-based estimates of aerosol radiative effects is their exclusive reliance on polar-orbiting satellite sensors, with solar-fixed orbits that repeat at nearly the same time of the day and thus fail to capture the complete cloud diurnal cycles. Here we quantify the all-sky direct dust radiative effects using hourly cloud observations from geostationary satellite data and aerosol optical properties from the Modern-Era Retrospective-analysis for Research and Applications- Version 2 (MERRA-2), constrained by Dust Constraints from joint Observational-Modelling-experiMental analysis (DustCOMM) and the NASA Earth surface Mineral dust source InvesTigation (EMIT) dust mineralogy data sets. We also assess how mineral dust influences diurnal cycles of various cloud properties and quantify cloud adjustments to all-sky dust radiative effects.

490846.title: How Good Are Today’s AI Weather Forecasts Over the Northeastern United States?
490846.authors: Sandeep Chinta, MIT, Cambridge, MA; and H. Baki, P. Salunke, and C. A. Schlosser
490846.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have rapidly expanded the number of operational weather forecasting systems available to users, including both locally executable AI models and provider-issued operational AI forecast products. Despite this rapid evolution, independent evaluations of these forecasting systems within a common verification framework remain limited. This study evaluates the performance of state-of-the-art operational AI and numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems over the Northeastern United States during the summer of 2026. The comparison includes locally executed AI models, operational AI forecast products from multiple providers, and established operational NWP systems. All forecasts are standardized to a common regional framework and evaluated using consistent verification metrics for near-surface temperature and related atmospheric variables. Seasonal forecast performance is assessed across the summer, with particular emphasis on the major Northeastern U.S. heatwave of early July 2026, enabling comparisons of forecast accuracy, event onset, intensity, persistence, lead-time behavior, and systematic biases across forecasting systems. In addition to forecast skill, the evaluation documents forecast provenance, initialization source, and operational configuration to support transparent and reproducible comparisons. The results provide insight into the strengths, limitations, and systematic biases of contemporary operational forecasting systems and establish a reproducible approach for evaluating the rapidly evolving ecosystem of AI weather prediction technologies.

490851.title: Kilometer-Scale to Large-Eddy Simulations of Impactful Deep Convection Alongside Retrieved Vertical Velocity at the Bankhead National Forest, Alabama
490851.authors: William I. Gustafson Jr., PNNL, Richland, WA
490851.abstract: High-resolution simulations of deep convection provide useful details regarding spatial scales and magnitudes of air motions within convective systems. For example, vertical velocity within plumes lifts up air from the boundary layer, but the extent of this lifting is impacted by mixing of laterally entrained air along the cloud boundaries. In-cloud vertical velocity in combination with microphysical processes also drives cloud electrification. Prior work demonstrates the grid-scale dependence of resolved vertical velocity in atmospheric models, with kilometer-scale models systematically biased toward stronger cloud updraft cores due to unresolved mixing. However, the accuracy of large-eddy simulation (LES) updraft characteristics is not well documented, particularly given the more bubble-like behavior that becomes resolved as the model resolution increases. The US Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility is in the process of generating a new set of simulations as part of its LES ARM Symbiotic Simulation and Observation (LASSO) activity. This new scenario focuses on nested LES of deep convection that impacts the water and energy systems around ARM’s Bankhead National Forest (BNF) campaign site in northern Alabama. For this scenario, we use a nested modeling approach with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to provide simulations with a range of grid spacings from 2.5 km down to 100 m. Combining these with radar retrievals of in-cloud vertical velocities made possible by the BNF deployments, the suite of simulations and observations will be a valuable tool for studying the resolution dependence of clouds and related dynamical processes. Initial prototype simulations include three cases: a quasi-linear convective system on 2-May-2025, a tornadic case on 20-May-2025, and isolated deep convection on 7-Sep-2025. Each case includes an ensemble based on varying the data source used for the initial and boundary conditions combined with microphysics parameterization options. Horizontal and vertical air velocity retrievals are available from dual-Doppler retrievals using the C-band ARM Scanning Precipitation Radar (CSAPR), the X-band Scanning ARM Cloud Radar (XSACR), the National Weather Service Next Generation Weather Radar (NEXRAD) network, and a complement of guest radars deployed near the BNF site. When complete, the LASSO-BNF scenario will contain roughly a dozen case dates spanning different types of deep convection at BNF. Case dates are being evaluated on an ongoing basis through the coming one to two years. The resulting simulations will be available for researchers to download, or to access directly through requesting resources on ARM’s high-performance computer.

490853.title: Developing Impact-Based Flood Hazard Thresholds to Improve National Water Model Forecast Communication
490853.authors: Suffiyan Safdar, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT; and R. Diehl, R. Van Der Heiden, A. Dadkhah, A. J. Jefferson, D. M. Rizzo, and E. Doran
490853.abstract: Interpretable and actionable flood hazard communication is crucial for improving public preparedness and reducing risk to life and property. The National Water Model (NWM) Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM) service provides forecast of inundation extent; however, it does not directly convey the full range of potential flood hazards posed to people, vehicles, property, and infrastructure. Hydraulic variables, including flood duration, depth, velocity, and specific stream power influence the severity and nature of flood impacts but are not currently translated from model outputs into actionable hazard information. Consequently, there is a need to establish connections between flood forecast outputs and hazard metrics that communicate the risks associated with floodwaters. To begin to address this need, we compiled flood impact case studies of fatalities, erosion, and inundation damages across the United States to develop hydraulic-based flood hazard thresholds that can be integrated into NWM FIM forecasts communication. We extracted 330 events from the NOAA Storm Events Database spanning 2005 to 2025 using the keywords “wash” and “erosion”. Associated storm reports and newspaper articles were reviewed to geocode and categorize case studies into flood impact classes, including drowning fatalities, vehicles swept away by floodwaters, roads and bridges washed out by erosion, and damages due to inundation. Maximum event specific stream power was derived, and velocity was retrieved at the reach scale from NWM retrospective and operational dataset and HAND-FIM data. Preliminary results showed that 70% of erosion-induced flood impacts occurred during storm events with NWM-modeled specific stream power greater than 35 W/m2. In contrast, a lower frequency of drowning fatalities (56%) and inundation damages (53%) occurred above 35 W/m2, suggesting that specific stream power alone is less predictive of these impact types. These findings suggest that specific stream power thresholds can provide operationalizable metrics for geomorphic disturbance within the stream channel as a primary driver of damage to low-water crossings and structures along stream corridors, whereas flood depth and velocity are more relevant for assessing inundation damage and risks to human and vehicle stability. This work demonstrates the potential of impact-based thresholds to improve the communication of NWM flood forecasts.

490856.title: Applying the Tropical Cyclone Logistic Guidance for Genesis (TCLOGG) to output from the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS)
490856.authors: Daniel J. Halperin, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; and R. E. Hart, S. T. Barnier, and D. Murphy
490856.abstract: The Tropical Cyclone Logistic Guidance for Genesis (TCLOGG) has produced well-calibrated probabilistic forecasts of tropical cyclone genesis out to seven days using a suite of deterministic global numerical weather prediction (NWP) models (CMC GEM, ECMWF, GFS, NAVGEM, UKMO). This technique has recently been applied to output from the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS). While the TCLOGG probabilities from deterministic NWP data rely on the most recent seven years of TC genesis forecasts to serve as a training data set, storage limitations prevent archiving an analogous training data set of ensemble forecasts. However, the regression equations developed from the deterministic NWP output can readily be applied to ensemble forecast system output since all of the relevant predictor variables are available. Here we test the reliability of TC genesis probabilities using this approach and introduce visualizations of the genesis probability and timing distribution for each forecast TC genesis event. Preliminary verification of forecasts during calendar year 2026 will be presented.

490858.title: The East Saharan Heat Low Enhancement and Excessive Wet Years In the Central and Eastern Sahel: Potential Physical Causes and Trends
490858.authors: Appolinaire Derbetini Vondou, University of Yaounde, Yaounde, Cameroon; and A. H. Fink, M. Maranan, A. Jong, P. Knippertz, and C. C. Funk
490858.abstract: Recent years have been marked by increasing wetness across the central and eastern Sahel and extending into the southern Sahara, culminating in exceptional rainfall and flooding in 2024. Using ERA5 reanalysis, CHIRPS V3 precipitation, and NOAA OLR-CDR datasets for 1981-2024, this study investigates the atmospheric drivers of these hydroclimatic extremes and the role of the eastern part of the Saharan Heat Low. Results show that the 2024 event was characterized by anomalously high total column water vapor, elevated near-surface dew point temperatures, and strengthened monsoonal westerlies that enhanced Atlantic moisture transport and convergence over the Sahel. Concurrently, the eastern part of the Saharan Heat Low intensified and shifted northward, reinforcing deep convection and moisture accumulation. Although African Easterly Waves were active during August 2024, their amplitude was not unusually strong, indicating that synoptic-scale wave activity was not the principal cause of the rainfall extremes. An accompanying long-term climatological analysis reveals: i) Significant positive precipitation trends across the central/eastern Sahel and adjacent southern Sahara; ii) a pronounced intensification and poleward migration of the eastern part of the Saharan Heat Low, accompanied by northward displacement of the Intertropical Discontinuity and monsoonal westerlies; and iii) evidence that the Saharan Heat Low enhancement is driven by extratropical dynamics, with little contributions from a reduced ventilation and water vapor feedback at its northern and southern boundaries, respectively. Taken together, this work highlights some worrying climate trends and the need for further studies regarding Saharan Heat Low changes and the role of thermodynamic vs. dynamic factors, as this may have consequences for the continuation of the Sahel wetting.

490859.title: TROPICAL - Aerospace Approach to Detect Extreme Rain Events
490859.authors: Devika Mukundan, Christ College of Engineering, Irinjalakkuda, KL, India; and A. T. Byju, S. Ramachandran, N. P. Olakkengil, H. P. Abdul Jalal, K. Pradeep, S. Balagopalan, and N. M. Komerath
490859.abstract: This Abstract describes progress to detect precursors to Extreme Rain Events (EREs) in time for useful warnings. Interest is limited for now to EREs from monsoon rain between 32 degrees N and S. Problem: Rising frequency of EREs is associated with rising moisture and energy in the atmosphere, and Atmospheric Rivers [1,2]. The 2026 North Indian Ocean SouthWest Monsoon has sunny days interspersed with very strong localized rainfall. Cities are flooded; soaked soil leads to catastrophic landslides. Sudden rain on watersheds forces dams to open at the worst times, with flooding and misery downstream. Computational approaches hit a practical limit with near-surface features: local models offer a way to improve. In the near term, data-based predictions refine models. When accuracy of both converge, meaningful longer-term Climate Predictions can support warnings as well as interventions. The technical problem is to predict ERE with at least a few hours of lead time, to move cars and possessions to higher levels, and evacuate people. Present satellite data resolution is between 13km and 22 km: Keralam State is 600km N-S and 70 km E-W, with microclimates, terrain and vegetation non-uniformity plus the sharp, steep Western Ghats. Fewer than 300 functioning rain sensors and AWS around the State, compare to 36,000 needed for average 1km grid resolution. Hypothesis: A 100X increase in high-quality data on weather parameters will enable data-based predictions. Physics-based computational prediction will be validated and demonstrated in time by reference to the data. As a first urgent step we postulate detectable anomalies above the cloud layer preceding EREs, inaccessible to ground sensors. A companion abstract deals with that. A fleet of UAVs flying slowly for 8 hours a day at 5km to 10km, or 24 hrs/day at mid-stratosphere, can detect much using different sensors. Dense cumulonimbus walls rising to 14000 m are easily visible from the sunlit zone above the lower cloud layer. Strong humid Atmospheric Rivers (AR) are experienced in the troposphere. Methods and Data Sources: AR bring huge amounts of water vapor. Using a newly developed software system, we track property variations in the global NOAA/NASA/ESA satellite and ocean buoy databases, with 1hr resolution for 7 days centered on each ERE, at 8 different altitudes, to capture the end of Rising Air phase and starting descent. This is done for 3 grid points centered on the ERE. Events analyzed are Chooralmala, KL, India July 2024, Kavalappara, KL, Aug. 2019, KL Floods Aug. 2018, Mumbai Floods, July 2005, Dubai April 2024, Sharjah, March 2026, Morgoro, Tanzania 2025, Umargram, GJ, India July 2026. round rain tracking closes the loop. Results: A mechanism for rapid rise of the moist AR is seen in most events: a mountain range is a physical obstruction (Keralam, Sharjah). At coastal Umargram AR moisture was drawn into an existing depression and vortical rise. A characteristic double spike evolved. The second one brought strong rise to above 14300m, leading to sudden rise reversal, with deluge-level rain. By 2026 end with our automated software, we expect to classify ERE signatures into 3 types. Next the database will be scanned in tropics/subtropics, to capture similar events. Training on these, a further refined classification of signatures will refine confidence to predict EREs with improving lead time, linking to national weather forecasters in 2027. A condensation/descent physical model is being added. Conclusions: State of the Art (NCMRWF, NCUM) shows near-term need for predictions based on finely-resolved data. UAVs in mid-troposphere can obtain such data, detect precursors of ERE and link to ground measurements. Data analysis confirms typical ERE signature over tropics with AR bringing high IVT, uplift, and rapid IVT decrease. AR lifts moisture from warm seas over mountain ranges. Western Ghats cause heavy Orographic rainfall. EREs over British Isles, UAE and E. Africa do not show AR as a factor. Searches through interpolated global database are demonstrated. Capability developed to-date, enables linking with ground and flight-based data. Broader Impacts: We start with a clearer understanding of EREs. Atmospheric conditions (wall of dark cloud rising to high altitudes, for instance) simulated, will depict what can be seen from above the lower cloud bank. We fully expect that a developing ERE can be seen from 25 to 50 km away by UAVs in the troposphere, so that reliable warnings can be sent to the probable area of impact, giving time and extent, and perhaps also intensity and cumulative rainfall, enabling accurate prediction of flooding, and perhaps pre-emptive dam openings to reduce need to open dams later. In the longer term we will be able to predict less significant rain events as well, refining weather prediction and dam water conservation management. Evolving “Best Signature” Model: The graphic shows Umargram data contours, what a UAV might have seen before it, and how to predict where rain actually falls. AR typically above 1000hPA level, get lifted above Dew Point level. Droplets rise and fall in parabolic trajectory, reaching ground as rain perhaps 50km and over 1 hour later unless vaporized. Descent and condensation interact into massive downpour, determined by gravity, relative humidity and wind. High IVT combined with uplift above DewPoint altitude should trigger focused computing. First rainfall triggers warning with more precise estimate of location and timing. Increased rainfall triggers Red Alert. Umargram (July 22-24, 2026) data especially at 850hPA indicate that a warning was possible up to 5 hours before IVT peaked, followed by the heaviest downpour. Reliable location and maximum cumulative rain enable flood contours and rates. This model will be refined and tested in the coming weeks. References: [1] Mohandas, et al., Dyn. Atm. & Oceans, 91,2020. [2] Bowen, Aus. J. Sc. Res. A: 3, 2, 1950. [3] Ji et al., Th. & App. Climatology, 115,1, 2014. [4] Zhu and Xue, Adv. in Atm. Sc, 33,11, 2016. [5] Xie, K. et al. J.Hydrology, 603, 2021. [6] Root, B. et al. J. Applied Met. & Clim., 46, 7, 2007. [7] Kumar, et al. Atmosphere, 11,7, 2020. [8] M. Nair, et al, Met. & Atm. Physics, 137, 6, 2025.

490861.title: Giant Cloud Condensation Nuclei (GCCN) Dampen Precipitation Susceptibility to Submicron Aerosol
490861.authors: Robert Wood, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and K. E. Mifsud and J. Barr
490861.abstract: This presentation examines the role of giant cloud condensation nuclei (GCCN)—large, hygroscopic aerosol particles, primarily sea salt—in regulating warm rain formation in marine low clouds. Using theory, observations, and a new minimal Lagrangian cloud model, we show that aerosol impacts on precipitation depend strongly on particle size, not just number concentration. While submicron (accumulation‑mode) aerosols tend to suppress precipitation by increasing cloud droplet numbers and reducing droplet size, GCCN with dry radii ≳1 µm act as efficient precipitation nuclei, accelerating condensational growth even at very low supersaturation. This rapid growth allows GCCN‑formed droplets to reach sizes favorable for collision–coalescence much faster than droplets formed on standard CCN. A minimal parcel‑based model is developed that includes condensational growth, collision–coalescence, and sedimentation of GCCN and drizzle embryos. Model results demonstrate that precipitation enhancement scales approximately linearly with GCCN mass loading, making GCCN mass a better predictor than number concentration. GCCN are especially important in polluted or marginally raining clouds, where they can enable precipitation and substantially reduce precipitation susceptibility to submicron aerosol. Overall, the work concludes that GCCN dampen aerosol–precipitation sensitivity, help reconcile models with observations, and are largely missing from current cloud and climate model parameterizations, despite their potentially important role in marine cloud–climate interactions.

490862.title: Incorporation of GNSS Zenith Total Delay Data in the NOAA RRFS/JEDI System
490862.authors: Hui Liu, Lynker, NOAA NWS Office of Model Development (OMD), Riverdale Park, MD; and S. Liu, D. Holdaway, S. K. Degelia, T. Lei, D. E. Lippi, X. Zhang, M. E. Pyle, and D. T. Kleist
490862.abstract: The GNSS Zenith Total Delay (ZTD) observations contain valuable information on water vapor in the lower troposphere, with hourly refresh from ~500 stations across the Continental United States (CONUS). This data is being incorporated into the NOAA Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) using the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) as the data assimilation framework, with the goal of improving forecast of convective precipitation. Two ZTD forward operators are evaluated on the 3-km CONUS grid: the existing MetOffice pointwise operator and a newly developed NWS/OMD Field-of-View (FOV) averaging operator. Retrospective assimilation experiments using either a hybrid 3D-EnVar or a Gain-form Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter were conducted over the 3-km CONUS domain for May 6-12, 2024. The results demonstrate that the FOV operator produces smaller RMS error of ZTD innovations than the MetOffice operator. Assimilation of ZTD data also reduces moisture forecast RMS error relative to radiosondes and aircraft observations (up to 2.5%) and increases moisture in the FV3 model background in the lower troposphere. These improvements translate into improved forecasts of convective precipitation events. In particular, the Equitable Threat Scores (ETS) for forecast of radar composite reflectivity is improved (see attached figure), demonstrating the potential of ZTD data to improve prediction of convective rainfall in the RRFS.

490866.title: Urban Atmospheric Boundary Layer Evolution and Surface–Atmosphere Coupling in the Washington, DC Metropolitan Area Using UrbanNet Tower and Doppler Lidar Observations
490866.authors: Praveena Krishnan, NOAA, Oak Ridge, TN; and S. Baidar, F. Ngan, N. Lichiheb, D. Christensen, and R. White
490866.abstract: The urban atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) plays a critical role in regulating the exchange of heat, momentum, and mass between the surface and the overlying atmosphere. As cities continue to expand and face increasing challenges related to climate change, heat stress, air quality, and urban scale weather prediction, an improved understanding of urban boundary layer processes has become increasingly important. However, complex interactions among surface energy exchange, turbulence, urban morphology, and atmospheric dynamics make urban ABL evolution challenging to characterize. Despite its importance, long-term observations that directly connect urban surface fluxes with the vertical structure and evolution of the ABL remain limited. This study investigates urban atmospheric boundary layer structure and dynamics over the Washington, DC metropolitan area using three years (2023-2025) of continuous, high-resolution observations from NOAA/ARL’s UrbanNet rooftop tower network, with observations available since August 2023. UrbanNet provides observations of urban surface meteorology, radiation balance, and turbulent exchange processes. High-frequency sonic anemometer measurements are used to estimate turbulence statistics, friction velocity, momentum flux, and sensible heat flux using the eddy covariance method. To examine the relationship between urban surface processes and boundary-layer evolution, UrbanNet tower observations are integrated with measurements from the NOAA/CSL HALO Doppler scanning lidar located at the Herbert C. Hoover Building in Washington, DC. The lidar provides vertically resolved observations of atmospheric structure, including boundary-layer height estimated using a fuzzy-logic algorithm, wind profiles, vertical velocity variance, and turbulence characteristics. The study evaluates multi-scale variability of the urban ABL across diurnal (daytime and nighttime), monthly, seasonal, and annual timescales, including morning boundary-layer growth, daytime mixed-layer development, evening transition to the nocturnal boundary layer. Surface turbulent exchange measurements are coupled with vertical atmospheric observations to examine how thermal and mechanical surface forcing influences atmospheric mixing under varying meteorological conditions. The integration of continuous urban surface observations from UrbanNet with vertically resolved lidar measurements provides a unique multi-year observational framework for understanding urban surface - boundary layer coupling. These observations advance understanding of urban atmospheric processes and provide valuable benchmarks for improving representation of ABL dynamics in weather prediction and dispersion models.

490874.title: Influence of Surface Type and Observational Data Source on Understanding Tropical Cyclone Integrated Kinetic Energy
490874.authors: Keloni Rio Laws, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and C. M. Rozoff and J. L. Vigh
490874.abstract: Integrated kinetic energy (IKE) can be used to assess the size and magnitude of a tropical cyclone (TC) wind field. When a TC makes landfall, it is imperative that wind information is as accurate as possible to protect infrastructure and lives. The Tropical Cyclone Surface Wind Model (WTCM) is currently being tested to be used for forecaster support as soon as next year. To evaluate the performance of WTCM’s surface wind representation, we examine Hurricane Laura (2020) and Hurricane Delta (2020) as case studies, comparing the model wind field to flight-level observations after applying a flight level-to-surface reduction factor. Analysis reveals that IKE levels prior to landfall are significantly different between WTCM and the flight data, particularly for Laura. Upon examining threshold wind radii, we observe further disagreement in the winds prior to landfall, predominately seen in the stronger winds. Wind profiles from both storms before landfall reveal that the WTCM struggles with capturing TC asymmetry and winds from their max to the eye and the outer wind field, though it successfully captures the peak winds. Finally, we find that generally, the WTCM quickly tapered winds off from the center of the storm as it approached landfall, compared to a more expansive wind structure in the flight-level data. We believe these discrepancies are likely due to the fitting of the to storm parameters designed to emphasize maximal aspects of the storm (maximum intensity, maximal radial extent of winds) vs. “most-likely” wind values at a given radial location.

490877.title: A Novel Algorithm for Detecting and Characterizing Lake-Breeze Fronts at Lake Victoria
490877.authors: Musa Ssemujju, Institute of Meteorology and Climate Research, Karlsruhe, Germany; and M. Maranan, A. H. Fink, and S. Ageet
490877.abstract: Lake Victoria, the largest tropical lake globally, is a driver of a mesoscale Land-Lake-Breeze (LLB) system due to its vast surface area and diurnal thermal contrasts between the lake and surrounding land. This LLB system significantly influences cloudiness, deep moist convection, and heavy precipitation, making their accurate representation in global forecast systems essential for regional weather prediction and climate modeling. Past studies focused on the well-known strong thunderstorms over the lake that are related to the nighttime Land-Breeze and cause many fatalities of fishermen each year. Studies on the daytime Lake-Breeze are surprisingly infrequent also due to the paucity of surface and upper-air stations. This study therefore benefits from a dense network of 45 automated weather stations (AWS) for the six-year period 2017–2022 at the Ugandan shores. It will present a novel Objective Lake-Breeze Detection Algorithm (OLBDA) to detect the daytime Lake Breeze Front (LBF) based on 15-minutely observations of air temperature, dewpoint temperature and wind from which climatological LBF characteristics are derived. Using short-term forecast of the ECWMF Integrated Forecast System (IFS), the representation of the LBF in the hourly station and hourly, 9 km gridded IFS data is compared using thresholds derived from the same percentile-based methodology for the three parameters. Finally, the three-dimensional structure of the lake breeze and single suitable identification parameters to detect the LBF in IFS are discussed. First, a database of 609 LBF days for the twice-yearly dry seasons, December-February (DJF) and June-August (JJA), has been created in a labor-intensive visual inspection of visible imagery of Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) aboard NASA’s Terra and Aqua satellites, as well as the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) onboard the Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 satellites. After testing a variety of sudden changes in AWS parameters for rainless LBF days in a performance diagram, a combination of the lowest 30% of air temperature drops and highest 30% of dewpoint and wind speed increases were identified as the optimal thresholds for OLBDA. Using these thresholds, isochrones of the daytime LBF progression are plotted. Most of the stations record LBF mean arrival time between 1400 and 1600 LT, with the coastal stations showing a start around 1200 LT and showing the highest LBF frequency of 54%. The LBF penetrates around 130 km inland until 1800 LT, with the propagation speed being 8 m/s towards the west and 6 m/s towards the north, most likely related to the easterly background flow. The DJF, with January being the peak month, has more LBF days than JJA due to the stronger thermal contrast. IFS overestimates the LBF days by 26% and tends to simulate a too fast inland propagation, yet basic structures are realistically represented. The best single IFS parameter to delineate the LBF is the boundary layer height. Composite vertical cross-section confirms the contrasts between western and northern transects. The NW-SE transect shows stronger vertical motion and deeper inland penetration when compared to the North-South transect. The depth of the BLH in the late afternoon is 3 km. Overall, the study sheds new light on the diurnal cycle of the LBF at the western and northern shores of Lake Victoria. In absence of available high-resolution AWS data, IFS short-term forecasts yield a reasonable, though somewhat biased representation of the LBF. Future studies shall ideally employ high-resolution Large Eddy Simulations to learn more about the reasons of the asymmetric propagation speed and the biases in ECWMF IFS.

490878.title: How Do Atmospheric Scientists Learn to Communicate? Student and Faculty Perspectives from a Nationwide Qualitative Interview Study
490878.authors: Kierstin Blomberg, University of Nebraska - Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and D. M. Kopacz
490878.abstract: Effective science communication is an essential competency for atmospheric scientists; however, relatively little is known about how these skills are developed within undergraduate education. Guided by Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT), this qualitative, semi-structured interview study explores experiences with and perceptions of science communication education among students and faculty representing atmospheric science programs across the United States. Interview questions examined science communication training experiences, the value placed on science communication skills, and barriers to communication learning and instruction. A distinguishing feature of the study is the intentional comparison of weather and climate communication to explore similarities and differences across these contexts. Preliminary analysis of student interviews suggests that science communication is widely viewed as an essential professional competency for atmospheric scientists. Emergent themes highlight the importance of translating scientific concepts, using audience-appropriate language, and assessing prior knowledge when communicating scientific information. Students also frequently describe a belief that strong communication is rooted in a solid foundation of disciplinary knowledge and identify barriers including time, effort, and limited opportunities for explicit science communication instruction. Preliminary review of faculty interviews suggests several themes may overlap with those emerging from student interviews. Ongoing analysis will further explore student and faculty perspectives on effective science communication, communication training, and its role within undergraduate atmospheric science programs.
