This work provides foundational insight into how atmospheric science programs prepare future atmospheric scientists for communication responsibilities and informs future research aimed at strengthening science communication education across the discipline.

490879.title: Role of Tropical Waves on Rainfall Variability and Extremes In Western and Central Equatorial Africa
490879.authors: Andreas H. Fink, Institute of Meteorology and Climate Research, Karlsruhe, Germany; and P. Knippertz, M. Maranan, A. D. Vondou, I. Mantho, C. C. Funk, and S. E. Nicholson
490879.abstract: The recent two decades have seen a plethora of studies quantifying the role of tropical waves (TW) on rainfall and rainfall extremes in western and central equatorial Africa. Most of these studies used the Wheeler and Kiladis (1999, henceforth WK99) space-time filtering approach using Outgoing Longwave Radiation or Satellite Rainfall Estimates (SRE) for the convective signal of the wave. Due to the paucity of daily rain gauge (RG) data, SRE were also often utilized to assess the impact of TW on rainfall variability. Fewer studies, including several of the authors of this contribution used RG data. And rarely did studies investigate the mechanisms of rainfall modification by TW or used more than one TW identification methods (like WK99 plus the method presented in Yang et al. (2021, henceforth Y21) based on equatorial zonal wind fields). Yet, in a review of wave identification methods, Knippertz et al. (2022) demonstrate for the example of the equatorial Kelvin wave (KW) that different methods lead to different amplitudes and propagation speeds. The presentation will first provide a quick overview on past studies. In West Africa, Tropical Disturbances (TD), which in this region are largely reflecting African Easterly Wave (AEW) activity, are the dominant rainfall modulator including favoring extreme events. The fast TD and KW appear to favor organized convection by influencing low-level convergence, vertical wind shear and instability while the slower waves, like Equatorial Rossby (ER) Waves and the Madden-Julian Oscillation, enhance total columnar water vapor over the course of a few days. Note, however, that waves other than TD explain a much lower fraction of rainfall variability, although positive wave interference has been observed. TWs, especially TD, have also been considered in recent climate change and weather forecasting studies by the authors. Significantly enhanced TD activity may have contributed to the observed significant increase in monsoon rainfall in the central Sahel since the early 1980s, and observed TW amplitude and phase information provide skill in statistical forecasting of rainfall for the following 24 hours. In central equatorial Africa, including the Congo Basin, KW plays a dominant role, while over Eastern Equatorial Africa, the MJO is known to be more important, including for extreme events. However, for results of a study using 19 years of daily rain gauge and SRE rainfall for Cameroon, a comparison of the WK99 and Y21 methods will be presented that show relevant difference in the assessment of the role of KWs on rainfall variation in Cameroon. Based on 850-hPa zonal wind, the Y21 method captures a Kelvin wave signal that propagates more slowly than in WK99, with its longitudinal propagation influenced by mountain ranges, unlike the global propagation seen in WK99. This difference is absent at 200 hPa. On average, the KW passage is associated with greater rainfall and a higher probability of heavy rainfall events in WK99 than in Y21, although such events occur during the wet phase in both methods. Overall, this study, in line with Knippertz et al. (2022), suggests the use of more than one filtering method and its application to both the convective and dynamical signal to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of the role of TW in rainfall modulation.

490889.title: Atmospheric Research at a Crossroads (Invited Presentation)
490889.authors: David Allan Randall, Atmosperic Science, Fort Collins, CO
490889.abstract: Global atmospheric models have served as an organizing framework for my research over the years. Stratocumulus clouds, land-atmosphere interactions, numerical methods, cumulus parameterization, and multiscale modeling all fit in that framework. My work, and the work of all of us, has been made possible by a national culture that recognized and embraced the intrinsic value of scientific research, which is first of all about understanding nature. The earliest numerical models of the atmosphere were built to help us understand the circulation. Today, our field is in the midst of four highly disruptive transformations: 1) The funding model that has sustained us for more than seventy years is being replaced by something else, but we don’t know what yet. 2) Some global models are explicitly resolving mesoscale convective systems, which allows them to simulate important aspects of the weather for the first time. 3) Inscrutable machine-learning models are producing some of the best weather forecasts available, and climate-change simulation may be next. 4) Artificial intelligence is utterly transforming the nature of day-to-day scientific work and scientific education. Disruption is disorienting, but it's not always a bad thing. Where will we be in ten years? I will hazard a few predictions.

490890.title: Modeling Lightning Activity with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks based Poisson Regression for Lightning Count Prediction
490890.authors: Ashley Marines, Code-Ag, Corpus Christi, TX; Code-Ag, Corpus Christi, TX; and Z. Wei and C. Liu
490890.abstract: Lightning occurrence exhibits highly nonlinear behavior while also containing a large proportion of zero observations, making accurate count prediction challenging for conventional regression and deep learning approaches. We propose a Zero-Inflated Poisson Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (ZIP-KAN) that combines a statistically principled zero-inflated likelihood with the nonlinear function approximation capabilities of Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) to model lightning count data. To investigate both predictive performance and interpretability, we first evaluate the proposed framework using simulated nonlinear zero-inflated count data with known generating functions. Results demonstrate that the ZIP-KAN substantially improves recovery of nonlinear count relationships compared with conventional linear ZIP regression. We then explore symbolic interpretation of the learned KAN representation using symbolic extraction techniques. While automatic symbolic extraction produces simplified expressions, our experiments reveal an important tradeoff between symbolic interpretability and model expressiveness: increasing symbolic simplicity can substantially reduce predictive accuracy. To address this limitation, we investigate surrogate polynomial approximations that preserve much of the learned nonlinear structure while providing an interpretable mathematical representation. This work highlights the potential of combining statistical count models with interpretable neural architectures for atmospheric applications. The proposed framework provides an avenue toward physically interpretable machine learning models capable of modeling complex nonlinear lightning processes while balancing predictive performance with scientific interpretability.

490892.title: Is Missing the Butterfly Effect a Good Thing for AI Weather Models?
490892.authors: Pedram Hassanzadeh, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL; and W. Li, Y. Q. Sun, J. Wang, A. Wikner, J. M. Finkel, Z. Liu, and J. Weare
490892.abstract: AI weather prediction (AIWP) models now outperform the best physics-based models on standard skill metrics, at a fraction of the cost. This superior accuracy comes despite long-standing skepticism of data-driven weather forecasting. Yet these models lack the butterfly effect: vanishingly small initial perturbations do not grow exponentially, defying fundamental understanding of the multi-scale chaotic atmosphere and numerical results. We probe this puzzle from a new direction: backcasting. We train neural networks identical to AIWP models except for one change: they predict the past. For a dissipative system like the atmosphere, skillful backcasting should be practically impossible: time reversal turns dissipation into anti-dissipation, so backward numerical integrations blow up; backcasting appears to violate the second law of thermodynamics. Yet across a hierarchy spanning ERA5, an intermediate-complexity GCM, and the multi-scale Lorenz 96 system, AI models backcast skillfully, e.g., 6.4 days into the past for ERA5 z500 (versus 9 days forward; see figure). Stranger still, the butterfly effect is missing from forecasting and backcasting AI models alike, across deterministic, generative, and neural-operator architectures. We show that these three surprises (superior forecasting accuracy, skillful backcasting, and the missing butterfly effect) are symptoms of one cause: not the architecture, the loss function, or deterministic versus generative design, but the training data. In practice, training data are coarse-grained: small/fast scales are filtered out and some state variables often excluded, leading to missing physics. Reducing coarse-graining brings back the butterfly effect and yields AI models that behave more like numerical integrations, but with lower forecast accuracy. We discuss which behaviors are features, which are bugs, and the implications for the growing use of AIWP models in ensemble forecasting, predictability research, and climate projection.

490893.title: The Quest for Bioluminescent 'Milky Seas'—a Missing Link in the Chain of Coupled Earth System Science
490893.authors: Steven D. Miller, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Hudson, S. H. D. Haddock, C. Seaman, W. C. Straka III, M. Wang, W. Shi, and S. Nam
490893.abstract: The term ‘Milky Seas’ describes a remarkable yet seldom witnessed form of bioluminescence where vast swaths of the ocean surface glow steadily. Mariner accounts describe their surreal appearance as a snowfield extending the horizon in all directions, accompanied by a sensation of hovering above the glowing surface on an unseen swell. Milky seas are thought to be caused by luminous bacteria, but the circumstances for how these ~2 nanometer-sized organisms combine en-masse to produce a structure observable from space (at times exceeding 100,000 km2), remain unclear—the phenomena remains a modern-day science mystery. Owing to the remote, ephemeral, and elusive nature of milky seas, Earth-viewing satellites equipped with low-light sensors offer our best hope for learning more about them. The Day/Night Band (DNB) on NOAA's Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) has demonstrated the ability to detect and quantify milky seas. Nightly DNB imagery sequences reveal the spatial and light emission characteristics of these glowing waters as they drift and morph with the currents, persisting from days to months in the waters of the Northwest Indian Ocean and the Maritime Continent. This presentation updates the state the science around milky seas. We recover, update and curate a compendium of eye-witness mariner accounts spanning four centuries. This database forms the basis for a statistical predictive model that regresses sightings against major coupled air-sea processes such as the Indian and Australian Monsoons, the Indian Ocean Dipole, and the El Nino Southern Oscillation. Based on the output of this model, we discovered an overlooked milky sea event south of Java in 2017. These tools, together with DNB satellite observations, open the first realistic possibility of deploying to an active event for in situ sampling. Understanding the nuances of milky seas can shed light how primary production in the ocean—a major sink for atmospheric carbon—may respond to a changing climate. In particular, milky seas represent a heretofore unknown anomalous behavior of the microbial carbon pump response that can generate more bacteria in one modest-sized event than previous estimates of the global coastal population. The story told by milky seas is one of unanticipated coupled earth system processes. Getting to the heart of this scientific mystery will require breaking down the traditional silos of atmospheric science, oceanography, and marine ecosystems / microbial ecology, and considering feedbacks that connect from the microscopic to global scales.

490900.title: A 22-Year Two-layered Cloud Climatology through the fusion of MISR & MODIS on Terra
490900.authors: Larry DiGirolamo, University of Illinois at Urbana Champaign, Urbana, IL; University of Illinois at Urbana Champaign, Urbana, IL; and G. Zhao, A. Mitra, M. V. De Vera, M. D. Zelinka, H. A. Mahmoud, and K. J. Mueller
490900.abstract: Satellite measurements of multilayer cloud properties are critical for applications ranging from radiative flux estimation and atmospheric model evaluation to the development of long-term cloud data records.Our longest single-satellite cloud record providing stable and multi-decadal observations comes from NASA’s Terra mission. Cloud properties are derived separately from Terra’s MODIS and MISR instruments using a single-cloud-layer assumption. Extensive validation of cloud top heights (CTH) for these two datasets using the ISS-CATS lidar showed significant issues with these datasets for conditions of thin cirrus over low cloud (~30% of global cloud cover). In these conditions, MISR accurately retrieves the low cloud CTH rather than the CTH of the thin cirrus, while MODIS underestimates the CTH and overestimates the opacity of the thin cirrus. This poses significant challenges in characterizing CTH and cloud optical property variability in the Terra record. Here, we present advances in a physics-based MODIS+MISR fusion algorithm for accurately determining the height of both layers, as well as the cirrus emissivity and optical depth, for conditions of thin cirrus over lower cloud. We evaluate our two-layered retrievals against collocated ISS-CATS lidar observations. Relative to CATS, the mean bias of the upper cloud top pressure and emissivity are reduced by ∼90% and ∼75%, respectively, in the MODIS+MISR fusion algorithmcompared to the standard MODIS products. We develop an error model for the two-layered retrieval accounting for systematic and random errors and find up to 87% of all residuals lie within modeled 95% confidence intervals, indicating a near-closure of the error budget. Through the NASA MEaSUREs program, we are working towards an open access, pixel-level two-layered cloud product over the MISR swath for the first 22 years of the Terra record. This will lead to a first-of-its-kind two-layered cloud climatology from Terra’s morning orbit.

490901.title: The Role of Eddy Moisture Fluxes in ITCZ Breakdown
490901.authors: Victor C. Mayta, University of Wisconsin, Madison, Madison, WI; and Á. F. Adames-Corraliza, Q. J. Lin, and J. M. Windmiller
490901.abstract: The spatial organization of column water vapor (CWV) is fundamental to tropical convection, defining distinct moist and dry regimes separated by a ``moist margin." Using a CWV aggregation index, we analyze the spatiotemporal evolution of convective aggregation within the Pacific and Atlantic Intertropical Convergence Zones (ITCZ) in the ERA5 reanalysis. Our analysis shows that variability in ITCZ aggregation arises from the combined influence of transient eddies spanning synoptic to intraseasonal timescales. Furthermore, we use theory to show that large eddy energy fluxes are not necessary to cause convective disaggregation and ITCZ breakdown. This is because deep convection is highly sensitive to moisture, and even small eddy-driven moisture fluctuations can have a large impact on the distribution of precipitation. As a result, eddies play a larger role in tropical weather and climate than would be inferred from their contribution to atmospheric energy transport alone.

490902.title: Pressure Spectrum Scaling Under Atmospheric Stability: Evidence from the M2HATS Field Campaign
490902.authors: Mauro Ghirardelli, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria; and G. G. Katul and I. Stiperski
490902.abstract: Static pressure fluctuations regulate turbulent kinetic energy transport and redistribution in turbulent flows, yet remain one of the least understood variables in atmospheric turbulence. This is because pressure obeys the (elliptic) Poisson equation, so that energy at any given scale is tied to the dynamics of every other scale, complicating the identification of mechanisms controlling pressure. Spectra scaling laws are one of the main diagnostic tools for probing these mechanisms. The slopes of the spectral scaling regions in atmospheric applications are predicted to equal -7/3 in the inertial subrange under the assumption of local isotropy, while Townsend’s attached-eddy framework predicts a −1 mid-frequency overlap regime arising from the superposition of inner (wall-scaled) and outer (boundary-layer-scaled) motions. Both scalings find support in the literature under neutral, high-Re conditions, mostly stemming from wind-tunnel experiments. How atmospheric stability affects this picture, however, remains a significant gap in the field. Here we use high-frequency pressure and eddy-covariance measurements from the M2HATS field campaign, conducted over flat, horizontally homogeneous but rough terrain to examine the dependence of spectral slopes in the mid-frequency and inertial subrange to the effects of stratification. The results show a clear monotonic signature of stratification: a progressive narrowing of the -1 region and flattening of the -7/3 slope in the inertial subrange as stratification becomes progressively more stable. We further relate these changes to shear and buoyancy metrics, boundary layer height, and bulk anisotropy, and set it within the arguments of the Poisson equation.

490903.title: Investigating the Effects of Geometric Scale and Orientation of Structures Relative to Tornado-Like Vortices on Aerodynamic Loading: An LES Study
490903.authors: Samuel Hanson, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and M. A. Hasan and F. Khaled
490903.abstract: From 2015 through 2024, tornadoes were responsible for nearly $11.5 billion in property damage in the United States and caused just under 6,000 injuries and 500 deaths (National Weather Service, 2025). An improved understanding of the interactions between tornadic wind fields and structures is critical to work towards improving building design standards and better protecting life and property. There is a significant knowledge gap between tornadic wind fields and their interactions with the built environment. Atmospheric science field projects dealing with low-level tornadic winds are limited by the increase of radar beam height with horizontal distance and feasibility challenges of placing observational probes in the path of tornadoes. Radars used in such field projects are also deployed in open areas away from structures to avoid beam blockage, further reducing the chances of observing wind interactions with the built environment. Traditionally, the engineering community has relied on modeling tornadoes using tornado vortex generators (TVGs) to create tornado-like vortices (TLVs). The major TVGs include the WindEEE Dome at the University of Western Ontario, Texas Tech University’s VorTECH, and the TVGs at Iowa State University and the University of Birmingham. TVGs generate pseudo-stationary or wandering TLVs through a combination of near-ground fans oriented to create cyclonic circulation around a larger fan in the ceiling that serves as an updraft. To study vortex-induced loading on a structure from a TLV generated by a TVG, a downscaled building is often fixed to a stationary floor of the simulator, fixed to a sliding plate that is translated under the TLV. This works in the opposite manner as the real world, where tornadoes translate over structures. Some facilities allow for a small degree of translational TLV movement; however, the majority of TVGs produce wandering TLVs at best. Khaled et al., (2025) introduced a novel method of generating a TLV inside of the University of Florida Boundary Layer Wind Tunnel (UF BLWT). This method utilizes a blockage mechanism composed of a wall and transverse barrier placed part-way down the BLWT (Figure (1a)) that creates horizontal shear instability as the flow passes around it (Figure (1b)), creating a translating TLV. This type of TLV formation follows Goodnight et al., (2022), which states that some tornadoes generated from quasi-linear convective systems (QLCS) also develop through a type of ‘horizontal shearing instability’. The initial idea behind the experiments was explored and tested using LES with the stationary wall arrangement, which is also reported in Khaled et al., (2025). The TLVs generated in the virtual framework agreed with the physical results from experiments and field observations. CFD offers a plethora of advantages over physical simulators, as virtual probes can be placed inside the domain that gathers flow velocity and dynamic pressure data at near-infinite spatial and temporal resolutions. The goal of this project is to use the transverse wall blockage mechanism introduced by Khaled et al., (2025), and place a structure inside of the computational domain and examine the loading induced by a translating TLV. The virtual UF BLWT domain used in Khaled et al. (2025), seen in Figure (1b), serves as the test domain for this study. The structure placed inside of the CFD domain is a scaled down 1:46 version of Texas Tech University’s Wind Engineering Research Field Laboratory (WERFL) building located at Reese Center, TX, USA. The 1:46 scale was chosen to achieve the same ratio of the TLV radius to the length scale of the test structure as used in simulations conducted at the TTU VorTECH TVG. The building is placed downstream of the wall blockage mechanism and in the center of the domain such that the vortex center passes directly over the center of the structure. To test loading differences from building orientation relative to the TLV, additional building versions of each scaling were created by applying a 25° and 45° counterclockwise rotation around the building center. 374 virtual probes were placed in the domain on the roof of the structure that measure instantaneous velocity and kinematic pressure. These observations are used to calculate the pressure coefficient (Cp) used to estimate TLV-induced loading on the roof of the structure when compared to reference values. The large-eddy simulations are performed using OpenFOAM v11. The domain has a mesh consisting of 2.97 million cells, with refinement zones placed around the blockage mechanism and the test structure. The boundaries are assigned no-slip conditions, and an incompressible flow is used. The pimpleFoam solver is used because of its ability to resolve transient incompressible, turbulent flow. The nutUSpaldingWallFunction is the wall function used to define flow around the walls, blockage mechanism, and structure due to its ability to model a wide range of flow regions. Initial results from a non-rotated single pulse simulation display that as the TLV wind field approaches the structure, the aerodynamic pressure component created by the flow being forced over the structure dominates the Cp distribution. This is partly due to the creation of conical vortices as the flow interacts with the bottom wall of the structure and leads to a concentrated Cp maximum at that location. However, when the TLV is directly on top of the structure, the static pressure drop associated with the TLV dominates, leading to a more even Cp magnitude distribution, with some hotspots, such as the one toward the bottom-right of the roof, formed as conical vortices from residual flow create aerodynamic pressure contributions. To test whether the observed differences are true features of the TLV-structure interactions or a property of vortex inconsistencies, a number of pulses for each WERFL scaling and rotation angle will be conducted to create a database of instantaneous quantities of interest from each pulse, allowing for the creation of ensemble mean Cp plots as well as skewness and kurtosis analysis.

490904.title: Operationalizing Wildfire Smoke Forecasts for Population-Level Warnings and Patient-Centered Health Action
490904.authors: Yunyao Li, The University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, TX; and S. Shahriar, D. Tong, K. Cromar, L. Myers, B. D. Baker II, R. Ahmadov, A. S. Darmenov, E. J. Hyer, D. Figueras-Nieto, and J. Chen
490904.abstract: Air quality forecasts have the potential to reduce wildfire-smoke exposure, but forecast skill alone does not ensure effective public health action. Forecast information must identify where hazardous conditions will occur, how many people will be affected, and whether warnings can be delivered with sufficient accuracy and lead time to support protective decisions. We present an exposure-oriented framework that connects probabilistic smoke forecasting with population warnings and patient-centered health communication. The framework is built upon the Hazardous Air Quality Ensemble System (HAQES), which synthesizes six operational atmospheric composition models to generate hourly PM2.5 forecasts and exceedance probabilities across the contiguous United States. During a major Canadian smoke episode in July 2026, HAQES reproduced smoke transport into the Great Lakes and northeastern United States with correlations of 0.82 and 0.80 at 24- and 48-hour lead times. For the PM2.5 exceedance, both forecasts achieved a hit rate of 0.83, with false-alarm rates of 0.10 and 0.09. We translated these forecasts into spatially explicit population warnings and evaluated their potential public health value. The 24-hour forecast would have correctly alerted 165.9 million people, representing 87% of the population subsequently exposed to unhealthy smoke. Under a hypothetical protective-action scenario that following a successful alert, total population exposure could have been reduced by 76%. To address limitations in the raw forecasts, we developed complementary AI and exceedance-based prediction approaches using operational model output, recent AirNow measurements, satellite observations, and observed pollution trends. These approaches improved the identification and spatial delineation of hazardous smoke conditions; during a July 2025 Chicago event, the AI forecast yielded a potential exposure reduction of 56% under the same scenario. In partnership with Kaiser Permanente, we are translating location-specific ensemble and AI forecasts into a prototype patient-messaging test bed. The collaboration evaluates how alert thresholds, lead times, forecast confidence, and health guidance can be tailored for patients at elevated risk from smoke exposure. This work demonstrates how verified atmospheric predictions can be operationalized across scales, from regional population warnings to targeted health communication, while explicitly accounting for missed events, false alarms, and forecast uncertainty.

490908.title: Decadal Changes in Atmospheric Circulation Detected in Cloud Motion Vectors
490908.authors: Larry DiGirolamo, University of Illinois at Urbana Champaign, Urbana, IL; and G. Zhao, G. Zhang, Z. Wang, J. R. Loveridge, and A. Mitra
490908.abstract: Climate model and atmospheric reanalysis datasets show changes in recent decades of atmospheric circulations, including changes to the strength and width of the Hadley circulation and latitudinal shifts in the polar fronts. However, these datasets do show discrepancies in magnitude and even direction of circulation changes, underscoring an urgent need for validation with independent, climate-quality measurements. Here, we show the first direct observations of decadal changes in cloud-conditioned atmospheric circulation throughout the tropopause using our longest, and only climate-quality record from space that’s capable of doing so, namely the height-resolved, cloud motion vectors from the Multi-angle Imaging SpectroRadiometer (MISR) onboard the Terra satellite. Upper tropospheric cloud motion speeds in the midlatitudes have increased by up to ~4 m s⁻¹ decade⁻¹. This acceleration is primarily due to the strengthening of meridional flow, which could potentially indicate more poleward storm-track trajectories or intensified extratropical cyclones. The northern and southern hemisphere tropics shifted poleward at a rate of 0.42±0.22 and 0.02±0.14 °latitude decade⁻¹ (95% CI), respectively, while the corresponding polar fronts shifted at 0.37±0.31 and 0.31±0.21 °latitude decade⁻¹ (95% CI). We also show that the widely used ERA5 reanalysis winds subsampled to MISR are in good agreement with MISR’s climatological values and trends but indicate likely ERA5 biases in the upper troposphere, as well as potential problems in ERA5’s ability in representing clouds. Our assessment of changes to the atmospheric circulation is specific to the 2000-2020 period, containing both natural internal climate variability and human-induced changes.

490923.title: The Precipitation Prediction Grand Challenge: From the First to the Last Mile (Invited)
490923.authors: David R. Novak, NWS/Weather Prediction Center, College Park, MD; and J. E. Ten Hoeve III, J. Huang, Ph.D., and V. S. Tallapragada
490923.abstract: The impacts from extreme precipitation are deadly, damaging, and increasing. In just the past year, the nation experienced the deadliest flash flood in recent history, and extreme rainfall events have caused billions of dollars in damages and economic loss. Accurate prediction in concert with eye-to-eye decision support services saves lives. Unfortunately, NOAA models (global models in particular) have seen marginal improvement in precipitation skill (~15%) over the past 2 decades. Further, partner needs in terms of accuracy, specificity, and lead time often exceed current capabilities. Finally, even the best forecast needs to result in action to be useful (the ‘Last Mile’). In response, NOAA has developed a strategy for a multi-year effort to improve precipitation forecasts and decision support (from mesoscale weather to seasonal timescales) - called the NOAA Precipitation Prediction Grand Challenge. The goal of this effort is to dramatically improve precipitation forecast accuracy, lead time, and reliability. The challenge demands investment across the value chain from the ‘First Mile’ of basic understanding of precipitation processes and predictability limits, to enhanced observations, data assimilation, improved models, post-processing and tools for the human forecaster, – to the ‘Last Mile’ eye-to-eye provision of understandable and actionable decision support. The initiative works hand-in-hand with the NOAA Moonshot effort to transform modeling - an essential component of the challenge. An initial suite of projects are coming to fruition, while a new set supported by Congressional investment is being launched. These projects and results will be highlighted, including UFS modeling improvements, a prototype Atmospheric River Forecast System, the Urban Rain Rate Dashboard, and eye-to-eye stakeholder engagements. Further, the presentation will emphasize the need for an ‘all-hands-on-deck’ approach to build national strength in the face of precipitation extremes. The strategy to achieve this result will be described, with attention focused on opportunities for community involvement.

490924.title: Air–Sea Coupling and Distinct Transverse Clouds in an Extratropical Cyclone: Kilometer-Scale SHiELD–MOM6 Simulations
490924.authors: Biao Zhao, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; GFDL, Princeton, NJ; and K. Gao, J. Mouallem, L. M. Harris, B. G. Reichl, and J. Chen
490924.abstract: Strong air–sea exchanges in the cold sectors of extratropical cyclones fuel vigorous marine boundary layer convection, yet their characteristics and also their representation in high-resolution models remain poorly understood. Using GOES-16 satellite imagery and GFDL’s kilometer-scale SHiELD-MOM6 atmosphere-ocean coupled model, we investigate a transverse cloud pattern in the cold sector of a North Atlantic extratropical cyclone. Unlike the common cloud streets that align approximately with the prevailing wind, these coherent cloud bands are oriented nearly perpendicular to the boundary layer flow. Our simulations successfully reproduce their occurrence, spatial scale, and orientation. The coupled experiment produces more pronounced transverse cloud features than the uncoupled experiment, indicating the potential role of interactive air-sea coupling. Analyses of their three-dimensional structure reveal they are signatures of transverse convective rolls. The eddy kinetic energy budget analysis further indicates that buoyancy production is a main contributor in the middle boundary layer, while shear production peaks near the boundary layer top. Their orientation is more closely associated with upper-boundary-layer shear. These results reveal an underrecognized mode of boundary layer cloud organization in extratropical cyclones and demonstrate the value of kilometer-scale coupled modeling for resolving fine-scale cloud structures.

490926.title: Using the Integrated Observing System for Air Quality to Improve Our Understanding of Urban NO2 Pollution in New York
490926.authors: Tabitha Lee, NASA Langley Research Center/Oak Ridge Associated Universities (ORAU), Hampton, VA
490926.abstract: Urban environments present a challenge for air quality models to simulate surface ozone and interpret satellite observations due to the modification of local meteorology or chemical properties by urban characteristics. Chemical transport models such as GEOS-CF do not properly treat such characteristics, creating questions on their influence in simulating O₃ and its precursors. In this work, we address this question through the simulation of the diurnal and vertical profiles of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) over New York City, NY (USA) during the AEROMMA/STAQS deployment using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF)-driven GEOS-Chem (WRF-GC) model version 3.0. WRF-GC is run at urban scales (~4km) and includes a 2023 US EPA National Emissions Inventory (NEI) which is updated to include CRACMM v2 chemistry from Pye et al. (2024). WRF-GC includes the treatment of urban areas through the building environment parameterization (BEP) (Martilli et al., 2002), coupled with the building energy model (BEM) (Salamanca et al., 2010). Non- and urban WRF-GC results are evaluated against observations from the AEROMMA/STAQS field campaigns as well as TEMPO and TROPOMI retrievals and in situ ground monitors to test WRF-GC’s ability to reproduce the magnitude, diurnal evolution, and shape of the urban plumes. The effects of urban characteristics on O₃ chemistry were evaluated through changes in O₃ production and the distribution and evolution of its precursors. We show here the first inclusion of urban characteristics in WRF-GC and its improved ability to represent urban atmospheric chemistry in New York City in addition to insight into feasible changes that could be made to GEOS-CF without the addition of a complex urban scheme to improve performance for urban satellite retrievals.

490928.title: A Video Library for Atmospheric Sciences, Educators and Students
490928.authors: John M. Wallace, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and H. J. Witte
490928.abstract: Much of the attractiveness of atmospheric sciences as a career option or as a hobby derives from the color and dynamism of atmospheric phenomena. Making use of state-of-the-art graphics imagery, it is possible to produce animations that convey the grandeur, the mysteries, and the challenges of atmosphere science, and to elucidate the phenomena themselves. NOAA, NASA, university scientists, storm chasers and landscape photographers have already produced a veritable treasure trove of videos, but they are scattered across numerous websites, some of which require that the viewer watch advertisements before they can see them. In our talk we will introduce a collection of short (mostly under a minute), silent videos of atmospheric and climate-related phenomena which is accessed by way of an index at https://animalib.atmos.washington.edu/ We will also seek input from the community on how the user interface can be improved to make it easier for viewers to see what’s available in the library and to choose the particular videos they want to see, and on how the collection can be expanded to better serve the needs of educators and students. https://animalib.atmos.washington.edu/

490931.title: AI Integration at the Weather Prediction Center
490931.authors: David R. Novak, NWS/Weather Prediction Center, College Park, MD; and M. Youngman
490931.abstract: The NOAA/NWS Weather Prediction Center is interwoven into the emergency management and security infrastructure of the US -- providing expert weather forecasts and datasets with particular focus on precipitation and temperature extremes. The advent of AI has provided an opportunity to transform operations, with potential for more accurate forecasts with greater efficiency. This talk will provide a view into this transformation, covering success stories, surprises, and lessons learned. For example, the rapid development and maturation of AI emulator guidance was met with quick adoption. First, through critical examination of verification, to real-time website viewing, confidence grew that the first generation of AI emulators would be skillful for synoptic weather - particularly at the Days 3-7 timeframe. Datasets such as the AIFS and AIGFS were quickly incorporated into product generation software. At the same time, the promise of skillful AI applications for convective rainfall, winter weather, and S2S forecasts has not come to fruition. Coarse resolution, lack of AI-ready datasets, and limited sample sizes appear to have hindered the first generation of AI emulators for these phenomena. The Center also has also developed several aids for ‘first-guess’ guidance on critical products, such as the Excessive Rainfall Outlook and Surface Analysis. Forecasters report these aids have proven helpful for a ‘gut check’ on complicated scenarios, and helping flag any areas or features that were not initially considered (a weak cold front or area of enhanced probabilities) for further investigation. To date, these aids generally lag the skill of the operational products, which benefit from human oversight and intervention, but have aided efficiency. Another key application of AI is the emergence of chatbots as a ‘tap-on-the-shoulder’ assistant. Operational meteorology is rife with complex protocols and thresholds of action that can be difficult to remember or find under urgent circumstances. The Center trained a Gemini assistant with volumes of protocol and technical documentation, and refined it with exploratory testing. The AI assistant has been found to be a helpful check for operational forecasters to use internally – ultimately aiding efficiency. These use cases will be explored further in the talk. Overall, an innovative spirit and the use of verification has aided the rapid and responsible integration of AI into WPC operations - ultimately fostering more accurate forecasts with greater efficiency.

490933.title: Beyond Streamflow: Predicting Flood Impacts Across Scales
490933.authors: Gabriele Villarini, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ
490933.abstract: Advances in meteorological forecasting, distributed hydrologic modeling, remote sensing, and high-performance computing have substantially improved our ability to predict precipitation and streamflow. Yet, the quantities predicted by scientists often differ from the information needed by decision makers, emergency managers, and communities. While streamflow remains a fundamental descriptor of flood hazard, flood impacts ultimately arise from the complex interaction among hydrologic response, inundation dynamics, infrastructure, exposure, and vulnerability. Using examples from flood forecasting, continental-scale hydrologic modeling, reservoir operations, flood inundation mapping, and climate change applications, I highlight the growing need to move beyond the prediction of streamflow toward the prediction of impacts across a range of spatial scales. These examples illustrate both the opportunities and challenges associated with connecting weather, hydrology, infrastructure, and societal vulnerability within a common predictive framework. Key scientific and operational challenges remain, including the representation of human influences on hydrologic systems, the propagation of uncertainty across modeling frameworks, and the development of scalable approaches for supporting both present-day risk management and future climate adaptation.

490936.title: Expanding Lunar and Planetary Space Weather Modeling Capabilities at the CCMC: Supporting Artemis and Moon-to-Mars Exploration
490936.authors: Yihua Zheng, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD; and T. J. Stubbs, C. J. Mertens, G. Gronoff, G. Toth, L. Rastaetter, P. Chamberlin, M. L. Mays, M. Petrenko, C. C. Inko-Tariah, and S. Kumar
490936.abstract: As NASA’s Artemis program and the Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative accelerate the return to the Moon and future crewed missions to Mars, the requirement for robust, validated, and community-accessible space weather modeling has expanded into the deep-space domain. The Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) is addressing this need by onboarding a suite of advanced modeling capabilities designed to characterize the plasma and radiation environments from the lunar surface and its vicinity to the Martian environment by working closely with model developers. A primary focus of this effort is the operationalization of the community-validated Stubbs et al. (2014) current-balance model. The lunar surface is exposed to a dynamic space plasma and solar UV environment that produces hazardous electrostatic charging, with potentials ranging from a few volts positive in sunlight to hundreds or thousands of volts negative near the terminator and during space weather events. These conditions pose direct risks to Artemis crew, EVA suits, and landed infrastructure through electrostatic discharge (ESD) and the mobilization of charged dust. We present the implementation of this model at CCMC as both a Run-on-Request research tool and a real-time diagnostic, augmented by a new secondary electron emission algorithm, coupling to the FISM2 solar irradiance model, and plasma environment specifications from global MHD magnetospheric models. Complementing the surface charging effort, we detail the integration of the Nowcast of Atmospheric Ionizing Radiation System (NAIRAS) and its extension to Mars. Originally developed for aviation safety, NAIRAS is being utilized to provide real-time, and retrospective assessments of ionizing radiation dose rates from galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) and solar energetic particles (SEPs), providing critical information for trans-lunar and trans-martian trajectories and radiation impact assessment at Mars. We will also highlight the integration of the Space Weather Modeling Framework (SWMF) for the Moon and Mars, enabling high-fidelity simulations of the solar wind interaction with the lunar environment and the Martian ionosphere/magnetosphere system.

490937.title: Interior Roof Polygon Creation and Feature Extraction From LiDAR Data for Snow Load Analysis
490937.authors: Brennan Bean, Utah State University, Logan, UT; and J. Newlun, K. Sullivan, Z. Fair, P. Hawkins, D. Tree, A. B. Liel, C. Vuyovich, and A. Albayrak
490937.abstract: Structural failure due to excessive accumulation of snow on roofs presents a persistent risk in cold regions motivating the need for scalable, building-level data on roof geometry and snow accumulation. Existing approaches for characterizing these accumulations, referred to as roof snow loads, are largely survey-based and limited in spatial extent resulting in small sample sizes and substantial uncertainty when extrapolated to broader building inventories. Although LiDAR has been widely adopted for topographic mapping, its application to roof snow load analysis remains largely unexplored. This thesis develops a complete, transferable methodology for extracting interior roof polygons and snow-load-relevant building characteristics from airborne LiDAR data, demonstrated using a high-resolution acquisition in Fairbanks, Alaska. The workflow differences snow-on and snow-off elevation rasters to estimate snow depth and addresses several challenges inherent to LiDAR-based building analysis including (1) missing-not-at-random data within LiDAR swaths, (2) automated identification of interior roof polygons, and (3) robust extraction of roof geometry metrics including building height and roof slope. Roof angle extraction employs a plane fitting approach with per-building uncertainty quantification, and the full pipeline is implemented in a documented, open-source R package called rasterpolygonizer designed to support reproducibility and adaptation to new LiDAR extents. Results demonstrate that high-resolution LiDAR enables reliable extraction of interior roof polygons and associated geometric characteristics across a large and diverse building inventory with hit rates sufficient to drastically increase the population of buildings available for snow-on analysis. The methodology remains effective under moderate reductions in spatial resolution suggesting applicability to existing LiDAR archives collected for purposes beyond snow load analysis. Substantive snow load characterization will ultimately require repeated acquisitions across multiple accumulation events within a season; the contribution of this thesis is the analytical framework that makes such analysis tractable when that data becomes available. Using Fairbanks, Alaska as a model case, this work establishes a defensible, scalable foundation for building-level roof geometry and snow load extraction in cold-region environments.

490938.title: Flavors of Marine Heatwaves on the Northeast U.S. Shelf and Associated Large-Scale Environment
490938.authors: Yifei Fan, Pennsylvania State University, STATE COLLEGE, PA; and K. Chen and L. Li
490938.abstract: The Northeast U.S. continental shelf, home to a highly productive ecosystem and of great economic importance,has emerged as a hotspot of extreme ocean events, particularly marine heatwaves (MHWs). Traditional MHWs identification relies on fixed percentile and duration thresholds applied to predefined domains, with focuses on individual events and their summary statistics. Here, we identify MHWs across the entire Northeast U.S. continental shelf using Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs), an unsupervised machine-learning technique that identifies recurring patterns by clustering similar observations. This pattern-based approach preserves the complex spatial structures of MHWs and their temporal evolution. A 3×6 SOM trained using 2004–2024 daily sea surface temperature (SST) fields from the 1/12° Global Ocean Reanalysis and Simulations (GLORYS) identifies three distinct flavors of MHWs over the Northeast U.S. continental shelf. They are characterized by warming hotspots in the Gulf of Maine (GM), the Mid-Atlantic Bight (MAB), and the South Atlantic Bight (SAB), respectively. The GM-centered MHWs have an average occurrence frequency of 4.9%, with most frequent occurrences during 2012. Analysis of node transition probability reveals that the GM-centered MHW has a typical residence time of 10 days. In addition, over half of the GM-centered events evolve from precursor nodes with statistically significant reductions in surface latent heat flux and a weakening of the subtropical high during the preceding month. This suggests an important role of atmospheric circulation in driving these MHWs through reduced turbulent heat loss, consistent with previous diagnoses of the 2012 case study. In contrast, the SAB-centered MHW exhibits the longest residence time and coincides with subsurface heat extremes. It is accompanied by anomalous northeastward upper-ocean currents (statistically significant), suggesting a role of oceanic heat transport. The least persistent MAB-centered MHW appears to represent a transitional state between the GM- and SAB-centered MHW patterns. These results demonstrate distinct regional expression of MHWs on the Northeast U.S. continental shelf, which cannot be readily identified using traditional threshold-based definition. It thus highlight the value of SOMs as a framework to investigate the spatiotemporal evolution and large-scale environmental drivers MHWs.

490939.title: Evaluating the Performance of CONUS404 Dataset during the 29 June 2012 Derecho
490939.authors: SeanPaul F. Padilla, UCAR, Boulder, CO; University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and Y. Tian and J. H. Kim
490939.abstract: This study aims to evaluate the performance of the 4-km resolution CONUS404 dataset, a hydroclimate reanalysis dataset simulated using the Weather Research and Forecasting Model (WRF), during the June 29th - 30th, 2012, Derecho event in the central and eastern US. To examine the sensitivity of simulated convective environments to spatial resolution and physics suites, a 10-km horizontal resolution control (CTRL) simulation was initialized as a comparative framework against CONUS404. To validate the CONUS404 and CTRL simulation, we compared the model outputs to sounding observations that measured the environment before the MCS developed (Wilmington, OH), and during the event (Sterling, VA). Despite the local kinematic and thermodynamic discrepancies, the CTRL simulation reasonably captured the temporal evolution of the MCS development and the mean vertical profiles of temperature and water vapor. In contrast, the CONUS404 dataset depicted a significantly drier planetary boundary layer (PBL) than the CTRL, leading to a noticeable temporal delay in convective initiation. Furthermore, CONUS404 severely underestimated the low-level jet, resulting in a substantial underprediction of low-level moisture. While CONUS404 and the CTRL simulation use different PBL and microphysics schemes, these results highlight the importance of physics combinations alongside spatial resolution. In future work, we aim to eliminate resolution differences within the CTRL simulation and compare to CONUS404 as a foundational framework.

490941.title: Separating ENSO's Unstable Coupled Feedbacks from Uncoupled Atmospheric Noise with an Interactive Ensemble in CESM2
490941.authors: Cait Martinez, University of Miami, Miami, FL; and B. Kirtman, N. Perlin, and S. Larson
490941.abstract: The El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the dominant mode of climate variability in the tropical Pacific, playing an essential role in modulating the global climate through its numerous teleconnections. ENSO predictability in fully coupled models is limited by the entanglement of unstable coupled feedbacks and uncoupled atmospheric noise, that is, internal atmospheric variability at the air-sea interface that acts as a stochastic forcing of the ocean.Yet ocean dynamics alone cannot account for all ENSO variability: CESM2 ensembles initialized from ENSO-neutral March states readily develop events without any ENSO cycle preconditioning. Perhaps then, the noise is a fundamental component of the physical climate system. Do the characteristics of the stochastic forcing depend on the ENSO state itself? Understanding that role requires a sophisticated characterization of its spatiotemporal structure, but a more fundamental prerequisite remains unaddressed: separating unstable coupled feedbacks from uncoupled atmospheric noise.This work leverages a novel integrated model framework. The interactive ensemble (IE) couples multiple atmospheric realizations to a single ocean through their ensemble-mean surface fluxes, reducing the stochastic forcing while preserving the coupled feedbacks. We present the first implementation of the IE in CESM2 and examine two 10-atmosphere simulations: a CESM2-IE control, and a NoENSO-IE that embeds the IE within a mechanically decoupled framework—the first IE over an ENSO-neutral ocean.We characterize the amplitude, spatial structure, and seasonal cycle of the forcing to diagnose whether it is state-dependent or state-independent, and we quantify how ENSO variance, periodicity, and skewness respond when the forcing is minimized. Because fully coupled models are unconstrained by a priori assumptions about the regime governing ENSO, any regime, or transitions between them, can emerge naturally, opening the possibility that predictability itself varies across climate states or epochs. This nuanced understanding of when and where atmospheric noise most critically limits ENSO predictability is important for both improving seasonal forecasts and disentangling ENSO's dynamical complexities.

490942.title: The Importance of Convective Downdrafts
490942.authors: Kerry A. Emanuel, MIT, New Harbor, ME
490942.abstract: Most atmospheric scientists think of moist convective primarily in terms of updrafts driven by latent heat release. Some early parameterizations omitted downdrafts altogether. Yet observations leave little doubt that downdrafts mass fluxes are of the same order as updraft fluxes, and downdrafts play a central role in interpretive frameworks such as boundary layer quasi-equilibrium. In this talk, inspired by George Kiladis’s work on tropical convective modes, I will examine how downdraft effects on surface winds may influence large-scale tropical disturbances.

490943.title: Modal Interference Drives Madden-Julian Oscillation Diversity
490943.authors: David H Marsico, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and M. Gehne, J. R. Albers, and J. Dias
490943.abstract: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) exhibits diverse behaviors, including "standing," "jumping," and propagating events of varying speeds, as well as occasional decay over the Maritime Continent (the so-called "barrier effect"). This behavioral diversity points to complex underlying physics, complicating efforts to establish a unified dynamical theory. Specifically, understanding the dynamical drivers of these events is hindered both by a limited number of observations and by the difficulty of disentangling tropical signals that have overlapping spatial signatures but evolve on different timescales. To overcome these challenges, we apply a data-driven dynamical filter to separate tropical processes based on their distinct temporal evolutions. Building on recent work that isolated tropical variability into two primary propagating patterns, specifically an "MJO-fast" eigenmode with a 45-day period and an "MJO-slow" eigenmode with a 70-day period, we evaluate the underlying dynamical drivers of diverse MJO events, and the extent to which the drivers seen in observations persist in longer data samples. We find that the apparent diversity of the MJO, including the fast, slow, jumping, and standing types, is governed by modal interference. Specifically, fast, slow, and jumping events result from interference between the MJO-fast and MJO-slow eigenmodes, with the MJO-slow eigenmode modulating the amplitude and propagation speed of the total MJO signal. Meanwhile, standing events are characterized by a set of "fast-decaying" eigenmodes that span a continuum of frequencies and represent synoptic-scale variability. These modes act to effectively mask the underlying, weakly propagating signal of the MJO-fast eigenmode. By framing MJO evolution as the consequence of overlapping dynamical modes, we provide a unified framework for understanding the diverse characteristics of the MJO.

490946.title: Synoptic-Scale Moisture Modes in a Convection-Permitting Aquaplanet Experiment: Evidence and Relationship to ITCZ Breakdown (Invited Presentation)
490946.authors: Rosimar Rios-Berrios, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and R. Rotunno and J. A. Ocegueda Sanchez
490946.abstract: Westward-propagating disturbances are fundamental for organizing tropical convection and modulating precipitation. While classic theories attribute their existence to dry dynamics with a reduced effective static stability, recent evidence suggests moisture-flow interactions are the primary driver. Isolating these mechanisms in nature is difficult; therefore, this study investigates them using a convection-permitting aquaplanet simulation. Previously, aquaplanet experiments identified ambiguous ``advective disturbances" that seemingly lacked the rotational characteristics of standard equatorial waves. Using a composite approach, we find that these disturbances exhibit coherent cyclonic circulation coupled with moisture and precipitation anomalies. Moisture variability dominates the rainfall and thermodynamic variability of these disturbances, supporting our hypothesis. While vorticity and moisture budgets support the growth of these disturbances via moisture-vortex instability, their decay is driven by non-linear eddy processes not accounted for in existing theory. These findings resolve previous ambiguity regarding aquaplanet wave classification and demonstrate that westward-propagating moisture modes are fundamental tropical phenomena arising from the interaction between convection and meridional moisture gradients. To determine whether these moisture modes affect tropical cyclogenesis, this study will also explore the link between westward-propagating moisture modes and ITCZ breakdown in the aquaplanet simulations.

490948.title: Tracking Cold Front Precipitation in the CoURAGE Domain
490948.authors: Matthew Woody, Sonoma State University, Rohnert Park, CA; and M. Deng
490948.abstract: Cold fronts are synoptic-scale events that affect tens of millions of people, yet their precipitation effects remain difficult to predict. Improving predictions of precipitation location, duration, and intensity supports Department of Energy (DOE) efforts to evaluate weather models and strengthen energy resilience. Our study aims to improve understanding of cold front precipitation and provide constraints for predicting how terrain contributes to differences among fronts. We combined Next-Generation Weather Radar (NEXRAD) precipitation observations with surface measurements from the DOE Atmospheric Radiation Measurement User Facility’s Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE). Using cold-front passage times identified from CoURAGE measurements at three sites, we retained 18 multi-site events and tracked precipitation as the fronts moved eastward through the domain. We analyzed events using an Orienteering Tape Recorder (OTR) diagram, which tracks how radar-observed conditions evolve over time along a fixed direction. Because conventional thresholding could not isolate the frontal region from background weather, we developed an OTR-based method that detected the leading edge and extended a selection region according to its slope. We combined observations across fronts to examine how precipitation properties varied with location and surface type. We observed precipitation enhancement over mountainous regions and possible modification near bay breeze boundaries. Urban transect portions generally had lower maximum rain rates, accumulation, and duration than mountain portions despite comparable mean rain rates, suggesting shorter-lived precipitation and possibly greater spatial localization, although precipitation area was not directly evaluated. These findings provide benchmarks for evaluating how DOE-supported weather models represent cold front precipitation across heterogeneous environments.

490949.title: Diagnosing Ocean Memory in ENSO Initial Conditions: Insights from CESM2 Release Experiments
490949.authors: Cait Martinez, University of Miami, Miami, FL; and B. Kirtman, S. Larson, and R. W. Payne Jr.
490949.abstract: Subsurface preconditioning—anomalous ocean heat content in the equatorial Pacific—is widely considered necessary for ENSO event development, but not all ENSO variability can be explained by such deterministic dynamics. Recent studies reveal that ENSO-like events can initiate and grow independently of preceding events, preconditioning, or large-scale wind stress triggers. Meanwhile, forecasts initialized from preconditioned states exhibit reduced spread and shifted outcome distributions. The extent to which this "ocean memory" constrains event evolution, however, remains unresolved. We test this in CESM2 with a suite of release experiment ensembles initialized from contrasting climate states within a predictability experiment context. The initial states come from long control simulations in which tropical Pacific wind stress is prescribed to manually control the frequency and amplitude of the ENSO cycle. This mechanically decoupled model (MDM) framework builds subsurface preconditioning of a chosen character: neutral states with suppressed ENSO, and recharged and discharged states from prescribed cycles differing in frequency and amplitude. From each, ensemble members are initialized on March 1 and integrated twelve months fully coupled and fully unrestrained from the prescribed cycle that built their initial conditions. Events readily develop from the neutral states without any preconditioning, while members initialized from strongly preconditioned states often evolve opposite to their subsurface signal by December. This is a stark departure from previous work where preconditioning reliably constrains outcomes, suggesting the initial conditions carry not only an anomalous subsurface state but an imprint of the oscillation that produced it. What, exactly, in these initial conditions carries that ocean memory forward? In this talk, we explore what characteristics of the preconditioned initial state determine whether ensemble members develop into events that match or oppose the subsurface signal. Understanding these sensitivities is critical for improving seasonal prediction when preconditioning should theoretically provide the greatest predictive advantage.

490950.title: Beyond The Lab Manual: Authentic Research as a Driver of Curriculum Innovation in 2YC - 4YC Atmospheric and Environmental Science Programs
490950.authors: Melanie Will-Cole, Central New Mexico Community College, Albuquerque, NM
490950.abstract: Community colleges (2YCs) are vital to building a diverse atmospheric and environmental science workforce, yet two-year students rarely have early access to authentic research. This presentation details a scalable, hybrid model that merges apprentice research with course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) across two-year and four-year (4YC) institutions. By pairing core atmospheric content with active learning and community-engaged research, this framework strengthens scientific identity, deepens conceptual understanding, and improves STEM retention. The curriculum guides students through the complete research lifecycle: formulating hypotheses, conducting literature reviews, designing sampling protocols, collecting field measurements, analyzing data, creating visualizations, and presenting findings. Replacing traditional cook-book labs with inquiry-driven fieldwork and collaborative problem-solving provides students with hands-on practice in critical thinking and scientific reasoning. We present actionable strategies for selecting semester- and year-long projects that balance scientific rigor, local relevance, instrumentation limits, and feasibility. Example topics include urban heat islands, air quality, wildfire smoke, microclimate dynamics, drought impacts, and local climate resilience. Key emphasis is placed on developing foundational research skills, including critical evaluation of literature and data visualization using GIS, statistical software, and scientific graphing tools. Finally, we explore pathways to sustain these research initiatives through multi-institutional and external funding partnerships, including NSF (IUSE, ATE, REU), NOAA, NASA, state agencies, and local industry. Adaptable delivery models, such as modular field experiences, hybrid courses, learning communities, and faculty mentoring networks, demonstrate how institutions can broaden access to authentic research while equipping a modern workforce for careers across the geosciences.

490951.title: Multisensor Observations of Environmental and Land-Surface Controls on Isolated Convective Cell Evolution
490951.authors: Oluwafemi Omitusa, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook , NY; and K. E. McKeown, N. Allwayin, M. Oue, and P. Kollias
490951.abstract: Deep convective cells play an important role in the vertical transport of heat, moisture, and momentum. Their evolution is controlled by interactions among storm dynamics, the surrounding environment, and the underlying land surface. No single observing system, however, captures all aspects of the convective lifecycle. Radar resolves storm structure, geostationary satellites characterize cloud-top evolution, lightning observations document electrical activity, and environmental datasets describe the thermodynamic conditions that support storm development. Combining these observations provides a more complete view of how isolated convective cells initiate, intensify, and dissipate. This study uses multisensor observations collected in Huntsville, Alabama, between June and August 2025 to investigate the evolution of isolated warm-season convective cells. Convective cells are identified and tracked using gridded radar observations and classified as isolated, merging, or splitting based on their interactions with neighboring cells. Radar observations are then combined with geostationary satellite, lightning, thermodynamic, and land-cover datasets to examine how storm evolution varies across different environments and land-surface types. The presentation will examine how multisensor observations improve the characterization of isolated convective cell lifecycles and quantify the relative roles of environmental conditions and land-surface characteristics in storm evolution. These results demonstrate the value of multisensor data fusion for understanding convective processes and provide a framework for future studies of storm predictability and land–atmosphere interactions.

490952.title: The Radiometric Imperative in a Congested Spectrum Environment - Keeping the Earth Visible to Passive Band Sensors
490952.abstract: Preserving radio frequency (RF) spectrum for Earth Exploration-Satellite Service (EESS) passive bands is critical for weather forecasting and environmental intelligence. Passive microwave sensors detect natural thermal emissions governed by immutable physical laws and molecular resonance (e.g., absorption at 50–60 GHz and water vapor at 23.8 GHz). These non-relocatable measurements are essential inputs for Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models. However, expanding commercial wireless services—including 5G mm Wave deployments, Direct-to-Device (D2D) mega-constellations, and reallocations under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) in bands like 1675–1680 MHz—threaten passive sensing by elevating global thermal noise floors and causing radio frequency interference (RFI). Operating at high sensitivity (), passive radiometers are acutely vulnerable to active out-of-band emissions (OOBE) and aggregate noise. Per Recommendation ITU-R RS.2017, interference exceeding 20% of the minimum discernible power change () corrupts data integrity. On-orbit analyses, such as Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) observations over urban centers, confirm 5G-induced RFI bias. Furthermore, regulatory models like "light licensing" fail for passive protection because they address co-channel jamming rather than aggregate noise accumulation. To address these risks, the IEEE GRSS FARS Technical Committee is pursuing joint technical and regulatory mitigations. Key initiatives include developing the IEEE P4006 standard for RFI impact assessment. Internationally, joint preparations for WRC-27 focus on enforcing Resolution 750 unwanted emission limits (AIs 1.1, 1.3), protecting raw downlink spectrum (AI 1.7), and securing sea surface temperature allocations (AI 1.19). Essential priorities include requiring aggregate interference modeling for satellite mega-constellations, establishing standards for satellite Unintended Electro-Magnetic Radiation (UEMR), extending regulatory review cycles, and deploying on-board DSP RFI mitigation across passive sensor hosting satellite architectures to safeguard NWP accuracy and public safety.

490954.title: Satellite Use of DCS Concept Validation: Operational Results, Organizational Transition, and Path Forward
490954.abstract: The Data Collection System (DCS) has served as a vital environmental data relay since 1975, utilizing UHF (401–402 MHz) uplinks to geostationary satellites including GOES, Meteosat, and Himawari. The Satellite DCS Use Concept Validation Project—a collaborative initiative between NOAA, NASA Ames Research Center, and international partners—was established to evaluate whether Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) smallsat platforms could interface with these geostationary receivers to deliver continuous, low-bandwidth (100–1200 bps) data links for spaceborne sensors and hazard monitoring. Flight validation progressed through NASA’s TechEdSat (TES) nanosatellite series. Following initial tests on TES-8 and the proof-of-concept demonstration on TES-10 in 2020, the TES-11 mission (launched July 2024 into a 520 km polar orbit) achieved full operational success. TES-11 transmitted thousands of error-free DCS messages through GOES-16/18 and Meteosat-9/10/12 transponders. Key technical milestones included validating dynamic pre-Doppler shift compensation algorithms, closing links at transmit powers as low as 1 , and diagnosing multipath Earth reflection phenomena (manifesting as spectral ghosting over land and smearing over ocean surfaces). Having successfully demonstrated LEO-to-GEO link feasibility, characterized orbital propagation mechanics, and fulfilled its primary joint research objectives, the NOAA/NESDIS Office of Systems Architecture and Engineering (SAE) has ended its participation in the project. The accumulated technology heritage and engineering findings now provide a baseline for future operational stakeholders and space architecture developers. The recommended path forward highlights advancing LEO-to-GEO communication architectures through the Enhanced DCP (EDCP) standard, incorporating Reed-Solomon forward error correction and dynamic baud rate switching to mitigate multipath interference. Future priorities also include establishing a dedicated 21 kHz spectral reservation within the 401–402 MHz band to prevent co-channel impacts on terrestrial weather sensors, as well as developing geostationary return-link commanding capabilities to enable bi-directional control of orbital environmental constellations.

490957.title: Short-Term Solar Influences via the MJO on the Northern Hemisphere Storm Tracks
490957.authors: Lon L. Hood, Univ. of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and C. A. Hoopes and T. J. Galarneau
490957.abstract: Prior work has shown that the Northern Hemisphere storm tracks are modulated by the tropical Madden-Julian oscillation (MJO) and that the modulation is strongest during the easterly phase of the stratospheric quasi-biennial oscillation (Guo et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018). Prior work has also identified a ~27-day solar rotational modulation of the MJO and its eastward propagation (e.g., Hoopes et al., 2024). Here, lagged composite analyses of storm tracks relative to 126 strong solar UV peaks occurring under solar maximum conditions during the northern cool season (Nov. to April) over a 68-year period demonstrate a significant weakening and southward shift of the N.H. storm tracks, especially in the North Pacific, near and following UV peaks. This occurred for more than 64% of the 126 strong UV peak dates, significant at 97% confidence. During the most recent solar maximum, of 23 UV peaks, 16 had a weakened and southward shifted storm track on the date of the peak. Evidence is presented supporting the hypothesis that reduced MJO convection in the Indian Ocean region occurring on average prior to solar UV peaks produces a positive Rossby wave source that results in a cyclonic circulation anomaly in the North Pacific, tending to suppress the westerly zonal wind leading to less baroclinic wave activity, thereby causing the weakening and southward shift of the storm tracks. These results highlight the need for a better understanding of how stratospheric influences (QBO and solar) can produce significant differences in MJO amplitude and eastward propagation. 1 Guo, Y., Shinoda, T., Lin, J., and Chang, E. K. M. (2017). Journal of Climate, 30, 4799-4818. https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469(2004)061%3C0023:TEOVIJ%3E2.0.CO;2. 2 Wang, J., Kim, H.-M., Chang, E. K. M., & Son, S.-W. (2018), Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 123, 3976-3992. https://doi.org/10.1029/2017JD027977 3 Hoopes, C. A., Hood, L.L., & Galarneau, T. J., Jr. (2024). Geophysical Research Letters, 51, e2023GL107701. https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GL107701

490959.title: Preliminary results of applying Stochastically Perturbed Parameterizations (SPP) to a cumulus convection scheme in MPAS
490959.authors: Haiqin Li, CIRES/CU at NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; and G. A. Grell, N. Wang, S. Freitas, and C. Evans
490959.abstract: Cumulus convection parameterization is essential for representing sub-grid scale convective processes that significantly influence large-scale atmospheric circulations and precipitation forecasts across the gray-zone resolutions. However, significant uncertainties remain in the process representation of the convection parameterization. Recently, the Grell-Freitas scheme (GF) has been generalized as the Grell-Freitas-Li (GFL, https://github.com/NOAA-GSL/GFL) submodule for different community modeling systems, including the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS), the Weather Research & Forecasting (WRF) model, and the Common Community Physics Package (CCPP). In this study, we implement the Stochastically Perturbed Parameterizations (SPP) framework in the MPAS model, and apply stochastic perturbations to the momentum transport, convective mass flux, and closure assumptions of GFL. The stochastic implementation preserves the mass-conserving properties of the GFL parameterization. We present preliminary results evaluating the impacts of these convective stochastic perturbations on MPAS forecasts. In addition, we introduce a new Community Convective Clouds Parameterization (C3P), which builds upon the GFL framework, and these convective stochastic features will also be available in C3P.

490961.title: Applying Reason's Swiss Cheese Model to Studying Weather-related Disasters: An Update
490961.authors: John M. Lanicci, University of South Alabama, Mobile, AL
490961.abstract: At the inaugural symposium on Disaster and Emergency Management held at the 2026 AMS Annual Meeting, the first author proposed the idea of employing Reason’s Swiss Cheese Model of system accident investigation (Reason, 1990, 2000) to weather-related disasters (Lanicci, 2026). To review, the model, which has been used to investigate aircraft accidents, large industrial accidents, and most recently, medical system failures, compares a complex human system to slices of Swiss cheese, where individual slices represent layers of ‘defense’ against human and system errors, and the alignment of errors (Swiss cheese holes lining up) produces a major accident. At the talk, the first author posed the question “Do weather-related disasters represent system failures?” Given the community’s enthusiastic reception to this idea and the interest in examining significant weather events in a system-like setting (e.g., Philips, 2026), we have decided to pursue the application of the Swiss Cheese Model to the 27 April 2011 tornado outbreak in the southeastern U.S. as a test case. The second author, a junior undergraduate meteorology student, is presently conducting the study in several stages. The first stage is a literature review of the event, from the perspectives of the meteorology itself (e.g., Knupp et al., 2014), NWS operations (NWS, 2011), and social science aspects of the case (e.g., Klockow et al., 2014; Wallace et al., 2015). Following this phase, in which the lit review essentially doubles as the data collection, applications of the Swiss Cheese Model in various disciplines will be examined and analyzed. We hope to be able to study applications in aviation and medicine, with the assistance of subject matter experts in these fields. We hope that these conversations will help inform our instantiation of the model for this case. This talk will outline the progress made thus far and describe some of the challenges we are currently facing. Here are a few examples. First (and perhaps most important) is the determination of slices, holes, and hole alignment, since this is the first time the model is being applied to our field. For instance, in this outbreak, there were 247 documented fatalities in Alabama alone (Chiu et al., 2013); how will the vulnerabilities be depicted? Will we need multiple models, or will one comprehensive model be sufficient? Another challenge is the question of whether there is an implied time dimension in this application of the model where different 'slices' of the model operate in some type of sequential order, or if it makes more sense for the model to represent an overall ‘snapshot’ of events on that day. Yet another challenge has to do with the fact that this case occurred over 15 years ago. We must ensure that the formulation of the model depicts the state-of-the-art and circumstances that existed at that time. To help us maintain accuracy in this aspect of the study, it may be necessary to conduct structured interviews of key personnel who were working on that day as part of the study methodology.
