490962.title: Twists and Turns in George Kiladis’ Research Path
490962.authors: Gerald Allen Meehl, NCAR, Boulder, CO
490962.abstract: George has a broad range of science interests that have steered him along a winding road through his very interesting and multi-faceted career, but one primary focus of his research involves tropical waves and the MJO. I learned this when I first met George when we were both grad students at CU in the mid-1980s. During evenings and weekends working on our research at NCAR, we discussed various science topics as well as our shared interest in hikes in the Rockies west of Boulder. Shortly after we finished our PhDs, a new field project was being proposed to take place in the early 1990s called TOGA COARE. We first heard about this at the AMS annual meeting in February of 1988. The objective of TOGA COARE was to study air-sea interaction and convective processes and systems, including the MJO, over the western Pacific warm pool. This was right down George’s alley of course, so George and I, along with Klaus Weickmann, submitted a total of eight versions of a research proposal over three years (from 1989 to 1992) until the proposal was finally funded in early 1992 (“Synoptic-scale convective events and westerly wind bursts in the western Pacific”). We proposed to deploy four of NCAR’s Integrated Sounding System (ISS) units on remote islands in the equatorial western Pacific to obtain unique vertical profiles of winds and temperature to complement the large-scale array of existing radiosonde stations in the western Pacific. Our goal during TOGA-COARE was to obtain better observations of the large-scale structure and evolution of westerly wind bursts and MJO events as they transitioned from the Indian Ocean to the Pacific over the warm pool region. The TOGA-COARE ISS observations, supplemented by other radiosonde observations, directly led us to write four subsequent papers as well as a follow-up TOGA COARE proposal that George led in 1995. During the TOGA-COARE Intensive Observing Period in late 1992 and early 1993 at the operations center in Townsville, Australia, we met a very perceptive Australian undergrad student named Matt Wheeler. The funding from our TOGA-COARE grant enabled us to subsequently bring Matt to Boulder where he received a PhD from the University of Colorado. His work with George on tropical waves formed the foundation for a number of novel insights that produced, for example, the now iconic “Wheeler-Kiladis diagram” (Convectively-coupled equatorial waves: Analysis of clouds and temperature in the wavenumber-frequency domain. Wheeler and Kiladis, J. Atmos. Sci., 1999). In addition to subseasonal timescale processes, another facet of George’s evolving research path involved seasonal to interannual and longer timescale phenomena involving ENSO and Southern Hemisphere climate. He and I were both mentored on these topics by NCAR scientist Harry van Loon. Harry’s keen interests and insights into physical processes in the Earth system inspired us to attempt to understand in greater detail the processes and mechanisms in the system. George’s work with Harry was evidenced by his authorship on parts 7 and 8 of Harry’s “parts is parts” series of papers on ENSO (The Southern Oscillation. Part VII: Meteorological anomalies over the Indian and Pacific sectors associated with the extremes of the oscillation, Kiladis and van Loon, Mon. Wea. Rev., 1988; The Southern Oscillation. Part VIII: Model sensitivity to SST anomalies in the tropical and subtropical regions of the South Pacific Convergence Zone, von Storch, van Loon, and Kiladis, J. Climate, 1988) as well as a foundational paper on the SPCZ (Origin of the South Pacific Convergence Zone, Kiladis, von Storch, and van Loon, J. Climate, 1989).

490973.title: Aerosol Impacts on Convective Storms in the Texas Gulf Coast: Insights from the Regionally Refined SCREAM (Invited Presentation)
490973.authors: Youtong Zheng, University of Houston, Houston, TX; and R. K. T. Oware, D. Rosenfeld, Y. Zhang, H. Y. Ma, P. A. Bogenschutz, J. Zhang, H. Beydoun, S. Xie, and C. Tao
490973.abstract: A widely debated hypothesis is that human-generated air pollution can make storms more intense worldwide, a phenomenon commonly known as “aerosol invigoration”. Coastal urban regions are especially vulnerable to this effect. The sea breeze circulation across the coast can initiate isolated convective cells that are exposed to urban air pollution, increasing the likelihood of aerosol invigoration. These aerosol-invigorated storms can cause severe hydrological events that significantly influence the economy and livelihoods of densely populated coastal urban regions. Therefore, there is a pressing need to improve the representation of air pollution’s impact on coastal storms in global climate models. Unfortunately, current global climate models cannot represent this effect due to the coarse grid resolution that fails to capture the intricate details of storm dynamics and microphysics. With advancements in computational power, a new generation of climate models has emerged, allowing for more detailed and accurate simulations at the kilometer scale. One such model is the DOE's Simple Cloud-Resolving E3SM Atmosphere Model (SCREAM). This presentation uses the regionally refined version of SCREAM to investigate the aerosol impacts on costal storms for a “golden” sea-breeze convection case during the DOE TRACER field campaign. We explore possible mechanisms including suppression of warm-rain formation, delayed precipitation onset, changes in condensate and latent-heating profiles, and altered updraft structure.

490976.title: Air-Sea Flux Parameterization - a Data-Driven Approach and Implementation In a Coupled Climate Model
490976.abstract: Accurately quantifying air-sea fluxes is important for understanding air-sea interactions and improving coupled weather and climate systems. This study introduces a probabilistic framework to represent the uncertain nature of air-sea fluxes. Assuming Gaussian distributions conditioned on the input variables, we use artificial neural networks and eddy-covariance measurement data to estimate the mean and variance by minimizing negative log-likelihood loss. The trained neural networks provide alternative mean flux estimates to existing bulk algorithms, and quantify the uncertainty around the mean estimates. Stochastic parameterization of air-sea turbulent fluxes can be constructed by sampling from the predicted distributions. I will discuss test results first in a single-column forced ocean model and then in the coupled Community Earth System Model.

490985.title: Building an AI-Ready Calibration/Validation Reference Knowledge Base for JPSS: Automated Knowledge Preservation Across ATMS, VIIRS, CrIS, and OMPS
490985.authors: Manik Bali, Global Science and Technology, Lanham, MD; and S. Iacovazzi and L. Zhou
490985.abstract: Calibration and validation (cal/val) records for the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) programs instruments ATMS, VIIRS, CrIS, and OMPS are fragmented across NASA and NOAA/STAR. As the LEO missions extend from JPSS/S-NPP through JPSS/J4 and Quicksounder, this dispersion erodes traceability between algorithms, coefficients, and product versions, and risks permanent loss of institutional knowledge during staff and contractor transitions. We present the LEO Science Cal/Val Reference Knowledge Base (KB), a NOAA-centered framework for consolidating and preserving cal/val documentation and derived calibration products. This KB effort is neither a science investigation nor a replacement for operational archives, and excludes the approximately 270 TB of pre- and post-launch test data held elsewhere. Establishing AI readiness across four dimensions, data quality, infrastructure, workforce skills, and governance, enabled the KB’s defining capability: automated manifest generation of thousands of files using ITAR compliant AI models. In place of manual cataloging, we developed a pipeline comprising repository scan, folder-structure analysis, metadata extraction, and description generation using an ITAR-compliant large language model. Cataloging of ATMS holdings (~400 records) fell from 2.5 days to approximately 10 minutes; VIIRS holdings exceeding 7,000 records were cataloged in 30 minutes, work previously estimated at several weeks. The resulting manifests permit quantitative characterization of the archive. The VIIRS library is 86% pre-launch testing material (1,703 records), supplemented by 40 waivers, 17 look-up-table records, and 205 on-orbit validation records. ATMS inventories are led by Quick Sounder (113) and J3 (107), with S-NPP (35) representing a compact, mature baseline. The validated ATMS structure now serves as the template for CrIS and OMPS repository construction. We describe a prototype discovery interface, a defined path toward final storage, and planned AI capabilities including completeness monitoring, missing-record identification, risk and schedule tracking, and semantic question-answering over the CAL/VAL records.

490987.title: Trends in Precipitation Pattern Controls for Windward Hawaii in a Warming Climate
490987.authors: Aren Wang, Cornell University, Kailua, HI
490987.abstract: Trade winds are the source of much of the moisture that results in rainfall for the windward coasts and slopes of the Hawaiian islands. These winds form when warm equatorial air rises and travels poleward, eventually sinking and traveling back equatorward in a cycle known as a Hadley cell. When this air is orographically lifted by mountains, water vapor condenses into clouds, often resulting in precipitation. A warming climate is projected to expand Hadley cells poleward, but uncertainties remain as to how trade winds (and therefore rainfall) will be affected. Previous studies focused overwhelmingly on the speed and frequency of trade winds to predict changes in rainfall (Fandrich et al. 2022; Garza et al. 2012) without considering subsidence and inversion height. This study aims to forge a multifaceted understanding of how anthropogenic climate change will impact trade winds and rainfall for the Hawaiian islands. Findings will empower Hawaiians and those dependent on trade winds to become more climate-resilient. In this study, we investigated how long-term environmental changes affect the primary drivers of windward rainfall in Hawaii using ERA5 reanalysis, airport station data, and radiosonde observations from 1979 to 2024. We used ground-based NCEI data from Hawaii sensors in airports in Hilo (19.7°N, 155.0°W) and Lihue (22.0°N, 159.3°W). Using ERA5 data for the Hilo and Lihue regions, we analyzed five regulating factors of rain showers related to trade winds: frequency, speed, low-level moisture, subsidence, and inversion height. Subsidence and inversion height are phenomena directly associated with trade winds in Hawaii and the rest of the outer tropics. We calculated that the fraction of days per year with winds from the trade direction (estimated at 45° - 120°) is linearly related to the total annual rainfall. In Hilo, we also found trade wind speed positively correlated with precipitation. Further findings included a weakly negative correlation between low-level moisture and annual rainfall in both Lihue and Hilo. We posit that this is due to strong surface moisture being trapped by subsidence (downward air movement), which would lower the inversion height and hinder orographic cloud formation. We confirmed this hypothesis with our finding that lower inversion height and high subsidence are robustly correlated with reduced rainfall. Overall, our results show a significant shift in trade wind strength and moisture, with a lowering inversion height and subsidence zone. Of the five controls we analyzed, we found inversion height to be the primary driver of rainfall totals in Hawaii. This study will contribute to the climate field by highlighting the importance of other variables beyond wind speed in predicting rainfall. Our results will give more accurate insight into how climate change will hydrologically impact Hawaiians as well as other residents of the outer tropics. These findings will also help governments and communities to create healthier outcomes for people with climate risks such as drought in mind.

490992.title: Modernization of the Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) Globally-Distributed Data Infrastructure
490992.presenter: Hoffman, Forrest M., PhD, Earth System Science
490992.authors: Forrest M. Hoffman, PhD, Earth System Science, ORNL, Oak Ridge, TN; and P. Kershaw, S. Ames, R. Ananthakrishnan, S. Kindermann, C. Pagé, A. Radhakrishnan, and A. Robinson
490992.abstract: The Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) is an international consortium that delivers a global network of enterprise data systems for the management, dissemination, and analysis of Earth system model output and related forcing, reanalysis, downscaled, and observational data. The consortium also develops and maintains the necessary software for the network. Constructed and operated primarily in support of the WCRP Working Group on Coupled Modelling’s (WGCM’s) Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP), ESGF infrastructure catalogs, stores and delivers Earth system model output to the scientific community for Earth system science research. The majority of the data, in excess of 10 petabytes for the recent CMIP phase 6 (CMIP6), are open and freely accessible to stakeholders, industry, and the general public. To better serve the community and in preparation for CMIP7 Assessment Fast Track, the ESGF consortium has modernized the software architecture by adopting new data management standards and improving performance and resilience. The new software tools and capabilities are incrementally deployed on expanding storage and analysis hardware infrastructure. System enhancements include a new core architecture based on synchronized indexes that use the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalogs (STAC) specification; a message queueing system to manage data publication, replication, and retraction; more user authentication options; additional data access and transfer technologies; server-side data subsetting and summary product generation; and, at some regional data centers, user computing platforms that enable data-proximate computing via JupyterHub environments. With an expanding focus on artificial intelligence, the ESGF team has developed an agentic large language model-based ESGF Assistant for data discovery and access and is testing data storage and access configurations that enable optimal automated data analytics and foundation model training over wide area networks.

490993.title: Using the SSEC Portable Atmospheric Research Center (SPARC) as a Centerpiece of a Field Study Course
490993.authors: Timothy J. Wagner, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and J. Gero, Z. Buckholtz, E. Olson, M. R. Hilario, and M. Mulligan
490993.abstract: When students gain hands-on experiences with atmospheric observations in support of authentic research experiences, it can foster a lifelong connection to scientific inquiry. The Space Science and Engineering Center (SSEC) Portable Atmospheric Research Center (SPARC) is a mobile instrument laboratory designed to observe the vertical structure of the atmosphere with a level of detail that is challenging to achieve with conventional platforms. SPARC has been deployed in a variety of challenging environments to monitor the evolution of the atmospheric state as impacted by numerous phenomena, from severe weather to solar eclipses. However, SPARC has participated in several educationally-focused deployments to help provide some of these real-world unique research opportunities. As a member of the National Science Foundation’s Community Instruments and Facilities (CIF) program, educational institutions (including two-year universities and primarily undergraduate institutions) can request SPARC as the cornerstone of a classroom experience. SPARC scientists first work with instructors and their students to craft a plan to integrate the facility into the class. With deployment, these staffers will then be available to lecture in the classroom and to train students how to operate the instruments and interrogate the data. After the field phase, the team passes along processed and quality-controlled data so that students can carry out their own investigation of the study they helped design. This presentation will illustrate some of SPARC’s past successes as a classroom tool and discuss how interested instructors can work with the SPARC team to request and deploy this valuable tool. Feedback from previous instructors and students will also be shared.

490994.title: SPARC: A Deployable Mobile Platform for Intensive PBL Observations
490994.authors: Timothy J. Wagner, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and J. Gero, Z. Buckholtz, M. R. Hilario, and M. Mulligan
490994.abstract: The University of Wisconsin Space Science and Engineering Center (SSEC) Portable Atmospheric Radiation Center (SPARC) is a ground-based mobile instrument platform designed for intense studies of the planetary boundary layer (PBL) and lower troposphere. With multiple remote sensing instruments, including a hyperspectral infrared spectroradiometer for measuring thermodynamic profiles, a Doppler lidar for wind profiling, and a high spectral resolution lidar (HSRL) for measuring aerosol profiles, SPARC is capable of providing high-temporal resolution observations that capture the evolution of the atmospheric state in fine detail. SPARC also hosts in situ instruments, including radiosonde launches and surface meteorology observations. The recent addition of a Microorifice Uniform Deposit Impactor (MOUDI) to directly measure surface aerosol type and concentration expands SPARC’s capabilities for more direct investigation of air quality. SPARC is a National Science Foundation (NSF) Community Instrument and Facility (CIF), which means it is available to researchers and academics for scientific and educational deployments. As part of the CIF program, SPARC has been deployed to environments as diverse as the shores of the Great Lakes and the heart of a total solar eclipse to observe the evolution of the PBL in order to better understand key PBL processes. This presentation will showcase some of SPARC’s previous research successes as well as demonstrate how members of the scientific community can apply to include SPARC as a key component of their research projects or classrooms.

490998.title: Validation of Contrail Model Predictions with Surface-Based Instrumentation
490998.authors: Timothy J. Wagner, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and T. Dean, T. Abbott, and M. Shapiro
490998.abstract: Contrail models, like the Contrail Cirrus Prediction (CoCiP) model, are an important tool for diagnosing the initiation, evolution, and dissipation of contrails. CoCiP generates contrails from individual flights when appropriate environmental conditions are present and uses numerical weather prediction (NWP) output to propagate and disperse them with time. However, validating CoCiP output can be challenging due to the paucity of microphysical and radiative measurements. The global network of Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) ground-based atmospheric observatories have the infrastructure required to serve as contrail observation laboratories. Instruments such as all-sky cameras, lidars, microwave and infrared radiometers, and cloud radars all monitor clouds and the rest of the atmospheric state at very fine temporal resolutions. Mature retrieval algorithms can be applied to these collocated observations to retrieve valuable quantities like thermodynamic structure of the atmosphere and cloud microphysical characteristics. Observations from these instruments and their associated retrieved quantities can be used to evaluate how well CoCiP is simulating contrail characteristics. A year’s worth of observations from the ARM Southern Great Plains site in north central Oklahoma, USA, was compared against CoCiP for the same location. These observations show that CoCiP does well at predicting the overall timing and optical depth of contrails, though it may be overestimating the rate at which contrails subside after formation. Additional results depicting the performance of CoCiP as a function of contrail age will also be presented. It is important to note that results are limited to sky conditions that are otherwise clear, as ground-based instruments are unable to view contrails when lower-level clouds lie in between.

490999.title: When the Lights Went Out: Modeled and Observed Characteristics of the Evolution of the Planetary Boundary Layer During Solar Eclipses
490999.authors: Timothy J. Wagner, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and D. D. Turner, J. M. Simonson, G. N. Raghunathan, and T. Heus
490999.abstract: Solar eclipses provide a unique opportunity to investigate the processes at work in the planetary boundary layer (PBL) during diurnal transitions. The eclipse acts as an accelerated diurnal cycle, in which a rapid sunset and sunrise follow in quick succession. Coincident with the diminished insolation during the eclipse’s growth phase, observations indicate a collapse in PBL height, the reduction of low-level turbulence, and the development of a weak “nocturnal” inversion. As the sunlight returns, we see a rapid return of the turbulent mixing, the erosion of the nocturnal inversion, and regrowth of the PBL height back to its pre-eclipse level. However, these impacts are not experienced equally in all environments. Maritime, polar, and snow-covered locations all experience reduced impacts on PBL evolution when compared to dry continental locations, thus showing the importance of land surface-atmosphere interactions for these events (and by extension, for evening and morning transitions in general). By investigating eclipses in such detail, we are thus able to learn more about the processes underlying more typical evening and morning transitions. This presentation will show the behavior of the thermodynamic and kinematic characteristics of the evolution of the PBL during several North American solar eclipses as observed by ground-based high temporal resolution instruments, including hyperspectral infrared radiometers and Doppler lidars. These results will be accompanied by output from large eddy simulations and single column models to further quantify the impact that solar eclipses have on the local environment.

491000.title: Hadley Cell vs. Surface Forcing: Modeling Inversion Height in a Warming Pacific
491000.authors: Aren Wang, Cornell University, Kailua, HI
491000.abstract: The proximity of the inversion height to the Lifted Condensation Level (LCL) is the most crucial factor in determining rainfall for Hawaii. How climate change will affect inversion height is uncertain due to two main conflicting factors. On one hand, an expanding Hadley cell could increase bulk subsidence and depress the inversion layer, decreasing rainfall. Conversely, the increase in evaporation of ocean water could release latent heat, lifting the layer and potentially increasing extreme events. This study analyzes the relative strength of these two forcings affecting the trade wind inversion, a heavily overlooked variable controlling Hawaiian rainfall. We build on our prior research into trade winds and give insight into better forecasting of rainfall anomalies so that Hawaiian governmental and community organizations may better adapt to climate change. We develop a model that predicts inversion height, focusing on trade-wind regime days to eliminate synoptic precipitation events like Kona lows and hurricanes. We use ERA5 data (1950-to-present), quantifying conditions along the trade wind direction toward the Hawaiian Islands. Based on wind speeds, we separate the data into weak, moderate, and strong regimes. Our model uses various inputs including surface wind, vertical velocity aloft, and surface net thermal radiation. Preliminary NCEI data shows a moderate downward trend in inversion height over the past 20 years, suggesting the Hadley Cell forcing has prevailed so far. We validate our model against high-quality NCEI radiosonde data, excluding pre-2000 records that may contain sensor-wetting biases. This study details the fine-tuned model and discusses whether the Hadley Cell forcing will continue to dominate (lowering the inversion further) or whether latent heat forcing will take over (causing the inversion height to rebound.) In doing so, we call attention to the inversion height as an often-ignored factor in Hawaii’s rainfall. We hope this research contributes to a better understanding of which natural disasters (e.g., floods vs. droughts) will impact the outer tropics so regions like Hawaii and Polynesia can better adapt to and mitigate their impacts.

491001.title: Strateole-2 Balloon Ascent Trajectories and ECMWF Forecast Representation of Tropical Waves above the Indian Ocean
491001.authors: M. Joan Alexander, NorthWest Research Associates, Boulder, CO; and L. Luan, M. Bramberger, M. Norgren, L. Kalnajs, A. Hertzog, R. Plougonven, F. Sielmann, and N. Žagar
491001.abstract: New measurements from the Strateole-2 field campaign in 2026 will include the launch of 22 long-duration super-pressure balloons from Victoria Airport on Mahe Island, The Seychelles (55.4oE, 4.6oS) in the Indian Ocean. Launches are planned for October-November-December, the season when climatological surface winds are a minimum. Balloon ascent trajectory forecasts based on European Center for Medium-range Weather Forecasting (ECMWF) Integrated Forecast System (IFS) fields will be compared to ascent trajectories from balloon-borne Global Navigation Satellite System position measurements as balloons rise from the surface to the lower stratosphere. Accuracy of these trajectory forecasts is an indicator of the quality of local wind profile forecasts, which are strongly influenced by tropical waves that vary with time through the season. In addition, real-time modal decomposition of ECMWF IFS deterministic forecasts of tropical winds into different tropical wave mode contributions is routinely performed and graphically reported on the MODES website (https://modes.cen.uni-hamburg.de). The decomposition includes both balanced (Rossby wave) and unbalanced (Kelvin/gravity wave) modes in forecast wind fields and further evaluates components of the wind associated with the specific modes that tend to dominate the energy spectrum: symmetric Rossby, Kelvin, mixed-Rossby-gravity, and eastward and westward inertia-gravity wave modes. The modally decomposed fields permit attribution of the accuracy or inaccuracy of the forecast trajectories to the quality of the representation of different tropical wave modes in the forecast. The presentation will include an introduction to the array of Strateole-2 measurements most relevant to tropical wave dynamics that will be acquired from the Lagrangian super-pressure balloon flights expected to continue through February 2027.

491007.title: Thermospheric Density Nowcasting and Forecasting by Assimilating Multiple Monthsof Commercial Constellation Data into NOAA/SWPC’s WAM-IPE model
491007.authors: Ching-Chung Cheng, University of Colorado at Boulder,Space Weather Technology, Research, and Education Center, Boulder, CO; and E. Sutton, T. W. Fang, N. Y. Wang, Z. Li, T. E. Berger, and T. Fuller-Rowell
491007.abstract: Whole Atmosphere Model (WAM) is operated by NOAA’s Space Weather PredictionCenter (SWPC) and simulates the whole atmosphere neutral compositions in realtime, while WAM tended to have a positive bias compared to various observations.SpaceX is operating thousands of Starlink satellites, and the orbit-averageddensities can be derived by monitoring the dissipation of orbital energy. TheStarlink density estimates from April 2022 – April 2023 were assimilated to WAM,using the Iterative Driver Estimation and Assimilation (IDEA) data assimilation (DA)technique. Results show that the data assimilative WAM density (WAM-DA)effectively captured the Starlink orbit-averaged density during both quiet and stormtime, with a root-mean-square error (RMSe) at 4.6%. In addition, a cross-comparison was conducted with the accelerometer estimates of neutral densityfrom GRACE-FO. The good agreement (RMSe = 6.5%) between WAM-DA andGRACE-FO shows that the Starlink neutral density estimates could be used toimprove the WAM neutral density outputs in the IDEA DA scheme. A 2-day neutraldensity forecast has also been performed to evaluate the performance in theforecast mode with DA initial conditions and issued forecasted solar wind drivers.With the rapid growth in the number of spacecraft and debris objects in LEO (LowEarth Orbis), reducing neutral density uncertainty remains one of the most effectiveways to improve orbit prediction and collision avoidance, and this study can be ofbenefit to improve thermospheric neutral density specification.

491008.title: TROPICAL - Mid-Troposphere Diagnostics Using Ultralight Solar-Powered UAV
491008.authors: Sidharth Menon, Christ College of Engineering, Irinjalakkuda, KL, India; and S. Ramachandran, R. Robert, S. Shaju, F. Kuttikat, S. Raman, S. John, A. Sobhanan, S. Balagopalan, and N. M. Komerath
491008.abstract: Problem: Improved weather prediction is urgent, as Extreme Weather Events (ERE) become more frequent [1]. Computational meteorology [2] is helped by flow models around known terrain features at low altitudes, and a database much finer-resolved than satellite data [3]. This is a progress report on a long-term, community-led collaborative non-commercial, unrestricted approach [4,5] to integrate the full range of sensing into a network towards 100x improvement in resolution. Methods: This is an effort to set up a large research project, so results at this point are multifaceted. We report progress on 6 aspects: Multi-sensor Bosch BME680/690 chips [6] have been connected to store and/or transmit data on pressure, temperature, humidity and gas resistance (VOCs interacting with heated MOS sensor) for air-quality estimation. MEMS 690 adds AI to DSP for improved signal. An ESPC32-C3 Super Mini board is used to evaluate different modes of connection. UAV-compatible packages are successful in ground testing and being installed for flight (awaiting break/end of SW Monsoon). Ground-based calibration is satisfactory. Other packages are destined for 6 initial locations including an urban heat island, 2 rural campuses, and mountain locations at 800m, 1400m and 1500m. Nominal data acquisition rate of even 200 samples/s on each channel and frequency resolution of 0.39Hz would be enough to resolve a 10-meter diameter plume at planned flight speed of 20m/s or lower. Aircraft control data with GPS and flight dynamics will provide wind components and location data. First flight data are from a fixed-wing UAV (FT Guinea Pig, built from a kit). A a 3m ultralight upper wing is added to the 1.7m wing to match low-speed, low altitude tests to flight simulation. Vehicle is in ground testing. Flight simulation trains the pilots, and sees what the UAV will see above the base cloud layer as thunderstorms approach. Results include integrating flight simulation with design-build-fly in a lower-division STEM undergraduate setting. A 4m span LiPo battery-powered UAV is being built, prelude to the solar-powered autonomous UAV. This will sweep areas between ground nodes, getting high-resolution profiles across low to mid troposphere. The construction metric here is low Wing Loading and Zero-Lift Drag Coefficient at small scale. This is to validate design of HALE versions to survive a 12-hr night in unpowered glide above controlled airspace. The Gold Standard is 1.25N/sq.m. [4,5] Present materials and construction have achieved 0.94N/sq.m upper wing loading, promising success for 72m HALE. Sheet stability and structural strength at required dynamic pressure are demonstrated in steady, yawed and gusting conditions. Test validation through routine use will prepare for an 8m UAV flying between Keralam coast and Lakshadweep inside a sunlit day. Results presented are on flight simulation, design and construction to achieve specified weight, wing loading and net thrust. An interesting result is that even at 4m scale, the FLT can operate with solar PV or battery directly, and solar-charge the battery. With this, 4MFLT can take off from sunlit or partly cloudy but dry East (TamilNad) side of Western Ghats, rise through clouds to sunlight, and fly through the day at 1500 m or higher, descending to safe, dry evening landing. Operation from typical school cricket-sized grounds has been confirmed. A concept for soft-rough field takeoffs has been developed, keeping on-board landing gear light. Rain measurement is best done at ground level, since satellite data on cloudtop luminescence do not tell us where, when and how much rain actually falls. Keralam, has about 300 official Automatic Weather Sensing Stations, and 50-odd sites operated by NGOs. We have installed about 20 Rain Cans operated by community friends: our results match reliable data in low to moderate rain – and seem to do significantly better than “tipper” type AWS in heavier or very light rain. Data since May 1, will cover the entire SW Monsoon and part of the NE Monsoon by conference time, meaning over 90% of an annual cycle. Requirements refinement from evolving Meteorology knowledge on EREs. A companion abstract describes linkage to global satellite and ocean database, to identify precursors to EREs from satellite data. These will also tell us what to expect from UAV confirmation above the lower luminescent cloud layer. We expect that UAV-based detection will provide at least 5 hours' reliable warning, compared to 2 hrs from usual satellite meteorology. A major result is the lessons from how this STEM student/community – built project has evolved and grown, following our prior work [6], including aspects such as safety and operator training apart from theoretical knowledge. Conclusions to-date: A grassroots project aims at high-resolution local weather measurements. It implements Glitter Belt architecture to mitigate Climate Change. Simulation-in-loop design builds 4-meter UAVs for meteorology. Process includes training student team, operating from aboratories and campus playground. Flight training has progressed from a small Bluetooth UAV, to flight simulation using XPLANE 12. A kit-built <2kg UAV with flight simulation is the first vehicle. Focus is on Safety protocols and regular documentation. Ground stations are testing sensors at schools to calibrate vs. altitude up to 1500meters, and urban heat island. A simple laws-of-physics traceable rain gauge community effort has tracked official data with excellent accuracy. Divergence at high rain rates warns of problems with Automated Rain Gauges. The project has started helping to face a major threat in Keralam Graphic shows UAV above luminescent cloud, seeing vertical dark wall of incipient ERE. RainCan and data are compared to official statewide average data. Present rain predictor model shows role of AR, IVT, Dew Point, vortical rise (rather than physical mountains). Other images show sensor connection of instrument package, CAD of 4mFLT, 4m FLT rendering and eventual 8-FLT HALE (FL) view from 30km. References [1] Mohandas,S. et al. Kerala flood. Dyn. 491010.title: Evaluation of a Data-Driven Model In the Data-Sparse Arctic
491010.authors: Melissa Westland, UBC, North Vancouver, BC, Canada; and R. Stull, T. N. Nipen, E. M. Nordhagen, R. H. White, and R. Lagerquist
491010.abstract: We present an evaluation of a data-driven weather forecasting model during the 2026 Canada-Sweden Arctic Expedition onboard the icebreaker Oden. The expedition will take place from August 10 to September 20, 2026, leaving from Svalbard and touring the Arctic circle. End-to-end AI weather forecasting models are typically trained on reanalysis and/or NWP analyses; however, there are known biases in such datasets in underobserved areas like the Arctic due to a lack of assimilated data and poor representation of physical processes specific to the domain. Thus, the expedition provides a unique opportunity to evaluate the performance of end-to-end ML weather forecasting models in the Arctic. The model we chose to evaluate is Bris, MET Norway’s operational data-driven weather model, which is a graph transformer model with a stretched grid. MET Norway has spent significant time developing and tuning stretched-grid graph transformer models. When trained as an ensemble with probabilistic loss, such a model has demonstrated competitive skill when compared to its high-resolution NWP equivalent over the Nordics. However, the ML model has the additional advantage of generating a forecast in minutes instead of hours. The model presented here is trained on a coarse global grid and a fine-resolution grid over the Arctic. The model is pre-trained on 43 years of ERA5 reanalyses and 6 years of IFS operational analyses. The model is subsequently fine-tuned with the high-resolution grid on three years of AROME-Arctic operational analyses at 2.5km grid spacing. We will present results of verification of the data-driven model’s forecasts against measurements taken onboard the icebreaker Oden during the expedition. The ship's observations include a weather station, radar, ceilometer, and 4-times daily radiosoundings. We include both qualitative and quantitative evaluations of the forecast model, including biases in different variables as a function of lead time. Additionally, we review the model’s ability to predict frontal passages, vertical atmospheric profiles, and cloud cover. The evaluation of this model informs potential improvements to training methods, thereby improving the operational model at MET Norway.

491014.title: Bridging the Last Mile: Pairing Expert Analysis with AI-Assisted Topic Modeling to Synthesize a Decade of VORTEX Social Science Research
491014.authors: Emily K. Laidlaw, NOAA (contractor through FedWriters), Ridgway, CO; and C. A. Williamsberg, A. Arnold, J. Dale, and I. M. Renta López
491014.abstract: This presentation asks a simple but powerful question: What becomes visible when we stop examining funded studies one at a time and begin looking at them as a connected body of evidence? Research findings are often dispersed across projects, programs, and publications, while responsibility for who should connect those findings with operational needs is not always clear. Researchers may not always have sufficient insight into how, when, or why practitioners might apply their findings in their day-to-day work. Conversely, practitioners and other operational staff often lack the time and capacity to synthesize research alongside their primary responsibilities. Research program managers face similar constraints because much of their time is devoted to administering, tracking, and reporting on active projects, leaving limited time to revisit previously funded work and identify opportunities for operational use. Together, these constraints create a need for a more systematic and scalable way to synthesize research findings, identify recurring themes, and surface connections to bridge the last mile between research and operations. In response to a 2023 request for an evaluation of NOAA’s National Weather Service tornado forecasting and warning services, NOAA’s Weather Program Office developed a unique approach to undertaking a comprehensive literature review, with the National Severe Storms Laboratory-funded Verification of the Origins of Rotation in Tornadoes EXperiment (VORTEX) social science portfolio as the first use case. This presentation will showcase the value of using our approach pairing extensive human analysis, refinement, and synthesis with AI-assisted topic modeling, and highlight VORTEX examples about how the public receives, perceives, and responds to tornado risk information, with an emphasis on findings that are unlikely to have emerged from either human or AI analysis alone. This presentation will show how our replicable process can efficiently examine how a research portfolio has evolved, what it collectively suggests, what gaps remain, and how its findings might be more consistently integrated into operational decision-making. By helping funders and practitioners see the forest rather than the trees, this approach offers a scalable new way to turn years of research investment into clearer priorities, stronger connections between research and operations, and knowledge that is far more likely to reach the people who can use it.

491022.title: Dynamical Influence of Tropical and Subtropical Deployment of Marine Cloud Brightening on North American Surface Temperature
491022.authors: Siyu Zhao, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, 33, China; and L. Cao, Y. Fang, P. Dai, and J. Zhang
491022.abstract: Marine cloud brightening (MCB) aims to reduce global warming, but its regional impacts remain uncertain. Here we implement MCB in CESM2 over tropical and subtropical oceans that occupy approximately 5% of the global ocean area. Under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, this deployment strategy would stabilize global mean warming near 1.5 °C above the pre-industrial level by the end of the century. Despite widespread cooling over most of the global land area, MCB produces a pronounced winter–early spring (JFM) warming over mid-eastern North America. During JFM, MCB reduces downward top-of-atmosphere (TOA) shortwave flux, cooling the atmospheric column and inducing a La Niña-like sea surface temperature (SST) pattern over the tropical and subtropical eastern Pacific. The resulting column cooling induces upper-tropospheric convergence over the equatorial eastern Pacific. It is accompanied by westerly wind anomalies over the equatorial Pacific, symmetric cyclonic circulation about the equator, and an anticyclonic circulation over the extratropical North Pacific. These circulation anomalies represent a Gill-type response to MCB forcing and the propagation of Rossby waves into the northern extratropics through the upper-tropospheric westerly window. The changes in the upper-level background circulation modify lower-level circulation and air temperature, producing positive near-surface temperature advection anomalies over mid-eastern North America. Meanwhile, the MCB-altered background flow suppresses the growth of synoptic disturbances over mid-eastern North America, reducing low- and mid-level cloud formation and enhancing downward shortwave radiation at the surface. Together, these dynamical and thermodynamic processes lead to the winter–early spring warming over mid-eastern North America. During JAS, MCB similarly reduces atmospheric shortwave absorption and cools the underlying tropical and subtropical oceans. However, it induces a much weaker atmospheric teleconnection response than in JFM. This seasonal contrast reflects the strong seasonality of the background circulation, including seasonality variations in the equatorial zonal winds and the associated Gill-type and Rossby wave responses. Consequently, the dynamical and thermodynamic responses to MCB that produce the JFM warming over mid-eastern North America are much weaker during JAS, resulting in little or no warming. In addition to mid-eastern North America, we also investigate the seasonal temperature variability over northwestern North America. This region exhibits substantial cooling anomalies during JFM under MCB, while such cooling is weaker during JAS. Overall, the spatial correspondence between the cooling anomalies and the associated dynamical and thermodynamic surface influences is less pronounced than that over mid-eastern North America, likely reflecting the more complex high-latitude Arctic environment. Our results highlight the potential for unintended seasonal continental warming in response to MCB, which should be carefully considered in the design and evaluation of MCB interventions. More broadly, a deeper understanding of the underlying process-level responses and coupled atmosphere–ocean mechanisms in response to solar radiation modification (SRM) is essential for reducing unintended risks and regional consequences associated with SRM deployment.

491031.title: Intensification and Spatial Expansion of Heatwaves across Eurasia Since 1950
491031.abstract: Extreme heatwave events are becoming more frequent and intensified over many parts of the world as warming climate leads to greater temperature anomalies, causing wide-spread negative impacts on human health, terrestrial ecosystems, social economy. Many parts of Europe and Asia are among the regions that increasingly experienced a series of extreme heatwaves over large areas. However, quantitative assessments regarding their spatial expansion and extremity evolution at the continental scale remain limited. In this study, we used multiple datasets and a unified framework to assess long-term changes in heatwave frequency, intensity and spatial clustering across 15 reference regions of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in Eurasia from 1950 to 2023. Multiple datasets include daily maximum temperature () from the Berkeley Earth Surface Temperatures (BEST), the NOAA Climate Prediction Center (CPC, 0.5°×0.5°), and ECMWF Fifth Generation Reanalysis dataset (ERA5, 0.25°×0.25°). We employed two metrics to quantify heatwave characteristics: heatwave frequency (HWF) and heatwave intensity (HWI). In Eurasia, heatwaves have shifted toward more extreme conditions since the 1990s. The spatial extent of rare events, which represent the most extreme conditions exceeding the 90th percentile of the 1991–2020 baseline period, expanded most rapidly. The annual mean area affected by rare heatwaves during 2014–2023 has tripled relative to the climatological mean of the 1991–2020 baseline period. Temporally, both the frequency and intensity of heatwaves in Eurasia have accelerated since the 1990s, with most record-breaking years occurring after 2010. Spatially, major expansions were not limited to traditional low-latitude heatwave-prone regions but have extended into mid- and high-latitude areas. In mid- and high-latitude regions such as Northern Europe, Eastern Europe and the Russian Arctic, frequency was 1.1–1.4 times and intensity was 1.2–2.2 times higher in the recent period (1994–2023) than in the early period (1964–1993). In these regions, the occurrence probability of rare events in these areas reached 15% in the recent period. The non-linear increase in Eurasian heatwave extremity reflects the combined influence of internal climate variability large-scale circulation changes and land surface feedbacks, meanwhile, the increasing mid- and high-latitude heatwave extremity is closely linked to Arctic amplification. These findings highlight a shift in heatwave climatology across Eurasia under climate change and provide new insights into the evolving risk of extreme heat events. Although we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the long-term change characteristics of historical heatwaves, future efforts are needed to leverage future projection to explore how the climatology of heatwave extremity may evolve under further warming. Advancing mechanistic understanding also remains vital for attributing and anticipating ongoing changes.

491032.title: Disentangling Prediction and Flood Driver Attribution in Explainable Machine Learning: The Role of Drainage Area
491032.authors: Kaili Zhu, Newcastle University, Newcastle, United kingdom; and H. J. Fowler, M. Herrera, C. Manning, S. Jiang, J. Song, and F. Wang
491032.abstract: Floods are among the most damaging natural hazards worldwide, and understanding their generating mechanisms is essential for effective flood risk management. Explainable machine learning provides new opportunities to investigate flood-generation mechanisms across large samples of catchments, yet the robustness of AI-based flood-driver attribution to differences in model formulation remains poorly understood. In this study, we analysed 2,459 catchments across North America using two explainable machine-learning frameworks to investigate the influence of drainage area information on flood-driver attribution. The first model incorporated drainage area and predicted flood discharge, whereas the second excluded drainage area and predicted runoff depth. The two models were compared in terms of predictive performance, overall predictor utilisation, and SHAP-based flood-driver attribution under positive-driver and dominant-driver attribution frameworks. The two models exhibited different patterns of predictive performance and predictor utilisation. Despite these differences, both models produced consistent spatial and temporal patterns of flood-driver attribution. While the positive-driver and dominant-driver frameworks emphasised different aspects of predictor contributions, both yielded highly consistent attribution results across the two model formulations. These findings suggest that AI-based flood-driver attribution is considerably more robust than predictive performance to differences in model formulation. Although drainage area substantially influences model performance and predictor utilisation, its influence on inferred flood-generation mechanisms appears much more limited.

491033.title: Synoptic-Scale Characterization of North Atlantic Tropical Cyclone-Linked Atmospheric Rivers Affecting Western Europe
491033.authors: Sachit Parekh, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA; and M. N. Malasala, K. Wu, X. Wu, and V. S. Tallapragada
491033.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are long, narrow channels of atmospheric water vapor that are responsible for significant impacts across the subtropical regions, subjecting areas to heavy rains and strong winds. During the Atlantic hurricane season, moisture associated with an active tropical cyclone (TC) can become incorporated into a water vapor transport feature akin to that of an AR. Such an AR can further impact western Europe, leading to periods of intense rainfall. This research defines this phenomenon as a tropical cyclone-linked atmospheric river (TCLAR) and aims to characterize the synoptic structure of TCLARs that form over the North Atlantic and affect western Europe. Prior events in the Western Pacific and North Atlantic were previously analyzed by Cordeira et al. (2013) and Doiteau et al. (2021), and this research aims to contextualize this phenomenon in the North Atlantic as a whole. AR catalogs developed by Rutz et al. (2014) and Guan and Waliser (2015) are used in conjunction with HURDAT2 to visually identify TCLAR events from the 2000-2015 hurricane seasons. Multivariate ERA5 data is then used to analyze their synoptic-scale atmospheric environments. A total of 28 TCLAR events lasting at least 24 hours are identified among 241 named tropical cyclones during the 15-year period. Preliminary observations suggest that TCLAR formation in the North Atlantic is the result of the influences of lower- and upper-level jets and an extratropical cyclone centered over northern Europe. The analysis also suggests that the subtropical high during a TCLAR event is shifted to the southeast. Composite analyses of the synoptic-scale atmospheric setup throughout the evolution of the 28 observed events are conducted, with particular emphasis being placed on the TC-jet stream interaction at the onset of each event. Additional analyses examine relationships between the TC’s water vapor content, the intensity of the European extratropical cyclone, and the strength and orientation of the resulting AR. TCLAR events are further compared based on the post-event status of the associated TC.

491037.title: UAV Icing Risk Classification via Multiple Field of View Lidar and Machine Learning
491037.authors: Lars-Stephan Klein, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, 16, Norway
491037.abstract: Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are vulnerable to atmospheric in-flight icing, where rapid ice accretion severely degrades aerodynamic performance and flight safety [1]. Currently, limited atmospheric situational awareness forces operators to adopt overly conservative flight constraints, frequently resulting in mission cancellations to ensure vehicle safety. Enabling active risk mitigation, such as dynamic path re-routing or automated de-icing activation, rather than preemptive mission cancellation, requires localized, real-time awareness of cloud microphysical properties, specifically Liquid Water Content (LWC) and droplet size distribution. Multiple Field of View (MFOV) lidar systems are distinctively capable of probing these atmospheric parameters by capturing the spatial and temporal decay of the multiple-scattering halo [2]. However, classical analytical inversion techniques used to isolate the multiple-scattering component are often computationally intensive and rely on rigid a priori assumptions, limiting their utility for real-time pilot decision-making such as emergency re-routing or the deployment of onboard anti-icing countermeasures [3]. To bridge this operational gap, this study investigates two machine learning architectures for rapidly inverting MFOV lidar backscatter profiles into atmospheric parameters. The first approach, based on a Random Forest Regressor, utilizes a transparent, decision-tree-based model trained on discrete statistical parameters extracted from the scattering halo. The second approach employs a convolutional neural network designed to directly ingest the raw, uncompressed volumetric backscatter tensors in a fully end-to-end configuration. By evaluating these algorithms against MFOV datasets of various environmental conditions, the computational latency and retrieval accuracy of both architectures are compared against traditional analytical approaches. Ultimately, the objective is to translate these microphysical retrievals into a real-time 'Icing Hazard Index'. Rather than exclusively outputting exact physical values, the algorithms categorize the environmental hazard level, providing UAV operators with immediate, data-driven thresholds for mission changes or, if available, deploying anti-icing or de-icing countermeasures. [1] Hann, R. (2022). Hazards of in-flight icing on unmanned aircraft [Conference paper]. SCI-328 Symposium on Flight Testing of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), Segovia, Spain. [2] Bissonnette, L. R., Roy, G., & Roy, N. (2005). Multiple-scattering-based lidar retrieval: Method and results of cloud probings [Journal article]. Applied Optics, 44, 5565–5581. [3] Zhang, H., Bu, L., Gao, H., Huang, X., & Kumar, K. R. (2018). Retrieving homogeneous liquid cloud microphysical properties using multiple-field-of-view lidar [Journal article]. Journal of Applied Remote Sensing, 12(4), 046021.

491039.title: Data Skills Pathways for Undergraduates to go from Curricula to Internship to Employment
491039.authors: David J. Delene, Univ. of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND
491039.abstract: Undergraduate students are increasingly expected to enter internships and the workforce with skills in programming, data processing, quality control, analysis, documentation, and scientific communication. Yet many students encounter these skills only through small, pre-cleaned datasets or late-stage capstone projects. Moreover, access to authentic experiential learning opportunities and research experiences often depends on informal faculty connections, prior technical experience, or a student’s ability to accept unpaid work. These barriers can be particularly significant for first-generation and Pell-eligible students. The University of North Dakota (UND) Data Skills Pathway addresses this gap through a structured, credit-bearing program that connects undergraduate coursework to authentic experiential learning opportunities, paid research positions, and internships. Anchored in data science and open to students from multiple disciplines, the program has already attracted seven students from atmospheric sciences, aviation, engineering, physics, and chemistry during the first six months of a funded four-year project. Students progress through four connected pillars: (1) orientation to data-intensive careers; (2) programming through complex analysis; (3) guided-to-independent collection, documentation, and visualization tasks; and (4) simple-to-complex tasks involving observational and model datasets. The Pathway includes a capstone mini-project consisting of a written report and presentation. Emphasis is placed on data provenance, reproducible workflows, analytical judgment, uncertainty, and clear communication rather than mere code development. Beyond purpose, sustained success in data-intensive careers requires passion. The Pathway sparks it through an ever-expanding list of opportunities that connect students' interests to careers, which currently includes working with data from meteorological instruments, field platforms, research aircraft, uncrewed aircraft systems, numerical weather models, and computational fluid dynamics simulations. Students are encouraged to begin by playing with data to get familiar with a topic they care about. Students who successfully complete the Data Skills Pathway receive priority consideration for paid research assistantships and internships with university research groups and external partners. UND's Experiential Learning Center supports recruitment, advising, placement, and follow-up, helping broaden access to structured research opportunities. The project evaluates student participation, completion, skill development, career awareness, research products, and transitions into paid work-based learning. Over four years, approximately 80–100 students are expected to complete the Pathway program. The broader goal is to create a sustainable, adaptable model that transforms fragmented undergraduate research experiences into a coherent pathway linking curriculum to workforce participation.

491040.title: A Generalized 3D Richardson Number for Boundary-Layer Diagnosis over Complex Terrain: Application to the TEAMx Campaign
491040.authors: Mohamed Foudad, University of Reading, Reading, RDG, United kingdom; University of Reading, Reading, RDG, United kingdom; and M. A. C. Teixeira, M. Lehner, P. Sheridan, and P. D. Williams
491040.abstract: The classical gradient Richardson number (Ri) is widely used to diagnose atmospheric stability and turbulent mixing, but it assumes horizontal homogeneity and considers only vertical shear of the horizontal wind. This assumption may be inadequate over complex terrain, where thermally driven valley and slope flows generate substantial horizontal shear that also contributes to turbulence production. Here, we extend a recently developed generalized Richardson number, Ri_new, derived from the turbulent kinetic energy budget, to the Mountain Boundary Layer (MoBL). The formulation retains horizontal shear and gradients of the vertical velocity, while accounting for anisotropic turbulent mixing through the ratio of horizontal to vertical eddy viscosities (K_mh/K_mv). The diagnostic is applied to a 1 km convection-permitting Met Office Unified Model simulation for TEAMx summer IOP18 (18 July 2025) over the Inn Valley, Austria, a case characterized by thermally driven boundary-layer flows and valley-exit jets. Ri_new is compared with the classical Richardson number and the model turbulent mixing height. The simulation is evaluated against radiosonde observations, with further validation using ground-based lidar and research-aircraft measurements collected during the TEAMx campaign. Compared with the classical Richardson number, Ri_new diagnoses a deeper turbulent boundary layer in regions of significant horizontal shear. At 18:00 UTC, Ri_new diagnoses a deeper boundary layer over 34–42% of grid points, with median boundary-layer depths approximately 2 and 2.5 times those diagnosed by the classical Richardson number over the Inn Valley and Alpine Crest Target Area, respectively. The model turbulent mixing height generally lies between the classical and Ri_new estimates, consistent with the new formulation capturing additional turbulent mixing associated with horizontal shear. Ri_new also identifies larger turbulent regions during both daytime and nighttime conditions. These results demonstrate that incorporating horizontal wind shear into the Richardson number provides a more physically realistic representation of turbulent mixing over complex terrain and offers a promising framework for boundary-layer diagnosis and parameterization development in high-resolution numerical weather prediction models.

491041.title: The Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) Level 0-1 Processor – Algorithm Updates
491041.authors: Heesung Chong, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, Cambridge, MA; and X. Liu, D. E. Flittner, J. Houck, J. Carr, W. Hou, J. Park, G. Gonzalez Abad, C. R. Nowlan, H. Wang, L. E. Flynn, S. Marchenko, J. E. Davis, R. M. Suleiman, J. Fitzmaurice, K. Chance, B. Baker, and B. Luo
491041.abstract: The Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) is North America’s first geostationary air quality satellite mission. The TEMPO instrument, flying on the Intelsat-40e satellite, measures Earth radiance and solar irradiance with two charge-coupled device detectors covering the 293–494 nm and 538–741 nm ranges. Raw measurement data downlinked from the satellite are converted on the ground into Level-0 digital counts and then into Level-1 spectra in physical units. The Version 4 TEMPO Level 1 products were released in September 2025, with updates to absolute radiometric calibration, solar diffuser transmittance correction, stray light correction, and spectral calibration. The TEMPO Level 0-1 processor is currently undergoing further enhancements in preparation for Version 5. The planned major updates include instrument degradation correction, dynamic bad pixel detection, and polarization correction, all newly enabled for the mission. We also plan to enhance existing calibration methods, including etalon correction, stray light correction, spectral calibration, and absolute radiometric calibration. In this presentation, we provide an update on the status of each planned algorithm enhancement.

491042.title: Improving Upper-Level Aviation Turbulence Detection Using a Generalized Richardson Number and Machine Learning
491042.authors: Mohamed Foudad, University of Reading, Reading, RDG, United kingdom; and P. D. Williams, M. A. C. Teixeira, T. Kaluza, K. Ng, and K. M. R. Hunt
491042.abstract: Turbulence in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere poses a significant hazard to aviation safety and is projected to increase in frequency and intensity under climate change. Despite advances in numerical weather prediction, diagnosing turbulence at cruise altitudes remains challenging due to its small-scale, intermittent nature and the limitations of existing turbulence diagnostics. We present a two-part contribution addressing both physics-based and data-driven approaches to upper-level turbulence detection. First, we introduce a generalized Richardson number (Ri_new) derived from the full turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) budget, which incorporates both vertical and horizontal shear components weighted by the ratio of horizontal to vertical eddy viscosities — a term neglected in the classical Richardson number formulation. Using ERA5 reanalysis and a large dataset of more than 247 million in-situ aircraft EDR observations from the MADIS archive (2017–2024), we show that Ri_new consistently outperforms the classical Richardson number and the widely used Ellrod turbulence index (TI1) across a range of turbulence intensity thresholds (light, moderate, and severe-or-greater). Furthermore, combining Ri_new with existing shear-based diagnostics leads to significant improvements in predictive skill. In particular, the combination of TI1 with Ri_new outperforms TI1 alone, indicating that the generalized stability criterion in Ri_new provides complementary information beyond existing diagnostics. This simple and computationally inexpensive combination has strong potential for implementation in operational turbulence forecasting algorithms and offers a robust diagnostic for climatological studies of upper-level turbulence. Second, we explore the application of machine learning (ML) using the same large EDR dataset. An XGBoost classifier is trained on ERA5-derived predictors, including GOES-16 infrared brightness temperature. The model achieves high predictive skill, with ROC AUC values exceeding those typically reported in the literature. Feature importance analysis highlights vertical wind shear and total deformation as dominant predictors, with satellite information becoming increasingly important for severe turbulence. These results demonstrate that advances in physical turbulence diagnostics and machine learning together improve the detection of upper-level aviation turbulence.

491043.title: HELIO TODAY — Deterministic Space Weather Forecasting
491043.authors: Larisza D Krista, Helio Physics LLC, Denver, CO
491043.abstract: What and Why: Operational space weather forecasting — including NOAA's own products, from short-term nowcasts to 24–72 hour outlooks — is fundamentally probabilistic. Helio Today takes a different approach: deterministic, event-specific forecasting. Rather than a probability of disturbed conditions, our system issues a forecast tied to a specific flare, CME, or high-speed stream, with a defined lead time. This is the difference between "conditions may be disturbed" and "this event is coming" — a distinction that matters directly to satellite operators, airlines, and power grid operators who need a decision point as well as a risk percentage. How: Helio Today is built on three automated detection systems developed from two decades of solar physics research, using adaptive, real-time image processing of GOES and SDO data. DEFT identifies solar flare precursors before the flare occurs. CoDiT detects coronal dimming, the earliest observable signature of a CME, often hours before the ejection is visible in coronagraph imagery. CHARM identifies coronal holes and forecasts the resulting high-speed solar wind streams days in advance. All three operate continuously and autonomously, with no forecaster in the loop ad available through subscription 24/7. Validated Performance: Helio Today's detection methods are peer-reviewed (Krista 2021, 2025a, 2025b; Krista et al. 2013, 2017, 2022; Krista et al. 2009, 2011, 2018) and have been benchmarked against operational NOAA alerts, with Helio Today issuing warnings measurably ahead of comparable NOAA notifications for recent X-class flares and CME events. The research underlying Helio Today has been supported over many years by NSF's Solar-Terrestrial Research and SHINE programs. Helio Today is a product of Helio Physics LLC. We welcome discussion with the space weather community on deterministic forecasting and its applications to operational decision-making.

491046.title: Ventilation Efficiency of Street Canyons Subject to Diurnal Heating: A Large Eddy Simuation
491046.authors: Brian Nguyen, ASCE, Princeton, NJ; and H. Soeda and E. Bou-Zeid
491046.abstract: Urban areas consist largely of street canyons that shape atmospheric contaminant and heat transport through the built terrain. Studies often compute the bulk air exchange rate across the top of these canyons, but actual effectiveness of ventilation remains poorly characterized since some parcels can leave and return to the canyon without much mixing. The large eddy simulation PALM is used to investigate turbulent thermal and scalar transport over street canyons aligned perpendicularly to the prevailing synoptic flow. Simulations of steady-state dynamics are first conducted for verification against existing literature. Then, transient diurnal heating is simulated using a radiation model compatible with PALM. Temporal and spatial averages of the ventilation efficiency are calculated as averaged and maximum flux rates Favg and Fmax, respectively, in different locations within the canyon. We show that Favg is proportional to the spatiotemporal average of the covariance wC, where C is the scalar concentration, while Fmax scales with the gradient of scalar concentration and the volumetric air exchange rate ACH across the horizontal plane of interest. In unheated street canyons, ventilation into the free atmosphere above the canyon is controlled by shear-dominated turbulence generation. In heated street canyons, the ventilation efficiency of pollutants depends on both shear and buoyant processes, altering the ventilation efficiency.

491047.title: AQUA-CLIME: Linking Microsensors, Modeling, and Water with Stakeholders
491047.authors: Raju Badireddy, Univ. of Vermont, Burlington, VT; and V. Gadhamshetty, D. W. DuBois, W. J. Capehart, E. Doran, E. Gnimpieba Zohim, M. Geza, and T. Kulkarni
491047.abstract: The NSF-funded “Advancing Quality and Climate-Resilient Water Management with Community Partnerships and Enhanced Sensor Network” (AQUA-CLIME) project addresses water issues in rural areas of Vermont, South Dakota, and New Mexico. A key element of this project is to provide a cost-effective knowledge orchestration toolkit (e.g., capturing, managing, analyzing, monitoring) for stakeholders' benefit. This aims to fill existing data gaps in water quantity and, specifically, water quality. Printable microsensors are being developed and tested in underserved areas, and the results are integrated through process-based and expert-in-the-loop AI/ML (artificial intelligence and machine-learning models) and LLM-powered semi-automatic reporting frameworks. Broader goals include stakeholder outreach and engagement, climate change impacts and climate resiliency strategies in our impacted regions, and workforce development. Here, we present our results to date, including integrated assessments of climate change impacts on water resources, development and testing of our microsensors, and sensor acceptability, data access, and results featuring our decision support tool framework.

491049.title: Impact of Submesoscale Wave-Current Interactions on Tropical Cyclone-Induced Sea Surface Cooling
491049.authors: Qian Xiao, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; NOAA, Princeton, NJ; and B. G. Reichl
491049.abstract: Accurate modeling of sea surface cooling during tropical cyclones (TCs) is essential for intensity forecasting. This cooling is significantly influenced by wave-current interactions involving Stokes drift. At small scales ($<$1km), Langmuir turbulence enhances vertical mixing, while at larger scales, resolved wave-current interactions couple Stokes drift to model resolved ocean currents. This study investigates the spatial scale dependence of these effects using a coupled MOM6-WAVEWATCH III model under idealized TC conditions, with horizontal resolutions from 50km to 500m. Many of our coupled model simulations yield a cold-wake with the primary horizontal scale of the SST pattern being related to the size of the storm. In the no-wave reference state with a 50km radius of maximum wind, a 10km horizontal grid captures broad cold-wake patterns. In these simulations, using a finer grid resolution (e.g., $<$1km) produces little change. We find that adding a Langmuir turbulence parameterization on top of this baseline provides a resolution-insensitive driver of enhanced cooling in the ocean response. Conversely, adding the grid-resolved Stokes drift interactions into the model yields a weak resolution dependence of the SST response that is modified slightly when refining the grid-spacing. A second set of coupled model simulations is conducted with reduced vertical mixing, which reveals a scenario where the TC forcing generates a cold-wake front with structures that are unstable to submesoscale filaments. These submesoscale structures modify SST cooling by several degrees in the baseline case. They also strongly energize the resolved wave-induced contributions, indicating complex interactions between resolved wave forcing and submesoscale dynamics. However, these features and their interactions with Stokes drift require horizontal resolutions of 1km or finer to resolve. These findings demonstrate that resolved Stokes-wave effects depend strongly on the ocean's dynamical state. While mesoscale (e.g., $\sim$10km) resolution suffices for the ocean response to TCs in stable submesoscale regimes, kilometer-scale resolutions are critical when TC forcing triggers submesoscale instabilities that modify cooling and reorganize wave-induced responses. Consequently, high-resolution modeling is vital for representing upper-ocean responses in active submesoscale environments.

491058.title: Nonlinearity and Tropical Anchoring in the Asymmetric Extra-Tropical Response to Warm and Cold Tropical ENSO Forcing
491058.authors: Benjamin Paul Kirtman, University of Miami, Miami, FL
491058.abstract: The observed atmospheric response to warm and cold phases of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is well known to be asymmetric, yet the dynamical mechanisms underlying this asymmetry remain incompletely understood. Here we present a suite of idealized experiments using a dry primitive equation atmospheric general circulation model (Kirtman et al. 2025) designed to systematically isolate and diagnose the sources of asymmetry in extra-tropical teleconnections to warm and cold tropical forcing anomalies. First, a fully nonlinear formulation with a weakly prescribed background state allows the zonal eddy field to evolve freely while constraining the climatological mean state through Newtonian relaxation and Rayleigh friction. Second, a nonlinear formulation with a strongly prescribed background state constrains both the mean state and the eddy field, providing precise control over the atmospheric background against which teleconnections develop. Third, a linearized version of the model, solved via a novel method (bred vectors) that avoids the resolution limitations of traditional matrix inversion approaches, provides a benchmark for quantifying the role of nonlinear dynamics. Results from this hierarchy of experiments reveal: the atmospheric circulation does not respond symmetrically to equal-and-opposite tropical heating anomalies, with the nonlinear residual exhibiting a coherent large-scale pattern. Furthermore, topographic forcing is shown to play a critical role in anchoring the teleconnection response, particularly in the Northern Hemisphere, modulating both the amplitude and spatial structure of the asymmetric circulation anomaly. These findings highlight the importance of nonlinear dynamics and orography in shaping ENSO-forced teleconnections and have implications for seasonal prediction.

491063.title: The Complexity of the Coastal Urban Boundary Layer and Implications for Urban Atmospheric Composition: Results from CoURAGE
491063.authors: Kenneth J. Davis, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and S. R. Hill, N. E. Prince, A. LaPorte, B. J. Ahlswede, S. Murphy, J. P. Horne, W. E. Foust, H. Y. Spears, R. C. Sullivan, D. Zhang, D. W. Waugh, P. J. Walter, M. Deng, M. P. Jensen, M. E. D. Roots, T. Leblanc, F. Chouza, S. Pal, and N. Subhash
491063.abstract: Many cities are located within complex geography. Baltimore is such a city, bordered by the I-95 corridor, the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains and the Chesapeake Bay. This geography, in addition to the complexity of the urban surface, yields potential for a highly complex urban atmospheric boundary layer (ABL). The Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE) and the Baltimore Social-Environmental Collaborative (BSEC) are complementary, multi-disciplinary, Department of Energy funded studies of the atmospheric environment of the city of Baltimore. CoURAGE, which took place in calendar year 2025, was a deployment of the DOE Atmospheric Radiation Measurement Program Mobile Facility to the city and its surroundings. One objective of CoURAGE and BSEC is to understand the factors governing the atmospheric composition of the city, including the urban ABL. The Baltimore ABL is influenced both by the urban land cover and the heterogeneity of the coastal region. Observations reveal significant differences in urban vs. rural ABL development, especially at night. These differences are broadly consistent with the surface fluxes observed within and around the city. The contrasts in urban vs. rural ABL cloud cover have a strong seasonal component. The regional geography supports frequent mesoscale flows. Low-level jets (LLJs) are observed roughly 50% of the nights during the experiment and typically extend across the entire northwest to southeast extent (~100 km) of our observational network. The LLJs have been associated with near-surface turbulent mixing at some locations within the city. Bay breezes, while not as common as the LLJs, are observed fairly often and are associated with high lidar reflectivity air masses likely containing elevated aerosol concentrations. Vigorous turbulence associated with cold front passages were found to bring elevated aerosol plumes (e.g., wildfire smoke) into the urban ABL. We are in the process of evaluating the links between these ABL features and regional air quality, as well as our ability to simulate the urban ABL. Initial simulations of the urban ABL reveal limited ability to simulate urban surface fluxes and intra-urban temperatures. The extensive meteorological network was complemented by two atmospheric composition ‘supersites,’ one in Baltimore and one at a rural boundary location, an ozone lidar network, multiple AERONET stations, instrumented aircraft, a tethered-balloon campaign and an intra-urban network of particulate matter sensors. New numerical studies of urban atmospheric composition have not been initiated to date due to limited funding. Great potential exists for this data set to serve as a test bed for testing and improving our understanding of urban atmospheric composition.

491064.title: Tracking Drought Propagation Across Soil Moisture, Streamflow, and Vegetation in Illinois Using Predictive Machine Learning Models
491064.authors: Anika Raj, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Naperville, IL; and K. Wolski and A. Goodwell
491064.abstract: Drought impacts in the US Corn Belt propagate through the land surface: precipitation deficits reduce soil moisture, and sustained deficits can later appear in streamflow and vegetation conditions. However, these stages are observed by separate systems, complicating direct comparison of their timing and severity. In this study, we integrate observations from the 19-station Illinois Climate Network (ICN), U.S. Geological Survey stream gauges, and satellite-based vegetation indices to place these three types of drought impacts on a common scale and study their predictability. We first predict the 5 cm and 50 cm soil-moisture anomaly one day ahead using linear, ridge, lasso, and random-forest models. To test how much predictive information is retained in longer-term antecedent soil conditions, we withhold the most recent 14 days of soil measurements; the model sees soil conditions from 14 days before the issue date, or 15 days before the prediction target. Because soil moisture is strongly autocorrelated, this is a more demanding test than initializing from the present state, which would draw substantial skill from persistence.
