Five predictor sets isolate the information sources: weather alone, the delayed soil readings alone, and weather plus the delayed 5 cm reading, the 50 cm reading, or both. Splits are chronological: training before 2023 (106,159 samples), model selection on 2023–2024, and 2025 held back entirely. Using weather together with both delayed soil layers reduced RMSE by 26% at 5 cm (R² = 0.70) and 48% at 50 cm (R² = 0.75) relative to weather alone. It also outperformed the persistence baseline—the delayed reading carried forward unchanged—by 43% at 5 cm and 12% at 50 cm. This difference reflects the much stronger persistence of deeper soil moisture: the delayed reading alone explains 5% of anomaly variance at 5 cm but 68% at 50 cm, leaving substantially less room for improvement at depth. The information sources also reverse rank with depth. Using only the delayed soil readings, the best model explains 67% of variance at 50 cm compared with 6% for weather alone, essentially matching the persistence baseline; at 5 cm, this reverses to 44% for weather and 28% for soil. The best model class also changes with depth. Random forest is most accurate at 5 cm, consistent with more nonlinear near-surface soil-moisture dynamics. Meanwhile at 50 cm, which integrates forcing over longer periods, linear regression performs best. During 2023–2024, the observed 50 cm soil-moisture anomaly averaged −0.30 relative to the pre-2023 seasonal climatology, indicating persistently drier-than-normal conditions at depth. Weather-only models instead predicted a mean anomaly near zero, producing a positive bias of 0.32. Adding the delayed 50 cm soil observation reduced this bias to 0.10, whereas adding the delayed 5 cm observation produced little change. This suggests that recent weather alone did not capture the persistent subsurface dryness, while the older deep-soil observation retained that information. The streamflow and vegetation components are being incorporated using the same anomaly framework. Daily discharge at long-record Illinois U.S. Geological Survey gauges is converted to a 14-day rolling mean, log-transformed, and standardized seasonally, while satellite NDVI anomalies surrounding each station will represent vegetation response. Station–gauge linkage is determined by watershed containment rather than proximity, since a station can lie near a gauge while draining elsewhere; 36 pairs across 16 gauges currently qualify, with 18 overlapping the modeling period. We will present evaluation on the withheld 2025 period, station-level variation in prediction skill, soil–streamflow relationships at verified pairs, and progress on the vegetation component. This study contributes to the understanding and prediction of multiple facets of drought in the US Midwest.

491065.title: Asymmetric Mean-State Influence on Pacific Kelvin Waves
491065.authors: Qiao-Jun Lin, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and Á. F. Adames Corraliza, V. C. Mayta, and K. C. Tseng
491065.abstract: Convectively coupled Kelvin waves (CCKWs) over the central Pacific exhibit an equatorially asymmetric circulation, wherein convection shifts northward toward the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), unlike the Kelvin waves in Matsuno’s shallow water theory. Using ERA5 reanalysis, we identify two distinct antisymmetric components associated with Kelvin waves. An eastward inertio-gravity-like structure develops near the equator, while a broader antisymmetric structure appears within the ITCZ. To isolate the role of the asymmetric mean state, we perform idealized shallow-water simulations, in which a zonally elongated reduction in equivalent depth is prescribed north of the equator to represent the background state of the northward-displaced ITCZ. As the Kelvin wave response propagates, its geopotential maximum remains centered near the equator, whereas low-level convergence shifts toward the equivalent-depth minimum. Meanwhile, two antisymmetric circulation components emerge, closely resembling those identified in the reanalysis. These results demonstrate that an asymmetric mean state alone can reorganize Kelvin-wave circulation, generating antisymmetric components even in the absence of interactive moisture.

491067.title: Numerical Modeling of Graupel Riming
491067.authors: Sage Branham, CU Boulder, Boulder, CO; and B. Baker
491067.abstract: Riming, the freezing of super-cooled water droplets onto ice particles, is a fundamental process in mixed phase clouds. Actively riming graupel seems to play a central role in thunderstorm electrification. During the riming of graupel, latent heat released by freezing maintains a riming droplet near 0°C, while it is freezing. When the graupel is substantially colder, this results in strong localized gradients in temperature and water vapor density that enhance vapor deposition onto the nearby graupel surface. It has been hypothesized from laboratory models of mixed phase cloud electrification that these regions of enhanced growth of the graupel are key to understanding charge transfer during ice-ice interactions, in the lab and in clouds. Existing analytical descriptions of this process are limited to simplified geometries and idealized assumptions. We develop a numerical model that explicitly represents a graupel particle, a freezing super-cooled droplet, and the surrounding air as coupled domains. The model simultaneously handles heat conduction, phase change, and vapor diffusion, allowing the evolution of temperature and vapor density fields to be simulated for realistic geometries throughout the period during which the droplet is freezing. The numerical model is intended as an open and extensible research tool for studying localized vapor deposition during graupel riming and its potential implications for thunderstorm electrification.

491069.title: Subseasonal-to-Seasonal Forecast of Total Water Levels Using a 3D Ensemble System
491069.authors: Yinglong Joseph Zhang, Virginia Institute of Marine Science, Williamsburg, VA
491069.abstract: This study focuses on downscaling a global model to US East and Gulf coasts for sub-seasonal to seasonal time scales (S2S) prediction of coastal total water levels (TWL), in particular extreme water levels that are important for coastal flooding. Because the global model (SPEAR+MOM6) resolution is 1/12º at best but finer than 500 m resolution is needed for coastal inundation forecasts, a key gap exists between the coarse global model ensembles used to make S2S prediction and the fine resolution desired for coastal flooding prediction. Previously, we have demonstrated the utility of a high-resolution coastal model (STOFS-3D-Atlantic) to capture tidal, sub-seasonal and seasonal variation of the TWL (Cui et al. 2024; Yoo et al. 2025). Here, we use a simplified version of STOFS-3D-Atlantic as the base for ensemble prediction; the end product will be an ensemble of downscaled hindcasts for leads of up to at least four (and possibly six) weeks, initialized at the same frequency as the ensemble GEFS v.13 hindcasts (roughly twice weekly). The skill of the downscaled sea surface height prediction ensemble will be assessed using standard deterministic and probabilistic metrics such as ROC Area Under Curve.

491075.title: Global Urban-Rural Differences In Precipitation: Cities See More Light Rain but Milder Extremes
491075.authors: Mingze Ding, Boston University, Boston, MA; and X. T. Zheng, T. Sun, Z. Li, H. Chen, and D. Li
491075.abstract: Ample evidence has shown that cities modulate regional hydrometeorology and hydroclimatology. Because different precipitation intensities have distinct hydrological and societal impacts, it is important to understand whether and how urban effects vary with precipitation intensity. Based on global satellite-based observations, we demonstrate that 70.1% of large cities experience increased light precipitation frequency, while 69.9% exhibit milder extreme precipitation magnitude than their rural counterparts. By further dividing the rural areas into upwind and downwind regions, we find that the frequency of light precipitation events is enhanced within cities, but such enhancements shift to the downwind rural areas as the precipitation intensity increases, notably for heavy precipitation (> 20 mm) frequency and extreme precipitation indices. The contrasting influence of cities on light and extreme precipitation suggests an underappreciated role of urbanization in improving local climate conditions.

491081.title: The Forcing behind the Coastal Urban Atmospheric Environment: Observational results from the CoURAGE/BSEC Urban Eddy-Covariance Flux Network
491081.authors: Kenneth J. Davis, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and S. R. Hill, S. Murphy, J. P. Horne, C. Ross, B. J. Ahlswede, Y. Pan, C. Keener, N. E. Prince, and R. C. Sullivan
491081.abstract: Studies of the urban atmospheric environment are often motivated in part by the need to understand how the urban surface modifies the urban atmospheric boundary layer (ABL). Direct measurements of these land-atmosphere interactions, however, are often lacking. We present the findings of an urban eddy-covariance (EC) flux network deployed in Baltimore, Maryland, USA in support of studies of the urban ABL. The Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE) was a deployment of the DOE ARM Mobile Facility to Baltimore from 1 December, 2024 through 30 November, 2025. CoURAGE and the Baltimore Social-Environmental Collaborative (BSEC) combined to deploy and operate seven EC flux towers in and around the city during this time period. The urban sites include a central, commercial area, residential neighborhoods and urban turf grass. Fluxes were also measured at a farm northwest of the city and over the Chesapeake Bay. These flux measurements show, not surprisingly, differences in sensible and latent heat fluxes and friction velocity that are consistent with the formation of an urban heat island. Urbanized surfaces generally exhibit a larger daytime Bowen ratio, minimal nocturnal cooling over the urbanized surface and larger friction velocities than the rural surroundings. The urban surface, however, is far from uniform and fluxes within the city can be very similar to the rural background conditions. The rural-urban differences in sensible heat flux are not as dramatic as suggested by the Bowen Ratio, perhaps due to increased ground heat fluxes in the city. Differences in fluxes at urbanized sites within the city appear to be governed to first order by variations in vegetation cover but surprising differences that are counter to this trend have emerged from two contrasting residential neighborhoods. Fluxes from the Chesapeake Bay remain small year-round, varying mostly as a function of season. Initial comparisons with Noah-MP suggest the broad ability to represent rural-urban-bay flux differences but challenges in representing intra-urban flux variability. We suggest paths forward to improve urban land surface flux modeling, an essential area of improvement in the effort to improve our ability to simulate the urban atmospheric environment.

491084.title: A New Time-Series Analysis Algorithm for Measuring TKE Dissipation and the Inertial Subrange
491084.authors: Robert M. Banta, Retired, Boulder, CO; and C. J. Senff
491084.abstract: Accurate profile measurements of turbulence variables are needed to close the TKE budget under diverse atmospheric conditions. Such measurements are needed to better understand how turbulence dynamics behave under a range of steady conditions and how they respond to non-steady conditions in the real-world atmospheric boundary layer (ABL). Enhanced understanding is also essential to improve NWP modeling of turbulent processes. A key variable is TKE dissipation ε. It has been shown to be a major control on the subresolution-scale (SRS) transport term in mesoscale NWP models. Commonly, time-series analysis approaches to finding ε use relationships proposed by Kolmogorov, which describe the time-scale dependence of the power spectrum S and structure function D of velocity fluctuations in the turbulent inertial subrange ISR, where these functions are directly related to ε. According to these relationships, the spectrum follows a f -5/3 dependence on frequency f in the ISR, and D is proportional to τ 2/3, where τ is a time offset. Most often researchers have used the spectra, calculated using a Fast Fourier Transform FFT after several preconditioning steps to the time series, which alter the input data series. The result is a rather noisy-appearing plot against f, even when S is modestly smoothed. Because of its broad dynamic range, the spectrum is typically plotted on a log-log grid, where departures of the measured spectrum from the -5/3 theoretical slope appear diminished. These can make assessing the accuracy of the estimates difficult, because to estimate ε, one must try to find an appropriate value for the noisy S function at corresponding values of f. Here we present a more straightforward approach using the structure function D, which needs no preconditioning (other than standard outlier and mean removal) and no transform. It also produces a smooth curve over the regions of interest. The ultimate goal is to make the scheme objective and thus automatable. We aimed to determine ε in a straightforward manner, while also assuring that data used for the analysis were from the ISR portion of D. To simplify the process, we multiply D by τ -2/3 to obtain a function gw(τ) that is constant for τ within the ISR. A plot of this function, known as the compensated structure function, has a benchlike form resembling a geological mesa, with small values at the largest and smallest scales and an elevated middle region that is constant—flat and level—according to Kolmogorov’s theory. To test this approach’s ability to produce internally consistent values of ε while demonstrating that these estimates were based on ISR values, we used sonic-anemometer measurements of vertical velocity w from 6 levels at 50-m vertical intervals on the 300-m Boulder Atmospheric Observatory (BAO) tower, a High Plains site in moderately complex terrain. Our dataset consisted of hour-long midday samples from two consecutive hours on three convective days in March and April 2015, for a total of 36 time-series samples. The log-log spectrum plots for all the time series appeared to have a -5/3 slope, and the structure functions, a 2/3 slope. Plots of the compensated structure functions gw(τ) on a log-log grid appeared flat and level in most cases as anticipated (Figure 1, middle). When plotted against a linear ordinate (Fig.1, top), however, departures from constancy—representing barely perceptible departures from the 2/3 log slope of the structure function itself—were revealed, due to the inherent natural variability of the real-world ABL. Several gw(τ) plots did show a relatively flat bench- or mesa-like shape containing minor bumps and wiggles but clearly consistent with Kolmogorov theory. Other curves showed a more mounded rather than flat structure and other larger departures, most likely indicating more complex ISR dynamics or other influences on the time series such as nonstationarity or ε intermittency. Although the departures may seem significant on the linear ordinate, they still produce a slope of -5/3 or 2/3 on log-log plots, so they would be considered part of the ISR according to a so-called ‘eyeball test’ comparison against the appropriate slope. In most cases, therefore, the elevated portion of the gw(τ) plot should be considered part of an ISR. The challenge in developing an objective structure-function algorithm to identify the ISR thus means finding an acceptably constant, flat region of the gw(τ) curve. This is accomplished by selecting all gw values that fall within a certain prescribed tolerance (tol) of a representative reference value. In line with previous studies, we used a value for tol of 25%, but 20% and 30% gave nearly identical results in most cases. With tolerance values as the only input, we developed an objective algorithm to determine the extent of the ISR and the median value of gw(τ) over that range, and ε is directly computed from that median gw(τ). Because of the diversity of shapes of gw(τ) due to atmospheric variability, the algorithm was somewhat complicated, involving two steps and two kinds of tolerance, but it yielded reasonable, consistent results that were insensitive to tol over a range of tolerance values. The algorithm also provided estimates of the upper and lower τ limits of the ISR. Profiles of ε from z=50 to 300 m determined for the three days by this method were gradually decreasing with height as typical of the upper portion of an unstable surface layer, and the magnitudes of 10-3 to 10-2 m2s-3 are also characteristic of these conditions. Reliable measurements of ε have many benefits. Profiles of ε have been shown to provide a definitive indicator of the ABL top. Because the area under the power-spectrum curve equals the variance of the time-series sample, superimposing the extent of the ISR determined by our algorithm onto the spectrum gives an estimate of the fraction of the variance that is pure turbulence, which is modeled as diffusion. For our samples we find that a significant fraction is from low-frequency, non-turbulent disturbances, which in general are not diffusive. This result has important implications for verifying SRS modeling parameterizations that rely on TKE or other velocity variances.

491090.title: Unstable ITCZ Rainfall Gradients Promote Tropical Cyclone Genesis
491090.authors: Qiao-Jun Lin, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and Á. F. Adames Corraliza, S. N. Wu, and V. C. Mayta
491090.abstract: Recent theoretical and diagnostic work has shown that steep moisture and precipitation gradients of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) are unstable and can lead to increased easterly wave activity. The easterly waves in turn dry the ITCZ by transporting moisture poleward. In this study, we show that tropical cyclone genesis (TCG) is also associated with this ITCZ instability, quantified by the product of planetary vorticity and the meridional rainfall gradient. A higher instability metric is associated with enhanced TCG frequency on seasonal-to-interannual timescales across all six major TC basins. Daily composites reveal that prior to TCG, the ITCZ is stronger, the precipitation gradient is steeper, and easterly wave activity is increasing. After a disturbance develops into a TC, poleward eddy moisture flux increases and the ITCZ weakens. These results link ITCZ variability, easterly waves, and TCs to the distribution of moisture and precipitation: the strong moisture and precipitation gradients of the ITCZ not only increase easterly wave activity but also promote TCG. In turn, TCs strengthen eddy moisture fluxes that weaken the ITCZ.

491092.title: Hysteresis in Global Atmospheric River Activity under Carbon Dioxide Removal
491092.authors: Seohyun Chung, Seoul National University, Seoul, 41, South korea; and C. Park, Y. Kwon, S. W. Son, A. C. Winters, and W. Dong
491092.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are key agents regulating global hydroclimate and extreme precipitation. Climate models project the increase and intensification of ARs in a warming climate, but their responses to CO2 mitigation remain unclear. Based on large-ensemble climate model experiments in which CO2 concentrations are systematically increased and then decreased, we show that AR frequency and intensity do not fully return to their present-day states when CO2 concentrations are reduced. Instead ARs are projected to remain more frequent and intense, particularly along the western coasts of North America, Europe and South America, in East Asia, and along the Antarctic coast, leading to increased extreme precipitation in the midlatitudes and potential impacts on Antarctic ice mass balance. The hysteresis pattern of AR frequency results from the competition between effects of thermodynamic and dynamic processes, both of which are closely related to the delayed recovery of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation and the Southern Ocean temperature.

491093.title: Revisiting the Streamwise Velocity Variance in Stable Atmospheric Surface Layers
491093.authors: Xin Shao, Nanjing University, Nanjing, 32, China; Boston University, Boston, MA
491093.abstract: The streamwise velocity variance is an important parameter for understanding boundary layer dynamics and developing turbulence parameterizations in meteorological and climate models. It is also commonly required as an input parameter in footprint modelling and pollutant dispersion studies. It is known that atmospheric stability has a strong impact on the streamwise velocity variance in atmospheric boundary layers. However, the atmospheric stability effect on the streamwise velocity variance normalized by the friction velocity cannot be described by the Monin-Obukhov similarity theory inspired way by expressing the normalized streamwise velocity variance as a function of the stability parameter. Currently, focusing on stable conditions, there are two existing phenomenological models for the normalized streamwise velocity variance. These two models predict a decrease in the normalized streamwise velocity variance with increasing atmospheric stability under weakly to moderately stable conditions. However, observational data indicate that the normalized streamwise velocity variance increases with increasing atmospheric stability. Two explanations are proposed for the observed increase in the normalized streamwise velocity variance as the atmospheric stability increases: (1) vertical velocity fluctuations are damped by atmospheric stability more strongly than horizontal velocity fluctuations, and (2) in order for the normalized streamwise velocity variance to satisfy the z-less scaling under strongly stable conditions, it must increase with the atmospheric stability under weakly to moderately stable conditions. To describe the increasing trend for the normalized streamwise velocity variance with stability under weakly to moderately stable conditions, a model based on the budgets of second-order turbulence statistics is proposed and compared to measurements. The model adequately explains the stability dependence of the normalized streamwise velocity variance under weakly to moderately stable conditions, but does not recover the logarithmic behaviour of the normalized streamwise velocity variance under neutral conditions. These findings highlight a persistent gap between engineering and atmospheric science approaches in modelling the normalized streamwise velocity variance. Bridging this gap is needed for developing unified turbulence representations across disciplines.

491094.title: Revisiting the Relationships between Lightning Activity and Rapid Intensification of Tropical Cyclone
491094.authors: Weixin Xu, School of Atmospheric Science Sun Yat-sen University, Zhuhai, China
491094.abstract: Lightning activity has been popularly linked to the rapid intensification (RI) of tropical cyclone (TC), as lightning is an excellent indicator of intense convection. While eyewall lightning outbreaks were found prior to or during RI in some TCs, certain studies reported a contradictory negative relationship between inner-core lightning and TC intensity change. However, most previous studies only considered RI during a 24h period but not the whole RI lifecycle. This study revisits the lightning-RI relationships by examining the evolutions of TC lightning and precipitation in a large sample (~1500) of full lifecycle RI events. Results show that lightning substantially increases 12-18h prior to the RI onset but quickly decreases afterward. In contrast, the precipitation and deep convection increase after the RI initiation and maximize in the middle of the RI lifecycle. We further find that convective clouds before RI have a shallower convective depth, but stronger mixed-phase signature compared to that after RI. RI events are further categorized into short, medium, and long duration events, and the lightning evolution through their life cycles are fully examined. RI events with greater intensification rate and longer duration are featured by more active lightning activity before the RI onset, which is likely due to the more favorable thermodynamic storm environments such as SST and CAPE. In short, this study investigates the lightning-RI relationships from a new perspective (event-based) and reconciles the previous seemingly contradictory results, offering a roadmap for monitoring TC intensity change using the global lightning detection network.

491099.title: Assessing Lightning Risk in Africa: A Framework Integrating Hazard, Exposure, and Vulnerability via the African Lightning Incident Database
491099.authors: Daile Zhang, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and I. Sanford, R. L. Holle, and M. A. Cooper
491099.abstract: Lightning is a significant yet underreported hazard across Africa, with casualty rates far exceeding those in developed nations. This study analyzes 1,290 lightning incident reports from the African Lightning Incident Database (ALID), covering 44 countries between 2018 and 2023, documenting 3,047 fatalities and 3,703 injuries. We characterize African lightning risk through the Hazard-Exposure-Vulnerability framework. Seasonal casualty patterns closely follow hemispheric thunderstorm activity (hazard). National casualty rates in several central and southern African countries exceed 20 per million annually, which is roughly 20 times higher than developed nations. Only 13% of African incidents involve single victims compared to 90%+ in the U.S. and U.K., with an average of 5.3 casualties per event reflecting concentrated exposure in group settings. Nearly half (49.6%) of casualties occur indoors in buildings lacking lightning protection, and children account for 57.4% of known casualties, often at unprotected schools (vulnerability). Risk assessment for 15 countries identifies five Very High Risk countries (DRC, Rwanda, Uganda, Malawi, Guinea) where hazard, exposure, and vulnerability interact to produce extreme casualty risk. Despite reporting limitations, ALID provides foundational evidence for risk characterization and supports targeted interventions including improved building standards for schools and public spaces, region-specific safety education, and expanded early-warning systems to reduce Africa’s disproportionate lightning impacts.

491100.title: Warming weakens downslope winds and slows simulated nighttime spread of the 2018 Camp Fire
491100.authors: WEICHEN LIU, Department of Atmospheric Science, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and S. Rahimi, F. Zhao, M. E. Frediani, B. J. Hatchett, A. Hall, C. W. Thackeray, E. Taciroglu, K. Singh, and T. W. juliano
491100.abstract: Warming is generally expected to increase wildfire hazard, but projections tend to carry that expectation through fuel aridity alone, holding the meteorology that drives spread at present-day conditions. The assumption has rarely been tested for downslope windstorm fires, which are disproportionately destructive. We tested it with coupled WRF-Fire simulations of the 2018 Camp Fire in northern California, run under a baseline and under conditioned warming of +1.5 to +6 K, each with six members: a control plus five initial-condition perturbations. Nighttime spread slowed in all members. Between 2100 and 0300 LST, when the nocturnal downslope flow was strongest, the ridge-to-valley sea-level pressure difference fell by about 1.6 hPa at +6 K. Over the grid cells in the top quartile of spread rate, the most rapidly advancing part of the fire, near-surface wind weakened from 4.12 to 3.46 m/s and the spread rate from 0.52 to 0.42 m/s, roughly 93 to 75 chains per hour. These reductions, 16 and 20 percent, exceed the ensemble spread by an order of magnitude. That spread fell proportionally more than wind follows from the nonlinear wind dependence of the spread parameterization. We attribute the wind response to the hypsometric relationship: uniform warming lowers sea-level pressure more over the elevated interior than over adjacent lower terrain, weakening the inland high and relaxing the cross-barrier gradient that drives the easterly downslope flow. Gradient-boosted tree models (XGBoost) interpreted with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) provide an independent check, ranking wind speed as the leading control on spread across its full sampled range; other predictors matter only within narrow bands. Because the mechanism rests on column warming over high terrain rather than on conditions specific to this event, it may extend to other downslope wind regimes such as foehn and bora, though we did not test that here. Projections holding winds fixed may therefore overstate future hazard for this class of fires.

491106.title: MicroPulse DIAL (MPD) for Continuous Thermodynamic Profiling: Technological Advancements and Multi-Unit Inter-Comparisons
491106.authors: Scott M. Spuler, NCAR, BOULDER, CO; NSF NCAR, Center Green Dr., CO; and R. A. Stillwell, M. Hayman, and B. Garby
491106.abstract: Continuous, high-resolution thermodynamic profiling in the lower troposphere is vital for improving numerical weather prediction and boundary layer research. The MicroPulse DIAL (MPD) provides a cost-effective, diode-laser-based active remote sensing architecture integrating water vapor DIAL, O2 DIAL, and High Spectral Resolution Lidar (HSRL) to deliver self-calibrating thermodynamic observations without relying on external priors. Recent algorithmic and hardware advancements—including a Global forward-modeling framework and Multi-Pulse Mode (MPM)—address historical near-range blind zones and signal noise, extending the nominal retrieval range to 100 m - 6 km AGL. This presentation will highlight findings from a recent field study at the DOE ARM Southern Great Plains (SGP) Central Facility in Oklahoma. Multiple co-located MPD units were operated to quantify unit-to-unit consistency and hardware-specific biases. Data availability as a function of range is also characterized; it is not uniform within the nominal span, varying with time of day and retrieval method, and it is not yet validated throughout. Preliminary water vapor observations compared against co-located radiosondes and HRRR model output are shown in Figure 1. The data in this figure were generated using a fast, direct-inversion retrieval (DIAL equation). These rapid diagnostics resolve hardware performance and transient behaviors without the smoothing effects of regularized inversion, and the per-unit biases they expose inform ongoing development of the Global forward-model retrieval, which will produce the final data products with improved accuracy and noise suppression across all channels. The inter-comparisons presented here are an intermediate step toward validating that product.

491111.title: Modulation of Convective Mass Flux by Echo-Top Height Across Storm Modes in a Kilometer-Scale Climate Simulation
491111.authors: Justin Hassel, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and K. L. Rasmussen, Ph.D. and H. Yu
491111.abstract: Deep convective storms vertically transport heat, moisture, and momentum through the troposphere, shaping storm dynamics, precipitation intensity, and severe weather. Convective mass flux (CMF) characterizes the upward transport of air and water within convective updrafts. The magnitude and vertical structure of CMF are influenced by storm organization, with organized systems often transporting substantially more mass through a deeper layer of the troposphere than isolated convection. Despite its importance, existing CMF observations are short-duration and spatially limited, leaving relationships between storm organization, convective vigor, and CMF poorly constrained at climatological scales. We therefore aim to determine how storm organization and convective vigor shape the magnitude and vertical structure of CMF across storm modes. Using the 43-year, 4-km CONUS404 hydroclimate reanalysis, we compute hourly, vertically integrated upward CMF and partition it among Deep Convective Cores (DCCs), Wide Convective Cores (WCCs), and Deep and Wide Convective Cores (DWCCs) using TRMM-heritage storm mode definitions applied to simulated three-dimensional reflectivity. Across the full record, total hourly CMF scales nearly linearly with storm mode area, but the area-normalized intensity differs systematically among modes, with DCCs producing the strongest transport and WCCs the weakest. Incorporating 30-dBZ echo-top height (ETH) reveals additional variability in CMF production associated with convective vigor. Within organized, spatially extensive systems, higher mean ETH is associated with increased total CMF at a given storm mode area, while across all storm modes, pixel-level ETH is positively related to local CMF production. We further assess how these relationships vary across seasons and distinct regions characterized by different convective regimes. Finally, we examine how ETH-dependent CMF variations relate to the vertical distribution of convective transport, including the height and intensity of peak updrafts. Together, these results show that storm mode area strongly constrains total CMF, while ETH further modulates its intensity and vertical structure. This work provides a storm-mode-resolved climatological reference for interpreting future observations of CMF from the upcoming NASA INvestigation of Convective Updrafts (INCUS) mission across diverse convective systems.

491113.title: Atmospheric Circulation Constraints on Future Changes in Tropical Cyclone Activity
491113.authors: Megha Rao, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and G. Zhang and K. Reed
491113.abstract: Climate models simulate potential changes in tropical cyclone (TC) activity but show substantial disagreement across projections. While various physical relationships have been proposed to explain these simulated changes, it remains unclear whether those relationships help narrow projection uncertainty. Here we investigate zonal-mean large-scale circulation changes, such as Hadley cell expansion, ITCZ migration, and shifting vertical wind shear (VWS), and ask whether they function as emergent constraints (ECs) for global TC projections. We analyze HighResMIP simulations from three model families, including 25 configurations spanning atmosphere-only and coupled runs at 25–130 km atmospheric resolution. We regress historical circulation metrics against projected mid-century changes in Northern Hemisphere TC metrics and constrain projections using ERA5 observational data. Most relationships drawn from the literature do not provide strong constraints. The Hadley cell edge correlates significantly with poleward migration of lifetime maximum intensity (LMI) latitude, but the relationship reverses sign when considering atmosphere-only and coupled model subsets. Constraints on LMI latitude derived from VWS and from jet-edge position oppose in sign, indicating sensitivity to metric choice. Subtropical VWS and ITCZ latitude each imply an additional ~0.15° poleward LMI shift but narrow model spread by only ~7%. Although TC frequency lacks significant relationships with the ITCZ or Hadley cell strength, mean tropical shear (10–20°N) more effectively constrains projections, narrowing intermodel spread by ~15%. Overall, circulation-based ECs for global TC projections are achievable but deliver only modest uncertainty reduction. Additional tests with more climate simulations are underway and will be presented.

491114.title: Student Perceptions of Climate Change in University Classrooms
491114.authors: Lindsay C. Maudlin, Department of Geological and Atmospheric Sciences, Ames, IA
491114.abstract: Student perceptions of climate change are evaluated at the beginning and end of the semester in two climate-focused courses at a large R1 university. With data from 1,083 students over five years, changes in self-reported levels of confidence in their understanding of climate concepts, the degree to which they feel informed about climate change, their awareness of the scientific consensus, and the extent to which they are sure climate change is occurring are explored. Increases are observed in student confidence, the degree to which they feel informed, and the extent to which they are sure climate change is occurring. Minimal changes are observed in student awareness of the scientific consensus; nearly 90% of students are already aware of the scientific consensus at the beginning of the semester. Additionally, these changes are compared to their scores on a climate concept inventory (CCI) taken at the same time. The level of confidence of students in the upper-level course is correlated with average score at both the beginning and end of the semester; the most confident students perform the best on the CCI. In the lower-level course, the highest performers tend not to be the most confident. The extent to which students feel informed is positively correlated with performance on the CCI, and scores are similar across groups of students who are aware of the scientific consensus and those who are not. Findings from this study can inform climate educators about student perceptions of climate change and topics to emphasize or not in the classroom.

491115.title: Data Acquisition Systems: A Configurable, Open-Source Design
491115.authors: Tori Lang, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and C. Owen and K. Lesko
491115.abstract: Data Acquisition Systems (DAQs) are essential for all weather instrumentation. The DAQ acts as the translator between the instrument and the computer where data is stored. While these systems are not new or novel technology, commercially available DAQs are often quite expensive and non-configurable. A typical observations-based project would require multiple DAQs that cost anywhere from $200-$1000+. The focus of this project is to provide a low-cost, easy reproducible DAQ design. This design is called the Lesko Owen Lang DAQ (LOLDAQ). Several constraints were applied to this project so that it exceeded in both functionality and efficiency: the system must be as small as possible, must be inexpensive and open source, must meet certain input-output requirements, and must be flexible in its placement. The LOLDAQ is designed to take digital, analog, and UART inputs and turn them into RS485 communication for maximum data transmission distance. The hardware selection for the evaluation board includes an Arduino R4 Minima (chosen for its inexpensive price, extensive documentation, onboard 14-bit ADC, and onboard RTC), MAX485 transceiver (used to convert all signals into RS485 communication), RS485 to USB serial converter, breadboard, and jumper wires. Code was compiled and uploaded through the Arduino IDE. The LOLDAQ successfully translates input digital, analog, and UART signals into RS485 communication. However, to be the most effective in scientific campaigns, more features, such as input commands and counters, will be added in the future.

491117.title: Educate, Simulate, Protect: Teaching Drought and Flood Preparedness Through Tabletop Exercises
491117.authors: Margaret A Holzer, Science Curriculum Design Consultant, Somerset, NJ; and D. A. Robinson
491117.abstract: New Jersey’s changing climate is creating profound direct and indirect consequences for our daily lives, with few systems more vulnerable than our state’s water supply. As global temperatures rise and weather patterns shift, our water infrastructure faces compounding threats from both intense droughts and severe, localized flooding. Water resource managers and emergency personnel must continuously adapt to these environmental pressures to ensure reliable, clean access for all residents. A key mechanism for building emergency readiness is the Tabletop Exercise (TTX) - an informal, discussion-based practice session designed to evaluate responses to hypothetical crises. During a TTX, a diverse group of key stakeholders gathers around a table to walk through their respective roles, refine communication protocols, and stress-test action plans against a simulated disaster scenario. Because these sessions prioritize exploratory dialogue and collaborative problem-solving over high-stress simulation, they offer an ideal environment for low-stakes learning and strategic planning. To bring this authentic planning framework into the classroom, we developed two Problem-Based Learning (PBL) units for middle and high school students across New Jersey. These units explore the complex interplay between climate change, regional hydrology, and public policy by placing students in the driver's seat of localized water management crises. The curriculum is fully adaptable across grade bands: Middle School Track: Focuses on foundational Earth science concepts, localized environmental impacts, and community awareness. High School Track: Expands into advanced data analysis, policy evaluation, and systemic infrastructure challenges. Both tracks are anchored by a central driving question: How does climate change impact water resources in New Jersey, and what strategies can ensure equitable access to clean, safe water for all communities? The curriculum follows a multi-phase structure that mimics real-world disaster management—guiding students through how communities prepare for, respond to, and recover from severe flood and drought events while embedding long-term resilience into their solutions. The unit begins with an anchor lesson to establish the crisis context, builds core scientific knowledge across Lessons 1 and 2, and culminates in a multi-stakeholder Tabletop Exercise in the final lesson. Although these units were designed for New Jersey students, they can be implemented in schools across the country. This presentation outlines the instructional design and implementation framework of these units, provides actionable insights for educators, and shares empirical feedback from initial classroom implementation.

491118.title: Operational Verification of the Rapid Refresh Forecast System Using NOAA's Evaluation and Verification System (EVS)
491118.authors: Marcel Gabriel Caron, OMD, College Park, MD; NOAA, Riverdale Park, MD; and A. Benjamin, M. P. Row, B. Zhou, and H. C. Huang
491118.abstract: The NOAA Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) is preparing to implement the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) and RRFS Ensemble Forecast System (REFS) into operations. The RRFS is a rapidly updating high-resolution deterministic weather prediction system and will replace several legacy regional systems, including the North American Model and High-Resolution Window Forecast System. The REFS is a high-resolution ensemble forecast system composed of current and time-lagged forecasts from the RRFS and High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and will replace the High-Resolution Ensemble Forecast and Short-Range Ensemble Forecast systems. To provide routine objective evaluation of NOAA's new operational high-resolution modeling suite, the OMD is updating version 2 of the Evaluation and Verification System (EVS) to include verification of the RRFS and REFS. Using publicly available EVS verification products, we compare objective EVS-based performance metrics for the RRFS, REFS, HRRR, and Rapid Refresh (RAP) model. Our comparison focuses on recent short-range surface and upper-air forecasts, precipitation products, simulated radar reflectivity, and 2-5-km updraft helicity-based surrogate severe forecasts. We also highlight recent enhancements to EVS developed for preoperational field evaluation of the RRFS and REFS, including new radar reflectivity and surrogate severe verification products and web pages. Finally, we discuss ongoing development of regional verification capabilities within EVS.

491120.title: Visualizing Forecast Uncertainty: A Predictive Learning Approach to Highlight Targets of Opportunity with the National Blend of Models
491120.authors: Monika Von Cyga, CUNY Queens College, Flushing, NY; NOAA NWS, Tucson, AZ; and T. Dang
491120.abstract: The National Blend of Models (NBM) is an established starting point for highly accurate and consistent gridded weather forecasts, consisting of blends of global, regional, and convective Numerical Weather Prediction models. While it is designed for calibrated forecast guidance, there are often cases where the NBM’s deterministic ‘Core Blend’ performs poorly in comparison to true events, particularly when forecasting extreme weather events and shifting seasonal patterns. The purpose of this project is to provide National Weather Service meteorologists with enhanced decision guidance while using the Core Blend. This is done by developing a machine-learning based dashboard that visualizes when the NBM may output irregular forecasts that are inconsistent with historical data for maximum/minimum temperatures, quantitative precipitation forecasts (QPF), and snowfall. By analyzing over- and under-forecast probabilities exceeding specified thresholds, users can evaluate if there is a need for NBM output fine-tuning. This dashboard incorporates zonal statistics for 3850 NWS public zones across the contiguous United States, using data from the NBM, versions 4.0 through 4.3, along with observational measurements from the Parameter-elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) 24-hr dataset. The general feature space for the ML model includes NBM forecast day, week of the year, public zone number, and the 60-day and 7-day rolling windows for model/observations difference values. A gradient boosting algorithm, LightGBM, was selected to be the learner behind this dashboard due to fast training speed and a high multiclass ‘area under the curve’ (AUC) score, which evaluates the ability of a model to capture correct anomalous forecasts. The average AUC score across all thresholds for minimum/maximum temperature, QPF, and snowfall were 0.752, 0.720, 0.890, and 0.914 respectively. These metrics represent the model’s strong ability to distinguish rarer NBM underperformances from common instances of accurate NBM outputs. In general, the test set metrics for NBM v5.0 saw a high recall score across all variables and their associated thresholds, implying high model sensitivity to any potential high impact, anomalous events. This dashboard is ultimately designed to highlight targets of opportunity of where, when, and under what weather conditions the NBM Core Blend could be improved upon, along with improved operational risk assessment and forecast skill.

491121.title: Inverse Energy Cascade in Typhoon Boundary Layer Turbulence
491121.authors: Xin Shao, Boston University, Boston, MA; Nanjing University, Nanjing, 32, China
491121.abstract: Boundary layer turbulence plays an important role in the formation and evolution of typhoons. In conventional atmospheric boundary layers, turbulent kinetic energy is transferred from large to small eddies, forming the direct energy cascade. However, observations show that a part of energy flows inversely to larger scales within the inner-core region of typhoons, forming the inverse energy cascade, while the other part continues to flow downscale to the dissipative scales. However, physical mechanism controlling the observed inverse energy cascade in typhoon boundary layers remains unrevealed. Using eddy covariance data collected within typhoon boundary layers, this study shows that this inverse energy cascade arises from the rapid rotation of typhoons. The transition between the inverse and direct energy cascade can be characterized by the Zeman length scale. Symmetry analysis further shows that the ratio of the inverse energy cascade flux to the direct energy cascade flux is proportional to the turbulence Rossby number with a power of -2. These findings offer a pathway to incorporate the effects of the inverse energy cascade into the boundary layer parameterizations and improving typhoon modelling.

491122.title: Causal Drivers of All India Summer Monsoon Precipitation Using Graph Based Bayesian Networks
491122.authors: Naman Kishan Rastogi, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and B. Rajagopalan
491122.abstract: Identifying the causal climate drivers of precipitation variability remains a challenge in seasonal forecasting. We present a generalized three stage framework combining Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA), network pruning, and Bayesian causal network inference, and apply it to All India summer monsoon precipitation over a 124-year record. In the first stage, EGA uncovers the natural community structure among precipitation and candidate drivers, with bootstrapped stability analysis confirming robust groupings. In the second stage, a Bayesian network directed acyclic graph (DAG) is constructed from this structure and pruned using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and significance criteria. In the third stage, Bayes Factors for wet and dry precipitation regimes, defined by the 70th and 30th percentile thresholds, are computed through network mutilation and posterior querying on the pruned DAG. Applied using El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) indices Nino1+2, Nino3, Nino4, and the Trans Nino Index (TNI), the Dipole Mode Index (DMI), and the Western Pacific index (WPI), the framework reveals community structure evolving through the monsoon season. In June all variables form a single community, but by July a two-community split emerges, separating the ENSO cluster from the Indian Ocean and Warm Pool cluster. Precipitation, isolated in July, joins the ENSO community by August and September, coinciding with Nino3's explained variance rising from 7.1 to 18.1 percent and adjusted R squared improving from 0.056 to 0.172. Individual Bayes factors vary by month, while the aggregate seasonal network remains stable, with Nino3 and the DMI surviving pruning.

491123.title: Revisiting Sutton's Advection Problem with Satellite Land Surface Temperature Boundary Conditions
491123.authors: Octavia V Crompton, ARS, Sebastopol, CA; ARS, Beltsville, MD; and G. G. Katul
491123.abstract: Quantifying water losses due to advection is increasingly necessary for water resource management in irrigated landscapes. The effects of water vapor advection are most pronounced near abrupt land condition transitions, such as the edges of irrigated fields or bodies of water. Advection can enhance evaporation from lakes and reservoirs, increase evapotranspiration (ET) in irrigated fields downwind of fallow land, and accelerate ice melt in snow-covered soils. While advection impacts on ET have been widely studied in micrometeorology and agricultural sciences, the integration of remote sensing approaches to infer these effects at scales relevant to water resources management remains limited. Here, Sutton’s 1934 problem of advection across a dry/wet boundary is revisited under the simplified assumption that momentum roughness length remains unchanged across the transition. We introduce an approach that considers the coupled mean conservation of water vapor and air temperature, where the dominant balance is between the mean advective flux and the turbulent flux gradient. Bridging remote sensing methods into Sutton’s problem requires reformulating the lower boundary conditions to utilize satellite-derived land surface temperature (LST). Within this modeling framework, advective impacts on heat and water vapor transport are resolved for the case of repeated wet-dry land-cover transitions. Finally, landscape-scale ET enhancements due to advection are estimated and compared to prior experimental and literature values.

491124.title: Model Biases In Quasi-Stationary Waves and Projections for the Future: Impacts of Ocean Forcing and Resolution
491124.authors: Olivia Belle Samolej, Univ. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and V. T. Narinesingh, S. P. Raghuraman, and N. Johnson
491124.abstract: Quasi-stationary waves (QSWs) are persistent, midlatitude atmospheric patterns that can lead to extreme weather lasting from days to weeks. Improving our understanding of QSWs and accurately simulating QSWs in weather and climate models can enhance forecast accuracy and increase lead times for impactful weather events such as heat waves and extreme cold outbreaks. These advancements are imperative to building weather ready communities worldwide. In this work we examine the impact of ocean forcing and atmospheric resolution on climate model fidelity in capturing QSWs. Using NOAA Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory’s (GFDL) atmosphere only model, AM4 (1° atmospheric resolution), and its coupled-ocean counterpart, CM4 (1° atmospheric and .25° ocean resolution), we find that regardless of if the model is forced by sea surface temperatures (SST) matching reality, the models are able to reproduce the spatial pattern of climatological QSW amplitude in the Northern Hemisphere. During winter, however, the models: (1) oversimulate climatological QSW amplitudes over North America and Southern Eurasia, and (2) undersimulate over northern Europe. On the other hand, in summer, AM4 and CM4 yield dissimilar biases, showing an increased sensitivity to SST compared to winter. In addition, large ensemble simulations using .25° atmospheric resolution (GFDL SPEAR-HI) yielded similar biases to 1° simulations (SPEAR-LO) regardless of season, suggesting this increase in atmospheric resolution is not the primary issue. We also examine mid and end of century projections of climatological QSW amplitudes in moderate and extreme greenhouse gas forcing scenarios. Each scenario yields mixed regional responses for both winter and summer, but some regions may experience increased severe weather.

491125.title: Visualizing Forecast Uncertainty: A Predictive Learning Approach to Highlight Targets of Opportunity With the National Blend of Models (NBM)
491125.authors: Monika Von Cyga, CUNY Queens College, Flushing, NY; NOAA NWS, Tucson, AZ; and T. Dang

491130.title: Gas-Surface Interactions on Satellites in Very Low Earth Orbit
491130.authors: Timothy K. Minton, University of Colorado Boulder, BOULDER, CO
491130.abstract: There is intense interest in the utilization of very low Earth orbit (VLEO, roughly 100 – 350 km altitude) for commercial and military purposes. Despite the obvious proximity advantages of VLEO, these altitudes have long been avoided because of the high density and harsh oxidizing environment of the residual atmosphere. VLEO environments contain predominantly atomic oxygen (AO) and molecular nitrogen (N2), which collide with ram surfaces on spacecraft at relative velocities of ~7.5 km s-1. Momentum exchange in collisions between these species and satellite surfaces results in aerodynamic drag. Aside from drag, materials on the external surfaces of VLEO satellites may react chemically with AO, resulting in oxidation, erosion, roughening, and degradation of function. Minimizing and predicting drag and maximizing AO resistance are crucial for proliferated VLEO operation. A laser-driven breakdown source was used to produce molecular beams of O atoms at orbital velocities of ~8 km s-1, which were used to investigate the AO resistance of various polymeric materials that may have applications on VLEO satellites. Silicon-containing polymers, for example, form an AO-resistant SiO2 layer upon exposure to AO, which leads to a negligible erosion yield for some of these materials. The laser-driven source was also used in molecular beam-surface scattering experiments, employing a rotatable mass spectrometer detector, to characterize the scattering dynamics of O atoms, Ar atoms, and N2 molecules on both polymeric and inorganic material surfaces. These experiments enabled us to investigate the relationship between the nature of a surface and its potential to promote low drag. The scattering dynamics were measured as a function of both polar (θ) and azimuthal (φ) scattering angles on pristine and pre-exposed sample surfaces. The velocity and angular distributions of scattered O-atoms (or Ar atoms or N2 molecules) depend strongly on the incident angle of the impinging atoms, the roughness of the surface, and the local atom/molecule-surface interaction potential. The attached image illustrates the relationship between the experimental gas-surface scattering dynamics, the measured surface topography, and the development of a gas-surface scattering model based on a washboard approach, which uses a gamma function roughness model and a coupled CL model for the local atom-surface scattering kernel. These results may be used in simulations of drag, calculation of lift-to-drag ratios on control surfaces, and gas concentration in inlets for air breathing electric propulsion.

491131.title: On the Nucleation Pathways of Common and Some Emerging Seeding Agents
491131.authors: Tom DeFelice, ASCE/EWRI AWM SC, Sheboygan, WI
491131.abstract: This presentation briefly reviews atmospheric aerosol fundamentals, and highlights nucleation pathways for common cloud-seeding agents and teases relevant considerations of environmental and socio-economic perspectives. Nuclei size and composition influence whether aerosols function as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) or ice nuclei (IN). Studies show that cloudwater contains chemically complex mixtures, challenging the simplifying assumptions used in many atmospheric models that treat droplets as pure water and nuclei as single salts. New aerosol measurement technologies are beginning to enable rapid analysis of individual particles, and revealing their size, morphology, and composition. This improves targeting effectiveness and evaluations of seeding operation efficiency and more, particularly weather forecast accuracy, and will ultimately begin to inform on the importance and improvement in seeding agent placement, timing, and dispensing method(s). The nucleation pathways will focus on glaciogenic agents like silver iodide, hygroscopic salts, biogenic particles, and ion-based methods. Finally, responsible, standard cloud seeding practices require attention to environmental impacts, seeding agent composition transparency, and effective public communication. All toward a robust understanding of aerosol-mediated cloud modifications across scales

491132.title: A Global Decline in Atmospheric Dust during the 21st Century
491132.authors: Ashok Kumar Gupta, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN; and J. F. Kok, V. Amiridis, A. Gkikas, K. Rizos, E. Proestakis, S. A. Logothetis, E. Marinou, and C. P. Garcia-Pando
491132.abstract: Mineral dust influences Earth’s energy budget, clouds, and biochemistry, yet the evolution of the global dust cycle in recent decades remains shrouded in uncertainty. Here we reconstruct the global dust cycle during the early 21st century by integrating a suite of global dust aerosol optical depth (DAOD) products from satellite-borne lidar, infrared sounders, and multi-spectral imagers; three aerosol reanalyses; and a compilation of dust-dominated AERONET sites into a large-ensemble inverse modeling framework. We show that North Africa has remained the dominant global dust source, yet it has experienced a decline in DAOD of −10 ± 8 % between 2003 and 2023. A comparable reduction is observed across Asia (−10 ± 12 %), together driving a global decrease of −10 ± 8 %. Similar declines in dust loading, emissions, and deposition indicate a coherent reduction of the global dust cycle. Individual satellite products converge on overall similar trends, providing the strongest evidence to date that the planet has become less dusty in the early 21st century. This decline in atmospheric dust has exerted a positive effective radiative forcing of +0.02 ± 0.05 W m⁻² over 2003–2023, implying that declining atmospheric dust might have modestly contributed to the rapid warming of the past two decades.

491133.title: Observing atmospheric and laboratory clouds at centimeter scales using single-photon counting lidars (Invited Presentation)
491133.authors: Fan Yang, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Mastic, NY
491133.abstract: In this talk, I will present recent progress in applying time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC) lidars for cloud observations at centimeter resolutions in the atmosphere and in a laboratory cloud chamber, and demonstrate the value of high-resolution lidars for advancing fundamental understanding of cloud microphysical processes. We developed a ground-based, vertically pointing, time-gated TCSPC lidar (T2 lidar) that resolves atmospheric clouds at ~10 cm. The T2 lidar captures fine structure near cloud base, and its highly resolved backscatter profiles can be inverted to retrieve cloud droplet number concentration. In a recent deployment, we collocated the T2 lidar with a Doppler lidar to observe a boundary-layer stratiform cloud. We found that cloud base height increases with vertical velocity, consistent with the hysteresis effect. We also built a TCSPC lidar that profiles clouds in a convection cloud chamber at 1 cm resolution. High-resolution lidar profiles indicate that turbulent mixing tends to homogenize the cloud in the bulk, while sedimentation-induced droplet size sorting generates inhomogeneity near cloud top. They further indicate that entrainment mainly affects the upper cloud layer under clean conditions, but it influences the entire cloud layer under polluted conditions, owing to competition for limited water vapor and haze–cloud recycling.

491136.title: Coastal Redistribution of Tropical Cyclone Precipitation and a Discrete Shift from Thermodynamic to Dynamic Control
491136.authors: Eric Peino, NOAA/AOML, Miami, FL; and G. Foltz and J. A. Zhang
491136.abstract: Predicting tropical cyclone (TC) rainfall at landfall requires understanding how environmental forcing and storm intensity interact across the coastal transition. Using satellite precipitation composited in a shear-relative framework, with radii normalized by the radius of 34-kt winds (R34) and cases stratified by intensity and by coastal phase, we track how TC rainfall magnitude and spatial structure evolve from the open ocean through landfall. Over open ocean, the azimuthal-mean rain rate is concentrated within 0.25 R34 and intensifies with intensity (from about 6.5 mm/h in tropical storms to over 15 mm/h in category 3-5 storms), whereas wavenumber-1 asymmetry peaks beyond R34, with the rainfall maximum in the downshear-left quadrant. Approaching land, rainfall within 0.2 R34 is suppressed in every intensity class (19 to 29 percent at landfall), but the response at larger radii (0.2-1.5 R34) diverges. Tropical storms and category 1-2 storms damp near-uniformly and lose up to 35 percent of domain-total rainfall, whereas category 3-5 storms conserve it (a 6 percent decline) through a structural dipole: suppression near the center paired with areal expansion and an 11 percent mean rainfall increase between 0.2 and 1.5 R34. The downshear-left orientation is preserved throughout. Environmental control shifts discretely rather than gradually. Over the open ocean, sea surface temperature (SST) explains 34.5 to 46.1 percent of rainfall variance through a direct thermodynamic pathway (more than 90 percent unmediated by intensity) that amplifies the extreme tail. At landfall, vertical wind shear emerges as a leading control on magnitude (21.5 percent of variance). Shear acts in two modes: it increases rainfall asymmetry at the same rate from open ocean to landfall, and it controls rainfall magnitude near land, where the rain-shear relationship, weak over open ocean, becomes strongly negative: stronger shear reduces rainfall in tropical storms and category 1-2 storms (r = -0.83 for tropical storms). These results show that weakening near the center of a category 3-5 storm does not signal reduced rainfall risk, since the footprint expands outward. They also argue for phase-dependent predictor weighting: SST to gauge rainfall volume and extreme tail risk during the oceanic approach, and the shear vector at landfall to anticipate suppression in weaker systems.

491137.title: Evaluation of GFSv16, GFSv17, and AIGFS for Atmospheric River Precipitation Forecasts over the U.S. West Coast
491137.authors: Keqin Wu, NOAA, Riverdale Park, MD; and X. Wu, B. Zhou, M. N. Malasala, M. Aristizabal Vargas, X. Wang, V. S. Tallapragada, F. Yang, and J. Wang
491137.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are long, narrow corridors of enhanced integrated vapor transport (IVT) that account for most poleward water vapor transport outside the tropics. Although ARs are a vital source of freshwater, they also produce many of the most damaging heavy precipitation and flooding events along the U.S. West Coast. Accurate prediction of AR-related precipitation is therefore essential for flood forecasting, water resource management, and hazard mitigation. This study evaluates the performance of NCEP Global Forecast System versions 16 and 17 (GFSv16 and GFSv17) and the AI-based Global Forecast System (AIGFS) version 1.1 in forecasting precipitation during landfalling AR events. Forecasts are verified against CCPA precipitation analyses for AR cases occurring during January-March 2026 using precipitation verification metrics across multiple forecast lead times. Preliminary results indicate that GFSv17 consistently outperforms GFSv16 and provides significant improvements in precipitation forecasts over the U.S. West Coast. Relative to GFSv16, GFSv17 more accurately predicts precipitation intensity and spatial distribution, reduces systematic forecast biases, and better captures moderate-to-heavy precipitation associated with landfalling ARs. The improvements occur over the complex terrain of the western United States, where accurate prediction of orographic precipitation remains a longstanding forecasting challenge. Compared with both GFSv16 and GFSv17, AIGFS demonstrates superior skill in forecasting the occurrence and spatial distribution of light-to-moderate precipitation. However, its performance degrades for the heaviest precipitation, tending to underpredict extreme rainfall during the most intense AR events. These findings suggest that while AIGFS effectively represents large-scale moisture transport, additional development is needed to improve the representation of mesoscale processes and terrain-enhanced precipitation associated with extreme rainfall. These evaluations are intended to provide guidance for the continued development and operational application of both numerical and AI-based weather prediction systems for high-impact precipitation events.

491140.title: The Missing Butterfly and the Role of Small-Scale Dynamics: Deterministic vs Stochastic AI Weather Models
491140.authors: Weidong Li, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL; and P. Hassanzadeh, Y. Q. Sun, A. Wikner, J. Wang, J. M. Finkel, and J. Weare
491140.abstract: In the multi-scale chaotic atmosphere, the butterfly effect originates in the fast dynamics of small scales: errors there grow rapidly, saturate early, and cascade upscale, so reducing the initial-error amplitude does not extend skill beyond a finite predictability limit. AI weather prediction (AIWP) models lack this behavior, though they outperform physics-based models on several standard metrics. A common explanation blames the loss function or learning paradigm: deterministic models trained on mean-squared error blur small scales, whereas generative models such as GenCast produce far more accurate spectra, so a stochastic generative formulation should restore the missing dynamics. Accurate spectra are not sufficient. We train deterministic (Swin Transformer, Spherical Fourier Neural Operators), and stochastic (Diffusion Transformer, Stochastic Interpolants) AIWP models on output of PlaSim, an intermediate-complexity GCM, with time step dt = 24 h. All reproduce the nearly perfect spectrum, yet none shows the butterfly effect: ensemble dispersion saturates as the initial-perturbation amplitude is reduced. Matching small-scale variance is not the same as learning the dynamics of small-scale error growth. We use difference kinetic energy (DKE) to follow how error grows scale by scale, comparing the same model trained with dt = 24, 6, and 1 h. We also examine the effects of the type of initial perturbations and the GPU numerical precision. The 1 h models show much faster DKE growth at early lead times, comparable to physics-based PlaSim ensembles, whereas the 24 h models grow error slowly from the start (figure). The time step therefore appears central, for deterministic and stochastic models alike. At large dt, small-scale errors saturate within a single step, leaving no signal from learning their growth. We discuss implications for modeling design and predictability research.

491141.title: ICEPyUS: A Python Tool for Calculating ETCCDI Precipitation Indices and Analyzing Climate Trends Using Weather Station and NetCDF Data Abstract
491141.authors: Omar Ramos Pérez, Universidad de Sonora, Hermosillo, SO, Mexico; and C. M. Minjárez Sosa
491141.abstract: Detecting changes in climate extremes, particularly precipitation, requires standardized and reproducible methodologies capable of integrating both in situ observations and gridded climate datasets. Although several well-established tools are available in other programming languages, limitations remain in the implementation of ETCCDI index calculations in Python in an accessible, flexible, and reproducible manner, particularly when working with weather station records and NetCDF datasets. We developed ICEPyUS (ETCCDI Precipitation Climate Indices in Python from the University of Sonora), an open-source package designed to automate the processing and analysis of daily precipitation data. The tool computes the 11 precipitation-related ETCCDI indices for both individual weather station time series stored in text files and gridded datasets in NetCDF format. In addition, it provides functions for generating time series and spatial maps, estimating trends using Sen’s slope and the Mann–Kendall test, evaluating spatial significance, and exporting results for further analysis. ICEPyUS facilitates the application of standardized methodologies in climate variability and climate change studies, reduces dependence on manual processing, and enhances the reproducibility of analyses. Its modular architecture enables the comparison of weather stations, regions, and climate products within a unified workflow. The package can support studies focused on precipitation extremes, hydroclimatic risk assessment, water resources management, and the development of climate adaptation strategies. It is intended for researchers, academic institutions, and organizations involved in climate services, environmental management, and evidence-based decision-making.

491143.title: From Road to Runway to Rocket: Altitude- and Species-Resolved Mission Screening
491143.authors: Jack Gao, St Paul Academy, St Paul, MN
491143.abstract: Transportation emissions are often compared by fuel consumption or carbon dioxide mass. These measures are useful, but they overlook a key difference among road vehicles, commercial aircraft, and launch vehicles: the altitude at which exhaust, in this case greenhouse gases, enters the atmosphere. Road vehicles emit near the surface, commercial aircraft release much of their cruise exhaust in the upper troposphere, and launch vehicles carry combustion products through the stratosphere and into the mesosphere. As launch activity grows, this distinction becomes increasingly important because rocket exhaust introduces gases and particles into atmospheric layers where removal and radiative and chemical responses differ from those near the surface. This realization raises a central question: Can emission mass alone capture the potential climate significance of a mission? The working hypothesis is that atmospheric response depends not only on the amount of material emitted, but also on the species involved, the altitude at which they are released, their atmospheric persistence and radiative effects at that altitude, and the useful service or payload the mission provides. To explore this hypothesis, representative screening cases are considered for a Falcon 9 launch, a Starship/Super Heavy launch, a modeled 1,500-kilometer (km) Airbus A320 flight, and travel in an average gasoline-powered passenger vehicle. Direct emissions of carbon dioxide (CO₂), water vapor (H₂O), and black carbon (BC) are estimated for each aerospace mission and distributed among five atmospheric layers extending from the surface to 85 km. Published vehicle specifications provide the propulsion architecture and nominal low Earth orbit payload capacities [1,2]. Within the study boundary, the central Falcon 9 case produces an estimated 405 metric tonnes (t) of CO₂, 158 t of H₂O, and 0.129 t of BC. The Starship/Super Heavy case produces 2,530 t of CO₂, 2,070 t of H₂O, and 0.0092 t of BC. The A320 mission simulated using the open-source OpenAP aircraft-performance model [3] produces 16.78 t of CO₂, 6.53 t of H₂O, and 0.00016 t of BC. For road travel, the comparison uses the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency estimate of approximately 400 grams (g) of tailpipe CO₂ per mile for an average passenger vehicle [4]. Based on direct CO₂ mass alone, the Falcon 9 and Starship cases correspond to approximately 24 and 151 modeled A320 missions, respectively, or about 1.01 and 6.33 million average vehicle miles. These familiar-scale comparisons represent direct-CO₂ mass equivalence, not total climate-impact equivalence. To examine how the interpretation changes with release altitude, the analysis introduces a dimensionless response-enhancement ratio. For each species and altitude band, the ratio compares the assigned response per unit mass with a near-surface reference. A ratio of 1 indicates no enhancement, while a value above 1 indicates a stronger screening response. Published atmospheric studies support the need for this species- and altitude-resolved approach. Previous studies have shown that rocket BC injected into the stratosphere can persist, absorb solar radiation, warm the surrounding air, and alter atmospheric circulation and ozone [5,6]. H₂O effects also depend strongly on emission altitude because water above the rapidly cycling lower troposphere can persist and interact differently with chemistry and radiation [8]. The literature, however, does not provide a universal mission-level multiplier for Falcon 9 or Starship. The numerical kernel used in this study is therefore a literature-informed sensitivity test, not a measurement of radiative forcing. CO₂ is assigned a weight of 1 at all altitudes; H₂O weights increase from 0.02 below 10 km to 6 in the 60–85 km band; and BC weights increase from 1 below 10 km to 120 in the 60–85 km band. These weights are explicit assumptions informed by the literature’s qualitative ordering of responses, not by values reported in the cited studies. Applying the altitude-dependent weights shifts attention toward emissions released above conventional aircraft cruise altitudes, particularly BC and high-altitude H₂O. A weighted emission score (WES) summarizes the test by multiplying each species mass by its response weight and summing across species and altitude bands. The score uses weighted metric tonnes (t_w), a bookkeeping unit specific to this screening analysis. The central WES values are 576 t_w for Falcon 9, 4,917 t_w for Starship/Super Heavy, and 17.5 t_w for the modeled A320 mission. These values are not radiative forcing in watts per square meter (W m⁻²), effective radiative forcing (ERF), or carbon dioxide equivalent emissions (CO₂e). Instead, the WES identifies influential species–altitude combinations and priorities for improved engine measurements, vertical inventories, and chemistry–climate modeling [6,7]. A payload-normalized comparison provides an additional perspective. Using published nominal low Earth orbit (LEO) payload capacities [1,2], the estimated direct-CO₂ intensity is 17.8 t of CO₂ per tonne of payload for Falcon 9 and 25.3 t of CO₂ per tonne of payload for the Starship scenario. The corresponding weighted intensities are 25.3 and 49.2 t_w per tonne of payload. These values illustrate the effect of normalization but do not provide a general ranking of vehicle efficiency. The two launch cases are not harmonized with respect to destination orbit, achieved payload utilization, reusable configuration, return burns, engine operating conditions, re-entry emissions, or lifecycle effects. Global inventory work likewise supports three-dimensional treatment of launch and re-entry emissions [7]. Together, the results show why emitted-mass comparisons are informative but incomplete. Direct mission emissions can be compared transparently when the system boundary and the delivered service are stated clearly. Altitude also matters, but its importance cannot be separated from species, atmospheric lifetime, chemistry, and optical behavior. Most importantly, similarity in direct CO₂ mass does not imply similarity in total climate impact. A physically calibrated comparison would require time-resolved trajectories and propellant flow, engine-specific emission indices, plume afterburning and chemistry, recovery and re-entry inventories, and species- and altitude-specific response functions evaluated over a defined time horizon [5–8]. By separating published evidence, model-derived quantities, and assumptions, the framework provides a reproducible path toward rigorous assessment of launch effects on atmospheric composition and climate.

491144.title: User-Informed Research to Guide Space Weather Research Priorities: A Pilot Study of the Space Traffic Management and Coordination Sector
491144.authors: Soudeh Kamali, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Demuth and R. Prestley
491144.abstract: As reliance on technologies vulnerable to space weather continues to grow, so too does the need for space weather predictions that are grounded in the real-world decision-making contexts of the people who use them. To ensure space weather research priorities keep pace with this evolving landscape, the National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) is undertaking a broader effort to systematically engage and study space weather users to directly inform space weather predictability research based on their needs. As an initial milestone toward this goal, this project establishes a multi-year plan for conducting research with space weather users and initiates a pilot research effort with a select user group. This pilot focuses on the Space Traffic Management and Coordination (STM/C) sector, one of the rapidly growing user communities with emerging needs shaped by the proliferation of commercial satellites and constellations, increasing reliance on space-based services, and expanding space situational awareness needs. This pilot project has two primary goals. First, using a semi-structured interview methodology, the project seeks to understand STM/C users' needs, risks, and decision-making contexts. Including how they use and interpret predictive space weather information, specifically with regards to neutral density variability in Low Earth Orbit. Second, the project will apply these insights to guide research priorities for NCAR High Altitude Observatory (HAO) and the broader space weather research community. This work builds on and complements recent broad-based efforts, such as the national survey of user needs for space weather conducted by the Space Weather Advisory Group.
