This transdisciplinary research combines social science, specifically risk communication research, with systems engineering tools and frameworks to translate user needs into prioritized space weather research requirements. The findings from this research will directly inform NSF NCAR HAO's current and future space weather observation and modeling efforts. By grounding future research priorities in a rigorous understanding of user needs, this project aims to strengthen the pipeline between space weather science and user decision-making, ultimately improving the resilience and safety of an increasingly crowded and weather-vulnerable orbital environment. This talk will present preliminary findings from the interview process, including emerging themes in user risk perception, current gaps in available data and tools, and opportunities for more targeted space weather research in support of the STM/C community.

491148.title: Impact of Active Learning on Student Performance in an Introductory Atmospheric Science Laboratory Course
491148.authors: Kassidy Kjos, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and M. Etten-Bohm
491148.abstract: Little investigation into pedagogy in atmospheric sciences has been conducted. While numerous studies across STEM disciplines have examined and demonstrate active learning (AL) education is beneficial to student performance, fewer than fifty explored atmospheric sciences classrooms specifically. This work expands upon the few existing atmospheric science pedagogical studies that examined AL by evaluating a diverse set of AL strategies implemented into introductory meteorology laboratories at the University of North Dakota. Five AL techniques (Think-Pair-Share, Game-Based, Role-Playing, Diagramming, and Gallery Walks) were implemented across multiple laboratory sections in the 2025-2026 Academic Year. Student performance is analyzed using the laboratory and its accompanying lecture curriculum assessments, as well as through pre- and post-tests. Results indicate students exposed to AL performed better than students not exposed on most assessments. Pre- and post-test data suggests students have opportunity to understand material more after experiencing AL compared to students in traditional laboratories, although, there is variability in the extent of the learning gains and which topics benefit more from AL intervention. The most effective strategy identified was Game-Based (top performing for the most topics: Humidity, Stability, Force Balances, and General Circulation), but, overall, top strategy varied depending on topic taught and assessment analyzed, demonstrating that further analysis across various modalities is needed.

491149.title: On the Development of our Understanding of Boundary Layer Halogen Photochemistry in Polar Regions
491149.authors: Paul B. Shepson, Stonybrook University, Stonybrook, NY
491149.abstract: It has been known for ~40 years that there is halogen chemistry involving unusually high concentrations of the halogens chlorine, bromine, and iodine in the boundary layer above ice and snow in polar regions (in the beginning, just in the Arctic). In the 1980s it was discovered that that chemistry may be depleting ozone and elemental mercury to near-zero concentrations, in the springtime, in the highly stable boundary layer. At first there was only a hypothesis that this was caused by bromine atom chemistry, with an unknown source of the reactive bromine. However, game-changing developments in optical spectroscopy and in mass spectrometry led to the observations of Br atoms and BrO radicals, in the process enabling proof that most of the chemical loss of ozone and Hg was due to reaction with Br atoms. It was also found through mass spectrometry observations that chlorine and iodine atom chemistry was also occurring and important. Field experiments in the Arctic showed that reactive halogen species were photochemically produced in the saline snowpack, and then released into the stable boundary layer, where a chain reaction could lead to efficient destruction of ozone and mercury. That chain reaction was found to be sustained in part by reactions on surfaces, including the snowpack and aerosol particles in and aloft of the boundary layer. This rather remarkable exhibition of nature requires a conspiracy of forces - complex photochemistry in the condensed phase, efflux from the surface to the atmosphere, entrapment of the halogen gases near the cold surface due to boundary layer stability, and the consumption of other species that initially revealed the complex phenomenon. Here I will discuss the combination of technical innovations and scientific experiments in the field and in the laboratory, as well as model development, that led to our current understanding of these processes. I will also briefly discuss how climate change may impact these processes, and future work that may help us with predictability related to these processes in a changing climate.

491152.title: George Kiladis: A Master at Linking Tropical and Midlatitude Circulations and Extreme Weather Events
491152.authors: Lance F. Bosart, University at Albany/SUNY, Albany, NY
491152.abstract: Dr. George Kiladis has had a highly fascinating and extremely productive scientific career "making waves” almost everywhere, but mostly in the tropica l eastern North Pacific Ocean and lower middle-latitude troposphere..I have the great honor to participate in the upcoming January 2027 George Kiladis Symposium where I will overview George’s remarkably productive scientific career with NOAA. During my presentation in George’s upcoming AMS Symposium, I will focus on several of his published papers in refereed AMS journals that focused on linkages of Rossby waves to deep convection in the tropical Eastern North Pacific Ocean during Northern Hemisphere winter. These papers include (e.g., 1) Kiladis et al. 1989, "The Origin of The South Pacific Convergence Zone”; 2) Kiladis and Weickmann 1992, "Extratropical Forcing of Tropical Pacific Convection during Northern Winter", and 3) Kiladis 1998 “Observations of Rossby Waves Linked to convection over the Eastern TropicalPacific." Key takeaways from the aforementioned Kiladis papers include: 1) Kiladis 1989: "Results show that the presence of South America and the equatorial Pacific upwelling zone does not appear to be crucial to the SPCZ, but that the removal of Australia destroys the southern monsoon and substantially weakens the western part of the SPCZ, 2), "Kiladis et al. 1992: ”Statistical evidence is presented to support the notion that tropical convection in the eastern Pacific and Atlantic intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) during northern winter can be forced by disturbances originating in the extratropics”, and 3) Kiladis et al. 1998: "The transient wave activity appears to be a crucial component of the momentum balance of the eastern tropical Pacific circulation. There is substantial interannual variability in the wave activity, consistent with observed changes in the large-scale basic state associated with the Southern Oscillation.

491153.title: Advancing the Weather and Climate Enterprise: The Value of Certified Consulting Meteorologists in a Changing Scientific and Professional Landscape.
491153.authors: Thomas C. Moore, ACM - Association of Certified Meteorologists, Hendersonville, NC; and C. L. Suffern
491153.abstract: The weather and climate enterprise continually evolves to meet growing societal demands. For example, AI has made it easier for the general public to gather information on current and past weather events. A positive result is that access to weather information has and continues to improve. However, this evolvement has also increased the need for educated meteorologists to interpret, and perhaps more importantly, verify the data. In fact, the demand for highly skilled, adaptable, and credentialed meteorologists continues to grow—particularly in the private sector. The Certified Consulting Meteorologist (CCM) program, administered by the American Meteorological Society since 1957, represents a rigorous standard of excellence, professionalism, and independent expertise in the private sector. This poster explores the vital role CCMs play in today’s diverse weather-related industries, provides insight into the CCM certification process, and highlights how the CCM credential can position professional meteorologists to meet emerging challenges in both a competitive job market and an evolving field of science. By emphasizing interdisciplinary knowledge, ethical character, and communication skills, CCMs are uniquely equipped to bridge gaps between science, business, and public service—helping to shape a more resilient and responsive weather and climate enterprise.

491154.title: Exploring Music Ensemble Participation Among Atmospheric Sciences Students
491154.abstract: At the University of North Dakota (UND), many students pursuing degrees in Atmospheric Sciences voluntarily participate in collegiate music ensembles despite having no curricular or professional requirement to do so. Anecdotal observations have highlighted a recurring overlap between high-performing students and sustained participation in instrumental and vocal music. This observation raises a broader question: what motivates STEM students participate in and remain involved with collegiate music, and how do they perceive that participation as contributing to their overall experience as students? This exploratory study aims to investigate the motivations of these students, with particular attention to students’ musical identity and sense of belonging, as well as perceived connections between music and their cognitive, academic, and personal development. Rather than assuming a causal relationship between music participation and academic success, the study seeks to understand these connections from the perspectives of the students themselves. Initial data will be collected through surveys of STEM students who participate in music, non-STEM students who participate in music, and STEM students who do not participate in music. Survey responses will identify patterns and themes across these groups and inform semi-structured interviews with STEM students participating in music. Thematic analysis of survey and interview data will explore recurring motivations, experiences, and perceived benefits to better understand why students in rigorous technical disciplines devote substantial time and effort to music and what, if anything, they perceive music provides that their STEM coursework does not. Findings may also provide insight into the roles of identity, belonging, cognitive contrast, and co-curricular engagement in the broader STEM student experience while establishing a foundation for future research into potential connections between musical engagement and the analytical and pattern-recognition skills used in STEM disciplines.

491163.title: Mapping the Evidence for Legal Cases: Storm Surge, Shadows, and Forensic Meteorology
491163.authors: Caroline Larsen Suffern, Equus Weather, Wake Forest, NC; and T. C. Moore
491163.abstract: AMS Certified Consulting Meteorologists (CCM) are retained by those in the legal field who represent a plaintiff or defendant when a case involves injury or property damage due to adverse weather conditions. The ability to create visually appealing maps of the weather observations and data for a case improves communication between the CCM and client, and can be helpful as an exhibit for a judge and/or jury to review, should the case go to trial. For storm surge claims due to tropical weather, detailed and property specific information on the storm surge inundation at the property of interest is required. In slip and fall cases (most frequently occurring during the winter months), consideration of land cover and subsequent irradiance at the location of the accident is necessary. Storm surge investigations often necessitate the interpolation of data from the closest United States Geological Service (USGS) gauges sites. Using the Environmental Systems Research Institute’s (ESRI) suite of software, Atlantic States Weather, Inc. (ASW) has developed GIS processes to map the timing of water inundation at a specific property and a process to visualize high water marks specific to structures at a specific property. Using high resolution Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), Digital Surface Models (DSMs), and building height information ASW maps the height of water from storm surge compared to a building’s height. This is crucial as typically, there are different insurance coverages for wind versus water damage at a property. ASW has employed the use of ESRI software to create a process to determine the timing of maximum storm surge at a USGS gauge. The process utilizes USGS storm tide (or the total height of the storm surge plus the normal astronomical tide) datasets that are filtered for maximum water depth then plotted in both 2D and 3D using ArcGIS Pro tools. Both the 2D and 3D visualizations show the timing of water levels at a property. The 3D visualizations depict when water levels reach parts of a building such as the first floor or second floor, and indicate potential water inundation into specific building levels. Cloud cover is an essential consideration for slip and fall claims as it impacts snow and ice melt. Using a combination of observations from climate sites, radar imagery, and satellite imagery from the date of the claim, ASW can construct a narrative of the cloud/sky conditions for the claim date. Slip and falls occur both at night and during the day. For those during daylight hours, irradiance is a consideration. Accident sites refer to specific areas of a property such as a back stairway, a street corner, or a parking space. Using the 2D ArcGIS Pro ‘Hillshade’ tool, the 3D ArcGIS Pro ‘Sun Shadow Volume’ tool, the specific latitude/longitude of a slip/fall, and the date/time of accident, shadows from the surrounding landcover are mapped. These shadowed areas enable ASW to determine the likelihood of snow and/or ice melt and provide visualizations helpful in discussions with clients.

491179.title: Interannual Variability of the Stratospheric Hydrogen Chloride simulated with SD-WACCM in Recent Years
491179.abstract: The quasi-biennial oscillation (QBO) is a dominant mode of variability in the tropical lower stratosphere and global models have only been able to generate the QBO in the past ~20 years. In this study, we examine the characteristics of the QBO and its impact on large-scale transport processes in the stratosphere using both the free-running and specified-dynamics (SD) versions of the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model version 6 (WACCM6) at 2° horizontal resolution. Potential modulation of the QBO by perpetual El Niño and La Niña conditions is also examined by conducting model simulations with the composites of sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies constructed for the QBOi project. Interannual variability of stratospheric hydrogen chloride (HCl), a long-lived tracer, is also examined using monthly mean mixing ratios of HCl simulated from the SD-WACCM and measured from NASA’s Aura Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS) for 2005-2020. The perpetual El Niño (EL) case tends to speed up the QBO, producing an average period of ~18 months and the perpetual La Niña (LA) case tends to slow down the QBO (period of ~35 months). Our results show that both the changes in the meridional circulation related to the stratospheric QBO and the QBO teleconnections to the sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) appear to have significant impacts on the year-to-year variability of stratospheric HCl in the midlatitudes of the Northern Hemisphere in recent years.

491180.title: Drizzle-State Dependence of MODIS Cloud Droplet Number Retrieval Bias in Marine Stratocumulus
491180.authors: Fatma Emin, DRI, RENO, NV; and J. G. Hudson
491180.abstract: Drizzle-State Dependence of MODIS Cloud Droplet Number Retrieval Bias in Marine Stratocumulus Satellite-derived cloud droplet number concentration (Nc) from MODIS is widely used to investigate aerosol–cloud interactions, yet comparisons with aircraft observations show substantial variability in marine stratocumulus. Here we examine whether MODIS–aircraft Nc bias is systematically organized by aircraft-observed drizzle state. We use 52 MODIS-matched vertical cloud profiles from the POST, MASE, and VOCALS-REx field campaigns. Aircraft Nc is defined from Cloud and Aerosol Spectrometer (CAS) cloud-droplet measurements, while drizzle state is classified independently using Cloud Imaging Probe (CIP) observations. MODIS Nc is calculated using both profile-specific values of k, fad, and cw, and a fixed literature-based parameter set. The profile-specific calculation is used as the main analysis, while the fixed values are used to test whether the observed bias depends on the retrieval assumptions. The MODIS–aircraft bias is not well represented by a single uniform offset. The median Nc bias decreases from 1.18 in non-drizzling profiles (n=21) to 0.90 in transition-drizzle profiles (n=23) and 0.74 in heavy-drizzle profiles (n=8). The heavy-drizzle regime provides the most robust signal, showing systematic MODIS Nc underestimation that persists across retrieval-parameter choices, effective-radius channels, and leave-one-out sensitivity tests. Because drizzle occurrence and aircraft Nc are correlated, we tested whether the drizzle-state dependence could be explained only by differences in Nc. Drizzle fraction remained significantly related to MODIS–aircraft bias after accounting for aircraft Nc, indicating that drizzle state contributes independently to the observed bias. We calculated the MODIS–CAS difference for each drizzle state and found a similar median offset of about +2.7 μm across all three states. Because retrieved Nc is proportional to re-5/2, this positive difference tends to lower MODIS Nc. In heavy-drizzle profiles, the observed Nc underestimation is close to what is expected from the difference alone. In non-drizzling and transition-drizzle profiles, the observed bias is less negative than expected, suggesting that other factors partly compensate for the effect of . These results indicate that MODIS-derived Nc should not be interpreted as having a single state-independent bias. Our results indicate a tendency toward MODIS Nc underestimation in heavy-drizzle profiles. In the transition regime, the near-unity median bias may reflect compensating errors rather than consistently accurate retrievals. Drizzle-dependent retrieval bias may therefore influence aerosol–cloud and cloud–precipitation relationships inferred using MODIS Nc.

491183.title: Higher-Order Reynolds-Stress and Temperature-Flux Cospectra In the Convective Atmospheric Surface Layer: Theory and Validation
491183.authors: Chenning Tong, Clemson University, Clemson, SC; and K. V. Barskov, A. H. Syed, S. D. Mayor, and P. Dérian
491183.abstract: Turbulence (co)spectra are often characterized by their scaling exponents, which represent the leading-order contributions and physics. However, actual (co)spectra contain higher-order contributions (deviations from the leading-order scaling) due to additional physics, and usually are only obtained empirically using data. We derive the higher-order velocity and temperature (co)spectra for scales larger than the height from the surface ($h$) in the convective surface layer using the method of matched asymptotic expansions. Starting from the (co)spectral transport equations, we identify an outer ($z_i$, the inversion height) and two inner ($L$, the Obukhov length and $h$) length scales, forming a singular perturbation problem. The perturbation parameters, $(-z_i/L)^4/3$, $(-z_i/L)^2/3$, and $-h/L$ represent the magnitudes of shear production in the outer scale, time derivative in the inner-outer scale, and gradient and shear production, and buoyancy production in the inner-inner scales, which are the physical origin of the higher-order contributions. The approximate solution, the higher-order (co)spectra in each scale range, are written as asymptotic expansions. Matching between the adjacent scales using a new matching method as an implementation of van Dyke's matching principle, yields the higher-order expansions for the convective (for scales larger than $-L$) and the dynamic ranges (for scales larger than $h$ and smaller than $-L$, see Tong and Nguyen 2015). The no-dimensional expansion coefficients are obtained using the data from the M2HATS field campaign (Tong et al. 2026). The agreement between the predicted and measured (co)spectra is excellent, despite the relatively large statistical uncertainties in the data, validating the theory. The results show that the seemingly random scatter in the measured (co)spectra is mainly due to systematic higher-order contributions. This work highlights the importance of the underlying physics of the perturbation parameters in obtaining the higher-order (co)spectra. Chenning Tong and Khuong X. Nguyen 2015 Multipoint Monin-Obukhov similarity and its application to turbulence spectra in the convective atmospheric surface layer. J. Atmos. Sci. 72, 4337-4348. Chenning Tong, Shane D. Mayor, Steven P. Oncley, Chris Roden, William O. J. Brown,c Scott M. Spuler,c Matthew Hayman,c Bruce M. Morley,c Jacquelyn Witte, Pierre Dérianb Stephan F. J. De Wekker,d Jielun Sun, Kirill Barskov, and Davoud Pourabdollah 2026 Multipoint Monin–Obukhov Similarity Theory Horizontal Array Turbulence Study (M2HATS), Bull. Amer. Meteorol. Soc. E501

491187.title: Meteorology Movies Hollywood Needs to Make Next
491187.authors: Roger D. Turner, Science History Institute, Carlisle, PA
491187.abstract: Films like Pressure (2026) and The Aeronauts (2019) show that the history of meteorology has amazing stories that can soar on the silver screen. This paper playfully considers what could be next. Should director Christopher Nolan follow Oppenheimer (2023) with Rossby, dramatizing that Manhattan Project of meteorology, the invention of numerical weather prediction? Would The Carrington Event be a (box office) disaster today, or could it stimulate space weather preparedness? Could Cate Blanchett bring the right emotional depth and intellectual heft to a biopic about the troubled, brilliant tropical meteorology giant Joanne Simpson? The presentation introduces compelling history books that could spark great screenplays, while thinking through some inspiring stories that can help us engage with science-skeptical audiences today. Come argue over casting choices or pitch your own script. Inspired by true events.

491191.title: Seasonal Wind and Boundary Controls on United States Gulf Coast Sea-Level Variability
491191.authors: Christopher M. Little, AER, Lexington, MA
491191.abstract: Monthly-to-interannual coastal sea-level variability raises the background water level on which weather-driven extremes occur and is therefore an important contributor to coastal flood frequency. Unlike extremes, however, much of this lower-frequency variability is coherent across the entire Gulf Coast. Here, as part of the iGROWL (improving submonthly Gulf Regional Outlooks of Water Level) project, we investigate the dynamical origin of Gulf-wide coastal sea-level coherence, the processes controlling its local amplitude, and its seasonal dependence. By analyzing monthly dynamic sea-level variability over 1993–2018, we find that shared coastal variability is prominent year-round, explaining about 70% of local variance across 10 Gulf tide gauges. This shared variability is not a simple basin-wide sea-level offset: it is amplified at tide gauges relative to gridded altimetric sea-surface-height products and is larger and more spatially coherent in the cool season than in the warm season. Cool-season Gulf coastal sea-level variability is associated with broad western North Atlantic wind anomalies and positive shelf sea-level anomalies extending around Florida toward the South Atlantic Bight, whereas warm-season variability is more localized to the Gulf. Idealized numerical simulations reproduce key features of the observed coastal amplification and indicate that shared variability reflects two nonlocal, temporally correlated contributions: a broad shelf/eastern-boundary sea-level anomaly and a coastally and western-amplified response controlled by integrated alongshore wind stress and shelf geometry. The boundary-forced contribution is most important for eastern Gulf locations and during the cool season. These results show that monthly Gulf tide-gauge variability cannot be inferred from offshore sea-surface height or local winds alone; it is a dynamically modulated coastal expression of seasonally varying atmospheric and boundary forcing.

491198.title: Learning from the Oracle: Prioritizing Gulf Coast high-Tide Flood Forecasting Efforts
491198.authors: Christopher M. Little, AER, Lexington, MA; and M. J. Widlansky, G. Dusek, Y. Wang, and A. Rateb
491198.abstract: Current generation high-tide flood (HTF) outlooks exhibit limited skill in locations such as the United States Gulf Coast, where non-tidal residual (NTR) variance is large relative to tidal amplitudes. The 5-year IGROWL project — Improving submonthly Gulf Regional Outlooks of Water Level — aims to improve the relevance and accuracy of flood outlooks by: 1) relating tide-gauge water levels to inland impacts and 2) accounting for time-dependent distributions of submonthly NTRs. Here, to guide these efforts, we analyze perfect-information ("oracle") forecasts, in which selected measures of target-month NTR distributions are assumed known. These analyses provide a quantitative basis for assessing which NTR measures (e.g., monthly means and/or upper tails), locations, and lead times offer the greatest potential for forecast skill improvement. Relative to a Gaussian baseline, empirical climatological distributions better represent positive tails, increasing total expected flood counts at 8 of 10 Gulf Coast tide gauges. However, daily and monthly skill gains remain minimal, because climatologies do not resolve month-to-month variability in NTR distributions. In contrast, oracle forecasts indicate that improved NTR information can substantially increase skill. For example, a perfect monthly oracle reduces Gulf-wide mean monthly flood-count RMSE by approximately 25% relative to the Gaussian baseline. The relative value of complete, monthly-mean-only, and upper-tail-only information differs widely among stations, reflecting local differences in tide regime, tail behavior, and tide-surge phasing. Based on our analyses, we propose that Gulf Coast HTF outlooks use a lead-time-dependent continuum of dynamical and statistical forecast tools that explicitly communicate their capabilities and objectives. Monthly-to-seasonal products can emphasize regional-scale flood burden and the probability of high-NTR regimes, whereas shorter-lead products are needed to resolve individual flood days at specific locations.

491207.title: Observations and Trends from the Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) Gridded Products prior to, during, and after Strong Tornadoes
491207.authors: Joseph Patton, CISESS - Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies, College Park, MD; and S. D. Rudlosky
491207.abstract: Changes in observed lightning activity have long been associated with changes in the frequency of observed severe weather events. Prior research has shown that sudden increases in lightning activity (i.e., lightning jumps) often precede damaging severe weather events such as large hailstones and tornadoes. This research explores the observations of lightning flash characteristics as detected by the Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) instruments, which produce gridded products of lightning flash density, area, and brightness. Strong tornado events are analyzed within the context of these gridded products from the GLM instruments. Lightning flash characteristics are tracked from thirty minutes before tornado touchdown, through the lifespan of the tornado using verified damage reports, through to thirty minutes after tornado cessation for the storm associated with each tornado. On average across all tracked storms, a marked decrease in lightning flash brightness is observed in the minutes immediately following tornado cessation. This demonstrates the utility of incorporating space-based lightning imagery such as the GLM gridded products into the severe weather warning decision-making process for operational weather forecasting.

491210.title: Dissemination of STAR-Processed GNSS Radio Occultation Products to Support NWP Data Assimilation
491210.authors: Yan Bai, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD
491210.abstract: Title: Dissemination of STAR-Processed GNSS Radio Occultation Products to Support NWP Data Assimilation Yan Bai, and Xi Shao Abstract Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) Radio Occultation (RO) data has become one of the cornerstones of the global observing system, providing high-vertical-resolution, all-weather bending angles, from which atmospheric temperature, and moisture profiles can also be derived. The timely assimilation of these data into Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models is mission-critical for maximizing global forecast skill. This poster provides an overview of the operational framework at the NOAA Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR) for generating and disseminating GNSS RO neutral atmosphere and space weather products from both commercial data-buy (PlanetiQ and Spire), and COSMIC-2 missions. The STAR end-to-end processing pipeline transforms raw satellite data into science-ready Level 1 (bending angle) and Level 2 (retrieved atmospheric temperature and humidity profiles) neutral atmosphere products, and into Total Electron Content (TEC) products for space weather. To meet the strict timeliness of operational data assimilation, the data processing and distribution framework relies on low-latency data pipelines routing real-time data streams through the NOAA’s NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF) and distributed through the Product Distribution and Access (PDA) and the Global Telecommunication System (GTS). Continuous RO product quality monitoring is integrated into the pipeline, utilizing automated, near-real-time validation systems that evaluate the products against weather models. Concurrently, comprehensive satellite constellation monitoring tracks health, spatial distribution, and daily RO profile counts for each RO satellite across multi-GNSS constellations (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, and BeiDou). The complete portfolio of STAR GNSS RO data products, system performance statistics, and access portals can be explored at the website: https://ncc.nesdis.noaa.gov/.

491211.title: Simulation of Mesoscale Convective Systems and Extreme Rainfall Event over West Africa Using MPAS-A.
491211.authors: Ayodeji Olatunde, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA; and L. V. Carvalho, J. Done, and J. Berner
491211.abstract: Mesoscale Convective Systems (MCSs) are the dominant source of extreme rainfall and flooding in West Africa, driving most high-impact precipitation events in the region. This study investigates an extreme rainfall event that occurred over Mokwa, Niger State, Nigeria between May 26 and May 30, 2025. The event led to severe flooding that submerged the town, destroyed over 4,000 homes and recorded at least 500 casualties. To understand the physical process responsible for this extreme event, we use the Model for prediction Across Scales-Atmosphere (MPAS-A), a global cloud-resolving model to simulate the development and evolution of the convective system and its interaction with large-scale environmental conditions. The analysis focuses on the atmospheric processes that support the initiation and maintenance of the system, including moisture transport, thermodynamic instability, and low-level circulation associated with the West African monsoon environment. To assess surface impacts, the study also examines land surface responses during the event, including soil moisture variability and runoff generation in response to intense rainfall. These diagnostics are used to link atmospheric dynamics with hydrological outcomes at the surface. Overall, this work provides a process-based case study of a high-impact MCS event and evaluates the ability of MPAS-A to represent key characteristics of convective systems and their associated hydrological impacts in West Africa.

491213.title: Towards The Next-Generation Low-Earth Orbit Hyperspectral Microwave Sounding
491213.authors: Antonia Gambacorta, GSFC, bethesda, MD; and N. Shahroudi, S. D. Nicholls, A. E. Kotsakis, M. S. Yabra, J. A. Caraballo-Vega, R. Kroodsma, V. Torres III, P. Mohammed, M. Stephen, B. Bulcha, M. Frittz, S. Kalluri, L. Zhou, W. McCarty, and A. E. Emory
491213.abstract: Through multi-year investments, NASA and NOAA have advanced hyperspectral microwave technology for Earth remote sensing from technology incubation to mission formulation. Key programs include the Near Earth Orbit Observatory network (NEON) Series-1 and the Decadal Survey Incubation Planetary Boundary Layer Mission. This presentation examines the development of operational hyperspectral microwave sounding capabilities within the context of the international joint satellite remote sensing system. We present spectral design trade studies, noise tolerance analyses, and observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs) that evaluate the impact of hyperspectral microwave measurements through data addition and denial experiments. Results demonstrate the potential operational benefits of integrating these capabilities into the combined LEO and GEO observation framework, informing strategic planning for next-generation international satellite coordination and data utilization.

491216.title: In-Flight Performance of the Pyro-Atmosphere Infrared Sounder (PIRS) Airborne Spectrometer
491216.authors: Thomas S. Pagano, JPL, Thousand Oaks, CA; and S. Wong, R. C. Wilson, A. Soibel, Y. Maruyama, R. Chao, and R. Toda
491216.abstract: The PIRS instrument was developed under the NASA Earth Science Technology Office (ESTO) FireTech program and recently completed its first flight demonstration during part of the NASA FireSense campaign. PIRS is designed to measure temperature and water vapor profiles in the lower troposphere. The instrument incorporates a compact grating spectrometer operating in the 4.0-5.2 µm spectral region and uses an immersion grating together with High Operating Temperature-Barrier Infrared Detectors (HOT-BIRD) fabricated by JPL’s microdevices laboratory. These features enable a compact instrument while allowing higher operating temperature with excellent uniformity of the Focal Plane Assembly. Unlike conventional infrared sounders, which primarily rely on longer wavelengths spectral regions for temperature and humidity sounding, PIRS operates in the 4.0-5.2 µm band. Recent studies have highlighted the high information content in this spectral region for sounding temperature and humidity profiles in the lower troposphere. However, solar reflected energy contributes significantly to the measured signal in this band alongside thermal emission. Accurate retrieval of atmospheric profiles therefore requires careful estimation of the solar reflected component. PIRS provides a platform for evaluating these retrieval challenges using real observational data. PIRS has a native sounding footprint of better than 250 m, and includes a built-in imaging mode that provides 40 m spatial resolution across a wide ±40° cross-track swath. The instrument radiometric sensitivity is better than 0.7 K in the CO2 sounding band and 0.4 K in the water vapor band at a scene temperature of 280 K. Its spectrometer provides 640 spectral channels with spectral resolution ranging from ~3.5 nm at the shortest wavelengths to ~5 nm at the longest wavelengths. This presentation will focus on the instrument radiometric, spatial and spectral performance and examples of data obtained during the NASA FireSense campaign.

491225.title: New Opportunities for Sampling the Atmospheric Boundary Layer Using ARM Data (Invited Presentation)
491225.authors: Larry K. Berg, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA; and J. M. Comstock, D. Dexheimer, N. L. Hickmon, C. Kuang, F. Mei, J. R. O'Brien, B. Schmid, M. Spychala, and A. Theisen
491225.abstract: The Department of Energy’s (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility has a long track record in atmospheric boundary layer measurements. ARM currently operates three fixed observatories: the Southern Great Plains, the North Slope of Alaska, and the Eastern North Atlantic. In addition to these locations, ARM deploys three ARM Mobile Facilities (AMFs) globally with one AMF beginning a five-year deployment at Bankhead National Forest (BNF) in 2024. Both the fixed observatories and the AMFs deploy similar instrumentation, including remote sensing systems to measure key variables within the boundary layer and into the free troposphere. The BNF observatory is distinguished by a 42.7-meter instrumented tower to sample key variables over the depth of the forest canopy. ARM is also developing two portable profiling systems to measure profiles of temperature, humidity, and winds to temporarily augment spatial coverage during AMF campaigns. In addition to the ground-based observatories, ARM operates multiple airborne observation platforms, such as the tethered balloon system (TBS) as well as an uncrewed aerial system (UAS). The TBS can carry an instrument payload of approximately 50 kg to altitudes as high as 1.5 km. Instrumentation deployed with the TBS can measure aerosol properties, atmospheric state, and gas phase properties. The ArcticShark is the ARM UAS. It is a fixed-wind vehicle with a 6.7 m wingspan and the ability to carry a scientific payload of approximately 45 kg, including high-frequency cloud and aerosol observing instruments. This presentation will include a review of ARM instruments that are applicable to studying turbulence in the atmospheric boundary layer and will focus on new measurements being made at the BNF observatory as well as those made using platforms like the TBS and UAS.

491229.title: Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS) on Aqua: Operations, Calibration and Data Products
491229.authors: Thomas S. Pagano, JPL, Thousand Oaks, CA; and Q. Yue, J. P. Teixeira, R. C. Wilson, T. Wang, R. Monarrez, and W. Mathews
491229.abstract: Hyperspectral infrared sounding of the atmosphere has become a vital element in the observational system for weather forecast prediction at National Weather Prediction (NWP) centers worldwide. The NASA Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS) instrument, launched in 2002, was a technology and science demonstration of hyperspectral infrared observations and was designed to provide accurate atmospheric temperature and water vapor profile information in support of weather prediction. AIRS demonstrated key technologies that afforded high performance and long life and is still operational today. AIRS data represent the longest continuous record of high spectral resolution infrared radiometric spectra from Earth in the 3.7-15.4 µm region. In addition to AIRS use in weather prediction, its exceptional radiometric, spectral and spatial stability make it useful for weather process studies and climate science. AIRS has operated nearly continuously with only periodic temporary outages for several days a few times during its operational history. AIRS exceptional radiometric stability can be attributed to its full-aperture on-board blackbody and space view combined with a temperature controlled optical bench and focal plane. Small changes in mirror polarization have been accounted for in the most recent release of the Level 1B version 8 product. This presentation will review the nearly 25 year history of AIRS in orbit with a focus on the instrument operations, calibration and currently available data products.

491231.title: TROPICAL - The Effect of Polydisperse Evaporating Sea Spray on Hurricane Boundary Layer: A Multi-Fluid Approach
491231.authors: Yevgenii Rastigejev, North Carolina A&T State Univ., Greensboro, NC; and S. A. Suslov and W. B. Dong
491231.abstract: Despite decades of research, sea spray remains an important yet not well-understood component of air-sea interaction under hurricane-strength winds. Powerful winds tear large amounts of ocean spray from breaking waves and carry it into the marine boundary layer. These droplets act as an intermediate medium in the exchange of momentum and heat between the ocean and the atmosphere, modifying turbulent transport and, consequently, the mechanical and thermodynamic structure of the boundary layer. In this work, we have developed an Eulerian multifluid framework to simulate the effects of evaporating polydisperse sea spray on the vertical heat and momentum transport in the hurricane and severe-storm marine atmospheric boundary layer. In this framework, the air and droplet phases are represented as distinct, interacting continua, each with its own velocity, temperature, and turbulence fields. This formulation provides a more consistent description of air-spray coupling than conventional empirical or mixture-type models and resolves the interaction between droplets and turbulent flow. In particular, the multi-fluid approach enables us to capture two mechanisms by which sea spray suppresses turbulence: (1) frictional dissipation of turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) caused by the relative motion between air and droplets, and (2) loss of turbulent-eddy energy associated with suspending droplets against gravitational settling. Both reduce TKE and eddy viscosity, leading to wind acceleration and a lower air-sea drag coefficient. Sea spray also exerts a thermodynamic effect: as droplets evaporate, they exchange heat and moisture with the air, modifying vertical temperature and humidity profiles and, as a result, sensible and latent heat fluxes. Since spray-driven turbulence suppression also affects these thermodynamic processes, it further amplifies the influence of sea spray on heat fluxes and on the moisture and temperature distribution in the boundary layer. Using the multifluid model, we examine the influence of sea spray on turbulent air-sea drag and bulk enthalpy transfer coefficients. Enhanced heat exchange combined with reduced drag is widely considered essential for hurricane intensification and maintenance. In particular, it has been suggested that hurricanes reaching wind speeds of 50 m/s or higher require an enthalpy-to-drag transfer coefficient ratio of at least 0.75. Consistent with theoretical predictions, observations indicate that this ratio approaches 0.7 at tropical-storm wind speeds. However, extrapolation from lower wind speeds yields values of only 0.3–0.4 at hurricane-strength winds. This discrepancy suggests that an additional physical mechanism becomes important at high wind speeds. Our simulations show that including sea spray approximately doubles the ratio, increasing it to 0.6–0.75 at hurricane-strength winds, in close agreement with theoretical predictions and observations. At lower wind speeds, typical of tropical storms, the effect of spray is small because of its low concentration. These results support the hypothesis that sea spray contributes to the increase in the enthalpy-to-drag transfer coefficient ratio at high wind speeds.

491233.title: Abstract: Advancing Biogenic Ice Nucleating Proteins for Precipitation Enhancement: New Validation from University CollaborationsAuthor: Sabina Simjee —Real Baarish, Newport Beach, CA,UnitedStates
491233.authors: Sabina Aslam Simjee, Real Baarish, Chino hills , CA
491233.abstract: Advancing Biogenic Ice Nucleating Proteins for Precipitation Enhancement: New Validation from University Collaborations Sabina Simjee —Real Baarish, Newport Beach, CA, United States Abstract Building on our 2026 introduction of biogenic ice nucleating proteins (INPs) as a biodegradable alternative to silver iodide (AgI). Real Baarish presents new results advancing both the science and the manufacturability of organic seeding agents. Since our last presentation, a new collaboration with the Atmospheric Science Laboratory at Colorado State University, to continue independently validating the performance of our material by continuing aerosol studies. AgI remains constrained by an activation ceiling near −6°C, leaving the large volume of atmospheric moisture in warm winter storms unreachable by legacy technology. Our latest results demonstrate that Real Baarish’s organic seeding agents nucleate ice at temperatures as warm as −3.5°C deep within this “thermal dead zone”. We will present preliminary data grounded in the foundational work from Boise State and Colorado State University confirming that biological INPs are more effective at than current industry agents at glaciogenic freezing. Suggesting a better material for cloud seeding operations. By pairing dramatically higher warm-temperature efficiency with a 100% biodegradable, non-toxic profile, our seeding agents remove the environmental and regulatory barriers that have historically kept cloud seeding out of the agriculture and global drinking water sectors. As water scarcity and wildfire risk intensify globally, these results establish biogenic INPs as a proven, high-yield, and operationally ready bridge to a secure water future.

491234.title: Inherited Climate Forcing versus the Forward Climate Commitment of Annual Transport Activity
491234.authors: Jack Gao, St Paul Academy, St Paul, MN
491234.abstract: Transportation influences climate through processes that operate over very different timescales. As illustrated by previous studies, carbon dioxide (CO₂) accumulates and persists for centuries, whereas contrails, nitrogen-oxide-driven changes in ozone and methane, aerosols, and high-altitude rocket emissions act over periods ranging from hours to decades [1–4]. This difference creates a practical problem for cross-sector comparison. Effective radiative forcing (ERF) in a given calendar year reflects the accumulated legacy of past activity, whereas current technology and policy decisions primarily affect emissions from activity occurring now and in the future. Road transportation dominates direct transport CO₂ emissions; aviation has substantial non-CO₂ effects; and spaceflight introduces an emerging, altitude-sensitive source of emissions [1,5–7]. A single present-day forcing value, therefore, cannot fully describe both inherited climate influence and the forward consequence of an additional year of activity. This study compares these two perspectives for global road transportation, aviation, and a provisional spaceflight sensitivity pathway from 2018 to 2060. The first metric, inherited forcing, estimates sector-attributable ERF present in a calendar year. Historical and projected CO₂ emissions are propagated through a multi-timescale carbon-cycle impulse-response function, which represents the rapid initial removal of an emission pulse and its long atmospheric tail [2]. Aviation CO₂ is combined with assessed aviation non-CO₂ forcing components [1]. The second metric, forward climate commitment, integrates the ERF initiated by one annual cohort of activity over 10-, 20-, and 100-year horizons. Aviation cohort responses are anchored to published global-warming-per-activity (GWA) estimates for CO₂, contrails, short-lived nitrogen-oxide (NOₓ)-driven ozone warming, and longer-lived NOₓ-driven methane and ozone cooling [3]. Integrated forcing is reported in milliwatt-years per square meter (mW yr m⁻²). ERF itself is expressed in milliwatts per square meter (mW m⁻²), where 1 mW equals 10⁻³ watts. The two metrics intentionally preserve physical timescale differences rather than merging them into a universal aviation multiplier. Persistent contrails generally last for hours; the short NOₓ–ozone response is represented on an approximately one-month timescale; the longer NOₓ–methane-related response evolves over roughly 12 years; and the CO₂ response extends across multiple timescales, including a centuries-long tail [2,3]. This structure allows a calendar-year stock-like measure and an annual-cohort flow-like measure to be evaluated side by side without implying that they answer the same question. The main methodological novelty is the explicit separation of inherited forcing from forward commitment within one transparent cross-sector framework. The comparison also keeps the operational atmospheric boundaries visible, so that apparent sector crossovers can be traced to included species, response timescales, and selected integration horizons. In the central scenario, accumulated road CO₂ forcing remains larger than the combined aviation and provisional spaceflight screening pathway through 2060. The annual-cohort metric produces a different ordering. For activity in 2018, aviation initiates estimated integrated ERF values of 77.6, 80.4, and 132.6 mW yr m⁻² over 10, 20, and 100 years, respectively. The corresponding road CO₂-only values are 68.4, 122.9, and 432.8 mW yr m⁻². Aviation is therefore near the same as, and modestly above, the road CO₂-only comparison at 10 years, but remains below it over the longer horizons. Under the central activity and technology pathways, the aviation-only annual commitment exceeds the road CO₂-only comparison around 2032 for a 20-year horizon and around 2056 for a 100-year horizon. These crossover years are conditional scenario results, not forecasts; they depend on sector growth, technology assumptions, the selected time horizon, and the atmospheric effects included in each sector boundary. The most robust scientific learning is not a specific crossover date but the divergence between the two metrics. Inherited ERF describes the climate influence already present due to accumulated historical emissions and ongoing short-lived effects. Forward climate commitment asks a different question: how much time-integrated ERF is initiated by the next year of transport activity? Because aviation combines long-lived CO₂ with short-lived warming and cooling responses, its relative importance changes with the integration horizon [1,3,4]. The analysis, therefore, demonstrates why the ranking of transport sectors cannot be treated as a fixed property independent of metric choice. It also shows why direct CO₂ shares, present-day ERF, and prospective annual commitment should be reported separately rather than combined into a single multiplier. The comparison remains deliberately bounded. The road pathway currently includes CO₂ only, whereas aviation includes CO₂, contrails, and coupled short- and long-lived NOₓ responses. Road-related ozone, methane lifetime, and black carbon effects must be accounted for before interpreting the modeled crossover as a complete sector comparison. Spaceflight remains a screening sensitivity because its atmospheric response depends on emitted species, propellant, and engine type, injection altitude, plume chemistry, and re-entry processes [6,7]. These boundary differences do not invalidate the metric comparison; instead, they identify the evidence required for a physically harmonized assessment. The resulting framework provides two complementary views of the influence of transport climate: one measures the inherited forcing visible today, and the other measures the forward commitment created by new activity. As a result, the policy implication is additive rather than substitutive, while the prospective importance of aviation and spaceflight supports targeted mitigation of distinct atmospheric effects but does not reduce the need for continued decarbonization of road transport.

491237.title: Midlatitude Cyclone Patterns Resulting in Significant Snowfall over Metro Denver
491237.authors: Kendall Custer, South Dakota School of Mines, Rapid City, SD
491237.abstract: Denver, Colorado, is a metropolis located along the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains, a topographic barrier that alters weather patterns and makes accurate forecasting difficult, especially when forecasting significant snowstorms. Between 2000 and 2024, Denver has experienced numerous significant snowfall events, some of which are associated with midlatitude cyclones. There is a lack of research on the patterns associated with these synoptic-scale systems that influence significant snowfall rates over Metro Denver and the Adjacent Foothills. This leads to the goal of this research: to find how many of Denver’s significant snowfall events between 2000 and 2024 are associated with midlatitude cyclones, and what patterns emerge from these systems that result in significant snowfall accumulation over Metro Denver and the Foothills. This research is important because, by finding these associated patterns, the scientific community can better understand what to observe when forecasting significant snowfall events. Using heavy snowfall criteria from the National Weather Service’s Boulder/Denver Weather Forecasting Office, “significant snowfall events” were defined as those with an average total accumulation of 8 inches or greater and an average maximum snowfall rate of 8 inches or more in 24 hours. Historical snowfall accumulations were gathered using seven co-op/CoCoRaHS stations around Metro Denver and the Foothills on NOAA’s Regional Climate Centers’ xmACIS 2 database. This snowfall data was used to develop a list of dates when significant snowfall events occurred. Using these dates as references, the National Center for Atmospheric Research’s ERA5 database was utilized to gather data at the 250 mb, 500 mb, 700 mb, 850 mb, and surface levels to establish which dates have an associated midlatitude cyclone. Moving forward, the plan is to trace the centers of the midlatitude cyclones and their upper-level features, including cut-off lows and upper-level cyclogenesis, to find patterns associated with their proximity to Colorado and whether their locations result in significant snowfall events over Metro Denver and the Foothills. As mentioned, this research is important for understanding the patterns associated with midlatitude cyclones and could greatly improve the forecasting accuracy of significant snowstorms in the Denver Metro Area.

491238.title: Project EXCEED for PMP: AI Model Development to Downscale Reanalysis for Extreme Precipitation - Preliminary Results, Lessons Learned, and Future Work
491238.authors: Imme Ebert-Uphoff, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and A. Libardoni, P. Schumacher, K. A. Hilburn, L. Slivinski, S. Frolov, and K. M. Mahoney
491238.abstract: The goal of Project EXCEED (EXtreme preCipitation Estimates from Enhanced Downscaling) is to pursue improved estimates of probable maximum precipitation (PMP) by downscaling reanalysis precipitation data, which have a very low resolution, to much higher resolution. Project EXCEED includes both physical and AI-based approaches. The focus of this presentation is solely on discussing AI-based approaches. Our ultimate goal is to develop AI models to downscale precipitation fields from the Twentieth Century Reanalysis (20CR) dataset, which is currently available from 1806 to 2015 and has a resolution of about 75km, to a desired target resolution of roughly 3km. The target ground truth is the NOAA Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC) Dataset, a radar-based estimate of precipitation, which is available from 1979 to near-present and has a native resolution of about 800m, and is coarsened to 3km. Emphasis is on modeling extreme precipitation well. If successful, these models will be applied to downscale historical precipitation records in order to better estimate civil infrastructure needs in the immediate future. In future projects, these models may also serve as a starting point to downscale the output of climate models to better understand infrastructure needs further into the future, but that task is not part of this current project. Downscaling precipitation is known to be a difficult problem and achieving the large downscaling factor, about 25x, makes this task particularly challenging. Furthermore, AORC and 20CR both have biases in precipitation location and amounts, especially for extreme events, making it hard to match AORC exactly. This presentation will cover our journey of approaches tried so far, including selection of atmospheric variables to utilize from the 20CR input dataset, neural network architectures tried, and loss functions, to yield both deterministic and probabilistic AI downscaling models for this task. We describe preliminary results obtained, challenges encountered, lessons learned, and proposed future work. Links to datasets: Twentieth Century Reanalysis (20CR) dataset: https://psl.noaa.gov/data/20thC_Rean/ NOAA Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC) Dataset: https://registry.opendata.aws/noaa-nws-aorc/

491239.title: The Relationship between Tropical Cyclone Rainfall Intensity and Vertical Wind Shear
491239.authors: Ting-Yu Cha, NSF NCAR, Fort Collins, CO
491239.abstract: Vertical wind shear (VWS) is well known to modulate tropical cyclone (TC) intensity and structure, but its effect on TC rainfall remains less understood. Simple parametric models addressing the relationship between rainfall intensity and VWS magnitude often assume steady-state asymmetries, which fail to capture early-stage, less organized TCs that are often influenced by transient mid-tropospheric vorticity anomalies. To understand this relationship better, we use 38 years of TC-PRIMED radar-radiometer observations across all basins, applying a distributional Natural gradient-boosting framework (NGBoost) that decouples environmental drivers of rainfall's typical value (location) from its variability (scale) — rather than the storm-mean and azimuthal-mean metrics used in prior climatologies. We show that the effect of VWS is concentrated almost entirely in the tail: median rainfall is nearly insensitive to shear, while upper-percentile rain rates, convective echo-top heights, and intense low-level reflectivity cores all increase with VWS, and VWS ranks among the top drivers of rainfall's variability across all environmental predictors considered. This effect is not strongest in early-stage TCs — it persists across the life cycle and has the largest impact on major TCs. These findings indicate that VWS influences extreme TC rainfall risk throughout the life cycle and underscore the importance of distributional analysis for examining TC rainfall.

491247.title: Connecting Weather and Climate As Part of Ocean Literacy By Using Conceptual Flow Diagrams.
491247.authors: Howard Joe Witte, American Meteorological Society, Los Angeles, CA
491247.abstract: "The Ocean is a Major Influence on Weather and Climate", Principle #3 in The Handbook for Increasing Ocean Literacy, Tool for Educators. A free updated reference booklet you will want on your bookshelf. This will be a quick review of the authors' development of easy-to-use conceptual flow diagrams aligning with the NGSS framework for elementary, middle, and high school teachers. Beside the weather and climate section, the handbook provides an Earth Systems perspective of the ocean with 28 conceptual flow diagrams of The Ocean Literacy Scope and Sequence for Grades K–12, and am article explaining the theoretical basis for the Scope and Sequence

491248.title: Constraining Sectoral NOx and CO2 Emissions over East Asia and Japan by Leveraging High-Resolution GOSAT-GW NO2 and GHG Measurements
491248.authors: Chia-Hua Hsu, National Institute for Environmental Studies, Japan, Tsukuba, Japan; and H. Tanimoto, K. Ikeda, S. Chatani, T. Fujinawa, H. Lim, S. Okamoto, S. Inomata, Y. Niwa, J. Bisht, M. C. Rajwar, N. D. Thien Chi, T. Sugita, A. P. Mizzi, L. M. Judd, and S. Janz
491248.abstract: Nitrogen oxides (NOx) and carbon dioxide (CO2) are key drivers of air pollution and climate change, respectively. Accurate quantification of their emissions is essential for developing effective pollution control and climate mitigation policies. Because these gases are co-emitted during fossil fuel combustion processes, simultaneous observations of NOx and CO2 offer a unique opportunity to jointly constrain these anthropogenic emissions. The Global Observing SATellite for Greenhouse gases and Water cycle (GOSAT-GW) mission provides concurrent global nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and CO2 measurements through its TANSO-3 spectrometer, which features two observing modes: a wide-swath mode providing observations with a swath width of 900 km and a pixel resolution of 10 km, and a Focus Mode providing unprecedentedly high-resolution (1–3 km) NO2 and CO2 data targeting for urban areas. This fine spatial resolution provides the capability to resolve NO2 plumes—which exhibit high signal-to-noise ratios relative to background levels—to serve as precise proxies for pinpointing fossil fuel CO2 emission sources that are otherwise obscured by biospheric fluxes and background variability. This study aims to use GOSAT-GW data alongside other satellite products (e.g., TROPOMI, OCO-2) to optimize NOx and CO2 (may also include CH4) emissions from regional to urban scales at high spatial resolution. We set up a nested 15-, 3-, and potentially 1-km WRF-Chem simulation framework over East Asia and Japan, with the finest domain specifically targeting the complex urban source mixtures of the Tokyo Metropolitan Area. We directly constrain emissions from different sectors (e.g., transportation, power generation) and investigate how GOSAT-GW Focus Mode observations enhance sectoral top-down emission estimates. Posterior model simulations are evaluated against field campaign aircraft observations and in situ measurements from ground networks to verify the accuracy of the emission inversion. Furthermore, top-down CO2 emissions are compared with other local and global inventories (e.g., Climate TRACE) to evaluate emission uncertainties. We will present preliminary results from our joint NOx and CO2 emission inversion, highlighting the potential of GOSAT-GW to improve urban-scale emissions quantification.

491253.title: The Global Impacts of CO2 Plant-Physiological Feedbacks on Fire Weather Risk
491253.authors: Ashley Ellen Cornish, University of Georgia, Athens, GA; Univ. of Georgia, Athens, GA; and G. J. Kooperman, J. Mao, and J. Kumar
491253.abstract: Recent literature has demonstrated that increased CO2 emissions and associated warming are causing higher likelihood for wildfire development in many regions around the globe. In addition to the radiative warming effect of rising CO2, higher atmospheric CO2 concentrations may also modify fire weather dynamics through plant-physiological forcing. As CO2 increases, there are reductions in stomatal conductance, which reduces water lost through transpiration. This reduces the water content in the near-surface atmosphere, contributing to increases in air temperatures via increased sensible heating; however, it may lead to retention of water in the soil and in the plants themselves. To analyze the impact these competing effects may have on vegetation fire and fire weather dynamics, we make use of idealized CMIP6 simulations (1%/year CO2 increase) that isolate radiative, plant-physiological, and combined impacts of rising CO2. In our assessment, we investigate the plant-physiological contribution to changes as indicated by several fire and fire weather indices, including output directly from the models (e.g., burned area) and derived metrics using the Canadian Fire Weather Index System (CFWIS). Results show regional differences in terms of overall change, with physiological forcing amplifying fire weather risk in some regions (e.g., Amazon) while dampening in others (e.g., Western Australia). To evaluate the drivers of these differences, we utilize machine learning and Shapley value analysis to determine contribution of each meteorological variable to the change, with preliminary results showing temperature and relative humidity being the dominant variables. When changes in meteorological-derived fire risk are compared with model output burned area and fire carbon emissions, sign changes are not consistent in all regions, highlighting the need to consider changes in soil moisture and vegetation when assessing changes in fire potential.

491254.title: Employing Residual Circulation Variables to Improve AI Model Skill in QBO Prediction
491254.authors: Wenyuan Du, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI; Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and Y. Sun and M. H. Hitchman
491254.abstract: The stratosphere is one of the few recognized sources of forecast skill on subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) time scales. In the stratosphere, the Quasi-biennial Oscillation (QBO) is the most regular oscillation. Living in the tropical stratosphere, the QBO features alternating layers of easterly and westerly winds that descend from about 10 hPa to 100 hPa, with a period between 22-34 months. The phase of the QBO can affect the polar vortex, tropical convection, and extratropical surface climate. A model that predicts the QBO skillfully therefore holds value far beyond the tropical stratosphere. However, the stratosphere is exactly where the new Artificial Intelligence (AI) weather models are weakest. In most current machine learning (ML) models which focus on tropospheric weather and climate, the optimization weighting is proportional to pressure, so that stratospheric levels contribute little to the loss. Current AI model tops usually do not extend above 50 hPa (in the lower stratosphere), and benchmarking stratospheric skill is not usually a primary focus. In such a situation, the prediction skill of ML models in the stratosphere stays largely unexplored. Under the topic of QBO prediction, there have been some neural networks (NN) models that have developed specifically for QBO prediction. One of them included Eliassen-Palm (EP) fluxes in the tropical upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS) as input, and their results show that the inclusion improves NN forecast skill for the QBO. Since EP-fluxes represent momentum and heat transport in the transformed Eulerian mean (TEM) framework, we extend this approach by employing not only EP-fluxes 10-250 hPa but also more eddy and transient variables to train a NN QBO prediction model. We find enhancement of the NN-based QBO model performance across all levels between 10 hPa and 100 hPa by using more residual variables, which extends useful forecasting out to 26 months. However, we also find that incorporating the zonal mean wind data is critical among the training inputs to obtain a skillful model.

491265.title: Ice Loading Controls the Vertical Distribution of Radiative Heating in Tropical Cirrus: Implications for Cirrus Cloud Thinning
491265.authors: Ashok Kumar Gupta, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN; and R. Bennartz
491265.abstract: Cirrus cloud thinning seeks to reduce the radiative warming of high clouds by altering their ice properties, yet its consequences may depend not only on changes in top-of-atmosphere radiative effects but also on where radiative heating is deposited within the cloud. This vertical heating structure influences in-cloud stability and may therefore affect subsequent cirrus evolution. However, how radiative heating is distributed vertically through tropical cirrus and how that distribution changes with ice loading have not been characterized from long-term observations. Here we show, using four years of combined spaceborne radar and lidar retrievals of tropical single-layer cirrus with no liquid-containing clouds elsewhere in the column, that the ice water path (IWP) is the primary parameter organizing the vertical structure of longwave heating. As IWP increases, the longwave-heating centroid descends 3.6 km toward cloud base, and the vertical heating gradient reverses sign, from positive (stabilizing tendency) in thin cirrus to ~−1.8 K day⁻¹ km⁻¹ (destabilizing tendency) in thick anvils. The reversal occurs at IWP values of approximately 9–10 g m⁻² at night and 18–24 g m⁻² during the day, whereas the daytime shortwave gradient remains positive at all ice loadings, which isolates the reversal as a longwave phenomenon. Observation-constrained radiative-transfer calculations reproduce both the centroid descent and the gradient reversal. An idealized thinning perturbation that halves each cloud's IWP and doubles its effective radius reduces the occurrence-weighted tropical-mean longwave cloud radiative effect by 2.7 ± 0.2 W m⁻² and local in-cloud heating by up to 1.2 K day⁻¹. These results establish ice loading as a key control on tropical cirrus radiative heating structure and provide an observational constraint for assessing how cirrus thinning may modify in-cloud stability, cloud evolution, and radiative effects.

491267.title: State-Dependent Vertical Organization in an Aerosol-Loaded Boundary Layer: Implications for the Subcritical Aerosol-Moisture Feedback
491267.authors: Stephen M. Jessup, Columbus State University, Columbus, GA
491267.abstract: Numerous radiative, microphysical, and thermodynamic processes operate in aerosol-loaded boundary layers, yet coupled interactions between particulate matter and atmospheric moisture remain difficult to represent within a unified framework. Aerosol water uptake and loss respond strongly to environmental humidity, altering particle size and optical properties, while aerosol loading modifies radiative transfer and heating and cooling rates influencing boundary-layer temperature, stability, and mixing. These processes are individually well established, but their coupled evolution may produce feedbacks not captured when aerosol microphysics, radiation, and boundary-layer thermodynamics are considered independently. Jessup and Enfinger (2025) observed steady air and dewpoint temperatures within a smoke plume as shortwave radiative forcing changed rapidly during the 8 April 2024 solar eclipse in Columbus, Georgia, and proposed the Subcritical Aerosol-Moisture Feedback (SAMF) to explain these observations. Let G, H, and R represent hygroscopic aerosol growth, environmental humidity, and infrared radiation, with subscript ₀ denoting reference states. For system response F, SAMF may be represented by the irreducible three-way interaction S_SAMF = F(G,H,R) − F(G,H,R₀) − F(G,H₀,R) − F(G₀,H,R) + F(G,H₀,R₀) + F(G₀,H,R₀) + F(G₀,H₀,R) − F(G₀,H₀,R₀) which isolates the response beyond individual and pairwise effects. Whether the anomalous thermodynamic response during the eclipse represented an unusually salient expression of this interaction, and whether it operates detectably under ordinary radiative forcing, remains unknown. Without directly estimating that term, we seek to bound its possible influence on particulate matter (PM) and relative humidity (RH) time series by decomposing common-trend, common-mode, and remaining variability during noneclipse conditions. One Temtop M2000 sensor and two M2000 sensors were deployed on an approximately 2.5-m ladder during 17 days in December 2025 and January 2026, providing simultaneous 1-min PM2.5, PM10, and RH measurements. Sensors were manually calibrated before each deployment. Sampling frequently occurred under aerosol loading associated with local burning. Statistical analysis tested whether vertical variability could be represented by common temporal trends and a dominant shared mode, as might arise from advection or other common forcing, or whether additional vertically structured covariability, potentially consistent with SAMF, remained. Measurements were divided into 15-min windows and classified by mean cross-level slopes into dataset-relative near-zero, gentle, moderate, and steep rates of change. Vertical correlations were calculated before and after independent linear detrending of each sensor record, separating shorter-timescale cross-level covariability from simultaneous monotonic changes. Date-clustered permutation and bootstrap inference with false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction tested persistence and state dependence of detrended cross-level correlation. Principal-component analysis/singular-value decomposition (PCA/SVD), with PCA-aware surrogate nulls, quantified whether remaining covariance could be represented by a single dominant shared mode and whether significant multilevel structure remained after its removal. Significant positive cross-level correlation persisted after detrending for PM2.5, PM10, and RH, indicating synchronized short-timescale variability not attributable solely to simultaneous increases or decreases throughout the array. The clearest state dependence occurred in particulate matter. PM10 detrended cross-level correlations varied significantly among slope regimes and increased with greater upward and absolute concentration-change magnitude. PM2.5 detrended cross-level correlations increased systematically with upward, downward, and absolute slope magnitude, although its global slope-bin test narrowly missed the FDR threshold. RH detrended cross-level correlations remained significantly positive but showed no comparable systematic dependence on RH rate of change. Thus, significant state-dependent modulation of detrended cross-level correlation was evident in particulate matter but not RH, qualitatively echoing the eclipse observations in which aerosol scattering changed rapidly while thermodynamic state remained comparatively steady. Among particulate regimes with significant steep-versus-near-zero enhancement, only steep PM10 decreases retained significant residual structure after PC1 removal, during the strongest observed aerosol-loading decline, consistent with dispersal. PCA analysis therefore focused on this regime to determine how much internal covariance could be attributed to broad concentration trends, a dominant shared mode, and secondary multilevel structure beyond that mode. During steep PM10 decreases, raw cross-level correlation significantly exceeded that of detrended data (q = 0.0058), while substantial positive cross-level correlation remained after independent trend removal (r = 0.322; q = 0.0005). PCA/SVD of detrended PM10 identified two principal modes accounting for approximately 57% and 30% of total detrended variance, averaged first within each date and then across dates. Of the 43% variance remaining after PC1 removal, PC2 captured an average of 72% using the same date-first averaging, significantly exceeding the approximately 65% expected under the PCA-aware conditional surrogate null (q = 0.0037). Together, PC1 and PC2 accounted for approximately 87% of detrended variance within the steep PM10 decrease regime, leaving about 13% to PC3. Because all valid PCA windows contained three measurement heights, PC3 was the final orthogonal mode rather than an unmodeled residual; its geometry is interpreted descriptively below rather than subjected to a separate significance test. In a separate post-PC1 test, root-mean-square (RMS) cross-level correlation was approximately 4.7% greater than its PCA-aware null expectation (0.566 versus 0.541; q = 0.046), providing additional evidence of statistically detectable multilevel structure beyond the dominant shared mode. Neither PC2 variance concentration, the post-PC1 correlation excess, nor the approximately 13% of detrended variance in PC3 can be attributed specifically to SAMF coupling in the steep PM10 decrease regime. Qualitatively, PC1 was vertically distributed, with comparable contributions from all three heights, consistent with common influence from advection, turbulent mixing, or other shared forcing across the sampled layer. PC2 generally expressed a localized vertical contrast dominated by one height: in the 15-min analysis, its strongest loading accounted for approximately 76% of total squared loading magnitude and averaged about 2.5 times the next strongest loading, although the dominant height varied among window durations. PC3 represented a smaller but more distributed contrast, with the two strongest loadings more comparable (approximately 50% and 39% of squared loading magnitude; ratio ≈ 1.15). This distinction between single-height-dominated PC2 geometry and more distributed PC3 geometry persisted in 10- and 20-min sensitivity analyses. Although SAMF coupling cannot be directly attributed, these results suggest that statistical signatures potentially compatible with SAMF may be detectable beyond the original eclipse case. Smaller-scale advection, turbulence, heterogeneous sources, and other vertically structured processes remain viable explanations. These findings provide a specific basis for continued direct investigation using more precise aerosol microphysical, radiative, and vertically resolved thermodynamic measurements.

491281.title: What Controls the Formation and Propagation of Sumatra Squall Lines?
491281.authors: Rubaiat Islam, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and C. Schwartz, Z. Liu, J. Dudhia, and R. Rios-Berrios
491281.abstract: Sumatra squall lines are one of the most common mesoscale convective systems in the Maritime Continent, causing heavy rainfall, strong winds, and sometimes even flash floods. Many previous studies reported in the literature suggest that these squall lines originate as an initial thunderstorm over Malacca Strait that subsequently propagate eastward and make landfall over Singapore and adjacent regions. However, the September 17, 2024 squall line originated much further west over the mountainous Sumatra island, despite giving a characteristic bow echo structure and producing up to 80 km/hr wind gusts and 130 mm/hr precipitation. This event challenges the conventional expectation of Sumatra Squall Lines forming over Malacca Strait as an initial thunderstorm. In this study, we analyze the meteorological conditions leading up to the September 17, 2024 squall line event using satellite imagery, radar data, and numerical weather prediction model simulations. Our findings indicate that the squall line was influenced by a combination of factors, including a strong low-level jet over the western part of Sumatra, enhanced moisture convergence, and favorable upper-level wind patterns. These conditions created an environment conducive to the development of deep convection and the organization of thunderstorms into a linear structure. Our results underscore the need for a systematic study of squall line formation mechanisms in the Maritime Continent, in which the role of regional topography, land-sea interactions, and synoptic-scale influences may be more significant than previously thought. Further research is warranted to explore these alternative mechanisms and improve forecasting capabilities for such severe weather events in the region.

491283.title: The Damage Is the Data: EF-SELF Report for Property-Level Forensic Wind Speed Estimation
491283.authors: C. Justin Van De Wiele, APEC Engineering and Laboratory, Shallowater, TX; AEOLUS Analytics, LLC, Shallowater, TX; and A. J. Reese and M. B. Phelps
491283.abstract: Accurate determination of wind speed at a specific property remains a problem in forensic meteorology. Surface observing stations, storm reports, radar-derived products, and commercial weather reports are useful for defining the larger meteorological environment, but the wind actually experienced at an individual property may differ substantially from the nearest observation. Severe convective wind fields are spatially variable, observing stations are often several miles away, and in many post-storm investigations there simply is no instrument located where the damage occurred.
