The physical evidence, however, remains. The Enhanced Fujita Scale was developed specifically around the relationship between wind and observed damage. Damage Indicators (DI) and Degrees of Damage (DoD) associate recognizable damage to buildings, structures, trees, and other objects with published Lower Bound, Expected, and Upper Bound wind-speed estimates. Although developed primarily for tornado assessment, the underlying concept is fundamentally broader: if wind leaves a measurable damage signature, that damage contains information concerning the wind that produced it. AEOLUS Analytics developed the Enhanced Fujita Self Report, or EF-SELF, to use that concept at the property level. EF-SELF converts geotagged photographs of observed wind damage into a transparent, damage-constrained wind-speed assessment. Each photograph is associated with a location, a Damage Indicator, a Degree of Damage, and its corresponding published EF-scale wind-speed interval. Rather than relying upon a single damage observation, EF-SELF evaluates multiple observations surrounding the property and combines them into a single representative estimate. The photographs, geographic locations, DI/DoD selections, wind-speed ranges, and mathematical calculations remain visible to the user so that the result can be examined rather than simply accepted as the output of a proprietary model. The current methodology combines three complementary measures. An uncertainty-range-weighted expected wind speed gives greater influence to observations having narrower published EF wind-speed ranges. Maximum interval-support analysis identifies the wind speed supported by the greatest number of observed LB–UB intervals. A global-bound midpoint evaluates the relationship between the maximum lower bound and minimum upper bound when the observations do not share a complete common intersection. These three measures are combined using a fixed-weight ensemble to produce the EF-SELF wind-speed estimate. Additional diagnostics quantify interval overlap, discordance, leave-one-out stability, and sensitivity to perturbation of the input observations. These statistics describe the internal agreement and stability of the damage-based estimate and are not presented as direct wind measurements or ground-truth error rates. A representative EF-SELF application was performed at a property in Gainesville, Texas using ten geotagged damage observations representing four Damage Indicator types, including hardwood trees, manufactured homes, small barns and farm outbuildings, and a grain bin. The published expected EF wind speeds associated with the observations ranged from 56 to 91 mph. Nine of the ten damage intervals supported the maximum-support portion of the analysis, producing an overlap ratio of 0.90. The fixed-weight ensemble produced a property-level wind speed estimate of 74.9 mph. Leave-one-out analysis produced a mean of 75.2 mph, with estimates ranging from 74.4 to 79.0 mph and a standard deviation of 1.37 mph, indicating that the final estimate was not controlled by any single damage observation. An important feature of the approach is that the wind-speed estimate is tied directly to observable physical evidence rather than to spatial interpolation alone. The nearest available observing station may adequately characterize the regional storm environment while still failing to resolve local variations in wind speed caused by storm structure, terrain, exposure, and distance from the observation site. EF-SELF provides an independent damage-based estimate that can be compared with surface observations, radar-derived estimates, storm reports, and commercial wind products. Agreement among these independent lines of evidence strengthens the interpretation of the event, while disagreement identifies where additional investigation may be necessary. The method also provides a framework for reproducibility and quality control. Because each observation retains its photograph, location, DI/DoD assignment, published wind-speed interval, and contribution to the ensemble, a second analyst can examine the same evidence and reproduce or challenge the result. Future work will evaluate inter-analyst agreement in DI/DoD selection, compare EF-SELF estimates with independently measured or well-constrained wind events, and examine the sensitivity of the fixed ensemble weights to different damage populations and storm environments. EF-SELF is not intended to replace surface observations, radar, engineering analysis, or conventional post-storm meteorology. Instead, it provides another source of information where one is commonly missing: what the damage itself says about the wind at the location of interest. Event timing and attribution remain separate questions and should be evaluated using radar, surface observations, storm reports, eyewitness information, and other independent evidence. The practical value of EF-SELF is its simplicity and transparency. A user can document damage with photographs, locate those observations geographically, apply established EF-scale Damage Indicators and Degrees of Damage, and produce a repeatable property-level wind-speed assessment whose underlying evidence can be reviewed photograph by photograph. This creates an opportunity to supplement conventional post-event observing and analysis methods with the enormous amount of physical wind information that is already present after virtually every damaging storm. With continued evaluation, inter-analyst testing, and development of automated quality-control tools, EF-SELF has the potential to evolve from a forensic reporting application into a scalable platform for high-resolution, damage-based documentation of wind events.

491284.title: Characterizing 2018-2026 Fire Activity, Emissions, and Variability with the GOES Eastern U.S. Fire Emissions Inventory, Version 2 (GEUFE 2)
491284.authors: Gavin A. White, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and C. H. Fite, C. C. Schmidt, and C. D. Holmes
491284.abstract: The eastern United States (U.S.) experiences frequent agricultural and wildland fires, the vast majority being intentional or prescribed. The GOES Eastern U.S. Fire Emissions (GEUFE) inventory was developed to better represent the emissions from these numerous, short-duration fires using geostationary satellite data and detailed, region-specific emission factors. This work presents GEUFE version 2 (GEUFE 2), which improves the land cover classification, adapts to changes in the operational Fire Detection and Classification (FDC) algorithm, and expands the inventory to span 2018-2026. As in version 1, GEUFE 2 estimates fuel consumption and atmospheric emissions of 8 pyrogenic compounds for the eastern U.S. We evaluate how land cover data impacts estimates of dry matter consumption and show that GEUFE 2 is consistent with version 1 for the overlapping period. The estimated dry matter consumption of GEUFE 2 is compared to four other biomass burning emissions inventories: GFAS, GFED, QFED, and RAVE. The longer data record of GEUFE 2 enables the characterization of seasonal and interannual variability of fires in the eastern U.S. Additionally, we use GEUFE 2 to separately estimate emissions from wild vs. prescribed fires and fires on public vs. private lands. Wildfires that occur on public lands are found to contribute more dry matter consumption per fire than that of the average private land wildfire. GEUFE 2 offers further insights into the complex nature of eastern U.S. fire activity, characterizing it over a nine-year period with respects to land cover, wildfire vs. prescribed fire designation, and land ownership.

491285.title: The Enterprise Microwave Rain Rate and Type Retrieval for AMSR3 and WSF-M MWI
491285.authors: Veljko Petkovic, Univ. of Maryland College Park, College Park, MD; and H. Meng and R. Ferraro
491285.abstract: The constellation of conical-scanning passive microwave imagers supporting NOAA's operational precipitation monitoring is being renewed. The Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 3 (AMSR3), aboard JAXA's Global Observing SATellite for Greenhouse gases and Water cycle (GOSAT-GW), carries forward the AMSR-E and AMSR2 heritage. The Microwave Imager (MWI) aboard the Department of Defense Weather System Follow-on – Microwave (WSF-M1) satellite takes over the early-morning orbit held for decades by SSMIS, succeeding the DMSP series. Further imagers will follow. Each must deliver validated rain rate and precipitation type early in its mission, and each arrives with its own channel set, footprint geometry, and latency requirement. Giving every sensor its own retrieval package multiplies maintenance with each addition. NOAA's Enterprise Microwave Rain Rate and Type (EMRRT) retrieval is instead designed as a single system that hosts multiple passive microwave imagers within the NOAA Low Earth Orbit program. The retrieval core is the Goddard Profiling Algorithm (GPROF), a fully parametric Bayesian scheme that inverts observed brightness temperatures against an a priori database linking radiances to radar-observed precipitation, screened by total precipitable water, two-meter temperature, and surface type. A unified front end performs ingestion, geolocation, radiometric quality control, and ancillary preparation for any supported instrument. Each sensor then retains its own retrieval core, preserving the channel configuration and a priori database appropriate to its frequencies and field-of-view geometry, and a common back end writes a standardized product carrying rain rate, the convective contribution to it, probability of precipitation, and per-pixel quality. Because the sensor-specific work is restricted to that core, supporting an additional imager extends the existing package rather than duplicating it, and it is this new configuration that is now entering operations. An ongoing work, intended for a subsequent release of the enterprise package, applies convolutional neural networks that relate brightness temperatures directly to rain rate and precipitation type, trained on collocated observations from current and heritage instruments against Global Precipitation Measurement mission radar. We present NOAA operational EMRRT retrievals for both AMSR3 and WSF-M MWI, evaluated against the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor ground reference over the contiguous United States and against the GPM Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar. Additionally, we demonstrate that the ML-based retrievals match the accuracy of the operational Bayesian scheme at substantially lower processing cost, and models trained on one instrument successfully transfer to another. The same package is being prepared for additional imagers as they enter operational service, including the EPS-SG MWI, with refinement against on-orbit observations, continued evaluation against independent references, and near-real-time performance monitoring.

491287.title: Passive Microwave Convective/Stratiform Precipitation Type Retrieval for the GPM Constellation
491287.authors: Veljko Petkovic, Univ. of Maryland College Park, College Park, MD; and M. Orescanin, B. Manfre, J. Tan, G. J. Huffman, P. Kirstetter, L. Ji, D. Watters, and M. Arulraj
491287.abstract: Whether precipitation is convective or stratiform governs a storm’s latent heating profile, its morphology, and the error characteristics of nearly every satellite precipitation retrieval. Despite this, no global observational record of precipitation type exists. Ground radar networks resolve type regionally; the TRMM Precipitation Radar and the GPM Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar (DPR) resolve it with high fidelity but sample only a narrow swath. As part of a larger ongoing effort, we are producing an observation-based convective/stratiform type dataset at 0.05°, 90°S–90°N, half-hourly, spanning 1998–2027, combining low-Earth-orbit passive microwave (PMW) retrievals with geostationary infrared (IR) retrievals, each carrying per-pixel uncertainty. This presentation reports results from the PMW component. A Bayesian U-Net maps multichannel brightness temperatures to DPR-referenced convective probability at 5 km scale. Trained on GMI–DPR coincidences, the retrieval transfers across the GPM constellation and is produced for a number of sensors, including GMI, AMSR2, ATMS, and SSMIS. Precipitation class is computed everywhere, allowing users to impose the precipitation mask of their choice, with retrieval scale set by the DPR training footprint rather than sensor field of view. We present the evaluation of PMW-predicted precipitation class against DPR, including skill by class, by sensor, and by precipitation regime, together with the spatial and zonal structure of performance across the constellation. Retrieval skill depends on label-scheme design: a two-class scheme operating behind an external rain/no-rain mask outperforms a self-contained three-class scheme on the raining classes, while the three-class model usefully flags its own rain/no-rain ambiguity. Decomposed predictive uncertainty shows that the dominant limitation is the intrinsic ambiguity of the microwave signature rather than insufficient training, and identifies the regimes where added training data would pay off the most. The results are placed in the context of a continuous, high-resolution record of precipitation type, its extension across the full observational period, its evaluation against independent references, and the combination of information from multiple observing systems.

491288.title: High-Resolution CO2 Emission Pattern Reconstruction Using Observation-Constrained Pollutant Emissions over China
491288.authors: Wei Feng, IAP, Beijing, 11, China; and X. Tang and F. Fang
491288.abstract: Timely and spatially resolved anthropogenic CO2 emission inventories are essential for regional carbon monitoring and atmospheric inversion. However, conventional bottom-up inventories are often released with substantial delay, and their gridded spatial distributions commonly rely on historical patterns and proxy data that change only gradually. Because CO2, NOx, and CO share major combustion and industrial sources, observation-constrained pollutant emission posteriors may provide complementary information for updating CO2 emission patterns. We develop a hierarchical, mass-conserving framework for reconstructing monthly CO2 emission patterns over mainland China at a spatial resolution of 15 km. Historical MEIC-global-derived CO2 emissions are used as the supervisory reference, while monthly CAQIEI NOx and CO posterior emissions provide observation-constrained inputs. Grid-cell emissions are decomposed into national monthly totals, provincial shares, and within-province spatial compositions. The principal model begins with training-period monthly mean spatial patterns and estimates spatial corrections using pollutant emissions, land cover, and geographical information. Province-wise normalization ensures nonnegative emission fractions and exact mass closure. Fixed emission-ratio, linear-regression, and gradient-boosting approaches are evaluated using common learning targets and rolling temporal experiments. Current results show that fixed-ratio and linear approaches capture the average relationships between CO2 and co-emitted pollutants but are less effective in representing differences among regions, cities, and high-emission areas. Gradient boosting provides more stable spatial reconstruction. In an observable NOx-to-CO experiment, directly applying relationships learned from MEIC to CAQIEI produced a national bias of approximately −56% in 2020. Training the model using information from both inventory systems reduced the bias to approximately +1%. For CO2 reconstruction, using MEIC-global as the evaluation reference, the model reduced the Jensen–Shannon divergence of within-province emission-share distributions by approximately 28% at 45 km during 2021–2023 relative to training-period monthly mean patterns. Similar improvements were obtained during model development and historical evaluation. Hierarchical attribution further indicates that national emission magnitude, interprovincial allocation, and within-province spatial patterns control distinct families of reconstruction errors. These results support a modular inventory design in which external activity information constrains emission totals, while observation-constrained pollutant emissions inform high-resolution spatial allocation. The framework provides a practical pathway for extending spatially resolved CO2 emission estimates to years without contemporaneous CO2 training labels.

491290.title: Seeing the CME as One Object: Multi-Instrument Composites and Feature Tracking from the Solar Disk through the PUNCH Field of View
491290.authors: C R Gilly, NorthWest Research Associates, Denver, CO; and S. Gibson
491290.abstract: PUNCH images coronal density structures out to 45 degrees from the Sun on a 4-minute cadence, yet anyone following a single CME across that range still assembles it by hand from instruments with different fields of view, cadences, and intensity scales. We have built that assembly into JHelioviewer, the open-source client maintained by the Helioviewer Project. We demonstrate a CME followed continuously from the solar disk through the PUNCH field of view, and we use that view to identify what still stands between this imagery and routine operational work. JHelioviewer now loads PUNCH mosaics beside SUVI, AIA, MLSO K-Cor, LASCO C2 and C3, CCOR-1, and PROBA-3 ASPIICS, and we render them as one continuous scene rather than a row of panels. We use radial projections to keep structure far from the Sun from collapsing into the last few pixels of the frame, a radial histogram equalization filter to make the faint outer corona and the bright low corona legible in a single image, and feature tracking to hold a propagating front in view from roughly 9 solar radii out to the edge of the PUNCH field. We also render three-dimensional point clouds in context with the imagery, which is how we connect this view to the polarization-based CME reconstructions the team is developing. The official release now carries the PUNCH data source and the filter, so anyone can use them without a local build. We note that the filter is intended for visualization and feature detection; it is not suitable for absolute photometry, and quantitative brightness work should return to the calibrated products. The imagery across this instrument ladder is contiguous while the event list behind it is not: the Heliophysics Events Knowledgebase holds no CME entries from K-Cor, CCOR-1, or PUNCH anywhere in 2026. Continuous imagery with a discontinuous catalog behind it limits what can be automated on top of it, and we suggest that closing that gap is where the next useful work lies.

491292.title: Accounting for Humidity in Projections of Cooling Demand and Household Energy Vulnerability in North Carolina
491292.authors: Matthew Menon, North Carolina State University, Apex, NC; and W. A. Robinson, G. E. Tierney, and J. H. Bowden
491292.abstract: Households face increasing energy demands for warm-season cooling as climate change alters both temperature and atmospheric moisture. Cooling degree days (CDDs), a commonly used metric for estimating temperature-driven cooling demand, account for temperature but do not explicitly capture the influence of humidity on cooling requirements. In this study, we evaluate how incorporating humidity into cooling-demand metrics affects projected changes in household cooling needs and how physical climate risk is distributed amongst counties in North Carolina with varying socioeconomic circumstances impacting homeowners' ability to afford warm-season cooling. We use monthly temperature and humidity data from 20 CMIP6 global climate models statistically downscaled to 6-km resolution using LOCA (Localized Constructed Analogs) version 2. We compare conventional temperature-based CDDs with a humidity-adjusted cooling metric for the historical period of 1985–2014 and the near-term future period of 2025–2054 under multiple Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios. We quantify differences in projected cooling demand across climate models, emissions scenarios, and geographic regions to assess the relative contributions of each source of uncertainty. We further combine projected changes in cooling demand with county-level measures of household energy burden and socioeconomic characteristics to develop a more rigorous assessment of energy vulnerability. Comparing vulnerability estimates based on temperature-only and humidity-adjusted metrics allows us to evaluate whether accounting for humidity changes the magnitude or geographic distribution of projected risk. This analysis provides insight into how conventional temperature-based measures may impact future cooling-related energy demands and identifies communities that may face disproportionate challenges in maintaining affordable household cooling as the climate changes.

491293.title: Coupled Weather–Fire Forecasting Under Operational Constraints: Predictability, Skill, and Evaluation
491293.authors: Janice Lynn Coen, NCAR, Boulder, CO; University of San Francisco, San Francisco, CA; and G. W. Johnson, N. LaHaye, D. S. Saah, W. Schroeder, and V. Waeselynck
491293.abstract: Forecasting wildfire growth requires predicting how an evolving fire responds to atmospheric flow that varies across terrain and in time, heterogeneous fuels, and an imperfectly known fire state. At convective scales, the fire can also modify the local airflow driving its subsequent spread. Errors in forecast winds, fire location or state, or the timing of changes in fire behavior can therefore produce increasingly different outcomes as a forecast proceeds. Successful retrospective simulation does not by itself establish an ability to forecast. Retrospective studies can be calibrated through adjustments to spread parameters or inputs or configured with knowledge of the event. A forecast instead must use information available at initialization and be completed sufficiently far ahead of the evolving fire to provide advance information. Input latency, computational cost, domain extent, resolution, and model execution time therefore become part of the forecasting problem. We examine retrospective and real-time forecasts of several recent high-impact wildfires produced with the CAWFE coupled weather–fire model during its integration into the PyreCast forecasting framework. Forecasts use information available within realistic operational latency, are configured to complete rapidly enough to support 24–36-hour predictions, and are initialized from operational numerical weather prediction at different times and lead times. The cases span contrasting wind-driven, plume-influenced, and terrain-controlled fire behavior. We examine whether forecasts capture consequential aspects of fire evolution, including periods of rapid growth, direction and rate of spread, changes in behavior, and distinctive transient features, and how predictability changes with initialization time and atmospheric uncertainty. Evaluation is an integral part of this problem. A fire growth forecast contains more information than its eventual perimeter, and final perimeter agreement alone cannot distinguish a simulation that reaches a similar outcome for the wrong reasons from one that captures important aspects of the event but differs somewhat in location or timing. As in severe convective forecasting, exact timing and location may lose predictability while other characteristics of hazardous evolution remain forecastable. We therefore ask what aspects of wildfire evolution retain forecast skill, at what lead times, and how that skill should be assessed under operational conditions. This work draws on operational forecasting, model evaluation, and decision-support research funded by the California Energy Commission, NASA FireSense, the National Science Foundation, and the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture Small Business Innovation Research program.

491297.title: A Climatology of Austral Spring Relative Extreme Heatwave Characteristics for Southern South America
491297.authors: Joshua M Gilliland, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, TX
491297.abstract: This study investigates the relative extreme heatwave (REHW) characteristics of the southern cone (Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay) during austral spring (SON) from 1971 to 2025. European Reanalysis Fifth Generation (ECWF-ERA5) product is used to calculate and establish the REHW characteristics for the region. In addition, exploratory data analysis and visualization of multi-level mandatory atmospheric pressure (850, 700, 500, and 250 hPa) conditions are performed through principal component analysis (PCA). Synoptic-level scenarios are completed to demonstrate how REHWs are temporally and geographically changing over the 55-year study period. Results from this paper can provide additional context on how near-surface and upper-level temperature characteristics are shifting and what possible impacts it may have on the short and long-term applications for Southern South America.

491298.title: Radar-Informed Reconstruction of Sub-daily Extreme Precipitation for Probable Maximum Precipitation Estimation
491298.authors: V. Chandrasekar, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and Y. Pulipati, S. K. Biswas, and K. M. Mahoney
491298.abstract: Probable maximum precipitation (PMP) is a critical design quantity for dams and other high-hazard water infrastructure, yet conventional estimation remains limited by the sparse temporal and spatial information contained in long-term rain gauge records. Daily observations provide valuable long-term information on rainfall magnitude but cannot resolve the sub-daily evolution or spatial organization of extreme storms. This study develops a radar-informed framework for PMP estimation at a regional scale with California as an example, where extreme precipitation is strongly influenced by landfalling atmospheric rivers and orographic enhancement. Stage IV radar precipitation estimates are used to characterize the spatial and temporal structure of extreme storms and to derive multisite fragments for temporal disaggregation. These fragments are applied to the long-term daily gauge record to reconstruct hourly and sub-hourly precipitation series. Candidate extreme events are further screened using circulation-pattern classification based on ERA5 atmospheric fields relevant to rainfall-generating mechanisms, allowing storms with similar rainfall totals but differing atmospheric characteristics to be distinguished and representative fragments to be selected. PMP estimation is subsequently performed using complementary approaches that reflect established empirical, hydrometeorological, and statistical perspectives. The conventional Hershfield approach provides an empirical benchmark based on the statistical characteristics of annual precipitation maxima, while a statistical formulation based on precipitable-water maximization and an upper-bounded Pearson Type-I precipitation distribution provides an alternative physically motivated estimate. The reconstructed series are then used to derive PMP estimates across multiple durations within the radar-informed framework. Separately, L-moment regional frequency analysis is applied to the reconstructed rainfall extremes to characterize return-period precipitation magnitudes and regional behavior across durations. The analysis also evaluates whether regional homogeneity varies with duration and how different storm types, particularly atmospheric rivers, contribute to the upper tail of the precipitation distribution. By integrating radar-derived rainfall estimates, multisite rainfall disaggregation, and the long-term daily gauge record, the framework extends the historical record of extreme precipitation into realistic spatial and sub-daily dimensions and provides a consistent basis for deriving PMP estimates across durations for hydrologic design and hazard assessment in California.

491304.title: AR-AFSv2: Near-Real-Time Forecasting of Atmospheric Rivers on the U.S. West Coast and Alaska
491304.authors: Keqin Wu, NGI at EMC/NCEP/NOAA, College Park, MD; and X. Wu, M. N. Malasala, M. Aristizabal Vargas, B. Zhou, X. Wang, and V. S. Tallapragada
491304.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are the primary drivers of extreme precipitation along the U.S. West Coast, yet operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) models often struggle to capture their landfall timing, location, and intensity. To advance NOAA’s Research-to-Operations (R2O) goals, the Atmospheric River Analysis and Forecast System (AR-AFS) was developed as a standalone, high-resolution (3-km) regional model based on the FV3 dynamical core within the Unified Forecast System (UFS) framework. This study details the transition to AR-AFSv2, incorporating system-level upgrades aligned with the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System version 2 (HAFSv2). Key enhancements include increasing vertical resolution (64 to 82 levels), expanding the domain to include Alaska, and optimizing the physics suite by using Thompson microphysics with the TEDMF planetary boundary layer (PBL) scheme to improve moisture transport and precipitation forecast. We will present the evaluation of near-real-time AR-AFSv2 forecast during the 2026 Water Year (November 2025 to March 2026), along with an assessment of heavy precipitation events associated with landfalling ARs. Model performance for 24-hour accumulated precipitation is validated against Stage IV observations, and Integrated Vapor Transport (IVT) compared with GDAS analysis. Case studies highlight the capability of AR-AFSv2 to improve forecasts of AR landfall and watershed-scale precipitation. These results demonstrate the potential of AR-AFSv2 for 1–5 day operational applications. Finally, we introduce a prototype Atmospheric River Ensemble Forecast System (AR-EFS) leveraging high-resolution multi-physics ensembles to quantify forecast uncertainty and provide probabilistic guidance for atmospheric river prediction.

491315.title: Doppler Performance of a HAPS-Borne Phased-Array Weather Radar for Observing Convective Storms
491315.authors: Victor-Benjamin Villain, The University of Osaka, Suita, Osaka, Japan; and E. Yoshikawa, M. Kondo, T. Ushio, and T. Iguchi
491315.abstract: Persistent, high-resolution observation of extreme weather over oceans remains a major gap, due to the limitations of current ground-based and spaceborne systems. High-Altitude Platform Stations (HAPS) operating in the stratosphere can provide continuous, wide-area monitoring, while Phased-Array Weather Radars (PAWR) enable rapid three-dimensional volumetric scanning through electronic beam steering, together offering a compelling solution to this issue. In this study, we investigate the feasibility and performance of a Doppler-capable HAPS-borne PAWR for improved severe weather monitoring. The expected Doppler accuracy of the proposed system is assessed using an I/Q measurement simulator based on high-resolution 3D synthetic data from a cloud-resolving model, including realistic noise levels and attenuation. Performance is evaluated in two convective scenarios, focusing on the impact of platform speed and nonuniform beam-filling (NUBF) on velocity measurements, a major error source for faster airborne and spaceborne radars that usually requires specific corrections. Results show that a low-power, compact antenna (200 W peak power, square aperture below 40 cm, X-band) can successfully observe the structure of convective storms from cloud top to the surface despite significant attenuation. Flying at low speed, HAPS keeps NUBF velocity errors negligible at a cruising speed of 100 km/h, requiring no correction and yielding a raw accuracy of about 0.5 m/s. At a higher cruising speed of 200 km/h, a raw accuracy of the order of 0.6 m/s is obtained, and improves to less than 0.4 m/s after correction. These results support HAPS-borne PAWR as a viable option for storm observation at high spatial and temporal resolution.

491319.title: Tropical Cyclone Observation at NIMS/KMA: From Atmospheric to Oceanic Observation Platforms
491319.authors: Baek-Jo Kim Sr., KMA, Seogwipo, Jeju, South korea
491319.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) making landfall on the Korean Peninsula—typically two to three per year, most passing through the East China Sea—remain one of Korea's most damaging weather hazards, as illustrated by the record seven TCs affecting the peninsula in 2019 and continuing decadal shifts in landfall track and frequency. Since the Korea Enhanced Observing Period (KEOP, 2000), the National Institute of Meteorological Sciences (NIMS) of the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) has conducted intensive in-situ observations of landfalling TCs, expanding from atmospheric to oceanic platforms, to better understand TC structure, intensity change, and TC–ocean interaction. Aerosonde and autosonde soundings of Typhoons Rusa (2002), Nakri (2008), and Kongrey (2018) revealed a strong lower-tropospheric temperature inversion linked to adiabatic compression and precipitation-induced cooling, boundary-layer relative humidity exceeding 65–90% within the inner core, and an abrupt low-level wind shift from easterly to westerly as each TC passed—together with terrain- and synoptic-scale modulation of wind direction below 2.5 km during landfall. On the oceanic side, more than 272 Argo floats deployed across the Northwest Pacific since 2000 show that in the long-term variability of ocean heat content in the Ulleung Basin of the East Sea calculated from Argo float observations, the ocean heat content in 2025 was about 2 GJ/m² lower than in 2024. At the trend of long-term fluctuations over a year, there is the 10-year periodicity in the variability of the ocean heat content around Ulleungdo-Dokdo. Multi-year glider-based intensive observations in the East China Sea (2022–2025) shows Ocean heat content is governed more by the sub-thermocline cold-water layer than by surface temperature. These twenty years of coupled atmosphere–ocean observations underscore the value of sustained in-situ monitoring for TC–ocean interaction research and inform NIMS/KMA's plan for an integrated three-dimensional ocean observation network—including next-generation and cost-effective coastal Argo floats—to improve TC intensity and track forecasting in the East Asian seas.

491324.title: A Cloud-Based Framework for Real-Time Processing, Monitoring, and Distribution of COSMIC-2 and Commercial GNSS Radio Occultation Data
491324.authors: Xinjia Zhou, ERT LLC, Riverdale Park, MD; NOAA/NESDIS, College Park, MD; and J. Zhou, Y. Chen, X. Shao, M. Chen, X. Jing, and B. Zhang
491324.abstract: Commercial GNSS radio occultation (RO) observations are vital for numerical weather prediction (NWP) and space weather applications. We present a cloud-based, end-to-end system developed within NOAA’s NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF) for the real-time processing and distribution of data from missions including COSMIC-2, Spire, and PlanetiQ. Our system automates the ingestion of Level 0 and Level-1A to generate neutral atmospheric and ionospheric products. The processing chain integrates precise orbit determination and clock estimation, excess phase processing, bending-angle retrieval with integrated quality control, BUFR generation for NWP data assimilation, and total electron content (TEC) retrieval for space weather monitoring. By leveraging event-driven workflow orchestration and parallel processing, the framework ensures scalable, low-latency operations and facilitates the transition from the Sandbox to the Moderate Cloud environment. To guarantee reliability, we integrated a real-time monitoring and alerting framework that tracks mission-specific processing metrics, including profile counts, quality-control (QC) pass rates, height of straight line (HSL), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), processing latency, and ionospheric TEC arc coverage. Anomaly detection algorithms identify performance bottlenecks and ingestion failures, enabling rapid operational response. Furthermore, we implemented a data quality assessment framework that evaluates RO product performance through the NOAA Integrated Calibration and Validation System (ICVS). By comparing RO observations against GFS forecasts, ECMWF forecasts and ERA5 reanalysis, this system provides comprehensive insights into RO data quality and long-term stability. Together, these developments establish a robust, cloud-native operational framework for processing, monitoring, distributing, and evaluating GNSS RO data, accelerating the integration of commercial GNSS RO capabilities into NOAA's operational weather and space weather enterprise while providing a scalable foundation for future commercial GNSS RO missions.

491328.title: Reflections on AI Model Development for Earth Science - Progress, Gaps, and Opportunities (Invited Presentation)
491328.authors: Imme Ebert-Uphoff, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO
491328.abstract: AI models already provide huge benefits for countless earth science applications and their use in earth science is expected to increase even more rapidly in the coming years. Future progress will partially be driven by the emergence of even more powerful AI algorithms being developed by the computer science community. However, there are also fundamental challenges to the success of AI models in earth science which need to be addressed by earth scientists, in collaboration with social scientists and computer scientists. Here we focus on two such challenges: The alignment problem: For many applications we still struggle to mathematically define what exactly we want our AI models to optimize. This issue is known as the Alignment Problem in the AI community [1]. It is a crucial challenge in environmental applications, where trade-offs abound and many outcomes are hard to define (e.g., how do we define the accuracy of capturing a meteorological feature?). Furthermore, we still have a long way to go to model and adequately include the resulting social impacts we ultimately seek to achieve. The interpretability/uncertainty/accountability problem: In spite of significant progress in the areas of Explainable AI, Interpretable AI, and Uncertainty Quantification in AI, we still struggle to fully understand the internal reasoning processes of most AI models. This is exacerbated by the increasing complexity of many AI models. Large Language Models (LLMs) are the newest and most extreme example of this tension, as they offer sweeping new capabilities, yet are notoriously bad at providing uncertainty estimates of their own output, raising questions about who should be accountable for answers provided by a LLM. This presentation is not about novel results or even posing new problems. Rather, we hope that by providing a collection of our experiences and perspectives on these urgent challenges, we might provide food-for-thought for the next generation of earth scientists, and sow the seeds for more interdisciplinary collaboration, in particular between earth scientists and social scientists. Reference: [1] Christian, Brian (2020), The Alignment Problem: Machine Learning And Human Values. New York: WW Norton & Company, 329 pages, Oct 2020.

491333.title: Hydroclimatic Whiplash Across the United States: Observation, Modeling, and Forecasting
491333.authors: Wei Zhang, Utah State Univ., Logan, UT; and M. M. Fathi and M. Kumar
491333.abstract: Hydroclimatic whiplash is defined as the rapid transition from dry to wet conditions, or vice versa, within a relatively short period in the atmosphere or hydrologic system. Understanding the characteristics of hydroclimatic whiplash can strengthen community preparedness and resilience to related hazards. Here, we investigate hydroclimatic whiplash events in both the climate and hydrologic systems by characterizing their spatial and temporal variability, predictability, and real-time forecasting skill based on numerical weather prediction models. Whiplash events are identified using precipitation- and discharge-based indices derived from the Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies (CAMELS) dataset. We characterize the spatial and temporal variability of hydroclimatic whiplash in terms of event magnitude, duration, transition period, and other key metrics. We identify a significant decrease in the transition period of whiplash events in the climate system, suggesting that transitions between dry and wet conditions are becoming more rapid in observations. Regional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models consistently outperform local models in detecting drought, flood, and transition events, with the performance gap widening for high-severity events and rapid transitions. Both ECMWF and NOAA CFSv2 forecasting systems exhibit limited skill in predicting hydroclimatic whiplash across HUC-2 basins at a one-month lead time. Real-time precipitation and temperature forecasts improve hydrologic forecasts, but the added predictive skill is generally limited to lead times of up to seven days.

491338.title: Water Availability Predictions of a Coupled Earth System with a Knowledge-Guided AI Surrogate
491338.abstract: Managing water-intensive energy infrastructures requires accurate, fine-scale water availability predictions at critical weeks-to-years timescales. However, existing coupled Earth system models, such as the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM), often exhibit structural and parametric biases that limit their utility for long-term predictions. To address this challenge, we present the Water Intelligence System for Energy infrastructures (WISE), a physics-informed AI surrogate modeling framework designed to deliver robust predictions of water availability. Our approach combines physical knowledge of the coupled earth system, deep neural network surrogate, and multiple datasets to learn and predict water availability dynamics. Using Texas as a proof-of-concept, we present preliminary results demonstrating that the fine-tuned AI surrogate achieves high predictive skill and significantly reduces biases while executing orders of magnitude faster. Finally, we project water availability from 2027 through 2031 to identify potential water-stress hotspots and potential impacts on critical cooling water-dependent energy infrastructures. This work demonstrates how AI can bridge the gap between complex Earth system simulations and actionable decision-making to safeguard national energy security.

491340.title: A Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Precipitation Downscaling: Getting Ready for NOAA PMP/EXCEED Applications
491340.authors: Yongxin Liu, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and H. Chen, K. M. Mahoney, L. Slivinski, and S. Frolov
491340.abstract: High-resolution precipitation estimates and forecasts, in both space and time domains, are critical for applications such as flood monitoring, and water resources management and planning. However, the long-term precipitation records available from climate models and reanalysis datasets such as ERA5 (~25 km) are too coarse for these applications. Convection-permitting models provide physically consistent precipitation at fine scales but at a computational cost that limits large-ensemble uncertainty assessment. The project EXCEED (EXtreme preCipitation Estimates from Enhanced Downscaling) aims to improve the historical record of extreme precipitation by developing and evaluating physical and machine learning-based methods for super-resolving reanalyses of precipitation over the US. To support this project, this paper develops a hybrid machine learning framework for precipitation downscaling. In our initial design, a super-resolution transformer produces a deterministic baseline, and a residual diffusion model then restores the fine-scale texture and spatial structure to generate a calibrated ensemble through DDIM sampling (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models). This design separates the downscaling problem into two aspects: the deterministic stage predicts the precipitation placement, while the generative stage recovers the stochastic fine-scale variability that a one-to-many mapping requires. To demonstrate the downscaling performance, we have trained and tested this hybrid model using 25-km ERA5 data as input, and 4-km CONUS404 precipitation data as target labels to generate high-resolution precipitation analysis over the contiguous U.S. based on low-resolution ERA5 data. Evaluation results show that the diffusion stage restores realistic spatial texture and spectral characteristics that the deterministic baseline lacks, but also reveals a persistent underestimation of the heaviest precipitation. To address this intensity gap, we use quantile mapping (QM) as the third step to correct the intensity, with the QM fitted entirely on independent training years. The final products are extensively evaluated across different precipitation events, including convective precipitation in the southeast U.S. and atmospheric-river events in the western U.S., which shows that the QM correction has effectively recovered the precipitation intensity while maintaining the spatial placement represented by the Fractions Skill Score. Overall, this hybrid machine learning framework offers a physically realistic, ensemble-capable, and computationally efficient option for precipitation downscaling.

491344.title: Local Energetics of Extratropical Transition: A Case Study of Typhoon Hagibis (2019)
491344.authors: Yeeun Kwon, Seoul National University, Seoul, South korea; Seoul National University, Seoul, South korea; and S. W. Son
491344.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) moving into the midlatitudes often undergo notable structural changes as they transition into extratropical cyclones (ETCs). This transition, known as the extratropical transition (ET), results from interactions between the TC and the midlatitude baroclinic environment. To elucidate the dynamical processes underlying ET, this study proposes a cyclone-following local energetics framework and applies it to TC Hagibis (2019) in the western North Pacific. The energy cycle intensifies during the ET phase, with its spatial structure becoming markedly asymmetric relative to that in the TC phase. In both the TC and ET phases, eddy available potential energy increases as its generation and energy conversion from background flow dominate over the baroclinic energy conversion. During ET, enhanced diabatic heating, warm temperature anomalies, and vertical motion appear ahead of the cyclone due to its interaction with the midlatitude jet. This leads to an asymmetric distribution of enhanced energy sources and energy conversions for eddy available potential energy. While eddy kinetic energy also increases in the TC phase as baroclinic energy conversion exceeds lateral boundary flux, it decreases and redistributes asymmetrically during ET due to enhanced divergence of eddy geopotential flux along the boundary of the western North Pacific subtropical high and the upper-level divergent TC outflow associated with jet-TC interaction. These results show that local energetics can effectively capture asymmetric thermal and dynamical processes during ET, offering a physical interpretation of TC-to-ETC transition processes.

491348.title: Decadal Variability and Mechanism of the Summer North Atlantic Subtropical High
491348.authors: Yan Pan, Duke University, Durham, NC; and W. Li
491348.abstract: The North Atlantic Subtropical High (NASH) exerts a strong influence on summertime climate variability over the southeastern United States, Central American, and Caribbean region. Across subseasonal to interannual time scales, variations in NASH strength modulate moisture transport and atmospheric stability, influencing regional precipitation. A systematic understanding of NASH variability is therefore important for improving our understanding of regional climate variability and its predictability. Previous studies have linked summer NASH variability to North Atlantic sea surface temperature (SST) on interannual time scales. Because North Atlantic SST itself exhibits pronounced low-frequency variability on decadal to multi-decadal scales, it remains to be unanswered that whether summer NASH also varies on these long-term scales, and what physical processes may control such variability. Using multiple reanalysis datasets, we systematically investigate low-frequency summer NASH variability and oscillation periods and investigate the associated physical mechanisms. Prescribed-SST experiments are conducted to examine the atmospheric response to North Atlantic SST anomalies to explain the decadal NASH variability. Finally, we discussed the possible physical origin of the identified decadal variability and mechanisms.

491350.title: Open Oceanography: Using Storytelling and Open Data to Connect with the Ocean
491350.authors: Drew Arlen Burrier, RAFT, Honolulu, HI
491350.abstract: I have spent my entire life drawn to the ocean, charting my course by a childhood memory of bottlenose dolphins off the Florida Gulf Coast. Today, that beach no longer exists due to storm surge and rising sea levels. The loss of cherished coastal habitats is a reality many face daily in coastal communities, including my own on the island of O'ahu. While my formal training is in physical oceanography, my professional career spans the tech sector, building advanced meteorological and oceanographic forecasting systems as a senior data scientist and engineer. Here in the tropical Pacific, we are on the front lines of climate change, navigating the immediate threats of drought, wildfires, habitat loss, and intensifying tropical cyclones. Open Oceanography, an open access science storytelling initiative, translates my applied knowledge in marine science and data engineering into accessible community resources. Rather than relying on abstract theory, the initiative is built on authentic observations, drawing directly from data I gathered personally in the Gulf of Alaska as a researcher for the World Ocean Circulation Experiment under Moss Landing Marine Laboratory as well as other publicly available datasets from public institutions like WMO, NOAA, and NASA. By demystifying this caliber of institutional science, the project gives the public the vital tools they need for awareness and preparedness during major environmental shifts. This initiative steps away from traditional academic lectures and leans heavily into accessible narrative to teach physical oceanography and build public awareness. By sharing stories of working in extreme environments like the Bering Sea, the project connects audiences to the visceral reality of the ocean, offering a perspective most people never have the opportunity to experience. The goal is to move beyond simply telling people about the weather. When a tropical cyclone threatens O'ahu, the community does not just get a forecast. Through Open Oceanography, they are equipped with the ability to track the storm system, as well as the oceanic heat content and the water properties driving the storm using the exact same public data that scientists use. Teaching data literacy, however, is only half the battle. Open Oceanography explicitly highlights the vital role of the public agencies that collect this information. These monitoring systems are public resources, funded by and belonging entirely to the citizens they protect. As public science infrastructure increasingly finds itself in the political crosshairs, with real threats emerging to dismantle the agencies that monitor our waters, data literacy becomes a form of advocacy. Making science accessible is about more than just providing numbers. It is about giving people a reason to care and a reason to defend their right to know. This presentation will explore how we can use authentic storytelling to ignite curiosity, demystify complex Earth system science, and build a more informed public that is actively engaged in protecting both our shared natural resources and the public data systems we rely on to survive.

491351.title: Evaluating Ozone Production across the Northern Colorado Front Range during Summer 2025 with Observationally Constrained Box Modeling
491351.authors: Andrey Marsavin, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and A. Sullivan, Y. Zhou, J. Ban, J. P. Stickney, D. C. Guevara, B. McGuire, E. Cope, A. Deters, W. Permar, L. Hu, B. C. Sive, S. R. Hall, E. Mattson, A. Frazier, T. Moore, E. V. Fischer, and J. L. Collett Jr.
491351.abstract: The Denver Metro/Northern Front Range (DM/NFR) region of Colorado frequently exceeds the US EPA’s National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for ground-level ozone (O3). To better understand the processes driving persistent O3 pollution and to inform future emission control strategies, measurements of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and speciated volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were collected at four sites spanning the DM/NFR during summer 2025 as part of the Front Range OZone Éxperiment (FROZÉ) field campaign. The present analysis examines O3 production during FROZÉ using the Framework for 0-D Atmospheric Modeling (F0AM) box model constrained by in situ, multi-site observations of NOₓ and VOCs. The monitoring sites represent a range of emission environments, including suburban Denver, an area influenced by oil and gas (O&G) activity south of Greeley, and the Rocky Mountain foothills west of Denver and Fort Collins. At the Fort Collins site, additional measurements of the NO2 photolysis frequency (jNO2), peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), formaldehyde (HCHO), and other oxygenated VOCs (OVOCs) are used to further constrain and evaluate F0AM performance. Output from F0AM will be used to quantify and compare the O3 production rate and efficiency (OPE; molecules of O3 produced per molecule of NOₓ consumed) across the four sites. Sensitivity simulations will be performed by applying scaling factors to observed NOₓ and VOC concentrations to evaluate the response of O3 production to changes in precursor levels. VOC perturbations will be applied by emission source category using results from a positive matrix factorization (PMF) analysis, which identified vehicle traffic, O&G activities, biogenic emissions, and solvent use as key regional VOC sources. Simulations in which individual source categories are independently perturbed will provide a source-specific assessment of O3 production sensitivity, allowing the relative importance of different VOC emission sectors and their impact on O3 production to be quantified across the DM/NFR.

491362.title: ENSO- and PDO-Related Spring Land-Surface Preconditioning of Early-Summer Great Plains Soil Moisture in E3SM
491362.authors: BO-YI LU, Albany, Albany, NY; and R. D. Torn and Q. Tang
491362.abstract: Subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction of warm-season hydroclimate over CONUS remains challenging because atmospheric memory decays rapidly, while land and ocean states can provide longer-lived predictability. This study examines how eastern Pacific and central Pacific ENSO, and the Pacific decadal oscillation, individually and in combination, modulate spring-to-early-summer soil moisture over the Great Plains of the USA using idealized E3SMv2 AMIP-style atmosphere–land simulations. In general, negative-phase single-forcing simulations are associated with broad CONUS drying, with maxima over the central Great Plains, whereas positive-phase simulations favor a north–south contrast, with drier northern Great Plains and wetter southern Great Plains. Combined ENSO–PDO responses depend on phase relationship, reinforcing the Great Plains as a focal region of soil-moisture sensitivity. Over the northern Great Plains, SST-forced simulations generally reach peak soil moisture earlier than CTRL and exhibit lower May–June soil moisture, with April rainfall deficits responsible for the reduced spring recharge, and differences in snowmelt adding experiment-to-experiment variability. Over the southern Great Plains, April soil-moisture variability is primarily rainfall-driven. Circulation and moisture-transport diagnostics indicate that recurring upper-level circulation features reorganize Gulf moisture transport, providing a dynamical framework for the contrasting Great Plains soil-moisture responses.

491369.title: Arctic Climate Hysteresis under CO2 Removal and the Related Physical Processes
491369.authors: Seok-Woo Son, Seoul National University, Seoul, South korea; and M. I. Cajada, Y. C. Liang, E. S. Chung, Q. You, and S. I. An
491369.abstract: Arctic warming is projected to weaken under reducing atmospheric CO2 concentrations. However, climate model experiments under carbon dioxide removal (CDR) scenarios robustly show that Arctic surface temperature during the CO2 ramp-down period is higher than that during the ramp-up with the CO2 concentrations being identical. Here, the underlying mechanisms of such Arctic climate hysteresis is elucidated by conducting forcing-feedback analysis. A large-ensemble CDR experiment reveals that the warmer Arctic surface temperature during the CO2 ramp-down period is associated with stronger temperature (Planck plus lapse-rate) and surface-albedo feedbacks, which are closely linked to the delayed recovery of Arctic sea-ice extent. The ocean heat uptake also contributes to warmer temperature, but its effect is largely offset by the atmospheric heat transport. These results highlight the critical role of sea-ice change in the Arctic climate hysteresis and the dependence of Arctic climate change on the forcing trajectory.

491372.title: Distinct Meteorological Drivers of Warm-Season Ozone Exceedances across China Under Different Synoptic Patterns
491372.authors: Jiandong Li, Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China
491372.abstract: Warm-season ozone (O3) pollution remains a major air-quality challenge in China, yet how different synoptic patterns regulate regional ozone exceedances remains unclear. Here, we combine synoptic weather classification, meteorological normalization, and explainable machine learning to investigate the meteorological pathways driving O3 exceedances across China. Six dominant warm-season circulation patterns were identified using a self-organizing map approach. These patterns exhibited distinct regional ozone enhancement patterns, indicating strong dependence of ozone variability on synoptic background. Meteorological-normalization models revealed that anticyclonic regimes associated with enhanced radiation, high temperature, low humidity, and stagnant conditions produced substantial ozone enhancements over the North China Plain, Bohai Rim, and Chuan-Yu regions, whereas transport-favorable regimes promoted ozone increases in northeastern and central China. A multiclass XGBoost classifier combined with SHAP analysis further demonstrated that the meteorological controls of moderate and high-concentration ozone events were not identical. Temperature, humidity, radiation, and ventilation conditions showed strong but regionally varying contributions, with extreme ozone events characterized by stronger combinations of heat, dryness, and stagnant conditions. These results reveal that ozone exceedances across China arise from distinct synoptic-dependent meteorological pathways, providing new insights for weather-based ozone prediction and regional pollution management.

491376.title: QBO–TC Relationship in the Western North Pacific is Nonstationary
491376.authors: Jeong-Hyeon Kim, Seoul National University, Seoul, South korea; and C. H. Park, S. H. Lee, H. Yoon, E. Nawo, and S. W. Son
491376.abstract: The Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (QBO) has been proposed as a key factor modulating tropical cyclone (TC) tracks in the western North Pacific, but its robustness remains controversial. This study revisits the QBO–TC relationship by extending the analysis period to 2024. The results reveal that the relationship is nonstationary and has changed sign around the 2000s. Before the 2000s, the westerly QBO phase was associated with an anticyclonic circulation anomaly over southeast Japan, favoring TC movement toward the East China Sea. After the 2000s, however, an anticyclonic circulation anomaly developed south of the East China Sea, hindering TC movement toward the region. This decadal change is likely influenced by internal climate variability rather than changes in the QBO itself or TC frequency. Consequently, the QBO may not serve as a robust predictor of western North Pacific TC tracks.

491381.title: QBO–MJO Connection is Mediated by Cloud-longwave Radiative Feedback
491381.authors: Seok-Woo Son, Seoul National University, Seoul, South korea; and S. Y. Back and J. H. Kim
491381.abstract: Observational studies have shown that the boreal winter Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is significantly stronger during the easterly phase of the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (EQBO) than during the westerly phase (WQBO). While this relationship has been partly attributed to QBO-induced cloud-longwave radiation feedback, the extent of its impact remains unclear. This study presents the first modelling evidence of the critical role of cloud-longwave radiation feedback in the QBO-MJO connection. Although weaker than the observations, the high-resolution modelling successfully reproduces the QBO-MJO connection. The fractions of deep convective, stratiform, and anvil clouds are significantly higher under the EQBO condition than under the WQBO condition. However, when clouds are made transparent to longwave radiation, this difference becomes insignificant. This result suggests that the QBO-MJO connection is at least partly mediated by cloud-longwave radiative feedback.

491383.title: Solution Analysis and Intelligent Radar Concept to Advance an Airborne Weather Phased Array Radar for Observing Hazardous Weather Conditions
491383.authors: Bradley Klotz, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and L. Clifford, W. C. Lee, A. Karboski, P. Kollias, and J. Vivekanandan
491383.abstract: After the conclusion of the National Science Foundation (NSF) supported Airborne Phased Array Radar (APAR) program in Spring of 2025, continued development toward an airborne precipitation radar was viewed as significantly important for National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and it’s role to serve the research community to understand hazardous weather. An initial phased development pathway was created to investigate commercially available PARs, their feasibility for weather observations from an aircraft, and minimally invasive aircraft mounting solutions on a C-130. The authors explicitly searched for options with X-band operating frequency because they are typically more readily available and more affordable. Understanding these outcomes was vitally important to establishing a baseline for future development. Several specific tasks were completed in this solutions analysis phase. Firstly, an airborne testbed feasibility study was performed using specifications of commercially available PARs with installation in pod or side door mount configurations. Simulated field of view analyses were conducted and indicate that all investigated locations have sufficient azimuthal and vertical scanning space to perform dual Doppler analyses. Associated radar weather retrievals were performed using the APAR Observing, Processing, and Research Environment (AOSPRE) tool to evaluate the scientific output of commercially available X-band PARs at these locations. While there is variation in the performance capabilities, it is clear that installing and operating a PAR on the C-130 is feasible for weather observations. Another task performed in this study was integration of a PAR digital twin model into AOSPRE to create a more realistic evaluation of existing systems. The results from this portion of the work are presented with scientific and technical scores and highlight the capabilities and limitations of a given radar solution for airborne weather observation. The second phase of this work is focused on technology maturation and risk reduction, whereby incorporating autonomous and intelligent radar solutions enable improved temporal and spatial scanning. Using the PAR integrated digital twin as a base, the Radar Environment for Predictive Learning and Intelligent Convective Analysis (REPLICA) project serves as a closed-loop, end-to-end simulation platform where specific artificial intelligence procedures are a training environment to understand optimal radar and flight operations. Subsequently, the Autonomous Airborne Side-looking Phased-array Intelligent Radar Experiment (AASPIRE) will serve as the means to test intelligent radar concepts in a real environment. Therefore, combining the teaching and training of REPLICA with ground validation of an intelligent radar solution will enable future deployment of an intelligent, airborne PAR. A description and initial scope of work for these projects will be provided.

491386.title: The 2026 NSF NCAR Radar Technology Community Workshop: Outcomes and Recommendations for Advancing the U. S. Weather Radar Enterprise
491386.authors: Bradley Klotz, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and P. Kollias, B. Baeuerle, R. Tanamachi, M. M. Bell, A. Rowe, J. Vivekanandan, S. W. Nesbitt, T. Y. Yu, Z. Liu, and M. Killinger
491386.abstract: In 2023, NSF NCAR hosted the Facilities for Atmospheric Research and Education (FARE) Users Workshop to showcase the broad resources and facilities that NSF NCAR and its partners provide for community research. A key outcome was the recommendation to hold periodic workshops on specific subthemes to encourage continued community engagement with NSF NCAR’s current and future instrumentation. The “Radars” subtheme emphasized the importance of maintaining access to mobile radars, investing in new centimeter wavelength phased array radars, advancing open source radar software, and improving data access and processing. Support across these areas remains strong but there was a sense of urgency to explore new approaches for advancing radar capabilities. In particular, there is a growing interest in applying Phased Array Radar (PAR) technology across airborne, shipborne and ground-based platforms. Therefore, the National Science Foundation (NSF) supported the Radar Technology Community Workshop (RTCW) in March 2026. Held at the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, CO, the workshop brought together over 180 people across all career stages from federal agencies, industry, and universities. Because the most recent iteration of this workshop was held nearly 15 years ago, much has changed across the radar landscape. The workshop steering committee designed a program to accommodate four major themes, including: next generation radar technology, sustainable facility operations and partnerships, community software and data integration, and workforce development. During the two and a half day workshop, sessions were structured with selected topical presentations and small group discussions. Synthesis of these presentations and discussions helped determine recommended actions for the radar community across near to long term time scales. These recommendations include: Balance existing and emerging technologies, such as phased array radar, to enable growth and discovery Build networked and adaptive radar observing systems through investment in real-time software integration, cyberinfrastructure, and multi-agency coordination Invest in advanced airborne precipitation radar capabilities through a phased development strategy Adopt artificial intelligence responsibly and strategically to enhance scientific research with radars Establish a centralized radar software and data hub for the purposes of consolidating open-source software support, benchmark datasets, data standards, and training resources. There is an expectation that NSF and other funding agencies can take action on these recommendations to ensure the continuation of a robust radar community and research infrastructure designed to support national weather readiness and resilience. It was also agreed upon through the discussions and post-workshop survey that holding more frequent, specific topic workshops and advisory meetings would help the community stay accountable to these recommendations and ensure the field is advancing in the right direction. This presentation will provide more details on RTCW design, implementation, recommendations, and actionable steps NSF and other federal agencies can pursue to fulfill the community needs. It is clear that the five recommendations above with detailed implementation descriptions in the final workshop report must come through a coordinated, cross-agency and industry effort.

491389.title: Declining Anthropogenic Aerosols Amplify Northern Hemisphere Hadley Circulation Weakening in the 21st Century
491389.authors: Seok-Woo Son, Seoul National University, Seoul, South korea; and S. Y. Kim, Y. Ming, D. C. Hong, X. Gu, and R. Park
491389.abstract: The Hadley circulation plays a key role in transporting atmospheric heat from the tropics to the subtropics, shaping the climate in low latitudes. While its projected weakening has been largely attributed to rising greenhouse gas concentrations, the long-term impact of future anthropogenic aerosol concentrations remains underexplored. Here, we show that the projected changes in anthropogenic aerosol concentrations can account for about one-third of the Northern Hemisphere Hadley circulation weakening between 1980 and 2080, emerging as a major driver of tropical circulation change throughout the 21st century. This impact is linked to altered diabatic heating patterns in the northern tropics, driven by precipitation changes under reduced aerosol forcing. These results highlight a critical trade-off of aerosol mitigation: while improving air quality, it may amplify tropical atmospheric circulation changes driven by greenhouse gases.

491390.title: Droughts are Dominated by Anomalous Circulation Not Anomalous Atmospheric Moisture Content
491390.authors: Seung Uk Kim, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and F. Dominguez and D. Miralles
491390.abstract: Agricultural drought is caused by reduced net moisture flux to the land surface that is precipitation minus evaporation. Using global reanalysis data and moisture budget analyses, we show that drought-related drying is driven primarily by atmospheric circulation anomalies rather than anomalous atmospheric moisture. Historical droughts have occurred under both anomalously low and high atmospheric moisture conditions, but consistently associated with enhanced low-level divergent flow and rising geopotential heights aloft. Regardless of the signs of anomalous evaporation, decreased surface relative humidity is observed, suggesting that anomalous circulation is suppressing formation of precipitation. Moisture budget decomposition further reveals that anomalous wind divergence explains spatial patterns of precipitation minus evaporation, while anomalous moisture advection often offsets drying. Thus, drought reflects reduced precipitation efficiency rather than limited moisture supply: moisture is exported by anomalous divergence, and what remains does not condense. Circulation-based indicators may therefore provide more robust drought diagnostics than atmospheric moisture content.

491392.title: Investigating the Impact of Cold Front Passages on Near-Surface Turbulence Using Collocated Lidar and Tower-Based Measurements In a Complex Terrain Environment
491392.authors: Danielle E. Harr, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and T. R. Lee and S. Pal
491392.abstract: Improvement of parameterization schemes used within numerical weather prediction (NWP) models requires both a comprehensive understanding and a proper representation of exchanges of heat fluxes and turbulent kinetic energy occurring between the land surface and overlying surface layer (SL) and atmospheric boundary layer (ABL). Empirical findings reporting turbulence features during airmass exchanges typically involved in cold front passages have remained underexplored in literature. Additionally, many NWP models struggle in regions with complex and mountainous terrain, as the models largely rely on SL and ABL parameterizations formulated from flat terrain observations. The southeastern United States, including eastern Tennessee, frequently experiences cold front passages, in which cold, continental air masses generally originate from the Great Plains and the northern United States. Convergence at the cold front interface often generates severe weather, including damaging winds and thunderstorms. We aim to investigate the impact of cold front passages on turbulence features during both winter and summer using systematic studies with observational data. To this end, we explored the changes in near-surface turbulence features across cold front boundaries in the mountainous region of eastern Tennessee. To evaluate cold-front-relative turbulence characteristics in this region, we used a combination of measurements from a WindCube V2.1 lidar, a local automated surface observation station (ASOS), and a 60-m micrometeorological tower along a ridgetop and outfitted with a suite of meteorological and flux measurements within and above the forest canopy obtained over the period of 1 June 2023 to 31 May 2024. Cold front passages were initially identified using Weather Prediction Center surface analyses and then narrowed down based on the availability of data from each instrument during the cold front passage period. Mean turbulence statistics, including vertical velocity variance and skewness, were obtained from the lidar and used to quantify turbulence intensity and vertical motion tendency within the prefrontal, frontal, and postfrontal environments. The lidar observations were also used to quantify low-level wind shear, whereas the 60-m tower observations were used to quantify changes in within- and above-canopy turbulence, heat, and momentum fluxes. Impacts of the time of day, season, and wind shift timing will be discussed, and two cases from the period of study will be presented. The cases compared will include a more classical wintertime cold front passage and a less classical summertime cold front passage. These analyses will lay the groundwork for a more comprehensive understanding of the typical behavior of front-relative turbulence features in regions with complex terrain.

491412.title: Objective Estimation of Atmospheric Turbulence Intensity Near Convective Clouds over East Asia Using Machine Learning and Satellite Observations
491412.authors: Yoonjin Lee, Seoul National University, Seoul, Seoul, Korea, Republic of (South); and J. H. Kim and D. B. Lee
491412.abstract: Atmospheric turbulence poses a significant hazard to aviation safety and operational efficiency, making its timely detection and prediction essential. Turbulence diagnostics derived from numerical weather prediction (NWP) models provide valuable forecast guidance, while ground-based and airborne radars provide real-time information during flight operations. Radar observations are particularly effective for identifying deep convection and supporting the tactical avoidance of convectively induced turbulence. However, ground-based radar coverage is limited, particularly over oceanic regions, and radar observations cannot readily detect clear-air or mountain-wave turbulence. Geostationary satellites provide an important complementary source of observations because of their broad coverage and high spatial and temporal resolution. Water vapor channels can capture features associated with tropopause folding and gravity waves, whereas infrared window channels provide information on deep convective clouds and their surrounding environments. Nevertheless, the lack of direct vertical information has generally limited satellite-based turbulence detection to broad altitude ranges, with most existing applications focused on the upper troposphere. This study develops a machine learning framework for estimating warm-season turbulence intensity at multiple vertical layers using observations from GEO-KOMPSAT-2A (GK-2A) (Lee et al., 2025), a geostationary satellite operated by the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA). A U-Net model integrates information from seven GK-2A infrared channels to estimate turbulence intensity across four atmospheric layers over East Asia and the western Pacific. The model is trained using turbulence diagnostics employed in the Global–Korean aviation Turbulence Guidance (G-KTG) product, an operational turbulence forecasting system of KMA’s Aviation Meteorological Office. Evaluation against in situ eddy dissipation rate measurements demonstrates generally good performance in the lower three layers, with reduced skill near and above the tropopause. Case studies further show that the model successfully identifies moderate-or-greater turbulence within and near convective systems, including over oceanic regions with limited radar coverage, although it tends to produce broader turbulent areas and underestimate severe-to-extreme turbulence intensity. These results demonstrate the potential of geostationary satellite observations to provide real-time, multilayer turbulence guidance that complements existing radar- and NWP-based systems over East Asia. References Lee, Y., D. B. Lee, and J. H. Kim, 2025: Machine learning‐based turbulence intensity estimation near convective clouds in East Asia using GK‐2A satellite observations. Geophysical Research Letters, 52(23), e2025GL119119. Acknowledgements This work was supported by the Korea Meteorological Administration Research and Development Program under Grants RS-2022-KM220310 and RS-2022-KM220410.

491416.title: Post-Extratropical Transition Behavior of North Atlantic Tropical Cyclones: A Climatology of Track and Intensity Changes
491416.authors: Rupsa Bhowmick, University of Wisconsin- La Crosse, La Crosse, WI; and A. Fleury
491416.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) undergoing extratropical transition (ET), hereafter referred to as ETTCs, can generate widespread high-impact weather across North America and Europe, including heavy rainfall and damaging winds. This study quantifies long-term changes in ET completion location and post-transition track evolution of North Atlantic ETTCs. It also characterizes the spatiotemporal climatology of post-transition intensity evolution from ET completion through subsequent stages of the storm life cycle. Using the IBTrACS six-hourly best-track dataset, statistical analyses and spatial mapping are used to quantify temporal trends, geographic shifts, and climatological patterns in ETTC tracks and intensity. Preliminary analyses identified 296 TCs completed ET during 1980–2025. ETTC occurrence has increased significantly over the past four decades, with approximately one additional transition event per decade. ET completion is strongly seasonal, with nearly three-quarters (77%) of all transitions occurring during August to October and a pronounced peak in September (36%). The mean transition latitude declined from approximately 43°N during the 1980s to 39°N during 2016–2025, representing an average southward shift of 3.75°. However, TCs completing transition at higher latitudes (>50°N) are maintaining stronger maximum winds, and a Generalized Additive Model revealed a significant nonlinear relationship between latitude and post-transition intensity.
