The resulting climatology provides a benchmark for future machine-learning-based prediction of ETTC intensity change and identification of its environmental controls.

491417.title: Controls on Orographic Convection Initiation Timing across RELAMPAGO/CACTI Events: Insights from LASSO Ensemble Simulations
491417.authors: Andres Yamil Lopez, McGill Univ., Montreal, QC, Canada; and D. J. Kirshbaum
491417.abstract: During the austral warm season, the Sierras de Córdoba (SDC)—a north-south mountain ridge in north-central Argentina—frequently initiates deep moist convection. These events exhibit a wide range of outcomes, from short-lived storms to mesoscale convective systems, including some of the world’s deepest thunderstorms with cloud tops exceeding 21 km. The initiation of these convective events is governed by a complex interplay of processes acting across multiple scales, including orographically induced flows and moisture transport driven by the South American Low-Level Jet. To better understand these processes, this study focuses on five convective events originating on the eastern slope of the SDC, where convection frequently initiates. These events were observed during the Cloud, Aerosol, and Complex Terrain Interactions (CACTI)/Remote Sensing of Electrification, Lightning, and Mesoscale/Microscale Processes with Adaptive Ground Observations (RELAMPAGO) joint field campaigns. 33-member convective-scale ensembles from the Large-Eddy Simulation (LES) ARM Symbiotic Simulation and Observation (LASSO) dataset provide a unique opportunity to systematically analyze how local pre-convective conditions influence convection initiation (CI) timing. To quantitatively define CI timing for each simulation, cloud properties and their life cycles are characterized using the open-source Python FLEXible object TRacKeR (PyFLEXTRKR) tracking algorithm. Potential predictors of CI timing are derived from the pre-convective SDC environment and include parameters representing moist instability, dry instability, relative humidity, large-scale winds, and mountain circulation strength. The relationships between these parameters and CI timing are quantified for each ensemble using multiple linear regressions, testing all combinations of three parameters, each drawn from a different category. The best-performing statistically significant combinations are then used to identify the main predictors of CI timing and assess the contribution of additional predictors that may be overlooked when considered individually. Preliminary results indicate substantial variability in the predictors of CI timing across events. Moist instability parameters are, by a small margin, the most frequently identified main predictors, while large-scale wind parameters appear most frequently among the top-performing combinations overall.

491418.title: Lightning Studies at the Large-Area Cosmic-Ray Telescope Array Surface Detector (TASD) in Central Utah
491418.authors: Paul R. Krehbiel, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, NM; New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, SOCORRO, NM
491418.abstract: Utah storms have a wide variety of electrical structures and lightning types that are well documented by Lightning Mapping Array (LMA), dual broadband VHF interferometer, fast sferic measurements and high speed video observations being obtained at the large-area TASD in central Utah. The TASD observations constitute an important additional instrument in that they detect downward terrestrial gamma ray flashes (TGFs) that are sometimes produced by lightning, providing significant insights into the lightning discharge processes themselves, as well as helping understand upward TGFs and gamma ray glows being detected by satellites.

491420.title: Retrieval of Low-Level Water Vapor Transport over East Asia from Microwave and Infrared Satellite Observations Using Machine Learning Techniques
491420.authors: Yoonjin Lee, Seoul National University, Seoul, Seoul, Korea, Republic of (South)
491420.abstract: Low-level water vapor is a key ingredient for initiation and intensification of heavy rainfall over Korea. Substantial moisture is frequently transported toward the Korean Peninsula across the East China Sea, where conventional observations are insufficient for continuous, high-resolution monitoring of low-level water vapor. The GEO-KOMPSAT-2A (GK-2A) provides observations with high spatial and temporal resolution over East Asia. Although its water vapor channels are primarily sensitive to the middle and upper troposphere, the split-window difference (SWD) between infrared window channels contains information related to lower tropospheric moisture. However, infrared-based retrievals are restricted to clear-sky conditions, and the relationship between SWD and low-level moisture is generally more robust during daytime than at night. In contrast, microwave-derived products such as Advected Layer Precipitable Water (ALPW) provide vertically resolved precipitable water information and are less affected by clouds, although their retrieval accuracy can decrease in areas of strong precipitation. Their relatively coarse spatial and temporal resolution also limits their ability to resolve the narrow and rapidly evolving moisture transport corridors associated with heavy rainfall over Korea. This study therefore develops a machine learning framework that integrates microwave-derived ALPW with GK-2A infrared observations to exploit the complementary strengths of the two observing systems. The model retrieves precipitable water within the 1000–850 hPa layer, which is subsequently combined with low-level numerical weather prediction model winds to estimate the magnitude and direction of low-level water vapor transport. The model is trained using ERA5 reanalysis data and independently evaluated against ERA5 and radiosonde observations. Its performance is compared with that of retrievals based on GK-2A or ALPW alone to quantify the contribution of multisensor integration under different environmental and observational conditions. Heavy rainfall cases over Korea, especially mesoscale convective system, are further examined to assess whether the integrated product can represent the spatial structure and temporal evolution of low-level moisture transport. The developed framework is expected to provide more spatially detailed and temporally continuous monitoring of moisture transport toward the Korean Peninsula, supporting the detection and analysis of environments favorable for heavy rainfall. Acknowledgments This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Korea government (Ministry of Science and ICT) under Grant RS-2025-00519412, and by the Korea Meteorological Administration Research and Development Program under Grant RS-2025-02219688.

491421.title: Quantitative Analysis of the Fine Structure of Water-Waves Excited by Impulsively Applied Wind
491421.authors: Lev Shemer, Tel-Aviv University, Tel-Aviv, Israel
491421.abstract: Wind-generated waves on the surfaces of lakes, oceans, and reservoirs are ubiquitous. Nevertheless, despite decades of research, the mechanisms responsible for their generation are not yet fully understood. Improving our understanding of wind-wave excitation is important not only because it represents a long-standing physical problem, but also because wave forecasting depends on accurately formulated energy-balance equation. While considerable effort has been devoted to understanding nonlinear effects, the source and sink terms in the balance equation remain represented by phenomenological estimates. Wind input is commonly modeled using the empirical Plant’s (JGR, 1982) relation, which is loosely based on the shear-flow instability theory introduced by Miles (JFM, 1957). Miles’ inviscid approach was later extended to include viscosity by Valenzuela (JFM, 1976) and Kawai (JFM, 1976). All those formulations describe a two-dimensional, linear instability of a mean airflow (in the viscous case, wind-induced water flow is also incorporated), and predict the exponential temporal growth of a deterministic wave with prescribed wavelength. In reality though, wind-waves are random, characterized by broad spectra, directional spreading, and rapidly decreasing spatial and temporal coherence. The stochastic nature of wind waves motivated Phillips (JFM, 1957) to relate the appearance and subsequent growth of surface disturbances to interactions between waves and random pressure fluctuations in turbulent airflow. His three-dimensional nonlinear theory identified several possible mechanisms governing wind-wave evolution but did not provide predictive capabilities. Both the deterministic, 2D shear-flow instability theory and the 3D stochastic approach of Phillips assume spatially homogeneous conditions. Consequently, Fourier components of the surface elevation are defined by their wave vectors, and numerical studies are typically conducted using periodic boundary conditions. These assumptions imply spatially uniform temporal evolution, corresponding to the duration-limited problem. In contrast, most laboratory experiments are performed under steady wind forcing, in which the wave field remains statistically stationary at each location and evolves in the spatial, or fetch, direction. The fetch-limited configuration requires a reference location, such as the shoreline in field experiments or the wind-inlet position in laboratory facilities. Shear-flow instability is generally accepted as the primary mechanism responsible for wave excitation on an initially smooth water surface. However, direct experimental verification remains elusive. Such verification is essential because of the substantial gap between the simplifying assumptions of existing theoretical models and the conditions governing real wind waves, both in nature and in the laboratory. Reliable verification requires statistically robust, well-resolved measurements under controlled conditions, which can be obtained most effectively in laboratory experiments. With this objective, Zavadsky and Shemer (JFM, 2017) measured wave parameters in a 5-m-long wind-wave facility at several fetches following the effectively abrupt initiation of wind over an initially calm water surface. For each wind velocity U0 and fetch x, the instantaneous surface elevation, η(x,t), and the two surface slope components, ηx(x,t) and ηy(x,t), were recorded over numerous independent realizations. The initiation time of the blower provided a common temporal reference. These measurements enabled the determination of reliable ensemble-averaged, time-dependent integral quantities that characterize wind-wave field, including the root-mean-square (rms) wave amplitude, the rms slope components fdom(x,t). These findings, together with extensive experimental results obtained in our laboratory and summarized by Shemer (Atmosphere, 2019), motivated Geva and Shemer (PRL, 2022) to develop a quasi-linear stochastic model describing the complex spatial and temporal evolution of these parameters. The model assumes that the wind-wave field consists of multiple, equally probable, random unidirectional harmonics with wavenumbers kj . Each harmonic is assigned an initial ensemble-averaged energy and undergoes exponential growth at a temporal rate γ(kj) determined from the viscous shear-flow instability model based on the coupled Orr–Sommerfeld equations for the air and water. The initial exponential growth of each harmonic is eventually limited by nonlinear effects such as a maximum wave steepness or the maximum propagation time, τ(kj) =x/cg(kj), where cg(kj) is the group velocity. The model successfully reproduces the distinct fetch-dependent stages of wave evolution observed experimentally and captures the development of the wave field both qualitatively and, in most cases, quantitatively. Several assumptions as well as predictions based on the Geva–Shemer model were subsequently supported by Kumar and Shemer (JFM, 2024a, b). The model therefore represents significant progress toward understanding wind-wave excitation. Further verification and refinement are nevertheless required, particularly moving from the integral quantities to the details of evolution of individual spectral harmonics during the transient linear and post-linear stages that define the fine structure of the wind-wave field at each instant. In the present study, numerical solutions of the coupled Orr–Sommerfeld equations obtained by Kumar and Shemer (JFM, 2026) for a range of operational parameters are used as a background to provide theoretical estimates. The experimental data of Zavadsky and Shemer are revisited using quantitative wavelet analysis to investigate the temporal and spatial evolution of individual coexisting spectral harmonics over the whole spectrum. The wavelet analysis yields the temporal variation of the amplitude of each harmonic represented by its instantaneous rms value ensemble-averaged over multiple realizations. Results obtained independently from measurements of the wavelet frequency spectral components of surface elevation and the along-wind slope component are compared. For all spectral harmonics, the rate and the timing of the initial temporal growth of the root-mean-square values of both quantities agrees reasonably well with the theoretical predictions based on the Orr–Sommerfeld equations. Deviations from exponential growth of each harmonic during the later stages are examined in relation to the maximum attainable wave steepness, wave breaking, and spatial modulation associated with the boundary conditions at the facility entrance and the finite wave energy propagation velocity cg(kj). The group velocity of each harmonic is calculated from the Orr–Sommerfeld solutions that yield the dispersion relation between fj and kj for each experimental condition. The new findings on the temporal variation of the fine structure of young wind waves generally corroborate the 2D stochastic approach suggested by Geva & Shemer but suggest numerous refinements and clarify the physics of the process. The new understanding shed further light on modeling the effective dissipation of different spectral harmonics in the wind-wave field, as well as assessment of contribution of nonlinear wave-wave interactions.

491427.title: Global Atmosphere–Ocean Kinetic Energy Transfer via Surface Waves: Evidence of Upscale Correlation
491427.authors: Xuanting Hao, SIO, UC San Diego, La Jolla, CA; UC San Diego, La Jolla, CA
491427.abstract: The atmosphere–ocean kinetic energy flux, i.e., the wind work on the ocean, shapes the global ocean energy budget and spans a wide range of spatial scales. Among the various pathways, the energy flux through surface waves is nearly two orders of magnitude larger than all other pathways combined, yet its spatiotemporal characteristics remain poorly understood. Using ERA5 data, we compute the global integral of the wind work on surface waves over the past eight decades (1945–2025) and obtain a time-averaged value of approximately 83 TW, which is higher than previous estimates. The zonal and temporal mean of the energy flux per unit area exhibits a distinct peak in the Southern Ocean, whereas substantial variability is observed in the Northern Hemisphere. Both the spatial distribution and the interannual variability of the wind work on surface waves show strong correlations with those of large-scale currents and inertial waves reported in the literature, suggesting that cross-scale interactions are missing from conventional ocean energy budget frameworks.

491428.title: A Century of Observations Reveals a Seasonal Shift in Extreme Heat in Phoenix
491428.authors: Sudhansu Sekhar Rath, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ; and M. Georgescu
491428.abstract: The evolving nature of extreme heat is commonly examined via seasonal analysis of temperature magnitude, frequency, or duration. Less attention has been paid to whether the timing of extreme heat is also changing. This is particularly relevant for cities because shifts in the timing of extreme heat can extend the period of heat exposure and increase stress on people, energy systems, and urban infrastructure. Here, we examine this question using daily maximum temperature observations from Phoenix, Arizona, from 1933 to 2026. We track the first and last annual occurrence of three societally relevant temperature thresholds: 100°F (37.8°C), 105°F (40.6°C), and 110°F (43.3°C). Analysis of the observational record shows a clear shift in the seasonal timing of extreme heat. The first occurrence of (37.8°C) and 105°F (40.6°C) conditions has shifted more than three weeks earlier in the observational record (by 24 and 22 days, respectively), while the last occurrence of extreme heat has shifted similarly later in the year. Together, these changes have substantially expanded the window of the calendar year during which Phoenix experiences extreme heat. The number of extreme-heat days, duration of consecutive heat events, and cumulative heat above these thresholds have also increased. These results show that warming in Phoenix is changing not only how hot the city has become, but also when hazardous heat begins and how long it persists. This cross-seasonal threshold-based perspective complements more conventional climate metrics, providing a direct bridge between climate change detection and societal relevance. Our results demonstrate a considerable shift in the timing of heat adaptation needs that traditional seasonal analyses cannot capture.

491429.title: Global Mineral Constraints on Dust Shortwave Radiative Effects (Invited Presentation)
491429.authors: Longlei Li, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, NY; University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China; and N. M. Mahowald, R. L. Miller, C. Perez Garcia-Pando, M. Gonçalves Ageitos, P. Ginoux, V. Obiso, Q. Song, P. G. Brodrick, D. R. Thompson, R. N. Clark, G. Okin, B. L. Ehlmann, B. Zhou, O. V. Kalashnikova, and R. O. Green
491429.abstract: Mineral dust aerosols affect Earth’s energy balance in multiple ways, including interactions with solar radiation, but this effect remains poorly quantified. A central limitation has been the lack of reliable global information on dust mineral composition, particularly light-absorbing iron oxides. An imaging spectrometer, placed aboard the International Space Station by the Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation mission, provides high-resolution, near-global retrievals of surface mineralogy. Here we incorporate these retrievals into four Earth system models to constrain the dust shortwave direct radiative effect. Analysis shows that the retrievals reduce the radiative effect uncertainty by more than a factor of six in both present-day (2007–2011) and late twenty-first-century (2090–2094) climates. This improvement is enabled by tighter constraints on iron oxide content, which reduce its uncertainty contribution from 0.62 W m−2 to 0.10 W m−2. Greatest improvement occurs over the Sahara, where high dust abundance and surface reflectance amplify the influence of iron oxides. Orbital spectroscopy thus shifts the primary uncertainty from mineral composition to processes controlling the spatial distribution of dust. These findings mark a transition towards confident aerosol composition modelling and provide an improved basis for assessing how dust alters Earth’s energy balance today and in a warming future.

491431.title: Storm-Relative Controls on Drag Variability in the Air-Sea Transition Zone During Hurricane Erin (2025)
491431.authors: Otoniel Palacios, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and H. Potter
491431.abstract: Air-sea momentum exchange during hurricanes is governed by rapidly evolving interactions among wind forcing, directional wave structure, turbulence, and sea-state evolution within the Air-Sea Transition Zone (ASTZ). Despite recent advances in coupled atmosphere-wave models, the physical processes controlling sea-state-dependent drag variability remain incompletely understood, particularly under rapidly rotating hurricane winds. Processes such as spectral partitioning, swell directional memory, mixed sea states, directional asymmetry, and slanting-fetch dynamics are expected to influence momentum transfer, yet their relative contributions remain poorly constrained. This study investigates the storm-relative physical controls on air-sea drag variability during Hurricane Erin (2025). Directional wave observations were collected by A-size Directional Wave Spectra Barometer Drifters (ADWSBDs) during the Office of Naval Research (ONR)-funded Study of Air-Sea Coupling with Waves, Turbulence, and Clouds at High Winds (SASCWATCH) field campaign. These observations are integrated with Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) wind field observations, the HURDAT2 best-track dataset, and COAMPS-TC wind fields and wind stress. Directional wave spectra are partitioned into dominant swell and high-frequency (HF) wind-sea components to quantify directional wave memory, local wind-wave adjustment, and the evolution of mixed sea states. Wind-wave misalignment, directional asymmetry, and slanting-fetch conditions are then investigated as interconnected physical mechanisms governing air-sea momentum exchange. Results reveal a broad range of wind-wave misalignment regimes associated with systematic differences in the directional response of swell and HF wind-sea to the evolving hurricane wind field. Whereas HF wind-sea remains closely coupled to the local wind forcing, swell exhibits stronger directional memory, producing persistent directional offsets and mixed sea states. These observations advance understanding of the physical mechanisms governing sea-state-dependent drag variability under extreme winds. They also provide new observational constraints for the development and evaluation of sea-state-dependent drag parameterizations in coupled atmosphere-wave models, ultimately improving the representation of air-sea momentum exchange within the Air-Sea Transition Zone under hurricane conditions.

491435.title: Spatial-Scale Dependence of Extreme Summer Precipitation Changes over Metropolitan Phoenix
491435.authors: Sudhansu Sekhar Rath, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ; and J. Karanja, R. C. Balling Jr., and M. Georgescu
491435.abstract: Urban influences on precipitation are difficult to isolate because cities may enhance, suppress, or alter rainfall through multi-scale interactions with the broader atmospheric environment. Assessment of urban-induced precipitation is particularly challenging for cities in complex terrain, where multiple forcing mechanisms can interact with the built environment to produce a precipitation signal. We examine historical (1980-2024) summertime rainfall trends using the high-resolution NOAA Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC) dataset for the Phoenix Metropolitan Area (PHX-Metro), located in the southwest US and lying within the North American Monsoon (NAM) region. Whereas prior research has shown contrasting effects of urban-induced precipitation changes over PHX-Metro, our analysis demonstrates weak and spatially heterogeneous multi-decadal trends. However, we demonstrate that rainfall exceeding the 95th and 99th percentiles shows significant increases in exceedance total, intensity, and localized frequency. Importantly, the interpretation of these changes depends strongly on the spatial scale of assessment and on how PHX-Metro is framed relative to the surrounding terrain and broader monsoon environment. These changes are strongly embedded within the broader NAM domain, making it difficult to separate a distinct urban precipitation signal from regional controls

491436.title: Architecture and Design of the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA)
491436.authors: James David Campbell, Raytheon, El Segundo, CA; and M. A. Cook, J. Rodriguez, K. R. Gedin, E. O. Monroy, A. J. Fernandez, L. Wu Yuen, A. C. Petty, M. Henry, and M. K. Belal
491436.abstract: The Raytheon–Spire architecture for the Sounder for Microwave Based Applications (SMBA) integrates proven technologies into an instrument designed for next generation atmospheric sensing. The SMBA architecture supports the NOAA Near-Earth Orbit Network (NEON) program with a precision calibrated hyperspectral backbone. The SMBA design provides improvements in sensitivity, spectral resolution, and on-board radio frequency interference (RFI) detection. We will describe the architecture and the improvements for establishing a traceable calibration standard, hyperspectral capability, and flexible RFI detection.

491438.title: Interface-Resolving Simulations of Secondary Droplets Produced By Ocean Precipitation
491438.authors: Xuanting Hao, UC San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and H. H. Kuo
491438.abstract: Secondary droplets produced by raindrop interaction with ocean surface play a critical role in air-sea interaction and yet their dynamics are extremely difficult to capture because of their size. We use direct numerical simulations to investigate the dynamics of secondary droplets generated by raindrop-liquid pool interactions. The raindrop parameters feature a realistic speed of ~7 m/s, average diameters of ~1–4 mm, and surface tension values ranging from 25% to twice the typical air–water interface value. The numerical configurations include both a single raindrop and two raindrops separated by distances between two and four times the raindrop diameter. The secondary droplet size distribution, Nd, is found to scale with the droplet radius, rs, as Nd(rs)∝rs-5/2, with additional dependencies on surface tension and raindrop diameter. When normalized according to this new scaling law, the droplet size distribution obtained from simulations with different parameter values collapses onto a single curve. Analysis of the impact morphology reveals distinct stages of raindrop interactions and identifies the formation and breakup of a central liquid film. Spatial and temporal analyses of the secondary droplets show that raindrop interaction can influence both the percentage of droplets captured by the cavity and the duration over which they re-merge with the pool. These behaviors arise from the combined effects of differences in the birth times of secondary droplets of various sizes and aerodynamic forcing associated with the cavity airflow.

491446.title: On the Accuracy of P3 Microphysics Schemes in Predicting Ice Crystal Growth in Winter Storms: Results from IMPACTS
491446.authors: Peter Anthony Brechner, Univ. of Oklahoma/CIWRO, Norman, OK; and G. M. McFarquhar, J. C. Douglas, Y. Huang, P. Yeh, B. A. Colle, D. J. Delene, C. Nairy, K. L. Thornhill, J. A. Finlon, D. Noone, A. J. Heymsfield, and A. Bansemer
491446.abstract: Accurate modeling of ice growth processes in ice- and mixed-phase clouds in winter storms requires that ice growth process rates (GPRs) predicted in models accurately represent those occurring in nature. Errors in modeled GPRs lead to errors in particle size distributions (PSDs) that compound the GPR errors since modeled PSDs are used to calculate GPRs. To date, however, few studies have quantified discrepancies between GPRs predicted in bulk microphysics schemes and those derived from in-situ observations that may offer a reasonable representation of those occurring in nature. To address this, PSDs derived from simulations of a rapidly deepening snowstorm that produced heavy snow in multiple bands on 7 February 2020, conducted using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model with the 2-moment P3 1-category and 2-category bulk microphysics schemes, were compared to PSDs observed in-situ from a NASA P-3 aircraft that sampled the same storm during the Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) campaign. GPRs derived directly from in-situ observations using equations for various process rates were also compared against those prognosed from the WRF simulations. Data from multiple in-situ cloud probes on the P-3 aircraft are input to a phase classification algorithm to categorize each 1-s period in cloud as ice-, liquid-, or mixed-phase. A spatial and temporal analysis of the observed and modeled reflectivity, Doppler velocity, wind, and temperature fields determined times and locations for comparing modeled and derived PSDs and GPRs so that storm properties (e.g., proximity to fronts, convection, temperature, cloud phases) included in both the model and the observations were as similar as possible. The observed ice- and mixed-phase PSDs were fit to gamma distributions for easier comparison to the model assumed/prognosed gamma distributions for the same cloud phases; all model species contributing to each phase were added to determine the model PSD and fit for comparison. Estimates of GPRs derived from the in-situ observations used the formulas from the P3 schemes. Gamma fit parameters, both modeled and observed, decreased with temperature, ice water content, and median mass diameter. Both bulk microphysics schemes underestimated the highest plausible values for μ, regardless of environmental conditions. The 2-category microphysics scheme systematically overpredicted N(D) for higher D and underpredicted N(D) for lower D. Aggregation rates, both modeled and derived, were larger in regions with higher temperatures and ice water contents but were biased high in the 2-category microphysics scheme even after controlling for ice water content. Causes of errors in modeled GPRs, including the overestimation of aggregation rates, are examined and discussed.

491454.title: Coastal Effects on the Evolution of Mesoscale Convective Systems over the Seoul Metropolitan Area during the KPOP-MS Field Campaign
491454.authors: Seung Hee Kim, Institute for Earth, Computing, Human and Observing, Schmid College of Science and Technology, Chapman Univ., Orange, CA; and J. H. Jeong, J. E. Lee, K. S. Lim, G. Lee, and M. Kafatos
491454.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) affecting the Korean Peninsula frequently develop or propagate over the shallow, warm Yellow Sea before reaching the western coastline and moving inland during the warm season. The western coastal region adjacent to the Seoul Metropolitan Area is characterized by a complex coastline and strong land–sea thermal contrasts, providing a unique environment that can substantially influence convective initiation, organization, and intensification. Understanding these coastal effects is therefore essential for improving forecasts of high-impact precipitation, particularly over the densely populated Seoul Metropolitan Area. This study investigates interactions among MCSs, coastal circulations, complex terrain and the thermodynamic environment using multi-platform observations collected during the Korea Precipitation Observation Program: international collaborative experiments for Mesoscale convective system in Seoul metropolitan area (KPOP-MS) field campaign, together with high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations. Three-dimensional wind fields are retrieved using the Wind Synthesis System using Doppler Measurements (WISSDOM), which integrates observations from 11 Doppler radars surrounding the Seoul Metropolitan Area. In addition, balloon-based Storm Tracker measurements collected during intensive observation periods provide high-resolution vertical profiles of the thermodynamic and kinematic environment, offering further insight into convective initiation and subsequent MCS evolution over the coastal region. In this presentation, we examine several MCS events observed during the KPOP-MS field campaigns since 2023. These cases demonstrate that coastal processes can substantially influence MCS initiation and evolution through modifications of atmospheric instability, sea-breeze forcing, cold-pool dynamics, and microphysical–dynamical feedbacks. The results highlight the importance of accurately representing coastal mesoscale processes for improving forecasts of convective initiation, MCS evolution, and extreme precipitation over the Korean Peninsula, with broader implications for other coastal regions. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea(NRF) grant funded by the Korea government(MSIT) (RS-2026-25488670)

491455.title: Reanalysis - The Enabling Technology for a New Space Weather R2O Paradigm
491455.authors: Thomas P. O'Brien III, The Aerospace Corporation, Chantilly, VA; The Aerospace Corporation, Chantilly, VA; and J. Green and R. Redmon
491455.abstract: A reanalysis is typically the result of a long-term, data assimilative, physics-based model run. As such, it combines observations and simulations into an optimal global or regional estimated state of the environment. Recent advances in tropospheric weather prediction have shown that machine learning (ML) models trained on decades of reanalysis data can match and even surpass conventional numerical weather prediction models that solve partial differential equations (PDEs) in real time with data assimilation. It is likely far easier to deploy and maintain an ML space weather forecast model in operations, compared to the complex super-computing environments often required for PDE solvers. This is partly a consequence of the relatively simpler computing resources needed to evaluate a trained ML model, like a neural network. It is also partly a result of being able to use established software libraries that can perform core ML functions in a variety of computer languages suitable for operations. To realize these potential operational benefits, first we must build reanalyses on which to train the ML models. This will require detailed understanding and curation of our long-term data sets, introduction of data assimilation into new space weather domains, execution of long-term reanalysis runs, and training and deploying large operational ML forecast models.

491460.title: Land-PBL-Cloud Coupling in ARM Ground-based Observations and DOE’s Global Storm Resolving Model
491460.abstract: Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program (supported by US Department Of Energy, DOE) hosts longterm ground-based observations at multiple locations, providing high resolution comprehensive profiling and scanning data from subsurface soil layers to the top of atmosphere. In this study, these data are used to characterize the interactive processes among land surface, planetary boundary layer (PBL), clouds and precipitation and focus on the terrestrial and the atmospheric feedback between soil moisture, surface fluxes, radiation and precipitation at the surface, PBL turbulence and convective triggering. On the other hand, global earth system models have approached kilometer scale to resolve convective systems in recent years, which significantly bridged the gap between models and ground-based site observations for model validation and improvement of their representation on physical processes. In this study, we adopt a hierarchy of modeling tools developed by DOE Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) including decadal-long global simulations by Simple Cloud-Resolving E3SM Atmosphere Model (SCREAM) and golden-case-wise regional simulations by a stand-alone doubly periodic SCREAM (DP-SCREAM). In this study, we focus on several ARM sites to systematically evaluate SCREAM’s performance on representing land-atmosphere interactive relationships under local-coupling regimes including clear-sky PBL, surface-forced fair-weather shallow cumuli and their transition into deep convection and soil moisture-precipitation feedback across multiple time scales from diurnal to seasonal. By doing so, we aim to dissect model biases and attribute model error sources to advance mechanistic understanding of physics and to provide insights on possible pathways of model improvement. This work was performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under contract DE‐AC52‐07NA27344, Lawrence Livermore National Security, LLC.

491464.title: Assessing the physical consistency of AI weather models through idealized experiments
491464.authors: Zhen-Qiang Zhou, Fudan Univ., Shanghai, China
491464.abstract: Deep‐learning weather prediction models have demonstrated skill in simulating large‐scale climate modes, but their physical interpretability remains a critical challenge. Here, we apply a 360‐member Green's function‐like ensemble to the Pangu‐Weather model to diagnose the optimal forcing configuration of the tropical western North Pacific anomalous anticyclone. The model reproduces the observed optimal forcing structure, including cooling over the western North Pacific and warming over the tropical Indian Ocean, demonstrating its ability to simulate physically consistent large‐scale responses. However, the model exhibits systematic biases, including a spurious westerly anomaly east of Indian Ocean heating and underestimated response to tropical Atlantic heating. These findings highlight both the physical consistency of Pangu‐Weather in capturing key climate modes and the challenges arising from its data‐driven nature. Our results underscore the need for hybrid modeling approaches that combine data‐driven learning with physical constraints to improve climate predictability and interpretability.

491471.title: Hail-StormScope: A Regional High-Resolution Nowcasting System for Hailstorms Built on NVIDIA StormScope Architecture
491471.authors: V. Chandrasekar, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and C. Radhakrishnan, S. K. Biswas, S. Abbas, and R. R. P. Kumar
491471.abstract: Short-term prediction of severe hailstorms remains challenging because operational forecasts must capture the rapid motion and structural evolution of localized convective cores. Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models provide valuable guidance, but initialization and spin-up time limit their ability to represent rapidly evolving convection at short lead times. Traditional extrapolation-based nowcasting methods propagate existing storms to some extent but struggle to represent a storm's convective nature, intensification, and decay. These limitations motivate data-driven, machine learning (ML)-based approaches that learn storm evolution directly from high-resolution radar observations. This study presents a modification of NVIDIA's Earth-2 StormScope architecture for regional application and short-term prediction of intense convection over Colorado and Wyoming (CO-WY) region. StormScope is a generative model based on a diffusion transformer (DiT). The resulting framework, referred to as Hail-StormScope, was trained on a high-resolution composite reflectivity dataset generated from 12 NEXRAD radars covering the CO-WY region. The dataset spans 2021 to 2025, with four years (2021 - 2024) used for training and 2025 reserved for testing. Two ensemble-of-experts (EOE) models were trained for low and high noise ranges, respectively, with each fine-tuned on the CO-WY hail season (May–August) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). At inference, Hail-StormScope combines the low- and high-noise range models to produce composite reflectivity nowcasts at 3-hour lead time with 10-minute temporal resolution. The model was evaluated against 15 independent severe hail events from 2025 hail season using the Fractions Skill Score and Structural Similarity Index Measure, with verification focusing on echoes exceeding 40 dBZ. This threshold highlights vigorous convective cores and regions with hail potential. Forecasts were compared against traditional extrapolation-based nowcasting and the operational High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model. Hail-StormScope showed strong skill at short lead times and retained useful forecast information out to three hours. The model also generated nowcasts whose storm morphology closely resembled the original observations. In contrast, traditional extrapolation methods tended to advect the storm closer to persistence with little to no change in structure. Hail-StormScope uses a single radar composite frame to initialize each forecast. Subsequent nowcast frames are generated autoregressively, each predicted frame conditioning the next step. A notable strength of the StormScope architecture is that the model accurately learns the motion of multiple, spatially distinct storm cells within the same domain, even when those cells move in different directions. Hail-StormScope captures the distinct direction of each individual storm cell, even as different cells move in different directions across the domain. A general description of the StormScope architecture, training methodology, and validation process will be presented.

491474.title: From Hazard to Harm: Leveraging AI to Collect and Attribute Societal Weather Impacts
491474.authors: Joanne Robbins, UKMO, Exeter, United kingdom
491474.abstract: High-impact weather events are increasingly affecting societies worldwide, resulting in fatalities, injuries, disruption to critical services, infrastructure damage, economic losses, and wider social consequences. While considerable advances have been made in forecasting hazardous weather, the systematic collection and attribution of societal impacts remain a significant challenge. Understanding how meteorological hazards translate into real-world consequences is fundamental to improving risk assessment, evaluating warning effectiveness, developing impact-based forecasting and warning systems, and identifying pathways to increase societal resilience. However, impact information is often fragmented across multiple sources, inconsistently reported, and rarely linked directly to the hazard conditions responsible for the observed outcomes. These limitations hinder efforts to build comprehensive evidence bases for decision-making and forecast evaluation. This presentation will describe new and novel approaches being developed under the AWAKEN (AI Weather for Action, Knowledge and Early response through Networks) project and the ANTICIPATE Network – Extended-range multi-hazard predictions and early warnings. It will explore emerging methods for collecting, harmonising, and attributing societal impact observations associated with high-impact weather events. We will focus on recent advances in automated impact collection techniques that leverage natural language processing and artificial intelligence and discuss the methods for integrating information from diverse sources (e.g. governmental & emergency management records, humanitarian datasets, media reports). The presentation will also review key methodological challenges for hazard-to-impact attribution, including inconsistent spatial and temporal reporting, uncertainty in event boundaries, the presence of cascading and multi-hazard processes, and the difficulties associated with linking impacts to hazard footprints. Ultimately, the challenge is no longer simply predicting the weather but understanding and anticipating its consequences. By leveraging AI to connect hazards with their societal consequences, we can transform impact observations into actionable risk intelligence and support more effective decisions before, during, and after extreme weather events.

491477.title: Seasonal and Geographical Differences in the Marine Thermal Influence on US Coastal Air Temperatures
491477.authors: Eric A Schmitt, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA; University of Miami, Miami, FL; and A. C. Clement
491477.abstract: The ocean is often thought to moderate temperatures along adjacent coastlines, but its influence varies by region, season, and time of day. This study quantifies the ocean’s influence on coastal air temperatures along the East and West Coasts of the United States using a ten-year record of land-based weather observations and satellite derived sea surface temperatures. By calculating ocean-land temperature differences and estimating temperature advection, we identify distinct seasonal and geographical differences in marine thermal influence. Generally, the ocean has a moderating influence on daily average coastal air temperatures, warming in winter and cooling in summer. However, this does not hold at all latitudes. On the East Coast south of 35°N, warm coastal ocean waters have a year round warming influence on nighttime temperatures that exceeds the cooling influence on daytime temperatures, resulting in a net warming effect on daily average coastal air temperatures. In contrast, the west coast is more uniform latitudinally, with oceans providing a generally cooling influence on coastal land temperatures, but more variable between nearby stations, likely due to topography. These findings challenge the assumption that the ocean uniformly cools coastal regions in warmer months and highlight the need to consider spatial, seasonal, and daily dynamics in adaptation strategies for coastal heat hazards.

491481.title: Machine Learning-Based Sea-Surface Temperature Prediction Using Himawari-Derived HIMSST
491481.authors: Takeshi Enomoto, Disaster Prevention Research Institute, Kyoto University, Uji, 26, Japan
491481.abstract: Geostationary satellites observe the infrared and visible radiation from the atmosphere and the surface of the Earth, providing rich information for monitoring and numerical weather prediction. Himawari geostationary satellites have been operated by the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) since 1977, monitoring the western Pacific. HIMSST (High Resolution Merged Satellite and In-situ Data Sea Surface Temperature) provides daily sea-surface temperature (SST) in the western north Pacific (100°E–180°E, 0°–60°N) since February 2017 at a horizontal resolution of 0.1 degree. HIMSST merges observations from Himawari, polar-orbiting satellites and in-situ platforms to achieve high spatial resolution. In this study, lightweight machine-learning techniques are examined to predict SST five days ahead using HIMSST. For the subdomain of 120°E–150°E and 20°N–50°N (301 x 301), the data is divided into training (four years), validation (two years) and test (two years). The data is standardized with the daily climatology and standard deviation. To extract horizontal features, the singular value decomposition (SVD) or convolutional autoencoder (CAE) is applied to the standardized data. The inputs are the leading ten modes and their day-to-day changes, and the outputs are the daily changes of SST anomalies during the next five days. XGBoost and MLP (multi-layer perceptron) are used for direct five-day prediction. In addition, a temporal convolutional network (TCN) is used for autoregressive (AR) prediction using the CAE outputs. A bottleneck architecture is required for the MLP to perform comparably to XGBoost. The root-mean-squared errors (RMSE) for the test data are 0.7403 K for persistence, 0.6805 K for the initial anomalies extrapolated with the seasonal cycle, 0.6728 K for XGBoost, and 0.6779 K for MLP. Welch's t-tests indicate that XGBoost yields significantly lower errors than the extrapolation and persistence baselines and MLP. The improvement in the Sea of Japan primarily arises from the seasonal cycle, whereas that in the subtropics arises from the machine-learning model. The errors are particularly large in the Kuroshio Extension (KE), indicating the importance of ocean dynamics. Replacing SVD with a CAE yields similar results for XGBoost. While the AR prediction using the CAE and TCN yields the smallest five-day forecast RMSE of 0.6644 K, the errors in the KE remain large.

491484.title: COASTAL - Estimating Spectral Diffuse Light Attenuation from Remote-Sensing Reflectance to Support Seagrass Restoration
491484.authors: Harshit ` Singh, Boston University, Boston, MA; Edison Academy Magnet School, Edison, NJ; and K. Moon, S. Ranasinghe, S. Tierney, and C. G. Fichot
491484.abstract: Seagrass habitats face increasing threats, and identifying locations with adequate underwater light is vital to their successful restoration. The diffuse attenuation coefficient, Kd(λ), describes how rapidly light at a given wavelength decreases with depth. In order to calculate Kd, researchers typically collect in situ light profiles through the water column, limiting data to directly surveyed locations and times. Remote-sensing reflectance, Rrs(λ), can be measured in situ and retrieved from observations by satellite sensors such as the Sentinel-2 Multispectral Instrument (MSI). To enable broader spatial estimates of spectral light attenuation, we developed and evaluated Sentinel-2-compatible models to reconstruct Kd(λ) spectra from Rrs(λ). We analyzed 257 Rrs–Kd observations collected from 2017–2026 across estuarine and coastal Massachusetts waters with varied optical conditions, which included Boston Harbor, Plum Island Sound, and Stellwagen Bank. Rrs was measured at each station using a portable spectroradiometer, and Kd(λ) was determined from downwelling irradiance measured at multiple depths using a C-OPS optical profiler. We converted hyperspectral field Rrs(λ) into Sentinel-2-equivalent band reflectances by weighting the spectra with the sensor’s spectral response functions. Using these bands, we developed regression-based and machine-learning models to estimate Kd(λ) at 18 wavelengths from 305 to 710 nm. The models used individual Rrs bands and derived spectral variables, including band ratios and normalized differences. Location-based holdout tests and repeated 80/20 train-test splits were used to assess the generalization of the models. Across the 18 wavelengths, selected field models achieved a mean repeated 80/20 R2 of 0.92 and MAPE of 13.8%. Performance was strongest at ultraviolet and blue-green wavelengths and declined toward the red end of the spectrum. Seven Sentinel-2 scenes were selected for validation based on the availability of 30 in situ observations collected within ±1.5 hours of overpass. Field-trained models were applied to the ACOLITE dark spectrum fitting (DSF)-processed imagery, using the median Rrs from a 5×5-pixel window at each station. All field observations from the matchup dates were excluded from model training. The strongest satellite performance yielded a mean R2 of 0.77 and MAPE of 14.8% across the same wavelength range. Satellite performance was lower than field-based model performance, likely due to uncertainties in satellite Rrs retrieval. With further satellite validation, Kd(λ) estimates could be combined with surface irradiance and water depth to estimate benthic light availability and facilitate spatial evaluation of potential seagrass restoration sites.

491485.title: Anabatic Flows over Idealized Mountain Ridges and the Relation between Slope Angle and Turbulence Anoisotropy
491485.authors: Andreas Rauchöcker, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, 7, Austria; and M. S. Wedel, A. Gohm, and I. Stiperski
491485.abstract: The boundary layer structure in mountainous regions is heavily influenced by thermally-driven wind systems of various scales. On the smallest scale, anabatic (upslope) flows develop over slopes that are heated and thus warmer than the atmosphere adjacent to the slope. While the along-slope component of the buoyancy force triggers the rising motion, a horizontal pressure gradient develops due to the horizontal temperature contrast between the heated air close to the slope and the cooler ambient air at the same elevation and forces the air to rise along the slope. Anabatic flows are characterized by a distinct jet-like wind profile, and previous observational studies suggest that the wind maximum over steep slopes is below 10 m above the ground. According to analytical models and data from numerical simulations, the strength and depth of the anabatic flow layer are sensitive to the slope angle. Since increasing slope angles results in anabatic jets that are stronger and have jet maxima closer to the surface, a fine vertical grid spacing is necessary to resolve the vertical structure of anabatic flows near the surface. Such grid spacing is especially important for Large-Eddy Simulations (LES), since the jet height limits the size of the largest, most energetic eddies that govern the vertical exchange between the surface and the anabatic flow above. In addition, measurement results suggest that the slope angle is a potential driver of anisotropy, thus correctly resolving the jet maximum in LES is especially important. Most existing LES studies of anabatic flows over steep slopes, however, were unable to reproduce a well-defined jet profile. In this study we explore the influence of the slope angle on turbulence anisotropy, which has not been investigated in numerical simulations so far. To evaluate the influence of ridge height, slope angle and slope curvature on turbulence anisotropy, we conducted large-eddy simulations of anabatic flows above idealized ridges using the Cloud Model 1 (CM1) with an unprecedented vertical resolution of 1 m close to the slope. Based on different ridge heights and widths, we performed 7 simulations each for sinusoidal ridges and ridges with a constant slope angle, equal to the average angle in sinusoidal ridge simulations. The simulations were dry, and initialized with a constant potential temperature gradient throughout the domain and a constant surface heat flux of 0.12 K m s-1. In agreement with previously published results, the anabatic jet was stronger and closer to the surface for larger slope angles. An increase of the slope angle along the slope also led to an acceleration of the flow along the slope and a decrease of the anabatic jet height. An anabatic jet was reproduced for all simulations except those with slope angles larger than 35 degrees. Anisotropic turbulence dominated below the anabatic jet, while turbulence was more isotropic above the jet. In addition, larger slope angles were associated with more anisotropic turbulence. Turbulence reaches an isotropic state already closer to the surface over convex sections of sinusoidal ridges compared to the concave sections. Since turbulence was also more isotropic above slopes with constant slope angles compared to concave slopes of sinusoidal ridges, terrain curvature has a pronounced effect on the spatial distribution of the degree of anisotropy.

491486.title: ACCESS-A/AE: A National Convective-Scale NWP System for Australia
491486.authors: Shaun Cooper, BoM, Docklands, VIC, Australia; and B. Roux, C. Franklin, I. White, S. Rennie, Y. Xiao, and S. Wales
491486.abstract: The Australian Bureau of Meteorology has developed a regional, high-resolution numerical weather prediction (NWP) system with a domain that provides convective-scale forecasts across all of Australia. Spanning 5 – 50oS, ACCESS-A/AE is one of the world’s largest km-scale NWP systems. This system includes a deterministic model, Australian Community Climate and Earth Systems Simulator Australia (ACCESS-A), which has a horizontal grid spacing of ~1.5 km and includes convective-scale data assimilation and large-scale blending. ACCESS Australia Ensemble (ACCESS-AE) is the convective-scale ensemble counterpart with 12-members and a horizontal grid spacing of ~2.2 km. ACCESS-A/AE have 90 vertical levels and use the UK Met Office Unified Model. Australia experiences a range of weather regimes, from tropical weather in the north, to temperate midlatitude weather in the south. In between, conditions range from subtropical to arid. Previous generations of the bureau's convective-scale systems have run several smaller domains only covering highly populated regions of the country and using either a tropical or midlatitude science configuration. ACCESS-A/AE use the Regional Atmosphere and Land version 3.2 science configuration, which has unified the tropical and midlatitude configurations. This system represents a significant advancement in convective-scale modelling capability at the bureau by replacing multiple smaller domains with a single system that provides convective-scale NWP guidance for the whole country, including regions that were not previously covered. The large domain pushes the lateral boundaries further from the area of interest, reducing the influence boundary errors and allowing the development of mesoscale circulations that are less constrained by the driving model. It allows the life cycle of long-lived systems to be consistently modelled as they move through the domain without transitioning through lateral boundaries. The single domain also simplifies operational workflows and provides convective-scale guidance over spatial scales not previously possible at the bureau. ACCESS-A/AE provides a unique opportunity to assess the performance of the unified science configuration across Australia's varied climatic regimes and to investigate interactions between synoptic, mesoscale and convective-scale processes. The system also provides a foundation for future forecast-system development, including advances in post-processing, calibration, and emerging data-driven forecasting approaches. Preliminary verification of ACCESS-AE against the current operational convective-scale NWP domains shows an improvement in precipitation forecasts. It also demonstrates generally lower RMSE in 10 m wind, 2 m temperature and dewpoint which, in conjunction with an increase in ensemble spread, is resulting in a general enhancement of spread/error ratios. This presentation will discuss aspects of the general performance of the system, and the ability to forecast high-impact weather events including thunderstorms, heavy rainfall and tropical cyclones. It will also discuss some of the challenges in evaluating a large domain convective-scale system that spans such diverse weather regimes and observationally sparse regions.

491490.title: Influence of the Interdecadal Variation of the Extratropical Southern Indian Ocean SST on East Asian Summer Monsoon Precipitation
491490.authors: Qingquan Li, National Climate Centre, China Meteorological Administration, Beijing, China; and X. Li, Y. Ding, and S. Yang
491490.abstract: Observations indicate that East Asian summer precipitation exhibits significant interdecadal variability, with an alternating reverse phase distribution of rainfall from south to north, which is different from the consistent increase or decrease of precipitation in the whole region. The East Asian summer monsoon mainly affects the spatial pattern of meridional tripole precipitation on the interdecadal timescale. Moreover, the interdecadal sea surface temperature variability in the extratropical southern Indian Ocean is the most significant in the boreal summer. When there is anomalous warming in the extratropical southern Indian Ocean, the Somali cross-equatorial flow weakens and then alternating positive and negative waves propagate to central East Asia. In contrast, the New Guinea cross-equatorial flow experiences interdecadal enhancement with cyclonic circulation anomalies over the Northwest Pacific and anticyclonic circulation anomalies over the Philippines, which leads to a weakening of the South China Sea monsoon trough. On one hand, the cyclonic-anticyclonic coupling over the Philippines and Northwest Pacific results in an anomalous eastward transport of water vapor and reduced water vapor input over southern East Asia. On the other hand, the coupling strengthens the water vapor transport from the mid-latitude Northwest Pacific to central East Asia. These circulation anomalies favor the development of a meridional tripole pattern, i.e. a “negative – positive – negative” pattern of East Asian summer monsoon precipitation anomalies on the interdecadal timescale, which is specifically manifested in the abnormal increase of precipitation in central East Asia and the decrease of precipitation in northern and southern East Asia.

491491.title: A New Benchmark for Convective Boundary Layer Flows over Complex Terrain - the Terrain-Induced Atmospheric Boundary-Layer Flow: Large-Eddy Simulation Model Intercomparison Study (TABLES)
491491.authors: Andreas Rauchöcker, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, 7, Austria; and C. Barthlott, M. Cassiani, S. R. de Roode, L. L. Donati, L. Huusko, M. Fritz, V. Fuka, M. G. Giometto, B. Kosović, N. Krieger, C. Kühnlein, S. Marras, D. Munoz-Esparza, L. Papritz, E. G. Patton, J. A. Sauer, J. Schmidli, S. Serafin, I. Stiperski, G. Svensson, A. van Ginkel, S. J. A. van der Linden, H. Wang, and H. C. Ward
491491.abstract: Due to ever-increasing computational resources in recent years, large-eddy simulations (LES) have become one of the most important tools to study boundary layer turbulence. The application of LES in boundary layer research ranges from idealized simulations of flow over horizontally homogeneous and flat terrain to hindcasts of realistic meteorological events nested in mesoscale simulations. The wide range of potential applications of LES models led to the development of a large variety of different LES codes. These codes differ in various aspects, including the spatial and temporal discretization, the dynamical cores, the sub-filter-scale turbulence models, and the representation of terrain. While comparative studies of different LES models already exist for a variety of scenarios and weather regimes (stable boundary layer, very stable arctic boundary layer, stratocumulus, idealized convective boundary layer flow) exist for flat terrain, a benchmark study for complex-terrain flows has not been conducted yet. To adress this research gap, the Terrain-induced Atmospheric Boundary Layer flow: Large-Eddy Simulation (TABLES) model intercomparison Study was designed to provide a benchmark for convective boundary layer flows above idealized 2D bell-shaped hills, with and without background flow. In this simple scenario, a thermally-driven circulation is generated by baroclinicity triggered by differential heating along sloping surfaces and modified by the presence of large scale flow of various magnitudes. Due to the thermally-driven circulation, turbulence in the boundary layer exhibits strong heterogeneity that is dependent on the location along the ridge transect. The project consists of 12 research groups bringing 12 different LES codes. While all models use the same initial and boundary conditions, the models differ in the dynamical core and spatial discretization, as well as in the implementation of terrain, sub-filter-scale model and surface model. Each research group was asked to provide simulations of free convection and forced convection, both over flat terrain and over a 100-m-high ridge. In addition, research groups working with compressible models provided also one free convection and one forced convection simulation over a 1000-m-high ridge. First results indicate that mean variables and turbulence statistics of the different models agree remarkably well for the flat simulations and for the general flow structures in the convective boundary layer flows above idealized ridges. However, differences in both the strength of these terrain-induced flow structures and their location across the ridge between the different models are more pronounced with important implications for understanding the turbulence structure of these flows.

491494.title: Variable Droplet Evaporation during Dilution-Drivenexpansion of Shallow Cumuli
491494.authors: Fabian Hoffmann, Freie Universität Berlin, Berlin, Berlin, Germany; and G. Bagheri, B. Thiede, Y. Kim, A. Pumir, B. Mehlig, and E. Bodenschatz
491494.abstract: The lifetime and spatial extent of atmospheric clouds depend on the turbulent mixing between cloudy and environmental air. This process generates droplet heterogeneities across scales that remain poorly constrained by observations. Here, we present in-situ measurements of shallow cumulus cloud edges ranging from 1 mm to 20 m, revealing sharp cloud boundaries and strong variability in cloud microphysical properties. A comparison with a high-resolution microphysical model shows intermittent droplet evaporation at the cloud edge but also reveals that average cloud microphysical properties are scale-independent, thereby allowing the large-scale cloud response to be inferred.

491495.title: Kite-Based Atmospheric Measurements in the Classroom: NASA's AREN Program as a Model for Student-Collected Data
491495.authors: Michael Jabot, SUNY Fredonia, Fredonia, NY
491495.abstract: Understanding near-surface atmospheric dynamics — temperature, humidity, and wind behavior close to the ground — typically requires instrumentation and access that place this kind of data collection out of reach for most classrooms. NASA's AEROKATS and ROVER Education Network (AREN) addressed this gap by using kite-lofted instrument payloads to collect atmospheric measurements at low cost, giving students direct, hands-on access to a type of data collection normally reserved for research-grade equipment. This presentation and activity describes the implementation of AREN's atmospheric measurement activities, walking through the full mission arc: planning a launch, preparing the sensor payload, conducting the flight, and analyzing the resulting data. Students constructed simple vertical profiles of temperature, humidity, and wind from their own collected readings, directly observing how atmospheric conditions shift with altitude even over short vertical distances — a concept often taught abstractly but rarely measured firsthand by students. We will discuss the practical and pedagogical aspects of running this kind of activity in a classroom, including safety and logistical considerations for kite-based data collection, how student-collected data compares to and can be contextualized against broader datasets through The GLOBE Program and My NASA Data, and what evidence of student learning and engagement resulted from this work. We aim to share this work as a replicable, low-cost model for bringing authentic atmospheric science data collection into classrooms, and to invite discussion on how it might be adapted across different educational contexts.

491496.title: Bringing the Atmosphere Down to Earth: Using NASA's AREN Project to Teach Atmospheric Boundary Layer Concepts in Secondary Classrooms
491496.authors: Michael Jabot, SUNY Fredonia, Fredonia, NY
491496.abstract: The atmospheric boundary layer is a foundational concept which remains challenging for students to grasp because its dynamics are invisible, scale-dependent, and rarely addressed with hands-on tools. This presentation, reports on a Discipline-Based Education Research (DBER) effort to bring authentic atmospheric boundary layer data collection into classrooms through NASA's AEROKATS and ROVER Education Network (AREN) project. Using low-cost, kite-borne sensors and instruments, students collected in situ vertical profiles of temperature, humidity, and wind, generating real atmospheric soundings that parallel the observations gathered by NASA's Earth-observing satellites—but at a local, tangible scale. This place-based approach allowed learners to connect classroom instruction on atmospheric structure and stability directly to data they gather themselves, bridging the gap between abstract disciplinary concepts and lived, observable phenomena. This session shares findings from classroom implementation of AREN-based atmospheric boundary layer activities, including shifts in student understanding of boundary layer processes, engagement outcomes, and practical lessons for integrating remote sensing and field-based data collection into existing instruction. We also discuss how this work exemplified the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) by iterating on instructional design based on classroom evidence. By grounding disciplinary content in authentic, project-based data collection, this work contributes to the growing body of ASER scholarship aimed at preparing a scientifically literate public and a future atmospheric science workforce equipped to address pressing environmental challenges.

491497.title: Source Apportionment of VOCs in European Cities
491497.authors: Archita Rana, Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Jülich, Germany; and R. Wegener, M. G. Adam, R. Dubus, L. Kesper, D. Klemp, R. Franz, S. Schmitz, D. van Dusseldorp Saskia, P. G. Rivera, G. Jibuti, N. Kalivitis, F. S. Domingues, S. O. Barrault, E. van der Gaag, M. Pikridas, R. Baalbaki, M. Van Poppel, and E. von Schneidemesser
491497.abstract: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs), are key ozone precursors and a target pollutant under the EU’s newly adopted air quality directive (EU/2024/2281), yet standardized datasets linking VOC composition, OH reactivity and emissions source across European urban traffic environments remain limited, making it difficult to compare the local air quality drivers or design targeted mitigation measures. The Net4Cities project addresses this gap by establishing an integrated network of air quality and noise measurements across 11 cities in 10 European countries: Tbilisi, Antwerp, Zurich, Berlin, Duesseldorf, Limassol, Heraklion, Rotterdam, Oslo, Barcelona, and Southampton. The project focuses on capturing exhaust and non-exhaust emissions, particularly near urban traffic locations and around major transport hubs such as ports and airports. Along with VOC sampling, the network monitors ultrafine particles (UFPs) (as particle number concentration (PNC) and lung-deposited surface area) and ammonia (NH₃). From March 2025 to April 2026, ambient air samples were collected monthly (on the first Wednesday of each month, 08:00–09:00 AM local time) in all partner cities using evacuated silco-steel canisters, then the canisters were analyzed using GC-MS/FID for VOCs quantification. Carbon monoxide (CO), carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrogen oxides (NOx), and nitrous oxide (N2O) were also quantified for each city, with CO2 used as a normalization tracer for comparison across city. Since more than 90% of VOCs are processed by OH radicals, the atmospheric impact of VOCs is determined by their OH reactivity, which is the product of the VOC concentration and its reaction rate constant with OH. Together with the prevailing VOC/NOx ratio, OH-reactivity characterizes local ozone production as a single comparable parameter across cities with different VOC mixtures. Across all cities, alcohols, aldehydes, alkenes, and ketones dominate the VOC mixing ratio with ethanol, methanol, acetaldehyde, and acetone as leading individual contributors. OH reactivity however was dominated by monoterpenes and aromatics despite their comparatively low mixing ratios, limonene contributed 4-5 times more to reactivity than any other terpene, toluene and 1,2,3−trimethylbenzene led among aromatics. Semi-volatile alkanes such as dodecane and decane remained low and stable through winter but spiked sharply in summer, most strongly for dodecane, consistent with temperature-driven evaporative release from fuels, lubricants, and asphalt rather than a change in emission sources. Toluene-xylene and ethylbenzene-xylene pairs correlated strongly across cities, while benzene showed weaker correlation with other BTEX (benzene, toluene, xylene, and ethylbenzene) species, likely reflecting its longer atmospheric lifetime or more mixed source profile. Beyond VOCs, the N2O/CO2 ratio was highest in Heraklion and Limassol and lowest in Tbilisi, consistent with differences in catalytic converter usage, also supported by high CO concentration in Tbilisi, likely due to older vehicles and less complete combustion. CH₄ concentration was highest in petrochemical-dominated port cities (Antwerp, Rotterdam), while CO₂ was highest in Zurich and lowest in Limassol. Substantial heterogeneity in ∑VOC/NOx ratios among different cities further points to different local emission profiles, mixes of traffic composition, and photochemical aging across the network. Based on the meteorological and BTEX-ratio patterns, chemical mass balance (CMB) receptor modelling will be applied to apportion the ambient VOC concentrations among source profiles such as gasoline and diesel exhaust, evaporative fuel losses, solvent/industrial use, biogenic emissions, and residential/shipping combustion, supporting source-targeted mitigation under the EU Zero Pollution Action Plan. This work is co-funded by the European Union under Project 101138405—Net4Cities, the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) under the UK government’s Horizon Europe funding guarantee (grant no. 10107404), and the Swiss Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI) (grant no. 23.00622).

491498.title: Kites as a Gateway: Cultivating Pre-College Interest in Atmospheric Science Through NASA's AREN Program
491498.authors: Michael Jabot, SUNY Fredonia, Fredonia, NY
491498.abstract: Building lasting interest in the weather and climate professions among pre-college students depends on giving them authentic, hands-on contact with atmospheric science early — not just instruction about it. NASA's AEROKATS and ROVER Education Network (AREN) offered exactly this kind of experiential entry point: using kite-lofted sensor payloads, K-12 students collected their own near-surface atmospheric data — temperature, humidity, and wind speed — through a complete, self-directed mission arc of planning, launching, collecting, and analyzing data. This presentation describes the implementation of AREN's atmospheric measurement activities in in collaboration with regional education partners connected to the AREN network. We discuss how the program lowered the barrier to real atmospheric science practice: no specialized aircraft, licensing, or costly instrumentation was required, allowing the activity to run in a standard school setting while still producing data that connects to larger frameworks like The GLOBE Program and NASA's My NASA Data resources. Students moved through the same procedures used in professional atmospheric field campaigns at a scale appropriate for a classroom, building both technical familiarity and a sense of ownership over real scientific data. We will share what this experience revealed about student engagement and interest in atmospheric science as a field of study or career, discuss the logistical and collaborative aspects of bringing a kite-based program into a K-12 environment, and offer this model as a low-cost, replicable way for other pre-college programs — whether school-based or informal — to cultivate early, hands-on connections to the weather and climate sciences. We aim to contribute to the broader conversation on how experiential learning at the pre-college level can help build the next generation's involvement in atmospheric science, professionally and personally.

491499.title: Small-Scale Anisotropy in the Stable Boundary Layer: A Scale-Resolved Pressure-Strain Budget from Ultra-High Resolution LES
491499.authors: Maja-Sophie Wedel, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, 7, Austria; University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, 7, Austria; and M. Ghirardelli, A. Rauchöcker, and I. Stiperski
491499.abstract: The stable boundary layer (SBL) represent a particularly challenging version of boundary layer where the exchange of momentum, heat, and scalars between the surface and the free atmosphere is strongly impacted by stratification. Especially in conditions of very stable stratification, where turbulence is often intermittent and strongly anisotropy, SBL turbulence is not well represented in operational weather forecast and climate models. Even in Large-eddy simulation (LES), the small size of turbulent structures in the SBL requires extremely fine grids to resolve energy containing eddies, while isotropic assumption of the subgrid-scale (SGS) closures is not often met. At larger scales, where turbulent kinetic energy is generated, flows are generically anisotropic as shear preferentially energizes the streamwise component, while buoyancy acts as a sink. This produces the pronounced suppression of vertical fluctuations characteristic of the SBL. Isotropy is only expected to be recovered at sufficiently small scales, below a transition nominally set by the Ozmidov scale. Yet the sharpness and universality of this transition remain debated. Here we explore the role of pressure-strain correlations, which redistributes energy between the velocity components, on the onset of small-scale isotropy in wall-bounded stably stratified flow. We use large-eddy simulation data with a grid spacing of 20cm of the GABLS1 stable boundary layer case, obtained from the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database, under two stability regimes. A scale-resolved second-moment budget is computed by filtering the resolved velocity field across a range of scales. Each budget term is then evaluated as a function of filter width and height. First results suggest that the vertical pressure-strain term reverses sign as a function of scale: it is positive and consistent with the Rotta model at large scales, but negative and anisotropy-generating below a threshold scale. This mirrors the sign reversal previously reported in the convective boundary layer, but occurs at the opposite end of the scale range. In weakly stable case the scale that best predicts the sign reversal appears to be the Thorpe scale rather than the Ozmidov or buoyancy length scale. Preliminary analysis further indicates that this anomalous small-scale behavior is compensated almost exactly by the nonlinear interscale energy transfer term, with the residual consistent with dissipation. These findings suggest that the apparent small-scale isotropy seen in bulk anisotropy diagnostics is not a passive relaxation, but a dynamic equilibrium between opposing terms. This can have direct consequences for the grid-spacing criteria required for isotropic SGS closures to be valid.

491500.title: Variability and Trends in Tropospheric Ozone over the Equatorial Americas Based on SHADOZ Observations
491500.authors: Debra E. Kollonige, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD; ADNET Systems, Inc., Bethesda, MD; and R. M. Stauffer, A. M. Thompson, M. Cazorla, A. Piters, I. Nedeljkovic, T. Warsodikromo, F. Raimundo Silva, J. A. Diaz, and E. Corrales
491500.abstract: Global tropospheric ozone trends are important for studying climate forcing and surface pollution. With current satellite products and model tropospheric ozone trends diverging, observations from the Southern Hemisphere Additional Ozonesondes (SHADOZ) network are a reference for tropical and subtropical tropospheric ozone. Over the past almost 30 years, tropical free tropospheric (FT) ozone changes are modest, to within ~±3%/decade, except over southeast Asia (Thompson et al., 2025). Recent analyses (Stauffer et al., 2024; Millet et al., 2025; Thompson et al., 2025) of ozone trends and variability in the troposphere and lowermost stratosphere (LS) reveal signatures of changing convection, a perturbed tropopause and impacts of COVID-19 in the tropics and subtropics. We perform analyses similar to those in Stauffer et al. (2024) and Thompson et al. (2025) to examine tropospheric ozone changes (1998-2025) over SHADOZ locations, focusing on the Equatorial Americas region: Costa Rica, Paramaribo, Natal, San Cristobal and Quito (Figure below) stations, specifically. The GSFC MLR model is used for trends determination with monthly mean profiles from ozonesondes and radiosondes. Monthly averaged dynamic properties from satellite data and MERRA-2 reanalyses (e.g. cloud-top brightness temperature, OLR) are also analyzed with the MLR model. Satellite CO from AIRS and IAGOS CO/O3 aircraft profiles are used as a proxy for FT anthropogenic pollution. Additionally, tropopause height trends give insight into upper troposphere (UT)/LS structure regionally and seasonally.
