We also use the method of quantile regression to demonstrate differences in trends regionally for the 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles of tropospheric ozone (ie, low or background versus elevated tropospheric ozone.) This study summarizes region-specific drivers in the Equatorial Americas influencing tropospheric ozone.

491503.title: Evaluation of an MPAS-A Simulation of Tropical Storm Isaias: Comparison with Offshore Floating LiDAR Observations and WRF simulations
491503.authors: Patrick Michael Miller, University of Albany State University of New York, Albany, NY; and D. J. M. Freedman
491503.abstract: Accurate prediction of offshore winds during tropical cyclones is important for offshore operations and maintenance (O&M), structural design, and characterization of extreme wind conditions. This study evaluates the performance of the Model for Prediction Across Scales– Atmosphere (MPAS-A) in simulating the offshore wind environment as Tropical Storm Isaias affected the northeastern U.S. coastal waters. The simulation is conducted using a 2-km interpolated regional mesh derived from a larger global MPAS mesh, allowing convection to be represented explicitly. The MPAS-A simulation is run for 48 hours, with a 12-hour model spin-up excluded from the primary analysis. Simulated offshore wind speeds are validated against observations from two New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) floating LiDAR buoys. MPAS-A results are also compared with a previously completed Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulation of Tropical Storm Isaias conducted at the same 2-km horizontal resolution. Model performance is assessed through comparisons of observed and simulated wind speeds, vertical wind profiles, and the timing and magnitude of peak winds. Our results will identify strengths and limitations of MPAS-A in representing high-impact offshore wind conditions during Tropical Storm Isaias and determine how its performance compares with WRF for the same event. The study provides insight into the potential application of MPAS-A for offshore wind forecasting and the simulation of extreme wind events relevant to offshore wind-energy systems.

491504.title: A GPU-Native, Differentiable CRTM: Connecting Satellite Radiative Transfer, Data Assimilation, and AI Weather Modeling
491504.authors: Xiaoxu Tian, Independent Researcher, Clarksville, MD
491504.abstract: We present a GPU-native, differentiable reimplementation of the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) in PyTorch. Rather than emulating CRTM with a learned surrogate, the implementation re-expresses the underlying CRTM physical algorithms as differentiable tensor operations, including gaseous absorption, surface emissivity, cloud and aerosol optical properties, and multi-stream scattering. The same computational graph therefore provides both forward radiances and Jacobians through automatic differentiation, without a separately implemented tangent-linear or adjoint model. Satellite radiance assimilation sits at the intersection of some of the largest computational and methodological changes now occurring in weather forecasting: rapidly increasing observation volumes, heterogeneous GPU computing, emerging machine-learning forecast systems, and growing interest in differentiable and hybrid data-assimilation methods. Yet the physical observation operators connecting atmospheric states to satellite measurements largely predate these recent advances. For the operational sensor configurations examined to date—including ATMS, AMSU-A, CrIS, AIRS, IASI, ABI, and AHI, spanning microwave and infrared, clear-sky and all-sky conditions—the double-precision forward calculation reproduces the Fortran CRTM reference near machine precision. Autograd-derived Jacobians likewise reproduce CRTM K-matrices within machine-precision tolerances for the validated fields and configurations, including gradients through the all-sky scattering solver. GPU batching provides substantial throughput acceleration, particularly for computationally intensive all-sky radiative transfer. Beyond acceleration, a differentiable physical observation operator creates a new interface between traditionally separate parts of the weather enterprise. It can support conventional variational assimilation, GPU-native and hybrid DA architectures, observation-space sensitivity studies and OSSEs, and physics-based radiance objectives for training or adapting machine-learning weather models directly against satellite observations. In this sense, the work provides an enabling computational layer through which established satellite radiative-transfer physics can participate directly in emerging differentiable Earth-system workflows.

491505.title: Withdrawn: Cloud Microphysics - Turbulence Interactions: Insights from Experiments at LACIS-T
491505.authors: Dennis Niedermeier, Leibniz Institute for Tropospheric Research, Germany, Leipzig, SN, Germany; and S. Schmalfuss, S. Melnik, K. Goharian, P. E. Lloyd, R. A. Shaw, R. van Loon, W. Frey, J. P. Mellado, and F. Stratmann
491505.abstract: Clouds in general and cloud microphysical processes in particular are fundamental to the Earth's hydrological cycle and radiative budget. While studying these processes in isolation is already challenging due to the complexity of aerosol-water interactions, the atmospheric reality is far more complex. Turbulence is omnipresent, inducing stochastic fluctuations in temperature, water vapor concentration and consequently saturation, creating a dynamic environment that fundamentally alters microphysical pathways compared to homogeneous conditions. Determining and quantifying the occurring interactions is critical to generally understand the behavior of clouds. To do so, large efforts have been taken during the last decades including numerical simulations, field studies, as well as laboratory investigations, with the latter offering a unique opportunity to simulate turbulent environments under well-defined and reproducible initial and boundary conditions. This presentation focuses on results obtained from the Turbulent Leipzig Aerosol Cloud Interaction Simulator (LACIS-T) which is a closed-loop moist-air wind tunnel. This facility allows for the systematic investigation of cloud microphysical processes within a controlled turbulent temperature and saturation field. A key aspect of this work addresses turbulent mixing processes. We analyze how the turbulent mixing of two air flows with different thermodynamic properties (which leads e.g., to saturation fluctuations) affects particle deliquescence, cloud droplet activation, and the subsequent growth, with a specific emphasis on the evolution of droplet size distributions under fluctuating conditions. Furthermore, we examine the impact of turbulent temperature fluctuations on the immersion freezing of cloud droplets, a process highly sensitive to temperature variability. Overall, the results can provide essential constraints for the parameterization of cloud microphysics in cloud-resolving models. This study also highlights the necessity of accounting for turbulence-induced fluctuations to accurately describe and predict cloud behavior. Acknowledgement This research has been supported by: German Research Foundation (grant nos. NI 2231/1-1 and STR 453/14-1); Federal Ministry of Education and Research (grant nos. 01LK2001A-K and 01LK2002A-G) in the context of ACTRIS-D, which is the German contribution to the Aerosols, Clouds and Trace Gases Research Infrastructure (ACTRIS); European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under the Marie Skłodowska Curie grant agreement no. 835305

491506.title: Joint CCOR-1 and STEREO-A observations: Developing a 3D CME Measurement Dataset for Machine Learning Validation
491506.authors: Laura Balmaceda, George Mason University, Fairfax, MD; George Mason University, Fairfax, VA; and N. Kuroda, D. Lloveras, and A. Thernisien
491506.abstract: The deployment of the NOAA Compact Coronagraphs series (CCOR-1,-2) represents a vital new asset for monitoring Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) from the Earth-Sun line. However, single-view coronagraph observations inherently suffer from projection effects, leading to ambiguities in apparent CME speeds, widths, and trajectories. To resolve these geometric uncertainties, we present an analysis of over 40 CME events observed simultaneously by CCOR-1 and STEREO-A (STA) in the period November - December, 2024. Leveraging a ~28-degree separation angle between Earth and STA, we apply 3D stereoscopic reconstructions to calculate deprojected, true kinematics, and include CME mass as an improved constraint (Kay et al. 2025, Sol. Phys.). This joint observation effort yields a comprehensive, manually measured catalog of CME parameters, including height-time (H-T) tracking of the leading edge, apparent and true angular widths, and brightness profiles. The primary objective of this manual dataset is to provide a high-fidelity dataset for validating automated machine learning (ML) architectures. Advanced ML models for automated CME segmentation have been already successfully tested using STEREO/COR2 data (Iglesias & Lloveras 2025, Sol. Phys.). However, adapting and verifying these pipelines for the new CCOR-1 instrument requires robust, cross-validated baseline measurements. By comparing our manually single viewpoint measurements and derived 3D kinematics against the outputs of the automated segmentation models applied to STA and CCOR-1 imagery, we can accurately quantify algorithmic performance, identify potential cross-instrument biases, and refine automated detection capabilities. This presentation details our joint CCOR-1 and STA methodology, highlights the geometry-corrected kinematics of our dataset, and demonstrates how this manual catalog serves as a critical benchmark for expanding proven ML segmentation models to next-generation space weather monitoring assets.

491511.title: Tracking CMEs Across the Solar System with PUNCH
491511.authors: Craig E DeForest, Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO
491511.abstract: The Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) is a NASA mission that images the entire inner solar system every four minutes, in polarized visible light over a 90 degree field of view centered on the Sun. PUNCH is specifically designed to study and understand how the corona gives rise to the solar wind, and how transients such as coronal mass ejections (CMEs) evolve and propagate across the inner solar system. Although PUNCH is a scientific mission, it is demonstrating the importance of wide-field imaging for space weather forecasting as well as for direct science. Continuously tracking CMEs through the PUNCH data yields order-of-magnitude improvements in CME arrival time forecasting accuracy. Initial "retro-forecast" studies with a simple front-tracking method yielded continuously improving forecasts that converged to within 30 minutes of CME arrival at Earth, some eight hours before arrival. The convergence was clearly identifiable in the sequence of forecasts generated by the method.

491512.title: A GPU-Native, Differentiable MPAS Atmospheric Dynamical Core
491512.authors: Xiaoxu Tian, Independent Researcher, Clarksville, MD; and D. Holdaway
491512.abstract: We present an implementation of the Model for Prediction Across Scales–Atmosphere (MPAS-A) dynamical core in PyTorch, designed to explore GPU-native and differentiable numerical weather prediction. The implementation retains the underlying MPAS numerical formulation while expressing the dynamical-core calculations within a modern accelerator-oriented computational framework. The growing use of GPUs and machine learning in weather prediction is creating demand for atmospheric-model architectures that can efficiently exploit modern accelerators while interacting naturally with differentiable and machine-learning workflows. Most established atmospheric dynamical cores, however, were developed around software architectures that well predate the maturation of these capabilities for large-scale scientific applications. The current prototype supports global simulation at approximately 60-km horizontal resolution on a single GPU. Numerical comparisons with the reference MPAS-A implementation demonstrate agreement near machine precisions. Preliminary performance measurements also show substantial acceleration relative to serial CPU execution. Further kernel fusion, GPU-oriented optimization, systematic comparison against modern multicore CPU configurations, and extension to distributed multi-GPU execution remain areas of active development. Because the dynamical core is expressed natively within PyTorch, automatic differentiation can be applied through model integration, providing a foundation for applications including sensitivity analysis, parameter estimation, variational data assimilation, and hybrid physics–machine-learning approaches. More broadly, this work investigates whether the numerical foundations of established atmospheric prediction systems can be carried forward into a computational architecture that unifies physical modeling, accelerator computing, automatic differentiation, and machine learning. Such an approach could provide a pathway toward progressively modernizing not only individual model components, but the wider weather-modeling workflow around them, while retaining the scientific structure and verification heritage of existing numerical systems. We will present numerical verification, current GPU performance, demonstrations of differentiability, lessons from the implementation, and remaining challenges toward scalable multi-GPU execution and broader model integration.

491513.title: Improving HAFS Track Predictions via Spectral Nudging toward AI-GFS Forecasts
491513.authors: Xu Lu, Lynker at NOAA/NWS/OMD, College Park, MD; and L. Zhu, B. Liu, Z. Zhang, F. Yang, Y. Weng, J. Cheng, B. Thomas, and V. S. Tallapragada
491513.abstract: Machine-learning (ML)-based weather prediction systems, such as AI-GFS, have demonstrated substantial skill in forecasting tropical cyclone (TC) tracks, partly because of their ability to represent large-scale environmental steering flows at relatively low computational cost. This study investigates a hybrid ML–physics approach in which spectral nudging (SN) is applied only within the parent domain of the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) to constrain the large-scale components of the horizontal wind and temperature fields toward corresponding AI-GFS forecasts. Experiments are conducted for major Atlantic TCs during the 2025 hurricane season to evaluate the feasibility and potential benefits of this new capability. Preliminary results indicate that the AI-GFS spectral nudging configuration (AISN) effectively brings the large-scale HAFS environment into closer agreement with AI-GFS guidance while retaining the regional model’s high-resolution storm-scale structure. Overall, AISN improves track forecasts relative to the control configuration (AICN), particularly beyond day 3, while maintaining comparable intensity forecast performance. Individual storm analyses show track-error reductions of approximately 20%–30% in several cases. The impacts are case dependent, however, and may become unfavorable when the underlying AI-GFS guidance contains substantial forecast errors. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using ML-based large-scale environmental guidance to improve forecasts from a high-resolution, physics-based regional hurricane model. Additional results and detailed diagnostics of AISN performance will be presented at the conference.

491514.title: Preparing The UK For The Next Big Storm
491514.authors: Krista Hammond, UKMO, Exeter, DEV, United kingdom; UKMO, Exeter, Devon, United Kingdom; and S. Machin
491514.abstract: Severe space weather has been recognised as a significant risk to the UK since 2011, when it was added to the National Risk Register. In response, the Met Office took ownership of the risk, with the Met Office Space Weather Operations Centre (MOSWOC) commencing 24/7 staffed operations in 2014. Since then, MOSWOC have worked alongside government, defence, industry and academic partners to continue to build an understanding of the risk of severe space weather to critical services and infrastructure. As our technology and vulnerabilities continue to change, so must we continue to evolve to maintain national resilience. In his presentation, we will give an overview of the ongoing developments within the UK to prepare for impactful severe space weather events. We will explore how this has involved working directly with users across multiple sectors to understand their unique vulnerabilities and requirements, including local, national and international exercising, to refine our products and communication during severe events, as well as helping to inform mitigation measures across government, defence and critical infrastructure providers. Finally, we shall look at how recent studies including the National Audit Office report into the UK’s preparedness to severe space weather takes a holistic view of the threat to the UK from severe space weather, and how this will help to inform the UK government’s update to the Severe Space Weather Preparedness Strategy.

491520.title: Changing Aerosol–Cloud Sensitivity over the Northwest Pacific under East Asian Emission Reductions
491520.authors: Jingyi Liu, University of Leeds, Leeds, United Kingdom; and K. Carslaw
491520.abstract: Cloud droplet number concentration (Nd) provides a key link between aerosol perturbations and cloud radiative properties, yet aerosol–cloud interactions remain a major source of uncertainty in estimates of anthropogenic radiative forcing. Over East Asia, substantial reductions in anthropogenic emissions over the past two decades provide a natural experiment for investigating how marine clouds respond to a changing aerosol environment. Here, we combine satellite retrievals, anthropogenic emission inventories, reanalysis data, and Lagrangian particle dispersion modelling to quantify how changes in China's anthropogenic emissions influence marine stratocumulus clouds over the Northwest Pacific through seasonally varying continental outflow. Over the past two decades, SO₂ and black carbon emissions over East China decreased by 48.1% and 24.0%, respectively, accompanied by a 23.0% decline in aerosol optical depth (AOD). Downwind over the Northwest Pacific, AOD decreased by 15.3% and marine Nd by 15.4%. Winter–spring northwesterly flow produces the strongest continental outflow, and the southern Northwest Pacific exhibits pronounced seasonal coherence between Nd and transport from East China (R = 0.88). During peak outflow months from February to April, East China accounts for nearly 50% of the potential anthropogenic influence on air masses reaching the downstream marine cloud region. At the daily timescale, Nd is approximately 32% higher under strong than weak transport conditions, while its response becomes progressively weaker at high transport intensity, indicating a nonlinear and potentially saturating response to increasing aerosol influence. At the decadal timescale, the sensitivity of marine Nd to AOD increased from approximately 0.3 before 2013 to approximately 1.0 thereafter, suggesting a transition toward a more aerosol-sensitive cloud regime as regional aerosol loading declined. Consistent with this shift, during February–April, Nd decreased at −2.2 cm⁻³ yr⁻¹ and the shortwave cloud radiative effect weakened at −0.22 W m⁻² yr⁻¹, whereas corresponding trends were small during months characterized by weak continental transport. These results demonstrate that reductions in anthropogenic emissions over China have propagated far downstream and altered both marine cloud microphysics and associated radiative effects over the Northwest Pacific. More importantly, they show that aerosol–cloud sensitivity is not stationary, but evolves with the background aerosol state and with the meteorological pathways connecting continental source regions to marine cloud systems. We further explored how variations in lower-tropospheric stability, boundary-layer structure, and synoptic circulation modulate the translation of aerosol perturbations into cloud responses.

491521.title: Machine Learning Analyses of AWAKEN Wind Turbine Wake Characteristics
491521.authors: Rebecca J. Barthelmie, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and S. C. Pryor
491521.abstract: Modeling of wind turbine wakes is challenging due to the large number of atmospheric drivers that generate high stochastic variability around predicted values of wake characteristics such as the velocity deficit, wake width and height from engineering and high-order models. Understanding these metrics and how they change in time and space is fundamental to modeling power output from large wind farms. This study applies machine learning tools (including regression trees) to wind turbine wake characteristics from a new data set comprising over 60,000 individual wakes. The machine learning tools are used to extract physical dependencies and develop predictability, utilizing high-fidelity remote sensing data. Here we use a long time-series of wake observations determined from scanning Doppler lidar (high resolution 3D wind fields) and vertically pointing lidar (turbulence intensity profiles) measurements during the AWAKEN field experiment. To provide a coherent dataset, flow from the south is selected where data from a Halo scanning Dopler lidar characterizes both the freestream wind profile and the wind field over the King Plains wind farm at high temporal and spatial scales. During a six-month time period over 60,000 wakes were characterized in terms of (i) the maximum velocity deficit and its height above the terrain, plus (ii) the horizontal width and vertical extent as wakes move downwind from each wind turbine. The Monin-Obukhov length (MOL) is used to define atmospheric stability based on measurements from a sonic anemometer at the site. Boundary-layer height (PBLH) is estimated based on the Halo lidar Vertical Azimuth Display data and these data are also used to detect the presence, height and core wind speed of low-level jets. Analysis of the wind fields at the wind farm are used to quantify wake characteristics from four wind turbines that have wakes that can be detected between 100 and 1100 m from the wind turbines. The normalized velocity deficit (NVD defined by [Ufreestream-Uwake]/Ufreestream) is more than 0.6 at 100 m distance at low wind speeds when the thrust coefficient is high. NVD decreases as the distance downstream and/or the wind speed increase but does not reach zero over these distances i.e. the wakes do not fully recover. Consistent with physical expectations and engineering models average NVD at each distance downstream is highly correlated with the distance from the wind turbine that generated the wake (regression coefficient squared (r2) for a linear fit exceeds 0.95). However, predicting individual wake characteristics is challenging. Individual NVD observations at given downstream distances exhibit very large variability. For example, at 100 m downstream when the average NVD is 0.62, the interquartile range (25th-75th percentile) is 0.58. Accordingly, a number of regression models (Linear, Ridge, Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (Lasso), elastic net (Enet), Support vector machine (SVM) and Tree) are trained to predict the velocity deficit as a function of a wide range of potential predictands including; MOL, turbulence intensity, freestream wind speed, PBLH, presence/characteristics of LLJ, downstream distance. The best results as defined by standard metrics such as r2, root mean square error and mean absolute error are from Tree regression. Further training of models based on binned downwind distances illustrate that the relative predictor importance varies as wakes develop over distances of up to about one kilometer.

491524.title: Causes and Projections of Global Warming Hiatus and Warming Spikes
491524.authors: Sara C. Pryor, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and J. J. Coburn
491524.abstract: Even in the absence of changes in atmospheric composition, paleo and historical records of global mean air temperature exhibit notable variability on annual to decadal timescales. This variability includes periods of near-zero warming over the last century that occurred despite secular increases in atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases. One period with relatively slow increases in global mean near-surface air temperature warming (a so-called warming “hiatus”) occurred during ~1998-2012 [Medhaug et al., 2017]. Although the precise duration and intensity of the warming slowdown is variable across different data sets, it is broadly accepted as a hiatus. The HadCRUT.5.1.0.0 dataset shows that in the 15-years prior to 1998 the mean rate of increase of global mean air temperature was 0.03+/-0.007 ºC/year, while the mean rate between 1988 and 2012 was 0.012+/-0.005 ºC/year and the 13 years after 2012 the mean rate of change was 0.06+/-0.006 ºC/year. The rate of change of global mean near-surface air temperature during the hiatus period was thus less than half that of the prior and subsequent periods of near equivalent length. Internal variability, and specifically extended periods with anomalously cool sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean due to a dominance of La Niña conditions in the tropical Pacific and negative (cool) Pacific Decadal Oscillation led to increased heat uptake by the oceans and thus were critical drivers of the warming hiatus [Medhaug et al., 2017]. The moderately strong La Niña that persisted between 2020 and 2022 (RONI index from NOAA dataset = -0.6) contributed to suppression of the rate of global temperature increase, while the subsequent strong El Niño (annual mean NOAA-RONI index = 0.9) has been identified as a major cause of the 0.31 ºC (HadCRUT.5.1.0.0 analysis dataset) increase (spike) in 2023 relative to 2022. One analysis of simulations performed with 64 different models without anthropogenic forcing found that such ‘spikes’ in global mean temperature occur only rarely (1.6% of the time) but their probability of occurrence increased six-fold when a multi-year La Niña immediately precedes El Niño conditions [Raghuraman et al., 2024]. The emergence of an intense El Niño event during 2026 has reinvigorated interest in understanding the interaction between internally and externally forced climate change on global air temperatures. Research presented in this talk employs historical datasets and large ensemble simulations from CMIP6 and MESACLIP to investigate the causes/mechanisms and characteristics (probability/duration/intensity) of warming hiatuses and spikes in both the historical and future periods. A robust and repeatable method is used to identify the presence of warming peak and hiatus periods in global average temperature so that the duration and characteristics of “hiatus periods” wherein global warming may appear to have stalled, stopped or reversed can be identified and assessed. This approach is first demonstrated on historical datasets (ERA5, MERRA, HadCRUT5.1, NOAA v6, GISS GISTEMP v4 and BEST) and correctly identifies warming peaks in 1982/83, 1997/98, 2015/16 and 2022/23, all of which correspond to major El Niño events. Then the same method is applied to 150 CMIP6 ensemble members and MESACLIP simulations. Our results indicate that: Periods with relatively stable mean global air temperatures (nominal hiatus periods) are longer and exhibit a wider range of trend magnitudes and signs in the historical period. The duration and variability of the hiatus periods reduce as warming accelerates. For example, analyses of output from the 10 historical and 10 future (RCP 8.5 Wm-2) MESACLIP simulations indicate that the median hiatus duration during 1850-1949 is 42 years, decreasing to 15 years for hiatus periods that start during 1900-1999, to 6 years for hiatus periods that commence during 1950-2049 and to 4 years for hiatus periods during 2000-2099. However, hiatus periods do not disappear from the record even under very high forcing. The mean magnitude of warming peaks(i.e. increments from the prior year) is 0.24 °C which is ten times the average decadal warming rate in the historical records and across the CMIP6 and MESACLIP simulations. Individual warming peaks of up to 0.8 °C are manifest in some simulations. Warming peaks earlier in simulations are almost uniformly associated with significant El Niño episodes (Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) > 1.5), while higher RONI values are not as necessary to trigger similar peaks in near-surface global mean air temperature toward 2100 under high radiative forcing (RCP8.5 (MESACLIP) or SSP5-8.5 (CMIP6)). These analyses indicate the continuing importance of ENSO in dictating the time evolution of global mean air temperatures including the occurrence of periods with anomalously rapid rises in global mean temperature. The presentation will conclude by discussing these results in the broader context of understanding the interaction between internally forced seasonal to decadal climate variability and externally forced climate change. Acknowledgements SCP acknowledges funding support from the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0016605) and computational resources provided by the NSF Extreme Science and Engineering Discovery Environment (XSEDE2) (award TG-ATM170024). References Medhaug, I., M. B. Stolpe, E. M. Fischer, and R. Knutti (2017), Reconciling controversies about the ‘global warming hiatus’, Nature, 545(7652), 41-47. Raghuraman, S. P., B. Soden, A. Clement, G. Vecchi, S. Menemenlis, and W. Yang (2024), The 2023 global warming spike was driven by the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 24(19), 11275-11283.

491527.title: The Influence of Atmospheric Rivers on Streamflow Extremes over U.S. Watersheds
491527.authors: Emily A. Slinskey, Center For Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) Scripps Institution of Oceanography University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and J. Cordeira
491527.abstract: The extreme precipitation produced by atmospheric rivers (ARs) is an important source of runoff generation for watersheds across the U.S. This study extends previous regional Western-focused studies on the linkage between variability in daily streamflow extremes and AR occurrence to watersheds throughout the contiguous U.S. Over 5,000 USGS streamflow gauges are analyzed annually and seasonally against the Guan and Waliser tARget v4 AR catalog between 1940–2024. The results show AR contribution to extreme streamflow (i.e., annually defined top-5% threshold) is highest within West Coast watersheds (up to 100%) with secondary maxima over New England and the Mid-Atlantic watersheds (upwards of 80%) in the winter and autumn. A smaller contribution (up to 50%) is evident across the Central U.S. where ARs are less common. The fraction of annual maximum streamflow days associated with ARs is equally as high (up to 100%) within Pacific Northwest Coast watersheds and throughout the Mid-Atlantic and Ohio River Valley watersheds. Detailed case studies further illustrate the relationship between impactful AR storms, extreme precipitation, and peaks in the 3-day streamflow percentile over Western and Eastern U.S. watersheds. Results from this analysis aim to improve our understanding of the different storm types responsible for runoff generation in support of flood risk assessment and situational awareness in water resources management.

491528.title: Wind Turbine Blade Erosion Atlases: Method to Derive Them and Potential Uses
491528.authors: Sara C. Pryor, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and R. J. Barthelmie, J. Coburn, X. Zhou, C. Hasager, A. Vinod, L. D. D. S. Toft, and K. Dimitriadou
491528.abstract: Hundreds of thousands of wind turbines are installed and operating worldwide. Over the 30 years in service, they are subject to harsh operating conditions that can reduce reliability and power production and cause the need for maintenance/repair/replacement. The likelihood of blade damage depends on operating conditions at each site and, specific to this presentation, materials stresses caused by solid and liquid hydrometeors impinging on rapidly rotating blades. Wind turbine blades have an outer coating layer that protects the underlying glass or carbon fiber reinforced polymer that is applied to a load-carrying shell. Once the coating is damaged or removed the substrate is rapidly eroded causing reduction of blade aerodynamic efficiency and power production. Wind turbine blade coating lifetimes and thus blade durability can be extended by: Redesign/reduction of manufacturing defects. Application of commercially available leading edge protection products. Using erosion-safe-mode (ESM) wherein rotor speed is reduced during damaging events (i.e. curtailment). The cost-efficiency of mitigation options to increase the time to onset of blade erosion at each site can be computed for a given location if the following information is available: (1) Estimates of the blade coating lifetimes and the time histories of material stresses that reduce coating lifetimes. (2) Annual Energy Production (AEP) and the time history of electricity production. (3) Time history of wholesale electricity price (WEP) and other revenue sources (e.g. subsidies). (4) Estimates of capital expenditures, typical operational expenditures, discount rates and costs for blade repair/replacement. Items (1) and (2) are components of Erosion Atlases. Here we present and contrast novel and transferable Erosion Atlas workflows to quantify time evolution of material stresses and wind turbine blade coating lifetimes plus electricity production based on wind turbine power and blade rotational speed (RPM) curves and observed or modeled meteorological conditions (wind speeds and precipitation) for Europe and North America. The first approach uses 5-minute time series of precipitation and wind speed from surface observing systems combined with hail metrics from scanning Doppler radar as input to the Springer model and wind turbine power curves to compute time series of electricity power production and coating accumulated distance to failure at > 800 sites across the USA. The second uses observed rainfall rate measurements at 1- and 10-minute intervals plus satellite-based (IMERG) rainfall rates and 30-minute wind speeds from the New European Wind Atlas as input to an impingement model to derive coating lifetime estimates. We contrast the strengths and weakness of each workflow and present results from detailed uncertainty propagation analyses wherein the precise wind turbine and curtailment duration are varied, and meteorological conditions are resampled. We then illustrate examples of how these Erosion Atlases can be used to evaluate how much and when (time of day and month of year) ESM curtailment is needed to minimize the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCoE) and illustrate the impact of that curtailment on blade coating lifetime extension and wind farm operational revenues in the USA and at the measurement site in Denmark which is located in the Nord Pool power exchange market. An example of the information flow and utility is illustrated here using 18 years of 5-minute meteorological data from an individual site in the US state of Oklahoma which is within the Southern Power Pool Independent System Operator (ISO). For the WINDPACT 3 MW wind turbine, the mean modeled AEP is 10,000 MWh (which equates to a capacity factor of 38%). The modeled wind turbine blade coating lifetime is 8 years. In this environment the time series of damage increments (formerly called accumulated distance to failure, ADF) is extremely heavy tailed. A few extreme (very intense precipitation with embedded hailfall at rated wind speeds) events dominate coating lifetimes, with one-third of the 18-year ADF occurring in approx. 1200 of the almost 1.9 million, 5-minute periods. The optimization algorithm is then run to determine the level of ESM curtailment associated with minimized LCoE. We then compute what is the impact of that curtailment on coating lifetime extension and gross revenue according to the WEP during the month and hour of the day when each curtailment period is enacted. The optimization indicates that curtailment to avoid the top 0.245% of erosive periods doubles the coating lifetime thereby deferring repair costs and power losses due to reduced aerodynamic efficiency. That curtailment reduces revenues by < 0.2%. Acknowledgements Support for this research was provided by U.S. National Science Foundation (2329911) and Sandia National Laboratory (DE-NA0003525), plus the European Union AIRE project (grant agreement 101083716). Computational resources used in these analyses are provided by the NSF Extreme Science and Engineering Discovery Environment (XSEDE2) (award TG-ATM170024).

491531.title: Operational Application of Real-time River Flood Forecast System with CaMa-Flood at Weathernews: Use case in Southeast Asia
491531.authors: Ikuto KAMBE, Weathernews Inc., Chiba, 12, Japan
491531.abstract: Climate change is projected to increase both the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, with riverine flooding among the most destructive consequences. Southeast Asia is particularly vulnerable due to dense populations on low-lying floodplains, intense monsoonal precipitation, and complex transboundary river systems, underscoring the urgent need for accurate, real-time forecasting systems capable of providing actionable early warnings. In response, Weathernews Inc. has developed a real-time river flood forecasting system for Southeast Asia using CaMa-Flood. The prediction pipeline consists of three sequential components. Atmospheric forcing is provided by "COMPASS", a weather forecasting system developed and operated by Weathernews Inc., at a horizontal resolution of 0.1 degree. These meteorological fields — including precipitation, temperature, and radiation — drive the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) land surface model, which computes surface runoff through the simulation of evapotranspiration and soil moisture dynamics. The resulting runoff is subsequently fed into CaMa-Flood as lateral inflow for river routing, yielding spatially distributed forecasts of river discharge, water depth, and flood inundation extent across Southeast Asia. Forecast accuracy is evaluated through hindcast experiments based on historical flood events in the region. Simulated discharge and inundation patterns are assessed against observational records and post-event reports. Model validation further leverages locally available hydrological observations across the region, providing a level of ground-truthing that complements globally consistent forecast products and strengthens confidence in operational deployment. Additionally, predictions are benchmarked against Google Flood to provide an objective comparison of the two operational systems and to highlight where local data integration offers a distinct advantage. Finally, we discuss the requirements and needs of local meteorological agencies in Southeast Asia as essential steps toward full operational deployment. Key considerations include data-sharing frameworks, integration of ground-based observations for model calibration, and effective communication of forecast uncertainty to end users and decision-makers. Bridging the gap between technical development and operational practice remains a central challenge in advancing flood early warning capabilities across the region.

491533.title: Impacts of Ocean Data Assimilation on HAFS Hurricane Fiona (2022) Forecasts
491533.authors: Hyun-Sook Kim, NOAA/OAR/AOML, MIAMI, FL; and H. kang, B. Thomas, B. Liu, G. Vernieres, and Z. Zhang
491533.abstract: This study evaluates the impacts of ocean 3DVar-FGAT data assimilation (DA) on the predictions of Hurricane Fiona (2022) using the U.S. Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) configured with a weakly coupled DA framework (WCDA-HAFS). The ocean DA incorporates the Marine JEDI (Joint Efforts for Data Assimilation Integration) system within the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6), which serves as the ocean component of HAFS. Numerical experiments were performed using both 3DVar and 3DVar-FGAT schemes, alongside two sets of the background error covariance (B-matrix): a parametric model and a MOM6 ensemble-based approach. The findings indicated that ocean analysis was improved with all the three approaches, as evidenced by a comparable reduction in observation-minus-background errors. Besides, each approach successfully captured a warm mixed layer, a subsurface salinity maximum, and a mesoscale anti-cyclone eddy characterized by high ocean heat content (OHC; <150 kJ cm-2) similar to the AVISO SSH and NESDIS OHC products. Forecast verifications for 36 homogeneous cases revealed up to a 20% improvement in both track and intensity skills when employing the 3DVar-FGAT scheme relative to the baseline configuration without ocean DA. Validations against Saildrone observations indicated that the baseline simulation consistently underestimated air temperature throughout the storm passage with a maximum of ~2oC, and also the baseline sea surface temperature was underestimated prior to the storm and overestimated following its passage by up to 2oC in each phase, which interestingly resulted in an overestimation of storm intensity by a mean of approximately 5.5 ms-1 for a 48-h period. To the contrary, the 3DVar-FGAT simulation provided similar estimates as the Saildrone for both air and sea surface temperatures, while reducing the mean intensity discrepancy to 3.7 ms-1. The 3DVar DA experiments utilizing the B-matrix overpredicted minimum pressure and maximum sustained winds, while degrading track forecasting skill by up to 35% compared to the baseline. Details of the results will be presented.

491534.title: The Evolution of R2O2R in the UK - Research and Partnerships
491534.authors: Simon Machin, UK Met Office, Exeter, Devon, United kingdom; and K. Hammond
491534.abstract: The Met Office Space Weather Operations Centre (MOSWOC) is the UK national capability for space weather monitoring and forecasting which provides operational support and information for government, industry, military and the public. Now in its 12th year of full operations, a number of new models, instruments and data sources are being operationalised, which is enhancing capabilities to meet the critical needs of users and to ensure the UK is prepared for and able to respond effectively to severe space weather events, to ensure the resilience of critical services and infrastructure. During this presentation we will share some of the past successes from the SWIMMR programme, including ground breaking new procedures and datasets, alongside addressing some of the challenges that come alongside transitioning our new models and monitoring capability into operations. This spans understanding user needs through structured engagements using User Centric Design approaches, ensuring that our development platforms are robust as well as being accessible to external partners and ensuring our operational models and systems meet the appropriate standards for operations. Finally, but not least we will outline the next steps towards an enduring research to operations pipeline, which will be delivered through the new Met Office Space Weather Partnerships Programme (MOSWePP), through four key thematic research pillars. We will showcase the MOSWePP programme and illuminate the developing opportunities this will provide to work together across international boundaries for mutual benefit.

491536.title: Nowcasting Precipitation with an Observation-Conditioned Diffusion Transformer using Dense GNSS Water Vapour and New York State Mesonet Data
491536.authors: Alexandros Matakos, Skyfora, Helsinki, Uusimaa, Finland; Skyfora, Helsinki, Finland; and M. Aichinger-Rosenberger, J. Maelan, K. Kaisti, B. Shrestha, N. Bain, and J. Wang
491536.abstract: Flash-flood warning at lead times of 0 to 3 h rests almost entirely on radar extrapolation, which carries skill only once precipitation exists to advect. Convective initiation, the failure mode behind many urban flash floods, is exactly where radar history is empty. Ground-based Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) senses the water-vapour loading that precedes initiation, in all weather and at 5-min cadence. In this study we rely on more than 470 geodetic GNSS stations across the wider New York region, 69 of them inside the state, together with a dedicated micronet of 25 Skyfora StreamGNSS meteorological GPS antennas in New York City. New York State Mesonet (NYSM) supplies the surface meteorology through 127 stations at 5-min resolution, anchoring the water-vapour retrieval and the precipitation truth the model trains on. We present an observation-conditioned diffusion transformer for probabilistic precipitation nowcasting, building on NVIDIA's openly released StormScope architecture. The system learns directly from observations, with no NWP or reanalysis fields in the loop: each station's 12-h vapour history, radar imagery, and NYSM surface observations condition a generative ensemble designed to deliver sharp, physically coherent precipitation scenarios at 2-km, 15-min resolution out to 3 h; training draws on a 552-event storm catalogue over New York State (2023 to 2025). The moisture contribution is isolated through paired ablations: identical architecture, training, and sampling, with the GNSS stream withheld. Station-level evidence already locates the signal: where radar and rain gauges have been dry for hours, GNSS-derived features raise ranking skill by up to 0.10 AUC and roughly double per-event detection at 2 to 3 h lead. We report the diffusion system's paired evaluation across New York State cases, foremost the 20 May 2026 New York City flash flood, where the newly deployed micronet recorded a pronounced vapour surge before the first echo. Applications span flash-flood early warning for emergency managers, forecaster guidance, and weather-critical operations across New York State, each gaining lead time in the minutes before radar sees rain. The method scales with the network it conditions on: GNSS at every NYSM site is the immediate extension, and the receivers already deployed across telecom and 5G infrastructure a denser one still.

491540.title: Convective Cold Pool Induced Turbulence and CO2 Transport within and Above the Amazon Forest Canopy: Insights from ATTO. (Invited Presentation)
491540.authors: Luca Mortarini, Università degli Studi di Milano, Milano, Milano, Italy; and M. Oliveira, O. C. Acevedo, D. D. V. Brondani, C. Q. Dias-Junior, V. Ferreira, and L. I. Reis
491540.abstract: Convective cold pools generated by deep moist convection produce abrupt changes in wind, temperature, and turbulence over the Amazon rainforest, yet their role in redistributing scalars within and above the forest canopy remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how convective cold pool passages modify turbulence and the vertical distribution of carbon dioxide (CO2) at the Amazon Tall Tower Observatory (ATTO) in central Amazonia. We analyze 410 cold-pool events identified between August 2021 and December 2023 using multilevel observations from the 81-m INSTANT tower and the 325-m ATTO tall tower, which together provide measurements spanning the forest canopy and the atmosphere up to 316 m above ground. Events are classified according to cold-pool intensity and background boundary-layer stability, allowing the dynamical effects of cold-pool passage to be examined in the context of the pronounced diurnal cycle of forest–atmosphere CO2 exchange. Cold-pool arrival produces a rapid and vertically coherent increase in CO2 concentration throughout the observed layer, generally developing within 10–20 min of gust-front passage. The CO2 enhancement is closely associated with the characteristic circulation at the cold-pool leading edge: convergence and upward motion are followed by strong post-frontal downdrafts, enhanced horizontal winds, and pronounced cooling. This overturning circulation redistributes CO2 rich air from the canopy and lower atmosphere through the boundary layer. Background stability strongly controls the magnitude of the CO2 response, with substantially larger enhancements under stable conditions, when respiratory CO2 accumulates within and above the canopy. Cold-pool intensity primarily modulates the strength, vertical extent, and persistence of the post-frontal response, with stronger events producing longer lasting CO2 enhancements. Vertically integrated CO2 anomalies confirm substantial changes in the CO2 content of the layer extending from the canopy to the upper levels of the ATTO tower. These observations show that convective cold pools provide an important intermittent mechanism linking deep convection, canopy-scale scalar accumulation, and boundary-layer transport over the Amazon forest. By rapidly reorganizing turbulence within and above the canopy, cold pools create short lived but intense forest–atmosphere exchanges.

491548.title: Sea Ice and Topographic Influences on Greenland Sea Polar Lows: Insights from three cases.
491548.authors: Maria Luisa Rocha, Brown University, Providence, RI; and A. H. Lynch
491548.abstract: Arctic maritime activity has grown by approximately 40% over the past decade as declining sea ice has made Arctic waters increasingly accessible. This increased activity exposes more vessels and coastal operations to weather hazards, and presents challenges for preparation and response. Polar lows are particularly consequential weather hazards because their rapid development, strong winds, heavy snowfall, and high waves can produce severe local conditions. Shipping activity is particularly sensitive to these hazardous conditions in the fishing grounds and community resupply routes of the Greenland Sea. To better understand development processes of these mesoscale phenomena, we simulate three polar lows using 9-km Polar WRF ensembles under conditions that perturb sea ice. We further seek to quantify the role of the Greenland ice sheet in focusing storm activity in the region by simulations that remove the topographic barrier. We evaluate storm intensity, surface heat fluxes, low-level baroclinicity, and vertical structure around the tracked storm centers. Comparisons with available observations show that control ensembles reproduce cyclone evolution reasonably well. Removing sea ice increased surface heat fluxes and lowered minimum pressure, but the response was variable in strength. Increasing sea ice weakened the storms consistently, raising minimum pressure and reducing maximum winds. The response was more pronounced when storms interacted with the marginal ice zone during early development. Removing Greenland’s topography prevented the coastal circulation from consolidating into a distinct mesoscale vortex in two cases. Across the cases examined, sea ice regulated polar low intensification, while Greenland’s topography influenced storm organization. These results suggest that assessments of the impacts of a changing climate on polar low incidence should focus on the development stage, as well as the proximity to the marginal ice zone, synoptic forcing, and coastal topography, rather than relying on sea ice extent alone.

491554.title: Marine Boundary-Layer Height from Wind Forecast Improvement Project 3 (WFIP3) Observations and Simulations
491554.authors: Adrien Tirouvanziam, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and N. Bodini and J. K. Lundquist
491554.abstract: The height of the planetary boundary layer (PBLH) defines the elevation separating the boundary layer from the free troposphere. PBLH is a key property in atmospheric science, governing pollutant dispersion, cloud formation, wind speed profiles, and generation of turbulence kinetic energy (TKE). It is also an important parameter in atmospheric models and applied models such as wind turbine wake models. PBLH can be measured using a variety of methods and instruments: thermodynamic methods like potential temperature gradient, modified parcel method, and Heffter method; turbulence methods checking for mean backscatter coefficients, backscatter ratio, and velocity variance; and alternative methods characterizing vapor and aerosol concentrations. While the boundary layer over land experiences a strong diurnal cycle due to the solar heating of the land, the boundary layer over water experiences more subtle diurnal variations. However, stronger seasonal variations have been observed in the marine environment, with a larger occurrence of unstably stratified boundary layers in autumn and winter. Compared to boundary layers over land, marine boundary layers are more rarely observed and therefore not as well understood. This analysis uses a unique offshore dataset to quantify seasonal and diurnal variability of PBLH, and compares results to several simulated datasets, including the NOW-WAKES dataset, ERA5 reanalysis, and the High Resolution Rapid Refresh Meteorology, Energy, and Transmission (HRRR MET) Toolkit to assess the ability of simulation tools to represent marine PBLH variability. The Third Wind Forecast Improvement Project (WFIP3) was a measurement campaign launched by the Department of Energy, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and several university and commercial partners from November 2023 to August 2025, characterizing the coastal and marine boundary layer near Massachusetts and Rhode Island. During the experiment, a 45-meter barge was moored at a site 46 km south of Martha’s Vineyard, Massachusetts, collecting data for 83 days between June and September 2024. The barge hosted a 25-meter observational tower with several sonic anemometers, profiling and scanning Doppler lidars, an infrared (IR) spectrometer, a ceilometer, and a W-band radar. We use observations from the barge to assess marine PBLH diurnal and seasonal variability, and its relationship with atmospheric stability, wind speed, wind direction, and cloud cover. As a first evaluation of the likely variability in marine PBLH at the barge location, we first interrogate the NOW-WAKES dataset, based on 2km x 2km WRF simulations from September 2019 to August 2020 (not concurrent with the barge deployment, but sampling a different year). These simulations show significant monthly variability, with a deeper winter boundary layer contrasting with a shallower summer boundary layer (Figure 1), consistent with prior analyses of the dataset. Average PBLH in November is 801 meters, compared to 182 meters in June.. September, the last month of the barge deployment, shows significantly deeper boundary layers than June-July-August. Additionally (not shown), preliminary analysis of the NOW-WAKES diurnal cycle from June-September shows an early morning peak in PBLH during June and July contrasting with a mid-day peak in August and September. These simulated patterns, as well as those from the ERA5 reanalysis and the HRRR MET Toolkit, will be compared to our analysis of the marine PBLH from the barge observations. Data from Doppler lidars will show mean backscatter coefficient, backscatter ratio, and velocity variance, while the IR spectrometer will measure PBLH using a variety of thermodynamic methods, and the ceilometer will show mixing layer height. Figure 1. Monthly PBLH distribution from the NOW-WAKES dataset based on WRF simulations from Sept 2019-Aug 2020. Horizontal bars represent minimum, 25th percentile, 50th percentile, 75th percentile, and maximum values from each month.

491555.title: Overcoming Systematic Biases In Soil Moisture: A Hybrid Machine Learning Approach for high-Resolution Regionalization
491555.authors: Patricia M. Lawston Parker, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD; and S. V. Kumar, T. M. Lahmers, and R. Anand
491555.abstract: Land surface model (LSM) states, particularly soil moisture (SM), often suffer from large systematic errors. While traditional parameter optimization reduces bias, it is computationally expensive and difficult to regionalize outside the calibration space. This study demonstrates a hybrid approach, combining traditional calibration and machine learning to optimize, regionalize, and downscale parameters for the NoahMP LSM. First, a genetic algorithm is used to calibrate soil and vegetation parameters against SMAP SM at 25-km resolution over the CONUS, Asia, and Europe. Next, a Random Forest algorithm is used to downscale and regionalize the optimized parameters to 1-km resolution over North and Central America. By utilizing ML to extend calibrated parameter information across space and scale, this hybrid approach offers a computationally efficient alternative to traditional, resource-intensive calibration methods for generating high-resolution parameter fields. Results show this hybrid approach successfully reduces average bias in top-layer SM in regions across the United States.

491560.title: assetra: Integrating Metrological Data into Resource Adequacy Modeling for the Power Sector
491560.authors: Martha Vierra, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI; and I. Bromley-Dulfano, S. Sundar, and M. Craig
491560.abstract: As electrification, the transition to low-carbon energy sources, and changes in weather patterns from climate change occur simultaneously, understanding the changing Resource Adequacy (RA) of the electricity grid is vital. RA analyses typically use historic weather data to simulate the availability of generators across a range of operating conditions. As climate projections are integrated into RA planning, researchers and practitioners need light-weight, flexible tools to incorporate large volumes of metrological data into their analytical frameworks. The ASSET Lab RA package (assetra) presents an easy-to-use and extensible Python package that offers a concise and intuitive interface for constructing representations of energy systems, running probabilistic simulations, and evaluating common RA metrics under a variety of meteorological data types. NetCDF, GRIB, Zarr and other metrological data that integrates with Xarray can all be used with assetra to model changing wind and solar capacity factors, temperature dependent forced outage rates, and storage dispatch. With these features, assetra offers researchers and practitioners a tool for maintaining system reliability while advancing decarbonization and climate adaptation. Our methodology reflects a tighter coupling between RA and meteorological modeling, and the need for tools that cater to interdisciplinary researchers.

491562.title: Ocean Dynamics Are Driving the GHG-Induced Strengthening of the Zonal SST Gradient across the Equatorial Pacific and Models Get It Wrong
491562.authors: Richard Seager, LDEO, Palisades, NY; and F. Jiang and M. A. Cane
491562.abstract: Tony Busalacchi has been at the center of research into the tropical oceans and their role in the global climate system for decades. He was a key figure in the development of the theoretical understanding of ENSO and the practical implementation of its prediction which is one of the major advances in the Earth sciences of the last century. But despite everything Tony did, there is still much we do not know about the tropical ocean-atmosphere system. Not least is how they respond to radiative forcing. It is now widely accepted that the observed long-term strengthening of the zonal SST gradient across the tropical Pacific cannot be captured by state-of-the-art models which, instead, predict the zonal contrast should weaken in response to rising greenhouse gases. Less widely acknowledged is that the discrepancy between observations and models is not just an SST phenomenon: instead, the disagreement is a zonal rearrangement of the entire tropical Pacific ocean-atmosphere system from the thermocline to the tropopause. We propose the following sequence of events. In the real world GHG heating warms least in the central equatorial Pacific where it is opposed by cold upwelling; the atmosphere responds with westerlies to the west and easterlies to the east; the westerlies shallow the thermocline while the easterlies reduce shear-driven vertical mixing; both results in shallowing and cooling of the thermocline; mean upwelling and active mixing bring the cooling into the mixed layer enhancing the zonal SST gradient. In models, by contrast, enhanced thermal stratification wins, reduces mixing and intensifies surface warming, the zonal SST gradient and Walker circulation weaken. In models the subsurface still cools but via reduced mixing and weakened subtropical cells and this remains isolated from the surface. The tropical Atlantic provides a test of this hypothesis. The absence of a strong mixing environment in the real world allows stratification to win and SSTs to warm with only weak dynamical opposition. However, models still get this wrong, but for reasons different to those in the Pacific. Sadly, or happily, after decades of work by Tony and others, there is still much to do in tropical oceanography keeping Tony’s former students, postdocs and colleagues busy for the foreseeable future.

491564.title: Controls on Arctic Maritime Cyclone Intensification.
491564.authors: Amanda H Lynch, Brown Univ., Providence, RI; and M. L. Rocha
491564.abstract: Arctic maritime cyclones threaten shipping, fisheries, coastal communities, and infrastructure through strong winds, high seas, icing, and storm surge. As sea ice retreats, it has been postulated that greater open water will strengthen these storms by increasing surface fluxes of heat and moisture. Using a new ERA5 climatology (1950–2024), neither cyclone frequency nor peak intensity shows a significant trend over the satellite era (1979-2024), though the fraction of warm-core and transitioning systems rises from roughly 40% to 53%. Here we analyze 138 intensifying cyclones occurring in the Greenland–Iceland–Norwegian, Barents, and Kara Seas, stratified by the sea-ice environment at genesis. A diabatic quasi-geostrophic omega-equation decomposition separates the ascent into upper-air forcing and diabatic contributions. While the diabatic share of forced ascent is larger over open water than over consolidated ice, the deepening rates do not differ significantly among sea-ice environments. Surface latent heat flux, open-water exposure, and marine cold-air-outbreak intensity carry no positive deepening signal. Rather, deepening is most strongly and independently associated with where and how sharply moisture is released within the storm rather than on the magnitude of surface input. The dominant control also evolves as the storm develops: upper-air forcing leads during initiation, and latent heating becomes the stronger independent influence as the cyclone matures. At the synoptic-to-meso-α scales that ERA5 resolves, sea ice thus shapes the life-cycle evolution of cyclone forcing but does not determine storm initiation and deepening. Whether continued Arctic warming and sea ice retreat will intensify hazardous storms likely depends on smaller-scale convective and mesoscale processes that require finer-resolution analysis.

491565.title: Use of Drift Echoes to Characterize Long-term Effects of Radiation Damage on GOES-16 MPS-HI Proton Fluxes
491565.authors: Juan V Rodriguez, University of Colorado, BOULDER, CO; and F. Inceoglu and B. Kress
491565.abstract: Proton fluxes of 10's-to-100's of keV energy observed by NOAA's solid-state radiation telescopes in low-earth orbit (LEO) and geostationary orbit (GEO) have been observed to decrease gradually with time. This common problem has been attributed to the growth of a dead layer within a few micrometers of the silicon detector surface that is caused by radiation damage by the protons being measured. As the dead layer grows, protons deposit less energy in the active part of the detector. Higher incident proton energies are thus required to satisfy the fixed channel logic based on energy deposition. As a result, the channel effective energy increases and the observed fluxes decrease over the long term. We have used the energy-dependent periodicities of proton and electron drift echoes to characterize changes in GOES-16 Magnetospheric Particle Sensor - High Energy (MPS-HI) channel energies over its mission duration (January 2017 - March 2025). This physics-based method was originally developed to cross-calibrate electron measurements from multiple Van Allen Probes instruments (O'Brien+, JGR, 120, 2076, 2015). We identified drift-echo candidates automatically by applying an iterative CLEAN (Inceoglu & Loto'aniu, Scientific Reports, 15, 36661, 2025) spectral algorithm to high-pass-filtered MPS-HI flux time series in fixed sliding windows, with the high-pass cutoff scaled to the expected drift period at geostationary orbit. Within each window, the dominant FFT peak was localized via a Hanning-window-aware sinc² fit, its sinusoidal component subtracted from the residual, and its significance assessed against AR(1) red-noise surrogates re-fit to the residual at each iteration. The application of this method to GOES-16 MPS-HI fluxes reveals that, while the electron channel energies were stable, the proton channel energies increased of order 100 keV over the mission duration. We discuss plans for using this information to correct the MPS-HI data, and we use the 8+ years of drift echo detections to study the behavior of drift echoes at all local times as a function of several magnetospheric and solar wind parameters.

491566.title: CRTM v3.2.0: Forward Operator Support for Next-Generation Sensors from the Sub-Millimeter to the Ultraviolet
491566.authors: Benjamin T. Johnson, UCAR, COLLEGE PARK, MD
491566.abstract: The Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM), developed by the Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA) and its partner agencies, is the fast forward operator used operationally in United States satellite data assimilation systems, computing top-of-atmosphere radiances and brightness temperatures together with the tangent-linear, adjoint, and Jacobian sensitivities that variational assimilation requires. This presentation describes the v3.2.0 release, which extends the model's spectral reach in both directions while completing coefficient support for the next generation of operational sensors. At the high-frequency end, a new lookup-table-driven physical reference ocean emissivity model, PARMIO, serves sub-millimeter sounders of the AWS and TROPICS class: microwave water channels at and above 200 GHz route to PARMIO automatically when its table is present, while every legacy sensor below 200 GHz remains bit-identical to v3.1.x on the FASTEM path. At the opposite end of the spectrum, ultraviolet sensors can now run through the forward operator for the first time: the surface optics dispatch gained a UV branch, OMPS coefficients were regenerated as per-platform NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 products, and a new scene-dependent NO2 transmittance component allows UV-VIS air quality spectrometers of the TEMPO and GEMS class to respond to a supplied NO2 profile, with full forward, tangent-linear, adjoint, and K-matrix support; a companion microwave ozone transmittance component was added as well. In between, the release adds or regenerates coefficients across the operational fleet: IASI-NG, MWS, and MetImage on Metop-SG-A1; the GeoXO imager; the GOES ABI infrared family, rebuilt with per-flight-model spectral response functions after a measured 1.67 K channel 16 bias was traced in the previously shipped GOES-19 product; the complete FY-3C through FY-3G microwave suite (MWHS-2, MWTS-2/3, MWRI, MWRI-2, MWRI-RM); AMSR3, whose three highest humidity channels had spectral response functions up to 2.72 times too wide against WMO OSCAR, a correction that reduces the 183 GHz water vapor Jacobian error from 9.5 to 0.3 percent; INSAT-3DS visible channels; and the new GEMS2-Amethyst 24-channel smallsat microwave sounder, validated to 0.04 K against line-by-line truth. Surface modeling advances include an opt-in TELSEM2 microwave land emissivity atlas, analytic microwave land surface Jacobians for all physical land state variables, and an experimental SNICAR visible snow reflectance table. The vector (polarimetric) radiative transfer path was substantially repaired: the surface is handed to the solver in the Stokes basis, the third and fourth Stokes components survive to the top of the atmosphere, clear-sky polarimetric runs are supported, and tangent-linear, adjoint, and K-matrix consistency is verified at four Stokes components. New level-resolved downwelling and upwelling radiance profile outputs are fully differentiated. Infrastructure changes include the transition to netCDF as the canonical coefficient format, a rebuilt ODPS transmittance group registry with load-time validation of coefficient files, and runtime OpenMP thread control with corrected single-profile threading behavior. We present the release scope, the coefficient change census against v3.1.4, validation evidence, and migration guidance for v3.1.x users.

491569.title: Drought Recurrence or Bust?: Examining the Compounding Effects of Tropical Cyclones and Droughts in the Carolinas
491569.authors: Kaitlin Karaffa, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and S. Larson, G. E. Tierney, and J. H. Bowden
491569.abstract: The Southeast United States (U.S.), including North and South Carolina (i.e., the Carolinas), is susceptible to two climate events at opposite ends of the hydrological spectrum, tropical cyclones and droughts. Tropical cyclones (TCs) account for approximately 4-10% of all rainfall during the TC season in the Southeast, and as much as 15% in the Carolinas. The TC season, spanning June through November, coincides with periods of increased drought activity during the summer and fall in this region. When considering interactions between these two events, most studies analyze tropical cyclones as drought busters or drought ameliorators. A drought bust occurs when a storm, in this case a TC, moves through an area and entirely removes drought from that area. Drought amelioration is a similar process in which the drought is weakened rather than entirely removed. Several studies have looked at drought busts and ameliorations by TCs in the Southeast U.S.; however, few studies have looked past the initial interaction to see if the drought returns after being removed or weakened. In this study, we analyze the interactions between droughts and TCs by considering drought recurrence, as well as drought busts and ameliorations. We define a drought recurrence as a drought event that is fully removed from an area by the passage of a TC, and that same area returns to drought conditions within 30 days of the storm passage. We use the HURDAT2 dataset to identify TCs that track through a bounding box of the river basins for the Carolinas, and identify 122 storms for the period 1980-2024. We use the Evaporative Demand Drought Index (EDDI) and the Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) to identify droughts before and after TC passage. Overall, we find that droughts are more likely to be busted by TCs in the Piedmont of the Carolinas compared to the Mountains or Coastal Plain, where drought recurrence is more common. The observed regional differences in drought busts, ameliorations, and recurrences may be caused by storm track location, strength of storm, or local factors, such as land use or soil type. By including drought recurrence into analysis of TC and drought interactions, this study provides a more complete view on droughts and TCs as compound hazards in the Carolinas.

491573.title: Identifying Cost Effective Structural Mitigation Actions under Five Future Climate Scenarios using the NC Flood Resiliency Blueprint
491573.authors: Alyssa L Griffin, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and C. H. Halbert and S. Brown
491573.abstract: North Carolinians often find themselves in the wake of flooding brought on by orographic precipitation, extratropical cyclones, and tropical cyclones. As a response to this need, the NC General Assembly tasked the North Carolina (NC) Department of Environmental Quality to develop the NC Flood Resiliency Blueprint (henceforward “Blueprint”). The Blueprint is an online decision support tool used to strengthen flood resilience planning and implementation in NC. This study utilizes the Blueprint to quantify the number of structures that are potentially susceptible to flooding during the 100-yr storm under five future climate scenarios across 51 counties in NC. The feasibility and cost of performing four precipitation mitigation actions (dryproofing, elevation, relocating, and acquiring) were assessed from factors including the structure's foundation type, heated square footage, and projected flood depth above the first floor of elevation. Cost-effectiveness ratios were used to deem what action was the most physically, economically, and socially plausible per impacted structure. Buildings that had at least one qualified mitigation action were quantified and counties with the greatest number of structures with applicable actions were identified for further analysis. Onslow and Nash counties are some of the most susceptible due to the different water features that are a part of them. Onslow County is along the seacoast and encompasses several inlets and straits that are vulnerable to both sea level rise and changes in extreme precipitation. 792 unique buildings qualify for at least one mitigation action across the different climate scenarios. Elevation is the most common measure under the two middle-of-century scenarios (low and high emissions). Relocation, however, is the most suitable under the three end-of-century scenarios (low, high, and severe emissions). The median cost-effectiveness ratio for elevation and relocation is between 1.0 - 1.50, demonstrating that performing these flood mitigation actions are slightly less costly than the potential damages that may occur during a 100-yr storm. The Tar River flows through Nash County along with many brooks and creeks that feed into it. These waterbodies may flood more in the future due to changes in rainfall frequency and magnitude. There are 173 unique structures that qualify for at least one mitigation action. Acquisition is the most common and has the highest cost-effectiveness ratios; the majority of these buildings are located along the Tar River and are projected to experience flood heights of eight feet or more. Less than 50 residential buildings qualify for elevation and relocation. These flood mitigation actions have median cost-effectiness ratios of 1.5-6.0, proving that floodproofing is less costly than potential damage costs. Overall, this work highlights some counties in NC that are most at risk to future flood events. By providing decision makers with adaptation mitigation recommendations at the structural level, communities in NC can increase their resilience to future flooding events more quickly.

491576.title: Observational Uncertainty is the Primary Source of Climate Uncertainty in Projections of Climate Damages
491576.authors: Kevin Schwarzwald, Columbia University, New York, NY; LDEO, Palisades, NY; and N. Lenssen, T. Bearpark, A. Bonanno, R. Horton, and G. Wagner
491576.abstract: Projections of future climate damages underpin risk management but depend on inherently uncertain climate data. These projections are affected by uncertainty in climate data through multiple pathways, only some of which are regularly accounted for. We investigate the importance of the choice of gridded historical data products used to fit impact models and bias-correct and downscale global climate models (GCMs) on the spread in projections of climate impacts. This decision is often either ad hoc in econometric or financial climate impact studies or made for reasons orthogonal to a given product's performance for metrics and regions of interest, despite known limitations of any particular gridded product and difficulties in product evaluation in regions most vulnerable to climate damages. We re-estimate three climate impact models from the statistical econometric literature, relating exposure to daily mean or max temperature to annual GDP per capita growth, mortality, and payroll, using four different reanalysis products as a proxy for the spread across different observational climate records commonly used in climate impacts studies. We then project damages for each dose-response function using a novel ensemble of near-global daily temperature projections, bias-corrected and downscaled to the same four reanalyses to estimate this “observational” uncertainty, and incorporating up to 86 runs from all available CMIP6-generation Large Ensembles of GCMs to estimate model uncertainty and internal variability, and publicly available in analysis-ready, cloud-optimized (ARCO) format. Armed with this Bias-Corrected and Downscaled Massive Ensemble (BCD-ME), the spread in projections of climate impacts can be partitioned into contributions from model uncertainty, internal variability, reanalysis uncertainty, and the statistical uncertainty from training impact models. We find that the choice of reanalysis contributes more to the spread in future projections of GDP per capita growth, mortality, and payroll than uncertainty within or across GCMs for most parts of the globe, particularly in the mid-latitudes. Addressing observational uncertainty through the use of multiple reanalyses more than triples the spread of climate uncertainty and raises our 95th-percentile damage estimate by up to 104%. Most of this increase comes from training impact models; even small differences in historical weather records can lead to substantially different estimates of climate–society relationships, and these differences are amplified when projected into the extreme temperatures that become increasingly common under climate change. Since in common practice this source of uncertainty is not considered, existing climate risk assessments likely underestimate uncertainty in future damages, possibly undercounting the possibility of plausible but extreme damages. We thus recommend that (1) users of climate data test the sensitivity of their results to the choice of historical data product and use products that have been evaluated for the metrics and regions of interest whenever possible, (2) developers of climate risk models consider how the choice of functional form may cause the range of out-of-sample impacts to be more or less constrained, especially given the reality that ‘perfect’ historical climate observations are unattainable, (3) auditors of climate risk information take care to note what observational data were used to produce damage estimates, and (4) the climate science community to increase research into constraining uncertainties about past estimates of the climate, especially given recent decreases in the density of available weather records in many parts of the world.

491577.title: Meteorology Education and Generative AI - When, Where, and Why?
491577.authors: Kevin H. Goebbert, University of Tampa, Tampa, FL; and T. M. Bals-Elsholz, K. A. Barber, C. A. Clark, and C. E. Phillips
