491577.abstract: Since November 2022 with the public launch of Chat GPT 3.5, large language models (generative AI) have rapidly evolved and become integrated into countless leisure and work activities; this AI use has grown exponentially. Collegiate education in meteorology has been greatly impacted by this disruptive technology in numerous ways, especially with regard to writing assignments and computer code. While there has been some level of conversation within the field on how to use it in our work, there has not been broad discussion of when and where generative AI should be used within meteorology education. This interactive poster is the beginning of that discussion where the authors look to gather insights from all attendees (and we do mean ALL attendees regardless of whether you are a student, faculty member, or professional) on when and where generative AI is currently utilized (or should be) with the goal of using the collected insights to inform the development of an interactive session at the Education Conference of the 108th AMS Annual meeting where our field can more fully wrestle with how and where this tool should impact meteorology education.

491579.title: The Fall 2024 Drought over the Northeast US and its impact on the New York City Water Supply System
491579.authors: Jason M. Cordeira, UCSD/Scripps Institution of Oceanography, Delmar, NY
491579.abstract: The Fall 2024 drought over the Northeast U.S. rapidly evolved during September–November and affected water supply availability within the New York City Water Supply System (NYCWSS). Beginning in August, an extended period of record-low rainfall led to reduced streamflow, declining reservoir storage, and an upstream advance of the Delaware River salt front. By mid-November, many locations across the Mid-Atlantic were in severe drought and New York City issued its first drought warning in 22 years. The drought coincided with the Rondout–West Branch Tunnel repair project, which reduced reservoir storage and conveyance capacity available for water supply operations. This overlap created major management challenges, including maintaining water supply reliability for New York City and surrounding communities while sustaining downstream releases to meet flow targets, support cold-water fisheries, and mitigate salt front intrusion in the Delaware River. The drought was associated with a persistent ridge of high pressure over eastern North America that suppressed storm track activity. Subseasonal variability, potentially linked to La Niña conditions and a convectively active Madden–Julian Oscillation, may have reinforced the dry pattern. Forecast guidance at seasonal, subseasonal, and 10-day lead times consistently portrayed wetter conditions than observed, producing false expectations for reservoir replenishment, underestimating drought severity, and contributing to a pause in the tunnel repair project. Drought relief arrived in late November with a cutoff low, followed by an early December atmospheric river, that increased streamflow, reversed the salt front intrusion, and partially alleviated drought conditions. This event highlights the importance of accurate precipitation prediction for water resource management in highly regulated systems.

491580.title: Impacts of Traffic-Driven Diurnal Emission Profiles on MUSICAv0-Simulated Aerosols over Metro Manila, Philippines
491580.authors: Shane Marie Aurelio Visaga, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and R. B. Pierce, R. Holz, W. Tang, L. K. Emmons, E. W. Eloranta, R. A. Ferrare, C. Hostetler, L. Ziemba, M. A. Shook, M. Cambaliza, and J. Simpas
491580.abstract: Global anthropogenic emission inventories provide broad spatial coverage but are limited to a coarse monthly temporal resolution which cannot represent the hourly variations in anthropogenic activities. This gap can bias air quality forecasts that rely on these input emissions. Existing diurnal profile estimates, when available, rely on generalized assumptions that remain largely untested in data-sparse regions. Here, we address Metro Manila, Philippines, a megacity lacking an hourly emission inventory, where diurnal variability can instead be inferred from ground-based records of local anthropogenic activity. We use the Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols (MUSICAv0), a variable-resolution global chemistry model refined to ~7 km over Metro Manila, Philippines, configured with specified oxidants and a simplified secondary organic aerosol (SOA) mechanism, for 24 August to 5 October 2019. Driven by monthly CAMS-GLOB-ANT emissions, the default MUSICAv0 simulation overestimates surface PM2.5 at night and into the early morning over an urban mixed background monitoring site, Manila Observatory, reaching a bias of 60 µg m-3 (~348%) at 06:00 local time (LT). Modeled nighttime planetary boundary layer height underestimates the ground-based High Spectral Resolution Lidar aerosol mixed layer height retrievals by up to 63 m (25%), explaining only part of the PM2.5 overestimate and pointing to the absence of diurnal profile in the emissions as the larger contributor. With vehicular sources dominant in the Philippine annual national emission inventory, traffic is expected to control the diurnal emission shape. We construct an hourly profile from 06:00 to 19:00 LT vehicle counts along Katipunan Avenue, Quezon City, Metro Manila extended overnight using Manila City traffic volumes from Madueño et al. (2019), in which traffic subsides after 19:00 LT to one-fifth of the daytime mean at 03:00 LT. Applying to CAMS-GLOB-ANT across Metro Manila grid cells, we examine whether this nighttime emission drop improves the early-morning PM2.5 concentration bias. The MUSICAv0 experiments are evaluated against hourly Beta Attenuation Monitor PM2.5 measurements over Manila Observatory, within 1 km of the daytime vehicle count site. To assess aerosol vertical distribution and speciation, we used the remote sensing and in-situ aircraft measurements from the NASA Cloud, Aerosol, and Monsoon Processes Philippine Experiment (CAMP2Ex) Metro Manila missed approach flight of 4 October 2019. We will present changes in simulated diurnal surface PM2.5 and speciated aerosol vertical distribution, with insights on the simple SOA mechanism behavior under resolved diurnal emissions. Results from this study aim to contribute to future air quality forecasting applications in the region.

491582.title: Analysis of the 24-26 January 2026 Winter Storm: Meteorological Drivers and Socioeconomic Impacts
491582.authors: Stacie H Hanes, NWS, Blacksburg, VA; NWSFO, Blacksburg, VA; and A. M. Sava and E. Taylor
491582.abstract: A potent wintertime storm brought life-threatening and widespread wintry hazards to much of the southern and eastern United States from January 24 through 26, 2026, resulting in significant snow, sleet, and freezing rain. The system's vast geographic footprint extended from northern Mexico to Canada, ultimately claiming 173 lives and prompting 24 gubernatorial state-of-emergency declarations, making it one of the deadliest North American winter storms of the 21st century. Within the National Weather Service (NWS) Blacksburg forecast area, heavy sleet served as the primary precipitation hazard, yielding historic accumulations of 5 to 20 cm (2 to 8 in) alongside localized snow and freezing rain. These accumulations, compounded by subsequent days of sub-freezing temperatures, resulted in tens of thousands of power outages, widespread structural and transit disruptions, and hundreds of traffic accidents. This study examines the thermodynamic profiles and atmospheric mechanisms driving this substantial sleet event, while focusing heavily on the execution of Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS) and risk communication during a complex, evolving winter hazard. We evaluate how the NWS Blacksburg operational forecast team leveraged advanced probabilistic guidance tools- including the National Blend of Models (NBM), the Dynamic Ensemble-based Scenarios for Incident Decision Support Services (DESI), and the Probabilistic Winter Storm Severity Index (WSSI-P)- to quantify forecast uncertainty and communicate potential impacts. Finally, we assess how the delivery of this actionable, probabilistic information to core partners, including school administrators, emergency managers, and municipal and state officials, influenced localized decision-making, optimized resource allocation, and shaped regional operational recovery efforts.

491583.title: Advancing Aerosol Data Assimilation in the NOAA Global Chemistry and Aerosol Forecast System (GCAFS)
491583.authors: Yaping Wang, SAIC @ NOAA/NWS/OMD, College Park, MD; and A. Kliewer, B. D. Baker II, and D. Holdaway
491583.abstract: The Global Chemistry and Aerosol Forecast System (GCAFS) is NOAA’s next-generation global aerosol prediction framework. GCAFSv1 employs the Finite-Volume Cubed-Sphere (FV3) dynamical core and Goddard Chemistry Aerosol Radiation and Transport (GOCART) aerosol module to generate high-resolution (~25 km) global forecasts. To constrain the aerosol components, the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI)-based Global Constituent Data Assimilation System (GCDAS) was developed to assimilate 550 nm Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instruments. The performance of GCDAS had been evaluated using nine-month (Dec 2023–Sept 2024) retrospective experiments. Compared to a free-running control experiment, GCDAS reduces the global total AOD background errors, maintaining a positive forecast impact throughout the entire 5-days period. However, diagnostics reveal localized errors: the model overestimates organic carbon during wildfire seasons in North and South America and degrades the sulfate forecast. This study investigates the underlying causes of these challenges and explores DA optimization strategies, including refining background error covariance and adaptive bias correction techniques, as well as integrating new observations from different platforms. The tuned system will be evaluated against independent reanalysis datasets and observations.

491585.title: Toward Global Storm-Scale Modeling: A Comparison Across High-Resolution Domains
491585.authors: Matt Oehler, University of Wisconsin Madison, Madison, WI; Univ. of Wisconsin, Madison, WI; and C. Evans and M. I. Oyola-Merced
491585.abstract: In January 2026, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) launched the "Moonshot" initiative, aiming to establish a global 3km convection-allowing model, built on the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS), as the next-generation operational and research model. While MPAS is widely used for regional and global variable-resolution applications and has seen some global demonstrations at storm-scale, how the global storm-scale simulations compare to regional storm-scale simulations that require lateral boundary conditions or global variable-resolution simulations that require cumulus parameterizations remains largely unknown. This study evaluates the impact of domain size and configuration on storm-scale forecast performance through the analysis of a weakly forced severe weather outbreak in the midwestern United States coinciding with a large influx of wildfire smoke from the southwest. Four MPAS forecast simulations were conducted and evaluated: 1) a global uniform 3.75km grid, 2) a global variable-resolution (15-to-3km over the contiguous United States) grid, 3) a regional 3-km domain over the contiguous United States, and 4) a regional 3-km domain over the contiguous United States incorporating aerosol feedback. Preliminary evaluations focus on simulated composite reflectivity, surface hail diameter, and upper-air dynamics across each configuration. Preliminary evaluations suggest that the cumulus parameterization present in the global varied resolution domain may be having a greater impact on the forecast than the regional vs global 3.75km forecasts. Additionally, the global variable resolution domain forecasted severe hail production at a significantly reduced rate compared to the other model runs. The shifts in convective cell placement and intensity in the global variable resolution domain may have had impact on the latent heating processes altering the forecasted jetstream intensity compared to the other domains.

491586.title: Forecasting ENSO up to 12-Months Ahead with Physics-Guided Deep Learning and Multi-Resolution SST Observations
491586.authors: Pratik Shukla, University Of Maryland Baltimore County, Halethorpe, MD; and M. Halem
491586.abstract: Skillful long-lead prediction of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) remains a major challenge because the coupled ocean–atmosphere processes that govern ENSO span a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. This work develops DUNE2, a physics-guided deep learning framework for predicting tropical Pacific sea-surface temperature (SST) variability and ENSO evolution up to 12 months in advance. Building on the original Deep UNet++ Ensemble (DUNE), DUNE2 integrates convolutional architectures to learn localized spatial features with State Space Models (SSMs) to efficiently model long-range temporal dependencies. This hybrid design is intended to capture both fine-scale spatial variability and the persistent, evolving ocean–atmosphere interactions that influence ENSO development over seasonal-to-annual timescales. A central objective of this study is to quantify the impact of SST observation spatial resolution on long-lead ENSO prediction. Experiments will compare SST products spanning substantially different resolutions, including ERA5 at 0.25°, NOAA Coral Reef Watch SST at approximately 0.05°, and JPL MUR SST products at approximately 0.01°. By training comparable forecasting models across these datasets, we systematically assess how SST spatial resolution influences ENSO prediction skill and whether finer-resolution observations better capture important oceanic features and evolving temperature anomalies that contribute to predictability at seasonal-to-annual lead times. The framework uses physically relevant atmospheric predictors, including near-surface winds (U10/V10), moisture flux, wind divergence, and surface heat fluxes, as well as static inputs (land–sea mask and orography). Physics-guided loss functions emphasize the Niño 1+2, Niño 3, Niño 3.4, and Niño 4 regions and place additional weight on anomalous ENSO conditions. Forecasts are evaluated using RMSE, ACC, Niño-region indices, and lead-dependent ENSO event skill, with particular attention to the spring predictability barrier. DUNE2 is benchmarked against persistence, climatology, conventional CNN-based architectures, and representative dynamical forecasting systems (e.g., CanCM3/4, CCSM3/4, GFDL-A06/B01). The study addresses both a modeling question and an observing-system question: how much can physics-guided deep learning improve year-ahead ENSO forecasts, and how much additional predictive value is gained from resolving SST at increasingly finer spatial scales?

491589.title: Identifying Urban Heat Island Circulations and their Influence on Downwind Air Pollutants
491589.authors: Jackson Fenner, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor , MI; and A. Raudzens Bailey
491589.abstract: The Urban Heat Island Circulation (UHIC) is a thermally driven overturning circulation at the city scale that occurs under favorable meteorological conditions. Through its influence on boundary layer growth and vertical mixing, the UHIC may influence urban air quality by diluting pollutants within the boundary layer. It may also export pollutants into the free troposphere, much like a thermally driven mountain venting process. To test this idea, we focus on four U.S. cities—Minneapolis, MN; Detroit, MI; Kansas City, MO; and Columbus, OH—and use CONUS404, an ERA5-constrained WRF meteorological data product, to diagnose days in which a UHIC develops. We require UHIC days to exhibit low-level convergence and upper-level divergence over the city center (144 km2), as well as a clear mixed layer, measured by potential temperature. To evaluate the impact of the UHIC circulation strength on pollution venting, we identify ozone profiles retrieved by Sentinel-5P TROPOMI downwind of each city center on July days during the TROPOMI record. We compare the lowest-level ozone concentrations to ozone concentrations in the lower free troposphere between UHIC and non-UHIC days. Across all four cities, we find that UHIC-days experience higher mixing heights than non-UHIC days. This confirms that UHICs support conditions favorable for pollutant dilution within the boundary layer. However, their venting potential remains unclear. While there is a slight tendency for ozone concentrations to decrease near the surface on UHIC days, lower free tropospheric concentrations are similar between UHIC and non-UHIC days. This ambiguity may be due to a timing mismatch between UHIC peak strength in the late afternoon and the TROPOMI overpass at approximately 1:30PM local, or to the chemical complexity of ozone. Ongoing analysis will examine TROPOMI NO2 as another tracer of pollutant venting by the UHIC.

491594.title: Cross-Seasonal Impacts of the Atlantic Niño on Arctic Winter Surface Air Temperature
491594.authors: Xin Hao, Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China
491594.abstract: The Arctic has warmed at more than twice the global mean rate, with winter anomalies over the Barents-Kara Seas (BKS) linked to remote tropical forcing. While El Niño Southern Oscillation is often emphasized, the role of the Atlantic Niño remains poorly understood. Using reanalysis data and CESM2 large-ensemble simulations, we show that summer Atlantic Niño sea surface temperature anomalies persist into autumn and induce cross-basin atmospheric circulation adjustments that extend their influence to the Arctic. These changes trigger wave activity that propagates into the stratosphere, where the signal is stored and released downward in winter, producing a negative NAO-like circulation. This response reinforces a dipole in Arctic surface air temperature, with cooling over the BKS and Eurasia and warming over Greenland and northeastern Canada. These results identify the Atlantic Niño as a predictable driver of Arctic variability, with implications for seasonal prediction.

491595.title: Improving Forecast Skill for Atmospheric Rivers and Hurricanes Through Targeted Observations
491595.authors: Palmer Gilliard, NCEP, Daytona Beach, FL
491595.abstract: IMPROVING FORECAST SKILL FOR ATMOSPHERIC RIVERS THROUGH TARGETED OBSERVATIONS Palmer Gilliard¹˒², Vijay Tallapragada², Xingren Wu², Keqin Wu², Murali Malasala² ¹ Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, Florida ² National Weather Service, NOAA, Riverdale Park, Maryland Targeted atmospheric observations are collected to improve forecasts by reducing uncertainty in the most meteorologically important parts of the flow, but their value depends strongly on atmospheric River (AR) structure, environmental regime, forecast lead time, and how well observations sample the evolving features that control downstream impacts. This study examines how targeted observations improve forecasts of ARs affecting the U.S. West Coast. The goal is to determine when, where, and why targeted observations provide the greatest forecast benefit and to translate those results into practical guidance for future observing strategies. For ARs, 42 AR Reconnaissance (AR Recon) intensive observation periods (IOPs) from the 2025-2026 season were classified using AR core structure, moisture environment, and integrated water vapor transport (IVT) characteristics. These mission classes were evaluated together with dropsonde deployment patterns, forecast sensitivity guidance, environmental structure, and precipitation-response metrics. The results show that the most forecast-relevant AR missions were concentrated in stronger, more coherent, and more moisture-connected regimes rather than weak compact cases. Forecast improvement was not controlled by sensitivity overlap alone. Instead, the strongest outcomes occurred when observations sampled a favorable combination of key AR core structures, elevated forecast sensitivity, and the larger-scale synoptic environment, including jet structure and interacting extratropical features. The analysis also showed a clear lead-time dependence in optimal observing strategy: upstream environmental sampling provided the greatest value for medium-range forecast improvement, while sampling landfalling AR structure and coastal conditions became more important at shorter lead times for improving hazard prediction along the U.S. West Coast. IMPROVING FORECAST SKILL FOR HURRICANES THROUGH TARGETED OBSERVATIONS Palmer Gilliard¹˒², Vijay Tallapragada², Zhan Zhang², Bin Liu², Yonghui Weng² ¹ Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, Florida ² National Weather Service, NOAA, Riverdale Park, Maryland Targeted atmospheric observations are collected to improve forecasts by reducing uncertainty in the most meteorologically important parts of the flow, but their value depends strongly on storm structure, environmental regime, forecast lead time, and where observations are placed relative to the evolving features that control downstream impacts. This study examines how targeted observations improve hurricane forecasts affecting vulnerable U.S. coastal communities. The goal is to determine when, where, and why targeted observations provide the greatest forecast benefit and to translate those results into practical guidance for future observing strategies. For hurricanes, reconnaissance impacts were evaluated across the 2025 storm set, including all four major hurricanes, with emphasis on storm-specific behavior across forecast lead times, life-cycle stages, and intensity classes rather than on seasonal averages alone. Results show that reconnaissance benefit was not uniform across cases, with the largest gains concentrated at selected medium and longer forecast lead times and especially pronounced for rapidly intensifying and major hurricanes. Storm-by-storm analysis demonstrated that some systems experienced clear simultaneous improvement in track and intensity, while others showed split responses or more limited value. A detailed case study of Hurricane Melissa showed that the strongest positive forecast response occurred during an active error-growth period, when the recon-enabled forecast remained much closer to the observed rapid-intensification pathway than the no-recon comparison. Taken together, these results show that improving forecast skill through targeted observations requires more than simply sampling storms more often. The greatest forecast value comes from sampling the right features, in the right environment, at the right time in the forecast cycle. This work provides an operationally relevant framework for prioritizing future reconnaissance observations to improve forecast skill, reduce hazard uncertainty, and strengthen decision support for high-impact tropical cyclone threats.

491596.title: Assessing Structural Differences in Multivariate Uncertainty between Ensemble Kalman Filters and Local Particle Filters
491596.authors: Maria Nikolaitchik, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD; and J. Poterjoy
491596.abstract: Ensemble data assimilation leverages a sample of model states to quantify uncertainty in dynamical systems during prediction and update steps. Linear filters, such as ensemble Kalman filters (EnKFs), rely on Gaussian approximations of error, which are suboptimal for most geophysical applications. Additionally, the development of data-driven emulators to replace physics-based models decreases computational load and supports larger ensemble sizes, potentially reducing sampling deficiency for data assimilation. Nonlinear filters, such as the local particle filter (LPF), have the potential to better leverage these large ensemble sizes and have previously been shown to be nearly as skillful as EnKFs for high-dimensional Gaussian applications, even with small ensemble sizes. For both nonlinear filters and data-driven emulators, a clear understanding of how each impacts the quantification of multivariate uncertainty during data assimilation remains unstudied. The present study utilizes Analysis Error Covariance Singular Vectors (AEC SVs) to quantify and compare the evolution of error covariances between an Ensemble Square Root Filter (EnSRF) and a LPF in a global application of the Unified Forecast System (UFS). The data assimilation application is constructed to reproduce forecasting challenges encountered when producing the 20th century reanalysis; states are conditioned on a sparse network of surface pressure observations assimilated at 6-h intervals. AEC SVs quantify the fastest growing perturbations within an optimization interval, with perturbations constrained by an initial analysis error covariance. In addition to providing an in-depth comparison of error covariances, AEC SVs preserve the multivariate relationships between model state variables. Furthermore, to examine the effects of data-driven emulators on ensemble covariance evolution, we compared estimates of AEC SVs between ensembles forecasted with the UFS and GraphCast using the same assimilation method. Preliminary results using AEC SVs suggest the LPF demonstrates comparable estimates of covariance structure to the EnSRF, despite not explicitly estimating the background covariance during updates. Additionally, AEC SVs suggest that the Relaxation to Perturbation Spread (RTPS) inflation scheme serves to dampen perturbation growth at the smallest scales, especially for model variables directly observed. Further research will examine the effects on utilizing GraphCast on the ensemble covariance evolution in a cycling system.

491597.title: Technology to Tackle Uncertainty: Developing a HAFS Ensemble for the Cloud with an Eye to an AI Future
491597.authors: Aaron J. Poyer, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; NOAA, Riverdale Park, MD; and J. Peng, Z. Zhang, W. Komaromi, F. Yang, V. S. Tallapragada, K. Garrett, J. King, R. Panda, U. Kurandumkara, M. Long, L. J. Gramer, S. Gopalakrishnan, X. Zhang, and G. J. Alaka Jr.
491597.abstract: Current National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Weather Service (NWS) operational tropical cyclone forecasting relies heavily on a combined suite of deterministic forecast models from multiple agencies across the world, including NWS flagship deterministic Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) model. These models collectively create a probabilistic forecast output from the NWS Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program (HFIP) Corrected Consensus Approach (HCCA). As a direct ensemble model approach, NWS relies on the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for uncertainty quantification in forecast scenarios, particularly for track. However, global ensembles fail to fully capture mesoscale details of the forecast due to insufficient horizontal resolution and their focus instead on capturing the large-scale flow pattern. As such, the development of a HAFS-based regional ensemble system that excels in predicting intensity, storm structure, and localized impacts has become a top priority. Over the past several years the NWS Office of Modeling & Development (formerly Environmental Modeling Center) has been developing an experimental HAFS based ensemble known as the Hurricane Ensemble Run on the Cloud (HERC). HERC was developed from funding provided from the Disaster Relief Supplemental Act (DRSA) as well as additional funds from the HFIP program and cloud computing from the NOAA Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) through commercial cloud providers. These allocations served as the primary near real-time testbed for HERC for both forecast performance and as a proof of concept for moving from on-prem computing to cloud computing for time critical forecast models and products. However, the high computational demands of fully physics-based high-resolution ensembles increasingly exceed available high-performance computing (HPC) allocations, creating critical latency bottlenecks for forecasters, emergency managers, and decision makers requiring actionable lead times. To overcome these constraints, the NWS is exploring a paradigm shift from traditional numerical models to physics-aware, hybrid Artificial Intelligence (AI) frameworks built and trained on high-resolution model reanalysis, in this case from HERC. The OMD and the Office of Atmospheric Research (OAR) Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory (AOML) Hurricane Research Division (HRD) along with the HFIP community are working together to create a high-resolution AI training set from a 2-km resolution HERC for potential development of a physics-aware AI-HERC model. This project employs a similar development philosophy to the Experimental AI Global and Limited-area Ensemble forecast system (Project EAGLE), which led to rapid deployment of the AI Global Ensemble Forecast System (AIGEFS) and the Hybrid Global Ensemble Forecast System (HGEFS), to produce robust probabilistic guidance in much less time and resource use than traditional deterministic and probabilistic physics-based models. By requiring less computational power, these types of hybrid frameworks alleviate HPC resource limits, while dramatically accelerating multi-model ensemble generation. The resulting hyper-efficient, storm structure-informed guidance directly supports forecast uncertainty and by extension Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS), drastically improving community risk awareness and meteorological resilience. Given the impacts and high risk nature of hurricanes, advancing skills and capabilities to forecast further in advance as well as to quantify probability of these risks is critical to reducing human and financial impacts.

491599.title: Enabling Accelerations In Science and Operations through AI Enabled Data Fusion
491599.authors: Kevin Johnson, Entarian, McLean, VA; and J. Arnold, Ph.D., K. Ryan, and R. Boyd
491599.abstract: A future view of Earth science data velocity appears to be uncapped. NASA and NOAA alone already account for enormous daily new data volumes (NISAR alone is over100 TB/day) that add onto a collective data store of over 200 Petabytes of historical data that is used by government, academia, and private industry for everything from new science, situational awareness, and even verifying your insurance claim after the last microburst left a tree on your car. The number and sizes of the repositories is vast, however, which results in far too much time spent searching for, accessing and normalizing these heterogeneous data streams. To address this challenge, we will display a cloud-agnostic data fusion prototype across both NASA and NOAA Earth science archives. It demonstrates the ability harmonize distributed environmental datasets regardless of their physical storage location. By integrating artificial intelligence into the data orchestration plane, the system intelligently optimizes query paths, automates metadata extraction, and accelerates data access layers for complex meteorological formats (e.g., NetCDF, GRIB2, and cloud-optimized Zarr). This presentation details the vision, architectural framework, and performance benefits of a recently developed prototype built in collaboration with government partners. Preliminary results demonstrate a significant reduction in data retrieval latency, enabling scientists to bypass traditional infrastructure hurdles and drastically accelerate operational workflows.

491600.title: Exploring 15+ Years of NASA GPM GV Disdrometer Data over the Globe
491600.authors: Charanjit Singh Pabla, Science and Technology Corporation, Hampton, VA; and D. B. Wolff and A. Tokay
491600.abstract: NASA’s Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Mission Ground Validation (GV) program has spent over a decade validating satellite-based precipitation and particle size distributions (PSDs) using ground-based disdrometers. These direct validation efforts are accompanied by physical validation efforts, where disdrometer-derived relationships between PSD parameters are incorporated into GPM precipitation retrieval algorithms. By measuring the size and fall speed of individual hydrometeors, these point instruments help scientists understand storm mechanics—such as distinguishing between convective and stratiform precipitation—and hydrometeor phase. Furthermore, when combined with ground-based weather radars, instantaneous disdrometer measurements help scale precise point data to match the larger spatial volumes captured by satellite footprints, allowing for the derivation of empirical relationships between various precipitation parameters. Understanding global precipitation variability is critical for remote sensing, satellite calibration and validation, and the parameterization of microphysical processes in numerical models. Since 2010, the GPM GV program has collected liquid and frozen PSDs from over 100 disdrometers across highly diverse environments, spanning mid- to high latitudes, tropical and oceanic regions, and complex terrain. Historically, accessing and processing these extensive datasets have been challenging, often requiring researchers to develop custom tools. To address this, the GPM GV program decided to collaborate with Disdrometer Database (DISDRODB; https://disdrodb.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) developers to import our extensive datasets into this unique open-source framework to streamline data processing, analysis and visualization. Using this framework, this study explores over 15 years of global in-situ disdrometer data, analyzing precipitation rates, PSD parameters (including mass-weighted mean diameter, normalized intercept parameter, and maximum diameter), and disdrometer-derived polarimetric radar variables.

491601.title: Urban Vulnerability to Extreme Hail: A Worst-Case Scenario for the 2024 Calgary Hailstorm
491601.authors: Madeleine Richer, Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory, Western University, Canada, London, ON, Canada; and J. Brimelow, G. A. Kopp, and T. Schmidt
491601.abstract: Insured losses from hail have been steadily increasing and, in 2023, hailstorms accounted for a majority of the $71 billion in losses from severe convective storms globally. Despite the substantial financial and infrastructural risks posed by hail, large-scale mitigation and adaptation measures remain limited. In Canada, the province of Alberta records the most hail days, with a national maximum in hail occurrence found along the Rocky Mountain foothills. Since 2010, eight major hail events have affected the Calgary area in Alberta, generating nearly 400,000 insurance claims and approximately $6.4 billion in losses. Two of Canada’s costliest natural disasters are hail events that have struck Calgary. The August 5th, 2024 storm was the costliest hailstorm in Canadian history, with insured losses that were significantly higher than reported for Canada’s first billion-dollar hail event in June 2020 that also hit Calgary. Large hail (>45 mm) observed during the 2024 event was accompanied by strong wind gusts of up to 65 km h-1, which increased the destructive power of the hail. Even though the storm only affected the far northern and northeastern portions of the city, the storm had a huge impact, with over 123,000 residential and auto claims resulting in insured losses of $2.81B. As the costs and risk of hail continue to increase, it is critical to continue taking mitigative measures. Where to invest the funds to do this depends on the risk and exposure. For instance, the insured losses due to the 2024 Calgary hailstorm could have been much worse had the storm followed a different track over the city. One of the goals of this study is to identify the assets most vulnerable to hail damage under a worst-case scenario for the 2024 Calgary hailstorm. The foundation of this investigation requires the construction of a building and vehicle inventory across the city. Without access to insurance data beyond the coarse Forward Sorting Area (FSA) level, asset vulnerability and exposure had to be determined through surveys and open access data. The residential building inventory for this study was derived from a LiDAR-generated 3D building map completed by the City of Calgary in 2020. Residential building wall and roof surface areas were extracted from the LiDAR data and aggregated for the 290 Census Tracts (CTs) across the city. To evaluate exposure to hail, particular attention was given to building envelope materials, as vinyl siding and asphalt roof shingles are known to perform poorly under severe hail conditions. Manual surveys were conducted in the summers of 2025 and 2026 to determine the spatial distributions of vinyl siding, asphalt shingles, and personal vehicle exposure. The vehicle inventory was calculated using expected exposed vehicles in residential areas and large parking lots using an expected maximum occupancy. The total vinyl siding, asphalt shingle, and personal vehicle exposure were estimated by CT and the costs per unit were then assigned to determine total expected asset exposure. Using the NSSL’s Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor System, a relationship was found between the Maximum Estimated Size of Hail (MESH) and insurance claims results for three of Calgary’s recent hail catastrophes observed on June 13th 2020, July 2nd 2021, and August 5th 2024. A sigmoid function was found to best describe the relationship between the median MESH values and percentages of claims at the FSA level, for both personal and auto claims, with R2 values of 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. This relationship was applied to the building inventory at the CT level and used to recreate losses for the August 2024 event. Loss estimates using the cost model showed a strong correlation (R2 > 0.90) for expected asset counts and losses for both personal and auto when aggregated to FSA levels and compared with the CatIQ losses. To investigate other plausible outcomes, the 2024 MESH track was transposed across the city in 20 orientations (avoiding overlap between MESH swaths). The loss model was then used to determine the insured losses to the affected residential buildings and personal vehicles. Findings from this analysis will be presented, with a focus on which areas of the city are most vulnerable to insured hail losses. This research has identified vulnerable hotspots across the city and provides critical insight for targeted mitigation strategies, risk-informed policy development, and long-term urban resilience planning. For example, following the 2020 hailstorm, a cost-benefit analysis of buildings with hail-resilient materials found that installing impact-resistant shingles on roofs yields a 3:1 cost-benefit ratio, rising to 8:1 in more hail-prone areas. Results from our research will aid the municipality of Calgary in identifying where to focus investments to achieve the best outcomes in mitigating future hail damage.

491604.title: Future Heat Wave Characteristics in Dynamically Downscaled Projections of Wet Bulb Globe Temperature
491604.authors: Kaitlin Karaffa, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and S. Larson, G. E. Tierney, and J. H. Bowden
491604.abstract: Extreme heat is the leading weather-related killer in the United States (U.S.), and is expected to occur more frequently and become more intense under a warming climate. Heat waves are a subset of extreme heat that can disproportionately impact vulnerable populations, including the elderly, children, and outdoor workers. Many previous studies and most NWS forecast offices define heat waves using heat index as an indicator. However, heat index may not be the most representative indicator of heat stress, as it only considers air temperature and humidity, and is measured in the shade. Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) is another metric of heat stress that is representative of the human body’s response to heat, but is not often used to measure heat wave events. WBGT is a weighted average of the natural wet-bulb temperature, black globe temperature, and surface air temperature. Wet bulb temperature simulates how the human body cools through perspiration, and black globe temperature measures how solar radiation impacts the skin. The incorporation of these two variables in WBGT makes it useful for characterizing how heat directly impacts humans and their health. We use the EPA Dynamically Downscaled Ensemble (EDDEv2) to calculate WBGT on hourly increments for both historical (1985-2014) and future (2040-2069; 2070-2099) periods. EDDEv2 provides atmospheric variables at a high temporal and spatial resolution for multiple Shared Socioeconomic Pathways across the continental U.S. and U.S. Virgin Islands. This dataset allows for the unique opportunity to study these heat waves using WBGT, because it provides highly variable components, such as wind speed and solar radiation, on an hourly basis. When calculating WBGT, it is important to use datasets with variables provided at a high temporal resolution, because variables like wind speed and solar radiation can fluctuate rapidly, which quickly changes the WBGT in that area. In this study, we define heat waves using WBGT as a metric for both the historical and future time periods, and compare these results with established extreme heat metrics, such as heat index and surface air temperature.

491610.title: Precipitation Network Densification Without a Maintenance Ceiling: A Vertically Pointing 61 GHz Radar Precipitation Sensor That Resolves Individual Hydrometeors
491610.authors: Mikko Krapu, Vaisala Oyj, Vantaa, 18, Finland; and R. Keranen, L. Wickramanayake, L. Kauppinen, K. Heyn, and S. M. Mackaro
491610.abstract: World Meteorological Organization minimum gauge density requirements for annual precipitation monitoring are met over only 13.4% of the global land surface, falling to 1.9% when long-record stations alone are considered, and a quarter of the global land area already requires urgent network expansion on the basis of precipitation variability alone (Su et al. 2026). Among the causes the authors identify is the cost of network construction and maintenance. Where gauges are present, wind-induced undercatch reduces rainfall estimates from modern tipping-bucket gauges by 5–46% depending on design, siting, and ambient conditions, and recorded amounts may fall below one-third of the actual amount when precipitation is frozen or the gauge is exposed (Dunn et al. 2025). Correction factors are routinely applied and demonstrably improve the data, but no single factor is widely accepted and different formulations yield significantly different rainfall estimates (Dunn et al. 2025). Correction also addresses undercatch rather than absence: a clogged funnel and a dry sky produce the same record, and no factor recovers an event that was never registered. Maintenance workload, as much as hardware cost, constrains how far a network can extend. This contribution presents a vertically pointing 61 GHz Doppler radar precipitation sensor (Vaisala PRECICAP RM60) that resolves individual hydrometeors, allowing precipitation properties to be derived from physically interpretable measurements of single particles rather than from empirical relationships applied to bulk returns. Near-field measurement at 61 GHz gives the sensitivity to detect and characterize individual particles down to light drizzle, while narrow-beam geometry confines the measurement volume to a small column directly above the sensor, eliminating the need for the shields, fences, and rain pits used to mitigate wind effects on catchment gauges. For each particle the sensor measures fall velocity from the Doppler shift and the backscattered echo power; particle size is then reconstructed from that power using the known size–terminal-velocity relationship of hydrometeors. From these the sensor derives precipitation intensity, accumulation, type, drop size distribution across 22 size classes, and reflectivity factor. The design has no collection surfaces, no moving parts, no optics, and no heating, draws 0.5–1.3 W, and requires neither cleaning nor scheduled maintenance. Continuous self-diagnostics flag anomalies rather than allowing degraded data to pass unmarked. Units have operated in the field since 2020, accumulating more than 700,000 sensor-hours across a range of climates and operating conditions. As one example, during Atlantic Storm Bert in November 2024, a unit on an unshielded coastal mast measured through sustained winds of 14 m/s and gusts above 23 m/s in close agreement with a collocated pit-mounted operational reference. Across pilot deployments the sensor has required no scheduled servicing or cleaning. Two further findings of the same global assessment indicate where such a capability is most valuable. The global station distribution is biased toward lower elevations, leaving high-altitude regions underrepresented despite the importance of orographic effects there — the headwater catchments that supply much of the world's surface freshwater. And while the indirect methods that provide spatial coverage, principally radar and satellite, deliver spatially continuous and high-frequency data, they carry systematic biases and estimation errors and cannot substitute for ground-level measurement, which remains essential for their validation; in Africa the scarcity of gauge data makes it impossible to evaluate the accuracy of satellite-based precipitation products at all. Sensors that can be sited in these gaps without a service commitment therefore contribute in two ways: as direct observation where none exists, and, deployed in numbers, as part of the surface reference on which radar- and satellite-based products depend — a reference that includes precipitation type and drop size distribution, not accumulation alone. The presentation closes by considering the implications for AI-based precipitation analysis and prediction, where surface reference quality and representativeness remain limiting factors.

491614.title: Characterization of a Hydration Spectrometer (HySpec) System for Studying Aerosol-Cloud Interactions
491614.authors: Ogochukwu Yvonne Enekwizu, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY; and E. Lewis and A. Sedlacek
491614.abstract: Aerosol-cloud interactions contribute the largest uncertainties to estimates of the Earth’s energy budget because of the poor quantification of fundamental microphysical and chemical processes. A key process is the formation of cloud residuals – aerosol particles that undergo cloud processing and are left behind after cloud drop evaporation. These aerosol particles reenter the atmosphere with different microphysical, chemical, and optical properties than the cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) that formed the cloud drop and thus interact with incoming solar radiation or influence clouds differently. The measurement of cloud residuals is, however, challenging and often limited to either aircraft campaigns or mountain site stations that employ a counterflow virtual impactor (CVI) to separate the generally larger cloud residuals from smaller aerosol particles based on their inertia. Here, we integrate a pumped CVI (PCVI), developed for laboratory applications, with a modified CCN counter to isolate and sample cloud residuals in a controlled laboratory setting. Dry aerosol particles introduced to the CCN-PCVI, which we refer to as a Hydration Spectrometer system, are first exposed to supersaturation conditions in the CCN counter that will cause some particles to activate. The resulting population of cloud droplets and non-activated particles are immediately drawn into the PCVI, where a particle-free flow of gas directed opposite the particle-laden flow provides a controllable means of separating the non-activated aerosol particles while allowing cloud droplets to be transmitted. Cloud droplets exiting the PCVI are dried prior to subsequent analysis, forming residuals, and their microphysical and optical properties are quantified. We report the efficacy and performance of the Hydration Spectrometer system for different particle types and sizes over a range of flow and supersaturation conditions.

491615.title: Valuing Extreme Temperature and Hurricane Mitigation: An Economic Assessment of the NOAA NEON Microwave Sounder
491615.authors: Joseph Conran, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and R. Chittilla, M. Grasso, P. Kelly, J. Wielgus, and T. Wodajo
491615.abstract: The NOAA Chief Economist Team alongside the Office of Low Earth Observations (LEO) developed a study with Aerospace and TBD Economics to support the justification of the upcoming Near-Earth Orbit Network (NEON) program and its foundational payload, the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA). As legacy polar weather satellites retire, the loss of critical orbital coverage threatens to create a major data gap for global forecasting models. To prevent this forecast degradation, the NEON program will deploy a disaggregated, multi-satellite architecture. By placing satellites across complementary orbital planes, the SMBA measures atmospheric temperature and moisture profiles directly through dense cloud cover. Weather model simulations confirm this configuration significantly reduces forecast errors, particularly in tracking two-day tropical atmospheric steering flows. To measure the economic and societal impacts of these forecast improvements, this study uses a Value of Information framework that evaluates and quantifies these socioeconomic benefits from 2027 to 2045. Traditional economic assessments often overstate the value of a satellite by improperly attributing the cumulative benefits of the broader forecasting enterprise to a single asset. To address this limitation , our model isolates the marginal value specifically generated by the SMBA payload, focusing on three highly vulnerable domains: extreme temperature events, electric power grid operations, and hurricane damage mitigation. We evaluate the net economic benefits through a three-part framework. First, we define the baseline economic exposure subject to weather hazards in these target domains. Second, we measure the forecast sensitivity, which translates improved forecast accuracy into direct dollar savings. Finally, we apply a real-world response factor that adjusts for the physical and operational limits preventing emergency managers, local authorities, and utility dispatchers from acting instantly or perfectly. By grounding theoretical forecast gains in realistic operational constraints, this model provides a transparent assessment of how next-generation satellite data protects society and key economic sectors.

491616.title: Constructing Severe Convective Storm Event Sets using GCM and Reanalysis-Derived Environments Using Machine Learning
491616.authors: Victor A. Gensini, Northern Illinois Univ., DeKalb, IL; and W. S. Ashley, A. Haberlie, and L. R. Bundy
491616.abstract: Robust characterization of severe convective storm (SCS) risk under present and future climates requires a large and physically consistent event set that adequately sample the tails of environmental distributions. Traditional approaches using SCS reports are limited by the relatively short observational record and/or the computational expense of convection-allowing simulations. This work introduces a scalable framework for generating large event sets of SCS-favorable environments using bias-corrected output from the Community Earth System Model (CESM). We train machine learning models on reanalysis-derived environmental fields with target outputs defined by practically perfect hindcasts of severe weather occurrence. This approach enables the identification of environmental patterns most strongly associated with observed severe convective hazards. The trained models are then applied to bias-corrected CESM simulations to diagnose SCS-relevant environments across a substantially larger sample space than is available from reanalysis alone. To further enhance sampling of extreme, but plausible, environments, stochastic techniques are employed to perturb and augment the CESM-derived event set, preserving key multivariate dependencies while expanding representation of low-probability, high-impact scenarios. The resulting dataset provides a physically grounded and computationally efficient means of generating large ensembles of severe storm environments suitable for risk assessment, catastrophe modeling, and climate change attribution studies.

491618.title: Improving Prediction of Highbush Blueberry Bud Break, Bloom, and Harvest Timing Using Optimized Chilling and Heat Accumulation Models
491618.authors: James Shope, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ; and P. Oudemans, D. A. Robinson, and R. Muldowney
491618.abstract: Blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum L.) phenology influences production decisions such as pesticide applications, when to use bees for pollination, or deploying labor. Often, predictive phenological models solely utilize calendar dates or heat accumulation, which may be less accurate with variable weather. We present seasonal prediction models of peak truss bud stage (T3), bloom onset, and harvest start in the 'Duke' highbush blueberry cultivar that incorporate both chilling and forcing. Using 22 years of phenological observations and hourly meteorological observations from Hammonton, New Jersey, we trained multivariate predictive models incorporating chilling units and growing degree day interactions. A systematic grid-search hyperparameter optimization was used to identify chilling and forcing integration windows for predicting each crop development stage, and model generalizability and predictive skill were assessed using leave-one-out cross-validation. Models using a single variable had limited predictive accuracy, whereas multiple linear models incorporating chilling and growing degree days showed improved performance. The best combined models predicted T3 with cross-validated R2 values exceeding 0.85 approximately 20 days in advance and bloom onset with cross-validated R2 values exceeding 0.75 approximately 30 days in advance. These timings coincided with the end of dormancy and the preceding weeks before bud break or bloom. Harvest predictive accuracy was lower, with cross-validated R2 values between 0.57 and 0.60 at 20 days in advance. The resultant models improve the prediction of phenology for blueberry production management, and this work provides a transferable workflow to refine local, cultivar-specific prediction models in other regions through optimization and the incorporation of chilling units.

491619.title: Scale-Dependent Coupled Boundary Layer Energetics: New Metrics for km-Scale Model Evaluation and Parameterization
491619.authors: Momme C. Hell, WHOI, Woods Hole, RI; and B. Fox-Kemper and A. Ayouche
491619.abstract: Kilometer-scale coupled climate models are beginning to resolve processes that fundamentally alter how energy is exchanged between the ocean and atmosphere—but we currently lack diagnostic frameworks to evaluate whether these models capture the right physics for the right reasons. Here, we present a structure-function-based analysis of scale-dependent kinetic energy budgets in the coupled boundary layer and apply it to km-scale COAS simulations of the California Current System. We identify two coexisting routes of cross-interface energy transfer: (1) synoptic-scale atmospheric events drive mesoscale wind-work on the ocean and forward cascades to smaller scales in both fluids; (2) ocean submesoscale instabilities generate inverse (upscale) energy cascades and induce their own wind- and pressure-work responses. These competing up- and downscale cascades coexist in both fluids' Boundary layers but are overlooked in bulk flux formulations based on homogeneous similarity theory. Comparison with airborne Doppler scatterometer observations from the S-MODE field campaign validates the scale-dependent variability seen in the model and demonstrates that remote sensing can constrain these cross-scale energy transfers. This framework provides process-based metrics for evaluating km-scale coupled models—particularly the scale at which energy exchange transitions from synoptic-forced to submesoscale-driven regimes—and offers a path toward scale-aware, stochastic air-sea flux parameterizations for use in coarser-resolution climate models. We discuss implications for high-resolution model hierarchy design and how resolving coupled boundary-layer turbulence changes estimates of near-surface energy budgets relevant to climate sensitivity.

491622.title: Analytic Formulation of Turbulent Aerosol-Cloud-Precipitation Interactions: Drizzle Initiation and Droplet Growth in the Presence of Ordinary and Giant Cloud Condensation Nuclei
491622.authors: Robert McGraw, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY; and Y. Liu and V. P. Ghate
491622.abstract: An analytic formulation of drizzle initiation theory that considers the combined effects of turbulence and aerosols has been lacking. We address this gap by extending previous studies on droplet growth using a Brownian drift-diffusion model for condensation in turbulent clouds alongside the kinetic potential (KP) of nucleation theory. This framework is adapted to describe drizzle initiation and subsequent droplet growth. By incorporating Köhler activation of water-soluble aerosols, we provide an integrated description of how ordinary cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), particles having dry radii < 0.5 , and giant CCN (GCCN) impact drizzling and non-drizzling clouds. Water-soluble GCCN in the 0.5 - 3 radius range are shown to significantly lower the KP barrier required for drizzle initiation. Near the high end of this range (circa 2 radius for marine clouds) the barrier vanishes and drizzle occurs spontaneously. The extended model yields predictions for drizzle formation and seasonal dependence consistent with observations. This framework provides a theoretical foundation for understanding how turbulence impacts aerosol-cloud-precipitation interactions and the effectiveness of cloud seeding.

491624.title: Photometric and Pointing Calibration of CCOR-1 and CCOR-2 Observations
491624.authors: Karl Battams, NRL, Washington, DC; and A. Gutarra-Leon, N. Kuroda, A. Thernisien, and G. Dima
491624.abstract: We present details of the photometric and astrometric calibrations for the CCOR-1 and CCOR-2 coronagraphs. Through the application of aperture photometry to stars observed in instrument data from launch to the present, we have developed a photometric database of several million data points. This database can be used to conduct a number of crucial calibration and characterization tasks for the instrument. Primarily, we have determined the global photometric calibration factors to convert digital values to the community-standard physical units of mean solar brightness. Secondarily, analysis of variability in the light curves of individual stars enables exploration of the sub-pixel properties of the detectors, including pixel-edge and pixel-corner effects that can induce substantial variations in derived photometry. Finally, iterative algorithms enable us to derive high-precision World Coordinate System (WCS) pointing-correction parameters on an image-by-image basis. The parameters include roll and absolute-pointing corrections, as well as corrections related to the optical distortion and optical axis of the instrument. With these model parameters, together with our improved understanding of sub-pixel detector response, we achieve post-fit stellar positional residuals of approximately 0.16 px RMS in CCOR-1, while application of these techniques to SWFO/CCOR-2 data is still ongoing.

491631.title: The Connective Tissue: Constructing a Guidebook for Earth Science Communities of Practice.
491631.authors: Aimee Neeley, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and D. Fritz and M. Beig
491631.abstract: Developing long-lasting communities of practice (CoPs) centered on intricate datasets requires bringing together specialized data user groups to collaborate on challenges and solutions. Within the Earth Sciences ecosystem, these CoPs facilitate vital knowledge exchange, enabling participants to stay abreast of technological and scientific progress. Because a comprehensive framework for establishing durable groups does not currently exist, our primary objective is to design a foundational "guidebook" for building resilient CoPs. To accomplish this, we hosted a collaborative session at the Earth Science Information Partners (ESIP) meeting, gathering valuable insights from both virtual and in-person participants via a digital whiteboard. These shared experiences form the basis of a web-hosted guidebook intended to bridge institutional and geographical gaps between researchers and data users. To ensure the resource remains dynamic and responsive to new ideas, the text is hosted in a community-editable repository where all contributors receive formal credit. This presentation outlines the guidebook's structure, highlighting its real-world case studies designed to guide the initiation or optimization of CoPs. Key chapters focus on foundational steps such as defining and engaging a community, establishing robust governance frameworks, and evaluating the long-term effectiveness of the CoP's core mission.

491633.title: Variations in Drop Size and Drop Size Distribution Across the Rural-Urban-Coastal Gradient during the Warm Season of the CoURAGE Field Experiment
491633.authors: Kaitlyn Anne Potucek, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and K. Lombardo
491633.abstract: Land-surface heterogeneities, such as the rural-urban-coastal transition in the Mid-Atlantic, impact the development and intensification of regional convective storms. Difference in local environments (rural, urban, marine) can also impact precipitation properties and processes in convective storms. Therefore, we investigate the impact of the local environment (rural, urban, marine) on convective storm precipitation properties. During the Coastal-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE), precipitation properties were measured within the Baltimore urban environment, the rural mid-Atlantic environment east of Baltimore, and the Chesapeake Bay marine environment west of the city from December 2024 – November 2025. Utilizing laser disdrometer measurements from the CoURAGE dataset at Mt. Airy (S2; rural), Baltimore city (M1; urban), and Kent Island (S3; marine), we evaluate differences in drop size distribution in various storm modes and environments. Warm season convective rainfall events (when rainfall is ≥ 10 mm hr-1) are identified at CoURAGE sites (S2, M1, and S3) and classified as one of four warm season storm modes: 1. single-cell, 2. cluster, 3. mesoscale convective system (MCS), and 4. non-linear. From these groups, the number density of drops, binned by diameter, from each convective rainfall event are grouped by location only (3 groups), storm mode only (4 groups), and location plus storm mode (12 groups). The objectives of this study are to 1. Identify variations in drop size distribution properties across warm season storm modes, 2. Identify variations in drop size distribution properties in rural, urban/coastal, and marine environments among common convective modes, and 3. Assess potential environmental conditions associated with differences in precipitation properties. Preliminary findings show that median drop sizes are generally larger at the marine site (S3) than at the rural (S2) or urban (M1) sites. Of the two onshore sites, M1 exhibits the smallest median drop sizes for single-cell and cluster storm modes. We observed greater differences across sites for single-cell storms than other modes, perhaps due to weaker storm-scale forcing. Considering only the MCS storm mode, the median drop size is largest at the urban site, M1, rather than at the marine site, S3, where it is largest for all other storm modes. However, there is more substantial variation in the precipitation distribution among MCS events at M1 than among MCS events at S2 and S3. MCSs are largely dynamically driven, and perhaps the nearby coastal boundary along the Chesapeake Bay increases convergence and thus drives a stronger updraft within MCSs, augmenting rain drop size. These results will be investigated further and linked to potential processes contributing to variations in precipitation properties.

491634.title: An Update on the Evolution of the 2026-27 El Nino
491634.authors: Michelle L. L'Heureux, NOAA/Climate Prediction Center, College Park, MD
491634.abstract: The predictability provided by El Niño may only be exceeded by its newsworthiness. Here, we examine the evolution of an already remarkable El Niño, which began to emerge as a possibility in mid-2026 with the NOAA Climate Prediction Center (CPC)’s El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) team’s December 2025 update. Despite La Niña being present at the beginning of 2026, an El Niño Watch was issued in March and was shortly followed by an El Niño Advisory in June. We will assess several oceanic and atmospheric diagnostics that CPC uses to monitor and forecast ENSO, including the new Relative Oceanic Niño Index. We will also evaluate the recent forecasts and their multi-model consolidations, which have suggested a potentially historic El Niño event in 2026-27. Finally, we will summarize potential impacts on global temperature and precipitation anomalies that were observed through December 2026.

491636.title: R2O - Evaluating Zonal Wind and Temperature Performance in the USF Reanalysis Scout (ScoutV2) Relative to ERA5
491636.authors: Sherrie Mae Fredrick, CIRES, Louisville, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; Univ. of Colorado CIRES, Boulder, CO; and A. Schneider, G. P. Compo, J. M. Souza, H. H. Wei, L. J. Spencer, and P. Pegion
491636.abstract: High-quality, multi-decadal reanalysis datasets are essential for establishing consistent initial conditions for retrospective forecasting, benchmarking model performance, and training next-generation AI applications. This study evaluated the global performance of the UFS Reanalysis Scout (ScoutV2) relative to ECMWF Reanalysis V5(ERA5) for the years 1997 and 1998. Daily zonal wind (U) and temperature (T) fields were evaluated across three vertical levels(250,500, and 850 hpa) using grid-area weighted global mean bias and anomaly root-mean-square error(RMSE). Spatial pattern agreement was quantified using Pearson anomaly pattern correlations(r) and spatial variance (R²). These reanalysis-to-reanalysis comparisons are supplemented with direct comparisons to the assimilated conventional and satellite observations. Daily zonal wind fields showed strong spatial agreement globally (r > 0.95, R² ≈ 0.85–0.95), peaking at 250 hpa (r ≈ 0.97–0.98). These high zonal wind correlations across levels align with recent global reanalysis evaluations (Wu et al., 2024). Temperature biases display distinct vertical stratification: 250 hpa exhibits near-zero bias (≈ ±0.2 K), 500 hpa shows a persistent warm bias (+0.2 to +0.6 K), and 850 hpa displays a consistent cold bias (-0.2 to -0.6 K). Temperature anomaly RMSE increases toward the surface (0.8–1.3 K at 250/500 hpa vs. 1.5–2.0 K at 850 hpa). Extratropical temperature pattern correlations routinely exceed 0.90 (R² > 0.81), whereas tropical performance degrades (r ≈ 0.50–0.85), particularly at 250 hpa during the 1997/98 El Niño–La Niña transition. SCOUTV2 demonstrates high overall spatial fidelity and interannual stability across strong climate anomalies, though tropical temperature skill and lower-tropospheric biases remain key targets for UFS reanalysis production runs.

491637.title: Cyclonic Rossby Wave Break Event’s Impact on Labrador Sea Convection in Winter 2009-2010
491637.authors: Jackson Samuel Quinn, University of South Alabama, Mobile, AL; and M. Gervais and K. A. Bowley
491637.abstract: Deep convection in the Labrador Sea helps drive the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Given the current and projected slowdown of the AMOC, understanding the mechanisms that affect the strength of deep convection is crucial to understanding future climate change. The winter of 2009–2010 was characterized by an extraordinarily negative NAO phase, which has been linked to a decrease in deep convection in the Labrador Sea. Cyclonic wave break events have been linked with the negative phase of the NAO. This study examines atmosphere-ocean interactions during the winter of 2009-2010 through the lens of synoptic forcing. We identify a series of cyclonic wave break (CWB) events in the winter of 2009-2010 that impact the Labrador Sea region. We find that these events can impact the Labrador Sea deep convection through surface heat fluxes and Ekman pumping. CWBs are often associated with a decrease in surface heat flux, owing to an increase in warmer moist air over the Labrador Sea linked with the warm sector. Furthermore, the formation of surface cyclones acts to increase Ekman pumping–driven upwelling and reduce the mixed layer depth. We conclude that the seasonal decrease in deep convection in the Labrador Sea is due in part to the aggregated effects of these synoptic scale systems.

491638.title: Latent Under-Canopy Inundation Delineation (LUCID): Remote Sensing-Derived Basin Flood Mapping
491638.abstract: Tree canopy routinely obscures detection of flood water in traditional remote sensing-derived flood inundation mapping (FIM), leaving the true extent unknown and fracturing flood detections into a ‘patchwork quilt’ of isolated flood signatures separated by riparian forest cover. National Water Center (NWC) Operations has developed a novel, sensor-agnostic, hydrologically connected and land-cover informed approach to gap-filling remote sensing-derived flood signatures, producing a contiguous flood extent. These improved flood extents are used operationally to assist in validating modeled FIM from the National Water Model (NWM) as well as creating a catalog of analog flood extents from historical observations to characterize impacts for future flood events. LUCID Basin is a Python-based pipeline that converts observed flood pixels into seeds that can be grown under canopy using a least-cost surface built from USGS National Land Cover Dataset Tree Canopy Cover, slope, distance to streams, and height above nearest drainage (HAND) as cost parameters. Comparison of LUCID extents against NWM FIM derived from Analysis and Assimilation forcings and Categorical HAND flood categories at RFC forecast gages shows strong agreement, except where NWM FIM is constrained by catchment boundaries inherent to its HAND-based methodology. Because LUCID operates without pre-determined catchment boundary constraints it operates over larger areas. This makes it far less susceptible to this catchment-boundary limitation, giving a fuller picture of flood extent for comparison. This approach to mitigating a well known remote sensing liability in FIM enables NWC Operations and partners to understand how well NWM FIM will perform before the flooding occurs. Operationally, LUCID extents are archived into an ArcGIS Online feature service storing remote sensing origin provenance and hydrologic conditions of the flood itself. In several instances, these historical flood observations have been used to evaluate NWM FIM ahead of the forecast flood wave which served to increase confidence in NWM FIM extents as well as understand areas where NWM FIM may not be representative. LUCID is not limited to historical imagery, however, as it can produce flood extents within four hours of a Sentinel-1 acquisition, which is fast enough to inform decisions during an active event. Looking forward, development is focused on generalizing LUCID Basin’s flood classification engine to be sensor-agnostic, allowing the same under-canopy growing methodology to ingest flood seed pixels from multiple SAR and optical sources rather than a single platform. Additional work refining the vector pipeline and attribute schema to better support automated, event-driven activation, and expanding the historical analog library to strengthen the tool’s use in describing plausible impacts ahead of forecast events is planned. Together, these efforts aim to mature LUCID from a validation and research tool into a resilient, multi-sensor operational capability within NWC’s remote sensing portfolio. This presentation will detail both LUCID's theory of operations demonstrating how observed flood pixels are utilized as seeds to infer contiguous under-canopy inundation and showcase its application across varying scales. Through case studies ranging from annual flooding in the Ohio River Valley to extreme events like Hurricane Harvey, we will highlight comparative analyses against NWM FIM outputs to demonstrate the tool’s operational value.

491640.title: How Can the MJO and Convectively Coupled Kelvin Waves Both Propagate by Kelvin Wave Dynamics and Move at Different Speeds?
491640.authors: Paul E. Roundy, Univ. at Albany, Albany, NY
491640.abstract: Recent results demonstrate that the MJO upper tropospheric wind signal in the equatorial plane emerges mostly from Kelvin waves interacting with the mean flow, and that this is the dominant mechanism governing propagation of MJO convection. The slow phase speed of the MJO emerges from upper tropospheric Kelvin waves advected westward by easterly background wind over the Indian Ocean. However, convectively coupled Kelvin waves are also dominated by Kelvin wave dynamics, but they often propagate faster than the MJO through the MJO convective envelope. It is unclear how these two types of disturbances could move at different speeds through the same environment, driven by dynamics that yield non dispersive signal. Analysis of ERA5 data shows that the dominant heights wherein these disturbances demonstrate Kelvin wave structures are different, with the MJO's Kelvin wave dynamics centered in the upper troposphere and the synoptic waves dominated by the lower troposphere, where they are subject to weaker background flow than the MJO's Kelvin wave, allowing them to move more rapidly eastward.

491641.title: The Evolution Of Space Weather Forecasting in the UK
491641.authors: Krista Hammond, UKMO, Exeter, Devon, United Kingdom; and S. Machin
491641.abstract: The Met Office Space Weather Operations Centre (MOSWOC) is a UK national capability, that provides operational support and information for government, industry, defence and the public. Now in its 12th year of full operations, the capability has continually expended to meet user requirements in a constantly evolving world. In this presentation we will give an overview of the current state of forecasting in the UK, including the ongoing improvement of our current forecasts, models and procedures, and our efforts to integrate new forecasting models and monitoring tools into our operations. Finally, we look to the future and our plans to further develop our capabilities, including where AI and machine learning has a place, our intentions to grow and enhance the network of ground, atmospheric and space-based sensors, how this can help with data assimilation in our current and future models. This session will emphasise the importance of strong collaboration both within the UK and internationally to help enhance the global response to severe space weather.

491647.title: Advancing Operational Satellite Fire Detection with the Next Generation Fire System
491647.authors: Jason A. Otkin, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and M. Pavolonis, J. Sieglaff, S. Batzli, B. Bellon, C. Calvert, L. Cronce, T. Jasmin, D. Parker, R. B. Pierce, C. Schmidt, and F. Wang
491647.abstract: The Next Generation Fire System (NGFS) is a sensor-agnostic framework designed to generate analysis-ready active fire information from observations acquired by geostationary and low Earth orbiting satellites. The NGFS is scheduled to become NOAA’s operational fire detection system for GOES in 2026, with operational implementation for additional sensors planned thereafter. This artificial intelligence method uses an event-based data model, several static and dynamic ancillary datasets, and measurements from visible, shortwave infrared, midwave infrared, and longwave infrared spectral bands to automatically detect, characterize, and track fires in a manner consistent with expert interpretation of satellite imagery. The use of robust detection metrics and atmospheric correction procedures makes the resulting fire detection and fire radiative power products highly resilient to clouds and smoke. This presentation will describe recent efforts to enhance the sensitivity, utility, and operational readiness of the NGFS. Particular emphasis will be placed on discussing results from event-based comparisons of detections produced by the NGFS and the current GOES operational Fire Detection and Characterization algorithm. These analyses show that the NGFS (1) detects approximately twice as many fire features while producing substantially fewer false detections, (2) is much more sensitive to weaker thermal signals, (3) identifies new fires 15-20 minutes earlier on average, and (4) captures substantially more fire radiative power throughout a fire event because of its enhanced sensitivity and more continuous detection of thermal signals across a wide range of environmental and viewing conditions. Recent enhancements to the detection methodology and the development of higher order products will also be discussed.

491649.title: Training Deterministic and Probabilistic Kilometer-scale Numerical Weather Prediction Models over North America and Europe.
491649.authors: Montgomery L. Flora, NSSL, Norman, OK; and T. M. Hamill and P. Neilley
491649.abstract: Although global AI numerical weather prediction (NWP) models have achieved significant milestones, they predominantly rely on ECMWF Reanalysis version 5 (ERA5) data, which is too coarse in both spatial and temporal resolution to capture kilometer-scale evolution. While kilometer-scale efforts are emerging, most focus on downscaling global predictions rather than directly learning to emulate those scales. The primary bottleneck for direct emulation is the data requirement: grid spacing of ≤ 4 km and sub-hourly timesteps. These are the bare minimum requirements to begin partially resolving complex 3D deep moist convection, orographic flow, and cold-pool evolution and outflow boundaries (Weisman et al. 1997). To address these data limitations, TWC has developed a global reforecast dataset using our in-house Global Hi-Resolution Atmospheric Forecast System (GRAF), which uses an MPAS dynamics core with mesh refinements to 4 km over the US and Europe. We are also collaborating with MITRE to leverage their recently developed 2-year reforecast dataset from the 1-km Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model over the contiguous US (known as Weather 1K). The GRAF and MITRE datasets have 15-min and 10-min timesteps, respectively. Our initial efforts focus on deterministic forecasting. Given the success and computational efficiency of the Diffusion transformer (DiT) architecture (as in NVIDIA’s Atlas, StormScope, and STRATA models), we’ve adopted a deterministic variant. For the attention mechanism, we leverage 2D neighborhood attention (NATTEN; Hassani et al. 2023).
