Our prognostic variables include U, V, potential temperature, and water vapor mixing ratio at 17 model levels up to 16 km AGL, as well as surface variables such as 2-m temperature, composite reflectivity, and 15-min precipitation rate. Our goal is to extend the surface variables to include instantaneous precipitation rate, 2-m dew point, 10-m u and v components, precipitation type, and winter precipitation fields, such as total snowfall and snow depth. The model is trained using tile-based sampling from CONUS and Europe. Our results will evaluate how faithfully our deterministic emulators match physics-based forecasts out to 18 h, including subjective comparisons, storm-object-based verification, and other objective verification statistics. If time permits, we will highlight our early efforts towards probabilistic emulation with CRPS-based and diffusion-based training. Weisman, M. L., Skamarock, W. C., & Klemp, J. B. (1997). 491651.title: Pathway to Operations: Achievements and Lessons Learned from the WoFS Demonstration Project
491651.authors: Sikchya Upadhayay, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and Y. Jung, K. Garrett, A. Rabassa, C. M. Gravelle, J. Huang, K. S. SPEROW, P. C. Burke, P. Heinselman, A. J. Clark, L. J. Wicker, J. Martin, K. H. Knopfmeier, B. C. Matilla, N. Yussouf, and M. Silcott
491651.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) has been demonstrating the Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS) capability, developed by the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL), to enhance warning and pre-warning decision-support, since October 2024. The WoFS is an end-to-end, on-demand system with one or more relocatable regional ensemble forecast domains running on a cloud-computing platform. Its domain covers a 900x900 km2 footprint at 3-km grid spacing, generating probabilistic forecast guidance at 5-minute intervals for timelines spanning up to 3 to 6 hours, renewed every 30 minutes. The system is optimized to support a spectrum of severe convective weather hazards. Since the NWS WoFS Demonstration Project began, WoFS ran for 174 days, comprising 234 total domains through 12 July 2026. The system has generated guidance across a wide spectrum of high-impact events. Operational feedback from NWS Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) indicates a transformative impact on localized Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS). For example, post-event evaluations across multiple significant tornado events in Oklahoma demonstrated that WoFS enabled forecasters to message significant tornado potential in specific counties nearly two hours in advance, compared to a traditional warning lead time of 23.7 minutes. This extended decision window can enable local emergency managers to proactively staff Emergency Operations Centers (EOCs) prior to convective initiation, activate community warning sirens earlier, and pre-position public emergency shelters in advance of severe weather. Beginning in 2026, the protocol for WoFS was expanded to support Department of Homeland Security designated Special Event Assessment Rating (SEAR) events, including the Super Bowl and high-profile 2026 FIFA World Cup matches, President of the United States (POTUS) events, and Search and Recovery missions. This presentation outlines the recent updates on operational status and key milestones achieved during the NWS WoFS Demonstration Project. Finally, we share critical lessons learned that are guiding the programmatic pathway to formal operations, demonstrating how WoFS fundamentally optimizes community preparedness, communication of uncertainty, and public safety.

491653.title: Satellite Near UV Aerosol Observations over North America from GEO, LEO, and L1 orbital configurations.
491653.authors: Omar Torres, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD; and C. Ahn and H. Jethva
491653.abstract: Multi-satellite observations of aerosol optical depth (AOD) and single scattering albedo (SSA) over North America will be discussed. Retrieval results from the NASA near-UV aerosol algorithm applied to the IntelSat40-TEMPO, DSCOVR-EPIC, and S5P-TROPOMI sensors observations from distinct orbital configurations (GEO, L1, and LEO respectively) over the area of regard of the TEMPO sensor will be inter-compared. The aerosol inversion algorithm uses Oxygen-B band observations at 680 and 688 nm to derive an effective aerosol layer height (ALH) to characterize the aerosol load vertical distribution as a single layer. The derived ALH information is then fed to a two-channel (354 and 388 nm) inversion algorithm to retrieve near-UV AOD and SSA. The inter-consistency of the multi-platform aerosol product, and their accuracy in relation to independent ground-based AERONET observations will be examined.

491657.title: NESDIS Antennas as a Service (NAaaS) - Transforming NESDIS Antenna Ground Enterprise Architecture
491657.authors: Kenneth I Watts, NOAA, Neavitt, MD
491657.abstract: Title: NESDIS Antennas as a Service (NAaaS) - Transforming NESDIS Antenna Ground Enterprise Architecture Authors: Toni Lord, Ken Watts, John Gosnell, Nicolaie Todirita, Ron Smilek Conference: 107th American Meteorological Society (AMS) Annual Meeting Session: 23rd Symposium on Operational Environmental Satellite Systems AMS Session: Next Generation Satellite Ground Architecture and Technological Advances Topic Keywords: antenna, commercial services, enterprise, multi-mission, digital ground The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) operates and manages the critical ground architecture for the nation’s operational environmental satellites. NESDIS Antennas as a Service (NAaaS) represents an enterprise-wide shift from legacy, stovepiped satellite tracking networks to an integrated, flexible, and highly cost-efficient common ground architecture. The NESDI Antennas-as-a-Service (NAaaS) program aims to transform legacy ground antenna infrastructure into a modernized, multi-mission architecture. Operating across a multi-mission, multi-orbit paradigm, NAaaS leverages cloud-native architectures, standard network-centric protocols, digital ground capabilities (e.g., Digital IF and Software-Defined Radios), and commercial Ground Segment as a Service (GSaaS) integration. Primary Objectives of the NAaaS Program Consolidation & Asset Reusability: consolidating single-mission antennas into shared, reusable assets supporting LEO, GEO, and SWO simultaneously Cost Efficiency & Optimization: reducing operations and maintenance costs through elimination of redundant systems and maximized infrastructure utilization Commercial GSaaS Integration: integrating commercial Ground Segment-as-a-Service (GSaaS) capabilities to provide scalable telemetry, tracking, command, and data downlink services . Modernization & Digital Ground Transition: modernizing ground systems via software-defined radios, tri-band antennas, phased arrays, and cloud-based mission management platforms . Enhanced Cybersecurity: strengthening cybersecurity through FISMA High zero-trust frameworks, FIPS 140-3 encryption standards, and automated threat monitoring. This comprehensive approach enables cost-effective, flexible, and secure ground segment operations across diverse mission portfolios. This briefing will provide an update on current NAaaS projects, support to the NESDIS LEO, GEO and Space Weather Office flight programs, ongoing transformational objectives, special studies, and the utilization of commercially provided capabilities to augment NAaaS Services.

491659.title: Integration of Satellite-FRP-Constrained Wildfire Emissions in Air Quality Forecast
491659.authors: Abu Ubayeda Ibnal Zarrah, Washington State University, Pullman, WA; and J. Meng
491659.abstract: Wildfire emissions remain a major source of uncertainty in regional air quality forecasting, because operational fire emissions rely on simplified assumptions regarding fuel load, heat release, and temporal variability. This study presents an improved Fire Radiative Power (FRP)-based wildfire emissions framework implemented in the new AIRPACT-6 forecasting system, which produces hourly PM2.5 and O3 forecasts at 4-km spatial resolution across the Pacific Northwest. The framework estimates wildfire emissions from satellite fire detections using literature-constrained fuel consumption, top-down heat flux, and an empirically derived diurnal profile from multi-year satellite FRP observations. Sensitivity simulations were conducted for the 2025 and 2026 wildfire seasons and evaluated against EPA AQS observations. We found the revised FRP formulation improves the spatio-temporal distribution of fire emissions over the previous BlueSky-based emission framework while preserving physically consistent plume rise calculations, resulting in up to a 50% improvement in PM2.5 correlation. In addition, the empirically derived temporal profile further enhanced hourly PM2.5 correlations and better captured smoke transport during major wildfire episodes. Ozone forecasts remained comparable to the current operational system, suggesting the necessity of improved smoke chemistry for future improvements. These results demonstrate the value of physically constrained FRP-based wildfire emissions for regional air quality forecasting and establish a baseline for future integration of advanced chemical mechanisms and satellite data assimilation within AIRPACT.

491661.title: The Different Types and Modes of International Research Collaboration under the GEWEX Umbrella: Showcasing the Regional Hydroclimate Projects
491661.authors: Petrus (Peter) J. van Oevelen, COLA, Broomfield, CO
491661.abstract: The Global Energy and Water Exchanges (GEWEX) core project of the World Climate Research Programme (WCRP) has been established in the late 80's and hence represents well over 3 decades of international research collaboration support. Much has changed over this time yet the Regional Hydroclimate Projects (RHPs) formerly Continental Scale Experiments (CSEs) have continued to be successful in establishing an large international regional network of scientists and their activities to support the water, weather and climate enterprise. In this overview I present the various styles of collaboration, timelines, support mechanism and types of success that were a direct result of these regional projects and what has changed over the years. As such these projects can provide useful examples of how to collaborate and what the various trade offs are.

491662.title: Onset of the Rainy Season Sub-Seasonal Forecasts Tailored to Agricultural Users In Southern Mexico
491662.authors: Alan Andres García-López, Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, Palisades, NY; Columbia University, New York, NY; and J. L. Garcia Franco
491662.abstract: The first rains of the annual cycle in southern Mexico are crucial for crop planting and a range of agricultural decisions during the early rainy season. Forecasts of this rainfall characteristic are not yet operational, but subseasonal forecasts of rainfall onset show sufficient skill at lead times of up to 30 days. From the users’ perspective, there is an identified need for this climate information within the Local Technical Agroclimatic Committees (LTACs), which are forums where the standard practice is to disseminate seasonal forecasts only. This work presents an academia-to-practice pipeline in which subseasonal forecast data are tailored to the needs of the LTACs through a co-production process. We present and evaluate different forecast products designed to communicate information about onset date shifts and rainfall intensity using deterministic and probabilistic categories at the local scale, while balancing technical capabilities with users’ needs. The products are based on ECMWF S2S reforecasts and are verified against multiple observational rainfall datasets, including CHIRPS and MSWEP, as well as data from local stations. We also discuss best practices for data visualization in the context of the LTACs, considering the quantitative skill of each format and providing guidelines for incorporating verification results into forecast communication.

491664.title: Assessing the Impact of Assimilating WSR-88D Derived Planetary Boundary Layer Height for Convection Initiation Forecast Using MPAS
491664.authors: Ayoola Olumide Abe, Howard Univ., Washington, DC; and N. N. Karle, S. Chiao, and Z. Yang
491664.abstract: Accurate predictions of the location and timing of convection initiation (CI) remain an emerging topic in convection-permitting numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. A relatively small error in the pre-convective planetary boundary layer (PBL) can greatly alter low-level moisture, instability, convective inhibition, mesoscale convergence, the location of focused ascent, and subsequently the CI. Many necessary processes for CI are rooted in PBL, which NWP is eager to represent accurately. This study examines a dryline cold-front severe convective event that occurred across the southern Great Plains on 16-17 May 2017. During which convection developed near the intersection of the dryline and an advancing cold front. The Model for Prediction Across Scales - Atmosphere (MPAS-A) was used with approximately 3-km horizontal grid spacing. The ensemble consists of 20 members, and observations are assimilated using the local gain-form ensemble transform Kalman filter (LGETKF) implemented within the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework. To improve ensemble forecasts of the PBL structure and subsequent CI forecasts, we utilized the differential reflectivity data from the national network of WSR-88D radars to estimate the observed daytime planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) to better describe PBL structures. To evaluate the influence of each observation type of data on CI, conventional, WSR-88D PBLH, and Multi Radar/Multi Sensor (MRMS) reflectivity observations are assimilated separately over a 3-h period and a 15-minute cycling window, and the resulting ensemble analyses and forecasts are compared with available observations. Preliminary results show that PBLH assimilation modifies boundary-layer depth and the vertical distribution of low-level temperature and moisture, reducing errors associated with excessively deep mixing in portions of the pre-convective environment. The analysis increments are spatially heterogeneous, with distinct responses in the dry and moist air masses on opposite sides of the dryline. Compared to the experiment without PBLH assimilation, the PBLH experiment strengthens low-level thermodynamic gradients along the dryline, improves the representation of the pre-convective environment, and produces CI timing and placement more consistent with radar observations.

491666.title: Oceanic Variability and Seasonal Precipitation Forecasts of Opportunity in East Africa
491666.authors: Andrew J. Hoell, NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and R. M. Robinson and M. L. Breeden
491666.abstract: We diagnose forecasts of opportunity related to oceanic variability, and those that failed, for East Africa (7.5°S–7.5°N and 32.5°E–50°E) precipitation since 1993 during the region's two principal wet seasons, October–December and March–May, using a 100-member multi-model ensemble of dynamical forecasts initialized one month prior. Precipitation predictability shows a notable asymmetry between the two wet seasons, with October–December considerably more predictable than March–May owing to the differing effects of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). October–December produced 13 forecasts of opportunity (a forecast of the upper or lower tercile exceeding a 50% chance), of which 10 proved correct (observed precipitation fell into the predicted tercile). All of these forecasts of opportunity occurred during forecast ENSO or IOD events, or both. When the two modes of ocean variability acted in tandem, they substantially increased the chances of above- and below-average precipitation relative to either mode acting alone. El Niño paired with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole produced highly confident above-average precipitation forecasts, while La Niña paired with a negative Indian Ocean Dipole produced highly confident below-average precipitation forecasts. March–May, by contrast, yielded just four forecasts of opportunity, of which only two verified. These occurred during forecast El Niño and La Niña events. The scarcity of forecasts of opportunity in this season reflects the fact that ENSO is typically transitioning between phases during March–May, leaving forecasts uncertain even several months in advance. We also examine failed forecasts of opportunity, defined as confident above- or below-average precipitation forecasts in which observed precipitation did not fall into the predicted tercile, to better understand the mechanisms behind such outcomes. In both wet seasons, the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) played a key role in disrupting the forecast effect of oceanic variability on East Africa precipitation. When observed precipitation was above average despite a below-average forecast, the MJO drove exceptional rainfall over a few weeks that reversed the seasonal outcome. When observed precipitation was below average despite an above-average forecast, the MJO suppressed rainfall over several weeks during the wettest parts of the season. Notable failed forecasts of opportunity include October–December 2022 and March–May 2023. We conclude with a retrospective of the October–December 2026 precipitation season, examining how the strong El Niño drove high forecast confidence in above-average precipitation, how observed precipitation compared to that forecast, and whether factors such as the MJO contributed to a failed forecast of opportunity. These results offer early warning systems a framework for identifying not only when confident seasonal forecasts are likely to verify, but also the subseasonal conditions under which they are more likely to fail.

491669.title: A Hybrid Physics-Machine Learning Model for High-Resolution Operational Snow Depth Mapping
491669.authors: Jeremy M Johnston, University of New Hampshire, DURHAM, NH; and M. Moradi, C. Pan, and J. M. Jacobs
491669.abstract: The spatial distribution of snow properties at fine spatial scales (< 100 m) influences wintertime mobility for recreation, logging, military operations, and more. However, ground-based observations and physics-based models often lack the spatial resolution needed to represent snowpack variability at these scales. In this work, we developed and evaluated an operation-ready hybrid fine-scale snow depth modeling framework. Unlike previous studies, which rely on site-specific models, we train a single ML model to predict local redistribution factors using nearly 100 UAS-derived snow depth fields collected across several unique sites and winter seasons. The framework combines a coarse-resolution physical model (ERA5-Land, 9 km), which represents the evolving regional snow state, with a machine learning model trained on repeated meter-scale UAS snow depth observations to learn transferable fine-scale snow redistribution patterns and produce daily 10 m snow depth estimates. Model performance is evaluated using statistical and computational metrics across three distinct 1,000 km² regions in New Hampshire, USA. Evaluation regions include (1) southeastern ephemeral snowpacks (<0.5 m in depth), (2) north-central mixed-forest foothills of the White Mountains (0.5 – 1 m), and (3) the northern White Mountains and Mt. Washington region (high snow depth variability, wind drifts exceeding 10 m). Model transferability is assessed using independent in-situ observations and lidar surveys during time periods withheld from model training. This work establishes a transferable hybrid modeling framework for integrating detailed snow observations with operational physical models, providing a scalable pathway toward daily high-resolution snow mapping. As new observations become available, the framework can be iteratively updated to improve predictive skill, expand to previously unseen environments, and be integrated with other physical models to support next-generation operational snow monitoring and forecasting.

491671.title: The Evolution of Cloud Liquid Water Profiles under Different Precipitation and Sub-Cloud Dynamical Conditions
491671.authors: Emina Hafiz, McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada; and J. Kim, A. Battaglia, M. D. Lebsock, and P. Kollias
491671.abstract: The vertical distribution of cloud liquid water influences cloud radiative properties, precipitation formation, and cloud evolution. Although liquid water path is routinely measured, vertically resolved observations of cloud liquid water content (LWC) remain difficult, particularly in precipitating warm clouds where cloud and drizzle droplets coexist. Quantifying how LWC profiles vary with precipitation intensity and sub-cloud-layer dynamics can improve our understanding of warm-rain development. This study uses collocated Ka-, W-, and G-band radar observations collected during the Cloud And Precipitation Experiment at kennaook (CAPE-k) as part of the second Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Mobile Facility (AMF2) deployment from April 2024 through September 2025. LWC profiles are retrieved from differential hydrometeor absorption between the three radar frequencies, while differential scattering is used to estimate drizzle properties. Clouds are classified as non-precipitating, lightly precipitating, or moderately precipitating using radar reflectivity immediately below cloud base, and Doppler lidar observations are used to distinguish sub-cloud-layer updraft and downdraft conditions. The presentation will describe the triple-frequency retrieval methodology from Doppler spectra and present the first statistical characterization of LWC profiles as a function of precipitation intensity and sub-cloud-layer dynamics. The results will illustrate how cloud liquid water is redistributed as precipitation develops under different dynamical conditions and demonstrate the value of combining triple-frequency radar and Doppler lidar observations to study warm-cloud microphysical processes.

491679.title: A Modernized Development and Implementation Lifecycle for NWS Modeling
491679.authors: Jacob R. Carley, EMC, College Park, MD
491679.abstract: Together the Environmental Modeling Center, the Meteorological Development Laboratory, and NWS Central Operations are responsible for developing, maintaining, and implementing the majority of the complex suite of analysis and prediction systems that form much of the foundation of our nation's weather forecasts. However, the increasing complexity of these systems, coupled with a growing reliance on community-developed scientific software, has exposed the limitations of our traditional development and implementation methods. Our current "waterfall" approach, characterized by infrequent, high-stakes "big bang" implementations, is becoming unsustainable. We propose a fundamental modernization of our development-to-operations lifecycle, inspired by the proven principles of DevOps and Agile methodologies. Our vision is to transition from our current high-risk, multi-year release schedule to a predictable and sustainable rhythm of smaller, more frequent upgrades. This will be achieved by restructuring our processes, investing in modern tools, and fostering a culture of collaboration and continuous improvement. The end result will be faster delivery of improvements to our models, more predictable update cycles, and reduced transition friction. In this talk we will present the basic premise for this endeavor and review our status in the early stages of this transition effort.

491680.title: Exploring Glacier Boundary Layers (Invited Presentation)
491680.authors: Ivana Stiperski, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria; and M. Haugeneder, S. Mosso, R. Mott-Grünewald, L. Nicholson, R. Prinz, T. Sauter, L. Schlagbauer, M. Schroeder, and J. E. Sicart
491680.abstract: Mountainous regions cover 20% of the Earth’s land surface and house 20% of the Earth’s population. Still, our understanding of mountain boundary layers and their turbulence structure remain incomplete, which translates to the lag in the development of theoretical foundations that can be used to model turbulence in these regions. A particularly challenging sub-group of mountain boundary layers are the glacier boundary layers that develop over alpine glaciers in summer. Characterised by their strongly stable stratification, shallow nature, persistent katabatic flows, and their setting the within the larger mountain boundary layers, the glacier boundary layers integrate the very local surface processes with non-local topographic influences, as well as larger-scale mountain boundary layer processes such as valley winds or downslope windstorms. How these larger-scale influences are communicated down to the surface remains an open question. Here we explore the principial findings from several major recent measurement campaigns focusing on the understanding of glacier boundary layers within the larger mountain boundary layers. We cover both boundary layers developing over alpine glaciers from the HEFEX II and III campaigns that took place on the Hintereisferner glacier, Austria, set within the larger TEAMx campaign, and turbulence measurements on ice-cliffs on Kilimanjaro, Tanzania. The focus is on surface-atmosphere exchange, processing governing it, and similarity scaling, as well as spatial variability of turbulence statistics, and the vertical coupling of the flow between the glacier surface and the overlying atmosphere.

491681.title: Impact of Assimilating the GOES-16 ABI Surface-Sensitive Channel Observations on the Prediction of the Second Rapid Intensification of Hurricane Ida (2021)
491681.authors: Seoyoun Jo, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
491681.abstract: Predicting hurricane development, particularly rapid intensification (RI), remains challenging due to multiple sources of uncertainty. In particular, complex interactions within the ocean–atmosphere boundary layer, including heat and energy exchanges and boundary layer recovery, are difficult to represent in numerical models. Assimilation of geostationary surface-sensitive infrared radiances can provide valuable lower-tropospheric information with high spatiotemporal resolution over oceans, where conventional observations are sparse. However, their sensitivity to both cloud tops and the surface introduces substantial nonlinearity, making it difficult to distinguish the sources of observation errors. As a result, their use in data assimilation (DA) has been limited compared to that of water vapor channels. In this study, clear-sky radiances from GOES-16 ABI channel 15 (the dirty window channel) over the ocean were assimilated to evaluate their feasibility and benefits when properly treated. The objective was to improve the prediction of the second RI event of Hurricane Ida (2021) by enhancing the representation of lower-atmospheric environmental conditions. A cycling DA experiment assimilating ABI channel 15 radiances together with conventional observations (ABI_SFC) was compared with a corresponding cycling experiment assimilating only conventional observations (CTRL). Results indicate the potential of assimilating surface-sensitive channels to improve intensity forecast accuracy when appropriate quality-control procedures are applied. Backward trajectory analysis and lower-level moist static energy (MSE) distributions suggest that assimilation-induced changes in the surrounding thermodynamic environment can be transported into the hurricane vortex, substantially influencing storm intensity. The impacts of cycling configurations and observation-error settings will also be discussed.

491685.title: A Longitudinal Analysis of Self-Efficacy in First-Year Undergraduate Meteorology Majors
491685.authors: Eli Blackwelder, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte, NC; and C. Davenport
491685.abstract: Previous studies have demonstrated that student self-efficacy, or the belief that one can reach their goals, is a critical predictor for student success. Self-efficacy can be tied to undergraduate outcomes such as persistence in the major (particularly in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics disciplines) and time to graduation. Note that self-efficacy is not a static measure of perceived competence; rather, it is sensitive to student experience, as well as family, social, and educational environments. In particular, the shift from high school to college or changing from a community college to a four-year institution represent a substantial academic and social transition period. This transition has a large influence on student self efficacy and early academic success, particularly for new transfer students, who tend to perform worse than their “traditional” entry counterparts. However, limited research exists with regards to changes in self-efficacy over time in college settings and its relationship to the shifting demands occurring over the course of an academic year. This study evaluates the evolution in self-efficacy in two cohorts of incoming meteorology majors (comprised of both new college freshmen and transfer students) at a large research intensive university in the southeastern US, along with its relationship to academic performance in coursework. Regularly administered surveys were conducted using the Beliefs in Educational Success Test (BEST) assessment to quantify students’ self-reported self-efficacy at multiple points throughout each of their first 4 semesters on campus. Qualitative response questions were also included to solicit relevant context to reported self-efficacy scores. This presentation will describe broad trends in self-efficacy, along with shifts in various components of the BEST and sensitivities to student demographics and specific courses. Most notably, reported levels of self-efficacy were dependent on the nature of the academic activity in question. For example, analysis of year 1 data indicates that students reported overall improvement in self-efficacy over time related to future courses and interacting with faculty, while showing diminished self-efficacy over time regarding individual assignments and collaborative work with their peers. Students who enrolled in rigorous (non-meteorology) general education courses with lower course-wide average grades did not appear to negatively influence self-efficacy, regardless of their individual grades in those courses. Additional trends, along with preliminary results from year 2 of the first cohort and year 1 of the second cohort, will also be discussed.

491692.title: Advancing Science and Services for Improved Heat Preparedness through NOAA's Climate Program Office
491692.authors: Laura Petes, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and M. Zabow and A. Mariotti
491692.abstract: The NOAA Climate Program Office (CPO) advances science and services to support NOAA’s mission, including providing information useful for societal preparedness. Extreme heat is a growing threat, requiring increased knowledge, tools, and resources. To meet this challenge, CPO/NOAA has worked with agencies across the federal family to establish and implement the National Integrated Heat Health Information System (NIHHIS). NIHHIS’ vision is a heat-resilient nation empowered to effectively address extreme heat and its impacts. This presentation will highlight CPO’s work, through NIHHIS and coordinated research investments, informing understanding of, preparedness for, and response to extreme heat. Through coordinated heat island mapping campaigns, support for tabletop exercises, creation of communities of practice, and heat-focused communications and engagement campaigns, NIHHIS is raising awareness of the impacts of heat across the Nation. This became particularly timely and relevant in Summer 2026, with several heat dome events that impacted wide swaths of the country, coinciding with several large, high-profile outdoor events. CPO has also invested in cross-NOAA and extramural research, including through competitive granting processes, to advance science related to heat prediction and impacts. This has advanced heat predictability and understanding of heat mechanisms, and has provided insights into phenomena such as marine heat waves, with implications for key economic sectors such as fisheries and infrastructure. Collectively, these investments are improving understanding of heat and are advancing science that supports societal decision making through sustained partnerships among scientists, stakeholders, and communities. Opportunities for future research, services, and engagement related to heat will also be discussed.

491695.title: A Physics-Guided Neural Network T-Matrix Emulator for Simulating Dual-Polarization Radar Variables
491695.authors: Jacob T. Carlin, NSSL, Norman, OK
491695.abstract: Dual-polarization radar variables offer enhanced insight into the size, shape, phase, composition, and orientation of scattering particles. As such, the ability to link precipitation particles with their attendant scattering behavior has many applications, including understanding the microphysical processes behind observed radar signatures, evaluating numerical weather prediction models, and developing forward operators for data assimilation. T-matrix calculations offer a robust way to calculate the scattering behavior of spheroidal particles, particularly for large particles that experience complex resonances for which the simplified Rayleigh equations are invalid. However, the computational expense of T-matrix calculations may prohibit their real-time operational use. Instead, large sets of multidimensional look-up tables (LUTs) are often used, but may introduce errors due to interpolation or fixed assumptions about particle characteristics during their generation. This work develops a Python-based physics-guided neural network T-matrix emulator. A comprehensive training data set of S-band scattering amplitudes representing a wide range of hydrometeor characteristics (e.g., size, shape, and composition) is generated from explicit Fortran-based T-matrix calculations. This data set is used to train a Sinusoidal Representation Network (SIREN) model that predicts the residual (i.e., non-Rayleigh) component of complex forward- and back-scattering amplitudes in the horizontal and vertical planes from particle size, shape, and dielectric constant, from which dual-polarization radar variables can be calculated. Results indicate that the model accurately emulates scattering amplitudes, with linear-space mean absolute errors of 1–7% (r2 > 0.99). The attendant radar variables are similarly well predicted, with KDP exhibiting the largest errors. However, the impact of radar variable errors for individual particles is mitigated when integrating across the full particle size distribution. Sensitivity analysis highlights that prediction errors are largest for particles that are either large, highly nonspherical, or have small absorptive losses. This generalized emulator calculates particle scattering amplitudes approximately an order of magnitude faster than the full T-matrix code and provides users flexibility by alleviating the need to recreate LUTs for custom particle characteristics. Future work will seek to extend this approach to shorter wavelengths and pursue a two-layer T-matrix emulator to more accurately calculate the scattering characteristics of water-coated hail.

491701.title: Discovering Missing Physics from Analysis Increments with Symbolic Regression: Toward Improving MPAS Tropical S2S Forecasts
491701.authors: Peng-Xiang Lai, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and P. J. van Leeuwen
491701.abstract: The forecast skill of numerical weather prediction (NWP) is still limited by missing or poorly represented physical processes. The framework we present unites data assimilation (DA) with machine learning (ML) to extract model error equations from the analysis increment. Because we use a data-assimilation method that provides updates at subsequent time steps, the increment covers one step and remains a direct measure of model error over that time step: it is not affected by nonlinear error growth over several time steps, and it does not mix with the model's own dynamics over several time steps. For equation discovery, we use symbolic regression, which is a branch of machine learning that finds the mathematical equations that best describe the data. The system evaluates all possible combinations of input variables with mathematical operators and constants to create potential equations, which it evaluates based on their predictive power and their structural simplicity. The research work makes use of the Python package PySR, which Cranmer developed in 2023. The data-assimilation-equation-discovery framework has been tested in simple models (Lorenz-63 and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky), where it correctly recovers the removed terms without using the true equations as a reference. We implemented the framework in the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) through the JEDI data assimilation system. The main challenge is that multiple physics schemes together with the dynamical core act within a single model time step, which prevents direct association between the one-step increment and any specific physics scheme. We developed several methodologies to solve this issue, which differ in what can be extracted from the model runs. We first explore this methodology to improve tropical convection parameterization schemes, because systematic biases in these schemes have profound influence on medium range mid-latitude weather prediction. The presentation will show preliminary findings along with a method to distinguish scheme-related errors from convection errors, which will allow us to improve tropical convection parameterization and MPAS S2S forecast performance through data-driven methods.

491703.title: An Operational Forward Looking Instrument Siting Tool for Large-Scale Wildfire Observing Campaigns using Remotely Sensed Data and Coupled Fire-Atmosphere WRF-SFIRE Forecasts: A Planning and Decision Support Tool
491703.authors: Kathleen Nicole Clough, DRI, Reno, NV; and A. Farguell and T. J. Brown
491703.abstract: Wildfire observation campaigns that utilize ground-based platforms collocated with airborne platforms to obtain remotely sensed and in-situ measurements of wildfire face unique challenges in selecting target fires that are accessible to both ground-based and airborne platforms. Access expands beyond whether or not there are roads around a wildfire, but if those roads offer the proper amount of line of sight or viewing points for ground assets, like radar and LiDAR, to successfully collect observations. In campaigns that have a large region of interest, such as the entire western United States, it is nearly impossible to assess the viability of every potential target fire manually, especially when target fires or fires of interest are changing daily. In order to support target prioritization decisions, ground-based sampling viability assessments, as well as provide deployment targets for ground crews along with incident-level situational awareness in near real-time, the Observational Fire Atmosphere Mapping Suite (OFAMS) was developed. By utilizing all paved and unpaved road information, a digital elevation model (DEM), estimated vegetation height (EVH) from LANDFIRE2025, and 48-hour forecasted fire spread from the coupled fire-atmosphere model WRF-SFIRE, all road points around a fire were assessed for each hour of forecasted fire growth to determine if fire activity is visible from that point based on user inputs such as minimum distance from active fire, maximum distance from active fire, or whether or not to prioritized paved roads for safety reasons. Once the user has chosen their settings, OFAMS provides a list of the top ten viewing points per hour or per observational period, which is defined as a 6-hour period, allowing ground crews to plan ahead and strategically pick observing locations that are viable for longer periods of time. This tool and subsequent dashboard were deployed for the 2026 Injected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE) campaign, but have utility for a variety of applications outside of wildfire.

491712.title: An SSP-Consistent Framework for Projecting Future Urban Climate and Thermal Comfort across Megacities
491712.authors: XIAO JIN, Institute of Science Tokyo, Tokyo, N/A, Japan; and A. C. G. Varquez, D. N. Khanh, M. Sekiya, S. Kumar, J. Wei, J. Cao, and M. Kanda
491712.abstract: Climate change and urbanization jointly reshape urban thermal environments. Climate change alters regional meteorological conditions, whereas changes in urban morphology and anthropogenic heat emissions (AHE) modify land–atmosphere exchange, heat storage, ventilation, and radiative exposure. Yet projections that differentiate both urban morphology and AHE among Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) alongside climate change remain limited. Future urbanization is often represented through urban land expansion or broad urban classes, while studies that incorporate detailed future urban change have focused mainly on near-surface air temperature. Outdoor thermal comfort, however, also depends on humidity, wind speed, and mean radiant temperature (Tmrt), and may therefore change differently from air temperature. The Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) is used here to assess outdoor thermal comfort from the combined effects of these meteorological variables. However, conventional grid-scale Tmrt diagnostics do not fully exploit the urban-canyon radiative information represented by SLUCM. Here, we develop and evaluate a pedestrian-level Tmrt parameterization that uses SLUCM facet temperatures, canyon geometry, and shading information. This study develops an SSP-consistent framework for simulating present-day and 2050s urban climate and UTCI across megacities with contrasting climatic backgrounds. The Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model version 4.6 coupled with SLUCM is applied at 1.5-km horizontal grid spacing using Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6)-based pseudo-global-warming perturbations under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP3-7.0. Spatially heterogeneous present-day fields of five urban parameters, together with AHE, provide the baseline urban conditions. For the 2050s, a data-driven workflow is used to generate separate gridded urban-parameter datasets aligned with SSP1, SSP2, and SSP3, each comprising mean building height, plan area index, frontal area index, zero-plane displacement height, and aerodynamic roughness length. Each dataset is combined with an AHE projection for the corresponding socioeconomic pathway. Together, these constitute urban-development inputs aligned with SSP1, SSP2, and SSP3 and are paired, respectively, with the CMIP6 climate perturbations under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP3-7.0. Hourly Tmrt is estimated using an improved canyon-aware diagnostic that incorporates SLUCM facet temperatures and urban-canyon radiative information, and UTCI is calculated from air temperature, humidity, wind speed, and Tmrt. Factorial simulations separate the individual and combined contributions of climate forcing, urban morphological change, and AHE. For each megacity, simulations target the calendar month with the highest present-day climatological mean 2-m air temperature, with the same calendar month analyzed in all present-day and future experiments. Conditions exceeding the UTCI strong-heat-stress threshold of 32 degrees Celsius are evaluated in terms of intensity, persistence, spatial heterogeneity, and diurnal evolution. Particular attention is given to daytime radiative loading, post-sunset persistence of thermal stress, and nighttime cooling and recovery. Factorial contrasts attribute these responses to climate forcing, urban morphological change, and AHE, while concurrent changes in air temperature, Tmrt, humidity, and wind speed identify the meteorological pathways through which urban development modifies UTCI. Comparisons across climatic backgrounds and socioeconomic pathways examine how the dominant controls on future thermal stress vary among megacities and across the diurnal cycle. By pairing CMIP6 climate perturbations with urban-parameter and AHE inputs aligned with the corresponding socioeconomic pathway, the framework improves the scenario consistency of future urban-climate projections. Incorporating SLUCM facet temperatures and urban-canyon radiative information into Tmrt also strengthens the linkage between SLUCM surface-energy calculations and UTCI diagnosis. The framework quantifies how pathway-dependent urban development amplifies or offsets climate-driven UTCI changes and why these responses differ among megacities, thereby providing a scenario-consistent evidence base for city-specific urban planning, anthropogenic heat mitigation, and climate adaptation under alternative development pathways. This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI (Grants JP25K03366 and JP25K00040) and JSTSPRING (Grant JPMJSP2180).

491713.title: Sea Ice Motion and Dynamics Retrievals Through the Blending of Satellite Retrievals
491713.authors: Jay P. Hoffman, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and Y. Liu and A. Ross
491713.abstract: Sea ice motion and understanding underlying ice dynamics are critical for marine navigation, climate modeling, and monitoring the rapidly changing cryosphere. This study presents a novel approach to estimating sea ice kinematics by blending retrievals from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer (AMSR), and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR). While passive microwave sensors like AMSR provide continuous, all-weather monitoring, their coarse resolution limits the detection of small-scale dynamic features such as fine leads. VIIRS offers superior spatial detail but is limited by clouds, and SAR provides high-resolution, all-weather imagery but often lacks continuous pan-polar spatial and temporal coverage. By applying a Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) framework alongside robust feature-tracking algorithms, we optimally combine the clear-sky, high-resolution kinematic fields from VIIRS, the all-sky, moderate-resolution motion vectors from AMSR, and the targeted, ultra-high-resolution observations from SAR. Validation against drifting buoy data demonstrates that this multi-sensor blended product significantly reduces root mean square errors and directional biases compared to single- or dual-sensor retrievals. These blended results mitigate the limitations inherent in standalone observations, providing a more continuous, detailed, and reliable characterization of sea ice motion to enhance our understanding of complex ocean-ice-atmosphere interactions.

491714.title: What Comparing the Southern and Northern Hemispheres Teaches Us about Aerosols
491714.abstract: The ATom mission was a unique opportunity to compare and contrast the Northern and Southern Hemispheres as well as study seasonal trends. I will summarize some of the published results that utilize the hemispheric comparison to study atmospheric aerosols. For example, on a single mission sea salt could be very different in the two hemispheres, but the multiple deployments show that this was due to seasonal changes rather than a hemispheric difference. Mixed organic-sulfate aerosols were broadly similar between the hemisphere, with perhaps surprising amounts of biomass burning aerosol in the Southern Hemisphere. Dust was present in both hemisphere but was less evenly distributed. Some stratospheric aerosols were very different. There was a source of new particle formation specific to the Northern Hemisphere lower stratosphere. Concentrations of perchlorate were much higher in the Southern Hemisphere stratosphere.

491717.title: A Road Map for Continental Flood Risk Assessment Under a Pseudo Global Warming Approach
491717.authors: Alexander Timothy Michalek, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN; and L. N. Tobias-Tarsh, R. Amorim, G. Villarini, and J. Done
491717.abstract: Development of high-resolution flood risk maps is important for preparing communities across the United States for expected changes in extreme weather events driving flooding in the future. However, assessing future changes in risk is difficult as there are large uncertainties associated with changes in land use, population, and demographics. One way to overcome this uncertainty is to use a pseudo global warming (PGW) approach where historical weather events are simulated under warming conditions. This allows us to assess how the warming component may change future flood risk while maintaining representative present-day population and building datasets. In this study, we use 4-km outputs from historical and PGW hydroclimate simulations provided by CONUS404 from water years 1980–2020 to develop flood hazard maps for eight annual exceedance probabilities (AEPs). Outputs are coupled with hydrologic and hydraulic models. The underlying hydraulic model is Triton 2D hydrodynamic model with 30-m digital elevation and land cover maps. For pluvial conditions, six-hour storm events are estimated for each AEP at all 4-km grid cells and input to Triton. For fluvial conditions, runoff, precipitation, and temperature from CONUS404 feed the Tiger-HLM framework to generate streamflow via direct routing and precipitation/temperature runoff generation. Peak flows are extracted to estimate AEPs input into Triton. Historical coastal surge heights from USCoastEX dataset inform coastal maps. Mosaicking these yields 32 total maps. Comparison with FEMA 100-year flood maps reveal a Critical Success Index of 0.83. Expected losses are computed using 2022/2026 National Structure Inventory datasets. To assess foundation uncertainty, 2000 Monte Carlo simulations sample foundation type/height, yielding six loss sets. National average annual losses range from 0.4–0.8 Trillion dollars (2–3% of GDP). For extreme AEPs (e.g., 0.02%), loss differences between fluvial models and building datasets mirror historical vs. PGW scenario differences. Annual losses increase most in West Virginia and Louisiana, with Appalachian and Texas counties having the least recovery ability. A thought experiment evaluates adaptation costs by estimating the expense of raising residential structures to offset warming-driven losses.

491723.title: Storm-Type Contributions to Seasonal and Interannual Precipitation Variability over CONUS in CONUS404 and Observations
491723.authors: Qien Huang, University of Utah, Salt Lake City; and A. M. Stansfield
491723.abstract: Precipitation over the continental United States (CONUS) is produced by weather systems spanning synoptic to convective scales, yet precipitation climatologies often combine events with substantially different dynamics and structures. This study uses the Unified Tracking System (UTS), a novel object-based framework, to link precipitation and storm-mode structures to objectively identified low pressure systems (LPSs), frontal regions, and mesoscale convective systems (MCSs). Hourly precipitation objects are identified in CONUS404, a 40-year WRF simulation with 4 km grid spacing over CONUS forced by reanalysis, and GPM IMERG fields. In parallel, connected storm-mode objects are extracted from categorical masks derived from CONUS404 simulated reflectivity and GridRad radar observations for five modes: deep convective cores, ordinary convective cores, wide convective cores, deep-and-wide convective cores, and broad stratiform regions. Object overlap with LPS impact zones, LPS-related fronts, other frontal regions, and MCS masks is used to assign precipitation and storm modes to a final analysis group: Tropical, Extratropical, Dry, Extreme High Altitude, Front, Monsoon Trough, MCS, or Others. UTS calculates object geometry and precipitation-related metrics. We use these diagnostics to (1) compare precipitation characteristics among storm types, (2) quantify the fraction of seasonal and annual CONUS precipitation associated with each type, (3) assess whether extreme precipitation is preferentially associated with particular storm types, and (4) determine how storm modes vary across the storm types. Seasonal cycles and year-to-year anomalies in storm-type precipitation contributions will be evaluated in CONUS404 and compared with observation-based estimates over a common period. This study will assess how well CONUS404 represents those contributions.

491726.title: Translating the Urban Rainfall Effect From Research to Applications: Assessing the Role of Urbanization on Flash Floods [INVITED]
491726.authors: J. Marshall Shepherd, Univ. of Georgia, Athens, GA; and J. T. McLeod
491726.abstract: An overarching goal of within our research framework is to advance the concept of the urban rainfall effect (URE) from theoretical paradigms to applied hydrometeorological prediction. Using recent flash flooed events in Atlanta, Georgia, we leverage observational and mesoscale modeling methodologies to study the concept of "flashiness." Our results support previous studies that the urban environment can serve as an amplification mechanism when an environment is primed for convective processes. A key finding is that extreme rainfall – urbanization – flash flooding connections are partially explained by a “prime and pump” mechanism. Urban destabilization primes the environment with enhanced convective available potential energy (CAPE), while surface-based convergence spatially focuses the extreme rainfall. To further quantify how the URE translates to a flood hazard, we introduced a new model-based metric to represent hydrological “flashiness.” The newly proposed Flash Flood Potential Index produced credible signals of flood potential that were consistent with previous observational studies. While there was some variability, this may be one of the first attempts to quantify flashiness within a hydrometeorological modeling framework.

491727.title: Integrating GFSv17 Physics into the Standalone MPAS Atmosphere Model for Global High-Resolution Forecasting
491727.authors: Helin Wei, NOAA/NWS/OMD, College Park, MD; and J. Dong, W. Li, F. Yang, and B. yang
491727.abstract: The Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) atmosphere model has been selected as a candidate dynamical core for next-generation global numerical weather prediction systems. To facilitate a direct assessment of MPAS relative to existing operational configurations, we have integrated major components of the Global Forecast System (GFS) version 17 physics suite into the standalone MPAS atmosphere model. The current implementation includes the GFS surface layer scheme, the scale-aware TKE-EDMF planetary boundary layer (PBL) scheme, and the scale-aware Simplified Arakawa-Schubert (SAS) deep and shallow convection schemes. Integrating these physics packages required substantial modifications to the coupling interface between MPAS and GFS physics because of differences in model infrastructure, variable definitions, vertical coordinates, and data layout. Particular attention was devoted to consistent transformations of thermodynamic variables, pressure fields, and prognostic tendencies between the MPAS dynamical core and GFS physics. Several numerical challenges were encountered during the coupling process, particularly for high-resolution global integrations. These challenges primarily involved maintaining numerical consistency and tracer positivity when coupling the MPAS dynamical core with the GFS physics suite. Localized tracer-positivity violations associated with the TKE-EDMF planetary boundary layer scheme were addressed using level-by-level positivity-preserving limiters for water vapor, cloud water, and cloud ice tendencies. The resulting coupled system successfully completed stable multi-day global forecasts while the positivity corrections were applied to only a negligible fraction of model columns. The coupled MPAS–GFS physics system has successfully completed global 60-km forecasts, providing confidence in the robustness of the physics integration. Ongoing work focuses on evaluating the system at convection-permitting global resolutions. A series of 7-day global 10-km forecasts initialized daily from 1–10 July 2024 is being conducted to assess the impact of the integrated GFS physics on forecast skill, precipitation, boundary layer structure, and surface meteorological fields. Comparisons with the baseline MPAS physics configuration will quantify the scientific benefits and remaining challenges associated with coupling operational GFS physics to the MPAS dynamical core. This work establishes a unified framework for evaluating operational GFS physics within an alternative global dynamical core and provides a foundation for future MPAS-based operational and research applications within the Unified Forecast System (UFS).

491732.title: Development of a JEDI Data Assimilation System for WACCM-X
491732.authors: Simin Zhang, University of Colorado Boulder, BOULDER, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, BOULDER, CO; and M. Miesch, N. Pedatella, H. Shao, B. C. Ruston, L. J. Hayden, and T. E. Berger
491732.abstract: The Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) is a state-of-the-art unified data assimilation (DA) system developed by UCAR’s Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA), which is slated for operational implementation at many agencies and will also serve as a community system for research. To extend this capability to the ionosphere-thermosphere (IT) system, we developed a JEDI-based data assimilation system for NSF NCAR Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model with thermosphere and ionosphere extension (WACCM-X) through the cam-jedi interface. The cam-jedi model interface is developed as the JEDI interface for the Community Atmosphere Model (CAM) to couple the WACCM-X to the JEDI framework. The current implementation of cam-jedi supports the CAM finite-volume dynamical core geometry, enables parallelized I/O and computational operations and exchanges information through file-based data communication. The model interface provides the infrastructure for CAM to leverage JEDI's existing capabilities for forward observation simulation (H(x)) and LETKF (Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter)-based ensemble data assimilation through standardized model-specific classes. Ongoing work integrates the cam-jedi interface with the JCSDA Skylab workflow (powered by the Ewok workflow engine) for automated testing and cycling ensemble data assimilation experiments, with R2D2 providing storage and management of model and observation data. This work extends the JEDI ecosystem into the IT system, providing community DA capability and creating a foundation for space weather research and operations.

491735.title: A Framework for Addressing Parameter Uncertainty and Model-Form Error In Parameterizations Using Scale-Resolving Large-Eddy Simulations
491735.authors: Ethan YoungIn Shin, MIT, Cambridge, MA; and B. Kale and M. F. Howland
491735.abstract: Physical processes such as planetary boundary layer turbulence and surface-atmosphere interactions are parameterized in the weather and climate models that drive predictions used for decision-making, representing a primary source of error and uncertainty. The uncertainties in parameterizations stem from both their imperfect model form, and from uncertainty in the tuned model parameters. Deciding which uncertainty to address is rarely straightforward, since either can be adjusted to reduce discrepancies between models and data. Here we introduce a framework that attributes the discrepancy to either model parameters or model form, and then treats both in a principled manner. We apply the framework to the MYNN and YSU turbulence parameterization schemes in the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, where parameterization uncertainty is learned based on scale-resolving large eddy simulations (LES). When model-form error is the primary driver of the discrepancy, we use a derivative-free, ensemble-based method to infer an embedded, functional correction term acting directly on the closure, rather than an additive correction to an observable model output state. Because the closure error acts inside the model, it is not directly measurable. Field inversion lets us infer an internal model-form correction for a given flow regime. Pairing the correction with nondimensional quantities of the regime yields training data for a map from flow inputs to correction. Inferring the embedded correction term across multiple flow regimes lets us learn algebraic expressions that generalize beyond a single flow regime. On the other hand, when model parameter uncertainty is the primary driver, the standard framework to subsequently derive parameter sensitivity is forward uncertainty propagation, but this requires physically plausible parameter distributions that first must be learned from scale-resolving data. Bayesian or inverse uncertainty quantification offers a principled approach to learning these parameter distributions, but can become ill-posed when observations weakly constrain parameters – a condition difficult to know prior to inference. On this challenge, we perform both forward and inverse uncertainty quantification of parameters in WRF and show that parameter sensitivities from forward uncertainty quantification can guide a non-iterative strategy for identifying observations informative to inverse uncertainty quantification. To overcome the computational bottleneck of O(105) model evaluations required for both analyses, we leverage Gaussian process emulators trained on only O(102) WRF simulations. We introduce nondimensional diagnostics based on global sensitivity analysis that target regions in the observable model output space in which a parameter's contribution to the variance exceeds the observational noise and its independent effect exceeds its interactions with other parameters. Emulator-accelerated Bayesian inversion for parameters in WRF based on LES demonstrates that observations drawn from these targeted regions yield narrower posteriors. By treating parameter uncertainty and model-form error under a consistent, scheme-agnostic procedure rather than ad hoc judgment, the proposed framework aims to improve predictions across multiple flow regimes relative to parameter calibration or model-form correction alone. *This research is supported by the Office of Naval Research, Young Investigator Program, grant no. N000142512045. Simulations were performed on the Stampede3 super-computers under the NSF EXPLORE project EES240114, NSF ACCELERATE project EVE240008, and NSF MAXIMIZE project ATM170028.

491739.title: On the Immersion Freezing Ability of Biomass Burning Aerosols Across Multiple North American Environments
491739.authors: Naruki Hiranuma, The University of Texas at El Paso, El Paso, TX; and J. M. Harris
491739.abstract: Give a title to it. Abstract: Biomass burning aerosols (BBA) from events like wildfires or prescribed burnings are a major source of atmospheric aerosols globally, however their role as ice-nucleating particles (INPs) are not well understood. There is significant disagreement about the ice nucleation efficiency of BBA in previous studies, and understanding this gap in mixed phase cloud regime would be instrumental in improving climate and weather models. In this study, we leveraged immersion mode INP data collected at the ground level during several field campaigns across diverse environments in North America using the Portable Ice Nucleating Experiment (PINE) and freezing assay. These measured data were combined with long with airmass backtrajectory path, satellite, meteorological, and aerosol data to examine the impact of biomass-burning plumes. We have identified multiple instances where our data in the Arctic, Rocky Mountains, Southern Great Plains, and other regions reflected the influence of BBAs. Across these diverse environments, our preliminary results suggest no substantial increase in observed INP concentrations, despite an often substantial increase in total particle and cloud condensation nuclei concentrations. These findings imply that BBAs act poorly as immersion mode INPs while biomass burning events may contribute to INP concentrations in cirrus cloud regime must be studied in the future.

491740.title: Diurnal and Seasonal Variability of Planetary Boundary Layer Height Observed by COSMIC-2 and Radiosondes over the Texas Gulf Coast
491740.authors: Delaynie Barbara Peters, Texas A&M Univ.—Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX; and F. Xie and L. Adhikari
491740.abstract: The planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) is critical parameter for quantifying the extent of surface-atmosphere interactions and improving numerical weather predictions and climate modeling. Although space-borne GNSS Radio Occultation (RO) observations have proven effective for detecting PBLH over relative homogeneous land and ocean surface, their performance in coastal regions remain less understood because of strong land-sea contrasts, sharp moisture gradients, and mesoscale circulations. To investigate these effects, PBLH observations from the COSMIC-2 GNSS RO were evaluated against the six-hourly Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Tracking Aerosol Convection Interactions Experiment (TRACER) radiosonde observations collected near Houston, Texas, between October 2021 and September 2022. PBLH was identifiedusing a multi-layer refractivity-gradient-based approach. COSMIC-2 RO successfully captured the diurnal evolution of the boundary layer observed by radiosondes, including daytime growth and nocturnal collapse,despite the complexity of the south Texas coastal environment. COSMIC-2 PBLH estimates showed the closest agreement with radiosonde measurements during daytime, when the PBL top was characterized by a well-defined, sharp refractivity gradient. Larger discrepancies occurred at night and during summer, when weaker or multilayer refractivity-gradient structures are more prevalent. COSMIC-2 RO also reproduced the seasonal evolution of the diurnal cycle, accurately capturing the phase of the daytime maximum and nocturnal minimum with a median timing error within ~2.1 hours, and the diurnal amplitude with a median difference of 0.12 km.These results demonstrate that GNSS RO can reliably detect PBLH in dynamically complex coastal environments, particularly when refractivity gradients are well defined, thereby increasing confidence in refractivity-based PBLH diagnostics derived from GNSS RO observations.

491744.title: The Blizzard of 2026: Forecasting and Communicating a Historic Southern New England Snowstorm.
491744.authors: Hayden Frank, NWS, Norton, MA, MA
491744.abstract: On 22–23 February 2026, a historic blizzard struck Southern New England as a rapidly deepening cyclone underwent bombogenesis near 970 mb and tracked near the Benchmark. Storm-total snowfall of 37.9 inches at Rhode Island T.F. Green International Airport shattered the Providence record of 28.6 inches set during the Blizzard of 1978 and established a new validated 24-hour Rhode Island state snowfall record. Persistent mesoscale banding produced totals exceeding 30 inches across Rhode Island and Southeast Massachusetts; blizzard conditions persisted for more than three hours, over 300,000 Massachusetts customers lost power, and a storm surge of 2.1–2.5 feet drove coastal flooding from Boston to Nantucket. Significant model track disagreement characterized the Day 3–5 window, with most guidance placing the storm too far east. The GFS correctly anticipated a faster positive-to-negative longwave tilt, yielding an amplified, coast-hugging track. Probabilistic tools proved decisive: the NAEFS ensemble situational awareness table flagged a low-level jet 5–6 standard deviations above climatology, while the ECMWF Extreme Forecast Index approached 1.0 with a Shift of Tails exceeding 2.0. NBM 5.0 underresolved the extreme coastal snowfall gradient, underforecasting Rhode Island and Southeast Massachusetts while overforecasting the distant interior. Significant track uncertainty in the Day 3–5 window shaped the decision-support approach. Partner communication began during the 17 February weekly emergency-manager video briefing, which appropriately emphasized the probabilistic range of outcomes rather than a single deterministic solution. As ensemble guidance converged 2–3 days before the event, messaging escalated to a high-confidence, high-impact outlook, giving emergency managers actionable lead time. DESI-based hourly snowfall-rate graphics and WSSI coordination supported protective action across the region. Post-storm, staff conducted a T.F. Green site visit, and a State Climate Extremes Committee convened on 17 March 2026 to validate the record. This presentation shows how disciplined communication of uncertainty — followed by timely escalation as confidence grew — translated a rare, high-end blizzard into empowered protective action. Attendees will gain insights into multi-model ensemble interpretation during a high-uncertainty track scenario; application of probabilistic tools (NAEFS SAT, ECMWF EFI/SOT) for historic-event recognition; limitations of NBM 5.0 in resolving extreme coastal snowfall gradients; IDSS best practices for a potentially destructive Nor’easter; and the post-storm observational verification process required to establish a new state snowfall record.

491746.title: Improving Objective Drought Outlook With NCEP Seasonal Forecast System (SFS)
491746.authors: Li Xu, CPC, College Park, MD; and M. Robjhon, Y. Liu, Y. Pan, W. M. Thiaw, and Z. Segele
491746.abstract: The development of the Seasonal Forecast System (SFS) version beta 1 (including beta 1.0 and beta 1.1) has significantly enhanced the Climate Prediction Center's (CPC) subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction capability. This advancement represents a major milestone for NCEP's coupled modeling, as the system is designed to replace the currently operational Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2). By leveraging improved dynamical processes and coupling with higher-resolution ocean and ice models, the SFS provides more accurate and reliable forecasts for sea surface temperatures (SST), regional precipitation, and temperature anomalies. These enhancements are critical for strengthening the international desk drought early warning system in support of the Department Of State (DOS) Famine Early Warning System (FEWS) NET. This research outlines the essential post-processing techniques used to integrate SFS data into objective monthly drought projections. Primary development efforts focus on three key areas: Model Evaluation and Validation to assess S2S prediction skill benchmarked against the operational CFSv2; Regional Downscaling & Bias Correction to achieve improved local resolution and minimize systematic errors; and the utilization of sophisticated statistical and hybrid statistical-dynamical methods to enhance weak forecast signals.Through the refinement of these data products, the project is currently designing and prototyping early warning products. These routines convert raw meteorological data into actionable, impact-based forecast products applicable to vital sectors such as agriculture, public health, and water management. Ultimately, these improvements provide enhanced accuracy and reliability in monthly drought forecasts, which are essential for food security, water resource management, and addressing societal, economic, and environmental challenges in vulnerable regions.

491748.title: An Overview of NWS Efforts to Transition FAA Weather Research into Operations
491748.authors: Alex Patrick Korner, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; CIRA/AWC, Kansas City, MO; and R. M. Hepper and N. E. Starzec
491748.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) Aviation Weather Center (AWC) in collaboration with the Colorado Institute for Research of the Atmosphere (CIRA) has a long history of supporting and transitioning research into operations for the NOAA National Weather Service (NWS) that supports the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and other aviation interests. The AWC through the Aviation Weather Testbed (AWT) provides a path to NWS operational use for experimental products and services, promotes collaboration among stakeholders, provides a test environment for the purpose of refining and optimizing experimental technologies, verifies the scientific validity of experimental products, educates stakeholders about experimental tools and the latest research related to aviation weather, and educates researchers about operational needs and constraints. This presentation will summarize the activities conducted by the AWC/CIRA through the AWT including: Implementing the Domestic Aviation Forecast System (DAFS) on the NWS supercomputer, WCOSS, featuring the integration of upgraded Forecast Icing Product version 2 (FIP2) and Graphical Turbulence Guidance version 4 (GTG4) algorithms into NCEP’s Unified Post Processor (UPP) libraries. Successfully implementing the Graphical Turbulence Guidance Nowcast (GTGN) and the Current Icing Product (CIP) version 2 as standalone applications on WCOSS. Transitioning the Localized Aviation MOS Program (LAMP) Ceiling & Visibility (C&V) dashboard to operations. Prototyping 15-minute Gridded LAMP (GLMP) data streams into the Graphical Forecasts for Aviation - Low Altitude (GFA-LA) interface to improve temporal granularity for low-altitude pilots, supported by FAA Aviation Weather Demonstration and Evaluation (AWDE) user assessments. Prototyping gridded NBM C&V guidance for Hawaii into the GFA. Leading facilitation of global icing and turbulence algorithm upgrades. By seamlessly translating complex research algorithms into robust operational code, these initiatives enhance safety across the National Airspace System (NAS), support International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) commitments, and ensure a highly sophisticated and consistent operational picture for the aviation enterprise. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the FAA. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

491759.title: IKCCF: Indigenous Kinship Circle for Climate Futures
491759.authors: Elinor R. Martin, University of Oklahoma, NORMAN, OK; and A. Cook, E. Iralu, E. Kuster, J. Mosely, L. Paquin, and L. Tsinnajinnie
491759.abstract: “Connecting with Community” was the guiding theme of our inaugural, multi-state summer program to cultivate relationships and shared learning among students and community members interested in weaving together Indigenous and Western approaches for community-driven climate adaptation. We called the program Indigenous Kinship Circle for Climate Futures as kinship is our guiding value and a practical approach for climate adaptation. During the two summer program, undergraduate and graduate students from Oklahoma and New Mexico embarked on a learning journey to explore climate science, Indigenous planning and design, and community-based adaptation practices. Guided by the Two-Eyed Seeing framework, students engaged with climate-related concepts through both Indigenous and Western perspectives and developed a deeper understanding of how these knowledge systems can inform one another. The internship spanned across two summers, with the first summer focused on building knowledge and community partnerships and the second focused on implementing a community-led project and a community-engaged portfolio. Over each summer, students also participated in PhotoVoice to capture their learning journey as they learned about climate change and co-developed an adaptation project with a local community. As part of this brief presentation, we will showcase the power of collaborative programs for fostering intercultural and intergenerational discussions and community resilience and share preliminary results from our research on how students experience this type of learning. This project is funded by the National Science Foundation and is a collaborative effort between the University of Oklahoma, The Chickasaw Nation, and the University of New Mexico.

491761.title: UK Heatwaves of 2026 - An Exceptional Season of Multi-Hazard Impact Events
491761.authors: Mike Silverstone, UK Met Office, Exeter, United kingdom
491761.abstract: The UK heatwaves of 2026 represented one of the most significant periods of weather-related societal risk experienced in recent years. While exceptional temperatures attracted public attention, the operational challenge extended far beyond heat alone. Successive periods of extreme temperatures, prolonged overnight heat, drought conditions, infrastructure disruption, pressures on health and emergency services, heightened wildfire risk, water resource concerns and outbreaks of convective weather combined to create a season of sustained multi-hazard impacts across the UK. This presentation explores the forecasting, warning, communication and response challenges arising from these events, drawing on operational experience, rapid event reviews, stakeholder feedback and post-event learning. Particular attention will be given to understanding compound and cascading impacts, communicating uncertainty, maintaining situational awareness during prolonged periods of operational activity and translating meteorological information into effective decisions. The presentation will also discuss lessons emerging from the events and how these are informing future developments in impact-based warning services, hazard management and decision-support capabilities. The heatwaves provided a valuable opportunity to examine how forecasting science, operational delivery, stakeholder partnerships and service design can work together to enhance resilience and societal outcomes during high-impact weather events.

491763.title: Regional Contracts in the Evolution of Tropical Mesoscale Convective Systems over the Western and Eastern Pacific
491763.authors: Yi-Chien Chen, Nagoya University, Nagoya City, Aichi, Japan; and H. Masunaga
491763.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) are major contributors to tropical precipitation and play a vital role in the redistribution of heat and moisture. However, their characteristics and lifecycle evolution can vary substantially across tropical ocean. This study examines regional contrasts in the evolution of tropical MCSs over the western Pacific (WP) and eastern Pacific (EP), with a focus on system size, lifetime, precipitation structure, and the large-scale environment. Tropical MCSs are identified and tracked using the global MCS dataset of Feng et al. (2021), generated with PyFLEXTRKR by tracking cold cloud systems and their associated precipitation features. MCSs are first classified into different lifetime groups. Within each group, individual MCS lifecycles are normalized by system duration to examine their evolution on a common relative timescale. Satellite-based observations are combined with ERA5 reanalysis to investigate the evolution of precipitation, vertical motion, and energy and moisture transport throughout the MCS lifecycle. Initial analyses indicate regional differences in MCS characteristics and evolution.
