WP systems tend to attain larger horizontal extents, whereas EP systems appear to persist for longer periods on average. Differences between the two regions become particularly evident for longer-lived MCSs, which exhibit contrasting evolutions in vertical motion, energy and moisture transport, and the contribution of large-scale precipitation. Preliminary results further suggest that EP MCSs are associated with stronger and more persistent large-scale environmental support during the mature and decaying stages of their lifecycles. By systematically comparing MCS lifecycle evolution between the western and eastern Pacific, this study aims to clarify the processes regulating regional differences in convective organization and maintenance. These results may provide new insight into how tropical MCSs evolve differently under distinct large-scale environmental conditions.

491770.title: Disentangling Aerosol–Cloud Interactions Using Ground and Satellite Observations across Contrasting Environmental Regimes
491770.authors: Shujun Zhou, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD; and Z. Li
491770.abstract: Aerosol–cloud interactions (ACIs) remain a major source of uncertainties in climate predictions. Quantifying these interactions is challenging because cloud properties respond simultaneously to aerosol perturbations and meteorological variability, and aerosol-induced cloud adjustments may involve competing physical processes. Using long-term ground-based observations from three Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) sites representing continental, marine, and coastal environments, we applied an explainable machine-learning framework combining eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) with Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to disentangle aerosol effects from meteorological controls. Strong regime dependence is revealed in the relative importance of aerosol and meteorological influences. Cloud variability at the Southern Great Plains (SGP) and Eastern North Atlantic (ENA) sites is predominantly controlled by meteorological factors, whereas aerosol effects are strongest in the stable coastal regime observed during the Eastern Pacific Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment (EPCAPE). The aerosol–liquid water path relationships are generally negative, suggesting net evaporation–entrainment control in sampled regimes. However, this ground-based analysis focuses on non-precipitating warm clouds. A growing body of observational and modeling evidence suggests that aerosol-induced LWP adjustments can be bidirectional, reflecting competing effects of evaporation/entrainment and precipitation suppression, with their relative importance depending on environmental and precipitation conditions. Following our ground-based study, ongoing work extends the explainable machine-learning framework to satellite observations by integrating CALIPSO aerosol extinction profiles, MODIS and CloudSat cloud retrievals, and ERA5 meteorological fields around the SGP, ENA, and EPCAPE sites. We will first evaluate the consistency of aerosol–cloud relationships derived from ground-based and satellite observations; we will then separate precipitating and non-precipitating warm-cloud populations to investigate whether precipitation state modifies aerosol–LWP relationships and the relative roles of entrainment and precipitation processes. Together, a cross-platform assessment will be conducted of the robustness of ACIs together with the physical mechanisms governing aerosol-induced cloud-water adjustments across contrasting environmental regimes.

491772.title: Enhanced Organic Aerosol from Sea-spray Mitigates Global Warming
491772.authors: Yiyang Sun, School of Earth System Science, Tianjin University, Tianjin, 12, China
491772.abstract: Sea-spray aerosol is a major natural source that modulates marine clouds and contributes to uncertainty in climate projections. Its primary organic fraction—Sea-spray primary organic aerosol (SSPOA), derived from ocean biological activity, dominates fine sea-spray aerosol that seeds cloud droplets, yet its global climate effects remain poorly quantified. Here, using a fully coupled Earth system model that incorporates a dynamic SSPOA emissions module, we show that SSPOA exerts a cooling effect, reducing global annual mean surface air temperature by −0.31 ± 0.18 K. This cooling offsets ~20% of the warming attributable to enhanced greenhouse gas emissions from preindustrial period to present day, while including SSPOA emissions reduces the present-day warm bias relative to reanalysis data by ~80%. This cooling is strongest over the North Pacific with high biologically productivity, where SSPOA increases cloud droplet number and liquid water path, strengthens cloud forcing, and cools surface air by −0.52 ± 0.45 K. With global warming, SSPOA emissions will be intensified resulting in a reduced warming trend during 2025–2100 of ~5%. These findings suggest that enhancing marine ecosystem productivity can achieve a stronger cooling effect through increased production of SSPOA beyond the increased global carbon sink.

491780.title: Understanding Land-Atmosphere Exchange of Reactive Nitrogen through Tiered and Machine Learning Assisted Monitoring
491780.authors: Da Pan, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA
491780.abstract: Atmospheric reactive nitrogen (Nr ), including its reduced form ammonia (NH3 ) and oxidized forms (NOy ), is a critical component of the Earth system that significantly impacts air quality, ecosystem health, and climate. While essential for agriculture, excess Nr is lost to the environment, initiating a cascade of detrimental effects, including the formation of ground-level ozone and fine particulate matter (PM2.5 ), ecosystem acidification, and biodiversity loss. As emissions of oxidized nitrogen decline, the role of agricultural ammonia in driving these impacts has grown, yet it remains the largest source of uncertainty in the U.S. nitrogen budget due to a lack of direct flux observation. To address these significant knowledge gaps, we propose a novel Tiered and Machine Learning Assisted Monitoring (TMLAM) framework designed to provide comprehensive and cost-effective NH3 flux data. The framework synergistically combines: Tier 1) direct, high-fidelity eddy covariance flux measurements at a few "supersites" to develop and evaluate process models; Tier 2) inferential modeling driven by low-cost sensors to expand spatial coverage into critical regions; and Tier 3) upscaling using existing air quality monitoring networks and reanalysis data. A key innovation of the TMLAM framework is a data-driven site selection strategy that moves beyond traditional ecoregions. We hypothesize that coherent regions for NH3 land-atmosphere exchange are defined by multivariate environmental drivers, including soil, vegetation, and atmospheric composition. Using unsupervised machine learning (K-means clustering) on principal components of high-resolution environmental data, we identify these "Nitrogen Exchange Similar Areas" (NESAs). This approach allows for strategic placement of Tier 1 sites in highly representative areas and Tier 2 sites at the boundaries between NESAs to characterize model uncertainty. This presentation will detail the TMLAM framework and the ML-based methodology for NESA determination. In addition, we will discuss sensors suitable for each tier and recent advances in inferential modeling for Tier 2 sites. Finally, we will also evaluate and rank potential sites for the future implementation of TMLAM for NH3 or Nr fluxes.

491781.title: Characterizing PM2.5 Data in Low-Cost Air Quality Sensors
491781.authors: Kaylena Dinh Pham, UCAR, Boulder, CO; University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA; and S. Shams, K. Payne, W. Nicewonger, and A. Frazier
491781.abstract: Short and long-term exposure to fine particulate matter, specifically particles with a diameter below 2.5 μm (PM2.5) is attributed to severe human health impacts. Conventional air quality monitoring for PM2.5 is limited on their spatial resolution and costs, often requiring high-cost instrumentation and time-intensive work to record observations. Low-cost air quality sensors offer the ability to measure air pollutants at higher network density compared to conventional methods. 3D-Printed Automatic Weather Station (3D-PAWS) is a low-cost weather and environmental monitoring system that seeks to provide accessible and reliable environmental observations. Each station is modular in design and portable, giving us the ability to expand air quality networks to a wider network of communities. Given the potentials of 3D-PAWS Air Quality Sensors (3D-PAWS AQ), we find that they have an important role in measuring PM2.5. In this work, we characterize the 3D-PAWS AQ through analyzing its biases and uncertainties to improve its usability. Our study area focuses on Athens, Georgia; Boulder, Colorado; and Lee Park, Virginia, where we evaluate 3D-PAWS data collocated with air quality data sourced from EPA reference-grade air quality monitors (Teledyne 640x) for comparison. This helps establish their reliability as a monitoring system for comparison of reported concentrations to improve sensor agreement. We use a temporal sequence analysis to clean out the dataset and make it more robust for statistical analysis. Then, we apply a rolling standard deviation and mean, allowing to smoothen our dataset and reduce noise. Afterwards, we apply a regression analysis to understand the correlation between our reference and instrument data as well as defining correction factors that are needed to calibrate the data. The results show that final calibrated data saved the enhancement features, while improving its performance proficiency as reflected in statistical metrics. We find that 3D-PAWS is capable of capturing features that are reflected in reference monitors and a calibration process can be applied to mitigate biases. Our results emphasize the importance in evaluating the accuracy of low-cost sensors to improve PM2.5 monitoring across varied environmental regimes and communities.

491782.title: A Hybrid Observation and Reanalysis Method for Hyper-Local Subseasonal-to-Seasonal high Tide Flood Prediction
491782.authors: Gregory Dusek, ; and R. T. Searcy and B. Glazer
491782.abstract: Coastal flooding in the United States has more than doubled in frequency over the past two decades due to sea level rise, and is projected to accelerate further, becoming a chronic problem for most coastal communities. In response to this growing hazard, communities have started to invest in local observing networks to monitor and prepare for flood impacts, driving a rapid increase in available water level data. For instance, Hohonu now operates more than 200 sensors across 18 states, enabling a much broader application of data-driven approaches to flood prediction than previously possible. Those approaches, however, typically need a long data-record. Resolving the seasonal characteristics that drive prediction ideally takes 20 years of observations, while most sensors in the Hohonu network have only a few years or less. Here we present a hybrid method for subseasonal-to-seasonal high-tide flood prediction. We fuse climatological data from the NOAA Coastal Ocean Reanalysis (CORA), a 40+ year hourly wave and water level reanalysis spanning the U.S. East and Gulf coasts, with mean sea level, tide predictions, and non-tidal persistence from water level sensors. The resulting hybrid model outperforms predictions built from short-term observations or CORA alone. By turning a newly installed sensor into a skillful forecast within months rather than decades, this approach lets communities realize the flood-preparedness benefit of their observing investment on a timescale that matters for planning and response.

491783.title: Experimental Outlook Graphics for Aviation Hazards
491783.authors: Diandong Ren, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and A. P. Korner
491783.abstract: The Aviation Weather Center (AWC) produces an expansive array of aviation hazard products for use within the National Airspace System (NAS), including warnings, advisories, and forecasts like the Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA). While these serve the primary needs of many customers, there is great interest from the general aviation community to have more extended range guidance. However, this guidance must be communicated to pilots graphically in a clear, salient, and easily digestible manner. The AWC, in collaboration with Colorado Institute for Research in the Atmosphere (CIRA), is developing an Outlook Graphic system to produce hazard guidance for Days 2-4. This system highlights five key hazards: Ceiling and Visibility (IFR), Icing, Turbulence, Thunderstorm Potential, and Mixed Precipitation across four timeframes: Day 2 AM (09Z–18Z), Day 2 PM (18Z–03Z), Day 3 (09Z–03Z), and Day 4 (09Z–03Z). Guidance is driven by numerical weather prediction (NWP) data from the National Blend of Models (NBM) and the World Area Forecast System (WAFS). This presentation details the technical framework and the potential operational pathway of the Outlook Graphic product.

491784.title: Evolution of International Air Navigation Weather Services at the Aviation Weather Center (Invited Presentation)
491784.authors: Austin E. Cross, NWS/Aviation Weather Center, Kansas City, MO; and N. E. Starzec, D. Vietor, and J. Rush
491784.abstract: In order to meet the need for aviation weather information worldwide, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) developed requirements for the operation of two World Area Forecast Centers (WAFCs), one operated by the National Weather Service (WAFC Washington) and one by the UK Met Office (WAFC London). The NWS Aviation Weather Center serves this role, on behalf of the Federal Aviation Administration, the US aviation meteorological authority. To make data available for international flight operations, the WAFCs each operate Internet data services, the World Area Forecast System (WAFS) Internet File Service (WIFS) in the case of the NWS. Efforts by NWS in partnership with UK Met Office have increased grid resolution of aviation variables by an order of magnitude, providing much greater fidelity forecast information. As the horizontal resolution of WAFC gridded forecasts increases and observations transition to XML/GML formats, more advanced product delivery mechanisms are required. Updated API services aim to advance availability and push the boundaries of several international standards including ICAO Meteorological Information Exchange Model (IWXXM), Systemwide Information Management (SWIM), and the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) Environmental Data Retrieval (EDR) delivered through cloud providers with minimal latency. These upcoming standards are expected to be an increasing part of all meteorological service provider product delivery in the future as we evolve beyond traditional alphanumeric products and file-based download paradigms toward cloud and integrated data provisioning. This presentation will provide an overview of the technologies and standards being used and other related developments.

491787.title: Value of Information Analysis of the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) in LEO
491787.authors: Katherine A Hawley, NESDIS, Lanham, MD; NOAA, Greenbelt, MD; and S. Kalluri, V. Grycenkov, J. M. Valenti, H. Hope, T. Walsh, S. E. Groot, M. Johnson, K. Klockow McClain, B. Smith, C. Smith, and H. E. Brooks
491787.abstract: The Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) program marks a fundamental paradigm shift in NOAA’s approach to space-based Earth observations. Representing the agency’s first transition toward a disaggregated architecture in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), NEON moves away from the traditional model of large, multi-instrument platforms, such as the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS), in favor of a more agile, distributed network. This modernized approach ensures critical data continuity while enabling rapid adaptation to emerging operational and user requirements. To support this new architecture, the Office of LEO Observations conducted a Value of Information (VoI) study evaluating how, when, where, and why microwave sounders (MW) provide value to the nation through the lens of NOAA’s National Hurricane Center (NHC) track and intensity forecast. This presentation highlights key findings, including return on investment (ROI) of NEON’s Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) concept across four candidate architectural configurations.

491799.title: Beyond Anomaly-Based Linear Models: Generalizable Nonlinear Prediction of Large-Scale Low-Cloud Regime Occurrences from Cloud-Controlling Factors
491799.authors: Daeho Jin, UMBC/NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, MD
491799.abstract: Accurately predicting low-cloud occurrences from environmental drivers is essential for reducing uncertainties in cloud-climate feedbacks. This study evaluates linear and non-linear frameworks—specifically anomaly-based ridge regression and neural networks (NNet) predicting raw target values—to predict cloud regime (CR) occurrence frequency from low-cloud-amount-indices (LCAIs) and other cloud-controlling factors at monthly, 4° resolution. While incorporating multiple LCAIs notably improves linear model performance within training domains, these models exhibit poor geographic transferability, reflecting the diversity of cloud-environment relationships across regions. In contrast, an NNet trained on pooled data from diverse subtropical regions consistently outperforms the linear models and captures established physical mechanisms, including the capping inversion effect. However, global application of the baseline NNet model reveals a "generalization gap," particularly in extra-tropical and tropical warm-pool environments that are poorly represented in the training data. To address this limitation, an expanded NNet model is trained using additional samples from poorly predicted regions. This approach reduces global biases and improves mean absolute error by 30-50%, while substantially reducing regional biases. However, the broader training domain also introduces increased nonlinearity and regional trade-offs, including slightly degraded performance within the original training regions. These results suggest that a generalizable cloud-regime prediction model requires both high-capacity non-linear architectures and diverse sampling strategies to represent the geographically varying relationships between cloud and their controlling factors. Once successfully constructed, such a framework coud provide a computationally efficient alternative to satellite simulators for CR-based evaluations of Earth System Model outputs.

491802.title: Evaluating Performance and Operational Utility of Cloud-Based WindNinja for Fire Weather Decision Support
491802.authors: Ansley Baring, GSL Fire Weather Testbed, Boulder, CO; Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and J. J. Brost, K. Fenton, J. Forthofer, L. McMeeking, PhD, K. J. Thiem, P. N. Schumacher, J. Vickery, N. Wagenbrenner, and R. Walsh
491802.abstract: Localized winds significantly influence fire behavior and both strategic and tactical firefighting operations. Even subtle shifts in wind direction or speed can compromise firefighter safety or dramatically alter fire behavior and spread. As such, wind forecasts that are accurate and at the appropriate scale for wildland fire decision making are critical to operations. WindNinja, a tool developed by the U.S. Forest Service’s Missoula Fire Sciences Laboratory, downscales coarse resolution weather forecasts (~1-10km) as low as 100m in complex terrain. While the desktop version is widely used by burn bosses, fire behavior analysts (FBANs), and incident meteorologists (IMETs) to support operations, leveraging its capabilities in the field has historically faced challenges such as computational constraints, managing file formats, and visualization challenges. This has limited WindNinja from being used to its full potential. To enhance operational efficiency, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Global Systems Laboratory’s (GSL) Fire Weather Testbed (FWT) adapted WindNinja to run on a robust cloud-based server via the National Weather Service (NWS) Operations Proving Ground (OPG). The output is then visualized dynamically in GSL’s Dynamic Ensemble-based Scenarios for Impact-based Decision Support (DESI) to be used for Spot Forecasts or for deployed IMETs to customize WindNinja runs. To evaluate WindNinja in the cloud-based environment, the FWT implemented a dual-track evaluation framework that highlights the physical results of a quantitative verification study and complements these metrics with a qualitative value and utility assessment involving 33 NWS forecasters. By pairing statistical verification of high-resolution downscaled winds from WindNinja with targeted user diaries and task-based scenario comparisons, this design allows quantitative metrics to explain forecasters' operational experiences, while user feedback provides context for statistical findings. In the quantitative verification evaluation, downscaled wind speed and direction forecasts at both 10-meter and 20-foot heights are verified against weather observations across the diverse, complex terrains of the CONUS, Alaska, and Hawaii. Initialized using HRRR, RRFS, and deterministic NBM datasets, the verification evaluates performance metrics for the mass only solver and the conservation of mass and momentum solver in WindNinja. Additionally, the quantitative verification examines how WindNinja performs across wind regimes (e.g. diurnal winds, synoptically driven winds) in complex terrain to identify optimal default settings for automated cloud-based runs and best practices for forecasters when using WindNinja guidance. To complement the quantitative verification, qualitative data collection, including a task-based usability simulation and a longitudinal field study, captured how end-user/forecaster confidence, decision making, and trust evolved in using WindNinja under active operational pressure.

491803.title: Exploring the Contributions of Course Materials to the Growth of Spatial Thinking Skills in Meteorology Majors
491803.authors: Lauren Elise Augusta Burns, The University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte, NC; and C. Davenport
491803.abstract: Spatial thinking, or the ability to reason about objects, processes, and relationships in space, is fundamental to student success in the geosciences, including meteorology, which inherently requires the application of spatial reasoning to accurately interpret, understand, and predict the four-dimensional atmosphere. Previous research on spatial thinking skills in meteorology demonstrated that coursework in the middle of an undergraduate meteorology program (i.e., sophomore through junior year) contributed to substantial growth in students’ spatial thinking skills. However, the underlying factors driving this growth remain unclear. Notably, prior work has identified three kinds of behavior that were involved in an individual’s comprehension of information when it is shown in written or symbolic form: translation (e.g., describing content), interpretation (e.g., searching for relationships among variables), and extrapolation and interpolation (e.g., identifying trends and implications perceived in the data). This mental manipulation of information underlying the use of multi-dimensional atmospheric data and associated processes and equations students are exposed to in intermediate courses suggest that practicing quantitative reasoning may also be relevant. To better understand how coursework supports the development of spatial thinking skills and any connections to quantitative reasoning, this study will evaluate content that students interact with or are exposed to four required courses: Synoptic Meteorology, Physical Meteorology, Dynamic Meteorology I, and Climate Dynamics. Course content evaluated in this study includes homework assignments, assessments, in-class activities, and lecture slides. This evaluation, completed with the use of a rubric, focuses on the presence or required application of four different spatial thinking skills: disembedding, spatial orientation, spatial relations, and perspective taking, as well as identifying the presence of quantitative reasoning through either explicit calculations or conceptual reasoning. Student assignment and assessment grades are also collected to evaluate the relationship between frequency of exposure and required use of various spatial thinking skills with the degree of successful application. Results indicate differences in the specific spatial thinking skills students are frequently using when completing coursework among the various intermediate courses. Disembedding and Spatial Orientation were used most frequently in Synoptic Meteorology, while Disembedding and Spatial Relations were emphasized in Physical Meteorology. Additionally, of the four intermediate courses included in this study, Physical Meteorology and Dynamic Meteorology I emphasize quantitative reasoning more frequently than Synoptic Meteorology and Climate Dynamics. Preliminary results found that the majority of lecture slides in Physical Meteorology included explanations of meteorological phenomena using mathematical concepts, whereas 50% of the lecture slides in Synoptic Meteorology did. Further details regarding spatial skills and quantitative reasoning in assignments and assessments will also be presented, as well as connections between grades, use of quantitative reasoning, and measures of spatial thinking skills.

491806.title: Painless RGB Recipe Development Using GeoIPS
491806.authors: Shane Michael Ciardelli, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and E. Rose, G. Uttmark, and J. E. Solbrig
491806.abstract: This presentation will introduce a new set of plugins for the Geolocated Information Processing System (GeoIPS) implementing many different RGB recipes, and how the development of these plugins demonstrates reduced barriers for visualizing geolocated data according to standard RGB recipes. GeoIPS is an open-source Python framework that facilitates development of scientific algorithms. It comes with pre-installed plugins for recipe development, and because of its modular and open-source nature, new readers, writers, and workflows can be developed with minimal effort. Scientists who want to quickly and easily see certain RGB recipes applied to satellite data, as well those who wish to quickly test recipe ideas with real-world datasets, can leverage GeoIPS’ pre-developed infrastructure such as readers, interpolators, and output formatters. With this open-ended approach, over 90 different RGB recipes agreed upon by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) at the 2025 Norrkoping Workshop were implemented into one GeoIPS plugin package. These plugins support multiple satellite sensors, including ABI and SEVIRI. Even with this variability, each plugin runs on the same infrastructure, and required only a few minor tweaks to configure. GeoIPS plugins and plugin packages can be installed from GitHub and used in any GeoIPS instance. Right now, GeoIPS is used by the US Navy and Colorado State University, and assists in the rapid development of new algorithms and sensors for eventual transition to operational use.

491808.title: Radiation Environments during the Artemis Missions
491808.authors: Joseph Minow, NASA, Marshall Space Flight Center, Huntsville, AL
491808.abstract: Understanding and mitigating space radiation impacts on space system hardware is critical to ensure safe and successful human and robotic exploration missions to the Moon, Mars, and other planetary bodies. The Artemis missions to the Moon transit the Earth’s radiation belts on their way to and from the Moon, may be exposed to transient solar particle events (SPE) when outside the protective shield of the Earth’s magnetic field, and operate in the ever present background of penetrating, energetic galactic cosmic rays (GCR). This presentation will describe the radiation protection strategies used by NASA to mitigate the effects of space radiation on sensitive flight hardware for the Artemis missions to the Moon. First, we will discuss NASA’s natural environments definition standard—the M2M 30519, Design Specification for Natural Environments (DSNE)—which includes conservative radiation design environments. Flight hardware designed to meet or exceed the standard will be unlikely to ever experience more severe radiation environments during a mission. Next, we compare SPE and GCR environments during the Artemis I and II missions in 2022 and 2026, respectively, to show how the mission environments compared to the standard and discuss the radiation impacts on the missions. Finally, we will compare the DSNE SPE and GCR environments to more severe historical space weather events to show how the design environments compare to significant space weather events that have occurred in the past.

491810.title: How to Make a Cirrus Cloud: A Case Study of Novel Theory for Ice Microphysics within a Lagrangian Cloud Model
491810.authors: Julian Christopher Schima, Penn State University, University Park, PA; and K. K. Chandrakar, H. Morrison, and J. Y. Harrington
491810.abstract: The ingredients required to make a cirrus cloud are deceptively simple. A cirrus cloud generally requires a source of ice supersaturation at cirrus-like temperatures below -30°C, and ice nucleating particles (INP) upon which excess water vapor can deposit as ice. However, predicting the extent, radiative properties, and lifetime of cirrus clouds in a cloud model is a task that is anything but simple, due to uncertainty in the rates at which ice crystals will nucleate from INPs, grow or sublimate, fall, and absorb or scatter light. This uncertainty is magnified by the complex shapes (habits) of ice crystals. Historically, models have treated small ice crystals as spherical with capacitance theory, and an assumed bulk size distribution. These are necessary assumptions, but are not always physically realistic. However, in recent years, new theories have been developed that can treat the evolution of more realistic ice crystal shapes and growth processes. Further, with the development of Lagrangian particle-tracking schemes, the need to assume a bulk size distribution is eliminated, and properties of individual crystals can be preserved. With these developments, a path theoretically exists for convergence between model simulations of cirrus, and their real counterparts. In this work, we attempt to achieve such a convergence by implementing a new theory for depositional growth of ice in Cloud Model 1 (CM1), while also employing the Lagrangian “superdroplet method” (SDM). In contrast to the latest theory, we also run CM1 with bulk capacitance theory. To compare with observations of real cirrus, CM1 is initialized with a set of atmospheric conditions representative of one day of the Ice Cryo Encapsulation by Balloon (ICE-Ball) field campaign, a day in which widespread cirrus were observed. Modeled ice crystal shapes and sizes are viewed alongside environmental, cold-stage electron microscopic images of actual crystals collected during ICE-Ball. Remotely sensed properties of the cirrus, such as radar reflectivity, velocity, and spectral width, are quantitatively compared to observations from the Ka-Band Scanning ARM Cloud Radar (KASACAR) and a doppler lidar taken during the field campaign.

491811.title: Localized Ensemble Data Assimilation in Learned Spatial Latent Space
491811.authors: Xingchao Chen, The Pennsylvania State Univ., University Park, PA
491811.abstract: Latent-space data assimilation (DA) has emerged as a promising approach for exploiting learned low-dimensional structure of high-dimensional dynamical systems to improve DA performance. However, its advantages relative to well-designed ensemble DA remain unclear, because physical-space DA can be substantially improved through the tuning of inflation and covariance localization. Localization is also a central challenge for latent-space DA: strong compression can degrade autoencoder reconstruction and decoder accuracy, whereas weak compression may leave the latent dimension large enough for finite-ensemble sampling error to remain important. Moreover, many existing latent-space approaches use global latent vectors, for which spatial localization is not naturally defined. Here we develop localized ensemble latent-space DA methods. For global latent vectors, we introduce a serial update strategy that localizes decoded physical-space analysis increments. We also propose a spatial-latent approach in which a convolutional autoencoder preserves a coarsened spatial grid, enabling direct latent-space localization. Results show that localization improves latent-space DA performance for both global and spatial latent representations. Localized spatial-latent DA outperforms a physical-space DA even when inflation and localization are tuned for the physical-space DA. This advantage is robust in observation density/error and ensemble size sensitivity experiments. Diagnostics indicate that spatial latent variables reduce finite-ensemble sampling-error sensitivity while preserving spatial structure needed for meaningful localization. These results suggest spatially structured latent variables offer a practical compromise between dimension reduction and locality preservation, providing a pathway for improving ensemble DA in high-dimensional geophysical systems.

491815.title: Impact of Directly Assimilating GOES-16 ABI All-Sky Radiances on Hurricane Vortex Tilt Evolution and Subsequent Rapid Intensification: CADRE HAFS-JEDI System Development and a Case Study
491815.authors: Yue Yang, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and X. Wang
491815.abstract: Previous observational and simulation studies have found a close relationship between vortex tilt evolution and subsequent intensity change in relatively weak tropical cyclones (TCs). Accurately estimating the transition of vortex tilt from misalignment to alignment is crucial for TC rapid intensification (RI) forecasts. Vortex tilt is influenced by multiscale interactions between external environment forcing and the TC’s internal structure. The all-sky radiances (ASR) from the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) aboard the GOES-16 satellite can sample both the TC inner-core features and the ambient environment with high spatial and temporal resolution. ASR data assimilation (DA) has the potential to improve vortex initialization and its evolution, leading to more accurate RI forecasts. This study investigates the impact of directly assimilating ABI radiances using the ensemble–variational (EnVar) method within CADRE HAFS-JEDI, a Python-based workflow that integrates the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration framework (JEDI) into the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS). CADRE HAFS-JEDI is designed as a self-cycled, dual-resolution, regional convection-allowing system with various DA algorithms. As a starting point, the performance of assimilating clear-sky radiances (CSR) is examined to primarily improve the ambient environment for Hurricane Ida (2021). Results show the superiority of CSR DA in improving TC intensity forecasts, including two episodes of RI, as it captures the evolution of observed vortex tilt. Enhancing the assimilation of ASR to further improve the TC inner-core features requires additional efforts, such as specific quality control procedures and the use of brightness temperature as a state variable to avoid the cost function gradient imbalance. Results regarding the impact of directly assimilating ASR will be presented at the conference.

491819.title: The Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) Research, Development, and Product Roadmap
491819.authors: Robert A. Clark III, NOAA / OAR / National Severe Storms Laboratory, Norman, OK; and J. Zhang, C. Langston, K. Cooper, M. Taylor, S. Martinaitis, A. P. Osborne, J. A. Schultz, R. Silver, C. Pieper, and W. MacKenzie
491819.abstract: The Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system, jointly developed by NOAA’s National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) and the University of Oklahoma’s Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), produces high-quality, rapidly-updating analyses of various atmospheric conditions for a wide range of stakeholders across the weather enterprise. The system has been operational at the NWS since the fall of 2014, with regular updates incorporating new science and technology developed and deployed by NSSL and CIWRO. As part of the NWS Transformation, NSSL will be supporting an effort to migrate the operational version of MRMS into the NWS Enterprise Cloud. In parallel, NSSL is also supporting the NWS’s Radar Next Program’s planning for the follow-on to the existing network of WSR-88Ds operated by the NEXRAD program. In this talk, we will lay out a current high-level roadmap encompassing MRMS’s research and development activities in support of the Radar Next Program, the NWS Transformation, and NSSL and CIWRO priorities. New MRMS products and capabilities are planned for prototyping and eventual deployment into operations and will be described. Associated MRMS R&D activities include exploration of new sensor networks for incorporation into the system and new techniques for successfully merging and mosaicking these sensors into existing products. Plans for the transition of the operational MRMS into the NWS Enterprise Cloud will also be described. Finally, we will present an associated timeline of key milestones.

491821.title: Out with the Old, In with the New? Evaluating Artificial Intelligence Weather Models for Circulation Regime Forecasting
491821.authors: Rohan Shroff, Prescient Weather, Chantilly, VA; and J. Ross and R. James
491821.abstract: Over the last several years, meteorologists and decision makers have rapidly adopted Artificial Intelligence (AI) based weather models alongside traditional dynamical (physics-based) models, a result of their rapidly improving capabilities and ease of accessibility. Furthermore, a substantial body of verification work has shown these models can match or exceed the skill of dynamical models on standard grid point metrics (RMSE, CRPS). However, less is known regarding the performance of AI-based weather models in large-scale circulation regime forecasting. Regimes, also referred to as circulation regimes, classify the 500 mb circulation pattern over a particular region into predefined categories that describe typical modes of behavior. By allowing forecasters to quickly categorize the most likely 500 mb flow pattern for a particular day or date, regimes are a powerful tool to help understand the likely state of the atmosphere and determine the probable weather impacts. For this work, we evaluate the performance of dynamical models (ECMWF, GEFS, GEPS) and AI models (AIFS, WxNext2, Aurora) for regime forecasting using both Simon Lee’s and Christian Grams’ regime frameworks. Forecasts are verified against ERA5 regime truth with the multicategory Brier Skill Score (BSS), alongside reliability diagrams computed both overall and per regime. We separately test, for ECMWF, whether substituting the model's own hindcast forecast climatology for the ERA5 reanalysis climatology as the reference affects skill. Finally, motivated by the established "windows of opportunity" framework for flow-dependent predictability, we search for lead times, active regimes, and teleconnection phases (e.g., MJO) at which the AI ensemble's relative skill against the dynamical ensembles is systematically higher or lower. Preliminary results indicate that AI models are competitive with dynamical models and maintain their competitiveness for the entire evaluation period (days 0 to 15). We will present results quantifying the skill of AI weather models for regime forecasting, discuss skill changes that arise from using ECMWF’s own climatology instead of ERA5 and the potential applications to AI models, and finally identify any windows of opportunity where AI weather model skill exceeds that of dynamical models.

491822.title: Evaluating VOC Reactivity and Ozone Production In Houston, TX: Insights from Airborne Observations and Photochemical Box Modeling
491822.authors: Chelsea Stockwell, NOAA, Longmont, CO; and S. Albertin, K. Bates, M. J. Carter, M. M. Coggon, W. S. Chace, C. Womack, N. Schafer, S. S. Brown, A. Rollins, I. B. Pollack, J. Gilman, A. Middlebrook, A. G. Negron, S. Baidar, R. Alvarez II, B. J. Carroll, M. W. Holloway, S. Sandberg, R. Marchbanks, and C. Warneke
491822.abstract: Ground-level ozone (O3) formation in the Greater Houston metropolitan area is driven by complex photochemical evolution of emissions from urban, industrial, and biogenic sources. While long-term control strategies have reduced regional peak ozone levels over the past two decades, determining the present-day sensitivity of O3 production to changing emissions is possible using observation-based photochemical modeling. In this study, high-resolution in situ trace gas and volatile organic compound (VOC) measurements collected aboard research aircraft during the recent 2026 Texas Air Quality Study as part of the larger NOAA Airborne and Remote sensing Multi Air Pollutant Surveys (AiRMAPS) are used to constrain a zero-dimensional photochemical box model. By integrating measured VOC species and nitrogen oxides (NOx), we evaluate total hydroxyl radical (OH) reactivity, model instantaneous ozone production rates, and identify key VOC species driving photochemistry across mixed urban and industrial plumes. To assess decadal shifts in regional photochemistry, these observationally constrained simulations are compared against chemical conditions measured during the 2006 Texas Air Quality Study (TexAQS 2006). We will investigate how both the primary emissions and chemistry have changed between the two campaigns. Preliminary modeling results highlighting dominant VOC reactivity drivers and updated chemical regime indicators will be presented.

491823.title: Probing kappa-Köhler Equivalence in the Pi Convection-Cloud Chamber
491823.authors: Kristin Joy Swartz-Schult, University of Notre Dame, South Bend, IN
491823.abstract: Weather and climate models employ significant simplifying assumptions in representing cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and their turbulent environment. These assumptions affect their ability to accurately capture aerosol-cloud interactions, and, subsequently, cloud droplet size distributions (DSDs), among other cloud properties. In this work, we focus on one such assumption — that aerosols of differing size and hygroscopicity, but theoretically matching kappa-Köhler activation characteristics, behave identically as CCN under the same supersaturation forcing. To do this, we utilized the Pi Convection-Cloud Chamber at Michigan Technological University to generate steady-state warm clouds using aerosols which, according to kappa-Köhler theory, have identical critical supersaturations: 70 nm NaCl, 200 nm phthalic acid, and 125 nm maleic acid. Additionally, we measured the residuals and interstitials during steady state and cloud decay for a heterogenous mix of CCN (70 nm NaCl and 200 nm phthalic acid) in order to determine if one aerosol type preferentially activates over the other. Preliminary assessment suggests subtle but systematic differences in the DSDs between the three Köhler-equivalent CCN, whereas the theory would predict identical DSDs. This talk will present analysis of the experimental results, including the ensemble-averaged steady-state DSDs for each CCN along with a comparison of the ratio of NaCl to phthalic acid upon injection, in activated droplets, and in interstitials during the steady state and decay phase. Further, the results of direct numerical simulations (DNS) designed to mirror the experimental configuration will be considered and compared to experimental data.

491824.title: From Air Quality Prediction to Public Health Action: Neighborhood Ozone Forecasting for Environmental Justice Communities
491824.authors: Divyansh Kumar, Montgomery Blair High School, Silver Spring, MD
491824.abstract: Environmental justice communities often experience disproportionate air pollution burdens and associated respiratory and cardiovascular risks. Yet regional ozone forecasts can mask neighborhood scale differences in air quality and health risk. This study developed and evaluated a machine learning forecasting system for four monitoring locations relevant to environmental justice communities in the Washington, D.C., metropolitan region. Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression, and a CNN–bidirectional LSTM with attention mechanism were trained on March–October data from 2017–2019 and 2022 and independently tested on 2023. Hyperparameters were selected using Bayesian optimization with five-fold time-series cross-validation. The models predicted ozone one hour ahead using either a 1-hour input window or a rolling 24-hour input window containing meteorological variables, temporal indicators, and ozone lagged by 24 hours. For each target day, 24 hourly predictions were combined to calculate the daily maximum 8-hour-average ozone concentration and corresponding AQI and color category. The best performing model was selected separately for each site. XGBoost with a 1-hour input performed best at McMillan, XGBoost with a 24-hour input at Prince George’s Equestrian Center, and Random Forest with a 24-hour input at HU-Beltsville and Rockville. Selected models achieved test R² values of 0.71–0.86, and the 24-hour configuration performed slightly better at three of four locations. Compared with the official regional forecast, the site-specific models improved agreement with observed AQI color categories by 8–24 percentage points, depending on location. Because the site-specific gains over a common 24-hour Random Forest configuration were small, a uniform Random Forest approach was used in the automated research forecasting system to simplify implementation and maintain a consistent workflow across sites. The automated system retrieves recent ozone observations and forecast meteorology, constructs site-specific inputs, produces 24 hourly ozone forecasts for the target day, calculates the maximum 8-hour value, AQI category and associated color code, and updates a public website. Rare high ozone episodes were challenging. Among only 2–8 Code Orange or worse days per site in the 2023 test set, none were classified into their observed AQI category. On three wildfire related ozone days, forecasts across the four sites underestimated observed daily maximum 8-hour ozone by 5–35 ppb, with a mean actual-minus-predicted bias of +19 ppb and AQI-category agreement of only 8.3%. These results highlight the need to improve rare event performance, with upwind ozone observations, smoke indicators, and wind trajectory information representing promising additions for health relevant high ozone forecasting.

491828.title: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible Trend Analysis of Long-Term Atmospheric Observations
491828.authors: Adam Theisen, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, IL; and N. L. Hickmon and S. Collis
491828.abstract: Long-term atmospheric observing facilities produce measurement records that continue to grow over decades, creating valuable opportunities to evaluate environmental variability, identify persistent trends, and compare conditions across sites and time periods. However, traditional publications provide only a fixed snapshot of an evolving observational record. As new data becomes available, analyses can quickly become outdated, while differences in processing, completeness criteria, data quality, and visualization methods can make results difficult to reproduce or extend. We present an open-source framework for reproducible trend analysis using observations from the U.S. Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility. Implemented through a GitHub repository, the framework provides standardized and version-controlled workflows for generating monthly and annual statistical summaries, seasonal-cycle analyses, long-term trend estimates, user-defined baseline comparisons, and departures from reference-period averages. Over 40,000 files from ARM are processed into quality controlled Zarr data stores for easy analysis and statistics generation. The repository is designed to function as a maintained scientific reference rather than a static collection of figures. Periodic releases incorporate new observations, methodological improvements, additional variables, and new locations while preserving previous versions for transparency, reproducibility, and citation. The repository serves both as an analysis framework and as an evolving record of the scientific interpretation of ARM’s long-term measurements. A companion interactive dashboard extends these capabilities by allowing users to evaluate trends, select baseline periods, examine seasonal behaviour, and compare variables. Together, the repository and dashboard provide a consistent pathway from quality-aware data aggregation to reproducible analysis and interactive exploration.

491832.title: Impacts of Sensible Heat Flux Modifications in Urban Areas on the Development of Afternoon Thunderstorms
491832.authors: Tetsuya Takemi, Kyoto University, Uji, 26, Japan; Kyoto Univ., Japan, Kyoto, Japan; and M. Tanaka and S. Tanji
491832.abstract: In urban areas with high-rise and densely distributed buildings, highly turbulent flows are generated, which affects sensible heat flux from urban surfaces to the overlying boundary layer. Furthermore, such heat transfer is considered to affect the development of isolated thunderstorms during the daytime because of the modifications of the urban heat flux. In Irie and Takemi (2025, Theoretical and Applied Climatology), it was demonstrated that constantly reducing the sensible heat fluxes from urban surfaces by 10% resulted in the reductions in accumulated rainfall by 18% and in peak rainfall by 13% through the stabilization of the urban boundary layer due to the sensible heat reduction. This study numerically investigates the sensitivity of the development of isolated thunderstorms and precipitation to changes in the heat release from urban surfaces within a limited time period. The Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model are used to conduct a set of numerical experiments in which sensible heat flux within a limited area having urban land use is systematically changed within a limited time period. Cases of the afternoon thunderstorm development in the Osaka metropolitan area in Japan during the summertime are chosen. Different from the numerical experiments conducted in Irie and Takemi (2025), this study examines the changes in the time duration of the reduction in the urban heat flux and the impacts of the changes in the duration on the convective development. In changing the sensible heat flux, a certain percentage of the original flux is reduced within a limited time. It is found that reducing the sensible heat flux, only by 10% relative to the original flux, just before the development of isolated thunderstorms in the afternoon effectively decreases the intensity and amount of local-scale precipitation in urban areas. In addition, it is shown that the reduction of the heat flux for the duration of only one hour significantly affects the precipitation. Increasing the reduction rate of the heat flux leads to the gradual enhancement of the decrease in the precipitation intensity and amount. The impacts of the sensible heat modifications in urban areas on the convective development appear because of the stability changes in the urban boundary layer and hence the suppression of the cumulus development.

491834.title: Trends of Variability in Pennsylvania’s Growing Season Length and Diurnal Temperature Range
491834.authors: Ciaran Murphy, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA; and S. Baugh
491834.abstract: Growing Season Length (GSL) is a crucial metric of atmospheric influence on global agriculture. This project seeks to identify trends in GSL Variability (GSLV) and understand GSL’s ties to Diurnal Temperature Range (DTR) and other variables, using observational and reanalysis data from 180 stations in Pennsylvania. To guide this analysis, we evaluated four hypotheses: we expect (1) stations with large DTR values to have smaller GSL, (2) GSLV to decrease over time, (3) GSLV to decrease as DTR values increase, and (4) mean temperature to mediate the impact of DTR on GSLV. Using Bayesian heteroskedastic regression modeling, GSLV was found to decrease by 26.75% (Credible Interval, CI: 12.73– 38.58%) from 1960 to 2025. Additionally, contrary to hypothesis (3), GSLV was found to increase by 13.07% (CI: 9.78 – 16.48%). Finally, a DTR increase of 1°C was found to decrease GSL by 9.51 days (CI: 8.76 – 10.26 days) and mean temperature was not found to mediate DTR’s impact on GSLV more than other covariates. This work provides a baseline understanding of trends in GSLV, and these results can be used for future research on forecasting GSL to aid agricultural sustainability and food security in a changing world. Keywords: Growing Season Length, Growing Season Length Variability, Diurnal Temperature Range

491839.title: Field-Deployable Ground-Based High Spectral Resolution Lidar for Range-Resolved Aerosol Monitoring of Fire Emissions
491839.authors: Dylan Joseph Maxwell, Montana State University, BOZEMAN, MT; Montana State University-Bozeman, BOZEMAN, MT; and K. S. Repasky and L. Colberg
491839.abstract: The design of a ground-based high spectral resolution lidar (HSRL) is presented. The instrument architecture utilizes a diode-laser-based architecture that transmits 780 nm light. Scattered light is collected using a 40 cm diameter telescope. The optical receiver uses two separate channels with photon-counting avalanche photodiodes: the first measures the total backscatter signal, and the second uses a rubidium atomic vapor cell as a spectral filter. This second channel allows the molecularly scattered signal to be determined. The HSRL is housed in an environmentally controlled enclosure for field deployments and provides eye-safe operation at the exit of the environmental housing. The HSRL instrument provides vertical profiles of the backscatter ratio (ratio of the total backscatter to the molecular backscatter) with a 37.5 m range resolution and a five-minute averaging time. Data collected at Montana State University will be presented demonstrating the instrument capabilities. Data from the HSRL instrument will be combined with data products from the NOAA High-Resolution Rapid Refresh model. NASA satellite images, a co-located AERONET instrument, and local air quality monitoring will be presented showing the long-range transport of wildfire smoke, the entrainment of the smoke within the mixing layer, and the effects of the smoke on air quality. Finally, a brief discussion on the planned future deployment of the instrument at controlled burns will be presented.

491840.title: Investigating Boundary Layer Transitions Using Observations and Data Assimilation During JCRDP and COURAGE 2025 Field Campaigns
491840.authors: Zhifeng Yang, Howard University, Beltsville, DC; Howard Univ., Beltsville, DC; and S. Chiao, N. N. Karle, R. K. Sakai, A. Flores, B. Demoz, and R. D. Rossi
491840.abstract: This study aims to advance our understanding of the evolution of the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) during transitions between daytime and nighttime, as well as between urban and suburban environments, strongly influences weather forecasts, especially during extreme events, e.g., heat waves. This study utilized data collected from the Joint Collaborative Research and Development Project (JCRDP, 14 July - 03 August 2025) and the Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE, December 2024 - November 2025) field campaigns in the Baltimore-Washington metropolitan area during. The campaigns provided a comprehensive set of high-resolution observations, including radiosonde profiles, ceilometer backscatter profiles, microwave radiometer temperature and humidity retrievals, and continuous surface measurements. In this study, we investigate boundary layer structure and dynamics during diurnal and urban-suburban transitions, focusing on vertical mixing, stratification, and pollutant transport. MPAS-JEDI and WRF-Chem/DART are employed to assimilate radiosonde, ceilometer, tower and other observations to improve the representation of ABL evolution. Comparisons between baseline and assimilation experiments highlight the impact of integrated observations on capturing boundary layer height, stability transitions. Preliminary results show that assimilating high-frequency profiles significantly improves the timing and intensity of daytime boundary layer growth and evening collapse. The findings demonstrate the critical role of dense observational networks and advanced data assimilation for resolving boundary layer processes in complex urban-suburban regions. This work contributes to ongoing efforts to advance understanding of diurnal boundary layer transitions and to improve forecasting capabilities in metropolitan regions.

491841.title: Higher-Order Mean Temperature Profile In the Convective Atmospheric Boundary Layer
491841.authors: Abdul Haseeb Syed, Clemson University, Clemson, SC; and C. Tong and K. V. Barskov
491841.abstract: The leading-order scaling of mean potential temperature profiles in the convective atmospheric boundary layer is well established within the Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory (MOST) framework. The dimensionless mean potential temperature gradient in the surface layer is scaled using the height above the surface (z), the Obukhov length (L), and the temperature scale (Θ*). The resulting stability function (Φh) depends on the stability parameter (z/L). Several empirical formulations for the temperature-gradient leading-order scaling have been introduced using experimental data. However, theoretical predictions beyond leading order are still lacking. In this study, we apply the method of matched asymptotic expansions to derive the higher-order temperature profile for the mean temperature in the convective atmospheric boundary layer. We identify an outer region (scales with zi, the boundary layer height), an inner-outer region (scales with -L), and an inner-inner region (scales with ho, the thermal roughness length). The three scaling layers form a singular perturbation problem. The asymptotic matching between the outer and inner-outer regions yields the leading-order scaling (-z/L)-1/3 of the local free-convection layer and higher-order scalings: (-z/L)-5/3, ε3' (-z/L)-1, ε3' (-z/L)1/3, ... where ε3'= (-zi/L)-2/3. The matching between the inner-outer and inner-inner layers produces the leading-order surface-layer scaling of ln(z/h0) and higher-order scalings: ε3'' (z/h0), ε3''2 (z/h0)2, ..., where ε3'' = h0 / (-L). We validate the theoretical predictions using unstable boundary-layer datasets from two measurement campaigns: the M^2HATS field campaign at Tonopah Valley in Nevada, conducted from July to September 2023 and the classic 1973 Minnesota Boundary Layer Experiment. In the surface layer (z/(-L) < 1), both sites yield an excellent fit to the expansion form, with both leading and higher-order coefficients well determined. The inferred thermal von Karman constant differs between the two sites (0.39 at M2HATS and 0.46 at Minnesota) due to site-specific characteristics and possible differences in Prandtl number. For the local free-convection layer, only the Minnesota temperature profiles were used due to the availability of suitable data. The fit with the campaign data showed a good agreement with the derived leading and higher-order scaling terms. This validation signifies the value of extending the MOST framework beyond the leading-order scaling. It also demonstrates that the method of matched asymptotic expansions provides a physics-based framework for deducing higher-order corrections with high certainty.

491845.title: The Storms Without Names - Translating Everyday Weather into Healthcare Emergency Management Decisions
491845.authors: Arthur B. Ditzel Jr., WMCHealth Good Samaritan Hospital, Suffern, NY; WMCHealth Good Samaritan Hospital, Suffern, NY
491845.abstract: Hurricanes Katrina and Sandy fundamentally changed how emergency managers think about healthcare preparedness, response, evacuation, infrastructure resilience, communications, and continuity of operations. These historic storms became case studies that continue to influence emergency planning decades later. Yet most weather-related disruptions affecting healthcare will never receive a name, a presidential disaster declaration, or national media coverage. They are winter storms, extreme heat and cold, heavy rainfall, high winds, thunderstorms, flooding, drought, poor air quality, and combinations of otherwise routine weather hazards. Individually, these events may not appear extraordinary. Within a healthcare system, however, even an ordinary weather event can create extraordinary operational consequences. For healthcare emergency managers, the forecast is only the beginning of the decision-making process. A forecast of six inches of snow is meteorological information. The emergency management question is what those six inches mean for hospital operations. Will road conditions deteriorate during shift change? Can staff safely reach the hospital? Will ambulances experience longer response and transport times? Will oxygen, pharmaceuticals, food, linen, and other critical supplies arrive? Can patients scheduled for discharge safely return home? Will outpatient healthcare services close and shift additional demand toward the emergency department? Similar translations occur across weather hazards. Extreme heat creates concerns involving electrical demand, HVAC reliability, medically vulnerable populations, patient surge, and staff safety. Heavy rainfall can affect transportation routes, facility infrastructure, EMS access, staffing, and supply chains. High winds introduce concerns involving utility failures, communications, generator operations, and transportation. Wildfire smoke and poor air quality can affect respiratory patient volumes, building filtration systems, outdoor operations, and community healthcare demand. The challenge becomes even greater when hazards combine. Snow accompanied by high winds, extreme cold, and utility interruptions presents a fundamentally different healthcare risk than any of those hazards considered independently. This presentation examines weather events from the perspective of a healthcare emergency manager and explores the critical translation that occurs between weather information and operational action. Using lessons from major named disasters alongside examples of the more frequent “storms without names,” the presentation will demonstrate a simple operational progression: Effective emergency management requires more than knowing what the weather will be. Emergency managers need to understand when conditions will begin to affect operations, how rapidly they may deteriorate, the confidence associated with the forecast, the reasonable worst-case scenario, and when improved information will become available. These factors influence decisions including Emergency Operations Center or Incident Management Team activation, staffing adjustments, resource staging, continuity measures, alternate communications, supply-chain actions, patient movement, and coordination with community partners. A forecast indicating four to eight inches of snow may describe the expected hazard, but the healthcare emergency manager may need a different question answered: Will the 7:00 a.m. shift be able to reach the hospital? That distinction illustrates the importance of the relationship between meteorologists and emergency managers. Weather data becomes most valuable when it helps decision-makers understand not simply what may occur, but when operational consequences are likely to develop and what uncertainty exists around those consequences. Historic disasters such as Hurricanes Katrina and Sandy provide essential lessons about healthcare resilience, evacuation, infrastructure, communications, logistics, and continuity. However, the value of those lessons is not limited to preparing for the next catastrophic hurricane. They should inform decisions made during the winter storm next month, the heat wave next summer, or the heavy rainfall expected tomorrow. Healthcare operates continuously, regardless of weather. Hospitals cannot simply close when conditions deteriorate, and many healthcare services become more important precisely when community infrastructure is under stress. This creates a unique requirement for healthcare emergency managers to continuously translate meteorological information into operational risk. Most of these events will never become historic disasters. They will not receive memorable names or dominate national news. But they will disrupt transportation, challenge infrastructure, affect staffing, increase patient demand, strain EMS and healthcare resources, and require emergency managers to make consequential decisions with incomplete information. These are the storms without names; and they are where much of emergency management actually happens.

491847.title: Development of a New Balloon-Based Electrostatic Aerosol Sampler for the Collection of Upper Tropospheric Ice Nucleating Particles.
491847.authors: Ryan Patnaude, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and J. Schwarz
491847.abstract: Direct measurements of ice-nucleating particles (INPs) in cirrus clouds remain limited, leading to uncertainties in predictions of cirrus cloud formation and radiative effects. Previous investigations of cirrus INPs have included targeted laboratory studies of known aerosol sources and airborne measurements of ice crystal residuals. In this study, we report on the development of a small, lightweight, and low-power aerosol sampler designed for deployment aboard weather balloons to collect aerosol particles relevant to cirrus ice nucleation. We discuss the major challenges associated with this approach, including optimizing airflow and aerosol collection efficiency at low pressure and minimizing aerosol contamination at the surface and outside of cirrus-relevant atmospheric conditions through sealed sampling surfaces and careful preparation of the sampler before and after balloon launches. Finally, we present initial sampler designs and results from experimental testing.

491853.title: A Climatology of Convection Initiation Attempts Associated with the Dryline
491853.authors: Michael J. Hosek, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; and P. S. Skinner
491853.abstract: Drylines are a key mechanism for convection initiation (CI) in the central United States. Forecasting dryline CI, even at short timescales, is a significant challenge. A climatological dataset of all dryline-associated CI attempts is presented for spring 2015-2025. FrontFinder AI applied to hourly ERA5 reanalysis is employed to identify drylines and fronts, and 5-minute MRMS data is used to track CI objects (radar reflectivity exceeding 20 dBZ) and storm objects (exceeding 40 dBZ) which develop within the dryline CI region. Statistics including the distribution of CI attempt frequency and success rate, the location and timing of CI attempts, and related storm outcomes (longevity, association with NWS-issued warnings and severe storm reports) will be presented. Environmental conditions, including dryline characteristics, will be compared between successful and failed dryline CI attempts to begin an investigation into factors influencing dryline CI outcomes that may be useful in forecasting.

491855.title: Improving Shortwave Radiation Prediction in WRF During Winter Storms: A Microphysics-Based Correction of Snow Optical Properties in Thompson–RRTMG
491855.authors: Fatemeh Azizpourshoubi, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; and U. Khaira, B. Filipiak, and M. Astitha
491855.abstract: Bulk microphysics schemes supply hydrometeor effective radii to the radiation scheme, so the simulated cloud and precipitation optical properties depend directly on how particle sizes are represented. In the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, the Thompson microphysics scheme paired with the Rapid Radiative Transfer Model for General Circulation Models (RRTMG) shortwave scheme exhibits a persistent positive bias in downwelling shortwave radiation (SWDOWN) during winter storms over the Northeastern United States. This bias is not confined to the surface energy budget: because near-surface temperature responds to SWDOWN, an overestimate can shift the model's precipitation-type diagnosis from snow to rain, which in turn suppresses predicted snowfall accumulation. We trace the bias to how the snow effective radius supplied to radiation is diagnosed from the Thompson scheme's assumed snow size distribution. Because this effective radius is dominated by the sparse population of large snow aggregates, it is too large and underestimates the snow optical depth, particularly in heavy snow. We develop physically based corrections that recompute the snow optical properties from the underlying size distribution, increasing the snow optical depth seen by RRTMG and reducing the solar radiation transmitted to the surface. Evaluation against surface stations and satellite-derived irradiance across multiple Northeastern U.S. winter storms demonstrates a substantial reduction in SWDOWN bias, with improved correlation and root-mean-square error relative to the standard configuration. By correcting the microphysics–radiation coupling, the approach also reduces precipitation-type misclassification and improves predicted snowfall.

491857.title: Summer Drying over the Pacific Northwest (1982-2024)
491857.authors: Sara Rauscher, University of Delaware, NEWARK, DE; and A. P. Williams
491857.abstract: Regional precipitation change due to increased greenhouse gases is difficult to observe and quantify due to its spatial and temporal heterogeneity. In the Pacific Northwest (PNW) of the United States and Canada, the summer season is its driest, particularly inland of the Olympic Mountains, the Oregon Coastal Range, and the Cascades. We report on a statistically significant late spring and summer drying trend over the Pacific Northwest of the United States and Canada first documented by Holden et al. (2018) for the US. This drying has persisted from 1982 through 2024 and it is consistent among four observed precipitation datasets (NOAA's nClimGrid-Daily Version 1, Climate Prediction Center's Unified Gauge-Based Analysis of Global Daily Precipitation, Combined Merged Analysis of Precipitation, and the Global Historical Climate Network stations), the ERA5 reanalysis, and the NASA/DLR Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and NASA/GFZ Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-On (GRACE-FO). Drying occurs in May through August, with the largest drying trends in July. The drying extends from the US PNW eastward to Montana and northward to British Columbia and Alberta, Canada. The ERA5 reanalysis shows a similar drying pattern peaking in July. Analysis of the three water cycle components (precipitation, evaporation, and vertically integrated moisture convergence) using ERA5 indicates reductions in moisture convergence dominate along the coast while evaporation reductions contribute to drying in the interior east of the coastal mountain ranges. Further, evaporation is declining faster than precipitation alone predicts based on a regression analysis of evaporation and precipitation, suggesting that evaporation is limited by supply (i.e., the available moisture at the surface and subsurface). This is supported by a significant decrease in water storage from 2002-2024 across Washington State and southern British Columbia and Alberta from the GRACE and GRACE-FO data. These precipitation and water storage changes are associated with an increasing trend in 500 hPa geopotential heights over the eastern Pacific and West Coast of North America and lower heights further inland over the interior US and Saskatchewan and Alberta. Winds at all levels have become more northerly along the coast and inland from 200 hPa down to 850 hPa. The circulation trends suggest ridging events are associated with the drying. Therefore, we assess the frequency and length (in days) of West Coast ridging events and the number of ridge days (days when there is a ridge event present). Ridges have been present on more days over the eastern Pacific, and the length of the 90th percentile ridging event has increased by three days over the 43 year period. Meanwhile, ridge days have decreased further inland. The decrease in late spring and summer precipitation and water storage over parts of the Pacific Northwest and longer 90th percentile ridging events are concerning since summer drying can exacerbate droughts and lead to water restrictions, particularly in the drier interior of the PNW. They are also associated with heatwaves and enhanced forest fire activity. A question remains as to what is driving these trends - do they represent the effects of internal atmospheric variability or greenhouse forcing? The Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), an El Niño-like pattern of sea surface temperature variability, largely affects winter PNW precipitation. Regardless, during the 1980s the PDO was positive, and in the 2020s, it was in a negative phase. The positive phase is associated with drying over the PNW, and the negative phase is associated with higher precipitation, contrary to the trends shown here. As for greenhouse gas forcing, our results are consistent with CMIP5 and CMIP6 model projections for more frequent and longer-lasting summer ridging events over the PNW in the 21st century and historical CMIP6 simulations, but the forcing mechanisms may not be the same. Further investigation is necessary to determine what, if anything, is forcing these trends. Holden, Z. A., Swanson, A., Luce, C. H., Jolly, W. M., Maneta, M., Oyler, J. W., R. Parsons, and Affleck, D. (2018). Decreasing fire season precipitation increased recent western us forest wildfire activity. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115 (36), E8349-E8357. Image Caption: Decadal precipitation trend for May (left), June (left center), July (right center), and August (right) for GHCN (a-d), nCLMGRD (e-h), CPC (i-l), and CMAP (m-p) in mm/day/decade. For a-d, trends are significant when station circles are outlined in black; for e-p, stippled areas are significant. Stipple spacing for gridded datasets has been thinned for a target spacing between stipple dots in degrees, independent of native resolution. Brown shading indicates a negative trend in precipitation, and green shading indicates a positive trend.

491859.title: Development of a New ICESat-2 Atmospheric Research Product: Daytime Denoising, Feature Subtyping, and Planetary Boundary Layer Height Retrievals
491859.authors: Kenneth Christian, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and P. Selmer, N. Midzak, J. E. Yorks, A. Cresanti, J. Gomes, and M. J. McGill
491859.abstract: Spaceborne lidar observations provide a unique capability for observing the vertical structure of clouds and aerosols, which is critical in understanding the Earth’s radiative balance, improving weather forecast models, and monitoring global air quality. Following the retirements of the Cloud-Aerosol Lidar and Infrared Pathfinder Satellite Observations (CALIPSO) and Cloud-Aerosol Transport System (CATS) missions, the Ice, Cloud, and Land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) is currently NASA’s only operational space-based lidar providing atmospheric profiles. However, because ICESat-2 was primarily designed for cryospheric and surface elevation measurements, its atmospheric capabilities face limitations such as poor daytime signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) and a lack of linear depolarization measurements, which restrict its utility for atmospheric research and applications. To overcome these constraints and improve upon the current atmospheric product, we have developed a new ICESat-2 atmospheric research product. This enhanced product introduces advanced daytime denoising techniques to mitigate low SNR, allowing for the retrieval of planetary boundary layer (PBL) height. Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Application, version 2 (MERRA-2) reanalysis data is incorporated to allow for feature subtyping capabilities (cloud phase and aerosol type) enabling layer optical depths to be retrieved using established lidar ratios. Initial evaluation of the derived aerosol classifications across major regimes such as marine aerosols, North African dust, and West African biomass burning areas shows strong similarities to those derived from CALIPSO observations. Additionally, comparisons with Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) aerosol optical depths show favorable agreement in both magnitude and spatial distribution. Ultimately, this expanded research product enhances the scientific utility of ICESat-2 observations, providing critical continuity in atmospheric measurements between legacy missions, the Earth Cloud, Aerosol, and Radiation Explorer (EarthCARE), and future spaceborne lidars.

491860.title: FrontFinder 2.0: Updating a UNet for Identification of Baroclinic Boundaries in NOAA's Unified Surface Analysis Domain
491860.authors: Taylor S. Mandelbaum, Brightband, Nyack, NY
491860.abstract: Locating baroclinic boundaries is a complex process that involves a combination of lower-tropospheric observations, multiple scales of meteorological phenomena, and a human forecaster’s intuition in interpreting these inputs. In forecasting organizations such as NOAA’s National Weather Service, forecasters apply their knowledge to estimate these boundaries, drawing them manually onto a map. Determining these boundaries is time-consuming, and in some organizations meteorologists are required to produce maps as often as every three hours. FrontFinder, a UNet-based machine learning model, provides a probabilistic output to guide the process of where to locate and draw these boundaries and is in use operationally at several NOAA centers. We introduce FrontFinder v2.0, which builds on the original FrontFinder to locate boundaries, including cold fronts, warm fronts, occluded fronts, stationary fronts, and drylines and adds other boundaries including troughs, tropical troughs, and instability axes. FrontFinder v2.0 also utilizes a proper scoring rule, the neighborhood brier score, as the loss function to approximate the target distribution and to avoid the risk of hedging towards a certain outcome. Combined with an updated training dataset, the updated model improved on the existing FrontFinder's metrics such as probability of detection, critical success index, and false alarm ratio. A case study is provided showing the evolution of a significant mid-latitude cyclone within the contiguous United States (CONUS). Given the intent of this model to make decisions of consequence, we approach all aspects of the project - data, code, and model outputs - in a transparent and strictly governed manner with the goal of upholding FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles.
