491864.title: The Operational Verification of NWS Chemical and Transport Models
491864.authors: Ho-Chun Huang, Lynker at the NOAA/NWS/OMD, Leesburg, VA; Lynker at the NOAA/NWS/OMD, Leesburg, VA; and A. M. Bentley, A. Benjamin, and M. P. Row
491864.abstract: As wildfire activity has increased in recent years, wildfire smoke has not only impacted the health of communities near the source areas but has also degraded air quality in downwind regions far from the fires. The National Weather Service (NWS) has developed global and regional chemical and transport models to predict air pollutants originating from both anthropogenic and natural sources, including wind-blown dust, thereby mitigating adverse public health and economic impacts. To assess the performance of these models, the NWS Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) developed the Evaluation and Verification System (EVS). The EVS serves as a daily monitoring tool to detect model dropouts and provides a foundation for future model enhancements. Additionally, it establishes a common platform for inter-comparing the performance of various models within the NWS operational modeling suite. This presentation will discuss EVS verification methodologies alongside the diverse observational sources utilized to evaluate each model based on temporal availability and model products. The location of the publicly accessible verification websites and illustrative verification graphics featuring standard performance metrics will also be presented.

491871.title: Top-Down Estimates of Ammonia Emissions In China Using FY-4B/GIIRS Observations
491871.authors: Yixuan Gu, Nanjing Univeristy of Information Science and Technology, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China; and D. K. Henze, Z. C. Zeng, Z. Chen, and H. Liao
491871.abstract: Ammonia (NH3) is a key precursor of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), yet its emissions remain highly uncertain because of substantial spatial and temporal variability in sources. Geostationary satellite observations provide an emerging opportunity to constrain NH3 emissions with comprehensive observational information at high temporal frequency. Here, we develop monthly top-down estimates of NH3 emissions over China using observations from the Geostationary Interferometric Infrared Sounder (GIIRS) onboard the FengYun-4B (FY-4B) satellite. GIIRS NH3 retrievals are assimilated into the GEOS-Chem chemical transport model using an adjoint-based inverse modeling framework. The geostationary observing capability of GIIRS provides multiple observations per day over China, enabling improved characterization of the spatial and temporal variability of atmospheric NH3 compared with conventional polar-orbiting satellite measurements. Monthly inversions are conducted throughout 2023 and the resulting posterior emissions are evaluated against GIIRS observations and compared with prior bottom-up emission inventories to identify regions and seasons with systematic emission discrepancies.

491872.title: Key Considerations for Modernizing AWC Convective SIGMETs
491872.authors: Jilliann A. Dufort, CIWRO, Norman, OK; and J. Godwin and B. A. Smith
491872.abstract: Convective SIGMETs (C-SIGs) are issued hourly by NOAA/NWS Aviation Weather Center (AWC) forecasters to highlight regions where convective weather will be hazardous to flights. Typically, a single forecaster is responsible for issuing and updating several polygons within the hour; however, polygon issuance can increase substantially during summertime convection. Therefore, discussions with the AWC and FAA are underway to determine if and how C-SIGs can be modernized to assist forecaster workflow. Here, we will provide an overview of the proposed changes and cover the important factors that must be addressed before they can be implemented. One proposed modernization is the use of an automated C-SIG algorithm, designed to simulate human decision making and produce a first-guess C-SIG polygon for the forecaster. While this seems straightforward, several considerations are needed to ensure that the automated C-SIGs accurately represent forecaster expectations. We will discuss the importance of obtaining forecasters' opinions and preferences on the creation of the automated C-SIGs and how they are merged, simplified, and adapted for special or challenging weather events. Finally, we will frame these considerations by outlining plans for a future user evaluation within the NOAA AWC testbed.

491884.title: Advancing QES-Plume: GPU-Accelerated Transport in Complex Environments
491884.authors: Fabien Margairaz, Univ. of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and P. Willemsen, W. Mahaffee, E. R. Pardyjak, and R. Stoll
491884.abstract: A fast dispersion modeling is crucial for predicting the transport of airborne material in complex environments, particularly when accurate concentration fields are required for decisions related to emergency response, urban air quality, wildfire smoke, and pathogen transport. The Quick Environmental Simulation (QES) framework is a cross platform, low-computational-cost, GPU-accelerated, open-source modular modeling environment that can rapidly predict wind, turbulence, and particle dispersion in atmospheric boundary-layer flows (https://github.com/UtahEFD/QES-Public). It uses a Lagrangian stochastic dispersion model (QES-Plume) with a time-implicit integration scheme to calculate particle trajectories from mean-flow and turbulence fields provided by QES-Winds (GPU-accelerated mass-conserving wind-field solver) and QES-Turb. To further accelerate dispersion modeling, we developed parallel implementations of QES-Plume using NVIDIA CUDA for GPUs and OpenMP for multicore CPUs, taking advantage of the independent nature of Lagrangian particle trajectories. Improvements to memory management and data transfer reduce computational overhead and support simulations with large particle populations. Together, these developments accelerate particle release, transport, boundary interactions, concentration sampling, and deposition calculations while retaining a serial CPU pathway for systems without GPU hardware. In addition, shapefile-based inputs allow realistic buildings and vegetation distributions to be incorporated more easily into urban and agricultural domains. Additional refactoring of the QES framework architecture has resulted in greater modularity facilitating a broader range of model configurations, environmental processes, and applications. The GPU version was evaluated against the original CPU and OpenMP models using analytical solutions and complex environment test cases by examining concentration distributions, plume spread, and numerical consistency across implementations. Computational performance was assessed using wall-clock time, computational cost per particle and time step, and speedup relative to the serial CPU implementation. The OpenMP implementation scales with the number of cores used while the GPU acceleration is highly dependent on the size of the problem, with speedup around 100x in optimal cases. The analyses considered different particle populations, simulation durations, and levels of environmental complexity to determine how buildings, boundary interactions, concentration sampling, and deposition processes affect simulation cost. Overall, the accelerated framework retains the modeling capabilities of the original implementation while reducing the cost of high-resolution dispersion simulations and enabling much faster than real-time predictions for the rapid assessment and mitigation of airborne hazards in complex environments.

491888.title: Multi-Mechanism Detection of Precipitation-Generating Weather Systems over CONUS: Historical and Future Climate Simulations
491888.authors: Madhusmita Swain, North Carolina State University, Asheville, NC; and K. E. Kunkel
491888.abstract: Extreme precipitation across the contiguous United States (CONUS) arises from multiple synoptic- and mesoscale mechanisms such as tropical cyclones (TCs), extratropical cyclones (ETCs), atmospheric rivers (ARs), and weather fronts, each of which may respond differently to a warming climate. Here we use the EPA's 12-km regional climate downscaling ensemble (EDDEv2, driven by MPI-ESM1-2-HR) to characterize how these mechanisms and their associated precipitation change between a historical period (1985–2014) and end-of-century future periods (2070–2099) under SSP3-7.0 scenario. TCs, ETCs, and ARs are objectively identified using TempestExtremes (Ullrich et al., 2021), applying mechanism-specific detection criteria for sea-level-pressure minima and closed contours (TCs, ETCs), warm-core structure (TCs), and Laplacian ridges in integrated vapor transport (ARs). TC genesis and track density decline in most basins in future scenario, most sharply in the Caribbean (genesis: −30.6%; track: −49.8%) and Eastern Pacific (genesis: −29.8%; track: −28.1%), while the Atlantic Coast shows a divergent signal: genesis density decreases modestly (−10.8%) even as track density increases (+8.0%), suggesting a redistribution of storm activity toward the coast independent of local genesis. ETC activity also declines overall, with the total number of strong ETC tracks falling from 1,257 (1985–2014) to 1,125 (2070–2099), concentrated north of 40°N in both periods. AR frequency exhibits a clear northward shift, increasing by up to 4–5% across the Pacific Northwest, Upper Midwest, and Northeast while decreasing by a similar magnitude across the Gulf Coast and Southeast; despite this redistribution, AR-attributed total precipitation increases across nearly all of CONUS in future period, most substantially over the Southeast and Ohio Valley. We are extending this multi-mechanism framework with a deep learning-based front detection model, building on prior CNN-based approaches (e.g., DL-FRONT; Biard and Kunkel, 2019); results for fronts are in progress and will be presented alongside the TC/ETC/AR findings above. Together, these results provide a unified, mechanism-resolved picture of how the primary drivers of U.S. extreme precipitation are shifting under climate change, with direct relevance for nonstationary IDF curve development and extreme design metrics.

491889.title: Development, Testing and Evaluation of a JEDI-Based Data Assimilation Framework for the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS)
491889.authors: Jing Cheng, NOAA, College Park, MD; Axiom Consultants Inc., Rockville, MD
491889.abstract: As part of the ongoing modernization of the data assimilation (DA) platform for the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS), continuous development has focused on implementing and refining a Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI)-based DA framework. This presentation highlights the key technical, structural, and methodological upgrades integrated into the HAFS-JEDI system following its initial testing phase. Significant advancements have been made to the core infrastructure, including updates to underlying JEDI submodule, a redesigned model interface, and the integration of a broader suite of observation types equivalent to the legacy Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) system. Furthermore, we present the integration of specific DA configurations selected for the framework, which were actively evaluated through both retrospective and real-time experiments during the 2026 hurricane season. To better align with current operational HAFS baselines, the system was configured to utilize the 80-member Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) ensemble for background error covariance, rather than the 40-member HAFS ensemble from previous iterations. Additionally, configuration choices were implemented to ensure full system compatibility with updated GFSv17 inputs and model physics packages. While introducing these experimental frameworks, this presentation will focus primarily on the architectural evolution, observation integration, and technical configuration strategy of the JEDI-based framework, setting the technical foundation for the future HAFSv3 operational transition.

491891.title: When Borders Get in the Way: How Emergency Managers Overcame Geographic Challenges During the 4 November 2022 Red River Valley Tornado Outbreak
491891.authors: Taylor Maciag, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. Hogg, H. Obermeier, M. Krocak, and K. L. Berry
491891.abstract: On 4 November 2022, a significant severe weather outbreak took place across the Red River portions of Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas, and Louisiana. Several tornadoes, including two EF-4s, crossed multiple NWS County Warning Areas (CWAs), television markets, and jurisdictional boundaries. With each boundary crossed, the storms entered different communication and operational environments, raising some challenges for Emergency Managers (EMs) and their partners in both receiving and disseminating weather information. Interviews conducted with 13 EMs in impacted areas revealed details about these challenges, such as monitoring the weather in a “radar hole”, piecing together forecast information from multiple NWS Weather Forecast Offices, and coordinating resources and information across multiple political borders. This talk will discuss how EMs addressed these challenges given their unique geography.

491894.title: Evaluating Wind Farm Wake Recovery Using a Mesoscale 3DPBL Parameterization and Large-Eddy Simulation
491894.authors: William Correa Radünz, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and J. Kasper, R. J. A. M. Stevens, and J. K. Lundquist
491894.abstract: Offshore wind farms cluster near the best wind resource areas and can be within tens of kilometers from each other. Within this relatively short distance, the energy extracted from the wind can impact downstream wind farms. The region with weaker winds behind a wind farm is called the “wake”. Relative to onshore conditions, the offshore wake persists up to tens of kilometers because of the weak ambient turbulence found over sea. Therefore, accurately quantifying inter-farm wake losses is crucial for wind farm planning and development in clustered offshore areas. Mesoscale simulations with Wind Farm Parameterizations (WFPs) are a powerful tool for quantifying future or current scenarios of inter-farm wake effects. This framework can simulate wind farm clusters under realistic meteorological conditions at a reasonable computational cost. Thus, understanding biases in these simulations is important for accurate cluster wake predictions. Idealized mesoscale simulations under neutral conditions displayed slow wake recovery behind the wind farm using the MYNN Planetary Boundary Layer (PBL) scheme (Radünz et al., 2026). The mechanism that controls wake recovery depends on the grid resolution and the spatial gradients in the wake. Thus, a three-dimensional PBL (3DPBL) scheme (Juliano et al., 2022) may be more suitable than traditional PBL schemes for situations with strong spatial gradients and can potentially improve the representation of wake recovery. We compare mesoscale simulations using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) version 4.4 model with large-eddy simulations (LES) of an idealized offshore wind farm with aligned layout under neutral conditions (Kasper et al., 2024). Idealized simulations enable the evaluation of the WFP and wake recovery in a more controlled setting than in realistic cases. This idealized westerly inflow has a hub height (119 m) wind speed of 9.12 m/s and a surface roughness of 0.002 m. Mesoscale simulations at 1246 m horizontal resolution employ either the MYNN or 3DPBL scheme with the Fitch et al. (2012) WFP including the axial induction correction factor (Vollmer et al. 2024). The LES employs grid resolutions of 50, 20, and 10 m in the x, y, and z directions, respectively, with turbines represented using an actuator disk model. The 3DPBL scheme improves wake recovery relative to the MYNN scheme at kilometer-scale resolution (Figure 1). Future studies will employ the same approach at finer resolutions (< 1 km), where the enhanced treatment of spatial gradients by the 3DPBL scheme can further improve wake recovery representation.

491895.title: Advancing NOAA's Subseasonal and Seasonal Applications: Stakeholder Engagement and Communication in Support of the NWS Weeks 3-4 Program/Seasonal Forecast System Project
491895.authors: Steven Michael Simon, IBSS Corporation, Silver Spring, MD; NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and Y. Xue and K. Garrett
491895.abstract: NOAA is undergoing a critical transition in its modeling strategy by adopting a modern, fully coupled Unified Forecast System (UFS) architecture and rapidly integrating artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) applications, which ultimately will necessitate the retirement of legacy forecast systems like the Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2) and the Climate Forecast System Reanalysis (CFSR). At the core of these modernization efforts managed by the NWS Modeling Weeks 3-4 Program and Seasonal Forecast System (SFS) Project is the development and implementation of SFSv1, a fully coupled, UFS-based replacement for the legacy CFSv2. Concurrently, the ongoing Global Ensemble Forecast System version 13 (GEFSv13) development will establish a fully coupled global ensemble forecast system that significantly upgrades the NWS's subseasonal forecast capabilities. To expand predictability boundaries further, our programs are actively driving related AI innovations, including extending the Artificial Intelligence Global Ensemble Forecast System (AIGEFS) toward 48-day forecasts and developing hybrid AI and physics-based models within the GEFSv13 framework. Transitioning these subseasonal and seasonal (S2S) applications into operations requires robust programmatic strategies to connect modelers with researchers, stakeholders, and end-users. This community integration is formally driven by a Weeks 3-4/SFS Project Stakeholder Engagement Plan that provides swift, early integration strategies to ensure continuity of operations for downstream users amidst a highly compressed transition-to-operations (T2O) timeline. To execute this plan, we leverage two vital recurring community forums: the Monthly Weeks 3-4/S2S Webinar Series connects modelers, researchers, forecasters, and end-users to create a direct feedback loop aligning modeling priorities with evolving technology and stakeholder needs, while the Monthly SFS Community Evaluation Meeting establishes an interactive platform to evaluate SFS prototype performance and provide actionable feedback to developers. Furthermore, to ensure that these modernized modeling systems meet sector-specific stakeholder requirements, our program applies the community framework of S2S applications metrics established by the NCAR-facilitated S2S Land-Atmosphere Interactions Workshop Working Group. This structured, multi-tier approach bridges the persistent gap between traditional deterministic and probabilistic forecast skill assessment and practical decision relevance by evaluating core forecast variables alongside derived hazard and impact indicators and decision-relevant metrics, such as stakeholder usability and lead-time adequacy. A cornerstone of our strategy for stakeholder engagement and scientific advancement is maximizing data accessibility through the cloud-based NOAA Open Data Dissemination (NODD) Program. By leveraging NODD for the storage and public dissemination of critical forecast, reanalysis, and reforecast datasets in cloud-optimized formats, we provide the essential historical baselines required to train next-generation AI/ML models. Executing this cloud-forward strategy is essential, as the retirement of the legacy CFSv2 and CFSR deeply affects downstream S2S products and the diverse array of stakeholders who heavily rely on these models for sector-specific long-term planning and impact-based decision support. Ultimately, successfully implementing SFSv1 and GEFSv13 will significantly improve guidance for Weeks 3-4 and Seasonal Outlooks, winter storm severity, marine and sea ice hazards, drought, streamflow forecasts, water resource management, and food security applications. By ensuring actionable information flows to decision-makers, this transition sustains essential operations, including the National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS) for drought and wildfire predictions, the Forecast-Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO) for water resource management, and the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) for global food insecurity, thus empowering the Weather Enterprise and the vulnerable global communities that rely on it.

491896.title: From Signal Structure to Forecast Skill: Deep Learning of Coastal Sea Level Variability along the U.S. Atlantic and Gulf Coasts
491896.authors: Dafrosa John Kataraihya, Florida International University, MIAMI, FL; and W. SHIMON
491896.abstract: Reliable short-term sea-level (SL) forecasting is important for coastal flood preparedness. This study evaluates SL forecasts at 18 tide-gauge stations along the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts using three workflows: standalone deep learning (DL), standard signal decomposition combined with DL (SD+DL), and a corrected, leakage-free SD+DL workflow. The standalone and corrected workflows produced comparable results, whereas standard SD+DL yielded artificially high results due to leakage of future information. Autocorrelation and intrinsic mode function (IMF) variance analyses explained spatial differences in forecast performance. Stations along the US Northeast Atlantic coast exhibited short temporal persistence and dominant high-frequency variability, and DL forecasts lost skill beyond day 2. In contrast, stations along the Southeast US Atlantic coast showed longer persistence and greater medium-low frequency variance contributions, supporting forecasts up to day 3-4. These findings provide explainability on DL model performance, spatial differences, and support leakage-free model evaluation, therefore providing reliable forecasting methods.

491898.title: Reducing Time Integration Error for Microphysics Parameterizations with SPAECIES
491898.authors: Sean Patrick Santos, PNNL, Richland, WA; and J. Dong, S. Roberts, C. Vogl, and C. Woodward
491898.abstract: Parameterizations of cloud and precipitation microphysics are used across variety of models with differing spatial and temporal resolutions. The time step sizes used for these microphysics parameterizations can range from seconds in LES models to several minutes in low-resolution global models. Unsurprisingly, this can lead to large time integration errors and time step sensitivity, and potentially contributes to the need to retune these parameterizations for different resolutions. In our work, we have tested alternative time integration methods for the rain processes in the version of the P3 microphysics scheme implemented in E3SMv3, using a simple rainshaft model designed to reproduce the conditions that would typically be input to the microphysics scheme in an E3SM run. In addition to the original P3 method, we have tested several second- and higher-order methods provided by the SUNDIALS library, including methods with an adaptive time step size. This experimentation is facilitated by the SPAECIES framework, which separates out numerics from physical processes, allowing different time integrators to be used for the same physics parameterization. Although P3's original time integration method converges to first order in time, in our rainshaft model this behavior is only visible for quite small (~2 second and lower) time step sizes, and reducing the time step size is not an efficient way to reduce error. In the same model with the same inputs, higher-order SUNDIALS methods are able to achieve remarkably low errors (less than 0.1% estimated relative error in rain mass mixing ratios) in exchange for a 2.5x increase in computational cost over the E3SM configuration (which uses a 300s time step). Furthermore, the adaptive time stepping allows us to run stably without limiters and without specialized substepping of the sedimentation scheme, allowing much of the parameterization's complexity to be offloaded to the SPAECIES and SUNDIALS codes without changing the solution that the P3 rain microphysics converges to. This suggests that by using adaptive time stepping with higher-order schemes, developers may be able to affordably reduce time integration error to very low levels, allowing developers to focus on other sources of parameterization uncertainty without worrying about mistuned limiters or excessive time integration error complicating evaluation of microphysics schemes and afflicting simulations in production.

491901.title: OVERCAST: Producing a Global 3D Cloud Product using GeoIPS and Courier
491901.authors: Evan William Rose, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and G. Uttmark, J. E. Solbrig, Z. Ruan, S. D. Miller, J. M. Haynes, J. Fluke, and Y. J. Noh
491901.abstract: This presentation will introduce how the Geolocated Information Processing System (GeoIPS) and an orchestration package, Courier, are being used to produce a global 3D cloud product for the OVERCAST project. Production of this product requires orchestration because it is derived from data from five geostationary and multiple low-earth orbiting satellites and requires over a dozen different algorithms, and needs to be produced in both batch and near real-time modes. Courier is an open-source Python package responsible for the orchestration of jobs and data. It’s been built on top of interchangeable message broker systems and can be configured to wait for data and spawn jobs intelligently. Using just a single YAML configuration file, users can direct Courier how to create data products in a near real time (NRT) fashion. The latency for this software package is extremely low, on the order of milliseconds. GeoIPS is responsible for running individual scientific jobs. It is an open-source Python framework that facilitates the development and dissemination of scientific algorithms. A large suite of readers, algorithms, and other plugins are included in GeoIPS by default and are responsible for data manipulation and processing. The framework can be used to produce many output formats like imagery or datasets, such as NetCDF or GeoTIFF files. Large updates to GeoIPS have recently been released as v2.0 to support a new method of processing. The ‘Order Based Procflow’ is a series of operations on a hierarchical data object. A user can create reproducible workflows that can be run in NRT on HPC or locally with the same configuration. GeoIPS is used within the US Navy and GeoIPS is publicly maintained and available through GitHub.

491902.title: Designing for Serendipity: Unexpected Discoveries, Instrument Innovation, and the Case for the Next ATom
491902.authors: Patrick Veres, NCAR, Broomfield, CO; and J. Peischl, G. M. Wolfe, A. Rollins, and B. Stephens
491902.abstract: The NASA Atmospheric Tomography (ATom) mission ran from 2016-2018 and was designed to quantify the reactivity of the remote troposphere through near-continuous vertical profiling of the Pacific and Atlantic basins using the heavy-lift NASA DC-8 aircraft. A decade on, however, some of its most consequential discoveries were never part of the original proposal. This talk revisits ATom from the perspective of its unexpected discoveries and the technological innovations they generated, and contends that both are central to the case for an ATom-style follow-on. One of the clearest examples of ATom serendipity is the discovery of hydroperoxymethyl thioformate (HPMTF), a previously unobserved intermediate of dimethyl sulfide (DMS) oxidation that reshaped our understanding of remote sulfur chemistry. Detecting this novel compound depended on adding new instrumentation to ATom-3 even though the original science plan never targeted the DMS budget. This was possible because the mission maintained enough fiscal and payload flexibility to add capabilities mid-campaign. That timing is the point: the instrument did not exist when ATom's payload was first proposed. Had the payload been frozen at ATom-1, neither the instrument nor the discovery it enabled would ever have flown. As the payload evolved across deployments, these additions dynamically expanded the mission's goals in response to its originally planned observations. The mission's instrument development also paid dividends far beyond ATom. A dynamic humidity-control scheme devised during ATom to stabilize chemical ionization mass spectrometer sensitivity is now standard on nearly every commercial instrument of its class. Meanwhile, inlet design driven by the requirements of a broad set of instruments across the payload was iterated from deployment to deployment into a standard inlet design adopted widely across the community. Critically, repeated deployments in close succession, rather than a single campaign, allowed instruments to be assessed, improved, and re-flown, so that data quality improved from ATom-1 through ATom-4. Continuing to evaluate emerging technologies during a multi-year program will ensure that each deployment benefits from the most up-to-date payload achievable. ATom also exposed significant observational needs that were not able to be addressed. The absence of high-time-resolution (1 Hz) volatile organic compound (VOC) measurements limited our view of the atmosphere's filamentary fine structure, which governs processes from DMS oxidation to halogen cycling. Further, unresolved discrepancies between co-located measurements (for example, disagreements in DMS observations) still complicate mechanistic interpretation. A more capable heavy-lift platform, such as the new NASA Boeing 777, would allow these gaps to be addressed. Its greater payload capacity would accommodate complementary instruments, adding confidence in the resulting data and identifying discrepancies that still require reconciliation. We will show that one enduring lesson of ATom is the flexible, complete payload and repeatable mission design enabled by the NASA Earth Venture program approach. The next iteration should offer achievable science objectives as well as the flexibility to support additional measurements to enable the opportunistic, exploratory science that produced some of ATom's most far-reaching results. The challenge for an even more successful follow-on mission is to enhance the scientific, budgetary, and payload flexibility that greatly benefited ATom. Serendipity, it turns out, can be designed into a mission, and ATom's original architects, whether by intention or instinct, showed us how. A decade of unplanned discoveries is a lesson worth reading closely as we plan the next one.

491906.title: Development of a Dual-Pol Snow QPE for NEXRAD and MRMS
491906.authors: Dean Meyer, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; and P. Bukovcic and J. Zhang
491906.abstract: Water management in the mountainous western United States, real-time snow depth calculations during high-impact Nor’easter snow events, and numerical weather prediction (NWP) models all depend on accurate estimates of the snow water equivalent (SWE). Herein, we estimate the SWE using a radar quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) method. Current operational QPE products at S-band within the NEXRAD and Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) systems use the radar reflectivity in their S(Z) snow rate functions. These tend to substantially underestimate the SWE in heavy snow events because Z alone cannot account for the full variability of snow particle size distributions, densities, shapes, and orientations. As a result, to match precipitation gauge and reanalysis data, the MRMS S(Z) must be increased by up to a factor of 1.5. We propose an S(Kdp, Z) function that adds the specific differential phase (Kdp) product to better capture the snow characteristics and more accurately estimate the SWE. Recent tests have shown that the S(Kdp, Z) improved the mean absolute error (MAE) of operational products by 19% and 52% in two high-impact Nor’easter snow events, for example. Efforts to implement the S(Kdp, Z) in the NEXRAD and MRMS systems are currently underway. Challenges are discussed including the verification of the snow QPE method against gauges in the presence of wind-induced undercatch. Estimating snowfall from lake level data à la Pritchard et al. (2021) may be a valuable independent check when high winds or freezing temperatures render most other conventional gauges unreliable.

491907.title: Risk Assessment Indices for Peak Loads Under Extreme Weather & Electrification
491907.authors: Kaiden Patrick Sookdar, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY; and J. P. Montoya-Rincon, J. E. González-Cruz, C. Kirkpatrick, R. Hinkley, J. Hanle, and A. Mohamed
491907.abstract: In the past several years, power grids nationwide have come under increased stress due to the frequency and severity of extreme heat events. The combination of rapid data center capacity growth and the electrification of transportation and buildings make it imperative to quantify the growing exposure to demand in the medium-to long-term. However, many existing projections do this too coarsely to enable targeted planning at scales useful to utilities, potentially exposing them to unaccounted risk. In this study, we compile projections of electric vehicle and data center electricity demand through the 2050s combined with high-resolution physical simulations of climate and building energy. The Thermodynamic Global Warming dataset modifies ERA5 reanalysis with time-evolving thermodynamic signals from two climate scenarios: Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) 4.5 and SSP8.5, representing historical and future warming trajectories. These projections are dynamically downscaled to the Urbanized Weather Research and Forecasting Model (uWRF), coupled with the Building Effect Parameterization (BEP) and the Building Energy Model (BEM), which together simulate building energy use and its feedback on the urban microclimate, enabling uWRF to capture key urban-sensitive processes such as radiative exchange and heat storage. Crucially, the variable adoption of electric heating technologies (such as heat pumps) is woven into the model. Temporal coverage of these simulations is hourly through 2058, and the spatial coverage is the entire Northeast at 4km grid spacing, with a nest of 1.33 km in the New York City Metro Area. The net result is a total future load forecast through 2050 at the grid, starting with New York Independent System Operator (NYISO) Zone,and substation levels. We develop a comprehensive risk and readiness assessment mapping for projected peak loads across Northeastern service areas through mid-Century, including a quantitative index. The high-resolution nature of the dataset allows us to study local-scale weather and infrastructure impacts by assessing load management at specific transmission and distribution points. The risk index includes factors that indicate future stress at these locations, such as a large increase in the load relative to historical values and main drivers of surging peak loads. In this presentation, we identify and locate disproportionately high-risk chokepoints in the transmission grid, starting with the NYISO Zones and substations within the Zones. We show that suburban to rural load zones have the greatest risk of substation capacity exceedance and that this largely occurs during the winter due to electrification, regardless of scenario. This study’s initial focus is New York State; however, it is designed for scalability across the Northeastern US and nationwide. This abstract was prepared by Kaiden Sookdar with support from NYSERDA. The opinions expressed do not necessarily reflect those of NYSERDA or the State of New York, and references do not constitute an implied or expressed recommendation or endorsement.

491911.title: Exploring the ACRE (Agricultural Conservation for Resilient Environments) Portal
491911.authors: Madelynn Wuestenberg, Iowa State University, Ames, IA; and A. M. Pearson
491911.abstract: The ACRE (Agricultural Conservation for Resilient Environments) portal is a science-based online tool for exploring suites of climate-smart conservation practices, designed to support farmers, educators, Extension and outreach professionals, and agricultural advisors. This portal connects research-backed practices with USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) conservation practice standards and aims to address the benefits and limitations of conservation practices for commercial row and specialty crops, and livestock. Developed through a multidisciplinary effort, the portal integrates scientific research and expert knowledge across agricultural systems, including agroforestry, corn and soybean rotations, extended rotations, grazed livestock, horticultural crops, and perennial crop systems. The portal serves as a launch point for exploring conservation practices and research supporting their use in agricultural systems. Rather than prescribing a single solution, it allows users to compare conservation practices, evaluate potential benefits, limitations, and tradeoffs, and identify strategies that align with production goals and resource concerns. Information is provided on outcomes related to soil health, water and nutrient management, agricultural productivity, biodiversity, greenhouse gas emissions, and economic considerations, with supporting case studies that demonstrate practical applications. The portal was developed using gamification strategies to define climate-smart agricultural systems and identify needs and barriers to adaptation. Players utilize pieces representing traditional and climate-smart agricultural practices to build their “farm.” These pieces are not labeled as traditional or climate-smart, allowing players to make authentic choices about the practices they believe make sense. The facilitator sets the scene and describes their current climate challenges. After two rounds of gameplay, points are totaled, and the activity ends with a full-group discussion. Participants answer questions about the opportunities and challenges their “farms” faced under future climate scenarios. The ACRE Portal helps guide conversations between Extension and outreach professionals, agricultural advisors, and farmers about climate concerns and building resilient agricultural systems through conservation practices. By translating research into practical, evidence-based guidance, the portal supports more informed conservation planning and management decisions.

491912.title: High-Rate Airborne Measurements of Condensed Water Mass Across Different Cloud and Turbulence Regimes.
491912.authors: Shane Richard Martrich, Univ. of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and S. Woods, P. Zuidema, G. M. McFarquhar, B. Geerts, and J. R. French
491912.abstract: Mixed-phase clouds influence cloud radiative properties, precipitation development, and cloud lifetime, yet many of the microphysical processes governing their evolution occur at spatial scales smaller than those typically resolved by airborne observations. Turbulence may be particularly important at these scales by redistributing condensed water and influencing the persistence and spatial organization of liquid and ice (Korolev and Milbrandt 2022). Mixed-phase clouds may persist longer when the timescale of turbulent mixing occurs more rapidly than that of glaciation which is driven by microphysical processes. High-rate Nevzorov hot-wire probe measurements provide a potential pathway for observing condensed-water variability at meter- to tens-of-meter scales as a way of determining which, turbulence or microphysics, drives heterogeneity in mixed-phase clouds. In this study, high-rate Nevzorov liquid, total, and derived ice water content measurements are analyzed across multiple airborne field campaigns (e.g. CAESAR, SNOWIE, and WINTRE-MIX) spanning a range of cloud environments and flight-level turbulence conditions. In-cloud observations are classified using the magnitude of vertical-velocity perturbations, |w′|, as a proxy for turbulence intensity, with weak (< 2 m/s), moderate (2–5 m/s), and strong (>5 m/s) regimes. Fourier spectral analyses of the Nevzorov signals are compared across turbulence and cloud-phase regimes, with the vertical-velocity spectra providing an independent dynamical reference for the turbulent cascade. This analysis evaluates whether the spatial scales of physically meaningful condensed-water variability change systematically with turbulence and whether differences among LWC, TWC, and IWC remain consistent across environmental conditions. These results aim to constrain when high-rate Nevzorov measurements reliably resolve fine-scale cloud structure and identify the atmospheric conditions governing their effective spatial resolutions.

491916.title: 2026 HAFS Real-Time Experiments: Demonstrating JEDI-Based Hurricane Inner-Core Data Assimilation and Toward Basin-Wide High-Resolution Self-Cycled Analysis System
491916.authors: Bin Liu, Lynker at NOAA/NWS/OMD, Riverdale Park, MD; and Z. Zhang, X. Lu, Y. Weng, J. Cheng, B. Thomas, L. Zhu, W. Wang, J. Shin, C. K. Wang, J. Peng, M. Aristizabal Vargas, F. Yang, and V. S. Tallapragada
491916.abstract: The Hurricane Analysis and Forecasting System (HAFS) serves as NOAA's flagship regional operational hurricane model, providing critical numerical guidance on hurricane track, intensity, and storm structure. Since the implementation of HAFS initial operational capability (HAFSv1) in 2023, the system has undergone rapid annual upgrades, including HAFSv2 (2024), HAFSv2.1 (2025), and the upcoming HAFSv2.2 (2026), driven by collaborative developments and real-time parallel and multi-season retrospective experiments. A primary objective for the next major HAFS upgrade (HAFSv3) is to transition the atmospheric data assimilation (DA) system from the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) to the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework. Based on the HAFSv2.2 configuration with specific physics and dynamics fine-tunings for the upcoming GFSv17 upgrade and building upon the 2025 HAFSv2.1.1J real-time JEDI-DA experiment, the 2026 HAFSv2.2.1A real-time parallel experiment implements the JEDI-based 4DEnVar DA system utilizing an 80-member GDAS ensemble covariance and enabling the assimilation of additional observation types. Toward expanding hurricane analysis capabilities, the development of the HAFSv2.2.1D prototype explores a self-cycled, high-resolution, basin-wide hybrid 4DEnVar-EnKF analysis system for the North Atlantic basin. By pairing a 2.4-km resolution deterministic analysis with 40 self-cycled 7.2-km EnKF ensemble members, this system aims to provide high-resolution analysis for North Atlantic hurricanes with improved representation of storm intensity and structure, which can also be used for developing combined dynamical and AI/ML-based HAFS deterministic and ensemble forecasting.

491919.title: Neutral Pressure Spectra: Role of Height, Roughness, Slope and Anisotropy
491919.authors: Ivana Stiperski, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria; and S. E. Smith
491919.abstract: Earth’s boundary layers are strongly influenced by the complexity of the Earth’s surface, as well as the multi-scale interactions that drive the flow anisotropy. From salt flats to vegetative canopies, features such as surface roughness, canopy heterogeneity and buoyancy impose a strong control on the anisotropy production mechanisms and pressure-strain interactions that act to destroy the anisotropy. The non-local nature of turbulent pressure in particular integrates the influences not only originating from the surface, but also those of outer-layer structures, making the pressure spectra particularly sensitive indicator of complex nature of atmospheric boundary layer. This study explores the impact of realistic landscapes on neutral turbulent pressure spectral scaling through the lens of Reynolds stress anisotropy by comparing wind tunnel boundary layers to field observations under a range of surface conditions. Wind tunnel experiments cover smooth and rough wall flat-plate boundary layers over a range of surface roughnesses and pressure gradients, and provide time-resolved microphone pressure and hotwire anemometry measurements. Nanobarometer field observations cover the Salt Lake Test campaign (SLTEST), Multi-point Monin-Obukhov similarity horizontal array turbulence study (M2HATS), the Shallow Cold Pools (SCP) campaign and the Sublimation of Snow Campaign (SOS) and examine the spectral characteristics of pressure under neutral stratification (determined through the Obukhov length and friction velocity criterion) as a function of height, roughness, slope angle and bulk anisotropy. The results highlight the joint role of bulk anisotropy and roughness in driving the spectral exponents of distinct spectral ranges found at all sites.

491920.title: Recent Advancements in the Common Community Physics Package
491920.authors: Ligia Bernardet, NOAA Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; Developmental Testbed Center (DTC), Boulder, CO; and D. J. Swales, G. Firl, D. Heinzeller, C. Peverley, S. Rasmussen, T. J. Hertneky, M. J. Kavulich Jr., and L. Xue
491920.abstract: The Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) consists of a library of physical parameterizations (CCPP-Physics) and associated infrastructure (CCPP-Framework) that enables its use in generic host models in a way that is agnostic of the dynamical core (dycore). The design of the CCPP-Framework encompasses many features that enable technical interoperability. Those include the absence of dycore-specific dependencies (such as grid structure), the use of standardized APIs, and respect for the host model parallelization strategy. In addition, the CCPP is developed publicly and is highly portable to foster its utilization in the large community. The CCPP is a major component of the Unified Forecast System (UFS) and supplies physical parameterizations for NOAA’s operational systems such as the Hurricane and Analysis Forecast System (HAFS) and the Air-Quality Modeling System (AQM). It is also slated for inclusion in all upcoming UFS operational systems, such as the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) v1 and the Global Forecast System (GFS) v17. Additionally, the CCPP is implemented in the soon-to-be-operational Navy Environmental Prediction System Using a Nonhydrostatic Engine (NEPTUNE) and in the next-generation NSF NCAR’s Community Atmospheric Model (CAM) as part of the System for Integrated Modeling of the Atmosphere (SIMA). Finally, the CCPP is distributed with a Single-Column Model to enable hierarchical development and software testing. In the last year, the community contributed to the CCPP a number of scientific updates aimed at supporting the modeling systems above. Highlights include the addition of the Thompson-Eidhammer Microphysics Parameterization for Operations (TEMPO) v3 and a rewrite of the Community Convective Cloud (C3) parameterization. Additionally, a new standard has been implemented requiring that all parameterizations not update the model state directly but instead return tendencies. This development allows host models to use process-split or time-split methods to update the mode state and shifts control of physics-dynamics coupling from the parameterizations to the host model. Ultimately, this development enhances the CCPP interoperability and makes it suitable for use the atmospheric component of the UFS Weather Model, which now includes two dynamical cores: the Finite-Volume Cubed Sphere (FV3) and the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS). In 2026 the CCPP Framework was upgraded to provide greater functionality, allow for a cleaner and more functional interface to the host model, and simplify the implementation process for physics parameterization developers. It now provides dynamic (runtime) configurability of atmospheric constituents, allowing for chemistry to be implemented in tight coupling with the physics. In this presentation we will provide a status update on the CCPP development and current capabilities, on its use within the UFS, and of capabilities available to the broad community.

491922.title: Beyond the Continent: Extending Antarctica’s Blowing Snow Climatology to Sea Ice with ICESat-2
491922.authors: Joseph Robinson, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and L. Jaegle and S. P. Palm
491922.abstract: Blowing snow plays a critical role in Antarctic ice sheet mass balance by driving substantial redistribution and sublimation. Space-borne lidar observations have been a cornerstone for constraining blowing snow processes in recent studies, including establishment of the first decade-long climatology of blowing snow occurrence and sublimation over the Antarctic ice sheet. In this work, we use observations from the lidar system aboard the ICESat-2 satellite to continue this record and expand it to Antarctic sea ice by optimizing the blowing snow detection algorithm for use in these regions. Using this framework, we explore the occurrence and properties (layer geometry and optical depth) of blowing snow across the Southern Hemisphere in the ICESat-2 record (2018-2025). We compare blowing snow characteristics between the ice sheet and sea ice and evaluate how they correlate with local meteorological drivers such as wind speed, which can serve as an effective proxy for boundary layer turbulent processes. Relationships with broader modes of climate variability will also be explored to examine the multi-scale drivers of blowing snow. Furthermore, we will quantify blowing snow transport and sublimation fluxes using the ICESat-2 observations, placing them in context of snowfall to highlight the impact of blowing snow on the snow mass budget across different regions and seasons. Finally, we compare the ICESat-2 derived fluxes against current model-based estimates, thereby providing an updated observational benchmark to guide future model refinements. By extending the baseline Antarctic blowing snow record established by previous observation and model-based studies, this work offers preliminary insights into how blowing snow processes interact with an evolving polar climate.

491924.title: Modulation of Winter Daily Temperature Variability and Extremes by NAO, PNA, and ENSO
491924.authors: Emily J. Becker, Univ. of Miami, Miami, FL; and S. Larson, R. W. Payne Jr., M. Hasan, and I. Gifford
491924.abstract: The variability of daily winter surface temperatures, including extremes, over North America and Europe is known to be modulated on subseasonal timescales by the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and the Pacific-North America pattern (PNA), and on intraseasonal timescales by El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO). The NAO is dynamically distinct from ENSO, while PNA variability is modulated by stronger ENSO events, and the observational record is too brief to understand their combined influence, especially on extreme temperatures. We investigate the interaction of these three modes and their influence on winter daily temperature using three idealized preindustrial CESM2 experiments: moderate and strong ENSO cases, each with at least 100 warm and cool ENSO events, and a no-ENSO control. We focus on January–March, the period when NAO’s modulation of daily temperature is the greatest. NAO and PNA indices are calculated for the separate CESM2 experiments, and daily minimum and maximum temperature variability, measured by interquartile range and 10th/90th percentiles, is evaluated for El Niño and La Niña years separately, with significance assessed via permutation testing. While the observational record is short, we compare model output against reanalysis and observed NAO, PNA, and Niño3.4 indices (1950–2025). Preliminary results show the NAO’s modulation of winter daily temperature variability is largely independent of ENSO phase, particularly over Europe.

491931.title: Overview of the Next Global Forecast System, Version 17
491931.authors: Jessica Meixner, NOAA, College Park , MD; NOAA/NWS/OMD, College Park, MD; and C. A. Thomas and R. Sun
491931.abstract: The Office of Modeling and Development is in the process of updating the Global Forecast System (GFS) to version 17 in collaboration with the Unified Forecast System and Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) communities. GFSv17 will include a fully coupled atmosphere, land, ocean, ice and wave model, utilizing the UFS weather model. The coupled model will be part of a weakly coupled data assimilation system, with new non-atmospheric data assimilation components for snow, ocean and sea ice based on JEDI software. The existing atmospheric data assimilation algorithms will be updated with the inclusion of multiscale atmospheric data assimilation. The existing atmospheric parameterizations have been upgraded, notably moving to use of the Thompson Microphysics Scheme and the NOAH-MP land model. The atmospheric horizontal resolution has increased from 13 km to 9 km for the deterministic forecast. This presentation will provide an overview of the GFSv17 system and share details and evaluations of the pre-implementation retrospective and real-time testing which have been completed.

491935.title: Hyperspectral Microwave Channel Grouping and Retrieval Performance: Results from the WH²yMSIE Campaign
491935.authors: Narges Shahroudi, NASA GSFC ; Univ. of Maryland, ESSIC, Silver Spring, MD; and A. Gambacorta, S. D. Nicholls, R. Kroodsma, A. E. Kotsakis, M. S. Yabra, and S. Kalluri
491935.abstract: Future low-Earth orbit (LEO) hyperspectral microwave (HMW) sounders will provide thousands of spectral channels, requiring new approaches for channel grouping and operational retrieval. In this study, we use simulated datasets together with airborne observations collected by the CoSMIR-H radiometer during the WH²yMSIE campaign to evaluate channel grouping strategies and retrieval performance for future operational applications. To address this challenge, we grouped hyperspectral measurements from the CoSMIR-H radiometer into reduced channel configurations while preserving the essential atmospheric information content required for operational applications. Results show that the grouped configurations retain the radiometric and atmospheric sensitivity characteristics of the original hyperspectral observations while substantially reducing the number of channels and lowering the effective noise equivalent differential temperature (NEDT). We then compared temperature and water vapor profile retrievals using a physics-based retrieval system applied to grouped hyperspectral CoSMIR-H observations, CoSMIR-H ATMS-equivalent observations, and collocated ATMS observations from the WH²yMSIE campaign. The results include detailed comparisons of the resulting temperature and water vapor retrievals and their implications for future operational retrieval systems. This work provides guidance for future LEO hyperspectral microwave mission design, channel grouping strategies, and operational retrieval development for numerical weather prediction and data assimilation.

491937.title: Evaluating Atmospheric Boundary Layer Turbulence Stationarity Utilizing Bayesian Changepoint Detection
491937.authors: Kevin Ferguson, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. Killick, S. W. Hoch, and E. G. Patton
491937.abstract: The assumption of statistical stationarity of turbulence underlies many common analysis and parameterization techniques in boundary layer meteorology, including eddy covariance flux calculations, computation of turbulence statistics, and self-similar scaling relationships. This assumption is often violated at geophysical scales as boundary layer turbulence is frequently non-stationary or transitions between stationary states due to the influence of mesoscale processes and spatiotemporal variability in forcing. As a consequence, analysis and parameterization of atmospheric boundary layer turbulence must assess how well the flow is represented by the assumption of stationarity. Traditional stationarity tests (e.g., Foken and Wichura 1996; Cava et al. 2014) perform this assessment utilizing temporal windows of a fixed size and predefined thresholds of statistical moments. However, recent work (Stiperski et al. 2025) has highlighted a need to generalize upon these methods as fixed-window approaches may not work well in some conditions, such as under very stable conditions. To this end, we present a novel method for assessing turbulence stationarity utilizing Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (BOCPD). Rather than assessing stationarity over a window of fixed size, this technique identifies locations in a turbulent signal where the statistical description of the turbulence prior to that point is inconsistent with its description after that point. This has the effect of identifying windows of arbitrary size over which turbulence in the boundary layer is reasonably represented by an assumption of stationarity. We test this technique against synthetic signals with known properties, simulated stationary turbulent flow, and observational data where large-scale sea breeze fronts impact an observational site at known times. Strengths and weaknesses of this technique in each context are discussed.

491941.title: Identifying and Addressing Gaps in Hydrometeorological Monitoring Networks in Support of Forecast Informed Reservoir Operations
491941.authors: Ava Cooper, Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, Univ. of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and J. Wilcox, S. Yoon, A. Wilson, J. F. Kalansky, L. Delle Monache, and F. M. Ralph
491941.abstract: Forecast Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO) is an approach to reservoir management that uses improved weather and water forecasts to inform operational decisions while maintaining flood risk management objectives. Reliable hydrometeorological observations are central to FIRO because they provide the information needed to understand watershed processes, evaluate and validate models used to produce forecasts, and verify forecast performance. The Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) has developed a framework for identifying and addressing gaps in hydrometeorological monitoring networks to support these objectives. The framework is designed to be adaptable to different watersheds and regions and to identify observations needed to characterize the spatial and temporal variability of relevant hydrometeorological processes. Monitoring networks across the Western United States are composed of stations operated by many different agencies, each with its own objectives and constraints. As a result, stations are often sited according to individual agency priorities and practical limitations such as permitting, accessibility, and challenging terrain, which can result in gaps in spatial and temporal coverage. This presentation summarizes the application of CW3E’s monitoring network evaluation framework to the Willamette River Basin in Oregon, highlighting how an integrated assessment of existing observations can identify gaps and inform recommendations for observations that support FIRO.

491942.title: Automated Detection and Modeling of Icebergs and Ice Islands in the Western Arctic
491942.authors: Abigail Dalton, EC, Ottawa, ON, Canada; and L. Pogson
491942.abstract: Since the 1980s, the ice forecasting service in Canada, now the Canadian Ice Service (CIS), has provided iceberg information for navigation in the North Atlantic. Today, year-round monitoring of icebergs in “Iceberg Alley”, the region between the coast of Labrador to the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, is a shared responsibility between CIS and the International Ice Patrol. CIS uses both visual analysis for iceberg monitoring, and since 2018 has automated part of the operational workflow. Following the breakup of the Milne Ice Shelf on Northern Ellesmere Island in 2020 and increasing risk to ships navigating waters of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, the CIS Applied Science team has initiated a multi-phase project with the objective of proposing improvements to the operational iceberg monitoring program. Started in 2024, this work uses a combination of RADARSAT Constellation Mission satellite imagery and in-situ observations to evaluate the applicability of existing automated detection and modelling methods for monitoring icebergs and ice islands drifting in open water in the western Arctic. Ice islands that calve from Canadian Arctic ice shelves, thick masses of floating ice that are attached to land, can drift in the Beaufort Sea for years to decades. From 2023 to 2025, CIS used historical and opportunistic ice island observations to manually adjust an iceberg limit on ice charts in the western Arctic. Since 2025, all open water on ice charts in the western Arctic has been classified as ‘bergy water’. Using commercial iceberg detection software to automatically identify icebergs/ice islands and a North American Ice Service (NAIS) iceberg drift and deterioration model, the goal of this project is to develop a method for creating products showing areas of known icebergs in open water of the western Arctic. Preliminary results show that automated detection and drift of ice island fragments in the western Canadian Arctic is possible with results comparable to those from the East Coast. Next steps will involve the development and evaluation of iceberg product prototypes from model and detection software output.

491943.title: A Machine Learning Model to Predict Solar Irradiance Relevant to Ionospheric and Thermospheric Models based on Solar EUV Images and Far-side Helioseismic Phase Maps
491943.authors: Thomas E. Berger, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and N. Flyer, N. Holland, S. Webber, and M. Vincent
491943.abstract: We report on the development of a machine learning (ML) model to accurately and reliably forecast a new index relevant to the solar extreme ultraviolet (EUV) irradiance at Earth using NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) EUV images from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) instrument in combination with helioseismic phase shift maps of the solar far-side hemisphere from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) instrument. The new index is called B10.7 and is an adaptation of the commonly used F10.7 index that approximately isolates the bremsstrahlung ("B") component of solar 10.7 cm radio emission from the gyroresonance component to more directly correlate with solar EUV irradiance. B10.7 is directly useable in place of the F10.7 index in thermospheric and ionospheric modeling and produces, e.g., more accurate thermospheric density profiles in empirical models such as MSIS when the F10.7 flux is above approximately 120 sfu. The ML model predicts the adapted B10.7 index by fusing front-side EUV image data with helioseismic phase map data that indicates magnetic activity on the far side of the Sun in a multi-channel recursive CNN architecture with attention layers to produce B10.7 predictions with up to 14-day lead times. Here we report 7-day B10.7 predictions using the AIA 94, 171, 193, and 304Å bandpasses that achieve relative Mean Absolute Error (MAE) values below 5.5% for 5-day lead times and below 6.5% for 7-day lead times, offering significant skill advantage over both persistence forecasts and the human heuristic F10.7 forecasts produced by the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center. The model will eventually be adapted to use NOAA/GOES SUVI EUV images and GONG far-side phase maps, both of which are used in NOAA operations.

491944.title: Unified Forecast System (UFS) Applications Across Scales: Status and Progress Toward NOAA Operations
491944.authors: Fanglin Yang, NOAA, ELLICOTT CITY, MD
491944.abstract: NOAA, in close collaboration with the broader U.S. weather and climate science community, is rapidly advancing a fully coupled Earth system modeling capability through the Unified Forecast System (UFS). As a community-based modeling framework, the UFS is designed to unify research and operations across a broad range of temporal and spatial scales. By replacing a collection of disparate legacy models with a unified modeling system, it supports applications spanning sub-hourly, convection-allowing local forecasts to subseasonal and seasonal global predictions, serving as the cornerstone of NOAA's strategy for next-generation environmental prediction. This presentation provides an update on several key UFS applications that are in advanced stages of development and are being prepared for operational implementation within the National Weather Service (NWS), including the Global Forecast System (GFS), the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), the Seasonal Forecast System (SFS), the Global Chemistry and Aerosol Forecast System (GCAFS), the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS), the Air Quality Model (AQM), and the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS). Recent evaluation cycles demonstrate substantial improvements across a few forecasting applications. These include, for instance, enhanced medium-range weather prediction, improved subseasonal and seasonal predictability of phenomena such as the Madden-Julian Oscillation and ENSO events, more accurate guidance for tropical cyclone rapid intensification and improved aerosol forecasts enabled by aerosol data assimilation. Despite these advances, transitioning each experimental application into NWS operations presents its unique technical and programmatic challenges. This presentation will discuss these challenges, outline the roadmap for operational implementation, and highlight future directions for UFS development.

491946.title: Proxy-Based Linear Models of Near-Booth PM2.5 at Two U.S.–Mexico Ports of Entry: Shift-Specific Predictors of Outdoor Occupational Exposure
491946.authors: Josdell Maria Guerra Ruiz, The University of Texas at El Paso, El Paso, TX; and V. Fontes, C. A. Flores, and G. IBARRA-MEJIA
491946.abstract: Exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is a leading environmental risk factor for morbidity and mortality worldwide, and economic impacts across the population. In [year] PM2.5 exposure was associated with 231.5 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) globally. Furthermore, in the U.S., between 2015 and 2018, it was estimated that a 1 µg/m3 increase in PM2.5 exposure is associated with between 9.5 and 12.8 million person-days and an average economic cost of $2.7 billion (Meng et al., 2024). Moreover, there was not found data regarding the health and economic impact of PM2.5 exposure on outdoor workers. However, the Occupational Information Network (O*NET) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Occupational Employment Projections Program indicated that there are more than 20 million outdoor workers at potential risk for occupational exposure to ambient air pollution in the U.S. (MacMurdo et al.,2025) To better predict and understand the contaminant’s trends and tailor improved mitigation strategies that can help alleviate the air quality burden, researchers across different fields have developed several predictive models for fine particulate matter (PM2.5).This include but are not limited to, land-use regression models, chemical transport modelss, satellite AOD-based models, low-cost sensor networks, and econometric models. However, modeling this criteria air pollutant is challenging and varies by monitoring platform for several reasons: regulatory monitoring networks are sparse and spatially uneven when representing air quality at a broader scale and tend to miss fluctuations across microenvironments that may better reflect personal exposure. In addition, some of these microenvironments may show concentration variations due to site-specific infrastructure, proximity to emission sources, and meteorological conditions. International Border Ports of Entry (IBPEs) along the U.S.-Mexico border are no exception. Nevertheless, these sites are characterized by a distinct primary anthropogenic source, constant high flux of slow-moving vehicles producing heavy traffic congestion. Particularly, concerns on air quality levels have been raised in the El Paso del Norte Region. This region is not only host to six IBPEs, but its air basin topography favors the accumulation and entrapment air pollutants. Occupational exposure assessment under OSHA is framed around 8-hour time-weighted averages, whereas the EPA's National Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5 are set on 24-hour and annual averaging periods. Discrepancies between regulatory frameworks governing these institutions result in a gap in oversight on outdoor workers’ safety. The only nominally applicable OSHA limit is the Particulates Not Otherwise Regulated PEL (5 mg/m³ respirable), which exceeds ambient concentrations by roughly three orders of magnitude and is therefore protective in name only. Commonly, personal sampling remains the reference method because it captures the breathing-zone microenvironment. Nonetheless, some occupations, such as inspection booth offciers,restrict the use of such instrumentation due to security screening protocols, uniform and equipment restrictions, and federal facility constraints. As a result, proxy methods are used to estimate worker exposure by using nearby station measurements when direct monitoring is not feasible. We therefore aimed to (i) characterize near-booth PM2.5 concentrations across operational shifts at two structurally distinct IBPEs, and (ii) evaluate whether traffic throughput and meteorology explain sufficient variability to support proxy-based shift exposure estimation. This research project collected 12 months of air quality data at two targeted IBPEs (IBPE 01 and IBPE 02) to model pollutant exposure across booth and near-booth workers. IBPE 01 is a peri-urban site, whereas IBPE 02 is an urban-core location with high-volume crossings used for comparison. The study used a standalone Federal Equivalent Method (FEM) monitor with a Real Time Particulate Profiler (RTP) for PM2.5 concentrations and an all-in-one weather station for meteorological records. Monitoring consisted of 24 continuous hours of data collection following a 1-in-6 systematic random scheme. PM2.5 and meteorological data were then averaged into hourly concentrations and matched with passenger-owned vehicles (no commercial vehicles) and buses (at IBPE 02). Data management and linear econometric models were analyzed for 8-hour operational work shifts (morning, afternoon, and night) at each IBPE through R. Final models comprised 464 hours of observation across 58 sampling dates. The dependent variable across all econometric models was the natural logarithm of the hourly PM2.5 mass concentration, and the vehicular throughput predictor was retained at all times. For both IBPEs, the morning shift exhibited the strongest model fit with the smallest residual error, indicating that its retained predictors captured a meaningful portion of the variability at the booth-level PM2.5 concentrations. In addition, both IBPEs’ afternoon models retained the most predictors. Nevertheless, the large residual error and lower adjusted R² value suggests that substantial variability from the contaminant remains unexplained by the candidate predictor set. On the other hand, the night shift model produced the lowest explanatory power across all shifts, consistent with the reduced traffic and meteorological variability available to drive PM2.5 concentrations during nighttime operations. Lastly, inter-site contrasts indicated that the morning and afternoon models at IBPE 01 were higher than those at IBPE 02, showing that the candidate meteorological predictor set captures a materially larger share of PM2.5 variability at the open peri-urban site compared to the urban-core site. This is consistent with structural differences in the assessed IBPEs, the peri-urban site's less constrained airshed allows regional meteorology to dominate, whereas the urban-core site's confined microenvironment and denser local emissions introduce variability that a linear meteorological specification cannot capture. Our model's lower explanatory power suggests that additional unmeasured factors influence afternoon PM2.5 concentrations, including cross-border traffic queuing patterns and congestion, or secondary aerosol formation processes. Moreover, although the resulting models used 12 months of data to showcase sufficient variability across the year, single-year data cannot separate interannual meteorological anomalies from systematic site effects. Shift-resolved proxy models can provide defensible near-booth exposure estimates for outdoor federal inspection personnel in settings where personal sampling is operationally prohibited, offering a practical basis for occupational surveillance in the absence of an applicable PEL. 491947.title: AI Weather Prediction: EAGLE Train-Infer-Verify Pipeline in the Cloud
491947.authors: Rayette Toles-Abdullah, Amazon Web Services, Upper Marlboro, MD
491947.abstract: The Earth Prediction Innovation Center's EAGLE (Experimental AI Global and Limited-area Ensemble) system is an end-to-end machine-learning weather prediction pipeline that produces forecasts from a trained graph neural network and verifies them against observations. We ported EAGLE to a managed cloud high-performance computing environment that provisions a Slurm-based GPU cluster on demand, and we ran the inference and verification workflow on it. Because EAGLE already submits its work through Slurm, the port required essentially no changes to the pipeline's Python code. Platform support reduced to a small configuration file naming the cluster's compute partitions, together with infrastructure-as-code templates that provision a matching cluster, a high-performance shared filesystem, and networking. The pipeline reads operational global and regional forecasts and conventional observations directly from public cloud object storage co-located with the cluster, which eliminates the data-transfer bottleneck that constrains on-premises runs. We generated forecasts and scored them over global and limited-area domains, including a case study of Hurricane Helene, with output written to durable object storage and read back independently of the cluster. This work demonstrates that platform-abstracted machine-learning weather systems can move to managed cloud HPC with minimal engineering, lowering the barrier for researchers without dedicated supercomputing allocations.

491950.title: Propagation of Radar-Derived Quantitative Precipitation Estimation Errors Through Hydrologic Processes Across Scales
491950.authors: Bong Chul Seo, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO; and S. Maharjan
491950.abstract: Reliable characterization of uncertainty in hydrologic predictions is critical for advancing our understanding of watershed dynamics and improving risk management for extreme weather and water-related hazards. Streamflow prediction uncertainty originates from several sources, including uncertainties in model inputs (e.g., precipitation), hydrologic process representation, and model parameterization. This study focuses on uncertainty associated with quantitative precipitation estimates (QPEs) and investigates how QPE errors propagate through hydrologic processes to influence streamflow predictions. Radar-derived polarimetric QPEs are generated for multiple rainfall events spanning 2013–2024 over the Kansas City metropolitan area, where a dense network of tipping-bucket rain gages provides reference rainfall observations. These observations are interpolated to produce gridded reference rainfall fields, which are then used to quantify QPE error characteristics, including systematic bias, random error, and their spatiotemporal correlation structures. The primary objective is to determine how spatiotemporally correlated random QPE errors are transformed by watershed processes and how they contribute to uncertainty in streamflow predictions. Whereas previous studies have largely assumed that uncorrelated precipitation errors diminish through spatial or watershed aggregation, this work evaluates whether correlated precipitation errors are attenuated, preserved, or amplified during hydrologic response across watershed scales. To address this question, both distributed and lumped hydrologic models are employed to examine uncertainty propagation across watershed systems.

491951.title: Recent MPAS-JEDI Research and Development at NSF NCAR
491951.authors: Craig Schwartz, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and B. J. Jung, C. Snyder, Z. Liu, I. Hernandez Banos, J. Ban, R. Kong, S. Toedtli, J. H. Kim, X. Zhang, J. Wittig, Z. Ying, and R. Islam
491951.abstract: Since 2018, the National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) has been developing a data assimilation (DA) system using the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) interfaced to the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS); i.e., “MPAS-JEDI”. MPAS-JEDI is now fairly mature and provides atmospheric DA capabilities for global, regional, and variable-resolution MPAS applications. This presentation provides an update on recent MPAS-JEDI research and development at NSF NCAR. Specifically, we report on progress concerning: i) convection-allowing DA of radar observations, including development of a new forward operator for dual-polarization applications; ii) DA experiments where ensemble-based background error covariances were provided by an artificial intelligence-based model emulator, rather than MPAS; iii) developments assimilating satellite-based reflectivity observations from EarthCARE’s Cloud Profiling Radar (CPR) and GPM’s Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar (DPR); iv) enhancements for clear- and all-sky radiance DA from infrared and microwave sensors; and v) experiments using MPAS-JEDI for global variable-resolution applications with multiple areas of convection-allowing horizontal cell spacing. Plans for the next year of MPAS-JEDI development at NSF NCAR will also be discussed

491957.title: Retrieval of Raindrop Size Distributions and Vertical Air Motions from Coherent Doppler Lidar
491957.abstract: The US Department of Energy’s Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program operates pulsed coherent Doppler lidars at all its fixed and mobile sites. These instruments provide accurate range- and time-resolved measurements of line-of-sight (radial) velocity and aerosol backscatter in the atmospheric boundary layer under clear-air conditions. As a result, they have been used extensively to study winds and turbulence in the atmospheric boundary layer, while their ability to measure precipitation properties has received much less attention. In this study, raw spectra from a vertically staring coherent Doppler lidar are used to retrieve raindrop size distributions (RSDs) during multiple convective precipitation events at ARMs Southern Great Plains site. RSDs derived from the lidar’s lowest valid height bin are compared to a nearby surface-based laser disdrometer. The median correlation coefficient between RSDs was found to be 0.92 and the median percent difference in the modal diameters was found to be 4%, with the lidar producing slightly higher estimates. Significantly better agreement is obtained if the disdrometer is used to essentially calibrate the backscatter efficiency.
