In that case, median correlation coefficient increases to 0.96 and the median percent difference in the modal diameters decreases to -2.3%, with the lidar producing slightly lower estimates than the disdrometer. These results indicate that coherent Doppler lidar could be used operationally to obtain accurate height-resolved RSD retrievals.

491959.title: An Overview of Global Verification in the NOAA/NWS Office of Modeling and Development Evaluation and Verification System (EVS)
491959.authors: Alicia M. Bentley, NOAA/NWS/Office of Modeling and Development, Riverdale Park, MD; and J. J. Levit, A. E. Benjamin, M. P. Row, Q. Shi, S. R. Shields, L. G. Chen, S. Ardani, H. C. Huang, B. Zhou, M. G. Caron, Y. Mao, L. B. Stefanova, and S. Banihashemi
491959.abstract: The NOAA/NWS Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) has implemented version 2.0 of the Evaluation and Verification System (EVS)—an operational software system used to verify and validate forecasts from the NWS operational modeling suite. EVS uses the enhanced Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) developed by the NCAR/NOAA Developmental Testbed Center (DTC) to generate verification statistics for many NWS global and regional models, as well as a subset of global models from international modeling centers. EVS verification graphics are produced operationally using Python and are routinely disseminated to the public via the OMD Verification website. A critical component of EVS version 2.0 is its expanded global verification capabilities, which encompass both deterministic and ensemble skill scores and metrics. This presentation highlights key upgrades in the latest EVS release, including the addition of AI-driven NWS global models: AIGFS, AIGEFS, and HGEFS. Global wave verification now includes low-level wind direction skill scores and additional significant wave height validation datasets (e.g., satellites). Global aerosol (GEFS-chem) verification has also been added. Finally, we will discuss the development of Summary Assessment Metrics (SAMs), such as the NWP Index, for inclusion in future EVS releases.

491965.title: Impacts of Storm Mode on Turbulence
491965.authors: Cole Thomas Hartman, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
491965.abstract: Convectively induced turbulence (CIT) poses a hazard to aviation, with severe encounters occurring large distances from visible storm boundaries. Avoidance protocol that treats all storms as equal does not consider that turbulence risk is not distributed symmetrically around storms, and preliminary observational work suggests that storm-scale morphology, rather than proximity alone, may be a key control on hazard extent. Despite this, no study has systematically linked turbulence risk to objectively classified storm mode and geometry. This work addresses that gap by pairing eddy dissipation rate (EDR) observations from commercial aircraft with GridRad-Severe, a high-resolution, automatically tracked radar dataset that classifies storms into single-cell, multicell, MCS, and supercell modes. EDR reports are spatiotemporally matched to tracked storm objects, and relative risk of moderate-or-greater turbulence is computed as a function of horizontal distance from the storm's 10-dBZ boundary and vertical separation from echo top, stratified by storm mode and geometric characteristics (eccentricity, orientation, maximum dimension). We hypothesize that organized systems, including MCSs and supercells, will exhibit the most spatially expansive and intense risk regions, while isolated single-cell storms will produce more spatially confined turbulence signatures. Additionally, we predict that storms that are more elongated will produce non-uniform risk environments surrounding the storm. These results are intended to establish a morphology-dependent framework for CIT risk, providing physical information that can inform future guidance.

491966.title: Synthesizing Regional and Global Atmospheric Chemistry, Wet Deposition, and Biometeorological Networks for Dry Deposition Estimates
491966.authors: Adrien Tirouvanziam, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and D. Pan
491966.abstract: Dry deposition and wet deposition are the two processes by which chemicals in the atmosphere reach the surface . Dry deposition budgets are a key component of nitrogen and biogeochemical cycles, but currently lack rigorous estimates at all scales because monitoring infrastructure is unevenly distributed globally. This analysis visualizes the state of global monitoring infrastructure from 25 flux networks, overlain with the NASA MODIS Land Cover Classification dataset, to contribute to a methodology paper about the state of science for dry deposition. Dry deposition networks come in three types: atmospheric chemistry networks measure pollutants and tracers like ammonia, sulfate, sulfur dioxide, ozone, and particulate matter; wet deposition networks measure precipitation rate and wet concentrations of pollutants; and biometeorological networks measure carbon dioxide, temperature, humidity, soil, and canopy properties to improve aerodynamic resistance estimates. These regional-to-continental-scale flux networks measure key components of chemical fluxes, and are most densely located in North America, Western Europe, and China. The MODIS Land Cover Classification dataset uses a variety of parameters and a decision tree algorithm to analyze land use from surface meteorology. The 17 land types include water, desert, croplands, and a variety of forest and grassland climates. This dataset is used as a basemap, and is extrapolated onto a 0.1º x 0.1º grid to reduce computational time. The finalized map displays flux networks split between atmospheric chemistry, wet deposition, and biometeorology, along with sites containing a mixture of atmospheric chemistry and wet deposition measurements. Zoomed-in portions of the map are displayed for the global regions with densest network coverage. We look at co-location of sites and analyze the gap, since inferential modeling requires all three types of measurements in close proximity. These co-location sites are categorized by ecosystem type. Alongside the map, a multi-tiered monitoring strategy can help select new sites and improve data access. In areas with many measurements, ecological, meteorological, and chemical measurements can already be cross-verified, while tiered models can help portray large-scale patterns in areas with sparse measurements. In sparser areas or less commonly measured biomes, this map can identify opportunities for site clustering and measurement collocation, which would improve global flux data accessibility. Combined with labels depicting years of operation and a linked table for accessing site coordinates and measurements, this map can serve as a valuable tool for atmospheric chemists, climate scientists, and ecohydrologists studying atmospheric and biogeochemical cycles.

491968.title: Creating a Global High-Resolution Convective or Stratiform Type Product
491968.authors: Jackson Tan, Univ. of Maryland Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; and V. Petkovic, D. Watters, P. E. Kirstetter, G. J. Huffman, and M. Orescanin
491968.abstract: Precipitation is commonly classified as convective or stratiform (C/S) type, representing intense but spatially variable precipitation versus widespread lower-intensity precipitation, respectively. C/S type classification is critical for numerous applications, including storm-type identification, extreme event detection, and numerical model evaluation, as well as serving as a prerequisite to satellite-based latent heating profiles. While C/S types are typically inferred from radar observations, the limited spatial coverage of ground-based radars and sparsity of spaceborne radars preclude global C/S type products at monitoring scales. This presentation provides an overview of ongoing efforts to create a global C/S type product at 0.05° every 30 minutes, complementing high-resolution precipitation rate products such as the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG). Leveraging machine learning capabilities in spatial pattern classification, we adopt a framework parallel to IMERG, utilizing the GPM constellation of passive microwave and infrared sensors with the GPM Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar (DPR) as reference. We present initial results from a merged 0.05° gridded product of C/S type probabilities with uncertainty quantification enabled by a Bayesian framework. We demonstrate the skill of the C/S type retrievals and assess the representativeness of their uncertainties through evaluation against DPR and ground-based radar observations. We also present case studies to demonstrate its capability to provide insights into the precipitation processes beyond just surface precipitation rates. Test products are currently available for user exploration and feedback as development continues, with details on specific algorithm components discussed in companion presentations. The project aims to deliver a high-quality global C/S type dataset at 0.05° and 30-minute resolution spanning 1998–2027.

491969.title: Incorporating the CRACMM Multiphase Mechanism into UFS-Chem
491969.authors: Rebecca Helen Schwantes, NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and B. D. Baker II, M. Bruckner, B. Koziol, B. Murphy, J. He, Q. Z. Rasool, Z. Moon, W. Li, K. Shores, M. Dawson, D. Fillmore, A. Hodzic, M. C. Barth, G. Pfister, R. Ahmadov, J. Schnell, and B. C. McDonald
491969.abstract: The Unified Forecast System with Chemistry (UFS-Chem) is an effort to unify atmospheric chemistry and composition in NOAA's UFS with the goal to both improve air quality, smoke, and weather forecasts for Research to Operation activities and address stakeholder concerns especially related to improving understanding of air quality for Research to Application activities. Chemical mechanisms like CRACMM (Community Regional Atmospheric Chemistry Multiphase Mechanism) have been designed to accurately represent air toxics, aerosols, and ozone together in one common mechanism by leveraging community knowledge to efficiently incorporate the latest scientific advancements while remaining computationally feasible for 3D modeling applications. Because the interactions between gases and aerosols (e.g., heterogeneous chemistry processes occurring on aerosols, secondary organic aerosol formation, and aqueous phase chemistry) are intrinsically linked in the atmosphere there is a growing need for modern software architecture systems to evolve to accurately represent this multiphase chemistry in 3D models. In this work, we will 1) share our initial progress on incorporating CRACMM into UFS-Chem through the use of NOAA’s CATChem (Configurable ATmospheric Chemistry) library and modeling component and NSF NCAR’s MUSICA (Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols) library, 2) describe how we are designing our new system to efficiently and accurately represent these multiphase chemistry processes important for accurately representing air quality in 3D models, and 3) get feedback from the community on the progress and vision.

491972.title: Developing Week 2 Severe Weather Predictions through Decoder-Only Transformer Postprocessing of Weather Model Forecasts
491972.authors: Michael J. Hosek, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; and T. J. Galarneau
491972.abstract: Experimental medium-range (days 3-8) daily severe weather predictions derived from the application of a decoder-only transformer (DOT) to both physics-based and AI-emulated numerical weather prediction forecast models have demonstrated impressive skill (Hua et al. 2026). This work extends the DOT technique to the prediction of severe weather through week 2 (days 8-15). While daily forecast skill degrades with increasing lead time, alternative types of severe weather forecasts including rolling multi-day windows and the weekly frequency of high-impact severe days relative to climatology are investigated. These results will preview an experimental extended-range severe weather forecast product to be tested by participants of the NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed Extended Range Severe Weather Forecasting and Verification Experiment (SWERVE) 2027.

491973.title: Terrestrial Water Cycle Evolution During Soil Moisture Whiplash
491973.authors: Kristen Marie Whitney, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, Greenbelt, MD; NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and S. V. Kumar, W. Nie, and J. Bolten
491973.abstract: Hydroclimate whiplash, characterized by rapid transitions between extreme dry and wet conditions, has emerged as an increasingly important manifestation of an intensifying water cycle across many regions in recent decades. Because these transitions often occur before natural and human systems have fully adjusted to the preceding extreme, they can produce greater disruption than either extreme occurring in isolation, resulting in cascading impacts on water resources, ecosystems, agriculture, and infrastructure. Recent studies have shown that surface soil moisture mediates land-atmosphere feedbacks governing rapid wetting and drying transitions, with the dominant pathways varying across hydroclimatic environments. However, how the terrestrial water cycle evolves through these transitions remains poorly understood. Using a physically consistent global land-surface reanalysis constrained by satellite observations (2003–2021), we identify dry-to-wet (DW) and wet-to-dry (WD) whiplash events from transitions between extreme dry and wet surface soil moisture states and delineate coherent hotspot regions of recurrent whiplash activity. We quantify hotspot whiplash behavior, including whiplash frequency, abruptness, seasonal occurrence, dominant transition direction (DW or WD), and directional asymmetry. We then compare the evolution of terrestrial hydrologic and vegetation conditions among hotspots exhibiting contrasting whiplash behavior. The presentation will examine what these differences reveal about terrestrial evolution among global whiplash hotspots.

491974.title: Accelerating Process Representation Research into Operations using Hierarchical UFS/SCM/NoahMP Simulations
491974.authors: Michael J. Barlage, Office of Modeling and Development, Boulder, CO; and Y. Cheng, Z. Guo, and W. Zheng
491974.abstract: The current NoahMP implementation in UFS and MPAS assumes a two-tile representation of the surface where the two tiles are quasi-independent. Separate energy balances are calculated over a vegetated and non-vegetated surface, then area-averaged to send back to the atmosphere. These tiles overlay a single soil column, where the total soil/snow interface flux is used as a top boundary condition for soil/snow thermodynamic updates. In addition, for the vegetated tile, the energy balance is calculated first for the canopy and then for the sub-canopy. This approach, though conservative, can make the calculated fluxes inconsistent with the diagnostic temperature/moisture calculated in the model. Furthermore, due to the low roughness length of bare ground and decreased turbulent interactions below canopy, this method can result in a decoupling of the soil with the atmosphere. A new approach is implemented and tested where a single “blended” tile is used to represent distributed vegetation elements producing a single energy and water flux for the model tile. The method also attempts to better represent land-atmosphere interactions through approximating the impact of turbulent mixing between canopy elements resulting in stronger coupling between the atmosphere and the soil. To achieve a better representation of the surface, increased communication and collaboration with NOAA/NESDIS has been established to provide additional datasets to estimate the vegetation cover using satellite imagery. As part of this work, a hierarchical testing environment in the CCPP single column model (SCM) was developed to assess systematic impacts of model changes on land atmosphere coupling. This presentation will show the impact of incorporating a new representation of the NoahMP vegetation structure in SCM simulations evaluated against surface temperature/moisture measurements and flux tower observations.

491976.title: Developing a Seasonal Index for Tropical Easterly Wave Activity
491976.authors: Carolyn Joy Emerson, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and V. Misra
491976.abstract: Tropical Easterly Waves (TEWs) are synoptic-scale seed disturbances that regularly spawn from the African Easterly Jet (AEJ) and travel westward across the tropical Atlantic. Approximately 60-65 TEWs are tracked across the Atlantic annually, with 14-17% developing into tropical cyclones (TCs). TEWs are a significant contributor to Atlantic TC activity with 75% of TCs and 85% of major hurricanes originating from a TEW. The seasonal climatology of TEW activity is well understood, with the climatological active window occurring during June-October, largely matching the Atlantic hurricane season. However, TEWs have been noted to have complex interannual and decadal variability, often relating to other large-scale climate modulations. Furthermore, TEWs exhibit distinct characteristics depending on whether they follow a northern or southern track, suggesting these sub-populations may possess unique low-frequency variations and climatic sensitivities. This work aims to develop a seasonal index for TEW activity that can be used to better understand the long-term variations in TEW activity and their dominant climatic drivers.

491977.title: Evaluating Regional Air Quality over the CONUS with a Variable-Resolution Global UFS-Chem Model
491977.authors: Jian He, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA/Chemical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and L. Zhang, L. M. Harris, M. Lin, V. Naik, R. H. Schwantes, C. Lyu, C. Harkins, M. Li, Q. Z. Rasool, M. Bruckner, B. D. Baker II, W. Li, R. Ahmadov, J. Schnell, L. Bernardet, S. Kondragunta, C. Warneke, S. S. Brown, and B. C. McDonald
491977.abstract: Simulating atmospheric chemistry across multiple spatial scales remains a significant challenge for both operational forecasting and regional air quality research. Traditional nested regional models often suffer from lateral boundary condition errors that limit their application for long range transport of air pollutants, while uniform global models are computationally constrained from resolving localized chemical features. These challenges have motivated the development of variable-resolution global chemistry-climate models with regional grid refinements, such as GFDL AM4VR and NCAR MUSICA. Here we present a stretched-grid configuration of NOAA’s Unified Forecast System with Chemistry (UFS-Chem) for regional air quality applications. We employ a stretched cubed-sphere grid centered over the Continental United States (CONUS), with regional resolution comparable to a C768 grid (~12.5 km near the stretch center), and compare its performance against a standard uniform C384 global UFS-Chem simulation (~25 km). This work extends UFS-Chem with a stretched-grid capability, enabling seamless multiscale weather–chemistry simulations within a fully coupled global forecasting system. To assess the multiscale fidelity of this modeling framework, we simulate the summer 2023 period and conduct a multi-platform validation using both spaceborne and airborne measurements. We use satellite observations to evaluate the model's representation of large-scale chemical distributions and localized gradients. Furthermore, we utilize extensive airborne data from the 2023 Atmospheric Emissions and Reactions Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas (AEROMMA) field campaign to diagnose the model's performance in simulating regional air quality over CONUS. Preliminary results indicate that the stretched-grid configuration improves regional air quality simulations relative to the uniform-resolution C384 simulation while maintaining consistent large-scale chemical distributions, supporting the use of UFS-Chem as a seamless global-to-regional air quality modeling framework.

491978.title: Implementation of Explicit Volatile Chemical Product Chemistry in CAMx: Implications for Regulatory Ozone Modeling
491978.authors: Marco Rodriguez, Ramboll, FORT COLLINS, CO; and K. Tuite, T. Tran, T. Shah, C. J. Chien, and R. Morris
491978.abstract: Volatile chemical products (VCPs), including personal care products, cleaners, coatings, adhesives, pesticides, and other solvent-containing products, represent an increasingly important share of anthropogenic volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions in urban areas. However, many oxygenated VOCs, siloxanes, and large alkanes used in VCPs are not explicitly represented in conventional chemical mechanisms. Instead, they are assigned to surrogate species which can have lower reactivity, potentially underestimating their ozone-forming potential. To address this limitation, this study first developed an explicit treatment of VCP-associated emissions and chemistry within the Comprehensive Air-quality Model with extensions (CAMx). The study then evaluated this treatment using the CAMx modeling platform developed for ozone planning in the Denver Metro/North Front Range (DM/NFR), Colorado nonattainment area for a 2022 base-year and 2026 future-year scenarios. The explicit VCP treatment was implemented and evaluated using the CAMx model with nested model domains at 36-,12-, and 4-kilometer resolution developed for the DM/NFR Serious ozone State Implementation Plan (SIP). The modeling episode extended from May 26 through September 15, 2022, following a 15-day spin-up period. The 2022 base-year and 2026 future-year emissions scenarios were based on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) 2022v1 platform and incorporated Colorado-specific updates. VCP-associated emissions were first identified in the solvent and non-electric-generating-unit inventories using Source Classification Codes. This analysis estimated 42,890 tons per year of VCP-related VOC emissions in Colorado, including 40,733 tons per year from solvent sources and 2,158 tons per year from industrial point sources. To represent these emissions more explicitly, the Carbon Bond chemical mechanism was updated to add 16 explicit gas-phase VCP species and their associated hydroxyl-radical oxidation chemistry. These species represent compound classes that are not adequately characterized by conventional surrogate assignments, including alcohols, ethers, esters, siloxanes, and large alkanes. Emission mappings were revised for the new mechanism, and 2,676 VOC speciation profiles were generated from the EPA SPECIATE database version 5.3 (https://www.epa.gov/air-emissions-modeling/speciate-4). The affected emissions sectors were then reprocessed using the Sparse Matrix Operator Kernel Emissions (SMOKE) processing system to produce CAMx-ready emissions both with and without explicit VCP speciation. The 2022 base-case simulation had previously undergone a model performance evaluation against available ozone observations. The model performed adequately for its intended use in the ozone SIP, although it tended to underpredict the highest observed ozone concentrations. The sensitivity simulations conducted in this study therefore assessed whether explicit VCP speciation and chemistry improved the representation of peak ozone. Comparisons of the 2022 base-case simulations with and without the explicit VCP treatment showed that the resulting changes in modeled ozone varied by location and time but were generally too small to meaningfully improve overall model performance. Additional 2026 sensitivity simulations evaluated the effects of explicit VCP treatment and VCP-associated emissions on projected ozone design values. The changes in modeled ozone concentrations due the implemented VCP chemistry were observed in urban areas, particularly near metropolitan Denver, consistent with the spatial distribution of VCP-associated emissions. Maximum hourly differences were small and ranged from +0.27 to −0.13 ppb in 2022 and from +0.18 to −0.11 ppb in 2026. Ozone generally increased during the morning, when freshly emitted VCP-associated VOCs entered the atmosphere, and decreased more often during the afternoon. This diurnal pattern indicates that the explicit treatment affects the timing of modeled VOC sensitivity, but overall impacts on ozone chemistry are minor. Accordingly, projected 2026 ozone design values differed by less than 0.1 ppb at all monitoring sites between simulations with and without explicit VCP treatment. The sensitivity simulation that removed all VCP-associated emissions produced a larger, although still modest, response, reducing projected design values by 0.1 to 0.7 ppb at a subset of monitors. The results show a practical implementation of chemically explicit VCP treatment in an operational photochemical modeling platform. Better representation of VCP composition improves the chemical representation and traceability of emissions. Although ozone impacts were small, the VCP updates to CAMx represent an improvement to the model as the importance of VCP chemistry has been noted by several researchers. The larger response to removing VCP-associated emissions, although still modest, shows that the rate of emissions and their spatial distribution have an important influence on projected design values. These results could help planning agencies develop more accurate and effective control strategies in consideration of VCP sources, as relevant for their nonattainment area. The latest version of CAMx (v7.40, released on July 30, 2026) provides explicit VCP treatment as an available chemical mechanism and is freely available for public download.

491982.title: Modernizing EMC's Global Workflow to Balance Development and Operational Needs Through Templates
491982.authors: Travis J. Elless, EMC, College Park, MD; and D. Huber, A. Fernando, A. Smoot, T. McGuinness, A. Hrabski, and J. R. Carley
491982.abstract: The NOAA/NWS Environmental Modeling Center (EMC) maintains a global workflow codebase that has historically included all the necessary scripting that allow development and operational users to run the Global Forecast System (GFS) on multiple high performance computing platforms. Over the past 5 years, the complexity of this codebase increased significantly. Coupled model development for GFSv17 and the addition of several other systems to the global workflow package as part of the NWS Unified Forecast System effort [Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), Seasonal Forecast System (SFS), and Global Chemistry and Aerosols Forecast System (GCAFS)], resulted in the need to build and maintain functionality for these different components and systems. Additionally, developers and operational users currently use different workflow schedulers (Rocoto vs ecFlow) which further increases the code maintenance activities and complexities of the global workflow. This presentation will highlight the efforts made so far to address some of these complexities through centralizing commonly used code and the use of system-specific configurations. We will examine how these strategies have worked well for development users but have fallen short in addressing operational needs. This presentation will then pivot to a discussion and examples of our adoption of a templating strategy to modernize and improve the workflow. In particular, a focus on increasing our use of Jinja-templated configurations will allow for more easily testable, maintainable, and deployable code for both our developers and operational users. Finally, we will look forward to our plan to utilize the Unified Workflow (UW) tools to generate more dynamic, maintainable and developer-friendly ecFlow code in the global workflow. This will help eliminate the barrier of entry for developmental users utilizing ecFlow and reduce the need to maintain two separate workflow schedulers.

491985.title: Leveraging Guided Random Forest Machine Learning to Advance Gridded Composite Drought Indicators for Operational Drought Monitoring
491985.authors: Brian Fuchs, National Drought Mitigation Center-University of Nebraska, LINCOLN, NE; and M. D. Svoboda
491985.abstract: . Weekly operational drought monitoring requires objective guidance tools that balance multi-scalar physical data with expert validation. While historical "objective blends" supporting the United States Drought Monitor (USDM) relied on manual weighting of coarse climate division data, modern operational timelines demand high-resolution, gridded data fusion. To address this need, the National Drought Mitigation Center (NDMC) developed a digital data library of operationally available climate variables, utilizing guided random forest machine learning (ML) models to optimize inputs and predictive weights across diverse timescales. This ML-driven approach automatically identifies flash, short-, mid-, and long-term drought episodes while actively accounting for climate non-stationarity, regional microclimates, and seasonal nuances. By pairing historical expert consensus with guided random forest decision architectures, the resulting composite drought indicators provide objective, gridded spatial guidance that mirrors the reality observed on the ground. Operationally deployed at https://ndmcblends.unl.edu, these tools allow USDM authors and regional contributors to isolate specific atmospheric and terrestrial drivers affecting localized systems week-to-week to best categorize drought spatial extent and intensity. Furthermore, ongoing developments leverage these synchronized composites to train predictive artificial intelligence pipelines capable of generating an automated, weekly "first guess" of the final USDM map via a composite of the composites. This predictive evolution directly enhances the climate enterprise's capacity for rapid-response extreme event tracking, providing actionable, localized intelligence for agricultural, water resource, and municipal decision-makers grappling with expanding climate extremes and will continue to enhance and improve the weekly United States Drought Monitor.

491987.title: Participation of the Canadian Ice Service in an Antarctic expedition
491987.authors: Alexandra Cournoyer, EC, Montréal, QC, Canada
491987.abstract: The Ice Service Specialists of the Canadian Ice Service (CIS), a division of the Meteorological Service of Canada, are professionals with expertise in the observation and analysis of meteorological and ice conditions in support of maritime and environmental operational planning, as well as in the management and development of partnerships with a range of stakeholders. In March 2026, the CIS participated in the Canadian Antarctic Research Expedition aboard the Chilean Navy vessel Almirante Viel. This participation supported the expedition's scientific planning, including the identification of sampling areas, through the provision of real-time observations and analysis of ice and weather conditions. The deployment also provided an opportunity for knowledge and expertise exchange with Chilean counterparts operating in polar waters, enabling a comparison of service levels, operational procedures, and data practices between Canada's Arctic operations and Chile's Antarctic operations. This collaboration generated positive feedback while also identifying areas requiring further development to achieve full operational capability.

491989.title: Intercomparison of Optical and SAR-Derived Sea Ice Concentration Products over Alaskan Waters for Improved Operational Arctic Sea Ice Monitoring and Forecasting
491989.authors: Olivia Smith, University of Virginia, Fairfax Station, VA; NOAA, College Park, MD; NWS/NCEP/Ocean and Tsunami Center (U.S. National Ice Center), Hillcrest Heights, MD; and S. R. Helfrich, W. Clark, and R. C. Julian
491989.abstract: Monitoring sea ice is a fundamental aspect of numerical weather prediction, climate tracking, polar ecology, and maritime operations in the Arctic. Despite advances in remote sensing, validating and tracking Arctic sea ice remains difficult due to uncertainties arising from limited in-situ data, persistent cloud cover, seasonal polar darkness, and surface melt and snow cover. Currently, ice analysts rely on all-weather, high-resolution synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery to create generalized charts of the Arctic and Antarctic to guide mariners, however it is a time-consuming and expertise-dependent process. Combining optical sensors and SAR imagery through blending has the potential to improve both the accuracy and speed in estimating sea ice concentrations, allowing for applications in atmospheric and oceanic models and improved operational sea ice forecasting. This work aims to inform such future dataset blending by quantifying systematic differences across ice concentration ranges and seasons between two products: the NOAA Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), an infrared and optical sensor limited by cloud cover and polar darkness, and the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI)-Automated Sea Ice Products (ASIP) SAR-derived L3 sea ice concentration product, a CNN trained on Sentinel-1 SAR imagery and ice charts providing all-weather coverage. The differences were characterized over Alaskan waters in the Beaufort, Chukchi, and Bering Seas. Comparison days spanning winter and summer seasons were selected to maximize clear-sky VIIRS coverage and capture both the melt-out and maximum ice coverage cycles of sea ice. Both products were co-registered to a common polar stereographic grid and compared across 10% concentration bins using traditional error metrics (e.g., bias, RMSE, STD) and performance diagrams (e.g., probability of detection, success rate). DMI-ASIP consistently estimated higher ice concentrations relative to VIIRS across all bins in both seasons, with mean seasonal bias lowest in the 90-100% range (summer = 1.2%, winter = 2.4%) and largest in the 10-20% range (summer = 54.5%, winter = 72.9%), consistent with known retrieval challenges along the marginal ice zone. Winter biases were significantly larger than summer across 9 of 10 bins (p < 0.01), potentially associated with differences in new-ice detection. These initial findings suggest that future blending of VIIRS and DMI-ASIP products must account for seasonal and concentration-dependent biases, particularly in the marginal ice zone, for improved operational sea ice monitoring and forecasting.

491990.title: Radiation Parameterization In the Age of Data (Invited Presentation)
491990.authors: Robert Pincus, LDEO, Palisades, NY; and D. J. X. Ho and P. Czarnecki
491990.abstract: The representation of radiation in atmospheric models is a particularly clear example of parameterization: the governing equations are known so the task is “simply” about balancing computational cost with the requisite accuracy. The computation of radiative fluxes requires two integrals: one over all the angles in each hemisphere, and the other over the electromagnetic spectrum, which varies in opacity by orders of magnitude over very small spectral intervals. I’ll describe two parameterizations develop in the last five years to address these problems. Data-driven quadrature identifies a small (order 50) number of spectral locations and associated weights that reproduce benchmark calculations of spectrally-integrated fluxes, where the spectral locations and weights are determined by minimizing an explicit cost function over a finite set of atmospheric conditions. This explicitly empirical approach circumvents many of the conceptual and practical problems inherent in correlated k distributions. Angular integration, typically avoided by using two-stream methods, can also be approached using simple empirical methods including interpolation to map the optical properties of the atmosphere directly to the required layer-integrated reflectance and transmittance, avoiding pitfalls introduced by unrealistic structural assumptions made in the development of the two-stream equations. The theme in both efforts is the transparent and careful use of empiricism that respects the governing equations.

491995.title: The Evolving Global Satellite Observing System: WMO Priorities for the Weather Enterprise
491995.authors: Natalia Donoho, WMO, Geneva, GE, Switzerland
491995.abstract: Space-based observations are fundamental to today’s weather and Earth-system prediction capabilities, while the environment in which operational satellite systems are planned, operated, and used is changing rapidly. New observing technologies, expanding commercial capabilities, increasing demands for Earth-system information, evolving data architectures, and growing pressure on the radio-frequency spectrum are reshaping the global observing landscape. This invited presentation will provide an update on key World Meteorological Organization (WMO) priorities and developments relevant to the operational environmental satellite and broader weather enterprise. It will highlight progress toward the WMO Integrated Global Observing System (WIGOS) Vision 2050 and WMO’s work to translate evolving user requirements into priorities for future space-based observing capabilities. Particular attention will be given to the increasing integration of observations across weather, climate, atmospheric composition, oceans, cryosphere, greenhouse gases, and space weather. The presentation will also examine several cross-cutting issues that will influence the resilience and effectiveness of the future observing system. These include protection of the radio-frequency spectrum required for passive and active Earth observations; implementation of the WMO Unified Data Policy, including the identification and international exchange of Core data needed to support essential weather, climate, and related Earth-system services; the evolution of data discovery and access through WMO Information System (WIS) 2.0; and the opportunities and challenges presented by new technologies, commercial observing systems, and increasingly diverse data providers. The presentation will conclude with a forward-looking perspective on how WMO is responding to this changing landscape and how the weather enterprise can help shape the next generation of operational environmental satellite systems, ensuring that advances in space-based observations translate into improved forecasts, warnings, climate services, and societal benefits.

491998.title: Drone-Based Glaciogenic Seeding and Radar Signatures: Operations, Case Study, and Statistical Characterization from the 2025–2026 Rainmaker Season
491998.authors: Martin Satrio, Rainmaker Technology Corporation, Norman, OK; and J. Aikins, A. Dixon, A. Dobracki, C. Wessel, M. Decker, and K. Suski
491998.abstract: During the 2025–2026 winter season, Rainmaker Technology Corporation conducted operational glaciogenic cloud seeding campaigns in several target areas, including Pendleton, Oregon, the Bear River basin of Idaho, and several domains across Utah. Seeding utilized weather-resistant uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) developed in-house to disperse silver iodide (AgI) via burn-in-place flares directly into supercooled liquid water (SLW) regions of winter orographic and stratiform cloud systems. UAS-based delivery offers several advantages over ground-based generators and manned seeding aircraft, including precise targeting of SLW zones, operation in conditions that may preclude manned flight, and reduced operational cost. Collectively, the season's physically-validated seeding signatures are estimated to have produced several hundred acre-feet of additional water, a meaningful contribution to water resources in each target area. A comprehensive observational strategy characterized the atmospheric environment before, during, and after each event. The instrument suite included ceilometers for cloud-base height, radiosondes with SLW sensors for thermodynamic profiling and supercooled liquid detection, UAS-mounted in-situ sensors measuring pressure, temperature, relative humidity, and SLW within the seeding environment itself, and remote sensing from NEXRAD S-band radars, a dedicated gap-filling X-band radar atop Sedgwick Peak in southeastern Idaho, and the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES). This presentation first summarizes the operational domains, UAS capabilities, and measurement and validation strategy. A case study from 23–24 January in the Pendleton, Oregon domain is then examined in detail, tracing localized reflectivity enhancements consistent with AgI-induced ice nucleation and subsequent precipitation development, radar-derived quantitative precipitation estimates attributable to seeding, and the evolution of dual-polarization variables within the seeded plume as it advected downwind. Changes in the ZDR and ρHV distributions are used to infer the microphysical evolution of seeded hydrometeors. Finally, a statistical analysis of the 71 radar-identified seeding signatures observed across the season characterizes seeded plumes under varying operational and environmental conditions. Temporal metrics are quantified, including time to initial detection, peak reflectivity, maximum precipitation production, and maximum spatial extent, while composite analyses characterize signature morphology, horizontal structure, and areal coverage of anthropogenic precipitation. Segmentation by mission characteristics reveals preliminary results on how signature evolution and detectability vary with flare burn time, number of flares, and ambient temperature and wind speed. These results demonstrate UAS-based glaciogenic seeding as a scalable approach to winter orographic precipitation enhancement and offer a repeatable framework for radar-based validation of seeding effects.

492001.title: LEMS v3: An Open-Source Distributed Platform for Microclimate and Air-Quality Monitoring
492001.authors: Fabien Margairaz, Univ. of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and T. Wright, K. Baldino, L. Ulmer, A. Yousuf, W. Mahaffee, E. R. Pardyjak, and R. Stoll
492001.abstract: Complex environments such as cities and agricultural fields contain strong spatial variations in wind, temperature, humidity, surface energy exchange, and air quality. Conventional meteorological towers provide high-quality observations, but their cost, size, and deployment requirements limit the number of locations that can be sampled. Distributed low-cost sensor networks offer an alternative approach by providing the spatial coverage needed to characterize heterogeneous environments and evaluate atmospheric models. The Low-cost Energy-budget Measurement Stations (LEMS) were originally developed as open-source, Arduino-based weather stations for continuous environmental monitoring. The platform measured wind speed and direction, air temperature, relative humidity, barometric pressure, incoming solar radiation, surface temperature, soil temperature, and soil moisture. Laboratory and field evaluations demonstrated that LEMS could provide useful measurements at approximately a tenth of the cost, compared to similarly instrumented research-grade towers. These deployments also identified practical limitations related to power consumption, connectivity, sensor performance, and scalability. This work presents LEMS v3 (https://github.com/UtahEFD/LEMSv3), a redesigned open-source platform that improves flexibility, ease of deployment, and long-term operation. The updated system combines low-cost, off-the-shelf sensors with modular interfaces for digital, analog, and SDI-12 instruments. Integrated positioning, local data storage, wireless communication, solar power, and a compact mounting system support deployments across a wide range of environments. In addition to standard micrometeorological measurements, LEMS v3 extends the platform to air-quality applications through measurements of ozone and particulate matter. This flexibility allows individual stations to be configured for specific scientific objectives while maintaining a common measurement and data-management framework. When deployed as a distributed network, LEMS v3 provides the spatial density needed to resolve local gradients, identify sources and sinks, quantify horizontal transport, and characterize variability that cannot be captured by isolated stations. Two current projects illustrate these capabilities. In the USDA-funded FRAMEwork project, a network of 26 LEMS is deployed across vineyards in five states. The stations collect vineyard-scale microclimate observations to support crop-phenology estimates, disease-risk mapping, improved timing of fungicide applications, and resistance monitoring. In the NSF-funded VBUS project, a gridded network of nine LEMS is combined with centralized turbulence measurements to document changes in microclimate, urban energy budgets, ozone, and particulate matter before a after the redevelopment of an entire city block in Salt Lake City, Utah. Together, these applications demonstrate how LEMS v3 can provide high-resolution environmental datasets for model development, agricultural management, urban planning, and science-based assessment across a changing landscape.

492003.title: Success or Bust of Project Pen Pal: The Evaluation of an Inter-Collegiate Course on Collaborative Research
492003.authors: Katelyn A. Barber, Valparaiso Univ., Valparaiso, IN; and R. Stenz and Y. Wang
492003.abstract: Research Collaborations (affectionately known as Project Pen Pal), was an in-person/virtual course offered for the first time at three universities (Valparaiso University, the College of DuPage, and SUNY Oswego) during Spring 2026. This course aimed to replicate real-world research experiences, such as those in major research institutions. Twenty-six students from the three universities were placed into research groups based on their scientific interests, academic level, and institutions with a goal of completing a research project from the ground up, concluding with a 20-minute virtual group seminar on the their topics. Each week of the semester, a new research component was covered complementing the students project tasks, such as formulating a research question, open-source coding repositories, meteorological datasets, scientific writing, and interpersonal communication strategies (in-person and virtually). An “all-hands” meeting was held at the fourth week for all students to meet each other virtually. A career panel with personnel from various meteorological landscapes was held virtually where the topic was collaboration. In the end, research projects were completed with varying success and both students and faculty did experience the highs and lows of research. After reflection by the faculty instructors, advice and considerations are provided for similar future courses.

492007.title: Expanding the UFS Community through the Unifying Innovations in Forecasting Capabilities Workshop (UIFCW)
492007.authors: Jennifer Vogt, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and A. Gregory, J. Wheeler, and A. C. Jones
492007.abstract: The Unifying Innovations in Forecasting Capabilities Workshop (UIFCW) has evolved over the past five years into a critical nexus for the Weather, Water, and Climate Enterprise, serving as a primary venue for advancing the Unified Forecast System (UFS). This presentation highlights the growth of UIFCW from its inception to the 5th Annual Workshop held in 2026, demonstrating how this annual gathering has become essential to fostering a cohesive, collaborative UFS community across government, academic, and private sectors. Beyond the workshop events, this talk examines the strategic outreach efforts that have significantly strengthened the UFS community during this period. These initiatives include the implementation of targeted training sessions, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Numerical Weather Prediction, the UFS Ambassador Program, and the expansion of student travel grants that have broadened global academic interest. Notably, specific efforts to bridge the gap between research and operations (R2O), combined with deliberate outreach to Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) and NOAA Cooperative Science Centers, have been instrumental in fostering inclusivity and nurturing a diverse talent pipeline. By analyzing the longitudinal successes and community engagement metrics from 2022–2026, this presentation outlines how these workshops and outreach programs have accelerated innovation, optimized new technologies, and ultimately enhanced operational forecasting capabilities.

492010.title: Passive Microwave Water Vapor Sounding Retrievals via Gaussian and non-Gaussian Formulations
492010.authors: Steven J. Fletcher, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and J. M. Forsythe, T. H. VonderHaar, and S. Liu
492010.abstract: The existing NASA Water Vapor Project Making Earth System Data Records for Use in Research Environments (NVAP-M) dataset spans 1988-2009. It consists of daily, global total column water vapor (TCWV) and layer water vapor fields. NVAP-M characterizes global water vapor, an Essential Climate Variable. It supports users from both a weather case study and climate standpoint. NVAP-M was evaluated under the GEWEX Water Vapor Assessment (GVAP) efforts of the past several years. NVAP-M is constructed from blended multisatellite observations with minimal reliance on reanalysis products. This makes it valuable for comparison to the reanalyses. Satellite microwave observations provide the core data for observationally-based datasets like NVAP, which provide an alternative approach to reanalyses. Hypersectral infrared instruments such as AIRS, IASI and CrIS provide a foundation for the 21st century portion of the time series. However, there have been several studies recently that have indicated that both reanalysis and water vapor datasets appear to overestimate the water vapor over semi-arid regions. As most 1DVAR retrieval systems are based upon a Gaussian assumption for the errors, this maybe causing this incorrect state. Differences in water vapor fields between the Gaussian and non-Gaussian formulations will be presented.

492012.title: Energetic Fluxes during Northern Hemispheric Rain-on-Snow and Non-Precipitation Snowmelt Events
492012.authors: Zachary Suriano, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and S. Adhikari and R. D. Dixon
492012.abstract: The combination of liquid precipitation during snowmelt, a rain-on-snow (ROS) event, is a common but hydrologically impactful occurrence, where the dual inputs of runoff have the potential to generate substantial flooding and other hazards. Our team’s recent work evaluating ROS has demonstrated that latent heat fluxes into the snowpack, which lead to faster melt rates, are often underrepresented in models. However, this work has been focused on case studies across the Central and Eastern United States. To better understand when and where these fluxes are important for proper snowmelt forecasts, we investigate the timing and spatial patterns of turbulent fluxes during ROS and compared to snowmelt events without precipitation (NP). In this study, we used hourly reanalysis from ERA5 from 1980-2024 to identify periods of ROS and NP and quantify the corresponding energetic exchange across the Northern Hemisphere. Results indicate turbulent heat fluxes account for approximately half of the total energy during ROS, but with substantial spatial variability and an increasing contribution of turbulent heat fluxes with progressive larger ROS events. The percentage contribution to total energy from turbulent heat fluxes during ROS more than doubles when comparing our smallest (0.5 mm/hr; ~29%) to largest (2.0 mm/hr; ~62%) event magnitude thresholds. Further, the magnitude of turbulent vs. radiative fluxes during ROS are, in-part, a function of elevation, where over half of the variance in the spatial pattern of shortwave radiation fluxes during ROS can be attributed to variations in elevation. In contrast, NP snowmelt events do not exhibit meaningful differences in turbulent vs radiative fluxes, on average, with net radiation (primarily shortwave) contributing over 95% of energetic inputs.

492016.title: Evaluating Spatial Calibration Strategies for Regional Soil Moisture and Agricultural Drought Prediction: An Illinois Testbed
492016.authors: Tahsina Alam, University of Illinois, Urbana, IL; and D. Lafferty, T. Avila, T. Ford, S. Zuidema, and R. Sriver
492016.abstract: Accurate simulation of root-zone soil moisture is fundamental for drought monitoring, hydrologic forecasting, and assessment of future water availability. Hydrologic models are commonly calibrated independently at individual monitoring stations, limiting parameter transferability and reducing predictive skill in ungauged regions. Although spatial calibration has the potential to overcome these limitations, there is limited understanding of which approaches best balance regional consistency with local hydrologic realism. We use Illinois as a well-instrumented testbed to systematically evaluate spatial calibration strategies for scalable hydrologic modeling. Using the differentiable Python Water Balance Model (pyWBM) and long-term soil moisture observations from the Illinois Water and Atmospheric Resources Monitoring (WARM) network, we compare multiple spatial calibration approaches, including geographically weighted calibration, environmentally based parameter regionalization, hierarchical calibration, and spatially regularized optimization. These methods integrate soil properties, land cover, and meteorological information to estimate transferable hydrologic parameters while preserving local hydrologic characteristics. Their performance is evaluated against conventional station-by-station calibration using leave-one-station-out cross-validation and multiple objective functions, including RMSE, KGE, KGE′, and drought-focused performance metrics. The best-performing calibration strategy is subsequently applied with LOCA2 downscaled CMIP6 meteorological projections to generate regional projections of future root-zone soil moisture and agricultural drought. By systematically comparing alternative spatial calibration methods, this study identifies approaches that improve parameter transferability, preserve local hydrologic variability, and enhance prediction in data-limited regions. While Illinois provides an ideal testbed because of its long-term, high-quality observation network, the methodology is designed to be transferable to other regions where sparse in situ observations must be integrated with spatial environmental data. The results provide practical guidance for regional hydrologic model calibration and support improved drought monitoring, future water-resource assessment, and water management under changing environmental conditions.

492018.title: Improving Estimates of Western US Snow Water Resources By Assimilating Process Based Models and Deep Learning SWE Estimates
492018.authors: Justin M Pflug, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and S. V. Kumar, A. Getirana, M. Wrzesien, K. M. Whitney, K. Locke, M. T. Dodson, D. M. Mocko, and F. Z. Maina
492018.abstract: Seasonal snow in the western US is a critical source of water for municipalities, local ecosystems, and agriculture. However, models used for operational decision making are often heavily parameterized, dependent on sparse networks of point snow observations, or do not represent the interrelationships between snowpack, soil moisture, and runoff generation important for streamflow. Here, using results from NASA’s North American Land Data Assimilation System, version 3 (NLDAS-3), we evaluate the impact on seasonal runoff and water supplies from assimilating snow water equivalent (SWE) generated from a remote sensing-based deep-learning model. We focus on gaged and unmanaged headwater regions contributing to US Bureau of Reclamation dams in years with anomalously high and low snow amounts, which are currently the most challenging to simulate with existing operational models. Results show 1) improvements to simulated SWE relative to Western US snow pillows and historical reanalyses, and 2) improved characterization of runoff pulses as compared to observed streamflow in snow-dominated watersheds. Provided feedback from state, regional, and federal collaborators, we also discuss how low-latency hydrologic outputs from NLDAS-3 could be used to assess forecasted water supplies across both short-range (2-week) and seasonal (multi-month) periods important for decision making activities. By constraining snow hydrology using deep learning, we develop low-latency hydrologic data into the insight and decision support tools necessary for resilient water management in increasingly anomalous years.

492019.title: CIMSS Satellite Blog Highlights of the Uses of GOES Imagery
492019.authors: Mathew Gunshor, CIMSS, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; CIMSS/SSEC, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and T. J. Wagner, A. S. Bachmeier, and W. Line
492019.abstract: The CIMSS Satellite Blog highlights interesting meteorological and environmental phenomena that can be observed with satellite imagery and products. GOES imagery is the most frequently used imagery for this purpose because of the temporal frequency and coverage area available. The blog format allows for timely reporting on impactful events, provides material for training, and serves as a form of public outreach highlighting the usefulness of satellite imagery. The CIMSS Satellite Blog has been around for over 20 years and this presentation will focus primarily on highlights from the GOES-R series Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) from 2026, including blowing dust, convection, low clouds and fog, wildfires, and winter weather. GOES is not the only satellite that is featured on the blog and so VIIRS and other imagery will be presented, as well as other types of data such as RAOB and model data. The blog provides scientists with examples of products and techniques that are useful for various types of situations. Examples of how meteorologists can apply satellite data and products during real events is useful for training and helps the public better understand why these instruments are so necessary.

492022.title: Unlocking the Value of SMBA: A Value of Information (VoI) Approach to Satellite Mission Design
492022.authors: Katherine A Hawley, NESDIS, Lanham, MD; and S. Kalluri, V. Grycenkov, J. M. Valenti, S. E. Groot, M. Johnson, K. Klockow McClain, B. Smith, C. Smith, and H. E. Brooks
492022.abstract: The Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) program marks a fundamental paradigm shift in NOAA’s approach to space-based Earth observations. Representing the agency’s first transition toward a disaggregated architecture in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), NEON moves away from the traditional model of large, multi-instrument platforms, such as the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS), in favor of a more agile, distributed network. This modernized approach ensures critical data continuity while enabling rapid adaptation to emerging operational and user requirements. To support this new architecture, the Office of LEO Observations conducted a Value of Information (VoI) study evaluating how, when, where, and why microwave sounders (MW) provide value to the nation through the lens of NOAA’s National Hurricane Center (NHC) track and intensity forecasts. This presentation communicates key findings, details how the Office of LEO Observations defines value, and traces the VoI analytical process used to reveal the value of NEON’s Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) concept across four candidate architectural configurations. Furthermore, it details how a rigorous VoI methodology and targeted user engagement can be leveraged to directly inform satellite mission design, establishing a repeatable framework to assess the value of earth observations across diverse user communities.

492023.title: Spatiotemporal Variability of Organic Aerosols Across the Los Angeles South Coast Air Basin During Summertime
492023.authors: Sarah Albertin, Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and A. Middlebrook, A. Piasecki, M. A. Robinson, M. M. Coggon, W. S. Chace, J. Gilman, J. Peischl, I. B. Pollack, A. Rollins, N. Schafer, C. Stockwell, E. Waxman, C. Womack, C. Warneke, S. S. Brown, and T. AEROMMA Science Team
492023.abstract: Organic aerosol (OA) is a major component of urban air pollution, with photochemical secondary OA (SOA) formation representing a primary driver of poor summertime air quality. The Los Angeles South Coast Air Basin (SoCAB) exemplifies persistent urban air quality challenges, as fine particulate matter (PM) levels continue to exceed health-based standards despite decades of emission regulations, with a growing contribution of SOA. Here, utilizing data collected during NOAA’s Atmospheric Emissions and Reactions Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas airborne campaign, we present an updated spatiotemporal characterization of OA across the SoCAB during August 2023. Across all sampled regions, OA dominated submicron nonrefractory aerosol mass (>60%), peaking directly downwind of downtown Los Angeles in the early-to-mid afternoon, while a gradual increase over the afternoon was observed further east toward San Bernardino. We extend previous ground-based OA source apportionment studies to the scale of the SoCAB and investigate the diurnal variability of OA components. Locally formed SOA drove more than 70% of the OA temporal variability downwind of Los Angeles. Daily repeated sampling of the SoCAB enabled near-Lagrangian analysis of SOA production, revealing a clear increase in dilution-corrected SOA with photochemical age across the basin. These results provide a quantitative characterization of OA spatiotemporal variability, highlighting the combined role of topography and photochemistry in sustaining elevated SOA in the SoCAB.

492029.title: Cloud-Based Software Deployments for NWS R&D and Operations
492029.authors: Alexander J.W. Richert, Lynker Corporation, Leesburg, VA; and T. McGuinness, A. Stahl, J. R. Carley, R. Mahajan, S. Earle, H. Lei, and A. Hrabski
492029.abstract: The upcoming transition of the NWS production forecast suite to a cloud-based environment represents a significant milestone and technical transformation for the NWS transition-to-operations (T2O) paradigm. The software dependency stack for the operational suite consists of dozens of direct and indirect dependencies providing libraries and utilities for supporting various scientific file formats, numerical routines, model infrastructure, and various low-level functionality. Past approaches for implementing the software dependency stack have been accompanied by a range of technical and logistical challenges. The increased use of cloud resources in R&D and operations represents an opportunity to improve the way that the production software stack is implemented. As a step in this direction, we first discuss our increasing adoption of automated workflows and containers, including for continuous integration (CI) workflows, along with some of the benefits and challenges of bare-metal and containerized approaches for large model R&D. We then present our preliminary work implementing an operations-ready software stack in an HPC-in-the-cloud environment, and discuss possible future approaches to facilitating DevOps-oriented code delivery in a cloud-native production suite.

492030.title: A Non-Gaussian Data Assimilation Solution for Updating State Quantities Constrained By Their Sum: Application to Sea Ice and Potential for Other Geophysical Variables
492030.authors: Molly M. Wieringa, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Anderson
492030.abstract: Two-step ensemble data assimilation adjusts a model state by updating a model estimate of the observed quantity and then transferring that update to unobserved state variables in some manner. In some geophysical applications, the second step involves category variables that are constrained by physical bounds on their sum. Sea ice, a relevant example, is commonly modeled using an ice thickness distribution that partitions grid cell sea ice concentration amongst several ice thickness categories. Concentration in each ice thickness category is bounded between 0 and 1, as is the sum of all category concentrations. Traditional Gaussian state-space update approaches, which treat each categorized state variable independently, lead to both analysis inaccuracies and non-physical changes to total sea ice concentration. A novel solution for updating categorized state variables constrained by their sum is introduced. The solution, based on probit probability integral transforms and a normalization of the state, is explored in a simple autoregressive model and then applied in a single-column sea ice model. When compared to existing state update methods for the sea ice application, the new solution produces accurate state updates that more appropriately reflect the observation update. These results have implications for data assimilation with other geophysical variables such as cloud fraction, snow layer categories, water storage compartments, and gas tracers.

492031.title: Transitioning the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) Data Assimilation to the JEDI Framework
492031.authors: Shun Liu, NWS/OMD, Riverdale Park, MD; and D. Holdaway, M. Hu, S. K. Degelia, D. E. Lippi, T. Lei, X. Zhang, H. liu, J. R. Carley, D. Klest, M. E. Pyle, G. Ge, D. Dowell, C. Zhou, R. Li, T. T. Ladwig, C. R. Alexander, and C. R. Martin, PhD
492031.abstract: The Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) version 1, operating on a 3-km grid over North America with the FV3 dynamical core, is scheduled for operational implementation in 2026 utilizing the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) data assimilation system. To modernize this infrastructure, the RRFS is actively transitioning from GSI to the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework, serving as a critical bridge (RRFSv1.x) to the future RRFSv2. This presentation details the development, validation, and performance of the JEDI-based RRFS Data Assimilation System (RDAS). Core data assimilation algorithms and observation forward operators have been successfully transitioned to the new framework, and cycled retrospective and real-time parallel experiments demonstrate that the JEDI-based EnKF matches the GSI baseline performance. Finally, we will discuss the ongoing integration of JEDI components into the RRFS workflow and report on the overall performance of the JEDI-equipped RDAS.

492033.title: Evaluation of Satellite-Based Ozone Sensitivity Indicators of Ozone Exceedance Episodes Using Multi-Source In-Situ Measurements and CMAQ over the Northeast US
492033.authors: Siyi Wang, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, New Brunswick, NJ; and X. Jin
492033.abstract: Ground-level Ozone (O3) exceedances persist across nonattainment areas of the Northeast US, where effective emission controls depend on correctly diagnosing whether peak O3 is NOx-limited or VOC-limited. Satellite formaldehyde-to-nitrogen-dioxide ratios (FNR = HCHO/NO₂) provide spatially and temporally continuous indicators of ozone sensitivity, but the regime transition thresholds used to diagnose ozone sensitivity are model- and satellite-dependent, and their reliability on high-O3 exceedance days has not been evaluated at the process level. We establish these thresholds and map the spatiotemporal evolution of FNR-based ozone sensitivity and subsequently use ground-based observations to quantify the uncertainties arising from both the model-based thresholds and the satellite NO₂ and HCHO densities and their propagated errors in the computed FNR values, across contiguous United States (CONUS). Next, we compare the CMAQ high-order decoupled direct method (HDDM-3D)-derived sensitivity regimes with the satellite-FNR classifications to characterize where the observational indicator holds and where it diverges. We also use the model to interpret how meteorology and emissions jointly shape the sensitivity regime and its transitions during ozone exceedance.

492040.title: Exploring the Value of Ground-Based Infrared Thermometers for Operational and Research Uses
492040.authors: Frédéric Fabry, McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada; and R. Tellier and V. Meunier
492040.abstract: It has been long recognized that insufficient information about the planetary boundary layer and the free atmosphere are limiting our ability to forecast severe weather. As such, there have been many calls for additional measurement constraints in the lower atmosphere, but most proposed approaches are prohibitive; this has limited their deployment for operations and research as well as their spatial density. Yet, given the scale of convective systems, higher resolution measurements are required, and information of appropriate density are only available from dense networks of surface stations. A solution would be to find robust sensors of sufficiently low cost that they could be installed on a surface station yet provide routine constraints on the atmosphere above. Infrared thermometers measure the amount of medium- or long-wave infrared radiation coming from a specific direction and derive the source’s brightness temperature from it. The atmosphere being semi-transparent to the infrared, when pointing at high elevations, we get constraints that primarily depend on cloud base temperature and on the amount of precipitable water; at lower elevations, emissions from the atmosphere gradually saturate, and the data depend increasingly on boundary layer temperatures. While the information content of any single IR thermometer measurement is limited, the wealth of possible measurements of poorly constrained atmospheric properties intrigued us: Could infrared thermometers be useful instruments for operations and research? We explored the ability of infrared thermometers to provide such information. Two sets of experiments were performed to gauge the value of IR temperature measurements in an operational and in a research context: In the first, we pointed an infrared thermometer at a fixed elevation angle (20°) from the end of the Montreal winter to the summer; in the second, we scanned the thermometer in elevation and/or azimuth to obtain a greater diversity of information from a given sensor. With its lower brightness temperature limit of −55°C, the IR thermometer we tested (Optris CTi) could obtain measurements in winter under most cloudy conditions, but it sometimes was incapable of obtaining valid measurements in clear skies, at least when using a 20° elevation angle. In all seasons, from the characteristics of the signal itself, variable cloudiness conditions are easy to identify, but clear skies and overcast conditions are difficult to distinguish except through the brightness temperature measured, but that temperature remains a useful constraint for a data assimilation system. When the instrument scanned, the information became considerably richer as we could obtain nearly simultaneously measurements from surface emissions, the lower boundary layer (if the visible horizon is low enough), clouds and vertically integrated humidity, and temperature and humidity fluctuations in the convective boundary layer. The main artifacts affecting data quality were biological observations and the resetting of the sensor when overheating.

492044.title: A Bayesian Framework for Uncertainty Quantification of Surface Parameters within Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory
492044.authors: Michael F. Howland, MIT, Cambridge, MA; and E. Y. Shin
492044.abstract: Surface parameters aggregate the unresolved effects of surface morphology and roughness into effective surface properties, providing surface flux boundary conditions to atmospheric models. Although these parameters are understood to depend on both surface and flow characteristics, both of which exhibit significant variability, existing estimation methods give deterministic estimates with no characterization of uncertainty. In this study, we present a Bayesian framework for inferring and quantifying uncertainty in surface parameters, which in turn allows unresolved surface–atmosphere interactions to be represented through probabilistic boundary conditions. Here, we derive closed-form expressions for the posterior and posterior predictive distributions in the case of inferring the aerodynamic roughness length z0 within Monin--Obukhov similarity theory (MOST). We verify the new surface parameter estimation method by recovering the prescribed z0 from mean flow statistics obtained from wall-modeled large-eddy simulations, in which z0 is specified within a MOST-based wall model. Following verification, we apply the method to field observations from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement Southern Great Plains Atmospheric Observatory to produce site-specific, probabilistic estimates of z0. Here, we examine how the choices of conditioning variable --- considering month, wind direction, and their combination --- and time-averaging length, applied to the training and testing observations, affect both the parameter and prediction uncertainties. The Bayesian method propagates z0 uncertainty into predictive intervals that capture the spread in out-of-sample wind speeds whereas deterministic predictions do not. Quantitative analysis shows that the inferred z0 based on the Bayesian approach lowers both point-forecast scores (root mean square error and mean absolute error, evaluated at the posterior mean) and probabilistic-forecast score (continuous ranked probability score) relative to the deterministic baseline. *This research is supported by the Office of Naval Research, Young Investigator Program, grant no. N000142512045. Simulations were performed on the NSF ACCESS Stampede3 supercomputer under the project ATM170028.

492045.title: Integration of Machine Learning in Environment and Climate Change Canada's Operational Global Weather Prediction System
492045.authors: Leo Separovic, ECCC, Dorval, QC, Canada; Environment and Climate Change Canada, Dorval, Quebec, Canada, QC, Canada; and S. Z. Husain, J. F. Caron, and C. Subich
492045.abstract: Machine learning-based weather prediction (MLWP) is increasingly challenging the state of the art in physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP), with several MLWP models now matching or exceeding leading NWP systems for many standard measures of medium-range forecast skill. Nevertheless, current deterministic MLWP models remain limited by their coarse effective resolution and their restricted representation of atmospheric variables, preventing their direct replacement of NWP in operational forecasting and motivating the development of hybrid NWP-MLWP approaches. To obtain the best of both worlds, ECCC developed a hybrid system using the physics-based Global Environmental Multiscale (GEM) model and its machine learning counterpart, the Global Environmental eMuLator (GEML). This hybrid approach, implemented within the Global Deterministic Prediction System (GDPS), is based on spectral nudging, in which the large-scale components of GEM are relaxed toward those of GEML while allowing GEM to generate physically consistent small-scale structures essential for representing weather extremes that are dynamically consistent with the adjusted large-scale flow. Crucially, the hybrid system retains the complete set of forecast variables required for operational meteorology. In May 2026, this system became the first of its kind to be deployed operationally, making ECCC the first national weather service to deploy an operational hybrid NWP-MLWP forecasting system. This presentation will describe the methodology and development behind this milestone. We will present an in-depth analysis of the unprecedented forecast improvements achieved at medium ranges and outline our ongoing research for further integrating machine learning into operational forecasting systems.

492052.title: Integrating Soil, Water, and Atmospheric Monitoring to Evaluate Ecosystem Restoration and Regenerative Agriculture in Northwest Indiana: Implementation Process
492052.authors: Katelyn A. Barber, Valparaiso Univ., Valparaiso, IN; and C. E. Phillips, L. Blind-Doskocil, and J. P. McCool
492052.abstract: Northwest Indiana is a cacophony of land surface types, with the urban environment of Chicago, IL drastically influencing the regional meteorology. On a local level, a concerted effort of native land restoration is gaining momentum and agricultural fields are actively changing farming practices or donating parcels of land for restoration. This rapid change in landscape offers a unique opportunity to understand the impacts of land surface type on the micrometeorology and soil composition of the area. A planning grant was awarded to Valparaiso University to install two, 10-m instrumented weather towers and two wells for soil monitoring at various depths, along with nitrate sampling. The towers are on a restored wetland and an agricultural field slated for restoration less than half a mile away from one another. While weather towers are not an unusual platform deployed for meteorological purposes, the tower sites themselves came along with unique challenges for investigators. This presentation provides an overview of the scientific objectives, the deployment strategies, preliminary results, and highlights student contributions.

492057.title: Rapid Evaluation and Operational Integration of Cutting-Edge NOAA Observing Systems and Other New Technologies through the Hurricane and Ocean Testbed
492057.authors: David A. Zelinsky, National Hurricane Center, Miami, FL; and P. Santos, E. Bookbinder, S. M. Camposano, M. Onderlinde, A. D. Mahoney, R. Zelinsky, A. Brammer, and J. A. Sippel
492057.abstract: The National Hurricane Center (NHC) Hurricane and Ocean Testbed (HOT) provides a cloud-based framework for the rapid evaluation and operational integration of cutting-edge technologies, including new NOAA observing systems and novel forecasting tools. The HOT cloud allows NHC and HOT staff to access and display experimental and operational data from NOAA and external partners in real time. The HOT cloud looks and feels exactly like NHC’s operational software, but without any risk of disrupting critical operational systems. If a data type is deemed useful and viable for operations, it can then be rapidly transitioned into NHC’s operational systems since the required configuration and associated software has already been tested in parallel in the cloud. This process has allowed NHC to rapidly integrate several new technologies into operations including uncrewed drone observations (UxS), radar and satellite imagery from NOAA partners, and AI models, ultimately improving human-in-the-loop analysis and forecasting at the NHC. Specific examples of models that have gone through this transition process during the last two years include the HAFS models and the Google DeepMind model plus its derived products. Observational datasets that have gone through this transition include OSCAT, SAR, Tomorrow.IO, Meteosat, LightningCast, Himawari ProxyVis, GREMLIN, Climavision RADARs, UxS observations, and SOFAR buoys. Experimental ROARS, new UxS atmospheric and oceanic observations, and additional marine observations are being evaluated in the cloud during the 2026 hurricane season. This talk will demonstrate how the NHC is leading efforts to rapidly integrate new technologies into operations, including the use of AI assistants through a NOAA AI pilot project.
