It will also discuss how this process does not need to be exclusive to NHC’s current operations and can be a model for NWS integration of new observing or forecasting technologies in future cloud-based operational systems.

492067.title: Wildfire Aerosols and the Indoor Chemistry Threats to Artwork
492067.authors: Liora Mael, Mount Holyoke College, South Hadley, MA; and O. Ryder and S. J. Kramer
492067.abstract: Wildfire frequency and severity have increased substantially across North America in recent decades due to climate change and evolving land management practices. While public health impacts of wildfire smoke are well documented, a less-visible but also consequential impact affects irreplaceable cultural heritage collections housed in museums, galleries, and historic buildings throughout the United States. Wildfire smoke intrusion into museum spaces poses a dual threat: it threatens the health and safety of visitors and staff, and it creates chemical and physical hazards to cultural heritage that has been preserved under strict climate and air quality controls for decades. Museum collections are composed of materials including organic binders, pigments, varnishes, ceramics, adhesives, cellulosics, metal, and glass that are chemically reactive when exposed to wildfire smoke. Indoor surface chemistry and gas-phase reactions can irreversibly degrade artwork. The increasing frequency and intensity of wildfire smoke events now exceed the protective capacity of many museum building envelopes and ventilation systems. To assess the scale of this threat and develop evidence-based mitigation strategies, we present novel results from two complementary approaches: (1) continental-scale air quality modeling using the Community Multiscale Air Quality (CMAQ) model and satellite observations to map the geographic extent and temporal evolution of wildfire smoke impacts on museum locations across the United States, and (2) direct indoor-outdoor air quality monitoring (PM1, PM2.5, PM10, CO2) at Baltimore Museum of Art and Winterthur Museum (Winterthur, Delaware), especially during the June 2026 Canadian wildfire smoke event that severely impacted the Eastern United States to determine the degree and extent of smoke infiltration into the buildings. This work bridges atmospheric science, air quality modeling, and cultural heritage preservation, demonstrating how detailed air quality observations, surface chemistry investigations, and forecasting tools can quantify threats to museum collections and inform mitigation strategies. It also highlights the need for museums to develop emergency strategies for future smoke events, and underscores the importance of including cultural heritage in climate resilience planning.

492070.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning Prediction of Tornado, Severe Hail, and Severe Thunderstorm Wind Occurrence Using ERA5 Reanalysis
492070.authors: Nana Ofosuhene Pinkrah, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and X. Fan, Z. Suriano, and M. Singh
492070.abstract: Severe convective hazards occur on spatial and temporal scales that are not directly resolved by global reanalyses, but the atmospheric environments supporting them can be characterized using reanalysis-derived diagnostics. This study develops and evaluates a machine-learning framework for estimating 3-hourly probabilities of reported tornado, severe-hail, and severe-thunderstorm-wind occurrence across the Ohio River Basin and surrounding region using ERA5 reanalysis and NOAA storm events reports. A total of 107 thermodynamic, kinematic, moisture, and composite diagnostics were calculated from 3-hourly ERA5 fields for 1996–2025. Storm reports were matched to the 0.25° ERA5 grid using a 25-km spatial radius and forward 3-hour interval to construct binary labels for each hazard. Random forest (RF) and XGBoost models were trained using 1996–2016 data, with model selection based on 2017–2018 validation period. The selected models were retrained using 1996–2018 data, and isotonic regression and categorical thresholds were determined using 2019–2020 data. Model performance was evaluated using an independent 2021–2025 test period. Observed report frequencies showed distinct seasonal cycles, with tornado reports peaking in April, severe hail in May, and severe thunderstorm wind in June. XGBoost produced the strongest overall discrimination for all three hazards. Receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) values were 0.986 for tornado, 0.987 for severe hail, and 0.978 for severe thunderstorm wind. Corresponding average-precision (AP) values were 0.035, 0.060, and 0.091, respectively, substantially exceeding the no-skill values determined by the hazard-specific event frequencies. XGBoost generally produced higher average-precision lift, critical success index, and precision, whereas random forest generally produced higher probability of detection. Differences in probabilistic skill were smaller than differences in discrimination, particularly for severe hail and severe thunderstorm wind. Model probability fields reproduced the main seasonal behavior of observed event rates, including spring maxima for tornado and severe hail and a later warm-season maximum for severe thunderstorm wind. The models also captured the broad west-to-east concentration of report-based event rates, although predicted probability fields were smoother than the observed spatial patterns. Permutation importance showed that each hazard relied on a different combination of environmental information. Tornado probabilities were sensitive to low-level and deep-layer shear, Bulk Richardson Number components, moisture, and lapse rates. Severe-hail probabilities were sensitive to midlevel lapse rates, precipitable water, instability, deep-layer shear, and the significant hail parameter. Severe-thunderstorm-wind probabilities were sensitive to precipitable water, low-level moisture transport, lapse rates, shear, and low-level wind components. These results show that ERA5-derived environmental diagnostics can support hazard-specific, subdaily probability estimates of reported severe-weather occurrence at regional scales.

492071.title: Regionally Contrasting Daily Winter Rainfall Responses to ENSO Amplitude in the CONUS
492071.authors: Alyssa L Griffin, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and S. Larson, R. W. Payne Jr., and E. J. Becker
492071.abstract: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) generates well established impacts on seasonal precipitation variability in the U.S., especially during boreal winter. However, little is known about the daily precipitation patterns and extremes that comprise those seasonal impacts and how they change with ENSO amplitude. This analysis uses idealized ENSO amplitude experiments in CESM2 to compare boreal winter daily precipitation characteristics over the United States during ENSO-neutral conditions and low, moderate, and high amplitude ENSO events. Patterns that emerged include increased anomalous precipitation in the Pacific Northwest during La Niña and Southeast during El Niño compared to ENSO-neutral conditions. While the magnitude of the daily precipitation pattern in the Southeast U.S. increased with El Niño amplitude, it did not in the Pacific Northwest during La Niña amplitude. Instead, as La Niña amplitude increased, so did the frequency of precipitation events in the Pacific Northwest. This result may be linked to the stronger, more zonal upper-level jet during El Niño, which results in more intense rain events in the Southeast compared to the more orographically forced, slower moving stratiform precipitation that occurs in the Pacific Northwest during La Niña. Overall, this study provides a new insight as to what daily precipitation patterns can be expected from different ENSO conditions.

492072.title: An Interactive Visualization and Raster-Tile Server API for Seasonal-to-Subseasonal Hydrometeorology Forecasts in the Amazon Basin
492072.authors: Qibo Kris Su, The Johns Hopkins Univ., Baltimore, MD; and P. Kansara and B. F. Zaitchik
492072.abstract: Subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) land-surface forecasts can provide actionable information for applications ranging from water-resources planning and wildfire-risk monitoring to epidemiology early-warning systems. Against the backdrop of the 2026 El Nino, the potential hydrometeorological extremes in ecological hotspots such as the Amazon Basin increases the importance of timely access to S2S forecast data. However, the size and multidimensional structure of forecast datasets can make these products difficult for end-users to access and interpret. This project develops an interactive web interface of a raster-tile server API for delivering S2S categorical tercile-probability hydrometeorological forecast products of the Amazon Basin generated by downscaling forecasts of the NASA GEOS-S2S ensemble forecast system and applying them to customized hydrological simulations using Noah-MP and HyMAP in the NASA Land Information System (LIS). The platform processes CF-compliant LIS output on a 0.05-degree equidistant cylindrical grid and converts large multidimensional datasets into web-accessible map-layers. Available variables include precipitation, evapotranspiration, surface-runoff, soil moisture, soil temperature, specific humidity, air temperature, and streamflow. Users can query forecasts at lead times of up to six months, and view the probabilities of below-normal, near-normal, and above-normal conditions. The tercile thresholds and the associated probabilities are calculated against a climatological baseline of 20 years of hindcast data. Vertical profiles are available for soil-moisture and soil-temperature, represented across four layers with thicknesses of approximately 10, 30, 60, and 100 cm. The tile-server API supports on-demand rendering and allows forecast layers to be incorporated into other web applications. The poster presents the system architecture, the processing workflow from forecast output to map-ready products, and examples of interactive forecast visualization across the Amazon Basin. The platform is intended to support governmental and private agencies by improving access to geospatial information relevant for the ongoing ENSO planning and response activities, including drought, wildfire, and epidemiological risk management. This work demonstrates how interoperable web services can help translate land-surface model output into accessible decision-support products.

492073.title: Leveraging NASA TROPICS Observations to Advance Predictability of African Easterly Waves
492073.authors: Robert G. Nystrom, Iowa State University, Ames, IA
492073.abstract: African easterly waves (AEWs) are the primary precursors to Atlantic tropical cyclones, yet substantial uncertainty remains regarding the convective processes that distinguish developing waves from those that do not undergo tropical cyclogenesis. This talk highlights the utility of observations from NASA's Time-Resolved Observations of Precipitation Structure and Storm Intensity with a Constellation of Smallsats (TROPICS) mission for improving our understanding and prediction of AEW evolution. First, we introduce a new dataset of collocated TROPICS observations and objectively tracked AEWs during the 2023 Atlantic hurricane season. Using this dataset, we examine differences in the convective and thermodynamic characteristics of developing and non-developing waves, with particular emphasis on the organization, intensity, and temporal evolution of deep convection observed by TROPICS' high-frequency microwave measurements. Results provide new insights into the environmental and convective signatures associated with AEWs. Building on these observational analyses, we evaluate convection-permitting simulations performed with the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) to assess their ability to reproduce the convective characteristics observed by TROPICS. Through direct comparisons between simulated storms and satellite-derived metrics, we investigate how well the model captures the structure, variability, and evolution of AEW convection and identify key strengths and biases. Finally, we discuss how this observational and modeling framework is being used to prepare upcoming data assimilation experiments that will directly incorporate TROPICS observations into MPAS-JEDI and assess their potential to improve AEW analyses, forecasts, and tropical cyclone genesis prediction. Together, these results demonstrate how emerging spaceborne observations and high-resolution numerical modeling can be combined to improve process understanding and advance forecasting capabilities for AEWs and tropical convection.

492075.title: Beyond Individual Cities: Two Decades of Regional Urban Heat Change Across the Atlanta–Charlotte I-85 Corridor
492075.authors: Kathy Osei, Univ. of Georgia, Athens, GA; and J. M. Shepherd
492075.abstract: Urban heat is typically characterized at the scale of individual cities, yet expanding urban development increasingly connects urban areas into larger regional systems. Understanding heat across these broader spatial scales is critical for characterizing patterns of chronic heat that extend beyond individual municipal boundaries. While regional urban heat studies have documented broader thermal patterns, less attention has focused on how the extent, persistence, and spatial configuration of these patterns change over time across multi-city systems. Using the urban heat archipelago framework, which conceptualizes multiple urban centers as components of a broader regional thermal system, this study quantifies summer land surface temperature (LST) changes along the Atlanta–Charlotte I-85 corridor from 2004 to 2024 using MODIS Aqua LST observations. Summer LST was classified into five thermal intensity classes relative to a 2004–2006 baseline using a pixel-wise mean ± standard deviation approach. Annual summer LST composites were organized into a space-time cube, and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) was used to identify statistically significant spatiotemporal hotspot patterns. Results reveal substantial regional thermal intensification, with High and Extreme High thermal intensity classes more than doubling from 13.5% of the corridor in 2004 to 29.5% in 2024. The most pronounced expansion occurred around the Atlanta, Greenville-Spartanburg, and Charlotte metropolitan regions. EHSA identified persistent hotspots within major metropolitan areas, while emerging hotspot patterns developed across surrounding urbanizing landscapes, demonstrating that high-temperature clustering is becoming increasingly widespread across the corridor. A complementary pixel-wise standard deviation analysis identified areas of elevated interannual thermal variability beyond these persistent metropolitan hotspots, providing additional insight into regional thermal heterogeneity. Ongoing analyses of fragmentation and connectivity will further characterize changes in the spatial configuration of these thermal patterns. Together, these findings establish a two-decade quantitative baseline of regional thermal change along the I-85 corridor, advancing understanding of chronic heat patterns across interconnected urban systems and providing a basis for subsequent regional heat exposure and vulnerability assessments.

492078.title: Impacts of Regional CO2 Fluxes and Meteorology on CO2 Simulations over South Korea
492078.authors: Hyeong-Ahn Kwon, University of Suwon, Hwaseong-si, Gyeonggi-do, Korea, Republic of (South); and Y. J. Oak, G. Lee, S. Kim, H. Lin, H. Kim, M. Kim, R. Park, and S. Jeong
492078.abstract: To support the assessment of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement, numerical modeling can provide an independent approach for evaluating national greenhouse gas emissions. In particular, inverse modeling can estimate CO2 surface fluxes based on observations, for which reliable forward modeling is essential. In this study, we use WRF-GC, which couples the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model with GEOS-Chem, to evaluate regional CO2 fluxes over South Korea and investigate meteorological factors affecting model performance. A simulation using global anthropogenic emissions from ODIAC and net ecosystem exchange (NEE) from MiCASA was used as a control run, and simulations using national CO2 emissions and NEE estimates from the Korean Carbon Project (KCP) were compared with the control simulation. Compared with CO2 observations from the World Data Centre for Greenhouse Gases (WDCGG), the simulation using the KCP estimates showed a higher temporal correlation than that using the global inventories, increasing the correlation coefficient from 0.77 to 0.89 and improving the normalized mean bias (NMB) from –1.5% to –0.5%. In particular, changes in biospheric CO2 fluxes had the largest impact on the simulated temporal variability, indicating the importance of representing regional biospheric fluxes for reproducing observed CO2 variations. However, the model showed relatively high CO2 concentrations during periods with a low planetary boundary layer (PBL) height. This suggests that simulated CO2 enhancements near strong emission sources are sensitive not only to anthropogenic emissions but also to vertical mixing within the boundary layer. Therefore, our results show that improved regional CO2 flux estimates can better reproduce the observed temporal variability of atmospheric CO2 over South Korea. However, uncertainties in meteorological processes, particularly PBL mixing, should be carefully considered in the evaluation of regional CO2 fluxes. These results provide a basis for developing a reliable forward modeling framework for future inverse modeling of CO2 fluxes over South Korea.

492080.title: Benchmarking Generative Models for Weather Data Assimilation on Real Station Observations
492080.authors: Ruizhe Huang, MIT, Cambridge, MA; MIT, Cambridge, MA; and Q. Yang, J. Giezendanner, and S. Wang
492080.abstract: Weather forecasting relies on computationally intensive data assimilation methods that require repeated numerical weather prediction model integrations. Recent advances in generative AI have motivated learned alternatives that shift much of this cost from inference to offline training, potentially enabling much cheaper assimilation. However, existing generative approaches have largely been evaluated on synthetic observations or under inconsistent datasets and evaluation schemes, making it unclear which design choices actually improve real-world data assimilation. We present the first controlled benchmark of generative weather data assimilation on real weather station observations. Using 11,849 NOAA MADIS stations across the contiguous United States, four surface variables, and 360 assimilation snapshots from 2023, we evaluate methods under both dense and sparse observation regimes while holding the dataset, observation operator, and network backbone fixed. The benchmark compares the major design choices proposed for generative data assimilation, including diffusion versus flow matching, pixel versus latent-space formulations, and multiple inference-time conditioning strategies, against a classical 3D-Var baseline. The benchmark reveals four clear conclusions. First, generative methods outperform the 3D-Var baseline (35.7% vs. 33.3% root-mean-square error (RMSE) improvement over ERA5) despite using no ERA5 background field at inference, with the advantage widening as observations become sparse (+7.9 pp vs. +2.4 pp dense). Second, diffusion and flow matching perform nearly identically under matched conditions (35.4% vs. 35.7%), indicating that the choice of generative framework matters little. Third, full-gradient guidance consistently outperforms stop-gradient and initial-noise optimization, particularly under sparse observations. Fourth, several commonly adopted architectural choices, including latent-space variable mixing, provide little measurable benefit. Together, these results identify which components of generative weather data assimilation materially improve performance on real station observations and establish a standardized benchmark for future work.

492081.title: Drifting into the Future: Evolving Canada's Arctic Marine Observations
492081.authors: Alexander Zucconi, MSC, Toronto, ON, Canada
492081.abstract: The Arctic is undergoing rapid environmental change, while marine activity and the need for safe and reliable navigation continue to increase. As seasonal sea ice extent declines and access to Arctic waters expands, timely environmental information is becoming increasingly important for mariners, forecasters, weather and sea-ice models, and operational decision-making. Yet, obtaining sustained observations in the Arctic remains exceptionally challenging due to its remoteness, harsh environmental conditions, limited infrastructure, and difficult access. More than a decade ago, recognizing the potential for increased Arctic shipping, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) established five Arctic METAREAs to extend the Maritime Safety Information (MSI) service of the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) to the North Pole. As Canada's designated meteorological information authority for METAREAs XVII and XVIII, the Meteorological Service of Canada (MSC) has an international responsibility to provide marine meteorological forecasts, warnings and information across this vast region. A key component of Canada's contribution is the MSC's Arctic drifting buoy observation program, now entering its tenth year of operation. Each summer/fall, approximately 10–15 drifting buoys are deployed in and around the Beaufort Sea to establish and attempt to maintain an observation presence in an otherwise data-sparse region. The buoys provide hourly observations of parameters including air temperature, atmospheric pressure, and sea-surface temperature, together with their geographic position. Observations are transmitted via satellite and are made available for use in operational marine weather services, numerical weather prediction, environmental modelling, forecasting, and other applications. The MSC also collaborates with the Canadian Ice Service (CIS) to deploy ice beacons on Arctic ice islands that calve from the rugged northern coast of Ellesmere Island in Nunavut. These beacons track ice-island movement, supporting monitoring of an emerging hazard to marine navigation and offshore operations. After nearly a decade of operation, the program is evolving in response to changing operational realities. Historically, deployment has relied heavily on Canadian Department of National Defence (DND) support. However, increasing competition for military resources, logistical constraints, and the difficulty of sustaining dedicated Arctic deployment missions have highlighted the risks of relying on a single deployment model. The MSC is therefore diversifying its approach by pursuing opportunistic ship-based deployments and partnerships with vessels already operating in Arctic waters, while continuing to leverage air-based opportunities when available. This more flexible model provides opportunities to increase deployment options, reduce reliance on dedicated missions, and improve the resilience and sustainability of the observing network. The program also provides an operational opportunity to explore new deployment approaches, observing platforms, and technologies suited to Arctic conditions. This presentation will review the first decade of Canada's Arctic METAREA drifting buoy program, from its establishment and operational challenges to lessons learned that are driving its evolution. It will conclude by exploring how innovation, collaboration, and diversified deployment strategies are creating a more resilient and sustainable observing program for the future.

492084.title: The Beginnings of Space Weather Support in the US Air Force
492084.authors: William B. Cade III, Baylor University, Waco, TX
492084.abstract: With the advent of the space age and the creation of the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), Colorado Springs became the epicenter of space weather support for the United States Air Force in the 1960s. This talk will discuss the earliest steps that led to the beginning of the Air Force’s space weather warning and forecasting system, its early evolution, and the timely role it played in preventing a world war.

492093.title: AI Foundation Model of U.S Coastal Waters in Support of Safe and Efficient Marine Navigation and Disaster Mitigation
492093.authors: William James Pringle, ANL, Chicago, IL; and S. Moghimi, C. Blakely, A. Alipour, D. Fytanidis, F. Daneshvar, S. R. Brus, S. Mani, and R. Kotamarthi
492093.abstract: Safe and efficient navigation in U.S. coastal waters requires timely predictions of tides, waves, currents, and hazards such as storm surge and extreme ocean conditions. These predictions are also critical for disaster mitigation and emergency response. While AI foundation models have recently achieved skill comparable to numerical weather prediction at substantially lower computational cost, similar capabilities have not yet been developed for coastal and continental-shelf waters, where complex bathymetry, land-ocean interactions, and multiscale processes create unique challenges. This project brings together expertise in coastal ocean modeling, operational forecasting, machine learning, and high-performance computing to develop an AI foundation model for U.S. coastal waters. NOAA’s National Ocean Service operates coastal ocean forecast systems including the two- and three-dimensional Surge and Tide Operational Forecast System (STOFS). These systems provide valuable operational guidance, but their computational cost and complexity limit the ability to generate large ensembles and forecasts at extended lead times. Our objective is to complement these capabilities with an AI model that enables computationally efficient forecasting, longer lead times, and large ensembles for marine navigation and hazard mitigation. The approach builds on the highly scalable weather-forecasting framework developed at Argonne National Laboratory and trained on Aurora [1,2], Argonne’s exascale supercomputer ranked the fourth fastest in the world at the time of this work. The Argonne Earth Systems Model for Reliable and Skillful Predictions (AERIS) has demonstrated competitive skill and stable ensemble performance at subseasonal-to-seasonal lead times, providing a strong foundation for adaptation to coastal ocean prediction. A 25-year high-resolution STOFS-3D hindcast provides the training and evaluation resource. In this presentation, we will describe the project team and approach, including the model architecture, training methodology, and strategies for representing coastal processes and handling complex, unstructured grids and domains. Preliminary results will be presented, along with opportunities and challenges in applying AI forecasting methods to coastal environments in support of safe navigation and disaster mitigation. References: [1] Hatanpää, V., et al. (2025). AERIS: Argonne Earth Systems Model for Reliable and Skillful Predictions. arXiv. http://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13523 [2] Stock, J., Arcomano, T., and Kotamarthi, R (2026). Swift: An autoregressive consistency model for efficient weather forecasting. Machine Learning: Earth 2(2):025004. https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/3049-4753/ae802a

492097.title: Updates on Global Machine Learning-Derived Cloud Condensation Nuclei Based on EarthCARE ATLID Observations and Their Use in Aerosol-Cloud-Interaction Studies (Invited Presentation)
492097.authors: Jens Redemann, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and L. Gao, B. F. Lamkin, C. J. Flynn, L. Kang, W. K. Jones, S. De, M. Ritman, P. Stier, K. von Salzen, M. El Abdioui, R. Wood, D. Donovan, and G. Jan van Zadelhoff
492097.abstract: The EarthCARE mission provides new observations of aerosol extinction, backscatter, and depolarization from the ATMospheric LIDar (ATLID) system. These observations are proving to be superior to past satellite-based lidar observations in accuracy partly because of the use of the high-spectral resolution lidar (HSRL) technique. These high-accuracy lidar observations can be used as input to machine-learning (ML) models to estimate cloud condensation nuclei (CCN at 0.4% supersaturation) and aerosol absorption (ABS at 532nm). We present ML-based CCN and ABS retrievals using the first two years of ATLID observations (September 2024 to August 2026) of aerosol backscatter, extinction, and depolarization along with RH and temperature data from reanalyses as predictors. We provide validation results of the ML-based CCN retrievals against airborne and ground-based in situ observations and retrievals from airborne HSRL systems. These validation efforts indicate mean relative errors less than 30% for CCN concentrations greater than 200/cm3. New approaches for improving the accuracy in clean conditions are discussed, including the development of two-ML-model solutions with one model specifically trained for low aerosol loadings. Based on the first two years of ATLID observations, we present global vertically-resolved distributions of ML-derived CCN, which indicate a relatively clean boundary layer in the Southern hemisphere and a middle-tropospheric maximum in CCN near the equator. Finally, we discuss preliminary results on cloud susceptibility studies and validation of Earth System Models facilitated by these new retrievals.

492099.title: The Evolution of TOLNet: From Research Deployments to an Operational Network
492099.authors: Fernando Chouza Keil, JPL, Pasadna, CA; JPL, Wrightwood, CA; and T. Leblanc, M. E. D. Roots, M. Newchurch, J. Burden, D. Phoenix, G. Gronoff, R. Alvarez II, S. Baidar, F. Moshary, Y. Wu, M. S. Johnson, C. M. Bernier, J. Su, L. Twigg, J. Flynn, M. A. Shook, C. Gummo, C. Gao, J. T. Sullivan, and K. E. Knowland
492099.abstract: For over a decade, the Tropospheric Ozone Lidar Network (TOLNet) has provided high-resolution vertical profiling of tropospheric ozone across North America. To meet the growing demand for continuous monitoring, TOLNet is transitioning from a diverse, research-focused network into a sustained operational framework driven by standardized Small Mobile Ozone Lidars (SMOLs). This operational shift enables quasi-continuous, long-term profiling to fulfill several network mandates. First, it provides essential ground-truth vertical data to validate lower-tropospheric retrievals from the recently launched TEMPO satellite and evaluate regional chemical transport models, such as GEOS-CF. Second, this sustained data equips state and local environmental agencies to identify drivers of air quality degradation —including stratospheric intrusions and transported wildfire smoke— while helping assess long-term tropospheric ozone trends. This presentation will review TOLNet’s operational transition and highlight extended profiling results from recent deployments in Baltimore, Houston, Phoenix, and San Bernardino. Ultimately, we will discuss the network's enhanced capacity to unravel the dynamics of extreme ozone events in complex urban environments.

492102.title: Using Large-Eddy Simulations to Assess Mesoscale Wind Farm Parameterizations
492102.authors: Amelia J. Adcroft, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and J. K. Lundquist, W. C. Radünz, L. Vollmer, B. A. M. Sengers, and M. Dörenkämper
492102.abstract: As many areas experience increasingly dense deployment of wind farms, accurately representing how wind farms interact through cluster wakes has become an important challenge. Many researchers and developers use representation of wind farms in mesoscale simulations (horizontal resolution on the order of 1 kilometer or coarser), such as the Fitch Wind Farm Parameterization (Fitch WFP) in the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, to accomplish this purpose. While computationally efficient, these parameterizations cannot resolve turbine-scale flow features such as induction zones and near wakes. Finer-resolution large-eddy simulations (LES), with grid resolutions on the order of 10 meters, can represent such features and thus can provide evaluations of mesoscale parameterizations. The recent Axial Induction Factor (AIF) modification (Vollmer et al. 2024) and Analytical TKE Coefficient (ATC) correction (Sengers et al. 2026) to the Fitch WFP change wind turbine induction and modify the implementation of turbine-added turbulence, but have not yet been evaluated with LES. To assess these modifications to the Fitch WFP in controlled idealized simulations, we perform use WRF-LES in a range of wind speeds and for unstable, neutral, and stably stratified conditions. Our wind speeds range from 6 m/s to 18 m/s, emphasizing the range of wind speeds where changes to the Fitch WFP exert significant impacts. Initial simulations have used actuator disk models of standard 2.8, 5, and 10 MW turbines. Differences emerge between the LES and the mesoscale parameterizations. For example (see figure), while both the LES (dotted lines with points) and the mesoscale AIF (solid lines) predict stronger induction with decreasing grid cell size in stable conditions than in neutral conditions, the AIF predicts about 20% weaker induction than LES. The presentation will incorporate simulations with other turbines and wind farm geometries to generalize the performance of the AIF and the ATCC with regard to induction and wake recovery. These comparisons validate the assumptions underlying the modified Fitch WFP and support its application to future cluster-wake simulations, which are important for assessing and predicting wind farm performance and the integration of renewably generated electricity into power grids. Figure: Comparison of mean wind speed deficit due to induction in WRF-LES with generalized actuator disk (GAD) turbine model (dotted lines) and predicted by AIF for mesoscale WRF simulation with Fitch WFP (solid lines), normalized by freestream wind speed, for both stable (blue) and neutral (purple) atmospheres. Shaded regions indicate the range of standard error in normalized hub-height induced wind speed from LES. Both simulations use a hub-height freestream wind speed of ~10 m/s and a single NREL 2.8 MW turbine. References Sengers, B. A. M., H. Kassem, L. Vollmer, J. Theron, and K. Gunn, 2026: Analytical equation for the TKE coefficient in mesoscale wind farm parameterizations. J. Phys.: Conf. Ser., 3224, 032015, https://doi.org/10.1088/1742-6596/3224/3/032015. Vollmer, L., B. A. M. Sengers, and M. Dörenkämper, 2024: Brief communication: A simple axial induction modification to the Weather Research and Forecasting Fitch wind farm parameterization. Wind Energ. Sci., 9, 1689–1693, https://doi.org/10.5194/wes-9-1689-2024.

492107.title: From Shallow to Deep: Easterly Wave Modulation of the East Pacific ITCZ
492107.abstract: Organized tropical convection in the eastern Pacific is influenced by a variety of synoptic-scale disturbances, including easterly waves and convectively coupled equatorial waves. Together with the underlying sea surface temperature gradients, these disturbances shape the structure and variability of the East Pacific Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). This presentation explores how easterly waves modify the shallow and deep meridional overturning circulations during the Organization of Tropical East Pacific Convection (OTREC) field campaign in 2019, in which George and I participated. Using field campaign observations, satellite precipitation estimates, and ERA5 reanalysis, I examine three well-defined easterly wave events observed during OTREC. The results show that easterly waves consistently alter the climatological overturning circulation of the East Pacific ITCZ. During the convectively active phase, the cyclonic circulation associated with the easterly wave strengthens the deep meridional circulation through enhanced moisture convergence and moist static energy transport. As the wave transitions into its suppressed phase, the anticyclonic circulation strengthens the shallow overturning circulation, promoting shallow convection over the southern ITCZ. These findings highlight the important role of multiscale interactions between easterly waves, convectively coupled equatorial waves, and the background tropical circulation in organizing convection over the eastern Pacific. This work also reflects the lasting impact of George Kiladis’ scientific leadership and mentorship. As one of his mentees, George’s guidance shaped my research and the way I approach meteorology today. The scientific foundation I developed through his mentorship continues to guide my work as Manager of the Applied Meteorology team at AccuWeather, where we apply atmospheric science to improve weather forecasting, support better decision-making and help save lives, prevent injuries and help people and businesses prosper.

492112.title: Space Weather Analysis and Prediction Activities Supporting End-Users with Planetary Exploration by NASA GSFC’s Moon to Mars Space Weather Analysis Office
492112.authors: Teresa Nieves-Chinchilla, NASA/GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and M. Romano, M. Aronne, C. Alden, M. Anastopulos, A. Chulaki, F. Di Mare, A. Iampietro, E. Juelfs, M. Kane, R. D. Loper, M. Pasanen, N. Romanelli, and C. A. Young, Ph.D.
492112.abstract: The Moon to Mars Space Weather Analysis Office (M2M SWAO) at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) carries out space weather analysis and prediction for NASA missions throughout the solar system. As NASA plans for new exploratory missions to the Moon and Mars through the current Artemis, Moon Base, and Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) programs, M2M SWAO supports interdisciplinary activities to help identify how planetary environments are impacted by space weather hazards, including solar energetic particle events. These efforts have informed M2M SWAO about future operational needs for mission control, astronauts, and other end-users requiring real-time space weather analysis and prediction capabilities. We present our ongoing work to understand connections between solar, heliospheric, and planetary domains to ensure the evaluation of space weather hazards is appropriately communicated for mission success. In this presentation, we highlight specific space weather assessments for planetary environments alongside real-time analysis statistics from Solar Cycle 25. To conclude, we identify critical gaps in current data and modeling, sharing key lessons learned that will help refine space weather services and ensure the safety of sustained human exploration beyond Earth.

492114.title: Breaking the Distribution Wall: Modernizing NOMADS via Cloud-Native Architectures
492114.authors: Margaret B Curtis, NWS, College Park, MD; and A. Myckow and D. Hood
492114.abstract: The National Operational Model Archive and Distribution System (NOMADS) is a critical component of the National Weather Service's operational infrastructure, providing timely access to numerical weather prediction (NWP) guidance for internal operations, partners, researchers, and the public. As operational computing environments evolve, modernizing NOMADS is essential to improve scalability, maintainability, and operational resilience while supporting increasing data volumes and user demand. This presentation describes the ongoing modernization of NOMADS through the adoption of cloud-native software engineering practices and deployment architectures. Key initiatives include containerizing NOMADS to improve portability, scalability, and operational consistency across computing environments, as well as implementing continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) workflows to streamline software delivery, testing, and system maintenance. These efforts are designed to enhance system reliability, reduce operational complexity, and provide a more flexible platform for future enhancements and service expansion. The presentation will discuss the architectural approach, implementation strategy, and early operational experience gained during this modernization effort. By applying modern software development and deployment practices to a mission-critical operational system, this work advances the National Weather Service's modernization strategy and establishes a foundation for more resilient and scalable delivery of operational weather prediction products in support of forecast operations and public access.

492116.title: Unprecedented Continental Drying, Shrinking Freshwater Availability, and Increasing Land Contributions to Sea Level Rise (INVITED)
492116.authors: James S. Famiglietti, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ; and H. A. Chandanpurkar
492116.abstract: Changes in terrestrial water storage (TWS) - all of the ice, snow, canopy water, surface water, soil moisture, and groundwater - are a critical, holistic indicator of freshwater availability. As global patterns of precipitation, evaporation, and streamflow change, TWS has been shifting rapidly in response. Shifting patterns of TWS threaten water availability and sustainable water management for people and the environment, putting livelihoods and food security at risk, while acting as a trigger for climate migration, and transboundary conflict, both intra- and internationally. Here, we use more than two decades of observations (April 2002 to May 2026) from NASA/DLR’s Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) missions to evaluate how and why TWS has changed since 2002. We find that the continents (all land excluding Greenland and Antarctica) have undergone unprecedented rates of drying, and that the continental areas experiencing drying are increasing by about twice the size of the State of California in the United States each year. The rapid expansion of dry areas has resulted in the emergence of four “mega-drying” regions, by the interlinking of previously known drying hot spots, particularly since the strongest recorded El Niño of 2014, and across the Northern Hemisphere. The newly-identified mega-drying regions include Northern Canada and Alaska, Northern Russia, southwestern North America and Central America, and MENA/Pan-Eurasia. While most of the world’s dry areas continue to get drier and its wet areas continue to get wetter, we note that dry areas are drying at a faster rate than wet areas are wetting. At the same time, the area experiencing drying has increased, while the area experiencing wetting has decreased. Only the tropical region between 10º south and 20º north experienced a net TWS increase. We show that changes in TWS since previous global studies are robust, and are driven primarily by high-latitude water losses in Canada and Russia (most likely due to ice and permafrost melt), by the extreme Central American and European droughts of the past several years, and by continued global groundwater depletion, which accounts for an astounding 68% of the TWS trend over the non-glaciated continents. We refer to the phenomenon of global-scale reduction in TWS as measured by the GRACE missions as “continental drying.” Our definition of continental drying implicitly includes melting of glaciers and ice caps (GICs) on land (distinct from the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets). The expansion of drying regions reported here, however, occurs in the non-glaciated regions. We note that this continental drying affects most of the population and countries in the world. Roughly 75% of the global population lives in the 101 countries that have been losing freshwater water since 2002. Within the global water budget, the continents are now contributing more freshwater to sea level rise than either of the individual ice sheets. Furthermore, the drying regions on the continents now contribute more to sea level rise than GICs on land. While efforts to slow climate change may be sputtering, there is no reason why efforts to slow rates of continental drying should do the same. Key management decisions and new policies, especially toward regional and national groundwater sustainability, and international efforts toward global groundwater sustainability, can help preserve this precious resource for generations to come. Simultaneously, such actions will slow rates of sea level rise. We hope that the findings of this work will serve to raise awareness of the urgent, global need to prepare for shrinking freshwater availability on land; greater vulnerability to sea level rise along coastal regions; and the interconnected, widespread impacts of continental drying on people, the environment, and the economy. Major coordinated, national, international, and global, transdisciplinary efforts are critically needed to elevate the level of awareness and action around continental drying and decreasing freshwater availability to that of the carbon cycle. Without such urgent attention, the findings presented here will continue to worsen, leading to far-reaching accelerations in water, food, and human insecurity and sea level rise.

492117.title: Integration of Weather Predictions into Space Operations
492117.authors: Tracy Copp, US Space Force, Colorado Springs, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO
492117.abstract: Space, as a domain, is congested, contested, competitive and critical. Given the increased number of assets in space, along with a spectrum of diverse asset types, designs, and function it is necessary to revisit the integration of weather predictions to space operations. Ensuring resiliency, availability and utility of space assets depend significantly on understanding weather predictions, the impacts of weather to operations, and crucially how to assess the risk and potential mitigations of those impacts. Current efforts towards understanding the risk assessment and mitigations of weather impacts, integration of weather predictions will be discussed.

492129.title: Speaking to the Hollers: Workshop Perspectives on Rural Appalachian Vulnerabilities to Hazardous Weather
492129.authors: Michelle E. Saunders, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State, MS; and E. H. Marold
492129.abstract: A key objective of Rural Region Readiness (RRR), a NOAA VORTEX-USA study, is to record, analyze, and share rural Appalachian vulnerabilities that overlap with tornado weather hazards as discussed during Integrated Warning Team (IWT) Workshops. The primary goal of RRR is to provide the NWS with guidelines for how to plan and run IWT workshops to improve impact-based decision support services (IDSS). Over three summers, RRR researchers worked with three Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) to plan and host four IWT workshops in rural Appalachia. One in Morristown, TN (2024), one in Charleston, WV (2025), and two in Roanoke, VA (2026). IWT attendees varied by workshop and included NWS meteorologists, emergency management, police, fire, emergency medical services, and emergency dispatch personnel. Other attendees included local broadcast meteorologists, university staff, Community Emergency Response Teams (CERT), and National Voluntary Organizations Active in Disaster (VOAD) members. Detailed observation notes were recorded during each IWT by two researchers who served as “participant observers” during the IWTs. Thematic Analysis was used to analyze two researchers’ observation notes across all four IWT workshops. This method was used to identify meaning in the form of themes within text-based data guided by two research questions. RQ1: How are vulnerabilities to tornadoes discussed during the IWT workshops? RQ2: In what ways are (a) physical geography and (b)human geography discussed as a cause for vulnerability to weather hazards by RRR participants? Findings from our thematic analysis will be discussed in this presentation.

492134.title: Diversity of Developing El Niño Events and Its Relationship with the Zonal Contrast SSTA Mode in Summer
492134.authors: Run Wang, Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences, Beijing, Beijing, China; and H. L. Ren
492134.abstract: El Niño exhibits spatial diversity during its mature stage and is commonly categorized into eastern Pacific (EP) and central Pacific (CP) types. However, contrasting with matured warm sea surface temperature anomaly (SSTA) centers distributed around the Niño-3.4 region, intense warming or cooling often occurs in the far eastern equatorial Pacific in developing summer, like the 2023 extreme coastal event. Interevent differences of developing El Niño have been unintentionally overlooked. In this study, two tropical Pacific modes—the conventional El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) mode and zonal contrast SSTA mode—are found to play crucial roles in the diversity of developing El Niño, as they are comparable factors influencing zonal gradients of equatorial SSTAs. The former features a prominent SSTA center along the Peru–Ecuador coast. The latter features opposite SSTA centers located around 90°W and 180°, respectively. According to the spatial structure in summer, developing El Niños are classified into two types: the coast-centered (CC) type governed by the ENSO mode and the ocean-centered (OC) type regulated by the zonal contrast SSTA mode. These two types own different dynamic processes, where the CC type is driven by the thermocline feedback (TH), but the OC type is initially dominated by TH, with an increasing contribution of zonal advective feedback over time. The CC and OC developing types can be precursors to the EP and CP mature types, respectively, with approximately 70% of them developing into the corresponding mature types. These results enhance our understanding of ENSO diversity and provide new references for ENSO categorized monitoring.

492136.title: Dust Storms across the United States: Spatial and Temporal Distributions and Impact
492136.authors: Karin Ardon-Dryer, Texas Tech Univ., Lubbock, TX
492136.abstract: Dust events are one of the main natural contributors to atmospheric aerosols. They impact millions of people across the US and can affect the climate, environment, air quality, economy, and human well-being and health. Dust storms are the most severe form of dust events, defined by horizontal visibility ≤ 1 km. However, their frequency and spatial or temporal distributions remain uncertain. Using ground meteorological measurements, we were able to identify times with dust storms. Our results will show how many dust storms occurred across the western US over the last 20 years (2000-2020), where and when they occurred, and how long they lasted. This information is part of a new dust database, under development, that will shed light on the spatial and temporal distributions of these dust storms and their impact.

492137.title: An Evaluation of Historical Drought Representation in Texas in the LOCA2, STAR-ESDM, and C-PrEP2 Statistically Downscaled Datasets
492137.authors: Oliver T. Millin, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and R. Juluru, H. Omidi, and A. Wootten
492137.abstract: Drought arises from sustained precipitation deficits and is often compounded by anomalously high temperatures and evapotranspiration. Anthropogenic climate change is altering the processes that govern drought onset and intensification, with growing evidence that both the frequency and severity of drought events are shifting in response. These changes carry substantial societal costs. In the United States (US), drought and associated heatwaves caused approximately $328 billion in damages between 1980 and 2022, with impacts including stressed water supplies, reduced agricultural productivity, and depleted major reservoirs. Texas is particularly exposed to this risk, experiencing recurring drought alongside projected increases in drought frequency and severity in a warming climate. Robust projections (especially of high resolution) of future drought risk in Texas therefore have direct value for water resource planning and impact mitigation. Although statistically downscaled datasets are increasingly used for future climate projections, there has been limited evaluation of how well they reproduce historical drought characteristics, especially over Texas. However, confidence in these projections depends on their ability to first reproduce observed drought behavior. Previous studies have emphasized that evaluating historical drought representation is a critical prerequisite for establishing confidence in future climate projections. However, comparatively few studies have systematically assessed how well multiple statistically downscaled datasets reproduce historical drought characteristics over Texas. High-resolution, statistically downscaled climate projections offer a key opportunity to evaluate whether such datasets can accurately capture the key statistical characteristics of Texas drought, providing the necessary foundation for interpreting and trusting future projections built upon them. In this presentation, we evaluate drought frequency, intensity, and duration (both maximum and average) across Texas in three statistically downscaled datasets, benchmarking each against its respective training data: (1) Localized Canonical Analogs version 2 (LOCA2) between 1950-2014, (2) the Seasonal Trends and Analysis of Residuals Empirical Statistical Downscaling (STAR-ESDM) between 1951-2014, and (3) the Climate Projections Evaluation Project version 2 (C-PrEP2) between 1981-2014. Historical simulations and training data are first converted to monthly precipitation accumulations, then transformed into the Standardized Precipitation index (SPI) and mapped to corresponding US Drought Monitor categories. We focus specifically on the 6-month (SPI-6) and 12-month (SPI-12) timescales to characterize longer-term drought behavior. Initial results show that for all collective dry/drought conditions (D0-D4) using SPI-6, the LOCA2 and STAR-ESDM datasets on average oversimulate drought occurrence in western Texas and oversimulate drought intensity in northern Texas, while frequency, intensity, mean duration, and maximum duration are underestimated in central to eastern Texas. SPI-12 drought in LOCA2 and STAR-ESDM shows an overestimation in intensity in western Texas, with mostly overestimation (underestimation) in mean duration in northwest (southeast) Texas, while maximum duration is largely underestimated in south-central Texas. We will also show results delineated by drought monitor category, as well as bias results from C-PrEP2 and analyses of trends and trend biases in all datasets. Overall, this work will help toward supporting the selection of reliable downscaled datasets for future drought projections and water resource planning in Texas.

492138.title: Modernizing NOAA Operational Model Archive and Dissemination (NOMADS) with Kerchunk and grib2io: Next-Generation Data Accessibility on the NOAA Ingtegrated Modeling Backbone for Unified Super Computing (NIMBUS) Cloud Supercomputer
492138.authors: Margaret B Curtis, NWS, College Park, MD; and R. Mahajan and D. Hood
492138.abstract: Global Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) providers have long utilized the GRIB2 format for operational data delivery. However, as data volumes grow, traditional access methods create bottlenecks for cloud-native workflows. This presentation outlines the ongoing architecture and deployment of a modernized, cloud-based NOMADS framework utilizing Kerchunk and the grib2io engine, running on the new NOAA Integrated Modeling Backbone for Unified Supercomputing (NIMBUS) cloud supercomputing system developed in partnership with cloud provider Google. By generating lightweight reference manifests, this approach enables users to interact with legacy, operational formats (such as GRIB2) as if they were cloud-native, chunked datasets (like Zarr) without requiring costly, time-consuming, and duplicative data translation pipelines. This technical innovation sits at the center of Modernizing Operations, Planning, and Assets. By optimizing the research-to-operations (R2O) pipeline through virtualized Zarr access, we accelerate the transition of emerging technologies and scientific research directly into the hands of stakeholders, significantly enhancing operational readiness and organizational effectiveness. Furthermore, this deployment advances U.S. efforts in Leading the World in NWP. Implementing Kerchunk via grib2io provides the highly scalable, low-latency data access required for modern AI integration and model consolidation. It allows researchers to train and run machine learning models directly against historical and real-time GRIB2 archives without the overhead of data conversion.

492142.title: Northern Hemisphere Rain-on-Snow and non-Rain-on-Snow Ablation: Frequency and Trends
492142.authors: Sanskar Adhikari, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and Z. Suriano
492142.abstract: Snow ablation plays a vital role in altering water availability, soil moisture, groundwater supplies, and the risk of hydrological hazards such as Rain-on-snow (ROS) flooding across cold regions. Most studies have predominantly focused on ROS ablation at regional scales, leaving a gap in large-scale hemispherical analyses of ROS and nROS (melt occurring in the absence of rainfall) ablation events. Here we present a climatology of ablation events across the Northern Hemisphere (20°N-90°N) over a 46-year period (1980 - 2025), focusing on their frequency and trends. This study uses the ERA5 hourly reanalysis to examine spatiotemporal variations across three separate thresholds (0.5mm, 1.0mm, and 2.0mm per hour) to assess the sensitivity of climatology and trends to varying event intensity. Across thresholds, a large majority of total events are snowmelt occurring in the absence of precipitation (≈78–89%). Spatially, these events frequently occur in high-elevation regions across Europe, the west and northeastern North America, Alaska, and the Himalayas. Interseasonally, both events peak in late spring (≈ May); ROS events persist year-round and experience a second peak in winter (DJF), whereas nROS events eventually zero out after peaking. The trends reveal spatially heterogeneous patterns across most of the seasonal snow zone, with a coherent decline in ablation frequency, especially in coastal and high-latitude regions, and some increases in mid-latitude inland regions. These results present snow-cover regions where rainfall versus rainfall-free melt governs snow ablation, with implications for flood risk, water management, and hazard resilience.

492149.title: Comparing Satellite Observed and Large Eddy Simulated Ship Track Signatures in Open-Cell Mesoscale Cellular Convection
492149.authors: Elizabeth O'Meara, Florida State University, Coral Gables, FL; and M. S. Diamond
492149.abstract: Ship tracks, which are disruptions in marine stratocumulus clouds created by exhaust aerosols, serve as an ideal natural experiment for exploring aerosol-cloud interactions. Open cellular convection, characterized by cloud-free centers ringed by drizzle-driven cloudy walls, represents a particularly sensitive regime in which to examine this interaction. This study compares ship track signatures propagating through open-cell mesoscale cellular convection (MCC) in MODIS satellite retrievals against those produced by large eddy simulations (LES). MODIS Cloud Optical Thickness, Cloud Effective Radius, Liquid Water Path, and cloud droplet number concentration (Nd) are retrieved or calculated for two ship tracks for direct comparison with LES output, which is run under three surface aerosol emission scenarios with each different aerosol surface fluxes to assess sensitivity of the simulated open-cell response to aerosol loading. Preliminary comparisons show differences between observed and simulated cloud properties, with the LES underestimating background cloud effective radius while producing stronger ship track perturbations in cloud optical thickness and Nd. Future work will extend analysis to characterize open-cell size and aspect ratio under varying aerosol conditions, aiming to understand the mechanisms driving differences in cell geometry across the low/mid/high emission scenarios. It is also planned to examine how aerosol-driven perturbations impact boundary-layer circulation, including the extent to which elevated aerosol injection produces a clearing effect within the open-cell field, and how the magnitude and spatial extent of this clearing depends on both aerosol injection rate and background aerosol concentration.

492151.title: Impacts of Period of Record on the Uncertainty of Estimates of Hourly Precipitation Extremes
492151.authors: Janice L. Bytheway, NOAA, Loveland, CO; and K. M. Mahoney and G. S. Karlovits
492151.abstract: Multiple US agencies are currently working towards improving and updating estimates of extreme precipitation and its hydrologic impacts at a variety of spatial and temporal scales. Many of these efforts will include estimates of the frequency and potential magnitude of extreme precipitation in modeled future climates. Increases in extreme precipitation have been observed with a warming climate, with sub-daily precipitation extremes increasing at a faster rate than extreme precipitation at longer durations. The reliability of modeled future extreme precipitation characteristics can be estimated by evaluating the ability of a model to represent the statistics of extreme precipitation during the current climate. Because of the rarity of extreme precipitation, long period of record reference datasets are needed to adequately capture the tails of the precipitation distribution. Gauge datasets such as the Global Historical Climatology Network (GHCN) provide in situ estimates of precipitation with some records extending back to the mid-1900s. However, gauge data is spatially discontinuous, particularly difficult to quality control for sub-daily precipitation, and has many locations with much shorter periods of record. Gridded precipitation datasets provide spatially continuous precipitation estimates with high temporal resolution, but often have limited periods of record or inconsistent inputs through time. We hypothesize that, for some regions or datasets, a shorter period of record may be sufficient to estimate the characteristics of precipitation, including extremes, with reasonably low uncertainty. This would increase confidence in evaluations of gridded QPE from gauge locations with shorter periods of record, and potentially support the use of high resolution radar-based datasets to evaluate modeled precipitation characteristics. In this study we quality control the GHCN-hourly gauge precipitation dataset over the CONUS and select stations with at least 40 years of data. We then calculate extreme precipitation statistics using subsets of the data to represent shorter periods of record at each site, using bootstrapping with replacement to estimate the confidence intervals of the calculated statistics, examining how the uncertainty changes with increasing years of available data. We then compare the calculated statistics and confidence intervals to those from several regional gridded precipitation datasets with varying periods of record, including Stage IV, CONUS404 and the Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC), to identify regions where the gridded datasets adequately represent the statistical characteristics of precipitation compared to the gauges and to better understand the uncertainty in the tails of the estimated precipitation distribution. In this way, we infer where spatially continuous gridded datasets with a relatively short period of record may be more or less robust references for the evaluation of model output.

492152.title: Toward Rapid-Cycling Global Artificial Intelligence Data Assimilation Using Progressively Available Observations
492152.authors: Chong-Chi Tong, NOAA/OAR/PSL, Boulder, CO; and L. Slivinski, S. Frolov, C. Miller, J. DaRosa, N. Silverman, A. Gupta, and N. D. Brenowitz
492152.abstract: More frequent data assimilation can improve short-range forecasts by incorporating observations more promptly and better addressing the rapid error growth associated with fast-evolving weather systems. However, increasing the cycling frequency of traditional data assimilation and numerical weather prediction systems from the current six-hourly synoptic cycle (i.e., 00, 06, 12, and 18 UTC) to higher frequencies, such as hourly cycling, substantially increases computational demands and workflow complexity. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based data assimilation and forecasting therefore offer a promising pathway toward more timely and efficient use of observations. Toward this goal, we have been developing and testing AI-based data assimilation and forecasting capabilities. However, several challenges remain before a fully self-cycling, hourly system can be implemented. These include the AI forecast model’s dependence on two initial states separated by six hours, the limited assessment of existing AI forecasting components outside conventional synoptic times, the lack of reliable one-hour cycling global backgrounds, and the latency of observations available for real-time assimilation. As an initial step, we propose a prototype to evaluate whether progressively incorporating newly available hourly observations into a 6-h background forecast from an existing global DA system can improve the latest synoptic-time initial condition used to initialize AI forecasts. This design preserves the existing six-hour initial-condition requirement, remains within the synoptic-time framework in which current AI models have been trained and evaluated, and initially avoids the additional complexity of fully cycling the system. Additional details on the prototype architecture, integration of the AI data assimilation and forecast components, workflow implementation, and planned evaluation strategy will be presented at the conference.

492157.title: How Variable are Observed and Simulated Cold Pools?
492157.authors: Leah D. Grant, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Bukowski, S. W. Freeman, P. J. Marinescu, M. Nieto-Caballero, R. J. Perkins, I. Singh, and S. C. van den Heever
492157.abstract: Cold pools play important roles in a multitude of atmospheric science and societal topics including aerosol transport and health hazards; severe winds impacting property, urban infrastructure, and airports; convection initiation and suppression; convective system behavior; and land-atmosphere interactions. Cold pools are notoriously difficult to simulate, being turbulent and vertically thin atmospheric features located close to the surface. In this presentation we ask the question, do large-eddy simulations (LES) of cold pools accurately capture observed variability in their properties, both spatio-temporally and across different environmental regimes? To address this question, we utilize a database of observations collected from recent field campaigns focused on observing cold pool properties, along with long-term surface observations, in the U.S. High Plains, Germany, the tropical Atlantic, and the Amazon. We also analyze cold pool properties in an extensive suite of LES simulations conducted with multiple models and microphysical schemes for the upcoming NASA INvestigation of Convective UpdraftS (INCUS) satellite mission. Initial results indicate that simulated cold pool properties are less spatially variable than observed cold pools despite indications that the largest observed perturbations are captured by the simulations. Physical mechanisms explaining the variability differences are explored.

492159.title: VEDA: NASA's Cloud-based, Open-source Cyberinfrastructure for Sharing Earth Science Data
492159.authors: Jeanné le Roux, MSFC, Huntsville, AL; and B. Freitag, A. Barciauskas, S. Adhikari, S. Chaudhary, and B. Corremonte
492159.abstract: Here we present the Visualization, Exploration, and Data Analysis (VEDA) platform, a cyberinfrastructure that integrates existing open-source community standards to deliver Earth science data to end users. Designed for the cloud, VEDA leverages cloud-native data formats and tools to enable data discovery, scientific storytelling, and interactive data visualization within a deployable platform package. VEDA has been adopted across multiple NASA and interagency efforts, including the U.S. Greenhouse Gas Center, NASA Disasters Program, Earth Information Center, Air-quality Resource for the United States (AIR4US), and other emerging applications. The platform consists of reusable services spanning the scientific data lifecycle. These include cloud-native data ingestion pipelines, SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC)-based data cataloging, dynamic visualization via TiTiler, centralized authentication using Keycloak, modular web-based dashboards, and shared cloud computing environments through JupyterHub. To ensure efficient access to archival datasets without data duplication, the system supports both cloud-native formats and optimized workarounds like Virtual Zarr. These components can be deployed independently or combined to rapidly build new science applications and make data accessible to a wider audience. We will provide a high-level summary of the VEDA architecture and explore how it’s been leveraged for the development of multiple Earth science applications. We also plan to discuss lessons learned from supporting diverse science domains and outline the future direction of the project.

492160.title: Fewer Drops, but They Look the Same: Why Inhomogeneous Mixing Appears to Dominate in Cumulus Clouds and Implications for Climate Model Representations (Invited Presentation)
492160.authors: Nithin Allwayin, Michigan Technological University, Houghton, MI; Stony Brook Univ., Stony Brook, NY; and G. Roberts, E. M. Rosky, K. Bala, A. Bansemer, K. Ranjbar, and R. A. Shaw
492160.abstract: How cloud droplets respond to the entraining dry air determines their longevity, affects precipitation and most importantly, determines how much sunlight they reflect. We find from observations of cumulus clouds made during the Experiment of Sea Breeze Convection, Aerosols, Precipitation, and Environment (ESCAPE) field campaign that this mixing process appears inhomogeneous-like, the scenario where a subset of droplets fully evaporates. The term “inhomogeneous-like” is used intentionally, as we've found that the cloud microphysical response is similar irrespective of the mixing scenario; from a microphysical perspective, inhomogeneous mixing dominates. The mixing process is visualized using traditional mixing diagrams and a two-dimensional phase space, that captures the interplay between the three relevant timescales- the mixing, phase relaxation and droplet evaporation times that dictate the entrainment process. The microphysical response is inhomogeneous-like; we have fewer cloud drops with the same mean diameter. A mixing slope parameter used to distinguish mixing types also aligns with this picture of inhomogeneous mixing. To explain these findings, we develop a simplified diffusive turbulent-evaporation model that captures the dynamic evolution of the entrainment process. The results indicate that the first evaporating droplets humidify the region around the cloud and unmixed dry air rarely reaches the core, explaining why mixing appears inhomogeneous. As mixing at these later stages is with preconditioned air of high relative humidity, the microphysical response is indistinguishable for homogeneous and inhomogeneous mixing scenarios. Based on these results, we propose a simple parameterization for cloud optical properties suitable for coarse-resolution models.

492161.title: Mean and Turbulent Flow Over a Forest, With and Without Canopy Breaks
492161.authors: Jerome Fast, PNNL, Richland, WA; and R. Krishnamurthy, R. Newsom, Y. Liu, H. Liu, and S. Wharton
492161.abstract: Forest canopies as well as their spatial variability in height and density affect wind and turbulence within a few hundred meters of the ground. These effects are not represented by operational weather forecast models such as HRRR. While idealized Large Eddy Simulations (LES) have been used to investigate the effects of canopy heterogeneities, there are relatively few coincident wind and turbulence observations within and above forest canopies. In this study, we analyze new long-term boundary layer measurements collected by the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program’s Bankhead National Forest (BNF) site in northern Alabama. While the BNF site has a full suite of meteorological measurements, we focus on data from three scanning Doppler lidar locations: one located in the forest, one located in a small forest break, and one located in cropland north of the forest. Over a two-month period during the summer of 2025, these lidars were operated to obtain high temporal resolution of the winds interspersed with RHI scans over a 10-min period for each hour. In addition, a profiling lidar was deployed at the forested site during the summer of 2026 to obtain high-temporal resolution winds up to ~300 m. Turbulent kinetic energy and momentum fluxes were derived from the high-temporal resolution profiles. Sonic anemometer measurements on a 43-m meteorological tower at the forested site are merged with lidar measurements to obtain wind and turbulence profiles from the ground up to several hundred meters above the forest. The observations among the three sites are compared to examine the sensitivity of mean of turbulence profiles to differences in vegetation variability. RHI reveal differences between the forest and forest break sites in how eddies within the growing convective boundary layer erode shallow low-level jets that frequently form at night. These datasets are also used to evaluate HRRR predictions of boundary layer properties over the forest as functions of season and synoptic regime.

492163.title: Impact of AORC Processing Changes on the Representation of Hourly Precipitation
492163.authors: Janice L. Bytheway, NOAA, Loveland, CO; and K. M. Mahoney
492163.abstract: The Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC) was created to provide hydrologic forcing variables for use in calibrating hydrologic models at the NWS Office of Water Prediction’s National Water Center. It provides wind, humidity, temperature, pressure, radiation, and precipitation estimates at hourly time steps and 800m grid spacing over the period from 1979 to near-real-time. This makes it one of the few long period of record datasets offering quantitative precipitation estimates (QPE) at high spatial and temporal resolution. AORC precipitation estimates combine observations and analysis from different sources to provide hourly QPE over the CONUS, as well as Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Alaska, and the US Virgin Islands. Because these sources are not available for the entire dataset period of record, there are potential discontinuities in the climatology of precipitation when data sources and the methods to combine them change. Specifically, AORC is divided into three periods with different disaggregation and blending methods: Historical (1979-2009), Interim (2010-2015), and Near-real time (2016-present). While the impacts of changing inputs and processing methods have been examined for daily precipitation accumulations, to date most evaluations of hourly AORC QPE have focused on regional performance during subsets of the dataset period of record. This talk will discuss how the changes to input datasets and blending methodology impact the climatology of precipitation from AORC, including extremes, as well as the impacts of these changes on the performance of the dataset when compared to quality controlled hourly rain gauge data from the Global Historical Climatology Network.

492166.title: Introducing NIMBUS - NOAA Integrated Modeling Backbone for Unified Super Computing
492166.authors: Anne Myckow, NWS, College Park, MD; and M. B. Curtis and D. Hood
492166.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) is undertaking the modernization of the Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System (WCOSS) to support the next generation of operational numerical weather prediction (NWP). As cloud computing capabilities continue to mature, migrating operational modeling systems requires careful evaluation of how best to leverage cloud-native technologies while maintaining the performance, reliability, and resiliency required for mission-critical forecast operations. This presentation describes the ongoing architectural design of a cloud-based environment NIMBUS - NOAA Integrated Modeling Backbone for Unified Super Computing. The effort includes evaluating strategies for matching operational workloads to appropriate computing resources, including traditional compute nodes, high-performance computing resources, and graphics processing units (GPUs). In parallel, multiple storage architectures—including parallel file systems, cloud object storage, and hybrid approaches—are being assessed to support the diverse I/O requirements of forecast production, post-processing, and operational data services. The presentation will also discuss considerations for integrating cloud-native services, supporting operational resiliency, and enabling a phased transition from existing on-premises infrastructure. By establishing a flexible and scalable cloud architecture for operational NWP, this work advances the NWS modernization strategy and provides a foundation for future innovations in forecasting capabilities. The architectural approaches and lessons learned are intended to inform the design of resilient, cloud-enabled operational computing environments that can adapt to evolving scientific and operational requirements.

492170.title: From Weather Information to Protective Action: NWS Support to Core Partners During the 2026 FIFA World Cup Timeframe
492170.authors: Stephanie D. Sipprell, NWS, KANSAS CITY, MO; and R. A. Garcia, M. Solum, R. Wolcott, and R. A. Graham, NWS
492170.abstract: National Weather Service (NWS) operations in support of core partners during the 2026 FIFA World Cup timeframe placed meteorologists directly into complex public-safety decision environments across 11 match cities and more than 40 federal, regional, state, and local coordination centers. Emergency managers, public-safety officials, and other core partners faced repeated decisions involving large outdoor gatherings, crowd movement, sheltering, and medical response. Lightning, excessive heat, severe thunderstorms, damaging winds, and flooding required more than routine forecast delivery. Core partners needed timely weather information connected to the specific actions available to them. Several operational needs became especially important ahead of this timeframe. Meteorologists working from core partner locations required dependable access to lightning information so they could provide public-safety decision makers with the most current assessment of rapidly evolving threats. Local Weather Forecast Offices also needed specialized short-term forecast support when convection threatened multiple locations or when small changes in storm timing could significantly affect public-safety operations. Warn-on-Forecast System guidance provided additional insight into potential storm development and evolution, while Remote Mesoscale Analysis experts helped translate high-resolution environmental information into operational context for offices supporting core partners.
