Together, these capabilities strengthened meteorologists’ ability to communicate timing, confidence, expected impacts, and evolving threats, helping core partners make timely protective decisions. During a lightning threat affecting a Miami Fan Festival, local officials suspended activities and moved approximately 3,000 attendees into shelter. In Houston and Sugar Land, emergency management partners reported that having NWS personnel onsite increased their confidence when clearing a public gathering location and later reopening a viewing party. In Philadelphia, forecast winds of 35 to 45 mph contributed to the early closure of an outdoor Fan Festival before the strongest conditions arrived. In Kansas City, repeated heat and thunderstorm threats required sustained coordination among emergency management, public safety, transportation, and multiple operational centers. Across the timeframe, operations documented more than 68 lightning-related incidents or impacts and more than 50 heat-related incidents or impacts. Heat support demonstrated the same forecast-to-action connection before hazardous conditions developed. NWS offices communicated excessive-heat conditions, HeatRisk, wet-bulb globe temperature, and expected timing to public-safety officials. Core partners subsequently adjusted activity schedules and locations, implemented heat-mitigation measures, increased medical readiness, and, in some cases, canceled activities in advance. Across all hazards, core partners used NWS weather information when determining whether to shelter people, suspend activities, close or reopen public gathering locations, adjust activity timing or location, increase medical and staffing resources, modify transportation operations, or take other protective actions Feedback from public-safety personnel highlighted the operational value of direct meteorological engagement. Core partners stated that onsite NWS support increased confidence during clearing and reopening decisions, praised the information provided during high-impact operations, and noted that some real-time decisions "couldn’t have been done without the NWS team and support provided". These examples demonstrate that the value of improved forecasting capabilities is realized when meteorologists translate them into trusted, decision-relevant information at the time and place core partners are making decisions. The primary outcome was not the deployment of a particular tool or dataset, but the connection of specialized weather information, local expertise, and trusted core partner relationships to real-world protective action. The experience provides a multi-hazard case study of how emerging capabilities and direct meteorologist engagement can strengthen weather-informed decision making. These lessons will strengthen NWS operational guidance for onsite support and help ensure more effective decision support for core partners during future complex public-safety operations.

492177.title: The National Atmospheric Deposition Program (NADP): Strategic Optimization for Long-Term Atmospheric Monitoring
492177.authors: Nichole Miller, Wisconsin State Lab of Hygiene, Madison, WI; and M. Shafer, C. Dahman, K. Blaydes, E. Osby, Z. Najacht, M. Kuether, and S. E. Benish
492177.abstract: Since 1978, the National Atmospheric Deposition Program (NADP) has provided publicly accessible, continuous, quality-assured measurements of atmospheric deposition chemistry across North America. From its origins as an acid deposition-focused wet deposition network (National Trends Network, NTN), the NADP has expanded into a coordinated system of networks including the Mercury Deposition Network (MDN), Ammonia Monitoring Network (AMoN), Atmospheric Mercury Network (AMNet), Mercury Litterfall Network (MLN), and the newly launched PFAS-NTN subnetwork (PFN). These long-term records underpin hundreds of peer-reviewed studies and federal and state assessment reports annually, informing evaluation of Clean Air Act policy effectiveness, nitrogen and sulfur critical load modeling, mercury and PFAS deposition tracking to terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, and satellite-derived air quality products. NADP is also piloting new efforts to extend its observational footprint, including a passive gaseous elemental mercury monitoring network and expanded wet deposition sampling for total nitrogen and total phosphorus. We present practical lessons from nearly five decades of network operation and adaptation, including cost-saving strategies that preserve data quality objectives, improved operational tracking and communication through shared digital tools, extension of rigorous quality assurance protocols to new trace-level inorganic and organic analytes, and cross-disciplinary engagement embedded in NADP’s committee governance structure. As demand grows for monitoring emerging contaminants alongside legacy pollutants, the NADP’s experience scaling long-term networks to incorporate new technologies and analytes offer a practical, transferable model for sustaining ground-based observational infrastructure without compromising data continuity or scientific rigor – directly relevant to community efforts to modernize total deposition monitoring and modeling.

492180.title: Elevating R2O: Scaling Dynamic Transition Planning for Optimized Usability
492180.authors: Annette Hollingshead, AOML, Miami, FL; NOAA, Miami, FL
492180.abstract: NOAA’s Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory (AOML) conducts a diverse portfolio of research aimed at advancing the understanding and prediction of complex atmospheric and oceanic phenomena. Central to maximizing the societal impact of this research is the effective transition of scientific outcomes into operational applications. While formalizing Research to Operations (R2O) processes through transition plans is a standard practice, scaling these requirements across AOML's wide array of projects—ranging from oceanographic observations to advanced numerical modeling—presents unique logistical challenges. Transition plans are most effective when they function as dynamic, "living documents" that evolve alongside the maturity of the underlying research. However, the manual overhead required to manage and update these plans for a growing, heterogeneous project portfolio can become a significant bottleneck. This presentation will highlight AOML’s recent efforts to modernize its approach to R2O. We will detail the development of a streamlined, highly adaptable transition plan framework designed to be usable across all AOML divisions. By integrating more dynamic data-tracking and standardized workflows, we have simplified the process for project leads to maintain compliant and actionable plans. Attendees will learn how these improvements have reduced administrative burden, fostered better cross-divisional alignment, and accelerated the overall transition pipeline from research to operational capability.

492184.title: Integrating Surface Observations and Numerical Weather Prediction Guidance for Wind Gust Nowcasting Using a Tabular Foundation Model
492184.authors: Chau Lam Yu, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY; SUNY, Albany, NY; and H. Baki and S. Basu
492184.abstract: Extreme convective wind gusts are characterized by short time scale, localized occurrence, and abrupt changes in magnitude, making accurate nowcasting challenging. Existing gust-nowcasting approaches generally rely on one of two complementary sources of predictability. Observation-based methods exploit the persistence of the local atmospheric boundary layer state observed from recent surface observations, whereas numerical weather prediction (NWP)-based methods utilize forward-looking guidance that describes the temporal evolution of mesoscale and synoptic-scale flows. In this study, we propose a hybrid wind-gust nowcasting framework using the Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN), a pretrained foundation model developed for general prediction tasks on structured tabular datasets. We utilize a multi-year observational database from the New York State Mesonet (NYSM) and a historical archive of NOAA’s High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model forecasts. Because both recent NYSM observations and HRRR forecast variables can be represented in structured tabular format, the proposed framework naturally integrates these complementary data sources within a single forecasting model. To account for spatial variability, we augment the predictor set with multiscale neighborhood-based meteorological features. We evaluate the performance of the hybrid framework against four different baselines: persistence, raw HRRR gust potential, TabPFN statistical post-processing of HRRR guidance, and TabPFN using only NYSM observations. The hybrid framework achieves the highest forecast skill throughout the 6-hour nowcasting window and more accurately predicts the spatial-temporal evolution of extreme wind-gust events than the baseline methods. Feature attribution using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) reveals a gradual transition in the relative importance of the predictors, with recent surface observations controlling short-lead forecasts and HRRR-derived predictors becoming increasingly important beyond approximately two hours. These results demonstrate that recent observations and NWP guidance provide complementary sources of predictability and that pretrained tabular foundation models offer a computationally efficient way for combining these data sources within one unified prediction framework.

492187.title: Enterprise Architecture for NESDIS Environmental Intelligence
492187.authors: Shawn Miller, Science and Technology Corporation, Denver, CO; and H. S. Kilcoyne and S. A. Hausman
492187.abstract: Within the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) plays a critical role in transforming observations from raw measurements to actionable environmental intelligence for a broad range of users, spanning from real-time weather forecasts and warnings through research and development of new science and capabilities. Multiple stakeholders within NESDIS contribute in significant ways to this enterprise. As both observations and observational needs evolve into the future, including increasing integration of new missions and commercial data sources, NESDIS stakeholders must continue to collaborate ever more efficiently, while retaining the integrity, timeliness, and quality of the data and metadata delivered to its user community. In this presentation, we describe the application of the Unified Architecture Framework (UAF) and The Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF) to a digital enterprise architecture model that captures the strategy, capabilities, operational activities, and technology roadmap required for NESDIS to achieve and maintain this enterprise vision.

492188.title: Effects of Green Space Layout and Canopy Parameters on Wind Environment and Pollutant Dispersion in Urban Street Canyon
492188.authors: QianFeng Liang, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, shanghai, China; University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, shanghai, 31, China; and Y. Huang and Y. Luo
492188.abstract: Abstract: With accelerated urbanization, the combined effects of traffic emissions and high-density built environments have led to increasingly severe pollutant accumulation in urban street canyons, seriously threatening pedestrian health and urban livability. This study focuses on a street canyon at an urban community intersection to investigate the influence mechanisms of green space layout, canopy height, and leaf area density (LAD) on the wind environment and pollutant dispersion. A wind-tunnel-validated CFD numerical simulation method was adopted to establish multiple case models with different green space layouts (upstream/downstream), canopy heights (8 m, 16 m, 24 m), and LAD values (1, 3, 5). The flow field, pollutant concentration distribution, and air exchange characteristics within the urban street block were analyzed. The results indicate that, with upstream greening, canopy height and LAD significantly affect the intra-block flow field and thus exert marked regulatory effects on pollutant dispersion. A canopy height of 8 m combined with LAD = 1 proves most favorable for pollutant dispersion, reducing pollutant concentrations at pedestrian breathing height by 9.90% relative to the no-greenery case; conversely, a canopy height of 16 m with LAD = 5 is the most unfavorable, increasing breathing-height concentrations by 4.82% relative to the no-greenery case. Downstream greening generally exacerbates street-block pollution, with the worst case increasing breathing-height pollutant concentrations by 31.37%. Furthermore, variations in canopy height and LAD have limited impact on the flow pattern under downstream greening, with pollutants mainly accumulating in the leeward region. This study provides a scientific basis for optimizing urban community greening patterns and mitigating traffic-related pollution. Keywords: green space layout; canopy height; leaf area density; pollutant dispersion; street canyon

492189.title: Persistence of Extreme Precipitation Across CONUS: Evaluating Downscaling Methods and Uncertainty in Historical Simulation and Future Projections
492189.authors: Graham Taylor, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and K. W. Dixon, L. Sun, and F. Lehner
492189.abstract: The persistence of extreme precipitation strongly influences flood risk, soil moisture, and other hydrologic impacts, yet is often overlooked in evaluations of downscaled climate datasets. This work evaluates historical and future multi-day clustering of extreme precipitation across the contiguous United States (CONUS) in observation-based datasets, coarse-resolution climate models (GCMs), and three widely used statistical downscaling products (STAR-ESDM, NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, and LOCA2). Future changes are additionally assessed using a dynamical downscaling product (WUS-D3) and a large ensemble (GARD-LENS) to place projected changes in the context of internal variability and dynamical-vs-statistical downscaling behavior. Observation-based datasets show substantial spatial variability in extreme precipitation clustering, with multi-day sequences most common in the coastally-adjacent western United States and least common in the Northeast. GCMs reproduce the broad spatial pattern but underestimate the clustering in western mountain ranges and overestimate clustering in the gulf-adjacent Southeast. STAR-ESDM and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 biases closely resemble those of the driving GCMs across much of CONUS (underestimating/overestimating where the GCM underestimates/overestimates), whereas LOCA2 reduces clustering biases in western mountains and southern Florida but introduces new biases, overestimating clustering, in parts of the northeastern United States. Future projections show increased multi-day clustering over the eastern United States and southern Great Plains, with statistical downscaling products generally inheriting the sign and spatial pattern of change from their driving GCMs. Projected changes in clustering appear less spatially consistent than changes in precipitation intensity, and large-ensemble simulations (GARD-LENS) indicate these projected changes are strongly influenced by internal climate variability. These results demonstrate that downscaling methodology can substantially influence the representation and projection of extreme precipitation persistence and should therefore be explicitly considered in hydrologic impact assessments and climate adaptation planning.

492190.title: 20 Years of High-Speed Camera Lightning Observations. What We Have Seen and What We Have Learned (Invited Presentation)
492190.authors: Tom Warner, ZT Research, Rapid City, SD; and M. M. F. Saba, C. Schumann, and H. G. P. Hunt
492190.abstract: The development and implementation of high-speed digital camera technology into lightning research has greatly enhanced our understanding of lightning processes and behavior. This presentation explores early use of high-speed digital cameras dating back to late1990s and the rapid integration and expansion of this observation method into lightning research over the last 20+ years. High-speed cameras have allowed researchers, as well as the general public, to see lightning like never before and in a way that is much easier to analyze and understand from previous optically-based observation methods. Analysis of high-speed camera data along with correlated electromagnetic, current and radiative data has greatly advanced our understanding of lightning physical properties and behavior. These advancements will be discussed and shown via high-speed camera recordings along with a discussion on the future evolution of digital high-speed optical technology.

492191.title: Building a Shared Cloud Storage Platform for Operations
492191.authors: Margaret B Curtis, NWS, College Park, MD; and A. Myckow and D. Hood
492191.abstract: As the National Weather Service modernizes its operational computing infrastructure, cloud-native storage architectures are becoming a critical component for both numerical weather prediction (NWP) and operational data dissemination. Historically, high-performance modeling systems and public data distribution services have relied on distinct storage solutions optimized for their individual workloads. The migration of operational modeling and dissemination capabilities to the cloud presents an opportunity to design a unified storage architecture capable of supporting both high-performance forecast production and large-scale public data access. This presentation describes the ongoing design and evaluation of a shared cloud storage platform intended to support operational NWP workloads alongside NOAA's National Operational Model Archive and Distribution System (NOMADS). The effort includes evaluating storage technologies, such as parallel file systems and cloud object storage, to balance the performance, scalability, resiliency, and cost requirements of diverse operational workloads. Architectural considerations include data lifecycle management, interoperability between modeling and dissemination systems, and support for cloud-native workflows. By developing a common storage foundation for both forecast production and operational data dissemination, this work supports the National Weather Service's broader modernization strategy while enabling more efficient operations, improved scalability, and a more flexible platform for future innovations in numerical weather prediction and data services.

492192.title: Ocean Advection Drives Mixed Layer Temperature Variance at 10-100 km in the Gulf Stream Extension.
492192.authors: Chaehyeong Lee, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and D. Giglio and A. C. Subramanian
492192.abstract: Upper-ocean temperature variability arises from both atmospheric forcing and oceanic processes, but the relative contribution of the ocean itself across spatial and temporal scales remains poorly constrained. Previous studies have relied on stochastic frameworks that infer the ocean's contribution rather than directly quantifying it across spatial and temporal scales. Here, we directly assess the dominant source and sink processes governing mixed layer temperature variability in the Gulf Stream Extension across spatiotemporal scales using a fully coupled mesoscale-resolving simulation (GEOS/ECCO C1440-LLC2160). We decompose the temperature budget into the frequency-wavenumber domain and evaluate the co-spectrum of each process with the mixed layer temperature tendency. Horizontal temperature advection emerges as the leading source of temperature variance at every resolved spatial scale, with a source that is positive across the resolved band and increases toward lower frequencies. Conversely, the surface heat flux acts as a source only at the largest scales and damps variance at all scales below 400 km. Horizontal advection is also the most scale-dependent term: 69% of its contribution comes from wavelengths shorter than 100 km, compared with 30% or less for every other term, with its high-frequency source shifting systematically toward smaller scales. Overall, these results suggest that ocean models that do not resolve 10–100 km motions significantly underestimate the advective source of mixed-layer temperature variance, particularly at high frequencies.

492194.title: Historical County Scale Extreme Weather Damages in Across Texas
492194.authors: William J. Baule, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and J. W. Nielsen-Gammon, A. Tarter, and V. N. E. Ford
492194.abstract: Historical estimates of total damages from extreme weather events in Texas are used in the State Hazard Mitigation Plan and as guidance to counties by the State of Texas, are based on storm reports produced by the National Weather Service and archived by the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). For many events affecting multiple counties, locations, and hazards, the damages appear to be indiscriminately distributed across multiple counties or assigned to the county specifically housing the local National Weather Service office and appears to be dependent on data source. This is a problem for resiliency and disaster management at the county and state levels. One such example is the Texas State Hazard Mitigation Plan (SHMP) relies on the distribution of monetary and human impacts drawn from the Storm Data database for assessing county-scale risk and identifying hot spots of vulnerability. Given apparent shortcomings in the current database an in-depth analysis was conducted for the State of Texas counties from 2000-2025 consisting of the following components. A careful analysis of historical damages for the period 2000-2025 counties in Texas was performed as many counties are highly susceptible to natural disasters, that span a wide range of urban and rural communities, and that fall within the areas of responsibility of multiple National Weather Service offices. The comparison of analyzed damages to damages reported by the NWS and stored in national databases, in order to determine the extent and nature of discrepancies and how they vary across different types of natural disasters. Interviews with NWS employees in WFOs around Texas discussed changes in procedure and reporting have taken place from 2000-2025, based on discrepancies found during an earlier pilot study.

492196.title: Porting to NOAA Integrated Modeling Backbone for Unified Super Computing (NIMBUS): Transitioning Operational Ingestion and Dataflows to the Cloud Era
492196.authors: Margaret B Curtis, NWS, College Park, MD; and A. Myckow and D. Hood
492196.abstract: As numerical weather prediction (NWP) models grow increasingly sophisticated—demanding ever-larger volumes of inbound data and generating massive outputs—the operational bottleneck has shifted from raw compute capacity to data orchestration. Every day, operational frameworks must sort through hundreds of inbound connections and ingest millions of multi-source environmental observations. Transitioning these workflows to the cloud, however, requires navigating a complex web of legacy infrastructure. The NIMBUS- NOAA Integrated Modeling Backbone for Unified Super Computing- framework must ingest these massive data streams currently coming from a variety of critical legacy systems: Local Data Manager (LDM) feeds, multi-protocol mirror sites (FTP, SFTP, HTTP), and the traditional dbnet data-routing and sorting system. Safely migrating these flows into NIMBUS is not merely a matter of changing target servers, but of architecting a highly resilient hybrid bridge that optimizes data access for model runtimes without risking operational reliability. This presentation outlines the ongoing migration and modernization strategy for NIMBUS. We focus on how legacy protocols are sustained during the transition, and how the file-trigger-based routing of dbnet is being mapped to cloud based architecture. By decoupling legacy ingestion endpoints from cloud-native processing layers, we preserve operational continuity for downstream NWP models. Finally, we discuss how we are validating this architecture to ensure uninterrupted, high-volume data delivery and operational stability . Ultimately, modernizing this critical data highway accelerates the transition of research data into real-time operations (R2O), ensuring that the next generation of probabilistic and AI-driven weather guidance is fed by seamless, optimized, and highly reliable observing data streams.

492197.title: Development of A Far-Infrared Extension of the CAMEL V3 Land Surface Emissivity Climatology for Radiative Transfer Applications
492197.authors: Michelle Loveless, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and E. Borbas, R. Knuteson, and J. Hocking
492197.abstract: A far-infrared (FIR) extension of the CAMEL infrared land surface emissivity product is presented here and addresses the need for a global emissivity dataset in the FIR region for use in radiative transfer modeling, with applications such radiative balance, numerical weather prediction, and climate modeling studies. This first version of the CAMEL far infrared extension (FIRE) is based on the CAMEL Version 3 (V3) Climatology and was developed using the limited FIR emissivity measurements available at the time of production. For this first CAMEL FIRE version, the UW SSEC Absolute Radiance Interferometer (ARI) measurements were selected for use due to the limited availability of more comprehensive observational datasets and due to the authors’ familiarity with these data. These observation-based data are supplemented with model FIR emissivity from Huang et al. (2016). The FIR extension method was developed so that lab datasets could be easily updated to incorporate new FIR emissivity measurements and models as they become available from recent campaigns and other efforts in the scientific community. Continued development in this area will further improve the accuracy and applicability of FIR emissivity representations for radiative transfer modeling and related applications. This work supports the recent efforts of the NASA PREFIRE and ESA FORUM missions, and the CAMEL V3 Climatology FIRE module is planned to be released as part of RTTOV v14.

492198.title: Investigating NOx Variability in the San Joaquin Valley Using Long-Term Stationary Monitoring Data
492198.authors: Georges Saliba, California Air Resources Board, Sacramento, CA; and M. Amini, A. Carrazco, E. Yang, J. Schroeder, M. Jiang, and M. FitzGibbon
492198.abstract: California's San Joaquin Valley (SJV) remains in extreme nonattainment for ozone national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS) and serious for fine particulate matter (PM2.5) NAAQS. Nitrogen oxides (NOx) are key precursors to both ozone and PM2.5. Comparisons between satellite images and air quality modeling outputs over agricultural areas reveal a NO2 discrepancy over the SJV for certain months and years, and some studies suggest that agriculture and soil NOx emissions may be underrepresented in current emission inventories. Long-term U.S. EPA Air Quality System (AQS) monitoring data from 5 rural sites were used to characterize ambient NOx trends and variability across the SJV, and to test for an agricultural soil emission signature in measured ambient concentrations. Ambient NOx generally declined at all sites, but reductions slowed at rural sites after 2017. Furthermore, summertime (May-September) rural NOx ambient concentrations were similar to or higher than those measured in urban Fresno. Statistical analysis combined tracer correlations, principal component analysis, and multi-linear regression analysis to reveal that NOx variability is positively correlated with a combustion tracer in winter but with an agricultural tracer in summer. Leveraging long-term precipitation data also indicated post-rain enhancements in NO, N2O, and CO2 concentrations – but not CO – in a rural site during summer, consistent with soil pulses. These results may suggest agricultural contributions to ambient NOx though this study characterizes variability rather than absolute emissions. Sustained NOx flux measurements in the SJV would yield deeper insights into the pulse effect, helping to constrain the soil emission parameterizations in models. The measurements can also provide important information for evaluating NOx contributions from other emission sources.

492205.title: NSF Unidata AWIPS Update
492205.authors: Tiffany C. Meyer, UCAR/NSF Unidata, Norman, OK
492205.abstract: UCAR’s Unidata Program Center continues to modify and redistribute the National Weather Service’s AWIPS build for the general public, with a focus on helping the needs of the University community. Unidata provides a public facing AWIPS EDEX data server on the NSF-funded Jetstream2 cloud. This EDEX instance serves real-time data to CAVE clients and allows users to use the python-awips to access, analyze, and plot data. The distributed architectural concepts of AWIPS allow for the ability to scale EDEX in the cloud to account for the desired data feeds (and size). Currently, Unidata AWIPS CAVE is available for Redhat8-based Linux, Windows, and MacOS as well as a virtual machine. The Windows installer is also available to install at the admin level (for all users) which has come in handy for labs. The backend server, EDEX, is available on Redhat8-based Linux operating systems. Updates, new features, and bug fixes are continually being incorporated in sub-releases. Updates are also incorporated into python-awips which is available on all three operating systems. We currently have a number of training resources available. There are two online training modules: Learn AWIPS CAVE and Learn Python-AWIPS as well as the AWIPS Manual available to the public. Additionally, there are a number of example python notebooks to show how to access and plot different EDEX datatypes. Previous AWIPS Tips blogs are accessible here. As the NWS continues its AWIPS modernization efforts with the cloud-based CIRRUS and HIVE initiatives, the future direction of AWIPS and related applications is still evolving. Unidata will continue to monitor these efforts while maintaining the existing Unidata AWIPS to support the university community. We will also work with NOAA/NWS and the broader AWIPS community to identify the best path forward as the efforts progress.

492207.title: Understanding and Predicting Weather-Driven Transmission Congestion Under Current and Future Climate
492207.authors: Martha Vierra, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI; and J. A. Lee, T. Ennis, P. Hawbecker, and M. Craig
492207.abstract: Transmission congestion costs electricity grid operators and downstream customers over $20 billion annually, drives curtailment of renewable resources, and is directly tied to atmospheric conditions that increase system losses and shift demand patterns. Extreme weather plays an outsized role in congestion, as exemplified by Winter Storm Elliott’s $350 million in congestion costs for the Midcontinent Independent System Operator. While prior work has examined weather impacts on electricity prices, grid stress, and renewable-driven congestion, the link between large-scale atmospheric patterns and transmission congestion remains largely unexplored in the United States. We present a AI/ML framework that connects multiscale weather patterns to grid congestion, applied to the PJM Interconnection. Using hourly nodal congestion prices alongside ERA5 and CONUS404 reanalysis data, we first cluster synoptic patterns associated with congestion events using self-organizing maps (SOMs). Within each synoptic cluster, k-means clustering of the 4-km CONUS404 fields isolates the mesoscale features that determine whether a given synoptic pattern produces congestion. We then train a graph neural network (GNN) that infers latent connectivity among PJM pricing nodes, capturing the spatial structure of congestion propagation, to predict congestion regimes from these multiscale atmospheric drivers. Finally, applying the trained GNN to the CONUS404 pseudo-global-warming dataset, we project how congestion regimes within PJM may shift under warmer-climate analogs of historical weather. We present the identified congestion-linked weather patterns, GNN performance, and projected regime shifts, along with implications for prioritizing transmission buildout under a changing climate.

492209.title: Using the ERF GPU-Enabled Model to Simulate LES to Mesoscale Meteorology
492209.authors: Jerome Fast, PNNL, Richland, WA; and A. Almgren, D. Fytanidis, C. Kaul, A. Lattanzi, J. D. Mirocha, K. Pressel, R. K. Rai, A. Wang, J. Wang, A. Wise, G. Xia, and R. Krishnamurthy
492209.abstract: High performance computing architectures can dramatically increase atmospheric simulation throughput, permitting larger and higher resolution grid configurations and shorter simulation times. Atmospheric models, like the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, are typically used for operational forecasting and research studies but can be computationally expensive when ensemble runs and high spatiotemporal resolutions are required. The Department of Energy (DOE) is supporting development of the Energy Research and Forecasting (ERF) model, a new regional atmospheric model built on the AMReX software framework (Lattanzi et al. 2025). ERF is designed to run on GPUs and is envisioned as a next-generation alternative to WRF. Physics parameterizations in ERF have been ported to C++, although interfaces can be used to couple with Fortran-based parameterizations. ERF goes beyond WRF by enabling portability across computer architectures, generality in meshing strategies, and an anelastic option in addition to fully compressible equations. ERF is new, however, and must be evaluated over a range of real-world weather conditions using both large eddy simulation (LES) and mesoscale configurations. This study, part of the Observationally driven Resource Assessment with CoupLEd models (ORACLE) project, utilizes data from DOE-supported field studies to test and evaluate ERF. The work is focused on the myriad of weather phenomena impacting generation and transmission, including lightning strikes, heatwaves, cold snaps, nor’easters, high winds and strong wind shears, freezing rain, and flooding at several locations across the United States. Preliminary simulations, currently still underway, indicate that ERF can capture key boundary-layer and mesoscale structures across diverse environments, although biases remain in representing extreme events and complex terrain flows. We will also compare WRF and ERF simulations with observations, determine the computational performance for similar domain configurations, and identify potential pathways for model improvement. The project team maintains close contact with ERF developers, so that bugs or issues with the code can be addressed quickly. Reference Lattanzi, A., A. Almgren, E. Quon, M. Natarajan, B. Kosovic, J. Mirocha, B. Perry, D. Wiersema, D. Willcox, X. Yuan, and W. Zhang, 2025: ERF: Energy Research and Forecasting Model. Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems, 17, e2024MS004884, https://doi.org/10.1029/2024MS004884.

492210.title: Utilizing Local Wave Activity to Analyze Eddy Mean Flow Interaction across Flavors of Tropospheric Rossby Wave Breaking Events
492210.authors: Grant LaChat, United States Naval Academy, Annapolis, MD; and K. A. Bowley and M. Gervais
492210.abstract: Rossby wave breaking (RWB) is a dynamical process that has been connected to the generation of multiple, high impact sensible weather features like atmospheric rivers, strong extratropical cyclones, and atmospheric blocking. Wave breaking manifests as substantial deformation of the potential temperature (θ) field on constant potential vorticity (PV) surfaces which occurs when highly amplified Rossby waves encounter strong horizontal shear near the upper tropospheric jet stream. In prior work, the machine learning algorithm self-organizing maps (SOM) was implemented to identify a set of archetypal patterns, or “flavors”, of anticyclonic wave breaking (AWB) and cyclonic wave breaking (CWB) events in the European Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis v5 (ERA5) dataset during the period December, January, and February 1980 - 2014. In this work, we use the local wave activity (LWA) framework to assess eddy mean flow interaction across the RWB flavors. Composites of the LWA and LWA budget were constructed for all of the AWB and CWB flavors which revealed a subset of flavors that were characterized by the combination of: very large LWA accumulation and negative zonal wind anomalies. Additional analysis of the LWA budget across the RWB flavors revealed that the primary source of LWA differs between the AWB and CWB flavors. The primary source of LWA during AWB is from convergence of the LWA flux while the primary source of LWA during CWB is from diabatic heating. This is noteworthy because it implies that there are multiple pathways leading to the accumulation of large LWA between AWB and CWB events. Additionally, the primary sink of LWA also differed between the AWB and CWB flavors. The residual (i.e., represents nonconservative processes) acted as the primary sink of LWA during AWB while strong LWA flux divergence was the primary sink of LWA during CWB. These findings will be utilized for assessing the representation of RWB flavors and their eddy mean flow interaction in a global climate model (GCM).

492212.title: Reevaluating PBL Metrics in Hurricane Rapid Intensification Using Large Eddy Simulation and Airborne Remote Sensing
492212.authors: Ethan Andrew Bruce, Hampton University, Newport News, VA; and S. R. Guimond
492212.abstract: This work examines the structure of turbulence in rapidly intensifying hurricanes using a large eddy simulation and high-resolution observational data captured by NOAA’s Imaging Wind and Rain Airborne Profiler (IWRAP) radar system. Both datasets capture the hurricane rapid intensification process, which is driven by convective bursts occurring within the inner core of the hurricane. The simulation was conducted at 60-meter grid spacing with a high-order continuous Galerkin (spectral element) dynamic core coupled to observational latent heating estimates from a real rapid intensification case. Previous studies investigated hurricane PBL definitions using dropsondes from numerous research flights. These studies could not define the PBL locally due to the large data gaps between sondes, which required averaging the data in space, time and even across multiple storms. The datasets used in this study mitigate such inconsistencies by providing a complete set of fine-resolution turbulence-resolving data, and they allow for a cleaner implementation of PBL heights defined in previous studies. For instance, several local maximums of TKE are seen to occur below and above the observed PBL height, thus suggesting that standard PBL metrics may need to be revised. Moreover, analysis from the LES suggests these vertically-stretched TKE formations are primarily induced by perturbation vertical velocities tied to horizontal spiral bands propagating outward from the vortex. Wave diagnostics conducted thus far have ruled out the possibility of these bands being products of vortex Rossby waves. As this study progresses, findings from the LES will continue to be validated with IWRAP. A coarse resolution simulation is also studied to investigate the performance of PBL parameterizations in capturing the characteristics of turbulence, which is useful for operational models.

492214.title: Preliminary Data Analysis of the 2023 ecoDemonstrator Explorer SAF Emissions and Contrail Project
492214.authors: Rose Miller, The Boeing Company, Seattle, WA; and S. Baughcum, T. Rahmes, C. Tully, W. Griffin, R. H. Moore, R. Miake-Lye, C. Voigt, D. Sauer, R. Maerkl, R. Dischl, T. Braeuer, and G. Dalakos
492214.abstract: In October 2023 Boeing and NASA conducted a joint flight and ground experiment based out of Paine Field in Everett, Washington. This experiment measured the emissions and contrail properties of a Boeing 737-10 equipped with CFM LEAP-1B engines, utilizing the NASA DC-8 airborne laboratory as a chase aircraft. The experiment measured and evaluated particulate emissions and contrail properties of three distinct fuels from 11 flights and two ground tests. In-situ flight measurements on the DC-8 were typically conducted at distances ranging from 1 to 20 nautical miles behind and within a vertical range of ±100 feet of the 737-10 for both visible contrail and non-visible plume sampling. Atmospheric conditions ranged from ice supersaturation for persistent contrails to subsaturated temporary contrails to non-contrail conditions. The fuels tested included low sulfur Jet A, 100% paraffinic sustainable aviation fuel, and locally available Jet A. Significant efforts were made to minimize fuel mixing to avoid contamination with sulfur and/or aromatics across fuels. Preliminary data analyses from both the ground and in-flight measurements are presented. This includes measurements of total particles, non-volatile particles measured after passing through a 350°C thermal denuder, and ice particle concentration measured using a Cloud Aerosol Spectrometer (CAS), and contrasting the results for the different fuels. Differences in particulate matter across fuels were also captured by the NASA high-spectral-resolution lidar (HSRL) High Altitude Lidar Observatory (HALO) Water Vapor differential absorption lidar (DIAL) instrument, which sampled approximately 1,000-5,000 ft above the contrails made by the Boeing 737-10. Challenges of using instruments originally developed for particle measurements in clear air in the more complicated environment of an ice cloud, such as a contrail, will be discussed. This presentation will also review challenges related to logistics, fuel handling, and sampling in contrails, which highlights the complex interactions between atmospheric chemistry and microphysical processes in cloud formation and ice nucleation. Next steps will encompass future campaign needs, outstanding research questions, and novel measurement techniques.

492215.title: Enhancing Great Lakes Ice Modeling: Integration of CICE6 and the Unified Forecast System
492215.authors: Ayumi Fujisaki-Manome, NOAA/GLERL, Ann Arbor, MI; and D. Titze and J. Kessler
492215.abstract: The short-term prediction capability of coastal ice is critical for safe and efficient navigation, coastal facility management, and planning for winter recreations. In the North American Great Lakes (hereafter referred to as the Great Lakes), NOAA’s Great Lakes Operational Forecast System (GLOFS) provides nowcast and 5-day forecast guidance for 3-dimensional hydrodynamic conditions such as lake current, water temperature, and water level. The ice model, based on the unstructured grid version of Los Alamos Sea Ice Model (CICE) within the Finite Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM), is added to the experimental version of GLOFS to provide 3-day forecast guidance for ice conditions (e.g., ice concentration and thickness). This ice model was calibrated and extensively verified with available observations, and is based on an older version of CICE (version 3-4). In the next generation GLOFS development, the newer version of CICE column physics based on Icepack is tested within the Semi-implicit Cross-scale Hydroscience Integrated System Model (SCHISM). On the other hand, the latest version of CICE (version 6) is fully compliant with the Unified Forecast System (UFS) infrastructure based on the Earth System Modeling Framework (ESMF) and the National Unified Operational Prediction Capability (NUOPC) layer, providing the opportunities to examine the infrastructure capability of efficient coupling across the model components and future streamlined development. This work demonstrates the capability of the CICE6 and the UFS-Coastal infrastructure for applications to coastal ice predictions through testing for Great Lakes short-term ice predictions. In the previous presentations, we showed hindcast simulations using a standalone CICE6 configured for the Great Lakes at 1-km resolution, driven by surface hydrodynamic data from GLOFS and atmospheric forcing from the High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and ERA-5 reanalysis, as well as preliminary test simulations using UFS-Coastal. In this presentation, we show further experiment results of CICE6 coupled with SCHISM within the UFS-Coastal for the Great Lakes.

492218.title: Stratospheric Intrusions of Ozone Coincide with New Particle Formation Over the Northwest Atlantic
492218.authors: Brooke Gabrielle Beran, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and L. W. Siu, Y. Choi, J. P. DiGangi, G. S. Diskin, M. A. Shook, K. L. Thornhill, E. Winstead, L. Ziemba, and A. Sorooshian
492218.abstract: New particle formation (NPF) is a critical source of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and contributes appreciably to the total particle concentration budget in the free troposphere. Using airborne data from the Aerosol Cloud meTeorology Interactions oVer the western ATlantic Experiment (ACTIVATE) collected across multiple summer and winter seasons from 2020-2022, we find that 11 of 15 previously identified stratospheric intrusion cases (SI; i.e., the downward transport of air from the stratosphere to the troposphere) coincide with NPF events over the northwest Atlantic Ocean. Observations of higher ratios of particle concentrations greater than 3 versus 10 nm (N3:N10 > 1.3) and elevated absolute particle concentrations between 3 and 10 nm (N3-N10) coincide with flight maximum O3 associated with SIs. For ± 30-seconds from the flight maximum O3 for the 11 SI cases, average N3:N10 values range from 1.33-2.16, while N3-N10 values range from 116.7-2445.9 cm-3. Mean N3:N10 and N3-N10 values associated with SI cases are on average 13.3% and 92.6% greater than values observed in background air (± 10 minutes within SI and ± 50 meters within SI altitude) in over half of the SI-NPF cases, respectively. Additionally, SI-associated air masses with stronger NPF signatures generally descend from the tropopause closer in time to the point of sampling than air masses with weaker NPF signatures. This work shows the importance of SI as a driver of NPF in the troposphere, with implications for global aerosol-cloud interactions and CCN budgets.

492219.title: Toward Federated Agentic Workflows For Numerical Weather Prediction
492219.authors: Christopher W. Harrop, Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences, NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; and I. Jankov
492219.abstract: Advances in numerical weather prediction (NWP) capabilities have traditionally relied on performance gains from high-performance computing (HPC) procurement cycles. Existing workflow management systems can seamlessly leverage these hardware upgrades. However, this traditional model is no longer sustainable as single-thread performance gains slow, cloud-based architectures go mainstream, and forecasting application components shift from classic HPC toward AI/ML paradigms. Tackling modern grand challenge problems requires diverse workflows and computational resources beyond the scale of a single site, making multi-site federation essential. To bridge this capability gap, we are developing Chiltepin—a workflow middleware designed specifically for federated NWP systems. This presentation details our progress with Chiltepin, focusing on new capabilities to enable agentic workflows and the integration of large language models (LLMs).

492223.title: Catching Marine Fog: Integrating Earth System Science Research and Education on Alaskan Cruises
492223.abstract: Cruise ships serve as a unique platform for Earth system science (ESS) research and education, combining access to remote sampling locations and sustained engagement with passengers. This presentation will share how a collaborative partnership between the U.S. National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) and HX Expeditions integrated novel marine fog research with ESS engagement activities for Alaska expedition cruise passengers. During the summer of 2026, NSF NCAR scientists installed instrumentation to quantify and characterize aerosols in the Alaska coastal environment. Alongside this research, we implemented a variety of passenger engagement activities designed to enhance public understanding of ESS. These activities included 1) a traveling exhibit on building resilience to weather hazards, which encouraged guests to reflect on meaningful actions for environmental protection, 2) citizen science initiatives, where passengers actively participated in weather observation and data collection using mobile technology, and 3) scientist-led educational presentations and workshops that translated complex research findings into accessible narratives and engaged passengers in interactive discussions and “doing science”. Together, these strategies fostered a deeper connection between passengers and active research on board. We will discuss the effectiveness across the different engagement activities, and strategies for sustaining engagement across a full sailing. More broadly, this partnership offers an innovative model for how research institutions and tourism can create meaningful bridges between science and public audiences.

492226.title: Observation Validation for NOAA's Rapid Refresh Forecast System Transition from FV3-GSI to FV3-JEDI
492226.authors: Donald E. Lippi, Lynker@NWS/OMD, Riverdale Park, MD; and X. Zhang, S. Liu, S. K. Degelia, K. C. Eure, S. Pan, G. Ge, T. Lei, H. liu, D. Holdaway, D. T. Kleist, and M. Hu
492226.abstract: The data assimilation (DA) framework of the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) is being modernized from FV3-GSI to FV3-JEDI, which uses the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) system. The FV3-JEDI capability provides an important intermediate step toward the planned RRFSv2 transition to MPAS-JEDI. An important part of this transition is demonstrating that FV3-JEDI can assimilate conventional and satellite radiance observations in a way that is consistent with the current FV3-GSI system. The focus of this work is validating observation processing in FV3-JEDI for RRFS. Key aspects of GSI observation handling, including quality control (QC), observation errors, and forward-operator behavior, were translated into FV3-JEDI configurations. Validation was performed in phases, moving from controlled observation-operator and QC tests to full workflow cycling experiments. Results focus on cycling experiments using comparable FV3-GSI and FV3-JEDI workflow configurations. For selected cycles, FV3-GSI and FV3-JEDI are compared using the same background fields to evaluate agreement between the two systems and identify remaining differences. This validation supports technical modernization of RRFS DA and helps prepare JEDI-based capabilities for future operational use.

492240.title: Incorporating Physically Informative Predictors into Generative AI for Global Aerosol Downscaling
492240.authors: Meng Huang, PNNL, Richland, WA; and A. Geiss, M. Christensen, A. Varble, PhD, and P. L. Ma
492240.abstract: Satellite instruments provide aerosol optical depth (AOD) retrievals at kilometer-scale resolution, but their spatial and temporal coverage is incomplete, particularly under cloudy conditions. In contrast, global aerosol reanalysis and model products provide continuous AOD fields but at resolutions too coarse to represent features important for understanding aerosol-cloud interactions. We develop an artificial intelligence framework that learns fine-scale information from satellite observations and combines coarse-resolution AOD with aerosol-controlling predictors, such as meteorology, cloud, and precipitation. The framework is ultimately intended to downscale coarse-resolution reanalysis and model products, thereby supporting process-level investigation of aerosol-cloud interactions. For initial model development and evaluation, we use the MODIS Level 2 AOD_550_Dark_Target_Deep_Blue_Combined product for 2007–2011, gridded at 1° and 0.1° spatial resolutions. Candidate predictors are objectively selected using correlation, mutual information, and U-Net ablation experiments. In these experiments, input variable(s) are systematically removed to quantify their contributions to model performance. This approach identifies predictors that are most useful for representing processes associated with aerosol transport, boundary-layer mixing, hygroscopic growth, cloud processing, and wet scavenging, while minimizing redundant model inputs. Preliminary results show that the selected predictors enable a deterministic U-Net to recover more spatial variability than downscaling from coarse AOD alone. However, the reconstructed fields remain smoother than the reference data and miss some localized aerosol structures. To address this limitation, we extend the framework with a conditional denoising diffusion model that generates ensembles of plausible fine-resolution AOD fields conditioned on the same coarse-resolution AOD and atmospheric predictors. The U-Net and diffusion models will be compared within a common evaluation framework covering prediction accuracy, high-AOD events, spatial structure, coarse-scale consistency, and uncertainty. This integrated predictor-selection and generative-modeling framework will evaluate whether conditional diffusion can produce more realistic fine-resolution AOD fields and provide process-level insights into relationships among aerosols, clouds, and precipitation.

492249.title: Surface Heat Fluxes Across the Gulf Stream Observed with Concurrent Shipboard Measurements
492249.authors: Nathan Moore, University of Utah Atmospheric Sciences, Salt Lake City, UT; AOML, Miami, FL; and S. Dong, M. Goes, and M. Andres
492249.abstract: The exchange of heat, freshwater, and momentum across the air-sea interface is critical for modulating weather and climate. In the North Atlantic, the Gulf Stream plays a key role in regulating regional weather patterns by transporting thermal energy poleward. To address a shortage of direct high-resolution observations, a targeted initiative was launched in 2024 under the eXpendable BathyThermograph (XBT) project to collect concurrent meteorological variables and upper ocean temperature profiles along fixed transects across the Gulf Stream. The goal of this study is to analyze these observed variables (2-m air temperature (T2m), sea-surface temperature (SST), relative humidity (RH), and mean sea-level pressure (MSLP)) over 16 cruises from Florida to Puerto Rico, compare them with ERA5 and CFSv2 reanalysis products, and evaluate their respective latent and sensible heat fluxes. While both reanalysis variables show strong correlations (≥0.95) with observations, RH correlations are somewhat lower (0.85 for ERA5 and 0.79 for CFSv2). Transitioning from the coast to the Gulf Stream core (~80°W), SST increases rapidly, generating a strong positive ocean–air temperature gradient alongside a marked drop in relative humidity. However, both ERA5 and CFSv2 smooth this intense transition, underestimating the peak SST over the jet while overestimating relative humidity across the domain. Consequently, both reanalyses undercalculate the severe sensible and latent heat exchange occurring at the Gulf Stream front. Case studies highlight two extreme air–sea interaction events: a late dry-season event in June 2024 (Cruise 1) that drove intense latent heat fluxes via dry, northeasterly flow, and an arctic cold-air outbreak in January 2025 (Cruise 9) with air–sea temperature differences reaching 15°C, resulting intense sensible and latent fluxes. These systematic biases show that ERA5 and CFSv2 smooth thermal fronts and reduce coastal variability, underestimating turbulent air–sea heat fluxes during extreme events. This vulnerability in current reanalyses and models can distort regional heat budgets and storm intensity forecasts.

492250.title: Examining the Shift in Large-Scale Biases and RMSE: From GFSv16 to the Fully Coupled GFSv17
492250.authors: Lydia Stefanova, NOAA/NWS/Office of Modeling and Development, College Park, MD; NOAA/NWS/Office of Modeling and Development, Riverdale Park, MD; and A. M. Bentley, N. Barton, D. S. Dukhovskoy, X. Luo, J. Meixner, R. Sun, and C. A. Thomas
492250.abstract: The transition to GFSv17 marks a significant evolution in NOAA’s global modeling, moving from the uncoupled ocean and prescribed sea-ice framework of GFSv16 toward a fully integrated Earth system. This updated system dynamically links the atmospheric model, operating at a higher 9km resolution with CCPP physics and Noah-MP, with active ocean (MOM6), sea ice (CICE6), and wave (WAVEWATCH III) components connected via the CMEPS mediator. As GFSv17 nears operational implementation, characterizing how these extensive physics updates and multi-component coupling have altered systematic error profiles is essential. This study compares the large-scale biases and Root Mean Square Errors (RMSE) of both versions, evaluating global forecast performance across multiple seasons. We present a seasonal analysis of errors in key variables to identify where long-standing biases have been mitigated and how total error magnitudes have evolved. Initial evaluations of seasonally aggregated forecasts demonstrate an overall reduction in RMSE and large-scale biases over most areas. By analyzing spatial and temporal patterns, we associate these forecast improvements with specific changes in model parameterizations and newly integrated feedback loops. Furthermore, we provide a diagnostic attribution for remaining system challenges and emergent regional errors. We evaluate seasonal performance extremes, including polar sea ice state and localized surface temperature biases, linking them to underlying physical drivers such as radiative fluxes and albedo feedbacks. These findings offer a practical assessment of the GFSv17 error climate and provide a baseline for ongoing tuning and development within the UFS framework.

492251.title: Exploring Uncertainty in Climate-Driven Electricity Demand Forecasts in California
492251.authors: Minda Monteagudo, LLNL, Livermore, CA; and S. Po-Chedley, J. C. Golaz, and J. P. Watson
492251.abstract: Power system planning studies such as capacity expansion require hourly load timeseries as input, for planning horizons 20-30 years from present. Load variability is largely driven by diurnal, day-to-day, and seasonal temperature fluctuations, with previous work showing that temperature alone is a good predictor of hourly demand in California. In this study we combine hourly temperature timeseries from the NOAA High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model with the mid-century warming signal derived from the ensemble mean of individual CMIP6 models. The resulting timeseries retain the observed high-frequency variability (weather) from individual HRRR years, with the addition of model and emissions scenario-specific warming trends, satisfying the need for both high temporal resolution (hourly) and far-term (mid-century) data. We use these different realizations of mid-century temperature to drive a temperature-dependent electricity load model to create a suite of possible demand forecasts for California. From this dataset, we explore the contributions of model, emissions scenario and historical weather year variability to the uncertainty in load forecasting for the mid-century. Prepared by LLNL under Contract DE-AC52-07NA27344 and supported by the LLNL-LDRD Program under Project No. 25-SI-007.

492256.title: Improving Polarimetric Radar Quantitative Precipitation Estimation Using Process-Oriented Vertical Profile (POVP) Guided 3D Analysis
492256.authors: Jiaxi Hu, University at Albany, Albany, NY; and A. V. Ryzhkov and P. Zhang
492256.abstract: Accurate quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) from polarimetric radar remains challenging due to the spatial variability of rain microphysics, drop size distributions (DSD), and precipitation type along the radar beam. Conventional QPE algorithms, including R(A) and R(KDP) relations, rely primarily on 1D (nearest-point) radar observations and fail to capture the three-dimensional microphysical evolution of precipitation systems. Recent refinements to the R(A) methodology have shown that incorporating temperature-dependent specific attenuation and a spatially variable α can reduce QPE bias, and new R(KDP) formulations now incorporate limited 2D information—yet substantial room for improvement remains. Building on these advances, this study introduces a novel QPE framework that leverages the Process-Oriented Vertical Profile (POVP) technique to integrate three-dimensional polarimetric radar data into precipitation estimation. By systematically extracting vertical profiles of reflectivity, differential reflectivity, specific differential phase, and cross-correlation coefficient within storm cores, the POVP-guided QPE approach enables real-time classification of warm- versus cold-rain contributions and optimization of rain-rate relations across the full column depth below the melting layer. Preliminary results using WSR-88D observations from multiple storm events demonstrate significant bias reduction and improved correlation with rain gauge networks compared to existing QPE methods.

492258.title: Toward Generalizable Bias Correction of Satellite Aerosol Optical Depth: Machine Learning Applied to VIIRS Dark Target Retrievals
492258.authors: Nora Wang, River Hill High School, Clarksville, MD; and Y. R. Shi and R. C. Levy
492258.abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites provide essential high-resolution measurements of global aerosols with global coverage that can be used for air quality monitoring and accurate atmospheric modeling. Machine Learning (ML) models have been used to bias-correct satellite retrieval products due to their ability to resolve nonlinear relations between product uncertainties, observational conditions, and diagnostic parameters. However, variance in environmental conditions, both spatially and temporally, demands that ML models become more generalizable and robust before they can be widely adopted in generating bias-corrected satellite products. In this study, we apply ML to a dataset that represents global collocations of aerosol optical depth (AOD) as observed from ground-based Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET) and retrieved from the Visible Infrared Imaging suite (VIIRS) aboard the Suomi-NPP satellite. Specifically, we assess uncertainties of the products (AOD at 554 nm) derived from the Dark Target retrieval algorithm between 2018 to 2021, and attempt to generate an unbiased AOD product. We use spatial-temporal cross validation to ensure the effectiveness and representativeness of the ML model by dividing AERONET ground stations and multiple years of data into distinctive spatial temporal folds, with the 60% of data given to the training split, 20% to the validation split, and 20% to the testing split. Our input features include satellite-retrieved AOD, viewing geometry, observed reflectances in different spectral channels, cloud condition, day of year, and topographic altitude. We choose to use an XGboost architecture as the ML algorithm due to its ability to capture complex, nonlinear relationships and interactions between variables from tabular data. The model set up is finalized using both the feature importance selection and hyperparameterization. Our preliminary results from baseline XGboost architecture shows consistent ability to correct DT VIIRS products closer towards the ground-truth AOD measurements at 554 nm across training, validation, and testing splits. The model performs the best at low-to-moderate AOD range (AOD ～0 to 1.0). Because not all input variables contribute substantially to model performance, we are identifying key predictive inputs. Further improving our understanding of retrieval production bias-correction, alongside XGboost we are exploring utilizing additional ML methods to model increasingly complex nonlinear relationships between variable inputs, spatial grids, and temporal sequences.

492259.title: Combined Influence of the Madden-Julian Oscillation and Convectively-Coupled Kelvin Waves on Asian Summer Monsoon Rainfall Onset
492259.authors: Sadiksha Rai, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and N. Sakaeda
492259.abstract: The Asian Summer Monsoon (ASM) produces substantial annual rainfall across South and Southeast Asia, yet the timing and evolution of local rainfall onset remain difficult to represent accurately in climate models. While the influences of the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) and other large-scale climate modes on ASM variability have been extensively studied, the combined influence of the MJO and Convectively Coupled Kelvin Waves (CCKW) during local rainfall onset remains less understood. This study investigates the combined influence of the MJO and CCKW on ASM rainfall onset using IMERG precipitation and MERRA-2 reanalysis. Local MJO and CCKW activity is identified from reconstructed precipitation fields, and their relationships with rainfall, low-level circulation, and moisture evolution are examined relative to the onset date. Results reveal distinct regional differences across the ASM domain. Over the southern South China Sea, Bay of Bengal, and Arabian Sea, rainfall onset occurs more frequently under active MJO conditions, while CCKW activity becomes increasingly prevalent after onset. MJO- and CCKW-associated rainfall contributions are also more evident over these oceanic regions than over much of the continental ASM region. Despite these rainfall contributions, constructive interference of MJO- and CCKW-associated low-level winds with the monsoonal flow primarily develops after rainfall onset and varies considerably among regions. Thus, the strengthening of characteristic monsoonal flow does not appear to provide a systematic dynamical precursor to local rainfall onset. Taken together, these results indicate that the combined MJO-CCKW influence on onset-related rainfall is spatially heterogeneous, with stronger associations over selected oceanic regions and comparatively limited influence elsewhere across the ASM domain.

492261.title: Impacts of Assimilating Novel High-Density Surface Pressure Observations in the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS)
492261.authors: Jason M. English, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and E. P. James, M. Hu, C. F. Mass, J. Baars, R. Steed, G. Pratt, and T. T. Ladwig
492261.abstract: High density pressure observations may help resolve important mesoscale weather features particularly in data sparse regions. We explore assimilation of surface pressure observations from several sources (PurpleAir, Tempest, and/or IBM Smartphone obs) in the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS), which is a convection-allowing (3-km grid spacing) ensemble-based data assimilation and forecasting system. We compare forecasts from retrospective simulations with and without the high density surface pressure observations in the data assimilation to available verification datasets, including the implementation of a new surface pressure verification dataset. We explore short-term evolution of the lower atmosphere in the RRFS model in response to the added surface pressure observations to the data assimilation system.

492262.title: Clearing the Air: The Impact of Air Quality on Student Success, A Proposed Study
492262.authors: Rebekah Rose Hackett, NCAS, Baltimore , MD
492262.abstract: Air pollution is a significant contributor to climate change and continues to disproportionately affect urban areas where air quality is often substandard due to their proximity to industrial zones. This leads to the emission of pollutants such as carbon dioxide (CO2), often linked to respiratory and cardiovascular diseases (i.e. asthma, stroke, chest pain, shortness of breath, etc.), increased heat, asbestos, mold, and other harmful substances. Urban schools, often with limited resources compared to suburban schools, are vulnerable to the effect of poor air quality. Students in these settings may experience decreased concentration, fatigue, absences, and impaired cognitive development. This study aims to examine the impact of air quality on student academic achievement in urban schools. The study emphasizes the need for improved air quality monitoring for schools in urban settings, the implementation of air filtration systems, and policies to reduce pollution to foster a more productive learning environment. Addressing these environmental concerns is crucial for improving academic performance and awareness to society and climate.

492264.title: Supporting GFDL Climate Model Workflows through an Ecosystem of Earth-System Modeling Tools and YAML Configurations
492264.authors: Dana Singh, SAIC, Flemington, NJ; and C. Blanton, I. Laflotte, C. Brown, A. Kiihne, T. E. Robinson Jr., M. K. Lee, R. Mulhall, L. Chilutti, C. Whitlock, K. E. Rand, J. Lentz, U. Ramirez, and B. Chang
492264.abstract: The Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Lab (GFDL) of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) strives to understand the Earth’s climate through high resolution computer models. These models are tested for reproducibility, run, post-processed, and analyzed using tools created in the Flexible Model System (FMS) Runtime Environment (FRE). Built upon an original set of Perl and shell scripts, FRE Bronx, encompasses one monolithic workflow. While FRE Bronx functions well, its original design was to facilitate a very specific production workflow within on-premise HPC systems. As a result, it functions as a “black box” with little configurability and has proven difficult to adapt the various phases to the needs of developers. In order to make NOAA GFDL models more user-friendly and easier to develop, the next generation of FRE is being rewritten with the foundations of portability, flexibility, and simplicity through three core components: a pythonic and modular toolset, YAML configurations to define parameters, and workflow configurations to orchestrate the tools. The new pythonic toolset deconstructs the functionality of the monolithic tools into a “tool subtool” structure through a re-envisioned user interface called FRE-cli. Reforming the FRE tools with python allows for a modernization of code and increases maintainability and extensibility. FRE then leverages user-defined YAML configurations to encapsulate GFDL model parameters, compilation information, and experiment-specific components. To align with the modularity design of FRE, these YAML files are broken down into distinct configurations to cover specific segments of an end-to-end workflow. Furthermore, in order to ensure they are compatible in the FRE ecosystem, JSON schema files are used to validate the configuration. Finally, to orchestrate and run a coherent workflow, FRE utilizes Cylc, a workflow engine and scheduler. The Cylc workflow engine was chosen for its distributed, scalable, and flexible nature, and provides a powerful user interface. Driven by information from the YAML configuration, the workflow configuration defines a task dependency graph that leverages the FRE-cli toolset. With tasks mapped, the workflow creates batch jobs for each task which are then submitted to run in a comprehensible fashion. Now that the core framework has been established, FRE is flexible to meet the needs of individual developers and can be extended to support additional workflows.

492268.title: Making Flood Risk Clear: Enhancing the Usability of Probabilistic Flood Inundation Maps
492268.authors: Snigdha Nautiyal, University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN; and A. Joshi, S. Kandel, A. J. Jefferson, A. Stumpf, J. L. Follum, M. Follum, D. Giardino, and M. A. Kenney
492268.abstract: More frequent and intense flood events in the United States over recent decades have prompted increased use of flood forecasting decision-support tools such as NOAA’s deterministic Flood Inundation Maps (FIMs) that communicate high-resolution and location-specific flood information to users. Advances in computation and ensemble modeling are now leading to increasing integration of probabilistic forecast information into public-facing tools so that users can be further empowered to take timely and well-informed decisions. However, visual communication of probabilistic FIMs remains a big challenge since representing and accurately interpreting probabilities is notoriously difficult and places a huge cognitive load on users.. Thus, it becomes imperative to understand how best to visually represent probabilistic information to users through FIM products designed to be intuitive and clearly facilitate decision-making. The goal of this project is to test how design elements such as color scales, legend design, and information layering influence the usability and understandability of probabilistic multi-model FIM visualizations. The project applies a mixed-methods approach in two phases. In the first phase, semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted with FIM producers who are developing models for visualizing, comparing, and communicating probabilistic FIM results. The interviews built a common vocabulary around key technical terms such as ‘multimodel’ ‘ensemble’ and ‘probabilistic’ that are central to interpreting probabilistic communication to users. The interviews also illuminated goals and challenges producers see in user interpretation of the uncertainty underlying their models, such as thinking about how many ensembles should feed into the probabilistic FIMs. In the second phase of this project, we are conducting a public-facing survey and A/B testing of alternative graphic prototypes based on the challenges recognized above combined with design considerations and evidence-based best practices for effective probabilistic communication. Results will identify design choices that improve accurate interpretation and efficient use of probabilistic information, providing operational insights for the design and effective deployment of NOAA’s probabilistic FIMs. Overall, this research supports the effective translation of flood-forecast decision-support tools that help users better manage flood risk and make timely, life-saving decisions.

492271.title: What WAS That?
492271.authors: Walter A. Lyons, FMA Research, Fort Collins, CO
492271.abstract: Here's a chance to test your skills at identifying TLEs - transient luminous events. We present rapid fire videos of some of the glowing creatures that reside in the mesopheric zoo. Can you name them all?

492272.title: NOAA’s Surge and Tide Operational Forecast System (STOFS) and S-104 Water Levels/S-111 Surface Currents Navigation Products
492272.authors: Greg Seroka, NOAA, NOS, OCS, Silver Spring, MD; and Y. Funakoshi, Z. Yang, L. Shi, A. Kluge, T. Thompson, S. Mani, A. Alipour, M. A. Jisan, F. Cassalho, F. Daneshvar, C. George, S. Moghimi, M. Rostaminia, L. Tang, E. Myers, C. Allen, A. Tejaswi, A. R. Cerrone, J. Westerink, F. Ye, H. C. Yu, H. Yoo, Y. J. Zhang, C. Seaton, and M. Swirsky
492272.abstract: NOAA’s National Ocean Service (NOS) has leveraged a close partnership with the National Weather Service (NWS) and the academic community for over 15 years to lead the research-to-operations (R2O) of the Surge and Tide Operational Forecast System (STOFS). NOAA STOFS provides operational model nowcast (analyses of near present conditions) and forecast guidance of water levels, water currents, water temperature, and salinity for coastal resilience, marine navigation, and other end users across the globe. STOFS includes a global 2D depth-averaged component [with ADvanced CIRCulation (ADCIRC) core, STOFS-2D-Global], a 3D component for the U.S. East Coast, Gulf of America, and Caribbean [with Semi-implicit Cross-scale Hydroscience Integrated System Model (SCHISM) core, STOFS-3D-Atlantic], and a new 3D component added in 2026 for a vast portion of the Pacific, from the Bering Strait to 33°S latitude [with SCHISM core, STOFS-3D-Pacific]. Efforts are underway to develop STOFS-3D-Alaska, an ocean-sea ice-wave coupled system using the Unified Forecast System Coastal coupling infrastructure (UFS Coastal). One of the most important end user applications of STOFS is to support marine navigation by dynamically updating Electronic Navigation Charts (ENCs), which provide real-time ship positioning, as well as collision and grounding avoidance. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has mandated a transition from International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) S-57 to S-100 chart standards. This transition is voluntary in 2026, but mandatory in 2029 for new builds of Electronic Chart Display & Information Systems (ECDIS). In this transition to S-100, new S-101 ENCs will integrate high-resolution bathymetry (S-102), real-time/forecast water levels (S-104), gridded forecast surface currents (S-111), and in the future sea ice (S-411) and weather/wave warnings (S-412). The enhanced ENC will have dynamically adjusted charted depths and safety contours (S-102, S-104) and overlaid gridded surface current velocity vectors (S-111) for better ship route planning (e.g. fuel efficiency) and maneuvering (e.g. hazard avoidance). In this presentation we will describe the different components of STOFS, and then detail NOAA’s development of S-104 and S-111 products sourced from STOFS.

492275.title: From Science to Human Outcomes - Designing the Systems Between Knowledge and Action (Core Science Keynote)
492275.authors: Christian B. Rathke, National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS), Silver Spring, MD; Captain, U.S. Public Health Service, Silver Spring, MD; Director, Total Worker Health (TWH), Silver Spring, MD
492275.abstract: Meteorological and environmental science have become increasingly sophisticated at observing, modeling, and anticipating hazards. Yet human outcomes are shaped not by hazards alone, but by the conditions in which people live, work, make decisions, and act. Drawing on public health, occupational health, work design, human factors, and systems thinking, this keynote explores what happens between scientific knowledge and human outcomes. It examines how exposure, vulnerability, communication, organizational conditions, and capacity can determine whether accurate science becomes protective action. Rather than asking every discipline to solve the entire problem, the presentation considers how we can better connect specialized expertise across scientific, health, organizational, and community systems. The challenge is not to reduce scientific depth, but to design stronger connections between what we know and what people are actually able to do.

492276.title: Evaluating the Implementation of GOCART2G Aerosols in the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS)
492276.authors: Rajesh Kumar, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and F. Lacey, S. W. Wei, M. W. Wong, J. Park, M. C. Barth, S. Ha, G. Pfister, J. Pereira, and M. Duda
492276.abstract: The MPAS-GOCART2G model has been developed as part of the NSF NCAR’s vision to move towards a unified modeling framework. The GOCART2G module adds 30 new scalars to represent seven tropospheric aerosol species and their precursors. Major aerosol species represented by GOCART2G include black carbon (BC), brown carbon (BrC), organic carbon (OC, both primary and secondary), sulfate, nitrate, dust, and sea-salt.
