This new capability will soon be released to the community. Here, we present the implementation of GOCART2G aerosols in the MPAS-A modeling system along with a comprehensive global evaluation of this modeling system using a 60 km global uniform mesh simulation for 15 October to 30 November 2024. Specifically, we will showcase atmospheric spin-up dynamics, global mass budgets, aerosol optical depth (AOD), and deposition pathways across primary (mineral dust, sea salt, carbonaceous) and secondary inorganic (sulfate, nitrate, and ammonium) aerosols. To assess the impact of analysis nudging on aerosol simulations, we evaluate a suite of numerical experiments comparing a free-running baseline against analysis nudging of dynamics and thermodynamics (UVT) and full state variables (UVTQ). UVT-nudging preserves internal cloud microphysical consistency while constraining wind-driven emissions and synoptic transport, while nudging water vapor (Q) alters the hydrological balance, impacting local precipitation fields and wet scavenging rates. The model captures many important features of the global distribution of AOD, Angstrom Exponent, meteorological parameters, and surface fine particulate matter. Process analysis shows that the removal of submicron secondary inorganic aerosols is governed by wet scavenging, whereas mineral dust is dominated by dry gravitational sedimentation.

492279.title: Coupled Pathways from Large-Scale Climate Variability to Antarctic Ice-Shelf Melt in a Southern Ocean–Refined E3SMv3 Ensemble
492279.authors: Carolyn Branecky Begeman, LANL, Santa Fe, NM; LANL, Los Alamos, NM; and D. Comeau, A. F. Roberts, X. Asay-Davis, J. Wolfe, S. Zhang, W. Lin, S. Price, C. Zender, E. E. Thomas, and M. Hoffman
492279.abstract: Large-scale modes of climate variability can reorganize atmospheric circulation, sea ice, and ocean heat transport around Antarctica, creating pathways by which remote climate anomalies influence ice-shelf basal melt. Here, we use a 15-member ensemble of the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 3 (E3SMv3) to quantify how seasonal-to-interannual climate variability propagates through the coupled Southern Ocean–sea ice–ice shelf system. Our global, fully coupled configuration includes enhanced ocean and sea-ice resolution throughout the Southern Ocean and within thermodynamically active ice-shelf cavities, together with data-driven iceberg fluxes. Following spin-up under repeating 2010 forcing, ensemble members branch into transient simulations spanning 2010–2050. We combine statistical and spectral analyses with a multi-view Transformer architecture to characterize contemporaneous and lagged relationships in the ensemble among El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Southern Annular Mode (SAM), sea-ice concentration, continental-shelf ocean heat content, and ice-shelf basal melt. By connecting remote climate variability to coupled polar processes in an Earth system model with explicit ice-shelf cavities, this work advances understanding of how internal climate variability is communicated to the Antarctic margins and shapes near-term variability in ice-shelf melt.

492283.title: Tropopause-Overshooting Convection in Tropical Cyclones in 1-minute GOES Imagery
492283.authors: B. Ryland McClure, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and C. R. Homeyer and K. M. Bedka
492283.abstract: The sensitivity of Earth’s radiative equilibrium to changes in trace greenhouse gases including water vapor has inspired interest in processes through which stratosphere-troposphere exchange (STE) occurs and modifies stratospheric composition. Tropical cyclones (TCs) have been suggested as disproportionate contributors to STE in the tropics and have been shown to be associated with increased stratospheric water vapor content; recent simulations have shown overshooting convection to be the dominant process by which troposphere-to-stratosphere transport of water vapor occurs in TCs. However, the few case studies that have been performed have produced disagreements such as in the primary location of overshooting convection within the TC eyewall or outer rainbands. Additionally, the limitations of available instruments have posed obstacles to the inspection of the characteristics of overshooting convection in tropical cyclones in observations. This study used automated detection and tracking of overshooting cloud tops (OT) in high resolution visible and IR imagery of North Atlantic basin tropical cyclones obtained by the Mesoscale Domain Sectors of the GOES-R series of geostationary satellites during 2019–2024 to examine the relationship between the occurrence and properties of overshooting convection and TC intensity, rate of TC intensification, distance from TC center, and environmental vertical wind shear (VWS). TC center positions were interpolated from HURDAT and deep-layer VWS was obtained from ERA5 reanalysis. Preliminary results showed that the majority of overshooting convection in tropical cyclones occurred within the eyewall, primarily in the downshear-left quadrant. Eyewall OT (defined as OT within 100 km of the TC center) occurrence was greatly increased during periods of intensification and decreased during periods of weakening; however, eyewall OT detection was maximized in weak hurricanes and was decreased in major hurricanes below the level of OT observed in tropical depressions and storms. Total OT detection was similar for the regions within 100 km of the TC center and 100–500 km from TC center in tropical depressions, tropical storms, and TCs experiencing strong VWS. The relationship between OT and TC intensity and intensification rate may warrant study of whether observed or predicted trends in tropical cyclone intensity and intensification rates could influence the occurrence of STE in the tropics; this association might also indicate that automated detection of OT could be useful as an additional remote proxy of TC intensification rate.

492284.title: Peering Beyond the Storm: Emergency Manager Decision-Making During Severe Weather
492284.authors: Donald Long Jr., NOAA Center for Atmospheric Sciences and Meteorology, Beltsville, MD
492284.abstract: Emergency managers are the essential link between meteorologists and the public during inclement weather. They must understand and relay large amounts of complex information in a non-standardized field. Previous researchers derived emergency manager decision-making models for various inclement weather conditions to better understand this complexity. Baumgart et al. (2008) developed one of the most recent models for severe weather event application. They sought to improve an emergency manager training program in Oklahoma called OK-FIRST by developing a categorical decision-making model based on a simulated severe thunderstorm event. This research investigated how well the Baumgart et al. (2008) model could represent a real, non-simulated tornado event using emergency managers’ decisions made during the December 10th-11th, 2021, Ohio River Valley tornado outbreak. Thematic analysis was employed to code 16 transcripts using NVivo version 1.7.1. The sample consisted of 10 emergency managers, two fire chiefs performing the duties of emergency managers, and four National Weather Service Weather Forecast Office managers. Participants were interviewed in early 2022 by the National Severe Storms Laboratory and the Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations. Deductive and inductive analyses of emergency managers' decisions during the event revealed that while the model framework can represent a real tornado event, further research is needed to incorporate preparedness and interpersonal relationships into the model. These factors were the most salient for emergency managers when making decisions.

492286.title: Quantifying the Influence of Diabatic Heating Processes on Atmospheric Blocking Characteristics and Climatology
492286.authors: Jacob Lee Fields, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
492286.abstract: Atmospheric blocking is a phenomenon in which upper-level atmospheric flow becomes quasi-stationary for an extended period (i.e., several days to weeks). When a blocking pattern develops, nearby weather patterns become essentially locked in place, inducing severely impactful weather events in the mid-latitudes (e.g., droughts, heatwaves, and flooding). While the existence and impacts of blocking have been long recognized, the physical factors responsible for blocking formation and maintenance are not well understood, presenting a challenge for the development of accurate long-range weather forecasts. Recent studies have identified diabatic heating processes as an important influence on the blocking lifecycle, especially initial onset. Despite this, quantitative assessment of the impacts of these processes on block characteristics and climatology remains lacking. We hypothesize that diabatic heating has a measurable effect on blocking frequency and distribution, as well as characteristics such as duration and intensity. We use ERA5 reanalysis data for block identification and diabatic heating analysis. Blocks are identified via a detection algorithm utilizing meridional gradients of 500hPa geopotential height, creating a repository of blocking events in the Northern Hemisphere from 1950-2024. To quantify diabatic heating, mid-tropospheric diabatic heating rates are calculated as residuals from the atmospheric thermodynamic energy equation. Lag compositing (including centered composites) and regression analysis is used to examine the influence of diabatic heating processes on blocking. Results show statistically significant correlations between diabatic heating and the intensity, duration, and spatial area of Northern Hemisphere blocking events. These correlations are shown to vary between season and geographical region. Additionally, the characteristics of different blocked flow patterns (i.e., ridge vs. dipole blocks) are affected differently by diabatic heating processes. These results contribute to an improved understanding of the dynamical factors responsible for blocking formation and maintenance, potentially providing an enhanced source of predictability for long-term prediction of weather in the mid-latitudes.

492288.title: A Regional Weather-Stress Framework for Quantifying Future Agricultural Risk and Uncertainty Across CONUS Croplands
492288.authors: Srishti Vishwakarma, ORNL, Oak Ridge, TN; and M. Ashfaq, D. Rastogi, and P. Thornton
492288.abstract: Rising exposure to extreme weather stress, including heat, precipitation variability, and drought, poses growing risks to agricultural productivity and food security. Although numerous weather-stress indices have been developed to assess cropland vulnerability, single-index approaches often fail to capture the region-specific combinations of stressors that shape agricultural risk. This study develops a regional weather-stress framework to quantify historical and future changes in stress divergence and similarity across major cropland regions of the conterminous United States (CONUS), with the goal of supporting resilient agricultural planning. We use an ensemble of downscaled CMIP6 projections consisting of six driving Earth System Models (ESMs) and seven downscaling products for the period 1980–2059. Temperature- and precipitation-derived stress indices are aggregated using agroecological-zone-specific weights to reduce redundancy among correlated variables while retaining regional stress signatures. For each grid cell and year, projected stress conditions are compared with the local historical baseline conditions to derive two complementary weather-stress metrics: divergence, representing the magnitude of departure from baseline conditions, and similarity, representing the displacement required to identify an analogous historical stress state elsewhere. We further quantify uncertainty across product–ESM members, separating variability associated with individual downscaling products and ESMs. Preliminary results indicate a consistent increase in cropland weather-stress divergence and reduced similarity by the 2050s, with ESM uncertainty accounting for a substantial fraction of projected anomaly spread. Results reveal regional differences in the magnitude and uncertainty of future agricultural stress, highlighting areas where weather-related risks may challenge agricultural productivity. This framework provides a spatially explicit assessment of where agricultural weather stress is intensifying, where projection uncertainty is greatest, and where adaptation planning may be most urgently needed to sustain future crop production, while integrating multiple weather stressors and their uncertainty to support agricultural decision-making and strengthen food production resilience.

492298.title: The Challenges of Assessing a Turbulence Nowcast Product
492298.authors: Dana Uden, CIRA, Boulder, CO; NOAA Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and L. D. Melling, L. R. Blank, K. Y. Wong, A. Hewett, and M. S. Wandishin
492298.abstract: In summer of 2026, the Graphical Turbulence Guidance, Nowcast (GTGN) product successfully transitioned to operations. The FAA transition included an evaluation by the Quality Assessment Product Development Team. This presentation will highlight the improvements of GTGN over the forecast version, GTG4. However, the focus will be more on the challenges encountered: unevenly distributed observations (due to both nature and the observation platforms), highly-skewed distributions, and, relatedly, the limited effect of changes because of the low base rates of high-impact events, among others.

492299.title: An Adjoint-Free Method of Optimizing initial State and Wind Forcing of a Regional Wave Model
492299.authors: Gleb Panteleev, US Naval Research Laboratory, Stennis Space Center, MS; and N. Evdokimova, D. Nicolsky, M. Yaremchuk, and O. P. Francis
492299.abstract: An extension of the adjoint-free data assimilation method for a regional configuration of a spectral wave model is proposed. Performance of the technique is tested with the Simulating Waves Nearshore (SWAN) model in a series of Observation System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) and with real data from Sofar Spotter buoys deployed in the Beaufort Sea in August 2022. The types of observations constraining the model are directional spectra, significant wave height (SWH) and wind speed estimated from point measurements by stationary buoys. Numerical experiments demonstrate computational feasibility and robustness of the method for integration periods of up to 24-48 hours. Validation against independent SWH observations from satellites shows that the approach significantly improves regional wave forecasts. Optimization of the wind forcing reduces bias in the wind forcing and, in addition, provides a natural expansion of the search subspace used for optimization of the initial conditions, accelerating convergence of the minimization algorithm. The largest improvement of the model forecast skill is due to optimization of the wave spectrum, while additional assimilation of the wind observations may deteriorate the quality of the wave forecast.

492301.title: Measuring Space Weather Literacy: Development and Validation of a Space Weather Concept Inventory
492301.authors: Anthony L Williams, Auburn University, Auburn, AL; and K. McNeal
492301.abstract: Space weather poses growing risks to the technological systems modern society depends on, yet educational and training efforts have lacked a validated diagnostic tool for measuring literacy in this area across both professional and public audiences. This study describes the development and validation of the Space Weather Concept Inventory (SWCI), a 24-item diagnostic instrument designed to assess space weather literacy. Item development drew on a literature review and consultation with a five-member expert panel representing government, private, and academic sectors. The instrument was first tested in a pilot study of approximately 250 participants, then administered to an independent validation sample of 750 participants recruited through Prolific, with a final analytic sample of 719 respondents. Data were analyzed using classical test theory, confirmatory factor analysis, Rasch modeling, and linear regression. The SWCI demonstrated strong internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .877) and stable measurement properties across a range of item difficulties, largely reflecting a single broad dimension of space weather understanding. Engagement with space weather content and prior training were considerably more predictive of performance than demographic variables such as age or education. Open-ended responses revealed that public uncertainty clustered around no prior exposure, catastrophic framing of infrastructure risk, and confusion between fundamental phenomena. As the first validated concept inventory developed specifically for space weather, the SWCI provides a shared diagnostic foundation that researchers, educators, and practitioners can build on in support of broader public and professional preparedness.

492302.title: Continuous Data Assimilation Modes in JEDI
492302.abstract: Abstract: In operational settings, useful observations valid in a given data assimilation (DA) window may arrive after a data assimilation cycle has begun leading to a loss of potentially important information in the assimilation step. Continuous DA allows us to avoid that information loss by adding newly arrived observations between outer loops. JCSDA is developing three new continuous DA modes for the JEDI system. In the first any newly arrived observations are added before beginning the next outer loop. The second also adds newly arrived observations but allows for a shift forward of the end of the DA window. And finally, the third adds newly arrived observations while shifting both the beginning and the end of the DA window between outer loops. The genericity of JEDI extends these abilities to any model with a JEDI interface. In this talk I will present the implementation of these new modes and present initial results on how they affect DA when cycling.

492306.title: Toward Consistent Navigation of Six Decades of Geostationary Satellite Observations
492306.authors: Jerrold Robaidek, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and D. Santek, S. T. Wanzong, W. E. Lewis, S. Gunshor, A. De Smet, J. Feltz, and D. Stettner
492306.abstract: The University of Wisconsin–Madison Space Science and Engineering Center (SSEC) maintains a geostationary satellite archive extending from Applications Technology Satellite (ATS) observations beginning in 1966 through the present GOES-R era. Recent work is improving the navigation and geolocation of several generations of these observations, with the goal of producing a more spatially consistent long-term record suitable for climate studies, reanalysis, and artificial intelligence and machine-learning applications. For the GOES GVAR record beginning in 1994, modern geostationary observations from GOES ABI, Himawari AHI, and Meteosat Third Generation FCI are combined to construct nearly cloud-free reference imagery. Coastal features and other identifiable landmarks in historical GOES imagery are matched against this navigation standard to measure line and element displacement. The resulting landmark residuals are used to estimate corrections to spacecraft/instrument attitude parameters, including roll, pitch, and yaw. Preliminary analysis of approximately 2.06 million GVAR images shows the median combined landmark residual decreasing from approximately 1.15 pixels before correction to 0.38 pixels after correction. The same landmark-based methodology is being applied to the pre-GVAR GOES record. These observations present a more difficult navigation problem, with larger initial errors and substantially different orbital and attitude metadata. Preliminary results for approximately 350,000 images from GOES-1 through GOES-7 show the median landmark residual decreasing from approximately 3.67 pixels to 0.95 pixels. Where usable original navigation information exists, the spacecraft orbital and attitude state is adjusted using landmark-derived offsets. For imagery lacking reliable navigation, an initial navigation estimate can instead be generated from orbital information, including Two-Line Element sets, and subsequently refined using landmarks. These techniques are also being extended farther back in the geostationary record. Approximately three months of digital SMS-1 observations from 1974 are being navigated using similar methods. Scanned and digitized daily SMS and GOES imagery from 1974-1978 is being geolocated and provided with rudimentary radiometric calibration. For these scanned observations, satellite subpoint estimates and a perspective-view geometry provide an initial navigation that is subsequently refined through landmark matching against the same modern reference imagery. Similar techniques are being developed for scanned ATS imagery from 1966-1974. The use of a common modern navigation reference and landmark-fitting methodology across these substantially different satellite generations provides a path toward a consistently geolocated geostationary satellite record spanning nearly 60 years. Improving the spatial consistency and usability of these historical observations will increase their value for quantitative long-term studies and for emerging AI/ML applications that can benefit from multidecadal satellite training datasets.

492311.title: Spatial Variability of the Atmospheric Boundary Layer Across an Urban-Rural-Coastal Gradient in the Washington DC - Baltimore Region.
492311.authors: Akye C Johnson, NOAA, Capitol Heights, MD
492311.abstract: The atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) mediates surface-atmosphere exchange, yet its spatial variability across adjacent urban, rural, and coastal surfaces remains poorly constrained. We characterize ABL height (ABLH) across a four-site gradient in the Washington-Baltimore-Chesapeake Bay region during July 2025 to investigate how contrasting land surfaces, including urban and coastal environments, influence ABL structure and development : Mt. Airy, MD (rural), Baltimore, MD (urban), Kent Island, MD (bay), and Washington, DC (urban core). ABLH is retrieved from HALO Doppler lidar and ceilometer observations and paired with co-located eddy-covariance measurements of sensible and latent heat flux, with all sites referenced to Local Standard Time for direct diurnal comparison. Observations from the CoURAGE and UrbanNet campaigns are evaluated against WRF simulations using correlation, bias, and RMSD at each site. Across all sites, daytime ABLH is strongly associated with sensible heat flux and near-surface air temperature under convective conditions, highlighting the role of surface heating in boundary - layer growth. The urban sites depart from this baseline in both magnitude and timing: the urban heat island sustains a deeper boundary layer through the afternoon and delays evening collapse well past sunset, when the rural site has already stabilized. The bay site behaves oppositely - cool marine air advected over Kent Island suppresses sensible heat flux and air temperature, limiting ABL growth while producing the largest day-to-day variability of the four sites. Comparisons among the urban, rural, and coastal sites highlight the distinct influences of urbanization and marine processes on ABL characteristics. These results quantify the surface heterogeneity that mesoscale models must resolve to represent boundary layer structure across the urban-rural-coastal transition, while evaluation against Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations provides insight into model performance across contrasting environments. Together, these findings improve understanding of lower - atmospheric processes across heterogeneous landscapes and provide guidance for improving representation of the ABL in numerical models.

492313.title: Simulating Near-Surface Environments In Neighborhoods Using WRF-LES: Case Study of an Urban Atmospheric Boundary Layer during a Heatwave Event.
492313.authors: Jason Patrick Horne, The University of Massachusetts, Broomfield, CO; and Y. Pan, K. J. Davis, D. W. Waugh, B. J. Ahlswede, and N. E. Prince
492313.abstract: This study presents an in-depth comparison of meteorological observations and simulations from a high-resolution numerical weather model during an urban heatwave in Baltimore, MD. The simulations use a multi-nested downscaling approach to bridge the mesoscale and neighborhood-scale environments and incorporate high-resolution static data sources to better represent the urban surface. The nested Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model employs planetary boundary layer (PBL) or large-eddy simulation (LES) closure depending on the horizontal grid spacing of each domain. Comparing simulation results with observations demonstrates the successful replication of a daytime convective boundary layer (CBL). Meanwhile, the results reveal several model biases that are insensitive to updating the static land surface data. Firstly, the simulated boundary layer is too cool, too dry, and approximately 500 m too deep at midday. This overestimation of the daytime convective boundary-layer depth is likely due to an overestimation of the surface sensible heat flux, partly attributable to a misrepresentation of urban vegetation. Secondly, for forecast-relevant variables such as 2-m air temperature and humidity, little benefit is obtained by reducing the horizontal grid spacing below the typical kilometer scale. An exception is the simulated nighttime temperatures, which benefit from both higher-resolution static data and finer grid resolution. Overall, the WRF simulation biases reported here are not eliminated by decreasing the horizontal grid spacing or by improving the land surface data. The model biases identified in this work suggest directions for future improvements to urban parameterizations.

492314.title: Spray-Mediated Fluxes In High Winds: A Large-Eddy Simulation Investigation
492314.authors: David H. Richter, University of Notre Dame, South Bend, IN; and G. H. Bryan, J. Sun, J. M. Dennis, and S. Voelz
492314.abstract: The large uncertainty in air-sea fluxes momentum, heat, and moisture at high winds in the marine boundary layer is a longstanding problem, despite their pivotal role in hurricane dynamics. In particular, the role of sea spray on air-sea transfer remains largely unconstrained, owing to the difficulty of measuring spray influence directly, and the untested assumptions that must be made in various spray parameterizations. In this work, we aim to close this gap by conducting large eddy simulations of the high-wind marine boundary layer, while explicitly resolving spray generation and feedback via a Lagrangian method (the so-called “superdroplet” or Lagrangian cloud model). This explicit treatment avoids the need for making ad hoc assumptions about the spray dynamics and thermodynamics, and naturally incorporates the complex interplay between the boundary layer turbulence and the suspended droplets. We find that spray can have potentially large impacts on the thermodynamic flux coefficients, depending on background humidity. Furthermore, certain key assumptions which form the basis of spray-mediated bulk models are shown to be problematic, including the role of background environment, assumed droplet lifetimes, and the neglect of small droplets which do not re-enter the ocean.

492315.title: One Mission, Many Locations: Building NWS Readiness for Complex Public-Safety Operations
492315.authors: Stephanie D. Sipprell, NWS, KANSAS CITY, MO; and S. Johnson and M. Solum
492315.abstract: National Weather Service (NWS) operations in support of core partners during the 2026 FIFA World Cup timeframe presented a complex coordination challenge. The NWS needed to sustain trusted local forecasts, warnings, and impact-based decision support services while connecting 11 match cities, more than 20 operational hubs, and multiple federal, regional, state, and local coordination centers. Emergency managers and other public-safety partners were operating within different jurisdictions, authorities, and decision environments, yet all required timely access to locally relevant weather information. The scale and geographic reach of the mission required a national approach that could strengthen coordination across the system without replacing local expertise or established core partner relationships. To meet that need, the NWS established and operationally tested a flexible national readiness framework that connected local Weather Forecast Offices with national forecast expertise, aviation support, deployed meteorologists, technology, logistics, leadership, and other mission-support functions. The framework combined common readiness expectations, defined communication and escalation pathways, exercises, local planning, and an agency-adapted Incident Command System structure. Together, these elements helped align NWS operations with the broader network of emergency management and public-safety coordination already in place. Execution revealed several lessons relevant to large-event readiness. First, geographically distributed operations require clear pathways for elevating problems beyond individual offices. Staffing shortages, communications barriers, equipment failures, network issues, employee safety concerns, and other operational needs could be routed to personnel positioned to respond, reducing the burden on local offices during periods of active weather. Second, a shared national operating picture improved awareness across the system while still allowing local meteorologists to tailor services to emergency managers, public-safety officials and other core partners. Third, continuity depended on people and processes as much as technology: defined roles, cross-office relationships, shift handoffs, and practiced escalation pathways were essential when normal workflows were disrupted. The operation also became an early real-world test of the newly organized NWS Operations Pillar. Mission Execution and Mission Support functions worked together during a sustained national mission, revealing opportunities to improve role clarity, technology access, staffing and deployment processes, continuity procedures, and the integration of scientific and technical capabilities into frontline operations. These findings provided direct feedback on how the NWS can operate more effectively as part of the broader preparedness and response system. The main outcome was a tested, scalable model for connecting national resources with local public-safety needs across multiple jurisdictions and coordination environments. The experience showed that national consistency and local flexibility can reinforce one another when responsibilities are clear, escalation pathways function, and local decision environments remain central to service delivery. Lessons from the post-event review are informing future staffing, training, continuity planning, technology access, and operational coordination. They provide an initial blueprint for NWS operations in support of core partners during the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games and offer transferable lessons working across complex, multi-jurisdictional disaster and emergency management systems.

492318.title: Analysis and Emission Constraints of NSF’s Experimental Air Quality Forecasting System over Colorado Using MELODIES-MONET
492318.authors: Gabriele Pfister, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. Kumar, P. Lichtig, F. Lacey, and J. Boehnert
492318.abstract: Evaluating model simulations with observations is an integral part of any modeling effort but is complicated by the different data formats and spatiotemporal resolutions of observations and in the case of remote sensing products, the need to apply special observation operators. To address these challenges, NOAA and NSF NCAR have developed an open-access, user-friendly Python Package called MELODIES-MONET, which is targeted at atmospheric chemistry applications. It systematically compares model output from a range of models with a suite of available observations, providing the community with a tool to reproducibly evaluate atmospheric chemistry simulations. Under a Colorado Air Quality Enterprise (AQE) grant, we adapted the framework for the evaluation of the Colorado State of Implementation (SIP) modeling. In this presentation we will showcase the framework and the observations that were added as part of the AQE project, such as trace gas retrievals from the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI) and the Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO). Using the NSF NCAR experimental WRF-Chem air quality forecasting system, we further demonstrate the added benefit of including remote sensing data in assessing model performance over using surface data only as has been done traditionally for SIP modeling. We will also present results from a simple mass-balance approach that has been applied to paired model-observation output for TEMPO and TROPOMI from MELODIES MONET to constrain nitrogen dioxide (NO2) emissions. This approach will allow for easy first-order adjustment of NO2 emissions for forecasting and other applications.

492323.title: The Weather Effect: Using AccuWeather’s Comprehensive Data Suite to Predict Retail and Dining Trends in the Holiday Season
492323.authors: Crystal Francis Camron, AccuWeather, Inc., Loveland, CO
492323.abstract: AccuWeather's mission is to deliver the most accurate weather forecasts available with proven Superior Accuracy™, better protecting lives and property while helping businesses plan with greater confidence. That same forecasting accuracy underpins AccuWeather's Data Suite on Databricks, which packages more than 300 weather parameters spanning a 35-plus-year historical archive, real-time conditions across millions of global locations, and forward-looking forecasts, giving retail and restaurant operators a better foundation for demand forecasting, staffing, and disruption planning. Weather shapes where people go and what they buy every day, yet its influence on retail and dining traffic is rarely measured with the same rigor applied to economic or demographic drivers. This study puts AccuWeather's Data Suite to work alongside foot traffic data from a location analytics company to quantify that influence, using the holiday season, a period of peak consumer activity and heightened weather sensitivity, as a proving ground. Retail and dining visits rose broadly across most U.S. states during the season, with value-oriented and open-air, experiential formats outperforming traditional and luxury channels, while weather departures in temperature, precipitation, snow, wind, cloud cover, and AccuWeather’s RealFeel® temperature traced closely similar regional patterns. Pearson correlation analysis identified multiple weather parameters of interest that showed a strong relationship with changes in retail and dining foot traffic. These weather drivers were used to build single-variable linear regression models to predict the direction of week-over-week percent change in retail and dining traffic; the retail model correctly predicted the direction of sales change in roughly 60% of states, while the dining model showed weaker but still informative predictive skill. These findings demonstrate that weather is a measurable, quantifiable driver of consumer foot traffic, and that fusing granular weather data with location-based visitation analytics offers retailers and restaurants a path from reactive decision-making to proactive planning around staffing, merchandising, marketing timing, and operational preparedness. AccuWeather's weather data is built to support exactly this kind of work: accurate, reliable, flexible, customizable, and accessible. AccuWeather APIs give developers direct access to this same global, detailed, and local weather data, available today directly from AccuWeather or through plug-and-play platforms such as Databricks, Snowflake, and Azure, allowing individuals and organizations to integrate it effectively into their own weather-related planning and decision-making.

492331.title: Preferential Impacts of the Asian-Australian Monsoonal Subtropical Highs on the Indian Ocean Dipole Phases
492331.authors: Hong-Li Ren, Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences, Beijing, Beijing, China; and Z. Li, M. Liu, and R. Wang
492331.abstract: The influence of the Western-Pacific Subtropical High (WPSH) and Australian High (AH) on the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) phase is investigated in this study. We refer to this influence as phase-preferential impacts. The results show that 14 out of 15 IOD events since 1990 have co-occurred with anomalous WPSH and AH during boreal summer. These circulation anomalies induce variations in the meridional sea-level pressure (SLP) gradient spanning the Maritime Continent (MC), which play a key role in IOD formation. A strong and westward-extended summer WPSH can weaken the meridional SLP gradient over the flanks of MC by increasing SLP over the South China Sea, thereby suppressing monsoonal cross-equatorial southerlies. This reduction in winds decreases both surface evaporation off Sumatra and coastal ocean upwelling, leading to positive sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies in the southeastern tropical Indian Ocean (TIO) and then the negative IOD. In contrast, when the AH is strong, the subsidence and SLP over the southeastern TIO increase, strengthening the inter-hemispheric pressure gradient and the southeasterlies off Sumatra. These winds enhance evaporation and ocean upwelling, leading to an SST cooling in the southeastern TIO and then the positive IOD. Conversely, weak AH-induced northwesterlies promote SST warming in this region, facilitating the negative IOD growth. The IOD phases are further strengthened through exciting the positive air-sea feedbacks over the TIO. These results highlight the phase-preferential role of the two subtropical highs in modulating IOD, with a strong WPSH favoring the negative phase and a strong (weak) AH favoring the positive (negative) one.

492332.title: NUCAPS Emissivity Evaluation: Comparisons with CAMEL V3 Climatology
492332.authors: Michelle Loveless, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and E. Borbas, R. Knuteson, and K. L. Pryor
492332.abstract: NOAA NESDIS STAR maintains the NOAA Unique Combined Atmospheric Processing System (NUCAPS) Environmental Data Record (EDR) software for the operational retrieval of atmospheric profiles of temperature, moisture, and trace gasses as well as cloud-cleared radiances from the JPSS CrIS and ATMS Sensor Data Records (SDRs). The calibration and validation of these products is ongoing at STAR to characterize product quality through comparison with external validation sources and to identify areas where improvements can be made. One of those areas of improvement has been identified by STAR to be the infrared surface emissivity and the related surface temperature. This poster details an independent assessment of the NUCAPS surface emissivity scientific integrity using the NASA CAMEL infrared land surface emissivity database and makes recommendations for improvements. The CAMEL database used for comparison is available from the NASA LPDAAC, is a monthly product with high spectral and 0.05 degree (~5 km) gridded resolution and is based on the MODIS and ASTER narrowband emissivities. The assessment shown here makes use of the CAMEL Version 3 (V3) Climatology, which covers the years 2003 – 2021, and the NOAA-20 NUCAPS Version 3.2 emissivity product downloaded from NOAA CLASS. Select validation sites were chosen to cover a range of surface types and environmental conditions. Comparison results show that the NUCAPS retrieval adds variability to the first-guess emissivity across most channels. It is recommended that the CAMEL V3 Climatology is updated to the NUCAPS first guess to represent surface emissivity more accurately in partially snowy scenes, and that the covariance is used to constrain the emissivity retrieval to physically reasonable values (Knuteson et al., 2019).

492333.title: Adding a Stratosphere to the E3SM Atmosphere Dynamical Core
492333.authors: Jason Louis Torchinsky, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM; and T. S. Ehrmann
492333.abstract: Accurate simulation of stratospheric transport in high-resolution Earth system models requires robust numerical treatment of wave propagation, vertical resolution, and troposphere–stratosphere coupling. We are working to extend vertical extent of the dynamical core of the E3SM Atmosphere Model (EAM) to accurately represent a high-resolution stratosphere. Our numerical experiments include the following: 1) tropical convection in a vertically-extended Doubly-Periodic configuration of the Simplified Cloud-Resolving E3SM Atmosphere Model (DP-SCREAM) with sponge layer at 2 hPa and model top at about 60 km, and 2) a modification of the Polvani-Kushner 2002 numerical experiment in the EAM dynamical core, called NH-HOMME, with a northern hemisphere polar vortex, non-uniform surface topography, and a regionally-refined horizontal mesh. These numerical experiments both feature different sources of gravity waves, deep convection and topography, respectively, that penetrate the stratosphere. We resolve these gravity waves with a high-resolution (3-km) domain to study their sensitivity to vertical grid spacing. By performing convergence testing, we have identified a vertical configuration that best preserves the wave spectra while minimizing the increased computational cost of additional levels. We present this novel 192-level grid along with a modified sponge-layer needed for a high-resolution stratosphere.

492336.title: Trends of Variability in Growing Season Length and Diurnal Temperature Range in Pennsylvania, 1960 - 2025
492336.authors: Ciaran Murphy, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA
492336.abstract: Growing Season Length (GSL) is a crucial metric of atmospheric influence on global agriculture. This project seeks to identify trends in GSL Variability (GSLV) and understand GSL’s ties to Diurnal Temperature Range (DTR) and other variables, using observational and reanalysis data from 180 stations in Pennsylvania. To guide this analysis, we evaluated four hypotheses: we expect (1) stations with large DTR values to have smaller GSL, (2) GSLV to decrease over time, (3) GSLV to decrease as DTR values increase, and (4) mean temperature to mediate the impact of DTR on GSLV. Using Bayesian heteroskedastic regression modeling, GSLV was found to decrease by 26.75% (Credible Interval, CI: 12.73– 38.58%) from 1960 to 2025. Additionally, contrary to hypothesis (3), GSLV was found to increase by 13.07% (CI: 9.78 – 16.48%). Finally, a DTR increase of 1°C was found to decrease GSL by 9.51 days (CI: 8.76 – 10.26 days) and mean temperature was not found to mediate DTR’s impact on GSLV more than other covariates. This work provides a baseline understanding of trends in GSLV, and these results can be used for future research on forecasting GSL to aid agricultural sustainability and food security in a changing world. Keywords: Growing Season Length, Growing Season Length Variability, Diurnal Temperature Range

492339.title: An Overview of the 2026 NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed Spring Forecasting Experiment
492339.authors: Adam J. Clark, NSSL, Norman, OK; and I. L. Jirak, T. J. Galarneau, T. A. Supinie, K. H. Knopfmeier, D. R. Harrison, J. Vancil, M. Silcott, D. E. Jahn, C. Karstens, A. Wade, K. A. Hoogewind, C. K. Potvin, N. Yussouf, S. R. Ernst, J. Picca, M. E. Baldwin, J. A. Duarte, J. Martin, and B. C. Matilla
492339.abstract: The 2026 Spring Forecasting Experiment (2026 SFE) was conducted from 27 April - 29 May by the NWS/Storm Prediction Center (SPC) and OAR/National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL). Since 2023, SFEs have used a hybrid format, with both in-person and virtual participation. We have found that the hybrid format is ideal because we can engage those that cannot attend physically, while in-person participation enables invaluable science-based discussions and establishment of new collaborations. SFE 2026 featured model contributions from NOAA Global Systems Laboratory (GSL), NOAA/NCEP Environmental Modeling Center (EMC), NOAA/OAR National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL), and the Global Modeling and Assimilation Office of NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center. Industry contributions included Google DeepMind, Nvidia, Brightband, and OpenSnow. With implementation of the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) and RRFS Ensemble Forecast System (REFS) expected in October 2026, a major point of emphasis was once again evaluating these systems relative to the operational systems they are designed to replace. Additionally, with the recent announcement that the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) will be the future dynamical core for global and regional UFS applications, several MPAS evaluations were conducted, including MPAS-based RRFSv2 prototypes contributed by GSL and a new MPAS-based version of NSSL’s Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS). Finally, SFE 2026 expanded upon evaluations of AI NWP emulators from the previous two years. Highlights include first-time evaluations of GSL’s HRRRCast, next-day evaluations of an improved version of WoFSCast, which was also used in an afternoon forecasting activity, and a first-time examination of 0-3 h forecasts from a data-driven model contributed by Nvidia. The main goals of this talk will be to summarize SFE 2026 activities and highlight some notable results.

492340.title: Mapping Two Decades of Surface Ozone in the US: Integrating Satellite Observations, Monitoring Networks, and Atmospheric Modeling
492340.authors: Weizhi Deng, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; Univ. of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; and J. Wang, M. Zhou, X. Chen, H. Zhang, G. Brasseur, C. Granier, and L. Rouil
492340.abstract: Surface ozone monitoring networks cover only about 2% of the contiguous US, limiting assessments of population exposure, ozone standard exceedances, and long-term trends outside monitored locations. We integrate satellite observations, surface measurements, and CAMS atmospheric composition reanalysis within a deep-learning framework to generate a daily 1-km surface ozone dataset across the contiguous US from 2003 to 2024. Out-of-sample evaluation shows high overall accuracy (R2 = 0.88) and improved skills in capturing ozone exceedance events compared to the benchmark CAMS reanalysis (+2.5 exceedance events per station-year). High-resolution satellite features on population distribution, nighttime lights, vegetation, land use, and topography further enable the model to resolve ozone variability at the neighborhood scale, which could be useful for more targeted mitigation strategies. The spatially complete dataset also uncovers new ozone hotspots in sparsely monitored regions, such as the Permian Basin. Importantly, the dataset reveals a nationwide setback in reducing ozone pollution beginning around 2015, an insight not fully captured by sparse monitoring network alone. Policy-relevant ozone concentrations declined broadly through 2015 as anthropogenic precursor emissions decreased, but subsequently increased across large areas, particularly in the western and midwestern US. By combining the long-term ozone record with model-based fire influence estimates, we show that increasing wildfire emissions are the dominant driver of this trend reversal. Wildfire-driven ozone has increased the associated premature mortality by more than 300 deaths annually since 2013, and resulted in an additional 43 million people living in areas exceeding the ozone standard during 2022-2024. These results show how fusing observations from various platforms and atmospheric modeling with machine learning can extend the reach of sparse monitoring networks and support air quality management, especially in the context of increasing wildfire activity in North America.

492342.title: Evaluating the Metawatt Weather-to-Power Framework for Wind and Solar Generation Using High-Resolution Meteorological Data
492342.authors: Jungmin lee, LLNL, Oakland, CA; and R. S. Arthur, C. McGrath, X. Li, C. Bracken, and S. C. Dhulipala
492342.abstract: Accurate weather-driven wind and solar energy generation datasets are increasingly important for power system planning, production cost modeling, and studies of wind and solar energy integration. However, evaluating these datasets remains challenging because available observations often do not match the spatial and temporal resolution required by power system models. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of Metawatt, a weather-to-power framework that converts gridded meteorological data into hourly, plant-level wind and solar energy generation time series across the contiguous United States. Metawatt is evaluated using two high-resolution meteorological inputs: the 3-km High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model and the 4-km CONUS404 regional hydroclimate reanalysis. The framework combines meteorological fields with plant-specific characteristics and physics-based wind and photovoltaic power models to estimate hourly wind and solar energy generation. Simulated generation is evaluated against U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) reports, using monthly plant-level generation from Form EIA-923 to assess generation magnitude and hourly balancing-authority-level generation from Form EIA-930 to evaluate temporal variability. Independent observations of 100-m wind speed and surface solar irradiance from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Southern Great Plains site are also used to evaluate the underlying meteorological forcing. The evaluation demonstrates that Metawatt reproduces the major spatial and temporal characteristics of observed wind and solar energy generation when driven by either HRRR or CONUS404. Across most balancing authorities, modeled hourly generation exhibits strong correlations with EIA observations, particularly in regions with substantial installed wind and solar capacity. A multi-year evaluation of HRRR-driven Metawatt generation from 2019–2024 further demonstrates consistent performance as U.S. wind and solar capacity expanded rapidly, with the framework capturing both long-term growth and year-to-year variability in generation. Independent meteorological evaluation provides additional confidence that the high-resolution weather fields used by Metawatt realistically represent the atmospheric conditions controlling wind and solar energy generation. The analysis also highlights challenges associated with validating weather-to-power datasets. In several regions, apparently large solar generation errors are associated with inconsistencies between EIA-930 and EIA-923 rather than deficiencies in Metawatt's representation of hourly variability. In addition, sensitivity experiments using zero-, one-, and two-hour HRRR forecasts show that Metawatt generation estimates are only weakly sensitive to forecast lead time, supporting the use of HRRR analysis fields for retrospective weather-driven power modeling. Overall, the results establish confidence in Metawatt as a robust framework for translating high-resolution meteorological information into multi-year, hourly wind and solar energy generation datasets. Its ability to produce realistic generation characteristics using multiple meteorological inputs makes Metawatt well suited for power system studies examining wind and solar variability, grid operations, and the increasing integration of weather-dependent energy resources.

492343.title: Building the Next Generation of NASA Earth Science Data Systems
492343.authors: James O'Sullivan, NASA, Washington, DC; NASA, Washington, DC; and K. Baynes and C. Durachka
492343.abstract: NASA's Earth Science Data Systems (ESDS) program continues to enact a comprehensive strategy to address the growing volume and complexity of Earth science data. This presentation will overview NASA Earth science data activities, including data processing, stewardship, cloud-based distribution, user services, and support for open science. The talk will cover the transformation of the Earth Science Data and Information System (ESDIS) Project over the past year and into 2027. This transformation includes the realignment of its archive centers into thematic science teams and the consolidation of its core services. It will also cover the new Foundational Data Products (FDP) project, which centralizes stewardship and continuity of essential Earth system observations. The talk will discuss the completion of the Earthdata Website Unification and the migration of the data archive to the cloud. The talk will highlight ESDS's role in enabling scientific discovery in an increasingly data-rich environment, including ESDS's new AI strategy for FY27–FY30, which defines how the program applies artificial intelligence across the full data lifecycle, from infrastructure and production to data access and analysis. Throughout, ESDS continues to prioritize FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, AI-ready data curation, and robust access and discovery capabilities as NASA transitions to scalable commercial cloud infrastructure and modular processing architectures.

492345.title: A Climate-Informed Compound Event Impact Assessment for New York State
492345.authors: Jacola Roman, Eagle Rock Analytics, Sacramento, CA; and O. Doherty, H. Inda Diaz, A. Ordonez, and S. A. Saki
492345.abstract: New Yorkers are increasingly threatened by extreme weather hazards that endanger lives, devastate property, and disrupt critical infrastructure. While a single event can be severe, impacts amplify when multiple hazards interact—creating compound events. Local factors, such as the socioeconomic status of residents or unique local geographies, can amplify the impacts of compounding or cascading hazards. Characterizing how hazards are amplified or dampened by the interplay across time, space, human and natural systems; and in turn how the interplay determines impacts to society provides a more comprehensive risk assessment to enable trusted, climate-informed decisions that protect and benefit all New Yorkers. To ensure effective climate-informed planning and design for compound events in New York, a clear understanding of the following components is required: What are the critical underlying environmental drivers of these kinds of compound events? What factors further exacerbate the impact of these compound events? How will the frequency and intensity of these events change under a warming climate? Eagle Rock Analytics, in partnership with NYSERDA, are performing a climate-informed impact assessment of compound events in New York State (NYS) by developing a set of tools in the form of open-access notebooks that analyze past compound extreme events in NYS, quantify their compounding effect, and provide compound event insights across disparate datasets, including future climate projections. We will provide a detailed description into the compound events identified as most impactful and the key environmental drivers behind them. We will discuss our engagement and open-source development strategies so as to better align with user needs enabling actionable science to make climate-informed decisions through reproducibility and future extension to novel applications.

492347.title: Characteristics and Spatial Scales of Natural and Seeding Ice Nucleating Particles in the Colorado Rockies (Invited Presentation)
492347.authors: Russell James Perkins, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and R. Zhou, D. Juergensen, K. Ayars, C. Hume, K. R. Barry, O. Dutton, G. McMeeking, E. Levin, A. L. Hodshire, L. Gibson, E. Emerson, P. J. DeMott, J. M. Creamean, and S. M. Kreidenweis
492347.abstract: Ice Nucleating Particles (INPs) impact cloud characteristics and precipitation likelihood. They are available as a very small portion of natural aerosol and are emitted anthropogenically by cloud seeding efforts aimed at increasing wintertime precipitation, snowpack, and water resources. The DOE ARM Surface Atmosphere Integrated Field Laboratory (SAIL) campaign in 2021-2023 near Crested Butte, Colorado, included long-term measurements of INPs, with spatially distributed INP and aerosol measurements provided by the co-located SAIL-Net campaign. These measurements and others are used to inform the sources of natural INPs, the natural and seeding-modified seasonal cycle of INPs, seeding INP-cloud interactions and deposition in precipitation and the spatial heterogeneity of INPs in the Rocky Mountain region and beyond.

492348.title: Global Variability In Fire VOC Emissions Characterized from Space
492348.authors: Julieta Fernanda Juncosa Calahorrano, University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN; and D. B. Millet, K. Wells, C. Hu, and V. Payne
492348.abstract: We use satellite observations in the thermal infrared (IR) to explore how fire VOC emissions vary globally as a function of ecoregion and fire intensity. Thermal IR observations provide access to a range of pyrogenic VOCs and are largely unaffected by the fine aerosols that are abundant in smoke. Here we use single-footprint hyperspectral range indices (HRIs) from the Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) to map the distribution of methanol, ethene, ethyne, and HCN over and downwind of a global ensemble of fires spanning 14 years of data. Inclusion of ethene, with its short lifetime to oxidation, allows the freshest portions of smoke plumes to be readily identified and separated from scenes with diluted or no smoke. We leverage the similar vertical sensitivities of ethene and methanol to quantify their relative abundance in smoke without requiring any plume height information and build on prior work over North America suggesting that this ratio can be used to infer the pyrolysis conditions of the underlying fire. We explore the degree to which this relationship holds globally, and assess how well the variability in VOC:VOC ratios seen from space can be understood based on ecoregion, fire radiative power, and other physical observables. Finally, we use case studies encompassing large fire events and isolated plumes to investigate the lifetime of ethene in fresh smoke, and its implications for the oxidation capacity in these plumes.

492351.title: Across Model Structure and Configuration: Strong Historical Cooling from Warm-Phase Aerosol-Cloud Interactions
492351.authors: Jacqueline M. Nugent, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and H. Y. Brown, D. McCoy, L. Regayre, K. Ghosh, G. S. Elsaesser, Y. Bhatti, J. Mülmenstädt, C. Song, S. M. Burrows, D. Watson-Parris, K. Carslaw, A. Gettelman, and T. Eidhammer
492351.abstract: The historical cooling from aerosol-cloud interactions remains the largest uncertainty in our ability to infer future Earth system behavior from the historical record. This reflects the huge gap in scale between the processes that underpin aerosol-cloud interactions and the top-of-atmosphere radiative forcing that informs temperature variability in the Earth system. Earth system models (ESMs) remain the tool that we can use to estimate historical forcing, but they must mathematically abstract (parameterize) aerosol-cloud interactions – leading to substantial parametric uncertainty and potential structural error in their estimates of historical cooling. Here, we unite a set of perturbed process ensembles (PPEs) hosted in four different ESMs to constrain historical aerosol forcing through constraints on changes in warm cloud microphysics and subsequent aerosol-cloud adjustments. Across this multi-model PPE, we find a wide range of ESM behaviors with both decreasing and increasing cloud liquid in response to historical increases in aerosol and consequently both very strong and very weak historical cooling. We find that when confronted with observations, all ESMs produce a net increase in liquid cloud in response to increased aerosol during the historical period and consequently a strong historical cooling. We find that when combined with top-down constraints from historical temperature record, this yields a tighter constraint on future Earth system behavior.

492355.title: Comparative Assessment of the Next Generation Fire System (NGFS) and the VIIRS I-band Active Fire Product During the 2026 Alaska Wildfire Season.
492355.authors: Owen Larson, Univ. of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and J. Delamere, C. Dierking, J. Cable, B. Buechler, M. Pavolonis, J. Sieglaff, J. A. Otkin, PhD, and J. Jenkins
492355.abstract: Satellite-based fire detection is critical to wildland fire management in Alaska, with a sparse population spread across a large landscape. Polar-orbiting satellites are ideal for fire detection in Alaska due to frequent overpasses at high latitudes. The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) carried onboard Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) satellites has 22 visible and infrared channels, among them 5 I-band channels with 375-meter resolution. These I-band channels, including shortwave infrared, provide the source of the VIIRS I-band Active Fire Product which is used operationally for wildfire management by the Alaska Interagency Coordination Center (AICC). The high temporal frequency of revisits from the 3 operational JPSS satellites leads to as many as 20+ overpasses in Northern AK. The Next Generation Fire System (NGFS), a relatively new system undergoing active development by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NOAA NESDIS) and the Cooperative Institute for Meteorological Satellite Studies (CIMSS) at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, is a multi-sensor system that uses advanced spatial and temporal metrics to deliver analysis-ready data complete with ancillary data sources to end users. Relative to the VIIRS I-band Active Fire algorithm, the NGFS fire detection algorithm has the capability to detect heat below clouds and smoke and weaker heat signatures. The Geographic Information Network of Alaska (GINA), located at the University of Alaska, Fairbanks, has two antennas receiving direct-broadcast data from JPSS satellites and a production processing system that delivers low-latency fire detection products to AICC in as low as 8 minutes from time of overpass over Alaska. In addition, GINA provides support and training to AICC staff for use of fire detection products alongside a suite of supporting VIIRS imagery. GINA has deployed and tested the NGFS on VIIRS data over Alaska since 2024 and has been delivering an experimental output with ArcGIS map services to AICC designed to integrate into existing decision support systems. In addition to providing support to AICC, and feedback to the NGFS development team, GINA has monitored the performance of NGFS as a successor to VIIRS Active Fire. In this presentation, we will discuss the relative performance of NGFS and VIIRS Active Fire on GINA direct broadcast data during the 2026 Alaska fire season. Fire-extent polygons from the National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) provide a reference for fire growth and extent, and data from AICC provides context for discovery and management of fires. Analysis will focus on metrics important to operational use by AICC. Preliminary results on the current, in-development NGFS indicate the NGFS algorithm frequently provides the earliest known detection for remote wildfires, has a higher number of detections within fire extent perimeters, but also may have a higher proportion of false detections due to solar cloud reflection. We will also discuss our work in building out our production deployment of NGFS, the close collaboration amongst AICC, GINA, CIMSS, and NOAA NESDIS, and future considerations, such as the inclusion of Metop SG as an additional satellite data source.

492367.title: Prelaunch Simulation of JPSS-4 VIIRS Sensor Data Records for Calibration and Validation Readiness
492367.authors: Xi Shao, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, Riverdale, MD; and X. Jing, T. C. Liu, S. Blonski, W. Wang, and C. Cao
492367.abstract: The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) aboard the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) provides critical observations for numerical weather prediction, environmental monitoring, and hazard detection. With the launch of JPSS-4 (J4) planned for late 2027, comprehensive prelaunch calibration and validation (Cal/Val) activities are essential to ensure continuity and consistency with the operational NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 (N21) VIIRS data record. To reduce scan-to-scan underlap, the J4 VIIRS optical design incorporates a shorter effective focal length (EFL), requiring an increased instrument scan rate. To accommodate the new scan rate, the Interface Data Processing Segment (IDPS) has reduced the J3/J4 SDR granule duration. In addition, J4 VIIRS adopts the Total and Spectral Solar Irradiance Sensor (TSIS) model for reflective solar band radiance. These changes can impact downstream Environmental Data Record (EDR) algorithms, making realistic proxy J4 SDRs essential for algorithm development and testing prior to launch. We developed an end-to-end J4 VIIRS SDR simulation framework that generates J4-equivalent SDRs from N21 observations by incorporating all major anticipated instrument and calibration changes. The framework first generates J4-specific pixel geolocation grids using actual J4 Science RDRs from satellite pre-launch testing combined with simulated J4 Spacecraft Diary RDRs based on N21 ephemeris and attitude data and processed through ADL (Algorithm Development Library) software, accounting for the updated scan rate. N21 radiance, reflectance, and brightness temperature observations are then resampled onto the J4 geometry while preserving pixel- and scan-level quality information. Radiometric differences resulting from spectral response function (SRF) differences between J4 and N21 are corrected using Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) to derive channel-dependent adjustment factors. In addition, the framework incorporates the transition from the Thuillier solar irradiance model to the TSIS reference by applying band-specific solar irradiance corrections to the reflective solar bands. The simulated J4 SDRs provide a unique capability to quantify the impacts of scan rate and geometry modifications, SRF differences, and the TSIS solar irradiance reference before launch. Statistical analyses of radiance, reflectance, and brightness temperature differences are performed over diverse surface types and illumination conditions, with particular emphasis on spectrally sensitive channels such as the M13 (fire band). The impact of the TSIS transition is further quantified by relating simulated radiometric differences to band-integrated solar irradiance changes. These prelaunch assessments provide critical guidance for calibration strategy, EDR algorithm development, uncertainty characterization, and calibration readiness, helping ensure a seamless transition and long-term continuity between NOAA-20/21 and J4 VIIRS observations.

492379.title: Redi or Not? An AI-Assisted Decision-Support Tool for Assessing R&D Readiness
492379.authors: Abigail Arnold, NOAA, Springfield, MO; FedWriters Supporting NOAA's Weather Program Office, Silver Spring, MD; and C. A. Williamsberg
492379.abstract: Readiness levels (RLs) are widely used across federal agencies to assess how close research and development activities are to real-world use. However, researchers and practitioners alike have reported persistent challenges applying the framework consistently, including subjective differences in how people judge a project’s progress, difficulty distinguishing between levels, and challenges applying the same framework to many different types of research and development (Olechowski et al. 2020; NOAA 2020). To address these concerns in NOAA, the Line Office Transition Manager Committee (LOTMC) established a Readiness Level Task Force in 2020, which developed revised guidance, training modules, and examples to make RL assessments more intuitive and practical. Even with these resources, NOAA’s Weather Program Office (WPO) staff, grantees, and applicants continued to report challenges navigating the framework. In response, WPO developed Redi, a Gemini-based agent (called a Gem) that helps users apply NOAA’s RL framework to the specific context of their project. Redi considers a project’s objectives, methods, intended users, evidence of progress, and planned milestones to recommend a readiness level and/or map future activities to readiness level advancement. To help users understand how the framework applies to their project, Redi explains the reasoning behind its recommendation, provides a confidence assessment to communicate the level of certainty in its interpretation, and identifies the critical gap preventing advancement to the next readiness level. Together, these features help tailor a broad, general framework to their specific project, making the RL assessment process more relevant, practical, and easier to navigate. This presentation will take attendees behind the scenes of Redi’s development, testing, and refinement, including where the tool struggled, what was learned when it got things wrong, and how user feedback reshaped its design. It will demonstrate how Redi moves beyond simply assigning a readiness level and in doing so, offers a new way to turn readiness levels from a frustrating box-checking exercise into an actionable roadmap for moving innovation from research to real-world use.

492387.title: Investigating Satellite-Based Precipitation Retrievals at ARM Sites for Long-Term Climatology, Validation, and AI-Driven Anomaly Detection and Forecasting
492387.authors: Siddhant Gupta, ; and L. L. Briggs, J. R. O'Brien, R. C. Jackson, B. A. Raut, A. Theisen, and N. L. Hickmon
492387.abstract: Precipitation measurements are critical for addressing aerosol-cloud interactions, providing observational constraints on seasonal transitions, investigating subseasonal-to-seasonal variability, and for site operations in remote environments. Surface precipitation is linked to meteorological conditions and atmospheric phenomena from the synoptic scale to micrometer scale. These ties are studied using Department of Energy’s Atmospheric Radiation Measurement User Facility (ARM) observations over daily timescales and synoptic regimes identified using an artificial neural network (self-organizing maps) to constrain synoptic variability over decadal timescales. While ARM deployments provide ground-based sensors and radars to measure surface precipitation rates or retrieve Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (QPEs), these measurements are unavailable before the deployment, have limited spatial coverage, or contain large uncertainties farther away from the site. This work provides precipitation context for ARM deployments (starting with Bankhead National Forest (BNF), Southern Great Plains, and the Amazon sites) using satellite-based estimates of surface precipitation from the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Mission (GPM IMERG) dataset and the NOAA Global Historical Climatology Network daily (GHCNd) dataset. For the Amazon site, GPM data are used to identify the dry to wet season transition, and the output is compared with the self-organizing map regimes based on 500 mb geopotential heights. Separately, for the BNF site, comparisons between IMERG and ARM daily precipitation showed significant correlation (r = 0.67) for days with moderate rain from October 2024 to September 2025. During this period, 13 days with high rainfall (over 38 mm d-1) exhibit higher biases and the radar scenes are classified into convective organization regimes to identify sources of uncertainty in IMERG and ARM observations of daily precipitation. This study presents 25-year precipitation climatology at three ARM sites and uses Long Short-Term Memory model to identify precipitation patterns and anomalies over 25 years of GHCNd and IMERG data to predict the frequency and distribution of extreme rainfall events. For the duration of ARM deployments, IMERG precipitation is compared with ARM in-situ observations and radar products like Extracted Radar Columns and In-Situ Sensors (RadCLss) and Surface Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (SQUIRE) to evaluate IMERG and ARM radar retrievals.

492392.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Communication of Total Water Level Visualizations Through User Testing of Compound Flood Products
492392.authors: Snehalata Sainjoo, University of Minnesota, College Station, TX; and S. Kandel, P. Singh, A. Stumpf, T. A. Sudol, L. A. Mariolis, S. Hettige, A. Luscher, B. Sweetman, R. Atkins, D. Giardino, F. Moser, A. J. Jefferson, and M. A. Kenney
492392.abstract: Total Water Level (TWL) products are designed to provide forecasting of compound flood risk in coastal communities by combining multiple drivers, including tides, storm surge, waves, and inland flooding. However, these products are complex and present interpretive challenges for coastal emergency managers, planners, and other end users who rely on them during time-sensitive decisions. To date, NOAA has limited empirical evidence on how users actually read, interpret and act on TWL visualizations, creating a gap between product design and operational use. This project addresses that gap through a user-centered evaluation approach aimed at identifying communication barriers, assessing users' understanding of TWL products, and generating evidence to guide NOAA's development of TWL products ahead of full operational release. In collaboration with NOAA's National Ocean Service (NOS) and Office of Water Prediction (OWP), we are conducting a multi-phase, mixed-methods evaluation. This includes (1) a structured empirical diagnostic assessment of six federal coastal flooding visualization products to identity the communication barriers and areas for improvement; (2) virtual focus groups with 15 NOAA and USGS TWL producers to surface communication goals, design priorities and trade-offs, and risk communication challenges; and (3) forthcoming interviews with NOAA OWP producers and focus groups with users across coastal watersheds to characterize user needs and test alternative visualization designs. Results from these activities will directly inform the co-design and empirical evaluation of alternative TWL visualizations and the development of TWL training modules, which will subsequently be evaluated with approximately 25 stakeholders across two major coastal watersheds. Collectively, this work will generate evidence-based guidance for improving the usability of NOAA's TWL products and establish a user-centered framework for evaluating next-generation coastal flood decision-support tools. By bringing together producer insights, user needs, and empirical usability testing before operational deployment, the project directly supports NOAA's operational transition of TWL products and its broader mission of delivering impact-based decision support services for coastal flood preparedness and climate resilience.

492397.title: Observation and Prediction of Horizontal Wind Gradients in the Delaware Coastal Environment
492397.authors: Emmanuel Olamiriki, University of Delaware, Newark, DE; and D. E. Veron, PhD and A. TREMBANIS
492397.abstract: The Delaware coastal region is shaped by the interaction of multi-scale atmospheric forcing with coastal processes governed by complex coastline geometry, the Delaware Bay-Atlantic shelf system, and spatially variable sea-surface temperatures (SST), which result in the development of steep horizontal wind gradients. Despite knowing that these gradients affect coastal and offshore wind forecasting and resource assessment, sufficient observation and accurate prediction remain a challenge. This study examines horizontal wind gradients along the Delaware coast in the late fall of November, 2022, using observations from Wave Glider, National Data Buoy Center (NDBC) buoys, and Delaware Environmental Observing System (DEOS) stations, together with weather radar observations, 1-km Multi-scale Ultra-high Resolution (MUR) SST analyses, and Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations. We analyzed storm and calm cases representing contrasting synoptic regimes to characterize the spatial and temporal evolution of the coastal wind field and to evaluate the representation of observed wind gradients in WRF simulations. In addition, Wave Glider observations were used to examine fine-scale and diurnal variability in SST that may not be fully resolved by daily SST analyses, highlighting the value of autonomous observations for characterizing coastal air-sea conditions. WRF simulations of several case studies provide insight into model representation of these same features. Improved characterization and prediction of coastal wind field and variability can support more accurate offshore wind forecasts, and operational decision-making for offshore wind applications.

492398.title: The Development and Evaluation of SMART: A Comprehensive In-Situ Cloud Microphysics Dataset
492398.authors: Jonathan Connor Douglas, CIWRO, Norman, OK; The University of Oklahoma/CIWRO, Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and G. M. McFarquhar, Y. Huang, P. A. Brechner, A. M. Dzambo, C. Knowles, and C. Kotlarz
492398.abstract: Weather systems such as hurricanes, supercells, and snowstorms are among the largest causes of humanitarian and economic disasters in the world today. Accurate representations of cloud processes and radiative forcing are paramount for the development and evaluation of remote sensing and modeling parameterizations. To quantify the properties of clouds in a variety of systems, numerous field studies have sampled clouds with in-situ probes and remote sensing instruments. These campaigns span a wide range of latitudes, surface conditions, aerosol loadings, and synoptic conditions, ranging from deep tropical convection and convective systems over the United States to low-level polar marine clouds and synoptically forced clouds in regions of large-scale ascent. Knowledge about how cloud properties vary with environmental conditions sampled in different campaigns is critical for enhancing the understanding of cloud processes needed for parameterization development. However, because there are no standard instruments for sampling cloud properties in-situ and no common algorithm for processing in-situ cloud probe data, nuances exist when comparing data from one campaign to another. Further, there is no common repository with all data and finding available cloud probe data can be difficult for those unfamiliar with the campaigns. These complexities often restrict research efforts and may introduce artificial error when comparing field campaign datasets. The Standardized Microphysics Airborne Repository Toolkit (SMART) represents the first step toward the development of a consistent and comprehensive in-situ cloud physics database. Preprocessed size distributions (SDs) and environmental variables are used as the only inputs to the first version of SMART to make the development of a consistent algorithm feasible. SMART rebins the input SDs to a common set of bins and subsequently calculates bulk cloud properties such as total number concentration (N) and liquid and ice water content (LWC, IWC) using a common algorithm. A simplified phase identification scheme sorts each sample as clear air or ice, mixed, or liquid phase cloud.
