Since input particle information is limited to SDs, IWC is estimated using simple mass-dimensional relationships rather than more complex methods that utilize area ratio or habit. An assessment of error introduced by SD rebinning and simplified IWC calculation is examined here. The rebinning process reveals no artifacts in resultant SDs and bulk properties derived from the input and output distributions match 1:1. SMART IWC calculations show some discrepancy compared to more sophisticated algorithms included in the University of Illinois/Oklahoma Optical Array Probe Software (UIOOPS), but still exhibit strong correlation with a best-fit slope of 0.8 and a regression coefficient of 0.91. Lastly, the agreement of SMART-processed datasets using input SDs from various sources reveals and quantifies the uncertainty arising from using pre-processed SD inputs. To highlight the utility of consistent data, SMART is used to process an array of cloud campaign datasets. SDs from CAESAR are prepared using a variety of processing codes and SMART outputs are compared to determine if similar dependencies on environmental variables such as cloud height, temperature, and cloud source are obtained between datasets. Preliminary findings from this analysis not only reveal which environmental variables have the largest effect on cloud properties during CAESAR, but also demonstrate the research possible with a comprehensive dataset.

492401.title: Using Global Ensemble Forecasting System Variables in U-Nets to Predict Vapor Pressure Deficit at Three- and Four- Week Lead Times
492401.authors: Christina E. Kumler, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and M. L. Breeden and R. Worsnop
492401.abstract: Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD) can be a useful meteorological predictor for wildfire potential. The higher the VPD, the higher potential for wildfire ignition and spread. This study utilizes 31 ensemble members in the Global Ensemble Forecasting System (GEFS) as inputs into U-NET models that then predict 31 VPD forecasts at 3- and 4- week lead times. The final product is a single 2D forecasted probability of exceedance for the desired lead-time for the CONUS domain. To do this, U-NET models were trained over portions of the Pacific and CONUS from each ensemble member in the GEFS forecast as an individual input. Different weekly minimums, means, and/or maximum values were calculated over GEFS grid cells to represent the input week conditions and forecast the corresponding targeted lead-time. Once trained, the U-NETS produced an ensemble of VPD forecasts. To analyze performance, a mean VPD was calculated from the ensembled forecast and compared to a baseline. These were compared to a mathematically calculated week-of-year VPD from those same GEFS forecasts for the corresponding lead-time. While the Brier Skill Score (BSS) generally seemed to show that U-NET performance was at or just below the skill of that of a calculated predicted VPD, regions in the west, specifically wildfire prone areas, during summer and late summer/fall did show positive BSS. The ensembled VPD that were then used to calculate a probability of exceedance of the week-of-year mean VPD from the climatological VPD average. Areas indicated either below, at, or above percent exceedance based on the 20-year climatological record from the week-of-year VPD calculated from ERA5 data.

492406.title: Do Data-Driven Weather Models Learn Similar Internal Representations of the Atmosphere?
492406.authors: Kirsten I. Tempest, Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich, Munich, BY, Germany; and M. Beylich, L. Peralt, and G. C. Craig
492406.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models now outperform traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) systems on several benchmark metrics, but it remains unclear whether independently developed models achieve this skill by learning similar internal representations of the atmosphere. We investigate whether four state-of-the-art models, AIFS-CRPS, GraphCast, ArchesWeather, and Aurora, develop aligned representations. We hypothesise that the models will have learned similar internal representations, although differences in model architecture may influence the degree of alignment. We compare representations extracted from the final processor step of each model, primarily using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), with scores calibrated against a null baseline that accounts for temporal and spatial dependencies in the data. Similarity is evaluated across the global spatial grid and across forecast lead times. Within each model, we also compare representations across successive processor steps. Complementary measures, including orthogonal Procrustes, are in addition used to assess how estimates of similarity depend on the invariances and sensitivities of the chosen metric. Results indicate representational similarity across all model pairs, although the degree of similarity varies with both the metric used and the models compared. The metrics are also found to be influenced by high-variance components of the representations to varying degrees. This is particularly evident for CKA, where high-variance components inflate similarity scores while under-emphasising lower-variance but potentially physically meaningful structure. These results highlight the importance of combining complementary similarity measures with appropriate calibration to obtain a more comprehensive assessment of internal representations. This work provides a systematic comparison of internal representations in data-driven weather models while also assessing the strengths and limitations of different similarity measures. Because each metric is sensitive to different properties of the representations, future work will extend the analysis to a broader range of measures and evaluate their suitability in greater detail. This will support a more comprehensive understanding of shared and model-specific atmospheric representations and advance interpretability in data-driven weather forecasting.

492410.title: Investigating Connections of Colorado River Water Supply and Wildfire Activity on Interannual to Decadal Timescales
492410.authors: Lydia Conger, Utah State University, Logan, UT; and Y. Chikamoto, W. Zhang, and L. Yocom
492410.abstract: The Colorado River Water Supply (CRWS), a drought indicator for the Upper Colorado River Basin, is highly correlated with fire activity across the Western United States on interannual to decadal timescales. Low CRWS can enhance wildfire potential through dry conditions but suppress wildfire activity through reduced vegetation cover. This counteracting effect produces diverse spatial patterns and temporal evolutions of wildfire response in the Western United States. Why this Upper Colorado River Basin drought indicator is linked to fire activity across the larger Western United States remains unresolved. Here we show that CRWS is significantly negatively correlated with annual burned area from 1984–2024 for all western states, excluding Nevada and Idaho. Positive correlations of soil moisture anomalies with CRWS, and negative correlations of fire weather days with CRWS, further support this Western United States connection. Composite analysis of high- and low-CRWS years shows that low precipitation and high temperature anomalies during fall–winter initiate low soil moisture anomalies that persist from winter into the following summer across the West. In contrast, higher fire weather index anomalies and lower Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) anomalies emerge over the Southwest in winter and shift northward from spring to summer, reaching northwestern states in late summer. Ongoing analysis further examines the roles of vapor pressure deficit and atmospheric forcing in these drought–fire connections.

492411.title: Associations Between Daily Minimum Temperature and Heat-Related Illness among Workers in Washington State, 2006-2022
492411.authors: Xinyuan Hao, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and J. A. Casey and J. T. Spector
492411.abstract: Objective. Heat-related illness (HRI) is of major health concern among workers, with a heat-related fatality rate of 0.22 per 1 million workers per the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Exertional heat stroke can develop among outdoor workers when the body cannot adequately dissipate heat. Incomplete recovery during the preceding night may compound this risk, while a cooler ambient home environment may reduce the risk of HRI. In recent years, nighttime temperatures are rising faster than daytime temperatures and warm nights are becoming more frequent across many areas, including parts of Washington State, compressing the window available for overnight recovery from heat. We explored the associations of elevated daily minimum temperature (Tmin), as a proxy for nighttime temperature, with same-day occupational HRI risk among Washington State workers. Materials and Methods. We spatiotemporally linked 1347 Washington State Fund HRI workers’ compensation claims (2006-2022) to 4 km2 gridded daily Parameter-elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) meteorological data at the date and location of each claim. Using a time-stratified case-crossover design, in which each HRI claim serves as its own control, we compared Tmin conditions on claim days with referent days on the same day of the week, month, and year as the claim and fit conditional logistic regression models. Dichotomous Tmin indicators were specified at multiple thresholds (60, 65, and 70°F) to reflect the Tmin distribution in the dataset, which also aligns with published temperature ranges for optimal sleep. Models were adjusted for same-day maximum temperature (Tmax) and humidity (dew point temperature) to isolate the independent effect of Tmin. Results. HRI days were warmer than referent days (mean Tmin 56.4 vs. 53.2˚F; mean Tmax 87.0 vs. 79.5˚F, respectively). Tmin reached 60°F or higher on 31.3% of case days compared with 15.4% of referent days. Across all days (median Tmin 54.3°F), 19.0% of days had a Tmin of 60˚F or higher, and 1.3% had a Tmin of 70˚F or higher. After adjustment for Tmax and humidity, Tmin retained an independent positive association with HRI across all three binary thresholds: OR = 1.68 (95% CI 1.37, 2.06) at Tmin ≥60°F, OR = 2.22 (1.69, 2.91) at Tmin ≥65°F, and OR = 3.37 (2.04, 5.58) at Tmin ≥70°F. A continuous Tmin specification yielded an OR of 1.09 (95% CI 1.07, 1.10) per 1˚F increase in Tmin, corresponding to 9% higher odds of HRI for each elevated degree of Tmin. Conclusion. In this study, an exposure-response pattern was observed, with higher Tmin thresholds corresponding to progressively greater HRI risk, even after adjustment for daytime maximum temperature. Warm nights carry HRI risk beyond that attributable to hot days, consistent with impaired overnight thermoregulatory recovery, without which workers may begin the following work shift with residual heat strain. Tmin in this study was a gridded ambient proxy rather than a real-time measurement of the sleeping environments workers actually experience, and future studies should include indoor sleeping temperature and sleep monitoring data to further explore associations and mechanisms of night-time temperature with occupational HRI risk. These results have implications for public health, occupational health, and worker housing policies. Acknowledgements: Safety & Health Assessment & Research for Prevention (SHARP) Program, Washington State Department of Labor & Industries (L&I)

492416.title: Predicting Passive Microwave Precipitation Biases Using Meteorological Information
492416.authors: Eric Goldenstern, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO
492416.abstract: Errors in satellite precipitation products are difficult to quantify due to the lack of a high quality, globally available ground truth dataset. Because of this, satellite precipitation errors cannot be directly quantified over much of the world, leaving crucial gaps in our understanding of product performance which must be filled. A method which utilizes information that can be gathered with relative ease over the whole Earth is thus desired. Since the large-scale environment dictates the formation of precipitating systems, this information should also provide some insight into their representation in satellite precipitation products and the errors therewithin. This study provides a first-steps investigation in using meteorological information to directly quantify satellite precipitation errors. The method presented here, termed the Satellite PRecipitation Errors from Ancillary Data (SPREAD) model, utilizes support vector regression to translate the information from multiple ERA5 parameters into observed precipitation errors. Tests of this method in the Tropics shows promising utility, while its application to the midlatitudes indicates further refinement is necessary. In all, this method presents a means by which to begin investigating the application of meteorological reasoning to fill gaps in the observational network’s bias quantification capabilities.

492417.title: Comparing The Vertical Exchange of Scalars Parameterized by Planetary Boundary Layer Schemes to LES in a Heterogeneous Convective Boundary Layer.
492417.authors: Jason Patrick Horne, The University of Massachusetts, Broomfield, CO; and Y. Pan and K. J. Davis
492417.abstract: Planetary boundary layer (PBL) parameterizations are critical for representing vertical exchange in climate and numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. Yet the assumptions underlying most schemes become questionable as horizontal grid lengths approach 1 km or finer, particularly over highly heterogeneous surfaces. Here we use a nested Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulation spanning the mesoscale to the neighborhood scale, with the innermost domain centered over Baltimore City, Maryland, to simulate two idealized afternoon periods during a summer heatwave. The nested configuration allows direct comparison between the exchange parameterized in the outer domains and that captured by the large-eddy simulation (LES) in the innermost domain. Vertical fluxes of temperature and moisture differ substantially between the two, indicating that the PBL scheme does not capture the profile nonlinearity captured by the LES. Despite these differences in flux divergence, the temporal evolution of the associated scalar profiles is remarkably similar between the two, as the divergence differences are balanced by advective tendencies. Examination of the prognostic budget of resolved covariance reveals terms that depart from profiles expected under horizontal homogeneity and are not in equilibrium, which is related to the characteristic length scale of heterogeneity and the numerical grid length. These results highlight the risks of applying conventional PBL parameterizations at finer NWP grid spacing and motivate the continued work towards schemes that relax classical assumptions such as horizontal homogeneity.

492418.title: Spatial and Seasonal Climate Trends across Mexico during 1961-2017
492418.authors: Evi Becerra-Acosta, University of Leon, Leon, Spain; and A. I. Calvo, J. M. Polanco-Martinez, and R. Fraile
492418.abstract: Long-term climate change across Mexico exhibits substantial spatial and seasonal variability, reflecting the country's complex topography and diverse climatic regimes. The present analysis investigates changes in maximum temperature (TX), minimum temperature (TN), precipitation (P), and diurnal temperature range (DTR) across Mexico from 1961 to 2017. Emphasis is placed on the robustness of these patterns under explicitly quantified spatial uncertainty, the degree to which ERA5-Land reproduces observed trends, and whether asymmetric changes in daytime and nighttime temperatures are reflected in DTR. Seasonal trends were estimated using Sen’s slope estimator, and their statistical significance was evaluated with the non-parametric Mann–Kendall test. Station-level trends were further analyzed within a hierarchical Bayesian spatial framework that incorporated elevation as a covariate, yielding spatially continuous estimates of trend magnitude and associated uncertainty. The diurnal temperature range (DTR) was calculated as the difference between maximum and minimum temperatures and analyzed to determine whether daytime and nighttime temperatures have changed at different rates. The results demonstrate widespread warming in both maximum and minimum temperatures, although the magnitude and spatial distribution of these changes vary significantly across Mexico. Maximum temperature exhibits particularly consistent warming during the dry season, while minimum temperature displays distinct regional patterns, including localized areas of weaker warming or cooling. These contrasting TX and TN responses underscore the relevance of analyzing DTR as an indicator of asymmetric daytime and nighttime warming. Precipitation trends are notably more heterogeneous, with generally weak changes during the dry season and more pronounced positive trends during the wet season, especially in southern Mexico. Comparison with ERA5-Land reveals broad agreement in large-scale climate variability but highlights important differences in trend magnitude, particularly for minimum temperature and wet-season precipitation. These findings reveal pronounced regional and seasonal contrasts in climate change across Mexico and underscore the importance of accounting for asymmetric daytime and nighttime warming, as well as spatial uncertainty, when interpreting long-term climatic trends.

492420.title: Advancing Flood Inundation Map Design Through Testbed Development and User Testing
492420.authors: Prabhjot Singh, University of Minnesota, St. Paul, MN; and S. Kandel, D. Munasinghe, M. Singh, P. Halalae, A. Patel, K. Abshire, J. Dobur, C. Gobs, S. Cohen, and M. A. Kenney
492420.abstract: Interactive decision support tools are increasingly used by federal agencies to translate complex forecasts into actionable information. Effective flood risk communication depends not only on the forecast accuracy of flood inundation maps (FIM) but also on how the information is presented and interpreted by end users. To better understand how to improve the presentation of information and increase the understandability of decision support tools like NOAA's National Water Prediction Service (NWPS), this research 1) designed and developed a web-based usability testing platform that emulates NWPS, and 2) uses that platform to rigorously evaluate how design and communication interventions affect the usability of NWPS FIM products. With guidance from NOAA Office of Water Prediction partners, decision support social scientists at the University of Minnesota’s Institute on the Environment collaborated with front-end web developers at the University of Alabama to design and inform the development of an experimental research platform that mirrors the layout and interactivity of NOAA NWPS and its embedded FIM services. This platform provides a controlled testing environment for conducting usability and understandability studies of flood data and forecast information available on NWPS. Building on this platform, we conduct an experimental study testing how specific design and communication interventions influence users' ability to navigate, interpret, and use NWPS flood data and visualizations. This work will generate empirical evidence on effective visualization and communication strategies and inform operational design recommendations for improving the usability of interactive flood-data products. The impact of this work reaches beyond its initial application and institutional partnership by providing a reusable research testbed for experimentally evaluating an interactive decision support tool. Because the platform allows researchers to modify experimental conditions, it can support future studies designed and run by the broader environmental decision support community and other social scientists. In doing so, it sustains the collaborative, interdisciplinary spirit that shaped its development, while extending its value far beyond this project alone.

492422.title: Multi-Model Comparison of Machine Learning Approaches for AI Enhancement of Satellite Microwave Precipitation Retrievals
492422.authors: Wei Wang, NOAA, College Park, MD
492422.abstract: Accurate satellite-based precipitation retrievals are essential for weather nowcasting, hydrologic forecasting, and hazard monitoring, among many other applications. NOAA's Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS) provides operational precipitation retrievals from passive microwave observations using a physically based one-dimensional variational (1DVAR) retrieval framework. While the baseline MiRS algorithm effectively captures large-scale precipitation patterns across diverse observing systems, systematic regional biases and challenges in representing complex precipitation structures remain. Recent advances in machine learning provide new opportunities to enhance physically based retrievals through data-driven post-processing while preserving the physical consistency of the original retrieval. This study presents a comprehensive comparison of four machine learning architectures for improving MiRS precipitation retrievals: a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), a Residual Neural Network (ResNet), a U-Net, and a Vision Transformer for Precipitation Retrieval (ViT-PR). Rather than replacing the operational retrieval algorithm, each model learns the systematic errors in the baseline MiRS product and generates refined precipitation estimates. Training samples are constructed directly from the native satellite scan geometry, preserving the original spatial characteristics of microwave observations. The input features include MiRS-retrieved atmospheric, hydrologic, and surface parameters together with ancillary geometric information, while the difference between the MiRS precipitation retrieval and the corresponding MRMS precipitation estimate is used as the target for learning the systematic retrieval error. Model performance is evaluated over the contiguous United States using Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) precipitation as the reference dataset. All four models are trained and evaluated using identical datasets (NOAA-20 observations) and verification procedures to ensure a fair comparison. Performance is assessed using both continuous and categorical verification metrics, including root-mean-square error (RMSE) and Heidke Skill Score (HSS). The comparison also examines each model's ability to reproduce precipitation spatial structures, rain-rate distributions, and regional precipitation characteristics. The results highlight the strengths and limitations of different machine learning architectures for satellite precipitation retrieval enhancement. The MLP provides an efficient baseline, while ResNet improves feature representation through residual learning. U-Net more effectively captures multi-scale spatial patterns and preserves precipitation morphology, leading to improved retrieval accuracy. The Transformer demonstrates the potential to model long-range spatial dependencies but requires greater computational resources and larger training datasets to fully realize its advantages. This comparative study provides practical guidance for selecting AI architectures for operational precipitation retrieval enhancement and supports the continued development of hybrid physics-AI retrieval systems within the NOAA MiRS framework for current and future microwave sensor constellations.

492425.title: Combined Convective Cloud Analysis Using Ground-Based ARM AMF3 Surface and GOES-19 Satellite Observations
492425.authors: Darby Stevenson, UAH, HUNTSVILLE, AL; and J. R. Mecikalski, J. A. Otkin, PhD, and D. S. Henderson
492425.abstract: With the advent of the ARM Mobile Facility-3 (AMF3) surface and boundary layer observations in the Bankhead National Forest of North Alabama in October 2024, research continues on combining select ground observations, GOES-19 satellite cloud property retrieved fields (i.e. in-cloud updraft estimates), and numerical weather prediction datasets toward forming new insights into the evolution of cumulus clouds before, during, and after convective storm initiation (CI). The analysis is being done as a function of planetary boundary layer (PBL) structure and land surface conditions, with a focus on mainly daytime hours in the humid months of June-August for several summer seasons. One project goal is to determine how AMF3 ground-based observations of convective clouds can augment cloud top information provided by geostationary satellites, which together can be used to understand PBL and environmental conditions influencing cumulus cloud updraft structure and in-cloud updraft velocities, and subsequently cloud growth rates, depth and type evolution. Furthermore, the research seeks to discern macrophysical cumulus cloud properties in combined ground- and satellite- observations, and how the science community can gain more information on convective clouds and the CI process from satellite-based fields than is presently known. Specifically, we are investigating how these factors interact with conditions in the lower troposphere to ultimately determine CI success or failure. This presentation will discuss the methodology that co-locates AMF3 datasets in time, as spatial averaging is performed to match the GOES-19 5-min resolution cloud datasets within ~1.5° x ~1.5° latitude/longitude surrounding the AMF3 site. The analysis also combines ARM surface-based observations cloud base and in-cloud updrafts (from the KAZR vertically pointing, 915 MHz radar wind profiler, and Doppler lidar) with GOES-19 derived in-cloud updrafts, to help determine relationships between PBL structure and in-cloud updraft characteristics. Environmental measurements from radiosonde, surface meteorology and tower observations are included to identify how thermodynamic and surface flux conditions relate to cloud evolution and updraft behavior. To separate the types of cloud transitions observed during the study period, a GOES-19 based unsupervised classification, convective cloud mask product is applied across the study domain to identify the coverage of various cloud types, to find distinct “cloudy-day” types based on the spatial and temporal evolution of low-warm and convective clouds. Through K-means cluster analysis, six cloudy-day types are identified, which relate to how low cloud cover (in terms of percentage across the study domain) and cloud types evolve from ~1200 UTC to 0000 UTC on all days. The study days are further separated by weak synoptic forcing to isolate the influence of local PBL processes on cumulus cloud development and CI, to highlight where land-atmosphere coupling has a larger impact. Our results will be in the form of both statistical and case study analyses to help explain updraft characteristics as a function of cloud evolution (cloud coverage and type changes), from morning through the afternoon on all study days.

492429.title: DLESyM-v2: A Coupled Earth-System Model for Simulation of the Current Climate
492429.authors: Dale R. Durran, Univ. of Washington, Seattle, WA; and N. A. Cresswell-Clay, Z. I. Espinosa, R. A. Moreno, W. J. Yik, A. Subramaniam, P. Harrington, D. Pruitt, S. Janardhan, and M. Pritchard
492429.abstract: Stable highly realistic 1000-year simulations of the current climate were achieved by DLESyM-v1, a deterministic convolutional neural network coupling a 9-variable atmosphere model with an ocean model that included only SST. Here we report on the climatology of our coupled v2 model that includes 37 atmospheric variables and 22 oceanic variables including sea ice. As before, the model variables are defined on a globally uniform 110-km HEALPix mesh. Atmospheric variables in each atmospheric column are trained to satisfy an error-tolerant hydrostatic balance. From 100-year autoregressive simulations, we examine the performance of DLESyM-v2 on leading modes of extratropical variability such as the Northern and Southern Annular Modes (the NAM and SAM) and blocking. We examine tropical cyclogenesis and the model’s representation of El Nino, as well as the model’s representation of sea ice and tropical waves. Historical simulations from 1970-2010 conducted as part of the 6th Coupled Model Intercomparison Experiment are used, along with ERA5 reanalysis, as standards of comparison against the climate generated in century-long free-running DLESyM-v2 simulations. UFS-replay data is used to evaluate sub-surface oceanic fields. The sensitivity of these results to training loss functions, checkpoint selection and initial conditions on ensemble mean forecasts for 100-year simulations is also discussed. The performance difference between MSE and variants of CRPS loss is of particular interest.

492432.title: Assembly and Quantitative Analysis of Burn Scar Induced Flash Flood and Debris Flow Events in Colorado (2000-2025)
492432.authors: Addison Meyer, National Weather Service Boulder / University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL
492432.abstract: Wildfire burn scars promote highly impactful and sometimes deadly flash flood and debris flow (FFDF) events across much of the western United States. Colorado lacks a comprehensive, robust, database of burn scar induced FFDF events. Additionally, very little quantitative analysis of FFDF events has ever been attempted in Colorado. Quantifying burn scar sensitivity and year-over-year trends would both improve the understanding of FFDF events, and aid in National Weather Service (NWS) warning operations for future burn scars. This study builds the foundation for a historical Colorado burn scar induced FFDF event database by compiling 264 FFDF event reports since 2000. Extensive quality control techniques were utilized to ensure FFDF reports could reliably be linked to rainfall on a particular burn scar. Additionally, the study examines the connections across four prominent (multiple years with FFDF reports) Colorado burn scars in an attempt to establish rainfall thresholds to be used in warning operations by NWS offices. Using Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) quantitative estimation precipitation data, extensive analysis of basin specific maximum and mean rainfall totals at least an hour before a given event shows that most burn scars recover quickly. Within the first year of the examined fires, FFDF events occurred with a mean basin average rainfall total of 0.23”, with a maximum of 0.66”. Within two years of the initial burn, mean basin average totals increased to 0.38” as maximum increased to 1.08”, an increase of 0.15” (65.2%) and 0.42” (63.6%) respectively, indicating the total rainfall required to generate high impact FFDF events increases year over year as recovery progresses. Rainfall total trends were computed as the burn scar recovers with the goal of utilizing similar methodologies to develop dynamic rainfall total thresholds for future burn scars. Finally, this work also developed a Google Sites-based burn scar induced FFDF page that NWS forecasters across Colorado can visit to view detailed information on the 264 FFDF events since 2000.

492435.title: NOAA’s Coupled Weather and Smoke/Dust Forecast Model - RRFS-Smoke/Dust
492435.authors: Ravan Ahmadov, NOAA/OAR/GSL, Boulder, CO; and J. Romero-Alvarez, H. Li, S. Bhimireddy, J. Schnell, E. P. James, G. Ferrada, G. A. Grell, M. Hu, J. B. Olson, L. Bernardet, C. R. Alexander, P. S. Bhattacharjee, S. Kondragunta, C. Xu, H. Zhang, B. Koziol, C. Evans, D. D. Turner, F. Li, B. D. Baker II, M. E. Pyle, B. Blake, J. R. Carley, and F. Yang
492435.abstract: NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory, in collaboration with partner laboratories, has developed the Rapid Refresh Forecast System with Smoke and Dust (RRFS-SD), a next-generation coupled weather-aerosol forecast model. Currently running in real time, the RRFS-SD model will be fully operational at NOAA/NWS by the time of the AMS conference. The model grid covers all of North America at a 3 km spatial resolution. RRFS-SD ingests the fire radiative power (FRP) from Regional ABI and VIIRS Emissions (RAVE) product to estimate biomass-burning emissions and fire heat fluxes in real-time. The model parameterizes plume injection based on these heat flux estimates and prevailing meteorological conditions. Additionally, we have implemented the Hourly Wildfire Potential (HWP) index, which leverages model-predicted meteorological variables, including hourly air temperature, humidity, wind gusts, and soil moisture. The RRFS-SD explicitly simulates fine particulate matter from biomass burning and both fine and coarse dust aerosols generated by windblown emissions. The model includes their radiative feedback as well. Initialized hourly by assimilating meteorological observations and ingesting the RAVE FRP data, the model cycles smoke and dust tracers between forecasts. Forecast lengths extend to 84 hours for 00, 06, 12, and 18 UTC cycles, and to 18 hours for other cycles. Forecast products are accessible via the NOAA-developed interactive visualization tool, DESI, and other sources. This presentation will detail the capabilities of the RRFS-SD and show the results of evaluation for the model performance during the 2026 U.S. fire season, a period marked by significant wildfire activity across the western United States. During these wildfires millions of people in the US were impacted by poor air quality and visibility. I will present evaluation results comparing smoke forecasts against ground-based in-situ and remote sensing data, as well as satellite observations from JPSS and TEMPO, and conclude by discussing lessons learned and future model improvements.

492443.title: Updated Hazard Services Threats in Motion Testing at the National Weather Service Operational Proving Ground.
492443.authors: Kevin L. Manross, CIRA, Ft. Collins, CO; and J. J. Brost, G. J. Stumpf, D. Tomalak, R. Walsh, D. M. Kingfield, and N. R. Hardin
492443.abstract: Changes within the National Weather Service (NWS) are nothing new. Throughout its existence personnel arrive, retire, and change duty offices. Other changes are occurring with programmatic restructuring, new concepts, and new technologies. The NWS Operational Proving Ground (OPG) is where many of the science driven changes make their way into operations and the personnel that will be using these new techniques. The Threats-in-Motion (TIM) concept - the idea of updating existing warning polygons by moving them with the storm, as opposed to “stacking” new warnings at the end of expiring ones - has been tested and refined over several years, including at the OPG. However, several factors are coming together that would benefit from another round of testing TIM at the OPG. Among those changes are an influx of new forecasters, a new software platform for all NWS offices known as the Hydrometeorological Interactive Virtual Environment (HIVE), and a new workflow for TIM. This presentation will explore the new TIM workflow as well as the effort to have forecasters become aware of the concepts and use cases for TIM in the warning process through exercises at the OPG. The experience gained through these exercises aims to both prepare the forecaster for TIM operations, as well as set the standard for implementation of TIM within the new HIVE environment.

492450.title: A High Resolution Nested Replay Simulation for Extreme Precipitation and PMP Modernization
492450.authors: Brett M. Basarab, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and K. M. Mahoney, S. Frolov, B. Liu, and L. Bengtsson
492450.abstract: Datasets that accurately represent extreme precipitation at high resolution have numerous applications, including ongoing efforts at NOAA to modernize estimates of Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP). We introduce initial multi-year results from a novel UFS-based “Nested Replay” simulation which includes a 3-km grid spacing nest covering the conterminous United States (CONUS) within a 12.5-km global grid. In place of traditional data assimilation, the Replay methodology calculates the analysis increments between the UFS forecast and an external precalculated analysis (in this case ERA5). We demonstrate that Nested Replay is skillful in the detection and placement of precipitation events within its high-resolution nest when verified against the 4-km Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC) precipitation dataset. For the time periods evaluated, Nested Replay also shows improved depictions of precipitation compared to the CONUS404 dataset, specifically in the placement of larger precipitation events such as central US mesoscale convective systems. For several extreme precipitation case studies evaluated, Nested Replay is skillful in the spatial and temporal depiction of the event and simulates amounts that agree reasonably well with AORC. Future work will include refining the Nested Replay workflow within the Cylc framework to facilitate expanding the dataset to at least 30 years (likely 1994-2024). Additionally, we will undertake a comprehensive evaluation of Nested Replay’s performance for extreme precipitation. It is expected that Nested Replay will support a variety of future purposes such as the aforementioned PMP modernization efforts while serving as a suitable alternative to traditional reanalyses.

492451.title: Improving Extreme Precipitation Forecasts via Cascade Binary Classification with Diffusion Post-Processing
492451.authors: Huiling Yuan, Nanjing Univ., Nanjing, China; Nanjing University, Nanjing, 32, China; and L. Dai
492451.abstract: Accurate forecasting of extreme precipitation remains a critical challenge, owing to its heavy-tailed distribution and severe class imbalance that limit conventional deep learning approaches. This study presents a two-stage cascade-diffusion framework for extreme precipitation forecasting over eastern China (110°–130°E, 20°–40°N). The first stage employs a cascade binary classification module comprising 15 independent U-Net models. Each model is trained for a specific precipitation threshold and integrated via hierarchical stacking, producing a coarse-resolution (0.25°) diagnostic field with reliable spatial localization across intensity levels. The second stage employs a diffusion-based post-processing module for simultaneous bias correction and probabilistic spatial downscaling from 0.25° to 0.1°. This step recovers distributional continuity and preserves the heavy-precipitation tail via higher-percentile ensemble aggregation (P80, P90). The framework uses ERA5 reanalysis and GPM IMERG over 2013–2023, with 2023 as an independent test year. Results demonstrate that the cascade module achieves Critical Success Index (CSI) improvements of 25%–54% over regression and multi-task learning baselines at the 50–100 mm 6h⁻¹ thresholds. The diffusion post-processing module further improves distributional fidelity, with P80 and P90 aggregation both achieving strong detection skill at high thresholds. While P90 attains the highest CSI at extreme thresholds, P80 provides a more balanced performance with better-controlled frequency bias. Variable importance analysis via sequential feature selection reveals physically interpretable, threshold-dependent pressure-level contributions. Near-surface levels dominate across all intensities, while upper-tropospheric levels provide progressively greater marginal skill for extreme events. These results establish the cascade-diffusion framework as a practically viable approach for operational extreme precipitation forecasting.

492452.title: The July, 2026 Wildfire Smoke Outbreak: Challenges and Impacts for New York
492452.authors: Nick P. Bassill, University at Albany, Albany, NY; and S. J. Breslin
492452.abstract: 2026 has seen numerous wildfire events associated with significant reductions in air quality for locations downwind of those fires. One significant event occurred in July 2026, originating from wildfires across central and southern Canada, as well as far northern Minnesota. Wildfire smoke from this event was carried eastward into the Great Lakes and eastern U.S. states, including New York (NY). A similar - and high impact - event occurred approximately three years earlier, which increased concern over the potential effects of this event in NY. Unlike most traditional weather hazards (winter storms, hurricanes, heatwaves, etc.), air quality associated with wildfires is unusually difficult to predict due to several factors. Two primary factors are (1) the presence and extent of ongoing wildfires (which can change day to day) and (2) the vertical distribution of smoke, which can frequently be plentiful aloft, but which may not always reach the surface. Relatedly, there are few smoke forecasting models with significant lead time, in contrast to the multitude of widely available models used to forecast other types of weather hazards. As is typical in many states, the National Weather Service (NWS) offices in NY relay air quality advisories produced by a state organization: in this case, the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC). The NYSDEC issues air quality alerts up to one day in advance for various regions in NY, and for both fine particulates and ozone. Concurrently, a relatively new organization in NY titled the NY State Weather Risk Communication Center (NYSWRCC) is tasked with assisting the state’s emergency management infrastructure relating to weather events. Like NWS, this organization primarily relays and interprets (where needed) products issued by the NYSDEC. They also make ancillary products regarding wildfire smoke derived from other sources, to assist with interpretation. This presentation will briefly describe the July 2026 wildfires, before discussing the forecasting and communication challenges inherent in wildfire-induced air quality forecasting. Products and tools produced by the NYSDEC and NYSWRCC will be shown, and the relationship between these respective organizations and others in NY will also be discussed. Finally, a brief comparison between the impacts of this event to a similar event three years prior will be highlighted.

492453.title: Aerosol Influence on Radiative Feedback During Tropical Cyclone Intensification
492453.authors: Mitchell David Voelker, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL
492453.abstract: In a developing tropical cyclone (TC), the deep convection and high clouds aggregate near the developing storm center. The high clouds reduce longwave radiative cooling in the cloudy core compared with the clear, dry surroundings because less longwave radiation is allowed to escape the TC. The radiative feedback of reduced cooling (or, radiatively driven warming) occurs at the core of the TC and acts as a greenhouse effect within the TC. The radiative feedback of the high ice clouds accelerates the warming that occurs at the center of circulation, so the total thermodynamic energy of the column increases. Thus, the moist static energy (MSE) – a measure of the total thermodynamic energy contained in a parcel of moist air – aggregates faster. Alongside this radiative feedback, surface evaporation off the ocean surface supplies warm, moist air to the boundary layer of the developing cyclone while the low-level inflow of the TC concentrates it at the center. Deep convection lifts the moist air, producing condensation and freezing that releases latent heat within the storm core. These processes drive self-aggregation of MSE in TCs, but cloud-radiative feedback accelerates self-development of TCs. Wing (2022) found that including the radiative feedback in convection-permitting simulations accelerates TC development by a factor of 2 or more. This project uses the System for Atmospheric Modeling (SAM) with the Morrison et al. (2005) two-moment microphysics scheme to investigate tropical cyclone intensification. SAM simulations initialize with varying concentrations of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) concentrations and ice nucleating particles (INP). The control experiment will have a medium number of ice nuclei and a medium number of cloud condensation nuclei. The rest of the experiments will vary initial CCN from low to high concentration and initial INP from low to high concentration. For example, one experiment would have a high number of CCN with a low number of INP, another experiment would have a high number of INP with a low number of CCN. Different CCN and INP conditions produce different hydrometeor mass and number concentrations that evolve with time. Consequently, the varying hydrometeor size distributions alter precipitation processes, sedimentation, cloud lifetime, and anvil structure. The altered cloud properties change the longwave and shortwave radiative feedback. Those feedback changes influence the rate and spatial pattern of frozen moist static energy (FMSE) aggregation, which is connected to TC organization and intensification. Therefore, this experimental setup allows for the advantage of determining the aerosol and microphysical conditions that produce the ice cloud structures that strengthen or weaken the cloud-radiative feedback.

492455.title: The Convective Engine: Results from Modeling and Field Experiments of Initiating Convection via Updraft Generation
492455.authors: Tyler Pardun, Convective Technology Company, San Jose, CA; and W. Winograd, D. Anderson, T. Kosaraju, S. Letizia, A. Rybchuk, and A. Scholbrock
492455.abstract: Since the Météotron campaigns of the 1960s in France, Cuba, and the Soviet Union, researchers have used large ground-based heat sources to study buoyant plumes, vortices, and cloud formation. Deliberate initiation of moist convection could support future water-resource and hazard-mitigation applications, but causal attribution remains a central scientific challenge. Many historical experiments, however, lacked quality remote sensing and cloud-resolving models needed to trace and model a source-driven plume from surface forcing to condensation and, eventually, deep convection. We present observations and simulations from a summer 2026 field campaign using the Convective Engine, a combustion-based surface heat source designed to initiate atmospheric convection. Experiments were conducted at a flat midlatitude site during periods of high lower-tropospheric moisture and weak boundary-layer winds. During the campaign, the engine generated a coherent updraft followed by cumulus development within the source plume. A scanning Doppler wind lidar detected the induced updraft in radial velocity and the subsequent cloud signature in signal-to-noise ratio. A collocated Atmospheric Emitted Radiance Interferometer retrieved environmental temperature and water-vapor profiles used to characterize the lifting and condensation environment. Together, the measurements resolve the sequence from source activation through plume ascent to condensation in time, space, and thermodynamic context. This continuity supports attribution of the observed cumulus to the engineered source. We compare the observed evolution with simulations using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model, focusing on surface forcing, entrainment, cloud-base attainment, and sensitivity to the ambient environment. Implications for future study and operational precipitation enhancement are discussed.

492456.title: Advancing Water Literacy: Communicating Snow Drought and Runoff Efficiency for Actionable Decision Making
492456.abstract: Persistent water supply challenges across the Western United States highlight the need to align evolving snow drought and runoff efficiency science with critical decision making. Addressing measurement uncertainties, nuanced definitions, and communication needs at the regional scale requires digestible, user-centric information tools in order to make water management more streamlined. Working in conjunction with NOAA’s National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS), a synthesized report of the key takeaways from the Science Informed Spring Runoff Management Workshop, held on March 31st, 2026, in Glenwood Springs, Colorado, an updated snow drought resource page, and an expanded standardized snow drought glossary on Drought.gov were created to help support improved understanding of drought preparedness, mitigation, and response. Throughout the development of these products, key themes regarding communication and science needs emerged, which are detailed further in this presentation. Capturing these themes required establishing ongoing interdisciplinary dialogue across all key stakeholders, including researchers, forecasters, and operators. Understanding user interests and their challenges is an iterative process that can aid in the refinement and expansion of contextual resources. Improving the interpretation and communication of snow drought and runoff efficiency would make this emerging field of research more actionable for stakeholders, addressing the continuous challenge of empowering decision making with accessible, user-centric tools.

492459.title: Observations of Large Lake Ice Thickness Using ICESat-2: A Framework for Monitoring Freshwater Coastal Environments
492459.authors: Isabella Peter, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and E. J. Anderson, N. Kurtz, M. R. Siegfried, and B. Villas Boas
492459.abstract: More than 80% of Earth's liquid surface freshwater is contained within only ten large lakes, yet regional observations of lake ice freeboard and thickness remain limited. The Laurentian Great Lakes support extensive commercial navigation and coastal communities, but limited ice observations constrain the development, evaluation, and operation of coastal hydrodynamic and ice forecasting systems. Satellite laser altimetry provides a unique opportunity to address this observational gap by directly measuring surface elevations across large freshwater systems. We present a novel framework for retrieving lake ice freeboard and thickness from ICESat-2 Inland Surface Water (ATL13) observations, using the Laurentian Great Lakes as a testbed. The methodology integrates satellite laser altimetry with multisensor remote sensing products and operational model output to develop algorithms for (1) ice and open-water surface classification, (2) estimation of water surface elevations beneath and adjacent to ice cover, and (3) incorporation of snow depth and snow water equivalent information required to convert freeboard to ice thickness. The resulting framework produces the first regional, observation-based dataset of lake ice freeboard and thickness across the Great Lakes. Algorithm performance and uncertainty are quantified throughout the retrieval process, providing confidence estimates for the derived ice thickness observations. Beyond demonstrating a new application of ICESat-2, this work introduces a novel observational dataset that can support validation and improvement of coastal hydrodynamic and ice models, evaluation of coupled forecasting systems, and future data assimilation efforts in seasonally ice-covered freshwater environments. By expanding the observational record available to modelers and operational forecasting systems, these measurements provide new opportunities to improve winter navigation, coastal hazard prediction, and long-term assessments of changing ice conditions across Earth's largest freshwater lakes.

492464.title: Hygroscopic Seeding to Trigger a Natural Secondary Ice Process and Potential for Rain Enhancement
492464.authors: Paul Lawson, SPEC Incorporated, Boulder, CO; SPEC Inc., Boulder, CO; and P. Morris, S. Calderón, and S. Romakkaniemi
492464.abstract: Results from several filed projects show that cumulus clouds with warm cloud-base temperatures (e.g. 23 °C) and broad cloud drop size distributions (DSDs) will form a strong coalescence process, supercooled large drops (SLDs) and a secondary ice process (SIP) via the fragmentation of freezing drops (FFD) (Lawson et al. 2015, 2017, 2022, 2023). The FFD SIP in these clouds generally results in heavy rain at cloud base. On the other hand, cold-based (e.g., 0 °C) cumulus clouds with narrow drop distributions do not produce SLDs via coalescence and the FFD SIP does not occur (Lawson et al. 2022). Cumulus clouds with intermediate cloud-base temperatures and DSDs may form weak coalescence, which is inadequate to trigger the FFD SIP. Seeding at cloud base with appropriate hygroscopic material may enhance coalescence and trigger the FFD SIP. Once the FFD SIP is triggered in clouds where it would not normally occur, the resulting generation of abundant small ice particles will be dispersed via turbulent motions and freeze other SLDs, thereby creating an avalanche process that rapidly freezes the supercooled cloud region. In this presentation we present results from seven recent field projects and compare with modeling studies. Simulations from the UCLA-SALSA model show that the FFD SIP initiates after SLDs form near – 12 °C in a cloud with base temperature of 17.5 °C and broad drop size distribution (Calderón et al. 2025), which agrees with measurements from Lawson et al. (2023). Subsequent to the FFD SIP, rime splintering and ice-ice collisions further enhance ice particle concentration. The model also suggests that once SLDs form after hygroscopic seeding and SIP processes dominate, rainfall is enhanced at cloud base. We present results from simulations with a range of cloud base temperatures, aerosol (CCN) size distributions and CAPE, and compare with measurements from the seven field projects. Calderon, S. 492466.title: The Consortium for Enhancing Resilience and Catastrophe Modeling (CERCat): Strengthening Academic-Private Sector Partnerships for Climate Adaptation
492466.authors: Scott Weaver, CLIMET Consulting, LLC, Gaithersburg, MD
492466.abstract: As impacts from extreme weather events continue to increase, it has become clear that strengthened climate adaptation strategies are necessary to ensure our Nation’s prosperity and security, through its ability to effectively rebound from weather, water, and climate disasters. Given their multi-causal nature (e.g., hazard intensity & societal factors), reducing impacts from these disasters requires interdisciplinary scientific partnerships. However, recent changes in federal science priorities, coupled with unique interpretations of federal appropriations law, highlight great uncertainty in future federal support for applied climate adaptation research. Therefore, new partnerships are being forged and developed to continue effectively integrating new science and technology advancements into our response to the Nation’s most pressing issues in meteorological disaster resilience. The Consortium for Enhancing Resilience and Catastrophe Modeling (CERCat) is a new academic-private sector partnership led by the Engineering Departments at Lehigh and Rice Universities, forged by investments from an array of public and private sector disaster sensitive member organizations. CERCat provides the environment for these critical research partnerships to thrive, not only advancing fundamental understanding of the climate-weather-disaster interface, but exploiting that knowledge to develop practical and actionable solutions to reduce extreme weather impacts. The discussion will focus on a brief history of CERCat, the motivation for its proposed research and development activities in weather and climate, a description of selected inaugural projects, advantages of leveraging both financial and research resources across consortium members, and a vision for CERCat’s future.

492470.title: Analysis of Heavy Precipitation, Antecedent Soil Moisture, and Subsequent Streamflow within the Upper Washita River CEAP watersheds
492470.authors: Paul X. Flanagan, ARS, El Reno, OK; and A. M. Fortuna and S. Hunt
492470.abstract: Agricultural watershed conservation practices are created to protect the ecosystem from known threats, primarily agricultural runoff and soil erosion. In the Southern Great Plains, the natural drivers of these threats take the form of meteorological and climatological extremes, such as high magnitude precipitation events (floods) and prolonged periods of little to no precipitation (droughts). This study seeks to further the understanding of heavy and extreme precipitation events within two monitored conservation watersheds in the Upper Washita River linked to the Conservation Effects Assessment Project (CEAP), the Little Washita River and Fort Cobb Reservoir experimental watersheds located in southwestern Oklahoma. Using observed data from both watersheds this study will investigate heavy and extreme precipitation events across both watersheds, linking their inputs of water to antecedent soil moisture, or the average daily soil moisture the day before the precipitation event, and increased surface runoff. Further, the heavy and extreme precipitation events will also be linked to subsequent stream discharge, to quantify how the high inputs of water impact the hydrology of the watersheds. In both watersheds, heavy (~ 70% of annual total precipitation) and extreme precipitation (~ 25% of annual total precipitation) events made up a large portion of the annual total precipitation between 2006 and 2024. Analysis into heavy and extreme precipitation events illustrate that while increased soil water content (above median, or ~ 10 – 20%) leads to an increased probability of a larger subsequent streamflow event (> 10 m3 s-1), high streamflow was depicted at all soil water content levels. Given the noted erodibility issues of the two CEAP experimental watersheds, these results provide area stakeholders more information on the environmental conditions that lead impactful precipitation events within the Upper Washita River subwatersheds.

492471.title: Automated Fire Forecasting and Monitoring Using Satellite Fire Detections
492471.authors: James Haley, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and K. Hillburn, A. Farguell, and J. A. Otkin
492471.abstract: Wildfire forecasting and monitoring are critical for proactive fire management and emergency response. We present a fully automated wildfire forecasting and monitoring system that continuously detects new wildfires from near real-time satellite observations, initializes and executes fire spread forecasts without manual intervention, and provides an integrated web-based interface for monitoring active incidents. The system ingests active fire detections from GOES-R geostationary satellites and JPSS polar-orbiting satellites through the Next Generation Fire System (NGFS). These observations initialize WRF-SFIRE, a coupled atmosphere–fire model controlled with WRFXPY, while interactive visualization tools integrate current satellite detections with active forecasts to provide situational awareness, monitor forecast evolution, and evaluate forecast performance across all active incidents. The system has generated forecasts for more than 10,000 wildfire incidents across the United States and continues to operate in near real time. This presentation highlights recent advances to the operational system, including integrated web-based monitoring tools that combine current satellite observations with active forecasts in a unified display, incorporation of enhanced NGFS satellite products, and algorithmic improvements to the forecasting pipeline that reduce the time between satellite detection and forecast availability. Together, these developments improve situational awareness, accelerate forecast delivery, and enhance the operational value of automated wildfire forecasting for emergency management and fire response.

492473.title: Enhancing Public Engagement through Weather History: A Climate Library for the Commonwealth of Kentucky (CLoCK)
492473.authors: Jerald A. Brotzge, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and A. Nemon, M. Gripshover, D. Klein, M. Menig, and A. Oldham
492473.abstract: In 2024, the Kentucky State Climate Office, the Kentucky Climate Center (KCC), received a seed grant from NSF EPSCoR to build an online “climate library”. Before this time, the KCC had little online presence, with no state records or historical data available to the public. With this new funding, the KCC set out to design what is now called the “Climate Library for the Commonwealth of Kentucky (CLoCK)”. Once complete, CLoCK will be an online, GIS-based, interactive library available for education and research. CLoCK is comprised of several key components: (1) Listing of state and county records; (2) Timeline history of high-impact and notable weather and climate events; (3) Links to historical accounts (e.g., newspapers, diaries) describing the events; (4) Quality-controlled lists of all known tornado, severe hail, and severe wind events; (5) GIS-mapping of notable climate and weather events; and (6) Story maps of regional high-impact weather and climate. The end goal of this work is to create a “living” resource where local historical societies and weather enthusiasts contribute to building a collective climate narrative for multi-disciplinary education.

492476.title: Observations from the Lightning-Ignited Wildfire Campaign In Western Australia
492476.authors: Patrick N. Gatlin, MSFC, HUNTSVILLE, AL; and P. Bitzer, M. Wingo, J. C. Burchfield, and P. de Souza
492476.abstract: In 2025, an autonomous lightning mapping system was deployed to Western Australia for a field study on lightning-ignited bushfires. This system includes NASA’s portable Lightning Mapping Array (LMA) and UAH’s electric field change meters (FCM) that are both solar powered and utilize the cellular network to transfer data. The data is combined to locate cloud-to-ground lightning strikes within the domain, map their source regions within the cloud, and measure continuing current. These are the first such measurements in this region of Australia, which is very prone to bushfires October-February. During the 2025 bushfire season, many bushfires were reported within the LMA and FCM domain. This presentation will include an overview of the lightning activity recorded during that time and highlight the observations for a few bushfire events where lightning likely served as the ignition source.

492478.title: Intercomparison of Nighttime Aerosol Optical Depth Retrievals from Both Reflectance-Based and City Light-Based Methods Using VIIRS DNB Data
492478.authors: Aanan Schlief, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. W. Marquis, J. Zhang, J. S. Reid, and S. D. Miller
492478.abstract: Nighttime retrievals of Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) from conventional imaging radiometers in space is an inherently challenging problem, but imperative to completing the diurnal picture of this key atmospheric parameter. In this study, we intercompared two methods that retrieve nighttime AOD using Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) Day/Night Band (DNB) data over Dakar and Dakar Belair, Senegal for 2017-2019. Similar to the conventional daytime AOD retrieval methods which use reflected sun light, the first method retrieves nighttime AOD using reflected moonlight (lunar reflectance-based method). The second method derives nighttime AOD through measuring the changes in spatial homogeneity over regions with artificial light sources such as city lights (city light-based method). Through intercomparisons against daytime and nighttime Aerosol Robotic NETwork (AERONET) and daytime Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) AOD data, the performance of both nighttime aerosol retrieval methods is evaluated. Uncertainties in nighttime AOD retrievals due to cloud contamination and moon status are also investigated. In comparison with nighttime lunar AERONET AOD, the lunar reflectance-based method produces a correlation (r) of 0.57 and RMSE of 0.30, while the city light-based method has a correlation of 0.72 and RMSE of 0.16. Furthermore, this study reveals the limitations in data sampling for both retrieval methods and shows that a joint application of the two methods yields a more than 50% increase in nighttime AOD retrieval sampling rates.

492484.title: Reassessing Global Fire Emissions through New Satellite Constraints of Combustion Efficiency
492484.authors: Weizhi Deng, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; Univ. of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; and J. Wang, M. Zhou, L. Chutia, H. Zhang, L. Castro Garcia, A. da Silva, and W. Tang
492484.abstract: Large uncertainties remain in state-of-the-art fire emission inventories at regional and even global scales. One major unresolved source of uncertainty is the assumption of static modified combustion efficiency (MCE) values based on biome type, which fails to capture MCE variability within the same biome or its evolution throughout the fire life cycle. However, even small changes in MCE can significantly alter fire emission composition. Field measurements indicate that a 0.2 increase in MCE is associated with a fivefold reduction in CO emissions and a threefold increase in NOx emissions. We use new satellite constraints of MCE from the VIIRS FILDA-2 product to characterize the magnitude, spatial patterns, and temporal variability of combustion efficiency across global fire regimes. We find that global fires are generally more smoldering than assumed, and that MCE exhibits substantial spatial and temporal variability not captured by existing inventories. Using the QFED fire emission inventory as an example, we show that incorporating VIIRS MCE constraints significantly changes the composition of fire emissions, increasing annual global fire CO emissions by ~38% while decreasing NOx emissions by ~46%. GEOS-Chem simulations with MCE-constrained QFED emissions demonstrate improved representation of both the magnitude and seasonal variability of CO and NO2. Evaluation against MOPITT CO and OMI NO2 observations shows increases in explained variability of 10% and 8%, respectively, while reducing model mean biases by 88% and 80%. With the improved fire emissions, we then reassess the contributions of fires to the global tropospheric ozone budget. Finally, we demonstrate that the monthly MCE climatology derived from VIIRS observations can be applied to constrain historical fire emissions prior to the VIIRS era, providing a pathway to improve long-term fire emission and atmospheric composition reanalysis datasets extending into the MODIS period.

492485.title: Implementation of Probabilistic Hazards Information in Hazard Services for the 2026 PHI-Derived Warnings Evaluation at the NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed
492485.authors: Kevin L. Manross, CIRA, Ft. Collins, CO; and K. M. Calhoun, J. Monroe, J. Madden, P. A. Campbell, R. B. Steeves, A. V. Bates, G. J. Stumpf, K. L. Berry, and N. R. Hardin
492485.abstract: Improvement in warning performance is a never ending goal within the National Weather Service (NWS) along with providing better Impact-based Decision Support Services (IDSS) to partners. The NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory has developed Machine Learning (ML) based Probabilistic Hazards Information (PHI) recommenders aimed at helping forecasters diagnose storm severity and longevity as well as the likelihood of needing a new warning or continuing an existing one. Partnering with the NOAA Global Systems Laboratory, these PHI recommenders were ingested into Hazard Services to provide initial parameters, like location, area, motion and duration as well as probabilistic information to forecasters for new warnings or for deciding whether or not to continue a warning using the Threats-in-Motion (TIM) paradigm. A companion presentation (Calhoun et al.) will focus on results and forecaster feedback. This presentation will concentrate on the design and implementation of ingesting PHI into Hazard Services as a first guess for warning creation along with its relationship with the decision making process for TIM. This presentation will also discuss impacts PHI and TIM have on the NWS’s future forecasting software platform for forecasters - Hydrometeorological Interactive Virtual Environment (HIVE).

492489.title: Over the Moon: Global-Nested and Global-Storm Resolving Models with FV3, FMS, and SHiELD
492489.authors: Lucas M. Harris, GFDL, PRINCETON, NJ
492489.abstract: The next generation of ultra-high resolution weather and climate models requires modeling systems that are robust, accurate, efficient, and with the appropriate level of complexity. The Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory, in collaboration with external partners, is developing new modeling systems that enable frontier predictions. This is made possible through three core technologies: the highly-accurate and efficient FV3 Dynamical Core used in all NOAA and NASA global models; the unified SHiELD prediction model; and the elegant FMS infrastructure and Coupler. Together this tight coupling, lightweight software, flexible grid structure, and massive scaling permits new applications to be rapidly built, advanced, and applied to new scientific problems. SHiELD and the broader community of FV3-based models has led to significant advances in tropical cyclone prediction and extended-range kilometer-scale prediction, including of convective storms and atmospheric rivers. Unprecedented years-long X-SHiELD global storm resolving model simulations enable new uses transcending traditional global models or limited-area regional models. Further new applications are enabled through sub-kilometer telescopic nesting, Coupled-SHiELD with MOM6 and LM4, and GPU-accelerated PyFV3 and PySHiELD. You can learn more about FV3 and SHiELD from www.gfdl.noaa.gov/fv3 and www.gfdl.noaa.gov/shield.

492491.title: From the Microscale to the Exascale: Adventures in Clouds and the General Circulation
492491.abstract: The future trajectory of the earth system and the general circulation of the atmosphere are heavily modulated by clouds. The effect of cloud microphysical processes is paramount for distributing water and energy in the earth's atmosphere through precipitation processes and the radiative effects of clouds. The need to cross scales from the microscale to the global has motivated lots of explorations in simulating cloud physics at the global scale through new and novel developments in sub-grid parameterization of clouds. As compute power has increased, our ability to simulate more details in clouds, their interaction with turbulence, and their effects on the circulation has expanded. This presentation will highlight the many advances in cloud parameterization and their impacts on community earth system modeling championed by Dave Randall, from convective parameterization to super parameterization through to km-scale earth system modeling. It will also discuss recent work attacking these problems, including new detailed microphysical treatments enabled with Machine Learning approaches and cross-scale turbulence effects embedded in larger scale models, and future prospects for understanding cloud impacts at global scales.

492496.title: Multi-Timescale Emulation of the Community Atmosphere Model for Parameter Optimization
492496.authors: Grace Liu, Penn State University, University Park, PA; and C. M. Zarzycki
492496.abstract: Due to computational limits, Earth system models are run at relatively coarse resolutions and rely on parameterization schemes to capture subgrid-scale processes. These parameters are traditionally calibrated through careful, iterative experimentation, but the high computational cost of climate simulations constrains the speed of model development and increases the risk of converging to a local minimum where biases become more difficult to eliminate. In contrast, short simulations on the order of days are cheap to run and can provide abundant training data for machine learning methods, which excel at learning nonlinear parameter-response relationships. However, short runs alone are inadequate for tuning models designed to be run for multiple decades as they lack information about slow processes and compensating feedbacks that take weeks, months, or even years to emerge. In this presentation, we describe a two-step approach to emulating the Community Atmosphere Model version 7 (CAM7). We first train a short-term emulator on a large perturbed parameter ensemble (PPE) of 3-day simulations to capture fast parameter sensitivities. We then train a long-term emulator on a small subset of 30-year simulations to capture nonlinear feedbacks, slow responses, and long-term modulation of the mean climate. We primarily vary parameters from the CLUBB turbulence, Zhang–McFarlane deep convection, and PUMAS microphysics schemes. We evaluate the ability of the two-step framework to reproduce CAM7 responses across parameter space and explore surrogate-based parameter optimization to identify parameter values that match target climate statistics.

492497.title: Scalable and Operational Neighborhood-Level Air Temperature Forecasting across CONUS Cities Using Mixtures of Gaussian-Process Experts
492497.authors: Yutong Yao, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and P. Li and A. Sharma
492497.abstract: Neighborhood-scale air temperature forecasts are increasingly needed for urban heat-risk assessment, infrastructure and energy management, emergency response, and climate adaptation. Operational numerical weather prediction models provide the large-scale meteorological evolution required for these applications, but their kilometer-scale grid spacing does not resolve much of the spatial variability associated with urban development, vegetation, impervious surfaces, terrain, and land–water transitions. Consequently, locations within the same operational model grid cell can experience substantially different near-surface thermal conditions. Producing neighborhood-scale forecasts therefore requires a downscaling framework that combines regional meteorological information with high-resolution geographic characteristics and surface observations while maintaining computational feasibility for operational applications. We develop a scalable machine-learning framework for producing hourly, sub-kilometer 2-m air temperature forecasts across U.S. metropolitan areas. The framework integrates operational High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) meteorological fields, National Land Cover Database (NLCD) characteristics, U.S. Geological Survey 3D Elevation Program (3DEP) terrain information, and crowdsourced surface weather observations. These datasets provide nationally consistent meteorological, land-surface, and observational inputs and support model transfer across metropolitan regions without requiring specialized local urban simulations or city-specific geographic datasets. HRRR provides the evolving synoptic and mesoscale atmospheric state, while the higher-resolution geographic predictors characterize spatial heterogeneity within individual HRRR grid cells. The relationship between regional meteorology, geographic characteristics, and local air temperature is heterogeneous across the urban environment. Dense urban cores, suburban development, vegetated areas, open land, elevated terrain, and land–water transition zones can occupy distinct regions of the multidimensional predictor space and exhibit different temperature responses under similar regional atmospheric forcing. The modeling framework therefore applies fuzzy clustering to identify multimodal structure within the combined meteorological and geographic feature space. Each location is represented by a vector of membership values rather than assignment to a single discrete cluster. This formulation permits gradual transitions between environmental regimes and provides overlap among locations with similar predictor characteristics. A mixture of Gaussian-process (GP) experts is used to represent the resulting environmental modes. Each GP expert is trained using a selected subset of labeled observations that is representative of its corresponding region of feature space. Training-sample selection is used to maintain coverage of relevant environmental conditions, reduce redundancy among densely sampled conditions, and limit the computational cost associated with GP regression. Fuzzy membership values provide the weighting structure for combining predictions from multiple experts. Locations strongly associated with one environmental mode receive larger contributions from the corresponding expert, while locations near mode boundaries receive contributions from multiple experts. The weighted combination produces spatially continuous temperature fields and reduces discontinuities associated with hard clustering or spatially segmented models. The GP formulation also provides predictive uncertainty for each expert. Combined uncertainty fields are used to characterize confidence in the predicted temperature and identify conditions that are weakly represented by the available training observations. Locations with sparse training support, unusual combinations of meteorological and geographic predictors, or disagreement among relevant experts can therefore be identified during inference. These diagnostics provide information on extrapolation risk and can guide subsequent refinement of the training dataset or individual local experts. The framework is designed for repeated application over large metropolitan prediction grids and operational forecast horizons. Model training and forecast inference are separated so that trained experts can be applied repeatedly to successive HRRR forecast cycles. Prediction grids are processed in batches, allowing parallel and GPU-enabled inference over large spatial domains and multiple forecast lead times. The mixture structure also supports localized refinement because individual experts can be retrained or updated for underrepresented environmental conditions without reconstructing the complete modeling system. Evaluation includes conventional pointwise prediction statistics as well as assessment of whether the framework credibly reconstructs fine-scale spatiotemporal temperature structure. Experiments examine predictor selection, training-sample design, fuzzy-clustering configuration, expert weighting, localized model refinement, and output grid spacing from approximately 500 to 50 m across multiple metropolitan areas. Point-based evaluation uses independent observations and metrics including root-mean-square error, mean absolute error, bias, and predictive uncertainty. Spatial evaluation examines temperature gradients, neighborhood-scale variability, transition zones, spatial continuity, and localized artifacts within the reconstructed temperature fields. Additional analysis evaluates model behavior for environmental conditions with limited training representation and compares performance across different metropolitan regions and meteorological conditions. The experiments emphasize the interaction among predictor resolution, observational representativeness, local model complexity, output resolution, uncertainty, computational cost, and spatial-field fidelity. Increasing nominal output resolution does not necessarily increase the amount of physically credible temperature information recovered by the model, particularly when high-resolution geographic variability is weakly represented in the training observations. The proposed mixture-of-GP-experts framework provides a probabilistic and computationally scalable approach for representing heterogeneous urban environments while retaining information on local model support and prediction uncertainty. The framework provides a portable pathway toward operational neighborhood-scale air temperature forecasting and urban climate services across CONUS metropolitan areas.
