492498.title: HRRRCast: Advancing High-Resolution Probabilistic Weather Prediction with AI
492498.authors: Isidora Jankov, NOAA, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and D. S. Abdi, M. Baldwin, V. Vargas Jr., J. Jacobson, and E. White
492498.abstract: HRRRCast is a CONUS-wide, 3-km convection-resolving ensemble prediction system that uses data-driven methods trained primarily on HRRR analyses. The system is designed to complement traditional numerical weather prediction by providing high-resolution probabilistic guidance at substantially lower computational cost. The latest version expands the ensemble to 18 members, uses higher-frequency training data to better represent rapidly evolving weather systems, and provides hourly forecasts through 24 hours, with additional forecasts extending to 48 hours at 00, 06, 12, and 18 UTC. Recent development has focused on improving the representation of precipitation and convective structure, addressing artifacts identified during the 2026 Spring Experiment, and improving the physical and temporal consistency of forecasts. A score-based data assimilation capability is also being developed to improve initialization and provide a pathway toward more observation-informed, rapidly updating AI forecasts. This presentation will highlight the evolution of HRRRCast, recent advances in ensemble generation and forecast frequency, evaluation results from high-impact weather cases, and ongoing efforts to assess its potential as a new source of high-resolution probabilistic guidance for operational weather prediction.

492501.title: 3D Volumetric Time-Resolved Measurements of Diurnal Atmospheric Surface-Layer Turbulence with Field-Scale Lagrangian Particle Tracking
492501.authors: William Deng, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA; and B. Cornell, C. Bianco, and N. J. Wei
492501.abstract: Winds in the atmospheric surface layer (ASL) over complex surface topography, such as cities, forests, and wind and solar farms, are dominated by strong variations in space and time. Within urban street canyons and between photovoltaic panels in a solar farm, turbulent flow structures vary over minutes in time and tens of meters in space. These hyperlocal flow phenomena have outsized impacts on surface fluxes in complex terrain, including scalar transport and convective heat transfer over natural and human-built structures. They are also difficult to study and predict at full scale, as they are too localized for weather and climate models to resolve and too large to be replicated in most lab-scale experiments. High-fidelity simulations can capture these multiscale physics, but generating large enough ensembles to represent real-world conditions is often prohibitively expensive. Furthermore, field-scale measurement techniques such as meteorological towers and scanning LiDAR are limited by spatial resolution, cost, and logical constraints. To address these gaps and provide 3D, volumetric, and time-resolved measurements of ASL turbulence in the field, we are developing a field-scale 3D Lagrangian particle-tracking (3D-LPT) system, composed of four commercially available movie cameras and air-filled soap bubbles from off-the-shelf bubble machines as flow seeding. The cameras are placed around the measurement volume and record images at 4K resolution and 60 Hz. The soap bubbles, ranging in diameter from 1 to 4 cm, are nearly neutrally buoyant. Natural sunlight illuminates two glare points on the bubbles, allowing them to be isolated from background features in the images at distances exceeding 20 m. This differentiates the present approach from prior methods that relied on high-powered lighting and were limited to nocturnal conditions, thus increasing the range of applicability and lowering costs. A wand calibration procedure enables accurate 3D triangulation of the particle positions, and a multi-step predictive tracking algorithm is used to reconstruct Lagrangian particle trajectories. Our group is also developing a data-assimilation method to reconstruct 3D volumetric pressure and temperature fluctuations from these trajectories. This field-scale 3D-LPT method enables unprecedented 3D volumetric measurements of spatiotemporal variations in diurnal ASL turbulence over length scales ranging from ~10 cm to ~10 m. The system is easily deployable and is composed of relatively low-cost, off-the-shelf components. Initial measurements have been conducted in the urban canopy layer of Philadelphia, with results validated by an ultrasonic anemometer. Lagrangian trajectories over an 8 m x 8 m area were captured at a rate of approximately 2,500 tracks per minute of data collection. Lagrangian and bin-averaged Eulerian statistics were computed. The 3D-LPT data demonstrate good agreement with the data from the ultrasonic anemometer, with significantly broader coverage of spatial variations and extreme events. A field campaign to measure turbulent flow structures and convective cooling over solar photovoltaic panels in a utility-scale solar farm in central Pennsylvania is planned for October 2026. Future deployments will investigate non-equilibrium turbulence and Lagrangian transport in urban street canyons, sand dunes, and other contexts with complex surface topography.

492513.title: Simulating Climate Change Impacts on Great Lakes Hydrodynamics Using a PGW-Forced FVCOM Structure
492513.authors: Jack Austin Easterday, GLERL, Ann Arbor, MI; and D. Cannon, A. L. Hutson, J. Wang, and A. H. Young
492513.abstract: The Great Lakes region (GLR) is uniquely affected by climate change because of the lake-atmosphere interactions that shape regional climate. Although global climate models (GCMs) provide context for future changes, these lake interactions are often ignored (or poorly parameterized), leading to large biases in seasonal climate patterns in the GLR. Regional climate models (RCMs) provide another option for modeling future scenarios using GCMs as boundary conditions; however, this method can be prohibitively expensive, and downscaling needs to be repeated as new GCMs are developed. The Pseudo Global Warming (PGW) method offers a computationally efficient alternative by superimposing projected long-term changes in climate (“deltas”) onto a high-resolution historic reanalysis baseline to estimate probable future climate conditions. In this study, we estimate long-term average changes in regional climate conditions using GFLD-CM4 (Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory Climate Model version 4), focusing on changes from historic data (1970-2000) to mid-century and end-century for both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. Individual climate deltas are estimated for 15 thermodynamic, radiative, and kinematic parameters, including wind speed, air temperature, and solar radiation. These deltas are applied to the North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR) atmospheric forcing product by interpolating horizontally onto the NARR grid and vertically along the NARR vertical pressure levels. PGW scenarios are compared to published RCM simulations to estimate seasonal biases in climate change signals associated with the approach. Finally, PGW simulations are used to force the Finite-Volume Community Ocean Model to evaluate changes in Great Lakes climate and ice cover dynamics over the next century.

492517.title: Validation of ASOS/AWOS Actual Versus Documented Locations and Adherence to Siting Specifications
492517.authors: Randall G. Bass, Bass Weather Services, LLC, Waynesboro, VA
492517.abstract: The Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) detects and measures atmospheric conditions occurring at designated airports and other locations across the United States. The program is a joint effort between the National Weather Service (NWS), the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and the Department of Defense. The Automated Weather Observing System (AWOS) is a similar system to ASOS but for use beyond the federal government. AWOS was designed to provide basic weather observation data, while the more sophisticated ASOS was developed to support weather forecast activities for aviation operations. Systems not owned and operated by the FAA are termed “Non-Federal” systems. While these systems were primarily developed for aviation, they are the backbone of the certified surface observations across the nation and are indispensable as the ground truth for the entire weather observation network. Almost 2500 ASOS and AWOS systems are currently in operation throughout the US, including Alaska, Hawaii, and territories. A database is maintained by both agencies regarding the location of these systems and their suite of sensors. These systems must meet strict guidelines from the NWS and FAA when initially installed regarding placement of the systems. This placement depends on factors such as distance from structures and other obstructions and even the type of surface the sensors are placed on. Antidotal stories about improper placement of sensors, sensors in a different location than the reported location, and even incorrect observations from the sensors due to obstructions from new construction and vegetation growth have been reported to the FAA and NWS for years, but no formal study has occurred to determine the scope of these anomalies. Bass Weather Services is conducting an independent, on-going study to validate the actual location of the ASOS/AWOS sensors versus the documented location in official publications. Additionally, an analysis of each ASOS/AWOS suite is being performed to determine if they still meet siting specifications. This presentation will discuss the results found so far and provide examples of well-placed sensors as well as those that are poorly sited or have obstructions and other issues that could be contaminating the critical output of these weather sensors.

492522.title: Variability and Evolution of African Easterly Wave Structures Associated with High and Low Dust Loading
492522.authors: Christian Wilder Barreto-Schuler, UALBANY, Menands, NY; and C. D. Thorncroft, C. H. Lu, and S. W. Wei
492522.abstract: African Easterly Waves (AEWs) were objectively identified at ≈30°W using MERRA-2 data and classified into High and Low Dust Loading groups (HDL-AEWs and LDL-AEWs, respectively) based on area-averaged Dust Aerosol Optical Depth (DUAOD) anomalies near their trough centers. The AEWs in both groups were then tracked backward to West Africa, and composite analyses were used to compare their mean structures and evolution. The results reveal distinctive evolutions between HDL-AEWs and LDL-AEWs. Over land, in the lower troposphere, HDL-AEWs exhibit a stronger, broader, and vertically deeper northern vortex consistent with stronger dust emissions. Despite their weaker northern vortex, LDL-AEWs maintain a stronger southern midlevel vortex throughout their westward evolution from West Africa to the eastern Atlantic. As the waves propagate toward the eastern Atlantic, the northern vortex becomes co-located with the southern midlevel vortex near 20°W in HDL-AEWs, whereas in LDL-AEWs, this co-location occurs earlier, near 15°W, after which low-level vorticity progressively intensifies. By 30°W, HDL-AEWs exhibit weaker convection and lower-tropospheric vorticity than LDL-AEWs. These average differences over the eastern Atlantic are likely due to enhanced lower-tropospheric static stability associated with positive temperature anomalies between ≈850 and ≈700 hPa, produced by the direct radiative effects of the pronounced dust plume located within and west of the HDL-AEW troughs, at around the same pressure levels. Furthermore, because dust intrusion into the trough region is more pronounced in HDL-AEWs than in LDL-AEWs, wave-relative circulation composites and backward trajectories were used to investigate the mechanisms underlying this difference. The results suggest that the greater persistence of the northern vortex over the ocean in HDL-AEWs favors dust transport toward the trough. In addition, below 700 hPa, the circulation around the trough remains relatively open to the surrounding environment in both groups, especially in HDL-AEWs, allowing dust-laden air to enter the AEW trough center primarily from the northwestern and southwestern quadrants. Finally, HDL-AEWs also tend to occur in environments with elevated preexisting dust concentrations, highlighting the importance of background dust conditions.

492523.title: NOAA Science and Risk Preparedness for the 2026-2027 El Niño
492523.authors: Annarita Mariotti, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and R. S. Pulwarty, M. L. L'Heureux, N. Johnson, and M. J. McPhaden
492523.abstract: An El Niño is developing in the Tropical Pacific, likely becoming very strong at its peak during winter 2026-2027. This event offers a significant scientific opportunity to deepen our understanding and improve predictions of El Niño/Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and its impacts. Simultaneously, it presents a challenge for the scientific community to share critical knowledge that informs local, regional, and national risk preparedness. Across NOAA and its partner organizations, decades of ENSO research and engagement will be brought to bear to advance understanding of this phenomenon and its impacts, and to deliver actionable information that assists society in planning and responding to these events. This presentation will showcase examples of work by NOAA and its partners that leverage the 2026-2027 El Niño to continue advancing our understanding and response to ENSO events. These examples will include efforts to observe ENSO processes, the environmental hazards they create and their impacts on vulnerable communities. We will highlight predictability analyses utilizing diverse observational data and ensemble model forecasts, as well as real-time forecast assessments that inform NOAA’s modeling and prediction systems. Beyond observation, modeling, and prediction advancements, this presentation will portray the practical application of this ENSO research in bolstering risk preparedness (e.g., drought, fire, heat) through communication and engagement. We will illustrate collaborative and applied research activities aimed at identifying ENSO risk vulnerabilities and testing solutions that support resilience for local decision-makers and critical sectors like agriculture and energy. Furthermore, we will provide examples of strategies for communicating integrated, targeted ENSO information. Through these examples, we highlight how close coordination across NOAA and engagement with stakeholders advance ENSO scientific knowledge, effectively translating it into relevant, actionable guidance for addressing the current and emerging risks posed by the ongoing El Niño event and what may come next.

492531.title: Ten Things I Hate About DART (and Why I Love It Anyway): A Field Guide for Enthusiastic Collaborators
492531.authors: Helen Kershaw, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and M. Smith, J. Anderson, M. El Gharamti, B. Raczka, and K. Raeder
492531.abstract: Since the last DART-focused AMS session in 2023, DART has continued to evolve as a community software facility, now supporting more than 50 models, novel data assimilation methods, broader observation capabilities, and continued modernization of tooling, testing, and build infrastructure. This talk is a field guide to sustaining and improving DART's scientific software ecosystem. We examine persistent sources of friction, including legacy design decisions; the Fortran/Python boundary; build complexity; developer onboarding; observation interface diversity; scalability challenges; documentation debt; testing gaps; experiment workflow complexity; and the tension between research flexibility and long-term software sustainability. Rather than simply cataloging these challenges, we present each as a practical entry point for collaboration, inviting new contributors to help shape the next generation of DART. Recent efforts show these lessons already being applied. The CROCODILE project demonstrates integration across previously separate infrastructure by combining CESM-based regional MOM6 ocean and carbon-cycle data assimilation, CrocoLake observations, model verification, and DART workflows. Emerging interoperability with observation frameworks such as JEDI’s IODA further highlights the need for flexible interfaces across the data assimilation community. Looking ahead, DART must adapt to increasingly complex Earth system applications, convection-allowing and high-resolution ensembles, and emerging AI-based prediction systems. DART is at an inflection point: AI emulators challenge the long-standing assumption that ensemble DA is inherently computationally prohibitive, opening up new possibilities while introducing new software and algorithmic challenges. Meeting these demands will require continued innovation in algorithms, interfaces, workflows, and community practices. This is a field guide meant to be used: the future of DART will be shaped by the community willing to tackle its hardest problems. Attendees are invited to bring their scientific questions, software expertise, and ideas to help build what comes next.

492532.title: Updates to NOAA Space Weather Next Program Objectives
492532.authors: Irfan Azeem, NOAA, Washington DC, DC; and E. M. Lynch, N. J. Zaremba, Y. Collado-Vega, and D. Vassiliadis
492532.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Office of Space Weather Observations (SWO) provides the operational space weather measurements that underpin critical forecasting and warning services. By maintaining continuous observations from multiple orbital regimes, SWO delivers an uninterrupted stream of space weather data, products, and alerts that support government, commercial, and scientific users. As the nation's dependence on space-based technologies continues to grow, so does the demand for more advanced, resilient, and timely space weather observations and products. To address these future needs, NOAA's Space Weather Next program will extend observational capabilities beyond the current Program of Record (POR2025). This presentation summarizes recent updates to the Space Weather Next Program Objectives (PO), which establish the requirements supporting NESDIS strategic objectives. We describe the evolving aspirational functional and performance requirements for the Space Weather Next System, envisioned as an integrated architecture of space-based observatories and instruments, ground infrastructure, and data processing capabilities. Together, these elements are designed to detect, quantify, and continuously monitor the physical conditions of the space weather environment, enabling improved operational products and enhanced national space weather resilience.

492533.title: Using Digital Sub-banding to Detect and Lessen the Impact of RFI for the Weather-System Follow-on Flight 2 Microwave Imager
492533.authors: David Draper, BAE Systems, Boulder, CO; and B. Davis, G. Moroney, S. Griebel, R. Hofer, and G. Gibson
492533.abstract: The Weather System Follow-on (WSF-M) Flight 2 Microwave Imager (MWI) incorporates digital sub-banding techniques to mitigate the impact of Radio Frequency Interference (RFI). The technique allows downlink of multiple sub-bands for the 10 GHz, 18 GHz, and if needed, 36 GHz channels. Each of the bands already utilize a digital receiver to generate the fully polarimetric outputs necessary for Ocean Surface Vector Winds. The digital receiver will be reprogrammed prior to flight to segment each of the fully polarimetric channels into multiple sub-bands. The design also provides an RFI survey mode, where up to 64 sub-bands can be downlinked to the ground over several orbits providing knowledge of the spectral distribution of the RFI. Using the information gleaned from the on-orbit RFI survey, the design affords flexibility to modify the sub-band configuration and integration time on-orbit to adapt to the measured on-orbit RFI environment. Sub-banding provides RFI mitigation capability by removing contaminated portion of the spectrum while retaining a portion that is RFI-free. The sub-banding architecture drives less complexity into the on-board processing and more flexibility into ground-implemented RFI mitigation approach versus purely on-board mitigation techniques. In the paper, the WSF-M RFI mitigation approach is contrasted with purely on-board techniques. The idea of an on-board mitigation technique that produces clean output data from RFI contaminated inputs is understandably alluring and is the topic of much research and debate. On-board techniques promise lower downlink bandwidth, but with some additional bandwidth to telemeter the information on omitted sub-bands/samples for calibration. On-board techniques by necessity operate on the raw uncalibrated data, which require techniques such as spectral flattening or gain tracking to provide the best sensitivity. They also require on-board maintenance of thresholds to provide the best trade-off of false alarms vs. missed detections. Tuning must be done with limited insight into the spectral and temporal characteristics of the RFI. If the RFI characteristics are well suited for the on-board algorithms, on-board techniques can provide good rejection of RFI with the lowest impact to data rate. Ground mitigation techniques require telemetering of the multiple sub-bands. Data rate limitations may preclude full spectral/temporal sampling, resulting in a few sub-bands or sub-samples sent to the ground. The lower spectral resolution of the wider sub-bands can reduce the sensitivity of the RFI detection for narrow-band sources. To compensate, additional techniques not available on-board can be used to recoup the detection sensitivity such as spatial averaging, spatial dilation around RFI sources, or use of geolocation information to identify persistent fixed ground sources. Also, ground detection techniques have the advantage of using calibrated data rather than raw data to detect the RFI. Ground mitigation with as little as 2 or 3 sub-bands can be effective, especially if the RFI sources are broadband. The on-board capability to survey the environment at higher spectral resolution provides additional sensitivity by adjusting the sub-bands via ground command. This paper lays out the design of the WSF-M RFI mitigation system, the pros and cons with on-board vs ground mitigation techniques and investigates the detection sensitivity of the WSF-M architecture.

492538.title: A Geostationary Satellite Based Cloud-Top Cooling Rate Peak In-Cloud Updraft Algorithm Calibrated to high-Resolution WRF Model Simulations and Ground-Based Observations
492538.authors: John R. Mecikalski, UAH, Huntsville, AL; and J. Strandgren, S. Joro, and T. Bölle
492538.abstract: Past research has developed cumulus cloud-top cooling rates (CTCR) for growing and moving clouds (Mecikalski et al. 2016). As initiated by an EUMETSAT study in 2023, these CTCRs data were used in a merged way to estimate in-cloud updrafts for actively growing cumulus clouds, as observed in 2 km x 2 km Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) GOES-16 satellite imagery. The EUMETSAT study outcome was a Cloud Updraft Detection product, and while impactful, required further validation of its methods and data processing procedures toward assessing the accuracy of the in-cloud updraft magnitudes. The goal of this presentation is to highlight recent and ongoing research that was done to form an enhanced GOES-16/-19 satellite in-cloud updraft algorithm. These GOES-16/-19 retrieve updraft magnitudes are compared to high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations and ground-based updraft observations. Within the initial updraft algorithm, a 1 km x 1 km resolution ABI convective cloud mask (CCM; Berendes et al. 2008) product identifies and differentiates between pre- and existing deep convective cloud types, with the CCM being an unsupervised classification using all GOES-16/-19 visible and infrared channels. For pre-convective storm cumulus clouds identified by the CCM product, the CTCRs (in °C/15 min) are converted into cloud-top rising rates using results from prior studies (e.g., Adler and Fenn 1979; Romps and Charn 2018), and then into estimated peak in-cloud updraft magnitudes (in m/s). These updraft estimates are essentially based on parcel theory, with adjustments made to account for satellite resolution of cumulus clouds and implied entrainment rates. In a recent study by Mecikalski et al. (2026), the initial CTCR-based updraft magnitudes are increased by factors consistent with the CCM cloud object resolution, and further to match 500 and 250 m WRF model simulation results. Importantly, this upscaling conforms with prior LES and observational study’s conclusions related to updraft thermal behavior, and suggests that an optimal satellite resolution to obtain maximum updrafts in growing convective clouds is 375-400 m. The retrieved updrafts also seemingly apply to mature convective storms, given they estimate updraft velocities consistent with convective available potential energy. In late 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program finalized the installation of the ARM Mobile Facility-3 in the Bankhead National Forest (BNF) of North Alabama. This BNF site hosts a number of ground-based instruments, with several designed to observe cloud-base and in-cloud updrafts. Cloud-base vertical motions are retrieved directly from Doppler lidars (Haliczer et al. 2025), while other updraft information is provided by the KAZR vertically pointing radar and 915 MHz radar wind profiler. Hence, the main presentation will also focus on comparing the GOES-16/-19 CTCR-based in-cloud updraft estimates to the ground-based updraft magnitudes. As the updraft algorithm matures, the research described above can be applied to other geostationary satellite datasets (e.g., Meteosat Third Generation Flexible Combined Imager using 2.5 min Rapid Scan Service data over the European Domain; Himawari-8/-9), or be useful in algorithms and applications that would benefit from such in-cloud convective updraft information (e.g., data assimilation, the aviation industry).

492539.title: NASA Continuity MODIS-VIIRS Imager-Sounder Cloud Products
492539.authors: Dongwei Fu, Space Science and Engineering Center, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and P. Veglio, R. Holz, K. Meyer, S. Platnick, S. Dutcher, E. Borbas, D. Botambekov, G. Quinn, C. Peterson, E. Zhan, and A. Gumber
492539.abstract: The NASA Continuity MODIS-VIIRS Cloud Products were developed to maintain a consistent cloud climatology across MODIS and VIIRS, forming the basis for an approximately 40-year satellite record of global ocean, land, and atmospheric observations. To ensure cross-sensor continuity, the imager-only algorithm is restricted to spectral channels common to both instruments. However, VIIRS lacks key thermal infrared absorption bands, including water vapor and CO2 bands, reducing cloud detection during polar night and degrading cloud-top height retrievals, especially for tropical high cirrus where infrared absorption channels provide enhanced vertical sensitivity. We present the development and validation of the Continuity MODIS-VIIRS Imager-Sounder Cloud Products. The approach integrates collocated hyperspectral infrared sounder observations with imager measurements using a simplified, traceable fusion methodology: sounder radiances are spectrally averaged to match MODIS thermal emissive bands and spatially mapped to the imager pixel grid. This preserves spectral consistency while augmenting infrared information. Validation focuses on cloud-top height and cloud mask. For cloud-top height, the updated retrieval uses convolved sounder infrared radiances for CO2 slicing in ice and cirrus scenes while retaining original high-resolution imager channels for split-window retrievals and structured low clouds. Comparisons with collocated CALIOP show improved performance for thin cirrus, consistent with stable hyperspectral sounder calibration and reduced uncertainty from imager calibration and spectral response. The resulting lower cirrus cloud-top heights have climatological implications, particularly for longwave flux calculations and radiation budget studies. For cloud mask, the imager-sounder product closely reproduces MODIS MYD35 retrievals while improving agreement with CALIOP, particularly over snow- and ice-covered surfaces and during nighttime conditions. This imager-sounder framework restores missing infrared information while preserving imager spatial detail. It improves both cloud-top characterization and cloud masking, extends MODIS heritage retrieval capability into the VIIRS era, and supports a consistent multi-decadal cloud climate record.

492540.title: Characterizing the 2024 Extreme Heatwave Events over the West African Sahel Region: Physical Drivers, Population Exposure, and Socioeconomic Vulnerability
492540.authors: Aissatou Faye, NOAA, College Park, MD; NOAA Climate Prediction Center, College Park, MD; and C. Niang, E. B. Bekele, B. Mayala, M. Tall, Z. Segele, and W. M. Thiaw
492540.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive characterization of the record-breaking heatwave events that affected the West African Sahel during the March-June (MAMJ) 2024 hot season. It investigates their physical drivers and assesses the associated population exposure and socioeconomic vulnerability. Utilizing ERA5 reanalysis data, we quantify heatwave intensity, duration, and spatial extent relative to the 1991-2020 baseline. Population exposure is estimated using gridded population datasets, while socioeconomic and health indicators derived from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) are used to assess vulnerability across affected populations. The results show that the 2024 MAMJ hot season was unprecedented over the Sahel, with persistent extreme temperatures, prolonged heatwave episodes, and a spatial extent exceeding that of any event during the 1991–2020 reference period. The The areal-average cumulative heatwave duration reached 34.92 days, nearly twice the previous maximum recorded, highlighting the exceptional severity of the 2024 season. Our investigation into the physical drivers identifies persistent large-scale atmospheric circulation anomalies, coupled with favorable ocean-atmosphere interactions and subseasonal variability from the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), as the key mechanisms behind the sustained warming and suppressed heat dissipation. As a result, population exposure increased substantially, amplifying health risks for vulnerable groups, including older adults, pregnant women, individuals with pre-existing medical conditions, low-income households, and outdoor workers. By integrating climate information with socioeconomic vulnerability indicators, this study provides a comprehensive assessment of heat risk across the Sahel. The findings demonstrate the value of combining physical and social dimensions of extreme heat to improve heat-risk assessment, forecasting, and heat–health early warning systems. They also provide actionable evidence to support regional climate centers, national meteorological services, and public health agencies in strengthening heat preparedness, climate services, and long-term adaptation strategies in one of the world's most climate-vulnerable regions.

492542.title: A Practical Approach to Assigning Uncertainty in Coastal Flood Forecasts
492542.authors: Alexander R. Davies, U.S. Naval Academy, Annapolis, MD; and S. Loeffler and J. P. Smith
492542.abstract: Coastal flooding increasingly impacts communities throughout the Chesapeake Bay, including Annapolis, Maryland, where local stakeholders rely on water level forecasts from the National Weather Service (NWS) Baltimore/Washington Weather Forecast Office (WFO) to prepare for and mitigate flooding impacts. This presentation summarizes a recent evaluation of NWS Baltimore/Washington WFO water level forecasts for forecasted coastal flooding events in Annapolis from 2018 through 2022. The analysis identified a systematic high bias in both the mean and median forecast errors, with the largest errors occurring in the 12- to 36-hour forecast window—the period during which many stakeholders begin implementing protective actions. Across all forecast lead times, the magnitude and variability of forecast errors associated with coastal flooding events indicate that deterministic water level forecasts alone do not adequately convey the uncertainty needed to support risk-informed decision making. In the absence of operational probabilistic water level guidance for the Chesapeake Bay, this presentation introduces a practical, data-driven framework for communicating forecast uncertainty. The approach uses historical forecast errors to assign uncertainty bounds to deterministic water level forecasts, analogous to how the National Hurricane Center communicates tropical cyclone track uncertainty through the forecast cone. Case studies of coastal flooding events in Annapolis demonstrate how this methodology provides stakeholders with a more actionable representation of forecast uncertainty while remaining compatible with existing operational forecasting practices.

492543.title: Physical Drivers of Wind–SST Co-Variability on Timescales of a Few Days Along the California Coast
492543.authors: Thamirys Cavaton Rocha, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and B. Villas Boas
492543.abstract: Investigation of wind–SST variability on daily timescales and oceanic submesoscales O(1–10 km) has recently become possible through high-resolution coupled ocean–atmosphere models because they provide the spatial and temporal resolution needed to resolve air–sea interactions that cannot be fully captured by satellite and in situ observations alone. Although recent modeling studies have identified a global co-oscillation between wind speed and sea surface temperature (SST) on time scales of a few days, the duration, intensity, seasonality, and physical drivers of this variability remain poorly understood. This raises several key questions: Does the strength of the wind–SST co-oscillation vary with season? How does it differ among geographic regions? Which physical processes control the observed variability? Do coastal upwelling systems exhibit stronger coupling than regions dominated by high eddy kinetic energy? Addressing these questions is essential for understanding the mechanisms governing short-term air–sea interactions and improving their representation in coupled models used for weather and climate prediction. Here, we present a characterization of the duration, strength, and physical drivers of wind–SST feedbacks along the California coast. We quantify the seasonality of this variability using lag-correlation analysis and estimate the relative contributions of coastal upwelling and surface heat fluxes. To accomplish this, we use observations from National Data Buoy Center (NDBC) buoys to evaluate simulations from the coupled MITgcm–GEOS model. Then, the model output is used to generate lag-correlation maps and diagnose the dominant physical processes responsible for the observed variability. Understanding how the wind–SST co-oscillation varies with season and geographic location, and identifying the mechanisms that control it, may help explain uncertainties in bulk air–sea flux estimates and inform improved parameterizations in coupled weather and climate models.

492546.title: Cloud and Surface Radiation Interactions on Daytime Boundary Layer Evolution from Long-Term NOAA SURFRAD Observations
492546.authors: Vanessa Caicedo, CIRES, Longmont, CO; and J. Sedlar, L. Riihimaki, L. M. Bruhwiler, and A. Jacobson
492546.abstract: Surface heating and cooling drive daytime boundary layer (BL) evolution and regulate the exchange of energy and moisture between the land surface and atmosphere. Clouds both respond to and modify these processes by altering the surface radiation budget. Low clouds reduce incoming shortwave radiation while enhancing downwelling longwave radiation, and clouds aloft can further influence BL evolution through their radiative effects on the surface energy balance. As a result, the timing and magnitude of daytime BL growth emerge from coupled interactions among cloud properties, surface radiation, and atmospheric thermodynamic structure. These coupled processes remain difficult both to observe and to represent in numerical weather and climate models because they span a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. To investigate these relationships, we developed a long-term collocated dataset of lidar-derived BL height, cloud typing, and surface radiation observations from the NOAA Surface Radiation (SURFRAD) network. Using this dataset, we examine how cloud regimes and atmospheric conditions modify the daytime evolution of the BL across multiple climate regions. Long-term observations show that the daytime BL response varies substantially with climate regime, cloud regimes, and throughout the daytime evolution of the BL. We also evaluate the representation of these relationships in the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh version 4 (HRRRv4) model and the TM5 global atmospheric transport model. In particular, we assess model biases in the timing and magnitude of BL evolution under different cloud and atmospheric conditions, their ability to reproduce long-term BL evolution across diverse climate regimes, and how model resolution influences the representation of BL evolution. These results provide insights into cloud-BL-radiation interactions and establish an observational benchmark for evaluating BL evolution in numerical weather prediction and climate models, with implications for atmospheric transport, air quality, cloud evolution, and land-atmosphere coupling.

492548.title: Keynote Speaker Colorado Insurance Commissioner Michael Conway - A Regulatory Perspective on Insurance in the Current Era of Extreme Weather
492548.abstract: This 30-minute session would combine a presentation with audience discussion, offering a regulatory perspective on how weather and climate information can support practical decisions across insurance and reinsurance markets. Extreme weather is testing how insurance markets balance affordability, availability, solvency, consumer protection, and long-term resilience. The presentation would examine how a state insurance regulator evaluates forward-looking catastrophe risk, including the usefulness of hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and loss information in regulatory oversight. It would consider the roles of model transparency, validation, uncertainty communication, mitigation evidence, and public-private collaboration as insurers and reinsurers respond to evolving hazards and changing exposure. It will also examine the regulatory strategy and what needs are to address from a regulatory perspective the ability to maintain healthy markets through pricing and other incentives for both individual insured parties and communities to make investments that reduce risks. The discussion would address questions such as: Which scientific and financial indicators are most decision-useful for regulatory oversight? How should regulators assess climate-conditioned scenarios, catastrophe models, public data, and emerging risk-transfer approaches? What evidence can connect mitigation investments to insurance outcomes? How can public policy support consumer protection while sustaining a stable and responsive private insurance market? The session would connect the Forum’s focus on weather and climate science with the operational, financial, and policy decisions that shape insurance markets. It would also provide a foundation for the roundtable that follows by identifying shared challenges and practical opportunities for regulators, insurers, reinsurers, scientists, modelers, and communities.

492549.title: A Knowledge Network Framework for Diagnosing Social Science Integration within Interdisciplinary Earth Science Teams
492549.authors: Alison Gregory, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and H. Love and E. Dickman
492549.abstract: Earth science programs and social scientists share a common goal: producing knowledge that serves communities. Achieving that goal requires that social science knowledge be integrated and structurally embedded in research design, decision-making, and collaboration. This paper introduces a framework for characterizing that integration and a method for measuring it. Using knowledge network theory and Baran's (1964) network topologies, we first examine what meaningful social science integration looks like as a structural property of knowledge networks. In this regard, social network analysis nodes don’t represent specific people but rather the flow of knowledge. We then introduce a brief four-tier framework that helps programs identify where their knowledge network currently stands and what level of social science integration their work actually requires. This framework is diagnostic, not prescriptive. Social Network Analysis (SNA) serves as the measurement strategy, making knowledge integration visible and quantifiable. We then present a Field case study of NOAA's Unified Forecast System (UFS) community of practice (with a goal of R2O—research to operations) in which we use SNA data to assess the positioning of social science knowledge in alignment with stakeholders commitment to community engagement. We conclude by discussing implications for practice and outlining a Knowledge Integration Alignment Tool (KIAT), currently under development, that can be used as a practical diagnostic tool to help programs assess the gap between the integration their work requires and the integration their network currently reflects. Recommendations include various structures for embedding social scientists within teams depending on the desired outcome.

492550.title: Adding Value to Downscaling Coarse Global Models : Ensemble Calibration and Transfer Efficacy in Tomorrow.io's FOCUS model
492550.authors: Maxfield E Green, Tomorrow.io, Salt Lake City, UT; Tomorrow.io, Fort Collins, CO; and F. Cannon, R. Chase, A. Evans, M. Pope, B. Taylor, and A. Chawla
492550.abstract: High-resolution probabilistic numerical weather prediction (NWP) is computationally expensive to deploy at global scale, motivating methods that can recover fine-scale structure and calibrated uncertainty from coarser, lower-cost forecasts. FOCUS is a generative postprocessing model designed to spatially and temporally downscale coarse NWP forecasts into high-resolution surface weather fields. Spatially, FOCUS maps coarse atmospheric fields onto kilometer-scale tiles. Temporally, it uses a cascaded architecture that combines an estimated deterministic high-resolution initial state with a residual generative component predicting 15-minute increments. FOCUS is first pretrained to reconstruct high-resolution structure from artificially coarsened High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) fields under a Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) objective, and is subsequently fine-tuned to downscale operational IFS HRES forecasts to HRRR targets. We address two questions: how effectively high-resolution structure learned from HRRR transfers to a global NWP input domain, and how much probabilistic information the generative model recovers from a reduced input ensemble. Both are tested on matched seasonal suites pairing coarsened-HRRR and IFS HRES inputs against shared HRRR targets, with additional verification against station observations outside of the HRRR domain. Driven by HRES inputs, the pretrained model shows a clear domain gap relative to coarsened-HRRR inputs. The baseline HRES fine-tuning is designed to close this gap. The generative ensembles remain underspread, yet match full NWP ensemble CRPS to within 1% using half the NWP members. This talk offers an examination of the skill and calibration of generative ensembles coupled to a spatial-temporal downscaling system applied in and out of training domains.

492557.title: Wind Speed Calibrations at the Oklahoma Mesonet and a Well Sampled Significant Wind Event on 4 July 2026
492557.authors: Ethan John Becker, Oklahoma Climatological Survey, Norman, OK; and C. A. Fiebrich, C. M. Luttrell, and D. Grimsley
492557.abstract: Since 1999, the Oklahoma Mesonet has been calibrating both propeller vane and cup anemometers at an outdoor facility comprised of test sensor mounts surrounding a NIST traceable reference anemometer at a height of 4 meters. This sensor calibration methodology has been touched on in the literature, but after a relocation of the network’s outdoor wind speed calibration facility in 2024, a detailed review of the process is warranted. Starting threshold evaluation and mean errors are documented for the range of wind speeds observed for each test run. The refurbishment process and resulting calibration archive has allowed lab and data quality personnel to establish guidelines for acceptable errors for both pre- and post-field wind speed sensor performance. Additionally, the wind speed reference instrument and a suite of test sensors were deployed during a significant high wind event on 4 July 2026. This occurrence provided a unique opportunity to evaluate the performance of test sensors and the reference during strong winds alongside an official 10 m wind measurement from the Norman Mesonet site. This presentation will overview the Mesonet's anemometer calibration procedures, as well as the unique observations recorded during the 4 July 2026 event.

492561.title: Horizontal Flash Expansion Sustaining Continuing Current in Winter Stratiform Lightning
492561.authors: Jessica L. Losego, Georgia Tech Research Institute, Smyrna, GA; and M. J. Peterson
492561.abstract: Winter thunderstorms over large bodies of water produce distinctive lightning behavior characterized by extensive horizontal propagation through stratiform cloud layers. The Lake Effect Electrification (LEE) field campaign conducted during winter 2022-2023 near Lake Ontario captured detailed observations of this phenomenon, which is typically difficult to study due to its occurrence over remote oceanic regions. During 17-20 November 2022, a Lightning Mapping Array (LMA) network consisting of 16 sensors deployed by NSSL and Georgia Tech's Severe Storms Research Center detected 150 lightning flashes. This study examines the phenomenon of Continuing Current (CC) in one exceptionally long-horizontal stratiform lightning flash from 18 November. Cloud-to-ground strokes can produce CC lasting tens or hundreds of milliseconds, causing sustained optical emission that can be amplified by continued leader development into new pockets of charge within the cloud. Our analysis demonstrates how flash expansion can drive the complex light curves observed in long-horizontal stratiform lightning, including those found in lake-effect and sea-based winter lightning environments. These findings provide new insights into the electrical structure and evolution of winter stratiform thunderstorms and contribute to understanding extreme lightning events in cold-season convective systems sustained by bodies of water.

492564.title: Analysis of Model-Tracked Moisture Prior to High Magnitude Precipitation Events in the American Intermountain West
492564.authors: Kyle Johnson, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and T. W. Aerenson, D. Caulton, and D. McCoy
492564.abstract: Water is one of nature’s most powerful forces, and the American intermountain west is no stranger to this force. Both flash flooding and areal flooding can occur within this region of the United States on a regular basis due to a combination of atmospheric, geographic, and topographic factors. High magnitude precipitation events have been responsible for many of these flood events, some of which have caused severe damage and loss of life. One such example would be the Front Range Floods of September 2013, which impacted portions of the Colorado Front Range from Fort Collins all the way to Pueblo and were responsible for the loss of 8 lives and over $1 billion in damages. A more thorough understanding of the moisture sources and transport mechanisms that contribute to these high magnitude events would have multiple potential benefits, such as increased levels of preparedness for at-risk areas, higher rates of success when attempting to forecast future events, and an improved understanding of atmospheric teleconnections within and among North America and the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. This study attempts to gain a higher level of understanding of these events through utilizing a preexisting dataset of daily tracked moisture. This dataset, known as Evaporation Dataset of Regional Precipitation Sources (E-DRoPS), was created by applying a WAM2layersV3 model to ERA5 reanalysis data that spans from 1990 to 2024. The E-DRoPS dataset provides spatial distributions for evaporation and precipitation for each of the 22 USGS 2-digit hydrological units (HUs). Dates of high magnitude precipitation events were determined by isolating the geographical intermountain west region within ERA5 reanalysis data and taking the top 0.12 percent of daily total precipitation between 1990 and 2024 within that region. These dates were then used to obtain the modeled evaporated moisture for each of the 7 days prior to each event, which were then summed up to produce a cumulative moisture source dataset for each event. Statistical clustering algorithms, such as gaussian process clustering, allowed these source datasets to be sorted into groups based on geographical location and amount of moisture. Preliminary analysis shows that high magnitude precipitation events over the intermountain west are not the result of any one specific source region and transport pattern. Instead, the data indicates that the moisture responsible for these events can come from multiple different source regions and can arrive in the intermountain west via multiple transport pathways. Further analysis and interpretation of these results will be presented as well as any trends and changes observed over the 34 years spanned by the original E-DRoPS dataset.

492566.title: Advancements for Remotely Sensed Detection and Alerting for Rapid Upgrowth Convective Turbulence
492566.authors: Brian Pettegrew, The MITRE Corportation, Parkville, MO; and T. Thrasher, N. Bonds, S. Menon, S. Liu, and A. Shay
492566.abstract: According to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), turbulence remains the leading weather-related cause of serious injuries in commercial aviation, accounting for more than 70% of weather-related incidents. The frequency of severe turbulence encounters has increased substantially over recent decades. Although pilots and dispatchers rely on a combination of weather observations, forecasts, and pilot reports to mitigate risk, it is difficult to operationally remotely sense turbulence without first encountering it, particularly in the case of rapidly developing convection that yes to produce a visible signature. To address this challenge, The MITRE Corporation, through its Independent Research and Development Program, is developing a remotely sensed turbulence detection capability that leverages rapidly updating imagery from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES-19) to identify and alerts for atmospheric signatures associated with Rapid Upgrowth-Convectively Induced Turbulence (U-CITTM). Building upon previous research, recent efforts have focused on integrating physics-informed machine learning techniques to better exploit the rich multispectral satellite observations, improve feature extraction, and increase the precision and accuracy of U-CIT identification while maintaining the physical interpretability of the detection process. The enhanced detection capability is being assessed through comparisons with observed convective development from Multi Radar Multi Sensor (MRMS) and objective turbulence reports in the form of in-situ observed Eddy Dissipation Rate (EDR). This paper presents recent advances in the U-CIT™ alerting, including physics-informed machine learning and updated technical validation against independent observational datasets. It also outlines the approach for assessing operational applicability and informing continued capability maturation and future transition planning. Data from the U-CIT™ alerting algorithm are shared with aviation industry partners to support operational utility. Approved for Public Release; Distribution Unlimited. Public Release Case Number 26-1576 © 2026 The MITRE Corporation. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

492569.title: Whence "Atmospheric Tomography": From Barroom, to Concept, to ATom.
492569.authors: Steven Wofsy, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA; and P. A. Newman
492569.abstract: This presentation reviews the development of the Atmospheric Tomography Mission (AToM) NASA Earth Venture Suborbital proposal for acquiring global-scale cross sections of atmospheric composition. Critical lessons were learned from precursor missions (GAMETAG (NSF, NCAR Electra), ASHOE/MAESA (NASA, ER-2), STRAT (NASA, ER-2), and HIPPO (NSF, G-V) ), including the availability of a suitable long range platform, agency commitment, and appropriate TRL-9 instrumentation. A group of lead scientists collaborated to develop the ATom mission concept with sufficiently specific science goals to meet reviewers' demands, while preserving the capability to address a wide range of aspirational science questions. The flight plans and payload needed to be coherent and comprehensive while allowing for flexibility and strictly avoiding mission creep. ATom succeeded beyond expectations through the efforts of the flight crews to safely navigate the globe, and by measurement teams to make accurate, traceable data maximally available to the international science community via fully open, accessible data policies. Abbreviations: GAMETAG-78: Global Atmospheric Measurements Experiment on Tropospheric Aerosols and Gases - 1978 ASHOE/MAESA: Airborne Southern Hemisphere Ozone Experiment / Measurements for Assessing the Effects of Stratospheric Aircraft -- 1994 STRAT: Stratospheric TRacers of Atmospheric Transport Mission -- 1995 - 1997 HIPPO: HIAPER Pole-to-Pole Observations project -- 2009 - 2011 TRL: Technical Readiness Level

492570.title: Rain within Arctic Marine Stratocumulus Clouds: Comparison of Measurements and Calculations
492570.authors: Jeff Snider, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and E. Weissburg, A. Robertson, A. Rodi, S. Woods, C. G. Kruse, A. Bansemer, L. Cai, S. Mahant, and M. D. Petters
492570.abstract: We analyzed measurements acquired over the Norwegian and Greenland Seas during the CAESAR campaign, focusing on measurements collected during airborne profiling of stratocumulus. Results are presented for 14 profiles with cloud base temperature between -21 and -6 C, including ice water content, mean updraft, cloud geometric thickness, cloud water content, cloud droplet concentration, droplet spectral dispersion, and liquid at diameter larger than 55 µm. The latter is the threshold we define as the boundary between droplets and rain drops. Rain drop concentration and ice water content were derived using measurements from two complimentary optical imager probes. The ratio of ice water path divided by cloud liquid water path was significantly smaller than one. A parameterized two-moment model of liquid hydrometeor coalescence was used to predict rain drop concentration based on measurements of cloud droplet concentration, dispersion, mean updraft, cloud base altitude, and cloud top altitude. Observed rain drop concentrations exceed those modeled by a factor of 300 and even though the model is documented as a fast producer of rain drops when compared with explicit integration of the stochastic collection equation. Measurements of eddy dissipation rate in CAESAR were approximately five times that in subtropical marine boundary layers, which is noteworthy but cannot fully explain the rain drop concentrations that were observed compared to those modeled.

492576.title: Characterizing Downslope Windstorms at NCAR's Marshall Field Site: Toward a Site-Specific Observing Strategy
492576.authors: Simran Ambuja LaBore, NWS, St. Louis, MO
492576.abstract: Downslope windstorms along Colorado's Front Range and beyond pose significant hazards, including fire and infrastructure risk. NCAR's Marshall Field Site, at the Front Range's base with an in-situ and remote-sensing instrumentation suite, is uniquely positioned to study these events. Dynamical flow features such as sweeping flows, rotors, and hydraulic jumps dictate hazard extent; hydraulic jump location shaped fire spread in the 2021 Marshall and 2023 Lahaina Fires. Across a two-year observational period (January 2024–April 2026), we identified 16 downslope windstorm events using tower observations, ERA5 reanalysis, and Doppler lidar scans, supporting case-study and statistical analysis. We define these events as periods of strong, westerly cross-barrier flow exceeding 20 m/s. The observational record was limited by power outages during severe events, and lidar coverage was available for 6 of these events. We developed a technique to visualize the spatiotemporal evolution of critical flow features, such as hydraulic jumps and rotors, both essential to hazard assessment, and used it to identify a hydraulic jump signature during the 12 March 2026 case study. Increased lidar scan frequency will better resolve this feature evolution. Future work includes a dual-Doppler approach using co-planar scans from NOAA's additional wind lidars, turbulence characterization via vertical velocity variance (σw), and comparison to Froude number theory and model output (HRRR, WRF), sharpening detection of the flow features that govern fire and infrastructure risk at Marshall and similar sites.

492580.title: NOAA’s Software Engineering for Novel Architectures Program: Laying the Foundation for the NOAA Moonshot
492580.authors: Thomas Edward Robinson Jr., GFDL, Raritan, NJ; and J. R. Carley, I. Jankov, R. Benson, J. King, and R. Lyons
492580.abstract: In early 2026 NOAA announced the ambitious “Moonshot” initiative to deliver a global fully coupled Earth-System model at convection-allowing resolution (~3 km) for operational Numerical Weather Prediction. Realizing such a vision will require scientific and technological advances over the years, especially in the realm of High Performance Computing (HPC). Fortunately, the Software Engineering for Novel Architectures (SENA) program has been providing support for applied research into the latest technology trends for over a decade through NOAA’s Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) to the Global Systems Laboratory (GSL), the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL), and the Office of Modeling and Development (OMD). This cross-line office effort was initially focused on transitioning NOAA’s model code bases to fine-grained architectures defined as supporting more than 60 concurrent threads in hardware, which at the time meant GPUs or other emerging accelerators. However, over the last decade, traditional HPC nodes have come to support much more than 60 threads, and GPU porting has expanded to many different methodologies. Additionally, new trends in computing such as cloud and AI have emerged as commercial drivers for the industry. As a result, this presentation will serve to update the decade-old goals of SENA to meet the current and future needs of NOAA’s computing capabilities. SENA will focus on four strategic pillars: cross-platform support for both traditional HPC and cloud systems including systems based on x86 and ARM while considering GPUs; applied research into maximizing usage of GPUs through porting legacy code, using the latest developments in coding standards and methods while maintaining code readability, leveraging generative and traditional AI; developing AI weather prediction models; and creating synergistic projects that serve OCIO, GSL, GFDL, and OMD. NOAA will continue to work with commercial industry partners to ensure that their software and hardware meets the computational needs of earth science modeling. The SENA program has enabled NOAA to readily engage with today's technology by supporting a sustained effort to explore the latest technology for our applications such that NOAA is well-poised to meet the ambitious goals set forth by the Modeling Moonshot. NOAA will continue to leverage the decade’s worth of expertise that has been built and expand this knowledge to navigate the changing landscape of hybrid cloud and on-prem systems to ensure readiness of our flagship applications, such as the UFS, for years to come.

492581.title: Connections Between Mid-Level Stable Layers, Humidity Gradients, and Congestus Clouds in the Tropical Atlantic During ORCESTRA
492581.authors: Macintyre M Syrett, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. Colón-Burgos, S. A. Kennison, A. Trosits, J. H. Ruppert Jr., A. A. Wing, and M. M. Bell
492581.abstract: During the ORCESTRA field campaign, which took place from early August to late September 2024 and investigated convection in the tropical Atlantic, sounding observations revealed the presence of elevated stable layers displaced several kilometers (at an altitude of ~6 km) above the freezing level. This is in conflict with existing literature, which suggests that tropical stable layers are instead collocated with the freezing level at around 4-5 km. Analysis of the vertical distributions of stable layers across the ORCESTRA, DYNAMO, EUREC4A, and OTREC field campaigns lends credence to the idea that the formation of mid-level stability is not inherently related to freezing-level processes. Instead, statistical analysis of soundings from the aforementioned field campaigns reveals a robust statistical linear relationship between a mid-level stability index and strongly vertically decreasing relative humidity. Additionally, experiments with a radiative transfer model demonstrate that these observed vertical humidity gradients are sufficient to induce the formation of a mid-level stable layer over diurnal timescales without incorporating latent heating or cloud processes. Recent research using data from multiple remote sensing instruments and soundings launched on board the RV Meteor during the ORCESTRA campaign reveals statistical relationships between mid-level stable layers, congestus cloud populations, and convective organization metrics. Higher stability indices are associated with decreased cloud fraction above 6 km. A similar radiative transfer model experiment reveals the impact of congestus clouds on the formation of a mid-level stable layer.

492583.title: A Convection-Permitting, Observation-Verified Assessment of Aviation Turbulence over the Last 40 Years Above North America
492583.authors: Martina Bramberger, NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and W. Deierling, H. Shin, and G. Meymaris
492583.abstract: Turbulence is the leading cause of in-flight injury to passengers and crew, yet multi-decadal assessments of how it has changed rest almost entirely on coarse-resolution reanalyses and on clear-air turbulence alone. We analyse turbulence between 1980–2021 over North America using Graphical Turbulence Guidance product output computed on a 4 km convection-permitting Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model reanalysis dataset called CONUS404, resolving convectively induced (CIT), clear-air (CAT) and mountain-wave (MWT) turbulence across seven flight levels. Because mean energy dissipation rate conflates how often turbulence occurs with how strong it is, we decompose each trend into an occurrence component and a severity component. Results investigating the changes in occurrence and severity of turbulence will be shown. Findings include increases of moderate and greater turbulence between 1980 and 2020 depending on mechanism and flight level. The decomposition shows that turbulence occurrence and intensity respond differently: for MoG the rise is dominated by frequency, the severity contributing only 10–30%. Changes are also strongly non-uniform across the United States. We also verify the CONUS404 derived turbulence distributions against gridded in-situ energy dissipation rate observations (2009–2021). Modelled MoG rates agree within ~10% where aircraft actually fly, although severe turbulence is underpredicted by 30–40%. CAT and CIT reproduce the observed spatial pattern (rₛ = 0.45 and 0.42) against an observational reliability ceiling of ~0.9. A portion of this research is in response to requirements and funding by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

492585.title: Real-Time, Multi-Species VOC Detection with Picarro Broad Band Cavity Ring Down Spectroscopy
492585.authors: Alexis Rae Badder, PIcarro, Inc., Santa Clara, CA; and J. Bhattacharya, K. Skog, L. McHale, and C. Rella
492585.abstract: Monitoring Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) in the ambient atmosphere has become increasingly critical as their role in air quality degradation and human health impacts grows clearer. VOCs contribute to tropospheric ozone formation and can be hazardous at parts-per-billion (ppb) to parts-per-trillion (ppt) concentrations, with several species linked to respiratory complications and elevated cancer risks. Reflecting these concerns, the U.S. EPA has recently proposed more stringent fence-line monitoring requirements for six high-priority air toxics: benzene, ethylene oxide, chloroprene, 1,3-butadiene, vinyl chloride, and ethylene dichloride. To address the need for sensitive, robust, and field-deployable VOC monitoring solutions, Picarro has developed Broad Band Cavity Ring-Down Spectroscopy (BB-CRDS), a laser-based analytical platform capable of quantifying a wide range of VOCs in real time at ppb–ppt levels. The system can simultaneously measure ten or more compounds selected from a library of nearly 700 spectrally characterized species, spanning both VOCs and key inorganic gases such as H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, etc. Designed for operational simplicity and deployment in challenging environments, the analyzer requires minimal consumables and maintenance. This presentation will describe the BB-CRDS technology and demonstrate its analytical performance, highlighting advances that support enhanced air-quality management, scientific research, and emerging regulatory compliance needs.

492586.title: A Simplified Near Real-Time (NRT) Geolocation Monitoring System for GOES ABI
492586.abstract: Observations from the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) on GOES satellites are vital for routine weather forecasting, nowcasting, environmental hazard detecting/tracking, and more. Accurate geolocation is a key requirement of the ABI data quality since it ensures that observations are precisely aligned with real-world situation. The NOAA NESDIS GOES Calibration Working Group (CWG) Extended Navigation and Registration Analysis and Improvement System (CENRAIS) was developed to monitor the ABI image navigation and registration (INR). However, the CENRAIS system is computationally intensive since it evaluates a comprehensive suite of INR metrics, which causes significant delays and limits operational responsiveness. To address the latency, we present a simplified ABI geolocation monitoring system that’s derived from CENRAIS but optimized for rapid real-time assessment. Instead of processing all 16 spectral channels and complex inter-channel metrics, the new system focuses on evaluating navigation residuals in two key representative channels (one visible and one thermal infrared) by cross-correlating ABI images against high-resolution Landsat landmark chips. Operating as a continuous anomaly detector, this system can trigger offline CENRAIS for deep-dive diagnostic analysis whenever a navigation residual threshold is exceeded. Furthermore, this system can be easily adapted to monitor future geostationary instruments, such as those on the GeoXO satellite series.

492587.title: Event-Based Evaluation of NOAA Coastal Ocean Reanalysis (CORA) Water Levels at Department of War Coastal Installations During High-Impact Coastal Flooding
492587.authors: Alexander R. Davies, U.S. Naval Academy, Annapolis, MD; and S. Loeffler
492587.abstract: Coastal flooding poses an increasing threat to infrastructure, operations, and mission readiness at U.S. Department of War (DoW) installations. While many coastal installations rely on nearby NOAA tide gauges to assess flood risk, numerous locations lack long-term observational water level records needed to evaluate historical flooding, characterize local vulnerability, and support resilience planning. The NOAA Coastal Ocean Reanalysis (CORA) provides hourly water level estimates along the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts from 1979–2022, offering a potential solution for extending water level analyses beyond locations with in situ observations. Previous validation efforts have demonstrated good agreement between CORA nodes and NOAA tide gauges over long-term records. However, the ability of CORA to accurately represent the relatively infrequent but operationally significant high-impact coastal flooding events has not been comprehensively assessed. This study evaluates CORA performance during high-impact coastal flooding events at multiple DoD coastal installations spanning a range of hydrodynamic regimes. Event-based comparisons between NOAA Tides Gauges and nearby CORA nodes examine water level magnitude, peak timing, and event duration, with case studies highlighting impactful flooding events.

492593.title: You Say You Want More Resolution: The Transition of Aviation Weather Products from 13 to 3 km.
492593.authors: Matthew S. Wandishin, NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; and L. D. Melling, L. R. Blank, D. M. Uden, and A. Hewett
492593.abstract: During calendar year 2026, new versions of icing and turbulence forecasts produced by the NWS for the FAA transitioned to operations, marking another transition: The input model has switched from the 13-km Rapid Refresh (RAP) model to the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model. Quality Assessment evaluations were performed as part of the transition process. This presentation will focus on the impacts of the increase in resolution beyond mere comparisons of skillfulness. This will include the introduction of high-frequency (or small physical scale) variability and changes in the underlying distribution of intensity values. When one then considers that many systems are as yet (and will remain for some time) unable to display the products at their full, new resolution, several questions arise about how the 3-km data should be upscaled back to 13 km. These questions will be introduced and initial answer attempted.

492594.title: Commercial and COSMIC-2 Radio Occultation TEC and Electron Density Profile Retrievals at NOAA/STAR for Space Weather Studies
492594.authors: Xi Shao, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, Riverdale, MD; and Y. Chen, T. C. Liu, X. Jing, X. Zhou, J. Zhou, C. Cao, and S. R. Shrestha
492594.abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) radio occultation (RO) observations provide unique measurements to characterize ionospheric structure and variability with high vertical resolution and global sampling. At NOAA's Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR), we have developed an end-to-end cloud-based framework to retrieve absolute total electron content (aTEC) and electron density profiles (EDPs) from multi-GNSS RO observations collected by the COSMIC-2 and commercial PlanetiQ missions. These products improve space weather monitoring by providing critical ionospheric data for satellite communications, navigation, and positioning applications. Our TEC retrieval algorithm incorporates carrier phase–pseudorange leveling, multipath correction, and differential code bias (DCB) estimation to produce high-accuracy aTEC. The EDP retrieval algorithm derives altitude-resolved profiles from calibrated limb TEC observations through an iterative onion-peeling inversion under a local spherical symmetry assumption. The algorithm also retrieves key ionospheric parameters, including F-region peak electron density (NmF2), peak height (hmF2), vertical TEC (VTEC), and associated geolocation information. Product quality is assessed through comparisons with PlanetiQ, CDAAC, and the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) model. TEC product quality is further evaluated using metrics including DCB stability, inter-center relative bias consistency, anomalous outlier detection, and relative uncertainty derived from paired GNSS observations tracked simultaneously by the same LEO satellite. System performance is further verified by assessing latency, throughput, and data yield within the NOAA NCCF cloud environment. The ionospheric products are applied to investigate ionospheric responses during the severe geomagnetic storms of 12–13 November 2025 and 19–20 January 2026 (Kp index 8.7). These case studies characterize the storm-time evolution of total electron content, highlighting latitudinal dependence and the temporal lifecycle of ionospheric disturbances. The results demonstrate that integrating commercial and COSMIC-2 GNSS RO observations enhances global ionospheric monitoring capabilities, improves space weather situational awareness, and provides a strong foundation forl space weather nowcasting and forecasting.

492595.title: A Spatio-Temporal Analysis of Tropical Cyclone-Induced Tornadoes Along Southern Coastal Georgia
492595.authors: William Burgett-Merkel, University of Georgia, Athens, GA
492595.abstract: A Spatio-temporal Analysis of Tropical Cyclone-induced Tornadoes along Southern Coastal Georgia. William Burgett-Merkel, Dr. James Marshall Shepherd The University of Georgia Tropical cyclone-induced tornadoes are not often the most prevalent hazard in tropical cyclones; however, tornadoes can be a major risk as seen in Hurricane Milton, which formed a major tornado outbreak that caused multiple fatalities. Tornadogenesis generally occurs in the right front quadrant of the hurricane. Using ArcGIS, tornado tracks will be paired with tropical cyclone tracks, with a range of Tropical Storm to Category 5, in the southeastern US. The climatology of tropical cyclone tornadoes and to what extent of the annual tornado production is due to tropical cyclones, tropical cyclone tracks and their relationship to tornadogenesis, and the intensity of the tropical cyclones that produce tornadoes are studied using IBTRaCS, TCTOR, and SVRGIS Tornado Report Database data over past decades and covering a 500 km radius around Southeast Georgia. Analysis of the climatology of tropical cyclone tornadoes shows the region saw a 310% increase in tropical cyclone tornadoes compared to national studies, but a comparable distribution in rating. Additionally, analysis shows that 2020-2024 was the most productive five-year span for tropical cyclone tornadoes since 2000-2004. Investigation into the intensity of the tropical cyclones during tornadogenesis reveals that tropical storms yielded the most tornadoes within the region of interest. The next phase is to look at the frequency of each tropical cyclone category and how many tornadoes are formed by each category. The final research question’s framework is looking at the tropical cyclone track and seeing the distance the tornadoes form from the eye. This research aims to advance studies into tropical cyclone hazards using spatio-temporal analysis, as well as advance our understanding of tropical cyclone tornadoes, especially in the southeastern United States.

492597.title: Bridging the Latency Gap: The Operational Impact of CSPP LEO Direct Broadcast Products on Local Decision Support
492597.authors: Kathleen I. Strabala, SSEC/CIMSS, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and L. E. Gumley, D. Schumacher, G. Cureton, M. Odle, T. Rink, and J. Braun
492597.abstract: As high-impact weather events become increasingly volatile, the necessity for low-latency environmental data has never been more critical for operational forecasting. While centralized data distribution hubs provide comprehensive global coverage, the inherent "ground-to-user" latency can limit the utility of polar-orbiting data in quickly evolving situations. This presentation explores the operational implementation and value of satellite products generated locally via the Community Satellite Processing Package (CSPP) software for Low Earth Orbiter (LEO) satellites. CSPP LEO includes 15 software packages that generate everything from calibrated and geolocated JPSS Sensor Data Records (SDR) to NOAA science products for low-latency decision support. By utilizing local antenna sites to capture direct broadcast feeds from constellations including JPSS, Metop and GCOM-W, forecasters gain access to high-resolution science and imagery products - including VIIRS Day/Night Imagery (DNB), Active Fire retrievals, Flood Detections, NUCAPS sounding retrievals, MiRS microwave products, and GAASP AMSR products - often 30 to 90 minutes faster than traditional distribution channels. We present case studies demonstrating how this reduced latency directly impacts decision-making in diverse operational scenarios, including detection of Floods and Fires using the JPSS VIIRS imager. The results indicate that tailoring these low-latency products to specific local geographic domains significantly enhances the environmental decision maker's ability to provide timely, Decision Support Services (DSS). We conclude by discussing the future of CSPP LEO in an evolving satellite architecture.

492601.title: Using Lightning Data to Diagnose Dynamic Changes in the TLE Producing MCS on May 27th 2025
492601.authors: Zoe Bush, Texas A&M, College Station, TX
492601.abstract: Between May 26th and May 27th 2025, a mesoscale convective system (MCS) moved through the southeast Texas area over the domain of the Houston Lightning Mapping Array (HLMA). This research aims to use lightning data to diagnose the dynamics of each phase of the MCS along with the tracking algorithm for mesoscale convective systems (TAMS) and the experimental lightning burst metric (LBUG) products. TAMS uses cloud top temperatures from the GOES Satellite to organize and label MCS's while overlaying various atmospheric variables. LBUG uses the spatial and temporal evolution of VHF source points from the HLMA data to identify the strongest area of organized electrical activity within a storm based on changes in location of source points. The combined use of Earth Networks Total Lightning Network (ENTLN), HLMA, GOES, and NEXRAD data will be used for the analysis. The electrically active storm observed between 0200 UTC and 1000 UTC produced various TLEs which each occurred individually across the three MCS stages identified: the upscale growth phase from 0200 - 0500 UTC with sprite-TROLLS, the mature phase from 0500 - 0700 UTC with sprites, and the dissipation phase with megaflashes from 0700 - 1000 UTC. The bipole structure of the ENTLN pulses varies between the different MCS phases and lightning types. The final results will compare and contrast the bipole pattern and the overall flashes in the stratiform and convective regions of the MCS.

492605.title: Spatial and Temporal Patterns in Climate across a Small Urban Area: A Case Study from a New Micronet Deployed across Bowling Green, Kentucky.
492605.authors: Kamal Biswakarma, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and J. A. Brotzge
