492605.abstract: Urban heat islands (UHIs), in which urban areas are warmer than their rural surroundings, are well documented in major metropolitan regions but remain less studied in small and mid-sized cities. This study investigates the spatial and temporal characteristics of UHI across Bowling Green, Kentucky, using observations from 35 weather stations(Micronet) distributed across the city, with average station spacing of less than 1.1 km and 1-minute temporal resolution throughout 2025. Stations are characterized using the Local Climate Zone (LCZ) classification system to evaluate differences in UHI intensity across urban and rural environments. Preliminary results reveal a pronounced diurnal and seasonal cycle in UHI intensity. UHI intensity was generally weak during daytime hours but increased substantially during evening and nighttime. Maximum UHI intensity reached 4.2°C at 1900 local time in September, while nighttime intensities exceeded 3°C during several hours in June and September. In contrast, daytime UHI intensity was generally below 1°C and occasionally became slightly negative. These results indicate that urban–rural temperature contrasts are strongest after sunset and during late summer and early fall. Ongoing analysis will evaluate the influence of wind speed, atmospheric stability, temperature, humidity, and impervious surface fraction on UHI variability. Satellite-derived land surface temperature will also be compared with ground-based air temperature across LCZ classes and times of day to assess LST as a UHI proxy in small cities. This study provides a high-resolution characterization of UHI variability in a small U.S. city and offers insights relevant to urban climate research and heat mitigation planning.

492610.title: For Algorithms and Science: High-Resolution Simulations of Tropical and Subtropical Deep Convection for the NASA INCUS Mission
492610.authors: Itinderjot Singh, Colorado State University, Longmont, CO; and J. Bukowski, P. J. Marinescu, L. D. Grant, R. L. Storer, G. R. Leung, B. Dolan, R. Schulte, S. Prasanth, D. J. Posselt, K. L. Rasmussen, and S. C. Van Den Heever
492610.abstract: The INvestigation of Convective UpdraftS (INCUS) is a NASA Earth Ventures Mission targeting launch in early 2027. It will produce the first global estimates of convective mass flux within tropical and subtropical cloud systems using temporally consecutive reflectivity profiles from a convoy of three smallsats each carrying a Ka-band radar and supported by a multi-channel passive microwave radiometer housed on the middle smallsat. As part of the development of retrieval algorithms and in support of the mission’s science objectives, the INCUS team is producing a comprehensive database of updrafts and their local convective environments using high-resolution simulations of convective clouds. The goals of this talk are to: (1) provide an overview of the INCUS simulation database and explain how it contributes to the mission, and (2) present statistics of convective mass flux, convective environmental parameters, tracked updrafts along with their anvils, and reflectivity profiles as captured by high-resolution multi-model simulations in the database. The simulation database includes more than 30 cases of deep moist convection across the tropics and subtropics, encompassing convective morphologies from isolated cells to hurricanes and mesoscale convective systems. Each case is simulated three times: once with the Regional Atmospheric Modeling System (RAMS; 2-moment, bin-emulating microphysics) and twice with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model (2-moment Morrison and Thompson aerosol-aware microphysics). All simulations are configured using three nested grids, with grid spacings of 1.6 km, 400 m, and 100 m. Across our 100-m simulations, we find maximum vertical velocities ranging from 12 m/s in ITCZ convection over the Eastern Atlantic to about 50 m/s within supercells in Argentina. Similarly, we capture a wide range of convective environments, with CAPE and deep-layer shear values reaching up to 6000 J/kg and 40 m/s, respectively. Post-processing of this extensive model output involves running the Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds (tobac) algorithm offline to characterize the three-dimensional evolution of storm updrafts and associate them with their anvils and storm environments. These tracked updrafts and anvils feed directly into INCUS algorithm development. Additionally, the simulation output is passed through various instrument simulators to forward-model geostationary infrared brightness temperatures, INCUS radar reflectivity, and INCUS microwave brightness temperatures. We systematically evaluate these simulations against available observations to (1) ensure that the model output is realistic, and (2) identify underrepresented convective environments, updraft profiles, storm morphologies, and reflectivity signatures. The INCUS simulation database continues to expand as new cases are completed and will serve as a valuable community resource for advancing understanding of tropical and subtropical deep moist convection.

492612.title: Improving Ensemble Data Assimilation with Quantile Conserving Ensemble Filters in the Data Assimilation Research Testbed
492612.authors: Jeffrey Anderson, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and M. Gharamti, H. Kershaw, M. Smith, K. Raeder, B. Raczka, and M. Wieringa
492612.abstract: Traditional ensemble data assimilation methods make explicit or implicit assumptions of normality for both prior distributions and observation likelihoods. Variables like tropospheric temperature or surface pressure are examples where normality is generally a good assumption. However, Earth system applications include many quantities that are associated with distributions and likelihoods that are distinctly nonnormal. For example, concentrations of tracers in the atmosphere and ocean are nonnegative with associated distributions and likelihoods that are bounded below. Tracers that can completely disappear, like cloud ice, are bounded but also have mixed distributions and likelihoods; the probability of zero can be finite while positive values are associated with a continuous probability distribution. Rainfall rate and amount have similar characteristics. Wind speed is also bounded below at zero and observation likelihoods have mixed distributions given a lower bound for instrument detection. The fractional amount of cloud cover, ice cover, or snow cover have additional complexity since they are also bounded above and may have finite probability of both zero and one. The Data Assimilation Research Testbed implements quantile conserving ensemble filters (QCEFs) that can use arbitrary families of probability distributions to represent both prior distributions and likelihoods. Basic QCEFs for cases of continuous distributions are reviewed first and the rank histogram distribution is introduced. The extension to mixed distributions requires more careful algorithmic design. Ensemble members with duplicate values are interpreted as sampling discrete probability and non-duplicate ensemble members are treated as representing a continuous distribution as in existing algorithms. A key part of the algorithm is extending the definition of quantile. Poor definitions can lead to biased ensemble updates. Even these methods do not solve the problem of “creating something from nothing” and future work on this challenge is discussed.

492615.title: MODIS Collection 7 Clear-Sky Radiances and Products: Updates and 20-Year Trends
492615.authors: Eva Borbas, Space Science and Engineering Center, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and E. Weisz, W. P. Menzel, C. Moeller, P. Veglio, P. Hubanks, and R. Holz
492615.abstract: The University of Wisconsin–Madison has developed and is responsible for the MODIS Cloud Mask, IR Cloud Top Properties and Phase, and Clear-Sky Atmospheric Profile products for the Terra and Aqua instruments. As part of the preparation for Collection 7 (C7), we collaborated with the MODIS Characterization Support Team to refine the calibration of the MODIS photoconductive photovoltaic longwave infrared (PVLWIR) bands (27–30), with particular focus on Aqua Band 29 and Terra Band 30. The updated calibration addresses cross-talk effects that became increasingly evident after 2016 and may have been further impacted by instrument events, including the Aqua safehold in April 2022. To further reduce radiance biases in the MODIS infrared observations, we also revisited the spectral response function (SRF) shifts using Simultaneous Nadir Overpasses (SNO) between Aqua and Terra MODIS and the Metop-A, Metop-B, and Metop-C IASI instruments. The analysis provides an independent assessment of the MODIS spectral response functions and their potential contribution to observed radiance biases. This presentation will summarize the revised SRF shifts derived from the IASI SNO analysis and assess their impact, together with the C7 radiance calibration updates, on the temporal behavior of clear-sky C7 Level-1B infrared radiances and the resulting clear-sky Atmospheric Profile Products. The results demonstrate the importance of accounting for both radiometric calibration changes and SRF shifts when assessing the long-term stability of MODIS infrared observations and downstream atmospheric products.

492617.title: Investigating Seasonal Changes in Highly Oxygenated Organic Molecule Composition and their Influence on Particle Formation and Growth in a Rural Agricultural Area
492617.authors: Maxwell Lee, University of Colorado, Boulder, Boulder, CO; and D. Katz, B. Dobson, and E. Browne
492617.abstract: Ambiguity in aerosol cloud interactions contributes substantial uncertainty to radiative forcing estimates. New particle formation (NPF) and the subsequent growth of the particles is estimated to account for around half of the global cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) number. Thus, understanding this process is critical for correctly predicting aerosol-cloud interactions. Agricultural areas are understudied with respect to NPF and growth particularly considering that agricultural regions account for ~40% of land area. NPF in agricultural environments is influenced by a variety of factors, including emissions of biogenic volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from crops and vegetation, and nitrogen oxides from soils. Transport of anthropogenic VOCs and biomass burning products will also impact atmospheric composition. Thus, real time gas phase measurements are required to determine the influence of each of these sources on particle formation and growth in agricultural areas. With its location in a rural agricultural region and its long history of aerosol measurements, the Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement Southern Great Plains user facility (SGP) is a good location to conduct such measurements. Although aerosol composition and size distribution has been measured for several years at SGP, only limited information on the species that will grow particles exists. A previous modeling study has suggested that anthropogenic VOCs may be important, while measurements in the fall of 2016 suggested that monoterpene and sesquiterpene oxidation products were the main compounds that would contribute to particle growth. However, local emissions that influence the chemistry and formation of compounds that contribute to particle formation and growth vary throughout the year, leaving open questions about how the seasonality of emissions influences NPF and growth at SGP. We investigate differences in the chemical make-up of the organic compounds that influence particle formation and growth using measurements made at SGP in October 2021, April 2022, and May 2023. We show that while monoterpene and sesquiterpene oxidation products dominate the highly oxygenated organic compound composition in all seasons, the chemical pathways responsible for their formation differ. In the spring, monoterpene-derived oxidation products are dominated by organonitrates formed via night-time reactions with NO3 radical and/or via daytime NO chemistry. In contrast, relatively more non-nitrate products are observed in the fall. For the sesquiterpene-derived oxidation products, there is evidence for relatively more RO2 + HO2 chemistry in the spring compared to the fall. Understanding how these different chemical formation processes impact the speciation and volatility of the highly oxygenated organic molecules will help explain observed differences in NPF behavior between the spring and the fall.

492618.title: Correcting the Stereo Opacity Bias for Multi-Angle Passive Imagers Using Deep Learning
492618.authors: Joseph Nied, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and J. R. Loveridge and L. DiGirolamo
492618.abstract: Cloud-top height (CTH) retrievals from space-borne multi-angle passive imaging systems, such as the Multi-angle Imaging SpectroRadiometer (MISR), provide a key constraint for characterizing cloud vertical structure and reconstructing three-dimensional (3D) cloud fields. These imaging systems use stereoscopic techniques, whereby features are matched across multi-angle views to triangulate height. The emerging radiation field of these features are assumed to be localized to a surface. For clouds, however, this assumption is violated. Recent studies have shown that stereo-derived CTHs are subject to a systematic “stereo opacity bias,” whereby the retrieved cloud top is displaced downward into the cloud volume by as much as several hundred meters. This bias could have important implications for using stereo-derived CTH for in meteorological studies and in constraining 3D tomographic retrievals of cloud microphysics. Here, we explore the use of deep learning to correct the stereo opacity bias. The model is trained and evaluated using both synthetic observations generated from stochastic cloud fields and real MISR observations collocated with ISS-CATS lidar measurements. Particular attention is given to identifying the physical information exploited by the model, including multi-angle parallax signatures and spatial texture characteristics. We assess the model's ability to recover unbiased cloud-top heights and discuss implications for improving existing MISR cloud-height products and future retrievals of 3D cloud volume from passive multi-angle observations.

492620.title: Observation-Based Deep Learning Models for Short-Term Regional Cloud Fraction Forecasting
492620.authors: Evan Andrew Krell, NRL, Monterey, CA; and J. Nachamkin, C. Camacho, T. M. McHardy, D. Sidoti, J. Gull, and M. Fernandez
492620.abstract: We apply deep learning (DL) methods to produce skillful short-term, regional forecasts of cloud fraction directly from geostationary satellite observations. Speciﬁcally, we use the infrared bands from the Advanced Baseline Imagery (ABI) aboard the Himawari 8/9 geostationary satellites to produce cloud fraction ﬁelds for the Western Paciﬁc at quarter-degree resolution for lead times up to 6 hours. While Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) systems represent the state-of-the art in weather forecasting models, advances in DL have led to substantial research effort toward AI-based NWP (AINWP) systems. Traditional NWPs require massive computational resources to compute physics equations. Alternatively, after a computationally intensive training phase, AINWP models can produce forecasts within minutes on modest hardware. However, they typically rely on reanalysis data which increases their complexity. So, there is interest in purely observation-based AI models that produce forecasts without reliance on NWP outputs or reanalysis data. Once trained, these models can rapidly produce forecasts in the absence of high performance computing systems. We develop observation-based AI models by training a U-Net, a DL architecture that produces gridded output based on gridded input predictors composed of satellite observations and various auxiliary fields. These models are trained to predict a binary cloud mask. Rather than applying a single model autoregressively, we train a unique model for each lead time hour. While this requires additional computation effort, the models are optimized for their given lead time which alleviates the rapid error accumulation associated with autoregressive models. This presentation focuses on the results of substantial training experiments. These include comparing single-region to multi-region models, the choice of loss function, and strategies for formulating the target. We analyzed model performance for lead times up to 6 hours across several skill metrics including FSS, Equitable Threat Score, Probability of Detection, and False Alarm Rate. Pixel-wise loss functions tend to promote blurry, low-confident forecasts. Based on a published study by Lagerquist and Ebert-Uphoff (2022), we show that the Structural Similarity Index Measurement can produce sharper forecasts that exhibit improved skill across multiple metrics. There is inherent uncertainty in cloud prediction from satellite observations; without NWP, the model must infer the atmospheric state from a sequence of cloud top images. As expected, performance degrades with lead time but remains skillful relative to persistence. Lagerquist, Ryan, and Imme Ebert-Uphoff. "Can we integrate spatial verification methods into neural network loss functions for atmospheric science?." Artificial Intelligence for the Earth Systems 1.4 (2022): e220021.

492623.title: EPIC: Accelerating Community UFS Applications and Powering the Moonshot
492623.authors: Eric A. Aligo, STC @ NOAA/OAR/WPO/EPIC, Crofton, MD; NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and M. Lueken, R. Vasic, C. Book, M. Huang, and J. Vogt
492623.abstract: The Earth Prediction and Innovation Center (EPIC) has made it easier for the community to collaborate, innovate and enhance the R2O process by fueling foundational applications within the Unified Forecast System (UFS). Current and future enhancements to the UFS will help further bridge the gap between research and operations, putting NOAA on the path to fulfill one of the modeling moonshot goals for a global, convective-scale, fully coupled, ensemble-based Earth-system model based on the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS). One of the contributing factors to the success of the UFS is the technical support that EPIC provides to the community. This includes contributing to, deploying, and maintaining spack-stack, which provides a framework for setting up and managing software libraries on a wide range of software platforms, allowing internal and external partners to more easily use UFS applications. Furthermore, NOAA and the community use the UFS Short-Range Weather (SRW) application to run the UFS Weather Model (WM) and the Finite-Volume Cubed-Sphere (FV3) dycore, typically over short time scales and convective-scale horizontal resolutions. The SRW app encompasses both the UFS Fire model and the UFS Air Quality Model (AQM), with the AQM becoming operational in May 2024. Additionally, EPIC’s June 2026 Global Workflow release supports medium-range global forecasting configurations. Enhancements to the UFS and its applications, including the planned integration of the MPAS into UFS, will enable the research and operational community to run a global system at high temporal and spatial scales. A second goal of the NOAA modeling moonshot includes an ensemble based forecast system, within which stochastic physics pattern generator has been demonstrated to be a technique that provides sufficient spread and improves probabilistic forecasts. EPIC already maintains the stochastic physics component of the UFS-WM for the FV3 dycore, which gives developers the tools needed to determine its usefulness in probabilistic forecasting, and allows them to fine tune results to improve forecasts. EPIC will continue to provide user support and expand documentation for stochastic physics to include MPAS-UFS, which will be essential in achieving the second moonshot goal. NOAA aims to place the community at the forefront of weather forecast innovation, advancing its third moonshot goal of driving R2O2R. One effective way to bridge the gap between NOAA, academia, and the private sector is through Hierarchical System Development (HSD) test cases. Working alongside key partners, EPIC has developed and released several test cases accompanied by comprehensive documentation on execution and implementation. While the National Centers for Environmental Prediction maintains a list of high-profile cases—often representing operational model failures—EPIC has the potential to expand this library with real-world test cases that directly highlight and inform the community of National Weather Service needs. This presentation will demonstrate how EPIC can help achieve some of NOAA’s moonshot goals by building upon its current technical support and community collaborations while expanding future capabilities, such as the integration of MPAS into the UFS, supporting stochastic physics and adding additional HSD test cases.

492625.title: NH3 Emissions from Concentrated Beef Animal Feeding Operations Derived from Airborne In Situ Observations
492625.authors: Lena Low, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. Davis, B. Dobson, J. F. Juncosa Calahorrano, D. B. Millet, and E. V. Fischer
492625.abstract: Livestock systems are a major source of ammonia (NH3) emissions, stemming from the full chain of manure management activities. NH3 is released during the microbial-mediated breakdown of nitrogen-containing proteins, uric acid, and urea in animal feces and urine. Influenced by various storage and treatment systems and environment conditions, NH3 fluxes have high spatiotemporal variability. NH3 is emitted from manure deposits of indoor facilities and outdoor pastures, open-air pile and lagoon storage, and manure-fertilizer soil application. Volatilization levels depend on livestock and feed type, farming system, manure type, housing and storage systems, and meteorological and soil conditions. Since agricultural regions are historically understudied, and emissions are largely unregulated, uncertainty in the magnitude, variability, and fate of agricultural NH3 emissions is a major limitation to understanding agricultural emission impacts. Concentrated beef and dairy operations across the U.S. are hotspots for livestock NH3 emissions. Cattle feeding operations across Texas (TX), Oklahoma, New Mexico, and Colorado (CO) collectively account for >30% of national beef production. As such, the FarmFlux airborne campaign in Fall 2026 sampled emission plumes from several large beef facilities in northeastern CO and northern TX to better understand NH3 emissions rates and downwind plume evolution. These colder and wetter season NH3 measurements presented in this work provide contrast to previous warm season studies in CO that have sampled emission during primarily hot and dry conditions. Here we report preliminary analysis of NH3 plume magnitudes, emission ratios, and fluxes from selected beef cattle operations in TX and CO and contrast them with summer values.

492626.title: Tuning the GFDL Atmosphere Model (AM5) Using Perturbed Parameter Ensembles and Machine Learning
492626.authors: Ryan Kramer, NOAA/GFDL, Princeton, NJ; and H. Guo, Z. Tan, G. S. Elsaesser, K. Loftus, Q. Yang, M. van Lier-Walqui, D. J. Paynter, B. Xiang, V. Naik, M. Zhao, and S. Malyshev
492626.abstract: In general circulation models (GCMs), physical parameterizations contain empirical constants and simplified representations of unresolved physical processes, giving rise to uncertain or tunable parameters. These parameters can substantially influence model performance. Traditionally, parameter tuning has relied heavily on expert knowledge and experience. This process is often subjective, difficult to reproduce, and requires significant human effort and expertise. To develop a more objective, efficient, and automated tuning framework, we apply a machine learning (ML)-based parameter calibration strategy to a prototype version of the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's (GFDL) latest atmospheric model, AM5. In this study, we calibrate the model mean climate against a suite of observations, including metrics of the global radiation budget, hydrological cycle, cloud properties, and other key aspects of the climate system. Our approach begins by identifying a physically informed set of tunable parameters and constructing a Perturbed Parameter Ensemble (PPE) using the AM5 prototype. The resulting ensemble simulations are used to train an ML-based emulator and then generate promising parameter configurations. The promising parameter configurations are used for another round of PPE simulations and then emulator training. This iterative cycle of simulation, emulator training, and parameter calibration continues until the model performance metrics converge toward observational constraints. After a few iterations, we achieved a few alternative parameter configurations that produce a realistic mean climate in good agreement with the target observations. These results demonstrate that combining PPE simulations with an ML-based emulator provides an effective framework for calibrating complex climate models. This approach offers a reproducible and scalable pathway for parameter optimization and has the potential to accelerate the development and improvement of next-generation Earth system models.

492627.title: A New Approach to Reduced Nitrogen Identification and Quantification from Aerosol Mass Spectrometry Measurements
492627.authors: Guy Symonds, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and P. Campuzano-Jost, D. Kim, D. Day, Q. Zhang, X. Ge, B. A. Nault, H. Guo, D. Pagonis, and J. L. Jimenez
492627.abstract: Aerosol reduced organic nitrogen (ARON) species, such as amines, amides, and amino acids are often present in ambient particles but are seldom identified by standard analysis techniques. Smaller amines are known to participate in nucleation of particles. While some techniques do exist for detection of ARON species in aerosol mass spectrometer (AMS) data, they are limited. A new diagnostic was developed for detecting the presence of ARON species with the Aerodyne HR-AMS and evaluated with ambient data covering a wide range of locations and conditions. The new diagnostic relies on deviations in the ratios between reduced nitrogen ions (NHx+) in AMS spectra. These ion ratios (NH+/NH2+ and NH3+/NH2+) are generally very consistent for ammonium salts, both in calibrations and ambient data (0.068 ± 0.010 and 1.23 ± 0.04, respectively). Small differences between instruments can be corrected for based on the routine NH4NO3 sensitivity calibration. Most ambient datasets show results very similar to ammonium, so these ratios are not routinely examined. Analysis of dozens of ARON laboratory standards shows that these ratios deviate significantly from NH4+ values for at least one of these ratios. Thus, a 2D framework of these ions in ambient data can help identify the presence of ARON species. Ongoing work is investigating the information content of this diagnostic and its potential for quantification and apportionment, including comparisons with other techniques. Fresh biomass burning smoke often contains significant ARON. The lifetime of ARON from the analyzed biomass burning plumes is relatively short, on the order of several hours. Patterns in the 2D NHx fragmentation ratio space allow excluding many common amines as contributing majorly to ambient ARON. On the other hand, the 2D diagnostic suggests that dimethylamine and trimethylamine could be major components of ARON with further analysis ongoing.

492628.title: ATom-like Missions for the NASA B777-200ER
492628.authors: Paul A. Newman, Univ. of Maryland, Baltimore County, Greenbelt, MD; and L. Lait, S. Wofsy, and M. D. Rutovic
492628.abstract: The Atmospheric Tomography Mission (ATom) was amongst the most successful NASA Earth Venture Suborbital field campaigns (2016-2018). ATom utilized the NASA DC-8 long-rang aircraft, and was defined by its: 1) comprehensive payload that sampled key radical species, aerosols and aerosol properties, radiation, and meteorological parameters; 2) multiple profiles from the near-surface (boundary layer) to 13 km meridionally spanning the Pacific and Atlantic from the Arctic to the Antarctic, 3) a focus on the remote atmosphere for unbiased sampling, 4) one full global circuit during each of the four seasons, spread out over the three-year campaign, and 5) daytime flights to maximize the photochemistry sampling. The four ATom deployments accomplished 44 science flights over 416 flight hours with a total of 645 vertical profiles. The new NASA Boeing 777-200ER is an opportunity to expand and extend atmospheric science research with an ATom-like field campaign. The max-range ATom DC-8 flight was 4,400 nautical miles (8,166 km) from 34.7˚N (Palmdale, CA, USA) to 0.9˚N (near-Equator) and return (28 Sep. 2017, ATom-3) with a 50,000 lb. payload. In contrast, the NASA B777-200ER could fly 7,400 nautical miles (13,700 km) and carry a 100,000 lb. payload. With only the 50,000 lb. ATom-4 payload, the B777 can fly 9,000 nautical miles (16,600 km). New and existing questions provide the science rationale for global-scale atmospheric observations. While ATom provided a global snapshot of the Earth’s chemistry, new missions will be more than a decade following this sampling. For example, carbon dioxide (CO2) will likely have increased 20-25 ppm, CH4 by 50-110 ppb, and N2O by another 10 ppb by the late-2020s since ATom. How are these GHG increases changing the global photochemistry? The 2026 summer was characterized by severe heat waves in Europe, extensive wildfires in the NH, the development of a super-El Nino. How does this change aerosol concentrations and the global chemistry? Do we understand the cross-equatorial transport of chemical species? In this presentation, we describe ATom-like hypothetical deployments. The first scenario is a repeat of the ATom mission utilizing the B777-200ER to contrast with the NASA DC-8. The second scenario describes a tropical “longitudinal” mission that samples across the Pacific Ocean, the maritime continent (Indonesia, the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Malaysia, and surrounding shallow seas), the India Ocean, Southern Africa, and Atlantic Ocean. This 2nd scenario has multiple crossings of the ITCZ and regions where the ITCZ is ill formed such as the maritime continent.

492629.title: Vortex Initialization with Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Tropical Cyclone Forecasting
492629.authors: Shay Gilpin, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and G. Melka, R. Beeson, G. A. Vecchi, and H. A. Camp
492629.abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) forecasting is a crucial component of modern weather prediction, where communities rely on TC forecasts to prepare for and mitigate the impacts of these severe weather events. In recent years, TC track forecasting has improved considerably due to advancements in numerical weather models, data assimilation algorithms, and increased global observation availability. However, similar improvements in forecasting storm intensity have lagged behind. Accurately predicting TC intensity is challenging due to complex dynamical behaviors, particularly during rapid intensification, and limited data availability within the vortex itself. Vortex initialization (VI) methods have been designed to help improve TC forecast by adjusting the structure and intensity of the initial vortex field. State-of-the-art operational models combine VI with data assimilation to produce a “best” initial guess for the TC forecast. However, this approach can be limited by the simplicity of the semi-empirical VI procedures and missing physics knowledge of the governing cyclone dynamics. We introduce a physics-based machine learning approach to VI with the goals of (i) improving intensity forecasts, and thereby forecast skill, for tropical cyclones that undergo rapid intensification, and (ii) improving our understanding of the dynamics driving rapid intensification events. Specifically, we train a physics-informed neural network (PINN) to satisfy the first-order governing equations for TC dynamics, further constrained by model output from the Hurricane Analysis and Forecasting System (HAFS) and observations of TCs from dropsonde data and tail doppler radar. The trained PINN is then used to construct an estimate of the vortex field to initialize forecasts with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. We perform a case study for Hurricane Fiona (2022). We compare the forecast skill of WRF initialized with three different initial conditions: the vortex field estimated by the trained PINN, a vortex field constructed by the HAFS VI procedure modified for the WRF model, and model data from HAFS. For each forecast, we compare the accuracy of the cyclone track relative to the HURDAT best track data, and the vortex structure relative to estimates from the HAFS model. This work serves as a first step towards developing a physics-based machine learning VI procedure, which can help answer open questions about cyclone dynamics and become part of a VI-data assimilation framework to help improve tropical cyclone forecasts.

492632.title: Distinct Changes in the QBO Vertical Amplitude due to Tropical Upwelling and Wave Forcing
492632.authors: Hong-Li Ren, Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences, Beijing, Beijing, China; and W. Xu
492632.abstract: The quasi-biennial oscillation (QBO) dominates variability of the equatorial stratosphere and shows a weakening trend in the lower levels in recent studies. This study focuses on the vertical structure of QBO amplitude changes in observation, the dynamic reasons involved, and possible changes under future scenarios. The QBO amplitude has an increased trend in the upper levels of stratosphere and a decreased one in the lower during 1960–2022. Results indicate that the QBO amplitude changes are mainly controlled by the tropical upwelling and wave forcing, where the former dampens the lower QBO but the latter primarily maintains the whole QBO amplitude. In addition, the entire QBO could be weakened in the future, responding to the high emission scenario in CMIP6. Under the high scenario, the enhanced tropical upwelling would weaken the amplitude of QBO at lower levels of stratosphere, and meanwhile, the reduced wave forcing, mainly caused by the increased tropospheric stability and weakened convection activity, would make the QBO amplitude maintenance hard.

492633.title: Convective Organization in Developing and Non-Developing Tropical Cyclone Seed Disturbances
492633.authors: Jacob Hamil, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and A. A. Wing, G. Muesing, S. J. Camargo, D. Kim, and J. Moon
492633.abstract: Tropical Cyclone (TC) seed disturbances are the precursors to tropical cyclones (TCs) and are defined as a broad cyclonic area of moist convection that may or may not develop into a tropical cyclone. Recent work has suggested that TC frequency, the number of global annual TCs, is a function of the number of tropical cyclone seeds and their survival rate, which is the percentage of TC seeds that strengthen to a TC. The large-scale environmental impact on the survival rate has a greater body of literature than TC seeds and their frequency. Therefore, this work aims to increase our understanding of TC seeds through the development of diagnostics to assess their respective convective organization. These diagnostics were first applied to an ERA-5 reanalysis TC seed dataset from Moon et al. (2025), and now will be applied to global climate model (GCM) simulations from HighResMIP. We distinguish between “developing” seeds that eventually develop into a TC and “non-developing” seeds that never do. After distinguishing the seeds, we calculate convective organization metrics in a 10°-10° box centered on the seed and then composite by seed intensity. We consider several types of organization metrics, including simple metrics that capture the area coverage of convection as well as more complex clustering metrics that capture the spatial proximity of heavily raining pixels. These diagnostics will allow for direct comparisons between ERA5 reanalysis and GCM simulations representations of convection organization in TC seed disturbances. Preliminary results show developing seeds have a greater area coverage of deep convection, while the clustering metrics generally show non-developing seeds are more organized due to a smaller area where deep convection can develop. Therefore, convective organization metrics alone cannot definitively answer whether a seed will develop or not, one must also account for large-scale environmental variables such as vertical wind shear, relative humidity, and sea surface temperatures.

492634.title: Impact of Solid Inorganic Aerosols on Ice Clouds
492634.authors: Veronica Nicole Vologodskaya, The University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC, Canada; and E. Rowlandson, T. M. Seifried, C. N. Rapp, and A. K. Bertram
492634.abstract: Climate intervention strategies such as stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) have been proposed to limit warming due to greenhouse gases. Solid inorganic aerosols are promising SAI candidates because they can reflect incoming solar radiation more efficiently while absorbing less outgoing terrestrial radiation than sulfate aerosols. Most research on these materials has focused on their role in heterogeneous chemistry, while their potential to nucleate crystalline polar stratospheric clouds and ice in mixed-phase clouds is neglected. Crystalline polar stratospheric cloud particles can facilitate heterogeneous reactions that activate halogen species and promote catalytic ozone depletion. Furthermore, once SAI particles are transported into the troposphere, they may also act as ice-nucleating particles in mixed-phase clouds. Here, we investigated six proposed SAI materials: anatase TiO2, rutile TiO2, γ-Al2O3, α-Al2O3, α-SiC and nano-diamond. Their ability to nucleate ice under conditions relevant to polar stratospheric and mixed-phase clouds was evaluated through immersion freezing experiments in suspensions of 24.4 wt% HNO3 in water and pure water to study each system, respectively. We determined that these materials do nucleate ice relevant to polar stratospheric conditions; however, the predicted ice crystal number densities were lower than measured background ice concentrations. Their ice-nucleating activity under mixed-phase cloud conditions was also lower than that of mineral dust. These results provide constraints on the potential impacts of solid SAI materials on cloud formation.

492640.title: AI-Enabled Prediction of High-Impact Weather and Its Effects on Energy Infrastructure Resilience
492640.authors: Sha Feng, PNNL, Richland, WA; and B. Daniel, J. Rice, J. Zeng, N. Lalo, J. Tian, K. Balaguru, S. M. Hagos, and R. Krishnamurthy
492640.abstract: Extreme weather events, including atmospheric rivers (ARs), derechos, and tropical cyclones (TCs), pose growing and increasingly interconnected risks to U.S. energy infrastructure, grid reliability, and coastal energy assets. Flooding associated with ARs can disrupt West Coast substations, transmission corridors, and generation facilities. TC-driven winds and flooding threaten Gulf and Atlantic transmission networks, coastal assets, and oil and gas platforms. Derechos can produce widespread, high-severity, multistate power outages with limited warning. Although physics-based hazard models remain foundational, their computational cost can constrain the large ensembles, high spatial resolution, and rapid event throughput needed for infrastructure-focused probabilistic risk assessment and decision support. To address these challenges, we showcase two AI-enabled hazard risk assessment frameworks (DeepAR-Torrent and RAFT-Wind) and an AI-based hazard impact assessment model (DerechoGrid). They combine generative and discriminative AI with physics-based hazard and impact models across three complementary extreme-weather regimes. These frameworks link hazard prediction, and infrastructure-impact assessment to deliver spatially resolved, uncertainty-aware products for operational planning and long-term energy-system resilience. DeepAR-Torrent addresses AR-driven precipitation and flooding risks to West Coast energy infrastructure by coupling DeepAR, a generative AI system for producing large AR ensembles with 96-hour lead time, with Torrent, a computationally efficient Lagrangian hydrodynamic model that generate broad-area inundation maps at 10–30 m resolution. Targeted refinements at 1–3 m resolution incorporate detailed building footprints to support energy-asset-scale risk assessment. RAFT-Wind integrates an AI-enabled three-dimensional wind model that better resolves the vertical and horizontal structure of damaging TC wind fields in the existing Risk Analysis for Tropical Cyclones (RAFT) framework to provide more spatially detailed damage-probability estimates and supports grid-reliability analysis, operational planning, and infrastructure-damage tolerance assessments under present and future environmental conditions. DerechoGrid is an AI-enabled probabilistic hazard-to-impact framework that translates derechos into grid-relevant outage metrics, including outage probability, outage severity, and the number of customers interrupted. Using a hybrid U-Net and conditional diffusion architecture, DerechoGrid predicts probabilistic county-level outage footprints. The resulting products are designed to support grid-reliability planning, situational awareness, and outage preparedness. This integrated effort demonstrates how generative and discriminative AI can complement physics-based modeling to improve the speed, resolution, and probabilistic characterization of extreme-weather risks to energy infrastructure. By delivering ensemble-based and infrastructure-aware risk information, the project supports operational early warning, probabilistic decision-making, emergency preparedness, and long-term resilience planning for a more secure and reliable U.S. energy system.

492646.title: NOAA’s Fire Weather Testbed: A Year in Review and Future Evaluations
492646.authors: Ken Fenton, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and A. Baring, B. J. Hatchett, S. M. Hoekstra, L. McMeeking, PhD, P. N. Schumacher, K. J. Thiem, J. Vickery, and E. Wells
492646.abstract: NOAA’s Fire Weather Testbed (FWT) is a joint effort between three NOAA Line Offices: NOAA’s Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR), National Weather Service (NWS), and National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS). Functioning within NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) based in Boulder, Colorado, the FWT conducts evaluations and experiments both physically and virtually. As part of a transdisciplinary approach to fire weather research, evaluation, and user needs assessments that involves meteorological, social science, and on-the-ground expertise, the FWT and Decision Support Research and Evaluation (DSRE) Branch at GSL work together to conduct user needs assessments, research, and evaluations. The FWT also works alongside other NOAA Testbeds and Proving Grounds to facilitate the evaluation and transition of cutting edge fire weather tools and products into operations. Here, we intend to share an update on the last year of FWT evaluations, including three evaluations of how WindNinja can support Spot Weather forecasts and high-resolution fire models, and look ahead to upcoming work on Red Flag Warnings and coupled atmospheric and fire behavior models.

492647.title: Dust Events in Lubbock, Texas: Examining their Concentration, Chemical Composition, and Toxicity
492647.authors: Lauryn Fox, Texas Tech University, Seminole, FL; and K. Ardon-Dryer
492647.abstract: Dust is a prevalent concern in the Lubbock area as particles from dust storms have the potential to be toxic to human health. Particle size, concentration, and chemical compositions are each unique and changing variables of dust storms, all of which could affect their toxicity. Respiratory health in particular is especially vulnerable to changes in air quality conditions, with dust exposure being known to cause inflammation, trigger asthma, and lead to spikes in hospitalizations. This study aims to investigate the effects of different dust events that occur in Lubbock on human health using in vitro experiments with human epithelial lung cells (A549). Particle samples were collected from the AEROS station at Texas Tech University during dust events on May 17, 2022, and March 24, 2024. These events each had unique particle concentrations and size distributions and originated from different locations. By tracking individual A549 cells over 48 hours of exposure, the frequency and rate of cell division, as well as death, can be observed across different particle concentrations. A chemical analysis of these particles will help identify the primary compounds present in each dust event. Additionally, meteorological data from each dust event can be analyzed to provide insight on how forecasted dust conditions compare to observations. This analysis may improve the understanding of the impact dust events have on human health - potentially contributing toward better hospital preparation and eventual prediction of health outcomes related to dust forecasts.

492648.title: Wintertime Severe Convective Storms in the United States: Climatology, Trends, and Compound Hazards
492648.authors: August Kaapcke LePique, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and A. A. L. Lang and J. E. Martin
492648.abstract: Severe convective storms (SCS) are among the highest loss-causing catastrophic events in the United States, totaling an estimated $514.3 billion in damages between 1980 and 2024. When focusing exclusively on the winter months (December through March), SCS have become the leading type of billion-dollar disaster, accounting for nearly half of all losses (averaging 47.9% per year so far in the 2020s), representing a substantial increase relative to prior decades. These cold season severe weather outbreaks are typically organized by the environment and dynamics associated with mid-latitude cyclones. Despite the outsized impacts of cold season SCS events on infrastructure and economic loss, the climatological frequency and drivers of these systems remain under-examined compared to their traditional warm-season counterparts. A further complication is that many of the same cyclones that produce SCS hazards (e.g., tornadoes, hail, severe winds) in their warm sector simultaneously generate significant cold-side snowfall, creating a compound hazard that has received little attention in the literature and not well represented in catastrophe models. This research highlights a developing climatology of winter SCS events, compiled using data from the NCEI Storm Event Database, the NOHRSC National Gridded Snowfall Analysis, and ERA-5 Reanalysis, with the goal of characterizing both the SCS and snowfall hazard from a cyclone-relative perspective. At the synoptic scale, we use cyclone-relative composites to distinguish outbreak-producing cyclones (OCs) from non-outbreak cyclones (NOCs) following the Tochimoto and Niino (2016) framework. Preliminary results show OCs have substantially greater warm-sector instability than NOCs, driven primarily by low-level thermodynamic differences tied to a stronger low-level jet, while shear differences between the two populations are minimal. While the frequency of outbreak cyclones shows no statistically significant long-term trend, we investigate whether outbreak severity and associated environments have evolved over time. The frequency of OCs indicates large-scale variability (e.g., ENSO, MJO, stratospheric polar vortex) influences the wintertime SCS environment.. At the mesoscale, we use Kernel Density Estimation to isolate discrete outbreak “cores” within each cyclone, allowing characterization of core-level environments (e.g., CAPE/CIN, helicity) and hazard type.

492653.title: From Regulatory Insight to Insurance Action: A Roundtable on Weather, Climate, and Financial Risk
492653.abstract: Immediately following the 30-minute keynote, this 60-minute roundtable discussion would extend the regulatory perspective into a cross-sector discussion of how weather and climate information can inform decisions across the insurance and reinsurance value chain. Effective translation requires alignment among scientific evidence, financial objectives, regulatory responsibilities, and operational needs, including shared attention to data, time horizons, spatial scales, and uncertainty. Invited speakers will include, subject to confirmation, the Colorado Insurance Commissioner Michael Conway or a representative he designates from the Colorado Division of Insurance; an insurance value-chain and pricing-risk speaker from Allstate, Aon, Liberty Mutual, or Prudential; a reinsurance, capital-markets, or catastrophe-risk speaker from BlackRock, Moody’s, USAA, FM Global, or Alpha Geo; and academic and industry experts in catastrophe modeling, climate science, and risk management, with Hussam Mahmoud among the prospective academic participants. The discussion will focus on practical pathways from hazard intelligence to decisions about underwriting, pricing, portfolio management, reinsurance, mitigation, claims planning, capital allocation, and consumer protection and what are the innovations, research, and changes in practice neeeded to effect those pathways. Topics may include the regulatory use of forward-looking risk information; transparency and validation of catastrophe models; public data and climate-conditioned scenarios; communication of uncertainty; evidence for mitigation and resilience investments; changing reinsurance conditions; and opportunities for public-private partnerships. The roundtable will prioritize audience engagement and concrete lessons. Participants will identify the information, standards, validation practices, and institutional relationships needed to turn increasingly sophisticated weather and climate analytics into decisions that support resilient communities, functioning insurance markets, and effective management of financial risk. Participation by any proposed speaker is not yet confirmed.

492656.title: Simulated Tropospheric Vertical Transport by Amazonian Mesoscale Convective Systems and its Dependence on Model Grid Spacing
492656.authors: Sheng-Lun Tai, PNNL, Richland, WA; and J. D. Fast, A. Varble, PhD, M. Shrivastava, and H. Xiao
492656.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) play a significant role in altering the vertical distribution of aerosols and trace gases within the Amazon. However, the exact characteristics and effectiveness of upward and downward transport—and how they respond to changes in model grid spacing—are not well understood. To investigate this, we conducted WRF-Chem simulations with horizontal grid resolutions of 10, 4, 1, and 0.25 km using passive tracers introduced at various tropospheric levels. We analyzed transport during a prominent MCS event over central Amazonia on April 1, 2014, as part of GoAmazon2014/5. Simulations were compared with satellite infrared brightness temperatures and radar wind profiler observations, and vertical transport was assessed using the vertical mass transport rate (VMTR). Our findings show that, when comparing model-resolved vertical motions, convection-permitting and large-eddy simulations closely match the observed double-peaked vertical velocity structure and produce significantly higher upward and downward VMTR than the 10-km simulation, with the 0.25-km run yielding more than twice the VMTR below approximately 6 km. High-resolution models also highlight relatively stronger downward transport from the upper troposphere to the boundary layer, contrasting with the 10-km model’s weak upper-to-lower tropospheric transport. Adding subgrid contributions to vertical mass flux caused excessive downward transport likely due to overestimated deep convection. Composite cross-sections based on the LES simulation demonstrate a two-stage process: mesoscale descent beneath the anvil transfers upper-tropospheric air into the mid-troposphere, followed by convective and stratiform downdrafts moving tracer-rich air into the boundary layer. These results indicate that coarse-resolution convection-parameterized models may have large uncertainties in both ventilation effect of Amazonian MCSs on the free troposphere and the return flow of upper-tropospheric air, which has substantial implications for aerosol budgets and aerosol-cloud interactions in atmospheric chemistry modeling.

492657.title: Advancing Spire's GNSS Space Weather Observations: TEC Validation, Receiver Improvements, and Scintillation Product Readiness
492657.authors: Vu Nguyen, Spire Global, Arvada, CO; and M. Talpe and P. Jales
492657.abstract: Spire Global's space weather products are derived from a constellation of approximately 40 satellites equipped with proprietary multi-GNSS STRATOS receivers, operating in sun-synchronous orbits across a range of Local Times of Ascending Node. Following a successful 2023 NOAA data pilot, Spire's GNSS-derived total electron content (TEC) products have matured to operational readiness, positioning them for NOAA's operational data buys and improved space weather forecasting capabilities. This presentation details recent advancements in observational technique and data quality, drawing on both on-orbit collections and ground-based simulator testing, and provides an update on scintillation product development toward a future evaluation pilot. First, we describe an optimization of code tracking through refined correlator tap spacing. Implemented on orbit, this reduced GPS pseudorange noise by nearly 50%, directly improving the leveling procedure that ties absolute pseudorange TEC to higher-precision relative phase TEC. The 2023 NOAA data pilot evaluated only GPS-derived TEC; this analysis extends that assessment to Galileo and BeiDou, whose modernized, wider-bandwidth signals exhibited pseudorange noise approximately 25% of GPS levels under default tap-spacing settings. Second, we assess TEC quality using an ionospheric trough analysis, focusing on nighttime observations when ionospheric activity is minimal. Using three months of GPS data from eight Spire satellites, the standard deviation of slant TEC is under 3 TECu for Spire-processed data, lower than that of UCAR-processed values, reflecting better precision. We examine how transmitter and receiver differential code bias (DCB) estimation and correlator tap spacing affect these results. Third, we compare slant TEC between co-located Spire and COSMIC-2 observations. Over a two-month period, the daily standard deviation of these differences is approximately 3.0 TECu. Longer-timescale analysis shows that the transition from STRATOS v1 to v2 receivers — which included a new wideband radio architecture and enhanced EMI shielding, and has been rolling out across the constellation since 2022 — is associated with a roughly 1.5 TECu reduction in this standard deviation. Fourth, ground-based testing using a STRATOS receiver with simulated GNSS signals (Skydel system) quantifies the temperature stability of DCB, informing on-orbit calibration. Finally, we present progress on Spire's scintillation products, including the addition of sigma-phi indices, performance improvements toward meeting observation requirements, and enhanced flagging of radio-frequency interference (RFI). These advances position the scintillation product for a second NOAA data pilot. Together, these results characterize the current maturity of Spire's space weather observations from its constellation of nanosatellites and outline the technical path toward expanded operational use.

492658.title: Sea-Pol Derived Estimates of Precipitation Induced Dissipation during the PICCOLO Campaign
492658.authors: Rosa M. Maria Vargas Martes, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada; Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and A. A. Wing, M. M. Bell, S. A. Kennison, D. Colón-Burgos, J. H. Ruppert Jr., and M. E. O'Neill
492658.abstract: The atmosphere is a highly entropic and irreversible system in which the hydrologic cycle plays a leading role in the dissipation of kinetic energy. In spite of its relevance in quantifying the energetics of the atmosphere, direct observation-based estimates (i.e., radar) of precipitation-induced dissipation remain elusive, with few studies providing satellite-derived estimates. Thus, in this study we provide the first ship-borne radar estimate of precipitation-induced dissipation. We employ data from novel measurements of tropical rainfall attained from the Colorado State University Sea-Going and Land Deployable Polarimetric (Sea-Pol) radar on board the RV Meteor during the Process Investigation of Clouds and Convective Organization over the atLantic Ocean (PICCOLO) field campaign, part of the 2024 ORCESTRA field campaign. The three-dimensional precipitation retrievals from the Sea-Pol radar allow the identification of virga (i.e., rain that evaporates before reaching the ground), and consequently attain a more constrained observation-based dissipation estimate. We compare our high-resolution measure of dissipation to coarse resolution reanalysis- and satellite-based estimates. We find that previous estimates from GPM DPR underestimate the value of precipitation-induced dissipation in the tropical atmosphere, while integrated datasets such as IMERG overestimate it. To assess the potential constraints different convective states may have on the energetics of the atmosphere, we partition by deciles of low-level precipitation and consider how, for a given decile, dissipation depends on the spatial morphology of convection. We further assess the contribution of convective type (i.e., stratiform, mixed, convective) and height (i.e., shallow, congestus, deep) classifications to precipitation-induced dissipation. We find that states with broad areas of scattered convection are more dissipative than those with small areas of clustered convection. Finally, we show that convective and deep classifications of convection contribute the most to the estimated dissipation. This observational constraint will inform future model development and tropical entropy budget studies.

492662.title: Impacts of Assimilating Mode S EHS Aircraft Data from Portable Aircraft Derived Weather Observation Systems (PADWOSs) in the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS)
492662.authors: Jason M. English, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and M. McPartland, Ph.D., T. Bonin, E. P. James, and M. Hu
492662.abstract: Aircraft observations are known to be the most important type of data assimilated by short-range Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models for predicting winds and temperatures (James et al. 2020), yet current aircraft data systems (such as MDCRS, a.k.a. ACARS) only obtain observations from a small percentage of large commercial aircraft. Over 95% of commercial jets plus many smaller aircraft are equipped with Mode Selective (S) Enhanced Surveillance (EHS) transponders which, if they are appropriately interrogated, can be used as a source of wind and temperature estimates. Six Portable Aircraft Derived Weather Observation Systems (PADWOSs) have been deployed across four states in the southern United States via a joint program between NOAA and MIT Lincoln Laboratory. These systems can interrogate Mode S EHS equipped aircraft that fly within 60 nautical miles of a PADWOS and provide temperature and wind estimates in real-time. We assimilate data from PADWOSs into the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS), which is a convection-allowing (3-km grid spacing) ensemble-based data assimilation and forecasting system. We conduct retrospective simulations using two different versions of RRFS, which use different data assimilation systems and dynamical cores: RRFSv1 (FV3-GSI) and RRFSv2 (MPAS-JEDI). We quantify the impact of assimilating PADWOS data on model forecast accuracy.

492663.title: Looking Ahead: Using GXI's 0.91 μm Channel for Daytime Monitoring of Water Vapor over the Continental United States.
492663.authors: Jack Dostalek, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and J. M. Haynes and K. McCants
492663.abstract: NOAA’s Geostationary Extended Observations (GeoXO) is the successor fleet to the current geostationary series, GOES-R. Starting with the second GeoXO launch, the GeoXO satellites will feature a new imaging instrument, the GeoXO Imager (GXI). One of the advances of the GXI over NOAA’s current geostationary imager, the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), is the addition of two new channels sensitive to water vapor. The first is an infrared band centered at 5.15 µm. The second, and subject of this presentation, is a near-infrared channel centered at 0.91 µm. This channel can be viewed alone or, perhaps more useful, in conjunction with the 0.86 µm window channel (the combination of the two is known as the water vapor transmittance product, or WVT) to monitor the total precipitable water (TPW) of the atmosphere. Although these shortwave channels cannot be used for nighttime operations, they do offer two advantages over their infrared counterparts. First is increased spatial resolution. The infrared bands normally used for water vapor detection, the so-called split window channels (10.35, 11.2, and 12.3 µm), will have a 2 km (nadir) footprint from the GXI. The 0.91 µm channel will have a footprint of 1 km. Secondly, methods of determining water vapor from infrared bands are complicated by the strong signal from the surface skin temperature. That problem is nonexistent at near-infrared wavelengths. The WVT product is the ratio of the reflectance at 0.91 µm to that at 0.86 µm. It is analogous to the infrared split window brightness temperature difference, usually 10.3 µm – 12.3 µm. The atmosphere is relatively transparent to radiation at 0.86 µm and 10.3 µm, but is somewhat absorbent to radiation at 0.91 µm and 12.3 µm. Taking the ratio of, or difference between, a window channel and an absorbing channel helps to isolate the water vapor signal from surface effects. This WVT product has shown promise over Europe and Africa using the channels of the Flexible Combined Imager aboard Meteosat Third Generation geostationary satellite operated by the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites. Since the ABI instrument does not carry a channel at 0.91 µm, examples of its use at geostationary orbit over the United States will be given via synthetic imagery created by the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) using fields from the High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model. After a demonstration of the creation of the WVT product, a discussion of it use for weather analysis and forecasting will be given. Severe weather forecasting is perhaps the most obvious use for the WVT product, so its ability to capture moisture in thunderstorm environments will be highlighted. Other potential areas of use, such as fire weather forecasting and sea breeze moisture, will also be explored. The 0.91 µm channel represents one of the advancements afforded by the GXI instrument aboard the upcoming GeoXO satellite series. Its ability to monitor water vapor will give forecasters another tool for the analysis and forecasting of weather in various scenarios.

492666.title: CoCoRaHS (The Community Collaborative Rain, Hail and Snow Network) - Citizen Science through collaboration and innovation... Engaging the public and professionals with a rich menu of information for over 28 years.
492666.authors: Henry W. Reges II, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO
492666.abstract: CoCoRaHS, the Community Collaborative Rain, Hail and Snow Network, consists of over 28,000 volunteer precipitation observers throughout the United States, Canada, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Bahamas, and Guam. It is currently the largest source of daily precipitation observations in North America. Now in its 28th year, it provides high-quality data to many organizations, including the NWS, State Climate Offices, the NDMC, Municipalities, and Agriculture, just to name a few. With a simple manual rain gauge, observers report daily precipitation measurements. They also report landscape conditions, which help with early drought detection. CoCoRaHS is all about collaboration with numerous entities, the public, and weather professionals. Through innovation over its existence, the network has evolved into an example of excellence among Citizen Science/crowdsourcing, providing an important educational link between end users of the data and those taking observations. CoCoRaHS's outreach, current innovations, and future opportunities for growth will be highlighted.

492668.title: Modernizing the NWS Storm Events Database
492668.authors: Liz Batty, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and G. Strassberg
492668.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) Storm Events Database (SED) is the basis for publicly available weather impact data published by the National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI). This data is used for NWS for verification purposes and by academics, the media, the insurance sector, and emergency managers. Historically, the data has not been formatted in a way that is easy for researchers within and outside of the NWS to use, and pertinent information is often missing. The current modernization effort improves data formatting and adds variables to the database, completes an improved user interface and database known as Storm Dat 2.0, and moves the application and database to the cloud. These enhancements will improve social science research by providing specific demographic and geospatial information related to weather impacts in a uniformly formatted way. Researchers will have access to variables including age, gender, city, state, and location of residence when provided, which will help them establish statistical patterns in the data by weather event. This will lead to a better understanding of fatality data and demographic risk for both the NWS and emergency managers to use in their operations. With the completion of Storm Dat 2.0, database entries will have enhanced georeferencing options that will improve the verification process and provide social scientists and researchers with more accurate geospatial data. The new database will be connected to the Damage Assessment Toolkit (DAT) in order to improve the accuracy and consistency of SED, DAT, and local storm reports (LSRs). Lastly, hosting the application and database in the cloud will facilitate the movement of data to NCEI in a more efficient manner and align with NOAA’s priority to move to cloud-based systems.

492671.title: A Synthetic Green Band for GeoColor True Color Imagery
492671.authors: Stephanie M. Ortland, CIRA, Loveland, CO; and C. White, J. M. Haynes, C. Seaman, S. D. Miller, and D. Lindsey
492671.abstract: True color satellite imagery is produced using red, green, and blue spectral bands. The Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) aboard the GOES-R series of satellites lacks a “green” (0.51 µm) band, making the creation of true color imagery non-trivial. Currently the GeoColor product uses a look-up table (LUT) approach to obtain green band values, but the LUT technique is limited in certain scenarios including shallow water, algae blooms, and smoke. To address these issues, we utilize advances in machine learning to create a synthetic green band. We use a variation of a U-Net convolutional neural network and train it with a diverse set of images representing a wide array of solar and viewing geometries from Himawari-9 Advanced Himawari Imager (AHI). The model currently uses Rayleigh-corrected 0.47 µm, 0.64 µm, and 0.86 µm channels from AHI, which have roughly similar spectral response functions to ABI sensors aboard GOES-R series satellites, to generate a Rayleigh-corrected 0.51 µm synthetic green band at 1 km resolution. We demonstrate whether a machine learning model can match or outperform the current LUT-based approach by comparing the synthetic green band values to the LUT-based synthetic green currently used within GeoColor. Additionally, we apply the model to the GOES-R ABI domain and integrate the machine-learning synthetic green band into the GeoColor pipeline.

492675.title: Reconstructing Indiana’s First F5 Tornado: A Case Study of the April 1, 1884 Oakville, Indiana Tornado
492675.authors: Lindsey Peterson, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX
492675.abstract: On April 1, 1884, a violent tornado struck parts of Delaware and Henry Counties in eastern Indiana. The first of only four F/EF5-strength tornadoes to occur in the state, the tornado was highly visible and caused parts of Oakville to “literally vanish,” leaving only three of the 30 houses in town still standing. Despite the significance of this event, detailed documentation remains limited. This case study reconstructs the tornado event through newspaper articles, cemetery records, and other historical resources to better understand its track and impacts. A strong emphasis is placed on reconciling discrepancies among contemporary accounts, including conflicting fatality totals and inconsistent biographical information for identified victims. An approximately 12-mile path across two counties and eight fatalities were identified, along with additional details uncovered about the destruction of Oakville, the individuals affected along the tornado’s path, and the recovery of the town. The resulting reconstruction provides a more comprehensive account of the event while demonstrating the challenges of interpreting fragmented and sometimes contradictory primary sources from the nineteenth century. This case study illustrates how integrating meteorological, archival, and genealogical sources can refine the historical tornado record, recover details lost to time, and preserve the memories of individuals and communities affected by significant tornadoes.

492676.title: Evolution of Turbulence and Precipitation Structure from Convective Core to Anvil with Adaptive Radar Observations
492676.authors: Jialin Yan, Stony Brook University, STONY BROOK, NY; and M. Oue, N. Allwayin, K. E. McKeown, E. Luke, and P. Kollias
492676.abstract: Deep convective clouds evolve rapidly as convective cells develop, mature, and spread into anvils, accompanied by changes in turbulence, airflow, and precipitation structure. Conventional radar scanning strategies often miss much of this evolution because they cannot continuously observe individual cells at high spatial and temporal resolution. Adaptive radar observations now make it possible to follow individual convective cells through key lifecycle stages while resolving their evolving internal structure. The Multisensor Agile Adaptive Sampling (MAAS) framework was deployed during the Tracking Aerosol Convection Interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER) and Experiment of Sea Breeze Convection, Aerosols, Precipitation and Environment (ESCAPE) field campaigns in Houston, Texas. Adaptive range–height indicator (RHI) observations were linked in a Lagrangian, cell-relative framework, enabling direct comparison of turbulence, airflow, and precipitation structure throughout the convective lifecycle. The observations reveal systematic spatial and lifecycle-dependent differences in turbulence and precipitation structure. Enhanced turbulence is displaced above the strongest low-level precipitation signatures and extends horizontally through the middle and upper portions of the cell toward the surrounding anvil. The mature stage exhibits the largest upper-level EDR together with broader regions of enhanced differential reflectivity and specific differential phase, while EDR decreases during dissipation. Vertical-velocity composites further reveal a vertically stacked draft structure, including an upper-level updraft overlying a lower-level downdraft within the broader region of elevated EDR. These observations establish a direct observational link between convective lifecycle evolution and the internal organization of turbulence, airflow, and precipitation structure. They provide new observational constraints on the transition from active convective cores to surrounding anvils and new benchmarks for evaluating convective turbulence and storm evolution in cloud-resolving models.

492690.title: Freezing Level Forecast Skill and Uncertainty During Atmospheric Rivers Along the U.S. West Coast.
492690.authors: Shawn C Roj, Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, Univ. of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and R. Weihs
492690.abstract: Accurate freezing level forecasts are critical for predicting precipitation phase in mountainous watersheds along the U.S. West Coast, where small errors can lead to large discrepancies in modeled runoff and reservoir inflows. These forecasts are particularly important for situational awareness and operational decision-making in watersheds implementing Forecast-Informed Reservoir Operations. This study evaluates deterministic freezing level forecast skill and uncertainty during atmospheric river (AR) events using three forecast configurations. Observations come from the National Weather Service, the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) radiosondes, and dropsondes collected as part of the AR Reconnaissance program over the eastern Pacific. The forecast configurations evaluated include the CW3E 9 km West-WRF, initialized at 00 UTC using GFS and ECMWF initial and boundary conditions, and the California–Nevada River Forecast Center (CNRFC) freezing level product initialized at 12 UTC. Forecasts and observations are evaluated for AR days at 24-hour lead intervals across days 1–4, with corresponding analysis times included, providing a baseline for comparison. Results indicate that forecast skill degrades systematically with increasing lead time, with notable differences among model configurations. The ECMWF-forced West-WRF configuration generally demonstrates the highest skill among the WRF configurations, exhibiting lower MAE and higher r² than the GFS-forced configuration across lead times, while RMSE differences are more variable. Mean errors indicate a persistent negative bias across all models, with the magnitude of the bias generally increasing at longer lead times. This systematic underestimation may be influenced by the vertical resolution and interpolation methods used to identify freezing level height. Standard deviations also increase with lead time, indicating greater forecast uncertainty and error variability at extended lead times. At longer lead times, RMSE values are on the order of several hundred meters, comparable to the vertical thickness of individual model layers in the lower to mid-troposphere. This suggests that forecast errors can approach the scale of the model's vertical resolution, highlighting the importance of vertical discretization when interpreting freezing-level forecast uncertainty. These results improve our understanding of freezing level forecast uncertainty in support of more reliable precipitation phase prediction and more informed hydrologic decision-making in complex terrain.

492693.title: Diagnostics and Monitoring of Satellite Radiance Data Assimilation for RRFSv2X
492693.authors: Ethan Chang, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA; NOAA/OAR/GSL, Boulder, CO; and L. Lin, G. Ge, H. Lin, K. C. Eure, and A. Back
492693.abstract: Efforts are underway at NOAA across both the Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) and the National Weather Service's Office of Modeling and Development to develop version 2 of the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFSv2X), an experimental next-generation numerical weather prediction system using the Model for Prediction Across Scales dynamical core and the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration framework. Rapidly refreshing systems such as the RRFS conduct hourly data assimilation (DA) cycles that ingest millions of satellite radiance observations over North America, and the overall forecast quality is highly dependent on the performance of extensive quality control procedures. As real-time DA capabilities advance, it is becoming increasingly critical to monitor assimilation diagnostics in detail. The Assimilation and Verification Innovation Division at GSL is developing pyDAmonitor, a Python-based real-time monitor for data assimilation that generates various diagnostics and metrics for the assimilation of observations into RRFSv2X. pyDAmonitor supports the monitoring of conventional DA, but has limited tools to diagnose the performance of radiance DA. This project extends the capabilities of pyDAmonitor by providing initial real-time radiance DA diagnostics for multiple instruments, including CrIS, ATMS, and ABI. For example, observation-minus-background (O-B) diagnostics can reveal spatial patterns and assess the quality of assimilated observations, while time series plots convey information on the volume of assimilated observations. The results of this work will provide valuable insight into the radiance DA process and support the continued advancement of RRFSv2X data assimilation strategies.

492695.title: Evaluation of Machine Learning Weather Prediction Over the Southern Polar Region
492695.authors: Saurav Dey Shuvo, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; The Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH; and B. C. Rakoczy, D. H. Bromwich, and S. H. Wang
492695.abstract: Machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models are increasingly being explored as alternatives to traditional numerical weather prediction systems. This study evaluates the performance of four MLWP systems, namely Aurora, GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and FourCastNet. The MLWP systems examined in this study are heavily trained on ERA5 reanalysis in combination with other numerical weather prediction analyses and forecast datasets. MLWP model output is obtained from the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere (CIRA) and NOAA-GSL. The output is evaluated poleward of 50°S from August 2025 through February 2026 against automatic weather station observations from the Antarctic Meteorological Research and Data Center (AMRDC) and staffed station observations. This period encompasses the primary Antarctic operational season when activity at staffed research stations and field sites increases substantially, and weather forecasting is particularly important for aviation, logistics, and field operations. Forecasts initialized using GFS analyses and ECMWF IFS analyses are compared to assess initialization impacts on forecast skill. Forecast verification focuses on key near-surface variables including 2 m temperature, 10 m wind speed, surface pressure, wind direction, and specific humidity. Verification is conducted using daily 00 and 12 UTC initializations with 6-hourly forecasts extending to 240 hours (10 days). Model output is bilinearly interpolated to station locations and compared using RMSE, bias, correlation coefficient, and derived thermodynamic diagnostics. Preliminary results indicate generally skillful performance across all four MLWP systems for surface pressure and temperature forecasts, with relatively small variations in error magnitude between models. All forecast systems exhibit common spatial error structures, including coastal wind speed underestimation and enhanced temperature errors near the northern Antarctic Peninsula.
