Forecasts initialized from IFS analyses generally demonstrate improved performance relative to GFS initialized forecasts. This work provides an observation-based benchmark and validation of emerging MLWP systems within the challenging high-latitude Southern Hemisphere environment, identifying regional strengths and limitations relevant to their use as complements to traditional numerical weather prediction systems.

492701.title: Accelerating Heat-to-Extreme Precipitation Transitions across the CONUS: Contrasting Dry and Humid Heat
492701.authors: Nari Im, Boston University, Boston, MA; and P. W. Keys
492701.abstract: Rapid swings between heatwaves and extreme precipitation have been increasingly observed globally in a warming climate. Such sequential compound extreme events can threaten ecosystems and cause substantial socioeconomic losses due to short recovery time. Yet, historical trends in successive hot-wet extremes remain less understood, particularly the distinct ways that dry or humid heatwaves influence conditions for extreme precipitation. We examine how sequential hot-wet extremes have evolved in recent decades across the contiguous United States (CONUS), using ERA5 reanalysis. Given the CONUS region’s diverse climate, we compare the characteristics of dry and humid heat using a locally defined extreme humidity threshold. We find that rapid transitions from heatwaves to extreme precipitation have become more frequent across the CONUS, with humid heat-to-wet events occurring more often than dry types. Hotspot regions for dry events are concentrated in the Southwest and Southeast, where enhanced instability and moisture transport are observed. Meanwhile, humid events are dominant along the Gulf of Mexico and the East coast, with trends in increased moisture transport and reduced local instability. These findings strengthen our understanding of these climate extremes, and could support climate adaptation strategies and local resilience to cascading weather extremes.

492702.title: Architecting Distributed Data Resilience: Transferring 14 PB of Geoscience Data across Research Networks
492702.abstract: The Geoscience Data Exchange (GDEX; https://gdex.ucar.edu) at the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) provides a centralized repository of 1,700+ curated datasets integrated with NSF NCAR high-performance computing resources to support atmospheric and geosciences research. Serving as the primary data commons for NSF NCAR, GDEX promotes collaborative discovery through open science practices, maintaining alignment with FAIR principles while providing targeted datasets optimized for AI/ML research requirements. In 2025, to ensure long-term data durability and resilience, GDEX staff initiated a project to establish a geographically and organizationally distributed disaster recovery repository. Collaborating with the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC) at the University of Texas at Austin, the team moved 14 PB of data from NSF NCAR to TACC via research and education (R&E) networks, supplementing existing tape archives. The initial transfer process, spanning February to May 2026, involved rigorous route evaluation and performance testing. Ongoing end-to-end performance assessments now inform strategies for sustained, optimized data synchronization. This presentation outlines the preliminary design, architectural trade-offs, and methodology required for petabyte-scale data migration. We will demonstrate how such transfers are not only feasible but can become standard practice for the broader research community, while also discussing future plans to enhance data accessibility.

492705.title: Three-Phase Machine Learning for PM₂.₅ Forecasting: A Comparative Study with Deep Learning and Transformers
492705.authors: Rokeya Siddiqua, Morgan State University, Baltimore, MD
492705.abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is a major air pollutant of significant concern because of its adverse effects on human health, environmental quality, and overall air quality conditions, while its concentration can change rapidly in response to variations in atmospheric, meteorological, and temporal conditions. Accurate and temporally resolved PM2.5 forecasting is therefore essential for effective air quality management, public health protection, pollution-warning systems, environmental monitoring, and timely decision-making. However, reliable short-term PM2.5 prediction remains challenging because particulate concentrations are governed by complex and nonlinear interactions among meteorological conditions, atmospheric aerosol characteristics, temporal patterns, and local emission processes. Conventional ground-based monitoring networks provide valuable measurements but may not adequately capture the spatial and temporal variability required for high-resolution forecasting. The increasing availability of satellite-derived aerosol observations, particularly aerosol optical depth (AOD), provides an important complementary source of information that can enhance ground-based observations and improve the representation of atmospheric particulate conditions. Nevertheless, integrating multi-source environmental data introduces additional challenges related to temporal alignment, feature representation, nonlinear relationships, model complexity, and the realistic evaluation of forecasting performance. This study addresses these challenges by developing and systematically evaluating a three-phase machine learning framework for high-resolution PM2.5 forecasting that integrates satellite-derived AOD with ground-based meteorological observations and compares optimized conventional machine learning models with deep learning, hybrid, and Transformer-based architectures. The primary objectives of the study are to investigate the influence of temporal resolution on PM2.5 forecasting accuracy, determine whether systematic temporal and nonlinear feature engineering can improve predictive performance, identify the most informative predictors through feature selection, evaluate the relative performance of different machine learning approaches, and assess whether more complex deep learning and Transformer architectures provide meaningful advantages over optimized tree-based ensemble models. To accomplish these objectives, data from three monitoring stations in the DMV region—Howard, Padonia, and Beltsville—were collected for the period from 2019 to 2022 using publicly available U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) observations and GEO-LEO Dark Target satellite datasets. The satellite-derived AOD observations were integrated with ground-based meteorological and environmental variables to construct two datasets at 60-minute and 30-minute temporal resolutions, enabling a direct assessment of the effect of increased temporal granularity on forecasting performance. The proposed framework consists of three sequential phases: baseline modeling, temporal and nonlinear feature engineering, and feature selection. In the feature-engineering phase, lagged variables were introduced to capture temporal dependencies, rolling statistical features were generated to represent short-term variability and local trends, interaction features were incorporated to capture nonlinear relationships among predictors, and cyclic features were developed to represent recurring temporal patterns. These procedures expanded the predictor space to 87 variables, after which feature-importance analysis was applied to identify the 10 most informative predictors and construct optimized feature sets. Ten supervised machine learning algorithms representing linear, tree-based, boosting, and instance-based learning approaches were subsequently evaluated using both random train-test splitting and chronological TimeSeriesSplit validation. While random splitting was used to assess conventional predictive capability, chronological validation was emphasized to provide a more realistic evaluation of future forecasting performance and to reduce the potential for overly optimistic results caused by temporal dependence and information leakage. The optimized machine learning models were further benchmarked under time-series validation against eight deep learning and hybrid approaches, including recurrent neural networks, convolutional models, CNN-LSTM architectures, and STL-XGBoost, together with two structured Transformer configurations. Model performance was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (R2), mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE), providing complementary measures of explanatory power, average prediction error, overall error magnitude, and relative forecasting accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that increasing temporal resolution from 60 to 30 minutes consistently improves predictive performance across the evaluated models, indicating that higher-frequency integrated observations can provide more useful information for capturing short-term PM2.5 variability. The proposed temporal and nonlinear feature-engineering and feature-selection strategy also produces substantial improvements over baseline machine learning configurations. At the 30-minute temporal resolution, ensemble boosting methods, particularly CatBoost, XGBoost, and LightGBM, achieved R2 values of approximately 0.89–0.92 under random train-test splitting and 0.84–0.89 under chronological time-series validation, while simultaneously producing substantial reductions in RMSE and MAE compared with their corresponding baseline models. These results demonstrate that appropriate feature representation can be as important as algorithm selection for high-resolution PM2.5 forecasting. Although the deep learning, hybrid, and Transformer-based models demonstrated competitive predictive performance and were capable of learning complex temporal relationships, the optimized tree-based ensemble models achieved stronger overall predictive performance and more stable generalization under chronological validation. This finding suggests that increasing model architectural complexity does not necessarily translate into superior forecasting accuracy when conventional machine learning models are supported by carefully engineered and selectively refined predictors. Overall, the study demonstrates that an integrated multi-source forecasting strategy combining satellite-derived AOD, ground-based observations, systematic feature engineering, feature selection, and time-aware validation can provide an accurate, robust, and computationally practical approach to high-resolution PM2.5 forecasting. The findings further indicate that optimized tree-based ensemble methods can serve as effective alternatives to computationally intensive sequence-based deep learning and Transformer architectures, particularly when the primary objective is reliable future-oriented prediction rather than architectural complexity. The proposed framework also emphasizes the importance of evaluating environmental forecasting models under chronological validation, which provides a more realistic indication of their ability to generalize to unseen future observations. By combining high temporal resolution with multi-source environmental information and rigorous model comparison, this study contributes a practical and systematic framework for operational PM2.5 forecasting and provides useful evidence for the development of air quality monitoring, early-warning, environmental management, and public health decision-support applications.

492708.title: The Invisible Depletion: Compound Drought, Groundwater Collapse, and Maladaptation in the Middle East and Southwest Asia
492708.authors: Mahmoud Osman, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and A. McNally and B. Cook
492708.abstract: The Middle East and Southwest Asia (MESWA) region is experiencing severe hydro-climatic non-stationarity, transitioning from cyclical precipitation deficits and surpluses to a state of structural water bankruptcy. This review synthesizes the compounding atmospheric and anthropogenic drivers of this crisis, highlighting the region’s shift towards a regime defined by frequent, concurrent extremes of drought and heat ("Hot Drought" regime). Earth System Models and observational records confirm that while fundamental ocean-basin teleconnections (e.g., ENSO) remain intact, their hydrological impacts have become asymmetric. In recent years, (1) expected moisture delivery to MESWA has been frequently deflected by persistent atmospheric blocking and (2) escalating temperatures and extreme evaporative demand have reduced snow water storage and the ability of precipitation events to recharge surface moisture and water resources. To compensate for these losses in surface water availability, the region has increasingly relied on unregulated groundwater extraction. We present case studies in the region of different ways that the changing hydrological and climate dynamics are influencing water availability and water management for agriculture and other sectors. We argue that operational Early Warning Systems (EWS) must expand beyond solely traditional, precipitation-centric meteorological forecasting by additionally tracking absolute water availability accounting for increasing groundwater and evaporative demand

492711.title: A Machine Learning Approach to Predicting Winter Weather-Related Motor Vehicle Crashes
492711.authors: La Ditra Kelina Mason, Southern Illinois University- Edwardsville, Edwardsville, IL
492711.abstract: Winter weather events such as snow, freezing rain, and subfreezing conditions present major challenges to transportation systems and are associated with increased motor vehicle crash risk. There is an existing general relationship between winter precipitation and crash frequency, however there is a paucity of impact-based systems that capture the nonlinear interactions between atmospheric, roadway and traffic variables. This study addresses these limitations by developing a machine learning framework to predict crash risk for motor-vehicle crashes during winter weather-related events. Crash data from Iowa Department of Transportation (IowaDoT) are integrated with 6-hr gridded snowfall data from NOAA’s National Operational Hydrologic Remote Sensing Center (NOHRSC) and meteorological variables (precipitation type, road surface temperature, wind speed, and visibility) from the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ERA5 reanalysis. Logistic Regression, Linear Regression and Random Forest models are used to identify which atmospheric variables most strongly associated with crash occurrence, evaluate how crash risk changes during specific phases of winter weather events (pre-event, onset, peak, and post-event), and assesses how models perform across different roadway classifications. Model performance is evaluated utilizing classification metrics (accuracy, precision, F1-score and AUC-ROC) and regression metrics (RMSE and bias). By integrating meteorological conditions and crash occurrence, this research aims to advance impact-based forecasting to increase public safety and reduce socioeconomic cost.

492712.title: Machine Learning for Downscaling and Bias Correction of Global Forecasts to Enhance NBM Probabilistic Guidance
492712.authors: Adam D. Schnapp, NWS, Silver Spring, MD
492712.abstract: The National Blend of Models (NBM) is a nationally consistent and skillful suite of calibrated forecast guidance based on numerical weather prediction (NWP) model data. The NBM is instrumental in the National Weather Service’s (NWS) efforts to provide decision support services to protect life and property by minimizing time spent on forecast generation and maximizing time spent on customer and core partner needs. The NBM uses recent data to bias-correct NWP and works well when recent biases are likely to persist, but is less effective during seasonal transition periods. To improve the performance of the NBM in these situations, the Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) is pursuing machine learning techniques with neural networks to optimize the calibration of postprocessed NWP using longer training samples. This presentation will highlight the machine learning efforts to improve bias correction and downscaling techniques for NWP models and produce guidance to populate the NWS probabilistic guidance database. Initial work to derive high-resolution temperature, dewpoint, and 10-m winds and gusts from Global Forecast System (GFS) quarter-degree inputs using a combination of convolutional neural networks and point-based models will be discussed, alongside verification and evaluation plans.

492714.title: Advancing Research to Operations Across the CIROH Enterprise
492714.authors: Erin White, University of Alabama, Cooperative Institute for Research to Operations in Hydrology, Tuscaloosa, AL; and S. J. Burian
492714.abstract: The NOAA Cooperative Institute for Research to Operations in Hydrology (CIROH) brings together academic, federal, and private-sector partners to accelerate the transition of water research into operational capabilities and other applications. Achieving successful research-to-operations (R2O) requires more than scientific innovation alone; it depends on sustained coordination among researchers, operational partners, developers, and users throughout the research and development lifecycle. This panel contribution will provide an enterprise-level perspective on CIROH’s approach to advancing R2O across its four thematic research areas: Improving Water Prediction Capabilities; Advancing Community Water Resources Modeling; Innovating Hydroinformatics Solutions; and Enhancing the Design, Communication, and Use of Hydrologic Information. Examples from across the CIROH portfolio will illustrate pathways by which research advances are translated toward operational use, including development and testing within community modeling frameworks, advancement of forecasting and modeling capabilities, development of data and hydroinformatics infrastructure, and translation of hydrologic information into decision-relevant products and services. The discussion will also highlight lessons emerging from CIROH’s R2O enterprise, including the importance of early operational engagement, clearly defined transition pathways, collaborative testing and evaluation, and sustained public-private-academic partnerships. Together, these practices help align research with operational requirements, reduce barriers to transition, and increase the likelihood that scientific advances ultimately deliver usable improvements in water prediction and decision support.

492720.title: Influence of Sea Surface Temperature Variability on Dangerous Caribbean Heat
492720.authors: Allan Cruz, UCAR, Bayamon, PR; and V. T. Narinesingh, K. Mandli, G. Seijo, and J. T. Fasullo
492720.abstract: The Caribbean region has experienced increases in heatwave frequency and intensity mostly driven by diabatic heating, which may be influenced by external factors like El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Atlantic Niño. In this study we look at how sea surface temperature variability of the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean basins surrounding the Caribbean Sea may influence the regional heat index (HI). We show that warm phases of ENSO and Atlantic Niño increase daily maximum HI and surface temperature over the Caribbean. We also show that the influence of ENSO with a neutral Atlantic is much smaller than that of Atlantic Niño with a neutral ENSO. When analyzing the rare case where both oceans are warm at the same time, we found that daily maximum HI anomalies during the early rainfall season (ERS) go over 4°F in most of the Caribbean, which is higher than during the HI peak in the late rainfall season (LRS). When comparing distinct types of Atlantic Niño, we show temperature anomalies are influenced by Eastern Atlantic Niño but not the Central Atlantic Niño. Relative humidity and surface winds did not show significance, further analysis on specific humidity and higher-level winds is needed. The influence of ENSO and Atlantic Niño on HI, temperature, and relative humidity shown here expands our understanding of important external factors to consider when forecasting dangerous heat seasons in the Caribbean.

492726.title: An Overview of the Data Assimilation Research Testbed: Past, Present, and an Exciting Future
492726.authors: Jeffrey Anderson, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and K. Raeder, H. Kershaw, M. Gharamti, B. Raczka, M. Smith, D. Amrhein, T. Hoar, and N. collins
492726.abstract: 2027 marks 25 years since the initial development of the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) at the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research. DART is a community facility for ensemble data assimilation (DA) overseen by the Data Assimilation Research Section (DAReS) at NCAR. The mission of DAReS is: “To accelerate progress in Earth System Science at NCAR, UCAR Universities, and in the broader science community by providing state-of-the-art ensemble DA capabilities”. DAReS continually improves existing capabilities and adds new ones while retaining transparent support for existing users. The selection of new capabilities is driven by user requests and by the development of novel ensemble DA algorithms. Our goal is to maintain DART's unique position as an accessible, state-of-the-art, research facility, for driving scientific inquiry across the spectrum of Earth system applications. The talk will begin with a very brief history of DART including key algorithmic and software decisions that have been foundational in supporting scientific collaborations across Earth system science. In particular, the use of a two-step implementation of ensemble filters and an interface design that does not require modifications to existing model code are crucial for past and ongoing success. An overview of many powerful, new DART capabilities will follow. These include Quantile Conserving Ensemble Filters, a generalized strongly coupled DA capability, hybrid ensemble filters, advanced visualization tools, rigorous software engineering enhancements to facilitate collaborations, and tools to easily access a vast array of Earth system observations. While all these capabilities are mature, many have yet to be applied broadly for many new Earth system and DA science applications. The talk will conclude by looking forward to the next generation of DART capabilities. These include further enhancements to our software to make DART easier to learn and use. The nexus with AI/ML tools will provide a chance to reduce computational costs and explore hitherto impossible ensemble sizes with advanced DA algorithms. Similarly, implementing DART on the most modern high-performance computing will also allow much larger DA applications. We will enhance our existing collaborations, including numerous operational applications of DART for Earth system prediction, and catalyze exciting new science explorations in the years to come.

492727.title: Summary of RaXPol Data Collection During the 2026 Spring Field Program with its New, Low-Power, Solid-State Transmitter
492727.authors: Howard B. Bluestein, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and A. Naik, T. Y. Yu, B. Cheong, D. J. Bodine, M. D. TZENG, H. W. Hsu, S. Emmerson, A. Schueth, M. Rajagopal, L. Shedd, F. De Martin, J. W. Thiesing, B. K. Cohen, V. GOEDE, and D. Schvartzman
492727.abstract: RaXPol data were collected in severe convective storms in parts of Oklahoma, Kansas, and Nebraska on nine days during the latter half of April and the first several weeks in May. The data collected were important not just for their scientific value, but also because these were the first severe-storm data collected with a new, low-power, solid state transmitter and different signal-processing techniques than the ones used on the older version of RaXPol. Pulse compression was successfully implemented and used while collecting operations in rapid-scan mode. To our knowledge, this is the first time rapid-scan volumes have been collected with a solid-state transmitter. Experiments were conducted to determine the optimum ways of collecting high-quality data for various severe-storm phenomena. RaXPol remains capable of collecting data by traditional frequency hopping, which was demonstrated during our field operations. However, the sensitivity and data quality collected via traditional frequency hopping were degraded, as judged by qualitative intercomparison with rapid-scan data collected via pulse compression. Additional signal processing and future modifications to the radar are expected to improve the RaXPol’s sensitivity by 5–10 dB. A summary of our results and suggestions for further improving data quality are described. The highlights of the season include the following: Surveillance scans and some raw I/Q data collection suitable for polarimetric spectral analysis in a large tornado and a satellite tornado on 23 April in Braman, OK. This was the most significant dataset collected this past season (see below). RHIs through mamma underneath the anvil of an MCS on 15 April in Purcell, OK Attempted bistatic data collection in an MCS in NW OK, on 17 April, on embedded supercells; an “Owl’s Horn” echo was documented in one of the developing supercells. This dataset was notable for the documentation of supercells behind an outflow boundary/front. Bistatic data collection in a supercell behind an outflow boundary/front in SE OK on 25 April. The radar reflectivity and Doppler velocity were retrieved by Sam Emmerson’s bistatic receiver and a 2-D wind field was synthesized. Surveillance data were also collected in another supercell, in central Oklahoma, with a funnel-shaped cloud at the occlusion point, but no tornado was observed. High-based multicells with some supercell characteristics were surveyed just W of Norman on 8 May. Bistatic data were also collected, and reflectivity and Doppler velocity were successfully retrieved. Surveillance scans and attempted I/Q data collection were conducted in a tornadic supercell in Nebraska and in an LP storm in south-central Nebraska on 17 May. One weak tornado was also documented, but the range to both tornadoes was too great for analyses of acceptable quality. Surveillance scans were collected in E central Kansas in a string of supercells, one of which was tornadic during data collection, but only very briefly, on 18 May. Some examples of data collected on 23 April are shown in the figures.

492740.title: Improving Machine-Learning Snowfall Forecasts for Extreme Events with Generative Data Augmentation
492740.authors: Fatemeh Azizpourshoubi, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; and M. Astitha
492740.abstract: Reliable prediction of high-impact winter storms remains difficult, and it matters: extreme snowstorms are relatively rare, but they strain transportation, the power grid, and emergency services, so accurate guidance for these events is valuable for decision-makers. For data-driven forecast systems, the main obstacle is the skewed distribution of snowfall accumulation. The largest, most damaging storms fall in the tail of the record, where training examples are scarce. We present a deep learning framework that combines physics-constrained generative modeling with discriminative prediction to address this imbalance. A variational autoencoder is trained on atmospheric fields from the CONUS404 reanalysis (Rasmussen et al. 2023) over a 4-km grid across the northeastern United States, learning a compact representation of each storm's structure. A diffusion model, conditioned on storm intensity, then generates new, physically plausible storms for the extreme categories that are underrepresented in the record. We add these synthetic storms to the observed record and use the combined dataset to train several snowfall prediction models, including gradient-boosted trees, convolutional networks, and encoder-decoder networks. We measure forecast skill with the Critical Success Index across a range of accumulation thresholds, focusing on the heavy and extreme categories, and we check whether the predicted snowfall patterns stay physically consistent with the atmospheric fields that drive them. The question we set out to answer is whether these synthetic storms can fill the gap in rare events without introducing unrealistic patterns that would hurt forecast skill, which is the main risk in applying generative augmentation to extreme weather.

492748.title: Analysis of Reprocessed MiRS Retrievals from the NOAA-18 AMSU-A/MHS Mission
492748.authors: Wei Wang, NOAA, College Park, MD
492748.abstract: The Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS) algorithm has undergone numerous version changes since first becoming operational in 2007, when it began processing NOAA-18 AMSU-A/MHS data, with some updates containing science improvements that significantly impacted the accuracy and precision of retrieval products. As a result, the official time series of MiRS contains potential discontinuities of key retrieval products, including temperature, water vapor, precipitation rate, and snow water equivalent. Users with the need to go back to the archive in support of retrospective studies or downstream algorithm assessments or recalibration must currently contend with inconsistent retrieval performance characteristics, which diminishes the confidence in results and any conclusions drawn from the studies. The user community strongly supports an effort to achieve this goal as they see it as benefitting their long-term research and development plans. In this study, we effectively extended the reprocessed data record backward in time by leveraging the availability of operational AMSU-A/MHS data from the NOAA-18 satellite. NOAA-18 was launched in May 2005. By reprocessing this data using a consistent version of the MiRS algorithm, the time series of retrieved geophysical variables would be extended by approximately 12 years from shortly after launch (May 2005) through 2017 (until AMSU-A/MHS channels are healthy with an overlap with SNPP from October 2011). Some MiRS retrieval outputs, such as TPW, will be discussed and also the comparison with SNPP ATMS retrieval outputs will be included as needed.

492750.title: Towards Parametrizing Misaligned Wind-Wave Interaction Using a Two-Phase DNS model
492750.authors: Jinshi Chen, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and N. Scapin and L. Deike
492750.abstract: Winds blowing at an oblique angle to ocean surface waves are ubiquitous, particularly during storms and in coastal regions. Accurate parametrization of momentum and energy exchanges under misaligned wind-wave conditions is crucial for predicting sea surface roughness and the mean wind profile, improving wave forecasting models and optimizing the performance of offshore wind turbines. Most existing parameterizations represent wind–wave misalignment as an equivalent aligned condition by projecting the wind velocity onto the wave propagation direction. Yet such assumption has not been systematically evaluated across a broad range of wind and wave conditions. Here, two-phase Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) with adaptive mesh refinement are employed to investigate misaligned wind–wave interactions over a range of wave steepnesses (ak), friction-velocity-to-phase-speed ratios (or inversed wave age, u*/c), and wind–wave misalignment angles (θw). The drag coefficient of the mean airflow is related to the effective wave steepness, akcos(θw). The form (pressure) drag and pressure-driven energy input depend on ak, u*/c and relative streamwise wind velocity. The predicted pressure-driven energy input is consistent with the parameterization implemented in WaveWatch III. The growth of shear-driven subsurface drift current is consistent with the prediction from a 1D diffusion equation. The direction of surface shear stress deviates from that of the freestream wind, with the deviation angle related to ak. In the wave-averaged momentum flux balance, turbulent momentum flux dominates for slow waves (large u*/c), while turbulence and viscous stresses are in primary balance in fast wave (small u*/c) or when streamwise wind opposes the wave. The wave coherent component of the turbulence structure will be examined and compared with previous parametrizations. A preliminary physical framework that integrates concepts from critical-layer and perturbation theories will be discussed.

492752.title: Ice Nucleation Ability of Tire Wear Particles Affects Their Long-Range Transport In the Atmosphere
492752.authors: Gurcharan Uppal, The University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC, Canada; and T. M. Seifried, D. Tatsii, C. Varcoe, C. Lam, S. N. Rogak, S. Bucci, A. Stohl, and A. K. Bertram
492752.abstract: Microplastics are continuously released into the environment, yet their fate in the atmosphere is poorly constrained. A major source of atmospheric microplastics are emissions from road traffic, mainly being tire wear particles (TWP). When these particles are transported into clouds, they may act as ice nuclei leading to mixed-phase clouds. This process could indirectly affect the climate by altering cloud reflective properties, cloud lifetime, and precipitation. Also, this process could limit the long-range transport of tire wear particle to remote regions. Therefore, it is crucial to determine if tire wear act as ice nucleating particles. Here, we investigated the ice-nucleating ability of TWP in immersion freezing mode and evaluated through an atmospheric transport model whether ice nucleation, followed by precipitation, can influence the transport and global distribution of these particles in the atmosphere. We measured the ice nucleation ability of one reference sample, a cryo-milled tire tread standard material, and one field sample, collected during operation of a truck on a dynamometer. Both tire wear samples nucleated ice heterogeneously with median temperatures ranging from -22 to -25 °C. Atmospheric transport model FLEXPART simulations suggest that, under the emission scenarios considered, tire wear contributes only marginally to the total atmospheric INP population under mixed-phase cloud conditions and ice nucleation slightly enhances TWP wet scavenging in polar regions.

492754.title: Relationship Between Lightning Characteristics and Hurricane Intensity
492754.authors: Jacquelyn S. Ringhausen, ; and D. T. Haliczer, P. Bitzer, J. Lapierre, E. A. DiGangi, and Y. Zhu
492754.abstract: This study utilizes the Earth Networks Total Lightning Network (ENTLN) combined with the Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) to investigate lightning activity in hurricanes relative to hurricane structure and evolution for 5 years of hurricane seasons. This combination enables a more complete estimate of lightning activity than one detection method can provide alone, including the derivation of the cloud flash fraction (CFF) for each hurricane. Additionally, lightning characteristics for each individual hurricane as well as average trends and correlations to hurricane wind speed and brightness temperatures are explored. Overall, this research has the potential to provide further insight into tropical cyclone intensification and weakening.

492755.title: Evaluating the Conditional Relationship between Atmospheric Rivers and Precipitation Across Observations, Reanalyses, and Climate Models
492755.authors: Siofra Linden, Univ. of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA; and K. Lu, W. Ma, E. Yanez Jr., and G. Chen
492755.abstract: Atmospheric Rivers (ARs) produce a substantial fraction of midlatitude precipitation, making their accurate representation vital for understanding the hydrological cycle and projecting future climate change. Despite widespread reliance on reanalysis and climate models to examine AR behavior, uncertainties remain in the representation of ARs and their associated precipitation. In this work, we develop a conditional relationship to better understand the sensitivity of conditional mean AR precipitation to changes in AR characteristics such as integrated water vapor (IWV), integrated water vapor transport (IVT), and wind speed. Particularly, we employ a binned scatter approach to divide the independent variable (e.g., IVT) into discrete bins and find the conditional means of a dependent variable (e.g., precipitation), similar to the convective onset statistics for tropical convective precipitation against changes in column water vapor (e.g., Peters & Neelin, 2006). The conditional analysis is applied globally to satellite observations, reanalyses, and a climate model (CESM2) to establish an observational baseline and examine the uncertainties across these products. The global analysis is further analyzed through the AR-precipitation relationships across ocean basins, seasons, and hemispheres. We find that there is a general increase in precipitation with increasing IVT and IWV across satellite products and reanalyses, while the precipitation-wind relationship exhibits greater variability at high wind speeds. We will assess whether the diagnostic yields consistent qualitative conclusions across multiple AR-detection algorithms from the Atmospheric River Tracking Method Intercomparison Project (ARTMIP), while also examining quantitative differences among the resulting estimates. Finally, upon applying these algorithms to CESM2, the reliability of the climate model in representing AR characteristics and precipitation relationships will be evaluated, with important implications for the model projection in ARs due to climate change.

492757.title: Mie–Raman–Fluorescence LiDAR Observations of Wildfire Smoke and Pollen in the Baltimore-Washington Region
492757.authors: Parker Coye, UMBC/JHUAPL, Laurel, MD; and A. Willitsford and B. Demoz
492757.abstract: Laser-induced fluorescence provides an observable for aerosol characterization and classification that is not typically available from elastic backscatter lidar alone. Biological particles and biomass-burning aerosols can exhibit measurable fluorescence signals, which may assist in distinguishing them from predominantly inorganic particles and provide additional context for interpreting aerosol layers with similar backscatter characteristics. When combined with conventional elastic and Raman measurements, fluorescence observations may therefore improve the ability of lidar systems to examine differences in aerosol type, source, and atmospheric processing. Here, we present initial observations from the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC) ultraviolet (UV) Mie–Raman–fluorescence lidar. The instrument simultaneously measures UV elastic backscatter, nitrogen Raman scattering, and aerosol fluorescence, enabling altitude-resolved retrievals of aerosol backscatter, extinction, and fluorescence capacity. Two contrasting aerosol case studies are examined: a springtime period likely influenced by locally generated pollen and a transported smoke intrusion associated with the 2026 Canadian wildfires. For each case, we evaluate the vertical and temporal evolution of observed aerosol layers, their fluorescence signals, and the relationship between fluorescence capacity, aerosol backscatter, and extinction. Concurrent measurements from a water-vapor differential absorption lidar at Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (JHU APL) provide information on the vertical distribution of atmospheric moisture. These measurements enable the fluorescence observations to be interpreted within their environmental context and allow potential moisture-related influences on the retrieved aerosol properties to be assessed. This is particularly important because changes in particle size, water uptake, and backscatter under humid conditions may influence fluorescence-capacity measurements even when the underlying aerosol composition remains similar. The analysis also considers uncertainties associated with signal background, geometric overlap, atmospheric attenuation, channel calibration, and the use of a single fluorescence detection band. These measurements demonstrate the feasibility of incorporating fluorescence detection into a conventional UV Raman lidar and provide an initial assessment of its value for characterizing biologically influenced aerosol and transported biomass-burning smoke in the lower troposphere.

492760.title: The Rise and Decline of Desert Dust: Changing Climate Impacts Since the Pre-Industrial Era
492760.authors: Jasper F. Kok, University of California, Los Angeles, Santa Monica, CA; and D. M. Leung and A. K. Gupta
492760.abstract: Atmospheric desert dust has changed substantially since the pre-industrial era, but its historical evolution and contribution to climate forcing remain poorly constrained. We combine a reconstruction based on sedimentary records with satellite-era constraints to assess changes in dust abundance and the associated effective radiative forcing (ERF). Dust abundance increased through much of the industrial period, reaching a maximum in the 1980s of 75 ± 40% above the pre-industrial level. This increase likely produced a progressively more negative dust ERF, partly offsetting anthropogenic greenhouse-gas-driven global warming. Dust abundance has since declined steadily, but remains 25 ± 20% above the pre-industrial level. The post-1980s decline reduced dust cooling, likely shifting dust from slightly opposing to enhancing global warming due to anthropogenic greenhouse gases. This sign reversal may have contributed modestly to the acceleration of climate warming over the past few decades. Current climate models do not reproduce the reconstructed historical evolution of dust, limiting their ability to represent its time-varying forcing, slightly biasing the interpretation of historical temperature changes and the prediction of future changes.

492762.title: Airborne Lidar-Polarimeter Instrument Development for Enhanced Aerosol Detection
492762.authors: Jackson L Begolka, University of Iowa, Iowa, IA; and M. J. McGill, G. Finneman, S. M. Vlk, and S. Kuang
492762.abstract: Accurate, low-latency, vertical and spatial distributions of atmospheric aerosols are critical for real-time climate, aerosol, and air quality forecasting. We present a miniaturized airborne sensor suite combining a 946 nm lidar system with a polarization sensitive FLIR Blackfly S camera system (BFS-PGE-51S5P-C). A dedicated NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX handles the lidar data processing. The camera is hardware-triggered via a custom FPGA, with frame acquisition and image processing handled by a second NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX computer. The lidar system delivers highly accurate, vertically resolved profiles of clouds, boundary layer heights, and aerosol layers, while the polarimetric camera provides added multi-angle spatial scene context. In our retrieval pipeline, multi-angle polarimetric measurements from the camera will help constrain the initial lidar ratio guess, improving our backscatter and extinction profile accuracies. The airborne payload is scheduled for flight demonstration aboard the University of Iowa’s L-39 research aircraft in Spring 2027. This instrument architecture provides a compact, low-latency solution for monitoring aerosol plumes and planetary boundary layer characterization.

492769.title: Predictability of Sea Level Anomaly Provided By Ocean Dynamic Memory
492769.authors: Xue Feng, University of Hamburg, Eimsbüttel, CA; and M. J. Widlansky, T. Lee, O. Wang, M. Balmaseda, H. Zuo, G. Dusek, W. Sweet, and M. F. Stuecker
492769.abstract: Seasonal prediction of sea-level anomalies along the U.S. Atlantic Coast and Gulf Coasts is challenging in part because of the lack of seasonal predictability of Atlantic atmospheric forcing. Rapid memory loss of the initial ocean state by coupled models also their prediction skills. It raises the question of what predictability the initial state can provide through ocean dynamics without knowledge of future atmospheric forcing. Here, we address this question by performing 12-month hindcasts of the 3-D ocean state using the ECCO (https://ecco-group.org/) global ocean model initialized monthly from ECCO ocean state estimates but forced by climatological atmospheric forcings. Nonseasonal anomalies in the hindcasts reflect dynamic evolution of the initial ocean state without knowledge of future atmospheric forcing, coined as Ocean Dynamic Persistence (ODP). ODP hindcasts of U.S. Atlantic Coast and Gulf Coast generally outperformed the predictions based on the altimetry-based damped persistence (a commonly used statistical prediction method) and the state-of-the-art ECMWF SEAS5 climate forecast system when evaluated against observations. At a lead of 4 months, ODP hindcasts have the highest anomaly correlation coefficients with tide-gauge data at 22 out of 39 coastal locations (mostly south of Cape Hatteras). The sea-level predictability from ODP comes from ocean dynamic memory of the initial states that contain anomalies associated with open-ocean Rossy waves generated by prior atmospheric forcing. The Rossby waves propagate slowly from the open Atlantic Ocean towards the U.S. Atlantic Coast and subsequently transmitted into the Gulf Coast via Coastally Trapped Waves, giving rise to significant se-level predictability along these coasts. We also highlight many regions in the world ocean where ODP has a significant skill in predicting sea level anomalies months in advance and discuss the potential difference in the underlying physics. The significant predictability offered by ODP underscores the importance of improving coupled models to maximize the predictability offered by initial ocean state. The ODP method is a general approach that is applicable to predictability studies for other phenomena and time scales.

492770.title: Back-To-Back Years of Historical July Floods in Texas? A NASA Earthdata Access Driven Retrospective Utilizing IMERG Precipitation.
492770.authors: Brandon Oren Mitchell, GES DISC, Greenbelt, MD; and A. Savtchenko, PhD, NASA/GSFC/ADNET
492770.abstract: In July 2025 and July 2026 residents along the Guadalupe River in portions of South Central Texas experienced extreme floods caused by heavy rains. These flood events resulted in large casualties and loss of life across the region, with 2025 being the more notable of the two events. The experience of back-to-back years of floods raises the question of how historical was the rainfall that induced such events? The Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Mission unifies advanced precipitation measurements from its constellation of partner satellites and core observatory to produce global precipitation products, most notably the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) collection. This case study leverages the continuous high-resolution spatial coverage of IMERG (10 km) daily data to compute statistics regarding precipitation extremes over Texas to better provide perspective of these two flood events in terms of the nearly 30-year IMERG record (1998-present). Additionally, the GPM IMERG collection is one of the many data holdings that reside in NASA’s Earth Science Data Systems (ESDS). In recent years, NASA data ingest and archive centers (DAACs) have migrated their data archives to the Earthdata Cloud in line with a programmatic vision of unifying methods of data access —— further lowering the barriers of enabling science by simplifying user workflows. Here we also take this case study as an opportunity to demonstrate the advantages of the different enterprise workflows such as Cloud OPeNDAP and other data services available through NASA Harmony, for users to download data. Benchmarking of several different data access methods will help provide users with the information for choosing their NASA Earthdata workflows.

492772.title: A Global Evaluation of AI and NWP Models for Precipitation Forecasting During Atmospheric River Events
492772.authors: Marina Vicens-Miquel, AES, Norman, OK; University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and T. S. Mandelbaum, A. McGovern, A. J. Hill, and D. A. Rothenberg
492772.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are responsible for transporting large amounts of atmospheric moisture and producing many of the world's most impactful precipitation events, contributing substantially to regional water resources while also causing floods, landslides, and other hydrometeorological hazards. Despite advances in numerical weather prediction (NWP), accurately forecasting precipitation during AR events remains challenging because precipitation depends on complex interactions among large-scale moisture transport, topography, atmospheric dynamics, and cloud microphysical processes. At the same time, recent artificial intelligence (AI)-based weather prediction models have demonstrated skill comparable to or exceeding traditional NWP models for many atmospheric variables, yet their performance for precipitation during high-impact AR events has not been comprehensively evaluated. This study presents a global evaluation of precipitation forecast skill during AR events using the Extreme Weather Bench framework. A globally distributed dataset of AR events is constructed to evaluate 24-hour accumulated precipitation forecasts from multiple state-of-the-art AI and physics-based forecasting systems, including GraphCast, the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS), the Global Forecast System (GFS), and the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS). Forecasts are evaluated at lead times from 1 to 10 days using a comprehensive suite of deterministic, spatial, and event-based verification metrics that quantify forecast accuracy, precipitation intensity, spatial structure, and localization. Complementing the global analysis, three regional case studies focused on North America, Australia and New Zealand, and Europe provide a more detailed assessment of model performance across well-established atmospheric river regions. These regions were selected because they experience frequent AR landfalls that contribute substantially to annual precipitation while also producing many of the most impactful flood events. Evaluating model performance across these diverse climatic and topographic environments provides additional insight into regional forecast strengths, systematic biases, and the challenges of predicting precipitation across different atmospheric river regimes. Across all verification metrics, AIFS and GraphCast consistently outperform GFS and GEFS, with comparable performance between the two AI models. The AI advantage is greatest for extreme precipitation, where GraphCast and AIFS retain meaningful skill while GFS and GEFS rapidly lose the ability to accurately predict heavy precipitation. The AI models also better reproduce the spatial organization of AR-related precipitation and maintain higher forecast skill through 10-day lead times, although all models exhibit declining performance with increasing lead time. While AI models generally provide more accurate forecasts, systematic biases remain with GraphCast and AIFS overpredicting moderate-to-heavy precipitation but underpredicting the most extreme precipitation at longer lead times, while GFS and GEFS exhibit a persistent dry bias that intensifies with precipitation magnitude. This work establishes one of the first global benchmarking frameworks specifically designed to evaluate precipitation forecasts during atmospheric river events. By leveraging the open-source Extreme Weather Bench framework, all datasets, evaluation procedures, and verification metrics are fully reproducible, providing a standardized benchmark for future comparison of AI and NWP forecasting systems and supporting continued development of operational weather prediction models.

492773.title: From STOFS to UFS-Coastal: Advancing NOS Operational Forecasting Systems
492773.authors: Saeed Moghimi, NOAA, North Potomac, MD; and G. Seroka, S. Mani, M. A. Jisan, F. Cassalho, L. Shi, W. J. Pringle, Z. Yang, F. Daneshvar, Y. Sun, A. Alipour, Y. Funakoshi, A. L. Kurapov, C. George, and E. Myers
492773.abstract: NOAA's National Ocean Service (NOS) is leading the transition toward a unified, high-fidelity coastal ocean modeling enterprise. The NOS Office of Coast Survey (OCS) spearheads the development of NOS's coastal ocean modeling infrastructure, with the NOS Storm Surge Modeling Team dedicated to continually advancing the Surge and Tide Operational Forecast System (STOFS) to deliver high-quality guidance to end-users and stakeholders. Beyond STOFS, our team provides critical research, development, and operational support for the entire NOS coastal ocean modeling portfolio and other impactful NOAA-wide modeling capabilities. In partnership with OAR, NWS, USACE, and the broader academic community, the team is leading the development of the UFS-Coastal , a specialized coupling infrastructure integrated into the NOAA Unified Forecast System (UFS) portfolio. This framework represents a paradigm shift from siloed regional models to a standardized, interoperable Earth System approach. By leveraging the ESMF/NUOPC coupling architecture, UFS-Coastal integrates community models (including ROMS, ADCIRC, SCHISM, and FVCOM) with other physical domains such as sea-ice, inland hydrology, and surface waves (WW3). In this presentation, we will update the community on recent advances and future plans in these key areas, supporting the Blue Economy and Coastal Resilience : STOFS Version 3 Upgrade: Includes STOFS-2D-Global (ADCIRC), STOFS-3D-Atlantic (SCHISM), and the new STOFS-3D-Pacific (SCHISM), becoming operational August 2026. UFS-Coastal System: NOS's next-generation coastal ocean modeling framework and its mission-critical downstream applications (ufs-coastal-app): STOFS-3D-Alaska & SECOFS: 3D unstructured coupling of SCHISM, WW3, and CICE for high-latitude and regional navigation safety. NOS Workflow: Modernized operational pipelines ensuring 99.9% up-time and standardized delivery of navigational products. On-demand unstructured 3D coastal ocean modeling: Rapid, flexible simulations tailored to event-driven and stakeholder-specific coastal forecasting needs. List of partners: NOAA: NOS-OCS, NOS-NGS, NOS-IOOS, NOS-CO-OPS; NWS-NHC, NWS-EMC, NWS-OWP, OAR-EPIC; University of Notre Dame; Virginia Institute of Marine Science; Argonne National Laboratory; National Center for Atmospheric Research; Texas Advanced Computing Center; Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission; Louisiana State University; Oregon State University;

492774.title: Characterization of Smoke-Related Impacts on Air Quality in Wildland Fire Campsites Using Ground-Based Measurements, Geostationary Satellite Data, and Atmospheric Transport Analysis
492774.authors: Dorian Isabel Schwartz, University of Colorado at Boulder, Boulder, CO; and A. Gaudel, A. J. Milkman, T. West, and K. E. Goldfarb
492774.abstract: Wildland firefighters are routinely exposed to smoke-related air pollutants during fire suppression activities, but the air quality in wildland fire campsites where firefighters rest in between shifts remains a relatively under-studied component of occupational exposure. There is potential for elevated air pollution exposure in fire camps not only because they are located near active wildfires, but also because they are often set up in valleys where meteorological factors may cause pollutants to linger for extended periods. To address the lack of prior investigation into air pollutant exposure in fire camps, this study aimed to characterize the air quality in fire camps and evaluate the extent to which wildfire smoke influences pollutant concentrations using in-situ measurements along with atmospheric transport analysis. Ground-level measurements of ozone (O3), fine particulate matter (PM2.5), and carbon monoxide (CO) were collected at three fire camps associated with an Oregon wildfire in July and August of 2023. These measurements were compared with data from nearby U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Air Quality System (AQS) monitoring sites. Satellite imagery of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) GOES-ABI surface PM2.5 data and the NOAA HRRR-Smoke model output were used to contextualize the location of the fire camps relative to the fire’s domain. Backward trajectories computed with the NOAA’s HYSPLIT model were used to show the air transport patterns in the surrounding area and identify periods when the air quality in the fire camps was likely influenced by the nearby wildfire. During the sampling campaign, multiple periods with concurrent, prolonged elevated levels of O3, PM2.5, and CO were observed with concentrations reaching up to 120 ppb, 438 µg/m3, and 4 ppm, respectively. These concentration increases were distinct from the typical O3 summertime diurnal pattern, suggesting that the air quality at the fire camps was being impacted by smoke. Additionally, HYSPLIT backward trajectories for these periods indicated that the air at the impacted fire camps was approaching from the direction of the fire, indicating that the concentration increases may have been due to the transport of smoke from the nearby fire. For most days within the sampling period, the concentrations of O3 and PM2.5 at the fire camps exceeded those at the nearby AQS sites, although the overall temporal trends observed at the fire camps were similar to those observed at the AQS sites. These findings demonstrate that fire camps can experience substantial elevated exposure to smoke-related air pollutants, and that this exposure may not be fully represented by nearby regulatory monitoring sites. This highlights the importance of further characterizing the air quality in occupational exposure environments for wildland firefighters. Key words: Wildfire smoke, fire campsites, ozone, PM2.5, carbon monoxide.

492779.title: UFS-Chem Modeling of 2023 Canadian Wildfires Evaluated with TEMPO
492779.authors: Brian Charles McDonald, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and C. Lyu, S. Wang, K. L. Chang, O. R. Cooper, J. He, M. Bruckner, R. H. Schwantes, H. Zhang, F. Li, J. Przybocki, S. Kondragunta, H. Huynh, A. Ahern, J. W. Hair, and L. Judd
492779.abstract: Wildfires remain a difficult challenge for weather-chemistry models to simulate air quality, including for both ozone and fine particulate matter (PM2.5). Given the dynamic nature of wildfires, geostationary satellite observations (e.g., TEMPO) offer an ability to track diurnal changes in emissions, plume-rise, long-range transport, and chemistry. TEMPO retrievals of aerosol optical depth (AOD), aerosol layer height (ALH), and ozone profile potentially provide a capability to track long-range transport and chemical evolution of smoke that can improve air quality forecasting and reanalysis products. Here, we utilize the first version of the Unified Forecast System with Chemistry (UFS-Chem) model to simulate wildfires and air quality during the Atmospheric Emissions and Reactions Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas (AEROMMA) and Synergistic TEMPO Air Quality Science (STAQS) airborne field campaigns in 2023. During the campaign, the NASA DC-8 aircraft intercepted lofted wildfire plumes over Chicago, New York City, and Toronto from Canadian boreal forests coincident with TEMPO. UFS-Chem is simulated at both coarse (1 degree x 1 degree) and finer resolution (0.25 degree x 0.25 degree), utilizing wildfire emissions from the Blended Global Biomass Burning Emissions Product (GBBEPx) and Regional ABI-VIIRS Emissions (RAVE). TEMPO AOD provides insight on how well the UFS-Chem model simulates emissions and long-range transport of aerosols, while TEMPO ALH provides insight on wildfire plume-rise algorithms. Overall, there is general agreement between UFS-Chem and airborne field campaign data for AOD. However, there is greater disagreement for ALH by up to a factor of 2 suggesting a need to improve plume-rise algorithms or better define how to compare modeled ALH with satellite ALH. Similar analyses are performed on TEMPO v4 beta ozone profiles validated with AEROMMA-STAQS observations to explore photochemical production and long-range transport. Lastly, we model the full year of 2023 with and without wildfires to estimate the premature mortality associated with smoke for ozone and PM2.5.

492780.title: Investigating Historical North Atlantic Extratropical Cyclone Characteristics Using High Resolution Modeling
492780.authors: Diana Katherine Apoznanski, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ; and A. J. Broccoli and R. Kopp
492780.abstract: Extratropical cyclones (ETCs) are mid-latitude, large scale storm systems that bring frequent, costly impacts such as flooding and strong winds to the Northeast US. Despite their impacts, ETCs are understudied, and historical observations of these storms have yielded unclear trends in their characteristics, partially due to a short record length. Climate models provide many years of data, and may produce physically possible, but not yet recorded extreme storms. Our analysis uses the high resolution MESoscale Atmosphere-Ocean Interactions in Seasonal-to-Decadal CLImate Prediction (MESACLIP) to evaluate ETCs in a historical climate scenario. In comparison with ECMWF Reanalysis 5th Generation (ERA5), we evaluate the changing climatology of ETC characteristics (e.g. central pressure, surface wind speeds, and average precipitation) over the course of the historical period 1920-2005 for multiple ensemble members. The results from this study inform current efforts to understand how climate models simulate ETCs, and provide metrics that can inform climate risk analysis.

492781.title: Fostering Hope Amid Fear: How Positive Eco-Emotions Can Protect Adolescent Mental Health and Promote Climate Activism
492781.authors: Lexi Nutkiewicz, Colorado School of Public Health, Aurora, CO
492781.abstract: Nearly half of the world’s children live in high-risk areas threatened by extreme weather events and other environmental crises that may affect their health, education, and safety. Adolescents (ages 10-19) are uniquely vulnerable to the impacts of climate change and related extreme weather events due to physiological vulnerabilities, limited agency over decisions affecting their future, disruptions to their academic progress, and disproportionate exposure to negative messaging about climate risk. Many adolescents experience significant climate anxiety, or chronic fear, stress, and worry about climate change. These concerns can manifest into various eco-emotions, such as eco-anxiety, eco-grief, and eco-anger. Despite this vulnerability, most scientific research on climate anxiety and eco-emotions has centered on adult populations, leaving a critical gap in understanding how young people experience and articulate these emotions. While it is increasingly recognized that youth experience anxiety related to environmental issues, there is a lack of systematic examination of both positive and negative eco-emotions, such as hope and guilt. The purpose of our study is to examine positive and negative emotions about climate change reported by older adolescents living in northern California and explore how these emotions are linked to climate anxiety, activism, and other measures of well-being such as optimism and compassion. We conducted a cross-sectional survey on 521 ethnically diverse first- and second-year college students in northern California (mean age = 19; 78% non-white) about their feelings toward climate change, engagement in climate activism, and well-being. Variations in positive and negative climate emotions by demographic characteristics were examined in bivariate analyses. Relationships between indicators of climate anxiety (eco-emotions, eco-anxiety, eco-impairment) and activism and well-being were assessed with Pearson correlations. We used General Linear Models (GLM) to examine how eco-emotions were related to key variables while accounting for demographic characteristics. In these models, climate emotions were entered as covariates, and eco-anxiety, eco-impairment, activism, and well-being were treated as dependent variables, with a separate GLM model conducted for each outcome, controlling for gender, race, and income. Positive and negative eco-emotion scales were entered simultaneously into each model, which allowed us to assess the overall contribution of climate emotions and directly compare how positive versus negative feelings related to each outcome. Nervousness (84%) and frustration (82%) were the most common negative emotions felt when thinking about climate change, while determination (71%) and motivation (70%) were the most common positive emotions reported by respondents. Female and non-binary students reported significantly more negative emotions about climate change than male students, and minority students reported significantly fewer negative emotions compared to their peers. Climate anxiety was linked to greater activism and confidence that actions matter. However, positive climate-related emotions were more strongly associated with activism and optimism about the present and future compared to negative emotions, which were linked to higher eco-anxiety and greater compassion for others. Lastly, participants did not report greater disruptions in their daily functioning (eco-impairment), suggesting that they may maintain serious climate concerns without these concerns significantly affecting their everyday lives. To our knowledge, this is one of the first investigations of positive and negative eco-emotions in older adolescents. The findings suggest that cultivating positive eco-emotions may be a more effective way to encourage activism while also protecting adolescent mental health and well-being, offering dual benefits that negative eco-emotions do not. While negative eco-emotions can lead to increased activism, the mental health burden associated with a pessimistic view of climate change may outweigh those benefits. As climate change and extreme weather events continue to affect adolescents, environmental education and climate messaging aimed at them should emphasize hope and agency to effectively motivate them to engage in activism and climate solutions.

492784.title: 'Why Are the East African Long Rains Weakly Predictable? Diagnosing Sources of Seasonal Predictability Beyond ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole'
492784.authors: Jane Elizabeth Umhofer, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and K. Pegion
492784.abstract: The March to May (MAM) long rains are an important part of the hydroclimatology of East Africa, contributing to rainfed agricultural production, water resource management, and food security for millions of individuals across East Africa. Though they are economically important, the MAM rains show considerably less seasonal predictability compared to the October to December (OND) short rains, thus posing a limitation on the effectiveness of operational seasonal forecast systems. Studies have found that MAM rainfall variability is associated with the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), Indo-Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) variability, and anomalous circulation in the region, such as changes in the Walker circulation and the Congo Basin zonal winds. However, the relative importance of these mechanisms remains uncertain, and it is unclear whether SST variability outside the canonical ENSO and IOD regions contributes additional sources of seasonal predictability. Furthermore, the extent to which operational seasonal forecast systems represent these observed SST–rainfall teleconnections remains poorly understood. This study investigates sources of MAM rainfall predictability across East Africa using CHIRPS rainfall observations, global SST fields, and forecasts from the North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME). Correlation analysis and Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) are used to identify coupled modes of SST and rainfall variability and to quantify the contribution of SST anomalies beyond the canonical ENSO and IOD regions. By comparing observed SST–rainfall relationships with those represented in NMME forecasts, we assess whether deficiencies in forecast skill arise from weak oceanic forcing or from an inadequate representation of large-scale teleconnections. We also investigate whether East African MAM rainfall contains predictable nonlinear relationships that are not captured by current dynamical seasonal forecast models. A U-Net–based deep learning framework is applied to NMME forecast fields to determine whether nonlinear post-processing can recover additional predictive information from large-scale climate patterns and improve seasonal rainfall prediction. Model performance is evaluated against CHIRPS observations using correlation, root-mean-square error, and forecast skill metrics. This work tests whether (i) the variations in SST outside the traditionally known areas for ENSO and IOD influence the seasonal predictability of East African MAM rainfall; (ii) the teleconnection patterns identified above are adequately represented in operational NMME forecasts; and (iii) the application of nonlinear machine learning techniques recovers any forecast skill beyond what is contained in the dynamical model outputs. Through this study, it is intended to gain insights on the mechanisms behind the variability of East African MAM rainfall and potential ways to improve its seasonal predictions.

492786.title: Propagating Tropical Cyclone Forecast Uncertainty from Atmospheric Forcing to Flood Impacts
492786.authors: Renato Amorim, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and L. N. Tobias-Tarsh, A. T. Michalek, M. Binjolkar, G. A. Vecchi, and G. Villarini
492786.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) and their post-tropical remnants can produce devastating freshwater flooding, posing major threats to communities, infrastructure, economies, and ecosystems. These impacts can extend far beyond their landfall location, where communities are often less exposed to warnings and less prepared. In recent years, TC forecasts have improved considerably, including predictions of storm track, intensity, and associated precipitation. These advances, together with the increasing availability of convection-allowing hurricane models (e.g., HAFS, T-SHiELD) and ensemble forecasting systems, have improved our ability to characterize the range of possible meteorological outcomes and their associated uncertainties, especially at longer lead times. However, the extent to which improvements in TC forecasting translate into more reliable and actionable predictions of flood hazard and risk remains unclear, particularly at lead times relevant for emergency management and evacuation planning. A key challenge is understanding how uncertainties in numerical weather prediction propagate through hydrologic and hydraulic models and ultimately shape estimates of TC flood impacts. To address this challenge, we develop a framework to quantify how rainfall forecast uncertainty propagates through the flood modeling chain and influences predictions of flood extent, water depths, and property impacts across forecast horizons. We apply this framework to the Raritan River Basin during Hurricane Ida (2021), whose extratropical remnants produced extreme rainfall, record flooding, and widespread societal impacts across the northeastern United States from September 1 to 5, 2021. The event provides an ideal case study for evaluating how uncertainty in TC rainfall forecasts propagates into estimates of flood hazard, exposure, and impacts. Our framework integrates outputs from hydrologic and hydraulic modeling with rainfall fields from multi-model ensembles of numerical weather prediction models to estimate flood hazard, exposure, and vulnerability at lead times up to 168 hours. The products in these ensembles vary with lead time, including global ensembles from the THORPEX Interactive Grand Global Ensemble (e.g., IFS, GEFS), hurricane models such as T-SHiELD, and short-range, convection-allowing models like the HRRR. Following validation against observations and simulations driven by gridded rainfall datasets (e.g., AORC), each rainfall forecast realization is propagated through a hydrologic model and a high resolution two-dimensional hydraulic model to simulate streamflow, flood extent, and water depth across the Raritan River basin. The resulting ensemble of inundation maps is then combined with building-level information to quantify flood exposure and structural damage. By integrating results across ensemble members and forecast lead times, we empirically estimate the probability of flooding and associated structural damage at each location, allowing forecast uncertainty to be systematically propagated through the complete modeling chain from precipitation to streamflow, inundation, exposure, and impacts. Moreover, this framework provides a basis for understanding how forecast uncertainty propagates through the complete modeling framework and influences estimates of flood hazard, exposure, and impacts.

492788.title: AI-HAFS: A Data-Driven Weather Model for Tropical Cyclone Prediction
492788.authors: Lin Zhu, SAIC at NOAA/NWS/OMD, Riverdale Park, MD; and Z. Zhang, B. Liu, B. Thomas, X. Lu, Y. Wen, L. Cui, J. Wang, V. S. Tallapragada, and F. Yang
492788.abstract: Recent advances in data-driven weather prediction systems, such as AIGFS, have demonstrated promising skills for global weather forecasting. However, accurately predicting Tropical Cyclone (TC) structure and intensity remains challenging because of the need to resolve fine-scale processes while simultaneously representing a large-scale environment. To address this challenge, we are developing AI-HAFS, a data-driven weather prediction model for TC within the Anemoi framework. AI-HAFS employs a stretched-grid graph architecture that enhances spatial resolution over the North Atlantic basin while preserving a global computational domain to maintain large-scale atmospheric context. The model is trained using multi-year atmospheric reanalysis data. By concentrating model capacity over the region of interest, the stretched-grid approach enables substantially higher effective resolution for tropical cyclone prediction without incurring the computational cost of uniformly increasing global resolution. The current development focuses on evaluating the capability of AI-HAFS to reproduce the evolution of TCs and regional weather patterns. Preliminary experiments are to optimize prediction skill over the TC basin. AI-HAFS represents an initial step toward a regional AI-based forecasting system that combines the efficiency of graph neural networks with enhanced spatial resolution over tropical cyclone-prone regions. Ongoing work includes further optimization of the grid configuration, incorporation of additional training strategies, and comprehensive evaluation during historical hurricane seasons.

492797.title: FloodTrace, Realtime Post Flood Ground Truth
492797.abstract: The United States experiences over 300 flood events per year. Emergency management agencies at every level — municipal, county, state, and federal — respond to these events with limited field resources and compressed decision timelines. FloodTrace is a tool built to increase the volume, speed, and spatial coverage of the ground-truth data these agencies collect, using hardware they already have, within workflows they already follow. FloodTrace operates on three levels: a field tool for rapid, guided high-water mark collection; a SaaS platform for real-time observation, field coordination, and data quality control; and a secure data storage system adaptable to customer infrastructure. The tool runs on iOS devices, using LiDAR and onboard sensors to capture a detailed 3D model of each high-water mark site along with GIS and metadata. The capture method is simple — point, paint, and tap — and the process is procedural and step-based, requiring minimal training. Data is secure from capture to database. The collection device is also the communication device — the operator in the field is reachable on the same phone they're collecting with. And when collection is done, it disappears into a pocket. It can reacharge from a one-pound backup battery. There is no equipment to pack, stage, or maintain. On the SaaS side, the tenant organization registers devices through a secure device-to-terminal handshake, allowing them to expand or collapse their fleet of registered collection devices as operations scale up or wind down. The dashboard shows incoming survey points in real time with their status. Each point has a detailed survey page with tools to visualize the 3D capture, correct mark placement, or discount questionable points without returning to the field. Integrated HAND modeling software generates ad hoc flood extent models that update on the fly as new points arrive — giving coordinators a progressively sharper picture of the event while collection is still underway. The data storage layer is adaptable to most cloud platforms, simple to set up, and secure. Tenant organizations maintain authoritative control of their data from the moment of capture. Every point, mark, point cloud, model, and product belongs to the tenant — now and forever. No lock-ins. No data walls. Because the collection is fully digital, real-time adjustment becomes possible in ways that analog field methods cannot support. The HAND feedback loop is the clearest example: as marked points come in, the flood extent model refines itself with observed data. Each new point sharpens the projection. Coordinators are not waiting for a post-processed deliverable — they are watching the model improve while collectors are still in the field. The capture process walks the operator through a fixed sequence: GPS lock, point cloud capture, on-screen mark identification, bare earth base point for later rover tie-in, field notes, and site photos. At transmit, the system auto-generates a rapid report. Each step completes before the next begins — the operator always knows where they are in the workflow. This procedural design opens the method to crowd sourcing — because you can control the crowd. The guided workflow ensures that every collector, regardless of experience, produces a structured, reviewable record. A dozen emergency responders working an impacted area can tag high-water mark locations across a wide footprint simultaneously, each producing the same data format, each following the same steps. Quality reviewers can filter incoming data in real time. Survey professionals who arrive later inherit a map of known mark locations with 3D records they can verify or upgrade. This does not replace or interfere with current survey methods or gold-standard survey practice. It enhances and accelerates it. More ground truth is available to data leads. Flood projections update as collection progresses. A larger spread of possible survey points becomes available because more personnel are contributing to the collection effort. Finally, it is cost effective. The collection device is a phone. The guided process requires little training. For communities and agencies where traditional flood data collection has been inaccessible due to high equipment and personnel costs, FloodTrace offers an entry point that did not previously exist. FloodTrace is a post-event flood data collection platform built for the people already on the ground. It produces observable, correctable, three-dimensional ground-truth records in real time on hardware that fits in a pocket. It expands who can collect without compromising data quality. It feeds a HAND model that sharpens with every point. It keeps data under the collecting organization's control.
