And it does all of this without replacing the survey methods that agencies already trust — it makes them better. This poster presents the platform and invites discussion with emergency management professionals on how FloodTrace fits their post-event operations.

492798.title: Application of the Earth Model Column Collaboratory (EMC²) v1.4 to Diagnose Model Parameterization Inconsistencies and Deficiencies
492798.abstract: The Earth Model Column Collaboratory (EMC²) is an open-source Python package that simulates active remote-sensing instruments and generates subcolumns to statistically emulate higher spatial resolution by accounting for sub-grid-scale variability. EMC² was designed to represent Earth system and high-resolution model physics with minimal internal assumptions, enabling statistically robust and consistent evaluation of models against measurements from ground-based, airborne, and spaceborne radars and lidars. The package has a primary focus on instruments from the U.S. Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility, and also supports direct model-to-model comparisons. EMC² Version 1.4 introduces multiple updates, including faster processing through code optimization, implementation of the Predicted Particle Properties (P3) microphysics scheme logic (Morrison and Milbrandt, 2015), and representation of key Cloud Layers Unified by Binormals (CLUBB; Bogenschutz et al., 2013) turbulence closure assumptions, with particular attention to sub-grid-scale vertical motion. To demonstrate these new capabilities, we apply EMC² to column output from the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 3 (E3SMv3) corresponding to a selected set of ARM sites. Analyses of both the raw model output and EMC²-processed data suggest parameterization inconsistencies with observations (such as in ice particle size distributions), along with model-internal deficiencies that may extend to other models — findings that offer guidance for future model development.

492803.title: A Study of Severe Weather Risk Based on Warning Frequency Within the Jackson Mississippi National Weather Service County Warning Area
492803.authors: Alison Nicole Hart, NCAS-M II, Jackson, MS; and R. S. Reddy
492803.abstract: I will be investigating the frequency and location of severe thunderstorm and tornado warnings within the Jackson County Warning Area served by the National Weather Service office in Jackson, Mississippi. The main objective of this research is to develop a Climatology identifying areas that often experience severe storm and tornado development. Historical severe storm and tornado warning data will be analyzed to examine temporal and geographic trends across the forecast area. In this study I will evaluate patterns in warning frequency and identify locations with recurring severe weather potential. By compelling and interpreting this data, I aim to improve understanding of how severe weather risk varies throughout the region and to highlight areas that may require increased preparedness, monitoring and outreach efforts. In support of my research, the internship experience provided will allow me to gain real operational meteorology experience and new understanding of the forecasting process used by the National Weather Service. Participation in forecasting operations and community outreach opportunities will help connect my climatological analysis with real-time weather operations and public safety communication. My research has the potential to support operational awareness by helping forecasters and emergency management partners to better recognize areas that routinely meet the necessary environmental criteria for severe storm development. The resulting climatology will serve as a resource for outreach, education and preparedness initiatives designed with community awareness in mind. I am hoping to provide valuable insight into localized severe weather vulnerability and contribute to future outreach, preparedness and education initiatives.

492804.title: Update on the AMS Community Modeling Committee
492804.authors: Frederick H. Carr, University of Oklahoma, NORMAN, OK; and J. L. Kinter
492804.abstract: In Fall 2025, the Ad hoc Community Modeling Committee (CMC) was formed within the AMS Weather, Water, and Climate Commission to promote the advancement of world-leading, fully coupled, Earth system models (ESM) for research, operations, and applications. Its primary activities are to: (1) Increase private, public, and academic participation in research and development of Earth system prediction modeling; (2) Enhance coordination among U.S. modeling centers, with a focus on advancement and community use of the Unified Forecast System (UFS); (3) Serve as a catalyst for leveraging community expertise on modeling innovations and advancements to benefit the UFS; and (4) Identify best practices and innovations to the UFS and assess how to best facilitate community use of the UFS. The CMC has 15 members from across the ESM community and 12 liaisons from within ESM centers. Its activities include the initiation of three studies by the following working groups: (1) Ease of Use of UFS; (2) Best Practices for Effective R2O; and (3) Strategic Plan for Community Engagement. Our talk will summarize the progress of and initial findings from these working groups.

492807.title: The Development and Applications of an ML Classifier for Precipitation from New York State Mesonet Camera Images.
492807.authors: Brian T Horan, University of North Dakota, South Haven, MI
492807.abstract: The New York State Mesonet standard sites contain cameras mounted at 2 meters AGL for monitoring of site conditions and situation awareness. These cameras are also capable of observing precipitation in real time during the daytime, which is used to train an ML classifier to classify falling precipitation in images. The data is labeled from 22 of the 127 NYSM sites, utilizing best practices in trustworthy dataset creation for ML training. Sites are identified for labeling with a novel algorithm for coreset selection of geographically varied images. The model is trained using a shifted window vision transformer on the 22 labeled sites. This work shows different applications of this classifier, including onset and cessation time, time series predictions, rain/snow line, applicability to other networks, and more.

492809.title: SuPerPoV: Score and Evolution of the Stratospheric Polar Vortex Via Persistent Homology
492809.authors: Jake Austen Cordes, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY; and Z. Wu and B. Giunti
492809.abstract: Classifying the stratospheric polar vortex provides predictability for surface weather on extended-range timescales. In detail, a stratospheric polar vortex is a cyclone of cold wind that forms over the North Pole in the winter months. When a stratospheric event occurs, it can cause the vortex to either become displaced or split. However, all definitions of these events proposed in over 60 years of study depend on empirically chosen parameters and yield different results when they change. Moreover, as previous definitions are based on static thresholds, it is not straightforward to use them to study the spatiotemporal evolution of the vortex. Here, we introduce SuPerPoV, a score system that computes height, and displacement and split scores using tools from Topological Data Analysis (TDA). The computation is entirely threshold-free, open source, and does not require familiarity with TDA to be used. The scores generally recover previous definitions of SSWs and ESV events, and are output for a user-defined number of days, thus showing the evolution of the event. SuPerPoV offers a paradigm shift in the study of the polar vortex, bringing a deeper understanding of the polar vortex and related extreme events.

492810.title: Toward Assimilation of Spaceborne Active Sensors in MPAS-JEDI
492810.authors: Junmei Ban, NSF-NCAR, Boulder, CO; and C. Schwartz, Z. Ying, B. J. Jung, C. Snyder, Z. Liu, I. Moradi, B. C. Ruston, and B. T. Johnson
492810.abstract: This study presents recent progress toward assimilating spaceborne active-sensor observations within the MPAS-JEDI data assimilation framework. Radar reflectivity observations from the EarthCARE’s Cloud Profiling Radar (CPR) and Global Precipitation Measurement Microwave Imager (GMI) Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar (DPR) are being incorporated to provide additional information on hydrometeors and cloud structures to the assimilation system. The forward operator is based on the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM), which has been extended by the Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA) to support active-sensor applications. Preprocessing, quality control, and an observation error model tailored to spaceborne active-radar observations are being developed and evaluated. Preliminary evaluations for this ongoing work indicate that the simulated observations are physically consistent and the corresponding Jacobians exhibit reasonable sensitivity to hydrometeor variables. Early results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating active sensor data into MPAS-JEDI and highlight their potential to improve the forecasts of precipitation and cloud processes in numerical weather prediction systems.

492812.title: LLM Agents Meet Aviation Weather: What Worked, What Broke, and What It Cost
492812.authors: Brandon Rose, Jataware Corp, Washington, DC
492812.abstract: Aviation, range, and aerospace meteorology draws on data sources that differ widely in access method and format: TAFs and METARs from the Aviation Weather Center, gridded forecasts from ECMWF and NOAA, output from AI weather models such as GraphCast, GenCast, and WeatherNext, space weather products from SWPC and NASA DONKI, and flight data from operational APIs. Analysts who combine these sources spend much of their time writing data access code rather than doing meteorology. We built a set of specialized weather, aviation, and space weather agents on top of Beaker Notebook, an open-source AI computational notebook platform. Each agent runs an LLM inside a live notebook session, where it writes and executes Python against roughly twenty data sources and applies domain skills for tasks such as turbulence EDR computation, synthetic TAF generation, evaporation duct modeling, and forecast verification with METplus. A human reviews and steers each step from the notebook. This talk covers what we learned building these agents. We trace the progression of agent tooling from raw tool calling, to Model Context Protocol servers, to skills, and describe the problems that drove each transition. We describe the techniques that made the agents reliable in practice: progressive disclosure of documentation to stay within context window limits, caching known-good query examples for reuse in later tasks, and AI-assisted conversion of API documentation into skills. We also report failure modes: frameworks that support multiple LLMs still require per-model handling because model behavior differs; open-weight models trail frontier models on multi-step tasks; usage costs can spike without guardrails; and human review of multi-step agent workflows requires specific user interface support. We close with a request to the community: weather data providers are the right parties to publish well-designed, agent-ready skills for their own services, and we would like to see more of them do so.

492813.title: Assessing Contrails and Aviation Climate Impact Using Fuel Hydrogen Content
492813.authors: Ziming Wang, Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Mainz, RP, Germany; IPSL, Paris, France; and C. Voigt, A. Marsing, A. Lecouffe, M. Juchem, G. Smallwood, S. Kirschler, D. Piontek, G. Eckel, R. Dischl, R. Maerkl, D. Sauer, U. Schumann, K. Widmaier, R. Teoh, M. Stettler, B. Rauch, and N. Bellouin
492813.abstract: Contrail cirrus clouds are among the largest non-CO2 climate impacts of aviation. Today, theory links engine soot particle emissions to contrails and climate impact, yet the relationship between chemical fuel properties and contrail ice crystal number remains poorly constrained. Here we show that fuel hydrogen content (FHC), previously included in fuel specifications, provides a mechanistically grounded predictor of soot and contrail ice particle numbers, with the first validation using in-flight measurements showing agreement within ~±20%. Increasing FHC by 1.4 percentage points within the observed range of aviation fuels substantially reduce soot emission and ice particle numbers, contrail optical depth, and lifetime, leading to a calculated 52% reduction in contrail energy forcing. Global deployment scenarios based on fuel policies for alternative aviation fuels, including sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) and hydroprocessed fuels, indicate that by 2050 the widespread adoption of fuels with an estimated mean hydrogen content of 15.0% could reduce aviation-induced global surface temperature increase by 21%, largely offsetting the projected growth in aviation CO2-equivalent emissions. Our results establish FHC as a physically based and operationally measurable metric linking fuel composition, soot emissions, contrail properties, and aviation climate impact across scales. As a practical fuel metric independent of fuel type (e.g., kerosene, SAF blends, neat SAF, and hydroprocessed fuels), FHC provides a means of mitigating aviation climate impacts alongside decarbonization strategies focused on lifecycle CO2 emissions. These findings provide a scientific basis for incorporating FHC into future fuel standards and climate mitigation strategies, supporting the transition toward more climate-compatible aviation.

492815.title: A Benchmarking Suite for Multimodal Wildfire Prediction
492815.authors: Andrew Rittenbach, Information Sciences Institute, University of Southern California, Arlington, VA; and J. J. Mason, H. Siegel, J. P. Walters, D. W. Pack, and T. Hall
492815.abstract: In recent years, there has been great interest in the collection of large-scale multimodal datasets suitable for training deep learning-based models for both wildfire detection and wildfire spread prediction. These datasets provide datacubes with imagery from a variety of sources, such as elevation or wind models, climate measurements, and remote sensing imagery. Datasets of interest also incorporate fire products such as the NASA VIIRS Active Fire Product, which are used as labels for wildfire. The scale, range, breadth, and perhaps most importantly, the widespread availability of these datasets have accelerated the development of training models for wildfire detection and spread prediction. However, it can be very challenging to make fair comparisons between different research products derived from these datasets. As a simple example, studies utilizing the same dataset splits, may employ different detection metrics (e.g. mAP vs F1 Score). Comparison becomes even more challenging when different datasets are used, due to the natural variability found across these datasets. Due to variations such as these, it is challenging to fairly compare the underlying ideas between research products, such as data preprocessing techniques or the neural network architectures used. In this work, we developed a benchmark suite to facilitate model evaluation across different datasets. To this end, we offer the following contributions: We curated multiple wildfire detection dataset and built a standardized data format for deep learning model training. We collected a model zoo with standardized training and evaluation tools for a variety of wildfire prediction neural network architectures. We present a newly collected multimodal fused dataset consisting of thousands of multiday wildfires derived from the US Monitoring Trends in Burns (MTBS) dataset, as well as open-source tooling used for collection of the dataset. The model training components of our toolset have been validated by replicating performance metrics of published models. Similarly, our dataset generation tools have been validated by comparing newly generated stacked datacubes with publicly available burn maps of historic fires. Ultimately, we hope to standardize deep learning-based wildfire detection research conducted across different datasets, which will help us to understand which model training approaches transfer well across datasets. From the initial validation conducted using our toolset, we believe that this is an easily achievable goal, which will help to advance the current state-of-the-art of deep learning-based wildfire detection and spread prediction. With time, we hope that the tools produced by this work will be adopted by the wildfire research community and help to accelerate wildfire AI research.

492817.title: Artificial Intelligence - Enhanced Versions of the National Hurricane Center Operational Statistical-Dynamical Tropical Cyclone Intensity and Size Forecast Models
492817.authors: Galina Chirokova, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and M. DeMaria, E. Brown, M. N. Razin, and J. Knaff
492817.abstract: The National Hurricane Center (NHC) and the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) use multiple statistical-dynamical models for forecasting tropical cyclone (TC) intensity and size. The Statistical Hurricane Intensity Prediction Scheme (SHIPS) has been operational at NHC since 1991 and at JTWC since 2014. More recent additions include the Decay-SHIPS Wind Radii model (DSWR), the DeMaria Radii Climatology and Persistence (DRCL) model at NHC and the Markov Model Climatology and Persistence (MMCL) at JTWC. SHIPS and DSWR are used as both standalone guidance and as input for the consensus models, and DRCL is used by NHC and JTWC as a baseline for evaluating the skill of wind radii forecasts. All of these models are based on multiple linear regression, which is likely limiting their performance. We developed NN-SHIPS, an artificial intelligence (AI) version of the NHC’s SHIPS model, and demonstrated that replacing linear regression with a fully connected neural network could significantly improve forecast performance relative to the operational SHIPS model. Further, in addition to capturing nonlinear relationships, the new model makes it much easier to test additional predictors and different formulation architectures. This presentation will discuss NN-SHIPS and preliminary results for neural network versions of the NHC’s wind radii models, NN-DSWR and NN-DRCL. We will discuss the model architectures, their performance using real-time inputs, and the use of explainable AI to understand the contributions of different predictors and better understand the physical processes important for changes in wind structure. We will also discuss potential pathways for transitioning the new models to operations and developing similar AI versions of JTWC statistical-dynamical models. The new AI models also establish a foundation for developing more advanced versions enhanced with low-Earth-orbiting satellite-based predictors. Disclaimer: The scientific results and conclusions, as well as any views or opinions expressed herein, are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect those of NOAA or the Department of Commerce.

492823.title: Designing and Delivering Trusted AI/ML Products for Short-term Weather Driven Hazard Prediction and Resilience at the NASA SPoRT Center
492823.authors: Emily B. Berndt, NASA MSFC, Huntsville, AL
492823.abstract: The Short-term Predication Research and Transition (SPoRT) Center at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center is an innovation hub for short-term weather driven hazard predication and resilience. In order to transition NASA Earth Science research, observations, and modeling capabilities to operations and applications SPoRT focuses on 1. Proactive Prediction, 2. User-Driven Research, and 3. Transition and Impact. For nearly 25 years, SPoRT has refined a co-development paradigm that accelerates the maturation of experimental products for sustained use by stakeholders- often increasing situational awareness, improving forecasting, and enhancing decision-making. SPoRT focuses on key domains including Weather & Air Quality, Land & Hydrology, and Coastal & Marine hazards with stakeholders that span federal, state/local agencies, academia, and the private sector. This presentation will highlight SPoRT’s co-development approach and the development of AI/ML predication and decision support systems. These include overviews of SPoRT’s DustTracker-AI, Streamflow-AI, and Lightning-AI as well as newer efforts to co-develop AI/ML derived surface pollutants from the TEMPO (Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution) mission observations and approaches to Lightning Initiated Wildfire. This presentation will highlight how SPoRT has used AI/ML to translate research into trusted operational assets. SPoRT has a history of designing and delivering AI/ML products that meet user challenges with the goal of providing actionable insights that benefit decision-making and society.

492824.title: Implementation of Space Weather Data Assimilation Capabilities in the JEDI System
492824.authors: Lindsey J. Hayden, UCAR, Arvada, CO
492824.abstract: The Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) data assimilation system is a model agnostic data assimilation software that is the product of a coordinated effort by the Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA) and its partner organizations: NASA, NOAA, US Navy and Air Force, and the UK Met Office. It is developed with the goal of rapid adaptation and integration of new and emerging sensors and data types. To that end, the JEDI software is designed with reusability in mind, so that new models and techniques can be implemented with ease and minimal repeated code. This work details the space weather data assimilation capabilities in the JEDI system. The background of the electron density for JEDI is provided by the Python implementation of the International Reference Ionosphere (PyIRI). It is a climatological model that was developed at the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) in order to run the widely used, climatological International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) model at significantly reduced computational cost. Ionosonde and space-based Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) total electron content (TEC) measurements are used. Both measure electron density. Ionosondes are profile measurements of electron density produced by a ground based high frequency radio transmitter. GNSS based observations measure the total electron density along the path of the GNSS signal through the atmosphere. The capability to assimilate these observations has been developed in JEDI and is demonstrated using a pseudo cycling system with a simplified Gauss-Markov forecast model. Similarly, a framework to use the Mass Spectrometer and Incoherent Scatter (MSIS) and Horizontal Wind Model (HWM) climatological models along with upper atmospheric observations such as Global-scale Observations of the Limb and Disk (GOLD) satellite measurements in an assimilation system for the neutral thermosphere has been developed. These simplified assimilation systems will be used to develop assimilation techniques for both the ionosphere and neutral thermosphere that can be used with physics based models in order to improve the forecast capabilities in these regions.

492825.title: Validation and Quality Assessment of NOAA/STAR Multi-Mission GNSS Radio Occultation Neutral Atmosphere Products
492825.authors: Xin Jing, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD; and T. C. Liu, Y. Chen, X. Zhou, J. Zhou, X. Shao, M. Chen, B. Zhang, W. Miller, and C. Cao
492825.abstract: The rapid expansion of Global Navigation Satellite System Radio Occultation (GNSS-RO) observations, from operational missions like COSMIC-2 and MetOp-SG to commercial constellations such as Spire and PlanetiQ, provides unprecedented opportunities to improve global atmospheric sounding for numerical weather prediction (NWP). Given the critical needs for consistency, accuracy, and long-term stability in these multi-mission datasets, this study presents a comprehensive evaluation of the quality of NOAA/STAR’s GNSS-RO neutral atmosphere products, with particular emphasis on bending angle and refractivity retrievals across these key platforms. We employ a multi-faceted validation approach to assess data quality. Overall data quality is characterized through analyses of global and regional sampling, local-time coverage, penetration depth, quality-control retention rates, and inter-comparisons of excess phase and bending angle products across processing centers. Furthermore, inter-mission consistency is evaluated using the simultaneous radio occultation (SRO) method and collocated observations among COSMIC-2, MetOp-SG, Spire, and PlanetiQ, enabling direct comparisons of bending angle and refractivity profiles while minimizing spatiotemporal mismatches. We perform Observation-minus-background (O–B) analyses against GFS and ECMWF reanalysis data to quantify global, latitudinal, and solar zenith angle-dependent biases. Additionally, we conduct independent validation using collocated radiosonde to assess vertical structure, lower-tropospheric performance, and retrieval accuracy under varying atmospheric conditions.Our evaluation also focuses on the performance of COSMIC-2 and commercial RO datasets across multiple GNSS constellations (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, and BeiDou), examining factors such as antenna viewing geometry, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), penetration depth, and regional sampling. Finally, supported by enhanced Integrated Calibration and Validation System (ICVS) monitoring, our long-term time-series analyses confirm data stability and consistency across missions. The results provide a comprehensive characterization of the precision, bias, uncertainty, and long-term stability of multi-mission GNSS-RO observations, supporting their readiness for NWP data assimilation and broader atmospheric science applications.

492830.title: Multi-Fidelity Modeling of Wind-Wave Interactions Using Scale-Resolving Simulations and Emulator-Accelerated Uncertainty Quantification
492830.authors: Baris Kale, MIT, Cambridge, MA; and E. Y. Shin and M. F. Howland
492830.abstract: Modeled representation of air-sea exchanges of momentum, heat, and moisture remains a major source of uncertainty in predictions of the marine atmospheric boundary layer (MABL). At operational grid resolutions, models such as the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model typically employ Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS)-type boundary layer closures with computationally efficient, wave-phase-averaged bulk parameterizations that represent sea-state effects through aerodynamic roughness. These parameterizations cannot explicitly capture wave-coherent airflow, phase-dependent form drag, nor their dependence on wave age and steepness. In this study, we facilitate parameterization learning within a unified WRF framework, where fully wave-phase-resolved large-eddy simulation (LES) provides the highest-fidelity representation by explicitly resolving the moving wave geometry and associated pressure field, but at substantial computational cost. The mesoscale (RANS) WRF configurations consist of two wave-phase-averaged parameterizations based on wind-speed- and wave-age-dependent Charnock formulations. In order to reduce error and uncertainty in the mesoscale WRF RANS-based wave-phase-averaged parameterizations, we utilize a Bayesian inverse uncertainty quantification approach to quantify the parametric uncertainty of the wave-phase-averaged models across fifteen wave regimes that span a range of wave steepness and wave age values, using data generated by the scale-resolving LES as reference. Next, we quantify parametric uncertainty jointly with that of the turbulence parameterization, treating the surface and turbulence parameterizations that represent the MABL as a coupled system rather than as independently calibrated components. Finally, we describe a sensitivity-based method that enables us to identify the LES data to generate that improves parameter identifiability and reduces parameter uncertainty, providing a basis for targeting future field measurements that provide maximum uncertainty reduction in parameterizations of turbulent flow over waves. Together, this framework quantifies uncertainty in modeling interactions between turbulent wind and waves in mesoscale weather models within a unified meso-microscale framework, accelerated by efficient data-driven emulators. Acknowledgements The authors thank Dr. Jeff D. Mirocha, Dr. Tianyi Li, Dr. Peiyun Zhu, and Prof. Oliver Fringer for their contributions to the development and validation of the moving-wave framework in WRF-LES. This work was supported by the Office of Naval Research Young Investigator Program (YIP), grant N000142512045, with computational resources provided by TACC Stampede3 through NSF ACCESS project ATM170028.

492831.title: An Analysis of the Delta Flight 175 Encounter with Severe Turbulence over Atlanta, Georgia, Using MPAS-A
492831.authors: Idamis Enid Rodriguez Nazario, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and M. I. Oyola-Merced
492831.abstract: The encounter with severe turbulence poses a significant risk to safety and comfort due to abrupt variations in an aircraft’s speed and altitude. In this study, we examine the international flight, Delta Airlines 175 (DL175), from Milan Malpensa (MXP), Milan, Italy to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) on 29 August 2023. DL175 encountered severe turbulence over Atlanta, Georgia, during descent at 22:31, resulting in 4 passengers seriously injured and 13 sustained minor injuries. The atmospheric conditions were complex due to the presence of two major hurricanes, one in the Gulf (Idalia) and the other in the Atlantic basin (Franklin), and a stationary front that extended across Mississippi and New York. Predicting turbulence remains a challenge because high-resolution numerical simulations are needed to capture small-scale atmospheric processes that lead to rapid turbulence development. The Model for Prediction Across Scales–Atmosphere (MPAS-A) was used to perform a 3-km regional simulation over CONUS. MPAS-A is a high-resolution numerical modeling framework that allows for explicit representation of fine-scale atmospheric dynamics in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere. As a result, vertically resolved MPAS-A diagnostics were sampled along the reconstructed DL175 flight track, and a rapidly developing cloud was observed. These results showed that the probable cause of this accident was the encounter with severe convectively induced turbulence (CIT). This is consistent with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) report; hence, this creates an opportunity to use high-resolution models like MPAS-A to recreate these incidents and better understand turbulence mechanisms, improving flight safety and comfort in a changing atmosphere.

492832.title: Forays into Event-based Verification
492832.authors: Matthew S. Wandishin, NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; and D. M. Uden, L. R. Blank, L. D. Melling, and A. Hewett
492832.abstract: Much of forecast verification involves evaluating areal forecasts for each lead time, separately. Less frequency, time series for a single location (or averaged over an area, such as a river catchment) are compared with observations at set time steps (typically based on either forecast or observation frequency). This presentation will draw from three separate verification efforts focused on the timing of event onset and cessation. One involved deterministic forecasts of thunderstorms (that is, binary or yes/no events) in the vicinity of airports. The second involved probabilistic forecasts of snowfall (also binary) at airports, while the third examined deterministic forecasts of flight categories (based on thresholds of cloud ceiling heights and visibility distances, that is, multicategory). Commonalities and unique aspects of these efforts will be discussed.

492834.title: Advances in Representing Land-Atmosphere Interactions using the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART)
492834.authors: Brett Raczka, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Anderson, M. El Gharamti, K. Raeder, H. Kershaw, and M. Smith
492834.abstract: Land processes interact with the atmosphere in important ways that influence sub-seasonal to seasonal forecasting, air quality, and radiative forcing (atmospheric CO2). The proper initialization of land surface states such as vegetation, soil moisture, soil temperature and snowcover within Earth system models is essential to improve predictability of these atmospheric processes. Proper initialization of land surface states is challenging, however, because of errors related to initial and boundary conditions, model structure, and parameters. Furthermore, the land, unlike the atmosphere, is chronically under-observed. Ensemble data assimilation (DA) techniques combined with an expanding network of Earth system observations present an opportunity to reduce these errors and improve forecasts. Ensemble DA has a built-in advantage through the generation of a background error covariance which improves the representation of unobserved regions such as sub-surface soil and vegetation properties. First, we provide a review of land state estimation experiments using NCAR’s Community Land Model with DART that constrain carbon, water, energy and nitrogen cycling through a complementary set of observations including leaf area, soil moisture, snow, and solar-induced fluorescence. Next, we discuss the implementation of joint parameter and state estimation to further improve land model forecast skill. We evaluate to what extent the inclusion of parameter calibration extends the persistence of the model forecast skill. Finally, we discuss the use of joint parameter and state estimation as a tool to diagnose shortcomings in land-atmosphere coupling with potential applications for sub-seasonal atmospheric forecasting.

492835.title: An Independent Implementation of MPAS-CMAQ: 3-km Regional Air Quality over California's Central Valley Evaluated Against WRF-Chem
492835.authors: Simona Renee Seastrand, Nextgen Federal Systems, Bellevue, NE
492835.abstract: The Model for Prediction Across Scales–Atmosphere (MPAS-A) offers a globally consistent, variable-resolution alternative to traditional nested limited-area models. However, fully coupled gas- and aerosol-phase chemistry applications remain rare due to significant technical challenges. We present one of the first independent, non-EPA implementations of EPA's MPAS-CMAQ (MPAS-A coupled online with CMAQ v5.5) on a ~3-km regional limited-area domain over California's Central Valley. We compare the system against a WRF-Chem simulation for a wintertime stagnation episode on 18 December 2022. The configuration uses meteorological initial and lateral boundary conditions from GFS/GDAS, chemical initial and boundary conditions from NCAR CAM-Chem mapped to the CB6R5M_AE7_AQ mechanism, EDGAR v8.1 anthropogenic emissions, and inline MEGAN biogenic emissions. For surface ozone, MPAS-CMAQ reproduces both the magnitude and the broad west-to-east spatial gradient simulated by WRF-Chem, while the variable-resolution Voronoi mesh better resolves terrain-driven gradients along the Coast Ranges and Sierra foothills. Ongoing work extends the evaluation to wintertime PM2.5 and ammonium-nitrate aerosol, the dominant cold-season pollutant in the valley. This work demonstrates that MPAS-CMAQ is a viable platform for high-resolution regional air quality modeling. We document the major technical barriers encountered and the solutions implemented, and we developed a containerized, reproducible workflow to lower the barrier to entry for the broader MPAS-Chem community.

492837.title: Standardizing Emissions Processing in the UFS with the Community Emissions Computing Engine (CECE)
492837.authors: Barry D Baker II, EMC, College Park, MD
492837.abstract: As the Unified Forecast System (UFS) advances toward a comprehensive, multi-scale meteorological modeling framework, the need for standardized, reproducible, and flexible emissions processing has become paramount. Historically, emissions handling has been fragmented across different forecast suites, complicating Research-to-Operations (R2O) transitions and limiting scientific consistency. To address this challenge, we introduce the Community Emissions Computing Engine (CECE). CECE operates as a dual-purpose framework within the UFS. As a core UFS infrastructure component, it is optimized for I/O-intensive operations such as ingesting anthropogenic emissions and performing regridding. Simultaneously, CECE integrates with the Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) to support dynamic, physics-driven emission processes directly during model execution. By decoupling these functions from the core model, CECE provides a standardized interface for handling diverse emission sources, ensuring consistency across all UFS applications—whether global, regional, or sub-seasonal to seasonal. This presentation will detail the technical architecture of CECE, highlighting its capability to streamline the incorporation of new emission inventories and improve forecast reproducibility across different UFS runs. We will demonstrate how the decoupling of emissions processing from model physics simplifies the R2O timeline and enhances the scientific rigor of air quality and coupled chemistry-climate applications. This work underscores the role of CECE as a foundational component for the next generation of UFS atmospheric composition modeling, facilitating a more cohesive and sustainable forecasting system.

492839.title: Driving Innovations in Atmospheric Science and Technology Applications at NESDIS/STAR
492839.authors: Krishna V. Kumar, Science & Technology Corporation (STC) @ NESDIS/STAR, Riverdale, MD; NOAA, College Park, MD; Science and Technology Corporation, Columbia, MD; and L. Hembeck, M. G. Divakarla, A. Allegrino, and M. LaJoie
492839.abstract: NESDIS Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR) transforms satellite observations into actionable information essential for environmental, security, and economic decision-making. The center provides scientific guidance for satellite missions, sensors, and Earth-observing capabilities, while also developing and distributing high-quality, fit-for-purpose, multi-sensor satellite data products from both NOAA and non-NOAA missions. This presentation focuses on specific research and operational support contributions by our team of scientists at NOAA/STAR. The critical activities range from scientific algorithm development and implementation to ongoing refinements for JPSS/GOES Environmental Data Records (EDRs) derived from satellite Sensor Data Records (SDRs). These EDRs are vital for environmental monitoring, situational awareness, numerical weather prediction (NWP), and the extension of Climate Data Records (CDRs). Our work includes product development, calibration and validation (Cal/Val), data quality assurance, scientific monitoring, application demonstrations, the transition of algorithms from research to operations (R2O), and ongoing user support and stakeholder engagement for both Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO) products. The LEO Team, such as the NUCAPS team, has advanced algorithm augmentation for upcoming JPSS-4 and EPS-SG hyperspectral sounders, including integrating AI/ML frameworks to modernize first-guess retrieval and support cloud-based mission-long reprocessing. The LEO Team continues to conduct rigorous product validation using ground-truth networks, supporting applications such as heatwave and ozone hole monitoring. For data accessibility, a near-real-time global mapping and visualization tool hosted by STAR JPSS called JSTAR Mapper has enhanced reliability through a modernized dashboard and tile production, while the NOAA Products Validation System (NPROVS) now provides enterprise-level EDR validation via a modular, cloud-ready architecture. The Aerosols Detection Project (ADP) and Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) teams have improved air quality monitoring by integrating AI/ML models to enhance Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) and geostationary retrieval accuracy, transitioning Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) algorithms to operations, and supporting stakeholders with robust validation resources. In wildfire analysis, the fire detection (Active Fires) team uses sensor intercomparisons and machine learning to refine identification via EFire and NGFS, while the fire emissions team upgrades RAVE and GBBEPx algorithms for long-term emissions records. The ozone team supported the delivery and adaptation of enterprise Version 8 algorithms for OMPS, GOME-2, and UVNS, with recent accomplishments including upgrading NOAA-20 OMPS resolution, reprocessing ozone data records, maintaining the NOAA Cohesive Dataset, and developing trace gas algorithms. The JPSS/LEO support team successfully coordinated the delivery of J4-compatible enterprise algorithms across STAR-Interface Data Processing Segment (IDPS) - NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF) stakeholders while rigorously tracking schedules, milestones, and deliverables. The GEO team has significantly advanced the GOES-R program by providing robust operational support and serving as a critical liaison for algorithm refinements. Key accomplishments include leading the complex transition of GOES-R ground systems to the cloud, complemented by the development of innovative products, such as high-resolution tropical cyclones and polar winds, and advanced stereo-based cloud height methodologies. Furthermore, the team has enhanced data quality and utility through extensive validation tool development, improved radiation budget, fire and aerosol monitoring, optimized characterization of cloud texture for precipitation analysis, the maintenance of specialized web interfaces, and rigorous cross-platform validation against datasets like RAOB and Lidar, ensuring the program's long-term scientific reliability and operational readiness. Collectively, both LEO and GEO efforts demonstrate a strategic focus on expanding research and operational flexibility while maintaining rigorous data quality standards. By addressing sampling challenges, integrating new datasets, and automating workflows, the team has strengthened NOAA’s atmospheric monitoring capabilities. These advancements not only support the immediate needs of current operational systems but also lay a solid technical foundation for future satellite missions and inter-agency scientific collaborations.

492840.title: Changing Rain-on-Snow Events across Alaska: Historical Trends, Atmospheric Drivers, and Future Projections using Dynamically Downscaled Datasets
492840.authors: Patricia Hutton, Univesrity of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and P. A. Bieniek, U. S. Bhatt, C. F. Waigl, and R. Lader
492840.abstract: Rain-on-Snow (ROS) events occur when rain falls on snow-covered frozen ground, often refreezing and forming a layer of ice. In high northern latitude regions such as Alaska, ROS events can cause significant risks to transportation, wildlife, and power infrastructure as ice cover on vegetation and built-up surfaces may persist until the spring thaw. Understanding the spatial and temporal distribution of ROS events across Alaska is critical for emergency preparedness and climate adaptation strategies. Alaska’s complex terrain and scarce observational data coverage limit detailed analysis, but gridded reanalysis datasets help bridge this gap by capturing fine-scale regional variability. Newly developed dynamically downscaled ERA5 4km data spanning from winter season 1950–2025 provide a long-term dataset to examine historical trends and regional differences of ROS occurrences across Alaska's diverse landscapes. Prior analysis demonstrated that the 4km dataset more accurately represents winter rainfall than the coarser resolution product, and identifies increasing ROS hours and associated rainfall, particularly during the early and midwinter, indicating a shift towards warmer winter conditions and changes in the seasonal snowpack dynamics. These historical trends provide strong evidence of changing ROS characteristics, but raise important questions regarding the evolution and underlying drivers of these events. Rather than focusing solely on monthly and seasonal ROS frequency, this study will examine whether changes are driven by an increasing number of individual ROS events or by longer-lasting consecutive episodes. This study will also identify the large-scale synoptic conditions associated with ROS events across Alaska to help determine the atmospheric patterns that favor ROS development. A key objective is to evaluate whether observed changes in ROS characteristics are primarily driven by increasing winter temperatures, allowing for precipitation to fall as rain rather than snow, or by changes in the frequency or intensity of favorable synoptic weather patterns. To extend the historical analysis, a dynamically downscaled 4km MIROC6 climate projection will be used to assess how ROS frequency, duration, seasonality, and associated synoptic drivers may evolve under future climate conditions. Comparing projected changes to the historical ERA5 record will provide insights into whether the controlling mechanisms of ROS events remain consistent or shift as the climate continues to warm. Together this work aims to improve understanding of the physical mechanisms driving ROS events and how their duration, seasonality, and atmospheric drivers may be evolving under a warming climate. The resulting historical and projected climatologies will provide a scientific foundation for improving hazard assessments and informing climate adaptation and resilience planning across Alaska.

492842.title: Source and Air Toxics Characterization of Urban Air Pollution in Denver Using Combined Positive Matrix Factorization of Multi-Instrument ASCENT Data
492842.authors: Seonsik Yun, CIRES, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and D. A. Day, A. V. Handschy, E. Mattson, R. Bahreini, A. M. Dillner, S. M. Raffuse, A. G. Russell, N. L. Ng, and J. L. Jimenez
492842.abstract: Air pollution in the Denver metropolitan area has increased in recent years, raising concerns about adverse health effects and visibility degradation. Major sources include traffic, industrial activity, cooking, biomass burning, and long-range transport. Source apportionment is essential for effective air quality management, but is often limited by the time resolution and chemical specificity of routine networks and short-term campaigns. Since May 2023, we have operated long-term, high-time-resolution measurements of aerosol composition, trace metals, and black and brown carbon in Denver as part of the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry mEasurement NeTwork (ASCENT), supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation. This new multi-instrument monitoring infrastructure overcomes these observational constraints. We present results from a combined Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF) approach that integrates co-located non-refractory aerosol, trace element, and multi-wavelength absorption datasets into a single matrix (collected with three separate instruments). Single-instrument PMF often lacks sufficient chemical contrast to separate some key aerosol sources. In contrast, leveraging complementary cross-instrument tracers significantly improves source factor separation, particularly for isolating biomass burning organic aerosol (BBOA). Incorporating elemental potassium as a biomass burning tracer alongside multi-wavelength absorption parameters allows better differentiation between fresh and aged biomass burning smoke, which cannot be clearly distinguished using single-instrument data alone. Overall, aerosol in Denver is dominated by oxygenated secondary organic aerosol with a regional character, alongside substantial primary contributions from traffic and cooking activities. Measured trace metals are predominantly linked to anthropogenic emissions as well as re-suspended road and soil dust. Furthermore, these high-sensitivity measurements facilitate the evaluation of air toxics, including trace metals, revealing that several species routinely approach or exceed health-based reference thresholds on annual and daily scales. These findings underscore the distinct advantage of integrated multi-instrument PMF frameworks for disentangling complex pollution sources and advancing air toxics exposure assessments in urban environments.

492845.title: Benchmarking an ML Classifier for Precipitation Observation from New York State Mesonet Camera Images Against Observations and Other Algorithms
492845.authors: Brian T Horan, University of North Dakota, South Haven, MI
492845.abstract: The New York State Mesonet contains cameras mounted at 2 meters above ground level along with the suite of other observing instruments. These cameras are able to observe falling precipitation during the daytime from a static view. These images are used to train a Machine Learning model which identifies falling rain and snow in real time. However, a benchmark is needed to verify that predictions from the ML model are realistic, consistent, and useful. This work compares the ML model to different benchmarks, including radar, NYSM observations, ASOS/AWOS observations, and others. This will be shown in case studies, and larger statistical inference across the NYSM.

492849.title: Starting the AI Conversation: A Student's Lens on Connecting Learners and Educators in the Unidata Community
492849.authors: Tara Elizabeth Staresinic, UCAR, Gibsonia, PA; The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA
492849.abstract: AI has rapidly changed the education industry, leaving students and educators unsure of how to adapt. Conversations with university faculty revealed common struggles with incorporating AI in the classroom. These include a lack of personal understanding of AI, minimal policy and resources from higher administrations for AI education, little awareness of student perspectives, and limited time to adjust curriculum. Based on feedback, we wrote a series of four articles about various AI topics for university faculty. The articles are mainly authored by an undergraduate university student, to provide a student’s perspective on AI in their education. They are short and easy to read. The goal of the articles is to provide readers with a quick overview of each topic, and encourage them to learn more about what interests them. Each article contains a list of further reading materials for easy access. We focused on incorporating a wide variety of peer-reviewed research, along with anecdotes and news from popular culture. The articles are published on the Unidata website blog, an established platform where Unidata shares news with the community.

492850.title: Bridging Research Operations, and People for Atmospheric Science and Technology Application
492850.authors: Linda Hembeck, STC, College Park, MD; and K. V. Kumar
492850.abstract: Effective research-to-operations (R2O) requires more than scientific innovation—it depends on strong program management, technical collaboration, and continuous workforce development. Building on lessons learned from our first year managing a multidisciplinary team of approximately 40 scientists supporting NOAA/STAR research and operations, this presentation highlights how leadership practices evolved to further strengthen collaboration, software development, and operational readiness. We discuss strategies for managing a diverse research portfolio, aligning scientific priorities with mission needs, and coordinating diverse stakeholders—including researchers, software engineers, and government partners. We will present initiatives, such as GitLab training to promote version control best practices, AWS bootcamps to increase cloud computing proficiency, and an AI/ML working group to facilitate cross-team knowledge sharing. Finally, we share practical lessons on building a culture of continuous learning and technical excellence that accelerates the transition of research into operations while fostering leadership pathways for scientists combining technical expertise with program management.

492858.title: Toward a Regional Training Network: Strengthening Caribbean Scientific Capacity for Climate Resilience
492858.authors: Alexandra N. Ramos-Valle, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. Haacker
492858.abstract: In addition to scientific advances, developing a resilient Caribbean requires sustained investment in human capital, institutional capacity, and stronger links between research and practice. While regional expertise exists, significant gaps remain in how academic programs, governmental institutions and broader academic stakeholders collaborate to support the next generation of scientific leaders. This presentation reports on a community-driven workshop held in Puerto Rico that brought together researchers, educators, Governmental agency representatives, and practitioners to explore workforce development priorities across the Caribbean. Participants examined key barriers to effective knowledge transfer and professional development, highlighting the need for a structured, regional training network. Workshop discussions explored topics such as bridging the gap between early-career education and operational practice, expanding research and internship opportunities, interdisciplinary skill-building, artificial intelligence integration, and locally relevant hazard mitigation strategies. The workshop also examined sustainable training models capable of retaining talent and addressing regional vulnerabilities. The findings, recommendations, and identified priorities emerging from the workshop discussions will be presented at the conference, providing a roadmap for future workforce development efforts and regional collaboration across the Caribbean.

492859.title: Prediction of High-Altitude Atmospheric Turbulence over CONUS Using an Operational NWP Model and NASA Airborne Field Campaign Data
492859.authors: Soo-Hyun Kim, NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, CA; and R. Ueyama, J. H. Kim, J. Dean-Day, and R. Sharman
492859.abstract: Atmospheric turbulence in the upper troposphere to lower stratosphere (UTLS) plays an important role in total energy dissipation and in the transport and mixing of heat, momentum, and atmospheric constituents, while also posing significant hazards to aviation, including high-altitude platform systems (HAPS) operating around 20 km. Given that current turbulence forecasting systems have been developed and validated primarily for commercial cruising altitudes below 15 km, reliable high-altitude turbulence prediction remains limited, despite the increasing interest in HAPS and its applications. In this study, we develop a high-altitude turbulence prediction method over the contiguous United States (CONUS) using 3-km hourly forecasts from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model, and is evaluated against the high-altitude in situ turbulence observations from eight NASA airborne field campaigns. The method computes the multiple turbulence diagnostics from the 3-km HRRR forecasts, and then we apply not only a conventional average ensemble approach but also machine-learning-based techniques to obtain an optimal solution. Detailed results of high-altitude turbulence prediction will be presented at the conference.

492860.title: Flash Drought Intensification and Concurrent Land-Atmosphere Coupling In the Contiguous United States from ERA5
492860.authors: Tobias Gerken, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA; and Y. Zhong, J. A. Otkin, PhD, P. C. Stoy, A. M. Girard, and Z. Sealfon
492860.abstract: While drought development is often considered to be a slow process in response to lack of precipitation, rapidly intensifying flash droughts have the potential to cause significant socioeconomic impact over a timeframe of just a few weeks. This rapid intensification makes them challenging to predict and manage. Rapid drought intensification has been linked to local and regional land-atmosphere feedbacks mediated by boundary-layer processes that accelerate drying of the land-surface, but it is unclear if this is a ubiquitous feature of flash droughts that can guide predictability. We have previously shown that local land-atmosphere coupling metrics including Convective Triggering Potential and Lower Tropospheric Humidity Index (CTP-HILow) can serve as integrated measures to track feedback processes and are responsive at the timescales of flash drought intensification. Using the Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds (TOBAC) algorithm, we identified and tracked 883 drought objects within the Contiguous U.S. during the growing seasons between 1979-2023. The drought objects represent a continuum from conventional to rapidly accelerating droughts based on the total fraction of drought area affected by flash drought. The average flash drought duration is also calculated within each drought object using the Flash Drought Intensity Index (FDII). Evaluation of land-atmosphere coupling and feedback during drought using CTP-HILow calculated from ERA5 atmospheric profiles on 137 model levels archived at the NCAR Research Data Archive (doi: 10.5065/XV5R-5344) revealed that drought objects with flash drought areas in excess of 50% were strongly associated with positive CTP and HILow anomalies, suggesting that abnormally high CTP and HILow are necessary, but not sufficient conditions for the development of flash drought. At the same time, correlation analysis revealed substantial year-to-year differences in the sensitivity of flash drought development to land-atmosphere coupling for reasons unknown. The association of abnormally high CTP-HILow and flash drought intensification highlights the potential importance of reinforcing land-atmosphere feedback for drought onset speed and might provide a promising avenue for monitoring and predicting drought development at seasonal to subseasonal scales.

492864.title: Probability of a Cloud Free Line of Sight Analysis Using the EarthCARE ATLID
492864.authors: Adam Willitsford, JHU/APL, Laurel, MD; and P. Coye
492864.abstract: The Atmospheric Lidar (ATLID) aboard the Earth Cloud Aerosol and Radiation Explorer (EarthCARE) mission provides new opportunities to characterize clouds and aerosols from space. In this study, we use ATLID observations to update a previous CALIPSO-based climatology of the statistical probability of a cloud-free line of sight, p(CFLOS), and extend the analysis to account for cloud optical depth and atmospheric transmission. These statistics are relevant to free-space optical communications, electro-optical and infrared sensing, and other systems whose performance depends on atmospheric transmission. More broadly, characterizing cloud occurrence and optical properties supports studies of cloud climatology, atmospheric radiative transfer, and aerosol–cloud interactions. Cloud-free-line-of-sight statistics are commonly derived from binary cloud masks, in which an atmospheric column is classified as either cloudy or clear. While useful for describing cloud occurrence, this approach does not distinguish between opaque clouds and optically thin layers that may retain meaningful transmission. ATLID’s high-spectral-resolution lidar capability provides vertically resolved aerosol and cloud extinction profiles, allowing each observed column to be evaluated according to both cloud presence and cumulative optical attenuation. Using ATLID cloud and extinction products, we calculate p(CFLOS) and related transmission-based statistics over a range of geographic regions and seasonal periods. The analysis quantifies the frequency of optically thin clouds, their vertical and regional distributions, and their effect on estimates of optical availability. It also examines changes in estimated cloud occurrence and optical availability associated with differences in instrument sensitivity, retrieval methodology, sampling, and the use of extinction rather than cloud detection alone for CALIPSO versus EarthCARE. These results demonstrate how EarthCARE ATLID can extend cloud climatologies beyond binary occurrence to provide a more complete characterization of cloud optical properties and their influence on atmospheric transmission.

492866.title: Regional and Seasonal Trends in Mean and Extreme Dust Activity Across the Contiguous U.S. from Observations and E3SM
492866.authors: Rylen Pereira, ANL, Lemont, IL; ANL, Lemont, IL; and Y. Feng, X. S. Li, X. Xi, R. C. Sullivan, W. Lin, and J. C. Golaz
492866.abstract: Atmospheric aerosols, particularly mineral dust, play a pivotal role in Earth’s climate system by influencing radiative forcing, cloud microphysics, and air quality. This research characterizes spatiotemporal trends in dust aerosol optical depth (DAOD) across the contiguous United States (CONUS) over the last two decades (2003-2022) using combined observations from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Aqua and Terra satellites alongside ground-based AErosol RObotic NETwork (AERONET) retrievals. Mann-Kendall trend tests and regional monthly anomaly analyses were performed on satellite, ground, and model time series using consistent completeness and quality control filters. No statistically significant CONUS-wide trends were found in mean DAOD or annual extreme dust days (daily DAOD >95th percentile) in MODIS satellite observations. However, pronounced regional and seasonal trends emerged. Monthly DAOD anomalies increased significantly in the Southwest (0.00015 yr⁻¹), while significant decreases occurred in the Southeast (-0.00032 yr⁻¹) and Midwest (-0.00023 yr⁻¹), with these regional trends largely driven by changes during specific seasons. In contrast, AERONET observations generally indicate localized decreasing tendencies, including at several southwestern sites, although station-level trends exhibit substantial spatial variability, likely reflecting the sparse sampling of the network. When compared against the DOE’s Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM), the model shows strong spatial concordance with MODIS in DAOD trends. E3SM demonstrates its highest performance in the Southwest and Southern Great Plains regions, exhibiting strong correlation with satellite observations for annual DAOD (r > 0.5, p < 0.05) while exhibiting reduced skill in representing extreme dust occurrence frequency. By integrating satellite, ground-based, and modeling perspectives, these findings provide critical constraints on regional dust behavior and observational sampling limits, ultimately supporting efforts to improve aerosol parameterizations and predictive fidelity in Earth system models.

492867.title: Impacts of Machine-Learning and Numerical Weather Prediction Forcing on High-Frequency Ocean Surface-Current Forecasts
492867.authors: Luyu Sun, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and J. Carton, L. Chen, S. Carton, and S. G. Penny
492867.abstract: Accurate atmospheric forcing is essential for forecasting rapidly evolving ocean surface currents, particularly their wind-driven component. Emerging machine-learning weather prediction (MLWP) systems offer computationally efficient alternatives to conventional numerical weather prediction (NWP), but whether differences in atmospheric forecast skill translate into meaningful differences in downstream ocean prediction remains poorly understood. We investigate how atmospheric forecast errors propagate into six-hourly surface-current predictions and whether ML-based atmospheric forcing can provide skill comparable to conventional NWP. Atmospheric forecasts from NASA's Prithvi-WxC Earth foundation model are compared with NOAA's Global Forecast System (GFS), using the ERA5 reanalysis as a common atmospheric reference. Ten-meter winds from each forecast system are mapped to a common 0.25° grid and converted to surface wind stress using a common formulation. These forcings are then introduced into the same hybrid AI-physics ocean forecasting framework. An altimetry-based sea-surface-height (SSH) forecast emulator, trained on the DASHv1 dataset, provides the evolving geostrophic-current component, while an explicit tidal contribution represents additional high-frequency variability. The SSH and tidal components are held fixed across experiments, allowing differences in surface-current forecasts to be attributed specifically to atmospheric forcing. Initial Prithvi-WxC experiments reveal geographically structured errors in 10-m winds and derived wind stress, with enhanced errors at higher latitudes that propagate into the wind-driven current estimate. We examine how these errors evolve from 6 to 48 h lead times, whether similar error structures occur in GFS, and, critically, whether differences in atmospheric forecast skill produce comparable differences in total surface-current forecast skill. ERA5-forced experiments provide an additional benchmark for estimating the fraction of surface-current error associated with atmospheric forecast uncertainty. Evaluation is conducted globally and across dynamically distinct ocean regimes, including the Gulf Stream and the Agulhas Current, using atmospheric and surface-current verification metrics together with surface drifters and high-frequency radar where available. This study provides a controlled assessment of how MLWP and NWP errors propagate into downstream ocean prediction and evaluates whether Earth foundation models can provide atmospheric forcing competitive with conventional NWP for high-frequency ocean forecasting.

492870.title: Unifying Composition in the UFS through CATChem and CECE
492870.authors: Barry D Baker II, EMC, College Park, MD
492870.abstract: The Unified Forecast System (UFS) is evolving into a comprehensive meteorological modeling system spanning sub-seasonal to seasonal, global, and regional applications; however, a critical challenge remains in the historically fragmented nature of atmospheric chemistry representations within forecast suites. To establish a cohesive, flexible, and scientifically rigorous representation of atmospheric composition across UFS forecast applications, we present a unified framework integrating two key community-developed components: the Configurable Atmospheric Chemistry (CATChem) package and the Community Emissions Computing Engine (CECE). CATChem serves as the modular chemical solver, providing a consistent interface for gas and aerosol transformations ranging from computationally efficient schemes for global operational forecasts to detailed mechanisms for high-resolution regional air quality predictions. Complementing this, CECE standardizes emissions handling by acting as a centralized engine for anthropogenic, biogenic, and fire sources. By decoupling emissions processing and chemical solvers from the core model physics, this integrated approach ensures scientific consistency between UFS components, improves forecast reproducibility, and significantly reduces the Research-to-Operations (R2O) timeline for novel atmospheric chemistry parameterizations. This work provides the foundation for the next generation of UFS meteorological and coupled chemistry-climate applications. CATChem serves as the core chemical solver, designed to provide a single, consistent interface for managing atmospheric transformations with gas and aerosol species. Its modular design allows users to select from a library of chemical mechanisms—ranging from simple, computationally efficient schemes necessary for long-range global forecasts, to complex, detailed mechanisms required for regional air quality predictions—without altering the underlying transport model structure. This configurability ensures scientific rigor while maintaining the necessary computational efficiency across the UFS's diverse applications. Complementing CATChem, CECE standardizes the crucial process of emissions handling. CECE acts as a centralized engine for ingesting and processing all relevant emission types (anthropogenic, biogenic, and fire). By decoupling emissions pre-processing from the model physics, CECE ensures that emissions data are consistently handled, interpolated, and coupled to the UFS, facilitating the rapid incorporation of new emission inventories (e.g., global fire products or evolving national emissions data) and improving reproducibility across different UFS runs. The unification of chemistry within the UFS through the CATChem and CECE framework represents a significant step towards a truly cohesive and sustainable forecasting system. This presentation will detail the technical implementation strategy, demonstrate the flexibility of CATChem's mechanism switching for different forecast scales, and present initial validation results from UFS testbed simulations. We will specifically highlight how this unified structure improves consistency between UFS components—such as the seamless transition of chemical states between global and nested regional domains—and significantly reduces the Research-to-Operations (R2O) timeline for novel atmospheric chemistry parameterizations. This work provides a foundation for the next generation of UFS air quality and coupled chemistry-climate applications, bridging the gap between meteorological forecasting and atmospheric composition.

492876.title: Changing Modulation of Easterly Waves and Tropical Cyclones by the Madden-Julian Oscillation in a Warming Climate
492876.authors: Amanda F. M. Bowden, DOE CSGF Fellow, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado, Boulder, Boulder, CO; Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences, University of Colorado, Boulder, Boulder, CO; and K. Karnauskas, E. D. Maloney, A. C. Subramanian, W. Lin, and K. A. Reed
492876.abstract: Understanding the processes that influence tropical cyclone (TC) development is critical for improving subseasonal predictions of these high-impact events. Easterly waves (EW) are synoptic-scale tropical disturbances that can serve as precursors to TCs, while the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) modulates the large-scale environment in which these disturbances develop. By altering tropical moisture, precipitation, and low-level winds, the MJO can enhance or suppress EW activity and associated tropical cyclogenesis. Our previous work has shown that the MJO is expected to strengthen, while EWs tend to weaken in a warmer climate. However, an intensified MJO could strengthen its modulation of EWs, with consequences for subseasonal prediction of TC activity and severity. We use the Community Earth System Model Large Ensemble (CESM2 LENS) and Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SMv3), including projections for 2081–2100. We compare boreal summer EW responses to warming and MJO modulation between the models. We then apply TC tracking algorithms (e.g. ClimateNet & Tempest Extremes) to examine changes in TC frequency and intensity. Results indicate decreased EW activity across the tropics in a warming climate, although MJO amplitude increases in both models. Ensemble mean E3SMv3 MJO OLR activity is stronger in the central to western Pacific, whereas CESM2 LENS EW OLR activity is stronger in the Gulf and Atlantic. In a separate comparison, composite analysis indicates that MJO is stronger in CESM2 LENS than E3SMv3 and exhibits a higher frequency of weak MJO states. Preliminary analysis suggests that MJO modulation of African Easterly Waves (AEWs) strengthens in a warmer climate by enhancing positive AEW anomalies during phases 2–3 and intensifying negative anomalies during phases 1 and 8. These results have implications for subseasonal TC prediction and emerging risks in a warming climate.

492880.title: Revisiting Radar-Based Estimates of Atmospheric Turbulence in Deep Convection: The Role of Sampling Strategy and Retrieval Methodology
492880.authors: Songchen Li, Stony Brook University, STONY BROOK, NY; Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY; and J. Yan, N. Allwayin, M. Oue, E. Luke, and P. Kollias
492880.abstract: Radar measurements of Doppler spectrum width provide a physically based means of estimating the cube root of the turbulent kinetic energy dissipation rate (EDR), the standard metric used to quantify atmospheric turbulence. However, EDR estimates depend on both the radar sampling strategy and the assumptions used to separate turbulence from other sources of spectrum broadening. In rapidly evolving deep convection, sequential volume scans, range-dependent beam broadening, and coarse vertical sampling can smooth localized turbulent structures, while velocity shear and hydrometeor fall-speed variability introduce additional uncertainty into retrieved EDR. This study examines the relative importance of these two uncertainty sources by comparing rapid-scanning range–height indicator (RHI) observations collected with reflector-based and phased-array radars to pseudo-RHI observations reconstructed from conventional weather radar volume scans. EDR is retrieved using both the NCAR Turbulence Detection Algorithm (NTDA) and a physics-based spectrum-width variance budget framework adapted for scanning RHI and phased-array radar observations, which explicitly accounts for velocity shear and hydrometeor fall-speed variability. The results show that the radar sampling strategy often has a larger influence on retrieved EDR than the choice of retrieval methodology. Conventional volume scans reliably identify the dominant turbulent convective cores but progressively lose the intensity and fine-scale structure of turbulence with increasing range. Differences between retrieval algorithms become most pronounced near asymmetric coherent updraft and downdraft structures, where non-turbulent contributions to Doppler spectrum width are largest. Using high-temporal-resolution phased-array radar observations, we demonstrate these effects directly for the first time. These findings provide new guidance for interpreting radar-derived turbulence products and for designing future radar observing strategies aimed at resolving convective turbulence.

492882.title: Disentangling the Influence of Mesoscale Cloud Organization on Aerosol-Cloud Interactions
492882.authors: Jonathan Roland Irving, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada; and X. Zhou, Y. S. Chen, T. Yamaguchi, and G. Feingold
492882.abstract: Marine stratocumulus responses to anthropogenic aerosol perturbations remain a major source of uncertainty in estimates of anthropogenic climate forcing. This uncertainty reflects coupled feedbacks among cloud microphysics, thermodynamics, and dynamics. Recent studies suggest that mesoscale cloud organization, including characteristic cellular size, can modulate aerosol-induced changes in cloud albedo. Because current climate models generally do not resolve these mesoscale structures, their representation of aerosol–cloud interactions may be systematically biased. In this study, we investigate how mesoscale cloud organization influences aerosol–cloud interactions using an ensemble of 242 large-eddy simulations of diurnally evolving nonprecipitating marine stratocumulus. The simulations span a range of initial temperature and moisture profiles, boundary-layer depths, and aerosol concentrations. These environmental and aerosol conditions are treated as concurrent predictors of the evolving cloud system. Each simulation is divided into three stages of the diurnal cycle: nocturnal cloud development, daytime cloud decay, and late-afternoon cloud recovery. Within each stage, we examine how the characteristic cloud-organization scale covaries with cloud fraction and liquid water path, and how these relationships depend on the environmental state. This stage-specific analysis reveals how the coupling between mesoscale organization and bulk cloud properties evolves during diurnal cloud evolution. We then train an interpretable supervised machine-learning model on the LES ensemble to separate the influence of cloud-organization scale on aerosol–cloud interactions from the effects of covarying environmental conditions. This framework provides a process-oriented assessment of the role of mesoscale organization in regulating aerosol-induced cloud responses and offers insights relevant to improving their representation in climate models.

492887.title: Surface Heterogeneity Impacts on the Formation and Evolution of Dust-Devil-Like Vortices
492887.authors: Isaiah Montgomery, The University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and E. J. Kerr, S. Bailey, A. C. Blackford, and U. S. Nair
492887.abstract: The role of land-atmosphere interactions in modulating coherent vortices in the planetary boundary layer (PBL) is not well understood. Dust-devil-like vortices (DDLVs) are one type of coherent vortices that form on the corners of convective cells under unstable and low wind PBL conditions. These vortices are responsible for significant movement of dust in the lower atmosphere on Earth and especially on Mars. While it is recognized that land-atmosphere interactions play an important role, the surface heterogeneity aspect has not been studied in detail. This study investigates how land-use and land-cover heterogeneity influence DDLV formation using high-resolution (10 m) idealized Cloud Model 1 (CM1) simulations. Land cover type and heterogeneity patch size are varied across simulations using the heterogeneity framework from Bou-Zeid et al (2020). Simulations show that as the size of heterogeneity decreases (patch size at or below 200 m), the DDLV count becomes equivalent to the homogeneous land use case, as the atmosphere reaches a statistically homogeneous state. Contrast between land use patches as a function of roughness length and albedo was examined to assess the impact of different land use types on DDLV formation. Simulations with high roughness length patches led to enhanced DDLV activity surrounding the square, indicating a stronger impact on the surrounding environment. Simulations initialized with random patches of land use led to higher counts of DDLVs on the surfaces with low roughness length and high albedo. Preliminary analysis of the simulations using temporal tracking also indicate that variations in land cover increases the median DDLV path length to 82.8 m, up from the control case median of 68.7 m. Large heterogeneity also generally reduced the number of DDLVs, indicating a decrease in the number of shorter-lived dust devils.

492894.title: Learning Across Sensors: AI-Enabled Multi-Sensor Retrievals of the Planetary Boundary Layer
492894.authors: Jordan A Caraballo-Vega, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and A. E. Kotsakis, S. D. Nicholls, N. Shahroudi, and A. Gambacorta
492894.abstract: Accurate characterization of the planetary boundary layer (PBL) requires observations capable of resolving its coupled thermodynamic, moisture, aerosol, and cloud structure. Individual observing systems provide only part of this information, motivating approaches that can exploit complementary measurements across sensors. Recent observing efforts, including the 2024 Westcoast & Heartland Hyperspectral Microwave Sensor Intensive Experiment (WH²yMSIE) and APEX, provide coincident hyperspectral microwave, lidar, and in situ observations that offer a unique opportunity to investigate AI-enabled multi-sensor PBL retrievals. We present an AI framework that integrates passive and active hyperspectral microwave, lidar, and in situ observations to retrieve PBL properties.
