Convolutional, transformer-based, and hybrid architectures are evaluated to capture spectral and vertical dependencies while accommodating the high dimensionality of emerging hyperspectral instruments. Rather than treating each observing system independently, the framework learns from complementary measurements and evaluates how different sensor combinations influence retrieval performance. Explainable AI experiments are used to quantify the contribution of individual spectral channels and observing systems to retrieved PBL properties. This connects retrieval performance with observational information content and provides a quantitative approach for assessing the value of complementary measurements. The framework demonstrates how AI-enabled multi-sensor fusion can improve PBL retrieval development while informing sensor and spectral-channel combinations for future atmospheric observing systems.

492899.title: Storm Surge Impacts from High-Resolution Downscaled Extratropical Cyclones in the Northeast US
492899.authors: Alexandra N. Ramos-Valle, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. Jaye
492899.abstract: Extratropical Cyclones (ETCs) can produce high-impact weather in mid-latitudes leading to extreme precipitation, winds, and storm surge events. A recent study used CESM2 Large Ensemble (LENS2) and the variable-resolution capabilities of the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) to evaluate systematic changes in end-of-century ETC characteristics including intensity, translation speed and storm size, with a particular focus on evaluating how wind hazards related to ETCs are expected to change under future climate conditions in the Northeast US. MPAS was used to downscale 600 extreme ETCs, comprising 200 storms each from the present-day, mid-century, and end-of-century period, from LENS2 to a 3-km grid spacing. In this study, we build on that work and use these simulations as atmospheric forcing for the Advanced Circulation Model (ADCIRC) to evaluate storm surge impacts under present-day, mid-century, and end-of-century conditions. We hypothesize that end-of-century ETCs will drive disproportionately larger storm surge events, according to projected changes in storm tracks along the Northeast US, broadened wind fields and overall increased storm intensity.

492902.title: Examining Southeast U.S. Convective Environments with Doppler Wind Lidar Observations
492902.authors: Sabrina Roche, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY; and B. Saba and M. D. Flournoy
492902.abstract: In 2022 and 2023, the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) participated in the Propagation, Evolution, and Rotation in Linear Storms (PERiLS) field campaign. PERiLS was designed to characterize the near-storm environments associated with tornado-producing quasi-linear convective systems (QLCS). One of the NSSL’s instruments operated during this project was a mobile scanning doppler wind lidar (DWL). The research goal of the DWL was to observe the evolution of storm inflow properties to gain a better understanding of the storm environment surrounding an evolving QLCS. An optimal estimation technique (windOE) was designed to incorporate colocated rawinsonde and surface observations into the wind retrievals that provide data between the surface and 75 m. The result is continuous surface to 6 km wind profiles with associated uncertainty information. Retrieval configuration resulted in wind profiles every 5 minutes, providing high resolution observations not captured using other methods (e.g., balloons). The tornadic environment featured a more significant hodograph evolution as the storm approached. This included increases in SRH, particularly in the 0-1 km and 0-3 km layers. Synoptic-scale features also (e.g., nocturnal low-level jet) appeared to heavily influence the evolution of the storm environments. These findings can provide operational insight into differences between tornadic and non-tornadic storm environments in the Southeast U.S..

492904.title: Characterizing Evolution of Biomass Burning Smoke Using Dual-View Geostationary Satellite Retrievals
492904.authors: Sonia M. Kreidenweis, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and T. Johnson, J. C. Chiu, I. L. McCoy, and J. Limbacher
492904.abstract: Biomass burning is a major source of aerosols and greenhouse gases, affecting air quality, human health, and the Earth’s radiation budget. While monitoring of the evolution of individual wildfire smoke plumes is possible via geostationary satellite observations, current retrieval methods do not necessarily identify them as smoke, nor do they retrieve how smoke properties other than aerosol optical depth change with plume evolution. We present a case study demonstrating how integration of observations from both GOES-16 and GOES-17 Advanced Baseline Imagers can be used to diagnose smoke properties with both time and distance (atmospheric age) in a plume. The case study is from 12 August 2021 near Kelowna, Canada, where a smoke plume from nearby wildfires passed directly over the Kelowna Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET) site, providing a unique opportunity for evaluation. Our retrievals showed good agreement with AERONET aerosol optical depths, and indicated that fine-mode brown carbon models contributed about 30% of the AOD in the plume. Analysis of smoke evolution revealed that, as the plume aged, non-absorbing aerosol models constituted larger fractions of the total aerosol optical depth, and the average single-scattering albedo increased from 0.92 to 0.95.

492905.title: Translating Climate Warming into Fire Danger: Seasonal Mean and Peak Drought Code Trends Across Alaska's Predictive Service Areas
492905.authors: Benjamin Bown, IARC, Fairbanks, AK; and R. Lader
492905.abstract: High-latitude climate warming is fundamentally altering fire regimes across sub-Arctic and Arctic ecosystems. Across northern Canada and Alaska, escalating fire weather severity and severe organic soil drying are pushing wildland fires into ecosystems and sub-Arctic zones that have historically burned infrequently. During the fire season in Alaska (April 1 - Sept 30), widespread solar noon temperature increases (+0.23 to +0.33°C per decade from 1959–2025) and reduced snow cover duration are accelerating seasonal drying of deep organic soils, despite limited changes in precipitation To quantify these shifts, this study evaluates multi-decadal trends in both seasonal mean and seasonal maximum Drought Code (DC) across 5 Alaska Predictive Service Area (PSA) groups. The Drought Code, a component of the Canadian Forest Fire Danger Rating System (CFFDRS), represents moisture conditions in deep organic fuels, providing a useful indicator of the fuel conditions underlying persistent northern wildfires. Using historical gridded climate baselines, we analyze spatial and seasonal trends in DC, surface temperature, and precipitation. Results reveal statistically significant increases in Drought Code (1959–2025), where regional mean trends were +1.92 DC per decade in the Eastern Boreal region and +1.19 in the South Central region, while localized maximum trends reached up to +2.56 and +3.77 DC per decade, respectively—demonstrating that peak trends most relevant for fire management substantially exceed regional averages. Seasonal analysis highlights pronounced early-to-mid-summer soil drying. Regional case studies—including the 2004 Taylor Complex in the Interior, the 2007 Anaktuvuk River Fire on the North Slope, and the 2014 Funny River Fire in Southcentral—illustrate how Drought Code anomalies corresponded with observed fire activity, burn severity, and late-season persistence. These elevating DC trends carry cascading ecological and operational impacts. Severe organic layer drying increases vulnerability to lightning ignitions, promotes deep smoldering combustion, and strips the protective soil organic layer, exposing underlying permafrost to accelerated thaw. Furthermore, altered burn severities are triggering non-traditional vegetation trajectories, such as shrubification and repeat-fire grassification. By contextualizing climatological DC shifts with land-atmosphere interactions and operational danger rating thresholds, this analysis translates long-term climate information into an operationally relevant fire-danger metric, providing critical decision support for wildland fire management, pre-suppression resource allocation, and carbon cycle monitoring across changing northern landscapes.

492907.title: Our Current Best-Estimate Ozone Depleting Substances Scenario and its Impact on Stratospheric Chlorine and Ozone Recovery
492907.authors: Eric L. Fleming, NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center and ADNET Systems, Inc., Greenbelt, MD; and Q. Liang and J. S. Daniel
492907.abstract: Due to successful Montreal Protocol regulations, atmospheric abundances of the controlled ozone depleting substances (ODSs) continue to decrease, with observations showing clear signs of ozone recovery in the upper and middle stratosphere and the Antarctic spring lower stratosphere. However, emissions of the long-lived ODSs from feedstock-related applications, which are not controlled by the Montreal Protocol, are occurring and will likely increase in the future. This increase is driven by rapidly expanding polymer industry and the production for low-GWP alternatives. The multimodel simulations from the CCMI-2022 RefD2 experiment which follows a “middle of the road” climate scenario (SSP2-4.5) and the WMO 2018 A1 ODS scenario show that global total column ozone (TCO) is projected to return to 1980 values around 2040 and the Antarctic spring TCO is expected to return to 1980 levels during the 2060s. Our most recent WMO 2026 ODS baseline scenario, which accounts for our best knowledge of all ongoing ODS production and consumption, both in controlled and not-controlled applications, predicts that the effective equivalent stratospheric chlorine (EESC) return date is approximately a decade later that that predicted with the WMO 2018 A1 ODS scenario. This results in a delay of ozone recovery. In this study we use the GSFC2D model to conduct simulations with the updated WMO 2026 ODS baseline scenario projection, and quantify the changes in return years of EESC, stratospheric equivalent chlorine (chlorine + bromine), and TCO to their 1980 levels. We compare these results with previous projections using the WMO 2018 A1 ODS scenario. Additionally, we conduct sensitivity simulations comparing emissions-based simulations vs. mixing ratio boundary conditions, as well as empirical parameterized EESC estimates to evaluate how methodological differences and underlying assumptions and configuration differences impact projected recovery timelines.

492911.title: Who Uses Medium-Range Severe Weather Forecasts? Awareness, Use, and Evaluations Among the Public and Emergency Managers
492911.authors: Benjamin Jacob Fellman, School of Meteorology, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; Storm Prediction Center, Norman, OK; Institute for Public Policy, Research and Analysis (IPPRA), University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and J. T. Ripberger, A. L. Bitterman, M. Krocak, A. C. Wanless, H. E. Brooks, and P. T. Marsh
492911.abstract: Advances in forecasting have increased the ability to identify severe weather threats several days in advance. For nearly two decades, the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) has issued medium-range severe weather forecasts, defined here as forecasts issued three to seven days before a potential event. While research has devoted considerable attention to evaluating the quality of these medium-range forecasts, less is known about whether users seek out severe weather information at these lead times and how different audiences use and evaluate medium-range forecast products. Using data from three surveys, this study investigates when members of the public and emergency managers (EMs) seek severe weather information and their awareness, use, and perceptions of medium-range severe weather forecasts. Results suggest that although EMs typically access severe weather information earlier than members of the public, a majority of members of the public are aware that severe weather forecasts are available three to seven days in advance. Among individuals who are aware of these forecasts, both groups report using them on at least an occasional basis. Members of the public generally view medium-range forecasts as accurate, reliable, and sufficiently detailed for decision-making, while a majority of EMs report moderate levels of trust in the medium-range SPC severe weather outlook. Together, these findings highlight both the value of medium-range severe weather forecasts and important differences in how public and professional audiences engage with forecast information across lead times.

492912.title: Attributing Tropospheric Ozone Variability In Boulder: Insights from Multiple NDACC Instruments and Models
492912.authors: Irina Petropavlovskikh, CIRES, BOULDER, CO; and P. Effertz, B. Noirot, J. W. Hannigan, I. Ortega, S. A. Strode, P. Cullis, G. A. Morris, R. M. Stauffer, D. E. Kollonige, and A. M. Thompson
492912.abstract: The Tropospheric Ozone Assessment Report (TOAR-II) focus working group "Harmonization and Evaluation of Ground-based Instruments for Free-Tropospheric Ozone Measurements" (HEGIFTOM) recently evaluated 2000–2022 global ozone records to assess changes in partial tropospheric ozone columns below 300 hPa, identifying regionally distributed ozone changes (Van Malderen et al., 2025). This paper is focused on high-quality Boulder, Colorado records derived from ozonesondes, a Fourier-Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectrometer, and Dobson Umkehr instruments maintained under the Network for Detection of Atmospheric Composition Change (NDACC). Despite strict protocols, intermittent biases and data gaps in these records contribute to discrepancies in derived trends. We investigate mean ozone biases driven by instrument-specific temporal sampling and vertical sensitivities, utilizing respective Averaging Kernels for the FTIR and Umkehr retrievals. Discrepancies in long-term trends (2000-2025) are assessed with an emphasis on seasonal patterns, data gaps, trend shifts, and record endpoints. We combine the LOTUS statistical model with the GEOS-CCMI global chemistry-climate model. This approach simulates tropospheric chemistry and transport at the NDACC station to interpret interannual ozone variability. Finally, we propose strategies for future intercomparisons of surface-based ozone instruments.

492913.title: Evaluation of MRMS and Stage IV Precipitation Products under NASA’s Global Precipitation Measurement Mision Ground Validation Program
492913.authors: Ali Tokay, JCET/Univ. of Maryland, Greenbelt, MD; and D. B. Wolff, C. N. Helms, S. D. Nicholls, J. L. Pippitt, B. Filipiak, A. V. Chibisov, and M. J. Boulanger
492913.abstract: As part of the NASA’s Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Ground Validation (GV) program, the Platform for In-Situ Estimation Rainfall Systems (PIERS) has been fabricated at NASA Wallops Flight Facility, Wallops Island Virginia. PIERS consists of dual tipping bucket gauges, a solar panel, and a cell modem. PIERS+ is an upgraded version with the addition of a laser-optical PARSIVEL disdrometer. Both versions have been distributed at granted institutions under the NASA Headquarters program, Increasing Participation of Minority Serving Institutions (https://wallops-prf/gsfc.nasa.gov), across the United States. PIERS+ is an affordable, low maintenance, easy to operate platform plays a key role in developing precipitation products. This study uses nine (9) PIERS+ sites for evaluating two publicly available precipitation products, the NOAA National Severe Storm Laboratory (NSSL) Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS), and the River Forecast Center (RFC) based Stage IV. Both products are used to validate spaceborne, reanalysis, and model-based precipitation estimates. Among those, the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) is evaluated by MRMS. MRMS is a gauge-adjusted radar precipitation product over contiguous US at 1-km spatial and 2-minute temporal resolution. This study uses a 30-minute averaged version of MRMS, known as GV-MRMS. Stage IV is an ensemble of RFC’s Multi-Sensor Precipitation Estimate (MPE) product over the contiguous US and is an hourly temporal and at 4-km spatial resolution. Unlike MRMS, Stage IV has a strong dependency on operational decisions by the RFC forecaster who may use MRMS radar only or MRMS final products to initialize the MPE processing. Thus, Stage IV is not uniformly constructed across the US. In this study, most of the PIERS+ sites are deployed in the Mid-Atlantic within the Mid-Atlantic RFC with two additional sites in Texas with the West Gulf RFC, and another additional site in Colorado within the Missouri Basin RFC. Two of the sites in the Mid-Atlantic and Texas are coastal, while the site in Colorado is at a higher elevation (1656m asl). The sites have been operating since late 2023 and early 2024 and this study focuses on the rain only events that occurred in 2024. This study presents direct comparisons between the PIERS+ event rainfall point measurements and the event rainfall totals from the MRMS/Stage IV gridded products. The comparative study includes individual sites as well as merged regional and US sites. The “regional” category of the sites includes the four PIERS+ sites in the Delmarva Peninsula, all under a single operational radar, KDOX. The “US” category of the sites includes six PIERS+ sites only one of which is also a Delmarva regional site, spread across different climatic regimes and in proximity of different operational radars. A key novelty of this study is the presence of a PARSIVEL disdrometer, which is used as a reference for event definition as well as for the event duration and rain intensity. One of the two tipping bucket gauges is the reference for the event rain total. Previous validation studies relied on gauges the comparative studies were based on fixed periods (e.g. hour, day, month). However, gauges are not ideal to determine the rainfall at a given period, rain duration and intensity. In this study, the year-long rainfall observations provide more in-depth analysis to evaluate the precipitation products not only for overall performance but also for specific conditions (i.e., short versus long events, light versus heavy rain intensity). Both MRMS and Stage IV missed about 10% of the rain events at US sites and 5-6% at Delmarva sites. For event totals, MRMS outperformed Stage IV at three sites, while they had about the same error at two sites. Stage IV, on the other hand, outperformed MRMS at four Delmarva sites where KDOX had extremely low differential reflectivity values resulting in unreasonably high MRMS rainfall at several events. It seems that this is where RFC forecaster input becomes crucial in Stage IV rainfall estimate. Excluding Delmarva sites, the rainfall errors were relatively high for both MRMS and Stage IV at coastal Texas and Colorado sites. Other than those sites, MRMS and Stage IV had an error at 18-28% and 18-31% intervals, respectively. Except one site, both MRMS and Stage IV had a wet bias, and correlations were above 0.9 for most of the sites. By dividing events to three sub-categories, the events with higher accumulation, longer duration and moderate rain intensity had lower rainfall errors. For heavy rainfall (mean rain rate > 5 mm h-1), MRMS and Stage IV had up to 24% and 27% rainfall errors, respectively. The radar data quality, radar-gauge distance, orography, available gauge and gauge data quality are perhaps the most common features in MRMS and Stage IV production. One key difference between the two products is the inclusion of daily gauges in Stage IV. This may increase or decrease performance of the product. The disaggregation of daily gauge rainfall to hourly rainfall based on radar observations may be beneficial in the absence of any other nearby gauges for the targeted pixel but could not be useful in the presence of reliable hourly nearby gauge.

492921.title: Knowledge-Guided Machine Learning Improves Soil Moisture Estimation and Drought Detection Across the Conterminous United States
492921.authors: Zachary H. Hoylman, University of Montana, Missoula, MT; and T. Colligan, D. Ketchum, K. Bocinsky, C. Brust, N. L. Edwards, and K. Jencso
492921.abstract: Accurate soil moisture information is essential for agriculture, drought monitoring, and water-resource management, but sparse in situ observations cannot characterize conditions continuously across the United States. We developed a knowledge-guided machine-learning (KGML) framework that combines process-model simulations with station observations. A one-dimensional temporal U-Net was pretrained on NASA SPoRT-LIS simulations from approximately 20,000 locations across the conterminous United States during 2005–2022 and then fine-tuned using observations from more than 700 stations for shallow (0–10 cm) and mid-depth (10–50 cm) soil layers. In 10-fold cross-validation, KGML increased median Kling–Gupta efficiency relative to SPoRT-LIS from 0.34 to 0.60 in the shallow layer and from 0.35 to 0.47 at mid-depth. In a controlled comparison with an otherwise identical model trained only on observations, SPoRT-LIS pretraining increased median KGE from 0.47 to 0.60 and from 0.34 to 0.48, respectively, demonstrating that process-model pretraining provided skill beyond observational training alone. Comparable performance at fully independent stations supported generalization to previously unseen locations. Model skill increased approximately linearly as the training network expanded from 100 to 650 stations, with no clear plateau. Fine-tuning with post-2015 observations also improved estimates at independent sites during 2005–2010, demonstrating transfer across space and time. KGML reduced standardized anomaly errors across all drought and wetness classes and captured the rapid development of the 2017 Northern Great Plains flash drought. These findings demonstrate a scalable approach for integrating process simulations and expanding observation networks to improve operational soil moisture estimation and drought characterization.

492928.title: An Analysis of 125 years of Weather-Related Fatalities across Kentucky (1901-2025)
492928.authors: Benjamin Woodson, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and J. A. Brotzge
492928.abstract: Between 1901 and 2025, an approximate 1,068 fatalities occurred across the state of Kentucky from a wide array of natural hazards, including tornadoes, floods, lightning, severe wind (non-tornadic), extreme temperatures, and winter weather. These direct (e.g., tornado projectiles) and indirect (e.g., carbon monoxide poisoning) deaths occurred, in part, due to a variety of influencing factors, such as storm strength, seasonality, time of day, and mobility, among others. As part of an ongoing five-year NSF EPSCoR grant focused on hazard resiliency, this study examined Kentucky’s hazard archive in-depth to identify the major factors contributing to the state’s weather hazard fatalities. Databases were created for each hazard, and where possible, individual victim metadata and death circumstances were captured from public (online) sources. Extensive newspaper, journal, book, and grave archive information were reviewed and combined with NOAA records to develop a comprehensive database of hazard and victim information. This presentation will share results from this study including spatial and temporal trends of fatalities from each hazard as well as commonalities noted across hazard types. These results will be used to build a better understanding of how to reduce weather fatalities across the state moving forward.

492931.title: How Does the Environment at Meso-γ Scales Affect the Sensitivity of Convective Mass Flux to Horizontal Grid Spacing?
492931.authors: Itinderjot Singh, Colorado State University, Longmont, CO; and J. Bukowski, P. J. Marinescu, G. R. Leung, S. Prasanth, R. Schulte, L. D. Grant, and S. C. van den Heever
492931.abstract: Prior work has established that the sensitivity of various properties of simulated deep moist convection to horizontal grid spacing is not uniform across all convective environments, even for the same storm morphology. We still lack a comprehensive understanding of how the near-storm environment modulates the relationship between deep convection properties and grid spacing, partly because such a study would require a very large number of samples of deep convection across a wide range of environments, simulated at multiple grid spacings. Here, we systematically quantify how convective mass flux (CMF) depends on horizontal grid spacing across a broad range of subtropical and tropical convective environments. We use the state-of-the-art INvestigation of Convective UpdraftS (INCUS) simulation database, which comprises over 30 case studies of deep moist convection spanning diverse convective morphologies, from isolated deep convection to mesoscale convective systems and tropical cyclones. Each case is simulated using three modeling frameworks: the Regional Atmospheric Modeling System (RAMS) with a 2-moment, bin-emulating bulk microphysics scheme; the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model with Morrison microphysics; and the WRF model with Thompson aerosol-aware microphysics. All simulations employ three one-way nested grids (Δx = 1.6 km, 400 m, 100 m) with approximately 230 vertical levels. For each simulation, we track individual updrafts over their lifetimes using the cloud object tracking tool, tobac. To isolate environmental controls on the sensitivity of CMF to resolution, we apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the high-dimensional environmental state of each updraft to two scalar variables. We then bin the updrafts by equivalent environments, allowing us to examine how CMF varies with grid spacing within each environmental regime. This approach reveals the convective environments in which vertical mass transport is most sensitive to model resolution. We find that the maximum CMF in the kilometer-scale simulations (Δx = 1.6 km), on average, is roughly double that seen in the large-eddy simulations (Δx = 100 m). The largest differences between these two resolution regimes appear in tropical convective environments associated with scattered, isolated convection. The two resolutions agree with respect to maximum CMF in high-terrain, high-shear environments. We discuss the physical processes behind these findings. We also discuss inter-model differences and the general dependence of CMF on CAPE, CIN, shear, and various commonly used environmental descriptors.

492934.title: Drought Monitoring Enhancements from the Third Phase of the North American Land Data Assimilation (NLDAS-3)
492934.authors: David M. Mocko, SSAI, Greenbelt, MD; and S. V. Kumar, C. R. Hain, J. L. Case, K. M. Whitney, F. Z. Maina, M. Hashemi, K. Locke, and R. A. Wade
492934.abstract: The North American Land Data Assimilation (NLDAS) is a surface meteorological and land-surface model (LSM) dataset that produces gridded fields of precipitation, soil moisture, snow, and numerous other fields. While NLDAS is used for countless applications, one of its primary applications is for drought monitoring and analysis. NLDAS Phase 2 runs in operations at NOAA, with a long-term archive and daily updates stored at NASA’s GES DISC. As part of NASA’s Water Insight project, the third phase of NLDAS is being developed. The spatial extent is being expanded from NLDAS-2, to now include Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Central America, and nearly all of Canada. The grid spacing is reduced from 12.5-km to 1-km, and the expected latency will be reduced from ~4 days to under 10 hours. A new precipitation analysis and advanced downscaling are used for the surface meteorology. The Noah-MP LSM is used in NASA’s Land Information System (LIS) software framework, and includes data assimilation of soil moisture, snow, vegetation, and terrestrial water storage. Details of these enhancements will be presented, with a focus on benefits to drought monitoring. Case studies on drought extent/severity improvements demonstrating the impacts from land data assimilation will also be shown.

492949.title: Assessing the Relative Impact of GOLD Tdisk and O/N2 Observations on Thermospheric Neutral Density Using OSSEs
492949.authors: Fazlul Laskar, Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, Boulder, CO; and N. Pedatella, M. Miesch, T. E. Berger, S. Zhang, and E. Sutton
492949.abstract: Accurate specification of thermospheric neutral density is important for understanding thermosphere-ionosphere variability and for applications such as satellite drag and orbit prediction. Data assimilation improves thermospheric state estimates by combining observations with physics-based models. NASA's Global-scale Observations of the Limb and Disk (GOLD) mission provides measurements of disk temperature (Tdisk) and column O/N₂, which can constrain thermospheric temperature and composition, respectively. To evaluate the relative contributions of these observations to neutral density specification, we perform a series of Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) within a whole-atmosphere data assimilation framework based on state estimation. Four experiments are conducted: (1) assimilation of lower-atmosphere (LA) only observations (meteorological, SABER and MLS measurements), (2) LA + GOLD Tdisk, (3) LA + GOLD O/N₂, and (4) LA + both GOLD Tdisk and O/N₂. Within a state-estimation DA framework, results show that assimilating GOLD Tdisk + O/N₂ with LA observations produce the largest improvement in thermospheric neutral density, demonstrating the value of jointly constraining temperature and composition. Assimilation of Tdisk alone yields greater improvement than assimilation of O/N₂ alone, indicating that thermospheric temperature provides a particularly strong constraint on neutral density. However, inclusion of O/N₂ further improves density specification when combined with Tdisk. These findings highlight the benefit of assimilating multiple thermospheric state variables and provide guidance for optimizing future upper-atmosphere observing systems and data assimilation strategies for space-weather applications.

492952.title: Evaluating the Cloud Exit Response of Water Content Measurements by the Multi-Element Water Content System
492952.authors: Summer Marie Coleman, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and D. J. Delene and A. Neumann-Skow
492952.abstract: Liquid water content (LWC), defined as the mass of liquid water droplets per unit volume of air, and total water content (TWC), which includes both liquid and ice mass, are fundamental microphysical cloud quantities relevant to hydrologic and climatologic disciplines. The Science Engineering Associates (SEA) Multi Element Water Content System (WCM) is a hotwire type probe for in-situ measurement of both LWC and TWC. In-flight comparison of WCM LWC and TWC measurements against the King Probe and Cloud Droplet Probe (CDP) during the NASA Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) airborne campaign demonstrates that the WCM exhibits a slow response when exiting a cloud, expressed by a time constant of 3.4. Based on laboratory experiments, new coefficients for the WCM Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller were developed to reduce the WCM cloud exit time lag. Three new PID configurations, with reduced proportional and derivative constants, were tested during cumulus cloud penetrations conducted by the Citation II aircraft. The time constant across all test flight cloud exit periods remained unchanged for each updated PID configuration. To further evaluate the contribution of the WCM PID configuration to the cloud exit time lag, a new set of laboratory experiments is conducted. A high-resolution camera with an adjustable frame rate examines liquid water retention on the WCM probe head when the water supply is cut off. The PID configuration producing the lowest time constant during simulated cloud exit periods is presented.

492953.title: Observations of the Atmospheric Electric Field during Blizzards
492953.authors: Malachi Bowen, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and D. Zhang and A. D. Kennedy
492953.abstract: Blizzards are a winter hazard characterized by high winds and visibility below ¼ mile due to falling and/or blowing snow. The reduction in visibility creates extremely hazardous travel conditions and significantly impacts local economies due to extended road closures. In addition to the aforementioned impacts, the electrification of blowing snow particles has been found to disrupt radio communications. While the electrification of blizzards has been widely studied in the Arctic and Antarctic, observations in the CONUS have been limited to the mid-1990s. Three blizzards were sampled in Grand Forks, North Dakota during the 2025-2026 winter using an ensemble of instruments, including an electric field mill, ceilometer, rawinsonde launches, and the Open Snowflake Camera for Research and Education (OSCRE). Results show that the electric field (E-field) peaks during periods of blowing snow, despite reduced particle size and number concentration, likely due to the smallest, charge-carrying particles being below OSCRE’s pixel resolution. During a period of both falling and blowing snow, the E-field was strongly correlated (R-squared of 0.8) with wind speed above a threshold of 6 m/s and trends in E-field closely followed visibility. The E-field is predominantly of negative polarity and exceeds 10 kV/m. The evolution of the E-field, snow particle size, number concentration, depth of blowing snow layer, and other meteorological variables during the sampled blizzards will be explored.

492955.title: Radiative Simulation Studies Using Enhanced Water Vapor and Smoke Aerosol Inputs In a Clear Sky
492955.authors: Marco Giordano, The Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV; and E. M. Wilcox and K. Pistone
492955.abstract: We focus on studies relevant to the Southeast Atlantic (SEA) region where the stratocumulus cloud regime is prevalent and seasonal biomass burning in the African sub-Sahel contribute to smoke aerosol loading. We construct canonical vertical profiles (characteristic "shape" curves) of column water vapor and smoke aerosol from records in the historic sub-Sahel burn season window, and within the geographic rectangular boundaries of interest. These canonical curves are constrained to be distributed vertically such that their integrated sum matches to specific bulk columnar values of relevance to measured observations. The vertical layer values are normalized to fractional coefficients of the columnar total for each canonical profile. These coefficients then are distributed as layer coefficients of the bulk columnar values; thus, preserving the canonical profile shapes. This results in vertically resolved profiles for specific geo-regions which can be fed into a radiative transfer model (RTM) to result in total layered heating rates (TLHR) and aerosol layered heating rates ALHR) expressed in K/day. The RTM is employed, firstly baselining clearsky (no cloud) water vapor only effects, then combining variations on profile water vapor and aerosol concentrations as inputs. The model outputs are expressed as instantaneous and diurnally averaged values. We found smoke aerosol plumes in the SEA during the August to October season tend to bimodally develop between a characteristically higher plume and a lower plume, separated by approximately 1 km vertically with their layer heating rates developed accordingly. For this presentation we present methodology applicable to a diverse set of geographic regions, model and study developments, and some specific cases of these studies. We find for our experiments in the SEA region that enhanced water vapor in the atmospheric column results in shortwave column heating rates on the order of 3K/day above a seasonal norm for the no aerosol load cases. We see the combined effects of enhanced column water vapor with enhanced column aerosol loads result in shortwave combined heating rates of 6+ K/day with extreme cases of 8+ K/day.

492956.title: Evaluating Variable Resolution Ensemble Hindcasts of Tropical Cyclones with the Model for Prediction Across Scales
492956.authors: Lara Natasha Tobias-Tarsh, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and G. Villarini, S. Nong, and A. Werner
492956.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) are among the costliest and most deadly hazards globally, accounting for over $1,500 billion in damages between 1980 and 2024 in the United States alone. Minimizing these impacts requires precise modeling of TC’s characteristics (track, intensity, and structure) and its non-linear multiscale vortex-environment coupling, which dictate highly destructive hazards like flooding and wind. Substantial progress in predicting these hazards has been made through the use of convection-allowing models. However, significant uncertainties remain in forecasting these characteristics, especially during complex environmental interactions that reduce predictability, such as the sudden northwestward turn of Super Typhoon Doksuri (2023) following interaction with the monsoon trough or Hurricane Sandy’s “left hook” during extratropical transition. In these scenarios, running ensemble simulations over domains large enough to capture both fine-scale TC features and the broader synoptic environment is critical for characterizing the full range of possible outcomes and quantifying forecast uncertainty. The Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) has emerged as a useful tool to address these challenges, especially when run in a global, variable resolution configuration. MPAS utilizes unstructured Voronoi meshes and scale-aware convective parameterizations, enabling regional refinement to convection-permitting resolutions over TC-vulnerable regions while smoothly transitioning to coarser resolutions globally. This allows both the representation of deep convection in the TC and the broader synoptic environment without prohibitive computational costs. This investigation focuses on how TCs are represented in MPAS, especially at initialization, and their sensitivity to factors such as physics configuration, initial conditions, and the extent and size of the variable resolution domain, remains necessary. This study explores global ensemble hindcasts of selected TCs to evaluate how varying sources of variability including microphysical, planetary boundary layer and scale-aware cumulus parameterizations and initial conditions affect TC representation in MPAS. Understanding these sensitivities is a critical first step toward improving predictions of post-landfall hazards, for example, rainfall-induced inland flooding.

492958.title: Preparing Physical Science Students for Careers in Financial Risk Management
492958.authors: Gary M. Lackmann, Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, Raleigh, NC; and G. Characklis, A. Sebastian, and S. Bennett
492958.abstract: Times have changed for students in the physical sciences, including meteorology. In addition to traditional careers, there are exciting opportunities in risk management and weather-linked economics. It is easy for students to get excited about studying extreme weather, but perhaps it is more challenging to motivate them on the economic side. In this session, we will explore the following questions: What are the essential components of a curriculum that blends physical science and risk management? What resources are available to students and instructors that can help to connect these areas? How can and should physical science programs best prepare students for careers in applied science such as risk management? How can physical science students best add value to the risk management enterprise? The success of the Institute for Risk Management and Insurance Innovation (IRMII) at UNC Chapel Hill offers a novel model for how to set up a program that addresses both workforce development and interdisciplinary connection aspects. It is valuable for students to understand industry perspectives and motivations, including topics such as credit risk and market response. Courses providing an overview of the risk-management value chain, translating geohazard information into risk and financial terms, and understanding the different classes of risk management tools can provide valuable career preparation. An overview and basic understanding of the various industry components can go a long way toward helping students to be competitive in this field.

492966.title: On the Past, Present, and Future Role of a Human Forecaster in Aviation Weather (Invited Presentation)
492966.abstract: This presentation reflects upon the evolving role of a human observer and forecaster in the aviation weather arena, covering aspects of the past and present, and providing a look into the future. It builds upon a growing scientific understanding of how the atmosphere behaves and technological advances in capabilities to observe, communicate, and process information. In parallel, the needs of the aviation industry are evolving as well, making it a dynamically evolving environment to work in.

492968.title: Non-Intrusive Sensing of the Ocean Tangential Viscous Stress at the Air-Sea Interface
492968.authors: Christopher J Zappa, LDEO, Palisades, NY; and N. Laxague, J. Liu, L. Hogan, S. Soumya, I. Savelyev, M. P. Buckley, and B. K. Haus
492968.abstract: Recent research has shown that physical interactions between the earth’s atmosphere and ocean are inadequately described, with a need for improved measurements of aqueous viscous sublayer forcing processes. In contrast to wind flow over flat surfaces, the ocean surface prominently features waves that form, grow, interact with each other, and eventually break. In the course of this process, the waves alter the turbulent properties of the airflow near the surface and thus change how the atmosphere and ocean exchange momentum and energy. While this effect has been studied extensively in the laboratory and through numerical modeling, it is exceptionally difficult to observe, and therefore quantify, in the real ocean. To address this fundamental knowledge gap, a multi-spectral thermal infrared imaging instrumentation system, the MultIR, was developed. This novel device enables the observation of viscous (i.e., molecular-scale) stress and heat transfer in the uppermost layer of the sea (top 100 microns) without disrupting the flow. This study presents a first-test of the MultIR system in the wind-wave tank of the Surge Structure Atmosphere Interaction Facility (SUSTAIN) at University of Miami in August-September 2022 and March 2024. We tested the system over a range of wind speed (3-14 m/s) over calm surfaces at 10 m fetch. The MultIR measurements compare well with PIV measurements of the air-side and aqueous viscous tangential stress in 2022. For the 2024 campaign, the comparison of the tangential viscous stress from the MultIR with the profiled hot-wire anemometry of the air-side Reynolds or total stress provides insight into the wave-related stress (or form drag) as a function of wind speed. Results from SUSTAIN are also shown to be comparable with previous tangential viscous stress estimates of Banner & Peirson (1998), Grare (2009a,b), Peirson et al. (2014), Bopp (2018), and Yousefi et al. (2020). These 21st-century measurements will yield crucial insight into basic air-sea transfer processes, thereby directly improving the way in which atmosphere-ocean interactions are treated in weather and climate models.

492977.title: Can Painting Mountains White Protect High-Elevation Snow and Ice? A CESM2 Experiment under SSP3-7.0 Warming
492977.authors: Jairo Michael Valdivia Prado Sr., University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and J. Kay, A. C. Subramanian, and K. Friedrich
492977.abstract: Mountain glaciers and seasonal snowpacks are shrinking under anthropogenic warming, putting water resources at risk from the tropics to the mid-latitudes. We test whether brightening high mountain surfaces—an idealized “paint the mountains white” intervention—can cool mountain climates and increase snowpack. Using the Community Earth System Model version 2 at about 1° resolution, we run a fully coupled experiment for 2015–2030 under a high-emissions pathway (SSP3-7.0). Surface albedo is set to 0.6 over land above 1000 m between 60°S and 60°N to represent white paint. The modified run is compared with an otherwise identical control simulation and with a 100-member large ensemble under the same scenario, so forced changes can be distinguished from natural variability. The intervention produces strong extra reflection of sunlight over the modified mountains and cools the climate. Global near-surface air temperature falls by about 0.8°C relative to the control, with much larger regional cooling over the Himalayas (about 6°C), the Rockies (about 7°C), and the Andes (about 2°C). Cooling is strongest in boreal summer, when glacier melt is typically most intense. Snowpack increases in all modified regions: snow water equivalent roughly quadruples over the Himalayas (about +50 mm), rises by about 30 mm over the Rockies, and increases from a near-zero baseline over the Andes. Snowfall increases over the Rockies and Andes (about +35–40%), but decreases over the Himalayas, where total precipitation also declines. Globally, total precipitation changes little. Idealized mountain whitening therefore yields robust, ensemble-detectable cooling and snowpack gains across major ranges, including a clear positive snow response in the tropical Andes, consistent with cooler surfaces retaining more snow. Hydroclimate responses differ by region, however, and a 1° global model cannot resolve individual glaciers. Finer-scale simulations are needed before these results can be translated into glacier mass balance or water-resource decisions.

492987.title: Evaluating Pixel Brightness Analysis for Automated Snow Detection From Highway Traffic Cameras
492987.authors: Michael J Davies, Utah State University, vernal, UT
492987.abstract: Automated assessment of winter road conditions from existing traffic camera networks is attractive because the cameras are already deployed, already maintained, and already streaming. This work evaluates whether pixel brightness analysis, in which snow coverage is inferred from the luminance, saturation, and color balance of each image, can exploit that infrastructure. Brightness thresholding was selected for defensible reasons: it needs no labeled training data, runs in milliseconds, degrades gracefully at low resolution, and is transparent enough that a transportation agency can audit any individual classification. We implemented it in an operational public platform covering 46 state DOT traffic cameras integrated with 9 Road Weather Information System stations, serving roughly 600 to 1,050 monthly unique visitors through its first winter season. To evaluate against ground truth rather than our own judgment, we validated on an independent benchmark from a separate state DOT network: 138 usable images from four fixed cameras, each labeled by six trained coders, with almost perfect inter-coder agreement on the collapsed three-class set. We swept 180 threshold combinations across three road-isolation strategies. Full-image analysis reached 26.1 percent accuracy, a rectangular road crop reached 39.1 percent, and hand-drawn per-camera road masks isolating only pavement pixels reached 44.2 percent. No combination in any configuration exceeded 45 percent, and all three configurations selected identical optimal thresholds, showing the failure is threshold independent rather than a tuning problem. Under those thresholds the detector predicted no snow for 118 of 138 images, including all 30 heavy-snow images and 27 of 33 moderate-snow images. The cause is physical. Dry pavement in daylight registers 15 to 32 percent qualifying pixels, driven almost entirely by bright sky, while snow on a trafficked road under overcast registers 1 to 8 percent and at night 0.1 to 5 percent. Compaction, tire tracking, grit, and brine drive road snow toward a mid gray that never fires a white-pixel test. Adding meteorological gating changed the picture: on a 49-image subset with recoverable air temperature, accuracy rose from 38.8 percent image-only to 69.4 percent with RWIS temperature gating, with all 16 reclassifications correct and concentrated above 40 degrees Fahrenheit. A snapshot across 136 deployment cameras during an active storm reproduced the same signature, with 18.2 percent recall at cameras reporting snow or ice surfaces and a 28.3 percent false positive rate at cameras reporting dry surfaces. We describe ongoing work replacing brightness with a machine learning cascade combining road surface segmentation, supervised classification, and confidence scoring, trained on a 43-month archive of 12.4 million images from 115 highway cameras, and discuss the domain generalization gap between held-out training cameras and live deployment.

492988.title: On the Wind-Wave Forcing of Multi-scales Ocean Surface Slope Statistics
492988.authors: Junzhe Liu, LDEO, New York, NY; LDEO, Palisades, NY; and C. J. Zappa, N. Laxague, L. Hogan, and A. Cifuentes-Lorenzen
492988.abstract: The classic Cox and Munk (1954) wind–mean-square-slope (MSS) relation provides a foundational framework linking ocean surface roughness to wind forcing, which underpins many optical and microwave remote-sensing applications over the ocean. However, relatively few studies have examined scale-dependent surface roughness, particularly in the ocean, largely due to observational challenges in resolving short-wave dynamics. In this study, we use advanced visible polarimetric measurements collected during the ASIT-2019 field campaign to investigate the ocean surface roughness across a wide range of spatial scales -- from long-period swell to gravity–capillary waves with wavenumbers up to approximately 700 rad m⁻¹. We examine the mean response of sea-surface slope statistics, including variance, skewness, and kurtosis, to wind and other environmental forcing. We also present observations of long-wave phase-coherent modulation of gravity–capillary roughness. This modulation is quantified and interpreted in terms of contributions from free-wave components, influenced by airflow perturbations and hydrodynamic interactions, and bound-wave components associated with the long-wave field. These results advance our understanding of ocean gravity–capillary wave forcing and modulation, with important implications for interpreting and modeling radar Bragg-scale roughness across multiple frequency bands.

492989.title: Three-Dimensional Shear Stress Tensor and Flux Estimation with a Fleet of Multicopter UAS across Multiple Campaigns.
492989.authors: Norman Wildmann, DLR, Oberpfaffenhofen, Germany; and J. Kistner and A. Alexa
492989.abstract: Turbulence is a primary driver of small-scale dynamics in the Atmospheric Boundary Layer (ABL), yet accurately measuring its characteristics continues to be a fundamental observational challenge. As numerical weather prediction (NWP) models increasingly push towards sub-kilometer resolutions, the need for high-resolution, three-dimensional empirical data has become critical. On scales of a few hundred meters, turbulence is often highly anisotropic and spatially inhomogeneous. This non-homogeneity is frequently driven by complex topography, secondary circulations, and technogenically modified flows, such as those found within wind farms. Traditional single-point measurements from meteorological towers are insufficient to capture this complex spatial variability and rarely reach a height of more than 100 m. Furthermore, towers are expensive, inflexible, and logistically difficult to arrange in remote or highly structured environments. To bridge this observational gap, we present a novel approach utilizing true multi-point measurements acquired by a fleet of multicopter Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS). The SWUF-3D fleet utilizes up to 30 synchronized drones to establish flexible measurement arrays at virtually any location throughout the ABL. To capture turbulent dynamics, the 3D wind vector at each node is calculated directly from the high-frequency avionics data of the drone. Concurrently, a fast-response platinum fine-wire resistance thermometer measures temperature fluctuations at a turbulence-resolving resolution of 5 Hz. While the SWUF-3D fleet supports diverse flight geometries—including lines, crosses, and planar grids—we specifically Focus on the so-called "cube pattern" in this study which is explicitly designed for the estimation of the 3D shear stress tensor and the spatial variability of turbulent fluxes within the probed volume. Featuring a side length of approximately 100 meters with different values of vertical stretching, this volumetric configuration allows for the concurrent calculation of Reynolds stresses and sensible heat fluxes at each individual measurement location within the cube. Leveraging the multi-point nature of the datasets, we can derive the actual shear tensor, spatial velocity increments and coherence to characterize the turbulent flow field. Measurements utilizing this cube pattern were successfully conducted across four distinct campaigns at two contrasting sites: the WiValdi research wind farm in the flat terrain of Northern Germany, and the Nafingalm alpine pasture site in highly complex topography during the TEAMx campaigns. While full quantitative analyses are ongoing, preliminary findings reveal distinct structural differences in the flow dynamics across these environments. As anticipated, the principal axes of the shear tensor and the Reynolds stresses demonstrate a stronger alignment in the undisturbed flat terrain of the WiValdi site. Conversely, this alignment is significantly disrupted in the complex alpine topography and within the wind turbine waked flows, underscoring the pronounced anisotropy and flow distortion characterizing these regimes. Ongoing and future analyses are incorporating additional flight geometries and deployment locations to further characterize ABL dynamics. Future advancements of the SWUF-3D fleet will feature enhanced automation and extended flight endurance. This development will enable long-term spatial measurement capabilities, significantly expanding the so far limited observational database and improving the statistical robustness of spatial turbulence measurements with UAS.

492991.title: Role of Potential Intensity in Tropical Cyclone Future Projections
492991.authors: Suzana J. Camargo, Columbia University, Palisades, NY
492991.abstract: Potential intensity (PI) plays a crucial role in future projections of tropical cyclones (TCs). Here, I’ll give an overview of various ways that PI is used in future TC projections. Analysis of future environmental conditions relevant for TC activity frequently use PI as a key proxy for projections of TC activity, by itself or combined with other variables, e.g. as one of the components of the ventilation index or the recently developed ventilated PI. PI is also typically one of the main ingredients of various formulations of genesis indices and depending on the formulation of the index PI can be critical to determine if that genesis index will increase or decrease in the future. In most cases, future projections based on PI and environmental variables that include PI are performed without taking into account the PI biases present in climate models, as well as issues associated with the SST pattern. Importantly, the definition of PI bias itself is very sensitivity to the reanalysis dataset used to determine the baseline “observed” PI. PI also has a key role in various statistical-dynamical models used to downscale climate models and generate synthetic TCs, used to make future TC risk projections. Awareness and understanding of these issues are essential in order to determine the robustness of future TC projections which are dependent on PI.

492994.title: Embedding Research-to-Operations Hydrologists to Support Forecast-Informed Reservoir Operations at the Northwest River Forecast Center
492994.authors: Matt Lurtz, Lynker, Leesburg, VA; and E. Schwat, K. Haleakala, A. Chen, T. Dixon, S. Horvath, J. R. Zimmerman, F. M. M. Ralph, T. Vo, and J. C. Jankot
492994.abstract: Bridging the gap between hydrologic research and operational forecasting remains a major challenge, and beneficial scientific advances are often limited or delayed within operational hydrology. In this presentation, we discuss a newly-developed role, the Research-to-Operations (R2O) Hydrologist, funded by CIROH and embedded at NWS River Forecast Centers (RFCs). These positions bring hydrologic research to operational forecasts and facilitate the implementation of Forecast Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO) across the United States. R2O hydrologists serve as liaisons, facilitating the exchange of information between the operations-focused RFCs, the research-focused Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E), and the resources- and public-safety-focused US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE). The position begins with three months of in-depth training in the RFC’s operational forecasting systems: the Community Hydrologic Prediction System (CHPS) and the Hydrologic Ensemble Forecast Service (HEFS), which together produce ensemble streamflow predictions across the United States. The primary objective of the R2O hydrologist is to support the development and implementation of FIRO at reservoirs across the United States. The training program introduces CHPS, HEFS, and CW3E forecast systems in the context of supporting FIRO viability assessments. For example, the R2O hydrologists at NWRFC produce streamflow hindcasts at key FIRO locations, including the Howard A. Hanson Dam (Washington) and multiple sites in the Willamette Valley System (Oregon). Hindcasts are critical for evaluating the risks and robustness of FIRO at individual locations prior to implementation. The secondary objective of the R2O hydrologist is to test FIRO-relevant research capabilities within the RFC’s strict operational context. Recently, R2O hydrologists have tested the assimilation of modern evapotranspiration datasets into CHPS calibration routines and have helped demonstrate the value of CIROH-supported deep learning-based ensemble weather predictions in the RFC CHPS and HEFS systems.

492996.title: Quantifying the Influence of Climate Change on Global Marine Heat Waves in Near-Real Time
492996.authors: Brandon Bourassa, Climate Central, Princeton, NJ; and Z. M. Labe, PhD, K. Dahl, J. Giguere, and A. Pershing
492996.abstract: Marine heat waves (MHWs) are becoming increasingly widespread, persistent, and intense as the global ocean warms, with profound consequences for marine ecosystems, extreme weather, and coastal communities. However, quantifying the influence of anthropogenic climate change on evolving MHW conditions remains a major challenge. To enable near-real-time attribution of MHW impacts, we leverage Climate Central's Climate Shift Index: Ocean, an operational attribution system that integrates daily observational sea surface temperature data with state-of-the-art global climate model simulations to reconstruct a counterfactual sea surface temperature record representative of a world without human-caused warming. This approach also preserves the timing and structure of internal variability. MHWs are then independently identified in both the observed and counterfactual climates, which enables their direct attribution for a range of local and global MHW diagnostics. Using this framework, we find that anthropogenic climate change has fundamentally transformed global MHW characteristics. In 1982, about one-third (33%) of the global ocean remained free of MHW conditions throughout the entire year. By 2025, that had fallen to just 11%, meaning nearly 90% of the ocean experienced at least one MHW during the year. MHW persistence has also changed in response to anthropogenic warming, with the average ocean location experiencing only about 14 MHW days per year from 2020-2025 in the counterfactual simulation instead of 99 in the factual world. Human-caused warming also increased peak MHW intensity by approximately 0.3°C, therefore shifting MHWs toward higher-impact severity categories, especially the area experiencing Strong (Category II) and Severe (Category III) events. Together, these results demonstrate that climate change has transformed MHWs from brief, localized extremes into widespread, persistent conditions that now dominate large regions of the global ocean, while also providing a framework for rapidly disentangling climate change's contribution to evolving MHW hazards in near-real time.

492998.title: IDSS Engine Operational Integration into NWS Connect and Future
492998.authors: Ken Fenton, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and D. Atrash, M. Davis, M. Grimes, R. Howlett, M. Rabellino, J. Schulz, and M. Willis
492998.abstract: The IDSS Engine automates key components of the Impact-based Decision Support Services (IDSS) workflow by integrating partner-defined thresholds with real-time and probabilistic forecast weather data. By continuously evaluating model output against pre-established criteria, the system proactively identifies weather risks and alerts meteorologists when further interrogation is required. Built as a cloud- and web-based application, the platform provides tailored visualizations—including plan-view maps, time series, and risk matrices—that enable forecasters to rapidly contextualize weather hazards within specific partner operational thresholds. Following its integration into NWS Connect in September 2026 across all Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs), the IDSS Engine has modernized how the National Weather Service engages with core partners. The tool streamlines risk identification and communication while keeping forecasters at the center of decision support, ensuring meteorologists retain full authority over final messaging. As the NWS shifts toward a probabilistic, impact-based forecasting framework, the IDSS Engine provides a crucial step toward efficient, targeted decision support. This presentation reviews the operational rollout within NWS Connect, synthesizes initial field feedback from forecasters, and outlines plans for future development.

493005.title: A Lightweight Coastal Digital Twin for Transferable and Adaptive Water Level Forecasting
493005.authors: Soheil Radfar, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and N. Lin
493005.abstract: Machine-learning coastal forecast systems are often developed and evaluated at individual locations, yet operationally useful systems must function across coastlines with different tidal regimes, storm climatologies, geometries, and hydrodynamic responses. We examine the portability of coastal water-level forecasting across U.S. East and Gulf Coast environments and ask when a model trained at one location can provide useful information at another. Cross-location experiments show that direct transfer can substantially degrade surge prediction and that transferability is strongly directional: performance depends on which location provides the training information and which receives it. We then evaluate whether limited observations from the target site can recover useful forecast skill. Local updating using relatively short observational records substantially reduces the transfer penalty, including for extremes and threshold exceedances, while feature-attribution diagnostics reveal how the dominant forecast relationships change after adaptation. These forecasting experiments are embedded within a lightweight coastal digital-twin workflow in which NOAA observations, multi-lead ensemble prediction, observation assimilation, rapid inundation modeling, and impact estimation operate sequentially. During extreme conditions, newly available observations are used to update the evolving forecast ensemble, improving short-lead estimates of peak water levels and forecast uncertainty before propagation into flood-impact calculations. The results indicate that portability should not be treated as an intrinsic property of a coastal machine-learning model. Instead, transferable coastal forecasting requires explicit adaptation to the receiving environment and continued updating as observations characterize the realized event.

493006.title: The Modulation of Air-Sea Momentum Flux by Breaking Waves
493006.authors: Lindsay Hogan, Columbia University, Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, Palisades, NY; and C. J. Zappa, S. Soumya, N. Laxague, I. Savelyev, and J. Liu
493006.abstract: Accurate description of air-sea momentum flux relies on partitioning the wind stress into viscous tangential stress and form drag (wave-related stress). The wind stress partition and viscous sublayer properties vary with wave phase due to poorly resolved processes such as airflow separation and breaking waves. Microscale breaking waves are a ubiquitous feature of the sea surface that influence air-sea momentum flux and the partitioning of wind stress between form drag and viscous components. Sheltering and air-flow separation induced by breaking waves reduce the viscous stress and increase the form drag. In addition to modulating the wind stress partition, breaking waves transfer momentum from the wave field to the near-surface current. We investigate the effects of microscale breaking waves on momentum flux with measurements from laboratory experiments conducted in the wind-wave tank of the Surge Structure Atmosphere Interaction Facility (SUSTAIN) at University of Miami in March 2024. A novel method is used to directly measure the viscous stress for winds from 3-14 m/s. Specifically, the viscous stress is measured with multi-spectral infrared imagery and thermal marking velocimetry, directly measuring the velocity shear profile in the aqueous viscous sublayer. In addition to direct measurements of the viscous stress with multi-spectral thermal infrared imaging, we examine the momentum flux through breaking wave statistics evaluated from infrared imagery, the Reynolds stress estimated from profiling hot-wire anemometry, and wave spectra from wave wires. The laboratory measurements of wind-wave coupling under strongly-forced conditions are evaluated in the context of non-linear stress partitioning models and agree well both with previous laboratory measurements of viscous stress and with stress partitioning models. Additionally, these results present direct observations of the modulation of the viscous stress by microscale breaking waves: enhanced viscous stress on the crest of the breaking wave and diminished viscous stress on the leeward side where air-flow separation is expected. These results are pertinent wind-wave coupling in wave models, including decomposition of the total wind stress, modulations of the viscous stress by microscale breaking waves, and momentum flux into near-surface currents by breaking waves.

493007.title: The 2024 Tornado Season: The Impacts of Communication and Societal factors on Oklahoma's Tornado fatalities
493007.authors: Hayley Grimes, American Meteorological Society, Jupiter, FL
493007.abstract: The 2024 tornado season: The Impacts of Communication and Societal factors on Oklahoma’s Tornado fatalities Hayley Grimes Department of Ocean Engineering and Marine Sciences, Florida Institute of Technology MET3403: Data Analysis in Meteorology and Geosciences Dr. Milla Costa Alex Boreham(T.A.) January-August 2026 The 2024 tornado season was extremely active in Oklahoma and even with frequent tornado events at a national and state level, fatalities were well below what was normally expected. The state recorded 178 tornadoes alone and the United States experienced 1,796, possibly the most on record. Despite the high tornadic activity, fatalities totaled only 54 nationwide and 8 for the state of Oklahoma. The study was performed with a desire to investigate why the fatality count was low focusing on the role of communication and societal vulnerability. An understanding of how these factors influence the outcome for the season is crucial for improving risk reduction and management in the future as well as a mitigation of fatalities. Data was collected from many authoritative sources including the Storm Prediction Center, the NOAA Storms Event Database, the NWS Fatality dataset, the IOWA Environmental Mesonet Archive, the American Community Survey, the U.S. Census Bureau, the Tornado Archive, NWS, NCEI, and FEMA Open Data. Analysis was performed for the entire season specifically focusing on tornado characteristics, warnings, population density, and societal vulnerability. A case study of the events on May 6th, 2024 was also performed. Upon completion of the study, many results were made including critical periods for the public’s awareness including the months of April, May, and November as well as the hours of 18, 19, 20, 22 local time. Tornado path length and the amount of tornado occurrences made a connection between the overall risk and the tornado occurrences more frequently in less populated areas of the state. The top ten counties were highlighted in a darker red while the lighter reds indicated less of a SVI. Many counties of the state were red or darker red. A larger circle in a county of the state indicates a higher impact and the possibility of an event occurrence for a county with a lower to moderate SVI. The May 6th, 2024 tornado outbreak including an EF4 passing through Osage and Washington County was expected to have a more significant impact. Even with the dense cluster of tornado paths and the EF4, fatalities remained limited. This was suggestive that the fatality outcome was shaped primarily through effective communication and societal vulnerability even in an extremely active season and suggests overall effectiveness of the warning systems and public preparation.

493009.title: Severe Weather Preparedness in the Upper Midwest: Insights from Emergency Managers in Wisconsin
493009.authors: Rebecca Rose, American Meteorological Society, Madison, WI
493009.abstract: Wisconsin is expected to face more frequent and severe weather events such as extreme heat and cold, floods, and severe storms, all of which impact human health, economic activity, and infrastructure. To better understand how local governments in Wisconsin prepare for and respond to severe weather, we conducted interviews with emergency management officials at the county, regional, and state level. Here, we share their perspectives about the hazard mitigation planning process, how these plans translate into on-the-ground action, challenges faced, and ideas for improving severe weather preparedness. We also integrate findings from analyzing FEMA datasets on hazard frequency and severity and reviews of hazard mitigation plans. Major themes include difficulties and strategies in communication and public engagement, federal uncertainty around funding and policy, compounding hazards and vulnerabilities, progress made and success stories, and potential benefits of broadening what is considered to be hazard mitigation and severe weather preparedness.

493010.title: Long-Term Observations of Carbon Monoxide in the UTLS over the United States: Insights from AirCore, MLS, and WACCM
493010.authors: Xander Moss, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and X. Wang, PhD, J. Li, B. Baier, and C. Sweeney
493010.abstract: Variability in upper troposphere-lower stratosphere (UTLS) carbon monoxide (CO) provides insight into surface emissions, convection, and large-scale circulation. CO is also closely linked to methane oxidation chemistry in the upper troposphere. Our study aims to characterize the long-term variability and vertical structure of CO in the UTLS. In this study, we compare the NOAA GML AirCore vertical profile measurements with observations from NASA Aura MLS (v5), and use these observations to evaluate CO simulated by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). We focus on observations over Colorado with a latitude range of 37º N to 43º N and a longitude range of 102º W to 109º W. We analyze AirCore vertical profiles from 2012-2025, including 29 flights from the summer months (JJA) and 29 from the winter months (DJF). Overall, AirCore CO shows consistently lower mixing ratios than MLS in the UTLS, and both observational datasets show higher CO than WACCM. During JJA, AirCore CO is 7.6 ppb (19.8%) lower than MLS at 100 hPa and 8.0 ppb (16.1%) lower at 146 hPa. Relative to AirCore, WACCM underestimates CO by 11.0 ppb (35.8%) at 100 hPa and 7.0 ppb (15.5%) at 146 hPa. During DJF, AirCore CO is 12.7 ppb (36.2%) lower than MLS at 100 hPa and 5.2 ppb (13.6%) lower at 146 hPa, while WACCM underestimates AirCore CO by 9.2 ppb (33.4%) and 7.9 ppb (20.2%), respectively.

493015.title: Drought Information and Data for the Masses: The United States Drought Monitor Portfolio
493015.authors: Brian Fuchs, National Drought Mitigation Center-University of Nebraska, LINCOLN, NE; and M. D. Svoboda, C. J. Riganti, and L. Johnson
493015.abstract: Effectively managing escalating climate extremes requires robust, transparent, and multi-scalar environmental intelligence that is accessible to all sectors of society. To meet this operational demand, the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) digital portal (https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/) has evolved into a cornerstone public climate service ecosystem. Rather than serving as just a static mapping archive, the modernized platform delivers a dynamic suite of interactive products designed for a diverse user base—spanning government agencies, agricultural producers, emergency managers, municipal planners, media professionals, resource managers, economic decision makers, and the general public. This presentation explores the operational architecture and user utility of the complete USDM online portfolio. We highlight advanced web offerings including the GIS Data and Metadata clearinghouses, various tools, customizable Map Export configurations, and automated Web Services for seamless API data integration. Furthermore, the portal enhances targeted stakeholder decision-making via specialized applications like the Farm Service Agency (FSA) Eligibility Tool, localized State Impact archives, and community-sourced Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR). By providing transparent access to weekly data tables, time-series graphs, and multi-scalar drought indices, the platform bridges the gap between complex geophysical datasets and local risk management. This session demonstrates how the USDM web ecosystem empowers users to independently analyze regional drought footprints and track fast-evolving anomalies, serving as an international benchmark for how academic, federal, and citizen-science partnerships can democratize vital climate information.

493024.title: Environmental Controls on Cross-Barrier Precipitation over the Narrow Northern Wasatch Barrier
493024.authors: Zachary Alexander Atkins-Weltman, University of Utah, Salt lake city, UT; University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and A. Stansfield and J. Steenburgh
493024.abstract: Orographic wintertime precipitation in mountainous regions can vary dramatically over short distances, producing sharp contrasts in snowfall that influence water resources, avalanche risk, transportation, and winter recreation. This study examines how upstream environmental conditions influence precipitation distribution in a small set of winter storms observed during the Seeded and Natural Orographic Winter Storms Catchment Processes and Evaluation (SNOWSCAPE) field campaign in the northern Wasatch Mountains. Using coordinated scanning Doppler radar observations, vertically pointing Micro Rain Radar (MRR) observations, atmospheric soundings, and surface measurements, the study relates variations in stability, crossbarrier flow, and moisture structure to differences in precipitation organization, echo depth, and spillover across the mountain barrier. The selected events span a range of conditions, including weak orographic precipitation, post-frontal convection, and frontal passages, allowing comparison of how differing atmospheric states influence cross-barrier precipitation distribution. These results provide insight into the physical processes that control precipitation distribution across a narrow mountain barrier.

493026.title: A Generalized Framework for Detection and Mitigation of RFI in Dual-Polarization Weather Radars
493026.authors: Shashank S Joshil, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and V. Chandrasekar, M. Vaccarano, P. Rossi, and J. Selzler
493026.abstract: Radio Frequency Interference (RFI) has become an increasingly important challenge for weather radar systems because of growing spectrum congestion and expanded use of wireless technologies. Operational weather radars encounter interference with diverse characteristics. Therefore, mitigation methods designed for a single RFI type may not perform reliably across different systems and environments. This is particularly important for dual-polarization radars, where interference in either channel can bias polarimetric variables and compromise hydrometeorological interpretation. This study presents a generalized processing framework for identifying and mitigating various forms of RFI directly in dual-polarization weather radar data while preserving the underlying meteorological signal. The framework integrates complementary detection strategies that target different interference characteristics and combines their outputs to generate a unified RFI mitigation system. Contaminated samples are subsequently reconstructed using techniques designed to minimize impact on the weather echo measurement and maintain continuity in the resulting radar variables. The processing architecture is highly modular, allowing detection parameters and mitigation strategies to be adapted to different radar configurations and interference environments. Computational efficiency is also emphasized to support real-time implementation. The approach is evaluated using observations from multiple C-band dual-polarization weather radars operating in different environments, including radar datasets from Europe and the US. Results demonstrate effective suppression of interference signatures in both horizontal and vertical polarization channels while retaining meteorological observations and improving the quality of derived radar products. The proposed framework provides a practical and extensible approach for managing RFI interference in operational weather radar systems.

493035.title: Cloudflow: A Python Workflow for On-Demand High-Performance Computing in the National Ocean Service Coastal Cloud Modeling Sandbox
493035.authors: Patrick Tripp, Tetra Tech, Inc., South Kingstown, RI; and J. A. Ducker, M. Alvis, Z. Wills, T. C. Vance, M. Lalime, B. Vanderplow, M. J. Wengren, K. Powell, and K. Knee
493035.abstract: On-demand high-performance computing is increasingly important for coastal modeling, yet cloud-based execution continues to present challenges for workflow portability, reproducibility, and systematic evaluation across multiple compute configurations.
