We present Cloudflow, a Python-based workflow package for the Integrated Ocean Observing System’s (IOOS) National Ocean Service (NOS) Coastal Cloud Modeling Sandbox. The underlying IOOS Cloud Sandbox project began in 2019 and was expanded to NOS in 2023 as the NOS Coastal Cloud Modeling Sandbox. Since then, it has matured into a framework for executing and evaluating a range of ocean and coastal applications. Cloudflow workflows are implemented in Python using Prefect and related scripts, while cloud-specific implementation details are abstracted from the user-facing workflow, enabling users to interact with a consistent Python-based interface rather than provider-specific infrastructure. A distinguishing feature of Cloudflow is that it does not rely on a traditional cluster job scheduler such as Slurm. Instead, it integrates existing model submit and run scripts within a Python-based workflow, allowing jobs to be launched directly on selected virtual machine types and node counts. This design requires model-specific integration, but it provides flexibility for exploring instance families, memory, and core counts in cloud environments, thereby supporting scalability and resource-efficient execution across a broad range of configurations. Cloudflow also supports non-model workflows, including parallel Dask-based workflows across multiple nodes for pre-processing and post-processing of data. The workflow was intentionally designed for cloud extensibility. The current implementation includes an Amazon Web Services (AWS) AWSCluster class and classes for AWS-specific storage services such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) and Amazon FSx for Lustre (FSx). The object-oriented design is intended to support additional cloud providers, including Google Cloud Platform (GCP), by substituting provider-specific cluster and storage implementations while leaving end-user workflows unchanged. The Sandbox has supported a broad set of applications, including the National Ocean Service Operational Forecast System (NOSOFS) suite of Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) and Finite Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM) models, ADCIRC-based Coastal Ocean Reanalysis (CORA), LiveOcean, the East Coast Community Ocean Forecast System (ECCOFS), the Northeast Coastal Ocean Forecast System (NECOFS), the Southeast Coastal Ocean Forecast System (SECOFS), the Office of Water Prediction’s National Water Model (OWP NWM), Semi-implicit Cross-scale Hydroscience Integrated System Model (SCHISM), and the Unified Forecast System (UFS) Coastal Application. One notable use case was the CORA effort, in which the Sandbox enabled completion of a 400-day Pacific-domain run in 36 hours after limitations were encountered on the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Gaea high-performance computer. This result demonstrates the Sandbox’s ability to support demanding coastal modeling workloads, ensuring timely and accurate data is delivered to decision makers. Cloudflow is now being extended to GCP, consistent with NOAA’s broader migration of operational forecasting to GCP and the need to support research-to-operations and operations-to-research workflows. More broadly, Cloudflow illustrates a Python-centered approach to on-demand high-performance computing in atmospheric and ocean sciences that supports flexible execution, reproducible experimentation, and portable cloud-based coastal modeling across providers.

493038.title: Evacuation Lessons Analyzed from Hurricane Ian 2022
493038.authors: Joel William Cline, DOC / National Institute of Standards and Technology, Vienna, VA
493038.abstract: Hurricane Ian's catastrophic landfall in Southwest Florida on September 28, 2022, as a Category 4 hurricane, resulted in 161 fatalities. Ian was the deadliest hurricane in Florida since 1935 and exposed critical vulnerabilities at the intersection of meteorological forecasting, risk communication, and evacuation decision-making. Under the authority of the National Windstorm Impact Reduction Program (NWIRP), NIST launched a research study to evaluate the various impacts of Hurricane Ian and produce recommendations. This volume will focus on the evacuation process during Hurricane Ian as a case study, alongside a comparative analysis of seven major and distinct U.S. hurricanes (Charley 2004, Katrina 2005, Sandy 2012, Harvey 2017, Irma 2017, Michael 2018, and Milton 2024) to identify systemic patterns in evacuation performance. Ian exhibited rapid intensification and a late-stage southward track shift compressing the evacuation window for Lee County. Nearly 40% of the residents surveyed in the hardest hit areas sheltered in place. This is likely a result of the late track shift and anchoring in decision-making. Analysis of the evacuation efforts of Hurricane Ian, along with comparative studies of seven other hurricane evacuations were performed. The study examines forecast uncertainty, public risk perception, infrastructure and logistical constraints. The results indicate that under the "just-in-time" evacuation strategy, and public anchoring on the deterministic forecast track cone, consistently undermined perceived risk. Poor risk perception manifests itself in a lack of evacuation. Forecast lead times were analyzed along with a persistent tradeoff between under- and over-evacuation as part of this study. The findings support moving toward impact-based, probabilistic hazard communication, which needs to be anchored in storm surge and inland flood risk rather than the forecast cone track centerline. The work could lead to recommendations for federal, state, and local agencies, along with public/private partnerships, to strengthen evacuation strategies and standards to reduce preventable loss of life in future tropical cyclones.

493039.title: Deep Learning Probabilistic Precipitation Forecast Postprocessing to Improve HEFS and Enhance FIRO
493039.authors: Alex Chen, Center For Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E), La Jolla, CA; and T. Dixon, K. Haleakala, S. Yu, L. Delle Monache, A. Sengupta, and B. Whitin
493039.abstract: The Hydrologic Ensemble Forecast System (HEFS) is the U.S. National Weather Service’s operational river forecasting framework, providing probabilistic short-term flood and long-term water supply hydrologic forecasts. The primary engine of HEFS is the Meteorological Ensemble Forecast Processor (MEFP), which generates post-processed ensemble forecasts of precipitation and temperature that serve as inputs to HEFS. However, operational experience has shown that MEFP tends to exhibit low bias and inadequate spread, with forecast skill declining beyond 2-3 days of lead time, particularly during impactful precipitation events. To address these limitations, we developed the Deep Learning Ensemble Prediction (DLEP), a flexible and operationally focused framework designed for seamless integration into existing River Forecast Center (RFC) forecasting workflows through compatibility with MEFP inputs and outputs. DLEP was evaluated for postprocessing six-hourly accumulated, basin-scale precipitation forecasts from Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) reforecasts, during the wet seasons of 2000–2019 across 495 basins within the California-Nevada River Forecast Center (CNRFC) domain. Compared to MEFP hindcasts that reflect the operational configuration as the baseline, DLEP improves probabilistic precipitation forecast skill by 10-30% across basins and lead times ranging from 1-16 days, with comparable improvements for events exceeding the 95th percentile. The greatest improvements in overall skill occur at lead times of 3-7 days, a forecast window that is particularly valuable for Forecast-Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO). Case studies of significant flood events in the FIRO watersheds in California further demonstrate that DLEP better represents ensemble spread during extreme precipitation events and produces forecasts that more closely resemble the operational quantitative precipitation forecasts (QPFs) issued by CNRFC (that are informed by higher-resolution inputs than the GEFS). Overall, the improved precipitation forecasts from DLEP can complement MEFP to enhance HEFS with more reliable and skillful river forecasts during critical FIRO lead times, providing reservoir managers with additional time to make informed decisions. Ongoing work focuses on implementing DLEP within the existing RFC modeling framework in near real-time to support probabilistic forecasting at CNRFC, demonstrating how research-to-operations collaboration can translate advances in hydrometeorological prediction into operational decision support.

493040.title: Cloud-Native Access to NOAA's VIIRS Global Area Coverage Dataset
493040.authors: Philip Casey, North Carolina Institute for Climate Studies, Asheville, NC; and K. R. Knapp and D. Rao
493040.abstract: Satellite climate data records require not only compatible observations, but accessible archives. The VIIRS Global Area Coverage (VGAC) dataset bridges the legacy AVHRR Global Area Coverage record with the modern VIIRS instrument across multiple JPSS satellites by reformatting VIIRS data into single-orbit files. This format is compatible with existing AVHRR climate data records while adding VIIRS's enhanced radiometric accuracy and stability. The dataset maintains AVHRR's 4 km global coverage and temporal sampling characteristics, allowing integration with established climate time series spanning from 1981 to present. With the VGAC data publicly available on AWS through the NOAA Open Data Dissemination Program (NODD), we address how modern, cloud-native tools can improve access to satellite data. We use VirtualiZarr and Icechunk to create and store virtual chunk references without duplicating any legacy netCDF files. By indexing at the chunk level, users can read only the variables and regions needed for analysis, drastically reducing data loading times compared with downloading and opening entire orbit files. This provides an analysis-ready cloud dataset suited for climate research and ML/AI workflows. Practical lessons from building and maintaining this system within an operational satellite processing pipeline are also discussed. This work demonstrates a reproducible pattern for making large legacy-format climate data more accessible and usable for research, with direct relevance to the broader community of satellite climate data record producers and users.

493042.title: Diagnostic Comparison of CONUS404 and AORC Precipitation for Development of SST Storm Catalogs
493042.authors: Gregory Karlovits, Dewberry, Fairfax, VA; and A. H. Dietrich, S. Janke, and C. Williams
493042.abstract: Stochastic storm transposition (SST) is a nonparametric simulation framework used to estimate the frequency and magnitude of extreme precipitation events beyond the limits of at-site observations. Instead of relying on fitted statistical distributions, SST uses a space-for-time substitution approach in which storms observed across a meteorologically homogeneous region much larger than a study watershed are considered plausible events within the watershed. By using a larger regional sample of historical storms, SST increases the effective record length available for estimating the probability of rare precipitation events and supports precipitation-frequency analyses at return periods that exceed the period of record for available observations. SST requires long-term, high-resolution precipitation datasets to identify, characterize, and rank storm events. Storms are extracted from a transposition domain and evaluated according to the precipitation they could produce if relocated to the study area. The most severe storms are retained in a catalog that preserves realistic storm structure, spatial organization, and temporal evolution. During simulation, storms are repeatedly resampled and transposed within the domain, and their impacts are evaluated through a Monte Carlo framework. SST has been widely applied to estimate extreme precipitation and flood risk, particularly when coupled with hydrologic models to develop precipitation-frequency and flow-frequency relationships across watersheds. The Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC; Fall et al., 2023) Version 1.1 dataset (1 km, hourly, 1979 to present) has been successfully applied in SST studies, including the development of watershed-scale flow-frequency relationships through coupling with hydrologic models. However, operational use of AORC has revealed challenges such as spatial discontinuities, data gaps, resolution and assimilation artifacts, and temporal inconsistencies. While these issues have generally not limited the utility of AORC in probabilistic analyses, they can affect the representation of individual storms, particularly for large magnitude events and precipitation in complex terrain. The CONUS404 dataset (Rasmussen et al., 2023; 4 km, hourly, 1979 to 2024) is derived from atmospheric reanalysis and modeling and may alleviate several of the data-quality issues observed in AORC. This study evaluates the suitability of CONUS404 for SST applications by comparing storm catalogs developed from both datasets for a common transposition domain. Results highlight differences in storm representation, catalog composition, seasonality, and storm spatial distribution, as well as their implications for precipitation-frequency estimates. The findings provide insight into the strengths and limitations of each dataset and inform dataset selection for future SST-based hazard assessments.

493046.title: Training New York State’s Emergency Managers: The State Weather Risk Communication Center’s Introduction to Weather Interpretation Course
493046.authors: Michael S. Michaud, University at Albany, SUNY, Albany, NY; and N. P. Bassill
493046.abstract: Emergency Managers rely heavily on weather information to make decisions on how to prepare and respond for their communities. However, weather training varies among emergency managers, from some with no formal weather education or training, to those with degrees in meteorology or other earth sciences. To help fill this education gap, the New York State Weather Risk Communication Center developed a course to provide foundational knowledge about what leads to different kinds of weather, how it is measured and observed, basic forecasting techniques, publicly available tools and how to use them, common impacts, and how to best communicate weather information to various audiences. Participants who complete the course receive a credential from the University at Albany. This presentation will share the pedagogy behind the course, course objectives, course content, and outcomes after five course offerings.

493047.title: Dynamic Meteorology-Aware Emissions to Improve UFS Air Quality Model Predictions
493047.authors: Patrick C. Campbell, George Mason University, College Park, MD
493047.abstract: Background/Objectives: Emissions representation remains a key limitation in air quality forecasting, as current approaches rely on static, offline inventories with limited sensitivity to meteorological variability. This mismatch introduces structural inconsistencies that degrade forecast skill, particularly for short-term air quality and high-impact events. Under the NOAA Joint Technology Transfer Initiative (JTTI), we are advancing the research-to-operations transition of the Meteorology-aware Emissions (MetEmis) dynamic coupler to address this gap. MetEmis enables online, meteorology-aware emissions that evolve consistently with modeled atmospheric conditions within the UFS. Methods: MetEmis onroad mobile emissions have been integrated into the NOAA Emission and Exchange Unified System (NEXUS) for the Unified Forecast System-Air Quality Model (UFS-AQM). Implemented as an online extension within Harvard’s Harmonized Emissions Component (HEMCO), MetEmis applies meteorology-dependent adjustments using ambient temperature and relative humidity, improving spatiotemporal emissions variability relative to static inventories. Ongoing development expands MetEmis to additional meteorology-sensitive and operationally relevant sectors, including agricultural livestock emissions, residential wood combustion, and fugitive dust. Results: Preliminary results indicate improved boundary layer ozone predictions, particularly reduced summertime daytime overestimates in humid regions. Additional MetEmis sectors show substantial impacts on fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅) predictions, with reduced overpredictions during both winter and summertime in some U.S. regions. Conclusions: MetEmis advances fully coupled meteorology–chemistry modeling in the UFS and provides a scalable pathway for improving operational air quality forecasting for the UFS-AQM and the next-generation atmospheric composition systems at NOAA. Keywords: MetEmis, UFS-AQM, Air Quality Forecasting, Meteorology-aware Emissions, Atmospheric Composition

493048.title: The SupraThermal Ion Sensor (STIS) Onboard the Space Weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1 (SOLAR-1) Spacecraft: Data Calibration and Validation Progress
493048.authors: Athanasios Boudouridis, University of Colorado at Boulder, BOULDER, CO; and J. V. Rodriguez, X. Wei, B. Kress, D. Larson, R. Jolitz, A. Rahmati, P. Dunn, N. Miles, L. A. Rachmeler, and D. Vassiliadis
493048.abstract: The Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1 (SOLAR-1) spacecraft is the newest space weather satellite of the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). It was launched on September 24, 2025, and it is currently stationed in a stable orbit around the Sun-Earth Lagrange 1 (L1) point. It became operational in June of 2026. It is designed to deliver real-time observations of the solar corona to help improve forecasts of solar events that can impact Earth. These include coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and other plasma structures emanating from the solar atmosphere, as well as the geomagnetic storms resulting from the interaction of CMEs with the Earth’s magnetosphere. The storms may induce numerous space weather effects, including power grid outages, satellite communication disruptions, and radiation harmful to humans in space. One of the instruments onboard SOLAR-1 is the SupraThermal Ion Sensor (STIS). STIS has two telescopes, one for electrons and one for ions, both equipped with solid state detectors that measure electrons in the range 25-300 keV, and ions in the range 25-6000 keV. Both telescopes have an 80° x 60° Field-of-View (FOV) pointing at 50° from the Sun direction, on the ecliptic and along the Parker spiral. The main purpose of STIS is to measure gradual Energetic Ion Enhancements (EIEs) that result from solar wind plasma acceleration by an interplanetary shock as it propagates out from the Sun. The Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) monitors the flux enhancements at 47-68 keV in order to provide an advance warning of an incoming geomagnetic storm (several hours to a day), as opposed to the actual detection of the shock at L1 in the magnetic field and plasma, which gives only 10s of minutes of advanced warning. The STIS data products consist of differential particle fluxes with 2-s cadence plus 1-min averages provided by NOAA’s National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI) and used for space weather alerts by SWPC. In this presentation we discuss the calibration/validation steps taken to ensure accurate and reliable STIS products for operational and scientific use.

493051.title: Experimental Measurements of Lagrangian Statistics and Scalar Transport in Unsteady Urban Street Canyon Flows
493051.authors: Christopher Bianco, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA; and N. Wei
493051.abstract: The Urban Boundary Layer (UBL), where the lowest part of the atmosphere interacts with urban structures, is home to a complex canopy layer characterized by buildings and the street canyons between them. Strong surface heterogeneity and flow unsteadiness vary simultaneously, which can be difficult to represent and measure. Thus, fluid flows in this layer remain poorly understood despite their wide-ranging effects. They drive local weather patterns, which impacts everything from contamination of air and water due to scalar transport to the effects of storms and wildfires. Even in a statistically stationary boundary layer, large-scale coherent structures still cause low-level street canyons flows to remain highly unsteady. Furthermore, accurate parametrizations of UBL flows and processes are crucial for accurate meso- to micro-scale atmospheric modeling. Currently, most models use Monin-Obukhov similarity theory to represent these effects, However, this approach treats buildings as frictional elements which quickly breaks down within the urban canopy layer. These flows are also highly three-dimensional and vary strongly in both space and time. In order to fully capture this wide range of flow physics, we pursue a Lagrangian approach to flow measurement. This method is inherently 3D and provides high temporal resolution. Additionally, it directly captures particle transport effects. We present data from laboratory experiments in recirculating free-surface water channel flow over idealized urban environments. Street canyons with aspect ratios ranging from 1 to 2 and building height Reynolds numbers from 50,000 to 100,000 were examined. Flow measurements were conducted by tracking neutrally-buoyant tracer particles with four cameras to obtain 3D Lagrangian particle tracks. An active grid upstream of the urban models produced unsteady pulsatile inflow, mimicking large scale gusts passing over street canyons. The effects of unsteady inflow on turbulent mixing of scalars within street canyons and exchanges with the canopy layer were analyzed. Turbulent statistics and Lagrangian correlations were computed. Impacts on scalar and momentum transport are also discussed. This work provides key insights into non-equilibrium urban atmospheric flows, which informs parametrizations of urban areas in mesoscale weather and climate models and helps us to understand the influence of complex urban topography and coherent flow structures on 3D scalar transport.

493053.title: Investigating Drivers of the Unexpected Rapid Weakening of Hurricane Lee (2023)
493053.authors: Alexander James DesRosiers, National Research Council, Monterey, CA; NRL, Monterey, CA; and P. Finocchio and D. P. Stern
493053.abstract: Extreme tropical cyclones (intensity ≥ 113 kt) frequently undergo rapid intensity changes throughout their life cycle, including rapid intensification (RI) and rapid weakening (RW), which present major forecasting challenges. While there have been significant advances in our understanding of environmental and internal factors related to RI, research into RW mechanisms has received less attention. Hurricane Lee (2023) serves as a recent example of this forecasting challenge, having undergone a sudden and poorly predicted RW event over the open waters of the tropical Atlantic shortly after its historic rate of RI to a Category 5 storm. Understanding the physical mechanisms responsible for such unexpected weakening is critical for improving predictions of TC intensity and reducing the associated large forecast errors. To isolate the potential mechanisms responsible for this unexpected RW event, we use Cloud Model 1 (CM1) to generate an idealized numerical model simulation that recreates the basic intensity evolution of Hurricane Lee. Rather than relying on generic profiles of environmental background flow, we nudge the simulation with more realistic conditions derived from ERA5 reanalysis data specific to the kinematic environment surrounding Hurricane Lee during its large intensity fluctuations. Tail Doppler radar (TDR) analyses from NOAA hurricane hunter reconnaissance aircraft during the RW of Hurricane Lee document a degradation of the tangential wind field in the upper-troposphere without significant changes to the low- to mid-level vortex tilt. Comparisons between the structural evolution of the model TC and TDR composites from NOAA hurricane hunter reconnaissance aircraft during RW help to anchor the simulation to the observed evolution of the storm. Analysis of the simulation is focused on understanding and characterizing the evolution of the TC vortex and warm core in the upper levels of the troposphere during RW.

493054.title: A General Capability for Strongly Coupled Data Assimilation in DART
493054.authors: Kevin Raeder, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and B. Raczka, J. Anderson, H. Kershaw, M. Smith, and M. Gharamti
493054.abstract: The Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) currently provides ensemble data assimilation (DA) capabilities for many Earth system models. This includes sea ice models, atmospheric and oceanic chemistry models, more than a half dozen each of land and ocean models, and more than a dozen atmospheric models. DART also provides capabilities to assimilate a wide range of observation types for the Earth system. Developing DART interfaces to models is a straightforward process that does not require modifications to the model code. While the DART infrastructure has supported weakly coupled data assimilation with multiple component models for years, it has not included a mechanism for strongly coupled assimilation. Both types use the same model coupling, but, in this context, strongly-coupled means that observations of a component are assimilated into other component(s). This talk describes new DART infrastructure that supports a general strongly coupled assimilation capability. This allows DART users to do strongly-coupled assimilation with any set of models and observations that have existing DART interfaces. No modification to existing code is required. The key scientific challenge to strongly-coupled assimilation is localization. The DART implementation supports localization of observations from one component onto state from another component. General localization algorithms are supported and do not require modifying any existing code. This work highlights the interactions between algorithms and software implementations that lead to powerful and efficient coupled DA. Results are shown for strongly coupled DA with the Community Atmosphere Model (CAM) and Community Land Model (CLM) components of NCAR’s Community Earth System Model (CESM).

493055.title: A WRF-FastEddy Multiscale Modeling Demonstration of Urban Heat Variability in Augusta, Georgia
493055.authors: Bradford D Johnson, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and J. Sauer, M. D. Williams, and J. M. Shepherd
493055.abstract: Fine-scale meteorological variability in built environments can influence heat exposure, infrastructure resilience, and conservation and resilience planning. However, traditional mesoscale modeling systems often cannot explicitly represent the neighborhood-scale flow and thermal structures produced by heterogeneous land cover, urban morphology, and boundary-layer turbulence. As part of an exploratory SERDP effort to establish a multiscale atmospheric modeling framework for Department of Defense built-environment applications, this study demonstrates a prototype workflow using WRF-ARW to force the GPU-accelerated FastEddy®large-eddy simulation model for urban heat cases in the Augusta, Georgia region. The demonstration is motivated by observed warm-season temperature differences between Daniel Field and Augusta Regional Airport and the possibility that these differences are influenced by wind-direction-dependent advection of the Augusta urban heat island. Candidate events were selected from anomalous maximum temperature days and inter-site temperature differences, with additional consideration of afternoon wind speed and direction during the period of maximum heating. Selected cases include 13, 17, and 22 June 2022, representing different low-level wind regimes. WRF simulations provided mesoscale atmospheric context and initial and boundary condition information for a 50 km × 50 km FastEddy domain. The workflow included WRF preprocessing, generation of FastEddy initial and boundary conditions, FastEddy integration over afternoon through early evening focus periods, and extraction of tower-based time series for comparison with available observations. Although this effort is not intended as a comprehensive validation exercise, model output was compared with 5-minute ASOS/METAR observations at KDNL and KAGS to assess whether the demonstration reproduced major features of the observed near-surface evolution. The comparison focused on air temperature, wind speed, and wind direction, with METAR-derived. Preliminary results indicate that the WRF–FastEddy simulations captured several observed temporal trends and abrupt meteorological changes during the selected afternoon periods. While both models, exhibited a general warm bias, particularly at KAGS, complicating interpretation of inter-site urban heat island contrasts, the LES does tend to show more distinction between stations relative to the mesoscale results. Wind speed comparisons were generally reasonable with the LES demonstrating improved agreement with observations and the ability to capture distinct wind characteristics at the disparate stations. Additional WRF sensitivity testing suggests that urban and planetary boundary layer physics materially affect the thermal structure passed to FastEddy. In particular, a BouLac PBL/BEM urban configuration produced a more pronounced urban thermal signal than a YSU-based configuration, including approximately 5°C differences in urban skin temperature. These results demonstrate the feasibility of applying WRF–FastEddy downscaling to built-environment heat applications while highlighting key considerations for future work, including urban/PBL physics selection, diagnosis of systematic thermal biases, and wind-regime-dependent interpretation of urban heat advection.

493058.title: Graph-Based Spatiotemporal Learning for Probabilistic Coastal Water Level Simulation and Updating
493058.authors: Soheil Radfar, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and N. Lin and M. Rahnemoonfar
493058.abstract: Coastal water-level hazard analysis increasingly requires simulations spanning long historical periods, large ensembles, and multiple climate-forcing datasets. Physics-based hydrodynamic models provide the necessary representation of coastal response but become computationally expensive when repeatedly applied across these large forcing ensembles. We investigate whether a learned regional representation can reproduce coastal water-level dynamics while remaining transferable across distinct atmospheric forcing products. A deep spatiotemporal model is trained using ADCIRC simulations along the U.S. Mid-Atlantic and Northeast coasts and represents regional wind and pressure evolution, coastal-location characteristics, temporal dependence, and interactions among gauges. Rather than directly predicting total water level, the model estimates the meteorologically driven component and combines it with astronomical tide, allowing atmospheric and tidal contributions to remain physically distinguishable. Evaluation using reanalysis-driven simulations and multiple historical and future climate-model forcings shows that the learned representation reproduces the spatial and temporal structure of modeled coastal water levels while reducing the computational burden of large-ensemble simulation. Comparison against NOAA observations further reveals an important limitation: agreement with a hydrodynamic training target does not guarantee agreement with the realized coastal state because discrepancies in the parent model are inherited by the surrogate. We therefore examine whether information retained within the learned regional representation can support observation-based updating. The results suggest that learned coastal-response representations can serve two complementary roles: accelerating ensemble hazard simulation and providing a compact state description for incorporating observations into regional coastal water-level prediction.

493061.title: Extreme Precipitation Associated with Quasi-Linear Convective Systems over the Central and Eastern Conterminous United States under Intermediate and Pessimistic Climate Change Scenarios
493061.authors: Nathan Daniel Sonntag, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL; and A. Haberlie, W. S. Ashley, V. A. Gensini, A. C. Michaelis, and M. Van Den Broeke
493061.abstract: Quasi-linear convective systems (QLCSs) have pronounced impacts on the hydroclimate of the conterminous United States east of the Rocky Mountains (ECONUS) and contribute to hydrological hazards such as flash flooding, which cause immense economic losses and can pose a substantial threat to life. Furthermore, anthropogenic climate change may influence these systems in various ways, including regional reduction or intensification of short-duration, high-intensity precipitation, potentially increasing the societal impacts of these events. However, few studies have examined potential future ECONUS spatiotemporal changes to hourly extreme precipitation (EP) produced by QLCSs. This study analyzes changes in hourly EP produced by QLCSs over the ECONUS, using convection-permitting, dynamically downscaled regional climate model output for three 15-year epochs. These epochs include a historical baseline (HIST; 1990–2005) and two end-of-21st-century periods (END; 2085–2100) under either an intermediate (END4.5) or pessimistic (END8.5) representative concentration pathway (RCP). An updated segmentation, tracking, and identification machine learning method identifies QLCS events across epochs, which are spatiotemporally compared to hourly EP occurrences. Results suggest that overall mesoscale convective system-associated EPs (MEPs) will become more frequent east of the Mississippi River under both future climate scenarios, with the largest increases in spring and fall. Decreases in MEP days are projected over the summer, primarily in the Great Plains. Regional analysis highlights the Northeast as most likely to be affected by changes in MEPs, with significant increases across all four seasons. Largely driven by increases in MEPs, EP frequency is also projected to increase in future climates east of the Mississippi River. Overall, this research provides insight for forecasters, stakeholders, and the public into how these events may change and, moreover, inform resilient measures to mitigate and adapt to precipitation-based hazards.

493062.title: Area-Weighted and Physics-Based Gaussian Oversampling of TROPOMI NO2 for Analysis of Village-Level Air Pollution Disparities Across India
493062.authors: Alexander Michael Cherny, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and X. Jin
493062.abstract: India’s existing air quality monitoring network provides limited spatial coverage relative to the country’s vast geographic extent and large rural population. Satellite remote sensing from the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI) helps address this gap by providing near-daily observations of tropospheric nitrogen dioxide (NO2) across nearly the entire country. However, TROPOMI observations are provided as satellite pixels that do not align with the administrative and statistical boundaries commonly used to organize census, demographic, and socioeconomic data. Effective exposure analysis therefore requires methods for converting pixel-based TROPOMI NO2 observations into village-level estimates. Building on a framework originally developed to oversample satellite NO2 observations over U.S. neighborhoods, we compare two oversampling approaches—area-weighted oversampling (AWO) and physics-based Gaussian oversampling (PGO)—for more than 600,000 villages across India. AWO assigns satellite observations to villages according to the area of spatial overlap, whereas PGO represents each satellite observation as a continuous spatial sensitivity distribution, assigning greater weight to villages closer to the center of the satellite field of view. We aim to determine which method more effectively represents village-level NO2 column densities, spatial gradients, and data availability in India, where village geometries and cloud patterns differ substantially from the U.S. context in which the approach was originally developed. Using both AWO and PGO, we have developed village-level NO2 column density datasets covering all of India. Although the two approaches produce broadly similar large-scale spatial patterns, PGO shows a systematic low bias relative to AWO in regions with higher NO2 column densities. These datasets are being integrated with demographic and socioeconomic information to investigate potential disparities in air pollution exposure across India. Specifically, we will examine differences in NO2 between urban and rural communities, assess whether particular socioeconomic groups are more likely to reside in areas with elevated NO2, and determine whether communities near major industrial and mining corridors experience disproportionately high NO2 exposure. Ultimately, this work aims to establish a framework for using satellite remote sensing to characterize highly localized air pollution patterns and identify populations that may experience disproportionately high NO2 burdens.

493063.title: Resolving Convective Dynamics with High Spatiotemporal Resolution Adaptive Radar Observations
493063.authors: Edward Luke, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY; and N. Allwayin, M. Oue, J. Yan, O. Omitusa, B. Dolan, S. W. Freeman, P. N. Gatlin, and P. Kollias
493063.abstract: Rapid changes in convective updrafts, downdrafts, and turbulence occur on spatial and temporal scales that are often poorly resolved by conventional weather radar scanning strategies. Over the past five years, the Multi-sensor Agile Adaptive Sampling (MAAS) framework has been developed to coordinate radar, satellite, and surface observations and automatically guide radar measurements toward rapidly evolving atmospheric phenomena. MAAS was first demonstrated during the TRACER and ESCAPE field campaigns in Houston, Texas, and since 2025 has supported operations of the Huntsville Integrated Radar Testbed (IRT), a hybrid network of reflector-based and phased-array radar systems. This presentation will summarize what we have learned from high spatiotemporal resolution range–height indicator (RHI) observations of convective cores collected during these field campaigns. Adaptive RHI observations resolve the evolution of convective updrafts, downdrafts, turbulence, and coherent dynamical structures at spatial and temporal resolutions that are difficult to achieve with conventional volume scans. These observations provide new insight into the relationships among convective intensity, turbulence, storm evolution, and environmental conditions such as convective available potential energy (CAPE) and vertical wind shear. The presentation will also discuss future opportunities for adaptive radar observations, given continued operation of the Huntsville Integrated Radar Testbed in 2027. Together with emerging multistatic and phased-array radar capabilities, this will enable increasingly comprehensive observations of convective dynamics and turbulence, providing new datasets for understanding storm evolution and evaluating next-generation cloud-resolving numerical models.

493064.title: Full Day/Night High Spatial Resolution Cloud Mask as part of the NASA Continuity MODIS/VIIRS Products
493064.authors: Paolo Veglio, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and R. Holz, K. Meyer, S. Platnick, A. Heidinger, and E. Zhan
493064.abstract: With the launch of the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) in 2011 the NASA Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Cloud Mask needed an update to account for the different spectral characteristics of the new sensor. For this reason, the NASA Continuity MODIS/VIIRS Cloud Mask (MVCM) was developed, which allows to produce a consistent record of cloud coverage leveraging only the spectral bands common to both the MODIS and VIIRS instruments. The algorithm uses a series of spectral tests in a fuzzy logic approach, each with assigned low and high confidence thresholds. Specific sets of tests are run on a given pixel based on surface type such as land, water, coast, desert, snow or ice, and solar illumination, i.e., day or night. Each individual test that belongs to the sets describing the current scene returns a clear sky confidence value and eventually gets combined with all the other test outcomes to create the overall clear sky confidence as reported in the final output. For this work we modified the existing MVCM to ingest both VIIRS M-bands (750m spatial resolution) and I-bands (375m spatial resolution) and created a new set of tests, while maintaining those from the original algorithm that were still relevant for the I-bands. We then fine-tuned the old thresholds and defined additional ones to account for the new tests. As opposed to MODIS, that has high-resolution bands only in the visible, VIIRS I-bands extend from the visible (0.64µm) to the infrared window (11µm), allowing for multiple spectral tests for cloud detection to be performed during both daytime and nighttime. We will show case studies to highlight how the use of the I-bands helps detect finer cloud features focusing on challenges in working with nighttime data and the limited amount of information available to produce a retrieval. Moreover, now that the algorithm is fully operational and the data publicly available, we will also analyze L3 global statistics to determine how the high-resolution data changes the cloud detection compared to the regular MVCM. The high-resolution cloud mask is included as part of the V2 NASA VIIRS cloud mask. This will help building an unprecedented multi-decadal record across multiple platforms from early 2012 with S-NPP and well into the 2030s and beyond with NOAA-20, NOAA-21 already flying, and the future JPSS-4 and JPSS-3 currently scheduled for 2027 and 2032, respectively.

493066.title: Evaluating Regionally Trained CNNs for Radar-Based Quantitative Precipitation Estimation in the Pacific Northwest
493066.authors: Enrique Saldivar, Howard University, Washington, DC; and A. P. Osborne and O. V. Chimborazo
493066.abstract: Accurate quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) remains challenging in complex terrain, where radar coverage limitations and orographic effects can introduce substantial errors. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a type of machine learning, have shown potential to improve Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) radar derived QPE in the western United States. This study evaluates two CNN configurations over the Pacific Northwest (PNW; 45°–49°N, 125°–116°W) that use the same 29 radar, terrain, and numerical weather prediction input variables but differ in their training regions. The CA CNN29 was trained over California, while the WA CNN29 is a multi-seed ensemble trained over the PNW. Both configurations include models trained using mean absolute error (MAE) and fractional mean absolute error (FMAE) loss functions. A four-case study is conducted using three cold season atmospheric river (AR) precipitation events during 2025 and one convective event during 2026. CNN derived QPE is compared with the operational MRMS radar based QPE with evaporation correction (Q3EVAP) and independently evaluated using quality-controlled Community Collaborative Rain, Hail and Snow Network (CoCoRaHS) observations. Performance is assessed using mean bias ratio (MBR), Pearson correlation coefficient (CC), and MAE. The CA CNN29 FMAE model outperformed Q3EVAP during two AR events. During the 8–9 December 2025 AR, CA CNN29 FMAE reduced MAE from 0.391 to 0.373 in., shifted MBR from 1.131 to 0.966, and increased CC from 0.861 to 0.903. During the May 2026 convective event, CA CNN29 MAE reduced MAE from 0.105 to 0.089 in. and increased CC from 0.618 to 0.799 relative to Q3EVAP. The WA CNN29 models did not outperform Q3EVAP for the four cases examined. Permutation importance testing showed that WA CNN29 performance was more sensitive to Reflectivity at Lowest Altitude (RALA) than CA CNN29, motivating further investigation into how radar derived predictors influence regional model performance. Overall, the results highlight the influence of training region, loss function, and predictor importance on machine learning based precipitation estimation. Across these four cases, the California trained model demonstrated the potential to retain skill when applied to the complex terrain of Washington.

493068.title: Evaluating the Thermodynamic Structure of Saharan Air Layer Events Using the Galvez-Davison Index
493068.authors: Charles Henry Dolce, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA; and P. W. Miller
493068.abstract: The Saharan Air Layer (SAL) is a warm, dry, and stable air mass that carries millions of tons of dust annually, disrupting otherwise intense convection in the tropical North Atlantic Ocean. Because the SAL is a statically stable air mass, convective instability parameters can help identify the presence of a SAL event, though most convective indices are designed for forecasting mid-latitude convection, and struggle when applied to more barotropic settings. The Galvez-Davison Index (GDI) was developed to improve the skill of traditional instability metrics in tropical latitudes, accounting for thermodynamic factors that both enhance and inhibit tropical convection. This study uses a pre-established dataset of SAL events to evaluate their thermodynamic structure and evolution by leveraging the GDI as a proxy for convective instability. The GDI was calculated for 45 years of MERRA-2 reanalysis over the tropical North Atlantic. GDI characteristics near SALs were found to reflect the known intra-SAL stability patterns, though they also reveal large spatial and temporal variations. The most apparent pattern discovered was that intra-SAL GDI was lowest at the end of the SAL’s life cycle, which most frequently occurs in or around the Caribbean Sea. This eastward displacement of minimum GDI relative to maximum dust transport suggests that the strongest convective suppression occurs after prolonged exposure to SAL-modified air rather than at the time of highest dust concentration or transport. Specifically, the lag in GDI decline following the SAL passage can assist in evaluating total air mass modifications in the wake of a SAL.

493070.title: REFRAIN: Era-Consistent Radar Precipitation Reanalysis with Quantified Uncertainty
493070.authors: Yagmur Derin, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; and D. B. Wright and J. A. Smith
493070.abstract: Long-term radar rainfall reanalyses can characterize the climatology of extreme precipitation at the fine space and time scales that are required for hydrologic design. Given that NEXRAD archives span a quarter of century, the recent National Academies (NASEM) report “Modernizing Probable Maximum Precipitation Estimation” (2024) recommended high-resolution radar rainfall reanalysis from 2000 to present. Operational products such as the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) have continually evolving algorithms, leaves us with a mixture of hydroclimatic signals with algorithm-era changes. In this study we present REFRAIN (REanalysis FRamework for rAdar-derived precipitation with uncertainINty) an open source QPE system which implements specific attenuation R(A) rainfall with dynamic α, model-derived melting layer and VPR corrections, evaporation correction and advection-corrected accumulation and multi-radar mosaicking. It is designed to run as a fixed, documented algorithm over the entire NEXRAD archive, producing hourly, kilometer scale precipitation fields. The single to dual polarization transition is handled by two fixed branches of the full polarimetric chain and reflectivity only chain. Lastly, REFRAIN quantifies retrieval uncertainty using a Monte Carlo ensemble. Algorithmic uncertainty is represented by perturbation of the physically-constrained retrieval parameters. Preliminary evaluation over the state of Iowa conducted against independent hourly gauges for both REFRAIN and MRMS Radar only data across warm and cool season convective regimes. Results show that seven radar REFRAIN mosaic has lower multiplicative bias compared to MRMS across regimes. For example, REFRAIN bias, correlation and mean absolute error are reported as 1.48, 0.66 and 2.18 mm while MRMS Radar only reported as 1.49, 0.57 and 2.62mm. This study aims to provide a path to a multi-decade, uncertainty quantified radar precipitation reanalysis product.

493071.title: An Extreme Precipitation Event Database for the Contiguous U.S.
493071.authors: Daniel Christopher Watters, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and P. Kirstetter, A. J. Newman, A. W. Wood, and G. Tang
493071.abstract: No database currently exists which quantifies extreme precipitation events across the Contiguous U.S. (CONUS), limiting our ability to understand the causes and underlying processes of these natural hazards. To address this gap, we produce a CONUS extreme precipitation event database derived from the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system. MRMS enables this database production by providing a suite of hydrometeorological products (e.g., precipitation rate, type, phase, and various other parameters) from 2014 to present, produced from the fusion of CONUS ground-based dual-polarization radars, rain gauges and atmospheric model analyses. The high spatiotemporal resolution of MRMS (0.01° x 0.01°, 2-minute), combined with its stability and uniformity as an observational system, make it an ideal product for tracking the high variability of extreme precipitation events and bridging in-depth and consistent hydrometeorological process characterization from sub-hourly to daily timescales. The novelty of this database lies in the automated detection of extreme precipitation events at the daily timescale and subsequent diagnosis of these daily events at the 2-minute timescale. In this analysis, we utilize the MRMS-based CONUS extreme event database to evaluate key hydrometeorological quantities (e.g., time of maximum precipitation, maximum 2-minute, hourly and daily precipitation intensity, event accumulation, convective accumulation fraction) and uncertainties across precipitation hazards from 2014 to present. This innovative application of the database is potentially one of many, with it originally produced to support the verification of a novel multi-decadal probabilistic 2-km surface precipitation product for CONUS. Other potential database applications include emergency management, model evaluation, precipitation process studies, and ground validation of spaceborne precipitation observations.

493072.title: Nonlocal Deep Learning Parameterization for Climate Model Representation of Gravity Waves: Towards a Hybrid CAM7 Atmospheric Model
493072.authors: Aman Gupta, Stanford University, Stanford, CA; and A. Sheshadri, J. Bacmeister, T. Meltzer, and L. Rousseau
493072.abstract: Gravity waves (GWs) make crucial contributions to the middle atmospheric circulation.Yet, their representation in climate models remains inaccurate, leading to key circulation biases. In this work, we develop high-fidelity deep learning schemes, trained on high-resolution CAM7 simulation output, to more physically represent atmospheric gravity waves in a coarse-resolution CAM7 atmospheric model. We develop two neural networks(NNs) that learn to predict GW fluxes from multiple years of high-resolution CAM7 output, which resolves the mesoscale spectrum of gravity waves. The two NNs—a 1x1 ANN and a periodicity-enforced Attention UNet—embed different levels of horizontal nonlocality in their architecture and are capable of representing nonlocal GW effects that are missing from current operational GW parameterizations. The NNs are first evaluated offline on time-averaged statistics and time-evolving flux variability. The Attention UNet accurately reproduces the global gravity wave flux distribution in both the troposphere and the stratosphere and predicts the transient evolution of GWFs over prominent orographic and nonorographic hotspots. In a first effort of its kind, we develop a framework to couple the nonlocal UNet to a spectral-element-based CAM7 dynamical core to assess its online performance, thus creating a hybrid version of the CAM7 atmospheric model. This framework can be generalized to nonlocal emulators of other subgrid processes. Upon successful coupling, the online performance of the schemes is evaluated using the resulting stratospheric variability and sudden warming frequency. This work represents an advance in creating the next generation of hybrid climate models with coupled high-fidelity nonlocal NNs to represent subgrid atmospheric variability.

493074.title: An Update on the Hemispheric Airborne Measurements of Air Quality (HAMAQ) Field Study
493074.authors: James Crawford, NASA LaRC, Hampton, VA; and L. Judd, B. C. McDonald, and M. Kleb
493074.abstract: Under NASA’s Earth Venture Suborbital program, Hemispheric Airborne Measurements of Air Quality (HAMAQ) will conduct a series of campaigns in 2028 under the Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) geostationary satellite instrument. HAMAQ plans include two deployments, including the Mexico City megalopolis and Metro Atlanta. NASA’s B777 will be used for remote sensing, and NASA’s P-3B will be used for in situ sampling. These aircraft will be used to complete a system of integrated observations, combining satellite observations, ground-based monitoring and research observations with air quality modeling. HAMAQ field intensives will serve multiple objectives to include: improving the use of satellite observations in concert with traditional ground monitoring to inform air quality; assessing emissions to better understand their timing and source apportionment; advancing the development of satellite proxies for air quality; and assessing the factors controlling local air quality in each location sampled. Given the long lead time for this campaign, the HAMAQ team welcomes discussion from the community on flight strategies. HAMAQ is also planning to expand the scientific value of the study by including remote sensing observations to better understand the drivers and evolution of the planetary boundary layer.

493076.title: State-Dependent Tendency Bias Correction for NASA GEOS-S2S-3 using a U-Net-based AI approach
493076.authors: Min-Seop Ahn, NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and A. Molod, N. Arnold, and D. Barahona
493076.abstract: Systematic model biases remain a major source of error in subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction because they depend in large part on the evolving atmospheric state and cannot be adequately represented by conventional climatological bias correction methods. To address this challenge, we are developing a State-Dependent Tendency Bias Correction (SDTBC) framework for the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System Subseasonal-to-Seasonal prediction system version 3 (GEOS-S2S-3) based on a three-dimensional U-Net deep learning architecture. The SDTBC model is trained using the GiOCEAN coupled atmosphere-ocean reanalysis, which employs the same Earth system model as GEOS-S2S-3. Atmospheric state variables, including winds, temperature, specific humidity, and surface pressure, are used as predictors, while Incremental Analysis Update (IAU) analysis increments are used as training targets representing model tendency biases. The SDTBC model learns the nonlinear relationship between the background atmospheric state and analysis increments. The SDTBC model is trained using data from 1998–2019 and evaluated on data from 2020. It successfully infers the three-dimensional fields of analysis increments, with temporal correlation coefficients of approximately 0.6–0.7, substantially higher than those obtained using climatological analysis increments. The SDTBC model is being integrated into the GEOS-S2S-3 model through the existing IAU infrastructure, enabling AI-based tendency bias correction to be applied during model integration with minimal changes to the forecast system. Preliminary forecast experiments for year 2020 show that SDTBC reduces the mean biases of atmospheric state variables and mitigates forecast drift in GEOS-S2S-3. In addition, the forecasts exhibit improved prediction skill for the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) and El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), two major modes of subseasonal-to-seasonal predictability. These results demonstrate the potential of AI-based state-dependent tendency bias correction as a practical framework for improving both the mean state and predictive skill of S2S forecasting systems.

493078.title: Predict, Warn, Protect: Advancing a Unified Wildfire Warning System for US Public Safety and Resilience
493078.authors: Elizabeth Fairchild Meister, ; and D. Hogg, A. C. Wanless, M. Krocak, J. T. Ripberger, M. O. Mattox, P. S. Skinner, A. Fox, K. Gupta, and V. Dunham
493078.abstract: As wildfires continue to increase in frequency and impact, the United States still lacks a unified warning-scale alert system for fire, unlike other extreme hazards such as severe thunderstorms or tornadoes. The work showcased in this presentation integrates three core elements: improving the basic science of fire atmosphere prediction, understanding public response and organizational response to wildfire alerts, and building a unified fire warning roadmap through targeted outreach and workshops across disciplines in both research and practice. This presentation will provide an overview of the project and highlight findings from comparative case studies, detailing the importance of early and accurate fire prediction and the importance of cross-agency coordination and communication strategies that align with public and organizational decision-making. Overall, this presentation will showcase this collaborative project that advances the scientific, institutional, and behavioral foundations needed to support a unified wildfire warning system.

493080.title: Momentum Transport over Valley Terrain with Heterogeneous Canopy Cover: Wind Tunnel Experiments
493080.authors: Alec Petersen, Duke University, Durham, NC; and M. Placidi, M. Carpentieri, G. G. Katul, and T. Banerjee
493080.abstract: Atmospheric boundary-layer flow over terrain covered by a uniform canopy has received increasing research attention through experiments, theories, and simulations. The significance of such flows is not in dispute, given their relevance to a plethora of applications such as biosphere-atmosphere exchange of mass, energy, and momentum, wind energy and turbine placement, pollution spread, particle dispersion, biocontainment zones, and gene flow in forestry, among others. A less studied but more pressing issue is the effects of inhomogeneous canopy cover situated over complex terrain. It has been known for some time now that even for symmetric topography and uniform canopy cover, non-linearities in the governing equations can lead to anomalous features such as mean circulation zones within the canopy. Forest canopy edges and gaps introduced by heterogeneity lead to additional complications – especially in terms of wakes, mean advection, pressure buildup and release, and horizontal transport of energy by turbulence. To this end, experiments at the EnFlo aerodynamics wind tunnel at the University of Surrey were conducted using Particle Image Velocimetry to measure turbulence induced by varying spatial configurations of a canopy around complex terrain. To simulate a forested canopy, we used coarse aquarium sponge filter pads with 10 pores-per-inch, which provided a pressure drop similar to that of full-scale field maple (Acer campestre) in its foliated state. The flow without a canopy was compared to five canopy configurations around a central valley: 1) upstream canopy, 2) downstream canopy, 3) canopy gap in the valley, 4) canopy only within the valley, and 5) total forest cover of the whole domain. We first compare the spatial structure of the mean velocity, turbulent stress, and mechanical production of turbulent kinetic energy fields, followed by an examination of the relative strength of the various terms in the integrated horizontal mean momentum equation. We relate these observations to the drag force exerted by the various canopy and terrain configurations, both locally and in bulk over the entire imaged domain. We further investigate the spatial distribution of sweep-ejection events relative to the terrain and canopy edges. Implications to representing canopy-, local-, and bulk- drag in wall models and meso-scale atmospheric models over complex terrain covered by canopy inhomogeneities are discussed with reference to the depth- averaged and domain-averaged mean momentum balance. In the absence of a canopy, the leading order pressure perturbation appears to be in phase with the topographic undulation. The addition of a non-uniform canopy breaks the symmetry in such pressure perturbations due to wake generation, mean vertical advection, and recirculation. The strength of these ‘symmetry-breaking’ terms in the pressure is first tracked to mean advection, longitudinal variance transport, and turbulent stresses – and then to distortions in local and bulk drag models that consider geometric features of the canopy.

493081.title: Multi-Scale Cloud Influences on Air-Sea Interaction During Monsoon Onset Over the Northern Indian Ocean
493081.authors: Alex Kinsella, WHOI, Woods Hole, MA; and A. O. Gonzalez, Z. Davidson, and A. Mahadevan
493081.abstract: Clouds modify the ocean surface energy budget across a wide range of scales from individual convective cells to seasonal monsoon transitions, but quantifying their combined radiative and turbulent effects and their influence on ocean mixed-layer temperature remains challenging. The Enhancing Knowledge of the Arabian Sea Marine Environment through Science and Advanced Training (EKAMSAT) campaign provides a new observational framework for studying these processes across the 2023 Arabian Sea and 2024-2025 Bay of Bengal monsoon onsets. Using complementary in-situ and satellite-based datasets, we quantify SST-flux feedbacks, identify transitions between ocean- and atmosphere-controlled air-sea interaction regimes, and investigate the cloud processes underlying the observed surface flux variability. At seasonal timescales, an analysis of 25 years of satellite-derived radiative surface fluxes and SST reveals surface shortwave and longwave radiative feedback magnitudes over the Bay of Bengal reaching up to 25 W m-2 K-1. There is a distinct transition in longwave feedbacks across monsoon onset: a positive clear-sky longwave feedback during the pre-monsoon period transitions toward a negative cloudy-sky longwave feedback after onset. We separately assess the direction of air-sea coupling using the symmetry properties of lagged SST–flux relationships. This air-sea interaction regime analysis indicates strong oceanic control of longwave flux variability both before and after monsoon onset, with atmospheric control becoming more important during the onset transition itself. Together, these diagnostics suggest that the ocean plays an important role in establishing both the pre- and post-onset feedback regimes even as the radiative mechanisms coupling SST to surface fluxes change across monsoon onset. At hourly to daily timescales, we find that cloud processes produce large perturbations to the surface energy budget. During the monsoon onset, the daily-mean surface shortwave cloud radiative effect strengthened from roughly -10 W m-2 in pre-monsoon conditions to near -100 W m-2 post-onset, averaging -55 W m-2 across EKAMSAT Bay of Bengal deployments. Low clouds contribute about 7 W m-2 to time-mean downwelling longwave radiation but can produce instantaneous longwave perturbations approaching 60 W m-2. Cloud-generated cold pools provide an additional turbulent pathway, generating localized heat-flux perturbations comparable in magnitude to the radiative effects. A neural-network-based classification of shipboard all-sky imagery into clear, low-cloud, high-cloud, mixed, and deep-convective scenes links these cloud regimes directly to measured surface radiation and SST tendency: clear-sky scenes are associated with daytime surface warming, while deep-cloud scenes are associated with weak daytime cooling. Low, high, and mixed cloud scenes lie at intermediate values of SST tendency. We further use coincident upper-ocean temperature profiles to examine how these cloud-dependent surface flux perturbations affect mixed-layer temperature and near-surface stratification. These results show that monsoon air-sea interaction is shaped by cloud processes spanning from the individual cloud scale to the seasonal scale. Combining long-term feedback and coupling diagnostics with in-situ observations of cloud state, surface fluxes, and upper-ocean structure provides a framework for connecting short-timescale cloud variability and its ocean response to changes in the large-scale air-sea interaction regime.

493082.title: Predicting Post-Displacement Vulnerability: A National Household Survey Analysis of High-Risk Populations in the First Month After U.S. Natural Disasters
493082.authors: Tonghui Xu, University of Houston, Houston, MA; and L. Xu, S. Chavez, and O. E. Adepoju
493082.abstract: Background The first month following a natural disaster represents a critical period during which displaced households face acute and compounding challenges including disruptions to water, electricity, housing, and basic safety that can shape both immediate wellbeing and longer-term recovery trajectories. Objective The objective of this study was to develop a predictive model using national survey data to identify individuals at elevated risk of experiencing multiple challenges during the first month following disaster-related displacement. Data This study used nationally representative data from 21 waves of the U.S Household Pulse Survey (HPS), collected between December 9–19, 2022 (Week 52) and August 20–September 16, 2024 (Cycle 09). The outcome variables comprised seven survey items assessing the extent to which participants experienced the following challenges during the first month after a natural disaster: (1) food shortages, (2) loss of electricity, (3) shortages of drinking water, (4) unsanitary conditions such as inadequate toilet facilities, (5) feelings of isolation, depression, anxiety, nervousness, or being on edge, (6) fear of crime, and (7) offers that appeared to be scams. Each item was rated on a four-point scale: 1 = Not at all, 2 = A little, 3 = Some, and 4 = A lot. The covariates included sex, region, race and ethnicity, age, education, household size, presence of children in the household, metropolitan residence, military service by the participant or spouse, last annual household income, type of natural disaster experienced in the past year, and level of property damage. Methods Because the study included seven outcome items, we first conducted latent class analysis (LCA) using the poLCA package in R version 4.4.2 to classify participants into distinct outcome classes. We estimated one- through five-class solutions and compared model fit using the Akaike information criterion, Bayesian information criterion, and entropy to identify the optimal class solution. We then developed three classification models in python version 3.11: logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and Brier score. Calibration curves were generated using the test dataset. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analyses were conducted in both the training and test datasets to compare feature-importance patterns and assess their stability. Finally, multivariable logistic regression was conducted as an interpretability analysis. Results The LCA results supported the three-class solution as the optimal model (Figure 1). Participants in Class 2 had average scores ranging from approximately 3.5 to 4.0 across the seven items. Participants in Class 1 had average scores ranging from approximately 2.0 to 3.0. Participants in Class 3 had average scores ranging from approximately 1.0 to 2.5. Together, these patterns suggest three distinct profiles of disaster-related challenge severity: low, moderate, and high. Latent classes were collapsed into a binary outcome to support prediction modeling and maintain adequate group sizes. No class was free of disaster-related challenges, suggesting that displacement-related difficulties varied primarily in severity rather than presence. Therefore, Classes 1 (moderate challenge) and 2 (high challenge) were combined to form the positive class (1 = moderate or high disaster-related challenge), while Class 3 (low challenge) served as the reference category (0 = no or low challenge). A total of 12,264 participants aged 18 years or older were included in the analysis, of whom 6,201 (50.6%) were in the moderate- and high- challenges classes and 6,063 (49.4%) were in the low- and no- challenges classes during the first month of displacement. Compared with the other models, XGBoost without post-hoc calibration adjustment showed the most appropriate overall performance, with a Brier score of 0.20 and an AUC of 0.75. Precision, recall, and F1 scores ranged from 0.68 to 0.70. The null-model Brier score was 0.250. The calibration curve (Figure 2) closely followed the line of perfect calibration across most probability ranges, indicating that the predicted probabilities were generally well calibrated. The SHAP results (Figure 3) were highly consistent with the findings from the supplementary interpretability regression analysis. Compared with adults aged ≥65 years, all younger age groups had significantly higher odds of moderate-to-high challenges, with the highest odds among those aged 45–54 years (aOR = 2.20, 95% CI: 1.61–3.00). Compared with non-Hispanic White participants, higher odds were observed among Black (aOR = 1.62, 95% CI: 1.19–2.21), Asian (aOR = 1.80, 95% CI: 1.09–2.99), Other (aOR = 2.28, 95% CI: 1.54–3.39), and Hispanic participants (aOR = 1.46, 95% CI: 1.05–2.02). Higher odds were also found among participants with a high school education or less (aOR = 1.60, 95% CI: 1.19–2.16) or some college/associate degree (aOR = 1.37, 95% CI: 1.09–1.70), compared with those holding a bachelor’s degree or higher. Relative to household incomes ≥$100,000, incomes of $50,000–$99,999 (aOR = 2.16, 95% CI: 1.67–2.80) and <$50,000 (aOR = 3.66, 95% CI: 2.80–4.77) were associated with higher odds. Military service by participants or spouses was also associated with higher odds (aOR = 1.96, 95% CI: 1.05–3.63). Compared with hurricanes, floods (aOR = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.41–0.78), fires (aOR = 0.37, 95% CI: 0.26–0.52), tornadoes (aOR = 0.55, 95% CI: 0.39–0.76), and other disasters (aOR = 0.55, 95% CI: 0.42–0.72) were associated with lower odds. Greater property damage showed a dose-response pattern, with aORs of 2.24 (95% CI: 1.71–2.94) for some damage, 3.57 (95% CI: 2.63–4.84) for moderate damage, and 5.14 (95% CI: 3.83–6.88) for a lot of damage versus no damage. Conclusion This study effectively identified individuals at risk of experiencing moderate-to-high levels of challenges during the first month of displacement following a natural disaster and developed a predictive model using only participant characteristics that demonstrated good performance. SHAP and interpretability analyses indicated that structural social factors remained important predictors of challenges during the first month following disaster-related displacement. Timely identification of high-risk populations during the first month of displacement is essential for guiding equitable resource allocation, targeting outreach efforts, and informing disaster response policy before hardship compounds into longer-term adverse outcomes.

493083.title: Foundation Models Challenge Dynamical Models for Seasonal Tropical Cyclone Prediction
493083.authors: Hiroyuki Murakami, Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory, Princeton, NJ
493083.abstract: Foundation models are far cheaper than dynamical seasonal prediction systems and have shown skillful tropical cyclone (TC) prediction under persisted sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies, but their skill under dynamically predicted ocean boundary conditions, benchmarked against an operational system, is untested. We evaluate eight seasonal hindcast systems against NOAA's GFDL-SPEAR, the coupled model behind GFDL's real-time forecasts, over 1993-2025 for the July-November season in the western North Pacific, eastern North Pacific, and North Atlantic. The hybrid NeuralGCM and data-driven ACE2 use predicted SST and sea ice from operational systems; six NeuralGCM configurations differ only in their SST source. Their advantage over SPEAR is basin-, metric-, and lead-dependent. At zero-month lead, seven of eight other systems achieve North Atlantic rank correlations of 0.60-0.76, versus SPEAR's 0.59. At the grid-point scale, nearly every AI-based system exceeds SPEAR's significant-skill area in the eastern North Pacific and North Atlantic by up to 20-25 percentage points, and one retains skill at four-month lead where SPEAR does not; SPEAR remains unmatched for accumulated cyclone energy in the western North Pacific. ACE2 produces almost no hurricanes. A skill-based subset does not reliably outperform pooling all nine equally, regardless of basin or initialization month. TC prediction skill reflects a complex interplay among biases in a system's TC climatology, large-scale environment, and genesis response to it, so higher skill can arise from compensating biases rather than a physically valid mechanism. Overall, foundation models are best viewed as complements to dynamical prediction, with SST boundary-condition quality a first-order control on skill.

493085.title: Synoptic Environments for Extreme Rainfall in the Ohio River Basin.
493085.authors: Joycelyn Adjekum, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and X. Fan
493085.abstract: Extreme rainfall is a major driver of flooding and other hydrologic hazards in the Ohio River Basin, yet these events exhibit substantial variability in their duration, spatial organization, and atmospheric forcing. Although previous studies have examined daily precipitation extremes and individual high-impact events, objective event-based classifications of basin-wide extreme rainfall remain limited. This study develops an event-based climatology of extreme rainfall to objectively identify recurring rainfall regimes and provide a framework for investigating their associated synoptic environments. Daily 4-km PRISM precipitation data from 1981–2025 were used to identify extreme rainfall events using a modified Peak-Associated Region (PAR) approach. The method objectively identified spatially coherent rainfall events and reconstructed their complete duration, producing a catalog of 476 extreme rainfall events, including 331 one-day events and 145 multi-day events lasting two to seven days. Event-total precipitation fields were normalized to emphasize spatial rainfall organization independent of event magnitude in order for rainfall pattern analysis. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was then applied to reduce the dimensionality of the rainfall fields while preserving the dominant spatial variability. Principal components explaining approximately 90% of the total variance were retained and subsequently classified using Ward's hierarchical clustering to objectively group rainfall events with similar spatial characteristics. The resulting PCA–Ward classification demonstrates that extreme rainfall over the Ohio River Basin is not represented by a single characteristic spatial pattern but instead consists of several recurring rainfall regimes distinguished by differences in the location, orientation, spatial extent, and concentration of event-total precipitation. The predominance of one-day events (69.54%), together with the occurrence of numerous multi-day events, highlights the diversity of extreme rainfall characteristics across the basin and the value of an objective event-based classification framework. The classified rainfall regimes are subsequently related to composite ERA5 reanalysis fields to identify the dominant synoptic environments associated with each rainfall regime. The analysis focuses on large-scale pressure patterns, upper-level circulation, low-level flow, and moisture transport to determine the atmospheric processes governing the development, organization, and persistence of each rainfall regime. Linking objectively identified rainfall regimes with their characteristic synoptic environments is expected to improve understanding of extreme rainfall across the Ohio River Basin and provide insights that can support future flood forecasting and hazard assessment.

493087.title: Benchmarking Operational Forecasts on Extreme Weather Events
493087.authors: Amy McGovern, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. A. Rothenberg and T. S. Mandelbaum
493087.abstract: The United Nations and the World Meteorological Organization have an initiative to provide early warnings for major disasters across the globe (Early Warnings for All). A key part of achieving this goal is providing skillful forecasts for such disasters. As a part of this, the Weather Prediction Model Intercomparison Project (WP-MIP) has a curated archive of forecasts from operational centers around the world for 2024. These forecasts include AI models, hybrid physics and AI models, and traditional physics-based numerical weather prediction models. Many of the models are initialized from a common analysis. The archive currently includes only single-member, deterministic forecasts. The goal of this project is to facilitate a prediction of operational-scale forecasts across paradigms and to develop evaluations that can be used for by weather forecasting centers to fairly evaluate new models and paradigms. In this work, we use Extreme Weather Bench (McGovern et al, 2026) to compare the WP-MIP forecasts across five categories of extreme weather: heat waves, freezes, severe convective weather days, tropical cyclones, and atmospheric rivers. We compare the forecasts across centres as well as by type of forecast, including AI-only forecasts as well as hybrid and traditional physics-based models. We take a deeper look at example events for each of the extreme weather categories and demonstrate that Extreme Weather Bench can be used to fairly evaluate forecast models focusing on extreme weather, achieving one of the goals of the WP-MIP project. Figure 1 shows a scorecard analyzing heatwave performance over three metrics. Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) is the traditional metric used by WeatherBench and indicates strong performance by the AI models while a deeper dive on the performance of the intensity of the heatwave, as measured by the maximum temperature and the maximum lowest temperature, show that none of the methods outperformed HRES (serving as a baseline) on these metrics. Figures 2-4 show examples of specific forecasts for individual centers and models. We highlight a specific forecast for an atmospheric river that affected the west coast of the United States, a severe weather outbreak in Australia, and a hurricane forecast.
