In this talk, we will dive more deeply into each of our events and highlight cases where the forecasts went wrong and where they worked well.

493089.title: The Role of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation in the Projection of Sahel Precipitation
493089.authors: Emmanuel Ogwuche Audu, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and R. D. Dixon
493089.abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is widely anticipated to weaken by the end of the 21st century, although there is considerable disparity among state-of-the-art Earth System Models (ESM) from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) regarding the magnitude of this weakening. Notably, the weakening of AMOC has been shown to influence future precipitation patterns across different regions, including across West Africa. Uncertainty in projections of Sahelian precipitation has persisted across generations of ESMs and remains a significant challenge for stakeholders. Towards the end of the 21st century, many climate models predict a dipole pattern, characterized by a drought across western Sahel and an increased rainfall across the central Sahel. Recent work has shown that models displaying this zonal dipole pattern tend to predict a southward shift in the position of the Atlantic Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), while those that do not show this dipole tend to predict a northward shift in the Atlantic ITCZ. Furthermore, for the models that do produce this dipole, variability in the longitude where drying transitions to increased precipitation remains difficult to explain. In this study, we seek to elucidate the relationship between changes in AMOC and changes in Sahel precipitation, particularly exploring the potential influence of AMOC on the Atlantic ITCZ and its connection with zonal variability across the Sahel. We use an ensemble of CMIP6 models and statistical analysis to connect the weakening of the AMOC to structural changes in Sahel precipitation across models. Finally, we explore potential mechanisms, including changes to the subtropical high, that may connect these critical climate signals.

493090.title: Interactions Between Boundary Layer Thermodynamics, Surface Fluxes, and Sea-Breeze Circulations During TRACER
493090.authors: Siddhant Gupta, ANL, Lemont, IL; and V. P. Ghate, M. Jones, N. Pszeniczny, D. Wang, and M. P. Jensen
493090.abstract: Previous studies have shown sea/bay breeze circulations affect the meteorology, aerosol, cloud, and precipitation systems around Houston metropolitan area. However, the impact of these circulations on surface fluxes, boundary layer turbulence, clouds and the resulting radiative effect is still unclear. To address this issue, the Tracking Aerosol Convection Interactions Experiment (TRACER) field campaign was conducted from 1 October 2021 to 30 September 2022. During TRACER, an Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Mobile Facility (AMF) deployed at La Porte, Texas made detailed observations of surface, dynamic, thermodynamic, aerosol, cloud and radiative properties. In this work, we utilized these observations to 1) characterize the regional annual and diurnal cycle of boundary layer thermodynamics and dynamics, 2) characterize the the coincident changes in the surface, boundary layer, cloud and radiative properties immediately before, during, and after the sea/bay breeze frontal passage over the site, and 3) probe the factors affecting the timing and intensity of the breeze front passages. The surface air temperature, humidity, fluxes, and turbulence were higher during the summer season as compared to the winter season with the exception of winds. During the summer season (Jul to Sep), 2m air temperature, surface fluxes, turbulence and cloud fraction, exhibited a distinct diurnal cycle, however the 2m water vapor mixing ratio and precipitable water vapor did not. Diurnal wind vector hodographs revealed a clockwise rotation during the summer season with higher magnitude during breeze days as compared to the non-breeze days. Compositing of the 35 breeze front passages revealed the peak-to-peak changes in 2m air temperature, water vapor mixing ratio, air pressure, zonal wind and meridional wind to be 0.6 K, 1.41 g/kg, 5.82 Pa, 2.7 m/s and 1.2 m/s respectively. This resulted in average updraft of 1 m/s within the boundary layer increasing boundary layer cloudiness by 26% and changing cloud radiative effect by 338 W/m2. This suggests that it is necessary for atmospheric models to accurately represent the breeze passages and the associated changes in turbulence and cloudiness to accurately represent the Earth’s radiation budget.

493091.title: Comprehensive Treatment of C4-C6 Alkanes and Their Oxidation Products in CAM-chem: The MOZART-T3 Mechanism
493091.authors: Duseong S. Jo, Seoul National University, Seoul, Seoul, Korea, Republic of (South); and J. J. Orlando, R. H. Schwantes, L. K. Emmons, R. S. Hornbrook, E. C. Apel, A. Hills, K. Ullmann, L. G. Huey, C. Granier, C. Thompson, and J. Peischl
493091.abstract: Most global atmospheric chemistry models lump ≥C4 alkanes into a single surrogate species, obscuring the chemistry of their oxygenated products and leaving many measured compounds without model counterparts. We present MOZART-T3, a new chemical mechanism for CAM-chem that explicitly represents individual C4–C6 alkanes and includes more detailed propane chemistry. We evaluate T3 using the NASA ATom campaign, whose global, vertically resolved measurements of diverse VOCs and oxygenated VOCs provide unusually comprehensive constraints on alkane oxidation chemistry. While total alkane burdens change little, the budgets and distributions of alkane-derived products are substantially reshaped. T3 substantially lowers simulated methyl ethyl ketone concentrations and enables direct evaluation of previously unrepresented species, including individual alkane isomers, propanal, and peroxypropionyl nitrate (PPN). Comparisons with ATom show improved representation of several oxygenated products but persistent underestimation of alkane concentrations with both emission inventories tested. Because observed branched-to-total ratios for butanes and pentanes are well reproduced, the remaining bias points to underestimated emission magnitudes and highlights the need to revisit alkane emissions in global inventories.

493095.title: Salinity-Driven Barrier Layer Dynamics in the Equatorial Pacific
493095.authors: Yuan-Jen Lin, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and A. C. Subramanian, K. Karnauskas, C. A. DeMott, J. Sprintall, and R. Sun
493095.abstract: Barrier layers in the upper ocean suppress the upward entrainment of cold thermocline water, trapping heat and momentum near the surface and thereby influencing tropical air-sea interaction. However, the mechanisms governing their spatial and temporal variability are not fully understood. This study highlights the importance of salinity-induced vertical stratification in shaping the climatology and variability of the barrier layer in the Pacific Ocean on subannual and interannual timescales. Compared to observational and reanalysis data, coupled ocean-atmosphere models simulate a less eastward-extending warm pool, along with a thin barrier layer bias. This bias is linked to a saltier upper western Pacific and can be attributed to weaker precipitation and stronger easterly winds along the equator. Consistently, models with a more eastward-extending warm pool tend to exhibit a thicker barrier layer and lower salinity over the western Pacific. On interannual timescales, models agree with observational and reanalysis data that anomalous westerly winds and increased precipitation develop 10--13 months before the peak eastward shift of the warm pool eastern edge (WPEE), accompanied by an upper-ocean freshening. These anomalies peak with the WPEE shift and persist for another 9--10 months. Subannual variations exhibit more complex temporal patterns. Anomalous westerly winds and increased precipitation emerge 3--4 months prior to the WPEE peak extension and reverse rapidly one month after the peak. While models capture the timing and magnitude of wind and precipitation changes, they fail to reproduce subannual salinity variations. Improving salinity climatology and subannual variability in models remains essential for simulating barrier layers.

493098.title: Calibrating Weather Impacts Between Forecasters and Practioners: The New York State Perspective
493098.authors: Michael S. Michaud, University at Albany, SUNY, Albany, NY; and D. Lewis
493098.abstract: Emergency managers rely on timely and accurate forecasts to mitigate, prepare, and respond to emergencies and disasters in their communities. Extreme events can cause major impacts, but so can everyday weather. The New York State Weather Risk Communication Center uses a color-coded impact level scale in a daily briefing to communicate to emergency managers and other partners about the risk for different hazards in a quick and visual way. However, this scale communicates threats from hazards, which can be difficult to translate into impacts. To bridge this gap, the Center conducted focus groups with state and local partners to understand their perceptions of impacts from weather hazards. This presentation shares the outcomes from these conversations, and how they influenced a revised version of the scale to more accurately communicate potential impacts.

493099.title: Lightning Data Assimilation Development for MPAS- and JEDI-Based Regional UFS
493099.authors: Amanda Back, NOAA, Fort Collins, CO; and A. Burke, D. Dowell, K. C. Eure, and M. Hu
493099.abstract: With the operational implementation at NCEP of the first version of the Unified Forecast System’s short-range, convection-allowing regional component, the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS), comes a groundbreaking ensemble-variational lightning data assimilation capability. In the GSI-based RRFSv1 data assimilation framework, an ensemble of perturbed members at convection-allowing scales assimilate lightning flash densities from the GOES-R GLM instruments, along with numerous other observation types, in an hourly, cycled fashion. Short forecasts from the ensemble members then inform a pure EnVar capability to assimilate radar data and lightning flash extent density into the control member, along with providing the flow-dependent covariance for the hybrid assimilation of other observation types. Both the control member and a selection of the ensemble members provide forecasts as long as 3.5 days, with the control member producing forecasts at each hour. The GLM instruments provide coverage for nearly all of RRFSv1’s domain comprising North America and surrounding oceans, and past work has shown the benefit of EnVar lightning data assimilation in RRFSv1 on very-short-range convective forecasts, up to 3-4 hours in lead time. As NOAA Global Systems Lab develops and tests capabilities for a proposed future RRFS version using the MPAS dynamical core and JEDI data assimilation system, work is underway to adapt the lightning assimilation strategy to these systems. The theory underlying the lightning assimilation capability will be detailed, along with the results of calibrating the forward operator to a new forecasting system and testing optimal correlation length scales. Preliminary demonstrations of forecast skill, both with and without radar data assimilation, will highlight the potential impacts of lightning assimilation for data-sparse areas outside of CONUS.

493101.title: Disentangling Turbulence, Surface, and Particle Controls on Submicron Dry Deposition Velocity: A Chamber Study
493101.authors: Jonah Hazelwood, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and N. Meskhidze and M. D. Petters
493101.abstract: Accurate quantification of size-resolved particle dry deposition velocities (vd) requires resolving transport across the viscous sublayer immediately adjacent to a surface, a layer only millimeters thick where boundary-layer turbulence and molecular diffusion control particle transport. Field methods such as eddy covariance cannot resolve this layer directly, and existing parameterizations built from indirect flux measurements differ by more than an order of magnitude among established schemes. Here we report controlled experiments in a spherical aluminum chamber (91.4 cm diameter, ~0.4 m3) that isolate how turbulence intensity, surface complexity, and particle physicochemical properties independently govern size-resolved vd. Deposition velocities were determined by two complementary methods, chamber concentration decay and filter collection with re-atomization, using three particle types spanning distinct morphologies and densities (NaCl, polystyrene latex, and black carbon aggregates) at RH < 30% and fan speeds of 0-1500 RPM. Friction velocity (u*) and viscous sublayer thickness were derived directly from the size-resolved vd data, yielding u* = 0.16-0.25 m/s and sublayer thicknesses of 0.30-0.46 mm across the turbulence range tested. Turbulence exerted a strong, non-monotonic, size-dependent control on vd: for particles in the 70-150 nm transitional range, introducing low mechanical turbulence (250 RPM) produced a viscous sublayer thicker than the natural-convection layer present under quiescent conditions, suppressing vd below the 0-RPM baseline, a suppression that only reversed as further increases in turbulence thinned the sublayer. Surface complexity modified vd through two distinct mechanisms: flow-permeable vegetation surrogates enhanced normalized vd 10-15× for 20-50 nm particles relative to the smooth-wall baseline, consistent with combined flow penetration and local turbulence generation within the canopy-like structure, while impermeable bluff-body obstacles alone enhanced vd 2-5× through wake-turbulence-driven sublayer thinning, with no flow penetration. These results directly challenge how surface resistance is represented in the Zhang et al. (2001) scheme (used in CMAQ, GEOS-Chem, and LOTOS-EUROS), which assigns land-use-category deposition rates independent of actual canopy flow permeability. Particle morphology and density independently produced up to an order-of-magnitude spread in vd at a given mobility diameter; black carbon fractal aggregates exceeded smooth-sphere model predictions by a mean factor of ~10 (range 1.8-15.7) across 30–300 nm. The filter and decay methods agreed within a factor of 2 across the PSL sizes tested, establishing filter collection as a quantitative standalone tool for size-resolved vd determination. These results provide direct experimental constraints on near-surface boundary-layer parameterizations of particle transport over complex, permeable, and heterogeneous terrain.

493105.title: JEDI Unified Forward Operators (UFO) Overview and Progress
493105.authors: Francois Vandenberghe, JCSDA, Boulder, CO; and B. C. Ruston, L. J. Hayden, R. Chidambara, B. Johnson, C. Dang, and H. Zhang
493105.abstract: The Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA) leads the development of the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI), a flexible and model-agnostic assimilation framework. JEDI separates environmental models from forward operators, enabling the use of a wide range of observation operators—from simple linear interpolation to advanced applications such as radiances with the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM), bending angles with the NOAA Bending Angle Model (NBAM), and radio occultation with the EUMETSAT Radio Occultation Pre-Processor (ROPP). This talk will demonstrate how JEDI’s configurable filters, observation functions, and bias correction options provide powerful tools for quality control, error modeling, and predictor development. Through its YAML-based configuration, JEDI enables rapid testing of new methods without code modifications, significantly shortening development timelines and supporting efficient trade-space exploration. We will also highlight recent extensions to JEDI’s Unified Forward Operator (UFO) system, including enhanced handling of surface observations, forward operators for ground-based radar reflectivity, reconstructed radiances for hyperspectral sounders, and new capabilities for ionospheric observations. Together, these features illustrate JEDI’s flexibility and its growing potential as a unified data assimilation framework across the atmosphere and space weather domains.

493109.title: Air-Sea Exchange and Surface-Layer Turbulence Observations from a Novel Ship-Based Profiling System
493109.authors: Ryan Yamaguchi, NPS, Monterey, CA; and Q. Wang, J. Kalogiros, E. D. Creegan, R. Y. W. Chang, D. Fernandez, H. J. S. Fernando, J. Ruiz-Plancarte, and D. G. Ortiz-Suslow
493109.abstract: Accurate measurements of turbulent air-sea fluxes in the wave-affected marine surface layer remain challenging becauseconventional shipboard observations are often affected by flow distortion around the vessel and are limited in their abilityto sample close to the ocean surface. To address these observational gaps, we investigate near-surface momentum, sensible heat, and latent heat fluxes using the Crane-mounted Cloud and Aerosol Measurement System (C-CAMS), a novel ship-crane-based platform designed to obtain high-quality turbulence measurements within the lowest levels of the marine atmospheric boundary layer. C-CAMS is suspended from a shipboard crane, allowing measurements to be made away from the ship hull and deck while providing vertical profiling capabilities from near the sea surface to heights exceeding 10 m. The platform supportsresearch-grade instrumentation that measures three-dimensional wind velocity, temperature, humidity, sea-surfacetemperature, radiative fluxes, surface height, and aerosol and fog microphysical properties. This unique measurementconfiguration minimizes aerodynamic and thermal contamination while enabling direct eddy-covariance estimates ofmomentum, sensible heat, and latent heat fluxes. This study highlights observations from C-CAMS deployments during the Fog and Turbulence in the Marine Atmosphere (FATIMA) field campaigns. The measurements provide rare observations within the wave-affected surface layer, a regionthat plays a critical role in regulating exchanges of momentum, heat, moisture, and aerosols between the ocean andatmosphere. We examine the variability of turbulent fluxes and their relationship to surface wave conditions, atmosphericstability, wind forcing, and fog occurrence. Results demonstrate the value of C-CAMS as a new observational tool for characterizing air-sea exchange processes and improving understanding of the dynamics of the wave-affected marine surface layer.

493110.title: Case Study Evaluations of Experimental Ensemble Forecasts Toward Rapid Refresh Forecast System with JEDI and MPAS
493110.authors: Amanda Back, NOAA, Fort Collins, CO; and D. Dowell, T. T. Ladwig, C. Zhou, M. Hu, and J. Chamberlain
493110.abstract: The newly-operational Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) v1, the first regional, convection-allowing component of NOAA’s Unified Forecast System, features an ensemble forecast capability with five perturbed RRFS members launching forecasts four times daily and producing high-resolution forecasts with lead times up to 3.5 days. While RRFSv1 uses the FV3 dynamical core and GSI data assimilation system, a prototype RRFS based on MPAS runs both hourly deterministic and ensemble data assimilation cycles over the CONUS 3 km grid for real-time evaluation. As the NOAA Global Systems Lab develops and tests candidate configurations for RRFSv1’s successor using the MPAS dynamical core and JEDI data assimilation system, a new ensemble component has been run experimentally in near-real-time, as well as retrospectively, for 2026 case studies capturing high-impact weather events including flooding and severe convection. In contrast to the mixed-model ensemble forecast systems currently and previously operational at NCEP, the prototype ensemble attempts to achieve the necessary forecast diversity to capture low-probability, difficult-to-forecast events strictly through initial condition perturbations and stochastic physics parameterizations. While the prototype ensemble is still under active development, performance of the experimental configuration on notable 2026 events will be assessed in terms of reliability, spread-skill, and overall ability to represent weather extremes. Probabilistic forecast skill will also be examined in relation to storm mode, hazard type, lead time, time of day, and region to illuminate strengths and possible deficiencies ahead of the next year of RRFSv2X development.

493119.title: Interactions between Short-Wave Troughs and Atmospheric Rivers and Their Impacts on AR Landfalls Along the U.S. West Coast
493119.authors: Zhenhai Zhang, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and F. M. Ralph, W. S. Lin, J. Cordeira, M. Zheng, X. Zou, L. Delle Monache, J. D. Doyle, and C. A. Reynolds
493119.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) play a key role in water vapor transport and precipitation in the midlatitudes, including along the U.S. West Coast. ARs often interact with other essential atmospheric structures, and these interactions can have significant impacts on AR development. Upper-level cold short-wave troughs (SWTs) are one important example. Over the North Pacific, SWTs often approach ARs from the northwest and influence their development and propagation. This study investigates the key dynamical and physical processes associated with SWT–AR interactions over the North Pacific through selected case studies and assesses their impacts on landfalling ARs along the U.S. West Coast. Results show that when SWTs approach an AR, they can induce ascent above or within the warm, moist air of the AR, weakening its moist stability and promoting condensation and precipitation in the lower-to-mid troposphere. The associated latent heat release can then substantially influence the low-level circulation and subsequent AR evolution. In particular, an intensified low-level cyclonic circulation can enhance the meridional component of water vapor transport within the AR, thereby modifying its intensity, structure, and orientation. These changes can substantially influence precipitation when ARs encounter the complex terrain of the U.S. West Coast. Overall, changes in moist stability and diabatic processes associated with SWT–AR interactions can strongly modulate storm development, influencing AR landfall characteristics and precipitation along the West Coast. These findings suggest that improved understanding of SWT–AR interactions can help diagnose forecast errors in landfalling ARs and their associated precipitation.

493130.title: Extreme Weather and the Economics of Cows
493130.authors: Jon B. Davis, Everstream Analytics, Barcelona, Spain
493130.abstract: Rising frequency and severity of extreme weather events—heat waves, droughts, floods, and cold snaps—are exerting mounting pressure on global cattle production systems, with significant implications for both dairy and beef economics. This session will examine recent events and the impacts on the industry. Topics covered within this session will include the 2026 historic summer heat wave in Europe and impacts on milk production and forage, trends in THI (temperature-humidity index) in the central US and impacts on beef cattle and the El Niño no related impacts on cattle in Asia.

493143.title: Future Kilometer-Scale Climate Simulations on Microsoft Azure’s Cloud Computing System: Downscaling the CESM2 Large Ensemble over the Conterminous United States
493143.authors: Alexander Thompson, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA/OAR/PSL, Boulder, CO; and K. M. Mahoney, L. Xue, C. He, A. F. Prein, B. Liu, and S. Adili
493143.abstract: The 2024 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report on modernizing probable maximum precipitation recommends creating a multi-model large ensemble of kilometer-scale climate simulations to update extreme precipitation guidance across the United States. An ongoing effort in NOAA’s Physical Sciences Laboratory is producing this large ensemble, termed CONUS-Futures, by downscaling future decades from global climate models to a 4-km conterminous United States (CONUS) grid. Here, we present the first ensemble member of CONUS-Futures, which dynamically downscales the mean state bias corrected member 1031.002 from the CESM2 Large Ensemble with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model version 4.6.1. This simulation uses a more recent version of WRF but near-identical settings (e.g., grid, physics) as the NCAR-USGS CONUS404 dataset, enabling seamless temporal comparison between the two. Temporally, it will span an initial 5-year period that closely resembles the CONUS-mean 2-m air temperature in ERA5 from 2021 to 2025 and a subsequent future 35-year period. This 40-year simulation is currently running on Microsoft Azure’s cloud computing system in automated monthly increments with the cylc workflow engine. We anticipate that this dataset will be publicly available on Microsoft’s Planetary Computer in early 2027.

493156.title: Spatiotemporal Variability and Trends in Aerosol Optical Depth and PM2.5 Across Texas, with a focus on Lower Rio Grande Valley
493156.authors: Ibrahim-Anyass Yussif, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, BROWNSVILLE, TX; University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, BROWNSVILLE, TX; and M. Rizwan, S. D. Pinakana, A. M. Mestas-Nunez, M. Dahal, and A. U. Raysoni
493156.abstract: We present a 16-year (January 2010 – December 2025) analysis of spatiotemporal trends and variability in fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and aerosol optical depth (AOD) across Texas, focusing on the Lower Rio Grande Valley (LRGV), a Gulf-influenced U.S.-Mexico border region subjected to transboundary emissions and seasonal long-range dust transport. PM2.5 and AOD are derived from the MERRA-2 reanalysis, with data from ERA5 providing meteorological covariates (boundary layer height, wind, temperature, humidity) to help quantify meteorologically driven variability and the humidity-related effects in AOD and PM2.5. Trend analyses will be presented using the Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimator. The study area was compartmentalized into four macro-regions (West: Trans Pecos; North: High Plains, North Central and Low Rolling Plains; East: East Texas and Upper Coast; and South: Edwards Plateau, South Central, South Texas and Lower Valley) based on NOAA NCEI Climate Divisions, enabling comparisons of trends, seasonal patterns, and variability across distinct meteorological and emission environments. MERRA-2-derived PM2.5 will be evaluated against ground-based observations for PM2.5 obtained from Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) Continuous Ambient Monitoring Sites (CAMS) stations, with performance assessed by region and year using data completeness, bias, and correlation with ground-based observations. We will also examine the relationship between MERRA-2 AOD and PM2.5 to assess the consistency between column aerosol loading and near-surface particulate concentrations. Ground-based observational coverage varies substantially across Texas: West, North, and East Texas have sites with near-continuous records over the study period, whereas observations in the LRGV are limited. The analysis will characterize regional aerosol variability, long-term trends, and the performance of MERRA-2 products across diverse Texas environments, while assessing the utility of reanalysis datasets for air-quality applications in a data-sparse border region.

493160.title: Long-Term Spatiotemporal Variability of Criteria Air Pollutants and Meteorological Parameters in Three Regions of South Texas
493160.authors: Mahad Rizwan, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, Brownsville, TX; and I. A. Yussif, A. M. Mestas-Nunez, S. D. Pinakana, M. Dahal, and A. U. Raysoni
493160.abstract: Over the past two decades, South Texas has experienced enormous growth in economic, industrial and cross-border activities. However, the effect of these developments on the long-term air pollution patterns and the role of meteorological parameters on these patterns is a crucial field of study. This research examines a multi-year spatial and temporal variability in PM2.5, PM10, ozone, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide in three South Texas regions of Rio Grande Valley, Laredo and Corpus Christi starting from 2005 until 2025. We took into account various meteorological parameters such as wind speed, wind direction and temperature to evaluate their relationship with pollution trends throughout the years. The hourly concentrations and meteorological observations were measured at 14 Continuous Ambient Monitoring sites (CAMS) at the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) stations. Generalized Additive Model (GAM) will be used in our analysis to evaluate the non-linear association between meteorological observations and pollution concentrations. Seasonal and annual assessments will also be conducted using the Thielsen trend analysis to compare the pollution trends across the regions as well. This long-term study provides us with a valuable insight into the evolution of pollution trends in South Texas amid continued growth in the oil and gas industry along with an increase in the cross-border activities.

493163.title: µWMS: Serverless Cloud-Native Web Map Service for Environmental Data Visualization
493163.authors: David Hahn, NCAR, Boulder, CO; UCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO
493163.abstract: Web Map Services continue to play a vital role in the data visualization of geographic data sets, including meteorological, hydrological, and climatological data. However, current implementations are designed to run on dedicated servers, increasing complexity for system maintenance and scalability. Cloud-native deployments can offer a large advantage in terms of scalability, maintenance, and cost-efficiency. NSF NCAR/RAL has developed a Web Map Service implementation with a serverless, cloud-native architecture called micro Web Map Service (µWMS). By leveraging Amazon Web Service’s (AWS) API Gateway, Lambda, and S3 services with the data stored in the cloud-optimized Zarr format , the system eliminates infrastructure management, automatically scales to accommodate changes in user demand, and has proven highly cost-efficient, serving approximately 70,000 map tile requests for about $1 (USD). This approach eliminates the need for capacity planning and hardware acquisition phases, and in practice, has proven to be extremely inexpensive. µWMS has been deployed in three publicly available web applications: (1) COSMIC’s GNSS-RO Dashboard, where µWMS provides NOAA’s Global Mosaic of Geostationary Satellite Imagery (GMGSI) as a backdrop against the GNSS-RO observations; (2) RAL’s Fuel Moisture Content Display uses µWMS to render satellite-derived fuel moisture content for CONUS, Alaska, and Hawaii domains to show data related to wildfire risks; and (3) RAL’s Climate & Environmental Hazards Explorer, which displays select climate indicators affecting sensitive populations. Data storage costs are comparable to standard AWS S3 ($0.023/GB-month), with lifecycle costs further reduced by migrating older data to lower-cost tiers like S3 Glacier, either manually or automatically using S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Using cloud services effectively can be challenging. µWMS has simplified cloud deployments through automated infrastructure provisioning using Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) and pre-built components, enabling users to deploy the system with minimal technical expertise. The µWMS python package includes command line tools for ingesting data, which converts NetCDF to Zarr formats and pushes files to AWS S3 data storage. µWMS was built with security as a top priority. Three access modes support different use cases: (1) fully open access for public datasets; (2) API key with referrer validation for public-facing web applications; and (3) user authentication via username/password or passkeys for restricted datasets. All API requests are logged in a searchable database with full metadata and links to CloudWatch Logs. These features provide data access controls and comprehensive audit trails for enhanced security. µWMS demonstrates how cloud-native serverless architecture can transform a Web Map Service from a resource-intensive and complex deployment into a cost-efficient, scalable visualization platform. By eliminating infrastructure management, it enables environmental science organizations to rapidly deploy data visualization services with robust security controls. The proven track record across three operational deployments underscores its viability for both open science initiatives and mission-critical applications with restrictive data.

493170.title: Cloud and AI Based Management of Big Data: A Case Study, Scaling Water-Column Acoustic Big Data: Cloud-Native and AI Assisted Data Processing Pipelines, and Visual Exploration of NOAA's Open Access Sonar Archive
493170.authors: Stephanie C. Herring, NOAA/NESDIS, Rollinsville, CO
493170.abstract: Summary: TugBoat and EchoFish represent a modern model for managing big-data challenges in marine science and atmospheric-oceanic observing networks. By transitioning from legacy binary storage to an automated, cloud-native transformation pipeline (TugBoat) and pairing it with a web-based exploration engine (EchoFish), NOAA converts hundreds of terabytes of raw sonar data into an open, scalable, and analysis-ready cloud resource. This framework accelerates scientific discovery, enhances ecosystem-based management, and unlocks new cross-disciplinary applications. 1. Introduction and Background - Active ocean soundings—specifically water-column sonar and high-frequency multi-frequency echosounders—serve as a cornerstone technology for non-invasive observations of marine ecosystems. By emitting acoustic pulses into the water column and recording the intensity and arrival time of the returning backscatter, oceanographers and marine scientists can continuously map physical and biological phenomena. Over decades of research cruises and routine operational deployments aboard National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) ships, academic research vessels, and uncrewed surface vehicles (USVs), NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) has accumulated hundreds of terabytes of water-column sonar data. While this vast dataset represents an irreplaceable repository of long-term biological and physical oceanographic observations, its immense scale and legacy data formats present significant barriers to data stewardship. Traditional workflows create severe computational bottlenecks, prevents cross-survey comparative analyses, restricts interoperability with atmospheric and oceanic reanalysis datasets, and effectively transforms an open archive into a "data swamp" where data is accessible in theory, but intractable in practice. To solve these challenges, NOAA—in collaboration with the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES) and academic partners—developed TugBoat and EchoFish. Together, these two integrated systems form an end-to-end cloud-native pipeline designed to convert raw, legacy water-column sonar holdings into Analysis-Ready Cloud-Optimized (ARCO) formats and deliver interactive, web-scale visual analytics to the global scientific community. 2. Data Ingestion Pipeline (TugBoat) - The backbone of this modernization effort is TugBoat, an automated, cloud-based data transformation pipeline built on Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure. TugBoat handles the massive compute load required to parse, calibrate, standardize, and store raw sonar files into open-standard, distributed data structures. Raw echosounder data files are ingested directly from NCEI's public S3 bucket on AWS via the NOAA Open Data Dissemination (NODD) program. TugBoat leverages Echopype—an open-source scientific Python package. TugBoat converts acoustic backscatter into Zarr stores following Earth Science Information Partners (ESIP) ARCO standards. Zarr allows multidimensional arrays—indexed by range/depth, timestamp, and acoustic frequency—to be broken into uniform, compressed chunks. By leveraging parallel processing frameworks like Dask, TugBoat processes multiple cruises simultaneously in serverless or containerized cloud compute nodes, scaling on-demand to handle petabyte-scale archives without local hardware limitations. 3. Interactive Web Visualization & Analytics (EchoFish)- While TugBoat transforms raw data into cloud-optimized formats, EchoFish provides the user-facing discovery platform that exposes these Zarr stores to scientists, resource managers, and the public without requiring advanced programming skills. Subsetting and Interactive Echograms: EchoFish serves as an AWS-hosted web visualization and analytical platform. EchoFish enables rapid spatial and temporal subsetting. Users can query a region of interest or a specific ship track, and EchoFish dynamically retrieves only the specific byte chunks needed to render high-resolution interactive echograms in the browser. Because each measurement in the Zarr store is coupled with high-frequency NMEA GPS coordinates (latitude, longitude, UTC timestamp), EchoFish aligns acoustic backscatter directly with geospatial boundaries. This capability allows users to inspect target strength differences across frequencies to visually differentiate between physical targets (e.g., seabed topography), fluid targets (e.g., pycnoclines, internal waves), and biological targets (e.g., swim-bladdered fish versus gelatinous zooplankton). 4. Impact, Applications, and Future Work - The deployment of TugBoat and EchoFish fundamentally changes how hydroacoustic sonar data can be used across multidisciplinary Earth science domains, and sets an example for how large, complex data sets can be managed in the future. Key Scientific and Operational Benefits: (1) Democratization of Acoustic Data: By eliminating the requirement for expensive desktop licenses, specialized local software, and massive local storage setups, high-resolution ocean sonar data is made accessible to climate researchers, educators, and policy makers worldwide. (2) Ecosystem-Based Fisheries Management (EBFM): Managers can perform cross-decade comparisons of marine biomass distributions, evaluate habitat impacts, and track shifts in pelagic species ranges caused by changing ocean temperatures and marine heatwaves. (3) Multidisciplinary Climate & Atmosphere-Ocean Research: Standardized ARCO structures facilitate the direct fusion of water-column acoustic datasets with satellite sea surface temperatures (SST), atmospheric reanalysis products (e.g., ERA5), ocean color imagery, and hydrographic Argo float profiles.

493178.title: How Can We H.E.L.P.? The Present and Future of Mutual Aid Efforts in the National Weather Service
493178.authors: Trevor M Boucher, NOAA/NWS, Salt Lake City, UT; and K. Sherburn
493178.abstract: Historically, the National Weather Service (NWS) has leveraged nearby service backup offices or physically deploying meteorologists to fill critical staffing gaps that arise in operations. More recently, the agency has begun to supplement local offices with remote, specialized expertise. While successful, sustaining these efforts requires a transition to a robust, centralized framework. Under the NWS Transformation initiative, the newly established Mutual Aid Unit within the Office of Mission Delivery represents a fundamental, agency-wide operational paradigm shift. By formalizing and consolidating these efforts into a unified, virtual operations support system, the NWS aims to create a scalable, modernized expertise-based paradigm under the Operations Pillar and make it a core component of its future operating model. Recent milestones achieved over the last year have proven the necessity and practical application of this vision. This presentation will focus on the immediate and future goals of the new Unit post-reorganization. In short, by integrating geographically dispersed expertise into this new unified system, the future of mutual aid will align with the "One NWS" philosophy, ensuring the NWS remains agile and capable of delivering superior services in an evolving operational landscape. More broadly, we seek to highlight how an agency can effectively leverage remote technology and geographically dispersed talent to promote optimal service delivery during high-impact events.

493182.title: Education and Workforce Development for Trustworthy AI (Core Science Keynote)
493182.authors: Amy McGovern, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
493182.abstract: As the use of AI is exploding across the workforce, it is critical that we train both current and future workforce in how best to make use of AI in an ethical and trustworthy manner. In this fireside chat, we discuss best practices learned from the NSF AI Institute for Research in Trustworthy in AI for Weather, Climate, and Coastal Oceanography (AI2ES). AI2ES provided training for students of all levels as well as provided workforce development opportunities, including summer schools and other online training. We also introduced a novel trust-a-thon (McGovern et al, 2023).

493183.title: High-Fidelity Instrument Simulation for the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) Constellation
493183.authors: Adam Bell, Tomorrow.io, Boston, MA; and S. J. J. Munchak and R. Chase
493183.abstract: Instrument simulators are central to realizing the operational value of commercial microwave sounder constellations. They enable pre-launch trade studies, observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs), vicarious calibration, harmonization across a constellation, and physically based Level 2 retrievals. We present the passive microwave simulation framework developed for Tomorrow.io’s Microwave Sounder (TMS) constellation and successor instruments, and describe how comparison with current observations is being used to refine the forward model. The simulator ingests high-resolution model fields, such as the NASA GMAO DYAMOND Phase II 3-km global nature run and the operational HAFS regional hurricane model. A preprocessor constructs an oversampled, realistic orbital viewing geometry, and resamples the model fields along individual lines of sight. Radiative transfer is performed on a fine spectral grid and convolved with the measured spectral response functions (SRFs) and 3D antenna beam patterns of each payload, thus capturing the differences among individual instruments in the constellation that matter for intercalibration. Surface emission combines an ocean emissivity model with an emissivity atlas derived from satellite observations over land, snow, and sea ice. Scattering by frozen hydrometeors draws on single scattering databases spanning multiple particle habits and size distribution assumptions, including a parameterization of the polarization signal produced by oriented ice crystals. We evaluate the simulations against collocated TMS observations of tropical cyclones by comparing distributions of simulated and observed brightness temperature (TB). These comparisons motivated corrections to surface emissivity models, improved our understanding of how measured versus idealized SRFs impact simulated TB, and confirmed that the 91 and 204 GHz window channel simulations realistically reproduce observed ice scattering signatures of deep convection. These results, and the forward model improvements they drive, bring simulations into closer agreement with observations. This agreement underpins intercalibration across a large constellation and directly improves operational products delivered to end users, and builds trust in trade studies for instrument performance improvements. Here we present the updated simulation architecture, validation results across the 91 to 205 GHz channels, and lessons learned for operational use of commercial sounder data.

493189.title: The Prevalence of Meteoric-Sulfuric Aerosol within the Stratospheric Aerosol Layer
493189.authors: Graham Mann, Univ. of Leeds, Leeds, YOR, United kingdom; and J. Brooke, M. Yoshioka, L. Marshall, S. Dhomse, W. Feng, C. G. Bardeen, N. Bellouin, M. Dalvi, N. L. Abraham, T. Deshler, L. Thomason, and J. Plane
493189.abstract: In-situ stratospheric aerosol measurements show highly-elevated refractory particles within the wintertime polar vortex, consistent with a meteoric-origin source of condensation nuclei within descending polar vortex air. The presence of meteoric-signature metal ions within laser-ablation mass spectrometer aerosol composition measurements has also emerged from high-altitude aircraft missions in the mid- and high-latitude lowermost stratosphere. In this study, we analyse the global distribution of meteoric smoke particles (MSPs) and their presence within a subset of stratospheric sulphate particles simulated with an interactive stratospheric aerosol microphysics model. The simulations apply the same GA4 UM-UKCA stratosphere-troposphere aerosol-chemistry-climate model submitted to two recent ISA-MIP intercomparison papers, this standard version predicting the formation, transport and tranformation of two types of sulphate aerosol, those heterogeneously nucleated on MSP cores (meteoric-sulphuric particles), alongside also sulphate particles formed from homogeneous nucleation. The model enacts a source of MSPs in the uppermost model level (above 50km) via a monthly-varying two-moment climatology from multi-annual simulations with the WACCM-CARMA model. The source is mapped to one of the size modes of the GLOMAP aerosol microphysics module, MSP coagulation occurring during descent to the high-latitude stratosphere within each winter's polar vortex. Predicted MSP particle concentrations in the winter polar stratosphere are ~500 cm-3, for particles larger then 10nm dry diameter (CN10) at 40km, reducing steeply to a few per cc at ~25-30km the altitude they enter the uppermost high latitude stratospheric aerosol layer. The model predictions find sulphate particles form readily on the smoke particles as they descend into H2SO4-supersaturaated air, generating a distinct mode of MSP-core sulphate aerosol at ~20-25km, at sizes ~50-70nm dry-diameter. Inter-particle coagulation between these non-volatile particles reduces their number, The model predicting MSP-sulphate refractory CN10 at around 1-5 particles per cm3 at 15-20km. Within the January Arctic vortex, the model predicts MSP-core sulphate comprises ~90\% of CN10 particles at 25km, this high-latitude wintertime non-volatile CN10 fraction reducing to ~40% at 20km, and ~10% at 15km. Far from being restricted to high-latitudes, the model predicts meteoric-sulphuric particles remain a significant proportion of the mid-latitude stratospheric aerosol layer throughout the year, the tropical lower stratosphere the only portion of the stratophere where MSP-core aerosol are below 5% of total sulphate CN10. To evaluate the simulations, we compare to mid-latitude balloon-borne particle concentration measurements from quiescent-period soundings, in all 4 seasons. We test the model primarily from comparing simulated CN10 to condensation nuclei profile measurements from Laramie, but evaluate also simulated particle concentrations at radii larger than 150nm and 250nm, as measured from the Wyoming optical particle counter balloon measurements. The model is consistent with the Wyoming mid-latitude balloon measurements, and captures a key observed variation in the vertical CN10 profile, a decreasing profile in the lowermost stratosphere changing to be approximately constant above 20km, the MSP-nucleated sulphate particles by far the dominant Aerosol type in the uppermost statospheric aerosol layer. In light of anticipated increased space debris adding to the ablation-generated meteoric smoke input, we ran sensitivity simulations with a factor-8-elevated MSP input climatology. The simulations generate higher numbers of meteoric-sulphuric particle concentrations, but a competition effect meaning fewer sulphate particles reach 100nm, causing a counter-intuitive reduction in the stratospheric aerosol layer's light extinction, that would cause a small positive radiative forcing (surface warming effect).

493190.title: Beyond the Clouds: The Ripple Effect of Mentorship, Leadership, and Community (Invited Presentation)
493190.authors: Melissa A. Burt, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO
493190.abstract: David Randall’s impact on atmospheric science extends far beyond his groundbreaking and innovative contributions to climate modeling. His legacy is also defined by his extraordinary commitment to mentoring, education, and building communities where scientists can thrive. In this presentation, I will share my personal journey as a mentee and colleague of Dave’s, from my experiences as a graduate student studying Arctic climate, to my role as Education and Diversity Manager for the NSF Science and Technology Center for Multiscale Modeling of Atmospheric Processes (CMMAP), and to my current position as an associate professor and associate dean. Through these experiences, I have witnessed firsthand the power of intentional mentorship and the lasting impact of a leader who invested deeply in people. Dave’s commitment to educational leadership was evident not only through his support of CMMAP’s Education and Diversity efforts, but also through the countless ways he nurtured students, early-career scientists, and colleagues through generous guidance, encouragement, and opportunity. He understood that advancing atmospheric science requires not only scientific excellence but also cultivating the people and communities that sustain the field. This talk will reflect on the lessons I learned from Dave’s leadership, including the importance of creating pathways for others, fostering belonging within scientific communities, and recognizing mentorship as a critical aspect of science. I will highlight how Dave’s mentorship shaped my own career trajectory and continues to influence my work in atmospheric science education research, workforce development, and efforts to create more supportive and inclusive scientific communities.

493197.title: An Interactive Webpage for Exploring the Synoptic Conditions Related to Historical Extreme Precipitation Events
493197.authors: Alexander Thompson, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA/OAR/PSL, Boulder, CO; and P. N. Schumacher, C. Smith, and K. M. Mahoney
493197.abstract: We present an interactive webpage hosted by NOAA’s Physical Sciences Laboratory that shows the synoptic conditions, precipitation development, and recurrence intervals associated with numerous historical extreme precipitation events spanning several decades. The webpage allows a user to display multiple durations of quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) at both a regional and continental United States (CONUS) scale. Average recurrence intervals (ARIs) from 1 year to 1000 years are also available for multiple durations at a regional scale to highlight the severity of each event. In addition, six meteorological variables can be shown at intervals from seven days prior to the event throughout the entire duration of the event. These variables are 500 mb geopotential height, precipitable water, integrated vapor transport (overlain by sea level pressure), soil moisture, 2-m temperature, and convective available potential energy. This webpage is designed to be continually updated with new events over time. The data sources used for precipitation are the Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC, period of record: 1979 – present) and the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor Pass 2 (MRMS, period of record: October 14, 2020 – present). The data source for meteorological variables is ERA5 reanalysis. We intend for this webpage to be used by a broad community including probable maximum precipitation (PMP) practitioners, weather and climate researchers, and the general public. In particular, understanding the meteorological conditions that produced an extreme precipitation event, not just the precipitation amount, is critical for applications to PMP, comparison of storm types across extreme events, and distinguishing physical drivers of a storm from its antecedent land surface conditions. This project is a joint effort between NOAA’s Physical Sciences and Global Systems Laboratories and the cooperative institutes CIRES and CIRA in support of NOAA’s PMP Estimation Modernization project.

493198.title: Quantifying the Radiative Lever Available for Arctic Mixed-Phase Cloud Thinning
493198.authors: Jasper F. Kok, University of California, Los Angeles, Santa Monica, CA; and L. M. Zamora and A. T. Evan
493198.abstract: Rapid Arctic warming has prompted interest in regional cooling interventions that might supplement greenhouse-gas mitigation by slowing Arctic warming. Mixed-phase cloud thinning (MCT) would deliberately glaciate wintertime Arctic mixed-phase clouds to weaken their longwave warming. However, the magnitude, location, seasonality, and seeding-agent dependence of the radiative effect available to MCT remain poorly constrained. Here we quantify this radiative “lever”: the surface and top-of-atmosphere (TOA) cloud radiative effects (CREs) of low-level, liquid-containing mixed-phase clouds potentially susceptible to seeding. We use CloudSat/CALIPSO cloud-phase and radiative-flux retrievals resolved by month, location, and cloud-top temperature (CTT). The available surface CRE is strongly seasonal and geographically concentrated, peaking over open ocean in winter where susceptible-cloud occurrence is high, longwave CRE is strong, and shortwave CRE is weak. The corresponding TOA CRE is substantially smaller, showing that MCT effects on surface and planetary energy budgets cannot be inferred interchangeably. Surface and TOA CREs are also much larger using a CTT threshold of −5 °C, approximating susceptibility to silver iodide, than using −15 °C, approximating susceptibility to mineral dust. These results provide an observation-based map of MCT’s physically available radiative lever for subsequent climate and sea-ice response calculations.

493203.title: Precipitation, Mass Flux, and Cloud Shield Characteristics Throughout the Lifecycles and Upscale Growth of Simulated Mesoscale Convective Complexes
493203.authors: Miles Harmala, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Hassel, K. L. Rasmussen, and S. C. van den Heever
493203.abstract: Mesoscale Convective Complexes (MCCs) are a distinct class of mesoscale convective system characterized by long lifecycles and persistent, cold, quasi-circular cloud shields. They often exhibit extreme variability in precipitation structure and intensity throughout their lifecycle, particularly at the incipient stage. A theorized mechanism for MCC upscale development involves latent heating-induced deep-tropospheric gravity waves, which are hypothesized to produce a meso-beta-scale cycle in volumetric rain rate followed by a longer-lived meso-alpha-scale cycle. While this signal has been shown to be robust across several MCC case studies, it has yet to be investigated and validated across large samples of MCCs. There is also large uncertainty as to what extent the mass flux of MCCs influences cloud shield properties, and other storm-scale characteristics. While there have been some previous explorations of the mass flux-cloud anvil extent relationship in globally modeled convective storms, the exploration of this relationship in large, organized convective complexes is relatively limited. The overarching goal of this study is to investigate the relationship between mass flux, precipitation fields, and cloud shield properties in MCCs, and to examine how these evolve through their lifecycle and upscale growth. To address our stated goal, we examine rainfall, mass flux, and cloud shield morphologies as a function of MCC lifecycle. We use the Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds (tobac) algorithm to identify and track MCCs in 40+ years of convection-allowing CONUS404 reanalysis simulations. Within the tobac-tracked MCC cloud segments, volumetric rain rate and mass flux are computed, each partitioned into stratiform and convective components. Then, the evolution of volumetric rain rate, mass flux, and anvil extent across storm lifecycle are analyzed in the database of tracked MCCs. We investigate the degree to which signals of theorized mechanisms of MCC upscale growth are evident in large sample sizes of MCCs, and how well resolved they are at the 1-hour temporal resolution of CONUS404. We find that the meso-beta-scale cycle is coarsely resolved at 1-hour temporal resolution with additional diagnostic signatures consistent with the proposed upscale growth mechanism. Additionally, we find that the degree of correlation between MCC mass flux and the cloud shield extent is strongly modulated by system-scale characteristics such as total mass flux, precipitation, and degree of system organization.

493204.title: Airmass Source Regions and their Relationship to the Mesoscale Structure of the Comma Head Regions of Winter Cyclones over the U.S. Great Plains
493204.authors: Matthew William Perry, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and R. M. Rauber, T. J. Zaremba, and K. R. Jesmonth
493204.abstract: Past air parcel trajectory studies within the comma head of winter cyclones from the NSF Profiling of Winter Storms (PLOWS) and the NASA Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation in Atlantic Coastal-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) have suggested that much of the precipitation occurring in cyclones over the central and eastern United States originates at high altitude from moisture that sources from the Pacific Ocean, rather than the Gulf of Mexico. Low-level moisture, however, may provide the bulk of the precipitation mass and may originate from more local sources, such as the Gulf and the Atlantic Ocean. In this talk, we present a modeling investigation of the moisture source regions of extratropical cyclones over the central United States that produced heavy snowfall across the northern Great Plains and Midwestern U.S. Specifically, we conducted Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations of the storms using moisture tracers and back trajectories to identify the moisture sources as a function of altitude within the comma head. We show that a seeder-feeder process occurs within the comma head of the storm whereby ice particles form in the upper parts of the storm from moisture sourced from the Pacific Ocean but gain the majority of their mass at lower altitudes from moisture sourced from the Gulf of Mexico. We also show that the vertical distribution of Gulf and Pacific moisture differs across the comma head of each storm. We investigate potential mesoscale causes of these differences. Finally, we analyze links between snowfall totals across the comma head and the vertical profile of moisture source regions. This is the first study to quantify the relative contributions and mesoscale impacts of Pacific and Gulf moisture sources in winter storms.

493205.title: Optimizing Future Surface Observations to Improve Earth System Predictability
493205.authors: Daniel McCoy, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and J. M. Nugent, D. Caulton, B. D. Rodenkirch, J. D. Small Griswold, and G. Torri
493205.abstract: Earth system models (ESMs) remain the tool we use to offer predictions at annual-to-decadal time scales. This is a time scale that is extremely useful for decision makers planning infrastructure. ESMs are also the tool that allow us to interpret processes linking different parts of the Earth system at these time scales. However, a substantial portion of the uncertainty in our ability to predict the Earth system at this time scale originates from small, fast processes related to phenomena such as clouds, rain, turbulence, and aerosol. Many of these processes will not be resolvable by ESMs for the foreseeable future and are a source of both structural and parametric uncertainty in ESM predictions. Field observations are well-suited to studying these processes, but must be carefully scoped and planned as they occur with limited spatial and temporal coverage and must make decisions about which instruments to deploy. Here, we present a new field deployment planning framework based on a suite of perturbed process ensembles (PPEs) combined with large eddy simulation (LES). We demonstrate the utility of this framework to suggest a deployment focused on decreasing uncertainty in the historical cooling due to aerosol-cloud interactions in the context of a surface observation deployment such as a Department of Energy (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) mobile facility. A set of candidate observables and different deployment locations are objectively identified and the effects of different hypothesized constraints are discussed.

493207.title: The Remote Mesoanalyst: An Emerging Operational Function in the Evolving National Weather Service Operations Model
493207.authors: Michael Jurewicz Sr., NOAA, State College, PA; NWS, State College, PA; and C. M. Gravelle and K. Sherburn
493207.abstract: During high-impact weather events, the forecast and warning decision-making process is increasingly extending beyond the local National Weather Service (NWS) Weather Forecast Office, requiring expertise, collaboration, and decision support from across the NWS. The remote mesoanalyst is emerging as a critical operational function that strengthens warning operations, collaboration, and impact-based decision support, with important implications for the evolving NWS Operations Model. Since the inception of the Remote Mesoanalyst Mutual Aid Program, NWS meteorologists have identified key practices that strengthen forecast and warning operations and maximize the effectiveness of the remote mesoanalyst. First, remote mesoanalysts strengthen warning decision making by communicating probabilistic scenarios, the meteorological reasoning supporting those scenarios, and evolving environmental trends that might otherwise go unrecognized. Second, dedicated local mesoanalysts have emerged as the critical operational link between the remote mesoanalyst and warning meteorologists, translating expert environmental analysis into actionable information for real-time warning operations..Finally, remote mesoanalysts are accelerating the operational adoption of emerging NWS capabilities, including the Warn-on-Forecast System and the cloud-based Aircraft Communications Addressing and Reporting System (ACARS) sounding viewer, by integrating these tools into real-time operations, and demonstrating their operational value. Operational examples will demonstrate how expert remote mesoanalysts are at the forefront of applying these practices to improve warning effectiveness, strengthen collaboration, accelerate the adoption of emerging capabilities, and provide a framework for incorporating the remote mesoanalyst as a foundational operational function within the evolving NWS Operations Model.

493210.title: Observed Changes in Compound Drought-Heat-Wave Occurrence and Severity across the Contiguous United States, 1951-2025.
493210.authors: Nana Ofosuhene Pinkrah, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY
493210.abstract: Concurrent drought and heat waves can amplify impacts on water resources, ecosystems, agriculture, and human health. Their occurrence and severity across the contiguous United States (CONUS) during 1951-2025 are examined using NOAA's nClimGrid-Daily dataset. Drought was defined primarily as a one-month Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI-1) below -0.8, and heat waves as at least three consecutive days with daily maximum temperature (Tmax) above the local 95th-percentile threshold (T95) derived from 1961-1990. A compound month required drought and at least one heat-wave day. Compound severity was measured with a locally standardized Compound Drought and Heat Wave Magnitude Index (CDHMI). CONUS area-weighted compound occurrence increased by 0.059 months decade⁻¹ (95% CI: 0.028-0.090; p < 0.001); mean occurrence during 1996-2025 was 45.3% higher than during 1951-1980. After false-discovery-rate correction, significant regional trends were confined to the West (+0.221 months decade⁻¹), Northwest (+0.152), and Southwest (+0.143). The West also had the highest fraction of drought months accompanied by heat waves (31.7%) and the highest mean annual CDHMI (0.413). Estimates were much more sensitive to drought definition than to the T95 reference period: in the West, mean occurrence was 1.074 months yr⁻¹ using SPEI-1 but only 0.231 months yr⁻¹ using the SPI-1, whereas using a full-period (1951-2025) T95 changed occurrence much less. The observed increase is therefore strongly concentrated in western CONUS and depends substantially on how drought is represented, providing a high-resolution observational baseline for monitoring compound drought-heat-wave risk and for evaluating how climate models reproduce it.

493218.title: Towards Improved Lake Temperature Simulation in Global UFS
493218.authors: Benjamin W. Green, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and S. Sun
493218.abstract: NOAA’s Unified Forecast System (UFS) provides a framework to consolidate physically-based Earth system modeling products across many temporal and spatial scales. Currently, global-scale applications of UFS – namely, the Global (Ensemble) Forecast System (GFS/GEFS) and the experimental Seasonal Forecast System (SFS) – treat lakes with a simplistic relaxation to climatology for temperature and ice coverage. While there are efforts to eventually incorporate a three-dimensional lake model into UFS for larger lakes, progress has been slow. To bridge this gap, we implement a simplistic model ENLOAN (for “energy loan”) that can prognose lake skin temperature and ice coverage (allowing for both freezing and melting). Preliminary tests show that, compared to the control climatological lake treatment, use of ENLOAN in GEFS- and SFS-like environments improves the realism (and, at shorter time scales, the accuracy) of surface lake conditions. While ENLOAN does not systematically change the global large-scale circulation at seasonal timescales, it can still be advantageous in the local vicinity of (large) lakes. Work is currently underway to expand the Community Land Model (CLM) one-dimensional lake model’s capability from regional UFS applications, to global UFS applications. Results from both ENLOAN and the CLM lake model in global UFS will be presented.

493226.title: Machine Learning-Based Tropical Cyclone Boundary Layer Wind Retrieval Using Aircraft Observations
493226.authors: Juhyun Lee, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. M. Bell
493226.abstract: Understanding tropical cyclone boundary layer (TCBL) wind structure is crucial for understanding air-sea interactions during TC intensification. Dropsondes provide fine-scale vertical resolution that is highly valuable for analyzing boundary layer wind structure, but they have low temporal and horizontal resolution due to deployment and cost limitations. The tail Doppler radar (TDR) provides complementary measurements with relatively continuous vertical profile information in precipitating regions, but there are numerous missing values in TDR retrieval caused by lack of scatterers and sea clutter contamination. Measurements from flight-level wind with other relevant storm information such as intensity, radius of maximum wind, and storm motion provide additional, indirect information on the TCBL structure and surface wind speed (DesRosiers et al. 2025). Given the diverse spatial and temporal characteristics of these datasets, machine learning (ML) is useful for capturing nonlinear relationships to retrieve relevant information from proxy measurements. In this study, we proposed machine learning-based approach for estimating TC boundary layer wind profiles by integrating multiple observations available from the NOAA WP-3D aircraft and best track. The technique predicts high-resolution (15m vertical resolution) TCBL vertical wind profiles from operationally-available aircraft measurements and TC information, facilitating continuous along-track TCBL analysis. We proposed a novel latent space bridging model built on a multi-modal learning framework that enables data dimensionality reduction and fusion for reconstructing simulated boundary layer wind profiles. In effect, the model estimates dropsonde wind profiles everywhere along an aircraft flight track from an integration of operationally available TCBL information trained on prior dropsonde measurements and auxiliary data. We utilize dropsonde, TDR, flight-level, and TC information from IBTrACS (International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship). Datasets from 2018 to 2023 August are used for training and validating, and dataset from 2023 September to 2024 data are utilized for testing and evaluation. The prediction evaluation shows reasonable evaluation results with a median absolute error of approximately 3–4 m/s relative to dropsonde observations throughout the boundary layer from the surface to 2 km. Furthermore, the proposed framework enables retrieval of pseudo-dropsonde profiles corresponding to historical aircraft flight-leg datasets, thereby facilitating investigation of wind-structure variations associated with tropical cyclone intensity changes. Applications to the Office of Naval Research-sponsored SASCWATCH (Study on Air-Sea Coupling with WAves, Turbulence, and Clouds at High winds) field program will also be discussed.

493227.title: Assessment of Compound Extreme Precipitation and Temperature Events Using Empirical and Quantile-Based Techniques
493227.authors: Nirajan Dhakal, Spelman College, Atlanta, GA; and D. W. Werth
493227.abstract: Compound extreme events (CEs) have broader and more significant impacts on natural and social environments compared with individual occurrences. To this end, detection, and quantification of changes in the compound extreme events under a warm climate are important for making reliable risk projections and for understanding changes in compound extremes. This study quantified the characteristics of compound events based on i) empirical approach, and ii) quantile-based approach using both observed (1964–2014) as well as dynamically downscaled climate model data (2025–2075) for select locations in the USA. Compound events were defined based on the combination of temperature and precipitation (cold-wet, cold-dry, warm-wet, warm-dry) using 25% and 75% thresholds of temperature and precipitation. The empirical approach for the analysis of CEs was executed through counting the number of CEs on annual and seasonal scale and evaluating their trends for both the historical observed period and the future periods. Trend analysis shows marked increasing trends of CEs for future climate conditions during RCP 8.5 scenario. Quantile regression method was used to detect the changes in conditional probabilities of CEs. Results show that conditional trends of upper quantiles/tails have increased for warm-wet events and lower quantiles have increased for cold-wet events as compared to mean trends indicating that both warm and cold dominated compound extreme events are becoming more severe. Results from this study provide better understanding of the changes in compound events.

493228.title: Can we Utilize Pyrocumulonimbus Events as Proxies for Stratospheric Aerosol Injection?
493228.authors: Isabel L. McCoy, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. C. Chiu, S. M. Kreidenweis, and P. C. Lin
493228.abstract: Our work seeks to investigate whether pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) events may be an informative proxy for stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) and under what environmental conditions pyroCb are most SAI-like. Sufficiently strong wildfire events give rise to pyroCbs that inject smoke into the stratosphere. Whether the smoke properties align with those of proposed particles for SAI is still in question. Our work applies a newly developed Bayesian smoke retrieval to pyroCb cases to address this. This retrieval allows us to extract aerosol optical depth, particle size, and composition from high resolution geostationary observations. Preliminary analysis indicates pyroCbs produce a reflective stratospheric layer with majority light-scattering and sub-micron sized particles, desired attributes for SAI deployment. However, statistical case compositing allows us to examine the generalizability of this potential SAI-proxy behavior. Specifically, the smoke particle property sensitivity to varied environmental conditions, their behavior under wider stratospheric dispersion, and the implications for radiative impacts will be discussed.

493229.title: Integrated GNSS Water Vapor Measurements with NYC Micronet for Improving Operational Heavy Precipitation Monitoring and Forecasting
493229.authors: Junhong Wang, SUNY at Albany, Albany, NY; and A. Gallagher, J. E. González-Cruz, M. Leszak, J. Maelan, A. Matakos, MSc, D. Radell, B. Shrestha, K. P. Sookdar, and Z. Wu
493229.abstract: New York State (NYS) has experienced the largest increase in the nation in the heavy precipitation rate over recent decades. Flash flooding in NYS occurs most frequently in the coastal area (NYC and Long Island regions), causing enormous damage to property and infrastructure and even deaths. The dense NY City Micronet (NYCM) operated by New York State Mesonet (NYSM) at University at Albany has played an important role in real-time, high resolution precipitation measurements, informing operations and decision making for forecasters, emergency managers and other sectors. However, the quantitative precipitation forecasting (QPF) skill during extreme rainfall events remains challenging because of lack of continuous atmospheric water vapor monitoring. The NYSM is partnering with Skyfora to build a dense ground-based Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) network based off Skyfora low-cost, low-power, state-of-art GNSS technology (StreamGNSS) using the existing NYCM’s infrastructure to continuously map out 3D water vapor field, which is critical but missing in current measurements. Twenty-seven StreamGNSS units were deployed to the NYCM and the NYSM stations in the surrounding regions during Spring 2026. The GNSS precipitable water vapor (PWV) data are validated against NYSM profiler and radiosonde data. By fusing current NYCM dense, high-quality weather data with real-time GNSS water vapor data and next-generation AI/ML and physical urban weather forecasting models, we are working towards improved nowcasting of heavy precipitation events. To support operational applications, user-tailored dashboards will be developed for real-time situation awareness and actionable projections of extreme precipitation events (e.g. flood, flash flood, heavy rain). On May 20, 2026, a line of thunderstorms developed and merged over NYC, produced localized flash flooding with 1-hour rainfall rates 1.5” to 2” in Brooklyn and Queens and caused submerged vehicles and subway suspension. The heavy rain started shortly after PWVs exceeded 50 mm and increased by 5 mm in one hour or even in 5 minutes in some cases. The preliminary results show that the PWV data are useful for nowcasting localized heavy rainfall. Future work includes continuation of impact studies for May 20 and other cases, and improvements, operational deployments and evaluation of the dashboard for NYC’s weather forecasting office, emergency managers and utilities and scientifically by the research community.

493231.title: Development of an Operational Interpolation Tool for Verification of West-WRF Water Vapor Flux Forecasts against CW3E Radiosondes in Northern California
493231.authors: Sarah Dixie Burnett, SIO, La Jolla, CA; University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and R. Weihs, J. Wilcox, A. Wilson, D. F. Steinhoff, L. Delle Monache, and F. M. Ralph
493231.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are characterized by concentrated corridors of water vapor flux and are often associated with extreme precipitation, particularly over complex terrain where orographic enhancement can occur. Accurate representation of the water vapor flux, both in magnitude and vertical structure, are important for diagnosing numerical weather prediction model skill of extreme events. In this study, a high-resolution regional forecast model is assessed by evaluating water vapor flux characteristics and related environmental factors using radiosonde data collected during targeted AR events in Northern California. One element of this analysis involved developing an operational tool that efficiently interpolates model forecasted values from multiple lead times to the locations of the radiosonde data. 518 radiosonde launches were used between two launch locations to evaluate the forecast skill of the model. For each launch, the most concentrated portion of the vapor transport, called the IVT core layer, is determined by finding the thinnest vertical region of the atmosphere which contains an integrated water vapor flux that is equal to 25%. The vertical placement and thickness of the observed IVT core layer is then compared to the forecasted IVT core layer at different lead times. To better quantify model performance in representing this feature, a novel verification metric, termed the Core Score, is introduced to assess model agreement of the location and intensity of the most concentrated layer of water vapor flux. Applications of this metric reveals that the model captures the thickness well, but lacks skill in the vertical placement of the concentrated water vapor flux.

493232.title: AMOC Weakening Enhances Equatorial Pacific Warming in the 21st Century Through an Oceanic Pathway
493232.authors: Xiaodan Chen, Fudan University, Shanghai, Shanghai, China; and A. Dai
493232.abstract: Future tropical Pacific warming patterns affect weather and climate over the U.S. and other regions but remain uncertain in 21st century climate projections. Most climate models project an El Niño-like warming pattern with varying magnitude characterized by enhanced warming over the equatorial central-eastern Pacific. Existing studies emphasize the role of atmospheric and upper-ocean processes in the formation of such a warming pattern. Here we analyze various climate model simulations to show that the weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) enhances equatorial Pacific warming through a deep ocean pathway. Moderate AMOC weakening in the 21st century reduces Atlantic deep ocean flow into the Southern Ocean, which weakens the Indo-Pacific overturning circulation and the associated heat export. This builds a heat reservoir below the thermocline that is transported upward by background upwelling to enhance the warming in the equatorial upper Pacific Ocean. Our findings reveal a new Atlantic–Indo-Pacific oceanic pathway that complements local atmospheric and upper-ocean processes for explaining the El Niño-like warming pattern and helps constrain future equatorial Pacific warming projections, as the magnitude of the AMOC weakening can account for ~45% of the inter-model spread of the projected El Niño-like warming pattern among CMIP6 models.

493246.title: Aircraft Operated by the Research Aviation Facility at NSF NCAR
493246.authors: Cory A. Wolff, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO
