493246.abstract: The NSF NCAR Research Aviation Facility (RAF) has been operating research aircraft for the atmospheric and geophysical research community since 1964. After NCAR was founded in 1960, there was an immediate recognition that the science community would benefit from a facility that could provide airborne project support, which were beyond the capabilities of a university to establish or maintain. A National Aircraft Facility Survey Group was formed to study the requirements for a research aircraft, instrumentation, and data handling. This group’s work resulted in the founding of the “NCAR Aviation Facility”, which later became RAF. Its initial role was to provide non-operational assistance to atmospheric researchers across the nation, to include dissemination of information, technical assistance, training, and liaison services. Since its founding RAF has operated nine different types of research aircraft to fulfill its original mission in support of the scientific community: Beechcraft Queen Air, Sabreliner, Schweizer Explorer sailplane, Beechcraft King Air, WB-57, de Havilland Canada Buffalo, Lockheed P3 Electra, Lockheed C-130, and Gulfstream V. A brief overview of each aircraft will be presented, including pictures from the NSF NCAR archives, operating characteristics, operational period, and highlights from research projects they were involved in.

493248.title: Commercial Satellite Observations of Tornado Damage Morphology and Surface Heterogeneity
493248.authors: Andrew Caleb Blackford, The University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and E. J. Kerr, I. Montgomery, U. S. Nair, and K. Horn
493248.abstract: High-resolution commercial Earth observation imagery has demonstrated considerable potential for post-storm tornado damage assessment, yet most satellite-based studies have focused on individual events. Building upon a remote sensing methodology developed for the 21 May 2024 Greenfield, Iowa EF-4 tornado, this study evaluates the applicability of satellite-based damage assessment techniques across a five-year climatology of EF-3+ tornadoes using imagery acquired through NASA's Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) Program. The analysis includes all EF-3 and EF-4 tornadoes occurring across North America between 2019 and 2024. Following quality control, suitable commercial imagery was obtained for 157 tornadoes, comprising 1,281 PlanetScope multispectral scenes. Supplemental Vantor multispectral imagery was acquired for an additional 16 tornadoes lacking suitable PlanetScope coverage, expanding the dataset to 173 of the 189 tornadoes identified during the study period. Standardized workflows generate derived products to characterize tornado-induced surface change and damage morphology across diverse environmental settings. Using the Greenfield methodology as a baseline, this work evaluates the applicability of satellite-based tornado damage assessment across diverse environmental settings. Particular emphasis is placed on understanding how vegetation condition, terrain variability, and other forms of surface heterogeneity influence satellite-observed damage signatures and damage morphology. This dataset provides a framework for identifying environmental controls on remote sensing performance and assessing the generality of methodologies developed from individual case studies. Preliminary analyses indicate that environmental conditions have a measurable influence on satellite-observed tornado damage signatures, with vegetation phenology representing one important factor affecting damage detectability. Further analysis examines the roles of terrain variability, land cover, and surface roughness in modulating observed damage morphology. These results will help establish the strengths and limitations of commercial satellite observations for objective tornado damage assessment across diverse landscapes.

493253.title: Operationalizing Gridded NFDRSv4 Analyses and Forecasts at SPC
493253.authors: Adam David Werkema, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; and N. J. Nauslar, R. Barnes, M. S. Elliott, and D. E. Jahn
493253.abstract: The Storm Prediction Center (SPC) is developing operational, gridded, percentile-based fire danger analyses and forecasts using the National Fire Danger Rating System version 4 (NFDRSv4). Marking a transition from traditional point-based methods, this gridded approach better captures the spatial gradients and topographical complexities of modern fire environments. This framework produces CONUS-wide real-time analyses, 7-day forecasts, and an 8-year climatology to support fire environment decision-making. Constructing this system requires optimal, temporally consistent meteorological inputs across historical, real-time, and forecast timeframes. To ensure consistency with traditional data, candidate gridded analysis and forecast inputs were rigorously evaluated against Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS) observations. Additionally, the analyses and forecasts were intercompared to verify that their underlying statistical distributions align. Based on these evaluations, the Unrestricted Mesoscale Analysis (URMA) and Snow Data Assimilation System (SNODAS) provide the NFDRSv4 inputs to construct the 8-year climatology. Real-time inputs are sourced from the Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis (RTMA), SNODAS, and Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) Pass 2 Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (QPE), while forecasts rely on the National Blend of Models (NBM). Collectively, these selections establish a robust, operational framework for spatially continuous fire danger assessment across the United States.

493258.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Predict Impact to Communities During Hurricane Events
493258.authors: Felix Fuentes III, Texas A&M Univ.-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX; and J. J. Alland and J. R. Rhome
493258.abstract: Hurricanes impose wide-ranging consequences on the communities in their path, from power outages and structural damage to injuries and loss of life. Anticipating these impacts before landfall is central to the National Hurricane Center’s mission of protecting life and property, yet most operational guidance characterizes the physical hazard (wind, storm surge, rainfall) rather than its consequences for people. This project develops artificial intelligence models that translate hurricane hazard forecasts into predictions of community-level impact. Our framework combines forecast hazards with measures of population exposure and vulnerability, following a risk-based approach, to estimate consequences at the county level across the United States. Operational prediction models that were developed include power outage severity, power outage duration, and monetary damage. Trained and validated on historical landfalling storms, the models forecast categorical predictions at the county-level and skillfully identify the counties most likely to experience power outages and infrastructure damage days ahead of landfall. Building on this foundation, the models are able to identify the most important factors in each individual county that drive the prediction for operational risk communication. By predicting not just where a storm will strike but how it will affect communities, this work supports emergency managers and the public in preparing for hurricane impacts. The results demonstrate that consequence modeling is both feasible and operationally valuable, and they lay the groundwork for an impact-based decision-support capability at the National Hurricane Center.

493259.title: Observed and Simulated Ice Water Content in Updrafts and Downdrafts of Arctic Mixed-Phase Clouds: A Lagrangian Perspective
493259.authors: Jung-Sub Lim, CIRES, Boulder, CO, Germany; and N. Schnierstein, M. D. Shupe, F. Hoffmann, R. Neggers, and G. Feingold
493259.abstract: The spatial organization of supercooled liquid droplets and ice particles in Arctic mixed-phase clouds emerges from complex interactions among cloud dynamics, supersaturation, and microphysical processes. Yet models differ in how they represent this organization, while observations often show enhanced ice water content in updrafts relative to downdrafts. Here, we compare large-eddy simulations using two-moment bulk and Lagrangian particle-based microphysics with high-resolution radar observations from wintertime stratiform mixed-phase cloud cases during the MOSAiC campaign. Although both modeling frameworks reproduce several bulk cloud properties, they differ substantially in vertical phase structure, spatial heterogeneity, and the relationship between vertical motion and ice water content. The Lagrangian framework, using stochastic ice nucleation without saturation adjustment, more closely reproduces the observed heterogeneity and vertical-motion–ice relationship, as assessed using observed and forward-simulated radar reflectivity and Doppler velocity, together with retrievals of liquid and ice water content. By tracking individual ice particles through updraft and downdraft regions, we further examine how their growth histories contribute to this relationship. Together, these results help clarify the processes shaping the observed relationship between vertical motion and ice water content and illustrate how differences in microphysical representation can influence the internal variability of simulated mixed-phase clouds.

493260.title: The Influence of the Gulf Stream Fine-Scale SST Gradient on Frontal Structures within Extratropical Cyclones and Bomb Cyclones
493260.authors: Jacob D. Hair, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and R. Parfitt, R. J. Wills, J. Müller, and R. E. Hart
493260.abstract: It is well established that western boundary currents can significantly influence the development of extratropical cyclones (ETCs). However, it remains challenging to disentangle the relative importance of absolute sea-surface temperature (SST) versus the various spatial scales of the SST gradient. This study isolates the role of the fine-scale (~25 km) Gulf Stream SST gradient in the development and structure of atmospheric fronts within ETCs by smoothing the fine-scale SST gradient. We utilized two atmospheric simulations with the Community Atmospheric Model Version 6, one having an atmospheric regional grid refinement of 14 km encompassing the North Atlantic Gulf Stream region, and the other a 111 km global resolution. The SST is specified and has a resolution of 0.1°. It is shown that atmospheric warm fronts are significantly influenced by the fine-scale SST gradient perturbation when they are collocated with the Gulf Stream Front (GSF). Mechanistically, this is associated with the reduction in the diabatic frontogenesis. When the fine-scale SST gradient is smoothed, within the warm front there is a significant reduction in frontogenesis, vertical velocities, and vertical diabatic heating averaged over the lifecycle of ETCs in high-resolution simulations. These perturbations are magnified within rapidly developing ETCs, known as bomb cyclones. All aforementioned responses by the atmospheric warm front are not seen in the low-resolution simulations. This work suggests that: (1) the strength of the diabatic frontogenesis of atmospheric fronts within ETCs passing over the GSF is modulated by the strength of the fine-scale SST gradient, with the largest influence to bomb cyclones, and (2) a high-resolution atmospheric model can better represent the fine-scale SST gradient influences on atmospheric fronts throughout the free troposphere.

493262.title: Multilayer Simulation of Wind-Forced Breaking Waves
493262.authors: Luc Deike, ; and R. Yang, J. Wu, S. Popinet, J. T. Farrar, and B. Chapron
493262.abstract: Wave breaking under moderate to high winds occurs within broad-band ocean wave fields and drives turbulence and mixing in the upper ocean. However, the inherently multiscale nature of wind-forced wave breaking presents challenges for accurately characterizing the wave field, in terms of balance between wind input, nonlinear wave interactions, and dissipation due to breaking, as well as the associated turbulence generation. We extend a recent multilayer framework from Wu, Popinet and Deike (2023, 2025) to resolve broadband wave fields with waves spanning from O(1) to O(100) m, including breaking, in wind-forced conditions. We introduce a physical-space wind forcing that represents aerodynamic pressure forcing induced by the wind on the waves and compare it to wind input models commonly used in spectral space. We perform relatively long-duration simulations (O(100) peak wave periods) under both pseudo-steady and growing wave conditions, and evaluate key features of wind-wave statistics, including classical fetch and duration-limited relationships and the shape of the wave spectrum. We quantify the wave-breaking statistics, directionality of the waves and breaking fields, turbulence generation, and vertical turbulence profiles, and demonstrate consistency with field observations. These results provide a physically consistent framework for the evolution of nonlinear wave fields and the associated coupling between wave-induced turbulence and mixing, with the potential to improve parameterizations in ocean boundary-layer models.

493268.title: Linking Agrivoltaic Configurations to Microclimate, Crop Production, and Solar Energy Generation Trends
493268.authors: Jason Montagna, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and Z. R. Frey, E. R. Compton, A. R. Cervenka, O. Fercak, S. Smith, D. Denham, R. B. Cal, and M. Calaf
493268.abstract: Agrivoltaics is the combination of solar energy harvesting with crop production. This is a relatively new practice that emphasizes the synergy of both approaches traditionally disconnected with the goal of helping meet food and energy challenges of the 21st century enable crops and solar energy to be produced simultaneously, potentially playing a major role in sustainably meeting growing global energy demands while also minimizing competition for land. This has become an even more pressing matter in the age of massive datacenters, hungry for water, land, and energy. It has long been understood that crop production is affected by excess solar radiation, and that the efficiency of traditional solar photovoltaics is significantly affected by increased solar panel temperature above the standard test conditions of 25˚C. Therefore, agrivoltaics appeared as the perfect synergy, where additional shading could reduce crop stress, and crop evapotranspiration could lead to increased power output. Yet for this approach to be widely applicable significant challenges remain. For instance, what is the impact of solar modules spacing and height in terms of crop and power yield? Traditional approaches tend to only consider engineering challenges, or agricultural practice needs, yet there is a lack of a holistic analysis. In this project we use a combination of field measurements in an in-house built solar farm, together with high-resolution numerical simulations to shed light into the problem. The experimental measurements track the solar radiation, soil temperature and moisture, and crop production at different locations, as well as solar panel temperature and power harvested. The numerical simulations consist of a one-way coupling between the Energy Research and Forecasting (ERF) model with the Photovoltaic Agrivoltaic Simulation Environment (PASE) together with a thermoelectric model for solar panels. Results shed light in the interplay between solar array spacing, installation height and inclination angle, together with soil properties, and crop production.

493272.title: Development and Evaluation of a Real-Time Prototype MPAS-JEDI-Based Next-Generation Rapid Refresh Forecast System
493272.authors: Chunhua Zhou, CIRES, Boulder, CO; CIRES and NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; and G. Ge, J. Hu, S. Pan, S. K. Degelia, A. Back, D. Dowell, R. Li, H. Wang, L. Lin, M. Hu, T. T. Ladwig, J. Beck, and S. Liu
493272.abstract: Hourly updating convection-allowing numerical weather prediction is essential for severe weather forecasting. Following the success of the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR), NOAA is developing the next-generation Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS). While the first operational RRFS release is based on the FV3 dynamical core and GSI data assimilation, ongoing development has shifted toward the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) and the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI). A major milestone is the development of RRFSv2X, the first real-time MPAS-JEDI-based RRFS prototype. Operating continuously since spring 2026 over a 3-km CONUS domain, RRFSv2X employs an hourly cycling, two-way coupled data assimilation system that combines a deterministic hybrid 3DEnVar analysis with a 30-member ensemble data assimilation cycle. The observing system has expanded to include aircraft, surface, radiosonde soundings, radar reflectivity. The analysis functions also include non-variational cloud analysis and continuous land-surface cycling. Real-time forecasts from RRFSv2X were evaluated during the 2026 Hazardous Weather Testbed Spring Forecasting Experiment and received positive feedback for guidance on convective initiation and storm evolution. Based on these results, substantial efforts have been made to improve all major system components, including the MPAS model, JEDI data assimilation, and workflow infrastructure, with a focus on both scientific performance and computational efficiency. The system has been upgraded to a fully cycled configuration with both spin-up and continuous cycling to help us evaluate possible operational configurations. Ongoing development and evaluation are supported through both real-time operations and retrospective experiments. This presentation describes the development, real-time implementation, and evaluation of RRFSv2X, highlighting the scientific and engineering advances, real-time readiness, and remaining challenges of the MPAS-JEDI-based next-generation rapid-refresh forecasting system.

493277.title: A Precipitation-Tracking Perspective on MJO Diversity and Its Environmental Controls
493277.authors: Yakelyn R. Jauregui, NCAR, Boulder, WA; and J. Berner and K. Huang
493277.abstract: The Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) exhibits substantial event-to-event diversity in its zonal propagation and meridional structure, yet existing diversity frameworks classify events from cluster analysis of intraseasonal OLR Hovmöller diagrams. Here we develop a complementary diversity framework based on Large-scale Precipitation Tracking (LPT), classifying MJO-related precipitation tracks in ERA5 (1970–2025) by Indian Ocean origin, Maritime Continent crossing and non-crossing behavior, and meridional excursion off the equatorial band (10°S–10°N). We composite ERA5 atmospheric fields along each category's mean propagation pathway to characterize the large-scale thermodynamic and dynamical environment governing equatorial deflection. Because off-equatorial excursions can reshape the extratropical wave trains MJO convection excites, identifying their environmental controls has direct implications for subseasonal teleconnection forecasts and S2S prediction of MJO-forced circulation anomalies.

493278.title: Isolating the Effects of Immersion-Freezing Parameterizations on Ice Crystal Number Budgets in a COMBLE Cold-Air-Outbreak Cloud
493278.authors: Yijia Sun, SUNY, Stony Brook, NY; and F. Tornow, A. M. Fridlind, N. Riemer, and D. A. Knopf
493278.abstract: Immersion freezing of supercooled cloud droplets contributes to primary ice production and can thereby influence the evolution of marine cold-air outbreak (CAO) mixed-phase clouds. Yet predicted primary ice production depends on how immersion freezing is parameterized. Ice nucleation active surface site (INAS) density and time-dependent nucleation-rate formulations are both used to represent this process, but the uncertainty associated with this parameterization choice remains poorly quantified under realistic CAO conditions. CAO cloud environments provide a stringent test because they combine time-varying temperatures with persistent supercooled liquid water, making both temperature history and exposure time relevant. Here we evaluate immersion-freezing parameterization dependence for the 13 March 2020 CAO observed during the Cold-Air Outbreaks in the Marine Boundary Layer Experiment (COMBLE). We use a one-dimensional aerosol–cloud model informed by time-varying temperature, cloud liquid water, and cloud droplet number fields from a large-eddy simulation of the COMBLE Model Intercomparison Project. We compare two temperature-dependent INAS density formulations with one time-dependent heterogeneous ice nucleation-rate formulation. The INAS density formulations represent freezing through temperature-dependent active-site densities, whereas the rate formulation accumulates freezing probability by integrating a surface-area-normalized nucleation rate over time. All simulations use the same time-varying LES inputs and advance the same aerosol population through time. Each formulation prognoses its own ice-nucleating particle (INP) availability, while all simulations advance ice crystal number through modeled production, transport, and loss tendencies. The parameterizations yield primary ice production rates spanning nearly three orders of magnitude and distinct time–height patterns of ice formation. Analyses of accumulated primary ice production and ice crystal number tendencies show how these production differences carry into simulated ice number. For the rate formulation, cloud-mean ice number also changes by about 14% between alternative definitions of the aerosol-mixing top. Even so, order-of-magnitude separation in ice number among the parameterizations remains when sedimentation, sublimation, and turbulent mixing are included. These processes therefore do not substantially diminish the spread established during primary ice production. Under the same LES-derived cloud evolution, primary ice production and ice number remain strongly sensitive to immersion-freezing parameterization choice. Applying these laboratory-derived formulations within a COMBLE-constrained cloud history links nucleation-scale assumptions to cloud-scale ice production. The persistent separation in simulated ice number provides a pathway for immersion-freezing uncertainty to influence CAO cloud evolution in coupled simulations.

493281.title: TTUKa Mobile Doppler Radar Analysis of Tornado Structure from the Low-Level Internal Flow of Tornadoes (LIFT) Experiment
493281.authors: Ethan B. Steward, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and C. C. Weiss
493281.abstract: Tornadoes are highly destructive and pose a significant threat to life and property. When considering their high frequency (1,200 per year on average) in the United States, understanding tornadic wind fields and behavior becomes crucial to saving lives. As a result, many studies have been conducted to investigate tornado structure. However, tornadic radar observations have been mostly confined to altitudes greater than 100 m above ground level (AGL), leaving the lowest levels of the tornado - most critical for its maintenance and impact - largely unobserved. The Low-Level Internal Flow of Tornadoes (LIFT) field project was focused on resolving the tornadic wind field at the lowest levels near the surface. Tornadoes were scanned using the two Texas Tech University Ka-band mobile (TTUKa) radars, which allow for high-resolution, close-range observations of the near-surface flow of tornadoes. Notable LIFT cases include the 23 May 2024 Eldorado, Oklahoma, EF-2 tornado; the 2 June 2024 Silverton, Texas, EFU tornado; and the 25 April 2025 Sudan, Texas, EFU tornado. Plan position indicator (PPI) scans from these cases correspond to 17-35, 9, and 31-36 m AGL, respectively. Additionally, range-height indicator (RHI) scans capture the vertical structure of each tornado’s core and outer region down to the surface. The Generalized Velocity Track Display (GVTD) technique is used to retrieve the near-surface axisymmetric tangential and radial wind fields from PPI data. Results from the GVTD analyses for the three tornadoes indicate structure more closely matching the Burgers-Rott Vortex (BRV) overall than the Rankine-Combined Vortex (RCV). However, both idealized vortex models decrease tangential velocity too rapidly in the outer region compared to observed velocities. Tornadic RHI data are interpolated to a uniform 25 m Cartesian, vortex-relative grid in order to create vertical profiles of horizontal wind speed both inside and immediately surrounding the vortex core. Mean vertical profiles in the maximum outbound and inbound Doppler velocity regions for the three tornadoes indicate overall wind speed reductions with height in the 0-1 km layer. However, each tornado features a considerably different variation of wind speed in the opposing regions of Doppler velocity maxima. Observed corner flow swirl ratio values are calculated for the Eldorado and Sudan tornadoes using a combination of GVTD output and vertical integration of the tornado inflow layer in RHI scans azimuthally closest to the tornado center. A median corner flow swirl ratio of 3.97 was calculated for the Eldorado tornado from multiple estimates of the corner flow mass flux, indicating a tornado with multicellular structure and possible multiple vortices. In contrast, a median corner flow swirl ratio of 0.77 was calculated for the Sudan tornado, suggesting a single-celled vortex structure. These observational results raise open questions about how tornado- and storm-scale processes interact to influence tornado structure and evolution. Asymmetries in the horizontal flow, including subvortices, remain difficult to characterize spatially and temporally in observational datasets. Ongoing work extends this analysis beyond individual case studies using idealized Cloud Model 1 (CM1) simulations, with the goal of generalizing low-level tornado wind field characteristics and investigating the physical mechanisms driving them. Progress on this next stage, along with recommendations for future modeling efforts, will be discussed.

493283.title: Evaluating Probabilistic Diffusion Downscaling for Short-Range Fire-Weather Prediction in Complex Terrain
493283.authors: Nicholas Silverman, The MITRE Corporation, McLean, VA; and D. S. Abdi, N. Krall, I. Jankov, and C. J. Lewellyn
493283.abstract: Fire-weather conditions can change rapidly in complex terrain, where fine-scale variations in topography modulate near-surface wind, temperature, and relative humidity. Reliable 0–12 hour forecasts of these conditions are needed to support wildfire situational awareness and operations, but producing accurate, high-resolution probabilistic guidance remains challenging due to large computational demands and complex atmospheric dynamics. To address these challenges, we developed Weather-1K, a one-of-a-kind, high-resolution numerical weather prediction (NWP) dataset, created using the AceCast weather model, a GPU-accelerated version of the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. AceCast was run at 1-km resolution across the contiguous United States, with 10-minute time steps for 2022–2023. Leveraging the dataset’s high spatiotemporal resolution, we use NVIDIA’s Correction Diffusion (CorrDiff) generative AI model to downscale the operational High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model’s hourly, 3-km forecasts to 10-minute and 1-km resolution. Preliminary evaluation against held-out Weather-1k data indicates that learned downscaling substantially reduces error relative to interpolated HRRR input fields for temperature, near-surface relative humidity, and 10-m wind components. CorrDiff’s deterministic regression reduced RMSE relative to HRRR from 2.18 to 1.70 K for temperature (22%), from 15.11 to 9.35 percentage points for relative humidity (38%), from 2.73 to 1.62 m s⁻¹ for 10-m u wind (40%), and from 2.23 to 1.35 m s⁻¹ for 10-m v wind (39%). CorrDiff’s diffusion ensemble also improved upon HRRR and produced realistic fine-scale patterns and uncertainty unavailable in standard HRRR forecasts. Ongoing evaluation examines whether this probabilistic information improves reliability and captures localized wind and humidity conditions relevant to fire weather. In addition, we will evaluate these results, along with an AI emulator approach, in NOAA’s Fire Weather Testbed in fall 2026; these results will be included in our presentation.

493287.title: Transitioning to a New (UFS) Governance Framework for Modeling at NOAA
493287.authors: Jennifer Vogt, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and N. Jacobs
493287.abstract: NOAA’s ability to rapidly transition cutting-edge research into operational environmental forecasts has historically been hindered by fragmented modeling governance. Legacy structures suffered from split decisional authority, siloed resource allocation across Line Offices (LOs), and micro-project-level management that created operational redundancies. Furthermore, traditional paradigms struggled to nimbly integrate external scientific breakthroughs or effectively leverage NOAA’s expanding High-Performance Computing (HPC) footprint beyond individual project silos. To maintain global leadership in Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) and accelerate key initiatives like the Modeling Moonshot, NOAA required a modernized, agile modeling governance framework. The new Modeling (UFS) governance structure is centered around three core pillars: The NOAA Modeling Decision Board(NMDB): Chaired by the NOAA Administrator, the NMDB drives strategy, authorizes resources (including HPC), and ensures alignment with operational requirements. The AMS Community Modeling Committee (CMC): Serving as the primary interface with the broader research community (academia, private sector, NGOs), the CMC captures community priorities, advocates for user needs, and provides community input. The Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC): Acting as the operational engine, EPIC accelerates community-developed innovations into the UFS by supporting software infrastructure, managing code releases, and coordinating testing and evaluation. Additionally, technical execution is distributed among specialized UFS subteams—including Architecture & Infrastructure, Component Development, Performance & Evaluation, Education & Outreach, and Release Coordination—to codify software standards, eliminate cross-agency redundancies, and foster cross-sector collaboration. This new modeling (UFS) governance implementation aims to accelerate research-to-operations (R2O) pathways, enhance transparency, and foster a more collaborative and efficient UFS enterprise. I will present the structural framework, the roles of these key entities, and the mechanisms established to harmonize community contributions with NOAA's operational objectives.

493292.title: Updated Meteorological Data Dissemination Process to Characterize Terrestrial Environmentsfor Space Vehicle Applications
493292.abstract: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s Marshall Space Flight Center Natural Environments Branch (MSFC NE) maintains the near real-time acquisition and dissemination of meteorological data for assessing the terrestrial environment experienced by spacecraft and launch vehicles. Continuous, reliable transmission of terrestrial environment data in Meteorological Data Transfer Format between Kennedy Space Center, Johnson Space Center, and MSFC is critical on day of launch for use in characterizing and evaluating the atmospheric wind and thermodynamic profile. In the long-term, archived data is used by analysts within MSFC NE to define the environment climatologically, compute launch availability and probability against constraints, and evaluate instrument performance. This presentation outlines the historical database distribution and archiving framework used by MSFC NE, highlights challenges encountered within that system, and describes recent improvements such as implementing redundant data backups. The instrument source network, automated data transmission software processes, and a brief overview of downstream quality assessments, machine learning quality control, and a few application use cases are detailed.i i Artificial Intelligence (AI) Usage Disclosure: This document was created with assistance from Microsoft Copilot for sentence structure and flow. The content has been reviewed and edited by Kelly Welch.

493294.title: Using Narratives to Understand the Multi-Hazard Impacts of Tropical Cyclones: A Florida Case Study
493294.authors: Yao Zhou, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL
493294.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) expose coastal regions to multiple hazards—storm surge, heavy rainfall and freshwater flooding, strong winds, tornadoes, and rip currents—that interact with populations, the built environment, infrastructure, and natural systems to produce compound and cascading impacts. Understanding the full range of impacts from historical TCs can strengthen hazard mitigation and resilience planning. Yet existing impact studies typically rely on a narrow set of metrics, such as mortality, property damage, and economic loss, or focus on individual events at limited spatial scales—constraints driven largely by the scarcity of systematic, detailed disaster-impact data. We develop a large language model (LLM)-based approach that makes detailed, multi-system impact information accessible at a breadth and scale not previously available. Drawing on storm event narratives from the NOAA Storm Events Database and an impact taxonomy of 11 systems and 47 categories, we extract and classify hazard and impact information for 2,670 TC events across Florida from 2007 to 2025. We validate the approach against independent human annotation of a 10% sample by two coders. With this dataset, we examine (1) the range of systems and assets affected by TCs, (2) the extent to which impacts co-occur across multiple systems within individual county-level events, and (3) the hazard characteristics associated with different types and combinations of impacts. Three patterns emerge. First, reported impacts span a wide range of systems, with vegetation, transportation, buildings and facilities, utilities, and populations most frequently affected. Second, impacts commonly span multiple systems within the same TC process and location, reflecting the interconnected nature of TC impacts. Third, distinct relationships link hazard types to observed impacts, particularly between wind- and water-related hazards; multi-system impacts are more strongly correlated with the multi-hazard character of TCs, underscoring the need to consider interacting hazards rather than examining them in isolation. These findings demonstrate the value of weather narratives for building a more comprehensive understanding of TC impacts and for informing multi-hazard mitigation and coastal resilience planning. We conclude by discussing the opportunities and limitations of LLM-based methods for extracting structured impact information from historical weather narratives.

493299.title: Global 3D Cloud Data Construction Adapting Multiple Sensors and Flexible Mapping Frameworks
493299.authors: Brandon John Daub, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO
493299.abstract: Level-2 cloud retrieval products using NOAA Enterprise Cloud Algorithms are currently available from GOES-R and JPSS satellites, including Cloud Top Height (CTH), Cloud Phase (CP), Cloud Base Height (CBH), Cloud Cover Layers (CCL), etc. Previous validation efforts have shown that these products meet program requirements in relation to surface observations and other space-borne active sensors. With an emphasis on extending the benefits of satellite observations into the vertical dimension, as part of the OVERCAST project, we have broadened our work to a global scale by constructing a global 3D cloud field from multiple geostationary and polar-orbiting satellite observations with supplementary data. Blending techniques between geostationary satellites (GOES-18, GOES-19, Himawari-9, Meteosat-10, and Meteosat-9) are adopted to produce 3D cloud data on a 0.02° × 0.02° horizontal grid domain with 40 vertical levels at a 500-m interval between 70°S and 70°N. Polar-orbiting VIIRS sensors (NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and Suomi NPP) are used to produce the same 3D cloud data, but on a reduced Gaussian grid for the north (70°N to 90°N) and south (70°S to 90°S) polar regions to complete full global coverage. The current blending technique uses a flexible weighting function (currently based on solar zenith angle) that allows inputs from multiple sensors that have differing spectral coverage, spatial resolution, and temporal resolution to provide a more seamless boundary between sensors. This work is actively being expanded with ongoing updates and new additions. The introduction of temporal correction will allow for a more accurate boundary matchup between sensors that have different scan patterns. Alternative mapping frameworks are currently being evaluated such as a global HEALPix grid, a globally uniform equal area grid, in order to fully merge the GEO and polar grids into a single, global equal area grid. Other efforts include replacing Meteosat-10 with the new Meteosat-12 FCI data and adding the MetOP-SG A1 METimage sensor from EUMETSAT to improve coverage around the polar regions. Validation and code optimization efforts continue to improve our 3D global data processing. This work will highlight technical updates and continuing work in the construction of satellite-based global 3D cloud data.

493301.title: Atmospheric Tomography in the 2030’s: Airborne Sampling to Uncover How Atmospheric Composition Responds to Changing Human Activities and Climate Change.
493301.authors: Eric A. Kort, Max Planck Institute for Chemistry, Mainz, Germany
493301.abstract: Measurements of atmospheric composition made from airborne platforms as part of global-scale surveys provide unique insights into the chemical composition of the atmosphere, the influence of anthropogenic activities, how natural systems dynamically respond and in turn change composition, and how chemistry in the atmosphere itself leads to changes. At the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry, we are planning a new set of global airborne surveys to be made in the 2030’s to study how and why the atmosphere’s composition is changing. I will discuss possible flight campaigns that leverage the HALO aircraft and its ability to sample from the boundary layer to the lower stratosphere, over land and water. I will address how this sampling can help tackle questions about dynamic natural and anthropogenic fluxes of methane and carbon dioxide as well as possible changes to atmospheric oxidation capacity. I will further discuss how international coordination, with instrumentation and with aircraft such as the NASA 777 can greatly expand the science impact.

493304.title: Comparative Evaluation of LOCA2 and STAR-ESDM Downscaled Precipitation Products for Climate Applications over the Conterminous United States
493304.authors: Liqiang Sun, GFDL, Princeton, NJ; and K. W. Dixon, K. E. Kunkel, X. Sun, and D. R. Easterling
493304.abstract: High-resolution downscaled climate datasets are increasingly used to support climate impact assessments, infrastructure design, and adaptation planning. Understanding the strengths, limitations, and sources of uncertainty in these products is therefore essential for selecting appropriate datasets for applied climatology. This study compares two widely used CMIP6-based statistical downscaling products, Localized Constructed Analogs version 2 (LOCA2) and the Seasonal Trends and Analysis of Residuals Empirical–Statistical Downscaling Model (STAR-ESDM), both highlighted in the Fifth National Climate Assessment (NCA5), using a common 16-model CMIP6 ensemble to facilitate a direct comparison of uncertainties associated with observational training data and downscaling methodology. Historical performance is evaluated against the Livneh and nClimGrid observational datasets using metrics including annual and seasonal precipitation, the number of rainy days, annual maximum daily precipitation, precipitation variability, and sub-GCM-scale spatial variability. Future projections are also examined to evaluate the sensitivity of projected precipitation changes to downscaling methodology. Both products reproduce the observed large-scale precipitation climatology and substantially improve upon their parent GCM simulations. However, important differences remain in regional bias patterns, precipitation variability, precipitation extremes, and projected future changes. For a given parent GCM, differences in the number of rainy days among the downscaled products are primarily associated with uncertainties in the observational training datasets, whereas differences in annual maximum daily precipitation and annual and seasonal total precipitation are largely driven by the downscaling methodology. Compared with LOCA2, STAR-ESDM generally projects larger and more spatially coherent changes in precipitation variability. These findings demonstrate that the dominant source of uncertainty depends on the precipitation metric being evaluated: observational training data primarily influence the simulation of rainy days, whereas downscaling methodology exerts a larger influence on precipitation totals and extremes. This distinction provides practical guidance for selecting downscaled climate datasets and underscores the importance of accounting for both observational and methodological uncertainties in hydrologic, infrastructure, and climate-risk applications.

493306.title: Setting the Standard: Recommended Practices for Data Preprocessing in Data-Driven Climate Prediction
493306.authors: Jason C. Furtado, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and M. J. Molina, M. Arcodia, W. Anderson, T. Beucler, J. A. Callahan, L. M. Ciasto, V. A. Gensini, M. L. L'Heureux, K. Pegion, J. S. Perez-Carrasquilla, M. Sonnewald, K. Takahashi, B. Xiang, and B. Zimmerman
493306.abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) methods are rapidly transforming prediction across subseasonal-to-decadal timescales. However, over time, the field has focused heavily on model architecture and explainability rather than the importance of data preprocessing, arguably a more foundational determinant of model trustworthiness. Climate datasets present unique preprocessing challenges (e.g., strong spatiotemporal autocorrelation, nonstationarity, non-Gaussian and multi-modal distributions, and class imbalance for extreme weather and climate events). Without careful handling, these properties can silently inflate apparent skill and undermine the generalizability of AI/ML-based climate prediction models. This presentation offers a set of recommended practices for preprocessing climate data used in AI/ML prediction studies on subseasonal-to-decadal timescales. We specifically focus on the following: (1) minimizing data leakage through proper train/validation/test splitting; (2) computing anomalies, detrending, and standardization in ways that avoid incorporating future information or overinflating skill; and (3) handling non-normal distributions, outliers, and class imbalance common in the field. We demonstrate the practical consequences of these choices through two specific case studies. The first case study examines North American weather regime classification using ERA5 500 hPa geopotential heights and k-means clustering, showing that seemingly minor preprocessing decisions (e.g., local versus domain-averaged standardization) can alter the optimal number of identified regimes and their spatial structure, subsequently affecting their interpretation and application by practitioners. The second case study uses a neural network to predict Southwest United States temperature anomalies, comparing a "clean" preprocessing pipeline against common missteps used by scientists. Each misstep produces artificially-inflated apparent skill within the same model, with trend leakage alone nearly tripling the adjusted error relative to reported skill. Together, these case studies provide evidence that data preprocessing is not just a technical detail in AI/ML-based prediction studies. Instead, data preprocessing represents a key lever controlling whether AI/ML climate predictions are scientifically sound and trustworthy in applied research. These findings are synthesized into an actionable workflow intended as a practical template for researchers, model developers, and operational forecasters alike. As such, following these recommended steps for data preprocessing for AI/ML climate prediction applications will build community trust, enable more equitable model comparison, and ensure that reported forecast skill reflects genuine predictive capability rather than artifacts of incorrect data preprocessing.

493310.title: Operationalizing a Memory-Intensive Analog Ensemble Forecast System using Cloud-Based Computing
493310.authors: Thomas Brummet, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO
493310.abstract: Analog ensemble (AnEn) methods produce probabilistic forecasts by identifying historical conditions similar to a current numerical weather prediction forecast. While AnEn provides a useful framework for generating probabilistic guidance from deterministic forecasts, operationalizing the system presents significant computational challenges, primarily due to the intense memory demands and the strict time constraints required for operational forecasting. This presentation describes the design and implementation of a cloud-based architecture developed to run a memory-intensive AnEn system operationally. The AnEn runs within an operational DICast forecasting system, producing deterministic hourly forecasts out 15 days for over 10,000 global sites. Running AnEn at this scale requires processing large historical forecast and observation datasets while maintaining sufficient memory to perform analog searches across many locations, variables, and forecast lead times. These requirements made resource selection, workflow orchestration, and cost-efficient scaling key components of the operational design. The application was containerized with Docker and deployed on Amazon Web Services using Elastic Container Registry (ECR), AWS Batch, EC2, and S3. AWS Batch manages job scheduling and dynamically provisions high-memory EC2 resources when forecasts are generated, allowing compute capacity to scale down when processing is complete. Containerization provides a reproducible runtime environment while separating application deployment from the underlying compute infrastructure. The presentation will examine the resulting software and cloud architecture, including container design, data movement, job orchestration, compute-resource selection, memory profiling, and monitoring. The presentation will also highlight lessons learned regarding AWS resource selection and EC2 right-sizing for workloads with substantial memory requirements. The resulting framework demonstrates how elastic cloud computing can be used to transition a computationally demanding probabilistic forecasting technique into a scalable operational weather forecasting system.

493311.title: A Global Approach to Neighborhood-Scale Weather Modeling with uMORPH and Urban-Physics-Aware AI
493311.authors: Luis E Ortiz, George Mason University, Arlington, VA; and M. Jain and T. McPhearson
493311.abstract: High-resolution urban canopy parameters (UCPs) are a persistent bottleneck for both physics-based and AI-driven neighborhood-scale weather modeling. Existing products are either city-specific and non-scalable or too coarse to resolve important intra-urban structure. This introduces a major challenge to truly generalizable urban-scale models, as the combination of a lack of global UCP data coupled to the high computational cost of urban-scale physics, makes this information inaccessible for most of the world and impractical for most businesses. Here, we present work to address both issues. We will introduce uMORPH, a global, open access, 100-meter resolution UCP and building heights dataset derived by a hierarchical integration of openly available urban and building data. uMORPH provides UCPs and individual building data required by all urban physics parameterizations in the Weather and Research Forecasting Model (WRF) in native geogrid binaries as well as in ML/AI model-ready cloud-optimized GeoTIFF. We demonstrate uMORPH's utility across two complementary modeling pathways focused on extreme heat. First, we drive WRF coupled with the multi-layer urban parameterization using uMORPH UCPs for 12 cities across the globe. For each city, we simulate 500 summer days across representative years (from coolest to warmest) and produce physically coherent near-surface fields at a native spatial resolution of 500 meters and temporal frequency of 3 hours. Second, using these WRF outputs as training data, we develop an urban physics-aware machine learning downscaler model that bridges reanalysis scales to sub-kilometer resolution fields. The residual U-Net architecture-based ML model ingests uMORPH UCPs as static morphological features and to emulate neighborhood-scale 2-m air temperature. Our model reproduces the diurnal temperature cycle and spatial heterogeneity of the physics-based WRF simulations across all 10 US cities, indicating that uMORPH's morphological signal is both dynamically meaningful to a mesoscale NWP model and learnable by a data-driven emulator. In addition, results show that inclusion of detailed UCP predictors lead to better representation of the spatiotemporal features of summer temperatures across all cities when compared to a no-UCP scenario, including out-of-training holdouts and out-of-validation samples. To demonstrate the value of our approach, we estimate economic losses due to extreme heat across a wide range of US cities using publicly available methods for labor losses and infrastructure disruption. Together, these results position uMORPH as reusable infrastructure that couples consistently to both physics-based and ML/ AI-based urban modeling frameworks, offering a scalable pathway for neighborhood-scale climate and urban heat applications. As our model is trained across a large set of cities under a wide range of climatological and urbanization conditions, it offers a truly generalized predictions of near-asset scale fields at a fraction of the cost of traditional models.

493314.title: Fast and Efficient Constrained Capon Beamforming for Phased Array Weather Radars using Deep Neural Networks
493314.authors: James M. Kurdzo, MIT Lincoln Laboratory, Lexington, MA; and M. L. Weiss, F. Nai, S. M. Torres, and C. D. Curtis
493314.abstract: Meteorological rotating phased-array radars (RPARs) can achieve substantially faster volumetric updates than conventional dish radars by leveraging advanced beamforming strategies. Without such strategies, the narrow pencil beam of an RPAR offers little volumetric update-rate advantage. Elevation beam spoiling is one promising approach, but no real-time adaptive digital beamforming method that maintains acceptable weather data quality currently exists, making this a key barrier to operational RPARs. We have recently developed the Constrained Capon Beamforming (CCB) technique, which provides adaptive sidelobe suppression while preserving the beam shape of a Fourier beamformer, resulting in properly calibrated weather data without significant sidelobes. However, CCB is extremely compute intensive, making it untenable for real-time use. This work accelerates CCB processing speed by training a deep neural network (DNN) to match the CCB output in milliseconds instead of hours, enabling real-time CCB and unlocking new capabilities for meteorological RPARs. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Advanced Technology Demonstrator (ATD) is a phased array with an overlapped-subarray architecture that enables receive-side adaptive digital beamforming that could enhance dynamic antenna pattern adjustments to improve radar variable estimates when a spoiled beam is used, especially in regions with sharp reflectivity gradients. As part of the DNN-based CCB development, we built an ATD beamforming simulator to generate large machine learning-ready datasets for DNN training and evaluation. The technique ingests emulated Weather Surveillance Radar – 1988 Doppler (WSR-88D) in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) data and simulates 5-degree spoiled transmit beams and 0.5-degree beamformed receive beams from the ATD. In this work, we detail WSR-88D case selection and data curation strategies, as well as subarray I/Q simulation, gradient detection techniques, analysis metrics, and approaches to mitigate data imbalance, all compared between Fourier, Capon, CCB, and DNN-based CCB methods. We also explore DNN architectures that leverage complex-valued layers to retain phase information in the subarray weights, assess velocity, spectrum width, and polarimetric variable estimates, and outline a roadmap for future work.

493317.title: NWP Array: Access NWP Forecast Archives as Xarray Datasets
493317.authors: William May, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY
493317.abstract: Even though it's a common requirement for many tasks, organizing historical forecast datasets (for example, for the GFS or HRRR) is challenging and time consuming. Forecasts are stored across hundreds of thousands, or even millions of files, in a format not designed for long-term analysis. The Python package nwparray simplifies this task by allowing users to open an entire forecast file collection as a single dataset in xarray. Each array in the xarray dataset is created by the parallel processing tool Dask, using templates from the Herbie Python package to find the required data files. Using Dask, users can easily spread the work across hundreds of workers to enable massive parallel downloads and parallel processing. The results can be written from xarray to standard formats such as netcdf and zarr. This can shorten the downloading and processing time from days or even weeks to hours, thus speeding up tasks such as forecast calibration, forecast evaluation, and AI model training.

493319.title: Investigating Climatological Relationships Influencing Tropical Cyclone Tornado Environmental Favorability
493319.authors: Kailey R Jones, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN; and D. R. Chavas and B. A. Schenkel
493319.abstract: After making landfall, most tropical cyclones produce tornadoes, an extreme weather event co-occurring with the costliest and deadliest natural disaster in the United States. These tropical cyclone tornadoes (TCTs) have been historically overlooked as a secondary hazard, leaving much unknown about how environmental parameters and land surface properties shape TCT hotspots. With this, existing research has largely been confined to case studies, leaving a limited understanding of TCT climatological patterns. Our study addresses this gap by using the CONUS404 reanalysis (4km, hourly data from 1980-2024), to conduct a 40-year climatology of TCT production across the continental U.S. To identify and distinguish short and long-lived potentially tornadic storms, or TCT-surrogates, we add spatiotemporal tracking to an existing framework combining maximum updraft helicity and radar reflectivity thresholds [1]. From these tracks, we quantify the relationships between TCT production and environmental variables like storm-relative helicity, low-level shear, and instability, as well as land surface types like orography, elevation roughness, and surface roughness in order to characterize regional TCT environmental favorability. Finally, we compare these results with the same methodology and analysis applied to the CONUS404 Pseudo-Global Warming dataset, allowing us to assess how these environments may evolve under future climate change. Carroll-Smith, D. L., Dawson, L. C., & Trapp, R. J. (2019). High Resolution Real-data WRF Modeling and Verification of Tropical Cyclone Tornadoes Associated with Hurricane Ivan 2004. E-Journal of Severe Storms Meteorology, 14(2), 1–36. https://doi.org/10.55599/ejssm.v14i2.72

493324.title: QuickPUNCH: Demonstrating Low-Latency Imaging with NASA’s Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere Mission to Support Space Weather Forecasts and R2O2R
493324.authors: Daniel B. Seaton, Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO; and J. M. Hughes, C. E. DeForest, S. Gibson, D. Lamb, C. Lowder, K. Kenny, J. Kobayashi, R. Patel, C. Peck, J. Redfern, S. Van Kooten, A. Adeyeye, M. Burek, G. Dima, J. Johnson, T. Meisenhelder, M. Middlebusher, G. Millward, D. J. Schmit, and N. Y. Wang
493324.abstract: PUNCH is a coronagraphic and heliospheric imaging NASA Small Explorer comprising four spacecraft: three Wide Field Imagers (WFI) and one Near Field Imager (NFI), which generates polarization-resolved observations of the corona and heliosphere between 6–180 solar radii. PUNCH observations can be used to track solar wind flow and coronal mass ejections continuously from near the Sun nearly to 1 AU, which is useful for space weather forecasting. However, the processing required to remove contributions from stray light and the F-corona also introduce significant delays in producing PUNCH’s primary science data. QuickPUNCH was conceived as a way to demonstrate how specially processed low-latency data could support space weather forecast operations. There are two QuickPUNCH products, produced both in FITS format, for science analysis, and JPEG2000, for use in analysis tools like JHelioviewer. The QuickPUNCH NFI images provide coronagraphic views of the solar atmosphere covering 6–32 solar radii that can be used to identify and characterize nascent coronal mass ejections. These observations can serve as a tertiary backup for NOAA’s Compact Coronagraph observations from GOES-19 and SOLAR-1. The QuickPUNCH WFI images provide views of the heliosphere from 12–180 solar radii, enabling new capabilities to track outflow from the Sun throughout the heliosphere. In addition to being sent directly to NOAA at minimum-latency, all QuickPUNCH data products are archived in and are publicly available from the NASA SDAC with only slightly increased delay. Here we describe the status of the QuickPUNCH project and summarize our preliminary analysis of these products’ suitability for future space weather forecasting operations. We compare the benefits and limitations of QuickPUNCH and PUNCH science observations for both operations, R2O2R, and research applications. We present several ongoing R2O2R efforts using PUNCH data, and highlight some lessons learned from the experience of adapting these science data to provide new capabilities for real-time space weather forecasting activity.

493330.title: AI Ensembles: Forecasts for the Curious
493330.authors: Leif Mark Swenson, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and K. M. Mahoney and M. L. Breeden
493330.abstract: This study investigates the performance of ensemble machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models for the medium-range forecasting of atmospheric river (AR) events impacting the Western United States. With the proliferation of machine learning weather prediction models (MLWPs) the need for process-based evaluation of these novel models becomes crucial. ARs are a useful lens through which to analyze MLWP models because they are filamentary features exhibiting large gradients in thermodynamic and kinematic fields that may not be well represented within the machine learning loss function framework. Furthermore, ARs showcase the strengths of ensemble forecasts relative to deterministic forecasts because the average landfalling error in forecasts is large relative to the typical area of extreme precipitation. Ensemble forecasts, therefore, can give decision makers a better idea of the distribution of possible precipitation impacts than can a single deterministic model. The introduction of ensemble MLWPs, most notably GenCast from Google DeepMind, gives us the opportunity to investigate both the ensemble and MLWP representation of ARs and AR risks. Additionally, the advances claimed in GenCast addressing the problem of overly smooth forecasts observed by many in existing MLWPs makes GenCast an exciting target for examination. We compare forecasts of AR associated precipitation across GenCast, NOAA’s Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), and ECMWF’s IFS ENS during the winter seasons from January 2021 through December 2025. We compare the ensembles across skill metrics, like critical success index and fraction skill, for multiple precipitation thresholds. Additionally we investigate the characteristics of the underlying precipitation distributions, and perform a probabilistic, object based evaluation.

493331.title: Preparing the CHAPS Hyperspectral Imaging Spectrometer for Space Demonstration
493331.authors: William H. Swartz, Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD; and J. L. McDermott, C. B. Gardner, S. L. Disque, and M. F. Morgan
493331.abstract: CHAPS is a next-generation hyperspectral imaging spectrometer currently being matured for spaceflight under NASA’s Earth Science Technology Office Instrument Incubator Program. CHAPS is designed to address emerging requirements for high–spatial resolution atmospheric composition measurements from low Earth orbit, providing observations of trace gases such as nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) at spatial scales down to 1 × 1 km². CHAPS represents a new sensor and small-satellite payload design concept that combines hyperspectral sensing (300–500 nm, 0.6-nm spectral resolution) with advanced enabling technologies, including freeform optics, topology optimization, and additive manufacturing. These innovative optical and structural technologies significantly reduce instrument mass, volume, and complexity while maintaining science-grade performance, enabling deployment on small satellites, hosted payloads, and future satellite constellations. The instrument’s focal plane assembly is currently being upgraded with a space-qualified detector, along with space-ready electronics and onboard processing systems, to prepare the instrument for space flight. The project builds upon the CHAPS-D precursor system, which served as both a laboratory testbed and airborne simulator. Laboratory characterization, calibration activities, and a flight campaign have demonstrated the performance of the sensor architecture and form the basis for the space demonstration. The instrument employs established differential optical absorption spectroscopy (DOAS) retrieval techniques and supports future integration with atmospheric models and in situ observations for improved emissions quantification. Beyond air quality applications, the CHAPS architecture is scalable across ultraviolet, visible, and shortwave infrared wavelengths (270–2400 nm), providing a flexible foundation for future hyperspectral Earth science and applications missions. The combination of a compact sensor, innovative optical technologies, advanced calibration approaches, and constellation-enabled observing strategies offers a pathway toward next-generation remote sensing systems. This paper presents a summary of ground and airborne testing to date and ongoing development for a planned space demonstration.

493334.title: Translating Environmental Information into Agricultural Financial Decision Support: The DAWN Financial Tool
493334.authors: You Wu, University of Maryland, COLLEGE PARK, MD; and X. Z. Liang
493334.abstract: Agricultural producers and stakeholders increasingly face complex decisions under uncertainty arising from environmental variability, production risks, and market fluctuations. Although advances in environmental monitoring and prediction provide valuable information, a persistent challenge remains in translating this information into actionable financial insights for agricultural decision-making. This study presents a financial decision-support tool developed within the DAWN (Decision-support system for Agricultural Water use and Nutrient management) project to address this gap by translating environmental and production information into decision-ready financial outcomes. The DAWN financial tool integrates multi-source environmental, crop, and economic datasets to connect production conditions with financial consequences and supports county-level analysis. The tool supports user-selected scenarios and automatically performs the associated financial and risk calculations. Applying enterprise budgeting principles, the tool incorporates production costs, commodity prices, and revenue estimates to assess gross and net margins, return on investment, break-even metrics, and profitability under alternative environmental and production conditions. It also generates downside-risk probabilities and sensitivity-based tradeoff advice. These outputs support pre-season profitability assessment, risk planning, and evaluation of management tradeoffs, translating complex environmental and economic information into practical financial decisions. A key contribution of the DAWN financial tool is its integration of environmental information, enterprise budgeting, uncertainty assessment, and actionable financial decision support within a useful, usable, and user-friendly framework. By integrating county-level information and user-selected scenarios with automated financial calculations and clear, actionable outputs, the tool enables producers, extension professionals, and policy stakeholders to interpret complex environmental and economic information and evaluate financial tradeoffs without directly managing the underlying data or performing the associated financial calculations. This approach helps close the gap between environmental information and agricultural action by linking environmental and production conditions to decision-ready financial information.

493350.title: Investigating Spatial Error of QPE and QPF in the Northern Great Plains for Increased Agricultural Production and Decreased Waste
493350.authors: Kayla Kenow, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. W. Marquis and J. Zhang
493350.abstract: Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (QPE) derived by NOAA’s Next Generation Weather Radars (NEXRAD) have substantially improved hydrological outlooks and forecasts for the Contiguous United States. While these radars provide high-resolution spatial and temporal precipitation data, the accuracy of precipitation estimates is highly dependent on distance from the radar. While verification shows good comparisons between radar-derived estimates such as National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) Stage IV QPE and observations, comparisons have not been analyzed as a function of distance from nearest radar. Additional analyses of High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model data have been performed to determine the effectiveness of including a short-term modeled precipitation forecast. In this case, the root mean squared error (RMSE) and mean squared error of HRRR precipitation values, along with QPEs are being analyzed in comparison to distance from radar. Meanwhile, the rise in precision agriculture has led to the rise in sub-field level prescriptions for fertilizer and pesticides built upon variables such as soil moisture. As such, accurate analyses of soil moisture are necessary to optimize agricultural production and food security. As soil moisture estimates are largely derived from precipitation estimates, it is necessary to understand the full spatial uncertainties of QPEs and modeled precipitation to provide the best possible inputs. This work investigates the combination of radar-derived precipitation estimates, modeled precipitation, and in-situ measurements as a means of error reduction. Potential mitigation strategies and techniques are explored, as well as any limitations related to the quantity of radar sites over a geographical area. This work utilizes the North Dakota Agricultural Weather Network (NDAWN), radar derived QPE, and HRRR precipitation forecasts for the growing season months of May through September. Preliminary results of a weighted precipitation forecast model from the years 2015-2024 have been established and are used as a historical baseline against which 2025-2026 precipitation estimates will be evaluated.

493352.title: Preparing for Climate-Driven Migration: Insights and Strategies for Receiving Communities
493352.authors: Mona Behl, William and Mary's Batten School and VIMS, Gloucester Point, VA
493352.abstract: As climate change and extreme weather events intensify, an increasing number of individuals are compelled to relocate, shifting national attention toward the unique dynamics of receiving communities. Funded by the National Science Foundation’s Coastlines and People (NSF CoPe) program, the People on the Move in a Changing Climate (PEMOCC) Research Coordination Network fosters cross-sector collaboration to address the socioeconomic and resilience consequences of climate-induced human mobility in U.S. coastal and Great Lakes regions. This presentation outlines core findings from PEMOCC’s national initiatives—including a foundational 2024 national workshop in Corvallis, Oregon—and highlights frameworks for understanding how communities absorb and integrate newcomers. While receiving communities often face significant pressures, such as heightened demand for housing, healthcare, education, and physical infrastructure alongside potential social and cultural tensions, they can also experience substantial benefits. These advantages include a revitalized workforce that mitigates labor shortages, economic growth, cultural enrichment, and increased diversity. Drawing from these insights, this talk explores critical issues affecting receiving communities, with a particular focus on local planning, community-led resilience, social networks, and equity. Attendees will gain a better understanding of what it means to be a receiving community, the multifaceted challenges and opportunities involved, and essential tools, resources, and future action items required for researchers and practitioners to support communities anticipating or experiencing an influx of climate-displaced populations.

493353.title: Extending ARM Observations for Boundary-Layer Studies
493353.authors: Nicki L. Hickmon, ANL, Lemont, IL; ANL, Lemont, IL; and J. M. Comstock, A. Theisen, J. H. Mather, and G. Prakash
493353.abstract: The U.S. Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility is developing a new portable profiling system capability designed to provide easily relocatable, integrated observations of the atmospheric boundary layer and its interactions with the surface. Two systems are planned to complement the next ARM Mobile Facility 2 (AMF2) deployment by enabling measurements at distributed pre-determined locations, within 150 km of the AMF2 main site, for weeks at a time. This capability is intended to provide users additional observations for characterizing the spatial variability and evolution of boundary-layer structure, thermodynamics, winds, clouds, precipitation, and surface forcing. This highly mobile, trailer-based platform will integrate power, data acquisition, and communications to deploy where there is limited infrastructure. These coordinated measurements will provide vertically resolved thermodynamic structure, boundary-layer depth, winds, and precipitation measurements while supporting development of merged retrievals and gridded data products. Integration with ARM data standards and value-added products will facilitate utilization of measurements with other field campaigns measurements, remote sensing networks, models, and potentially future autonomous observing systems.

493360.title: CREDIT Gen 2: The Future of ML Weather Prediction Is Coupled and Composable
493360.authors: David John Gagne II, Computational and Information Systems Lab, Boulder, CO; NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and C. Becker, J. Schreck, and K. Yang
493360.abstract: The first generation of ML weather prediction models focused on predicting larger scale features of the global atmosphere and demonstrated significant prediction accuracy improvements at this task. Tackling the frontiers of weather prediction across timescales from convection to teleconnections will require more than bigger data and models. It requires a new foundation for efficiently coupling Earth system components together and composing physics and machine learning operations together in clever ways to promote both improved predictions and understanding. At NCAR, we have built the second generation of the Community Research Earth Digital Intelligence Twin (CREDIT), an open platform for developing ML Earth system prediction emulators. CREDIT Generation 2 focuses on adding reproducible physics transformations and constraints throughout the pipeline, reducing latency bottlenecks, and improving the user experience. Composable PyTorch physics transforms both before and after the ML model enable direct alignment of grids, calculation of derived quantities, and differentiable operations through the entire pipeline. Registries for pipeline components allow users to connect custom objects into CREDIT config files without having to modify the CREDIT source code, allowing it to be used purely as a foundational library for further modeling research. CREDIT Generation 2 is already being used to train a new generation of emulators across the Earth system, including paired satellite and radar nowcasting, coupled atmospheric chemistry with forced emissions, and coupled atmosphere ocean models. CREDIT Gen 2 has enabled significant speedups and accuracy improvements and has enabled even undergrads to reduce their time to science. Examples of CREDIT Gen 2 use cases will be demonstrated in the presentation, and plans for further development will be discussed.

493361.title: The Origins of the NCAR Dropsonde Program
493361.abstract: The dropsonde systems developed at NCAR made remote and dangerous regions of the atmosphere accessible to previously impossible in situ observations of the thermodynamic and kinematic state. The origins of this technology date back to the 1960s, when NCAR scientists recognized that measurements of wind profiles over the oceans, which cover two thirds of the planet’s surface, are essential to the understanding of large-scale atmospheric dynamics. The development of global radionavigation systems (Omega and LORAN) in the 1950s and 1960s opened new possibilities for measuring winds using dropsondes especially over open oceans. A key advance was the retransmission of Omega and later LORAN radionavigation signals to measure wind profiles below the airborne platform, either from aircraft or balloons. Equally important was the design of dropsondes that could withstand the launch from fast-moving aircraft, or from cold-soaked balloons that floated in the upper troposphere/lower stratosphere for weeks. In the early 1970s, three independent programs developed dropsondes at NCAR. Two aircraft-borne programs targeted atmospheric dynamics over the tropical Atlantic as well as hail-producing thunderstorms. A third balloon-borne program targeted equatorial large-scale observations. While the dropsondes developed for the National Hail Research Experiment (NHRE) were not successful, the dropsondes designed for the Global Atmospheric Research Programme (GARP) Atlantic Tropical Experiment (GATE) laid the foundation for the dropsonde program that continues strong over 50 years later. During GATE, three aircraft launched 412 NCAR dropsondes, which yielded the first wind measurements below the aircraft flight level over open oceans. This program was so successful that Robert Simpson, then at the University of Virginia, commented: "I think the dropwindsonde developed at NCAR is one of the really important instrumental developments of recent years. Surely it is the route all operational reconnaissance aircraft should go in the future for comprehensive data acquisition." Following GATE, NCAR worked with NOAA and the Air Force to add dropsonde observations to operational hurricane surveillance missions, dramatically improving the value of these missions for predicting such dangerous storms. The long-duration Carrier Balloon System (CBS), which was built at NCAR at the same time, conducted several test flights and two larger deployments at Kourou, French Guiana. The last flights in 1975 successfully demonstrated the capabilities of this balloon-borne dropsonde system; however, this program was discontinued in favor of the aircraft-deployed dropsonde system. Today, this idea is implemented by several commercial companies. Well into the 1990s, improvements to the Omega and LORAN sondes and to the sensor technology laid a strong technical and scientific foundation that established NCAR as the leader in dropsonde technology worldwide. The next generation of the NCAR-developed technology started using Global Navigation Satellite System signals for an even better determination of winds and was adopted on research aircraft around the world.

493363.title: Using Small Drone Data to Analyze Low-Level Saharan Dust
493363.authors: Madison Anne Turner, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and S. W. Freeman, T. A. Gobble, K. Britton, N. M. Falk, C. A. Neumaier, M. Nieto-Caballero, R. J. Perkins, S. C. van den Heever, R. Zhou, and L. D. Grant
493363.abstract: The Saharan Air Layer (SAL) remains largely unobserved within the lower marine boundary layer (MBL) despite its impact on Earth’s radiative balance, severe weather, and cloud formation. During the summer of 2025, the Relating Atlantic Marine Convection, Ice Nuclei and Cold pools (RAM-CINC) team collected thermodynamic and cold pool data in the Atlantic Ocean MBL using small multirotor drones. Additional measurements included aerosol concentrations and size distributions, aerosol filter samples, and surface microlayer water and rainwater samples for analysis of ice-nucleating particles. During the campaign, two Saharan dust events were observed on July 8th and July 14th, 2025, providing an opportunity to measure the thermodynamic impact of the SAL on the lower MBL. The drones measured thermodynamic changes in the lower MBL during SAL days, compared to days surrounding SAL events. Average temperatures increased by approximately 3 K compared to the preceding day and the days following each dust event, suggesting that a combination of the radiative properties of SAL dust and the strong inversion at the top of the boundary layer associated with SAL contributed to warming in the lower MBL. HYSPLIT back-trajectories indicated that Saharan dust was transported downward from the free troposphere to within 250 m of the ocean surface during the measurement period. Water vapor mixing ratios showed a similar trend to temperature, increasing on both July 8th and July 14th compared to the surrounding days. These observations suggest that the SAL significantly changes the thermodynamics of the lower MBL.

493364.title: Order-Based Procflow : The Foundational Building Block of GeoIPS 2.0
493364.authors: Srikanth Gampa, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and J. E. Solbrig, G. Uttmark, E. Rose, C. McClelland, M. Surratt, C. Camacho, C. Selman, and A. Thorpe
493364.abstract: This presents the Order-Based Procflow (OBP), the foundational building block of the Geolocated Information Processing System v2.0 (GeoIPS).
