The OBP enables users to define processing pipelines as declarative YAML Workflows plugins composed of reusable plugin steps. By separating the Workflow orchestration from underlying complex code implementation, it empowers meteorologists and scientists to focus on the science rather than writing code from scratch. GeoIPS users can build complex satellite meteorological imagery products and analyses through configuration, with flexibility to integrate their own algorithms into GeoIPS or incorporate GeoIPS as a modular component into their existing scripts or Workflows. The OBP builds on Xarray's DataTree to hierarchically organize datasets and metadata. It also captures provenance information for intermediate and nested steps processing results throughout the workflow. This unified representation enables seamless data exchange between processing steps while naturally supporting nested workflows, allowing complex processing pipelines to be composed of smaller, reusable workflow components. As a result, developers can encapsulate common functionality, improve code reuse, and construct sophisticated processing chains with minimal duplication. This is an added advantage as GeoIPS’s plugin-based architecture already enables new algorithms, sensors, and products to be integrated while maintaining a consistent execution framework. By combining a hierarchical data model, reusable nested workflows, and hardware-agnostic execution, the OBP serves as the foundational building block of GeoIPS 2.0. It provides a scalable and extensible framework for developing next-generation Earth observation processing systems while improving maintainability, reproducibility, and scientific collaboration. The OBP is currently in the validation process to replace the legacy workflows used operationally by U.S. the Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) Marine Meteorology Division. GeoIPS is an open-source, plugin-based framework for scientific discovery, near real-time (NRT) applications, and operational data processing. It comes with a variety of pre-built plugins for reading, manipulating, and writing data. Its plugin architecture allows scientists and developers to build their own plugins without editing the main GeoIPS code. These plugins can be used either by importing them in Python scripts/packages for scientific use or combined in configurable, human-readable workflows to create reproducible, infrastructure-as-code pipelines for NRT applications.

493366.title: Long-Term Regional Trends In Lightning across the U.S.
493366.authors: Clifford F. Mass, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and J. Baars, K. S. Virts, and R. H. Holzworth
493366.abstract: Understanding the regional trends in lightning frequency is important for many reasons, including the role of lightning in initiating wildfires over the western U.S. This presentation will present lightning trends over extended periods (from decadal to ~50 years) using two networks: the University of Washington WWLLN (World Wide Lightning Location Network) and the Vaisala NLFD (National Lightning Detection Network) collections. Trends in surface-station thunder reports will also be evaluated. This presentation will describe lightning trends over the continental U.S., examining both regional and seasonal trends.

493371.title: Improving Week 3-4 Precipitation Forecasts by Leveraging Forecasts-of-Opportunity Identified via Explainable Machine Learning
493371.abstract: Accurate and reliable subseasonal precipitation forecasts provide sufficient lead-time to the public, water resource managers, and the energy and agriculture sectors. However, Week 3–4 precipitation prediction remains particularly challenging due to limited model skill and large forecast uncertainty. Building on recent work demonstrating that machine learning (ML) can identify predictable climate states that result in subseasonal forecasts-of-opportunity, this project applies eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to detect these forecasts-of-opportunity and to quantify associated uncertainty in Week 3–4 precipitation anomalies for Miami, Florida. We conduct numerous experiments spanning three ML architectures, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a Vision Transformer (ViT), and a hybrid CNN-ViT, each trained under two data regimes: (1) solely on ERA5 reanalysis, and (2) pre-trained on 9 members of a 10-member ensemble of high-resolution CESM historical simulations via the MESACLIP Project before fine-tuning on ERA5. This approach aims to isolate the impact of transfer learning from large climate datasets and to evaluate whether transformer self-attention offers complementary interpretability to CNN-based feature extraction. XAI attribution in the CNNs reveals that high-skill windows coincide with large-scale climate features such as El Niño–Southern Oscillation and the Gulf Stream, while lower-skill time frames are characterized by the disappearance of these coherent signals. Attention-based attribution is used to test whether self-attention maps reveal additional sources of predictability beyond those captured by the preliminary CNN architecture. Together, this multi-architecture, XAI-driven approach aims to advance predictability and uncertainty quantification across S2S timescales while supporting the development of operational precipitation forecasting tools for decision-making in vulnerable regions such as South Florida.

493373.title: Keynote Speaker Victor Gensini: Translating Severe Convective Storm Science into Actionable Risk
493373.authors: Victor A. Gensini, Northern Illinois Univ., DeKalb, IL
493373.abstract: Severe convective storms (SCSs)—including large hail, tornadoes, and damaging straight-line winds—generate persistent and highly volatile losses for insurers, reinsurers, property owners, and communities. SCS losses emerge from the intersection of hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and human behavior, each of which is evolving on different spatial and temporal scales. Consequently, increasing losses cannot be attributed to a single cause, and historical loss experience alone may not adequately represent future risk. This keynote will examine the current scientific understanding of severe convective storm risk and its application to insurance and financial decision-making. Topics will include the strengths and limitations of historical storm reports, radar-derived climatologies, environmental proxies, machine-learning methods, and convection-permitting climate simulations. Particular attention will be given to the spatial and seasonal variability of hail, tornado, and wind hazards; the challenge of representing localized and tail-risk events; and the evidence for, and uncertainty surrounding, changes in severe convective storm environments under a warming climate. Drawing upon research and industry engagement through the Center for Interdisciplinary Research on Convective Storms (CIRCS), the keynote will conclude with pathways of collaboration among atmospheric scientists, catastrophe modelers, insurers, reinsurers, engineers, and public-sector partners. Such collaboration is essential for converting improved understanding of storms into more credible risk estimates and more resilient communities.

493374.title: Update on UXarray: A Community Driven Python Package for the Analysis Kilometer-Scale Model Outputs on Native Unstructured Grids
493374.authors: John Clyne, NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and H. Chen, N. W. Cherukuru, O. Eroglu, R. L. Jacob, R. Jain, B. P. Medeiros, P. Ullrich, A. Virapongse, C. M. Zarzycki, C. Dupuis, S. Evans, and D. Nelson
493374.abstract: UXarray is an open-source scientific Python package that provides analysis, visualization, and post-processing capabilities for Earth system data defined on horizontally unstructured, kilometer-scale global grids. UXarray supports output from several weather and climate models, including MPAS, CAM-SE, E3SM, ICON, and HEALPix-based models. By operating directly on native unstructured meshes, UXarray eliminates the need to resample data to regular grids, preserving the native representation of modern Earth system models. UXarray extends the widely used Xarray package by inheriting its core functionality and providing unstructured-grid-aware implementations, allowing many existing structured-grid analysis workflows to be adapted to unstructured grids with minimal code changes. UXarray is designed to integrate broadly with the scientific Python ecosystem. Its visualization capabilities leverage the HoloViz stack, including HoloViews, Datashader, and GeoViews, to enable scalable and interactive exploration of large unstructured datasets, while also supporting traditional Matplotlib and Cartopy workflows. These capabilities can be used both to explore mesh structure, and to visualize scientific data using color plots, contours, and related techniques. Through its integration with Xarray, UXarray also benefits from the broader Xarray ecosystem, including Dask for parallel computation and support for cloud-ready data formats such as Zarr. Together, these capabilities provide a familiar Python-based environment for scientists working with increasingly complex atmospheric, land, and oceanic model output. As the resolution and size of unstructured datasets continue to increase, particularly with the emergence of global storm-resolving models, scalable implementations of core analysis operations are essential. UXarray uses Numba, a just-in-time compiler that translates Python code to machine code, to accelerate spatial and geometric operations such as bounding-box calculations, intersection algorithms, and rasterization. This allows computationally intensive Python routines to approach the performance of compiled languages while retaining the productivity and maintainability of a Python-based implementation. UXarray is developed using an open-source, community-driven development model in which users and contributors participate throughout the project lifecycle, from establishing the roadmap and designing new capabilities to software development, testing, and documentation. In this talk, we will provide an overview of UXarray's current analysis, visualization, and post-processing capabilities; demonstrate how it integrates with established scientific Python workflows; and describe the project's development roadmap. We will also discuss upcoming community engagement and training opportunities, supported by our recent NSF POSE award.

493375.title: Atmospheric Blocking in the Great Lakes: From Scientific Understanding to Operational Needs
493375.authors: Claire Pettersen, Univ. of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI; and A. L. Hutson, D. M. Wright, L. Fry, and A. H. Young
493375.abstract: The Cooperative Institute for Great Lakes Research (CIGLR), a NOAA Cooperative Institute, recently sponsored the Great Lakes Summit on Atmospheric Blocking; providing a collaborative forum to advance the scientific understanding, monitoring, and prediction of the downscale impacts of persistent large-scale circulation regimes. These systems are often classified as “atmospheric blocks”, and include diverse high pressure patterns such as Omega and Rex blocking, which can strongly influence weather and climate variability across the Great Lakes region. These quasi-stationary atmospheric features can stall synoptic weather systems for days to weeks, increasing the frequency of occurrence, duration, and severity of high-impact events such as heat waves, heavy and continuous precipitation, flooding, drought, extended periods of poor air quality, and cold-air outbreaks leading to lake-effect snowfall. Through their influence on lake-atmosphere interactions, hydrologic processes, and regional climate, atmospheric blocking events have far-reaching implications for water resources, lake levels, ecosystems, infrastructure, transportation, agriculture, energy, and public safety. During the Summit, participants organize into break-out groups that are composed of complementary expertise on Great Lakes processes to strengthen regional understanding of the science of atmospheric blocking events, impacts, and forecast and operational needs. This outcome of this Summit is designed to strengthen Research-to-Operations (R2O) pathways by bringing together academics, operational forecasters, and model developers from a variety of backgrounds and expertise to identify current scientific capabilities, operational needs, and future research priorities to advance a national weather ready framework and improve societal outcomes.

493381.title: Development of an Adaptive sUAS-Enabled Atmospheric Observing Infrastructure for Persistent Boundary-Layer Measurements Using Cooperative Tether-Riding Robotic Profilers
493381.authors: Daniel A. Rico, University of Nebraska - Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and J. M. Bradley and F. Munoz-Arriola
493381.abstract: Atmospheric processes in the lower planetary boundary layer (PBL) govern the exchange of heat, moisture, trace gases, and energy between the Earth's surface and the free atmosphere. Yet, these processes remain among the most challenging to observe with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution. Existing observing systems, including eddy covariance towers, Mesonet stations, radiosondes, remote sensing platforms, and conventional small uncrewed aircraft systems (sUAS), each provide essential but inherently incomplete views of the PBL. Fixed infrastructure offers persistent measurements but is spatially constrained, whereas mobile platforms provide greater flexibility at the expense of endurance, revisit frequency, or continuous vertical sampling. Consequently, rapidly evolving atmospheric phenomena such as nocturnal temperature inversion formation, moisture stratification, intermittent turbulent mixing, and localized carbon dioxide accumulation remain difficult to characterize using existing observational strategies alone. Addressing this observational gap requires sensing systems capable of autonomously redistributing observational resources in response to evolving atmospheric conditions. To address this observational need, we present an adaptive sUAS-enabled atmospheric observing infrastructure built on the Tethered Aircraft Uncrewed System (TAUS), a persistent power-over-tether small uncrewed aircraft system capable of sustained lower-atmospheric operation. Rather than mounting environmental sensors directly on the sUAS platform, where measurements may be biased by rotor wash and other platform-induced disturbances, the observing infrastructure employs multiple autonomous tether-riding robotic profilers (TetherBots) that traverse a shared, aircraft-hoisted power tether. Each TetherBot serves as a mobile node within an autonomously coordinated atmospheric sensing network. The robotic profilers are equipped with actively aspirated, triply redundant, consensus-integrated ambient temperature, relative humidity, and barometric pressure sensors, providing robust altitude-resolved meteorological measurements while remaining mechanically decoupled from the aerial platform. Collectively, these robotic profilers transform a single power tether into a persistent, vertically distributed, and dynamically reconfigurable observing infrastructure capable of reallocating its measurement geometry in response to evolving boundary-layer conditions. Unlike conventional vertical profilers that repeatedly traverse the atmospheric column, the adaptive atmospheric observing infrastructure continuously redistributes its mobile sensing nodes based upon real-time sensor feedback and network topology. Rather than maintaining fixed sampling intervals throughout the atmospheric column, individual TetherBots autonomously reposition along the shared power tether to increase measurement density within dynamically active regions of atmospheric interest, including developing temperature inversions, moisture stratification, intermittent turbulent mixing, and localized trace-gas plumes. This adaptive sUAS sampling strategy concentrates observational resources where evolving atmospheric structure produces the greatest scientific uncertainty while maintaining persistent coverage throughout the remainder of the atmospheric column. By reducing revisit times within rapidly evolving atmospheric features and increasing spatiotemporal sampling density where thermodynamic gradients are strongest, the adaptive atmospheric observing infrastructure provides a dynamically reconfigurable representation of the lower atmosphere that is not achievable through static instrumentation or sequential single-platform profiling alone. The adaptive atmospheric observing infrastructure is designed to integrate with, rather than replace, established atmospheric observing systems through coordinated field validation and complementary deployment strategies. Field deployments evaluate altitude-resolved measurements by comparing them with collocated eddy covariance towers, Mesonet stations, conventional sUAS profiles, and complementary reference instrumentation to characterize measurement agreement, quantify observational uncertainty, and assess the scientific value of adaptive robotic sampling. By integrating persistent mobile observations with established observing infrastructure, the adaptive atmospheric observing infrastructure improves characterization of transient boundary-layer processes, including inversion development, moisture stratification, intermittent turbulent transport, and vertically resolved carbon dioxide variability. These complementary observations support atmospheric field campaigns and investigations into boundary-layer evolution, ecosystem-atmosphere exchange, and atmospheric transport processes that remain difficult to resolve with a single observing system. Beyond the immediate sensing capabilities demonstrated here, this work establishes a foundation for a new class of adaptive atmospheric observing infrastructure capable of persistently responding to evolving environmental conditions. Future deployments may integrate additional sensing modalities, coordinated multi-tether observing networks, and hybrid sampling strategies to support atmospheric field campaigns across agricultural, urban, forested, coastal, and other environmentally complex landscapes. The ability to dynamically allocate observational resources in both space and time has the potential to integrate with and complement existing meteorological observing networks, enhance gaseous carbon monitoring, improve characterization of lower-atmospheric processes, and provide high-resolution datasets for numerical weather prediction, ecosystem science, and climate research. By bridging persistent atmospheric observing infrastructure with autonomous robotics and persistent sUAS technologies, this work represents a step toward intelligent atmospheric in situ observatories capable of adapting to the atmosphere as it evolves rather than observing it from fixed or distant locations alone.

493383.title: The Impacts of a Storm Merger on Rear Flank Downdraft Formation and Updraft Intensification During Supercell Tornadogenesis
493383.authors: Adam J. French, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD
493383.abstract: Past research has shown that tornadogenesis in supercell thunderstorms is often observed after a merger with another thunderstorm. In particular, mergers that occur near the rear flank of the supercell appear to be particularly favorable for tornado formation. However, the physical processes that explain why some mergers may lead to tornado formation are still poorly understood. This research used dual polarized Doppler radar data from the National Weather Service and a high-resolution numerical simulation to examine a storm merger that produced an EF-3 tornado near Hermosa, SD on 13 June 2016. The tornado formed as a segment of a quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) merged with the rear flank of a developing supercell thunderstorm. Doppler radar data indicated that tornadogenesis occurred shortly after the QLCS outflow boundary overtook the rear flank of the supercell. As the line of 40 dBZ radar reflectivity in the QLCS merged with the rear flank of the supercell, a region of enhanced inbound Doppler velocities developed within the merged outflow in the vicinity of the supercell’s hook echo. This region of strong velocity progressed northeastward toward the supercell’s inflow notch and evolved into a tornado vortex signature. Mid-level radar scans indicated this velocity feature was preceded by weak mid-level radial convergence, consistent with a downdraft. Following the merger, a pronounced differential reflectivity (ZDR) column and low-level ZDR arc were observed within the supercell, and it’s mid-level mesocyclone rapidly strengthened. These signatures are consistent with the supercell’s updraft strengthening following the merger with the QLCS. The case was also simulated using a high-resolution (333 m horizontal grid spacing) Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulation. The simulation captured many of the salient features of the case, including the overall merger geometry and the development of a near-surface vortex that evolved similarly to the observed tornado. In the simulation, the vortex formed on the leading edge of a downdraft that developed along the rear flank of the supercell as the line segment merged with it. As air from the downdraft descended toward the surface and the gust front surged eastward, an elongated region of vertical vorticity developed along the gust front and quickly evolved into a discrete vortex. The vortex intensified further as it moved under the supercell’s updraft to the north of the surging outflow. As this is occurred, the low-level (0-3 km) updraft associated with the merging line segment overtook the supercell. This created a strong, broad, low-level updraft within the merged system that promoted further vortex intensification via vorticity stretching. The stormscale evolution seen in the radar observations and numerical simulation is conceptually consistent with tornadogenesis in a discrete supercell thunderstorm. Near-surface vertical vorticity was first produced by a rear flank downdraft and then stretched to tornado intensity by the low-level updraft. In this case, the timing, location, and structure of the rear flank downdraft suggest that it was connected to the storm merger. The subsequent updraft merger between the line segment and supercell led to a rapid intensification of the merged system’s low-level updraft, facilitating stretching of the near-surface vorticity to tornado strength. Thus, for this particular case, the storm merger modulated processes common in supercell tornadogenesis rather than representing a unique tornadogenesis pathway.

493385.title: On Fifty+ Years of Weather Decision Processes and Technology (Invited Presentation)
493385.abstract: In this serious yet light-hearted keynote address, Matt Fronzak will look back on his 50+ years of experiences in the world of aviation weather, beginning with being bitten by the aviation bug in the 1960s, his introduction to the science and voodoo art of meteorology in the early 1970s, putting the wonder of the Limited Fine Mesh (LFM) model to work in the late 1970s, the magic of advanced automation and the changes it wrought from the 1980s-2020s, the power of collaboration from the 1990s through the 2020s, and the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML) in the mid 2020s. He will identify what he considers pearls of wisdom discovered along the way and leave behind several key open questions, some of which his heroes, mentors, collaborators and friends will attempt to wrestle to the ground in other session presentations.

493389.title: When Does Machine Learning Improve Rainfall Gap Filling? An Evaluation for Pacific Climate Records
493389.authors: Hannah Marley, Earth Sciences New Zealand, Wellington, New zealand; and T. Meyers and S. O'Neill
493389.abstract: Across the Pacific, missing observations, or gaps, are a persistent feature of many meteorological datasets. This challenge is especially relevant for automatic weather station records, which provide valuable high-frequency observations but may contain gaps caused by instrument and communications failures. Station remoteness, difficult access, and limited resources for maintenance and repairs can also make maintaining continuous observations challenging. In a region where rainfall observations are often sparse and climate variability is high, these gaps can substantially reduce the usefulness of otherwise valuable high-frequency rainfall records for climate analysis and climate-service applications, including the calculation of rainfall totals, wet-day frequencies, and rainfall extremes. This study will evaluate statistical and machine-learning approaches for imputing gaps in 10-minute rainfall records, with the aim of identifying methods that are both accurate and practical for use by Pacific National Meteorological and Hydrological Services. Artificial gaps of increasing duration will be introduced into complete periods of observed rainfall so that imputed values can be evaluated against known observations. Several infilling approaches will be applied to the same artificial gaps and compared: a simple method based on rainfall at a nearby station, multiple linear regression, and tree-based machine-learning methods such as Random Forest and XGBoost. Performance will be evaluated across gap lengths and rainfall conditions using measures of prediction error, bias, wet/dry detection, accumulated rainfall, and performance during high-intensity rainfall. The study will test whether imputation skill declines systematically with increasing gap length, whether nonlinear machine-learning methods provide meaningful improvements over simpler approaches, and whether differences among methods become more pronounced during wet and high-intensity rainfall periods. Rather than assuming that a single machine-learning method will be universally preferable, the study will determine when additional model complexity provides sufficient benefit to justify its use. This work is currently in progress, with results to be used to develop practical guidance for selecting rainfall-infilling approaches according to gap characteristics and data availability. The findings could support more consistent use of incomplete rainfall records for climate monitoring, analysis, and data rescue across data-sparse Pacific observing networks. More broadly, the work aims to demonstrate how applied machine-learning methods may help improve the completeness and usability of existing Pacific observational datasets and expand their value for climate analysis and climate services.

493393.title: Addressing Extreme Heat Impacts in Oklahoma City: Longitudinal Coproduction Between Scientists and Stakeholders
493393.authors: Rachel E. Riley, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. Bertrand, T. O. Bowman, C. Cruickshank, C. A. Fiebrich, E. Kuster, E. H. Marold, G. McManus, D. Na-Yemeh, S. Terry-Cobo, and A. Yang
493393.abstract: Extreme heat is a persistent hazard in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. On average, the air temperature reaches 90°F about 70 days each year and 100°F about 10 days each year. During the record-breaking year of 2011, the city experienced 63 days of ≥ 100°F temperatures. Though the surrounding population is moderately used to the heat, impacts to people and infrastructure still occur. Extreme heat causes an increase in heat stroke and all forms of cardiovascular diseases to worsen. It also causes roads to buckle, water main breaks, and stresses electricity grids. So far, long term warming trends in the Oklahoma City area have largely shown up as an increase in winter and overnight low temperatures. Climate projections indicate that by mid-century the area could see 10 to 30 more days of ≥ 100°F temperatures each year. Over the last decade, city staff (stakeholders) have engaged with several scientists about extreme heat and other climate-related topics that affect Oklahoma City residents and visitors. Scientists provided climate data, research products, and information to the stakeholders, and the stakeholders used the information to inform planning and mitigation efforts. Enabling factors for this longitudinal coproduction include stakeholder interest in the subject, baseline federal grant funding, leveraging organizational resources, and framing problems and solutions in ways that are relevant to city departmental contexts. Progress has been made not through a single project but multiple efforts over the years. These endeavors have been complementary and collaborative rather than duplicative. This presentation will describe how scientific information has informed planning and operations within the city. It will highlight a subset of coproduction activities, including the city’s first sustainability plan adaptOKC, a heat-mapping campaign, extreme heat tabletop exercise, and mayoral heat awareness proclamation. The presentation will conclude with the city’s plans for future projects and risk reduction initiatives followed by recommendations for scientists who desire to have their work inform more real-world applications at local scales.

493398.title: Smoke Transport and Radiative Forcings within Wildfire-Generated Thunderstorms
493398.authors: Phoebe C. Lin, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and S. M. Saleeby, S. D. Miller, and S. C. Van Den Heever
493398.abstract: Pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) are vigorous convective storms driven by wildfire heating which can influence local atmospheric dynamics, impact wildfire behavior, and even start new fires by lightning ignition. Wildfires serve as significant sources of sensible heat fluxes and smoke aerosols, both of which impact the dynamics and microphysics of pyroCb anvils. Strong updrafts driven by the sensible heat fluxes from fires can transport smoke vertically into the stratosphere, where it may persist for several months, impacting the atmospheric radiative balance. Smoke also modifies the radiative forcing of pyroCb anvils through both direct and indirect aerosol effects. Smoke particles absorb radiation, thereby warming the layer in which they reside. They can also serve as cloud condensation nuclei, leading to numerous but small cloud droplets and subsequent cloud-top ice crystals, thereby impacting the anvil cloud albedo. The opposing warming and cooling effects lead to uncertainty in the radiative impacts of pyroCb. In this study, we focus on the effects of fire characteristics on stratospheric smoke transport and anvil cloud-radiative forcing. We do so by running a suite of high-resolution idealized model simulations of pyroCb storms with the Regional Atmospheric Modeling System (RAMS). Sensitivity simulations are conducted by varying fire heating rates, smoke aerosol fluxes and sizes, and convective environments, in order to explore the impacts of a wide variety of fire, aerosol and environmental conditions on pyroCb storm properties. We analyze the effects of these changing variables on the cloud lifecycles and hydrometeor evolution, as well as their subsequent effects on the anvil radiative forcing. Areas of smoke are found to heat the lower levels of the atmosphere, leading to a redistribution of heat in the vertical with implications for atmospheric static stability and convective suppression. Furthermore, the enhanced reflection of incoming solar radiation by small cloud-top ice crystals found in pyrocumulus is found to dominate the cloud-radiative effect. These findings may improve our understanding and predictability of the impacts of pyroCb on stratospheric processes and the atmospheric radiative balance.

493400.title: Madden–Julian Oscillation Modulation of East Pacific Easterly Wave Evolution and the Wave-to-Tropical Cyclone Transition
493400.authors: Yu-Cian Tsai, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and E. D. Maloney
493400.abstract: East Pacific easterly waves (EWs) are the important precursors of tropical cyclones (TCs) over the eastern Pacific, making their accurate representation essential for subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecasts. However, recent evaluations of NOAA's Unified Forecast System (UFS) indicate that systematic biases in simulated EW activity remain a major source of forecast uncertainty. Although previous studies have shown that both EW activity and TC genesis are enhanced during the convectively active phases of the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO), the physical processes through which the MJO preconditions EWs for subsequent tropical cyclogenesis remain incompletely understood. Using ERA5 reanalysis for 1984–2023, we investigate how the MJO modifies the large-scale dynamical and thermodynamical environment governing EW growth to establish a physical framework for interpreting these forecast biases. EW tracking reveals substantially greater wave activity during wet MJO phases than during dry and neutral phases, including higher track density, longer-lived disturbances, and enhanced synoptic-scale eddy kinetic energy. Composite analyses show that wet MJO conditions are characterized by enhanced low-level vorticity, stronger meridional moisture gradients, and a background flow more favorable for barotropic instability. These environmental changes strengthen moisture–vortex instability, resulting in greater EW amplification before and during genesis. A moist static energy (MSE) budget further reveals that the interaction between meridional wind anomalies and the background meridional MSE gradient provides the primary energy source for wave growth, whereas interactions with the perturbation MSE gradient act to damp the disturbance. As EWs mature, enhanced deep convection produces stronger longwave cloud-radiative heating that provides an additional diabatic energy source, enabling mature waves to more effectively extract energy from the background environment and sustain continued growth favorable for TC development. These results support a two-stage mechanism linking the MJO to tropical cyclogenesis over the eastern Pacific. The MJO first establishes a large-scale environment favorable for moisture–vortex instability and accelerated EW growth, after which cloud-radiative feedback sustains and intensifies mature disturbances, increasing their likelihood of transitioning into TCs. This observational framework provides a physical interpretation for recent UFS findings that EW activity is highly sensitive to the background moisture environment and offers process-based diagnostics for evaluating and improving the representation of tropical wave evolution and wave-to-TC transition in S2S forecast systems.

493404.title: Recent Advances and a New Testbed for a Short-Term Tornado Prediction and Detection Model using Deep Learning Techniques
493404.authors: James M. Kurdzo, MIT Lincoln Laboratory, Lexington, MA; and T. C. Reis
493404.abstract: Weather radar remains the primary tool for real-time warning operations and has advanced in several ways, including the key additions of polarimetric data and Supplemental Adaptive Intra-Volume Low-Level Scan (SAILS) cuts. While tornado warning performance is much improved in recent decades, there continue to be high false alarm rates nationwide. Current radar-based tornado detection and warning algorithms are limited in their ability to provide useful human-machine teaming success, especially for rapidly developing tornadoes. This work aims to enhance forecaster situational awareness and tornado prediction capabilities by testing and evaluating the Intelligent Tornado Prediction Engine (ITORPE), a tornado detection and prediction algorithm based on deep neural networks. This presentation will detail recent updates to the open-source, radar-based TorNet dataset that drives ITORPE’s train/test pipeline, as well as improvements to tornado detection and prediction at 5-, 10-, and 15-minute lead times. Additionally, a new partnership with the United States Air Force (USAF) has enabled a real-time, non-operational, parallel testbed to evaluate ITORPE during Spring campaigns in both 2027 and 2028. Multiple USAF weather groups and operational squadrons will take part in the evaluations, leading to an accelerated, iterative research and development process, allowing us to directly engage with end-users, facilitating rapid prototyping and testing. Our partner squadrons operate specifically in regions prone to tornadoes, including responsibility for over 130 assets across the Southeast and the southern Plains. In addition to collecting qualitative feedback from end-users via detailed notes and post-event interviews, quantitative analyses of standard performance metrics against existing algorithms will provide critical data on the effectiveness of ITORPE in an operational environment.

493407.title: Investigating the Atmospheric and Land Surface Conditions Conducive for Non-Mesocyclonic Tornadoes
493407.authors: Ethan James Kerr, The University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and U. Nair
493407.abstract: Non-mesocyclonic tornadoes (i.e. landspouts and non-mesocyclonic waterspouts) are a meteorological phenomenon of limited research. While they cause minimal damage, non-mesocyclonic tornadoes provide a unique pathway for studying the influence of surface conditions on all tornadoes. It has long been hypothesized that changes in land use-land cover (LULC) have impacts on the morphology of tornadoes. Without the supercell processes that contribute to mesocyclonic tornadogenesis, many confounding variables contributing to vertical vorticity generation are absent in non-mesocyclone tornadoes. Since landspouts are less dynamically complex, the influence of surface conditions and land-atmosphere interactions can be more directly isolated and studied, which has implications on tornadoes more broadly. The authors hypothesize that surface conditions such as LULC can have an outsized impact on landspout tornadogenesis. Prior case studies have found that convergent boundaries caused by horizontal temperature and moisture gradients play an important role in landspout formation. LULC heterogeneity can generate or modulate these convergent boundaries. A climatology of landspout tornadoes has never been curated, nor has there been a systematic study of the atmospheric conditions and LULC conducive to their formation using a large sample. In this study, a climatology of over 1,100 landspout events documented by the National Weather Service since 1995 was compiled. Convective parameters from ERA5 reanalysis and the Rapid Refresh (RAP) model were compiled. With average 0-3 km CAPE of only 37 J/kg and average 0-1km lapse rates of 10 K/km across events, preliminary results indicate that anomalous lapse rates are more important in determining landspout environments. Using the National Land Cover Database (NLCD), a disproportionate amount of landspout events were found to occur over cultivated cropland as opposed to grassland. Initial analysis of GOES land surface temperature (LST) reveals a preference for landspouts over surfaces with elevated LST. Further analysis of surface fluxes, land cover/LST gradients, vegetation, and soil moisture with NASA remote sensing data is expected to yield more insight on if certain land surface conditions favor non-supercell tornadogenesis.

493409.title: Snow Sublimation-Driven Cold Pools in Marine Cold-Air Outbreaks: A Mechanism for Open-Cell Transition?
493409.authors: Steven K. Krueger, Univ.of Utah, SALT LAKE CITY, UT; and A. Raudzens Bailey and C. A. Yang
493409.abstract: Marine cold-air outbreaks, or CAOs, occur when frigid air streams off of sea ice or ice-covered land and flows out over exposed and relatively warm ocean waters. Under these conditions, the advection of cold air drives extreme sensible and latent heat fluxes, fueling convection and facilitating the development of complex and intricately structured cloud formations. Horizontal convective rolls, organized by moderate wind shear within a convective boundary layer, form streets—or quasi-regularly spaced rows—of clouds close to the ice edge. These “roll clouds” typically transition to large areas of deeper cumuliform (open cell) clouds downstream. Similar boundary-layer cloud transitions occur worldwide but under different thermodynamic and microphysical conditions. Unlike subtropical cloud transitions, marine CAO cloud transitions are characterized by much more extreme environmental conditions and complex microphysics. CAO clouds are also typically mixed phase which means that precipitation-size particles can grow by either vapor deposition or by the accretion of supercooled liquid. As a result, boundary-layer deepening and precipitation initiation proceed through pathways that differ substantially from (and are less well understood than) those in warmer environments. One hypothesis for the transition from closed to open-cell convection involves cold pools formed by snow sublimation. Once cold pools form, we propose that precipitation, cold pools, and convective updrafts become linked in a self-perpetuating cycle which maintains the open-cell structure. A key aspect of the proposed cycle is snow sublimation, which quantitatively depends on precipitation rate, surface temperature, and surface relative humidity. We will present a detailed analysis of snow sublimation and its relation to cold pools and subsequent updrafts in a Lagrangian LES of a marine CAO in the Norwegian Sea, under winter conditions similar to those that occurred during the COMBLE and CAESAR field programs. We will focus on determining the conditions that are most favorable for large snow sublimation rates.

493414.title: Evaluating Precipitation Characteristics in Different Storm Structures Using EXPRESS Stations
493414.authors: Ian Earley, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY; and S. Gunter
493414.abstract: Various forms of mobile meteorological instrumentation have been used to study severe and hazardous weather from the Great Plains to the Great Lakes. These often rapidly deployable research-grade weather stations have provided valuable data in transient events with short forecast horizons, such as landfalling hurricanes, the near-tornado environment, and intense lake effect snowstorms. The value of these systems is demonstrated not only in being able to capture highly localized and poorly sampled meteorological conditions, but also in maintaining data collection abilities when other systems that depend on grid power fail during extreme events. The valuable data collected by research-grade mobile meteorological instrumentation have been used to further the state of the science surrounding these hazardous events as well as contribute to more accurate numerical modeling. Through generous support from the National Science Foundation, the University of Louisville has been tasked with the development of a similar mobile instrumentation array that will focus on collecting in-situ characteristics of extreme precipitation across the Commonwealth of Kentucky and surrounding areas. This project is part of a larger effort to address climate resilience across Kentucky by exploiting a rich history of meteorological data as well as collecting targeted observations in hard-to-access areas of the state, such as the Eastern Appalachian region. This project, titled CLIMBS: Climate Resilience through Multidisciplinary Big Data Learning, Prediction and Building Response Systems, includes the development of rapidly deployable meteorological instrument towers as well as funding for an initial field project. The mobile towers, called EXPRESS stations (EXtreme PREcipitation Surface Stations), were designed to include an All-in-One weather sensor capable of measuring standard meteorological parameters, including a precipitation gauge for mobile rainfall totals. Precipitation characteristics are quantified by a Parsivel Present Weather Sensor manufactured by OTT HydroMet. This laser disdrometer can provide high-resolution drop size distribution, precipitation fall speed, and equivalent radar reflectivity data. This presentation introduces the full capabilities of the array and presents initial results from a Spring and Summer 2026 field project. Deployments of EXPRESS stations were conducted across the state of Kentucky and Ohio Valley region and limited to within a 150 km radius of WSR-88D radar sites within the region. Multiple convective modes such as single-cell pulse thunderstorms and mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) were targeted during the project. A combination of both in-situ and remotely sensed data were used to provide insight into convective processes that lead to flash flooding. Five Intensive Observation Periods (IOPs) were conducted, spanning from April-July. Preliminary comparisons of the data were conducted between each sensor within each EXPRESS station and against a nearby Kentucky Mesonet site. When compared to each other, the data from each sensor showed close agreement, with minimal differences between sensors. When compared to the Kentucky Mesonet site, the EXPRESS sensors showed good agreement with the Mesonet sensors. Individual events within the IOPs demonstrated large rainfall totals (e.g. > 80 mm) and high rain rates (e.g. > 30 mm/hr). These data will be compared to available radar data, in particular dual-polarimetric moments along with flash flood warning issuance. The synthesis of these different data types will ideally provide insight into characteristics of flash flooding rainfall. Keywords: Extreme Precipitation Characteristics, In-Situ Observations, Convective Modes, Flash Flooding

493418.title: AI - Explainability Does Not Imply Causality: Two Lessons from Causal Inference
493418.authors: Caren Marzban, University of Washington, SEATTLE, WA; and Y. Zhang, N. Bond, and M. B. Richman
493418.abstract: Explainability in AI is often based on correlations. As such, there is no assurance that an explainable pattern discovered by AI reflects true/physical processes. One obstacle in elevating a correlation to a causal relation is the phenomenon of confounding, wherein an association between two variables is observed only because they are both caused by another variable. This presentation summarizes two methods designed to account for such confounding. Both methods are based on what is called the potential outcomes framework in causal inference. While one method assumes that the confounding variable is known and observed, the second method assumes that it is known but unobserved.

493419.title: GLOBE for Research: Applying NASA Earth Science’s Crowdsourcing Capabilities for Atmospheric and Environmental Research
493419.authors: Marile Colon Robles, ADNET Systems Inc., NASA Langley Research Center, Hampton, VA; and T. M. Rogerson, A. D. Clark, and J. Taylor
493419.abstract: The Global Learning and Observations to Benefit the Environment (GLOBE) Program engages a global network of volunteers to collect standardized, open-access environmental data in support of NASA Earth science research priorities. Operating across Earth's spheres, GLOBE has provided millions of in situ observations since 1995. Data includes sky cover, cloud type, and almost 3 million sky and cloud photographs. There are additional data collection protocols for a variety of observables including surface and air temperature, phenology, water quality and land cover. All data are ingested in near-real-time and accessible within minutes of submission. Crowdsourced observations offer critical spatial and temporal flexibility, capturing atmospheric phenomena in regions and at scales often unreached by traditional, fixed surface station networks. The GLOBE community of volunteers is made up of students, teachers, and adults. This community includes nature enthusiasts, interpreters at national parks, families, and educators at museums and libraries. Observations are sent in through the GLOBE website or through the GLOBE Program’s GLOBE Observer app. Both methods use steps to maximize data quality through the data ingest process. Observations are received from all continents including Antarctica. Integrating citizen science into atmospheric analytics requires tailored methodologies to harness data volume while accounting for observational variability. To enable robust data fusion and machine learning application, the GLOBE platform generates curated, multi-source data packages that collocate volunteer ground observations directly with satellite overpasses (e.g., MODIS, VIIRS, GOES, OCI), and unique atmospheric events, such as solar eclipses and regional dust storms. Cloud reports include sky photographs from the volunteer’s point of view that can be used to study cloud scenes collocated to satellite data, or to detect unique atmospheric events. These fused datasets provide valuable ground-truth validation for remote sensing algorithms and atmospheric modeling. Beyond an archive exceeding millions of atmospheric observations, GLOBE provides a flexible framework for scientists to deploy custom, campaign-style data collection calls. Researchers can partner with NASA’s crowdsourcing team to design regional or global data calls tailored to specific research questions. Learn about past request examples such as requesting specialized sky obscuration photos to study blowing snow dynamics or timing observations at sunrise or sunset to advance algorithm development related to the solar terminator. This presentation outlines the data archive, science protocols, and data fusion capabilities of the GLOBE platform. Attendees will explore GLOBE data retrieval options including an API for integrating crowdsourced in situ observations into open-science cloud analytics, accessing pre-matched satellite-ground datasets, and collaborating with the GLOBE infrastructure to execute targeted data collection campaigns for Earth system research.

493424.title: Coverage and Verification Statistics of Tropical Cyclone Wind Fields by Synthetic Aperture Radar
493424.authors: Sydney Walters, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. Carstens
493424.abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) offers a precipitation-penetrating, high-resolution measurement of the tropical cyclone (TC) surface wind field, which may include the 34-, 50-, and 64-kt wind radii that define storm size and structure operationally. However, SAR sampling of any individual TC is irregular and orbit-dependent. It remains unclear how often a SAR overpass resolves the full tropical storm-force wind field of a TC, and how those retrievals compare against the best-track record. This study quantifies SAR coverage and verification statistics for TCs globally from 2015-2025, using NOAA STAR 3.0-km SAR wind products and a processing pipeline to identify qualifying SAR passes and extract wind radii estimates. Coverage is assessed for each wind radius threshold as the fraction of TC synoptic fixes captured by a qualifying SAR pass, stratified by best-track maximum sustained wind, basin, and year. Verification statistics compare SAR-derived R34, R50, and R64 against concurrent best-track values by quadrant, characterizing systematic bias and its sensitivity to storm intensity, size, and time offset between SAR pass and best-track fix. These coverage and verification statistics characterize the practical sampling limits of SAR for the full TC wind field, and the degree to which SAR-derived wind radii are consistent with operational best-track estimates. This is meant to assess SAR’s practical utility as a comprehensive source of TC structural information. As one such application, we apply SAR-derived wind radii to refine integrated kinetic energy (IKE) estimates from best-track wind radii, an effort that will be expanded in future work to include analysis of motion- and shear-relative wind asymmetry.

493427.title: Sub-Seasonal Variations of the Asian Summer Monsoon Anticyclone and Its Impact on UTLS Composition
493427.authors: Dong Huang, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and X. Wang, PhD, W. Randel, W. Smith, and M. Park
493427.abstract: The Asian Summer Monsoon Anticyclone (ASMA) is the dominant circulation system in the upper troposphere–lower stratosphere (UTLS) during boreal summer. Its strong anticyclonic circulation confines convectively lofted pollutants and water vapor, regulating UTLS transport with important implications for stratospheric composition. During the ACCLIP field campaign in August 2022, the northern flank of the ASMA extended northward, accompanied by positive carbon monoxide (CO) and negative ozone (O₃) anomalies in the UTLS. The summer of 2022 was an anomalous year in the context of climate variability based on the EOF analysis of 200 hPa zonal winds from the ERA5 reanalysis (1979-2025). The first leading mode captures the northward shifts of the northern flank of the ASMA, indicating dynamical and chemical patterns similar to those observed in August 2022 have occurred in other years. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we performed composite analyses of subtropical jets for ACCLIP-like years and opposite-phase years. Our results show that the first leading mode exhibits a period of approximately 20 days, with temperature and wind anomalies closely coupled through thermal wind balance. In northward (southward) shift events, warming (cooling) was developed in the 200–500 hPa layer accompanied by cooling (warming) in the 50–200 hPa layer over 30°–50°N, with temperature anomalies of opposite sign over 50°–70°N that formed a meridional dipole. Consistent with these circulation changes, robust positive (negative) CO and negative (positive) O₃ anomalies appeared at 200 hPa over the Asian summer monsoon region, demonstrating the meridional variability of the ASMA systematically modulates the trace gas transport from the troposphere into the UTLS.

493428.title: Regional Drivers and Subseasonal Predictability of Atlantic Tropical Cyclones
493428.authors: Mahdi Hasan, NOAA/AOML, Miami, FL; Northern Gulf Institute (NOAA/Mississippi State University), Miami, FL; and H. Lopez, S. K. Lee, R. West, D. Kim, and A. E. Mercer
493428.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) rank among the deadliest and most destructive natural hazards affecting the United States, yet their forecast capability varies significantly across timescales. TC prediction on weather timescales (up to 8 days) has improved steadily over the last two decades, while seasonal outlooks now derive useful skill from slowly evolving oceanic boundary conditions such as sea surface temperature and large-scale climate modes. In contrast, subseasonal Atlantic TC prediction, which bridges the gap between weather and seasonal timescales, remains the least skillful. This deficiency persists despite its immense value for providing actionable guidance to critical sectors such as agriculture, energy, insurance, water resource management, and emergency response. Subseasonal Atlantic TC activity is affected by a range of factors, including environmental conditions, tropical waves, and climate modes such as the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) and the El Niño Southern Oscillation. While prior studies have largely emphasized linear connections between environmental predictors, climate indices, and TC activity, the mechanisms driving TC genesis are highly nonlinear. For example, the MJO influences TC genesis by modulating the same environmental fields, such as low-level absolute vorticity, that serve as predictors. Beyond these nonlinear interactions, the relative importance of individual drivers also varies by region, with genesis in the eastern tropical Atlantic responding differently from the Caribbean or the Gulf of America. In this work, we use a hybrid dynamical machine learning framework to investigate the subseasonal predictability of Atlantic TC genesis. Bias-corrected environmental fields from the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) are combined with climate mode indices to train classification-based machine learning models (e.g., random forest, gradient boosting). Importantly, instead of treating the tropical Atlantic as a single domain, we partition the basin into objectively defined subregions using unsupervised clustering of the historical TC genesis locations. For each subregion, we analyze probabilistic outlooks of the genesis potential index rather than individual TC counts at two to four week lead times, since the index provides a continuous sample distribution for model training and testing. Forecast skill is assessed against climatology, persistence, and genesis potential computed directly from the bias-corrected GEFS fields. This framework is intended to quantify the regionally varying drivers of subseasonal Atlantic TC genesis and to eventually guide efforts toward improved subseasonal prediction of TC activity.

493430.title: Characterizing the Spatial and Temporal Distribution of Wind-Wave Alignment Under Time-Varying Winds in Tropical Cyclones
493430.authors: Anna Williams, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; WHOI, Woods Hole, MA; and J. Davis, B. Villas Boas, and S. R. Jayne
493430.abstract: The transfer of heat, moisture, and momentum at the air-sea interface influences tropical cyclone (TC) intensity. Thus, accurate modeling of these exchanges is crucial for storm forecasting. The momentum flux, one of the largest sinks of energy in a TC, is often parameterized through the drag coefficient and is poorly constrained at high wind speeds. Recent studies suggest that wind-wave alignment plays an important role in modulating the drag coefficient and, consequently, the momentum flux. This study uses a simple 2D parametric tropical cyclone wave model and high-fidelity WAVEWATCH III simulations with idealized wind-forcing experiments to help understand the spatial and temporal variability of wind-wave alignment in TCs. We compare our results to a large data set of wave buoy observations collected during Hurricane Erin (2025) through the Study on Air-Sea Coupling with WAves, Turbulence and Clouds at High winds (SASCWATCH) field campaign. Models forced with realistic Hurricane Erin winds produce spatial patterns of wind-wave alignment consistent with observations. Preliminary modeling results reveal that modulating storm translation speed and heading induces large variability in the coherent spatial pattern of wind-wave alignment. This suggests storm speed and track can affect the spatial distribution of momentum fluxes through their dependence on wind-wave alignment. The results of this study directly support ongoing efforts to improve TC forecasting by advancing the understanding of sea-state-dependent drag in high winds.

493434.title: Characterizing the Evolution of Monsoon Convection Using a Four-Stage MSE Phase Plane Framework
493434.authors: Soumili Chakraborty, IIT Bombay, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India; and A. C. Nikumbh, V. Maithel, B. Wolding, and B. P. Medeiros
493434.abstract: A tug-of-war between large-scale processes that build atmospheric instability and convection that consumes it gives rise to a wide range of spatiotemporal scales of tropical convection. How these interactions shape the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) variability remains an active area of research. Here, we investigate daily atmospheric state over the Monsoon Core Zone (MCZ) from a moist thermodynamic perspective, focusing on how the atmosphere evolves when perturbed from its moist equilibrium state. We capture the evolution by expanding the traditional two-phase recharge–discharge paradigm into a finer four-stage framework: Build-up, Cresting, Decay, and Recovery, providing a comprehensive description of the complete trajectory. Using 25 years (2001–2025) of ERA5 reanalysis data, we construct a two-dimensional phase space based on column-integrated Moist Static Energy (MSE) and its tendency to study the evolution of convection during the ISM. The moist equilibrium state represents the modal point in phase space, reflecting the balance between slow accumulation of instability by large-scale processes and rapid convective consumption. The four stages of this observed cyclic variability are then analyzed to describe how this balance and the different processes (advective, radiative, and surface fluxes) change when the atmosphere moves away from its equilibrium state. We map the individual terms of the MSE budget as departures from moist equilibrium, allowing us to first qualitatively characterize their roles throughout the convective cycle and then quantify their relative contributions using specific scores, following the conceptual approach of Anderson & Kuang (2012). Through this, we delineate distinct thermodynamic and dynamic processes across the cycle: horizontal advection acts as the primary driver of net energy tendencies independent of the column’s equilibrium state (highest evolution score), while vertical advection serves as a restoring mechanism, exporting energy whenever the column exceeds moist equilibrium to pull it back toward balance and vice versa (highest relaxation score). Meanwhile, radiative fluxes act as a positive feedback that opposes this restoration, sustaining the energetic state and delaying the return to equilibrium (highest maintenance score). This analysis offers a physically interpretable framework with potential applications for improving the diagnosis and predictability of monsoon convection.

493442.title: Automatic and Efficient Determination of Adaptive Scale-Separation and Scale-Dependent Localization for Multiscale Ensemble Data Assimilation
493442.authors: Naicheng Xu, Multiscale data Assimilation and Prediction lab, School of Meteorology, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
493442.abstract: Accurate numerical weather predictions require data assimilation (DA) to analyze the state and quantify the background error statistics across multiple scales. Multi-scale DA, achieved through scale-dependent covariance localization (SDL), has been examined and demonstrated to obtain multiscale analyses. However, proper scale decomposition and optimization of the localization radius at each scale, which are essential for SDL, typically require extensive parameter-tuning experiments, leading to substantial computational costs. These tuning experiments are often conducted over multiple retrospective cases and thus neglect the varying nature of the background error covariances. This study develops an observation innovation-based maximum likelihood method (MIL) to adaptively, efficiently, and automatically determine the parameters for scale separation and localization radii. This study evaluates MIL using a one-dimensional statistical model and the Surface Quasi-Geostrophic (SQG) model within the MLGETKF framework (Wang et al. 2021). In the statistical model, MIL achieves the same level of analysis accuracy while reducing computational cost by 95%, compared to the tuning experiments. In the SQG cycling experiments, MIL adaptively adjusts radii for scale separation and localization across cycles, resulting in slightly better, comparable analysis and forecast performance while achieving an 80% reduction in computational cost compared with the tuning experiments.

493443.title: The Global Planetary Boundary Layer
493443.authors: Joao P. Teixeira, JPL, Pasadena, CA
493443.abstract: While modern atmospheric turbulence science started more than 100 years ago, the focus on a global perspective of the planetary boundary layer (PBL) grew with the advent of global atmospheric models and satellite observations in the 1960s and 70s. The global PBL plays an essential role in weather, air quality and climate prediction, from extreme weather to PBL dispersion and cloud-climate feedback. Initially, most PBL regimes were not well (if at all) represented in global models, and PBL characteristics were virtually not sensed from space. During the last 25 years, much progress has been achieved in developing unified PBL parameterizations capable of representing a large variety of PBL regimes in a unified manner in global models and in extracting PBL thermodynamic structure information from satellite measurements. In this presentation, these recent achievements will be reviewed in some detail and a future global PBL observatory from space will be presented.

493444.title: From Prototype to Operations: Modernizing Product Processing for GOES-R and SWFO in the NESDIS Cloud
493444.authors: Tony Paullin, L3Harris Technologies, Inc., Melbourne, FL; and B. Brown-Bergtold
493444.abstract: Over the past three years, the GOES-R mission has defined the architecture for and executed the migration of its mission data processing to NESDIS’ enterprise cloud environments, establishing the foundation for scalable, resilient, and more operationally flexible product generation. In June 2026, that effort reached a major milestone with qualification and transition to operations. This presentation provides an update on the operational cloud-native processing system now supporting real-time GOES-R and SWFO mission data processing within the NESDIS GEO Cloud Compute Subsystem (GCCS). The operational system uses a service-based, data-agnostic architecture built on containerized microservices, Kubernetes orchestration, reliable messaging, distributed in-memory data caching, and cloud-native monitoring and control. It is designed to satisfy the demanding latency, throughput, availability, and cybersecurity requirements of continuously operating geostationary and space weather missions, including 24x7 ingest, complex Level 0, Level 1b, and Level 2+ processing chains, and dissemination to downstream users and enterprise services. Since entering operations, the system has generated more than 200,000 GOES-R and SWFO products per day while satisfying product delivery and system availability service-level agreements. The presentation summarizes the final operational architecture, the path from prototype to mission operations, and lessons learned integrating live mission interfaces, GCCS enterprise cloud services, observability, cybersecurity, and sustainment workflows. These results show that cloud-native product processing has matured from a promising modernization concept into an operationally viable foundation for current and next-generation environmental satellite ground systems.

493448.title: Minutes to Warning: A Novel Approach to Flash Flood Prediction for Impact-Based Forecasting
493448.authors: Jon Tarleton, Baron Weather Inc., Saint Charles, MO; Baron Weather Services, Huntsville, AL
493448.abstract: According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), flash floods account for nearly 85% of all flooding-related fatalities worldwide and result in economic losses exceeding $50 billion annually. The greatest challenge with flash flooding is lead time. Most agencies define a flash flood as flooding that occurs within six hours of a rainfall event, and many events unfold far more rapidly. High-resolution numerical weather prediction (NWP) models can identify approximate locations of pending flood threats; however, the precise location and timing often remain uncertain until convective signatures become apparent on weather radar. At that point, it may be too late to initialize a new model run with updated radar data assimilation factored into a revised forecast. We will demonstrate a novel technique using a local weather radar is coupled with a artificial intelligent rapid-refresh flood impact model, enabling meteorologists to predict flooding impacts hours in advance. The most significant feature of this new modeling capability is that it can be executed on demand, delivering actionable output within minutes for an area approximately 25,000 square kilometers in size. The model ingests Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (QPE) derived from local radar to assess recent rainfall accumulations, and Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPF) from a high-resolution NWP model to project future precipitation. The presentation will focus on examples where the system performed in real world situations to deliver timing decision making information. In a flash flood situation, meteorologists have very little time to warn communities of rapidly developing and life-threatening conditions. A solution that delivers guidance within minutes is therefore far more operationally valuable than one optimized purely for absolute accuracy. This capability represents a meaningful advancement in impact-based forecasting and has the potential to save lives across vulnerable communities worldwide.

493449.title: A Case Study on the Impacts of Land Usage on Diurnal Convection in the Southeast United States
493449.authors: Michael Eppley-Ishida, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI; and D. S. Henderson, J. A. Otkin, PhD, and J. Mecikalski
493449.abstract: Weakly-forced convection across the southeast United States (SE USA) delivers a substantial amount of summertime precipitation, but forecast models struggle to accurately predict the locations where the first convective cells initiate. These initial cells create the outflow boundaries that trigger more convection, leading to the upscale growth into multicellular clusters. Where these initial storms develop is important for the sensible weather and local hydrology. The SE USA has large areas of both forests and croplands, and these different land types absorb different amounts of incoming solar radiation, driving gradients in sensible and latent heating, which result in thermally direct circulations known as “forest breezes”. These forest breezes result in near-surface convergence which can lift parcels to their LFC in the weakly stratified environment common during the summertime in the SE USA. In the absence of synoptic-scale forcing, this can be the primary mechanism for convective initiation (CI) before outflow boundaries initiate more convection. This work examines the impact different land types have on convective initiation location and cloud characteristics. The Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds (tobac) Python package determines CI timing and location, as well as tracks cloud characteristics before and after CI. The Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model is used to examine the impact of land use on CI locations for a case study on 8 July 2025 in northern Alabama and Mississippi. Model sensitivity experiments are used to examine the sensitivity of CI location and cloud characteristics, such as updraft width and velocity, cloudtop temperature and extent, and microphysical properties, related to variations in forest density, boundary shape, and boundary size.

493452.title: Tropical Cyclones and Vertical Wind Shear Interactions in the High Resolution ECMWF Climate Model.
493452.authors: Mark Andrew McGarry Jr., University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. Carstens
493452.abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) asymmetry greatly influences intensity and the distribution of wind, rainfall, and storm surge hazards. Global climate models (GCMs) have improved in simulating axisymmetric TC structure, but resolving structural asymmetries and vortex tilt associated with environmental vertical wind shear is also important for accurately capturing the lifecycle of these systems. In particular, a tilted vortex is associated with asymmetric deep convection in the inner core and outer rainbands, and is more susceptible to ventilation of cooler, drier environmental air. This study uses the ECMWF-IFS high-resolution climate model from the High-Resolution Model Intercomparison Project (HighResMIP) to investigate how accurately GCMs can simulate vortex tilt, as well as kinematic and thermodynamic asymmetry, relative to observational records. TCs are tracked objectively using TempestExtremes, which identifies colocated 300-500 mb geopotential thickness and surface pressure minima relative to the surrounding environment. Three-dimensional model data is then processed to create six-hourly snapshots following the TCs throughout their lifecycle, in both storm- and shear-relative space. Composite TC structures will be analyzed based on intensity and wind shear magnitude in simulations with two resolutions: “High-Resolution” (ECMWF-IFS-HR, 0.5 degree grid spacing) and “Low-Resolution” (ECMWF-IFS-LR, 1 degree grid spacing). The successful simulation of TCs in this work is a stepping stone toward a better understanding of how TC structure and their impacts may change in the future.

493453.title: Unraveling the Physics of Marine Heatwaves: Atmosphere–Ocean Dynamics in the Tropical Atlantic and the Caribbean
493453.authors: KENESHIA HIBBERT, CUNY Graduate Center, brooklyn, NY; and B. Huang, X. Yin, F. B. Oppong, T. M. Smith, and J. E. Gonzalez-Cruz
493453.abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) in the tropical North Atlantic and Caribbean affect coral reefs, fisheries, and coastal economies, yet the physical processes that control how these events form, grow, and decay remain poorly understood. Most existing work in this region has focused on documenting long-term trends in MHW frequency and duration; here we take a different approach, using detailed event-by-event characterization as the foundation for identifying the atmospheric and oceanic drivers behind events. Using daily SST data from the NOAA OISST v2.1 dataset spanning 1982–2025 and a domain-scale application of the Hobday et al. (2016) detection method, including a requirement that at least 15% of the basin exceed its local 90th-percentile threshold on a given day, we identify 108 distinct MHW events across the region. These events are strongly skewed: the median event lasts 11 days, but mean duration climbs to 43 days because a handful of long-lived events pull the average up. Spatial extent follows the same pattern, with a median footprint of about 8 million km² and a maximum exceeding 25 million ². These events are not spread evenly through the year: activity peaks during the late rainfall season (August–November), which also produced the individual most active years in the record (2015, 2019, and 2024), while the dry season (December–March) and early rainfall season (April–July) show comparatively fewer events. Duration, footprint, and intensity are closely linked. Footprint grows with duration, and that growth accelerates the longer an event persists; peak intensity, a median of 2.4°C above threshold, versus a median mean intensity of just 0.3°C, also rises with event size. A correlation analysis across nine event metrics shows duration, footprint, persistence, and cumulative thermal stress clustering tightly together (r > 0.85), while mean intensity and spatial growth rate behave independently, hinting that different physical mechanisms may govern how an event grows versus how intense it is. These size and intensity-dependent relationships carry direct implications for the surrounding atmosphere-ocean system: the largest, most persistent events are also the ones most likely to force compound atmospheric extremes, and place sustained stress on regional marine ecosystems. These relationships motivate the central question of this work: what atmospheric and oceanic conditions separate events that stay small and short-lived from those that grow large, persist for months, and reach extreme peak intensities? We present our approach to this question, linking large-scale climate modes (ENSO, the NAO, the AMO, and the PDO) with local atmospheric forcing and upper-ocean conditions across the onset, growth, and decay phases of MHW events in the tropical North Atlantic and the Caribbean.

493454.title: Observing Convective Updrafts with Heterogeneous Radar Networks
493454.authors: Brenda Dolan, Colorado State University, Longmont, CO; and P. N. Gatlin, C. Schumacher, P. Kollias, S. W. Freeman, K. L. Rasmussen, Ph.D., S. C. van den Heever, E. Luke, T. J. Lang, K. E. McKeown, E. I. Ebbert, C. G. Amiot, V. Chandrasekar, S. Tanelli, D. J. Posselt, and M. Oue
493454.abstract: Measuring vertical velocity and convective mass flux (CMF) is challenging, owing to the fine temporal and spatial variability of updrafts, as well as difficulties in obtaining in situ measurements. Observations commonly rely on remote sensing retrievals, such as from radars, most often derived from Doppler radial velocity. These types of measurements often include significant contributions from hydrometeor fall velocities, require coordinated or special scanning, and resolve different temporal and spatial scales. We investigate various sampling techniques from different types of radars, from scanning C-band dish radars to X-band phased array radars (PAR) to profiling radars at different frequencies with the goal of understanding the capabilities of different measurement techniques for determining vertical velocities in convective updrafts. Estimating vertical velocity and CMF is a central objective of the upcoming NASA INvestigation of Convective UpdraftS (INCUS) satellite Mission. INCUS, which is planned to launch in 2027, will measure CMF across the tropical and subtropical latitudes using a constellation of three SmallSats flying in close formation, each carrying a Ka-band radar. Data collected from two recent field campaigns, Tracking Aerosol Convection Interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER) and Testing INCUS Methods Experiment -Suborbital preLaunch Investigation of Convective Evolution (TIME-SLICE), will be used to study the uncertainties and spatial and temporal scales of different methods of deriving vertical velocity from ground-radar measurements. First, we examine multiple Doppler retrievals using both scanning-dish radars and PAR. Second, a novel “updraft mapping” mode is employed with a vertically pointing PAR. Third, we look at high-elevation angle retrievals from both scanning dish radars and PAR. Lastly, we utilize co-located profilers of different wavelengths to understand the effects of attenuation and scattering by hydrometeors on velocity retrievals above the melting layer. The results of this study underpin the validation efforts for INCUS. Planned post-launch field campaigns in Huntsville, Alabama in 2027 and Key West, Florida in 2028 are being designed with heterogeneous radar networks to statistically measure a wide variety of updrafts from the ground. These field campaigns will sample convective updrafts, their environments, and associated anvils, across different storm morphologies providing ground-based statistics for comparisons with INCUS.

493455.title: Investigating Atmospheric River Characteristics and Hydrologic Impacts on Alaskan Communities
493455.authors: Marc Sailer, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; Univ. of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and A. C. Winters and K. Musselman
493455.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs), defined as long, narrow, transient corridors of strong horizontal water vapor transport, are responsible for heavy precipitation in Alaska and contribute a large portion of the state’s annual precipitation. Low intensity ARs bring precipitation that provides beneficial ecological and social impacts. However, extreme precipitation events associated with high intensity ARs produce floods and landslides with deleterious consequences for Alaskan communities, many of which are remote and/or rural. For example, extreme precipitation associated with an AR impacted western Alaska during October 2025. In Kipnuk, water levels rose 2 m above normal high tide, damaging every home and destroying 90% of them. Landfalling ARs can also impact sea ice coverage, a key surface state for Alaskan ecology and many communities.
