This study provides an improved understanding of synoptic-scale and mesoscale conditions that produce ARs in Alaska utilizing reanalysis data and newly available high-resolution atmospheric and hydrologic data from the Arctic Rivers Project. The study develops a catalogue of AR events in Alaska between water years (WY) 1990–2021 using a combination of three AR detection algorithms (ARDTs) available from the Atmospheric River Tracking Method Intercomparison Project (ARTMIP), as well as ERA5 reanalysis data to identify key event characteristics such as maximum integrated water vapor transport (IVT) and total precipitation. Preliminary results show patterns of seasonality of AR event frequency across different Alaskan regions. Long duration, high IVT AR events occur most frequently between July and October, primarily impacting southern Alaska during the summer and western Alaska during the Fall. Distinct moisture transport pathways prompt synoptic-scale analysis of their accompanying circulation patterns and evolution using ERA5 reanalysis data. Subsequently, high-resolution model data from the Arctic Rivers Project will be used to investigate the mesoscale characteristics of these AR events.

493456.title: Evaluation of GOES Satellite Data for Use In the Grassland Fire Danger Index
493456.authors: Philip N. Schumacher, CIRA, Sioux Falls, SD; and E. Centeno, B. Wu, K. Gallo, and S. M. Hoekstra
493456.abstract: Large and fast spreading wildfires that impact life and property have become more common in the Great Plains of the United States due to high winds and low humidity in the presence of dry fuels. Determining fire fuel moisture status remains a challenge across the Great Plains of the US where grasses and shrubs are the primary land covers and fuels for fires. At the same time, surveyed fire partners expressed a desire for more current fuel moisture information included when Red Flag Warnings are issued by the National Weather Service (NWS). While many NWS offices in the Great Plains relied on visual examination of fuels or modeled fuel moisture as the Energy Release Component, some offices had begun to use satellite data to estimate fuel moisture. This study compared two methods of estimating the Curing Index, an indicator of the moisture level of vegetation, that is included in the Grassland Fire Danger Index (GFDI): i) a satellite method using data acquired by the GOES Advanced Baseline Imager and ii) a method using a Growing Season Index (GSI), which includes observed meteorological conditions to estimate plant growth. Curing Index values were calculated for 2021 and 2022 at 47 Remote Automated Weather Stations (RAWS) that had dominant land cover types of either grassland or shrubland vegetation. Differences in the Curing Index of greater than 50% were observed at various times from spring through autumn between the two methods. Differences in Curing Index between the two methods resulted in differences in GFDI which changed the fire danger rating category within the National Fire Danger Rating System. The greatest differences in grassland and shrubland GFDI values included greater values of GFDI in the summer months when GSI was used to compute the Curing Index. Also, during both years, the Curing Index computed with the GSI displayed an autumn green-up during a dry early autumn that was not observed by satellite data. The early autumn green-up displayed by the GSI-based Curing Index, when vegetation is normally in senescence, was attributed to a decrease in the vapor pressure deficit component of the GSI. These differences in how the Curing Index is calculated led directly to differences in the forecast fire danger which can impact decisions from whether NWS forecasters issue Red Flag Warnings to what actions fire responders take to prepare for extreme fire behavior.

493458.title: 30 Years of the NSF NCAR EOL Field Catalog and Its Role in Modern Field Campaigns
493458.authors: Carol Ruchti, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Allison, S. M. Loehrer, S. Stringer, and W. C. Lenhardt
493458.abstract: Since its inception in 1995, the National Science Foundation (NSF), National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), Earth Observing Laboratory (EOL) Field Catalog (hereafter Field Catalog) has evolved from a centralized website for cataloging atmospheric field campaign data products into a sophisticated, customizable, real-time application for planning campaigns, tracking field campaign research platforms, and displaying real-time data products. The catalog team has managed over 100 catalogs across various atmospheric science disciplines, working with numerous Principal Investigators (PIs), and using data from hundreds of unique instruments to easily share near real-time data products. As technology continues to improve and real-time earth science data is more accessible, the Field Catalog continues to evolve to align with the needs of the atmospheric science community and PIs by collecting user feedback. Users continue to emphasize how essential the Field Catalog is to efficiently collaborate and accomplish the science goals of the field campaigns before, during, and after deployment. Thanks to the managers, developers, scientists, and users who contributed to the creation of the Field Catalog, it has become a cornerstone of the atmospheric field science community. After creating V1 and V2 of the Field Catalog, the team has started to envision and plan the next iteration of the catalog to create an even better user experience supporting evolving science needs. This talk will outline the Field Catalog’s historical impact, current capabilities, and plans for the future. The Field Catalog has the potential to tell the stories of science across the various earth science disciplines. In the future, this same Field Catalog application could be used to tell science stories of the past. For example, a social science case study of Hurricane Ian from 2022 could be visually displayed with operational data products (satellite, radar, NWS watches/warnings) and citizen survey data. Thus, research spanning earth science or even multidisciplinary science could utilize the Field Catalog in a newly imagined way for visual science story telling. Then, NCAR’s Field Catalog application would be available for an even broader science audience, and the Field Catalog would continue to evolve and adapt as has been the case for the last 30 years.

493463.title: The Role of Mesoscale Cloud Morphology in Aerosol Radiative Forcing
493463.authors: Isabel L. McCoy, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and D. McCoy, J. J. Gristey, G. Feingold, and J. C. Chiu
493463.abstract: Boundary layer clouds can organize into mesoscale structures that influence both their coverage and brightness. Globally, these morphology patterns are diverse and responsive to their environmental conditions. This analysis investigates the role that organization may play in modulating aerosol radiative forcing. We utilize organization identifications from a supervised neural network applied to satellite observations from 2003-2018 in combination with reanalysis meteorological variables and a cloud droplet number proxy, a measure for aerosol influence. We use a random forest to learn the relationships between key environmental factors and morphology occurrence frequencies in the Northern Hemisphere. To test this model, we use an opportunistic experiment: aerosol decline off the Eastern Seaboard. This enables evaluation of the contributions from changes in meteorology and aerosol to organizational shifts. Test scenarios are developed using the random forest to predict organization under varied pairings of constant and temporally varying environmental factors, disentangling their respective influences and co-variability. The resulting dependencies enable an estimation of the contribution from organizational shifts to radiative forcing since 2003, since the pre-industrial, and under possible future cloud brightening efforts.

493464.title: Observational Evidence of Boundary Layer Modification by Anvil Shading and Evaporative Cooling
493464.authors: Michelle Rose Storm, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. W. Hoch
493464.abstract: Anvil clouds can produce substantial reductions in surface shortwave radiation well before precipitation reaches the ground, altering the thermodynamic and dynamic structures of the planetary boundary layer (PBL). Despite the frequency of anvil clouds associated with continental convection, relatively few observational studies have examined the atmospheric response to anvil shading events. Previous observational studies have relied on sparse radiosondes or surface measurements, while modeling studies have primarily focused on storm evolution and subsequent convection through idealized modeling configurations rather than PBL evolution. Additionally, discrepancies exist between observations and models in the magnitude of surface cooling and shortwave radiation reduction associated with anvil shading events. To our knowledge, no observational studies examine the effects of anvil shading, from shading onset to precipitation onset, through the depth of the PBL by utilizing profiling measurements. This study examines the evolution of the surface and PBL during an anvil shading event on 25 May 2024 in northern Oklahoma using a suite of observations from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Southern Great Plains (SGP) site. Surface radiation measurements are used to identify the shading onset and magnitude of anvil-induced radiation changes, while Doppler lidar and surface flux observations are used to characterize changes in PBL turbulence, winds, and fluxes. Ka-band radar data is used for virga identification beneath the anvil leading up to surface-observed precipitation. Preliminary analysis reveals 5°C surface cooling through the duration of the anvil shading event, accompanied by an increase in wind speed through the depth of the PBL. Turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) initially decreases after shading onset, consistent with the suppression of surface-driven turbulence following the reduction in solar radiation. Shortly before precipitation reaches the surface, TKE increases, suggesting a transition toward enhanced mixing associated with changes in the thermodynamic and kinematic structure of the PBL. These observations provide an opportunity to evaluate whether the magnitude of the observed surface and PBL response is consistent with the radiative forcing alone.A second objective is to quantify the contribution of precipitation evaporation to the observed cooling. Vertically pointed radar and thermodynamic observations will be used to characterize the evolution of hydrometeors and atmospheric moisture beneath cloud base and estimate the associated evaporative cooling as precipitation falls and evaporates through the boundary layer. Comparing this estimated evaporative contribution with the observed temperature evolution and radiative forcing will provide an observational constraint on the mechanisms responsible for boundary layer cooling during anvil shading events.This case study provides an observational framework for investigating anvil shading as a PBL process rather than solely as a radiative perturbation to the surface or a precursor to storm evolution. The results aim to establish whether precipitation evaporation represents a substantial additional source of boundary layer cooling and provide a basis for evaluating the representation of anvil shading and associated PBL responses in atmospheric models.

493467.title: Act Two: NOAA Weather Radio's Next Half Century
493467.authors: Bruce T. Jones, Midland Radio Corporation, Kansas City, MO
493467.abstract: In the aftermath of the deadly 1974 Super Outbreak of tornadoes, President Gerald Ford designated NOAA Weather Radio "America's Official Federal Warning System". A half century later the world's largest single-operator transmitter network continues to save lives and protect property with instantaneous alerts direct from the originator - the 122 WFO's of the National Weather Service. In 2027 the second half-century of NOAA Weather Radio opens with Partial County Alerting (PCA), allowing radar operators to issue more targeted warnings. What is PCA, how does it work, and how can it be leveraged to better protect and serve a Weather-Ready Nation? And then, after PCA, what might be the next improvement? An overview of the the past, present and future of the USA's federal alerting system gives you a better grasp of the tools available to help you save lives.

493469.title: Specialized LEO Products and Training for IMETs in Alaska
493469.authors: Carl F. Dierking, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and L. Byerle, J. Delamere, J. Cable, B. bartos, J. Chriest, T. W. Quarterman, J. K. Zajic, M. Foster, M. Pavolonis, H. Mair, and R. Rickey
493469.abstract: The deployment of a National Weather Service (NWS) Incident Meteorologist (IMET) in Alaska presents unique challenges without a direct equivalent in the Continental United States (CONUS). The vast size and remoteness of the state demand logistical planning that is more complicated than typical CONUS deployments. Additionally, fires are often managed as complexes covering areas up to the size of some states with very little surface observation data. The Fire Weather Meteorologist, based at AICC headquarters in Fairbanks, provides guidance to all federal and state agencies on fire weather and fire potential — a statewide coordinating role unique to Alaska's multi-agency structure that bridges NWS Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) and on-site IMETs. Alaska's wildfire season is relatively short but intense, officially spanning April 1 through September 1, with peak activity from June through August. The ruggedness and scale of the state, combined with a limited road network, present significant operational challenges. Fires frequently burn in remote boreal and arctic terrain, and vast areas of the state go largely unobserved due to sparse transportation routes. As a result, satellite-derived products are critical for early fire detection and monitoring by fire managers, meteorologists, and wildland firefighters. Alaska's high-latitude position offers a distinct observational advantage: the three Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites equipped with Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) sensors provide more than 20 overpasses per day over the Interior, where fire activity is most concentrated. The 375-meter resolution I-band channels on VIIRS, which include a shortwave infrared band highly sensitive to fire heat emissions, form the basis of numerous fire-specific detection and monitoring products. The Geographic Information Network of Alaska (GINA) at the University of Alaska Fairbanks (UAF) operates three Direct Broadcast antennas capable of processing satellite products within 10 minutes of overpass and distributes these products to Alaska WFOs via LDM for display in the Advanced Weather Interactive Processing System (AWIPS). In 2021, NWS began testing a cloud-based AWIPS implementation for IMETs, running the Common AWIPS Visualization Environment (CAVE) application remotely to eliminate the dependency on hardware only available at a supporting WFO. CAVE is widely viewed as the best platform to analyze satellite data, however, LEO satellite products were initially unavailable in this cloud environment due to distribution challenges. In 2026, to address this deficiency, a collaboration among NWS Total Operational Weather Readiness - Satellites (TOWR-S), GINA, and the NWS Office of Systems resolved these challenges, establishing procedures to deliver LEO satellite data to the AWIPS IMET cloud service and creating a dedicated CAVE menu providing streamlined access to LEO products for fire detection, smoke monitoring, and precipitation assessment. Achieving cloud-based AWIPS access to LEO fire products represented a significant milestone for IMET operations. However, many CONUS IMETs deployed to Alaska are often unfamiliar with VIIRS and other LEO satellite products. Prior to the 2026 fire season, GINA staff delivered presentations at national and regional IMET training sessions that described LEO products applicable to wildfire monitoring, precipitation assessment, and smoke tracking. The Next Generation Fire System (NGFS) development team also presented their new fire detection application, which was made available within the AWIPS cloud implementation. Additionally, an ArcGIS Story Map titled "Exploring JPSS Fire Products" and fire product Quick Guides were developed to support individual self-paced training. This presentation highlights the contributions of the many agencies and institutions whose collaboration made these advancements possible.

493473.title: MRMS Software Architecture: Infrastructure Evolution, RAPIO, and Future Algorithm Integration
493473.authors: Carrie Langston, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma - CIWRO, Norman, OK; and R. E. Toomey, K. Cooper, M. Taylor, T. Miller, G. Fisher, T. M. Smith, and R. A. Clark III
493473.abstract: The Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system is a critical, advanced weather analysis framework utilized by the National Weather Service (NWS) for severe weather detection, aviation, and quantitative precipitation estimation. Over the past two decades, the MRMS codebase has expanded significantly to support a diverse and growing suite of algorithms, including hydrometeorological (HMET) applications, the Flooded Locations And Simulated Hydrographs (FLASH) system, and ProbSevere. To ensure reliable research-to-operations (R2O) transitions and accommodate increasingly complex data streams, MRMS requires a modernized, highly modular coding infrastructure. This presentation outlines the ongoing evolution and future direction of the MRMS software architecture. A focal point of this modernization is the continued integration of the Real-Time Algorithm Parameter and I/O (RAPIO) system. By consolidating decades of legacy libraries into a cohesive framework, RAPIO abstracts I/O processes, parameter management, and event notifications, allowing developers to focus purely on scientific computation. This poster will detail the current state of the MRMS coding infrastructure, highlight recent architectural transitions (including RAPIO applications and broader algorithm integrations), and provide a roadmap for future software development within the MRMS ecosystem.

493474.title: A Case Study of Atmospheric River Induced Extreme Convective Precipitation Over San Diego in January 2024
493474.authors: Emilio Yanez Jr., Scripps Institution of Oceanography (SIO), Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E), UCSD, San Diego, CA, USA, La Jolla, CA; and M. Zheng, J. Wang, L. Delle Monache, S. P. Xie, and F. M. Ralph
493474.abstract: On January 22, 2024, a weakening atmospheric river (AR) moving through Southern California produced heavy convective precipitation over San Diego. Rainfall totals of >3 inches far exceeded ensemble model guidance, causing severe flooding that overwhelmed storm drainage infrastructure in low-lying communities. Despite the widespread underprediction, some of the 200 ensemble members in the West-WRF model successfully captured the observed precipitation. We investigate the mesoscale processes that led to convective precipitation and why a majority of ensemble members missed the event. We apply EOF decomposition of 24-hr accumulated precipitation forecasts to explore dominant error modes. The leading EOF (42% variance) describes a domain-wide wet/dry bias, while the second EOF (21% variance) describes a north/south shift of the precipitation maxima within the San Diego region. Composites of members that best captured the observed precipitation show strong dynamic support for convective precipitation relative to poor members, with a stronger coastal low-level jet (LLJ), low-level moisture flux, and 850-hPa frontogenesis. Ensemble statistics show large uncertainty in the location and magnitude of the water vapor plume, with low-level zonal winds and moisture having fractional spreads of 60% and 15%, respectively. These analyses suggest that the largest uncertainty wasn’t in moisture availability, but rather how the mesoscale dynamics reorganized that moisture to produce convective precipitation. We hypothesize that the localization of convective cells near downtown San Diego is a signature of conditional symmetric instability (CSI) release within an environment preconditioned by a mesoscale frontal wave (MFW), which focused coastal LLJ-driven moisture convergence and frontally forced ascent along the AR’s leading flank. The observed cell latitudes suggest that San Clemente Island may have further modified this environment by disrupting and reorganizing the MFW’s low-level vorticity anomaly, reinforcing convergence patterns favorable for downstream CSI release. These results highlight the importance of high-resolution, large-ensemble modeling for resolving embedded mesoscale processes driving AR precipitation extremes as well as the role of mesoscale initial condition uncertainty.

493476.title: Investigating Atmospheric Chemistry on the African Continent as an Example for the Need for a Global ‘GEO-Belt’
493476.authors: Pieternel Felicitas Levelt, UCAR, Boulder, CO
493476.abstract: The Geostationary Air Quality (GeoAQ) constellation comprising TEMPO, Sentinel-4, and GEMS has revolutionized atmospheric composition monitoring by providing continuous, diurnal observations of short-lived pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide (NO2), ozone (O3), formaldehyde (HCHO), and aerosols. However, this capability is currently limited to major economic centers in the Northern Hemisphere, creating an observational divide. This paper suggests expansion of the GeoAQ constellation into a comprehensive, global ‘Geo-Belt’ by deploying four additional geostationary satellites over under-monitored regions: Africa, South America, the Middle East and India, and Oceania. Rapid urbanization, escalating anthropogenic emissions, and climate-driven extreme events such as megafires and severe dust storms are disproportionately impacting these unmonitored regions leading to poor health outcomes. Current Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites, which typically provide once-daily snapshots that are inadequate for capturing the rapid diurnal evolution of local atmospheric chemistries. Single daily observations miss the morning accumulation of household combustion emissions in Africa, the midday intensification of photochemical smog in Indian megacities, and the rapid overnight evolution of biogenic emissions and wildfire plumes in South America and Oceania. To address this global information gap, this paper outlines a strategic, technical, and collaborative framework for the Geo-Belt. It details the specific regional measurement gaps and complex chemical regimes that mandate high-temporal-resolution monitoring. Furthermore, it evaluates the technical feasibility of leveraging the proven design heritage of existing GeoAQ spectrometers to cover these regions. The paper argues that orbiting hardware alone is insufficient and recommends establishment of a multi-level international consortium linking space agencies, regional institutions, and the private sector to pair these spaceborne assets with robust, on-the-ground infrastructure. In this paper Africa will be used as an example scientific case for the need for the GEO-Belt. In the next decades a large increase in population is expected to occur on the African continent, leading to a doubling of the current population by 2050 (2.5 billion) and air pollution emissions increasing considerably with health impacts to people in Africa. The time has come to determine the evolving role of Africa in global environmental change.

493483.title: When Projections Become Observable: Independent Evaluation of 2015–2025 Projections in a Paired 4-km CMIP6-WRF and ERA5-WRF Framework
493483.authors: Xingang Fan, Western Kentucky Univ., Bowling Green, KY
493483.abstract: High-resolution mesoscale weather information is needed to investigate potential changes in precipitation extremes and severe-weather environments. However, evaluating climate projections against observations remains challenging because of differences in spatial and temporal scales and because free-running climate models are not expected to reproduce the timing of individual observed weather events. This study develops a paired 4-km Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) dataset consisting of an ERA5-driven simulation (EW) and a CMIP6-driven simulation (CW) over the Ohio River Basin using the same regional modeling framework and a systematically evaluated WRF configuration. The CMIP6 simulations are driven by the bias-corrected CMIP6 forcing dataset of Xu et al. (2021), which was specifically developed for dynamical downscaling and incorporates information from 18 CMIP6 models and ERA5 data through 2014. A set of 21 WRF physics configurations was evaluated using multiple aspects of model performance, including continuous precipitation statistics, categorical precipitation verification, neighborhood-based verification, object-based diagnostics, and synoptic-scale atmospheric fields. The resulting evaluation is used to identify a physically and statistically robust configuration for the production simulations. A particular focus of this study is the 2015–2025 period. When the CMIP6 projections and the Xu et al. forcing dataset were developed, this period was part of the prospective projection period and extended beyond the ERA5 information used in the bias-correction procedure. The period can therefore now be evaluated retrospectively against observations, providing an independent observational test of the originally prospective projections. Rather than expecting correspondence between individual weather events, the evaluation focuses on climatological distributions, frequencies, variability, and extremes arising from mesoscale atmospheric conditions. The paired EW and CW datasets also provide an opportunity to investigate analog-based statistical connections between projected and observationally constrained atmospheric states. As an initial demonstration, CW atmospheric states will be matched with statistically similar EW states, and the corresponding precipitation outcomes will be compared without requiring the simulations to share the same dates or individual weather events. This analysis will assess the feasibility of using the observationally constrained EW simulation as a statistical bridge between for verification of CMIP6 projections against observed regional precipitation. The resulting datasets and evaluation framework are intended to support subsequent investigations of extreme precipitation and severe-weather environments under future climate change.

493487.title: Intelligent Reconstruction of Over 140,000 Vertical Profiles in China Driven by Multi-Source Space-Air-Ground Observations
493487.abstract: Addressing the structural shortcomings of traditional meteorological observation networks—such as uneven spatial distribution and the existence of observational blind spots—which make it difficult to meet the demands for constructing high-precision three-dimensional real-time meteorological fields, this paper proposes an intelligent reconstruction method for over 140,000 vertical profiles across China, driven by multi-source observations from ground, air, and space. The method integrates ten types of heterogeneous ground-to-space observations, including data from automatic weather stations, radiosondes, microwave radiometers, wind profiling radars, weather radars, tower-based observations, AGRI L1 data from the FY-4B satellite, atmospheric temperature and humidity profiles from the FY-4B satellite’s GIIRS instrument, and FY-4B cloud-tracking winds. After applying differentiated quality control measures, the method has accumulated more than 400,000 valid observation points below an altitude of 15 km, thereby establishing an integrated ground-air-space observation data foundation. On this basis, using kernel density estimation and spatial correlation analysis, we reveal the uneven distribution characteristic of the existing station network—denser in the east and sparser in the west. By optimizing the layout through spatial homogenization and employing intelligent interpolation to generate virtual ground observation stations, we increase the number of discrete ground stations from over 100,000 to 145,307 profile observation stations, thereby shifting from a dominance in station quantity to a dominance in spatial coverage. By leveraging a K-D tree spatial index, we achieve rapid inference of neighborhood relationships and introduce a KL-divergence-based weighting correction scheme to realize precise spatial similarity measurement. We built a factor graph model based on Markov random fields and used the iterative message-passing mechanism of the belief-propagation algorithm to complete their data with high accuracy. Meanwhile, we incorporated atmospheric statics constraints and adaptive regularization to ensure the physical plausibility of the completed results. We construct a ground-to-air associated point cloud training dataset based on KNN neighborhood search. Subsequently, we develop a physics- and data-driven fusion model based on the Transformer architecture, embedding atmospheric dynamics and thermodynamic conservation equations into the deep-learning framework. By balancing fitting accuracy with physical consistency, we generate stable and reliable three-dimensional meteorological analysis fields. This product covers 145,070 meteorological profiles across all of China, with a vertical range extending up to 15 km and a vertical resolution of 50 m. It is updated every 10 minutes and provides outputs for 7 3D key variables: temperature, relative humidity, specific humidity, atmospheric pressure, U/V winds, and vertical wind, and one surface variable: hourly accumulated precipitation. This product can provide precise and reliable data support for refined weather services, disaster prevention and mitigation efforts, as well as applications in industries such as aviation and energy.

493488.title: Bridging Radar and Entrainment-Plume Theory to Nowcast Supercells in Hurricane Milton
493488.authors: Terrence John Corrigan Jr., NRL, Honolulu, HI
493488.abstract: On 9 October 2024, Hurricane Milton made landfall across the Florida peninsula as a category three hurricane. Its preceding warm sector produced an unprecedented severe weather outbreak that included life-threatening storm surge, rainfall exceeding 500 mm, and 45 confirmed tornadoes, the most ever recorded for the state in a single day. Nowcasting (0–3 h) such all-hazard, multi-storm events is exceptionally challenging, yet essential for timely warnings of hazard timing, location, type, and severity. This study tests a hybrid, computationally inexpensive, nowcasting framework that bridges radar extrapolation and numerical weather prediction by applying recent entraining-plume theory to ongoing convection. We hypothesize that, despite known biases from dual-Doppler, wind retrieval vertical velocities, the geometric properties of storm updrafts, such as their radius, depth, base height, vertical tilt, and propagation speed, are more accurate representations of true updraft structure than retrieved magnitudes alone, and that incorporating them into entraining-plume theory improves nowcasting of storm initiation, intensity, and longevity. To test this, the Pythonic direct data assimilation (PyDDA) package is used to produce 5 minute, three-dimensional wind fields at 500 meter resolution, by assimilating Florida’s dense NEXRAD weather radar systems (WSR-88D) network with High Resolution Rapid Refresh model, Version 4 (Dowell et al. 2022) (HRRRv4) model fields. The tracking and object-based analysis of clouds (tobac) Python module is then used to identify, segment, and track three-dimensional updraft geometric properties whose trends in geometry, vertical velocity, and storm-relative winds covary in time consistent with entraining-plume theory. Three nowcasting experiments of progressively increasing observational constraint from tobac and radar are applied to three isolated tornadic supercells in Milton’s warm sector to evaluate key convective properties incorporating entrainment impacts. Experiments that directly incorporated updraft geometry most consistently aligned diagnosed storm efficiency, intensity, and longevity with observed tornado occurrence, supporting our hypothesis and demonstrating the utility of volumetric updraft properties as an effective observational constraint for nowcasting severe convection.

493491.title: Deep Convective Cell Properties Under Varying Meteorological and Aerosol Conditions: Insights from TRACER Observations and Ensemble Large-Eddy Simulations
493491.authors: Dhwanit J Mise, CAPS, Norman, OK; and Y. Huang, G. M. McFarquhar, M. Xue, A. V. Ryzhkov, J. C. Snyder, L. Xue, W. Y. Cheng, M. Oue, P. Kollias, M. P. Jensen, M. Taszarek, C. Kuang, and T. Subba
493491.abstract: Deep convective clouds, with strong updrafts, downdrafts and frequent lightning, are key modulators of Earth’s energy budget and hydrological cycle. However, the mechanisms governing convective lifecycle evolution, particularly its coupling with the ambient environment, remain poorly constrained. Using observations from the Tracking Aerosol Convection Interactions Experiment (TRACER) Intensive Operational Period (June–September 2022), this study characterizes isolated convective cells across diverse meteorological and aerosol regimes using the second-generation C-Band Scanning ARM Precipitation Radar (CSAPR2) and collocated instrumentation. Over 400 deep convective cells (DCCs) were identified from CSAPR2 observations, with full lifetimes constructed using observations from the nearby NEXRAD KHGX radar. Long-lived cells were wider (~13.2 km at 2–4 km height) and deeper (~11.4 km) than short-lived DCCs (~6.4 km wide, ~7.3 km tall). A Random Forest (RF) analysis identified precipitable water vapor (PWV) as the most important environmental predictor of convective cell lifetime. A modeling framework was developed to investigate the linkages between aerosol loading, meteorological conditions, and convective evolution. To represent the range of meteorological environments sampled during TRACER, K-means clustering was applied to classify meteorological soundings from all DCCs based on temperature, humidity, and horizontal winds at multiple pressure levels into nine sounding clusters. Five representative clusters were selected, with 10 soundings each used to initialize deep convective simulations in the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model in Large-Eddy Simulation (LES) mode with the Fast Spectral Bin Microphysics (FSBM) scheme. LOW, MOD, and HIGH aerosol conditions were derived from ground-based Scanning Mobility Particle Sizer (SMPS) observations and their observed variability. In total, a 150-member LES ensemble was used to systematically evaluate aerosol effects across contrasting meteorological environments. Across meteorological clusters, higher aerosol loading was generally associated with delayed first radar echo, reduced radar reflectivity, and shorter-lived, shallower DCCs, whereas lower aerosol conditions produced deeper, longer-lived convection. Clusters with higher PWV showed longer lifetimes and greater cell heights than lower-PWV clusters. Process-level analysis suggests that differences in diffusional growth (both ice and liquid) at upper levels play a dominant role in controlling lifetime differences between low and high-aerosol scenarios. Stronger diffusional growth under low-aerosol conditions enhanced latent heating and sustained convection, while high-aerosol conditions favored evaporation and likely increased entrainment leading to suppressed convective development. Notably, aerosol sensitivity also depended on the initiating thermal perturbation's radius, with smaller warm-bubble size producing stronger aerosol effects, likely due to increased entrainment in narrower DCCs. These results indicate that aerosol impacts on deep convection are not uniform but depend jointly on the ambient thermodynamic environment and the scale of convective initiation.

493495.title: Developing the High-Resolution Urban Meteorology for Impacts Dataset (HUMID) Version 2: Applications to Urban Heat and Snow Hazards
493495.authors: Tzu-Shun Lin, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and A. J. Newman, C. He, and O. Wilhelmi
493495.abstract: Urban areas host a large and growing portion of the population and are featured by complex land surface characteristics, building morphology, and multiple physical and anthropogenic processes that influence urban environments. High-resolution and long-term gridded meteorological datasets across cities are therefore needed to understand urban hazards, such as heat stress and rooftop snow loading, and to support applications including urban planning and risk assessment. Building on the previous successful HUMID products—including a 1-km model–observation fusion product spanning 1981–2018 across the CONUS at daily temporal resolution, developed using an offline land–urban modeling system; and the HUMID-Atlanta product, spanning 2010–2023 over the Atlanta metropolitan area at hourly temporal resolution, developed using a coupled atmosphere–land–urban modeling system. This study develops a new prototype of the HUMID version 2 (HUMID v2). HUMID v2 integrates state-of-the-art urban datasets, an updated modeling framework, and newly developed urban rooftop snow processes. The new product leverages 1-km meteorological data from the third phase of North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS-3), updated urban land cover types, and annual impervious surface datasets. A machine-learning-based bias-correction method is also incorporated into the workflow to fuse the model outputs with in-situ measurements. In addition, multiple urban-related variables, including road, building-wall, roof temperatures and various heat indices, are provided at hourly temporal resolution. A prototype of HUMID v2 is developed over the Denver metropolitan area using the single-layer urban canopy model within the High-Resolution Land Data Assimilation System (HRLDAS). Beyond the prototype applications in Denver, newly developed urban rooftop snow loading processes are being integrated into the coupled Building Effect Parameterization–Building Energy Model (BEP–BEM) within the HRLDAS framework to quantify rooftop snow loading hazards in Anchorage, Alaska. Overall, the improved modeling framework, updated input datasets, enhanced bias-correction approach, tailored output indices, and newly developed rooftop snow processes establish a more comprehensive framework for HUMID v2 and expand its potential applications in urban hazard monitoring, planning, and early warning.

493497.title: SOLAR A-B Missions; Continuing Resilience for Space Weather Forecasting
493497.authors: Yaireska Collado-Vega, NOAA, Lanaham, MD; and A. Greeley, I. Azeem, E. M. Lynch, J. F. Spann Jr., J. Morrissey, J. Panek, C. DeLee, R. G. Marlow, R. Ullman, and E. Guerrero-Martin
493497.abstract: The Space Weather Next (SW Next) program at NOAA NESDIS Office of Space Weather Observations was designed and is being implemented to provide low latency data resiliency from different vantage points that include the Geostationary and Low Earth orbits, as well as Lagrange 1 (L1) and Lagrange 5 (L5), in collaboration with the European Space Agency (ESA). The first project of the SW Next program, already in Phase B, is the Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness (SOLAR) project, composed of two spacecraft, SOLAR-A and SOLAR-B, with SOLAR-A currently planned to be launched by 2029. The main objective for the SOLAR project is to provide continuity of observations beyond the SOLAR-1, previously known as Space Weather Follow On – Lagrange 1 (SWFO-L1), mission launched in September 2025 with a design life of five years. SOLAR will include six instruments that include a coronagraph, a plasma sensor, a magnetometer, a suprathermal ion sensor, an X-ray irradiance sensor and a particle contributed instrument. In this presentation, we will describe the observational requirements from the L1 vantage point, how the project is working to continue critical observations, and how these observations will support the space weather operational environment to safeguard the Nation and to support government and commercial human exploration missions.

493498.title: Dual Physical Pathways Shape Subseasonal-to-Seasonal Predictability of North American Summer Heat Extremes
493498.authors: Baoqiang Xiang, GFDL, Princeton, NJ; and L. M. Harris, G. Zhang, and X. Ding
493498.abstract: Improving the subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction of heatwaves is a critical scientific challenge due to their severe societal impacts and the limited predictability at these lead times. Here we show two dominant and physically distinct sources of S2S predictability for the weekly hot days across North America. The leading predictable mode, with its strongest loading over the southern U.S., reflects an ocean-forced mode associated with a Pacific Decadal Oscillation-like sea surface temperature pattern. In contrast, the second most predictable mode, with centers of action over northwestern and southeastern North America, is dominated by atmospheric internal variability associated with the summer Arctic Oscillation and summer North Atlantic Oscillation. Skillful week-3 forecasts of hot days are further characterized by quasi-stationary wave patterns coupled with regional soil moisture deficit, revealing dynamical and land-surface “windows of opportunity” for extended S2S predictability. These findings identify the physical mechanisms governing North American heat extreme predictability and provide a scientific basis for improving extended-range early warnings of heat extremes.

493499.title: Toward AI-Enabled and Latent Space DA within DART
493499.authors: Mohamad El Gharamti, NCAR, Boulder, CO
493499.abstract: As the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) enters its next 25 years, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer new opportunities to extend ensemble data assimilation (DA) beyond traditional approaches. Emerging directions include emulators for expensive and complex forward operators (e.g., radiances), fast and large emulated physical ensembles, ML-assisted inflation and localization schemes, and further hybridization of DART’s existing covariance capabilities with ML-generated ensembles to better represent model error and systematic bias. The work will highlight already existing ML capabilities within DART such as group filters and empirical localization functions. These tools serve as prototypes that could guide more powerful AI products in the near future. We will also discuss recent efforts of integrating AI-based weather models (e.g., PANGU) into DART and demonstrate their efficacy for predicting extreme weather events, such as hurricane tracking. DART will further focus on a transformative direction which involves conducting the DA update in a learned latent space. Forecast ensemble members can be encoded into a lower-dimensional nonlinear representation, updated using DART’s advanced ensemble algorithms, and decoded back into physical model space. This approach could reduce the computational complexity associated with high-dimensional systems, improve covariance estimation, preserve correlations and multivariate structures, and provide new ways to handle nonlinear and non-Gaussian relationships. The work will also explore the scientific challenges associated with these AI tools, including uncertainty representation, physical balance and constraints, localization, and inflation.

493501.title: Aerosols, Clouds, and Lightning in Tropical Maritime Clouds: Evidence from IMO-2020
493501.authors: Emily Katherine de Jong, Lawrence Livermore National Lab, Livermore, CA; and T. Schneider, J. P. Jalkanen, and P. O. Wennberg
493501.abstract: Oceanic lightning frequency was previously shown to correlate with the location of two major shipping corridors in the tropical Indo-Pacific, suggesting an aerosol contribution to enhanced lightning occurrence. In 2020, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) restricted shipping fuel sulfur concentration, providing an opportunity to reassess the response of oceanic lightning to a perturbation in aerosol conditions in this region. Based on previous findings, a reduction in shipping aerosols is expected to lead to a decrease in lightning over shipping corridors relative to unpolluted regions, yet this work finds that only one of the two investigated shipping lanes displays a robust aerosol-lightning response. Through a multivariate regression of meteorological, convective, and cloud microphysical quantities with lightning flash rate, we detangle the contributions of large-scale meteorological conditions from those of aerosol emissions to lightning in both shipping regions. Using these results, we estimate the sensitivity of cloud water path to cloud number concentration using scaling arguments based on a microphysical pathway through which aerosol impacts lightning frequency. Our results offer new insights into the role of aerosol-cloud interactions in deep convection.

493508.title: LAFT: An LLM-Assisted Fortran translation and Validation-Gated HPC Workflow for Modernizing Fortran Atmospheric Physics into GPU-optimized JAX
493508.authors: Iris Linck, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Schreck, J. M. Dennis, D. J. Gagne II, and K. Stengel
493508.abstract: Atmospheric models contain decades of validated Fortran physics that are difficult to integrate with Python/JAX-based machine-learning workflows or to execute efficiently on GPU-accelerated systems. We present LAFT (LLM-Assisted Fortran Translation), a framework that converts large-language-model code generation into a reproducible HPC modernization workflow for atmospheric physics parameterizations. LAFT combines a deterministic Fortran front end, bridge-based language interoperability, multi-pass LLM translation, iterative correction based on validation tests, and hardware-level performance profiling. An automated Fortran analysis step identifies procedures, variables, module state, and dependencies, then organizes the code into translation units, while an automatically generated bridge preserves Fortran memory layout and module state across the Fortran/JAX boundary. The translation stage can use either frontier agentic coding systems or locally-served open-weight LLMs. Generated code is then checked through structural linting, a semantic audit against the Fortran source code, GPU runtime validation, an end-to-end numerical comparison with the Fortran reference, and a profiling/diagnosis loop that guides repair. We evaluate LAFT across three atmospheric microphysics codes of increasing complexity: the two-procedure Kessler warm-rain scheme, the 49-procedure P3 scheme, and a 71-procedure, 8-module kernel subset of the SCALE-SDM super-droplet model. Kessler and P3 are validated end-to-end, while translation of the SCALE-SDM kernel subset is underway. Across these targets, framework extensions were target-agnostic rather than code-specific, suggesting that LAFT can scale beyond a single microphysics case study. For Kessler and P3 configured with 10⁴ columns, translated JAX implementations achieve end-to-end speedups of 34× and 11×, respectively, over the serial Fortran references when host-device transfers and layout transposes are included. Device compute alone is 216× faster for Kessler and 140× faster for P3. These results identify the language-interoperability overhead and host-to-device data transfers, rather than the physics kernels, as the remaining bottleneck. All validated Kessler and P3 translations reproduce the Fortran references to machine precision and generate production-ready GPU performance profiles. However, the repair burden, differed substantially across model classes: frontier models generally produced validation-ready translations with minimal intervention, whereas open-weight models more often required iterative repair. Recurrent open-weight failure modes include placeholder scaffolding (placeholder stubs replace translated procedure bodies), positional omissions consistent with lost-in-the-middle behavior, and non-idiomatic JAX designs that preserve sequential Fortran loop structure instead of vectorizing across columns. These findings show that LLM-assisted translation can accelerate atmospheric-code modernization, but only when combined with deterministic interfaces, rigorous validation, and hardware-aware profiling feedback.

493514.title: Recent Advancement of JEDI Local Ensemble Solvers for Coupled UFS Applications
493514.authors: Bo Huang, CIRES, BOULDER, CO; and S. Frolov, C. Thomas, J. Waller, D. Simonin, A. Shlyaeva, J. Whitaker, C. H. Bishop, M. Zidikheri, N. Eizenberg, C. R. Martin, D. Holdaway, S. Herbener, and Y. Tremolet
493514.abstract: The computational efficiency of the local ensemble solvers in the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) has been significantly improved, enabling testing in real applications including the atmosphere, ocean, sea ice and atmospheric compositions. We are currently focusing on implementing advanced techniques and science to further improve the background error covariance estimates in the JEDI local ensemble solvers. Recently, a cross-validation capability was implemented to utilize independent subsets of ensemble members for member updates and thus mitigate filter inbreeding. We are now implementing an efficient muti-scale localization method for local ensemble solvers in JEDI to better represent physical correlations across varying spatial scales. These new developments will be evaluated within the NOAA Unified Forecast System (UFS) global atmospheric model using near-operational observation datasets. Detailed implementation strategies and experiment results will be presented.

493515.title: Developing Actionable Heat Index Data for Health Applications from a Climate-Information Generation Perspective
493515.authors: Keith William Dixon, NOAA, Princeton, NJ; and W. Xu, L. Sun, and J. R. Lanzante
493515.abstract: Translating climate data and model simulations into actionable insights for public health and other stakeholders requires more than simply distributing data files, as it benefits from a robust transfer of knowledge regarding appropriate data application. Bridging the atmospheric sciences and public health realms often involves evaluating whether observational and/or model-derived climate datasets are “fit for purpose” without “allowing the perfect to become the enemy of the good.” Here, we share perspectives drawn from our team’s experience at NOAA’s Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory, addressing the topic primarily from the climate-information generation vantage point. We illustrate approaches and findings based on three studies completed within the past two years, each of which examines the frequency of extreme summertime heat conditions as measured by the heat index (HI), a function of temperature and humidity. Though the analyses focus on HI, the results can inform studies that employ other multivariate climate indices. First, challenges related to suboptimal temporal resolution of climate variables in observations and model output are illustrated. Specifically, it is shown that a not uncommon approach for estimating the daily maximum HI from daily maximum temperature and daily minimum relative humidity underestimates the frequency of extreme HI days, and the causes of these regional differences are explained. Next, methodological options are considered when bias correction and/or statistical downscaling are used to produce statistically refined daily maximum HI time series from climate model output. The results expose limitations in computing a multivariate index such as HI from component variables individually bias-corrected with univariate methods. Computed in this way, HI inherits shortcomings in the climate model’s representation of the temperature–humidity covariance. Improved results are obtained either by using a multivariate bias correction approach (e.g., MBCn) that transfers the observed temperature–humidity covariance to the bias-corrected output, or by computing HI from the model output first and then applying univariate bias correction (e.g., QDM) to the resulting HI series. Finally, the seasonal prediction skill and reliability of summertime HI in GFDL SPEAR hindcasts across the contiguous United States are assessed. Regional differences in prediction skill are linked to SPEAR’s ability to reproduce temperature–humidity relationships and the regional influence of large-scale sea surface temperature variability. Together, these studies illustrate that generating application-ready heat index information requires careful attention to temporal resolution, multivariate dependence, bias-correction strategy, and forecast skill. These considerations are essential for translating climate data into reliable information for heat-health preparedness and other climate-risk applications.

493517.title: Past and Future NOAA Space Weather Missions at GEO.
493517.authors: Nicholas John Zaremba, NOAA, Lanham, MD; and I. Azeem, E. M. Lynch, L. A. Rachmeler, and A. Heidinger
493517.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is mandated to provide operational space-based environmental data that are essential for a modern society. NOAA is currently planning its next generation of environmental satellites to meet evolving user needs. Operational space weather observations aboard the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) program continue to play a foundational role in advancing NOAA’s ability to monitor, forecast, and respond to space weather-related hazards. The GOES constellation has existed for over 50 years, with its initial launch in 1975. The modern GOES-R generation introduced significant improvements in space weather monitoring. In addition, other missions have provided essential observations from geostationary orbit (GEO), including the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). As part of its Space Weather Next program, NESDIS’s Office of Space Weather Observations (SWO) is exploring options for data continuity and refinement of space weather observations from GEO, alongside other relevant orbits, such as Lagrange point 1 (L1) and Lagrange 5 (L5). As part of this process, SWO is assessing the current use of GEO-based observations. This includes, but is not limited to, products produced by the Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) or the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) that are essential for space weather stakeholders and users. SWO also recognizes the space weather community is interested in products and datasets derived from GEO to develop new and innovative methodologies to advance space weather science. SWO is currently undergoing a number of activities to refine space weather observations at GEO including an analysis of alternatives (AoA) and multiple instruments studies. This presentation discusses the historical evolution of space weather instruments aboard GOES, the data over time and considerations for the future.

493519.title: AMS SATMOC Virtual Short Course in 2026
493519.authors: Jun Wang, Univ. of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; Univ. of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; and M. Christiansen, C. Smith, M. Zhou, M. N. Razin, Y. Fan, J. Fain, J. Torres, J. J. Gerth, J. Cintineo, E. Goldenstern, S. S. Morris, and G. B. McWilliams
493519.abstract: The American Meteorological Society's (AMS) Committee on Satellite Meteorology, Oceanography, and Climatology (SatMOC) offered a virtual short course to demonstrate the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in developing new and improved environmental satellite data applications. This short course, titled “AI Applications Using Environmental Satellite Remote Sensing Data”, continues an effort SatMOC began in 2022 to provide virtual training on environmental satellite data applications. This presentation provides an overview of the 2026 course and reflects on the achievements and feedback gained, which will guide planning for the 2027 short course. Held across four 4-hour training sessions in June: 'An Introduction to Environmental Satellite Remote Sensing,' 'Creating AI-Ready Datasets,' 'Understanding Machine Learning in Land Cover Classification,' and 'AI for Atmospheric Applications’, the courses included interactive exercises and Q&A. Registration included 948 participants from 109 countries. The University of Iowa facilitated online registration and hosted virtual sessions via the Zoom platform. The Colorado State University Cooperative Institute for Research on the Atmosphere (CIRA) website provides the publicly accessible recordings and presentation materials. Although tailored for students and early-career professionals, the SatMOC training attacted a broad audience, including professionals transitioning into roles requiring satellite data knowledge. Participant feedback indicates a strong intent to apply knowledge regarding the preparation of AI-ready datasets, preprocessing workflows, and general machine learning techniques to their research and operational projects. Survey results also highlight a significant interest in deepening knowledge of foundation models, physics-informed machine learning, and deep learning architectures—specifically for uncertainty quantification, bias detection, and anomaly identification. This feedback will serve as a foundational guide for determining topics for future SatMOC-sponsored short courses.

493525.title: A High-Resolution Coupled MPAS-A/MOM6 Model for Multiscale Air-Sea Interaction Research and Forecasting
493525.authors: Benjamin W. Barr, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. Amrhein, B. Dobbins, M. Duda, A. Janney, Y. R. Jauregui, F. Judt, S. Kamali, G. Marques, S. Voelz, R. C. Mullis, R. Oehmke, G. Seijo, A. Tsay, and U. U. Turuncoglu
493525.abstract: High-resolution, km-scale coupled atmosphere-ocean models allow representation of physical processes and air-sea interactions that are relevant to research and forecasting at weather and seasonal-to-subseasonal (S2S) timescales. Here we present an overview and preliminary validation for a new high-resolution system coupling the Model for Prediction Across Scales – Atmosphere (MPAS-A) with the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6). The model leverages existing coupling capabilities used by NSF NCAR for the Community Earth System Model (CESM), namely ESMF and NUOPC tools for field handling and communication, CMEPS for defining and managing exchanges, and CDEPS for data forcing. The system is being configured and developed for both regional and global applications, with target usage up to global km-scale (~3-km horizontal resolution, ~65 million horizontal grid columns). We will report on development to date and ongoing test cases, including forecasts for tropical cyclones and Indo-Pacific coupled air-sea phenomena, which show realistic physical features and promising computational performance for large domains. After completing the atmosphere-ocean coupling, the team plans to further leverage CMEPS and CESM tools to expand the framework into a full Earth System model with coupling to advanced land, ocean surface wave, sea ice, and river runoff components, enabling comprehensive multiscale study of the coupled Earth System at high resolution and weather to S2S timescales.

493526.title: Extreme Fire-Weather: Downslope Winds and Hydraulic Transitions in WRF-CFBM Simulations of the Eaton and Palisades Fires
493526.authors: Masih Eghdami, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and M. E. Frediani, P. A. Jimenez, M. J. Kavulich Jr., A. Wang, and A. Habib
493526.abstract: Extreme downslope windstorms over complex terrain can produce attached downslope jets that transition into hydraulic jumps and turbulent rotor regions, creating sharp spatial and temporal gradients in near-surface wind, turbulence, and flow separation. The location of an ignition, fire front, or community relative to these flow features can result in large differences in fire spread and its impacts. These structures may also modify plume rise and near-surface smoke transport through localized ascent, descent, and recirculation. Diagnosing these localized structures remains challenging because of sparse observations, model-resolution limitations, model sensitivity, and the movement of small-scale flow features. This research analyzes the terrain-modified boundary-layer flow of two major fire-weather events: the Eaton and Palisades fires. This is the first real-world case study using the Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled with the Community Fire Behavior Model (WRF-CFBM, available in WRF v4.8.0). Simulations use three nested atmospheric domains with 900, 300, and 100 m grid spacing and a 25 m refined fire-spread mesh. The analysis combines flow-aligned vertical cross-sections, plan views, and time-evolution diagnostics of potential temperature, along-flow wind, and vertical velocity. Simulations with and without two-way fire-atmosphere coupling are compared to assess how fire-generated heat and moisture modify downslope winds, turbulence, and hydraulic-transition evolution, and how the flow affects simulated fire behavior. We also compare plume heights and near-surface smoke distribution among the diagnosed flow regimes. Results show a range of regimes, including hydraulic jumps that satisfy local supercritical-to-subcritical transition criteria, organized transitions that remain supercritical, and strong downslope flow without an organized jump near the fire. Cross-case and resolution comparisons, together with available observations, assess the robustness of these regimes and evaluate whether they can be distinguished using upstream wind and stability, changes in flow speed and layer depth across each feature, or both.

493530.title: Celebrating 25 Years of DART: Advancing Community-Driven Ensemble Data Assimilation
493530.authors: Mohamad El Gharamti, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Anderson, H. Kershaw, B. Raczka, K. Raeder, and M. Smith
493530.abstract: The Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) is a community facility for ensemble DA, developed and maintained at the National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research. For a quarter of a century, DART has enabled research and operational applications across the Earth system, including the atmosphere, ocean, hydrology, cryosphere, land surface, chemistry, and coupled modeling systems. Its flexibility, scalability, and broad model support have established DART as a leading DA framework with an active and growing international user community. This poster celebrates 25 years of DART by showcasing the framework’s capabilities, recent scientific advances, and expanding community. It also serves as an introduction for students, postdoctoral researchers, and DA practitioners interested in adopting ensemble DA, while also highlighting the latest developments for experienced users. Featured topics include recent high-impact applications spanning numerical weather prediction, ocean forecasting, hydrologic prediction, and coupled DA. DART’s diverse observational capabilities and support for new observing platforms will also be highlighted. The poster will further focus on major improvements to the DART documentation, including modernized online documentation system, expanded tutorials, step-by-step workflows, and numerous new examples and notebooks designed to lower the barrier for new users while improving the productivity of experienced ones. Additional highlights include software enhancements and emerging directions (e.g., AI) that illustrate how DART continues to evolve in support of the next-generation Earth system prediction. We welcome attendees to learn about DART, meet the development team, and explore opportunities for collaboration.

493531.title: Use of Machine Learning for More Diurnally Consistent Geostationary Satellite Cloud Retrievals
493531.authors: Cecilia W Fleeger, Analytical Mechanics Associates, Hampton, VA; and W. L. Smith Jr., L. Nguyen, D. Painemal, T. Chee, R. Palikonda, K. Khlopenkov, D. Spangenberg, J. Hicks, C. R. Yost, and K. Ayers
493531.abstract: Retrieving cloud properties from geostationary (GEO) satellite observations remains challenging under difficult observing conditions, including sunglint, high solar zenith angles, twilight, and nighttime. The uncertainties in cloud detection and cloud-property retrievals increase in these challenging observing regimes due to changes in solar illumination and viewing geometry, sunglint contamination of visible and shortwave infrared observations, rapid surface temperature fluctuations at twilight, or the loss of reflected-solar information at twilight and night. We have developed a temporally adaptive machine learning (ML) approach to improve the diurnal consistency of cloud retrievals across the GEO satellite constellation under these challenging conditions within the NASA Langley Satellite ClOud and Radiation Property retrieval System (SatCORPS). The ML approach uses satellite geolocation and infrared (IR) observations as input features. The corresponding cloud retrievals provide reference cloud properties in multidimensional training datasets. K-dimensional trees, using satellite-specific training data, are constructed for different observing regimes to conduct efficient nearest-neighbor searches. The ML-based retrievals, including cloud mask, cloud phase, nighttime cloud optical depth, and particle size, are selected where conventional approaches have greater uncertainty. We also developed a dedicated preprocessing system to generate and maintain quality-controlled training datasets for implementing the ML applications into the SatCORPS Global Cloud Composite (GCC), a near-real-time operational processing system. The system is updated in real time with the most recent 24 hours of satellite observations and corresponding cloud retrievals, allowing the ML retrievals to adapt to recent atmospheric and surface conditions. This study presents recent advances in training-data preprocessing, the ML algorithms, and their implementation within the SatCORPS GCC processing system. The updated ML algorithms will be validated using SatCORPS GCC retrievals for April 2020, with collocated CALIPSO cloud products serving as the validation reference.

493533.title: Generative Neural Operators for Multi-Variable Postprocessing of High-Resolution Ensemble Weather Forecasts
493533.authors: Josh Jacobson, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and I. Jankov and D. S. Abdi
493533.abstract: Ensemble forecasts can capture physical and model-based uncertainty but suffer from bias and dispersion errors that require postprocessing. Standard postprocessing methods are often applied to one weather variable at a time, which erodes inter-variable dependencies and can yield unphysical combinations in coupled fields. We present an ongoing multi-variable postprocessing framework for HRRRCast version 3, a diffusion-generated ensemble trained on NOAA’s High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) analyses for convection-allowing forecasts over the contiguous United States (CONUS). Building on feedback from NOAA’s 2026 Spring Forecasting Experiment, which highlighted overconfidence in severe convective forecasts, our approach aims to jointly calibrate composite reflectivity and precipitation. We propose a generative neural operator that maps the uncalibrated HRRRCast ensemble to a physically coherent bivariate distribution over the CONUS domain. Formulated for training against Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor (MRMS) observational analyses, the model optimizes a composite loss combining multivariate proper scoring rules in both spectral and physical domains to preserve spatial structure and inter-variable dependence. By leveraging direct operator forward passes rather than iterative diffusion steps, the system is designed to generate hundreds of postprocessed bivariate fields per second. Rather than storing these massive samples, we produce on-the-fly Monte Carlo estimators for the bias-corrected ensemble mean, calibrated tail quantiles, and joint hazard exceedance probabilities that can be tailored to operational alerting. In ongoing evaluation, we expect this framework to reduce bias and overconfidence while preserving convective cell morphology, rapidly delivering calibrated single-variable and multi-variable forecast products for severe weather hazards.

493535.title: Role of Shear-Driven Boundary Layer Rolls in QLCS-Supercell Mergers within High-Shear, Low-CAPE Environments
493535.authors: Joshua S. Ostaszewski, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and C. C. Weiss
493535.abstract: High-shear, low-CAPE (HSLC) environments have garnered increasing scientific attention over the past decade due to their frequent association with significant severe weather events, including tornadoes; their disproportionate impacts on vulnerable populations, particularly during nighttime events; and, more recently, their propensity to support both supercells and quasi-linear convective systems (QLCSs) within the same environment, which can produce a range of merger outcomes. The latter remains virtually unexplored, owing to the scarcity of high-resolution, four-dimensional observational datasets and the challenges of sustaining HSLC convection in idealized modeling, particularly when attempting to maintain both a QLCS and a supercell simultaneously. This research aims to address this gap by using CM1 to simulate an HSLC QLCS and preceding supercell(s) using observed ambient soundings from the Propagation, Evolution, and Rotation in Linear Storms (PERiLS) field campaign, while varying lower boundary conditions (free-slip, semi-slip). The simulations will be used to quantify favorable and unfavorable interactions that contribute to mesovortexgenesis, and potentially tornadogenesis, within the pre-line supercell, during the merger, and in the post-merger QLCS segment. HSLC QLCS-supercell mergers frequently enhance low-level vertical vorticity within both the pre-line supercell and the post-merger mesovortex; however, the processes that initiate, amplify, and maintain this rotation remain poorly understood. The semi-slip QLCS produced stronger rear-to-front flow aloft (in comparison to the free-slip QLCS), promoting a stratiform-leading structure. Evaporative cooling aloft within this regime produces a 25 km-wide zone of weak potential temperature deficits ahead of the line. In conjunction with shear-driven turbulent boundary layer roll vortices, numerous ancillary convective cells develop within this zone. As these cells mature and merge along the QLCS gust front, they provide a mechanism for tilting and reorienting pre-existing horizontal vorticity, promoting mesovortexgenesis and, in some cases, tornado-like vortices (TLVs). With time, some ancillary cells evolve into “mini-supercells,” intensifying as they propagate toward the QLCS and interact with the increasingly organized boundary layer rolls near the line. More robust leading-QLCS supercells were also initiated via instantaneous warm bubbles, yielding mergers that are dynamically distinct from interactions involving weaker ancillary cells/mini-supercells. Comparisons to the free-slip QLCS-supercell mergers will also be presented.

493536.title: 30 Years of the NSF NCAR EOL Field Catalog: An Application for Science Connection
493536.authors: Carol Ruchti, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Allison, S. M. Loehrer, S. Stringer, and W. C. Lenhardt
493536.abstract: Since its inception in 1995, the National Science Foundation (NSF), National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), Earth Observing Laboratory (EOL) Field Catalog (hereafter Field Catalog) has evolved from a centralized website for cataloging atmospheric field campaign data products into a sophisticated, customizable, real-time application for planning campaigns, tracking field campaign research platforms, and displaying real-time data products. The catalog team has managed over 100 catalogs across various atmospheric science disciplines, working with numerous Principal Investigators (PIs), and using data from hundreds of unique instruments to easily share near real-time data products. As technology continues to improve and real-time earth science data is more accessible, the Field Catalog continues to evolve to align with the needs of the atmospheric science community and PIs by collecting user feedback. Users continue to emphasize how essential the Field Catalog is to efficiently collaborate and accomplish the science goals of the field campaigns before, during, and after deployment. Thanks to the managers, developers, scientists, and users who contributed to the creation of the Field Catalog, it has become a cornerstone of the atmospheric field science community. After creating V1 and V2 of the Field Catalog, the team has started to envision and plan the next iteration of the catalog to create an even better user experience supporting evolving science needs. This talk will outline the Field Catalog’s historical impact, current capabilities, and plans for the future. The Field Catalog has the potential to tell the stories of science across the various earth science disciplines. In the future, this same Field Catalog application could be used to tell science stories of the past. For example, a social science case study of Hurricane Ian from 2022 could be visually displayed with operational data products (satellite, radar, NWS watches/warnings) and citizen survey data. Thus, research spanning earth science or even multidisciplinary science could utilize the Field Catalog in a newly imagined way for visual science story telling. Then, NCAR’s Field Catalog application would be available for an even broader science audience, and the Field Catalog would continue to evolve and adapt as has been the case for the last 30 years.

493537.title: Advancing Multiscale Soil Moisture Research Through the RUBISCO Soil Moisture Working Group
493537.authors: Jiafu Mao, DOE, Oak Ridge, TN; and Y. Wang, F. M. Hoffman, A. K. Ambika, A. Chen, J. Fisher, Y. Hao, G. J. Kooperman, G. Koren, M. Kumar, C. Li, L. Li, E. Massoud, H. Moreno, P. Raghav, P. Ray, V. Sehgal, M. Shi, H. Zhang, H. Thakur, Y. Wang, Y. Xu, W. Zhang, and X. Zhang
493537.abstract: Soil moisture plays a central role in global hydrologic, energy, and biogeochemical cycles and is a key control on land–atmosphere interactions, ecosystem responses, and hydroclimate variability. Yet major challenges remain in developing multiscale soil moisture datasets, characterizing land–atmosphere and ecosystem feedbacks, assessing links to climate extremes and predictability, and benchmarking Earth system models. To address these challenges, the U.S. Department of Energy RUBISCO project established the Soil Moisture Working Group (SMWG) in early 2023 as a collaborative forum for the international soil moisture research community. The SMWG brings together observational, modeling, machine-learning, and application-focused perspectives through regular meetings, topical discussions, collaborative publications, and the development of datasets and model benchmarks. The working group is organized around two complementary research themes. The first focuses on integrative approaches to soil moisture science, ranging from sustained in situ observations and machine-learning-enhanced products to satellite remote-sensing evaluation, global ecohydrological modeling, and model benchmarking. These efforts support improved characterization of soil moisture variability across spatial and temporal scales and provide a foundation for evaluating land-surface processes and their influence on atmospheric conditions. The second theme examines interdisciplinary connections among soil moisture dynamics, environmental hazards, ecosystems, and human impacts, including applications related to drought, agriculture, vegetation, land-use influences, and land–atmosphere feedbacks. This presentation synthesizes progress across the SMWG topical areas, highlights opportunities to connect in situ observations, satellite remote sensing, data-driven methods, and process-based models, and discusses how these coordinated efforts can advance understanding of soil moisture controls on hydroclimate extremes and land–atmosphere interactions. We also identify priorities for future collaborative research aimed at strengthening multiscale soil moisture datasets, improving model evaluation and representation of land-surface processes, and supporting studies of predictability and Earth system responses across timescales.

493540.title: The Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes' Atmospheric River Reconnaissance (AR Recon) Coordinated University Soundings Program (CUSP)
493540.authors: F Martin Ralph, Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and A. C. Michaelis, A. M. Wilson, T. A. O'Brien, and B. Demoz
493540.abstract: Expanding research into the topic of atmospheric rivers (ARs) and establishment of the AR Reconnaissance (AR Recon) research and operations partnership highlight the importance of collecting observations for forecast improvement, as well as enhancing our own understanding of these impactful storms. To aid in this effort, we created the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) AR Recon Coordinated University Soundings Program for (CUSP) as a unique partnership between CW3E and universities to collect targeted upper-air observations in support of AR Recon. The AR Recon CUSP university network plays an important role in broadening observational coverage to sample environments downstream and within high-impact weather regimes involving ARs. These observations are disseminated in real time, improving the accuracy of the forecasts during impactful weather events that communities, emergency managers, and water operators depend on. This dataset is also publicly available for broader use across the meteorological community for research and education purposes. AR Recon CUSP is entirely powered by faculty, staff, and student teams at participating universities with students helping to lead launch planning, weather balloon deployment, and tracking of radiosonde output through the upper atmosphere. University participants can also join daily AR Recon briefings to learn how science teams across agencies work together in real time to plan missions in response to evolving storm forecasts. Student participants were overwhelming positive about their AR Recon experience, noting the value of experiential learning for reinforcing classroom concepts, building community with inter- and intra-university peers, and gaining necessary skills for entering the workforce. During the 2026 AR Recon CUSP season, we collected 477 profiles across our 15 university sites with much of the data being shared with local National Weather Service forecast offices and assimilated directly into global forecast models. We plan to expand to 25 universities for the upcoming 2027 AR Recon CUSP season.
