493543.title: Meteorological Patterns Associated with the Onset and Demise of Persistent Cold-Air Pools in the Northwestern United States
493543.authors: Arielle G. Sherbak, Portland State University, Portland, OR; Portland State University, Portland, OR; and P. C. Loikith and H. K. Lee
493543.abstract: Persistent cold-air pools (PCAPs) are multi-day episodes of stable atmospheric stratification in valleys and basins that can strongly influence wintertime air quality, fog development and persistence, low-temperature extremes, and freezing-rain hazards. Although the large-scale circulation patterns associated with established PCAPs are relatively well understood, the meteorological conditions supporting their onset and demise remain less clearly defined, and a comprehensive PCAP climatology has not been established for valleys and basins of the U.S. Northwest. Using radiosonde observations, we identify PCAP events over a 1995–2025 record in the Northwest. K-means clustering is then applied to 500-hPa geopotential height, sea-level pressure, and 700-hPa temperature fields to identify recurring meteorological patterns before, during, and after the events. The clustering reveals several distinct pathways associated with PCAP development. These include low-level cold-air advection into valleys and basins, extended periods of radiational cooling beneath persistent upper-level ridging, and PCAP development following the passage of a cool-season trough or frontal system, as precipitation and cloud cover give way to ridging and increasing surface stability. These pathways vary between locations, suggesting that similar large-scale circulation patterns can produce different local response. Cold-air advection and radiational cooling represent direct mechanisms for establishing and strengthening low-level stability, while the post-frontal pattern highlights a broader synoptic sequence in which PCAP formation follows the transition from unsettled weather to clearing, subsidence, and surface cooling. Clustering of conditions surrounding event demise further shows that PCAP erosion can occur through multiple pathways rather than a single characteristic circulation pattern, including changes in large-scale flow that weaken stability, increase mixing, or alter low-level temperature advection. Because PCAPs are shallow, localized, and strongly dependent on complex terrain, they are often difficult for numerical weather prediction models and reanalysis to represent directly. Using radiosonde observations to identify events reduces reliance on uncertain model representations of low-level inversions while allowing reanalysis data to characterize the larger-scale meteorological context. A clearer understanding of PCAP onset and demise may improve forecasts of event development and erosion, support air-quality and biomass-burning bans, and provide a foundation for evaluating how these events may change in a non-stationary atmosphere.

493544.title: Temporal Evolution of Secondary Eyewall Formation Revealed by Synthetic Passive Microwave Imagery
493544.authors: Taiga Tsukada, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and K. Haynes, K. Musgrave, and I. Ebert-Uphoff
493544.abstract: Introduction Passive microwave (PMW) observations from Earth-observing satellites are indispensable for characterizing tropical cyclone (TC) structure and are particularly important for diagnosing secondary eyewall formation (SEF) and the eyewall replacement cycle. Vaughan et al. (2020) reported that 79% of SEF cases exhibited a Stationary Banding Complex (SBC) in PMW imagery prior to SEF, and that the logarithmic spiral geometry of the SBC evolved toward the secondary eyewall by exhibiting greater azimuthal extent and a smaller crossing angle beginning 12–24 h before SEF. Cheung et al. (2024) further demonstrated an alternative pathway in which an outer rainband gradually wraps around the TC to become the secondary eyewall. However, the relatively low temporal sampling of PMW observations (approximately ~4.5 h on average) currently precludes characterization of the temporal evolution of SEF at high temporal resolution. At CIRA/CSU, an AI model has been developed to generate Synthetic Passive Microwave (SPM) imagery from geostationary satellite visible and infrared observations, providing global TC-centered SPM imagery at 10-min intervals (Haynes et al. 2025). The objective of this study is to use SPM imagery to characterize the detailed temporal evolution of SEF and improve our understanding of its typical evolution and variability. Data and Methods The SPM model was trained using TCs that occurred during 2017–2021 within the observational domains of the Himawari-8 AHI and the GOES-16/17 ABI. The SPM model uses 15 spectrally corresponding channels between the two sensors, along with various inter-channel difference images, distance to land, and vegetation cover information as input variables, and outputs 4-km-resolution imagery at 89 and 37 GHz for both horizontal and vertical polarizations (Haynes et al. 2025). Because visible imagery is included among the input predictors, retrieval accuracy exhibits a pronounced diurnal dependence, with higher performance during daytime. Accordingly, this study focuses on daytime SEF cases in which the secondary eyewall is clearly identifiable in observed PMW imagery, and examines their temporal evolution using SPM. Here, we present results for Typhoon Kong-Rey (2024), one of the independent test cases. The analysis primarily uses polarization-corrected temperature (PCT) imagery at 89 GHz. Results Observed PMW imagery at 0500 UTC 30 October 2024 clearly showed the presence of both a primary and a secondary eyewall (Fig. 1a). Although the secondary eyewall was not completely closed, it satisfied the objective criteria for concentric eyewalls adopted in many previous studies. The corresponding SPM image accurately reproduced the observed PMW brightness temperature distribution (Fig. 1b). Visible and infrared imagery (Fig. 1c,d) indicated the presence of thin cirrus clouds over the moat region. An SBC-like rainband connected to the primary eyewall was evident in the southeastern quadrant ~6 h earlier (~2300 UTC), around local sunrise (not shown). Between 0130 and 0230 UTC, the moat region developed in a manner that progressively separated the SBC from the primary eyewall, accompanied by an increase in the azimuthal extent of the SBC and a decrease in its crossing angle (not shown). Furthermore, prior to moat formation identified in the SPM imagery, infrared brightness temperatures over the moat region gradually decreased (not shown). These results suggest that the development of subsidence within the moat region detached the SBC from the primary eyewall, ultimately producing a structure recognized as a secondary eyewall. Additional case studies will be presented to discuss the characteristic temporal evolution of SEF. Acknowledgement: This study was supported by CIRA/CSU and by AI Institute Grant ICER-2019758 of the US National Science Foundation (AI2ES; McGovern et al. 2022). Figure 1. (a) Observed 89-GHz PCT, (b) AI-generated SPM 89-GHz PCT, (c) Himawari-9 0.64-µm visible reflectance, and (d) Himawari-9 10.4-µm infrared brightness temperature for Typhoon Kong-Rey (2024) at 0500 UTC 30 October 2024.

493549.title: Forecast Evaluation of a Numerical Model with Coupled Urban and Eddy-Diffusivity Mass-Flux Schemes
493549.authors: Kaiden Patrick Sookdar, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY; and J. C. Pena, J. Wang, and J. E. González-Cruz
493549.abstract: The paradigm of operational weather forecasting models is shifting to include a mass-flux component in their planetary boundary layer (PBL) schemes, typically improving model clouds and forecast evolution. Many operational forecast models implement such schemes yet lack detailed urban physics due to both computational cost and speed. It is hypothesized that an eddy-diffusivity mass-flux (EDMF) PBL scheme with a multi-layer urban canopy model will improve the forecast evolution of lower-tropospheric variables when deployed over a limited-area domain. We test this by deploying the Mellor-Yamada-Nakanishi-Niino EDMF (MYNN-EDMF) and Building Effect Parameterization (BEP) with Building Energy Model (BEM) parametrizations within the Weather Research and Forecasting Model, known as Urban-WRF (uWRF), for the weather forecasting of a coastal megacity, New York City. We conduct a pilot test of the new configuration with daily initialization across the months of February and July 2026 to 52 hours with hourly output intervals. The objective is twofold: determine the skill and error metrics of uWRF across this forecast period and cross-validate with existing models using community verification tools and observational networks, including the New York State Mesonet’s surface and boundary layer profiler networks as well as NWS operational radar. Preliminary results show significantly improved skill relative to other models, particularly in stable nighttime regimes. The presentation will highlight future considerations for urban model physics and potential for applications as operational urbanized forecast system. Due to growing needs for accurate short-range, high-resolution forecasts in major metropolitan areas, it could support a wide range of efforts ranging from wildfires and extreme precipitation to energy demand forecasting.

493552.title: When Summer Stays: Shifting Energy, Water, and Carbon Exchanges Based on a Three-Decade Record from a Colorado Subalpine Forest.
493552.authors: Peter D. Blanken, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and S. P. Burns, A. Turnipseed, D. Bowling, J. Knowles, and R. Monson
493552.abstract: Forested mountain ecosystems play an important role in the regional water, carbon, and energy cycles, and are sensitive to climate change. As in many similar locations world-wide, high-elevation forested watersheds provide most of the surface water critical for lower elevation water resources. For example, an estimated ~80% of Colorado’s water supply originates from the high elevation forest watersheds, and ~75% of that water is derived from the springtime snow meltwater. During the past 30 years, changes in Colorado’s subalpine forest environment have been observed. The date of the snowpack’s peak water content has advanced by roughly 5 days per decade, and the total water content has decreased 10-15% with increased interannual variation. Atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations have increased. The CO2 concentration has increased at a rate of roughly 2 μmol/mol per year, from 366 (1998) to 428 μmol/mol (2025). Methane has increased at a rate of roughly 7 nmol/mol per year, from 1800 (1998) to 1990 nmol/mol (2025). And nitrous oxide (N2O) has increased at a rate of roughly 1 nmol/mol per year, from 313 (1998) to 340 nmol/mol (2025). Concurrently, the Front Range population has increased over 60% from 3.3 million in 1998 to 5.3 million in 2026. This combination of changes in the atmospheric and hydrologic environments means that understanding the forest’s surface-atmosphere exchanges of water, carbon, and energy has never been more important. Recognizing the importance of these forests while meeting the challenges of making high-quality continuous measurements in mountain environments, the Niwot Ridge Flux tower was established November 1998 in the subalpine forest of Colorado, near Boulder, at an elevation of 3050 m asl. A 26-m-tall scaffold tower with AC power and remote network connection has provided continuous eddy covariance flux measurements of CO2 (NEE), H2O, sensible heat, and momentum fluxes. Several ancillary measurements including radiation (upward and downward shortwave and longwave radiation), meteorological (wind speed/direction, air temperature, humidity, precipitation), soil (heat flux, moisture, temperature) and snow properties (depth, temperature), are publicly available to interpret the flux measurements. The tower is located close to other programs with long-term measurements such as SNOTEL, NOAA’s Climate Reference Network, and the Niwot Ridge LTER. The site has participated in many field campaigns over the years, and endured winter and summer droughts, floods, nearby fires and insect outbreaks. In this presentation we will summarize how the subalpine forest has (or has not) responded over the past 30 years to the changing environment and interpret these results in the context of research that has contributed to our understanding of forest micrometeorology and tree physiology, not only in the subalpine forest, but forests in-general. We will also describe the challenges and benefits of making long-term measurements, through the perspective of trends and changes we have observed over the past 30 years. A general finding is that although changes in the springtime snowpack (less snow and earlier melt) do affect surface-atmosphere exchanges, we also see significant changes in the conditions that affect these exchanges during the late summer and fall. In many ways the extension of the summer into the fall has a greater impact than an earlier start to the growing season. Annually, air temperatures are 1.2 °C higher now than in 1998, with a slightly higher increase in the daytime (+1.3 °C) compared to nighttime (+1.1 °C) temperatures. The monthly distribution is not even. The rate of warming is, by far, highest in September (daytime and nighttime), at a warming rate nearly twice the next highest month (June) followed by December, August, October, and November. The rate of increase in vapor pressure deficits was largest in August and September, however, large decreasing trends occurred in May and especially in July. Incident solar and net radiation increased in all months except May, with the largest increases in August. Wind speeds decreased in all months (significantly in May, June, and September) except for increases in February and April (slight increase). Trends in soil temperature, moisture, and heat flux showed statistically significant trends more so than any other variables. Soil temperature increased significantly in all months except May through August. Soil volumetric water content decreased in all months with the largest decreases in fall (September, October, November). The greatest increases in the soil heat flux occurred in the spring (May, June), followed by late summer/fall (August, September). Although there is little doubt that the quantity and timing of water delivered to the subalpine forest during spring snowmelt is critical for growing season’s carbon and water cycling, in this presentation we highlight the importance of the often-overlooked fall period. As described above, the trends in key variables that influence the carbon and water cycles are changing more in the fall season than during any other season. It could be argued that fall is a more critical time than spring, since the forest is more susceptible to disturbances such as fire and disease outbreaks. In spring, the forest can quickly shift from a carbon source to a sink when soil moisture increases with snowmelt and temperatures increase. With limited summer rainfall and higher temperatures and a diminishing snowpack, soil moisture becomes depleted during the summer months. Positive feedback between soil moisture and temperature may begin in the late summer with drying soils warming and warming further drying soils. We see some evidence of this as the sensible heat flux has been increasing in all months except winter (decreasing in November, December, January) with the largest increases in Spring (March, April, May) likely due to the decreasing snow cover, and in late summer/fall (August, September, October). We also observed the largest increases in the latent heat flux in the summer months (June, July, August) supporting the notion of depleting summer soil moisture. The extension of summer into the fall will likely also influence the forest’s carbon cycle. We discuss if a tipping point is reached when soil moisture is inadequate to support net carbon uptake despite the extended summer, and how ecosystem respiration responds to the increased soil temperature concurrent with decreased moisture.

493553.title: Influence of Wildfire, Urban, and Oil and Gas Pollution on Ozone Formation
493553.authors: Seth Lyman, Utah State University, Vernal, UT; and T. O'Neil
493553.abstract: Smoke plumes from wildfires emit reactive organic compounds that are key precursors to ozone formation. When these organics combine with high levels of oxides of nitrogen (NOX) emitted from vehicles and other urban sources, they can increase the ability of urban atmospheres to produce ozone. Oil and gas activity is also an important source of ozone-forming organic compounds. The city of Roosevelt, Utah, has abundant oil and gas development combined with urban emission sources, and frequent influence from wildfire smoke. In the absence of smoke, ozone stays below U.S. EPA standards. When wildfire smoke influences the area, the Roosevelt monitoring station usually has higher ozone than other cities in the region, and higher than oil and gas pollution without urban influence. We measured ozone, a suite of 13 carbonyls, a suite of 56 hydrocarbons, three light alcohols, methane, total non-methane hydrocarbons (TNMHC), carbon monoxide, particulate matter, NOX, and total reactive nitrogen (NOY), along with meteorological parameters, in summers 2024 and 2026 at Roosevelt during smokey and smoke-free periods. We used the F0AM box model with the Master Chemical Mechanism to investigate ozone chemistry on smokey and smoke-free days. We used correlation with ethane on smoke-free days to identify oil and gas-related pollutants and compared smokey and smoke-free days to estimate pollutant levels (organics and reactive nitrogen) attributable to wildfire smoke. In this presentation, we will use the results of this study to discuss (1) the contributions of smoke, oil and gas, and urban pollution on ozone production rate and the ozone production efficiency of NOX at Roosevelt, (2) how this compares to urban areas without oil and gas influence, and (3) whether reductions in non-fire NOX or organic compound emissions in the Roosevelt area are likely to decrease ozone production on smoke-impacted days.

493555.title: The Influence of Indian River Lagoon Temperatures on Local Heat Stress Using Ultra-High-Resolution WRF-LES
493555.authors: Buddhi Prakash Jangid, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; and S. M. Lazarus, S. S. Maitra, and F. Salamanca Palou
493555.abstract: In east-central Florida, heat stress is often driven more by atmospheric moisture than extreme air temperatures. Along Florida’s Space Coast, high humidity associated with the nearby Indian River Lagoon (IRL), a shallow estuary, can produce locally elevated heat stress conditions despite relatively modest daytime temperatures. To investigate local-scale processes contributing to extreme heat stress, events were identified using cooling degree days obtained from National Weather Service observations. The WRF model was configured with three nested domains at horizontal resolutions of 2.5 km, 500 m, and 100 m. Large-Eddy Simulation (LES) was employed in the innermost domain to explicitly resolve turbulent motions within the boundary layer. Initial conditions were derived from both the North American Mesoscale (NAM) and High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) analyses. The lateral boundary conditions were updated every 6 h during a 48-h simulation period. High-resolution sea surface temperatures from the Group for High Resolution Sea Surface Temperature (GHRSST) and 30-m land use data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) were incorporated into the model configuration. Simulations were conducted to assess the sensitivity of heat-stress forecasts to the representation of IRL water temperatures. Because the GHRSST analysis underrepresented observed lagoon temperatures by up to 5 °C, observed IRL temperatures were used as the lower boundary condition for the estuary. Preliminary model results were evaluated against observations from the Melbourne International Airport ASOS station and a U.S. Department of Energy neighborhood meteorological station network. Simulated near-surface temperature and relative humidity fields produced heat-stress patterns that were in good agreement with observations. Sensitivity experiments are being conducted to evaluate how interactions between the warm Indian River Lagoon and the east-coast sea breeze modify local temperature, humidity, and heat-stress conditions.

493557.title: Measuring the Atmospheric Temperature Profile at V-band in the Time of Satellite Communications Uplinks
493557.authors: Giovanni de Amici, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and A. Bringer, E. J. Kim, M. Sammons, H. Yang, S. Abraham, and J. Fuentes
493557.abstract: We calculate the percentage of time that an ATMS-like passive radiometer [1] will be illuminated by the uplink beam of one of the proposed V-band communication system and estimate the damage resulting from such exposure. Using a combination of openly available information and educated guesses about the location and characteristics of the up/down link terminals, we constructed the ground segment of a hypothetical high-speed communication network. The space segment of the network was constructed from the orbital data of an existing constellation [2] of 6223 communication satellites (comsats). It is shown that without a very delicate balance of frequency allocations (science vs telecommunications), coupled with extremely steep and deep bandpass-defining filters, and strict adherence to the agreed limits (i.e. no out-of-band transmissions) the deployment of the telecommunication network leads to almost-complete loss of some important geophysical data. For the analysis we use the spectral characteristics of the ATMS instrument and the ephemeris of the NOAA-21 satellite [3]. The analysis is conducted for the USA and the simulation covers consecutive days in July 2024. It is urgent to assess how communication networks will affect passive microwave remote sensing because Eefective and reliable measurements of the atmosphere depends on the availability of interference-free spectrum windows at frequencies which are prescribed by physical processes [e.g. 4]. The family of resonant lines of the oxygen molecule near 60 GHz provides a unique opportunity to sample the vertical distribution of temperature and density from space, and it has been exploited for weather and climate studies from polar-orbiting satellites since 1978 (MSU on TIROS-N [5]). It remains a staple in the payloads operated by Russia, China, USA, Japan, France, India, UK, Ukraine [6] which are built around a common blueprint: a few wide-band (hundreds of MHz) channels around 50 GHz to sample the atmosphere and the surface while several more channels with high spectral resolution (few MHz) sample the individual resonant lines. Accurate retrieval of the environmental parameters depends upon the data provided by both sets of channels, and their location in frequency space is not arbitrary and cannot be altered at will [7, 8]. Some form of regulation or spectrum sharing is needed to preserve the societal benefits of accurate weather forecasts. Telecommunication companies have requested (and been granted) more and more bandwidth to be dedicated for up/downlink between satellites in low-earth orbits and terminals connected to fiberoptics network for distribution to high-speed local internet services. This additional bandwidth is only available in spectral regions, such as the V-band between 50 and 60 GHz, traditionally reserved for environmental and astrophysical research, The power broadcast by the uplink communication leg is many orders of magnitude greater than the natural thermal signal emitted from the Earth scene and it can overwhelm the radiometer’s electronics. While a direct boresight-to-boresight conjunction is extremely unlikely (even with a large constellation of satellites the fraction of the celestial sphere occupied by the satellites remains minuscule) the finite size of the ground station’s antenna beam in the sky suggests that a space-borne receiver will be in the background (as seen from the ground station) of one of the communication satellites and will be illuminated by either the main lobe or the near sidelobes of the uplink antenna more often than it is desirable. The analysis is conducted for the case when the uplink transmits within the radiometer’s passive channels (in-band scenario) and for the case when the uplink is limited to frequencies adjacent to the ATMS channels (out-of-band scenario). The antenna of the ground station is modelled as having a HPBW (Half-Power Beam Width) of 0.16 deg and the uplink has EIRP (Equivalent Isotropic Radiated Power) of 70 dBW. The geometric dissipation caused by the satellite orbital altitude, the attenuation induced by atmospheric gasses at 51 GHz and the mismatch between the circular polarization of the ground-based transmitting antenna and the linear polarization of the satellite-borne receiving antenna are considered. The effects on the radiometer's data are extrapolated from bench-level measurement conducted at the ATMS’ manufacturer facilities [unpublished]. References [1] H. Yang, F. Weng and K. 493565.title: Shifting Flood Regimes in the Western U.S.: Insights from Large Ensembles
493565.authors: Farshid Felfelani, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and A. J. Newman, A. W. Wood, N. Mizukami, A. Stone, K. Holman, S. Hartke, and K. Walker
493565.abstract: The western U.S. is highly vulnerable to climate variability, with particularly significant implications for its hydrological systems and future flood regimes. This study undertakes a comprehensive investigation into how future climate conditions will affect various flood characteristics, including magnitude, duration, and frequency, and seeks to identify the major hydrologic drivers behind these changes. A robust dataset of 200 ensemble members from three single-model initial-condition large ensembles (SMILEs), i.e., CESM2 (100 members), CanESM5 (50 members), and EC-Earth3 (50 members), is leveraged to characterize future hydrologic changes and to quantify components of uncertainty associated with these future scenarios. Sub-daily forcing fields are generated through the disaggregation of the daily precipitation and temperature data using the MetSim meteorological simulator. These sub-daily forcing fields are then used to drive a hydrological modeling system comprising SUMMA and mizuRoute. SUMMA is configured using USGS HUC12 catchments, whereas mizuRoute uses catchments and river reaches from Merit-Basin dataset. Based on the large-ensemble hydroclimate modeling framework above, we present the following key findings. (1) Late-century projections of GCM precipitation and subsequent SUMMA simulated total runoff exhibit substantial increases (up to 200 mm per year) across the northern portion of the domain, the Pacific Northwest and along the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains. Among the major river basins in the Western U.S., the Pacific Northwest, Upper Colorado, and Upper Missouri exhibit robust increases in late-century runoff. (2) Late-century projections show a consistent decrease in the return period of historical 100-year flood, indicating more frequent occurrences of such extreme event across all three SMILEs and in most river reaches in the western U.S. (3) All three SMILEs identify May as the month with peak probability of annual maximum floods during both historical and late-century periods. However, future projections reveal distinct seasonal shifts: the spring snowmelt-driven flood peak (April–July) dampens and shifts earlier in the year, while the probability of winter atmospheric river-driven floods (November–January) increases. Finally, the large number of ensemble members from each model allows us to perform initial uncertainty contributions to flood characteristics across the climate models and internal variability.

493567.title: Internship Opportunities at NOAA’s Office of Space Weather Observations (SWO)
493567.authors: Nicholas John Zaremba, NOAA, Lanham, MD; and M. Gauthier, I. Azeem, and D. Vassiliadis
493567.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) Office of Space Weather Observations (SWO) develops, deploys, and sustains NOAA operational satellite systems that monitor space weather and safeguard society. Essential to this mission is the cultivation of new talent through summer internships, where students work directly with SWO scientists. Recent student contributions have included the analysis of ionospheric anomalies using Constellation Observing System for Meteorology, Ionosphere, and Climate (COSMIC) and COSMIC-2 data, visualization of space weather data from instruments aboard Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES), and the quantification of Earth-produced eclipses on coronagraph imagery. The most recent SWO internship project required data analysis of Space Weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness – 1 (SOLAR-1) data and the application of machine learning and neural networks to explore forecasting techniques and capabilities. SWO actively recruits or plans to recruit summer interns through two primary programs. The Ernest F. Hollings Scholarship: A competitive program for undergraduates, who apply in sophomore year, providing two years of academic funding and a 10-week paid summer internship at a NOAA facility. The William M. Lapenta Internship Program: A 10-week paid summer program targeted at both undergraduate (sophomore/junior) and graduate students, offering robust operational and research experience.

493569.title: Boundary-Layer and Terrain Modulation of the Simulated Tornadic Supercell Environment during the 2 March 2012 Kentucky Tornado Outbreak
493569.authors: Alexander Honeycutt, Western Kentucky Univ., Bowling Green, KY; and X. Fan
493569.abstract: The 2 March 2012 tornado outbreak produced several long-track significant tornadoes across Kentucky, including supercells that remained organized and discrete while traversing the complex terrain of the Appalachian Plateau. This study examines how boundary-layer variability and terrain-modified flow influenced the near-storm environment across central and eastern Kentucky. Complex terrain can change near-surface winds through blocking, channeling, upslope flow, and downslope acceleration, producing localized changes in low-level vertical wind shear, storm-relative helicity (SRH), and horizontal vorticity. A high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model simulation with 1-km horizontal grid spacing is used to investigate these variations and their relationship to the environment met by the mature supercells. As the supercells advanced eastward, the simulated thermodynamic environment remained only modestly unstable, with surface-based CAPE around 1000–1500 J kg⁻¹ ahead of the storms and weakening as the event progressed. Meanwhile, the low-level kinematic environment became increasingly favorable. Simulated lifting condensation level heights decreased from approximately 750 m to near 550 m, while low-level shear, SRH, and effective-layer significant tornado parameter (STP) developed localized enhancements across central and eastern Kentucky. Several of these fields also contained narrow, quasi-periodic bands, showing that the near-storm environment varied significantly over relatively short distances. A particularly prominent feature was a series of southwest–northeast-oriented bands in the 0–1-km bulk-shear field. Similar structures appeared in the 250–500-m AGL vertical-velocity field, where alternating bands of ascent and descent broadly corresponded with variations in low-level shear. Vertical cross sections through these features showed repeated horizontal wind perturbations extending through much of the lowest kilometer, accompanied by alternating ascending and descending branches. Successive perturbation centers were separated by 7–10 km, producing repeated areas of wind acceleration, wind deceleration, ascent, and descent across the simulated environment. This structure is consistent with an organized boundary-layer wave- or roll-like circulation. Horizontal convective rolls and related boundary-layer circulations can redistribute momentum, moisture, and horizontal vorticity while producing periodic variations in vertical motion and low-level winds. In the simulation, the same banded structure was evident in 0–1-km shear, SRH, and effective-layer STP, showing that the circulation affected multiple tornado-relevant environmental parameters. Mature supercells moving east northeastward across Kentucky therefore encountered repeated areas of enhanced and reduced low-level kinematic favorability rather than a horizontally uniform inflow environment. The 7–10-km spacing of the simulated perturbations is larger than wavelengths produced in some idealized simulations of boundary-layer rolls but remain within the range documented in observational studies of terrestrial horizontal convective rolls. Because boundary-layer depth and additional thermodynamic perturbation fields have not yet been fully diagnosed, these features are conservatively interpreted as an organized boundary-layer wave–roll circulation rather than definitively classified as horizontal convective rolls or gravity waves. The interaction of the broadly southwesterly low-level flow with the rolling terrain of Kentucky likely contributed to the generation and organization of these boundary-layer circulations. Although individual perturbation bands did not correspond directly to specific ridges or valleys, their structure became increasingly irregular as they entered the more dissected terrain of the Appalachian Plateau. Terrain-induced lifting, blocking, channeling, and localized acceleration likely modified the amplitude, orientation, and vertical structure of the circulations while also introducing additional variability into the near-surface wind field. These changes produced localized differences in 0–1-km shear and SRH ahead of the mature supercells and suggest that terrain-related processes were an important component of the evolving low-level environment. The 1-km WRF simulation shows that these supercells traversed a highly heterogeneous low-level environment containing organized variations in vertical motion, near-surface winds, 0–1-km shear, SRH, and effective STP. The results of the simulations suggest that terrain-generated boundary-layer organization, continued terrain modification, and storm-induced environmental changes combined to produce localized corridors of enhanced and reduced kinematic favorability across central and eastern Kentucky. Although the present analysis does not establish a direct relationship between individual boundary-layer perturbations and tornado evolution, these kilometer-scale variations demonstrate why the broader mesoscale environment alone may not fully describe the conditions encountered by supercells in complex terrain. Further analysis of boundary-layer depth, thermodynamic perturbations, individual STP ingredients, and terrain-sensitivity simulations will help isolate the relative contributions of these processes.

493570.title: Different Stratospheric Aerosol Layer Responses to Volcanic and Wildfire Perturbations
493570.authors: Alexandre Albert Baron, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and K. Smith, E. Asher, and T. Thornberry
493570.abstract: The stratospheric aerosol layer is continuously impacted by volcanic eruptions and extreme wildfire events, yet the resulting aerosol evolution differs substantially depending on the nature of the perturbation. Since 2019, the NOAA Balloon Baseline Stratospheric Aerosol Profiles (B2SAP) network has provided routine in situ measurements of aerosol number concentration and size distributions from the surface to approximately 28 km, capturing multiple volcanic eruptions, pyrocumulonimbus smoke injections, and periods of background conditions. Here we present a multi-year analysis of B2SAP observations above Boulder, CO, spanning perturbations including Raikoke (2019), La Soufrière (2021), Hunga (2022), Ruang (2024), and recent boreal wildfire events. By comparing changes in particle loading and their size distribution, we examine how the stratospheric aerosol layer microphysics responds to different injection types and compositions. While all major perturbations increase the stratospheric aerosol burden, they do not produce a consistent relationship between aerosol concentration and particle size. Instead, differences in sulfur injection, co-emitted species (e.g. fine ash, water vapor), injection altitude, and the pre-existing stratospheric state lead to distinct microphysical responses, emphasizing the complexity of aerosol growth and optical properties evolution following volcanic eruptions and wildfire smoke injections. Our long-term in situ observations provide constraints on aerosol size distributions that cannot be directly retrieved from satellite observations but are critical for interpreting satellite-derived extinction and effective radius products and for evaluating aerosol-climate models. These results highlight the diversity of stratospheric aerosol responses to natural perturbations and provide new observational benchmarks for improving representations of aerosol microphysics in climate models.

493572.title: The New NASA GMAO GEOS FLASH Lightning Forecasting Algorithm - Statistical Results
493572.authors: Retha Matthee Mecikalski, GESTAR II, Morgan State University, GMAO, Greenbelt, MD; and W. Putman, S. Pawson, and V. Shah
493572.abstract: Lightning parameterization schemes in Earth System Models (ESMs) are relatively under-developed and many of these schemes rely on proxy variables, such as cloud top height. Recent studies show that cloud top height is not a good predictor of the amount and location of lightning and their associated lightning-produced nitrogen oxides, particularly in a changing climate. Our goal is therefore to develop a new lightning forecast algorithm that uses only infrared (IR) channels from the NASA Global Modeling and Assimilation Office’s (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) ESM (hereafter the “GEOS model”). The aim of this new scheme is to improve the location and amount of forecasted lightning flashes compared to the current lightning parameterization schemes in the GEOS model. As such, we have developed a new GEOS FLASH (FLash Algorithm derived from Satellite Harmonization) lightning forecast scheme to improve the lightning amount and spatial coverage in GEOS. The advantage of our algorithm is that it only uses IR satellite fields, and does not include cloud top height. The GEOS FLASH algorithm was applied to the stretched grid of the GEOS forecasted satellite IR fields for approximately 350 consecutive days from 22 April 2025 through 27 May 2026. The stretched grid has a resolution of 2 km over the Contiguous United States (CONUS) and up to 12 km outside of CONUS. To test the accuracy of the GEOS FLASH forecast we applied the algorithm to four different forecast times (at 30-minute temporal resolution) for 24 hours: 1) 12 to 36 hours, 2) 24 to 48 hours, 3) 36 to 60 hours, and 4) 60 to 84 hours. Figure 1 (Top Row) shows the comparison between the observed and 24-hour forecasted gridded flash counts on August 11, 2025. The panels show the gridded lightning flash counts from (a) GOES-19 GLM observations, (b) the 24-hour FLASH forecast, and (c) the 24-hour GEOS Chemistry flash rate (GCHEM) forecast, which is a current lightning parameterization scheme in the GEOS model. Note that we currently only have 177 days to compare to the GCHEM algorithm; future work includes expanding the GCHEM dataset. Overall, the statistical comparisons show that the new GEOS FLASH algorithm consistently outperforms the current GCHEM lightning scheme, except for having a lower probability of detection (POD). However, the higher PODs for the GCHEM algorithm is because the GCHEM algorithm always over-estimates the spatial coverage of lightning occurrence (as shown in Fig. 1c), which leads to False Alarm Rates (FARs) of up to 0.4 for the GCHEM algorithm compared to maximum FARs of 0.15 for the FLASH algorithm. Therefore, the FLASH algorithm has higher accuracies, higher threat scores (TS), and higher success ratio’s (SR) than the GCHEM algorithm, which is shown in Figure 1 (Bottom Row). Work is ongoing to improve the FLASH algorithm as well as to add more test cases from the GCHEM model. In addition, future work includes expanding the algorithm to regions outside of GOES-19, including to regions covered by GOES-18 and EUMETSAT’s Meteosat Third Generation, thereby expanding the region in the GEOS model that would use satellite IR fields to simulate lightning location and amount. Figure 1. Top Row: Comparison between the observed and 24-hour forecasted gridded flash counts on August 11, 2025, during NH Summer. The panels show the gridded lightning flash counts from (a) GOES-19 GLM observations; (b) the FLASH forecast; and (c) the GCHEM forecast. Bottom Row: Scatter plots showing (a) the POD versus SR, (b) the TS versus SR, and (c) the accuracy versus SR for the GCHEM algorithm that is shown as a “|” symbol and the FLASH algorithm that is shown as an “X” symbol. The colorbar respresents the month of the year.

493573.title: Attenuation and Differential Attenuation within the Melting Layer at Different Radar Wavelengths
493573.authors: Alexander V. Ryzhkov, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; and J. T. Carlin
493573.abstract: Supplementing the existing WSR-88D S-band weather radars with the shorter wavelength radars operating at C or X bands is one of the priorities of the Radar Next Program spawned by NOAA and NWS. Shorter wavelength radars usually experience much larger attenuation in precipitation compared to WSR-88Ds that may restrict their operational range and affect the quality of their measurements. Various methodologies exist for attenuation / differential attenuation correction of radar reflectivity Z and differential reflectivity ZDR at C and X bands in pure rain. Attenuation / differential attenuation in the melting layer can be an order of magnitude higher than in rain and require quantitative analysis. Attenuation within the melting layer may cause large negative biases in Z and ZDR above it which should be taken into account. Vertical profiles of specific attenuation A and specific differential attenuation ADP along with other polarimetric radar variables through the melting layer are simulated using a model of the melting layer in stratiform clouds with spectral bin microphysics linked to the polarimetric radar forward operator. It is shown that the maximal values of A, ADP, and specific differential phase KDP at C and X bands in the melting layer (ML) are much higher than the corresponding values within rain below the ML. However, the observed radial profiles of these variables within the ML are strongly affected by the antenna beamwidth as well as the effects of nonuniform beam filling and backscatter differential phase which can be quite high in the ML. The results of a theoretical analysis of these radial profiles at S, C, and X bands for snow with different sizes and degrees of riming above the ML are provided in this presentation and compared with some observational data within and above the ML collected by X-band polarimetric weather radars. The ideas for correcting attenuation-related biases in Z and ZDR within and above the ML will be also discussed.

493582.title: Withdrawn: The unstable ABL of the Amazon rainforest using multicell-LES-ODT
493582.authors: Livia S. Freire, University of Sao Paulo, Sao Carlos, SP, Brazil; and A. C. de Jesus and M. Popoff
493582.abstract: Large-eddy simulation (LES) of the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) over the Amazon rainforest is central to understanding canopy-atmosphere exchange of momentum, heat, and scalars, but resolving the flow field within and immediately above a ~36-m-tall canopy while simultaneously capturing the full ~1–2 km depth of the ABL is computationally prohibitive with a single uniform grid. Traditional algebraic wall models (e.g., log-law formulations) are poorly suited to this problem because they treat the near-surface region in a Reynolds-averaged sense, which breaks down over the strongly heterogeneous, multi-scale turbulence generated by a forest canopy. The One-Dimensional Turbulence (ODT) model, coupled to LES as a stochastic near-wall closure, resolves the instantaneous velocity and scalar fields along a vertical line while representing three-dimensional turbulent motions through stochastic eddy events, offering a physically richer alternative to algebraic wall models. In its original formulation, however, the ODT domain was constrained to the height of a single LES cell, forcing an unreasonably coarse LES resolution (~36 m) when applied to the Amazon canopy. This work applies the recently developed multicell-LES-ODT coupling, which decouples the LES vertical resolution from the vertical extent of the ODT domain by allowing ODT to replace multiple wall-adjacent LES cells, to simulate the unstable Amazon ABL with the near-wall region resolved at 1-m resolution while the LES grid spans the full boundary-layer depth. Simulations were performed using the LESGO-based multicell-LES-ODT code, with the ODT domain extending N = 3 LES cells (48 ODT grid points, 1-m spacing), providing 36 points across the canopy height (h = 36 m). The LES domain covers the full ABL depth with 128 vertical grid points, and canopy drag is represented through a leaf-area-density profile with LAI = 6, Cd = 0.4, and isotropic drag projection. Two unstable regimes were simulated to bracket the range of convective conditions observed over the Amazon: a forced-convection case (geostrophic wind of 16 m/s, surface heat flux of 0.11 Km/s) and a free-convection case (geostrophic wind of 5 m/s, surface heat flux of 0.20 Km/s), yielding final friction velocities of u* = 0.75 and 0.43 m/s and stability parameters h/L = −0.08 and −0.8, respectively. These configurations were chosen to reproduce the stability regimes identified from eddy-covariance measurements collected at nine heights within and above the canopy during the GoAmazon2014/15 campaign, which were classified into quasi-neutral, forced-convection, and free-convection subsets based on h/L. Results show that the multicell-LES-ODT model reproduces the essential features of canopy-modulated turbulence under both unstable regimes without any case-specific recalibration of the ODT tunable parameters beyond those established for the channel-flow benchmarks. Mean streamwise velocity, velocity variances, and momentum flux profiles from the ODT region through the canopy and into the roughness sublayer are in good qualitative and, for most quantities, quantitative agreement with the GoAmazon field observations, capturing the characteristic velocity-variance maxima near the canopy top and the associated inflection in the mean velocity profile associated with the mixing-layer analogy for canopy flows. The streamwise skewness profiles reproduce the sign changes with height reported in the field data, but not for the spanwise and vertical skewness. As found for the neutral case, the vertical velocity variance within the canopy is somewhat underestimated relative to observations, a known limitation inherited from the stand-alone ODT model's underrepresentation of variance. A key outcome of extending the coupling to unstable stratification is the analysis of coherent structures across the depth of the domain. In the forced-convection case, horizontal cross-sections above the canopy retain the elongated, streak-like organization associated with shear-driven mixing-layer instabilities, consistent with the classical roll-vortex paradigm for near-neutral canopy flows, while progressively more cellular, plume-like patterns emerge closer to the surface and with increasing instability. Snapshots of the resolved velocity fluctuations within the ODT region itself are physically realistic and capture canopy-scale coherent structures directly: near the canopy top, narrow, elongated streaks of alternating high- and low-momentum fluid are visible in the horizontal planes, consistent with the head-up/head-down hairpin-vortex packets that populate the roughness sublayer, while the vertical cross-sections through the sub-canopy ODT domain show these structures tilting and penetrating downward into the trunk space, reproducing the sweep-ejection organization associated with canopy-top shear instabilities. In the free-convection case, the flow organization transitions toward the broader, more isotropic convective cells expected when buoyancy dominates shear production, in agreement with conceptual models of the transition from shear-dominated to buoyancy-dominated coherent structures in vegetated canopies. Because the multicell approach resolves both the full convective boundary layer and the sub-canopy flow simultaneously, these simulations offer a unique opportunity to examine how canopy-scale coherent structures interact with, and are modulated by, boundary-layer-scale convective circulations. These results demonstrate that the multicell-LES-ODT coupling extends robustly from previously validated channel-flow and neutral ABL configurations to realistic, unstably stratified, vertically heterogeneous-canopy environmental flows, providing a computationally tractable pathway to simultaneously resolve canopy-scale and boundary-layer-scale turbulence. Future work will further quantify the interaction between canopy-generated turbulence and convective boundary-layer structures across the full range of observed Amazon stability conditions.

493583.title: Fine Particulate Matter Trends and Ground Validation Coverage in the Lower Rio Grande Valley: A 16-Year Reanalysis-Based Assessment
493583.authors: Ibrahim-Anyass Yussif, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, BROWNSVILLE, TX; and M. Rizwan, S. D. Pinakana, A. M. Mestas-Nunez, M. Dahal, and A. U. Raysoni
493583.abstract: We present a 16-year (January 2010 – December 2025) analysis of spatiotemporal trends and variability in fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and aerosol optical depth (AOD) across Texas, focusing on the Lower Rio Grande Valley (LRGV), a Gulf-influenced U.S.-Mexico border region subjected to transboundary emissions and seasonal long-range dust transport. PM2.5 and AOD are derived from the MERRA-2 reanalysis, with data from ERA5 providing meteorological covariates (boundary layer height, wind, temperature, humidity) to help quantify meteorologically driven variability and the humidity-related effects in AOD and PM2.5. Trend analyses will be presented using the Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimator. The study area was compartmentalized into four macro-regions (West: Trans Pecos; North: High Plains, North Central and Low Rolling Plains; East: East Texas and Upper Coast; and South: Edwards Plateau, South Central, South Texas and Lower Valley) based on NOAA NCEI Climate Divisions, enabling comparisons of trends, seasonal patterns, and variability across distinct meteorological and emission environments. MERRA-2-derived PM2.5 will be evaluated against ground-based observations for PM2.5 obtained from Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) Continuous Ambient Monitoring Sites (CAMS) stations, with performance assessed by region and year using data completeness, bias, and correlation with ground-based observations. We will also examine the relationship between MERRA-2 AOD and PM2.5 to assess the consistency between column aerosol loading and near-surface particulate concentrations. Ground-based observational coverage varies substantially across Texas: West, North, and East Texas have sites with near-continuous records over the study period, whereas observations in the LRGV are limited. The analysis will characterize regional aerosol variability, long-term trends, and the performance of MERRA-2 products across diverse Texas environments, while assessing the utility of reanalysis datasets for air-quality applications in a data-sparse border region

493586.title: Early Cloud Initiation along Highway Corridors near Houston, Texas: Satellite Observations and Idealized Large-Eddy Simulations
493586.authors: Dhwanit J Mise, School of meteorology, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations(CIWRO), Norman, OK; CAPS, CIWRO, SOM, The University of Oklahoma Norman OK, Norman, OK; CAPS, Norman, OK; and Y. Huang, G. M. McFarquhar, M. Xue, L. Xue, and W. I. Gustafson Jr.
493586.abstract: Cloud initiation along interstate highway corridors near Houston, Texas has recently been observed in high-spatiotemporal-resolution Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) imagery, drawing increasing public and scientific attention to linear cloud development spatially aligned with interstate roadway networks. This phenomenon raises the question of whether fine-scale, anthropogenic surface heterogeneities such as roadways, with thermal and emission properties distinct from their surroundings, can locally perturb boundary-layer processes and advance shallow cloud initiation. Understanding this has broader relevance beyond Houston: as transportation infrastructure expands, quantifying how narrow, linear thermal anomalies interact with an already-favorable thermodynamic environment could inform our understanding of small-scale land-atmosphere feedbacks in rapidly urbanizing regions. We analyze 4.5 years (January 2022–June 2026) of GOES imagery over the Houston region and manually identified five cases of cloud initiation aligned with interstate highway corridors. All cases occurred during the morning rush-hour period between 12–13 UTC (7–8 AM local time), with four events in June and one in August, indicating a strong diurnal and seasonal preference consistent with summertime boundary-layer conditions. In each case, the highway-aligned cloud signature persists only a few minutes before widespread cloud development across the broader domain obscures it, suggesting that the highway accelerates cloud onset relative to the surrounding environment rather than sustaining an independent, persistent feature. ERA5 reanalysis thermodynamic profiles show a near-saturated, near-surface environment (RH 80–100%) with weak near-surface winds (< ~3 m/s) at the time of initiation, under which a small, localized perturbation could plausibly induce an early onset of cloud formation. Landsat land surface temperature composites show systematically elevated surface temperatures along highway corridors relative to adjacent non-highway land cover within the study domain. Based on these observations, we hypothesize that the elevated thermal signature of highway surfaces from pavement thermal properties and from sensible heat and aerosol emitted by rush-hour traffic acts as a localized thermal and microphysical perturbation on an already near-saturated boundary layer, initiating cloud earlier over the highway than in its surroundings. To test this hypothesis, we conduct idealized large-eddy simulations (LES) using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, initialized with thermodynamic soundings derived from ERA5 reanalysis for the observed cases, and with a conceptualized road network prescribed with elevated skin temperature. A sensitivity analysis is performed by systematically varying road temperature, road width and length, surface flux parameterizations, aerosol initial conditions, microphysics schemes, and model grid spacing (20–50 m) including simulations that isolate the highway thermal and aerosol perturbations and their combined effects to identify the combination of surface, aerosol, and grid conditions that reproduce the observed early-onset, short-lived cloud signature.

493588.title: Harmonizing Global Atmospheric Carbonyl Sulfide (OCS) Observations: Initial Progress on NDACC FTIR Trends and Satellite Inter-calibration
493588.abstract: Carbonyl Sulfide (OCS) is the atmosphere's largest sulfur reservoir, serving as both the primary non-volcanic source for stratospheric aerosols and a proxy for biospheric CO2 uptake. Despite its importance, the global OCS budget remains highly uncertain, underscoring the critical need for long-term observations in both the troposphere and stratosphere. Supported by NASA’s Earth System Science Research (ESSR) program, our project aims to develop a harmonized global OCS dataset, derived from satellite records bias-corrected against ground-based and aircraft observations, and assess sensitivity simulations using the Community Earth System Model (CESM). This presentation details our initial progress in observational data synthesis. First, we present updated (1986 - 2026) long-term atmospheric OCS trends derived from high-resolution ground-based Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) measurements across the Network for the Detection of Atmospheric Composition Change (NDACC). In addition to providing a crucial baseline for evaluating global spatial and temporal variability, we demonstrate how these observations capture significant inflection points, notably the recent positive shift observed at Northern mid-latitude sites since ~2024. Second, we detail our initial inter-comparison of OCS retrievals from multiple satellite platforms (including TES, ACE-FTS, and MIPAS). Because current satellite products vary significantly in resolution and vertical sensitivity, we outline preliminary bias-correction methodologies that leverage the NDACC network alongside in-situ and suborbital datasets to evaluate and intercalibrate the satellite records.

493593.title: Expanding NASA Cloud Physics Lidar Algorithms Beyond Traditional Threshold-Based Retrievals
493593.authors: Natalie Midzak, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and J. E. Yorks, J. A. Finlon, P. Selmer, K. Christian, and M. J. McGill
493593.abstract: NASA’s Cloud Physics Lidar (CPL) has provided high-resolution, multiwavelength observations of clouds and aerosols from high-altitude aircraft for more than two decades. Operating at 355, 532 and 1064 nm, CPL delivers measurements of attenuated backscatter and depolarization ratio that have supported studies of cloud phase, aerosol and cloud vertical structure and optical properties across numerous field campaigns. These observations have also served as a critical airborne dataset for evaluating and developing satellite lidar retrievals. Most recently, CPL participated in the INjecyed Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE) campaign which aimed to characterize pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) through an extensive suite of remote-sensing and in-situ sensors. While traditional CPL processing algorithms have relied on well-established physics-based approaches, they are often threshold-based and rely on assumptions of particle properties. Therefore, recent techniques have been explored which exploit multidimensional information contained within CPL retrievals. Clustering approaches developed using the Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) field campaign data have explored relationships among multiwavelength backscatter, depolarization, and cloud microphysical properties, enabling particle-type classification based on combinations of observables rather than individual thresholds. Additionally, convolutional neural network (CNN) methods have been developed for automated detection and characterization of cloud and aerosol layers in the airborne CPL data. Therefore, this presentation will highlight initial results of smoke plumes captured during INSPYRE and discuss the evolution of CPL processing algorithms and consider how these new algorithms can support the development and validation of next-generation airborne and satellite lidar retrievals.

493595.title: Toward Operational Continental-Scale, High Resolution Hybrid Data Assimilation in JEDI: Progress from 3-km North American FV3-JEDI Experiments
493595.authors: Ting Lei, Lynker@NWS/OMD, Riverdale Park, MD; and S. Liu, R. J. Purser, M. Oigawa, D. kokron, S. K. Degelia, D. E. Lippi, X. Zhang, F. Hebert, M. Wlasak, M. Pondeca, H. liu, M. Rancic, A. Shlyaeva, and D. Holdaway
493595.abstract: The 3-km North American domain represents one of the most computationally demanding data assimilation applications pursued within JEDI. Its combination of continental-scale coverage, convection-allowing resolution, large model state, extensive observations, and hybrid variational assimilation exposes limitations and development needs across nearly every component of an operational data assimilation system. This presentation summarizes progress toward operational 3-km North American FV3-JEDI hybrid analyses using MGBF ensemble localization and GSIBEC static background-error covariance modeling. Particular attention is given to computational bottlenecks associated with ensemble localization. Recent MGBF/SABER developments include MGBF-based scale- and variable-dependent localization, treatment of spatially inhomogeneous grids, an a posteriori normalization-correction procedure, implementation of calibrated filtering formulations, and substantial code modernization and optimization. These enhancements further strengthen MGBF as a powerful covariance-modeling and ensemble-localization capability applicable across FV3-JEDI and MPAS-JEDI systems. Acknowledgement : Ting Lei is grateful to Benjamin Menetrier at MET Norway for his continued help with SABER

493597.title: Evolving the Meteorology - Air Traffic Management (MET-ATM) Integration Framework for Increased Operational Value and Returns on Investments (Invited Presentation)
493597.authors: Michael Robinson, Aeris LLC, Louisville, CO
493597.abstract: The Meteorology – Air Traffic Management (MET-ATM) framework provided the foundation for advancing weather information, services, and operational integration within the National Airspace System. It fostered a shared understanding of how meteorological capabilities support complex air traffic management (ATM) decisions, facilitating sustained investment and collaborative technology development. Specifically, the framework aimed to automate the manual translation of aviation weather information and forecasts into clear insights and predictions for airspace constraints and operational impacts, reducing cognitive bottlenecks and inconsistent planning among stakeholders. Despite years of supporting applied research and FAA-targeted solutions, MET-ATM outcomes have been mixed, often falling short of goals for integrated weather-impact mitigation and operational benefits. This presentation examines the challenges that have limited the value of MET-ATM integration to date and proposes a framework evolution. This new approach seeks to rebalance R&D across core translation and integration components, accelerate the transition from research to operational value, and better align meteorological services with the emerging needs of air traffic operations.

493598.title: The Impacts of the 2026-27 El Niño on Global Commodity Markets
493598.authors: Jon B. Davis, Everstream Analytics, Barcelona, Spain
493598.abstract: The Super El Niño event emerged in 2026 and rapidly strengthened to become one of the strongest warm episodes in history. The impacts on global circulation were widespread and significant. This session examines the transmission of the event's climatic anomalies into global commodity markets, with particular attention to agricultural, energy, and supply chain impacts. The panel will assess historical price responses to comparably strong El Niño events (1997–98, 2015–16) as a benchmark for the current episode and examine early-cycle price and volatility signals across commodity markets.

493600.title: Dual-Doppler Radar Analysis of Convective Core Structure in Houston, Texas During the ESCAPE and TRACER Field Campaigns
493600.authors: Katherine McKeown, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY; and M. Oue, O. Omitusa, and P. Kollias
493600.abstract: Ordinary convective cells are the most common type of deep convection and play a fundamental role in the vertical transport of heat, moisture and momentum throughout the atmosphere. The evolution of these cells is governed by the interaction of updrafts and downdrafts, which control storm intensity, precipitation production, and lifecycle. Despite the importance of these features, direct observations of them remains limited because conventional radar observations only measure radial velocities. Dual-doppler radar retrievals use two radars in close proximity to provide the full three-dimensional wind field, enabling the identification and characterization of updrafts and downdrafts. During the ESCAPE and TRACER field campaigns in Houston, Texas, dual-Doppler retrievals from the CHIVO and CSAPR2 C-band radars were used to analyze ordinary convective cells over a two-month period between August and September 2022 tracked with the Multisensor Agile Adaptive Sampling methodology (MAAS). This dataset contains more than 15,000 downdrafts and 13,000 updrafts in ~1400 cells, representing one of the largest collections of objectively identified convective drafts. The majority of the updraft and downdraft cores are less than 1 km2 in vertical slices. Results show that updrafts and downdrafts observed in these ordinary cells exhibit consistent geometric relationships, with draft width and depth increasing together across shallow and deep convection. Additionally, larger and deeper drafts are associated with stronger vertical velocities, taller echo top heights, and higher radar reflectivity. These findings provide a large-sample observational characterization of the three-dimensional dynamical structure of ordinary convective cells and offers new observational constraints for understanding storm evolution and large eddy simulations.

493606.title: Diurnal Variations in Urban Heat Island Intensity and Surface Energy Balance in Nanjing, China
493606.authors: Christina Li, West Morris Mendhem High School, Chester, NJ; and D. Li
493606.abstract: A major effect of urbanization is the urban heat island (UHI) effect, in which a city is warmer than nearby rural land, especially at night. Understanding the UHI effect can improve climate models and help guide vegetation, irrigation, and heat-reducing urban design. The surface energy balance is essential for understanding UHI intensity because it explains how urban and rural surfaces absorb, use, store, and release energy differently throughout the day. This study used half-hourly observations collected from May through August 2013 at urban, grassland, and cropland sites near Nanjing, China. The data were converted to hourly averages and organized into average diurnal cycles of air temperature, shortwave and longwave radiation, net radiation, sensible and latent heat fluxes, and estimated ground or storage heat flux. UHI intensity was calculated by subtracting the grassland or cropland air temperature from the urban air temperature. The urban site was approximately 1.8–2.0°C warmer during much of the night but slightly cooler around midday. Cropland had the greatest daytime latent heat flux because more energy was used for evapotranspiration, while grassland and urban surfaces used more energy for sensible heating. The urban site released stored heat after sunset and had higher sensible heat flux and outgoing longwave radiation. Overall, these results demonstrate how land-cover-dependent energy partitioning and heat storage shape the diurnal evolution of urban heat island intensity during the warm season in Nanjing.

493608.title: Developing Pathways to Innovation Through Team Building Activities -- Aligning Values to Practice to Build Psychological Safety on Research Teams
493608.authors: Becca Edwards, CIRES, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO
493608.abstract: Research teams strive for innovation and often get stuck when barriers arise due to lack of communication skills and structure in the daily workflow. Given that innovative research processes require the ability to challenge assumptions and learn from failure, it is critical that teams develop open communication and intellectual risk-taking. Building psychological safety on your team can create an environment where team members feel comfortable sharing ideas and asking questions without fear of embarrassment or retaliation. When team members trust that their perspectives will be respected, they are more likely to identify potential problems early and propose creative solutions. This openness enhances collaboration and builds flexibility into everyday practices such that each individual feels valued and supported for their unique work needs. Defining your group norms, and therefore bringing structure to your team process, has wide benefits. Research has shown that a team functions best when the members digest information slowly, avoiding assumptions that everyone is on the same page, embrace a common set of values to guide their work, and make space for a variety of ideas coming from different lived experiences. These practices cultivate psychological safety, which involves interpersonal trust and a shared belief that it is safe to take risks with the group. In this session, participants will hear about a team building activity to create a “group norms” document for a research team. Many research teams at the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at CU Boulder have completed this activity and developed their own unique group norms document. This activity includes a training on psychological safety, followed by identification of current team practices regarding meeting facilitation, communication, file or equipment storage and relationship building. After evaluation of whether the current practices create psychological safety, the team determines if they need to modify current practices and also design new practices to help build a collaborative work environment. They align values to these practices, and create a group document to share with new employees. The teams also discuss the process of “calling in” and determine how they will interact with each other if a norm is not honored. This activity has also addressed practices for field work campaigns, designing conversations that illuminate communication barriers and potential supportive processes during intense work days. Participants will hear about the benefits of this process and various struggles with implementing the process sustainably across a large institute. Citations: Duhigg, C. (2016, Feb 25) What Google learned from its quest to build the perfect team. NY Times.https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/28/magazine/what-google-learned-from-its-quest-to-build-the-perfect-team.html Edmondson, A. C. (2018). The Fearless Organization: Creating Psychological Safety in the Workplace for Learning, Innovation, and Growth. John Wiley & Sons. Rock, D., Grant, H. & Grey, J. 493609.title: Quantification of the Effect of Kinetic Uncertainties on Photochemical Loss of Ozone in the NH, Mid-Latitude Stratosphere Using DCOTSS Observations
493609.authors: Ross J. Salawitch, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; University of Maryland, College Park, COLLEGE PARK, MD; and L. Howar, D. Wilmouth, J. Hare, J. G. Anderson, E. Delaria, J. St. Clair, T. F. Hanisco, E. J. Hintsa, B. Hall, F. L. Moore, E. Atlas, S. Schauffler, K. Smith, S. Donnelly, V. A. Treadaway, J. B. Smith, D. Sayres, J. Pittman, B. Daube, P. T. Bui, J. Dean-Day, Y. Li, S. Wofsy, C. R. Homeyer, F. Keutsch, and K. Bowman
493609.abstract: In-situ observations of NO2, ClONO2, and ClO obtained in the summer of 2022 during the NASA Dynamics and Chemistry of the Summer Stratosphere (DCOTSS) mission are used to examine the photochemistry controlling catalytic ozone loss in the Northern Hemisphere, mid-latitude stratosphere. Model calculations employing kinetics recommendations from the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) kinetics compendium (JPL-2019) systematically overestimate observed NO2 and ClONO2 by 20−30% and 25−50%, respectively, in the 18 to 21 km altitude region, whereas good agreement (differences commonly less than 5%) is found between modeled and measured ClO at most altitudes. We perform Monte Carlo (MC) simulations, in which the rate coefficients of key reactions are perturbed to their ± 2σ uncertainty limits, to quantify the specific combination of perturbations to rate coefficients that is needed to better simulate observed NO2, ClONO2, and ClO. This analysis suggests an increase in the rate of formation of HNO3 and a decrease in the rate of formation of ClONO2, relative to the JPL-2019 kinetic recommendation, are the most important revisions needed to provide good agreement between the measured and modeled NO2, ClONO2, and ClO. The kinetic adjustments that allow for good model-observation agreement suggest that models using current JPL kinetic recommendations may underestimate the halogen contribution to ozone loss in the NH mid-latitude lower stratosphere by about 25%. Finally, we will also evaluate the comparison of measured and modeled NO2, ClONO2, and ClO using the kinetic recommendations of the just released JPL-2025 compendium.

493610.title: Surface Layer Structure and Evolution during M2HATS: An Observational Overview
493610.authors: Shane D. Mayor, California State University Chico, Chico, CA; and P. Dérian, C. P. Young, T. M. Green, A. M. King, J. Kyeyune, A. R. Lewis, C. D. Pappas, H. Peterson, S. J. Roman, H. N. Smith, D. Threlkeld, J. Sun, and C. Tong
493610.abstract: The M2HATS field campaign collected a rich set of in situ and remote-sensing observations of the atmospheric boundary layer under a range of meteorological conditions. This study presents an observational overview of boundary-layer structure and evolution during the campaign, with emphasis on relationships among near-surface turbulence, surface meteorological conditions, boundary-layer depth, and spatial structures observed by lidar. Measurements from the M2HATS in situ observing systems will be combined with observations from the Raman-shifted Eye-safe Aerosol Lidar (REAL) to characterize selected periods spanning different boundary-layer regimes. Analyses will include the diurnal evolution of temperature, wind, stability, turbulent fluxes, and boundary-layer depth, together with lidar imagery revealing the horizontal organization and evolution of aerosol structures within the boundary layer. Particular attention will be given to relationships between features observed remotely and simultaneous measurements of turbulence and meteorological conditions near the surface. The objective is to provide an accessible synthesis of the boundary-layer conditions sampled during M2HATS while identifying individual periods and phenomena suitable for more detailed investigation. The analysis is being conducted collaboratively with students enrolled in a Boundary Layer Meteorology course at California State University, Chico, providing students with experience working with field observations while contributing to the continuing scientific analysis of the M2HATS dataset.

493615.title: Processes that Maintain Cloud Ice in “Warm” Arctic Mixed-Phase Stratiform Cloud Systems
493615.authors: Amy B. Solomon, CIRES and NOAA/PSL, Boulder, CO; and E. Crosbie, A. V. Korolev, P. Lawson, R. J. Perkins, K. S. Schmidt, and P. Zuidema
493615.abstract: Arctic mixed-phase stratiform cloud systems are observed to occur approximately 45% of the time on the North Slope of Alaska, with a significant increase in occurrence during spring and fall transition seasons (Shupe, 2011). Due to the presence of liquid water in these clouds, they play an important role in determining the structure of the Arctic atmospheric boundary layer and magnitudes of surface energy budget terms. However, models at all scales are challenged to maintain the phase partitioning between cloud liquid and cloud ice at cold temperatures. This is fundamentally an issue with simulating ice processes, from potential sub-grid variability that allows the maintenance of liquid in the presence of cloud ice to uncertainties in secondary ice formation processes and sources of ice nucleating particles. In this study we investigate these issues using a case study from the NASA ARCSIX (Arctic Radiation-Cloud-Aerosol-Surface Interaction Experiment) aircraft campaign that took place out of Pituffik, Greenland in Spring-Summer 2024. During this case, an aircraft intensively measured the microphysics and dynamics in a warm (cloud top temperatures ~-6 C) mixed-phase stratocumulus with ice number concentrations up to 15 L-1 (see figure). It is hypothesized that warm mixed-phase stratiform cloud systems will occur more frequently in a warming climate and therefore need to be adequately simulated in weather-to-climate models. The observed cloud system is studied in large eddy simulations with 10-50m horizontal grid spacings. Secondary ice formation mechanisms, such as rime splintering, ice-ice collisions, and sublimation break up, and changes in crystal habits are included in bulk microphysics to investigate how ice concentrations up to 15 L-1 can be maintained at these warm temperatures. The role of potential interactions between turbulent surface layers and cloud-driven turbulence in maintaining phase partitioning in these cloud systems will also be discussed.

493621.title: Equilibrium Droplet Size Distributions in Entraining Parcels: From Condensation to Coalescence
493621.authors: Steven K. Krueger, Univ.of Utah, SALT LAKE CITY, UT
493621.abstract: Collision–coalescence and precipitation onset depend sensitively on the upper tail of the cloud droplet size distribution (DSD), which is shaped by the combined effects of mean condensational growth, turbulent supersaturation fluctuations, and entrainment followed by mixing. For hygroscopic seeding, an important issue is how the unseeded pre-coalescence DSD is established and how its characteristics influence subsequent coalescence growth. We develop a limiting-case analytical model that isolates these processes in an entraining cloud parcel before coalescence becomes important. In squared-radius space, mean condensation produces systematic droplet growth, stochastic supersaturation variability broadens the distribution, and entrainment limits the time droplets remain in the parcel. Their competition produces a compact equilibrium DSD characterized by a radius scale that increases with condensational growth and stochastic broadening and decreases with increasing entrainment loss. The graphic illustrates how the no-diffusion characteristic radius varies over a range of supersaturations and entrainment-loss rates. We then use the Explicit Mixing Parcel Model (EMPM) to test how accurately the analytic solution describes equilibrium DSDs and their large-droplet tails when individual droplets, entrainment, and mixing are represented explicitly. This comparison provides a way to identify where the limiting-case assumptions remain useful.
