Finally, we use the equilibrium DSD as a physically based starting point for examining the transition from condensational growth to collision–coalescence, including time-scale measures that indicate whether droplets remain in the parcel long enough for coalescence to substantially modify the large-droplet tail.

493625.title: Wildfire Smoke and Health: Impacts, Collaboration, and Remaining Challenges
493625.authors: Mahshid Ahmadian, American Meteorological Society, Washington, DC, DC; and P. A. Higgins, R. Rose, K. L. Seitter, and E. Tipton
493625.abstract: Wildfires pose serious risks to public health; beyond the immediate dangers of the fire itself, the smoke from wildfires can affect communities located many miles away. Weather and climate factors shape the conditions that lead to the ignition and spread of wildfire, and with it, wildfire smoke. The health impacts are notable: smoke exposure affects the heart, lungs, and kidneys, while the trauma of the fire itself contributes to long-term mental health issues like anxiety and depression. Additionally, from a societal viewpoint, many individuals often underestimate the risks posed by smoke since it is perceived as secondary to fire; moreover, social norms may shape whether protective action is taken since people take their cues from how others around them respond. As such, there is high potential for increased and improved collaboration between the meteorological and health professions to develop new approaches to the understanding and communication of the impacts of wildfire smoke. This presentation shares findings from a two-day workshop on wildfire smoke and health, held in July 2026 by the American Meteorological Society’s Policy Program. The workshop brought together scientists and practitioners in meteorology, wildfire management, and public health from across the United States. Participants engaged in discussions covering a wide range of challenges and opportunities, including forecasting, community preparedness, and the health effects associated with wildfire smoke. A key finding from the workshop was a gap that appears to be between what is known and understood about wildfire risks and the protective actions those who are affected take: the data reaches people, but the advice on what to do with it often does not. Smoke movement is directly related to weather, and as people already trust meteorologists for weather information, forecasters are well-positioned to offer guidance on smoke conditions as well. A forecast is most effective when it provides the insights people need to make informed decisions about whether and how to respond based on their specific circumstances. Bridging the gap between forecast and action, so that reliable science actually reaches the people who need it, is where the meteorological and health communities can do the most together.

493628.title: Outcomes of the NASA Mars L1 Space Weather Workshop: Observational Requirements and Operational Architectures for Deep Space Forecasting
493628.authors: Michele Cash, NASA, Washington, DC; and S. Savage, J. Favors, C. O. Lee, P. Chamberlin, Y. Collado-Vega, C. N. Arge, and D. Pawlowski
493628.abstract: As humanity prepares for sustained robotic and human exploration beyond Earth, understanding and mitigating space weather impacts is critical for operational safety and mission success. Currently, space weather analysts, forecasters, and exploration end-users face significant operational gaps in real-time radiation specification and advanced warning capabilities at Mars. A continuous, upstream monitor positioned at the Sun-Mars L1 point offers a vital vantage point for watching space weather arrive at Mars, providing essential advanced warning of solar energetic particle events, solar wind evolution, and coronal mass ejections. To explore potential concepts for a Mars space weather mission, the NASA Space Weather Program hosted the NASA Mars L1 Space Weather Workshop at NASA Ames in October 2026. Bringing together exploration end-users, space weather analysts and forecasters, industry, academia, and government partners, the workshop evaluated the critical decision-making processes, observational requirements, and mission architectures required for safe operations at Mars. This presentation synthesizes the key consensus outcomes, user needs, and mission concepts established during the workshop. We present the identified user needs and broad measurement requirements, focusing on critical observational needs rather than specific instrument hardware, as well as the real-time data architectures and autonomous systems essential for supporting space weather analysis and forecasting. Furthermore, we highlight the enabling science opportunities afforded by a sustained Mars L1 mission, including solar wind evolution and multipoint measurements of the Sun. Finally, we outline interdisciplinary pathways to integrate a Mars L1 space weather asset into broader heliospheric observation architectures, fostering collaboration between the heliophysics community and exploration end-users.

493629.title: A Scenario-Based Decision-Support Tool for Flash Flood Forecasting
493629.authors: Domenic C Brooks, Research Triangle Institute, Washington, DC; and K. van Werkhoven
493629.abstract: Flash flood forecasting and warning remain uniquely challenging tasks. Key decisions require coordination between multiple stakeholders in situations that transpire in very short periods using inherently uncertain forecasts. Through stakeholder engagement with forecasters and emergency managers, we identified a need for a way to test hypothetical precipitation and flash flood scenarios to assist their decision-making. Here we present the prototype for such a tool, developed under the Cooperative Institute for Research to Operations in Hydrology (CIROH), that allows users to transpose and modify existing spatial-temporal precipitation patterns to test different hypothetical precipitation scenarios and model their respective hydrologic responses. The tool uses NOAA Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) grids for depicting the spatial-temporal precipitation patterns and the Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting (SAC-SMA) hydrologic model for simulating the hydrologic response to modified precipitation scenarios. We are also exploring a stochastic modeling approach to allow users to input a range of values for various conditions, such as soil saturation and maximum rain rate, to create an envelope of potential scenarios that can be used to evaluate hydrologic response to different storm characteristics. The prototype is currently being tested for the Hawaii domain with plans for expansion into other domains. We envision this tool supporting both training and operational applications by allowing forecasters and emergency managers to explore historical and hypothetical events, develop a better understanding of local hydrologic response during blue-sky periods, and investigate a range of plausible outcomes when precipitation forecasts are uncertain.

493630.title: Can We Use the Community Earth System Model Version 3 (CESM3) to Understand and Communicate Future AR-Related Hydroclimate Hazards In National Park Service Units?
493630.authors: Kyle M Nardi, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and C. A. Shields, A. Rhoades, M. C. Crump, and A. Herrington
493630.abstract: The National Park Service (NPS) oversees a variety of parks, monuments, battlefields, and historical sites throughout the United States. These units protect vital ecosystems, preserve cultural heritage, and provide valued physical and mental health benefits for visitors. However, NPS units are vulnerable to the impacts of hydroclimate extremes driven by atmospheric rivers (ARs), such as the November 2006 rain-on-snow (ROS) flooding event in Glacier National Park. Therefore, it is critical for the weather and climate community in general, and the AR community in particular, to partner with NPS to understand and prepare for current and future hazards associated with AR-driven extreme events. In this study, we leverage a variable-resolution configuration of the Community Earth System Model version 3 (CESM3) to recreate the November 2006 ROS event in historical, contemporary, and future environments. We first use reanalysis of atmospheric and ocean conditions from November 2006 to initialize a CESM3 hindcast of the ROS event. We establish “adequacy for purpose” for CESM3 by comparing modeled physical processes and impacts to observed conditions during the event. Upon establishing the model’s realistic depiction of key physical mechanisms in the historical event, we generate the same AR-driven ROS storm in a variety of different background environments, under a spectrum of plausible future scenarios. We compare modeled event impacts, including precipitation, snowmelt, and river discharge, between the different environments. We further detail ongoing efforts to partner with NPS decision-makers to effectively transition this modeling effort to actionable information for NPS personnel and community partners.

493633.title: Overview of Aerosol Properties Across Southeast Asia During the ASIA-AQ Campaign
493633.authors: Sayantee Roy, NASA, Hampton, VA; and F. Gallo, C. E. Jordan, E. Winstead, M. A. Shook, G. Symonds, D. Kim, S. Yun, D. A. Day, P. Campuzano-Jost, J. L. Jimenez, L. Ziemba, and R. H. Moore
493633.abstract: NASA’s 2024 Airborne and Satellite Investigation of Asian Air Quality (ASIA-AQ) campaign deployed the NASA DC-8 aircraft across the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand, and Taiwan to better understand the air quality across Southeast Asia. The Langley Aerosol Research Group (LARGE) measured real-time aerosol microphysical and optical properties, while other research groups measured aerosol composition, trace gases, and meteorological parameters. Here, we characterize aerosol optical properties using scattering and absorption coefficients, single scattering albedo (SSA), mass absorption coefficient (MAC), and mass extinction coefficient (MEC) over the four locations and examine their relationships with aerosol mass, particle size-distribution, and chemical composition. The analysis will include spatial and vertical variability in aerosol properties across the regions and examine how differences in aerosol composition modify the relationship between aerosol loading and its optical impacts. This study is expected to provide an understanding of how aerosols with similar burdens can exhibit different optical efficiencies and, consequently, different potential radiative impacts.

493635.title: Anticipatory Action in Northern Central America: Gaps and Opportunities
493635.authors: Diego Pons, University of Denver, Denver, CO
493635.abstract: In this session, we discuss the results of two projects in Northern Central America regarding decision-making and adaptive behavior in the context of anticipatory actions based on seasonal precipitation forecasts to manage drought. First, we present fieldwork conducted in the Corozal, Orange Walk, and Cayo districts of Belize between 2024 and 2026. There, a participatory process involved a thorough investigation of the provision of climate services by the Belize National Meteorological Service as well as the demand by users for climate information to support decision-making across multiple sectors (energy, agriculture, tourism, conservation, and forestry). Our analysis suggests that in this case, climate information is not the limiting factor for decision-making on the ground. Operationally, the National Meteorological Service is providing what users demand, and users have Standard Operating Procedures, but these are not connected to critical triggers. The second project took place in the Huehuetenango and Quiché departments in the highlands of Guatemala, where subsistence crop cycles appear to be increasingly diverging from theoretical norms, thereby complicating drought adaptation efforts. In both cases, the evidence suggests a need to re-examine the assumptions underlying the provision of climate services for risk management in the region.

493636.title: Beyond the "Secondary" Peril: Why Severe Convective Storms Have Become Insurance's Costliest U.S. Catastrophe Risk
493636.authors: Steven G. Bowen, Gallagher Re, Rolling Meadows, IL
493636.abstract: According to Gallagher Re, severe convective storms (SCS) in the United States, including hail, tornadoes, and straight-line winds, have generated more than $542 billion in inflation-adjusted insured losses since 2010, compared to approximately $367 billion from tropical cyclones. As a result, SCS has become the costliest U.S. catastrophe peril for insurers during that period. The data also demonstrate that hazard activity alone does not explain the loss trajectory. Gallagher Re estimates that 80% to 90% of the nominal growth in U.S. SCS loss costs since 2008 has been driven by non-hazard factors, including replacement-cost inflation, rising construction and labor costs, energy-driven material price increases, social inflation, exposure growth, and the expansion of vulnerable assets. Drawing on a reinsurance perspective, this keynote examines how the industry's understanding of severe convective storm risk is evolving and what that evolution means for underwriting, portfolio management, reinsurance purchasing, capital allocation, and resilience planning. It challenges the usefulness of rigid labels such as "primary" and "secondary" peril when they obscure the actual risk profile of a portfolio. A more practical approach is to understand where exposures are concentrated, how loss costs are changing, and which combinations of hazard and socioeconomic drivers matter most for individual insurers, reinsurers, and capital providers. The 45-minute keynote and audience discussion will explore the limitations of relying solely on historical loss experience to assess future risk. While historical data remain essential, insurers increasingly require real-time observations, enhanced event reconstruction, atmospheric and climate indicators, and broader socioeconomic datasets to evaluate risk over decision-relevant time horizons. Modern catastrophe models must do more than simulate hazards; they must connect hazard science with rebuilding costs, claims settlement trends, infrastructure disruption, supply-chain impacts, and emerging concentrations of high-value assets. The session will conclude by highlighting research and market priorities that can make severe convective storm science more actionable. These include improved characterization of hail, tornado, and straight-line wind risk; more integrated approaches to modeling hazard and loss-cost drivers; clearer communication of uncertainty; and stronger collaboration among scientists, modelers, insurers, reinsurers, capital providers, and public-sector partners. Translating these advances into practical risk-transfer and resilience solutions can help narrow the protection gap and strengthen the industry's ability to manage one of its most significant and rapidly evolving sources of loss.

493642.title: Real-Time, Microscale Visibility Forecast Decision Support for Improved Low-Altitude Airspace Operations In Complex Domains
493642.authors: Kyle Niezgoda, Aeris LLC, Louisville, CO; and M. Robinson, F. Shryock, B. Waltman, and O. Lopez
493642.abstract: Hyperlocal variability in low-visibility conditions is a persistent challenge to aviation operations. Limitations in forecasting the timing, duration, intensity, and recovery of low-altitude fog, which often occurs irregularly across localized airspace, pose safety risks and operational inefficiencies that may otherwise be mitigated. Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) providing critical transport among hospitals in the Cincinnati river valley are routinely disrupted by these conditions. Visibility can differ dramatically between Cincinnati Municipal Lunken Airport (LUK), whose observations often dictate HEMS flight opportunities, and nearby Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG) or local hospital heliports. Terrain, proximity to the Ohio River, and land-type variability frequently create significant visibility gradients over short distances, complicating preflight planning and in-flight decision-making for time-critical missions. To help mitigate these challenges, Aeris is supporting a collaborative initiative to develop and demonstrate a real-time, microscale, low-altitude fog and visibility forecast and prototype decision support capability. This system aims to improve predictions of the onset, severity, recovery, and hyperlocal extent of impactful low-visibility conditions, enabling stakeholders to expand flight operations without compromising safety. The system is powered by the Joint Outdoor-indoor Urban Large Eddy Simulation (JOULES) modeling and real-time forecasting system, which provides meter-scale predictions of wind, turbulence, and visibility by accounting for terrain, land type, and three-dimensional urban infrastructure. This presentation will summarize the capabilities of JOULES to predict evolving near-surface moisture and fog conditions within the Cincinnati airspace and translate these boundary layer conditions into operationally meaningful visibility constraints. We will also describe the prototype decision support service and user interface developed to deliver these forecasts to Cincinnati HEMS pilots, dispatchers, and stakeholders. Finally, we will discuss results from live stakeholder evaluations and demonstrate how these applied, microscale forecast capabilities extend to general aviation, Uncrewed Aircraft System (UAS) Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) operations, and Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) services.

493645.title: Operationalizing GONG
493645.authors: Andrew R. Marble, CIRES/SWPC, Boulder, CO
493645.abstract: Originally designed for a three-year helioseismology research program, the Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG) began measuring vibrations on the Sun’s surface in 1995 in order to study the solar interior. Subsequent upgrades expanded GONG’s capabilities and transformed it into a critical asset for operational space weather forecasting. Today, it’s high-cadence magnetograms drive the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center’s (SWPC’s) Wang-Sheeley-Arge (WSA)-Enlil model of the solar wind and the propagation of Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) from the Sun to the Earth. SWPC forecasters additionally use both GONG magnetograms and continuum intensity images to characterize active regions on the Sun and inform solar flare forecasts, as well as GONG H-alpha imagery to monitor such activity. SWPC has used GONG observations operationally since 2010, financially supported GONG Operations & Maintenance since 2015, and hosted its near-real-time space weather data processing since 2021. We review GONG’s transformation from a purely scientific mission to a critical operational asset and the factors that made it a success.

493646.title: GeoXO Sensor and Hardware Development: Progress Toward Next-Generation Geostationary Observations
493646.authors: Monica Todirita, NOAA, Greenbelt, MD; and E. Grigsby, C. Carlisle, S. W. Bidwell, M. Rizzo, K. Gonzales, E. M. Kline, and M. M. Coakley
493646.abstract: The Geostationary Extended Observations (GeoXO) satellite system is being developed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) serving as acquisition and development partner, in collaboration with industry partners. GeoXO will carry a new generation of instruments designed to provide significant advances in spatial resolution, spectral coverage, temporal refresh, and vertical sounding capability over geostationary orbit. The first GeoXO spacecraft will fly an Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), providing continuity with GOES-R imaging capability, alongside the GeoXO Sounder (GXS). The second spacecraft will introduce the GeoXO Imager (GXI), a next-generation imager offering multi-band visible and infrared imagery with finer spatial resolution and faster revisit rates than ABI, paired again with GXS. GXS will deliver hyperspectral infrared sounding with the vertical resolution needed to resolve temperature, moisture, and wind profiles critical to numerical weather prediction and severe storm forecasting. The GXI program has progressed into hardware fabrication, with Engineering Development Unit (EDU) integration and long-lead component deliveries demonstrating readiness in detector, optical, and electronics subsystems. The GXS design continues to mature through targeted refinements addressing spectral uniformity, thermal management, and optical performance as the instrument progresses toward its design baseline. Meeting the stringent performance specifications for these instruments also demands careful spacecraft accommodation. The spacecraft platform is being designed to support the size, mass, thermal, pointing, and data handling requirements of these two large instruments, ensuring that spacecraft-level integration preserves instrument-level performance margins. Accommodating both instruments on a common platform has required attention to structural mounting, thermal isolation, jitter environments, and data interface architecture. Beyond hardware development, the instruments must integrate with the broader NESDIS enterprise responsible for translating raw measurements into operational products. NESDIS offices provide algorithm implementation services for Level 0 to Level 1b calibration and Level 2+ geophysical retrievals, as well as science stewardship, data archival, and distribution to the user community. GXI and GXS development is being coordinated with these offices and with the program's calibration/validation and operations teams under a streamlined NESDIS concept of operations designed to ensure a seamless transition from instrument commissioning to sustained operational service. This paper will provide an overview of GXI and GXS development status, the spacecraft accommodation challenges involved in hosting two large and demanding instruments, and the risk reduction and integration activities underway as the program advances toward its planned 2030s launch sequence.

493653.title: When Past Leads to Present: Exploring Response Actions and Risk Perception Across Varying Forecast Lead Times
493653.authors: Sean Robert Ernst, OU Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis, Norman, OK; Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations and NWS Storm Prediction Center, Norman, OK; and J. T. Ripberger
493653.abstract: Although hazardous weather warnings are often considered to be the point at which decision-makers under risk should take protective actions, decision-making and forecast reception research suggest that protective action decisions unfold over larger timescales with less precise forecasts. In particular, the Protective Action Decision-Making model suggests that Information Search behaviors, similar to Milling behaviors that have been previously discussed in weather risk response research, are often performed at longer lead times and can help decision-makers perform more effective protective responses more quickly when a risk is realized. In this study, we attempt to identify whether members of the public perform information search behaviors when exposed to long-range tornado forecasts, whether exposure to those long-range forecasts increases their likelihood of immediately performing protective response actions when they receive a tornado warning, and whether an extended period of forecasts for a dread-inducing hazard like tornadoes has meaningful impacts on feelings of exhaustion and trust in the forecast whether the hazard is realized or not. Results will present participant responses from a national survey that posed participants with a range of tornado forecast scenarios, and qualitatively and quantitatively compare the protective action decisions and forecast perceptions across different participant groups. These findings may help inform future efforts to survey members of the public about anticipated convective hazards, as well as inform forecast producers on the potential value that their long-range, less precise forecasts can generate for decision-makers in the public.

493654.title: Nitrosat, a Satellite Mission Concept for Mapping Reactive Nitrogen at the Landscape Scale Conference
493654.authors: Pieternel Felicitas Levelt, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and P. Coheur
493654.abstract: Two key forms of reactive nitrogen (Nr) in the atmosphere are nitrogen oxides (NO+NO2) and ammonia (NH3). Both species are abundantly emitted from anthropogenic sources (fossil fuel combustion, agriculture) with devastating consequences on the environment, human health and climate. Complementing sparse ground-based measurements, current satellite sounders provide daily coverage of their global distribution. However, the spatial resolution of these instruments (>20 km² for NO2 and >100km² for NH3) is orders of magnitudes greater than the typical size of the main Nr sources (industries, farms, roads), which makes identification of the emitters, and corresponding quantification of their emission strengths particularly challenging. To understand and address the impacts of a perturbed nitrogen cycle, and in response to the current observational gap, a dedicated satellite for the monitoring of NO2 and NH3 at high spatial resolution has been conceptualised, called Nitrosat. Its main objective is to quantify simultaneously the emission sources of NH3 and NOx at the landscape scale (<0.25 km²) and to characterize seasonal patterns (<1 month) in their emissions. The two imaging spectrometers onboard Nitrosat will operate respectively in the infrared for NH3 and the visible for NO2, offering gapless coverage in a single swath. Starting from representative examples of measurement techniques that are presently used to derive emission fluxes from NH3 and NO2 satellite observations, we discuss the limitations of current sounders. We introduce the Nitrosat measurement concept and, exploiting both model simulations and aircraft campaign data, provide examples from the ESA EE11 Phase 0 studies of how Nitrosat will enable retrieval of emission fluxes from local and diffuse sources in a way that will not be possible with other current or planned missions. New developments in Europe will be addressed.

493656.title: Implementation and Testing of Stochastic Physics for MPAS in UFS in Preparation for RRFSv2
493656.abstract: After adding stochastic physics capabilities including Stochastically Perturbed Parameterization Tendencies (SPPT) for the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) in preparation for its inclusion in the Unified Forecast System (UFS), the Developmental Testbed Center (DTC) has continued work to implement and test additional schemes in MPAS. Of critical importance to prepare MPAS for use in the Rapid Refresh Forecast System version 2 (RRFSv2), is the implementation and testing of Stochastically Perturbed Parameterizations (SPP). In SPP the stochastic pattern is used to perturb individual parameters closer to sources of uncertainty within physics schemes. Code was added to the physics schemes, and simulations were conducted to ensure stability of the model under each new perturbation and validate correct application of the perturbation pattern in all schemes, beginning with MYNN PBL and MYNN surface. These initial schemes were previously implemented by collaborators I-Han Chen and Judith Berner at NSF NCAR MMM, and after adding them the MPAS code base, DTC's work continues with some or all of TEMPO, GSL GWD, RRTMG, RUC-LSM, NOAH and GFL schemes. Further tests were included to assess impact on forecasts in kinetic energy spectra and estimate effective magnitudes for each parameter perturbation. Through this work, the DTC provides critical functionality for and expedites the transition of MPAS into the UFS framework in preparation for use within RRFSv2.

493664.title: Using AI in Research-to-Operations Pipelines: Successes, Challenges, Toolkits, and What I’m Still Learning
493664.authors: Daniel M. Gilford, Climate Central, Princeton, NJ
493664.abstract: AI has upended the way I work. While my goals remain the same—namely, converting rigorous climate change research into compelling online tools for media and public consumption—each step in the research-to-operations pipeline is now often touched or informed by large language models (used by myself or others). I use LLMs during research planning stages, across large and small code bases, over internal or public-facing documents, and for many other tasks. The landscape has remained relatively constant, while the landscaping is now being done with new and evolving tools. The evolution in tools requires an intentional and foundational change in me: in how I think about and solve problems, in what I delegate to a model and what I choose to do myself, in how I communicate both internally and externally, and in what my roles are in a task when I choose to use LLMs. In this talk I discuss and explore personal pathways and pitfalls in integrating AI into my day-to-day professional activities. Using example tasks, such as validating an operations codebase or debugging a decades-old tropical cyclone intensity theorem, I illustrate where AI was useful, where it failed me, where I failed, and where (together) we were useful. I touch on the challenges I have experienced using AI on a daily basis, including the needs and stress of role shifting, unclear policies and boundaries, and mental health impacts. I share some practical lessons learned, like the 80/20 rule, choosing the right model to fit each task, and the difficulty of knowing when I’ve found “sufficiently robust” between “first draft” and “perfect,” when using AI. I also demonstrate parts of the AI-Science-Toolkit, which is designed to optimize and smooth my work with AI. The toolkit is freely available, open-source, honed for climate- and atmospheric-relevant research, and actively being developed. Relevant tools for my AI-assisted workflows include domain-specific personas and Claude code skills like /commit-batch, /unstale, and /reviewer-2. The talk will conclude with a discussion on the development of my own AI personal policies, how I’m staying apprised and engaged in a rapidly changing space (e.g., hosting weekly AI office hours), and final takeaways on community responses and professional responsibilities. Transparency statement: AI was not used in the writing of this abstract. Any em-dashes or run-on sentences are mine.

493665.title: Urban Microscale Weather Modeling to Support City Interventions for Extreme Heat
493665.authors: Michael Robinson, Aeris LLC, Louisville, CO; and K. Niezgoda, F. Cochran, J. Alberque, and J. Kottamala
493665.abstract: The increasing frequency and severity of high-heat events, compounded by the urban heat island effect, present significant challenges to metropolitan infrastructure, public health, and community well-being. To address these challenges, the City of Raleigh has implemented a Community Climate Action Plan that incorporates extreme heat mitigation and adaptation strategies. These efforts are supported by Raleigh’s advanced Geographic Information System (GIS) services and dynamic digital twin capabilities, which provide an integrated, data-driven virtual model of the city and its environment. To optimize the implementation of these strategies, there is a growing need for comprehensive, very-high-resolution weather and heat data to objectively identify vulnerabilities and inform targeted resiliency and sustainability initiatives. Aeris is collaborating with the City of Raleigh to provide urban microscale weather simulation data for hyperlocal heat metrics across a range of high-heat days and scenarios. To achieve this, Aeris employs its Joint Outdoor-indoor Urban Large Eddy Simulation (JOULES) model to estimate 3-meter resolution (“street” scale) temperature, heat index, wet bulb globe temperature, and horizontal wind speed and direction across the entire city (approximately 30 square kilometers). JOULES is a well-validated atmospheric physics and forecasting model that resolves three-dimensional building and land types (e.g., grass, trees, roads, water). It has been employed extensively by various government agencies and has demonstrated accurate representations of variable, hyperlocal urban environmental conditions, including heat and humidity. This presentation will summarize simulated microscale heat results for Raleigh spanning select daytime and nighttime periods from 2024 to 2026. Results will include comparisons with available historical Raleigh intercity weather observations to validate the accuracy of the estimated heat conditions. Opportunities for integrating modeled microscale heat data with the City of Raleigh’s GIS and digital twin capabilities will be presented. Finally, we will present practical use cases for embedding JOULES-modeled data into city processes to prioritize objectives and initiatives for heat interventions, mitigations, and adaptations.

493668.title: Convective Boundary Layer (CBL)
493668.authors: Yufei Chu, Rice University, Houston, TX; and J. A. Zhang, G. Lin, Z. Wang, L. Xue, W. Li, H. Shin, M. Deng, D. Zhang, H. Guo, and L. Jin
493668.abstract: The convective boundary layer (CBL) governs surface–atmosphere coupling, pollutant dispersion, and cloud formation, yet its key properties — mixing-layer height (MLH), turbulence dissipation rate (EDR), and lower-tropospheric stability (LTS) — remain poorly resolved at ~100-km Earth-system-model grid scales and are costly to observe continuously. Using four years (2018–2021) of Doppler-lidar and collocated surface-flux observations from a dense five-site network at the ARM Southern Great Plains (SGP) observatory (C1, E32, E37, E39, E41), spanning ~100 km, we present an integrated, physics-guided, explainable machine-learning (ML) framework that retrieves and interprets all three CBL properties from the same lidar-centered observing network — effectively turning a single station's routine instrument suite into a multi-variable profiling capability, without dedicated sensors for each property. Building on our published physics-informed AutoML framework (TPOT + AutoKeras), which explains and predicts CBLH with high skill (R² = 0.74–0.86) and identifies LTS as the dominant, physically consistent driver via SHAP attribution, we extend the approach along three lines. First, we reconstruct the spatiotemporal structure of EDR from routine surface observations using a surface-constrained ML mapping trained on Doppler-lidar EDR retrievals, explaining ~70% of near-surface EDR variance, with skill decreasing with height (R² 0.7–0.5) as entrainment and shear processes take over, and robust cross-site transferability (R² ≈ 0.67). Second, we retrieve continuous LTS from routine surface-flux and lidar-derived MLH observations (R² = 0.78, MAE = 2.39 K) and introduce a new transferability diagnostic, ΔKL×|SHAP|, that combines Kullback–Leibler divergence in predictor distributions with SHAP sensitivity to identify where and why a station-trained retrieval will degrade at another site. Third — and central to this synthesis — we show that segmenting the diurnal CBL evolution into four physically distinct stages (Initiation, Growth, Peak, and Decay) and training stage-specific MLH models outperforms both a single bulk model and four separate seasonal models (R² = 0.88, MAE = 0.18 km at C1; R² = 0.83–0.86 transferability to nearby sites), with stage-to-stage driver variability exceeding season-to-season variability. Across all three variables, SHAP-based attribution consistently reveals distinct, physically meaningful drivers: surface heat flux and near-surface turbulence scales for EDR; mixed-layer height and cloud-base height for LTS; and stage-specific mechanisms — mechanical turbulence, cumulative heating, entrainment, and radiative cooling — for MLH. Retrieval skill tracks each variable's physical directness rather than any single confounding factor: MLH, a bulk quantity directly forced by the surface energy balance, attains the highest skill; LTS, which reflects the state of the free troposphere above the CBL rather than surface forcing alone, still retrieves well; and EDR, which captures instantaneous, small-scale turbulence and is intrinsically noisier, shows the lowest overall skill and is the only variable whose skill further declines with height as entrainment and shear dynamics take over. LTS itself proves to be a physical hinge linking the three properties — independently retrievable and, at the same time, the dominant SHAP driver of MLH during the Peak stage — evidence of genuine physical coupling rather than three independent fits. Together, these results demonstrate that a lidar-anchored, physics-guided, and diurnally stage-aware ML framework can jointly characterize CBL height, turbulence, and stability from a single ground-based profiling network, offering a transferable, low-cost, and interpretable pathway — requiring only routine surface-flux and lidar instrumentation — for extending point observations toward network- and regional-scale CBL monitoring.

493670.title: Evaluating Multi-Sensor Aerosol Optical Depth Retrieval Uncertainties for Wildfire Smoke Characterization and Climate Applications
493670.authors: Andrew Dai, Montgomery Blair High School, North Potomac, MD; and Y. R. Shi and R. C. Levy
493670.abstract: Satellite-based aerosol optical depth (AOD) retrievals have been essential for monitoring wildfire smoke transport, assessing aerosol impacts on air quality, and quantifying aerosol-climate interactions. However, significant discrepancies have existed among satellite aerosol products, introducing uncertainties in the characterization of smoke emissions and their atmospheric impacts. These uncertainties have been particularly important during extreme wildfire events, where accurate representation of aerosol loading has been necessary for understanding smoke evolution, aerosol-cloud interactions, air quality, and climate effects. This study investigated discrepancies between Dark Target (DT) aerosol optical depth retrievals from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite on Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (VIIRS SNPP) and the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS Aqua) sensors using XAERDT products from 2019–2020. Although both instruments applied the same DT retrieval framework, systematic differences remained due to variations in observation geometry, sensor characteristics, cloud screening, surface representation, and aerosol model assumptions. Targeted wildfire smoke cases were first analyzed to identify retrieval divergence patterns, followed by a broader statistical evaluation across diverse aerosol loading, surface, and atmospheric conditions. The analysis demonstrated that inter-sensor AOD differences were strongly influenced by retrieval geometry and algorithm assumptions, with distinct bias patterns emerging under varying smoke conditions and observation scenarios. Factors including viewing and scattering angles, pixel resolution, cloud contamination, and Fine-Mode-Fraction representation contributed to inconsistencies in satellite-derived aerosol distributions. These findings highlighted the importance of improving aerosol models, surface characterization, and cloud-aerosol treatment to reduce artificial biases in long-term wildfire smoke monitoring. More consistent multi-sensor aerosol datasets will improve the ability to quantify wildfire aerosol impacts on atmospheric composition, cloud interactions, and climate variability.

493673.title: Multi-Sensor Satellite Mapping of Severe Thunderstorm Impacts
493673.authors: Hannah Gayle Pankratz, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and A. L. Molthan, J. Bell, and A. Melancon
493673.abstract: Rapid and accurate mapping of severe thunderstorm impacts is critical for National Weather Service (NWS) storm assessments, emergency management, and public-private disaster response stakeholders. While ground surveys determine localized intensity and EF-scale ratings, they are constrained by resource limitations and physical accessibility. Utilizing satellite remote sensing can provide continuous spatial coverage across the larger impacted area, which is particularly beneficial in rural or hard-to-reach regions. Optical imagery is often leveraged to assess storm damage but is frequently hindered by cloud cover. More recently, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) has shown success in identifying specific storm damage by using Interferometric SAR (InSAR) coherence to determine the location of tornado damage tracks. To help bridge the gap between data availability and operational use, this study demonstrates a multi-sensor framework leveraging publicly available optical and SAR observations across a targeted subset of tornado tracks and hail and wind damage swaths (HWDSs) from 2025 and 2026. A pipeline was developed using Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) multispectral observations across tornado paths and HWDS events through localized composite differencing, multi-feature random forest classification, and ancillary datasets (e.g., NWS warnings, storm reports, weather radar). To provide data continuity, a complementary SAR processing workflow was established integrating Sentinel-1 C-band and newly released NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) L-band observations. To generate the final SAR-derived products, InSAR Coherent Change Detection (CCD) and backscatter intensity outputs were combined with dynamic land-cover thresholds. The output damage products were validated against official NOAA/NWS Damage Assessment Toolkit (DAT) survey data for tornadoes and hand-drawn assessments for HWDSs. Results demonstrate that while optical imagery delivers high-quality damage maps under clear skies, SAR workflows are essential for filling cloud-induced data gaps that hinder operational use. Though Sentinel-1 C-band suffered from decorrelation during summer green-up, NISAR’s longer L-band wavelength successfully maintained coherence through dense vegetation, enabling the detection of summer tornado tracks and wind and hail damage that were previously unresolvable. Combining optical and multi-band SAR observations highlights how these complementary datasets can be incorporated to create a reliable, year-round supplemental product that can assist NWS Weather Forecast Offices and emergency managers in conducting damage assessments after high-impact severe weather events.

493674.title: Evaluation of AI, Hybrid, and NWP Forecast Performance for Continuous Variables Using METplus
493674.authors: Christina P. Kalb, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and K. M. Newman, V. Vargas Jr., G. Ketefian, J. Halley Gotway, M. A. Harrold, G. P. McCabe Jr., and M. Win-Gildenmeister
493674.abstract: Verification and diagnostic efforts play a critical role in both the application and advancement of numerical weather prediction models. With the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence–based Weather Prediction (AIWP), there is a growing need to not only to evaluate the performance of these models, but also to assess the unique challenges associated with AIWP. Some of these challenges include forecast sharpness and the ability to produce physically realistic atmospheric states. The World Meteorological Organization’s Weather Prediction Model Intercomparison Project (WP-MIP) provides a testbed for addressing some of these needs. WP-MIP is uniquely designed to evaluate AIWP and hybrid models, alongside traditional numerical weather prediction models, with an emphasis on assessing physical consistency, atmospheric balance, and the ability to represent and predict key meteorological features. Using contributed datasets from participating modeling centers, the results presented here provide a comprehensive evaluation of continuous variables such as temperature, wind, and pressure. The evaluation is conducted using the enhanced Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) system, which is designed to provide a consistent and reproducible framework for verifying model performance. Forecasts are initialized every three days and extend sufficiently far in time to sample synoptic-scale variability. The analysis will incorporate techniques designed to address characteristics of AIWP forecasts that may not be fully captured by conventional measures including sharpness metrics and featured based methods.

493677.title: Accelerating Weather Prediction: In-Memory Observation Data Redistribution in the JEDI Framework
493677.authors: Stephen Herbener, UCAR/UCP/JCSDA, Boulder, CO; and S. Vahl, MA, L. Napper, S. K. Degelia, A. Shlyaeva, R. McLaren, F. Hebert, M. Cooke, and Y. Tremolet
493677.abstract: As numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems increase in resolution and ensemble complexity, computational efficiency of the data assimilation (DA) process is critical. A persistent bottleneck in the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) workflows, such as the Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (LETKF), has been the reliance on intermediate file I/O to perform necessary redistribution of observation data between application phases. Within JEDI, the Interface for Observation Data Access (IODA) manages the I/O and handling of diverse observational data. We present a refactoring of the IODA reader architecture that resolves this bottleneck by decoupling the task of distributing data across MPI tasks from the task of transferring data from file to memory. By enabling an in-memory redistribution capability, we eliminate the need for intermediate file writes and reads, allowing data to be repartitioned between MPI tasks "on the fly." We demonstrate that this software-level improvement significantly reduces runtime for LETKF applications at NOAA, moving workflows previously limited by I/O bottlenecks toward meeting research and operational time requirements. This work underscores the essential role of performance engineering in modern NWP, demonstrating how targeted software improvements directly enable more capable, efficient, and timely weather prediction science.

493679.title: Feasibility of Diffusion-Based Generative AI for Generating Large Ensembles for Convective-Scale Data Assimilation.
493679.authors: Thomas M. Hamill, The Weather Company, Boulder, CO; and C. Schwartz
493679.abstract: Large ensembles with appropriate variability at the scale of thunderstorms would likely be useful for convective-scale data assimilation. A large ensemble would ideally have realistic variability of thunderstorm position, intensity, and morphology. It would also reduce the sampling variability, necessitating less of the covariance localization that introduces initial condition imbalances. Unfortunately, with conventional models, large ensembles (hundreds or thousands of members) are prohibitively expensive to generate. In this pilot study, we will use a past time series of ensemble members from the 10-member, 3-km NCAR convective-scale ensemble (https://gdex.ucar.edu/datasets/d300000/) to train a diffusion algorithm to generate a larger synthetic ensemble. We will start by examining the diffusion algorithm’s ability to generate a synthetic ensemble of surface precipitation that realistically simulates the NCAR ensemble. The potential operational concept would then be that a limited-size convective-scale ensemble is generated with conventional methods. Before the data assimilation update, that ensemble is augmented by synthetic members to boost the sample size of the background forecasts used to estimate error covariances. Ensemble-based data assimilations then update the conventional ensemble, which is cycled forward to the next assimilation time, whereupon the process is repeated. In this study, we will examine whether the enlarged ensemble may improve the update step in ensemble-based data assimilations of radar data in a synthetic environment where one reserved ensemble member is treated as surrogate observation data. Pending a successful demonstration of this univariate assimilation problem, we will explore a more full 3-dimensional ensemble generation and whether the ensemble can realistically provide ensemble members with appropriate balances and cross-variable correlations. Methods, data, and results will be presented at the conference.

493681.title: A Qualitative Understanding of How Small Businesses in the Southeastern U.S. Perceive, Process, and Prioritize Hazardous Weather Information
493681.authors: Jada Rosalyn Lamar, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State, MS; and M. E. Saunders
493681.abstract: Businesses are impacted by natural disasters and severe weather hazards every year. A single event can disrupt normal operations, damage inventory, decrease revenue, and even place the lives of employees and patrons at risk. Being properly warned and prepared can increase the chances of survival for employees, staff, and patrons. Although businesses with more than 10 employees are required to have a written emergency action plan under Occupational Safety and Health Standards (OSHS) 1910.38 (OSHA, 2002), it remains unclear how many plans include severe weather safety procedures or whether employers routinely implement weather safety training. Many small businesses may rely on publicly available weather information rather than professional meteorological services, leaving weather-related decisions to owners or managers who may lack formal meteorological training. The specific thresholds businesses use to initiate protective actions, the weather information they rely on, and who is responsible for decision-making remains unclear. Thus, it is important to identify how designated decision-makers perceive, integrate, process, and prioritize hazardous weather information to ensure the safety of employees and patrons. The purpose of this study is to understand how small businesses perceive, integrate, process, and prioritize sources of weather hazard information. This study focused on small businesses across Mississippi and Alabama. Using a purposive sampling approach, small business owners or upper-management employees from multiple industries were selected to provide diverse perspectives and experiences. Data were collected through face-to-face or virtual semi-structured interviews lasting approximately 60 to 90 minutes. Participants were asked open-ended questions regarding how they access weather information and their current weather safety protocols and procedures. Participants were also presented with two severe weather scenarios and were asked to describe how they would implement protective actions for employees and patrons during a tornado event and flash flooding event. Interviews were audio recorded with participant permission, transcribed using an online transcription service, and analyzed in MAXQDA using qualitative methods to identify common themes related to how hazardous weather information is received, interpreted, and used to inform decision-making. The presentation discusses the results and analyses from the interviews.

493682.title: Propagating Generative River Bathymetry Uncertainty into Flood-Inundation Predictions
493682.authors: Saeed Memari, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and M. Morshed, E. J. Anderson, and V. Boddeti
493682.abstract: Accurate channel geometry is essential for flood modeling, yet river bathymetry remains one of the least observed and poorly constrained sources of uncertainty. National DEMs commonly represent river corridors as hydro-flattened water surfaces and therefore do not resolve submerged channel depth and morphology that govern conveyance, stage–discharge relationships, backwater effects, and floodplain connectivity. Available topobathymetric and hydrographic surveys cover only a small fraction of river networks, while conventional estimation approaches often require local observations, hydraulic calibration, or regional empirical relationships that limit transferability. This study develops a conditional diffusion framework to reconstruct missing river bathymetry from surrounding topography, river-corridor information, and optional sparse observations. The model is trained on more than 21,000 terrain tiles derived from USGS topobathymetric products and USACE hydrographic surveys, with complete river reaches withheld to evaluate spatial generalization. River-specific constraints on longitudinal slope, channel morphology, and volume improve hydraulic consistency. Initial evaluation on a subset of withheld test tiles yielded masked-area RMSE values of 0.05-0.64 m, with a median of approximately 0.19 m. Diffusion sampling produces multiple plausible bathymetric surfaces, providing an ensemble representation of channel-geometry uncertainty. To quantify the hydraulic consequences of this uncertainty, bathymetry ensembles are propagated through hydrodynamic simulations under identical forcing. Variability in water levels, flow distribution, and inundation extent is used to quantify flood sensitivity to channel geometry and generate ensemble-based inundation probabilities. Hydrodynamic simulations using hydro-flattened, reconstructed, and survey-derived bathymetries evaluate reconstruction performance through its effects on water levels and inundation, extending the assessment beyond elevation error alone. The workflow links scalable bathymetry reconstruction with uncertainty-aware flood-inundation modeling and improved channel representation in large-scale hydrofabrics.

493687.title: Pattern-Dependent Influence of Internal Tropical Pacific Temperature Variability on Southern Hemisphere Hadley Circulation Trends
493687.authors: Mahdi Hasan, Northern Gulf Institute (NOAA/Mississippi State University), Miami, FL; North Carolina State Univ., Raleigh, NC; and S. Larson
493687.abstract: The Hadley circulation critically influences tropical climate by redistributing heat and moisture between tropics and higher latitudes. Although global warming is expected to weaken the Hadley circulation following thermodynamic constraints, we observe a strengthening trend, especially in the Southern Hemisphere. Climate models also poorly agree on both the sign and magnitude of historical trends and sources of this uncertainty remain unclear. Using the Community Earth System Model version 2 (CESM2) historical large ensemble, we demonstrate that internal tropical Pacific sea surface temperature variability modulates Southern Hemisphere Hadley circulation on multidecadal timescales, contributing to the historical trend uncertainty. Both internal warming and cooling in the tropical Pacific can drive similar circulation trends, albeit through distinct spatial patterns and mechanisms. Hemispherically symmetric tropical Pacific warming strengthens the circulation through enhanced tropical diabatic heating and increased poleward atmospheric energy transport in both hemispheres. Conversely, hemispherically asymmetric tropical Pacific cooling, with a relatively cooler Southern Hemisphere, also strengthens the Southern Hemisphere Hadley circulation indirectly through southward cross-equatorial atmospheric energy transport. The results underscore the need to account for low-frequency tropical Pacific sea surface temperature patterns when attributing the Southern Hemisphere Hadley circulation trend to external forcing over recent and coming decades.

493691.title: Regulatory and Economic Drivers of Methane, Non-Methane Organics, and NOx Emissions from Oil and Gas Activity In the Uinta Basin, Utah
493691.authors: Seth Lyman, Utah State University, Vernal, UT; and L. Dhar
493691.abstract: Emissions of methane from the oil and natural gas industry have been well studied, but fewer studies of non-methane organic compound (NMOC) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions from the industry have been conducted. In Utah’s Uinta Basin, NMOC and NOx from oil and gas are the key contributors to wintertime ozone exceedances that occur in some years, and they also influence summertime air quality in other parts of North America. In this work, we used the Integrated Methane Inversion (IMI), an inverse emissions estimation method that relies on the TROPOMI satellite instrument and the GEOS-Chem transport model, to estimate annual methane emissions in the Uinta Basin from 2019 through 2025. We compared IMI results against those from a surface measurement-based inversion method developed by Lin et al. (2021) and found good agreement (r2 = 0.89), with the exception of one year during which the surface-based method appeared to be biased by a nearby emission source. We combined results from the two methods to create an annual time series spanning 2012 through 2025. We then used enhancement ratios with methane taken from daily surface measurements to extrapolate annual Uinta Basin-wide emissions of speciated NMOC and NOx. We found that methane emissions and emissions intensity (emissions relative to energy production) have both declined over the 13-year study period. Declines appear to have been driven by a combination of (1) declining gas production as the basin has transitioned from mostly gas-producing to mostly oil-producing, and (2) regulatory controls. In particular, a 2024 federal rule that required substantial emissions reductions to existing facilities appears to have had a larger impact than a series of rules targeting only new and modified facilities. NMOC emissions held steady through 2019 and then dropped to a low in 2020 and remained relatively low thereafter. The reason for the drop in 2020 and beyond is unknown. Also, the 2024 rule that strongly impacted methane emissions did not appear to influence NMOC, perhaps because most older wells in the Uinta Basin that were impacted by the 2024 rule were gas wells, which emit mostly methane. NOx emissions did not exhibit a decline over the study period, perhaps because no new regulations have been promulgated to target oil and gas NOx. Annual NOx emissions correlated strongly with drilling and well completion activity.

493695.title: Nonhydrostatic High-Altitude Modeling: Pressure Gradient Force and Vertical Coordinate
493695.authors: James F. Kelly, U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, DC
493695.abstract: High-Altitude (HA), ground-to-exosphere models rely on a Dynamical Core (DyCore) that must robustly handle large variations in density, variable composition, and high-amplitude gravity waves. To address these issues, a nonhydrostatic DyCore requires: 1) proper treatment of the pressure gradient force (PGF) and 2) an appropriate vertical coordinate that minimizes computational modes. These modeling challenges are addressed using a horizontal spectral element dynamical core and three equation sets that incorporate variable composition: Hybrid Virtual Potential Temperature (HVPT), specific internal energy (SIE), and total energy (TE). Novel logarithmic PGFs are derived for these equations sets to accurately represent the hydrostatic balance. Several vertical coordinates, including a staggered Lorenz and Charney-Phillips grid. A classical normal mode (Lamb wave) solution is used to test 1) and 3), while idealized mountain wave profiles are used to evaluate 2). Preliminary results indicate that HA modeling is sensitive to both factors, and recommendations for future operational HA models are presented.

493697.title: The Role of Radiative Canopy Heating on Flow over Forested Hills and Valleys
493697.authors: Gregory Q Torkelson, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA; and M. Chamecki
493697.abstract: Forested terrain covers vast regions of Earth's surface and plays a vital role in atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) dynamics that redistribute heat, moisture, and trace gases between the canopy sub-layer and overlying roughness sub-layer. Large-eddy simulation models of the ABL often neglect realistic surface properties and atmospheric conditions leading to poor comparison to observations. Here, we aim to bridge this gap through the coupling of two forms of increased realism, convective atmospheric stability, arising from solar heating on the canopy elements, and complex idealized topography. In this study, we present a suite of large eddy simulations of momentum, heat, and moisture in weakly to moderately unstable atmospheric conditions over idealized topography that includes hills, valleys, and periodic features. Radiative heating in the forest canopy drives an increased jet of fluid along the upslope resulting in enhanced mixing, shear, and turbulent kinetic energy across the canopy top. In the valley cases, the downslope recirculation, which results from a topography induced pressure gradient, grows significantly with stability as fluid is pushed up the downslope and out of the canopy. This enhanced recirculation results in a high concentration of moisture and a pooling across the valley floor.

493698.title: Development and Operational Evaluation of a Skillful Thunderstorm Nowcasting Model
493698.authors: Peter Harrington, NVIDIA Corporation, Santa Clara, CA; and J. Pathak, S. Abbas, D. R. Durran, C. K. Potvin, A. J. Clark, P. S. Skinner, A. Gupta, T. Ge, N. D. Brenowitz, S. Ravuri, and M. Pritchard
493698.abstract: Forecasting the first few hours of severe convective weather is critical for early warnings, yet remains difficult as storms evolve on time scales of minutes. The variables that matter most such as rain, hail, and lightning are imperfectly represented by numerical model physics and are difficult to initialize correctly, limitations that are inherited by AI models trained to emulate numerical models. We introduce StormScope, a generative forecasting system that learns storm-scale evolution directly from satellite, radar, and lightning observations over the continental United States with no numerical model used for training or initialization. StormScope produces coherent, well calibrated physically plausible ensembles of storm trajectories with state-of-the-art skill. We describe the development of StormScope and evaluation of its skill through a collaboration between NVIDIA and the NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory.

493708.title: Reeb Graph Based Topological Analysis for Hurricane Trajectories
493708.authors: Anantajit Subrahmanya, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA; and S. Chatterjee, S. Sivam, and B. S. Manjunath
493708.abstract: Hurricanes pose substantial risks to coastal populations and infrastructure, motivating methods that characterize the spatial organization of storm trajectories across large historical populations with an evolving climate. In this work, we introduce the first application of Reeb graphs to population-level hurricane trajectory analysis, constructing topological summaries from over 2,000 Atlantic Basin storms in the historical best-track record. Our framework transforms storm trajectories into spatially-embedded edge-weighted graphs that capture dominant pathways, genesis regions, and structural transitions without requiring predefined geographic clustering or heuristic tracking methods. We evaluate the resulting Reeb graphs across seasonal windows, multi-decadal periods, and varying spatial resolutions. The recovered topology reproduces established climatological structures and their characteristic progression over the course of hurricane seasons. Longitudinal comparisons further reveal changes in corridor structure across decades, including earlier-season emergence and increased prominence of tropical storms in recent periods. These results demonstrate that Reeb graphs provide an interpretable and scalable representation of population-level hurricane trajectories, enabling structural comparisons across seasons, decades, and potentially changing climate regimes.

493710.title: The Story of Adapting an Existing Atmospheric River Detection Tool to Broaden Scientific Utility and Enhance User Accessibility
493710.authors: Kyle M Nardi, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. Massa
493710.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) present public safety, environmental, and economic impacts for diverse populations globally. Many studies focused on quantifying past, present, and future AR impacts rely on a chosen definition for an AR, often based on objective detection tools (ARDTs). ARDT choice presents a key source of uncertainty in understanding AR hazards, so it is critical for ARDT developers to consider how effectively their tools characterize ARs globally. Meanwhile, rising public awareness of AR impacts necessitates increased consideration of public understanding of how we characterize ARs. In this poster, we detail efforts to enhance the effectiveness and accessibility of the Mundhenk ARDT for societally-relevant decision-making. First, we explore methodological enhancements aimed at improving the Mundhenk ARDT’s depiction of observed moisture and impacts globally. Previous iterations of the Mundhenk ARDT, which explored the sensitivity of AR detection to changes in the moisture and geometry thresholding requirements, showed the detectability of ARs is most sensitive to the chosen moisture threshold, compared to AR geometry. Building upon this understanding, the current generation of the model seeks to refine the moisture thresholding process by defining latitudinally varying thresholds. The use of this type of thresholding method deviates from previous generations, which employed a 94th percentile for the full globe. A shift to latitudinally varying percentile fields is subsequently shown to account for the natural variance in moisture content across the globe. As a result, the algorithm improves in its ability to not only capture ARs within the midlatitudes, but in more arid regions of the globe as well, such as the poles. In parallel to methodological development, we aim to enhance the accessibility of the Mundhenk algorithm for AR scientists, students, and community partners. In this poster, we additionally describe specific improvements to reduce barriers to access, and to enhance interpretability for end users. User-focused adaptations include hosting on a GitHub repository, increasing documentation, modernizing coding practices, and providing easier access to standardized input datasets. We also explore pathways toward leveraging the Mundhenk algorithm as an educational tool for individuals seeking to learn more about AR detection. We discuss possible applications of this modified Mundhenk algorithm for teachers and students in the classroom, as well as for decision-makers like emergency managers and weather forecasters. We hope that these adaptations will increase societal understanding and awareness of AR science and impacts.

493714.title: AICRTM-EPD: Jacobian-Trained Neural Network for CRTM
493714.abstract: Operational numerical weather prediction relies heavily on satellite radiances, yet the radiative transfer models used to simulate them, such as the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM), are computationally expensive, limiting how much satellite data can be assimilated. We present AICRTM (Artificial Intelligence Community Radiative Transfer Model), a machine-learning emulator trained on CRTM outputs, allowing it to learn not only simulated brightness temperatures but the underlying sensitivity structure. AICRTM uses an Encode–Process–Decode architecture that explicitly separates surface and pressure-level variables and processes vertical profiles with convolutional layers, improving on prior emulators. The model achieves an overall RMSE of approximately 0.2 K, falling below 0.1 K for most clear-sky infrared channels, while running roughly 400 times faster than CRTM for the forward calculation alone and about 80 times faster for the full observation simulation pipeline. Because AICRTM is fully differentiable, its Jacobian can be generated automatically via PyTorch autograd. We show that this automatically derived Jacobian closely matches CRTM's own. SHAP analysis confirms the network learns physically meaningful sensitivities rather than spurious correlations, supporting its use as a practical, differentiable observation operator for variational data assimilation. Unlike prior studies limited to offline, short-duration evaluation, AICRTM was deployed and validated within the JEDI-Skylab data assimilation experimental framework. Benchmarking for GOES ABI clear-sky and cloudy radiances against both CRTM and RTTOV shows AICRTM matches the accuracy of established radiative transfer models at a fraction of the cost.

493719.title: High Performance Computing, Agentic IA and Data Convergence: Moving from Data to Decision on AWS
493719.authors: Chris Stoner, Amazon Web Services, Upper Marlboro, MD; and R. Toles-Abdullah
493719.abstract: This talk will explore how Agentic AI can unlock data from trusted agencies like NOAA, turning these data into actionable insights through a chat interface. We will take an example, such as numerical weather prediction (NWP), and show how autonomous agents can ingest observations, perform some quality control, select optimal assimilation strategies and verify results with transparency to the Human In the Loop (HIL).

493725.title: High-Resolution Urban Flood Intensity Modeling Using Satellite Information in Data-Scarce Cities
493725.authors: Ali Haider, The City College of New York, New York, NY; and N. Devineni, S. Kamali, A. Mondal, M. D. Goldberg, and R. M. Khanbilvardi
493725.abstract: Urban flood modeling in rapidly urbanizing, data-scarce cities remains constrained by limited in situ observations and incomplete drainage-network information. This study develops a satellite-driven, event-based machine-learning framework for high-resolution urban flood-intensity modeling by integrating Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) observations, high-frequency rainfall measurements, and urban surface characteristics. Rather than representing flooding as a binary inundation state, flood intensity is expressed as a continuous normalized difference index derived from dry–wet SAR backscatter contrast, enabling characterization of spatial variations in flooding at 10 m resolution. The framework is evaluated using 34 monsoon flood events in Mumbai, India. Event-specific Random Forest regression models demonstrate predictive skill across heterogeneous rainfall conditions, with test R² values ranging from 0.05 to 0.61 and mean absolute errors of 0.06–0.08. To evaluate whether relationships learned during individual events are transferable, an exhaustive cross-event experiment comprising 1,122 source–target event combinations is conducted. Cross-event predictions achieve a mean R² of approximately 0.45, with about 88% of event combinations reaching R² ≥ 0.40 and exhibiting near-zero median bias. Spatial diagnostics further indicate that reductions in cross-event performance primarily arise from localized spatial displacement rather than systematic over- or underprediction. Most predicted flooded pixels remain within approximately 25–50 m of observed flooding. Feature-importance analysis reveals a physically interpretable hierarchy of controls: rainfall accumulation and short-duration rainfall intensity dominate event-level variability, while elevation, rainfall timing, and imperviousness influence the spatial organization of flooding. These results demonstrate that transferable urban flood-intensity relationships can be learned directly from satellite observations and geospatial predictors without requiring a calibrated hydrodynamic model. The framework provides a scalable approach for high-resolution urban flood assessment and risk characterization in data-limited megacities.

493726.title: Strong summertime temporal correlation of CCN across three sites in the BNF region: what are the drivers?
493726.authors: Gourihar Kulkarni, PNNL, RICHLAND, WA; and J. Fast, J. E. Shilling, F. Mei, Y. Chen, A. Zelenyuk, A. Varble, PhD, Z. Yang, C. Kaul, and L. K. Berg
493726.abstract: Complex land-type heterogeneity across the Bankhead National Forest (BNF) region may influence the spatial distribution of boundary-layer winds, temperature, moisture, aerosols, and cloud condensation nuclei (CCN). Accurately quantifying the spatial and temporal variability of CCN concentrations in parcels lifted to form clouds is essential for understanding the properties of shallow and deep convective clouds that are observed in this area. The BNF observatory includes a main central site (M1) located within the forest, along with multiple supplemental sites situated both within and outside the forest. In this study, we deployed CCN instruments from Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) at the S20 and S30 supplemental sites during June–August 2025, to measure CCN concentrations over a supersaturation range of 0.1 to 1%. Measurements from S20 and S30 enabled characterization of how different regional landscapes influence observations compared to the dense forest at the main site. The S20 site, situated northwest of the BNF, captured conditions over predominantly agricultural and rural areas, whereas S30, located northeast of the BNF, reflects a mixed landscape of pasture, rural residential, and open terrain. At S20, a dual-column CCN instrument was used: Column A measured CCN properties of ambient particles, while Column B measured CCN properties following heat treatment to assess the contribution of volatile aerosols. At S30, a single-column CCN instrument was deployed. For a shorter period, we deployed PNNL CCN instruments at the M1 site to intercompare with the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement baseline CCN measurements. The intercomparison was performed under similar supersaturation conditions to identify any instrumental biases. Relative to the overall campaign mean, CCN concentrations at 0.4% supersaturation showed positive anomalies at M1, S20, and S30 on 42, 29, and 39 days, respectively. The M1 (forest) site displayed the largest amplitude fluctuations in CCN concentrations. The S20 (agricultural) site captured the timing and phase of the major peaks observed at M1 but with slightly reduced amplitudes. In contrast, S30 (mixed) showed smaller magnitude variability while retaining the overall temporal structure of CCN anomalies. The CCN efficiency of thermodenuded particles was lower than ambient aerosols, indicating reduced hygroscopicity due to the removal of volatile and semi-volatile components. Our preliminary results show strong temporal correlations in CCN anomalies among the three sites, suggesting that large-scale meteorological conditions and regional background factors dominated the observed summertime variability. The differences in amplitude among the sites could be attributed to several factors such as variations in local biogenic, biomass burning, and anthropogenic aerosol emissions, wet scavenging, and dry deposition that will require further investigation. We plan to perform correlation analyses to elucidate the importance of these factors, across different wind directions and diurnal cycles, to identify their specific impacts on our CCN results.

493730.title: The US Drought Monitor: Unanswered Questions
493730.authors: John W. Nielsen-Gammon, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX
493730.abstract: The US Drought Monitor has been a highly successful tool for communicating the status of drought throughout the United States. Its simple approach of designating drought by one of four categories (plus abnormally dry) with qualifiers (short-term and long-term) makes drought easily trackable across space and time and, seemingly, easily understood. Yet drought itself is notoriously difficult to define. So how can something so complex possibly be represented so simply? I argue that five key ambiguities in the US Drought Monitor make its interpretation and communication challenging. Clearing up these ambiguities would make the US Drought Monitor's meaning more evident and easier to convey, but possibly at the cost of its present status as seemingly representing drought in all its complexity. Issue #1: Does the US Drought Monitor represent drought severity or drought risk? In a nonstationary climate, drought risk is the probability that drought of a similar or worse intensity would happen in the present climate, while drought severity is the probability that drought impacts would be similar or worse if historical conditions recurred. Both representations have multiple problems. Most fundamentally, in a risk-based approach climate change cannot drive an increase in the risk of D3 or D4, which seems contrary to the way we normally speak of changing drought. Conversely, in a severity-based approach it is possible that a drying climate would lead to permanent drought, which is contrary to the normal definition of drought. Issue #2: What is the relationship between US Drought Monitor levels and drought impacts? In some very wet climates, significant drought impacts might not be present until precipitation reaches the lowest 10th percentile or even the lowest 5th percentile. It is sometimes asserted that drought cannot be present if there are not impacts. Should drought categories be redefined in very wet climates so that D1 starts when impacts start? If so, what does that mean for D2, D3, and D4? What about locations with highly seasonal precipitation? Is short-term drought impossible in some locations and seasons? Issue #3: T How frequently should a given location be in, say, short-term drought? 20% of the time, corresponding to the D1 cutoff? Or should a given location be in drought of any sort 20% of the time, implying that short-term drought should be present much less than 20% of the time? Issue #4: Short-term drought primarily impacts agriculture. Certain crops are highly sensitive to precipitation during some parts of the year but not others. Should this sensitivity be reflected in Drought Monitor levels, so that the US Drought Monitor is closely correlated with agricultural impacts? If so, does that mean (in, say, a monoculture county) that short-term drought can only occur during certain times of the year? And if that is the case, what fraction of the acreage in a given county must be planted with a particular crop for it to impact the drought depiction? Conversely, is it possible to have short-term drought without impacts? Issue #5: The US Drought Monitor uses a "consilience of evidence" approach. What does that mean in the context of drought products that of varying quality and comprehensiveness? For example, the SPI and SPEI are very similar indices, except that the SPEI takes temperature into account in addition to precipitation. Assuming the SPEI does so in a valid manner, why should the SPI influence the US Drought Monitor? And if soil moisture models or observations were available for the past hundred years, why should either index be given weight in the face of direct information regarding the impact of drought on soil moisture?

493735.title: Dynamical Pathways of Summertime Heatwave Variability Across Spatial Scales in the Pacific Northwest
493735.authors: Satveer Sandhu, Univ. of Washington, Seattle, WA; and E. P. Salathé Jr.
493735.abstract: Summertime heatwaves in the Pacific Northwest (PNW) arise from interactions across synoptic, mesoscale, and local spatial scales, yet the relative contributions of these processes to individual events remain difficult to distinguish. This study develops a framework for identifying distinct dynamical pathways of PNW heatwaves using high-resolution ERA5-WRF simulations.
