Previously identified empirical orthogonal teleconnection (EOT) modes of summertime temperature variability are used to characterize the spatial evolution of heatwave events rather than as an end in themselves. Heatwaves are first identified using an established temperature-based detection method and then represented by their temporal evolution across seven EOT modes spanning the broader PNW, coastal range, Puget Sound, and eastern Cascades. These event trajectories are clustered to identify recurring heatwave structures and subsequently composited to diagnose their associated atmospheric dynamics. Composite analyses examine geopotential height, winds, temperature advection, surface temperature, and surface energy fluxes across multiple vertical levels to distinguish contributions from synoptic circulation, orographic modification, mesoscale processes, and localized land-atmosphere interactions. The resulting classification establishes a physically interpretable baseline of heatwave variability in the PNW and provides a reference framework for evaluating historical and future CMIP6-WRF simulations. Ultimately, this approach enables heatwaves to be compared not only by magnitude, but by the dynamical pathways through which regional and localized extremes develop and decay.

493736.title: Recent Updates to the Graphical Turbulence Guidance and Graphical Turbulence Guidance Nowcast Algorithms
493736.authors: Wiebke Deierling, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and C. Zuck, G. Meymaris, D. Munoz-Esparza, J. Sauer, H. Shin, J. A. Craig, and R. Sharman
493736.abstract: The Graphical Turbulence Guidance Product (GTG) has been developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) for strategic avoidance of turbulence aviation hazards. GTG utilizes a number of larger scale turbulence predictors that are combined to produce turbulence forecasts including clear-air turbulence (CAT), mountain wave turbulence (MWT), low-level turbulence (LLT) and in cloud convectively induced turbulence (CIT). It currently runs operationally at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Environmental Modeling Center based on NOAA’s High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model, NOAA’s Global Forecast System (GFS) and UK Met Office global models to provide turbulence forecasts. Recent work is focusing on upgrading the GTG algorithm to utilize machine learning capabilities. Furthermore, NCAR has developed a Graphical Turbulence Guidance Product Nowcast (GTGN) that is running operationally at NOAA to provide pilots, dispatchers and other aviation stakeholders with turbulence nowcasts updated every 15 minutes. Work is ongoing to update GTGN to include more observations, such as including Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADSB) derived Energy Dissipation Rate estimates. Initial results of updates towards future GTG and GTGN upgrades will be presented. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

493737.title: Development and Evaluation of a Machine Learning-Based Supercell Adaptive Scanning Algorithm for Phased Array Radars
493737.authors: Brandon K. Cohen, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. J. Bodine, H. Kim, J. C. Snyder, D. Schvartzman, C. M. Kuster, A. A. Alford, T. J. Schuur, T. Y. Yu, and M. Yeary
493737.abstract: Doppler weather radars, including the current WSR-88D radar network, have long been used to detect weather hazards and inform real-time operational decisions. However, with the WSR-88D network nearing the end of its service life between 2035–2040 and radar technology continuing to advance, phased array radars (PARs) are being evaluated as a possible contributor to future weather radar networks. PARs offer substantial flexibility through agile electronic beam steering, enabling faster volumetric updates and scanning techniques beyond traditional pencil beam observations, including digital beamforming (hereafter imaging) and multi-beam techniques. However, this flexibility introduces additional trade-offs between spatiotemporal resolution and data quality, which complicates the selection of scanning strategies for rapidly evolving hazards. These considerations motivate the development of machine learning (ML)-based approaches to assist with adaptive scanning decisions for PARs. Previous work developed an ML model that predicted the combined data quality and temporal resolution error associated with 1D imaging in elevation at varied spoiling factors using reflectivity (Z) and radial velocity (Vr) for multiple tornadic and non-tornadic cases observed by KOUN, a research-focused WSR-88D radar located in central Oklahoma that can be operated in sector mode enabling faster volumetric updates. Since then, this project has been expanded into an ML-based adaptive scanning algorithm that uses these predictions to recommend scanning configurations for supercells. This algorithm provides a framework for future expansion to a broader range of imaging configurations and PAR-enabled scanning strategies, such as multi-beam or beam multiplexing. This study evaluates the output of the prototype algorithm by varying imaging parameters and storm representations to determine how these changes influence recommended scanning strategies and radar-observed storm structure. We will characterize the conditions under which adaptive scanning recommendations are stable or sensitive to changes in scanning parameters and provide considerations and guidance for incorporating the algorithm’s recommendations into an operationally constrained adaptive scanning framework. Ultimately, this work represents an important transition from demonstrating the feasibility of ML-based adaptive scanning to evaluating the consistency and physical relevance of its recommendations for PAR observations of supercells. If meaningful data are available, performance comparisons with the fully digital S-band Horus PAR will also be presented.

493738.title: Impact of Perceived Snowfall Characteristics on Automotive LiDAR Performance: A Moving-Vehicle Field Study
493738.authors: Mohammadsadegh Moradi Ghareghani, Ontario Tech University, Oshawa, ON, Canada; and W. Y. Pao, M. Elewah, I. Gultepe, M. Agelin-Chaab, and H. Hangan
493738.abstract: Automated driving technologies have the potential to improve road safety and reduce traffic accidents; however, the reliability of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) and autonomous vehicles (AVs) remains a significant challenge under adverse weather conditions, particularly snowfall. Falling and wind-driven snow can degrade automotive LiDAR performance through laser backscatter, signal attenuation, false returns, and partial or complete occlusion of surrounding objects. Importantly, the precipitation encountered by a moving vehicle can differ substantially from that measured by a stationary weather station because vehicle motion and wind alter the relative particle flux and particle size distribution (PSD) perceived by vehicle-mounted sensors. This study experimentally investigates the performance of an automotive-grade Livox HAP LiDAR under natural snowfall conditions using a moving vehicle. Two LiDAR configurations were evaluated: an in-cabin configuration behind the windshield, which minimized direct sensor soiling, and an externally mounted configuration exposed directly to snowfall. Field experiments were conducted over a range of vehicle speeds and travel directions, with reference targets positioned along the test route to quantify changes in LiDAR detection performance. Concurrent meteorological measurements, including data from two laser precipitation monitors (LPM), were used to characterize the precipitation environment and the particle flux encountered by the moving vehicle. Rather than representing snowfall solely by conventional precipitation intensity, the perceived precipitation was characterized using the measured PSD and its statistical moments. Different PSD moments were examined to capture changes in particle concentration, size, and the relative contribution of larger snow particles. The experimental results demonstrate that LiDAR performance is more closely associated with the microphysical characteristics of the perceived snowfall than with precipitation intensity alone. Changes in PSD moments corresponded to systematic variations in target detection capability and LiDAR signal quality, with conditions characterized by greater concentrations and larger particles producing stronger degradation. Vehicle speed and direction further influenced the precipitation encountered by the sensor and consequently its performance. The resulting relationships between PSD moments and LiDAR performance provide a physics-informed framework for quantitatively describing the severity of snowfall from the perspective of automotive perception systems. These findings can support the development of weather-aware sensor performance models, improved adverse-weather testing methodologies, and more representative evaluation criteria for ADAS and automated vehicles operating in winter road environments.

493743.title: Urban-Bay Differences In Vertical Ozone Distributions during CoURAGE
493743.authors: Paul J. Walter, St. Edward's University, Austin, TX; and M. Deng, M. P. Jensen, T. Leblanc, F. Chouza, M. E. D. Roots, E. Strobach, N. E. Prince, and K. J. Davis
493743.abstract: We investigate the differences in vertical ozone distributions between Baltimore and the Hart Miller Island (HMI) in the Chesapeake Bay during the Summer 2025 portion of the Department of Energy (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE). Small Mobile Ozone Lidars (SMOLs) that are part of the Tropospheric Ozone Lidar Network (TOLNet) were deployed to the CoURAGE Baltimore Core Facility (M1) and HMI. We make composite plots of data at altitudes and times when data from both SMOLs was available. While the overlapping data coverage is limited, we observe more near surface ozone overwater at HMI (up to ~1 km above ground level (AGL)) than at the Baltimore M1 site, consistent with the pollution being confined to a shallower marine boundary layer than the terrestrial boundary layer. While more pronounced in the late afternoon, the higher levels of ozone overwater in the marine layer is observed at all hours, potentially a reflection of less titration of ozone overnight than in the city. There is a distinct ozone minimum at the the top of the boundary layer (and residual layer) at HMI compared to M1. That minimum extends anywhere from 1 - 3 km AGL. We identified days with a bay breeze (BB) using ARM data using Doppler lidar and surface meteorological measurements as well as NEXRAD observations and Orienteering Tape Recorder (OTR) diagrams that enable identifying and characterizing BB events. On non-BB days, we observe larger afternoon near surface differences between HMI and M1, with more near surface ozone over the Chesapeake Bay. Near surface ozone is less at HMI in the late afternoon on BB days than non-BB days. Near surface ozone is similar at HMI and M1 in the afternoon on BB days. During the early timing of the BB episodes the near surface ozone over Baltimore (M1) may be more than at M1 on non-bay breeze days before decreasing later in the day, perhaps due to advection of overwater pollution. Overall, the composite TOLNet observations provide an effective approach to compare vertical ozone distributions over land and overwater, and for observing the impacts of BB circulations.

493744.title: Enhancing ABI Reflectance Imagery with Solar Zenith Angle Adjustments
493744.authors: Kevin Thiel, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; and W. Line, J. W. Monroe, and J. G. Madden
493744.abstract: National Weather Service (NWS) forecasters routinely view satellite imagery in the visible and near-infrared frequencies to perform an array of operational duties including mesoanalysis, convective and fire weather nowcasting, decision support, and more. From the GOES-R Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), visible and near-infrared imagery are provided as reflectance factor values that are not locally adjusted for changes in solar zenith angle. In scenes with decreased solar irradiance (e.g. near local sunrise and sunset) the operational utility of visible and near-infrared imagery are limited due to the loss of brightness, gradients, and textures. Using the solar zenith angle, can we dynamically brighten satellite imagery to increase its operational utility? This presentation describes the development of a Solar Zenith Angle-Adjusted (SZA) imagery product, which applies a dynamic brightness adjustment to ABI reflectance factor values. SZA imagery was demonstrated with NWS forecasters in NOAA’s Hazardous Weather Testbed (HWT) and at the Storm Prediction Center. Based on forecaster feedback and numerical estimates, NWS forecasters in the conterminous United States can leverage an extra 60-90 minutes of reflectance factor imagery each day. Examples of SZA imagery applications and forecaster feedback will also be presented.

493745.title: Identifying Early Environmental Signals Associated with Severe Convective Storms
493745.authors: Weikang Qian, Unversity of Florida, Gainesville, FL; and Y. Wen
493745.abstract: Severe convective storms (SCSs) produce hazards such as tornadoes, large hail, and damaging winds that pose substantial risks to communities and infrastructure. Improving forecasts of these hazards requires a better understanding of how the atmospheric environment evolves before severe convection develops. SCS environments are commonly characterized using conventional diagnostics such as CAPE and vertical wind shear. Data-driven models can incorporate full radar and NWP fields, but their predictions often provide limited physical insight into the sequence of environmental changes that precedes severe convection. Consequently, the transition from synoptic-scale preconditioning several days in advance to mesoscale storm development remains incompletely characterized. This study examines how multilevel temperature, moisture, wind, and geopotential height fields evolve before, during, and after SCS events. We seek to determine when severe-event environments first become distinguishable from background variability, how these differences develop toward event onset. Spatially and temporally clustered tornado, hail, and thunderstorm-wind reports from the NOAA Storm Events Database are used to define event regions and times. Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor (MRMS) products characterize the intensity, spatial extent, and temporal evolution of the associated convection. Hourly High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) analyses provide pressure-level temperature, dewpoint, horizontal wind, and geopotential height, along with conventional diagnostics including CAPE, CIN, vertical wind shear, and storm-relative helicity. Each event is examined from 7 days before onset through 3 days afterward, providing a common window for analyzing environmental preconditioning, storm development, and post-event evolution. Temporal analysis is used to quantify how time-varying directional relationships among dominant vertical and spatial patterns change with lead time. Severe events are compared with less-severe convective cases and matched non-event periods while controlling for region, season, and time of day. The multilevel fields are also evaluated against conventional diagnostics to determine whether their evolution provides additional information for distinguishing severe events. The analysis will identify early environmental signals, determine when they become detectable.

493749.title: Not Enough Information? Predicting Intent to Revise Protective Decisions After Hurricane Ian
493749.authors: Robert Prestley, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Demuth, A. B. Schumacher, G. Wong-Parodi, R. E. Morss, N. Herbert, and M. Ng
493749.abstract: After a high-impact weather event like Hurricane Ian, it would make sense that those who were affected would reflect on their experiences, including the behaviors they did and did not take to mitigate harm, and think about whether they would make different decisions next time. Such decision revision intent, a form of counterfactual thinking, is closely tied to future decision-making in both the short-term and long-term, making it an important but under-theorized mechanism for understanding how individuals make decisions during and across hazardous weather events. We study decision revision intent through an online panel survey fielded several weeks after Hurricane Ian’s landfall, part of a broader longitudinal panel that surveyed the same participants three times before landfall in addition to this post-storm wave. Participants, drawn from YouGov’s panel, were located within 100 miles of the U.S. Gulf and Atlantic coasts from Mississippi to North Carolina. The revision-intent measure asked participants, in yes/no/not sure format, to reflect on their experiences during Ian and assess whether they would make each of six protective decisions differently next time. The decisions ranged from low-effort behaviors like gathering supplies and gassing up vehicles to high-effort behaviors like boarding up windows and doors or evacuating. We combined the revision intent measure with a parallel measure of self-reported action-taking for the same six decisions (collected on the post-storm survey) to construct a joint measure capturing the direction of revision intent, for example, distinguishing those who took an action and would revise it from those who did not act and would revise that choice. We then performed latent class analysis on this joint measure, which identified four classes. Two of the four - accounting for 65% of the sample - had near-identical rates of taking actions but differed sharply in their intent to revise those actions. In this presentation, we will focus on exploring this contrast in more depth, examining which pre-event and storm-related factors predict membership in the high-action, high-revision class relative to the high-action, low-revision class. These factors include the demographic and geographic composition of both groups, whether the two classes differed in the severity of impacts they experienced during Ian, and whether the classes sought out different types of information during the predictive phase of Hurricane Ian. Preliminary analyses show no association with information-seeking (by source or channel) or with the importance placed on different types of storm information. Instead, revision intent was predicted by race, income, and the severity of impacts experienced. This pattern suggests that the critical factors that influence decision revision intent are not communication failures or missing links in the prediction-to-decision pathway, but rather issues of constrained capacity to act. One potential exception: respondents who self-reported being affected by tornadoes, a hazard less often a part of individuals’ mental models of tropical cyclone impacts, also had higher membership in the high-action, high-revision class. This result may suggest that hazard-specific risk perception, rather than general communication volume, may be a relevant factor in post-event decision revision intent. By and large, however, these findings suggest that closing the gap between forecast and action may depend less on information design than on removing the material barriers that keep information from being actionable in the first place.

493759.title: Investigating Improvements in Subseasonal-to-Seasonal Streamflow Forecast Skill Using an Adaptive Probabilistic Precipitation Correction
493759.authors: Runze Li, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI; and M. Basirifard, S. Du, T. Yang, K. M. Dresback, C. Szpilka, and R. L. Kolar
493759.abstract: Flood-risk management, reservoir operations and drought preparedness depend on accurate subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) streamflow and precipitation forecasts. The skill of the streamflow forecasts depends on the precipitation ensembles; however, improvements in precipitation skill do not always translate to better streamflow predictions. Many efforts exist to postprocess the S2S precipitation forecasts; however, streamflow forecast skill remains poorly quantified from these improved precipitation probabilities. Herein, we utilized a machine-learning based adaptive probabilistic correction framework to update the S2S precipitation ensemble forecasts, which are then used to drive a process-based hydrologic model, Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting Model (SAC-SMA), over the contiguous United States (CONUS). In determining the corrected precipitation ensemble forecasts, we are calibrating the full predictive distribution rather than individual members or ensemble statistics. For the precipitation, the daily ECMWF S2S ensemble precipitation forecasts were calibrated against PRISM from the years of 2005-2024 and then used to force the SAC-SMA with the addition of the SNOW-17 model across the 511 CAMELS basin within the US. Additionally, the raw S2S precipitation forecasts were also utilized within the SAC-SMA/Snow-17 and compared to the results with the corrected precipitation forecasts. In these tests, all the other forcings were held fixed so we can isolate the hydrologic propagation of the skill of the improved precipitation forcing. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) results showed a 5.9% reduction at the grid scale (89.2% of cells improved) and by 6.6% after basin aggregation (94.7% of basins) for the precipitation with the corrected precipitation. After processing the precipitation through SAC-SMA model, the streamflow CPRS decreased by 5.6% (66.7% of basins). Additionally, these gains did not fade with lead time – by week 6 the mean reduction reached 6.6% (59.1% of basins still improved). The gains in the precipitation probability skill thus propagate effectively into the S2S streamflow predictions. Therefore, the adaptive probabilistic correction to the S2S precipitation provides a practical pathway towards more skillful forecasts, which can be utilized in flood-risk management, reservoir operations and drought preparedness.

493760.title: The Stratospheric Intrinsic Frequency Spectrum As a Superposition of Many Random Gravity Waves
493760.authors: Brian Green, Stanford University, Stanford, CA; and A. Podglajen and A. Sheshadri
493760.abstract: Time-average frequency spectra of super-pressure balloon motion have been shown to be broadly consistent with predictions from linear gravity wave theory. For example, the total wave energy is approximately equally split between potential and kinetic energy. Here, we find that time-varying frequency spectra of those same data depart significantly from this prediction, indicating interference between overlapping waves. In Concordiasi super-pressure balloon data from over the Southern Ocean and Antarctica, and in Strateole-2 data from over the tropics, variability in continuous wavelet transform spectra of the ratio of potential to total wave energy is consistent with the pattern of interference produced by a spectrum of steady, random, linear gravity waves. Much of the gravity wave amplitude variability (intermittency) in the data is also indistinguishable from the interference produced by steady, overlapping waves. By analyzing phase differences between balloon altitude and pressure data we find that, most of the time, the energy spectrum is approximately equally split between upward- and downward-propagating waves. The exception is for high-amplitude (> 80% quantile) waves, which propagate preferentially upward and are responsible for variability that cannot be explained by interference alone. Taken together, our results describe a stratospheric gravity wave field comprised of many random, quasi-steady, overlapping waves propagating both upward and downward, occasionally punctuated by large-amplitude upward-propagating waves.

493763.title: Ten Years of PROGRESS: What We’ve Learned About Mentoring and Belonging in the Geosciences
493763.authors: Melissa A. Burt, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and E. V. Fischer, S. Clinton, M. Estrada, M. Guajardo, P. Hernandez, L. Luo, and S. Schanz
493763.abstract: Despite the critical need to broaden participation in the geosciences, undergraduate women and students from minoritized groups continue to encounter barriers, including informational gatekeeping, limited access to effective mentorship, and challenges developing a sense of belonging. To address these barriers, we developed PROmoting Geoscience Research, Education, and SuccesS (PROGRESS), an NSF-supported program combining a professional development workshop with a longitudinal mentoring model. Over the last decade, PROGRESS has served multiple cohorts across U.S. regions and institution types. The one-day workshop emphasizes collaboration and community building while helping students identify and expand their mentoring and professional networks. Longitudinal surveys and interviews demonstrate that PROGRESS participation strengthens students’ science identity, sense of belonging, and persistence in the geosciences. Our research also highlights the importance of intentional mentor matching; connecting relationships grounded in shared undergraduate majors, gender identities, and disciplinary interests are more likely to be perceived by students as relevant and successful. Building on a decade of implementation and research, we have developed an evidence-based, adaptable, and comprehensive implementation guide. We will share key findings, lessons learned, and practical strategies for adapting the PROGRESS model to strengthen mentoring, belonging, and persistence across the geosciences.

493765.title: Drivers of North American Extratropical Cyclone Variability Across Timescales: Verification of the SPEAR Ensemble
493765.authors: Michael Igbinoba, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. R. McCrary, J. Stuivenvolt-Allen, S. McGinnis, and M. R. Tye
493765.abstract: Extratropical cyclones (ETCs) are a major source of cool-season hazardous weather across North America, yet their variability is strongly influenced by large-scale atmospheric and oceanic modes. This study evaluates how the El Nino–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), Pacific–North American pattern (PNA), and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) modulate North American ETC activity and assesses whether these relationships are reproduced by the 30-member GFDL SPEAR Large Ensemble relative to ERA5. Spectral analysis shows that SPEAR generally reproduces the dominant periodicities of ENSO, PNA, and NAO, although differences in spectral amplitude remain. SPEAR also captures the characteristic spatial structures of the PNA and NAO and the major North American storm-track corridors, while producing greater ETC track point densities than ERA5 in several regions. Composite analyses reveal particularly strong similarities between ENSO- and PNA-related storm-track responses, including a west-to-east redistribution of ETC activity across North America. In contrast, NAO-related variability is concentrated primarily at higher latitudes and over the North Atlantic. These results demonstrate that SPEAR reproduces many observed relationships between large-scale modes of variability and North American ETC activity whileexhibiting systematic differences in response magnitude and statistical robustness.

493766.title: Impacts of Fire Aerosol Absorption on Boundary-Layer Dynamics and Precipitation in E3SM (Invited Presentation)
493766.authors: Yan Feng, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, IL
493766.abstract: Absorbing aerosols from biomass burning perturb the atmospheric energy balance through atmospheric heating and surface dimming, with important consequences for atmospheric temperature structure, boundary-layer dynamics, convection, and precipitation. These initially localized perturbations may also interact with atmospheric and coupled-system feedbacks to produce responses over broader spatial and temporal scales. However, their representation remains uncertain in Earth system models because aerosol absorption depends strongly on the composition, mixing state, aging, and vertical distribution of carbonaceous aerosols. Recent developments in the U.S. Department of Energy’s Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SMv3) improve the representation of biomass-burning aerosol evolution and absorption. These developments include improved secondary organic aerosol aging and removal and a machine-learning representation of aerosol mixing state trained on particle-resolved simulations. Together, these improvements better reproduce observed aerosol evolution and reduce biases in the absorption of aged biomass-burning smoke. Building on these developments, we investigate how uncertainties in fire aerosol absorption propagate into atmospheric stability, boundary-layer dynamics, and precipitation, using North America as a regional testbed. We examine how aerosol-induced atmospheric heating and surface dimming alter vertical temperature structure, surface turbulent fluxes, PBL depth, and convective environments across different fire and meteorological regimes. We further place these regional responses in a global context by examining whether relationships between aerosol absorption, vertical distribution, and atmospheric stability are consistent across major biomass-burning regions. By connecting particle-scale representations of aerosol evolution and mixing state to regional atmospheric responses, this work provides a process-level framework for understanding how short-lived fire aerosol perturbations can influence atmospheric dynamics and precipitation across spatial and temporal scales, with implications for Earth system prediction.

493772.title: Advancing a Machine-Learning Tool for Identifying Hazardous Weather for Roadways
493772.authors: Andrew A. Rosenow, CIWRO - Cooperative Institute for Severe and High Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; and J. J. Gourley and J. A. Duarte
493772.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence and machine learning has created the opportunity to utilize existing datasets in new ways. As part of an ongoing effort supported by the Missouri Department of Transportation (MoDOT), a decision support system (DSS) is being developed aimed at detecting weather capable of causing roadway disruptions or closures. This DSS, the All-weather Road Impact Prediction System (ARIPS), is being built by pairing MoDOT records of weather-related road closures with meteorological data from the Multi Radar Multi Sensor (MRMS) system, static geographic and vulnerability data, and numerical model prediction forecasts. After analyzing MoDOT’s flash flood road closure database alongside those model predictors, a database of negative events was developed - times and locations where precipitation fell, but roads were likely not flooded, in order for the model to learn the difference between closures and non-closures. The methodology used to develop the negative events dataset using MRMS data will be described, including the challenges in creating a useful “no flood” dataset for training the ARIPS AI/ML model. The initial version of the model will be presented, and the parallel development of ARIPS’ winter weather DSS capability will be described, including the issues related to the winter road dataset when paired with meteorological data.

493773.title: Why Do Aerosol Reductions over North America and Europe Warm the Arctic More Than Larger Aerosol Reductions over East Asia?
493773.authors: Doyeon Kim, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada; and P. J. Kushner
493773.abstract: Why Do Aerosol Reductions over North America and Europe Warm the Arctic More Than Larger Aerosol Reductions over East Asia? Doyeon Kim1 and Paul J. Kushner1 1Department of Physics, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada Anthropogenic aerosol emissions are projected to decline substantially during the 21st century, yet the Arctic climate response depends strongly on the region of emission reduction. Using simulations from the Regional Aerosol Model Intercomparison Project (RAMIP), we show that aerosol reductions over North America and Europe (NAE) induce stronger Arctic warming than substantially larger reductions over East Asia (EAS). This contrasting response arises because the stronger loss of black carbon over EAS decreases atmospheric shortwave absorption, thereby suppressing atmospheric heating over the forcing region. Consequently, EAS drives weaker poleward latent energy transport into the Arctic, leading to smaller increases in Arctic atmospheric temperature and water vapor than NAE. Radiative kernel and Approximate Partial Radiative Perturbation (APRP) analyses reveal that this atmospheric warming and moistening enhances downward longwave radiation—the primary driver of the stronger Arctic surface warming. Ultimately, the Arctic response is governed by the net atmospheric energy balance determined by aerosol composition rather than the total magnitude of aerosol reductions, emphasizing the importance of both the geographical location and composition of aerosol reductions in shaping future Arctic warming.

493775.title: Interpretable AI-Optimized Analogs Reveal Oceanic Sources of Long-Lead Precipitation Predictability
493775.authors: Kinya Toride, NOAA, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and M. Newman, A. J. Hoell, and M. L. Breeden
493775.abstract: Seasonal precipitation forecasts provide critical information for managing climate-related risks, yet forecast skill remains limited at long lead times (>6 months), particularly outside the tropics. Here we introduce "AI-optimized analogs," an interpretable machine learning framework that learns spatially varying weights over initial ocean states to define the distance metric used for selecting analogs from climate model simulations. By learning these dynamic weights, the AI-Analog framework achieves skill comparable to the North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME) for ENSO and global precipitation, while providing significant skill gains in long-lead forecasts over extratropical land. These improvements are concentrated in seasons and events with strong predictable signals, particularly during strong ENSO years. The learned analog-selection weights emphasize the role of sea-surface temperature and sea-level structures in the tropical Pacific as key predictors of future precipitation. Regional weight perturbations demonstrate that Pacific information is necessary for these skill improvements and retains most of the full-weight gain, with broader Indo-Pacific information becoming increasingly important at longer lead times. Furthermore, across single-model analog libraries, larger skill improvements are associated with a more observation-consistent relationship between spring Pacific warm-water volume and subsequent winter precipitation, rather than the contemporaneous surface ENSO state alone. These results illustrate that interpretable AI-Analog can improve seasonal precipitation prediction, identify physically meaningful sources of predictability, and diagnose model-specific fidelity in representing oceanic precursors and their global impacts.

493778.title: Forecast-Driven Adaptive Tasking of a Microwave Sounder Constellation for Tropical Cyclone Observations
493778.authors: Kelly Patterson, Tomorrow.io, Golden, CO; and S. Gagnard and E. L. Nelson
493778.abstract: Tomorrow.io operates a commercial weather intelligence platform that integrates forecast, nowcast, and observational data for government and commercial decision support. A growing component of this observing system is the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) constellation: 6U CubeSats carrying passive microwave radiometers with 12 channels spanning W-band, temperature sounding channels near 118 GHz, and water vapor sounding channels near 183 GHz. These observations are designed to support precipitation analysis, nowcasting, and short- to medium-range forecasting, where both data value and latency are strongly dependent on when and where observations are collected and downlinked. This presentation describes an autonomous, adaptive tasking workflow that uses tropical cyclone forecast guidance to prioritize satellite observations of high-impact weather. These inputs identify areas with elevated likelihood of severe weather and provide a dynamic basis for observation prioritization. Opportunities for observation and other potential spacecraft activities are evaluated by a score-based mission planning algorithm that accounts for target priority, spacecraft availability, data latency, and near-term operational constraints, then used to construct a schedule according to the relative value of various activity components. Scheduled activities are re-evaluated as the forecast evolves, and may be shifted or cancelled to accommodate anticipated observation of significant cyclone events. The workflow leverages a distributed network of 23 ground stations to support frequent downlink opportunities and rapid tasking turnaround. An internal workflow engine and external vendor APIs are used autonomously to modify ground resource allocations, regenerate mission plans, and prepare updated tasking products for upload without human intervention. We will present the concept of operations, planning architecture, examples of priority storm overrides, and observed impacts on responsiveness for severe-weather collection opportunities. Finally, we discuss operational tradeoffs between downlink latency, observation value, contact availability, and constellation-level coverage. Future enhancements will incorporate more sophisticated optimization across orbit types, predicted revisit rates, and multiple spacecraft hardware platforms to balance rapid delivery with the scientific and operational value of each observation while maintaining a unified, highly automated tasking system.

493782.title: Preserving the Physical Structure of Regional Weather Extremes: A Hierarchical Evaluation of Machine Learning Downscaling over the United States
493782.authors: Sourav Taraphdar, PNNL, Richland, WA; and H. Tran, A. Gettelman, A. Geiss, C. Tebaldi, P. L. Ma, and N. Voisin
493782.abstract: High-resolution atmospheric information is essential for assessing severe weather event impacts, yet convection-permitting dynamical downscaling remains computationally expensive. Machine learning (ML) downscaling has emerged as a promising alternative; however, its applicability depends on whether it preserves the physical characteristics of the Earth system while reproducing long-term statistics. Here, we evaluate ML-based downscaling with a generative diffusion model, trained on dynamically downscaled mesoscale model simulations. We perform inference using large-scale historical weather patterns or synthetic emulated weather patterns and compare against another dynamically downscaled simulation and high-resolution observational datasets over the contiguous United States (CONUS) from 1980 to 2019. We adopt a hierarchical evaluation framework spanning mean state, seasonal variability, probability distributions, temperature and precipitation extremes, multivariate physical relationships, and temporal variability across various geographical regions over the CONUS. The ML products accurately reproduce the observed spatial patterns of precipitation and near-surface temperature and capture regional seasonal cycles and probability distributions with skill comparable to or exceeding the dynamical simulations. Extreme precipitation is realistically represented across most regions, although larger biases persist over the Pacific Northwest, where atmospheric rivers and complex topography dominate, and over the Great Plains, where mesoscale convective systems contribute to intense rainfall. Summer heat extremes are generally well represented but exhibit a coherent warm bias, whereas winter cold extremes show substantially improved agreement with observations relative to the dynamical simulations. Beyond reproducing the long-term statistics, the ML downscaling preserves the observed coupling among moisture, temperature, wind, and precipitation and realistically captures the dominant synoptic-to-mesoscale variability (2–16 days) governing extreme precipitation over the CONUS. These results demonstrate that physically consistent ML downscaling preserves the hierarchical organization of regional weather—from mean state and extremes to multivariate interactions and temporal variability—providing confidence in its application for regional Earth-energy impact and risk assessment, and next-generation Earth system modeling.

493790.title: Critical Roles of Fire and Soil Emissions in Trend Reversal of U.S. Air Quality
493790.authors: Jun Wang, Univ. of Iowa, Iowa City, IA
493790.abstract: Since the enactment of the Clean Air Act in the 1970s, tremendous progress has been made in improving surface air quality in the U.S. through regulatory policies that reduced anthropogenic emissions from power plants, transportation, and other industrial sources. However, the steady nationwide improvement observed up to around 2010 has recently faced dual challenges from non-regulatory emissions of wildfires and soils. By combining satellite data, atmospheric models, and surface observations with a machine-learning framework, we show that wildfire-driven increases in surface aerosol and ozone concentrations have reversed decades of air quality gains in the western U.S. over the past 15 years. Long-range transport of fire emissions has also contributed to stagnant or worsening air quality in parts of the central U.S. While wildfire emissions are episodic and often treated as exceptional events for compliance purposes, soil emissions are persistent during the growing season and have become an increasingly important factor in meeting the latest, more stringent air quality standards. For example, in regions such as California, we found that soil-derived NOx emissions may now account for up to one-third of surface ozone concentrations. Looking ahead, we argue that further improvements in air quality will likely depend on preventive strategies, including enhanced satellite monitoring, improved neighborhood-scale model predictions, and both regulatory and community-level initiatives, before a viable pathway toward meeting more stringent national air quality standards can be fully established.

493793.title: Tropospheric Brightening via Stratospheric Aerosols
493793.authors: Jake J. Gristey, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and G. Feingold and T. Yamaguchi
493793.abstract: Solar Radiation Management–the concept of intentionally increasing the amount of sunlight reflected back to space to cool the Earth–is receiving attention as a potential tool to alleviate the ongoing climate crisis. Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) and marine cloud brightening (MCB) are considered among the most viable approaches. In this presentation, we will show how SAI would cause substantial changes to cloud albedo without actively injecting aerosols into clouds as proposed by traditional MCB. Essentially, diffusion of the radiation field caused by stratospheric aerosols can result in sunlight entering clouds at steeper angles which increases cloud albedo, a mechanism we coin “diffusion-brightening” (Fig. 1). We will present idealized calculations to demonstrate that diffusion-brightening can lead to clouds reflecting up to 10% more of the incoming sunlight depending on stratospheric aerosol, cloud, and Sun conditions. We will also show that the top-of-atmosphere radiative effect from diffusion-brightening could exceed that from the reflection by stratospheric aerosols under many cloudy conditions, which has global relevance given that clouds cover around two-thirds of the planet. Steps toward global quantification of the diffusion-brightening effect and generalization to the cloud-free troposphere will be discussed. Fig. 1: Injecting particles into the stratosphere to deflect some of the incoming sunlight could also brighten marine clouds via the “diffusion-brightening” effect, thereby enhancing the overall cooling.

493803.title: What is a Snow Squall? What Eight Years of Snow Squall Warnings Tells Us.
493803.authors: Andrew A. Rosenow, CIWRO - Cooperative Institute for Severe and High Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK
493803.abstract: Snow squalls are short-fuse winter hazards with a quick onset of heavy snowfall. In response to the threat posed by snow squalls, the National Weather Service began issuing operational snow squall warnings in 2018. However, even to this day, there is not an accepted universal definition of a snow squall. The definition used for a snow squall warning is almost entirely qualitative, making it impossible to definitively declare whether or not events are snow squalls using that definition. To mitigate this problem, this talk presents analysis of the events that prompted snow squall warnings to better understand the underlying properties of the warned phenomena. Surface station observations within warnings show that the mean time to the minimum visibility is 23.2 min, but both inherent observation reporting interval and temporal averaging cause surface station observations to overestimate how long it actually takes to reach a given visibility during that sharp visibility drop. Composite model soundings were generated to show regional variability in snow squall environments, and the magnitude of the Banacos et al. (2014) snow squall parameter was also evaluated on a per-station basis. Finally, the perspective of a motorist experiencing a snow squall’s visibility drop is demonstrated with a case study, highlighting the requirement of making a mitigation decision in a minute or two when driving at highway speeds. Based on the results of this work, the rapid visibility drop is a defining characteristic of phenomena warned in an operational context, and that change in visibility represents a potential quantitative, testable, and verifiable way of defining a snow squall. Future work towards that goal is suggested.

493806.title: Rethinking Flash Drought: The Importance of State, Rate, and Timing
493806.authors: Lee Ellenburg, University of Alabama Huntsville, Huntsville, AL
493806.abstract: Flash drought has challenged how we think about drought onset and, more broadly, how we monitor drought. While traditional drought monitoring often focuses on the severity, rarity, or persistence of dry conditions, flash drought emphasizes two additional dimensions: how quickly conditions are changing and when that change occurs. Recent flash drought research in the southeastern United States demonstrates the importance of timing. A regional assessment from 2001–2023 found a distinct seasonal progression in flash drought occurrence. Importantly, drought occurrence alone does not determine impact. By coupling flash drought timing with crop development, the study showed that vulnerability varies substantially depending on whether rapid drought development coincides with sensitive growth stages. While demonstrated for agriculture, this concept extends to other time-sensitive sectors and systems where the same drought event may have very different consequences depending on when it occurs. Flash drought also raises broader questions about how we measure drought. The timescale over which change is evaluated, and the environmental stores or fluxes being monitored—from precipitation and soil moisture to evapotranspiration, vegetation, and streamflow—shape our interpretation of both drought severity and its rate of development. Shorter timescales may reveal rapid changes that are obscured within longer-term measures of storage, while longer timescales provide critical context for the underlying drought state. Rather than simply defining another category of drought, flash drought research provides an opportunity to rethink drought monitoring around state, rate, and timing: how dry the system is, how quickly it is changing, and when that change occurs. Together, these dimensions may provide a more complete and actionable picture of drought development and impacts.

493808.title: A Data-Driven Approach to Quantifying Forecast Uncertainty in HAFS and Understanding the Rapid Intensification and Rapid Weakening Phases of Hurricane Lee (2023)
493808.authors: Alex Alvin Cheung, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; and J. Poterjoy
493808.abstract: This study utilizes a data-driven approach to quantify forecast uncertainty in NOAA’s Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS). Here, the predictability of environmental conditions surrounding the storm and the quality of the model analysis state are considered. Using these considerations as predictors, a machine-learning model is developed to estimate forecast uncertainty during such events. Generally, the largest intensity errors are present near periods of rapid intensification (RI) and rapid weakening (RW). Prior to developing the machine-learning model, the RI and RW periods in Hurricane Lee (2023) are evaluated to identify potential predictors. Hurricane Lee was chosen because it was a uniquely challenging intensity forecast for most numerical models, including HAFS. From tropical cyclone genesis, Hurricane Lee rapidly intensified in a span of 66 h from 30 kt to a maximum lifetime intensity of 145 kt. Immediately after reaching its maximum lifetime intensity, Lee began to rapidly weaken for 42 h, until it reached a local minimum intensity of 85 kt. During the latter half of the weakening phase, Lee began to develop a secondary eyewall and underwent multiple secondary eyewall formations (SEFs) and eyewall replacement cycles before its extratropical transition. The combination of RI, RW, and structural changes in the TC eyewall contributed to extreme errors at certain valid times between the HAFS forecast intensities and the best-track intensity, ranging from an underprediction of 81 kt during RI to an overprediction of 65 kt during RW. During the SEF period, the forecasted intensity in HAFS generally remained an overprediction. In terms of environmental conditions, the Statistical Hurricane Intensity Prediction Scheme analysis indicates that shear was moderate (10–20 kt) for the first 36 h of RI, then became weak (< 10 kt) for the last 30 h. During and subsequent to RW, the shear became moderate once again, and remained so until extratropical transition. HAFS was able to generally capture this analyzed shear evolution throughout the lifecycle of Lee. This indicates that other errors in the model, such as in the wind or precipitation fields, could be responsible for the intensity forecast errors. To assess this, we will compare the HAFS model output to various observational datasets such as synthetic aperture radar, tail-Doppler radar, and satellite-derived precipitation estimates. The comparison will be performed at three critical times: 1) the extreme underpredictions during RI, 2) the extreme overpredictions during RW, and 3) the SEF period.

493810.title: Turbulence Trends from Climate Change: A Review of the Evidence
493810.authors: Paul D. Williams, University of Reading, Reading, United Kingdom; and L. Storer, M. Prosser, I. Smith, S. Lee, and J. D. Medeiros
493810.abstract: Increased turbulence is an important but under-appreciated consequence of anthropogenic climate change for aviation. This review presentation synthesises observational, reanalysis, and climate-model evidence for changes in atmospheric turbulence, with particular emphasis on the physical mechanisms linking greenhouse-gas forcing to changes in cruising-level wind shear, atmospheric stability, and turbulence production. Early modelling studies demonstrated that climate change could substantially increase clear-air turbulence (CAT) by modifying the jet streams and the conditions favourable for shear instability. More recently, observational evidence has emerged that these projected changes are already detectable. Analysis of four decades of atmospheric reanalysis data found large increases in diagnosed CAT since 1979, including a 55% increase in severe CAT over the North Atlantic, with significant increases also identified over other major aviation regions. These findings provide an important observation-based complement to earlier climate projections and strengthen the case for a detectable climate-change signal in aviation turbulence. The physical basis for these changes is examined in more detail through a recent analysis of upper-atmospheric wind shear. Climate-model projections indicate that vertical wind shear at typical aircraft cruising altitudes will increase substantially under continued warming, with multi-model simulations indicating increases in annual-mean strength of approximately 16–27% between 2015 and 2100. Over the same time period, the Brunt–Väisälä frequency is projected to decrease by 10–20%. The combination of enhanced shear and reduced hydrostatic stability decreases the Richardson number and creates conditions increasingly favourable for shear instability and CAT formation. Taken together, the above evidence indicates a coherent chain from greenhouse-gas forcing, through changes in jet-stream structure and upper-level shear, to increasing turbulence risk. Future projections suggest that severe CAT could become approximately two to three times more frequent on some flight routes later this century. Emerging evidence points to increases in near-cloud turbulence and mountain-wave turbulence too. The implications extend beyond passenger comfort, encompassing aviation safety, operational efficiency, aircraft design, and turbulence detection and forecasting.

493813.title: Measuring What We Can't See from Space: Heterogeneity in NO2 Pollution under Cloudy Skies
493813.authors: Rachel H. Mooers, Boston University, Boston, MA; and J. A. Geddes, C. Naughton, A. Pandey, B. Place, G. Gonzalez Abad, and N. Lombel
493813.abstract: Remote sensing of nitrogen dioxide (NO2), a prevalent and harmful urban air pollutant, can provide insights regarding its heterogeneity. We leverage the remote sensing capabilities of ground-based Pandora spectrometers and the geostationary TEMPO satellite to detect the influence of meteorology on NO2 heterogeneity. We developed a custom Pandora spectrometer methodology which measures NO2 in multiple directions around each of four sites in the Greater Boston area every hour. This methodology yielded high-quality, scientifically-valuable data, showing how NO2 hotspots move around and change hour-to-hour. We found that meteorology was a major driver of NO2 heterogeneity, with easterly and sea breeze winds resulting in an accumulation of NO2 over Boston whereas westerlies tend to vent pollution over the ocean. Furthermore, our experiment was used to understand whether TEMPO is performing well at observing hourly changes in urban NO2. The satellite is capable of observing the same changes we measured, however, our experiment has advantages over satellite observations by themselves. For example, we found that a bias in NO2 under cloudy versus clear conditions is present in Boston, driven by coastal meteorology. Easterly winds are associated with elevated NO2 concentrations but also clouds, causing satellites such as TEMPO to miss important pollution events. Previous work (Geddes et al., 2012; Goldberg et al., 2025) has corroborated that NO2 tends to be higher under cloudy versus clear skies. This bias presents a challenge for satellite remote sensing, which cannot observe NO2 underneath clouds. Our Pandora experiment can circumvent this limitation, providing observations of NO2 spatial heterogeneity even when clouds are present. Here, we present findings of NO2 heterogeneity in Boston as observed from our Pandora experiment and TEMPO, as well as leverage our experiment to fill gaps in the TEMPO record under cloudy skies.

493815.title: A High-Resolution Radar-Based Hail Climatology for the CONUS
493815.authors: Jacob Widanski, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and B. A. Schenkel, T. J. Galarneau, and C. J. Nixon
493815.abstract: Climatological analyses of hail enable quantitative assessments of hail risk, leading to improved awareness and preparedness that can mitigate the substantial hail-induced economic losses arising annually in the United States. While radar-based methods remedy the coverage and magnitude biases of report-based climatologies via gridded objective hail proxies, prior studies often applied them on coarse 80-km horizontal grids, obscuring more localized features. Additionally, existing literature largely overlooks sub-severe hail (<25.4 mm) despite notable impacts such as reducing the longevity and resiliency of common roofing material (i.e., asphalt shingles) with recurring exposure (Meisenzahl et al. 2025). Moreover, common gridded reflectivity-based products such as the Maximum Estimated Size of Hail (MESH) are severely limited in accuracy, and finer storm-scale details such as the length, width, direction, and longevity of hail swaths have yet to be robustly assessed. Using high-resolution (1-km) radar data from the Multi-Year Reanalysis of Remotely Sensed Storms (MYRORSS) and Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) archives, a multi-decadal gridded and object-based climatology for sub-severe (≥6.35 mm) and severe (≥25.4 mm) hail will be constructed over the contiguous United States (CONUS). Climatologies from MRMS MESH and a novel object-based machine learning algorithm utilizing MRMS and ERA5 fields will be compared. While the upscaled (80-km) analysis reveals similar spatiotemporal patterns as existing climatologies (e.g., a broad annual frequency maximum across the Great Plains shifting poleward over time during the spring and summer months), the fine MESH grid and hail swath objects provide spatiotemporal details otherwise not observed from coarser gridded climatologies (e.g., local terrain-following frequency maxima earlier in the afternoon). Moreover, notable shifts in the spatiotemporal patterns between sub-severe and severe hail exist (e.g., eastward shift of sub-severe maximum later at night in the central Plains), revealing broader patterns regarding storm mode and near-storm environments.

493820.title: Evaluation of Surface Downward Shortwave Irradiance Using the GLQ Method for Overcast Skies at the Southern Great Plains Site
493820.authors: Jordann Brendecke, Univ. of Arizona, Tucson, CO; and X. Dong, B. Xi, H. Barker, M. Li, and P. Pilewskie
493820.abstract: Quantifying the surface energy budget is vital to understanding the Earth's energy system. However, satellites are unable to directly observe downward and upward surface irradiance, leading to larger uncertainties compared to top-of-atmosphere (TOA) irradiances. Consequently, radiation transfer models (RTMs) are needed to determine global estimates of surface irradiance. While RTMs provide valuable information, they require significant computational resources for accurate global results. As a result, global gridded runs are typically performed at a 1° 1° resolution. Clouds, however, dominate the atmospheric conditions regulating solar energy and vary substantially over a 1° grid. Due to the nonlinear effects of cloud-radiation interactions, using averaged cloud properties does not produce accurate results. This study builds upon the work of Barker and Li (2018), which applies the Gaussian-Legendre quadrature (GLQ) method to liquid water paths to estimate surface irradiance. Comparing different Legendre points to the Independent Column Approximation (ICA), Li and Barker demonstrated a reduction in RTM calculation error from 2.8% to 0.11% when increasing from one to three Legendre points. This work extends the approach of Li and Barker (2018) by applying the method to satellite-retrieved data. The GLQ method is implemented over the Southern Great Plains (SGP) site using VIIRS cloud properties. More than 15 years of data are analyzed to identify overcast liquid clouds and compare them with surface site observations. The SGP site serves as an ideal test location because seven surface measurement sites are located within its 1° grid box, helping to better account for spatial variability. The ICA is also used to benchmark calculations against one, two, three, and five Legendre points. Results show the greatest improvement when moving from one to two Legendre points, with minimal differences observed between three and five Legendre points. Increased accuracy is also achieved when compared against observed surface irradiance. Overall, the findings demonstrate how high-accuracy surface irradiance calculations can be obtained with only a limited increase in computational cost.

493826.title: Machine Learning Coastal Compound Flooding Predictions for Corpus Christi, Texas
493826.authors: Felix Fuentes III, Texas A&M Univ.-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX; and P. E. Tissot and M. Vicens-Miquel
493826.abstract: With relative sea level rise, coastal communities are at increased risk of coastal flooding. As infrastructure height above sea levels decreases, it is becoming very important to include other drivers of coastal flooding models such as precipitation, river runoff and groundwater. Oso Creek, located near Corpus Christi, Texas, within the Oso Creek watershed, is prone to such compound flooding caused by the combined effects of heavy precipitation and tidal influences from Corpus Christi Bay. Traditional prediction systems often struggle to capture these interacting drivers, which motivates data-driven approaches. This study presents a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) forecasting model intended for operational use. The MLP is implemented in TensorFlow with architecture search using KerasTuner and optimization with the Adam optimizer. A custom loss function was developed to improve model skill, with particular emphasis on accurately forecasting large water level increases associated with heavy precipitation events. To enable forecasting, we include inputs such as High Resolution Rapid Refresh quantitative precipitation forecasts (HRRR QPF), ingested each hour and organized into fixed lead times from 1 to 15 hours. These operational predictions are combined with environmental time series: hourly precipitation from NOAA’s Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system over the Oso Creek watershed, primary water levels from two Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON) stations, and Oso Creek air gap measurements from a Conrad Blucher Institute sensor. HRRR QPF is clipped to the watershed and summarized as an area weighted average, creating consistent lead aware features for a data range of February 2015 through March 2021. The model forecasts Oso Creek water level at leads up to 15 hours. We will present forecast performance across lead times with an emphasis on accuracy and reliability. Integration of the HRRR predictions was challenging as significant precipitation is rare for this watershed, leading to slight decrease in overall performance when considering the full data set. However, results show that including the HRRR predictions as input to the model improves performance over baseline during the rain events themselves when the model is most needed. Benefits from the implementation of this compound flooding model include providing longer lead times to warn the community and better overall risk communication for the surrounding area impacted during Oso Creek overflowing events. The workflow is portable and can generalize to other coastal watersheds that face compound flood risk.

493829.title: Data-Driven Flux Parameterization for the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
493829.authors: Abed Hammoud, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; Princeton Univ., Princeton, NJ; and E. S. Titi, M. Bushuk, M. Calaf, K. Ghannam, and E. Bou-Zeid
493829.abstract: Turbulent fluxes in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) govern the exchange of momentum, heat, and mass between the surface and the atmosphere, thereby shaping the vertical structure of the ABL and influencing a wide range of engineering applications and atmospheric processes. Accurate parameterization of these fluxes in coarse resolution weather and climate models remains challenging, particularly under unstable conditions where flux transport is strongly nonlocal and under stable conditions where turbulence may become intermittent and partially decoupled from surface forcing. Traditional schemes generally prescribe fixed functional forms and empirical coefficients, which can limit their ability to represent changing transport mechanisms across stability regimes. Meanwhile, more flexible machine learning closures often sacrifice physical interpretability. In this study, we develop a data-driven parameterization of turbulent fluxes using a novel formulation in which nondimensional fluxes are represented as a convolution operation acting on the relevant nondimensional mean state profiles. A comprehensive high-resolution large eddy simulation (LES) dataset is generated for idealized flow over homogeneous surfaces across a range of stability conditions. We derive and test several first-order versions of this convolution flux parameterization, each based on different combinations of inputs, that map mean temperature and velocity profiles to heat and momentum fluxes. The results indicate that the proposed method improves predictive skill relative to a standard K-profile parameterization (KPP) benchmark. The present framework learns flux-profile relationships as operators constrained by the governing column dynamics, enabling the inferred operator kernels to reveal the spatial organization, locality, and nonlocality of turbulent transport across stability regimes. The resulting parameterization performs strongly across diverse stability conditions, and tests successfully in a posteriori single column model simulations, yielding state profiles that agree closely with the LES data. These findings suggest that data-informed operator closures can relax restrictive assumptions embedded in traditional closure schemes while providing a data-driven approach for transparent parameterizations.

493832.title: Adapt: A Real-Time, Open Source Framework to Drive Adaptive Radar Scanning and Convection Tracking
493832.authors: Siddhant Gupta, ; and B. A. Raut, R. C. Jackson, Z. Sherman, J. R. O'Brien, E. Schuman, P. Lech, S. Beus, S. Abernethy, S. Collis, N. L. Hickmon, and A. Theisen
493832.abstract: The U.S. Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility has produced an open-source, real-time convective feature identification system called Adapt to drive adaptive radar scanning. Typical radar scanning strategies for operational and research radars employ a fixed set of sweeps with consistent spatial coverage that are reproducible without human intervention. The temporal resolution can be too coarse to investigate dynamical and microphysical processes within rapidly evolving convective features. Therefore, adaptive scanning, wherein the radar scanning adapts to real-time meteorological observations from external datasets, is becoming an important tool for studying the lifecycle evolution of convection at high temporal resolution. Adapt is a reproducible and modular framework for adaptively scanning and analyzing the storm lifecycle. Adapt executes a configurable end-to-end analysis pipeline, integrating radar data ingestion, convective cell identification, motion estimation and projection, tracking, and lifecycle characterization. Adapt operates this processing chain in real-time and on historical data. The tracking system preserves events, including splitting, merging, and cell connectivity, and maintains reproducible storm IDs. A structured repository of outputs allows API-like queries for properties of tracked storms (e.g., size, intensity, echo-top heights, volumetric structure, and polarimetric signatures). Post-processing modules also associate observations from satellites, Lightning Mapping Arrays (LMAs), and other radars with tracked storm cells, enabling multi-sensor analysis of storm evolution. In this study, we demonstrate results from first-use cases of Adapt being used to drive adaptive scanning for the 2nd Generation C-band Scanning ARM Precipitation Radar (CSAPR2) at the Bankhead National Forest (BNF) in Alabama, USA. The high-fidelity radar retrievals will be used to address how the atmospheric thermodynamics, biogenic and anthropogenic aerosol emissions, and surface heterogeneity in Northern Alabama, marked by an urban-to-forest canopy corridor, influence the evolution of isolated convective cells as they propagate across the radar domain. Adapt will use rules-based criteria to select scan targets from the NEXRAD field and track isolated convective cells as they move across the urban-to-forest canopy corridor. This shows how Adapt can bridge the gap between raw radar data ingestion and real-time decision making to steer radar scanning.

493837.title: The Persistent Importance of Scientific Expertise in Sustaining the NSF-NOAA's GONG Project
493837.authors: Sushanta Chandra Tripathy, National Solar Observatory, Boulder, CO; National Solar Observatory, Boulder, CO; and L. Bertello, S. Gusain, A. Hamada, K. Jain, S. Kholikov, R. Komm, B. Lekshmi, G. Petrie, and A. A. Pevtsov
493837.abstract: The US National Science Foundation-National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG) provides continuous, full-disk solar observations (e.g. Doppler velocity, magnetic field, H-alpha and white-light intensity) using mature data processing pipelines. Even with the availability of well established pipelines, scientific expertise remains crucial to GONG operations—monitoring data quality, resolving unexpected anomalies, and updating analysis methods- to meet evolving operational and research needs. Furthermore, maintaining a reliable, consistent distributed network requires seamless collaboration between scientists and operation teams, especially during hardware repairs and upgrades that could disrupt data continuity. Furthermore, scientists drive the scientific value of GONG by developing new data products for space weather and a broad range of solar physics applications. In this presentation, we highlight key examples showing why ongoing scientific involvement is essential not only for maintaining the quality and reliability of GONG data, but also for preserving data integrity and unlocking GONG's full potential.

493838.title: Eye-Eyewall ‘Misovortices’ in a Rapidly-Intensifying Hurricane: Insights from 2D-4D Visualizations of a 222-meter, 0.3 Hertz Large Eddy Simulation
493838.authors: Michael Igbinoba, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and C. M. Rozoff and E. A. Hendricks
493838.abstract: Eyewall boundary-layer turbulence in mature hurricanes is strongly anisotropic within the intensely sheared flow surrounding the radius of maximum wind (RMW). The three-dimensional dynamical instabilities that arise from this configuration have been found to be favorable for the growth of coherent, energetic structures of cyclonically rotating turbulence at approximately 0.65–0.90 times the RMW diagnosed at 2 km AGL. This organized turbulence, often described dynamically as eyewall misovortices and visually associated with finger-like cloud features by recent literature, has horizontal scales on the order of a few kilometers and partially explains extreme gusts within the eyewall environment. The structures have been examined in literature through the lens of observations and modelling frameworks, and thus several hypotheses for their genesis, growth, and decay have been developed. However, few studies have examined the full three-dimensional characteristics of these vortices in time with sufficient resolution. We use the Weather Research and Forecasting model to simulate an idealized, rapidly intensifying hurricane reaching major-hurricane intensity, selecting a 20-minute period that encompasses the approximate lifetime of these vortical structures. The simulation employs 222-m horizontal grid spacing, 35-m vertical spacing within the lowest 1 km AGL, and 3-s output during the analysis period. This configuration permits kilometer-scale vortical structures to be explicitly resolved while sampling their evolution on timescales much shorter than their characteristic lifetimes. As in other small-scale atmospheric vortices, tilting of horizontal vorticity into the vertical contributes to the generation of cyclonic vertical vorticity, which is subsequently amplified through stretching; the 3-s output enables four-dimensional visualization of these processes throughout the vortex life cycle. We further examine their influence on the surrounding thermodynamic, microphysical, and kinematic fields and their potential contribution to three-dimensional mixing across the eye–eyewall interface.

493846.title: Multi-Modal Measurements of Sustained Emissions from Horizontally Propagating Leaders with a Low-Cost Commercial Off-the-Shelf (COTS) Detection System
493846.authors: Michael J. Peterson, Georgia Tech Research Institute, Smyrna, GA; and J. Burke
493846.abstract: Rare forms of lightning such as Transient Luminous Events (TLEs) and extreme flashes such as megaflashes are challenging to study due to the scarcity of research-grade observations that capture these events as they occur. The number of available observations is limited by multiple barriers to entry for citizen science, including hardware costs and technical complexity. The Raspberry Pi ecosystem is an attractive option to mitigate these barriers to entry. Hardware components are inexpensive and open-source software can be developed around different sensing strategies or targets. Where custom sensor components are needed, they can be created with 3D-printed parts now that makerspaces have become ubiquitous. Pre-planning, pre-developing, and pre-testing sensor hardware are key to making lightning chasing accessible to students, citizen scientists, and anyone limited by budget or available time. We have developed multiple iterations of lightning detectors around this vision since approximately 2014. To demonstrate the scientific value of one such system, we present joint optical and radio-frequency measurements of a lightning flash detected by the Geostationary Lightning Mapper that produced sustained optical emission resembling Continuing Current (CC), associated with the lateral expansion of a horizontal leader propagating along the cloud base.

493851.title: Seasonal Mountain Traffic Prediction In Colorado Using Basic Weather Data
493851.authors: Alex Alvin Cheung, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD
493851.abstract: In this study, basic daily weather data, such as temperature, precipitation, and snowfall, are used to predict traffic volume along the I-70 corridor in Colorado. Mountain congestion in Colorado, primarily due to outdoor recreational demand, is a serious consideration for travelers year-round. Traffic flow along several bottlenecks, such as the Eisenhower-Johnson Tunnels, Vail Pass, Floyd Pass, and Glenwood Canyon, is extremely sensitive to weather conditions. Here, a random forest model is trained to predict traffic volume at the Eisenhower Tunnel using daily weather data from a nearby weather station (Georgetown) obtained from the Colorado Climate Center. The traffic data is obtained from the Online Transportation Information System managed by the Colorado Department of Transportation. In the traffic data, two yearly local maxima in traffic volume exist: a summer peak around the end of July, and a ski season plateau that persists between January and March. On a day-to-day basis, traffic volume is dominated by the day of the week, with weekends yielding the highest traffic volumes, regardless of weather conditions. However, if the model is trained using a 30-day rolling mean of both the traffic data and weather data, a seasonal relationship exists between the two. The model is generally able to predict the winter and summer seasonal maxima in traffic volume, albeit slightly underpredicted. Among model feature importances, the 30-day rolling average of daily maximum temperature is the most important variable, followed by the day of year. Variables such as precipitation, minimum temperature, and surprisingly, snowfall, are less important. In the summer, the higher the daily maximum temperature, the greater the traffic volume. In the winter, a lower maximum temperature indicates higher traffic volume; however, some spread exists in traffic volume once the daily maximum temperature is below 50 F. This may be because during the shoulder seasons, more ski resorts operate in the spring, but not the fall. Further work in this model, such as incorporating future weather conditions, could help predict seasonal traffic demand along the I-70 corridor. Implications of this project include a traffic prediction model that can aid ski resorts in predicting future crowd volumes and planning for transportation partners, such as roadwork scheduling during low-traffic-volume seasons.

493856.title: An Introduction to FulminoSat – Ionospheric Measurement through Multi-Modal Detection of Lightning Signals of Opportunity
493856.authors: Michael J. Peterson, Georgia Tech Research Institute, Smryna, GA; and L. Boggs, M. Cohen, E. G. Lightsey, M. Birch, K. Prussing, and R. Warner
493856.abstract: Critical technologies—including radio communications, satellite positioning, and long-range radar—suffer performance degradation when their signals are distorted by the ionosphere's magneto-ionized plasma. Our ability to identify and correct for these distortions is limited by our knowledge of the electron density structure of the ionosphere across the globe and across scales. The availability and resolution of ionospheric measurements varies drastically from well-sampled regions on land to sparsely-sampled regions such as the open ocean. We can augment ionospheric measurements by recording trans-ionospheric radio signals of opportunity. These emitters are usually manmade, such as GNSS signals used in Radio Occultation (RO) measurements. Lightning-generated radio signals complement existing techniques by providing frequent, broadband measurements along flexible propagation paths worldwide, accessing ionospheric regions and structural scales unavailable to fixed transmitter-receiver systems. We present FulminoSat as a distributed radio-frequency (RF) and electro-optical / infrared (EO-IR) remote sensing concept to measure the ionosphere through wideband sensing of these signals of opportunity. Initial orbital simulations and progress on our on end-to-end system modeling and system design will be discussed, as well as measurement constraints, and remote sensing opportunities both within heliophysics and cross-cutting between disciplines.

493858.title: Enhancing Short-Range Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts for Flood Prediction Using a Generative Diffusion Nowcasting System
493858.authors: Stevenray Janke, Dewberry, Tucker, GA; and A. H. Dietrich and S. Lawler
493858.abstract: Quantitative precipitation forecast (QPF) error is a major source of uncertainty in operational flood forecasting.
