Hydrologic models used for flash-flood prediction are highly sensitive to the timing, placement, and intensity of rainfall forcing, yet convection-allowing NWP models such as the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) can exhibit substantial errors during the first several forecast hours. Model spin-up, convective initiation errors, and storm displacement degrade basin-scale rainfall estimates during the window when accurate forecasts are most consequential for warning dissemination and emergency response. Radar extrapolation techniques provide useful skill at very short leads (<60 minutes), but decrease rapidly as storms grow, decay, and reorganize. We present a generative nowcasting system based on the Elucidated Diffusion Model (EDM) framework and adapted from the proven architecture of NVIDIA’s Stormscope (Pathak et al., 2026). The system is configured over an approximately 600-km-wide domain centered on the Dallas–Fort Worth Metroplex at 3-km grid spacing. It consists of two coupled components: a satellite model that forecasts selected Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) Advanced Baseline Imager channels and a radar model conditioned on the satellite forecast. Each component uses two expert networks that operate at different stages of the diffusion process. At high noise levels, when the forecast field is still mostly unstructured, one expert learns the broad storm pattern and large-scale organization. At lower noise levels, after the general storm structure has emerged, a second expert focuses on refining smaller features such as convective cells and intense rainfall cores. This division allows the system to represent both large-scale storm evolution and the fine-scale details that are important for heavy-rainfall prediction. The models are also conditioned on the previous hour of observations, along with spatial location and time of day. Applying this architecture to a regional domain rather than the continental United States substantially reduces the computational cost of training and inference. The complete system can run on a single consumer GPU and is efficient enough to generate an ensemble of forecasts from the same initial conditions. These ensemble members sample multiple plausible storm evolutions and provide information about forecast uncertainty rather than only a single deterministic solution. Training uses a multi-year archive of NOAA's MRMS (Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor) national radar mosaic and GOES geostationary satellite observations. Critically, the radar model predicts precipitation rate directly as its primary output rather than forecasting reflectivity (dBZ) and converting it afterward. Radar nowcasting systems typically target composite reflectivity, which must then be mapped to rainfall through a Z–R relationship, a well-documented error source in hydrologic applications. The conversion follows a power law, so modest errors in dBZ become large errors in rain rate, and the error grows at the high intensities that drive flooding. MRMS mitigates this by using dual-polarization data and precipitation-type classification, so training on the MRMS rate product embeds that retrieval in the forecast itself and produces the variable most useful for hydrologic model input. The system is verified against gauge-corrected MRMS Pass2 Quantitative Precipitation Estimates over independent precipitation events withheld from training, using hourly accumulation windows initialized at the top of the hour and compared against operationally available HRRR forecasts at realistic data latency. Across accumulation thresholds, the nowcasting system substantially outperforms HRRR in the first forecast hour, with large gains in critical success index and fractions skill score and a corresponding reduction in RMSE. Advantages are largest at the heavier thresholds most relevant to flash flooding, and persist through the second forecast hour before converging toward NWP skill. The sub-basin response times that govern urban flash flooding are comparable to the lead times at which NWP skill is weakest, so improvements concentrated in the first two forecast hours translate directly into improved flood guidance. Sharper, more accurate rainfall forcing narrows the timing and location errors that carry downstream into predictions of peak water level and flood extent, and sub-hourly rate output provides both the variable and the temporal resolution that hydrologic models are built to ingest. Because the system is relatively computationally cheap, forecasts cost little to produce and can be refreshed as new observations arrive, keeping guidance current as a storm evolves. The resulting forecast product is being integrated into North Central Texas Council of Governments’ Stormwater Integrated Flood Forecasting Tool (SWIFT), where it is intended to support earlier and more confident decisions on road closures, warning issuance, and emergency response across a densely urbanized region prone to flash flooding.

493860.title: Improvements to and Performance of the Automated Real Time Unified Surface Wind Analysis (USWA) Product in the 2026 Hurricane Season
493860.authors: Katherine Sinclair Maclay Schwartz, CIRA, Cottage Grove, OR; and T. Tsukada, A. J. DesRosiers, K. Musgrave, J. Knaff, and M. DeMaria
493860.abstract: Tropical cyclone surface winds contribute both to wind and storm surge hazards, and their accurate estimation is vital for operational forecasting. The Unified Surface Wind Analysis (USWA; DesRosiers et al. 2026) product gathers and synthesizes data from the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere’s (CIRA) experimental multi-platform satellite-based SWA (MTCSWA; Knaff et al. 2011) product and an aircraft-based SWA (ACSWA; Knaff and Slocum, 2024) product with the addition of wind vectors from tail Doppler radar (TDR) and wind speeds from synthetic aperture radar (SAR) to provide automated, real-time analyses. The analyses provide surface wind fields with both inner-core and outer-core coverage. A variational fitting scheme is utilized to fill data sparse regions and individual observations are weighted based on quality and quantity. All observations are adjusted to a common flight level (700 hPa) for the analysis using a parametric adjustment, which is then reduced to 10 m for the final product. The Global Forecast System (GFS) forecasted wind field is used as the first guess field for the product. Based on USWA performance in the 2024 and 2025 seasons, there is a strong connection between the storm intensity and the accuracy of the product relative to best track estimates across all of the wind metrics (intensity, radius of maximum wind, and significant wind radii estimates). The presence of select data sets in a given analysis can also affect the accuracy of the different metrics. To assist in interpreting the USWA-derived wind metrics we have developed and added uncertainty estimates to the product. Furthermore, we are testing the addition of ultra high resolution ASCAT data and the use of Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) forecast fields instead of the GFS forecast fields for the first guess. The first guess fields are constructed from the inner, 2-km resolution moving nest. The performance of these test USWA products will be shown demonstrating future applicability to the real-time product. Previous study of the impacts of the addition of small Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (sUAS) data to the USWA product in the 2024 and 2025 seasons showed improvements particularly for radius of maximum wind estimates. Depending on the availability of data, the results of sUAS data for the 2026 season might also be shown to better understand the influence of this novel data in the USWA product metrics. Disclaimer: The scientific results and conclusions, as well as any views or opinions expressed herein, are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect those of NOAA or the Department of Commerce.

493861.title: Studying the Impact of Local Emissions on Ozone In Salt Lake City Using WRF-Chem
493861.authors: Audrey Gaudel, CIRES University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and M. Li, R. H. Schwantes, C. Harkins, M. M. Coggon, K. Bates, C. Stockwell, C. Warneke, J. Gilman, V. A. Treadaway, A. Rollins, E. Waxman, K. Zuraski, W. S. Chace, I. B. Pollack, N. Schafer, J. Peischl, B. C. McDonald, S. S. Brown, and C. Womack
493861.abstract: Northern Utah regularly experiences exceedances of the National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) for 8-hour ozone (O3) concentrations in the summer. The past two decades have seen continually decreasing precursor emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx = NO + NO2) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) due to improvements in technology and statewide emission reductions. However, the decrease in O3 exceedances has largely stagnated over the past decade, due in part to the non-linear and complex nature of O3 formation. To help answer questions related to this complex chemistry, the NOAA Utah Summer Ozone Study (USOS) occurred in the summer 2024 where ozone, NOx and VOCs were intensively measured between July 15 and August 18. We used this rich dataset along with satellite data from TROPOMI and TEMPO to tailor the GReenhouse gas And Air Pollutant Emissions System (GRA2PES) anthropogenic emission inventory used in the 3D chemistry transport model WRF-Chem to the Salt Lake City metro area. We quantified ozone variability due to reduced NOX and VOCs emissions scenario in Salt Lake City. In particular, we focused on emissions related to the copper mine activity in the southwest of the city, the on-road gasoline and diesel sector, as well as the cooking and volatile chemical products (VCP) emissions.

493865.title: Withdrawn: Curating Effective Severe Weather Communication for Non-Traditional Responders Using the Warn-On-Forecast System
493865.authors: Jackson Augustus Shumaker, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and J. E. Trujillo-Falcón, S. R. Ernst, and A. A. Taylor
493865.abstract: One of the key gaps in communicating convective hazard forecasts is in the watch-to-warning timeframe, the 30-minute to 4-hour period ahead of a storm’s arrival that sits between a National Weather Service (NWS) watch and warning. Effective communication of convective hazard information to end users during this gap is crucial to aid in protective action decision-making. Prior research has investigated how core partners of the NWS (e.g., emergency managers and broadcast meteorologists) as well as members of the public at-large make severe weather safety decisions during this timeframe. In this study, however, we focus on a specific group of non-traditional decision-makers that forecasts in the watch-to-warning timeframe would readily benefit: “designated decision-makers,” who we have defined as members of the public who are not traditional partners of the NWS, but whose role in their community makes them a potential critical link in the severe weather communication chain. These designated decision-makers include school principals, hospital managers, and large event coordinators. A key source of forecast information in the watch-to-warning gap is the Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS), a model ensemble developed by the NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory that is designed to provide high resolution and rapidly updating uncertainty information for mesoscale convective hazards. Using WoFS’ ensemble of forecasts, operational meteorologists foresee extending “effective” lead times for their partners and other decision-makers past the current average of 12 to 15 minutes–WoFS output can provide actionable forecast information one, two, or even six hours before a convective hazard occurs. However, some prior studies with members of the public have shown that forecasts with longer lead times are perceived to suggest lower risk and/or have higher location uncertainty. We apply sensemaking theory to determine how and at what point designated decision-makers interpret and respond to a hypothetical severe weather hazard. Through 20 qualitative interviews, we reveal the process through which these decision-makers conceptualize and understand a hypothetical severe weather event. With these results, in addition to feedback on example operational graphics created using WoFS output, we provide recommendations for how forecasters and designated decision-makers can collaborate to improve risk communication during the watch-to-warning gap and together utilize WoFS to inform critical decisions that help keep communities safe during severe mesoscale convective events.

493868.title: North Pacific Air-Sea Interactions Forcing Temperature Change in Pacific Decadal Oscillation Transitions
493868.authors: Rose Una, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR; and L. W. O'Neill, J. J. Wettstein, and N. T. Siler
493868.abstract: Abrupt regime shifts in the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), the leading mode of North Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) variability, have been linked to decreased physical-ecological covariance and extreme western North American climate events. These rapid transitions between positive and negative PDO phases typically occur on subseasonal-to-seasonal timescales. The statistical nature of PDO index computation and the timescales of known processes associated with the PDO make prediction of transitions challenging. We test the hypothesis that variability in air-sea coupling driven by explicit atmospheric circulation anomalies causes the large-scale SST anomaly changes associated with PDO transitions of different types and duration. We identify four types of transitions and compare the mixed layer heat budgets leading to each transition type: phase transitions (positive to negative, negative to positive) and transitory transitions (positive to positive, negative to negative). NASA Estimating the Circulation and Climate of the Ocean (ECCO) monthly closed ocean mixed layer heat budgets and fifth-generation European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Reanalysis (ERA5) are utilized to identify drivers of upper-ocean heat tendency leading up to and during transitions. We find that surface heat flux forcing and mixed layer depth anomalies are the primary drivers of North Pacific mixed layer temperature variability during transitions. Results from further analysis suggest interactions between anomalous mixed layer depth and net shortwave heat fluxes driven by synoptic events such as persistent large-scale ridging episodes are important factors in SST change during PDO transitions. The magnitude of these interactions and the timing of transitions indicate that boreal spring is important for the occurrence of PDO transitioning. Identifying physical indicators of and mechanisms driving PDO transitions improves subseasonal-to-multiseasonal predictability of the North Pacific atmosphere-ocean system.

493869.title: Local Impacts, Local Decisions: Understanding Extreme Cold Response in Western Washington
493869.authors: Mary Hannah Smith, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and J. Randazza, A. Bostrom, R. Wolcott, J. Vickery, and N. A. Errett
493869.abstract: The burden of illnesses, injuries, and deaths due to cold and extreme cold events (ECEs) is increasing in the United States. At the same time, the populations that face the highest risk of negative health impacts from cold, including people experiencing housing precarity, people unable to afford adequate heating, and older adults, are growing. In 2024, the National Weather Service (NWS) rolled out a new suite of cold alert products to streamline the forecast process, unify terms and warning frameworks across the United States, and clearly communicate the risks posed by extremely low temperatures. ECEs are unusual in Western Washington, and the NWS threshold for issuing these alerts is based on higher temperatures than in many other parts of the country. However, these cold product thresholds were primarily based on the average recurrence interval of ECEs, rather than on the potential for impacts to health or infrastructure, and represent temperatures very rarely experienced in the region. Some local response agencies rely on activation thresholds that differ from NWS alert criteria, incorporating observed impacts, other weather conditions, or differing and often higher temperature thresholds. However, there is little research that characterizes how response practitioners perceive and address ECE risk. This study, based on a series of interviews with forecast meteorologists and response practitioners in and around King County, Washington, reveals how agencies define actionable cold conditions and convert forecasts into response actions. Results suggest that agency cold weather response activation triggers are not consistently aligned with NWS alert thresholds, and that there is a need for additional decision-support services and alerting strategies that better align with local risk perception and public health and safety priorities. The ultimate goal of this convergent research is to improve early warning and response processes by describing the ways in which different agencies and organizations approach ECEs, their information needs, and integration of NWS products and warning frameworks into decision-making. Findings from this research will inform the development of decision support and forecast tools, including a proof-of-concept ColdRisk tool, to improve awareness of extreme cold impacts and response decision-making in Washington state while providing insights applicable to other regions.

493873.title: A Convectively Coupled Equatorial Wave Framework for Improving Subseasonal Rainfall Forecasts over Tropical Africa
493873.authors: Coumba Niang, CPAESS-UCAR, NOAA/Climate Prediction Center, College Park, MD; and E. B. Bekele, A. Faye, Z. Segele, and W. M. Thiaw
493873.abstract: The presentation builds on a previous study in which a wave-filtering diagnostic approach identified the mechanisms associated with extreme rainfall events in East Africa during the March-May 2018 season. The distinct contributions from equatorial waves, MJO, Kelvin, and Rossby were documented. A similar approach focuses on the June-September West African Monsoon incorporating African Easterly Waves (AEWs). Multi-wave alignment diagnostics reveal that constructive superposition among active Kelvin, ER, and AEW phases significantly enhances the organization of Mesoscale Convective Systems (MCSs) and localized extreme rainfall, whereas suppressed phases drive monsoonal breaks. Establishing unified multi-wave risk multipliers across both East and West Africa provides a transferable predictor for subseasonal rainfall extremes, offering an operational pathway to enhance flood forecasting and early warning systems across the region.

493874.title: Embracing Non-Uniqueness: A Probabilistic Machine Learning Framework for Lidar Aerosol Microphysical Retrievals
493874.authors: Matthew Hayman, NSF NCAR, Center Green Dr., CO
493874.abstract: Aerosol-cloud interactions remain a major source of uncertainty in climate models, requiring accurate, vertically resolved observations of aerosol microphysical properties. While lidar systems can measure aerosol layers at high vertical resolution, they fundamentally observe bulk volumetric optical properties. Retrieving microphysical quantities—such as effective radius and number concentration—from these observations is a mathematically ill-posed and non-unique inverse problem. However, decades of existing retrieval algorithms typically force a deterministic, single-point solution, masking fundamental uncertainties and relying on opaque priors. To address this, we introduce a machine learning framework that embraces the inherent non-uniqueness of lidar observations. Trained on a dataset of in situ aerosol size distributions coupled with Mie scattering theory, our model predicts the full Probability Density Function (PDF) of possible aerosol microphysical states rather than a single estimate. We leverage this framework to evaluate the theoretical capabilities and error sensitivities of distinct lidar architectures, ranging from advanced multi-wavelength Raman configurations (6𝛽+2𝛼, 3𝛽+2𝛼) to spaceborne-relevant systems like EarthCARE’s 355 nm HSRL (1𝛽+1𝛼) and multi-wavelength backscatter lidars (3𝛽). Under idealized, low-noise conditions, advanced multi-wavelength systems best constrain the microphysical solution space. However, under realistic observational uncertainties, the accuracy of these complex architectures degrades rapidly. In contrast, simpler configurations with direct extinction measurements (e.g., EarthCARE's 1𝛽+1𝛼) prove significantly more robust. Ultimately, we demonstrate that probabilistic retrievals can reliably constrain effective radius to approximately a factor of two and concentration to an order of magnitude, providing mathematically transparent observational constraints for global climate models.

493875.title: Advances on Ocean Surface Wind Retrievals in Storms with Satellite Microwave Radiometers
493875.authors: Lucrezia Ricciardulli, Remote Sensing Systems, Santa Rosa, CA; and T. Meissner and R. D. Lindsley
493875.abstract: Standard wind retrieval algorithms for Microwave (MW) Radiometers do not perform well in the presence of rain, because of the difficulty in separating the rain from the wind signal at these frequencies. Such algorithms result in a complete data loss in rain, estimated to be about 10% globally, but much larger in Tropical Storms. Radiometers with L-band frequency channels (~1 GHz, i.e. SMOS/SMAP) are an exception, as the wind signal is not affected by rain at this frequencies, and they have been successfully producing accurate wind retrievals in storms for the operational community for at least a decade now. Sensors with C-band (~ 5 GHz, i.e. AMSR2/3 and the decommissioned WindSat), allow wind retrievals in “all-weather” conditions, because the different impact of rain on C and X-band (~ 10 GHz) channels allows the separation of wind versus rain signal. For these C-band sensors, statistical algorithms were specifically developed for storm conditions (tropical and extratropical), and their retrievals have been used for TC operations. However, with the declining availability of satellite observations in TCs, the necessity arises to explore the capability of radiometers without L- or C-band (i.e. GMI, or the WSF-M Microwave Imager MWI) for wind retrievals in storms. Our presentation will describe the methodology for designing new wind-in-rain algorithms for radiometers with frequencies within 10-89 GHz. The major novelty of these new algorithm is the added use of the 89 GHz channel, which is very valuable as a proxy of cloud depth and liquid water content, and helps mitigating the rain impact These wind-in-rain algorithms are statistical regressions trained in Tropical Cyclones (TC) by precisely matching the satellite sensors brightness temperatures at all channels with ground truth winds in TCs from the HWRF model, and from SMAP, for a large number of satellite passes over TCs in all ocean basins. Similarly, we trained a statistical regression algorithm for extratropical storms in the presence of low to moderate rain. We applied these new wind-in-rain algorithm to GMI and WSF-M MWI, globally and for recent TCs in 2026. We will discuss the statistical performance, the skill in estimating storm intensity and radii, and present sample scenes of wind retrievals in storm. Our preliminary tests show promising skills, for rain rates below 8 mm/hour, thus allowing the recovery of a large portion of data lost with traditional rain-free wind algorithms.

493877.title: Full-System Testing of Operational Long-Lead Flash Flood Forecasting
493877.authors: Ana P. Barros, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; Univ. of Illinois Urbana Champaign, Urbana, IL; and S. Sohn, D. Gold, M. Liao, M. Jacobs, M. Kandage, J. Renfro, and M. Kulp
493877.abstract: Flood forecasting at long-lead times to enable effective warning of communities and save lives and property is especially challenging in headwater basins in regions of complex terrain where orographic effects organize and amplify heavy precipitation and rainfall-runoff response is very fast because of steep terrain producing flash floods. An AI-enhanced operational framework for flash-flood forecasting leveraging long-lead time weather forecasts, observations, physically based flood modeling, and risk assessment was developed building on previous work on Quantitative Flood Forecasting using Machine Learning. Albeit conceptually general and transferable to other regions, the framework was implemented to meet the needs of the National Park Service (NPS) for headwater basins in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park (GSMNP) in the Southern Appalachian Mountains. First, 48 hours of Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPF) fields at 3km resolution are extracted from each 6-hourly National Weather Service (NWS) High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) weather forecasts. Next, hourly precipitation corrections generated by an AI QPF error prediction model and downscaled to 250m are applied to the HRRR QPF fields. The corrected and 250 m hourly QPF fields drive a spatially distributed flood prediction model producing streamflow forecasts for over 1,020 km of streams and 20 basins within the GSMNP. The QPF error prediction model is a time-varying bias correction Random Forest Classifier trained with ground-based radar precipitation for extreme events along the Appalachian Mountains. The operational framework produces 8 time-lagged forecasts corresponding to 6,12, ..., up to 48 hour lead-time every 5 minutes across the stream network. It has been wrapped into a geospatial API (FloodView) and it has been in full-system testing mode for the GSMNP since May 2025. Performance statistics including Confidence metrics for the last 18 months of operations will be presented.

493880.title: Learning a Transferable Global Precipitation Prior with Mild Conditioning
493880.authors: Buddha Subedi, University of Minnesota- Twin Cities, Minneapolis, MN; Univ. of Minnesota-Twin Cities, Minneapolis, MN; and M. garshasbi and A. Ebtehaj
493880.abstract: Deep generative neural networks can synthesize realistic natural images that have no physical existence. This raises the question of whether they can similarly generate realistic global precipitation fields that reproduce both the probability distribution of precipitation and its geographically organized spatial patterns. Here, we investigate this question using a multi-head self-attention-based denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM). We first examine fully unconditional hourly global precipitation generation and then introduce mild conditioning based solely on geographic location, topography, and monthly precipitation climatology. The unconditional model captures broad statistical characteristics and precipitation structures but has limited ability to reproduce geographically organized patterns, including those associated with the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and midlatitude extratropical storm tracks. In contrast, mild conditioning leads to realistic generation of global near-surface precipitation fields that closely resemble those from Earth system models, while preserving both the precipitation probability distribution and its global spatial patterns. Both models are evaluated in terms of precipitation morphology and occurrence and intensity distributions, while the mildly conditioned model is further evaluated against reanalysis seasonal climatology and its latitudinal distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the precipitation prior learned by the mildly conditioned model transfers effectively to precipitation super-resolution, suggesting its broader utility as a probabilistic prior for climate model downscaling, satellite precipitation gap filling, and nowcasting with remarkable accuracy.

493886.title: A Real-Time Probabilistic Flash Drought Outlook from the NOAA Weather Prediction Center
493886.authors: Anthony M. DeAngelis, NOAA Weather Prediction Center, Extended Prediction Division & Entarian, Riverdale Park, MD; and H. Wang, M. Park, A. M. Badger, and J. Leung
493886.abstract: The NOAA Weather Prediction Center’s (WPC) Extended Prediction Division (EPD) is currently developing a new real-time probabilistic Flash Drought Outlook (FDO) product for the contiguous U.S., to provide flash drought forecast guidance with lead times of up to five weeks. Due to their rapid development and major impacts on agriculture and water resources, flash droughts pose a serious societal threat. The new probabilistic FDO will serve as a critical support tool for the WPC’s current week-2 Rapid Onset Drought (ROD) product as well as a stand-alone product for flash drought prediction for weeks 3-5, both of which will provide crucial flash drought prediction information for U.S. stakeholders. This presentation will document the datasets and methodology used to develop the real-time FDO. This includes first developing a real-time Flash Drought Monitor (FDM) based on a blend of meteorological and agricultural flash drought indices derived from low-latency observations, including CPC gauge-based observations and a Noah-MP land surface model analysis driven by CPC observations and the WPC’s Conventional Observational Reanalysis (CORe). The real-time probabilistic FDO is then generated from a blend of ensemble forecasts of flash drought indices. Bias-corrected meteorological forecasts from NOAA’s Global Ensemble Forecast System version 12 (GEFSv12) are directly used for meteorological drought indices or as forcing for the Noah-MP model to produce forecasts for agricultural indices. We will present a prototype of the new FDO and demonstrate its skill through a retrospective statistical evaluation and investigation of recent flash drought events.

493888.title: Modernizing the NOAA Space Weather Scales: Shaping the Next Generation of Space Weather Risk Communication
493888.authors: William Murtagh, Science and Technology Policy Institute, Berthoud, CO
493888.abstract: Introduced in 1999, the NOAA Space Weather Scales have served for more than 25 years as the Nation's standard framework for communicating the severity of geomagnetic storms, solar radiation storms, and radio blackouts. During that time, society's dependence on vulnerable technologies has grown dramatically, new operational users have emerged, and advances in forecasting and social science have highlighted opportunities to improve how space weather hazards are communicated. The Science and Technology Policy Institute (STPI), in support of NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center, is leading the first comprehensive modernization of the scales. Recognizing that one size does not, and cannot, fit all users, the effort includes evaluating updated severity descriptors, hazard terminology, frequency characterizations, and sector-specific impact information, while developing the implementation and stakeholder engagement strategies needed for a successful operational transition. This presentation will provide an overview of the proposed revisions and the rationale behind them. The proposed revisions reflect the extensive stakeholder input already gathered through STPI's engagement process and SWPC's subsequent development work. Rather than presenting final recommendations, the session will provide conference participants with an opportunity to offer additional observations that may inform targeted refinements and implementation planning. The goal is to ensure that the revised Space Weather Scales clearly communicate risk, support actionable decision-making, and meet the evolving needs of today's diverse space weather user community.

493891.title: Mixed-Phase Cloud Processes Improve Kilometer-Scale Simulation of Atmospheric River Extreme Precipitation over the U.S. Pacific Northwest
493891.authors: Sourav Taraphdar, PNNL, Richland, WA; and L. R. Leung, N. Sun, and X. Chen
493891.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are the dominant cause of the most damaging cold-season extreme precipitation events in the U.S. Pacific Northwest, yet accurately simulating the associated orographic precipitation over complex terrain remains challenging. This study investigates the physical processes controlling AR precipitation using kilometer-scale simulations with the Simple Cloud Resolving E3SM Atmosphere Model (SCREAM). Four flood-producing AR events affecting the Puget Sound basin are simulated using a regionally refined mesh (3.125 km) embedded within a 25 km global model. Two SCREAM configurations are compared that differ only in their representation of ice-cloud fraction: SCREAMv0 uses a relative humidity-based formulation, whereas SCREAMv0+ diagnoses ice-cloud fraction from the cell-averaged ice mass mixing ratio. Across all four events, SCREAMv0+ generates an orographic precipitation pattern that more closely resembles multiple observational products. Followed by diagnoses, SCREAMv0+ produces stronger low-level winds, greater precipitable water, and enhanced moisture transport than SCREAMv0, in closer agreement with ERA5. SCREAMv0+ also produces a deeper layer of cloud ice and mixed-phase hydrometeors. The associated changes in ice- and mixed-phase condensate likely modify latent heat release, induce a circulation response, and ultimately alter the precipitation distribution. Targeted sensitivity experiments confirm that these differences are primarily driven by interactions between ice-cloud fraction and cloud microphysics. Overall, the results demonstrate that changes in cloud macrophysics can substantially alter the coupling among microphysics, diabatic heating, large-scale circulation, and precipitation in kilometer-scale models. These findings highlight the importance of mixed-phase cloud processes for representing AR-driven orographic precipitation and demonstrate the ability of regionally refined SCREAM simulations to represent cold-season extreme rainfall over mountainous terrain.

493895.title: An Update on the Louisiana State Mesonet
493895.authors: Todd A Murphy, Univ. of Louisiana Monroe, Monroe, LA; and E. Newby, D. Hall, and K. Leppert
493895.abstract: Deployment of the Louisiana State Mesonet (LSM), managed by the University of Louisiana Monroe (ULM), began in August 2024 with installation of our first station on ULM’s campus. Since then, an additional 37 stations* have been installed across the state towards our initial goal of 50 stations. LSM stations collect typical weather and climate data, including temperature at three heights, relative humidity, pressure, solar radiation, wind speed and direction at two heights, precipitation, and soil conditions (moisture and temperature) to depths of 1-m. Each station also includes a camera to view the surrounding conditions. One goal of this presentation is to provide an update on the progress of the LSM to the broader weather and climate community, highlighting successes and challenges, how the data is being used internally at ULM, and by our partners across the state and region. Recently, ULM secured an additional round of funding to expand the LSM footprint by another 50 stations near and along the Mississippi River Delta, placing some stations into parts of Mississippi and Arkansas. Through this funding, the LSM will establish a regional forecasting center dedicated to high impact weather, with a specific focus towards flood and drought nowcasting and forecasting. This presentation will also detail the expanded scope of the LSM, including the new stations, target installation locations, and the spin up of the regional forecast center. Implementation and plans of the regional forecast center will be discussed, including how mesonet partners will play a critical role in its development. *38 stations installed as of the submission of this abstract on 8/11/26.

493900.title: Mapping Burn Scars Faster and Sooner for NWS Debris Flow Risk Assessment
493900.authors: Sam Batzli, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and D. Losos, W. Straka, and D. Parker
493900.abstract: The BRISK map portal emerged in response to a need from NOAA forecasters for timely burn severity maps in the immediate wake of wildfires. Post-fire hydrological risks like debris flows emerge instantaneously, but existing burn severity mapping programs deliver maps to end-users with data latency of weeks to months. Mapping efforts are stalled by waiting for a clear-sky satellite pass due to persistent cloud and smoke coverage. BRISK– Burned area Rapid Interim Severity RisK- is a decision support tool co-developed with NOAA WPO (Weather Program Office), National Weather Service (NWS) practitioners and guided by Google Cloud engineers. BRISK maps fuse multi-sensor active fire and reflectance data (from ABI, VIIRS, Landsat and Sentinel) to deliver daily burn severity maps that mosaic the most-timely and detailed information available. The portal interface allows end-users to view current BRISK maps across the Continental US (CONUS), customize map settings and filters, and download or stream high-resolution images to aid forecasting and modeling of post-fire impacts. In the backend, high speed cloud-based parallel computing is enabled by Google Earth Engine infrastructure. In this presentation, we will demonstrate the user interface operability and ongoing validation efforts. After one year of BRISK maps, we will also reflect on lessons from this public-private collaboration. We will discuss future directions for the BRISK portal, including plans to leverage GeoAI to improve high resolution near real-time mapping, new support from NASA to enhance accuracy, integrate BRISK maps with operational NWS platforms, and expand coverage beyond CONUS.

493902.title: Scaling Atmospheric Lidar Retrieval Speed and Robustness With Differentiable Forward Model Regularizers
493902.authors: Naowal Azraf Rahman, Columbia University, New York, NY; NCAR, East Elmhurst, NY; and B. Garby and M. Hayman
493902.abstract: Retrievals from photon-counting atmospheric lidar have traditionally relied on algebraic inversion, in which channel ratios cancel common instrument and atmospheric terms. While simple and interpretable, these estimators amplify photon-counting noise and force a trade-off between resolution and precision. Recent maximum-likelihood approaches such as Poisson Total Variation (PTV), solved with SPIRAL-TAP-class algorithms, instead invert the full instrument forward model under a Poisson noise model with total variation regularization, extending resolution and altitude coverage. However, these solvers depend on specialized proximal-operator methods that are computationally demanding, difficult to implement, and can introduce artifacts in scenes with high dynamic range. We present DiffraTorch (Differentiable Inversion Forward-model Fitting Regularized Algorithm), a PyTorch library that replaces total variation with smooth, differentiable regularizers such as the Charbonnier penalty, enabling the entire retrieval to be optimized with PyTorch's automatic differentiation engine. Eliminating the proximal solver reduces implementation complexity and computational cost, with retrievals running meaningfully on a laptop, and in some cases, improves convergence robustness. Our modular implementation also makes the framework straightforward for a non-expert to adapt to other lidar architectures and leverage alternative or fully custom optimizers. We validate DiffraTorch against SpiralTorch, the reference PTV implementation, on HSRL and DIAL retrievals, with validation losses agreeing to within 1% across retrievals. We will present these retrieval comparisons alongside runtime and robustness results, and discuss adapting the framework to other photon-counting lidar systems.

493905.title: User-Centered Design of Deterministic and Probabilistic Drought Outlook Visualizations to Improve Decision Support
493905.authors: Melissa A Kenney, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN; and A. Joshi, M. Gerst, J. Gottschalck, S. Sharma, A. Farris, A. Hartman, B. Pugh, A. M. Sheffield, and V. Deheza
493905.abstract: Drought outlooks are critical decision-support products used by water managers, agricultural stakeholders, emergency managers, and others to anticipate changing conditions and inform preparedness and response. However, scientifically robust forecasts can only support decisions if users correctly understand the information being communicated. Through a sustained collaboration among NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center (CPC), the National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS), and social scientists, we are applying an evidence-based, user-centered approach to improve drought forecast visualizations and support their transition from research to operations. This presentation will describe how research on NOAA’s deterministic U.S. Drought Outlooks is informing development and evaluation of new probabilistic drought outlook visualizations, with particular attention to designing a cohesive suite of products that communicate complementary but distinct forecast messages. Our work applies the Diagnose, Assess, Redesign, Test, and Synthesize (DARTS) framework, which integrates visualization, communication, and decision science with stakeholder engagement and empirical testing. The DARTS method that we developed has been deployed for a range of federal weather and sub-seasonal to seasonal data products, including the NOAA Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks, USGS Water Watches, NOAA Flood Inundation Maps, DAWN agricultural forecasts, and NOAA drought outlooks. For NOAA’s deterministic monthly and seasonal U.S. Drought Outlooks, we applied the DARTS framework by first conducting focus groups with forecasters, information translators, and end users to identify communication and interpretation challenges, which informed co-design of alternative graphics with CPC and NIDIS. Three redesigned graphics were subsequently evaluated against the existing outlook through a national control-treatment survey experiment with 813 U.S. adults. The research identified a fundamental mismatch between the product’s intended and perceived key messages: most participants interpreted the existing outlook as communicating forecast drought intensity rather than its intended message of forecast change in drought conditions. Redesigned graphics significantly improved understanding of this key message, were more intuitive, and included a modified legend that was significantly easier to understand. These findings informed evidence-based recommendations for proposed changes to NOAA’s deterministic U.S. Drought Outlooks. We are now extending the DARTS framework to the development of probabilistic drought outlooks, which are intended to communicate the likelihood of drought intensity across the U.S. This introduces additional communication challenges associated with probability and uncertainty while also creating a broader product-design challenge. The deterministic and probabilistic outlooks need sufficient visual consistency to function as a cohesive suite of drought information products while remaining sufficiently distinct for users to recognize and correctly interpret their different key messages. The research therefore engages CPC, NIDIS, NIDIS Regional Drought Early Warning System partners, and drought stakeholders to identify users, decision contexts, information needs, scientific and operational constraints, and potential interpretation challenges; co-design alternative graphical representations; and empirically evaluate prototypes. Planned testing will examine design elements including color scales, map-based representations, explanatory information, and representations of probability and uncertainty, with outcomes including interpretation accuracy, usability, confidence, and decision relevance. Together, this work demonstrates how a consistent decision support science framework can be applied across suites of NOAA drought products, using empirical evidence and sustained partnerships to move beyond designing individual graphics toward a coherent system of drought forecast information that supports accurate interpretation and actionable drought intelligence.

493906.title: Co-Developing a Flood Intelligence Card for the Rakiraki Catchment, Fiji: From Flash Flood Guidance to Impact-Based Decision Support
493906.authors: Viliame Vereivalu, Fiji Meteorological Service, Nadi, Fiji; and J. Reid, A. Horan, and R. Campbell
493906.abstract: Flash flooding is a significant and rapidly developing hazard in Fiji, where steep catchments, short hydrological response times, intense tropical rainfall, and growing exposure can produce damaging floods with little warning time. These conditions strain operational forecasting and underline the need to move beyond hazard-based information toward warnings that communicate expected impacts and support timely, proportionate protective action. The Fiji Meteorological Service (FMS), through its Meteorological and Hydrological Divisions, has strengthened its flash-flood forecasting capability through the Pacific Flash Flood Guidance System (Pacific FFGS), which integrates remotely sensed and forecast rainfall, soil-moisture conditions, terrain characteristics, and hydrological response information to identify catchments susceptible to flash flooding. FFGS provides valuable early hazard guidance, but does not by itself describe the consequences flooding may have for exposed communities, infrastructure, livelihoods, or critical services. Bridging that gap requires translating forecast guidance into locally meaningful impacts, actions, and decisions. This paper presents that translation through the Rakiraki catchment, where FMS worked with local stakeholders to co-develop a Flood Intelligence Card — a decision-support instrument that links FFGS guidance, forecast rainfall, and locally read water-level markers (staff gauges) at key river crossings to known areas of exposure, historical flood impacts, and defined response actions for the catchment. The card was co-developed through a stakeholder process that brought together FMS forecasters, the Secretariat of the Pacific Community (SPC), the National Disaster Management Office (NDMO), the Rakiraki Municipal Administration and the Ra Provincial Administration, community-based and civil-society organisations, government stakeholders, FemLinkPacific, and local school teachers — ensuring that thresholds and triggers reflect operational realities and locally recognised consequences rather than technical guidance alone. The card uses rainfall–river-level relationships and predefined river-level thresholds at Nakauvadra Upstream, Narara, and Rakiraki Town Centre to signal escalating flood impacts to roads, crossings, settlements, crops, and buildings, supporting timely alerts, warnings, and response actions. Tropical Cyclone Yasa (December 2020) is used as an operational case study to illustrate how the card functions in practice. Ahead of peak impacts, FFGS threat guidance and forecast rainfall indicated a rising potential for heavy rainfall and flash flooding across the Rakiraki catchment. As rainfall intensified, the guidance proved broadly consistent with the observed hydrological response, with runoff driving rapid rises in river levels; observations at Rakiraki Town Centre showed the river exceeding its warning threshold as flooding affected the town, roads, and surrounding low-lying areas. Crucially, while broad FFGS guidance was directionally correct, local observations showed that flooding could develop faster and more severely at specific sites than the catchment-scale forecast implied — the central reason locally read gauge levels are indispensable. Overall, the event demonstrated the value of combining FFGS threat products and forecast rainfall with real-time river-level observations to refine the timing and location of flood warnings. The case shows how impact-based decision support strengthens forecast confidence and enables authorities and communities to act ahead of flooding, while also revealing how limited observation density, telemetry gaps, and the need for better local threshold calibration can constrain the effectiveness of automated flood guidance and impact-based warnings. The Rakiraki experience demonstrates a practical, replicable pathway for extending FFGS from flash-flood hazard guidance toward impact-based forecasting and end-to-end early warning. Its central lesson is methodological: the Flood Intelligence Card works not because of any single model, but because stakeholder co-production embeds forecast information within local knowledge, exposure, and decision requirements. Remaining requirements include extending and standardising water-level observations at crossings (with a pathway toward telemetry), improved exposure and impact datasets, and systematic documentation of flood impacts. These lessons are directly relevant to other Pacific Island Countries and Small Island Developing States, and show how international partnerships and the global FFGS network — now spanning more than 100 countries — can underpin locally calibrated, people-centred early warning services under the Early Warnings for All initiative.

493907.title: Turbulence Measurements from ADS-B Out Reports
493907.authors: Larry Cornman, National Center for Atmospheric Research, longmont, CO; UCAR, Boulder, CO
493907.abstract: Due to efficiency and safety reasons, encounters with atmospheric turbulence remain a critical concern for the aviation community. Solutions to this problem can come partly from better turbulence nowcasts and forecasts, as well as from enhanced turbulence observations. Better measurements of turbulence would help enhance the physical understanding of the turbulence phenomenon and its operational predictability, as well as providing real-time data for tactical use. However, dense, routine, and quantitative observations of turbulence are still lacking, and without them it is difficult to provide usable information about the turbulent state of the atmosphere for tactical and strategic turbulence avoidance. Turbulence observations can be used as stand-alone measurements or fed into turbulence forecasting and nowcasting systems. Routine observations of turbulence are available through verbal reports from pilots (PIREPs) and through automated in situ measurements on some aircraft, and currently these are merged with NSF-NCAR’s Graphical Turbulence Guidance (GTG) product to generate the GTGN nowcasts. Inference of turbulence from radar and satellite imagery is also available, but all these combined sources are still not sufficient to provide prompt and accurate representations of atmospheric turbulence, which is well known to be an extremely dynamic physical process. One viable option to augment existing turbulence observations is to use the Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) Out position and velocity data to indicate the presence of turbulence. This information can be collected by ground stations and satellite-based receivers in near-real time and used to generate routine and quantitative measurements of turbulence across the globe. ADS–B is an element of the U.S. NextGen and Europe’s SESAR enhancements of the airspace system. Other nations across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, South America and Africa are also considering the adoption of ADS-B Out requirements. The amount of data available from ADS-B Out is unprecedented. For example, there are over 180,000 aircraft equipped with ADS-B datalink units. At any given moment, approximately 10,000 to 15,000 aircraft are airborne and actively reporting ADS-B data globally. Viewing each of the aircraft as a potential source of turbulence reporting is a paradigm-shifting scenario. In 2019, NSF-NCAR started providing technical support to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regarding the potential use of Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out reports for the detection of atmospheric turbulence. The purpose of the FAA turbulence project is to enhance the National Airspace System (NAS) safety and increase capacity through improved observation and forecasting of turbulence for strategic and tactical use by traffic flow managers, flight crews, airline dispatch operators, and aviation forecasters. These research efforts were initially focused on determining the feasibility of using ground-based ADS-B vertical rate reports for turbulence detection. The success of these efforts led to the development of a turbulence algorithm that produces accurate aircraft-independent measures of turbulence (e.g., energy dissipation rate, or EDR). Currently, NSF-NCAR is working closely with the FAA to transition the algorithm into operational deployment. The FAA efforts have been focused on using ADS-B Out data as received by a network of over 630 ground-based receivers covering the continental US, Alaska, Hawaii, and other locations. In 2023, NSF-NCAR began working with Aireon, LLC, to evaluate the feasibility of using their satellite-based network of ADS-B Out receivers to calculate EDR from aircraft all over the globe. This effort has also been successful and in 2025, UCAR (NSF-NCAR’s management corporation), licensed the technology to Aireon, which in turn has been running the algorithm operationally. The focus of the NSF-NCAR ADS-B turbulence detection algorithm effort has been to take an aircraft-dependent measurement, the vertical rate (VR), and convert it into an aircraft-independent measure of atmospheric turbulence intensity (i.e., EDR, the cube root of the energy dissipation rate). Key impediments to this process are the relatively low sampling rate of the ADS-B VR reports (1-2 Hz), relatively large quantization in the VR data (64 fpm, or ~0.325 m/s), and contamination due to non-turbulent sources such as maneuvers and wave-like atmospheric structures. Other considerations that required mitigation include resampling the asynchronous VR reports into a uniformly spaced time series (something exacerbated by the low sampling rate), data quality control issues, and scaling algorithms that transform an aircraft-dependent measure of turbulence into EDRs. The emphasis of NCAR’s efforts so far has been related to large transport aircraft. The rationale for this approach is that these aircraft dominate commercial air traffic, and that NSF-NCAR has access to higher-quality turbulence reports (i.e., NSF-NCAR in situ EDR reports) from a number of these aircraft types that can be used for algorithm tuning and verification. Work to apply the algorithm to ADS-B data from general aviation, business, and regional jets is also underway. Verification efforts have been ongoing using the aforementioned in situ reports, PIREPs, and high-rate recordings from certain aircraft. These verification efforts include both case studies and large-scale statistical analysis. NSF-NCAR has also performed an in-house demonstration to investigate the utility of ingesting ground-based ADS-B turbulence reports into the GTGN product, and a demonstration product is expected to go online later in 2026. Work towards a global GTGN, using ADS-B turbulence reports, is also underway. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

493909.title: Cocoa: A Fast, Modern, and GPU-Accelerated Coastal and Ocean Model for Local to Global Scale Simulation of Tides, Currents, Storm Surge, and Flooding
493909.authors: Zach Cobell, ICEYE, Irvine, CA; and S. Bunya, R. Luettich, and J. J. Westerink
493909.abstract: The architecture of modern high-performance computing has shifted dramatically since the time when many highly parallelized coastal hydrodynamic models in use today were originally developed. Whereas leadership-class supercomputers were historically dominated by CPU-based compute, the current generation of exascale systems, including the top three machines on the November 2025 TOP500 list (El Capitan, Frontier, and Aurora), derive the overwhelming majority of their floating-point performance from GPU accelerators, and now, more than half of all TOP500 systems are accelerated. Legacy coastal and ocean circulation models written in Fortran with MPI-based CPU parallelism were not designed for this paradigm and are unable to effectively utilize the accelerator compute that now constitutes the overwhelming majority of floating point operations available on modern HPC platforms, leaving the majority of available computational capacity inaccessible to the community. While directive-based approaches such as OpenACC and OpenMP offer a less invasive path to parallel execution on both CPUs and accelerated hardware for legacy Fortran codes, they are fundamentally constrained by CPU-centric data structures and often introduce unintentional performance pitfalls, both of which ultimately limit the achievable performance on modern accelerator hardware. We present Cocoa (Coastal and Ocean Circulation on Accelerators), a ground-up rewrite of the 2D depth-integrated ADCIRC model's physics and numerical methods targeted at GPU-based coastal and ocean circulation simulations on finite elements. Cocoa is written in C++ and leverages the Kokkos and Trilinos frameworks to achieve performance portability across x86 and ARM CPUs as well as GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel in both single- and multi-node configurations. Cocoa re-implements some of the most commonly used ADCIRC features such as astronomic tide forcing, wind and pressure forcing from multiple different input formats, parametric vortex models, ice coverage, and baroclinic forcing from external three-dimensional models. In a 28-day Hurricane Katrina hindcast comparison on a computational mesh containing 1.5M vertices, the ADCIRC model running on 1024 cores takes 99 minutes while a single NVIDIA H100 GPU takes 24 minutes. This represents a substantial reduction in both energy consumption and hardware cost for equivalent simulation throughput. Additionally, simulations that traditionally have required access to NSF-style supercomputing systems now can be conducted in local desktop environments at a fraction of the cost, broadening access and allowing many additional users can conduct large scale circulation simulations. We believe Cocoa can be impactful not only for traditional flood insurance studies where ADCIRC has traditionally been used to simulate hundreds to thousands of synthetic events, but also in real-time forecasting contexts where GPU architectures can be leveraged to provide high-resolution, full-physics, ensemble forecast simulations to generate probabilistic storm surge guidance where presently coarse, simplified models are used.

493915.title: Mixed-Phase Cloud Thinning Cooling Potential from Dust Indirect Effects in the Arctic
493915.authors: Kathryn A. Moore, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; and J. F. Kok, A. T. Evan, and L. M. Zamora
493915.abstract: Low-altitude mixed-phase clouds, which can contain both liquid droplets and ice crystals, are ubiquitous in polar regions and have a large influence on Earth's energy budget. Depending on the season, altitude, and cloud phase, mixed phase clouds can be cooling though reflection of shortwave (SW) radiation, and/or warming through absorption of longwave (LW) radiation. During polar winter, LW impacts dominate and these mixed-phase clouds are net warming. A recently proposed aerosol climate intervention technique known as mixed-phase cloud thinning (MCT) has suggested adding aerosols known as ice nucleating particles (INPs) to winter polar mixed-phase clouds to convert liquid droplets to ice crystals, thereby decreasing cloud optical thickness and cloud lifetime and reducing their LW warming. We use CloudSat and CALIPSO satellite cloud observations and aerosol concentrations from the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) Earth system model with new high latitude dust sources to assess the radiative cooling that may be achievable through MCT by seeding Arctic clouds with dust, a common natural INP. A generalized additive model (GAM) is used to determine how well modeled and reanalysis aerosol, including dust, and meteorological parameters can predict changes in Arctic cloud glaciation and LW cloud radiative effects (CRE). Prior to this statistical analysis, observations are binned using reanalysis meteorological parameters from MERRA-2 and ECMWF to limit the impact of meteorological co-variability on the results. Results will be used to assess whether a causative link between dust and CREs can be established for low Arctic nighttime clouds, and if so, whether further additions of dust can result in meaningful cooling at the surface or top of atmosphere.

493918.title: Recent Advances in Tuning JEDI Analysis Configurations for Applications in the MPAS–JEDI-Based Rapid Refresh Forecast System
493918.authors: Junjun Hu, CIRES/CU Boulder and NOAA/OAR/GSL, Boulder, CO; and G. Ge, M. Hu, C. Zhou, S. Pan, H. Wang, T. Lei, S. Liu, and T. T. Ladwig
493918.abstract: Over the past several years, NOAA has been leveraging advances in science and technology to develop the next-generation Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS): a rapidly updating, high-resolution weather prediction system. In parallel with the transition of the FV3-GSI-based RRFS to operations in 2026, active development of an RRFS configuration based on the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) and the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) has made substantial progress. The real-time experimental MPAS-JEDI-based RRFS configuration, RRFSv2X, operates over a 3-km CONUS domain with hourly cycling and a hybrid 3DEnVar data assimilation system. It was evaluated for the first time during the 2026 NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed Spring Forecasting Experiment and received positive feedback for its guidance on convective initiation and storm evolution. This presentation highlights recent advances in the data assimilation components of RRFSv2X, including the implementation of static background error covariance, localization strategies, and the hybrid 3DEnVar configuration. Single-observation tests and retrospective experiments have been conducted to evaluate analysis and forecast performance and to optimize data assimilation configurations. The scientific impacts of these developments, together with their computational resource requirements, are also assessed. Results from these experiments and their implications for the continued development of RRFS will be presented, along with ongoing efforts and plans toward improving system performance, computational efficiency, and operational readiness.

493920.title: Advancing Blowing Snow Prediction and Visibility Forecasting Through Coupled Modeling Techniques
493920.authors: Saurav Dey Shuvo, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and D. H. Bromwich, L. Bai, A. D. Kennedy, A. Sczepanski, and T. D. Kurtz
493920.abstract: Blowing snow remains one of the most challenging winter weather hazards in the northern Great Plains, where drifting snow and reduced visibility frequently disrupt transport and communications. This research advances both the predictive capability and the process-level understanding of blowing snow by integrating a newly coupled Polar WRF-PIEKTUK system with detailed observational and modeling analyses focused on the Red River Valley of North Dakota. The coupled framework enables explicit simulation of snow particles, especially their transport and sublimation, allowing blowing snow to be forecast in advance with substantially improved accuracy relative to traditional parameterizations. A major outcome of this work is the development of visibility forecasts that incorporate blowing snow physics directly into existing forecast systems. These forecasts demonstrated strong skill during multiple case studies, capturing both the onset and evolution of visibility reductions associated with snow transport. The ability to predict visibility at fine temporal resolution represents a major step toward operationally meaningful blowing snow guidance for transportation agencies and forecasters. Beyond forecasting, this research investigates the internal structure of blowing snow events, with particular emphasis on horizontal convective rolls (HCRs). High resolution simulations reveal that HCRs modulate snow particle concentration, vertical mixing, and localized visibility gradients. Their formation is strongly influenced by the unique topographic and surface characteristics of the Red River Valley, whose north-south orientation and shallow basin geometry enhance low-level wind channeling and mechanical turbulence. These findings highlight the Valley’s substantial role in shaping blowing snow dynamics and underscore the importance of regional physiography in winter weather prediction. Future work will expand this modeling framework using Large Eddy Simulation to resolve turbulent structures governing snow transport at a very high resolution. In parallel, a machine learning based visibility prediction system is being developed to fuse model output, surface observations, and remote sensing data. Together, these efforts aim to establish a hybrid forecasting approach capable of delivering highly accurate, operationally relevant blowing snow guidance for vulnerable regions across the northern United States.

493921.title: Toward Full-Diurnal MCE-Modulated Global Fire Emissions with VIIRS FILDA-3
493921.authors: Meng Zhou, Atmospheric and Environmental Research Laboratory, Iowa City, IA; and J. Wang, W. Deng, A. da Silva, and D. A. Peterson
493921.abstract: Biomass-burning emission inventories commonly estimate fire emissions using satellite-observed fire activity combined with emission factors prescribed according to vegetation or fuel type. While this approach captures broad differences among ecosystems, it does not explicitly represent the substantial spatial and temporal variability in combustion conditions associated with the evolving balance between flaming and smoldering combustion. Modified combustion efficiency (MCE) provides a physically meaningful indicator of this combustion state and offers a direct pathway for dynamically constraining combustion-dependent emission factors. Here, we develop a full-diurnal, MCE-modulated global fire-emission framework based on the Fire Light Detection Algorithm Version 3 (FILDA-3) and observations from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS). FILDA-3 extends the nighttime MCE capability established with VIIRS Day/Night Band fire-emitted visible light to daytime conditions using a physics-informed machine-learning framework, enabling consistent characterization of fire combustion efficiency across the diurnal cycle. Within the emission system, atmospherically corrected fire radiative power is aggregated by major vegetation class, while daytime and nighttime MCE are independently retained to characterize changes in combustion state. Rather than assigning emission factors solely from static vegetation classifications, species-specific emission factors are dynamically modulated by the satellite-derived MCE while retaining the underlying fuel-type dependence. Initial analyses reveal pronounced spatial and temporal variability in fire MCE that cannot be represented by vegetation class alone, resulting in substantial changes in combustion-sensitive emissions, particularly for species associated preferentially with smoldering or flaming combustion. The resulting framework provides a pathway from satellite-observed fire radiative energy and combustion state to full-diurnal, composition-resolved global fire emissions. By explicitly representing variability in combustion efficiency, FILDA-3-based emissions have the potential to improve simulations of trace-gas concentrations, emission ratios, and the atmospheric impacts of biomass burning.

493923.title: From Irrigation Status to Source-Resolved Water Demand: Transitioning Field-Scale ET Mapping to Operations
493923.authors: Peter ReVelle, DRI, Reno, NV; DRI, Reno, NV; and S. Majumdar, B. A. Minor, T. Ott, M. Bromley, D. Ketchum, Y. Xie, J. L. Atkin, C. Pearson, C. Morton, B. Daudert, and J. L. Huntington
493923.abstract: Field-scale evapotranspiration products are moving toward operational irrigation water accounting, but their value depends on knowing where individual fields are irrigated and how irrigation status varies across regions and years. Here, we develop a cloud-based testbed to improve irrigation status mapping across 17 western states and evaluate how this alternative product affects source-resolved agricultural water-use estimates, historical drought responses, and future projections in Nevada. Using labeled reference polygons from the IrrMapper training dataset, we trained state-specific XGBRF classifiers for 2016–2025 using OpenET evapotranspiration, Landsat NDVI, precipitation, and crop-type predictors. The classifiers produced annual irrigation-status estimates for approximately 4.5 million field polygons in Google Earth Engine, allowing labels to be revised and statewide models retrained within hours. Spatially independent holdouts and comparisons with IrrMapper and LANID were evaluated at field, county, and state scales, while the USDA-NASS Census county-level acreage provided an independent diagnostic. Across 11 overlap states, preliminary county-year agreement had mean state-level R² of 0.88 with IrrMapper and 0.85 with LANID. Initial results indicate reference-label quality influenced regional performance more than classifier selection: switching among three tree ensembles changed mean county-scale correlation with Census acreage across 15 states by less than 0.02, whereas revised training labels in Texas cotton counties increased correlation from 0.31 to 0.85. The contribution from adding evapotranspiration predictors was also region-dependent: improving held-out F1 scores by 0.02 to 0.18. For Nevada, we extended the classifier run through 1985–2025. We then evaluate how these irrigation-status product differences affect Nevada agricultural water use estimates. Combining 1985–2025 OpenET evapotranspiration, drought indices (SPI), irrigated acreage, and field-level water-rights attribution, we partition applied water between surface-water and groundwater sources and characterize historical drought responses. Historical basin responses differed depending on whether drought-related reductions occurred through less irrigated area, lower per-acre use, or both. We then use these historical basin-level relationships with future GCM precipitation estimates to project per-acre applied-water rates with a 40-member climate ensemble based on SPI. Finally, we repeat the projections using both irrigation-status products and compare the resulting source-resolved water use estimates to quantify their sensitivity to irrigation-status uncertainty. This work provides a reproducible research-to-operations pathway linking annual field-level irrigation status to source-resolved water-demand information, with rapid model retraining, independent diagnostics, and decision-ready outputs for water agencies.

493927.title: Bridging Meteorology, Emergency Response, and Research to Address Extreme Cold Risk in King County, Washington
493927.authors: Juliette Randazza, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and M. H. Smith, B. Kramer, A. Bostrom, J. Edge, R. Wolcott, T. Busch Isaksen, J. Vickery, and N. A. Errett
493927.abstract: While King County and its surrounding region are known for their often temperate winters, extreme cold events in the region have led to deaths, caused public and private infrastructure damage, and have compounded the effects of other winter hazards. Extreme cold is often overlooked compared to other hazards in the region, yet there is a growing regional effort to plan for and address the impacts of extreme cold events. Mitigating the risk posed by extreme cold requires close coordination between the National Weather Service (NWS) and its response partners. This coordination is bolstered by a clear understanding of populations vulnerable to extreme cold, how these populations may be impacted by this threat, and the potential response actions available to local agencies. In 2025, researchers from the University of Washington hosted a workshop that brought together meteorologists, representatives from response agencies including emergency management, public health, social services, utilities, and non-governmental organizations. This workshop sought to improve knowledge of both the impacts of extreme cold in the region and future approaches to extreme cold risk communication and response. Additionally, it sought to support the strong culture of emergency response collaboration in the region. All participants at the workshop had a response role in extreme cold events or knowledge of extreme cold health impacts, and were partners of the NWS Seattle Weather Forecast Office (WFO) or of Public Health - Seattle & King County. Workshop discussions covered pathways of exposure and vulnerability to extreme cold, cascading impacts and compounding hazards, and current or proposed response activities. University of Washington researchers guided the conversation using a modified World Café Facilitation approach and took notes on the discussion, which were qualitatively analyzed using an adapted rapid qualitative analysis method. Analysis of the workshop discussions identified that response agencies conceptualized cold risk differently based on their prior experiences with the hazard and their roles in response, demonstrating the importance of cross-disciplinary dialogue about weather-related hazards. Workshop discussions also highlighted the systemic factors that influence exposure and vulnerability, which extend beyond the mission and capacity of response agencies, suggesting that a broader coalition of organizations should be convened to strategize risk reduction for this hazard. Findings from this workshop have informed additional ongoing research about extreme cold information needs and decision-making in King County. The workshop also revealed a need for a statewide investigation of extreme cold impacts, strategies, and decision-support needs. This extreme cold body of research has since evolved to focus on the development of a proof-of-concept ColdRisk forecast tool for Washington State and beyond. More broadly, this project is an example of how the NWS Seattle WFO can catalyze cross-disciplinary and intersectoral collaboration among its response partners to strengthen regional collaboration and response planning, and to further tailor forecast and decision-support tools for local contexts.

493937.title: A Background-Conditioned Deep Learning Model for Short-Term Precipitation Prediction over CONUS
493937.authors: Shun Yao, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and H. Chen, K. M. Mahoney, and E. P. James
493937.abstract: High-resolution convection-allowing numerical weather prediction models such as the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model provide valuable short-range (up to 48 hours) precipitation prediction, but generating each forecast requires a computationally demanding numerical integration. To improve the prediction efficiency, this paper introduces a background-conditioned deep-learning model for short-range precipitation forecasting over the contiguous United States (CONUS). This model combines high-resolution regional atmospheric states with larger-domain background forcing to predict hourly precipitation together with a 60-channel auxiliary atmospheric state that is recurrently updated during autoregressive forecasting. The model is trained using CONUS404 data with ERA5 background forcing, while operational inference uses HRRR analysis states with background forecasts from the NOAA Global Forecast System (GFS). A dual-branch encoder integrates the regional and large-scale information, and a decoder predicts the next auxiliary state together with precipitation. Training combines group-weighted multivariable regression with precipitation-oriented spatial-gradient matching and multi-threshold binary cross-entropy. Three independent lead-specific models are trained for 1-, 3-, and 6-hour intervals and the results are composed hierarchically to generate enhanced forecasts up to 48 hours. Once trained, the models produce forecasts by fast neural inference rather than by a full convection-allowing numerical integration, significantly reducing computational cost relative to the HRRR model. In contrast to reflectivity-centered regional emulation studies such as HRRRCast, this model focuses on precipitation prediction and does not use operational HRRR forecasts as target labels, and the verification is based on Stage IV precipitation data which is independent from the training and inferences. Evaluations during the year 2022 using four initializations per day show that event-based and neighborhood scores are generally close to HRRR, although HRRR retains a modest advantage at longer leads and at the higher precipitation threshold. Encouragingly, the deep learning model forecasts have lower physical-space precipitation root-mean-square-error than HRRR across the examined lead times. These results demonstrate the potential of data-driven models for efficient, high-resolution regional precipitation forecasting, while identifying the representation, localization, and persistence of heavy precipitation as key remaining challenges.

493938.title: Compound Coastal Flooding Observations and Predictions with Low-Cost Water Level Sensors Along the Mid Coast of Texas
493938.authors: Juliet Cattell, Texas Sea Grant, College Station, TX; Texas A&M Univ.-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX; and P. E. Tissot, B. L. Estrada Jr., A. Taylor, H. M. Marrero Colominas, and R. Shelly
493938.abstract: Relative sea level rise, the combination of land subsidence and sea level rise, continues to progressively change our seaward boundaries. A growing impact along the US shorelines is the increased frequency of coastal flooding. The purpose of this research is to develop a prediction model for road flooding and other pain points using low-cost water level sensor (Hohonu Sensors) measurements along with data from long-term stations such as those of the Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON) and the National Water Level Observation Network (NWLON). These new low-cost sensors, although not as accurate and rugged as TCOON or NWLON stations, are much more portable, quick to install, and can be placed right next to locations prone to flooding. It is hypothesized that placing these sensors near the pain points will allow for better identification and quantification of the local drivers of flooding, provide data to calibrate predictive models, and provide observations that will help local officials better manage public safety concerns, such as vehicles attempting to cross flooded roads and the inability to provide emergency services to cut-off areas. The research consists of five low-cost sensors installed along the mid-coast of Texas, with those locations near Cove Harbor, Little Bay, Magnolia Beach, Six Mile Park, and Sargent. All sensors can be paired with TCOON stations two to ten miles away.
