The focus of the presentation will be the Six Mile Park location in Port Lavaca paired with the TCOON stations of Port Lavaca (8773259) and Port O’Connor (8773701). Findings indicate that good predictors for the water level model were time series of past water level and wind measurements from the Port Lavaca and Port O’Connor stations, wind predictions simulated using perfect prognosis, to be replaced by National Digital Forecast Database (NDFD) forecasts for operational predictions. These inputs are correlated to weather-driven changes in water levels, including those influenced by changes in the nearby Gulf and propagating to this back bay location. Inputs to the model also included rainfall amounts for the surrounding areas based on a county rain map and a nearby NOAA rain gauge (NOAA Station GHCND: US1TXCLH012) to attempt to predict the additional precipitation contribution to flooding, with operational predictions to come from the HRRR (High Resolution Rapid Refresh) operational model. Along with additional water level data from Port O’Connor to capture the longshore currents along the Gulf of Mexico shorelines. Water level measurements from the low-cost sensor located within Six Mile Park, Port Lavaca, and the nearby TCOON station were generally very similar but showed significant differences during several coastal flooding events due to compound flooding effects. After a three-day-long rain event with combined precipitation of 133mm (5.24 inches), road flooding started two and a half hours earlier at the pain point, and a difference of up to 18 cm in water levels between the two nearby locations was observed. At present, due to limited data, the predictive models are tuned based on the longer-term Port Lavaca and Port O’Connor data sets before being transferred to predict water levels at the Six Mile Park flooding location monitored by the low-cost water level sensor. The reason for the transfer is that Port Lavaca’s location is monitoring a wide open body of water not very sensitive to the influence of precipitation, while Six Mile Park (flooding location) is heavily affected by rainfall due to its location at the back of the same bay and runoff influencing its water levels.

493940.title: Improved Representation of High Latitude Mineral Dust Sources in the NASA GEOS Model
493940.authors: Kathryn A. Moore, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; and P. R. Colarco, J. R. Joshi, D. M. Leung, V. Amiridis, E. Proestakis, J. King, A. Downey, H. Skov, F. Hildebrand, C. Marsay, C. Buck, B. Koffman, D. Gaiero, C. Groot Zwaaftink, J. F. Kok, and L. M. Zamora
493940.abstract: Mineral dust aerosols play important roles in Earth’s climate, particularly by impacting aerosol direct radiative forcing and exerting indirect effects on clouds, including their phase and lifetime. Desert dust, primarily from low latitude sources, has received significant attention from both the observational and modeling communities, but dust emissions from high latitude sources remain understudied. Aircraft, ground, and satellite observations have indicated that high latitude dust sources may contribute up to 5% of global emissions. One challenge is the variability observed in high latitude dust concentrations between models, most of which do not consider local sources. This study aims to improve simulation of dust in polar regions in the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) Earth system model by adding local sources at high latitudes (≥50°). Two new source maps- one topographic dust emission map created for the FLEXPART model (FLEXDUST; Groot Zwaaftink et al. 2016), and a geomorphologically-based sediment supply map (SSM; Parajuli and Zender 2017) have been added to GEOS, both of which include sources at high latitudes. Simulations were then conducted with three emission schemes (Ginoux et al. 2011; Zender et al. 2003 (DEAD); Kok et al. 2014), the default Ginoux et al. (2001) topographic emission map, plus the new FLEXDUST and SSM maps. Finally, the DEAD scheme was updated to account for intermittent dust emissions caused by turbulent wind fluctuations (Leung et al. 2024), following a similar implementation in CESM2. New databases of high latitude dust concentrations have been derived from aerosol chemical measurements at ground sites in the Arctic and Antarctic, and also from the CALIOP lidar (LIVAS; Amiridis et al. 2015) in order to validate the simulations. In agreement with observations, GEOS simulations indicate a strong seasonality in Arctic dust emissions, which peak in summer and fall. Local sources contribute up to 80% of the surface-level dust mass in summer, with increased influence from long-range transport in winter. Initial results suggest the intermittency parameterization increases the frequency of simulated HLD events, improving agreement with satellite-observations.

493945.title: Beyond the Meteorological Tower: Evaluating Alternative Meteorological Data for Nuclear Facility Applications
493945.authors: Laura Marie Klein, Sargent & Lundy, Chicago, IL
493945.abstract: Meteorological data support a range of analyses associated with nuclear facilities and research institutions, including site characterization, environmental assessment, atmospheric dispersion analysis, and emergency preparedness. These activities have traditionally relied on dedicated onsite monitoring. However, expanded access to airport observations, regional mesonets, remote sensing systems, reanalysis products, and high-resolution numerical model output creates opportunities to use multiple sources of meteorological information. This presentation introduces a practical framework for evaluating whether an alternative meteorological dataset is appropriate for a defined application. The framework begins by identifying the decision or analysis the data must support and then considers dataset provenance, spatial and temporal representativeness, measurement or model uncertainty, quality assurance, terrain and surface characteristics, and, where available, comparison with independent observations. Particular attention is given to wind, atmospheric stability, and dispersion-related variables, for which datasets with similar summary statistics may produce different analytical results. The presentation shows how the framework can distinguish among datasets that may be appropriate for direct use, supplemental characterization, contextual analysis, or screening, as well as situations in which uncertainty or representativeness remains unresolved. The objective is not to prescribe a single data source, but to provide a transparent basis for understanding the capabilities, limitations, and appropriate uses of alternative meteorological information.

493946.title: Stomata: An Underappreciated Player in the Climate System (Invited Presentation)
493946.authors: Joseph A. Berry, Carnegie Institution for Science, Menlo Park, CA
493946.abstract: In the 1990s, Dave Randall led a program that linked the terrestrial biosphere to his atmospheric GCM - the so-called "greening of the CSU GCM." This was a first big step toward the Earth System models we have today. In fact, many of these still use approaches first implemented by Dave’s group at that time. These have evolved into a primary tool for understanding and predicting the trajectory of changing climate. Quite naturally, these are focused on the role of alternative trajectories of fossil fuel use on temperature, precipitation and carbon storage. Back at the time that Dave started all of this, our focus was more mundane - stomatal conductance was the issue. The first attempts at capturing the role of plants in controlling the partitioning of sensible and latent heat to the atmosphere didn't improve the simulated climate at all - in fact, large portions of the continents began to transition toward deserts - reminiscent of the collapse of the Green Sahara. Dave referred to this as "stomatal suicide." Modelers had tuned the surface conductance in their plant-less models to get the climate to behave. Implementing more mechanistic control by plant physiology and its interaction with atmospheric humidity and soil water availability threw this nicely balanced system out of whack. We found ways to correct this problem permitting other problems to take the stage. Nevertheless, our early experience with stomatal parameterizations is a good reminder of the importance of getting stomata right. In this presentation, I will revisit this topic and present some new ways we are developing to assess the role of stomata in the climate system.

493947.title: Machine Learning Embeddings for the Visual Exploration of Earth System Science Data
493947.authors: Nihanth W Cherukuru, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and M. Rehme, K. J. Mayer, D. J. Gagne II, J. Schreck, J. Clyne, and C. Becker
493947.abstract: Atmospheric and Earth system datasets are growing rapidly, driven by advances in both traditional, physics-based high-resolution modeling and evolving AI-based weather and climate models that can generate vast ensembles. The sheer volume and dimensionality of modern datasets make direct manual exploration impractical, limiting most current visualization approaches to rely on aggregated statistics or simplified summaries. As a result, much of the available data remains underexplored. Addressing these challenges requires not only scaling existing tools but also exploring novel approaches to exploratory data visualization. We present a general, domain-agnostic framework for visualization in the Earth system sciences. We present a machine learning (ML) assisted approach for semantic clustering, which groups datasets according to learned similarities in spatial and temporal patterns rather than fixed coordinates or time steps. The resulting cluster visualizations highlight relationships among ensemble members supporting new ways to browse, compare, and interpret complex data. They also enable practical applications such as visual similarity search, automated labeling of patterns for further analysis, and targeted model evaluation. Using pretrained models and open-source tools, we demonstrate a series of practical workflows that researchers can adapt for their own data.The goal is to highlight how existing machine learning models can serve as a tool for exploration as well as inspire the development of future ML models and human-in-the-loop visualization systems designed specifically for visualizing and communicating high-dimensional Earth sciences data.

493949.title: Characterization and Numerical Weather Prediction of Extreme Cool-Season Precipitation Events in Complex Terrain in Arizona
493949.authors: Tyler Anthony Maio, Univ. of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and E. H. Atallah, H. I. Chang, and B. Svoma
493949.abstract: While many precipitation studies in Arizona focus on the North American Monsoon season, almost 50% of annual precipitation occurs during the cool season, when extreme precipitation events can have substantial impacts on water resources and flood risk. Atmospheric Rivers (ARs) account for a large fraction of cool-season precipitation extremes in Arizona and produce widespread precipitation through interactions between synoptic scale forcing and complex terrain. Previous work identified two dominant synoptic regimes associated with extreme cool-season precipitation events in the Salt and Verde River Basins: Progressive Atmospheric Rivers (PARs) and Zonal Atmospheric Rivers (ZARs). However, the climatological prevalence of these regimes and their influence on numerical weather prediction remain less understood. In this study, we use Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) applied to more than 40 years of ERA5 500-hPa geopotential height data to examine the climatological occurrence of the PAR and ZAR synoptic patterns. The analysis demonstrates that both regimes are recurring large-scale wave patterns rather than characteristics of a limited event sample. We evaluate high-resolution numerical weather prediction simulations for an expanded set of 17 extreme cool-season precipitation events in the Salt and Verde River Basins, including 10 PAR and 7 ZAR cases, providing a more balanced assessment of precipitation forecast performance across the two synoptic regimes. The Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model is rerun using Global Forecasting System (GFS) forcing data to maintain consistency with the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) simulations. Sensitivity experiments are conducted using the Thompson and WSM6 microphysics schemes to investigate the influence of microphysical parameterization on precipitation forecasts. Model precipitation forecasts are evaluated using the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) precipitation estimates as a gridded dataset as well as multiple rain gauges throughout the Salt and Verde River Basins. Particular attention is given to differences in simulated hydrometeor fields, including mixing ratios of snow, graupel, and rain, to diagnose how cloud microphysical processes influence precipitation magnitude and spatial distribution across complex terrain. The expanded event set allows comparison of model performance and microphysical sensitivity between PAR and ZAR synoptic scale patterns. Results demonstrate that precipitation forecast errors vary between synoptic regimes and are associated with differences in the partitioning and evolution of frozen and liquid hydrometeors between the Thompson and WSM6 simulations. These findings provide insight into the physical sources of model precipitation biases and highlight the importance of synoptic regime and cloud microphysical representation when forecasting extreme AR precipitation events in the complex terrain of Arizona.

493952.title: Cloud Seeding Across Scales: Current Status and Future Research Needs (Invited Presentation)
493952.authors: Sarah A. Tessendorf, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO
493952.abstract: Cloud seeding is a technology primarily used for precipitation enhancement that was developed in the latter half of the 20th century following discoveries related to ice nucleation in the 1940s. Soon after these discoveries, researchers attempted to demonstrate the concept in numerous scientific studies, from precipitation enhancement to hail mitigation. The concept has even been utilized in research attempting to mitigate hurricanes and was used in military activities during Vietnam. In 1978, the Environmental Modification Convention (ENMOD) was signed prohibiting the use of environmental modifications, such as cloud seeding, as a form of warfare. After numerous experiments over multiple decades, in 2003 the National Research Council reported that the scientific consensus was that there was no conclusive evidence of the impacts of cloud seeding. In 2017, the Seeded and Natural Orographic Wintertime clouds: the Idaho Experiment (SNOWIE) project provided the first unambiguous observations of the impacts of airborne cloud seeding to enhance snowfall. Subsequent research and computer modeling developments have resulted in a renewed interest in the topic, especially for the purpose of precipitation enhancement given ongoing and worsening droughts in the western U.S. These efforts have largely focused on local-to-regional scale impacts over short timescales. In contrast, new research activities, such as the Japanese Moonshot Program, are studying if cloud seeding could mitigate natural disasters from larger-scale extreme precipitation and tropical cyclones. And on regional-to-global scales, some climate interventions research includes cloud seeding methods as a way of modifying cloud radiative properties to cool a warming planet, therefore seeking to impact not only larger spatial scales, but also longer timescales. These modern day research activities are advancing the science of cloud physics, meanwhile there are still numerous challenges to be addressed. This presentation shares the latest science about cloud seeding, how the technology is being used and how it’s being considered for use, as well as outlines some key challenges for research in the field.

493956.title: Potential Changes in Long-Duration Wind/Solar Energy Drought Events over the U.S.
493956.authors: Jared A. Lee, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. R. Siems-Anderson, S. E. Haupt, J. M. Wilczak, S. C. Pryor, X. Zhou, and R. J. Barthelmie
493956.abstract: While short-duration energy storage solutions like 4-h batteries can accommodate typical variability or forecast errors in wind/solar generation, longer-duration “droughts” in power output require different solutions for maintaining system resiliency and reliability. This is particularly true if droughts in both wind and solar generation simultaneously occur in a balancing region. To characterize the duration, frequency, and severity of wind and solar droughts in both historical and future climate, we use the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to generate high-resolution regional climate simulations to sample 40 years in both the historical (1960–1999) and future (2040–2079) climate states. The WRF domain covers North America at 12-km grid spacing and dynamically downscales a low-resolution climate model simulation (MPI-ESM1-2-LR, using shared socioeconomic pathway SSP5-8.5) performed for the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6). In this work we first convert the meteorological variables to estimated wind and solar capacity factors (CFs) using sample solar arrays and wind turbines at each grid point and hourly output time. Then we examine the size, intensity, frequency, and other climatological statistics of CF droughts for several durations (e.g., 1, 3, 7, and 30 days). We compare long-duration wind/solar energy production drought statistics in the WRF historical climate simulations to those derived from ERA5 reanalysis output. We also explore how wind/solar energy drought characteristics may change in the future climate scenario we downscaled with WRF.

493957.title: Machine Learning-Based Wind Gust Estimation Using Large-Scale Atmospheric and Geographic Predictors
493957.authors: Ekaterina A. Belash, SUNY, Albany, NY; SUNY, Albany, NY; SUNY, Albany, NY; and S. Basu
493957.abstract: Wind gusts are among the most hazardous atmospheric phenomena. Their short duration, strong spatial variability, and sensitivity to local surface characteristics make them difficult to represent accurately in numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. These NWP models also typically provide wind gust estimates at relatively coarse spatial and temporal resolutions. This study investigates the potential of machine learning to improve wind gust estimation by integrating large-scale atmospheric predictors with learned geographic representations. The proposed model uses key variables from a reanalysis dataset together with more than two hundred convective parameters from a simulated dataset. It also incorporates embeddings from a state-of-the-art geo- foundation model (Geo-FM). Wind gust observations from the New York State Mesonet (NYSM) are used as the target variable for model training and evaluation. A series of numerical experiments was conducted to assess the individual and combined contributions of the atmospheric datasets and to quantify the impact of Geo-FM embeddings. The inclusion of Geo-FM embeddings improved prediction accuracy at all NYSM stations relative to the reanalysis-only model. Improvements were also evident at the most challenging stations, where prediction errors were largest. Feature importance analysis was used to identify the atmospheric and geographic predictors that contributed most strongly to model performance. The analysis also revealed limitations related to the underrepresentation of extreme wind gusts in the training data and the coarse temporal resolution of the large-scale predictors. Case studies further indicate that warm-season convective wind events are more difficult to predict than cold- season events.

493958.title: Big Skies, Winding Paths: Finding My Place in STEM
493958.authors: Marissa Anne Vara, UCAR, Boulder, CO
493958.abstract: I grew up in the southern tip of the Texas hill country, surrounded by big blue skies, mesquite trees for miles, and roaring rivers to jump into. Long before I had language for it, these landscapes sparked a quiet curiosity about how it all worked together to create the world I saw around me. But I had no idea this curiosity was something I could study, and no sense that being an Earth scientist could be a career. I thought being a scientist was reserved for those headed into medicine. That changed when I was accepted into GeoFORCE Texas, a field-based outreach program connecting rural and urban students to the Earth system sciences (ESS) firsthand. That spark carried me through a B.S. in geoscience at the University of Texas at Austin and an M.S. in geography, focused on paleoclimatology, at Louisiana State University. My pathway since has been anything but linear, spanning environmental state government, federal science policy, K-12 science education, and academic research, before landing in my current role as a Higher Education Specialist at the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR) Center for Science Education, where I lead the U.S. National Science Foundation Significant Opportunities in Atmospheric Research and Science (NSF SOARS) program. In this presentation, I will trace how each stage of my journey, including moments of doubt about whether I belonged in STEM, shaped the mentoring strategies I now use with students across a range of communities and backgrounds. I'll offer practical takeaways on how a single moment of exposure, like a week in the field, can open a STEM pathway, and how embracing rather than hiding a winding career can make mentors more effective guides for the next generation.

493963.title: Effects of Ignition Technique, Method, and Pattern on Prescribed Fire Behavior and Downwind Population Exposure: A Case Study of Fort Benning
493963.authors: Zhuoxiao Wu, Colorado State University, FORT COLLINS, CO; and Z. Li, H. Zhu, C. Hoffman, J. R. Pierce, A. Wilson, J. Burkhardt, C. L'Orange, S. H. Jathar, and J. Volckens
493963.abstract: Prescribed burning is an effective land management tool for reducing wildfire risk. Unlike wildfire, it is intentionally ignited and carried out under controlled conditions. However, both wildfire and prescribed fire produce smoke that degrades air quality and harms human health. Therefore, a critical challenge is how to conduct prescribed burning safely and effectively to reduce fuel loads while limiting smoke exposure. Ignition technique (e.g. backing fire, flanking fire, and strip head fire), method (e.g. drip torch and helitorch), and pattern (e.g. number of ignition lines) are factors that burn managers directly control, yet their influence on fire behavior and downwind exposure has rarely been studied. In this study, we focused on a 1,043-acre unit in Fort Benning, Georgia burned on April 24, 2022. On that day, winds carried smoke toward Columbus County, Georgia, a populated area with several schools. To understand the effects of ignition technique, method, and pattern on fire behavior and downwind exposure, we used WRF-SFIRE, a coupled fire-atmosphere model that simulates fire spread, plume dynamics, and smoke transport. We designed seven simulations that varied only in ignition technique, method, and pattern. The base case simulated drip torch ignition with five strip head fire lines. To assess ignition method impacts, we increased the ignition line speed from 1.2 m/s in the base case to 20 m/s, an estimate of helitorch ignition speed. For ignition technique, defined as the orientation of the firing lines relative to the wind, we replaced the base case head fire with a backing fire, a flanking fire, and a center-and-ring fire. For the ignition pattern, we changed the number of ignition lines from five in the base case to two and ten. We analyzed fire spread rate, burned area, fuel consumption, emissions, and population exposure under different simulation scenarios. Compared to the base simulation, the backing fire had a slow spread rate and burned only 13% of the unit’s area during the ignition period (11:40 to 20:00 local time). Consequently, it also produced the lowest emissions and exposure. However, the ranking changes when exposure is normalized by emissions. The backing fire delivered the highest exposure per unit emission among all simulations, 22% above the baseline, while the center-and-ring fire was the most efficient at emitting smoke without exposing people, at 18% below the baseline. Overall, ignition design can affect both the effectiveness of fuel removal and the per-emission exposure of downwind communities.

493968.title: Seasonal Hybrid Prediction and Sources of Predictability of Eastern Pacific Tropical Cyclone Activity
493968.authors: Chuan-Chieh Chang, PNNL, West Richland, WA; and S. Zhao, L. R. Leung, S. W. Lubis, M.Sc, Ph.D.,, P. M. Kooloth, H. Li, and S. G. Yeager
493968.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) are among the most severe storm systems on Earth. Skillful seasonal prediction of TCs can improve preparedness and mitigate their destructive impacts, and is therefore of significant socioeconomic value. Seasonal forecasts are now routinely issued by several agencies prior to the hurricane/typhoon season for the North Atlantic and western North Pacific. Comparatively, fewer groups produce widely available seasonal TC forecasts for the eastern Pacific (EPAC), and the underlying sources of predictability remain somewhat elusive. In this study, we develop a hybrid statistical-dynamical model to predict the interannual variations of EPAC TC activity and investigate the underlying sources of predictability. A Poisson model is developed using predictors from initialized CESM2 and E3SMv2 hindcasts, including relative sea surface temperature (RSST) and upper-ocean heat content (UOHC) averaged over the EPAC main development region (MDR), RSST over the Atlantic subpolar gyre (SPG), and spring sea ice concentration over the Barents Sea. The hybrid model skillfully predicts June–November basinwide TC frequency, named storm days (NSD), accumulated cyclone energy (ACE), hurricane days (HD), and major hurricane days (MHD) over 1971–2019. Using May-initialized hindcasts, the correlation coefficients between observed and predicted TC frequency, NSD, ACE, HD, and MHD reach 0.62, 0.73, 0.71, 0.66, and 0.58, respectively. Sub-basin forecast experiments reveal that seasonal TC activity over the western portion of the EPAC (west of 112°W) is more predictable than that near Central America (east of 112°W). Further investigation of the contributions from individual predictors indicates that Atlantic SPG RSST provides the greatest added value to the overall predictive skill across the various TC metrics. Predictive information from EPAC MDR RSST and UOHC also improves the skill of the Poisson model, albeit to a lesser extent than Atlantic SPG RSST. The physical basis for the predictive power of Atlantic SPG RSST is further assessed. Anomalously warm SPG SST tends to occur in tandem with positive SST anomalies over the tropical North Atlantic. To disentangle the relative roles of tropical and extratropical North Atlantic SST anomalies in EPAC TC activity, we analyze idealized experiments in which SSTs are separately nudged over the tropical and extratropical North Atlantic. Results show that anomalously cool SSTs, stronger vertical wind shear, weaker mid-tropospheric ascent, and a lower genesis potential index are present over the tropical central-to-eastern Pacific when warm SST anomalies are imposed over the tropical North Atlantic. In contrast, these large-scale environmental conditions show no significant changes in experiments with SST restoring confined to the extratropical North Atlantic. Overall, the modeling evidence suggests that tropical North Atlantic SST anomalies exert a much stronger influence on EPAC TC activity than SST variations in the extratropical North Atlantic. The substantial added value of SPG RSST to predictive skill therefore arises, in part, from the linkage between tropical Atlantic SST variability and EPAC TC activity. Whether SPG RSST also implicitly captures the influences of climate modes beyond tropical North Atlantic SST variability warrants further investigation. Likewise, the physical mechanisms linking variations in RSST and UOHC over the EPAC MDR to regional TC activity remain to be clarified.

493970.title: Changing Autumn Storm Impacts In the Bering Strait: A Community-Engaged Assessment Using Coupled High-Resolution Community Earth System Model (CESM) Data
493970.authors: Alice DuVivier, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and M. W. Seefeldt, K. Erickson, M. M. Holland, K. M. Krumhardt, and L. L. Landrum
493970.abstract: Strong Autumn storms in the Bering Sea region have long been particularly impactful on local communities. During the months of September to November, when there is low to no sea ice cover, strong southwest winds associated with storms can act as a plow to push water inland and cause major community flooding. Flooding associated with these types of storms has been recorded in Nome since the late 1800’s. A large storm in November 1979 caused widespread Bering Sea flooding, and more recently there have been major regional flooding associated with autumn storms in 2011, 2022, 2024, and 2025. Additionally, in the past five years there have been three ex-typhoons that have impacted the Bering Strait region and caused widespread community damage. Climate change can lead to more extreme community impacts due to decreased sea ice cover, higher sea level, more storms, or stronger storms with higher wind speeds and increased precipitation rates. This study presents results of a community-engaged research project with local experts from three communities across the Bering Strait region: Savoonga, Shishmaref, and Unalakleet, Alaska. Through regular collaborator meetings we identify the major factors associated with autumn storms that pose hazards to communities. Then we use data from the MESACLIP dataset, which uses a high resolution coupled configuration of the Community Earth System Model (CESM) version 1 with historical and RCP6.0 greenhouse gas forcing. High resolution is important for this study to adequately resolve autumn storms, including those that may have originated as typhoons. Data from nine MESACLIP ensemble members are used with the method of self-organizing maps (SOMs), a machine learning algorithm, to categorize storm types and identify those that are most impactful for the Bering Strait communities. We find that these storms become more common in future decades when there is less sea ice. While events with exceptionally high waves (>15 ft.) and high precipitation (>1.5”/day) remain uncommon, there is a 2-3x increase in events in the local communities. Additionally, the frequency of compound hazards with both high waves and precipitation roughly doubles. This type of information can influence community members’ planning and preparation for future storm impacts.

493973.title: A comparative assessment of twenty-year air pollution and meteorology data in Corpus Christi, Laredo, and Lower Rio Grande Valley regions of South Texas.
493973.authors: Mahad Rizwan, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, Brownsville, TX
493973.abstract: Over the past two decades, South Texas has experienced enormous growth in economic, industrial and cross-border activities. However, the effect of these developments on the long-term air pollution patterns and the role of meteorological parameters on these patterns is a crucial field of study. This research examines a multi-year spatial and temporal variability in PM2.5, PM10, ozone, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide in three South Texas regions of Rio Grande Valley, Laredo and Corpus Christi starting from 2005 until 2025. We took into account various meteorological parameters such as wind speed, wind direction and temperature to evaluate their relationship with pollution trends throughout the years. The hourly concentrations and meteorological observations were measured at 14 Continuous Ambient Monitoring sites (CAMS) at the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) stations. Generalized Additive Model (GAM) will be used in our analysis to evaluate the non-linear association between meteorological observations and pollution concentrations. Seasonal and annual assessments will also be conducted using the Thielsen trend analysis to compare the pollution trends across the regions as well. This long-term study provides us with a valuable insight into the evolution of pollution trends in South Texas amid continued growth in the oil and gas industry along with an increase in the cross-border activities.

493975.title: Evaluating High-Resolution Prognostic Meteorological Data for Atmospheric Boundary Layer Parameterization and Regulatory Dispersion Modeling in Colorado's Complex Terrain
493975.authors: Gustavo Copstein Cuchiara, Colorado Department of Public Health & Environment, Denver, CO; and J. Turk, I. T. Ku, C. Youatt, A. White, P. McKean, M. Hacker, and V. Kumar
493975.abstract: Regulatory air dispersion models such as U.S. EPA’s AERMOD, a steady-state plume model used to estimate pollutant concentrations from industrial sources, depend on accurate meteorological inputs to produce reliable estimates of planetary boundary layer (PBL) structure and surface turbulent fluxes. In Colorado, traditional National Weather Service (NWS) surface meteorological observations are limited by large spatial gaps and the state’s complex terrain. These challenges are combined by recent nationwide helium shortages, which resulted in the elimination of upper air observations collected by radiosounds launched at Denver International Airport. The airport historically provided vertical soundings necessary to parameterize convective boundary layer heights and stability parameters in AERMOD meteorological datasets. To evaluate alternative data sets for regulatory modeling applications, this study performed a sensitivity analysis of a five-year (2020–2024) dataset developed from Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model output generated by the National Center for Atmospheric Research. Modeled at 1-km horizontal resolution, the prognostic meteorological dataset incorporated advanced data assimilation techniques to better represent meteorological conditions across Colorado's diverse regions. AERMOD simulations were completed using standard NWS observations and were compared with simulations using the 1-km WRF prognostic dataset across representative Colorado microclimates, including the Eastern Plains, Front Range and Foothills, Alpine and Subalpine regions near the Continental Divide, and the Western Slope. To isolate the effects of meteorological inputs on dispersion results, generic facilities representative of common Colorado air permit sources were developed, incorporating point, area, and volume emissions sources. Simulations using both meteorological datasets evaluated how differences in transport parameters (wind speed and direction) and turbulent diffusion parameters (e.g., Monin-Obukhov length, convective/mechanical mixing heights, surface roughness length, Bowen ratio, and sensible heat flux) affect short-term peak averaging periods (1-hour and 24-hour 1st highest concentrations), statistical design values representing the 98th percentile forms of the short-term NO2 and PM2.5 National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) (e.g., 8th highest concentrations) and Annual averaging concentration periods. Comparative analysis identified similarities and differences in micrometeorological parameters and resulting concentration fields between the NWS observational and WRF prognostic datasets. These findings highlight the strengths and limitations of high-resolution prognostic meteorology for regulatory dispersion modeling and provide insights on the feasibility of WRF-based inputs for AERMOD, particularly in complex terrain and regions with limited observational data.

493977.title: Beyond Spectral Signatures: Temporal-Spectral Machine Learning for Geostationary Cloud, Aerosol, and Aerosol Subtype Detection
493977.authors: Yingxi Rona Shi, Univ. of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC), Baltimore, MD; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD; and M. Humaira, X. Huang, H. Yu, Z. Zhang, J. Zheng, and C. Wang
493977.abstract: Accurate cloud and aerosol classification from geostationary satellites remains challenging, especially when distinguishing features that looks similar in spectral signals. We present six machine learning models: Random Forest, LSTM, CNN, ConvLSTM, ConvLSTM-UNet, and a novel hybrid LSTM-RF model, for classifying clouds, aerosols, and aerosol subtypes using nine GOES-R ABI channels plus three derived parameters. Training data were labeled by domain experts, with testing validated against collocated CALIOP retrievals. Our central contribution, the LSTM-RF hybrid, encodes temporal-spectral features via LSTM and performs final classification through Random Forest, achieving over 0.95 accuracy in training and testing. This design excels at separating thin aerosol plumes from temporally stationary surface features, a key limitation of spectral-only approaches. Monthly mean cloud fractions from the model align closely with MODIS climatology, confirming robustness at climatological scales. Compared against the NOAA Aerosol Detection Product (ADP) over ocean, the operational standard for dust/smoke detection, the LSTM-RF model shows improved classification performance, demonstrating the added value of temporal information in geostationary retrievals. These results demonstrate the potential of temporally-aware ML approaches to advance satellite-based aerosol and cloud characterization. We discuss remaining limitations, including large viewing angles, thin aerosol detection, and cloud-edge contamination, and outline directions for future model refinement.

493978.title: Precipitation Without Precipitation: Understanding and Diagnosing Precipitation from the Atmospheric State
493978.authors: Yongxin Liu, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and H. Chen and L. Xue
493978.abstract: Machine learning models are now widely applied to atmospheric downscaling and weather forecasting, typically ingesting large set of input variables selected by convention rather than by measured contributions. To understand and diagnose precipitation processes, it is often unclear how much the analytic models rely on the precipitation field itself or other atmospheric variables if precipitation field is used as an input. If other variables are used, which subset of them are the most important features that can infer precipitation. To address those questions, we train a transformer-based machine learning model over the contiguous United States using CONUS404 data as both input and target labels, in order to map the atmospheric state at times t and t−1 to the state at t+1 on the native 4 km CONUS404 grid. The input predictors include geopotential, temperature, horizontal winds, and relative humidity on eight pressure levels from 850 to 200 hPa, together with surface fields including 2 m temperature and dewpoint, 10 m winds, sea-level and surface pressure, surface CAPE, integrated vapor transport, total column water vapor, latent heat flux and soil moisture. Precipitation is excluded from the input, and the model is designed to infer precipitation from the dynamic and thermodynamic predictors. Predicted precipitation is then evaluated against the CONUS404 reference for placement, wet-area extent, and intensity distribution. Given that precipitation proves recoverable from the input variables, we apply gradient-based attribution to the trained transformer, accumulating the sensitivity of predicted precipitation to each input channel over testing samples to rank the variables that the model relies on. The resulting rankings provide a physically interpretable basis for input variable selection at convection-permitting scale, allowing forecast models to prioritize the variables that carry more information about precipitation.

493980.title: GOES-R EUVS Measurements and Degradation Calibrations
493980.authors: James Forest Mothersbaugh III, University of Colorado Boulder, Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES), Boulder, CO, Boulder, CO; NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), Boulder, CO, Boulder, CO; and J. Machol, S. V. Penton, M. Snow, and A. M. Mahon
493980.abstract: The Extreme Ultraviolet Sensor (EUVS) instrument on the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite R-Series (GOES-R) measures disk-averaged solar irradiance at 7 wavelengths in the ultraviolet region of the spectrum, and provide the Mg II index, used as a proxy for solar activity. These irradiance measurements are a unique record of high-cadence, long-term solar irradiance data. The instruments require regular calibration adjustments to correct for degradation in the irradiance measurements. These calibrations prevent incorrect trending in the irradiance data and are important for ensuring consistency between different satellites and across multiple solar cycles. Ongoing calibration updates are also important for maintaining accurate data for composite products that combine multiple data sources from different satellites, such as the Mg II composite as detailed in companion presentations by Penton et al. and Snow et al. at this conference. We present the methods used to model and apply the degradation corrections in the GOES-R EUVS instruments and show the effects of the degradation corrections in the irradiance data. Additionally, we present plans for future improvements to these degradation calibrations.

493982.title: Short History of LASCO and Its Role in Space Weather Forecasting
493982.authors: Russell Alfred Howard, Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD; and K. Battams and A. Vourlidas
493982.abstract: In this talk we will provide an abbreviated history of the SOHO/LASCO mission and the pivotal role it has played in the national and international space weather forecasting effort. Discussions of the instrument “The Large Angle and Spectrometric Coronagraph” (LASCO) began in 1983, when Dr. Rainer Schwenn of the Max-Planck-Institute for Aeronomy in Lindau, Germany, came to the Naval Research Lab for our collaboration comparing Helios in situ plasma and magnetic field data with images from the Solwind coronagraph on the USAF Space Test Program P78-1 spacecraft. We also discussed collaborating on a coronagraphic instrument to observe the corona for an upcoming mission being discussed by ESA – which became known as the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) and was an international collaboration between ESA and NASA. LASCO data have been prominent in advancing our understanding of coronal mass ejections and their significance for space weather, with four key differences from previous coronagraphic missions. First, it had a large field of view, extending out to 32 solar radii, over 3 times further out than previous instruments. Second, the charge-coupled-device detector provided a much greater dynamic range and lower noise than the previous film and vidicon detection techniques. Third, the SOHO mission was at the L1 Lagrangian point, which gave 24-hour coverage of the Sun, capturing all events, as opposed to the day/night cycle of previous missions. Fourth, the LASCO team was an international collaboration providing an innovative set of 3 complementary instruments leading to a diverse science team that greatly enhanced the science return and operational value from this instrument.

493985.title: Validation of Ionospheric Tomographic Models Assimilating PlanetiQ Radio Occultations and Ground-Based TEC Observations
493985.authors: Chunming Wang, PlanetiQ, Manhattan Beach, CA; and E. R. Kursinski and A. hunter
493985.abstract: Monitoring space weather and applications involving radio wave propagation requires accurate measurements of the ionosphere electron density profile. We develop regional ionospheric tomographic models using both Kalman Filter (KF) and Extended KF (EKF) that assimilate GNSS total electron content (TEC) measurements from PlanetiQ GNSS radio occultation (GNSS-RO) and from the International GNSS Service (IGS) ground-based stations. The ionosphere is represented by a regional 3D voxel grid. Three options for observation assimilation are evaluated: (1) GNSS-RO only, (2) IGS only, and (3) combined GNSS-RO and IGS TEC, to quantify their respective contributions to reconstructing the regional Ne structure. Both the KF and EKF use the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI-2020) to provide both the prior estimation for Ne, as well as, for its error covariance. While the state for the KF is the Ne at the model grid points, the state for EKF consists of an eight-parameter ionospheric representation derived from IRI. Tomographic reconstructions are evaluated against collocated incoherent scatter radar (ISR) and ionosonde observations. The OSSE results demonstrate that the EKF reduces the TEC RMSE by up to ~97% relative to its prior state. Assimilation of real GNSS-RO and ground GNSS measurements show promising performance when compared with ISR and ionosonde data. Specifically, the relative performance of the three observation configurations is analyzed to assess the complementary strengths of GNSS-RO and ground-based TEC observations. These results provide insight into the optimal integration of space- and ground-based GNSS observations for ionospheric tomography and future operational Ne specification and GNSS-RO constellation configurations.

493987.title: Withdrawn: Improving Global Atmospheric Composition Forecasts with the NASA GEOS-CF System
493987.authors: Viral Shah, Goddard Earth Sciences Technology and Research II, Morgan State University, and GMAO, Greenbelt, MD; and P. Wales, C. A. Malings, PhD, M. Abdi-Oskouei, J. V. Ardizzone, J. E. Barre, N. Balashov, S. Basu, F. Liu, M. Long, R. Lucchesi, M. E. Manyin, R. M. Mecikalski, S. Roberts, T. Tobin, K. Wargan, B. Weir, J. Sleeman, K. E. Knowland, L. Ott, and S. Pawson
493987.abstract: The NASA GEOS-CF (Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast) system offers near-real-time analysis and five-day forecasts of global atmospheric composition as part of the Global Modeling and Assimilation Office’s (GMAO’s) suite of forecast and reanalysis products based on the GEOS Earth System Model. The GEOS-CF system embeds the GEOS-Chem atmospheric chemistry model within GEOS, allowing chemistry and transport to be simulated at the same temporal and spatial resolution as the meteorology. GEOS-CF data are widely used for atmospheric chemistry research, air quality and health applications, and to support NASA’s satellite, suborbital and ground-based missions. We present an overview of GEOS-CF’s performance and capabilities and describe ongoing work to improve the system’s accuracy and efficiency. GEOS-CF was recently updated to include assimilation of satellite observations of ozone columns and profiles and new model physics and chemistry. Following these updates, the model shows broad agreement with observations of ozone, NO2 and PM2.5 in the stratosphere and troposphere. However, the model shows a high bias in surface ozone over the US, and we examine the sources of this error. Ongoing development efforts focus on increasing the model’s spatial resolution, advancing data assimilation, and improving computational efficiency. We present early results from experiments using a higher vertical resolution configuration of GEOS and evaluation of the performance of an AI forecast emulator for key GEOS-CF species.

493990.title: Future Changes In North Atlantic Tropical Cyclone Intraseasonal Variability Associated with the Madden-Julian Oscillation
493990.authors: Chuan-Chieh Chang, PNNL, West Richland, WA; and L. R. Leung, S. W. Lubis, M.Sc, Ph.D.,, Z. Chen, K. Balaguru, S. M. Hagos, M. Zhao, K. Yoshida, H. Murakami, and H. C. Liang
493990.abstract: A better understanding of how the influence of the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) on Atlantic tropical cyclones (TCs) will change in the future has important implications for emergency planning. In this study, we examine how future North Atlantic TC activity may be modulated by the MJO using the Database for Policy Decision-Making for Future Climate Change (d4PDF), a TC-permitting large-ensemble dataset. Consistent with observations, d4PDF simulates significant changes in basin-wide TC activity between phases 2–3 and phases 6–7 during the historical period. Future ensemble-mean projections indicate that phase-to-phase swings in basin-wide Atlantic TC activity may diminish, implying a weakened MJO influence. Nevertheless, projected changes in the MJO–TC relationship show pronounced uncertainty. Variations in intraseasonal TC variability are significantly correlated with changes in MJO convection over the Atlantic main development region (MDR). Compared with future simulations characterized by slightly enhanced MJO convection, projections with strongly suppressed MJO convection in the MDR exhibit weaker phase-to-phase fluctuations in lower-tropospheric diabatic potential vorticity production. Consequently, intraseasonal variability in African easterly waves (i.e., TC seeds) is reduced in these projections. Furthermore, relative to projections characterized by stronger MJO convection, those with muted MJO convection exhibit a thermodynamic mean state less favorable for sustained intraseasonal convection, as indicated by lower advective moistening efficiency (alpha), which is strongly modulated by local SST warming. Finally, changes in alpha alone cannot explain the response of MJO convection over the Atlantic MDR across different warming scenarios, whereas changes in alpha and mean-state saturation deficit together offer greater explanatory power.

493991.title: Machine Learning and Hyperparameter Tuning for Operational Cold-Stunning Predictions in Espiritu Santo Bay, Texas
493991.authors: Ayesha Khan, Texas A&M Univ.-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX; and H. M. Marrero Colominas, M. C. White, P. E. Tissot, C. Duff, B. Berger, A. Berger, and R. Hardy
493991.abstract: Green sea turtles are a threatened species in the United States and are at high risk of becoming cold-stunned during cold water events in Texas bays. Cold-stunning events, which occur when sudden drops in water temperature elicit a hypothermic reaction in cold-blooded animals, cause sea turtles to become weak and lethargic. In this vulnerable state, sea turtles float to the water’s surface and ashore which exposes them to harsher air temperatures, injury from boats, and predation. The water temperature threshold for significant sea turtle cold-stunning is 8°C which has recently been reached at least yearly in shallow water habitats. Espiritu Santo Bay is an extension of San Antonio Bay where green sea turtles are documented as year-round residents feeding on seagrass. Due to its shallow depths, the bay is prone to rapidly cooling temperatures during the cold front season, typically November through March, and is thus a known hub for significant cold-stunning of green sea turtles and other sea life. Rescue efforts necessitate gathering and organizing volunteers, preparing rescue boats, and planning for the transport of cold-stunned sea turtles to rehabilitation centers. As a result, there is a critical need for accurate predictions of the occurrence and timing of these events in this area so that stakeholders can make preparations. The goal of this research is to develop an operational machine learning model that accurately predicts cold-stunning events using a two-step modeling process. The model incorporates the most relevant temperatures measured at real-time Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON) stations to represent bay-wide air and water temperature conditions, while assuming the bay to be isothermal during cold-stunning events. In order to do so, this research utilizes data collected by four TCOON stations located around – but outside of – Espiritu Santo Bay and data from two air and water temperature measurement campaigns conducted during the winters of 2023-2024 and 2024-2025. Water and air temperature data were collected by Hobo sensors located within the bay during the winter of 2023-2024, and water temperature was collected using a modified Telonics buoy during the winter of 2024-2025. Exploration of this data revealed that the average temperatures measured within Espiritu Santo Bay corresponded relatively well with the mean temperatures measured by the four TCOON stations surrounding the bay (i.e., Port O’Connor, Seadrift, Port Lavaca, and Aransas Wildlife Refuge), thus leading to the provision of a representative nowcasting model of the bay temperature conditions. Subsequently, past air and water temperatures from the nowcasting model and air temperature predictions for Espiritu Santo Bay are used as inputs in the predictive water temperature model. A Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) model using the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) loss function was chosen to predict future water temperatures in Espiritu Santo Bay and trained utilizing four-fold cross validation based on yearly TCOON data from September 2020 through August 2025. This cross-validation approach was used to assess variability of the model calibration and performance during different cold water conditions. Additional data preprocessing steps included normalization of the data, which was critical for model performance during inference on the most extreme cold event since the eighties, 2021’s Winter Storm Uri. Performance of the MLP was analyzed with the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) metric for all water temperatures as well as for water temperatures below 12°C (a conditionalized metric designated as MAE12). Hyperparameter tuning was conducted in a 3-phase approach. The first phase consisted of a 3-repetition grid-search campaign for 21 forecast lead times and 4 folds with a search space consisting of activation functions, number of layers, number of neurons, and dropout rates. In phase 2, the top 20 combinations with the highest mean validation MAE12 were selected for further tuning to a total of 10 repetitions. Phase 3 consisted of manual analysis via a hyperparameter performance visualization tool and consisted of analyzing the stability of each hyperparameter combination across repetitions and cross-validation folds. One final selection was made for each of the 21 lead times based on rank stability score and MAE12 performance of the models. The operational model performance was tested on an independent testing set on 12, 48, 96, and 120 hour lead times. Outcomes of this research provide both a systematic method to calibrate operational AI models for the coastal environment, leveraging the network of state and federal tide gauges, and operational predictions specific to potential cold stunning events in Espiritu Santo Bay with up to a 120-hour lead time. The predictions give rescuers and stakeholders time to prepare for the events including planning for the rescue of cold-stunned sea turtles and other measures to help mitigate impacts on environmental and recreational activities.

493992.title: Using PlanetiQ Polarimetric GNSS Radio Occultation to Observe Cloud and Precipitation Features Across Spatiotemporal Scales
493992.authors: Kevin J. Nelson, PlanetiQ, Golden, CO; and E. R. Kursinski and X. Feng
493992.abstract: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) radio occultation (RO) is well established as an all-weather measurement of atmospheric pressure, temperature, and water vapor content in the form of atmospheric refractivity. Much like dual-polarized weather radar, GNSS right-hand circularly polarized (RCP) signals can be decomposed into their linear horizontally and vertically polarized components. When RO ray paths intersect precipitation or clouds where hydrometeors are preferentially oriented in the horizontal (vertical) direction (rather than stochastically), the propagation of the horizontal (vertical) polarization will be slowed slightly relative to the vertical (horizontal), resulting in a phase delay difference. Measuring this phase shift provides a measurement of the integrated cloud and precipitation particles along the ray path. In this way, the polarimetric GNSS-RO (GNSS-PRO) ray paths act as a forward-scattering, rather than traditional backscattering weather radar. Ground-based dual-linearly polarized weather radars produce significantly more accurate estimates of rain rate than their RCP counterparts. Furthermore, spaceborne radar and passive microwave observations are unable to detect the axial ratios of cloud and precipitation particles due to their downward looking geometry. As such, GNSS-PRO provides unique information critical to converting spaceborne radar and microwave observations to rain rates while also providing critical thermodynamic variables coincident with precipitation measurements via information about the preferential orientation of hydrometeors. This study examines PlanetiQ GNSS-PRO observations and assesses the noise level of GNSS-PRO differential phase shift observations from PlanetiQ. Colocations with other colocated ground-based and remote sensing observations are also performed, allowing for evaluation of GNSS-PRO data products. Observations from a variety of precipitating and cloudy regimes, such as atmospheric rivers, tropical cyclones, frontal precipitation, and differences across the seasons are also included. Previous observations of differential phase shift from PlanetiQ and ROHP-PAZ indicate differential phase shift maxima over 20-25 mm, which indicates heavy precipitation (e.g., R > 6.0 mm hr-1). Brightband-like features are also observed, much like those detected with weather radar at and just below the freezing level, which enhances the differential phase shift due to the particle surface melting. Additionally, cloud and precipitation signatures have been observed up to 16 km so far, indicating that the strongest updrafts could create differential phase shift signatures upward of 20 km along with signatures from surrounding anvil clouds.

493993.title: Next Generation Geostationary Atmospheric Composition Instruments: Performance Enhancements and Lessons Learned
493993.authors: Dennis Nicks, BAE Systems Space and Mission Systems, Boulder, CO; and T. Delker, B. Farris, M. Shogrin, and S. drobot
493993.abstract: The Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO), Geostationary Environment Monitoring Spectrometer (GEMS) and the Sentinel 4 UVN instruments represent a new era of monitoring atmospheric composition from space. These UV/Vis geostationary observatories provide hourly, high spatial resolution measurements of key trace gases such as nitrogen dioxide (NO2), ozone (O3), formaldehyde (CH2O), sulfur dioxide (SO2), glyoxal (C2H2O2), as well as aerosol optical depth. These high spatial and temporal resolution measurements have multiple societal and scientific benefits, such as improved public health protection, enhanced air quality forecasts, tracking harmful chemical plumes from wildfires, and monitoring point, and area sources of emissions. As a global expansion of these sensors is being envisioned and plans for replenishment of existing observatories are in development, there is an opportunity to enhance performance of these systems through the incorporation of modern technologies and lessons learned from the initial development. Improvements in detector technologies can increase sensor spatial coverage by at least 50%, while retaining both high spatial and temporal resolution. Enhancements to the instruments, first order impacts to the optical and mechanical designs and resulting benefits to observations for these next generation, geostationary atmospheric composition sensors will be presented.

493995.title: The Application of a Snowpack Runoff Decision Support System for Rain-on-Snow Events
493995.authors: Anne Heggli, DRI, Reno, NV; and B. J. Hatchett, A. Chen, T. Bardsley, J. Moore, M. Imgarten, and P. Fickenscher
493995.abstract: Accurately forecasting hydrologic outcomes of rain-on-snow (ROS) events is critical for water management and flood mitigation, not only in the western U.S., but globally. This study further refines a Snowpack Runoff Decision Support System (SR-DSS) using hourly Natural Resource Conservation Service SNOw TELemetry (SNOTEL) data to identify thresholds for present weather and antecedent snowpack conditions that favor liquid water input into soils. This study applies the revised SR-DSS to the unimpaired Upper Carson River watershed in the eastern Sierra Nevada, USA. We compare the SR-DSS detection of ROS liquid water input potential to observed soil moisture, streamflow, and an existing operational snowpack-runoff model framework (SNOW-17 and SAC-SMA). Information provided by the SR-DSS enables forecasters to make real-time adjustments to SNOW-17 parameters, including rain-snow temperature thresholds or melt factors, as conditions evolve in ways that the model alone might not capture. We provide the predictive probability (0.43–0.83) for the SR-DSS thresholds that identify the potential of ROS liquid water input from 2006 to 2022. Multiple case studies demonstrate that the SR-DSS alone captures the onset of liquid water input and provides evidence of how it can help performance assessment of operational models (SNOW-17 and SAC-SMA). Our results demonstrate that SR-DSS can enhance situational awareness by providing snowpack and weather conditions in a time-relevant manner for forecasting and decision-making. Increasing the technical readiness and capability for integration into operations of the SR-DSS through further development and evaluation will enhance the resiliency and flexibility of water management systems.

493996.title: Environmental Controls on Seasonal and Diurnal Cloud Fraction Variability Across Continental U.S. ARM Sites
493996.authors: Michael P. Jensen, DOE, Upton, NY; and M. Deng, K. Johnson, and A. Zhou
493996.abstract: Understanding the processes that govern cloud occurrence and precipitation is central to improving predictions of the terrestrial water cycle and supports the U.S. Department of Energy's Water for Energy mission. Long-term observations from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) user facility provide a unique opportunity to investigate how cloud evolution responds to large-scale forcing, regional thermodynamics, and mesoscale processes across diverse meteorological environments. In this study, we compare the seasonal and diurnal evolution of cloud fraction at three recent ARM deployments: Coastal-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE; Baltimore, Maryland), Tracking Aerosol Convection interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER; Houston, Texas), and the Bankhead National Forest site (BNF; Northern Alabama). Cloud occurrence is characterized using the Active Remote Sensing of CLouds (ARSCL) product derived from Ka-band ARM Zenith Radar observations. Radiosonde-derived thermodynamic parameters together with synoptic weather regime classifications are used to identify the environmental controls on cloud variability. The three sites exhibit distinct seasonal cloud regimes and markedly different summertime cloud evolution despite similarities in their large-scale circulation during portions of the warm season. Seasonal increases in tropopause height and convective available potential energy (CAPE) are associated with enhanced upper-tropospheric cloud occurrence and afternoon deep convection. Although anticyclonic weather regimes dominate during summer at both the CoURAGE and TRACER sites, their cloud diurnal cycles differ substantially, demonstrating that similar synoptic forcing can produce markedly different cloud evolution. At the TRACER site, mesoscale processes, including bay-breeze circulations and cold-pool outflows, strongly influence the timing and persistence of afternoon cloud development. Comparisons among the three sites further show that cloud vertical structure and diurnal variability are strongly modulated by geographic setting, moisture availability, and regional mesoscale processes. By combining long-term active remote sensing observations with thermodynamic and synoptic diagnostics across multiple ARM sites, this study identifies both common and region-specific controls on cloud evolution. These observational benchmarks improve our understanding of the physical processes linking clouds, precipitation, and the terrestrial water cycle, supporting DOE efforts to advance process understanding needed for Water for Energy applications.

493998.title: Weathering the Algorithm: Communicating Attribution Science with Clarity and Creativity
493998.authors: Shel D Winkley, Climate Central, Bryan, TX
493998.abstract: Attribution science has a hook most climate topics don’t: it helps to answer one of the “...but why?” questions many ask after extreme weather events. With every heat wave, flood, wildfire, or hurricane, meteorologists across the enterprise are being asked, “was this climate change?” The challenge we face in our current information and media landscape isn’t generating interest, but capturing the moment before it scrolls past. Audiences are increasingly finding scientists and meteorologists in short-form video and social feeds. Split-second decisions are being made about what’s worth more than a few breaths of attention – attribution findings, however stunning or rigorous, don’t automatically survive the format. This talk will break down best practices to translate extreme weather attribution into communication that is scroll-stopping rather than scroll-past, how to localize national and global data to a specific place or audience without sacrificing the science, and how to keep the conversation going once it starts – including in the comment sections where real engagement happens. Examining case studies from broadcast, digital, and social platforms, attendees will leave the room with sharper, ready-to-use approaches for turning attribution science into creative, engaging conversations – both in-person and online. When people ask why, this talk provides a moment to meet the question with clarity, credibility, and care...before the scroll moves on.

494000.title: Drivers of Coastal Flooding in Chesapeake Bay: Sea Level Rise and Land Subsidence Expand Flood Exposure
494000.authors: Shahryar K Ahmad, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and A. Getirana and S. V. Kumar
494000.abstract: Chesapeake Bay in the United States remains the most flood-prone region in the United States, where sea level rise, tides, storm surge, and land subsidence interact simultaneously at exceptional rates. Coastal flood impacts are often amplified by compound interactions among storm surge, heavy precipitation and river discharge. Yet most flood assessments remain event-focused, neglecting persistent coastal processes that continuously elevate baseline exposure. Here, using Chesapeake Bay as a high-exposure case study, we attribute coastal flooding over 1996-2024 to hydrologic forcing, tides, sea-level rise, and land subsidence by integrating decomposed tide-gauge observations with high-resolution hydrodynamic modeling. We find that tides dominate flood magnitude contributing most in six of eight events. In contrast, sea-level rise and land subsidence drive the multi-decadal increase in flooding with the former exposing 56% greater population than hydrologic flooding. This decoupling is overlooked in event-based hazard assessments and coincides with continued housing-market appreciation where flood trends are intensifying fastest. Our results show that coastal flood risk is increasingly governed by the timescale that a given driver operates on (event or trend), not only by elevation or coastal proximity, highlighting the need to reframe flood risk assessment around driver-specific temporal behavior rather than event magnitude in coastal regions worldwide.

494001.title: What's Behind the Map? Lessons from the U.S. Drought Monitor 101 Webinar Series
494001.authors: Lindsay E. Johnson, Univ. of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; National Drought Mitigation Center-University of Nebraska, LINCOLN, NE; and C. J. Riganti, B. Fuchs, and M. D. Svoboda
494001.abstract: The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) integrates multiple indicators, timescales, observed impacts, local expertise and author judgment to provide a weekly assessment of drought conditions across the U.S. While widely used to support drought planning and decision-making, the complexity of the assessment process can make it challenging for users to understand how classifications are determined, why conditions change and how different types of information contribute to the final map. Since 2024, the National Drought Mitigation Center (NDMC) has offered recurring USDM 101 webinars to explain the monitoring process and provide opportunities for users to interact directly with drought experts. Registration responses, live questions and post-webinar feedback provide insight into what users need from drought monitoring information and where barriers to understanding remain. Across multiple webinars, participants consistently express the greatest interest in the process behind the map. Questions frequently address how drought categories are determined, which datasets and indicators are considered, how evidence is weighed and how authors reach final decisions. Process and methodology represented the largest identified learning theme in both November 2025 and May 2026. Interest has continued as the audience has expanded, with registration for the August 2026 webinar reaching 500 participants. Participant questions also reveal an interest in how drought data become decisions. Users have asked how observed impacts and citizen-science reports are evaluated, how conflicting information is resolved, why classifications may respond slowly to precipitation and how timescale, local expertise and author judgment influence the map. Others want to know how they can contribute local information and apply USDM information within their own regions and professional roles. These questions highlight a key communication challenge: knowing which data are used does not necessarily explain how multiple sources of evidence converge into an actionable drought assessment. This presentation examines lessons from the USDM 101 webinar series from 2024 through 2026 as a case study in user-driven drought communication. The webinars provide a two-way feedback mechanism: drought experts can increase transparency around the monitoring and assessment process, while participant questions identify where users need additional context, explanation and opportunities to contribute. These lessons are informing future USDM education and communication efforts and demonstrate how sustained engagement between drought information providers and users can help make complex drought assessments more understandable, usable and relevant for decision-making.

494004.title: Machine-Learning Models for Retrieval of Cloud Properties from GNSS Radio Occultation
494004.authors: Chunming Wang, PlanetiQ, Manhattan Beach, CA; and K. J. Nelson and E. R. Kursinski
494004.abstract: Retrieval of cloud properties is a challenging area for environmental remote sensing. In addition to a cloud mask, properties such as cloud top and bottom heights, thickness, and cloud type are of critical importance for weather and climate prediction, as well as for determining the observability of the surface. Traditional passive imaging measurements of clouds at visible and IR wavelengths are largely limited to sensing cloud tops. In contrast, Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) signals received on Low Earth Orbiting (LEO) satellites penetrate through clouds. GNSS radio occultation (GNSS-RO) data from government missions like COSMIC-2 and from commercial entities like PlanetiQ have significantly enhanced numerical weather prediction (NWP) accuracy due to their very accurate, high vertical resolution measurements of atmospheric properties that complement traditional visible, infrared, and microwave satellite remote sensing platforms. While GNSS signals readily penetrate through clouds, the refractivity derived from GNSS-RO is proportional to atmospheric humidity and temperature, which are related to clouds, enabling the potential for characterizing cloud vertical structure indirectly. Furthermore, dual-linearly polarized RO, known as GNSS-PRO, can potentially sense certain types of ice clouds.These unique characteristics of GNSS-RO measurements present a valuable opportunity for cloud property remote sensing. First principle physics based retrieval of cloud property is extremely challenging due to the lack of additional parameters required by a physics-based model, as well as the extensive computational resources required. In similar applications of weather forecasting or remote sensing, empirical models trained by machine-learning methods using actual measurements have shown to be effective. PlanetiQ is developing a supervised machine-learning framework to retrieve cloud properties, including layered structures and cloud top/bottom heights from GNSS-RO observations. The model is trained on pairs of high-quality GNSS-RO observations from COSMIC-2 and PlanetiQ collocated with cloud properties from the European Space Agency's EarthCARE satellite cloud profiling radar, atmospheric lidar, and multispectral imager. Our models utilize GNSS-RO and NWP profiles—specifically pressure, temperature, humidity, and refractivity—as inputs to predict atmospheric cloudiness profiles, similar to those provided by EarthCARE data, which contains cloud flags and a number of microphysical and thermodynamic variables over 240 vertical levels along its ground track. Various ML techniques, such as logistic regression, support vector machines, and neural networks, are assessed to optimize retrieval performance. We will present initial RO-based cloud detection results from ML and comparisons to existing cloud and precipitation data for validation. As in all machine-learning experiments, the selection and preprocessing of components of the training data are essential in the success of the models. We also investigate the different options in preparation of training and verification datasets.

494005.title: Forecasting Snow Clearance on Behind-the-Meter Solar Assets: The Value of Downwelling Irradiance Forecasts for Cold-Weather Grid Operations
494005.authors: Marc Bremenkamp, Energy Forecasting Solutions, LLC, Norman, OK; and J. C. Collier
494005.abstract: Behind-the-meter (BTM) photovoltaic power generation challenges load forecasting for grid operators and, subsequently, grid reliability. Winter presents unique challenges for short-term solar power forecasting on grids exposed to cold weather climates. Heavy snow events can reduce the functional capacity of BTM assets by more than 90%. There is little visibility to snow coverage from installation to installation. Meanwhile, publicly available snow depth observations are limited in either temporal or spatial resolution and not always representative of snow depth on panels. Further, snow coverage can persist and impact generation for weeks after snowfall events, making the snow coverage condition at initialization of the solar power forecast critical to forecast accuracy. Currently, no ground-truth dataset documents the true effects of snow coverage on rooftop solar. Therefore, the performance of any snow cover model must be evaluated using the ratio of the actual solar generation to the delivered solar power forecast, and error in the power forecast introduces uncertainty in the evaluation of the snow cover model itself. For the short-term forecaster, BTM assets are distributed, but there may be little granularity available for building site-specific models. The distribution of panel orientations is unknown. However, panel orientation is a critical input to many snow cover models available in the scientific literature. While significant snow obscuration events can be forecasted days in advance by state-of-the-art numerical weather prediction (NWP), snow clearance—driven by melting, sublimation, gravity-driven slide-off, and manual removal—is not well forecasted, especially when 2-meter air temperatures remain below freezing. Therefore, clearance of snow is an acute challenge for load forecasting. Over-forecasting the rate of clearance creates tremendous downside risk and imbalance cost to the operator as cold air masses settle into a region and drive significant heating load. Meanwhile, a forecast that under-predicts the snow clearance rate can be costly if the operator purchases unnecessary ancillary reserves. This study demonstrates the value of predicted downwelling irradiance within the snow clearance component of a state-of-the-art, panel-orientation-independent snow cover model for grid operations. The parameterized model forecasts "effective capacity," the percentage of BTM capacity unaffected by snow coverage and available for power generation. The model is trained using actual BTM generation and power forecasts associated with historical snowfall events. Initial conditions are calculated using snow depth changes from the Snow Data Assimilation System (SNODAS) and categorical snowfall and 2-meter air temperature observations from Automated Surface/Weather Observing Systems (such as ASOS) within the region. The model evolves the initial conditions in time using snowfall and 2-meter temperature guidance from select NWP models, such as the NOAA National Blend of Models, and adds to this framework site-specific irradiance forecasts. Two versions of the snow clearance component of the model are compared to isolate the value of downwelling irradiance forecasts. Both versions include terms that quantify clearance associated with melting induced by ambient temperature and manual clearing. One version additionally introduces an irradiance-based snow clearance term to the model framework. We will demonstrate the value of this model and its clearing component to forecast accuracy, measuring performance during out-of-sample snow events, as well as associated load forecast and economic impacts to the grid operator. Importantly, applications to and/or adaptations for grid-connected front-of-the-meter solar generation during snow events will be described, as underperforming utility-scale assets, especially with fixed orientation, present a unique supply risk to utilities and grid operators.

494007.title: From Flash Flood Guidance to Decision-Making: Experiences Using the Central America FFGS in Costa Rica
494007.authors: Juan Diego Naranjo Díaz, Hydrologic Reseach Center, San Diego, CA; and A. Horan and R. Campbell
494007.abstract: Flash floods and rainfall-induced landslides are among the most dangerous hydrometeorological hazards in Costa Rica, where complex terrain, high exposure, and intensifying rainfall associated with a changing climate can turn heavy rain into rapid loss of life and serious damage to property and infrastructure. Many of these events can be forecast, and the Instituto Meteorológico Nacional (IMN) provides timely warning information, yet serious impacts still occur. A central challenge is not only forecasting the hazard, but understanding and communicating its likely impacts.
