For emergency managers, knowing that heavy rainfall or flash-flood conditions are expected is rarely enough; they also need to know where impacts are most likely and which areas warrant priority attention and resources. The Central America Flash Flood Guidance System (CAFFGS) has been central to meeting this challenge. In operational use in the region since 2004, it has given the IMN more than two decades of experience in forecasting flash floods and landslides. Daily use has deepened forecasters’ understanding of the relationship between rainfall, soil conditions, and flash-flood potential, and has strengthened the basis for hydrometeorological warnings. The same approach has since been extended by the World Meteorological Organization to more than 100 countries worldwide. Over more than two decades, this experience has allowed FFGS information to move beyond forecasting into the development of operational decision-support products. Forecasters combine FFGS guidance with rainfall observations, numerical weather prediction, antecedent rainfall and soil conditions, and local knowledge to produce a regionally resolved Flash Flood Risk and Landslide Threat Index that identifies areas likely to be seriously affected. This is delivered to the National Commission for Risk Prevention and Emergency Response (CNE) and the Emergency Operations Center (COE) through daily weather briefings and coordination meetings, supporting decisions on the deployment of personnel and financial resources before and during high-impact events. During the first week of August 2026, for example, a tropical wave crossed Costa Rica and left more than 100 mm of rainfall in six hours; these products informed the issuing of green and yellow alerts in Caribbean regions, enabling early activation of emergency protocols and pre-positioning of resources ahead of significant flood impacts. This experience shows that the value of an early warning system extends well beyond producing a forecast: information must be understood, interpreted, and communicated in a form useful to those making decisions. More than two decades of daily CAFFGS use in Costa Rica have strengthened the connection between weather forecasting and disaster risk management. This presentation shares the main experiences and lessons learned from CAFFGS use in Costa Rica, focusing on how forecast information has been transformed into products that support decision-making — lessons that can help other countries strengthen their early warning systems and advance the goals of the Early Warnings for All initiative.

494008.title: Accounting for Elevation in Model Surface Pressure Verification Against Observations
494008.authors: Natalie Babij, CIRA, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and J. A. Hamilton, R. Pierce, and J. English
494008.abstract: When evaluating gridded model output of continuous variables relative to point-based observations, it is common practice to interpolate the values of nearby model grid points to the observation location, e.g. using bilinear interpolation, and compare the interpolated value to the observation. This practice is insufficient for some variables, such as surface pressure, where factors, such as surface elevation, can have a stronger influence on the value than the horizontal distribution. By using simple horizontal interpolation of model surface pressure for verification against observations, we may be inaccurately characterizing model performance, especially in areas of complex terrain where the elevations of the neighboring model grid points may not be representative of the elevation of the observation location. At the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Global Systems Laboratory (GSL), we introduced a “normalized surface pressure” (NSP) variable into our Model Analysis Tool Suite (MATS). NSP adjusts the model surface pressure interpolated to an observation location to the elevation at that location, using interpolated elevations and temperatures from the neighboring model grid points and the hypsometric equation. This presentation will discuss how NSP is derived and how it is verified against observations in MATS. In addition, we will present the impact on verification statistics for models such as the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) and the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) over the continental U.S. and regional domains with varying topography, and demonstrate how GSL is using NSP verification to help assess impacts of assimilating different observations into the RRFS.

494009.title: Characterizing Intraseasonal and Interannual Variability in the Composition of the Asian Summer Monsoon Anticyclone Using 20+ Years of Aura Microwave Limb Sounder Measurements
494009.authors: Michelle L Santee, JPL, Pasadena, CA; JPL, Pasadena, CA; and G. L. Manney, L. F. Millán, and N. J. Livesey
494009.abstract: The Aura Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS) has made simultaneous co-located measurements of trace gases and cloud ice water content (a proxy for deep convection) in the upper troposphere / lower stratosphere (UTLS) on a daily basis for more than two decades. With its dense spatial and temporal sampling, extensive measurement suite, and insensitivity to aerosol and all but the thickest clouds, Aura MLS is well suited to characterizing UTLS composition in the region of the Asian summer monsoon (ASM) and quantifying the considerable spatial and seasonal variations therein. The long MLS data record is invaluable for assessing interannual variability in the impact of the ASM on the UTLS. In this talk we will use the final version of MLS measurements (version 6) of cloud ice and both tropospheric (CO, CH3Cl, CH3CN, HCN) and stratospheric (O3, HNO3, HCl) tracers, along with meteorological reanalyses, to provide an updated climatology of ASM anticyclone composition and place the 2017, 2022, and 2023 ASM seasons observed in detail by the StratoClim, ACCLIP, and PHILEAS field campaigns, respectively, into the spatial and temporal context of other monsoons in the last two decades. We will also briefly review the 2026 ASM season, likely one of the last to be observed by MLS.

494011.title: Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning for Global Generalization of Deep Learning-based Passive Microwave Precipitation Retrieval
494011.authors: Liping Wang, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and H. Chen and J. L. Bytheway
494011.abstract: Passive microwave (PMW) precipitation retrieval from low-Earth orbit satellites remains a cornerstone of global precipitation monitoring, yet deep learning approaches trained on high-quality ground radar networks face a fundamental domain transfer challenge: models supervised exclusively over regions with dense radar coverage—such as the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system over CONUS—often fail to generalize to the diverse precipitation regimes encountered globally. This study introduces a contrastive self-supervised learning framework that enables a transformer-based PMW retrieval model, trained on MRMS ground truth, to generalize globally through learned atmospheric state embeddings. Our approach employs a three-stage training pipeline. In Stage 1, a contrastive pretraining phase ingests millions of ATMS brightness temperature (BT) observations globally without any precipitation labels, learning an embedding space where scenes with similar atmospheric states—regardless of geographic location—cluster together. Augmentations designed for satellite observations (channel dropout, calibration jitter, spatial perturbation) enforce invariance to sensor-specific characteristics while preserving meteorological content. In Stage 2, a precipitation decoder is fine-tuned on the pretrained encoder using MRMS labels over CONUS. In Stage 3, sparse GPM Dual-Frequency Precipitation Radar (DPR) collocations provide globally distributed supervision, while a contrastive alignment loss pulls global embeddings toward physically similar CONUS scenes whose precipitation is known from MRMS. The embedding space reveals physically interpretable clustering: tropical deep convection, extratropical frontal systems, warm rain, and clear-sky scenes occupy distinct regions regardless of geographic origin. This structure enables MRMS-quality retrieval knowledge to propagate to physically analogous scenes worldwide through embedding proximity. Validation against held-out DPR observations demonstrates that the contrastive framework substantially reduces retrieval error in regions unseen during supervised training, compared to direct application of the CONUS-trained model. We present regime-specific performance analysis, embedding space visualization, and comparisons with operational retrievals (MIRS, GPROF), demonstrating the potential of self-supervised representation learning to bridge the gap between regional ground truth availability and the global applicability required for next-generation PMW precipitation products.

494014.title: Hands-on Air Quality Education Through Low-Cost Air Sensors
494014.authors: Lindsay Alison Nash, Spheros Environmental, Denver, CO; and J. Marrero
494014.abstract: Hands-on Air Quality Education Through Low-Cost Air Sensors Lindsay Nash, Josette Marrero Spheros Environmental, Denver, CO Emerging air quality sensor technology is creating new educational opportunities. Sensors with the ability to show data as it is being collected further engage students with the data collection process and encourage curiosity. We have developed a real-world hands-on science program, called Kids Making Sense (KMS), that leverages low-cost PM sensors. This Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) based environmental education curriculum teaches students to measure particle pollution using handheld mobile sensors and interpret the data they collect. The program encourages community engagement in air sensors, educates students about air pollution at a young age when they are forming their driving and consumption habits, and empowers students to engage with policy makers to create positive change in their communities. The accompanying curriculum meets Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) and has been successfully implemented in more than 400 classrooms worldwide. The curriculum begins with in-classroom experiments that teach students about the properties of air, sources and characteristics of particle pollution, and the health effects of air pollution. Working in teams, students use the scientific method to develop a research question and design a study to measure air pollution around their school or community. Using the handheld air sensors, students collect credible air quality data. The data is uploaded to a web platform that allows students to view their routes on a sharable map, identify key areas of pollution, and share their data with the global air quality community. The crowdsourced aspect of the web platform allows for critical conversations around disparities in air quality and environments. Finally, students develop an air quality awareness campaign to share what they’ve learned with members of their community. In the hands-on presentation, participants will use handheld air sensors to collect data. We will talk through the collected data and also highlight case studies where students have used the sensors and the program to enact real change at their schools or in their communities. Key Takeaways How to meaningfully engage students in hands-on science activities. How using sensors can enhance the quality and comparability of data, while increasing student engagement. How incorporating community-focused science activities can enhance outcomes for communities.

494016.title: Recent Developments on Vladimir Zakharov's Theory of a Wind Driven Sea
494016.authors: Patrik Vaclav Nabelek, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR; and S. Yim
494016.abstract: In 1968, Vladimir Zakharov published his revolutionary paper introducing the Hamiltonian formulation of the deep-water wave system. When we talk of Zakharov’s theory of a wind driven sea, we are referring to his body of works that explain many aspects of empirical observations of a wind driven sea using the Hamiltonian formulation as the primary mathematical first principle. Zakharov’s theory was a paradigm shift that facilitated some of the most important breakthroughs in modern models of wind driven waves: the inverse scattering transform (IST) for the focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation of Zakharov and Shabat, the higher order spectral (HOS) method of Dommermuth and Yue, the open-source Wave Watch III model developed and operated by NOAA and ERDC, and the statistical theory of rogue waves of Mori and Jannsen. Recently, many mathematical breakthroughs have been made with respect to a hypothetical statistical sea state called a soliton gas that can studied and simulated with closed form or limits of closed form solutions using the IST for the NLS equation in 1D. To study a soliton gas, instead of starting with linear superposition of water waves, one uses a nonlinear superposition of 1D breather solitons. We also apply the direct scattering transform (DST) which is the inverse of the IST to analyze numerical solutions in 2D. We have also been investigating approaches to include wave-structure interactions in numerical simulations based on Zakharov’s theory of a wind driven sea. In this talk, we will describe recent developments in the theory of soliton gasses in 1D and 2D that have important practical implications in the study of extreme waves generated by extreme winds and how they impact surface and subsurface crafts.

494022.title: Integrating Social Science into Research-to-Operations(R2O) for Flood Inundation Maps
494022.authors: Sajani Kandel, Univ. of Minnesota, STP, MN; and M. A. Kenney
494022.abstract: Advances in flood prediction can support better preparedness, response, and recovery only when forecast information is understandable, usable, and relevant to users’ decisions. Although research-to-operations (R2O) efforts often focus only on transitioning scientific and technological advances into operational systems, social science provides critical evidence for understanding product goals, user needs, decision contexts, and communication challenges. This presentation examines how interdisciplinary social science can be incorporated throughout the development and evaluation of operational flood decision-support products. We synthesize a multi-method, user-centered research effort supporting NOAA’s Flood Inundation Map (FIM) services within the National Water Prediction Service (NWPS). Interviews with product developers established a shared technical vocabulary and clarified product objectives, design considerations, operational constraints, and tradeoffs. Interviews with professional users examined their decision contexts, valued product features, and barriers to effective use. A comparative diagnostic evaluation of FIMs identified recurring strengths and challenges in how flood information was organized, visualized, and communicated. These findings subsequently informed empirical testing of alternative approaches to communicating and organizing flood-forecast information. The evaluation framework is now being extended across products, researchers, and testing environments. During the 2026 Water Prediction Innovators Summer Institute, students applied it to public and proprietary FIM products while developing decision-support evaluation skills. Building on this framework, FIMBox advances the research from diagnostic and static visualization evaluation to controlled testing in an interactive environment. NOAA’s NWPS testbed allowed alternative interface and communication designs to be tested with different user groups before potential operational implementation. This research demonstrates how social science can contribute throughout R2O—from defining operational needs and understanding user decision contexts to evaluating existing products and testing potential improvements. Throughout the research, emerging findings were shared with NOAA partners, allowing operational priorities to shape the research and helping the team interpret results within operational constraints. Social science methods connected operational expertise and user experiences with systematic empirical testing, supporting the translation of evidence into actionable, operationally feasible recommendations. This iterative engagement kept the research grounded in operational goals, product-development constraints, and user decision environments. The resulting evidence, methods, and evaluation infrastructure support the development of robust, understandable, usable, and actionable flood-forecast products and help translate advances in flood prediction into better operational decisions and more equitable flood-risk communication.

494025.title: More Talk, More Hope, More Action: Introducing the Talking Climate Collaborative
494025.authors: Elisabeth A. Cohen, Talking Climate Collaborative, Denver, CO; and B. Woods Placky, D. Fisher, and C. Jayko
494025.abstract: Trusted climate communicators are everywhere. They include health professionals, scientists, sustainability officers, creators, journalists, faith leaders, athletes, and many more. But too often, they're working alone. The Talking Climate Collaborative’s first-ever Landscape Assessment of climate communicators across the U.S. and Canada reveals both challenges and opportunities to amplify and scale efforts by individuals and organizations. This talk will present highlights from this survey and how it informs TCC’s goal to connect the science of effective climate communication to the trusted voices best placed to use it by turning research into practical tools, training, and ready-to-use resources. What could become possible if we truly invested in the people helping the world understand and talk about climate change? Come for the talk and help us build a stronger, better-connected climate communication ecosystem. We can't solve a problem we aren't talking about!

494026.title: Development of AI-Enhanced 3D Satellite Cloud Products for Weather Situational Awareness
494026.authors: Yoo-Jeong Noh, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and J. M. Haynes, C. H. White, and S. D. Miller
494026.abstract: Aviation forecasters and pilots make decisions for flight planning and safety management by monitoring environmental conditions based on a variety of weather observations and forecasts. As air transportation continues to increase rapidly, the need for high-quality aviation weather information has become more critical. Meteorological satellites have provided useful global weather observations for decades and remain one of the most valuable data sources for aviation, particularly over remote and oceanic regions where conventional observations are sparse. However, many satellite products often provide limited information on the vertical structure of clouds and aviation weather hazards. Recent advances in satellite remote sensing, combined with AI/machine learning (ML), are creating new opportunities to develop more quantitative and user-focused aviation weather products. To address this need, we have been developing a global framework of 3D cloud and environmental fields by integrating multiple satellite observations and numerical model information. One of new components is AI/ML-based estimation of cloud water vertical profiles, enabling improved characterization of cloud structure and aviation hazards such as in-flight icing associated with supercooled liquid clouds. This talk will present recent developments in satellite-derived 3D cloud products for both research and operational applications and discuss their potential to enhance weather situational awareness for aviation users.

494027.title: Shoulder-to-Shoulder: A Panel Conversation on Climate Attribution, Applications, and Creative Communication
494027.authors: Shel D Winkley, Climate Central, Bryan, TX; and D. M. Gilford and C. Martinez
494027.abstract: Climate attribution science and its communication have advanced rapidly over the past decade. Methods have improved, studies have multiplied, and the tools we use to compute attribution estimates have gotten faster and become more reliable. Yet, the scientists producing those estimates, the ones translating them for real-world applications, and the people communicating what they mean to the public and decision makers rarely have the opportunity to talk with each other in the same room, let alone on the same stage. This panel is designed to do just that: replace the usual sequence of individual talks for a single, moderated 60-minute conversation that puts different vantage points on these critical topics shoulder-to-shoulder for an in-depth discussion on the successes, challenges, and opportunities in climate attribution. This conversation will give attendees an in-depth view on the exchange, allowing them to hear directly from a researcher on best practices to turn attribution findings into usable tools, a communicator working to convey those tools and data through engaging, creative conversations with the public and media, a practitioner on how attribution is already landing in real-world policy and decision-making, and a scientist speaking to the growing range of attribution approaches applied across different extreme weather events. With time built in, this panel will also provide a space for those in attendance to ask questions from all four perspectives at once, furthering the dialogue and fostering future opportunities for reaching across these interdependent disciplines. This conversation will get to the heart of what the “Climate Attribution: Recent Advances, Applications, and Creative Communication” session is attempting to accomplish – bridging the science into real-world application and conversations. The end result will be a sharper grasp of the science across the community, a clearer sense of where climate attribution is headed, and the promotion of conversations still to come.

494031.title: Turbulent Droplet Collision Mechanisms and Cloud-Scale Coupling in Warm Rain Formation Across Developing Cumulus Cloud Regimes
494031.authors: Sasha Tolstoff, Stanford University, Stanford, CA; and Y. Wang and J. Cano
494031.abstract: Warm rain governs drizzle onset, cloud lifetime, and aerosol-cloud interactions. However, the initial process of liquid-to-liquid cloud droplet collision-coalescence (C-C) that leads to warm rain formation is often represented in cloud microphysics schemes without accounting for turbulent enhancement effects. Popular gravity-based kernels represent C-C based on differences in droplet mass and associated terminal velocity (differential sedimentation), which results in C-C estimates near zero for conditions including climate bias-prone drizzle cloud regimes where droplets are often small and similar in size. In reality, similar size droplets can still collide and coalesce with one another when experiencing turbulent transport, preferential concentration (clustering), and collector droplet collision efficiency enhancement. Although the physical role of each mechanism is well-defined by previous literature, their relative importance for rain formation and how they interact when coupled remains poorly constrained in realistic cloud simulations. We employ Chandrakar & Morrison’s (2025) coupling of the super-droplet method (Shima et al., 2009) with Cloud Model 1 to perform a factorial isolation of these mechanisms in large-eddy simulations of two contrasting shallow cumulus cloud regimes: precipitating (RICO) and non-precipitating (BOMEX) trade cumulus. Individual and pairwise sensitivity tests are conducted for each term of the Ayala-Wang (2008) turbulent kernel under varying aerosol loadings to quantify how each modifies cloud droplet size distribution, cloud liquid water path, rain water path, and precipitation susceptibility to aerosol effect. Furthermore, we introduce a cloud-scale coupling diagnostic to compare the collective response to the individual and pairwise responses. We find that turbulent enhancement of C-C is strongly regime-dependent even at comparable dissipation rates, and that the non-precipitating case is far more sensitive to turbulent activity than the precipitating case, with collision efficiency serving a dominant role when coupled with preferential concentration. Combining these turbulent mechanisms results in competing coupling effects rather than multiplicative amplification, which indicates that cloud-scale buffering may also play a role in determining the process dominance. We further extend this framework across various clean and polluted aerosol environments with additional cloud regimes covering a higher dissipation range to assess how this turbulence hierarchy and its dampening effect on aerosol susceptibility shift with cloud state.

494043.title: AI to improve Ground Clutter Filtering for Dual-Polarization Weather Radars
494043.authors: Shashank S Joshil, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and V. Chandrasekar
494043.abstract: Ground clutter is an important source of contamination in weather radar observations and can significantly affect the accuracy of radar-derived meteorological products. Conventional clutter filtering techniques generally rely on predefined spectral characteristics or filtering parameters and may have difficulty separating clutter from weather echoes when their Doppler characteristics overlap. This challenge is particularly important for dual-polarization weather radars, where preserving the integrity of both polarization channels is necessary for accurate characterization of precipitation. In this study, we investigate an Artificial Intelligence (AI) based approach for adaptive ground clutter filtering in dual-polarization weather radar data. The proposed framework operates on radar data and is trained to identify characteristics associated with meteorological echoes and ground clutter. The AI model provides a response that picks up the weather signal. The same processing framework can be applied to both horizontal and vertical polarization channels. The performance of the proposed system is evaluated using clutter-contaminated radar observations by comparing the retrieved weather observations from the reference data. Evaluation considers both the effectiveness of clutter removal and the preservation of meteorological information. The study demonstrates the potential of AI-based processing as an alternative to conventional ground clutter filtering.

494045.title: Teaching Weather Where We Are: Place, Culture, and Community in Atmospheric Science Education (Invited Presentation)
494045.authors: Jennifer D. Small Griswold, University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, HI; University of Hawaii at Manoa, H, HI
494045.abstract: Weather and climate are experienced in place. They shape landscapes and ecosystems, but also cultures, histories, livelihoods, and communities. Yet atmospheric science is often taught in ways that separate physical processes from the places where students encounter them. Place-based education provides an opportunity to reconnect those ideas, making atmospheric science more relevant and accessible while helping students understand relationships among atmosphere, culture, and community. At the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (UHM), I use Hawaiʻi and the broader Pacific as both a setting for and an integral part of atmospheric science education. This approach is most explicit in ATMO 102: Pacific Climate and Cultures, a course built around relationships among climate, people, and place across Oceania. However, place-based teaching is not confined to a course about culture. Across introductory, upper-division, and graduate atmospheric science courses, I use assignments, discussions, case studies, and locally relevant phenomena to connect disciplinary concepts to Hawaiʻi and the Pacific. These connections encourage students to see atmospheric science not simply as a collection of equations, processes, and concepts, but as a way of understanding the places where they live and the communities to which those places are connected. This presentation will share approaches for integrating place, culture, and community throughout an atmospheric science curriculum while maintaining disciplinary rigor. Drawing on examples from undergraduate non-major, undergraduate major and graduate student courses from UHM, I will discuss how place-based assignments, culturally situated discussions, and Hawaiʻi and Pacific case studies can create opportunities for students across disciplines and backgrounds to find connections to atmospheric science. More broadly, I will consider how teaching weather “where we are” can strengthen engagement and community connection while helping students recognize that atmospheric science is simultaneously local and global. Although these examples emerge from Hawaiʻi and the Pacific Islands, the underlying approach is transferable: every atmospheric science program exists in a place, and every place offers opportunities to connect atmospheric science with the people, cultures, and communities students encounter there.

494048.title: Diabatic Processes and Ice Microphysics in Tropical Cyclone Intensification: Examining Hurricane Ida Using gSAM
494048.authors: Ashlynne Gary, University of Arizona, Solvang, CA; and S. C. Sullivan, S. N. Wu, P. Blossey, M. Khairoutdinov, B. Gasparini, and A. M. Stansfield
494048.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) are the costliest natural disasters that affect the U.S. In 2021, Hurricane Ida evolved from a tropical depression to a Category 4 hurricane over the course of 3 days, causing between $31 and $44 billion in damage in the Gulf Coast region and Northeast. Investigating cases of rapid intensification is crucial for accurately forecasting risk for those in the path of developing storms. Although previous work has found strong correlations of TC intensification with larger ice water contents, the microphysical origin and radiative heating of this ice have not yet been clarified or quantified. To investigate the link between rapid cyclogenesis and the origin of upper-level TC ice, we complete multiple simulations of Hurricane Ida using the Global System for Atmospheric Modeling (gSAM) at 1-km resolution. We evaluate the simulation output with multiple observational data sources, including precipitation statistics from the NASA GPM Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals (IMERG), cyclone track and intensity metrics from the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS), and in-situ dropsondes from NOAA P-3 aircraft. We discuss implementation of microphysical tracers within the model to distinguish locally-formed and remotely-advected ice condensate; these tracers identify variations in cloud ice structure as intensification ensues. In line with recent studies of TC microphysics, we expect an important contribution of locally formed ice in the cirrus shield around the TC center. With three different schemes (one-moment, two-moment, and particle properties-based), we additionally test the microphysical sensitivity of the simulated TC track, intensity, rate of development, and cloud ice. Preliminary results indicate robust performance of gSAM in reproducing Hurricane Ida, although the intensification is slightly dampened and the simulated track is persistently eastward relative to observations with a ~120-km bias in landfall location. Uncovering the role of ice in strengthening tropical systems will allow for better scientific understanding of small-scale processes within storms and help forecasters identify environments conducive to rapid intensification.

494049.title: 'The Role of Aerosols, Turbulence, and Microphysics in Shaping Marine Boundary Layer Structure and Cloud Morphology Using LES'
494049.authors: Brianna Marie Salazar, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and S. T. Salesky and D. H. Richter
494049.abstract: Clouds play an essential role within the marine atmospheric boundary layer (MABL) due to their contributions to weather and climate processes. Climate models exhibit large uncertainty in representing the response of low-level marine clouds, including shallow cumulus and stratocumulus, to variations in environmental conditions. Recent studies have demonstrated that cloud morphology can influence cloud fraction and their associated radiative effects. Although previous work has identified several environmental factors that contribute to cloud organization, the relative sensitivity of cloud properties and MABL structure to modest perturbations in the thermodynamic and dynamical environment remain uncertain. In addition, few studies have explored how these environmental controls interact with turbulence, aerosols, and microphysical processes to regulate cloud morphology in a fully coupled way. Using a suite of idealized large-eddy simulations (LES) initialized using an environmental sounding from the Moisture and Aerosol Gradients/Physics of Inversion Evolution (MAGPIE) field campaign and configured using the canonical Barbados Oceanographic and Meteorological Experiment (BOMEX) forcings and simulation framework, we conduct a comprehensive sensitivity analysis to assess how perturbations in environmental conditions influence cloud morphology and MBL structure. To isolate the influence of each environmental control, individual forcing variables are perturbed one at a time while all other conditions are held fixed. Sensitivity experiments investigate variations in surface buoyancy forcing through changes in sensible and latent heat fluxes and evaporative fraction, in addition to boundary-layer moisture, large-scale subsidence, environmental wind conditions, and inversion strength. These simulations are evaluated using thermodynamic, dynamical, and cloud diagnostics to quantify changes in vertical structure, spatial organization, liquid water, and cloud amount. Simulations are first conducted using the standard Cloud Model 1 (CM1) with bulk (Eulerian) microphysics and will subsequently be extended using a modified CM1 framework that incorporates a Lagrangian representation of microphysics with fully two-way coupled droplet–fluid interactions. Findings from this research serve to improve the understanding of how interactions among aerosol, turbulence, and microphysics shape MABL structure while also supporting improved prediction of operationally relevant environmental conditions, including clouds and fog, visibility, precipitation, and electromagnetic/electro-optical propagation.

494054.title: Evolving the Thematic Real-time Environmental Distributed Data Services (THREDDS) Project: Crossing the Language Barrier
494054.authors: Sean C. Arms, UCAR, Boulder, CO
494054.abstract: The NSF Unidata Thematic Real-time Environmental Distributed Data Services (THREDDS) project aims to provide students, educators and researchers the ability to both access and provide real-time and archived datasets from a variety of environmental data sources. Currently, the project comprises data access libraries written in Java (netCDF-Java - both local and remote access) and Python (Siphon - focused on remote access), alongside the THREDDS Data Server (TDS). The TDS is a widely adopted tool used to support FAIR and Open Data dissemination, utilized by over 100 institutions globally. These institutions are represented by a fairly even distribution of educational, governmental, and non-profit organizations. This presentation will provide a brief review of the project's history and highlight current and upcoming efforts to evolve the TDS (and netCDF-Java) into a more sustainable, cross-language framework. Additionally, we will discuss the pros and cons of this transition relative to the existing installation base, along with specific mitigation steps being implemented to ensure our core community remains fully supported in their efforts to both access and provide FAIR and Open Data.

494056.title: United National Weather Team Alert System Uses For Actionable Emergency Management Guidance
494056.authors: Alicia Kay Hardimon, UNITED NATIONAL WEATHER TEAM, Eagle Bend, MN
494056.abstract: A unified digital‑alert system that blends technical meteorological data with AI‑driven public messaging — and adds explicit high‑ground and shelter guidance, or directions to safety or shelter in place, truly customizing any disaster risk imagined — can give both emergency managers and the public clearer, faster, and more actionable information during disaster events. Digital communication platforms increasingly serve as the primary bridge between complex hazard data and real‑world protective action. This Abstract presents an expanded AI‑supported alert framework known as the UNWT ALERT SYSTEM that integrates official meteorological warnings with geospatially targeted high‑ground locations for floods,shelter information after disasters, and ability to fully customize alerts and recovery information, even in multiple languages, to improve decision‑making for emergency managers and the public. Building on the UNWT Alert System model, the enhanced workflow consolidates a variety of alerts from federal and regional and local agencies, processes them through generative‑AI language models, and produces clear, audience‑specific narratives that emphasize immediate protective actions. A key innovation is the inclusion of customizable map‑linked high‑ground identifiers, image analysis and website scraping capabilities to provide custom disaster information. For emergency managers, these features provide operationally relevant, location‑specific cues that support evacuation routing, resource staging, and cross‑agency coordination. For the public, the same information is translated into plain‑language guidance that reduces interpretation burden during high‑stress events, helping individuals quickly understand where to go, what is safe, and how to act. The system demonstrates how digital technology can transform static hazard alerts into dynamic, action‑oriented communication products. Results highlight three core benefits: (1) centralized monitoring that reduces time‑to‑message, (2) AI‑assisted translation of technical risk data into accessible public instructions, and (3) Customizable interface that strengthen both professional response workflows and community‑level protective behavior. This approach illustrates a scalable pathway for pairing authoritative meteorological data with actionable, equity‑focused emergency communication designed to reach diverse populations across digital platforms.

494072.title: Boundary Layer Interactions with Urban Heat in a Coastal City: TRACER Case Studies
494072.authors: Elizabeth Spicer, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and P. M. Klein and M. R. Storm
494072.abstract: The phenomenon of higher near-surface air temperatures in cities compared to their surroundings, called the urban heat island (UHI) effect, is a known problem that has been repeatedly linked to a variety of health issues. While the impacts of UHI on human health and comfort are being increasingly studied, we can also learn more about the relationship between the UHI and the planetary boundary layer (PBL). The UHI is not a two-dimensional phenomenon, despite often being portrayed as one. Under weak wind conditions, a thermal circulation can form in the PBL due to the temperature gradient between urban and rural areas which can result in an urban heat dome. The disturbance of the PBL by the UHI is further complicated in coastal cities, where land and marine airmasses interact and various boundary passages—such as sea, bay, or land breezes—may further disrupt PBL processes. This presentation explores the interactions between the UHI and PBL during select summer cases in the Houston, TX area. Case studies are selected from the 2022 intensive observation period (IOP) of the U.S. Department of Energy’s TRacking Aerosol Convection interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER), utilizing prior work which identified anomalous heat events during the IOP. Thermodynamic and kinematic profiles collected continuously throughout the IOP from three sites within the greater Houston area allow for detailed PBL temporal and spatial analysis. Additionally, we focused on UHI at the canopy level, using a validated high-resolution reanalysis (2.5 km, hourly) to view temperature and related variables across the greater Houston area. The NOAA National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) Unrestricted Mesoscale Analysis (URMA) uniquely assimilates urban and rural near-surface observations from a variety of trusted networks. By analyzing near-surface temperatures and PBL profiles, we examine how the UHI and sea/bay breeze passages can impact the vertical extent of the urban heat dome and related mixing effects within the coastal PBL.

494074.title: METplus: Evaluating Numerical Weather Prediction Models Across Systems and Scales
494074.authors: Christina P. Kalb, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and M. A. Harrold, J. Halley Gotway, G. P. McCabe Jr., K. M. Newman, J. Prestopnik, M. Win-Gildenmeister, H. Soh, D. R. Adriaansen, T. J. Hertneky, M. B. Smith, M. J. Kavulich Jr., G. Ketefian, V. Vargas Jr., W. Mayfield, and J. L. Vigh
494074.abstract: Forecast evaluation requirements are rapidly evolving as the weather community adopts new modeling approaches that span convection-allowing numerical weather prediction (NWP), global prediction systems, unstructured-grid models, ensemble forecasting, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based prediction systems. These advances demand flexible verification capabilities that can be applied consistently across a wide range of forecast systems while remaining scalable, reproducible, and extensible. The enhanced Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) framework provides a comprehensive, community-developed verification and diagnostic system designed to meet these evolving needs. METplus integrates robust verification algorithms, workflow automation, statistical aggregation, visualization, and process-oriented diagnostics into a modular framework supporting both research and operational applications. The framework enables users to evaluate deterministic, probabilistic, ensemble, and neighborhood, and feature-based forecast characteristics using reproducible workflows. This presentation will highlight recent enhancements that expand METplus capabilities across modeling systems and applications. Some topics include growing support for unstructured-grid models such as the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS), expanded evaluation capabilities for AI/ML-generated forecasts, improved workflow flexibility and automation, and new verification capabilities supporting modern forecast systems.

494075.title: Calibrating an Auto-Differentiable Intermediate-Complexity Atmospheric Model with Reanalysis Data
494075.authors: Rebecca Gjini, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and M. Morzfeld, D. Watson-Parris, and O. Dunbar
494075.abstract: Advances in auto-differentiable climate modeling open new possibilities for gradient-based scientific discovery, e.g., the automatic calibration of physics parameterizations. For climate timescales, parameters can be learned by minimizing the misfit between modeled and observed climate statistics. However, the time window over which statistical observations are collected for calibrating parameterizations need not be equivalent to the projection timescale of interest after calibration. We present a calibration framework for learning parameters using different statistical observation timescales. We test this framework for calibrating physics parameterizations using an auto-differentiable atmospheric model called the JAX Circulation Model (JCM). To calibrate parameters over short time windows, we use stochastic gradient descent (SGD), a gradient-based optimizer, because of its success in large-scale machine learning applications. To calibrate parameters over long time windows, we use ensemble Kalman inversion (EKI), a derivative-free method, because JCM gradients are unstable beyond a few weeks. Our numerical experiments test both approaches by calibrating JCM in an idealized setting and against the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) reanalysis (ERA5) data. Results indicate that calibration using short time windows can achieve accuracy comparable to longer time windows in idealized settings, but struggles to capture the long-term variability of the ERA5 data.

494076.title: The Global Aerosol as Viewed by ATom: Lessons for Future Missions
494076.authors: Charles A. Brock, NOAA, Boulder, CO
494076.abstract: The Atmospheric Tomography (ATom) mission provided global-scale surveys of aerosol chemical, microphysical, and optical properties throughout the tropospheric column and into the mid- and high-latitude lower stratosphere in each season. The unique nature and scope of the measurements resulted in a remarkable number of high-impact findings that have helped improve understanding of aerosol distributions and characteristics and their representation in global models. Future in situ survey missions might focus on several remaining key issues related to aerosol-climate interactions. The species that condense on recently formed particles in the upper troposphere, growing them to climatically relevant sizes, are poorly known but likely to involve isoprene oxidation products and other organic species as well as sulfate from sulfur dioxide and dimethyl sulfide oxidation. The relative contributions of organics and sulfates likely vary substantially with latitude and airmass type. Aerosol sinks, including removal in warm conveyor belts, by deep convection, and by dry deposition to the surface, remains poorly quantified, with diverse model representations. Sea-spray particle fluxes to the boundary layer and free troposphere, and the fluxes of free tropospheric particles to the boundary layer, need to be better constrained. Hemispheric differences in aerosol properties, driven by differences in emissions, transport, and sinks between the hemispheres, are useful for identifying and quantifying model biases, especially as they relate to the abundance of the nuclei for liquid and ice cloud particle formation. Accomplishing these goals constrains the platform and payload, and emphasizes the need to sample at low altitude in the MBL, deploy fast-response instruments, use externally mounted cloud probes, and develop inlets for the quantitative sampling of particles with diameters up to 10 µm in diameter. Consistent cross-calibration of instruments and the integration of aerosol measurements into combined data products (data files that are based on chemical, physical, and optical parameters rather than instrument types) are needed to make the measurements most useful for scientists running global models and comparing in situ and remote sensing data. Models should pursue comparisons with measurements by focusing on relationships of aerosol parameters with tracer species, rather seeking matches in spatial distribution. Placing such comparisons in tracer space rather than comparing via geospatial matches elucidates limitations in model chemical and microphysical processes rather than emissions and transport.

494078.title: When and Why Wildfire Smoke Amplifies Ozone Exceedance Risk across the United States
494078.authors: Lixu Jin, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ; and X. Jin and Y. Li
494078.abstract: Wildfire smoke can enhance surface ozone (O3), yet the regions with the largest smoke-associated enhancements are not necessarily those where smoke most often pushes maximum daily 8-h average (MDA8) O₃ above the 70-ppbv standard. We integrate EPA Air Quality System (AQS) surface and TROPOMI satellite observations with chemical transport and trajectory model diagnostics to identify the controls on wildfire-driven O3 enhancement and exceedance risk. We show that smoke-associated ΔMDA8 O₃ was greater in the East than in the West, whereas sites with high smoke-pushed exceedance probabilities were more common in the West. The higher western exceedance risk reflected higher background O₃ (~50 versus ~40 ppbv), leaving western sites closer to the 70-ppbv standard. To explain why smoke-associated ΔMDA8 O3 was nevertheless larger in the East, we examined the smoke-associated change in local O3-production potential (ΔP(O3)) inferred from satellite observations. ΔP(O3) showed the opposite regional pattern, with positive values in the West but weak or negative values in the East. The positive ΔP(O3) response was strongest in the West and concentrated in fresh smoke; event-normalized ΔP(O3) declined by ~80% during the first 5 h of plume aging as ΔNO2 rapidly decreased while ΔHCHO remained elevated. In contrast, trajectory diagnostics indicated that the larger eastern O3 enhancement was more strongly associated with pre-arrival O₃ than with near-receptor O3-production potential. Chemical transport models such as CMAQ substantially underestimate wildfire-driven O3 risk. In our evaluation, CMAQ captured only ~21% of observed smoke-pushed exceedance site-days, reflecting biases in both background O3 and smoke-associated enhancement. The concurrent biases in smoke-associated precursor perturbations and ΔP(O3) suggest that incomplete representation of wildfire precursor emissions, plume chemistry, and transport may contribute to the underestimated O3 enhancement.

494080.title: Model-Agnostic Post-Processing Framework for Regional Weather Forecasts: Observation-Calibration and Learned Forecast Correction
494080.authors: Karan Jakhar, Pravah, San Francisco, CA; and Z. Wei, A. Gupta, H. Hilmarsson, and D. Suri
494080.abstract: Global weather prediction now follows two approaches: traditional physics-based numerical models (NWP) and modern AI-driven models (AIWP). Both yield strong global skills, but continue to exhibit two key challenges. First, they suffer from systematic biases, especially at the surface and near steep terrain, which persist across lead times. Second, reanalysis serves the two families differently: it is the training target for AIWPs alone, but the verification reference for both. In either role, the reanalysis is itself regionally biased, so both the models trained on it and the corrections verified against it inherit those biases. We present a two-stage, model-agnostic post-processing framework that transforms the output of any global forecast system, numerical or AI-based, to obtain a corrected regional forecast. The first stage comprises calibrating the gridded background field against in situ observations by optimal interpolation. This produces an observation-calibrated regional reanalysis that serves as both the training target and the verification reference for the next stage. The second stage comprises training and applying a neural network to correct the raw forecast toward the reference. Since the framework operates entirely on forecast output, it requires no access to the parent model's internals and is agnostic of either family of global systems. We instantiate the framework over the Indian subcontinent to calibrate ECMWF's ERA5 reanalysis and correct IFS-HRES surface forecasts against station observations from the NOAA Integrated Surface Database. Our two-stage approach reduces the forecast error for surface quantities ranging from the 2-m temperature, 2-m specific humidity, 10-m and 100-m wind speed, to surface pressure and surface solar irradiance, with skill gains retained across lead times of up to 10 days. Ablation shows that the two stages contribute independently and that omitting reference calibration caps improvements in regional skill. The framework offers a low-cost path to regional forecast improvement that requires neither retraining nor rerunning the parent global model.

494082.title: Does the Grid Matter? Exploring Verification of Unstructured Grids and Interpolated Model Output
494082.authors: Michelle A. Harrold, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and W. Mayfield, K. Newman, D. R. Adriaansen, and M. J. Kavulich Jr.
494082.abstract: As numerical weather prediction systems increasingly adopt unstructured-grid frameworks, new questions arise regarding how these models should be evaluated. Traditional verification workflows often require forecasts to be interpolated or otherwise post-processed onto a common structured grid prior to evaluation. While this approach simplifies comparisons with observations and other modeling systems, interpolation can modify spatial structures, smooth extrema, and alter forecast characteristics before verification statistics are computed. Verification directly on the native model grid may avoid these effects, but the magnitude and practical significance of the differences remain poorly understood. This study investigates the impacts of native grid versus post-processed verification using the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS), with experiments spanning approximately 12-, 3-, and 1-km grid spacing. Verification results computed directly on the native unstructured grid will be compared with results obtained after interpolation to structured grids to examine how verification methodology influences conclusions about forecast performance. The analysis will assess which verification measures and forecast characteristics are most sensitive to interpolation and explore how these sensitivities vary with grid length and interpolation methodology. The study will address when native grid verification provides meaningful additional information, when post-processed verification produces comparable conclusions, and where differences may influence interpretation of model performance for better or worse. Results will help establish best practices for evaluating emerging unstructured-grid prediction systems and inform verification approaches that enable robust comparisons across next-generation modeling frameworks.

494084.title: Exploring Economic Risk in Climate Tipping Point Scenarios Using Agentic AI
494084.authors: Marie McGraw, Jupiter Intelligence, Boulder, CO; and J. Hacker and J. Rogers
494084.abstract: Climate tipping point scenarios occur when a warming climate reaches a critical threshold that abruptly accelerates self-reinforcing and often irreversible changes across the Earth’s atmosphere, ocean, land surface, cryosphere, and biosphere. These scenarios are low-probability but very high-risk catastrophic events that represent major physical and economic modeling challenges. In the current climate risk modelling space, these consequences and cascading impacts of these events are frequently undervalued. In this study, we demonstrate how large language models and agentic AI can be used to explore the real-world consequences of climate tipping point scenarios. By exploring a wide variety of hazard-based, regionally diverse outcomes, agentic AI helps us construct plausible tail-risk scenarios across different climate tipping point scenarios. As one example, we explore the most well-known climate tipping point: an abrupt shutdown of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), an ocean circulation that affects European and North American climate by moving warm water from the tropical Atlantic Ocean to Greenland. Recent climate modeling studies have indicated that a full collapse of the AMOC is substantially more likely this century than had previously been thought. Using our agentic AI framework, we assess the increase in physical hazard exposure, and the subsequent increase in financial loss, following an AMOC collapse. We explore the socioeconomic impacts of severe weather events, such as hurricanes; as well as the rising costs of chronic hazards, such as increases in wintertime energy. For example, an AMOC collapse has been estimated to double coastal flood exposure in New York City. We estimate that the enhanced sea level rise and coastal flood risk that follows an AMOC collapse could mean that a 100-year flood event, such as a major hurricane impacting New York, would cost a sample real estate investment trust with concentrated exposure an additional $50M. Another firm with a strong presence in the United Kingdom and Ireland could see 15% increases in wintertime energy demands, as days below freezing increase by 200 - 400% in the U.K. and Ireland. We discuss the cascading risks of these climate tipping points that occur on top of sea level rise and warmer atmospheres; explore the complex outcomes that vary across geographies and emissions pathways; and show the value of agentic AI-based exploration in identifying risk and impact in the face of these abrupt, low-probability but high-consequence climate events.

494085.title: Phenology of NOAA VIIRS Green Vegetation Fraction: Evaluation and potential improvements
494085.authors: Corinne Minette Carter, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD
494085.abstract: Several land surface vegetation data products are produced at NOAA NESDIS on an operational basis from the VIIRS instrument aboard polar-orbiting environmental satellites. Two of these are the Vegetation Index (VI) and Green Vegetation Fraction (GVF). These are used in weather forecasting, agricultural monitoring, and other applications. GVF is defined as the fraction of horizontal vegetation surface that is covered by photosynthesizing vegetation, but in practice the NOAA GVF is determined from a scaled Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI). Potential issues with the GVF phenology have been flagged by users, and further investigation has determined that the greenup seen in the VIIRS GVF is often later and slower than that seen in in-situ observations. A lag is sometimes observed in the senescence phase as well, although this is a less consistent observation. This is likely because the operational GVF phenology depends on a 15-week historical data time series, a method used due to gaps in the VI upon which it is based. Improvements to the GVF and VI products are being made by the Land Products Development (LPD) research team at NOAA STAR. Part of the motivation of this work is to resolve these discrepancies in phenology between the VIIRS GVF and that of modeled vegetation and in-situ vegetation observations. A machine learning (ML) algorithm prototype has been developed to obtain GVF from the VIIRS VI without the use of the 15-week historical record. It is anticipated that the phenological lag will not be as much of an issue with the new method. Results of this evaluation will be presented here. It is likely that obtaining GVF directly from weekly VI and reflectance observations via the ML algorithm will produce unevenness in the GVF time series due to the variable quality of the input VI because of cloud contamination and other degraded quality pixels. Gap-filling methods for VI have shown promise in reducing the number of low-quality pixels. GVF will be obtained using the original and gap-filled VI. It is anticipated that GVF generated by the ML algorithm from the gap-filled VI will be both less uneven and have less phenological lag than the original operational or ML GVF. This presentation will demonstrate whether the ML algorithm results in improved GVF phenology performance when compared to the operational VIIRS GVF. ML and operational GVF time series over the years 2023 and 2024 will be plotted in comparison to the Copernicus Ground-based Observations for Validation (GBOV) fractional vegetation cover and PhenoCam Green Chromatic Coordinate and NDVI time series, and phenological transition dates will be determined for each time series at multiple sites representing different surface types over the continental US. It is anticipated that the ML phenology will more closely correspond to the ground-based observations. GVF obtained from gap-filled EVI is also anticipated to have smoother variation and be more consistent with ground-based observations than GVF from non-gap-filled EVI.

494087.title: Convective Storms: Easy-to-Use Demos and Resources for Better Student Sensemaking and Engagement
494087.authors: Robert Payo, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and M. S. Rummel
494087.abstract: Storms provide connections to real-world phenomena that illustrate key concepts related to physics, global temperatures, atmospheric interactions, and environmental changes. This session will feature two simple demonstrations included within a classroom lesson about convective storms from the UCAR Center for Science Education: a mylar-balloon convection demonstration and a saturation vapor pressure demonstration. We’ll also feature two online interactives: Make a Thunderstorm helps learners understand how the interaction of humidity and temperature are key ingredients for storm formation, and Share or Snooze which strengthens digital literacy through an online quiz where students evaluate social media posts about storms. Join us to explore and discuss these storm-focused activities to help learners engage in sensemaking and build conceptual understanding.

494088.title: Bridging the Gap: A JupyterHub for Introducing Earth System Science Programming to Undergraduates on the NSF Jetstream2 Cloud
494088.authors: Sarah Ravellette, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA; and A. V. Espinoza, J. Chastang, and D. D. Baldocchi
494088.abstract: Undergraduate Earth System Science students have varying levels of programming experience, with some having minimal to no experience. This project addresses this barrier by providing a cloud-hosted JupyterHub, known as The Littlest JupyterHub, running on the NSF Jetstream2 cloud platform to teach students Python. Jetstream2 handles the heavy lifting and places low computational demand on students’ personal computers. Access to Jetstream2 is provided by an NSF Advanced Cyberinfrastructure Coordination Ecosystem: Services & Support (ACCESS) allocation. The Littlest JupyterHub is a lightweight JupyterHub that can run up to 100 users; ideal for classroom environments and workshops, each with a personal isolated compute environment. Instead of participants’ valuable time being spent on setup, they simply sign in with a GitHub account using a web browser to access the preconfigured environment. Because setting up the infrastructure was difficult, each step was carefully documented to pass the JupyterHub on to future student administrators. Beyond improving accessibility and lowering the technical barrier, the JupyterHub provides a space for students to build their coding skills. To introduce students to Python, a small workshop was designed to cover some core scientific Python packages, and the materials are archived on a public GitHub repository for offline access. The workshop is built around the 2003 Cedar Fire, which had devastating impacts felt across San Diego County. This case study introduces atmospheric data analysis through a real-world event. Students approach the story from two angles: the total area burned and wind speeds during the fire. Finally, with the current documented infrastructure, this JupyterHub can have more workshops added over time within the current instance.

494090.title: Quantifying RTMA's Blind Spots for Decision-Ready Agriculture
494090.authors: Jaitun Vijaybhai Patel, AgWeatherNet, Washington State University, Pullman, WA; and L. khot and J. Ward
494090.abstract: NOAA’s Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis (RTMA) provides hourly near-surface conditions on a 2.5-km grid by combining numerical model backgrounds with surface and remote-sensing observations through variational data assimilation. Its spatial completeness makes it attractive for filling gaps where local observations are unavailable. However, for agricultural applications, its usefulness depends on whether gridded conditions adequately represent the local temperature and moisture environments that management decisions depend on. This study was therefore aimed at evaluating where and when RTMA diverges from quality-controlled in situ observations and whether those differences affect its suitability for frost risk assessment and other seasonal agricultural production management decision-making. The study compared hourly RTMA air temperature and dew point against approximately 1.5 million quality-controlled observations from 53 AgWeatherNet (AWN, managed by Washington State University) stations during 2023–2026. The stations span six climate divisions selected for agricultural and geographic contrast, including the Yakima Valley and Columbia Basin, Okanogan and Wenatchee valleys, East Cascade slopes, northeastern Washington, and the Palouse. Bias, mean absolute error (MAE), and root-mean-square error (RMSE) were evaluated by climate division, season, and day/night period, followed by station-level analysis to distinguish regional patterns from isolated site differences. RTMA reproduced daily mean temperature comparatively well, with seasonal mean biases generally within ±0.5°C, but this agreement masked a pronounced diurnal asymmetry. Daytime errors were primarily modest, while RTMA was systematically warmer at night across several interior divisions. Nighttime RMSE exceeded daytime RMSE in the interior divisions and reached about 3.3°C in northeastern Washington during summer months, when accurate overnight temperature is important for characterizing persistent heat exposure that governs tree fruit crop maturation and color progression, among other physiological aspects. Station-level patterns across divisions were spatially heterogeneous and were consistent with representativeness limitations associated with terrain and local processes unresolved at the RTMA grid scale. A decision-oriented evaluation of overnight freezing conditions showed that these temperature differences translate into meaningful discrepancies during the spring and fall frost seasons. AWN station data identified 7,173 sunset-to-sunrise episodes with air temperature ≤0°C, compared to 6,595 in RTMA, i.e., 8.1% fewer episodes, and a mean episode duration 14.4% shorter in RTMA. Of 6,512 station-nights on which AWN observed freezing conditions, RTMA classified 22.8% as above freezing, with the miss rate increasing to 25.0% in spring frost season. The discrepancy was greatest for marginal light-freeze nights between −2°C and 0°C, 39.3% of which RTMA classified as above freezing. Although exact nightly minimum-temperature category agreement was 87.4% across all spring and fall season nights, agreement fell to 48.5% among AWN-observed freezing nights, and nearly 70% of category disagreements placed RTMA in a warmer or less severe category. This directional error is agriculturally consequential because the risk of blossom-bud injury in fruit crops can change sharply over a narrow temperature range. For apples and sweet cherries near bloom stage, the average temperatures associated with 10% and 90% bud kill are only about 1.7°C apart. Errors of the magnitude observed with RTMA can therefore alter both the estimated severity of crop injury and frost-protection decisions. Dewpoint discrepancies were larger than those for temperature and showed coherent regional structure. RTMA was too moist in Division 5, representing the Cascades, with biases of approximately +4°C and RMSE values up to 9°C during spring and summer. Most interior divisions exhibited negative dewpoint biases that intensified during the summer, with dewpoint MAE exceeding 3°C in some divisions. These patterns are consistent with localized moisture influences, including irrigation, evapotranspiration, and valley moisture retention, occurring at spatial scales that may not be fully represented by the gridded analysis. Overall, RTMA's suitability as a substitute for local observations strongly depends on weather variables, location, season, and the risk associated with management decisions. RTMA provides a reasonable representation of broad daytime and daily mean temperature conditions, but it can underrepresent nighttime cooling, miss or underestimate spring and fall freezing exposure, and exhibit substantial regional dewpoint biases. For threshold-sensitive agricultural applications, these differences would matter, as using uncorrected RTMA alone could miss nearly one in four AWN-observed spring and fall freezing nights and nearly two in five marginal light-freeze nights. These findings thus help identify where gridded analyses can reasonably supplement local observations and where continued in situ monitoring remains important for agricultural production management decision-making.

494092.title: Data Assimilation in the Latent Space
494092.authors: Peter Jan van Leeuwen, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO
494092.abstract: Data assimilation has been transformed with the arrival of skillful machine learning. This has led to some wild growth along the edges, where the standard Bayesian view has been lost, but that viewpoint is gaining traction again as the fundamental building block of data assimilation and machine learning, simply because of its robust uncertainty quantification possibilities. In this talk, we explore multilayer perceptrons and transformers in an auto-encoder framework to build the lowest-dimensional latent representation of a numerical model. We then investigate non-Gaussian data-assimilation techniques in the latent space and compare its performance with data assimilation in physical space, while the model still propagates in the latent space. Specifically, we use the LES model CM1 in a 2-dimensional squall-line configuration with a Particle Flow Filter. We focus on the intricate interplay of dynamics, thermodynamics and microphysics via different observation networks and provide new insight into how we might move forward in this exciting new field.

494093.title: Development of a Two-Step EOF Statistical Postprocessing Algorithm to Identify Patterns of Systematic Error and Variance within CFSV2 Reforecasts
494093.authors: Sincere Miranda, SUNY, Albany, NY; and P. E. Roundy
494093.abstract: Errors in numerical weather prediction (NWP) grow over long lead times. A time-extended empirical orthogonal function (EEOF) analysis of Climate Forecast System Version 2 (CFSv2) model error suggests that biases in NWP generate large-scale patterns of error that grow to saturation with forecast lead. For 2-meter temperature (2mt) these systematic errors emerge as seasonally varying spatial-temporal structures sometimes consistent with land-surface processes such as snow-albedo and soil-moisture coupling, revealing coherent, continental-scale temperature errors that intensify with lead time. The systematic component of this error takes two distinct forms. First a seasonal cycle of model error: as a forecast loses the influence of its initial condition, the model drifts toward an exaggerated seasonal cycle, expressed in this study as a systematic cold bias over Northern Hemisphere continent in late winter a corresponding warm bias in summer. Second, the eddy error patterns that evolve with the forecast. While individual weather events do appear as noise, using the EEOF analysis, the leading continental-scale component of the error is isolated to show how these flow-dependent error patterns evolve with the forecast. In collaboration with NOAA-CPC, a statistical postprocessing algorithm identifies patterns of model error using linear transformation techniques and predicts model error from the projection of model forecast anomalies onto the patterns, relative to the separately calculated model seasonal cycle of error, onto these error patterns. Using EEOFs, the algorithm constructs error eigenmodes that evolve with further lead time, with the strongest and most coherent 2mt error signal concentrated over the high-latitude continents. To adapt the algorithm to a Research-to-Operations (R2O) workspace, the algorithm was projected onto real-time CFS ensemble forecasts to remove the historically derived model error in real time. Applied over a Northern Hemisphere domain and verified out-of-sample against a multi-year hindcast, the algorithm demonstrates error that grows with forecast lead, isolates the leading patterns of surface temperature bias, and produces an adjusted forecast with reduced error. Further analysis aims to extend this framework to additional atmospheric parameters and future operational ensemble prediction systems, with emphasis on implementing this framework into the Climate Prediction Center forecasting workspace.

494097.title: Using a Geostationary Imager Cloud-Tracking Algorithm to Understand the Effects of Environmental Variables on the Development Stage of Convection
494097.authors: Brianna Hauke, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and M. Saito
494097.abstract: Earth System Models (ESMs) poorly simulate the diurnal cycle of convective clouds, and cumulus parametrization used in ESMs tends to initiate convection of cloud systems several hours earlier compared to observations, leading to a systematic bias in convective initiation and precipitation timing. Improvements have been made to cumulus parametrization schemes, but convection still occurs 1-4 hours early. To better understand the environmental factors that influence convective initiation and growth of convective clouds, we use the Geostationary Operational Environmental Series-R (GOES-R) Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI)’s mesoscale sector that provides minutely IR images across a 1000 km x 1000 km area, which allows for the tracking of convective cells. Brightness temperature (BT) and cloud area pixels are retrieved from the imagery. A cloud tracking algorithm was created in order to track the initiation and growth of convective clouds using geostationary imagery. Clouds are only tracked in their initial growth stage. Multiple cloud clusters per case in a number of cases over 2024 are tracked. By estimating the increase in height of the cloud core from the decrease in BT and the increase in cloud core area, convective growth rate (CGR) and convective mass flux (CMF) estimations are calculated, assuming that air is only entrained and no precipitation falls from the cloud. The European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Reanalysis version 5 (ERA5) reanalysis dataset in the Southeastern (SE) U.S. provides environmental variables that affect convection, such as 2-meter temperature, convective available potential energy (CAPE), convective inhibition (CIN), wind direction and shear, aerosol optical depth, and vertical moisture profiles. In-depth statistical analysis between CGR and CMF calculated from GOES mesoscale imagery and environmental variables will reveal the most important variables to improve the modeling of convective clouds by cumulus parametrization. Results indicate slight significance in CAPE and CIN being contributing factors to CMF.

494100.title: Hyperspectral Radiometer (HSR1) Observations of Aerosol Optical Depth
494100.authors: Kelly A. Balmes, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA GML, Boulder, CO; and H. Telg, L. D. Riihimaki, and J. Wood
494100.abstract: The hyperspectral radiometer (HSR1) measures total and diffuse spectral irradiance from 360 to 1100 nm with a spectral resolution of 3 nm, which allows the spectral aerosol optical depth (AOD) to be retrieved. The HSR1 requires no moving parts to separate between the direct and diffuse shortwave components and ultimately retrieve AOD, which makes it unique amongst similar instrumentation and provides the opportunity to deploy on moving platforms and in remote environments. Previously, the HSR1 was a prototype instrument that was evaluated at the Department of Energy (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Southern Great Plains (SGP) site in Oklahoma and has also been a part of other short term deployments. Now, several of the instruments have been deployed in more locations for longer time periods including at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Surface Radiation Budget (SURFRAD) Network Table Mountain site in Boulder, Colorado as well as a part of the Collaborative Lower Atmospheric Mobile Profiling System (CLAMPS) in Colorado and Washington State. In addition, the HSR1 was a part of the Filter Radiometer Comparisons (FRC) at Physikalisch-Meteorologisches Observatorium Davos (PMOD) in Davos, Switzerland. The spectral AOD is retrieved and explored for these new environments and new atmospheric conditions for the HSR1, including for wildfire events. The insight and challenges of the AOD retrieval algorithm and measurements will also be presented. Other quantities possible from the HSR1 will also be explored, including photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), as well as the synergies with other collocated instruments to observe atmospheric conditions.

494102.title: Polydisperse Aerosol Activation In a Turbulent Convection Chamber (Invited Presentation)
494102.authors: Fan Yang, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Mastic, NY; and P. Hou, H. Fahandezh sadi, and R. A. Shaw
494102.abstract: Most cloud models using bulk or bin microphysics schemes rely on Twomey-type activation parameterization, in which an aerosol particle activates into a cloud droplet when the environmental supersaturation exceeds its critical supersaturation, and activated droplets are treated as pure water. However, properly simulating aerosol activation requires resolving unactuated haze particles and considering solute and curvature effects near activation. In previous studies, we developed a 1D haze-capable bin microphysical scheme that fully resolves droplet activation from monodisperse aerosol. In this study, we develop a 2D haze-capable bin microphysics scheme which resolves haze and cloud droplets while tracking the dry aerosol size within each, enabling simulations of activation from polydisperse aerosol. We compare monodisperse and polydisperse injections in the Michigan Tech Pi convection cloud chamber across a range of aerosol injection rates and temperature forcings. We find a universal behavior that governs the microphysical properties as long as the cloud is not in the haze-dominated regime. Certain aspects of the activation process are remarkably independent of the shape and mode radius of the aerosol size distribution. Our results provide new insights into polydisperse aerosol activation in turbulent environments.

494103.title: Future Automated and Electric Vehicle Operability During Various Weather Conditions
494103.authors: Curtis Louis Walker, Ph.D., A.M.ASCE, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. R. Siems-Anderson, B. M. Welch, D. Jaroszweski, and L. Chapman
494103.abstract: Future transportation technologies, such as automated and electric vehicles, continue to expand their footprint. The last few years have seen these technologies transition from lab-simulated concepts and closed test track operations to full scale, commercial ridesharing and mobility services. Increasingly, more automated and electric vehicles are entering the consumer market and expanding their market share. As the adoption and implementation of these technologies grows, so does their exposure to adverse weather conditions that can degrade their operability. Furthermore, non-stationary future weather conditions may pose presently unknown hazards to the safety and reliability of these technologies. The Clean Energy and Equitable Transportation Solutions (CLEETS) center is a global center established jointly between the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) and UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) to advance interdisciplinary research and accelerate use-inspired future transportation technologies.
