The center brings together weather, energy, data science, and transportation experts to research and engage with government, private sector, industry, and end-user communities with the goal to provide a global framework for researching and exchanging strategies. Ongoing work includes establishing an operability framework for defining and quantifying the weather sensitivity of these vehicle’s operational design domains based on the capacity of their sensors to safely navigate across various weather conditions. These impacts from precipitation events, temperature extremes, and visibility obstructions can be quantified in atmospheric modeling across scales. The results of this quantification can be leveraged to inform policy, future research, and identify critical needs for manufacturers and operators of these future vehicle technologies.

494105.title: Hail and Farewell to Algorithms and Sensors as NASA GPM Establishes Version 08
494105.authors: George J. Huffman, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and C. D. Kummerow, A. Loftus, W. S. Olson, S. Pfreundschuh, and E. F. Stocker
494105.abstract: The joint U.S.-Japan Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission has passed a decade of operations, and continues to pursue research, dataset production, and outreach related to precipitation. Key activities in the last year include upgrades from Version 07 to Version 08 of all GPM products and accommodating the rapid turnover of sensors. Key improvements in the Version 08 GPM products for which NASA has lead responsibility include: The Goddard Profiling (GPROF) algorithm has implemented a Machine Learning-based algorithm that shows solid improvements in computing retrievals from passive microwave (PMW) sensors, including improving the consistency of the partner satellite retrievals compared to the GPM Microwave Imager (GMI) retrievals. The Combined Radar Radiometer Algorithm (CORRA) now incorporates additional emphasis on GMI (and Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission [TRMM] Microwave Imager) data in regions where the radar lacks skill. Upgrades to the NASA Convective-Stratiform Heating latent heating product include two-moment microphysics, increased sampling, retrievals over higher terrain, and introduction of vertical velocity statistics retrievals. NASA’s Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) was upgraded to give more flexibility in using different-quality PMW sensors, and a new ML-based algorithm has been adopted for the Geosynchronous Earth Orbit infrared retrievals. Lessons learned from Version 07 focused attention on continuity for each product across the boundary in 2014 between the TRMM and GPM eras, as well as across the TRMM and GPM Core Observatory orbit boosts. The presentation also discusses how GPM has coped with the rapid turnover of PMW sensors. Key points include the requirement for standing groups to handle calibration and retrieval algorithm development, and the necessity of new sensors providing well-characterized, stable performance information at launch.

494106.title: Equatorial Pacific Westerly Wind Events and the Ocean Kelvin Wave Response in the Unified Forecast System Prototype 8
494106.authors: Charlotte A. DeMott, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and E. M. Riley Dellaripa, J. Cui, S. Ray, and E. D. Maloney
494106.abstract: Strong westerly wind events (WWEs) in the equatorial Pacific impart westerly momentum to the upper ocean and often initiate downwelling ocean Kelvin waves (OKWs) that propagate eastward across the Pacific basin. OKWs advect warm water eastward and suppress the thermocline. Changes to sea surface temperatures (SSTs) driven by these processes encourage eastward expansion of tropical Pacific convection and its upper-level divergent outflow that influences tropical-extratropical teleconnections. Additionally, OKWs foster scale interactions by linking episodic synoptic-to-subseasonal WWEs to seasonal and interannual ocean variability. Here, we examine WWE-OKW interactions in 35-day reforecasts by the Unified Forecast System (UFS) Prototype 8 (P8). P8 is a baseline prototype on which next-generation subseasonal (GFSv17), ensemble subseasonal (GEFSv13) and seasonal (SFSv1) operational systems are envisioned. It provides a relatively long period to assess its performance (April 2011-March 2018; 168 total forecasts). Using newly developed WWE and OKW metrics, we find that P8 generates WWEs that are too frequent, too strong, and too regular, and thus impart too much momentum to the upper equatorial Pacific. Amplitudes of the resulting OKWs are too large, both because of the too-strong wind forcing, but also because of an overly stratified upper ocean. Finally, we argue that the too-regular WWE that develops during forecast Week 3 is linked to convective activity supported by erroneous ocean feedbacks driven by model initialization shock.

494109.title: Adapting Science Demonstrations to Increase Access For All Learners
494109.authors: Robert Payo, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and M. S. Rummel
494109.abstract: Hands-on science activities can present challenges for some students, especially those with physical disabilities. Through the GLOBE Weather Pathways project, we apply Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles to a middle school weather curriculum to create adapted lessons that increase access and engagement for all learners. In this session, participants experience a hands-on demonstration that explores the movement of air during a cold front while wearing simulators to gain first-hand experience of challenges that students with physical disabilities may face. Building greater awareness of engagement barriers through the lens of students with disabilities often leads to adjustments that help all learners. We share a teacher-designed adapted lesson as well as strategies for increasing access for all learners during hands-on science activities and demonstrations.

494112.title: Fire Weather Seasonal-to-Multiannual Variability in a Super-Large Ensemble
494112.authors: Laura Hughes Thapa, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. W. Hurrell, D. Touma, and Y. Okumura
494112.abstract: Fire weather is an increasing concern across the western United States (U.S.), motivating improved understanding of its variability and potential predictability. Here, we use a 500-member ensemble of AMIP-style Community Atmosphere Model version 4 simulations (CAM4-SLE) to quantify the influence of sea surface temperature (SST) forcing on the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index (FWI). CAM4-SLE broadly reproduces the observed monthly seasonal cycle of FWI compared with MERRA2 and ERA5, particularly in winter months. However, regional biases – including overestimated summer FWI in the Great Plains and underestimated spring FWI in the western U.S – are evident, consistent with known temperature and rainfall errors in CAM4. Monthly EOF analysis shows that the region of greatest FWI variability shifts from the Southwest toward the Great Plains over the course of the year. Despite substantial atmospheric internal variability, distinct periods of strong FWI anomalies are reproducible across the 500 ensemble members, indicating an important role for SST forcing. Maximum covariance analysis further reveals significant associations between Pacific SST variability and regions of enhanced FWI variability, including patterns related to ENSO and lower-frequency Pacific variability. These results demonstrate the value of very large ensembles for separating SST-forced fire weather variability from atmospheric noise and suggest that Pacific SST variability may provide a source of predictability for seasonal and longer-timescale fire weather anomalies.

494115.title: Influence of Regional Sources on Baltimore Urban-Rural Gradient Atmospheric Composition During Winter-Spring Season Transition
494115.authors: Nahin Ferdousi-Rokib, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and K. N. Steiner, A. Pirone, D. Blomdahl, S. Jacoby, M. A. Zawadowicz, A. Asa-Awuku, C. Hennigan, B. A. Nault, and P. F. DeCarlo
494115.abstract: Regional aerosol sources can vary substantially during the transition from winter to spring. This transition is concurrent with changing emissions, including declining emissions from heating and increases in biogenic emissions with subsequent aerosol production due to warming temperatures. In urban-rural regions, atmospheric composition is further influenced by the mixing of urban and rural sources. As a result, particulate matter less than 2.5 micrometers in diameter (PM2.5) composition may differ between urban and rural environments and across seasonal transitions. Baltimore, as an urban center surrounded by rural, forested, and agricultural areas, represents a complex setting for studying these changes. However, observations of PM2.5 composition within urban-rural regions and understanding of seasonal influence are limited. Concurrent aerosol measurements in both the Baltimore urban core and rural region provide observational data for improved understanding of compositional changes over seasonal transitions and contributing regional sources. In this work, we obtain aerosol composition data using an Aerodyne Aerosol Composition Speciation Monitor (ACSM). Specifically, a TOF-ACSM-X located at the Department of Energy (DOE) funded Baltimore Social Environmental Collective (BSEC) super site and a Q-ACSM at the DOE Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE) Mt. Airy Rural S2 Site. Measurements were taken over the winter to spring season of 2025 and source apportionment was discerned using positive matrix factorization (PMF). The results of this work provide clarity on composition markers attributed to regional sources, changing temperatures, and impact on local air quality.

494116.title: Analysis of Flash Drought Characteristics and Trends over Sub-Saharan Africa from Evaporative Stress and Soil Moisture Perspectives
494116.authors: Stuart Galen Edris, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and A. McGovern, J. Hickey, and H. O. Olayiwola
494116.abstract: Flash droughts (FDs) are extreme dry events that dessicate the landscape and vegetation. Reliance on monsoonal rains for moisture supply often yields more impactful droughts in Africa, and potentially severe FDs. However, there are almost no studies of FD focusing on Africa. We conducted an analysis of FD over Africa using surface variables available from two reanalysis datasets. We used daily data from 1979 to 2024 and quantified FD using three identification methods (evaporative stress and soil moisture-based methods). All three methods found hotspots of FD (local maxima in FD frequency, duration, and severity) in the Sahel region, eastern Africa near the African Great Lakes, and in southern Africa, where precipitation climatology transitions from high to low average precipitation. In addition, we found increasing trends from 1979 - 2011 in FD characteristics in eastern Africa, while the Sahel region showed consistent decreases in FD, making it harder to experience rapid intensification in the region. Results also showed that while precipitation is an important first-order driver of FD, particularly in creating dry conditions, soil moisture was more strongly correlated with surface variables like potential evaporation and surface dryness. Evaporative stress had a stronger correlation with precipitation but was also strongly correlated with evaporative demand, indicating that precipitation alone is not the sole contributor to FD development in Africa and that additional variables are needed to monitor FD. Importantly, FD analysis using ERA5 data identified more FDs driven by precipitation deficits compared to GLDAS, which found a larger mixture of precipitation and energy demand driven FDs. This underscores the need for additional observations in Africa.

494117.title: Investigation of the Predictability of Droughts and Flash Droughts in a Transformer Based U-Net Machine Learning Model with Stochastic Decomposition Layer Ensemble
494117.authors: Stuart Galen Edris, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and A. McGovern and J. Hickey
494117.abstract: Droughts and dry extremes have severe impacts across the globe, from reducing reservoir supplies to food shortages and severe ecosystem stress in severe and prolonged events. Particularly, rapid intensification of drought conditions, termed flash drought (FD), has severe impacts due to rapid loss of moisture availability. Droughts, and in particular FD, have proven difficult to predict because of strong non-linearities and complexities in the hydrologic cycle and surface interactions that drive high energy demand and moisture deficits, as well as the rapid moisture drop for FD. Complexities in surface features that drive FD events have also proved difficult to forecast, with ensemble methods showing less than half of the ensemble members correctly identifying FD. Recently, advanced machine learning (ML) models have proven capable in forecasting weather and climate information, including drought-related variables, and ML has even shown some initial promise in identifying FD conditions. In particular, recent development of a large, state-of-the-art ML model, called DroughtFormer and based on NCAR’s Community Research Earth Digital Twin (CREDIT) framework, has shown high skill in predicting drought related variables and identifying when and where drought occurs. However, that model has difficulty in forecasting the magnitude of climate anomalies and in capturing precipitation forecasts. With the recent release of stochastic decomposition layers (SDLs) in the CREDIT framework to develop ensembles, this project seeks to examine drought and FD in DroughtFormer from an ensemble and probabilistic perspective. We build on DroughtFormer by adding SDL layers to improve on predictions of drought- and FD- related variables and to use the adjustable parameters in the SDL layers to examine the predictability of severe drought and FD events within a large, complex ML model. Early results show the ensemble version of DroughtFormer was able to make stable, realistic forecasts out to 90 day lead times with comparable skill to the deterministic DroughtFormer and outperforming the operational ECMWF ensemble in drought variables.

494119.title: Quantifying the Influence of Sea Surface Temperatures and Vertical Wind Shear on the Rapid Intensification of Hurricane Melissa (2025)
494119.authors: Sanaa Anaya Burke, NCAS-M II, Washington, DC; The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA
494119.abstract: Understanding how climate change impacts the intensification of tropical cyclones (TCs) is critical for preparedness, especially in regions disproportionately affected by landfalling TCs. Current climate projections suggest that there will be an increase in sea surface temperatures (SSTs), and prior research indicates that these warmer SSTs will serve as catalysts in the development and intensification of future TCs. In recent events, the impact that increased SSTs have on TCs has been demonstrated, with a great example of this being Hurricane Melissa. Hurricane Melissa, which formed on October 17, 2025, and dissipated on October 31, 2025, underwent a rapid intensification (RI) event from October 25 to October 26. The TC reached a maximum sustained wind speed (MSW) of 160 knots, tying it with both the Labor Day Hurricane of 1935 and Hurricane Dorian as one of the strongest hurricanes to make landfall in the Atlantic Basin. Hurricane Melissa’s RI occurred just southwest of Jamaica, where its translation speed slowed down significantly, allowing it to linger over a deep layer of warmer-than-normal SSTs. This research aims to quantify the impact of this layer of warmer ocean temperatures, combined with the extremely low mid- and upper-level shear during the RI event, on Melissa’s RI using the Weather Research & Forecasting Model (WRF). To accomplish this, a control simulation of Hurricane Melissa will first be conducted using GFS data to establish baseline atmospheric and oceanic conditions. A second set of simulations will then systematically vary vertical wind shear (VWS) across low, moderate, and high regimes while maintaining constant SSTs to isolate the influence of VWS on storm intensity. Finally, a third set of simulations will modify SSTs in accordance with projected climate conditions from Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) while holding VWS consistent with observed conditions. Comparing these simulations will allow for an assessment of the individual and relative contributions of VWS and SSTs to Hurricane Melissa’s intensification.

494123.title: Current Status and Future Directions of the Gochang and Boseong Standard Meteorological Observatories, Korea
494123.authors: Seo-A Ma, KMA, Seogwipo-si, Jeju-do, South korea; and S. R. In, K. H. Kim, and C. Lee
494123.abstract: Producing accurate and reliable meteorological and climatological data requires continuous evaluation of instrument performance and observing environments, together with long-term observational records with sufficient homogeneity and continuity. To this end, the National Institute of Meteorological Sciences (NIMS) operates the Gochang and Boseong Standard Meteorological Observatories to standardize meteorological observation techniques and improve observational data quality. The Gochang Standard Meteorological Observatory specializes in performance testing and intercomparison of operational surface meteorological instruments and produces high-quality surface reference observations. It also serves as a site of the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS) Surface Reference Network (GSRN). The Boseong Standard Meteorological Observatory, by contrast, specializes in vertical atmospheric observations and experimental research on upper-air observing instruments for wind, temperature, and humidity. It also serves as a World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Measurement Lead Centre (MLC), supporting the standardization and advancement of observing techniques. The 307 m meteorological tall tower at Boseong continuously measures temperature, humidity, and wind at 11 levels from 10 to 300 m. Wind measurements from multiple directions at each level are combined to minimize tower-induced wake effects and derive representative wind direction and speed, hereafter referred to as standard wind. These long-term, multi-level observations have been used to characterize local meteorological conditions and investigate long-term turbulence and flux variability. The long-term, high-quality datasets from the Gochang and Boseong Standard Meteorological Observatories provide a basis for evaluating instrument performance and consistency, as well as for a broad range of meteorological and climatological studies. In particular, long-term multi-level standard wind observations at Boseong can be used to examine seasonal and diurnal wind characteristics and height-dependent variability, providing a basis for evaluating and improving vertical wind-speed interpolation methods. This study introduces the major observing systems of the two observatories and the concept of standard wind derivation at Boseong, and discusses future directions based on these long-term observational datasets.

494126.title: Impact of Air Pollution and Poverty on Mortality in the United States
494126.authors: Taylor West, University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; and Y. Kuwayama, N. Miller, B. Demoz, K. Gribben, and J. E. Bell
494126.abstract: Knowing if poverty can amplify the risk of mortality associated with PM2.5 is important for designing fair, effective, public health policies and reducing preventable deaths. Despite the reduction in PM2.5 emissions, exposure remains widespread in both urban and rural areas. The human health impacts of PM2.5 exposure have been studied using long-term data on mortality, regulatory PM2.5 concentrations, and modeled PM2.5 estimates. Previous studies have shown that wildfire smoke, as indicated by PM2.5 concentrations, has contributed to mortality rates. While the relationship between air pollution and mortality rates has been studied, the role of poverty in modifying this relationship has not been widely examined in the literature. We estimate models for all contiguous U.S. counties using both satellite-derived and EPA monitor-based PM2.5 measures. In this study we used lagged PM2.5 exposure defined as the average PM2.5 concentration during the previous one, three, or five years, depending on the analysis. In addition, we estimate models separately for metropolitan and nonmetropolitan counties, as well as models using time-varying and time-invariant measures of poverty. I provide new evidence on the impacts of poverty on long-term trends in PM2.5 exposure and mortality by incorporating satellite-derived PM2.5 data, which offer more comprehensive spatial coverage than ground-based monitoring alone. Previous studies examining the relationship between air pollution and mortality have largely relied on regulatory air quality monitoring networks, which are concentrated in urban areas and provide limited coverage in rural and less-populated communities. Because rural and nonmetropolitan areas often have different socioeconomic characteristics, including higher rates of persistent poverty in many regions, this uneven monitoring distribution may lead to incomplete characterization of exposures and obscure important differences in air pollution-related mortality risk across rural and urban populations. The purpose of this study is to address this gap by examining the relationship between PM2.5, poverty, and mortality across all U.S. counties during 1999-2019 by examining (1) whether PM2.5 exposure is associated with higher mortality, and (2) whether the interaction between PM2.5 and poverty amplifies mortality risk. I examine associations in these variables for years prior to the COVID pandemic to exclude pandemic-related disruptions–such as changes in mobility, emissions, and healthcare access. Relationships between PM2.5, and mortality may vary across poverty levels. Therefore, we conducted a study that explores how poverty affects the impact of PM2.5 exposure on mortality rates. To evaluate this association, we combined county-level data on EPA Air Quality System (AQS) monitors and satellite-derived ambient PM2.5 levels, mortality rates, and poverty rates for the U.S. from 1999 to 2019. Daily EPA PM2.5 concentrations from sites were aggregated to compute annual county averages. For counties with one site, that site’s concentration was used; for counties with multiple sites, concentrations were averaged. Annual 1-km satellite-derived PM2.5 estimates from the Washington University in St. Louis group were aggregated to the county level using U.S. Census Bureau shapefiles. Annual all cause mortality rates were downloaded from the Center for Disease Control's (CDC’s) Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (WONDER) site. Poverty estimates were obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Small Area Income Poverty Estimates (SAIPE). A fixed-effects regression was used to estimate the relationship between poverty, PM2.5, and mortality, controlling for county and time fixed effects and state-specific time trends. The findings indicate that the relationship between air pollution, poverty, and death rates varies across different regions. Satellite-based PM2.5 data reveal stronger and more consistent connections between pollution and mortality, especially in areas outside major cities. While poverty is also linked to higher death rates, its combined effect with pollution does not uniformly increase health risks across all locations. These results emphasize the importance of using comprehensive pollution data that cover all areas and considering regional differences when studying environmental health issues. These findings highlight the importance of considering PM2.5 exposure and socioeconomic disadvantage in public health risk assessments, with future research conducting regional analyses to identify geographic disparities in air pollution–related mortality.

494127.title: Fate, Seasonality, and Long-Term Trends of Agricultural Pesticide Drift in Yuma County, Arizona: A 13-Year Modeling Study
494127.authors: Mohammad Amin Mirrezaei, Univ. of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and M. Furlong and A. F. Arellano Jr.
494127.abstract: Agricultural pesticide applications can contribute to ambient air pollution through dispersion and deposition; however, long-term observations are limited in many farmed areas. We characterize pesticide drift across Yuma County, Arizona, using CALPUFF driven by WRF meteorology. For 2000–2012, we simulated 48-hour transport and deposition following every reported application of the ten most-applied active ingredients in the region: zeta-cypermethrin, permethrin, methomyl, lambda-cyhalothrin, acephate, chlorpyrifos, dimethoate, bifenthrin, bensulide, and cyfluthrin. Simulations used a 160 × 160 km domain at 400 m resolution, with application amount, release height, and field geometry derived from Arizona Department of Agriculture records. The simulations show that approximately 98% of released pesticide mass leaves the domain in the vapor phase within 48 hours, whereas the particle fraction accounts for nearly all local deposition. Deposition is concentrated within about 1–2 km of treated fields and is dominated by dry deposition, with episodic wet-deposition events during the summer monsoon and winter. Weekly vapor concentrations span approximately 0.1–100 ng m-3 and show strong seasonality, with the highest burdens generally occurring in fall when application intensity is highest. We further analyze the distribution of grid-cell concentrations to distinguish near-source hotspots from the regional background. Results indicate declining concentrations through approximately 2010 followed by increases for several compounds, with differences between hotspot and background trends. Given the lack of monitoring in Arizona, modeled concentrations are broadly consistent with ambient measurements from California's pesticide air-monitoring network and reveal persistent spatial gradients in pesticide burdens near agricultural fields. These results provide a long-term characterization of pesticide transport, deposition, seasonality, and temporal change, while also highlighting the need for expanded atmospheric monitoring to better constrain pesticide exposure in intensively farmed regions.

494130.title: Hyperlocal Air Quality Modeling and Source Apportionment in Greater Boston
494130.authors: Yang Zhang, Northeastern University, Boston, MA; and Y. Wang, Y. Yang, and K. Farzad
494130.abstract: Air pollution is heterogeneous within cities, caused by a variety of emission sources such as buildings, vehicles, power plants, and restaurants, and their interactions with urban infrastructure and micrometeorology. Air pollution “hot spots” result in disproportionate exposure at hyperlocal scales (e.g., city block, neighborhood). There is a significant lack of hyperlocal measurements and modeling capabilities in characterizing those “hot spots,” their drivers, and their impacts—information that is necessary to design effective policy and mitigation strategies for affected communities. In this work, we integrate air quality measurements and modeling to understand the spatio-temporal distributions of hyperlocal air pollution and to quantify its source contributions in Greater Boston, USA. A suite of models is applied at multiple scales with a focus on hyperlocal scales (1-km and street-scale), including (1) an online-coupled meteorology-chemistry model, the Weather Research and Forecasting Model coupled with Chemistry and Greenhouse Gases (WRF-Chem-GHG); (2) the Comprehensive Air Quality Model with extensions (CAMx), encompassing the Ozone and Particulate Matter Source Apportionment Technology (OSAT and PSAT), driven by offline-coupled WRF meteorology; and (3) an advanced street-scale urban network model with detailed chemistry and aerosol formation mechanisms, the Model of Urban Network of Intersecting Canyons and Highways (MUNICH). WRF-Chem-GHG simulations show a strong gradient, with high concentrations of O3 and PM2.5 near sources, but insufficient grid resolution—even at 1 km—for resolving heterogeneity at a hyperlocal scale. MUNICH street-scale predictions show better capability in capturing PM2.5 hot spots on streets than the 1-km WRF-Chem-GHG predictions. WRF-CAMx source apportionment, with 15 emission sectors and 18 source regions, shows that while long-range transport affects air pollution in Greater Boston in both summer and winter months, significant local contributors include waste, commercial, residential, and vehicular emissions in both seasons, as well as biogenic sources in summer. These results provide invaluable insight into the drivers and impacts of hyperlocal air pollution and can inform emission control policies and related intervention strategies for cities in this region.

494131.title: Potential for Snow Enhancement in a Changing Climate: Environmental Conditions Govern the Added Benefit of Seeding Materials with Warmer Ice-Nucleation Temperatures
494131.authors: Sisi Chen, NCAR, Longmont, CO; and L. Xue, S. A. Tessendorf, and J. K. Wolff
494131.abstract: Silver iodide (AgI) is the most widely used material for glaciogenic cloud seeding because it can nucleate ice at a warmer temperature (~ −6 °C) than many natural ice-nucleating particles (INPs). As freezing levels rise and cloud thermodynamic structure changes under current and projected climate conditions, a greater fraction of the available supercooled liquid water (SLW) may occur at temperatures above the effective range of AgI. This could reduce the depth or frequency of cloud layers suitable for AgI seeding. We conducted complementary 2D idealized and 3D real-case WRF-WxMod simulations. 2D simulations over a bell-shaped mountain isolated sensitivity to temperature, moisture, wind speed, atmospheric stability, mountain geometry, and background aerosol concentration. For each environment, we tested ground-based and aircraft release of three hypothetical seeding materials with upper ice-nucleation temperatures near −6 °C (AgI baseline), −4 °C, and −2 °C. 3D simulations of real seeding events from past field campaigns are also conducted to examine whether the idealized response persisted with realistic terrain and storm structures. Both experiment sets show that seeding materials with warmer ice-nucleation temperatures consistently produce greater simulated precipitation enhancement. However environmental conditions remain the dominant control on snow-enhancement potential. The magnitude of the added benefit depends on cloud thermodynamic structure, SLW availability in cloud regions reached by the seeding material, natural ice production, and release method.

494133.title: Impact of Spatial Resolution on Climate and Atmospheric Chemistry Simulations in MIRAE-ESM v1.0
494133.authors: Seungun Lee, Seoul National University, Seoul, South korea; and R. Park
494133.abstract: The Multi-scale Integrated Research for Advanced Environment-Earth System Model (MIRAE-ESM) v1.0 is a newly developed fully coupled chemistry-climate model integrating the Global/Regional Integrated Model system (GRIMs), Noah-MP, GEOS-Chem, NEMO-OCE, and NEMO-SI3 via the OASIS3-MCT coupler. While the standard-resolution version shows stable long-term performance in historical simulations and future climate projections, testing how spatial resolution affects the model is key to understanding its overall capabilities. In this study, we evaluate resolution sensitivity by comparing a high-resolution version with the standard-resolution baseline. Instead of focusing only on specific regional weather events, this work aims to test the overall level of model improvement with higher spatial resolution. We analyze how higher resolution changes large-scale atmospheric circulation, key physical variables like surface temperature and precipitation, and air-sea interactions across the coupled system. In addition, we investigate how increased spatial resolution affects atmospheric chemistry through the GEOS-Chem module. By comparing different resolution setups, this study aims to show the general performance gains, chemical-physical coupling behavior, and overall model improvements of MIRAE-ESM v1.0 under higher spatial resolution.

494134.title: Urban and Coastal Urban Boundary Layers: Characteristics, Transport, and Extremes (Invited Presentation)
494134.authors: Prathap Ramamurthy, The City College of New York, New York
494134.abstract: This talk will explore the unique characteristics of urban and coastal urban boundary layers. Cities are defined above all by surface heterogeneity: the urban fabric is made up of materials with widely differing thermal and hygroscopic properties, with abrupt material boundaries that fundamentally reshape the radiation, energy, and water budgets. The buildings that dominate the urban environment have varying roughness lengths that lead to unique wind regimes and turbulent transport characteristics unlike anything found over flat, homogeneous terrain. Together, these modifications trap heat and suppress ventilation, leaving cities acutely vulnerable to heat and air quality extremes. While the impact of these surface features is well researched and represented in urban models, the boundary layer characteristics, particularly the transport in the urban mixed layer, are relatively less researched due to logistical and theoretical constraints. Here we will examine how urban momentum and thermal boundary layers behave under a range of local and non-local forcings, and where that behavior departs from conventional boundary layer theory. Drawing on multi-scale observations alongside numerical model results, we will characterize the properties of urban and coastal urban boundary layers, and how they shape extreme events such as heatwaves, thunderstorms, and air quality episodes. Finally, we will consider how sea breezes reshape the boundary layer over coastal cities.

494135.title: Evaluating Public Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence Applications in Early Warning Systems
494135.authors: Julia Adamczyk, NCAR, Boulder, CO; University of Florida, Gainesville, FL
494135.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming atmospheric sciences through advancements in forecasting, hazard detection, and environmental decision support. Recent developments in AI-based weather models and analytical tools have demonstrated the potential to improve prediction capabilities and enhance communication of hazardous weather information. However, the societal effectiveness of these technologies depends not only on technical performance but also on whether the public understands, trusts, and accepts AI-assisted warnings. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into operational meteorology and early warning systems (EWS), understanding public perceptions is essential for ensuring that these technologies support effective risk communication and decision-making. This study investigates public knowledge and perceptions of AI applications within EWS, focusing on factors influencing acceptance of AI-assisted warnings. A survey was conducted (n = 82) to examine respondents’ familiarity with AI, understanding of AI applications, perceptions of AI reliability, concerns regarding potential errors, preferences for human oversight, and willingness to act on AI-assisted hazard warnings. Relationship tests, including Spearman correlation and Chi-Square analyses, were used to evaluate associations between AI knowledge, transparency, trust, reliability perceptions, hazard scenarios, and behavioral intentions. Results indicate that greater interaction with AI does not necessarily translate into greater understanding of AI applications. While respondents generally recognized the potential of AI in meteorological contexts, familiarity with domain-specific applications such as AI-assisted EWS was more limited. These findings suggest that general exposure to AI alone may not be sufficient to improve AI literacy in meteorological-related contexts. Analysis of AI acceptance further demonstrated that trust and perceived reliability were stronger factors influencing acceptance than transparency alone. Although respondents expressed a strong desire to know when AI was used, transparency regarding AI involvement in EWS did not significantly determine willingness to act. Instead, concerns regarding AI errors were strongly associated with reduced trust and increased preference for human oversight. Respondents were not necessarily opposed to AI integration; rather, acceptance was higher when AI systems were perceived as reliable and supported by human review. These findings highlight the importance of considering societal factors alongside technological development when implementing AI in meteorological applications. Effective integration of AI into EWS will require not only accurate and reliable models but also targeted public education, clear communication strategies, and appropriate human oversight. Future work should investigate how different communication approaches, such as emphasizing AI generation, meteorologist verification, or combined human-AI decision processes, influence public trust and willingness to respond to AI-assisted warnings. Understanding public perceptions of AI provides an important foundation for developing trustworthy, accessible, and socially effective AI applications within weather forecasting and hazard communication.

494136.title: Drought in Context: Evolving U.S. Drought Monitor Communication Through Multimedia
494136.authors: Emily Case-Buskirk, National Drought Mitigation Center-University of Nebraska, LINCOLN, NE; and L. E. Johnson
494136.abstract: The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) provides a weekly assessment of drought conditions across the U.S., but communicating the story behind changes on the map can be challenging. Drought development and improvement often reflect a combination of precipitation, temperature, soil moisture, streamflow, snowpack, impacts and conditions occurring across multiple timescales. While the USDM map provides a concise representation of drought severity and extent, the map alone cannot communicate all of the context behind current conditions and weekly changes. The National Drought Mitigation Center (NDMC) developed the Drought Download video series as a way to expand USDM communication into a short multimedia format that combines maps, graphics and narration to provide additional context about drought conditions across the country. The Drought Download began as an effort to make USDM information more accessible and reach audiences through platforms and formats beyond the traditional weekly map and narrative. Producing the videos, however, quickly demonstrated that moving drought information from text and static maps into multimedia involves more than simply presenting the same information in a different format. Each video requires decisions about which drought developments are most important, how much scientific context audiences need, which maps and graphics best support the story and how to explain complex or rapidly changing conditions within a limited amount of time. As the series has continued, the Drought Download has evolved in response to lessons learned through the production process. Changes to the videos have focused on improving organization, pacing, visual presentation and the connection between what viewers see and what they hear. Experience producing the series has also highlighted the importance of moving beyond a description of where drought is located to explain why conditions are changing. Connecting changes on the USDM map with recent precipitation, temperature, impacts and other supporting information can provide audiences with a more complete drought story while helping explain why drought may improve rapidly in some situations but persist despite recent precipitation in others. The production process has also revealed challenges inherent in multimedia drought communication. More information does not necessarily produce a clearer video, and maps that are useful to drought experts may require additional explanation for broader audiences. Likewise, information that works well in a written narrative does not always translate effectively to narration or visual presentation. Developing the series has therefore required balancing scientific detail with clarity, video length and visual complexity while maintaining the context necessary to accurately represent drought conditions. This presentation will describe why the Drought Download was developed, how the series has changed over time and lessons learned from translating operational drought information into multimedia. Examples from the evolution of the videos will illustrate changes in content selection, storytelling, graphics and presentation and will highlight approaches that have worked as well as elements that required refinement. These experiences demonstrate the value of treating multimedia science communication as an iterative process rather than simply an additional outlet for existing information. Lessons from the Drought Download are helping inform how the NDMC communicates the USDM beyond the weekly map and narrative. More broadly, the experience illustrates both the opportunities and challenges involved in adapting complex climate information for multimedia audiences and provides practical lessons for organizations seeking to expand the reach of operational science products while maintaining scientific context and accuracy.

494137.title: A Retrospective Randall Experiment on the Sensitivity of an AI Emulator to Saharan Dust Heating (Invited Presentation)
494137.authors: Milton Halem, University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Rockville, MD; University of Maryland Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; and Y. Diggikar and A. Raman
494137.abstract: Early experiments by Randall, Carlson, and Mintz 1984, demonstrated that Saharan dust is not merely transported by the tropical circulation but can modify that circulation through radiative heating. Using the Goddard Laboratory for Atmospheric Sciences general circulation model, they found that prescribed dust heating narrowed and intensified the tropical Atlantic rain belt and weakened the low-level easterlies responsible for westward dust transport. Their pioneering work anticipated current questions concerning the interactions among Saharan dust, multi-scale 2-D cumulus cloud modeling, African easterly waves, and Atlantic tropical cyclogenesis. Subsequent aerosol-aware and cloud-resolving models GCM models such as Lau et. a. 2009, Strong et. al., 2018 and Chen et. al., 2021 have reproduced and substantially extended the original Randall–Carlson–Mintz experiment. In this talk we address the question of whether AI emulations can similarly validate these cloud physics based GCM experiments. Building on recent works by Diggikar, Halem and Raman on the performance of multi- AI OSSE emulations, the NASA–AI IBM Prithvi WxC foundation model is being adapted to validate the Randall et. al., results that Saharan dust emulation weakens low level Easterlies and intensifies the tropical rain belt over the Atlantic. Trained with post-2000 MERRA-2 data residuals, Prithvi will be able to resolve five dust tracer sizes, namely surface and column dust mass, aerosol optical properties, emissions, sedimentation, and wet and dry deposition. The model will be trained on MERRA-2 residuals to identify the roles of winds, boundary-layer depth, precipitation, particle size, and removal processes in dust biases during trans-Atlantic transport. Evaluations will be conducted against satellite products, AERONET, reanalysis, persistence, and climatology for assessing Prithvi for global dust forecasting and diagnosing regional altitude-dependent errors in dust emissions and transport. Thus, this OSSE experiment has two aims, (i) whether an AI model such as Prithvi has learned the two-way relationships between Saharan dust, radiative effects on circulation, and trans-Atlantic transport, (ii) to establish comparable Saharan dust sensitivity of the AI Prithvi foundation model with GCM global dust forecasting. Predicting global dust emission, transport, and deposition with an AI foundation model like Prithvi WxC thus directly attributes the involved processes and the key variables that drive uncertainties in dust vertical structure. This process-level understanding can help diagnose and correct regions where aerosol-shielding biases beneath overlying dust layers are highest in satellite trace gas retrievals.

494138.title: Remote Sensing of the Planetary Boundary Layer with PlanetiQ GNSS-RO High Vertical Resolution, All-Weather Soundings
494138.authors: Emil Robert Kursinski, PlanetiQ, Golden, CO; and X. Feng, J. Xu, K. J. Nelson, and P. H. Cheng
494138.abstract: PlanetiQ has developed - and is flying - an orbiting Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) radio occultation (RO) system that is profiling the atmosphere globally with very high vertical resolution. GNSS-RO is the only satellite system capable of profiling the planetary boundary layer (PBL) through any type of weather, over any surface type, with sufficiently high vertical resolution to resolve and profile the PBL. PlanetiQ’s system is unique in measuring GNSS-RO globally with very high signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), specifically to profile the PBL and detect radio frequency (RF) ducting conditions. PlanetiQ has also developed a new GNSS-RO processing system based on the sliding window phase matching (SWPM) method which, for the first time, can isolate results horizontally in the cross-track direction. The resulting GNSS-RO resolution is approximately 100 m in the vertical, 100 km in the along-track direction, and better than 10 km in the cross-track direction. The cross-track resolution has the potential to provide new information on mesoscale systems. We continue to refine our processing to better extract the wealth of information contained in the RO observations about the lower troposphere and boundary layer in particular. To quantify the accuracy of bending angle profiles retrieved from PlanetiQ GNSS-RO, we conduct retrieval intercomparisons, particularly in the lower troposphere and PBL, derived by UCAR, AER (running a version of UCAR’s retrieval system), and PlanetiQ’s own SWPM retrieval system. Retrievals are also compared to bending angle profiles derived from ERA5 reanalyses and GDAS analyses, as well as to collocated radiosondes. Radiosonde comparisons enable us to improve and refine our GNSS-RO retrievals. The comparisons with the analyses reveal systematic differences between the analyses and GNSS-RO demonstrating the need to better assimilate the GNSS-RO information into model forecasts and (re)analysis products and the potential impacts on produced results. We select interesting RO-retrieved global PBL examples to present, including from polar regions, marine and terrestrial tropical regions, atmospheric rivers and tropical cyclones, and horizontally-scanning occultations revealing variations in local PBL heights. Additionally, we explore how atmospheric turbulence affects GNSS-RO profiles both to improve the RO retrievals by accounting for turbulent scattering and defocusing of the GNSS signals passing through the atmosphere and to characterize properties of the turbulence.

494139.title: CANN2ONET: Integrating a Flux Tower Network, Study of Soil Processes and Improved Biogeochemical Modelling for Agricultural N2O Emission Mitigation
494139.authors: Claudia Wagner-Riddle, Univ. of Guelph, Guelph, ON, Canada
494139.abstract: Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a potent greenhouse gas emitted predominantly during crop production due to the addition of nitrogen fertilizer. N2O fluxes are challenging to measure due to their high temporal and spatial variability characterized as occurring in ‘hot spots’ (i.e. areas with high fluxes relative to surrounding areas) and at ‘hot moments’ (i.e. short periods of time with high fluxes relative to the intervening time periods). To capture emission events, it is imperative to use year-round measurement methods that integrate emissions over large field areas and with high temporal resolution such as is the case with micrometeorological methods. In addition, the need to assess mitigation practices requires side-by-side field comparisons that couple flux measurements with detailed studies of soil nitrogen cycling and microbial processes resulting in net N2O production. To address the challenge for improved measurements and better understanding of soil N2O flux drivers, we established CANN2ONET, a network of benchmark sites across Canada. This multidisciplinary network is a collaboration between academia, government and industry to achieve reductions in fertilizer-related N2O emissions. The network includes eight field tower sites in major grain and oilseed regions across Canada and a regional tall tower. Flux measurements are coupled to detailed soil process studies including mapping of microbial pathways generating N2O. High-frequency measurements collected at different scales are used to evaluate and improve biogeochemical models (e.g. DNDC), as well as data-driven approaches, including machine learning. Here we present an overview of CANN2ONET’s benchmark sites, instrumentation and measurement methods used, including recent data. Approaches used in integrating the findings to date and addressing the policy needs of partners will be discussed.

494142.title: Advances in a Compound Coastal Flood Modeling System
494142.authors: Christine Szpilka, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and M. Leonard, J. Parker, K. M. Dresback, and R. L. Kolar
494142.abstract: Flooding due to compound hazards is a complex problem that must be solved with coupled modeling systems; intense precipitation, overland flooding, and coastal surge often combine to create extreme hazards that cannot be linearly superimposed. With support from NOAA, NSF Coastlines and People (CoPe), and the NIST Center of Excellence on Risk-based Community Resilience Planning, a compound flood modeling system that combines multiple coastal hazards (precipitation, hydrology, wind, waves and surge) has been developed and continually refined over the past two decades. This presentation aims to summarize a few of the more recent advances with special focus on the precipitation, hydrology and hydrodynamic components. The framework has been applied to many different types of modeling exercises: when coupled to an evacuation model in forecast mode, it can provide guidance for emergency managers; ensemble studies can better identify hazards and “worst case scenarios” under different climate conditions; hindcast studies can assess the accuracy of each model component, as well as the framework as a whole; uncertainty propagation can be tracked, etc. For computationally efficient Monte Carlo simulations, the framework relies on ensemble tracks and a parametric model, P-CLIPER, to estimate precipitation. Recent upgrades to P-CLIPER are described in more detail in a companion presentation (Advances in the Parametric Tropical Cyclone Rainfall Model, P-CLIPER: Expanded Calibration and Asymmetry Implementation). In this presentation, we focus on the hydrologic and hydraulic response to the P-CLIPER improvements. Due to the system’s modular nature, a variety of hydrologic models can be used; in this presentation we compare the importance of resolution and accurate parameter estimation using one of NOAA’s operational models - the Ensemble Framework For Flash Flood Forecasting (EF5) - and discuss pros and cons. Finally, recent upgrades to the Advanced CIRCulation (ADCIRC) hydrodynamic model allow for direct ingestion of precipitation and hydrologic sources throughout the domain. An ongoing development is to allow the hydrologic input location for each feature to move upstream as the event progresses, so as to better capture the compound flooding in the coastal transition zone. Incremental model improvements for select historical events that impacted the North Carolina coast will be presented.

494148.title: An Overview of PlanetiQ's GNSS Remote Sensing Capabilities: Updates for 2027
494148.authors: E Robert Kursinski, PlanetIQ, Inc., Golden, CO; PlanetiQ, Inc., Golden, CO; and J. Brandmeyer, K. J. Nelson, PhD, X. Feng, C. Wang, and P. H. Cheng
494148.abstract: We present a summary of PlanetiQ’s state-of-the-art GNSS observing system’s capabilities and near-term plans. The observations consist primarily of both neutral atmosphere and ionosphere profiles starting in October 2021. By the time of the AMS Annual Meeting of 2027, PlanetiQ’s constellation of small satellites is scheduled to be producing more than 13,000 neutral atmosphere profiles and 14,000 daily slant total electron content (TEC) slant profiles each day. We have thus far acquired more than 2 million GNSS-RO profiles of the atmosphere and ionosphere, achieved by acquiring RO data from the 4 major GNSS constellations: GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, and BeiDou-3. Based on these data, we have contracts with NOAA, NASA, USAF, and USSF, as well as other commercial entities. Our GNSS observing system is unique in that it acquires neutral atmosphere RO data with very high signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), generally higher than that of COSMIC-2. This high SNR, plus our high-performance reference oscillators, reduces noise which enables the GNSS-RO profiles to extend to higher altitudes into the lower mesosphere. The bigger advantage of the high SNR is for profiling the planetary boundary layer (PBL) and lower troposphere, which the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) and NASA have identified as a key goal for weather, climate, and air quality monitoring, understanding, and forecasting. GNSS-RO’s ability to vertically profile the PBL from orbit, in all weather conditions, across the globe, is unique and critical to achieving these goals. High SNR GNSS-RO enables minimization of biases in GNSS-RO profiles in the lower troposphere and PBL. This includes detecting ducting conditions, which occur frequently over the ocean, that requires special processing of the GNSS-RO data to minimize biases, and therefore, knowledge of whether ducting is occurring. Two satellites in PlanetiQ’s constellation carry a proprietary high-gain, dual-linear polarization antenna that enables each satellite to acquire polarized RO (PRO) profiles for characterizing heavy liquid precipitation, snowfall, and certain ice cloud types in addition to acquiring the standard GNSS-RO profiles. The two satellites together acquire a total of more than 2000 GNSS-PRO profiles each day. The dual-linear polarization antennas also enable acquisition of reflected signals for grazing GNSS reflection (GNSS-GR) applications. We will discuss our Level-2 neutral atmosphere processing system and its performance, our low latency ionosphere acquisition and processing system (achieved with additional ground stations), work on electron density profiling including sporadic E-layer characterization, and acquisition of high-rate scintillation data to capture all scintillation events and enable geolocation and characterization of ionospheric inhomogeneities. We utilize the high SNR GNSS-RO observations together with our sliding window phase matching-based retrieval system to reduce biases and noise particularly in the lower troposphere and PBL to enable that information to be assimilated into NWP and reanalysis systems for weather, climate, and air quality. This includes fully recovering the largest bending angles from the RO data which are underestimated, better extraction of RO bending angle information with reduced noise, better uncertainty estimates needed to properly weight and maximize impact on weather forecasts and reanalyses for climate, and improving the vertical resolution to determine the PBL height (PBLH), and profile the refractivity structure within the PBL across the globe.

494150.title: Radiative-Convective Equilibrium with Mean Surface Wind and Wind Shear (Invited Presentation)
494150.authors: David S. Nolan, University of Miami, Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric and Earth Science, Miami, FL; and Y. Dai
494150.abstract: Radiative-convective equilibrium (RCE) is an idealization of the tropical atmosphere. It envisions a warm, moist atmosphere overlying a vast tropical ocean with constant surface temperature. Over the last few decades, RCE has been studied extensively in numerical simulations of many types and on many scales. A major finding from this work is that the random convection in RCE can organize into large-scale “aggregated” clusters, usually leading to formation of tropical cyclones (TCs) when the Coriolis parameter is nonzero. The positive feedbacks that lead to aggregation have been studied in great detail, and can vary fundamentally from case to case and model to model. However, the large majority of research on RCE and aggregation does not incorporate the effects surface wind and wind shear. Mean surface wind increases the evaporation rate everywhere, leading to an RCE state that is warmer and moister, and sometimes less responsive to some of the aforementioned feedbacks. Wind shear leads to organization of convection into bands, but also inhibits larger-scale aggregation. Some studies have used wind shear, but in many cases the wind profiles are overly idealized or unrealistic. We address these shortcomings by studying RCE with realistic mean surface winds and realistic wind profiles. Results show modification, and even suppression, of the aggregation phenomenon as surface wind and wind shear increase; these effects have been reported before, but have not been explored thoroughly. Effects of the diurnal cycle will also be considered.

494152.title: Rapid Tropical Cyclone Size Growth in Idealized GCM Experiments
494152.authors: Shuai Wang, University of Delaware, Newark, DE; and H. Murakami
494152.abstract: Rapid growth (RG), defined as the rapid expansion of the outer wind field of tropical cyclones (TCs), is a recently recognized structural mode distinct from rapid intensification, yet investigation has been limited by observational uncertainty. Here we show that both real-world and idealized general circulation model (GCM) simulations can reproduce observed TC outer-size characteristics and RG-related features. Two distinct RG regimes emerge near 30N. South of 30N, RG occurs in a tropical environment characterized by warm sea surface temperatures (SSTs), weak wind shear, and weak baroclinicity, accompanied by vortex axisymmetrization and intensification. North of 30N, RG occurs in a baroclinic environment with stronger shear and sharper SST gradients, associated with increasing surface wind asymmetry, weakening core intensity, and growing vortex tilt, consistent with extratropical transition. Despite uncertainties in observed TC outer size, our results demonstrate the potential of GCM frameworks for understanding rapid TC outer-wind growth.

494153.title: Three Ingredient Method: A Comparison of Tornadic and Non-tornadic Segments on the 15 April 2026 Southeast Michigan Severe Weather Event
494153.authors: Selena Ailis Centeno, NSF, Alpharetta, GA
494153.abstract: A Quasi-Linear Convective System (QLCS) moved across the state of Michigan during the overnight hours of 15 April 2026, producing widespread damaging winds and a series of weak tornadoes. This event presented the opportunity to investigate why mesovortex genesis occurred within certain portions of the convective line while other portions remained nontornadic despite being a part of the same QLCS. This research applied the Three Ingredient Method, along with confidence nudgers, to compare the evolution of tornadic segments of Washtenaw and Wayne counties and non-tornadic segments of Jackson County. Environmental conditions were evaluated using archived thermodynamic soundings and surface observational data, while mesovortic evolutions were examined using archived radar data (NEXRAD Level II). Special attention was given to changes in the low-level environment, orientation of shear vectors relative to the convective line, 0-3 kilometers bulk shear, and relationship between the cold pool and ambient shear. Results suggest that tornadic segments were characterized by a more favorable balance of ingredients than non-tornadic segments. The evolution of these ingredients also demonstrates the importance of investigating localized differences within a QLCS rather than treating these cases as having a uniform environment. These results support the utility of the Three Ingredient Method when assessing QLCS tornado potential, as it demonstrates the value of combining radar observation with environmental analysis when evaluating rapidly evolving severe weather.

494154.title: Closing the Radar Gap for Western Wisconsin Tornadoes
494154.authors: Elijah Conklin, Valparaiso University, Valparaiso, IN; and J. R. Beitlich and B. P. Hewett
494154.abstract: Western Wisconsin tornadoes currently present a difficult challenge for forecasters at the NWS Twin Cities office (MPX) due to the radar gap that exists for MPX’s nine Wisconsin counties in its county warning area (CWA). A radar gap is an area in which weather phenomena, especially at low altitudes, cannot be detected due to their far distance from the radar. To better identify this radar gap, an analysis of 83 tornado warnings and 17 unwarned tornadoes in western Wisconsin between 2013 and 2025 was conducted using GR2Analyst 3 to compare radar data from KMPX and neighboring radars at NWS La Crosse (ARX) and NWS Duluth (DLH). Radar beam height, distance from the radar, rotational velocity (VROT), and presence of a tornadic debris signature (TDS) were compared to determine which radar is best for nowcasting tornadoes across western Wisconsin. Near-storm environmental parameters were also compared to help distinguish tornadic from non-tornadic events. Results suggest that KARX radar provides greater utility in the southern tier of Wisconsin counties in the MPX CWA, while KDLH is more useful for the far northeastern counties. KMPX remains the most helpful radar for the remainder of the CWA. Storm mode also plays a role in accurately warning these tornadoes, as multicell systems appear to pose the greatest challenge for MPX forecasters, with eight of the 17 unwarned tornadoes being produced by this type of storm. Results from this research are now being utilized by MPX forecasters during warning operations.

494158.title: Static and Dynamic Diffusion Emulators: From Sampling Gray Swan Extreme Events to Suffering from Model Collapse
494158.authors: Karan Jakhar, Pravah, San Francisco, CA; University of Chicago, Chicago, IL; and P. Hassanzadeh, B. Lütjens, and J. Weare
494158.abstract: Characterizing rare extreme events is a major challenge in climate and other sciences, and AI emulators may offer a solution: The idea is that an emulator trained on a small dataset can generate large synthetic datasets with extreme events beyond those in the training set. In principle, AI cannot generalize beyond the training set (i.e., extrapolate), however, because the governing equations are fixed, there are speculations that generative models, especially those that learn from fast dynamics, can reproduce stronger events from the same dynamical system. Here, we investigate the most promising approaches using 2D geophysical turbulence test cases. First, we train an unconditional static emulator that samples plausible flow states from noise; second, an autoregressive dynamic emulator; and third, iteratively augment the training dataset using the emulator’s output. We show that both static and dynamic emulators can produce extreme events stronger than those in the training set, effectively creating “gray swans”. However, neither could accurately reproduce the frequency (return period) of these rare events. We show that both emulators are constrained by the small training set, and increasing the data size by iteratively training emulators on their own output leads to model collapse - a degenerative feedback that worsens extreme event estimates. Overall, we show that using a diffusion loss is an insufficient criterion for neural networks to learn the underlying equations or data-generating process.

494159.title: Physics-Guided Triphasic Nowcasting to Complement Warn-on-Forecast System During the First Forecast Hour
494159.authors: Marc J Crampe, The City College of New York, NYC, NY; and J. T. Carlin, J. J. Gourley, D. R. Stratman, C. A. Kerr, and R. M. Khanbilvardi
494159.abstract: Rapidly initiating and intensifying convection remains difficult to predict during the first forecast hour, when storm-scale numerical guidance may be affected by imperfect initiation timing, model spin-up, displacement errors, and the interval between forecast updates. Radar-based nowcasting provides a frequently updating representation of observed storm state, but its skill decreases as convective growth, decay, and new-cell development become increasingly important. Herein, we develop a physics-guided deep-learning nowcasting layer intended to complement, rather than replace, the Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS), with the goal of bridging observation-driven forecasts and convection-allowing ensemble guidance. The framework uses a triphasic U-Net that separates precipitation evolution into transport, intensity change, and new-cell generation. Radar observations anchor the forecast to the latest storm state, while satellite, environmental, and WoFS-derived guidance provide information on convective evolution beyond extrapolation alone. Pixel-level convection-initiation probabilities are being evaluated to condition the generation branch. The model produces 1-km precipitation forecasts at lead times from 10 to 180 min, with primary emphasis on the first forecast hour. A conditional adversarial refinement stage will subsequently sharpen localized structures and improve representation of the upper precipitation-intensity tail. The framework is being developed and evaluated using event-wise splits across more than 30 convective and flooding events in the northeastern United States. An initial comparison with WoFS for the 18–19 August 2024 Long Island flood event showed promising and complementary forecast behavior. While WoFS produced a more conservative ensemble forecast and underestimated the domain-mean and upper-tail precipitation, the rapid-update radar-based model provided stronger detection and spatial greement with the observed precipitation in this case.These encouraging results motivate an expanded evaluation of the complete triphasic system across additional events using continuous, categorical, probabilistic, and precipitation-intensity metrics. Current work is integrating additional satellite and storm-scale guidance into the triphasic system before the full WoFS evaluation. The goal is not to replace WoFS, but to determine whether rapid-update neural nowcasting can add value during the first forecast hour and provide a smoother transition to convection-allowing ensemble guidance. Broader generalization will require evaluation beyond the northeastern U.S. events currently used for training.

494160.title: Warm Season Drought in New England: Implications of a Changing Hydroclimate
494160.authors: Jordin Hubbard, University of Massachusetts Lowell, Lowell, MA; University of Massachusetts Lowell, Lowell, MA; and J. B. Basara, J. I. Christian, T. Schneider, S. A. Bakar, and V. Lakshmi
494160.abstract: New England’s hydroclimate is changing. Although the region exhibits an overall wetting trend, data analysis revealed an increase in anomalously warm and dry growing seasons over the past decade (2016-2025), during which three flash drought events (2016, 2020, and 2022) were identified via the United States Drought Monitor (USDM) and formal metrics. To investigate these events, multiple datasets were used including PRISM (precipitation and temperature), the ERA5-Land reanalysis (potential evapotranspiration), Harvard Forest Flux Tower observations (latent heat fluxes, net radiation, incoming shortwave radiation, and incoming longwave radiation), the United States Geological Survey (USGS) National Water Information System (NWIS; streamflow), and satellite remote sensing observation from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS; vegetation responses via the Land Surface Water Index; LSWI). Key characteristics include anomalously high temperatures, precipitation deficits, rapid streamflow declines, and elevated atmospheric demand indicated by increased potential evapotranspiration and net radiation. Despite these conditions, observations from the Harvard Forest EMS Flux Tower (HFR1) showed that latent heat fluxes remained near or above climatological norms during each event, resulting in elevated evapotranspiration (ET). LSWI data similarly showed enhanced greening in some areas despite persistent drought conditions, precipitation deficits, and increased atmospheric demand. This response differs from drought research in other regions, as latent heat fluxes, and thus evapotranspiration, kept pace with potential evapotranspiration. At the same time, rapid intensification of drought was first seen in the streamflow (versus vegetation) which rapidly declined from above the 50th percentile to below the 20th between May and June across New England. This response was consistent amongst the three events, pointing to rapid impacts in surface water as drought stress intensifies.

494161.title: Wave and current observations as proxies for Langmuir mixing beneath Hurricane Erin (2025)
494161.authors: Jacob Davis, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, MA; and S. R. Jayne, E. Sanabia, B. Villas Boas, D. H. Richter, M. Schonau, A. Williams, L. Centurioni, A. Ekholm, and L. Cen
494161.abstract: Wave-driven ocean mixing beneath tropical cyclones is explored using surface wave and upper ocean observations collected in Hurricane Erin (2025) as part of the Study on Air-Sea Coupling with WAves, Turbulence, and Clouds at High winds (SASCWATCH) project. Stokes drift profiles, estimated from directional wave spectra, and observed Lagrangian current profiles are combined with insights from the wave-averaged Craik-Leibovich equations to assess favorability for Langmuir turbulence development beneath the storm. Underlying wave spectra vary in development across low frequencies but mostly have saturated high frequency tails, limiting Stokes drift under the highest wind speed conditions. Stokes drift is substantially reduced in regions with misalignment between long waves (eventual swell) and wind-sea due to opposing contributions from low and high frequency wave components. Lagrangian current velocity profiles with low near-surface shear are common in regions of stronger Stokes drift, with low shear plausibly resulting from the Stokes return flow anticipated by the Stokes-Coriolis coupling term in the Craik-Leibovich equations. Counter-gradient Stokes drift and Lagrangian current profiles exist, but occur less frequently. Estimated directional Langmuir numbers vary widely throughout storm passage, with favorable conditions for Langmuir turbulence development during the forced stage. The largest changes are in the storm’s wake, where near-inertial oscillations repeatedly rotate current vectors in and out of alignment with Stokes drift vectors. Significant wave-current interaction is evident in the immediate storm wake, whereby wave height, slope, and Stokes drift are modulated at the inertial period. When combined with recent insights from coupled model studies, these observations advance understanding of wave-driven contributions to upper-ocean mixing and their influence on tropical cyclone intensity.

494162.title: How Do Surface Gravity Waves Organize Turbulent Currents into Jets?
494162.authors: Nicholas Pizzo, University of Rhode Island, Graduate School of Oceanography, Narragansett, RI; University of Rhode Island, Graduate School of Oceanography, Narragansett, RI
494162.abstract: We examine how surface gravity waves can organize turbulent currents into jets. This is done in the Craik-Leibovich framework, and we draw on the analogy between the vortex force term and the Coriolis term that enters into descriptions approximating flow on the rotating sphere. In certain asymptotic regimes the analogy is exact. Physically, the curl of the Stokes drift leads to a quantity akin to planetary vorticity. When this curl has a non-vanishing second derivative, the system supports the existence of vorticity waves. These waves can lead to jet formation, in line with Rhines's beta-arrest, when there is an inverse cascade present (the usual inverse cascade of two-dimensional turbulence on the beta-plane, and the inverse cascade due to Langmuir turbulence for the surface wave scenario). Numerical examples are given to support the theory.

494164.title: Coupled Earth–Human System Modeling in the Great Lakes Region (Invited Presentation)
494164.abstract: Interactions among the atmosphere, land, large water bodies, and human systems can substantially modify large-scale meteorological signals and associated risks. These interactions are particularly strong in the Great Lakes region, where lake thermal inertia, seasonal ice cover, complex coastlines, heterogeneous land use, and intensive water and energy management generate feedbacks that persist from weather to subseasonal-to-seasonal timescales. Accurately representing these processes remains a central challenge for regional prediction. The Coastal Observations, Mechanisms, and Predictions Across Systems and Scales—Great Lakes Modeling (COMPASS-GLM) project developed new capabilities for investigating these feedbacks through coupled, process-resolving simulations of the atmosphere, lakes, land surface, and hydrologic systems. These capabilities include a coupled atmosphere–lake–land modeling framework based on WRF-FVCOM-ELM for studying regional-scale processes. Together, they provide a foundation for determining which processes must be explicitly resolved, how uncertainties propagate among coupled components, and where reduced-order or machine-learning representations may be effective. This presentation reviews the modeling capabilities and applications developed through COMPASS-GLM and describes how they motivate the Great Lakes Earth System AI Modeling (GLEAM) project. GLEAM will extend this framework to investigate how interacting sources of environmental and societal memory, including lake heat storage, ice anomalies, soil moisture, groundwater, vegetation, land management, regulated water transfers, infrastructure decisions, and energy-system responses, influence regional predictability. The broader objective is to quantify the predictive skill gained by representing memory and feedbacks across natural and human systems while developing transferable approaches for next-generation regional Earth system modeling.

494167.title: Top-Down Validation of Regulatory Methane Inventories: A Case Study of Colorado Oil and Gas Facilities Using Backward Lagrangian Stochastic Modeling and Low-Cost Ambient Monitoring Data
494167.authors: Aaron Lamplugh, Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, Denver, CO
494167.abstract: Colorado Air Quality Control Commission Regulation 7 requires oil and gas operators in the state to monitor ambient air quality around their facilities during pre-production and early production activities (Section VI.C) and report estimated emissions of VOCs, NOx, N2O, CO2, CO, methane (CH4), and ethane (C2H6) from their facilities (Section V.B). While these operator-reported inventories form the foundation of regional tracking, top-down observational studies frequently reveal significant gaps between reported figures and actual emissions. This study leverages downwind ambient methane monitoring datasets submitted under AQCC Regulation 7 Section VI.C to independently quantify facility-level methane emissions across eight representative production sites in Colorado. Utilizing backward Lagrangian stochastic (bLS) dispersion modeling implemented through WindTrax (Thunder Beach Scientific), we derived monthly top-down methane emission fluxes and compared them directly against the corresponding bottom-up inventories reported under Section V.B. Preliminary results indicate a substantial disparity: top-down inverse modeling estimates typically exceed operator-reported inventory values across the monitored sites, suggesting that facility-level methane emissions during early production are under-reported on average. These findings demonstrate the utility of leveraging existing monitoring datasets to independently validate or challenge bottom-up accounting frameworks. Integrating observational dispersion modeling into state oversight offers a critical tool for improving greenhouse gas inventories and advancing Colorado’s broader climate and emission reduction targets.

494168.title: Observing Coastal Urban Effects on Thunderstorms with Radar
494168.authors: Jean Carlos Pena, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY; and S. Giangrande, P. Ramamurthy, E. C. Bruning, M. P. Jensen, and J. E. Gonzalez-Cruz
494168.abstract: Coastal cities face compound hazards from convective thunderstorms. This observational study aims to link potential urban boundary layer (UBL) influences on the rainfall and lightning cities experience by tracking multiple years of summer storms in Houston, TX. Isolated storm cells observed by NEXRAD operational radar are tracked using tobac, a feature detection algorithm. Lagrangian cell tracks are complemented by Houston Lightning Mapping Array and other field campaign data from the 2022 NSF-funded Convective-clouds Urban Boundary-layer Experiment (CUBE) and DOE Tracking Aerosol Convection interactions Experiment (TRACER) deployments. These datasets provide high-resolution lightning strike, frequent radiosonde, boundary layer profile, and surface flux observations to illuminate how the UBL may drive cloud differences. Reflectivity statistics of Lagrangian-tracked storm cells will demonstrate if the urban signal leads to differences in intensity, height, or duration. Preliminary profiler results for diurnal boundary layer patterns show that by late afternoon (1400 LT) a >1 K warmer, drier surface UBL corresponds to a >1.25 K cooler, more moist environment for urban cloud bases at 2.25 km. These differences drive non-precipitating urban cloud bases which are up to 1 km higher than their rural counterparts. This radar-based methodology may be used to trace how other cities with different morphologies respond to their weather, and their potential influence on flash floods, lightning, or other convective hazards.

494171.title: A Global Analysis and Inter-Basin Comparison of Tropical Cyclone Rapid Intensification Environments
494171.authors: Nicholas Mesa, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. M. Bell, P. J. Klotzbach, L. G. Silvers, S. Nebylitsa, S. J. Majumdar, Ph.D., and H. A. Ramsay
494171.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) that undergo rapid intensification (RI) remain a persistent global forecasting challenge. Intensification typically requires a favorable dynamic and thermodynamic environment to support critical mesoscale processes, such as sufficient surface enthalpy fluxes and vortex alignment.
