However, dynamic and thermodynamic environments often vary by region, which Majumdar et al. (2023) sought to quantify for North Atlantic TCs. Utilizing probability density functions (PDFs) of various TC-relevant variables from ERA5 reanalysis, they considered the distributions of sea surface temperature, deep-layer shear, and mid-layer relative humidity while subsetting by intensification rate, region, and time. In the current study, we expand this approach to evaluate basin-relative trends for rapidly intensifying TCs across the globe. Following the framework of Majumdar et al. (2023), we construct PDFs of ERA5 environmental factors for intensifying TCs across all global basins from 1990 to 2025. Using the global distribution of intensifying TC environments as a comparative baseline, we illustrate inter-basin differences in the RI distributions of our various environmental factors. Inter-basin differences are also present when considering these environmental factors using joint PDFs, highlighting how relationships between variables and preferences for RI vary across basins. To explore temporal trends, we evaluate shifts in the distributions of environmental factors and the poleward latitude of RI events. We find the most notable shift towards warming sea surface temperatures. Overall, this work offers a global synthesis of the variability in environments of rapidly intensifying TCs using a consistent methodology and provides a new basin-specific perspective of use to operational forecasters.

494174.title: Impact of Changjiang River Precipitation and Regional Atmospheric Conditions on Temperature and Salinity Changes In the Yellow and East China Sea
494174.authors: Juhye Kang, KMA, Seogwipo-si, Jeju-do, South korea; and B. J. Kim Sr., D. Kim, S. Moon, and C. Lee
494174.abstract: The Yellow and East China Seas (YECS) are a region where various water masses intersect, such as Tsushima Warm Current Water, Kuroshio Water, Yellow Sea Bottom Cold Water, and Changjiang (Yangtze) Diluted Water (CDW). The complex distribution of these water masses, combined with atmospheric conditions, has driven rapid warming and changes in the marine environment of the YECS in recent years. In particular, low-salinity water discharged from the Changjiang River due to summer precipitation significantly affects sea surface salinity variability in the YECS. In addition, as a result of global warming, summer sea surface temperatures (SST) exceeding 29℃ are occurring in the YECS, and the effects of this high-temperature phenomenon are increasingly felt not only in local weather patterns but also in regional ecosystems and fisheries, including mass mortality events in aquaculture. Therefore, it is essential to quantitatively understand how recent SST and salinity changes in the YECS are related to precipitation over the Changjiang River basin and atmospheric conditions such as heatwaves and low-pressure systems over the YECS. This study aims to examine the spatiotemporal variability of temperature and salinity in the YECS over the past 11 years (2016–2026), using data obtained from CTD (Conductivity Temperature Depth) observations conducted by the National Institute of Meteorological Sciences (NIMS). NIMS has conducted CTD observations bimonthly, beginning each January, with data reliability ensured through quality control (QC) procedures. We focus on July, when the Changjiang River discharge reaches its peak, to examine the spatial extent of low-salinity water and the corresponding characteristics of SST distribution. This allows us to quantitatively determine the impact of CDW expansion on SST and salinity in the YECS. In addition, we explore how this CDW expansion is related to atmospheric variables such as precipitation and wind, shedding light on the various factors driving temperature and salinity variability in the YECS.

494177.title: A Study of Flooding in Hanging Moss Creek in Jackson, Mississippi
494177.authors: Sydney Slaughter, NCAS-M II, Jackson, MS; and L. Maxie Jr., L. D. White, and D. Lamb
494177.abstract: Hanging Moss Creek, a tributary to the Pearl River, flows through North Jackson. The fast-responding creek has been known to flood from heavy rain and tended to back up when the Pearl River was flooded. Action or bankfull stage has long been established, but the impacts to the community were not well known to the Weather Service. This study will look at stream behavior, directly related to heavy rain, over the last 25 years to identify periods of flood, flood related impacts and determine if current products and services are meeting the needs of the community. This will be done by analyzing rainfall data, hydrographs, hydrological records, visiting the stream and interviewing members of the community.

494180.title: Bridging the Gap: The Lightning Safety Guide for Sports and Special Events
494180.authors: Kevin Kloesel, Event Safety Alliance, Salado, TX; and C. C. Woodrum and J. D. Durkee
494180.abstract: Lightning remains one of the most frequent and dangerous weather threats to outdoor sports and special events, endangering participants, spectators, and staff. Despite its predictability in a broad meteorological sense, the operational challenges of managing lightning risk—including detection, real-time decision-making, and evacuation logistics—often lead to fragmented safety approaches. This presentation introduces a comprehensive, scalable lightning safety framework developed to empower venue managers and event organizers with data-driven, actionable strategies. Drawing on findings from a National Center for Spectator Sports Safety and Security (NCS4) 2023 Needs Assessment, this guide addresses critical industry vulnerabilities such as conflicting safety protocols, misconceptions about lightning behavior (e.g., the "30/30" rule and "heat lightning" myths), and the lack of standardized incident management plans. We present a methodology that integrates meteorology with practical emergency and venue management, providing a pathway for organizations of all scales to: Standardize Decision-Making: Establish clear, flexible trigger points based on current lightning detection and prediction technologies rather than relying on outdated rules of thumb. Enhance Scalability: Implement tiered operations plans tailored to the proportionate level of risk, staffing, and facility infrastructure—ranging from small-scale youth sports to large-scale entertainment venues. Formalize Safety Protocols: Define the roles of designated Weather Safety Officials and Authorized Decision-Makers, ensuring seamless integration between weather monitoring and emergency response. By aligning professional meteorological guidance with the operational realities of the sports and entertainment industry, this guide aims to harmonize safety practices globally and move toward a standard of zero lightning-related injuries at outdoor events. Attendees will gain insights into deploying these resources to foster a safer, more resilient landscape for the future of outdoor events.

494183.title: Enhancements of Radar Quantitative Precipitation Estimation for Flash Flood Forecasting
494183.authors: James Anderson Smith, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and W. F. Krajewski and M. L. Baeck
494183.abstract: Analyses of storms producing catastrophic flash floods are used to develop recommendations for improving the effectiveness of QPE products from the NEXRAD network in reducing loss of life. Analyses of extreme flash flood events in Texas Hill Country, the Appalachian region of the Eastern US and the Intermountain West are presented. A key challenge for radar QPE is underestimation of rainfall for storms producing catastrophic flash floods. There is systematic bias in radar QPE for storms producing catastrophic flash floods. Over and above the systematic bias is a tendency for larger underestimation in the cores of peak rainfall. We show that vertical motion in downdrafts contributes to underestimation of rainfall in these settings and introduce approaches for addressing this problem. We recommend developing separate radar QPE techniques that specifically target storms producing catastrophic flash floods.

494188.title: The Science Behind the Chromospheric Magnetism Explorer
494188.abstract: The Chromospheric Magnetism Explorer, or CMEx (pronounced SEE-mehks), is a NASA Heliophysics Small Explorer mission concept to observe the sun’s magnetic fields from the photosphere to the base of the corona, with a particular emphasis on the solar chromosphere. CMEx is currently undergoing an extended Phase A concept study to refine the mission concept and conduct risk mitigation activities. CMEx has 2 over-arching science goals: to diagnose the magnetic nature of major solar eruptions and to constrain the magnetic sources of the solar wind. The Sun's magnetic field drives nearly every aspect of solar activity and Space Weather. CMEx is designed to observe that magnetic field where some of the most important physics happens—and where our observations are currently lacking. Here, I discuss the science questions that drove the CMEx mission concept, and how CMEx observations will answer them.

494189.title: MethaneSAT Global Dataset and Future Directions
494189.authors: Roisin Commane, LDEO, Palisades, NY; LDEO, New York, NY; Columbia University, New York, NY; and S. Wofsy, R. Gautam, T. Melendez, M. Lystrup, and S. Hamburg
494189.abstract: The emissions-monitoring satellite MethaneSAT was designed to help motivate and enable reduction of methane emissions. Commissioned by MethaneSAT LLC, a subsidiary of the Environmental Defense Fund, MethaneSAT actively mapped and quantified both concentrated and diffuse CH4 emissions from regions accounting for over 80% of global oil and gas production, with data now available for scenes captured between June 2024 and June 2025. MethaneSAT’s target observations consisted of a wide observing swath (~220 km @ nadir), high spatial resolution (~140 m x 400 m), and low detection threshold (2 ppb precision @ 4 km2 as determined on orbit), from a sun-synchronous orbit. MethaneSAT’s two imaging spectrometers (CH4/CO2: 1598-1683nm; O2: 1249-1305nm) were built by Ball Aerospace (now BAE) and integrated onto a spacecraft bus provided by Blue Canyon Technologies. Validation activities included targeting of Total Carbon Column Observing Network stations, coordination with controlled-release sites, and deployments of the airborne precursor instrument, MethaneAIR. In this presentation we will present an overview of the instrument performance, data products, lessons learned and recommendations for future plans.

494190.title: Evaluating Tropical Cyclone Forecasts using MPAS-JEDI: A Case Study of Typhoon Usagi(2024)
494190.authors: Feng Hsiao, NCAS, Washington, DC; Howard University, Washington, DC; and S. Chiao
494190.abstract: Typhoon Usagi (2024) presented a formidable forecasting challenge, characterized by explosive rapid intensification (RI) and a highly complex post-landfall trajectory. While the operational Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS-A) demonstrated initial skill in representing the synoptic steering flow, it exhibited significant deficiencies in predicting the storm's structural evolution and peak intensity. Verification against the Best Track dataset reveals that HAFS-A severely underestimated the magnitude of Usagi's RI, resulting in an approximately 20 hPa error in the minimum sea level pressure (forecast minimum of approximately 950 hPa versus the observed minimum of approximately 930 hPa). Qualitative comparisons with Himawari-9 Band 13 infrared observations indicate that this intensity error was associated with an underlying structural bias: the model simulated a broad, diffuse vortex that failed to reproduce the highly compact pinhole-eye structure observed in reality. Furthermore, forecast confidence degraded significantly during the storm's later stages, with operational guidance from both HAFS-A and HWRF exhibiting substantial track bifurcation following landfall. To address these critical limitations, this study evaluates the implementation of the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) coupled with the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) system. By assimilating clear-sky satellite observations to better constrain the surrounding environmental flow, this study aims to reduce track errors and improve tropical cyclone intensity forecasts.

494191.title: Object-Aware Probabilistic Forecasting of Convective Initiation from GOES and Radar Observations
494191.authors: Marc J Crampe, The City College of New York, NYC, NY; and S. A. Mejia Manrique, J. T. Carlin, J. J. Gourley, D. R. Stratman, C. A. Kerr, and R. M. Khanbilvardi
494191.abstract: Convective initiation (CI) remains a major challenge for short-term weather prediction and directly limits warning lead time for severe weather and flash flooding. Radar-based nowcasting can effectively extrapolate established storms but cannot reliably predict where and when new convection will develop. Progress is further constrained by the relative rarity of initiation events and the difficulty of constructing spatially and temporally consistent training labels. We develop a deep-learning framework that produces spatially explicit CI probabilities in four 15-min windows spanning the next hour. The model uses a 60-min history of GOES Advanced Baseline Imager infrared imagery observations and temporally matched Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor (MRMS) composite reflectivity, combining cloud-top evolution with the recent development of nearby radar echoes. An initial dataset was constructed from 31 convective events in the northeastern United States, with emphasis on the New York metropolitan region, and is currently being expanded to represent a broader range of environments and storm morphologies. Initiation events are identified using a radar-based detection and tracking algorithm that distinguishes newly developing convection from pre-existing echoes, and filters cases in which initiation cannot be reliably separated from the growth or advection of mature storms. Unlike conventional point-based or Gaussian labels, the proposed object-aware labels use adaptive footprints derived from the developing radar object and repositioned at its diagnosed initiation location. This formulation represents variations in storm size, morphology, and short-term displacement. A U-Net with residual-network encoder predicts the four lead-dependent probability fields corresponding to successive 15-min forecast windows. GOES-only and GOES-plus-radar configurations are compared using event-independent data partitions, and complementary pixel- and object-based verification. Initial experiments demonstrate the feasibility of learning spatial initiation probabilities but also reveal sensitivity to training-sample size, event imbalance, target definition, and storm-regime diversity. Ongoing work therefore focuses on expanding the event sample and improving the tradeoff between initiation detection and false alarms. The resulting probability fields provide stand-alone probabilistic guidance for forecasters, and transferable predictors for precipitation-nowcasting systems that require explicit information about where and when new convection may develop.

494193.title: Building a Community Verification Ecosystem with METplus
494193.authors: John Halley Gotway, NSF NCAR and Developmental Testbed Center, Boulder, CO; and M. A. Harrold, G. P. McCabe Jr., M. Win-Gildenmeister, M. Smith, C. P. Kalb, K. M. Newman, H. Soh, and J. Prestopnik
494193.abstract: Community-developed software has become an essential component of modern earth system modeling, enabling reproducible science, collaborative development, and rapid transition of new capabilities into operational practice. Since its inception, the enhanced Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) framework has evolved beyond a verification software package into a comprehensive community ecosystem supporting users worldwide, across government laboratories, operational forecasting centers, universities, and the private sector. METplus provides an open-source framework for forecast verification and diagnostics that combines robust scientific algorithms with community-driven software development, extensive documentation, reproducible workflows, and active user engagement. The project emphasizes accessibility through coordinated software releases, multiple installation pathways, comprehensive online documentation, example use cases, training materials, GitHub Discussions, and transparent development practices that encourage community participation and feedback. These resources have enabled widespread adoption across organizations including NOAA, the U.S. Department of Defense, the Naval Research Laboratory, the U.K. Met Office, Australia's Bureau of Meteorology, and numerous academic institutions. This presentation will explore the community practices that have enabled METplus to grow into a sustainable, open-source verification ecosystem and discuss how collaborative development continues to accelerate innovation in forecast evaluation.

494194.title: Hurricane Idalia in Future Climate Scenarios: Comparing Pseudo-Global Warming and Stratospheric Aerosol Injection Simulations
494194.authors: Emma K. Benedict, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and J. W. Hurrell, K. L. Rasmussen, and L. Sun
494194.abstract: As Earth’s global temperature continues to increase, severe weather events, such as tropical cyclones, tornadoes, and flooding are expected to increase in intensity, prompting interest in adaptation and potential climate intervention strategies. One proposed intervention strategy is stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI). SAI involves the injection of reflective particles, such as sulfur dioxide, into the stratosphere to increase Earth’s albedo, thus limiting the amount of incoming solar radiation reaching the surface. Previous studies have examined the influence of SAI on large-scale climate and atmospheric processes, however, its effects on severe weather remain less understood. To address this question, this study utilizes high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations to analyze how Hurricane Idalia (August 2023) reacts to different climate scenarios. The simulations span October 2022-2024 and include a present-day control, a pseudo-global warming (PGW) future, and an SAI-modified future climate (PSAI). Hurricane Idalia was selected as a case study to compare the large-scale environment and storm characteristics across these scenarios. An environmental analysis of sea surface temperature, atmospheric moisture, and windshear was conducted, followed by an evaluation of storm intensity through maximum wind speeds and precipitation. Initial results reveal that the environmental conditions surrounding Idalia and its intensity differ among the control, PGW, and PSAI simulations. These initial results illustrate how future climate change and potential SAI deployment may influence tropical cyclone behavior.

494198.title: From Sounding Parameters to Mesoscale Processes: The Meteorological Process Mapper Applied to Flash Floods
494198.authors: Stephen M. Jessup, Columbus State University, COLUMBUS, GA; Columbus State University, Columbus, GA
494198.abstract: Intense rainfall rates are a prerequisite for flash floods (FF). Doswell et al. (1996) identified three tightly coupled storm-scale processes necessary for sustaining intense rainfall: the development and maintenance of a vapor-rich air column, its efficient conversion to precipitation, and favorable rates of ascent within a storm’s updraft. Of these, only the resulting column moisture reservoir is readily quantified from sounding data. Precipitation efficiency depends on storm-scale processes, such as entrainment-induced evaporation, and involves distinct warm-, mixed-, and cold-phase microphysical pathways that each influence rainfall rate. Likewise, although a simple relationship (Emanuel 1994) can estimate ascent rate from convective available potential energy (CAPE), storm-scale processes such as entrainment and hydrometeor loading can inhibit vertical velocity. The Meteorological Process Mapper (MPM) addresses these limitations through a hierarchical, process-based architecture in which meteorological processes are decomposed into physically distinct components, each ultimately represented by sounding-derived parameters. Rather than treating sounding parameters only as individual descriptors, MPM uses them to construct explicit process representations. To quantify how precipitation efficiency and storm-scale ascent contribute to intense rainfall, each process can first be partitioned into physically meaningful mechanisms. For example, precipitation efficiency is divided into warm-rain, mixed-phase, freezing-layer, and wet-bulb-zero-layer subprocesses. Each subprocess is represented by distinct primary terms describing bounded, physically interpretable contributions to its parent process. Within this developing architecture, warm-rain processes are estimated using primary terms which include 1) whether warm cloud depth is deep and well-bounded, 2) whether the warm-cloud layer is sufficiently moist and 3) avoids dry layers and sub-cloud evaporative loss, and 4) whether ascent and warm-layer depth jointly support a) condensate generation, b) residence time for coalescence, and c) retention below the freezing level. Each primary term is then decomposed into secondary terms explicitly derived from sounding parameters. For example, in term 4), a) by whether updraft speed falls within a range favorable for condensate generation, b) by residence time estimated from warm-cloud depth and updraft speed, and c) by whether updraft speed and warm-cloud depth favor retention below the freezing level rather than rapid lofting above it. The same hierarchical construction governs the remaining warm-rain terms and the mixed-phase, freezing-layer, and wet-bulb-transition process representations, whose combined contributions are weighted and summed to compute a canonical process index for precipitation efficiency. A similar architecture estimates storm-scale ascent through an “updraft budget” whose primary terms ask whether buoyant acceleration is available, whether a parcel can access it, whether the environment resists entrainment-driven dilution, whether shear supports organized ascent, and whether the buoyant path is deep and continuous enough to be realized. As with precipitation efficiency, each primary term is represented by secondary terms explicitly defined from sounding parameters. MPM presently applies this architecture to about 60 mesoscale processes. Each term is normalized from zero to one, and, as for the process index, terms within each hierarchical layer are weighted so that the maximum possible value of that layer also sums to one. The resulting set of process indices and weighted component terms can therefore be compared across thermodynamic, kinematic, microphysical, and cross-domain process families. Broader process domains additionally aggregate related processes contributing to buoyancy, entrainment, cellular storm motion, broader system motion and regeneration, and other important modes of meteorological organization. To demonstrate MPM, a dataset of soundings representing 30 major FF events is analyzed using two standard parameters, CAPE and precipitable water (PW), together with select process indices, including precipitation efficiency and updraft budget. Their correlation matrix enables construction of network maps that quantify relationships among sounding parameters and process indices within the broader hierarchy. PW, CAPE, precipitation efficiency, and the updraft budget are among the highest-order nodes in the overall MPM network at both 12Z and 00Z, with PW occupying the central position at both times. CAPE exerts more influence within the network at 12Z, but the updraft budget becomes more central at 00Z, when both moist convection and processes that inhibit it are more strongly realized. To assess which processes become more important when total-column moisture is more modest, as is more common in drier climates and the cool season, a climatological sample was constructed by pairing each flash-flood sounding with the corresponding sounding from the same station and date in the preceding year. Here, total-column moisture is represented by column moisture reservoir structure (CRMS), the process analogue of PW, as the updraft budget is the process analogue of CAPE. Just as the predominant term in the updraft budget is a CAPE-derived estimate of vertical velocity, PW is the strongest contributor to CRMS. The dataset was divided into samples comprising the 15 highest and lowest CRMS indices and their climatological equivalents. Low-CRMS events exhibit significantly slower cellular storm motion while retaining near-climatological buoyancy, precipitation efficiency, entrainment, MCS motion and regeneration, and other quantified process families, despite spanning a range of convective modes. Thus, in environments climatologically less favorable for abundant column moisture, slower storm motion appears to increase the significance of rainfall duration. The dataset reveals systematic variation in the process pathways associated with different environments. For example, the updraft budget increases with decreasing PW among major FFs in the Desert Southwest, whereas the updraft budget and PW are positively correlated across events in all other regions. CAPE is uncorrelated with PW in both settings. The regional distinction therefore emerges in the process-based representation even though it is not apparent from the corresponding CAPE-PW relationship. These results highlight the broader potential of MPM. Although the process representations and the calibration of normalization and weighting remain under development, the preliminary results appear physically plausible and reveal relationships not clearly apparent from conventional sounding parameters alone. Conventional sounding parameters remain highly effective for discriminating hazards and their severity, while numerical simulations often anticipate convective organization well; MPM may complement these approaches by identifying limiting processes in edge cases and diagnosing process environments associated with forecast failures. More broadly, MPM provides an extensible architecture for using existing sounding parameters to quantify mesoscale processes, developing new process-informed parameters, and evaluating scientific questions quantitatively where process relationships have often been assessed qualitatively.

494199.title: Afforestation and Reforestation in China Amplifies Temperature Gradients through Biogenic Aerosol Effects
494199.authors: hao liu, Tianjin University, Tianjin, China
494199.abstract: Large-scale afforestation is critical for achieving China's carbon neutrality ambitions. Beyond carbon sequestration, afforestation increases biogenic volatile organic compound (BVOC) emissions, which enhance biogenic aerosol formation and reshape regional climate patterns. However, the magnitude and mechanisms of these climate responses remain unclear. Here, we developed a BVOC emissions model resolving 324 tree species across China, revealing a ~45% emission increase due to afforestation, which elevated biogenic aerosol burden by ~31%. The radiative effects of increased biogenic aerosols strengthened anticyclonic anomalies over southern China, facilitating northward moisture transport during July. This resulted in reduced cloud cover and increased temperature in the south, but enhanced cloud cover and decreased temperature in the north, amplifying the south-north temperature gradient by ~10% (0.33±0.05 °C). Moreover, different afforestation strategies, driven by variations in tree species selection, produced divergent BVOC emission strengths and spatial distributions, enhancing the temperature gradient to 0.40±0.09 °C. Our findings reveal complex atmospheric dynamical responses to biogenic aerosol radiative effects, challenging the conventional carbon and biophysical effect paradigm of nature-based solutions, and highlight the need to incorporate aerosol-climate feedbacks and tree selection to optimize climate benefits.

494200.title: Withdrawn: ATCHEM - Evaluation of GEOS-CF and Sentinel-5P TROPOMI NO2 Products Across Monitoring Stations in Peninsular Malaysia
494200.authors: Pauziyah Mohammad Salim, UKM, Bangi, Selangor, Malaysia; and M. T. Latif, L. ju Neng, and T. BANERJEE
494200.abstract: Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is one of the major air pollutants that can negatively affect air quality and human health. Continuous monitoring of NO₂ concentrations is important for understanding its spatial and temporal variations. This study assesses NO₂ concentrations Peninsular Malaysia for the year 2020 using multiple data sources, namely Sentinel- 5P TROPOMI satellite observations, GEOS-CF global model of Atmospheric Constituent Forecast, and ground-based observations from Continuous Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAQMS) Malaysia. These datasets' monthly mean NO₂ concentrations were analyzed to identify temporal trends and spatial distribution patterns across the study area. TROPOMI vertical column and GEOS-CF NO₂ surface concentration were co-located with the in situ ground stations for correlation and validation analysis. TROPOMI and GEOS-CF managed to identify similar NO2 hotspots which are the Central and Johor regions, corresponding to their urban and industrialized areas.TROPOMI have a high monthly correlation with ground observations throughout the year ranging from 0.7 to 0.9 although GEOS-CF also successfully reproduce the temporal variability of NO2 with strong monthly correlation that ranging from 0.6 to 0.8. GEOS-CF achieved its highest validation agreement with ground observations during the COVID-19 lockdown period of March and April, as indicated by the lowest monthly RMSE (3.432 and 1.586) and Mean Bias values (-2.501 and -0.525). Overall, GEOS-CF underestimates its surface NO2 measurement between the range of 15% to 60% for Peninsular Malaysia. The model also shows the weakest performance in the urban station category. This study gives an overall understanding of the GOES-CF data quality and validation study for this region.

494201.title: Coherent Structures in the Inner-Core Boundary Layer of Landfalling Typhoon Bebinca from Coordinated Multi-Platform Observations
494201.authors: Jie Tang, Shanghai Typhoon Institute,CMA, shanghai, shanghai, China; and X. Y. Zhou
494201.abstract: Coherent structures in the inner-core tropical cyclone boundary layer (TCBL) influence near-surface momentum exchange, but continuous, direct observations of their structural characteristics during landfall remain scarce. We analyze Typhoon Bebinca (2024) before landfall as the observing sites approached and entered its inner core, using two ground-based Doppler wind lidars and an X-band phased-array radar. The first three empirical orthogonal function (EOF) modes account for more than 80% of the vertical-velocity variance between 100 and 400 m, indicating that the vertical motions within this layer are highly organized and that most of their variability can be represented by a small number of dominant vertical structures. EOF1, which accounts for approximately half of the variance, describes vertically coherent ascent and descent, whereas EOF2 changes sign with height and represents the tilt of these structures. Based on the principal-component time series associated with EOF1 (PC1), strong coherent events are identified. These events contain alternating ascending and descending branches accompanied by along-flow velocity perturbations. The structures tilt radially with height, and the distances between their radial peaks are approximately 1.5–2.6 km. Most events occur beneath or adjacent to narrow convective bands and exhibit a structural configuration indicative of coupling with banded convection, whereas some are observed without detectable overlying radar echo. During both positive- and negative-PC1 events, the event-mean absolute vertical momentum flux exceeds the corresponding all-sample mean throughout the observed layer, with maximum event-to-all-sample mean ratios of 3.15 at DWL-1 and 1.91 at DWL-2. These observations identify tilted, roll-like structures in the inner-core boundary layer of Typhoon Bebinca as it approached landfall and quantify their contribution to vertical momentum transport.

494203.title: Tropical Cyclone Efficiency in the Western North Pacific Ocean under Different Climate Conditions
494203.authors: Yi-Chun Liao, National Taiwan Univ., Taipei, TPE, Taiwan; and I. I. Lin, J. Y. Yu, J. Y. Yu, C. C. Lien, and J. Y. Chan
494203.abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) thermodynamic efficiency is a component of TC potential intensity (PI) theory. Based on the PI theory framework, changes in TC thermodynamic efficiency depend on sea surface temperature (SST) and TC outflow temperature (To). Using reanalysis datasets from 1979–2024, we examine changes in TC efficiency in the western North Pacific (WNP) TC Main Development Region (MDR) under different El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) types and long-term trends. During ENSO events, efficiency changes depend on the ENSO types and regions. TC efficiency decreases during La Niña due to warmer To, and increases during Central Pacific (CP) El Niño, where upper-level cooling dominates. Eastern Pacific (EP) and Mixed El Niño display spatially variable responses. Overall, these efficiency changes during ENSO contribute to PI variability from −38 to +27%. In contrast, under long-term trends (1979–2024), both SST and To exhibit warming trends. Because their opposing effects on efficiency largely offset each other, thermodynamic efficiency shows minor variations, contributing slightly to PI. Reference: Liao, Y.-C., Lin, I.-I.*, Yu, J.-Y., Yu, J.-Y., Lien, C.-C., & Chan, J.-Y. (2026). Change in tropical cyclone efficiency under different ENSO conditions in the western North Pacific Ocean. Geophysical Research Letters, 53, e2025GL118850. https://doi.org/10.1029/2025GL118850

494205.title: Integrating Quasi-Operational WxUAS Operations into the Oklahoma Mesonet
494205.authors: Tyler M Bell, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and A. R. R. Segales, J. Gebauer, L. Bunting, E. N. Smith, C. A. Fiebrich, and C. M. Luttrell
494205.abstract: The University of Oklahoma (OU) and the Oklahoma Mesonet have achieved a significant operational milestone: the initiation of quasi-operational weather-sensing UAS (WxUAS) flights at a Mesonet station. Since late 2025, OU teams have collected hourly WxUAS atmospheric profiles at the Washington, OK Mesonet site at least once per week for an 8-hour period, with data transmitted in real time to the National Weather Service via the National Mesonet Program. This effort represents a meaningful and replicable step toward the routine integration of UAS-based measurements into existing operational surface networks. This presentation will cover: (1) key lessons learned from quasi-operational flights to date, including logistical, regulatory, and meteorological challenges; (2) real-time data visualization tools developed for use in NWS forecast offices; and (3) a roadmap for expanding the program to additional Mesonet sites and increasing flight frequency with fully automated systems

494208.title: Lidar Observations of Surface Layer Coherent Structures in Supercell Inflow
494208.authors: Joshua G. Gebauer, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; and M. Coniglio and R. A. Saba
494208.abstract: A supercell modeling study by Markowski (2024) identified a potential pathway for tornadogenesis facilitated by the vertical vorticity associated with atmospheric surface layer coherent turbulent structures in the storm's inflow. This simulation work has initiated a paradigm shift in tornadogenesis research, as most prior attention has focused on vertical vorticity generated in the outflow environment. Motivated by these simulations, the National Severe Storms Laboratory has deployed a truck-mounted Doppler lidar to scan surface layer coherent structures in the near-inflow of supercells during the Low-level Internal Flow of Tornadoes (LIFT) field experiment. We will show that over three years of deployments, the lidar has observed many cases of surface layer coherent structures serving as genesis locations for pretornadic vortices when the structures interact with the storm's updraft and boundaries. Observations of the near surface wind profile with the lidar indicate that development of these vortices is likely supported by tilting of the very large horizontal vorticity in the surface layer when this vorticity is streamwise relative to the storm's boundaries. These observations lend credibility to the simulations by Markowski (2024) and suggest that this potential tornadogenesis pathway deserves more research attention and collaboration between the severe storms and boundary-layer communities. Of particular interest is the potential for improving tornado forecasting by identifying the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) characteristics that produce the largest and most coherent surface layer structures, as these structures would have the greatest vorticity stretching potential. Our initial lidar observations indicate that vertical vorticity magnitude appears to scale with near-surface wind speed, as has been documented in past literature; however, further research is needed to address how these structures and associated near-surface shear are modified from their ambient environment characteristics in the highly unsteady near-inflow environment of supercell thunderstorms.

494210.title: Do Climate Models Need Microphysical and Convective Parameterizations to Simulate Precipitation? Learning from Observations with DLESyM
494210.authors: Raul Antonio Moreno, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and D. R. Durran
494210.abstract: Previously, we have shown that a convolutional neural network can be trained to derive the precipitation field from a small set of large scale atmospheric fields which can be readily assimilated. By training on satellite observations of precipitation (IMERG), the resulting model is capable of generating more realistic precipitation fields than can be achieved using traditional numerical weather prediction (NWP) parameterizations of convection and microphysics. Using reanalysis fields as inputs, the ML model produces precipitation estimates that reduce key biases in NWP precipitation estimates, including excessive light precipitation and underestimated extremes. The model also more closely reproduces the timing and amplitude of the diurnal cycle observed by the satellite than popular reanalysis datasets like ERA5. Here we extend this work to climate simulations by training DLESyM, a deep learning Earth systems model, on two sets of observations of precipitation (IMERG and MSWEP). In this implementation, DLESyM predicts precipitation as output only, meaning it does not include precipitation in the set of variables used to initialize or autoregressively advance the model. Notably, this version of DLESyM is probabilistic and trained using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), enabling the generation of ensemble forecasts. We assess the precipitation produced by DLESyM in a long-rollout simulation, using additional observations for evaluating seasonal and sub-seasonal variability as well as key characteristics that are typically poorly represented in NWP such as the diurnal cycle and extreme precipitation events. This work examines machine learning trained on observations as a viable alternative to parameterizations for simulating precipitation in a climate modeling context. The precipitation in DLESyM’s climate simulations is compared to that of CMIP style simulations of the current climate.

494211.title: Supplemental Radars in Support of Warning And Response: An Operational Perspective
494211.authors: Tara Goode, Climavision, Louisville, KY; and M. Simpson, M. R. Kramar, K. Ortega, L. Maynard, K. Grempler, and C. Goode
494211.abstract: Commercial supplemental gap-filling weather radars help improve situational awareness by providing observations close to the ground where distant government radars may overshoot due to the curvature of the earth. When such observations are delivered reliably with high spatial and temporal resolution and integrated into decision platforms used by National Weather Service forecasters, it allows them to issue more precise weather watches and warnings. Since early 2026, the Pittsburgh Weather Forecast office has had access to a commercial X-band weather radar located within their County Warning Area. The radar was installed and is operated by Climavision, a Kentucky based firm, to address a long-standing radar observation gap in West Pennsylvania. The radar was used actively by the office in the winter season of 2025-2026 to monitor snow squalls and lake effect snow arising from Lake Erie, revealing bands of intense snow missed by the neighboring WSR-88D radars. Later in the Spring, the radar was used to monitor the development of severe weather. In particular, the radar revealed low-altitude storm structure and velocity observations that helped inform the issuance of tornado warnings. Case studies from winter and severe-weather events during early 2026 will illustrate the supplementary information provided by the X-band radar and its application within NWS operational decision-making. The presentation will also discuss integration of commercial radar observations into existing forecast-office workflows, training requirements, communication between the radar provider and operational meteorologists, and lessons learned from the Climavision–NWS collaboration. These experiences provide an initial framework for evaluating how supplemental commercial radar networks could supplement the national WSR-88D system and be effectively incorporated into NWS field operations.

494216.title: Catastrophic Flash Flooding in Urban Environments: A Radar-Based Perspective [INVITED]
494216.authors: James Anderson Smith, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ
494216.abstract: Urban environments are especially susceptible to flash flooding from storms producing extreme short-duration, small-area rainfall. Radar provides the most effective approach for observing rainfall at time and space scales that are appropriate for flash flood applications. We examine rainfall extremes both from a precipitation frequency perspective and from the perspective of flash flood forecasting. In both cases, we focus on catastrophic flash flooding. For precipitation frequency analyses, concerns center on design of urban infrastructure to avoid catastrophic failure modes. For flash flood forecasting, the objective is to avoid catastrophic loss of life. Long radar rainfall data sets have an important role to play in precipitation frequency analyses, especially for short-duration, small-area rainfall extremes. Flash flood forecasting is grounded in accurate radar rainfall estimates for storms producing extreme rainfall. Major advances in radar rainfall estimation are needed to address the societal impacts of catastrophic flash flooding in urban environments. We illustrate the challenges through analyses of urban flash flood events in the US.

494218.title: How Similar is Similar Enough? Testing Scalar Similarity Across Moist Convective Boundary Layer Regimes (Invited Presentation)
494218.authors: Scott T. Salesky, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and B. Greene
494218.abstract: An assumption frequently employed in atmospheric boundary layer studies is scalar similarity—the statement that all scalar quantities (temperature, humidity, trace gas concentration, etc.) are transported similarly by a turbulent flow field. This assumption is often invoked when one wishes to estimate evaporation and trace gas fluxes when direct measurements via eddy covariance are not available. However, both prior observational and numerical modeling studies have provided evidence that scalar similarity does not always hold, with authors implicating a variety of different processes (advection, entrainment, land surface heterogeneity, different active/passive scalar roles, etc.). In particular, the similarity between heat and moisture transport in the atmospheric boundary layer contributes to the structure of the buoyancy field in moist CBLs, the initiation of deep convection, and electromagnetic wave propagation. Using a suite of 24 large eddy simulations of the moist convective boundary layer (CBL), spanning two values of global stability (-zi/L), three values of the evaporative fraction (Ef), and four values of the humidity entrainment flux ratio (φwq), we systematically examine the extent to which similarity between heat and moisture transport is influenced by temperature and humidity boundary conditions. We find that humidity plays an increasingly active role in moist CBL dynamics as evaporative fraction increases, which in turn heightens the sensitivity of moisture transport to the humidity entrainment flux ratio. Differences in heat and moisture transport are quantified through quadrant analysis, the temperature-humidity covariance budget, and a phase space approach, which allows us to identify the height at which deviations from scalar similarity begin to emerge. Using spectra and cross-spectra, we examine the scale-dependence of scalar dissimilarity for a given moist CBL state.

494220.title: A Comparison of In-Flight Icing Drop Size Categories from the Current and Forecast Icing Product (CIP & FIP)
494220.authors: Daniel R. Adriaansen, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. Jacobson and S. M. Ellis
494220.abstract: Recent additions to the National Center for Atmospheric Research’s (NCAR’s) CIP & FIP include new output fields that categorize supercooled liquid water drops into small, medium, and large sizes based on available data. In FIP, these categories are derived using Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) model forecast fields while in CIP observations are used and combined with the NWP model forecast fields when available. Recent collaboration with the Terminal Area Icing Weather INformation (TAIWIN) product development team has led to the exploration of using Time-Lagged Ensemble (TLE) NWP forecast fields of cloud liquid water content and cloud drop number concentration within the drop size category module in FIP. Initial results from comparison with in situ TAIWIN demonstration research data suggest this approach can help improve the skill of the small drop category forecasts. While the TLE fields were used in FIP, they were not tested in CIP. Results from CIP utilizing a TLE forecast of these fields will be presented, along with comparisons from additional in situ observations from the In Cloud Icing and Large Drop Experiment (ICICLE) field campaign. Attribution of differences in the CIP drop size category will be identified where observations were deemed to play a role in computing the drop size category when or if it is different from FIP, with a particular focus on the collision-coalescence scenario used within CIP and FIP. Additional opportunities for aligning methods used by the TAIWIN PDT for drop size categorization with methods used by CIP and FIP will be discussed. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the FAA. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

494224.title: Enhancing Aviation Turbulence Nowcasting: Integrating Statistically Optimised En-Route Turbulence In EDR (ETE) Thresholds with Special Air Reports Data Assimilation
494224.authors: Betty Mak, Hong Kong Observatory, Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong kong; and Y. L. Ng, X. Xiao, K. W. E. Chan, and M. H. Kok
494224.abstract: Clear-air turbulence (CAT) remains a critical, often invisible threat to aviation safety, underscored by the fatal Singapore Airlines Flight 321 incident in May 2024. Accurate turbulence nowcasting requires robust indices, reliable severity thresholds, and timely updates. This study presents a two-phase approach: first, establishing statistically optimised thresholds for the composite En-route Turbulence in EDR (ETE)[1], then, enhancing it through Special Air Reports (ARS) data assimilation for turbulence nowcasting. This study also benchmarks the performance of ETE against derived indices (TI2, VWS) based on both traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) model (ECMWF) and data-driven AI models (Pangu, Fengwu, and Fuxi). More than 60,000 pilot reports from May 2024 to May 2025 were used in the study, and the severe class imbalance was addressed by employing class-aware metrics (Cohen’s Kappa, G-mean, J-score, F2-score, CSI). Optimised ETE thresholds are determined as 0.336 (Light+), 0.379 (Moderate+), and 0.464 (Severe+). The ETEARS nowcast system then employs Gaussian kernel spatial nudging with exponential temporal decay to assimilate ARS observations into the forecast model, with the decay parameters optimised via Differential Evolution and Nelder-Mead methods. The performance of ETE is evaluated on a common dataset using POD, FAR, CSI, ROC-AUC, and Precision-Recall curves (PRC). For Moderate+ turbulence, although VWS yields a higher CSI, this metric alone hides operational limitations: VWS tends to over-forecast by covering large areas, while TI2 fails to capture convection-induced turbulence. Conversely, ETE delivers a more balanced performance across metrics (CSI of 0.506, AUC of 0.562). It potentially detects convection-induced turbulence signals without the excessive spatial coverage seen with VWS, thereby offering better spatial precision for operations. For Severe+ turbulence, ETE maintains superior performance (CSI: 0.079) over AI-derived indices, while ARS integration prevents over-warning inside jet streams. Case studies of CAT and convection-induced turbulence further validate ETE’s operational robustness in complex synoptic environments. This study provides validated thresholds and a nowcast enhancement framework for the operational use of ETE. The results confirm that ETE is one of the most effective turbulence indices for aviation safety, and the subsequent integration of real-time ARS data establishes a nowcasting system, supporting safer aviation operations. References: [1] Ng, Y. L., Cheung, C.N., and Fong C.F. (2025), Development of En-route Turbulence Index based on EDR and Exploring Turbulence Forecast using Machine Learning Techniques, Poster presented at the 22nd Asia Oceania Geosciences Society Annual Meeting (AOGS 2025), Singapore, 27 Jul–1 Aug.

494225.title: Monitoring Global Lakes and Reservoirs Using MODIS and VIIRS Observations
494225.authors: Huilin Gao, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and S. Zhang, D. Shah, and C. H. Huang
494225.abstract: Freshwater lakes and reservoirs are critical components of the Earth’s water and carbon cycles, yet our understanding of their long-term global dynamics—particularly in relation to climate variability, extremes, and water management—remains limited. The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) aboard the Terra and Aqua satellites, together with the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) aboard the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (SNPP) and NOAA-20 satellites, provides unique capabilities for developing long-term datasets to investigate these dynamics. Surface reflectance observations facilitate the estimation of water surface area, which can be used to infer storage variations, while land surface temperature (LST) observations improve the simulation of vertical thermal mixing and heat storage, thereby enhancing evaporation rate estimates. In this presentation, we introduce recent updates to the MODIS/VIIRS Global Water Reservoir (GWR) product suite, which provides estimates of surface area, water elevation, storage, evaporation rate, and evaporation loss for 164 large reservoirs worldwide. The GWR products provide reservoir storage and evaporation data at 8-day and monthly temporal resolutions. We evaluate the consistency between MODIS- and VIIRS-based GWR products to support the continuity of the 25-year MODIS observational record into the VIIRS era. In addition, we have expanded the dataset to include more than 2,700 large lakes and reservoirs worldwide and conducted broader product validation and MODIS–VIIRS continuity assessments. Using the GWR products and the expanded dataset, we demonstrate key applications, including monitoring reservoir-based droughts and comparing long-term evaporative losses from lakes and reservoirs at basin, regional, and global scales. These applications provide important insights into the long-term dynamics of global lakes and reservoirs and help address key knowledge gaps in their interactions with climate variability, hydrologic extremes, and human water management.

494228.title: Improving Wildfire Heat Flux and Plume Dynamics in WRF-SFIRE through Explicit Crown-Fire Representation for the NASA INSPYRE Campaign
494228.authors: Angel Farguell, San Jose State University, San Jose, CA; and C. Crawford, D. Moser, G. Cheng, A. Costes, and A. Kochanski
494228.abstract: Accurate prediction of wildfire plume dynamics and pyrocumulonimbus development requires realistic representation of fire heat release and its coupling with the atmosphere. We present an enhanced WRF-SFIRE configuration developed for NASA's INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE) that incorporates crown-fire behavior to improve representation of wildfire energetics and plume evolution. The crown-fire model accounts for the ignition and consumption of canopy fuels under conditions favorable for crown involvement, augmenting the heat release represented by the surface-fire model. Inclusion of canopy fuel consumption increases the magnitude and modifies the spatial distribution of sensible and latent heat fluxes transferred to the atmosphere. Compared with the baseline WRF-SFIRE configuration, simulations including crown fire produce stronger fire-induced updrafts, enhanced vertical plume development, and improved representation of smoke injection and pyroconvective processes. For INSPYRE, the enhanced WRF-SFIRE configuration was integrated within the WRFx operational forecasting system. Satellite active-fire detections and infrared fire perimeters were used to initialize ongoing fires, while dynamically estimated live and dead fuel moisture characterized fuel conditions. Coupled forecasts of fire spread, heat release, plume rise, and smoke transport were generated for fires considered as potential aircraft targets. We present simulations of INSPYRE fires illustrating how crown-fire representation modifies fire heat fluxes and the resulting atmospheric response. These results demonstrate that representing canopy fuel consumption is important for capturing the strong fire-atmosphere coupling associated with intense wildfires and provides improved predictions of plume dynamics for wildfire research and field-campaign applications.

494230.title: Divergent Trends in Post-landfall Decay of Strong and Weak Tropical Cyclones
494230.authors: Chenxi Hu, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX; and X. Sui, D. Niyogi, C. Dawson, and Z. L. Yang
494230.abstract: Tropical cyclone post-landfall decay strongly influences inland hazard exposure, yet most studies assume that environmental change affects storms of different intensities uniformly. Here we identify an intensity-dependent divergence in global trends of tropical cyclone post-landfall decay. Analyzing 885 observed events (1979–2024), we show that strong storms (≥ 29 m s⁻¹) now weaken 18.6% faster after landfall, whereas weak storms persist 14.5% longer inland. These contrasting trends arise from different environmental sensitivities. Weak storms respond primarily to thermodynamic factors, including sea-surface warming, enhanced atmospheric moisture, and increased oceanic influence along storm tracks, all of which favor prolonged inland persistence. In contrast, strong storms are more sensitive to dynamic and land-surface conditions, including faster translation speeds, increasing atmospheric stability, and drier soil, which collectively promote faster decay. Numerical experiments further demonstrate that weaker storms respond more strongly to thermodynamic enhancement, whereas stronger storms are more vulnerable to dynamic disruption. These results challenge uniform-response assumptions in tropical cyclone risk assessment, forging a dual-threat landscape: intensifying coastal impacts from faster decay strong storms alongside expanding inland risks from increasingly persistent weak systems. Our findings reveal pronounced intensity-dependent heterogeneity in tropical cyclones, urging refined hazard assessment and adaptation for vulnerable and unprepared regions worldwide.

494234.title: Radar Composite Analysis of Pyrocumulonimbus Clouds
494234.authors: Zachary James Esch, St Cloud State University, Farmington, MN; and M. D. Fromm, D. A. Peterson, T. M. McHardy, and N. P. Lareau
494234.abstract: Pyrocumulonimbus clouds (pyroCb) are a major source of stratospheric aerosols that are capable of atmospheric hazards such as lightning, erratic winds and tornadoes that can impact fire management operations such as lightning, erratic winds and tornadoes. Despite their significance, there are relatively few studies looking into the radar characteristics of pyroCbs. This study used NEXRAD dual-polarization radar data to create a composite of six different pyroCb events. Reflectivity and correlation coefficient (CC) data were gridded onto a common three dimensional domain centered on each pyroCb. The wind direction aligned plume cross section was converted to advection time using ERA5 vertical wind profiles. Results reveal a recurring feature, which we refer to as upscale hydrometeor growth (DUHG), and is characterized by high CC values (>0.8) located downwind of the fire updraft. The DUHG generally increases in size as the pyroCb evolves and is typically located above the convective condensation level. In contrast, the updraft region consistently lacks the high CC signature associated with hydrometeors found in general convection.

494237.title: A Comparison of HRRR and RRFSv2X In-Flight Icing Forecasts from the Forecast Icing Product
494237.authors: Daniel R. Adriaansen, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. R. Siems-Anderson and S. M. Ellis
494237.abstract: The currently operational Forecast Icing Product (FIP) version 2 utilizes Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) model forecast fields from the High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) version 4. A prototype FIP, under development by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), is scheduled to utilize Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) version 2 NWP model forecast fields once transitioned to operations. However, this prototype FIP has been developed using the HRRRv4, necessitating further testing and development using pre-production forecasts from RRFSv2X. The RRFSv2X utilizes improvements to the underlying microphysical parameterization, as well as a completely new dynamical core from the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS). Understanding how these changes affect the prototype FIP forecasts will be the focus of this exploratory work. Data from several cold season (October - March) cases will be obtained from both NWP models. Modifications to the prototype FIP to utilize the new RRFSv2X model forecasts will be reviewed, if necessary. Model input fields as well as FIP in-flight icing forecasts will be matched with voice Pilot Reports (PIREPs) of in-flight icing conditions. Differences in the identification of the scenario used to compute the in-flight icing forecasts, as well as the characteristics of clouds utilized by the FIP will be given particular attention. Opportunities for further development of the prototype FIP to best utilize the RRFSv2X forecasts will be discussed. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the FAA. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

494239.title: Some Historical Perspectives on the South American Low-Level Jet
494239.authors: Wayne H. Schubert, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; CSU, Fort Collins, CO
494239.abstract: One of the many contributions by George Kiladis and his research colleagues concerns the South American low-level jet (LLJ). This jet frequently occurs to the east of the Andes Mountains and is responsible for transporting large quantities of water vapor into central and southern South America. A major contribution to the dynamics of the jet is likely the effects of heating on the sloping terrain. Upper tropospheric jets are often interpreted in terms of the potential vorticity field. Can the LLJ be similarly interpreted? Such an interpretation (in simplified form) was advanced by Eliassen (1980). In this talk we update Eliassen's argument in light of recent observations.

494240.title: Tracking the Evolution of Hazard Exposure and Demographic Vulnerability across the United States between 2000 and 2025
494240.authors: Rakibul Ahasan, Esri, Redlands, CA; and S. Chatterjee and N. Noman
494240.abstract: Weather-related events and climatic hazards impose substantial and growing costs across the United States, and the burden falls unevenly across both region and population groups. Major hazardous events like, floods, extreme heat, winter storms, tropical cyclones, tornadoes, and drought each concentrate in distinct regions, and historical records indicate that those concentrations are not stationary. Reported damages have risen in areas where population and property have expanded, while the geography of where damaging events occur has itself shifted in ways that development patterns alone do not account for. Preparedness planning and response allocation depend on distinguishing these processes, and on knowing whether concentrated exposure in a given place is arriving, holding, or receding. Current hazard characterizations are limited in three respects. First, national products summarize decades of records as a single static surface, which conceals movement by construction. Second, delineating high-exposure zones requires substantial statistical analysis that requires sophisticated data. However, due to the nature of these data, they are often missing and existing pattern analysis methods depend more on subjective interpretation rather than the property of the distribution. This prevents comparison across hazards or between periods. Third, exposure is rarely reinforced by joining with the demographic composition of the populations that carry it, so the question of whether hazard burden falls disproportionately on particular communities is answered separately from the question of where hazards concentrate, if at all. This study uses NOAA Storm Events records from 2020 to 2025 across the conterminous United States, covering flood, extreme heat, heavy snow and winter storms, tropical cyclones, tornadoes, and drought. Damages are taken as reported property damage, converted to constant 2025 US dollars. These figures derive from local reporting rather than from systematic assessment, and reporting completeness varies by jurisdiction, hazard type, and period. We treat them accordingly and estimated a parallel unweighted surface for every hazard so that event frequency provides an independent check on any result driven by the loss field. Three-dimensional kernel density estimation is applied with time as the third dimension alongside the two planar coordinates, producing a continuous space-time density volume per hazard rather than a stack of annual maps. Estimates at any instant draw on adjacent periods, which separates short-term sampling variation from sustained change. Exposure zones are delineated using volume percentile contours, which enclose a fixed proportion of the estimated density volume. Because the enclosed share is held constant, contours are comparable across hazards, weighting schemes, and temporal windows, and nested levels distinguish persistent cores from broader intermittent envelopes. From the contour sequence, we derive the speed and bearing of core migration, change in enclosed area as a measure of consolidation or dispersal, core overlap between periods as a measure of persistence, and overlap between hazards as a measure of compound exposure. Exposure measures are then summarized to counties and joined to American Community Survey estimates covering income, age structure, housing tenure and vintage, vehicle access, disability, and language. We evaluate whether counties in persistent or intensifying exposure cores differ systematically in demographic composition from counties of comparable hazard frequency outside those cores, and whether any association strengthens or weakens over the study period (2000-2025). Comparisons are reported as associations, with the reporting characteristics of the underlying damage data treated as a source of potential bias rather than as noise. The estimation framework used in here is based on established practices, and it contributes to the progression from spatial exposure to temporal exposure to the demographic distribution of that exposure, built on measures that are comparable across hazards and reproducible without any analysis bias. Where exposure is intensifying and the resident population has limited capacity to prepare or recover, the two findings together identify priorities that neither analysis produces alone.

494241.title: Management, Not Just Climate: Agricultural Drought Risk in Interconnected Water Systems
494241.authors: Armen Konialian, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA; and B. Vangipuram, J. Medellin-Azuara, and A. Escriva-Bou
494241.abstract: Drought is often treated as a water-availability problem, where reductions in precipitation and snowfall are assumed to translate directly into reduced water supply and, in turn, greater economic losses. However, in highly managed water systems, such as California, the volume of water ultimately delivered to farms, districts, or regions is not determined by climate alone. It also depends on reservoir operations, the administration of water rights and delivery agreements, and the constraints imposed by environmental and regulatory requirements during periods of scarcity. Even where deliveries are comparable, two regions can experience different economic outcomes depending on the value and composition of the crops. A region planted in high-value permanent crops faces different consequences than one dominated by lower-value annual crops that can be fallowed in a dry year. As a result, regions exposed to similar hydroclimatic conditions, and even regions receiving similar deliveries, can experience different economic consequences, a distinction that matters directly for insurers, lenders, investors, and agricultural producers exposed to drought risk. Existing drought assessments often focus on hydroclimatic conditions or aggregate water demand without accounting for how allocation rules determine who bears a given shortage. Less attention has been paid to the consequences once a shortage occurs: these studies often represent vulnerability through composite indicators that vary in how clearly they connect to actual outcomes. The central risk question is therefore not only how severe a drought is in hydrologic terms, but also who bears the resulting shortage, what economic value is exposed, and how differences in adaptive capacity shape the resulting losses. To address this gap, we conceptualize agricultural drought risk as the interaction of hazard, exposure, and vulnerability, explicitly accounting for the role of water-system operations in translating hydroclimatic scarcity into agricultural impacts. Hazard is characterized by water shortages experienced by agricultural users under alternative hydroclimatic and management conditions. Exposure represents the agricultural land use and associated economic value subject to these shortages, while vulnerability captures differences in sensitivity and adaptive capacity under reduced water availability. Together, these components trace drought risk from the physical occurrence of water scarcity, through allocation decisions and agricultural responses, to spatially differentiated economic outcomes. We apply this framework to California's interconnected water system using CalSim 3, the state's planning and operations model for the State Water Project and Central Valley Project along with local water projects and groundwater in the Central Valley. CalSim 3 represents major reservoirs, conveyance infrastructure, water demands, environmental requirements, and operating rules governing water allocation across much of California. We simulate agricultural water deliveries under combinations of alternative hydroclimatic conditions and alternative management strategies, comparing management alternatives under identical hydroclimatic conditions to isolate how operational and regulatory choices alter the magnitude and spatial distribution of agricultural water scarcity, the hazard component of this framework. Exposure is quantified as the annual revenue associated with different crops. OpenAg, an agricultural production model based on Positive Mathematical Programming (PMP), then translates water shortages into changes in cropping patterns and irrigated acreage, from which we derive a region-specific damage function linking shortage to revenue loss, representing vulnerability. Together, these components yield spatially explicit, economically meaningful drought-risk indicators, allowing us to evaluate how management strategies, such as relaxing Delta salinity standards or expanding conveyance capacity, impact agricultural economic risk broadly or shift it toward specific water users. We hypothesize that economic drought risk will be disproportionately concentrated in regions where high-value, water-dependent agricultural production coincides with limited access to alternative supplies and lower adaptive flexibility. These differences carry direct implications for the assessment, pricing, and management of drought risk. For insurers, agricultural lenders, investors, and other institutions exposed to agricultural risk, hydrologic indicators describe the underlying hazard but not the distribution of realized economic exposure. By explicitly representing the institutional and operational processes linking hydrologic scarcity to agricultural outcomes, this framework identifies where similar climatic shocks generate different economic consequences and the mechanisms driving those differences. The resulting outputs can inform agricultural credit-risk assessment, insurance and risk-transfer design, investment stress testing, and other applications where the magnitude and spatial distribution of economic exposure are relevant. Although developed using CalSim 3, the framework is not California-specific. It can be applied to other highly managed, water-scarce basins by substituting locally appropriate hydrologic and operations models, institutional rules, and economic data. More broadly, it shifts drought-risk assessment from how much water will be available to who absorbs the shortage, where economic value is exposed, and how management decisions alter that distribution, translating aggregate measures of hydroclimatic and system stress into decision-relevant measures of economic exposure that can inform the pricing, allocation, and management of drought risk across interconnected water systems.

494243.title: Weather Support at the Regan Test Range, Kwajalein, Marshall Islands
494243.authors: John W. Conway, RedTown Technical Services, Norman, OK
494243.abstract: RedTown Technical Services, LLC (RTSLLC), headquartered in Norman, Oklahoma, provides meteorological support services for the Reagan Test Range (RTR) on Kwajalein Island in the Republic of the Marshall Islands under contract to the U.S. Army. The RTR is a critical national asset supporting missile defense testing and other missions that can involve stringent meteorological requirements. Kwajalein occupies a unique position within the meteorological observing network of the western and central Pacific. Although a National Weather Service upper-air stations are located at Majuro and Guam, ground-based Doppler weather radar coverage across the region is extremely sparse. Outside of Kwajalein, the nearest comparable location providing both routine radiosonde observations and operational Doppler weather radar data is Guam, approximately 2,500 km west-northwest of Kwajalein. This relative isolation makes locally collected meteorological data particularly important to mission planning and execution. The Kwajalein region is strongly influenced by the trade-wind regime and the Intertropical Convergence Zone, creating significant forecasting challenges. RTSLLC provides 24/7 meteorological support through a combination of on-island personnel and forecast support from company offices in Huntsville, Alabama, and Norman, Oklahoma. This presentation will describe the meteorological observing network supporting the Reagan Test Site, including its radar, upper-air, and surface observing capabilities; the operational forecasting responsibilities of the meteorological staff; and the challenges associated with providing mission-critical weather support from this remote Pacific island location.

494250.title: Fixed Storm Corridors over a Warming Ocean: Rapid Intensification Hazard and Coastal Exposure In the Gulf of Mexico
494250.authors: Rakibul Ahasan, Esri, Redlands, CA; and S. Mahmud, S. Chatterjee, and N. Noman
494250.abstract: Rapid intensification is the least predictable and most consequential behavior of Gulf of Mexico hurricanes, and the thermodynamic support it draws on is not stationary. Intensification depends on the heat available through the depth a storm mixes rather than on sea-surface temperature alone, and upper-ocean heat content has risen in every tropical cyclone basin over the satellite era. Coastal exposure has risen alongside it. Assessments intended to locate this rising danger are constructed in one of two ways: from storm track geography, with the ocean held as a stationary boundary condition, or from ocean climatology averaged over a fixed period, with time removed. Neither construction can determine whether growing coastal danger originates in the displacement of storm paths, in thermodynamic change in the upper ocean, or in the expansion of settlement, and each origin implies a different intervention. The Gulf of Mexico permits the three to be separated. It is a semi-enclosed basin with a well-observed upper-ocean record, short transit distances between rapid-intensification onset and landfall, and a densely settled shelf margin, so that a change in ocean state translates into a landfall consequence within a short and traceable interval. Upper-ocean conditions are derived from the GLORYS12 1/12° reanalysis for warm seasons (June–November) 1993 through 2026. Four fields are computed: tropical cyclone heat potential, depth of the 26°C isotherm, warm-season sea-surface temperature and its linear trend, and the density of extreme upper-ocean heat across space and time, the last identifying where anomalously high heat content recurs rather than where it occurs once. These are combined with coastal proximity into a rapid-intensification hazard index through an analytic hierarchy process (AHP) (heat potential 0.42, isotherm depth 0.26, coastal proximity 0.16, extreme-heat density 0.10, sea-surface temperature trend 0.06; consistency ratio 0.015). Tier boundaries are set once and held fixed across the record, so that measured change reflects the ocean rather than the classification, and weight uncertainty is propagated through 1,000 Monte Carlo runs with ±20% perturbation to yield a per-cell probability of top-tier membership. The index is recomputed in five-year slices, within which high-hazard cores are delineated as contiguous top-tier regions and characterized by footprint area and centroid position, so that intensification and displacement are measured separately. Track geography is taken from IBTrACS, measured as the annual intensity-weighted centroid relative to a 1985–1989 baseline and as a comparison of two equal twenty-year windows, 1985–2004 against 2005–2024. The hazard field is then intersected with built-up surface and population at five-year epochs and with an established social vulnerability index (SVI) from Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), partitioning observed exposure change into hazard, settlement, and interaction terms. The design uses no climate model, synthetic track generation, or emissions scenario, so the resulting hazard geography carries no scenario assumptions and is directly auditable against the source products. The findings from our analysis using these historical records indicate that track geography is statistically stationary over the decades. The intensity-weighted centroid differs by 60 km southward between the two windows, and neither displacement component carries a significant trend (−0.29° and −0.21° per decade in latitude and longitude; p = 0.36 and 0.57). The annual centroid deviation from the 1985–1989 baseline is flat to slightly declining across the record. However, the ocean beneath those tracks has changed. Warm-season sea-surface temperature has risen 0.25°C per decade (r = 0.75, p = 4×10⁻⁷), with the basin-mean anomaly moving from −0.29°C in 1993–1997 to +0.74°C in 2023–2026. The basin area supporting rapid intensification, defined as heat potential at or above 50 kJ cm⁻² for more than half the warm season, has grown from 24.7% to 60.6%. The composite high-hazard footprint has expanded from 28.8% to 61.7%, and its centroid has migrated westward, by approximately 2.3°, from 84.5°W (1993-2007) to 87.2°W (2013-2026), toward the Texas and Louisiana coast. The expansion is robust to weight perturbation across the Monte Carlo ensemble. Hazard growth in this basin is thermodynamic in origin and westward in direction, and it occurs beneath a track geography that has not moved. Two categories of hazard products are insensitive to that result. Track-based maps hold the ocean fixed and record no change because the tracks record none. In contrast, stationary-climatology maps hold time fixed and record no change because the averaging removes it. The fastest-growing component of Gulf hurricane hazard is, therefore, absent from the products most often used to communicate it. Storms following unchanged trajectories now traverse a greater extent of water capable of supporting rapid intensification before landfall, which compresses the interval between the last reliable intensity forecast and the arrival of damaging winds. This approach undercuts intensity assumptions embedded in coastal design standards calibrated on an earlier basin state and concentrates that burden on the Texas and Louisiana coast. Because the corridors are fixed, exposure change over the same period resolves into ocean change and settlement change without a confounding contribution from storm relocation.
