We expect that partition to show hazard-dominated growth along the western Gulf, where the high-hazard centroid has migrated and coastal populations have limited experience of rapid-intensification landfalls, against settlement-dominated growth in Florida, where the thermodynamic signal is weaker and coastal development has been faster. The broader significance is that a hazard can intensify substantially without moving trajectory from historical trends. Frameworks built on the geography of past storms cannot detect a change of this kind, however large, because the change resides in the water rather than in the record of where storms went. In the Gulf of Mexico, where the interval between intensification onset and landfall is short and the shelf margin is densely settled, that blind spot sits directly over the most consequential coastal risk in the basin. Reading hazards from the ocean rather than from the tracks is not a refinement of existing practice; it is the difference between seeing this change and missing it entirely.

494258.title: Expanding Storm Surge Observing with a 3D-Printed, Low-Cost Water-Level Gauge
494258.authors: Kathryn Payne, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. M. Halberstadt, R. Zieber, B. M. Smith, M. Steinson, and P. A. Kucera
494258.abstract: Storm surge is typically the most deadly phenomena during a tropical cyclone, but observational data to improve understanding of this hazard are scarce, both in some regions of the United States and internationally. The COMET program at the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR) has developed a low-cost solution to enhance storm surge monitoring and verification, in the form of the 3D-PAWS Storm Surge gauge. The 3D-Printed Automatic Weather Station (3D-PAWS) was developed at COMET over ten years ago to improve the monitoring of hazardous weather in data sparse regions, including in Small Island Developing States and Less Developed Countries. More recently, COMET has introduced a low-cost ultrasonic distance-to-surface sensor (MaxBotix MB7363) in a 3D-printed housing that can be used to monitor water level, including tides and storm surge. The 3D-PAWS Storm Surge uses PVC as a frame and runs on a solar panel and voltaic battery, with data being transmitted in real time every six minutes via a cellular datalogger. Additional meteorological sensors; including a pressure sensor, wind vane, and anemometer, can be integrated into the system as desired. A 3D-PAWS Storm Surge sensor was co-located with a USGS tidal gauge in Chincoteague, Virginia, and here we examine the performance of 3D-PAWS versus the USGS reference station. Water level observations from 3D-PAWS are found to closely mirror those of the reference station, and also capture the storm surge produced in Chincoteague Bay by Hurricane Erin in August, 2025. The 3D-PAWS’s observed water level rise aligns with that predicted by the National Hurricane Center (NHC)’s official storm surge forecast. In work supported by the U.S. State Department, National Weather Service, and the NHC, 3D-PAWS Storm Surge sensors are currently deployed in the U.S., Dominican Republic, Belize, the Cayman Islands, Turks and Caicos, and Fiji. Further testing and deployments in the U.S. and Caribbean are planned for the coming year. By expanding coastal water level observation networks, the 3D-PAWS Storm Surge gauge can help provide actionable data to inform an early warning response and verify numerical weather prediction for storm surge.

494262.title: Delivering the Next Generation of the Great Lakes Coastal Forecast Modeling System
494262.authors: Brooke Odstrchel, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI; GLERL, Ann Arbor, MI; and D. Titze, D. Cannon, M. Mattwig, Y. Hong, J. Anderson, Y. J. Zhang, C. Wu, and J. C. Feyen
494262.abstract: Across the Great Lakes, coastal infrastructure plays a major role in supporting commercial shipping, recreational activities, natural resource management, and flood preparedness. While regional forecast guidance relies on NOAA's Great Lakes Operational Forecast System (GLOFS), current operational products do not include many coastal areas of importance, such as estuaries, floodplains, ports, and harbors. To address this, we have developed a next-generation modeling system to extend model coverage to these missing coastal elements and to connect the land-water boundaries by coupling hydrodynamic and hydrologic domains. Next-generation models, developed using SCHISM, are directly coupled with the National Water Model (NWM), with more than over 300 explicitly resolved streams in the Lake Ontario mesh alone. . Both surface temperature nudging and an empirical stream temperature model have been incorporated to help improve temperature bias and thermal structure in the lakes. In this presentation, we discuss hindcasts for high ice (2025) and water level years (2017, 2019) in Lake Ontario, highlighting strong performance under extreme forcing conditions. Model performance is as good or better than the current operational model, with performance statistics calculated for surface temperature, thermal structure, water levels, and ice cover. Flood extent and inundation depth are validated against high water level mark data and SAR imagery where available. Working directly with regional stakeholders, we have also developed several new nowcast/forecast research products, including new graphics focused on zoomed-in areas of interest, highly populated areas, or areas prone to flooding around the lake. These new graphics will make it easier to see community-focused forecasting products, providing a value-added service to coastal communities in the Great Lakes. The methods and infrastructure used to develop the Lake Ontario model are currently being expanded to develop a consolidated next-generation forecast system that includes all five Great Lakes.

494264.title: State-Aware Dual-Stream Graph Neural Emulator of Lagrangian Ice-Particle Dynamics in Cirrus Clouds
494264.authors: Zesheng Liu, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA; and J. Liu, F. Li, J. Ko, K. D. Lamb, K. K. Chandrakar, and M. Rahnemoonfar
494264.abstract: Cirrus clouds play an important role in Earth’s climate, yet their evolution depends on ice-particle microphysical processes that occur at scales much finer than those resolved by global climate models. Cloud Model 1 (CM1), used in a large-eddy simulation (LES) configuration, enables high-resolution simulation of the three-dimensional atmospheric environment. Within CM1, the Super-Droplet Method (SDM) represents cloud microphysics by tracking Lagrangian superdroplets and the evolution of their positions and microphysical properties. The coupled CM1-SDM framework provides a detailed representation of cirrus cloud evolution, but the resulting particle-resolved simulations are computationally expensive. This motivates machine-learning emulators that can reproduce the evolution of SDM particles conditioned on the surrounding CM1 environment. We develop a state-aware emulator for superdroplet evolution in CM1-SDM cirrus simulations using a dual-stream architecture, where a graph neural network encodes the states and interactions of Lagrangian superdroplets, while a three-dimensional U-Net independently encodes spatially structured CM1 fields, including thermodynamic, humidity, and wind variables. The particle and atmospheric-field representations are combined through a structured fusion mechanism that separates particle self- and interaction dynamics, direct local atmospheric forcing, and learned three-dimensional environmental context. An adaptive gate controls the contribution of the learned environmental correction according to particle state and forecast horizon. The experiments use output from a CM1-SDM simulation of a cirrus case from the ICEBall field campaign. To accommodate coupled simulation outputs that may be archived at different temporal cadences between particle and atmospheric fields, the emulator uses a block-based, multi-horizon forecasting formulation. In the dataset considered here, SDM particle states are saved every 15 s, while CM1 atmospheric fields are saved every 60 s. From each CM1 output time, the model directly predicts particle positions and microphysical states at 15-, 30-, 45-, and 60-s lead times, with the 60-s prediction initializing the next rollout block. The state-aware component accounts for particles whose radius and effective density take fixed values in the SDM output, while separately modeling particles with continuously evolving microphysical properties. The training objectives capture particle trajectories, transitions between fixed-value and continuously evolving particle states, and population-level radius and effective density distributions. On particle-level tests, the dual-stream model substantially improves over particle-only multi-layer perceptron and graph neural network baselines. Under the inductive particle split, RMSE aggregated over all evaluated particle forecasts at 15-, 30-, 45-, and 60-s lead times was 2.08 m in x, 2.09 m in y, 4.29 m in z, 0.28 microns in equivalent radius, and 12.25 kg/m3 in effective density. Comparable performance between inductive and transductive particle splits further indicates that the learned representation is not dependent on individual particle identities. These results demonstrate the potential of coupled particle-field neural emulation as an efficient surrogate for resolving detailed ice-particle evolution within high-fidelity cirrus simulations.

494265.title: Increasing Exposure of Wet Bulb Globe Temperature Through Mesonet Observations
494265.authors: Blaine C. Thomas, White Sands Missile Range, White Sands, NM
494265.abstract: The wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT) provides a more comprehensive assessment of heat stress risk compared to standard metrics like air temperature or various apparent temperature measures (e.g., Heat Index). The adoption of WBGT in heat management policy has grown substantially in recent years, particularly for outdoor activities sponsored by high school associations in the United States. While on-site WBGT measurements remain the ideal standard, reasonably accurate estimations can be derived from standard meteorological variables (Liljegren et al. (2008), Dimiceli et al. (2011), Range Commanders Council Meteorology Group (2025)). Several mesonets are currently producing WBGT estimations with many others having requisite measurements (air temperature, humidity, wind speed, and solar radiation) to easily implement these estimations. This presentation showcases examples of how mesonets are deriving and sharing WBGT information to support heat stress decision-making. Mesonet-derived WBGT offers another valuable tool for heat-related situational awareness on local and regional scales. Expanding WBGT data points through mesonet estimations can deliver significant benefits to organizations providing heat-sensitive activity decision support or issuing public heat alert products, endeavors in line with the mission of mesonet organizations to protect lives through availability of their data.

494267.title: Impact of Far-Side Versus Polar Magnetic Fields on Coronal and Solar Wind Model Predictions
494267.authors: C. Nick Arge, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and E. Samara, C. Henney, S. Jones, S. Schonfeld, and D. G. Simpson
494267.abstract: Knowledge of the instantaneous global photospheric magnetic field is critical for accurate modeling of the corona and solar wind, as these data serve as the critical boundary condition to these models. Unfortunately, less than half of the Sun’s photospheric magnetic field is reliably measured from any given vantage point and thus it is common for the maps to have highly dated and unreliable measurements in them. Further, coronal models are extremely sensitive to the strengths of the Sun’s polar magnetic fields, which remain poorly observed. Recently, efforts to mitigate this problem include using flux transport models such as the Air Force Data Assimilative Photospheric Flux Transport (ADAPT) model, which evolves the field forward in time using well known transport processes occurring on the Sun. However, these models do not normally account for far-side emergence of new magnetic flux, which can significantly impact coronal and solar model predictions. Also, the strengths of the polar fields remain highly uncertain in these models, as meridional flows at high latitudes are not well specified there. Since the ADAPT model now includes the ability to include far-side active regions into the output maps it generates, we can now explore the relative importance and impact on coronal and solar wind model predictions of the inclusion of far-side observations versus the strengths of the polar fields. We study a nearly 1-year period near solar minimum from May 2010 to April 2011 where we include and exclude far-side active regions fields while varying the strength of the polar fields to quantitatively evaluate their importance and relative impact on coronal and solar wind models.

494270.title: From TRMM TMPA to GPM IMERG: Replicating Tropical Cyclone Precipitation Contributions in the Southeastern United States with Geomni
494270.authors: Kwo-Sen Kuo, GSFC, GREENBELT, MD; and M. R. Samperboyina, S. S. Ho, and G. J. Huffman
494270.abstract: Tropical cyclones make a substantial and highly variable contribution to warm-season precipitation in the southeastern United States, particularly along the Gulf Coast, Florida, and the coastal Carolinas. Prat and Nelson’s 2013 study used 12 years of TRMM Multisatellite Precipitation Analysis data from 1998–2009, together with IBTrACS tropical cyclone tracks, to quantify the seasonal, interannual, monthly, and intensity-dependent contribution of tropical cyclones to regional precipitation. Their results showed that tropical cyclones accounted for approximately 7% of June–November precipitation over land, with contributions reaching 15%–20% in some coastal areas, locally exceeding 40% in years with major landfalling hurricanes, and representing an increasing fraction of heavy rainfall events. This presentation reports a Geomni-assisted replication and adaptation of that study using a newer satellite precipitation record. Geomni, an expert-supervised agentic AI system for computational reproduction and workflow reuse, was used to recover the methodological structure of the original TRMM TMPA analysis, including the spatial domain, June–November tropical cyclone season, IBTrACS-based storm attribution, 500-km storm-centered precipitation association criterion, 3-hourly precipitation aggregation, and analyses of seasonal, annual, monthly, and heavy-rainfall contributions. After reproducing the logic of the original workflow, Geomni adapted it from TRMM TMPA for 1998–2009 to GPM IMERG for a later 11-year period, 2014–2024. The resulting comparison contrasts the original TRMM-era estimates of tropical cyclone rainfall contribution with those derived from the Geomni-replicated IMERG-era analysis. The comparison examines whether the spatial structure of tropical cyclone precipitation contribution remains concentrated along the Gulf and Atlantic coasts, whether inland gradients and monthly maxima are consistent with the original study, and how interannual variability and heavy-rainfall fractions differ between the two observing periods and satellite products. Differences may arise from changes in storm activity and tracks, the later climate period, the transition from TRMM TMPA to GPM IMERG retrievals, and differences in spatial and temporal sampling and algorithm design. By using Geomni to reproduce and adapt a published satellite-precipitation workflow, this study demonstrates how agentic AI can transform legacy environmental science studies into reusable analytical frameworks. The TRMM-to-IMERG replication provides both a scientific comparison of tropical cyclone precipitation contributions across two 12-year periods and a methodological example of AI-assisted reproducibility, replication, and extension of data-driven meteorological research.

494271.title: Heatwave Exposure During Pregnancy and Risk of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus in Arizona (2014-2021)
494271.authors: Paulina Luna, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and M. Furlong
494271.abstract: Exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy has been associated with a higher risk of adverse perinatal outcomes, but evidence regarding gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) remains limited. The purpose of this study was to identify the association between heatwave exposure during pregnancy and odds of GDM, while identifying gestational weeks of susceptibility. The analytical sample included 536,621 singleton births from Arizona birth certificates and a total of 43, 481 GDM cases. Heatwaves were defined as 3,4,and 5 consecutive days of a temperature higher than 42 degrees celsius. Distributed non-linear lag models were utilized to estimate the odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) across gestational weeks. Models were adjusted for birth year, infant sex, county, month of conception and maternal demographic characteristics such as age, race/ethnicity, and education. Additional heat index models were incorporated to assess temperature and humidity. For the maximum temperature models, significant associations were observed for 3-day, 4-day and 5-day heatwaves between gestational weeks 11 and 27 with odds ratios of 1.02-1.03 and a 95 %CI (1.01-1.03). Heat index models showed significant associations earlier in pregnancy. The highest associations were observed between gestational weeks 0-15 with an OR of 1.03 and a 95% CI (1.01- 1.05). These findings suggest that heatwave exposure during early and middle pregnancy increased the odds of developing GDM. Heat index models identified an association earlier, possibly indicating that combining temperature and humidity may be better at capturing the physiological response of heat stress. This highlights the importance of considering the gestational period and heatwave duration when identifying pregnancy outcomes related to heat.

494272.title: Creating Operational Products Using Supplemental Weather Radar
494272.authors: Tara Goode, Climavision, Louisville, KY; and M. Simpson, L. Maynard, R. A. Clark, S. Martinaitis, and C. Goode
494272.abstract: Supplemental weather radar networks provide observations in areas where the national Weather Surveillance Radar, 1988 Doppler (WSR-88D) network has low-altitude or inter-radar coverage limitations. The challenge is therefore evolving from determining whether supplemental radar observations can provide useful information to understanding how these data can be further refined, integrated, and transformed into reliable products within the National Weather Service (NWS) operational enterprise. Through collaboration among the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL), the Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), and Climavision, supplemental dual-polarization radar observations are progressing along this research-to-operations (R2O) pathway. Climavision operates a growing network of supplemental weather radars designed to improve low-altitude surveillance in areas affected by distance from existing WSR-88D radars, terrain blockage, and other persistent coverage limitations. Data from this network are already flowing to NWS Weather Forecast Offices (WFO) and are being used operationally by forecasters to enhance situational awareness during severe convection, winter weather, and other high-impact events. This operational use represents an important step, but it is not the endpoint. Continued research is focused on improving the quality, consistency, integration, and usability of supplemental radar observations and the products derived from them. A major component of this work is the integration of Climavision observations into the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) research program at NSSL. MRMS provides a framework for combining observations from multiple radars and wavelengths while applying sophisticated quality-control, mosaicking, and product-generation methodologies. Incorporating supplemental radar observations into this framework provides the opportunity to move beyond viewing individual commercial radars independently and instead assess their contribution as part of an integrated national radar mosaic. Through a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement (CRADA) with NSSL, significant progress has been made in data ingest, radar metadata handling, calibration assessment, quality control, and comparison with neighboring WSR-88D observations. Experimental MRMS integration is also enabling evaluation of how supplemental low-altitude observations affect the depiction of precipitation, storm structure, and other high-impact weather features. Case studies are being used to identify where additional radar coverage provides meaningful operational information while also revealing conditions under which wavelength, attenuation, non-meteorological echo, sensitivity, sampling characteristics, or other factors require additional consideration. These findings are helping guide continued refinement of supplemental-radar quality-control methodologies. Particular emphasis is being placed on developing approaches that preserve useful meteorological information while identifying and mitigating artifacts, with the broader objective of minimizing unnecessary filtering and improving consistency across differing radar technologies and wavelengths. As these methodologies mature, the same observations can support increasingly robust multi-radar products rather than serving solely as stand-alone supplemental displays. This collaborative research is being extended through activities associated with NOAA's Radar Next Broad Agency Announcement (BAA). That work provides a framework for more systematic exploration of supplemental radar data quality, performance characteristics, and potential operational requirements. Evaluations include objective comparisons with established radar observations, assessment of quality-control approaches, characterization of radar performance under differing meteorological conditions, and identification of remaining technical issues that must be addressed as supplemental radar becomes more deeply integrated into national applications. The presentation will describe the progression from delivery of Climavision radar observations to NWS WFOs and their current operational use, through integration into the MRMS research environment and development of increasingly mature quality-control and product-generation methodologies. Operational examples and initial evaluation results will illustrate both the value being realized today and areas where continued improvement is desired. Next steps include refinement of radar quality control, expanded quantitative evaluation across events and environmental regimes, continued assessment of precipitation and severe-weather applications, and development of increasingly consistent multi-radar products incorporating supplemental observations. These activities will also contribute to defining objective performance and data-quality criteria that can inform future operational use of commercial radar observations within the Radar Next program.

494276.title: Withdrawn: Predicting Subseasonal Forecast Skill of 2-m Temperature over East Asia Using a Multimodal Deep Learning Network
494276.authors: Xiaolei Liu, Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences, Beijing, 11, China; and J. Su
494276.abstract: The limited and highly sporadic subseasonal forecasting skill remains a major bottleneck in operational meteorology. Rather than attempting to improve average predictability, this study dynamically predicts the forecast skill itself to identify intermittent high- and low-skill forecast windows. To achieve this, a novel multimodal deep learning framework, SkillNet, is developed to classify the week-3 forecast skill (Top 30% high-skill versus Bottom 30% low-skill) of the ECMWF system for 2-meter temperature over East Asia. Driven by a dual-stream input architecture, SkillNet synergistically integrates two-dimensional large-scale spatial physical fields with one-dimensional low-frequency climate indices. Evaluations on an independent test set reveal that SkillNet effectively captures fluctuations in forecast skill, achieving peak ROC-AUC scores of 0.57 in the high-skill (Top 30%) task and 0.59 in the low-skill (Bottom 30%) task during summer. From a practical operational perspective, by utilizing a stringent decision threshold calibrated from the validation set, the model achieves a hit rate of approximately 60%. Furthermore, explainable machine learning diagnostics based on SHAP confirm that the discriminatory capacity of the SkillNet originates from intrinsic atmospheric/oceanic dynamics rather than artificial artifacts. Specifically, the SkillNet accurately captures key physical precursor signals such as ENSO/IOD-related SST anomalies and large-scale Z500 teleconnection wave trains. Ultimately, by proactively predicting predictability itself, this framework empowers forecasters to navigate the inherent uncertainties of the S2S timescale, transforming highly sporadic subseasonal forecast skill into actionable, risk-aware decision support.

494283.title: Enhancing the Radar Reflectivity Assimilation Capability of the Next-Generation Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFSv2): Constraining Hydrometeor Number Concentration in Double-Moment Microphysics for Ensemble Analyses
494283.authors: Chengsi Liu, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; and E. Mansell, Y. Wang, K. H. Knopfmeier, and N. Yussouf
494283.abstract: The next-generation Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFSv2), built on the MPAS dynamical core and the JEDI ensemble data assimilation framework, directly assimilates radar reflectivity to initialize probabilistic forecasts of severe convective storms. With double-moment microphysics, one reflectivity observation is used to constrain both hydrometeor mass and number concentration. Number concentration is much less constrained by physical processes and other observations, so analysis errors accumulate in this variable, producing unphysical particle sizes, degrading the retention of analyzed storms in forecasts, and generating spurious echoes in echo-free regions. This work develops an enhanced reflectivity assimilation capability for WoFSv2 based on three constraints on number concentration. A physical-bounds constraint inside the JEDI LETKF solver reparameterizes the hydrometeor control variable from mass and number to mass and the logarithm of mean particle mass, so that species-dependent particle diameter bounds are applied directly. A magnitude-consistency constraint rescales number concentration after the solver so that the reflectivity diagnosed from the hydrometeor analysis is consistent in magnitude with the analyzed reflectivity. A clear-air constraint removes residual hydrometeors where the analyzed reflectivity indicates no echo. The constraints are evaluated in a WoFSv2 prototype with the NSSL double-moment microphysics scheme, using rapidly cycled experiments for a May 2026 severe weather case in which MRMS reflectivity is assimilated together with conventional observations. Initial results show that the fully constrained configuration improves the neighborhood-based fractions skill score of composite reflectivity forecasts out to six hours and sharply reduces spurious echoes in clear air. Most of the forecast improvement comes from the magnitude-consistency and clear-air constraints, while the configuration that fits the reflectivity observations best at analysis time is not the one that produces the best forecasts. Detailed evaluations and implications for the operational configuration of WoFSv2 reflectivity assimilation will be presented at the conference.

494284.title: Impact of Vehicle Motion Coupled with Green Infrastructure on Pollutant Dispersion in Street Canyons
494284.authors: Yang Luo, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, shanghai, 31, China
494284.abstract: Moving vehicles act as primary emission sources and generate vehicle-induced turbulence (VIT), significantly influencing local flow structures and pollutant dispersion characteristics within street canyons. Combining wind tunnel experiments with numerical modeling using dynamic mesh technology, this study simulates dynamic pollutant emissions and systematically investigates the impacts of VIT and three green infrastructure configurations (street trees, hedgerows, and their combination) on canyon flow fields and pollutant dispersion (Fig.1). Results demonstrate that VIT substantially alters flow patterns and dispersion dynamics. Street trees impede canyon airflow, potentially hindering pollutant removal. Hedgerows significantly modify flow fields by generating leeward vortices that trap pollutants at canyon bases, increasing pedestrian-level concentrations by 7.10% and 5.88% compared to street tree-only and combined configurations, respectively, while exhibiting the lowest air change rate (ACH). In combined configurations, flow obstruction is primarily dominated by large-volume street trees and further hindered by hedgerows, weakening pollutant dispersion capacity while still outperforming hedgerow-only scenarios. This research provides practical insights and simulation foundations for optimizing vegetation typology and spatial arrangements in urban greening planning to mitigate adverse impacts on pollutant dispersion.

494287.title: Deep Convection Response to Aerosol in the Southeast using Tracking in Models and Observations
494287.authors: Sean William Freeman, The University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and K. Britton
494287.abstract: Understanding convective storm lifecycles, upscale growth, and how individual storms respond to changes in their local environment is crucial in understanding how, when, and why some storms develop from small cumulus clouds to deep cumulonimbus clouds. Cloud tracking has emerged as a valuable tool for quantifying this relationship through Lagrangian analysis of clouds and for linking individual cloud objects to local aerosol and meteorological conditions. Using the Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds library (tobac), we have developed multi-scale, multivariate databases of clouds in models and observations to examine the aerosol-meteorological-convection relationship. First, we have built a regional, multivariate database of clouds within the ARM AMF-3 domain in North Alabama, using satellite and multiple radar bands, from Ka to S, to quantify upscale growth from pre-precipitation to multicellular convective systems. Using this database, our initial results suggest that an increase in CCN suppresses upscale growth but increases convective cloud lifetime. Using this database and techniques developed for it, we have also examined the convective-aerosol-meteorological relationship in numerical models. We have developed a suite of high-resolution simulations around the AMF-3 site, using identical meteorology but varying aerosol concentrations with the direct and indirect effects enabled, to isolate the aerosol-convection signal. By combining the model and observations, we see a similar signal when increasing CCN concentrations in both the model and observations. These results provide observational constraints for improving aerosol-convection interactions in both regional and operational models, with implications for forecast accuracy in aerosol-active environments.

494294.title: Sources and Magnitude of Turbulence In Wintertime Cloud Systems during NASA IMPACTS
494294.authors: Alex Zielinski, University of Illinois of at Urbana/Champaign, River Forest, IL; and R. M. Rauber and T. J. Zaremba
494294.abstract: The comma head regions of extratropical cyclonic storm systems were sampled in coordinated flights during the Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) field campaign. The NASA P3-B Orion Turbulent Air Motion Measurement System (TAMMS) was deployed on the P-3 aircraft, which flew at altitudes between 2.5 and 5 km in the cloud systems to measure high-frequency wind components and calculate the Eddy Dissipation Rate (EDR), the standard metric for quantifying atmospheric turbulence intensity. Extensive calibrations were done during IMPACTS, with two flights completely dedicated to performing maneuvers to calibrate the angle of attack (speed maneuvers), the angle of sideslip (tailwags/crabbing), and the heading offset and pressure defect (reverse headings). Post mission analysis was done to remove any instances of icing contamination from the data. The NASA ER-2 flew at 20 km altitude along flight legs coordinated with the P-3. The ER-2 carried nadir pointing Doppler radars operating at W, Ka, Ku, and X band frequencies. In this talk, we present a statistical summary of the magnitude of EDR measured during the flights of the IMPACTS campaign. We provide case study analyses of regions of the storms that exhibited larger values of EDR. W-Band Doppler velocities are used to estimate vertical air motions in these regions, reflectivity from W and Ku Band radars are used to determine cloud structures, and high Resolution Rapid Refresh model data superimposed on the radar data is used to quantitatively relate the turbulent intensity to atmospheric stability, wind shear, frontal zones, and regions of evaporation, sublimation, and melting of hydrometeors.

494297.title: Taking on Snow and Ice Using Supplementary Weather Radar
494297.authors: Tara Goode, Climavision, Louisville, KY; and L. Maynard, M. Simpson, K. Ortega, K. Grempler, C. Zhang, J. van Doore, and C. Goode
494297.abstract: Taking decisions about road closures and diversions and actively adjusting snow and ice operations as a winter storm occurs remains a challenge for transportation agencies. Operational meteorologists look at weather radar to provide critical insights on storm timing and precipitation types. Scanning the lowest heights of the atmosphere with weather radar reveals storm structure, helps identify snow squalls, and lake effect snow positioning. Polarimetric radars help study hydrometeor type and distinguish precipitation type – snow, ice or rain. However, vast stretches of major transportation corridors and rural roadways in the United States still do not have adequate low altitude polarimetric weather radar coverage from the government weather radar network. Climavision operates a network of 30+ supplemental weather radars across the United States that provide the needed low altitude coverage between overshooting government radars. Climavision radars installed in Pennsylvania and Minnesota have captured snow squalls and Lake Effect Snow completely missed by the nearest WSR-88D radars. Over the last few years, government forecasters have used this data to issue snow squall warnings, and TV stations have used the data from these radars to alert the public of dangerous driving conditions. In addition, radar scientists at Climavision have developed a surface hydrometeor classification product that is able to distinguish between snow, freezing rain, and graupel, critical distinguishing factors for proper roadway planning. Examples of long duration snow squalls captured by the Climavision and neighboring WSR-88D radars will be shown side by side, along with examples of the new surface hydrometeor classification product. Integration of this new information into National Weather Service operations and broadcast meteorology will be discussed and examples of future products for snow and ice operations will be shown.

494298.title: Power Outage Exposure During Extreme Heat Under Pseudo-Global Warming: County-Scale Changes in Burden and Recurrence
494298.authors: Shah Afzal Saki, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; and G. Sofia, B. Kar, and E. N. Anagnostou
494298.abstract: Compound hazards during hot seasons, extreme heat, high winds and heavy rainfall, can turn a power outage into a prolonged public health emergency, yet outage severity is often measured only by the number of customers affected. That measure does not capture how long an outage overlaps dangerous heat or how warming may alter the location and recurrence of these compound events. We assess these changes across the contiguous United States by linking county-level wind and precipitation outage-response surfaces, developed from observed outage records with paired historical-control and pseudo-global warming regional climate simulations for 2000–2020. The analysis applies moderate and severe heat-index thresholds of 90°F and 105°F and estimates 5- and 10-year return levels for two measures: total customers exposed and customer-outage-hours accumulated above each threshold. We also compare urban, suburban and rural counties and evaluate how often historical return events recur in the warmer thermodynamic simulation. Preliminary results indicate that warming extends the seasonal period in which outages can coincide with hazardous heat. Changes in total customers exposed vary across space when present-day customer counts and settlement classifications are held constant. Customer-outage-hours, however, increase more consistently with larger changes for less frequent events. This pattern suggests that outage footprints of similar size may expose customers to dangerous heat for longer periods. The largest absolute burdens remain concentrated in regions with high historical exposure, while some of the strongest relative increases occur in suburban and rural transition areas and span several power-system regions. Events associated with historical 5-year and 10-year compound burdens also recur more often under pseudo-global warming and the reduction in recurrence intervals is greater for the severe heat threshold and higher return levels. Accounting for outage duration and climate-conditioned recurrence provides information that customer counts alone cannot supply for grid resilience planning, restoration readiness and protection of communities exposed to extreme heat.

494301.title: Where and When Is Seasonal Flood Risk Predictable? An Assessment Using GFDL SPEAR and Hydrological Modeling
494301.authors: Donghui Li, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and K. L. Findell, K. W. Dixon, A. Radhakrishna, and N. Johnson
494301.abstract: Seasonal prediction of flood risk can provide valuable lead time for disaster preparedness and water resources management. However, it remains unclear whether the climate information contained in seasonal forecast systems translates into useful hydrological information at regional and basin scales. This study investigates this question by combining meteorological forecasts from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory’s Seamless System for Prediction and EArth System Research (GFDL SPEAR) with hydrological modeling. SPEAR ensemble forecasts are used to drive the high-resolution, distributed Tiger–Hillslope Link Model (Tiger-HLM) and generate ensemble streamflow simulations at lead times up to several months. The analysis focuses on aggregated flood-risk characteristics, using indicators such as monthly maximum streamflow, the probability of exceeding high-flow thresholds, and the number of high-flow days. Initial analyses examine how forecast skill varies across selected regions, seasons, and lead times. Hydrological simulations driven by the Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC) provide a reference for interpreting differences between SPEAR-driven simulations and observation-based hydrological estimates. This modeling framework is designed to support broader evaluation of seasonal flood-risk predictability across the contiguous United States and the investigation of different flood-generating mechanisms. The study will present initial results from this framework and discuss where seasonal climate information shows the greatest potential to provide useful flood-risk information.

494302.title: Decadal Patterns of Surface-Atmosphere Exchange Seen from the Cross-Track Infrared Sounders
494302.authors: Dylan B. Millet, University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN; and K. Wells, C. Hu, J. F. Juncosa Calahorrano, J. Kearney, V. Payne, and J. D. Shutter
494302.abstract: Thermal infrared observations from the space-borne Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) enable detection of multiple volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are important for surface-atmosphere exchange and air chemistry. CrIS measurements began in 2012 with the launch of Suomi-NPP and are projected to continue through at least the late 2030s with successive instruments onboard the JPSS satellite series. In this presentation I will present some of our group’s recent work developing long-term, globally harmonized VOC records that span the 15-year CrIS record to date. I will first discuss the evaluation of these datasets in terms of their inter-sensor consistency and independent comparisons. Applications of the data will then be shown, including: i) the use of isoprene observations for characterizing biospheric fluxes, their interannual patterns of change, and impacts of climate variability and stress; ii) leveraging VOC:VOC ratios for mapping the atmosphere’s oxidizing capacity over biogenic source regions; and iii) using complementary pairs of pyrogenic VOCs for tracking fire pyrolysis conditions and smoke plume processing.

494305.title: 3D Tracking of a CME Observed by Both PUNCH and WISPR: Comparing Triangulation and Polarization-based Techniques
494305.authors: Sam Van Kooten, Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO
494305.abstract: On September 18, 2025, a coronal mass ejection was observed by both WISPR and PUNCH (an Earth-orbiting multi-satellite heliographic mission) while PSP was on the opposite side of the Sun from PUNCH. We triangulated this CME from these two distinct viewpoints, tracking it from about 20 to 70 solar radii and measuring a velocity increasing from 400 to 500 km / s. During this time, the CME in the PUNCH field of view moved from an elongation of about 5 deg to about 15 deg---a range of elongation that before PUNCH was not routinely observed from Earth. We compare this tracking result to the trajectory determined by analysis of the CME's polarization signal measured by PUNCH. This single-viewpoint polarization-based localization is a design feature and prominent science goal of PUNCH. Our study is one demonstration of PUNCH's ability to track CMEs outside traditional coronagraphic fields of view, which enables new science as well as significant advances in the ability to track and forecast Earth-directed CMEs. This also highlights WISPR's ability to complement other heliospheric missions.

494306.title: Geomni: An Agentic AI System for Reproducing and Replicating Earth Science Workflows
494306.authors: Kwo-Sen Kuo, GSFC, GREENBELT, MD; and M. R. Samperboyina, S. S. Ho, and G. J. Huffman
494306.abstract: Reproducibility and reuse remain persistent challenges in atmospheric and Earth system science, where published workflows often depend on fragmented data archives, incompletely documented code, and substantial expert labor. We present an application of Geomni, an expert-supervised agentic AI system for the end-to-end computational reproduction and adaptation of data-driven geoscience studies. Geomni extracts methodological intent from a target manuscript, identifies and retrieves required datasets, generates executable analysis code, recreates key figures, and evaluates results through structured expert intervention and verification gates. In this study, Geomni was used to reproduce a published precipitation analysis based on 12 years of TRMM TMPA data from 1998–2009. The system reconstructed the study workflow, including data acquisition, preprocessing, analysis logic, and figure generation, enabling comparison between reproduced outputs and the original published results. Beyond one-to-one reproduction, we then reused the extracted workflow and adapted it to the newer GPM IMERG precipitation data from 2014–2024 (11 years), demonstrating how agent-assisted workflow reuse can extend legacy analyses to updated satellite observing systems and more recent climate periods. This adaptation from TRMM to GPM demonstrates the broader scientific value of agentic reproducibility systems. These systems can reduce the manual effort required to recover previous methods, reveal gaps in documentation or data availability, and expedite hypothesis testing using modern datasets. Additionally, we have used Geomni to reproduce multiple geoscience data analysis publications. The results indicate that Geomni can assist in both verifying historical precipitation studies and efficiently reusing established analytical pipelines for contemporary satellite products. These capabilities provide a practical pathway toward more transparent, extensible, and reusable computational workflows in the fields of meteorology, hydrology, and climate research.

494307.title: Comparing Co-located Tipping Bucket and Weighing Gauge Extreme Rainfall Events
494307.authors: Emma L. Scott, North Carolina Institute for Climate Studies, Asheville, NC; and M. Palecki and J. Cacciamani
494307.abstract: Extreme rainfall events have serious implications for flash flooding and stormwater drainage design, but understanding of these events is limited by their relative scarcity, the fine spatial scale on which precipitation varies, and instrumentation challenges. The United States Climate Reference Network provides well-shielded observations of both tipping bucket and triple-wire weighing gauge precipitation for 114 sites across the conterminous United States. Differing instrument characteristics and observing capabilities may alter the depiction of intense rainfall events between these instrument types. The weighing gauge measurements show a greater frequency of exceedance of the NOAA Atlas 14 precipitation frequency estimates than the tipping bucket measurements. The distribution of differences in observed precipitation between the two instrument types was analyzed for spatial and temporal homogeneity. Additionally, station conditions for storms where the tipping bucket and weighing gauge showed large discrepancies were investigated. This study highlights the need for community understanding of limitations to tipping bucket observations and the need for corrective factors when studying extreme precipitation events using either tipping bucket networks or conglomerates of networks that are heavily composed of tipping bucket instruments.

494308.title: Evaluating Bias Correction in Radio Occultation Profiles for Hurricane Fiona (2022)
494308.authors: Preston Jackson, UCAR, Boulder, CO; UCAR, Boulder, CO; and H. C. Lin, J. J. Braun, and Y. H. Kuo
494308.abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) Radio Occultation (RO) is a remote sensing technique that uses signals from GNSS satellites, received by Low Earth Orbit satellites like COSMIC-2, to create highly precise vertical profiles of the Earth's atmosphere. RO soundings are valuable for numerical weather prediction because they provide high vertical resolution, all-weather atmospheric data globally, even over remote oceans. However, RO-derived refractivity in the lower troposphere has a well-documented negative bias, especially over subtropical and tropical oceans. This bias comes from atmospheric ducting. Sharp moisture drops and a temperature inversion at the top of the Planetary Boundary Layer trap GNSS signals, causing multiple signal paths to reach the same surface receiver simultaneously. This underestimates refractivity near the surface, and it is severe enough that forecasting systems often just throw this data away entirely. Instead of throwing this data away, Pham et al. (2024) developed a statistical regression method to correct this bias in FORMOSAT-7/COSMIC-2 RO profiles. Their approach combines two regional regression models, one using local spectral width as a predictor and one using temperature and specific humidity, blended using Minimum Variance Estimation and trained on winter-season COSMIC-2 profiles, validated against ECMWF reanalysis. In this research, I evaluate whether that correction actually improves refractivity accuracy in an environment that hasn't been studied much: the pre-genesis period of tropical cyclones, when lower-tropospheric moisture and thermodynamic structure matter most for understanding how storms form. I compared RO profiles across six hurricanes from the 2022 Atlantic season — Fiona, Ian, Julia, Lisa, Gaston, and Nicole — before and after bias correction, during each storm's pre-genesis period. The analysis was structured into three phases. Phase 1 focused on data ingestion and format verification using the Binary Universal Format for Data Representation (BUFR), validated using a single RO sounding from September 9, 2022, near Socorro Island, Mexico, to confirm the extraction of correctly isolated atmospheric refractivity against geometric height. Phase 2 scaled this pipeline to all six storms. I partitioned the dataset into storm-specific subsets and computed a raw refractivity bias — corrected or uncorrected value minus the ECMWF reference value — across the lowest 10 km of the troposphere, where negative refractivity biases are most pronounced. Aggregating across all six hurricanes produced a dataset exceeding 4 million RO data points, each matched between uncorrected, corrected, and ECMWF profiles using a shared timestamp key so only genuinely corresponding soundings were compared. Phase 3 introduced a percent error metric, which normalizes the bias by the magnitude of the ECMWF reference value so the relative severity of the error can be compared across altitudes and storms of differing intensity. When applied to all six storms, the resulting profiles crossed the zero-error baseline at different altitudes for each storm, making it difficult to tell just by looking whether corrected or uncorrected data was actually closer to the ECMWF reference. To resolve this, I calculated mean absolute percent error (MAPE) for each profile, which takes the absolute value of the percent error before averaging so positive and negative deviations cannot cancel out and hide the true error. This showed a consistent pattern across all six storms. Below 6 km, uncorrected MAPE ranged from 1.96% to 2.24%, while corrected MAPE ranged from 3.26% to 3.75%. The uncorrected data was closer to the ECMWF reference than the corrected data for every storm examined: Fiona, Ian, Julia, Lisa, Gaston, and Nicole. The next step was to look at the spatial characteristics of the bias, which meant tracking a specific storm's vortex center over time, not something that can be averaged across storms the way the MAPE analysis was. For this reason, I selected Hurricane Fiona for a focused case study. Isolating Fiona's profile showed that the corrected data did not sit at a constant offset from the ECMWF baseline. Instead, it overshot past zero near 5–6 km, while the uncorrected data stayed relatively flat. Below 5 km, the corrected data swung the opposite direction, pulling even farther from the reference than the uncorrected data. This pattern was also confirmed spatially. Within a 1,000 km radius of Fiona's pre-genesis vortex center, the raw refractivity fields and the delta maps both showed the same thing: uncorrected soundings tracked the ECMWF reference field more closely than corrected soundings, at most sounding locations inside the storm's environment. Taken together, these four lines of evidence — the six-storm MAPE comparison, the Fiona-specific percent error profile, the raw refractivity fields, and the spatial delta maps — point to the same conclusion. For the six tropical cyclones examined, the statistical bias correction developed by Pham et al. (2024) did not improve the accuracy of RO-derived refractivity in the pre-genesis environment. In most cases, it moved the data farther from the ECMWF reference than leaving it uncorrected, the opposite of what the correction is supposed to do. One likely explanation is the regression model's training data. The correction was trained on COSMIC-2 profiles from the winter season, while the storms in this study developed in September, and these two periods have very different atmospheric moisture and thermodynamic conditions in the lower troposphere. The regression models use local spectral width, temperature, and specific humidity as predictors, so a correction trained on winter conditions may not generalize well to the moist, convectively active environments of tropical cyclone pre-genesis. This seasonal mismatch is a plausible, testable explanation for why the correction underperforms here, even though it reduces bias in the original study's own evaluation. Future work should test this directly, by retraining the regression models on data from the same season and region as the storms being studied, rather than a model calibrated for a different time of year. Longer term, the same research team is already developing an AI-based alternative, which may generalize better across seasons and regions. Resolving this discrepancy matters beyond this dataset: improving RO refractivity in the pre-genesis environment is a meaningful step toward better predicting when and where tropical cyclones form, still one of the harder problems in operational forecasting.

494311.title: Evaluation of the Denver Metro/North Front Range NOx Emissions Inventory Using TEMPO
494311.authors: Liji David, Ramboll, Fort Collins, CO; and J. R. Johnson, B. de Foy, T. Shah, M. Rodriguez, and R. Morris
494311.abstract: Nitrogen oxides (NOx) are key precursors for ozone formation in the Denver Metro/North Front Range (DM/NFR) ozone nonattainment area, where complex terrain, mixed urban and oil and gas emissions, biogenic soil emissions, lightning, and episodic fire impacts complicate emissions evaluation. The Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) instrument provides hourly daytime tropospheric nitrogen dioxide (NO2) vertical column densities (VCDs) over North America, creating new opportunities to evaluate NOx emissions inventories at regional and subregional scales. This study combines TEMPO NO₂ retrievals, high-resolution Comprehensive Air Quality Model with Extensions (CAMx) source apportionment modeling, Pandora NO2 VCD observations, and multilinear regression (MLR) to evaluate the 2024 DM/NFR NOx emissions inventory and identify source sectors that warrant further investigation. A summer 2024 Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF)/CAMx modeling platform was developed with nested 12 km, 4 km, and 1.333 km grid resolution domains, with the finest grid focused on the DM/NFR ozone nonattainment area. The platform includes updated model-ready emissions for summer 2024 and CAMx source apportionment for major NOx sectors, including mobile sources, airports, oil and gas, electric generating units (EGUs), non-EGU point sources, biogenic soil NOx, lightning NOx, fires, and other sources. Emissions development for the 1.333 km domain included updated spatial allocation and temporal profiles for key sectors, EGU emissions based on 2024 hourly continuous emissions monitoring data, airport emissions based on Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR) takeoff and landing cycle and cruise emissions, lightning NOx, fire emissions and biogenic emissions from two biogenic emissions models: Biogenic Emission Inventory System (BEIS) and Model of Emissions of Gases and Aerosols from Nature (MEGAN). Episodic fire impacts were also considered because fires can strongly influence modeled NO2 VCDs and ozone during selected periods. TEMPO NO2 retrievals from V03 and V04 were processed for comparison with CAMx and evaluated independently against Pandora NO2 VCD observations in the 1.333 km domain. For the CAMx-TEMPO comparison, CAMx-derived air mass factors (AMFs) were applied to improve consistency between satellite retrievals and modeled NO2 vertical profiles. A key challenge in the V03 retrievals was a known surface pressure issue over complex terrain, which affected the AMF calculation and contributed to lower CAMx-adjusted NO2 VCDs at higher-elevation locations across the domain, including the Denver metropolitan area. This issue was corrected in V04, improving the CAMx-TEMPO comparison and producing clearer urban NO2 enhancement patterns. Pandora comparisons provide an independent check on both TEMPO and CAMx tropospheric NO2 VCDs and help assess whether model-satellite differences are also reflected in ground-based VCD measurements. MLR was applied to relate AMF-adjusted TEMPO NO2 VCDs to source-apportioned CAMx NO2 VCDs and evaluate sector-specific emissions sensitivities. Initial results indicate that the treatment of biogenic soil NOx is important, with BEIS and MEGAN producing different NO2 VCD responses. MEGAN shows a stronger biogenic NOx signal and a clearer daytime pattern over both the urban and plains subdomains, with behavior closer to TEMPO observations during late morning to early afternoon, although MEGAN-derived NO2 VCDs remain higher than TEMPO NO2 VCDs. These results suggest that soil NOx remains a key uncertainty and that the best representation may fall between the BEIS and MEGAN simulations. Initial MLR results also suggest that some non-EGU point source and on-road mobile contributions may be high relative to TEMPO-observed NO2 spatial patterns. Flux divergence analyses provide complementary spatial evidence, including a weaker match for non-EGU point source features. EGU-related signals appear more source-dependent, with larger sources more likely to be evident in TEMPO and smaller or less isolated sources less consistently resolved. These results identify biogenic soil NOx, non-EGU point sources, on-road mobile sources, EGUs, fires, and lightning NOx as sectors warranting further evaluation in the DM/NFR emissions inventory. These analyses demonstrate the value of combining hourly TEMPO NO2 observations, high-resolution source-apportioned CAMx simulations, CAMx-derived AMF recalculation, Pandora comparisons, and regression-based statistical methods for evaluating regional NOx emissions inventories. The study provides a framework for using geostationary satellite observations to diagnose model-satellite differences, identify source sectors requiring additional evaluation, and support future ozone planning efforts in the DM/NFR region.

494314.title: A U-Net Sequence-to-Sequence Framework for Satellite-Based Precipitation Nowcasting: Application to Atmospheric River Events
494314.authors: Sahar Mohsenzadeh Karimi, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and A. Bennett and E. Shamir
494314.abstract: This study develops a deep learning framework for short-term precipitation nowcasting via sequence-to-sequence image-to-image translation applied directly to satellite quantitative precipitation estimates (QPE). Using NOAA/NESDIS SCaMPR QPE fields, which provide 10-minute, ~4 km resolution retrievals well suited to resolving fine-scale rainfall structure, we train a U-Net-based architecture on six antecedent QPE frames to predict the subsequent three time steps (30–90 minute lead times), treating satellite-derived precipitation imagery as both the input and target variables. The framework is benchmarked against persistence and optical-flow baselines, which capture fine-scale structure poorly and degrade quickly with lead time. We apply the framework to landfalling atmospheric river (AR) events in Northern California, evaluating skill as a function of lead time, rainfall intensity, and storm structure, with particular attention to performance during the most extreme events relevant to compound flood hazard. Planned extensions include incorporating data assimilation of additional observation streams and generalizing the framework to Southwestern U.S. precipitation regimes, working toward an operationally relevant, satellite-based AI nowcasting tool for AR-driven hydrological extremes.

494315.title: Modernizing the Next-Generation UFS Weather Model and Navigating the Infrastructure Challenges Ahead
494315.authors: Daniel Perez Sarmiento, NOAA OMD, College Park, MD; and D. Worthen, B. D. Baker II, L. Bernardet, M. Huang, R. L. Jacob, R. Mahajan, D. J. Swales, V. S. Tallapragada, A. Tsay, and J. R. Carley
494315.abstract: The Unified Forecast System (UFS) is foundational to developing a community-based, coupled Earth system modeling framework, with the UFS Weather Model (UFS-WM) at its core. The successful adoption and advancement of the UFS-WM across the diverse U.S. weather enterprise is crucial for realizing improved prediction capabilities. The ongoing effort of integrating the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) dynamical core into the UFS-WM is a significant milestone for the community. This complex integration has acted as a direct catalyst for assessing and modernizing the UFS core modeling infrastructure. Currently, the UFS has a software stack that relies on multiple, overlapping frameworks, a resource demanding top-down testing workflow, and tools that are more focused on operational goals rather than community engagement. We propose an effort to modernize and create a Lean UFS architecture. To achieve the proposed Lean UFS architecture, the modernization strategy centers on three key initiatives: first, assessing and consolidating existing frameworks across the current set of UFS components; second, streamlining library dependencies to reduce the software's footprint and boost portability; and third, shifting the testing framework from top-level regression-based testing towards a more comprehensive unit and subcomponent-level style of testing. Implementing these approaches reduces the technical debt and software footprint, facilitating advances in other areas, such as adoption of GPU architectures and allowing for more rapid research to operations development cycles. Overcoming these core infrastructural barriers is paramount to unlocking the full collaborative potential of the UFS-WM community.

494317.title: Predicting AMOC Strength: A Validation Study of Climate Models and Ocean Reanalysis Products across Atlantic Latitudes
494317.authors: Zoya Sharma, Liberal Arts and Science Academy, Austin, TX; Austin Community College, Austin, TX
494317.abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) transports heat and nutrients from the tropics to the North Atlantic, regulating climate across the northern hemisphere. AMOC collapse could eliminate critical heat source triggering abrupt cooling of Northern Europe and accelerated sea-level rise along the U.S. east coast. As governments begin taking action to prevent destruction from a potential collapse, they require accurate AMOC strength predictions. There are a few methods to predict and reconstruct AMOC strength, including CMIP6 climate models, Ocean Reanalysis Products, and indirect proxies. There are also direct ocean monitoring systems such as the RAPID and OSNAP arrays that monitor ocean circulation across the Atlantic Ocean. This research evaluates the effectiveness of five CMIP6 models in simulating AMOC transport against both RAPID and OSNAP, and three Ocean Reanalyses against RAPID. Additionally, other proxies (sea surface temperature, air-sea heat-flux proxies) are evaluated in a literature review, as these cannot be directly compared with RAPID and OSNAP arrays. The review indicated air-sea heat-fluxes to be more effective than sea surface temperature proxies. Among CMIP6 models tested, MPI-ESM1-2-HR was the most accurate at RAPID. Overall, CMIP6 models performed better against RAPID than OSNAP, with four of the five models underestimating by > 5 Sv at OSNAP. This latitude-dependent bias reveals a structural model deficiency in subpolar water mass formation. Importantly, model bias and correlation skills were decoupled: ACCESS-CM2's smallest bias coincided with weakest variability correlation, while CESM2's larger bias better captured AMOC oscillations – indicating models cannot be selected by single metrics. Critically, Ocean Reanalysis Products achieved 45% lower error than CMIP6 (2.34 vs 4.26 Sv RMSE) indicating that the data-assimilation aspect of Ocean Reanalyses improves their ability to reconstruct AMOC patterns. The research supports a hybrid strategy of using constrained reanalysis products to establish recent AMOC trends and identify model structural flaws, while utilizing CMIP6 ensembles for future projections. The latitude-dependent model performance suggests that regional climate adaptation strategies must account for model skill variations across the Atlantic. Additionally, future research on converting OSNAP’s density driven transport to RAPID ‘s overturning in depth coordinates would be crucial for validating AMOC strength across latitudes.

494319.title: Direct Quantification of Ventilation Impacts on Tropical Cyclone Intensification Rate
494319.authors: Chau Lam Yu, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY; SUNY, Albany, NY
494319.abstract: Ventilation is widely recognized as an important mechanism governing tropical cyclone (TC) intensity, yet existing ventilation theories primarily quantify its impact on the steady-state intensity of a TC and do not provide a direct framework for predicting the associated intensity weakening rate due to reliance on the steady-state assumption of symmetric neutrality. Yu (2026) generalized maximum potential intensity (MPI) theory by relaxing the symmetric-neutrality assumption and showed that the balanced intensity of a TC is determined by the radial gradient of integrated entropy across the eyewall. Within this generalized non-symmetric-neutral framework, the impact of ventilation on TC intensity change can be directly quantified by relating ventilation-induced entropy forcing to changes in the integrated entropy gradient along eyewall absolute angular momentum surfaces. In particular, given the spatial distribution of ventilation forcing, expressed as the rate of change of saturation entropy associated with radial or downdraft ventilation, the TC intensity response timescale emerges naturally from the radial gradient of the integrated ventilation forcing along the eyewall absolute angular momentum surfaces. We evaluate this theoretical prediction using idealized CM1 simulations with prescribed ventilation forcing. For weakening rates below approximately 20 m s-1 h-1, the theoretical framework quantitatively reproduces the simulated TC weakening rates with nearly perfect agreement. At more extreme ventilation forcing, corresponding to weakening rates exceeding approximately 20 m s-1 h-1, the theory increasingly underestimates the simulated weakening rate. This discrepancy arises from the breakdown of the assumption that evaporation of eyewall cloud liquid is sufficiently rapid to maintain saturation of eyewall air parcels. The results suggest that sufficiently strong ventilation can produce a nonlinear enhancement of TC weakening, consistent with steady-state ventilation theory, in which ventilation beyond a critical threshold can no longer be balanced by thermodynamic recovery to sustain a steady ventilated intensity. These results provide a framework for directly quantifying ventilation-induced changes in TC intensification rate and establish a connection between transient intensity evolution and the steady-state limits imposed by ventilation.

494321.title: Characterizing Summertime Volatile Organic Compound Plumes from Waste Management Facilities during the Utah Summer Ozone Study
494321.authors: Maria J. Carter, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and C. Harkins, M. Li, B. C. McDonald, M. M. Coggon, C. Stockwell, I. B. Pollack, N. Schafer, J. Peischl, M. Zucker, C. Womack, C. Warneke, S. S. Brown, and K. Bates
494321.abstract: Waste management facilities, including landfills and wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), are ubiquitous sources of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), yet their emissions remain underrepresented in inventories used for air quality modeling and forecasting. This study characterizes waste sector VOC emissions using proton-transfer-reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometer (PTR-ToF-MS) data collected on the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory (CSL) mobile lab during the 2024 Utah Summer Ozone Study (USOS). Measurements of methane, a known compound emitted from landfills and WWTPs, are used to identify waste sector emission plumes. We characterize waste sector emission profiles using enhancement ratios of VOCs relative to methane, and find that oxygenates (e.g., methanol, ethanol, acetaldehyde) and aromatics (e.g., benzene, toluene) are the most abundantly emitted measured VOCs from both types of waste facilities. Observed waste sector VOCs contributed approximately 2% of total anthropogenic VOCs in Salt Lake and Davis counties. Of the observed VOCs, the majority (>54%) were hazardous air pollutants (HAPs). Estimated waste sector HAP emissions of methanol and benzene for Salt Lake and Davis counties were 9x and 40x higher than the corresponding 2020 National Emissions Inventory (NEI) estimates. A comparison of landfill observations with the GReenhouse gas And Air Pollutants Emissions System (GRA2PES) inventory found that landfill-emitted oxygenated VOCs were underestimated, indicating that further work is required to improve waste sector representation.

494324.title: Smoke Signals: Analyzing Wildfire's Influence on Atmospheric Pollutants over the Greater New York Region
494324.authors: Keana Alianna Beaufort, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. Franchin, R. R. Buchholz, and C. Cho
494324.abstract: Wildfire smoke transported over long distances can significantly worsen urban air quality. However, disentangling fire-driven contributions to existing anthropogenic pollution remains a challenge, particularly in a highly populated, chemically complex region like New York City. This project investigated how wildfire smoke, largely transported from Canadian fires in summer 2025, influenced atmospheric tracers across the Greater New York region. Using in-situ aircraft measurements from the GOTHAAM field campaign (July–August 2025), biomass-burning influence across flights was characterized using established combustion tracers, carbon monoxide (CO) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN), to classify flights as high fire-influenced or low-fire-influenced. NO2 concentrations were then compared between these two regimes, both across the whole sampling region and within distinct sub-regions, to identify whether smoke impacts overlapped with or amplified existing urban emissions. Aircraft-based findings were compared with NO2 retrievals from NASA's TEMPO instrument, a geostationary sensor capable of hourly daytime measurements over North America. Results aimed to clarify where and when wildfire smoke measurably elevated NO2 in the New York region, and whether satellite data could reliably supplement sparse aircraft sampling for tracking smoke-driven air quality changes. Accurately understanding the impact of fires on atmospheric chemistry has implications for forecasting air quality.

494325.title: Shear-Driven Instabilities as the Origin of Multibanded Cloud and Precipitation Structures in an Extratropical Cyclone
494325.authors: Stephen R. Guimond, Hampton University, Hampton, VA
494325.abstract: This paper investigates the dynamics governing multibanded cloud and precipitation structures in extratropical cyclones through a case study from the NASA Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) field campaign. On 1 February 2020, a low pressure system emerged off the North Carolina coast at 1200 UTC, deepening by 7 hPa in 6 h as it accelerated northeast over the Atlantic. High-resolution Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) visible imagery revealed multiple bands of high-reflectance cloud to the north/northeast of the center, along with clusters of convective cells closer to the core. Wavelet analysis identified a dominant multiband wavelength of 30 km and a secondary peak at 15–20 km. Airborne radar measurements from IMPACTS flights showed deep convection near the center and narrow, elevated reflectivity bands linked to the multiband features farther out. Numerical simulations reproduced the multibands, enabling exploration of their dynamical origin. Intrinsic phase speed and polarization relation calculations revealed that, contrary to several previous studies, the dominant multibands were not gravity waves. Instead, the bands were identified as manifestations of inflection-point instability due to the presence of counterrotating secondary circulations and the vertical wind shear profile with low Richardson numbers near the upper-level outflow. Gravity waves were present in the low- to midlevels generated by convection, but they did not account for the strong perturbations in the mid–upper levels. These new scientific insights into the governing dynamics of multibanded structures in extratropical cyclones highlight the role of shear-driven hydrodynamic instabilities.

494331.title: Development of the 2026 El Nino’s Precipitation Patterns in Comparison with Past El Ninos, including the Strong 2015 Even
494331.authors: Robert F. Adler, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; and G. Gu
494331.abstract: The evolution of the current 2026 El Nino is described in terms of its precipitation anomaly patterns and with comparison to previous El Nino’s during the last 40 years. Comparisons will be made to an overall El Nino composite consisting of the seven previous events, with a specific one-to-one comparison with the 2015 El Nino event, the strongest of the previous events and having roughly the same seasonal development evolution. These comparisons will be done using the Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) Version 3.3 Climate Data Record (CDR) analysis product, extended in time for the last few months with an Interim CDR (ICDR) to bring the record up to “real time” (about 10 days after the end of the month). Preliminary analysis through July 2026 indicates a rapid switch from La Nina rainfall anomaly patterns dominating the tropics early in the year to El Nino-type patterns across the tropical Pacific, Maritime Continent and South America regions as the RNino3.4 SST index went from negative to +1.4K in July. The spatial correlation of July’s tropical (40N-40S) rainfall anomaly pattern to an El Nino composite for the month of June is already +0.4, increasing rapidly from significant negative values a few months before. The current (July 2026) peak positive and negative anomalies in the tropics are similar in magnitude to those from 2015 at a similar stage of that strong event. An ENSO Precipitation Index (ESPI) used to measure the Maritime Continent to Central Pacific rainfall gradient has also already jumped to previous El Nino values in July. At the time of the conference we will present results through December 2026 and evaluate if the forecast strong 2026-2027 El Nino has continued to develop and how the resulting global precipitation anomaly patterns through December compare to the previous El Nino events both in magnitude and evolution.

494332.title: A Multi-National Multi-Sector Partnership to Re-Establish Typhoon Reconnaissance In the Western North Pacific Region
494332.authors: Kate Fossell, NSF NCAR, SUN PRAIRIE, WI; and E. D. Joseph, W. C. Lee, K. Tsuboki, S. K. Park, C. C. Wu, C. A. Wolff, and K. Golden
494332.abstract: The West-Northern Pacific (WNP) region is prone to impacts from landfalling typhoons that affect daily life and safety. Coastal regions of Japan, Korea, China, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the Philippines are densely populated and vulnerable to typhoon impacts, thus the prediction of these storms is critical for emergency management, government policy-making, and military operations in the region, including the U.S. Robust observations of the storm and environment are vital for skillful prediction of typhoon track and intensity. Routine aircraft typhoon reconnaissance in the region ended in 1987, and since then the WNP region has relied on satellite-based products to estimate typhoon tracks and intensity. The lack of in situ observations from dropsondes, airborne Doppler radar, and other advanced instruments in the region has led to disparities in intensity assignments among operational centers and hindered the accuracy of typhoon predictions. To address these gaps and foster international cooperation, leadership from NOAA and NSF NCAR began spearheading a collaboration in 2023 involving the U.S., Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan. This partnership explores re-establishing operational aircraft reconnaissance to tackle shared forecasting challenges, including tracking, intensity, rapid intensification, and heavy precipitation. This presentation provides an overview of the initiative goals, the multi-sector multi-national partnership structures to facilitate current and future coordinated international activities, and summarizes the 2025 and 2026 pilot studies using existing resources in the region.

494335.title: On the Relaxation of the Symmetric Neutrality Assumption of the Potential Intensity Theory of Tropical Cyclones
494335.authors: Chau Lam Yu, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY
494335.abstract: The potential intensity (PI) theory of tropical cyclones (TCs) provides a reasonable estimate of the maximum intensity a TC can achieve in a quiescent environment. Traditional PI theory relies on the symmetric neutrality (SN) assumption, under which surfaces of absolute angular momentum (M) are parallel to saturation entropy (s∗) surfaces within the saturated eyewall updraft. When symmetric neutrality is not satisfied, however, previous studies did not provide quantitative description on how s∗ constrains the vortex structure and, consequently, the balanced low-level wind intensity. In this study, I revisit PI theory without imposing the symmetric neutrality assumption and identify a new equipartition principle between the mechanical and thermal energies of a balanced vortex. This energetic principle provides a generalized vmax equation that accounts for both balanced and unbalanced contributions to the maximum tangential wind within the TC boundary layer. The generalized vmax equation naturally extends the traditional PI formulation from the SN state to the non-symmetrically neutral (non-SN) state. Specifically, under non-SN conditions, it is the gradient of s∗ with respect to M at fixed temperature (T) that constrains the vortex structure and determines the balanced component of vmax. Comparison with axisymmetric simulations demonstrates that the generalized vmax equation accurately quantifies the contributions of different physical processes to vmax throughout the rapid intensification period. These results provide new insights into the dynamics of TC intensification. First, they demonstrate that under non-SN and non-steady-state conditions, the s∗ gradient must be evaluated at fixed T to remain consistent with balanced vortex dynamics. Second, they reveal that this fixed-T s∗ gradient exhibits a distinctive, approximately linear vertical structure throughout the free troposphere during TC intensification, with large negative value of s∗ gradient near the tropopause.
