This result indicates that the development of a deep tall vortex that reaches tropopause preconditions the onset of TC rapid intensification. Furthermore, the non-uniform s∗ gradient provides evidence that the SN assumption does not hold during this stage of TC rapid intensification.

494336.title: Convective Organization in African Easterly Waves Observed During the NAMMA and CPEX-CV Field Campaigns
494336.authors: Delián Colón-Burgos, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. M. Bell
494336.abstract: Fundamental questions remain about where and when convection will occur within African easterly waves. In this study, we aim to better understand the dynamical processes that govern moist convective organization at the meso-alpha scale in tropical easterly waves using NASA airborne field campaigns and satellite observations. We employ the SAMURAI 3D variational analysis technique in a vortex-centric approach, integrating the fifth generation ECMWF (ERA5) reanalysis and research aircraft observations from 20 African easterly wave (AEW) cases sampled during the NASA African Monsoon Multidisciplinary Analyses (NAMMA) in 2006 and Convective Processes Experiment-Cabo Verde (CPEX-CV) in 2022. Infrared satellite imagery is used to obtain the frequency of occurrence within the wave of clear air, shallow/moderate convection, and deep convection relative to a potential vorticity (PV) centroid location. We identified four clusters of organized deep convection denoted as minimal deep, southern, southwestern, and widespread. Composites of the dynamical fields from the variational analyses show that high PV and relative humidity (RH) at mid-levels were approximately co-located with regions of low-level convergence and more frequent deep convection, particularly for the southwestern and widespread clusters, which had the highest frequencies of deep convection. Waves with a higher frequency of deep convection are characterized by stronger PV and higher RH at mid-levels compared to waves with a lower frequency of deep convection. The results suggest that improved understanding of the causal relationships between PV and RH and deep convection in easterly waves can lead to future forecast improvements of convective organization and tropical cyclogenesis.

494337.title: Coupled Development of the 2026-2027 El Niño: Historical Analogs of Ocean-Atmosphere Evolution
494337.authors: Terachet Rojrachsombat, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and S. Nigam and A. Ruiz-Barradas
494337.abstract: The 2026-27 El Niño has developed rapidly from La Niña conditions during boreal winter 2025-26. By July 2026, a recent downwelling Kelvin wave had deepened the thermocline in the eastern Pacific, while low-level westerly wind anomalies extended across the western and central equatorial Pacific. This rapid transition raises a simple question: when two El Niño events evolve similarly at the sea surface, how similar are the subsurface ocean and atmospheric conditions that accompany them? We first identify historical SST analogs using phase-aligned equatorial-Pacific longitude-time fields from NOAA ERSSTv6. Scaled relative SST anomalies are used for the main comparison. Historical events are ranked from their spatial pattern and temporal evolution using pattern correlation, field error, month-to-month change, and east-west gradients. With observations through July 2026, 1997-98 ranks first among 21 historical El Niño episodes in the catalog, followed by 1972-73 and 2023-24. A separate same-stage comparison of Niño-region structure gives a different ordering and places 1997-98 much lower. The 1997-98 comparison is also physically interesting because its onset was linked to intraseasonal atmospheric forcing and eastward-propagating equatorial Kelvin waves. Ongoing analysis extends the same framework to upper-ocean heat content and recharge, thermocline structure, equatorial zonal wind stress, and tropical convection. For each field, the 2026-27 similarity is compared with the distribution of same-stage similarities among historical El Niño events. This places the leading analog in historical context and tests whether its similarity is unusual or simply the closest match in a small sample. Cross-variable agreement provides a measure of whether one historical event remains a useful analog across the coupled ocean-atmosphere system. The analysis will also incorporate the late-2026 growth and early winter state of the event. If 1997-98 remains close across SST, upper-ocean state, winds, and convection, then the two events developed similarly through several parts of the coupled system. If the rankings separate, the analysis can identify where and when the resemblance breaks down. The 2026-27 event may also resemble different historical events in different parts of the system. These outcomes test how much information an evolving SST pattern contains about the underlying climate system, and how useful a single historical analog remains as El Niño develops. Understanding where historical analogs hold or break down may therefore help determine when past El Niño events are useful guides to the regional climate impacts of a developing event.

494339.title: Withdrawn: Seasonal Prediction Skill and Predictability of Physical and Biogeochemical Variables in the Caribbean Using the MOM6-COBALT-NWA12 Forecasting System
494339.authors: Milo Haniel Soto Pérez, GFDL, Aguada, PR; GFDL, Princeton, NJ; and J. Y. Luo, G. Negrete-García, and A. C. Ross
494339.abstract: Seasonal ocean forecasts can provide valuable information for marine resource management, fisheries, conservation, and blue economy planning in the Caribbean. Their usefulness, however, depends on the ability of forecasting systems to represent both physical ocean conditions and the biogeochemical processes that support marine ecosystems. This study evaluates seasonal prediction skill and predictability of physical and biogeochemical variables across Caribbean Sea ecoregions using the high-resolution MOM6-COBALT-NWA12 forecasting system. Retrospective 12-month forecasts initialized quarterly and spanning 1994–2023 were analyzed for sea surface temperature, sea surface salinity, bottom temperature, nitrate, phosphate, bottom oxygen, surface chlorophyll, and net primary production. Forecast performance and predictability were quantified across multiple lead times using the detrended anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC). Physical variables were additionally evaluated against available observational datasets to characterize forecast skill, while comparisons with corresponding model analyses were used to assess predictability. Results reveal substantial differences in seasonal prediction skill and predictability among variables and forecast lead times. Physical variables generally retain useful skill over longer lead times, whereas biogeochemical variables exhibit greater spatial and temporal variability. Detrended analyses further demonstrate that long-term trends can substantially influence conventional skill estimates, highlighting the importance of separating trend-related agreement from interannual predictability. These results improve understanding of physical and marine ecosystem predictability in the Caribbean and help identify where seasonal forecasting systems provide useful predictive information, supporting continued development of ocean and biogeochemical prediction capabilities for ecosystem management, conservation, and NOAA’s environmental prediction mission.

494340.title: From Source to Transport: Multi-Sensor Characterization of Black Summer Wildfire Aerosol and Its Representation in CESM2
494340.authors: Jennifer D. Small Griswold, University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, HI; and C. S. McCluskey
494340.abstract: The 2019–2020 Australian Black Summer fires produced an exceptional amount of smoke that was transported across the Southern Hemisphere, substantially perturbing regional and remote aerosol loading with potential impacts on radiation, clouds, and climate. Accurately representing these effects in Earth system models first requires models to reproduce the magnitude, spatial extent, vertical distribution, and evolution of the wildfire aerosol plume. Previous analysis of the Black Summer fires revealed substantial differences between satellite-observed aerosol optical depth (AOD) and simulations from the Community Earth System Model version 2 (CESM2), with the model failing to reproduce both the magnitude and spatial extent of the observed plume. Here, we use a complementary suite of satellite observations to characterize the Black Summer aerosol plume and diagnose processes contributing to these model–observation discrepancies. We first place the Black Summer event within the context of the long-term satellite record to distinguish the extreme wildfire-driven perturbation from typical austral summer aerosol conditions. MODIS Dark Target–Deep Blue (DTDB) AOD is used to characterize the magnitude and horizontal distribution of aerosol loading, while OMI ultraviolet aerosol index provides complementary information on the presence and evolution of absorbing aerosol. CALIOP observations provide constraints on aerosol vertical structure and subtype, including the occurrence and altitude of smoke and dust layers. We then focus on the evolution of the Black Summer plume during December 2019–January 2020 using higher-information-content observations. TROPOMI measurements of absorbing aerosol and carbon monoxide provide complementary constraints on smoke transport and the evolution of fire-influenced air masses. MISR multi-angle observations are used to constrain near-source plume height and aerosol spatial structure, while CALIOP profiles characterize the vertical distribution of smoke during downwind transport. MODIS AOD provides broader spatial context for the magnitude and extent of the evolving plume, and satellite fire observations provide constraints on the timing and intensity of wildfire emissions. These observational constraints are evaluated alongside CESM2 simulations to determine when and where discrepancies in the simulated Black Summer plume emerge. By separately examining fire activity, plume injection height, atmospheric transport, aerosol loading, vertical distribution, and downwind evolution, we investigate whether CESM2 biases are most consistent with errors in wildfire emissions, vertical injection, transport, aerosol removal, or aerosol optical properties. This process-oriented evaluation provides a framework for identifying the mechanisms limiting CESM2's representation of extreme wildfire aerosol events and, ultimately, for improving estimates of their aerosol–radiation and aerosol–cloud–climate impacts.

494342.title: Structuring Science for Integration: Designing Human Systems for Earth System Discovery
494342.authors: Jadwiga H. Richter, NSF NCAR, Longmont, CO; and D. Colgrove, M. Fowler, and S. Kamali
494342.abstract: The most consequential Earth system challenges do not adhere to disciplinary, institutional, or organizational boundaries. Yet most scientific institutions remain structured around them. As our scientific questions become increasingly interconnected—spanning physical processes, spatial and temporal scales, observations, modeling, prediction, and societal impacts—scientific progress depends not only on new tools and technologies, but also on how we organize people to work together. This presentation explores the deliberate design of human systems for integrative science, drawing on experience from NSF NCAR’s Earth System Predictability Across Timescales (ESPAT) initiative, team science literature, and principles from systems engineering. Rather than organizing around individual disciplines, models, or other traditional structures , ESPAT begins with grand scientific challenges that inherently require multiple forms of expertise. Interdisciplinary working groups then bring together researchers across institutions and agencies around shared science targets, with structures designed to enable connection, distributed leadership, and community ownership. Experience from ESPAT and related convergence efforts suggests that successful integration requires more than assembling diverse expertise. Teams need shared purpose and vision, clearly defined but flexible roles, boundary-spanning individuals who actively connect communities, mechanisms for sustained interaction, psychological safety, and pathways that allow leadership and ownership to evolve as initiatives mature. As Earth system science increasingly tackles coupled, multiscale problems, we should treat the organization of science itself as a design problem. By intentionally organizing teams around the problems we seek to solve—rather than the disciplines and institutions we inherited—we can create environments in which collaboration becomes more than coordination and where genuinely new science has the space to emerge.

494345.title: Screening and Predicting Global Solar and Wind Energy Investment Potential Accounting for Drought and Surplus
494345.authors: Mengjie Zhang, Columbia University, New York, NY; Columbia University, New York, NY; and A. Nayak and U. Lall
494345.abstract: As climate-dependent wind and solar energy account for a growing share of power systems, climate variability is creating new challenges for energy security by causing prolonged periods of renewable energy deficits and surpluses. Long-duration deficits can reduce the reliability of electricity supply, increase dependence on thermoelectric generation, and lead to contract penalties. Persistent surpluses can result in curtailment, lower electricity prices, and revenue losses. These risks can become more severe when renewable energy deficits occur simultaneously across regions or across wind and solar resources. Understanding when and where these events occur, how they vary across space and time, and whether they can be predicted in advance is therefore important for building reliable and climate-resilient energy systems. We develop a global framework to characterize and predict climate-driven renewable energy risks. First, a seasonally varying threshold is defined at each location to represent reliable and contractible wind and solar energy production. Deficit and surplus events are identified relative to this threshold and characterized by their cumulative magnitude and duration. This event-based representation allows us to distinguish short-term fluctuations from persistent renewable energy deficits and surpluses that are more relevant to energy system reliability and financial risk. We analyze their spatial patterns globally and examine the co-variability of wind and solar energy. This analysis identifies regions where wind–solar complementarity can reduce the severity of renewable energy deficits, as well as regions where simultaneous deficits can amplify energy security risks. We further investigate whether these renewable energy risks can be predicted using large-scale climate information. A non-homogeneous Hidden Markov Model (NHMM) is applied to sea surface temperature (SST) fields to identify latent climate states associated with different patterns of global climate variability. We then assess the predictability of renewable energy deficits and surpluses for different calendar months and climate states at seasonal lead times. The results show statistically significant predictability across multiple key regions, months, and climate states. The identified climate states provide information beyond individual climate indices by representing broader spatial patterns of SST variability. We also find evidence that wind and solar resources can either complement each other or experience amplified deficits under different climate conditions. Overall, this study connects the global characterization of renewable energy deficit and surplus risks with their seasonal predictability. By identifying where persistent renewable energy shortages are likely to occur and when their risks may be anticipated, the framework provides climate information that can support energy system planning before high-risk periods occur. These results can support forward contract design, predictive grid management, renewable energy investment and risk assessment, and broader strategies to strengthen energy security and system resilience under climate variability and extreme events.

494346.title: What Modulates Vorticity in the Atmospheric Surface Layer?
494346.authors: Robby M. Frost, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. Bodine, J. Gebauer, M. D. Flournoy, M. Coniglio, R. A. Saba, S. T. Salesky, and T. Y. Yu
494346.abstract: Recent numerical simulations and observations have highlighted turbulent coherent structures in the atmospheric surface layer (ASL) as potential seeds for supercell tornadogenesis (Markowski, 2024; Gebauer et al., 2026). These structures, colloquially referred to as “vorticity worms”, manifest as alternating streaks of positive and negative vertical vorticity in the lowest 100–200 m AGL in sheared planetary boundary layers (PBLs). Though there is not yet direct observational evidence of vorticity worms facilitating tornadogenesis in supercells, their potential impact warrants further investigation into what larger–scale features control vorticity in the ASL. Thus, we pose the question: How does the magnitude, coherence, and depth of ASL horizontal and vertical vorticity vary under different PBL geostrophic wind profiles? To investigate this, we perform large eddy simulations of the PBL with different geostrophic wind magnitudes using Cloud Model 1 and compare mean ASL vorticity profiles. We employ the wavelet transform (Rinoshika and Rinoshika, 2020; Frost et al., 2026) and the roll factor (Salesky et al., 2017; Frost et al., 2025) to analyze the wavelength and rotational symmetry of ASL vorticity, respectively. Additionally, we compare these results to observations by the MetroWeather Coherent Doppler Lidar (Hsu et al., 2026), which has performed low–elevation plan position indicator (PPI) scans collocated with twice daily soundings for much of the past two years. Connecting ASL vorticity to larger PBL conditions will give insight into which supercell environments support the existence of vorticity worms, and thus, potentially larger tornadic potential.

494349.title: Poisson Total Variation Lidar Retrievals with the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers
494349.authors: Bryce Garby, NSF NCAR, Center Green Dr., CO; and M. Hayman and J. Thayer
494349.abstract: Atmospheric lidar instruments observe a diverse dynamic range of signals across a variety of atmospheric features, ranging from dense low lying clouds to weak elevated aerosol layers and clear air. This range of features produces lidar signals which vary enormously in amplitude. Furthermore, features of interest often exhibit highly dynamic structure, making it critical to observe with high sensitivity and resolution. Poisson Total Variation (PTV) is a state-of-the-art lidar retrieval technique, originally developed as an image reconstruction method, which uses penalized maximum likelihood estimation in conjunction with a forward model to solve the retrieval while simultaneously denoising. PTV dynamically balances signal strength with resolution, making it well suited for the diverse features seen in the atmosphere. However, for extremely large signal dynamic ranges, the existing SPIRAL (Sparse Poisson Intensity Reconstruction ALgorithm) optimization procedure struggles to properly account for the curvature of the solution space, and the algorithm can either stall in areas of weaker signal (clear air or aerosols), or diverge in areas of high signal (clouds). This work presents a novel, alternative approach for solving the PTV estimation problem based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm, which realizes benefits in convergence in the presence of a large signal dynamic range. The ADMM approach for PTV lidar retrievals splits the combined objective function, consisting of Poisson Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) and Total Variation (TV) into two problems. The state is allowed to differ between the NLL and TV terms, however a constraint is added in the form of an augmented Lagrangian to penalize differences between the NLL and TV step solves. This results in a single, equivalent, shared solution at convergence. By splitting the NLL and TV problems, the curvature of the NLL surface can be described with quadratic approximation using a diagonal Hessian, in contrast to the scalar curvature used in the conventional PTV framework. The new approach has been demonstrated with observations from NSF NCAR’s next generation diode-laser High Spectral Resolution Lidar (HSRL), the ADiHSRL (Airborne Diode-Laser-Based HSRL), as well as with the MicroPulse DIALs (MPDs). Improvements in convergence speed and accuracy of the converged solution have been shown.This work introduces the new method and describes the theory and its benefits in depth.

494352.title: Capturing Extreme Weather Dynamics: Legacy Systems vs. Phased Array Radar
494352.authors: Stephen R. Guimond, Hampton University, Hampton, VA; and T. Mackey, A. N. Perez, and S. M. S. Karim
494352.abstract: Radar observations of extreme weather across the United States rely heavily on the NOAA National Weather Service’s legacy NEXRAD network, while airborne observations have traditionally employed systems such as the NOAA Tail Doppler Radar. Although these conventional radar systems provide extensive coverage and reliable observations, their spatial and temporal resolutions are typically insufficient to resolve the fine-scale structures that govern the evolution of many high-impact weather phenomena. Hazards such as flash flooding, severe wind gusts and tornadoes are strongly influenced by processes occurring at spatial and temporal scales associated with atmospheric turbulence that are not adequately resolved by these legacy observing systems. Resolving coherent turbulent structures within extreme weather systems therefore requires observations with substantially finer spatial and temporal resolution. This presentation evaluates the practical benefits of such observations through direct comparisons of high-resolution airborne (IWRAP) and ground-based (Skyler II) phased array radar measurements with those obtained from legacy NOAA radar systems. Comparisons are conducted across a range of extreme weather environments, including the hurricane boundary layer and the full lifecycle of deep convection, from initiation through growth and maturation to decay. These observations provide a framework for quantifying how enhanced radar resolution improves the characterization of fine-scale atmospheric structures and their evolution within high-impact weather systems.

494353.title: JEDI-based Multi-Resolution and Multiscale EnVar to Improve Forecasting of the Predecessor Rain Event Associated with Hurricane Helene (2024)
494353.authors: Erin A. Jones, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and X. Wang
494353.abstract: In ensemble-based data assimilation for numerical weather prediction, improving uncertainty estimation of the prior forecast, either through increasing the ensemble size or increasing the resolution of some or all ensemble members, is often associated with large computational costs. Prior work has aimed to address the cost limitation in ensemble resolution by introducing a multi-resolution ensemble (MR-ENS), which contains some members at high-resolution and others at a lower resolution. The MR-ENS method allows for retention of much of the smaller scale correlation structure at a substantially reduced cost compared with a purely high-resolution ensemble. Additionally, covariance localization can be applied differently for each resolution ensemble in the MR-ENS method. For example, prior work has applied a smaller localization radius for the high-resolution ensemble. Using this smaller radius for the high-resolution ensemble allows for the proper update of smaller-scale features. However, it ignores that the high-resolution ensemble also contains useful large-scale information since it reduces background error correlations at larger distances. Therefore, applying a scale-dependent localization (SDL) method in MR-ENS, could allow for more optimal correction of larger scales in the high-resolution ensemble. This study develops a method to utilize SDL with MR-ENS (SDL-MR-ENS) in a JEDI-based global data assimilation system. The combined multi-resolution and multiscale framework is applied to a case study of the predecessor rain event (PRE) associated with Hurricane Helene (2024). The study compares SDL-MR-ENS to a pure MR-ENS to determine the impact on the forecasted location and intensity of the PRE. Overall, SDL-MR-ENS creates a more consistently improved forecast of the location and intensity of the PRE compared to the pure MR-ENS framework. Results indicate that the improvement is associated with the ability of SDL to better analyze large-scale features, such as midtropospheric troughs and ridges, which contribute to the synoptic-scale forcing for the event.

494356.title: Hemispheric Cyclone Cloud Asymmetry Constrains Radiative Forcing
494356.authors: Grant Schlaff, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; Univ. of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and D. McCoy
494356.abstract: The effective radiative forcing due to aerosol-cloud interactions (ERFaci) remains a persistent uncertainty in interpreting the historical record and constraining future Earth system behavior. The major challenge is that the cloud changes must be inferred without having direct observations from the pre-industrial (PI) era. The southern hemisphere can act as a proxy for this unpolluted environment. Here, we examine how the north-south asymmetry in extratropical clouds across a perturbed parameter ensemble (PPE) relates to the difference in clouds between PI and present-day (PD). The northern and southern hemispheres have substantially different meteorology, making a direct comparison between the two difficult. To account for differences between hemispheres, we take advantage of extratropical marine cyclones. We argue that these storms are a natural laboratory to study how microphysical properties impact cloudiness in the context of synoptically enforced precipitation rate. Across the PPE, the hemispheric difference in the liquid water path (LWP) in the PD covaries with the change in the global mean LWP between PI and PD. Examination of the model processes across the PPE confirms that the hemispheric contrast in the cyclone LWP is controlled by similar processes that control the PI-PD change in LWP. We find that microwave radiometer observations of PD hemispheric contrast constrain the plausible range of PI to PD change in LWP to 1.28 ± 0.46 g m-2 and propagate to an ERFaci of -0.83 ± 0.52 W m-2.

494360.title: Air Mass Trajectories Moving into Colorado: What Do Backward Trajectory Models Say About Changes in Precipitation in Colorado?
494360.authors: Dylan Nahsjun, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and K. Friedrich and A. C. Winters
494360.abstract: Examining if and how atmospheric sources of precipitation in eastern and western Colorado have evolved over the last 75 years in Colorado is important to better understand the long-term changes in precipitation within the state. In our study, we determine where the most efficient moisture pathways moving into Colorado from the Pacific Ocean or Gulf of Mexico are located and how they have shifted during that period. We link the air mass trajectory pathways to integrated water vapor transport (IVT), precipitation, and other meteorological variables between the moisture source and Colorado. Air mass trajectories were derived from NOAA’s Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Integrated Trajectory (HYSPLIT) backward trajectory model using NCEP-NCAR Reanalysis 1 predictions, while the corresponding IVT values were calculated using the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts’ reanalysis ERA5 climatology data set, with the data from both ranging from 1948 to 2023. We observed the role of air mass trajectories of varying characteristics, such as ones featuring a significant decrease in IVT from when the air mass makes landfall on the West Coast to when it arrives in Colorado for different scenarios, including high IVT events and extreme precipitation events. This enables us to see which area in the Pacific Ocean is most influential under different regimes and which sources have become more prominent over time.

494362.title: Toward Standardized Methods and Metrics for Assessing Thermodynamic Profiler Performance: A MicroPulse DIAL (MPD) Case Study
494362.authors: Matthew Hayman, NSF NCAR, Center Green Dr., CO; and R. A. Stillwell, S. M. Spuler, and B. Garby
494362.abstract: A persistent challenge in atmospheric profiling is the lack of a standardized approach for evaluating and comparing instrument performance. Currently, reported metrics often reflect best-case scenarios or aggregate statistics dominated by canonical, easily forecast scenes. Furthermore, true performance is often obscured: maximum processed altitude is frequently cited as an effective range regardless of actual data availability, and reported capture resolutions often ignore the coarser effective resolution of processed output. Establishing rigorous, objective methods to assess what instruments truly deliver is essential for advancing observational capabilities. To address this, we present progress toward an instrument-agnostic methodology for evaluating thermodynamic profilers using a robust dataset from a summer/fall 2026 engineering deployment of four MicroPulse DIAL (MPD) systems at the DOE ARM Southern Great Plains (SGP) Central Facility. The MPD is a diode-laser-based lidar measuring absolute humidity, temperature, and aerosol optical properties via collocated water vapor DIAL, oxygen DIAL, and HSRL channels. The SGP deployment features collocated infrared and microwave radiometers, Raman lidar, and daily radiosonde launches, providing a rich basis for instrument cross-validation and assessment. This presentation details our progress in leveraging this diverse dataset to define a standardized, objective set of reportable metrics. By moving beyond idealized performance claims toward field-validated, directly comparable assessments, we aim to establish a rigorous framework applicable across all profiling instrument types.

494367.title: Revisiting the Extended Similarity Theory for Long-Lived and Nocturnal Stable Boundary Layers
494367.authors: Inanc Senocak, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA; and K. Chand and C. N. Xiao
494367.abstract: Monin–Obukhov similarity theory (MOST) and its associated flux-profile relationships form the backbone of surface-flux parameterizations used in numerical weather prediction (NWP) and large-eddy simulation (LES) of the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL). Classical MOST, however, is formulated for stationary, horizontally homogeneous conditions and does not explicitly account for the ambient stratification of the free atmosphere or Earth’s rotation — both of which strongly influence the ABL structure. Zilitinkevich and Esau (2007) proposed an extended version of MOST that addresses these limitations through a composite length scale, L*, which combines contributions from surface heat and momentum fluxes (via the classical Obukhov length), ambient stratification, and Coriolis forcing in a weighted manner. This composite scale is then used, under a local-scaling hypothesis, to parameterize the dimensionless gradients of velocity (φm) and potential temperature (φh). However, this extended framework has not been systematically validated against high-fidelity turbulence data for long-lived and nocturnal SABLs. To assess this framework against high-fidelity turbulence data, we present direct numerical simulations (DNS) of long-lived SABLs in which surface cooling and a constant, uniform ambient stratification act independently on the flow field. By contrasting cases of weak and strong ambient stratification at ReD = 900 against a nocturnal SABL without ambient stratification, we examine how these two stability mechanisms jointly modify the similarity theory and scaling relationships that are crucial for parameterizing turbulent mixing in the SABL. Here, we assess the extended similarity theory under surface-layer scaling, rather than the local scaling hypothesis originally adopted. Our analysis shows that the extended MOST framework performs well for the dimensionless velocity gradient φm, with DNS profiles collapsing satisfactorily onto the composite stability parameter z/L* across all three cases. This result is significant on its own, as it demonstrates that incorporating ambient stratification and Coriolis effects into the length scale meaningfully improves the representation of the momentum field relative to classical MOST, which typically struggles in long-lived and strongly stable regimes. Unlike the momentum field, the picture for potential temperature is more nuanced. When applied directly with the originally proposed empirical constants and functional form, the extended framework fails to adequately represent φh — consistent with the long-standing difficulty of parameterizing scalar gradients in stable conditions, where existing similarity functions are known to be less robust than their momentum counterparts. To address this, we perform a sensitivity analysis on the weighting of the different physical contributions (heat/momentum flux, stratification, rotation) within the composite length scale L*. Recalibrating these empirical constants under surface-layer scaling substantially improves the collapse of φh profiles onto z/L*, particularly within the region where similarity theory is expected to hold. Motivated by this recalibrated collapse of DNS data, we propose a new similarity relationship for φh expressed as a cubic function of the dimensionless composite stability parameter z/L*. This functional form captures the observed trend in the DNS data notably well across all three cases, offering a marked improvement over both the classical MOST scalar function and the original formulation of Zilitinkevich and Esau. The cubic relationship suggests that the interplay between ambient stratification, rotation, and surface fluxes introduces a higher-order nonlinearity in the scalar field’s response to stability that is not captured by the simpler forms traditionally used for φh. Beyond the flux-gradient relationships, the composite similarity parameter z/L* is further used to evaluate turbulent Prandtl number (Prt) profiles obtained from the DNS. Vertical profiles of Prt exhibit a slight decreasing trend with increasing z/L*, though not to a degree that challenges the common assumption of a constant Prt within the surface layer. Nevertheless, this approximately constant value shows a clear dependence on ambient stratification strength, increasing from Prt ≈ 0.82 in the nocturnal case to Prt ≈ 0.90 in the long-lived SABL with the strongest ambient stratification. This systematic shift indicates that ambient stratification exerts a clear influence on turbulent Prandtl number in long-lived SABLs, distinguishing it from the neutral or weakly stable predictions typically assumed in existing closure schemes. These results suggest that turbulence closure models for scalar mixing would benefit from explicitly accounting for ambient stratification effects, rather than relying on a single universal Prt or on local stability parameters such as the gradient Richardson number alone. Overall, our results indicate that the extended MOST framework, once properly recalibrated for surface-layer scaling, has strong potential to represent both momentum and scalar dimensionless gradients in long-lived and nocturnal SABLs — where accurate scalar-flux parameterization has historically been particularly elusive. The excellent collapse of φh over the surface-layer region, combined with the proposed cubic similarity function and the demonstrated sensitivity of the turbulent Prandtl number to ambient stratification suggest a revision of closure relationships for scalar transport in NWP and LES models, particularly for conditions dominated by strong and persistent stratification.

494368.title: Ground-Level Radio Frequency Emission Survey at K- and V-bands
494368.authors: Albin Gasiewski, University of Colorado at Boulder, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and M. Hurowitz, D. Baatarkhuyag, L. McAlexander, D. Orthel, M. Marques, R. Belter, A. Venkitasubramony, M. Bhat, D. Kraft, O. Montoya, S. McKee, and D. B. Kunkee
494368.abstract: Radio frequency interference into key bands that are uniquely suited for passive radiometric observations of the atmosphere present critical challenges to satellite weather forecasting. The CU Boulder Radio Frequency Emission (RFE) survey is an effort to understand the environment of radio spectrum emissions occurring in the U.S. that might either currently or in the future be affecting our nation's satellite weather forecast capabilities. Currently, much of the information used in numerical weather forecasts is obtained from passive microwave satellite imaging sounders that measure extremely faint thermal signals radiated by the earth’s surface and atmosphere in the microwave portion of the spectrum. Frequencies of greatest relevance and current risk fall in the water vapor and oxygen bands of 23.6-24 and 50-58 GHz (respectively). These bands provide unique sensitivity to maritime (including near coastal) humidity and global temperature. Passive sounder channels can be corrupted by small amounts of human-caused radiation emitted into these bands (as low as –159 dBm in a 1 MHz bandwidth for ~10 mK antenna temperature error), resulting in either antenna temperature data having to be discarded or (worse) the incorporation of erroneous antenna temperature data that that reduces weather forecast accuracy. The CU RFE survey uses state-of-art scanning microwave radiometers integrated into a vehicular platform (the CET Mobile Spectrum Laboratory, or MSL) to measure the antenna temperature spectrum in these key radio bands. The MSL permits continuous enroute scanning and acquisition of thermally calibrated radio emission spectra at ground level in PPI mode. Measurements are beginning to be made within several urban areas along with the less populated corridors in between them during road campaigns designed to sample a representative portion of CONUS. Survey excursions commenced in July 2026 with a focus on areas in Colorado. The near-surface data will be used to assess the current and future risks to weather satellite forecasts that are used regularly for health, safety, commerce, and defense, along with the development of radio frequency interference detection and mitigation algorithms for use on future passive microwave sounders. The survey is being conducted by the CU Center for Environmental Technology (CET) with the support of Weather Stream, Inc. and the National Science Foundation’s SpectrumX engineering research center.

494370.title: Retrofitting a Weather and Climate course to be Digitally ADA Compliant: Challenges and Unknowns
494370.authors: Matthew A. Lazzara, Madison Area Technical College, Madison, WI; Madison Area Technical College, Madison, WI
494370.abstract: As of 26 April 2027, there are requirements for all forward-facing materials from public entities (e.g. state and local government, educational institutions, etc.) ensure web content, mobile/computer applications, educational materials, etc. meet Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The requirements ensure that these applications and materials do not create barriers for those with disabilities. It enables tools such as screen readers to ensure the ability to access and deliver these same applications and materials to all. This is an essential need that must be met, not just for the regulatory requirement, but to ensure our students and the broader public have the proper access that is needed without barriers. The challenge to meet this requirement is often in the retrofitting of digital educational materials. As an example, a weather and climate course may require a host of updates including attaching metadata such as “alt text” descriptions to all images and usage of fonts screen readers are able to decipher. In short, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) must be followed. Additionally, there are some specific requirements that may not be obvious to the novice attempting to remediate content. These include captioning requirements, specific titling property requirements, required use of headings, and much more. There are some challenges including how different everyday software packages that now have built in accessibility checkers do not all enforce the WCAG rules the same or at the same level. Some learning management systems (LMS) have demonstrated to be stricter than common content creation software or worse, some LMS may have inconsistencies that are difficult to navigate. The largest unknowns however stem from within our own meteorological content. For example, what is the best way to provide the classic station model information and be completely compliant? How do complex diagrams such as thermodynamic diagrams (e.g. the classic Skew T Log P diagram) be best described in alt text or other supporting documentation, and meet our meteorological industry standards as well as meeting regulations? What are the best practices when introducing contouring (e.g. isotherms) in this digital arena and remain compliant? Furthermore, how should these elements be handled in assessments (e.g. quizzes, exams) and not have the answers to the questions given away in the required documentation such as alt text? This presentation brings these critical issues to light as they affect 4-year and 2-year educational institutions. The AMS Board of Higher Education has begun discussions surrounding this topic, and this is the topic of an AMS Town Hall meeting. Our collective future success to meet these regulations requires help and input from the community and ultimately, a check from those who need and will use these features. In being compliant, are the results of this effort valuable and useful?

494373.title: Assessing Physical and Mental Health Risks of Heatwaves in Megacity Shanghai under a Warming Climate
494373.authors: Jiacan Yuan, Fudan University, Shanghai, Shanghai, China; and C. Liang
494373.abstract: Extreme heat is a major climate-related health threat in megacities, where global warming interacts with urbanization to amplify exposure and vulnerability. By integrating long-term meteorological observations, health records, high-resolution regional climate simulations, and CMIP6 projections, we synthesize evidence from Shanghai and the Yangtze River Delta Urban agglomeration to understand how heat, humidity, and urban development jointly affect physical and mental health risks under current and future climates. A key finding is that humid-heat extremes pose substantially higher health risks than high-temperature extremes alone in Shanghai which is in a region of humid subtropical climate. When humidity is accounted for using metrics such as Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature, heat stress is significantly underestimated by air temperature alone. The health burden is especially severe during humid-hot nights, when limited nocturnal cooling reduces physiological recovery and increases risks of cardiovascular, respiratory, and mental health outcomes. These risks are projected to rise sharply under high greenhouse-gas emission scenarios, with both physical and mental health burdens increasing substantially toward the end of the century. We further show that heat-related mental and behavioral health risks are strongly sensitive to humid-heat exposure, with hospital admissions increasing under combined heat and humidity stress. Without demographic change, mental health-related morbidity is projected to increase markedly in future decades, while strong climate mitigation could substantially reduce this burden, preventing a large number of cases. A second major finding is that urbanization significantly amplifies heat-related health risks through land-use change and urban heat island effects. High-resolution simulations of the record-breaking 2024 heatwave reveal that urban expansion and anthropogenic heat emissions intensify local temperature extremes, particularly at night. In some urban areas of Shanghai, nighttime temperatures increase by more than 2°C due to urban effects, greatly reducing nighttime cooling and exacerbating heat exposure. This urban amplification substantially increases heat-related morbidity, highlighting the critical role of city structure and land-use patterns in shaping health outcomes. These results underscore the need to integrate urban climate processes and future climate changes with health impact assessments to improve heat-health warning systems, guide climate-resilient urban planning, and support effective mitigation and adaptation strategies in rapidly warming and urbanizing regions.

494374.title: Evaluating LES Representation of Boundary Layer Clouds Within the DOE PROCEED Initiative
494374.authors: Benjamin D. Rodenkirch, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, Honolulu, HI; and J. D. Small Griswold, G. Torri, J. M. Nugent, D. McCoy, and D. Caulton
494374.abstract: For many decades, Earth System Models (ESMs) have been developed and used to better understand and predict the global environment. While substantial progress continues to be made, ESMs continue to be limited in their predictive capacity by necessary yet imperfect parameterizations, including relating to cloud microphysics. In situ observations of clouds provide key insights into underlying cloud microphysical properties, which can help identify particular areas of improvement within relevant ESM parameterizations. However, direct evaluation of global-scale ESMs against process-scale observations is not an equitable comparison, and thus behooves an intermediary to bridge the gap between the differing scales. The U.S. Department of Energy Perturbed physics ensemble Regression Optimization Center for ESM Evaluation and Development (DOE PROCEED) in part seeks to address this need by developing a framework to better integrate process-scale observations with ESMs, specifically through the use of Large Eddy Simulations (LES), to ultimately help identify and improve ESM parametric uncertainty. Under the DOE PROCEED framework, this study investigates LES representation of marine boundary layer clouds in comparison with process-scale observations from the DOE Eastern North Atlantic Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ENA ARM) site. Using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, an LES suite is executed using nested domains centered over the ENA ARM site that resolve the boundary layer and cumulus convection, which in turn allow for comparisons with ENA ARM observations that are more equitable than that with an ESM. Individual simulations within the LES suite are designed with differing parametric configurations to determine the setup whose bulk cloud properties most optimally resemble those of ENA ARM observations. Statistical analysis of LES marine boundary layer cloud properties in the context of ENA ARM observations will be presented, including developed representativeness indices and “right answer, wrong reason” discernments. Emphasis will be placed on the LES configurations that best emulate the observations, which will subsequently inform future global-scale perturbed physics ensembles towards improving cloud microphysical parameterizations within the DOE Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM).

494375.title: What is Missing When Solar Photospheric Observations Are Only Available from Along the Sun-Earth Line
494375.authors: Marc DeRosa, Lockheed Martin Solar and Astrophysics Laboratory, Palo Alto, CA; and N. Nitta and M. Jin
494375.abstract: Space weather forecasting increasingly depends on knowledge of the Sun’s global photospheric and coronal magnetic state. Although observatories such as STEREO and Solar Orbiter occasionally provide magnetogram and coronal imaging observations from longitudes away from the Sun-Earth line, such data are not routinely available. At present, space weather researchers and forecasters typically rely on global magnetic maps of the solar photosphere that incorporate statistical assumptions about the evolution of known active regions as they rotate away from Earth-facing solar longitudes, due to the lack of regular observations of photospheric magnetism away from the Sun-Earth line. These photospheric magnetic maps then feed into the ensuing coronal magnetic models, thereby propagating these statistical assumptions. In the research presented here, we examine downstream consequences of having detailed observations mainly from along the Sun-Earth line, and consider how new instrumentation positioned at the L4 and L5 Sun–Earth Lagrange points are likely to enhance the capability to better characterize global photospheric and coronal magnetic fields.

494379.title: Understanding the Complex Interplay of Dynamics, Thermodynamics, and Microphysics, using Machine Learning
494379.authors: Peter Jan van Leeuwen, Colorado State University, Reading, United kingdom
494379.abstract: Machine learning has the potential to revolutionize the geosciences. It allows us to tackle one of the holy grails of finding the (strange) attractor of a chaotic geophysical system. As realized about a hundred years ago, the attractor of dimension D of a dynamical system can be represented by a Eulerian space of dimension 2D+1 at most. Using expressive autoencoders, this low-dimensional Eulerian space can be found, allowing us to study the structure of the attractor in this space. For example, it is known that the highly nonlinear and chaotic 1-D Kuramoto-Sivashinsky model with physical length-scale 100 has an attractor dimension of 22. We find that the minimal optimal latent space dimension for this system is 44, independent of the number of grid points used in the model (e.g. 128 or 1024). Our goal here is to explore the 2-D squall line modeled via LES model CM1, which displays an intricate interplay of dynamics, thermodynamics, and microphysics. We will explore the minimal optimal latent space, and study the dynamics in this space using recently developed techniques such as information flow to try to unravel what happens in this latent space and how that connects to physical space. The emphasis will be on how the latent space represents the interplay between dynamics, thermodynamics and microphysics, and how that connects back to physical space. This allows for a better understanding of how to represent the dominant physics with a small number of 'modes', both in latent and physical space. The area of skillful machine learning might allow for long-awaited serious progress in this intersection area.

494381.title: A Comparison of Vertical Profiles of Density, Speed, and Direction of Migratory Birds Between WSR-88D and TDWR Stations
494381.authors: Shawn Wallace, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and A. Dokter and Y. Deng
494381.abstract: Weather Surveillance Radar-1988 Doppler (WSR-88D) data are widely used to monitor nocturnal bird migration, while Terminal Doppler Weather Radar (TDWR) data in the United States have received comparatively little attention despite their higher spatial resolution. This study evaluated whether TDWR data could be used for quantitative migration monitoring by comparing measurements of nocturnal bird migration between nearby pairs of WSR-88D and TDWR stations. These TDWR stations have the potential to fill fine-scale spatial gaps in monitoring around major US cities, which are of special concern for migratory birds due to collision risks associated with attraction by artificial light at night. The information from TDWR systems may also have potential to tell us critical information regarding migration over major U.S. airports, helping us to reduce bird strikes across the aviation industry. Paired radar (WSR-88D and TDWR) data was processed using R-package bioRad, similar to the processing used for BirdCast. The resulting vertical profiles were compared in terms of bird density, flight speed, and the vertical distribution of migration. We cross-calibrated TDWR reflectivity measurements by TDWR on identical precipitation events detected by both sensors. We then evaluated the relationship between wavelength and reflectivity for bird-dominated migration events. Across most paired comparisons, WSR-88D (S-band) produced substantially higher estimates of bird density than TDWR (C-band), even after accounting for expected wavelength dependencies in scattering. We attribute these discrepancies to a complex resonant relationship between radar cross section and bird size. We find that reflectivity ratios between NEXRAD and TWDR varied between night as well as within nights, suggesting that radar cross section of birds is wavelength dependent and responding to the composition and size distribution of birds, which may change throughout the nights and between days. Early season migration in spring and late season migration in fall is often associated with a larger proportion of large-bodied birds, with small-bodied passerine species being overrepresented in late spring and early fall. We propose to use independent information on species composition from the citizen-science projects eBird and BirdFlow to account for seasonally changing radar cross sections. We conclude that onboarding of TDWR stations in the real-time continental-scale monitoring of birds is feasible, but will require careful cross-calibration with existing WSR-88D stations.

494386.title: The NSF NCAR Integrated Sounding System, a Brief History
494386.authors: William O.J. Brown, NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and T. Hock and C. Martin
494386.abstract: For the past 35 years, the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research Earth Observing Lab (NCAR / EOL) has operated the Integrated Sounding Systems (ISS) suites of instruments to profile the atmosphere. The ISS were developed together in partnership with the NOAA Aeronomy Lab for the TOGA-COARE campaign in 1992 (Parsons et.al. 1994) where six ISS were deployed around the western Pacific, four on island sites and two on-board research ships. The ISS consisted of a 915 MHz Radar Wind Profiler, radiosondes, surface meteorological tower, all connected to a central workstation computer where data was archived and integrated analysis tools were provided. The system was packaged into a seatainer that served as office space, and could be readily transported anywhere around the world. Together with the NCAR developed CLASS and GAUS radiosonde systems (Cross-chain LORAN Atmospheric Sounding System and GPS Advanced Upper-air Sounding system), the ISS have been deployed at over 60 field campaigns. The systems have been deployed across much of the US, in Europe, Asia and Oceania, on eight islands, and on seven ships sailing in the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, and Southern Oceans. The system started out with the TOGA COARE Tropical Meteorology study, but has contributed to studies in topics ranging from severe weather, mountain meteorology, boundary-layer meteorology, ocean-atmosphere exchange, precipitation, microphysics, fog, wind energy, agriculture, atmospheric chemistry, atmospheric gravity waves, to education and outreach. The ISS instrument suite has evolved over the years with the addition of equipment such as lidars (ceilometers and Doppler wind lidars), Micro Rain Radar, profiling IR spectrometer, visibility and aerosol sensors, and web cameras. The Radar Wind Profilers have long been a particular focus of development work for the ISS, especially the 449 MHz Modular Wind Profiler. This is a unique, scalable profiling radar for extended altitude coverage, and uses spaced antenna wind techniques for rapid wind measurements. The ISS are frequently deployed with the NCAR ISFS (Integrated Surface Flux System) for surface exchange balance studies, and these systems, along with the NCAR developed MPD (Micro Pulse DIAL) lidars, form the core instruments of the proposed LOTOS (LOwer Troposphere Observing System) integrated observing platform. Parsons, D., and Coauthors, 1994: The Integrated Sounding System: Description and Preliminary Observations from TOGA COARE. Bull. Amer. Meteor. Soc., 75, 553–568, DOI: 10.1175/1520-0477(1994)075<0553:TISSDA>2.0.CO;2.

494390.title: Mean and Extreme Precipitation Responses to ENSO Across Australian States at Different Global Warming Levels
494390.authors: Dhruba Jyoti Goswami, University of Exeter, Exeter, Exeter, United Kingdom; The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia; and R. Trancoso, R. Chadwick, J. Syktus, and M. Collins
494390.abstract: Climate extremes are projected to intensify under global warming, with annual maximum daily precipitation increasing by approximately 5.9-7.7% per degree of warming globally due to both thermodynamic and dynamic atmospheric processes. In Australia, the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a major driver of precipitation variability and extremes. Although CMIP6 General Circulation Models (GCMs) generally reproduce Australian precipitation patterns, they exhibit persistent dry biases, particularly in coastal and mountainous regions, highlighting the need for high-resolution downscaled climate data. While downscaled projections are broadly comparable to their host GCMs, high-resolution CORDEX simulations outperform the GCMs in representing rare precipitation extremes. Additionally, CMIP6 projections indicate that the intensity and frequency of El Niño events are likely to increase under future warming scenarios, emphasizing the importance of understanding ENSO-driven changes in Australian precipitation extremes. In this study, we investigate the response of mean and extreme precipitation (99th and 99.7th percentiles) during ENSO phases. We assess how ENSO and precipitation patterns evolve across different global warming levels (GWLs), and examine their regional variability across different Australian regions, such as climate domains, states, and major capital cities. We use observational gridded precipitation data (AGCD) as well as CMIP6-based GCM (host models) and CORDEX downscaled simulations. Our preliminary results show that while El Niño and La Niña conditions are generally associated with reduced and increased mean precipitation respectively across much of Australia, precipitation extremes remain pronounced during both El Niño and La Niña phases. The projected ENSO precipitation changes are greatest during DJF and MAM for all the GWLs, and the projections show weakening of teleconnection for higher GWLs. Among the CORDEX downscaled ensembles, BARPA-ACS showed the best overall performance, while NARCliM2.0 and QldFCP-2 exhibited dry biases and CCAM-ACS displayed a wet bias across parts of Australia. This study advances understanding of ENSO-driven changes in mean and extreme precipitation across Australia under different warming levels, with implications for climate risk management and adaptation planning.

494393.title: The Atmospheric Angular Momentum Budget across Time Scales
494393.authors: Klaus M. Weickmann, Retired, Boulder, CO; and D. Gold
494393.abstract: Weickmann, Kiladis, and Sardeshmukh (1997) examined global atmospheric angular momentum variations associated with the Madden-Julian oscillation, including the roles of momentum transports and exchanges with the solid Earth. That work motivated development of the Global Wind Oscillation, providing a broader angular-momentum perspective for describing subseasonal atmospheric circulation variability. This presentation will revisit the principal findings of the 1997 study, describe how the angular-momentum perspective evolved beyond an exclusively MJO-based view, and illustrate new real-time monitoring capabilities using the CORe global dataset. The presentation will conclude with evidence that the Southern Hemisphere momentum budget has occupied a distinctly different mean state since the 1990s, raising questions about the roles of tropical forcing, ozone depletion, and longer-term circulation change.

494394.title: An Experimental Lightning Metric to Diagnose the Evolution of Mesoscale Convective Systems during the Texas Hill Country Floods
494394.authors: Timothy Logan, Texas A&M Univ., College Station, TX; and K. M. Núñez Ocasio, Z. Moon, L. Zhao, and R. Zhang
494394.abstract: The Texas Hill Country floods, which took place from 3-5 July 2025, were among the most destructive weather events in terms of loss of life and property damage in Texas. Exceptionally elevated tropical moisture coupled with a meso-low pressure system interacting with a shortwave pressure trough led to the development of numerous storms in Central Texas. Some of the storms grew upscale into large mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) consisting of mesoscale convective complexes (MCCs) with embedded mesoscale convective vortices (MCVs). The storms produced copious amounts of rain prior to upscale growth (100+ mm) and became electrified as they rapidly transitioned to an MCS. The Guadalupe and San Gabriel River watersheds were strongly compromised by the late evening of 3 July 2025, and numerous search and rescue operations were carried out across the western Hill Country after midnight (0600 UTC 4 July 2025). The MCS responsible for the Williamson County Flood event developed at around 0300 UTC on 5 July 2025 and became electrically active from 0700-1200 UTC as observed by the Houston Lightning Mapping Array. Nearly three hours after lightning activity declined, the San Gabriel River rose above major flood stage at Liberty Hill (25 ft) and four hours later at Georgetown (35 ft). The core of electrical activity was nearly collocated with overshooting tops (satellite Tb < 201K) and displaced north and west of the maximum precipitation area (347 mm) suggesting dynamic, microphysical, and electrodynamic interactions. For the Kerrville Flood event, The Houston Lightning Mapping Array observed a smaller amount of lightning activity over the Guadalupe River watershed from 0000-1800 UTC on 4 July 2025 due to a more expansive, slow moving MCS. Both events featured storms that transitioned from warm phase to mixed-phase precipitation processes leading to storm electrification and increased flooding potential. This study addresses the following scientific questions: (1) how can Lightning Mapping Array data diagnose the evolution and strength of the flood-producing storms? and (2) how can the rapid cadence (1-minute sampling) of Lightning Mapping Array data complement other datasets such as satellite, radar, and meteorological observations? An experimental lightning metric has been developed and tested to illustrate upscale growth of thunderstorms as well as relate deep convection behavior to the timing of NWS flash flooding warning polygons. The Tracking Algorithm for Mesoscale Convective Systems (TAMS) software and Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor System (MRMS) product are used in conjunction with Houston Lightning Mapping Array datasets to track MCS and precipitation expansion with respect to the most concentrated lightning activity. This study also serves as a foundation to provide nowcasting support for emergency management, especially within the region of a Lightning Mapping Array. Future work will incorporate additional lightning and meteorological datasets.

494403.title: Cascading Impacts of Extreme and Compound Events Around the World
494403.authors: Laurie Huning, California State University, Long Beach, Long Beach, CA; and M. Brunner
494403.abstract: Built infrastructure and natural systems face numerous challenges each year as warming temperatures enhance the severity and frequency of many compound and extreme events (e.g., droughts, wildfires, heatwaves, floods) around the world. These events occur across different climate zones and landscapes, and have impacts that cascade across space, time, and sectors (e.g., water, energy, agriculture, recreation, trade, human health). Drawing on notable examples like the record-setting 2023 wildfires and heatwaves in Canada, snow droughts in the western U.S., heightened river temperatures during heatwaves in France, and other extreme events around the globe, we examine feedbacks associated with these natural hazards and their impacts. Such events and their interactions pose challenges for modeling, monitoring, and assessing risks, particularly when impacts span long periods of time or cascade to influence remote regions. For instance, we characterize the extent that the impacts of snowpack changes and drought and/or heatwaves can have in distant areas, particularly when agricultural regions are affected. We also highlight the critical need to include the feedbacks and cascading impacts of extreme and compound events in resource management practices and risk assessments. Since remote impacts are not yet well-understood or well-tracked, we must rethink approaches to hydrologic and impact modeling as well as disaster risk reduction strategies. We ultimately discuss gaps, opportunities, and ways forward to improve process understanding and impact modeling so that communities can move toward more resilient water, food, and energy systems.

494408.title: Beyond Headline Scores: Advanced Precipitation Verification of AI and Physical Numerical Weather Prediction Models for Operations
494408.authors: Kathryn M. Newman, DTC, Boulder, CO; and C. P. Kalb, V. Vargas Jr., M. A. Harrold, G. Ketefian, and J. Halley Gotway
494408.abstract: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence Numerical Weather Prediction (AIWP) have demonstrated substantial promise in improving forecast skill and computational efficiency. However, the rapid proliferation of AIWP systems has outpaced the development of robust, standardized approaches for testing, validation, and intercomparison. Traditional verification methodologies, while well-established for physically based models, may not fully capture the unique challenges associated with AIWP (e.g., spatial smoothing, temporal consistency, and physical realism). This gap motivates the need for advanced verification frameworks capable of evaluating intercomparisons of AI, hybrid, and physically based forecasts in a consistent and statistically reliable manner. The Developmental Testbed Center (DTC) is participating in the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Weather Prediction Model Intercomparison Project (WP-MIP), through evaluation of contributions using the enhanced Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) system. Contributed datasets from this coordinated intercomparison will be used to conduct a systematic evaluation of precipitation forecasts across several distinct regions. Particular focus will be placed on the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)’s AI Global Forecast System (AIGFS) vs. GFS. The results presented here will highlight feature based verification using the Method for Object-Based Diagnostic Evaluation (MODE), enabling evaluation beyond traditional verification approaches. The MODE results assess the representation of coherent features of precipitation objects (e.g., area, intensity, complexity, spatial placement), allowing for more physically interpretable comparisons. Further, AI-specific metrics (i.e., sharpness) for understanding how AIWP systems differ from traditional models will be incorporated. This presentation aims to not only benchmark model performance, but underscore the importance of advanced verification strategies to better understand the opportunities and challenges associated with AIWP systems.

494416.title: Directional Wave Organization Reflects Spectral Memory in Tropical Cyclones
494416.authors: Wyn Pauly, University of Hawai'i at Mānoa, Honolulu, HI; and H. Seo, J. Davis, and S. R. Jayne
494416.abstract: Observations of spectral wave properties under tropical cyclones are commonly interpreted using contemporaneous environmental descriptors such as local wind speed, wind direction, storm-relative position, and storm intensity. However, surface waves evolve over finite adjustment timescales through wind input, dissipation, and nonlinear wave-wave interactions, suggesting that instantaneous forcing alone may not uniquely determine the wave state. Here, we combine North Atlantic multi-storm Spotter directional wave spectra with collocated COAMPS-TC modeled atmospheric fields to quantify the first-order dependence of bulk and spectral wave properties on the local wind environment. Smooth, nonparametric baseline models are evaluated across independent storms to characterize the component of wave variability explained by the local wind environment, while residual variability is examined for systematic departures from a local equilibrium framework. While local wind forcing explains much of the variability in significant wave height, peak frequency, and other bulk wave properties, residual variability remains among observations experiencing similar instantaneous forcing conditions. Among these otherwise similarly forced wave fields, differences in peak-frequency directional spreading coincide with differences in significant wave height and mean square slope. These results are consistent with the interpretation that directional organization reflects spectral memory arising from the finite, spectrally dependent adjustment of the wave spectrum toward a changing equilibrium. The associated differences in mean square slope further indicate corresponding differences in short-wave roughness and high-frequency directional organization, with potentially important consequences for wave-supported stress and air-sea momentum transfer. Because these differences arise among wave fields subject to similar forcing, they represent a source of sea-state variability beyond that described by equilibrium-based bulk parameterizations. Together, these findings support a history-dependent description of tropical cyclone wave evolution in which spectral memory introduces an additional dimension of wave-state variability beyond that explained by instantaneous forcing.

494420.title: A Comparison of Random Forests and Echo State Networks for Extreme Subseasonal Temperature Forecasting over the Contiguous United States
494420.authors: Thomas Stephen Ehrmann, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM; and M. Holthuijzen, K. Goode, M. Brown, and J. Johnson
494420.abstract: Subseasonal temperature extremes pose major challenges for energy systems, agriculture, and public health, yet their prediction remains difficult due to weak atmospheric persistence and limited skill of physics-based models beyond 10 days. Here, we evaluate the ability of machine learning methods to forecast weekly mean and extreme temperatures at 1–4 week lead times across five regions of the contiguous United States. We compare a tree-based ensemble method (random forests, RF) and a recurrent neural network (deep ensemble echo state network, DEESN) against persistence and enhanced climatological baselines. Across all lead times and regions, RF slightly outperformed DEESN for most CONUS regions. To improve interpretability, we apply grouped permutation feature importance (PFI) to iteratively rank and select correlated predictor groups from an initial pool of over 1,100 atmospheric and land-surface variables. This approach reduces the input dimensionality to fewer than 10–150 inputs per model with no loss of skill. The selected predictor groups span a range of atmospheric and land-surface variables, including geopotential height, temperature, pressure, and surface fields, with the most important groups varying substantially by region and forecast horizon. These results demonstrate that RF offers a robust, interpretable baseline for subseasonal temperature forecasting, and grouped PFI provides an effective pathway for feature selection in high-dimensional forecasting tasks.

494422.title: A 26-Year Physics-Based Compound Flood Reanalysis for the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts
494422.authors: Fei Ye, Virginia Institute of Marine Science, Gloucester Point, VA; and H. C. Yu, Y. J. Zhang, H. Yoo, S. Moghimi, G. Seroka, Z. Yang, and E. Myers
494422.abstract: Coastal flood hazards arise from interactions among tides, storm surge, river discharge, precipitation, and their propagation through estuaries, tidal rivers, wetlands, and floodplains. Long-term assessments, however, often rely on isolated observations, event-based simulations, or statistical methods that do not represent these interacting processes consistently across the coastal transition zone. We present a 26-year, physics-based compound flood reanalysis for 2000–2025 covering the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts. The reanalysis is based on NOAA’s three-dimensional Surge and Tide Operational Forecast System for the Atlantic domain (STOFS3D-Atlantic), implemented with the Semi-implicit Cross-scale Hydroscience Integrated System Model (SCHISM). Its high-resolution unstructured mesh extends from the coastal ocean into the watershed to approximately 10 m above mean sea level and represents estuaries, floodplains, and watershed-scale river networks within a continuous hydrodynamic domain. An ensemble optimal interpolation framework with incremental analysis updating assimilates hourly sea-level observations while limiting artificial adjustment shocks. Evaluation against 161 NOAA water-level stations indicates strong domain-wide performance, with an overall correlation of 0.95, a root-mean-square error of approximately 9 cm, and a mean bias below 1 cm. The reanalysis also captures the timing and magnitude of water levels during several major hurricanes and broadly reproduces observed variations in extreme-water-level occurrence. Preliminary exceedance-day analyses indicate relatively few high-water days during the early part of the record and increased occurrence at many stations after approximately 2015, with broadly similar temporal patterns at coastal stations and stations within estuaries and tidal rivers. Ongoing analyses examine long-term water-level variability, seasonal tidal behavior, coastal-to-inland gradients, and the inland extent of elevated water-level excursions. Map- and transect-based analyses are being used to compare tidal transmission, seasonal tidal variability, and high-water behavior across representative estuaries and tidal rivers. These analyses are intended to characterize regional differences in the location, extent, and organization of dynamically active coastal transition zones. The reanalysis provides a physically consistent basis for regional compound-flood assessment, investigation of coastal transition zones, and data-driven studies, including AI/ML applications.

494433.title: Dynamical Control of Microphysical Evolution in Marine Cold-Air Outbreak Clouds from EarthCARE CPR
494433.authors: Jiseob Kim, McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada; and I. Tan, P. Kollias, and B. P. Treserras
494433.abstract: Marine cold-air outbreaks (MCAOs) strongly influence the radiative balance of high-latitude oceans. As cold air moves from the sea-ice edge over open water, shallow cloud streets deepen and reorganize into broken open-cell convection. Their rapid transitions in cloud structure and microphysics are tightly coupled to dynamics, but this interplay has not previously been observed from space. The Earth Cloud, Aerosol, and Radiation Explorer (EarthCARE) satellite, carrying the first spaceborne Doppler Cloud Profiling Radar (CPR), now provides observations of hydrometeor sedimentation velocity and vertical air motion across broad spatial and temporal scales. We analyze CPR observations of MCAO clouds over the Norwegian and Barents Seas from December 2024 to May 2025 and use Lagrangian trajectories to follow air masses after they leave the sea-ice edge. The CPR successfully captures a systematic downstream evolution in cloud structure, dynamics, and microphysics, despite the shallow depth, small horizontal scales, and substantial variability characteristic of MCAO clouds. The role of dynamics becomes particularly clear when MCAO clouds are compared with shallow mixed-phase clouds under non-MCAO conditions. We find that strong updrafts in MCAO clouds coincide with larger liquid water path (LWP). These conditions are accompanied by increases in sedimentation velocity and its vertical gradient, reflecting rapid riming-driven ice growth. In contrast, non-MCAO clouds show lower riming efficiency at similar LWP due to relatively weaker dynamical support. This highlights the importance of dynamics in shaping polar cloud structure and microphysics. Constraining these coupled processes from observations is expected to provide a benchmark for evaluating and improving the representation of MCAO cloud evolution in weather and climate models.

494442.title: Global Sensitivity Analysis of a Catch-Basin-Enabled Hydrodynamic Model for New York City
494442.authors: Niloufar Soheili, City University of New York, City College, New York, NY; and S. Kamali and R. M. Khanbilvardi
494442.abstract: Urban flooding in New York City (NYC) is driven by rainfall that exceeds the capacity of the street drainage system. Recent work has enhanced the LISFLOOD-FP hydrodynamic model for NYC by routing water off the street through individual catch basins. That work also introduced an NYC-specific clogging factor to represent reduced inlet efficiency, a condition that varies block to block and has never been measured. It remains unknown which input governs the simulated flood, and whether drainage matters more than roughness, rainfall, or terrain. Here we rank the inputs of this model through a global sensitivity analysis. Uncertain factors span surface roughness, rainfall forcing, terrain representation, and drainage parameters including inlet density and the clogging factor. Digital elevation model error enters as a spatially correlated field with sampled bias, standard deviation, and correlation length. Morris screening runs first and drops the factors whose average effect on the output stays small. Sobol decomposition then divides the output variance among the survivors, separating each factor's own effect from its interactions with others. Because a single simulation is expensive, the Sobol indices come from a Gaussian process emulator trained on a few hundred simulations of representative NYC catchments. Factor rankings depend on which output is examined, so indices are computed separately for flood depth, extent, timing, and recession. Depth, timing, and recession come from FloodNet sensors across recent NYC flood events. The analysis delivers a ranking of factors for each output metric and maps showing where in the city each factor dominates. Dropping the factors with negligible influence reduces the parameter space to a size that a full hydrodynamic ensemble can sample. Weighting that ensemble against FloodNet depth and recession then yields the target product: a probabilistic flood inundation map for NYC giving the probability of exceeding a given depth at each location.

494446.title: Joint Object-based Evaluation of Downscaled Precipitation and Near-surface Temperature Products over CONUS
494446.authors: Xiaodong Chen, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
