494446.abstract: High-resolution precipitation (P) and near-surface air temperature (T2) products, generated from dynamical or statistical downscaling, provide critical information for regional climate assessment and adaptation planning. Most downscaling evaluations emphasize grid-scale accuracy and largely overlook the storm-scale characteristics and the joint behavior of P and T2, both of which are critical in applications such as hydrologic modeling and analysis. This is particularly important in cold regions where snow processes are jointly controlled by P and T2 during individual storms. Therefore, standardized metrics are needed to evaluate how diverse downscaled products represent the storm-scale behavior and joint distribution of P and T2 fields within individual storms. To fill this gap, we built a joint analysis framework that extends the established object-based precipitation evaluation to P-T2 joint evaluation, focusing on the joint distribution of P intensity and T2 anomaly relative to 0°C. We evaluate each product’s ability to reproduce various observed P and T2 features at the storm-event level, including total precipitation volume, precipitation area, peak intensity, mean T2, T2 variability within the storm, P-T2 correlation, and the fraction of warm precipitation. Multiple metrics (Perkins score and non-parametric tests) are used to quantify product performance. The framework is applied to four downscaling products over their respective available periods from 1981 to the early 2020s. They include two dynamical products: Canadian Surface Reanalysis v3.2 and CONUS404, and two statistical products: LOCA2 and STAR-ESDM2. Product performance varies across Bukovsky regions and seasons. CONUS404 performs best in many region-season combinations, while LOCA2 achieves comparable performance across many evaluated characteristics. Based on this comprehensive evaluation, we provide guidance on choosing suitable downscaled products for specific regions, seasons, and applications. These findings and recommendations can inform precipitation-relevant modeling and analysis over CONUS, guide future developments to improve downscaling techniques, and provide actionable information for climate-impact assessments across hydrological and ecological systems.

494449.title: Current Status of Climate Information Disclosure Policies and Progress in Climate Risk Assessment and Management of Chinese Enterprises
494449.authors: huanping wu, National Climate Center, Beijing, China
494449.abstract: This paper first sorts out the origin, policy framework, layout of relevant research institutions and the latest development trends of climate-related information disclosure in the international community and China. It deeply analyzes the necessity and urgency of strengthening climate-related information disclosure, and systematically sorts out the main types and transmission mechanisms of climate risks, as well as the quantitative assessment methods of climate physical risks and transition risks. At present, the research and application of climate-related information disclosure in China are still in the initial stage, with obvious shortcomings in policy improvement, technical support, standard construction and professional services, which require multi-dimensional breakthroughs. Based on this, this paper puts forward targeted future suggestions: improving the service system and organizational mechanism of climate-related information disclosure, accelerating the construction of climate information data support capacity, strengthening the research on refined risk assessment methods for industries, constructing a demonstration platform and relevant technical standards for climate-related information disclosure services, and strengthening the integration of interdisciplinary technologies and collaborative development of teams. Finally, combined with the relevant work practices of the National Climate Center, this paper shares specific cases of cooperative application with Chinese banks, providing practical references and theoretical support for solving the key problems of psychical climate risk assessment and disclosure, constructing an ESG-oriented climate-related information disclosure system, enhancing enterprises' climate risk management capabilities and improving their ability to adapt to climate change.

494452.title: Impacts of Convectively Coupled Kelvin Waves on Tropical Cyclone Seeds Across Ocean Basins
494452.authors: Sunny Sharma, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; and M. J. Molina and Q. Lawton
494452.abstract: Convectively coupled Kelvin waves (CCKWs) have been shown to modulate tropical cyclone (TC) genesis, but most previous studies have linked CCKW activity directly to genesis events without tracking the precursor disturbances, or TC seeds, themselves. Here, using a global dataset of TC seed tracks and ERA5 reanalysis, we examine the evolution of developing and nondeveloping seeds before, during, and after CCKW interactions across tropical ocean basins. Analysis of the ventilation index shows that CCKWs reduce the ventilation index around TC seeds primarily through thermodynamic changes, providing reanalysis-based support for a mechanism previously identified in idealized aquaplanet simulations. CCKW interaction alone, however, is not sufficient to determine development. Seeds that ultimately develop are embedded in more favorable environments before CCKW interaction, with systematically lower pre-interaction ventilation indices than nondeveloping seeds. The Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) is one contributor to these background differences. Developing seeds, particularly over the Indian Ocean, preferentially encounter CCKWs during MJO phases associated with more favorable environmental conditions. These results suggest that CCKWs act as transient enhancers of TC seed environments, while development outcomes are conditioned by the background state in which the interaction occurs. This study provides a possible explanation for why CCKW interactions with TC seeds are associated with different genesis outcomes and highlights the combined influence of synoptic-scale and intraseasonal tropical variability on TC genesis.

494458.title: Future Changes of ENSO Precipitation Teleconnection Over Tropics and Subtropics
494458.authors: Dhruba Jyoti Goswami, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia; and R. Chadwick, M. Collins, R. Trancoso, and J. Syktus
494458.abstract: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the primary mode of interannual climate variability, arising from coupled ocean–atmosphere interactions in the tropical Pacific and oscillating between warm (El Niño) and cold (La Niña) phases on a 3–7 year timescale. Under increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, ENSO-related teleconnections are projected to undergo substantial changes in a warming climate. By the end of the 21st century, precipitation teleconnections are projected to intensify over more than 48% of tropical and subtropical land regions during El Niño events and over 45% during La Niña events. This presentation examines how ENSO teleconnections are projected to change across the tropics and subtropics, with a particular focus on the relative contributions of dynamic and thermodynamic processes. Using an ensemble of 25 CMIP6 climate models, we find that changes in mean atmospheric moisture strongly influence present-day ENSO-related precipitation, while uncertainties in the projected ENSO precipitation response from the present climate to the future are primarily associated with changes in ENSO-driven circulation. To further investigate the dynamical mechanisms underlying these projected changes, we employ a linear baroclinic model (LBM). The LBM successfully reproduces key features of future ENSO teleconnections simulated by CMIP6 models, including the eastward shift of convection and subsidence over the tropical Pacific. Our analysis aims to disentangle whether projected changes in ENSO teleconnections arise predominantly from modifications to the mean climate state or from changes in the spatial structure of ENSO variability under global warming.

494460.title: Impacts of Parameterized Deep-Convective Transport and Wet Removal on Aerosols in E3SM
494460.authors: Kai Zhang, PNNL, Richland, WA; and H. Wang, S. M. Burrows, M. Huang, X. Song, B. Singh, O. H. Diaz Ibarra, J. R. Overfelt, J. Johnson, J. W. Litzinger, M. Wu, C. R. Terai, H. Wan, P. L. Ma, and J. D. Fast
494460.abstract: Convective clouds influence the aerosol life cycle through vertical transport, aerosol activation, precipitation scavenging, and aerosol resuspension following rain evaporation. Global atmospheric models at typical (~100km) resolutions parameterize deep convection, whereas convection-permitting models represent much of convective cloud development and precipitation through resolved dynamics and cloud microphysics. These contrasting treatments can substantially affect the simulated aerosol distribution, burden, and lifetime. EAMxx, the next-generation atmospheric component of E3SM originally developed for global convection-permitting simulations, is incorporating the four-mode Modal Aerosol Module (MAM4) and being extended to coarser resolutions. Preliminary EAMxx-MAM4xx simulations without the Zhang–McFarlane (ZM) deep convection scheme overestimate aerosol burdens and lifetimes and exhibit weak wet-removal efficiency at both ~100 km and ~13 km resolutions. These results provide the clue that, in the configurations examined, the currently represented wet-removal processes are insufficient to constrain the simulated aerosol life cycle. Because EAMxx does not yet support the coupling of ZM to aerosol wet-removal parameterizations, we first conduct sensitivity experiments at coarse resolution using EAMv2, which is a predecessor of EAMxx that employs MAM4 and has aerosol tracer transport and wet removal coupled to ZM. We perform four simulations in a factorial design: a control, two experiments that separately disable convective wet removal and convective tracer transport, and one that disables both processes. Factorial contrasts isolate the individual effects of convective transport and wet removal and quantify their interaction. We will present how these processes affect aerosol vertical distribution, wet removal, aerosol burden, and lifetime. Once aerosol processes in EAMxx are coupled to ZM, we will repeat these experiments within EAMxx at different resolutions. Together, the EAMv2 and EAMxx experiments will clarify the relative roles of parameterized and grid-resolved convection in aerosol transport and removal and identify the mechanisms underlying weak aerosol wet removal in current EAMxx simulations.

494462.title: A Global View of Riming in Stratiform Clouds from EarthCARE Doppler Observations
494462.authors: Jiseob Kim, McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada; and P. Kollias, B. P. Treserras, A. Battaglia, and Z. Qu
494462.abstract: Riming is a key ice growth process in mixed-phase clouds that can rapidly increase particle mass and fall speed, significantly modulating precipitation efficiency, cloud lifetime, and resulting cloud radiative effects. Observational constraints on where riming occurs, however, remain sparse outside field campaigns and regional studies. The Earth Cloud, Aerosol, and Radiation Explorer (EarthCARE) carries the first spaceborne Doppler Cloud Profiling Radar (CPR). From its Doppler measurements, Level-2 processing derives an estimate of hydrometeor sedimentation velocity. We identify riming in stratiform clouds across the CPR’s near-global observations from sharp downward increases in retrieved sedimentation velocity. The detection threshold is derived from ice and snow regions where the Atmospheric Lidar (ATLID) signal remains unextinguished and no supercooled liquid water (SLW) is detected, separating the rapid fall speed increases associated with riming from those produced by vapor deposition and aggregation alone. We evaluate the detections in shallow mixed-phase clouds over ocean, where SLW amount and vertical extent can be more reliably constrained. They concentrate within the estimated SLW layer and become increasingly common as SLW amount increases. Riming probability frequently exceeds 50% within the layer once SLW path surpasses about 200 g m−2. Furthermore, aircraft particle imagery acquired during the EarthCARE overpass reveals rimed particles within and below detected riming regions, but predominantly unrimed crystals and aggregates in regions where little riming was detected. Ultimately, we provide the first near-global distribution of riming in stratiform clouds. This new observational constraint opens the way to examining how riming varies with cloud regime and meteorological environment and to evaluating its representation in weather and climate models.

494464.title: A Global Cold Wave Tracking Dataset, 1982–2024
494464.authors: Jianfeng Li, PNNL, Richland, WA; and L. R. Leung, K. Balaguru, and T. Chakraborty
494464.abstract: In contrast to heatwaves characterized by abnormally high temperatures, cold waves are periods of unusually cold temperatures that can strain public health systems, elevate energy demand, damage infrastructure, and disrupt ocean ecosystems and the aquatic economy. However, despite their societal relevance, their climatological characteristics remain understudied at the global scale. To address this gap, we develop a global tracking dataset of cold waves for 1982–2024 using a modified TempestExtremes framework and two observational products: NOAA OI SST v2.1 high‑resolution sea‑surface temperatures and the CPC global unified terrestrial surface temperature dataset. A cold wave is defined as a continuous spatiotemporal object lasting at least five days with negative temperature anomalies and a spatial coverage of at least 4×104 km2. Temperature anomalies are computed as deviations from the 10th‑percentile threshold of the daily temperature series from 1982 to 2024 after removing seasonal cycles and long‑term trends. We generate five versions of this dataset using distinct deseasonalization and detrending methods, and each version is further split into two components—one based on daily maximum 2‑m terrestrial temperature and the other on daily minimum temperature—yielding ten subsets tailored to diverse research and societal applications. These ten subsets exhibit consistent behavior across several cold‑wave statistics. Across all subsets, the annual number of events ranges from 927 to 1121 yr-1, and the mean lifetime is about 11 days. Annual spatial patterns of accumulated duration, event count, intensity, and spatial coverage broadly resemble those of heatwaves tracked using a similar approach—for example, marine regions exhibit higher accumulated duration but lower event counts than land areas due to the larger size and longer lifetimes of marine cold waves. Terrestrial cold and heat waves have larger intensities than their marine counterparts, reflecting the thermal inertia of water bodies. Globally, both cold and heat waves occur most frequently in January–March and the second most frequently in July–September. High‑latitude terrestrial regions experience more cold and heat waves than low‑latitude regions. Nevertheless, cold waves differ from heatwaves in several respects: (i) they are generally smaller within the same region; (ii) extremely intense cold waves can propagate into low‑latitude terrestrial areas more readily; and (iii) their detection is less sensitive to detrending choices. From 1982 to 2024, the dataset reveals consistent negative trends in cold wave event counts and positive trends in lifetimes across all ten subsets, whereas comparable trends in heatwaves become significant only when detrending is applied during temperature-anomaly computation. This long‑term observational dataset establishes a foundation for continued investigation into the formation mechanisms of cold waves.

494465.title: The INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE)
494465.authors: David A. Peterson, NRL, Monterey, CA; and N. P. Lareau and O. V. Kalashnikova
494465.abstract: The INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE) will constrain the role of pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) in the Earth system and characterize their physical links to extreme wildfire behavior. INSPYRE will test the hypothesis that: Increasing wildfire size and intensity will amplify pyroCb-driven smoke injection into the stratosphere resulting in measurable changes in Earth’s radiative balance. INSPYRE will address three science questions that establish links and feedbacks between the physical processes enabling pyroCb initiation, smoke injection into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS), and downstream consequences: (1) Which fires produce pyroCbs and why? (2) What mechanisms determine if a pyroCb will directly inject smoke into the stratosphere, and how much smoke is directly injected? (3) How do pyroCb-injected smoke plumes modify UTLS composition and radiation budget? INSPYRE will provide sustained measurements and modeling of co-evolving fire and pyroCb processes including fire energetics, plume development, pyroCb cloud properties, and smoke plume evolution. Measurements will span the spatial and temporal scales of pyroconvection, including non-pyroCb plumes, plumes capped by pyrocumulus, active pyroCbs, and downstream smoke plumes in the UTLS. The NASA ER-2 will be used in combination with the NSF/NCAR GV, along with ground-based measurements and support from modeling and forecasting teams. This presentation will provide an overview of the 2026 field deployment, as well as schedules and plans for 2027.

494468.title: Exploring Nonlinear Data Assimilation for Quantifying Indian-Atlantic Ocean Exchange
494468.authors: Hao-Lun Yeh, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and P. J. van Leeuwen
494468.abstract: The exchange of water from the Indian Ocean into the South Atlantic plays a key role in shaping global ocean circulation and the climate system. This exchange originates at the Agulhas Retroflection, where the current sheds Agulhas rings, eddies, and filaments, making the region highly turbulent and intermittent. Because these mesoscale dynamics are strongly nonlinear, both quantifying the exchange and understanding fundamental mechanisms that drive it remain substantial challenges. Our research uses a fully nonlinear data assimilation method, the Particle Flow Filter (PFF), to create a comprehensive ocean reanalysis specifically focusing on the Agulhas Retroflection area south of Africa. The PFF is implemented in the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) system, coupled with the MOM6 ocean model through the Sea-ice Ocean and Coupled Analysis (SOCA) system. MOM6 is run on a global OM4 0.25-degree rotated tripolar grid, with 5 km high resolution between South Africa and Antarctica. XBT and Argo float data, mooring data from several deployments, and satellite data, such as SWOT, across five years will be assimilated into the system. Results will be compared against the Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter experiments to demonstrate the advantages of the PFF in handling nonlinear dynamics.

494469.title: Global In-Situ Observations Reveal Aviation’s Impact on the Stratosphere
494469.authors: Andrew Rollins, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and A. Ahern, C. A. Brock, Z. Decker, S. D. Eastham, C. Gurganus, A. Kupc, M. Lyu, G. Novak, P. Rickly, J. P. Schwarz, T. Thornberry, E. Waxman, and C. Williamson
494469.abstract: Civil aviation is a source of continuous injection of combustion biproducts into the lower stratosphere including aerosols and aerosol precursor gasses. Key emissions include sulfur dioxide, NOx and fine particulates. While relative changes in the lower stratosphere due to aviation may be substantial and impactful both for climate and stratospheric ozone, these changes cannot be quantified using existing remote-sensing instruments, and therefore would go undetected without geographically-expansive in-situ observations. Airborne science missions such at the 2015-2018 NASA Atmospheric Tomography (ATom) mission are ideal and indispensable for discovering, illustrating, and quantifying the impact of such processes which have broad impacts on atmospheric chemistry. Using aircraft-based measurements including those from ATom and spanning ten years and a wide geographical region, we have mapped the vertical and latitudinal extent of civil aviation’s sulfur dioxide (SO2) and aerosol impact on the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UT/LS). Our analysis shows that SO2 is a key and persistent signature of aviation emissions in the northern LS which generate a roughly fivefold enhancement in stratospheric SO2. The in-situ observations show that atmospheric perturbations due to the current fleet include ubiquitous and dramatic increases in SO2 and changes in aerosol number and size distributions throughout the northern LS. Direct emissions of particles in jet exhaust are unlikely to explain the observed aerosol concentrations, and instead new particle formation from diluted trace gas emissions from aviation in the stratosphere likely contributes to increased numbers of nucleation and accumulation mode particles. These observations have important consequences for the understanding the aerosol optical depth of the stratosphere in its current state, and additionally under stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) climate intervention scenarios. The quantification of aviation’s impact on the stratosphere was not a mission objective from ATom, Nonetheless, this story illustrates one impactful example of an unanticipated advancement in the understanding of the atmosphere which was only made possible by repeated sampling of the atmosphere over multiple years, using a suite of cutting-edge in-situ instruments. In this presentation I will discuss the details of aviation’s impact on the stratosphere, as well as other outstanding and emerging questions in atmospheric chemistry which could be best advanced by an ATom-like mission in the future.

494471.title: Integrating Social Vulnerability in Climate-Resilient Flood Infrastructure Planning
494471.authors: Kwabena O Asante, GEI Consultants, Inc., Rancho Cordova, CA
494471.abstract: People with fewer social, physical, or financial resources face greater challenges before, during, and after a flood. Communities with higher concentrations of socially vulnerable populations also tend to lag behind in their efforts to implement resilient infrastructure solutions in a changing climate. This presentation describes efforts undertaken to identify and map socially vulnerable communities living in floodplains in California's Central Valley. The efforts aim to quantify the current and future flood risk outcomes for socially vulnerable communities, and ensure that they are not overlooked in regional flood management and mitigation planning. The development of a flood-specific social vulnerability index incorporating multiple indicators is described. The index is integrated into flood risk assessment models to evaluate damage and life loss under current and future climate scenarios. The performance of the flood protection infrastructure improvements in communities with higher social vulnerability is evaluated and compared with other parts of the system. The results are informing the planning of multi-decadal infrastructure and non-structural solutions in the 2027 Update of the Central Valley Flood Protection Plan.

494473.title: Strategic Priorities and Upcoming Research Opportunities in the NOAA WPO Subseasonal-to-Seasonal (S2S) Program
494473.authors: Christine Bassett, NOAA, Bethesda, MD; and M. Orr Hoeflich and M. Olsen
494473.abstract: Subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecasts provide critical decision support for water resource management, agricultural planning, energy grid operations, and emergency response. Guided by the priorities in the Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Act, the NOAA Weather Program Office (WPO) S2S Program supports research to advance forecast skill and predictability on two-week to two-year timescales. By partnering with universities, NOAA laboratories, and National Weather Service operational centers, the S2S Program aims to accelerate advances in S2S predictability. This presentation provides an overview of the S2S Program’s strategic priorities and outlines upcoming funding priorities centered around fostering collaborative research across the weather enterprise. Attendees will gain insight into overarching program goals, future competition themes, and pathways to collaborate with NOAA in advancing national S2S forecasting capabilities.

494474.title: Reliability of Extreme Ocean Surface Wind Observations: Unit- and Installation-Specific Errors in NOAA’s SFMR Fleet
494474.authors: Zorana Jelenak, UCAR, Springfield, VA; and H. Holbach
494474.abstract: Ocean surface winds govern air–sea momentum exchange and are critical to tropical-cyclone prediction, yet they are difficult to observe in high-wind, heavy-rain conditions. NOAA’s airborne Stepped Frequency Microwave Radiometers (SFMRs) retrieve surface wind speed and rain rate from multichannel C-band brightness temperatures along hurricane-reconnaissance flight tracks. In 2024, inconsistencies among the three P-3 units led to suspension of their operational dissemination and assimilation. We combined flight reanalysis with laboratory testing in 2026 to determine how radiometric errors affect this high-wind record. Three distinct mechanisms were identified. One unit exhibited a reversal in its frequency channels; per-channel offsets derived at 5 °C removed the reversal and transferred to 10 and 20 °C. A second error appeared as a 0.8 K spectral tilt that increased with target temperature and survived recalibration at any single temperature. Reverting a June 2024 coefficient change corrected milder flight cases but left residual channel differences of 0.6–2.3 K in the most severe cases. The remaining warm-up error was related more closely to measured internal temperature than to time after power-on. A per-channel nonlinear laboratory correction reduced mean absolute error during the first 30 minutes from 2.48 to 0.05 K. Temperature-ramp tests identified a radiometric lag near four minutes; accounting for it reduced hysteresis loops of 8–17 K to less than 0.3 K. Flight data from the 2026 season will determine whether these corrections transfer to wind retrievals and historical observations. A third signature was associated with aircraft installation. A reflection with an inferred path length near 10 cm changed amplitude between installations and disappeared when another SFMR occupied the same airframe, showing that bench calibration cannot guarantee post-installation performance. We recommend post-installation verification and real-time monitoring of channel spread, drift, and instrument health. Aggregate dropsonde comparisons met mission wind requirements but did not expose these internal errors. Reliable extreme-wind observations therefore require validation of individual channels, instrument state, and installation effects—not only agreement of final wind products with aggregate thresholds. This framework supports SFMR use in operational decisions and validation of satellite and model-based ocean surface wind products.

494476.title: Do Meteorological and Energy-System Evaluations of Statistical Downscaling Agree? A Comprehensive Assessment over ERCOT
494476.authors: Ziqi Wei, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA; and M. F. Howland
494476.abstract: It is essential to account for meteorological uncertainty when planning low-carbon, least-cost energy systems that will rely heavily on wind and solar power generation. However, a primary bottleneck in planning under meteorological uncertainty, driven by internal variability, model uncertainty, and long-term climate change, is the construction of sufficiently diverse and representative weather realizations that capture the kilometer-scale resolution necessary for both renewable generation and demand. Traditional numerical weather prediction (NWP) models can generate reliable data, but running sufficient ensemble realizations that capture modeling and climate uncertainty is typically out of reach. On the other hand, emerging statistical downscaling methods offer an opportunity to generate sufficient quantities of high-resolution realizations at lower cost, but incur additional uncertainty by not capturing physical processes directly. To elucidate the energy systems modeling uncertainty caused by statistical downscaling, we conduct a comprehensive assessment of statistical downscaling methods over the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) power grid region within the historical record. We compare a broad and extensible set of statistical downscaling approaches, including interpolation with quantile-based correction, such as Bias-Correction Spatial Disaggregation (BCSD) and Quantile Delta Mapping (QDM), a Multivariate Adaptive Constructed Analogs (MACA)-style method with shared or variable-specific hourly disaggregation, random-forest (RF) a posteriori correction, and the pretrained sup3rCC generative adversarial network (GAN). The 4-km hourly fields from the Wind Integration National Dataset Toolkit (WTK), generated by the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, and National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) serve as the high-resolution reference data for wind speed, solar irradiance, temperature, and other critical meteorological variables that affect energy systems. We use the statistical methods to downscale input European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis Version 5 (ERA5) aggregated to daily temporal resolution and approximately 100-km spatial resolution, which is commensurate with the spatiotemporal resolution of widely-available climate model data, with each method outputting 4-km hourly for evaluation. The resulting meteorological predictions are evaluated at four connected levels. First, statistical accuracy is assessed using conventional moment-based and distributional metrics. Second, physical consistency is examined through basic feasibility, scaling consistency, and multivariable consistency. Third, the downscaled fields are converted into renewable energy capacity factors and electricity demand, and their accuracy is quantified. Fourth, these power generation and demand predictions are propagated through energy system planning (capacity expansion) and dispatch models to compare power-system decision accuracy, including investment, siting, operations, costs, and reliability outcomes. This work receives financial support from the University Mohammed VI Polytechnic--MIT Research Program (UMRP). The authors thank Dr. Liying Qiu and Dr. Rahman Khorramfar for methodological guidance and support with the modeling framework. Computational resources were provided by the Engaging cluster at the MIT Office of Research Computing and Data (ORCD).

494479.title: GEMS Ozone Evaluation Using Consecutive Summertime Ozonesonde Measurements During the 2021–2022 ACCLIP Campaigns
494479.authors: Hyungyu Kang, Particle Pollution Research and Management Center, Kongju, Korea, Republic of (South); Kongju Natioanl University, Kongju, Korea, Republic of (South); and S. B. Oh, J. Kim, J. Bak, J. H. Koo, S. S. Park, W. J. Lee, S. A. Shin, and J. Park
494479.abstract: This study evaluated how well the Geostationary Environment Monitoring Spectrometer (GEMS) captures daily ozone variability during the Asian summer monsoon, using 62 daily ozonesonde measurements obtained at the Anmyeon station (36.54°N, 126.33°E) during the pre-ACCLIP (2021) and ACCLIP (2022) campaigns. Daily ozone variability across the troposphere and lower stratosphere is closely linked to Asian monsoon circulations and synoptic weather events, such as Rossby wave breaking and tropical cyclones. GEMS validation against ozonesonde measurements revealed substantial improvements in version 3 (v3) compared to version 2 (v2). GEMS versus ozonesonde total column ozone regression slopes increased from 0.78 to 1.14 (2021) and from 0.48 to 0.83 (2022), indicating improved daily variability. Layer-resolved evaluation over the lower troposphere (LT; 0–10 km), the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS; 10–20 km), and the middle stratosphere (MS; 20–30 km) showed the greatest v3 improvement in the LT, where correlations with ozonesonde increased from 0.56 to 0.74 (2021) and from 0.18 to 0.66 (2022). Consistent with these statistics, the lower-tropospheric ozone overestimation observed in v2 was reduced in v3 in the profile comparison. Process-based case studies of major synoptic events further supported these findings. GEMS v3 better captured the ozonesonde-consistent signatures of the 2021 stratosphere–troposphere exchange–related high-ozone intrusion and 2022 typhoon-related low-ozone episodes that were poorly represented in v2. Spatially, GEMS v3 showed more realistic ozone patterns and reduced positive bias in the troposphere than did v2. Overall, the improved v3 product more consistently reproduces observed daily ozone variability across the key vertical layers, supporting its use in studies on transport processes and regional air quality variability over East Asia.

494480.title: Field Deploying Complex Optical Systems for Long Term Operation
494480.authors: Genevieve Faria, NCAR, Bouler, CO; NSF NCAR, Center Green Dr., CO; and B. Crane, K. Gelatt, S. M. Spuler, R. A. Stillwell, and M. Hayman
494480.abstract: Continuous, broadly-distributed, high-quality observations of thermodynamic variables are vital for improving numerical weather prediction and boundary layer research. Of the many technologies that can contribute scientific quality observations, differential absorption lidar (DIAL) and high spectral resolution lidar (HSRL) show promise due to their continuous, quantitative, and fundamentally range resolved observations. DIAL and HSRL technologies have historically leveraged complex laser systems that require well controlled environmental conditions. As a result, DIAL and HSRL have historically been difficult to make robust for long term observations and for a field environment. Over the past 12 years, NSF NCAR has been developing the MicroPulse Differential Absorption Lidar (MPD), which is a field deployable lidar system that leverages both DIAL and HSRL using semiconductor lasers. Semiconductor lasers have lessened the requirement for well controlled laboratory conditions, but have not alleviated it completely. Consequently, the infrastructure needed to support the lidar is still very important to consider. In this presentation, we will describe the infrastructure needed to field deploy the MPD as well as lessons learned from its past field deployments.

494486.title: Learning Sparse HRRR 1-h Accumulated Precipitation with a U-Net: Roles of Physically Motivated Predictors and Rain-Aware Sampling
494486.authors: Oscar V Chimborazo, Howard University, Washington, DC; and S. Chiao
494486.abstract: Spatial intermittency challenges precipitation learning because domain-wide losses are dominated by dry pixels. We use controlled U-Net experiments to examine how training-patch sampling and thermodynamic information affect learning of High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) 1-h accumulated precipitation (APCP). At this stage, both the predictors and target are HRRR model fields. These experiments are intended to establish and refine the workflow before extending it to use observational precipitation as the target. We use hourly HRRR forecast-hour-1 fields from 1 January through 29 February 2024 on the native 3-km (1799 × 1059) grid. Composite reflectivity (REFC) and precipitable water (PWAT) are the base predictors. Training uses 256 × 256 patches, log1p-transformed APCP, L1 loss in log space, and a time-ordered split of 48 training days followed by 12 validation days. Full-domain evaluation is independent of training-patch sampling; only 4.87% of validation pixels contain at least 0.1 mm of APCP. We compared Uniform and rain-aware sampling in two independent experiments, each comprising 100 matched seed pairs, with only the training-patch sampler differing between paired runs. Analysis of these experiments showed that a terminal output rectified linear unit (ReLU) can cause training to collapse, leaving the model predicting zero precipitation throughout the domain. In subsequent experiments, we removed the terminal ReLU and used a linear output layer, imposing nonnegativity only after converting outputs from log space to precipitation for evaluation. Under this corrected architecture with centered 2-m temperature (TMP2m) included, a separate validation comparison using the best epoch from each of 100 matched pairs found that rain-aware sampling reduced all-pixel MAE by 1.00% (paired-bootstrap 95% CI: 0.30%–1.68%). To test predictor contribution, we added TMP2m to REFC and PWAT and evaluated 100 matched seed pairs over all grid points across 288 validation hours. Adding TMP2m reduced the ensemble-mean full-domain all-pixel and rainy-pixel MAEs by 2.83% and 1.68%, respectively. Paired-seed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for both mean differences excluded zero. TMP2m produced lower error in 89 of 100 pairs for all-pixel MAE and 74 of 100 pairs for rainy-pixel MAE. Results to date show modest ensemble-mean validation-error reductions from adding TMP2m in full-domain evaluation and from rain-aware sampling in the separate best-epoch comparison. Ongoing work evaluates additional physically motivated HRRR predictors using the same controlled, matched-seed framework to better characterize the role of predictor selection in learning sparse precipitation.

494490.title: Spatial Gradient of Sea State Driven by Internal Solitary Waves Observed by SWOT
494490.authors: Wyatt Conger, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and R. S. Du and B. Villas Boas
494490.abstract: Internal solitary waves are large-amplitude ocean interior waves that have distinct surface-height and surface-velocity structures. The recent Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission provides unprecedented, simultaneous measurements of sea surface height anomaly (SSHA) and significant wave height (SWH) at submesoscales (O(1-10 km)). This presents new opportunities for studying the dynamics of internal wave-surface wave interactions, compared to more traditional optical and synthetic aperture radar observations. While previous studies have demonstrated SWOT’s potential for studying internal solitary waves using its SSHA observations, the signature of internal solitary waves on SWH remains under-explored. Our analysis of SWOT’s synergistic SSHA and SWH observations reveals a consistent spatial relationship between anomalies associated with internal solitary waves, while the offset and sign between the two signals vary among events. We interpret the observed data through the theory of large-amplitude internal waves and surface wave physics. Our study provides a new perspective on the long-standing investigation of the surface manifestation of internal solitary waves by using novel satellite remote sensing observations. Additionally, these observations provide a unique evaluation of the SWOT SWH and SSHA products under the regime of strong spatial gradients, which could lead to improvement in the data products themselves.

494491.title: Building Confidence in Emerging Earth Observations
494491.authors: Zorana Jelenak, UCAR, Springfield, VA; and J. J. Braun, H. Mauriello, and C. L. Bruyere
494491.abstract: Commercial satellite constellations are expanding the volume and diversity of Earth observations available for meteorological research and operations. Realizing their value requires a scalable way to communicate how thoroughly an instrument and its products have been calibrated, validated, intercompared, and characterized for a particular application. We present a community-developed framework that builds on existing standards and subject-matter expertise to translate calibration and validation evidence into transparent, reproducible statements of data confidence. The framework uses a two-stage architecture. The first stage evaluates scientific confidence by considering both the rigor and scope of the calibration and validation process and the measured performance of the data. Evidence includes instrument and signal integrity, geolocation and observing geometry, radiometric calibration, measurement-level physics, data quality, algorithm provenance, verification datasets, constellation representativeness, uncertainty characterization, transparency, and continuity monitoring. Separate indices for validation rigor and measured performance are combined so that favorable performance statistics are interpreted in the context of the evidence supporting them. The second stage evaluates fitness for a defined use, recognizing that requirements for numerical weather prediction, tropical cyclone analysis, marine operations, and climate applications are not identical. We illustrate the framework through applications to Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R) measurements and derived products from Spire and Muon Space. Placing these datasets within a common evidence structure enables consistent assessment from calibrated observables through geophysical retrievals while retaining differences in instrument design, constellation sampling, processing, and product objectives. The applications demonstrate how cross-instrument and cross-provider intercomparison can be used together with independent reference data to distinguish measurement performance from effects associated with sampling, processing choices, environmental dependence, and the scope of available validation evidence. They also show how previously completed tests can be carried forward, how remaining evidence needs can be converted into targeted next steps, and how data maturity can be assessed progressively rather than through a single pass-or-fail determination. This approach creates a shared technical language for data providers, calibration and validation teams, and operational users. By making evidence, uncertainties, and application-specific requirements more visible, it can strengthen confidence in emerging observing systems, focus validation resources where they add the most value, and support faster, responsible use of commercial observations in meteorological decision-making.

494492.title: An Investigation of Regional and Seasonal Convective Mass Flux Characteristics by Storm Mode in CONUS404
494492.authors: Justin Hassel, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and K. L. Rasmussen, Ph.D. and H. Yu
494492.abstract: The organization of deep convection varies substantially across geographic regions, seasons, and background environments, with isolated convective cores and larger mesoscale systems contributing differently to precipitation, severe weather, and atmospheric transport. NASA’s INvestigation of Convective Updrafts (INCUS) mission will provide the first tropics-wide spaceborne observations of convective mass flux (CMF), yet the climatological distribution of CMF and its dependence on storm organization remains largely unquantified. This limits the context available for interpreting these observations across different convective regimes. We therefore aim to quantify the regional, seasonal, and diurnal characteristics of upward CMF and its contributions among convective storm modes. To address this gap, we use the 43-year, 4-km CONUS404 hydroclimate reanalysis to partition hourly, vertically integrated CMF among Deep Convective Cores (DCCs), Wide Convective Cores (WCCs), and Deep and Wide Convective Cores (DWCCs) using TRMM-heritage storm mode definitions applied to simulated three-dimensional reflectivity. Across the conterminous United States, convection occupies less than 1% of the spatiotemporal domain but contributes approximately 8% of total upward mass flux, highlighting the disproportionate role of localized convection in atmospheric transport. DCCs exhibit the greatest CMF intensity per unit area, while DWCCs provide the largest overall contribution among organized modes. The diurnal cycle reflects a transition from afternoon DCC-dominated convection toward increasing contributions from organized DWCCs during the evening and overnight hours, consistent with the upscale growth of convection. Storm mode composition also varies across seasons and regions, producing distinct CMF regimes across the subtropics and mid-latitudes and between land and water. These regional contrasts show that similar CMF contributions can arise from different combinations of storm mode frequency and intensity, with local DWCC contributions exceeding 60% in the South Plains during boreal spring before this dominance shifts to the Upper Plains by summer. These results demonstrate that the climatological distribution of CMF is strongly shaped by where, when, and in what organizational form convection occurs. This multi-decadal, storm-mode-resolved climatology provides a pre-launch baseline for interpreting INCUS observations and assessing how observed CMF varies across diverse convective regimes.

494493.title: Improved Representation of Photosynthetic Capacity in Noah-MP for Surface Energy and Water Flux Simulations
494493.authors: Peng Fu, Louisiana State Unviersity AgCenter, Baton Rouge, LA; Louisiana State University AgCenter, Baton Rouge, LA; and C. Qiu and C. He
494493.abstract: Photosynthesis regulates exchanges of water and energy between vegetation and the atmosphere through its coupling with stomatal conductance and transpiration. In Noah-MP, photosynthetic capacity is controlled primarily by the maximum carboxylation rate (Vcmax) and maximum electron transport rate (Jmax), which are commonly prescribed as fixed values for individual plant functional types. However, Vcmax and Jmax vary substantially across space and time in response to crop development and environmental conditions. This static representation may therefore limit the ability of Noah-MP to capture physiological controls on evapotranspiration (ET) and surface energy partitioning. This study will develop an observation-informed framework for dynamically representing photosynthetic capacity in Noah-MP. First, Vcmax and Jmax will be estimated from satellite observations using machine learning models trained with photosynthetic capacity derived from eddy covariance measurements. Long-term MODIS observations will be used to establish climatological patterns of photosynthetic capacity, while PACE hyperspectral observations will provide more accurate estimates of shorter-term variability. Deviations from the climatological baseline will then be related to satellite-derived vegetation state, phenology, and meteorological conditions to develop dynamic parameterizations of Vcmax and Jmax. These parameterizations will be implemented in Noah-MP and evaluated over soybean systems in Illinois, Iowa, and Louisiana. Simulations using dynamic versus conventional static photosynthetic capacity will be compared against observations to quantify impacts on ET, latent heat, and sensible heat fluxes. The study will provide a pathway for integrating satellite-constrained physiological variability into land surface models and will assess its importance for crop–atmosphere exchange.

494497.title: Development of a Dynamic CAPE-Based Convective Triggering Function: from Single-Column Model Testing to Global Earth System Model Application
494497.authors: Shaocheng Xie, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Tracy, CA
494497.abstract: Motivated by Randall et al. (1996), this work developed a dynamic convective available potential energy generation rate (dCAPE)-based convective triggering function using a single-column model (SCM) framework and observations from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program. The dCAPE trigger introduces an empirical dynamical constraint based on large-scale temperature and moisture advection to regulate the onset of deep convection. It assumes that deep convection occurs only when large-scale advection contributes positively to the existing CAPE. This constraint allows CAPE to accumulate before convection is initiated and links convective activity more closely to large-scale dynamical processes, including upward motion and low-level moisture convergence. The dCAPE trigger can therefore be considered as an empirical large‐scale parameterization of the dynamical triggering processes, including large‐scale upward motion, and warm and moist advection in the low levels. It also emphasizes convective persistence after initiation: convection can be maintained only when there is positive large-scale forcing, that is, under disturbed large-scale conditions. The dCAPE concept has since been extended to convective quasi-equilibrium closures used in traditional convection parameterizations. The dCAPE trigger and its variants have been implemented in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) and the operational weather prediction model of the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA), where they have improved simulations of precipitation and its diurnal cycle. This presentation will highlight the role of SCMs in linking field observations with Earth system model development, as advocated by Randall et al. (1996), and will present results from single-column simulations and applications in E3SM. Reference: Randall, D. A., K. Xu, R. J. C. Somerville, and S. Iacobellis, 1996: Single-Column Models and Cloud Ensemble Models as Links between Observations and Climate Models. J. Climate, 9, 1683–1697, https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0442(1996)009<1683:SCMACE>2.0.CO;2.

494503.title: Radar Observed Coastal Urban Effects on Isolated Thunderstorms
494503.authors: Jean Carlos Pena, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY
494503.abstract: Coastal cities face compound hazards from convective thunderstorms. This observational study aims to link potential urban boundary layer (UBL) influences on the rainfall and lightning cities experience by tracking multiple years of summer storms in Houston, TX. Isolated storm cells observed by NEXRAD operational radar are tracked using tobac, a feature detection algorithm. Lagrangian cell tracks are complemented by Houston Lightning Mapping Array and other field campaign data from the 2022 NSF-funded Convective-clouds Urban Boundary-layer Experiment (CUBE) and DOE Tracking Aerosol Convection interactions Experiment (TRACER) deployments. These datasets provide high-resolution lightning strike, frequent radiosonde, boundary layer profile, and surface flux observations to illuminate how the UBL may drive cloud differences. Reflectivity statistics of Lagrangian-tracked storm cells will demonstrate if the urban signal leads to differences in intensity, height, or duration. Preliminary profiler results for diurnal boundary layer patterns show that by late afternoon (1400 LT) a >1 K warmer, drier surface UBL corresponds to a >1.25 K cooler, more moist environment for urban cloud bases at 2.25 km. These differences drive non-precipitating urban cloud bases which are up to 1 km higher than their rural counterparts. This radar-based methodology may be used to trace how other cities with different morphologies respond to their weather, and their potential influence on flash floods, lightning, or other convective hazards.

494505.title: Sky Scouts: Assessing the Decarbonization Potential of Electric Vehicle Transition in Colorado’s Adams 12 Five Star Schools
494505.authors: Ansh Kumar, Rocky Top Middle School, Thornton, CO; and I. Sharma, A. Sharma, and R. Kumar
494505.abstract: Transportation remains a significant contributor to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions within municipal and educational infrastructures. For large school districts like Adams 12 Five Star Schools, the environmental footprint is shaped by diverse activities, including daily bus routing for thousands of students, staff commutes, and district-wide logistical operations. Understanding and quantifying these emissions is a critical first step toward achieving regional sustainability goals and mitigating local climate impacts. Our study develops a comprehensive GHG emissions inventory for transportation-related activities within the Adams 12 school district, using Rocky Top Mountain School as a case study. The inventory utilizes activity-based data to quantify emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), and nitrous oxide (N2O). We apply established emission factors to diverse fleet segments, including heavy-duty school buses and light-duty passenger vehicles used by staff and students. Following the baseline calculation, we will model a transition scenario where the district adopts Electric Vehicles (EVs) for its primary fleet. By demonstrating the potential for significant GHG reductions through EV adoption, the study will inform data-driven policy decisions for infrastructure investment and fleet management. Additionally, these efforts contribute to improved local air quality and the long-term health of the student population and the surrounding community.

494508.title: Deep Learning for ICESat-2 Atmospheric Lidar: Denoising, Cloud-Aerosol Discrimination, and a New Research Data Product
494508.authors: Joseph Gomes, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA
494508.abstract: We present a deep learning framework for enhancing ICESat-2 atmospheric observations through lidar signal denoising, layer detection, and cloud-aerosol discrimination. A U-Net convolutional neural network is trained using nighttime photon-count profiles augmented with realistic daytime background noise to reconstruct the underlying atmospheric signal. The reconstructed photon counts are converted to calibrated attenuated backscatter and analyzed using a second U-Net that performs pixel-wise atmospheric layer detection and cloud–aerosol discrimination. The resulting workflow preserves fine-scale layer structure and improves the identification of vertically stacked clouds and clouds embedded within aerosol. The presentation will conclude with ongoing development of an ICESat-2 research data product that combines denoised atmospheric profiles, calibrated backscatter, and machine-learning-derived layer and cloud–aerosol classifications for scientific applications.

494512.title: The Effects of Tropical-Extratropical Interactions on Snowstorms in the Central United States in a Changing Climate
494512.authors: Stephen Robert Foskey, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and P. E. Kirstetter and J. B. Basara
494512.abstract: Snowstorms are impactful events that can be destructive, causing loss of life and damage to property. At the same time, the water from snowstorms replenishes the soil when it melts, benefiting the hydrology of a region. The magnitude of these positive and negative impacts is likely to change in the future, as snowstorms are decreasing in frequency but increasing in intensity in the Central United States. However, preparing for snowstorms can be challenging due to predictability limitations at scales beyond a week. Tropical modes of climate variability, such as the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) and El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) have been shown to influence the amount of snowfall in the Central United States. MJO-induced convection over the Maritime Continent and the La Niña phase of ENSO have both been shown to be associated with increased snowfall in the Central United States. This study utilizes an event-based approach and examines how the MJO and ENSO affect individual snowstorms. In doing so, the frequency of snowstorms and characteristics of these storms such as their maximum accumulation, mean accumulation, area, volume, and location of maximum accumulation are all examined. Furthermore, trends in the effects of the MJO and ENSO on snowstorm characteristics over the past 45 years are quantified. Through this work, we seek to better determine how the MJO and ENSO impact snowstorms, with an aim towards future improvements in subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction of snowfall.

494517.title: BLT - The Nontraditional Coriolis Terms and Shallow Convection In LES and Parameterization
494517.authors: Hing Ong, Unaffiliated, Davis, CA; and V. E. Larson
494517.abstract: Trade-wind shallow convective clouds are important climate coolers because they reflect solar radiation and are widespread over tropical oceans. These cumuli bloom with a small areal fraction under a temperature inversion, but an additional layer of large-fraction stratocumuli will grow over the cumuli under a stronger inversion if the sea surface is cooler, marking a cloudiness regime transition modulating the climate cooling effect. The trade-wind cloudiness is driven by several physical processes, including subsidence, cloud radiative emission, and vertical turbulent mixing. However, previous studies omit the nontraditional Coriolis terms (NCTs), which can turn east–west turbulent activity into vertical owing to Earth’s rotation. This study comprises two parts, one with large-eddy simulations (LES) and the other with parameterization. The LES part of this study simulates the regime of stratocumulus-topped trade-wind cumuli in a case study and compares results with and without the NCTs. The results suggest that the NCTs substantially support the maintenance of the stratocumuli over cumuli. The NCTs enhance subcloud vertical turbulent activity, which then supplies more moisture flux to the cloud layer. Without the NCTs, the clouds yield insufficient radiative cooling against subsidence and entrainment warming, which causes the trade-wind inversion to descend. The inversion descending due to omitting the NCTs may be compensated by over-tuning cloud radiative parameters. The parameterization part of this study introduces the NCTs to the Cloud Layers Unified By Binormals (CLUBB) parameterization of clouds and turbulence. We design three single-column benchmarks to test the implementation of the NCTs in CLUBB. First, assuming that all except the Coriolis terms vanish on the right-hand side of the prognostic equations of the second-order moments of velocity, we derive an analytical solution in which the anisotropy of the moments rotates back to the initial state with a certain period. Our CLUBB results match this analytic benchmark. Second, assuming dry and neutrally stratified atmosphere with constant geostrophic winds, our results suggest that the NCTs make the Ekman layer deeper with geostrophic easterlies but shallower with westerlies. Third, under realistic conditions for the stratocumulus-topped trade-wind cumulus case, our CLUBB results are consistent with the LES. These benchmarks not only validate the Coriolis terms in CLUBB but also form a model hierarchy that aids our understanding of the effects of the NCTs on turbulence and convection. To summarize the LES and parameterization results, the NCTs enhance vertical turbulent activity in easterlies and suppress it in westerlies, marking a source of asymmetry in shallow convective systems.

494524.title: A Unified Deep-Learning Framework for Satellite Precipitation Estimation Across Land and Ocean
494524.authors: Yifan Yang, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and Y. Saqer and H. Chen
494524.abstract: Accurate precipitation estimation from geostationary satellites is important for providing spatially and temporally continuous observations, particularly over regions where ground-based measurements are limited or unavailable. However, satellite precipitation retrieval remains challenging because relationships between cloud-top observations and surface precipitation vary substantially across geographic regions and between land and ocean. In this study, we develop a deep-learning(DL)-based precipitation retrieval framework using geostationary satellite infrared observations and lightning information, and evaluate its applicability across both land and ocean environments. Over the land, precipitation observations from ground-based weather radars provide high-quality references for model development and evaluation, while ship-based precipitation observations are used to extend and assess retrieval capabilities over oceanic regions where radar coverage is unavailable. The framework is designed to improve precipitation detection and quantitative precipitation estimation while addressing changes in precipitation characteristics across different geographic domains. Results demonstrate the capability of the satellite-based DL approach to provide consistent precipitation estimates across diverse environments and highlight both the opportunities and challenges associated with extending retrieval algorithms from well-observed continental regions to data-sparse oceanic regions. This work represents a step toward a more unified satellite precipitation retrieval framework capable of supporting precipitation monitoring across land and ocean.

494526.title: Multidisciplinary Studies of Clouds and Precipitation Across a Coastal Urban Rural Gradient
494526.authors: Jean Carlos Pena, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY; and K. A. Potucek, M. Swain, S. Pal, E. J. Strobach, B. Demoz, S. Eagan, M. Deng, X. Li, Y. Pan, M. P. Jensen, J. E. Gonzalez-Cruz, and K. J. Davis
494526.abstract: A multi-institutional effort is underway to research the processes behind mid-latitude coastal precipitation. The Department of Energy (DOE) Coastal Urban Rural Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE) observed a range of events from summer thunderstorms to winter fronts using surface stations, surface-based remote sensing, radiosondes, flux anemometers, and laser disdrometers. The CoURAGE Precipitation sub-group spans researchers from the academic, federal, and private sectors. Efforts across synoptic- to canopy-scales fit mainly into three topics: precipitation processes, frontal passages & airmass dynamics, as well as land-surface influences on rainfall. Presented here are the highlights of scientific progress so far, spanning: a year-long calendar of campaign meteorology, drop size distributions across thunderstorm modes, thunderstorm surface convergence patterns, urban-frontal interactions, operational radar retrievals and campaign climatology, and a year-long urbanized forecast. Future research efforts will be discussed, highlighting the value of the dataset for an interagency model development workshop.

494527.title: Inferring Surface-Level Concentrations from Satellite-Based Column Measurements: Role of Atmospheric Boundary Layer Dynamics.
494527.authors: Sunil Baidar, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and R. Volkamer, S. S. Brown, B. J. Carroll, N. Malarich, W. A. Brewer, and C. Warneke
494527.abstract: Inferring surface-level concentrations from satellite-based column measurements of pollutants such as Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) is of tremendous interest to fill the gap in the ground monitoring network and associate exposure to air pollution with health risks. This interest has only increased with the advent of geostationary satellite measurements which provide hourly measurements at very high spatial resolution. However, inferring surface-level concentrations from satellite-based column measurements is challenging since satellite measurements are affected not only by emission sources, but also atmospheric boundary layer dynamics, topography, land use and time of day. Previous studies have found that satellite-inferred surface concentrations correlate well with in-situ observations but are biased low. Best agreements were observed over regions with flat terrain such as the U.S. Midwest and suburban sites away from major emission sources. In this study we use airborne measurements of column NO2, boundary layer in-situ NO2 and boundary layer dynamics in the New York metro area on the NOAA Twin Otter research aircraft during the Coastal Urban Plume Dynamics Study (CUPiDS) in summer 2023 to investigate the role of the local atmospheric boundary layer dynamics on the relationship between column and surface-level NO2 concentrations at a local/regional scale. Stacked flight legs above and inside the boundary layer were performed to measure column NO2 and boundary layer in-situ NO2 concentrations respectively, to explore this relationship. This near concurrent measurement in space and time probes our ability to infer ground-level concentrations from column measurement and tests the limitations and causes when the column-to-surface relationships break down. The ability of the TEMPO geostationary satellite instrument to capture spatial variability in complex urban areas of New York will also be evaluated.

494533.title: Evaluating Downscaling Uncertainty in High-Resolution Temperature Extremes and Regional Electricity Demand Projections
494533.authors: Deeksha Rastogi, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN; ORNL, Oak Ridge, TN; and H. Niu, S. C. Kao, and M. Ashfaq
494533.abstract: Temperature extremes are intensifying, increasing risks to public health and placing growing stress on electric power systems. Reliable regional impact assessments require high-resolution, long-term weather projections, yet the representation of temperature extremes remains sensitive to the choice of downscaling methodology. We analyze a 1/24° (~4 km) ensemble of downscaled Earth System Model (ESM) projections produced using one dynamical, two statistical, and two AI-based downscaling methods to characterize widespread and persistent hot and cold extremes across the 13 U.S. EIA-930 grid monitoring regions. We benchmark historical performance, quantify projected changes in extreme-event characteristics, and assess their implications for regional electricity demand. Across the ensemble, hot extremes become more intense, longer lasting, and more spatially extensive, while cold extremes become less intense and less frequent, with substantial regional variability. Although the overall direction of change is consistent across downscaling methods, the magnitude of projected changes varies considerably. Using variance decomposition and a Method Variability Index, we quantify the relative contributions of ESMs, downscaling methods, and reference observations to projection uncertainty. We further evaluate the implications of evolving temperature extremes for electricity demand using a Compound Load Stress Index. Our results identify where the choice of downscaling method influences grid-relevant projections and demonstrate the value of multi-method ensembles for supporting robust electricity system planning and resilience.

494534.title: Extreme Australian Wildfire Impact on Atmospheric Chemistry
494534.authors: Rebecca R. Buchholz, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and E. Keefe, W. Tang, L. K. Emmons, D. M. Leung, and H. Worden
494534.abstract: Smoke from the extreme Australian wildfire season in 2019/2020 was transported both regionally within the southeast of the continent, as well as at hemispheric scales. We use a combination of Earth system modeling and measurements to investigate the wildfire emission impacts on atmospheric chemistry. Primarily, we use the Community Atmosphere Model with chemistry (CAM-chem) within the NSF NCAR Community Earth System Model (CESM) to simulate sensitivity studies with and without fire emissions in the Australian region. We build on the HTAP-3 Fires multi-model intercomparison study to evaluate the 2019/2020 season relative to the historical record of Australian wildfires. Impacts of Australian wildfire on carbon monoxide (CO), a good tracer for wildfire smoke, as well as aerosols and ozone are highlighted. We also compare against satellite measurements, specifically the Measurements Of Pollution In The Troposphere (MOPITT) observations of CO, and the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) aerosol optical depth (AOD), to evaluate model performance.

494535.title: Multi-Pulse-Length Lidar: A Method to Simultaneously Improve Temporal and Spatial Resolution of Lidar Observations
494535.authors: Robert A. Stillwell, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Superior, CO; and M. Hayman and S. M. Spuler
494535.abstract: Continuous, broadly-distributed, high-quality observations of thermodynamic variables are needed by atmospheric scientists both for numerical weather prediction as well as process studies. In response to this need, we have been developing a field deployable lidar-based technology to measure absolute humidity and temperature leveraging differential absorption lidar (DIAL) and high spectral resolution lidar (HSRL). This system, the MicroPulse DIAL (MPD), leverages semiconductor lasers as its light source. Semiconductor lasers have a lot of desirable characteristics for atmospheric lidar including frequency stability, wide spectral coverage, reliability, energy efficiency, and low cost; their major drawback is low peak power. This tradeoff is similar to some design considerations present in modern radar systems, where influences other than peak power can drive hardware designs. One solution to low peak power is to use relatively long laser pulses, the cost of which is sacrificing range resolution as well as near field observations. For radar, pulse compression was introduced to address this trade but to our knowledge no analog is applied to lidar systems. We present a lidar-based method that allows us to emit a complex train of laser pulses that can be tailored to observational needs as well as a signal processing method to optimally combine data from pulses of different length. In this presentation, we will present multi-pulse length thermodynamic observations collected from instrument testing as well as from a recent field study at the DOE ARM Southern Great Plains (SGP) Central Facility in Oklahoma.

494537.title: Survey Results on Aurora Chasers' Preferences for Forecast Wording and Uncertainty Language
494537.authors: Vincent Ledvina, University of Alaska Fairbanks, NORTH POLE, AK; and T. Melnik, A. L. Williams, M. Kiczenski, E. MacDonald, L. Edson, C. Harris, and M. Cook
494537.abstract: Aurora chasers are a major public user group of space weather products and tools. Understanding preferences in forecast communication is important for public engagement, trust in science, and recognition of the societal value of space weather research. We conducted an IRB-approved online survey distributed through aurora-chasing communities and received 946 responses. Questions covered geography, chasing frequency, confidence in aurora science knowledge, forecast resources used, confidence in local news coverage, the impact of forecast uncertainty on chasing decisions, and preferred forecast wording. Multiple questions also collected open-ended responses, which we coded into themes. Self-reported aurora science knowledge confidence correlated with chasing activity level, and more frequent chasers reported substantially higher knowledge confidence in aurora science. Aurora chasing experience also correlated with preference for data streams used in decision-making, with more experienced chasers shifting from Kp to real-time solar wind data. Low-certainty forecasts affected the chasing decisions of casual and less frequent chasers more than those of frequent chasers, with the latter reporting they would likely chase regardless of certainty. In a forecast-format comparison, respondents preferred the more detailed forecast with explicit uncertainty discussion three to one, and more science-confident respondents chose wider CME arrival-time windows and reported lower confidence in precise 3-day Kp timing. Views on local news station coverage of space weather were mixed. The open-ended responses provided additional data about chasers’ approach to available information. Common themes included combining several resources for chasing decisions, relying on specific apps and websites, and trusting individual forecasters and social media groups alongside official products. Many weighed space weather data alongside cloud cover, moon phase, and their own schedules rather than a single number. The Kp index drew repeated criticism for being too coarse for real-time decision-making. On wording, respondents preferred defined levels of certainty over adjectives that read as the forecaster’s own judgment. To our knowledge, this is the first survey evaluating aurora chasers’ interaction with space weather data and forecasts. The sample does not represent the general public, but it shows that a survey of non-specialist users of space weather data can produce meaningful results that may inform communication strategies. Additional studies are

494540.title: Recent Changes in Dust-Rise Conditions over East Asian Dust Source Regions and Their Impacts on Dust Emission Modeling
494540.authors: Jae-Hyeong Lee, Kongju National University, Gongju, Chungcheongnam-do, South korea; and S. H. Lee and J. H. Cho
494540.abstract: Climate change has altered surface and meteorological conditions in East Asian dust source regions. This study examines threshold 10-m wind speeds between recent (2014-2022) and past (1998-2006) periods across four soil types (Gobi, Sand, Loess, Mixed), using ground meteorological observations. Threshold wind speeds, which typically range from 4.5 to 8.5 m s-1 depending on the soil type, increased by 0.5-3.0 m s-1 in most regions, particularly in the Loess, while changes in Sand areas were minimal. These increases are consistent with reduced dust occurrence and enhanced vegetation cover. Incorporating updated thresholds into the Asian Dust Aerosol Model, version 2 (ADAM2), reduced dust emission fluxes by ~9.0% overall, with decreases of 7.9% in the Gobi, 27.0% in the Loess, and 18.9% in Mixed soils. Model accuracy improved by up to 5% and bias scores decreased by up to 75, particularly in spring, underscoring the importance of realistic threshold wind speed conditions for dust emission modeling.

494547.title: Summertime Spatiotemporal Patterns of Nitrogen Oxides (NOx) and Ozone (O3) during the Colorado Front Range OZone Éxperiment (FROZÉ 2025)
494547.authors: Daniela Carolina Guevara, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and B. McGuire, M. Davis, A. Marsavin, J. Stickney, A. Sullivan, Y. Zhou, J. Ban, E. Cope, W. Permar, D. Ketcherside, A. Deters, L. Tan, E. Mattson, A. Frazier, D. Welsh, T. Moore, B. C. Sive, J. L. Collett Jr., L. Hu, and E. V. Fischer
494547.abstract: The Northern Front Range region of Colorado is designated as a serious nonattainment area for the 2015 8-hour ozone (O3) National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS). As part of the July-August 2025 Colorado Front Range OZone Éxperiment (FROZÉ), an Aerodyne dual channel Cavity Attenuated Phase Shift Monitor (CAPS NOx-NO2) and a 2B 211 O3 monitor were deployed in a mobile laboratory to quantify regional gradients and daily variability of nitrogen oxides (NOx = NO + NO2) and O3 across the Front Range. Our analysis for smoke-free data includes: (1) a total oxidant approach to determine NO2/NOx and NOx emission factors (EFNOx) from vehicle exhaust plumes and a comparison to other U.S. cities and the GRA2PES emission inventory; (2) a plume-filtering method to generate regional maps of NOx and O3; and (3) weekday-weekend differences in NOx and O3 using both mobile measurements and stationary observations. A total of 26 driving missions were conducted over 27 days, collecting ~131 hours of mobile observations. Preliminary results show an on-road NO2/NOx plume ratio of 14.6 ± 9.9%. Even after removing near-vehicle plumes, NOx concentrations showed an east-west and north-south gradient of ~7–11 ppbv. Both mobile and stationary measurements in the region show maximum abundances of NOx at La Salle Tower, an area near extensive oil and gas development, and at the CAMP site in downtown Denver, while the lowest are at the Rocky Mountain National Park - Longs Peak and the Fort Collins - West sites. Areas with higher NOx levels experience the largest reductions in pollution on weekends compared to weekdays.

494548.title: Identifying SST Precursors for Forecast Skill Windows of East Asian Winter Cold Surges
494548.authors: Xiaolei Liu, Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences, Beijing, 11, China; and J. Su and H. WANG
494548.abstract: Improving the Subseasonal-to-Seasonal (S2S) forecast skill for East Asian winter cold surges remains a grand challenge in operational me teorology. Utilizing ECMWF hindcast data, this study systematically identifies “high-skill windows” for week-3 cold surge forecasts. Results demonstrate that relying solely on atmospheric precursors leads to a high False Alarm Ratio (FAR) in identifying high-skill windows. Instead, stable boundary forcings from Sea Surface Temperature (SST) anomalies play a crucial modulating role in these high-skill windows. A “warm-west/cold-east” North Pacific SST dipole emerges as a consistent precursor during both El Niño and La Niña events. Under La Niña conditions, the SST dipole actively preconditions the atmospheric response; conversely, under El Niño conditions, initial atmospheric internal variability drives the formation of the SST dipole, which subsequently provides persistent oceanic feedback to anchor the circulation. Furthermore, this SST dipole can enhance subseasonal forecast skill via two dynamic pathways: (1) During El Niño and specific La Niña years, the SST dipole excites downstream Rossby wave trains that form a “coupled resonance” with Barents-Kara sea ice loss, providing robust predictable signals by sustaining Ural Blocking. (2) During other La Niña years, coherent interference from cold SST anomalies in the Indian Ocean confines wave energy to the North Pacific-Polar region, forcing a quasi-stationary meridional dipole structure that directly steers polar cold air southward. The SST-based screening technique effectively filters out low-skill cases lacking boundary support, achieving a high Hit Rate in specific La Niña years. These findings empower operational forecasters to transition from “blind forecasting” to “dynamic situational awareness”, enabling a priori pre- screening of forecast reliability based on SST precursors. This approach holds profound practical value for improving subseasonal decision-making and disaster prevention.

494550.title: Surface Visibility Forecasting and Risk Assessment for Maritime Operations
494550.authors: Kathryn Lynn Verlinden, Applied Ocean Sciences LLC, Clackamas, OR
494550.abstract: Inclement weather costs the shipping and transportation industry $3.5 billion each year, with hundreds of millions of dollars lost annually due to shipping transit delays alone. Small fishing and recreational vessels, which can have smaller radar footprints are also impact is low visibility overlaps with sea states inducing higher radar clutter. Visibility is a critical factor in maritime operations, impacted by various atmospheric conditions such as fog, heavy drizzle, large waves and spray under strong wind conditions, and other obstructions. Applied Ocean Sciences is developing a surface visibility prediction model by incorporating numerical weather prediction forecast fields and surface observations into a machine learning framework that takes into consideration unique fog formation processes at different locations (e.g., radiative, advective, upslope) and local influences on visibility.
