Current operational numerical weather prediction models traditionally parameterize temperature, moisture, and aerosol concentrations (if available), and struggle to accurately forecast visibility owing to the complexity of atmospheric dynamics at small scales and the high vertical resolution required near the surface. Due to these known issues, many numerical weather prediction visibility forecasts remain experimental and are not to be relied upon for operational uses. Our model outperforms current publicly available visibility forecasts with the goal of a producing high-fidelity forecasts with reliability to incorporate into planning for maritime operations. Expanding upon a generic risk assessment framework, using fuzzy-logic rules to classify probabilistic information based on the severity of the environmental states we create risk assessment codes. Probabilistic forecasts of visibility and additional meteorological and oceanographic fields are categorized utilizing international standards and industry-accepted definitions to classify their impacts on maritime operations. The rules governing the risk assessment codes have the ability to integrate criteria derived from multiple variables and consider forecast quality for each parameter. The resultant risk assessment codes are incorporated into a risk assessment tool for data dissemination, interaction, and integration by stakeholders and end-users. Validation datasets include historical maritime accident reports, pilot reports, and post-processed static imagery. A proprietary shipping economics model is used to explore, quantify, and communicate the impacts of reduced visibility on maritime operations. Initially, AOS is testing all off the models off the Gulf Coast and across the Caribbean Sea due to the importance of this region to US commerce and recreation.

494557.title: Correlation of In-Situ Coronal Mass Ejection Observations from Upstream to the First Lagrange Point
494557.authors: Caitlin Marie Magdanz, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte, NC; and E. Butler, A. Pacini, and E. Adamson
494557.abstract: Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) are the main driver behind geomagnetic storms which affect sectors such as power grids, satellite operations, aviation, and human spaceflight. While remote sensing observations (e.g, via coronagraphs) are indispensable for early detection and tracking of these events, they do not provide insight on the structure of the magnetic fields of these structures before they reach Lagrange Point One (L1), which is the primary factor for forecasting their effects on Earth. As L1 is not far from Earth, approximately a million miles away, these observations provide under one hour heads up. Past research has generated a common consensus that sub-L1 missions could provide information on CMEs well before they reach earth, allowing for preparation for their impacts in advance. However, these studies often utilize data from STEREO which is essentially at Earth’s orbit (~0.95 AU). Due to its location, it does not provide much lead time or the ability to analyse many CMEs, which makes it difficult to generate forecasting parameters from this information. This project addresses this gap by investigating how sub-L1 observations may be used to forecast the Interplanetary Magnetic Field (IMF) of CMEs at L1. We approached this by comparing CME arrivals at Solar Orbiter (SolO), which had observations from 0.3 AU to 0.93 AU and variable Sun-Earth line separations, and arrivals at the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE), which served as the primary operational satellite at the NWS Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) at the time of these events. SolO’s variable location allowed us to monitor how location influenced the IMF. The CMEs observed were initially selected from a NASA LArge Scale Structures Originating from the Sun (LASSOS) catalog ranging from October 2021 to November 2022. Once the max IMF was collected from each event at SolO and ACE, the following comparisons were made: heliocentric distance (HD) vs magnetic field (SolO), distance from Sun-Earth line vs magnetic field (SolO), and IMF at ACE vs IMF at SolO. We found a moderate correlation between the max IMF at SolO and ACE. The strong influence of HD on SolO’s IMF was addressed by using the quiet solar wind before each event at SolO as a control for HD. To further extend this project to aid forecasting geomagnetic severity, we also analyzed the BN and BZ IMF components from SolO and ACE respectively. This is important as SolO quickplots are provided for real-time analysis. As SolO quickplots are in satellite centric RTN coordinates (RTN) and ACE in geocentric GSM coordinates (XYZ) , understanding how these coordinate systems compare to each other is impertinent. The same trends observed in max IMF were observed in the IMF components, suggesting that SolO BN may be used as a forecasting tool for ACE Bz at L1.

494570.title: Cloud Thermodynamic Phase Classification using Spectrally Resolved Satellite Measurements for Cross-Platform Continuity
494570.authors: Nathaniel Miller, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and K. S. Mattingly, B. Kahn, T. Ochoa Peterson, and T. S. L'Ecuyer
494570.abstract: Hyperspectral remote sensing observations from satellite platforms are valuable for determining cloud phase in a variety of environmental conditions and over extended time periods. Over a 14-year period covered by observations from the Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS), Kahn et al. (2018) showed trends in the microphysical properties of clouds, pointing to the presence of cloud feedbacks in a changing climate. The Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) instruments aboard the SNPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 satellites provide the opportunity to assess trends in cloud phase starting in 2018 and into the future. Since AIRS and CrIS differ slightly in their spectral coverage, spectral channel grid, and instrument noise characteristics, agreement between AIRS and CrIS cloud products must be verified using similar retrieval methodology applied to all sensors. Additionally, in dry polar conditions and high cloud top scenes, spectra from the Polar Radiant Energy in the Far InfraRed Experiment (PREFIRE) mission offer a new perspective into the far-infrared (FIR) atmospheric window region to discern cloud microphysical properties. In this study, cloud phase determination is performed using brightness temperature differences (BTDs), sensitive to spectral signatures in cloud thermal emission, and thresholds that are indicative of either liquid or ice presence. Continuity between AIRS and CrIS retrievals is verified using collocated comparisons for overlapping time periods. In addition, adjusted CrIS BTD threshold values are determined from collocations with AIRS and then validated for several EarthCARE case studies. Seasonal statistics, as a function of latitude, quantify the extent to which cloud phase is changing from predominantly ice to liquid, especially in the polar regions. These temporal and regional differences in cloud phase provide insight into processes that are most likely to affect cloud feedbacks in projected warmer and wetter atmospheric conditions. Ultimately, continuity between AIRS and CrIS cloud retrievals provides a foundation to investigate long-term trends, while a new cloud phase estimate with adjusted CrIS BTD thresholds reduces the number of unknown scene classifications. Looking ahead to an era where FIR measurements may become widely available, a brightness temperature differencing technique that uses PREFIRE measurements is investigated, indicating that the FIR is useful for phase determination in dry conditions.

494572.title: Summertime Airborne Measurements of Nitrogen Oxides (NOx) and Ozone (O3) during the Salt Lake City Summer Ozone Study (SLC-SOS 2026)
494572.authors: Daniela Carolina Guevara, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and B. McGuire, M. Davis, K. A. Corwin, A. Marsavin, I. B. Pollack, F. Flocke, A. Robertson, A. Majewski, C. Grasmick, A. Deters, W. Permar, J. Tomlin, K. Ullmann, S. R. Hall, L. Hu, R. A. Hannun, A. G. Hallar, and E. V. Fischer
494572.abstract: The Northern Wasatch Front, the largest metropolitan region of Utah, is designated as a serious nonattainment area for the 2015 8-hour ozone (O3) National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS). As part of the July-August 2026 Salt Lake City Summer Ozone Study (SLC-SOS), an in situ payload was deployed in the University of Wyoming King Air (UWKA) research aircraft to measure O3 and its precursors and distinguish the presence of wildfire smoke. The UWKA conducted several flights over 2 months, collecting ~60 hours of airborne observations. An Aerodyne dual channel Cavity Attenuated Phase Shift Monitor (CAPS NOx-NO2) and the NASA Rapid OZone Experiment (ROZE) were deployed to quantify spatiotemporal (vertical and horizontal) gradients and daily variability of nitrogen oxides (NOx = NO + NO2) and O3 across the Wasatch Front. Our initial analysis for smoke-free data quantifies: (1) regional gradients and vertical profiles of NOx and O3, (2) NOx emission fluxes from the Bingham Canyon Mine and comparison to the current GRA2PES emission inventory, and (3) morning-afternoon and weekday-weekend differences of NOx and O3 over different land types (e.g., wetland, urban area, exposed playa, and open water areas of the Great Salt Lake). These measurements will help develop strategies to mitigate high O3 levels and improve air quality in the region.

494573.title: Ignition Risk Reduction Benefit of Advanced Power Flow Control
494573.abstract: While wildfire risk is a well-documented concern in the Western states of the U.S., the risk is increasing and expanding to the east. Meanwhile, energy affordability remains a top issue across the country. Electric utilities are presented with wildfire mitigation strategies that are costly and often unreliable, evaluated with unstandardized metrics. Innovative solutions to address excessive curtailment of renewable generation and defer transmission investments are being considered by utilities, policymakers, and regulators. One such solution is Advanced Power Flow Control (APFC), within the class of hardware and software technologies called Advanced Transmission Technologies. While APFC is typically considered as a reliability and optimization technology, it has potential ignition risk reduction benefits that have been largely overlooked in ratemaking procedures and cost-benefit analysis. By injecting a voltage in quadrature with current, APFC can reduce effective reactance on the transmission line on which it is installed, redirecting power flow toward less constrained lines to support topology optimization. In so doing, APFC reduces line current, thereby reducing resistive heating. This work applies the methodology used by Tandon et al. to quantify the ignition risk reduction benefit of dynamic line rating to the potential benefit of APFC. Novel application of this work includes introducing a causal chain that relates resistive heating to thermal expansion of transmission cable and vegetation contact in high ignition risk conditions. Ignition risk reduction potential emerges both from reduced conductor temperature and reduced line sag. This represents a potential benefit that, if realized, should be considered in cost-benefit analysis for future deployment of APFC. Power flow modeling can be used to assess the impacts of APFC activation for ignition risk reduction that redirects power along parallel lines in a meshed grid. Regulatory authorities can incorporate wildfire ignition risk reduction benefits into blue-sky ratemaking proceedings while considering the opportunity cost of avoided topology optimization during high ignition risk conditions.

494575.title: Weather Decision Support for Missile Defense Test Operations at the Regan Test Range, Kwajalein Atoll
494575.authors: Jake W. Evans, RedTown Technical Services, Kwajalein, AP; and C. Washington
494575.abstract: The Ronald Reagan Ballistic Missile Defense Test Range (RTR) at Kwajalein Atoll presents a unique weather decision-support environment distinct from traditional space-launch operations. Located in a remote, data-sparse region of the tropical Pacific, RTR operations rely on a limited observational network while facing frequent and rapidly evolving precipitation and convection. For ballistic missile defense (BMD) testing, these conditions can directly affect the collection of critical test data and introduce weather constraints that differ from those encountered during conventional launch operations. Weather decisions for BMD tests must therefore account for both the uncertainty in forecasting in a data-sparse tropical environment and the sensitivity of optical systems to evolving weather conditions. Forecasters integrate satellite imagery, surface observations, upper-air soundings, radar, and climatological knowledge to assess precipitation and convective threats throughout an extended decision window. This presentation provides an overview of the meteorological challenges and decision-support requirements associated with BMD test operations at RTR. Drawing on operational forecasting experience at Kwajalein and other launch environments, the discussion highlights how the range's remote location, limited observations, and unique weather sensitivities shape forecast strategy and mission support. The goal is to give the ARAM community a clearer picture of the meteorological support requirements unique to missile defense testing, an area less commonly represented in launch-weather literature compared to orbital and crewed spaceflight operations.

494579.title: SkyScouts: From the Grid to the Garage — A Middle School Study of How Electricity Sources Affect the Benefits of Electric Vehicles
494579.authors: Ishika Sharma, Granger Middle School, Aurora, IL; and A. Kumar, S. Wu, A. Wadhwa, R. Kumar, and A. Sharma
494579.abstract: Electric vehicles (EVs) do not produce pollution from their tailpipes, but the electricity used to charge them comes from different sources. It may come from solar and wind energy, nuclear power, natural gas, coal, or a combination of these sources. As part of the Sky Scouts program, this project asks: How much do EVs reduce carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions, and how does the source of their electricity affect that reduction? Using publicly available data, this Sky Scouts study estimates the number of EVs in Cook County, Illinois, and the amount of electricity required to charge them for one year. Vehicle registration data come from the Illinois Secretary of State. Information about EV energy use comes from FuelEconomy.gov, while electricity-generation and emissions data come from the U.S. Energy Information Administration and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The study compares four charging scenarios: the current regional electricity grid, a combination of household solar and grid electricity, fully renewable electricity, and electricity produced mainly from fossil fuels. It then compares emissions from EV charging with the tailpipe emissions produced by similar gasoline vehicles. The project also examines what happens when EVs make up 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% of vehicles in the county. The results show how EVs reduce CO₂ emissions under different charging scenarios and how the size of the reduction depends on how and when electricity is produced. Through Sky Scouts, this middle school study demonstrates how students can use public data to explore real transportation and energy questions. It also shows that switching to EVs reduces tailpipe pollution, while cleaner electricity sources can make EVs even more beneficial.

494583.title: Modeling Land-Atmosphere Feedbacks During the 2011 and 2012 US Great Plains Flash Droughts: Sensitivity to Vegetation and Irrigation
494583.authors: Mahmoud Osman, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and B. F. Zaitchik, S. Labhane, and N. Parazoo
494583.abstract: Flash droughts develop rapidly and cause significant agricultural and ecological damage. Predicting their onset and severity remains challenging due to complex land-atmosphere feedbacks and insufficient representation of vegetation and irrigation in models. This study investigates the influence of vegetation stress and irrigation on the spatiotemporal evolution of some major flash drought events. Using the fully coupled NASA Unified Weather Research and Forecasting (NU-WRF) and Land Information System (LIS) modeling frameworks with the Noah-MP land surface model, we conduct experiments applying satellite-derived, time-varying vegetation and spatial irrigation maps. Integrating observed vegetation anomalies leads to improved simulations of surface energy fluxes, atmospheric warming, and evapotranspiration patterns during the crucial onset and intensification phases during the observed 2011 Southern Great plains flash drought. For the 2012 Great Plains event, we examine how irrigation modulates soil moisture, surface energy partitioning, boundary layer dynamics, and their interaction with drought-stressed vegetation. Our findings highlights the critical importance of accurately representing vegetation variability and land-use practices to capture the physical mechanisms driving flash droughts, or mitigating their impacts and to improve early warning capabilities.

494586.title: A Reconstructed Record of June-July Lightning in Alaska (1959–2025): Climatology and Seasonal Predictability from March-April PNA
494586.authors: Joshua Hostler, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; Univ. of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; Univ. of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and U. S. Bhatt, P. A. Bieniek, T. J. Ballinger, C. Borries-Strigle, J. Chriest, R. Lader, H. Strader, R. Thoman, C. F. Waigl, and J. Coffey
494586.abstract: Lightning-ignited fires account for 97.5% of burned area in Alaska, and therefore fire managers would benefit substantially from seasonal outlooks of lightning activity. Dynamical forecasts, however, are limited to short-range guidance, and the brief observational lightning record precludes robust statistical prediction as identification of modest teleconnection signals requires more years than the lightning detection network has operated. We address this gap by reconstructing a 67-year proxy record of Alaska lightning and using it to evaluate the predictability of early-season lightning from preceding spring atmospheric variability. We train a histogram gradient boosted parameterization of daily June–July gridded lightning stroke density and apply it to ERA5 reanalysis to reconstruct lightning back to 1959. Hyperparameters are tuned with a cross-validation scheme that optimizes seasonally out-of-sample performance, and four fully held-out years verify that the model learned physical relationships between atmospheric state and lightning rather than overfitting to the systematic confounds of the detection network. The mean gridded Pearson correlation between daily observed and proxy lightning is 0.326, with 80% of grid points locally significant (p<0.05); the field is significant at p<0.001 against a null distribution that preserves seasonal and spatial autocorrelation structures as well as individual synoptic events. Interannual correlations of monthly statewide totals are 0.714 for June and 0.833 for July (both p<0.001). Using the proxy as predictand, we find that 12% of grid cells have a significant correlation between June lightning and the March–April Pacific–North American pattern (PNA; field significance of p=0.0342) — concentrated in the East Boreal region. Positive March–April PNA is associated with increased June lightning, earlier snowoff, warmer June Gulf of Alaska SSTs, and reduced June Beaufort sea-ice extent. The PNA–lightning relationship is robust to controlling for ENSO, the PDO, the North Pacific Index, and the Polar/Eurasia pattern. Snowoff timing is consistent with partial mediation; Beaufort sea-ice extent and Gulf of Alaska SST anomalies are plausible parallel pathways but fall below significance once the PNA is controlled. In leave-one-out cross-validation, the March–April PNA explains 17% of interannual East Boreal June lightning variance, enabling the first seasonal lightning outlooks for Alaska. The extended record also allows us to evaluate whether this predictability is stationary across decadal background states. The PNA–lightning correlation is stronger during positive PDO phases, yet the PDO itself is uncorrelated with lightning, and the mechanisms examined here do not fully account for the multi-decadal modulation. Snowoff does not vary with the PDO phase, and both the PNA–Beaufort sea ice and sea ice–lightning links are stronger during the recent negative phase, likely reflecting increased sea-ice variance rather than the PDO. Only the PNA–Gulf of Alaska SST and SST–lightning links strengthen during the positive phase. Even at 67 years, the record is unable to robustly resolve the role of decadal state across multiple collinear, cross-correlated pathways. Together, the proxy record confirms the PNA–lightning relationship suggested by the observational period and corroborates candidate mechanisms linking spring conditions to summer lightning, strengthening the case for operational use.

494587.title: Regional Climate Products and Local Watershed Observations: Hydroclimatic Variability in the Fraser River Headwaters, Colorado
494587.authors: Claudia R Corona, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and D. Stoughton, P. Glynn, and T. Hogue
494587.abstract: The Fraser River watershed in Grand County, Colorado is a headwater basin of the Colorado River that supports municipal water supplies, aquatic and riparian ecosystems, recreation, and transmountain water exports. Recent drought conditions, continued population growth, and increasing demands on limited water resources have heightened interest in understanding the hydroclimatic factors that influence water availability across the watershed. Historical context is particularly important because many local climate and hydrologic records span only recent decades, limiting the ability to place contemporary conditions within a longer-term perspective. This study evaluates hydroclimatic variability in the Fraser River headwaters using NOAA Climate-at-a-Glance temperature and precipitation products spanning 1931-2026 together with available local climate, streamflow, and water diversion records. The NOAA datasets provide a century-scale perspective on regional climate variability, while local observations are used to evaluate how well these regional products represent hydroclimatic conditions observed within the watershed and relevant to water-resource planning. Preliminary evaluation of the climate records indicates persistent warming during recent decades and substantial variability in precipitation across annual to decadal time scales. Comparisons among climate, streamflow, and diversion records are used to identify contrasting hydroclimatic periods and place recent drought conditions within a broader historical context. The objectives of this study are to: (1) characterize long-term temperature and precipitation variability in the Fraser River headwaters using century-scale climate products; (2) evaluate the consistency between regional climate products and available local observations; (3) examine relationships among climate variability, streamflow, and water diversions; and (4) identify representative hydroclimatic periods that provide context for future water-resource investigations. Results aim to provide a multi-decadal perspective on hydroclimatic variability in an important Colorado River headwater basin and assess the utility of regional climate products for interpreting watershed conditions. The study establishes a historical framework for understanding water availability and provides context for ongoing investigations of groundwater resources, watershed vulnerability, and long-term water management in the Fraser River watershed within the Upper Colorado River Basin.

494589.title: Contrasting Aerosol Effects on Elevated Updraft Pulses in Deep Convective Clouds: A Modeling Study from TRACER
494589.authors: Yongjie Huang, CAPS, Norman, OK; and D. J. Mise and G. M. McFarquhar
494589.abstract: Deep convective clouds (DCCs) substantially influence Earth’s energy balance and water cycle, yet limited understanding of their life cycles and interactions with meteorological and aerosol conditions hinders realistic representation in numerical models. During the 2021–2022 Tracking Aerosol Convection Interactions Experiment (TRACER) near Houston, numerous isolated DCCs were tracked across a wide range of environmental conditions using the C-band Scanning ARM Precipitation Radar (CSAPR) and other co-located instruments. This study uses a modeling framework to investigate the physical mechanisms linking aerosol and meteorological conditions to DCC updraft characteristics. Aerosol initial conditions were derived from ground-based Scanning Mobility Particle Sizer (SMPS) observations. The MODERATE case used a three-mode lognormal fit to the mean SMPS-derived aerosol size distribution, whereas LOW and HIGH aerosol cases used scaling factors of 1/3× and 3× of the mean, respectively, based on observed SMPS variability. DCCs were simulated with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model in large-eddy simulation (LES) mode using the Fast Spectral Bin Microphysics (FSBM) scheme. Among these simulations, cases were identified in which elevated updraft pulses formed over the DCC lifetime after the primary updraft. These simulations were classified into two groups. In the INC group, the number of elevated updraft pulses increased monotonically with increasing initial aerosol concentration, from LOW to MODERATE to HIGH; in the DEC group, it decreased monotonically across the same aerosol progression. Relative to DEC cases, INC cases were characterized by lower 0–1-km relative humidity (RH), weaker 0–6-km bulk shear, and a higher 2–6-km temperature lapse rate. In both groups, higher aerosol concentrations (HIGH) were associated with a later first echo (Z > 18 dBZ) than in the LOW cases. In INC cases, HIGH aerosol conditions were associated with enhanced ice diffusional growth at higher altitudes (~8-12 km) and greater latent heat release from diffusion than from other microphysical processes during both early (0-5 minutes after first echo) and later stages (10-20 minutes). In DEC cases, the early-stage response was consistent with INC; during later stages, however, LOW aerosol conditions were associated with stronger ice diffusional growth and greater latent heat release at higher altitudes, supporting stronger updrafts. Preliminary comparisons between simulated C-band radar reflectivity and observed range-height indicator (RHI) scans are also presented to place the simulated DCC evolution in observational context. These results highlight that aerosol effects on elevated updraft pulses are not unidirectional but depend on the background meteorological environment and stage-dependent ice diffusional growth, underscoring the need to represent these coupled processes in numerical models.

494590.title: Air Quality Impact of Rapid Data Centre Growth: Insights from Observations and Modelling In Melbourne, Australia
494590.authors: Robert G Ryan, University of Melbourne, Parkville, VIC, Australia
494590.abstract: Data centres (DCs) are emerging as critical infrastructure supporting digital economies of the world and the rapid growth of artificial intelligence. Their increasing electricity demand and widespread urban deployment present significant challenges for energy systems, water resources, and environmental sustainability. While much attention has focused on the energy requirements of DCs, the air quality implications of backup diesel generation and associated infrastructure remain largely unquantified. Despite rapid global expansion of the sector, there is currently limited understanding of the contribution of DCs to urban air pollution and associated public health risks. This study presents the first integrated assessment of DC-related air quality impacts in Australia. This study is urgently needed for Australia because several Australian state governments have positioned themselves as major global data centre hubs, but these findings are applicable to any place with large growth in DC infrastructure. We develop a regional emission inventory for DC operations, with a particular focus on diesel backup generators, and evaluate impacts on local and regional air quality using WRF-Chem chemical transport modelling. Model simulations are combined with observational analyses using Environment Protection Authority (EPA) monitoring data and air-mass back-trajectory techniques to identify pollution signatures associated with existing DC clusters and to characterize source-receptor relationships under varying meteorological conditions. Population exposure, health burden, and economic externalities are assessed using established epidemiological methodologies. The project further investigates the distribution of impacts across communities to identify potential environmental justice concerns associated with DC development. These results provide the first evidence base linking digital infrastructure growth to atmospheric composition and health outcomes in Australia. The framework developed here is transferable internationally and will inform environmental regulation, urban planning, and energy policy for one of the fastest-growing sectors of the global energy transition.

494591.title: Sensitivity of Tropical Cyclone Rapid Intensification to Sea-Spray Parameterization
494591.authors: Ha-Rim Kim, SEED Research Center, Institute of Environmental and Marine Science Technology, Pukyong National University, Busan, South korea; and Y. H. Kim, S. Yang, and B. M. Kim
494591.abstract: Rapid intensification (RI) remains a major challenge in tropical cyclone intensity prediction, partly because air–sea exchange under extreme winds is still subject to substantial uncertainty. Sea spray can modify sensible and latent heat transfer at the ocean surface, but its influence on RI simulations has not been systematically evaluated across multiple storms. Here, we assess the sensitivity of RI to two contrasting sea-spray parameterizations using recent RI events. Coupled atmosphere–ocean–wave simulations will be conducted with a conventional bulk formulation and a wave-tank-informed bag-breakup formulation that enhances spray production under extreme winds. Performance will be evaluated using maximum wind speed, minimum sea-level pressure, 24-h intensity change, RI timing, and peak intensity, together with surface heat-flux diagnostics. We hypothesize that differences between the parameterizations will emerge most strongly during RI, primarily through their influence on storm intensity rather than track. This study will quantify whether improved representation of sea-spray processes can reduce uncertainty in simulations of rapidly intensifying tropical cyclones.

494593.title: Asymmetric Strengthening of African Easterly Waves Driven By Differential North African Warming
494593.authors: Emily Bercos-Hickey, LBNL, Berkeley, CA; and C. M. Patricola-DiRosario and P. J. Klotzbach
494593.abstract: African easterly waves are synoptic-scale disturbances that are observed in two tracks north and south of the African easterly jet, and frequently serve as precursor disturbances to Atlantic tropical cyclones. Over the past four decades, there has been an increase in both African easterly wave strength and the number of tropical cyclones with African easterly wave origins. It is unclear, however, if the strengthening of African easterly waves has been uniform across both wave tracks or if it has predominantly affected one wave track. In this study, we use 46 years of reanalysis data (1980–2025) and an energetics-based analysis to examine trends in African easterly wave activity and the large-scale North African circulation. We found that differential warming between the Sahara and Sahel weakened the meridional temperature gradient south of the African easterly jet and strengthened it to the north. Via thermal wind, these changes to the meridional temperature gradient intensify the meridional shear of the zonal wind south of the African easterly jet, leading to an enhancement of barotropic energy conversion. As a consequence, the eddy kinetic energy of the southern African easterly wave track has strengthened 39% faster than the northern track. This result has important tropical cyclone implications, as previous research has shown that stronger African easterly waves and southern-track African easterly waves preferentially develop into tropical cyclones.

494596.title: Same Particles, Different Answers: Quantifying Algorithmic Uncertainty in Airborne Optical Array Probe Microphysical Retrievals
494596.authors: Yongjie Huang, CAPS, Norman, OK; and G. M. McFarquhar, A. Bansemer, M. Wolde, L. Nichman, and S. Woods
494596.abstract: Airborne optical array probes (OAPs) have been widely used in aircraft field campaigns to image cloud and precipitation particles and derive particle size distributions (PSDs) and bulk microphysical properties in diverse cloud systems. These retrievals provide critical constraints for investigating cloud processes, developing microphysical parameterizations, and evaluating numerical simulations and remote-sensing retrievals. However, the derived microphysical properties can depend substantially on the processing software and algorithms applied to the same OAP measurements, introducing uncertainties that are often difficult to quantify. To systematically characterize these uncertainties, we developed the Cloud OAP Processing Software (COPS), a new Python package for processing raw data from commonly used OAP instruments, including the Cloud Imaging Probe (CIP) and Precipitation Imaging Probe (PIP) manufactured by Droplet Measurement Technologies (DMT; now ENVEA), and the Two-Dimensional Stereo probe (2D-S) and High Volume Precipitation Spectrometer (HVPS) manufactured by Stratton Park Engineering Company (SPEC; now part of Weather Modification International), with raw probe data decoded into the Single Particle Image Format (SPIF) using a decoder that we substantially updated and extended from NRC-SPIFpy. COPS is evaluated using a benchmark synthetic OAP dataset generated by the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). COPS exactly reproduces the synthetic ground truth for both DMT and SPEC probes, giving confidence that subsequent sensitivity tests isolate algorithm choices rather than implementation errors. Controlled sensitivity analyses then quantify how individual algorithmic choices propagate into retrieved microphysical properties, examining uncertainties associated with the following: particle size definitions, including extents along the time and diode-array dimensions (Dt and Dp), mean box diameter (Dm), box hypotenuse (Dh), equivalent-area diameter (Deq), minimum-circle diameter (Ds), and Korolev-corrected diameter (DKorolev) for hollow spherical images; sample-volume calculations, particularly the constant used to calculate depth of field (DoF); corrections for out-of-focus particles or those not entirely in the field of view; and particle-phase classification as liquid, mixed phase, or ice. This approach attributes differences among processing software to specific algorithmic assumptions rather than to unexplained discrepancies among final products. Across the synthetic data for ice, columns, and drops, Ds and DKorolev most consistently reproduce the modeled reference diameter, whereas the other particle size definitions show larger habit-dependent biases and variability. For particles with D > 100 µm, sizing errors are the primary source of PSD retrieval bias. Number concentrations for D > 100 µm, N(D > 100 µm), are more sensitive to the DoF calculation (by up to 10% for drops and 15% for ice and columns) than to the choice of diameter definition (by up to 2% for drops and up to 9% for ice and columns). COPS, the NCAR System for OAP Data Analysis version 2 (SODA-2), and the SPEC processing software are further intercompared using Fast 2D-S observations from the Cold Air Outbreak Experiment in the Sub-Arctic Region (CAESAR) field campaign to evaluate algorithm performance in real atmospheric measurements. The three software packages agree on the evolution of total number concentrations but differ in PSDs, while COPS and SODA-2 assign different accept/reject classifications to 15–18% of particles. Uncertainties in other retrieved bulk properties (e.g., mass concentration, median mass diameter, and liquid/ice water content) are also quantified. This study identifies the processing assumptions responsible for much of the spread in OAP-derived PSDs and bulk microphysical properties and provides a pathway toward more consistent, transparent, and robust use of aircraft microphysical observations in cloud-process studies, model evaluation, and microphysics parameterization development.

494599.title: Can Differentiable Machine Learning Capture the Timing and Magnitude of Ecosystem Carbon and Water Flux Responses to Environmental Pulse Events?
494599.authors: Wenli Zhao, Columbia Univ., New York City, NY; and P. Gentine
494599.abstract: Environmental pulse events induce rapid changes in terrestrial carbon and water exchange, yet model evaluations dominated by seasonal covariation may not resolve performance at event timescales. Using observations from eddy covariance flux towers, we developed an observation-defined framework to assess whether differentiable machine learning captures ecosystem responses to soil-moisture pulses. We identified 542 events, including 239 in site-specific temporal test periods, and compared modeled and observed gross primary productivity (GPP) and evapotranspiration/latent heat (ET/LE) on matched event dates using response timing, magnitude, and frequency. The model reproduced the cross-site organization of ET/LE responses across these attributes (Spearman ρ=0.71–0.95), while both GPP and ET/LE retained strong daily correspondence with tower observations during pulse windows. Event-based agreement varied across fluxes and response timescales, providing information distinct from conventional daily performance metrics. Satellite vegetation proxies also covaried with modeled GPP during pulse periods, providing a complementary observational constraint. Together, these results indicate that differentiable machine learning can represent key dimensions of ecosystem pulse dynamics and support the use of observation-defined events for evaluating model behavior under hydroclimatic variability.

494600.title: NSF NCAR's Marshall Field Site - Past, Present, and Future of an Interdisciplinary Atmospheric Sciences Testbed
494600.authors: Sebastian W. Hoch, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. del Moral Méndez, Ph.D, K. Ferguson, S. D. Landolt, T. Hock, W. O. J. Brown, T. M. Weckwerth, J. C. Witte, C. Roden, J. C. Hubbert, J. Vivekanandan, B. Baeuerle, K. Barsanti, E. C. Apel, D. D. Turner, T. P. Meyers, J. Bednar, B. Adler, J. Sedlar, L. Bianco, B. Argrow, M. A. Wagner, and A. C. McComiskey
494600.abstract: For over 50 years, NSF NCAR’s Marshall Field Site (MFS) has been a place of observations, experiments, and discovery. The approximately 80 acres of land in the foothills southeast of Boulder were first leased, then purchased by NSF to provide NCAR with a readily accessible, flat and open area with no surrounding obstructions. It has been the birthplace of observational technologies that are foundational for our current understanding of atmospheric processes and their representation in current numerical weather prediction models. The MFS is ideally suited to observe the types of high impact weather occurring along Colorado’s Front Range: strong downslope windstorms, freezing precipitation, upslope snow storms, severe thunderstorms, red flag warning conditions, and hazardous air quality events. The MFS is the birthplace of the National Scientific Balloon Facility (NSPF). Established in 1961 by NSF, it was later moved to Palestine, TX, and is now NASA’s Columbia Scientific Balloon Facility. However, balloon operations at MFS continue, and are part of the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS) Reference Upper-Air Network (GRUAN). The site hosts the longest time series of stratospheric water vapor collected by NOAA’s Global Monitoring Laboratory dating back to 1980/81. Additional observations of long lived tracers using novel air core soundings are performed from this site by NOAA’s Chemical Sciences Laboratory. The MFS was, and continues to be, an initial test site for new radar technology developed at NCAR, including the use of polarimetric radar with the Cloud Physics Radar #2 (CP-2) and the S-band Dual Polarization Doppler Radar (S-Pol). S-Pol continues to operate at this site, collecting data during critical weather events, supporting NCAR-NOAA radar data quality research, and serving as a flagship system to test and develop new algorithms for calibration and data processing, as well as new and emerging technologies (e.g., phased-array). Collaborations across NCAR, and with other agency and industry partners have been centered around the MFS, which hosts permanent installations from the Research Application Laboratory (RAL), the Earth Observing Laboratory (EOL), the High Altitude Observatory (HAO), and the Atmospheric Chemistry Observation and Modeling (ACOM) laboratory, 3-D Printed Automated Weather Stations (3D-PAWS) from UCAR’s Cooperative Program for Operational Meteorology, Education and Training (COMET), as well as EarthScope seismic and geodetic instruments. The MFS served as a key site for the WMO Solid Precipitation Intercomparison Experiment (WMO-SPICE, 2012-2015) dedicated to developing the automated standard for snowfall measurement. The site was further used to evaluate precipitation-type detection sensors for the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) network and to evaluate winter weather forecast activities. Currently, NCAR EOL is deploying and testing an initial node of a next generation LOwer Troposphere Observing System (LOTOS), an integrated instrumentation suite offering transformative understanding of the lower atmosphere and its coupling to the Earth's surface. The LOTOS sensor suite is further compared to NOAA’s Collaborative Lower Atmospheric Mobile Profiling System (CLAMPS). Intercomparison activities and the development of synergistic observation strategies with the University of Colorado Mobile Uncrewed Systems for Atmospheric Science (MUSAS) facility are underway. In a partnership with the Colorado Department of Public Health and the Environment (CDPHE), ACOM is currently deploying a suite of instruments at the site in a year-long study that will provide critical information needed to improve the accuracy and reduce the uncertainty of air quality forecasting across the Front Range. Future efforts will focus on further coupling chemical observations provided by ACOM with the LOTOS provided by EOL. The southern section of MFS has been left undeveloped to allow unobstructed fetch from natural surfaces to facilitate the development and testing of micrometeorological instrumentation. Examples are intercomparisons for LOTOS sensor selection and platforms for the Horizontal Array Turbulence Study (HATS) experiments. Plans for a flexible micrometeorological tower network to allow for HATS-like studies and for intercomparisons and sensitivity studies with Large Eddy Simulations are under development. The MFS is a unique place for inspiring and educating the next generation of scientists, providing a comprehensive environment for rigorous instrument calibration, validation, and intercomparison studies against established ground-truth standards. Consequently, innovative strategic plans are underway to evolve the facility into a premier testbed and educational hub for research and workforce development. We envision this center to become a cornerstone of integrated research opportunities, providing hands-on training for the community from hardware design, signal processing, to field campaign deployment and data collection, bringing together national labs, industry and academia partners to address pressing atmospheric challenges. This presentation hopes to celebrate past achievements facilitated by observations at the MFS, to present ongoing activities, and to facilitate the discussion of the future of this unique place of discovery.

494601.title: Evaluation of Particulate Matter Retrievals from the Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) Mission in Urban and Rural North Carolina
494601.authors: Stella Foreman, The University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and E. Boakye Yiadom and I. Chang
494601.abstract: Fine particulate matter with diameter less than 2.5 μm (PM2.5) is a common pollutant associated with severe health complications, making monitoring critical. PM2.5 can be monitored via surface-based observations or estimated using satellite data, which fills spatial coverage gaps between surface monitors. TEMPO (Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution) detects small-scale spatial and temporal variations in air quality through hourly observations, capturing how PM2.5 changes throughout the day. Additionally, TEMPO is capable of detecting aerosol layer height, allowing for more accurate surface PM2.5 estimation from aerosol optical depth. We evaluated the performance of the TEMPO-ABI PM2.5 product by comparing values to EPA AirData hourly surface-based PM2.5 measurements. 22 EPA PM2.5 monitors across North Carolina and TEMPO pixels within 1500 m of those monitors were selected for comparison, with data selected for six dates between June 2024 and June 2025. Relationships between TEMPO-ABI and EPA AirData PM2.5 values were evaluated with a focus on diurnal variation and differences between urban and rural areas. Findings show that TEMPO-ABI PM2.5 estimations were strongly correlated with EPA surface PM2.5 measurements (R = 0.87) with similar diurnal variation trends. No trend was observed between population density and PM2.5 concentration; estimation error varied slightly with density but performance remained strong overall, with bias ranging from -0.14 μg/m3 in rural areas to -0.29 μg/m3 in urban areas. These findings confirm that TEMPO can detect diurnal variation in PM2.5 values across urban and rural areas and can provide highly localized, hourly PM2.5 data, filling gaps in areas without monitors.

494603.title: Storms in Global Convection Permitting Models
494603.authors: L. Ruby Leung, PNNL, Richland, WA
494603.abstract: Storms are primary drivers of extreme precipitation and high-impact flooding worldwide, yet unraveling their multi-scale drivers, local feedbacks, and societal impacts has long been constrained by coarse-resolution models and fragmented observational datasets. Recent advancements in global convection-permitting models (GCPMs)—operating at kilometer-scale resolutions—now offer a unified framework capable of resolving physical processes seamlessly from local to global scales. Paired with state-of-the-art tracking algorithms and atmospheric reanalyses, these models enable rigorous global benchmarking against observations. In this study, we evaluate a multi-model ensemble of global kilometer-scale models using multiple storm-tracking algorithms applied to observations to test two central hypotheses: (1) that storm-resolving models systematically improve the simulation of diverse storm types compared to low-resolution models, and (2) that better representation of observed physical behaviors yields reduced model uncertainty and spread. Our results demonstrate that GCPMs successfully reproduce the global distribution of various storm types, capturing organized convective systems that traditional low-resolution models miss entirely. However, the ensemble also reveals persistent model biases in storm statistics and differing representations of storm-environment relationships. While GCPMs mark a transformational shift in our ability to study convective systems, characterizing these model uncertainties remains essential for determining the specific applications and scientific questions for which these models are fit-for-purpose.

494606.title: An Evaluation of the Impacts of Meteorological Variables on Grass Fire Frequency in Barbados from 2014-2024
494606.authors: Adria Mia Leben, Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology, St. James, Barbados; and N. A. Collymore, A. Sealy, R. Chewitt-Lucas, and A. Taylor
494606.abstract: Grass fires represent a significant environmental hazard in Barbados, yet the meteorological conditions associated with their occurrence and the temporal variability of the island's fire season remain insufficiently investigated. This study examines reported 8,312 incidents of grass fires by the Barbados Fire Service (BFS) between 2014 and 2024. This is significant for an island that is 166 sq mi. The time period of 2014 to 2024 was used to (i) determine whether a fire season can be defined for Barbados, and (ii) investigate the correlation between meteorological variables and the frequency of grass fires recorded. The variables examined include air temperature, dew point temperature, relative humidity, rainfall, wind speed and atmospheric pressure, taken from the Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology (CIMH) Automatic Weather Station (AWS) archive. Findings indicate that Barbados’ fire season can be characterized by consecutive months in which there is one fire per day. This generally lags the beginning of the dry season in December. Additionally, fire weather conditions in Barbados appear to be strongly influenced by meteorological variables linked to atmospheric moisture and wind speed. The accuracy of these results may be biased by gaps in the weather data time series obtained from CIMH as well as assumptions made to generalize the localized data for the entire island. Furthering this research to include additional years and data, could further improve the definition of Barbados’ fire season and associated fire weather. Overall, this study contributes to a scientific understanding of the effects that individual meteorological variables have on grass fires in Barbados. This understanding provides a foundation for the second phase of this project which tests the performance of tree-based machine learning techniques as a means of developing the Barbados Fire Weather Index to support CIMH’s fire weather monitoring platform.

494607.title: Seasonal Malaria Early Warning In Tropical South America: Operational Methods and Forecasts Applied to the 2026-2027 El Nino
494607.authors: Benjamin F. Zaitchik, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; and P. Kansara, M. Janko, P. Chacón-Uscamaita, A. Gunderson, Q. Zheng, L. Benitez Ramirez, H. Cárdenas, A. Barbieri, A. Lescano, C. Mena, and W. Pan
494607.abstract: El Nino events have significant impacts on hydroclimatic conditions across the tropical South America. These impacts include elevated temperatures, extreme precipitation on the Pacific coast, and severe drought in much of the Amazon basin. This leads to coastal flooding, elevated fire risk in Amazon forests, disruptions to river transportation networks, unstable hydropower production, ecological shifts, and threats to agricultural productivity. El Nino (and La Nina) events also have substantial influence on infectious diseases, including malaria. Over the past fifteen years, our transdisciplinary team has worked to advance environmentally-informed malaria risk assessment and forecast in the Amazon region. Making use of satellite-informed land data assimilation systems (LDAS) for hydrometeorological monitoring and subseasonal-to-seasonal forecast, machine learning models that integrate these variables with landscape information, human systems data, and distributed health records to generate meaningful risk assessments, and interactive communication tools co-designed with operational health authorities, we have developed and deployed a system that offers malaria risk forecasts at the spatial scale of a district or health post with a lead of several weeks to several months. The 2026-2027 El Nino offers a test of this system. Here, we present an overview of the malaria early warning system, describe and evaluate its use in the ongoing El Nino event, and assess barriers and opportunities for malaria forecast and the operational use of those forecasts in countries of tropical South America.

494608.title: Google Weather, From Forecasts to Decisions: Turning Weather AI into Real-World Impact
494608.authors: Nofar Peled Levi, Google, NEW YORK
494608.abstract: Every day, billions of decisions are influenced by the weather. Some are as simple as grabbing an umbrella, others shape entire economies. And with an increase in extreme weather, the stakes are getting higher. Recent advances in AI are transforming weather forecasting, but better models are only the beginning. This talk explores how Google is translating cutting-edge weather AI research, including WeatherNext, into real-world impact at scale and draws lessons from that journey about what it takes to turn better forecasts into better decisions for people and organizations around the world.

494610.title: The Importance of a Self-Consistent Stefan-Boltzmann Constant in Earth System Models
494610.authors: Lili Manzo, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA; and A. Roberts, E. E. Thomas, and C. Zender
494610.abstract: Earth system model (ESM) development spans decades. Most modern models descend from older models and thus share components, algorithms, and numerical constants. This can lead to persistent biases inherited between models, and inconsistencies between model components that were developed independently of each other. One crucial example is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant (σ), which is used to compute broadband longwave (LW) radiation. Many surface components use an outdated value for σ, and in some cases σ even varies within the same component. Besides being physically inaccurate, this discrepancy can introduce inconsistency with the atmosphere model, which often computes LW flux as spectrally resolved rather than broadband. Here, we update σ to the latest value recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA) throughout the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM). The value of σ used in the latest releases of E3SM and other similar models is slightly smaller than the CODATA value. This induces a persistent energy leak between the surface and atmosphere components averaging 0.024 W/m2. After updating σ, the energy leak is reduced by 97%. Furthermore, an inaccurate Stefan-Boltzmann constant misrepresents long-term surface emission and ocean heat content (OHC) trends. In E3SM, surface emission changes by -0.0782±0.127 W/m2 per century. OHC declines at a rate of 54±5 petajoules per century, with the trend likely to continue on the timescale of deep ocean circulation. Other ESMs that overestimate σ will likely see opposite trends. These long-term changes in surface emission and heat storage have implications for the boundary conditions used to initiate model simulations. While the Stefan-Boltzmann constant is likely the most physically impactful constant that remains inconsistent across models, model-development workflows should include automated checks to ensure that all constants are up-to-date and consistent across coupled components.

494611.title: A Multi-Model Seasonal Forecast of June–July High-Lightning Days for Alaska with Daily SLP and 500-hPa Z SOM Patterns
494611.authors: Joshua Hostler, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and U. S. Bhatt, P. A. Bieniek, T. J. Ballinger, C. Borries-Strigle, J. Chriest, R. Lader, H. Strader, R. Thoman, and C. F. Waigl
494611.abstract: Lightning-ignited fires account for 97.5% of burned area in Alaska. Fire managers would benefit from seasonal outlooks of lightning, but dynamical seasonal forecast models cannot resolve the convection that produces lightning, and their direct convective output offers little usable skill at these leads. What these models do forecast with some skill is the large-scale circulation — and in Alaska, high-lightning days are synoptically driven. Self-organizing maps offer the means to categorize daily weather patterns, without the need for a labeled training data, into a set of physically recognizable patterns that supports both prediction — what fraction of the fire season occupies lightning-productive regimes — and diagnosis of why one forecast system outperforms another. Two self-organizing maps (SOMs) — unsupervised neural networks for nonlinear clustering — are trained independently on daily anomalies of ERA5 sea level pressure and 500-hPa geopotential height over Alaska for June–July of 2004–2022. These maps are carried over unchanged from prior work in which the resulting patterns were shown to explain daily lightning intensity. Each map uses a 4×5 array, and every day is assigned to its best-matching SOM node from each classification. Defining a high-lightning day (HLD) as one in the upper tercile of daily cloud-to-ground strike counts over interior Alaska, we tabulate the empirical probability of an HLD for each SLP–Z500 node combination. Forecasts are evaluated over June–July of 2004–2025, the period of consistent Alaska Lightning Detection Network (ALDN) coverage. Daily fields from ECMWF SEAS5, Météo-France System 9, and NCEP CFSv2, initialized in March, April, and May, are then evaluated at three levels. First, to test whether a forecast model generates the observed circulation patterns, we examine a SOM trained directly on March-initialized forecast June–July Z500 fields against the SOM trained from ERA5 fields. Second, to test whether it forecasts the frequency of observed patterns, forecast days are projected onto the ERA5 maps and scored by the earth mover's distance (EMD) between forecast and observed node-frequency distributions computed over the lattice. Third, to test the extent to which this process renders lightning skill, we evaluate each forecast day’s contribution by tabulating its probability as a fractional HLD, summed across June–July to yield a predicted seasonal count per member, and averaged into a single forecast for each model. The lookup table is rebuilt within each leave-one-year-out fold. The multi-model forecast is constructed from a leave-one-out multiple linear regression of each model’s z-score. From the March initialized forecasts, the multi-model ensemble attains an anomaly correlation of 0.58 between forecast and observed seasonal HLD counts, against 0.36, 0.62, and 0.21 for SEAS5, Météo-France System 9, and CFSv2, respectively. Each forecast system performs best in a different initialization month, and only SEAS5 monotonically improves as lead time decreases. Notably, the systems whose native SOM lattices most closely reproduce the ERA5 SOM lattice also produce the most skillful HLD forecasts.

494613.title: Our Recent Coordinated Effort In Engaging Rural Communities across New Mexico during the Current Extreme Drought
494613.authors: Dave W. DuBois, New Mexico State Univ., Las Cruces, NM
494613.abstract: This presentation summarizes an ongoing coordinated effort by the New Mexico State Climate Office with several key partners for education and outreach on water and climate. Here we highlight our interactions with the New Mexico Interstate Stream Commission, and the Navajo Sustainable Agriculture Program. The goal of this effort is to increase the awareness of rural community members to extreme water and climate events. One of our focus areas included communities on Navajo tribal land in northwestern New Mexico. We are partnering with the NSA staff for their support and knowledge and relationships to several rural communities. To reach these communities, we decided to first reach out to the Chapter Houses since they serve as hubs for community activities. As part of the education, we began with the introduction of CoCoRaHS to a small number of key Chapter Houses. Our initial outreach began with meetings with Chapter leadership to gage interest, a presentation to them on climate and how they can participate in monitoring precipitation. We encouraged community members to get involved with the monitoring as part of the long term data collection. Much of our efforts work towards increasing the awareness and fostering interest in how we as individuals are impacted by our environment, specifically the climate and our water resources. We will leverage this at additional communities where we have installed and continue to operate automated weather stations as part of the ZiaMet mesonet. At least one high school has invited us to talk about weather and climate to their students as a result of this connection. Our other partner has been the New Mexico Interstate Stream Commission Water Planning who have been busy in implementing the 2023 Water Security Planning Act in the face of challenges of reductions in water supply. As part of the planning, the group has helped our office in promoting CoCoRaHS in order to increase our knowledge of how much precipitation falls across the state but also in educating communities about water futures. We will be planning informal meet-ups with communities to reach out and talk about and listen for their stories on dealing with drought and other water issues. We have only been successful through the hard work from our other partners such as Soil and Water Conservation Districts, Cooperative Extension agents, our local National Weather Service forecast offices, the Navajo Department of Water Resources, and the Navajo Climate Change Program with the Navajo Fish and Wildlife Department. This is an ongoing effort and we look forward to strengthening our long-term connections to these communities and we anticipate reaching out to more in the near future.

494615.title: It's Getting Hot in Here: Assessing Public Interpretation of NWS Heat Products
494615.authors: Marissa K. Krautbauer, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; University of Oklahoma Student Chapter of the American Meteorological Society and National Weather Association (OU SCAN), Norman, OK; and N. Threlkeld, C. O'Donnell, C. Delconte, B. J. Fellman, and E. R. Martin
494615.abstract: Heat is the leading cause of weather-related fatalities in the United States, yet National Weather Service (NWS) heat products (such as graphics posted to social media sites) have historically struggled to elicit adequate public understanding and protective action. Recent changes to these products—including revised wording and the introduction of HeatRisk, a color-graded graphical tool designed to convey heat severity and potential health impacts—represented significant shifts in how hazardous heat is communicated. However, it remained unclear whether these updates improved comprehension or motivated protective decision-making among the general public. It was imperative to see what effects, if any, these changes had on public understanding and encouragement to take protective action. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of these changes by examining how people interpreted both the older and updated NWS heat products. To do this, we administered a survey to university students and faculty, capturing demographic information related to heat exposure and vulnerability. Participants were randomly assigned a selection of questions about either the old heat products or the updated heat versions, allowing for an unbiased comparison of comprehension, perceived severity, and likelihood of taking protective action. Additional questions assessed reactions to graphical tools such as HeatRisk. Particular attention was paid to whether terms like “extreme” function as jargon or convey meaningful risk. By analyzing how different forms of heat communication are interpreted, this research sought to identify language and visual elements that most effectively communicate hazardous heat. More generally, we aimed to gain insight into the kinds of language that best convey the true risk of dangerous heat. Through this insight, NWS products can be tailored to improve public understanding, encourage timely protective behaviors, and ultimately minimize heat-related injuries and fatalities.

494616.title: Exploring the Relationship between Arctic Cyclones, Atmospheric Rivers and Their Impacts on Energy and Moisture Transport in the Arctic
494616.authors: Chen Zhang, CIRES/NSIDC, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and J. J. Cassano and M. W. Seefeldt
494616.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are crucial pathways for atmospheric moisture and heat transport into, and within, the polar regions and play an important role in regulating the regional surface energy budget (SEB). Studies indicate that large SEB anomalies are often linked to increased cyclone activity. Because ARs frequently occur with extratropical cyclones, the relative roles of ARs and cyclones in driving Arctic heat, moisture, and surface radiation anomalies remain unclear. This study investigates AR-cyclone interactions over the Arctic Atlantic sector using ERA5 reanalysis, a region where AR-cyclone co-occurrence is most frequent due to the North Atlantic storm track. Approximately 76% of Arctic ARs are associated with cyclones, while the fraction of cyclones associated with ARs varies seasonally, reaching about 72% in summer but only about 50% in winter. Composite analyses reveal distinct synoptic environments for ARs with and without cyclones. ARs associated with cyclones are characterized by a strong pressure gradient between a northwestern low and a southeastern high, whereas ARs without nearby cyclones are maintained by a persistent southeastern anticyclone and upper-level ridge that efficiently transports moisture into the Arctic. Despite these contrasting circulation patterns, poleward integrated vapor transport associated with ARs is comparable regardless of cyclone presence, indicating that downstream ridging can be as effective as cyclones in supporting Arctic ARs. In contrast, cyclones without ARs are often disconnected from lower-latitude moisture sources and exhibit weaker heat and moisture transport than cyclones associated with ARs. Large positive downward longwave radiation anomalies accompany ARs regardless of cyclone presence, suggesting that AR-associated moisture is the primary driver of these surface radiative anomalies. Cyclones associated with ARs exhibit substantially stronger heat and moisture transport and larger radiative anomalies than cyclones without ARs. These results highlight the central role of ARs in Arctic heat and moisture transport and demonstrate how their interaction with cyclones amplifies their impacts on the Arctic surface radiation anomalies.

494617.title: Benchmarking AI-based Weather Models for Energy Applications: from Large-scale Dynamics to Local Conditions
494617.authors: Meghna Thomas, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA; and N. Bodini, V. Amatya, D. Fytanidis, L. M. Sheridan, G. Xia, H. Tan, C. Jung, P. Moriarty, J. Wang, R. Kotamarthi, and R. Krishnamurthy
494617.abstract: Effective operation of electric grids depends heavily on weather forecasts: anticipating extreme temperature events and understanding the conditions that affect diverse energy sources helps utilities prepare to keep the grid stable, meet demand, and minimize disruptions. Weather forecasting models based on artificial intelligence (AI) have advanced rapidly and are now increasingly competitive with numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems at medium-range lead times. These models are attractive for their ability to learn from decades of historical reanalysis data (such as ERA5), their fast inference once trained, and their capacity to capture physically consistent atmospheric structure. With several AI models now available, selecting one for a given purpose is difficult due to varying training datasets used during model development, algorithmic differences, horizontal and temporal resolutions, and unknown uncertainties for a given atmospheric process. Comparative benchmarking has typically evaluated these models at global or broad regional scales against reanalysis datasets like ERA5, which provide useful, general indicators of performance. However, such broad comparisons seldom capture the aspects that matter most for energy applications: the uncertainty associated with forecasts, model behavior during high impact weather events, and the representation of local atmospheric phenomena. Performance within the atmospheric boundary layer, the low-level region that governs many energy applications, remains especially underexplored. This talk will compare several AI-based foundation models, including deterministic and probabilistic models like WeatherNext2, FourCastNet3, Argonne’s Earth system AI foundation model AERIS, Swift and Stormer, NeuralGCM, and AIFS over 2023–2025. We evaluate how well these models capture large-scale dynamics by comparing them CONUS-wide against NOAA's HRRR analysis, and how well they capture local phenomena by comparing model output against high-resolution observations from the US East Coast and Southern Great Plains. We assess performance across multiple dimensions, such as accuracy by variable and vertical level, and across lead times, seasons, and time of day, to determine which models perform best in which regions, what the uncertainty of probabilistic models looks like, how the models behave during high impact weather events (such as heat waves, cold snaps, etc.), and how faithfully they represent local atmospheric phenomena. We additionally conduct a secondary error-modeling analysis to understand how input variables and local geographic characteristics may drive a model to be more or less accurate. Together, these results will map each model's strengths and limitations to the demands of energy-sector forecasting.

494622.title: The Scale of Detectability: Regime-Dependent Urban Turbulence Responses to Progressive Building Refurbishment in Paris
494622.authors: Nooshin Nowzamani, Leibniz University Hannover, Hannover, Niedersachsen, Germany; and B. Maronga
494622.abstract: While current building-resolving large-eddy simulation (LES) frameworks explicitly represent three-dimensional urban morphology at metre-scale resolution, building-envelope thermophysics is often neglected or represented by a single idealized building type. This disparity creates an informational scale gap between the spatial resolution of the atmospheric solver and the physical detail of the urban surface, potentially limiting the representation of building–atmosphere coupling. Here, we investigate whether increasingly deep energetic refurbishment systematically reduces atmospheric heat release or instead redistributes energy in time and space, producing nonlinear and meteorology-dependent responses in urban turbulence. Using the PALM model system, we perform building-resolving LES for the late-August 2023 heat-wave episode over Paris. A nested configuration with horizontal grid spacings of 32, 8, 2, and 1 m spans the urban-boundary-layer, neighbourhood, roughness-sublayer, and building scales. Time-varying meteorological forcing is derived from the HARMONIE mesoscale model. The urban building stock is represented using 40 TABULA-derived archetypes with detailed, layer-resolved thermophysical properties. Three scenarios--existing state, usual refurbishment, and advanced refurbishment--are evaluated while retaining the same urban morphology, thereby isolating the atmospheric response to changes in building thermophysics and refurbishment depth. The analysis traces the propagation of refurbishment-induced thermal perturbations from building surfaces through the urban canopy and roughness sublayer into the neighbourhood-scale atmosphere.The analysis prioritizes the thermal memory of the urban fabric and the afternoon-to-evening transition. Changes in volumetric heat capacity and thermal resistance modify the magnitude and phase of stored heat release, potentially altering surface sensible heat flux, buoyancy production, vertical turbulent heat transport, and vertical velocity variance. We further examine the competing roles of envelope insulation, thermal storage, and building-related waste heat rejection to determine whether the atmospheric response scales monotonically with refurbishment depth or changes with the evolving meteorological regime. Finally, the nested LES framework is used to quantify a scale of detectability: the horizontal and vertical scales over which refurbishment-induced thermophysical perturbations remain distinguishable in the atmospheric state. By linking building-scale energy redistribution to canopy turbulence and boundary-layer evolution, this study identifies when, where, and at what scale detailed building thermophysics becomes dynamically relevant to the urban atmosphere.

494625.title: Diagnosis of the Assimilation Impact of Observation Data In Chinese Global Numerical Weather Prediction System
494625.authors: Yan Liu, China Meteorology Administration Earth System Modeling and Prediction Centre, Beijing, China; China Meteorology Administration Earth System Modeling and Prediction Centre, Beijing, China
494625.abstract: Observation data is an important foundation for numerical weather prediction systems, and its quality and distribution directly affect the effectiveness of data assimilation and the accuracy of forecasts. With the rapid development of global observation systems, modern numerical weather forecasting centers need to process tens of millions of observation data daily from aircraft, radiosondes, ground stations, satellites, and ocean platforms. How to quantitatively evaluate the contribution of different observation systems to the analysis field and forecast field has become an important direction in the optimization design of observation systems and data assimilation research. Based on the theoretical basis and operational application of two mainstream observation impact assessment methods, namely the Observing System Experiment and Forecast Sensitivity to Observation Impact, this paper first introduces the theoretical framework of the FSOI method, and then discusses the contribution characteristics of main observation systems such as radiosonde observations, ground observations, aircraft observations, microwave radiation data, infrared hyperspectral data, and radio occultation data.

494626.title: Airport-Hour Aggregation Masks Within-Airport Structure in AMDAR-Derived Boundary-Layer Height: Retrieval Definition, Flight Leg and Land-Surface Context
494626.authors: Christopher "Chuck" C. Baker Jr., University of Maryland College Park, College Park, MD; NOAA Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR), Boulder, CO; University of Maryland, College Park, MD; University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and J. English, D. D. Turner, and X. Z. Liang
494626.abstract: Aircraft Meteorological Data Relay (AMDAR) profiles provide an unusually dense observational record of lower-tropospheric structure, but planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) is diagnosed rather than directly observed, and so each profile samples a slant-path corridor rather than a fixed atmospheric column. As AMDAR-derived PBLH climatologies and model comparisons commonly combine multiple commercial-aircraft profiles into a single airport-hour value, while this strategy makes a dense observing record usable at continental scales, it assumes that profiles collected using different retrieval definitions, flight legs and surface corridors represent an interchangeable population. We test that assumption and identify the structure hidden by airport-hour averaging. The analysis uses 1,524,101 quality-controlled daytime retrievals collected from 2018 through 2025 at nine western U.S. airports spanning coastal, interior, high-plains and arid regimes. Rather than beginning with an airport-hour mean, we preserve the flight-level observations, diagnose PBLH using both the potential-temperature-increase (TI) and bulk-Richardson-number (BR) methods, separate ascents from descents, and classify the land surface beneath each retrieval using the National Land Cover Database. Paired contrasts, airport-day bootstrap inference, exogenous airport-to-profile-base distance / directional-sector controls, and compositional land-cover analysis are used to distinguish reproducible structure from sampling imbalance. Three findings emerge. First, retrieval definition is not a minor technical choice. TI exceeded BR in 50 of 52 supported airport-by-cover groups (with a median paired difference of 156 m) and the network method gap approximately doubled as the daytime boundary layer deepened. Second, ascent and descent were not interchangeable sampling populations. Within-day ascent-minus-descent offsets ranged from +16 to +65 m at seven airports, were negative at Reno, and were approximately null at Phoenix; the sign and magnitude of a pooled estimate changed with the weighting and conditioning scheme, precluding one universal flight-leg correction. Third, land-cover class retained a 7.3-percentage-point incremental association with PBLH after controlling for airport-to-profile-base distance and directional sector, with a 95 percent airport-day bootstrap interval of 6.9 to 7.7 percentage points. Solar modulation and closure-safe compositional contrasts were broadly consistent with surface-energy partitioning, but terrain, trajectory history, advection, clouds, and correlated meteorology remain viable alternative explanations. Naturally, site and season remained larger organizers of PBLH than any of the three tested flight-level axes. These findings do not invalidate airport-hour AMDAR products, but rather show what those products average over and identify the metadata needed to interpret their representativeness. Within coordinated companion work on retrieval development and numerical-model evaluation, this study isolates the observational-representativeness link between measurement and application. Preserving retrieval definition, flight leg and sampled surface context makes AMDAR PBLH products more traceable and reduces the risk of misreading observational structure as atmospheric forcing or model error.

494627.title: Downscaling HRRR Wind Fields over Complex Terrain Using QES-Winds: A Yakima Valley Case Study
494627.authors: Behnam Bozorgmehr, Washington State University, Pullman, WA; Washington State Univ., Pullman, WA; and F. Margairaz, R. Stoll, W. Mahaffee, and H. Liu
494627.abstract: Numerical weather prediction models provide valuable regional atmospheric forcing but cannot resolve many terrain-induced variations in near-surface winds that influence transport and dispersion over mountainous landscapes. This study develops and evaluates a cross-scale modeling framework that downscales wind fields from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model using QES-Winds, a computationally efficient three-dimensional mass-consistent wind model. The objective is to produce computationally efficient, high-resolution wind fields that retain the larger-scale atmospheric conditions represented by HRRR while introducing the local influence of topography.
