Hourly HRRR meteorological fields at 3-km resolution are interpolated to a 100-m QES-Winds grid using bilinear interpolation. Atmospheric stability is represented using two approaches: The first uses Pasquill–Gifford stability classes based on near-surface wind speed, solar radiation, and cloud cover. The second estimates the Monin–Obukhov length directly from HRRR surface momentum and buoyancy fluxes. These methods allow QES-Winds to generate stability-dependent initial wind profiles before applying the mass-conservation adjustment. The framework is evaluated against near-surface tower observations collected in the Yakima Valley, Washington, during the 2020 wildfire season. The downscaled wind fields agree more closely with the observations than the original HRRR fields and provide more spatial detail around mountainous areas. The framework remains computationally efficient, making it suitable for high-resolution wind and smoke-transport applications. One limitation of the mass-consistent models is that they cannot generate terrain-induced flow separation and leeward recirculation. Ongoing work addresses this limitation through a geometry-based wake parameterization that identifies separation locations and represents recirculation regions downstream of hills and mountains. The Yakima Valley will serve as a real-world (not idealized) test case for evaluating how this parameterization affects local winds and wildfire-smoke transport estimates.

494628.title: Where, When, and How to Seed Marine Low Clouds: Emulating Lagrangian-LES Ensembles
494628.authors: Daisy Kerr, UC Berkeley, Berkeley, CA; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and J. Zhang, G. Feingold, and T. Yamaguchi
494628.abstract: The efficacy of marine cloud brightening (MCB) depends critically on how marine low clouds respond to aerosol perturbations. In particular, cloud adjustments arising from aerosol-mediated changes in cloud and precipitation processes remain a major uncertainty in determining where, when, and under what conditions MCB may be effective. These responses depend not only on the amount of aerosol introduced, but also on the timing and duration of seeding and the co-evolving meteorological conditions that govern cloud evolution. Here, we classify stratocumulus-to-cumulus transitions off the California coast according to their co-varying large-scale meteorological conditions, producing seven representative composites of Lagrangian trajectories. We then simulate these transitions using Lagrangian large-eddy simulations (LES). For each trajectory, we perform an ensemble of perturbation experiments spanning a broad range of aerosol injection rates, durations, and initiation times. The simulations reveal that cloud cover responses depend strongly on both the timing of seeding and the evolving meteorological state. Comparable aerosol perturbations can therefore produce substantially different cloud responses depending on when they are applied during the cloud transition. To generalize beyond the simulated cases, we develop a Gaussian process emulator for each trajectory, enabling rapid prediction of cloud responses across a broader range of seeding scenarios. By combining process-resolving atmospheric modeling with machine-learning emulation, we provide process-level insight into the response of marine boundary-layer clouds to aerosol perturbations and a computationally efficient approach for identifying favorable, and unfavorable, conditions and strategies for marine cloud brightening.

494629.title: Improving Radar-based Precipitation Estimation and Microphysics Retrievals Across Different Precipitation Regimes Using Deep Transfer Learning
494629.authors: Haonan Chen, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO
494629.abstract: Accurate and timely estimation of precipitation microphysics and surface precipitation rate is essential for understanding precipitation processes, as well as real-time applications in decision-making regarding water resources allocation and emergency management planning. Polarimetric weather radar is the primary tool used for quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) and precipitation microphysics retrievals. However, distinct features in topographical and meteorological environments in different precipitation regimes can degrade the generalization capability of a deep learning model trained in a specific region when applied to other regions. In addition, many areas have a lack of in situ and/or radar observations that are sufficient to train a deep learning model. This paper presents an adaptive transfer learning framework for polarimetric weather radar quantitative precipitation estimation and microphysics retrievals, which incorporates a long-distance regulation module and a short-distance adaptation module determined by the distribution similarity of polarimetric radar data across different precipitation regimes. To adaptively adjust the number of shared features in the neighborhood and alleviate the negative knowledge transfer problem, the proposed model adopts a dynamic adaptive layer and a novel loss function. The feasibility and performance of the transfer learning model are demonstrated and quantified using U.S. Weather Surveillance Radar-1988 Doppler (WSR-88D) observations and surface gauge measurements from five different precipitation regimes. Experimental results suggest that the designed transfer learning model can not only improve the accuracy of precipitation estimation and microphysics retrievals in data-scarce regions but also enhance the model’s generalization capability across diverse geophysical regions.

494630.title: Interactive H2 in CESM2.2/CAM-chem: Sources, Sinks, and Coupling to Atmospheric Oxidation
494630.authors: Mohammad Amin Mirrezaei, Univ. of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and B. Gaubert, A. Wong, G. Porter, I. Ortega, K. McKain, L. M. Bruhwiler, Y. Oh, G. Petron, X. Lan, R. Bordelon, L. Meredith, and A. F. Arellano Jr.
494630.abstract: Atmospheric H2 is controlled mainly by photochemical production from formaldehyde and microbial soil uptake, with smaller contributions from direct emissions and chemical loss by OH. In most global chemistry models, however, H2 is prescribed rather than calculated interactively, limiting its coupling with atmospheric chemistry. We use an emission-driven CESM2.2/CAM-chem simulation for 2010–2020 to represent atmospheric H2 interactively and compare it with the standard prescribed-H2 configuration. Both simulations include interactive tropospheric chemistry, including short-lived halogens. The emission-driven simulation uses direct H2 emissions from the recent Global Hydrogen Budget inventory and tagged H2 tracers separate the contributions of direct emission sectors and photochemical production. Comparisons with NOAA Cooperative Global Air Sampling Network flask measurements and NOAA GML aircraft profiles show that allowing H2 to evolve from its modeled sources and sinks improves the simulated spatial and seasonal distribution, reducing the mean absolute surface bias from 39 to 10 ppb and the campaign-mean aircraft bias from 67 to 49 ppb. We further constrain the dominant H2 source and sink by performing a companion simulation with an updated soil-uptake scheme based on soil physical properties and microbial activity, and by evaluating the photochemical source using formaldehyde observations from OMI satellite columns, ATom in situ profiles, and NDACC FTIR column measurements. Interactive H2 also changes the partitioning of OH loss within the troposphere, with H2–OH oxidation changing by up to 10% regionally. In contrast, total tropospheric OH production and loss change by less than 0.3%, as changes in H2oxidation are compensated by changes in OH loss through CO, CH4, and VOCs. These simulations provide a present-day baseline for future H2-emission scenarios while helping constrain uncertainties in the major H2 source and sink processes.

494631.title: The Amundsen Sea Low, Atmospheric Rivers, and the Climate of West Antarctica
494631.authors: Michelle De Luna, University of California Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA; University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA
494631.abstract: The polar cryosphere is maintained by the transport of moisture from low to high latitudes. Across Antarctica, one of the leading moisture transport mechanisms is the atmospheric river (AR), a transient corridor of enhanced water vapor transport known to produce both intense snowfall and surface melting over the polar region. Previous studies have linked Antarctic ARs to a surface high-low pressure couplet that forms over the Southern Ocean (SO) and redirects flow poleward in the meridional direction. While the high-pressure ridge has been identified as a vital component in the production of AR conditions, few studies have investigated the role of its low-pressure counterpart in modulating AR behavior. This study focuses on the region of West Antarctica and examines the relationship between ARs and the Amundsen Sea Low (ASL), a dynamic climatological low-pressure area in the Pacific sector of the SO. We investigate how variations in the position and magnitude of the ASL influence the spatial trajectory of Antarctic ARs. Furthermore, we examine how ASL-driven changes in AR activity affect the surface climate of West Antarctica during the period 1979-2025, with special attention paid to sea ice - a component of the Earth system that has undergone significant and unprecedented change in recent years. Our results show increased AR activity across the Bellingshausen Sea and Antarctic Peninsula during extremely strong ASL events, thus indicating an eastward shift in AR trajectory when ASL magnitude is strongest. During extremely weak ASL events, we identify a concentrated area of AR activity over the Ross Sea but a clear AR trajectory is not immediately apparent. Sea ice concentration and two-meter temperature anomalies align closely with AR trajectory and reflect local circulation patterns, which are influenced by ASL magnitude. The purpose of our study is to provide a comprehensive understanding of atmospheric moisture transport to West Antarctica as it relates to the ASL, a regional feature that strongly influences the climate of the study region. We suggest that changes to the ASL may affect the direction (and intensity) of meridional moisture transport via ARs and, moreover, consider the implications of such changes on the surface climate of West Antarctica at present and in a warmer future.

494635.title: Sliding Window Method for Adjoint Sensitivity under Nonlinear Evolution
494635.authors: Minori Fukushima, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Kyoto, Japan; and T. Enomoto and S. Nakashita
494635.abstract: Adjoint sensitivity analysis is an efficient method for identifying regions of the initial state to which a specified forecast metric is sensitive. However, because it is based on tangent-linear dynamics, its interpretation in terms of the response to finite initial perturbations can become less reliable as nonlinear effects accumulate. Separately, even when the tangent-linear approximation remains applicable, longer adjoint integrations can yield spatially diffuse sensitivity fields due to dynamical instability, making it difficult to isolate high-sensitivity regions at the initial time. This study introduces a Sliding Window Method (SWM) for adjoint sensitivity analysis and evaluates its effectiveness in identifying initial regions that influence the forecast metric under nonlinear evolution. The SWM divides the full analysis period into shorter time windows. Within each window, sensitivities are propagated backward with the adjoint model, and a spatial localization operator is applied at the boundaries between windows before the backward propagation continues. In contrast to the conventional adjoint method, which propagates sensitivity over the entire analysis period at once, the SWM sequentially restricts the spatial extent of the sensitivity during backward propagation. The SWM does not remove the underlying nonlinearity; rather, it is designed to control the spatial spreading of adjoint sensitivity while separating its backward propagation into shorter time intervals. The method was evaluated primarily using the Lorenz-96 model. The forcing parameter was varied from 4 to 8 to examine regimes with different degrees of nonlinearity and error growth. Analysis periods of 4, 8, and 12 days were considered, with window lengths equal to 1/2, 1/4, or 1/8 of the full analysis period and with several localization ranges. The conventional method and the SWM were evaluated using nonlinear forward integrations rather than by comparing the sensitivity fields alone. Initial perturbations were constructed from each sensitivity field and applied either over all grid points or only to the grid point with the largest sensitivity and its two neighboring points. Both perturbed and unperturbed states were then integrated with the nonlinear model to the verification time, and the configuration producing the largest perturbation amplitude at the verification location or region was identified. The comparison was performed over 200 background states and 40 verification locations for each parameter setting. The conventional adjoint method tended to be selected more frequently when nonlinearity was weak or the analysis period was short. When the initial perturbation was restricted to the three grid points around the largest sensitivity, however, shorter-window SWM configurations were increasingly favored as nonlinearity increased. In contrast, when perturbations were applied over all grid points, the conventional method remained the most frequently selected configuration in most cases, although the differences among the methods decreased as nonlinearity increased. These results suggest that the benefit of the SWM is not simply to narrow the sensitivity distribution, but to more selectively identify high-sensitivity regions that remain dynamically influential through nonlinear evolution. No single window length was optimal across all conditions; the preferred window length depended on the degree of nonlinearity, the analysis period, the localization range, and the construction of the initial perturbation. Supplementary experiments with the storm-track Lorenz-96 model, in which dynamical instability varies spatially, yielded results consistent with the Lorenz-96 experiments: shorter windows and narrower localization tended to be more effective in strongly unstable regions, whereas longer windows and broader localization tended to be favored in more stable regions. Together, these results suggest that effective window lengths and localization scales depend on the dynamical regime, motivating future work on selecting these parameters adaptively in more complex atmospheric systems.

494637.title: It's Getting Hot in Here: Assessing Public Understanding of NWS Heat Products
494637.authors: Marissa K. Krautbauer, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; University of Oklahoma Student Chapter of the American Meteorological Society and National Weather Association (OU SCAN), Norman, OK; and C. Delconte, N. Threlkeld, C. O'Donnell, B. J. Fellman, and E. R. Martin
494637.abstract: Heat is the leading cause of weather-related fatalities in the United States, yet National Weather Service (NWS) heat products (such as graphics posted to social media sites) have historically struggled to elicit adequate public understanding and protective action. Recent changes to these products—including revised wording and the introduction of HeatRisk, a color-graded graphical tool designed to convey heat severity and potential health impacts—represented significant shifts in how hazardous heat is communicated. However, it remained unclear whether these updates improved comprehension or motivated protective decision-making among the general public. It was imperative to see what effects, if any, these changes had on public understanding and encouragement to take protective action. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of these changes by examining how people interpreted both the older and updated NWS heat products. To do this, we administered a survey to university students and faculty, capturing demographic information related to heat exposure and vulnerability. Participants were randomly assigned a selection of questions about either the old heat products or the updated heat versions, allowing for an unbiased comparison of comprehension, perceived severity, and likelihood of taking protective action. Additional questions assessed reactions to graphical tools such as HeatRisk. Particular attention was paid to whether terms like “extreme” function as jargon or convey meaningful risk. By analyzing how different forms of heat communication are interpreted, this research sought to identify language and visual elements that most effectively communicate hazardous heat. More generally, we aimed to gain insight into the kinds of language that best convey the true risk of dangerous heat. Through this insight, NWS products can be tailored to improve public understanding, encourage timely protective behaviors, and ultimately minimize heat-related injuries and fatalities.

494639.title: Mission Specific Weather Decision Issues at the Regan Test Range, Kwajalein Marshall Islands
494639.authors: Charles W. Washington, RedTown Technical Services, Kwajalein, AP; and J. W. Evans
494639.abstract: The Ronald Reagan Ballistic Missile Defense Test Range (RTR) at Kwajalein Atoll presents forecasting requirements distinct from those of traditional space-launch ranges. Where launch weather support is built around Lightning Launch Commit Criteria and vehicle-specific constraints, ballistic missile defense (BMD) testing carries its own set of weather-sensitive thresholds, among which rainfall's effect on optical systems stands out as particularly unforgiving: optical assets go “red” at the first sign of rain, a frequent occurrence in this part of the tropical Pacific. Losing optics leaves range operators without critical visual data to evaluate system performance; while range safety and tracking can partially fall back on independent radar and telemetry systems, and terminal scoring may still proceed via ground-based assets, post-flight engineering analysis suffers a lasting data deficit, and a test may end up only partially meeting its data objectives. This precipitation-driven constraint is compounded by a sparse observational network: Kwajalein's radar is the sole operational unit in the entire Republic of the Marshall Islands, with no surrounding meteorological network for corroboration, and its products carry a 10-15 minute processing delay. Go/no-go decisions begin four hours before test time, with continuous updates through final countdown. In this high-stakes, low-margin environment, forecasters lean heavily on trained technique and experience, combining satellite imagery, 30-minute surface observations, upper-air soundings, and seasonal climatological knowledge, to anticipate the onset and duration of rainfall in a region shaped by ITCZ positioning, trade wind surges, and doldrums conditions. This presentation describes the weather decision-support process for BMD test events at RTR, contrasting rainfall-driven optics constraints with broader orbital launch weather criteria. Drawing on operational forecasting experience spanning both continental launch ranges (Patrick Space Force Base) and the remote, single-radar environment of Kwajalein, this talk examines the methodology used to protect a four-hour decision window against a rainfall threshold as sensitive as "first drop," and what's operationally lost when that threshold is crossed. The goal is to give the ARAM community a clearer picture of the meteorological support requirements unique to missile defense testing, an area less commonly represented in launch-weather literature compared to orbital and crewed spaceflight operations.

494640.title: Can a Front Detector Trained over North America Track Fronts Globally?
494640.authors: Hayoung Bong, NASA, New York, NY; and J. F. Booth, A. N. LeGrande, C. M. Naud, J. T. Allen, T. S. Mandelbaum, and A. McGovern
494640.abstract: Deep learning has produced skillful front detectors, but published detectors have largely been trained on hand-drawn analyses from Northern Hemisphere domains. One previous study extended such a detector to the Southern Hemisphere using mirrored training augmentation and reported the result as plausible but untested. This work asks whether hemispheric transfer can be measured, and when it fails, corrected without retraining and without new labels. We begin from FrontFinder, a published UNET3+ detector deployed operationally at NOAA's Weather Prediction Center, and retrain that architecture from scratch on a longer record of the same analyses. The labeled region is NOAA's Unified Surface Analysis Domain, reaching from the western Pacific across North America to Europe. It is far wider than a single continent, yet all of its labels come from one hemisphere. On years held entirely out of training the detector reaches precision between 71 and 92 percent depending on front type and reproduces the frontal area drawn by analysts. Carried directly south of the equator, it largely fails, finding orders of magnitude less frontal area at the same storm-track latitudes. Key dynamical fields change parity across the equator, so a Southern Hemisphere front presents a pattern the network was never shown. The remedy is a symmetry argument rather than more data. We reflect the inputs across the equator and reverse the sign of the parity-odd channels, the meridional wind and potential vorticity, 13 of the model's 77 inputs, then mirror the detection back. The frontal signal returns immediately, with no retraining. A control confirms the diagnosis. The same mirrored pass run over the Northern Hemisphere, where the detector normally works, fails there too, which places the fault in the handling of parity rather than in any real difference in frontal activity between the hemispheres. To test the mirrored half, we compare the catalog against two independent objective front products, one computed across the whole grid from thermal criteria and one cyclone-centered archive, on a different reanalysis, that locates fronts from wind shift alone. The wind-based reference uses no thermodynamic criterion, so agreement with it cannot come from an assumption our detector shares. Over ocean the mirrored hemisphere agrees with both at least as closely as the directly applied hemisphere does, in every front type. Over Southern Hemisphere land it does not, and both references say so, which we report rather than hide in a global average. Hemispheric transfer is therefore achievable by one transformation over ocean, and remains open over Southern Hemisphere land. The resulting catalog covers 1979 to 2025, six-hourly, at 0.25-degree resolution on the full global grid, with per-class probabilities retained so that thresholds can be recalibrated for a region or a period without retraining. We expect it to support climatologies of frontal frequency and motion, attribution of precipitation to fronts, and the evaluation of fronts in climate model output globally.

494647.title: Near Real Time LEO Level-2 Products via Direct Broadcast Using the Community Satellite Processing Package
494647.abstract: The Cooperative Institute for Meteorological Satellite Studies (CIMSS) has a long history of supporting the Direct Broadcast (DB) community for various low-Earth-orbit (LEO) sensors, previously with the International MODIS/AIRS Processing Package (IMAPP) for the NASA EOS polar orbiters Terra and Aqua, and currently with the Community Satellite Processing Package (CSPP) for the NOAA polar orbiters Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. CSPP has been significant in encouraging the early usage of Suomi-NPP data by US and international weather agencies, and this situation should continue with NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and beyond. Since 2021, CSPP support for NOAA polar orbiters has depended on the provision by NOAA of "Cloud Containerized Algorithm Packages (CCAP), developed by the Algorithm Scientific Software Integration and System Transition Team (ASSISTT). For selected science algorithms, CCAPs contain the source code and supporting scripting to enable building and containerizing the science algorithms and running them in a cloud processing environment. The CSPP team is tasked with taking the CCAPs and transforming them into deliverable software packages which can be run in a direct-broadcast/readout context. CSPP packages are targeted at execution on modest hardware, by potentially novice users, thus helping the increase and broaden the impact of NOAA funded scientific research. Example CSPP packages shown in this presentation include VIIRS Flood Mapping, OMPS Total Ozone / Profile, and OMPS SO2.

494649.title: Wildfire Smoke Influence on Ozone Precursors and Other Atmospheric Constituents during the Colorado Front Range Ozone Éxperiment (FROZÉ 2025)
494649.authors: Brandon McGuire, Colorado State University, FORT COLLINS, CO
494649.abstract: Colorado’s Denver Metro/Northern Front Range (DM/NFR) contains unique air quality challenges, including summer wildfire smoke coinciding with elevated ozone levels. Several studies have investigated the air quality impacts of wildfire smoke in the DM/NFR. The presence of smoke can elevate fine particulate matter (PM) concentrations, modify the distribution of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and increase the abundance of ozone (O3). Here, we report findings of wildfire smoke’s influence on gas-phase composition and PM abundance in northeastern Colorado using data collected from the summer 2025 Front Range OZone Éxperiment (FROZÉ). The campaign combined stationary and mobile measurements of O3, speciated VOCs, and NOx from June-August 2025 throughout the DM/NFR. Events of transported smoke allowed for investigation of smoke-driven differences in the abundance of a variety of trace gases at two stationary monitoring locations. This dataset includes measurements from both gas chromatography (GC) and proton-transfer-reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometry (PTR-ToF-MS), providing a large mix of alkanes, alkenes, aromatics, and oxygenated VOCs. Significant increases in formaldehyde, benzene, toluene, and other hazardous air pollutants (HAPs) were measured in the presence of smoke. Additionally, mobile measurements of smoke from the Lee Fire (located ~50 miles northeast of Grand Junction, CO) were observed near the mountain town of Estes Park, CO, prior to descending into the DM/NFR, and included enhancements in PM, O3, and other trace gases. Across these stationary and mobile datasets, measured composition were related to air mass trajectories, smoke age calculations, hydroxyl radical reactivity, and ambient meteorology to untangle the influence of smoke on air quality in the DM/NFR in the summer of 2025.

494650.title: Inverse Interscale Turbulent Transport over Idealized Urban Morphology
494650.authors: Ruiqi Wang, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; and Y. Hou, M. Qiu, W. C. Cheng, and C. H. Liu
494650.abstract: Surface-mounted roughness elements reshape energy transport in turbulent boundary layers (TBLs). This study uses large-eddy simulation (LES) of neutral atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) to trace out the full pathway from mean kinetic energy (KE) to turbulence then the redistribution of turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) in scale space. Alike flat-wall flows, roughness does not modify much forward mean KE transfer. However, notable inverse TKE cascades are observed within the roughness sublayers (RSLs). Our previous studies have proposed that rougher urban areas favor street-level ventilation and pollutant removal because of locally generated RSL turbulence [1]. Hence, small-scale turbulence is initiated on rough surfaces then evolves to large one (inverse energy transport) [2]. Recently, multiscale analyses evidenced that TKE is mainly entrained from ABL prevailing flows over ISLs down to RSLs and even urban canopy layers (UCLs) [3]. It is thus suggested that energetic (larger) scales at higher levels modulate their lower-level, smaller counterparts (forward energy transport) [4]. Because of the dissimilar findings, this study is conceived to demystify the forcing and mechanism of turbulent transport over (rough) urban areas. Continuity and momentum conservation in incompressible flows are solved by the open-source LES code LESGO [5]. Periodic boundary conditions (BCs) are applied in horizontal extents. Open-channel flows over arrays of explicitly resolved roughness elements are adopted that represent an isothermal ABL over idealized urban areas of different roughness. Prevailing flows are driven by a constant pressure gradient at friction velocity uτ (= 0.45 m sec−1). The computational domain is 8H (= 8,000 m) long x, 4H (= 4,000 m) wide y, and H (= 1,000 m) high z. It is discretized into almost 537 million cubes by uniform Cartesian meshes Δxi (= 3.9 m). After pseudo-steady, LESs are continued for another 70,000 steps (3.5 eddy turnover time H/uτ ) at time increment Δt (= 4.5×10−2 sec) during which data are archived at 100Δt interval. The maximum Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) number is therefore less than 0.1. Here, uτ and H serve as the characteristic velocity and length scales, respectively. As such, the Reynolds number Reuτ is almost 30×106. In addition to the flat-wall one (0x0), the LES datasets comprise 7 distinct cases of rough-wall flows (2x1, 8x4, 14x7, 20x10, 26x13, 32x16, and 38x19 with increasing packing density Λp) by surface-mounting identical square blocks of width 0.1H (= 100 m) and height 0.06H (= 60 m) represented by level set immersed boundary method (IBM) with a range of packing density 1.1×10−3 ≤ Λp ≤ 3.8×10−1. Logarithmic velocity profiles with roughness length z0 (= 0.1 m) are applied on all the solid boundaries. Interscale TKE cascade is predominantly forward ΓTKE for all the surfaces tested (Figure 1). In the flat-wall TBL, there is a notable forward TKE cascade and a tiny inverse TKE cascade, respectively, at cutoff wavelengths of λy,c about 0.03H and 0.1H. Such big difference in TKE cascade intensity (2 orders of magnitude in ΓTKE) is in line with existing studies using direct numerical simulation (DNS) [6] thought subgrid-scale (SGS) and wall models are used in this LES. Other than the cases 32×16 and 38×19, ground-level, negative ΓTKE emerges at wavelength longer than UCL scale (λy,c ≥ 0.1H). Nevertheless, these inverse-TKE cascade signatures are weak that are confined within UCLs. Elevated ΓTKE at cutoff wavelength λy,c ≈ 0.1H is distinct at roof level other than the TBLs over a flat wall or case 2×1. Rough surfaces thus plainly energize forward TKE cascade at motion scales comparable to the UCL ones. While roof-level, positive ΓTKE is strongest in the case 20×10, further increase in packing density Λp switches ΓTKE to negative (cases 32×16 or 38×19), initiating inverse TKE cascade. Hence, roughness elements at sufficiently dense packing (Λp ≥ 2.7×10−1) could generate TBL-scale eddies (λy,c ≈ H) at UCL roof level, cascading TKE inversely to even longer motion scales. Although the TKE cascade term ΓTKE originates from different formulations, scales, and processes, it systematically derives the forward/inverse interscale transport in ABL/TBL flows over rough surfaces of various packing density Λp. Rough (urban) surfaces with explicitly resolved roughness elements (buildings) promote forward mean KE transfer in RSLs and UCLs. Likewise, roughness triggers and modulates forward/inverse cascade of TKE. Additional analyses are needed to elucidate the detailed mechanism and forcing. References [1] C.-H. Liu, C.-T. Ng, and C. C. C. Wong, “A theory of ventilation estimate over hypothetical urban areas”, Journal of Hazardous Materials 296, 9 (2015). [2] F. Li, R. Wang, G. Chen, Z. Mo, N. Ikegaya, and C.-H. Liu, “Turbulence scale and strength analysis in the roughness and inertial sublayers over urban areas: A wind tunnel study”, Building and Environment 267, 112193 (2025). [3] R. Wang, C.-H. Liu, F. Li, and Z. Mo, “Turbulent transport mechanism in the roughness sublayers over idealized urban areas and its implication to street-level ventilation”, Sustainable Cities and Society 100, 105030 (2024). [4] R. Wang, C.-H. Liu, Y. Liu, F. Li, G. Chen, and Z. Mo, "Atmospheric surface layer turbulence: Intermittency and multiscale structure", Physics of Fluids 38, 065123 (2026). [5] LESGO, LESGO: A parallel pseudo-spectral large-eddy simulation code. [6] C. I. Chan, P. Schlatter, and R. C. Chin, "Interscale transport mechanisms in turbulent boundary layers", Journal of Fluid Mechanics 921, A13 (2021).

494651.title: Disruptive Novel Magnetograph Technology to Unravel the Physics of Solar Magnetism and Further Improve Space Weather Prediction
494651.authors: Georgios Chintzoglou, Lockheed Martin Advanced Technology Center, Palo Alto, CA; and N. Hurlburt
494651.abstract: Understanding the magnetic field of the Sun is central to predicting solar eruptions, understanding the heliosphere, and assessing space-weather hazards throughout the solar system. Current solar magnetographs are limited by the aperture sizes that can be launched on a single spacecraft, restricting spatial resolution and sensitivity. This disruptive technology introduces a fundamentally new approach: interferometric solar spectropolarimetric measurements are combined through computational imaging techniques to synthesize the resolving power of a much larger telescope for a fraction of mass (and cost) of conventional (heavy) space-based magnetographs. This technology leverages photonic integrated circuits, multi-aperture design with polarization, and advanced image reconstruction algorithms to recover high-resolution spectropolarimetric observations of the solar photosphere and chromosphere while significantly reducing mass, volume, and cost. The concept enables scalable architectures in which angular resolution can be including longer baselines for the aperture synthesis, opening a pathway toward sub-arcsecond and ultimately unprecedented magnetic-field measurements from space. Future observations with this instrumentation would address key science questions in solar and heliophysics research, including the formation and evolution of active regions, magnetic flux emergence and decay, flare and coronal mass ejection initiation, magnetic energy storage and release, the solar dynamo and other helioseismology problems, and the coupling of the solar atmosphere across multiple spatial scales. Thanks to the low mass and cost, multi-satellite constellation missions with such instruments could also provide simultaneous multi-vantage measurements of solar magnetic fields and Doppler velocities across photosphere and chromosphere, enabling stereoscopic constraints on three-dimensional magnetic structures, helioseismic inversions of the solar internal rotation, and improved data-driven models of the solar corona and heliosphere for the prediction of imminent eruptive flares. By combining interferometric imaging with low-mass multi-spacecraft constellations, this technology presents a transformative capability for future solar magnetic-field measurements and space-weather forecasting.

494658.title: A Conceptual Model to Demonstrate Equatorial Rossby-Gravity Wave Instabilities Under Meridional Wind Shear.
494658.authors: Pragallva Barpanda, University of Bergen, Bjerknes Center for Climate Research, Bergen, Norway; and S. N. Tulich, J. Dias, and G. N. Kiladis
494658.abstract: Equatorial Rossby, Kelvin, and gravity waves, first isolated theoretically by Matsuno (1966) as orthogonal solutions to the rotating shallow-water equations, are fundamental drivers of tropical atmospheric dynamics. Standard theoretical frameworks treat these modes as non-interactive, independent waves propagating over a quiescent background state. In reality, background zonal flows and horizontal meridional wind shear alter wave propagation, phase speeds, and their spatial structures. How background mean-flow variations mediate wave-wave interactions remains insufficiently understood. Here, we revisit Matsuno’s framework by incorporating an equatorially symmetric zonal flow with horizontal meridional shear. Using a transient linear shallow-water system and a reduced-order model with a finite meridional truncation (N>=2), we examine how background shear modifies classical equatorial modes. We find that meridional wind shear breaks mode orthogonality, forcing Rossby and Kelvin/gravity waves to couple and exchange energy through the background flow. In steady-state Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO)-like regimes, this coupling significantly alters horizontal flow structures and amplifies wave responses as the midlatitude subtropical jet strengthens. Under moderate shear conditions, these modes exhibit transient non-normal growth, while under extreme shear, wave-wave resonance between Doppler-shifted Rossby waves and Kelvin/gravity waves triggers a resonant instability which are distinct from classical barotropic or baroclinic instabilities. These results demonstrate that background meridional shear, even when remotely induced by subtropical jets, acts as a key mediator of equatorial wave interactions, mode hybridization, and planetary-scale wave instabilities relevant to Earth, tropical oceans, and other planetary atmospheres.

494663.title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning Retrieval of High-Resolution Spectral AOD from MTG-I FCI over Africa
494663.authors: Ahmed Khan Salman, University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and P. Gupta, J. Seo, A. Sayeed, and S. Neupane
494663.abstract: Africa sustains some of the strongest aerosol variability in the world, driven by Saharan dust, seasonal biomass burning, and rising anthropogenic emissions. Ground-based monitoring remains sparse, leaving aerosol and PM2.5 assessment undersampled. The Meteosat Third Generation Imager Flexible Combined Imager (MTG-I FCI) observes the full disk every 10 minutes with fine spatial resolution multi-channel measurements, an unprecedented capability for resolving rapidly evolving aerosol features. We present an uncertainty-aware deep learning retrieval of spectral aerosol optical depth (AOD) at 2 km from FCI, with pixel-level uncertainty estimates. Cloud-screened FCI visible and near-infrared reflectance, solar and viewing geometry, and visible surface albedo are collocated with AERONET spectral AOD using the nearest pixel-centered patch within ±10 minutes. A generalized TabM architecture, a deep learning framework embedding an efficient ensemble of 32 members within a single network, retrieves AOD at 440, 500, 675, 870, and 1020 nm simultaneously. Retrieving the full spectrum rather than AOD at 500 nm alone preserves the wavelength dependence of aerosol extinction and its particle-size information. The member-specific predictions provide an intrinsic basis for uncertainty estimation. We apply three complementary uncertainty approaches: TabM member spread, Monte Carlo dropout (MCD), and a probabilistic TabM that predicts conditional variance directly. Evaluation on 18 temporally independent test days, the last three of each month from June to November 2025, yields 61,713 collocations. Across 440–1020 nm, Pearson correlations are 0.93–0.94, index of agreement around 0.96, and RMSE is 0.032–0.055. Calibrated uncertainties align well with retrieval error, with spread-skill reliability errors of 0.001–0.005, while spread-skill ratios of 0.762–0.892 indicate residual under-dispersion. Probability integral transform deviations of 0.025–0.047 and prediction-interval coverage probability close to nominal confirm statistically reliable uncertainties. TabM member spread is best calibrated at 440–675 nm, whereas MCD and probabilistic TabM remain most reliable at 870–1020 nm. During the biomass burning season, the retrieval captures smoke-elevated AOD over south-central Africa, spatially coherent with Suomi-NPP VIIRS and extending well beyond AERONET locations. Coupling high-frequency spectral AOD with statistically reliable uncertainty provides an aerosol-informed future pathway for PM2.5 estimation over data-sparse regions.

494664.title: Linking Vertical Velocity and Microphysical Properties in Convective Cells: Multi-Doppler and Polarimetric Radar Observations from TRACER and ESCAPE
494664.authors: Lauren Marie Beard, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and B. Dolan, M. M. Bell, S. M. Saleeby, and V. Chandrasekar
494664.abstract: Convective updraft structure drives the evolution of raindrop size distributions (DSDs), but the timing between dynamical forcing and microphysical response remains poorly constrained. This gap limits quantitative precipitation estimation and the accuracy of microphysical parameterizations in numerical models. This study examines this timing using coordinated multi-Doppler and polarimetric radar observations from the DOE Tracking Aerosol Convection Interactions Experiment (TRACER) and NSF Experiment of Sea Breeze Convection, Aerosols, Precipitation, and Environment (ESCAPE) campaigns, conducted near Houston, Texas, during the summer of 2022. The campaigns deployed a coordinated four-radar network combining C-band and X-band polarimetric Doppler radars with operational NEXRAD coverage. The C-band radars used an adaptive sector-scanning strategy that tracked individual storm cells and directed 2-minute scan cycles toward actively evolving convection, resolving cell lifecycles at sub-kilometer scales much better than the standard operational volume scans allow. Three-dimensional wind fields were retrieved using a variational multi-Doppler synthesis technique, SAMURAI, drop size distribution parameters were derived from dual-polarization radar variables using established retrieval methods, and hydrometeor classification characterized the vertical distribution of precipitation type. We present several case studies of convective cells sampled by the adaptive multi-Doppler network. On 7 August 2022, two cells were tracked through their life cycles: Cell 1 developed a compact updraft core with strong vertical velocities despite its limited horizontal extent, while Cell 2 was sampled at an earlier developmental stage, with weaker but steadily strengthening updrafts. In both cells, peak drop size occurred before the time of maximum updraft strength, while the drop size distribution did not reach its equilibrium, high-concentration state until after the updraft peak. These results are compared to the dynamic and microphysical timing and interactions of two additional cells on 17 September 2022. This decoupling between the timing of peak drop size and peak drop concentration relative to updraft intensity offers a useful diagnostic for evaluating microphysics parameterizations in cloud-resolving models.

494668.title: Variability in Strength, Timing and Areal Coverage of Heat Waves in Different Regions of the World, 1940-2026.
494668.authors: Brandt D. Maxwell, Brandt Maxwell Meteorological Consulting, San Diego, CA
494668.abstract: As average temperatures have increased globally between 1940 and 2026, heat waves and associated 850 hPa temperatures have increased in many locations. The Continental United States (CONUS), western and central Europe, the Indian subcontinent, and Australia were analyzed (based on latitude and longitude bounds for each which include nearby oceanic areas) for changes in the strength, frequency and areal coverage of heat waves using 850 hPa temperatures based on ERA5 reanalysis (1940-2026) plus monthly average surface temperature anomalies based on Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS/NASA) data (dataset started in 1880, but only months and areas with 85% data coverage over the regions were used and thus mostly started around 1900 for this study). GISS/NASA data showed average temperatures in each of the summer months for the four regions (including April and May in India which are climatologically hot months) have increased at rates between 0.7°C and 1.4°C per 100 years since 1900, with an acceleration in the increase in heat after 2000. Europe had the highest rate of increase, followed by India, Australia, and the CONUS. There were 4 to 10 times the number of summer months with surface temperature anomalies greater than +1.0°C after 2000 versus 2000 and before in all the regions (despite the number of years after 2000 only being ¼ the number on and before 2000), and summer months with those anomalies sometimes occurring in consecutive years, even 16 in a row (2010-2025) for July in Europe (out of 22 after 2000), despite only 6 total between 1900 and 2000. Consecutive years before 2000 were restricted to the 1930s, which had several years of anomalous summer heat in the CONUS and Europe. Areal coverage of ERA5 850 hPa temperatures above 20°C in the summer months increased by 0.8% per 10 years since 1940. For the most extreme heat, all-time 850 hPa high temperature records were retrieved from the dataset (through June 2026), and they were disproportionately common after 2000 versus 1940-2000 in Europe, the CONUS, and Australia, with a year after 2000 for any given location being 3-5 times as likely to have an all-time record than the average of the years before in Europe and around twice as likely in the CONUS and Australia. India, despite increasing temperatures, had little difference in the pre- vs. post-2000 records. Specific excessive heat events, including the off-season anomalous heat in March 2026 (which had 42% of the March 850 hPa high temperature records between 1940 and 2026) in the United States and the heat event in Europe in June and July 2026, were also analyzed using the 500-hPa heights, air temperatures at selected levels aloft, air parcel trajectories, solar radiation, and antecedent soil moisture.

494671.title: The 2026 Wildfire Season: 420,002,026th Year of Biomass Burning on Earth
494671.authors: Timothy J. Brown, Western Regional Climate Center, Reno, NV
494671.abstract: Every year wildfire impacts some place on Earth. The year 2026 was no exception. This abstract is a general description as of mid-August. Summer heat waves across Europe with record high temperatures has been a major enabler for European wildfires. Fires occurred across many locations Europe, including France which had its largest wildfire in nearly 80 years. As of mid-July, Canada had nearly 950 active wildfires across the country. Wildfire smoke from Northwest Ontario created several days with poor air quality in southeastern Canada and northeastern U.S. In the U.S. as of mid-August over 45,000 wildfires have occurred burning nearly six million acres. Significant notable fires have occurred in the Pacific Northwest. Over numerous days throughout the summer fire season the U.S. EPA/U.S. Forest Service smoke and air map has shown large regions with wildfire smoke and degraded air quality. This presentation provides highlights of the 2026 global fire season, emphasizing the role of weather and climate, key events, actions, and impacts through pictures and narrative.

494672.title: Scale-Dependent Moisture Deficiency in Radar Assimilation: A Case Study of an Intense Afternoon Thunderstorm During TAHOPE/PRECIP
494672.authors: Shu-Chih Yang, National Central University, Taoyuan, Taiwan, Taiwan; National Central University, Jhongli City, Taiwan; and Y. W. Tseng, Z. H. Lin, S. H. Chen, and K. S. Chung
494672.abstract: Radar observation has traditionally served as the primary data source of convective-scale data assimilation. However, short-term prediction with WRF radar ensemble data assimilation (REDA) frequently underestimates intense convective precipitation. This study focuses on the REDA-related moisture deficiency and its impact on predicting an intense afternoon thunderstorm event on 31st May 2022, the #IOP2 during the TAHOPE field campaign. A three-hour radar ensemble data assimilation cycle was performed from 0900 to 1200 LST with a 12-minute update interval. Results reveal that an anomalous dry condition generated in the Taipei Basin during radar assimilation, and is attributed to large-scale moisture correction. This excessive drying suppressed convection initialization and subsequent cell-merging processes, ultimately leading to underpredicted rainfall intensity. To mitigate this limitation and improve short-term precipitation forecasting, two strategies were implemented. First, the scale-dependent inflation and localization schemes were adopted to improve the ensemble spread at convective-scales and optimize the small-scale moisture adjustments. Second, water vapor profiles from a Micropulse Differential (MPD) Absorption Lidar, deployed upstream of the afternoon thunderstorm, were additionally assimilated. Assimilating the MPD data increases moisture across at all scales. Both strategies show that enhancing the moisture field can significantly improve the efficiency of reflectivity assimilation and improve the short-term rainfall prediction. Further diagnostic analysis indicates that moisture corrections at distinct scales play critical, complementary roles in heavy rainfall development. While small-scale moisture corrections at the Taipei basin significantly increase local moisture statistic energy, large-scale moistening along the coast of northwestern Taiwan coupled with the enhanced westerly wind in the upper boundary layer promotes continuous moisture transporting into the basin. The synergy increases convective instability within the PBL. Once convection cells are initialized by orographic lifting over the southern slopes of the Taipei Basin, they intensified rapidly into higher altitude, leading to extreme heavy rainfall.

494673.title: Honoring Heroes During Historic Heat: Multi-Agency Support for the 2026 Bataan Memorial Death March
494673.authors: Rani M. Wiggins, White Sands Missile Range, White Sands, NM; and B. C. Thomas
494673.abstract: This project presents a case study regarding impacts of a historic March 2026 heat wave to a high profile, widely attended marathon. The Bataan Memorial Death March (BMDM) takes place within White Sands Missile Range (WSMR) in southern New Mexico each March, attracting veterans and runners from across the United States and beyond to participate in a trek across rugged desert terrain and potentially harsh conditions in honor of the World War II event by the same name. The WSMR Meteorology Branch is tasked each year with specialized forecasts leading up to the event for planning and decision making by leadership. An anomalous heat wave expected for the weekend of the 2026 BMDM sparked great concern for participants and ultimately resulted in the decision to shorten the course. This case study employs interviews by decision makers on the WSMR command team, medical crew members, and personnel from the Army Heat Center to demonstrate the risk analysis and decision-making process within a governmental agency regarding extreme heat events and their impact to a large public-facing race. Observed weather and heat casualty statistics from past BMDM events that shaped decision making and medical support for the 2026 event will be covered. This case illustrates the transdisciplinary approach and consistent communication needed to plan large race events effectively, underscoring the value of early preparation and event incident tracking. Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) observations and other environmental variables along the course during the march will be examined, demonstrating the high risk of heat stress during the 2026 event and reinforcing the case for using WBGT tracking at any event with heat casualty risk.

494675.title: Operational Deep-Learning Ensemble Forecast System for Tropical Cyclone Tracks in the Western North Pacific
494675.authors: Seungwoo Yoo, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea, Republic of (South); and I. Park, H. M. Cheung, W. Choi, J. Kim, S. Yang, and C. H. Ho
494675.abstract: The Tropical cyclone artificial Intelligence Model Ensemble (TaIME), an ensemble forecast system consisting of 32 deep-learning model members, has been developed for operational forecasting of tropical cyclone (TC) tracks in the western North Pacific for lead times up to 120 hours. The European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis version 5 (ERA5) and high-resolution Integrated Forecast System (IFS) data for 2001–2024 are utilized to learn the Regional Specialized Meteorological Center-Tokyo best track positions. Each member of TaIME consists of the Pangu-Weather encoder modified to incorporate multiple time steps and additional variables, in conjunction with a multi-layer perceptron decoder that extracts TC-specific features. During pretraining (fine-tuning), each member learns six-hourly ERA5 from −24-hr to 0-hr (−12-hr to 0-hr) and IFS forecasts from 6-hr to 12-hr (6-hr to 24-hr) in a 15° × 15° domain centered at the initial TC position to minimize the 6-hr and 12-hr (18-hr and 24-hr) track errors. The resulting 12-hr models are used to forecast six-hourly TC positions iteratively; with t increasing from 0 to 108 hours in 12-hr increments, (t−24)-hr to (t+12)-hr fields centered at the t-hr predicted position produce (t+6)-hr and (t+12)-hr TC track forecasts. TaIME reduces the mean and 90th-percentile test errors by up to 45% and 51%, respectively, compared to IFS forecasts. The spread-error relationships also remain reasonable, regardless of lead times. Training each member takes less than 3 hours on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. The improvement of both forecast skill and computational efficiency makes TaIME suitable for operational TC forecasting. This study was funded by the Korea Meteorological Administration Research and Development Program under Grant RS-2023-00236880.

494677.title: MapEval4OceanHeat (ME4OH): An Objective Assessment of Mapping Methods Used to Estimate Ocean Heat Content Change
494677.authors: Donata Giglio, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and M. D. Palmer, D. P. Monselesan, C. M. Domingues, A. Abele, R. Asselot, T. Boyer, L. Cheng, K. Christensen, R. Cowley, G. Forget, J. Gilson, M. Goes, M. Z. Hakuba, L. Hermanson, G. Johnson, R. E. Killick, N. Kolodziejczyk, M. Kuusela, W. Llovel, N. S. Lovenduski, J. M. Lyman, M. E. Maltrud, M. Martin, B. Meyssignac, K. Mills, C. Nissen, M. J. Roberts, A. Savita, F. Sebastien, C. Smith, D. M. Smith, T. Sukianto, C. Troupin, Z. Wang, and X. Zhang
494677.abstract: Knowledge of the spatiotemporal evolution of ocean heat content (OHC) is essential to our understanding of both past and future climate change. At global scales, ocean heat uptake is a key element of the global energy and sea level budgets and provides a powerful constraint on climate sensitivity and past climate forcings. At regional scales, OHC changes are important to our understanding of climate variability and for the development, initialization, and evaluation of seasonal-to-decadal prediction systems. However, international intercomparison efforts have repeatedly shown large spread in both global OHC change and the spatial patterns of change over the past decades estimated by various research groups. Even for the relatively well-observed 0-700 m ocean, the uncertainty introduced by the choice of mapping method remains large. MapEval4OceanHeat (ME4OH) initiative is an international collaborative project working on the objective assessment of a wide range of mapping methods based on “synthetic” ocean observations from high-resolution climate and ocean modeling systems. In the ME4OH framework, the model is sub-sampled according to the spatiotemporal distribution of in situ ocean temperature observations in the EN4 dataset. These synthetic observations are then used as the input to the same mapping methods routinely deployed to map observed changes in ocean temperature and heat content. This presentation will outline the experimental design of ME4OH and present results from comparing the model “truth” (based on a 1/10th degree ocean model simulation) with the output from spatial mapping methods used by the different international research teams. This approach allows us to evaluate the strengths and limitations of contemporary mapping approaches and assess our ability to constrain observed OHC change at global and regional scales.

494682.title: From Global Forecasts to Local Impact: Reconstructing Tropical Cyclone Wind Fields with Satellite-Guided HIWindCast
494682.authors: Enze Zhang, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; and H. Su, P. W. Chan, J. Zhao, X. Shi, C. Zhai, S. Yu, Y. Li, C. Wang, Y. He, Y. Wang, and L. Xu
494682.abstract: Accurate and timely forecasts of tropical cyclone (TC) winds are essential to protecting lives and infrastructure. Traditional numerical weather prediction models deliver detailed TC forecasts yet require hours of computation; artificial intelligence–based weather prediction (AIWP) models provide near-instantaneous inference, though they are hindered by coarse resolution and systematic TC intensity underestimation. We present the first multi-source satellite-based assessment of three leading AIWP models—Pangu, FuXi, and Aurora—focusing on their fidelity in reproducing observed TC wind structures. The models underestimate peak wind speeds by 49–55% and overestimate the radius of maximum winds by a factor of three. To overcome these limitations, we introduce HIWindCast, a deep learning framework that fuses high-resolution (~6 km) satellite observations with AIWP outputs to perform joint downscaling and bias correction. HIWindCast is model-agnostic and readily applicable to any ERA5-trained AIWP model. When applied to Pangu, FuXi, and Aurora, it reduces peak wind speed errors by up to 52% and radius-of-maximum-wind errors by up to 67% for lead times up to 120 h. This framework offers a critical operational tool, delivering timely and reliable predictions to support disaster preparedness and mitigate TC impacts.

494685.title: WeatherNext 3: Next-Generation Global Probabilistic Weather Prediction with Direct Observations
494685.authors: Stephan Rasp, Google DeepMind, Munich, BY, Germany; and B. Babenko, D. Masters, A. El-Kadi, S. Merchant, G. Shalev, I. Price, F. Zyda, R. Lam, A. Shysheya, M. Willson, S. Markou, S. Agrawal, S. Vora, B. Gaiarin, M. Alewi Hassen, S. Mak, M. Bela, F. Alet, A. Bell, P. Battaglia, and A. Sanchez-Gonzalez
494685.abstract: Current state-of-the-art machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models rely almost exclusively on atmospheric analyses for training and initialization, inheriting analysis biases and assimilation latency. Here we present WeatherNext 3 (WN3), an operational global probabilistic weather prediction system that moves beyond analysis-only modeling by directly incorporating low-latency observations into both model initialization and training. By combining higher spatial and temporal resolution with direct observational learning, WN3 delivers skillful and calibrated high-resolution forecasts across the globe.

494687.title: “People who are asleep are vulnerable”; Weather Experts’ Perceptions of Challenges during Nocturnal Rapid-onset Hazards
494687.authors: Jawata Afnan Saba, AER, Columbia, MO; University of Missouri, Columbia, MO; and J. First, K. N. Ellis, J. B. Houston, M. Waddle, and C. Brantley
494687.abstract: Rapid-onset nocturnal hazards, such as tornadoes and flash floods, are deadlier than comparable daytime events and occur frequently in the southeastern United States (SEUS). Despite these elevated risks, little is known about the operational challenges weather hazard professionals in the SEUS face when forecasting, communicating, and responding to nocturnal hazards. This study examined the experiences of emergency management and National Weather Service (NWS) professionals across nine states in the SEUS. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 27 weather hazard professionals (10 emergency managers and 17 NWS forecasters) to better understand the challenges associated with nocturnal hazard communication and response. Thematic analysis identified three overarching themes across ten subthemes. First, participants described unique overnight operational challenges, including limited visibility, forecast uncertainty, and communication delays. Second, they described workforce and resource limitations, including reduced overnight staffing and constrained resource mobilization. Third, participants described barriers to receiving warnings and taking protective action at night, including sleep-related challenges among the broader public and heightened barriers among socially vulnerable populations associated with housing conditions, disability, communication access, education and English proficiency, and socioeconomic disadvantage. The findings highlight that effective nocturnal hazard preparedness and response require addressing operational challenges and barriers to warning receipt and protective action, particularly among socially vulnerable populations in the SEUS.

494691.title: Combining PREFIRE Measurements with Antarctic Surface Observations During the SHIRE Campaign
494691.authors: Jonathan Gero, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI; and T. S. L'Ecuyer, D. Smale, S. Dean, H. D. Prince, and D. Feldman
494691.abstract: The Southern Hemisphere Polar Infrared Radiation Experiment (SHIRE) is a field campaign to study the role of water vapor, temperature and clouds on infrared radiation in the Antarctic atmosphere using ground-based and space-based observations. It brings together the unique capabilities of NASA's Polar Radiant Energy in the Far Infrared Experiment (PREFIRE) satellite system with ground-based measurements from an extended range Atmospheric Emitted Radiance Interferometer (AERI) and a suite of remote sensing and in situ instruments deployed at New Zealand's Scott Base, starting in November 2025. The combination of uplooking and downlooking thermal infrared measurements will allow an analysis of far-infrared heating rates and radiative closure of thermal emission over Antarctica for the first time. This unique dataset, spanning variable atmospheric states across seasons, can be used to evaluate general circulation models in Antarctica. We report preliminary results using this combined dataset.

494692.title: Fallowed Agricultural Dust in the United States: Implications for Regional Air Quality. (Invited Presentation)
494692.authors: Adeyemi A. Adebiyi, University of California – Merced, Merced, CA
494692.abstract: Dust is an increasingly important driver of particulate matter concentrations, air quality exceedances, and associated public health risks across the western United States. Yet the contribution of anthropogenic dust remains poorly constrained, introducing substantial uncertainty into estimates of total dust loading and its impacts on atmospheric composition. Among anthropogenic sources, agricultural dust, and specifically dust emitted from fallowed croplands, has emerged as a rapidly expanding component of regional aerosol burdens. These fallowed lands are themselves a consequence of prolonged drought, declining aquifer levels, and groundwater management regulations that restrict pumping, leading to large areas of previously irrigated farmland being taken out of production and exposed to wind erosion. Building on our recent work identifying fallowed lands as dominant anthropogenic dust sources in California’s Central Valley, this work will synthesize multi‑platform observations, including satellite observations, surface measurements, land‑surface datasets, and model simulations to characterize the spatial distribution and contribution of fallowed‑agricultural dust across multiple U.S. regions. Preliminary results suggest that fallowed lands are concentrated in a few agricultural regions in the western U.S, with expanding spatial extent that poses increasing potential risk to several downstream urban regions. In addition, satellite-identified anthropogenic dust sources are largely collocated with fallowed fields, and increases in dust event frequency occurred preferentially where fallowed fields are most spatially clustered. Furthermore, preliminary analysis also suggests that most models often omit or underestimate these fallowed lands, consequently underestimating the associated contribution to regional air quality. By understanding how evolving land‑use pressures amplify anthropogenic dust emissions, this work will highlight a growing pathway through which climate‑driven water scarcity can reshape regional air quality with implications for public health.

494697.title: Performance of an Analog Ensemble Applied to an Operational DICast Temperature Forecast System
494697.authors: Stefano Alessandrini, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and T. Brummet
494697.abstract: Analog ensemble methods are often used to generate probabilistic forecasts from deterministic numerical weather prediction output. In this work, we evaluate the use of an analog ensemble (AnEn) to add probabilistic guidance to an operational DICast forecasting system for 2-m temperature over more than 10000 stations around the world. DICast is a multi-model post-processing system based on linear regression, with weights that vary among the input models. Because DICast is already optimized to provide a strong deterministic forecast, this application provides a useful test of how much additional value AnEn can add when the input forecast has already been statistically post-processed. Several AnEn configurations were tested, including different bias-correction for rare events options, analog search leadtime windows, numbers of ensemble members, predictor sets, and weight-optimization approaches. The best AnEn configuration produced deterministic scores close to DICast, but did not clearly improve upon it. This suggests that much of the predictable signal in 2-m temperature was already captured by the DICast regression. In this case, the residual errors between observations and DICast may contain only limited systematic information for the analog approach to exploit. If these residuals are mostly random, the mean correction estimated from a finite set of analogs is limited by sampling uncertainty, which decreases only with the effective number of independent analogs. The results highlight both the strengths and the limits of using AnEn on top of a well-calibrated regression-based forecast. While the deterministic ensemble mean may not outperform DICast, the AnEn framework can still provide useful probabilistic information, including forecast uncertainty, ensemble spread, and probabilities of exceeding relevant thresholds. The operational implementation of this memory-intensive system was supported by a cloud-based workflow developed at NCAR, allowing AnEn forecasts to be generated at scale for a large number of forecast sites and lead times.

494702.title: Advancing Human Biometeorology: Collaborative Strategies for Research, Service Provision, and Societal Impact
494702.authors: Tanja Cegnar, Slovenian Environment Agency, Ljubljana, Slovenia
494702.abstract: As climate change accelerates, public health faces compounding pressures from extreme weather, shifting social dynamics, and rapid technological transformations. Addressing these multifaceted challenges requires not only advancing domain-specific science, but also bridging isolated disciplines, synthesizing existing knowledge, and translating research into actionable societal solutions. Central to this mission is the International Society of Biometeorology (ISB), which fosters interdisciplinary collaboration and promotes the study of relationships between living organisms and the atmospheric environment to enhance human well-being globally. This abstract presents the framework and objectives of the workshop Living with the Elements: Weather, Climate, and Human Health, organized by the Solco W. Tromp Foundation and ISB in collaboration with international partners. Robust communication within the scientific community is fundamental to advancing the ISB’s mission. By breaking down operational silos and connecting established scientific insights with modern societal needs, the biometeorological community can deliver more targeted, evidence-based services. This workshop—organized by the Solco W. Tromp Foundation and ISB alongside international partners—serves as a dynamic platform for experts, practitioners, policy advocates, and end-user stakeholders to align perspectives across four core pillars: Network Building & Inter-Community Communication: Strengthening internal scientific dialogue and fostering sustained international, interdisciplinary networks that link meteorology, public health, and environmental policy sectors. Tailored Operational Solutions: Showcasing innovative biometeorological services, early-warning frameworks, and media communication tools that adapt existing research into user-centric, real-world interventions for climate-resilient populations. Gap & Challenge Identification: Systematically analyzing scientific uncertainties, methodological limits, and communication barriers to better address environmental impacts alongside emerging technological and social shifts. Strategic Recommendations: Formulating actionable guidelines to drive future research priorities, refine service delivery, expand capacity development, and deepen institutional cooperation globally. By fostering interdisciplinary dialogue and stakeholder engagement, the workshop aims to strengthen the contribution of human biometeorology to climate-resilient and health-oriented decision-making in a rapidly changing world.

494705.title: Vertical Grid and Surface Representation Improvements in the CRTM for Hyperspectral MW Instruments and PBL Sounding
494705.authors: Patrick Stegmann, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; Univ. of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; and B. T. Johnson and S. E. Ringerud
494705.abstract: The Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) is a radiative transfer model widely used for satellite remote sensing and satellite data assimilation in numerical weather prediction (NWP). A project recently funded by the Decadal Survey Incubation (DSI) program aims at improving the efficiency and accuracy of the CRTM when used to perform planetary boundary layer (PBL) sounding and when used to simulate novel hyperspectral microwave (MW) instruments, particularly photonic MW instruments currently in development at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC). The first year of the project aims at introducing a new method to compute MW surface emissivity over land and a new internal vertical grid that is better suited for PBL sounding. Both of these new features are expected to have a significant impact on hyperspectral MW instrument brightness temperatures simulated with the CRTM. Earlier publications have shown evidence that the current default MW land surface emissivity model has increased biases compared to MWI retrievals for MW frequencies above 89 GHz and that an increased vertical resolution in the PBL will reduce the grid error in this layer of the atmosphere. Here we present the status of these two DSI tasks in the first year of the project.

494707.title: AI-Enabled Characterization of Cold-Air Outbreak Risk and Energy Grid Reliability in the Southeast United States
494707.authors: Aneesh C. Subramanian, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO
494707.abstract: The Southeast and mid-Atlantic United States face increasing vulnerability to winter extreme weather events that simultaneously stress electricity demand and impair generation capacity, a dual-stressor dynamic that conventional resource adequacy frameworks are poorly equipped to handle. Events such as Winter Storm Uri (February 2021), the December 2022 Christmas Eve storm, and the January 2026 Southeast ice storm illustrate how cold-air outbreaks (CAOs) driven by stratospheric polar vortex disruptions and Rossby wave breaking can trigger cascading failures across tightly coupled electricity and natural gas systems. Yet current grid planning relies on the historical observational record, at most a few decades of data, which provides only one or two realizations of 20-to-50-year return-period events, making tail-risk characterization deeply uncertain. We present early results from an AI-enabled Earth-Energy systems modeling framework designed to close this gap. Using AI atmospheric emulators (ACE2, CAMulator) driven by CMIP6 SST boundary conditions, we generate 1,000+ fifty-year weather realizations and analyze cold-snap precursor statistics over the SE/mid-Atlantic U.S. Composite analysis of ERA5 data reveals coherent large-scale circulation precursors, including 500 hPa blocking and stratospheric polar vortex anomalies, emerging 10-14 days prior to cold-snap onset, indicating meaningful predictability windows beyond current operational forecasts. We further show that single-ensemble estimates systematically underestimate exceedance probabilities for rare events compared to pooled large ensembles, directly demonstrating the value of the emulator approach for tail-risk characterization. These results motivate the development of weather-conditional generator outage models and coupled natural gas–power system reliability assessments that treat demand, generation, and fuel supply as correlated rather than independently distributed during cold extremes.

494708.title: Constraining Aerosol–Cloud Interactions in Midlatitude Marine and Coastal Boundary-Layer Clouds with Meteorological Regimes
494708.authors: Xiaojian Zheng, Stanford University, Stanford, CA; and Y. Feng, S. Xie, and Y. Wang
494708.abstract: Aerosol–cloud interactions (ACI) in marine boundary-layer clouds remain a significant source of uncertainty in anthropogenic effective radiative forcing, because the meteorological state co-determines aerosol and cloud properties and confounds observational estimates. This study constrains warm-cloud ACI by conditioning on the large-scale circulation. Using a deep clustering network trained on ERA5 reanalysis fields, we classify the daytime circulation into recurrent weather regimes at the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Eastern North Atlantic observatory in the Azores and the Eastern Pacific Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment (EPCAPE) in coastal Southern California, and evaluate regime-resolved ACI from ground-based remote-sensing and in situ measurements. The regimes span a subsidence-ridge-to-deep-trough continuum and recover each site's seasonal cloud cycle. A summertime subsidence-ridge regime, with a shallow, surface-coupled stratocumulus deck and elevated aerosol loading, emerges at both sites. In contrast, clean, deep post-frontal regimes are distinctive over the open ocean, whereas the coastal site exhibits dry, cloud-poor cool-season regimes with anthropogenically influenced aerosol and moist onshore transitions spanning a wide aerosol range. Cloud droplet number susceptibility to aerosol is strongest in the coupled subsidence-ridge regime over the open ocean and in the wide-aerosol-range onshore transitions at the coast, and dampened in the persistent coastal-stratus regime, whose circulation confines aerosol variability. The cloud liquid water path adjustment is negative at both sites and strongest in drier, subsiding aerosol-rich air masses. Evaluated at fixed cloud water and cloud fraction, the surface shortwave cloud radiative effect brightens with aerosol in the susceptible regimes, a response hidden from pooled regressions. These results establish meteorological regime clustering as a transferable framework for isolating and quantifying aerosol effects in marine low clouds.

494712.title: Flow Regimes and Turbulence Structure on a Steep Slope in Winter: Findings from the TEAMx wEOP
494712.authors: Ivana Stiperski, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria; and C. Brun, M. Ghirardelli, A. Gohm, M. Lehner, and M. W. Rotach
494712.abstract: During the TEAMx winter EOP, an extensive measurement campaign took place on a steep undulating slope in the Inn Valley, Austria. This six-week long campaign featured a suite of instrumentation, including a network of eight turbulence towers installed at two across-slope and an along-slope transects equipped with two levels of sonic anemometers, nano-barometers, and slow response sensors. In addition, four component radiation at two heights measured radiative flux divergence at a central location on the slope, a short-range Doppler wind lidar (Wind Ranger) at the bottom of the slope recorded wind speed and direction, while a fibre optic array at one along-slope and two-across slope transects, and two vertical sections complemented the set-up. Additional observations during intense observational periods included temperature profile measurements using a drone and wind speed and temperature observations using tethered balloon at the top of the slope. Here we present the measurement campaign design and focus on the first results that highlight the spatio-temporal variability of the flow on the slope, tightly coupled with the synoptic forcing and structure of the valley flow. During conditions of low synoptic forcing, persistent katabatic flows developed on the slope with acceleration down the slope and warmer conditions towards one side of this non-uniform slope. These flows were amplified by the transition of the flow regime within the valley brought about by the onset of the upvalley wind. On the other hand, during foehn conditions, very large differences in the mean and turbulence characteristics could be observed between the upper across-slope transect and lower stations that are more exposed to foehn. These differences translate to distinct behaviour of similarity scaling relations, as well as the importance of different terms in the momentum and TKE budgets.

494716.title: Does Forecast Skill Translate to Operational Value? Evaluating Rainfall Forecasts within Samoa's AWSOM-2 Hydropower Outlook System
494716.authors: Hannah Marley, Earth Sciences New Zealand, Wellington, New zealand; and J. Sturman, B. Miville, E. Etimani, S. O'Neill, and L. Wang
494716.abstract: Pacific Small Island Developing States face distinct energy challenges because of their reliance on imported fossil fuels and vulnerability to weather and climate variability. Hydropower provides an important renewable-energy opportunity for countries such as Samoa, but its reliability depends strongly on rainfall and the effective management of limited water-storage resources. Although advances in weather forecasting and hydrological modelling have increased the availability of forecast information, translating those forecasts into locally actionable guidance for hydropower operations remains challenging. The Afulilo Water Storage and Outlook Module (AWSOM-2) has been developed in collaboration with the Samoa Meteorological Service and Electric Power Corporation to support operational management of Samoa’s Afulilo hydropower reservoir. The underlying water-balance model was originally developed, calibrated, and validated using monthly inputs to produce monthly reservoir-storage forecasts. AWSOM-2 extends this approach to a daily operational forecasting framework, using numerical weather prediction model outputs to generate outlooks of future reservoir storage.
