This study will retrospectively evaluate this daily forecasting system and investigate how differences among rainfall forecasts propagate through the water-balance model and affect the reliability of operational water-storage guidance. Historical rainfall forecasts from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Regional Atmospheric Model for Samoa, the Global Forecast System (GFS), and the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) will be used as alternative rainfall forcings for AWSOM-2. Individual forecast rainfall products, and combinations of these products, will be evaluated over historical periods for which observed rainfall and reservoir conditions are available. The analysis will assess rainfall forecast performance and the skill of the resulting reservoir-storage outlooks across forecast lead times. A key objective will be to determine whether greater rainfall forecast skill translates into greater hydrological forecast skill, and whether the rainfall product that best reproduces observed rainfall also produces the most reliable reservoir-storage outlooks. Differences in rainfall forecast bias, timing, and magnitude may propagate through the water-balance model in ways that are not captured by rainfall verification metrics alone. The study will therefore seek to identify which rainfall forecast products, or combinations of products, provide the most reliable information for operational water-storage guidance at Afulilo. More broadly, it will highlight the importance of evaluating forecast performance within the hydrological systems in which forecasts are ultimately used. This work is currently in progress, with results to be used to identify the forecast rainfall inputs that provide the most reliable AWSOM-2 storage outlooks. The findings will directly inform refinement of the AWSOM-2 forecasting framework. More broadly, the study highlights how evaluating forecast skill in terms of downstream hydrological performance can help improve the translation of weather forecasts into actionable guidance for hydropower and water-resource management.

494717.title: Surface Observations Reveal Water Table Dynamics and Degradation In Tropical Peatlands
494717.authors: Rui Cheng, Claremont McKenna College, Claremont, CA; and S. Amin, A. Cobb, and C. Harvey
494717.abstract: Carbon emissions, land subsidence, streamflow, and fire risk in tropical peatlands all depend on the depth of the water table, yet neither sparse field wells nor existing remote sensing can monitor it reliably. Building upon the physics of energy transfer and water balance, we present an innovative method for estimating water table depth in tropical peatlands using only surface observations, such as air temperature, net radiation, and rainfall. We demonstrate the method at three tropical peat forests in Indonesian Borneo, with up to 19 years of water table observations but different disturbance histories (undrained, drained, and drained-burned sites). Across all sites, despite contrasting disturbance histories, the changes in water table depth follow the same form of hydrologic model. A simple statistical model, constrained by a hydrologic model, accurately predicts water table dynamics with root mean squared error (rmse) of 0.07-0.3 m, while simultaneously estimating hydraulic properties. Across sites, low specific yield and evapotranspiration track the peat collapse and vegetation loss caused by fire and drainage canals, which subsequently alter water table dynamics and their control on carbon emissions and fire risk.

494720.title: Proof-of-Concept for a Modular GNSS-Reflectometry Forward Operator
494720.authors: Patrick Stegmann, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; Univ. of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; and L. Liu
494720.abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) constellations in Medium Earth Orbit (MEO), such as the US GPS/Navstar, the Russian GLONASS, the European Galileo, and the Chinese BeiDou system provide stable, well-characterized, and quasi-monochromatic reference signals in the L band microwave (MW) frequency range that can be processed in various ways to obtain a wealth of information about the environment of the signal receiver. The most well-known applications include accurate Position, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) services and geodesy as a foundational technology of modern society. For remote sensing, planetary sciences, and meteorology however, the comparatively recent GNSS radio occultation (GNSS-RO) method is of greater importance. GNSS-RO is a well-established limb-sounding technique that exploits the refraction of GNSS signals in the terrestrial atmosphere to retrieve temperature and water vapor profiles at the tangent point. This approach can be used either as a standalone retrieval, or for satellite data assimilation in numerical weather prediction. An even more recent GNSS-based, passive remote sensing technique called GNSS-reflectometry (GNSS-R) allows for the retrieval of surface properties under all-sky conditions by determining the influence of surface dielectric properties and roughness state on the measured pseudo-range and Doppler shift of a GNSS signal reflected by said surface. Conceptually, this approach is similar to bistatic radar. Here, we present the prototype of a modular GNSS-R forward operator for all-sky surface property remote sensing that implements the Zavorotny-Voronovich model in modern Fortran. Given a suitable application-specific surface model, this modular forward operator can be used in a diverse range of applications, such as oceanography and monitoring of tsunamis, cryosphere, and soil moisture.

494721.title: MODIS Thermal Infrared Sounding (MOTIS): Estimating Tropical Cyclone Central Pressure from Warm-Core Anomalies
494721.authors: Jinghuai Yao, University of Wisoncin-Madison, Madison, WI; and P. Du, C. Y. Kwok, Y. Wang, and D. C. Herndon
494721.abstract: This study presents a novel framework for estimating the central sea-level pressure (Pc) of tropical cyclones (TCs) using infrared radiometers. We leverage the long-overlooked combination of high spatial resolution and sounding capability of the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) to measure warm-core anomalies in TC eyes. We develop the MODIS Thermal Infrared Sounding (MOTIS) framework, which performs instrument-specific preprocessing and estimates 𝑃c using multiple linear regression. MOTIS yields r^2 = 0.945 and RMSE = 4.3 hPa for high-intensity TCs with observed clear eyes (mean Pc = 937 hPa), outperforming all existing methods for intense TCs. We construct a dataset of 3288 (1082 clear-eye) MOTIS estimates from 2002 to 2025 and demonstrate its potential to improve the quality of Best Track Pc, roughly halving uncertainties in the absence of pressure observations. Although MODIS is nearing the end of its mission, the MOTIS framework could be extended to next-generation geostationary sounders to provide accurate real-time 𝑃c estimation for high-intensity TCs.

494725.title: Nonparameterized Representations for Atmospheric Deep Convection — the Anelastic Convective Entity Modeling Framework
494725.authors: Yi-Hung Kuo, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA; and J. D. Neelin and J. D. Huang
494725.abstract: Parameterizations of moist convection traditionally infer grid-scale heating and moistening by assuming 1) rapid gravity wave adjustment produces descent to compensate convective updrafts; and 2) the updrafts can be represented by simplified, steady plume models. Variants on the assumptions within the latter contribute greatly to the systematic errors and parameter sensitivity among climate and weather models. Randall and collaborators identified this convective parameterization deadlock and led an impressive effort to address it. Superparameterization/multiscale modeling overcomes assumption 2 using a sample of cloud resolving model grid cells—but ends up maintaining assumption 1. Here we outline a different approach to breaking the reliance on parameterization assumptions and outline some of the trade-offs among these approaches and brute force global high-resolution modeling. The Anelastic Convective Entity (ACE) model uses a combination of analytic work and numerical pre-solution to incorporate the nonlocal pressure-mediated response to buoyancy and diverging vertical momentum flux neglected in standard plume models. Important features of convection emerge, including time-dependent chains of coherent, inhomogeneous thermals, in which vortex-ring horizontal inflow below the updraft maximum dilutes the overall buoyancy of the thermal while maintaining strong positive buoyancy near the top. The updraft inflow layer adapts to draw air from conditionally unstable levels, and the convective cold top naturally appears and spreads, often associated with dynamic stratiform clouds; downdrafts can also emerge. These are solutions of the anelastic equations for the given geometry and thus sidestep closure assumptions including assumption 1 above. They thus offer an intriguing alternative between superparameterization and traditional parameterization that explicitly simulates the interaction between cloud-scale and large-scale dynamics.

494727.title: Bias Corrected Kilometer Scale Reanalysis for African region Using Machine Learning Station and Satellite Assimilation
494727.authors: Prakash Pithani Rama Durga Surya, Tomorrow.io, Boston, MA; and F. Cannon, A. Pattantyus, M. E. Green, and R. Chase
494727.abstract: High-resolution atmospheric reanalysis is essential for climate risk, hydrometeorological applications, and resilience planning across the globe, where terrain, lakes, coastlines, and deep convection create strong local gradients that coarse global products cannot resolve. ERA5 provides dynamically consistent large-scale atmospheric states but smooths critical near-surface structure at approximately 0.25° (~31 km) resolution. Kilometer-scale dynamical downscaling improves spatial detail, yet remains computationally expensive to regenerate and can exhibit systematic biases relative to dense in situ networks. Here we present FOCUS, a machine learning data assimilation framework from Tomorrow.io that produces a bias corrected ~4 km reanalysis over East and Southern Africa for 2016–2025 by learning residual corrections to high-resolution background fields and assimilating sparse observations in a single forward pass. The FOCUS model uses U-Net residual architecture with multi model meteorological, temporal, topographic, and land-water inputs. During training, masked high-resolution targets mimic station footprints so that, at inference, ground truth observations like TAHMO (ground observation network over Africa) and METARs can be injected and physically propagated across space, time, and related variables. We used temperature, relative humidity from ground stations (TAHMO & METAR) and IMERG precipitation for the assimilation product. This design anchors storm placement with satellite observations while using stations to improve local thermodynamic fidelity (temperature & relative humidity). A ten-year station evaluation shows clear gains for near-surface temperature and relative humidity. Against more than 10 million paired observations, FOCUS achieves correlations of 95.53% (temperature) and 89.38% (humidity), with mean absolute errors of 1.16°C and 6.03%, outperforming CBAM (Tomorrow.io’s customised regional model) and ERA5 and substantially reducing the strong dry bias in humidity. Production FOCUS with IMERG and TAHMO further tightens skill (temperature RMSE 1.62°C, r = 0.953; humidity RMSE 7.50%, r = 0.928). FOCUS precipitation exhibits low systematic bias and competitive continuous error relative to ERA5 and CBAM, while categorical heavy-precipitation discrimination remains an area of complementary skill. Diurnal, monthly, and spatial diagnostics indicate physically consistent responses to station and satellite assimilation, including sharper terrain and lake driven temperature structure and improved humidity bias behavior. These results demonstrate that AI-based assimilation can deliver cost effective, station aware kilometer scale reanalysis for Africa region, with particular strength for near surface temperature and humidity applications.

494729.title: European Heatwaves Aggravated by Recent Summer Arctic Changes
494729.authors: El Noh, Kongju National University, Gongju, Chungcheongnamdo, South korea; and J. Kim, Y. Kosaka, S. W. yeh, S. W. Son, B. M. Kim, D. Coumou, K. Kornhuber, S. Y. Jun, W. Moon, M. Mori, and J. H. Kim
494729.abstract: European heatwaves have become longer and more severe, with cumulative intensity increasing by over 50% in the recent decade. Here we identify the dynamical mechanisms by which recent summer Arctic changes drive this escalation. The Arctic has undergone pronounced regional changes since 2010: the Barents–Kara Seas have warmed by 2.3 °C per decade, while western Greenland has cooled by 0.6 °C per decade. These opposite temperature trends affect European weather through two separate pathways. First, Norwegian–Barents–Kara Sea warming weakens synoptic eddy activity over Eurasia. The suppressed eddies reduce daily weather variability, allowing persistently hot conditions over Northeastern Europe. Second, western Greenland cooling shifts the North Atlantic jet poleward. The displaced jet favors intrusions of the subtropical high and the advection of Saharan air, increasing heatwaves over Southwestern Europe. Both pathways have strengthened since 2010, amplifying heatwave risks across Europe. These circulation changes, and their link to the recent Arctic changes, are supported by CESM nudging experiments in which the observed Arctic surface temperature changes are constrained. Together, these mechanisms offer further insight into the ongoing and future increase in European heatwaves and highlight the evolving role of the Arctic.

494730.title: Crop Yield Estimation in Data Sparse Regions by Integrating Remote Sensing Phenology and Transfer Learning
494730.authors: Jiaying Zhang, China Jiliang University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China
494730.abstract: Accurate estimate of crop yield is crucial for agricultural planning and resource allocation. However, many countries and regions lack yield observations for accurate modeling. To address this challenge, this study integrates remote sensing–derived phenological information with transfer learning to improve crop yield estimation in data sparse regions. First, we build and train a phenology-aligned deep learning model to estimate crop yield based on rich field-level yield data from the U.S. Midwest. This phenology aligned model uses growing-season weather and satellite time series that are aligned with field-level phenology derived from satellite remote sensing. Compared with non-aligned model, which uses calendar-date based growing-season weather and satellite time series, this phenology-aligned model decreases the error of corn yield estimates from 34.1 bu/ac (or 21.8 %) to 29.2 bu/ac (or 18.7 %) and increase the explained yield variability from 61 % to 71 %, with significant improvement in extreme conditions, especially with phenology-related yield losses. Then, we transfer this phenology-aligned model for yield estimations in Brazil by fine-tuning the model with scarce state-level observations from Brazil. Despite differences in environmental conditions, crop phenology, and yield responses between the U.S. and Brazil, we show that transfer learning improves the municipal-level estimations by increasing the R2 from 0.29 (without transfer learning) to 0.44. Notably, this is achieved without using any municipal-level data and relying only on scarce state-level observations. These results demonstrate that phenology alignment captures environmental stress in crop yield estimates and shows great potential in accurate crop yield estimates, while transfer learning reduces the dependence of yield estimation models on dense high-resolution yield observations. Their integration provides an effective framework for accurate crop yield estimations in data-scarce regions.

494731.title: Full-Polarimetric Radar Measurements Using Orthogonal Waveform Multiplexing and Its Application to Thunderstorm Depolarization Signatures
494731.authors: Min-Duan Tzeng, Advanced Radar Research Center, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; School of Meteorology, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and T. Y. Yu, D. J. Bodine, and B. Cheong
494731.abstract: Dual-polarization weather radars face the fundamental challenge of measuring full-polarimetric scattering information, including both co-polar and cross-polar components, simultaneously. The Simultaneous Transmit Simultaneous Receive (STSR) mode provides high-precision co-polar variables (ZDR, ρhv, ΦDP) but lacks cross-polar (LDR, ρxp, Φxp) capabilities. Conversely, when a radar transmits single polarization to maintain cross-polarization isolation and measure cross-polar variables, co-polar measurements are restricted exclusively to the transmitted polarization, resulting in the loss of ZDR, ρhv, ΦDP. The Alternate Transmit Simultaneous Receive (ATSR) mode, the conventional benchmark for full-polarimetric observations, measures all the polarimetric variables at the expense of alternating transmit polarizations. This introduces inter-pulse decorrelation, reduces the unambiguous spectral domain, and degrades estimator precision. To overcome these constraints, this work applies Orthogonal Waveform Multiplexing (OWM), a novel technique that leverages software-defined radar and digital modulation to achieve simultaneous full-polarimetric measurements. OWM combines multiple waveforms during transmission and encodes polarization information by strategically allocating distinct waveforms across the polarization channels. During receiver signal processing, co-polar and cross-polar scattering components are extracted concurrently via individual matched filters corresponding to each designed waveform during pulse compression. Experimental validation using the solid-state X-band PX-1000 radar confirms that OWM yields co-polar moments comparable to STSR mode and cross-polar moments matching single-polarization transmit modes. Compared to ATSR, OWM significantly increases the precision of ZDR, ρhv, ΦDP measurements. Although power-splitting results in an approximately 3-dB power loss compared to traditional modes, leading to a minor loss of coverage at the periphery of weak echoes, OWM provides robust, uncompromised measurements highly beneficial for multi-phase cloud microphysics and hydrometeor classification. Finally, an initial evaluation of thunderstorm case studies collected during the summer of 2025 demonstrates clear cross-polar depolarization signatures corresponding to ice alignment signatures (IAS) induced by strong in-cloud electric fields. Cross-verification with Lightning Mapping Array (LMA) observations confirms the spatial consistency of these LDR and ρxp signatures with active lightning discharge regions. These observational results highlight the capability of OWM to provide high-fidelity, full-polarimetric observations for diagnosing storm electrification and lightning-related microphysical processes.

494733.title: Multiscale Micrometeorology in Urban Canopy Layer: A Large-Eddy Simulation
494733.authors: Yidi Hou, The University of Hongkong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; and M. Qiu and C. H. Liu
494733.abstract: With rapid urbanization driven by human activities and economic development, it is projected that 68% of the global population will live in cities by 2050 [1]. The rapid growth in urban inhabitants necessitates sustainability and environmental friendliness. In this connection, issues related to climate change, such as urban heat island (UHI) [2], thermal comfort [3], and micrometeorology [4], have attracted attention to safeguard public health and livability in modern cities. On top of atmospheric turbulence, diversified buildings and landuse lead to multiscale urban micrometeorology and nonlinear pedestrian-level winds, hindering the utilization of natural resources for urban resilience [5]. This paper aims to foster an in-depth, fundamental understanding of the nonlinear, multiscale transport in urban canopy layer (UCL) flanked by buildings using large-eddy simulation (LES) so as to elucidate the mechanism of microscale, pedestrian-level ventilation. Practically, it contributes to improving air quality management, inhabitant thermal comfort, climate-responsive urban design, as well as wind-environment assessment. With the growing demand for a more sustainable urban living environment, increasing attention has been paid to the urban microclimate and microscale environmental conditions. The complexity and heterogeneity of flow dynamics in the wake regions after buildings, coupled with the development of shear layers, highlight the significance of turbulence scales (Figure). We focus on investigating and comparing the multiscale turbulence characteristics in wake regions between the UCL and roughness sublayer (RSL). The signal processing method - Empirical mode decomposition (EMD) and Hilbert-Huang Transform (HHT) - is applied for in-depth analysis. The streamwise turbulence intensity (u’’) is lowest in the recirculation zone within the UCL and is peaked in the RSL, while the spanwise turbulence intensity (v’’) is highest among all zones. In contrast, the entrainment zone shows opposite characteristics, whereas the detrainment zone exhibits moderate u’’ and v’’ intensities. All three zones display relatively similar vertical turbulence intensity (w’’). The recirculation zone exhibits the strongest momentum flux (u’’w’’), followed by the entrainment zone, with the detrainment zone showing the weakest. The largest turbulence scales of streamwise velocity dominate in the entrainment zone, while cube-like scale prevail in the recirculation zone and medium-scale structures in the detrainment zone. The vertical turbulence scale w’’ is smaller in the recirculation and entrainment zones but becomes larger and more intense in the detrainment zone. This indicates that ventilation in the recirculation zone is primarily driven by recirculating flow. While in the upper UCL and RSL, it is dominated by shear layers. In the entrainment zone, enhanced ventilation is not solely due to flow entrainment but is also attributed to the presence of large-scale turbulence. In the detrainment zone, w’’ plays a key role in revealing the underlying ventilation mechanism. The recirculation zone contains coherent local flow structures in both u’’ and w’’ from the ground to z/h = 0.8, where z is the wall-normal distance and h the building height, characterized by reduced intensity, intermittency, and occurrence of extreme events. It has a more efficient local mixing ability associated with u’’ and w’’. This suggests that mixing in this region is primarily driven by coherent turbulence structure rather than intermittent turbulent bursts. Around the UCL roof level (0.8 ≤ z/h ≤ 1), the momentum flux u’’w’’ is driven by the shear layer and reaches the maximum. Besides, it has notable skewness and intermittency, indicating the asymmetric and burst-like turbulent events. The presence of strong ejection Q2 and sweep Q4 motions also enhances directional transport, contributing to the skewness and the temporal intermittency in turbulence signals. These flow dynamics characteristics reflect the transitional nature of the flow at the interface between UCL and RSL by the influence of the shear layer and recirculation. The entrainment zone is characterized by abundant multiscale turbulence with an enhanced plane mixing ability. The major finding in the entrainment zone is not only the more flow entrainment but the presence of the large-scale turbulence of u’’. This large-scale u’’ is the key energy carrier in UCLs and RSLs. Moreover, it is responsible for the majority momentum flux transportation. In contrast, vertical velocity w’’ exhibits more intermittent behavior with energy concentrated at localized smaller scale. This behavior suggests that, while the horizontal flow is governed by organized, energy-containing eddies, the vertical transport is driven by small-scale turbulence that intermittently inject or sweep momentum into the upper layers. The momentum flux has a wider vertical range in the detrainment zone due to less shear layer intensity. Although the turbulence scale of u’’ is smaller than that in the entrainment zone, the vertical velocity w’’ in the detrainment carries most of the energy by large scales. It is thus suggested that vertical transport is primarily governed by coherent, low-frequency structures. These discrepancies between u’’ and w’’ scales reflect the anisotropic energy distribution. Besides, it highlights that the vertical turbulence dominates the local mixing ability in the detrainment zone. References [1] U. Environment, Cities, https://www.unep.org/topics/cities. [2] G.Manolo, S. Fatichi,M. Schläpfer, K. Yu, T.W. Crowther, N.Meili, P. Burlando, G. G. Katul, E. Bou-Zeid, "Magnitude of urban heat islands largely explained by climate and population", Nature 573 (2019) 55–60. [3] B. Sayad, D. Alkama, H. A. Ahmad, J. Baili, N. H. Aljahdaly, Y. Menni, "Nature-based solutions to improve the summer thermal comfort outdoors", Case Studies in Thermal Engineering 28 (2021). [4] T. Foken, Micrometeorology, Springer Berlin, (2017). [5] I. Orlanski, "A rational subdivision of scales for atmospheric processes", Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 56 (1975) 527–530.

494736.title: Differential Backscattering Phase Estimation and its Application in Detection and Characterization of Storms
494736.authors: Rylan Lopez, University of Oklahoma, School of Meteorology, Norman, OK; and J. Ho, A. V. Raaijmakers, G. Zhang, J. Gao, J. T. Carlin, S. Kotturi, V. N. Mahale, P. McCrone, P. Bukovcic, and M. Johnson
494736.abstract: ABSTRACT: Differential phase (ΦDP) and its range derivative, specific differential phase (KDP), contain information about precipitation microphysics and have been used in quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE), particularly where traditional Z-R relationships fail. Measured ΦDP is composed of the differential propagation phase (φDP), differential backscattering phase (δ), and measurement error (ε). Most existing KDP estimators were developed based on the assumption of Rayleigh scattering, under which δ is negligible and ε can be substantially reduced through smoothing. However, this assumption does not hold when hail or melting snow are present, even in S-band radar measurements. Hail and melting snow can scatter S-band radar signals in a non-Rayleigh scattering regime, which can induce a nonzero δ and cause a localized departure from the otherwise monotonically increasing ΦDP field. Recent advances in KDP estimation algorithms show that this δ should not be neglected, both due to its tendency to contaminate operational KDP estimates and because it may provide useful information for characterizing storms. Nonzero δ signatures, which can have positive or negative values, appear as either bumps or dips in the raw ΦDP field. Most existing least-squares-fit (LSF) KDP estimators, including the operationally used algorithms on NEXRAD, do not account for or estimate δ. In this work, we utilize a classification-based linear programming (LP) method with physical constraints to separately estimate both KDP and δ. This estimation algorithm has been developed to be compatible with currently operational systems should this become an option. We analyze several cases in which positive and/or negative values of δ are present, and establish relationships between the present hydrometeors and the δ signature. Figure 1 depicts a case from Cleburne, TX, where large hail of 5 - 7.5 cm fell. It is important to note the apparent decreases in the measured ΦDP collocated with very low ρHV, indicative of negative δ. We find that large hail of approximately 5 cm (~2 inches) or greater in diameter tends to be moderately to strongly correlated with negative δ signatures. Our finding suggests that this signature may be important and useful in severe weather detection, potentially addressing part of the challenge of estimating hail size from polarimetric radar variables. The isolation of the δ contribution can additionally improve KDP estimation and, consequently, QPE and storm characterization.

494738.title: Why Does It Snow? An Idealized Single-Crystal Model of Snow and Graupel Formation in Mixed-Phase Clouds
494738.authors: Vaughan T. J. Phillips, University of Lund, Lund, Sweden
494738.abstract: Mixed-phase clouds contain both supercooled cloud liquid water and ice particles and are important for precipitation formation and the Earth’s radiation budget. A central question in mixed-phase cloud microphysics is why snowfall is commonly produced in stratiform clouds, whereas stronger convective ascent can promote riming and the formation of graupel or hail. Snow may be defined as ice precipitation with a rime fraction below 50%, with most of its mass derived from vapour growth or aggregation, whereas graupel has a rime fraction exceeding 50%. Snow formation therefore involves competition among vapour deposition, aggregation and riming. In stratiform clouds, weak ascent is often comparable to the fall speed of snow, allowing ice particles to remain within the mixed-phase region while undergoing aggregation. Stronger convective ascent, in contrast, can increase the availability of supercooled cloud liquid water and enhance riming. The physical basis of the transition between these regimes is investigated here using an idealized numerical model of single-ice-particle growth. Steiner and Smith in 1998, based on aircraft observations, identified a temperature–vertical-velocity phase space in which enhanced supercooled liquid water and predominant riming occupy a wedge associated with convective ascent. The wedge deepens with increasing ascent. Aggregation and snow production dominate under weaker stratiform ascent, whereas riming becomes increasingly important within the wedge at stronger ascent. We use their framework to investigate how the ambient conditions associated with basic cloud types determine whether an ice particle remains snow-like or evolves into graupel. The model follows the growth of an individual ice crystal initially by vapour deposition, including temperature-dependent crystal habits, followed by aggregation and riming. Temperature and ascent rate are prescribed to represent different cloud environments. The model does not attempt to simulate the cloud as a whole; instead, it isolates the response of a single particle to ambient conditions and follows its evolution through the mixed-phase region. A closed recirculation loop between convective and surrounding stratiform ascent is used to examine how repeated exposure to different environments affects the eventual hydrometeor type. The simulations reproduce a temperature–ascent phase-space structure similar to the Steiner–Smith riming wedge. Within the wedge, the availability of supercooled cloud liquid water is a key control on the conversion of snow to graupel. For sufficiently strong ascent, a snow particle can repeatedly recirculate through the mixed-phase region and encounter sufficient supercooled liquid water for substantial riming. In some conditions, conversion from snow to graupel occurs after at least three recirculation cycles. The lower half of the mixed-phase region is particularly important because the particle can repeatedly encounter liquid-rich conditions while retaining sufficient residence time for riming. At the weakest convective ascent, however, the available supercooled liquid water is insufficient to convert the snow particle to graupel. The particle remains predominantly snow-like and eventually falls out when its fall speed exceeds the imposed ascent. Thus, the distinction between snow and graupel is not controlled by temperature or ascent independently, but by their combined influence on liquid-water availability, particle residence time and the balance among aggregation, sticking and riming. The simulations also indicate why aggregation is important for maintaining snow under weak ascent. Habit-dependent sticking efficiencies and repeated aggregation produce a relatively low-density particle with a large cross-sectional area. This promotes subsequent interaction with supercooled liquid water, but the amount and duration of liquid-water exposure determine whether riming remains insufficient for graupel conversion or becomes dominant. Consequently, the same ice particle can remain snow-like in weak stratiform ascent yet evolve toward graupel when repeated recirculation through stronger convective ascent provides sufficient liquid water for riming. The results provide a process-based interpretation of why stratiform mixed-phase clouds can produce snowfall while convective environments favour graupel or hail. Snowfall is favoured not simply because ascent is weak, but because weak ascent, limited supercooled liquid water, aggregation and particle residence time combine to prevent efficient conversion of snow into graupel. Conversely, stronger ascent can maintain sufficient supercooled liquid water over repeated recirculation cycles for riming to transform snow into graupel.

494739.title: Unsupervised DDPM Parametrization Of Submesoscale Oceanic Turbulence
494739.authors: Mayank Kumar Bijay, International centre for theoretical Sciences - Tata Institute for fundamental research, Bangalore, India; and J. Thomas
494739.abstract: The dynamics of Oceanic flow change drastically with scale. While mesoscales (10-100km) are well-understood and containing 90% of the ocean's kinetic energy and characterized by geostrophically balanced flows, the submesoscale (<10km) is very different. This regime is characterized by unbalanced flows that create fine-scale structures requiring high resolution simulations, hence computationally challenging. This motivated developing high-resolution parametrizations and data-driven surrogate modeling. In this work, we develop a data-driven stochastic parametrization for submesoscale dynamics using an unsupervised conditional diffusion model. We focus on a two-vertical-mode ocean model, in which the evolution of the barotropic (vertically averaged) vorticity is coupled to baroclinic instabilities governed by multiple nonlinear equations. Instead of explicitly evolving the baroclinic modes, we replace their influence with an abstract field in a new surrogate barotropic vorticity equation. The abstract field modifies the surrogate flow such that the turbulent trajectory resembles the turbulence coming from the original two-mode-model equations. This term is sampled conditionally from the resolved barotropic state, without access to or supervision from baroclinic variables. The resulting learning problem is inherently unsupervised, as the target stochastic forcing is not observable and hence cannot be storable as target data. To ensure numerical stability and physical realism, we incorporate Lyapunov control operator that regulate the injected variance and enforce consistency with key flow statistics. We evaluate the surrogate model by comparing it with the full two-mode system using energy spectra, fluxes, and probability distributions. The surrogate model generalizes across forcings, initial conditions, and flow regimes. The surrogate model significantly accelerates simulations while retaining essential submesoscale characteristics. Building on insights from this quasi-2D framework, we further explore extensions to three-dimensional submesoscale turbulence parametrization and present preliminary results.

494740.title: Impact of Joint GNSS-RO and GNSS-R Data Assimilation on Tropical Cyclogenesis: Typhoon Gaemi (2024)
494740.authors: Shu-Ya Chen, National Central University, Taoyuan City, TAO, Taiwan
494740.abstract: Impact of Joint GNSS-RO and GNSS-R Data Assimilation on Tropical Cyclogenesis: Typhoon Gaemi (2024) Shu-Ya Chen, Quan Pham Xuan Global Atmospheric Observation and Data Application Research Center, National Central University, Taoyuan City, Taiwan Predicting tropical cyclogenesis remains challenging because of uncertainties in the pre-genesis environment, especially over data-sparse ocean regions. This study investigates the impact of GNSS radio occultation (GNSS-RO) and GNSS reflectometry (GNSS-R) data assimilation on the prediction of Typhoon Gaemi (2024). Experiments were conducted using the WRF model and the WRFDA hybrid 3DEnVar system. Four experiments were performed to examine the impacts of assimilating GNSS-RO and GNSS-R observations separately and jointly. The results show that GNSS-RO assimilation improves the mid-tropospheric moisture distribution and provides more favorable thermodynamic conditions for tropical cyclogenesis. GNSS-R assimilation improves the near-surface wind field and low-level circulation in the pre-genesis region. GNSS-RO plays a key role in successfully simulating the genesis of Gaemi. The joint assimilation of GNSS-RO and GNSS-R further improves the simulated genesis timing and location, as well as the subsequent track. The ensemble forecasts also show smaller genesis errors when both observation types are assimilated. These results suggest that GNSS-RO and GNSS-R provide complementary information on the thermodynamic and dynamical conditions associated with tropical cyclogenesis, leading to improved prediction of tropical cyclone genesis.

494742.title: Coherent Structures and Turbulence Anisotropy in Convective Urban Boundary Layers: Proper Orthogonal Decomposition
494742.authors: Mofan Qiu, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; and Y. Hou, L. yan, and C. H. Liu
494742.abstract: Convective buoyancy can strongly reorganize turbulent motions. However, its effects on energy distribution, characteristic frequency, coherent structures, and the anisotropic character of turbulence remain incompletely understood. It is especially true when shear and buoyancy coexist such that their relative contributions change continuously. Large eddy simulation (LES) data from neutral to strongly convective conditions are analyzed in this study. An idealized urban boundary layer is used as a controlled flow system that provides a wide range of balances between shear and buoyancy. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) is applied to velocity and temperature to identify coherent structures. The analysis first examines how convective instability modifies the POD energy distribution. Modal energy and cumulative energy fractions are compared among the stability conditions. Increasing instability concentrates a larger fraction of turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) in the dominant POD modes. The contribution from higher-order modes thus weakens relatively. The turbulent field can therefore be represented by fewer energetic modes under stronger convection. This change indicates that buoyancy strengthens the organization of large-scale motions and increases the energetic dominance of the dominant coherent structures. The comparison of cumulative energy also provides a direct measure of how the energetic representation changes with stability. The temporal behavior of the POD modes is then examined using the power spectral density (PSD) of the modal coefficients. Premultiplied spectra are used to identify the frequency ranges that contribute most to the individual modes. The characteristic frequency increases with increasing mode number in all cases. Low-order modes are dominated by low-frequency variability, whereas higher-order modes contain progressively higher characteristic frequencies. This ordering reveals a clear separation of time scales across the POD hierarchy. As convective instability increases, the dominant frequencies of the leading modes shift toward lower values. Their spectral peaks also become narrower and more distinct. These changes indicate longer characteristic time scales and stronger temporal coherence of the dominant motions. In contrast, higher-order modes retain shorter time scales, representing more rapidly varying fluctuations. The spectral results therefore show that buoyancy reorganizes not only the energy content of the modes but also their temporal hierarchy. The spatial organization of the POD modes changes together with the energy and frequency distributions. Spatial modes are compared under different stability conditions to identify changes in orientation, continuity, and vertical extent. Under neutral condition, the dominant structures are inclined that are elongated in the streamwise direction. Their geometry is consistent with turbulence organized primarily by mean shear. With increasing convective instability, the streamwise elongation becomes weaker and the vertical development becomes stronger. Under strong convection, the leading modes are dominated by nearly vertical thermal plume structures. These structures extend over a larger vertical range and show stronger vertical coherence. Higher-order modes also become more elevated as convection strengthens, though they remain smaller and more localized than the dominant modes. The spatial analysis therefore demonstrates a transition from shear-organized structures to buoyancy-organized motions. Turbulence anisotropy is further examined using POD-reconstructed velocity fields. The Reynolds stress anisotropy tensor is calculated for reconstructions containing progressively more modes. Its evolution is evaluated by the anisotropy invariant map at multiple heights. This analysis provides a scale-resolved view of how the component structure of turbulence is recovered across the POD hierarchy. Under neutral and weakly convective conditions, the anisotropy trajectories at different heights remain relatively close, illustrating limited vertical variation. As buoyancy increases, the trajectories become more dispersed and the dependence on height becomes stronger. Under strong convection, the lower region approaches a more balanced state among the three velocity components. In contrast, the upper region remains strongly anisotropic. This behavior is associated with coherent thermal plumes that preferentially strengthen vertical velocity fluctuations. The results show that the transition from shear dominated motions to thermal plumes does not correspond to a simple approach toward isotropy. Buoyancy redistributes TKE among the velocity components in a manner that depends on both scale and height. Large coherent motions can remain highly directional even when their geometry becomes more vertically organized. The recovery of a more complete three component turbulence state occurs gradually as additional POD modes are included. This result also demonstrates that low-order POD reconstructions can exaggerate the anisotropic character of the full turbulent field. Overall, the analysis connects modal energy, temporal frequency, coherent structure, and turbulence anisotropy within a POD framework. Increasing buoyancy produces a more compact, energetic hierarchy, shifts the dominant motions toward lower frequencies, transforms elongated shear structures into vertically coherent thermal plumes, and changes the pathway through which anisotropy is recovered across scales. The balance between shear and buoyancy therefore controls both the organization of the dominant coherent structures and the scale dependent component structure of turbulence.

494743.title: Cloud Regimes Driving Tropical Radiative Heating Variability Associated with ENSO
494743.authors: Fabian MullerDahlberg, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, WI; University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, WI; and D. S. Henderson
494743.abstract: Cloud radiative heating is an important component of the tropical atmospheric energy budget and is closely coupled to deep convection, precipitation, and large-scale atmospheric circulation. Previous work has demonstrated a strong relationship between tropical precipitation and atmospheric cloud radiative heating, particularly in regions dominated by deep convection and extensive upper-tropospheric cloud (Stephens et al., 2024). The cloud structures responsible for the strongest heating, however, are not fully characterized. It also remains unclear whether interannual variations in tropical radiative heating primarily arise from geographic shifts in similar convective cloud regimes or from changes in the cloud populations and vertical structures that characterize those regimes. Conventional passive satellite observations often infer cloud properties from column-integrated radiances, making it difficult to distinguish whether similar radiative signatures arise from different vertical cloud structures, cloud hydrometeor phase, or overlapping cloud layers. Using active vertical profiling from the NASA CloudSat and CALIPSO missions during the 2007-2017 observing period we directly relate observed ENSO-related radiative heating anomalies to the three-dimensional cloud structures that produce them. These vertically resolved observations, along with IMERG precipitation estimates and ERA5 environmental fields, let us examine the specific cloud characteristics contributing to heating variability in tropical diabatic heating profiles.

494744.title: Mechanism of Typhoon Weakening by Invigorating Non‑Axisymmetric Convection Using a Cloud‑Seeding Method
494744.authors: Masataka Murakami, Yokohama National University, Yokohama, Kanagawa, Japan; Yokohama National University, Yokohama, Kanagawa, Japan; and R. Yoshida, H. Fudeyasu, N. Orikasa, T. Tajiri, A. Iwata, and W. C. Kuo
494744.abstract: In this study as a part of Goal 8 of the MOONSHOT R&D PROGRAM, we are examining the feasibility of typhoon modification using cloud seeding method. Currently, we are investigating the possibility of weakening a typhoon by seeding high concentrations of CCN in a spatiotemporally limited area within the inner core region of the typhoon, suppressing warm rain processes, promoting the freezing of more cloud water in upper levels, releasing more latent heat of freezing, invigorating non-axisymmetric convection. Simulations on Typhoon Nanmadol, which occurred in September 2022, using 3D-NHM suggested that even limited CCN (hygroscopic particles) seeding for about 12 hours in the northern quadrant of the typhoon could disrupt the axisymmetric structure of the typhoon and weaken its strength (increases the central pressure by about 5 hPa and decreases IKE of wind>25m/s by 30%). Since the central pressure of a typhoon can be approximated by hydrostatic balance, the relative increase in central pressure due to seeding is considered to be directly caused by the relative cooling of the warm core. The warm core of the typhoon cools primarily due to the intrusion of eyewall clouds from regions with weak tangential winds, causing sublimation or evaporation of condensates. Secondarily, reduced air mass inflow from the eye into the eyewall weakens subsidence-driven adiabatic warming.

494746.title: Contrasting Regional Air Quality Responses: Climate-Driven Shifts in Anthropogenic–Biogenic VOC Interactions and Secondary Pollutant Formation over East Asia
494746.authors: Seung-Hee Baek, Pusan National Univ., Geumjeonggu, South korea; and H. J. Lee, Y. Kim, and M. J. Park
494746.abstract: Future air quality over East Asia will be influenced by climate change, vegetation responses, and anthropogenic emissions. Interactions among these drivers and local meteorological and chemical conditions are expected to produce spatially heterogeneous air-quality responses. The relative contributions of individual drivers and the processes underlying this spatial heterogeneity remain uncertain. This study investigates mid-century changes in ozone (O3), anthropogenic secondary organic aerosol (ASOA), and biogenic secondary organic aerosol (BSOA), focusing on the roles of regional meteorology and interactions between anthropogenic and biogenic volatile organic compounds. Mid-century air quality was simulated using the Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled with Chemistry (WRF-Chem), with future meteorological forcing derived from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5-8.5 (SSP5-8.5) scenario. Future vegetation was represented by a spatially explicit 2050 leaf area index (LAI) dataset generated using a random forest model trained with satellite-derived LAI observations and CMIP6 meteorological predictors. An independent evaluation using 2024 data yielded an R2 of approximately 0.9. Three simulations were conducted: (1) a 2019 baseline simulation, (2) a 2050 climate–vegetation simulation with anthropogenic emissions fixed at 2019 levels, and (3) a 2050 simulation incorporating the No Further Control (NFC) anthropogenic-emission scenario. Differences among these simulations were used to separate the effects of climate–vegetation change from those of future anthropogenic emissions. Climate–vegetation effects were generally stronger and more spatially extensive than anthropogenic-emission effects. Nevertheless, O3, ASOA, and BSOA showed substantial regional variability in both the magnitude and direction of their responses. Regional analyses indicated that these contrasting responses were governed by different combinations of LAI, temperature, solar radiation, biogenic emissions, oxidation chemistry, and atmospheric transport. Although similar drivers influenced multiple regions, their relative importance varied considerably, resulting in distinct pathways of secondary-pollutant formation and accumulation. These findings demonstrate that future air-quality responses over East Asia cannot be characterized by uniform changes across the region. Accounting for region-specific meteorological and chemical processes is essential for improving future air-quality projections and developing effective management strategies under a changing climate. * This research was supported by the Basic Science Research Program through the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) funded by the Ministry of Education (RS‐2020‐NR049592, RS-2022-NR069425, RS-2025-24873262).

494749.title: An Intercomparison of Sensing Technologies for Precipitation Amount & Type Identification Across Diverse Climates
494749.authors: Lasse Kauppinen, Vaisala Oyj, Vantaa, Finland; and K. Heyn, R. Keranen, M. Krapu, and L. Wickramanayake
494749.abstract: Accurate precipitation measurements, including precipitation type identification, are essential in meteorology, hydrology, climate monitoring, and for operational warning systems. Sensors of different technologies (such as optical, radar and gauge weighing) often respond differently to variations in precipitation intensity, hydrometeor sizes and types. Mechanisms of wind induced, and other environment related uncertainties vary for different sensing principles and implementations. Evaluations are complicated by the interplay between site characteristics (orography, shields, environmental exposure, seasonal aspects) and sensor specific characteristics (design features and actions of maintenance). Assessments of general suitability of a measurement (a sensor) for a particular application can be pursued, by studying an inter-comparison of precipitation measurement technologies deployed across multiple sites operated through multiple seasons representing different climatic and environmental conditions and extended to precipitation type identification, comparing how the radar- and optical-based technologies classify drizzle, rain, hail, and snow against one another, including their agreement during mixed-phase and transitional events and how their derived liquid-water-equivalent amounts compare against gauge measurements. The objective is to improve understanding of technology-dependent measurement behavior across varied climatic and environmental conditions, and to contribute to best practices for selecting suitable instruments for specific climates and deployment environments. The analysis considers time series of data from an ensemble of vertically pointing radar precipitation sensors (Vaisala PRECICAP RM60) compared to optical forward-scatter sensors (Vaisala FD70), and double-fenced weighing gauges (a shielding configuration widely used for reference measurement) and, at one site, against the pit-mounted operational reference gauge of a national observatory, all deployed at sites representing climatologies of tropical rainforest (Köppen Af), humid boreal (Dfb), elevated, cold semi-arid to humid subtropical (BSk/Cfa), and temperate maritime (Cfb) climate. Event-based and long-term performances are considered of precipitation intensity, accumulation, detection skills, temporal responses, and robustness in varied weather conditions.

494753.title: Transport of Carbon Monoxide to the Upper Troposphere and Lower Stratosphere through Daily Scale Convection in Asian Summer Monsoon
494753.authors: Grainne Rogacki, Columbia University in the City of New York, New York, NY; and Y. Wu
494753.abstract: The Asian summer monsoon (ASM) has been established as a dominant transport pathway for pollutants from the surface to the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS) where they can have major impacts on atmospheric chemistry, the radiative balance, and ozone levels. The seasonal cycle of this transport pathway has been well established, yet its exact mechanisms are not fully understood. This study investigates the role of daily convection compared to large-scale ascent on vertical transport. We used a model experiment with tagged CO, which allowed us to isolate the transport pathways for the two dominant source regions, South and East Asia, and visualize and analyze them independently. We used data from the monsoon’s active season, removing seasonal cycles and detrending to isolate daily fluctuations, and looked at the impact of individual convective events. We found that CO transport from the two regions is driven by different convective centers (aligned with the South Asian and East Asian monsoon subcomponents). South Asian CO is also most efficiently transported higher into the atmosphere than East Asian CO, although there is a lot of interannual variability in efficiency of this transport. Additionally, emissions from South Asia are more confined in the Asian monsoon anticyclone whereas East Asian emissions distribute throughout the entire region more freely. Our results showed that South Asian emissions to upper levels have a longer transport timescale (reaching a transport peak of 100hPa after 4 days) and transport may be more driven by large-scale vertical ascent compared to East Asia where the transport is quicker (reaching a transport peak of 150hPa after 2 days) and convection dominates.

494756.title: Observational Association between Aerosol and Precipitation with Smoke and Meteorology Constrained
494756.authors: Suqian Chu, State University of New York at Albany, Albany, NY
494756.abstract: Wildfire smoke is becoming an important aerosol source in New York State (NYS) recently, but its relationship with precipitation remains uncertain. This study combined 9-year hourly precipitation observations from the NYS Mesonet with satellite-based smoke product, aerosol and meteorological fields from reanalysis during 2017-2025. Smoke condition is classified at the station-hour scale using sub-daily smoke polygons and elevated organic carbon aerosol optical depth (AOD). Smoke periods exhibit substantially greater total AOD (a factor of 2.82) and surface PM2.5 concentrations (a factor of 2.62) than non-smoke periods and are associated with less frequent precipitation. Precipitation occurrence and intensity vary nonlinearly and nonmonotonically with AOD, increasing to maxima at AOD of approximately 0.4–0.5 before declining at higher aerosol loadings. Although precipitation rate and AOD in non-smoke condition showed larger correlation (r ~0.14) than smoke condition (r<0.1), the adjustment with meteorological constrained of the positive correlation, indicating that the observed precipitation-AOD relationship was largely attributed to meteorological covariation. Among the 14 meteorological variables, convective available potential energy and cloud base temperature exerted stronger attenuation. Under smoke conditions, extreme precipitation rate was negatively associated with AOD (r ~ −0.12) and remained significant with meteorology constrained, whereas the non-smoke association was negligible. However, this correlation weakened when extreme precipitation were represented by the maximum over the subsequent three hours, despite the persistent dependence. These findings emphasize the importance of separating smoke and non-smoke conditions as well as distinguishing between total and extreme precipitation when examining precipitation-AOD relationship.

494757.title: Advancing the Data Operations Service for GOES-R Satellite Observations with the GEO Cloud Compute Subsystem (GCCS)
494757.authors: Liliana Alvarado, NOAA, Clarksburg, MD; NESDIS, Greenbelt, MD; and M. Santilli, M. Burnett, S. Kashefi, T. Irons, and P. Serengulian
494757.abstract: The GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites) have been our “eyes in the sky” for over 50 years, so scientists could monitor dramatic events unfolding on Earth, the sun, and in space. Since the launch of GOES-A/1 on October 16, 1975, these satellites have continuously monitored everything from explosive volcanic eruptions and powerful hurricanes to intense blizzards and frightening wildfires. NOAA’s GOES satellites provide the only constant, real-time view of weather and environmental conditions across the U.S. and Western Hemisphere. The Ground System which captures, stores, and processes instrument observations from the GOES satellites is a complex architecture involving three geographically separated Government facilities. In total, these Government facilities have over 450 workstations and 550 servers deployed, 260 racks of IT equipment, 90 miles of rack cabling, 215 TFLOPS of processing power, millions of SLOC, thousands of firewall rules, and numerous external interfaces. Today, there is a need to reduce the on-premises GOES Ground System on-premise infrastructure size and complexity to align with the GOES-R sustainment budget. Migrating Ground System capabilities to the cloud addresses on-premises IT hardware obsolescence risks and simplifies software sustainment. The GOES Ground System (GS) is evolving, and its first capability migrated to the cloud is the Data Operations (DO) capability into a subsystem of the NESDIS Cloud System (NCS) called the GEO Cloud Compute Subsystem (GCCS). GEO DO in the GCCS is defined as: (a) L0, L1b, and L2+ Processing, (b) Product Generation (PG) Infrastructure and Service Management, (c) Product Monitoring and Product Performance, (d) Product Distribution (PD) of GOES Key Performance Parameters (KPPS) to the National Weather Service (NWS), and (e) Product Notifications (PN) to subscribed GEO Customers. This presentation and Q&A session will introduce the GCCS and its operational capabilities that are focused on the creation and publication of weather observation products for the GEO, NWS, and SWO missions. The presentation will convey the rationale and business drivers that led to the establishment of GCCS, an overview of the operational GCCS and its interfaces, a survey of key architectural features, and the path taken to operationalize and launch GCCS into operations. The interactive Q&A supports the sharing of lessons learned and experiences of the migration activities.

494760.title: Withdrawn: Beyond the Resolution Gap: Tri-Source Semantic Super-Resolution of Daily 100 m GK-2A NDVI
494760.authors: Seoyeong Ku, Korea Univ., Seoul, Seongbuk-gu, Korea, Republic of (South); and J. Baik, K. Park, M. Cho, S. Hwang, C. Oh, K. Kwon, and C. Jun
494760.abstract: Abstract The spatiotemporal trade-off between geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites limits the monitoring of vegetation dynamics relevant to land-atmosphere interactions. Conventional downscaling approaches often require fine-resolution imagery on each target date, thereby sacrificing temporal continuity, or rely on a single training label that may introduce sensor-specific radiometric biases. This study develops a tri-source semantic super-resolution framework to downscale GEO-KOMPSAT-2A (GK-2A) normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) from 2 km to 100 m over a region in central South Korea. The framework uses a U-Net with spatially adaptive denormalization (SPADE) conditioned on land cover and a water mask, together with atrous spatial pyramid pooling to capture multiscale spatial context. Training integrates complementary supervision from three satellite products at their respective spatial scales: 100 m Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) for fine-scale spatial detail, 2 km GK-2A for coarse-scale consistency, and 250 m MODIS MOD13Q1 for intermediate-scale vegetation patterns and values. Multi-source fusion is required only during training; daily inference uses GK-2A observations and static ancillary information. The model was trained using data from 2020-2022 and independently evaluated for 2023. Comparison with MOD13Q1 yielded a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.855 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.095. In contrast, an ablation model constrained only by the patch-level mean of MOD13Q1 achieved an R² of 0.720, indicating that the improvement arises primarily from learning intermediate-scale spatial patterns rather than simple radiometric rescaling. These results demonstrate the potential of multi-scale supervision to bridge the spatial-temporal resolution gap between polar-orbiting and geostationary observations and provide spatially enhanced daily GK-2A vegetation information at 100 m resolution. Keywords: GEO-KOMPSAT-2A (GK-2A); NDVI; Semantic super-resolution; Multi-source satellite fusion; Geostationary satellite; Vegetation monitoring Acknowledgement This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea(NRF) grant funded by the Korea government(MSIT) (RS-2024-00334564 & RS-2021-NR060085) and by the Korea Environmental Industry & Technology Institute (KEITI) through Wetland Ecosystem Value Evaluation and Carbon Absorption Value Promotion Technology Development Project, funded by Korea Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (MCEE) (RS-2022-KE002066), also by the Korea Railroad Research Institute through the Development of Intelligent Information-based Technology for Abnormal Climate and Complex Disaster Response. (PK26414A0)

494780.title: The NASA Micro Pulse Lidar Network (MPLNET): 25+ Years of Continuous Vertical Profiling of Aerosols and Thin Clouds
494780.authors: Jasper R. Lewis Jr., University of Maryland Baltimore County (UMBC), Baltimore, MD; and S. Stewart, S. Liu, V. K. Kayetha, B. Altner, and I. Adams
494780.abstract: Atmospheric aerosols and clouds play key roles in determining Earth’s climate through both direct and indirect effects as they interact with solar and thermal radiation. Furthermore, aerosols affect air quality and human health by penetrating deep into the lungs and bloodstream, which leads to increased morbidity and mortality. Therefore, studying the spatiotemporal distributions of these atmospheric constituents is a key goal of not only NASA, but the entire global community. Consequently, the Micro Pulse Network (MPLNET) began operations in 2000 in support of the NASA Earth Observing System Program. Most sites within the federated network are collocated with sunphotometers in the Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET), providing both columnar and vertical profile measurements. Continuous day and night observations are made at polar, midlatitude, and tropical sites using standardized instruments and data processing algorithms. Thorough uncertainty characterization makes for straightforward comparisons between sites. In this presentation, we highlight key scientific accomplishments from over twenty-five years of network operations including satellite validation, field campaigns, model intercomparisons, and international cooperation. Recent activities, including support for the INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE), will be used to demonstrate how continuous lidar measurements are utilized to determine injection heights for wildfire events and monitor the movement of smoke plumes throughout the troposphere and lower stratosphere. Coincident lidar measurements with overpasses from Cloud-Aerosol Lidar and Infrared Pathfinder Satellite Observations (CALIPSO) and Earth Cloud, Aerosol, and Radiation Explorer (EarthCARE) will be used to discuss the representativeness of observations from ground-based and spaceborne platforms. Finally, we present ongoing and future plans for MPLNET within the context of the Decadal Survey for Earth Science and Applications from Space 2028–2037, underscoring the critical need for vertical profiling of clouds and aerosols.

494783.title: Estimating Precipitation Through Measurements Referred to Physical Properties of Raindrops: the Case of Vertically Pointing High Resolution Doppler Sensor
494783.authors: Reino Keranen, Vaisala Oyj, Espoo, Finland; and K. Heyn, L. Kauppinen, M. Krapu, and L. Wickramanayake
494783.abstract: Estimating rain, precipitation generally, at a point on ground, is a task loaded by long-standing challenges, such as representativeness, measurement uncertainties induced by varied weather and site conditions coupled with vulnerabilities specific to sensor technology. Poor metrological consistency may hinder quick sensor deployments intended for immediate decision-making in communities. The ideal sensor simultaneously reports accurate measurements and classifications of precipitation in varied weather and climates, at a high level of meteorological performance, utilizes methodology with documented unbroken chain of calibrations to references, preferably SI units or physical constants (metrological traceability), is fit for utilization as an element of sensor networks, scalable to represent weather at high spatial and temporal resolutions, through automated operation, free of maintenance, and sustained meteorological performance (item 1.), and metrological consistency (item 2.), including verification of performance when the sensor measures precipitation. Technology development, such as Vaisala PRECICAP, has opened fresh perspectives in these aspects in comprehensive manner. Specifically, the skill to reconstruct rain as ensembles of distinct raindrop signals provides advantages in the viewpoints of meteorological measurement performance: raindrop number density classes can be estimated as counts of raindrops in predefined measurement volumes, and distinct raindrop signals allow for autonomous normalization of signal powers of bulk precipitation echo significantly mitigating the traditional uncertainties in utilizing echoes of vertically pointing Doppler radar as characteristics of rain. metrologically consistent traceability of the measurements, extending the validity of calibrations preset in controlled conditions to verification in sensor’s actual operating conditions, and realizations of a) and b) as individual autonomous sensor units. The viewpoints of meteorological measurement and metrological consistency of precipitation estimates are discussed in the context of PRECICAP technology, as a novel variant of non-catchment type of precipitation sensor.

494784.title: From Flat Disks to Dendroids: Settling Dynamics of Ice Crystals In Air
494784.authors: Robin Karl Barta, Max Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-organization, Göttingen, Niedersachsen, Germany; and Y. Wang, Y. Wang, T. Bhowmick, and G. Bagheri
494784.abstract: A comprehensive understanding of the settling dynamics of frozen precipitation is essential for atmospheric microphysics, yet this process is complicated by environmental conditions that produce a wide range of particle sizes, shapes, and velocities. Snow crystals broadly fall into columnar and plate-like forms; here, we focus on plate crystals. We investigate how shape controls the free-fall dynamics of plate-like ice-crystal analogs by combining numerical simulations with controlled experiments in quiescent air for four 3D-printed sub-millimeter particles designed to match in mass and aspect ratio while spanning increasing geometric complexity: a disk (P1), hexagon (P2), simplified snowflake (P3), and a realistic branched plate snowflake (P4); see figure 1(a). The particles were fabricated using a Photonic Professional GT 3D printer with a density of $\rho_{p}$ = 1200 kg m$^{-3}$. \ Following Willmarth, the free-fall behavior of plate-like particles, particularly idealized thin disks, is typically classified using a parameter space defined by the Reynolds number, $Re$, and a dimensionless moment of inertia, $I^*$: \begin{equation} Re = \frac{U\,D}{\nu}, \quad I^* = \frac{I}{\rho_{f}\,D^5}, \end{equation} where $U$ is the terminal velocity, $D$ is the maximum body dimension, $\nu$ is the fluid kinematic viscosity, $\rho_{f}$ is the fluid density, and $I$ is the smallest principal moment of inertia. Most studies emphasize low-inertia regimes ($I^* < 1$) and are carried out mainly in liquids. However, atmospheric snowflakes are often heavy particles in air with $I^* > 1$, where particle inertia dominates aerodynamic torques, which we cover in our experiments utilizing $Re \approx 5$ in the Göttingen turret. In this setup, particles are released into an air-filled settling chamber and recorded by two pairs of synchronized high-speed Phantom cameras with pulsed LED illumination; see figure 1(b). Our novel 3D particle tracking velocimetry method reconstructs trajectories, featuring the 3D shape as well as the translational and rotational motion of the falling particle at every frame; see figure 1(d). This allows us to resolve its full free-fall dynamics, with a specific focus on the inclination angle $\theta$ with respect to gravity and the angular velocity $\dot{\theta}$. Across all shapes, we identify two robust falling styles: an oscillating regime, where $\theta$ fluctuates at small amplitudes to maintain a near-horizontal orientation without inversion, and a flipping regime, characterized by repeated rotations that drive the particle between near-horizontal and near-vertical orientations. \ Following this observation, this study aims to characterize the settling velocity, stability criteria, and the resulting states of motion for the investigated plate-like shapes (P1-P4), with a particular focus on their angular dynamics. Alongside these experimental results, particle-resolved direct numerical simulations performed using the Palabos-Turret code reveal that snowflake-like particles can transition from a long-distance oscillatory descent to the flipping regime after sufficient fall distance; see figure 1(e). Ultimately, the resulting shape-informed settling dynamics for high-inertia flat ice crystals falling in air can be used to improve our fundamental understanding of snowflake dispersion and to enhance the modeling of collision-coalescence in numerical weather prediction.

494785.title: Turbulence and Droplet Clustering in Shallow Cumulus Clouds (Invited Presentation)
494785.authors: Gholamhossein Bagheri, MPI, Göttingen, NI, Germany
494785.abstract: Shallow cumulus clouds over tropical oceans play a fundamental role in Earth’s energy budget. Their microphysical properties strongly influence cloud albedo and climate feedbacks, yet the mechanisms responsible for rapid raindrop formation, particularly the role of turbulence, remain poorly understood. A major challenge has been the simultaneous characterization of turbulence and cloud microphysics across the wide range of spatial scales, from micrometres to kilometres, that govern cloud evolution. Here, we present unique airborne in-situ measurements obtained using a tethered balloon-kite hybrid platform equipped with high-speed digital holography and particle image velocimetry (PIV). These observations reveal the fine-scale structure and dynamics of tropical shallow cumulus clouds, providing unprecedented localized measurements of both cloud microphysics and turbulence. We examine turbulence dissipation rates and cloud droplet spatial distributions across a broad range of scales, from sub-millimetre to kilometre scales. Our results show that cloud droplet clustering is associated with regions of intense turbulence dissipation, particularly within precipitating clouds. The observed association between enhanced turbulence dissipation and droplet clustering is consistent with the hypothesis that turbulence influences droplet interactions relevant to warm-rain initiation.

494789.title: AI - Graph Machine Learning Data Assimilation Using a Global Icosahedral Shallow-Water Model As a Prototype
494789.authors: Miodrag Rancic, Lynker at NOAA/NWS/OMD, College Park, MD; and R. J. Purser, M. Pondeca, and A. Gholoubi
494789.abstract: Exploration of the most suitable pathway for the development of a fully machine-learning-based Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis (ML-RTMA) at NOAA/OMD is progressing along two parallel pathways, involving adaptation of the numerical frameworks of Aardvark and OCELOT, two end-to-end ML forecasting models. As research support for this effort, a Graph ML data-assimilation shallow-water prototype has been developed on a global hexagon–pentagon icosahedral grid. Such a synthetic framework provides complete knowledge of the true state, background field, and observations, allowing rigorous evaluation and improved understanding of the learned analysis operator before moving toward operational atmospheric applications. In addition, the developed baseline Graph ML-3DVAR system serves as the foundation for several complementary developments currently under investigation. The first examines the effects of incorporating physical constraints, including conservation of total mass, dynamical balance, and other properties, into the learning process. In addition to improving the physical consistency of the resulting analyses, such constraints provide explicit control over selected properties of the learned analysis operator, bringing machine-learning data assimilation conceptually closer to conventional variational methods, in which statistical and physical information can be introduced deliberately within the analysis formulation. By evaluating each constraint using both conventional analysis-error measures and diagnostics of the physical property it is designed to control, these experiments are intended to provide more general guidance for the development of machine-learning data-assimilation systems. The second development investigates type-specific observation weighting, allowing selected observations or observation categories to receive enhanced influence during the analysis. The third explores multiscale covariance guidance, transferring physically interpretable covariance information into the machine-learning framework. Together, these developments seek to establish a unified graph-based methodology that combines statistical learning, physical constraints, and covariance modeling for future ML-RTMA and graph-based data-assimilation systems.Work has also begun on an ML-4DVAR formulation using backpropagation through the neural network and an ML emulator in place of the physical forecast model. Consistent with the design of OCELOT, which performs forecasting in observation space, development has also been initiated on an ML Representer formulation using the simplified shallow-water framework as a prototype.

494792.title: Routine Atmospheric Profiling with Meteodrones as part of NOAA’s National Mesonet Program
494792.authors: Melanie Kobras, Meteomatics AG, St. Gallen, SG, Switzerland; and B. Guay and F. Ramelli
494792.abstract: NOAA’s National Mesonet Program leverages a network of public and private partners to provide timely, high-value weather observations across the United States, supporting the National Weather Service and weather-sensitive sectors and helping protect life, property, and economic activity. As part of this program and to enhance vertical profiling capabilities, Meteomatics is deploying its Meteodrone to demonstrate the feasibility of routine, remotely operated UAS-based atmospheric profiling in the continental United States. The initial deployment is located at the Washington Mesonet site in Oklahoma, co-located with the Kessler Atmospheric and Ecological Field Site, and is being conducted in collaboration with NOAA, Synoptic Data, KBR, and the University of Oklahoma. The Meteodrone performs repeated autonomous soundings to measure the vertical structure of key atmospheric variables, while requiring minimal on-site support for sustainable routine operations. This presentation will describe the operational concept and experience gained from establishing routine Meteodrone operations in Oklahoma, including the challenges that arise from these kinds of operations. Observations collected during the deployment will be used to illustrate the characteristics and potential applications of high-frequency vertical profiling and depending on the progression of the campaign, examples will highlight atmospheric structures and evolving boundary-layer conditions captured by the Meteodrone. The results will provide insight into the potential role of frequent UAS-based soundings in future operational observing systems and their use in weather analysis and forecasting.

494794.title: Global expansion of the sensitive aerosol-limited marine cloud regime under emission reductions (Invited Presentation)
494794.authors: Minghuai Wang, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China
494794.abstract: Aerosol-cloud interactions (ACI) are fundamentally nonlinear, with their strongest climatic effects emerging where cloud properties are highly sensitive to aerosol changes—the aerosol-limited regime. Quantifying this regime's evolution is therefore critical for constraining uncertainties in climate forcing and future projections. By integrating satellite observations with climate model simulations, we map this regime globally and track its recent change. We find it expanded by 4.8% per decade over the past twenty years, primarily due to a sharp increase (~14.7% per decade) in the Northern Hemisphere driven by anthropogenic emission reductions. Under a strong emission reduction pathway, its frequency is projected to double or triple in key ocean regions. This systematic shift pushes marine clouds into a state of heightened aerosol sensitivity, thereby amplifying the cloud-mediated radiative response to aerosol changes. Our findings underscore the need to account for this evolving sensitivity in climate projections.

494795.title: Building Resilience Against Disaster Exposure: Individual Disaster Resilience as a Protective Factor for Geriatric Depression
494795.authors: Alexis Merdjanoff, New York University, New York, NY
494795.abstract: Older adults are the fastest-growing age group in the U.S. and are the age group most vulnerable to extreme weather events, yet many reside in areas increasingly exposed to disaster exposure. Using data from the Aging in Risky Environmental Areas (AREA) Study, a nationally representative survey of community-dwelling adults ages 50+ conducted in November 2022, we examined how individual disaster resilience moderates the relationship between disaster exposure and geriatric depression.
