Multivariable moderation analyses evaluated associations between past 3-year disaster exposure, scores on the Disaster Adaptation and Resilience Scale (DARS) and depressive symptoms measured by the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS). Among 1,504 participants, 40.3% were exposed to ≥2 disasters or extreme weather events. Total disaster exposure (p = 0.002), any indirect exposure (p < 0.001), and any direct exposure (p = 0.005) were all negatively associated with total disaster resilience. However, higher individual disaster resilience significantly protected against geriatric depression across disaster exposure levels. Notably, disaster resilience demonstrated a stronger protective effect among individuals with direct and/or indirect disaster impacts (cohen's d: 0.64, 95% CI: 0.53, 0.74) compared to unexposed or exposed but unaffected individuals (cohen's d: 0.58, 95% CI: 0.51, 0.65). These results establish individual disaster resilience as a critical modifiable buffer, underscoring the urgency of integrating resilience-building interventions into public health and disaster preparedness strategies for older adults.

494800.title: Satellite Observations of Clouds and Atmospheric Thermodynamics for Weather and Climate Applications
494800.authors: William Leo Smith Jr., NASA, Poquoson, VA; and L. Nguyen, D. Painemal, T. Chee, A. DiNorscia, K. Khlopenkov, R. Palikonda, D. Spangenberg, C. R. Yost, and C. W. Fleeger
494800.abstract: Consistent, high space and time resolution observations of atmospheric conditions from satellite imagers can contribute to improved understandings of clouds and their representation in predictive models. This paper describes new historical and low-latency, high-resolution datasets of cloud properties, atmospheric thermodynamics and winds constructed from analyses of meteorological satellite imager data. The data products are produced in the NASA Satellite ClOud and Radiation Property retrieval System (SatCORPS) and made available for community use in research and operations. Global datasets of cloud properties are derived from Meteosat-9 and -10, Himawari-9, GOES-18 and-19, Aqua-MODIS, Terra-MODIS, and NOAA-20 VIIRS radiance data using algorithms that have been developed over many years to support NASA weather and climate programs such as the Clouds and Earth’s Radiant Energy System (CERES). The algorithms are state of the art, apply data fusion from active sensors, surface and aircraft observations to more accurately infer cloud vertical structure and water content, and they incorporate machine learning to reduce artifacts and to help provide more accurate and consistent information at all times of day. These data, referred to as the SatCORPS Global Cloud Composites (GCC) are currently produced hourly on a 3-km grid. A near real-time GEO-LEO Atmospheric Sounding System (GLASS) also operates in the SatCORPS producing vertical profiles of atmospheric thermodynamics every 30 minutes with a spatial resolution of ~ 3 km for an area extending from the mid Pacific across the continental United States into the western Atlantic. The vertical profiles of temperature and humidity are derived through the fusion of polar hyperspectral infrared and microwave soundings with geostationary satellite imagery and assimilated into a short-range weather forecast model to demonstrate the utility for these data to improve weather forecasting. The high-density GLASS fusion data have been found to resolve highly variable moisture features leading to enhanced knowledge of atmospheric stability and more accurate predictions of winds and severe weather. Together, the complementary information on clouds and atmospheric thermodynamics from satellites provide a powerful new tool for understanding high variability atmospheric moisture processes. A brief description of the methods highlighting the unique aspects of the SatCORPS data products, results from recent validation studies, and future plans will be presented.

494802.title: Meteodrone Strato: Automated Atmospheric Soundings Beyond 10 km
494802.authors: Enrico Ajanic, Meteomatics AG, St. Gallen, Switzerland; and B. Guay
494802.abstract: For several years, Meteomatics has operated Meteodrones that routinely perform autonomous atmospheric soundings up to 6 km, providing reusable, high frequency vertical profiles of the atmospheric boundary layer. Building on this operational experience, Meteomatics now introduces Meteodrone Strato, a high altitude multicopter for atmospheric profiling beyond 10 km. This drone enables repeatable in situ measurements from the surface to pressure levels near 250 hPa, resolving the diurnal evolution of the boundary layer and its transition into the free troposphere, the destabilisation preceding deep convection, the passage of mesoscale boundaries, and the mid-tropospheric moisture layering that are currently poorly sampled. Meteodrone Strato measures pressure, dew point, temperature, wind speed and wind direction throughout the vertical profile, with a full profile collected in about 20 minutes. The drone uses the proprietary Meteosense sensor system for high speed humidity and temperature measurements and is designed to operate in demanding environmental conditions , including temperatures down to minus 70 degrees C, wind speeds up to 35 m/s, icing conditions, and precipitation. The selectable flight altitude, launch timing, and operating location allow profiles to be tailored to specific meteorological conditions and observation needs. In this presentation, we introduce Meteodrone Strato from an engineering and measurement perspective. We present the aircraft design, measurement concept and first high altitude observations, and discuss the technical choices that enable rapid, reusable vertical profiling under challenging atmospheric conditions. We also discuss how targeted uncrewed aircraft soundings can complement radiosonde networks and support operational and research applications requiring more flexible upper air observations.

494805.title: Deploying LLM-as-a-Judge for GFDL’s Chatbots
494805.authors: Lauren Chilutti, NOAA, Princeton, NJ; and C. Brown, M. K. Lee, R. Mulhall, K. E. Rand, and D. Singh
494805.abstract: NOAA’s Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory developed a series of chatbots that ingest a database of code documentation to answer user queries about the software. The team prototyped these chatbots using two distinct approaches: a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline and a Google Gemini Gem. The RAG chatbot uses a Python program to search a database of code documentation for relevant context and instruct a locally running open-source LLM (such as Llama 3 or Mistral) to generate a conversational response. Alternatively, the Gemini Gem offers a “no-code” approach, leveraging Google’s Gems feature to create a task-specific version of Gemini configured with specific instructions and references to the code documentation. To systematically evaluate these chatbot prototypes, we developed an LLM-as-a-judge workflow. This presentation will focus on the methodology used to deploy the LLM-as-a-judge framework for both RAG and Gemini Gem chatbots. First, domain experts manually answered a set of predetermined queries to establish a “ground truth” evaluation dataset. Concurrently, an automated logging function was inserted into the chatbots to capture queries and responses in real time. Next, the same queries from the “ground truth” evaluation dataset were passed into the chatbot prototypes. The automated logging then collected and stored the chatbots’ responses. Finally, a secondary LLM was instructed to compare the chatbot responses against the "ground truth" database to evaluate correctness. This presentation will discuss the viability of automated LLM-as-a-judge evaluation frameworks for streamlining QA testing on technical documentation chatbots and share best practices and lessons learned from GFDL’s implementation.

494807.title: GNSS Micronet Employment In Small Areas for GNSS Meteorology Purposes
494807.authors: Kim Kaisti, Skyfora Oy, Helsinki, 18, Finland
494807.abstract: Skyfora has developed low cost GNSS antenna receivers (StreamGNSS) for GNSS meteorology. The purpose of the receivers is to install dense GNSS micronets in areas where there are insufficient GNSS observations. One such Micronet is installed around Manhattan area together with NYS Mesonet and results from that trial will be presented. There are two variants of the hardware; dual-band GNSS (L1/L5) and quad-band (L1/L2/L5/L6). All satellite systems (GPS/Galileo/Beidou/Glonass) are supported. QZSS (Japan) and NAVIC (India) systems can be activated also where additional regional satellite coverage is required. The receivers stream RTCM data (MSM7 messages @ 1Hz) over LTE (4G) using either a SIM card or using the embedded eSIM to Skyfora server. RTCM data is also available through RS485 for local access. The receivers are fully certified and Antex antenna calibration files are also available for antennas phase center offsets and phase variations corrections. Raw RTCM data from the antennas are converted to meteorological units (ZTD,PWV to mention a few) in Skyfora’s proprietary PPP-processing engine which is capable of handling tens of thousands of GNSS receivers residing in 5G telecom networks along with StreamGNSS antennas.

494808.title: Evaluating NaCl Solution Seeding in Thai Mixed-Phase Clouds Using SCALE-SDM: Preliminary Results
494808.authors: Arisara Nakburee, Department of Royal Rainmaking and Agricultural Aviation, A.Huahin, 77, Thailand; and C. Detyothin
494808.abstract: This study investigated the concentration-dependent and time-dependent effects of hygroscopic sodium chloride (NaCl) solution droplets on mixed-phase convective-cloud development and precipitation using the SCALE Large-Eddy Simulation coupled with the Super-Droplet Method (SCALE-LES/SDM). Four simulations were performed under common atmospheric initial conditions: an unseeded Control and three seeded cases containing NaCl solution mass fractions of 5% (Salt05), 15% (Salt15), and 25% (Salt25). The introduced NaCl solution droplets, representing seeding agents, had initial wet diameters of 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 µm with relative weights of 0.30, 0.40, and 0.30, respectively. The corresponding solution densities were approximately 1,034, 1,110, and 1,189 kg m⁻³ for the 5%, 15%, and 25% solutions. Mixed-phase SDM simulations included freezing/melting and sublimation processes and were integrated for 16,200 s (4.5 h) to resolve delayed precipitation responses over the cloud lifecycle. At 16,200 s, domain-mean accumulated rainfall was approximately 2.346 mm in the Control, compared with 2.479, 2.429, and 2.484 mm in Salt05, Salt15, and Salt25, corresponding to increases of approximately 5.69%, 3.56%, and 5.90%, respectively. Although Salt05 and Salt25 produced similar total rainfall, their temporal responses differed substantially. During the final 14,400–16,200 s interval, rainfall increments exceeded the Control by approximately 28.3% for Salt05, 56.6% for Salt15, and 39.2% for Salt25, indicating that precipitation responses remained active beyond four simulation hours. Microphysical diagnostics showed particularly persistent late-stage behaviour in Salt25. At 16,200 s, its mixed-phase condensate remained approximately 66.9% greater than the Control, while the liquid-particle mass for precipitation-sized droplets (D ≥ 200 µm) was approximately 8.71 × 10⁶ kg compared with 5.15 × 10⁶ kg in the Control. Salt25 also exhibited a larger mass-weighted droplet diameter, a substantial D ≥ 1 mm reservoir, a greater fraction of precipitation-sized particles below 2 km, and a shorter characteristic fallout-time proxy (derived from vertical distribution and terminal velocities) than the other simulations. These features are consistent with a delayed mixed-phase and fallout-supported precipitation pathway. Salt15 displayed a pronounced late-stage rainfall rebound despite reduced final mixed-phase condensate, suggesting a different timing of hydrometeor conversion, whereas Salt05 maintained a persistent cumulative enhancement with comparatively weaker mixed-phase support. The results demonstrate a nonlinear concentration–response relationship in which similar accumulated rainfall can arise through distinctly different microphysical pathways. The 25% NaCl case produced the largest accumulated rainfall at 4.5 h and retained the strongest evidence of an active delayed precipitation reservoir. These findings indicate that evaluation of hygroscopic cloud-seeding effectiveness should incorporate complete cloud-lifecycle evolution, precipitation-size distributions, mixed-phase reservoirs, and delayed fallout rather than relying solely on rainfall at an early simulation endpoint. Additional ensemble simulations are required to establish statistical robustness and separate treatment effects from stochastic cloud variability.

494810.title: The Future of Primary Ice Production In Mixed-Phase Clouds Simulated Using a New Parameterisation Constrained By GloPINE Observations
494810.authors: Ross Herbert, Institute for Climate and Atmospheric Science, Leeds, United kingdom; and B. J. Murray and K. Carslaw
494810.abstract: Ice-nucleating particles (INPs) are a rare subset of aerosols that drive primary ice production in mixed-phase clouds, influencing cloud properties and large-scale radiative flux profiles. The availability of INPs is strongly tied to the global distribution of aerosols, which are likely to change in future climates. However, global models typically treat primary ice production as a purely temperature-dependent process that is incapable of responding to aerosol perturbations. In this study, we exploit a novel dataset of 30,000 ambient INP measurements using the PINE instrument (GloPINE) to develop an optimized parameterisation for simulating temperature and aerosol-dependent INP concentrations in the UK Met Office climate model. We test this new method using INP measurements from offline filter-based methods from seven recent campaigns, and find that it reproduces INP global measurements, including the Southern Ocean, and outperforms existing alternatives. Having established a validated INP model, we have used CMIP6 scenarios to estimate the change in global distributions of INPs in the future. We show that there are significant changes to the distribution of INPs by 2100 (-0.84 L-1 globally) driven by altered aerosol emissions and transport (30 %) and higher ambient temperatures (70 %) that dominates the overall change in INP concentration.

494811.title: The Atmospheric Boundary Layer over the Marginal Ice Zone: Surface Pattern Characteristics, Convection Organization, and Flux Parametrization.
494811.authors: Joseph Fogarty, Princeton Univ., Princeton, NJ; and M. Bushuk, M. Allouche, M. Calaf, K. Ghannam, and E. Bou-Zeid
494811.abstract: Heterogeneous surface forcing organizes the convective boundary layer into secondary circulations that transport heat, scalars, and momentum; these physics remain outside the reach of conventional flux parameterizations. The marginal ice zone is a natural laboratory for this problem: the irregular shapes and uneven distribution of sea ice create intricate thermal patterns spanning scales from meters to tens of kilometers, and the resulting dynamics are difficult for climate models to simulate accurately. This gap has implications for predicting the future of the all-important polar regions that are warming faster than the rest of the planet. We conduct large-eddy simulations of the atmospheric boundary layer over realistic sea ice patterns obtained from satellites, and over simplified versions of those patterns that redistribute the ice while conserving its fraction. Our results confirm that the ice fraction on its own is insufficient to predict surface heat exchange. Three further descriptors of the surface pattern — encoding patch fragmentation, edge tortuosity, and size variability — also significantly modulate the strength of the induced circulations and the resulting fluxes. Changes in surface roughness between water and ice prove minor compared to the effects of the ice–ocean temperature contrast. A multi-linear regression on these descriptors reproduces the simulated fluxes, suggesting that aggregation rules for heterogeneous surfaces, in the marginal ice zone and elsewhere, can be improved by encoding pattern geometry more holistically, rather than relying on ice fraction alone.

494814.title: Storm Environment Measurements with PBL Mobile Active Profiling System (PBLMAPS)
494814.authors: Zhien Wang, SUNY-Stony Brook, Stony Brook, NY; and K. Yang, M. F. McGinnity, and J. Song
494814.abstract: The near-storm environment is highly heterogeneous and rapidly evolving, with strong spatial and temporal variability in thermodynamic, kinematic, and aerosol properties due to strong land-air and storm-environment interactions. These variations can strongly influence storm initiation, organization, intensity, and evolution. Yet, they remain poorly observed because conventional observing networks are too sparse to resolve the fine-scale structures surrounding storms. Rapid changes in boundary-layer temperature, moisture, winds, stability, and surface fluxes further complicate observations. To address these challenges and needs, the PBL Mobile Active Profiling System (PBLMAPS) was developed. PBLMAPS integrates a multi-function airborne Raman lidar (MARLi) and airborne Doppler lidar (ADL), two advanced airborne lidar systems, on a cargo van to provide simultaneous water vapor, wind, temperature, aerosol, and cloud structures in the PBL while driving around storms. This presentation provides a general overview of PBLMAPS instrumentation and highlights its capabilities with observations. PBLMAPS was deployed to northern Texas to sample dry line structures and associated convective developments in early June 2026. Inflow and cold pool structures of severe storms in central Illinois on June 11, 2026, will also be discussed.

494817.title: COASTAL - Nonlinear Interactions Between Tropical Cyclone Forcing and Estuarine Hydrodynamics During Compound Flooding in a Macrotidal Estuary
494817.authors: Lakku Naresh Kumar Goud, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Mumbai, MH, India; and A. Mohanty, P. K. Makhan, R. K. Dalai, C. G. Shankar, and M. R. Behera
494817.abstract: Extreme tropical cyclones (TCs) generate multiple hazards, including storm surge, wind waves, intense precipitation, and river flooding, which often occur simultaneously and interact through complex coastal and fluvial processes. The combined effects of these hazards, commonly referred to as compound flooding, have emerged as one of the most challenging problems in coastal hazard assessment because flood severity depends not only on the magnitude of individual drivers but also on their timing and hydrodynamic interactions (Wahl et al., 2015). Macrotidal estuaries are particularly vulnerable owing to large tidal ranges, shallow bathymetry, and convergent channel geometry that can substantially amplify cyclone-induced water levels and modify inland flood propagation (Pugh & Woodworth, 2014). Although storm surge, rainfall, and river flooding have been extensively investigated independently, relatively few studies have quantified their relative contributions and nonlinear interactions within a unified modelling framework (Silva-Aray et al., 2019). This study investigates how extreme TC forcing propagates through the atmosphere-ocean-river continuum and evaluates the dominant physical processes governing compound flooding in a tropical macrotidal estuary. An integrated numerical framework was developed by coupling atmospheric forcing, coastal hydrodynamics, machine-learning rainfall estimation, and hydraulic flood modelling, methodological framework has been shown in Figure 1. Historical Arabian Sea TCs were analyzed using extreme value statistics to estimate a 100-year design event. Maximum sustained wind speed and central pressure deficit were estimated using the best-fit Weibull distribution, and the resulting design hypothetical cyclone event was used to generate meteorological forcing. Storm surge, astronomical tides, and wave transformation were simulated using the coupled ADCIRC-SWAN model on an unstructured mesh designed to resolve offshore bathymetry, tidal channels, and estuarine geometry. Cyclone-induced rainfall was estimated using a hybrid CNN-LSTM model to reproduce the spatiotemporal evolution of precipitation associated with the TC. Flood propagation was simulated using a calibrated HEC-RAS 2D model (R² = 0.91), driven by downstream coastal water levels, spatially distributed rainfall, upstream inflows, and hypothetical dam-break hydrographs. Three physically representative scenarios were investigated: cyclone-induced coastal flooding, upstream extreme flooding, and compound flooding resulting from the simultaneous interaction of coastal and fluvial processes. Numerical simulations showed pronounced amplification of cyclone-induced coastal water levels within the estuary, reaching approximately 7.03 m near the estuarine entrance. This amplification was primarily attributed to the funnel-shaped estuarine geometry, shallow bathymetry, and tidal modulation, demonstrating the strong influence of local hydrodynamic conditions on the response to meteorological forcing. Flood characteristics were evaluated within the region of interest extending from downstream of the Ukai Reservoir to the coastal zone. Under the dam-break flooding scenario, simulated inundation depths ranged from 0 to 18.92 m, while the most frequently occurring depth was approximately 6.55 m. For the combined cyclone-induced flooding and dam-break scenario, inundation depths ranged from 0 to 19.47 m, with the highest frequency occurring at a depth of approximately 0.525 m. In comparison, the cyclone-induced flooding scenario produced depths ranging from 0 to 10.29 m, with the most frequently occurring depth being approximately 0.40 m. Although the combined scenario generated the greatest absolute inundation depth, the depth-frequency distributions indicate substantial spatial variability across the study area. The relatively shallow modal depths in the cyclone-induced and combined scenarios suggest that large areas experienced low-to-moderate inundation, whereas extreme depths were concentrated in localized sections of the river channel, floodplain depressions, or areas near hydraulic structures. The simulations therefore demonstrate that compound flooding cannot be represented as the simple addition of individual hazards. Storm surge primarily modified downstream boundary conditions, hydraulic gradients, and flood-propagation pathways, while dam-break discharge exerted stronger control over the largest inundation depths. Interactions among elevated coastal water levels, river hydraulics, and cyclone-induced rainfall substantially altered the spatial extent, depth distribution, and timing of flooding, emphasizing the importance of explicitly representing coupled coastal-fluvial processes. This study shows that compound flooding in macrotidal estuaries results from nonlinear interactions among storm surge, rainfall, and upstream discharge. While upstream flooding controlled the greatest inundation depths, storm surge altered downstream hydraulic gradients, flood extent, and propagation. The integrated framework provides a transferable approach for assessing cyclone-driven coastal–fluvial flood hazards under changing climate conditions. Keywords: Compound Flooding, Storm Surge, CNN-LSTM, HEC-RAS, Coastal Flooding

494820.title: Learning from the UK National Severe Weather Warning Service to Shape the Future of Impact-Based Public Weather Services
494820.authors: Mike Silverstone, UK Met Office, Exeter, United kingdom
494820.abstract: Weather services create value when scientific information is translated into decisions that help people and organisations prepare for, respond to and recover from high-impact weather. As societal expectations evolve and weather-related risks become increasingly complex, national warning services must continually adapt to ensure that they remain trusted, actionable and relevant. This presentation examines how learning from operational delivery, stakeholder engagement, post-event reviews and service development activities is helping to shape the future evolution of the United Kingdom's National Severe Weather Warning Service (NSWWS). Drawing on recent experiences across a range of severe weather events, the presentation explores the opportunities and challenges associated with impact-based forecasting and warning services, including communication of risk, understanding user behaviour, integration across hazards, improved use of impact intelligence and the development of more user-centred services. The session will consider how organisational learning and service design can support the development of future warning frameworks that better connect forecasting capability, hazard information, impacts, decision support and societal outcomes. Emerging areas of development include enhanced partnership working, common warning approaches, improved impact data, digital technologies and evolving roles across the wider weather enterprise. By sharing lessons from operational experience and ongoing service transformation, this work contributes to the broader discussion of how warning services can continue to evolve in support of community resilience, preparedness and public value.

494826.title: Building a Hail Event Catalog to Estimate Baseline Risk from Radar and Storm Reports
494826.authors: Alex Lapina, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; and Y. Amonkar, H. Zeff, and G. W. Characklis
494826.abstract: Severe convective storms, once considered a “secondary peril”, now drive rising insured losses across the United States, with hail among the leading contributors over the past decade. It remains unclear how much of this loss growth reflects increased exposure, changing vulnerability, or a genuine shift in the underlying hazard. This ambiguity persists largely because the baseline frequency and severity of hail itself is poorly characterized. A clearer picture of the spatial structure and intensity of hail would help property owners, government entities, and (re)insurers make better informed risk management decisions. Yet reliable hail data remains scarce. Radar-derived products tend to overestimate hail extent, while ground-observed storm reports are sparse and biased towards populated areas. This research draws on historical observations to estimate a baseline hail probability, first characterizing the deficiencies of each data source and then developing methods to reconcile and assimilate them. Using MESH (maximum expected size of hail) and POSH (probability of severe hail) we build a catalog of hail events from 2020 to present. We use clustering algorithms including DBSCAN to identify separate hail swaths, then adjust individual events using population density and latitude to incorporate storm report observations. Dataset level metrics including areal coverage and hail size, along with crop loss data, are used to validate this approach. With a robust catalog of events, hail risk management strategies can be evaluated by looking at exposure and vulnerability characteristics of individual assets. Solar PV power plants are deployed in hail-prone regions where their continued development creates a cascade of risk for investors, owners, and consumers. Using this catalog of hail footprints, we evaluate and quantify the effectiveness of risk mitigation techniques, such as increasing panel thickness and stowing, helping inform pricing and risk transfer decisions for property owners and insurers.

494828.title: Differences In Radiosonde and Aircraft Moisture Measurements Resulting In Misleading NWP Evaluation and Initialization
494828.authors: Stanley G. Benjamin, NOAA Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and D. D. Turner, E. P. James, and T. J. Wagner
494828.abstract: Accurate representation of clouds, precipitation, and convective storms within numerical weather prediction (NWP) models depends strongly on evolution of moisture, especially in the atmospheric boundary layer. We investigate a moisture puzzle in evaluating current NOAA/NWS operational NWP models (HRRR, RAP, GFS) over the US using radiosonde observation (RAOB) relative humidity (RH) observations indicating that these models have a moist bias in the lower and middle troposphere. In contrast, evaluating those same models using commercial aircraft (AMDAR – Aircraft Meteorological Data Relay) RH observations (available since 2015) show the opposite, namely that the models have a dry bias. In our study, we compare RAOB and AMDAR moisture observations using NWP models as a mediator and found RAOBs are about 4% drier than AMDAR. A new 2-year collocation study similarly showed RAOB RH to be 4% drier than AMDAR overall and by 7-10% when conditions are near saturation. This paper investigates these RH differences between aircraft and radiosonde measurements and discusses the implications for NWP models. A recent separate study (Benjamin et al. 2025, MWR) showed that the HRRR and RAP models have insufficient clouds and precipitation. The new assessment using AMDAR RH observations is consistent with these results and indicates that RAOB RH has provided misleading guidance for model development and even for atmospheric research in general. Moreover, assimilation of RAOB RH has added to the dry bias of models. Recommendations are made for RH model verification and for data assimilation of RH observations, including using a vendor-specific statistical correction for radiosonde RH values.

494830.title: Large Temperature Models: An Emerging Direction for AI-Driven Urban Climate Resilience
494830.authors: Jay Sadiq, FortyGuard, San Jose, CA
494830.abstract: Motivation. Cities worldwide are facing intensifying heat, and urban climate resilience has become one of the defining challenges of the coming decade. Yet the temperature intelligence that underpins resilience decisions, from cooling infrastructure planning to public-health response to grid load management, remains coarse. Standard weather models resolve at kilometers; many resilience decisions happen at the scale of a block, a building, or a street corner. Meeting the resilience challenge will require AI-driven near-surface temperature intelligence that operates at the scale where people actually experience the climate. The Emerging Direction: Large Temperature Models. This talk introduces Large Temperature Models (LTMs) as an emerging direction for AI in urban climate resilience. LTMs are a class of AI approaches that produce calibrated near-surface (2-meter) air-temperature intelligence at the resolution and cadence that resilience decisions actually require. FortyGuard is doing pioneering work in this space, and this talk is an invitation to the AMS AI community to help shape where LTMs go from here, what problems they should solve, what audiences they should serve, and what role they should play in the broader landscape of AI for environmental science. A Layered Approach. Conceptually, LTM approaches follow a layered pattern. At a platform layer, temperature-focused foundation models produce calibrated near-surface temperature intelligence. This intelligence then flows into downstream engines that translate it into decision-support for very different audiences and use cases: analytics and insights for urban planners, iterative design optimization for architects and landscape designers, temperature-aware routing for mobility and logistics, and integration into dashboards and APIs for enterprise workflows. The layered pattern matters because it explains how a shared foundation of temperature intelligence can serve a wide range of urban resilience needs without each needing to rebuild its own temperature science from scratch. Why This Direction Matters for Urban Climate Resilience. LTM approaches sit at the intersection of AI-for-environmental-science, urban climatology, and applied machine learning, and they open up questions the atmospheric AI community has not yet fully engaged with. What should near-surface temperature intelligence look like when it is designed from the outset for resilience decisions rather than adapted from forecasting or research products? What audiences should this intelligence serve, from municipal planners to grid operators to public-health responders to designers of urban interventions? How should the community think about the relationship between LTMs and the broader landscape of AI in environmental science, including weather emulators, physics-based urban models, and remote-sensing methods? These are questions the community is well positioned to help shape. FortyGuard's Position. FortyGuard is doing pioneering work on Large Temperature Models and their application to urban climate resilience. FortyGuard is a member of the NVIDIA Inception Program. This talk is to invite AMS AI community to engage with LTMs as an emerging direction, discuss where the science and applications should go, and shape the future of AI-driven urban climate resilience together. Contribution. This is a framing talk. Its contribution is to introduce Large Temperature Models as an emerging direction for AI-driven urban climate resilience, illustrate the layered pattern that connects near-surface temperature intelligence to a wide range of downstream applications, and invite the AMS AI community into an ongoing conversation about where this direction should go. We hope this session becomes an annual forum for that conversation, and we welcome co-organizers, discussants, and future presenters from academic, government, and industry groups working on adjacent problems.

494832.title: Operational Data-Driven Modeling for Subseasonal to Annual Net Basin Supply Forecasts in the Laurentian Great Lakes Region
494832.authors: David M. Wright, NOAA, Ann Arbor, MI; and L. Fry, D. Jones, Y. Hong, L. E. Fitzpatrick, N. Hernandez, J. Ward, A. H. Young, and D. Fielder
494832.abstract: Accurate predictions of subseasonal to annual net basin supply (NBS), encompassing precipitation, evaporation, and runoff in the Laurentian Great Lakes basin are necessary for the prediction of water levels. Accumulated changes in this value can lead to shifts in water levels on the lakes that can endanger key coastal infrastructure (e.g. shipping, navigation, and water intakes), making accurate forecasts of this value paramount for water level management. To improve water level forecasting capabilities and incorporate numerical predictions directly into forecasts, an ensemble of data-driven models, known as the NBS-Predictor, was developed in collaboration between the Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory (GLERL), the Cooperative Institute of Great Lakes Research (CIGLR), and the U. S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE). This model directly uses inputs from NOAA’s operational Climate Forecast System (CFSv2) and delivers first of its kind probabilistic outcomes of the NBS out to 12 months. The NBS-Predictor was transitioned to operations at the USACE in 2026 and created an additional tool to support operational water level forecasts over the region for decision-making stakeholders. This presentation will describe the performance of the current operational version and areas of on-going development, including the use of bias correction techniques on the CFSv2 input data and the use of teleconnections to increase predictability. Finally, early work on the evaluation and the transition to NOAA’s Subseasonal Forecast System (SFS) in the NBS-Predictor will be shared from a hydrological perspective.

494833.title: Integrating LCNN Nowcasting to Operations in IRIS Focus via a Scalable Algorithm Framework
494833.authors: Igli Balla, Vaisala Oyj, Vantaa, Finland; and P. Rossi and L. Thobois
494833.abstract: Weather nowcasting is one of the most important operational challenges in modern meteorology. Numerical prediction models present a number of drawbacks and often lose accuracy quickly. The use of radar observations has introduced improvements, but these techniques fall back into behavior more akin to transporting the observed objects passively, instead of also representing the terms that govern storm evolution in time. Machine learning-based nowcasting addresses this limitation directly: instead of assuming persistence, a deep-learning model can be trained on long radar archives to learn how precipitation systems grow and decay and should outperform traditional extrapolation at longer lead times. Such algorithms are hard to make operational, as they carry complex dependencies and must run as a monitored, uninterrupted 24/7 service once deployed. The algorithm framework introduced in Release 8 of Vaisala's IRIS Focus radar software intends to solve this issue: it standardizes how new and custom radar products are integrated, chained, and visualized alongside native ones, making it easier to move sophisticated algorithms from research into operations. The new algorithm framework, which acts as a modular processing backbone for radar product generation, is built on a recently introduced data layer based on Google Protocol Buffers (protobuf) format [1] for radar data and products, and the corresponding gRPC (Remote Procedure Call) data interfaces. Algorithms written in any language (Python, C/C++) only need to be adapted to these interfaces to request radar data and/or products from the IRIS Focus data manager as inputs, and to publish their outputs back into the system. Each algorithm is containerized and deployed on an existing IRIS Focus system as an independent, scalable microservice, so that new products can be added without rebuilding or restarting the core application. Users can configure the algorithm through the UI, setting its parameters, execution method, and triggers. Because outputs are published in the same protobuf representation as native products, they are immediately available for display, enabling downstream chaining, dissemination, and archiving. The use case presented is the integration of a modern machine learning nowcasting model into IRIS Focus through the algorithm framework: the Lagrangian Convolutional Neural Network (LCNN) [2], an open-source deep-learning model that numerically advects precipitation fields along a motion field generated from five previous observations, while a U-Net-based network predicts their growth and decay. This is the first ML integration using the new IRIS Focus algorithm framework, targeting a mature operational implementation rather than a research prototype: the model was also adapted to run over larger geographical areas than its original research configuration, using confidence-based tile merging, with outputs continuously adjusted against incoming observations through conformal calibration. A proof-of-concept version is running in IRIS Focus with model evaluation ongoing, and a more mature version is currently under development. The algorithm was evaluated on a Finnish radar dataset against standard nowcasting baselines and the IRIS Focus Legacy Model, using categorical and neighborhood-based metrics as a function of lead time. The LCNN detected rain substantially better than the baselines, with its advantage growing over lead time: probability of detection (POD) at the 0.1 mm/h threshold was 0.07–0.29 higher than the legacy model across the forecast horizon, at the cost of a marginally higher false alarm rate (FAR), up to 0.03 higher. For heavy rain the gain came without that trade-off: at the 10 mm/h threshold, the LCNN beat the STEPS [3] baseline by up to 0.24 in POD and 0.13 in ETS while simultaneously lowering FAR by up to 0.15, a ranking confirmed across neighborhood sizes from 5 to 100 pixels for FSS. The LCNN was also the least biased model tested, with a mean bias of −0.008 mm/h, about 60% smaller than that of LINDA [4]. To test generalization beyond this climatology, the evaluation was repeated without retraining on two unseen regimes: a landfalling tropical cyclone (Hurricane Dorian in Bahamas) and a monsoon season in Southeast Asia. In both cases the LCNN kept the lowest RMSE and highest skill score of all four models (0.285 and 0.270, respectively), and POD at 0.1 mm/h remained 0.06–0.26 and 0.08–0.30 higher than the legacy model, again at a modest FAR cost (up to 0.14 and 0.11, respectively). At higher rain rates the picture became more regime-dependent: for the cyclone, POD and ETS gains over the legacy model at 10 mm/h reached +0.19 and +0.15, with FAR up to 0.20 lower, though this advantage reversed at the longest lead time, and bias was higher than in the other two regimes; for the monsoon, the LCNN kept a POD/ETS edge of up to +0.11/+0.06 over the legacy model at 5 mm/h with FAR up to 0.11 lower, while a competing ensemble baseline nearly collapsed at the highest rain rates. Taken together, the case demonstrates that the algorithm framework shortens the path from a published, open-source machine-learning method to a supportable operational product, while preserving the configuration, visualization, and chaining behavior operators expect. This does not come at the cost of skill: the LCNN implementation outperforms the legacy model not only within its training climatology, but also across different regimes, from tropical cyclones to monsoon seasons. Looking ahead, the framework opens the door to integrating further functions from open-source libraries such as Py-ART and deploying additional data-driven products within IRIS Focus. References: [1] Thobois, L., Blankenbaker, P., Panov, S. I., Mitchell, T., & Selzler, J. (2025, August 28). Adoption of Modern Protocol Buffers Data Format with Interface Description Language for Weather Radar Data. AMS - 41st International Conference on Radar Meteorology. https://ams.confex.com/ams/41Radar/meetingapp.cgi/Paper/462773 [2] Ritvanen, J., Harnist, B., Aldana, M., Mäkinen, T., & Pulkkinen, S. (2023). Advection-Free convolutional neural network for convective rainfall nowcasting. IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing, 16, 1654–1667. https://doi.org/10.1109/jstars.2023.3238016 [3] Bowler, N.E., Pierce, C.E. and Seed, A.W. (2006), STEPS: A probabilistic precipitation forecasting scheme which merges an extrapolation nowcast with downscaled NWP. Q.J.R. Meteorol. Soc., 132: 2127-2155. https://doi.org/10.1256/qj.04.100 [4] Pulkkinen, S., Chandrasekar, V., & Niemi, T. (2021). Lagrangian Integro-Difference Equation Model for Precipitation Nowcasting.
