494837.title: Recent Physics Development and Optimization in the Operational HAFS
494837.authors: Weiguo Wang, SAIC, Riverdale Park, MD; SAIC at NOAA/NWS/OMD, Riverdale Park, MD; and J. H. Shin, J. Han, C. K. Wang, P. Zhu, A. Hazelton, R. Sun, B. Liu, Z. Zhang, and F. Yang
494837.abstract: Since its initial operational implementation in 2023, the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) has achieved significant performance improvements, with physical parameterizations playing a critical role. This presentation summarizes key physics developments in HAFS, highlighting both scheme advancements and extensive parameter optimization including calibration for hurricane applications. Specifically, three new developments have been implemented. First, a 3D-TKE formulation has been integrated into the traditional TKE-EDMF boundary layer scheme to improve subgrid-scale flux parameterizations in the gray zone (grid spacings of a few kilometers). Second, wind shear effects are now incorporated into the updraft and downdraft formulations within the Simplified Arakawa-Schubert (SAS) convection schemes, as well as in the parcel model for mixing length estimation. Third, fixed-value caps for mixing length calculations have been replaced by a physics-based, dynamically adjusting formulation. These developments have yielded positive impacts on HAFS forecast skills, particularly for storm intensity. Additionally, numerous sensitivity experiments have been conducted to optimize parameters within the PBL, microphysics, and convection schemes such as entrainment/detainment rates, detrained water conversion rates, and convective adjustment time scale.

494838.title: Mitigating Noise and Inter-Channel Correlation for Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounders
494838.authors: John Xun Yang, Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies, College Park, MD; and Y. K. Lee, S. Liu, X. Liang, W. Wang, H. Meng, C. Pan, and S. J. J. Munchak
494838.abstract: NOAA established the Commercial Data Program (CDP) to address the growing demand for commercial satellite observations. Through a series of pilot studies, commercial satellite datasets are evaluated to assess their potential value for numerical weather prediction and climate applications. The Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) is one of the commercial satellite systems participating in the CDP. TMS is a 12-channel microwave radiometer operating between 91 and 204 GHz. Unlike conventional microwave sounders, which use the 50 GHz oxygen absorption (V-band) channels for temperature sounding, TMS employs the 118 GHz oxygen absorption (F-band) channels, enabling a much smaller instrument suitable for CubeSat platforms. Eleven TMS satellites (S01–S11) have been launched, with additional satellites planned to complete the constellation. The current constellation already provides a median revisit time of less than 45 minutes, substantially improving temporal sampling and enabling near-real-time monitoring of rapidly evolving weather systems such as tropical cyclones. Despite its stable on-orbit performance, TMS exhibits noticeable striping artifacts and inter-channel correlation. Cross-track stripes with non-periodic sharp edges are observed across all channels, and the noise equivalent differential temperature (NEDT) is higher than that of ATMS. Significant inter-channel correlation is also observed, particularly among the F-band and G-band channels. These effects are primarily attributed to flicker (1/f) noise, which tends to be elevated in the compact CubeSat platform and miniature high-frequency microwave receiver. Unlike stationary, uncorrelated white noise, flicker noise is non-stationary and exhibits strong temporal correlation, leading to striping artifacts, elevated radiometric noise, and increased inter-channel correlation. Noise characteristics vary considerably among individual TMS sensors. For example, TMS S07 exhibits severe noise, with Channel 8 NEDT reaching up to 15 K and correlation coefficients exceeding 0.9 for several channel pairs. To address these issues, we developed a physics-based denoising algorithm that mitigates striping noise and reduces inter-channel correlation. The algorithm employs a noise model to decompose the measured noise into flicker and white noise components and estimates their respective amplitudes using observations of the onboard internal calibration target. It further exploits the distinct characteristics of the two noise sources: flicker noise produces sharp cross-track striping and exhibits short-term temporal autocorrelation on the order of tens of milliseconds, whereas white noise is spatially and temporally uncorrelated. These physical characteristics are incorporated into an optimization framework that iteratively estimates the noise-free radiances by minimizing the constrained loss function. The algorithm has been applied to both pre-launch test data and on-orbit Earth scene observations. Results demonstrate effective removal of striping artifacts, substantial reduction of radiometric noise, and preservation of fine-scale geophysical features. For the heavily-impacted S07 TMS, the NEDT of Channel 8 is reduced from 15 K to less than 2 K, restoring the sensor noise levels comparable to those of the other TMS instruments. In addition, inter-channel correlation is reduced by more than 90% for the most highly correlated channel pairs. These improvements enable the generation of higher-quality Level-1 brightness temperature data. The resulting higher-quality data have shown positive impacts in evaluations using the NOAA Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS) 1DVAR retrievals and numerical weather prediction, demonstrating the potential of the proposed approach to enhance the value of commercial microwave sounding observations.

494840.title: A 44-Year CONUS404 Analysis of Standalone and Heatwave-Compounded Wind Droughts
494840.authors: Emily Erickson, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; and G. Wang, T. Zaman, M. G. Bosilovich, C. Kirkpatrick, M. Astitha, and H. Moulik
494840.abstract: Wind is a major source of energy for the power grid, making up 10.5% of net electricity generated in the United States in 2025 (U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2026). Regional grids were as much as 40% dependent on wind for half the year in 2024 (Southwest Power Pool, 2025). The number of kilowatt hours generated from wind has more than doubled in the past decade. One major concern with increased use of wind power is the ‘wind drought’, a period of time where sustained wind speeds are too low for turbines to produce electricity. In this study, we carry out a historical analysis of wind drought occurrences and trends. We use outputs from the NCAR–USGS 4-km Long-Term Regional Hydroclimate Reanalysis over the CONUS (CONUS404; Rasmussen et al. 2023). This dataset provides weather variables at an hourly timescale for 44 years (1980-2023). We explore days with prolonged wind speeds (at least 6 hours) below the wind turbine cut-in speed (3-4 m/s) at hub height (100m). We present results related to frequency, duration, and spatial distribution of these wind droughts in the past 44 years. Additionally, we consider the impact of wind droughts compounded by heatwave events.. Heatwaves have increased in number, duration, and intensity over the past 60 years (EPA, 2024). They cause a higher energy demand and simultaneously decrease the efficiency of electricity flow. We analyze the trends of wind drought that co-occur with heatwaves over the same period, with a focus on urban areas and wind farm locations.

494841.title: WeatherGenerator: Learning and Forecasting a General Representation of the Earth System (Invited Presentation)
494841.authors: Christian Lessig, ECMWF, Reading, United kingdom; ECMWF, Tübingen, HH, Germany; and S. Hickman, S. Xhonneux, M. Karlbauer, J. Kuehnert, I. Luise, W. Almikaeel, J. Wang, T. Hunter, E. M. Nordhagen, C. Lussana, R. Heilemann Myhre, J. Pinon Rodriguez, T. N. Nipen, I. Seierstad, P. DUEBEN, and M. Schultz
494841.abstract: The WeatherGenerator is a multimodal foundation model for weather and climate prediction that is currently under development at ECMWF and its partners. It is designed to learn and evolve a general latent representation of the Earth system state from heterogeneous data sources, supporting both standard meteorological forecasts and adaptation to a wide range of downstream applications. We present results from a pre-operational prototype in which operational analyses are enriched with real-time observations, including satellite data. The WeatherGenerator represents these heterogeneous inputs as flexible data streams that may differ in spatial and temporal sampling, allowing observational information to be incorporated directly into the forecast system. We demonstrate how this additional real-time information can improve the representation of the initial atmospheric state and subsequent forecast skill. A central component of WeatherGenerator is self-supervised representation learning. We investigate masked-token learning and variants of JEPA for pretraining the encoder, and show how the resulting representations improve forecast performance across physical fields and lead times. Probabilistic forecasts are generated using latent diffusion, enabling ensemble prediction directly in the learned representation rather than independently modelling uncertainty for each output dataset. The resulting pre-trained WeatherGenerator model provides a general weather representation that can subsequently be fine-tuned for downstream applications. Forecasts can either be decoded into standard meteorological fields, as in conventional NWP systems, or exposed through their compact latent states, enabling application-specific models to make use of the same underlying forecast representation. Finally, we describe the pre-operational setup that is developed to make use of and quality-control real-time observations, generate probabilistic forecasts, and disseminate both conventional forecast products and latent representations. Together, these results demonstrate a path towards a flexible weather forecasting system in which real-time observations, self-supervised learning, probabilistic prediction, and downstream adaptation are combined within a common learned representation.

494842.title: GNSS Radio Occultation Observations in the MERRA-21C Reanalyses
494842.authors: Michael J. Murphy Jr., UMBC/GESTAR-II at GMAO/NASA, Baltimore, MD; and A. El Akkraoui, E. E. Jones, and M. Chattopadhyay
494842.abstract: The recent Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research Applications for the early 21st century (MERRA-21C) is currently being produced at NASA’s Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO). Its main purpose is to provide a detailed and consistent depiction of historical weather and climate since the start of the modern satellite era. Among the updates and improvements over previous reanalyses, the M21C includes changes to how Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) Radio Occultation (RO) observations are used. These observations form an important component of the global observing system utilized in operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems as well reanalysis products through data assimilation. A major update included in the M21C is the assimilation of the full set of GNSS-RO observations collected by Spire over recent years (peaking at approximately 20 thousand profiles per day) and made available for research by NASA’s Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) program. Changes have also been made to the algorithms for observation quality control and uncertainty specification for GNSS-RO within the Atmospheric Data Assimilation System (ADAS) used with the Global Earth Observing System (GEOS) NWP model employed to generate the M21C. These updates to the use of GNSS-RO in GMAO’s reanalysis efforts are presented along with an evaluation of the M21C product using in situ observations from radiosondes and remotely sensed observations, and compared with that of the more established MERRA-2 reanalysis product.

494844.title: How Does Tropical Updraft Speed Respond to Warming? Insights from a Simple Theoretical Model
494844.authors: John M Peters, Penn State University, State College, PA; Penn State Univ., State College, PA
494844.abstract: Despite buoyancy being the primary driver of upward acceleration in deep convective updrafts, many theoretical models of the tropical atmosphere assume zero buoyancy within a singular updraft plume. This assumption precludes a self-consistent prediction of vertical velocity (w). To address this limitation, we reformulate the zero-buoyancy framework by representing convection as an ensemble of plumes rather than a single updraft. The environmental temperature is constrained to equilibrate with the mass-flux-weighted mean temperature of the plume ensemble, allowing individual updrafts to attain positive buoyancy. This permits a self-consistent calculation of w. Analysis of the new model’s behavior yields the following insights: Although convective available potential energy (CAPE) increases exponentially with surface temperature, w only increases linearly. Moreover, w attains a maximum at a specific combination of surface temperature and updraft radius. Including freezing increases CAPE by 20–30 %, yet has little impact on w. Trends in CAPE and w with surface temperature are highly sensitive to how updraft radius evolves, and the responses of CAPE and w to changes in radius oppose one another. Finally, we show that the weak sensitivity of w to surface Bowen ratio found in previous simulations is an expected feature of radiative-convective equilibrium and does not contradict the positive relationship between updraft radius and lifted condensation level (LCL) height. This framework provides a self-consistent method for assessing the climate sensitivity of tropical updraft intensity and for diagnosing biases in reanalysis trends in CAPE.

494846.title: Geospatial Weather and Climate Impacts and Services Workflow Resilience through Turbulent and Steady Times
494846.authors: Michael Shaw, NOAA, Biddeford, ME; NOAA, Asheville, NC; and D. Burt, S. Ansari, and R. Bilotta
494846.abstract: Modern scientific and technical work increasingly relies on complex digital workflows, including continuous integration and deployment, containerization, migration to cloud-based platforms, and large-scale data generation and management. These workflows can now be closely intertwined with artificial intelligence and play a critical role in the reliability and resilience of research and societal infrastructure. At the same time, they face growing pressures: rapid technological change, evolving security requirements, and external constraints such as staffing, funding, and organizational instability. Meanwhile, emerging approaches—including automated and AI-assisted code refactoring, as well as new models for team organization and collaboration—offer promising if imperfect ways to adapt to these challenges. This moment presents an important opportunity to share and develop practical strategies that support sustainable, resilient workflows. By exchanging emerging best practices grounded in the FAIR and CARE principles, the community can better ensure continuity, transparency, and responsible stewardship of data and software amid both steady progress and inevitable disruption.

494847.title: ML Based Method for Water Level Gap Filling Based on Nearby Tide Gauge Measurements
494847.authors: Philippe E. Tissot, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX
494847.abstract: High quality water level data sets are important to a number of coastal applications, including the design of coastal infrastructure, community preparedness for increasing frequencies of coastal inundation, erosion mitigation, and the design of nature-based solutions. In the early 1990s, the Texas General Land Office and the Texas Water Development Board, along with the Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi Conrad Blucher Institute (CBI), with assistance from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the US Army Corps of Engineers, grew a small CBI network of tide gauges into a Texas coast-wide network, the Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON). While tide gauges in NOAA's National Water Level Observation Network (NWLON), and now most TCOON stations, benefit from measurements from both a primary and a backup sensor, historical TCOON data prior to about 2010 lack backup sensor measurements. This absence makes gap-filling in the primary water level time series more challenging. Filling such gaps facilitates the determination of tidal datums and is increasingly important for calibrating artificial intelligence models, which are sensitive to missing data. Given the spatial density of the TCOON network, most tide gauges are located relatively close to other gauges. We developed a method to fill gaps at a target station using measurements from a nearby tide gauge. While water level dynamics can change significantly across a bay or with distance inland, these differences are driven in large part by weather forcing, particularly wind. Data processing starts by a mostly automated QA/QC processing of the time series to remove, spikes, flats and other non-physical data. Our gap-filling method predicts water levels at a target gauge based on water levels measured at a nearby gauge while also incorporating wind forcing as an additional predictor if such measurements are available for the water body. Neural network hyperparameters are selected using a two-step grid search, comparing roughly 4,000 candidate configurations at each step: (1) all models begin from the same coarse grid, with (2) final hyperparameter values refined through a location-specific finer grid search. Prior to the gap-filling step, neural network predictions are linearly nudged toward observations using the average of the three measurements immediately preceding and following the gap. The method was evaluated using 1,000 synthetic gaps ranging from 1 to 150 hours in length, against a target accuracy of 2 cm average RMSE with minimal or preferably no outliers — a demanding threshold but necessary to give confidence to the eventual users that the gap filled time series can be used confidently. Performance varied considerably, with the maximum gap length fillable at RMSE below 2 cm ranging from as little as 1–2 hours to over 150 hours, depending on the distance between gauge pairs, the similarity of local hydrodynamics, and the water level range at the target station. Work is ongoing to produce and share broadly these improved time series.

494848.title: Retrospective Per-Flight Turbulence Estimation from Irregularly Sampled Mode S and ADS-B Observations
494848.authors: Marsha Burgess, FlightTurbulence.ai, London, United kingdom
494848.abstract: Passengers currently have no estimate of the turbulence experienced on a specific flight after it has landed that is derived from observations of that flight. This paper presents a method for estimating turbulence intensity for an individual flight from Mode S and ADS-B data already broadcast during that flight. A flight is identified from its flight number, date and route, which can be extracted automatically from an uploaded boarding pass and used to retrieve the corresponding aircraft track. Turbulence intensity is estimated primarily from divergence between the barometric and inertial vertical rates reported in BDS 6,0, with roll angle (BDS 5,0) and other flight-state parameters, including altitude, ground speed, track and position, used to distinguish candidate turbulence signatures from ordinary aircraft manoeuvres such as climbs, descents and turns. A central limitation is that Mode S observations do not form a uniformly sampled time series. Within airspace where Enhanced Surveillance is interrogated, as across much of Europe, the effective observation frequency varies with radar coverage, aircraft position and surveillance environment. Rather than treating missing observations as equivalent to smooth flight, the method characterises sampling interval and observational coverage alongside the estimated intensity, allowing poorly observed portions of a flight to be distinguished from portions where the available observations indicate low turbulence. The resulting estimate is treated as a surveillance-derived turbulence proxy rather than a calibrated EDR equivalent. Direct EDR observations provide a standardised measure of turbulence but are available only from aircraft that calculate and report them; the present approach can be applied to flights for which sufficient Mode S Enhanced Surveillance observations are available. Mode S parameters describe the aircraft response and are affected by aircraft type, flight state and control activity, while being sampled at substantially lower frequencies than measurements used for onboard EDR calculation. Estimates are therefore expressed on an ordinal turbulence intensity scale. The principal contribution is a framework for retrospective turbulence estimation and validation at the level of an individual flight. Because each estimate is tied to a uniquely identifiable flight and trajectory, it can be compared with independent evidence concerning the same encounter, including conventional turbulence reports and reports from passengers who were physically present on the aircraft. Passenger observations are subjective and are not treated as ground truth, but provide an independent source of encounter-level evidence that can be evaluated in aggregate. The approach provides a method for reconstructing per-flight turbulence encounters from surveillance data already broadcast by existing aircraft, without requiring additional onboard equipment, while explicitly identifying portions of a trajectory where the available observations are insufficient to support an estimate.

494849.title: Quantifying the Risk of Mississippi River Barge Delays under Low Water Conditions
494849.authors: Molly McKinley Alcorn, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; and H. Zeff and G. W. Characklis
494849.abstract: The Mississippi River is an essential shipping route for agricultural commodities in the United States, carrying grain by barge from the Midwest to Gulf of Mexico export ports. Low water levels have disrupted barge traffic during several recent harvest seasons (2012, 2022–2024), coinciding with the seasonal peak in transport demand. Grain exporters can hedge against the risk of higher spot barge freight rates with forward contracts but are still exposed to risks from shipping. Low water can slow vessel movement, extend travel times, and make delivery timing less predictable, complicating the coordination of barge deliveries with scheduled export operations at Gulf ports. This study quantifies the effects of low Mississippi River water levels on barge travel times along the Mississippi River. Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel tracking data is used to estimate travel times from St. Louis to New Orleans as a function of channel depth throughout the Lower Mississippi. River stage data is combined with U.S. Army Corps of Engineers hydrographic survey data to estimate available channel depth, capturing both water-level fluctuations and changes in riverbed elevation from dredging. Preliminary results indicate that even shippers insulated from spot rate spikes face meaningful scheduling risk. These findings offer grain shippers a way to assess delivery risk under forward contracts and plan transportation logistics ahead of low-water events.

494851.title: NOAA's Space Weather Observations Office: Current Plans and Future Planning
494851.authors: Richard G. Marlow, NOAA, Gaithersburg, MD
494851.abstract: The mission of the NESDIS Office of Space Weather Observations is to provide trusted space weather environmental data to safeguard society. The Nation’s increasing reliance on space and space-based systems for our economic vitality and security demands continuous improvement in both observational coverage and responsiveness to emerging requirements. Space weather events—such as geomagnetic storms, ionospheric disturbances, solar flares, and coronal mass ejections—create direct impacts across communications, navigation, timing, and power systems. Improving monitoring and forecasting requires a clear understanding of observational requirements and an integrated approach to data collection, measurement continuity, and operational transition. This presentation will describe the NESDIS observational program for monitoring the space weather environment, including the alignment of NOAA’s observing strategy with the PROSWIFT Act and Administration priorities and executive orders. At Lagrange Point 1, NOAA has transitioned from reliance on legacy research class data to the operational SOLAR-1 observatory, with a commitment to continuity through the future SOLAR-A mission. NOAA is also committed to multi-point, complementary measurements supported by partnerships such as the ESA collaboration with Vigil. Finally, planning is underway to ensure continuity of the critical and essential observations made by the current GOES-R series, including consideration of potential new operational measurements such as an operational solar magnetograph.

494853.title: Advancing Operational Success: Innovating and Growing in the Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences (SBES) Research Transition Space
494853.authors: Cassandra Shivers-Williams, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; WPO, Silver Spring, MD; and A. Krepp and K. Fillingham
494853.abstract: NOAA continues to make meaningful progress integrating social, behavioral, and economic science (SBES) research into its operations. However, the pathways by which knowledge generated through SBES research is operationalized vary. Understanding these pathways unlocks key insights to address persistent challenges and harness future opportunities necessary to achieving a holistic vision of operational success across the weather enterprise. The research landscape within NOAA is a key driver of these pathways. While NOAA’s physical science landscape is well established, the extreme weather SBES landscape within the agency is emergent and works with a vastly smaller bench, which is augmented by a robust network of extramural partners. As a result, a predominance of research that examines how the public perceives, understands, and responds to extreme weather is conducted outside of NOAA. Taken together, these realities shape the accessibility and expediency of research-to-operations pathways for SBES research and the role of the program office in setting priorities, cultivating connections, and fledging projects to operational use or societal application. A recent research-to-applications (R2X) evaluation conducted by the Weather Program Office characterized the operational pathways for SBES research in the following ways: As an Input to Technical Development: SBES shapes design decisions, clarifies user needs, and ensures tools fit naturally into a forecaster's workflow to enhance situational awareness rather than overwhelming it. As Independent Operational Outcomes: Some SBES outcomes are not tied to specific tools at all, such as visual communication products or new communication best practices. As Integrated or Standalone Tools: SBES can be added to existing tools to provide local vulnerability information or stand alone as independent capabilities. This presentation will draw upon past project transitions while also exploring future SBES transition opportunities.

494854.title: Investigating Thunderstorm Total Lightning Variability and Severe Weather Hazard Disposition in the Baltimore-Washington Urban Corridor: A Climatological Analysis of Observations and Climate Indices (2007-2017)
494854.authors: Aaron J. Poyer, University of Maryland Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; and J. Halverson and A. T. Poyer
494854.abstract: The Baltimore-Washington corridor warm season can be characterized by years with prolific severe weather driven by Mesoscale Convective Complexes (MCCs) producing high flash-count lightning, like the derecho of June 2012; by low-electrification systems with substantial flash flooding, like the 2016 Old Ellicott City flood; by primarily wind-driven damage with little to no electrification, like the dry microburst of August 2011; and by warm seasons with little severe weather, like 2007. The physical mechanisms separating highly electrified storms from rain-efficient, electrically quiet systems, and the large-scale climate drivers of this variability, remain poorly understood. Better characterization of these distinctions directly improves forecast skill, warning lead times for regional severe weather, and future preparedness. For this analysis, 11 years (2007-2017) of total lightning flash data from the NASA Washington DC Lightning Mapping Array (DCLMA) were used to characterize long-duration lightning statistics, seasonality, and extreme event frequencies throughout the domain. In this study, we investigate a novel approach integrating total lightning with Next Generation Radar (NEXRAD) reflectivity, velocity, and derived bulk wind shear from KLWX, along with radiosonde-measured thermodynamic parameters from KIAD, including freezing level height. Pairing the height of daily maximum-reflectivity echo detection and bulk wind shear with the ambient freezing level provides a physical basis for interpreting why some deep convection electrifies vigorously while other systems producing comparable or greater rainfall remain electrically quiet. A preliminary spatio-temporal climatology was performed to analyze possible interconnections between year-to-year convective characteristics and large-scale climate oscillations, including the North Atlantic Oscillation, Southern Oscillation Index, and Multivariate ENSO Index v2. Goals of this research are to refine our understanding of the interannual variability in thunderstorm electrification for the Baltimore-Washington metro area and to assess what large-scale, look-ahead climate factors may contribute to variability and predictability. This climatological analysis forms one component of a broader dissertation effort; a companion case-study investigation of impactful severe weather events spanning the same period of record is ongoing, with data collection and analysis underway.

494856.title: Fast and Slow Surfactants In Turbulence-Driven Bubble Breakup
494856.authors: Zhan Wu, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ
494856.abstract: Gas bubbles dispersed in turbulent flows play a fundamental role in air–sea exchange by mediating the transfer of mass, momentum, and energy across the ocean surface. Bubble bursting generates sea spray aerosols that influence atmospheric composition and climate, while underwater bubble fragmentation affects gas exchange. In natural waters, air–water interfaces are almost always contaminated by surface-active compounds of biological or anthropogenic origin, yet their influence on turbulent bubble breakup remains poorly understood. We experimentally investigate how surfactant adsorption kinetics modify the fragmentation of large air cavities in turbulence. During breakup, cavities undergo large deformations and generate cascades of ligaments and bubbles spanning a broad range of scales, with bubble formation governed by the interplay between turbulent stresses and capillary forces. We show that the fast-adsorbing surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) increases the production of sub-Hinze-scale bubbles by up to a factor of five while leaving the super-Hinze population essentially unchanged. The sub-Hinze bubble size distribution remains well described by a power law, but its exponent becomes progressively steeper than the classical -3/2 scaling as surfactant concentration increases, implying a substantial enhancement in the abundance of small bubbles. In contrast, the slow-adsorbing surfactant Tween 20 produces no measurable change in the bubble size distribution despite reducing the equilibrium surface tension by a similar amount. Cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), with intermediate adsorption kinetics, produces an intermediate response, increasing sub-Hinze bubble production only at sufficiently high concentrations. These contrasting behaviors are explained by comparing surfactant adsorption timescales with the characteristic deformation time of turbulent bubble breakup through the Biot number. Our results demonstrate that surfactant adsorption kinetics, rather than equilibrium surface tension alone, controls turbulence-driven bubble fragmentation, with important implications for air–sea gas exchange and sea spray aerosol production.

494858.title: Agentic AI for Earth Science Software: A Field Report from Building Worldscope (Invited Presentation)
494858.authors: David Matthew Hall, NVIDIA, Lafayette, CO
494858.abstract: What happens when AI agents are treated not as chatbots, but as full participants in an Earth science workflow? Worldscope is an interactive workbench I built to explore that question. It puts NVIDIA's entire Earth2Studio toolset on an interactive 3D globe alongside satellite imagery, climate archives, live weather feeds, and observational data, and it reads, writes, and visualizes many standard geoscience formats including NetCDF, GRIB2, GeoTIFF, and Zarr, and many grid types including our recent favorite, the HEALPix grid. Because every capability is exposed through the Model Context Protocol rather than through a chat window added afterwards, an agent can load forecasts, select variables, run models, compare results, and manipulate the same visualization a human user sees. Multiple agents can work on one scene at once. Worldscope is lightweight enough to run on any device while taking advantage of whatever NVIDIA hardware is present; with a single desktop DGX Spark it runs the vast majority of AI weather models locally. In under five months it grew from a proof of concept into a general-purpose environment for exploring Earth system models and data, standing at over 175,000 lines of source code across more than 1,400 commits. Every one of those commits was generated by an AI agent, split between two different assistants, while I served as architect, tester, and director. It is intended for open release. For well-specified features, agents produced implementations roughly a hundred times faster than I could have written them. This did not eliminate the work, it moved it, from implementation to specification, integration, and verification. Holding a coherent vision became more important as implementation became cheaper, since agents left to themselves converge on the generic. Verification was the hardest part, particularly for interactive behavior, and partly for a structural reason: the agents observed the browser through still screenshots and had to infer what happened in between. Features routinely looked correct and did not work, and fixing one silently broke others. Agent-generated tests helped but could not establish that a complex interactive workflow behaved correctly end to end. Running agents in parallel accelerated implementation while increasing the risk of conflicting assumptions and integration regressions. Meanwhile the tools themselves were in constant flux, each new assistant arriving with its own strengths, weaknesses, and personality quirks. The talk demonstrates a task progressing from a natural-language instruction through model execution to interactive visualization, alongside examples of failures that appeared successful to the agents that produced them, and reports where things stand at the time of the meeting. As the cost of intelligence drops rapidly toward zero, the scarce resource turns out to be artistic vision and judgment.

494859.title: Seasonal Drivers of Urban CO and CO2 Fluxes in Greater New York Informed by Tall Tower Eddy Covariance Measurements
494859.authors: Trey Andrew Maddaleno, Univ. of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN; and D. B. Millet, M. Vermeuel, K. Richard, J. Peischl, E. B. Franklin, D. Farmer, R. Commane, and T. J. Griffis
494859.abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO2) and carbon monoxide (CO) are key urban pollutants and widely used as tracers to differentiate combustion from other sources of pollutants and greenhouse gases. The importance of on-road CO and CO2 sources in the urban landscape has declined with improved fuel efficiency and emissions control technologies, with the result that less-understood fluxes now drive a greater share of their variability. Here, we present eddy covariance flux measurements for CO2 and CO across multiple seasons over an urban footprint during the Fluxes of Reactive Organic Gases in New York (FROG-NY) project. Measurements were made from two heights (32.5 and 60 m) on a cellular tower in Mineola, NY and compared to bottom-up estimates from the GRA2PES inventory. The measurements show net upward fluxes for CO2 and CO in both summer and winter, with a regular diel cycle characterized by a strong daytime peak. Wintertime flux measurements reveal the influence of residential and commercial heating; the associated CO:CO2 ratio indicates this source is much less efficient than predicted by GRA2PES, with implications for co-emitted pollutants including methane. Conversely, the observed weekday-weekend flux differences demonstrate that the on-road CO:CO2 signature agrees closely with the GRA2PES representation for this source. The paired CO and CO2 flux observations also provide a constraint on the biospheric CO2 flux associated with urban vegetation, and we find during summertime that this uptake is on the same order as the traffic emissions.

494860.title: From Forecast Skill to Operational Trust: Building Customer-Centered Validation Frameworks for Aviation Decision Support
494860.abstract: Forecast verification has traditionally focused on evaluating meteorological accuracy through statistical measures such as root mean square error, bias, and categorical skill scores. While these metrics are essential for model development, they often fail to answer the operational questions faced by aviation stakeholders: Can an aircraft safely depart? Will visibility fall below operational minima? How confident should a dispatcher be in a precipitation forecast? Bridging this gap between forecast verification and operational decision-making remains a key challenge in the transition from research to operations (R2O). This presentation introduces a customer-centered validation framework developed to evaluate weather forecasts in the context of real-world aviation operations. Rather than treating forecast verification as an end in itself, the framework begins with operational decision thresholds and selects verification approaches that quantify forecast value for those decisions. Traditional continuous metrics (e.g., RMSE and bias) are combined with categorical verification techniques, event-based analyses, and operationally relevant thresholds for hazards such as precipitation, visibility, wind, freezing temperatures, and crosswinds. The framework has been applied across multiple aviation use cases, including commercial airline dispatch, airport operations, and autonomous drone flight planning. Case studies demonstrate how combining statistical verification with targeted event analysis provides insight into forecast performance during high-impact weather events while identifying strengths and limitations that are not apparent from summary statistics alone. Examples also illustrate the importance of validating forecasts at the spatial and temporal scales relevant to customer operations, particularly in situations where localized hazards are not fully represented by conventional observing networks. By reframing forecast verification around operational decision support, this approach creates a repeatable pathway for translating advances in numerical weather prediction, artificial intelligence, and probabilistic forecasting into actionable guidance for end users. Although demonstrated through aviation applications, the methodology is broadly applicable to other weather-sensitive industries where forecast value is ultimately measured by the quality of operational decisions rather than forecast accuracy alone.

494861.title: An Introduction to NOAA's Enterprise GNSS-R Ocean Wind Processing System and Cal/Val Process
494861.authors: Faozi Said, STAR, College Park, MD; and Z. Jelenak and P. S. Chang
494861.abstract: The ongoing success of GNSS-R missions, such as CyGNSS, in retrieving geophysical parameters from space has recently led commercial satellite data-service providers in delivering data from their own fleet of GNSS-R small satellites. At NOAA-NESDIS-STAR, the ocean surface winds team (OSWT) was recently tasked to calibrate and validate level 1 GNSS-R data from commercial vendors such as Spire Global and Muon Space. This work has led the OSWT to adapt their in-house NOAA CyGNSS wind processor to retrieve wind speed from both Spire and Muon main observable (the normalized bi-static radar cross section). Promising results were obtained in terms of wind speed performance, from which NOAA decided to purchase commercial GNSS-R data for the long term. This has led the OSWT to develop an in-house GNSS-R wind speed processor capable of ingesting GNSS-R data regardless of the data provider. In this presentation, we will describe the key building blocks of the processor, including processing latency and output data description. We will also discuss the ongoing need for calibration and validation of the main observable prior to data ingestion. Specifically, we will highlight how the GNSS-R main observable calibration can differ greatly from one data provider to the next, leading to mission specific data filtering options and tailored geophysical model function development. The presentation will also highlight how the latest NOAA GNSS-R wind speed products compare to those derived from traditional scatterometers and radiometer missions, including numerical weather prediction models, and buoys from the National Data Buoy Center. 494863.title: Coupling Deep-Learned Data Assimilation and Forecasting Models for Improved Skill
494863.authors: Christopher William Miller, MITRE, McLean, VA; and J. DaRosa, M. Alam, C. Parker, S. Frolov, L. Slivinski, C. C. Tong, N. Silverman, and C. J. Lewellyn
494863.abstract: Traditional data-assimilation (DA) systems commonly use variational or ensemble methods and can be computationally expensive; machine learning offers a complementary approach that can learn nonlinear relationships between observations and atmospheric states from data. Furthermore, machine learned models for DA can be coupled directly to machine learned forecasting models and trained together to improve skill for various metrics. In this work we describe advances coupling pretrained DA models to data driven forecasting models based on the Aneomi framework. The DA model is pretrained to replicate the analysis increments from a fully cycling GSI 3dVar reanalysis, using background forecasts and observations from ATMS, AMSU-A, IASI, and conventional sensors as inputs. We further employ a novel loss based on deep-learned approximate satellite observation operators using held-out observations to enforce analysis consistency with observation. The DA module is then coupled to Anemoi forecasting model and fine-tuned to produce optimal forecasts at various lead times. We evaluate the approach against forecasts based on 3dVars analysis, demonstrating forecast skill improvement.

494865.title: Simulating Secondary Ice Production in Deep Convection with a Lagrangian Cloud Model
494865.authors: Benjamin David Ascher, Free University of Berlin, Berlin, Berlin, Germany; and F. Hoffmann
494865.abstract: Secondary ice production (SIP) is the process through which the number concentration of ice crystals increases to greatly exceed the number concentration of ice nuclei. Though recent field campaigns investigating SIP within deep convection have revealed important insights, the importance of different pathways to total SIP is still uncertain. To investigate these unknowns, we conducted large eddy simulations with Lagrangian microphysics of a subtropical oceanic deep convective cloud, in which four SIP pathways (freezing fragmentation of droplets, ice-ice collisional breakup, rime splintering, and splash freezing) were implemented. Our results indicate that SIP increases total condensate but reduces overall precipitation. Ice-ice collisional breakup is responsible for most SIP throughout the cloud’s lifetime; however, sensitivity experiments enabling and disabling specific SIP processes indicate that freezing fragmentation of droplets plays a crucial role in accelerating the onset of ice-ice collisional breakup in the cloud. Droplet fragmentation also reduces surface precipitation by a greater extent than ice-ice collisional breakup. Tracking the contribution of warm- and cold-rain processes to total precipitation reveals that SIP strongly reduces precipitation produced by purely liquid-phase processes, while increasing the amount of precipitation produced by melting ice. We also find that, of the four SIP pathways examined, only rime splintering increased overall precipitation. Increasing background aerosol concentration reduces total precipitation, with a stronger relative reduction when SIP is present. However, the effect of increasing background aerosol concentration on liquid and ice water content in the cloud is non-monotonic. Our work supports the feasibility of modeling SIP within a Lagrangian microphysical framework, and highlights the complex interactions between SIP, background aerosol concentration, and precipitation formation pathways.

494866.title: SuperDARN-Based Detection of Polar Cap Patches Using the Evolution of Echo Characteristics
494866.authors: Katarzyna Beser, New Jersey Institute of Technology, Newark, NJ; and G. Perry
494866.abstract: Polar cap patches (PCPs) are plasma density enhancements in the F-region that are ubiquitous features of the high-latitude ionosphere, posing a major space weather hazard to civil, commercial, and defense operations across geospace. Formed through complex macroscopic coupling between the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF), magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere, PCPs act as seeds for small-scale plasma density irregularities, which are a source of scattering in the radio spectrum, including in the high frequency (HF; 3 - 30 Hz) regime. Furthermore, PCPs significantly alter the ionospheric refractive index, causing geometric scattering, non-linear propagation path shifts, and signal degradation. At high-latitudes, they have been directly linked to the degradation of Over-The-Horizon Radar (OTHR) surveillance capabilities and HF communications. Identifying PCPs in the OTHR demands a robust, automated detection algorithm. In this study we present ionospheric HF radar backscatter characteristics for events with and without PCPs present. We analyze a three-year dataset from the Super Dual Auroral Radar Network (SuperDARN) Clyde River radar focused over Resolute Bay. These HF radar observations are spatially and temporally co-located with high-resolution plasma density measurements from the Resolute Bay Incoherent Scatter Radar-North (RISR-N), which was used to identify the presence of PCPs. Statistical evaluation of backscatter properties (power, spectral width, and Doppler line-of-sight velocity) reveals substantial overlap between PCP and non-PCP events, indicating that raw radar echo characteristics alone cannot uniquely isolate PCPs in SuperDARN’s backscatter data. We discuss the temporal evolution of SuperDARN parameters and demonstrate that incorporating ray-tracing models to account for dynamic ionospheric refraction is essential to resolve this ambiguity and enable PCP detection within SuperDARN data streams alone.

494870.title: The TPOS Equatorial Pacific Experiment (TEPEX): Multi-Platform Process Studies to Improve Weather and Climate Prediction
494870.authors: Jose Algarin, NOAA/OAR/CPO, Silver Spring, MD; and J. Huang, Ph.D.
494870.abstract: The tropical Pacific plays a dominant role in shaping global weather and climate, yet persistent biases in ocean-atmosphere coupling limit subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction skill. Emerging from TPOS 2020 recommendations, the Tropical Pacific Observing System (TPOS) Equatorial Pacific Experiment (TEPEX) is an upcoming multi-platform field initiative designed to address these critical predictability gaps. TEPEX will focus on process studies across two primary regimes: the Eastern Pacific Cold Tongue (TEPEX-East) and the Eastern Edge of the Warm Pool in the Central Pacific (TEPEX-Central). By deploying research vessels, uncrewed surface vehicles, aircraft, and enhanced moored arrays, the campaign will sample co-located interactions across the Air-Sea Transition Zone. These advances aim to resolve systematic model errors and improve predictions of extreme environmental events modulated by ENSO and the MJO, ultimately bridging field discovery with operational applications. This presentation provides a broad overview of TEPEX science objectives, campaign implementation plans for 2027–2028, and NOAA’s supporting program framework. The talk will highlight pre-campaign modeling progress and strategies for translating process observations into improved parameterizations, model evaluation, and coupled data assimilation. Opportunities for collaboration will also be discussed to maximize collective impact.

494871.title: Springtime Arctic Sea-Ice Leads Drive Convective Boundary-Layer Development and Mixed-Phase Cloud Formation (Invited Presentation)
494871.authors: Jose D. Fuentes, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and A. Cole, S. M. Lance, K. A. Pratt, P. B. Shepson, W. R. Simpson, K. Hajny, D. Jeong, P. Peterson, and S. Woods
494871.abstract: During winter and spring, sea-ice leads expose relatively warm ocean water to the cold Arctic atmosphere, supplying heat, moisture, and sea-spray aerosols to the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL). These inputs generate buoyancy-driven convection and warmer, moist plumes that promote cloud formation. This presentation examines how ABL thermodynamic properties evolve from conditions preceding lead formation to those associated with mature leads. Using in situ aircraft measurements and dropsonde observations conducted near Utqiaġvik, Alaska, during the 2022 Chemistry in the Arctic: Clouds, Halogens, and Aerosols (CHACHA) campaign, we evaluate how lead width and downwind distance influence convective boundary-layer depth, thermodynamic structure, and cloud microphysics. Dropsondes released upwind of, over, and downwind of active leads characterized the evolving ABL, while aircraft-mounted probes measured cloud properties. The observations reveal well-defined convective boundary layers that extend several hundred meters vertically and persist downwind of the leads. Mixed-layer depth varied systematically with lead width and downwind distance, demonstrating the influence of surface heterogeneity on ABL structure. Under mature lead conditions, convective circulations supported the development of mixed-phase cloud streaks near the top of the ABL. Aerosol particles activated to form cloud droplets, producing a supercooled liquid layer near cloud top. Ice particles subsequently developed beneath this layer, and the clouds progressively glaciated. These results reveal strong coupling among surface heat and moisture fluxes, boundary-layer dynamics, and cloud microphysical evolution. Accurately representing these fine-scale interactions is essential for improving estimates of surface energy budgets and the treatment of subgrid-scale surface heterogeneity in weather and climate models as Arctic sea-ice loss accelerates, and the data from CHACHA will help Arctic boundary layer scientists better evaluate such representations.

494872.title: Cloud Condensation Nuclei (CCN) Production by Fires
494872.authors: Aditya Kumar, Biosphere Research, Lucknow, India
494872.abstract: Cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) are necessary for cloud formation at realistic supersaturation levels. Fires in different ecosystems (forests, grasslands and agricultural burning) emit very different amounts of CCNs and at different altitudes (above or within the boundary layer). For example, biomass burning emission factors for temperate forests are twice that of agricultural fires and both temperate forests and agricultural fires are significant fire emissions sources in the United States. The CCNs emitted could have important effects on the local/regional meteorology during and after the fire event. This study uses typical cases of wildfires and agricultural fires to determine the differences in the CCN emitted by fires in different ecosystems across the United States.

494873.title: The Most Dangerous Intersection in the World that Almost Nobody Knows About - Educating Students on the Causal Structure of Disaster
494873.authors: Benjamin Reppert, Penn State University, University Park, PA
494873.abstract: The current generation of children and young adults has grown up in an era in which disasters make headlines in an almost continuous cycle. The most recent calendar year in which the United States experienced fewer than 10 separate billion-dollar weather and climate disasters was 2010. In recent years, the average has approached 25 events per year, with annual losses often exceeding $150 billion. Traditional and emerging media have played an important role in making the public increasingly aware of the devastating impacts of these high-profile events. However, the causes of disasters are often less well understood. Humans—and, consequently, the media—tend to attribute disasters to a single, easily identifiable cause. In reality, disasters rarely result from a single factor. Rather, they emerge when a series of hazards, vulnerabilities, and other contributing conditions align. Disaster occurs at the intersection of a physical hazard and societal vulnerability, an intersection that is becoming increasingly consequential in the modern world. The weather hazard typically receives considerable attention, while the societal factors that influence disaster risk often receive far less. This imbalance can create the perception that weather is the primary—or even sole—cause of disaster and, therefore, the only component that can be addressed through mitigation and preparedness. Yet, while society has limited ability to control day-to-day weather, it has considerable ability to reduce vulnerability and improve resilience. Doing so, however, requires people to first recognize that societal choices and conditions are an integral part of the disaster equation. A recently developed interdisciplinary general education course at Penn State University seeks to address this knowledge gap. The course has two primary goals. First, it explores the hypothesis that a majority of current college-age students do not fully understand the causal structure of disasters, particularly the relationship between hazards and societal vulnerability. Using survey data collected throughout the course, this presentation will examine students’ understanding of disaster causation and present the results of this investigation. Second, the course aims to equip students with the knowledge and strategies needed to better prepare themselves, their families, and their communities for future disasters. The presentation will conclude by highlighting several of these strategies and discussing how disaster education can help shift students from viewing disasters as solely weather-driven events toward understanding and addressing the broader societal factors that shape disaster risk.

494874.title: Known Unknowns: Sampling Variability and ENSO Teleconnections
494874.authors: Benjamin A. Cash, COLA, Silver Spring, MD
494874.abstract: Skillful subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) prediction depends critically on understanding and accurately representing the influence of long-lived boundary anomalies, such as the El Niño- Southern Oscillation (ENSO). A tremendous body of literature has been developed around identifying and quantifying these remote influences (teleconnections) on locations of forecasting interest. However, diagnosing these links from observations involves considerable uncertainty. Among the limitations of the observed record (length, changes in observing systems, etc.) is the fact that it is only a single ‘realization’ of the earth system. By its nature, every observation will include variability that is unrelated to the phenomena of interest (ENSO, Madden-Julian Oscillation, etc.) but may project onto the diagnosed teleconnections. This, in turn, can produce inaccurate assessments of the strength and location of the teleconnection centers of action and thus their utility as S2S predictors. In this work, we use a series of ensemble hindcasts from prototype versions of the new NOAA Seasonal Forecast System, as well as the GEM5-NEMO model, to assess the impact of uncertainty and unrelated variability on diagnosed ENSO teleconnections. We find that teleconnections can vary substantially in both magnitude and pattern based on the particular realization of atmospheric noise chosen, sufficient to impact both quantitative and qualitative assessments of their utility as predictors.

494875.title: Eastern Range Lightning and Megaflash Climatology
494875.authors: Nicholas P. Stewart, Midwest Weather Center, Cocoa, FL
494875.abstract: Analysis of Cape Mesoscale Eastern Range Lightning Information Network (MERLIN) observations from 2019–2025 reveals a pronounced seasonal cycle in lightning activity across the Cape Canaveral and the Eastern Range region. With increasing launch cadence, construction of new facilities and launch pads, and expanding launch operations, lightning hazards represent not only a safety concern for personnel working outdoors but also an obstacle to completing required work. For 2020–2025, summer accounted for 57.3% of all lightning minutes, compared with only 3.3% during winter. The 15-day climatological probability of a lightning day exceeded 90% from early June through mid-September and reached 100% during portions of the core summer season. Daily activity peaked in early August at approximately 585 lightning minutes per day within range of MERLIN, while the climatological lightning-active envelope expanded to nearly 20 hours, from an average first-lightning time near 13:44 UTC to a last-lightning time near 09:30 UTC the following day. Lightning flashes extending at least 100 km, commonly referred to as megaflashes, exhibited a stronger warm-season concentration than the broader lightning climatology. Of 246 MERLIN flashes with maximum spatial extents of at least 100 km, 63.8% occurred during June–August, with June alone accounting for 23.6%. These events also displayed a pronounced late-day preference, maximizing at 22–23 UTC. Despite substantial interannual variability, megaflashes occurred at an average rate of approximately 31 per year during 2019–2025. Cloud-to-ground (CG) activity was associated with 90.2% of megaflashes. Megaflashes produced a mean of 5.6 CG events per flash, with negative CGs comprising 63.1% of all associated CG events.

494876.title: Field Evaluation of a Compact Variance Bowen Ratio Instrument for Direct Evapotranspiration Measurements
494876.authors: Jeff Ritter, METER Group, Inc., Pullman, WA; and D. Beverly
494876.abstract: Eddy covariance and weighing lysimeter measurements remain the standard for direct evapotranspiration (ET) observations but are often constrained by instrument cost and complexity, limiting deployments across ecosystems. As a result, many agroecosystems and water-limited regions remain underrepresented in direct flux monitoring networks. The Variance Bowen Ratio (VBR) approach offers a simplified alternative by estimating turbulent exchange from high-frequency temperature and humidity variance measurements combined with energy balance closure methods. Here, we evaluate a compact implementation of the VBR method across diverse ecosystems and environmental conditions. During 2025, we developed a compact VBR system and conducted intercomparisons against eddy covariance towers and weighing lysimeters across irrigated and rainfed systems. These include agroecosystems, deciduous hardwood forest, and desert shrubland sites. ET was computed from high-frequency measurements of temperature and specific humidity combined with measured and modeled energy balance terms within the sensor footprint. Reduced infrastructure and power requirements enabled rapid deployment and distributed observations across multiple sites. Across the tested systems, ET fluxes computed from the VBR approach closely matched eddy covariance-derived fluxes, while remaining consistently 6–10% greater, consistent with expected differences between closed- and open-energy-balance approaches. Due to the reliance on energy-balance closure, the VBR method performed best in systems with moderate-to-high ET rates and relatively homogeneous footprints. More xeric environments exhibiting larger sensible heat fluxes will likely require additional constraints on energy balance terms, including soil heat flux, to optimize ET estimates. These results suggest that compact VBR implementations can provide a physically constrained approach for expanding the spatial density and replication of direct ET observations under appropriate surface and turbulence conditions. While not intended to replace eddy covariance measurements, such systems may complement existing flux networks in managed and under-observed ecosystems where conventional flux infrastructure is impractical.

494877.title: Substantial Aircraft Contrail Formation at Low Soot Emission Levels
494877.authors: Christiane Voigt, DLR, Weßling, Bavaria, Germany; and D. Sauer
494877.abstract: Contrail cirrus clouds are a major contributor to aviation climate forcing, yet the number of contrail ice crystals forming behind aircraft equipped with modern lean-burn engines remains poorly constrained. Current theoretical estimates span up to four orders of magnitude in ice crystal number concentrations, resulting in large uncertainties in predicted climate effects of contrails. Here, we present first in-flight observations of contrails forming behind an aircraft equipped with lean-burn engine technology. We observe a substantial reduction in soot particle number emissions, reaching levels up to three orders of magnitude below those of conventional rich-quench-lean combustors. Despite these very low soot emissions, volatile particle number emissions remain high, and contrail ice crystal number emission indices exceed 1015 kg-1 of fuel burned. These measurements provide direct experimental evidence that substantial contrail ice formation can occur on volatile aerosol particles when soot particles are scarce. Supported by microphysical theory, we investigate the transition from soot-dominated to volatile-particle-driven ice activation and quantify the sensitivity of contrail ice crystal numbers to engine technology, fuel composition, and ambient temperature. Our results demonstrate that reducing soot emissions alone does not necessarily lead to correspondingly low contrail ice crystal numbers. Instead, volatile particle formation can become increasingly important for contrail microphysics under low-soot conditions. Incorporating these processes into contrail models will improve predictions of contrail properties and their fleet-wide climate effects and provides guidance for the development of future low-emission engine and fuel technologies. Results of this study are published in Voigt et al., Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10286-0, 2026 and will be compared to results from recent aircraft campaigns.

494878.title: The Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications - Early 21st Century (MERRA-21C): A New Atmospheric Reanalysis from NASA.
494878.authors: Amal El Akkraoui, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; NASA, Greenbelt, MD
494878.abstract: Multi-decadal, physically consistent reanalyses of the Earth system provide a foundational record on which advances in integrated Earth system modeling and data assimilation are built and evaluated. MERRA‑21C is a new global atmospheric reanalysis produced by NASA’s Global Modeling and Assimilation Office as part of its suite of satellite‑era reanalyses. The system spans 1998 to present and uses a 25 km horizontal‑resolution cubed‑sphere grid with 72 vertical layers, upgraded GEOS atmospheric model and a hybrid 4D‑EnVar data assimilation framework. The observing system includes expanded, reprocessed satellite and conventional observations, all-sky microwave radiances from selected imagers and sounders, and radio-occultation profiles from operational and commercial providers, supported by updated bias‑correction procedures. The GEOS configuration for MERRA‑21C incorporates successive developments since MERRA-2, including RRTMG longwave and shortwave radiation with refined cloud optical properties, and updated deep convection and cloud microphysics parameterizations. A new land model with associated land and land‑ice diagnostics is used, and a refactored aerosol module now includes brown carbon and provides extended aerosol optical depth and mass diagnostics. Model precipitation is adjusted off‑line toward NASA’s IMERG dataset, updating the precipitation‑correction approach used in MERRA‑2. The MERRA‑21C data products provide global, regularly gridded diagnostics for atmospheric circulation, moisture, clouds, radiation, surface exchange, and aerosols from both control and ensemble streams. Dedicated collections support targeted process studies, including an expanded glacier collection and new planetary boundary layer diagnostics on constant‑height levels, while reduced‑resolution ensemble fields provide information on analysis uncertainty and sensitivity to changes in the observing system. This presentation will describe the MERRA‑21C configuration, highlighting key advances in the underlying model, observing system, and data assimilation framework. It will outline the main data products and diagnostic collections and discuss their target applications such as studies of atmospheric circulation, the planetary boundary layer, cryosphere, aerosols and air quality, fire weather, and the training of AI‑based DA and prediction systems. Selected examples will illustrate representative MERRA‑21C fields and comparisons with existing global reanalyses to provide context for future detailed evaluations by the community. Looking ahead, this atmospheric reanalysis effort lays the groundwork for future coupled reanalysis products that will introduce stronger coupling across the atmosphere, ocean, land, and cryosphere components of the Earth system.

494879.title: Beyond the Backup: National Weather Service Operations During the Smokehouse Creek Fire
494879.authors: Emily Elease Allen, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and J. Henderson and H. Obermeier
494879.abstract: Wildfires are a growing operational and public safety concern in the Southern Great Plains, where rapidly spreading grass fires can threaten communities with little notice. A prime example of this is the Smokehouse Creek Fire, which grew quickly after its ignition on 26 Feb 2024 and became the largest fire in Texas state history. During this event, National Weather Service (NWS) forecasters had to make fast-paced decisions about wildfire detection, warning issuance, and partner coordination. While efforts to develop new fire warning guidance for imminent wildfire threats are under way, little is known about how forecasters and their partners navigate real-time, high-impact events like Smokehouse Creek. The importance of this can be illustrated through what are known in the National Weather Service as backups, or when one NWS office takes over warning operations for another. The assumption is that knowledge of hazards in one place and the warning processes and technologies are interchangeable, with one office able to cover these processes at a distance. This thesis argues, however, that a backup for fire weather between two WFOS in the same region still faced critical obstacles with issuing warnings when requests for warnings for emergency management involve trust between partners that does not easily convey. That is, although a backup can provide critical operational support during extreme events, some resources remain difficult to replicate, including local expertise and established partner relationships. This type of expertise is not only place-based but highly relational, with collaborative decisions about fire warnings made based on trusting relationships and local knowledge between emergency management and forecasters. This presentation draws on nine semi-structured interviews conducted by an interdisciplinary team with NWS forecasters from two WFOs to illustrate backup operations in action and to highlight the problematic assumptions about the interchangeable nature of relational expertise and local knowledge necessary to issue fire warnings when one office must evacuate. Using thematic analysis to highlight the decision making and communication strategies forecasters engaged in during the Smokehouse Creek fire backup, this work raises important insights about the value of local relationships to warning operational processes and the need for further consideration of just how interoperable WFOs are in issuing life-saving products for those outside their respective County Warning Areas.

494882.title: Reconciling Seemingly Contradictory Modes of Land-Atmosphere Feedback: Implications of Simpson’s Paradox
494882.authors: Kirsten L. Findell, GFDL, Princeton, NJ; and Z. Yin
494882.abstract: Given the complexity of the processes coupling land, water, and energy, a myriad of metrics have been developed to assess the Earth’s water cycle and how it is changing. Many of these focus on land-atmosphere coupling strength or the sensitivity of one variable to changes in another. However, these metrics often assess different parts of the process chain, which extends from soil moisture and vegetation dynamics, through surface fluxes, to boundary layer properties and precipitation. Here, we reconcile two seemingly contradictory assessments of the impact of soil moisture (SM) on evaporation (E) and subsequent precipitation (P). We demonstrate that while part of the discrepancy stems from which specific links in the coupling chain are analyzed (SM-to-P versus E-to-P), a crucial factor involves Simpson’s Paradox. This is a statistical phenomenon where trends appear within distinct subsets of data, but reverse when those subsets are combined. In this case, the paradox manifests in the soil moisture–evaporative fraction relationship when data are stratified by the occurrence of subsequent precipitation events. Finally, we discuss how accounting for this statistical effect enables a more comprehensive, regime-dependent understanding of how the land surface influences key components of Earth’s hydrologic cycle.

494884.title: A Multi-Satellite Golden Dataset for Benchmarking Operational Tropical Cyclone Algorithms
494884.authors: Gian A. Villamil-Otero, NESDIS, Silver Spring, MD; and L. Soulliard, A. Garcia-Escovar, and J. McCullough
494884.abstract: Operational tropical cyclone satellite products are generated by algorithms that require continuous monitoring alongside regular software maintenance and rigorous evaluation before major upgrades are deployed. Testing these updates during the off season or during prolonged periods of low global storm activity presents a significant challenge for developers. Rare or complex environmental scenarios frequently push operational bounds and can expose bugs in the processing. Examples of these scenarios include rapid intensification, dual storm proximity, fast moving storms, and International Date Line crossings. To address these challenges, this talk introduces a curated multi-satellite “golden dataset” designed specifically to stress test and benchmark the tropical cyclone algorithms that NESDIS produces. This dataset supports the Advanced Dvorak Technique, Ensemble Tropical Rainfall Potential, the Hurricane Intensity and Structure Algorithm, Tropical Cyclone Formation Probability, and Multiplatform Tropical Cyclone Surface Winds Analysis along with various high resolution wind products. We establish a standard baseline by compiling a diverse arrangement of storm cases spanning from 2023 to 2026 that addresses not only the sensors supported by the different algorithms but also the complex scenarios that affect them. In this talk we will show how a standardized tropical cyclone golden dataset can establish a robust and repeatable offline environment. Additionally, this golden dataset can ensure that code updates, patches, or upgrades are able to be validated for scientific accuracy well before facing active real time operations.

494891.title: The ALGE Aqueous Contaminant Transport Model for Emergency Response
494891.authors: David W. Werth, Battelle Savannah River Alliance, LLC, Aiken, SC; and V. Turner
494891.abstract: During a release of an aqueous contaminant into a large body of water, emergency managers will require reliable predictions of contaminant concentration at critical locations to ensure the safety of public drinking water supplies, fisheries, and recreational areas. To assist with this need, a 3-dimensional hydrodynamic code, ALGE, was designed to predict the transport of an aqueous contaminant throughout a water body. The model dynamics include suspended sediment transport, dissolved and particulate chemical transport, radioactive decay, and dynamic salinity. It can be used to simulate a variety of bodies of water including rivers, lakes, large-scale bays and estuaries (Chesapeake Bay, Lake Michigan, etc.) and has been used to study previous events in water – simulating the fate and transport of tritiated water from an accidental release at the Savannah River Site, chlorine gas deposition into nearby bodies of water after a train collision in Graniteville, SC, and the Piney Point spill into Tampa Bay. It’s currently being converted from a research tool to a tool for emergency response managers in the event of a contaminant release. Our recent work involves i) incorporating new model physics and ii) making the model into an emergency response tool. To accomplish the first goal, ALGE has been recoded to account for two new processes: i) formation of sediment from dissolved clay, and ii) coagulation and breakup of sediment particles. This will act to alter the way sediment is distributed among 3 sediment size bins and, through adsorption, desorption, settling and resuspension, affect contaminant fate and transport. As part of the second goal, ALGE has been used to simulate the effects of an airborne release over a large lake and the subsequent transport of contaminant within the lake. A model of that lake was developed, and we then developed a process to convert dispersion model data to a source for ALGE – taking airborne material that has settled, introducing it to the uppermost water level, and simulating its transport to other locations. We will discuss the model and how it can serve the emergency management community.

494893.title: Atmospheric Stability Effects on Wind Farm Wake Recovery: A Multi-Fidelity Study Combining FAST.Farm with Large-Eddy Simulation
494893.authors: Gokhan Kirkil, Kadir Has Univ., Istanbul, 34, Turkey
494893.abstract: Wake recovery within wind farms is governed by turbulent entrainment from the surrounding atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), making thermal stratification a first-order control on both farm efficiency and turbine fatigue loading. This study investigates how ABL stability modulates wake structure and recovery rate through a multi-fidelity framework that couples offshore LiDAR observations, precursor large-eddy simulation (LES), and full aero-servo-elastic wind farm simulation. Stability characterization is grounded in a sub-hourly LiDAR dataset collected at Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts — a well-instrumented offshore reference site — from which wind shear profiles, turbulence intensity, and veer statistics are stratified into neutral, stable, and convective regimes using the bulk Richardson number and Obukhov length. These observed profiles serve dual roles: they define the physically realistic parameter space for the stability cases examined, and they provide turbulence spectral benchmarks against which precursor LES inflow fields are validated before driving the farm simulations. The farm consists of nine NREL 5-MW reference turbines in a 3×3 array (7D streamwise, 4D lateral spacing). For each stability class, LES-generated turbulent inflow fields — validated against LiDAR-measured spectra and length scales — drive FAST.Farm, where each turbine is represented as a complete OpenFAST aero-servo-elastic model. This coupling enables simultaneous quantification of farm-level power losses and individual turbine structural loads across stability regimes. The analysis targets three mechanistic questions: how buoyancy-driven mixing under convective conditions accelerates wake recovery relative to the neutral baseline; whether suppressed turbulence under stable stratification amplifies tower-base and blade-root fatigue loads through increased load oscillation amplitudes; and how dynamic wake meandering statistics scale with the stability parameter −z/L. By anchoring the simulation framework to field observations, the results provide a physically grounded basis for stability-aware wind farm control and ABL-parameterized layout optimization.

494894.title: LES Simulations of Windblown Polydisperse Particles Under Saltating Conditions
494894.authors: Logan Roy, University of Oklahoma, Edmond, OK; and S. T. Salesky
494894.abstract: Windblown particulate matter plays an important role in a number of weather and climate processes. For example, dust particles can serve as cloud condensation nuclei, while wind-blown snow impacts the mass balance of glaciated regions and the spatial distribution of snowpack, which can influence the timing of runoff in alpine watersheds. Most studies employ Lagrangian particle models to study these phenomena, but this approach is computationally costly, limiting what they can simulate. We use a two-fluid approach to model particle concentration in a turbulent boundary layer focusing on the impacts of various saltation representations on the particle size distributions of the overlying suspension layer. Our model consists of an unresolved 1-D saltation layer below the first grid point; a polydisperse finite volume Eulerian model for the particle suspension layer; and a wall model that accounts for the vertical fluxes between these two layers. This two-fluid approach allows us to simulate highly polydisperse particles without worrying about statistical convergence of Lagrangian particles. We test three different saltation schemes under two different representations of saltation initiation velocities, comparing mean profiles of particle properties and particle size distributions across the various models. The modeling approach considered herein allows us to assess differences between empirical saltation models and the consequences for wind-blown dust, sand, and snow transport.

494901.title: Creating Space for Conversations Around the U.S. Drought Monitor
