494901.authors: Brianne Louise Kendall Minton, Alabama Office of the State Climatologist, Huntsville, AL
494901.abstract: The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) is an ensemble product, drawing on multiple indicators and expert judgment to capture the varying dimensions of drought. Most people, however, experience only one version of drought: the one playing out on their land, in their community, and in their lives. Because the USDM supports numerous decision-making processes, including agricultural assistance programs, conversations about drought classifications often carry significant personal and financial implications. Effective drought communication is not about convincing people that the map is correct. It is about creating space for conversation. Communicating drought requires balancing scientific integrity with lived experience. Effective communication depends on transparency and trust, acknowledging local impacts while explaining how drought severity is determined and why broader assessments may not always align with perceived local conditions. This presentation explores how drought communicators can shift from a transactional approach to a conversational one. Rather than viewing differing perspectives as a challenge to the USDM, they can become opportunities to strengthen trust, encourage meaningful dialogue, and incorporate local observations through impact reporting. Citizen science programs such as Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR) provide an important pathway for people to share their experiences while helping inform broader drought assessments. By creating space for dialogue, drought communicators can strengthen trust while improving the impact information that supports drought monitoring.

494902.title: From Access to Leadership: Twenty Years of Building Pathways in Atmospheric Science in Puerto Rico
494902.authors: Hector J. Jimenez, University of Puerto Rico, Mayagüez, Mayaguez, PR; University of Puerto Rico at Mayaguez, Mayaguez, PR
494902.abstract: For more than two decades, the University of Puerto Rico, Mayagüez (UPRM) has developed pathways into atmospheric science for students in Puerto Rico. Beginning with a NOAA–UPRM partnership in the late 1990s and the establishment of an undergraduate meteorology curriculum in 2003, the program has evolved from a small curricular initiative into a multidisciplinary educational and professional-development enterprise. Its graduates have gone on to careers and advanced study at the National Weather Service, NOAA, NASA, NCAR, major universities, and other organizations throughout the United States. This presentation reflects on what 20 years of experience have taught us about increasing participation and, more importantly, creating pathways to success and leadership in the atmospheric sciences. We examine several elements that have been central to the UPRM experience: integrating atmospheric science with broader STEM education; providing early access to research and operational experiences; sustained mentoring; building partnerships with federal agencies, universities, and research laboratories; and connecting students' individual interests with authentic professional opportunities. A particularly important lesson has emerged from our long-running internship programs. Rather than asking students to compete for a fixed set of opportunities, our recent NSF-supported work has developed a student-driven model in which students identify their scientific and career interests and program faculty actively cultivate appropriate opportunities with external partners. From 2022–2025, this approach supported 22 undergraduate interns at institutions including NOAA, the National Weather Service, NCAR, NASA, and universities. The model builds on an earlier UPRM experience in which former interns became a substantial component of the operational workforce at the NWS San Juan office. We will discuss successes, failures, persistent challenges, and lessons learned from working within a Hispanic-Serving Institution in a geographically isolated region. We conclude with an outlook for the next generation of atmospheric-science education in Puerto Rico and a broader question for the geosciences: How do we move beyond recruiting underrepresented students toward building educational environments in which they can belong, succeed, and ultimately become the scientists and leaders who shape our field?

494908.title: Does Tropical Cyclone Frequency Self-Regulate? An Investigation Using Potential And Ventilation Indices in Global Climate Models
494908.authors: Gabriel Rios, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and G. A. Vecchi and W. Yang
494908.abstract: How will tropical cyclone (TC) frequency change with global warming? This question is among the most important in climate science, yet there remains considerable uncertainty in projections of TC frequency. In the satellite era, global TC frequency has remained relatively constant, with 80 +/- 10 TCs per year. To understand controls on changes to TC frequency, two thermodynamic indices are often used: potential intensity (PI) and ventilation index (VI). In this study, we compare hypothetical climates in a suite of global climate model runs featuring a range of TC frequencies, which is controlled by the modification of wind-induced surface heat exchange. We find that with increasing TC activity, PI decreases and VI increases. In other words, TC genesis and intensification become less favorable with additional TCs. These results suggest that TC frequency self-regulates, which may contribute to an explanation of the constancy of TC frequency in a warming climate.

494912.title: Using Score-Based Diffusion to Emulate Precipitation from a Convection-Permitting Regional Climate Model
494912.authors: Brandon Lee Weart, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL; and A. M. Haberlie, W. S. Ashley, V. A. Gensini, A. C. Michaelis, and R. C. Jackson
494912.abstract: Dynamical downscaling has improved the representation of precipitation and organized convection (e.g., supercells and mesoscale convective systems) but remains computationally expensive. To address these limitations, recent advances in deep learning, particularly score-based diffusion models, offer stable training and high-fidelity generation of gridded climate fields. Additionally, diffusion models have enabled kilometer-scale generative downscaling at a fraction of the computational cost of dynamical downscaling while preserving realistic spatial structure and intensity distributions of target atmospheric phenomena. This study applies a generative score-based diffusion framework for emulating precipitation at convection-permitting scales. Predictor data are derived from the ~100-km bias-corrected Community Earth System Model (CESM), whereas the target consists of 6-h accumulated precipitation from a 3.75-km horizontal grid spacing convection-permitting simulation. NVIDIA’s CorrDiff model is adapted to this application and trained on the existing dynamically downscaled dataset to generate ensembles of high-resolution precipitation. Water years (WY) 1990–2005 from the target historical simulation are divided into training (WY 1990–1999), validation (WY 2000–2001), and testing (WY 2002–2005) datasets. The approach is evaluated using metrics and diagnostics of performance and fidelity across the spectrum of precipitation intensity and coverage. Early results indicate that the CorrDiff diffusion step can reproduce precipitation structure and intensity across a range of spatial scales, with improved Fractions Skill Score (FSS) and power spectral density (PSD) characteristics relative to the deterministic baseline. A fully validated emulation framework could offer a more efficient way to generate ensembles of high-resolution realizations and to characterize uncertainty.

494913.title: Advancing NOAA's Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis: Three-Dimensional and AI Extensions
494913.authors: Manuel Pondeca, NOAA, Riverdale Park, MD; and T. T. Ladwig, M. T. Morris, T. Lei, A. M. Gibbs, G. Ge, A. Schein, A. Gholoubi, X. C. Jin, M. Craine, M. Rancic, G. Zhao, R. J. Purser, M. Hu, C. Hartsough, J. Hu, S. Pan, and D. Holdaway
494913.abstract: NOAA’s Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis (RTMA) and Unrestricted Mesoscale Analysis (URMA) provide critical, high-resolution, near-surface atmospheric analyses that support National Weather Service (NWS) forecast guidance, model verification, and downstream applications. This presentation starts by outlining efforts by the Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) and the Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) to upgrade the RTMA/URMA system. We detail the transition from 2DVar to a hybrid 3DEnVar framework—evolving from 3DRTMAv1 (GSI/HRRR) to 3DRTMAv2 (JEDI/MPAS)—to provide three-dimensional, high-resolution gridded analyses of hydro-meteorological parameters essential for digital forecasting. The second and main part of the presentation explores leveraging artificial intelligence to complement traditional variational and ensemble-based data assimilation. We discuss the ongoing development of the AI-RTMA framework: a modular, extensible system designed to integrate observation processing, target preparation, AI model development, post-processing, verification, and diagnostics into a unified workflow. By utilizing consistent datasets and evaluation metrics, this framework facilitates rigorous comparative testing of multiple AI-model pathways currently under evaluation, namely the Aardvark-based pathway for observation-to-analysis mapping, OCELOT-style observation-to-observation learning, Anemoi-based approaches for fusing observations with background information, and the artificial intelligence-based data assimilation framework (ADAF). Initial results from models evaluated within the AI-RTMA framework will be presented for surface sensible weather parameters.

494918.title: Mesoscale Organization of Updrafts and Cloud Microphysics in a Low-Latitude Polar Low Observed during IMPACTS
494918.authors: Troy Justin Zaremba, Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS; and R. M. Rauber, Z. Wang, K. P. Boyd, R. Wang, and L. A. McMurdie
494918.abstract: Polar lows are compact, rapidly intensifying maritime cyclones whose evolution depends strongly on the interaction between mesoscale dynamics, moist convection, and diabatic heating. Their small spatial scales and development over data-sparse oceans make them difficult to observe and forecast, and few direct observations exist of the vertical motions and cloud processes occurring within their circulations. Understanding how mesoscale ascent is organized within these storms, and how that ascent controls precipitation growth, is therefore important for both forecasting polar-low intensity and representing these systems in numerical models. On 15 January 2023, the NASA Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) field campaign sampled a low-latitude polar low over the western Atlantic during its convectively active phase. Four coordinated NASA ER-2 and P-3 flight legs crossed the storm at progressively lower altitudes, providing vertically resolved radar observations of the mesoscale cloud and kinematic structure together with in situ measurements of cloud and precipitation particles. The observations show a strongly organized mesoscale circulation characterized by deep convective updrafts surrounding a subsident eye and weaker vertical motions within the surrounding stratiform cloud shield. These differences in vertical motion produced sharp transitions in cloud microphysics over distances of only tens of kilometers. Within the convective eyewall, strong ascent supported enhanced supercooled liquid water, large cloud droplet concentrations, high ice particle concentrations, and vigorous riming. Outside the strongest updrafts, weaker ascent and longer particle residence times favored depositional growth and aggregation, producing the largest ice particles within the surrounding stratiform precipitation. Hydrometeor concentrations and particle sizes decreased sharply within the subsident eye. The observations demonstrate a direct linkage between the mesoscale organization of vertical motion and precipitation growth processes within a polar low. They provide a rare observational benchmark for evaluating how models represent convective ascent, diabatic cloud processes, and their coupling to the evolution of compact maritime cyclones.

494920.title: Developing a Methodology for Regionalizing In-Flight Icing Forecasts
494920.authors: Amanda R. Siems-Anderson, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. R. Adriaansen, S. M. Ellis, P. Prestopnik, and G. P. McCabe Jr.
494920.abstract: Alaska presents unique challenges in acquiring and utilizing the observation and forecast data necessary to identify in-flight icing hazards across the state’s airspace. With a greater reliance on general aviation to reach remote rural areas, the state has a unique icing exposure risk and different distribution of pilot reports and related observations than the similarly-sized contiguous US (CONUS). Along with unique geography and data, having a consistent methodology to evaluate the performance of icing-related forecasts aids research and development as advancements and updates to observing and/or modeling facilities become available. To that end, the National Science Foundation (NSF) National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) In-Flight Icing Product Development Team (IFIPDT) is in the process of developing a consistent methodology for evaluating the performance of the Forecast Icing Product version 2 (FIP2) in Alaska. This methodology isolates configuration parameters from model-obtained input data to systematically determine where differences between regions may lie and identify what if any configuration updates may be made to improve the performance of FIP2. Although first being developed for Alaska, this methodology may ultimately be applicable to any region-specific research across US airspace. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the FAA. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

494923.title: NSF NCAR EOL Field Data Archive: Sixty Years of Field Campaign Archives
494923.authors: Scot M. Loehrer, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Allison, D. Choi, W. C. Lenhardt, C. Ruchti, B. Snyder, and S. Williams
494923.abstract: The NSF NCAR EOL Data Management and Services (DMS) Facility Field Data Archive (FDA) maintains archives for over 600 field campaigns ranging from small educational campaigns to complex national and international campaigns. The campaigns have examined questions for a wide-ranging set of atmospheric and related science disciplines including tropical cyclones, tornadoes, mid-latitude and tropical convection, boundary layer, winter storms, cloud microphysics, windstorms, wildfire impacts, arctic, hydrology, oceanography, solar eclipses, and more. The depth of the archives varies depending on the requirements of the campaign and can range from just the EOL platform and instrument data to all research data from a campaign including those from government and university investigators. In addition to the campaign archives, the FDA also contains archives from some discontinued research facilities including the South Dakota School of Mines and Technology armored T-28 aircraft and the University of Washington Cloud and Aerosol Research Group Convair aircraft. We are taking the opportunity of the 60th anniversary of the Line Islands Experiment (LIE), the first large field campaign managed by NCAR, to provide an update on the current contents of the FDA including our digital and physical holdings, the FDA access interface, and our stewardship of these valuable one of a kind datasets.

494925.title: Assessing Ecologically Relevant Future Trends in Daily Flow Metrics Across the Continental United States
494925.authors: Catherine Anna Nikiel, USGS, Raleigh, NC
494925.abstract: Natural resource and water supply managers require projections of streamflow under climate and land use change to inform decision-making across diverse regions, including in areas that have high levels of aquatic biodiversity. Understanding how future changes in streamflow may affect freshwater species and habitats is therefore critical for managing these systems. However, high-resolution streamflow datasets are often large, difficult to interpret for non-specialists, and lack the ecological context needed for managers to quickly make connections between projected hydrological change and ecosystem impacts. This study utilizes a nationally consistent and locally calibrated dataset of daily stream flow projections from the Precipitation Runoff Modeling System (PRMS) to assess how hydrologic metrics relevant to ecological health may change over time and across emissions scenarios. This study assesses changes in hydrologic metrics between the historical period (1976-2005) and three future periods (2016–2045, 2046–2075, and 2075–2100) under two Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs): RCP4.5 and RCP8.5. Several general trends emerge across the continental United States: (1) Mean flows are projected to decrease across most regions under both scenarios in the multi model ensemble mean by the late 21st century with changes driven largely by decreases in the ecologically critical spring (April-June) and summer (July-September) seasons. (2) High flow magnitude and frequency metrics are increasing particularly in the Western United States across time and emissions scenario, while low flow metrics show a nationally consistent trend towards intensification. (3) Trends in some cases evolve across the east-west aridity spectrum and in the case of seasonal mean flows there are south-north trends that align with average shifts in temperature and precipitation. Areas where model simulations are more consistent with streamflow observations and have more agreement in the multi-model ensemble are highlighted to support confident application of model data to aquatic management decisions.

494927.title: Expanding the Scope of Flood Intelligence: New Developments for Nationwide Flood Inundation Mapping and Decision Support
494927.authors: Riley McDermott, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and C. Pruitt, D. Giardino, M. Jurewicz Sr., C. Evanego, J. Kirk, and F. Salas
494927.abstract: Flooding remains one of the most destructive and economically devastating natural hazards worldwide, demanding timely and accurate forecast information to enable effective risk management. While the hydrograph remains a cornerstone of flood forecasting, current RFC forecasts represent a single point and fail to capture the spatial representation critical for effective hazard mitigation. This gap in information leaves decision-makers blind to the full scale of impending hydrologic impacts. The National Weather Service’s Office of Water Prediction (OWP) has filled this critical gap in flood intelligence through its incremental releases of experimental Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM) capabilities that will cover nearly 100 percent of the United States beginning October 2026. These experimental flood maps provide five-day inundation extent forecasts at the 3,800 official river forecast points and an additional 2.7 million river reaches driven by National Water Model forecasts, alongside near-real-time snapshots of current flood conditions. The maps are provided in an open source format that enables easy identification of impacts to critical infrastructure needed for hazard mitigation. In addition to expanding the domain, the development team has produced several innovative prototype experimental services for internal decision support. These services support two of the three major milestones for OWP FIM, expansion to probabilistic services, evolution of rapidly updating FIM, and development of depth capabilities. The first new service is 'FLASH FIM', which leverages forecast maximum streamflow from the National Severe Storm Laboratory's Flooded Locations And Simulated Hydrographs (FLASH) project. This service provides frequently updating inundation maps every 15 minutes to better support rapidly-evolving flash flooding scenarios, a crucial application highlighted by the devastating flooding in Kerr County Texas in July, 2025. Another significant advancement is the addition of 'Likelihood FIM', a service that aims to quantify hydraulic and hydrologic uncertainty to deliver estimates of inundation likelihood. This service represents the first venture towards probabilistic FIM, providing end-users with critical insight into the inherent uncertainty associated with each forecast iteration. This presentation will explore the science behind these emerging FIM services, highlight recent innovations, dive into a real-world event review of these new services, and provide an outlook on the future evolution of OWP’s FIM as it transitions toward more comprehensive, probabilistic, and operationally relevant flood intelligence.

494928.title: Environmental Influences of the Chesapeake Bay on Supercell Thunderstorm Evolution and Hazard Production
494928.authors: Roger Ralph Riggin IV, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte , NC; and C. Davenport and C. R. Homeyer
494928.abstract: Foundational severe convective storm research has largely remained rooted in environments typical of the central and Midwestern United States, implicitly benefiting from the relative simplicity of this region's rural and level terrain. However, a growing body of literature highlights that convective evolution is highly-sensitive to localized heterogeneities within the boundary layer, often generated by air flow over varying surface features and land-use characteristics (e.g., complex terrain, coastal influences, and urbanization). These sensitivities are particularly notable during convective events across the densely populated East Coast, where the Appalachian Mountains, the I-95 urban corridor, and the Atlantic coastline introduce significant spatial variability. This variability in turn yields heterogeneous environmental gradients on spatial scales not well resolved by current observation networks. Although severe storms are less frequent and intense on the Eastern Seaboard compared to the Midwest, they remain a hazardous warm-season threat that presents significant operational forecasting challenges due to incomplete conceptual models regarding storm-scale responses to such heterogeneous environments. The Mid-Atlantic region of the Eastern Seaboard is a highly complex and geographically distinct domain. The inclusion of the Chesapeake Bay—situated between the Appalachians, the I-95 corridor, and the Atlantic Ocean—further compounds surface complexities, imparting substantial modulations in boundary-layer thermodynamic and kinematic profiles. Supercell thunderstorms are known to be sensitive to such low-level environmental heterogeneity and are frequently observed across the Mid-Atlantic throughout the warm season. However, a regional climatology of supercells has yet to be established, which is a critical first step in discerning how the maritime influences of the Chesapeake Bay affect storm evolution and hazard production. To address these gaps, this study develops a comprehensive climatology of isolated supercell thunderstorms across the Mid-Atlantic region during the warm-season months (March–August) of 2018–2024, with particular emphasis on supercells interacting with the Chesapeake Bay. A refined tracking and data analytics methodology utilizing raw, high-resolution NEXRAD Level-II and Level-III radar data is employed to capture storm-scale morphological changes with high precision during their interaction with the Bay. Furthermore, operational High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model analyses are utilized as a proxy to quantify the near-storm environment of each supercell. Additional spatiotemporal filtering of the dataset explores seasonal and local geographic sensitivities. Statistical analyses will discern which factors influence supercell maintenance within the Chesapeake Bay's maritime environment. Ultimately, these findings aim to aid short-term operational decision-making during high-impact severe weather events across the Mid-Atlantic, providing dynamical insights applicable to similar maritime environments.

494930.title: Historical Perspectives on GCM Research to Model the Tropical Circulation (Invited Presentation)
494930.authors: Wayne H. Schubert, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO
494930.abstract: When Dave Randall joined the UCLA general circulation modeling group (i.e., the Mintz-Arakawa group) as a graduate student in the early 1970's, the horizontal grid spacing of the GCM's being run at GFDL, NCAR, and UCLA was approximately 400 km. An important challenge for such coarse resolution models was to reasonably simulate the ITCZ, the Hadley circulation, tropical cloud clusters, and the non-precipitating shallow cumulus and stratocumulus clouds of the subtropics. Over his career, Dave has led many theoretical, modeling, and observational efforts that have substantially improved our understanding of these phenomena. This talk will highlight some of these advances.

494931.title: 3D Multi-Source Radar Fusion and Visualization
494931.abstract: NOAA’s Radar Next initiative will replace aging WSR‑88D radars with a modern, hybrid surveillance system that blends government‑owned and commercial sensors across multiple frequencies. Because of the heterogenous composition of radar technologies and sources, system availability, and economic factors, the National Weather Service needs a unified framework that integrates diverse environmental data—S-, C-, and X-band radar; satellite imagery; lightning detection; and numerical model output—for real‑time situational awareness. Multi‑frequency sensors introduce different resolutions, data formats, and quality characteristics, creating new demands for forecaster‑oriented integration, analysis, and display tools. Fast, efficient 3D data fusion and visualization are essential to meet operational latency and cost requirements, especially in cloud environments. Raytheon’s tile‑based, two‑tier fusion architecture addresses these challenges by delivering low‑latency integration, scalable product generation, and reliable information display. The system was evaluated using a complex rainfall event during the 2021 US Open in Flushing Meadows, NY, leveraging NEXRAD, TDWR, Skyler™ X‑band PAR, GOES and VIIRS imagery, GLM lightning data, GPM IMERG precipitation estimates, and HRRR output—a representative scenario for future Radar Next operations. In addition to highlighting performance results from this architecture, we introduce new AWIPS 3D visualization approaches that help forecasters rapidly interpret fused environmental information. ©2026 Raytheon Company. All rights reserved.

494933.title: Advancing Global Solar Photovoltaic Power Forecasting with Sub-Seasonal Climate Outlooks
494933.authors: Jung Choi, Yonsei University, Seoul, Seoul, South korea; Yonsei University, Seoul, Korea, Republic of (South); and S. W. Son
494933.abstract: Given the high weather dependency of solar photovoltaic energy, accurate weather information ranging from days to weeks in advance is required for stable plant operation and management. This study emphasizes that sub-seasonal climate outlooks can advance global solar power forecasting. We evaluate the capacity factor (CF) for standard test conditions (CFstc), calculated from atmospheric reanalysis of surface solar irradiance and ambient air temperature, by comparing it with actual CF from two solar plants in Korea. Results confirm CFstc as a reliable estimate of actual CF. Application of this methodology to four-week outlooks from two state-of-the-art sub-seasonal climate forecast systems shows a significant anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC) skill for global solar power forecasting at least one week in advance (5–11 forecast days). Regional ACC skills vary at extended lead times, with South Asia, eastern South America and eastern Australia maintaining ACC > 0.6 for up to two weeks (12–18 forecast days). Notably, useful ACC skill persists for up to four weeks (26–32 forecast days) across 70.9 % of global land areas. These findings suggest that sub-seasonal climate outlooks can provide decision-making information in developing more reliable solar energy strategies, highlighting the importance of transdisciplinary collaboration between renewable energy and meteorological sectors.

494935.title: Biomass Burning as a Source of Halocarbons
494935.authors: Aditya Kumar, Biosphere Research, Lucknow, India
494935.abstract: Biomass burning can produce a variety of atmospheric compounds that have a range of atmospheric lifetimes. Halocarbons (e.g. methyl bromide and methyl chloride) are a class of compounds produced by biomass burning that have hydroxyl radical oxidation as a major sink. This study uses theoretical calculations to determine the impacts of fires on halocarbons and the resulting impacts of halocarbons on the hydroxyl radical.

494937.title: Seasonal Drivers of Local Cloud Formation In the Colorado East River Basin: From Spring Snowpack to Summer Nocturnal Water Vapor
494937.authors: Ju-Hye Kim, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and E. D. Gutmann
494937.abstract: Understanding cloud formation in mountainous regions is crucial for accurately quantifying surface water and energy budgets over complex terrain. This study investigates the moisture sources and environmental mechanisms driving locally generated clouds in the Colorado East River Basin during spring and summer. Utilizing field-campaign observations from SAIL, SPLASH, and SOS alongside high-resolution CONUS404 simulations for water years (WY) 2022 and 2023, we evaluate seasonal cloud frequency in relation to snowpack volume, melt rates, local water vapor fluctuations, and the North American Monsoon. The results reveal a distinct seasonal transition in cloud-producing mechanisms. Specifically, the exceptionally heavy snowpack of WY2023 fueled spring cloud formation via enhanced surface latent heat fluxes. In contrast, summer cloud development is highly contingent upon nocturnal water vapor exceeding a distinct threshold of 6 g/kg during the early morning hours. Capturing the interplay between these local land-atmosphere feedbacks and large-scale monsoonal moisture supply is essential for predicting how shifting temperature baselines and accelerated snowmelt dynamics will reshape mountain ecohydrological cycles.

494940.title: Systematic Evaluation of Halo Photonics Doppler Lidar Against New York State Mesonet Deployed Doppler Lidar for Research and Operational Needs
494940.authors: Bhupal Shrestha, University at Albany, State University of New York, Albany, NY, NY; and J. Wang, N. Bain, J. F. Prego, J. Matheson, and J. Seely
494940.abstract: Doppler wind lidars provide wind and aerosol profiles at a high vertical and temporal resolution that are essential for operational meteorology, wind energy, advancing boundary layer research, model evaluation, and aviation. While all the Doppler lidars use the same Doppler principle based on moving aerosols/clouds to derive wind and aerosol data, the difference in hardware design, scanning strategies, signal processing and sensitivity to atmospheric conditions lead to variations in their performance, data availability, measurement accuracy, maximum range and operational flexibility. This study aims to conduct systematic evaluation of the Halo Photonics by Lumibird Streamline AllSky XR+ Doppler lidar against Vaisala Windcube 100S Doppler lidar that is deployed across New York State Mesonet (NYSM) Profiler Network for last 8 years. A comprehensive intercomparison of these two commercially available systems under identical atmospheric conditions provide insights into their relative performance and optimal applications. This study will present an evaluation of the Halo Photonics Streamline lidar against WindCube Doppler lidar - one deployed a few meters away at the University at Albany ETEC Building and another about 8 km away at the NYSM Profiler site at Albany since June 2026. The assessment of wind speed and direction, vertical velocity, turbulence characteristics, cloud base height and atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) evolution (height, growth rate and maximum depth) between two lidars will be presented. In addition, this study will show the lidar characteristic performance in terms of data availability and maximum measurement range along with system health reports (internal temperature and relative humidity). Independent observations from the NWS radiosondes will be used to evaluate the accuracy of the lidar winds and ABL height. The performance of two lidars during wildfire smoke, heat wave, heavy precipitation and thunderstorm events will be presented as well. Overall, this study will provide an objective evaluation of Halo Photonics Doppler lidar against Windcube Doppler lidar for boundary layer monitoring and research and operational reliability. The results will serve as guidance for deploying these lidars for future field campaigns.

494942.title: Uncovering Heat as a Hurricane Hazard Through Text Mining of Storm Event Databases
494942.authors: J. Marshall Shepherd, Univ. of Georgia, Athens, GA; and Q. Cao and A. J. Grundstein
494942.abstract: Heat is an underrecognized hazard in hurricane mortality, alongside better-tracked causes like flood drowning. Hurricane-attributable heat deaths, including fatalities from heat exposure triggered or worsened by power outages, evacuation, and post-storm cleanup, are not systematically tracked in official records. This study presents a large-scale text mining analysis of two authoritative databases, National Hurricane Center (NHC) Tropical Cyclone Reports and the NOAA Storm Events Database, covering 31 hurricane seasons (1995–2025). Using a pipeline combining keyword retrieval and large language model inference, we extracted structured fatality information from unstructured narrative text, including heat-relatedness, causal mechanism, timing, victim demographics, and death counts. We identified 385 deaths (182 direct cause and 203 indirect cause) among the 537 storms in our study. Most heat-related deaths occurred after storm passage, though pre-landfall fatalities during evacuation were also documented. NHC reports recorded heat-related deaths in only 5 storms, compared to 13 in the NOAA database, pointing to attribution gaps in official mortality records. These results suggest heat should be considered a hazard in hurricane risk planning and mitigation, alongside flooding and wind, and that text mining of existing reports offers a scalable method for retrospective mortality surveillance.

494943.title: A Dual-Transmitter Optical Particulate Sensor Architecture for Wide-Dynamic-Range Atmospheric Particle Measurements
494943.authors: Kaizhong Gao, Honeywell Aerospace Technologies, Plymouth, MN; and P. Badin, V. Drazan, J. Oklestek, Z. Drasal, J. Pekarek, and T. Dobbins
494943.abstract: Airborne measurements of atmospheric particles support aviation safety, icing characterization, engine protection, and environmental monitoring. Relevant particle populations include water droplets, ice crystals, volcanic ash, sand, dust, and other aerosols. A central instrumentation challenge is the broad particle-size range of interest. Particle diameters may span more than three orders of magnitude, producing scattered-light signals that differ by several orders of magnitude. Conventional optical systems often address this range with separate sensors, duplicated receive optics, or multiple detection channels, which increases size, weight, power, alignment burden, and aircraft-integration complexity. This work presents a compact optical particulate sensor architecture that combines two transmit channels with a shared receive path. Two laser beams with different beam profiles and optical characteristics illuminate adjacent interrogation regions. A narrow, higher-energy-density beam improves sensitivity to smaller particles, while a wider, lower-energy-density beam supports measurement of larger particles. Scattered light from both regions is collected through common receive optics, reducing hardware duplication while retaining channel-specific measurement conditions. Channel separation is provided by a wavelength-selective spatial filtering element with adjacent regions having different aperture characteristics and spectral passbands. The receive optics map signals from the two interrogation regions to the corresponding filter regions. The combined geometric and spectral discrimination separates the optical responses while preserving key functions of the slit, including sampling-volume definition and suppression of off-axis solar background. The architecture was evaluated using a non-sequential Ansys OpticStudio model containing the transmit optics, receive optics, detector assemblies, sensor housing, and optical filtering elements. The model verified formation and mapping of both interrogation regions and propagation of particle-scattered light through the receive system. The high-sensitivity channel produced an interrogation region of approximately 200 micrometers by 1200 micrometers, and the large-particle channel produced a region of approximately 5 millimeters by 5 millimeters, consistent with their respective design objectives. Water-droplet scattering simulations demonstrated distinct signal responses that support particle-sizing analysis. The modeled receive system collected backscattered light over an effective angular range of approximately 140 to 160 degrees, where 0 degrees denotes forward scatter and 180 degrees denotes backscatter. Separate solar-background analyses indicated strong rejection of off-axis illumination. The dual-transmitter, shared-receiver approach provides a practical path toward wide-dynamic-range atmospheric particle measurements in an aircraft-installable package. Integrating small- and large-particle measurements within one optical framework can reduce redundant hardware and support improved size, weight, and power characteristics. The architecture is applicable to future airborne icing instrumentation, atmospheric research, and detection of particulate hazards.

494946.title: Lower-Column Transport and Nocturnal Surface Coupling during a 2026 Canadian Wildfire Smoke Event over the Baltimore-Washington Corridor
494946.authors: Nakul Nitin Karle, Howard University, Washington, DC; and S. Chiao, Z. Yang, and D. Rosenberg
494946.abstract: In mid-July 2026, a long-range transport of dense Canadian wildfire smoke engulfed the Baltimore-Washington Corridor (BWC), raising the surface PM2.5 concentration above 180 µg m-3 at the McMillan Reservoir monitor in Washington, DC. We investigate the event using the co-located Vaisala CL61 ceilometer and HALO Doppler wind lidar observations at Howard University Interdisciplinary Research Building (HUIRB), along with radiosonde and ozone sonde profiles, regional AirNow measurements, and HRRR-Smoke analyses. The interaction between the smoke plume and the planetary boundary layer (PBL) on 16-17 July 2026 progressed in stages. On 16 July, PBL growth brought the mixed layer into contact with the aerosol layer aloft as CL61 optical variability and HALO vertical-velocity variance increased near the PBL top. The HRRR-modeled smoke increase occurred later under northerly flow, coincident with enhanced aerosol backscatter in the lower column. A shallow stable layer coincided with low surface PM2.5, consistent with temporarily limited surface exchange. Across 42 screened regional monitors, first-persistent, background-adjusted PM2.5 enhancement times were consistent with an approximately southward-moving phase feature, with an apparent speed of 5.6 m s-1. The 100-500 m AGL HALO wind component in the fitted propagation direction was comparable, providing kinematic consistency with regional advection. As the PBL subsequently deepened, a larger fraction of the HRRR-modeled smoke column fell within the diagnosed boundary layer. Observations and model results together support a progression from boundary layer preconditioning to lower-column advection, temporary surface decoupling, and subsequent vertical redistribution. This case shows why modeled smoke in the lower troposphere does not translate directly into surface exposure and demonstrates the value of paired aerosol and Doppler lidar profiling for resolving the timing and mechanisms of smoke impact.

494947.title: Advancing Multiscale Modeling of Wind Farm Wakes (Invited Presentation)
494947.authors: Cristina Lozej Archer, University of Delaware, Newark, DE; Politecnico di Torino, Torino, Torino, Italy
494947.abstract: As offshore and onshore wind energy expands globally, the ability to accurately predict the performance and environmental impacts of wind farms has become a critical engineering and meteorological challenge. Traditional mesoscale numerical models, which are vital for weather prediction, often struggle to resolve the sub-grid turbulence and wake interactions that strongly affect wind plant efficiency. This presentation synthesizes a decade of research into the multiscale modeling of wind turbine wakes, focusing on the development of robust parameterizations that bridge the gap between high-fidelity Large-Eddy Simulations (LES) and operational mesoscale weather forecasting (e.g., with the Weather and Research Forecast model and/or the Model for Prediction Across Scales, WRF and/or MPAS respectively). First, we will explore the “dual nature” of wind turbine wakes, moving beyond simple wind speed deficits to account for the complex transport, production, and dissipation of turbulence kinetic energy (TKE). By integrating LES-derived physical insights -- such as wake contraction and stability-dependent recovery -- into analytical and mesoscale frameworks (e.g., the Fitch, MAV, and Limited Domain parameterizations), I will demonstrate significant improvements in predicting power production and wake losses in both idealized and real-world conditions. Beyond energy yield, the talk will address the complex topic of the environmental footprint of wind farms. I will present evidence -- observational and computational -- on how wind turbine-induced turbulence enhances vertical mixing in the rotor region, while reduced wind shear decreases vertical mixing near the surface, causing small changes in near-surface temperature and precipitation under certain conditions and influencing, at times, regional air quality, specifically ozone and other pollutant transport. These findings underscore that wind farms are not just energy sources, but interact with the atmospheric boundary layer.

494949.title: A Unified Lightning Product for Operations: Demonstration and Developments
494949.authors: Sarah M. Stough, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and V. C. Chmielewski, K. M. Calhoun, and K. C. Thiel
494949.abstract: Operational use of lightning data extends from hazard awareness to thunderstorm diagnosis thanks to lightning’s relationship with deep convective processes. Multiple sources of lightning information are available over the conterminous United States, including the ground-based National Lightning Detection Network and Earth Networks Total Lightning Network as well as the satellite-borne Geostationary Lightning Mappers (GLMs). These networks and instruments measure either the radio or optical emissions of lightning, each detecting unique processes within lightning discharges. Used in concert, the combined data provide improved information about the coverage of lightning as well as value-added information about lightning characteristics. Lightning detections from these sources have been combined in the first iteration of a unified lightning product, a gridded boolean lightning dataset that implements storm-based GLM parallax correction to improve two-dimensional lightning location for hazard assessment. Preliminary results from a demonstration of near real-time product distribution are described, including impacts associated with data lag or dropout. Ongoing development to add quantitative lightning flash characteristics such as frequency, size, and energy are also discussed for improved thunderstorm diagnostic capabilities of lightning data in operations.

494950.title: Extending Predictability Limits of Tornadic Supercell Thunderstorms Using Self-Organizing Maps
494950.authors: Luke Justin LeBel, Iowa State University, Ames, IA; and B. A. Garcia and P. M. Markowski
494950.abstract: Despite their apparent steadiness, supercell thunderstorms are characterized by large internal variability. Manifestations of this variability are known to be important for the occurrence of supercell hazards, including tornadoes, and an improved understanding of storm-internal variability may therefore provide opportunities to extend hazard predictability. To explore and quantify the internal variability of supercells, the self-organizing map (SOM) method is applied at the storm-scale to the Markowski (2020) ensemble of 25 high-resolution simulations of supercells. To identify patterns of variability in the low-level updraft structure, a SOM is trained on 10-km by 10-km storm-centered horizontal cross sections of simulated vertical velocity at 1 km. The method effectively produces a range of updraft patterns, or nodes, that organize along axes of updraft intensity and updraft occlusion. The frequency of tornado-like vortices (TLVs) is variable across the SOM nodes. Although TLVs occur in association with all identified updraft patterns, TLVs are most common in the SOM nodes characterized by the strongest low-level updrafts. For several SOM nodes, TLV frequency remains anomalously high or low for up to 20 minutes after SOM node occurrence, suggesting that the supercell updraft structure conveys meaningful information about future TLV occurrence. In sum, the SOM approach is a powerful tool to explore the internal variability of supercells, and reveals that knowledge of the low-level updraft structure may meaningfully extend the predictability of tornadoes.

494951.title: Insights from Large Ensemble Modeling of Hydrologic Extremes across Kansas
494951.authors: Joshua K. Roundy, Univ. of Kansas, Lawrence, KS; and A. T. Michalek
494951.abstract: Advancements in high-performance computing, such as GPU–CPU-based hydrologic models (e.g., Tiger-HLM), enable rapid runoff and streamflow simulation across large domains at fine spatial and sub-daily temporal scales. High-resolution modeling is critical for isolating the influence of atmospheric forcing on hydrologic extremes (floods, droughts, and whiplash transitions) and identifying optimal parameters that maintain proper physical process representation. Delivering accurate forecasts and projections at these scales is essential for providing actionable, community-level decision support. Here, we model runoff and streamflow across all river basins in Kansas, a domain characterized by a sharp hydrologic performance gradient, where models traditionally struggle in the High Plains but improve toward the east. First, we use an ensemble of historical precipitation and temperature forcing datasets to generate initial hindcasts. Next, we integrate statistical learning with these simulations to refine parameterization and conceptual runoff representation across the state, establishing a finalized model framework. We then leverage these simulations to quantify uncertainty between input forcings and parameters during extreme flood, drought, and compound whiplash events. Finally, we evaluate the model's performance in operational forecasting and future climate projections across Kansas, disentangling the relative contributions of internal climate variability, global climate model uncertainty, and baseline reference uncertainty to inform resilient water management decisions.

494952.title: The Ideas Lab as a Mechanism for Enabling Interdisciplinary and Convergence Research
494952.authors: Alexandra N. Ramos-Valle, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. McCauley-Hartner, M. G. Cains, and P. Montaño, MS, MA
494952.abstract: The U.S. National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) Faculty Innovator Program supports faculty to co-develop interdisciplinary and actionable research projects in partnership with NSF NCAR scientists and engineers. The main goals of the program are to expand the capacity for interdisciplinary and convergence research and to build a network of expertise in the Earth system sciences. As the first step in selecting its fourth cohort, the Innovator Program invited applications from university faculty for an Ideas Lab workshop where applicants could co-develop research ideas with potential NSF NCAR collaborators. Here, we describe how the Ideas Lab workshop helped facilitate interdisciplinary and convergence research, focusing on how its structure, content, and participant composition were intentionally designed to maximize convergence potential. We present details of the workshop design, and discuss outcomes, challenges, and opportunities. We also include findings from the formal evaluation of the Ideas Lab to understand the extent to which the workshop achieved its intended outcomes. The Ideas Lab enabled new research by creating the space and structured time for participants to build collaborations and develop ideas. The Ideas Lab helped address common barriers to convergence research, including time constraints and short collaboration timelines, by extending the time available for team-building. Workshop participants reported connecting with researchers in disciplines they would not have met otherwise, achieving the workshop's intended outcome. These findings support the Ideas Lab as a valuable and effective model to catalyze convergence and interdisciplinary research process.

494953.title: Exploring Forecasters’ Ability to Identify Extreme Rainfall Location and Timing Through Forecasting Activities in the Flash Flood and Intense Rainfall (FFaIR) Experiment
494953.authors: Sarah Marie Trojniak, CIRES @ WPC-HMT, Sterling Heights, MI; and J. Correia Jr.
494953.abstract: The Weather Prediction Center (WPC) Hydrometeorology Testbed’s (HMT) Flash Flood and Intense Rainfall (FFaIR) Experiment focuses on evaluating experimental weather prediction datasets and tools in the context of heavy/extreme rainfall and its impacts. FFaIR assesses this information using objective and subjective verification methods. Forecasting tasks are also performed that utilize these datasets and tools to provide a way for participants to actively use the data and provide assessments. The latter of the two will be the focus of this talk. Since the summer of 2020, the FFaIR team has created a number of forecasting activities to investigate the question: can forecasters identify the region(s) at risk for extreme rainfall including, timing, location, footprint, and magnitudes? This presentation will discuss the evolution of the FFaIR forecasting products, participant insights on heavy rainfall forecasting, and how the “signal in the noise” at Day 2 and 3 lead times from the CAMs can highlight the where/when of heavy rainfall risks.

494954.title: Applying Machine Learning to Mapping the Slope Sea and Gulf Stream Subsurface
494954.authors: Elena Licia Pierce, Colorado State University, Littleton, CO; and J. Zavala-Garay, S. shekhar, J. Levin, and N. Nikolova
494954.abstract: The overarching goal of ocean modeling is to provide valuable hindcasts and forecasts to scientific communities and the general-public. These ocean state estimations are produced by numerical models which require observations to constrain the numerical models through data assimilation. While the surface variability is relatively well observed by satellite platforms, the subsurface of the ocean is poorly sampled. To address this data scarcity problem, this project experiments with leveraging machine learning to produce synthetic profiles of subsurface temperature and salinity in the slope sea and gulf stream regions. This project demonstrates that a neural network trained with in-situ Argo profiles and satellite analyses of surface variability can efficiently and accurately produce temperature and salinity profile predictions. The model accurately captures the vertical structure of large-scale and mesoscale ocean features such as the Gulf Stream and slope-sea eddies. We found that a data driven model is a considerably more efficient method for producing hydrographic profile predictions while still achieving a high level of skill. Including these synthetic profiles into data-assimilative forecasting models could improve forecast accuracy and efficiency. Given the global coverage of Argo floats and satellite observations, this study could have valuable implication for countries with limited resources dedicated to collecting ocean observations, as modeling offers an inexpensive way to gain critical information about the ocean, for example future effects of sea level rise.

494955.title: Advancing Non-Stationary Methods for Extreme Precipitation and Flood Estimation (INVITED)
494955.authors: Andrew J. Newman, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and N. D. Lybarger, F. Felfelani, A. W. Wood, T. Eidhammer, N. Mizukami, S. Hartke, K. Holman, A. Stone, E. D. Gutmann, J. F. England, and K. Walker
494955.abstract: Traditional extreme precipitation and flow estimation methods were developed largely under assumptions of climatic stationarity. Yet internal variability and warming are altering precipitation intensity and phase, storm tracks, and antecedent hydrologic conditions, creating a need for physically credible, uncertainty-aware methods that connect non-stationary extreme precipitation to extreme floods. We present progress towards this goal using Earth System Model (ESM) large ensembles, complementary downscaling methods, and continental-scale hydrologic simulation. First, we use multiple downscaling approaches to understand different aspects of uncertainty in extreme precipitation and flow estimation. Our downscaling approaches include GARD-LENS, which statistically downscales 200 members from three CMIP6 single-model initial-condition large ensembles to provide long, high-resolution time series of precipitation and temperature while explicitly representing internal climate variability. Further, convection-permitting WRF downscaling was performed for hundreds of extreme events from the CESM2 Large Ensemble across portions of CONUS, and for multiple 30-year time-slices across Alaska. Comparisons across CESM2, GARD-LENS, and WRF demonstrate that estimates of extreme-precipitation change can differ in magnitude, spatial pattern, and even sign. Dynamical downscaling additionally reveals changes in storm track and precipitation phase and intensity that are not consistently represented by the ESM or GARD-LENS. To translate these atmospheric changes into floods, we are taking two approaches. First, we use the traditional chain-of-models approach. The GARD-LENS data are used to drive the SUMMA–mizuRoute hydrologic modeling system across the western United States. Second, we are moving towards regional ESMs with fit-for-purpose online land and hydrology. Initial results from both domains show widespread increases in the frequency of historical high flows, declining and earlier snowmelt-driven flood peaks, and increasing contributions from winter rainfall. Internal variability is a substantial source of hydrologic uncertainty, while downscaling choices introduce additional uncertainty that may rival the projected precipitation signal. Together, these efforts support a probabilistic, process-based pathway from extreme precipitation through extreme flooding. They also highlight the need for 1) coordinated downscaling benchmarks and explicit uncertainty propagation; 2) continued methodological improvements to advance PMP and PMF modeling and applications including atmospheric and land state perturbations, and 3) continued advances in physically-based and AI-emulation for the coupled land-atmosphere system.

494957.title: We've Moved! The Status and Realignment of NOAA’s Weather Program Office within the National Weather Service
494957.authors: Gina M. Eosco, NOAA Federal, Silver Spring, MD
494957.abstract: Following a congressionally mandated transition in the Fiscal Year 2026 appropriations law, three major funding lines—the U.S. Weather Research Program (USWRP), the Joint Technology Transfer Initiative (JTTI), and the Phased Array Radar/Tornado Severe Storms Research lines—transferred from NOAA’s Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR) to the National Weather Service (NWS). Consequently, the Weather Program Office (WPO) and its personnel officially relocated to the NWS. This presentation updates WPO’s position within the revised NWS organizational structure. We outline key changes to administrative and operational integration while highlighting what remains constant: WPO’s core commitment to advancing weather research, supporting community partnerships, and driving research-to-operations (R2O) transitions. Attendees will learn how this realignment enhances research integration to better serve operational forecasting and public safety.

494958.title: An Updraft-Based Framework for Organizing Orographic Snowfall and Cloud Structure during S2noCliME
494958.authors: Troy Justin Zaremba, Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS
494958.abstract: Orographic precipitation in complex terrain reflects a wide range of flow regimes, yet a unifying framework for understanding variability in snowfall and cloud structure remains lacking. This study introduces an updraft-based framework that ranks events by terrain-tied ascent upstream of Storm Peak Laboratory (SPL), providing a physically grounded approach for interpreting cloud and precipitation variability in a mountain environment. The analysis focuses on the Snow Sensitivity to Clouds in a Mountain Environment field campaign (S2noCliME), conducted near Steamboat Springs, Colorado during the 2024–2025 winter season. Ground-based radar observations (Sea-Pol and KASPR) and in situ measurements collected during S2noCliME are combined with a season-long Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulation configured at 500-m horizontal grid spacing. Mean modeled vertical velocity within the lowest 5 km upstream of SPL is used to rank periods by updraft strength, enabling composite analyses that isolate the role of terrain-forced ascent. The WRF simulation is used to define the updraft-based ranking of time periods, which is then applied to the observational datasets (including ground-based radar such as Sea-Pol and in situ measurements) to construct composites of cloud and precipitation structure across regimes. The ranking framework reveals a coherent and physically consistent progression in cloud and precipitation structure across updraft regimes. Strong-updraft periods exhibit enhanced supercooled liquid water, increased radar reflectivity, and a pronounced downstream displacement of precipitation relative to the terrain crest. Composite cross sections show deeper cloud layers, more vertically continuous reflectivity structures, and enhanced hydrometeor growth extending downstream, consistent with sustained ascent followed by advection-driven growth in the lee. In contrast, weak-updraft regimes are characterized by shallow cloud depths, reduced liquid water content, and more spatially confined precipitation near the terrain. The transition across regimes is accompanied by systematic changes in environmental forcing. Stronger updraft periods are associated with higher low-level wind speeds and reduced static stability, indicative of more efficient flow-over and wave amplification, while weaker periods reflect more stable and/or blocked flow. Together, these results demonstrate that upstream terrain-tied ascent provides a unifying metric for organizing variability in orographic cloud structure and snowfall distribution. This framework offers a new pathway for linking environmental conditions to precipitation outcomes.

494959.title: Assimilating Dense Ground-based GNSS Zenith Total Delay and Tropospheric Gradient to Improve Afternoon Thunderstorm Prediction over Complex Terrain
494959.authors: Yi-Pin Chang, National Central University, Zhongli, Taiwan; and S. C. Yang, K. J. Lin, T. K. Yeh, F. Zus, R. Thundathil, and J. Wickert
494959.abstract: Predicting afternoon thunderstorms over complex terrain, such as the Taipei Basin, remains a major forecasting challenge. Taiwan features a unique, dense ground-based GNSS station network. Over 400 GNSS stations provide zenith total delay (ZTD) and tropospheric gradient (TG) observations at 30-minute intervals. These high spatiotemporal-resolution observations offer critical moisture information, which are essential for identifying precursors of rapidly developing convection and short-term heavy rainfall. This study utilizes a convective-scale ensemble data assimilation (EDA) system to assimilate ZTD and TG, aiming to capture fast moisture variations and their interactions with complex topography to improve afternoon thunderstorm prediction. Assimilation experiments were conducted on two afternoon thunderstorm events (June 24 and July 4, 2022) with distinct moisture distributions and precipitation intensities during the joint Taiwan-Area Heavy Rain Observation and Prediction Experiment (TAHOPE)/Prediction of Rainfall Extremes Campaign in the Pacific (PRECIP) field campaign. Results demonstrate that assimilating ZTD yields effective moisture corrections for each event. Incorporating TG further refines the moisture distribution by modulating localized features. These findings highlight the capability of dense ground-based GNSS data to capture timely and localized moisture variations, providing insights into the key thermodynamics driving the two events. Furthermore, sensitivity experiments evaluating optimal GNSS data assimilation strategies will be presented.

494962.title: From PROSWIFT to Operations: Advancing Aviation Resilience Through a National Space Weather Enterprise
494962.authors: Rondeau Flynn, APA, Ft. Worth, TX; Allied Pilots Association, Ft. Worth, TX
494962.abstract: From PROSWIFT to Operations: Advancing Aviation Resilience Through a National Space Weather Enterprise The aviation sector is among the Nation's most space weather-sensitive critical infrastructures, relying heavily on high-frequency communications, satellite-based navigation, surveillance systems, and the safe management of radiation exposure at flight altitudes. Recognizing these vulnerabilities, Congress enacted the Promoting Research and Observations of Space Weather to Improve the Forecasting of Tomorrow (PROSWIFT) Act of 2020, establishing a comprehensive national framework for space weather research, observations, forecasting, interagency coordination, and stakeholder engagement. The Act formalized the roles of federal agencies, strengthened the Space Weather Operations, Research, and Mitigation (SWORM) enterprise, established the Space Weather Advisory Group (SWAG), and emphasized the need to understand and address the requirements of operational end users. Since its passage, PROSWIFT has accelerated the maturation of the United States space weather enterprise by promoting research-to-operations transitions, advancing observational capabilities, fostering public-private partnerships, and creating formal mechanisms through which industry stakeholders can inform national priorities. A key outcome has been the elevation of aviation as a critical end-user community whose operational requirements help shape future investments in space weather products and services. Recent work by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine further underscored the importance of aviation resilience by identifying flight crewmembers as one of the most highly radiation-exposed occupational populations in the United States. Their assessment highlighted the need for improved monitoring, exposure assessment, dose tracking, risk communication, and mitigation strategies, particularly during solar energetic particle events capable of increasing radiation levels along high-latitude and polar routes. These findings reinforce the importance of integrating space weather information into aviation safety and operational decision-making processes. Complementing this work, SWAG's first national survey of space weather users documented aviation-sector demands for more actionable and impact-based forecasts, improved warning lead times, enhanced data accessibility, better characterization of operational risks, and decision-support tools tailored to flight operations. The survey demonstrated a growing need to translate scientific observations and forecasts into operationally relevant information that supports flight dispatch, route planning, navigation integrity monitoring, communications resilience, and radiation risk management. This presentation examines how the combined efforts of PROSWIFT, the National Academies, and SWAG, along with the FAA, NASA, and NOAA SWPC are transforming the relationship between space weather science and aviation operations. Together, these initiatives have strengthened national awareness of aviation vulnerabilities, improved engagement between end users and service providers, and established a strategic foundation for a more resilient National Airspace System. By connecting policy, science, and operational end-user needs, the United States is advancing toward a risk-informed aviation framework capable of mitigating the impacts of space weather events while enhancing national resilience through heightened awareness, education an advanced aviation technologies.

494963.title: Cloud Droplet Number, Precipitation Phase, and Precipitation Properties of Southern Ocean Boundary-Layer Clouds from the MISO Voyage
494963.authors: Gerald G. Mace, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT
494963.abstract: The MISO voyage aboard the Australian RV Investigator (Hobart–Antarctic coast–Perth, January–March 2024, 32–67°S) sampled marine boundary-layer clouds and precipitation across the Southern Ocean using dual-frequency (94- and 24-GHz) radar, depolarization lidar, and a microwave radiometer. We report retrievals of predominantly liquid cloud droplet number concentration (Nd), precipitation phase, and precipitation properties, and their control by aerosol source region. Optimal-estimation cloud droplet number, Nd, anchored to coincident MODIS retrievals and the measured CCN supersaturation spectrum, sits at CCN(0.2%) (Nd/CCN ≈ 1.0), indicating near-complete activation in these weak-updraft clouds. Nd is governed by air-mass history: an objective, residence-based Lagrangian classification of MERRA back-trajectories shows that continental Antarctic ice-sheet outflow yields the highest Nd and CCN (Nd ≈ 132 cm⁻³; CCN0.2 ≈ 222 cm⁻³), sea-ice/marginal-ice-zone air a secondary ~1.4× enhancement, and cryosphere-free oceanic air the clean baseline (Nd ≈ 57 cm⁻³). Nd decays monotonically with ice-sheet transit age (190 → 45 cm⁻³ over five days), consistent with a biogenic katabatic aerosol source. Ice-nucleating particle (INP) concentrations from daily filters are typically low but show sensitivity to air-mass source region. Consistent with this, sub-cloud precipitation is overwhelmingly supercooled liquid drizzle (83% of precipitating profiles; mean diameter ≈ 109 µm); ice is infrequent and light (median ice mass fraction 0.17; median rate 0.04 mm h⁻¹) and grows more frequent equatorward of the Polar Front. Retrieved drizzle validates against a shipboard disdrometer (mean-diameter ratio 1.00). The observed near-unity supercooled-liquid fraction contrasts sharply with CMIP6 models—five of seven glaciate these clouds—implicating an overactive ice process in their Southern Ocean cloud-phase feedback.

494965.title: From Hazard Signals to Financial Decisions: A Roundtable on Heat, Drought, and Water Risk
494965.abstract: Extreme heat, drought, and water scarcity are increasingly material risks for economies, communities, and financial systems. Their effects extend well beyond the physical hazard itself, influencing worker health and productivity, agricultural and livestock production, hydropower generation, energy demand, inland transportation, municipal water supplies, ecosystems, infrastructure, insurance markets, and regional economic stability. Because these impacts can compound and cascade across sectors and supply chains, decision-makers need climate intelligence that is both scientifically credible and usable under uncertainty. This 60-minute roundtable will examine how heat, drought, and water-related risks are measured, modeled, communicated, and translated into economic and financial decisions. Discussion will consider the strengths and limitations of drought prediction, including flash-drought monitoring and attribution; heat-stress indicators; hydrologic forecasts; water-availability assessments; exposure and vulnerability analysis; and financial risk metrics. Potential applications will span agricultural systems, energy and hydropower, urban heat and water impacts, inland transportation, and other weather-sensitive businesses and public services. Participants will explore how environmental intelligence can inform investment planning, resource allocation, energy reliability, resilience strategies, risk transfer, pricing mechanisms, and long-term sustainability in water-stressed and weather-sensitive systems.

494966.title: Moisture Structure and Mid-Level Clouds in Dusty Saharan Air Layers over the North Atlantic
494966.authors: Satyendra Kumar Pandey, University of California Merced, Merced, CA; and G. Gong and A. A. Adebiyi
494966.abstract: The Saharan Air Layer (SAL) is typically a warm, dry, dust-laden air mass that transports mineral dust from North Africa across the tropical North Atlantic. Recent aircraft data and long-term radiosonde observations found that on dust-dominated days, its vertical moisture structure is more complex, with drier air at lower levels and relatively moist air at upper levels. It remains unclear whether this pattern of moist upper and dry lower layers is common across the Atlantic, how it evolves during transport, and how well reanalysis datasets (such as CAMS: Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service reanalysis and MERRA2: Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2) capture this moisture structure. In this study, we examine the summer thermodynamic structure of dusty SALs in reanalysis data, using radiosonde observations over Tenerife as a reference for the eastern subtropical Atlantic and basin-wide satellite-retrieved temperature and moisture profiles. We compare temperature, water-vapor mixing ratio, relative humidity, and potential temperature under dusty and clean conditions to assess how accurately the models reproduce the observed SAL structure. We also analyze how the vertical moisture distribution varies with dust amount and distance from the African coast. Additionally, we use observations from active and passive satellite sensors to examine how mid-level cloud occurrence depends on moisture and dust loading within the SAL across the tropical North Atlantic. Thus, we evaluate whether enhanced upper-SAL moisture and mid-level cloud occurrence are characteristic of dusty SALs across the Atlantic or confined to specific episodes and regions. Improving this characterization is important for representing SAL thermodynamics and associated cloud environments in climate models.

494967.title: ESA Vigil: A New L5 Observing Capability for Operational Space Weather
494967.authors: Matthew John West, European Space Agency, Noordwijk, Netherlands
494967.abstract: ESA’s Vigil mission will establish a new operational space-weather observing capability from the Sun-Earth L5 Lagrange point, approximately (60°) behind Earth in its orbit around the Sun. This unique vantage point will complement observations made from the Sun-Earth line by providing earlier views of active regions rotating towards Earth, improved perspectives of Earth-directed coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and measurements of the solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field away from the near-Earth environment. Vigil will carry a suite of six remote-sensing and in-situ instruments designed to provide complementary observations from the solar surface, through the corona and inner heliosphere, to the local solar-wind environment at L5. Together, these measurements will support improved detection and characterisation of solar eruptions, tracking of CMEs through the heliosphere, monitoring of active regions and coronal holes, and forecasting of solar-wind structures that may subsequently affect Earth. Low-latency delivery of these observations will enable their integration into operational space-weather forecasting systems and heliospheric models, while their combination with measurements from other spacecraft and ground-based facilities will provide a substantially more complete description of the Sun–Earth system. This presentation will provide an update on the current status of the Vigil mission and its instrument suite, describe the observational capabilities that will become available from L5, and discuss how these measurements will complement existing and planned space-weather observing systems. Particular emphasis will be placed on the advantages of combining multiple observing geometries and instrument types, and on the role of Vigil within the evolving international space-weather observing architecture.

494970.title: Expanding Weather Observations in Historically Under-Observed Regions through the 3D-PAWS Initiative
494970.authors: Elizabeth Anne Wilson, Synoptic Data PBC, Raleigh, NC; and P. A. Kucera, K. Payne, W. Nicewonger, and B. M. Smith
494970.abstract: Reliable weather observations are the foundation for forecasting, situational awareness, and warning support. Observations are also important for improving modern forecast models. Yet many regions around the world remain observationally sparse, limiting the ability of local meteorological services to monitor severe weather, deliver timely warnings, and provide actionable information to the communities they serve. The 3D-Printed Automatic Weather Station (3D-PAWS) initiative was created to address this challenge by enabling the deployment of affordable, locally maintained weather stations in historically under-observed regions. Through a partnership with the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research’s (UCAR) COMET program and Synoptic Data, National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHS) in over 20 countries across the Caribbean, Africa, South Pacific, and beyond, now have access to 3D-PAWS network data through a centralized platform. 3D-PAWS is an open, modular weather and environmental monitoring system that helps make reliable observations more accessible. The weather stations combine 3D-printed enclosures with low cost, off-the-shelf microcontrollers and environmental microsensor technology to create weather stations that are affordable, replaceable, and easy to scale. The Synoptic platform provides access to the data from these weather networks and delivers critical, real-time information for monitoring, alerting, and forecasting, as well as data dissemination tools to quickly and easily share information with other agencies and the public. This presentation will explain how the partnership is helping close observational gaps by connecting innovative, locally deployed weather stations with modern data infrastructure. We will discuss how centralized visualization, network monitoring, quality control, customizable dashboards, and real-time data dissemination enable meteorological services to provide better services for their communities, while reducing technical barriers to operational weather monitoring. The presentation will also explore how observations collected in data-sparse regions contribute valuable surface observations to international forecasting systems. The 3D-PAWS initiative demonstrates that expanding access to weather information requires more than deploying sensors. It also relies on using reliable, scalable data technologies. Together, these elements allow underserved communities to benefit from the observations they collect and strengthen the global weather enterprise through improved data sharing and collaboration.

494972.title: The Python ARM Radar Toolkit and xradar: Updates and the Challenges and Opportunities of an Open Source Radar Toolkit in the Age of Agentic AI
494972.authors: Scott M. Collis, ANL, Lemont, IL; Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, IL; and R. C. Jackson, A. Ladino, Z. Sherman, K. Mühlbauer, B. A. Raut, J. R. O'Brien, M. A. Grover, and A. Theisen
494972.abstract: The Python ARM Radar Toolkit (Py-ART) is now over a decade old. It continues to power a large body of scientific research and has acted as a natural research to operations (and operations to research) pipeline, enabling over 600 publications. This presentation will cover several aspects of Py-ART. First, it will highlight our third, five year roadmap, which includes high priority items such as new countermeasures and policy with regards to AI usage. Second, it will highlight several new features added, some of which were aided by agentic coding agents. The presentation will also discuss the challenges of maintaining community code in an age where an AI agent can conceive, build code, and author a pull request with (on occasion) zero human input. In the 2022 Open Source Radar Developer’s Meeting in Locarno, Switzerland, a new xarray-based data model for weather radar data, xradar, was conceived as a universal data model based on Cf/Radial 2.0 for the open source radar stack. This talk also discusses those efforts and the adaptation of PyART to use the xradar data model. The xradar data model has also enabled the use of zarr stores, an Analysis Ready Cloud Optimized (ARCO) format that enables quick analyses of decadal radar datasets spanning tens of terabytes in size. Pulling it all together, we demonstrate examples of how xradar plus Py-ART plus Analysis Ready Cloud Optimized (ARCO) data supercharge agentically driven scientific workflows.

494973.title: Implementation of the RTTOV v14 C++ Interface in UFO and Its Application to Microphysics Sensitivity Testing in MPAS
494973.authors: Ju-Hye Kim, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Jang, J. Ban, B. J. Jung, and C. Schwartz
494973.abstract: This study presents the integration of RTTOV v14 into the Unified Forward Operator (UFO) system to support all-sky data assimilation and advanced satellite simulations. As a foundational validation, 5-day forecast experiments utilizing AMSU-A and MHS observations confirmed that RTTOV performs comparably to CRTM in both clear-sky and all-sky DA frameworks, establishing a robust and stable interface. Building upon this baseline, we have extended the JEDI forward operator framework to simulate GPM Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar (DPR) observations by leveraging the active sensor capabilities of RTTOV v14. Using this newly implemented radar simulator within UFO, we conduct sensitivity experiments to evaluate the performance of different cloud microphysics schemes in MPAS.
