We will present the calculated GPM DPR simulations (h(x)) and demonstrate how the simulated radar reflectivities respond to variations in hydrometeor distributions and partitioning across different microphysics options. This study establishes a robust diagnostic and validation framework using active radar simulators, providing critical technical baselines for improving model physics and advancing future radar data assimilation.

494975.title: Hydromex: A Python Package for Generating IHO S-104 Water Level and S-111 Surface Current Products from NOAA's Surge and Tide Operational Forecast System
494975.authors: John A. Kluge, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and G. Seroka, E. Nagel, T. Thompson, U. U. Turuncoglu, Y. Funakoshi, Z. Yang, L. Shi, S. Mani, A. Alipour, M. A. Jisan, F. Cassalho, F. Daneshvar, C. George, Y. Sun, S. Moghimi, M. Rostaminia, L. Tang, E. Myers, and C. Allen
494975.abstract: NOAA's National Ocean Service (NOS) continues to advance the Surge and Tide Operational Forecast System (STOFS), providing critical nowcast and forecast guidance for water levels and currents that support coastal resilience and marine navigation. Within NOS Precision Marine Navigation (PMN), these capabilities are being extended toward emerging S-100 navigation products and services. NOAA is developing dynamic S-100 navigation products in response to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) transition from International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) S-57 to S-100 chart standards. Under these new specifications, Electronic Navigation Charts (ENCs) will incorporate forecast water levels (S-104) and surface current products (S-111) to enhance route planning, fuel efficiency, and hazard avoidance. Translating raw, large-scale unstructured finite-element model output from ADCIRC and SCHISM into compliant IHO S-100 datasets presents significant computational and workflow challenges. We present hydromex (Hydrodynamic Model Extraction and Exchange), a Python package that automates generation of S-104 and S-111 products directly from cloud-hosted STOFS model output on AWS S3. The package uses components of the Earth System Modeling Framework (ESMF) and is being developed alongside evolving Unified Forecast System Coastal (UFS Coastal) workflows. hydromex generates S-104 on a structured regular grid using VDatum shifts from the model geoid to local mean sea level (LMSL) and mean lower low water (MLLW), which is the required chart datum. For S-111, the package supports both a regular grid and the native SCHISM unstructured mesh, preserving high spatial resolution in complex channels. To perform regular-grid transformations without writing temporary files to disk, hydromex uses the ESMF Python bindings (ESMPy) for bilinear regridding, helping to test and strengthen shared spatial remapping capabilities within the broader UFS Coastal framework. We also discuss our experience developing the package alongside terminal-based AI coding agents. AI coding agents were used throughout development to assist with software implementation, testing, and documentation. This approach supported development of the package, including architectural decision records, core data transformations, pipeline orchestration, and a comprehensive test suite. We will present package performance, regression testing against S-104 and S-111 test-bed datasets generated by existing command-line workflows, and lessons learned from applying AI tools to operational oceanographic software.

494976.title: Evaluating the Performance of the MPAS-JEDI System in Taiwan Using Observations from the TAHOPE (2022) Field Campaign
494976.authors: Kuan-Jen Lin, National Central University, Taoyuan City, Taiwan, Taiwan; and S. C. Yang and Y. P. Chang
494976.abstract: The Model for Prediction Across Scales coupled with the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (MPAS-JEDI) represents a new generation of numerical weather prediction systems. MPAS is designed to better capture multi-scale dynamic and thermodynamic interactions through its variable mesh structure, while the JEDI framework offers a highly flexible and modular infrastructure capable of integrating diverse observation types across global and regional scales. Previous studies have demonstrated the capability of the MPAS-JEDI system for global data assimilation and prediction at relatively coarse resolution. However, its performance regarding regional severe weather systems has yet to be thoroughly investigated. Therefore, this study conducts high-resolution experiments during the Taiwan-Area Heavy Rain Observation and Prediction Experiment (TAHOPE) field campaign in 2022. The severe weather events and dense observational network during TAHOPE provide an excellent opportunity to further evaluate the capabilities of MPAS-JEDI at the regional scale. The observations assimilated in this study include conventional data, such as radiosondes, surface stations, Atmospheric Motion Vectors (AMVs), aircraft reports, and GNSS-RO. In addition, remote sensing observations—including clear-sky and all-sky AMSU-A satellite radiances, as well as ground-based radar data in Taiwan—are also assimilated. Results indicate that the assimilation of all-sky AMSU-A data increases moisture from the surface to the mid-atmosphere, significantly reducing the dry bias and improving rainfall precipitation forecasts in Taiwan. Furthermore, the additional assimilation of radar radial wind and reflectivity data helps to better capture the detailed kinematic and thermodynamic structures of coastal rainbands. These findings highlight the value of the MPAS-JEDI framework for advancing regional severe weather prediction.

494977.title: Solar Energetic Particle Impacts on a Spacecraft Memory Register
494977.authors: Dimitrios Vassiliadis, NOAA, Rockville, MD; and P. Baltimore, D. Binkley, M. Devaney, D. Larson, A. Rahmati, A. Boudouridis, B. Kress, J. V. Rodriguez, R. Torbert, I. Dors, I. Azeem, J. Gronert, and M. Dahya
494977.abstract: NOAA’s Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1 (SOLAR-1) was launched on September 24, 2025 and declared operational on June 10, 2026. The spacecraft carries in situ instrumentation for measuring several heliospheric variables at its orbit around the Sun-Earth Lagrange 1 point (L1) including the SupraThermal Ion Sensor (STIS) measuring both ions (<6 MeV) and electrons (< 300 keV), and a suite of two fluxgate magnetometer sensors (MAG). One of the MAG memory registers is sensitive to high fluxes of suprathermal and energetic particles. There is no impact on the measurement accuracy or any other performance metric of the instrument. We report correlations between the register anomalies as they are reported in SOLAR-1 Error Detection And Correction (EDAC) tables and particle fluxes. For suprathermal particles we have used the STIS ion and electron measurements while for energetic particles we have used the 10-MeV and higher-energy proton measurements by the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite-19 (GOES-19) / Solar and Galactic Proton Sensor (SGPS). We discuss the impact of recent events including the solar radiation storms in 2025 (November 12-13) and 2026 (January 19, March 30, and June 30). Real-time SOLAR-1 and GOES data are available from NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC, https://spaceweather.gov). Archived versions of all environmental SOLAR-1 and GOES-19 data are available from the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) Space Weather Portal (SPOT, https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cloud-access/space-weather-portal/).

494978.title: Probabilistic Cloud Nowcast-to-Forecast Blending
494978.authors: James P Gibbons, MyRadar, Arlington, VA; and R. Lagerquist, I. L. McConnell, A. J. Wimmers, and S. Garimella
494978.abstract: Extrapolatory nowcasting provides high spatiotemporal resolution predictions, but quickly loses skill as lead time increases. Numerical forecasts suffer from spin-up issues, have poor skill in the first few hours, and forecast at resolutions too coarse to directly resolve many cloud processes. Combining the strengths of both nowcasting and forecasting can yield an integrated forecast that is skillful in both the nowcast range (nominally the next 3 hours) and the short forecast range (nominally 6+ hours). Many existing methods result in artifacts, unnatural motion, or an inability to model non-linear evolution realistically. There remains a need to improve skill in the intermediate range of 3–6 hours, provide a seamless transition between the nowcasting and forecasting regimes, and generally extend the skillful lead times of cloud forecasts. We propose a novel blending approach using deep-learning techniques. Our deterministic model has been extended into a probabilistic framework, using stochastic decomposition layers (SDLs; Schreck et al. 2025) to generate ensemble members and a latent processor architecture (Du et al. 2025) to forecast out to arbitrary lead times. This approach focuses on cloud properties, adaptively combining a nowcast of geostationary cloud retrievals and the GFS forecast of cloud fraction. We compare against a reduced-space ensemble Kalman filter method (EnKF; Nerini et. al 2019) at intermediate lead times and GFS at 6+ hour lead times. We provide a thorough evaluation of our approach via traditional regression metrics, spectral analyses, empirical CDFs, spread-skill ratio, CRPS/CRPSS, and rank histograms to assess ensemble calibration, and pooled spatial metrics (e.g., energy score) to evaluate spatial coherence of ensemble members. Evaluations at intermediate lead times of 3-6 hours will be compared against optical flow and the EnKF method. Extended lead times will be compared against GFS.

494980.title: Modeling Temporal Dependence and Dynamic Uncertainty In Ensemble Predictions of Tropical Cyclone Track and Intensity
494980.authors: Jonathan Martinez, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and A. Brammer, M. DeMaria, K. Musgrave, P. Santos, and D. A. Zelinsky
494980.abstract: The National Hurricane Center (NHC) Wind Speed Probability (WSP) model comprises 1000 ensemble members (realizations) of track, intensity, and wind radii predictions generated via Monte Carlo simulation. Previous work has demonstrated that individual ensemble members in WSP often exhibit unrealistic temporal variability that results in “jagged” trajectories. Furthermore, the ensemble track predictions in WSP comprise a crude representation of dynamic (situation-dependent) uncertainty, and there is currently no methodology implemented in WSP to account for dynamic uncertainty in its ensemble predictions of either intensity or wind radii. This study documents potential advancements to the Monte Carlo simulation framework underlying WSP that explicitly model temporal dependence and provide the foundation for modeling dynamic uncertainty. A brief overview of the autoregressive-like Monte Carlo sampling procedure for generating ensemble predictions of track and intensity in WSP will be provided, and the limitations of this approach will be highlighted. Ensemble predictions of track and intensity in WSP will be considered independently. To rectify the jagged behavior among individual track realizations and enable modeling dynamic uncertainty, the WSP framework for Monte Carlo simulation is reformulated with a multivariate normal sampling procedure. Through this framework, the underlying marginal distributions at each forecast hour are coupled through the prescribed multivariate normal distribution and thus conserved. Rectifying the jagged behavior among individual intensity realizations requires additional considerations given that marginal distributions of intensity forecast errors often exhibit non-normal characteristics such as skewness and heavy tails. A Monte Carlo simulation framework to generate intensity realizations that conserves arbitrary distributions while modeling temporal dependence and dynamic uncertainty will be discussed. A case study demonstrating temporally smooth trajectories and dynamic uncertainty will be shown for both track and intensity ensemble predictions generated from sampling error distributions predicted by the Tropical Cyclone Artificial Neural-network Error (TCANE) model. Bulk ensemble track and intensity verification measures will be shown for a three-year period to assess the performance of the expanded Monte Carlo simulation frameworks. Considerations will be given towards generating wind radii perturbations with the generalized framework for generating intensity perturbations. Furthermore, generating cross-correlated intensity and wind radii perturbations via Monte Carlo simulation will be discussed as the basis for unified wind and surge hazard products.

494982.title: Coronal and Solar Wind Activity In the Descending Phase of SC25: SOLAR-1
494982.authors: Dimitrios Vassiliadis, NOAA, Rockville, MD; and R. Ebert, D. Larson, A. Thernisien, R. Torbert, M. Aubrey, M. Burek, J. Johnson, N. Miles, G. Millward, M. Nakasone, A. Boudouridis, G. Dima, K. Horaites, N. Howard, F. Inceoglu, B. Kress, N. Merati, L. A. Rachmeler, R. Redmon, J. V. Rodriguez, W. Rowland, V. Salinas, D. J. Schmit, X. Wei, J. Carey, J. Declet, M. Devaney, M. Grotenhuis, J. Inskeep, J. Marshall, C. Merrow, and C. Pagan
494982.abstract: NOAA’s Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1 (SOLAR-1) was launched to the Sun-Earth Lagrange 1 point (L1) on September 24, 2025 and declared operational on June 10, 2026. On the same day, the Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) designated the mission as its primary solar wind monitor and started releasing real-time data (https://www.spaceweather.gov/products/solar-wind). The primary objective of the mission is to supply operational solar-coronal images and in situ solar-wind data to SWPC forecasters and to other users and thereby continue a long record of operationally used NOAA and NASA measurements from L1. This presentation will share several operationally-relevant highlights of the mission in its first year. These include CCOR-2 (coronagraph) observations of CMEs such as the January 18-19 and June 30 full-halo events, the March 30 fast CME, and others that produced strong or severe solar radiation storms and/or geomagnetic storms. In situ measurements from the three instruments for plasma (SWiPS), suprathermal particles (STIS), and IMF (MAG) have been useful for situational awareness and for driving geospace models at SWPC and other forecast centers. The program’s data products will be described, including types and levels, formats, latency, and documentation. Finally, the presentation will describe how users can access the data products, including the repository for real-time data at the Space Weather Prediction Center (https://spaceweather.gov) and the Space Weather Portal for archived data (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cloud-access/space-weather-portal/) at the National Centers for Environmental Information.

494984.title: GeoXO Sounder (GXS) Spectral Stability Assessment Including MTG IRS Data
494984.authors: Owen McElhinney, MIT Lincoln Laboratory, Lexington, MA
494984.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA’s) Geostationary eXtended Observations (GeoXO) series satellites are planned to follow the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES)-R series satellites in 2032 and beyond. GeoXO will provide the nation with continuity of environmental imagery over the western hemisphere. The GeoXO Sounder (GXS) will provide level 1b calibrated and navigated radiances in the midwave infrared (MWIR) and the longwave infrared (LWIR). The level 1b data will be used for vertical profile retrievals of atmospheric temperature and moisture. GXS data and associated retrievals will not only be employed by National Weather Service (NWS) forecasters in near real time but also will be used for numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. For NWP to fully utilize GXS data, the GXS spectral information must be precisely captured and spectrally corrected, as needed, for any instrument artifacts to provide a fixed spectral grid that is uniform over the full field of view and is temporally stable. A soft correction for spectrally oversampled systems that is based on the weighted sum of spectral samples is being employed for GXS to correct optical aberrations for a uniform spectral grid. Previous work discussed analysis of a scan procedure that enhanced the performance of this spectral correction by observing the same ground spot across the full field of view. This paper presents the results of simulated correction performance with inclusion of operational considerations. Results will employ simulated GXS observations using data from the Meteosat Third Generation IR Sounder (MTG-IRS) to further demonstrate the validity of the spectral correction method incorporating additional data and detector fidelity. DISTRIBUTION STATEMENT A. Approved for public release. Distribution is unlimited. This material is based upon work supported by the Department of Commerce under Air Force Contract No. FA8702-15-D-0001 or FA8702-25-D-B002. Any opinions, findings, conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of the Department of Commerce.

494985.title: Overview and Observed Storm Mode Diversity from the SNOWSCAPE Field Campaign
494985.authors: Nicholas Dawson, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and P. Brooks, A. Dugger, P. Golden, A. G. Hallar, J. D. Horel, J. Jennings, G. G. Mace, J. D. D. Meyer, B. Pokharel, M. Skiles, A. Dobracki, A. M. Stansfield, J. Steenburgh, S. A. Tessendorf, P. G. Veals, and D. Yorty
494985.abstract: Understanding the aerosol and microphysical processes that govern winter orographic precipitation and its transition to snowpack and runoff is essential for building water resource resiliency across the Interior West. The Seeded and Natural Orographic Winter Storms and Catchment Processes Evaluation (SNOWSCAPE) Project is a multi-institution field campaign addressing this need. Conducted in Utah's northern Wasatch Mountains by a consortium including NSF NCAR, the University of Utah, Utah State University, Rainmaker Technology Corporation, and the Utah Division of Water Resources, SNOWSCAPE ran its Special Observing Period from January 7 to March 6, 2026, executing 11 Intensive Observing Periods (IOPs), nine of which were seeded. The campaign deployed two dual-polarization X-band radars sited windward and leeward of the barrier with intersecting coverage along the southwesterly flow axis that prevails during precipitation. Additional observations include microwave radiometers, backscatter and depolarization ceilometers, radiosondes, micro rain radars, aerosol and ice-nucleating particle instrumentation, and snowpack and streamflow monitoring. Scientific objectives span four themes: aerosol-cloud-precipitation interactions, microphysical contrasts between seeded and natural precipitation including supercooled liquid water availability, hydrological responses to snowfall modification, and advancement of coupled WRF-WxMod and WRF-Hydro simulations through observation-driven evaluation. Initial review indicates convective and mixed convective-stratiform structures were common, with three IOPs producing lightning. Shallow post-frontal convection produced graupel and rimed snow under weak synoptic forcing. Several events were moisture-limited, with dry sub-cloud layers producing virga. We review campaign design, observing strategy, and execution, and present an observationally based storm mode classification with implications for seeding dispersion and model evaluation.

494986.title: Evaluation of CMIP6 Model Soil Moisture Performance for Environmental Assessment
494986.authors: Jacklynn K. Beck, Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS; and S. M. Quiring
494986.abstract: Soil moisture is a critical indicator of hydroclimatic extremes and plays an important role in land–atmosphere interactions, ecosystem dynamics, wildfire activity, extreme heat, and severe weather. As a result, soil moisture projections from global climate models are increasingly used to assess how environmental systems may respond to climate change. However, substantial differences among models can introduce uncertainty into these assessments. Model selection strategies range from comparing modeled soil moisture against observations to averaging all models together, but model selection strategies vary considerably and may not account for spatial and seasonal differences in model performance. This study evaluates the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project – Phase 6 (CMIP6) soil moisture performance across the contiguous United States (CONUS) to identify models best suited for environmental applications. We assess 19 CMIP6 models against an observationally based soil moisture dataset and evaluate model performance across multiple CONUS ecoregions.

494987.title: H3lioViz: Successes and Challenges in the Research to Operations to Research Transition of a 3D Heliosphere Visualization Tool
494987.authors: Christopher Pankratz, LASP - Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, Univ. of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and J. Knuth, E. Adamson, G. Lucas, B. McClellan, K. Brooks, and A. Ware
494987.abstract: H3lioViz is a three-dimensional visualization tool developed at the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics (LASP), funded in part by NASA Research to Operations to Research (R2O2R) grants and built through direct collaboration between developers, researchers, and forecasters. This presentation offers H3lioViz as a case study in both the successes and the challenges of the R2O2R model. H3lioViz visualizes output from ENLIL, a three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic model of solar wind and coronal mass ejection propagation through the heliosphere. ENLIL produces a full three-dimensional solution, but most operational displays in use today present two-dimensional slices of that output. H3lioViz makes the complete three-dimensional output available to forecasters and researchers, rendering fields such as solar wind density and velocity throughout the volume. Slices along the ecliptic and meridional planes do not always reveal glancing blows, near misses, or conditions along spacecraft trajectories outside those planes. A coronal mass ejection centered at some angle off the ecliptic can still reach Earth as these structures tend to be rather expansive and their leading edge widens with distance, and a two-dimensional view can obscure that outcome. H3lioViz presents the full model volume from any viewing angle, and it can show time series plots of model variables at selected locations. Forecasters can assess whether an off-ecliptic disturbance will reach Earth or another body, rather than inferring impact from two planar cuts. The tool also can compare model output with in-situ measurements, a capability especially valuable to researchers. H3lioViz is now transitioning into operations at NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) after a successful period of co-production. SWPC personnel continue to shape the production version, and the refinements developed for that version, including workflow improvements and backend performance gains, extend to a free community version that is available at https://swx-trec.com/h3lioviz. The community version ingests SWPC-generated runs as each completes. It runs in a standard web browser and requires no installation, data transfers, specialized hardware, logins, or registration, which keeps it open to the broader research and forecasting community. The development approach behind H3lioViz has been co-production: forecasters and researchers work directly with developers during design and testing, rather than receiving a tool designed separately and then handed over. This approach helped produce a tool aligned with forecasting needs and has drawn continued interest from forecasting centers and from researchers. Co-production is a central success, and it is the practice we advocate for developers building tools intended either for community use or for transition into operations. Co-production resembles the widely used Agile software engineering methodology, which advocates frequent interaction between developers and stakeholders. The transition also illustrated a challenge common to R2O2R efforts. Moving a validated research tool into sustained operations often depends on support directed at the transition itself, a stage that falls between programs oriented toward research and programs oriented toward operations. Recognizing and planning for that stage early, alongside the operational partners who will maintain the tool, can be as important to a successful transition as the underlying research and development. Tools like H3lioViz illustrate how sustained collaboration among developers, researchers, and forecasters can produce space weather capabilities suited to community use, and they inform the successes and challenges that others undertaking R2O2R efforts may encounter.

494996.title: Evaluating Governance Approaches to Support Federal Open Science and Public Data Access In Commercial Cloud Including Institutional Roles & Cost Responsibility
494996.authors: Joseph Fillingham, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and T. Lavoi
494996.abstract: Open data is fundamental to scientific collaboration, innovation, and economic growth, yet the implementation costs for open science standards remain poorly understood and are not always prioritized as a critical element of scientific investments. Commercial cloud storage and cloud-optimized data formats significantly enhance data reuse and efficiency across the atmospheric and Earth system modeling enterprise, however, federal mandates for rapid cloud migration introduce new governance and management challenges. As infrastructure transitions from on-premises systems, where public access costs are relatively low and well understood, to commercial cloud storage, compute, and high-performance computing (HPC) frameworks, the financial burden of accessibility can become prohibitive for legacy public access strategies. Federal agencies must now build on the success of limited scale programs, such as the NOAA Open Data Dissemination, or sole reliance on federal archive centers, for public access to sustainable enterprise frameworks and cost models in partnership with Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) that meet federal budget requirements and public access mandates. This presentation will explore four possible approaches to cost responsibility, institutional roles, and data governance to support open science principals for federal Earth science data in commercial cloud: 1) a comprehensive federal approach providing free public access, compute, and egress; 2) a cost-sharing model where federal agencies recover compute and egress expenses from either specific user groups or all users; 3) a CSP-managed framework where service providers oversee cost recovery; and 4) a third-party investment model leveraging philanthropies or non-profit endowments to subsidize community access. Each framework will be analyzed for its legal complexities, impacts on research and development across the weather enterprise, and the inter-agency and cross-sector collaborations necessary to resolve the governance challenges inherent in a rapidly modernizing federal data landscape.

494997.title: Toward a Best View of Severe Convective Storm Risk in the United States: Reconciling Catastrophe Models with Decades of Insured Hail Losses
494997.authors: Mark Ma, Mercury Insurance Services, LLC, Brea, CA; and J. Sheng, T. Ivancic, S. Levy, S. Purpura, M. Tran, S. Bennett, C. Rencurrel, J. Stephens, K. Shukla, D. Costello, W. Henry, F. Hedayati, and O. Payne
494997.abstract: Severe convective storms (SCS) — and hail in particular — have emerged as a leading driver of insured losses in the United States. Catastrophe models are the industry standard for quantifying this risk, yet they are necessarily refined to broad industry experience, and individual portfolios can exhibit meaningful differences from modeled expectations due to local exposure characteristics, building stock, and spatial concentration. This presentation develops a "best view" of SCS hail risk engine by integrating three complementary sources of information: a commercial catastrophe model, long-term hail observation and tracking, and decades of claims experience. We further outline a validation framework in which modeled hail hazard is benchmarked against independent ground observations and successive model refinements are evaluated against portfolio- and community-level loss experience. Special attention is given to the methodological challenges involved: placing historical claims on a like-for-like basis with model output, distinguishing spatial pattern from absolute level in hazard calibration, and recognizing what decades sample can and cannot say about tail risk. We conclude with perspectives on how meteorological observations, vendor models, and portfolio experience can be transparently combined — each contributing its distinct strength — into a scientifically defensible view of U.S. SCS risk, and on the broader opportunities for the meteorological community to support this integration.

494998.title: Instructor-Assessed Student Severe Storms Knowledge Gains from Field Work Often Exceed Self-Reported Gains
494998.authors: Robin Tanamachi, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN; and L. Carleton Parker, D. T. Dawson II, and M. Couillard
494998.abstract: Previously, we reported quantitative survey findings from the Students of Purdue Observing Tornadic Thunderstorms for Research (SPOTTR) 2023-2025 cohorts across constructs related to field work and careers. In that work, Likert scale responses were used to demonstrate medium to large knowledge gains. In this work, we analyze students’ pre- and post-course responses to the seven-question severe storms “concepts and context” inventory of Barrett and Woods (2012). Substantial knowledge gains are observed across the items queried, including large normalized gains on items specific to supercell structure and environments. Preliminary results indicate that students’ instructor-assessed knowledge gains are often larger than those self-reported by students on other parts of the survey. We hypothesize that students overestimate their pre-course severe storms knowledge, and assess themselves more accurately post-course. Implications for severe storms field work course design and assessment will be offered.

494999.title: Attribution of Precipitation Persistence Through Land-Atmosphere Coupling Regimes
494999.authors: Joshua K. Roundy, Univ. of Kansas, Lawrence, KS; and K. L. Findell and H. Hsu
494999.abstract: Extreme precipitation events have devastating impacts on many aspects of society, ranging from recreational to water and food supply, and ultimately result in significant socioeconomic losses. The ability to understand and predict extreme precipitation would allow for preparations that would reduce the severity of the impacts. While ocean sources of predictability exist at various timescales (i.e., NAO), interannual (i.e., ENSO), decadal (i.e., PDO), and multi-decadal (i.e., AMO) timescales, these oceanic sources of predictability are inherently weaker at S2S timescales. Especially during the warm season when land surface heating heterogeneity affects large-scale temperature and pressure gradients through land-atmosphere interactions. A long research history has shown the influence of soil moisture on the evolution of the boundary layer and the initiation of convection. The work of Findell and Eltahir demonstrated the preferential tendency for convective rainfall over wet (wet advantage) versus dry soils (dry advantage), depending on low-level atmospheric humidity (HI) and atmospheric instability (i.e., Convective Triggering Potential, CTP). This work was based on a combination of observations and modeling framework over the United States. This CTP-HI framework later became the basis for creating the Coupling Drought Index (CDI), which uses a data-driven approach to define global coupling regimes unique for each location. While the CDI and CTP-HI framework are similar, there are fundamental differences that have never been assessed on a global scale. Our primary research question is: Do both methods for defining the L-A coupling regimes show similar attribution between atmospheric and land-surface sources for the future occurrence of precipitation? To answer this question, we compare both methods for defining the coupling regimes and the resulting predictability of future gage-based precipitation through a hindcast experiment from 1980-2023. We also explore the sensitivity of the results to the choice of reanalysis data used to calculate the CTP and HI and discuss future work to better understand the preferential tendency for convective rainfall over dry and wet soils on a global scale.

495001.title: Biological Aerosol Impacts on Aerosol Budget and Cloud Microphysics over Bankhead National Forest
495001.authors: Tamanna Subba, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY; and A. L. Steiner, M. A. Zawadowicz, A. Singh, N. N. Lata, J. Cheng, G. Vandergrift, M. Guagenti, A. Rahman, D. Dexheimer, C. Longbottom, G. Whitson, C. Ruiz, S. Serbin, S. Giangrande, S. China, and C. Kuang
495001.abstract: Biological aerosols remain a poorly constrained component of aerosol-cloud interactions in Earth system models. Pollen, a major class of primary biological aerosol particles (PBAPs), can rupture to form smaller sub-pollen particles (SPPs), substantially altering aerosol number, size, mass, cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) concentrations, and cloud-relevant properties. We combine observations from the U.S. Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) user Facility at Bankhead National Forest (BNF), Alabama, with high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled with Chemistry (WRF-Chem) simulations to investigate potential pollen events (PPEs), interannual variability, vertical transport, aerosol and CCN responses, and associated cloud impacts during spring 2025 and 2026. PPEs occurred on up to ~40% of days and were more frequent and intense in 2025. Interannual differences indicate that growing degree days, boundary-layer evolution, humidity, winds, and vertical motion strongly regulate pollen release, rupture, and atmospheric transport. Observations and simulations show that pollen and SPPs can be transported several kilometers vertically, contributing to aerosol populations above the boundary layer. WRF-Chem sensitivity experiments include a no-pollen control, a primary-pollen-only case, and rupture cases producing 103 and 105 SPPs per ruptured primary pollen grain. Simulations indicate that pollen rupture modifies accumulation-mode particle number concentrations, PM10, and the condensation sink, with the largest enhancements near the surface and increased mid-level variability during vertical transport. Enhanced SPP production also alters CCN concentrations across multiple supersaturations and affects warm-cloud microphysics, reducing low-level cloud water while increasing rainwater below ~3-4 km. Ice-phase hydrometeors are redistributed aloft rather than uniformly enhanced, consistent with downstream responses to changes in CCN activation, liquid-cloud processing, and vertical transport. Overall, these results demonstrate that meteorology and pollen processing jointly regulate biological aerosol impacts on overall aerosol budget and regional aerosol-cloud interactions.

495002.title: Statistical Characteristics of Bolt-from-the-Blue Lightning and Their Implications for Lightning Hazard Area Delineation in Japan
495002.authors: Namiko Sakurai, National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience, Tsukuba, Ibaraki, Japan; National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience (NIED), Tsukuba, Ibaraki, Japan; and S. Shimizu, K. Shimose, R. Kato, A. Miyajima, and T. MAESAKA
495002.abstract: Bolt-from-the-blue (BFB) lightning is a cloud-to-ground discharge that strikes outside areas of surface rainfall, posing a particular hazard because the absence of rain may lead people to underestimate the lightning risk. To characterize BFBs in Japan and explore practical approaches for defining BFB warning areas, we analyzed 10 days with active lightning in the Kanto region during the summers of 2020 and 2022 using the Tokyo Lightning Mapping Array (LMA), Japanese Lightning Detection Network (JLDN), eXtended Radar Information Network (XRAIN), and Multi-Parameter Phased Array Weather Radar (MP-PAWR). We defined rain areas as regions near the surface with rainfall intensities of 1 mm h⁻¹ or more and identified 243 negative-polarity cloud-to-ground lightning strokes outside these areas. These strokes were grouped into 69 lightning flashes, accounting for multiple strokes within a single flash. Examination of their three-dimensional discharge paths using the LMA confirmed all 69 flashes as BFBs. All BFB flashes originated from regions with vertically integrated ice (VII), suggesting a relationship between BFB occurrence and regions containing substantial amounts of ice aloft. Although BFBs occurred outside the rain areas, most were located relatively close to their boundaries. For the 1, 10, and 20 mm h⁻¹ rain areas, 80% of BFBs occurred within 3, 4, and 5 km of the corresponding rain-area boundary, respectively, and 90% within 5, 6, and 7 km. In many cases, the distance from the BFB strike point to the VII region was smaller than that to the rain area, or the BFB strike point was located within the VII region itself. The results suggest that VII may provide additional information for identifying BFB-prone regions beyond surface rainfall. BFB leaders also showed directional variability among storms, with some preferentially propagating in a particular direction. The relationship between this directional variability and environmental wind conditions or the internal three-dimensional structure of thunderstorms remains to be clarified. The statistical characteristics identified in this study provide a basis for developing practical lightning risk information to support safer outdoor activities.

495004.title: Daily-to-Seasonal Boundary Layer and Cloud Cover Changes in the Baltimore Region
495004.authors: Sierra Robbin Hill, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and K. J. Davis, N. E. Prince, and D. Zhang
495004.abstract: The urban morphology of Baltimore, Maryland, poses a unique environment through which the atmospheric boundary layer dynamics and associated cloud formation interact. To explore this interaction, instruments were placed as part of the Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE) across the state of Maryland, United States, for one year, at one urban (M1), one rural (S2), and one coastal (S3) site. We use data from Doppler lidars and eddy-covariance flux towers deployed at all three sites, ceilometers deployed at the rural and urban sites, and radiosondes and a Ka-band radar deployed at the urban site. We analyze boundary layer height (BLH), cloud base height, and cloud fraction at all three sites. We show that the urban site experienced the highest average boundary layer heights over summer and spring during the early morning and late afternoon. The rural boundary layer was more stratified and shallower during the night at all times of year when compared to the urban or coastal boundary layers. These patterns are broadly consistent with the surface fluxes observed at each site. The non-urban sites show two distinct areas of higher frequencies of boundary layer cloud base height during the afternoon, one “low” at 500 meters, and one “high” at 2000 meters during the summer season. Comparatively, the urban site shows the presence of a continuous sequence of boundary layer cloud base heights as the afternoon progresses. Boundary layer cloud cover is more stratiform in the winter and thickest at the rural site, and follows the pattern of daily convective boundary layer growth in the summer. Lastly, the rural site shows higher rates of fog and low-level cloud fractions during the summer when compared to the urban and coastal sites. Future work will explore the dependence of these differences on syntopic state. These results will provide a benchmark for evaluation of numerical simulations of the urban atmospheric environment, which is essential for improving numerical weather prediction over complex coastal urban areas.

495005.title: Act Quickly to Protect Your Life: Understanding Protective Action Decisions During Flash Flood Warnings
495005.authors: Katy Herber, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Pflugerville, TX; and D. M. Kopacz
495005.abstract: On July 4th, 2025, torrential rainfall impacted the Texas Hill Country and surrounding area known as Flash Flood Alley. The Guadalupe River reached major flood stage, resulting in 137 deaths in Texas, 119 of whom were in Kerr County (Galarneau Jr. et al., 2026). The event highlighted the importance of understanding how residents interpret and respond to National Weather Service (NWS) flash flood products, including Flash Flood Warnings and a Flash Flood Emergency. Prior survey studies have examined public perception and comprehension of flash flood warnings, highlighting the need to better understand the factors that influence protective action decisions and the importance of engaging communities in efforts to improve flash flood risk communication (Morss et al., 2016). This study investigates how Kerr County, TX residents interpret NWS flash flood products and what factors influence protective action decisions. To achieve these goals, a survey was developed using the Protective Action Decision Model (Lindell & Perry, 2011), which provides a framework for understanding how individuals interpret hazard information and subsequent protective action intentions. Survey questions examine access to and trust in sources of flood information, perceptions of expertise and responsibility among information providers, information-seeking behavior, protective action intentions in response to three NWS flash flood products representing increasing levels of threat severity, evaluations of warning clarity, content, and usefulness, and demographic information. Paper surveys were mailed to 1500 randomly selected addresses in Kerr County, Texas in July 2026. There was an option to complete the survey online in case multiple people in a household wanted to complete the survey. This study will provide insight into how residents interpret NWS flash flood products and what factors influence protective action decisions. By examining how people respond to multiple flash flood products, this research addresses a key challenge in the forecast-to-decision pathway: understanding how people translate hazard information into protective action. The survey instrument developed for this project can be adapted to other communities to investigate hazard communication, public decision-making, and community-centered warning design. Findings will help identify opportunities to better align NWS flash flood products with the decision-making needs of at-risk communities. References: Galarneau, T. J., J. T. Carlin, R. A. Clark, J. J. Gourley, and J. Zhang, 2026: Hydrometeorological Analysis of the July 2025 Texas Hill Country Flash Flood Disaster. Bull. Amer. Meteor. Soc., , BAMS-D-25- 0227.1, https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-25-0227.1, in press. Lindell, M. K., & Perry, R. W. (2011). The Protective Action Decision Model: Theoretical Modifications and Additional Evidence. Risk Analysis, 32(4), 616–632. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1539-6924.2011.01647.x Morss, R. E., Mulder, K. J., Lazo, J. K., & Demuth, J. L. (2016). How do people perceive, understand, and anticipate responding to flash flood risks and warnings? Results from a public survey in Boulder, Colorado, USA. Journal of Hydrology, 541, 649–664. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2015.11.047

495006.title: Advancing Global Weather Services Through Public-Private Collaboration: Lessons from the Met Office and Synoptic Data
495006.authors: Elizabeth Anne Wilson, Synoptic Data PBC, Raleigh, NC
495006.abstract: National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs) increasingly rely on observations from diverse public, private, academic, and community-operated networks to enhance forecasting, situational awareness, and decision support. As the number of available observing systems continues to grow, so do the challenges of discovering, evaluating, integrating, and operationally managing these heterogeneous data sources while maintaining the quality, reliability, and governance required for mission-critical forecasting. This presentation examines the collaboration between the Met Office and Synoptic Data to modernize the Met Office's Third Party Observation Data Service (3PODS). As operational observing systems continue to expand, the Met Office is modernizing its 3PODS to improve the discovery, evaluation, integration, and operational use of observations from diverse external providers. The project provides a practical example of how public-private collaboration can strengthen operational weather services while allowing each organization to contribute complementary expertise. Observations are the backbone of weather forecasting, situational awareness, and warning support for meteorology operations. Drawing on the operational forecasting expertise of the Met Office and Synoptic's experience integrating observations from diverse environmental monitoring networks, this presentation will share best practices for governance, data stewardship, quality assurance, operational integration, public-private collaboration, and scalable approaches to incorporating third-party observations into national forecasting operations. Examples will be provided that demonstrate improved situational awareness, better public forecasts, and more informed decision-making across economic sectors. Rather than focusing solely on technical implementation, the presentation will highlight the collaborative framework that enabled the project, including shared responsibilities and trust between public and private partners. The lessons learned provide a practical model for other NMHSs seeking to modernize observation systems while maintaining operational reliability, transparency, and scientific integrity.

495007.title: Assessing the Impact of Lower-Atmospheric Wave Forcing on Reentry Prediction in Very Low Earth Orbit
495007.authors: Emmett Peters, CU Boulder, Boulder, CO
495007.abstract: The thermosphere is strongly influenced by a combination of solar, magnetospheric, lower-atmospheric forcing. While the impact of solar and geomagnetic drivers on thermospheric density variability is well established, the influence of lower-atmospheric processes, including atmospheric tides, remains comparatively understudied. Because of increased drag sensitivity in Very Low Earth orbit (VLEO), density variability due to atmospheric waves propagating up from the lower and middle atmosphere is likely a critical factor in orbit and reentry prediction particularly during solar minimum and geomagnetically quiet periods. This study quantitatively assesses the impact of lower-atmospheric waves on reentry prediction over the October 2019 - December 2021 period, encompassing mostly geomagnetically quiet conditions under quiet solar conditions. The period overlaps with the NASA Ionospheric Connection Explorer (ICON) mission. Using the atmospheric density fields simulated by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model with thermosphere and ionosphere extension, specified dynamics (WACCM-X SD), reentry trajectories are propagated from the final Two-Line Element (TLE) epoch reported in Tracking and Impact Prediction (TIP) messages. Predicted reentry times are evaluated against reported reentry times, with reentry prediction performance assessed across season and levels of geomagnetic activity. The analysis furthermore determines when and where realistic lower-atmospheric wave forcing in atmospheric density models leads to meaningful improvements in reentry timing predictions relative to empirical density models that do not account for wave forcing. The study provides guidance to space situational awareness and space domain awareness (SSA/SDA) operations when computationally intensive physics-based atmospheric models are warranted over more computationally efficient empirical models for reentry prediction.

495008.title: The Importance of Hyperlocal Meteorological Variables for Assessments of Urban Heat Stress (Invited) (Invited Presentation)
495008.authors: Sarah Berk, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; and T. Chakraborty, A. Hsu, S. Li, and X. Li
495008.abstract: Most assessments of urban heat exposure tend to focus primarily on air temperature as the predominant driver of heat stress. However, human heat stress is also influenced by humidity, radiation, and wind. These can vary substantially within an urban environment and work together to either amplify or reduce overall heat stress. Here, we examine the importance of representing hyperlocal spatial variability of air temperature and relative humidity for estimates of comprehensive heat stress in Durham, North Carolina. High-resolution (10 m) hourly air temperature and relative humidity gridded datasets were developed using observations from a stratified network of 41 sensors combined with a machine learning approach. These meteorological fields were then used as inputs to the SOlar and LongWave Environmental Irradiance Geometry (SOLWEIG) model to simulate mean radiant temperature (MRT) and the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI). Simulations using spatially varying meteorological inputs were compared with simulations using a spatially uniform, single city-wide value for air temperature and relative humidity, often used in the SOLWEIG literature due to data availability, to quantify how representing hyperlocal meteorological variability influences modeled heat stress. Results demonstrate that considering only air temperature or radiant heat exposure in isolation may misrepresent urban heat stress, particularly in cities with high humidity. Urban areas with higher air temperatures and MRT often have lower relative humidity, partially offsetting their influence on UTCI. Differences in MRT are strongly associated with differences in UTCI, but this relationship weakens under high-humidity conditions, highlighting the importance of considering high-resolution relative humidity measurements, alongside these other components of heat stress. These findings demonstrate that incorporating hyperlocal spatial information and interactions among meteorological variables provides a more complete characterization of human heat stress. Moreover, this spatially comprehensive approach can improve identification of locations and populations experiencing the greatest heat burden, assessed using socioeconomic data.

495014.title: Martian Winds from MRO and EMM Satellite Imagery for Dust Storm Investigations
495014.authors: Dean Klunk, Hampton University, Hampton, VA; and M. Friberg, M. A. Dorval, J. Carr, and H. Madani
495014.abstract: Direct, geographically distributed observations of Martian atmospheric motion remain too sparse to determine how regional circulation changes during dust-storm growth, persistence, and decay. This project will apply and characterize an emerging multi-view MARCI/EXI retrieval framework for quality-controlled regional dust-storm science. Multi-view satellite imagery from low-Earth and geostationary orbit has been utilized for Earth-based wind retrievals. With the Emirates Mars Mission’s (EMM) whole-disk view complementing Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s (MRO) close look, a similar wind retrieval done for Earth can be translated to the Martian atmosphere. The motivating science question of this project is: How do regional atmospheric dynamics change and affect the evolution of Martian dust-storms throughout their lifetimes? The first objective for this project to answer this question is to show initial results of MARCI/EXI derived Martian winds. This work will enable future dust-storm case study selection of regions across Mars with quality-screened wind data. The spatial and temporal coverage of multi-view imagery from MARCI and EXI will revolutionize dynamical study capabilities for the Martian atmosphere in ways previously restricted to Earth.

495015.title: Influence of ENSO Teleconnection on Surface Ozone Exceedances in Colorado’s Northern Front Range (1980-2024)
495015.authors: Joshua A Richards, Univ. of Maryland, Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; and G. A. Morris, I. Petropavlovskikh, and B. Demoz
495015.abstract: Ground-level ozone in Colorado’s Northern Front Range Metropolitan Area (NFRMA) remains in severe nonattainment of federal standards despite decades of anthropogenic emission regulations. While local emissions and complex terrain are known contributors, the role of large-scale climate modes in driving interannual ozone variability is less understood. This study investigated the influence of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) teleconnection on the timing, frequency, and meteorological drivers of ozone exceedances within the NFRMA. We utilized 45 years (1980-2024) of EPA surface ozone observations across six counties and collected ENSO phase classifications from the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI). The analysis integrated percentile trend analysis, synoptic typing via principal component analysis, and meteorological reanalysis to identify specific mechanisms of ozone enhancement and suppression. The analysis revealed that El Niño conditions shift the seasonal ozone peak from July to June, representing an earlier onset of the high-ozone season. During El Niño Junes, the frequency of exceedances above the 70 ppbv standard increased by 61.6% relative to neutral years. Meteorological data indicated this enhancement is driven by increased atmospheric stagnation and reduced synoptic ventilation, which favors the accumulation of ozone precursors. In contrast, El Niño Julys exhibited suppressed ozone levels due to cooler conditions and increased cloud cover. These findings demonstrate that ENSO exerts a marked influence on regional air quality, serving as a valuable tool for seasonal predictability and could provide insights to air quality mitigation strategies.

495018.title: On the Use of Tidal Information for Coastal Inundation Guidance in Microtidal Environments
495018.authors: Philippe E. Tissot, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX
495018.abstract: Relative sea level rise, the combination of land subsidence and sea level rise, continues to progressively change our seaward boundaries along the world’s coastlines. A growing impact is the increased frequency of coastal flooding leading impacted communities to look for guidance regarding both short term and long term predictions. Many coastal locations benefit from the presence of tide gauges from NOAA’s National Water Level Observation Network (NWLON) or state networks such as the Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON). In addition to these long term tide gauge networks, communities are increasingly installing lower cost water level sensors sourced from the private sector such as from Hohonu.io. Water level time series from these different sources allows for a much better monitoring of water levels around coastal inundation events. The time series also enable the computation of local tidal datums and tidal predictions which are very helpful for locations where tidal forcings represent a large component of the water level variability. This has allowed to share warnings of upcoming King Tides and the use of tidal information based dashboards. The importance of tidal information is however location dependent. For example, the Texas coast is microtidal with tidal ranges just below 1 foot on the Gulf coast and decreasing rapidly to half a foot or less when moving inland in bays and estuaries. The tidal influence completely disappears for water bodies such as the Laguna Madre. In such conditions, the tidal component can represent only a small fraction of the overall water level variability making the direct use of tidal predictions to predict coastal inundation events a poor choice. The seasonal and interannual variability of water levels along the Texas coast are also about a foot with their amplitude staying the same across coastal water bodies, tidal or non-tidal. Such information is more helpful to stakeholders and can be used in seasonal to subseasonal outlooks. Weather driven factors are however the larger drivers of coastal flooding in microtidal environments through wind driven set up or along shore currents or less directly through long period waves generated by more distant weather events. Short term predictions including weather drivers are essential for communities to prepare for such events although the seasonality of such events can also be communicated in flooding outlooks. Water level time series also allow for the computation of tidal datums used in different contexts such as Mean Lower Low Water (MLLW) used for navigation, Mean Sea Level (msl) used to track sea level rise, and Mean Higher High Water (MHHW) used land boundaries and increasingly as a warning level for the potential for coastal inundation. Similarly to tidal predictions, tidal datums are not a good indicator of the risk of coastal inundation along the microtidal Texas coast. An example will be shared for Port Aransas, Texas, where the MHHW is always under water or at least in the wet beach due to the local small tidal range and the importance of weather driven water level variability including wave runup. While the accuracy of computation of tidal predictions and tidal datums is not in question and these products provide enormous benefits to many communities, King Tides warning will not be of great use, and probably misleading, for microtidal locations with weather driven water level variability.

495019.title: Physical Sources of Subseasonal Predictability Uncovered in the Ai2 Climate Emulator
495019.authors: Marybeth Arcodia, RSMAS, Miami, FL; and S. Van Loon
495019.abstract: Recent breakthroughs in AI-based climate emulators enable century-scale simulations 100-1000x faster than traditional dynamical models, but their utility depends on capturing the predictable windows that inform critical decisions. By leveraging the Ai2 Climate Emulator (ACE2-ERA5), a neural network climate emulator trained on decades of historical reanalysis data, we generate thousands of climate simulations spanning 1941-2022. These ensembles encompass a range of climate states with sufficient sample sizes that allow for robust quantification of forecasts of opportunity, defined as predictions made during inherently more predictable climate states. Specifically, we focus on subseasonal temperature and precipitation predictability throughout the U.S., highlighting extreme heatwave, flooding, and drought events. Using explainable AI techniques, we validate whether ACE2-ERA5 represents physical processes, like tropical-extratropical teleconnections, consistent with theory and observations. This work assesses the trustworthiness of AI climate emulators through an intercomparison of subseasonal predictability sources in both AI-based and dynamical models, providing credibility for if AI climate emulators are not only accurately representing the climate system, but doing so for the right reasons. Our systematic approach to identifying forecasts of opportunity aims to provide scientific frameworks for understanding forecast confidence, ultimately translating prediction uncertainty into actionable guidance for water managers, agricultural planners, and emergency responders.

495022.title: Observational Evidence for Land-Cover Regulation of Heatwave Intensity Under Similar Synoptic Forcing
495022.authors: Yanjun Hu, Purdue University, WEST LAFAYETTE, IN; and L. Wang, L. Welp, M. Vermeuel, and D. Chavas
495022.abstract: Heatwave events are among the most impactful weather extremes, driven by large-scale atmospheric circulation and further intensified by land-atmosphere interactions. The land surface responds to atmospheric forcing but can also feed back to the atmosphere through land-atmosphere coupling, making it challenging to isolate the contribution of land processes alone to heatwave development. Several modeling studies have attempted to quantify the relative contributions of land-surface processes and overlying atmospheric circulation, while observational evidence remains limited. In this study, 22 pairs of FLUXNET sites with distinct land-cover types located no more than 100 km apart provide a natural experiment for isolating land-surface effects from synoptic-scale atmospheric forcing. Land-atmosphere interaction processes during heatwave events over these paired sites are analyzed. Results show significant differences in temperature anomalies between neighboring sites, with peak-day temperature anomaly differences exceeding the corresponding climatological temperature differences by as much as 1°C, as observed for the woody savanna-deciduous broadleaf forest pairs. Temperature anomaly differences are strongly correlated with differences in latent heat flux anomalies (r = −0.57), with the majority of site pairs exhibiting latent heat anomalies leading temperature anomalies, supporting a potential causal role of evaporative cooling in shaping land-cover temperature contrasts. In addition, where climatological temperature contrasts are already large, heatwaves tend to amplify them even further. Our findings provide observational evidence that land-cover heterogeneity regulates heatwave intensity after controlling for synoptic-scale atmospheric forcing.

495023.title: A Community Framework for Evaluating Subseasonal-to-Seasonal Forecast Applications: Metrics, Variables, and Data Requirements
495023.authors: Sanjiv Kumar, Auburn University, Auburn, AL
495023.abstract: Subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecasts provide critical information to support decision-making across application sectors including agriculture, water resources, energy, wildfire, public health, and hazard risk and disaster management. However, evaluation of S2S forecast systems has traditionally focused on the predictive skill of physical climate variables, with less attention to whether forecast information is usable for downstream applications and stakeholder decision-making. The rapid emergence of Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning-based S2S forecasting systems further increases the need for standardized, application-oriented evaluation approaches that assess both meteorological fidelity and downstream decision relevance. We present a community-informed framework for evaluating S2S forecasts in application contexts. The framework is informed by literature review, agency practices, international standards, community discussions, invited talks, and synthesis of inputs from S2S forecast developers, application researchers, and operational users. The framework links S2S forecasts to environmental variables, derived hazard indicators, impact models, and decision-relevant performance metrics. We organize evaluation approaches into a three-tier forecast-to-application structure. Tier 1 evaluates the fidelity of core S2S forecast variables using conventional deterministic and probabilistic metrics. Tier 2 translates forecast variables into derived hazard and impact-relevant indices, such as drought, heat-stress, fire-weather, snow-drought, and hydrologic indicators. Tier 3 evaluates sector-specific performance indicators tied to practical decision contexts, including crop stress, hydropower inflow, fire risk, water and energy management, heat exposure, and disaster preparedness. We also demonstrate implementation of the framework using U.S.-based S2S forecast models. The proposed framework provides a practical roadmap for advancing S2S forecast evaluation from traditional forecast skill assessment toward application utility and decision relevance.

495027.title: A Rigorous Spatial Upscaling Framework for Validating Satellite Passive Microwave Retrievals and Navy Models Using Airborne AMPR Data
495027.authors: Theodore M. McHardy, NRL, Monterey, CA; and E. K. Dolinar, T. J. Lang, and C. G. Amiot
495027.abstract: Satellite-borne passive microwave radiometers, such as AMSR2 and the GPM Microwave Imager (GMI), are critical tools for global observations of precipitation, atmospheric water vapor, and cloud liquid water. However, validating these satellite retrievals requires high-resolution, co-located measurements to account for significant sub-footprint spatial heterogeneity. This study utilizes multi-frequency airborne data from the Airborne Microwave Precipitation Radiometer (AMPR)—flown during the Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) campaign—to evaluate satellite Level 1B brightness temperatures, Level 2 environmental products, and operational Navy weather models. We’ve developed a highly configurable geospatial upscaling framework that accurately projects high-resolution AMPR measurements into coincident AMSR2 and GMI footprints. Utilizing precise elliptical footprint matching that accounts for satellite viewing geometry alongside strict temporal and data-quality filters, we generate robust statistical comparisons and bias distributions for both raw brightness temperatures (10–89 GHz) and derived Level 2 products. This approach provides a scalable method for assessing both satellite radiometer performance and model accuracy, highlighting the impacts of sub-pixel variability in remote sensing validation.

495030.title: Major Heat Waves over the United States and Europe During Summer 2026
495030.authors: Lance F. Bosart, University at Albany/SUNY, Albany, NY
495030.abstract: Impressive record-setting extreme waves characterized much summer 2026 over many parts of North America and Western Europe. The heat waves were notable both for their severity and their duration. July 2026 was the hottest month on record over the continental United States (CONUS) with an all-time record-breaking 76.9 F (24.9 C)......and the warmest month ever recorded in NOAA’s 132-year history (the previous hottest month on record was July 1936 during the dust bowl era when the average temperature was 76.8 F). In Europe, June 2026 was the hottest month on record. Temperatures frequently reached 40 C in many places. June 2026 was also the hottest month on record for Western Europe and the second warmest month globally. Likewise, sea surface temperatures were the highest on record globally during June 2026. The purpose of this presentation is to highlight both the summer 2026 extreme temperatures over the CONUS and Western Europe, and to discuss the configuration and evolution of the large-scale atmospheric flow patterns that facilitated the record heat.

495032.title: Bridging the Gap: NASA's Water Resources Program and Earth Observations for Actionable Water Resources Management
495032.authors: Jessica M. Erlingis, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and P. Oddo, C. Deval, S. W. Fleming, R. Frasson, B. Seegers, and E. Urquhart
495032.abstract: Satellite Earth observations (EOs) have become invaluable tools, providing consistent information about key hydrological variables such as precipitation, snow cover, groundwater, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and water quality over large areas, expanding the coverage available from in situ observations alone. The NASA Water Resources Program is committed to improving water resources management using EOs and Earth system models to increase resilience to water-related risks, improve economic security, and empower communities to make increasingly complex decisions about water use. Recent advancements in sensor technology, satellite data products, and advanced modeling have revolutionized our ability to co-design solutions with partners, a process that is fundamental to the adoption and long-term viability of water management tools that leverage NASA EOs and modeling technologies. In this presentation, we highlight applications of NASA EOs, including data from recently launched missions such as Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE), Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT), and NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR), showcasing their impact on a diverse set of water resources decision-making activities across the public and private sectors.

495033.title: Impacts of Electrification and Climate Shift on the Power Grid
495033.authors: Jorge E. Gonzalez-Cruz, University at Albany, Albany, NY; University at Albany, Albany, NY; and J. P. Montoya-Rincon, H. Gamarro, K. P. Sookdar, H. Hooshyar, and T. L. Nguyen
495033.abstract: The electrification of building and transportation systems is a cornerstone strategy for achieving deep decarbonization of the energy sector. However, the systemic implications of mass heat pump and electric-vehicle adoption for grid reliability remain poorly understood, particularly in cold climates. Here we present an integrated climate energy modeling framework that couples high-resolution urban weather simulations (uWRF at 1.3–4 km resolution) with building energy demand models and electric vehicle charging profiles to project electricity loads across New York State from 2010 to 2059 under multiple climate scenarios (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5). We demonstrate that widespread building electrification fundamentally shifts the grid’s vulnerability paradigm from well-understood summer peaks toward new winter peak constraints, while transportation electrification further amplifies total demand. Using the 95th (P95) percentile of daily peak load, we find that statewide peak demand increases from 27.31 GW in 2015–2019 to 28.88 GW under SSP2-4.5 in the 2055–2059 future analogue period, and reaches 31.86–34.93 GW when electric-vehicle adoption pathways are included. The seasonal structure of peak demand changes markedly, with statewide winter P95 growing by 7.78 GW between 2020–2024 and 2055–2059 while summer P95 remains nearly unchanged. By midcentury, statewide winter and summer P95 peaks become approximately equal, although NYC Metro remains slightly summer-peaking. These findings reveal that current grid planning frameworks, which focus predominantly on summer reliability, are inadequate for a decarbonized future. Reliability planning in cold-climate systems must account for winter peak growth, electric-vehicle load amplification and zone-specific transition timing.

495034.title: Evaluating Deep Convective Transport into the Upper Troposphere and Lower Stratosphere Using Coordinated Aircraft Observations and Global Chemistry Models
495034.authors: Colin Gurganus, NOAA, Louisville, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; CIRES, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and A. Rollins, E. Waxman, W. Smith, S. Tilmes, H. Bian, S. M. Davis, B. Baier, E. M. Bednarz, J. P. Schwarz, and T. Thornberry
495034.abstract: Deep convection is a primary pathway for transporting boundary-layer emissions into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS), where trace gases influence atmospheric chemistry, aerosol formation, and radiative forcing. Accurately representing the transport of anthropogenic tracer species such as carbon monoxide (CO) remains a significant challenge for global chemistry and Earth system models. During the 2022 Asian Summer Monsoon Chemical and Climate Impact Project (ACCLIP), coordinated measurements from the NASA WB-57 and NSF/NCAR Gulfstream V aircraft provided one of the most comprehensive vertically resolved in situ CO datasets collected in the UTLS, providing a unique opportunity to evaluate model representations of deep convective transport. Aircraft observations were compared with forecasts from GEOS-FP and simulations from GEOS-GOCART and CESM2-WACCM. While the models generally reproduced the large-scale distribution of CO, an intense convective outflow event sampled over the Yellow Sea on 19 August 2022 revealed substantial deficiencies in simulated transport. Both aircraft measured CO mixing ratios exceeding 325 ppb near the tropopause and a distinctive C-shaped vertical profile indicative of recent deep convective injection. Trajectory analyses traced the sampled plume to vigorous convection approximately 12 hours prior to the observations. GEOS-GOCART, using GEOS-FP specified dynamics, more accurately reproduced the observed vertical structure than CESM2-WACCM, using MERRA-2 specified dynamics, although both underestimated the magnitude of the transported pollution. These differences suggest that the choice of specified-dynamics meteorological forcing can strongly influence the fidelity of simulated deep convective transport, emphasizing the importance of accurately representing convective mass fluxes and vertical transport for realistic UTLS simulations. Satellite profile products from MLS, MOPITT, AIRS, CrIS, and IASI also failed to capture both the magnitude and vertical structure of the CO plume on 19 August, underscoring the limitations of assimilating current satellite profile products to represent localized deep convective transport. Together, these results demonstrate the value of coordinated high-altitude aircraft and balloon observations for evaluating deep convective transport in global chemistry models and highlight persistent challenges in representing the rapid vertical redistribution of boundary-layer pollution into the UTLS. Such observational constraints are critical for improving convective parameterizations, reducing uncertainties in atmospheric composition models, and increasing confidence in predictions of atmospheric chemistry and climate.

495036.title: Understanding Ocean Precipitation Product Uncertainty Through a Multi-Reference, Scale-Aware Evaluation Framework
495036.authors: Ali Behrangi, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and K. K. Kumah, Y. Song, G. Gu, O. Zandi, G. J. Huffman, R. F. Adler, C. C. Funk, D. T. Bolvin, E. J. Nelkin, and P. Peterson
495036.abstract: Ocean precipitation estimates from satellites and reanalyses are essential for understanding global water-cycle variability, but sparse and heterogeneous in situ observations make their evaluation challenging, particularly over the open ocean. Here, we assess seven widely used precipitation products, including four generations of the Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP), IMERG Version 07, ERA5, and MERRA-2, using a scale-consistent, multi-reference framework that combines Passive Aquatic Listener (PAL) observations, moored buoys, tropical Pacific atoll gauges, and OceanRAIN shipborne measurements. The assessment evaluates daily precipitation characteristics, high-latitude ocean performance, monthly-to-interannual variability, and tropical Pacific rainfall variability across complementary observational scales. At daily point scales, comparisons against 58 PAL deployments and 91 moored buoys show that newer GPCP products substantially improve upon the legacy GPCP v1.3 product, particularly in moderate-to-heavy rainfall distributions, while IMERG v07 provides the closest multiyear mean agreement with both reference datasets. Reanalysis products generally detect more precipitation events than satellite products, but this increased detection is often accompanied by higher frequency bias and false alarms. Extending the assessment to oceans poleward of 45° latitude using OceanRAIN reveals strong hemispheric dependence in product behavior. Products show systematic dry biases relative to OceanRAIN in the Northern Hemisphere, whereas most products become wet-biased in the Southern Hemisphere, demonstrating that precipitation evaluation outcomes depend strongly on region, sampling environment, and metric choice. At monthly-to-interannual scales, buoy and tropical Pacific atoll comparisons show that products generally reproduce the timing of rainfall variability more consistently than its amplitude. Agreement is strongest in the eastern Pacific, while larger differences occur in wetter and more convectively active regions such as the western Pacific and Indian Ocean. Among the GPCP products, GPCP v3.3 better preserves observed tropical Pacific atoll anomaly amplitudes, with regression slopes of 0.82–0.95 across four domains. These results demonstrate that no single reference or metric fully characterizes ocean precipitation product performance. A multi-reference, scale-aware evaluation framework is therefore essential for identifying product strengths, limitations, and uncertainty across diverse oceanic rainfall regimes.

495037.title: Scaling In Situ Soil Moisture Observations into Statewide Agricultural Drought Products in Missouri
495037.authors: Zachary Leasor, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO; and M. Sunde, B. Gyawali, A. Wolfgeher, and J. Travlos
495037.abstract: Following recent drought and flood events across Missouri, state, federal, and university partners initiated a coordinated effort to expand in situ soil moisture monitoring and develop operational soil moisture products for drought and flood assessment. As part of the Missouri Hydrology Information Center (MoHIC), a statewide network of soil moisture observations has been established to provide near real-time measurements across diverse soils and landscapes. To guide network expansion and ensure observations are representative of Missouri's environmental conditions, a soil moisture monitoring plan was developed using soil, ecological, and physiographic characteristics to identify priority monitoring locations. Soil moisture observations are combined with site-specific soil properties to derive plant available water metrics and agriculturally relevant condition categories. These products provide an assessment of water availability that is more directly related to agricultural drought impacts than volumetric soil moisture alone. In situ observations are further integrated with geospatial modeling approaches to produce statewide maps of soil moisture and available water conditions. This presentation describes the development of Missouri's soil moisture monitoring network, methods for scaling point observations into spatially continuous drought products, and approaches for communicating soil moisture information to diverse stakeholders. Applications for agricultural drought monitoring and climate services are highlighted, demonstrating how in situ soil moisture observations can improve drought assessment across Missouri.

495038.title: Using a Newly Developed Index to Investigate U.S. Droughts and Heatwaves
495038.authors: Matthew W. Perry, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and R. Obringer
495038.abstract: Droughts and heatwaves have several effects on regional populations, including water and food insecurity. These effects are exacerbated, however, when droughts and heatwaves occur simultaneously. A recent study developed a standardized compound drought heatwave index (SCDHI) by creating joint distributions of temperature and precipitation metrics. The index has been used to study compound drought heatwave events (CDHEs) in China. A similar analysis of CDHEs in the United States using this index has not yet been conducted. Our study aims to 1) recreate the SCDHI with temperature and precipitation products from the ERA5 database; and 2) identify changes in CDHEs across the United States since 1950 using the SCDHI.
