While the SCDHI was originally constructed using a Gaussian copula to study CDHEs in China, our index was built using a Student-t copula due to its ability to model extreme events. With the newly reconstructed SCDHI, we discuss CDHE trends across the country. We also describe efforts to use artificial intelligence and machine learning models to determine how CDHEs will change in future decades.

495040.title: Continuous Geostationary Monitoring of Aerosol Top Height over North America from the TEMPO-GOES Constellation
495040.authors: Yuhan Wu, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY; and G. Huang, M. Kim, J. Kim, and H. Zhang
495040.abstract: Aerosol vertical structure remains poorly observed needed for air quality and climate applications. Here we demonstrate that the TEMPO–GOES geostationary constellation can provide hourly aerosol top height (ATH) over North America from multi-angle stereo observations. Our retrieval captures major smoke plumes with broad spatial continuity and shows quantitative agreement with TEMPO and TROPOMI aerosol layer heights (ALHs) and qualitative consistency with airborne lidar profiles, with differences attributable to differing height definitions and limited lidar sample sizes. Initial comparison results have demonstrated the feasibility of TEMPO-GOES geostationary stereoscopy as a new approach to aerosol top height retrieval, providing spatially resolved, geometry-based observations for optically dense aerosol plumes that complement existing passive and lidar-based methods over North America. Comprehensive validation results based on the updated retrieval will be presented.

495041.title: Optimizing MPAS-JEDI for the experimental Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) v2 and the Prototype Atmospheric River Prediction System (AR-PS)
495041.authors: Guoqing Ge, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and M. Hu, C. Zhou, J. Hu, S. Pan, H. Lin, K. C. Eure, S. Liu, T. Lei, S. K. Degelia, S. Trahan, J. Beck, and T. T. Ladwig
495041.abstract: NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) and Office of Model Development (OMD) have been collaborating on the development of the experimental Rapid Refresh Forecast System version 2 (RRFSv2) based on Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) and Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI). In parallel, GSL has been developing a prototype Atmospheric River Prediction System (AR-PS) using the same MPAS+JEDI framework. As expected, experimental RRFSv2 and AR-PS share a large portion of their codebase, development work, and components. An operation-oriented, community-flexible hourly cycling MPAS+JEDI workflow (https://github.com/wx-workflow/wx-workflow) has been established, greatly facilitating scientific advancements in both modeling and data assimilation research. The workflow supports multiple domain and grid configurations—conus12km, conus3km, na12km, ar3.5km, global15km, global-15-3km, fx1.25km, etc —for a wide range of applications. Real-time experimental RRFSv2 and AR-PS experiments have been evaluated at the 2026 NOAA testbeds. Extensive retrospective experiments have been performed to access and refine data assimilation configurations. Current research spans a broad range of topics, including the evaluation of static and ensemble-based background error covariances, the development of hybrid data assimilation methods, and the assimilation of diverse observation types such as aircraft, surface, satellite, radar, and other conventional observations. Progress has also been made toward establishing a regional ensemble-based data assimilation and forecasting capability. For AR-PS, ongoing development emphasizes the assimilation of atmospheric river–relevant observations, including satellite radiances, GNSS radio occultation, dropsondes, and other remote-sensing data. Improving the representation of the marine boundary layer, a critical component for accurately predicting atmospheric river evolution and landfall, is another major focus. The latest experimental RRFSv2 and AR-PS developments and findings will be discussed at the conference.

495044.title: Wintertime Supercooled Liquid Cloud Frequency at Utqiaġvik: Implications for the Surface Energy Budget and Sea Ice Growth
495044.authors: Genevieve Rose Lorenzo Pearson, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and A. J. Buggee, R. Gillespie, C. Briggs, C. F. M. Coimbra, R. Sun, M. R. Mazloff, and L. M. Russell
495044.abstract: Supercooled liquid cloud (SLC) contributions to mixed-phase clouds, which are underestimated in models, impact the representation of downwelling longwave radiation in the winter, subsequently affecting the surface energy budget and the growth of sea ice. Surface-based vertically resolved DOE-ARM multi-sensor cloud phase measurements in Utqiaġvik, Alaska (NSA) spanning 5 winter seasons (October-March, 2022-2026) are used to analyze SLC frequency, timing, and duration. SLC are defined as those clouds existing in liquid phase during times with no precipitation at temperatures less than 0 °C and with liquid water path (LWP) > 2 g m-2. Non-precipitating SLC occur ~30% of the time from October to March, are mostly below 3 km, and are on average 300 - 600 m deep, with 80% (~1000 h) of cloud bases below 1.2 km. Greatest counts of SLC are observed from October to November (400 h mo-1) when they occur for more than 6 h day-1 and have a higher median liquid water path (LWP, 29 - 84 g m-2 in October). SLC occur for less than 6 h day-1 from December to March when they have lower counts and LWP (100 h mo-1 and median LWP of 9 – 26 g m-2 in February). SLC frequency of 30% is similar to other in-situ observations but higher than those retrieved by satellite for larger Arctic regions. The effects on surface radiation by these frequent SLC are estimated with semi-empirical multi-layered cloud models, showing their important contribution to the Arctic surface energy balance. Corresponding ice growth rates from sea ice model simulations are most sensitive over open water at the ice edges, where SLC occur most frequently, from October to November, underscoring the value of a targeted approach in assessing the impact of SLC on the surface energy budget and sea ice growth.

495045.title: An Analysis of the Occurrence and Predictability of an Anticyclonic EF2 Tornado Associated with a Left-Moving Supercell
495045.authors: Luke Justin LeBel, Iowa State University, Ames, IA
495045.abstract: On 18 May 2025, a tornado outbreak occurred across portions of the central United States. As part of this outbreak, an anticyclonic EF2 tornado was produced by a left-moving supercell in far northwestern Kansas. Significant (EF2+) anticyclonic tornadoes associated with left-moving supercells are very rare, and the 18 May 2025 case therefore provides a valuable opportunity to explore the occurrence and predictability of left-moving supercells and their associated hazards. This study documents the properties of the tornadic left-moving supercell and explores the predictability of left-moving supercells on 18 May 2025 more broadly. It is found that the several characteristics of the left-moving supercell likely made the anticyclonic tornado especially challenging for warning operations. First, the anticyclonic tornado occurred shortly after convection initiation. As a result, the near-surface reflectivity field associated with the supercell evolved very rapidly prior to tornadogenesis. Second, the tornadic supercell moved quickly in an atypical direction (towards the north-northwest). Despite these challenges, guidance from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model did indicate high likelihood of left-moving supercells in northwestern Kansas and eastern Colorado. Thus, operational numerical weather prediction models likely have utility in anticipating corridors of enhanced risk of left-moving supercells. In sum, the 18 May 2025 event highlights several important challenges in the operational prediction of left-moving supercells and their associated hazards, and moreover demonstrates that there are opportunities for improving forecasts of such events.

495046.title: Operational Space Weather Support for NASA Missions by NASA GSFC’s Moon to Mars Space Weather Analysis Office
495046.authors: Teresa Nieves-Chinchilla, NASA/GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and M. Romano, M. Aronne, C. Alden, M. Anastopulos, A. Chulaki, F. Di Mare, A. Iampietro, E. Juelfs, M. Kane, R. D. Loper, N. Romanelli, and C. A. Young, Ph.D.
495046.abstract: The Moon to Mars Space Weather Analysis Office (M2M SWAO) at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) provides real-time, human-in-the-loop space weather analysis and prediction to protect NASA missions and support operational decision-making. M2M SWAO carries out daily monitoring of solar-heliospheric activity, including solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs), to characterize space weather and its potential impacts throughout the solar system. Highlighting recent advancements in data synthesis, this presentation outlines our operational framework for assessing space weather using heterogeneous, multi-viewpoint observations available in near real time. We showcase how these data are integrated into experimental capabilities within the office’s broader prototyping framework to improve forecasting. Furthermore, we share updates about past and upcoming support activities for NASA space exploration programs, such as Artemis. We conclude by outlining the challenges, data gaps, and limitations in current operational forecasting tools that must be resolved to enable and protect future planetary exploration.

495047.title: When Being Wrong is Right: The GCCS Product Validation Paradox
495047.authors: Stephen Superczynski, NESDIS, Annapolis, MD; NOAA, Riverdale Park, MD; and H. Carrasco, K. Pitts, J. Fulbright, and D. Pogorzala
495047.abstract: In June of 2026, NOAA’s Office of Geostationary Earth Orbit Observations (GEO) completed the migration of its Data Operations capabilities from their on-prem Ground System to the new GEO Cloud Compute Subsystem (GCCS). The GEO Program Science and Ground Project teams were tasked with externally validating the GOES products produced by the GCCS against those produced by the then-operational system. Using a collection of internally developed Python tools along with publicly available tools like UW-Glance, products generated by the GCCS were matched against their corresponding products generated on-premises to show they were fit for operational use. The primary objective of the validation process was to confirm that products generated by the GCCS were scientifically indistinguishable from those produced by the on-premise system. Although minor variation in machine precision and routine metadata updates were anticipated, evaluating discrepancies that exceeded standard systemic deviations proved more complex. To address this, evaluations during the final phases of the project shifted to an individual case review to establish if these notable variances represented genuine defects or unexpected improvements. Ultimately, this thorough assessment successfully validated every product within the GOES-R series, providing the definitive evidence required to support and authorize the migration to GCCS.

495048.title: Software as a Socio-Technical System: Lessons from NSF NCAR's Community Software Facility
495048.authors: Soudeh Kamali, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. Voelz, J. Petch, K. Kuzemka, D. Colegrove, G. L. Mullendore, G. Romine, and D. C. Schuster
495048.abstract: NSF NCAR's Community Software Facility (CSF) is an initiative that set out to modernize how the center develops, supports, and sustains community models and tools to meet the current and future needs of scientific and engineering staff, as well as the broader Earth System science community. Modernizing scientific software is often framed as an engineering challenge which involves adopting better tools, improving code quality, or streamlining infrastructure. Early in this effort, however, it became clear that meaningful software modernization could not succeed as a purely technical undertaking. Conway's Law describes how the structure of an organization, its teams, reporting lines, and communication patterns become embedded in the architecture of the systems it builds. If NSF NCAR's software architecture reflects its organizational and communication structures, then modernizing that software requires just as much attention to how staff collaborate, communicate, and share ownership of the code. This recognition has shaped the CSF's approach from the outset: NSF NCAR's software ecosystem is not simply a collection of codebases and tools, but a socio-technical system, an interconnected network of people, processes, and technologies. The success of scientific software depends as much on engineering technical rigor as it does on building trust across disciplines, recognizing software engineers as equal scientific partners, and establishing team structures that support open communication and shared decision making. Developing and architecting the CSF has required coordinated investment not only in software engineering practices, but in the organizational culture, team structures, and collaborative processes needed to sustain them. This presentation will share the motivation behind the CSF initiative and reflect on key lessons learned so far as in building the collaborative structures and culture needed to support it. We will also share preliminary reflections on how these lessons might extend beyond NSF NCAR to inform collaboration with partner institutions and the broader Earth System modeling community. In doing so, we aim to demonstrate that the CSF is not only a technical catalyst for better scientific software, but also a cultural catalyst that shows how designing development processes around people, collaboration, and feedback leads to a more resilient, innovative, and connected research community. We hope these lessons offer a useful model for other organizations and community modeling efforts seeking to align technical modernization with the social and organizational structures that ultimately shape it.

495049.title: Assessing the Uncertainty of Precipitation Products In Modeling Streamflow Drought and the Associated Societal Risks
495049.authors: Alexander Timothy Michalek, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN; and J. K. Roundy
495049.abstract: Development of watershed-scale drought risk maps is important for preparing communities and water resource managers across the United States for streamflow deficits and water supply shortages. However, assessing and predicting drought hazard and risk is difficult due to compounding uncertainties originating from both precipitation forcing inputs and hydrologic model structure. Addressing these challenges requires first evaluating model performance against historical low-flow variability, followed by an ensemble framework designed to isolate input precipitation uncertainty from model structural errors. In this study, we present an ensemble framework to evaluate streamflow drought hazard, exposure, and vulnerability across the Contiguous United States (CONUS). First, we evaluate the GPU-based hydrologic model (Tiger-HLM) against historical streamflow observations across CONUS to benchmark its ability to capture low-flow regimes and historical drought metrics, implementing model refinements where discrepancies exist. To disentangle input forcing variability from structural model uncertainty, the evaluated Tiger-HLM framework is driven by an ensemble of precipitation products to simulate 7-day moving low flows and historical percentile thresholds. Next, to translate streamflow deficits into socio-hydrologic risk, hazard outputs are coupled with surface water reliance data from the USGS Water Use dataset for exposure and CDC Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) metrics for vulnerability. Composite drought risk indices are computed across all ensemble members and aggregated to watershed scales. This ongoing study will establish the utility of the framework by quantifying the relative contributions of precipitation input selection versus model structural uncertainty to spatial variance in drought risk. By mapping the spread across ensemble risk predictions, we will identify hydroclimatic regions where forcing uncertainty dominates over model structure in degrading operational low-flow predictability. The resulting framework will generate watershed scale risk maps that highlight regions where 7-day low-flow deficits coincide with high surface water reliance (i.e., USGS data) and elevated social vulnerability (i.e., CDC SVI metrics), advancing uncertainty-aware drought risk management.

495052.title: An AI/ML Framework for Distinguishing Real Fires from Persistent Thermal Anomalies in VIIRS Active-Fire Observations
495052.authors: Benjamin Marchant, STC – Science & Technology Corp., Columbia, MD; and W. Schroeder and I. A. Csiszar
495052.abstract: Persistent thermal anomalies associated with gas and oil flares, industrial facilities, volcanoes, solar panel farms, and greenhouse complexes can be repeatedly identified as active fires in satellite observations. These detections represent a significant source of false alarms in operational fire products and can reduce confidence in real-time fire monitoring. Existing static anomaly databases are useful for identifying known sources but require frequent updates as infrastructure and landscapes evolve. They can also incorrectly suppress real fires occurring within or near known anomaly locations. This study develops an artificial intelligence and machine-learning framework to distinguish real fires from persistent thermal anomalies in satellite active-fire observations. The initial framework was developed and evaluated using multiyear observations from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite aboard the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 satellites. Fire detections were organized using a hierarchical spatial indexing system to characterize their frequency, persistence, temporal recurrence, spatial distribution, and surrounding context. Known anomaly locations were labeled using high-resolution imagery and grouped into major source types, including gas and oil flares, solar panel farms, greenhouse complexes, industrial facilities, and volcanoes. The framework follows a hierarchical approach. A Random Forest classifier first estimates whether an individual satellite detection is more consistent with a real fire or a persistent non-fire thermal source. Predictors include thermal and contextual information, fire radiative power, viewing geometry, background-window properties, and the historical behavior of detections at and around each location. Additional machine-learning and deep-learning methods, including a Siamese neural network trained with high-resolution imagery, are used to characterize persistent-anomaly types and identify previously unclassified sources. Evaluation of the VIIRS fire-versus-non-fire classifier produced a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve of approximately 0.88 on a balanced evaluation dataset. A conservative decision threshold designed to minimize missed fires retained approximately 95% of real-fire observations while removing a substantial fraction of detections associated with persistent thermal sources. The framework also identified new anomaly candidates and distinguished real fires occurring near established anomaly locations, addressing two important limitations of conventional static masks. This adaptive framework provides a pathway toward probabilistic persistent-anomaly screening in NOAA operational VIIRS and ABI fire products. It can improve the reliability of active-fire detections while preserving sensitivity to real fires and adapting to newly constructed or changing thermal sources.

495055.title: NVIDIA StormScope at NSSL
495055.authors: John L. Cintineo, NOAA / OAR / National Severe Storms Laboratory, Madison, WI; and C. K. Potvin, P. S. Skinner, N. Yussouf, A. J. Clark, J. Pathak, P. Harrington, and S. Abbas
495055.abstract: StormScope, a generative AI nowcasting model, was designed by NVIDIA for short-term severe weather forecasting. Built on a diffusion transformer architecture, it ingests GOES-R ABI and MRMS channels to generate 3-kilometer-scale predictions of future satellite and radar fields out to 6 hours, at 10-minute resolution. StormScope was evaluated at the 2026 Spring Forecasting Experiment (SFE) in the Hazardous Weather Testbed, and demonstrated excellent skill with respect to state-of-the-art NWP models such as the Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS) at 0-3 hour lead times. In this research, we summarize StormScope results from the SFE and detail recent co-development of the model with NSSL, such as the inclusion of additional outputs, running inference on local-area domains, and improved horizontal resolution.

495056.title: NOAA Atmospheric River Forecasting Accomplishments (FY2023–2025)
495056.authors: Lingyan Xin, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and J. E. Ten Hoeve III, M. Huang, and L. Wolf
495056.abstract: Over fiscal years 2023–2025, Weather Program Office (WPO) oversees the project on behalf of NOAA, which involves stakeholders from across NOAA and the wider weather community. NOAA laboratories and centers - Physical Science Lab, Global System Lab, Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC), Office of Modeling and Development (OMD), Weather Prediction Center, and Office of Water Prediction (OWP) - together with partners Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E), Cooperative Institute for Research to Operations in Hydrology (CIROH), and WPO’s Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences (SBES), have achieved major milestones in Atmospheric River (AR) forecasting under the "Water in the West" initiative, advancing forecast skill, modernizing data assimilation, and integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) /Machine Learning (ML) to support real-time decision-making. Central to this effort is the Atmospheric River Analysis and Forecast System (AR-AFS), now in its second iteration (AR-AFSv2), which combines a convection-permitting 3 km grid with refined physics - including Thompson Microphysics and Turbulent Kinetic Energy (TKE)-based moist Eddy-Diffusivity Mass-Flux boundary-layer schemes - to outperform legacy systems like GFSv16 for heavy precipitation events at lead times up to 120 hours. Coupling with the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) has improved air-sea interaction and water vapor transport (IVT) representation, while development has shifted toward a globally nested MPAS framework, with early prototypes showing strong results in the 2025-2026 WPC PEAR experiments. Complementary physics advances - including hail-aware Thompson-Eidhammer Microphysics Parameterization for Operations (TEMPO) microphysics, scale-aware snow-cover parameterization, and boundary-layer sensitivity studies - have sharpened model fidelity in complex terrain, while research linking the Madden-Julian Oscillation to California precipitation has extended predictability to 14 days. On the data assimilation side, the GSI-to-JEDI transition has streamlined DA workflows and enabled higher-resolution, more frequent assimilation cycles, bolstered by expanded satellite and AMV observations. Through collaboration with the NOAA AI for NWP (AI4NWP) Working Group, the project enabled the development and release of the AI for numerical weather prediction (NWP) framework, Experimental AI Global and Limited-area Ensemble forecast system (EAGLE), for the broader weather enterprise, supporting rapid testing, development, and demonstration of near-real-time (NRT) forecasts. A nested EAGLE version entered NRT forecast mode in July 2026, while machine learning innovations, including HRRRCast and CIROH’s advances in hydrologic and snow water equivalent (SWE) prediction, further extended forecasting capabilities.

495058.title: Evaluating Estimates of Tropical Cyclone Maximum Potential Intensity Derived from NUCAPS Retrievals
495058.authors: Alex Libardoni, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and M. N. Razin
495058.abstract: Tropical cyclone Maximum Potential Intensity (MPI) provides a thermodynamically-based estimate for the maximum strength of the storm given its environment. Pairing current storm intensity with its MPI can give an indication of how much a storm may further intensify. Operationally, MPI is generally estimated using either sea surface temperature (SST) or from the Carnot Engine theory proposed by Bister and Emanuel (1998) using numerical weather prediction (NWP) model inputs. In this study, we use a method for estimating MPI that is independent of NWP inputs and follows the sounding-based method of Holland (1997). Combining current surface pressure, SST, and an atmospheric sounding, this method calculates the surface pressure response to a redistribution of all available moist energy at an assumed surface relative humidity. If the pressure drop is sufficiently large (>20 hPa), a further eye adjustment is included. For this work, we use atmospheric soundings from the NOAA Unique Combined Atmospheric Processing System (NUCAPS) to investigate their utility in estimating MPI. The NUCAPS soundings are globally available and can thus provide a basin-wide look at storm environments for already developed storms and regions where development may occur. We present the viability of using these retrievals in the sounding-based method and show our progress in the development of a real-time display of global MPI using these estimates.

495059.title: New Northeastern US Snowpack Climatological Products and Interactive Webpage
495059.authors: Eric P. Kelsey, Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH; Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH; and D. Zywiczynski
495059.abstract: Monitoring current snowpack snow water equivalent (swe) within a climatological context for water management, agricultural, and other hydrologic purposes is critical for operational decisions related to protecting life and property, and ensuring an adequate water supply for all private, commercial, and ecosystem uses. Recent Northeast US droughts (2025, 2020), a trend of decreasing snowpack swe, and earlier snow-out in spring highlights the decreasing reliability of spring snowpack meltwater to replenish groundwater and reservoirs in preparation for the increasing summer water demand by people and increasing evapotranspiration of ecosystems. A first-ever, observation-based climatology of over 250 snow course sites in the Northeastern US has been produced to address these critical water management needs. Snowpack products produced by this NOAA/National Integrative Drought Information System-funded project include daily climatological normals of swe, daily swe percentiles and record maximum and minimum values, median snow-out dates, current swe and depth updated daily, and more. Now, stakeholders can access a quantitative assessment of how much water is stored in the snowpack in near real-time relative to a climatological context. Plymouth State University’s Meteorology website hosts these snowpack data products on an interactive webpage. This presentation will introduce the snowpack data products, the webpage where users can access them, and current work to develop an operational Snowpack Drought Index.

495060.title: Using Generalized Additive Models to Quantify Sources of Variability in Severe Convective Storm Event Data across the CONUS
495060.authors: Jacob J Coburn, Verisk, Boston, MA; and S. Tolwinski-Ward
495060.abstract: Severe convective storms (SCSs) account for a major proportion of climate-related risk in the United States. Storm Prediction Center (SPC) reports on historical hazard from the major sub-perils (hail, tornadoes and damaging winds) are an important source of ground-truth information for SCS peril in the contiguous United States (CONUS) but are well known to contain biases and heterogeneities in space and time related to population-dependent reporting coverage, as well as temporal changes in observing practices and technologies. These features of the historical record can confound inference on the underlying hazard distributions, which already contain complex space-time structure due to physical climate variability, mesoscale and synoptic stochasticity, and climate change impacts. This study develops a generalized additive modeling (GAM) framework to characterize seasonal SCS sub-peril hazard while explicitly accounting for several of these confounding influences. Improved quantitative understanding of biases and patterns in SCS hazard has direct implications for climate-driven assessments of risk. Historical SPC records of SCS sub-peril event counts are aggregated into seasonal summaries on a regular grid across CONUS. The preprocessed data exhibit substantial spatial and temporal variability, including recurring seasonal patterns, interannual fluctuations and long term, though not necessarily monotonic, trends. The statistical models are designed with additive terms allowing for a description of these well-known climatological features with appropriately smooth space-time structure, and interactions with physically based predictors. Index representations of the state of important large-scale climate modes (e.g., ENSO) are included in the predictor set. Population data are also included as a predictor to separate historical record variability stemming from changes in observational coverage, rather than that inherent to the hazard climatology. Model inference is carried out using rigorous statistical practices to guard against overfitting, including techniques for choosing which candidate predictors should be retained as significant explanators of the data, and for choosing a robust amount of spatial smoothing in each model term. The final fitted models reproduce the observed seasonal SCS hazard variability with a high degree of fidelity, and the individual model terms to various predictor inputs can be studied to interpret the underlying drivers. On their own, the model terms making use of the population data can be used as a quantitative description of population-based undercount bias and provide direct guidance on best practices for using SPC data in other contexts. The analysis demonstrates that a proper accounting for population changes is especially critical to accurately capturing responses to external climate drivers (long-term trends due to warming from increasing CO2) and internal modes that influence interannual and decadal patterns. The model terms not related to the population effects can be parsed to decompose climatological SCS hazard into components attributable to seasonality, large-scale climate variability, climate change, and inherent local internal variability. The model quantifies major climatological features like the migration of peak activity regions across seasons, and for each sub-peril. The analysis also suggests that long-term changes vary spatially by sub-peril, and that SCS hazard response to observational and environmental factors are often nonlinear. Large-scale climate variability emerges as an important source of seasonal modulation, with effects that differ by region and time of year. While the models explain many broad patterns, considerable residual variability remains, reflecting the inherently complex and episodic nature of severe weather and the influence of processes that are difficult to represent within a seasonal statistical framework. The talk will conclude with exhibits showing how the model decomposition of hazard variability can be used in combination with a catastrophe risk model to quantify climate-driven variations in risk. This work demonstrates the value of flexible data-driven statistical modeling for rigorous, unbiased, and physically-interpretable quantification of the components of U.S. severe thunderstorm hazard. This type of modeling can bring value to both scientific and industrial applications through improved interpretation of historical severe weather trends, development of bias-adjusted event climatologies, and differentiation between the underlying drivers of SCS events and their associated losses across CONUS.

495061.title: Revisiting Estimation of the Oceanic Cool Skin: Limitations of Simplified Parameterizations and Recent Results with Physical Approaches
495061.authors: Gary A. Wick, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and S. L. Castro
495061.abstract: The existence of a cool skin at the ocean surface has long been known along with its impact on air-sea heat fluxes and satellite sea surface temperature retrievals. Following many years of work developing and exploring physical models for the skin effect, attention waned and shifted to more simplified approaches and the larger impacts of diurnal warming of the near-surface layer of the ocean. Simplified parameterizations based solely on the wind speed or humidity found wider use due to the relatively small magnitude of the effect and global mean behavior of the temperature difference. Recent results, however, show distinct limitations of the simplified parameterizations and specific conditions where they fail. A physics-based update to the skin-layer treatment in the widely used COARE heat flux model has also been recently published. The update attempts to better account for near-surface turbulent processes but leads to a different interpretation of the skin layer. In this work, data from multiple recent experiments are employed to assess the limitations of the simplified parameterizations and test the validity of recent refinements to physical models for the cool skin. The data include in situ observations from the Sub-Mesoscale Ocean Dynamics Experiment (S-MODE), the Australian Integrated Marine Observing System (IMOS), and a merged data set combining satellite skin retrievals from the Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR) and high-quality buoy observations of the near-surface temperature with traceability to observational standards. Results show the wind-only predictions break down in strong frontal regions and the assumed asymptotic behavior at high winds shows a clear heat flux dependence. Gains in accuracy are shown to be possible utilizing physically-based models. Further tests evaluate the appropriateness of the updated physical approach to estimating the skin effect.

495062.title: Diagnosing Communication Challenges in Online Coastal Flooding Products
495062.authors: Andrea C Stumpf, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT; and S. Sainjoo, S. Kandel, P. Singh, S. Nautiyal, T. A. Sudol, A. J. Jefferson, and M. A. Kenney
495062.abstract: The United States federal government provides a range of coastal flooding digital tools to inform users of historical, real-time, and expected conditions. These products are primarily designed to help technical users make informed decisions on how to respond to flood conditions. Displaying the multiple types of data required to sufficiently inform the users without overwhelming them remains challenging. As an interdisciplinary team of environmental and decision scientists, we used a task-based diagnosis that consisted of a series of questions designed to lead the user through the capabilities of each product. Following that, we had guided virtual group discussions to identify the enabling and challenging aspects of using six federal coastal flooding visualization products. The products use a wide variety of approaches to introduce new users to product capabilities (e.g., FAQs, video tutorials, pop-ups), and these approaches had varying success in promoting confident and accurate tool use in the task-based diagnoses. Within the products, early results indicate that areas for improvement include color schemes, the relationship between different visuals on a page, and navigating between different parts of the website. Information gathered from these diagnoses will be thematically coded. Synthesizing results with visualization literature and design theory, we will generate recommendations for future coastal flooding products. Future work includes collaboration with the intended user audience of these tools to assess their efficacy in translating complex data into easily actionable information.

495063.title: The Circumglobal Teleconnection as a Modulator of Rossby Wave Packets and Land-Atmosphere Coupling in U.S. Heat Wave Development
495063.authors: Ashley Fanning, University of Delaware, Newark, DE; and K. Malloy
495063.abstract: The Circumglobal Teleconnection (CGT), a quasi-stationary wavenumber-5 pattern embedded in the Northern Hemisphere summer subtropical jet, has been identified as a potential source of subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) predictability for U.S. heat waves, yet the pathways linking CGT phase to transient wave dynamics and land-surface conditions remain incompletely understood. Using ERA5 reanalysis data from 1951 to 2024, we classify CGT phase from monthly principal component values and examine how positive and negative phases modulate the spatial distribution, intensity, and dynamical evolution of 94 identified U.S. heat wave events. We find that CGT phase spatially shifts heat wave risk, with positive phases favoring the Northwest and Northern Plains and negative phases favoring the Southeast. CGT phase also modulates event intensity, with positive phases producing warmer peak anomalies. This difference in heat wave location and intensity corresponds to distinct Rossby wave packet (RWP) behavior and land-atmosphere coupling. Heat waves during positive CGT months develop from a diffuse, slower-propagating wave packet that arrives as an amplified ridge, while those under negative CGT months emerge from a zonally dominated, faster-moving packet that produces a weak ridge across the southeastern U.S. Land-atmosphere feedbacks reinforce this dynamical pathway, with sensible heat flux anomalies emerging earlier and stronger under positive CGT conditions, consistent with soil moisture deficits, possibly enhancing the intensity of heat waves. These results indicate that CGT phase modulates not only the likelihood of U.S. heat wave occurrence but also the location, intensity, and underlying physical drivers of these events, supporting the CGT as a potential window of opportunity for enhanced S2S predictability of extreme heat.

495066.title: Impact of Successive Nocturnal Low-Level Jets on the Vertical Redistribution of CanadianWildfire Smoke over the Mid-Atlantic during the CoURAGE Campaign
495066.authors: Sharad Pandey, UMBC, Baltimore City, MD; and M. E. D. Roots, B. Demoz, P. Coye, and K. Hoffman
495066.abstract: Long-range transport of wildfire smoke from Canada is an important source of air-quality degradation over the Mid-Atlantic United States, but the meteorological processes that control how elevated smoke reaches the surface are still not fully understood. This study examines a multi-day smoke episode that affected the Baltimore–Washington corridor between 3 and 7 June 2025, during the Coastal Urban Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE). Smoke transported from Canada first arrived in the free troposphere and then gradually descended into the lower atmosphere. We use a multi-instrument observational network spanning rural, urban, and coastal environments across Maryland, including lidars, wind profilers, microwave radiometers, radiosondes, and a differential absorption lidar (DIAL), together with reanalysis and model products (ERA5, MERRA-2, HRRR, WRF). The observations show that a sequence of nocturnal low-level jets (NLLJs) on 4–6 June produced persistent coupling between the elevated smoke layers and the near-surface environment. On 3 June, before the jets developed, the boundary layer was stable and capped, with moisture and smoke confined below 1 km. The following jets enhanced vertical mixing, eroded the stable cap, and allowed smoke initially aloft to repeatedly penetrate the boundary layer and reach the surface. This mixing also supported moisture recovery and deeper boundary-layer development. These results show that repeated NLLJ episodes can transform an episodic long-range transport event into prolonged surface exposure, highlighting a key dynamical pathway through which distant wildfires strongly influence regional air quality and offer insight for future smoke air-quality forecasting.

495069.title: Quantifying the NH3 Footprint of Global Diets Using Consumption-based Accounting
495069.authors: Rain Hin Wing Ho, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong kong; and X. Liu and A. Tai
495069.abstract: Agriculture is a primary driver of global environmental change, contributing significantly to freshwater withdrawal, land use change, soil acidification, and emissions of greenhouse gases and ammonia (NH3). To mitigate these impacts, nations need to evaluate their agricultural environmental footprints to gauge progress toward sustainability. Current indicators primarily rely on production-based accounting, which quantifies environmental costs based on the total volume of food produced domestically. However, this approach obscures environmental burdens embodied in international food trade and fails to isolate the specific impacts driven by individual consumption patterns from national population demographics. Here, we propose a consumption-based accounting framework to assess the NH3 footprint of representative national diets. We analyzed dietary profiles across countries and traced the origin of consumed food—domestic versus imported—for major food categories. Results indicate distinct trade dependencies: while India (1%), Brazil (6%), and Russia (9%) are largely self-sufficient, Saudi Arabia (71%), Germany (57%), Italy (55%), and the UK (52%) exhibit high import reliance, with China (12%), the US (15%), Canada (36%), and France (34%) falling in an intermediate range. We then derived country- and food-specific NH3 emission intensities using the Magnitude And Seasonality of Agricultural Emissions model for NH3 (MASAGE_NH3). These intensities vary substantially; for example, meat production emits 0.55 g NH3 g–1 meat in India compared to 0.10 g NH3 g–1 meat in China and 0.05 g NH3 g–1 meat in the US, reflecting disparities in agricultural management practices. By coupling these emission intensities with per capita dietary profile, we calculated the final NH3 footprint of national diets. We estimate that global diets result in per capita NH3 emissions ranging from 7 to 25 g per day. Unlike aggregate national totals, comparing individual dietary footprints effectively isolates the environmental impact of per capita consumption levels from differences in national population size, providing a more accurate metric for assessing the efficacy of demand-side mitigation strategies across countries. These findings provide an evidence base for designing targeted food system sustainability policies and advancing responsible consumption patterns worldwide.

495071.title: Development of an Improved Surface Stress Model for LES of the Atmospheric Boundary Layer (ABL) with Analysis of Daytime ABL Structure Modified by Hilly Terrain using an Immersed Boundary Method
495071.authors: Adhithiya Sivakumar, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and J. G. Brasseur, M. J. Churchfield, and T. Wei
495071.abstract: We investigate how complex topography modifies the turbulent velocity and temperature fields of the daytime atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) using a large-eddy simulation (LES) framework specifically designed for accurate prediction of the surface layer (SL), where LES is known to overpredict mean velocity gradient, and therefore the mean velocity profile, an error referred to as the “overshoot.” As discussed in [3], when the overshoot is suppressed oscillations in mean shear-rate are exposed that we show here result from a fundamental flaw in the total surface stress (TSS) model in the surface boundary condition (BC). To this end, we present two developments: (1) a new approach for the total surface stress (TSS) model in the LES BC that overcomes the fundamental flaw in the standard TSS model [4] and removes the error in mean velocity when the overshoot is suppressed [3] and its application to the development of a revised immersed boundary method (IBM) with the TSS exposed for modeling, and (2) the application of our improved TSS model and IBM framework—that we refer to as the “Surface Stress Terrain Forcing (SSTF)” framework— to study the impacts of ridge-like surface topography on the energy-containing eddy structure of the atmospheric SL. SL accuracy is important to our application: the development of knowledge to improve optimal placements of wind turbines within wind farms in hilly terrain, terrain that seriously alters the structure of SL turbulence where wind turbines reside, without completely removing the SL that exists in the canonical ABL. [1,2] have shown that the spatio-temporal structure of energy-containing eddies in the SL directly impacts the time-dependent loadings on utility-scale wind turbines, reliability and power. In the current study we address the micro-meteorological implications of hilly terrain on ABL mean and turbulence structure and on model improvements in LES-based model frameworks with immersed boundary methods to accurately predict ABL structure in the SL of the daytime ABL with ridge-like surface topography. An Improved Surface-stress Boundary Conditions for LES of the ABL and its Incorporation into an IBM for Non-Planar Topography TSS Model Improvement. The standard model of the TSS vector [4] is based on a representation with mean surface stress parameterized. We show that the predicted fluctuating TSS component is unphysical due to a spurious sink in streamwise velocity variance producing a sudden reduction of variance at the surface, as illustrated in Fig. (a). We show that this error generates spurious near-surface oscillations in mean shear-rate, and consequently in the mean velocity profile. These oscillations are generally masked by the near-surface overshoot which results from frictional content in the SFS model and algorithm. When these issues are addressed using the method in [3], oscillations in mean velocity gradient with distance from the surface appear which we show are associated with a fundamental error in the standard TSS model. To address this error we restructure the model into mean plus fluctuating TSS components with a separate model for the fluctuating part and the current model for the mean. Through systematic parametric variation in the fluctuating TSS component, we find that it is possible to eliminate near-surface oscillations in mean shear and correct the underprediction of streamwise velocity variance, recovering a monotonic profile that aligns well with experimental and field data. Improved IBM for Non-planar Topography. To apply these advancements to complex terrain, we utilize an extension of the “Immersed Boundary Forcing Method” (IBFM) outlined in [5]. In this approach, complex terrain is represented with explicit localized body forces designed to drive the fluid velocity to zero in cells within the solid surface. However, this method does not provide access to the TSS over the ABL surface. We modify the IBFM approach by specifying the velocity in fluid-adjacent terrain cells in a manner that forces the TSS vector to be that obtained by the standard TSS model and our modified TSS model that addresses the errors in mean velocity described above. Results of our new SSTF method with the standard TSS model are shown in the figure. Fig. (a) shows that whereas our new SSFT framework agrees well with a standard wall model simulation, the IBFM approach with TSS not explicitly modeled significantly mispredicts streamwise velocity variance, as well as mean shear-rate and other turbulence variables. Figures (b)-(c) show significant misprediction of turbulence structure by the IBFM in comparison to the SWM and the new SSFT, where both the magnitude, orientation, and elongation of the energy-containing eddies are predicted similarly. Characteristics of the Daytime ABL over Ridge-like Topography Our simulations use the NLR AMR-Wind code (now known as Kynema-SGF), an exascale CFD solver that relies on a fixed adaptively refinable Cartesian grid rather than a terrain-following one, requiring an IBM to represent non-planar surfaces. We have implemented our improved TSS model and SSTF framework into the solver and completed stable proof-of-concept simulations over flat and complex terrain. We will analyze effects of ridge-like topography on mean-flow and turbulence structure for presentation at the BLT AMS meeting. To this end, we will first conduct a flat-terrain precursor simulation to generate a baseline quasi-stationary moderately convective daytime ABL. Driven by specified geostrophic wind and surface temperature flux, we apply our improved TSS model with periodic horizontal boundary conditions. The resulting time-evolving resolved velocity fields will provide Dirichlet inflow boundary conditions for a topography simulation in a 10 km x 10 km x 6 km domain containing 3-5 spanwise-uniform ridges spaced ~500m apart and ~200m in height to modify the energy-containing structure in the SL without destroying it. Of particular interest are the impacts of up-flow at the first ridge and continual modifications by the ridges behind it on SL structure, in contrast with the turbulence eddying structure over a flat surface. Sciences 41. [5] D. Muñoz‐Esparza et al., 2020, J. Adv. Model. Earth Syst. 12.

495076.title: Understanding Differential Vulnerability to Heat from EMS Calls for Heat-Related Illness in Wisconsin
495076.authors: Rebecca Rose, American Meteorological Society, Madison, WI
495076.abstract: It is critical to understand the impacts of heat on health in order to take actions that increase heat resilience. Studying past heat-caused morbidity can tell us who or what groups are vulnerable to heat events, what places experience a higher burden of heat-related illness, which meteorological conditions generate elevated risk, anticipated capacity demands on emergency medical services, and where more interventions are needed. In this study, we utilize ambulance callout data to quantify heat-health relationships in Wisconsin, especially in understudied rural areas. We ask: What meteorological and sociodemographic conditions are associated with elevated rates of heat-related illness in Wisconsin? Who and what parts of the state are disproportionately impacted, and under what circumstances? Here we specifically investigate the demographics of gender, race, and ethnicity, rural vs. urban areas, counties, labor, and weather conditions. We find significant relationships between sociodemographic characteristics and health outcomes at the county level; evidence of successful adaptation and behavior change during the hottest days; disproportionate rural vulnerability; and a high prevalence of heat-related illness that occurs outside of the home. Furthermore, we note strengths and limitations of different data sources on health responses to heat.

495077.title: Long-Lead, Model-Specific NOAA Storm Prediction Center Convective Parameters for Power Outage Forecasting
495077.authors: Brent McRoberts, Itron, Richmond, TX; and S. M. Quiring
495077.abstract: Severe convective weather frequently causes widespread and prolonged power outages across the United States. Itron's Storm Impact Prediction (SIP) system enables electric utilities to prepare for weather-related disruptions by generating outage forecasts from multiple Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models. Accurate forecasts with sufficient lead time allow utilities to optimize resource allocation, crew staging, and storm response planning. NOAA Storm Prediction Center (SPC) severe weather outlooks are a critical input to SIP because they provide an authoritative assessment of severe convective weather risk by integrating expert meteorological analysis with guidance from multiple forecast models. However, SPC outlooks tend to become increasingly conservative at longer lead times as forecast uncertainty and model divergence increase. This research develops an objective framework for generating SPC-like severe convective weather forecasts, including categorical risk levels and probabilistic guidance, independently for each NWP model. The methodology combines key environmental predictors, such as Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE) and bulk wind shear, to derive model-specific estimates of severe weather potential. By preserving the unique signal from each NWP, the resulting forecasts provide a more detailed characterization of forecast uncertainty and storm risk than a single consensus outlook. We demonstrate how incorporating NWP-specific severe weather guidance into SIP improves outage prediction skill, particularly at extended lead times. This approach enhances situational awareness, enables earlier identification of high-impact events, and provides utilities with more actionable information for proactive resource planning and operational decision-making.

495078.title: Lessons Learned from the SABRE 2023 Airborne Campaign: Improving Representation of Carbonyl Sulfide and the Stratospheric Sulfur Budget
495078.authors: Colin Gurganus, NOAA, Louisville, CO; and E. M. Bednarz, A. Rollins, E. Ray, S. Montzka, J. P. Schwarz, J. Zhang, T. Thornberry, and E. Waxman
495078.abstract: Carbonyl sulfide (OCS) is the most abundant sulfur species in the atmosphere and the primary source of non-volcanic sulfur to the stratosphere, where it is ultimately converted to sulfate aerosol, influencing global radiative forcing. Direct observations of OCS throughout the atmosphere remain sparse, and historical datasets are limited, leading to major uncertainties in the global sulfur budget. During the 2023 Stratospheric Aerosol Processes, Budget and Radiative Effects (SABRE) airborne campaign, the NOAA Airborne Carbonic Oxides and Sulfide Spectrometer (ACOS) collected high-precision in situ OCS measurements throughout the Arctic lower stratosphere during boreal winter. These observations provided a unique opportunity to evaluate satellite retrievals, assess long-term trends, and identify deficiencies in global chemistry-climate models. The SABRE observations demonstrate excellent agreement with Atmospheric Chemistry Experiment–Fourier Transform Spectrometer (ACE-FTS) retrievals, providing one of the first comprehensive in situ validations of satellite OCS measurements in the lower stratosphere. Combining these aircraft observations with satellite retrievals and NOAA surface measurements revealed an approximately 8% decline in global OCS abundance since 2016 that is not represented in many current chemistry-climate models. Updating the prescribed boundary-layer OCS abundance substantially improves modeled agreement with both aircraft and satellite observations while reducing the simulated stratospheric sulfate burden. The revised simulations increase modeled shortwave radiative flux at the tropical tropopause by as much as 0.3 W m⁻² locally, demonstrating that relatively small changes in OCS abundance can produce measurable differences in the simulated sulfur budget and radiative balance. These results demonstrate how targeted airborne observations can identify biases in global chemistry-climate models and improve representations of atmospheric composition and climate-relevant processes.

495082.title: Idealized Simulations of Flight-Level Interactions Between Two Storms
495082.authors: Stacey M. Hitchcock, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and T. Lane and C. R. Homeyer
495082.abstract: Current Federal Aviation Administration guidelines recommend that pilots avoid thunderstorms by at least 20 mi (32 km), leaving at least 40 mi between echoes before flying between them. However, pilots, route planners, and air traffic controllers also have operational considerations (fuel, tight schedules, etc.) that often make identifying potential paths between storms desirable. Analysis of a case of severe turbulence observed 32 km from radar-based storm boundaries in one of these ‘gap’ regions between two MCSs suggest that both gravity wave processes and interactions between upper-level outflow from the MCSs contribute to the turbulence severity and location. To better isolate key processes and generalize the results from the observed case, we run a series of idealized CM1 simulations with two storms in which we test sensitivity to both aspects of the environment and distance between storms. Results will explore both gravity wave and upper-level outflow interactions between two storms.

495084.title: Hospital Revenue Disruption from Hurricanes: Insurance Coverage Gap and Community Exposure in North Carolina
495084.authors: Francois Daudelin, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; and A. M. Lord, H. Zeff, and G. Characklis
495084.abstract: Hurricanes can force hospitals to cancel or postpone appointments, limit services, or evacuate patients. These operational disruptions combine with hurricane-driven demand shocks in the service area, where damage to infrastructure and homes can force patient relocation and increase cancellations. This results in a drop in revenue which can lead to short-term liquidity problems and permanent losses in affected facilities. Standard commercial property insurance carried by most hospitals only covers business interruption losses resulting from direct facility damage or mandated closures, not indirect losses from service-area disruptions. These two exposures must be isolated to evaluate the full scope of uninsured risks facing hospitals. In this study, we use a monthly patient-level admissions and charges database covering all hospitals in North Carolina (NC) 2016-2019 to evaluate the impacts of hurricane Florence on hospital revenue while separating service area and facility exposure. Data on hospital service mix enables the evaluation of revenue impacts on inpatient, outpatient, and emergency services, which can vary significantly across facilities. Service area exposure is defined using a hurricane hindcast dataset and patient zip codes; facility exposure is based on news reporting of hospital damage. We estimate effects by service and exposure types using a difference-in-differences model. We then map these results onto current NC hospitals, overlaying existing vulnerabilities (payer mix, safety-net status, rurality, financial reserves) and measures of hurricane risk to identify which facilities face the greatest risk from hurricane-driven revenue disruption.

495085.title: NOAA One Health: Integrating Weather Driven Tools, Ecological Forecasts, and Environmental Intelligence To Advance Health Outcomes
495085.authors: Alice Cheung Lau, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD
495085.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is a U.S. government agency established in 1970 to unify and leverage the country’s expertise in ocean, weather, hazards, and water science, holding a unique, ever-evolving role in the One Health approach. As a global leader in oceanographic, meteorological, and atmospheric predictive science, NOAA is at the forefront of efforts to promote marine ecosystem health and environmental intelligence initiatives. Recognizing its crucial role, the NOAA Science Advisory Board established the Oceans and Health Working Group (OHWG) in 2010 to guide agency-wide health sector contributions, mitigate threats to ocean health, and highlight underrepresented opportunities across multiple sectors. With leading organizations within the One Health framework primarily focusing on human or animal health, NOAA is well-positioned to fill this gap in ecosystem health and play a crucial role in advancing global One Health efforts. The NOAA One Health Group is an essential, multidisciplinary nexus convening experts across NOAA, other federal agencies, researchers, non-governmental partners, and international organizations with cross-cutting expertise in the environment and health space. With ten thematic areas encompassing the agency’s diverse One Health portfolio, such as leading initiatives in air quality monitoring, sustainable aquaculture, weather forecasting, ocean health benefits, and vector-borne diseases management, NOAA One Health provides authoritative meteorological and ecological data and research at the intersection of environmental drivers and health outcomes. NOAA produces a suite of predictive models, forecasts, and weather-driven tools for infectious diseases and environmental hazards across aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. Examples include sea surface temperature products and a Vibrio harvest calculator to ensure safe shellfish harvesting and food security nationwide, the interactive messaging framework designed to assist both public health professionals and healthcare providers in communicating health risks and delivering clear, timely messages during drought, and the experimental pollen forecast that provides estimates and high-risk times of daily, location-specific pollen concentration by modeling weather impacts. The delivery of integrated advanced modeling tools enables actionable environmental health applications. NOAA One Health further builds capacity in One Health solutions through robust cross-sector partnerships, leadership, and engagement in professional and intergovernmental organizations, such as the U.S. One Health Coordination Unit, Group on Earth Observations, and the American Meteorological Society. From extreme conditions to emerging infectious diseases, developing environmentally based, weather-driven health outlooks and interdisciplinary action are paramount to tackling unprecedented, rapidly evolving public health and ecosystem threats. Focused on synthesizing, analyzing, and refining environmental data, NOAA provides critical environmental intelligence through its observing systems and models to support ecological and epidemiological forecasts and modeling across timescales. Through its mission, legislative mandate, and partnerships, NOAA holds a critical role in contributing to environmental protection and marine ecosystem health initiatives within the One Health framework.

495087.title: Quantifying Measurement and Sampling Biases in Low-Cost Urban Sensor Networks
495087.authors: Sarah Berk, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; and T. Chakraborty and A. Hsu
495087.abstract: Researchers are increasingly turning to low-cost sensor networks as a means of resolving fine-scale urban spatial variability in air temperature and moist heat stress. These may be fixed sensor networks, crowdsourced citizen weather stations, or mobile vehicle traverses. However, sensor placement is challenging in heterogeneous urban environments, and observed spatial differences may reflect both true microclimatic variability and variability introduced by instrumentation, siting, and sampling design. Here, we quantify these sources of uncertainty through a series of controlled and field experiments using 41 low-cost air temperature and relative humidity sensors in Chapel Hill and Durham, North Carolina. Sensors were evaluated under controlled indoor conditions, and colocated in urban lawn and rooftop settings to examine how measurement variability between sensors changes across locations. The importance of radiation shielding and proximity to anthropogenic heat sources was also examined. Despite close agreement in controlled conditions, cross-sensor variability increased substantially outdoors and exhibited a strong dependence on daily meteorological conditions. For sensors housed in unaspirated radiation shields, daytime air temperature measurement variability was strongly correlated with diurnal temperature range (lawn r = 0.86; unshaded rooftop r = 0.97), and unshielded sensors overestimated temperature by up to 0.7 °C relative to shielded counterparts. Humidity measurements exhibited a weaker dependence on diurnal range, with more consistent variability between sensors across days. These uncertainties propagated into heat index estimates, which combine air temperature and humidity, resulting in a standard deviation 14% greater than that of air temperature alone. The impact of spatiotemporal sampling bias on modeled estimates of moist heat stress was then investigated using the Urban Stratified Environmental Network for Spatiotemporal Exposure (UrbanSENSE), designed to capture systematic variations in land cover and shading. Training a machine learning model on a subsample of this network demonstrates that observations restricted to particular land cover or shading environments, or limited times of day, produce systematic biases. These biases can propagate into machine-learning-derived urban temperature and humidity maps, even when conventional model evaluation suggests strong performance due to often shared training and test domains. Together, these findings demonstrate that both how and where urban meteorological observations are collected can influence inferred spatial patterns of temperature, humidity, and thus, moist heat stress. They provide guidance for designing low-cost urban meteorological networks, and highlight sources of observational and sampling bias that should be considered when interpreting fixed, crowdsource, and mobile measurements of urban microclimates.

495089.title: AI - Unsupervised Machine Learning Applied to a 60-Year Daily Gridded SPI Dataset to Diagnose Coherent Drought Regimes over CONUS
495089.authors: Iype Eldho, CICS-NC, Asheville, NC; and O. Prat, D. A. Coates, B. Nelson, M. Shaw, and S. Ansari
495089.abstract: Drought evolves across multiple time scales, from short-term precipitation deficits to persistent multi-season events, and diagnosing that evolution is central to understanding regional drought behavior and improving drought monitoring. A recurring practical problem is that the regions used to aggregate, interpret, and communicate drought information are typically inherited from climate divisions, river basins, or administrative boundaries rather than derived from drought behavior itself. In this work, we ask which measurable characteristics of a drought event actually define coherent regions across the contiguous United States (CONUS), and we apply unsupervised machine learning (ML) to a long-term observational record to answer this question. Daily Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) fields are computed over CONUS at 5-km resolution from NOAA's nClimGrid-Daily in situ precipitation dataset for 1961-2020, using both a two-parameter Gamma (McKee et al. 1993) and a three-parameter Pearson Type III (Guttman 1998) distribution, with 90-day and 270-day accumulation periods. Drought events are identified when SPI falls below -0.5, equivalent to the US Drought Monitor (USDM) Abnormally Dry (D0) category, sustained for at least 30 days. Each event is described by its duration, accumulated precipitation, minimum SPI, date of minimum SPI, onset and termination dates, fitted distribution parameters, and location. Partition-based, hierarchical, probabilistic, and density-based clustering algorithms are evaluated across these feature sets, with silhouette analysis indicating approximately four dominant regimes; k-means and k-medoids with K = 4 yield the most interpretable partitions. Longer and more severe events require greater accumulated precipitation for relief, and the duration-accumulation relationship becomes progressively more organized geographically as the accumulation period lengthens. The central result is that this spatial organization is carried almost entirely by a single feature: clustering on accumulated precipitation alone produces a clean, contiguous three-domain partition of CONUS, comprising a western domain extending into the southern Plains, a central domain, and a southeastern and coastal domain, whereas clustering on drought onset, termination, or peak-severity dates yields spatially incoherent, speckled fields, and clustering on duration or minimum SPI collapses to a single cluster spanning nearly the entire domain. Combining features does not monotonically improve delineation: adding accumulation to a set of timing features restores regional structure, but adding minimum SPI dilutes it - the outcome depends on which features are combined rather than on how many. Clustering the fitted precipitation-distribution parameters separates an interior Mountain West and Great Basin domain from the remainder of CONUS under both the Gamma and Pearson Type III formulations; however, the two formulations disagree on how the eastern two-thirds subdivides. Longer accumulation periods produce more coherent regions than shorter ones, but only when the full record is used: repeating every experiment separately for 1961-1990 and 1991-2020 produces additional clusters that are not reproducible between the two sub-periods and do not match the full-record partition, indicating that they reflect the smaller number of events available per grid cell rather than a genuine change in drought behavior. Accumulation is the notable exception. It recovers essentially the same domains for both sub-periods, providing a basis on which period-to-period differences can be interpreted with confidence. Two such differences are robust. The first concerns seasonal timing. At 270-day accumulation, the modal season of drought onset, termination, and peak severity is stable across periods: the Great Plains are spring-dominated and the West Coast winter-dominated in every period, broadly consistent with the USDM-derived climatology of Leeper et al. (2022). The corresponding 90-day fields are not stable. They shift by up to two seasons between sub-periods, most extensively over the Great Plains, Pacific Northwest, and Upper Midwest. Second, mean drought duration has been redistributed rather than uniformly trended, lengthening over the interior West and the southern Plains while shortening over the northern Plains, Upper Midwest, and Northeast, with changes several times larger at 270-day than at 90-day accumulation and concentrated in the same regions where sub-period clustering diverges most. Taken together, these results demonstrate that unsupervised learning applied to a long observational record can produce objectively defined and physically interpretable drought regions, but that such an analysis is only as trustworthy as its feature selection and record length. For applied climatology, this carries a concrete recommendation: regional delineations intended to support drought monitoring and early warning should be built on accumulation-based features and on the longest record available, since partitions fitted to a single 30-year normal period are unlikely to be stable. More broadly, the framework provides a diagnostic basis for examining how drought episodes transition from local, short-term rainfall deficits toward persistent, spatially organized drought regimes, and for evaluating how ML-derived regions compare with the operational regions currently used for drought monitoring and communication.

495090.title: Evaluating GFSv17 Surface Temperature and Precipitation Biases over Complex Terrains of the Continental United States
495090.authors: Peter Zachary H'Doubler, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and X. Z. Liang and F. Yang
495090.abstract: Cold and wet biases are common and long-standing over mountains in atmospheric and Earth system models and have been identified in past and current NCEP operational Global Forecast System (GFS) and Unified Forecast System (UFS). Despite their persistence, the cause of these biases has yet to be explained. We will diagnose the comprehensive characteristics of temperature and precipitation biases over the Rocky Mountains in the experimental GFSv17, which is the first NOAA fully coupled earth system model developed for global weather forecasting. The diagnostics will enable the identification of the potential physical processes underlying the biases and thereby the development of improved parameterizations to reduce them. To deepen the process understanding, we will analyze Rocky Mountain biases in all worldwide General Circulation Models (GCMs) from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP). This CMIP analysis will provide a more comprehensive spectrum of physics realizations than an analysis of GFSv17 alone, providing a more objective understanding of the model performance. Once contributing parameterization deficiencies from CMIP, GFSv17, or both are identified, we will conduct a sensitivity analysis using the regional Climate-Weather Research and Forecasting model (CWRF) multi-physics ensemble to verify the root physical causes of these biases and thereby find an effective solution to reduce the biases.

495091.title: NOAA's Contributions and Preparations for ESA Vigil Mission to L5
495091.abstract: The ESA Vigil Mission is the planned European Space Agency's operational space weather mission at the 5th Lagrangian point (L5) between the Earth and Sun to provide observations for space weather nowcasting and forecasting and for event-based alerts and warnings when solar events take place. Vigil Mission is scheduled to launch in 2031. The observations from L5 complements space weather monitoring at the 1st Lagrangian point (L1) and space weather instruments on satellites orbiting the Earth. The multi-vantages observations together enable more accurate space weather impact predictions and early warnings of potentially hazardous solar weather conditions emerging. NOAA NESDIS Office of Space Weather Observations is cooperating with ESA Vigil mission by providing a compact coronagraph-3 (CCOR-3) instrument to ESA. CCOR-3 will observe the solar corona and track coronal mass ejections (CMEs) from a side-on perspective at L5. The 3-D imaging capability generated from the combination of CCOR-3 at L5 with CCOR-1 onboard of GOES-19 and CCOR-2 onboard of SOLAR-1 and planned SOLAR-A/SOLAR-B at L1 will improve coronal mass ejection (CME) speed and direction tracking, reduce projection effects, and improve arrival time for the Earth-directed CMEs. The presentation will discuss CCOR-3 flight instrument development status and offer initial thoughts and plans to integrate Vigil’s Photospheric Magnetic Field Imager (PMI) data from the Sun’s east limb with earth-facing magnetogram data.

495092.title: Assessing the Effects of the Appalachian Mountains on the June 29-30, 2012 Derecho-Producing MCS
495092.authors: Max Murtough, Ohio University, Athens, OH; and D. V. Blount
495092.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) are distinguished from other severe convective storm modes by their production of widespread rain and wind impacts over timescales of 6-12 hours or more. While the atmospheric processes that influence MCS genesis and decay are well studied and observed, the influence of the physical topography of Earth’s surface on MCS behavior has proven to be an area where more work is needed. Past research has shown that idealized ridge-and-valley mountain ranges of similar (or greater) height to the Appalachian Mountains are sufficiently large to disrupt continuous MCS forward propagation by blocking advancement of the gust front and delaying new updraft production. In anomalously strong MCS cases, however, the Appalachians have often proven to be insufficient in disrupting crossing. One example of this comes from June 29-30, 2012, when an intense MCS moved through the Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic regions, crossing the Appalachians while producing significant severe wind gusts (65 kt+) across the entire width of the mountains. This study recreates this case using the WRF model to examine its sensitivity to the ridges it traversed. This is done by altering the scale of the terrain in the Appalachians to 40% above and below its real-world height. The goal of this is to determine if anomalously strong MCSs like the June 2012 case simply require a greater terrain height to effectively disrupt new updraft formation at the gust front, or if some other characteristic of extreme cases (such as strong rear inflow) allows for continuous forward propagation despite gust front blocking.

495094.title: AI-RTMA: Purely AI-based High Resolution Data Assimilation for NOAA's Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis
495094.authors: Guoqing Ge, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and A. Schein, M. Craine, T. T. Ladwig, A. M. Gibbs, T. Lei, X. C. Jin, M. Rancic, M. Pondeca, and D. Holdaway
495094.abstract: The Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis (RTMA) and Unrestricted Mesoscale Analysis (URMA) provides the best estimates of the current atmospheric state for situational awareness and analysis of record (AOR). RTMA combines atmospheric observations with short term forecasts (typically 1-hour forecasts) to produce a physically consistent analysis using the hybrid 3DEnVar data assimilation method for 3D-RTMA and the 2DVar data assimilation method for 2D-RTMA. There is a growing need for RTMA products to become available as quickly as possible, ideally within minutes of receiving observations. Meeting such stringent latency requirements, however, is extremely challenging for traditional physics-based data assimilation systems because of their substantial computational cost. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming Earth system science by providing powerful new approaches for learning from observations, accelerating computation, and capturing complex relationships within the Earth system. Despite remarkable progress in AI-based weather forecasting, developing a purely AI-based data assimilation (AI-DA) system capable of producing high-quality estimates of the atmospheric initial state remains a significant challenge, particularly when assimilating sparse and irregularly distributed surface observations. NOAA’s AI-RTMA project aims to pioneer a purely AI-based approach to high-resolution surface data assimilation. AI-RTMA is expected to rapidly integrate observations, with or without atmospheric background information, and generate high-resolution analysis products within seconds, potentially reducing latency by orders of magnitude compared with traditional data assimilation systems. Significant progress has been made across multiple components of the AI-RTMA system. At the conference, we will present the AI-RTMA innovations and initial results demonstrating its potential for next-generation operational high-resolution atmospheric analysis.

495097.title: Hydrogen Peroxide as an Atmospheric Oxidant
495097.authors: Aditya Kumar, Biosphere Research, Lucknow, India
495097.abstract: Hydrogen Peroxide is an important atmospheric oxidant playing a role in tropospheric carbon monoxide and sulfur oxidation cycles. Several factors such as gas to aqueous phase partitioning and cloud composition affect its oxidation capacity. This study reviews the impacts of hydrogen peroxide in atmospheric chemistry, and quantifies how several factors influence its behavior in the atmosphere and interactions with other atmospheric species.

495098.title: Integrating Ceilometer Observations and Machine Learning to Investigate Boundary Layer Evolution in Urban and Suburban Environments
495098.authors: Tsunghau Peng, NCAS, Washington, DC; and N. N. Karle, Z. Yang, and S. Chiao
495098.abstract: An adaptive algorithm was developed using ground-based, high-resolution aerosol backscatter profiles from the Vaisala CL61 ceilometer to retrieve planetary boundary layer height (PBLH).
