More than three years of observations (2022–2025) from the U.S. National Capital Region (NCR) were analyzed to investigate the temporal evolution and controlling mechanisms of PBL dynamics across contrasting urban and suburban environments. Observations from the Howard University Interdisciplinary Research Building (HUIRB) in Washington, D.C., represent the urban environment, while observations from the Howard University Beltsville Campus (HUBC) in Beltsville, Maryland, represent the suburban environment. The resulting PBLH dataset provides a continuous observational framework for examining differences in boundary-layer development between the two environments. The PBLH exhibited a pronounced diurnal and seasonal cycle at both sites, with daytime PBLH generally increasing during periods of stronger surface heating and decreasing during nighttime. In contrast, the nocturnal boundary layer height (NBLH) displayed substantially greater variability and did not exhibit a simple seasonal pattern. Contrary to expectations that enhanced urban surface heating associated with the urban heat island (UHI) effect would lead to a deeper nocturnal boundary layer, the urban site did not show a systematic enhancement in NBLH relative to the suburban site. Instead, the suburban site generally exhibited higher NBLH values. These results indicate that differences in surface energy exchange and meteorological conditions may exert a stronger influence on boundary-layer development than urban heating alone. To investigate the environmental controls on PBLH and evaluate the potential for data-driven PBLH prediction, a machine-learning framework was developed using meteorological variables. Predictor variables included net heat flux, wind speed, pressure, relative humidity and equivalent potential temperature obtained from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model. Wind speed parameter from Doppler wind LiDAR can be fed in the machine learning model instead of the HRRR model result. Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost regression models were trained using the ceilometer-derived PBLH as the reference target. Model performance was evaluated against the algorithm-based PBLH using independent testing periods and compared across the urban and suburban sites. In addition to evaluating predictive skill, feature importance was examined to identify the environmental variables that contributed most strongly to PBLH variability. The machine-learning results demonstrate the potential of a data-driven framework to reproduce the observed variability in PBLH from meteorological and surface conditions without directly relying on aerosol backscatter profiles. This provides a complementary approach to ceilometer-based retrievals: the adaptive algorithm provides the observational PBLH reference, while the machine-learning models provide a means of predicting and interpreting PBLH variability from readily available environmental parameters. The results further indicate that the relative importance of meteorological and surface-energy variables differs between the urban and suburban environments, suggesting that the mechanisms controlling boundary-layer development are spatially heterogeneous. Precipitation events provided an additional framework for examining these differences. After precipitation, PBLH at the suburban site was generally elevated and subsequently decreased over time, whereas the urban PBLH exhibited substantially weaker sensitivity to precipitation. The observed post-precipitation evolution is consistent with a potential role of soil-moisture perturbations in modifying surface energy partitioning and subsequent boundary-layer development at the suburban site. The machine-learning framework provides an additional means of evaluating this relationship by quantifying the contribution of meteorological and surface variables to PBLH variability. Overall, this study combines high-resolution ceilometer observations, an adaptive PBLH retrieval algorithm, and machine-learning techniques to investigate PBL dynamics across urban and suburban environments in the NCR. The results demonstrate that machine learning can complement observation-based PBLH retrievals by providing a data-driven framework for PBLH prediction and for identifying the environmental controls responsible for differences in boundary-layer evolution. This approach could ultimately support PBLH estimation during observational data gaps and provide a pathway toward extending PBLH prediction to locations where continuous ceilometer observations are unavailable.

495100.title: Evaluating Low-Cost Air Quality Sensors for a GLOBE PM2.5 Protocol
495100.authors: Samantha J Adams, New York, NY; and M. Pippin, K. Okorn, and K. Czajkowski
495100.abstract: The GLOBE (Global Learning and Observations to Benefit the Environment) program is an international science and education program that connects students, teachers, scientists, and citizen scientists in hands-on environmental investigations. A key component of GLOBE is its data collection protocols, which help to ensure data quality. As GLOBE expands its crowdsourcing initiatives, a PM2.5 protocol is being developed, which will utilize low cost air quality sensors (LCS). As the protocol is developed, these LCS must be evaluated against reference-grade regulatory monitors to ensure data can be used for scientific research, air quality forecasting, and augmenting satellite measurements (e.g. NASA’s TEMPO mission). From July 2025 through August 2026, an intercomparison study of diverse LCS models was conducted at the Chemistry and Physics Atmospheric Boundary Layer Experiment (CAPABLE) site at NASA Langley Research Center. The site is co-located with the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality’s Hampton-NASA monitoring station, which utilizes a Teledyne T640 Federal Equivalency Method (FEM) real time mass monitor to measure fine particulate matter (PM2.5). This instrument was used as the reference standard. Three distinct LCS categories were evaluated: do-it-yourself (DIY) LCS, mobile LCS, and stationary LCS, all of which utilize laser-based optical particle counters (OPCs) to measure particulate matter concentrations. The majority of the LCS use Plantower OPCs: four use the PMS5003 (an Arduino-based DIY LCS, the Kids Making Sense AQgo, the AirGradient Open Air and the PurpleAir PA-II) and two use the PMSA003I (a ThingPlus-based DIY LCS and the Davis AirLink). The AtmoTube Pro uses a Sensirion SPS30 OPC. All of the LCS were evaluated using the EPA’s performance metrics for fine particulate matter air sensors; where possible, the suggested base testing protocols were utilized. However, true base testing could not be conducted on the DIY and mobile sensors because battery constraints and lack of weatherproofing meant they could not be continuously deployed. Additionally, the PurpleAir - which has a well established correction factor - was used to evaluate a correction factor applied to the AirGradient measurements. Although complete base testing protocols were only used for the stationary LCS, the performance metrics established a baseline for comparison and helped to evaluate reliability. The DIY LCS generally met or exceeded EPA performance metrics, though the Arduino variant had an average y-intercept over the recommended upper bound (>5 micrograms per cubic meter) and the ThingPlus variant exceeded the normalized root mean square error (>30%). Both of the mobile sensors failed to meet the majority of the performance metrics, struggling under high-temperature conditions (>30 degrees Celsius) - further evaluation is needed, but these results suggest the use of these types of LCS may be constrained by environmental conditions. All three stationary sensors performed well, the AirGradient in particular. By default, AirGradient applies a version of the PurpleAir correction factor, which improves AirGradient’s accuracy; this verifies vendor co-location evaluations. Data from the Davis AirLink cannot be evaluated with the EPA correction factor applied, as the raw data needed to use this formula is unavailable for download; this means that a different correction factor has to be developed using the available, processed data. Moving forward, more long-term, multi-climate co-location evaluations will be done to establish reliable correction algorithms and evaluate various LCS’ viability for the PM2.5 protocol.

495102.title: Multiyear Predictability of Flood Frequency Along the U.S. Southeast Coast from Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation Variability
495102.authors: Liping Zhang, UCAR, Boulder, CO; GFDL/NOAA, Princeton, NJ; and H. Murakami, T. L. Delworth, V. Koul, A. C. Ross, C. Stock, X. Yang, J. Lee, and A. Wittenberg
495102.abstract: Observations have shown a significant increase in flood frequency along the U.S. Southeast Coast (USSEC) since the year 2010. This increased flooding is driven both by increases in storm frequency and rising background sea level due to increasing greenhouse gases and internal low-frequency variabilities. While background sea levels are the primary factor driving the increase in flooding events, storms are responsible for the most extreme flooding events and play a crucial role in determining the maximum flood intensity. We describe here multiyear predictability of USSEC flood frequency, where much of the predictive skill originates from predictable decadal scale variations in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) which impact regional sea level. Using a 1/12o regional ocean model along with AMOC predictions from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL) global decadal prediction system, we generate skillful flood frequency predictions along the USSEC with significant skill three years in advance.

495103.title: Taking the Top Down Approach: Using Thunderstorm Overshooting Top Characteristics to Understand Deep Convective Updrafts in Supercells and Quasi-Linear Convective Systems
495103.authors: Melinda Berman, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and R. J. Trapp and S. Nesbitt
495103.abstract: Overshooting tops (OTs) are manifestations of deep convective updrafts that extend past the tropopause into the stratosphere. OTs can transport moisture and aerosols into the stratosphere and have been connected to the occurrence and intensity of hazardous convective weather, such as tornadoes and hail. Our recent observational and supercell studies have shown that overshooting top area (OTA) is relatively insensitive to stratospheric static stability and is more closely related to tropospheric updraft core area, which in turn depends on tropospheric vertical wind shear. In contrast, overshooting top depth (OTD) depends significantly on stratospheric static stability and vertical velocity in the upper-tropospheric (8-12.5 km) updraft core. Further questions remain, however, about the effect that storm mode has on overshooting top characteristics. Using idealized simulations of both supercells and quasi-linear convective systems (QLCSs), we will explore how changes to the environment manifest into changes in OT characteristics. Results indicate that OTA, regardless of storm mode, is at least somewhat related to vertical wind shear. OTA is also not correlated to stratospheric static stability, regardless of storm mode. OTD, however, shows variability across storm modes. In supercells, OTD is not correlated to vertical wind shear, while in QLCSs, OTD is correlated to vertical wind shear. Reasons for this divergence in OTD controls between storm modes will be explored.

495105.title: SatCORPS Global Cloud Composite (GCC): Increasing the Pace of the Research to Production Science Innovation Pipeline
495105.authors: Thad Chee, LaRC - NASA Langley Research Center, Bethesda, MD
495105.abstract: The NASA Satellite ClOud and Radiation Property retrieval System (SatCORPS) team has created an analysis ready and cloud-optimized data transformation pipeline and geospatial service of a Global Cloud Composite (GCC) product derived from global geostationary and Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite imagery. This geospatial service and generated information is available at high temporal and spatial resolution via the SatCORPS web mapping application for visualization and analysis. The SatCORPS GCC product takes advantage of the scalable processing resources provided by both the AWS batch service and the Langley Research Center Batch service (LaRC Batch) to provide new composites every hour. Information from each of the satellites is available on schedules specific to each satellite acquisition time so the processing algorithm temporally composites the final dataset as each satellite’s information becomes available. Since the SatCORPS team is primarily a research effort, one of the most important aspects of the GCC system is continually working on increasing the pace of scientific discovery and improvement. Towards this goal, the team has worked on creating a processing system that enhances the speed of transfer of discoveries and innovations in the science and technical research areas to our publicly available at no charge data streams. In this work, we describe the techniques, systems policies and architecture that underlies the GCC system and have been developed over time and prior experiences. In addressing the challenges that presented themselves, the SatCORPS team has evolved new ways that significantly enhance the speed that changes are deployed into operational systems. The SatCORPS Global GCC product provides sophisticated global composited cloud research products with very low latency that we see that as filling a rapidly growing need in the research and modelling community with no up-front nor ongoing costs associated with downloading or using the information.

495106.title: When It Rains, Does It Pour? A Likelihood-Based Framework for Evaluating Changing Precipitation Extremes in Climate Models
495106.authors: Sara Almadani, George Mason University, Alexandria, VA; and T. DelSole
495106.abstract: Insurance, reinsurance, infrastructure, and resilience decisions increasingly rely on climate-model information about changing heavy-precipitation hazards. The credibility of these applications depends on whether simulations reproduce both the statistical characteristics of observed extremes and their changes with warming. Existing evaluations often rely on visual comparisons of return levels rather than formal statistical decision rules. We introduce a transparent, likelihood-based framework for comparing nonstationary Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distributions fitted to annual maximum daily precipitation from climate simulations and gauge-based observations. The GEV location parameter is modeled as a linear function of the monthly global mean temperature anomaly corresponding to the month of each annual precipitation maximum. A likelihood-ratio test evaluates the null hypothesis that the location intercept, temperature sensitivity, scale, and shape parameters are equal between two datasets. We first assess the framework through all 10 pairwise comparisons among five ensemble members generated by the same climate model. At the 5% significance level, parameter equality is rejected in 6.7%–8.0% of analyzed land grid cells, indicating broad consistency across realizations despite internal climate variability and finite-sample uncertainty. In contrast, comparisons between individual ensemble members and observations reject parameter equality in approximately 84% of land grid cells, providing widespread evidence that the fitted distributions of simulated and observed precipitation extremes differ. This framework provides a reproducible approach for validating the hazard information underlying climate-risk assessments. By identifying where simulated precipitation extremes are statistically consistent with observations—and where additional scrutiny is warranted—it can support more transparent and informed use of climate-model information in insurance and reinsurance risk management, infrastructure planning, and resilience decisions.

495107.title: Shair: Transforming Hyperlocal Air Quality Information into Public Health Action
495107.authors: Courtney Taylor, Ramboll, Fort Collins, CO; Ramboll, Fort Collins, CO; and P. Vennam and M. Cheeseman
495107.abstract: Communities and local agencies increasingly face the challenge of making timely decisions about air quality with limited monitoring infrastructure, rapidly changing environmental conditions, and growing concerns regarding environmental justice and public health. While regulatory monitoring networks provide essential information, they are often too sparse to characterize neighborhood-scale variations in air pollution that can influence community exposure, public health outcomes, and local decision-making. Advances in sensor technologies, atmospheric modeling, data assimilation, and cloud computing now offer new opportunities to bridge this gap by transforming air quality observations into actionable information. Ramboll's Shair platform was developed to address this need by integrating real-time observations, advanced atmospheric science, and intuitive visualization tools into a single decision-support system designed for agencies, community organizations, and the public. Shair is a real-time air quality analysis, forecasting, and source attribution platform that combines low-cost sensor observations, regulatory monitoring data, meteorological information, traffic activity, emissions inventories, and advanced atmospheric models to generate high-resolution estimates of pollutant concentrations at neighborhood scales. The platform integrates scientifically established modeling frameworks, including weather prediction models, specifically the Weather Research and Forecasting Model, and photochemical grid models, specifically the Comprehensive Air Quality Model with Extensions (CAMx), with real-time data assimilation techniques that continuously adjust model predictions using observed measurements. This fusion of modeled and observed data enables Shair to provide spatially continuous air quality information, including in locations where no monitoring instruments exist. A key capability of Shair is its ability to convert complex air quality data into information that supports practical decisions. Rather than simply displaying monitored concentrations, the platform provides users with estimates of pollutant levels across entire communities, identifies pollution hotspots, and quantifies the contribution of different source categories to observed air quality conditions. Through interactive mapping and analytical tools, users can evaluate how air quality varies by neighborhood, census tract, school location, transportation corridor, or community-identified area of concern in urban or rural areas alike. This level of spatial detail helps agencies and community organizations better understand disparities in pollution exposure and prioritize mitigation actions where they can achieve the greatest public health benefits. The platform has been successfully implemented in partnership with community based organizations, transportation planning agencies, and private companies. Shair can integrate data from a network of community-deployed sensors with atmospheric modeling systems to generate real-time PM2.5 concentration maps at approximately 10-meter spatial resolution. The resulting analyses have revealed consistent differences in air quality between neighborhoods, identified higher concentrations near downtown transportation corridors, and provided insight into seasonal pollution patterns that are not visible through monitoring data alone. Another distinguishing feature of the platform is its ability to support environmental justice and community-centered decision-making. Shair combines community monitoring data with advanced scientific models to provide geographically specific information that can support local planning, grant applications, public outreach, and policy development. The platform also provides a foundation for evaluating long-term trends, assessing progress toward community air quality goals, and identifying opportunities to reduce disproportionate pollution burdens. This presentation will describe the scientific framework, data integration approach, and operational implementation of Shair, with emphasis on lessons learned from community-based applications. Case studies will demonstrate how combining monitoring, modeling, visualization, and community alerting can improve understanding of neighborhood-scale air quality and provide actionable information for protecting public health. By translating technical air quality analyses into accessible visualizations, Shair has enabled community members to engage directly with environmental data and participate more effectively in discussions related to air quality planning and mitigation strategies. Beyond providing publicly accessible, comprehensive air quality information, Shair provides public health protection by providing early-warning notifications and alerts enabling agencies and interested citizens take action to avoid or minimize exposure. A recent pilot initiative developed a community-focused, neighborhood-scale air quality alert system. The pilot leverages Shair's real-time capabilities to identify periods when localized air quality conditions may pose elevated health risks and communicate this information to residents, schools, community organizations, and local agencies. Real-time information can help local agencies communicate health risks, issue advisories, prepare for wildfire smoke events, and inform decisions related to schools, outdoor recreation, community events, and vulnerable populations. During episodic events, notification messages provide crucial situational awareness that can help decision-makers identify impacted communities and implement targeted interventions more rapidly than would be possible using traditional monitoring networks alone. The pilot project is designed to demonstrate how hyperlocal environmental intelligence can support proactive public health protection, improve resilience to episodic events such as wildfire smoke, facility releases and winter stagnation events thereby creating a model for more equitable and responsive community health interventions. Ultimately, Shair illustrates how integrated air quality intelligence systems can help agencies and communities move from atmospheric data to informed decisions that support healthier, more resilient communities.

495108.title: Evaluating Model Precipitation Extremes: Verification and Fitness for Purpose Assessments
495108.authors: James Correia Jr., CIRES / NWS Weather Prediction Center, College Park, MD; NWS/Weather Prediction Center and CU Boulder CIRES, College Park, MD; and S. M. Trojniak
495108.abstract: Demonstrating fitness for purpose in model evaluation frameworks is usually accomplished by model verification. Verification using bulk metrics can hide important characteristics that cloud fit for purpose assessments. Other means exist to statistically compare models and observations at spatio-temporal scales that are important for process level context, though not always process level understanding. Examples that demonstrate fit for purpose assessment of the HRRR and RRFS data over the last 3 years will be shown to highlight the complexity and dimensionality of model evaluation. We will focus on seasons and regions along with national perspectives to highlight recurring challenges in precipitation forecasting. In addition we will highlight some phenomenon based challenges of forecasting precipitation for mesoscale convective systems that do and do not produce extreme rainfall. The state of the science forecasting of extreme precipitation will be on display along with the challenges of using verification for rare events to make decisions about model quality, improvement, and fitness for purpose.

495111.title: Climate Justice through Local Climate Zones: Unequal Heat Exposure and Social Vulnerability in Chiayi City, Taiwan
495111.authors: Yu-Cheng Chen, Nanhua University, Chiayi County, CYI, Taiwan; Nanhua University, Tainan, Taiwan (R.O.C.), Taiwan; and Y. L. Su
495111.abstract: Climate change is intensifying urban heat; however, its impacts are not evenly distributed among communities. This study examines the spatial relationships among Local Climate Zones (LCZs), environmental exposure, and social vulnerability in Chiayi City, Taiwan, and evaluates the applicability of LCZs as a framework for climate justice assessment in a medium-sized city. Neighborhoods were used as the analytical units. Urban morphology was classified using the LCZ system, while social vulnerability was assessed using six indicators: population, wage income, comprehensive income tax, low-income households, lower-middle-income households, and older adults living alone. Temperature, relative humidity, PM2.5, anthropogenic heat, and a natural environment index were integrated using geographic information systems and analyzed through Pearson correlation analysis. The results reveal distinct socio-spatial inequalities in environmental exposure. Compact mid-rise areas (LCZ2), primarily located around Chiayi Railway Station and the central commercial districts, exhibited the highest anthropogenic heat levels. Compact low-rise areas (LCZ3), which dominate older neighborhoods in western Chiayi, experienced elevated heat loads because of dense buildings, restricted ventilation, and limited green coverage. These areas also overlapped with neighborhoods containing higher proportions of low-income households, lower-middle-income households, and older adults living alone. In contrast, open low-rise areas (LCZ6) and natural zones containing green spaces and water bodies (LCZG) showed lower heat loads and more favorable environmental conditions. Overall social vulnerability was positively correlated with winter early-morning temperature (r = 0.595) and summer afternoon temperature (r = 0.528). The risk associated with lower-middle-income households showed a stronger correlation with summer afternoon temperature (r = 0.583). Anthropogenic heat was positively associated with overall social vulnerability (r = 0.468), whereas the natural environment index was negatively correlated with both social vulnerability (r = −0.505) and anthropogenic heat (r = −0.606). These results suggest that vulnerable neighborhoods experience not only greater heat exposure but also cumulative environmental burdens, including limited access to natural resources and poorer air quality. The findings demonstrate that urban heat risk is shaped by the interaction between urban morphology and the unequal distribution of social and environmental resources. Integrating LCZ classification with social vulnerability assessment can identify priority areas where compact urban form, insufficient greenery, and socioeconomic disadvantage overlap. This framework transforms LCZs from a descriptive urban climate classification into an operational tool for climate justice, providing a scientific basis for equitable green infrastructure, accessible cooling shelters, neighborhood-scale cooling interventions, and priority-based resource allocation.

495114.title: Rapid Assessment of Drought-Impacted Stream Water Temperature With a Remote Sensing Model
495114.authors: Daniel Philippus, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and C. R. Corona and T. Hogue
495114.abstract: The 2026 snow drought in the Upper Colorado River Basin (UCRB), in the western part of the United States, was one of the worst on record, with droughts on a similar scale expected to become more common in the coming decades. The primary concern during such snow droughts is diminishing water supply to streams/rivers that are used for both human and environmental purposes. However, with diminishing supply, which visibly affects streamflow, also comes the concern of higher stream water temperatures (SWT) due to reduced cool water input upstream and less thermal mass available to buffer water temperature increases, making aquatic environments less tempered than ecological systems are accustomed to. While streamflow has been an important focus of drought effect studies in the UCRB, the same cannot be said for SWT monitoring, which currently depends on about 87 USGS stations across the UCRB reporting real-time SWT and local monitoring. Small and remote streams in particular are largely unmonitored, but are often key habitat and important water sources, so expanded monitoring of such streams would be an important advantage in understanding drought impacts. We address limitations in real-time SWT monitoring by predicting SWT impacts throughout the UCRB using a remote sensing SWT model for unmonitored streams called TempEst 2. TempEst 2 was chosen for straightforward modification for drought representation and applicability to thousands of sites over the UCRB. Additionally, the use of a remote sensing model like TempEst 2 allows for the opportunity to detect drought-related SWT shifts directly through perturbations in land surface temperature. TempEst 2 with the drought modification allows predictions of recent conditions up through seven days before the present, enabling rapid assessment of developing drought impacts. Preliminary testing shows that a drought-modified TempEst 2 is capable of identifying drought impacts to daily SWT and ecologically-relevant metrics such as maximum 30-day mean SWT. Current model objectives include producing a detailed spatiotemporal analysis of drought impacts to SWT in the UCRB through August 2026, derived from several thousand sites in the UCRB including small and remote streams, with an initial analysis already covering 762 stream locations, from first-order through major rivers, through July 2026. Results currently show that SWT impacts vary by upwards of 1 °C, which is similar to the magnitude of overall drought impacts to SWT, over tens of kilometers even within the same river. These results highlight the importance of distributed SWT estimates to characterizing drought impacts over large scales. Final analysis will examine the scope of drought-driven SWT increases throughout the UCRB, identifying the extent to which water quality is impaired alongside water quantity as a result of the 2026 drought.

495115.title: Improving Tropical Cyclone Track and Intensity Forecasts: An LSTM-Based Post-Processing Framework for Sequential Data Correction and Uncertainty Estimation
495115.authors: Hsiao-Chung Tsai, Tamkang University, New Taipei City, Taiwan; and F. Y. Lin, Y. L. Lin, N. N. Hsu, T. S. Huang, and R. L. Elsberry
495115.abstract: Traditional methods for estimating forecast confidence—such as deriving the Cone of Uncertainty (CoU) from historical climatological errors or relying on linear statistical combinations for intensity—often fail to capture complex, non-linear atmospheric interactions and unique case-specific synoptic conditions. This study proposes a unified post-processing framework utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to correct sequential forecast data and dynamically estimate tropical cyclone (TC) prediction uncertainties. For track uncertainty, we utilize a many-to-many LSTM architecture that leverages multi-model ensemble guidance to generate situation-dependent uncertainty radii, providing a continuous and adaptive representation of spatiotemporal forecast errors. For intensity, the LSTM model refines outputs from the Weighted Analog Intensity Prediction (WAIP; Tsai and Elsberry 2014; Tsai and Elsberry 2019) model. To overcome cross-agency inconsistencies in maximum sustained wind definitions, the intensity forecasting is centered on minimum central pressure (Pmin) coupled with pressure-wind relationship conversions in the LSTM. Furthermore, the model is optimized using a loss function designed for probability distribution functions (PDFs) to refine both deterministic forecasting and intensity spread. Preliminary results demonstrate that LSTM is highly effective for the post-processing and correction of sequential meteorological data. The dynamically estimated CoU radii effectively capture situational track uncertainty (Tsai et al. 2026), avoiding the stepwise discontinuity found in traditional methodologies. In addtion, the refined intensity spread more reliably encompasses observed data while narrowing the overall uncertainty range compared to the original WAIP model. By transitioning from static climatological statistics to an AI-based dynamic approach, this unified LSTM framework provides a robust, case-sensitive estimation of forecast confidence, offering significant advancements for operational guidance and disaster preparedness.

495116.title: A New Model for Inland Tropical Cyclone Wind Decay
495116.authors: Cameron Masiello, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and J. W. Cline and G. M. Lackmann
495116.abstract: Near-surface winds are among the most consequential inland hazards produced by landfalling tropical cyclones (TCs). Over water, observational and modeling studies show that near-surface wind speed varies logarithmically with height and is sensitive to both the height and strength of the boundary-layer jet and to surface roughness. Recent work on landfalling TCs recovers the same logarithmic structure inland, where the profile responds to the roughness of the underlying surface and to the wind at the top of the boundary layer. Building on these results, a parametric model of inland near-surface winds is developed for both forecast applications and post-event analysis. Wind at the boundary layer top is specified by blending a parametric pressure profile with dropsonde observations. Observationally derived parameterizations of pressure fill, radius of maximum wind expansion, and radial decay govern weakening after landfall. A logarithmic surface-layer profile, high-resolution roughness fields derived from WRF land use, and a turbulence-based gust parameterization then yield location-specific sustained winds and gusts at 10 meters and above. Evaluation against inland observations from Hurricanes Ian (2022) and Helene (2024) demonstrates skill in reproducing the magnitude and spatial footprint of observed sustained winds and gusts, while systemically having a slight positive bias. The computationally efficient framework provides a practical tool for rapid inland wind-hazard assessment, ensemble applications, and post-event reconstruction at a fraction of the computational cost of high-resolution NWP.

495121.title: WRF LES Simulation of Hurricane María Over Complex Terrain: Assessing Impacts on Puerto Rico's Power Transmission Network
495121.authors: Bianca Valeria Méndez Cruz, University at Albany, Department of Atmospheric and Evironmental Sciences and Atmospheric Science Research Center, Albany, NY; and J. P. Montoya-Rincon and J. E. Gonzalez-Cruz
495121.abstract: Puerto Rico is a tropical archipelago located in the Caribbean Sea, and on September 20, 2017, it was impacted by Hurricane María. The strong winds of 155 mph and the heavy rainfall on the island caused power transmission failure, and it left around 3.7 million customers without power. In addition, Puerto Rico has a mountain range in the central region of the island and the complex terrain poses additional challenges to the electrical grid. The purpose of this research is to gain deeper insight into the simulated hurricane boundary layer of María, specifically the conditions close to the power towers. By doing the analysis, we seek to comprehend how the complex terrain of Puerto Rico influences the damage of the power transmission towers. Due to the collaboration with Puerto Rico’s power company, we have access to the Hurricane María damage records that identify which towers failed and which did not. It is important to note that the island’s transmission network operates across three transmission lines: 230 kV, 115 kV, and 38 kV, though the damage report available covers only the 230 kV and 115 kV lines. The Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model with Large Eddy Simulation (LES) leads us to get a clearer comprehension of the stresses that the power infrastructure undergoes during events like María. The focus of this research is the transmission line that goes from the north to the south of the island, from the municipality of Manatí to Peñuelas, where we can evaluate how the complex terrain influences the damage in the transmission towers. To achieve this goal, we used 5 two-way nested domains centered on the municipality of Jayuya, with the innermost domain at a 111 m grid resolution and covering the mountain range, as shown in Figure 1. Preliminary results show a difference in the wind speed magnitude, where we compare the wind with and without the LES in the location of Jayuya (Figure 2). The 10 m wind speed mean difference was 2.5 mph, with the LES presenting the highest values. However, the largest difference between the two appears to increase with wind speed intensity. We selected two points, one with the highest wind speed and the other with the lowest. At 06:15 UTC, the wind speed without the LES was 25.7 mph, but with the LES, this goes up to 27.5 mph. The highest wind speed at the Jayuya location was at 09:45 UTC, where the simulated wind speed without LES was 56.8 mph, but with the LES, this value increased to 61.0 mph. As expected, the preliminary results suggest that LES resolves higher wind speeds, which may have implications for transmission tower damage. Future research will include an evaluation of the Hurricane Boundary Layer to compare the differences between the domain 3 and domain 5 values, while also studying the failure rates of the towers across the transect using Fragility Curves and Machine Learning Methods.

495122.title: The Influence of North African Vegetation on African Easterly Waves, Atlantic Tropical Cyclones, and the West African Monsoon
495122.authors: Braydon Paul Songer, Iowa State University, Ames, IA; and C. M. Patricola-DiRosario, E. Bercos-Hickey, P. J. Klotzbach, and D. K. Danso
495122.abstract: Although sea surface temperatures (SSTs) are a valuable predictor of seasonal Atlantic tropical cyclone (TC) activity, there have been times when TC activity corresponds weakly with SST variability. For example, there was an unexpected mid-season lull in the 2024 Atlantic hurricane season despite extremely favorable tropical Atlantic and Pacific SSTs. The lull has been linked in part to a northward shift of African easterly waves (AEWs), a common TC precursor, and to a concurrent northward extension of North African precipitation and vegetation, which can impact the meridional temperature gradient that maintains the African easterly jet (AEJ), and thereby AEWs. In this study, we investigated the impact of North African vegetation on seasonal Atlantic TC activity through its influence on AEWs, the AEJ, and the West African Monsoon (WAM). We used the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model at 27 km resolution to conduct 10-member ensembles of three Atlantic hurricane seasons characterized by above-average, near-average, and below-average TC activity, respectively: 2010, 2001, and 2015. The control simulations consist of seasonal hindcasts, while the experiments extend North African vegetation to 22°N by prescribing vegetation and associated land and soil conditions (e.g., leaf area index, albedo, soil moisture, and soil type). The experiment represents an environment in which anomalous precipitation, like what was observed in 2024, could support a northward expansion of vegetation. Preliminary results show that extending the vegetation northward reduces AEW activity, which is associated with a weakened AEJ and a stronger WAM. Additionally, Atlantic TC activity responds to the changes over North Africa, experiencing shifts in track location and extending activity into the late season. However, the seasonal number of TCs is relatively unchanged, despite decreases in AEWs. We plan to investigate changes in TC seeds and TC environmental favorability to understand the TC response. Our findings can improve subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction of Atlantic TC activity by understanding how North African vegetation can serve as a source of predictability through its role in the climate of Northern Africa

495124.title: Effects of Land Use and Land Cover Change on Extreme Rainfall from Mesoscale Convective Systems In a Convection-Permitting Model: Case Study of the Great Midwest Floods of 1993
495124.authors: Seth Colston, Iowa State University, Ames, IA; and I. N. Williams and D. McDermott
495124.abstract: Understanding the effect of climate changes on extreme weather events such as floods is of significant importance. In addition to climate changes, millions of acres of forest have been lost in the U.S. over the past few centuries, primarily due to changing agricultural activity. Although climate mitigation efforts include reforestation plans, the impacts of land use and land cover (LULC) change on precipitation extremes remain uncertain due to the inability of coarse-resolution climate models to explicitly resolve convective storms including heavy rain-producing mesoscale convective systems (MCSs). In this study the Weather Research and Forecasting Model (WRF) at a convection-permitting (3 km) resolution was paired with the Noah-MP land model to investigate whether LULC changes impact extreme precipitation in the Midwest. WRF was run with present day and preindustrial (1850) LULC classes to evaluate the impact of LULC on MCS formation, intensity, and coverage. Two periods were chosen for simulation: The Great Midwest Flood of 1993, which remains one of the costliest natural disasters and was driven in part by a higher than average number of MCSs, and the summer of 2009, chosen for its near average precipitation characteristics. Our findings show that MCSs either fail to form or their precipitation intensity is reduced in preindustrial WRF simulations, with the largest differences occurring in regions where present day croplands were forests in the preindustrial era. Differences in MCSs can be attributed to differences in thermodynamics, where forests result in less convective available potential energy, greater convective inhibition energy, and an increase in the level of free convection (LFC). Differences in thermodynamics are associated with LULC changes, as albedo is greater over forest, increasing surface temperatures. In addition, latent heat flux decreases over forests compared to croplands, reducing low level moisture. This study shows that changing present day LULC to preindustrial LULC results in 10% less average precipitation throughout the Midwest, due to the combination of reduced precipitation coverage and intensity.

495125.title: Developing Air Quality Risk Indices for Mixed-Pollutant Neighborhoods: A Census Block Group-level Analysis of the Denver Metro Region
495125.authors: Forrest Lacey, NCAR, Boulder, CO; NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and K. H. Nguyen, J. Boehnert, O. Wilhelmi, K. Fewless, L. Kessenich, R. R. McCrary, R. Kumar, and J. L. Vigh
495125.abstract: Effective air quality management in the Denver Metro area requires a nuanced understanding of localized pollution drivers, specifically regarding fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and ozone. These trace pollutants are significant determinants of community health and resilience, with clear links to various acute and chronic health outcomes. Assessing the sources, formation, and transport of these contaminants is essential for identifying populations at heightened risk and implementing targeted mitigation strategies. Utilizing WRF-Chem modeling at the 4km gridded scale and aggregating to the census block group level, we have identified distinct and opposing influences from geophysical and environmental modifiers for PM2.5 and ozone. For directly emitted pollutants like PM2.5, higher concentrations are associated with indicators such as increased population, industrial presence, commercial land use, and proximity to traffic corridors. Conversely, as a pollutant formed in the atmosphere, ozone concentrations exhibit an inverse relationship with these same modifiers as areas with higher density and industrial activity correlate to lower ozone levels, though increased greenspace and building density appear to associate with different patterns as pollutants from industrialized areas are mixed with biogenic VOCs. We also have identified distinct temporal patterns where PM2.5 concentrations are highest in the winter months due to the compression of the planetary boundary layer and stagnant air building up concentrations, whereas ozone is highest in the summer due to the high solar radiation and increased emissions and photochemistry critical to ozone chemistry. This divergence underscores the complexity of air quality dynamics in urban environments and creates a challenge for decision-makers when designing mitigation plans for neighborhoods impacted by a range of air quality issues. Interventions targeting one pollutant may not yield uniform benefits for the other, and have the potential for worsening air quality. Incorporating these high-resolution spatial models into risk assessment frameworks allows for more precise public information campaigns and strategic planning to address the unique environmental hazards facing different Denver communities and can be applied to other similar regions as well.

495127.title: NOAA Satellite Snowfall Rate Algorithm and its Applications
495127.authors: Jun Dong, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; and Y. Fan, Y. Hong, H. Meng, P. Xie, A. Jacobs, C. Dierking, E. B. Berndt, and K. D. White
495127.abstract: Winter snow events can significantly affect communities, and major snowstorms can cause substantial damage to infrastructure, transportation systems, and local economies. The NOAA/NESDIS snowfall rate (SFR) product provides global estimates of liquid-equivalent snowfall rates. It is derived from satellite passive microwave radiometers, including ATMS, MHS, GMI, SSMIS, and newer sensors such as MWR (AWS), MWS (Metop-SG), and AMSR3 (GOSAT-GW). The retrieval algorithm combines machine learning (ML) for snowfall detection with a 1DVAR-based physical inversion model for snowfall rate estimation. The radiative transfer model used in the 1DVAR has recently been enhanced to incorporate multiple ice habits to improve snowfall rate estimation. Lastly, the retrieved snowfall rate is further refined using a neural network (NN) bias-correction model. The SFR product provides observation-based snowfall estimates for applications in weather forecasting, hydrology, and cryosphere research. To support operational nowcasting, NOAA NESDIS and CISESS at the University of Maryland developed a near real-time Direct Broadcast (DB) SFR processing system with a latency of less than 20 minutes, which is significantly faster than the standard operational data stream. The DB SFR is merged with MRMS radar snowfall estimates to produce the merged Snowfall Rate (mSFR) product, providing improved spatial and temporal coverage for National Weather Service (NWS) nowcasting applications. Both the SFR and mSFR products are reformatted for AWIPS and provided to some NWS Offices in near real-time. The SFR product is also an important input to the NWS Climate Prediction Center (CPC) CMORPH2 dataset. In collaboration with the Geographic Information Network of Alaska (GINA) at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, the SFR team has also developed the Alaska Regional SFR (AKSFR) system to improve situational awareness and nowcasting in data-sparse regions of Alaska.

495129.title: A 26-year Radar Climatology Estimating Hail Likelihood at the Location Level
495129.authors: Tim Ivancic, Mercury Insurance Services, LLC, Brea, CA; and S. Purpura, C. Rencurrel, J. Stephens, J. Sheng, M. Ma, S. Levy, O. Payne, S. Bennett, K. Shukla, D. Costello, M. Tran, and W. Henry
495129.abstract: Severe hail results in several billion dollars worth of damage to homes per year in the United States. Much of this loss is absorbed by the insurance industry and passed on to consumers through insurance cost. An accurate understanding of severe hail likelihood at the property level can enable insurers to price their policies more equitably, better address fraudulent claims, and identify target areas for mitigation incentives (ex. impact resistant shingles). Unfortunately, due to limitations in data sources, existing climatologies nearly all fall short of quantifying the crucial annual likelihood at a property level that relates directly to property damage. In this presentation we introduce a data pipeline to mosaic together a 26 year history of radar based hail detections. The data is composed of MYRORSS reanalysis and archived MRMS output. Gaps in the record are filled using an in-house calculation of hail indices starting with archived Nexrad data. The hail signals are filtered using a machine learning classifier based on surface hail reports, and, crucially, bias corrected using CoCoRaHS in-situ detection data. This method, still in development, gives us a preliminary estimate of the actual likelihood of a specific property being struck by severe hail across the central and eastern United States. We will present current results and discuss model biases and potential improvements.

495133.title: Updates on The Development of A Machine Learning Algorithm to Detect Wind Turbine Clutter on Weather Radar Data.
495133.authors: Cesar Manuel Salazar, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and S. M. Torres
495133.abstract: Weather radar data quality plays a fundamental role in reliable weather surveillance and in the detection of severe and high-impact weather phenomena that affect the communities served by these systems. However, radar observations are frequently impacted by non-meteorological echoes, commonly known as clutter, which can introduce biases and reduce the accuracy of radar-derived products. While ground clutter has been extensively studied and several effective mitigation techniques have been developed, other sources of clutter contamination remain challenging to characterize and mitigate. In particular, wind turbine clutter (WTC) has become an increasing concern due to the expansion of wind energy infrastructure and the complex, time-varying radar signatures generated by their rotating blades, which introduces dynamic contamination that is significantly more challenging to mitigate than stationary ground clutter. Some methods have been proposed to filter the WTC; however, applying these techniques across all radar resolution cells can be computationally demanding and may introduce undesired negative impacts on uncontaminated weather signals. A reliable approach for identifying cells contaminated by WTC is therefore needed to enable targeted application of the filter and improve the efficiency of WTC mitigation. We have previously presented the methodology for developing a machine-learning approach to identify radar resolution cells contaminated by WTC, based on statistical features derived from Level-I radar data, along with two proof-of-concept implementations that demonstrated the feasibility of this approach. Those earlier iterations established the basic classification framework and highlighted both the promise of the approach and several limitations related to feature selection, training-set representativeness, sample labeling, and model generalization across different radar cases. This study presents a third iteration of the methodology and algorithm that directly builds on lessons learned from those previous implementations. The updated methodology incorporates an expanded and more diverse training and validation dataset. In addition, the supervised classification criteria used to generate labeled samples have been refined to reduce ambiguity between contaminated and uncontaminated resolution cells and to improve consistency across datasets. The current work also includes a more comprehensive evaluation of candidate statistical features, including their relative importance, redundancy, and contribution to model performance across multiple machine-learning classifiers. By comparing the performance of this updated implementation with the previous proof-of-concept versions, this work provides further insight into the robustness, transferability, and practical limitations of machine-learning-based WTC detection. The results are intended to support the development of targeted WTC mitigation strategies, in which clutter filters are applied only to radar resolution cells identified as likely contaminated, thereby improving computational efficiency and reducing the risk of degrading uncontaminated meteorological observations.

495134.title: An Ecohydrological Perspective on Convective Organization
495134.authors: Elizabeth Cultra, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and M. Bertagni and A. M. Porporato
495134.abstract: Land–atmosphere feedbacks couple soil water availability and vegetation fluxes to atmospheric moisture, convective instability, and rainfall. From an ecohydrological perspective, we seek to understand how these nonlinear feedbacks impact convective initiation and the spatial organization of convective systems. This perspective links plant transpiration trajectories, which depend on both plant traits and soil properties, to surface flux partitioning, boundary-layer growth, lifting condensation level (LCL) changes, convective available potential energy (CAPE), and ultimately rainfall patterns. Idealized studies of convection typically prescribe surface fluxes or hold soil moisture fixed. Because of this, how soil moisture and plant function shape the timing and spatial scale of convection remains an open question. Our minimalist model, consisting of set of coupled ordinary differential equations, ties the evolution of soil moisture directly to surface fluxes and thus to atmospheric properties. It also reveals long-term behavior that is difficult and computationally expensive to obtain with models that resolve convection explicitly. We then extend the dynamical model spatially by adding thermal circulations induced by sensible heat flux gradients over heterogeneous soil moisture, which shape the spatial distribution of rainfall, providing insight into hydroclimatic persistence and convective aggregation. Finally, we compare against idealized convection-permitting simulations to test which features the minimalist model reproduces without explicitly representing convection, and thus which processes are sufficient to reproduce convective initiation and organization.

495136.title: yamltools4jedi: Facilitating JEDI R2O with intuitive WYSIWYG Management of JEDI Super YAMLs
495136.authors: Guoqing Ge, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and H. Lin, M. Hu, T. T. Ladwig, and J. Beck
495136.abstract: NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL), in collaboration with its partners, has been developing MPAS-JEDI–based data assimilation and forecasting systems for potential operational implementation. These systems include the Rapid Refresh Forecast System Version 2 (RRFSv2), the Atmospheric River Prediction System (AR-PS), the three-dimensional Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis (3D-RTMA), as well as several preliminary global applications. All of these systems aim to assimilate all available weather observations. In JEDI, each type of observation is represented as an observer, and each observer requires specific observation operators and a series of quality-control procedures. JEDI provides a flexible mechanism for configuring these processes through nested YAML configurations. When working with only one or two observers or with YAML files containing a few hundred lines, managing such configurations is relatively straightforward. However, operational systems may involve hundreds of observers. To date, we have tested 65 observers, and the resulting final “super YAML” configuration file has grown to more than 23,000 lines. Managing a file of this size requires tools that can reliably add, modify, remove, and reorganize any section of the configuration while maintaining its readability and structure. PyYAML is a popular Python package that is well suited for loading YAML files into memory and manipulating their data structures in memory. However, it is well known that PyYAML does not preserve comments or the original formatting of a YAML file. Consequently, it is not suitable for managing large JEDI super YAML files, because the regenerated files may differ substantially from the originals (comments lost, formatting changed unexpectedly, etc). This also makes it almost impossible to use in YAML-generation CI/CD tests. To address this limitation, we developed hifiyaml, a high-fidelity, WYSIWYG (What You See Is What You Get) YAML parser and emitter that exactly preserves the original formatting of YAML files, including comments, anchors, aliases, blank lines, and indentation. Building on hifiyaml and taking advantage of the specialized structure of JEDI data assimilation YAML configurations, we further developed yamltools4jedi (https://github.com/hifiyaml/yamltools4jedi). yamltools4jedi provides an intuitive WYSIWYG way to develop and manage JEDI super YAML files. It makes it easy to read, inspect, edit, split, pack, and compare super YAML files, as well as to selectively modify, keep, or drop any portion of a configuration. Because the tools ensure human-readable YAMLs at any time by preserving comments, formatting, and structural organization, they support a consistent end-to-end workflow for configuration development and maintenance. These capabilities greatly facilitate both standalone and workflow-based JEDI testing, improve the maintainability and reproducibility of complex observation configurations, and accelerate the research-to-operations (R2O) process of JEDI-based applications.

495137.title: Long-Term Vertical Characterisation of Atmospheric Water Vapour over Granada Using Raman Lidar in the EARLINET-ACTRIS Network
495137.authors: Arlett Díaz Zurita, AER, GRANADA, GR, Spain; APL, Granada, GR, Spain; and V. M. Naval-Hernández, D. N. Whiteman, O. Rodríguez-Navarro, J. A. Muñiz-Rosado, D. Pérez-Ramírez, L. Alados-Arboledas, and F. Navas-Guzmán
495137.abstract: Water vapour is a crucial greenhouse gas that plays a major role in Earth's radiative balance, energy transport and photochemical processes. It can also indirectly affect the radiative balance through cloud formation and by altering the size, shape and chemical composition of aerosol particles. Moreover, monitoring water vapour remains challenging due to its high temporal and spatial variability. Consequently, systematic and accurate observations of water vapour are essential for understanding its role at local and global scales and for improving climate projections. Advances in remote sensing techniques have enabled routine measurements of precipitable water vapour (PWV) using sun photometry, microwave radiometry and the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS). Nevertheless, these instruments do not provide information on the vertical distribution of water vapour, which is particularly relevant considering that water vapour concentrations can vary by up to three orders of magnitude between the surface and the upper troposphere. In this context, Raman lidar has demonstrated its capability to capture the vertical and temporal evolution of water vapour throughout the troposphere. Accurate retrievals of the water vapour mixing ratio from Raman lidar measurements rely on accurate estimation of the differential atmospheric transmission (DT) term and robust and well-characterised calibration procedures. The DT term accounts for extinction differences between the molecular reference (nitrogen and oxygen) and water vapour wavelengths. It becomes particularly relevant in configurations employing rotational Raman filters, where the wavelength separation is larger. In this work, several approaches for estimating the differential atmospheric transmission term were assessed, and an automated methodology was implemented to account for the aerosol contribution using sun-photometer aerosol optical depth (AOD) measurements and assuming an exponential decrease in aerosol extinction with altitude, enabling the systematic uncertainties associated with the DT to be quantified. Regarding calibration, most studies rely on collocated radiosonde observations; however, the sporadic launches limit the temporal monitoring of the calibration constant. To overcome this limitation, a hybrid calibration method is proposed, combining correlative PWV measurements from collocated instruments with Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) data to reconstruct the water vapour profile within the incomplete overlap region of the lidar system, thereby enabling the calibration constant to be determined with high temporal resolution. The automated estimation of the differential atmospheric transmission and the hybrid calibration methodology were applied to Raman lidar observations acquired at the ACTRIS AGORA Granada station between 2009 and 2022. This enabled the determination of robust and temporally consistent calibration constants and the subsequent generation of a 14-year database of water vapour profiles with high vertical and temporal resolution. The long-term lidar dataset was first evaluated against independent PWV observations from GNSS and subsequently used to characterise the seasonal and interannual variability of the vertical water vapour distribution over Granada, representing the first long-term vertical characterisation of water vapour in this region. Analysis of this 14-year period shows a pronounced seasonal cycle, with the highest water vapour concentrations in summer and the lowest values in winter. The seasonal contrast is more marked below 3 km and decreases with height, although the summer enhancement can still be detected up to approximately 4.5 km. Interannual variability is also more pronounced in the lower troposphere. Similar year-to-year variations are observed across the vertical layers, with their magnitude progressively decreasing with height. Air-mass trajectory analysis indicates that changes in the relative frequency of the main transport pathways alone cannot explain the observed water vapour anomalies. Instead, these anomalies appear to be primarily associated with variations in the moisture content of air masses within the same trajectory clusters, whose moisture content can be lower or higher than the corresponding monthly mean during different periods and may reflect changes in the meteorological conditions affecting the air masses during transport. This behaviour was most evident when comparing the driest (2012) and wettest (2018) years, particularly below 3 km. Trend analysis shows positive water vapour trends throughout the 0–6 km range, which are statistically significant at the 95 % confidence level above 1.5 km. Collocated temperature profiles from ECMWF model data also show statistically significant warming (95 %), with the magnitude of the temperature trend decreasing with height. To investigate the relationship between these changes, the relative water vapour trends were expressed as the percentage change in water vapour per kelvin of temperature increase. Between 1.5 and 3 km, the observed water vapour response was close to that expected from the Clausius–Clapeyron relationship, whereas larger responses were found above 3 km, suggesting that relative humidity may not be conserved at individual atmospheric layers. However, the associated uncertainties limit the robustness of this interpretation. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of long-term, vertically resolved Raman lidar water vapour observations, combined with meteorological information and air-mass transport analysis, to improve our understanding of the roles of thermodynamic processes and atmospheric transport in regional water vapour variability and long-term change.

495139.title: From Vulnerable to Resilient: The Vermont Mesonet's First Steps Toward Flash Flood Preparedness
495139.authors: Samantha Cheung, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT; and J. Beneš, L. Muskin, and M. Dewey
495139.abstract: Flash flooding poses a growing risk to many Vermont communities that currently lack robust, real-time monitoring infrastructure. In 2025, the Water Resources Institute at the University of Vermont, with seed funding from the Leahy Institute, began developing a prototype mesonet station and a spatial analysis to guide deployment of additional stations in flood-vulnerable and rural areas. While the station design was aimed at creating synergies with monitoring in the neighboring northeastern states, the spatial analysis required creative adaptation to represent the Green Mountain State’s terrain while meeting World Meteorological Organization (WMO) siting specifications and the Recommendations and Best Practices for Mesonets (AASC, 2019). This study discusses the complexities of creating a network in a highly forested, mountainous state that can meet the needs of the people in Vermont. The spatial design process involved multiple stages, including identifying spatial resolution requirements, engaging stakeholders, balancing their needs and priorities, determining realistic and representative land plots, and working to gain the trust of potential site hosts and communities. The process revealed that to fully cover the state, the Vermont Mesonet will prioritize one station per HUC-8 watershed and county across the state. This will require a minimum of 21 stations. Many stakeholders were involved, including the National Weather Service Burlington Weather Forecast Office, Vermont Dam Safety Program, Vermont Agency of Transportation, Vermont Emergency Management, agricultural groups, and educational groups. Many of the needs identified by stakeholders overlapped, and the highest demand was for areas in major radar blockage zones in the state and flash-flood-prone areas. The needs were translated into a GIS map, then overlaid with WMO and AASC specifications to provide an estimate of the future station locations. Rollout of the stations will be prioritized in regions that have radar beam blockage of one degree or higher. Currently, the Vermont Mesonet is in the process of securing site hosts and working with communities to build support and trust. The prototype station was deployed in Lyndonville, VT, on May 5, 2026. Data from this station are available to the National Weather Service and Vermont Emergency Management. Data will be made public once the public-facing website is complete. As funding arrives, the Vermont Mesonet will deploy additional stations based on the established areas identified by the spatial analysis.

495144.title: Contextualizing Ice Crystal Chain Aggregates in Cold-Season Winter Storms using Airborne In Situ and Remote-Sensing Observations
495144.authors: Christian Nairy, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and D. J. Delene, S. Wagner, J. A. Finlon, and J. E. Yorks
495144.abstract: Ice aggregation influences particle growth, sedimentation, precipitation development, and cloud radiative properties. One comparatively understudied aggregate morphology is the ice crystal chain aggregate, defined here as three or more ice particles connected by small joints in an elongated, quasi-linear arrangement. In situ observations of chain aggregates have historically been concentrated in the mid- to upper-levels of summertime thunderstorms, where strong electric fields may influence particle aggregation. Laboratory cloud chamber experiments have demonstrated that chain aggregate formation is temperature dependent and can be enhanced by electric fields exceeding approximately 60 kV m-1. However, translating these laboratory findings to natural clouds remains challenging, and the environmental conditions and physical mechanisms associated with chain aggregate formation in storms are still uncertain. During the NASA Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) field campaign, airborne imaging probes aboard the NASA P-3 aircraft observed chain aggregates during multiple flights through the mid- and upper-level regions of weakly to moderately electrically active winter storms. A convolutional neural network (CNN) trained to distinguish chain aggregates from other particle morphologies is applied to Cloud Particle Imager (CPI) observations to systematically identify and map their spatio-temporal distribution across the multiyear campaign. Chain detections are compared with coincident in situ measurements of temperature, altitude, particle concentration, cloud water content, and other microphysical properties. Chain aggregate observations are further contextualized using collocated measurements from instruments aboard the NASA ER-2, including W-band radar reflectivity and Doppler velocity, Ku- and Ka-band radar observations, dual-frequency reflectivity ratios, as well as lidar backscatter and depolarization measurements. These measurements are used to evaluate whether chain-rich periods preferentially occur within cloud regions or near changes in particle scattering properties, cloud boundaries, and transitions in particle populations. Because the location where a chain aggregate is sampled may differ from where it formed, these observations cannot directly identify its formation mechanism. Instead, this study provides observational constraints on the thermodynamic, microphysical, and storm-scale environments in which chain aggregates occur and establishes a framework for evaluating their distribution and potential importance in cold-season clouds.

495147.title: Effects of Low Level Jets on the movement of Mai-Yu Front and Precipitation During a Heavy Rainfall Event
495147.authors: Pay-Liam Lin, National Central University, Taoyuan City, Zhongli District, Taiwan
495147.abstract: A heavy rainfall event associated with the Mei-Yu front occurred in northern Taiwan on June 2, 2017. A total of 645.5 mm of rain fell at the northern tip of Taiwan during this event. The Mei-Yu frontal system became quasistationary in northern Taiwan, and the event lasted 10 h. A strong barrier jet over the northwestern coast of Taiwan was present when the Mei-Yu front approached northern Taiwan. The strong jet brought moisture to the region and caused strong convergence along the frontal zone. The strong convection produced more than 600 mm of rainfall when the system became stationary. To determine how the barrier jet over northwestern Taiwan affected the movement of the Mei-Yu front, this study used the Weather Research and Forecasting model to reproduce this heavy rain event. Additionally, three sensitivity tests were conducted in a simulated environment. In one of the tests, the Taiwan was removed, which resulted in the front quickly moving southward. In this test, the accumulated rainfall was only 200 mm and the barrier jet was much weaker relative to that in a control test, demonstrating that topography obstructs the movement of the front. In another test, the southern Taiwan mountain range was removed, which resulted in the terrain of northern Taiwan having a partial blocking effect; however, the front still quickly moved southward without a strong barrier jet. In another test that included all of the terrain of Taiwan, the barrier jet was slightly stronger. In this test, the Mei-Yu front became stationary at a position further north than it did in the control test. The strong southerly wind also enhanced convergence, resulting in more rainfall; however, the rainfall did not fall over land. The results demonstrate that orographic effects partially contribute to the blocking of the frontal movement across northern Taiwan and that the southern mountains cause a barrier jet to form in northwestern Taiwan. The slow movement of the Mei-Yu front is significantly influenced by the barrier jet.

495148.title: The Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC) as a Catalyst for NOAA’s Future Earth Prediction System
495148.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) established the Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC) with a mission to be the catalyst for community research and modeling focused on informing and accelerating advances in operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecast modeling systems. In the past six years, EPIC invested in seven areas, namely, software engineering, software infrastructure, user support, cloud-based high-performance computing (HPC), scientific innovation, management and planning, and community engagement to advance EPIC’s mission. In this talk, we will highlight the EPIC program’s accomplishments toward (1) nurturing a representative and unifying modeling community; (2) developing a public accessible end-to-end testing and development environment to facilitate integration of innovations to improve forecast skill and computational performance in the context of the Unified Forecast System (UFS) and Machine Learning (ML)-based NWP; and (3) bringing in innovations to improve UFS forecast skill and computational performance. Built upon recent accomplishments, EPIC will continue transforming the landscape of Earth system prediction in the next few years. We will highlight EPIC’s role in implementing NOAA’s Modeling Moonshot Initiative toward a global, coupled, km-scale Earth system prediction system based on the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) dynamical core. Specifically, EPIC will play an essential role in modernizing NOAA’s Earth system modeling infrastructure to promote a new DevOps paradigm, including but not limited to optimizing UFS code for Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and refactoring UFS source code and testing framework to improve computational efficiency on modern computing platforms, and developing an open-source open development infrastructure for ML-based and hybrid NWP forecast systems. In addition to accelerating technical transformations, EPIC will continue championing partnerships across the weather enterprise, fostering a skilled workforce for Earth system modeling, and enabling a stronger community-driven process to guide future priorities for advancing Earth System Modeling capabilities through the UFS framework.

495150.title: Examining Rapidly-Evolving Processes Associated with Hail-Producing Storms Observed by the Horus Fully- Digital Polarimetric Phased Array Radar
495150.authors: Laura Shedd, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. J. Bodine, D. Schvartzman, A. E. Reinhart, and J. C. Snyder
495150.abstract: Rapid-scan polarimetric radar observations of hailstorms can enable a better understanding of the processes that drive growth and descent through improved tracking and characterization of polarimetric signatures associated with hail. Phased array radars (PARs) provide vertically dense volumetric observations on the order of tens of seconds, allowing for the full depth of a storm to be sampled essentially simultaneously when using advanced scanning strategies. However, since there are only a very small number of polarimetric PARs in use at this time, a very limited number of dual-polarization PAR-based datasets of hailstorms across the spectrum of storm types that are capable of producing severe hail have been examined. One such system is Horus, a mobile, fully-digital, S-band polarimetric PAR developed at the Advanced Radar Research Center with funding from NOAA’s National Severe Storms Laboratory. It was designed to explore the benefits of digital PAR technology for weather surveillance. This study uses high-temporal-resolution observations from Horus to examine the polarimetric processes associated with the formation and expansion of the hail core aloft and its descent to the surface. Using imaging scans, Horus collected data across a variety of storm modes, including right- and left-moving supercells and multicell thunderstorms in central Oklahoma. Volumetric data have been collected from the ground up to 16° in elevation with update intervals of 30 s or less. Horus has observed processes such as the initial formation and growth of severe hail-producing storms, providing insight into pathways that do and do not lead to severe hail production. Additionally, Horus has observed the rapid expansion of the hail growth zone and mixed phase region, with the hail growth zone marked in some cases by a rapid increase in the area of ZH > 55 dBZ and a co-located reduction in ρhv and ZDR. Rapid changes to a storm’s structure include the development and evolution of transient mesocyclones and ZDR columns as well as changes in the storm’s forward flank. These observations have enabled the development of a hail core algorithm that leverages both the high vertical density and the rapid-update characteristics of the polarimetric observations provided by PARs such as Horus. Using time derivatives, the hail core algorithm aims to better track and characterize the evolution of a storm’s hail core, including changes in hail-core volume and associated polarimetric characteristics.

495151.title: Citizen Radio Science in Solar-Terrestrial Physics: Recent Results
495151.authors: Gareth Perry, New Jersey Institute of Technology, Newark, NJ; and K. Pandey, N. Frissell, S. Fernandes, and J. Huba
495151.abstract: Over the past decade, collaborations with amateur radio enthusiasts (commonly known as “hams”) have increased dramatically within the solar-terrestrial physics community. A leading initiative in this effort is the Ham Radio Science Citizen Investigation (HamSCI). HamSCI has organized several campaigns to observe the effects of solar eclipses on the terrestrial ionosphere and radio wave propagation. The organization is also coordinating the design and deployment of Personal Space Weather Station (PSWS) nodes to expand ground-based coverage for remote sensing of the near-Earth space environment. In this presentation, we report on two recent scientific results stemming from these collaborations. First, we examine the effects of the 2017 and 2024 total solar eclipses on high-frequency (HF) radio communications using contact logs collected within the contiguous United States. Comparing these observations (2017 vs. 2024) demonstrates that HF propagation conditions exhibited disparate responses to the eclipses in the higher portion of the HF radio band, which we attribute to the differing phases of the solar cycle during each event. Second, we present results from a HamSCI PSWS study in which we analyzed data collected by a PSWS HF receiver at the New Jersey Institute of Technology (Newark, NJ). This receiver has monitored the Doppler variability of the WWV transmitter (Fort Collins, CO) for several years. Our analysis reveals the complexity of long-distance HF propagation modes and how they are influenced by daily ionospheric variations and transient phenomena, such as traveling ionospheric disturbances. These collaborations have matured to the point of generating impactful, peer-reviewed scientific results while driving the development of new scientific targets, methodologies, and instrumentation. We conclude with a brief outlook on future research directions with the HamSCI community.

495152.title: The Give-and-Take of Drought Communication: Insights from Missouri Stakeholders
495152.authors: Zachary Leasor, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO
