495152.abstract: The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) serves as the primary tool for assessing and communicating drought conditions in Missouri, but drought communication extends well beyond the weekly map. Missouri's drought monitoring process relies on regular engagement with agricultural producers, Extension specialists, natural resource managers, agency partners, and members of the public to better understand conditions and impacts across the state. These interactions provide critical context for weekly drought assessments and frequently identify emerging impacts that may not yet be evident in traditional drought indicator datasets. Stakeholder reports submitted through the Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR) system, and direct outreach help improve situational awareness and support better drought assessment. Missouri's experience has demonstrated the value of sustained stakeholder engagement with the USDM while also highlighting persistent challenges in explaining drought classifications, impacts, and recovery. A recurring challenge is the widespread perception that the USDM exists primarily to trigger eligibility for drought relief programs rather than to characterize the full range of drought impacts. This presentation explores the give-and-take of drought communication in Missouri and highlights lessons learned from stakeholders and efforts to improve public understanding of drought conditions and impacts.

495156.title: Toward Medium-Range Forecasting with OCELOT: A Comparison of Latent- and Observation-Space Rollouts
495156.authors: Mu-Chieh Ko, Lynker @ NOAA/NWS/OMD, College Park, MD; and A. Gholoubi
495156.abstract: Accurate medium-range weather forecasting remains a core challenge in numerical weather prediction due to chaotic error growth over extended horizons. OCELOT is an observation-space forecasting framework built on a Graph Neural Network (GNN) with an encoder-processor-decoder architecture, and predicts future atmospheric observations directly in observation space at 12-hour lead times. Extending this framework toward longer lead times can be enabled through recursive forecasting strategies. This ongoing work develops and evaluates two autoregressive rollout methods for progressively longer lead times: latent-space rollout and observation-space rollout. In both approaches, the model iteratively feeds its previous predictions back as inputs for the next time step. The two methods differ in where this recursion occurs and in the tradeoffs they introduce: latent-space rollout cycles predictions within the model's hidden representation, potentially reducing computational cost and avoiding repeated encoding/decoding errors, while observation-space rollout decodes each forecast to observation space before re-encoding it as input, providing stronger observational constraints at the risk of accumulating reconstruction errors. We are conducting a comparative evaluation of these configurations across four dimensions: forecast stability, error accumulation, computational efficiency, and forecast skill at increasing lead times. This analysis will inform which rollout strategy better supports stable extended-range prediction and guide future development of stable multi-day forecasting capabilities within OCELOT.

495157.title: Airborne L-Band Scatterometer Measurements for Ocean Surface Vector Wind Retrieval
495157.authors: Zach Kabelac, Aperture Earth, Waltham, MA
495157.abstract: Existing L-band ocean geophysical model functions rest on a narrow observational base. Aquarius provides coefficients at three incidence angles (29, 38, 46 degrees); PALSAR and SMAP add further constrained cases. Across most of the 20 to 60 degree range relevant to a scanning scatterometer, current L-band GMFs are extrapolations. This matters because L-band offers properties no operational ocean wind sensor currently exploits: two-way rain attenuation near 0.1 dB at rates where 7 to 40 percent of tropical C- and Ku-band retrievals degrade, and polarimetric channels expected to retain sensitivity at wind speeds where higher frequencies saturate. Closing that gap requires measurements rather than further modeling. We describe a software-defined L-band scatterometer and present initial results from its first airborne campaign. The payload performs direct digital synthesis and sampling at 1.28 GHz with waveform-level frequency diversity used to increase independent looks per dwell and drive radiometric uncertainty below Kp = 0.05 without increasing dwell time or narrowing swath. The prototype flew aboard a Twin Otter over Gulf coastal waters in fall 2026 in a fixed fan-beam, vertically polarized configuration spanning 35 to 65 degrees incidence. We report the radiometric calibration approach, achieved Kp relative to modeled values, and measured VV normalized radar cross section as a function of incidence angle under moderate wind conditions. We conclude with the extension to satellite based measurement and to the high-wind, high-precipitation regime that motivates the instrument.

495158.title: NASA SatCORPS Geostationary Satellite Cloud Properties Derived from 3-Km Gridded Radiances
495158.authors: Rabindra Palikonda, Analytical Mechanics Associates, Inc, Hampton, VA; NASA Langley Research Center, Hampton, VA; and L. Nguyen, W. L. Smith Jr., D. Painemal, C. R. Yost, C. W. Fleeger, T. Chee, K. Khlopenkov, and D. Spangenberg
495158.abstract: The Satellite ClOud and Radiation Property retrieval System (SatCORPS) algorithms are routinely applied to geostationary satellite imagers in native projection and pixel resolution, with the goal of deriving hourly real-time cloud properties, radiative fluxes, and other parameters globally between 70˚N and 70˚S. The SatCORPS group recently started producing hourly gridded radiance data at the equal-angle grid resolution of 0.027o(~3-km) from the constellation of geostationary satellites at full-disk scan. Satellite cloud properties derived from gridded radiances can be more easily integrated into applications, however, potential uncertainties of this method need to be properly characterized. This presentation will illustrate the cloud properties derived from the first application of the SatCORPS algorithms to gridded radiance data and evaluate their consistency with the standard (native resolution) SatCORPS cloud properties. Validations and comparisons against CALIPSO data will also be presented.

495159.title: Urban Atmospheric Variability along the San Antonio–Austin Corridor from Pandora and TEMPO Observations
495159.authors: Iyare Oseghae, University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX; Univ. of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX; and A. M. Mestas-Nunez
495159.abstract: The growing urban footprint in South-Central Texas along the San Antonio–Austin I-35 corridor, together with its exposure to local emissions, Saharan dust, wildfire smoke, and regional energy production, provide a unique setting for investigating urban and regional atmospheric variability. This study examines the first year of Pandora observations in downtown San Antonio to characterize the diurnal behavior of NO₂, O₃, and HCHO, evaluate weekday and weekend differences, and compare these patterns with observations from Austin over the same period. These measurements will establish a baseline of diurnal and weekday-weekend variability in atmospheric composition across the two cities, providing context for identifying departures associated with ozone episodes, wildfire smoke, and other anomalous pollution conditions. Pandora observations will also be compared with coincident TEMPO retrievals to evaluate agreement, assess differences between Versions 03 and 04, and determine how quality-control filtering, temporal matching, and spatial buffering influence the comparisons. Together, these analyses will characterize urban atmospheric variability along the San Antonio–Austin corridor while demonstrating how complementary Pandora and TEMPO observations can be integrated to investigate air quality across South-Central Texas.

495160.title: Evaluating the Impact of UAS Observations Collected with Different Sampling Strategies on Forecasts of the 10 March 2026 Severe Weather Outbreak Using OSSEs
495160.authors: Matthew Wilson, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. O. Pinto, Phd
495160.abstract: Thunderstorms pose a substantial hazard to aviation, but their formation and evolution are often profoundly impacted by features in or near the planetary boundary layer (PBL) which our current observing network is poorly equipped to resolve, whether in the horizontal (such as mesoscale boundaries or convergence zones) or in the vertical (such as capping inversions or layers of sharp vertical wind shear). This can lead to inaccurate forecasts. One observing platform which could help fill this PBL observation gap is Uncrewed Aerial Systems (UAS). This study will use a series of Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) to investigate the impacts of assimilating data from UAS collected using different sampling strategies on ensemble forecasts of the 10 March 2026 severe weather outbreak. This event produced numerous hazards to aviation and the general public, including a long-track supercell which produced several candidates for Illinois’s largest hailstone on record and an EF3 tornado, an elevated left-moving supercell which produced a swath of 2-4” hailstones that narrowly missed Midway Airport in Chicago, and a strong squall line that swept across much of the Midwest. Mesoscale features played a notable role in this outbreak, with the long-track supercell noted previously tracking along a lake breeze boundary which may have produced a locally more favorable environment for tornadoes, making it a useful test case for the impact of UAS observations of these features on model forecasts. After a brief overview of the observed evolution of the outbreak, this presentation will discuss the development of an MPAS-based nature run, the configuration of our WRF-DART DA system, and results from assimilating UAS observations from various network configurations. In particular, we intend to examine the impacts of horizontal spacing between UAS sites, the vertical extent of the UAS profiles, and how impacts differ between assimilating observations from a fixed network of profiling UAS or symbiotic observations from a network of delivery UAS. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

495161.title: Using Airborne MASTER Observations to Evaluate and Advance NOAA Satellite Fire Products from Heritage Algorithms to the Next Generation Fire System
495161.authors: Benjamin Marchant, STC – Science & Technology Corp., Columbia, MD; and M. Tsidulko, C. Xu, S. Kondragunta, I. A. Csiszar, M. Pavolonis, and W. Schroeder
495161.abstract: Accurate satellite detection and characterization of active fires are essential for operational fire monitoring, situational awareness, emissions estimation, and air-quality applications. However, evaluating satellite fire products remains challenging because fires evolve rapidly and because their observed thermal signals depend on spatial resolution, viewing geometry, atmospheric attenuation, smoke, and cloud cover. High-spatial-resolution airborne thermal observations provide an important intermediate reference between detailed ground measurements and continuous satellite monitoring. This study uses observations from NASA’s MODIS/ASTER Airborne Simulator (MASTER) acquired during the 2019 FIREX-AQ campaign and the NASA FireSense campaigns conducted in 2023 and 2025 to evaluate NOAA active-fire products derived from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) and the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite Advanced Baseline Imager (GOES ABI). MASTER fire observations were spatially and temporally collocated with satellite retrievals and aggregated to the corresponding VIIRS and ABI observing scales. The comparisons evaluated fire detection, omission and commission errors, geolocation, fire radiative power, and thermal characterization as functions of fire intensity, satellite viewing geometry, atmospheric attenuation, smoke, and cloud contamination. The analysis compares heritage NOAA active-fire products, including the VIIRS Enterprise Fire product and the ABI Fire Detection and Characterization product, against outputs from NOAA’s Next Generation Fire System (NGFS). Particular emphasis is placed on new NGFS capabilities, including atmospheric-transmittance-aware fire detection and intensity estimates, improved geolocation, the temporal association of individual detections within an event-based data model, and improved fire characterization under partial obscuration by clouds and smoke. By combining MASTER observations from multiple airborne campaigns, this work provides a consistent framework for assessing the transition from heritage NOAA active-fire products to NGFS and for identifying remaining limitations in satellite fire detection and characterization.

495163.title: Tree Damage or Wind Speed? Exploring Canopy and Exposure Bias in Severe Convective Wind Records
495163.authors: Sarah Purpura, Mercury Insurance LLC, Brea, CA; and T. Ivancic, C. Rencurrel, J. Stephens, J. Sheng, M. Ma, S. Levy, O. Payne, S. Bennett, K. Shukla, D. Costello, M. Tran, and W. Henry
495163.abstract: Severe convective storms are now a leading driver of US insured loss, and straight line wind is the largest non-hail share of it. But the wind hazard layer most risk modelers rely on is largely a record of observed damage, usually damage to trees, rather than measured wind. This work asks how much that distinction matters. Focusing on Texas and Oklahoma, a region spanning open plains in the west and dense woodland in the east and so, contains the full contrast within a single domain. We are testing a simple idea: that tree canopy shapes which of the two gets recorded. Where canopy is dense, moderate winds bring down trees and produce many damage reports, while that same canopy roughens the surface and lowers the peak gust measured. If that holds, hazard frequency and hazard magnitude would be biased in opposite directions in the same places. We combine five public datasets on a common grid: NCEI Storm Events wind reports, which flag each gust as estimated or measured; daily maximum winds from ASOS (Automated Surface Observing System) stations; URMA (Unrestricted Mesoscale Analysis) gust analyses; NWS severe storm warnings to filter ASOS and URMA gusts to convective wind; and NLCD (National Land Cover Database) tree canopy and developed land fractions. We present these preliminary findings and ask what they may mean for how convective wind hazard and exposure risk are being represented, and how we best use this data.

495168.title: Withdrawn: Connecting Students From a Minority-Serving Institution to Marine and Atmospheric Sciences
495168.authors: Katie Eaton, University of Miami, Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric and Earth Science, Key Biscayne, FL; and S. Rosales, E. J. Becker, and B. Kirtman
495168.abstract: Access to paid, hands-on undergraduate research experience remains a well-documented barrier to increasing minority participation in the marine, atmospheric, and earth sciences. Over the last five years, the Cooperative Institute for Marine and Atmospheric Studies (CIMAS) at the University of Miami Rosenstiel School has successfully developed and implemented an internship program in collaboration with Miami-Dade College (MDC), a minority-serving institution. The program offers paid research experiences to MDC undergraduate students in STEM disciplines. Many MDC students are first-generation college students, and immigrants, with over half of its student population classified as low-income. MDC is also one of the most diverse institutions in the country, with 167 nations and 63 languages represented in its student body. Since MDC is not a Research-1 institution, opportunities for hands-on research experience, particularly within marine, atmospheric, and earth sciences, are limited for its students. Our program addresses this gap by offering a paid 10-week experience where students work alongside CIMAS researchers at a NOAA facility, gaining hands-on exposure to NOAA research. The program is a part-time commitment with flexibility for hybrid work, allowing students to continue classes and/or jobs during the internship. CIMAS researchers design research projects, guide students through the execution of these projects, and serve as mentors. Since the program's onset in 2022, we have hosted 18 interns. Over the last two years, the program has grown substantially: we have dedicated staff to coordinate it, enriched the student experience with professional development activities, allocated additional funding to support more students, and expanded to Broward College, another minority-serving institution. We are also now placing interns beyond CIMAS with mentors from other labs within the Rosenstiel School. Student surveys and general feedback suggest students are highly satisfied with the program and would recommend it to others. The internship provides research experience students may not otherwise receive and has helped students transition from MDC into four-year degree programs in ocean, marine, or atmospheric sciences. Former interns have presented their research at local conferences, several are now pursuing bachelor’s degrees at the University of Miami or elsewhere, and others are exploring graduate school opportunities. We have also hired former interns as temporary or full-time staff at CIMAS. In honoring Professor Janet Liou Mark's legacy of increasing minority participation in the Earth and Geosciences, this presentation will share our program's structure, lessons learned over the last five years (as well as continued challenges), intern success stories, and practical recommendations for other institutions seeking to build similar partnerships with minority-serving institutions.

495171.title: Reviving Digital Course Materials in the Age of AI: A process for converting legacy web applications
495171.authors: David Lothers, Univ. of South Carolina, Columbia, SC; University of South Carolina, COLUMBIA, SC; and A. L. Hiscox, G. J. Carbone, and K. Beidel
495171.abstract: Interactive web applications are a common part of an introductory meteorology course curriculum. These applications allow students to change parameters to visualize concepts and understand system interactions. Unfortunately, changing web technologies requires consistent updates and technical knowledge to maintain such applications. The work presented here investigates the use of AI to modernize and maintain technologically outdated educational materials and tools to help instructors create, maintain, or update such modules. We use original web applications previously written in Flash as a data source for ChatGPT GPT-5.5 Pro. New applications were packaged using the software tool Vite, which substantially improved the ease of packaging for the apps. A specialized GPT was created to ease the conversion process and provide maximum information to the AI. The combined tool set described above, once tuned, was able to output a complete app that fit into an existing Github repository and was developed with 2-3 prompts. The ability to rapidly update existing web applications will allow teachers to revitalize interactive course materials with AI tools.

495176.title: Update on an Urban Digital Twin of Atmospheric Flow for Microscale Applications
495176.authors: Sue Ellen Ellen Haupt, NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and S. M. Dettling, K. Sha, T. Brummet, and B. Kosović
495176.abstract: Many real-world studies of urban flow require high-resolution information of atmospheric flow on the order of tens of meters or less for a host of applications, including wind energy, urban heat island assessment, contaminant dispersion, details of hurricane simulation, modeling wildland and urban interface fires, and more. Although it is becoming common to perform increasingly high-resolution simulations on the order of tens of meters or meters) for microscale atmospheric conditions with large-eddy simulation (LES) codes, it remains expensive in terms of computing time, and we are seldom able to perform these simulations faster than real time. Modern machine learning (ML) methods, however, may now be used to emulate such LES runs in a matter of seconds. At NSF NCAR, we are currently creating such emulators that 1) downscale from coarser resolution simulations, and 2) integrate forward in time using a neural operator. We report on using Diffusion Models to provide a 32-times downscale from mesoscale simulations (~200 m) into the microscale (~ 5 m) to resolve features in complex urban regions. We employ LES data for training, validating, and testing the ML methods and compare the downscaled results in terms of the statistical moments and ability to reproduce the turbulent energy spectrum for the regions of interest. We use a neural temporal operator to emulate behavior at fine temporal and spatial scales for urban areas and provide detailed information that can be used for a variety of applications. The temporal operator is periodically updated with results from the high-resolution downscale to preserve sharpness at those scales. The models reproduce expected features for a variety of wind and thermodynamic conditions. We’ll show results and discuss lessons learned.

495178.title: Real-Time Multi-Stop Flood Rescue Routing Using a Purpose Built Shallow Flow Simulator and Reinforcement Learning
495178.authors: Eshaan Sharma, Santa Clara High School, Santa Clara, CA
495178.abstract: During a flooding event, a significant challenge is getting an emergency responder to reach a victim's estimated location and extract them to safety, while navigating changing hazard conditions along the way. Risk minimized routing through active flooding depends on the dynamic values of water height, flow velocity, and soil saturation at a fine resolution, that if simulated, demands a high computational cost precluding route generation on the timescale of an active rescue. To address this, this research presents an optimized flow-physics informed reinforcement learning model to infer routing paths in real time. The optimized flow simulator departs from general-use hydrodynamic solvers in three ways: a) it uses elevation data directly to construct the mesh, avoiding meshing overhead, b) through a piped-network treatment of hydrostatic, momentum-flux, and friction pressures, it enforces mass and momentum conservation, and c) soil infiltration is approximated using a reduced model of Richards' equation, with soil structural integrity being derived from saturation and surface gradient. Together, these simplifications allow the simulator to generate large amounts of training data on low cost compute at various precipitation rates while capturing the flow and infiltration dynamics that govern route safety. The simulator was validated against three real world flooding events. Around Camp Mystic, TX, where a recorded precipitation rate of 5.1 inches-per-hour during the July 2025 flash flood produced a water height of 26 feet within 45 minutes, the simulator predicted 24.2 feet at the same mark. For the 2018 Ellicott City, MD flood, 9.71 inches of rain over 2 hours produced 10 feet of flooding, against a simulator prediction of 9.468 feet. For the 2023 Fort Lauderdale flood, roughly 3 inches-per-hour of rain sustained over 5 hours near the local stadium produced approximately 3 feet of flooding, while the simulator estimated 3.23 feet. The flow data over a specific area is then used to construct a graph with junctions, safe destination nodes and risk weighted connections through 120,000 simulations of a shortest path algorithm, while taking into account density of path and route divergence. Two neural networks are then trained on the graph to generate inferences of traversal time and hazard exposure for any connection between two nodes in the graph. Finally, a reinforcement learning policy is trained to navigate the graph, selecting routes based on these inferences. Additionally, to accommodate multiple rescue locations on a single path, the routing system is also built to enforce a required sequence of intermediate stops, each supplied as a raw coordinate rather than a predefined safety node, and resolved to its nearest node in the graph regardless of that node's safety. Further, a user adjustable safety priority parameter is introduced to govern the risk versus speed trade-off between stops, allowing the same trained policy to favor a faster, riskier route or a slower, safer one without retraining. This entire framework was applied to a 10 km by 10 km terrain area located in the Appalachian Mountains, over 12 potential precipitation rates with the following results: 1) across rainfall rates from 1 to 12 inches per hour, every evaluated stop sequence was reachable in 100% of 500 evaluation episodes, and 2) compared against a shortest path baseline that ignores time evolving hazard, the stop constrained routes reduced hazard exposure by 48.8% at an increased travel time cost of 15.6%, with the gap widening under heavier rainfall. Figures 1 through 5 demonstrate the functionality of the system, using terrain from the Appalachian Mountains. Figures 3 and 5 are severity maps pertaining to the distribution of water and mudslide risk during flooding respectively that were used for the graphing. In Fig. 3, green segments represent water heights of 0.1 to 1 m, yellow represents 1 to 3 m, orange represents 3 to 5.5 m and red represents above 5.5 m according to maximum water height attained for precipitation ranging from 1 to 12 inches per hour. In Fig. 5 red indicates greatest risk and brown indicates moderate risk of mudslide for the same precipitation rates. Fig. 4 demonstrates how the addition of a singular way-point for the emergency responder to cross second on the list, splits the middle segment of the route into two distinct paths to reach and exit that point.

495179.title: Doppler Wind Lidar Retrievals from a Moving Platform in Complex Terrain: Validation and Uncertainty
495179.authors: Jagdish Desai, Univ. of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA; and S. F. J. De Wekker, G. J. Duine, L. V. Carvalho, and C. Jones
495179.abstract: Obtaining representative observations of boundary-layer winds is challenging in complex terrain, where strong spatial gradients and rapidly changing conditions can limit the usefulness of fixed measurements. The University of Virginia Wind Observatory on Wheels (UWOW) combines Doppler lidar measurements with GPS and inertial navigation data to retrieve vertical profiles of horizontal winds while the observing platform is in motion. We quantify uncertainty associated with the production UWOW retrieval and its finite sampling volume using a controlled synthetic-lidar experiment for Intensive Observing Period 9 of the Sundowner Winds Experiment. Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model output is used as a known, dynamically consistent three-dimensional wind field. Synthetic radial velocities are generated for 844 observed scans using the actual trajectory, six-beam geometry, attitude, and platform kinematics, and are then processed with the same retrieval used for the observations. Retrieved winds are compared with a local WRF column above the platform and with a scan-volume reference formed from winds sampled at the beam and range-gate locations. Because no stochastic Doppler-velocity noise is added, the experiment isolates retrieval/forward-operator error and within-scan inhomogeneity rather than total observational uncertainty. The synthetic experiment yields a characteristic wind-speed RMSE of approximately 1.1-1.2 m s⁻¹, with mean biases below 0.13 m s⁻¹. Retrieval uncertainty varies with height and location, with larger errors occurring where the wind field changes rapidly within the sampled volume. Similar errors are obtained using the 1-km and 333-m WRF domains, indicating that the overall uncertainty estimate is not strongly sensitive to model grid spacing. When applied to the observed transects, WRF reproduces broad wind regimes but smooths or misses much of the sharper along-route and vertical variability observed by UWOW. These model-observation differences substantially exceed the synthetic retrieval error and therefore cannot be explained by retrieval uncertainty alone. Overall, the results demonstrate UWOW’s ability to resolve localized boundary layer structure in complex terrain and provide a quantitative basis for interpreting mobile wind profiles.

495180.title: Passive Microwave Sensor for the Spectrum Constrained World
495180.authors: Angel Christopher Madrid, Boulder Environmental Sciences and Technology, Boulder, CO; and M. M. Eble and M. Klein
495180.abstract: During the past 50 years, the spectrum above ~5 GHz was mostly used for remote sensing, both active and passive. However, the current demand for this part of the spectrum is greater than ever. Despite it only being 140 years since Heinrich Hertz (Wikipedia n.d.) demonstrated the existence of electromagnetic waves and stated that “it's of no use whatsoever”, our current society cannot get enough of the spectrum. The Microwave spectrum is not only useful for communications, security, and commerce, but it is also an irreplaceable natural resource. There is only one oxygen absorption spectrum between 50-70 GHz, and only one 22.235 GHz water vapor absorption line, both nature’s gifts for atmospheric profiling. These, among other natural properties of the electromagnetic waves’ propagation through the atmosphere and their interaction with various surfaces, ultimately enable nuanced environmental monitoring from air, space, or ground. Data observed by space-based microwave sensors have a significant impact on the forecast accuracy of numerical weather prediction systems in both the short and long-term (English, et al. 2013), (Lupu 2019), (Bormann, Lawrence and Farnan 2019), etc. Additional microwave sensors on orbit can positively impact numerical weather prediction skills. This is described in many studies, such as (Duncan, Bormann and Holm 2021), where the authors conclude that the “Addition of microwave sounder data shows a consistent, positive impact on short- and medium-range forecast metrics”. Another example which involves microwave sounders is the Arctic Weather Satellite (AWS), with channels spanning 50 to 325 GHz, that form the Polar System-Sterna (EPS-Sterna). An evaluation of the impact of up to 8 satellites in a constellation on various orbits on the numerical weather prediction model was done by (Rivoire, et al. 2024). “Significant positive improvements for the forecasts are found up to 96 hours, for every variable tested, with an impact increasing with the number of satellites.” One conclusion of the study is that the EPS-Sterna constellation will significantly improve forecasts up to +96 hours in the troposphere. Many more constellations are being planned or are currently being deployed. All of these studies assume that observations of passive microwave sensors will not be deteriorated by interference from active sources within the spectrum, such as communication systems, vehicle radars, satellite uplink and downlink systems, etc. There are numerous solutions for detecting interference within a channel, or a narrow bandwidth (e.g., up to ten of GHz). Such algorithms are currently used for the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) microwave radiometer, e.g., (Piepmeier, et al. 2014). These solutions provide detection within a relatively narrow radiometer band by digitizing microwave radiometer channels output. The digitizing hardware is, however, power hungry and thus expensive. BEST’s unique solution is a hyperspectral radiometer that does not use digitization, it is much simpler, low-power, and can be integrated into a compact, economic package. Moreover, BEST’s hyperspectral solution has a potential to improve observations with respect to the current state of the art, as documented by many authors, including (Maddy, Iturbe-Sanchez and Boukabara 2024). This class of hyperspectral sensors provides an economical solution, and could enhance the deployment of observational constellations, offering much improved spatial resolution (using deployable reflector antennas), temporal resolution (economical sensors), and spectral resolution. Our hybrid neural network RFI detection algorithm (WARD) enables observations in highly contested RFI environments. Data from the ECO1280 nature run (Hoffman, Malardel and Peevey 2018) were used for the simulation of observed radiances of a microwave sensor from orbit. ECO1280 data enabled training and testing WARD’s performance across a wide range of climatological conditions, including tropical cyclones. Synthetic RFI was applied to simulated radiance data, constructing a strong training dataset. During validation, WARD exhibits 0.9 Recall at RFI offsets of 1.6K for five simultaneously contaminated channels, and 0.99 Recall for a single contaminated channel, all while maintaining a false positive rate of ≤ 2% for both test cases. In addition to performing well in congested environments, performance is consistent across a wide range of climatologies and observing conditions. WARD can be further improved through use of time series data, incorporating RFI geospatial likelihoods, etc. We will present the results that only utilize single spectral footprints and simplified geospatial data, e.g., latitude and time. 1. References Bormann, N., H. Lawrence, and J. Farnan. 2019. Global observing systems experiments in the ECMWF assimilation system. Technical memorandum 839. Reading, United Kingdom: ECMWF. Duncan, D. 495181.title: How LEO Science Investments serve NOAA Mission Support Areas and help meet user needs
495181.abstract: The NOAA Office of Low Earth Observations (LEO) makes annual investments through its science program in order to further the exploitation of data from LEO satellites. Science program objectives include: enhancing LEO data utilization in support of the NOAA mission support areas; transitioning product algorithms to operations; supporting the calibration, validation, and long-term stewardship of LEO data; and exploring novel uses of LEO data and sensors. With increased government accountability oversight, this effort seeks to align LEO science program investments with validated NOAA observational requirements. Using the Consolidated Observation User Requirements List (COURL), LEO science projects are linked to NOAA Mission Service Areas (MSAs) through validated observational requirements that are enhanced or exploited through the respective project. Additionally, this effort will highlight some of the current accomplishments and transition to operations efforts of LEO investments. Through stakeholder engagement, many of the LEO investments have transitioned from research to meet a NOAA requirement to a user request for an operational product.

495182.title: Influence of Aging Wildfire Aerosols on Cloud Microphysical Properties
495182.authors: Chen-Hau Lan, NCAR, Boulder, CO; SUNY, Albany, NY; National Central University, Taoyuan City, Taiwan, Taiwan; and C. H. Lu, S. Ha, and P. L. Lin
495182.abstract: Wildfire smoke aerosols can be transported over long distances, influencing not only surface air quality but also cloud development and weather systems in downwind regions. While previous studies have focused mainly on near-source aerosol–radiation interactions (ARI), aerosol–cloud interactions (ACI) in remote regions remain less understood, particularly regarding how aging-induced changes in aerosol microphysics affect cloud evolution. In addition, traditional WRF-Chem configurations have limited representation of fully coupled aerosol–microphysics processes. This study examines an early August 2018 wildfire smoke transport event, during which aerosols from the western United States were transported to the Rocky Mountain region and interacted with developing cloud systems. Simulations are performed using WRF-Chem with a fully coupled GOCART–Thompson aerosol-aware microphysics scheme. Sensitivity experiments include a no-biomass-burning case (noBB), variations in aerosol aging timescale (EFOLD), and changes in the hygroscopicity parameter (κ) of secondary organic aerosol (OC2) (KAPPA). Results show that transported smoke enhances water-friendly aerosol (WFA) and increases cloud droplet number while reducing droplet size. Cloud response is more sensitive to CCN number concentration than to κ, highlighting the dominant role of aerosol loading. However, CCN effects are weaker under low vertical velocity due to limited activation. Increased CCN suppresses autoconversion and delays precipitation, while aerosol-induced changes in cloud water (qcloud) further influence ice mixing ratio (qice) in strong cloud cells. Overall, these results emphasize the importance of coupled aerosol–microphysics processes and cloud dynamics in shaping ACI during long-range transport events.

495183.title: Retrieval and Comparison of Planetary Boundary Layer Height from Microwave Radiometer and Lidar Observations
495183.authors: William Ligon, UMBC, Columbia, MD; UMBC, Baltimore City, MD; and S. Pandey, M. E. D. Roots, and B. Demoz
495183.abstract: The planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) is an important parameter for understanding air quality, pollutant mixing, and boundary-layer dynamics. Different instruments, however, often retrieve the PBLH using different physical principles, so it is important to compare them. This study retrieves the PBLH from microwave radiometer (MWR) observations and compares it with lidar-based estimates during the FP2 campaign. For the MWR retrieval, a pressure profile is first obtained from the temperature profile, and the potential temperature, its vertical gradient, and the wet adiabatic lapse rate (LR) are then calculated. The PBLH is identified as the lowest height where the potential temperature gradient exceeds the lapse rate. A flexible reading system was also developed so that the method can process netCDF files of almost any format. The results show a moderate agreement between the two instruments (R = 0.548), with better correlation during the day (R = 0.354) than at night (R = 0.195). The diurnal cycle shows that MWR generally retrieves a higher PBLH than lidar, especially at night, when the lidar values stay very low. When the days are separated into hot and cold cases, the difference between the two retrievals becomes clearer, and cold days show consistently higher MWR PBLH. These results demonstrate that MWR can capture the diurnal PBLH cycle and its temperature dependence, while also highlighting important day–night and instrument differences that should be considered in future boundary-layer studies.

495186.title: Regional Comparisons of Oceanic Observing System Impacts using the NASA GEOS-S2S-3 Forecasting System
495186.authors: Lindsay Noelle Chu, GMAO, Glenn Dale, MD; UMD ESSIC, College Park, MD; and A. Jersild and A. Molod
495186.abstract: Accurate prediction of large-scale climate processes relies on the quality of initial conditions generated through ocean reanalysis, and the assimilation of observational data into coupled ocean-atmosphere models. As ocean observing networks face increasing funding pressures, quantifying their distinct contributions to model accuracy becomes essential for informing future decision-making. However, the impacts of individual observation networks vary geographically and throughout the vertical ocean column. In order to understand how the roles and behaviors of observational data networks change across different regions of the world’s oceans, a series of Observing System Experiments (OSEs) were conducted within the NASA GEOS Sub-seasonal to Seasonal Version 3 (GEOS-S2S-3) forecasting system. To isolate the impacts of individual observation networks on the model’s ocean reanalysis, each OSE run excluded a different set of observing systems. All experimental OSE runs were evaluated for accuracy against a Control run, across a set of ocean variables (e.g., thermocline depth, subsurface salinity, heat content, etc.) and oceanic regions. Initial findings highlight the distinct impacts of Argo float data on resolving model analysis of the thermocline, eddy kinetic energy, and other subsurface variables, while altimetry data demonstrates impacts on constraining both subsurface and surface variables on a regional scale. Ultimately, this analysis demonstrates the necessity of observing systems in constraining prediction and analysis of ocean variables used for forecasting larger-scale weather and climate processes. It offers a systematic evaluation of observing system impacts for applications in broader society, and highlights the continued maintenance of such systems as an essential component of effective decision-making and global climate resilience.

495189.title: Ice Pressure Outlook Product: A Look at Mid-Range Marine Hazard Forecasting at the Canadian Ice Service.
495189.authors: Jessie Cluett, MSC, Ottawa, ON, Canada
495189.abstract: The Canadian Ice Service (CIS) is a part of the department of Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) and is the leading authority for ice and iceberg information in Canada's navigable waters. As part of its mandate to protect Canadians and support maritime shipping operations, the Canadian Ice Service has an ice warning program to identify and communicate hazardous ice conditions to marine users. The current program includes 3 types of short-range ice hazard warnings: unusual presence of ice warnings, rapidly closing lead warnings and the most frequently issued, ice pressure warnings. These warnings are all valid over a two-day forecast period (Day 1 and Day 2) and are disseminated through text forecast bulletins by the Canadian Ice Service and through marine radio broadcasts. Ice pressure occurs when a prolonged period of strong winds compresses and pressurizes the sea ice within an ice pack or along a coastline. Under strong ice pressure conditions, ships may lose the ability to navigate freely and be pushed towards potentially dangerous conditions. Growing marine traffic in Canadian waters and rapidly changing Arctic weather and ice conditions has led to increased demand for ice forecast products beyond the current 2-day forecast warning program valid time. In addition, there is also an increase in international users transiting Canadian waters for which French and/or English text bulletins may not be a preferred source of ice information. These changing client needs, as well as the Meteorological Service of Canada’s broader transformation initiatives to produce hazard-based forecast products, motivated the development of a Day-3 Ice Pressure Outlook graphical product. This presentation will discuss how the Canadian Ice Service assesses ice pressure hazards in the Arctic using RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) and Sentinel satellite imagery combined with forecasted ice stage of development information and numerical guidance. A discussion of the ice pressure numerical guidance will give insight into how the Regional Ice Ocean Prediction System Version 2 (RIOPS v2) ice pressure and convergence/divergence/ice shear fields are used by forecasters to assess areas of moderate and strong ice pressure. This presentation will also introduce the Day-3 Ice Pressure Outlook product and how to interpret the hazard map. The outlook map shows areas of forecasted moderate and strong ice pressure over our ice charting regions valid for a 24-hour period from midnight to midnight on Day 3, conforming to standards set by the ECCC marine guidelines. In addition to the ice pressure fields, the 24-hour average ice drift arrow is added over any region expecting pressure (valid for the 24-hour period of the chart) to help support decision-making. This Ice Pressure Outlook serves as a continuation of our current Day 1 and Day 2 warning program providing users with additional lead time for operational planning in Canadian waters. The target audience for this product includes weather and ice briefers, marine route coordinators for private shipping companies, ship captains and first officers on icebreaker and sealift vessels, weather coordinators for pleasure cruise ships and any other marine users travelling in ice infested waters.

495190.title: Turbulence-Resolving Weather Forecasting with the FastEddy® Model (Invited Presentation)
495190.authors: Domingo Munoz-Esparza, NSF NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and J. Sauer
495190.abstract: Large-eddy simulation (LES) of the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) is still predominantly used as a fundamental research tool. To enable actionable microscale weather forecasting, NSF NCAR’s Research Applications Laboratory has developed efficient, real-world LES capabilities using the GPU-accelerated FastEddy® community model (https://github.com/NCAR/FastEddy-model). During this talk, we will provide an update on recent efforts that couple mesoscale models (WRF and MPAS) with LES-to-LES nesting in FastEddy® to achieve downscaled weather at meter-scale grid spacings. We will show validation of this modeling approach against observations across several real-world cases with a focus on turbulence representation, demonstrating the accuracy and value of higher-fidelity ABL predictions.

495193.title: Mind the Gap Revisited: Assessing the Changing Private Sector Workforce in Atmospheric Science
495193.authors: Sarah Purpura, Mercury Insurance LLC, Brea, CA; and A. A. L. Lang, Z. J. Handlos, A. Markowitz, A. C. Wasula, M. A. Vido, A. Praino, C. L. Walker, J. M. Lanicci, S. Bennett, and D. Margolin
495193.abstract: The private sector has become an increasingly important part of the weather, water, and climate enterprise, while the pathways into that sector continue to change. Since the 2022 Mind the Gap survey, shifts in public-sector hiring and research funding have increased uncertainty for students and professionals considering careers in government and academia. At the same time, expanded use of artificial intelligence (AI) is changing expectations for technical work, raising questions about how organizations will develop and hire early-career talent. These changes make it important to revisit how academic programs, students, and employers understand preparation for private-sector careers. This presentation will describe a follow-up Mind the Gap survey effort designed to examine current workforce needs and identify opportunities to strengthen connections between academia and the private sector. The study will use two complementary surveys. The first will focus on students and early-career professionals, including their awareness of private-sector career paths and available resources, the skills they believe are most important, the barriers they face, and the types of mentoring, internships, coursework, and career guidance that would be most useful. The second will focus on private-sector hiring managers and will examine how hiring needs have changed since the 2022 survey, which skills and experiences now distinguish successful candidates, how employers expect early-career professionals to use AI, and whether hiring preferences are shifting among students, early-career applicants, and mid- or late-career professionals transitioning from government or academia. The survey will also explore the role private-sector organizations may play in supporting applied research, workforce development, internships, and academic partnerships. Results will be used to compare perceptions across students, early-career professionals, and hiring managers and to identify areas of alignment and continuing disconnect. The project is intended to produce practical guidance for academic programs, students, professional societies, and employers. By updating the 2022 perspective and incorporating current questions about AI, sector transitions, and research support, this work will provide a framework for developing more transparent, responsive, and collaborative pathways from atmospheric science education to private-sector careers.

495194.title: Model-Observation Comparison of the Chesapeake Bay Breeze Impact on Urban Boundary Layer Processes: Insights from the Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment
495194.authors: Nicholas E. Prince, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and K. A. Potucek, M. Deng, P. J. Walter, and K. J. Davis
495194.abstract: The Chesapeake Bay Breeze (CBB) is a regularly occurring phenomenon over the Baltimore metropolitan area that significantly impacts both the near-surface climate and air quality through the transport of marine air inland and the subsequent modification of the local urban boundary layer dynamics. This study explores the impact of the Chesapeake Bay Breeze on the urban boundary layer (UBL) and near-surface environment as well as the CBB structure using both the Weather Research Forecasting (WRF) model and observations from the Baltimore Social Environment Collaborative (BSEC) and Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE). By comparing WRF with the BSEC and CoURAGE observations, we also examine the model performance at simulating both the CBB structure and impact on the UBL. To that end, CBBs were identified using two Doppler lidars, the Baltimore-Washington International (BWI) terminal radar, five surface meteorological and three flux towers, a buoy, and radiosondes launched four times daily. Doppler lidars were located at the CoURAGE Baltimore Core Facility (M1) and at Morgan State University (MSU), roughly 3 km apart. Using these observations, we identified 42 CBB passages over Baltimore city using a decision tree approach, where criteria such as an increase in dewpoint temperature greater than one-degree Celsius over a 10-minute period, a positive terrestrial-marine air temperature, and a sudden shift in wind direction from the Chesapeake Bay were necessary in all identified passages. Preliminary findings show that the depth of the CBB inland propagating density current is on average about 400-500m and passes over M1 on average at about 14:30 LST and that the CBB has a greater impact on the near-surface moisture characteristics than the temperature. We hypothesize that the less pronounced impact of the CBB on the near-surface temperature is due to the high sensible heat flux provided by the impervious surface, moderating the thermal impact of the CBB. Moreover, the CBB has a robust impact on the turbulent mixing within the UBL, typically resulting in a strong reduction in turbulence following the passage of the CBB density current. Preliminary comparisons show that WRF tends to simulate CBBs on the days we observed them; however, the timing and structure of the simulated CBB differs from observations. Overall, results from this study illustrate the impact of the CBB on the UBL dynamics and near-surface climate as well as WRF’s capabilities at reproducing those effects which are instrumental for the future of urban weather and climate prediction.

495196.title: How Eddy Fluxes Shape Precipitation in the Midlatitudes
495196.authors: Pin-Chun Huang, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and S. Lee
495196.abstract: Most midlatitude precipitation during the cold season is produced by extratropical cyclones, and variations in midlatitude precipitation are often interpreted in terms of storm-track activity. From a large-scale dynamics perspective, previous research has shown a spatial relationship between eddy momentum flux (EMF) and precipitation. However, the dynamical pathway linking eddy fluxes and precipitation has not been fully established. Here, we examine how eddy fluxes, moisture transport, the residual mean circulation, and precipitation evolve during anomalously strong EMF events. We diagnose the residual mean circulation response and moisture transport by combining the transformed Eulerian mean (TEM) form of the Kuo–Eliassen equation with isentropic moisture budget analysis. We identify a two-stage transition in midlatitude precipitation during strong EMF events. During the early stage, approximately 48–24 h before the EMF maximum, anomalous eddy moisture flux convergence peaks in the mid-troposphere over the midlatitudes and is associated with enhanced large-scale precipitation. At the same time, the residual mean circulation is characterized by ascent in the subtropics, driven mainly by the strengthening of eddy heat flux (EHF). During the later stage, around and after the EMF maximum, mean-flow-driven moisture flux convergence becomes dominant in the lower troposphere. The residual mean circulation shows strong subtropical descent and midlatitude ascent, driven mainly by EMF, with convective precipitation anomalies becoming stronger during this phase. Anomalously strong EMF events tend to be associated with strong wave anomalies over preferred regions across the eastern Pacific, North America, and the Atlantic. Regional analysis shows that during the early stage, precipitation and moisture transport are concentrated near frontal systems, while the moisture transport and TEM circulation extend from the lower-tropospheric subtropics toward the mid- to upper-tropospheric midlatitudes, resembling a warm conveyor belt (WCB)-like transport pathway. By the later stage, the circulation and precipitation become more zonally coherent, with mean-flow moisture transport and upwelling in the lower troposphere over the midlatitudes. This evolution is consistent with previous studies showing the poleward movement of WCBs during the baroclinic life cycle.

495197.title: Photosynthetic Energy Storage: Improving Tower-Based ET Evaluation for OpenET Research-to-Operations
495197.authors: John Volk, DRI, Reno, NV; and Y. Kim, S. Sueki, S. Majumdar, C. Morton, B. A. Minor, J. L. Huntington, F. Melton, and P. Raghav
495197.abstract: Eddy covariance measurements commonly show that sensible and latent heat fluxes fall short of available energy, leaving a residual in the surface energy balance. Because energy-balance-corrected tower evapotranspiration (ET) is often used to evaluate remote-sensing ET products, choices in how the closure correction is calculated can propagate uncertainty into evaluation statistics. For operational data systems like OpenET, research-to-operations is adaptive and iterative, with advances in evaluation methods that help reduce uncertainty being critical for targeted subsequent improvements to the remote-sensing models themselves. One routinely neglected term is the chemical energy stored in carbohydrates during photosynthesis, which is small but systematic and biologically timed. We implemented a gross primary productivity (GPP)-derived photosynthetic energy storage (PES) term in the open-source flux-data-qaqc Python package. PES was calculated from nonnegative GPP using 0.422 J µmol⁻¹ CO₂. Across 50 AmeriFlux sites and 85,369 site-days, we compared available energy as net radiation minus ground heat flux (Rn − G) and Rn − G − PES, with active periods identified from seasonal daily GPP patterns. Across all days, median daily mean PES was 1.12 W m⁻², or 1.32% of available energy. Including PES increased the median closure slope from 0.80 to 0.82, improving closure at all 50 sites, and reduced median corrected ET from 2.63 to 2.58 mm d⁻¹. During active periods, PES increased to 3.13 W m⁻², closure slope increased from 0.81 to 0.83, and corrected ET decreased from 3.91 to 3.80 mm d⁻¹. Across 18 cropland sites, closure slope increased from 0.79 to 0.82 and corrected ET decreased by 3.26%, the largest response among ecosystem classes. We conducted a preliminary comparison of previously curated OpenET estimates with closure-corrected tower ET at 21 sites using 2,811 paired site-days. Including PES reduced closure-corrected tower ET by 2.28%, shifted the OpenET ensemble slope from 0.96 to 0.98, and reduced MAE and RMSE from 0.87 to 0.86 and 1.10 to 1.08 mm d⁻¹. For active croplands, tower ET decreased by 3.50%, while MAE and RMSE decreased by 10.0% and 8.7%. Although PES is a small energy term, preliminary results show that it can produce proportionally larger changes in remote-sensing ET evaluation, especially during biologically active, high-water-use periods. Accounting for PES may therefore provide a simple, process-based improvement to tower ET used for ET product evaluation. More broadly, these results demonstrate the iterative nature of research-to-operations: improving operational ET products requires continued refinement not only of remote-sensing methods, but also of the reference data and accuracy assessment methods used to evaluate them.

495198.title: Improving Extreme Precipitation Forecasts for Hydrologic Modeling using Mountain Mapper and Machine Learning Methods
495198.authors: Andrew D. Polasky, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and E. Towler, M. R. Abel, and K. Toride
495198.abstract: Ensemble streamflow forecasts are critical for assessing the risk of rare, high impact events. NOAA’s current operational Hydrological Ensemble Forecast System (HEFS) is known to underestimate the likelihood of extreme precipitation events. Using the GEFS v12 reforecasts from 2000-2019, we evaluate statistical and machine learning post-processing methods for improving the representation of extreme precipitation for a set of HEFS priority basins across the U.S. Benchmarking against the operational HEFS hindcasts, we test mountain mapper, a simple terrain adjustment approach, as well as several machine learning methods of varying complexity, ranging from Random Forest to a diffusion based model for increasing the size of the ensemble. We find that the mountain mapper approach improves forecasts of extreme precipitation in mountainous regions when used as a direct downscaling method, and provides a useful input adjustment for more complex methods. We test using the mountain mapper adjusted precipitation as an input feature for both operational statistical methods and deep learning approaches. Finally, we test how the precipitation post-processing approaches translate into streamflow forecasts by running the post-processed precipitation reforecasts through a lumped hydrological model similar to that used in HEFS.

495199.title: Teaching Non-Meteorology Undergraduate Students Data Analysis Through Evaluation of NASA Forecast Data
495199.authors: Hannah E. Attard, Daemen University, Amherst, NY
495199.abstract: Five undergraduate students conducted independent meteorological research from January 2025-January 2026 at a small, liberal arts university. These students were all health-science majors with no meteorology or coding background and utilized this opportunity to learn how to do independent, computational research. This research project culminated in poster presentations at the 2026 Student Meeting at the AMS Annual Meeting. This presentation will provide an overview of the research timeline, emphasizing the Spring 2025 semester in which the students learned how to code in Python and the basics of meteorology. During the Spring 2025 semester, the students completed the Geo-Python course that was created by professors at University of Helsinki, utilizing Jupyter Notebooks and GitHub. The cohort met twice a week with the research mentor to complete the Geo-Python course and conduct journal discussions on relevant topics. The semester culminated in a short presentation where each student presented an independent final coding project. The presentation will discuss lessons learned throughout this semester, including the feasibility of GitHub for grading assignments. Following the completion of the Spring 2025 semester, which emphasized learning the basics of both coding and meteorology, in Summer 2025, the cohort worked approximately 30 hours per week for 8 weeks conducting independent research on individual case studies. Students were provided Jupyter notebooks with templated code to edit and adjust for their individual needs. In Fall 2025, the students created posters for the AMS Annual Student meeting, which they then presented. This presentation will emphasize how research can be successfully completed with undergraduate researchers at either a university with a meteorology degree or without a meteorology degree.

495204.title: A History of Air Pollution Legislation in India
495204.authors: Aditya Kumar, Biosphere Research, Lucknow, India
495204.abstract: Air Pollution legislation is critical for controlling the degradation of air quality due to anthropogenic activities. Over the past several decades, joint efforts by policy makers and researchers have resulted in major advances in air pollution legislation globally. A most notable example is the development, implementation and success of the United States Clean Air Act. On the other side of the globe, India is balancing the effects of economic development and need for environment protection. This study reviews the history of air pollution legislation in India, the successes, failures and potential future steps to continue development and minimize environmental degradation.

495205.title: GeoXO Infrared Hyperspectral Sounder (GXS) Scanning for Level 1b and Level 2+ Product Needs
495205.authors: Monica M. Coakley, MIT Lincoln Laboratory, Lexington, MA; and A. Heidinger, S. W. Bidwell, O. McElhinney, C. A. Wheeler, N. Todirita, M. Todirita, and E. C. Grigsby
495205.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA’s) Geostationary eXtended Observations (GeoXO) series satellites are planned to follow the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES)-R series satellites in 2032 and beyond. GeoXO will provide the nation continuity of environmental imagery over the western hemisphere, with observational improvements where feasible. The GeoXO Sounder (GXS) will provide level 1b calibrated and navigated radiances in the midwave infrared (MWIR) and the longwave infrared (LWIR) for generation of level 2+ products such as vertical profiles of atmospheric temperature and moisture. New level 2+ product requirements and product parameter details in the GeoXO Program’s Mission Requirements Document are being defined and will be discussed here, with a focus on sounder-related products. L2+ temperature and moisture products will be employed by National Weather Service (NWS) forecasters in near real time, and the GXS L1b radiances will be assimilated into numerical weather prediction (NWP) models with ingest cadences of one to several hours. GXS scanned swath combinations can achieve scan regions up to the size of the sounding disk within 30 minutes. Because forecaster needs can be more dynamic than NWP data ingest cadences, the GXS instrument will be flexible to cover various scan regions to respond to dynamic tasking originating with the NWS Senior Duty Meteorologist. Scan patterns from user representatives discussed with the GXS vendor can be performed by GXS. Additional user feedback was solicited on these scan options to better determine anticipated operations. GXS operational scanning reflecting additional user feedback on scan options will be discussed as well. DISTRIBUTION STATEMENT A. Approved for public release. Distribution is unlimited. This material is based upon work supported by the Department of Commerce under Air Force Contract No. FA8702-15-D-0001 or FA8702-25-D-B002. Any opinions, findings, conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of the Department of Commerce.

495206.title: Determining Cloud Top Phase and Maximum Droplet Size Category using a Multi-Layer Perceptron and GOES-R ABI Emissive Bands
495206.authors: Joshua Lave, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. D. Landolt, B. Bernstein, and S. DiVito
495206.abstract: Atmospheric aircraft icing conditions pose a dangerous risk to aircraft operators and diagnosing and forecasting those conditions remains a challenge today. Over the past several decades, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has developed icing certification standards for aircraft based on droplet size; Appendix C certification covers cloud droplets less than 100 µm in diameter and Appendix O certification covers supercooled large drops (SLD) with diameters equal to or in excess of 100 µm. To facilitate compliance with certification standards, the FAA funded the Terminal Area Icing Weather Information (TAIWIN) project in early 2014 with the goal of providing reliable, highly resolved, and accurate diagnoses and forecasts of icing conditions on the ground and aloft in the airport terminal area, defined here as a cylinder from the surface to 12,000 ft AGL and with a 30 nm radius. The resulting TAIWIN Capability integrates a variety of in-situ and remote sensing observations and numerical weather prediction model output to produce 3D gridded total and SLD icing likelihood fields. Data from the GOES-R series satellites are a critical component of the Diagnostic Capability’s cloud top phase and drop size category sub-fields but are hampered by algorithm transitions during dawn and dusk (the solar terminator). To mitigate this issue and become independent of the solar zenith angle (SZA), a new cloud top parameterization scheme was developed using only GOES-R emissive band brightness temperature differences parsed by a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) neural network. Training and validation data were collected during the TAIWIN-sponsored In-Cloud Icing and Large-Drop Experiment (ICICLE), a flight campaign conducted in 2019 to collect in-situ observations of cloud microphysics parameters in icing conditions. Despite a limited training dataset, the MLP model performed similarly to the existing TAIWIN Capability algorithm and without artifacts along transition zones across the solar terminator. This presentation will discuss the required datasets, experimental design, and machine learning results and limitations before briefly exploring further opportunities to improve the model, including incorporating data from other flight campaigns into the training and validation datasets. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the FAA. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

495208.title: A Top Down Approach to Determining Cloud Boundaries for Single and Multi-layer Systems Using a Set of Neural Networks Trained with MODIS and CloudSat and CALIPSO data
495208.authors: Sunny Sun-Mack, Analytical Mechanics Associates, Inc, Hampton, VA; and P. Minnis, Y. Chen, D. A. Rutan, G. Hong, and W. L. Smith Jr.
495208.abstract: The vertical locations of clouds are important to many areas of weather and climate monitoring and research, particularly atmospheric and surface radiation, the hydrological cycle, and aviation. Typically, in passive satellite remote sensing clouds are treated as a single layer to retrieve cloud properties including cloud top height, CTH, and cloud base height, CBH. For clouds that are truly single-layered (SL), the retrieval accuracies have been increasing over the years, but still need improvement. For multilayered (ML) clouds, the errors are considerably greater than for their SL counterparts. Over the last decade, machine-learning approaches to detecting CTH and CBH for both SL and ML clouds have made significant strides in reducing the uncertainties in those retrieved quantities. To improve the characterization of cloud boundaries for monitoring the Earth’s radiation budget from satellites, a Cloud Height Artificial Neural Network System, CHANS, has been developed for Edition 5 of the Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System (CERES). The CHANS was trained with cloud boundaries determined from 2008 CloudSat and CALIPSO (CC) cloud profiles using MODIS radiances and CERES cloud property retrievals from the Aqua satellite to retrieve CTH and cloud geometric thickness, CGT, for SL clouds and for two-layer ice-over-water clouds. Instead of using standalone neural networks for each parameter, a set of individual parameter neural networks (PNNs) are trained in sequence from the highest CTH to the lowest CGT, adding to the MODIS data input the CTH and CGT results from the layers above. PNNs are trained separately for day and night, SL and ML clouds, and according to the CERES-MODIS cloud thermodynamic phase. Only data taken over areas free of snow and ice are considered since ML detection over cryogenic scenes is less reliable than elsewhere. CBH is computed as the difference between CTH and CGT. Validation is performed using 2009 MODIS data and CERES retrievals. For SL clouds, the standard deviations of the differences (SDD) between the CHANS and CC CTHs are 1.28 km and 1.23 km for day and night, respectively. The corresponding mean absolute errors (MAE) are 0.68 km and 0.67 km, while the mean bias errors (MBE) are 0.01 km and 0.03 km. For the ice-over-water ML clouds, the CTH for the upper layer has SDD = 1.19 km and 1.26 for day and night, respectively. The MAEs are 0.86 km and 0.91 km with MBEs of 0.02 km and 0.06 km. The errors are similar for the lower layer with SDD = 1.21 km during the day and 1.12 km at night. For these cases the MAEs are smaller than for the upper layer. The statistics for CBH are similar to those for CTH. For daytime SL CBH, SDD = 1.29 km, MAE = 0.69 km, and MBE = -0.03 km, a significant accuracy improvement compared with CERES Edition 4 with SDD = 2.61 km and MBE = -0.68 km. Similar results are found at night. Upper-layer ML cloud base heights are less accurate than their SL counterparts with SDD averaging 1.42 km overall and MAE at 1.06 km. For the lower layer CBH, SDD and MAE average 0.93 km and 0.60 km, respectively. Overall, these results represent the best accuracies to date for both SL and ML CTH and CBH. Additional details including other uncertainties and future efforts will be discussed at the conference. This approach to defining cloud boundaries from passive optical measurements is being employed by the CERES Edition 5 cloud products. Initial results indicate that it reduces the errors in downwelling long wave radiation by 40% compared to CERES Edition 4. This improvement was particularly pronounced for high clouds by approximately 60%. It should be applicable to both other low-Earth orbit and geostationary imagers. Thus, the CHANS should provide for more accurate continuous monitoring of cloud structure than is currently available.

495211.title: Well-Balanced and Higher-Order Finite Volume Schemes for River Flooding: A Regime-Dependent Assessment
495211.authors: Wisang Sugiarta, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and J. M. Moriarty and J. Brown
495211.abstract: Accurate flood forecasting is critical for disaster preparedness and risk management, yet the numerical schemes underlying large-scale flood models are rarely evaluated in the regimes they are most often deployed. For shallow water flow, where horizontal forces dominate, finite volume methods have become the primary choice due to simple discretization, exact mass conservation, and robust handling of wet/dry boundaries characteristic of flooding. Well-balanced and higher-order schemes within this framework were developed for ocean and coastal modeling, where continental shelf bathymetry causes non-physical oscillations and lake-at-rest imbalances, and first-order diffusion degrades fast-moving wave fronts over long domains. Whether these enhancements remain justified in friction-dominated river flooding, where friction dissipation dominates and event timescales are much shorter, has not been systematically assessed but are significant choices that directly affect forecast accuracy and computational cost. We address this within RDycore, DOE's performance-portable finite volume shallow water solver in E3SM, on unstructured triangular meshes with CPU and GPU backends. All four combinations of first- and second-order MUSCL reconstruction with and without well-balancing via hydrostatic reconstruction are evaluated on synthetic benchmarks and two real flood events: Hurricane Harvey (2017) in Houston, Texas and the 2013 Big Thompson River flood in northern Colorado. Both events compared to USGS stream gauge observations. Well-balancing eliminates spurious bed-slope-driven flow at negligible cost with strong impact on predicted flood extent and drainage pattern. Second-order reconstruction reduces numerical diffusion and better preserves flood wave structure and arrival times, but convergence rates degrade toward first order near wet-dry interfaces. We quantify the crossover resolution at which second-order schemes on a coarser mesh match first-order accuracy on a finer mesh, providing actionable guidance for forecasters balancing accuracy and computational budget. Overall, the cost-benefit of well-balanced and higher-order schemes is regime-dependent and cannot be assumed from ocean and coastal modeling experience.

495215.title: Beyond Stationarity: Characterizing Drought During a Changing Climate
495215.authors: Joshua Brinks, ISciences, LLC, Burlington, VT; and L. A. L. Dupigny-Giroux and T. M. Parris
495215.abstract: Drought has traditionally been defined as the difference between observed and expected meteorological, agricultural, and hydrological conditions expressed in terms of rarity derived from a probability distribution calculated over a baseline period. This framework was developed during a period of relative stability and is firmly embedded in operational public-facing capabilities to monitor and assess drought worldwide. However, we can now observe unmistakable trends in the data that violate this implicit assumption of stationarity and lead to distortions that compromise the effectiveness of drought analyses, planning, mitigation, and adaptation efforts by a broad spectrum of government, business, and civil society stakeholders throughout the United States. A fundamental reconceptualization of drought monitoring and assessment is required that explicitly accounts for non-stationarity. We will present the results of research in-progress that address this critical need by developing novel methods using structural time series decomposition to parse drought parameter time series and isolate long-term trends, changes in seasonality, and the effects of major ocean-atmosphere oscillations. These statistical models are used to estimate "dynamic normals" - expected daily drought parameter values that diagnose and account for non-stationarity in long-term trends, seasonal patterns, and co-covariates. We then compare current drought parameter values to the dynamic normal. This allows us to compute the peak magnitude, duration, and duration-integrated magnitude of each meteorological and flash drought event and assess the event rarity using distributions that account for non-stationarity while making use of the full observational record. We will illustrate our work using daily station data from the Global Historical Climatology Network (GHCN-daily) which includes Cooperative Observer Program (COOP) stations. The analysis in this presentation uses precipitation, temperature, and calculated reference evapotranspiration data from currently operating stations with at least 120 years of data and less than 2% missing data. We will assess multiple statistical methods for skill, interpretability, and computational cost with the goal of scaling this work up to work with raster reanalysis datasets such as the North American Land Data Assimilation System Version 3 (NLDAS-3) with additional parameters (e.g., soil moisture, runoff, streamflow).

495220.title: Development of the Next-Generation Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFSv2): Workflow and Initial Results
495220.authors: Yunheng Wang, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and C. Liu, K. H. Knopfmeier, D. Dowell, and N. Yussouf
495220.abstract: Abstract: The experimental Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS) aims to extend lead times for severe weather warnings through on-demand, adaptable domains and rapidly updating high-resolution ensemble analyses and forecasts. The version 1 (WoFSv1) uses the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model with the GSI-EnKF data assimilation system and is being demonstrated through the NWS WoFS Demonstration Project, with the NWS working toward an operational transition in FY27. To align with NOAA's Unified Forecast System (UFS) initiative, we are currently developing the next-generation WoFS version 2 (WoFSv2) based on the Model Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) dynamic core and the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework. The primary emphasis of the WoFSv2 workflow is its generalized, modular design, which separates machine-specific settings from scientific configurations to facilitate targeted tuning. The workflow is implemented using Bash and Python to ensure simplicity, flexibility, and portability. Key design objectives include accommodating on-demand domains, ensuring compatibility across multiple job schedulers, and implementing fault tolerance to allow the system to resume from checkpoints without redundant computation. In the experimental setup, WoFSv2 employs a Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (LETKF) solver for data assimilation every 15 minutes. The storm-scale ensemble consists of 30 members, initialized and driven by 1-hour Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFSv2) forecasts, with lateral boundary conditions provided by a 5-member RRFSv2 ensemble. The system utilizes a single-physics suite featuring the MYNN planetary boundary layer (PBL) scheme, the TEMPO microphysics scheme, and the RUC land surface model. To provide accurate, rapidly-updating analyses, the system assimilates radar reflectivity, radial velocity, GOES cloud water path, and conventional METAR observations. We will present initial results from experiments focusing on five high-impact convective cases from 2026. These case studies highlight the system's capabilities, design principles, and preliminary performance, demonstrating how modern technologies and methods can effectively inform watches, warnings, and impact-based decision support.

495221.title: Regional Air Quality Impact of Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S) Emitted from the Polluted Tijuana River Hotspot: A 1-Dimentional Lagrangian Modeling Study
495221.authors: Siyuan Wang, University of Miami, Miami, FL; and S. Zhao, B. Rico, K. Barsanti, W. Porter, K. Cysneiros de Carvalho, P. Stigler-Granados, and K. A. Prather
495221.abstract: For decades, toxic wastes and untreated sewage have polluted the Tijuana River, posing significant environmental and public health risks. Recent studies have shown that the contaminated Tijuana river water leads to severe air pollution by releasing a wide variety of pollutants (gases and aerosols) into the atmosphere, including hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), a toxic chemical known for its distinctive "rotten egg" smell (e.g. Rico et al. Science 2026). A hotspot at the Tijuana River crossing near Saturn Boulevard was identified as the dominant source of malodors and H2S in the area, consistent with the community odor complaints in the area. The regional air quality impact of this H2S source remains unclear. Point sources and small area sources are inherently challenging to represent in 3-D air quality models/chemical transport models, particularly at coarse spatial resolutions.
