To assess the air quality impact of H2S emitted from this river hotspot, we use a 1-D photochemical model operated in Lagrangian mode with detailed gas- and aerosol-phase chemistry. Driven by hourly observations of H2S, this Lagrangian model tracks the dispersion and chemistry of H2S (including its degradation products) in the atmosphere along dominant air mass trajectories. Preliminary results show that surface H2S in Tijuana River Valley and surrounding areas frequently exceeds established air quality standards (e.g. California Ambient Air Quality Standard: 30 ppb for odor control; California Office of Health Hazard Assessment: 7.3 ppb for chronic exposure), and the air quality impacts of H2S released from the polluted Tijuana river water are likely widespread in the San Diego-Tijuana border region.

495223.title: Observations of Coastal Atmospheric Duct Evolution using Multiple Lidars
495223.authors: Jia Su, Hampton University, Yorktown, VA; and T. Mackey, K. B. Herrera, R. Delgado, and M. Friberg
495223.abstract: Atmospheric ducts are special layers that trap and guide radio waves, allowing radar and communication signals to travel farther than normal. These layers are common near coastlines but are difficult to study because they can change quickly with temperature, humidity, and winds. To better understand the influence of atmospheric ducts on radio frequency (RF) operations, continuous high-resolution observations of temperature and water vapor are essential. Hampton University’s (HU) Raman-Mie lidar provides such measurements through rotational and vibrational Raman techniques, enabling detailed monitoring of refractivity gradients that drive duct formation. In this study, we analyzed a strong coastal ducting event from the evening of 22 May to the morning of 23 May 2019 over Hampton, Virginia, using a multi-lidar dataset that combines Raman-Mie thermodynamic profiles, US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM)-Army Research Laboratory (ARL) Doppler lidar wind fields, and NASA MPL aerosol and cloud observations. Results show that ducts developed between 200–330 m in association with the transition from a post-frontal cold air mass to a warm front. Water vapor depletion, rather than temperature inversion alone, was the primary driver of negative refractivity gradients. Wind shear was found to contribute to the persistence of a dry layer above the boundary layer, which in turn supported the formation of the duct. Doppler lidar further revealed that low-level jets (LLJs) elevated and weakened ducts through turbulent mixing, in some cases splitting them into two distinct layer processes rarely captured in previous studies. This case study demonstrates, for the first time in a coastal setting, how multi-lidar synergy resolves the fine-scale thermodynamic and dynamical processes that govern duct evolution. These findings highlight the importance of sustained, high-resolution coastal monitoring for improving refractivity forecasts and mitigating radar propagation uncertainties in littoral environments.

495225.title: Preparing for the Future: Exploring Hyperspectral Soundings with the Hyperlooper
495225.authors: Joseph K. Zajic, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and L. Wichrowski, E. Sorbella, J. Fulbright, M. Foster, A. Latto, J. Anderson, D. Pogorzala, and L. A. Byerle
495225.abstract: The future of environmental satellite observations will include unprecedented access to hyperspectral sounding information through the GeoXO era. To help prepare NWS forecasters and researchers for these capabilities, the NESDIS Total Operational Weather Readiness – Satellites (TOWR-S) team is working with the MTG IRS EUMETSAT Level 1 data from the Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Infrared Sounder (IRS), publicly released on July 30, 2026. Using its “Hyperlooper” application, the team is exploring new ways to visualize, analyze, and interact with hyperspectral sounding datasets. As GeoXO capabilities continue to mature, activities such as Hyperlooper provide an opportunity to better understand how next-generation sounding data can support forecasting, warning operations, and environmental analysis. Progress on this effort, including collaboration with NWS forecasters on both IRS and on early integration of MTG FCI imagery into National Centers, will be shared as the stakeholder engagement expands.

495226.title: The Solar Wind Plasma Sensor on the SOLAR-1 Mission: First Year of Observations at the Sun-Earth L1 Point
495226.authors: Robert Wilkes Ebert, Southwest Research Institute, San Antonio, TX; and P. Mokashi, R. Perryman, J. Carey, H. A. Elliott, R. Frahm, R. Gomez, K. LLera, P. Valek, B. Kress, N. Miles, and D. Vassiliadis
495226.abstract: The Solar Wind Plasma Sensor (SWiPS) measures solar wind ions onboard NOAA’s Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness (SOLAR-1) mission. Launched in September 2025 and having reached the Sun-Earth Lagrange 1 point (L1) in January 2026, SOLAR-1 was declared operational in June 2026 providing continuity of space weather observational requirements at L1 and enabling watches, warnings, and alerts for NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center. SWiPS contains two nested electrostatic analyzer-based sensors, each capable of measuring solar wind ions, mainly protons and alpha particles. Its primary data products include the solar wind ion velocity, temperature, density, and dynamic pressure for these two dominant ion species, while high resolution measurements of their 3-D phase space distributions and flows are also available. In this presentation, we summarize the SWiPS observations during its first year of measurements at the Sun-Earth L1 point, covering a range of conditions from slow (< 300 km s-1), cold (~104 K) solar wind to coronal mass ejections with speeds exceeding 1200 km s-1, along with our cross-calibration efforts with other solar wind instruments at L1. In addition, we report on the instrument health and the long-term outlook for providing continuous solar wind measurements onboard SOLAR-1.

495227.title: Satellite Observations of Top-of-Storm Behaviors and Tornado Production in Supercell Merger Events
495227.authors: Amy Conner, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and M. Brown and A. D. Kennedy
495227.abstract: Supercell interactions with other cells and their relationship to tornado production represent a large and growing body of recent severe storms research. A majority of this work utilizes base level radar data to characterize these interactions, including the low-level convergence of convective cells; however, this often fails to capture the role of upper-level interactions, which may begin in advance of what is observed via radar. Recent studies (e.g. Liu et al. 2025) have demonstrated the potentially critical role that these interactions have during merger events, emphasizing the need to study supercell mergers with a more holistic approach. This study utilizes GOES satellite imagery to study supercell mergers and other supercell interactions to examine the full, top-down evolution of the storm merger process. A machine learning model developed by Cooney et al. (2025) called SvrStormSig is applied to numerous tornado-producing supercell interactions identified in Nixon et al. (2024) to examine overshooting top (OT) behavior and above-anvil cirrus plume (AACP) production across a merger window. Furthermore, using the radar-based definitions provided in Nixon et al. (2024), the radar merger time is compared to a newly-defined satellite merger time to identify instances where these upper-level interactions may begin prior to the lower-level ones. These observations are conducted and compared across two robust sets of cases: one set which produced EF-2+ tornadoes following the interaction, and another set which did not. This allows potential satellite-based signals for tornadogenesis to be identified, which can be utilized by forecasters as early indicators of tornado production following supercell interactions. Early results indicate that during the time of tornado production, the OT associated with the supercell-producing storm is nearly always located to the north or northwest of the initial tornado report, rather than being directly collocated with it. Prior to tornado production, an organization and/or “consolidation” of multiple OTs is often observed, generally occurring in the 15-30 minutes prior to tornadogenesis. This leaves one or two “dominant” OTs associated with the tornado-producing supercell. AACP production associated with the dominant OT was also frequently noted during this window in tornadic cases, and may be a reliable indicator of the dominant OT when the convection is otherwise disorganized and turbulent. In some cases, an actual merging of the smaller individual OTs can be observed, creating one larger, higher-confidence OT prior to tornado production. While these behaviors are possible in a variety of circumstances, they may prove to be useful yet underutilized indicators of a tornado-favorable and strengthening storm, especially in cases where radar data alone cannot provide sufficient evidence. In addition to completing the satellite-based analysis, future additions to this study will include an analysis of the environments associated with each set of cases. This will allow the physical and environmental controls on the observed behaviors to be explored, including the differences between tornadic and non-tornadic mergers.

495230.title: Aerosol Perturbations Influence Tropical Anvil Persistence Through Heating-Driven Circulations
495230.authors: Ci Song, Stockholm University, Stockholm, N/A, Sweden; and C. J. Wall, B. Gasparini, and N. J. lutsko
495230.abstract: Anvil clouds play an important role in tropical climate by spreading far beyond deep convective cores and exerting strong radiative effects. Aerosols can alter anvil evolution by modifying cloud microphysics and the associated latent and radiative heating, but how these changes influence anvil persistence remains poorly understood. Here, we use cloud-resolving simulations of warm-bubble-triggered isolated convection to investigate the evolution of tropical anvil clouds and their response to perturbations in cloud droplet number concentration, representing changes in cloud condensation nuclei while excluding ice-nucleating particle effects. We find that aerosol perturbations modify anvil microphysical properties and ice sedimentation, leading to changes in both latent and radiative heating. These heating changes drive vertical motions and strengthen a circulation beneath the anvil that supports its continued evolution. While vertical motion during the early anvil stage is dominated by the initial convective disturbance, heating-driven circulations become increasingly important as this perturbation weakens. Our results reveal a mechanism through which aerosol-induced changes in cloud microphysics can influence anvil lifetime by altering heating and circulation. This provides new insight into aerosol–cloud–climate interactions in the tropical upper troposphere and suggests a potential positive contribution to aerosol–cloud radiative forcing from enhanced anvil persistence.

495231.title: Exploring the Gray Zone: Testing Scale-Aware PBL Models in Storm Forecasting
495231.authors: Joseph Michael Sean Payne, Ball State University, Muncie, IN; and T. Hahn and J. M. Peters
495231.abstract: As weather forecasting model resolution continues to increase, one of the limiting factors in forecast accuracy is how these models represent sub-grid scale turbulence in the Planetary Boundary Layer (PBL) “gray zone”. This “gray zone” consists of horizontal model grid spacing between 1 km and 100 m, where turbulence cannot be explicitly resolved, but parameterization is imprecise. Scale-aware parameterization schemes are a potential solution to this problem. They attempt to resolve turbulent currents where possible and adjust the influence of parameterization with grid spacing. To test the accuracy of these models, we ran a Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model on an 800 m horizontal grid twice; once with the Yonsei University parameterization scheme and again with the Shin-Hong scale-aware scheme. Next, we used a Lagrangian tracking algorithm to compare the properties of model-generated cells with NEXRAD observations during a convective event over Baltimore, MD on July 27, 2025. We found that the scale-aware scheme was marginally better at predicting maximum cell reflectivity area, but convective initiation was forecasted better by the parameterized scheme. Many other variables, including storm volume, lifetime, and perimeter were forecasted equally well by both models. Although both models’ maximum echo tops were consistent with one another, they were consistently higher than observed echo tops. Further research should evaluate the performance of scale-aware models at finer other grid spacings in the PBL gray zone.

495234.title: New and Emerging Measurements from the Pi Chamber
495234.authors: Will Cantrell, Michigan Technological Univ., HOUGHTON, MI; and J. C. Anderson, W. Chen, H. Fahandezh sadi, R. A. Shaw, J. Simmons, S. P. Singh, Y. M. Sua, A. Vakhtin, F. Yang, and J. Yeom
495234.abstract: Cloud chambers are a controlled complement to field and remote-sensing observations of cloud and precipitation physics. We present three examples of new and emerging measurement approaches from the Pi Chamber, a Rayleigh-Bénard convection cloud chamber at Michigan Technological University, each targeting a different observational gap. First, we discuss hygroscopic cloud seeding in mixed-phase conditions. A steady-state, well-characterized supercooled liquid water cloud is created in the chamber, then the perturbation from introduction of dust is observed. A fraction of the dust catalyzes ice formation, which is challenging to observe when the crystals are small. We discuss how we address this. We then observe perturbation to the mixed-phase cloud when a hygroscopic seeding agent (milled NaCl) is introduced to the chamber. Second, we highlight a new high-resolution, time-correlated single-photon-counting lidar, developed in collaboration with Brookhaven National Laboratory and Stevens Institute of Technology. Operating at roughly one-centimeter range resolution, this instrument resolves entrainment and sedimentation-driven droplet size sorting near a laboratory cloud top, revealing structure that bulk, homogeneous-cloud assumptions fail to capture and providing a benchmark for evaluating the algorithms used to relate lidar backscatter to cloud microphysical properties. Finally, we discuss a challenge. Can we measure cloud-relevant supersaturation in the chamber? The saturation ratio, S, is defined as the ratio of the actual vapor pressure (or mixing ratio) to the saturation vapor pressure (or saturation mixing ratio). A typical supersaturation (S-1) at cloud base is ~ 0.3%. Can we measure the mixing ratio and temperature accurately enough to determine values like this? Together, these efforts show that advancing understanding of cloud processes often starts by confronting how hard the measurement itself is.

495235.title: Air Quality and Health Impacts of Prescribed Fires: Case Studies in the Eastern United States
495235.authors: Christopher Louis Germano, Atmospheric Chemistry and Global Change Research Group, Tallahassee, FL; Florida State University, Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Science, Tallahassee, FL; and C. D. Holmes
495235.abstract: Prescribed burning is an essential land management tool for fuel reduction and ecological maintenance supporting the prevention of wildfires, yet the smoke emissions from these fires present air quality and public health concerns. Specifically, particulate matter (PM2.5) emitted from prescribed burns can degrade regional air quality and increase exposure risk for nearby and downwind populations. This study uses high-resolution smoke dispersion simulations with the Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Integrated Trajectory (HYSPLIT) model and mesoscale meteorological fields from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model. We present several case studies of prescribed fires in Florida for which burn area and fuels are known. Measurements of fire radiative power from geostationary satellites are used to constrain the timing and magnitude of heat release, which informs the simulated plume rise. The model simulates plume dispersion and downwind concentrations of PM2.5, which are compared to measurements. Simulated smoke PM2.5 concentrations are then combined with population data to assess several measures of public impacts: including number of people impacted and potential asthma episodes. We use this modeling framework to examine the relationship between burn-day meteorology and downwind health risk.

495236.title: Quantifying the Impact of Observing Systems on ENSO and Ocean Dynamics Using the GMAO S2S Forecast System
495236.authors: Annika Jersild, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; GMAO, Glenn Dale, MD; UMD ESSIC, College Park, MD; and L. N. Chu, A. Molod, E. Hackert, V. Ruiz-Xomchuk, S. Akella, L. Ren, and J. Carton
495236.abstract: El Niño/Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has a significant impact on climate and society, making it a critical focus for advancing predictability in seasonal coupled ocean-atmosphere forecasts. While the importance of observations for improving our understanding of the dynamics and prediction capabilities for ENSO is well recognized, optimizing observing networks to maximize return on federal investments requires a rigorous assessment of their impacts. Our research evaluates the impacts of selected data observing systems on the NASA GEOS Subseasonal to Seasonal Version 3 (GEOS-S2S-3) seasonal prediction system through a series of observation denial experiments (Observing System Evaluations – OSEs). Specifically, we assess the impact of Argo profiling floats and satellite altimetry observing systems within the data assimilation workflow, focusing on the tropical Pacific Ocean and ENSO predictions using reanalysis and forecasts starting in the year 2020. Experimental design compares three runs: the baseline control run, one with Argo excluded, and one with altimetry data excluded. Initial results indicate that withholding different observational systems alters temperature and thermocline reconstruction. Notably, these impacts exhibit seasonal variation, peaking in the boreal winter and spring, leading to larger impacts on our ENSO early forecasting capabilities. Application of these results is vital for constraining forecasts and optimizing Earth system modeling and data assimilation capabilities. This work supports strategic prioritization of observation networks and maximization of resource allocation efficiency, with international stakeholder and society benefits.

495238.title: Evaluation of Next-Generation Snow Depth Sensors for the ARM User Facility
495238.authors: Matthew Sturm, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and M. Oggier, D. Clemens-Sewall, K. Irving, J. Delamere, A. Theisen, and A. Glen
495238.abstract: Continuous, reliable snow-depth observations in cold Arctic marine environments pose significant operational challenges. The Department of Energy’s Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility deploys an array of 18 ultrasonic distance sounders to measure snow depth at the coastal North Slope of Alaska (NSA) observatory. These sensors experience frequent instrument failures and data dropouts caused by riming, moisture, extreme cold, and salinity. To identify the next-generation snow-depth sensor for ARM, the DRIFTS (Depth sensor Reliability and Intercomparison Field Test for Snow) project will deploy and analyze alternative snow-depth measuring technologies across multiple years and sites. Year 1 is planned for the 2026-2027 winter at the University of Alaska Fairbanks (UAF). Candidate and legacy sensors, basic meteorological instruments, and a time-lapse camera will be deployed within an existing terrestrial lidar footprint at a field site on the Troth Yeddha’ campus. One-minute sensor data, along with ground-truth snow depth, density, and stratigraphy, will be collected to assess integration, power, and performance in severe cold. In Year 2 (2027-2028), the evaluation instrument suite will be deployed at NSA during the Arctic winter. Continuous analysis will assess signal noise, dropout frequency, and accuracy relative to ground-truth measurements. Final evaluations will prioritize operational reliability, repairability, cost, data quality, and ease of integration into ARM data systems. The broader community is encouraged to get involved, especially during Year 2, by proposing additional guest instrumentation for deployment at NSA. This study aims to ensure the long-term reliability of observations at NSA, and the results may be of use to other snow-monitoring projects. Our presentation will provide an overview of Year 1 activities at UAF and planned data analyses, with a look ahead to Year 2 at NSA.

495239.title: Midwest Agrivoltaics for Resilient Communities (MARC): Building Community Economic and Energy Resilience to Extreme Weather
495239.authors: Daniel R Chavas, Purdue University, Indianapolis, IN, IN; and X. Lu, A. Thompson, K. Salazar, and J. Sesmero
495239.abstract: Rural energy security in the U.S. Midwest faces compounding pressure: extreme weather — hail, high wind, tornadoes, freezing rain, heat — increasingly drives rural power outages, while surging demand from AI and data centers intensifies competition for grid capacity and for farmland now sought for utility-scale solar. The Midwest Agrivoltaics for Resilient Communities (MARC) initiative, launched in 2025 through NSF's Regional Resilience Innovation Incubator (R2I2) program, is a Purdue-led effort to quantify how agrivoltaics — co-location of solar with active agriculture — paired with solar microgrids can strengthen rural energy security under weather extremes. MARC integrates four research tasks: (1) community engagement with Indiana farmers, utilities, and local officials to co-design trusted solutions; (2) a public-facing extreme-weather trends database ingesting NOAA Storm Events data (1955–2024) at county resolution for hail, tornado, thunderstorm wind, freezing rain, peak wind, and precipitation, with interactive "baseball card" and pannable county-map views for research and Extension use; (3) weather-dependent modeling of how agrivoltaics can build farm economic resilience by diversifying and stabilizing landowner income; and (4) weather-dependent modeling of how solar microgrids paired with agrivoltaics can reduce rural power outages. We present first-year outcomes across all four tasks: five completed regional stakeholder focus groups across Indiana, launch of the extreme-weather trends tool, proof-of-concept weather-driven economic and energy resilience models, and a partner network spanning rural electric cooperatives, utilities, and utility-scale solar developers. We describe plans to integrate these components into a stakeholder-facing decision-support pipeline for agrivoltaic + microgrid siting that strengthens rural energy security across the Midwest, along with the upcoming 2026 Indiana Land Use Summit anchoring ongoing community engagement.

495240.title: AWIPS Tsunami Operations Messaging Service (ATOMS): Modernizing and Unifying U.S. Tsunami Warning Message Generation and Dissemination.
495240.abstract: The United States operates two National Weather Service Tsunami Warning Centers: the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center (PTWC) in Honolulu, Hawaii, and the National Tsunami Warning Center (NTWC) in Palmer, Alaska. Historically, the centers have relied upon independently developed software and operational procedures to analyze tsunami threats and generate and disseminate warning products. While these systems have supported successful tsunami warning operations for many years, differences between the locally developed systems create challenges for software maintenance, consistency of warning operations, mutual backup, and continuity of operations between the two centers. The AWIPS Tsunami Operations Messaging Service (ATOMS) is being developed to modernize this capability by transitioning tsunami product generation and dissemination into the National Weather Service Advanced Weather Interactive Processing System (AWIPS). ATOMS provides the Tsunami Warning Centers with a common operational framework for creating and disseminating tsunami watches, warnings, advisories, information statements, and other tsunami-related products. The system leverages the NWS Hazard Services framework, providing a common, configurable platform while improving consistency between the two warning centers and supporting site backup and continuity-of-operations capabilities. ATOMS separates tsunami analysis and forecasting from the downstream warning-generation process. A major component of ATOMS is the Tsunami RECommender Software (T-RECS), which translates decision-tree elements from legacy tsunami warning systems into the Hazard Services framework. Development during 2025 and 2026 has focused increasingly on operational requirements and end-to-end functionality. Message-generation capabilities have likewise expanded. A new Tsunami Communications Test Message Tool supports center-specific communications-test hazard events in operational, practice, and test modes while using the same dissemination mechanism as other ATOMS hazard products. Recent use-case and acceptance testing encompasses initial and follow-up T-RECS procedures, multiple geographic product regions, tsunami hazard types, public and specialized product formats, non-seismic physical events, communications-test messages, localization, and operation in backup mode between Tsunami Warning Centers. This poster will provide an overview of the ATOMS architecture, demonstrate the Hazard Services tsunami workflow, highlight major capabilities developed during 2025–2026, and summarize recent integration, dissemination, training, and acceptance-testing activities at PTWC and NTWC.

495241.title: Characteristics of Rain-on-Snow Events Driven by Atmospheric Rivers
495241.authors: Ross D. Dixon, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA; University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and Z. Suriano
495241.abstract: When rain falls on a snowpack, a rain-on-snow (ROS) event, the combination of rain and snowmelt can lead to severe hazards such as flooding, avalanches, and landslides. Our recent work studying turbulent fluxes during these events has shown that latent heat fluxes into the snowpack, which lead to faster melt rates, are often underrepresented in models. Although this study focused on case studies across the Central and Eastern United States, further work has indicated that turbulent fluxes can drive ROS events across the Northern Hemisphere. Since turbulent fluxes are caused by low-level moisture and temperature gradients, which can often be enhanced by atmospheric rivers (ARs), we hypothesize that these turbulent flux driven ROS events may be associated with ARs. To test this, we use 6-hourly reanalysis data (ERA5 and MERRA2) from 1970 to 2019 to characterize ROS events across the globe. We also use tARget-v3 applied to both ERA5 and MERRA2 to identify AR events and their characteristics. We find that many regions have a large portion of ROS events during an AR. As we increase the threshold for the amount of snowmelt (greater than 0.5 mm/hr and 1 mm/hr) during the ROS event, we discover regions where the vast majority (greater than 70%) of strong ROS events occur during ARs. Several of these regions are well studied (e.g., US West Coast, Greenland), however, some understudied regions are highlighted (e.g., Central and Eastern US, Eastern Europe, Central Asia). We also explore the energetics of ROS events associated with ARs, and find that AR-ROS events produce stronger turbulent fluxes than non-AR-ROS events.

495244.title: The Predictability of Upward Wave Activity Flux and its Impact on the Predictability of Sudden Stratospheric Warming Events
495244.authors: Hannah E. Attard, Daemen University, Amherst, NY
495244.abstract: Previous work has shown that a primary driver for Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) events is from multiple pulses of upward wave activity flux (WAF) from the troposphere. This upward WAF acts to break down the climatological stratospheric westerly winds until the 10 hPa 60°N zonal-mean zonal wind eventually reverses to easterly and is thus categorized as an SSW. Though the upward WAF that impacts the stratosphere occurs on the planetary scale, synoptic weather events, such as blocking and extratropical cyclones, can constructively interfere with the planetary scale resulting in upward WAF. This study seeks to explore the predictability of SSW events through the predictability of the precursor upward WAF. The goal is to understand whether the predictability of tropospheric synoptic events impacts the predictability of the subsequent upward WAF and SSW. The results will address if stratospheric predictability is dependent on synoptic-scale features. To address the impact of tropospheric synoptic event predictability on the predictability of SSWs we explore by five SSWs (22 February 2008, 9 February 2010, 24 March 2010, 12 February 2018, 2 January 2019) with NASA’s new MERRA-21C forecast model, which is a high resolution dataset. Finally, this study also looks at the zonally varying state of the stratosphere to explore if inaccurate predictions of the stratospheric zonal-mean zonal wind can be explained through inaccurate predictions of the structure of the polar vortex and/or stratospheric high pressure systems such as the Aleutian High.

495246.title: From Risk to Resilience: An Accessible Framework for Assessing Physical Risk in the Built Environment
495246.authors: Taylor Ryan, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO; National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO; and K. Wegner Guilfoyle and L. Liu
495246.abstract: Natural hazards—such as flooding, wildfires, and hailstorms—have increasingly significant implications for financial and economic stability in U.S. homes, businesses, and communities. Hazards can damage buildings and critical building systems (e.g., heating, ventilating, and air-conditioning systems) and disrupt operations, which result in escalating costs over time if assets need to be repurchased or repaired. At the same time, there is a lack of accessible, transparent, and trusted data sources for assessing the financial impacts of physical risks in the built environment and identifying potential mitigation efforts. This gap creates significant challenges for commercial building owners (especially small asset owners), homeowners, tenants, and state and local governments, preventing stakeholders from making informed decisions and incentivizing and investing in resilience measures, such as hail-resistant roofs or wildfire defensible spaces. Investing in these measures could offer reduced insurance premiums, increase property resilience, and foster long-term weather hazard and economic stability for communities and insurance markets alike.This presentation will focus on findings from the Building Taxonomy research effort conducted by the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) to understand key challenges related to implementing building resilience investments. The research methodology was (1) assess data gaps in insurance and investment markets related to building science and resilience investments; (2) establish a conceptual “Building Taxonomy Framework” to bridge the gap by establishing data types, datasets, and financial outputs needed by commercial owners, homeowners, and insurance companies; (3) operationalize the Building Taxonomy Framework through the development of a platform concept and a singular use case prototype to validate the conceptual underpinnings; (4) validate the assumptions of the Building Taxonomy Framework through stakeholder interviews and market analysis; and (5) develop recommendations to inform decision-making by building owners, financiers, and insurance policy underwriters. The research identified key market failures hindering the current decision-making process, such as zero discounting of risks, lack of effective valuation mechanisms, asymmetry of information and timescales between stakeholders, and uncertainty in insurance. The research then addresses these market failures by developing key definitions and concepts, including: the Building Taxonomy framework that defines the level of building property risk assessment required to facilitate decision-making by commercial building owners, homeowners, and insurance companies; a concept for an online platform that combines high-quality data, building science, and integrated risk assessment approaches to identify natural hazard risks (e.g., flood, fire) for new and existing building properties and to evaluate risk mitigation strategies. The research found that tools that integrate building science data, weather hazards, and advanced risk quantification through financial modeling could incentivize broader adoption of building risk reduction strategies, strengthening market resilience and insurability across real estate markets and geographies. Such tools would also enable commercial building owners and homeowners to evaluate resilience investments that insurers recognize and reward. NLR will also present the second "phase" of this research effort, a collaboration with the insurance innovation non-profit InnSure, to develop the Building Taxonomy calculator. The calculator seeks to offer a minimum viable product (MVP) prototype to equip small asset owners, such as housing non-profits, small commercial operators, or a municipality's building stock, with information to answer practical questions like: Which building upgrades will reduce my risk, and by how much? Will performing building upgrades change what I pay for insurance, or whether I can get it at all? The development of this calculator is informed by findings of the first phase of the research effort and the "industry-led collaboration model" that establishes participation from all sectors- industry, research institutions, government, and other market actors. The second phase of research also includes partnerships with communities experiencing acute risk from natural hazards, including Massachusetts coastal communities, to "ground-truth" the calculator and establish working data pipelines for communities to provide feedback. This second phase puts the Building Taxonomy framework "into action". Through the integration of hazard data, building science, and financial modeling, this initiative enables stakeholders to quantitatively evaluate resilience strategies, unlocking pathways for new investments and products that address hazard-related risks. Based on stakeholder feedback, providing industry access to key datasets and vetted calculations will incentivize participation, foster buy-in, and close critical data gaps.

495247.title: Direct Numerical Simulations of Spume Production from Plunging Waves
495247.authors: Kaitao Tang, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom; and T. A. A. Adcock and W. Mostert
495247.abstract: The production of spume drops from the crests of ocean waves has long been considered to involve the direct action of wind on the crests of breaking waves. Here we study the phenomenon by conducting direct numerical simulations of wind blowing over waves which have been perturbed by small, high-wavenumber monochromatic perturbations. We solve the two-phase Navier-Stokes equations with surface tension, using both two- (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) configurations. First, in 2D simulations, a steep periodic wave is superimposed by an appropriate monochromatic perturbation wave. As the long wave approaches breaking, the perturbation wave undergoes explosive slope growth close to the crest of the long wave (see e.g. Maileybaev & Nachbin, 2019). The phenomenon can be reproduced in 3D simulations in the presence of turbulent winds and spanwise perturbations on the wave. In this case, the exploding perturbations can be inflated into bags (e.g. Troitskaya et al. 2017) and atomized by the wind above an appropriate threshold. In this talk, we will discuss the role of perturbation wavenumber and slope, effective inverse wave age, capillary and viscous effects, and pathways towards an appropriate parametrization describing spume drop production in complex open ocean conditions. References: Mailybaev & Nachbin (2019) J. Fluid Mech. 863, pp.876-892. Troitskaya, Kandaurov, Ermakova, Kozlov, Sergeev, Zilitinkevich (2017) Scientific Reports 7:1614.

495253.title: Assessment of the TEMPO Tropospheric NO2 Product for Local Air Quality Management in New York State
495253.authors: Shakirah Tahani Rogers, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY; and G. Huang
495253.abstract: This study investigates the potential use of TEMPO Tropospheric NO2 column density products to support local air quality management over the New York State area. The Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) mission is the first geostationary satellite instrument dedicated to hourly daytime air quality observations over North America. This study evaluates the TEMPO Level 2 Version 3 tropospheric nitrogen dioxide (NO2) product over New York State area (NY, CT, NJ, and PA) from March 1, 2023 to April 30, 2025. TEMPO tropospheric NO2 columns were compared with lower-tropospheric columns from thirteen Pandora spectrometer stations and correlated with in-situ surface NO2 concentrations from 31 EPA Air Quality System (AQS) monitors. TEMPO shows good overall agreement with Pandora, with a relative mean bias of 0.925 and an absolute bias of 0.1605, overestimating at low NO2 and underestimating at high NO2. Agreement degrades with increasing solar zenith angle and cloud fraction whereas biases are comparatively insensitive to hour of day and to planetary boundary layer height derived from High-Resolution Rapid Refresh meteorological fields. TEMPO columns are positively associated with AQS surface concentrations under quality-filtered conditions (TEMPO QF = 0, SZA < 75°, CF < 0.2, snow/ice fraction < 0.01, and AQS surface NO₂ > 0 ppb). These results support the use of hourly TEMPO NO2 observations for local-scale air quality assessment and management in New York State when scenes are appropriately filtered for solar geometry and cloud conditions.

495254.title: Interannual to Decadal Weather Hazard Forecasting for Operations Planning
495254.authors: Daniel B Kirk-Davidoff, EPRI, Washington, DC; and A. J. Newman, K. Sha, J. Lala, S. Alessandrini, S. G. Yeager, S. E. Haupt, D. Diaz, and C. A. Octaviano Villasana
495254.abstract: Reliable decadal forecast information for the next decade is needed for successful planning and operations of facilities exposed to extreme weather hazards. Progress in coupled climate model speed and resolution and in deep-learning based climate modeling promise to increase forecast skill and fidelity but this progress has not yet been systematically evaluated, used to produce easily accessible data, or paired with guidance for application in planning. In this work, we measure the skill of forecasting statistics of impactful weather 1 and 10 years in the future for the current state of the art. Using five test regions with installations of interest to the Department of War (Yuma Proving Ground, Fort Bragg, Pituffik Space Base, Fort Wainwright, and Naval Base Guam), we completed historical forecast operations and skill testing for statistical, coupled Earth System Model (ESM), and ML post-processed techniques. Statistical methods examined how weather statistics change with ENSO and other teleconnections; ESM work assessed ensemble CESM hindcasts globally and per site; and post-processing applied the Analog Ensemble (AnEn), EMOS, BMA, and regional AI-based downscaling. We identified a limited number of forecast settings and variables for which skill exists beyond one year. CESM has useful skill primarily for mean annual temperature across many leads, and temperature extremes at year-1 lead. Persistence forecasts of impactful weather events typically have little or no skill beyond the first year once trends are accounted for, while teleconnection-based forecasts perform slightly better. ML post-processing using the analog ensemble and other approaches generates improved statistics for multi-year forecasts, with CRPS improved for all sites at essentially all lead times, primarily through bias correction. Although deterministic skill beyond one year is never likely to be high, the generation of accurate simulations of many equally likely weather scenarios that correctly account for the changing statistics of climate due both to forced and unforced climate variability is an attainable goal.

495255.title: Rainfall Characteristics of Weakening Tropical Cyclones in the Northern Hemisphere
495255.authors: Kim Wood, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and A. Toms
495255.abstract: Increasing vertical wind shear and decreasing atmospheric moisture are known to induce tropical cyclone (TC) weakening, yet these environmental factors vary in magnitude and spatial coverage between the North Atlantic (ATL) and eastern North Pacific (ENP) despite over-ocean rapid weakening (RW) occurring in both basins. Dynamic factors (e.g., vertical wind shear) may be more conducive to ATL RW while thermodynamic factors (e.g., potential intensity) may be more conducive to ENP RW. However, the method by which shear is calculated may affect these observed relationships in addition to the size of the TCs that are undergoing RW. To assess the nature of these relationships beyond what can be provided by reanalysis fields, this study analyzes gridded rainfall data to capture TC structure. First, we compute vertical wind shear from ERA5 winds after removing the vortex following Davis et al. (2008), as we have found this approach more aggressively removes the TC vortex. We then evaluate rainfall using NASA’s Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM dataset (IMERG) within a motion-relative and shear-relative framework. We explore TCs from the IMERG era through the latest year available from the National Hurricane Center's best-track dataset (HURDAT2), which is 1998-2025. TCs from the western North Pacific (WNP) are added using best-track data from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center. We find that ENP TCs tend to retain a more symmetric rainfall structure as they approach RW onset and then begin rapidly weakening compared with ATL TCs which tend to gain asymmetry. Concurrently, convection in ATL TCs is strongly enhanced in the downshear left quadrant during RW in contrast to ENP TCs. Stronger shear for ATL cases likely contributes to this structural evolution. Based on spatial metrics computed for convective rain rates (e.g., Addington et al. 2025), ENP TCs are smaller than their ATL counterparts, which likely affects their weakening rate. Spatial metrics applied to cloud-top temperature thresholds exhibit a less distinct evolution, indicating the importance of rain rates in capturing convective intensity when exploring these storms that can span tropical and subtropical regions, with potential relevance to forecasting applications. If time allows, this presentation will also share findings from ERA5-based size metrics and evolutionary differences in rainfall extent and cloud-top temperature coverage relative to the TC diurnal cycle.

495259.title: Improving GBBEPx Trace Gas Emissions Through Harmonizing With Peatland Static Land Use Data and Dynamic Soil Moisture Datasets
495259.authors: Margaret Bruckner, NOAA CSL, Longmont, CO; and Q. Rasool, J. Romero-Alvarez, C. Lyu, P. C. Campbell, R. H. Schwantes, J. He, L. Zhang, R. Ahmadov, J. Schnell, and B. C. McDonald
495259.abstract: The Blended Global Biomass Burning Emissions Product (GBBEPx) from NOAA/NESDIS calculates daily aerosol and trace gas emissions by applying biomass conversion coefficients and emission factors to fire radiative power (FRP) retrievals. These factors are dependent on land cover classifications, although the operational GBBEPx omits peatland. This omission leads to underestimated CO and aerosol emissions for events such as the 2019 Indonesian and 2023 Canadian fires when significant peatland burning occurred, and results in inaccurate air quality forecasts. Within this project, we develop a workflow for incorporating peatland emissions into GBBEPx that harmonizes static peatland extent maps with dynamic soil moisture datasets, using soil dryness as a proxy for smoldering peat combustion susceptibility, to quantify the contribution of peat burning to detected fires daily.. Additionally, we apply peat-specific biomass conversion coefficients and trace gas emission factors. The resulting biomass burning emissions are tested within version 1 of NOAA’s Unified Forecast System with Chemistry (UFS-Chem) for May-September 1, 2023, capturing the period when Canadian wildfire smoke significantly impacted air quality in the Midwest and Northeast US. UFS-Chem simulations are evaluated against aircraft measurements from NOAA CSL’s AEROMMA (Atmospheric Emissions and Reactions Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas) field campaign, satellite retrievals of CO and aerosol optical depth (e.g., TROPOMI, VIIRS), and ground-based measurements. This work provides a pathway toward operational peat-aware fire emissions in NOAA's next-generation air quality forecasting.

495260.title: The Cascading Role of Topography in October 2015 South Carolina Extreme Precipitation and Flooding
495260.authors: Carolina Ann Bieri, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. A. Hence and J. M. Sepulveda
495260.abstract: In early October 2015, much of central and coastal South Carolina experienced extreme precipitation, with some areas reporting more than 20 inches of rain over a 5-day period. This resulted in widespread flooding and impacts on life and property, including 36 dam failures and 19 fatalities. The heavy precipitation was attributed to a combination of factors: a stationary front along the U.S. Atlantic coast, an upper-level low pressure area to the west, and abundant tropical moisture. Terrain modification experiments with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model were completed to ascertain the influence of the lower Appalachian Mountains on precipitation amount and spatial distribution during this event. These experiments involved an approach to artificially raise and lower terrain in the model, inducing shifts in precipitation in accordance with the altered flow regime. This research builds on this previous work by using meteorological forcing derived from the terrain modification experiments to drive WRF-Hydro simulations centered on South Carolina. We use a domain cutout of the National Water Model configuration of WRF-Hydro, which is used operationally for flood prediction. We carry out four simulations, utilizing meteorological forcing from the control WRF simulation (without terrain modification) as well as each of the terrain modification experiments. We compare WRF-Hydro streamflow output to observations and between experiments at United States Geological Survey (USGS) gauge locations in counties where dam failures were reported, including select sites upstream and downstream of failures. We find that discrepancies between observed and modeled streamflow from our control simulation also appear in the National Water Model CONUS retrospective dataset, signifying the challenge of modeling record-breaking precipitation events. Comparing between terrain modification experiments, we see there is not a consistent response among analysis sites. To explain this, we investigate the role of characteristics such as elevation, site type, and soil type. This work provides a multiscale overview of the hydrological implications of terrain modification experiments, considering not only large-scale changes in atmospheric variables such as precipitation, but also localized hydrologic impacts.

495263.title: Key Parameters Controlling initial Number Concentrations of Contrail Ice Particles: Development of Parameterizations for Global Applications
495263.authors: Fangqun Yu, SUNY, Albany, NY; and A. K. Khadka and G. Luo
495263.abstract: Aviation’s contribution to anthropogenic climate forcing is projected to grow substantially in the coming decades, with contrail cirrus clouds representing the largest single contribution, albeit with large uncertainty, to aviation’s net radiative forcing (RF). Global model simulations indicate that contrail RF is highly sensitive to initial number concentrations of contrail ice particles formed in the exhaust plume. As the industry pursues net-zero pathways through changes in fuel composition and the adoption of new engine technologies, a solid understanding of the physical processes and key parameters controlling the formation and number concentrations of contrail ice particles is critical for optimizing contrail-mitigation strategies. Here, we use an updated aerosol and contrail microphysics (ACM) model, previously validated against ECLIF and VOLCAN field measurements (Yu et al., doi:10.1021/acs.est.4c04340, 2024; Voigt et al., doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10286-0, 2026), to systematically investigate the dependence of initial contrail ice number concentrations on various factors, including the Schmidt–Appleman threshold temperature, the emission index and size of nonvolatile (soot) particles, fuel sulfur content, the emission index of low-volatility organic compounds, mixing processes, flight altitude, and the temperature, relative humidity, particle concentrations, and particle sizes of the ambient air. We show that volatile particles, formed through the nucleation and condensation of sulfuric acid and low-volatility organic compounds on chemi-ions produced during fuel combustion, generally dominate total particle number concentrations in the exhaust plume. These volatile particles can contribute significantly to contrail ice-particle formation and, consequently, RF under a variety of conditions, especially when the emission index of nonvolatile particles is lower, fuel sulfur content and/or low-volatility organic compound concentrations are higher, and ambient temperature is lower. The ACM model simulations also show that the coating of soot particles by condensable species enhances their activation and contribution to contrail ice particles under certain conditions. The contributions of nonvolatile and volatile particles to contrail ice formation and RF vary nonlinearly with many of the parameters mentioned above. To better capture the various factors influencing contrail properties and reduce uncertainties in contrail RF calculations, parameterizations in the form of multiple-variable lookup tables are developed and evaluated in (1) the Contrail Cirrus Prediction Model (CoCiP) (Schumann, doi:10.5194/gmd-5-543-2012, 2012) and (2) a Sectional Contrail Microphysics (SeCoM) model within the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SMv3). The impacts of the improved initial ice-number parameterizations on global contrail cirrus properties and RF, as well as their implications for contrail-mitigation strategies, will be discussed.

495264.title: Subseasonal Eastern North Pacific Tropical Cyclones in the S2S Models: Cluster Analysis and MJO Modulation
495264.authors: Tsung-Yung Lee, LDEO, Palisades, NY; and S. J. Camargo, C. Y. Lee, J. L. Garcia Franco, D. Kim, and E. D. Maloney
495264.abstract: This work investigates the probabilistic prediction of tropical cyclone (TC) genesis, track and precipitation in the Eastern North Pacific (ENP) in the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Subseasonal to Seasonal (S2S) Prediction Project database and the HURricane DATa 2nd generation (HURDAT2). Using cluster analysis, TCs in models and observations are categorized into 3 groups based on the geographical location of trajectories, especially by longitude. We identified three clusters: Cluster A: TC genesis close to the west coast of Central America; Cluster B: TC occurrence west of 110°W; and Cluster C with TCs forming west of 120°W, similar to previous observational analysis. Due to a westward bias in genesis location, some S2S models require an additional cluster (Cluster D: TCs occurrence west of 140°W) to describe the TC tracks, but there is no corresponding cluster in observations. We focus on the results of Cluster A since its high impact on the west coast of Central America. Cluster A shows a southeastward bias in genesis location, track pattern and accumulated TC precipitation distribution in most S2S models. The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) modulates the TC genesis in most clusters in the S2S models, while a statistically significant modulation is only present in cluster A in observations. A precipitation enhancement during MJO phases 8+1 and suppression during phases 4+5 are present for the total precipitation and TC precipitation associated with Cluster A in both observations and most of the S2S models. We are currently investigating the TC landfall rate and the MJO modulation of extreme precipitation in the S2S models. Key words: tropical cyclone, eastern North Pacific, MJO, cluster analysis, precipitation

495265.title: State of the Unified Forecast System (UFS) Subteams
495265.authors: Abigail Smith, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. E. Ten Hoeve III, K. Garrett, E. Myers, J. Vogt, and M. Huang
495265.abstract: The Unified Forecast System (UFS) modeling framework and its development community are experiencing high-stakes opportunities and challenges, and the community subteams of the NOAA Modeling Decision Board, established by the new UFS governance framework, will be a driving force of future innovation. Here we present an overview of these technical subteams and their evolution under the new governance structure. We highlight UFS subteam achievements, priorities, goals and current/anticipated issues. We describe the ways in which the subteams collaborate and communicate, emphasizing current opportunities for community involvement. We also outline common characteristics of groups that have experienced success in navigating the transitions between research and operations, including obstacles faced and lessons learned. Through these topics, we demonstrate the ways in which community members are progressing the strategic goals of the UFS. This presentation will be relevant to UFS users and developers seeking perspective on the broader community and how to make the most of their subteam participation, as well as those who are interested in the UFS and seeking entry points for engagement.

495268.title: Climate Whiplash Amplifies the Damages and Economic Consequences of U.S. Storm Events
495268.authors: Bailey Magers, City University of New York, New York, NY; The City College of New York, New York, NY; and J. F. Booth and N. Devineni
495268.abstract: Mechanisms by which climate, hydrological, and weather “whiplash”—rapid transitions between extreme dry and wet regimes—may amplify reported economic losses beyond individual hazards are documented, but quantitative evidence remains limited. Here, we combine NOAA Storm Events, local climate anomalies, and drought and climate-mode indices within a hidden Markov model to identify latent climate regimes and their rapid transitions across the contiguous United States from 1996–2025. Results show whiplash was rare, occurring in 0.8% of state-months and primarily in the western half of the United States. Dry-to-wet transitions were more common than wet-to-dry transitions, but both showed a significant increase in frequency over the last 30 years when aggregated nationally. Storm events during whiplash months produced more reported economic losses, on average, than comparable non-whiplash events, accruing $2.4 billion in total excess direct damages. The most damaging whiplash events by total excess losses include whiplash floods in the southwest and west, whiplash droughts in the south, and whiplash wildfires in the northwest. Whiplash exposure was also associated with economic disruptions. High-income counties experienced short-term earnings and income increases after whiplash events, but both significantly declined compared to expected growth 3 years after the events. Meanwhile, low-income counties experienced no significant changes to earnings but did show below expected income growth 1 year after whiplash events, followed by significantly increased transfer payments 2 years after the event, which seemingly stabilized income. These results associate whiplash with meaningful immediate economic losses and delayed economic disruption beyond typical storm events. However, the results here are observational and at broad spatial scales, highlighting the limitations of current datasets defining storm events and their related loss reporting.

495270.title: FEMA Phase-Out? Hyperclustered Storms Pose Risks to Decentralization of U.S. Flood Insurance (Invited)
495270.authors: Adam Nayak, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ
495270.abstract: The U.S. National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) faces growing solvency and affordability challenges amid proposals to decentralize FEMA and shift disaster management to states. Catastrophic floods often span state boundaries, exposing multiple decentralized insurance pools simultaneously. Using a path-independent simulation framework that integrates risk-based premiums, hydrometeorologically-clustered flood losses, and 2025 reinsurance contracts, we evaluate the stability of national and state-level pooling using historical data. In tandem, we assess tradeoffs for combinations of sub-national state pools using a novel multi-objective direct policy search framework across insurance pooling objectives. National pooling markedly reduces systemic insolvency through cross-regional diversification, while many state pools exhibit structural fragility. State-level deficits are dominated by hyperclusters—coherent spatiotemporal losses induced by common atmospheric drivers—indicating that correlated loss governs failure. Since states must balance budgets and face borrowing restrictions to cover large losses, pool liquidity constrains decentralized systems. Existing reinsurance (including insurance-linked securities) offers limited buffering due to its misalignment with the clustered, spatiotemporal nature of hydroclimatic risk, covering only single flood events in traditional contracts and individual named storms in FloodSmart catastrophe bonds. A resilient and affordable NFIP will require hybrid financial design aligning risk-based premiums and reinsurance to balance chronic and catastrophic risk.

495271.title: Extending Monin–Obukhov Similarity Theory with Turbulence Anisotropy in a High Resolution Large-Eddy Simulation Model
495271.authors: Benjamin Mark Udina, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and I. Stiperski and M. Calaf
495271.abstract: Monin–Obukhov similarity theory (MOST) remains the standard framework for representing turbulent exchanges of momentum, heat, and other scalars between the land surface and the atmosphere. Its widespread use in surface-layer parameterizations makes it a central component of numerical weather prediction and climate models. However, MOST is fundamentally based on assumptions of flat, horizontally homogeneous surfaces and stationary flow, conditions that are frequently violated over real-world surfaces. In these environments, departures from classical similarity relationships limit the reliability of conventional MOST formulations. A number of corrections and alternative parameterizations have been proposed for specific applications, but developing a framework that can accommodate a broad range of surface conditions remains an open challenge. Recent work has identified turbulence anisotropy as a potential additional non-dimensional variable capable of extending similarity theory beyond its traditional range of validity. In particular, generalized formulations for velocity variances and flux–gradient relationships have been proposed that incorporate the turbulence anisotropy invariant yB. Here, we take a further step toward the practical implementation of these anisotropy-dependent similarity relationships within the surface module of a high-resolution large-eddy simulation (LES) model. The anisotropy invariant yB is diagnosed on-the-fly from locally Lagrangian time-averaged Reynolds stresses. We test the implementation across a set of numerical experiments spanning different flow and surface conditions and examine its influence on the modeled surface-layer turbulence and associated fluxes. These simulations provide an initial assessment of the feasibility of incorporating turbulence anisotropy directly into surface-layer parameterizations and represent a step toward more general formulations capable of describing turbulent exchange over both idealized and complex surfaces.

495274.title: From Kite Soundings to Digital Archives: 140 Years of Data Stewardship at Blue Hill Observatory
495274.authors: Robert W. W. Maxson, GYRE LLC, Harrisonville, MO; and A. Joly, C. Cummings, and A. Evans
495274.abstract: Blue Hill Observatory (BHO), located on Great Blue Hill near Boston, Massachusetts, has maintained an essentially continuous series of daily weather observations since February 1, 1885. The longevity and scientific value of this record depend not simply on its duration, but on the Observatory’s long-standing commitment to consistent observing practices, careful documentation, and continuity through changes in instruments, observers, technology, and institutional stewardship. Founded by Abbott Lawrence Rotch in 1885, BHO quickly became a center for meteorological observation and innovation. Early work included the world’s first kite-based atmospheric sounding in 1894 and subsequent pioneering upper-air observations. At the same time, routine surface observations established the foundation of the long-term climate record that continues today. Several historic observing instruments and methods have remained in use for exceptionally long periods, while newer technologies have been introduced alongside them. Maintaining continuity across these transitions illustrates a challenge common to long-term observing systems: how to modernize observations and data access without compromising the consistency and comparability that give a historical record its scientific value. BHO’s institutional history presents a related stewardship challenge. Responsibility for the Observatory and its observing program has passed through multiple organizations since its founding, requiring successive generations of observers and partners to preserve the continuity of the record while adapting to changing scientific, operational, and financial circumstances. Recognition as a National Historic Landmark and a World Meteorological Organization Centennial Observing Station reflects the significance of this sustained observational commitment. However, institutional recognition alone does not solve the ongoing sustainability problem: as federal science funding contracts, the daily cost of keeping observations running increasingly falls to BHO's community-supported model, a tension we discuss candidly. Today, one of BHO’s major challenges is preserving and improving access to the historical observations themselves. More than a century of daily observations remains documented in handwritten records and other historical formats. Ongoing preservation and digitization efforts seek to safeguard these original records while improving the accessibility, documentation, quality control, and usability of the resulting datasets for future research. The process also highlights practical challenges associated with historical data rescue, including the interpretation of changing observing practices, instrument histories, metadata, and quality-control decisions across generations. At BHO, stewardship of the observational record extends beyond preservation and digitization to education. Through field trips, classroom programs, summer meteorology programs, and other outreach, students engage directly with meteorological observations, historic instruments, and the practices used to maintain a long-term climate record. These programs connect contemporary STEM education with BHO’s continuing observational mission, helping students understand not only how weather data are collected, but why consistency, documentation, and long-term observations matter. In this way, stewardship includes both preserving the record itself and passing forward the knowledge and practices necessary to understand and use it. The continuing scientific use of BHO observations demonstrates why this stewardship matters. Long-term records of temperature, precipitation, wind, sunshine, and other parameters provide opportunities to investigate environmental changes occurring over decades or longer; signals that shorter observational records may not adequately capture. Drawing on more than 140 years of observing experience, this presentation examines both the successes and unresolved challenges of maintaining a long-term meteorological record. BHO offers a case study in how continuity, documentation, institutional memory, historical preservation, modernization and funding continuity must work together to ensure that observations collected for one generation remain scientifically useful to the next.

495275.title: The Role of Quasi-Geostrophic Subsidence on the Onset of Moist Tropical Heat Waves
495275.authors: Sofia Avila Nevarez, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and Á. F. Adames-Corraliza
495275.abstract: Recent work has found that moist tropical heat waves (HWs) are a result of large-scale subsidence induced by atmospheric motions not in weak temperature gradient balance. This result leads us to hypothesize that quasi-geostrophic (QG) motions may be responsible for the development of many moist tropical HWs. To examine this, we compute the QG omega equation and focus on regions in the tropics that frequently experience moist heat waves. We find that QG forcing is evident in the days prior and after the onset of the HW, with both differential vorticity advection and the Laplacian of temperature advection playing non-negligible roles in their contribution to the vertical velocity. The importance of QG descent will be examined in the tropical regions identified.

495276.title: AI Ethics and Science Data Stewardship
495276.authors: Gerald J. Mulvey, Nighthawk Weather, San Antonio, TX
495276.abstract: “Data has become a high-value, high-risk asset tied directly to performance, regulatory compliance and organizational reputation”. High-quality traceable training data is required for high-quality solutions that meet the rigors of science. The system Data Curator exercises stewardship tasks including data lineage documentation, data cataloging, and data quality management. A second part of stewardship of the AI training data is data security. The training sets may contain private, restricted, company propriety, dual use, patten, copyright and government data as well as open data. Each of these data types may have different access control and storage requirements. The role of the Data Curator in the world of Artificial Intelligence is one focal point to ensure ethical design, development and operation of AI tools. Data primarily enters scientific AI tools during three phases. Foundational phase data is used to establish general basic functionality of the tool during development. Enterprise specific data enters the model during the adaption phase during which the foundational tool is adapted to a specific task or scope area. Finally, during operational phase, data enters the tool through continuing self-learning. expansion. This presentation will discuss the ethical responsibilities associated with data stewardship across the design, development and operations of AI tools focused on science for all people. Transform your data into an AI engine: The data foundation for trusted, scalable AI, 2026, https://www.sas.com/content/dam/sasdam/documents/20260302/transform-your-data-into-an-ai-engine.pdf

495278.title: Evaluating and Updating the Microburst Composite for Gulf Coast CWAs
495278.abstract: Microbursts are localized downdrafts that produce strong surface winds with the potential to have significant impacts on property and public safety. These events are difficult to forecast, particularly in the Southeastern United States and the Gulf Coast, where the region’s unique environment and atmospheric conditions pose challenges for current forecasting tools. This project builds on the current Microburst Composite Parameter and develops a different approach to more accurately predict downbursts in moist tropical convective environments using a probabilistic framework. The dataset consists of quality-controlled warm-season severe wind reports and null cases for the northern Gulf Coast CWAs (County Warning Areas). Environmental variables are calculated from RAP model soundings using model analysis programs such as SHARPpy and MetPy. The variables will be integrated into a logistic model that outputs a calibrated probability and a 0–10 MCP index. The model is compared to the current composite using AUC (Area Under the Curve), Brier score, and other reliability metrics. Statistical analysis indicates that the Gulf Coast Refined Parameter can better distinguish between wind report and null cases than the current parameter, achieving an AUC of 0.892 compared to 0.773. The results will be documented for further analysis and forecasting applications.

495279.title: How Important Are Equatorial Orbit Radio Occultation Observations, As Quantified By Data Denial Experiments of COSMIC-2 Data In GFS?
495279.authors: Agnes Lim, CIMSS, MADISON, WI; and S. E. Nebuda and Z. Li
495279.abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System radio occultation (GNSS-RO) observations have become a cornerstone of modern numerical weather prediction (NWP). By measuring the bending of radio signals as they pass through the atmosphere, GNSS-RO provides highly accurate, vertically resolved profiles of temperature, pressure, and moisture under nearly all-weather conditions. These observations are globally distributed, bias-resistant, and stable over time, making them particularly valuable for constraining model analyses in data-sparse regions such as the oceans and polar areas. Their consistent quality improves the representation of atmospheric structure in NWP systems, leading to more reliable initial conditions and, ultimately, more skillful weather forecasts across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. The FORMOSAT-7/COSMIC-2 provides highly accurate atmospheric profiles using GNSS radio occultation, delivering temperature, pressure, and moisture data with low bias for NWP. These observations significantly improve forecast accuracy, especially in tropical regions and during severe weather events. However, COSMIC-2 mission has passed its design life. While it remains operational, it is expected to degrade in coming years. The data quality degradation and eventual loss of COSMIC-2 would create a major observational gap in the global observing system, especially in the tropics, reducing forecast skill and weakening one of the most accurate and operationally impactful atmospheric sounding datasets available to NWP. The incremental value of each satellite will be quantified through successive single-satellite denial experiments, providing insight into the forecast sensitivity to constellation composition.

495286.title: Evaluating Giant Sea Salt Aerosol Transport in the Air-Sea Transition Zone; an In Situ and LES Comparison
495286.authors: Katherine L. Ackerman, Univ. of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, HI
495286.abstract: Sea salt aerosol (SSA) are produced at the ocean surface across several orders of magnitude in particle size, but the fraction of emitted particles that are transported from the near-surface layer into the well-mixed marine boundary layer remains poorly constrained. For Aitken- and accumulation-mode particles, gravitational settling is negligible relative to turbulent transport, allowing emitted particles to be efficiently mixed away from the surface. Giant sea salt aerosol (GSSA), however, have appreciable gravitational settling velocities that may compete with the relatively weak turbulent updrafts characteristic of the near-surface marine environment. Consequently, only a fraction of emitted GSSA may reach the mixed layer, with this fraction strongly dependent on particle size and near-surface turbulence. Here, in situ vertical profiles of GSSA size distributions are compared with particle transport simulated using large-eddy simulations (LES) in Cloud Model 1 (CM1) coupled to Lagrangian particle trajectories. Simulations spanning resolved and parameterized subgrid-scale turbulence regimes are used to quantify the size-dependent efficiency of particle transport from the ocean surface into the marine boundary layer and evaluate modeled vertical distributions against observations. These results characterize the ability of LES to reproduce observed GSSA transport and identify limitations associated with the representation of near-surface turbulent mixing. More broadly, this work evaluates the extent to which sea salt production at the ocean surface can be assumed to translate directly into aerosol concentrations aloft, particularly for the largest sea salt particles.

495288.title: Sparse Identification of Non-Linear Dynamical and Microphysical Processes In Precipitating Clouds
495288.authors: Samson M. Hagos, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA; and A. Varble, PhD, Z. Feng, and S. L. Tai
495288.abstract: Accurately representing cloud dynamical and microphysical processes in convection permitting Earth System Models remains a major challenge. Traditional cloud microphysics parameterizations in these models are often complex, manually tuned, and struggle to generalize across diverse meteorological regimes and geographical regions. In this work we present a novel framework aimed at discovering minimalist, fundamental governing laws for dynamic and microphysical evolution directly from observations. Leveraging the Sparse Identification of Non-linear Dynamics (SINDy) algorithm, we aim to identify the underlying differential equations that drive precipitation radar reflectivity evolution. Our approach utilizes extensive, aligned datasets that combine high-resolution model output from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model with observations from the C-Band Scanning ARM Precipitation Radar (CSAPR). By formulating dynamic and microphysical forcing as a sparse regression problem, we solve for the 3D radar reflectivity rate of change within a Lagrangian-constrained framework. We evaluate a library of 14 physically relevant terms, including advection, diffusion, condensation/evaporation proxies, and non-linear sedimentation power laws. The SINDy algorithm then prunes non-essential terms, revealing the most parsimonious mathematical structure that governs storm evolution. The roles of these processes in the lifecycle of the convective cloud systems and effects on precipitation under various atmospheric conditions will be discussed.

495290.title: Observational Data Impacts on the NASA GEOS-S2S-3 Model Analysis of the Ocean
495290.authors: Lindsay Noelle Chu, GMAO, Glenn Dale, MD; UMD ESSIC, College Park, MD; and A. Jersild and A. Molod
495290.abstract: Accurate prediction of large-scale climate processes relies on the quality of initial conditions generated through ocean reanalysis, and the assimilation of observational data into coupled ocean-atmosphere models. As ocean observing networks face increasing funding pressures, quantifying their distinct contributions to model accuracy becomes essential for informing future decision-making. However, the impacts of individual observation networks vary geographically and throughout the vertical ocean column. In order to understand how the roles and behaviors of observational data networks change across different regions of the world’s oceans, a series of Observing System Experiments (OSEs) were conducted within the NASA GEOS Sub-seasonal to Seasonal Version 3 (GEOS-S2S-3) forecasting system. To isolate the impacts of individual observation networks on the model’s ocean reanalysis, each OSE run excluded a different set of observing systems. All experimental OSE runs were evaluated for accuracy against a Control run, across a set of ocean variables (e.g., thermocline depth, subsurface salinity, heat content, etc.) and oceanic regions. Initial findings highlight the distinct impacts of Argo float data on resolving model analysis of the thermocline, eddy kinetic energy, and other subsurface variables, while altimetry data demonstrates impacts on constraining both subsurface and surface variables on a regional scale. Ultimately, this analysis demonstrates the necessity of observing systems in constraining prediction and analysis of ocean variables used for forecasting larger-scale weather and climate processes. It offers a systematic evaluation of observing system impacts for applications in broader society, and highlights the continued maintenance of such systems as an essential component of effective decision-making and global climate resilience.

495298.title: Evaluating Mesoscale Processes of Extreme Rainfall Using Idealized Numerical Simulations
495298.authors: Anastasia Joy Tomanek, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and R. S. Schumacher
495298.abstract: Understanding mesoscale processes and ingredients that lead to extreme precipitation is imperative for advancing numerical weather prediction and operational forecasting of these events. This knowledge motivated forecast analyses and observation comparisons from 26–28 March 2025 over the Texas Rio Grande Valley, where significant flash flooding was observed in Cameron County following prolonged rainfall that led to accumulations of up to 472 mm. Nocturnal Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) and Quasi-Linear Convective System (QLCS) evolution during the event informed idealized Cloud Model 1 experiments that sought to identify environmental conditions that maximized rainfall. Simulations used observed soundings as input from the National Weather Service in Brownsville, TX before and during the event. Expansive upscale growth, more intense rain rates, and notably higher surface accumulations resulted from the environment with ample 0–6-km shear. Additional tests perturb low-level moisture, shear, and other ingredients influenced by the low-level jet directed onshore from The Gulf over the identified area of isentropic moisture flux to exemplify their impacts on extreme-rain-producing MCS processes. Though processes and ingredients may align when applied to other cases, discrepancies are expected for events that occur in different climate regions or seasons. Accordingly, this work constructs a framework through which ingredients can be correlated between high-precipitation events.

495299.title: Regional Sensitivity of Tropical Deep Convection to a Future Climate Scenario
495299.authors: Quinlan Richard Mulhern, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and J. M. Peters
495299.abstract: Tropical deep convection plays a significant role in driving the climate system, and understanding of such convective processes is crucial for modeling both present and future climate impacts.
