Model output from CMIP6 simulations show increases in CAPE and alterations of vertical wind shear in tropical regions around the Earth. Background changes to these tropical environments may yield alterations to convective properties and impacts. This work investigates the effects of CAPE and shear changes on deep tropical convection in multiple tropical regions, including the Amazon, Sahel, and tropical Western Pacific. Using future projections from the CESM2 climate model, comparisons of historical (2000-2014) and late-century (2085-2100) high-CAPE environments were made for each of the tropical regions. For all regions, CAPE was larger in the late-century period, while shear changes were region-dependent. Composite soundings were gathered from each model period and were used to initialize large-eddy simulations in CM1. In regions with lower shear magnitudes, such as the Amazon and Western Pacific, single cell convection was dominant in the simulations. Despite large increases in CAPE and minimal changes in shear in these regions in the late-century simulations, updrafts and downdrafts were comparable in strength to those in the historical climate. However, with similar environmental changes found in the Sahel, where larger shear magnitudes are already present in the vicinity of the African Easterly Jet, the strength of convective updrafts increased. Downdrafts and cold pools associated with future Sahel mesoscale convective systems were stronger as well. Such differences in response between the unorganized convection of the Amazon and Western Pacific and the organized convection in the Sahel can likely be attributed to the larger magnitude of entrainment-driven dilution in the future climate, with narrow, unorganized updrafts more susceptible to detrimental effects compared to wider, more organized convection.

495302.title: Nitrate Substitution Alters the Fate of Monoterpene Alkoxy Radicals: An Experimental and Theoretical Study.
495302.authors: Anna Novelli, Forschungszentrum Jülich, Jülich, NW, Germany; and L. Vereecken, M. Färber, J. Fry, G. I. Gkatzelis, A. Grasse, E. Y. Pfannerstill, M. Riva, F. Rohrer, R. Wegener, A. Wahner, and H. Fuchs
495302.abstract: Despite its central role as a night-time oxidant, NO3-initiated chemistry has received comparatively little attention relative to OH-initiated pathways, leaving the degradation mechanisms of biogenic volatile organic compounds considerably less constrained. This gap is particularly consequential for monoterpenes such as α-pinene, β-pinene, and limonene, which are emitted in large quantities from forested regions and which react rapidly with NO3 after sunset. While mechanistic parallels exist between OH- and NO3-initiated oxidation, the literature suggests that nitrate substituents exert a distinct influence on the kinetics of the resulting peroxy (RO2) and alkoxy (RO) radicals compared to their hydroxy-substituted analogues — an effect that remains poorly quantified for the structurally complex, often cyclic, radical intermediates formed from monoterpene oxidation. This study investigates the chemistry of nitrate-substituted alkoxy radicals (nitrate-RO) derived from α-pinene, β-pinene, and limonene, combining experimental, theoretical, and modeling approaches. The theoretical component comprises quantum chemical and theoretical kinetic calculations targeting the ring-retaining and ring-opening decomposition and isomerization pathways characteristic of these monoterpene-derived alkoxy radicals, with results benchmarked against existing structure–activity relationship (SAR) predictions to refine SAR performance for cyclic and bicyclic systems. Complementary chamber experiments in SAPHIR at Forschungszentrum Jülich, Germany, together with box-model simulations, constrain the relative importance of unimolecular decomposition versus isomerization for the nitrate-RO derived from each monoterpene. These results are further used to assess implications for LIF-based detection of monoterpene-derived nitrated RO2 in the atmosphere, and to evaluate the broader impact of these reactions on the night-time degradation of biogenic VOCs.

495306.title: A High-Resolution Hydrodynamic Modeling Framework for Probabilistic Flood-Hazard Mapping: A Case Study for the Upper Tennessee River Basin
495306.authors: Sudershan Gangrade, ORNL, Oak Ridge, TN; ORNL, Oak Ridge, TN; and S. C. Kao, G. R. Ghimire, and M. Morales-Hernández
495306.abstract: High-resolution flood inundation mapping is increasingly important for regional flood-hazard assessment and infrastructure planning. Regulatory flood maps typically depict deterministic flood extents for selected annual exceedance probabilities (AEPs), providing limited characterization of uncertainties, including the spatially variability in flood probability, extent, and depth. We present a hierarchical modeling framework that integrates the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) hydrologic model with the GPU-accelerated, physics-based Two-dimensional Runoff Inundation Toolkit for Operational Needs (TRITON; https://triton.ornl.gov/) hydrodynamic inundation model to generate consistent, high-resolution probabilistic flood-inundation maps over large spatial domains. The framework is demonstrated for the Upper Tennessee River basin (HUC 0601). A historical hindcast inundation database for 1980–2019 is developed using Daymet-driven VIC-TRITON simulations and used to assess model performance. The framework is then applied using an ensemble of downscaled and bias-corrected meteorological forcings derived from multi-model Coupled Model Intercomparison Project – Phase 6 (CMIP6) projections. For each ensemble member, annual maximum flood events are selected based on VIC-simulated runoff over HUC 0601 and simulated with TRITON to generate high-resolution flood-depth and inundation-extent maps for baseline and future periods. Grid-cell-level flood-frequency analysis is applied to these event ensembles to estimate inundation associated with 1% and 0.2% AEPs, corresponding to 100- and 500-year return periods, respectively. These estimates are then compared with FEMA flood-hazard maps to assess differences in several aspects, including spatial agreement, mapped flood extent, and the availability of regulatory flood information across the basin. Simulations at 10- and 30-m spatial resolution are also compared to assess the sensitivity of derived flood-hazard patterns to model resolution. The resulting products characterize multiple characteristics of flood hazard, including inundation probability, flood-depth exceedance frequency, and maximum simulated flood depth. Together, they provide a scalable approach for generating high-resolution probabilistic flood-hazard information to support regional hazard assessment, infrastructure planning, and related applications.

495309.title: Snow, Rain, and Atmospheric Rivers in the Greenland-North Atlantic Region from 15 years of CloudSat Observations
495309.authors: Alanna Emma Wedum, University of Michigan, Ypsilanti, MI; University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI; and C. Pettersen, H. Guy, M. D. Shupe, K. S. Mattingly, T. S. L'Ecuyer, M. Mateling, and R. Bennartz
495309.abstract: Atmospheric rivers are long corridors of enhanced horizontal water vapor transport that are critical in moving moisture into the Arctic. The presented work uses CloudSat precipitation observations and retrievals from 2006-2020 to demonstrate and quantify how atmospheric rivers that reach the Greenland Ice Sheet accumulation zone impact the frequency, intensity, and phase of precipitation over the Greenland-North Atlantic region. We find that atmospheric rivers coincide with decreased snowfall frequency over the ocean and increased snowfall frequency over the ice sheet. Atmospheric river snowfall rates are enhanced over both ocean and the ice sheet, with the largest increases, an additional 0.32 to 1.2 mm hr—1, occurring over the accumulation zone of the Greenland Ice Sheet. Atmospheric rivers lead to an increase in the occurrence of rain over the region. We find that the rain-snow temperature threshold shifts poleward during atmospheric rivers in the area southwest of Greenland. Additionally, atmospheric rivers coincide with 30-50% of all rainfall occurrence, yet are present less than 10% of the time during the 15 year period. Although atmospheric rivers can efficiently produce snowfall within the accumulation zone, the associated warming and potential to produce rain mean that their effects on surface mass balance may not be uniformly positive.

495311.title: The Impact of Smart Autonomous Glider Sampling on Hurricane Intensity Forecasting
495311.authors: Alejandro Alvaro, Florida Atlantic University, Boca Raton, FL; NRL, Stennis Space Center, MS 39529 Balch Blvd, Stennis Space Center, MS; and A. W. Lawrence, C. Barron, J. Osborne, and P. Mukherjee
495311.abstract: The socio-economic and humanitarian impact of tropical cyclones, such as hurricanes, can be tied to the accuracy of storm intensity predictions. While track forecasting has steadily improved over the past several decades, predicting rapid intensification (RI) remains a critical operational challenge. Inaccurate intensity forecasts directly compromise public safety. A storm that intensifies faster than anticipated deprives communities of the 24-to-48-hour window needed to issue and receive effective evacuation orders, secure critical infrastructure, and plan a proper disaster response. On the other hand, over-predicting intensity can be costly, straining individual and governmental budgets. Therefore, accurate forecasting of Tropical Cyclone Heat Potential (TCHP) along a cyclone’s path is a fundamental necessity in the prediction of rapid intensification of tropical cyclones. When a tropical cyclone propagates over bodies of water, regions characterized by a deep 26°C isotherm or riverine-derived freshwater barrier layers resist upwelling-induced cooling, thereby sustaining the massive air-sea enthalpy fluxes required for rapid storm intensification. Collecting observations for use in assimilative ocean modelling produces ocean forecasts more true to the ocean state. Traditional observation infrastructure has limitations based on operational costs and platform capabilities. For example, manned research vessels are expensive to operate and dangerous to operate in proximity to intense storms. Floats are passive, slow-moving, uncontrolled, and rarely drift into specific Areas of Interest (AOI). While underwater gliders offer a compromise on these above issues, they remain labor-intensive to pilot and thus expensive to deploy at scale. This study seeks to demonstrate that adaptive sampling directly improves the representation of two critical thermodynamic metrics, TCHP and the depth of the 26°C isotherm, when compared to traditional geographically motivated sampling in assimilative ocean modeling. We test and evaluate glider guidance capabilities using GHOST (Guidance for Heterogenous Observing Systems Technology) within an Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) framework, examining the ocean conditions that supported the rapid intensification of Hurricane Ida. The forward ocean model used in this study is the Navy Coastal Ocean Model (NCOM). The data assimilation utilizes a 3DVAR technique as implemented in the Navy Coupled Ocean Data Assimilation (NCODA) system. We utilize NCODA to assimilate simulated profiles collected by gliders in the OSSE and quantify the accuracy improvement of TCHP and the depth of the 26°C isotherm in the ocean forecast model. OSSEs using adaptive sampling and geographically motivated guidance are compared against a high-resolution Nature Run. GHOST produces glider guidance by evaluating potential paths against a two-dimensional (longitude-latitude) “reward function” and selecting the best path. When gliders are in close proximity (~Rossby radius of deformation, 10-50 km in the Gulf of Mexico depending on bottom depth and ocean stratification), glider team behavior is accounted for to maximize the spatial coverage of assimilated glider data. Here, the reward is based on uncertainty in TCHP, derived from ocean model forecast uncertainty in temperature, which is updated with daily assimilation cycles. This allows GHOST to generate glider guidance in a way that reduces the number of redundant observations and maximizes the observation’s impact on the ocean forecasting model. Transitioning ocean observation networks from static or geographically motivated systems into intelligent, adaptive sensing arrays impacts the forecasting capabilities of operational oceanography systems allowing for more accurate ocean forecasting models, and uncertainty-driven autonomous navigation provides a scalable foundation for collecting real world data to where observations have the most impact on the ocean forecast.

495312.title: The AMS Certified Climate Science Professional (CCSP) Program: Establishing a Credential for Applied Climate Practice
495312.authors: Brian V. Smoliak, Weathervane, Minneapolis, MN; and P. Pasteris, N. Oakley, A. J. Hoell, K. O. Asante, E. L. Mecray, and I. Durre
495312.abstract: As climate science and future projections become mainstream inputs to infrastructure design, water resource planning, agriculture, public health, energy systems, and finance, demand has grown for professionals who can translate climate data into defensible, decision-relevant analysis. However, growing demand alone does not guarantee qualified professionals will meet it: anyone can claim climate expertise, and without a shared standard or maintained credential, clients have no reliable way to distinguish sound analysis from overconfident guesswork. Recognizing this, a group of AMS members proposed a new certification. This led to discussions within the community and AMS leadership, the establishment of an ad-hoc committee to develop the program, and now with AMS Council approval, the Certified Climate Science Professional (CCSP) program administered by the inaugural Board of CCSPs. The CCSP program targets scientists and engineers with at least five years of applied experience working at the intersection of climate science and practice, including climate risk consultants, water resource and geotechnical engineers, agricultural and public health climatologists, energy-sector forecasters, and other practitioners who need a portable, third-party credential attesting to both technical competence and communication skill. This presentation introduces the CCSP opportunity for applied climatologists and delves into CCSP's two-stage evaluation process: (1) a written examination (drawn from a question pool spanning historical climatology, water resources, drought, infrastructure, agriculture, health, energy, and climate change analysis, among others) paired with an original climate science essay scored on scientific accuracy, evidentiary reasoning, and clarity for non-technical audiences; followed by (2) an oral examination before a Board panel addressing the submitted essay, professional ethics, and weak areas in the written exam. We will outline the certification, renewal, and continuing-education requirements, as well as the Board's governance and conflict-of-interest safeguards. We invite discussion from the applied climatology community regarding credentialing standards, potential reciprocity with adjacent certifications like Certified Consulting Meteorologist (CCM), and how a CCSP designation might be leveraged by non-science professionals evaluating climate expertise for their organization.

495313.title: Evaluating Numerical Weather Prediction Improvements Using Simulated Honeywell HALAS LiDAR Observations: OSSE Results and CRADA Recommendations
495313.authors: Erik Horak, Honeywell Aerospace, Plymouth, MN
495313.abstract: In this presentation, we will explore the emerging role of lidar-based upper atmospheric observations in enhancing the quality of numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts, particularly through insights gained from a collaborative study between Honeywell and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). As part of our Cooperative Research and Development Agreement (CRADA), we are conducting Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) to assess how strategic locations and observing frequency of Honeywell's HALAS lidar observation network can improve the forecasting capabilities of the National Weather Service (NWS). The general OSSE process will be introduced with emphasis on resultant improvement to forecast skill. The outcomes of these experiments will be described, along with actionable recommendations on the integration of widespread LiDAR observations into the observing network, ultimately aiming to optimize weather prediction and response strategies.

495314.title: Direct Assimilation of Radar Reflectivity in Latent Space within CADRE MPAS-JEDI Data Assimilation System
495314.authors: Yongming Wang, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; CADRE, Norman, OK; and X. Wang
495314.abstract: Ensemble-based data assimilation (DA) is widely used for direct radar reflectivity assimilation because it provides a practical framework for estimating and applying flow-dependent background error covariances (BECs), which represent the evolving multivariate relationships among atmospheric variables. However, the quality of ensemble-derived BECs is strongly influenced by sampling errors and deficiencies in representing model uncertainties. To mitigate these limitations, considerable efforts have focused on improving BEC estimation and modulation, including adaptive ensemble spread inflation (e.g., Wang and Wang 2023a) and scale- and variable-dependent localization (e.g., Wang and Wang 2023b, 2024). Nevertheless, these approaches rely on empirical assumptions and parameter tuning, which can introduce additional complexity and require substantial computational effort to achieve optimal performance. Recent studies (e.g., Fan et al. 2026) have demonstrated the potential of latent data assimilation (LDA) to reduce dependence on explicitly estimated BECs by transforming atmospheric states into a latent space that preserves essential nonlinear relationships among variables. In this reduced-dimensional space, BECs become closer to diagonal, substantially simplifying covariance estimation and potentially improving DA efficiency. These advantages suggest that LDA may provide a promising alternative framework for radar reflectivity assimilation. However, several fundamental questions remain unresolved. First, to what extent is reflectivity-based LDA affected by model error and sampling error, which remain inherent challenges in ensemble-based DA? Second, existing LDA studies have primarily employed autoencoders (AEs) trained on smooth, continuous atmospheric fields, and applying such approaches to reconstruct highly intermittent and localized structures, such as radar reflectivity, remains unclear. This study develops a graph neural network (GNN)-based autoencoder trained with historical convection-allowing MPAS simulations to investigate its capability for reflectivity representation and reconstruction. The implementation of LDA within the CADRE MPAS-JEDI DA framework is currently underway. Single-observation experiments will be performed to examine the sensitivity of reflectivity LDA to model and sampling errors and to evaluate its potential for direct radar reflectivity assimilation. The corresponding results will be presented in the conference.

495315.title: The Influence of Soil Moisture on Subseasonal Temperature Predictability
495315.authors: Meg Devlan Fowler, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Berner, A. Jaye, N. Tavakoli, J. H. Richter, Z. Zhang, C. He, A. Glanville, S. W. Hoch, R. B. Neale, and P. A. Dirmeyer
495315.abstract: Soil moisture anomalies have the potential to enhance near-surface temperature predictability on subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) timescales as a result of their persistence. Across mid-latitude land, however, recent results from Richter et al. (2024) suggest that version 2 of the Community Earth System Model (CESM2) has almost no prediction skill that can be traced back to the land surface. Here we interrogate that result in more detail, investigating the degree to which wet and dry soil moisture initialization impacts prediction skill in the same model. Rather than assessing all mid-latitude regions, we focus on regions that exhibit strong land-atmosphere coupling under the hypothesis that if any land-based predictability does exist in CESM2, it should be most apparent in these regions. We find that in these particular regions, model initialization with anomalously wet or dry soil moisture can indeed drive enhanced temperature predictability on timescales of 3-6 weeks. We investigate the mechanisms that drive the sensitivity and robustness of signals across model simulations to better understand the physical processes underpinning fluctuations in predictability. We especially seek to understand if these variations form a soil-based indicator of forecasts of opportunity, where confidence in forecast skill could be determined a priori as a result of antecedent soil moisture conditions.

495317.title: Atmospheric Regimes and Aerosol-Cloud-Precipitation Interactions over the Coastal Northeast Pacific
495317.authors: Seethala Chellappan, NASA Langley /AMA, Hampton, VA; and D. Painemal, M. M. Thieman, and W. L. Smith Jr.
495317.abstract: Observations from the ARM Eastern Pacific Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment (EPCAPE), spanning February 2023 to February 2024 at Scripps Pier in La Jolla, California (32.8663°N, 117.2546°W), were used to investigate the regional-scale atmospheric factors controlling variability in marine low clouds and aerosols within the coastal boundary layer (BL). Using Self-Organizing Maps applied to ERA5 sea level pressure and near-surface winds, we classify the synoptic evolution of the subtropical anticyclone in spring and summer into nine regimes. These include, a regime characterized by an anticyclone over the domain with its core positioned towards the west of the pier, regimes depicting the cyclonic evolution from development to eastward advancement to southeastward dissipation, and a regime that captures the climatological mean state. GOES-18 cloud retrievals reveal that regimes associated with anomalous anticyclone cores closer to Scripps Pier produce reduced low-cloud fraction, shallower clouds, and low liquid water path (LWP); whereas regimes with a west/north-westward-displaced anomalous anticyclone provision extensive stratocumulus with higher LWP and elevated cloud tops. Regimes with a weak anticyclone centered adjacent to the Pier feature highest concentrations of smaller-sized particles, associated with a stable BL and stagnation under weak winds. Regimes with anticyclonic strengthening farther-offshore have lower aerosol concentrations. Partial inconsistency between cloud droplet number concentration (Nd) and aerosol concentration indicates BL turbulence critically influences aerosol activation into Nd. Ground-based ARM EPCAPE observations will be combined to quantify LWP, cloud fraction, and precipitation adjustments to aerosols.

495318.title: Global Daily Altimeter Sea Surface Height v1 – a JEDI Ocean Product
495318.authors: James A. Carton, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD; and L. Chen, L. Sun, D. A. Byrne, E. Leuliette, and T. Sluka
495318.abstract: Background Sea level is a critical indicator of phenomena ranging from storms and weather to climate variability and change. While in-ocean sensors like tide gauges provide precise temporal records, their spatial distribution remains extremely sparse. Satellite RADAR altimeter tracks, continuously available since the early 1990s, offer global spatial coverage but are constrained by significant spatial and temporal gaps between satellite orbital passes. Advanced swath RADAR missions, such as SWOT, can provide fine spatial details but suffer from long repeat periods. To fulfill the requirement for continuous, high-resolution global sea level fields, NOAA CoastWatch has relied on a legacy optimal interpolation system to produce daily global sea level anomaly analyses since 2017. This presentation describes the design, implementation, and evaluation of the Daily Altimeter Sea Surface Height (DASH) open-source software package. DASH serves as the next-generation system, utilizing variational filters within the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework to fill spatiotemporal gaps, filter bad observations, and supply rigorous error estimates applied to the Radar Altimeter Database System (RADS) database now containing more than satellite tracks. Methodology 2.1 Mapping: We use DASH to ingest virtually all historical satellite altimetry to build a publicly available, continuous 33-year record (1993–2025) of daily global sea level and surface currents at standard 1/4∘×1/4∘ and high-resolution 1/8∘×1/8∘ grids. 2.2 Variational Algorithm: DASH Version 1.0 implements a two-scale JEDI 3DVar filter. Prespecified background error covariance scales are designated separately for broad basin-scale dynamics (103-104 km) and energetic mesoscale/eddy-scale features (101-102 km), with error covariances that conform to the shapes of islands and continents. 2.3 Automated Quality Control: Satellite altimeter tracks occasionally introduce severe non-physical errors. Legacy protocols relied on manual human-in-the-loop (HITL) track deletion. DASH replaces HITL with an automated neighbor-comparison filter that evaluates and rejects suspect tracks, removing approximately 3–7% of erroneous satellite passes (identifying one specific satellite mission as a primary source of corrupted tracks). 2.4 Environmental Masking & Surface Currents: High-latitude RADAR interference from sea ice is mitigated using National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) Version 5 sea ice concentration fields. Daily ocean surface currents are derived from analyzed sea level gradients by combining pressure-gradient driven (near-geostrophic) flow with latitude-dependent corrections for wind drift and wave-induced Stokes drift. 3. Error Analysis & Uncertainty Quantification DASH total sea level error is partitioned into measurement and representation errors: 3.1 Measurement Error: Quantified using an ensemble of Observing System Experiments where unbiased, uncorrelated noise is introduced into individual observation tracks. The spread across ensemble members provides a direct estimate of measurement uncertainty. 3.2 Total Error & Increments: Total error is independently evaluated by analyzing daily analysis increments. Analysis shows DASH is unbiased with respect to altimeter observations and exhibits no spurious long-term trend. The standard deviation of analysis increments remains within 15–18% of the total background sea level variability. 3.3 External Validation: Independent validation against global tide gauge time series and surface drifters confirms the reliability of these internal error estimates. Comparisons DASH1 performance was evaluated relative to the legacy NOAA CoastWatch analysis and the Copernicus Marine Service (CMEMS) reprocessed products (DT-2021/DT2024): 4.1 CoastWatch Comparison: shows a daily difference standard deviation of approximately 4 cm, with correlation coefficients exceeding r=0.85 across most global ocean basins. 4.2 CMEMS Comparison: DASH retains 5–10% more power, predominantly in the intramonthly (1/dy to 1/month) frequency band (see Fig). While the older gridded products attenuate energy at high frequencies , DASH matches the slope and high-frequency spectral density of the in-situ tide gauge record. Future Outlook DASH1 is a significant infrastructure upgrade, providing an open-source, JEDI-based variational analysis that preserves high-frequency, eddy-scale variability without sacrificing stability or introducing artificial trends. Our future plans use DASH1 for training as a step towards incorporating machine learning and artificial intelligence capabilities. The inclusion of an emulator for short-term forecasts will be presented in a companion talk by coauthor Luyu Sun in the AMS 26th Conference on Artificial Intelligence for Environmental Science.

495326.title: The PREFIRE Anc-Sat Product: Development and Applications of CubeSat Collocations with Other Satellite Data
495326.authors: Kyle S Mattingly, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, WI; and C. Bean, X. Chen, B. Drouin, X. Huang, B. H. Kahn, T. S. L’Ecuyer, A. Merrelli, T. I. Michaels, N. Miller, and Q. Yue
495326.abstract: NASA’s Polar Radiant Energy in the Far InfraRed Experiment (PREFIRE) mission has been collecting spectrally-resolved radiance measurements out to far-infrared wavelengths since July 2024. The PREFIRE mission consists of two 6U CubeSats in sun-synchronous polar orbits, each carrying a Thermal InfraRed Spectrometer (TIRS) instrument. To maximize the utility of PREFIRE’s novel far-infrared observations, software tools have been developed for collocating observations and retrievals from numerous other low-Earth-orbiting (LEO) and geostationary (GEO) satellite instruments with TIRS footprints. This PREFIRE “ancillary satellite data” (Anc-Sat) product provides contextual information and opportunities for calibration and validation that expand the capabilities of the core TIRS instruments. In this presentation, we describe the development and some applications of the PREFIRE Anc-Sat product. We first discuss the product-specific characteristics that must be considered when collocating LEO and GEO satellite products with PREFIRE—such as their spatial resolution, orbital swath, data format, and quality flag scheme—and the product design decisions that were made in response to these particularities. Using the metadata provided in the Anc-Sat files, we analyze the spatiotemporal characteristics of collocations with other LEO products, demonstrating that the timing offset between the PREFIRE-SAT1 and PREFIRE-SAT2 orbits increases the latitude range across which close-in-time collocations are possible. We review ongoing applications of the Anc-Sat data, including calibration of the PREFIRE L1B spectral radiance geolocation using collocated GEO data, training of the PREFIRE L2 neural network cloud mask with collocated JPSS VIIRS data, and validation of L1 radiance and L2 retrieval products with several products from other satellites. We conclude by discussing opportunities for future product enhancements, such as expanding the number of collocated data products supported by the software, developing strategies for leveraging the high-fidelity but spatially sparse collocations with EarthCARE, and utilizing cloud computing resources to efficiently create larger batches of Anc-Sat product files.

495328.title: Smoke Evolution and Aerosol Optical Properties Over the Western United States Using HARP2
495328.authors: Clara Jane Bax, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and X. Xu, A. Puthukkudy, and A. Rocha Lima
495328.abstract: Increased wildfire activity in the western United States impacts air quality, human health, and Earth’s radiative balance. The Hyper-Angular Rainbow Polarimeter 2 (HARP2) onboard NASA’s Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, and ocean Ecosystem (PACE) satellite uses multi-angle, multi-spectral polarized observations of reflected sunlight to detect small aerosols emitted during biomass burning. Data from this instrument can provide information about aerosol concentration, size, and composition by estimating certain optical properties. This project analyzes several aerosol optical properties (e.g., aerosol optical depth, single-scattering albedo, fine-mode fraction, and Ångström exponent) from wildfires across the western United States. To validate HARP2 observations, results are compared to in situ measurements and prior studies that utilized multi-angle observations. Based on the spatial similarities and results from other studies on smoke evolution, the development of aerosol optical properties across the smoke plumes is expected to follow typical patterns seen elsewhere. All of the plumes studied were mapped using RGB imagery, with a cross-section and bounding box selected for each. Then, quality-controlled pixels within the cross-section were analyzed to understand the evolution of the optical properties of each plume. Each of the plumes showed an aerosol optical depth that peaked near the source and decreased as the distance from the fire increased. The Ångström exponent was higher than 1.5 near the fire sources, indicating the presence of fine-mode aerosols typical of biomass burning events. However, differences in single-scattering albedo and Ångström exponent were observed between individual plumes, highlighting variation in particle size and composition. These findings demonstrate that regional smoke evolution does not follow a single pattern, underscoring uncertainties in tracking wildfire smoke development and measuring aerosol optical properties.

495330.title: Elevating "Intermediate" Research Transitions and Communicating Their Impacts
495330.authors: Matthew C. Mahalik, NOAA, Boulder, CO; NOAA/OAR Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; NOAA/OAR/Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO
495330.abstract: NOAA’s weather research laboratories often struggle to identify and communicate the value of its research activities until they transition results into their final operational use. However, research and development occurs continuously, building off of a series of milestones that form the foundation of the next-generation tools and systems that shape the future of weather forecasting. By recognizing previously unsung successes, or “intermediate transitions,” between research phases throughout the readiness level spectrum, research organizations can more effectively demonstrate the value of their work. This presentation discusses examples from NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL), which leads the development of numerous, prominent earth-system forecast models and decision support tools, and conducts research at a wide variety of operational readiness. In 2025, its Program Management Office and Communications teams merged to establish a system that works directly with researchers to capture major milestones across all readiness levels and communicate the stories of how they benefit science, society, and the economy. This approach has been applied to research projects from field-campaign data collection to parameterization development, social science studies, and data distribution system builds. Through web and social media content, outreach, and innovative reporting strategies, GSL strives to increase the accessibility of the laboratory’s research results and more effectively and efficiently communicate their impacts to agency leadership, external stakeholders, and the public.

495332.title: Active-Passive Thermodynamic Retrieval Synergy to Improve Sounding of the Planetary Boundary Layer from Airborne Platforms
495332.authors: David M. Loveless, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and T. J. Wagner, A. R. Nehrir, M. Loveless, J. Taylor, and R. B. Pierce
495332.abstract: The 2017 Decadal Survey identified improving observations of the planetary boundary layer (PBL) as an area for future investment in order to improve our understanding of boundary layer processes and numerical weather prediction (NWP). NASA’s Planetary Boundary Layer Study Team Report in 2021 identified passive infrared (IR) sounding and water vapor differential absorption lidars as two instruments that would be critical for this objective. The University of Wisconsin-Madison Space Science and Engineering Center’s Scanning-High resolution Infrared Sounder (S-HIS) is a passive hyperspectral IR sounder that measures atmospheric emitted radiances between 3.5 and 17.3 μm (580 – 2850 cm-1 ) at 0.5 cm-1 resolution. S-HIS has been used in 37 field campaigns with deployments on the NASA ER-2, DC-8, Proteus, WB-57, and Global Hawk airborne platforms. S-HIS radiance measurements have been used for retrievals of thermodynamic profiles and trace gas concentrations, providing similar information content to current space-based IR sounders, such as the Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) and the Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer (IASI). The NASA Langley Research Center’s High Altitude Lidar Observatory (HALO) is a differential absorption lidar that has flown on the Gulfstream aircraft in a variety of campaigns, providing very high vertical resolution and accuracy estimates of water vapor profiles. During the West Coast and Heartland Hyperspectral Microwave Sensor Intensive Experiment (WH2yMSIE), S-HIS flew on the ER-2 and HALO flew on the G-III. While on different platforms, the flight tracks were designed to allow for numerous co-locations between these two instruments. An information content analysis for S-HIS shows that it provides temperature retrievals at 1-2 km vertical resolution and about 1 K uncertainty and water vapor retrievals at about 2 km vertical resolution and 10% water vapor uncertainty, as compared to the ambient water vapor mixing ratio. However, by including the HALO water vapor profiles and uncertainties in an optimal estimation type retrieval with the S-HIS radiances, we can significantly improve the water vapor profile (because of the very high signal provided by an active instrument) while also improving the temperature retrieval compared to using S-HIS radiances only. By constraining the water vapor profile with the HALO water vapor retrieval, additional information about the temperature profile can be extracted from the S-HIS radiances. Information content analyses suggest that the temperature information increases by 20% by including the HALO water vapor retrieval. This results in improved vertical resolution and reduced uncertainties to the temperature retrieval as well. This instrument synergy improves the retrieval throughout the profile but particularly at the top of the PBL where the vertical gradients in temperature and water vapor are often very large. Combined retrievals of S-HIS and HALO from the available co-locations during the WH2yMSIE campaign will be presented and compared with dropsonde profiles. Particular focus will be given to the improved representation of the PBL with this synergy.

495336.title: Successes and Challenges of R2O2R from NASA Space Weather Program - Implementation Office
495336.authors: Xia Cai, NASA, Hampton, VA; and S. R. Britton, E. B. Berndt, and A. Bergamini
495336.abstract: The NASA Space Weather Program – Implementation Office (IO) was established to actively manage and advance the transition of space weather Research-to-Operations and Operations-to-Research (R2O2R) projects. This effort is supported by collaborating with partner agencies and integrating insights from both space weather and terrestrial weather communities. In this presentation, we review recent successes and challenges in space weather R2O2R, highlighting how these experiences can improve project transitions and ultimately enhance tools for space weather forecasters. Following the Space Weather R2O2R Framework, the IO measures the technical maturity using the Space Weather Readiness Levels (RLs) from RL1 to RL9. A recent evaluation showed the average RL increased from 3 in May 2025 to 4 by May 2026. Projects that moved up significantly shared two traits: 1) strong user feedback from co-development; and 2) successful demonstration of end-to-end prototypes at the Space Weather Proving Grounds. The Framework illustrates the R2O2R process as a funnel showing while many projects begin at low RLs in the research phase, only a few reach high RLs and operational status. It is expected only a subset of R2O2R projects will ultimately achieve full operational capability. Determining the optimal transition rate requires more detailed analyses and comparisons with similar efforts in other fields. Moreover, as technology and technical requirements of operational facilities are evolving, transition plans must adapt accordingly. Developing a transition plan with the targeted user at an early stage, i.e., RL3 Proof of Concept, and updating it regularly proves highly beneficial. Despite ongoing challenges, the IO remains dedicated to: 1) actively fostering R2O and O2R connections between project principal investigators and users across NOAA, DoW, and NASA; 2) consistently aligning space weather research with real-world user needs and operational priorities; and 3) accelerating space weather research to serve society as a whole.

495337.title: The Long and Short of It: Mg II Index Measurements from GOES/EUVS and TSIS-1/SIM
495337.authors: Martin Snow, Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES), Boulder, CO, Boulder, CO; and S. V. Penton, J. Machol, J. Mothersbaugh III, and T. Woods
495337.abstract: The GOES-R series of satellites have provided high cadence solar irradiance measurements from the Extreme Ultraviolet Sensors (EUVS) since February 2017. The Magnesium II (Mg II) solar index, a quantitative indicator of solar activity, is measured operationally every three seconds. This observing cadence enables space weather relevant models of the solar spectral irradiance and satellite drag. The Total and Spectral Solar Irradiance Sensor/Solar Irradiance Monitor (TSIS-1/SIM) instrument on the International Space Station makes daily Mg II measurements with high precision and high accuracy. Its lower-cadence observations allow quantitative validation of the long-term degradation corrections to the EUVS dataset (see presentation by Mothersbaugh for details). This presentation will show the collaboration between these two datasets as well as their relationship with long-term Mg II composites and the ongoing F10.7 daily record. These comparisons are key objectives of the NASA solar irradiance science team: CATNIP.

495338.title: Changing How Aviation Manages Turbulence Through Space-Based ADS-B Data
495338.authors: Scott Young, Aireon, LLC, Reston, VA
495338.abstract: Turbulence causes more than $1 billion (USD) in damages and lost revenue annually around the world. In the National Airspace System (NAS) alone, moderate or worse turbulence events occur seven to eight times a day on average. As passenger traffic continues to grow, turbulence will be an increasing problem. Detecting, predicting and thereby avoiding turbulence is an urgent concern for commercial aviation. Aireon is the world’s leader in space-based Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) derived turbulence data. Partnering with the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), Aireon has developed a proprietary algorithm capable of calculating eddy dissipation rate (EDR) values for modelled aircraft, strictly from existing ADS-B data, with no onboard software or additional equipage. EDR values quantify turbulence, independent of aircraft type, allowing for predictive rather than reactive management of turbulence. This presentation will detail how global, real-time ADS-B derived turbulence data can transform how turbulence is detected and avoided. No longer dependent on moderate or severe turbulence occurring and then being reported, air traffic control and airlines can see where turbulence is and isn’t developing, all based on actual aircraft data, and then take proactive measures to avoid it. This presentation will show how Aireon’s turbulence data can be successfully used to avoid turbulence even when moderate or severe turbulence hasn’t been reported but is developing. Also, we will show how the data can be used to seed forecast models and train AI models, even further enabling proactive management of turbulence.

495339.title: Expanding Satellite Training in Alaska: Accelerating Operational Fluency with JPSS Data
495339.authors: Jennifer Delamere, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and C. Dierking, D. E. Levin, H. Mair, T. J. Wagner, W. Straka, J. Torres, E. Kutta, J. Troyke, A. Jacobs, M. Lawson, A. Stevermer, P. N. Dills, and S. Kalluri
495339.abstract: Observations from NOAA’s Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) provide essential weather and hazard coverage across Alaska, where geostationary coverage degrades. Operational applications using JPSS and partner polar-orbiting satellites span nowcasting (0–6 hours) and short-range forecasting, leveraging capabilities such as Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) imagery, NOAA Unique Combined Atmospheric Processing System (NUCAPS) soundings, and the Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS). Developing operational fluency with these satellite capabilities remains challenging because of the specialized nature of high-latitude satellite interpretation and the effort required to navigate dispersed training resources. To address this gap, satellite data liaisons and trainers sponsored by NOAA’s Office of LEO Observations, in collaboration with colleagues in the National Weather Service, are expanding the satellite training framework for Alaska. The initiative aims to establish a recommended training workflow that integrates existing LEO educational resources with new, event-driven ArcGIS StoryMap galleries. These galleries will deliver multi-sensor case studies focused on key high-latitude hazards, such as low fog and stratus, blowing snow, wildfires, and heavy precipitation. This effort accelerated during a collaborative LEO satellite workshop at the 2026 Arctic METOC Partnership Summit (AMPS) in Fairbanks. Participant feedback at AMPS underscored the need for structured, operational event examples to improve product integration. This presentation reviews existing resources, summarizes insights from AMPS engagement, and demonstrates the recommended workflow and expanded galleries.

495341.title: Current Status and Next Steps for the Multiscale Atmosphere-Geospace Environment Model.
495341.abstract: The Multiscale Atmosphere-Geospace Environment (MAGE) model is developed by the NASA DRIVE Science Center for Geospace Storms (CGS) to enable transformative advances in both heliophysics research and space weather applications. A distinguishing feature of MAGE is its coupling of all relevant regions of geospace at sufficiently high resolution to capture key cross-scale interactions within the magnetosphere-ionosphere-thermosphere system. Moreover, MAGE has now been extended all the way to the ground via a two-way coupling with the WACCM-X whole atmosphere model. This allows MAGE to investigate effects of driving of the ionosphere-thermosphere system from above and below. As a research model, MAGE describes the physical processes driving all essential space weather impacts including thermosphere expansion, space radiation environment, communications and geomagnetically-induced currents. However, bringing MAGE closer to the user and ultimately operationalizing it will require a large-scale concerted effort dedicated to understanding and quantifying its uncertainties and how the propagate through the model. This is a necessary requirement for data assimilation which, in turn, is a critical step toward an operationally viable model. In this presentation, we will describe the current status of MAGE and discuss ideas for next steps in its development, uncertainty quantification and data assimilation.

495343.title: Completing the AQPI Radar Network: Enhanced Atmospheric River Monitoring and Precipitation Estimation with a New C-Band Radar
495343.authors: V. Chandrasekar, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. George, S. K. Biswas, R. Bechini, D. Roberts, R. Cifelli, and J. Rutz
495343.abstract: The complex terrain of the San Francisco Bay Area presents significant challenges for observing precipitation. To improve regional precipitation monitoring, the Advanced Quantitative Precipitation Information (AQPI) project deployed several strategically located X-band radars to complement the existing NEXRAD coverage. Their low elevation and high resolution scans provide detailed observation of precipitation closer to the surface. However, low elevation radar beams can experience localized blockage in mountainous terrain. In addition, the shorter range of X-band systems limits observations farther offshore. To address these observational gaps, a new dual-polarization C-band Doppler radar has been deployed on Mount Barnabe in western Marin County. The addition of this longer range C-band radar further strengthens the AQPI network by complementing the X-band observations. The C-band system uses solid-state transmitters, providing a native range resolution of 150 m and high-quality observations over a radius of approximately 175 km. Its extended range provides broad offshore coverage over the Pacific, allowing precipitation structures associated with approaching atmospheric rivers to be detected before they reach the coast. At the same time, its different viewing geometry complements the existing X-band radars by providing observations in regions affected by terrain. Initial comparisons of reflectivity generated using NEXRAD observations alone and using the combined AQPI network demonstrate the added value of the C-band radar. The combined mosaic provides a more complete representation of precipitation systems across the AQPI domain, particularly over the ocean and within regions with previously limited radar coverage. The additional observations from C-Band also improve the representation of the vertical structure of precipitation and provide dual-polarization information related to precipitation microphysics in areas where observations were previously limited. This more complete three-dimensional characterization is expected to strengthen the multi-radar QPE product. Case studies will be presented to demonstrate improvements in radar coverage within terrain-blocked regions, and the resulting QPE after integration of the C-band observations.

495344.title: How Well Does CONUS404 Capture Storm Structure and Evolution? An Object-Based Evaluation Across U.S. Hydrologic Regions
495344.authors: Zhe Li, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and K. M. Mahoney, H. Chen, J. L. Bytheway, A. Thompson, and Y. Liu
495344.abstract: Recent advances in convection-permitting regional climate modeling have demonstrated strong potential for resolving extreme precipitation events and their changes at kilometer scales. These models can augment observation-based reconstructions of historical storms and provide physically consistent fields for tracking, classifying, and analyzing storm systems. Fully assessing their utility for storm characterization, however, requires evaluation at the event scale. Storm objects directly represent the spatial organization and temporal evolution of extreme precipitation systems, providing information that conventional grid-based metrics cannot capture. Here, we conduct a dedicated object-based evaluation of precipitation in CONUS404, a 4-km convection-permitting hydroclimate reanalysis-adjacent dataset, across the major hydrologic regions of the contiguous United States. Hourly CONUS404 precipitation and the observationally constrained Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC) are analyzed on a common 4-km grid for 2010–2021 across the 18 two-digit hydrologic regions. Storm objects are identified using a dual-threshold region-growing procedure and tracked through time. Each object is characterized by its centroid, projected area, mean, peak, and percentile intensities, major and minor axes, duration, orientation, and moving speed. CONUS404 and AORC storms are then paired using a three-dimensional mask-overlap approach in time-latitude-longitude space. The matched storms are used to assess probability of detection, false-alarm ratio, critical success index, spatial displacement, and overlap ratio. Both strict one-to-one and many-to-many matching approaches are considered to distinguish complete misses from differences associated with storm splitting and merging. CONUS404 exhibits pronounced regional and seasonal differences in storm-object occurrence, duration, area, intensity structure, and motion. Relative to AORC, it generally produces fewer one-hour objects but more objects at longer durations, with evidence of storm-life-cycle fragmentation in the Southeast and parts of the western United States. Projected storm area is typically underestimated, particularly in western hydrologic regions, although winter shows more mixed area differences. Within storm objects, upper-tail precipitation is generally enhanced whereas lower-intensity precipitation is reduced, indicating more concentrated rainfall around intense cores. Storm objects also move faster over much of the West and slower across parts of the central and eastern United States. Matched-object diagnostics show higher detection skill for larger and more intense storms. Allowing many-to-many correspondence substantially increases probability of detection and critical success index while reducing false alarms relative to strict one-to-one matching, demonstrating that storm splitting and merging contribute substantially to the apparent mismatch between CONUS404 and AORC. These findings provide an object-oriented basis for identifying where and for which storm attributes CONUS404 can reliably support regional extreme precipitation studies.

495348.title: Communicating Probabilities on Social Media: How Probability Expressions Shape Interpretation of Hurricane Forecast Graphics
495348.authors: Jinan N. Allan, Clemson University, Clemson, SC; and B. Remington, A. Baldwin, A. L. Bitterman, and J. T. Ripberger
495348.abstract: When communicating probabilistic forecast graphics on social media platforms, many risk communicators (e.g., emergency managers, broadcasters) often attempt to simplify the forecasted probabilities by using verbal probability expressions (e.g., “very likely”). Due to the wide range of interpretations for words and phrases used to convey probabilities, the use of verbal probability expressions could obfuscate the intended meaning of probabilistic forecasts (e.g., Lenhardt et al., 2020). The current study assesses the extent to which differing probability expressions on social media posts impact comprehension and protective action attitudes for two hurricane forecast graphics: the Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map and the Hurricane-Force Wind Speed Probability graphic. Simulated Twitter/X posts were presented to adult participants across the US (n = 3,355). The posts contained a hurricane forecast graphic and one of four possible accompanying text manipulations: (i) no text regarding probabilities, (ii) text with vague verbal probability expressions (e.g., “possible storm surge”), (iii) text with verbal probability expressions that include magnitude adjectives (e.g., “there is a small chance of storm surge”), or (iv) text with specific, numeric probabilities (e.g., “there is a 10% chance of storm surge”). Participants then answered questions related to forecast interpretation, risk perceptions, and protective action behaviors. For both graphics, posts that contained numeric probabilities were more likely to be correctly interpreted compared to posts in other conditions, F(3, 3353) = 47.62, p < .001. As such, participants were 1.67 times more likely to accurately interpret the forecasts when provided numeric probability information. Furthermore, statistical numeracy skills were positively related to forecast interpretation, such that highly numerate individuals were roughly 3 times more likely to accurately interpret the graphics, independent of the provided text. Finally, though the text manipulation did not directly impact protective action decisions, individuals who accurately interpreted the forecasts were 2.6 times more likely to recommend protective action. As people increasingly receive hurricane warnings and risk information from social media platforms, the current study reinforces the importance of providing numeric probabilities to support accurate risk assessments.

495351.title: Parameterized Cloud and Aerosol Processes Modulate the Spatial Distribution of Extreme Fire Weather over North America
495351.authors: Jiale Lou, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and D. McCoy, D. Caulton, H. Y. Brown, T. W. Aerenson, J. M. Nugent, and A. Kirby
495351.abstract: Cloud and aerosol processes remain among the largest sources of uncertainty in Earth system models because many governing microphysical processes occur at scales much smaller than those resolved by global models. These parameterized processes strongly influence energy balance, moisture transport, and cloud properties, all of which are closely linked to fire-prone weather extremes. Here, we leverage the perturbed physics ensemble (PPE) within a state-of-the-art Earth system model to investigate how uncertainties in microphysical parameterizations shape extreme fire weather over North America. Using 251 PPE members with perturbations applied to 25 parameters across the aerosol and stratiform and convective cloud microphysical schemes, we quantify how parametric uncertainty propagates into the spatial characteristics of extreme fire weather. We develop a parameter fingerprinting framework to identify the dominant parameters controlling simulated fire weather extremes and model–observation discrepancy. The leading mode of the parameter fingerprint matrix explains over 60% of the total variance, indicating that a relatively small subset of parameters governs the ensemble spread in fire weather extremes. Specifically, parameters associated with stratiform cloud autoconversion processes, which regulate the conversion of cloud droplets to rain, exert strong nonlinear controls on simulated fire weather extremes. The influence of these parameters is also sensitive to model configuration and large-scale dynamical constraints imposed through different nudging strategies and ocean surface conditions. Despite substantial parameter sensitivity, persistent regional biases remain, pointing to structural model challenges. Overly dry relative humidity biases appear to be a dominant contributor to the elevated fire weather biases. Building upon the existing PPE experiments and the parameter fingerprinting framework, we are also conducting targeted process-denial and parameter stress experiments to isolate the physical pathways linking cloud microphysical parameterizations to near-surface humidity and fire weather extreme. Preliminary results suggest that these targeted experiments provide valuable process-level constraints beyond statistical parameter attribution alone.

495353.title: Accelerating Subseasonal-to-Seasonal Prediction with a Standardized Coupling Framework for Hybrid Physics–ML Earth System Models
495353.authors: Ufuk U Turuncoglu, NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and W. P. Bruinsma
495353.abstract: Traditional Earth system models (ESMs) remain important tools for weather and climate research and operational prediction, yet they continue to face significant computational bottlenecks and persistent difficulty in accurately parameterizing complex sub-grid physical processes such as atmospheric convection, clouds, and radiation. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) offer a promising path forward by providing computationally efficient, data-driven surrogates for specific model components, including atmospheric solvers, sub-grid-scale parameterizations, ensemble generation, and data assimilation. Realizing the potential of these emulators within fully coupled modeling systems, however, requires infrastructure capable of integrating heterogeneous ML-based and physics-based components in a seamless, standardized, and reproducible manner. This is especially critical for longer prediction horizons, where the accuracy of the forecast is governed by slowly evolving, tightly coupled processes such as air-sea interaction and sea-ice feedbacks that cannot be captured by atmospheric ML emulators alone. This study introduces a novel coupling architecture designed to couple diverse ML-based models with traditional physics-based models to construct hybrid ESMs with minimal development effort. By leveraging the Earth System Modeling Framework (ESMF) and the National Unified Operational Prediction Capability (NUOPC) layer, a newly developed co-processing component, GeoGate, standardizes communication and data exchange among the different types of model components in a modeling-system-agnostic way. The design supports zero-copy data translation through a flexible plugin architecture, enables asynchronous execution, and allows physics components to be swapped with their data-driven counterparts, establishing a truly flexible hybrid modeling environment that is agnostic to any specific ESMF/NUOPC-based modeling system that allows to follow hieracical model development appraoch. We demonstrate this framework through a fully coupled, multi-component global Subseasonal-to-Seasonal (S2S) application, referred to as the Hybrid Earth System Model for S2S prediction (HESM-S2S). S2S forecasting aims to fill the gap between weather and climate prediction and represents a recognized priority area for operational centers because of its value in managing economic risk across sectors affected by climate variability. Skillful prediction at these time scales depends critically on the realistic representation of coupled ocean, sea-ice, and atmospheric processes and their two-way interactions. In the HESM-S2S configuration, inherited from the Unified Forecast System Weather Model, a fine-tuned version of the Aurora foundation model provides atmospheric forcing to prognostic physics-based ocean (Modular Ocean Model version 6; MOM6) and sea-ice (Los Alamos Sea Ice Model; CICE6) components, with the Community Mediator for Earth Prediction Systems (CMEPS) performing atmosphere-ocean flux calculation and orchestrating exchange among components. Aurora was fine-tuned at 0.25° resolution using ERA5 reanalysis and evaluated against the WeatherBench 2 benchmark, and the coupling design enables two-way interaction in which sea surface temperature (SST) generated by the physics-based ocean model is fed back to the Aurora atmospheric component at each coupling step. To assess performance, a set of 35-day coupled simulations initialized across four different seasons was conducted using several configurations, ranging from one-way data-atmosphere coupling to Aurora-forced autoregressive rollouts and fully two-way coupled experiments, and compared against a physics-driven reference simulation forced by ERA5 as well as OISST and satellite-based observational datasets. The results demonstrate that constraining the Aurora atmosphere with accurate SST is central to slowing error growth over the extended 35-day S2S horizon: configurations supplied with SST from the physics-based ocean model or from ERA5 exhibit consistently lower near-surface air temperature bias than the unconstrained autoregressive rollout across all analyzed seasons, and the two-way coupled configuration systematically reduces relative root-mean-square error for most surface variables by roughly 5–15% while improving anomaly correlation (Fig. 1). This improvement is geographically and physically coherent: the strongest gains appear in variables most directly influenced by air-sea heat exchange—2-meter air temperature, dew-point temperature, and specific and relative humidity—particularly where the air-sea temperature gradient is large, whereas variables such as shortwave radiation, precipitation, cloud cover, and mean sea level pressure show little sensitivity to the modified SST, consistent with the expected pathways of oceanic influence on the near-surface atmosphere. In parallel, the coupled system reproduces the spatiotemporal variability of SST consistently with the reference simulation and observations, maintains the stability of the underlying physics-based components, and yields sea-ice concentration and extent from CICE6 that agree with observations across both hemispheres, with the principal discrepancies confined to warm-season biases traceable to underlying ocean-model and reanalysis limitations rather than to the coupling with Aurora. Notably, these results were obtained without adjusting the configurations or initial conditions of the physics-based model components, indicating that the coupling framework introduces no additional degradation and that the fine-tuned foundation model is capable of driving realistic multi-component coupled behavior out of the box. Although the present study focuses on the S2S use case, the underlying coupling infrastructure is deliberately general and has been applied to additional configurations, including a regional two-way coupled atmosphere-ocean application used to study Hurricane Irene, demonstrating that the same framework can accommodate applications ranging from high-resolution regional coupling to complex, multi-component global prediction spanning a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. By enabling modular, interchangeable physical and ML components within a single standardized coupling framework, this approach enhances model development flexibility and paves the way toward next-generation, computationally efficient, and modular ESMs that can leverage the rapid innovation cycles of both physical and machine learning sciences while maintaining, and in some cases improving, simulation fidelity. This work has direct implications for the design of future operational hybrid prediction systems and for community efforts to integrate rapidly advancing AI/ML models into established Earth system modeling infrastructures without sacrificing the physical consistency and interpretability afforded by traditional coupled models. Acknowledgments: This material is based upon work supported by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), a major facility sponsored by the National Science Foundation under Cooperative Agreement No. 1852977. The authors thank the developer and maintainer communities of ESMF/NUOPC, CMEPS, CDEPS, MOM6, and CICE6, as well as the developers of the Aurora foundation model, for the tools and datasets used in this study. Computing resources were provided by the Climate Simulation Laboratory at NSF NCAR’s Computational and Information Systems Laboratory (CISL). We also thank colleagues from NCAR and NOAA for helpful discussions and feedback.

495355.title: Impact of Assimilation of MWS and AMSR3 Brightness Temperature Data in NOAA's Global Forecast System
495355.authors: Jianjun Jin, Lynker Corporation @ NOAA/NWS/OMD, Riverdale Park, MD; and A. Collard, R. Treadon, H. Liu, S. Stegall, I. Genkova, and D. Holdaway
495355.abstract: The Microwave Sounder (MWS) aboard the Meteorological Operational satellite - Second Generation (MetOp-SG) - A1 and the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 3 (AMSR3) aboard the Global Observation SATellite for Greenhouse gases and Water cycle (GOSAT-GW) were launched in summer 2025. These two instruments make microwave radiance observations at frequencies between 6.9 GHz - 229 GHz. These observations expand the microwave radiance datasets which are greatly beneficial to atmospheric data assimilation and numerical weather predictions. At NOAA National Weather Service's Office of Modeling and Development (OMD), we are implementing data processing and quality control measures in brightness temperature observations made by these instruments in order to assimilate these data within the current all-sky microwave radiance data assimilation framework in NOAA’s Global Forecast System (GFS). In this presentation, we will show our evaluations of data quality and the impact of these data in GFS’s analysis and forecasts. In addition, the GFS data assimilation system is in a transition from the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) based system to the Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA) Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) based system. We will also present the progress in assimilating satellite radiance observations within the new JEDI based data assimilation system.

495356.title: FAA Turbulence Program Updates
495356.authors: Chandler Kyle Zuck, FAA, Washington, DC; and W. Deierling, G. Meymaris, D. Munoz-Esparza, J. A. Sauer, H. Shin, J. A. Craig, and R. Sharman
495356.abstract: Turbulence remains the leading cause of weather-related aviation accidents within the National Airspace System (NAS). The mission of the Federal Aviation Administration's Weather Research Branch Turbulence Program is to improve the safety, efficiency, and capacity of the NAS. This is achieved through the research and development of products designed to reduce unnecessary rerouting of aircraft, decrease turbulence-related accidents, and equip planners and operators with the tools necessary for tactical and strategic avoidance. This presentation will provide program highlights like the recent operational implementation of the Graphical Turbulence Guidance Nowcast (GTGN) and integration of Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast Vertical Rate (ADS-B VR) data, progress on incorporating machine learning algorithms into GTG version 4.5, current efforts to support global harmonization for products like the global probabilistic GTG, and the Turbulence Project’s future role in supporting new entrant aviation technologies.

495359.title: The CGMS SWCG Task Group on Ionospheric Radio Occultation System Optimisation
495359.authors: Erin M. Lynch, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD
495359.abstract: The Ionospheric Radio Occultation System Optimisation Task Group was formed in the framework of the of the Coordination Group for Meteorological Satellites to address the high level priority objective to establish requirements for and recommend an implementation of an optimized system for radio occultation observation for ionospheric monitoring and prediction. The Task Group leverages the expertise of participants across the CGMS member agencies as well as coordination with the International Radio Occultation Working Group (IROWG). Objectives within the scope of work of the Task Group include an assessment of current and planned ionospheric RO capabilities of CGMS members and support for Observing System/System Simulation Experiments (OSE/OSSE) to address the sensitivity to changes in the latency, coverage, and counts of ionospheric observations to establish requirements. This presentation will discuss the past work and future plans of the Task Group and its members toward addressing latency, geographic and local time coverage, and number of ionospheric RO measurements needed to support operational ionospheric applications.

495362.title: Meteorology Across the Nation's Test Ranges: From Environmental Intelligence to Mission-Critical Decision Support at White Sands Missile Range
495362.authors: Scott A. Startz, White Sands Missile Range, WSMR, NM
495362.abstract: From missile and weapons testing to aviation, aerospace, directed-energy, and advanced defense-system development, the nation’s test ranges operate in environments where atmospheric conditions can determine whether a mission proceeds, how a system performs, and what conclusions can be drawn from a test. Meteorology is therefore an integral component of range operations, providing the observations, forecasts, analyses, and decision-support information necessary to characterize the environment and enable safe and successful testing. This presentation will provide a concise overview of the diverse missions conducted across the ranges represented by the Range Commanders Council (RCC) Meteorology Group, highlighting the distinctive testing and operational requirements at each location and the meteorological capabilities required to support them. From this national perspective, the presentation will then focus on White Sands Missile Range (WSMR), where a broad spectrum of equipment, munitions, weapons systems, and other materiel used by the U.S. military is tested and evaluated under controlled conditions before being fielded to soldiers and other operational forces. These tests help determine system performance, reliability, effectiveness, and safety under a wide range of environmental conditions. Accurate characterization of the atmosphere is fundamental to this mission, as weather and atmospheric variability can directly influence system performance, trajectories, sensor capabilities, communications, safety, and test results. The WSMR Meteorology Branch provides an extensive, integrated suite of capabilities spanning routine weather forecasting, mission-support forecasting, weather warnings and advisories, atmospheric profiling, real-time environmental monitoring, climatological analysis, and specialized meteorological instrumentation. Its observing network includes 10-, 20-, and 34-meter meteorological towers; more than 45 Surface Area Meteorological Stations (SAMS); WBGT Monitoring Stations; upper-air radiosonde and autosonde operations; lidars; wind-profiling radars; an X-Band Weather Surveillance Radar system; an AutoNowcaster radar system; and a three-dimensional Lightning Mapping Array. These observations are complemented by the 4DWX mesoscale weather model, specialized data products, archived climatological datasets, and SMART-IP Impact Prediction and Wind Weighting capabilities that transform meteorological information into actionable mission support. The presentation will highlight how these diverse systems are integrated to characterize the atmosphere before, during, and after testing and how meteorological information contributes to informed test decisions and the evaluation of military systems. The presentation will conclude with WSMR’s expeditionary “safari” capability—the ability to deploy meteorologists and specialized instrumentation beyond the range to provide mission-critical environmental support virtually anywhere in the world. Together, these capabilities demonstrate the evolving role of range meteorology: from forecasting weather to delivering integrated environmental intelligence and decision support that helps ensure the systems ultimately placed in the hands of the nation’s warfighters are tested, evaluated, and understood within their atmospheric environment.

495364.title: CoAgMET - Colorado Agricultural Meteorological Network Updates and Future Outlook
495364.authors: Kristie Mae Davis, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and L. Simmons, R. S. Schumacher, and P. Globe
495364.abstract: The Colorado Agricultural Meteorological Network (CoAgMET) serves as Colorado’s state mesonet, providing research-grade meteorological observations to support agricultural decision-making, water resource management, climate monitoring, research, and applied climate services. Originally established to address the need for localized weather information for agriculture, CoAgMET has evolved over more than three decades into a statewide network of 102 stations spanning Colorado’s diverse topography and climate. This presentation will highlight recent network updates, operational and technological developments, and future initiatives as CoAgMET continues to expand beyond its agricultural origins to serve broader weather and climate applications. CoAgMET originated in the early 1990s when plant pathology extension specialists at Colorado State University (CSU) and engineers with the USDA Agricultural Research Service (USDA-ARS) Water Management Unit recognized a shared need for localized meteorological observations; an informal coalition was established with a network of eight stations. As the network expanded, the Colorado Climate Center (CCC) at CSU assumed management, and CoAgMET developed into one of Colorado’s primary sources of high-resolution, long-term weather observations. Today, stations are distributed across mountain valleys, the Front Range, the western slope, and eastern plains, providing observations that complement traditional observing networks and gridded datasets. These data support applications including crop and irrigation management, drought monitoring, evapotranspiration estimation, hydrologic research, climate analysis, and validation of remotely sensed and modeled products. Continued network growth has also increased the challenges associated with maintaining a large, geographically distributed observing system. Recent efforts have focused on improving station reliability, modernizing instrumentation, standardizing station configurations and maintenance procedures, strengthening quality control, and improving data accessibility. Instrumentation upgrades include improvements to meteorological and soil observations, updated datalogger configurations, and installation and evaluation of new precipitation instrumentation. Quality assurance and quality control have become increasingly important as CoAgMET has transitioned into a broader state mesonet. Standardized quality control procedures and improved documentation provide a more consistent framework for evaluating observations while preserving the integrity of the historical record. CoAgMET’s expanding role has also broadened its user base beyond agriculture to include researchers, extension personnel, water managers, state and federal agencies, and the broader climate and weather community. Observations increasingly support statewide climate monitoring and analysis of precipitation, temperature, drought, evaporative demand, and other environmental conditions. Future development will focus on maintaining and improving this observational capacity while addressing emerging scientific and operational needs. Planned initiatives include continued station modernization, targeted expansion to address spatial gaps, improvements to precipitation measurement, and further development of automated quality control tools. As CoAgMET enters its fourth decade of operation, balancing modernization with preservation of the observational record will remain a central priority. Continued investment in instrumentation, field maintenance, data management, quality assurance, documentation, and personnel will be essential to sustaining the network. CoAgMET’s evolution from an eight-station agricultural network into a statewide mesonet demonstrates the growing need for weather observations across Colorado. Building on its agricultural foundation, CoAgMET is positioned to increasingly support climatological, hydrological, environmental, and applied weather applications while continuing to provide the observations needed to address Colorado’s changing weather and climate information needs.

495366.title: Leveraging High-Resolution Hydrologic Model Output and Quantified Flash Flood Reports for Conceptual Impact-Based Forecasting
495366.authors: Steven M. Martinaitis, Univ. of Oklahoma - CIWRO, Norman, OK; and A. J. Schroeder and J. J. Gourley
495366.abstract: High resolution hydrologic model output has become a prominent tool for helping with the prediction and warning of flash floods. The operational Flooded Locations and Simulated Hydrographs (FLASH) system has provided forecasters with maximum unit streamflow values generated by the hydrologic models running within the FLASH system. The normalization of modeled streamflow by the upstream basin area at each grid cell has provided the ability to identify areas of anomalous flow. There is general qualitative guidance on the relationship between FLASH maximum unit streamflow values and the considerations for warning issuance as well as impact-based warning tag application for flash flood events, yet there are limited quantified studies in this area.
