The information gathered through detailed multifaceted data collections across six significant flash flood events in 2024 has provided the ability to construct a more detailed mapping of the severity of flash flood events with the use of the Flash Flood Severity Index (FFSI); moreover, it allows for the opportunity to quantify the relationship between maximum unit streamflow values and the emerging FFSI classifications. This presentation will first evaluate the comparisons of quantified flash flood reports via FFSI classifications with hydrologic model output, including differences between model-defined overland grid points versus channels. The presentation will then address how relating these post-event evaluations and research will benefit future communication of flood risks. The presentation will then conclude with remarks on new hydrologic modeling advancements and probabilistic impact-based guidance development at the Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO).

495372.title: Projecting Climate Change Impacts on Electricity Demand at High Spatiotemporal Resolution Across Major U.S. Power-System Regions: Implications for Grid Resilience
495372.authors: Buket Sahin, Duke University, Durham, NC
495372.abstract: Electricity demand is strongly influenced by weather, but the dominant meteorological drivers and their effects vary across power-system regions and climate regimes. As climate change alters mean conditions and weather extremes, these differences can lead to substantial shifts in electricity use and periods of system stress. This study examines how future climate conditions may reshape electricity demand across major U.S. power-system regions and assesses the implications for grid resilience. Historical utility-level electricity demand is combined with high-spatiotemporal-resolution meteorological reanalysis data in a deep learning framework that captures nonlinear relationships between electricity use and regionally relevant weather conditions. Region-specific models are then driven by an ensemble of high-resolution, downscaled, and bias-corrected climate projections under different warming scenarios. The analysis quantifies changes in seasonal electricity demand and in the frequency, magnitude, and timing of elevated-demand periods, while variability across climate projections is used to characterize uncertainty in future utility-level responses. Projected impacts vary across power-system regions, reflecting geographic differences in future climate exposure and historical weather-demand relationships. Changes in the frequency and intensity of demand-driving weather conditions alter the magnitude and timing of high-demand periods and reshape seasonal heating- and cooling-related loads. These responses highlight where climate-driven changes in electricity demand may create greater operational and planning challenges. By translating future climate conditions into regional electricity demand estimates at high spatiotemporal resolution, this study provides decision-relevant information for resource adequacy, infrastructure planning, operational preparedness, and grid resilience under a changing climate.

495374.title: Benchmarking Operational Cloud Performance and Suitability for SCHISM and NWM Total Water Level Capabilities Ahead of NOAA's WCOSS Cloud Transition
495374.authors: Jason Alexander Ducker, NWS, Live Oak, FL
495374.abstract: With NOAA actively transitioning its Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System (WCOSS) infrastructure to cloud platforms by late 2027, evaluating the performance, scalability, and cost-efficiency of operational numerical models on cloud High Performance Computing (HPC) is critical. Historically, Research-to-Operations (R2O) initiatives for coastal models, such as the NOS Cloud-Sandbox project, have heavily leveraged Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud environments for benchmarking and workflow development. However, with NOAA selecting Google Cloud Platform (GCP) for future operational cloud supercomputing, understanding whether AWS-based R2O benchmarking directly translates to GCP operational performance is essential for the community. The National Water Model (NWM) Total Water Level (TWL) capability utilizes the SCHISM (Semi-implicit Cross-scale Hydroscience Integrated System Model) unstructured grid framework to generate compound flood guidance across coastal domains, providing a rigorous testbed for this transition due to its hybrid MPI/OpenMP execution model, unstructured domain decomposition, and heavy inter-node network communication requirements. To further explore this transition, performance and suitability benchmarks of SCHISM across AWS HPC and GCP H-Series environments are compared against NOAA’s operational WCOSS2 baseline. Evaluation of system performance under demanding operational conditions, included benchmarking a suite of production configurations, encompassing a major hurricane-induced coastal compound flooding event as well as operational forecast cycles that vary from rapid 18-hour short-range projections to 10-day extended-range guidance. This study addresses critical cloud transition barriers by profiling multi-node strong scaling over unstructured meshes, low-latency network fabric performance during heavy MPI message passing, asynchronous NetCDF data storage and I/O throughput, automated cluster provisioning, and cost-per-simulation efficiency. Ultimately, this work provides a comprehensive cost-benefit and suitability analysis demonstrating how computational optimizations and elastic cloud HPC can significantly shorten operational delivery windows, placing critical compound flood guidance into the hands of forecasters when they need it most.

495376.title: Microscale Urban Heat Island Impacts of Lakes on Human Body Stress
495376.authors: Gerald J. Mulvey, Nighthawk Weather, San Antonio, TX
495376.abstract: Urban planners have long sought to reduce the impacts of the urban heat island through the use of urban lakes and forests. The reasoning being that water of the lakes’ surfaces will evaporate and thus reducing the skin surface temperature and that of the air above the lake. In the case of urban forests, evapotranspiration will cool the forest air. Both approaches will lower the air temperature in the vicinity of the lake or forest, thus locally mitigating the thermal impacts of the urban heat island, but they add moisture to the air. (Jay et. al. 2012). The increase in humidity increases the stress experienced by humans in the outside environment due to a decrease in evaporative sweat cooling. Air conditioning systems also experience decreased efficiencies (increased cost of cooling) due to the increase in local humidity. Older, vulnerable and economically disadvantaged populations tend to be located in urban core where the temperature increases are the highest and indoor air conditioning may not be affordable. (Chakraborty et.al. 2019) An experiment was conducted during the summer of 2026 in the town of Williamsburg, Virginia to map the spatial extent of the humidity increase due to a lake in the city. The Heat Index calculated from these measurements were used to estimate the impacts on humans. The experiment was conducted using stationary weather stations to provide background temperature and humidity levels. It also used data from a weather station in the lake over the water surface. The mapping data was collected using a mobile temperature-humidity system based on the LabQuest system. Jay, O., A. Capon, P. Berry, C. Broderick, R. de Dear, G. Havenith, Y. Honda, R. Kovats, W. Ma, A. Malik, N. Morris, L. Nybo, S. Seneviratne, J. Vanos, and K. Ebi, 2012: Heat and Health 2 : Reducing the health effects of hot weather and heat extremes: from personal cooling strategies to green cities, Lancet; 398: 709–24 Chakraborty, A. Hsu, D. Manya, and G. Sheriff, 2019: Disproportionately higher exposure to urban heat in lower-income neighborhoods: A multi-city perspective. Environ. Res. Lett. 14, 105003 B. Wetherley, J. P. McFadden, D. A. Roberts, Megacity-scale analysis of urban vegetation temperatures, Remote Sens. Environ. 213, 18–33

495384.title: Congestus Clouds are Underrated: Precipitating Cloud Population in the Atlantic ITCZ from Sea-Pol Radar Observations
495384.authors: Delián Colón-Burgos, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. M. Bell, D. Klocke, A. A. Wing, and J. H. Ruppert Jr.
495384.abstract: Cloud and rainfall morphology in the Atlantic Inter-tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) has been a subject of interest for decades due to its impact on global precipitation and energy balance but has yet to be analyzed in detail with modern ship-borne radar observations. In this study we use 3D retrievals of convective structure from the Colorado State University Sea-Going Polarimetric (Sea-Pol) radar collected during the Process Investigation of Clouds and Convective Organization over the atLantic Ocean (PICCOLO) field campaign and satellite brightness temperatures during August and September 2024 to analyze the frequency, rate, height, and spatial distribution of precipitation in the Atlantic ITCZ. We calculate the height of the 10 dBZ echo and find three convection groups based on a trimodal division of frequency: shallow (1- 4 km), congestus (5- 7 km), and deep (8 km+). Congestus is shown to be a prominent cloud type in the ITCZ, constituting 41% of the echo population. Deep echoes, although infrequent, have higher rain rates per fractional area than other groups, but a significant fraction of the rain comes from marginally deep (8-9 km) clouds that have been considered congestus under different definitions. Deep and congestus convective echoes together contribute the most to the rainfall totals, despite being less frequent in occurrence than stratiform precipitation with the same echo top heights. Higher populations of deep and congestus clouds are often found in spatial proximity, while the cloud population of shallow convection is found to be more distinct in spatial frequency. This work motivates an assessment of convective definitions and supports the idea of viewing congestus clouds from 5 – 9 km as a ‘failed’ mode of undilute deep convective hot towers that are an important fraction of the cloud population and leading contributor of rainfall in the ITCZ.

495386.title: Fine-Tuning and Distilling Deep Optical Flow Stereo Winds Using Differentiable Geometric Solvers
495386.authors: Thomas J Vandal, Zeus AI, Arlington, MA; and D. L. Wu, J. Carr, D. J. Posselt, T. Ballard, E. penn, A. Posch, and K. Duffy
495386.abstract: Operational satellite atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) rely on numerical weather prediction (NWP) background states for height assignment, creating a circular dependency that accounts for up to 70% of total AMV uncertainty. While GEO–GEO stereo methods resolve heights geometrically from parallax to eliminate NWP reliance, traditional window-based tracking remains computationally expensive and yields sparse retrievals restricted to overlapping satellite coverage. We address these limits by replacing window matching with WindFlow, a deep optical flow architecture, enabling pixel-dense 3D wind retrievals. Feature tracking is fine-tuned end-to-end through a differentiable weighted least-squares solver supervised by sparse radiosonde wind profiles without explicit height labels. To overcome the spatial limits of dual-satellite coverage, we distill this stereo teacher into a single-satellite student model that predicts dense 3D winds, uncertainties, and learned quality metrics directly from three consecutive frames. On held-out test periods, fine-tuning reduces aggregate vector RMS error against radiosondes by more than 15% and removes systematic slow speed biases. Gains are largest in water vapor channels (6.2, 6.9, and 7.3 m), where vector error drops by up to 40%. Triple collocation demonstrates that fine-tuned stereo intrinsic wind errors outperform operational GOES-19 AMVs across water vapor bands by 0.5 m/s, with retrieved heights validated against EarthCARE cloud radar profiles. Finally, the distilled student transfers these 3D retrievals across the full-disk geostationary domain without requiring overlapping satellite geometry.

495387.title: Investigation of Resolved Spatial Scales in Tropical Cyclone Intensification
495387.authors: Chandler Xavier Jenkins, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. M. Bell and L. G. Silvers
495387.abstract: While there has been significant progress in tropical cyclone (TC) forecasting over the past few decades, forecasting TC intensity has remained challenging. One of the main reasons that intensity forecasting is so difficult is the prominence of non-linear interactions between both temporal and spatial scales in TCs. Previous research has shown that the largest scales, or the lowest azimuthal wavenumbers, contain the most asymmetric spectral power in TCs. It remains unclear, however, precisely which spatial scales contribute the most to TC mixing and development, and if they need to be explicitly resolved or can be parameterized as statistical turbulence within numerical modeling. This study addresses these uncertainties using an idealized cylindrical two-layer modeling framework to capture the essential dynamics of TC intensification. The cylindrical nature of our model allows us to easily modify the azimuthal wavenumbers of the TC wind field, giving us control over which scales are fully resolved in our model. We conducted a set of experiments that show the impact of varying the forcing parameter and sub-grid mixing scale parameter on the intensification of our vortex. We find that the largest scales, wavenumbers 4 and below, resolve adequate asymmetric processes to result in TC intensification. The inclusion of scales smaller than wavenumber 4 leads to minimal changes in the TC intensification, indicating these smaller scales do not contribute much to the development of the storm. The results from this study suggest that low resolution models can capture the essential dynamics of TC intensification. This could potentially reduce the computational cost of TC modeling, allowing for large ensemble forecasts of low resolution TCs to be utilized for forecasting.

495389.title: Improving Multiscale Representation of MAPCast Surrogate Background Error Covariances through a Modified Scale-Dependent Loss Function
495389.authors: Yongming Wang, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and X. Wang
495389.abstract: A convection-allowing MPAS emulator, MAPCast, has been developed to generate surrogate background ensembles for estimating flow-dependent background error covariances (BECs) toward multiscale ensemble-based data assimilation (DA). A systematic evaluation using 10 retrospective convective storm cases demonstrated that, although MAPCast reproduces short-term MPAS forecasts with high overall fidelity, notable discrepancies remain in convective-scale structures and storm-related variables. In terms of BEC estimation, MAPCast accurately reproduces the magnitude and spatial distribution of ensemble spread for most variables, whereas larger errors are found for convective variables. Likewise, both univariate and multivariate correlation structures are reproduced most faithfully at mesoscale and larger scales, with substantially degraded agreement at convective scales. Collectively, these results indicate that the current version of MAPCast underrepresents near-grid-scale variability in both deterministic forecasts and ensemble-based BEC statistics. Similar smoothing behavior has also been reported for other machine learning-based weather models, particularly in medium- and longer-range forecasting (e.g., Price et al. 2025; Slivinski et al. 2025). To address this limitation, Subich et al. (2025) proposed a spherical harmonic loss function that substantially improves the representation of fine-scale structures in GraphCast forecasts. Motivated by these results, we propose to develop a scale-dependent training objective for MAPCast by replacing the conventional gridpoint-based mean squared error (MSE) loss with a multiscale loss constructed from wavelet decompositions of both the predicted and target fields. This formulation explicitly constrains forecast errors across spatial scales and is expected to improve the representation of convective-scale features while preserving large-scale accuracy. Systematic experiments using the same 10 retrospective convective storm cases will be conducted to quantify the impact of the proposed loss function on both forecast quality and the reproduction of multiscale BEC statistics.

495392.title: Evaluating the Sensitivities of WoFSCast: Towards Robust Convection-Allowing AI-NWP
495392.authors: Jorge Alberto Duarte, (CIWRO) Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; and C. K. Potvin and P. S. Skinner
495392.abstract: Machine learning-based numerical weather prediction (AI-NWP) emulators have shown revolutionary potential for rapid, low-latency forecasting. This study presents a comprehensive physical sensitivity and architectural robustness framework for WoFSCast, a 50-million parameter, limited-area Graph Neural Network (GNN) designed to emulate the NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory’s Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS) at convection-allowing scales (3 km). While training WoFSCast is highly data-intensive, operational inference is extremely lightweight compared to WoFS. It requires only a single WoFS analysis state (t=0) and a single forecast state (t=10 min) to generate an 18-member, 6-hour forecast rollout in approximately 30 seconds on a single multi-GPU node. In this study, we systematically interrogate the GNN’s physical representation and optimal configuration through four core sensitivity experiments. First, we evaluate the impact of vertical resolution; while the baseline WoFSCast utilizes 17 of 51 available vertical levels, we test configurations using 10, 34, and all 51 levels. Second, we assess model sensitivity to temporal resolution by varying the integration timestep from the baseline 10 minutes to extended 30- and 60-minute intervals. Third, we perform systematic feature ablation on the current predictor set to quantify the relative physical importance of specific environmental inputs. Finally, we evaluate the impact of training data provenance by comparing models trained exclusively on analysis data against those trained directly on WoFS forecast data. Through these analyses, we quantify the rate of spatial blurring, spectral energy decay of composite reflectivity fields, and other key physical characteristics over the 0–6 hour forecast window. We evaluate model performance using grid- and object-based verification methods designed to isolate specific errors associated with short-term thunderstorm prediction, including errors in storm size, shape, and complexity. This work establishes a baseline physical interpretation and optimal configuration profile for WoFSCast, validating its ability to sustain realistic convective structures under varying architectural constraints. Ultimately, this research sets the stage for future advancements in operational robustness (e.g., resilience to missing data) and gradient-based attribution (e.g., using saliency maps to mathematically rank input variable importance for convective predictions).

495393.title: AI-Based Parameter Calibration for Wildland-Urban Interface Fire Spread Modeling
495393.authors: Huilin Huang, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA; and Z. Xia, S. Cheng, Y. Liu, Y. Chen, and T. Chakraborty
495393.abstract: Accurate, rapid prediction of wildland-urban interface (WUI) fire spread is critical for effective management, but the stochastic, fine-scale complexity of WUI fires makes traditional simulators slow and difficult to calibrate. Current fire spread models mostly depend on arbitrary parameters and lack calibration against real observations, making their performance unreliable and difficult to trust in operational settings. We present an enhanced, GPU-accelerated, fully differentiable version of PyTorchFire that calibrates its physical parameters using gradient descent (back-propagation) on observed fire lines. This AI-based calibration also identifies which physical parameters most strongly control fire spread at each stage of an event. The model assimilates near-real-time satellite fire detections, updating parameters as new observations arrive while maintaining numerical stability despite the noisy, unpredictable nature of fire spread. Applied to the 2025 Palisades Fire, back-propagation recovers the same optimal parameters as exhaustive grid search at a small fraction of the computational cost, enabling near-real-time calibration during an active event. The dominant drivers of fire spread shift from wind- to slope-dominated between the first and second 12 hours of the fire, revealing how fire behavior evolves within a single event.

495394.title: Environmental Controls on Hail Growth during ICECHIP IOP12: Insights from Ensemble Data Assimilation and Hail Trajectory Modeling
495394.authors: Tengdai Yang, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and X. Chen and Y. Zhang
495394.abstract: Hail growth within severe convective storms is strongly influenced by the thermodynamic and kinematic environment, yet the relative roles of different environmental factors and the physical pathways through which they affect hail production remain uncertain. This study investigates environmental controls on hail growth using Intensive Observing Period 12 (IOP12) from the In-situ Collaborative Experiment for the Collection of Hail In the Plains (ICECHIP). IOP12 occurred on 6-7 June 2025 in the Texas Panhandle near Lubbock, Texas. Convection initiated along a dryline near and west of the New Mexico-Texas border and subsequently moved eastward. The storm underwent a classic supercell-splitting process, with the resulting right-moving supercell producing a long hail swath and reported hailstones as large as baseball size (2.75 in) near Cochran, Texas. A convection-permitting ensemble data assimilation experiment is constructed using the Penn State WRF-EnKF system with 1.5-km horizontal grid spacing and 40 ensemble members. The experiment assimilates all-sky infrared brightness temperatures from GOES-19 ABI Channel 10, radar reflectivity and radial velocity from the Lubbock NEXRAD radar (KLBB), and conventional surface and upper-air observations at 5-min intervals. 40-member ensemble forecasts initialized from the EnKF analyses are integrated from 21 UTC on June 6 through 0300 UTC on June 7. Most ensemble members reproduce an east-southeastward-moving hail swath broadly consistent with observed hail reports, while substantial member-to-member variability occurs in storm evolution and hail-swath location, orientation, and length. Objective convective-cell tracking is then applied to each ensemble member to identify the simulated counterpart of the observed hail-producing supercell. Meteorological fields associated with each tracked storm are subsequently used to drive the Penn State Hail Trajectory Model, providing member-specific estimates of hail growth and surface hail size. Ensemble sensitivity analysis (ESA) is then used to relate variations in model maximum and mean surface hail diameter to differences in the pre-storm environment and storm structure represented by the EnKF ensemble. Preliminary results reveal a pronounced vertical dependence of the relationship between environmental moisture and hail size. Both maximum and mean surface hail diameters are positively correlated with lower-level relative humidity, particularly between surface and 800 hPa, but negatively correlated with relative humidity in the 750-600 hPa layer. The ESA further indicates that low- and mid-level vertical wind shear, including 0-1.5 km and 0-3 km shear, is closely associated with the early development and organization of the hail-producing storm, whereas hail size exhibits substantially weaker sensitivity to conventional 0-6 km deep-layer shear. These results suggest that the vertical distribution of environmental moisture and lower-tropospheric shear may influence hail production by regulating storm organization, updraft and downdraft structure, hailstone residence time within favorable growth regions, and melting during descent. The physical mechanisms underlying these statistical relationships will be further examined using targeted WRF sensitivity experiments.

495398.title: Future Weakening of Tropical Pacific Decadal Variability in High-Resolution CESM Simulations
495398.authors: Who Myung Kim, NCAR, Boulder, CO; IBS Center for Climate Physics, Busan, Korea, Republic of (South); and J. Y. Lee
495398.abstract: Future changes in tropical Pacific decadal variability (TPDV) are investigated in this study using a 10-member ensemble of high-resolution (HR) Community Earth System Model (CESM) historical and RCP8.5 simulations with a nominal horizontal resolution of 0.1º in the ocean and 0.25 º in the atmosphere. Results are compared with those from the low-resolution (LR) CESM Large Ensemble simulations. In contrast to a substantial increase in the canonical El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) under global warming in the LR-CESM, consistent with the response commonly simulated in low-resolution climate models, the HR-CESM exhibits a substantial decrease in TPDV despite little change in the canonical ENSO variability. The reduction in TPDV is accompanied by decreased decadal sea surface height (SSH) variability in the southwestern tropical Pacific. The TPDV in the HR-CESM appears to be initiated by variations in the South Pacific Convergence Zone (SPCZ) and associated wind stress curl forcing. Enhanced SPCZ and associated convergence of winds induce Ekman suction, depressing SSH in the southwestern tropical Pacific as Rossby waves propagate westward. A cyclonic circulation develops around the SSH depression, strengthening the equatorward western boundary current and enhancing heat convergence in the western to central equatorial Pacific. This equatorial warming weakens the trade winds and associated upwelling of cold waters in the central to eastern equatorial Pacific, further warming the region. The warming in the equatorial Pacific triggers the Pacific Meridional Mode in both hemispheres via extra-tropical teleconnections, generating the characteristic TPDV SST pattern. During the late 20th century, SPCZ variability appears to be linked to pronounced decadal SST variability in the Kuroshio-Oyashio Extension (KOE) region. The opposite-polarity response of the Northern Hemisphere Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) suggests that KOE SST variability modulates the SPCZ through an energetic constraint. By the late 21st century, the KOE SST variability weakens and consequently leads to weaker TPDV. These results suggest a new pathway through which extratropical SST variability influences TPDV by modulating the SPCZ through an energetic constraint, highlighting the importance of extratropical SST variability for understanding and projecting future changes in TPDV.

495399.title: AI-Based Forecast Representations of Sea Breezes In the WFIP3 Study Domain
495399.authors: Lindsay Marie Sheridan, PNNL, Richland, WA; and M. Thomas, N. Bodini, and R. Krishnamurthy
495399.abstract: The northeastern United States seaboard is characterized by two major features that influence local and regional energy supply and demand: 1) a variety of weather phenomena that can positively or negatively impact the availability and cost of energy and 2) dense urban populations that are experiencing growth. Accurate representation of impactful weather phenomena, such as sea breezes that impact energy demand and load over the region, is critical for establishing both long-term and short-term energy generation expectations. The ability of vetted forecast and reanalysis models to represent boundary layer phenomena, particularly winds, along the northeastern United States coast has been well established, thanks to a variety of land-based and water-based observational campaigns that occurred between 2015 and 2025. However, in recent years, significant investments have been made in the development of data-driven weather forecast models, particularly by for-profit companies. While early investigations into the performance of data-driven weather models show success on average metrics, recent studies have noted that such models can produce unrealistically smooth forecasts, with that trend becoming more pronounced with increased lead time. Using observations gathered along the northeastern U.S. mid-Atlantic bight during the third Wind Forecast Improvement Project (WFIP3), we establish the performance of several recently released AI-based weather models in their representation of large-scale forcing driving sea breezes. The AI-based models, including AIFS, FourCastNet3, and WeatherNext2, alongside a well-vetted physics-based model, HRRR, will be evaluated for their ability to 1) identify an observed sea breeze event and 2) represent the meteorological characteristics of each event over the duration of each model’s forecast lead times. For each model, errors during sea breeze events will be shared in the context of relevant meteorological variables and energy demand and load estimates.

495400.title: Introducing the NWS Office of Modeling and Development: Unifying NWS Numerical Weather Prediction, Guidance, and Application Development
495400.authors: Richard Bandy, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and D. T. Kleist
495400.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) established the Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) to unify the end-to-end modeling enterprise, strengthen coordination across the modeling lifecycle, and accelerate the transition of scientific advances into operational forecasting. OMD will be responsible for executing the full spectrum of modeling and development necessary for the provision of forecast information to support the National Weather Service Mission, including: observations ingest & processing; data assimilation; modeling; value added post-processing and guidance generation; verification evaluation; and visualizations and application development supporting service delivery. Another benefit of this unification would be centrally managed engagement with the research community and private sector for accelerated discovery and implementation of innovative science and technology solutions including a focus on implementations of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning solutions. The new office has a commitment to direct stakeholder engagement and collaboration, enabled by a shared technical infrastructure, to support rapid and continuous improvements through a user driven agile and continuous development process. In addition to providing more details on the new office, information will be provided about the new Center's strategic priorities and projects underway to fulfill that vision. Those efforts will be in alignment with the NOAA NWP Moonshot goals, which include: achieving a fully coupled, km-scale global model based on the MPAS dynamical core; advancing data driven (AI/ML) modeling efforts to supplement the traditional NWP; improving NOAA’s modeling infrastructure and accelerating the innovation to operational pipeline; and implementing user-driven probabilistic guidance improvements and service delivery tools.

495402.title: Air Quality Insights from a Dense Sensor Network and High-Resolution Land Use in Chicago
495402.authors: Grant Coleman, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and A. F. Dickens and Z. E. Adelman
495402.abstract: Reducing nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) concentrations is a central ozone-attainment strategy in the Chicago region, but the sparse regulatory monitoring network limits the ability to attribute urban NO₂ patterns to specific emission sources. This study tests whether data from a dense, low-cost sensor network can be used to characterise fine-scale variability in NO2 concentrations and investigate whether shared patterns in NO2 correspond to distinct urban source environments. The University of Illinois Chicago and the City of Chicago established a new network of air quality sensors, Open Air Chicago, with 277 Clarity Node-S NO2 and PM2.5 sensors arranged on a roughly 1.5-km grid across the city. We analysed nine months of hourly NO₂ observations (September 2025-May 2026) from the Open Air Chicago sensors comprising 7,153,586 observations. We characterised seasonal, weekly, and diurnal concentration behaviour of each sensor and applied principal component analysis, followed by hierarchical clustering, to group sensors. We then characterised land use, roadway traffic, and rail infrastructure within 0.5-, 1-, and 2-km buffers around each sensor using the land use inventory from Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning, the Illinois Department of Transportation’s Average Annual Daily Traffic, and the U.S. Census Bureau’s TIGER/Line data, and tested for associations between clusters and the land use variables. The NO2 sensors grouped into five clusters. Mean sensor-level NO₂ concentrations differed significantly (Kruskal-Wallis H = 206.5, p < 0.001), with approximately 6-7 ppb separating the highest- and lowest-concentration clusters. All clusters exhibited similar broad diurnal structure, including an early-morning peak, midday minimum, and evening enhancement, but differed in concentration magnitude and seasonal variability. The highest-concentration cluster increased from approximately 18-19 ppb in early fall to a winter maximum near 26 ppb. The strongest land-use signals occurred within the 0.5 km buffers of the sensors. Industrial land use accounted for approximately 15% of the buffer area surrounding the highest-concentration cluster, compared with minimal industrial land use in the lower-concentration clusters. Transportation-related land use was widespread and therefore provided limited discrimination when considered as a single category. However, separating roadway infrastructure from other transportation uses revealed stronger differences: rail right-of-way and intermodal facilities comprised approximately 85% of non-roadway transportation land use surrounding the highest-concentration cluster. This cluster also had the greatest mean rail length within the 0.5 km buffer distance. In contrast, roadway traffic volume alone did not consistently distinguish high- and low-NO₂ environments. These results indicate that near-source (< 0.5 km) NO₂ variability in Chicago is associated with distinct land use categories. Transportation, freight, and industrial infrastructure are associated with higher NO2 concentrations; open space is associated with lower NO2 concentrations. Integrating dense sensor observations with high-resolution urban land use data can therefore identify recurring urban concentration regimes and their associated source environments. Future analyses using this data framework that incorporates meteorology and facility-level emissions can be used to further evaluate source-receptor relationships and inform emissions control strategies that target the most impactful sources on sub-urban scales.

495403.title: Constraining Peroxy Radical Fate with Isoprene Chemistry
495403.authors: Michael A. Robinson, NOAA, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Univ. of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and M. M. Coggon, K. Bates, J. Peischl, C. Jernigan, S. Thakali, G. Novak, P. R. Veres, J. M. Roberts, D. Jeong, M. Rutherford, L. Xu, C. Stockwell, C. Warneke, A. Rollins, K. Ball, J. Crounse, P. O. Wennberg, and S. S. Brown
495403.abstract: Declining nitrogen oxide (NOx = NO + NO2) emissions across North America are changing atmospheric oxidation pathways, altering the production efficiency of tropospheric ozone and secondary organic aerosol. Organic peroxy radicals (RO2), key intermediates in volatile organic compound oxidation, dictate these photochemical regimes through competing bimolecular reactions with NO, HO2, and other RO2 radicals, or through unimolecular isomerization. During the summer 2023 NOAA-led AEROMMA mission, an iodide chemical ionization mass spectrometer (I− CIMS) was deployed to measure isoprene oxidation products. We formulate a measurement-based proxy (fNO*) for the fraction of RO2 reacting with NO by comparing isoprene hydroxy nitrates (∑IHN) from high-NO pathways to isoprene hydroperoxides and epoxydiols (∑[ISOPOOH + IEPOX]) from low-NO pathways. We evaluate this framework across major North American urban plumes characterizing variability in RO2 bimolecular lifetimes (τbi) and comparing in situ metrics against regional TEMPO geostationary satellite retrievals of column formaldehyde-to-NO2 ratios. To extend this framework beyond urban boundary layers, we evaluate observations from high-altitude convective outflow. In these low-NO, lower-temperature regimes, longer bimolecular lifetimes alter the competition between RO2 + HO2 and RO2 + NO reactions. Resolving these shifting RO2 fates from the urban boundary layer to convective outflow provides critical observational constraints for models evaluating RO2 chemistry.

495406.title: Physics Sensitivities in the Track and Intensity Forecasts of Hurricane Ian (2022): Analysis of a Multi-Scheme HAFS Ensemble
495406.authors: Myah Rather, Howard University, NW, Washington, DC; and A. Hazelton, F. Hsiao, S. Chiao, and S. Gopalakrishnan
495406.abstract: Hurricane Ian (2022) underwent significant track and intensity evolution as it approached the Gulf Coast of Florida, motivating continued investigation into the sensitivity of forecast outcomes to model physics configuration. This study uses an ensemble of 2023 Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) simulations, spanning multiple cumulus parameterization and physics schemes, to evaluate how cumulus parameterization and various physics schemes choice influences ensemble track and intensity spread for Hurricane Ian. Serial correlation analysis is applied to relate early-forecast position and motion to the final forecast position within each physics configuration, following methodology used in prior HAFS ensemble studies of tropical cyclone track sensitivity (e.g., Hazelton et al. 2023). Preliminary results reveal that forecast hour ~60, we see a significant increase with the ensemble’s interaction with Cuba and a northward turn is made in Ian’s tracks. Prior to this transition, early latitude is a stronger predictor of final longitude than early longitude itself, suggesting that the timing of each member's northward turn — rather than its early zonal (east–west) drift — was the dominant control on ultimate track position. This pattern is consistent across all five physics configurations examined, pointing to forecast hour ~60–70 as a critical window for further investigation of the synoptic steering features governing Ian's track evolution. This analysis contributes to a growing body of work using ensemble-based diagnostics to understand how convective parameterization affects tropical cyclone track and intensity predictability, with implications for physics scheme selection in operational HAFS configurations.

495407.title: Cloudy With a Chance of Misinterpretation: Why Accurate Forecasts Aren't Enough
495407.authors: Katie Rose Bachli, SUNY, Albany, NY; and M. S. Michaud, A. A. Jacques, and D. Van Hoesen
495407.abstract: Weather forecasts have never been more accurate; today’s five-day forecast matches the reliability of a 1980 one-day forecast. This progress is driven by advancements in remote sensing, numerical weather prediction, and computing power. However, improved accuracy does not automatically guarantee public safety. A critical gap persists between what a forecast intends to communicate and how the recipient interprets its severity and required response. Misinterpretations can cause underpreparedness, ultimately increasing injuries, fatalities, and emergency response demands. Announced in December 2023, the New York State Weather Risk Communication Center (NYSWRCC) bridges this gap by applying social science and human-centered design to operational meteorology. Rather than over-saturating stakeholders with raw data, the Center focuses on how individuals process risk information to build products aligned with actual decision-making behaviors. This poster explores how the NYSWRCC integrates meteorology, social science, and emergency management to transform complex data into actionable guidance. We detail the Center’s daily operations, strategic partnerships, and iterative product development. Furthermore, we highlight our empirical framework—utilizing surveys, focus groups, and human-centered design principles—to evaluate and optimize state weather briefings. A specific focus is placed on tailoring risk communication for vulnerable populations whose mitigation capacities differ from the general public. Ultimately, advanced forecasts are only as effective as a community's capacity to understand and act upon them. The NYSWRCC shifts the operational paradigm away from simply distributing forecasts toward communicating actionable risk. This approach supports optimized decision-making, sturdier preparedness frameworks, and safer communities.

495408.title: Improvements to MET Norway's Operational Data-Driven Weather Model Bris
495408.authors: Håvard Haugen, MET Norway, OSLO, OSLO, Norway; and T. Nipen, I. Seierstad, E. M. Nordhagen, and J. Kristiansen
495408.abstract: Bris is MET Norway's operational data-driven weather model, which uses a global stretched-grid architecture, combining a coarse resolution (31 km) global domain with a nested high-resolution (2.5 km) region over our Nordic and Arctic focus areas. Bris is initialized four times a day from global IFS and regional MEPS and AROME-Arctic analyses, providing ensemble forecasts at hourly resolution ten days into the future. Bris is a graph-transformer model developed within the Anemoi framework. This presentation describes some of the recent improvements to Bris. Firstly, we have introduced a wide range of surface physiography descriptors as forcing variables, giving the model the ability to distinguish grid points covering urban areas, lakes, forests, and glaciers. This significantly improves the forecasts locally, especially in urban areas where earlier versions of the model exhibited strong temperature biases. Near-surface wind speeds are also improved due to differentiation of surface roughness length. Secondly, we have introduced snow depth and sea-ice concentration as prognostic variables allowing the model to forecast their evolution jointly with the atmospheric state. These changes are enabled by a full retraining of the model on the newly released CARRA2 reanalysis, which provides a long record of high-resolution Arctic and sub-Arctic training data. We evaluate the updated model against its predecessor and against MEPS, MET Norway's operational NWP ensemble, using case studies and verification at surface observation stations across the Nordic and Arctic domains.

495409.title: Tropical Mesoscale Convective Systems under a Kilometer-Scale Future Climate Scenario
495409.authors: Kelly M. Núñez Ocasio, ; and E. M. Dougherty and Z. Moon
495409.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) across North Africa and the adjacent Atlantic Ocean are major contributors to regional precipitation, but they can also generate hazardous flooding and, particularly when associated with African easterly waves (AEWs), contribute to the development of Atlantic tropical cyclones. Here, we examine the response of African–Atlantic MCSs to climate warming using 3-km convection-permitting simulations with the Model for Prediction Across Scales–Atmosphere (MPAS-A). Convective activity during September 2006 is simulated under present-day and pseudo–global warming conditions, allowing us to isolate the effects of a warmer climate on MCS characteristics and behavior. Objective tracking of MCSs indicates that, despite a substantial increase in convective available potential energy (CAPE), the number of MCSs decreases in the future climate, primarily because of a pronounced increase in convective inhibition (CIN). Changes in MCS intensity based on brightness temperature are comparatively modest; however, both organized and disorganized systems produce greater rainfall under future conditions. The enhancement is particularly pronounced for organized MCSs over the Atlantic Ocean, where increasing relative humidity contrasts with a decrease over land and contributes to stronger precipitation responses. Future MCS activity also exhibits a southward displacement, with systems tending to propagate eastward across Africa and westward over the Atlantic. These shifts reduce the spatial overlap between MCSs and the African easterly jet while increasing their association with the West African monsoon and AEWs. The most extreme future MCSs are characterized by stronger updrafts and downdrafts and a drier mid- to lower troposphere, conditions that help explain enhanced rainfall evaporation. Building on these findings, we will also share results from new MPAS-A kilometer-scale simulations spanning the June–September (JJAS) season, including both historical and future climate periods, to further investigate how changes in the large-scale environment influence MCS characteristics, organization, and precipitation across the Africa–Atlantic region. These simulations provide an opportunity to assess the robustness of the September results and to explore the broader seasonal implications of climate change for high-impact convective systems.

495411.title: UAS and LiDAR-Based Digital Elevation Analysis: Characterizing Land-Surface Impacts on Tornado Dynamics
495411.authors: Lydia Bunting, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; and E. Tirone, A. W. Lyza, and E. N. Smith
495411.abstract: The Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO) and NOAA’s National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) deploy uncrewed aerial systems (UASs) to gather high-resolution multispectral imagery and three-dimensional data via aerial LiDAR and digital elevation models (DEMs). While these datasets offer critical insights into tornadic dynamics and structural damage, the specific influence of underlying terrain on storm evolution remains under-characterized. To better quantify terrain–tornado interactions, this study evaluates post-event DEM characteristics across affected landscapes. By assessing comparative surface metrics of terrain ruggedness, roughness length, and rugosity, this study aims to determine how these parameters can be leveraged to characterize land-surface impacts on tornado behavior and path geometry.

495412.title: Translating Seasonal Climate Predictability into Actionable Information for Energy Systems
495412.authors: Juan P. Montoya-Rincon, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and K. W. Dixon, K. L. Findell, and A. Radhakrishnan
495412.abstract: Weather and climate information supports a wide range of energy-sector decisions, from short-term operations and grid management to longer-term planning and infrastructure investment across hourly to decadal timescales. At seasonal timescales, climate forecasts can provide advance information about conditions that affect grid reliability, electricity demand, renewable-energy availability, and other weather-sensitive energy operations. However, translating seasonal climate predictions into reliable, decision-relevant information remains challenging because forecast skill varies across regions, seasons, lead times, and applications. Building on prior work aimed at understanding the effects of climate variability and long-term change on the energy landscape, this study extends that work toward seasonal timescales for the development of actionable climate information for energy systems. In this context, the study focuses on identifying relationships between seasonal climate conditions and observed energy-system behavior, with an emphasis on which compound climate conditions and patterns of occurrence are most strongly associated with energy-relevant outcomes, such as elevated demand during temperature extremes coinciding with reduced wind or solar resource availability. The analysis emphasizes how information contained in seasonal climate predictions can be related to observed energy conditions and translated into metrics relevant to energy-system applications. Historical energy-sector datasets, including regional electricity demand and renewable-generation records, are combined with meteorological observations and reanalysis products to characterize climate–energy relationships across regions and seasons. These observed relationships provide the foundation for identifying energy-relevant climate conditions and metrics that can ultimately be evaluated at seasonal lead times using prediction systems such as the NOAA Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL) Seamless System for Prediction and EArth System Research (SPEAR). The resulting framework is designed to enable the use of SPEAR hindcast archives to assess the predictability of compound climate conditions, with applications spanning energy demand, renewable generation, and other weather-sensitive operations. Moving forward, this analysis can be extended to explore the potential benefits of bias correction, statistical downscaling, and application-specific calibration for improved regional fidelity and predictive performance. These efforts contribute to a broader goal of developing reliable, actionable, and stakeholder-relevant seasonal climate products for planning, preparedness, and decision-making.

495415.title: Communicating Compound Wind and Water Hazards to English and Spanish-Speaking Audiences: Preliminary Results from a Bilingual National Survey of Broadcast Meteorologists
495415.authors: Rodolfo Andres Hernandez, NCAS, Washington, D.C., DC; Howard University, Washington DC, DC; and J. Henderson and E. R. Nielsen
495415.abstract: Broadcast meteorologists serve as critical intermediaries between National Weather Service forecasts and the public, particularly during landfalling tropical cyclones (LTCs) that generate compound wind and water hazards—tornadoes, storm surge, flash flooding, and inland flooding. For Spanish-speaking and bilingual (SP-EN) broadcast meteorologists, communicating these evolving, multi-hazard threats is complicated by a warning infrastructure built primarily around English-language conventions, including the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, which emphasizes wind over water hazards and does not capture the risks posed by post-landfall remnants (PTCs). This ongoing, NOAA-funded project examines how English and bilingual (Spanish-speaking) broadcast meteorologists across the U.S. assess, communicate, and adapt hazard information for their audiences during LTCs and their remnants. Building on prior qualitative work with broadcasters affected by Hurricane Ida, the research team developed and fielded a national, bilingual (English/Spanish) survey of broadcast meteorologists. The instrument captures hazard experience and audience demographics; strategies and channels used for non-English-language communication; perceived effectiveness of the Saffir-Simpson scale for compound hazards; and challenges in translating technical hazard terminology for vulnerable populations. This presentation will report preliminary results from the survey, focusing on how broadcasters characterize compound hazard risk for their audiences, the languages and channels used to reach non-English speakers, and broadcaster perceptions of the Saffir-Simpson scale’s utility for communicating wind-water hazard interactions. Findings will inform the development of Research-to-Operations (R2O) products and processes to support broadcast meteorologists who serve linguistically diverse audiences during landfalling tropical cyclones.

495417.title: Improving the Accuracy of Visibility Forecasting in the Chiayi and Kinmen Regions Using Neural Network Models
495417.authors: Chih-Ying Chen, Academia Sinica, Taiwan, Taipei, TPQ, Taiwan; and Y. C. Wang and S. C. Tsai
495417.abstract: This study focuses on the Chiayi and Kinmen stations to evaluate the potential impacts of winter low-visibility phenomena on regional aviation safety and to construct data-driven hourly visibility forecasting models. The dataset integrates hourly surface observations from the Central Weather Administration (CWA) and air quality monitoring factors (, ) from the Ministry of Environment, alongside exogenous inputs from a numerical weather prediction model (WRF) to simulate forecasting scenarios. Based on Pearson correlation coefficients and weighted hotspot analysis, relative humidity, historical visibility, and particulate matter (PM) concentrations emerge as the primary controlling factors. Specifically, low visibility in Chiayi is predominantly driven by pollutant accumulation, whereas Kinmen is more influenced by humidity conditions and advection fog environments. Methodologically, traditional empirical formulas (FSL, SW99) and Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) serve as baseline models, while sequential deep learning models, including LSTM and Transformer, are constructed to compare forecasting performance across different lead times. Model training incorporates normalization, regularization, and early stopping to mitigate overfitting. Comprehensive evaluations and case analyses are conducted using both continuous metrics (, ) and event-based threshold metrics (/). Event thresholds are set according to flight-operability standards, including , for Chiayi, and for Kinmen. The results indicate that traditional formulas have limited applicability across both stations, and while MLR partially reduces errors, it remains constrained by linear assumptions. In terms of continuous metrics, LSTM demonstrates higher overall stability and superior and values for both Chiayi and Kinmen, making it a suitable backbone model for continuous visibility forecasting. For event-based threshold metrics, the Transformer model exhibits better overall performance in identifying low-visibility events (/), though its efficacy varies significantly by site: the Kinmen Transformer shows higher skill in recognizing advection fog low-visibility events, offering effective hit rates for extremely low visibility thresholds at and . Conversely, in Chiayi, due to pollutant accumulation and complex underlying mechanisms, although the model enhances early warning capability at the threshold, predicting extreme events corresponding to the airport’s minimum operational standard of remains challenging—highlighting that predictability under high-PM-concentration scenarios remains a major limitation. Exogenous model scenario analysis further reveals a clear "exogenous data quality ceiling" in visibility forecasting: when WRF inputs contain systematic biases or temporal phase errors, the performance gains provided by AI models are constrained. To improve exogenous input quality, this study compares raw WRF data (), Quantile Delta Mapping ( via //), and XGBoost bias correction, applying variable-optimized corrections: pollutant variables (/) achieve the greatest bias reduction when pre-corrected via XGBoost; sea-level pressure () is better aligned using ; while pressure trend () and certain moisture/thermal variables remain more stable when retaining raw WRF data at specific stations. This highlights that exogenous variable bias exhibits strong variable-dependent and station-dependent characteristics.

495418.title: Impact of 50 GHz Band Radio Frequency Interference on Global Weather Forecasts
495418.authors: Agnes Lim, CIMSS, MADISON, WI; and A. B. Crews, D. K. Kwon, Y. Peng, R. A. Leduc, MPP, S. K. Avery, M. Knapp, S. Palo, and Z. Li
495418.abstract: Operational Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) centers have reported that microwave sounders that measure the earth’s temperature and humidity have the largest impact on reducing the global weather forecast errors. Microwave sounders carrying channels in the 50GHz bands and are used for data assimilation at NWP centers. Such sounders include the Advanced Microwave Sounding Unit (AMSU-A), the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS), and the Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS). As these instruments fly on multiple satellite platforms (such as the NOAA series, the METOP series, and the DMSP series), their observation counts contribute a significant proportion of the total observations being assimilated routinely for NWP. Radio Frequency Interference (RFI) in the 50 GHz channels can degrade the quality of these observations or even render them unusable. If the interferences are of a magnitude significantly larger than atmospheric variability, they are likely to be screened out prior to assimilation, thus losing all these microwave radiance measurements. If the interferences are of a similar magnitude as atmospheric variability, the data assimilation system may not be able to identify the degraded observations caused by RFI. Instead, the contaminated data will be assimilated into the model as valid information, potentially leading to forecast degradation. The Radio Science Coexistence Simulator (RSC-SIM) is a sophisticated Python-based framework initially developed to simulate the impact of RF signals from satellite constellations on radio telescope observations and instruments. It has since been expanded to model RFI affecting down-looking weather satellites. The weather satellite simulator component calculates RFI from sources beneath the satellite, including 5G mmWave ground networks and Starlink gateway ground stations, while accounting for atmospheric effects such as absorption by water vapor and oxygen, as well as attenuation by clouds and rain. The simulator then integrates the total calculated RFI into the weather satellite's baseline radiance measurements. Observing system experiments are used to assess the impact of RFI. This presentation compares two distinct RFI scenarios against a clean baseline where the 50 GHz band satellite radiances remain uncontaminated. The first scenario simulates a total loss of the 50 GHz band, while the second incorporates simulated RFI contributions generated by RSC-SIM.

495419.title: The Revolution in Water Vapor Detection and Tracking in the GeoXO Era
495419.authors: Dan Lindsey, NOAA / NESDIS / GEO, Greenbelt, MD; NOAA/NESDIS, Fort Collins, CO; and A. Heidinger and J. M. Haynes
495419.abstract: Atmospheric water vapor is a necessary and essential component of convection and plays a key role in the severity of storms. Low-level water vapor in particular is ingested by convective updrafts, and the amount of low-level water vapor is proportional to convective instability. Current geostationary imagers, such as the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) flying on NOAA’s GOES-R series, can be used to track mid- and upper-level water vapor, but they lack the ability to easily identify moisture in that critical layer near the surface. For these reasons, in planning for NOAA’s future geostationary satellite program, GeoXO (Geostationary Extended Observations), two new spectral channels were selected for the new imager (GXI) centered near 0.91 and 5.15 μm, both of which targeting low-level water vapor. In addition, for the first time, NOAA will be launching a hyperspectral infrared sounder (GXS) to sit side-by-side with GXI, and it too can be used to retrieve and track water vapor at multiple levels, including near the surface. Proxy data is now available over Europe and Africa from the new Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) geostationary satellites and serves as the ideal tool for studying water vapor retrieval methodologies. This presentation will describe the improvements that GeoXO instruments will offer in water vapor detection and tracking, and will show a number of examples from both MTG observations and numerical simulations.

495420.title: Integrating Post-Event UAS Imagery to Assess Surface Effects on Tornado Behavior
495420.authors: Elizabeth Tirone, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; and L. Bunting, A. W. Lyza, and E. N. Smith
495420.abstract: Uncrewed aerial systems (UASs) are utilized by the Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO) and the NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) to collect high resolution multispectral imagery and 3-dimensional data with digital elevation models (DEMs) and aerial LiDAR. While this information is critical in understanding spatial patterns in damage and characteristics of the tornado including path width, the location of tornado genesis and dissipation, on its own fails to provide information about the tornado’s winds near the surface. Using UAS derived aerial data collected after tornadoes in close proximity to radar provides an avenue to investigate how the land surface impacts the characteristics of the tornado. This study leverages statistical and machine learning techniques to isolate and attribute localized changes in tornado behavior to specific properties of the land surface. High-resolution surface metrics derived from UAS imagery and LiDAR (e.g., terrain slope, ruggedness, land use) are coupled with radar-derived metrics (e.g., low-level rotational velocity, radius of maximum winds, and storm structure). By synthesizing these observational datasets, this analytical framework aims to disentangle surface-induced perturbations from intrinsic storm dynamics, enhancing our ability to understand and predict low-level tornadic characteristics and track behavior.

495421.title: Amplified Warming In Tropical and Subtropical Cities Under 2 °C Climate Change
495421.authors: Sarah Berk, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; and M. Joshi, C. Goodess, and P. Nowack
495421.abstract: Urban areas face increasing heat risks due to increases in global temperatures due to climate change, and potential changes in their heat islands, which are influenced both by regional climate and land surface types. However, the relatively coarse spatial resolutions of Earth System Models (ESMs) limits their ability to resolve urban-rural temperature differences for small or medium sized cities. Consequently, current climate projections may not capture differences in how urban and rural areas respond to future climate change. To bridge this gap, we combine satellite observations, reanalysis data and CMIP6 ESM projections to develop a machine learning approach to estimate projections of changes in land surface temperature (LST) for 104 medium sized cities (population 300k to 1 million) in the tropics and subtropics. The model was trained to predict observed surface urban heat island (SUHI) magnitudes from climatic and land surface characteristics, then changes in climatic and vegetation drivers from five ESMs used to project SUHI changes at 2 °C global mean warming. Under this scenario, annual mean LST in 81% of these cities is projected to increase faster than the surrounding area, with a mean additional urban warming of 0.4 °C beyond regional ESM-projected warming.In 16% of cities, including several in India and China, this additional warming exceeds 50% of the projected regional warming. These results show that future urban warming may be underestimated in future projections, identifying potential key areas, and emphasizing the need for future study into the interaction between urban areas and climate change.

495423.title: The Institutional Integration of Social Science at NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory
495423.authors: Jamie Vickery, n/a, Boulder, CO; NOAA Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and K. Fenton, B. J. Hatchett, S. M. Hoekstra, L. McMeeking, PhD, and E. Wells
495423.abstract: This presentation examines the institutional evolution of NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL), highlighting an end-to-end approach that centers user needs across all research divisions. Spanning foundational social science research, early-stage model transitions, impact-based verification, decision-support tool co-design, and traditional atmospheric science, this cross-disciplinary framework demonstrates the measurable value and mission-relevant success of fully integrated decision science. Illustrative of this institutional change is GSL’s Decision Support Research and Evaluation (DSRE) Branch. The DSRE Branch serves as the organizational nexus for this shift, formalizing the integration of user needs research and social science methods in an interdisciplinary laboratory. Rather than confining social science applications to end-stage software interfaces, GSL is meaningfully integrating these methodologies throughout project lifecycles across its three science divisions. We examine this convergence through three primary efforts: 1) collaborative research and evaluation efforts with the Fire Weather Testbed (FWT); 2) prospective collaborations to apply user needs across the lab by collecting, documenting, and applying user thresholds into early-stage physical and statistical development; and 3) the ongoing shift toward impact-based verification frameworks that evaluate models by their societal utility rather than meteorological metrics alone. Finally, we provide a scalable roadmap and actionable lessons learned for other federal agencies and research institutions looking to leverage and integrate social science to ensure physical modeling provides real-world impact.

495425.title: Probing Cloud-Precipitation Processes with Radar, In-Model Instrument Emulation, and a Perturbed Parameter Ensemble (PPE)
495425.authors: August Mikkelsen, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and I. Silber, D. McCoy, and J. M. Nugent
495425.abstract: Marine cloud and precipitation processes are important to Earth system predictability but remain difficult to confidently observe at scale. Earth system model (ESM) representations of marine precipitation processes come with parametric and structural uncertainties that are challenging to disentangle, a problem made more difficult without a process-scale observational record to compare against. Data from the DOE Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility are uniquely useful in this regard, as even the lightest precipitation throughout the atmospheric column can be confidently detected with Ka-band ARM Zenith Radar (KAZR). Furthermore, ARM instrument deployments (including KAZR) have been stationed in strategic locations for the study of marine precipitation, including the long-lived Eastern North Atlantic (ENA) site, the Marine ARM GPCI Investigation of Clouds (MAGIC) campaign, and the Cloud And Precipitation Experiment at Kennaook (CAPE-K) campaign. In this project, we interrogate ESM cloud and precipitation processes with ENA ground-based active remote sensing observations by way of a perturbed parameter ensemble (PPE) hosted in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 3 (E3SMv3). This PPE, which perturbs many cloud and precipitation processes, can be used to investigate parametric uncertainty in models and delineate structural uncertainties when no parameter combination agrees with observations. To make faithful comparison with surface remote sensing observations, we leverage an instrument simulator and sub-column generator called the Earth Model Column Collaboratory (EMC2; doi:10.5194/gmd-15-901-2022) to generate emulated in-model KAZR observations. These simulated observables allow us to make apples-to-apples comparisons with the ARM observations, enabling a robust constraint of the E3SM PPE. With this constraint, we investigate the causal influences on model precipitation processes and their long-term effects on global radiative balance. While this analysis is currently limited to data from the ENA site, we plan to port this analysis to MAGIC and CAPE-K data for a more complete view of marine cloud-precipitation model physics.

495426.title: Human-Caused Global Ocean Warming Exacerbated the 2023 Europe-Africa Spatially-Compounding Flooding and Heatwave
495426.authors: Wei Sun, Chinese Academy of Meteorological Science, Beijing, 11, China
495426.abstract: Anthropogenic climate change has the potential of creating new compound weather and climate extremes with disproportionately amplified impacts. Diagnosing human influence on compound events is therefore crucial to assess emerging climatic risks. However, diverse compounding manners and complex physics, as showcased by the 2023 quasi-concurrent heatwaves and floods across Europe and Africa, pushes the established attribution methods to the limit. Here, we present a global variable-resolution storyline attribution framework that resolves interactions of planetary to regional dynamics fundamental to multi-scale events compounding. We show that human-caused global ocean warming has concurrently wettened the 2023 Spain, Greece, and Libya extremes by 7.4% and 15.7%, and 104.7% and simultaneously warmed the southern France heat by 0.2°C. Unfolding in a ~2°C warmer world under the same synoptics, these extremes would become 13.7%, 28.0%, 21.7%, 0.6°C wetter and hotter with the severely flooded areas expanded 2~3-folds. The results call for an urgent shift of preparedness against climate change-worsened single extremes to widespread concurrent climatic hazards.

495430.title: Developing a North American Freezing Rain Climatology Using Machine Learning and ERA5 Vertical Profiles
495430.authors: Art DeGaetano, Northeast Regional Climate Center, Ithaca, NY; and N. Zenes
495430.abstract: Freezing rain is one of the most severe and costly hydrometeorological events across North America with multisectoral impacts of ice accumulation including widespread power outages, transportation disruptions due to downed timber, and treacherous driving conditions. The current national extreme freezing rain accretion climatologies for the United States and Canada are based on a limited number of hourly reporting stations. Here we show that ERA5 data can be used to create a 46-year freezing rain climatology that spans the Continental US, Canada, and Alaska, accurately capturing the spatial patterns of freezing rain. The use of reanalysis data for this purpose was originally problematic as legacy diagnostic algorithms relied on thermodynamic assumptions that often misclassified freezing rain events. To address this limitation, LightGBM, a highly efficient machine learning algorithm that can accommodate high feature dimensions and is robust to class imbalances, is used. Here, LightGBM is trained on station precipitation type measurements and vertical atmospheric profiles of temperature and relative humidity using ERA5 hybrid-sigma model level data. From the vertical profile of meteorological variables, the model predicts what precipitation type is occurring at the surface. We show that this classifier model vastly outperforms ERA5 native precipitation type data, capturing 70% of freezing rain hours in the station record compared to 24% for the native precipitation typing. This reanalysis-based climatology can serve as a baseline for utility infrastructure planning and to applied to global climate models’ vertical profile data for diagnosing future freezing rain climatologies.

495431.title: Summer 2025 Compounded Extreme Heat and Ozone Episodes in Baltimore
495431.authors: Sabrina Eloisa Gonzalez, University at Albany SUNY, Albany, NY; and J. C. Pena and J. E. Gonzalez-Cruz
495431.abstract: Extreme heat threatens populations, a risk which is only amplified in built environments and by anthropogenic activity within cities. In coastal environments, where most populations reside, the sea breeze influence is typically linked with cooling off nearby urban areas. However, the associated humidity can also amplify the heat stress experienced by urban populations. Impactful heat mitigation strategies hinge on understanding the cascade of influences from heatwaves, sea breeze, the boundary layer, anthropogenic activity, and air quality. Despite the growing literature on heatwaves and urban heat islands (UHIs), gaps remain in understanding their structure and exchange with the background environment, particularly in coastal urban environments. To address these gaps, the present study utilizes observations from microwave radiometers, radiosonde launches, flux anemometers, lidars, and distributed surface stations during the summer of the 2025 US Department of Energy Coastal Urban-Rural Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE) in Baltimore, Maryland, paired with urban surface stations from the Baltimore Social-Environmental Collaborative (BSEC). This observational data is used to quantify the strength of two heatwave periods in June and July and how the surface meteorological conditions could relate to the development of enhanced tropospheric ozone and air quality degradation. Subsequent analyses are carried out to understand how the boundary layer development & decay relates to the structure of urban heat, moisture, and air quality under heatwave conditions. Results indicate that both heatwaves lasted 5 days, with the June heatwave reaching a maximum intensity of 104°F (114°F Heat Index) which ranked at the top 98th percentile in the 25-year record. The urban-rural differences point to a consistent enhancement of Heat Index temperatures in the urban environment and closest to the coast, along with a recurring UHI of 10°F during the peak of the heat event. The July heatwave manifested in an ozone episode with peak values of 100ppb closest to the urban core, representing the highest observed values over the summer. Ozone concentrations also exceeded 100ppb 1km aloft during this event shortly after maximum surface heating and during the onset of the bay breeze. These findings highlight how urbanization and coastal influence can enhance extreme heat and degrade air quality, and improving our understanding of this coupled process can support more effective heat mitigation strategies and urban planning, as well as public health preparedness.

495432.title: A Mobile Atmospheric Remote Sensing (MARS) Trailer for Synergistic Radar, Lidar, and Radiometer Measurements
495432.authors: Coltin Grasmick, Univ. of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and M. Saito, O. Cruikshank, and K. Li
495432.abstract: The Wyoming Cloud Radar (WCR) and Wyoming Cloud Lidar (WCL) are two of the University of Wyoming King Air Facility instruments designed for airborne remote sensing aboard the NSF UW King Air or NSF NCAR C-130 aircraft. When there are no ongoing airborne projects, the two instruments may sit for periods without use. The Mobile Atmospheric Remote Sensing (MARS) trailer enables a new platform for utilizing airborne instrumentation for ground-based research and educational activities. In Spring 2026, a UW college seed grant was used to modify an existing trailer to enable WCR and WCL installation. A WCR rack and WCL mount were designed for vertically pointing radar and lidar measurements through windows in the ceiling. The trailer can be powered using a nearby power drop or by a power generator for remote locations. The mobile system can be used for location-specific remote sensing research such as thunderstorms, winter weather, or even smoke or blowing dust events. The closely matched radar, lidar, and radiometer observations are optimal for comparative analyses and retrieval algorithms. On 1-3 April 2026, the MARS trailer was tested outside of Laramie, Wyoming including simultaneous measurements from WCR, WCL, and a HATPRO radiometer. The first day brought heavy rain during a cold front passage followed by a descending freezing level and a transition to snow. Operations on the second day observed snow triggered by cloud-top dynamics and a Kelvin-Helmholtz turbulence event. Lingering clouds and snow showers on day three were present during a visit from the UW Remote Sensing class. Example plots show the research-quality data achievable using the mobile trailer and the synergy between radar, lidar, and radiometry.

495435.title: Turbulent Transport and Vertical Distribution of Sea Spray Aerosols in a Coastal Marine Boundary Layer from Scanning Doppler LiDAR Measurements
495435.authors: Giacomo Valerio Lungo, University of Texas Dallas, Richardson, TX
495435.abstract: Sea spray aerosols (SSA) play a fundamental role in air-sea exchange processes by influencing momentum, heat, and moisture fluxes, as well as cloud microphysics and atmospheric radiative properties. Despite their importance, the transport mechanisms governing SSA distributions within the marine atmospheric boundary layer (MABL) remain poorly understood, particularly in coastal regions, where shoreline effects, wave-driven processes, and spatial heterogeneity lead to pronounced departures from classical surface-layer assumptions. Simultaneous measurements of wind turbulence and SSA concentration were collected using a scanning Doppler LiDAR deployed on Nantucket Island, Massachusetts. The LiDAR was operated with low-elevation scans aligned with the mean wind direction to probe the coastal MABL over the ocean. Relative SSA concentration was inferred from focus- and range-corrected backscatter coefficients, while wind velocity fluctuations were retrieved from Doppler radial velocity measurements. Profiles of mean velocity, turbulence intensity, aerosol concentration, and turbulent scalar fluxes were derived after applying quality-control procedures including signal-to-noise filtering, stationarity testing, and removal of mesoscale motions. The observations reveal persistent coastal induction effects in the mean flow and predominantly negative streamwise turbulent scalar fluxes, indicating enhanced aerosol concentrations associated with reductions in local wind velocity. Measured concentration profiles demonstrate the competing influences of turbulent diffusion, gravitational settling, and advective transport throughout the surface layer. The measurements are compared with analytical solutions of the Reynolds-averaged advection-diffusion equation, including classical logarithmic and power-law formulations. While existing models capture portions of the observed behavior, they do not adequately represent the influence of horizontal inhomogeneity characteristic of coastal environments. An extended turbulent diffusion-transport formulation is therefore developed to account for streamwise variability in both wind velocity and aerosol concentration. The proposed model provides improved agreement with LiDAR-derived concentration profiles and offers a physically based framework for describing SSA transport in coastal MABL conditions. These findings demonstrate the potential of scanning Doppler LiDAR to quantify aerosol transport processes and provide new insights into improving SSA parameterizations in atmospheric and weather prediction models.

495438.title: Assessing the Potential of the Ventilated Genesis Potential Index for Subseasonal Tropical Cyclone Predictability
495438.authors: Robert G. Nystrom, Iowa State University, Ames, IA
495438.abstract: The ventilated Genesis Potential Index (vGPI) has recently emerged as a promising framework for characterizing large-scale environmental controls on tropical cyclone (TC) genesis, but its utility for subseasonal prediction remains largely unexplored. This talk evaluates whether vGPI provides useful information on subseasonal variability in TC activity through a combination of reanalysis-derived self-organizing map (SOM) analyses and MPAS simulations.
