We first examine whether distinct large-scale vGPI patterns identified from reanalysis are associated with observed periods of enhanced and suppressed TC activity. Using SOM analysis, recurrent modes of environmental favorability are identified and evaluated for their correspondence with active and inactive TC periods, providing insight into the extent to which spatial variations in vGPI capture subseasonal fluctuations in TC occurrence. Building on this observational framework, we investigate whether MPAS captures the large-scale vGPI variability linked to observed TC activity. Specifically, we investigate whether the model reproduces the environmental patterns linked to periods of enhanced and suppressed cyclone activity. Finally, we examine the predictability associated with selected vGPI states by focusing on periods characterized by record-high and record-low vGPI values. Through targeted MPAS simulations initialized during these extreme environments, we evaluate whether anomalously favorable and unfavorable vGPI conditions are associated with differences in subsequent TC activity. Collectively, these analyses assess both the observational relevance and predictive value of vGPI, offering new insight into the role of large-scale environmental controls on subseasonal tropical cyclone activity.

495439.title: Evaluating Satellite Water Vapor And Downstream Precipitation Nowcast Performance During the 2026 Monsoon Over The Tropics
495439.authors: Saimy Davis, Tomorrow.io, Boston, MA; and A. Chawla, R. Honeyager, P. P. Rama Durga Surya, A. Pattantyus, J. J. Guerrette, and F. Cannon
495439.abstract: Accurate representation of atmospheric moisture is critical for anticipating the initiation and intensity of tropical precipitation. This study evaluates the impact of Tomorrow.io's satellite-derived water-vapor information on short-range nowcasting during the 2026 Indian monsoon, with emphasis on how skill is transferred across the operational pathway. This year, the monsoon was characterized by strong spatial and temporal variability, localized intense rainfall episodes occurring within an otherwise below-normal broader monsoon environment. Passive-microwave observations from the Tomorrow Microwave Sounder (TMS) constellation are transformed through AI-based and physics-informed retrieval methods into atmospheric moisture products. Tomorrow.io’s nowcasting product combines geostationary satellite imagery with passive-microwave observations in a deep-learning framework that produces spatially complete, frequently updated precipitation fields. The evaluated system generated approximately 4-km precipitation estimates every 10 minutes and demonstrated improved detection and intensity skill relative to near-real-time satellite products. Satellite-derived water-vapor profiles are validated using collocated radiosonde humidity profiles, while radiative-transfer-based brightness-temperature comparisons are used as an additional check on the underlying microwave observations. Nowcasts generated are evaluated using rainfall intensity, accumulation, spatial agreement, timing, and forecast-lead-time metrics. The two sets of verification results are then compared to determine whether periods and regions of higher water-vapor retrieval skill are associated with correspondingly higher precipitation-nowcast skill. Initial analysis of selected 2026 monsoon cases is being used to characterize this relationship across organized monsoon rainfall, coastal convection, and localized heavy-rainfall environments. The study provides an observation-to-prediction framework for evaluating satellite products not only by retrieval accuracy, but also by how effectively their information content is retained in downstream operational precipitation guidance. Water-vapor retrieval and precipitation-nowcast performance are evaluated jointly across tropical convective regimes to assess whether improved moisture representation translates into greater rainfall-prediction skill. *]:pointer-events-auto R6Vx5W_threadScrollVars scroll-mb-[calc(var(--scroll-root-safe-area-inset-bottom,0px)+var(--thread-response-height))] scroll-mt-[calc(var(--header-height)+min(200px,max(70px,20svh)))]" dir="auto" data-turn-id="request-6a586843-29c0-83ab-9be8-9f394ef23331-32" data-turn-id-container="request-6a586843-29c0-83ab-9be8-9f394ef23331-32" data-testid="conversation-turn-216" data-turn="assistant"> _:empty]:hidden">

495440.title: Climate Warming and Extreme Weather in the Caribbean: Insights from Convection-Permitting MPAS Simulations
495440.authors: Kwesi Twentwewa Quagraine, Texas A&M Univ., College Station; and E. M. Dougherty, K. M. Núñez Ocasio, and Z. Moon
495440.abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) impacts across the Mesoamerica–Caribbean region are expected to intensify under climate warming, yet the relative roles of changing large-scale circulation and storm-scale thermodynamics remain poorly understood. Using convection-permitting simulations with the Model for Prediction Across Scales–Atmosphere (MPAS-A), we investigate Hurricane Maria (15–30 September 2017) under present-day (CTRL) and pseudo-global warming (PGW) conditions to isolate the processes governing future TC behavior. The CTRL simulation reproduces the overall evolution of Hurricane Maria, while the PGW simulation exhibits a fundamentally different storm trajectory resulting from a strengthened and northwestward expansion of the North Atlantic Subtropical High (NASH). The altered steering flow redirects the storm toward the Gulf of Mexico, increasing land interaction and environmental vertical wind shear, ultimately shortening the storm lifetime. Despite this shorter duration, the PGW simulation produces approximately 12% greater maximum area-averaged precipitation, driven by enhanced atmospheric moisture and increased moist static energy that provide stronger thermodynamic support for deep convection. Storm-centered analyses further demonstrate that climate warming modifies moisture transport, storm organization, and precipitation distribution through the combined influence of evolving environmental dynamics and thermodynamics. Building on this case study, ongoing work extends these convection-permitting simulations to the entire 2020 Atlantic hurricane season, enabling a regional assessment of how climate warming influences multiple tropical cyclones, mesoscale convective systems (MCSs), and their interactions across the Mesoamerica–Caribbean basin. By moving beyond individual storms, this work aims to identify robust changes in tropical convection and precipitation extremes that are critical for future regional climate risk assessments.

495442.title: Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command Service Update
495442.authors: Joseph Calantoni, CNMOC, Stennis Space Center, MS; and E. E. O. Acosta and K. LaCroix
495442.abstract: The military and civilian professionals of the Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command stand watch around the clock, delivering decisive meteorology and oceanography (METOC) intelligence to U.S. Navy, Joint Force, and national leaders. Our core mission centers on the rapid collection, processing, exploitation, and dissemination of ocean, atmosphere, and space data. Our mission not only safeguards navigation but assures access and maximizes the combat power of the Joint Force. To accelerate "Data to Decision", Naval Meteorology and Oceanography is fielding modern capabilities that transform raw observations to enable planning and decision tools and the next generation modeling and simulation powered by AI. Our Office of Research and Technology Applications (ORTA) representative is exercising every available authority to partner with industry and academia to close critical sensing, transmitting, and edge processing gaps. Additionally, we are engaging our interservice, interagency, and international partners to ensure seamless interoperability across the spectrum of warfare. We will update our progress in three key areas that include global atmospheric modeling, enterprise data dissemination, and our efforts to provide sailors with a modernized forecaster tool suite.

495443.title: Subsidence in a Warming World: Translating Drought Risk into Asset-Level Financial Loss
495443.authors: Justin S Rogers, Jupiter Intelligence, Inc., San Mateo, CA; and H. Scannell, E. Dennis, M. McGraw, and J. Hacker
495443.abstract: Shrink-swell subsidence, the cyclical shrinking and swelling of clay-rich soils in response to changing moisture conditions, is a growing, climate-sensitive hazard causing billions of dollars in structural damage annually across the globe. Subsidence already costs the United Kingdom over £400 million per year, France over €600 million per year (with over €3 billion in claims reported in 2022), and the United States nearly $15 billion per year. As drought frequency and intensity increase under a warming climate, and as heat waves compound soil moisture deficits, subsidence risk to buildings and infrastructure is rising sharply in clay-rich regions worldwide. Despite losses comparable to wind, flood, and wildfire in some regions, subsidence has lacked a standardized, quantitative, forward-looking risk assessment framework. Existing tools are largely regional, hazard-only, or limited to present-day conditions. We present a global, asset-level subsidence hazard and financial loss model that links climate-driven drought risk directly to economic impact. The hazard component estimates annual subsidence probability from soil clay content, vegetation type, and drought risk (via the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index), calculated under present and future emissions scenarios at 90-meter resolution. This hazard output is combined with asset-level structural characteristics, including foundation type, building age, and construction material, to produce damage and financial loss estimates with quantified uncertainty. We present validation results comparing the hazard to other data models and loss results to aggregate country loss estimates from various sources. Applying this framework to case studies in the United Kingdom, France, the United States, and Australia, we project substantial increases in subsidence losses driven by rising drought risk: subsidence damages for UK single-family homes with vulnerable foundations could nearly triple by 2075, while French subsidence risk could increase by over 250% on average by 2070, alongside a 150–350% rise in drought risk. In Australia (where 20% of the country, including greater Melbourne, sits on subsidence-prone clay soils) losses are set to climb further as drought risk intensifies. We discuss implications for insurance pricing, portfolio risk management, and adaptation planning in water-stressed, clay-rich regions.

495445.title: LightningCast Research Improvements
495445.authors: Lena Heuscher, Univ. of Wisconsin, Madison, WI; and J. Cintineo, J. Sieglaff, and M. Pavolonis
495445.abstract: LightningCast (LC) is a deep-learning AI model (a U-Net) that predicts the probability of lightning within the next 60 minutes using single-timestamp GOES-R ABI data inputs. Core inputs to the model are the 0.64-µm reflectance (red portion of the visible 0.5-km resolution), the 1.6-µm reflectance (shortwave infrared, 1-km resolution), the 10.3-µm brightness temperature (longwave infrared, 2-km resolution), and the 12.3-µm brightness temperature (longwave infrared, 2-km resolution) with the truth dataset derived from the gridded Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) flash extent density product. National Weather Service (NWS) forecasters have noted concerns with current versions about the probability spatial extent, especially during storm mergers and MCSs. We are attempting to address this feedback through the following experiments: 1) using a centroid-gridded product of flash locations from the GLM, and 2) expanding the model to 3D by using a time series of ABI images. Results from each experiment are compared to LCv1 as a baseline to determine how these experiments may improve lightning predictions. Initial results from the first experiment show promise in the possibility of using a gridded truth dataset.

495446.title: Linking ENSO to Wisconsin Winter Snowfall: Implications for Seasonal Forecasting
495446.authors: Alexandra Vizcarra, University of Wisconsin, Madison, Madison, WI; and S. Vavrus
495446.abstract: The El Niño / Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a dominant mode of interannual climate variability with well-documented teleconnections to weather across the contiguous United States. However, its influence on snowfall in the Great Lakes region, particularly at the state scale, remains uncertain. In this study, we use Wisconsin’s extensive observational snowfall record to investigate the relationship between Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies and Wisconsin snowfall during boreal winter (DJF). After detrending both variables, we apply parametric and nonparametric statistical methods to characterize this relationship at both statewide and regional scales. Results reveal a statistically significant negative relationship between Niño 3.4 SST anomalies and statewide snowfall anomalies, with El Niño events associated with a more consistent reduction in winter snowfall and La Niña events exhibiting a broader range of snowfall responses across the state. This relationship is also observed across all nine Wisconsin climate divisions, with the most notable differences in snowfall responses occurring in the northwestern and north-central divisions. Although this asymmetry is not statistically significant, the observed tendency warrants further investigation. These findings suggest that ENSO is a meaningful predictor of Wisconsin winter snowfall variability, with potential applications for seasonal snowfall forecasting across the state.

495448.title: MAPCast v2: An Expanded Convection-Allowing MPAS Emulator for Generating Surrogate Background Ensembles in MPAS-JEDI
495448.authors: Daniel Lee Kubalek, University of Oklahoma, Broken Arrow, OK; and Y. Wang, X. Wang, and D. Dowell
495448.abstract: MAPCast is a convection allowing machine learning (ML) emulator with the goal of emulating the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) background ensemble to estimate background error covariances (BECs) for multi-scale data assimilation (DA). Evaluations of the first version of MAPCast (MAPCast v1; Wang and Wang 2026) have illustrated the promising potential of MAPCast v1 to provide surrogate background ensembles. Our recent simple model experiments (Kubalek et al. 2026) have shown that combining data-driven and physics-based ensemble estimates flow-dependent BECs better than either pure data-driven or pure physics-based ensembles. Motivated by this promising achievement, we develop MAPCast v2 to provide surrogate background ensembles more compatible with the MPAS background ensembles for examining the combined ensembles within MPAS-JEDI. Compared to v1, MAPCast v2 doubles the vertical levels to 40, with priority of the levels resolving boundary layer and meso-scale processes and includes all hydrometeors in addition to vertical velocity and reflectivity. These expanded configurations require extensive tuning experiments to obtain the optimal hyperparameters, such as variable-based and model-level-based weight classes assigned to loss function. This study develops MAPCast v2 trained with 5-season historical MPAS simulations. Systematic evaluation across 10 retrospective convective cases will be conducted to explore the agreement between MAPCast v2 surrogate and MPAS ensembles in the estimate of BEC statistics.

495450.title: What Would It Take for Aerosols to Invigorate a Cloud? (Invited Presentation)
495450.authors: David M. Romps, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA
495450.abstract: The hypothesis of aerosol invigoration states that an increase in aerosol concentration increases convective updraft speeds, e.g., by raising the latent heating harvested from supersaturation (warm phase) or by shifting more condensate to where it freezes (cold phase). This talk asks what it would take for that to happen, and what it would take for us to know that it had. The demands on nature are stiff. Warm-phase invigoration requires high supersaturation and an aerosol perturbation that collapses it. Cold-phase invigoration requires condensate that falls out below the freezing level, and an aerosol perturbation that carries it just above, but no higher. And either route must occur often enough to matter, but not so often that the stratification adjusts and erases the effect. The demands on us are also stiff. We cannot rely on correlations between aerosols and, e.g., lightning rates or cloud depths. Nor can we look at correlations between aerosols and vertical velocity without carefully excluding correlations with meteorology. And, when looking for high supersaturation, we must exclude samples outside the updraft core or in unsteady updrafts. Mapping these obstacles sets expectations: substantial aerosol invigoration is likely rare, and the evidence for it will be hard to come by. But our odds of unambiguous detection are higher if we recognize them.

495453.title: Verification of the New MPAS-A/MOM6 High-Resolution Coupled System across the Air-Sea Transition Zone In the Indo-Pacific
495453.authors: Yakelyn R. Jauregui, NCAR, Boulder, WA; and B. W. Barr, D. Amrhein, G. Marques, A. Janney, F. Judt, B. Dobbins, U. U. Turuncoglu, S. Kamali, M. Duda, and S. Voelz
495453.abstract: NCAR is developing a new high-resolution coupled atmosphere-ocean system, coupling MPAS-A with MOM6, targeting regional and global S2S applications. High-resolution, km-scale coupled atmosphere-ocean models allow representation of physical processes across the air-sea transition zone relevant to research and forecasting at weather and seasonal-to-subseasonal (S2S) timescales. We present verification and analysis of parallel 30-day simulations comparing standalone uncoupled MPAS-A and coupled MPAS-A/MOM6, with 3 km atmospheric resolution and 1/12° oceanic resolution. The study region is the Indo-Pacific domain, a region distinguished by strong scale interaction and the coupled MJO and ENSO phenomena central to S2S predictability, making the region ideal for testing and verification of the new coupled system. The comparison isolates the effect of coupling on atmospheric and oceanic boundary layer response across regimes relevant to MJO initiation and propagation and equatorial coupled variability. We discuss lessons learned from exercising the coupled workflow end-to-end, including current coupling limitations, and identify steps toward a configuration usable for both operational S2S forecasting and process-oriented research.

495454.title: WRF-speed: A GPU-native, Differentiable, Machine-Learning-Ready WRF
495454.authors: John Schreck, NSF-NCAR, Louisville, CO; and M. Jessey, I. Linck, M. E. Frediani, P. A. Jimenez, C. Becker, and D. J. Gagne II
495454.abstract: We built WRF-speed, a fully differentiable reimplementation of WRF and its wildland fire coupling (WRF-Fire) in PyTorch, for three reasons: (1) a differentiable model lets gradients pass directly through the physics for calibration and hybrid physics-machine-learning parameterization; (2) a native PyTorch implementation runs in the same GPU-first, Python-native ecosystem the machine learning community already builds on, rather than a bespoke Fortran and MPI stack; and (3) the result is far easier for the broader research community to read, extend, and experiment with than the original, since it's written in Python. The risk in any full reimplementation is correctness, so we hold the port to a 0-unit-in-last-place (ULP) standard: every prognostic field matches the reference Fortran model bit for bit, not approximately, verified against a real high-resolution simulation of the 2021 Marshall Fire (Boulder County, Colorado) over extended integration windows. The model runs natively on a GPU and needs no HPC cluster. On the validated Marshall configuration with fire and spotting active, a single B200 GPU matches the wall-clock speed of a 224-core MPI Fortran deployment of the same case. Against the same case on the Derecho HPC, the port runs 11.2x faster in double precision and 17.2x faster in single precision on a single A100 GPU than on a single Fortran CPU core. The port also supports exact multi-GPU domain decomposition, bit-for-bit identical to the single-GPU result. On four GPUs, this adds roughly 2x further throughput for larger domains. Fast fire simulation that scales from one GPU up makes large ensembles, reinforcement learning, and iterative model fitting tractable at a scale a CPU cluster workflow does not easily support. Because the model is differentiable end to end, gradients propagate through the full coupled physics and fire spread calculation rather than around it. This places WRF-speed alongside differentiable general circulation models such as NeuralGCM, which use gradient descent through a physical simulator to learn subgrid parameterizations at global scale. We bring that same paradigm to convection-permitting, fire-coupled regional simulation.

495461.title: Atmospheric Fate of Decamethylcyclopentasiloxane (D5): Global Multiscale Modeling of Multigenerational Oxidation and Secondary Organic Aerosol Formation
495461.authors: Saeideh Mohammadi, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; and C. E. Brunet, B. Roozitalab, D. S. Jo, A. Hodzic, K. C. Hornbuckle, G. R. Carmichael, and C. O. Stanier
495461.abstract: Decamethylcyclopentasiloxane (D5) is a chemical widely used in personal care products; it volatilizes into the atmosphere and undergoes multiple generations of OH oxidation in the atmosphere. Due to its potential for ecological effects, long-range transport, and bioaccumulation, it has been extensively modeled and measured. However, prior work has represented the oxidation chemistry as a single unresolved loss step that removes D5 without tracking its transformation products. We correct the oversimplification of prior work by adapting well established techniques from the global chemistry and climate community for gas-phase oxidation, treatment of semivolatiles, and aerosol formation. Specifically, we implement a silicon-conserving multigenerational oxidation mechanism in the chemistry–climate model CESM2, configured with MUSICAv0 on a regionally refined spectral-element grid (~14 km over the contiguous United States; ~110 km globally). The scheme resolves the full D5 chemical family including parent D5, volatile first-generation products, semivolatile gases across a volatility basis set, and secondary organic aerosol (SOA). Simulations for July 2022 are benchmarked against a conventional single-step representation and against gas- and particle-phase observations from the NYC-METS campaign. The revised model has important insights for managing volatile methyl siloxanes like D5, using it as a tracer of personal care products, and understanding anthropogenic organic silicon in the global atmosphere. The model-observation comparison in New York City yields good agreement for D5 and its total oxidation products, but underestimates aerosol partitioning, pointing to missing condensed-phase processes. Oxidation products constitute over half of the global D5 family burden, and have important implications for the details (location, amount, oxidation state) of deposited D5. Implications for future field and laboratory studies concerning this compound class are discussed.

495465.title: Variability of Supercooled Liquid Water over the Mountains of Utah: A Four-Site Microwave Radiometer Network
495465.authors: Kelvy Cardoso, Utah Climate Center, Logan, UT; and B. Pokharel and J. Jennings
495465.abstract: Utah is a global leader in operational wintertime cloud seeding, with the availability of supercooled liquid water (SLW) being a key factor influencing seeding opportunities and effectiveness. However, SLW exhibits substantial spatial and temporal variability across Utah’s complex mountainous terrain, and its characteristics across different mountain ranges have not been well documented using ground-based observations. During the winter of 2025–2026, four passive microwave radiometers (MWRs) were deployed for the first coordinated multi-site observation of SLW across several mountain ranges in Utah. Three radiometers were located in northern Utah, while one was deployed in the isolated La Sal Mountains of southern Utah. Observations covered the core winter period from January through March 2026. This study examines the vertical distribution and variability of SLW under different atmospheric conditions, including variations associated with cloud type (convective versus stratiform), temperature, and mountain location. The observations reveal substantial spatial and vertical variability in SLW across the observing sites. At the Snowbasin site in the northern Wasatch Mountains, located near the mountain peak at approximately 2,420 m MSL, SLW was generally observed up to about 4 km above ground level (AGL), whereas sites located at approximately 1,300 m MSL showed SLW extending up to about 6 km AGL. The mean liquid water path (LWP) over the northern mountain sites was approximately 400 g m⁻², nearly twice the mean LWP observed at the southern Utah. The presentation will focus on the vertical distribution of SLW across different temperature ranges and mountain locations, with particular emphasis on differences between convective and stratiform cloud systems. These observations provide new insights into the spatial and vertical variability of SLW across Utah’s diverse mountain ranges and have implications for improving the identification of favorable conditions for operational cloud seeding. Keywords: Supercooled liquid water; passive microwave radiometer; winter cloud seeding; Orographic clouds

495470.title: Designing Hurricane Wind Products With Communities: A Convergent, Weather-Ready Approach on the Gulf Coast
495470.authors: Christopher M. Rozoff, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), Boulder, CO; and O. Wilhelmi, X. Chen, E. A. Hendricks, J. C. Knievel, J. Boehnert, M. Casali, S. E. Haupt, S. Carboni, and S. M. Dettling
495470.abstract: Building a Weather-Ready Nation for hurricane wind hazards requires forecast products that communities actually use: products designed with users, not merely for them. We present a project overview and first-year progress of WHIRLTC (Wind and Hazards Investigation for Resilience to Landfalling Tropical Cyclones), a convergent effort on the Southeast Texas–Southwest Louisiana Gulf Coast that pairs advances in near-surface wind science with community-centered co-development of risk information. Landfalling hurricanes trigger cascading, compound hazards—including wind damage, prolonged power outages, and dangerous post-storm heat—all of which disproportionately affect socially vulnerable residents. New turbulence-resolving simulations and coastal radar analyses are sharpening estimates of sustained and gusty near-surface winds over land, giving a more reliable physical basis for wind and gust hazard products (the physical results are detailed in a companion tropical-cyclone presentation). We are aiming to translate that information into actionable guidance, in partnership with the NOAA/NWS Lake Charles Weather Forecast Office. Here we present key findings from the interviews with decision-makers, including forecasters, emergency managers, public-health, and industry professionals. The interviews provide insights on how hazard and risk information is generated, perceived, disseminated, and acted upon. We also present maps of wind, gust, surge, and heat hazards, alongside population exposure and vulnerability to reveal geographic patterns of risk. We share lessons for co-producing hazard information across disciplines, and with the communities it is meant to serve.

495474.title: Publicly Available Long-Term Snow Measurements in Utqiagvik, AK at the ARM User Facility
495474.authors: David Clemens-Sewall, Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and M. Sturm, M. Oggier, K. Irving, J. Delamere, and A. Glen
495474.abstract: The North Slope of Alaska is covered in persistent, yet shallow snow approximately 9 months of the year. This stands in contrast to many lower latitude snowpacks, which tend to be persistent and deep or ephemeral and shallow. Albeit shallow, the North Slope snowpack exhibits a high degree of spatial variability, varying from less than 20 cm to more than 1 m on horizontal distance of 10s of meters. To monitor this snowpack and its causes, long-term snow measurements were initiated in 2017 at the Department of Energy’s Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility at the North Slope of Alaska (NSA) observatory in Utqiaġvik, AK. These measurements consist of snow depth, precipitation (particle distributions and snow water equivalent), blowing snow mass flux, and 3D wind velocity. To address the spatial variability, snow depth measurements consist of two arrays of 9 depth sensors each. These measurements (and all data obtained through ARM) are monitored for quality and made available free of charge through the ARM Data Center via Data Discovery, typically in near real time (< 1 day). We present ongoing efforts to enhance the utility of these measurements to end users and solicit feedback from the community.

495476.title: Soil Moisture Preconditioning and Land-Atmosphere Coupling Enhance Central U.S. Heatwave Susceptibility
495476.authors: Valentina Castaneda, Purdue University, Lafayette, IN; Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN; and L. Wang, K. L. Findell, and V. T. Narinesingh
495476.abstract: Understanding which land-atmosphere processes on subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) timescales favor the most thermally intense heatwaves over the United States remains an open question. Previous studies have shown that soil moisture-temperature coupling is strongest in transitional regimes where ample energy is available to support latent heating but soil moisture is limited; in these conditions, temperature becomes highly sensitive to variations in soil moisture. However, the role of these coupling regimes in shaping real-world heatwave extremes across different U.S. regions remains poorly understood. In particular, we wish to determine whether enhanced land-atmosphere coupling increases regional susceptibility to heatwaves under weaker large-scale atmospheric forcing. Here, we characterize land-atmosphere coupling regimes associated with U.S. summer heatwaves using soil moisture and surface fluxes from GLEAM. We examine both subseasonal variability during heatwaves and spring soil moisture preconditioning to assess how land conditions influence heatwave susceptibility. Over the central U.S., we find that heatwave conditions are associated with stronger soil moisture-surface flux relationships. Locations that are climatologically energy-limited show stronger soil moisture-latent heat coupling during heatwaves than on non-heatwave days, while events occurring in regions with climatological transitional regime exhibit a disproportionately strong temperature response to soil moisture. We further identify a spring soil moisture pattern associated with an increased frequency of central U.S. heatwaves. Summers following this spring pattern exhibit enhanced sensitivity of sensible heating to soil moisture relative to climatological conditions, suggesting that spring soil moisture can precondition the land surface for stronger summer land-atmosphere coupling. Together, these results suggest that land conditions can increase central U.S. susceptibility to heatwaves, particularly when large-scale atmospheric forcing is comparatively weak. Ongoing work with GFDL climate models is also presented to verify whether GCMs are able to capture the aforementioned behavior.

495477.title: Point-Trained, Grid-Applied: Statistical Downscaling of Numerical Weather Prediction Guidance on a Variable-Resolution Mesh
495477.authors: Trevor Alcott, The Weather Company, Andover, MA; and M. Flora, T. M. Hamill, C. Guiang, J. P. Koval, J. I. Belanger, L. Gaudet, Ph.D., and P. Neilley
495477.abstract: Operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) guidance at 3-4-km grid spacing still fails to resolve the fine-scale terrain and land-use effects that drive local variability in sensible weather. We present a machine-learning downscaling framework that corrects gridded high-resolution forecasts toward station-scale accuracy by predicting a learned increment (observed minus forecast) at arbitrary point locations, rather than producing a downscaled gridded field directly. The approach trains residual multilayer-perceptron networks on quality-controlled surface observations paired with (1) time-matched NWP forecasts and (2) a suite of static terrain and land-use predictors. Those predictors include elevation, smoothed elevation and gradients at multiple length scales, land-use class, topographic position, and derived slope/solar and wind-terrain interaction features. Training stations are spatially thinned using a feature-stratified sampling scheme to reduce oversampling in densely instrumented regions, while preserving diversity of terrain and climate regimes. Separate networks for dynamic (wind speed/direction/gust) and thermodynamic (temperature, dewpoint) fields are combined at inference time to produce a full set of downscaled surface fields, evaluated on an adaptive, terrain-aware point mesh that refines in areas of complex terrain, coastlines, and urban centers. A terrain-aware bilateral smoother suppresses point-to-point noise while preserving physically justified gradients tied to elevation. We discuss lessons learned in building a robust, operational downscaling pipeline at full-CONUS scale, including feature-engineering choices that did and did not improve skill and practical strategies for efficient GPU-based inference and postprocessing. Verification against withheld surface observations shows the downscaled fields improve on raw NWP output for temperature, dewpoint, and wind, particularly where sub-grid-scale terrain variability is significant.

495480.title: A New Undergraduate Course in Building Deep-Learning AI Tools using PyTorch
495480.authors: Christopher E. Phillips, Valparaiso University, Valparaiso, IN
495480.abstract: Data-driven tools have long been used in meteorology, but in general have relied on algorithms that are limited in scope. Recently, however, there has been an explosion of very large deep-learning models for atmospheric science. These include NASA's Prithvi foundation model, the Pangu forecast model, and numerous others. These advancements are reflected in the job market with postings now requesting extensive experience in both meteorology and artificial intelligence development. In response to these new expectations, Valparaiso University has developed an "AI and Machine Learning in Earth Science" course that equips students with the skills for applying deep-learning algorithms to their field. This presentation describes the framework of the course, explains design decisions, and reports the student outcomes. The skills learned include when to apply machine learning algorithms, building training datasets, and programming deep-learning neural networks. The course heavily utilized the Scikit learn and PyTorch packages while also providing a basic theoretical understanding to demystify the AI black box. By the end of the course, each student could identify an Earth Science problem, construct training data, and build a neural network using Python to address the problem.

495481.title: Cascading Storms: Understanding Tornado, Thunderstorm, and Flood Hazards Connected to Tropical Cyclone Moisture Transport
495481.authors: Adam Nayak, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and N. Lin
495481.abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) impacts are conventionally attributed within a fixed radius of the storm track, an assumption that can sever the storm from the moisture it continues to transport through landfall, dissipation, and extratropical transition. We develop an objective attribution framework that follows the moisture itself. Using a computer-vision morphological transform on ERA5 integrated vapor transport, we extract transient TC moisture corridors, link them across time into a directed lineage graph, and resolve merger events by comparing integrated water vapor content, isolating the parcels a TC dominantly supplies. Applied to Atlantic TCs approaching the contiguous United States over 1978–2025, the method attributes flood insurance claims, disaster declarations and aid, and tornado and thunderstorm-wind reports to individual storms without imposing a distance threshold. We attribute thousands of tornadoes and thunderstorm-wind reports to TCs, and find TCs account for a substantial majority of national flood claim damage and household assistance aid. Comparison with FEMA's own event labels reveals a systematic attribution gap concentrated in remnant-stage impacts across the Midwest and Northeast. Annual counts of TC-associated convection show significant increasing trends in TC-induced thunderstorms and tornadoes, strongest among severe events, and significant covariability with ENSO. Nearly all TCs interact with additional moisture parcels, indicating that impacts arise from interacting weather systems rather than isolated storms. Most convective impacts occur before extratropical transition, in the symmetric warm-core phase, though remnant and post-dissipation stages often produce secondary thunderstorm clusters. Attributing hazards by moisture connectivity rather than proximity substantially expands the recognized footprint of TC risk, with direct implications for insurance pricing and disaster designation.

495483.title: Track Uncertainty in Tropical Cyclone Wind Speed Probability Products
495483.authors: Alan Brammer, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Martinez, M. DeMaria, K. Musgrave, P. Santos, M. Onderlinde, and D. A. Zelinsky
495483.abstract: The National Hurricane Center’s (NHC) Wind Speed Probability (WSP) model estimates point-specific probabilities of exceeding 34, 50, and 64 kt winds using 1,000 realizations. The ensemble has been based on 5-year track and intensity error distributions from NHC and Central Pacific Hurricane Center (CPHC) forecasts, generated via Monte Carlo methods with limited input from real-time dynamical model spread. This presentation will focus on the inclusion of dynamic forecast uncertainty into the track spread of the Monte Carlo ensemble members. While the statistically derived ensemble has previously incorporated 3 levels of uncertainty grounded in historical errors, recent work has expanded the model to include an option for direct forecast uncertainty from ensembles and statistical forecasts of uncertainty. This expands the uncertainty of the ensemble from terciles of along- and across-track errors, to full dynamic uncertainty that aligns with the major and minor axes of spread from the forecast inputs. In the verification process, the statistical ensemble utilized by the WSP model will be evaluated against other numerical weather prediction ensembles as well as new data-driven model ensemble outputs. This evaluation aims to assess the relative strengths and weaknesses of each approach regarding their ability to capture forecast uncertainty, and assess whether dynamical uncertainty provides reliable and consistent improvements to the statistical ensemble generation. The insights gained from this comparative analysis will be crucial for refining the WSP model and potentially integrating beneficial aspects from other advanced ensemble techniques to further enhance its operational utility.

495484.title: Accelerating Satellite Product Transition to Operations at NOAA/NESDIS
495484.authors: Melissa Zweng, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and W. W. Wolf, P. Roy, M. Hale, and K. Pinkney
495484.abstract: The National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) plays a vital role in providing secure and timely access to global environmental data and information. To support this mission, NESDIS has developed a modernized, agile lifecycle framework that leverages cloud computing and stakeholder engagement—including the Science and User Engagement Councils—to manage environmental data products from user needs and development to operations, archive, and retirement. As demand for weather and environmental information grows, driven by rapid advancements in AI and machine learning, the ability to transition scientific innovation and new data sources into operations is critical. This presentation describes how NESDIS is accelerating Transition to Operations (T2O) timelines by integrating an agile process with modern technological advancements, specifically through Algorithm Orchestration (AO) and GitLab CI/CD. AO empowers science teams to package algorithms into cloud-ready containers, utilizing automated GitLab CI/CD pipelines to build, test, and register their innovations seamlessly. Crucially, this approach bolsters security by enabling automated, standardized security scanning and continuous vulnerability monitoring within the CI/CD pipeline, ensuring that every containerized algorithm meets rigorous compliance standards before deployment. By leveraging this orchestration framework to automate data delivery, job scheduling, and container execution—supporting both near real-time and batch processing—NESDIS is reducing transition latency, enhancing developer autonomy, and ensuring that the most up-to-date environmental intelligence effectively reaches the Weather Enterprise and critical decision-makers.

495485.title: Developing a Long-Term (2002–2020), High-Resolution (1 km) Surface NO₂ Dataset over the CONUS Using Machine Learning Data Fusion
495485.authors: Beiming Tang, NOAA, fairfax, VA; and M. Tao, S. Ma, W. Li, and D. Tong
495485.abstract: Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is an important air pollutant that adversely affects human health and serves as a key precursor of ozone (O₃) and fine particulate matter (PM2.5). Although machine learning has been increasingly applied to estimate surface NO₂, existing datasets often fail to resolve urban-scale spatial variability due to uncertainties in emission inventories and the rapid chemical transformations of NO₂ after emission. Leveraging the George Mason University North America Chemical Reanalysis (NACR) project and Neighborhood Emission Mapping Operation (NEMO), we developed a machine learning data fusion framework that integrates satellite observations, chemical transport model simulations, and high-resolution anthropogenic emission data to reconstruct daily surface NO₂ concentrations at 1 km resolution across the continental United States (CONUS). Model predictors include tropospheric NO₂ column retrievals from the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), 1 km anthropogenic emissions from NEMO, Community Multiscale Air Quality (CMAQ) model simulations from NACR, reanalysis meteorology, population, elevation, and land-cover information. Sensitivity analyses showed that replacing TROPOMI and NEMO with coarser-resolution Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI) observations and the National Emissions Inventory (NEI) reduced the machine learning model performance but still produced acceptable results. So, for years without TROPOMI and NEMO, OMI and NEI were used as predictors. Using the optimal framework, we generated a 20-year (2002–2020) daily 1 km surface NO₂ dataset over CONUS. Evaluation against observations from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Air Quality System (EPA AQS) using ten-fold cross-validation yielded correlation coefficients (R) of approximately 0.97 and root-mean-square errors (RMSE) of 1.68–1.96 ppb. The reconstructed dataset successfully resolved urban-scale spatial features, including enhanced NO₂ concentrations along major highway corridors and within downtown areas. This long-term, high-resolution dataset provides a valuable resource for air quality analysis, human exposure assessment, and epidemiological studies.

495487.title: Combining Streamflow Forecast Machine Learning Models to Guide Water Management Decisions in New York
495487.authors: Nicole Zenes, Northeast Regional Climate Center, Ithaca, NY; and A. DeGaetano
495487.abstract: Although drought in the American West is more widely publicized, the Eastern US also faces significant drought impacts, especially in New England and the Mid-Atlantic Region. Drought conditions can negatively impact human health (e.g., water quality, infectious diseases), the agricultural sector (e.g., limited water available for irrigation), and tourism (e.g., water levels too low for fishing or boating). These regions experience drought, on average, every two to three years. This study addresses the need for effective water management during these events. To manage these recurring impacts, the Northeast Regional Climate Center (NRCC) paired with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYDEC), with guidance from a user advisory board, to develop a drought forecast tool to help meet the need for improved streamflow forecasts. NRCC scientists developed a machine learning model (Light Gradient Boosting Machine Classifier) that predicts the categorical change in streamflow (i.e., increase, decrease, persist) from current conditions to target forecast days (7 and 14 days out) using recent precipitation and streamflow conditions, and weather forecasts. Independent ML training for 26 streams in NY yielded models that were all more accurate than persistence baseline (mean skill score +0.25) and moderately dependent on the quality of the precipitation forecasts. To provide users with a more comprehensive view of drought conditions, the classifier forecasts are integrated with the U.S. Geological Survey’s (USGS) River DroughtCast tool into a combined, actionable decision-making data visualization. While the LightGBM classifier model captures the short-term directional momentum, the USGS long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network provides historical context, predicting the percentile the future streamflow will fall into (relative to the historical record for that calendar date) with uncertainty bounds. By displaying these tree-based and deep learning forecasts side-by-side, this tool allows stakeholders to make more informed drought management decisions.

495491.title: Improving Dust Detection with the Dynamic Enhancement Background Reduction Algorithm (DEBRA): Ancillary Data Sensitivity and Machine Learning Approaches
495491.authors: Zhixing Ruan, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; CIRA/CSU, Fort Collins, CO; and J. E. Solbrig and C. Seaman
495491.abstract: Lofted dust is transported over long distances and plays a role in air quality, visibility, weather, and climate, with direct impacts on human health, transportation, cloud microphysical processes, and the global radiation budget. Accurate detection of lofted dust is critical to National Weather Service (NWS) mission responsibilities, including dust storm warnings, blowing dust advisories, aviation hazard messaging, and Impact-Based Decision Support Services. The Dynamic Enhancement Background Reduction Algorithm (DEBRA), used operationally by the NWS and the U.S. Navy, combines five infrared channels (1.38, 8.6, 10, 11, and 12 μm) for cloud screening and dust detection. These channels alone yield reasonable detection in many circumstances but also produce frequent false positives, which are mitigated using a surface emissivity database and a surface temperature climatology to define a dynamic lower threshold for detection. This dynamic background correction is only as reliable as its ancillary inputs, both of which are static and do not reflect the surface conditions of individual dust events. We pursue two complementary approaches to improving DEBRA: evaluating the sensitivity of the dynamic background correction to its ancillary inputs, which offers a direct path to operational improvement, and exploring machine learning as a more adaptive alternative for difficult detection cases. Event domains were defined from a subset of the blowing dust plume initiation dataset of Line et al. (2025), covering southwestern North America. For each case, GOES ABI Level 1b radiances, brightness temperatures, geolocation, and viewing and solar geometry were processed alongside DEBRA output, producing a co-registered dataset suitable for both algorithm diagnosis and machine learning experimentation. Using this dataset, we replaced DEBRA's built-in surface temperature climatology with real-time GFS analysis 2-m temperature. Early results indicate that a more realistic background temperature reduces false detections arising from background misrepresentation, but thin and diffuse plumes remain difficult under both configurations. Because DEBRA's detection thresholds were empirically tuned around the ancillary datasets, fully realizing the benefit of improved inputs would require re-tuning these thresholds, and reliable performance would require that tuning to vary in both location and time. This manual, experience-driven process motivates a data-driven alternative. Machine learning approaches were therefore developed for dust detection from GOES ABI observations. Pixel-wise and patch-based neural networks trained on DEBRA-derived labels demonstrate that dust classification can be learned directly from the channel inputs without manually specified thresholds. Building on this proof-of-concept, ongoing work extends to spatially aware architectures that exploit plume texture and structure, together with an active learning strategy in which high-confidence DEBRA detections provide initial weak supervision and manual review is concentrated on ambiguous cases such as plume edges and optically thin dust. Results from these experiments, along with comparisons against the operational DEBRA product, will be presented.

495492.title: UFS Physics Process-Level Evaluation: Insights from the CCPP Single Column Model
495492.authors: Man Zhang, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and W. Li, E. Grell, J. Dudhia, T. J. Hertneky, J. Simonson, F. Yang, L. Bengtsson, L. Bernardet, and X. Zhou
495492.abstract: Advancing physics unification within NOAA’s Unified Forecast System (UFS) requires a process-oriented and scale-aware testing and evaluation framework that can identify the sources of systematic model biases and assess the behavior of physical parameterizations across applications and resolutions. The Developmental Testbed Center (DTC) supports this effort through systematic evaluation of operational and developmental UFS physics suites, including configurations associated with GFSv17 and GEFSv13. This framework is being extended to assess the applicability of these physics suites to NOAA’s Seasonal Forecast System (SFSv1), where coarser spatial resolution and longer prediction timescales introduce additional challenges for representing interactions among clouds, convection, radiation, and precipitation. In collaboration with UFS physics developers, we employ the Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) Single Column Model (SCM) as a process-level testbed to isolate and evaluate key physical processes governing cloud evolution across a range of meteorological regimes. Particular emphasis is placed on marine boundary layer clouds, tropical shallow cumulus, and Arctic mixed-phase clouds—regimes in which interactions among parameterized processes remain challenging for weather and climate models. The SCM framework enables controlled investigation of cloud microphysics, precipitation processes, subgrid-scale cloud representation, and cloud–radiation interactions while reducing complications associated with three-dimensional model dynamics. Through targeted SCM experiments and comparisons with available observations and reference datasets, this process-level evaluation provides insight into the mechanisms underlying physics sensitivities and systematic biases in UFS configurations. The results demonstrate how hierarchical, process-oriented evaluation with the CCPP SCM can inform physics development and help assess the robustness and scale awareness of unified physics suites across UFS applications ranging from weather to seasonal prediction.

495494.title: Untangling the Microphysics and Turbulent Factors Governing the Phase Structure of Arctic Mixed-Phase Stratiform Clouds
495494.authors: Kamal Kant Chandrakar, ; and H. Morrison, A. M. Dzambo, and G. M. McFarquhar
495494.abstract: The structures of liquid and ice phases and their co-variability in mixed-phase stratiform clouds are crucial for precipitation, radiative fluxes, and the timing of glaciation. Korolev & Milbrandt (2022) suggested: “phase composition of mixed-phase clouds is highly intermittent”. However, large-scale Earth System and Regional Models commonly assume homogeneous phase blending that artificially affects cloud glaciation. At the sub-mesoscale, interactions of turbulence with phase changes are hypothesized to help control phase partitioning in mixed-phase clouds. Apart from the availability of effective ice-nucleating particles, ice crystal sedimentation, as well as dynamics such as turbulence, entrainment, and wind shear, could also directly and indirectly affect the phase structure. Therefore, this study aims to untangle the contribution of these factors in controlling ice, liquid, and mixed-phase structures in polar stratiform clouds. Multiple Arctic mixed-phase stratus cloud cases during the Multidisciplinary Drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate (MOSAiC) expedition combined with high-resolution sensitivity simulations are analyzed. Cloud radar reflectivity and mean Doppler velocity from the ARM Ka-band Zenith Radar at high temporal (four-second) and vertical (30 m) resolution, interpolated sounding data, and derived microphysical properties from the Shupe-Turner cloud microphysics product are used to investigate cloud characteristics and structure. We complement these observations with high-resolution large-eddy simulations using the P3 bulk and particle-based Lagrangian microphysics schemes, which are initialized and constrained by observation data. Reflectivity length scales range from ~ 250 to 600 m across the various MOSAiC cases analyzed, varying with cloud depth and wind conditions (see Fig.1). The observed reflectivity spectra display the inertial-convective subrange turbulent cascade with a slightly steeper slope than -5/3 scaling. A detailed sensitivity analysis using LES reveals that ice variability is primarily controlled by sedimentation. The ice-phase correlation length is shorter than that of the liquid phase but slightly longer than vertical velocity within the cloud layer. The ice correlation length scale is also consistent with observations. Without ice, the liquid length scale is closer to the vertical velocity scale, suggesting liquid-ice interactions cause more spread in liquid structure. LES analysis also confirms that the spectral slope of ice is steeper than that of liquid and vertical velocity fields in the inertial subrange. This is due to the accumulation of ice in the updraft caused by differential vertical velocity and sedimentation, generating variability at forcing scales. Ice sedimentation acts as a low-pass filter, damping small-scale variability and faster decay of variance towards smaller scales. Overall, ice sedimentation organizes the phase structure in the large-eddy and inertial-convection range of Arctic mixed-phase stratiform clouds, driving potential for faster glaciation in updrafts than downdrafts. This is inconsistent with homogeneous phase blending commonly assumed in large-scale models.

495497.title: The MPAS Dynamical Core in the Unified Forecast System Weather Model
495497.authors: Dustin J. Swales, NOAA Global Systems Laboratory and Developmental Testbed Center, Westminster, CO
495497.abstract: Efforts are underway to implement the dynamical core from MPAS-Atmosphere within the Unified Forecast System (UFS) Weather Model (UWM). This is foundational to achieving NOAA’s goal of producing global storm scale (~3km) forecasts. Here we will provide an overview on the status of the technical effort to include the MPAS dynamical core within the UWM. This will include how we handle the atmospheric coupling between the Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) and multiple dynamical cores within the UWM ecosystem and highlight initial results. We will also discuss how the MPAS dynamical core integrates into the broader UWM ecosystem, and how the MPAS-UFS-Atmosphere will interface with other Earth system components in the UWM.

495498.title: From Satellite-Only to Gauge-Conditioned Precipitation Ensembles: Incorporating Sparse Rain Gauge Observations into STREAM
495498.authors: Zhe Li, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, 44, China; and D. B. Wright, K. Peng, S. Hartke, and C. Li
495498.abstract: Satellite precipitation products provide essential rainfall information in regions where ground observations are limited, but their uncertainties can be substantial during extreme rainfall events. Precipitation ensembles offer a means of representing these uncertainties through multiple plausible realizations of the unknown true rainfall field. The Space-Time Rainfall Error and Autocorrelation Model (STREAM) generates such ensembles by combining pixel-scale satellite precipitation uncertainty with spatiotemporal error-correlation structures inferred from satellite precipitation fields. In many regions, however, rain gauges are too sparsely distributed to independently characterize the complete rainfall field, despite providing accurate local rainfall information where observations are available. This motivates the development of a gauge-conditioned ensemble approach that uses limited ground observations without losing the probabilistic information provided by STREAM. We propose an extension of STREAM in which the satellite-only precipitation ensemble represents the prior distribution and is conditioned on gauge observations to generate a posterior ensemble. Gauge information is incorporated into the underlying probability structure of the STREAM ensemble, allowing the observations to constrain both precipitation occurrence and rainfall amount while retaining the spatial and temporal dependence represented by the satellite prior. The influence of each gauge is controlled by a localized covariance structure, such that its contribution is strongest near the observation and gradually diminishes with distance, while posterior uncertainty approaches that of the satellite-only prior in poorly observed areas. Gauge measurement and point-to-grid representativeness uncertainties are also considered to avoid unrealistically constraining a grid-cell precipitation estimate to a point measurement. The approach is designed to accommodate different gauge densities and spatial configurations and to be compatible with different satellite precipitation products and pixel-scale uncertainty models. The proposed approach will be demonstrated for extreme rainfall events in South China, including events associated with mesoscale convective systems and tropical cyclones. Existing satellite-only STREAM ensembles will serve as the prior and will then be conditioned using available gauge observations. The gauge network will be systematically thinned to represent different station densities and spatial configurations. The resulting gauge-conditioned ensembles, original satellite estimates, satellite-only STREAM ensembles, and gauge-only interpolated fields will all be evaluated against an independent CMA reference dataset. The analysis will examine how the benefit of gauge conditioning changes with station density, spatial configuration, and storm type, and identify when a satellite-based prior provides useful information beyond that available from sparse-gauge interpolation alone. The resulting approach is intended to more fully exploit the complementary strengths of spatially continuous satellite observations and locally accurate but sparse gauge measurements to produce better-constrained probabilistic precipitation estimates in data-limited regions.

495499.title: The ARTMIP Tier 2 Polar Synthesis: A Comparative Analysis of Polar Atmospheric River Tracking Methods In Historical and Future Climate States
495499.authors: Kyle S Mattingly, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, WI; and M. Maclennan, J. Schnaubelt, and C. A. Shields
495499.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are the conduit for the majority of atmospheric moisture transport to the polar regions and influence the evolution of polar ice sheets and sea ice. Their impacts on the polar cryosphere are expected to intensify as atmospheric moisture content and temperatures increase in a warming climate. Prior studies facilitated by the Atmospheric River Tracking Method Intercomparison Project (ARTMIP) show that quantitative and qualitative conclusions about the global climatology, impacts, and future changes of ARs depend on the choice of AR detection tool (ARDT) used in the analysis. There is a community need for a similar comparison of ARDTs in the polar regions (both the Arctic and Antarctica), where the unique atmospheric conditions require different parameters for AR detection relative to global ARDTs. Here, we present the ARTMIP polar synthesis experiment, a collaborative effort to provide community guidance on best practices for ARDT selection in polar studies. We build upon the existing ARTMIP framework to curate and compare AR catalogues from eleven ARDTs that have been developed for polar AR identification. We first analyze Arctic and Antarctic AR climatology across ARDTs in the historical record using MERRA-2 atmospheric reanalysis, focusing on similarities and differences among ARDTs linked to their algorithm design, and the effect of inter-ARDT differences on AR-attributed ice sheet and sea ice impacts. We then extend our analysis to future AR projections by applying a subset of ARDTs to three representative members of the CESM2 large ensemble under the SSP3-7.0 emissions scenario. Finally, we use a subset of four ARDTs in a case study to assess how existing ARDTs may be tuned to more accurately identify polar ARs. Our results show that polar ARDTs can generally be grouped into three categories based on their detection of AR frequency and impacts: (1) "global heritage" ARDTs that were originally developed for global AR studies and subsequently tuned for polar AR detection; (2) "Antarctic heritage" ARDTs that were developed from inception for AR detection in the interior of Antarctica; and (3) a "hybrid" ARDT (PIKART) that shares characteristics of both the other categories. The global heritage ARDTs generally show polar AR frequency and impacts that peak in the mid-latitude storm tracks of both the Northern and Southern hemispheres and decrease toward the poles, with little to no ARs identified in the interior of the Antarctic Ice Sheet. The Antarctic heritage ARDTs, conversely, show a less pronounced meridional gradient in AR detection in both hemispheres, and attribute a substantial proportion of precipitation in the Antarctic interior to ARs. Global heritage ARDTs show a large spread in future AR projections due to their varied algorithm design parameters, while Antarctic heritage ARDTs show more cross-algorithm consistency in projecting small increases in AR frequency. Our polar synthesis leads us to recommend that researchers carefully consider their research questions and study region when choosing which ARDT(s) to use, and following the guidance from previous ARTMIP experiments, we recommend using multiple ARDTs to constrain uncertainty related to AR detection where possible.

495502.title: Kansas Mesonet Fire Danger Data in A Changing Landscape
495502.authors: Chip A. Redmond, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS
495502.abstract: Kansas has sparse federal data collection for fire weather observations and calculations. With the recent transition between United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) United States Forest Service (USFS) Weather Information Management System (WIMS) to the multi-agency collaboration of Fire Environment Mapping System (FEMS), significant changes have occurred in the fire decision support landscape and data flow. Implementation of National Weather Service (NWS) Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) into the new FEMS system did improve data coverage. However, those locations typically migrated towards more populated areas of the state and are not representative of more exposed, wildfire prone rural portions of Kansas. Therefore, through efforts of FEMS collaborators/programmers, the National Mesonet Program (NMP) and state partners, the incorporation of Kansas Mesonet data has significantly expanded the coverage of supporting wildland fire decision data in Kansas. This complement of new data points incorporated into FEMS has substantially improved state fire managers, expanding their wildland fire support information. Most notably, the data inclusion into FEMS runs meteorological observations through the 2016 National Fire Danger Rating System (NFDRS). This provides output variables that address short and long term dryness, drought indices and dead fuel moisture calculations that support fire awareness and measurements of various fuel types. Resulting data availability had positive impacts on improving local preparedness, response and recovery from wildland fire. This presentation will discuss the improvements of data accessibility/quality, interaction between stakeholders and the methods by which data are integrated into state plans. This not only assisted at the state level but also improved fire district level decisions. Additionally, this presentation will use a case study to discuss the resulting preparedness and response to a rare, lightning wildfire outbreak which took place May 14, 2026 in Meade and Clark County, Kansas. This unique fire event was well captured with FEMS NFDRS data and provided management and suppression support, highlighting the improved fire weather data available. Integration of the Kansas Mesonet meteorological data into FEMS provides a great example for other state networks to integrate into a larger fire danger system.

495506.title: A Community Vision for Advancing Hydrologic Sciences In the Next Decade
495506.authors: Timothy L. Schneider, NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and E. Jack-Scott, S. Kumar, J. Reager, and J. A. Vano
495506.abstract: Supported by NASA’s Terrestrial Hydrology Program, a major community-led effort surveyed nearly 400 scientists, remote sensing experts, modelers, data scientists, and resource managers to establish strategic priorities for the next decade of space-based Earth observations. As environmental pressures mount, aligning satellite observational capabilities with actionable decision-making requires a coordinated framework across physical and applied sciences. This talk details the survey design, engagement methodology, and synthesized community findings across five core societal themes: floods, droughts, water quality, water supply, and water demand. We examine top recommendations at the intersection of satellite remote sensing, Earth system modeling and prediction, data science, and decision support. Special attention is given to cross-cutting priorities, including integrating human activities into physical water cycle models, closing data-to-decision gaps, and optimizing observational strategies under resource constraints. Finally, we present the high-level roadmap generated by this collective effort, offering a unified community perspective on how the next generation of space-based hydrological observations can advance foundational science while delivering tangible societal benefits.

495512.title: Advancing Precision in Estimating Hail Property Damage
495512.authors: Samuel Jeffrey Porter, The Ohio State University, Medina, OH; and R. Ding and S. M. Quiring
495512.abstract: Hail is one of the most financially consequential severe-weather hazards in the United States, however, substantial uncertainty remains in translating meteorological data into property-level damage and financial loss. Following a hail event, insurers and roofing contractors must rapidly determine the spatial extent of damage, identify properties with significant loss, prioritize inspections, and estimate the magnitude of near-future claims. Current workflows frequently rely on broad hail swaths, homeowner-reported damage, and property inspections. These approaches provide limited spatial resolution and introduce uncertainty and subjectivity into post-event damage assessment. Consequently, insurers face challenges in distinguishing potentially damaged properties from unaffected homes, while roofing contractors must efficiently identify and prioritize areas with the greatest actionable damage. This work, developed through Ohio State, addresses this gap with a real-time, property level hazard-to-loss modeling framework that meshes meteorological data with financial datasets and building footprints. Through a modelled framework, the results are delivered within an innovative live interactive dashboard, designed for rapid post-event assessments. As radar scans and additional datasets are processed, the platform produces interactive maps, property-level damage probabilities, and storm-level damage summaries. Users can analyze individual properties and spatial clusters of potentially impacted structures. This interface connects real-time atmospheric data with operational decisions to eliminate insurance fraud while improving the industry workflows post hailstorm. Development of the framework has been reviewed and discussed by nearly 80 interviews with insurance and roofing industry professionals, as well as multiple proof-of-concept feedback sessions, focusing on operational usability. As work continues, additional datasets, innovative model features, and platform accessibility will be added to link economics with financial impacts. Several hailstorm case studies are being evaluated to examine the relationship between observed meteorological data, modeled property-level risk, and reported damage. One case study focuses on the 30 May 2024 hailstorm (~2 Billion in Property Damage) in Denver, Colorado, providing an opportunity to evaluate model performance across a high-impact urban hail event with substantial property exposure. Additional case studies are being incorporated to assess the consistency of the framework across different storm environments. The presentation will highlight several hailstorm case studies and demonstrate how real-time meteorological events are transformed through the modeling framework into property-level damage and financial risk estimates. The presentation will also briefly speak on the development of the interactive platform, including visualization and user-accessibility to translate the data into operational decision-support systems.

495513.title: Vegetation-Atmosphere Interactions and Grid Vulnerability to Wildfires and Damaging Weather Events In the Northeastern U.S.
495513.authors: Jeffrey Michael Freedman, Atmospheric Sciences Reserach Center (ASRC) SUNY University at Albany, Albany, NY; and P. M. Miller, A. Mohammed, and M. Seymour, MS
495513.abstract: In the Northeastern US (NEUS), severe weather events (thunderstorms, icing, nor’easters, tropical cyclones, frontal systems) produce power outages affecting millions of customers and causing billions of dollars in economic losses. Wildfires, however, have had little impact on grid operations. For example, recent history shows New York State wildfire frequency and coverage is minimal—typically a few hundred acres annually. However, in the early 20th century, the NEUS experienced very large wildfires, especially in upstate New York and New England, including the Great Adirondack Fire, which burned nearly 500,000 acres in the spring of 1903; another large event burned several hundred thousand acres in 1908. After these two events, aggressive fire suppression efforts, in combination with the installation of large-scale fire tower networks, significantly decreased the amount of acreage burned. The current pluvial (wet) period (1968 - present) has also contributed to the overall decrease in the number of wildfires (Figure 1). In recent years, however, during periods of intense short-term drought, there has been an uptick in wildfire occurrence and size. The frequency and intensity of wildfires may increase further in response to higher probabilities of short-term drought and declining forest health, a consequence of invasive species, disease, and climate change. Here we present current research on vegetation–atmosphere interactions in the context of weather and ecosystem exchange, and the susceptibility of grid infrastructure to damaging weather events, with emphasis on wildfires, in a changing climate.

495514.title: The NASA Living With a Star Focused Science Team “Moving Beyond F10.7, Quantifying Solar EUV Flux and its Impact on the Ionosphere – Thermosphere – Mesosphere System”
495514.authors: Phillip Chamberlin, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and C. T. Hsu, C. N. Arge, S. Xu, M. Vincent, T. E. Berger, E. Thiemann, S. Webber, L. Balmaceda, S. Yu, S. Bahauddin, N. Pedatella, L. Qian, J. R. Gomez, F. Laskar, J. Thayer, T. Hoeksema, M. Wang, B. Schwab, N. Flyer, and N. Holland
495514.abstract: Solar Extreme-Ultraviolet (EUV) irradiance is a dominant heating and ionization source for the Ionosphere – Thermosphere – Mesosphere (ITM) system. Solar activity fluctuates on several temporal scales – from minutes (flares) to days (active region emergence and 27-day rotation) to decades (11-year cycle) – and initiates huge variations in the neutral density and temperature, ion and electron densities and temperatures, neutral winds, and electric fields in the ionosphere. Studies of the ITM often rely on the F10.7 index as a primary solar driver. However, it is currently known that this index does not fully describe the solar input in the EUV wavelength range. Using the F10.7 index will have an adverse effect on a wide range of ITM parameters (e.g., peak density of the F2 layer, total electron content (TEC), electron density in the D-region and topside ionosphere, nitric oxide concentration), but the quantitative impact is much less known/understood. The overarching goal of a 2022 Living With a Star Focus Science Team (LWS/FST) titled “Moving Beyond F10.7” is to develop the ability to reliably specify and predict the effects of solar variability on the ITM system. Specific objectives include: 1) identifying new and/or improved EUV indices for driving model predictions of ITM structure; 2) improved understanding of how particular portions of the EUV spectrum influence specific aspects of ITM structure (e.g., ionospheric profile shape, Thermospheric composition, density, or temperature); and 3) exploring new EUV observations characterizing the interactions between the ionosphere and thermosphere. It is now the fourth and final year of this FST, and this paper will be a summary of the team's accomplishments to date, other products/plans expected before conclusion of the project, as well as future potential projects that would be direct follow-ons to continue the momentum of this work.

495515.title: Multi-Sensor Precipitation Estimations from the MRMS System: From Initial Concepts to Current and Future Capabilities
495515.authors: Steven M. Martinaitis, University of Oklahoma - CIWRO, Norman, OK; and J. Zhang, R. A. Clark III, A. P. Osborne, C. Langston, and K. Elmore
495515.abstract: The multi-sensor aspect of the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system has been prominent within the development of MRMS quantitative precipitation estimates (QPEs) for over 20 years. This includes the initial operational capabilities of producing local gauge-corrected radar QPE and Mountain Mapper QPE products since 2014, which then evolved into the current multisensor QPE (MSQPE) product suite for both CONUS and OCONUS domains. The current operational MSQPE products are derived from a combination of mosaicked radar data, hourly rain gauges, model-derived precipitation forecasts, and other input fields, where these inputs are utilized based on radar coverage via the Radar Quality Index (RQI) and other weighting schemes. This presentation will first highlight the history of multi-sensor QPE within the MRMS system, ranging from conceptual designs to product development and testing prior to National Weather Service (NWS) operational implementation. The presentation will then provide current performance standards and results of the current MSQPE capabilities along with strengths and weaknesses of the MSQPE product based on comprehensive analyses and NWS feedback. And finally, the presentation will provide a future vision on what multi-sensor precipitation capabilities can look like within the MRMS system. This includes updates to our RQI and multi-sensor schemes, the future ingest and quality control of both hourly and daily gauge observations, the inclusion of satellite-based precipitation data, and how the work can align with next-generation weather observing capabilities.

495516.title: Scanning Doppler LiDAR Observations of Offshore Internal Boundary Layer Development
495516.authors: Giacomo Valerio Lungo, University of Texas Dallas, Richardson, TX
495516.abstract: Abrupt changes in surface roughness at coastlines generate an internal boundary layer (IBL) in which the mean flow and turbulence progressively adjust to the downstream surface. Offshore observations remain limited because resolving the spatial development of the IBL near the coastline requires measurements over the ocean. This observational gap is particularly relevant to offshore wind energy, where coastal transitions influence turbine-height wind speed, shear, and turbulence. In this work, the offshore evolution of the IBL is investigated using scanning Doppler LiDAR observations collected at Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, during the Third Wind Forecast Improvement Project. Repeated range–height indicator (RHI) scans were performed approximately aligned with the offshore wind direction. Each RHI scan was completed in approximately 8 s and contained about 18 lines of sight. Approximately 104 RHI scans were repeated during each 15-min measurement period, enabling the calculation of spatially resolved mean streamwise wind speed, the standard deviation of streamwise velocity fluctuations, and turbulence intensity. Along each line of sight, the LiDAR measurements were averaged over a 24-m range-gate length. However, overlapping range-gate processing provided estimates at approximately 1.5-m intervals, yielding nearly 1,800 measurement points in the horizontal direction over distances extending to approximately 2.7 km from the LiDAR. This high-resolution scanning configuration provides simultaneous measurements at numerous horizontal and vertical locations over the ocean, helping address the scarcity of spatially resolved offshore observations near land–sea transitions. The measurements, therefore, enable direct investigation of how wind speed and turbulence evolve as offshore flow adjusts from the rough land surface to the smoother ocean surface. A turbulence-intensity-based diagnostic is introduced to identify the IBL height as a function of the streamwise fetch.
