The method is motivated by the contrasting vertical turbulence structures over land and ocean. Below the IBL height, the flow progressively adjusts to the smoother ocean surface and turbulence intensity decreases, whereas the flow above the IBL retains the stronger turbulence signature of the upstream land surface. Their interaction produces a transition region and a local maximum in the vertical turbulence-intensity profile. The IBL height is therefore defined as the elevation of this local maximum, equivalently, where the vertical turbulence-intensity gradient changes from positive to negative. To evaluate the proposed method, an illustrative offshore RHI scan acquired on 22 January 2025 is analyzed. During this event, atmospheric conditions were near neutral over land but unstable over the ocean as colder air moved over warmer water, while the flow transitioned from the rough land surface to the smoother ocean surface. Vertical profiles of turbulence intensity are examined at multiple offshore fetch distances. A distinct local maximum is observed in each profile, and the elevation of this peak generally increases with fetch, confirming that the proposed turbulence-intensity-based diagnostic successfully captures the offshore growth of the IBL. Comparison with the corresponding upstream land profiles reveals a clear two-layer structure. Below the detected IBL height, turbulence intensity decreases and mean wind speed accelerates as the flow adjusts to the smoother ocean surface. Above the IBL height, both profiles retain trends and slopes comparable to those observed over land, indicating that the upper flow remains influenced by the upstream land boundary layer. Although both quantities capture the transition between the ocean-adjusted layer below and the residual land-influenced layer above, the IBL height is identified more clearly from the distinct local maximum in the turbulence-intensity profile than from the subtle kink in the mean wind-speed profile commonly used in previous studies. Quantitatively, the diagnosed IBL height increases from approximately 42 m at 300 m offshore to about 86 m at 900 m offshore. The turbulence intensity at the diagnosed IBL top is approximately 15–25% greater than the corresponding near-surface ocean value, while the mean wind speed near 50 m increases to approximately 11–12% above the upstream land value by about 2 km offshore. These results demonstrate that the lower part of the flow progressively adjusts to the smoother ocean surface, while the turbulence signature associated with the IBL top weakens with increasing fetch. Comparison with established IBL-height models shows that the Miyake diffusion-analogy model provides the closest agreement with the proposed turbulence-intensity-based method. Relative to the proposed estimates, the Miyake formulation yields a bias of 0.85 m, an RMSE of 10.35 m, a mean absolute percentage error of 8.97%, and a correlation coefficient of 0.982. This close agreement is physically meaningful because both methods are linked to turbulent transport: Miyake’s formulation relates IBL growth to vertical turbulent diffusion, whereas the proposed method identifies the IBL top from the local maximum in the vertical turbulence-intensity profile.

495517.title: Mathematical Feature Engineering for an Automated Gravity Wave Detection Algorithm in Day-Night Band Imagery
495517.authors: Lander Ver Hoef, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and S. D. Miller, I. Ebert-Uphoff, and J. M. Forsythe
495517.abstract: Atmospheric gravity waves (GWs) play an important role in energy transfer within Earth’s atmosphere, and have been studied extensively in the lower parts of the atmosphere where they can be detected in satellite imagery by their effects on clouds and water vapor fields. GWs also play a significant role in the middle to upper atmosphere, where they deposit their energy and momentum through breaking and absorption, influencing the circulation and accounting for important patterns such as stratospheric wind reversals (the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation) which go on to influence global seasonal to sub-seasonal weather patterns in the troposphere. However, the study of GWs in the middle-to-upper atmosphere is challenging due to few satellite observations providing sensitivity at these levels. The lack of data makes it more difficult to validate and improve upon current methods of parametrizing this energy transfer in numerical weather prediction models. A key breakthrough in our ability to observe these gravity waves came in 2015 when Miller et al. [1] reported that the Day-Night Band (DNB) sensor on the Suomi-NPP satellite was sensitive enough to view fluctuations in airglow near the mesopause on moonless nights caused by the pressure and temperature fluctuations induced by GWs. The GWs present in DNB imagery as a distinctive banding pattern that is often readily detectable by human analysts. However, due to the significant noise present in DNB imagery, the sparseness of observations (requiring the coincidence of significant airglow, a GW, and a satellite overpass on a moonless night), city lights, lightning, tropospheric clouds that reflect the downward airglow, and the lack of labeled data, building an automated detector has proved challenging, although recent work by Hozumi et al. [2] has shown that a conventional neural network model trained on non-satellite images then fine-tuned for this application is able to identify gravity waves in DNB imagery. Here we explore an alternative approach to try to build a simpler, more interpretable AI model from scratch for this application. We first identify the key information and patterns that human analysts use to identify GWs, and custom design a hybrid workflow leveraging that same information and patterns. To do so, we first utilize a new mathematical feature engineering technique (which we refer to as the Miller space) to highlight the characteristic signature of GWs in DNB imagery while suppressing noise and other potentially ambiguous features. We use these mathematically-defined features as input to a customized convolutional neural network with non-standard features such as asymmetric filters and unidirectional pooling, which is trained on a relatively small set of examples hand-labeled by a group of GW experts. Here, we present preliminary results, as well as details on the feature engineering technique and machine learning algorithm. In the future we plan to compare the results of our algorithms to those obtained by Hozumi et al. [2]. References: [1] Miller, S. D., Straka, W. C., Yue, J., Smith, S. M., Alexander, M. J., Hoffmann, L., Setvák, M., & Partain, P. T. (2015). Upper Atmospheric Gravity Wave details revealed in nightglow satellite imagery. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 112(49). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1508084112 [2] Hozumi, Y., Yue, J., Mostafa, S.A.M., Wang, C., Wang, J., Purushotham, S. and Miller, S.D., Machine-learning detection and variability of mesospheric frontal waves observed by VIIRS day/night band. Earth Planets Space 77, 179 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1186/s40623-025-02308-4

495519.title: The Multiscale Non-Gaussian Statistics of Free-Running 1000-Member General Circulation Model Ensembles
495519.authors: Man-Yau (Joseph) Chan, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and H. G. Chipilski, J. Schwartz, M. Albrecht, A. Q. Ridgway, and S. D. Shuvo
495519.abstract: Probabilistic atmospheric forecasts are useful for disaster management and a variety of socioeconomic activities. One avenue to improve these forecasts is through advancing our understanding of forecast distributions. This study advances that understanding through a multiscale investigation of 1000-member free-running ensembles of a coarse resolution intermediate complexity general circulation model (GCM). We found direct non-parametric evidence that a time-varying equilibrium forecast distribution manifests at long lead times (> 40% longer than the variance saturation time). Interestingly, the forecast distribution exhibits the strongest non-Gaussian characteristics prior to equilibration. That spike in non-Gaussianity is likely because the forecast distribution encountered the boundary separating physically realistic and unrealistic atmospheric states. The characteristics of the time-varying equilibrium distribution are also explored. Our findings thus imply that (1) useful information may be present in probabilistic forecasts beyond the variance saturation time, and (2) models of forecast distributions should account for the complicated structures that arise in multivariate forecast statistics prior to equilibration. These implications and our findings merit further investigation using more realistic GCMs.

495522.title: Moving Beyond Accuracy: Evaluating the Reasoning Chains of Vision-Language Models with ReasonBench
495522.authors: Gwyn Uttmark, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and R. Walsh, J. E. Solbrig, D. Nietfeld, and I. Ebert-Uphoff
495522.abstract: Operational forecasters receiving crowdsourced weather reports must manually retrieve and review radar or satellite imagery to determine meteorological plausibility. Vision-capable large language models could automate this triage by flagging reports clearly at odds with available meteorological data. However, no established methods exist for producing incremental and non-binary performance assessments of how such models evaluate meteorological imagery. Standard accuracy metrics do not reveal where reasoning breaks down and thus impede harness development and model selection. We are developing ReasonBench to benchmark both the final detection outcome of a vision-language model and the reasoning process it uses to reach its conclusions. The framework uses curated positive and negative report-and-imagery pairs from storm report data matched to radar and geostationary imagery for deep convection events. For each case the framework captures the reasoning and output tokens of the model under test which are then evaluated along two tracks. The first uses programmatic heuristics that verify whether a model's stated evidence, such as claimed high wind values, correspond to structures present in the data provided. The second uses a larger and more capable large language model to assess the meteorological soundness of the target model's reasoning chain, with evaluator judgments guided and calibrated by a human-reviewed data set. The framework is designed to be used to benchmark frontier and open source models with differing model sizes, quantizations, and temperature settings as existing vision-language benchmarks do not capture the specialized physical reasoning and operational decision logic that meteorological applications demand. Attendees will gain insight into an open source and reusable evaluation framework, data on model selection for meteorological imagery tasks, and contextual strategies for targeting commonly observed failure modes.

495523.title: Identifying Early Indicators of Mesoscale Rotation in Quasi-Linear Convective Systems with Ensemble Sensitivity Analysis and Sensitivity-Based Ensemble Subsetting
495523.authors: Michael L Brown, Texas Tech Univ., Lubbock, TX; and C. C. Weiss and D. Dowell
495523.abstract: While supercell tornadoes have average warning lead times of nearly 18 minutes, lead time drops by over 30% for quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) tornadoes due to several meteorological, socioeconomical, and geographical reasons. Moreso, these storm modes disproportionately affect the southeastern United States, a region made up of more vulnerable populations than other areas. Modern numerical weather prediction models (NWP) deploy several improvements compared to previous generation models yet still struggle to predict high-impact situations. Additional NWP improvements are costly and provide diminishing returns. Thus, post-processing techniques, including Ensemble Sensitivity Analysis (ESA) and sensitivity-based ensemble subsetting, are being evaluated for their efficacy in improving forecast skill. Here, both methods are applied to Verification of the Origins of Rotation in Tornadoes Experiment Southeast/USA (VORTEX-SE/USA) Intensive Observing Periods (IOPs) to assess improvements in forecasting QLCS thunderstorm rotation across the southeastern United States. Selected IOPs feature significant forecast uncertainty, high impact to the public, and are well-observed by VORTEX-SE/USA instrumentation. Simulations of these IOPs are generated with realistic Weather Research and Forecast (WRF) model ensembles that deploy operational High-Resolution-Rapid-Refresh (HRRR) model physics. Both qualitative and quantitative analyses are performed on the forecast sensitivities of updraft helicity (UH) and vertical vorticity (VV) response variables to several atmospheric state variables. Additionally, practical ensemble subsetting experiments are performed to evaluate forecast accuracy improvements achieved relative to the full ensemble family. Results show that the ESA technique can be successfully deployed to the nonlinear space of QLCSs at lead times of several hours. A simulation ensemble of VORTEX-SE/USA 2017 IOP4c (30 April 2017), reveals significant sensitivities to various coherent frontal, outflow, and warm-sector meteorological signals with respect to the UH maximum response analysis. Sensitivity-based ensemble subsetting experiments utilizing conventional and research-grade VORTEX-SE/USA observations explore the utility of a reduced subset of less error-prone ensemble members to exclusively predict the rotation response variable. This approach yields coherent forecasted rotation response error reductions with respect to the full model ensemble across multiple lead time durations and several projection definitions. An optimal ensemble subsetting configuration for this case study incorporates surface temperature observations from both the conventional ASOS observing network and the TTU StickNet research platform into the atmospheric state error calculations and has a subset size between 20% and 60% of the original model ensemble. While promising, caution regarding the case study’s nonlinear extension of the methodology and the definition of the observed proxy rotation response must be observed. An additional analysis centered on rotation responses located farther east in Alabama several hours later for the same IOP on 30 April 2017 also reveals significant coherent sensitivity features with respect to the QLCS of interest. This extension also provides further evaluation of practical ensemble subsetting methodologies utilizing more numerous and varied atmospheric observing platforms deployed during the IOP. A second simulation ensemble of the VORTEX-SE/USA Meso18-19 IOP8 (13 April 2019) also explores several meteorologically coherent sensitivity features that are linked to QLCS rotation response across the Southeast, as well as the utility of practical ensemble subsetting practices incorporating conventional and field observations to reduce forecasted mesoscale rotation error. Any commonalities in sensitivity feature presentations and practical ensemble subsetting performance evaluations across the cases will be explored to examine generalized behaviors of QLCS mesoscale rotation predictability.

495524.title: Using Machine Learning to Identify Potential Tornado Tracks for Post-Event Verification
495524.authors: Johnathan Alexander Strickland, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and C. Hammer
495524.abstract: In the wake of severe weather events, local National Weather Service (NWS) Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) are responsible for conducting post-event storm surveys to confirm the track and intensity of tornadoes. The NWS aims to complete surveys within 24 hours of an event so that accurate information can be gathered before substantial debris removal occurs. During large outbreaks, however, surveys may continue for days or even weeks after the event, hindering forecasters' ability to accurately estimate the storm's strength. To address this, we used machine learning to develop a model that identifies locations where tornado impacts are likely to help forecasters quickly and accurately determine where storm surveys are most needed. The model was trained on data from confirmed tornado tracks, unverified tornado warnings, and random points and times observed in the County Warning Areas (CWA) of the Northern Indiana (IWX) and Chicago (LOT) WFOs between January 1, 2020 and June 1, 2026. In training, the model achieved an accuracy of approximately 85%, indicating good skill at broadly identifying areas where storm surveys can be prioritized. In particular, the model showed relatively good skill at identifying areas where smaller, weaker tornadoes likely occurred. These tornadoes have the highest likelihood of going unnoticed by forecasters, highlighting a potential application of this model in an operational environment.

495525.title: Organizational Decision Making and Communication During Tornado Threats
495525.authors: Rhonda Plofkin, NCAS-M, Baltimore, MD; and J. Halverson and K. Klockow-McClain
495525.abstract: Although organizations may receive the same tornado warning, protective action decisions vary because operational priorities, regulatory requirements, and organizational responsibilities shape how warnings are interpreted and acted upon. Since businesses respond differently to disasters based on their own defined objectives, understanding the characteristics that define these differences is imperative for effective communication and preparedness during a tornadic event. This study used a qualitative approach to analyze seven in depth interviews across five business sectors located in the Midwestern United States. The data was analyzed through the lens of business characteristics such as mandate environment, life safety responsibility and sector. Despite receiving similar warning information, organizations described different communication and protective action strategies based on competing operational priorities, regulatory requirements, and responsibility for employee and patron safety. Organizational communication occurred through two pathways; internal communication between employees and external communication between employee and patron. Critical barriers emerged across all organizations revealing the tradeoffs businesses consider during tornado events. These findings suggest that improving tornado response requires more than accurate forecasts. Communication, emergency planning and policy guidance must account for the tradeoffs and barriers organizations face during severe weather.

495528.title: Forecast Skill and Propulsion as VLEO Design Parameters
495528.authors: Andrew Hermetet, Redwire, Chantilly, FL; and M. Holmes and S. Wise
495528.abstract: The space industry’s enthusiasm for Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) rests upon an uncomfortable bargain. The same low altitude that affords finer resolution, lower latency, and prompt post-mission disposal renders VLEO hostage to solar and geomagnetic events, wherein neutral density may double within hours. Compounding this, the electric propulsion (EP) that makes sustained VLEO operations tractable: superb in specific impulse, economical with propellant, is incapable of the impulsive response a density surge demands. The spacecraft that can afford to stay is often one that cannot flee. We interrogate this tension by way of the February 2022 space weather event, whose contribution to the loss of a newly launched Starlink tranche furnishes a well-documented natural experiment. Using the Redwire VLEO simulation stack: ACORN coupled to NASA DAC97, NRL MSIS, and NASA HWM14, we fly a generic box and wing bus and a VLEO-optimized configuration through the storm under three propulsion architectures (EP, chemical, and hybrid) and three tiers of forecast fidelity (none, NOAA SWPC, and HALE), yielding eighteen cases. The figure of merit is mission survival: whether the vehicle crosses the atmospheric conditions beyond which recovery is no longer possible. The heliophysics-driven forecast proves preferable in every configuration. Absent it, chemical propulsion, and its capacity to maneuver impulsively, emerges as the necessary hedge. Forecast skill, we submit, is not a convenience but a design parameter. In its absence, the deficit is settled in kilograms: the wet mass of a chemical or hybrid stage, carried for a storm that may never arrive.

495532.title: Irrigation-Atmosphere Feedbacks over the Southeastern United States
495532.authors: Georgios Priftis, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and A. T. White, D. T. Haliczer, L. Ellenburg, V. Mishra, U. Nair, V. Martin, and N. Magliocca
495532.abstract: Irrigation modifies surface-energy partitioning and may affect boundary-layer development, clouds, and precipitation beyond irrigated areas. Unlike the Great Plains and western Corn Belt, where irrigation creates a strong moisture contrast with the surrounding environment, the humid Southeast has abundant background moisture, frequent convection, and substantial terrestrial moisture recycling. Irrigation effects may therefore be weaker, more diffuse, or more dependent on prevailing atmospheric conditions. This study combines GOES-R observations with convection-permitting regional simulations to examine cloud variability and irrigation-induced atmospheric responses across scales. GOES-R Advanced Baseline Imager products are first used to characterize the diurnal cycle, frequency, and spatial distribution of clouds over agricultural regions. Cloud mask, cloud-top temperature and height, cloud optical depth, and cloud effective particle size describe cloud occurrence, vertical development, and microphysical and radiative characteristics under different land-surface and atmospheric conditions. This analysis provides an independent observational description of regional cloud behavior. Irrigation mechanisms are then investigated through paired irrigation and control simulations with identical atmospheric configurations but different agricultural land-surface conditions. Changes in soil moisture, surface heat fluxes, and Bowen ratio characterize responses over irrigated grid cells and surrounding areas. Associated changes in temperature, humidity, boundary-layer height, atmospheric stability, low-level convergence, clouds, and precipitation reveal how irrigation perturbations propagate through the lower atmosphere. The analysis emphasizes variations with time of day, background conditions, and spatial scale. By distinguishing local surface responses from indirect and nonlocal atmospheric effects, the study identifies when irrigation signals remain near the surface and when they influence environments favorable for cloud and precipitation development.

495534.title: TOWR-S Satellite Resources for NWS Mission Awareness
495534.authors: Luke Wichrowski, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and E. Sorbella, S. Koohpai, J. Anderson, M. Foster, J. K. Zajic, L. A. Byerle, and J. Fulbright
495534.abstract: The Total Operational Weather Readiness - Satellites (TOWR-S) Portal is a centralized outreach hub where forecasters can quickly access tools, data displays, and other mission support resources in one place. Primary examples include VuSkew, the Mission Map, and the Looper. VuSkew, an interactive multi-source satellite sounding viewer, combines radiosonde, aircraft, Geo and Polar satellite-based, and model soundings into one interface, allowing forecasters to compare profiles, evaluate stability, and analyze environmental evolution with intuitive controls. The Mission Map displays GOES mesoscale sectors and NWS alerts for real-time situational awareness. It details Weather Forecast Office (WFO) boundaries, soundings, severe hazards, observations, and other environmental features into an interactive display that supports rapid atmospheric interpretation. The Looper currently explores how satellite data can be integrated to provide tailored aviation support, while examining new techniques for satellite data visualization with cloud resources (e.g. zarr). The TOWR-S Portal also highlights reference procedures (thematic AWIPS bundles) provided by NWS forecasters; the Polar Planner tool; “SatCave” for connecting NESDIS and NWS colleagues to mission applications; and the NESDIS GEO and LEO Program-sponsored Satellite Book Club archive. All of these resources continue to evolve based upon feedback and collaboration with NWS forecasters.

495535.title: What Does the Future of the National Space Weather Enterprise Look like?
495535.authors: Geoff Crowley, Space Industry Consultants, Lafayette, CO; and J. Green
495535.abstract: The Space Weather Roundtable has held numerous meetings exploring the current state of the National Space Weather Enterprise. The Roundtable includes members from academia, government and commercial space weather service providers, and it is also attended ex-officio by representatives from NOAA, NSF, NASA and the DoD. In pursuit of its mandate from congress, the Roundtable has explored how the Nation might: (1) facilitate advances in space weather prediction and forecasting; (2) increase coordination of space weather research to operations and operations to research; and (3) improve preparedness for potential space weather phenomena. The Roundtable is currently asking whether the US National Space Weather Enterprise can be more effective, and we are looking for thoughts and opinions from the space weather community. The Roundtable is preparing for a major 3-4 day Workshop regarding the entire US Space Weather Enterprise that will be organized by the National Academies of Science, Engineering and Mathematics (NASEM). Our goal is to have a report produced from that Workshop with findings that can be referenced by policy makers, agencies and others in the future. The Workshop currently has a working theme along the lines of Evolving the Space Weather Enterprise to an “R2X” Framework, and will include discussion of a 'Fair Weather Report' for Space Weather. Potential discussion topics could include: What does the future of the National Space Weather Enterprise look like? Can new policies and processes be put in place to achieve a more effective and efficient Enterprise? Are there any User Needs that are not currently being met? Is the US ready to respond if a Carrington-level storm arises? What are the roles of NASA, NSF, NOAA, DoD and other agencies in the future ‘National Space Weather Enterprise’? What are the roles of commercial ‘Space weather service providers’ What is the role of Academia What is the role of CCMC and Space Weather Testbed How could the R2O2R program maintain and improve its effectiveness? What are the appropriate funding sources, levels, and contract vehicles for Space Weather Research and technology development? Can we improve the transition of space weather-related technologies to operational status? Is there really a Valley of Death (or a Cliff of Death) for new technologies? How can the Space Weather community respond to evolution of the Space Industry? Any other ideas or topics for discussion? Disclaimer: This presentation does not seek to reflect any official opinions or positions of the NASEM Roundtable.

495539.title: Studying Deep Meteorological Uncertainty in the Context of Energy System Planning
495539.authors: Srihari Sundar, National Lab of the Rockies, Golden, CO; and V. Carag, S. Cohen, and G. Buster
495539.abstract: The rapid evolution of the U.S. energy sector has increased the importance of power systems that are resilient to a large range of future weather conditions and events. Uncertainty in the characteristics and behavior of severe weather poses risks to the future stability and operation of the power systems. First, using a set of weather futures from five different global earth system models, we quantify long-term trends relevant to power systems, including regional, multi-sector load growth trajectories. We use the Regional Energy Deployment System (ReEDS), NLR's flagship capacity expansion model, to simulate how U.S. bulk power systems evolve under different socio-economic pathways and future weather scenarios. We stress test these future builds by quantifying system reliability using the Probabilistic Resource Adequacy Suite (PRAS) under unseen weather conditions. These unseen weather conditions include weather years and trajectories unused in the ReEDS simulations. Using resource adequacy (RA) metrics like loss of load expectation (LOLE) and expected unserved energy (EUE) we discover weather events and years that are particularly stressful for future power system portfolios. We also identify system builds that are robust against multiple weather futures. Finally, we explore methods from extreme value theory to compare return periods and levels of system RA failure events under different weather trajectories. This advancement will allow us to provide insights into robust investment strategies under deeply uncertain future weather conditions.

495540.title: Explainable Machine Learning for County-Scale Seasonal Drought Forecasting in Texas Using Remote Sensing and Land Surface Data
495540.authors: Ayantika Rinti Bose, University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX; and D. H. Sharif
495540.abstract: Agricultural drought produces recurring multibillion-dollar losses across Texas, yet county-scale forecasts at the 1- to 3-month lead times required for planting, stocking, and municipal water-supply decisions remain limited. The rapid onset of the 2011 and 2022-2023 events illustrates the need for guidance issued before drought conditions are fully established. Machine learning has demonstrated skill in seasonal drought forecasting, but the absence of physical interpretation has limited operational adoption. This study develops a forecasting framework, built on remote sensing and land surface data, that predicts U.S. Drought Monitor category for each of the 254 Texas counties at 1-, 2-, and 3-month lead times. Monthly predictors are derived from PRISM climate fields, gridMET reference evapotranspiration, NLDAS-2 soil moisture, MODIS vegetation indices, SMAP Level-4 surface and root-zone soil moisture, gNATSGO soil properties, and Pacific and Atlantic teleconnection indices. These fields yield SPI, SPEI, the Evaporative Demand Drought Index (EDDI), soil-moisture percentiles, and approximately 150 lagged, rolling-mean, and anomaly features covering 1981-2026, with the satellite predictors entering over their shorter records (MODIS from 2000, SMAP from 2015). Gradient-boosted decision tree models are trained separately for each lead time and benchmarked against a two-layer LSTM, monthly climatology, and persistence. Expanding-window walk-forward validation limits the inflated skill that drought persistence and temporal autocorrelation otherwise produce, and withholding entire Texas climate divisions tests spatial transferability. Skill is reported as class-specific F1 and as onset detection rate and lead time relative to the Drought Monitor. Predictor attribution uses Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) values at statewide, regional, and county-month scales, supported by permutation importance and partial dependence analysis. [INSERT 1-2 SENTENCES OF PRELIMINARY RESULTS: onset F1 at 1-month lead versus persistence; dominant predictor at 1 month versus 3 months.] Regional attribution maps separate counties where predictability derives from antecedent land surface memory from those governed by large-scale climate variability, and local explanations identify the drivers of individual forecasts and of forecast failures. The framework provides a transparent basis for a county-scale drought early warning capability supporting Texas water and agricultural management.

495541.title: The Tornado Detection Algorithm Improvement Project: Improving QLCS Tornado Detection
495541.authors: Adam Grayson Smith, University of Georgia, Athens, GA; and P. McCrone
495541.abstract: This project describes the Tornado Detection Algorithm (TDA) and its performance. National Weather Service (NWS) Operational forecasters have the TDA available for real-time guidance when issuing tornado warnings to increase confidence in warning decisions, extend tornado warning lead times, and reduce the possibility of undetected tornadoes. This study focuses on tornadoes within Quasi-Linear Convective Systems (QLCSs). QLCS tornadoes account for approximately 20% of all US tornadoes and for much higher proportions of total tornadoes across the Southeast and Midwest (Goodnight et al., 2022). These tornadoes are more likely to occur overnight and to have much shorter warning lead times, making them particularly dangerous despite their typically lower intensity (Goodnight et al., 2022). The NEXRAD Radar Operations Center (ROC) implemented the TDA capability operationally on the WSR-88D system in 1999. The TDA’s performance suffered due to poor data quality associated with Doppler velocity products of that era. Breakthroughs in data quality occurred, such as the Two-Dimensional Velocity Dealiasing Algorithm (2DVDA), which improved Doppler velocity data and increased the range of reliable data. As a result, the ROC adopted the goal of improving TDA performance in terms of range and other statistical measures of detection and skill. The team studied potential improvements to the TDA to enhance QLCS tornado detection. We analyzed results across different adaptable parameter values, focusing on combinations of adaptable parameters that NWS Operational meteorologists can alter at their Weather Forecast Offices. Our preliminary results support a recommendation to implement changes in the WSR 88D’s Radar Product Generator (RPG) adaptable parameters to extend the effective range to 230 km. This work prepares us to evaluate the Tornado Probability Algorithm (TORP) currently under development at the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) (Sandmael et al., 2023). In addition to providing a foundation upon which the ROC can evaluate future tornado warning support tools (like TORP), this project aligns well with NOAA's Weather-Ready Nation mission by promoting improvement of the already-operational TDA to enhance QLCS tornado warning operations for NWS forecasters.

495544.title: Understanding the Variability of Extreme Tropical Cyclone Precipitation Within Different Synoptic Regimes
495544.authors: Caleb Black, Iowa State University, Ames, IA; and R. G. Nystrom
495544.abstract: Extreme tropical cyclone (TC) precipitation leads to devastating impacts for coastal and inland communities through freshwater flooding and unpredictable landslides. The intensity of TC precipitation is well known to scale with increasing TC intensity and decreasing TC translation speed. Characteristics of TC precipitation have also been shown to vary within different oceanic basins and large-scale environmental conditions. However, little work has been done to quantify the variability of extreme TC precipitation and to understand how this may change within different synoptic regimes. We utilize a Self-Organizing Map (SOM), an unsupervised machine learning algorithm, to sort 82 U.S. landfalling TCs into three distinct long-wave patterns based on upper-level potential vorticity from ERA5. Our results suggest that the importance of different TC characteristics and environmental conditions in controlling extreme TC precipitation (ETCP) shifts across these regimes. Using a separate regression model for each node of the SOM, we highlight the key predictors of both ETCP intensity and areal coverage. We also demonstrate how these predictors vary across synoptic regimes. We further explore the variability in the spatial and temporal characteristics of ETCP across these patterns. Our results suggest that breaking down the variability of ETCP into distinct synoptic patterns provides new insight into the factors controlling ETCP variability and motivates future modeling studies focused on further understanding the implications for predictability.

495545.title: S2S Tropical Cyclone Tracks and Genesis Environments Across Uniform and Variable-Resolution MPAS-A Meshes
495545.authors: Abigail Jaye, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Berner and J. Done
495545.abstract: Subseasonal-to-Seasonal (S2S) prediction of tropical cyclones (TCs) sits in a unique middle ground between short-term atmospheric initial conditions and extended climate drivers. In this study, we evaluate how spatial resolution and mesh refinement affect TC forecast skill using 23 years of weekly initialized hindcasts from the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS-A). We assess model performance across four distinct horizontal grid configurations, including two variable-resolution meshes focused near CONUS. We apply the TempestExtremes framework to track TCs, evaluating general track density, trajectories, and extended-range skill from weeks 2 through 4 (out to week 6 for uniform meshes). In addition, we examine how well the hindcasts represent large-scale atmospheric environments conducive to TC genesis. By comparing uniform global configurations with CONUS-focused variable-resolution meshes, this work highlights how local grid refinement influences both explicit TC tracking and the representation of genesis-favorable environments on S2S timescales.

495546.title: Opening Remarks: NOAA's Scientific Highlights and Contributions (Invited Presentation)
495546.authors: Steven Thur, NOAA's Assistant Administrator for Research and Acting Chief Scientist, Silver Spring, MD
495546.abstract: Accurate environmental information is critical for our society’s ability to make decisions that protect life and property and sustain healthy ecosystems and economies. Rapid advances in observing technologies, significant increases in data volumes, advances in artificial intelligence, and the need for enhanced, hyper-local forecasts present both opportunities and challenges for the provision of this environmental information. NOAA is improving our understanding of the planet and equipping communities to make these informed decisions through modernization of our observing systems and enhancements to our forecasts. Grounded in NOAA's 10-Year Data Assimilation Strategy, this presentation will explore how enhanced observing networks and improved data assimilation capabilities combine to improve our understanding of the current state of the planet and enables NOAA to issue forecasts for a myriad of environmental phenomena, maximizing return on taxpayers’ investment. Remarks will touch on the vital role of the current global observational networks, highlight opportunities in public-private partnerships, and the research driving the next-generation technology and tools that support accurate weather forecasts and a sustainable future.

495547.title: Improved Airborne Radar Velocity Data Deliasing Using the Neural Net in Julia for Aliasing (NNJA) Algorithm
495547.authors: Jennifer C. DeHart, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Lee, M. M. Bell, D. A. Bryan, and P. D. Reasor
495547.abstract: Velocity and precipitation data collected in hurricanes by the NOAA P3 Tail Doppler Radars (TDRs) are critical for storm analysis by National Hurricane Center forecasters and data assimilation to improve numerical weather prediction. However, before the data and derived products can be used, the raw, noisy radar data must be quality controlled, which includes two tasks: 1) non-meteorological data and noise removal and 2) velocity dealiasing. The legacy code developed by researchers at the Hurricane Research Division (HRD) beginning in the 1990s to perform these tasks is a suite of FORTRAN components; although the software has been updated incrementally to process data in real time and address operational needs, software updates and bug fixes are onerous and increasingly impractical as the software ages. Recently, the Tropical Cyclones, Radar, Atmospheric Modeling, and Software Team (TC-RAMS) group at Colorado State University has developed a set of tools in modern, high-level programming languages that are easier to develop and maintain, but also improve analysis quality and computational speed. This presentation describes the Neural Net in Julia for Aliasing (NNJA) algorithm to dealias NOAA P3 TDR velocity data, which is an adaptation of the Veillette et al. (2023; hereafter V23) method for dealiasing NEXRAD data. In the current HRD workflow, velocity dealiasing is an iterative process, requiring a stable initial low-wavenumber analysis to manage missing data before adding in higher-wavenumber asymmetries. This process adds 5-6 minutes to the HRD processing workflow. In contrast, machine learning algorithms like NNJA can process data in seconds. Like the V23 method, NNJA is a convolutional neural network with a U-Net architecture. Where V23 used dealiased output from the Open Radar Product Generator as part of its training dataset, NNJA was trained using a large synthetic dataset from an observing simulation experiment. We generated virtual flights into Hurricanes Fiona (2022), Milton (2024), Erin (2025), and Melissa (2025). CfRadial flights from actual NOAA P3 flight legs are centered on the simulated storm and the geometry is used to resample velocity output from the regional domain of the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS). Velocity data are linearly interpolated to the TDR radar gates and the Doppler velocity is calculated according to the radar beam geometry. Precipitation mixing ratios are used to censor data in regions of weak radar signal. Through this method, the virtual sampling provides a large number of samples across a variety of storm intensities, structures, and flight tracks and the true Doppler velocity is known. Like V23, NNJA predicts the number of folds in the velocity data. The training dataset includes over 80,000 files across 54 synthetic flight legs across the four aforementioned storms. Although most velocity data points fall within the Nyquist velocity of the TDR (+/- 22.16 m/s), a fold number of at least 1 is present in all flight legs and the maximum fold number is 4, corresponding to Doppler velocities above 88 m/s. In this presentation, we benchmark NNJA against the performance of the V23 model and summarize the model’s overall performance. We evaluate NNJA using observational NOAA P3 data from Fiona (2022), Milton (2024), Erin (2025), and Melissa (2025). We evaluate how echo coverage affects the quality of the velocity fold detection, as missing data is a frequent cause of dealiasing algorithm failure. We also evaluate how storm intensity impacts the quality of the dealiasing as multiple folds are a small fraction of the training dataset, but require high accuracy for multi-Doppler synthesis. Finally, we will present our future plans, which includes adding manually-dealiased data from P3 observations to the training dataset, adding more realistic noise characteristics to the synthetic dataset, and additional planned validation.

495548.title: Resolving Boundary Layer Dynamics of Wildfire Smoke Transport: The High-Resolution FireWeather-Nest Model
495548.authors: Sudheer Bhimireddy, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA/OAR/GSL, Boulder, CO; and R. Ahmadov, J. Duda, J. Beck, J. Romero-Alvarez, J. Schnell, H. Li, M. Choi, E. P. James, G. Ferrada, J. A. Otkin, and M. Pavolonis
495548.abstract: Accurate forecasting of wildfire smoke transport and dispersion is critical for mitigating ground transportation, aviation, and air quality hazards and supporting public health decisions. This study evaluates the performance of the experimental FireWeather-Nest (FWx-nest) configuration based on the MPAS dynamical core, operating at 1.25km grid spacing over the western US. At this scale, the model explicitly resolves many of the complex terrain features, local circulations, and fine-scale planetary boundary layer (PBL) dynamics that heavily govern transport, mixing, trapping, and entrainment of wildfire smoke. We examine the model's capability in simulating complex smoke dispersion mechanisms—including daytime convective boundary layer growth, nocturnal drainage flows, low-level jets, and stable layer decoupling—across regions affected by major wildfires during the 2025 fire season. The model integrates satellite fire detections from the Next Generation Fire System (NGFS) to provide Fire Radiative Power (FRP)-driven heat fluxes over active fire pixels. This sensible heat feedback alters near-fire surface meteorology, resulting in enhanced turbulence, localized boundary layer growth, and pyroconvection over intense wildfires. Model outputs, such as vertical profiles of mixing depth, wind shear, and smoke concentrations, are systematically evaluated against surface air quality monitoring networks (AirNow) and remote sensing retrievals. To assess horizontal grid sensitivity, these outputs are compared against RRFS-Smoke operating at a 3-km grid spacing. Results demonstrate that the FWx-nest effectively captures terrain-driven PBL flows and sub-mesoscale transport pathways, improving the representation of smoke lofting, diurnal boundary layer dilution, and surface concentration peaks compared to coarser operational systems. These findings underscore the critical role of high-resolution PBL physics and fire-atmosphere coupling in advancing regional smoke and air quality forecasting.

495549.title: Training Weather Radar Quantitative Rainfall Retrievals on a Network of Non-Catchment 61 GHz Precipitation Sensors: A Proposed Method for Dual-Polarization Radars and Radar Networks
495549.authors: Aki Lilja, Vaisala Oyj, Helsinki, Uusimaa, Finland; and P. Rossi, M. McGoodwin, J. Brumley, and V. Chavez
495549.abstract: Quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) demands both spatial coverage and absolute accuracy, and no single instrument supplies both. Dual-polarization radar resolves the precipitation field across its coverage region, but its rainfall estimate is an inference drawn from the backscatter signal aloft. Catchment-type gauges anchor that field at individual points, but require undercatch correction and report only a rate — not the drop size spectrum that produced it. The retrieval relation and the radar calibration bias are therefore estimated together, against a reference that is both biased and microphysically blind. We propose a method that replaces the reference. The Vaisala PRECICAP Radar Precipitation Sensor RM60 is a vertically pointing 61 GHz Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) Doppler radar sensor that reconstructs precipitation as ensembles of individual hydrometeors within approximately two meters of an optimized narrow beam, over an effective sampling area of 700 cm². Having no orifice, no moving parts and no heating requirement, and measuring in the near field of a narrow, vertically pointing beam, it eliminates the wind-induced undercatch rather than corrects for it. It reports precipitation intensity from 0.02 mm/h, accumulation, precipitation type across 19 WMO 4680 SYNOP classes, drop size distribution in 22 bins spanning 0.17 to 6.2 mm, and the radar reflectivity factor computed directly from the measured drop spectrum; drop diameter and frequency are traceable to SI units. Drawing 0.5–1.3 W and requiring no scheduled maintenance, the instrument is economical enough in power and service to be deployed as a distributed network rather than as a supersite — which is what makes the method below feasible. We propose deploying a network of RM60 sensors across the coverage of a dual-polarization Doppler weather radar such as the Vaisala WRS300. Such a radar reports a full suite of weather radar dual-polarization moment data: horizontal, vertical and differential reflectivities (Zh, Zv, ZDR), specific differential phase (KDP), differential propagation phase (PHIDP), co-polar correlation coefficient (RHOHV), radial velocity, spectrum width and other moments, at resolutions down to 15 m in range. At each site and time step, the RM60 observation vector is paired with the vertical profile of radar moment vectors sampled at the co-located radar observation bins, together with the observing geometry: slant range, elevation angle, beam height and resolution volume, and geography: ground elevation. Sites are chosen deliberately to span that geometry space and the terrain and clutter regimes of the domain. This is facilitated by the light infrastructure requirements and the absence of scheduled maintenance of the RM60 sensor. A supervised machine learning retrieval learns a mapping from radar moment and geometry vectors to RM60-equivalent intensity and accumulation, allowing that mapping to vary with hydrometeor type and with the shape of the drop size distribution rather than holding one relation fixed. RM60 supplies both conditioning variable targets during training: the WMO 4680 precipitation type and the measured 22-bin drop spectrum. At inference both must be recovered from the radar observations themselves, with RHOHV and the vertical profile of the moments through the melting layer carrying phase and mixed-phase information, and ZDR together with Z constraining mean drop size and concentration. Because PHIDP accumulates along the propagation path, its inclusion among the predictors allows the model to absorb path-integrated attenuation implicitly, rather than through a separate correction step. The sensor network thus teaches the radar to read its own microphysical signatures. Automatically reported RM60 status flags can be used to select training samples, while hydrometeor fall time and advection can be used to set the time-matching window. Conceptually, it is possible to train the model to produce RM60 intensity, precipitation type, and parameterized drop size distribution by using the vertical profiles of dual-polarization radar moments. Once trained, the mapping is validated against RM60 measurements: either with a temporally independent data set or by leave-one-site-out cross-validation. Admitting geometry as an explicit predictor allows the model to be utilized outside the training points: the model learns how the retrieval varies with beam height, range and ground elevation, and can be applied wherever local geometry falls within the span the network samples. As a result, the dual-polarization weather radar or radar-network data yields expected RM60 rainfall intensity, accumulation and precipitation type for any location in the coverage area, leading to improved quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) in the coverage area of the radar. The method extends naturally to a network of dual-polarization radars whose composite coverage contains the RM60 network. Where coverage overlaps, a single RM60 site constrains several radars simultaneously at differing ranges, azimuths and beam heights, helping separate radar-specific calibration bias from precipitation regime and supplying a common, traceable reference for harmonizing radars within a mosaic. Because the mapping depends on observing geometry and microphysical signature rather than on azimuth, an RM60 network that spans the relevant geometry and precipitation regimes can train a retrieval that applies throughout the radar domain, including sectors that contain no sensors of their own. Across radars, a model trained where the network is dense likewise provides a starting point for domains where it is sparse — transfer learning across radars and coverage areas.

495550.title: Temperature and Humidity Retrievals from Atmospheric Refractivity using Particle Swarm Optimization
495550.authors: Jessica Hamilton, Coastal Carolina University, Conway, SC; and C. R. Sease, A. J. Kammerer, D. Flagg, and E. E. Hackett
495550.abstract: The marine atmospheric surface layer (MASL) is a highly dynamic environment where turbulent exchanges of momentum, heat and water vapor produce strong vertical gradients of temperature and humidity (Stull, 1988; Wang et al., 2018). These vertical gradients strongly affect radar wave propagation, communication systems, and are important for accurate numerical weather prediction (NWP) (Pastore et al., 2022; Stanek et al., 2023). However, obtaining thermodynamic profiles over the ocean remains challenging. In-situ observations are logistically demanding and expensive, while high-resolution NWP is computationally intensive and still requires approximations for near-surface processes. Several methods exist to remotely obtain estimates of atmospheric refractivity from radar measurements (Rogers, 2000; Pastore et al., 2022; Kariman et al., 2011; Gossard et al., 1998). As such, this study investigates the use of particle swarm optimization (PSO), a population-based metaheuristic algorithm (Kennedy & Eberhart, 1995), to retrieve vertical temperature and humidity profiles from atmospheric refractivity. In this framework, each particle represents a candidate set of atmospheric variables, temperature and humidity, that iteratively searches for an optimal match to the refractivity. Because this inversion is nonlinear and non-unique, a global optimization scheme such as PSO is needed. However, because PSO is inherently stochastic, repeated optimization trials are expected to produce variable solutions. The objective of this study is to examine the accuracy, convergence, and repeatability of PSO-based temperature and humidity retrievals, and their variance with algorithm hyperparameters. Retrieval numerical experiments were performed using verified NWP forecasts spanning multiple field campaigns. Temperature and humidity retrieval accuracies were evaluated while systematically varying key PSO hyperparameters to identify configurations that improve solution quality and algorithm consistency. Results provide insights into how effective application of a meta-heuristic algorithm for temperature and humidity retrievals from an estimated atmospheric refractivity could be. Retrieved temperature and humidity profiles exhibit substantial variability among PSO realizations due to random particle initialization and the non-uniqueness of the inversion problem even under the hyperparameter setup that yielded the lowest retrieval errors. Although the refractivity objective functions frequently converge to low-error solutions, the corresponding temperature and humidity profiles are often incorrect. Additionally, retrieved vertical profiles exhibit significant point-to-point variability with height, requiring smoothing and fitting to produce physically realistic vertical gradients. Constraining the PSO search interval alone does not consistently improve retrieval performance, especially for temperature. These findings quantify the uncertainty of PSO-based temperature and humidity retrievals and identify hyperparameter configurations that help improve algorithm consistency. This work highlights the challenges in estimating temperature and humidity from a measured refractivity providing valuable insights for advancements in atmospheric remote sensing. 495551.title: NOAA NWP Moonshot Goal 4: Ensuring the Mission-Centric Value of an Advanced NWS Modeling Suite
495551.authors: Sarah E. Perfater, Office of Modeling and Development, Silver Spring, MD; and G. M. Eosco, G. S. Manikin, M. Willis, J. E. Ten Hoeve III, D. T. Kleist, and R. Bandy
495551.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) established the Office of Modeling and Development (OMD), which is responsible for executing the full spectrum of modeling and development necessary for the provision of forecast information to support the National Weather Service mission, including: observations ingest and processing; data assimilation; modeling; value-added post-processing and guidance generation; verification evaluation; and visualizations and application development supporting service delivery. Over the next decade, through strategic enterprise partnerships, the NWS will thoroughly modernize its operational modeling suite and production schedule through a transformation to advanced software and HPC architectures, investments in high-resolution reanalyses, expansion of hybrid data-driven and physics-based ensemble prediction systems, and adoption of the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) atmospheric dynamical core. Implementing the vision will result in meeting stakeholder requirements for more accurate, timely, and actionable information tailored to the local level, increasing lead times and trust in forecasts, and realizing significant economic benefits across multiple sectors. High-resolution models, leveraging AI, provide decision-makers with more accurate "precision windows," reduce "missed" extreme events, and support the private sector with hyperlocal data to inform better business decisions. Rapid translation of weather variables into actionable thresholds using modern decision support tools optimizes emergency resource allocation. This transformation will be accelerated through a Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) Moonshot Initiative, led by the NOAA Administrator Dr. Neil Jacobs. As NOAA focuses on an overall NWP Moonshot, it is critical to ensure the provision of probabilistic information to support stakeholder decision making through NOAA’s NWP Moonshot Goal 4: “Advance seamless integration of probabilistic forecast guidance tools and services to increase access, reliability, and trustworthiness of tailored data to meet forecaster and societal demands.” This presentation will address the alignment of NWS operations, culture, and technology directly around a modernized and consolidated modeling suite. The sub-goals of this focus include 1) developing an advanced fully probabilistic, calibrated, global end-to-end probabilistic guidance suite augmented by machine learning techniques to enhance the official NWS probabilistic forecast database, 2) deriving bespoke products and services from the probabilistic guidance that lead to faster data interpretation and actionable information and 3) fusing probabilistic forecast guidance with impact-based decision support (IDSS) tools to support scenario-based communication with regional and local core partners.

495552.title: Characterizing Atmospheric Drag in VLEO Using CubeSat Flight Data
495552.authors: Angela B Crews, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and M. Pilinski, A. Bryant, N. Ratajczyk, A. Yenawine, C. Benson, C. Roseman, S. Swenson, G. Furlich, R. Marcusen, S. Flynn, C. Pankratz, S. Palo, and I. Boyd
495552.abstract: Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) offers significant advantages for spacecraft such as improved spatial resolution, reduced latency, and increased signal power. Operations in VLEO are complicated by interactions with the residual atmosphere at these altitudes. Elevated atmospheric drag, coupled with thermospheric density variability, presents significant challenges for spacecraft operations and trajectory prediction. Orbit tracking is further complicated by short ground station passes and uncertainties in atmospheric density and aerodynamic drag modeling, which can degrade orbit prediction accuracy. Flight data are therefore critical for validating aerodynamic models and improving the understanding of spacecraft behavior in this regime. In this work, we analyze flight data from the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics (LASP) Compact Spectral Irradiance Monitor (CSIM) CubeSat as it descends through VLEO. CSIM was intentionally operated in high- and low-drag configurations, providing a controlled experiment for characterizing aerodynamic forces and evaluating VLEO modeling approaches. Simulations of CSIM drag were performed over a range of spacecraft orientations using both MONACO, a Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) code, and VECTOR, a flat-plate analytical model. U.S. Space Force (USSF) Energy Dissipation Rate (EDR) products were compared with CSIM flight data to estimate surface energy accommodation and evaluate gas-surface interaction assumptions. We also examine how supplemental observations can improve orbit determination in the presence of increased atmospheric drag. Simulations and CSIM flight measurements demonstrate that Doppler and optical observations can substantially improve knowledge of VLEO spacecraft trajectories. Together, these results provide flight-based insight into aerodynamic modeling, gas-surface interactions, and observation strategies for future VLEO missions.

495554.title: Influence of Atmospheric Stability on Thermodynamic Retrieval Accuracy in the Marine Atmospheric Surface Layer
495554.authors: Lara Gonzalez Siaba Dillmann, Coastal Carolina University, Conway, SC; and C. R. Sease, A. J. Kammerer, D. Flagg, and E. E. Hackett
495554.abstract: Accurate estimates of atmospheric stability in the marine atmospheric surface layer (MASL) are essential to understanding boundary layer structure and processes. Understanding how atmospheric stability influences thermodynamic retrieval accuracy in the MASL can help improve these remote-sensing measurements. More readily accessible and continuous monitoring of thermodynamic vertical distributions in the MASL can help improve parameterization of small-scale processes in larger (mesoscale) weather models and greatly expand the data available for assimilation into numerical models; thereby improving weather forecasts particularly in conditions that are highly dependent on boundary layer processes including extreme weather predictions. Recently developed methods for retrieving MASL temperature and humidity vertical distributions from X-band radar propagation data have been shown to be accurate (Hackett et al., 2025; Sease et al., 2026). Specifically, retrieved humidity vertical distributions are nearly always accurate but errors in the temperature retrieval can occasionally occur potentially leading to misclassification of atmospheric stability, especially at the lowest altitudes (< 10 m), making them important errors to investigate. This study examines the relationships between atmospheric stability and temperature retrieval accuracy in the MASL to shed light on the atmospheric conditions that might be associated with these inaccuracies. To evaluate this relationship, both verified numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts and in-situ data are used for simulating thermodynamic retrievals from atmospheric refractivity. NWP and in-situ data are used for this study because they have known well-defined ground truths upon which to evaluate retrieval accuracy. Specifically, temperature and humidity vertical profiles are retrieved using an atmospheric refractivity vertical profile along with a reference measurement of temperature, humidity, and pressure at a single altitude for each NWP and in-situ profile (Hackett et al., 2025; Sease et al., 2026). These vertical profiles cover the lowest 100 meters of altitude and represent a range of geographic regions, seasons, and data types (in-situ measurements versus NWP forecasts). Together, this combination of data allows for a robust evaluation of atmospheric stability and retrieval accuracy across a wide range of MASL conditions. Furthermore, atmospheric stability is evaluated using a range of stability metrics to examine consistencies in relationships for varying stability parameters. Results from this study show that certain atmospheric conditions, including large deviations from hydrostatic pressure decreases, low surface modified refractivity gradients, high surface specific humidity, and stable atmospheric conditions, are strongly related to incorrect retrieved temperature gradient signs in the bottom 10 meters of the atmosphere. These sign errors occur even when the retrieved temperature profiles exhibit low temperature root-mean-square-errors (RMSEs) and high correlation coefficients with the known vertical profiles, when considering the entire profile. Other results include self-consistency of stability metrics and how they compare to the retrieval-based stability metrics as well as exploration of synoptic scale weather and how it relates to the observed retrieval accuracy trends with stability. Improved understanding of temperature retrieval errors and their relationship to certain atmospheric conditions can lead to more accurate fine-scale remote sensing in the MASL. References Hackett, E. E., D. M. Pastore, D. P. Greenway, A. E. Vaughan, and C. R. Sease, 2025: Remote sensing of humidity and temperature from X-band radar measurements in the marine atmospheric surface layer. 2025 U.S. National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM), IEEE. Sease, C. R., D. P. Greeway, A. J. Kammerer, D. D. Flagg, and E. E. Hackett, 2026: Evaluation of a humidity and temperature retrieval technique using ground-based radar. 106th American Meteorological Society Annual Meeting, Amer. Meteor. Soc.

495555.title: Effects of Wetlands Restoration on the Planetary Boundary Layer
495555.authors: Christopher E. Phillips, Valparaiso University, Valparaiso, IN
495555.abstract: Humans have extensively modified their environment, with agriculture alone now occupying almost half of habitable land. The impacts of these changes on the atmosphere are well-studied, but the consequences of restoring agricultural land to its natural state receive less attention. In areas restoring native ecosystems, it is important to quantify changes to the atmosphere to support regional water planning and climate adaptation policies. To address this need, two observation sites have been constructed in the Northwest Indiana region. The stations, one in a recently restored wetland and another in a neighboring agricultural field, are designed to monitor ongoing efforts to restore the native wetlands. Each site includes a ten meter tower monitoring temperature, pressure, wind speed, and surface heat fluxes as well as a soil monitoring system measuring soil moisture and temperature at various depths down to one meter. These observations are analyzed to determine the effects of wetland restoration on the surface layer, particularly regarding evapotranspiration, humidity, and temperature. Additionally, a single-column model is initialized using site observations to investigate the effects of land cover change on the boundary layer, including turbulent mixing, boundary layer height, and cloud formation.

495560.title: Investigation of Orographic Cloud Characteristics on Elk Mountain Utilizing High Resolution Numerical Simulations
495560.authors: Nolan Thomas Robertson, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY
495560.abstract: Elk Mountain is an isolated mountain in SE Wyoming, USA, that is located northwest of the Medicine Bow Mountains. It rises 4,000 ft above the surrounding plains with an elevation of more than 11,000 ft and a slightly lower saddle point just to the western (upwind) side, where Elk Mountain Observatory (EMO) is located. EMO was originally established in the 1960’s by the University of Wyoming for the study of cloud and precipitation physics, including glaciogenic cloud seeding. For several hundred miles upwind of the mountain, the terrain is relatively flat, allowing the orographic updraft and ensuing cloud formation at the mountain to be particularly consistent. Furthermore, Elk Mountain is in an isolated location with no public access and no significant upwind sources of pollution, minimizing anthropogenic influences that may perturb the clouds that form on the mountain. Due to this relative lack of external forcing mechanisms, Elk Mountain offers a unique opportunity for cloud and precipitation studies because the cloud formation can be almost purely attributed to the orography of Elk Mountain itself and the local meteorological conditions. Additionally, it provides a unique opportunity to intentionally perturb clouds that form near the mountain with aerosol to measure their microphysical response. Since the early 2000’s, EMO has largely remained unused. In order to take advantage of this unique facility for the study of orographic clouds, the University of Wyoming is currently revitalizing EMO. The overarching objective driving the work described here is to better understand cloud characteristics at EMO for planning future observational campaigns and in turn further evaluate and improve model performance. To further explore the favorable circumstances of studying cloud physics at Elk Mountain, a 25 year model-based wintertime climatology for Elk Mountain clouds was developed using RM1.3, a CONUS404 run down-scaled to 1.3 km and focused on the central Rocky Mountains. Cloud statistics were determined by taking all cloud cases from December through March of the 2000 through 2024 water years in which EMO was in-cloud. The model climatology demonstrates that there are about 32 cloud cases per season with EMO in-cloud about 35% of the time. The wind direction is unobstructed for about 62% of cloud cases, mean cloud top temperatures are between -10 and -20 C about 65% of the time, and cloud base is frequently between 0.5 and 1 km below cloud base. These statistics suggest that most of the clouds appearing on Elk Mountain are mixed phase and with cloud base frequently being below the observatory such that many of the wintertime cases are cap clouds where in-situ instruments placed at the observatory can make effective stationary measurements for most of its lifetime. Another objective is to conduct a comparison study of cloud conditions with the nearby (82 miles away) mountaintop observatory Storm Peak in North-central Colorado. The aim of this work is to understand how differences in orographic flow patterns from the relatively simple topography of Elk Mountain and the more complex topography of Storm Peak influences modeled clouds. Furthermore, it is expected that anthropogenic influences from the local ski resort and the upwind power plant at Storm Peak may lead to significant differences in cloud microphysical characteristics at the two sites. The outcome of this study will help better inform future observational work that will be conducted at one or both of the mountain sites.

495562.title: Overview of Data Assimilation Activities at the NWS Office of Modeling and Development
495562.authors: Daniel Holdaway, NOAA, College Park, MD; and C. S. Draper, A. Collard, C. R. Martin, PhD, C. A. Thomas, S. Liu, G. Vernieres, R. Treadon, and D. T. Kleist
495562.abstract: The Data Assimilation Division of NOAA's National Weather Service Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) supports several high priority efforts across the agency. This presentation gives a broad overview of ongoing work to transition operational forecast models to the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI), implement a new observation preprocessing paradigm, evaluate and incorporate commercial observations, and develop artificial intelligence techniques that supplement existing physically based data assimilation systems. OMD is implementing a fully coupled Global Forecast System with the adoption of version 17. We provide an overview of the JEDI based data assimilation systems developed for the marine and snow Earth system components, along with recent scientific advances in the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) based atmospheric and soil data assimilation systems. We also highlight progress toward a JEDI based implementation of the atmospheric and soil data assimilation systems. Observation preprocessing is a key component of any operational data assimilation framework. The transition to JEDI, the growing use of AI models, and the rising volume of commercial observations together motivate an overhaul of this part of our work. We are designing and prototyping a substantial refactor toward a more cloud friendly data format and methodology, along with modernized quality control procedures. A large number of new commercial and government observations have become available in recent years, and the share coming from commercial sources is expected to keep growing. We highlight ongoing work to evaluate these data types and bring them into operations. AI technology has driven several recent advances in operational modeling, including the adoption of AIGFS and AIGEFS. Within the Data Assimilation Division, we are developing direct observation prediction tools for both global and regional forecasting, and working to replace existing ‘record of analysis’ applications. We present results from this prototyping work and outline plans for the future.

495563.title: AccuWeather's Deep Learning Portfolio for Severe Weather Nowcasting
495563.authors: Timothy Patrick Loftus, AccuWeather, Lancaster, PA
495563.abstract: AccuWeather's Data Science team is advancing a family of deep learning nowcasting models that share a common architectural backbone — U-Net encoder–decoders fused with ConvNeXt blocks and Multi-axis Vision Transformers (MaxViT) — while targeting three of the most damaging and difficult-to-forecast convective hazards: hail, lightning, and precipitation. This session presents a unified view of that portfolio, illustrating how AccuWeather blends proprietary observation networks with cutting-edge AI to deliver proven Superior Accuracy™ guidance beyond what any single data source or legacy model can provide. The hail nowcasting model fuses MRMS radar, GOES-16 satellite imagery, and AccuWeather Lightning Network™ (ALN) stroke counts into an autoregressive latent-state framework to predict hail probability at four severity thresholds out to two hours. Over a 23-day spring evaluation, it achieved a best-threshold CSI of 0.46 at 30 minutes — outperforming the HRRR HAILCAST baseline by roughly a factor of five — and detected 69% of golf-ball-size hail reports with substantially fewer false alarms. Built on the same architectural philosophy, the lightning nowcasting model integrates ALN, GOES-16, and MRMS reflectivity to predict lightning occurrence at 10-minute resolution out to two hours, achieving a CSI of 0.49 for 30-minute forecasts and outperforming MRMS lightning probability products and NOAA-UW LightningCast on both CSI and AUC-PR. Rounding out the portfolio, AccuWeather's precipitation nowcasting model applies a time-distributed encoder–decoder wrapped around an embedded physical solver, advecting learned motion and intensity fields to evolve radar mosaics forward in time. Deployed operationally through a Databricks/MLflow pipeline for real-time inference, the model delivers measurable gains over AccuWeather's existing MinuteCast® benchmark, further extending the team's deep learning approach to precipitation guidance. Together, these efforts demonstrate a consistent design philosophy: pairing local convective detail with broader atmospheric context through hybrid convolutional-attention architectures, trained on AccuWeather's proprietary observation networks and rigorously verified against independent National Weather Service Local Storm Reports. This session highlights how AccuWeather's six decades of meteorological expertise, combined with modern deep learning, are translating into faster, more precise, and more trustworthy severe weather guidance — turning raw data into actionable intelligence that keeps people safer and organizations more resilient.

495564.title: Linking Planetary Boundary Layer Height and Tropospheric Nitrogen Dioxide over the Texas Gulf Coast using COSMIC-2 and TEMPO Observations
495564.authors: Kalyn Emma Utenis, Texas A&M University - Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX
495564.abstract: The planetary boundary layer (PBL) governs the exchange of heat, moisture, momentum, and atmospheric constituents between the Earth’s surface and the free atmosphere, making PBL height (PBLH) a critical parameter for both weather prediction and air quality studies. Along the Texas Gulf Coast, extensive industrial and urban emissions interact with coastal meteorological processes, particularly Gulf sea breezes, to influence pollutant transport, recirculation, and dispersion. This study will investigate the relationship between PBLH variability and tropospheric nitrogen dioxide (NO2) over the South Texas Gulf Coast by integrating satellite and ground-based observations. PBLH is derived from refractivity profiles observed by the Constellation Observing Satellite System for Meteorology, Ionosphere, and Climate-2 (COSMIC-2) Global Navigation Satellite System Radio Occultation (GNSS-RO) mission. Tropospheric NO2 vertical-column observations from NASA’s Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) mission are analyzed to characterize seasonal and diurnal variability. Ground-based Pandora spectrometer measurements are used to evaluate the TEMPO NO2 retrievals in coastal urban environments, while surface air-quality observations and Air Quality Index (AQI) data provide complementary information on near-surface pollution conditions. A multi-year (2020-2025) COSMIC-2 PBLH climatology has been developed for the Texas Gulf Coast with approximately 300-km spatial resolution. Integrating hourly TEMPO NO2 observations with this PBLH climatology enables an investigation of how boundary layer development and diurnal and seasonal variability affect the spatial and temporal distribution of NO2. The study will advance understanding of the interactions between boundary layer dynamics and air quality in a complex coastal industrial environment and demonstrate the synergistic scientific value of combining GNSS-RO and geostationary satellite observations for atmospheric and environmental applications.

495565.title: Nimbus: Reducing the HPC Barrier to Supercell Simulation
495565.authors: Victor Alexander Tiradoegas, Disaster Imaging Incorporated, Norman, OK; Disaster Imaging Incorporated, Norman, OK
495565.abstract: Convection-resolving supercell simulations often rely on high-performance computing queues, limiting rapid iteration, teaching, and exploratory ensembles. Nimbus is an independently developed, MIT-licensed open-source engine that examines how much of this workflow can move onto personal hardware without replacing physical equations with emulation. Nimbus advances compressible, nonhydrostatic dynamics using split-explicit Klemp–Wilhelmson integration and conservative scalar transport on a Cartesian C-grid. Its C++ engine combines aligned fields, OpenMP/SIMD CPU kernels, backend-neutral interfaces, and Vulkan compute. Persistent device residency, batched dispatches, reusable allocations, and pre-allocation memory admission reduce transfers, synchronization, and memory churn. Asynchronous output, bounded ZFP history, and interactive three-dimensional rendering separate science-resolution state from visualization products. Performance changes are accepted only when equations and declared precision remain fixed. Fail-closed configuration and state checks, deterministic mass/water/energy ledgers, CPU/GPU parity tests, checkpoints, and provenance-bearing output make scientific identity part of optimization. On an Apple M4 Max, a 1.05-million-cell solver-only C-grid case with Kessler microphysics and three-dimensional Smagorinsky closure achieved a median 84.1 ms per model step, or 11.9 simulated seconds per wall second, with 0.31 GB peak memory. A separate 4,500-s, 600-m translating-domain storm-lifetime case completed in 2,863 wall seconds on 12 CPU workers. Physical MoltenVK runs exercise Vulkan dynamics and physics with parity, restart, and ledger checks. Nimbus also implements constant translating domains and a transactional, fixed-capacity recycled window for flat, horizontally homogeneous experiments. These preserve Earth-relative output and export retired swaths instead of allocating an entire uniformly fine storm corridor.
