The results demonstrate a practical middle ground for selected idealized supercell workflows on laptop- class hardware, while very large domains, tornado-resolving grids, and large ensembles continue to require HPC.

495566.title: Updrafts in Waiting: INCUS Science Objectives and Progress on the Eve of Launch (Invited Presentation)
495566.authors: Susan C. Van Den Heever, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and D. J. Posselt, S. Tanelli, P. Kollias, K. L. Rasmussen, Ph.D., P. Partain, G. L. Stephens, R. Auth, J. Bukowski, A. Burzynski, B. Dolan, N. M. Falk, S. W. Freeman, P. N. Gatlin, L. D. Grant, M. Harmala, J. Hassel, G. J. Huffman, G. R. Leung, Z. J. Luo, G. G. Mace, P. J. Marinescu, M. Morris, A. J. Muehr, J. Pilewskie, S. Prasanth, S. C. Reising, R. Schulte, C. J. Schumacher, I. Singh, R. L. Storer, H. Takahashi, and H. Yu
495566.abstract: The NASA Investigation of Convective Updrafts (INCUS) mission will fly three Ka-band radar SmallSats in close formation, sampling the same convective system at 30-, 90-, and 120-second intervals to retrieve convective mass flux (CMF) via time-differencing. INCUS targets tropical and subtropical convection between 38°N and 38°S, with launch set for later in 2027, soon after this Annual Meeting. The mission is organized around four science objectives, each of which has been the focus of an extensive pre-launch effort combining high-resolution model simulations, forward modeling, cloud object tracking, and observational analysis. This talk will present the motivating background, planned approach, and pre-launch results to date for each objective in turn. Science Objective 1 asks how CMF is controlled by its local environment. Environmental wind shear, humidity, temperature, and instability are known to shape convective intensity, but the pathways connecting these controls to mass flux remain incompletely understood for the wide range of environments within the global tropics and subtropics. Pre-launch simulations have begun to quantify these environmental controls on CMF, laying groundwork for interpreting the storms INCUS will observe. Science Objective 2 examines how CMF shapes high anvil clouds, which influence Earth's radiation budget and upper-tropospheric water vapor. Updraft strength and microphysical processes are expected to govern anvil extent, depth, and the balance of thick versus thin anvil, and preparatory work has begun linking these updraft characteristics to the anvil properties INCUS will help constrain. Science Objective 3 addresses how CMF modulates storm severity. Convective organization strongly influences the transition from ordinary to severe convection, and team analyses have compared a range of proposed organization metrics, finding that they show a relatively large degree of consistency with one another. Machine-learning approaches have also been used to investigate relationships between CMF and severe weather, work that will guide how CMF-severity relationships are diagnosed from INCUS observations. Science Objective 4 evaluates whether the relationships identified in Science Objectives 1–3 hold across models and scales. Sensitivity studies show that CMF and the representation of convective processes change systematically with model grid spacing, underscoring the benchmarking value INCUS retrievals will offer once on orbit. Taken together, this pre-launch work provides a comprehensive picture of where the INCUS science team stands heading into the mission's launch year, positioning the community to translate on-orbit CMF retrievals into rapid progress across all four objectives.

495567.title: The Climate and Environmental Hazards Explorer: Provisioning Actionable Resilience Information to the City and County of Denver and its Residents
495567.authors: Jonathan L. Vigh, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and K. H. Nguyen, R. R. McCrary, D. Hahn, L. Kessenich, G. Pacheco, O. Wilhelmi, J. Boehnert, I. Simpson, R. Kumar, F. Lacey, K. Fewless, J. Taganova, W. Gram, and A. Smith
495567.abstract: The Denver metropolitan area faces considerable environmental, weather-, and climate-related hazards including wildfires, windstorms, hailstorms, tornadoes, flash floods, snowstorms, drought and water scarcity, vector-borne diseases, extreme heat, air pollution, and wildfire smoke. Denver’s residents, particularly communities disproportionately exposed or sensitive to environmental and climate-related hazards, and local government have a pressing need for actionable information to support resilience decisions. Yet, the information that is needed are not always well-defined, may not exist, or have not been translated into forms that are accessible for practitioners and residents. This abstract outlines a project which is developing information resources and tools to support Denver’s adaptation planning and risk mitigation decisions. Through Promotoras Climáticas, the City and County of Denver’s Office of Climate Action, Sustainability & Resiliency (CASR) engaged several community-based organizations (CBOs) and identified extreme heat and air quality as the two hazards of highest community concern. These hazards often occur together and can lead to significant impacts on Denver’s residents, including heat-related illnesses (cramps, heat exhaustion, heat stroke), respiratory illnesses (asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), and exacerbation of other chronic diseases or conditions such as diabetes, kidney disease, heart disease, neurological diseases (arthritis, multiple sclerosis, Long Covid), and mental health disorders. Impacts are especially pronounced among the approximately 10% of the population who lack access to central air conditioning. Through a baseline survey and eight working group meetings with city departments, the project developed a list of prioritized indicators and a risk-based framework which accounts for the interaction of hazards, population exposure, socio-demographic and health sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. The team has undertaken a high-resolution reanalysis of air quality conditions across the Denver metro area with air quality species constrained using NASA Earth Observation satellite data. Focus groups in August and September 2026 are examining resident’s perceptions of heat and air quality hazards, the impacts these have on them, and their level of adaptation. To make this information accessible to users, the team is creating ArcGIS StoryMaps and a public portal called the Climate & Environmental Hazards Explorer (hereafter, the Explorer). The Explorer contains several hazard-specific dashboards of prioritized and tailored climate and environmental indicators which have been selected or developed with input from the City. Each dashboard provides high quality visualizations of indicators specific to that hazard, including the trend (if applicable), a graph showing the potential ranges into the future under different scenarios, and tabular data. To help lay audiences interpret the information, guiding narratives are provided to help users understand what each indicator is, whether a robust trend exists, what the indicator is useful for, and what limitations the user should consider when using the indicator. To provision data in the most cost effective manner possible, the portal is implemented in Amazon Web Service using serverless functions and a micro web map service. To provide more details and narrative on the heat and air quality risk framework and what it means for various neighborhoods throughout the city, the portal will link to the StoryMaps. Looking ahead, the project seeks to develop decision support tools to guide residents and city planners in their daily and long-range resilience decisions. The Explorer, story maps, and tools will allow Denver city departments and residents to make risk-informed decisions to help address the consequences of extreme heat and air quality.

495569.title: Scientist Friendly Near Real-Time Data Pipelines
495569.authors: Gwyn Uttmark, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and S. M. Ciardelli, E. W. Rose, J. E. Solbrig, J. Fluke, S. D. Miller, Y. J. Noh, and J. M. Haynes
495569.abstract: This presentation will introduce Courier, a free and open-source Python orchestration package for near-real-time Earth-observation processing at scale. When data streams from multiple satellites arrive with irregular latencies, poll-and-wait schedulers often cause pipeline stalls that cascade and compound. Courier, with an event driven paradigm, was developed to address this issue. Courier decouples detection, assembly, and execution into independently scalable stages connected by interchangeable message broker backends. We developed Courier to drive CIRA's OVERCAST project (Optical Variability Evaluation of Regional Cloud Asymmetries in Space and Time), which blends five geostationary and several polar-orbiting sensors into a global three-dimensional cloud field. Each ten-minute cycle ingests approximately six full-disk high-resolution geostationary scans onto a 20,000 by 14,000 grid. As opposed to our bash-based system with a latency of approximately 3 hours, the end-to-end latency from observation to product availability with Courier is approximately 30 minutes. In addition, the pipeline is defined in a single YAML Courier config file that is considerably shorter and easier to maintain than the previously maintained set of bash scripts used to run the pipeline. Courier is publicly maintained on GitHub under a free and open-source license, and community contributions toward additional plugins are invited. We will discuss how Courier works to bridge the gap between industry DevOps and scientific processing for the benefit of the meteorological community and how event-driven orchestration out performs parallel polling in data monitoring and job creation.

495572.title: NWS Data and Dissemination Transformation: Decommissioning NOAAPort, Navigating Next-Generation Environmental Data Alternatives and Transitioning from VTEC to CAP
495572.authors: Brian J. Miretzky, NOAA, Sharon, MA
495572.abstract: The National Weather Service is currently working on a comprehensive modernization that includes our data formatting and dissemination. To remain up to date with technology we are rapidly transforming in the 2026-2028 timeframe. We want to inform the community of the planned changes and hear your feedback. For decades, the NOAAPort Satellite Broadcast Network (SBN) served as a primary, real-time mechanism for broad distribution of meteorological, hydrological, and environmental data to the broader Weather Enterprise. However, accelerating bandwidth demands driven by high-resolution numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, expanded GOES-R/JPSS satellite payloads, and dense radar suites have exposed the bandwidth limitations of legacy C-band satellite broadcasts. Rising operational costs, NWS infrastructure modernization, upcoming NWS transition from AWIPS to a centralized modern cloud environment (HIVE/CIRRUS), and planned 2027 ‘C’ spectrum auctioning by the FCC, all drive the need to decommission NOAAPort and mark a fundamental shift in how environmental data is distributed. This presentation will outline technical and operational implications of the NOAAPort sunset for key downstream stakeholders including: academia, commercial weather providers, emergency management agencies, and international meteorology partners. The sunset of NOAAPort will also affect National Weather Wire Service (NWWS) satellite users. Primary cloud-native and internet-based alternative dissemination pathways will be presented, such as: NOMADS/NOAA Open Data Dissemination (NODD) & Cloud Partners: Direct, scalable cloud ingest via public cloud providers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) for high-volume archive and real-time streaming access. National Weather Service Enterprise Dissemination System (NEC/CIRRUS): Low-latency web services and APIs tailored for critical warning text, alerts, and operational product suites. Satellite Alternatives: EMWIN and private satellite providers. In addition, as part of the NWS Transformation the NWS will be moving to Common Alerting Protocol (CAP) as our new standard. The National Weather Service (NWS) has relied on legacy text-based formatting—specifically the Valid Time Event Code (VTEC) combined with Universal Geographic Code (UGC)—to issue watches, warnings, and advisories. From the VTEC process we made CAP messages. CAP is an international XML standard that is more flexible and aligned with modern emergency communication. Now the NWS plans to transition fully to CAP. Finally, this presentation will present the next steps of the NWS to assist users in transitioning from NOAAPort and VTEC and a timeline for doing so.

495574.title: Understanding the Impact of Soil Moisture on Extreme Precipitation Intensity.
495574.authors: Faisal Mohammad Alvee, Univ. of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; and H. Qin, L. R. Leung, X. Sun, H. Hu, and G. Wang
495574.abstract: Extreme precipitation has significant impact on life and infrastructures. Studies have shown that extreme precipitation intensity (EPI) is strongly related to near surface air temperate (Ta) and atmospheric moisture availability. Soil moistute (SM) can influence both of these through its impact on the surface energy and water fluxes. However, the influence of soil moisture on EPI remains poorly understood. This study aims to fill this research gap through analyses of soil moistute data from SMAP L4 dataset, precipitation data from IMERGv7 final run and air temperature data from ERA5. The study is focused on multiple sample regions of 9x9 degrees representing different climate regimes. We limited our analysis to the summer season (JJA for Northern Hemisphere and DJF for Southern Hemisphere) when convective precipitation is dominant. SMAP L4 data was regridded to ~10km spatial resolution (from ~9km native resolution) using the nearest neighbor approach to match IMERG’s native resolution. Coarser resolution (~25km) ERA5 data was also regridded to ~10km using bilinear interpolation method, as both the air temperature and humidity have a lower degree of spatial heterogeneity than soil moisture and precipitation. Daily statistics, including mean and maximum, were then derived for all variables to support two types of analyses at the daily temporal resolution: 1) precipitation probability distribution comparison between dry and wet antecedent soil moisture conditions, and 2) bivariate scaling of EPI with temperature and soil moisture. For the first analysis, we derived the probability density function (PDF) of maximum daily or 3-hourly precipitation from IMERGv7 during staggered 2-week periods following “dry” and “wet” soil moisture conditions, respectively, where the “dry” regime refers to local soil moisture at or below its 25th percentile and “wet”regime refers to local soil moisture at or above its 75th percentle. Analyses are conducted with different lead times, so the precipitation data are from weeks 1-2, 2-3, and 3-4 from the time of soil moisture data. The bivariate scaling analysis is conducted by first “binning” the precipitation data according to the combination of concurrent daily mean air temperature Ta (from ERA5) and antecedent soil moisture (leading precipitation by 2-4 weeks), using a bin size of 1.0 °C for Ta and and 0.01m3/m3 for soil moisture; the EPI is then derived for each bin by averaging the precipitation intensity exceeding its 99th percentile. This allows us to examine how EPI varies with concurrent Ta following a given antecedent soil moisture and how Ta influences the EPI relationship with antecedent soil moisture. Preliminary results indicate that wetter antecedent soil moisture favors more intense precipitation and suppresses the occurrence and intensity of low-intensity precipitation, and the magnitude of EPI tends to increase with increased antecedent soil moisture.

495576.title: Particle Size and Mass Controls on Marine Cloud Brightening in ERF-SDM Simulations
495576.authors: Aya Ahmad, Georgetown University, Washington, DC; LLNL, Livermore, CA; and A. Donahue, H. Beydoun, E. K. de Jong, and E. Ware
495576.abstract: Marine cloud brightening (MCB) has been proposed as a climate-intervention strategy in which additional cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) are introduced into marine stratocumulus clouds to increase cloud droplet number, reduce droplet size, and enhance cloud albedo through the Twomey effect. However, MCB effectiveness depends not only on the amount of aerosol introduced, but also on particle size and the efficiency with which particles are activated and contribute to the cloud’s optical depth. Smaller dry aerosol particles can provide substantially more particles for a fixed mass of salt, while larger particles may have advantages in activation and growth according to Köhler activation theory. This study investigates the competing influences of particle number and activation efficiency by examining how dry aerosol diameter, injected mass, and injection strategy affect cloud brightening efficiency. We conduct small-domain simulations of warm stratocumulus clouds in DYCOMS-type cases and use the Energy Research and Forecasting (ERF) model in a large-eddy simulation configuration coupled to the Super Droplet Method (SDM) microphysics scheme. SDM retains particle-size information while representing large populations of physical aerosol and cloud particles as computational superdroplets, allowing injected aerosols to be followed as they humidify, activate, and grow through condensation. Where enabled, collision–coalescence is also represented. Cloud albedo is diagnosed from the simulated particle population using a two-stream optical-depth approximation. The experimental design proceeds in two stages to distinguish aerosol-size effects from the transport constraints associated with surface injection. The first iteration of perturbed parameter ensembles (PPEs) uses an idealized in-cloud injection configuration and varies dry aerosol diameter, total injected mass, and injection duration. Dry diameters of 80, 100, and 150 nm are tested, with approximately 1.9 and 19 kg total injected mass and injection durations of one and eight hours. Aerosols are introduced uniformly within the cloud layer at approximately 700–750 m, while collision–coalescence is disabled. At fixed injected mass, we observed that smaller particle cases produce substantially larger increases in domain-mean cloud albedo. The strongest responses occur for the 80 nm cases, while the 150 nm small-mass case is not distinguishable from control variability. This behavior is consistent with the cubic dependence of particle mass on diameter: for a fixed mass of salt, decreasing dry particle diameter permits the material to be distributed among many more particles. The first iteration therefore indicates that, within the tested range, particle-number efficiency can exert a stronger influence on brightening per unit mass than the activation advantage of larger particles. This result motivates testing smaller diameters and a more realistic surface-injection configuration. The second iteration extends the dry aerosol diameter range to 50, 80, and 100 nm and moves the injection source to the lowest 40 m of the domain, approximating a ship-based surface source. Aerosols are transported upward by turbulent mixing through the marine boundary layer. Simulations test clean and polluted background aerosol states and enable collision–coalescence. Cases implying unrealistically large particle populations or concentrations indistinguishable from background aerosols are excluded. Injection begins near hour two, allowing the pre-injection cloud state to develop. The mass-normalized trend observed in the first iteration persists under surface injection. The 50 nm small-mass case produces a strong albedo response, while the 80 and 100 nm large-mass cases also generate substantial increases. Within the two background aerosol concentrations examined, background aerosol concentration shows less influence on final albedo response than injected size and mass. This result should be interpreted cautiously because the experiments consider only two background states and are conducted on a set seed without duplicate runs. Size-resolved diagnostics provide a mechanistic explanation for the relationship between aerosol number and optical impact. Small interstitial aerosols can dominate particle number within the cloud layer while contributing relatively little to optical depth. The optical response is instead dominated by particles that have grown into cloud droplets, whose larger cross-sectional area gives them greater influence on cloud optical properties. Further testing is required to confirm that the calculated albedo from the size distribution is in agreement with the model’s built-in radiation diagnostics. Overall, the simulations demonstrate that injected aerosols can substantially increase domain-mean cloud albedo and that, within the tested parameter space, smaller dry particles produce greater albedo enhancement per unit injected mass. Particle number appears to be a major control on mass-normalized response, although no consistent optimum emerges when the response is normalized by particle number. As no fixed-number tests were performed, we do not attempt to determine the “ideal” particle size for activation and growth and solely attempt to observe efficiency from fixed-mass testing. We observed that surface-injected particles are mixed through the marine boundary layer and remain largely confined beneath the inversion, allowing a substantial population to reach the cloud layer and activate. The results remain subject to important limitations. The experiments use a single meteorological realization, limited background aerosol conditions, and simplified radiation diagnostics. Future work will examine multiple realizations, confirm agreement of albedo approximations with built-in radiation diagnostics, and further analyze the influence of droplet size distribution on domain optical depth. A parallel engineering analysis will attempt to connect simulated dry-particle sizes to realistic spray-generation technologies and their energy requirements. The ultimate objective is not simply to identify the particle size producing the largest albedo increase, but the strategy capable of producing the most robust cloud brightening per unit of mass and therefore energy required to inject the aerosols. Acknowledgement: This work was performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under contract DE-AC52 07NA27344 LLNL-ABS-2023054. This work was supported by a Clare Boothe Luce Scholarship from the Henry Luce Foundation.

495577.title: Advancing AI Capabilities for Weather Research: The Genesis Mission Collaboration between NOAA and Department of Energy’s Argonne National Laboratory
495577.authors: Mark Olsen, OAR, Silver Spring, MD; and S. W. Bieda III, PhD, R. Redmon, M. Youngman, M. Jones, R. Kotamarthi, T. Wall, and M. Neukomm
495577.abstract: In recent years, the scientific community has faced an exponential increase in data volume, widening the gap between data availability and effective utilization for model development and evaluation. Concurrently, the rising economic and humanitarian impacts of extreme weather events underscore the urgent need for actionable information across temporal scales, from medium-range to seasonal forecasting. Historically, data assimilation (DA) methods have been instrumental in improving predictability by refining initial conditions. However, their potential to reduce model error at longer time scales remains a promising, yet underutilized, pathway. The rapid growth of observational datasets presents a significant challenge for traditional model development. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer transformative solutions to these hurdles. By generating model surrogates and purely data-based earth system models, and by leveraging built-in backward propagation, these technologies can expand ensemble sizes and facilitate adjoint generation. This integration makes existing DA techniques more robust and adaptable to massive observational datasets. Recognizing these shared challenges and opportunities, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) are developing a burgeoning partnership to advance AI capabilities of mutual interest. A primary focus of this collaboration is the alignment of agency expertise, leveraging the best of NOAA’s environmental and weather intelligence from the National Weather Service (NWS), National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) and NOAA Research to advance the development of "AI-ready" reanalysis datasets while addressing the critical need for higher spatial and temporal resolution and improved data accessibility. Complementing this, Argonne is leveraging these improved datasets to pioneer the development of AI-supported Sub-seasonal to Seasonal (S2S) models. By integrating these AI-enhanced data streams with advanced modeling techniques, the collaboration seeks to provide the renewable energy industry with more dependable products for infrastructure siting and energy grid capacity analysis. As one of the first activities of the partnership, ANL and NOAA convened a small, focused workshop in September 2026 to explore a coordinated effort to provide high-resolution reanalyses supporting AI model training for weather prediction out to S2S time scales. This presentation will provide details of the NOAA/ANL partnership and goals. The workshop outcomes and conclusions will then be presented including an outline of the next steps in this interagency cooperation to facilitate future scientific innovation.

495578.title: Sub-Seasonal to Seasonal Prediction of Caribbean Extreme Heat Using Machine Learning
495578.authors: Frederick Boakye Oppong, University at Albany, Atmospheric Science Research Center, Albany, NY; and K. HIBBERT, J. P. Montoya-Rincon, P. Méndez-Lazaro, and J. E. Gonzalez-Cruz
495578.abstract: Weather forecasts provide useful guidance of extreme heat at short lead times, but actionable prediction of regional heat extremes several weeks to months in advance remains challenging. In the Caribbean, extreme heat is increasing at an alarming rate, influenced by oceanic, local and large-scale atmospheric mechanisms that may provide sources of extended-range predictability. This study asks: Can data-driven artificial intelligence identify the physical precursors of Caribbean extreme heat, determine when and where their predictive information emerges, and translate these relationships into reliable forecasts from two weeks to three months in advance? We develop an explainable, data-driven sub-seasonal-to-seasonal forecasting framework for the May-October Caribbean heat season. CHIRTS-ERA5 daily maximum temperature provides the observational target on a 0.05° grid, from which we derive multiple predictands including weekly extreme-heat frequency, weekly maximum-temperature anomalies, and heatwave occurrence. Unlike a single seasonal target, forecasts are formulated across Weeks 2-6 and monthly-to-seasonal lead times, allowing the evolution and limits of heat predictability to be quantified across the weather-to-climate prediction gap. The framework adapts an optimization-based climate feature-discovery approach to the tropical Caribbean. Approximately two millennia of MPI-ESM1-2-LR past2k simulations are used as a model-world discovery environment to search systematically across combinations of predictor variables, spatial regions, and precursor lead times. Candidate predictors characterize land memory, ocean memory, atmospheric circulation, moisture, convection, and surface climate, including soil moisture, sea-surface temperature, geopotential height, sea-level pressure, outgoing longwave radiation, precipitation, near-surface temperature, humidity, and low-level winds. Predictor domains encompass the Caribbean, tropical and North Atlantic, and tropical Pacific, enabling the framework to discover both local processes and remote teleconnections without restricting prediction to predetermined climate indices. Predictor relationships identified in the long climate simulation are subsequently transferred to the modern observational climate, using corresponding ERA5 and ERA5-Land fields to predict CHIRTS-ERA5 heat extremes. This model-to-observation transfer provides a stringent test of whether relationships learned from long-term climate variability contain predictive information applicable to present-day Caribbean heat. Multiple statistical and machine learning models are evaluated, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), permutation importance, and lead dependent feature attribution are used to quantify the relative contributions of predictor variables and identify the geographic regions and precursor timescales associated with forecast skill. Forecast performance is assessed using temporally independent hindcasts against climatology and persistence benchmarks, with deterministic and probabilistic verification used to evaluate both heat-frequency and heatwave-probability forecasts. Particular emphasis is placed on identifying where useful predictability originates, how it evolves from Weeks 2-6 to seasonal timescales, and whether land, Atlantic, or remote Pacific precursors dominate at different leads. The resulting framework extends data-driven seasonal heat prediction toward a seamless, physically interpretable, and probabilistic forecasting system. The framework provides a foundation for operational heat-risk guidance and seasonal outlooks supporting climate services and heat early warning across the Caribbean.

495579.title: Internal Climate Variability Mediates Atlantic TC Track Probabilities
495579.authors: Richard M Sullivan, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA; and A. Gori and B. S. Felzer
495579.abstract: Seasonal Atlantic tropical cyclone (TC) outlooks often emphasize basin-wide activity, but regional hazard depends on how storm tracks, and thus landfall probabilities, are distributed across the basin. Here, we use large synthetic TC sets statistical-dynamically downscaled from ERA5 reanalysis and CESM pre-industrial control simulations to identify recurrent seasonal track regimes and their associated climate states. Self-organizing maps identify six coherent track regimes in both datasets, reflecting zonal and meridional shifts in seasonal TC probabilities. Multivariate climate analysis identifies recurrent states characterized by coupled variability in tropical Atlantic and Pacific SSTs, Atlantic sea level pressure, and vertical wind shear, and shows that these climate states systematically alter the probability of individual track regimes. The recurrence of comparable track regimes and climate-track relationships in both reanalysis and pre-industrial model simulations indicates that internally generated climate variability is sufficient to organize regional Atlantic TC hazard at sub-decadal timescales. These relationships provide a framework for translating seasonal climate information into probabilistic estimates of regional TC hazard.

495580.title: On the Nature and Variability of African Easterly Wave Dust Relationships and its Impact on Downstream Tropical Cyclogenesis.
495580.authors: Christopher D. Thorncroft, Atmospheric Sciences Research Cetner, Albany, NY; and C. W. Barreto-Schuler, C. H. Lu, and S. W. Wei
495580.abstract: A common feature of African Easterly Waves (AEWs) leaving the West African coast is the presence of the Saharan Air Layer (SAL) Originating over the Sahara, the SAL is characterized by dry, warm and dusty air. The role of dry air on the probability of tropical cyclogenesis has been well documented but the role played by dust has been less studied in this context and is hence less well understood. While the presence of Saharan dust is often identified in the satellite products of AEWs leaving the West African coast and often referred to by forecasters in real time, its impact on the probability of tropical cyclogenesis, and associated mechanisms, remains relatively uncertain compared to that of the dry air and is the focus of the present study. This presentation will provide an overview of the nature and variability of AEW-dust characteristics and will include an assessment of the impact dust has on downstream tropical cyclogenesis. The talk will include a statistical and case-study view of the key downstream processes.

495582.title: Evaluation of a Next-Generation MPAS-based Warn-on-Forecast System Prototype During 2026 Spring and Summer Testbed Experiments
495582.authors: Brian C. Matilla, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; and N. Yussouf, P. S. Skinner, J. Martin, and K. H. Knopfmeier
495582.abstract: As the current WRF-based Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFSv1) continues its transition into operations within the National Weather Service, the next-generation version of WoFS with the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) dynamical core (WoFSv2) is being developed as part of continued efforts to align WoFS with NOAA’s Unified Forecast System framework. This initial version of WoFSv2 makes use of the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) software to assimilate similar types of observations as in WoFSv1. WoFSv2 was formally evaluated for the first time during the 2026 NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed Spring Forecasting Experiment (SFE) to assess its utility relative to WoFSv1 for 0–6-h severe convective hazard prediction. An additional evaluation was conducted in August 2026 for the HMT Flash Flood and Intense Rainfall (FFaIR) experiment using a displaced real-time framework. Participants evaluated WoFSv1 and WoFSv2 heavy-rainfall and flash-flood guidance for selected events. This study evaluates WoFSv2 relative to WoFSv1 for the 2026 SFE and FFaIR testbed cases using the Developmental Testbed Center’s Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) framework. Traditional and spatial verification statistics are computed for key forecast fields, including composite reflectivity, 1-km AGL reflectivity, and precipitation. Results from these evaluations will be presented at the conference.

495583.title: NOAA AMSU/MHS/ATMS Hydrological Bundle Climate Data Record (CDR), Version 2.0
495583.authors: James G. Beauchamp, UMD, College Park, MD; Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies, College Park, MD; and Y. You, J. X. Yang, and B. Nelson
495583.abstract: Previously, our team had generated Version 1.0 of the NOAA Hydrological Bundle Climate Data Record (CDR) using window channel (23.8, 31.4, 50.3, 89 GHz) observations from the Advanced Microwave Sounding Unit - A (AMSU-A) and humidity channel (89, 157, and 183 GHz) observations from the AMSU-B and Microwave Sensor Humidity (MHS) sensors. AMSU-A was aboard NOAA-15, -16, -17, -18, -19, and MetOp-A satellites, AMSU-B was aboard NOAA-15, -16, -17, and MHS aboard NOAA-18, -19, and MetOp-A satellites. This CDR extended from 2000 to the early 2020s, when most of the original sensors were no longer operating. Our team has completed a Version 2.0 CDR which includes these same historical data, plus has been extended with the addition of Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) window and humidity channel observations from the Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 satellites in addition to more AMSU-A and MHS observations from MetOp-B and MetOp-C. With this extension, it will be possible to eventually have a 30-year record of satellite inter-calibrated microwave brightness temperatures in this CDR. Where necessary, Version 2.0 employs a double difference method and simulates TBs from a state of the art radiative transfer model. Similar to Version 1.0, from the inter-calibrated TBs, hydrological products such as Total Precipitable Water (TPW), Cloud Liquid Water (CLW), Sea Ice, Land Surface Temperature (LST), Land Surface Emissivity (LSE), Ice Water Path (IWP), Rain Rate (RR), Snow Cover (SC), and Snow Water Equivalent (SWE) are generated using the Microwave Surface and Precipitation Products System (MSPPS). Both the inter-calibrated TBs (FCDRs) and the hydrological products (TCDRs) are available to the public through NCEI.

495584.title: Wave-State Effects on Turbulence in the Marine Atmospheric Boundary Layer for offshore Wind Applications
495584.authors: Alex Holguino, University of Puerto Rico, Mayaguez campus, Mayaguez, PR; and U. Ciri
495584.abstract: The marine atmospheric boundary layer (MABL) governs the exchange of momentum between the atmosphere and the ocean and strongly influences the turbulent structure of the lower atmosphere. Because the ocean surface is continuously deformed by surface gravity waves, different wave states modify the air–sea interface where momentum exchange takes place. Understanding how these wave states affect the atmospheric response is essential for improving the physical description of marine atmospheric flows and their interaction with the ocean. This understanding is critical for offshore wind energy because the mean and turbulent conditions of the MABL determine the atmospheric flow across a wind turbine rotor and can vary over the heights spanned by the rotor. A numerical study based on large-eddy simulation (LES) is conducted to investigate the atmospheric response over prescribed surface gravity waves. The simulations use a two-phase air–water configuration, with the air–water interface represented by a Level Set function. The instantaneous velocity field in the water region is prescribed from linear wave theory, while LES predicts the atmospheric response to this forcing, resulting in a one-way coupled configuration. The objective of this study is to investigate the impact of different wave states on the atmospheric response by considering variations in wavelength and wave height. These parameters modify the geometry of the air–water interface, allowing the atmospheric response to be examined across different combinations of wavelength and wave height. The analysis examines vertical profiles of mean wind velocity, shear stress, turbulence intensity, and resolved turbulent kinetic energy (TKE). Preliminary results for different wavelengths at a fixed wave height show that the strongest differences in the atmospheric response are concentrated in the lower MABL. Resolved TKE reaches its highest values near the air–water interface and decreases with height, with longer wavelengths exhibiting higher TKE levels near the surface. Differences in mean wind velocity, shear stress, and turbulence intensity are also observed among the different wavelengths. Future work will compare these wavelength-dependent responses at different wave heights to examine how changes in wave height modify the mean and turbulent structure of the MABL. The implications of these atmospheric responses for offshore wind energy will be discussed by considering different hub heights and rotor sizes across a variety of wave states.

495586.title: The Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI)
495586.authors: Yannick Tremolet, Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation, Boulder, CO
495586.abstract: Data assimilation systems have traditionally been built independently by each modeling center, leading to duplicated effort across agencies. The Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) addresses this by providing a unified, community-based data assimilation framework for research and operational use, for all components of the Earth system, and for different applications. The key goals are to reduce or avoid redundant work between government agencies and within the community, and to increase the efficiency of research and of the transition from development teams to Operations. After several years of development the code is getting mature and is planned for operational implementation by the JCSDA partner agencies (NOAA, NASA, US Navy, US Air Force, UKMO) in the next few years. JEDI cleanly separates the forecast model, observation handling, and data assimilation algorithms through well-defined interfaces, making the system generic with respect to the model it interfaces with — including atmospheric models (UFS, MPAS, LFRic, NEPTUNE), other Earth system components, coupled models, and AI/ML models. This separation of concerns lets specialists contribute independently without unintended side effects elsewhere in the system, and enables rapid prototyping of new science. For instance, a new observation type can be implemented once and immediately made available to all partner agencies — with no duplicated effort. The abstraction of code away from the specific implementation details allows for a very flexible system and fast prototyping of innovative data assimilation science. This talk presents the JEDI architecture and highlights recent progress toward operational readiness across multiple Earth system components and models.

495587.title: Assessing Lake-Atmosphere Coupling Approaches Against Observed Heat, Moisture, and Ice Dynamics in the Great Lakes
495587.authors: Aaron Bartlett, Cooperative Institute for Great Lakes Research (CIGLR), Ann Arbor, MI; and A. L. Hutson, A. H. Young, and D. M. Wright
495587.abstract: Lake-atmosphere interactions exert a distinct influence on the climate of the Great Lakes region, moderating regional air temperature, transferring moisture into the air, and governing lake ice cycles. These processes create feedbacks that are poorly represented by current land-surface parameterizations alone, making accurate lake modeling essential for reliable historical simulation and future projection of regional climate. This study evaluates three regional climate modeling frameworks, each using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to dynamically downscale ERA5 reanalysis over the Great Lakes Region: (1) GL-WRF, a Great Lakes regional climate model with WRF's native 1-D lake model; (2) Great Lakes FVCOM, a 3-D, unstructured hydrodynamic lake model designed for the Great Lakes, forced by bias-corrected GL-WRF output; and (3) COMPASS-GLM, a regional climate model in which WRF and FVCOM are coupled online with hourly bidirectional exchanges of surface conditions. Model performance is assessed through comparison of surface heat and moisture fluxes against eddy covariance observations from the Great Lakes Evaporation Network (GLEN), and through comparison of prevailing lake surface and overlake air conditions against satellite-based GLSEA and buoy-based NDBC observations. Together, these comparisons characterize the performance gaps of 1-D versus 3-D lake representations and offline versus online coupling. Results will directly inform the selection and implementation of lake-atmosphere coupling strategies for future climate simulations in the Great Lakes Region, guiding investment of computational and research resources toward the modeling frameworks best suited for the unique characteristics of the region.

495590.title: From Circulation to Degree Days: Weekly North American Weather Regime Relationships in ERCOT
495590.authors: Christian Bryce Bohon, Prescient Weather Ltd, State College, PA; and J. Ross, R. Shroff, and R. James
495590.abstract: Weekly heating and cooling degree days (HDD and CDD) provide temperature based proxies for electricity and natural gas demand, but they do not identify the persistent circulation pattern associated with a given weekly total. This study quantifies how weekly ERCOT degree days vary with the continuous amplitudes of the four World Climate Service (WCS) North American weather regimes. It evaluates which regimes have the largest relationships, how those relationships change between winter and summer, and whether population weighted and natural gas consumption weighted metrics respond similarly. The WCS year round classification includes Alaskan Ridge, Greenland High, Pacific Ridge, and Pacific Trough. It is based on ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis and closely follows Lee et al. (2023). Daily continuous regime amplitudes are obtained from the WCS observed weather regime daily archive. Daily population weighted and natural gas consumption weighted HDD and CDD observations from the WCS Point-in-Time Weather Forecast API for 1981 to 2026 are summed to complete seven-day calendar weeks, and regime amplitudes are averaged over the same weeks. This resolution is consistent with the observed persistence of North American regime episodes, which have a mean duration of 7.6 days and a median of 6 days. The principal weekly relationships are: For December and January, weekly HDD increases with Alaskan Ridge amplitude (r = +0.52, p < 0.001, n = 364 complete weeks). The highest amplitude decile averages 156 HDD, compared with 76 HDD in the lowest decile and a weekly climatology of 105 HDD. Weekly HDD decreases with Pacific Ridge and Pacific Trough amplitudes during December and January. The correlations are -0.31 and -0.25, and the differences between the highest and lowest amplitude deciles are 59 and 37 HDD, respectively. The Greenland High relationship is weak and is statistically significant only for November through March (r = +0.07, p = 0.02). Summer relationships are smaller. Pacific Ridge has the largest JJA CDD correlation (r = +0.21), with a difference of 18 CDD between amplitude deciles relative to a weekly climatology of 130 CDD. Across all regimes and time windows, correlations from the two weighting methods differ by no more than 0.009. These relationships provide a circulation based framework for weekly demand analysis. When paired with WCS forecast regime probabilities, the historical distributions can provide additional context for alternate HDD and CDD scenarios. For example, changes in forecast Alaskan Ridge probability can be compared with the observed weekly HDD distribution as Alaskan Ridge amplitude changes. The analysis does not assess added forecast skill, and HDD and CDD remain weather based proxies rather than observations of electricity load or natural gas consumption. It also does not estimate prices, system conditions, or trading outcomes.

495591.title: Toward a National Infrasound Network: Integrated Measurement and Prediction of Weather Hazards through Infrasound Testbeds
495591.authors: Michael H Zink, University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, MA; and C. A. Davis, B. J. Philips, Z. Clayton, H. Saplakoglu, and B. Regan
495591.abstract: Severe weather phenomena, including convection, extreme turbulence, and flash flooding, pose significant challenges to aviation safety, public welfare, and disaster preparedness. This research leverages infrasound detection—low-frequency pressure fluctuations—as a complementary observational approach for early warning and prediction of these societally critical weather hazards. We present an integrated measurement and prediction framework combining infrasound observations with complementary meteorological instrumentation including polarimetric radar, barometric measurements, GPS/GNSS water vapor, sonic anemometers, and unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). The Paros Center for Atmospheric Research is establishing three coordinated testbeds to validate infrasound capabilities: (1) a Western Massachusetts testbed focused on flooding and severe local winds, (2) a site in Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) Living Lab addressing severe convection and flash flooding, and (3) a deployment NSF’s NCAR Marshall Field Site in Colorado examining severe weather, wildfires, and turbulence detection. These integrated testbeds will generate cutting-edge observational and predictive insights while advancing infrastructure investments, technical expertise, and human capacity building. Each of these sites comprises three infrasound sensors and sonic anemometers and will integrate atmospheric measurement data from other sensors. For the Western Massachusetts site, this includes an X-band radar and weather station data (temperature, humidity, barometric pressure). At the Marshall site, our data will be complemented by data from LIDARS, precipitation and snow sensors, and sonar. In the DFW Living Lab, we will integrate data from five X-band polarimetric weather radars. Data from all sites are collected in a centralized processing, visualization, and archiving system. This system allows for immediate signal processing, data inspection, and dissemination to researchers. Raw and processed data are archived in a database, which provides easy data access to researchers. The system runs in a containerized environment, which can scale once the network of infrasound sensors is further expanded. We will give a detailed overview of the architecture and implementation of the data collection and signal processing system we implemented for our infrasound sensing network. In addition, we present results from our work that addresses wind filtering, which is a source of noise for infrasound measurements. Data from the infrasound sensors in Massachusetts and Colorado are used to evaluate several approaches, including one that is based on the approach of active noise cancellation. Our objectives over the next five years will focus on addressing fundamental gaps in observational meteorology, establishing a network of regional collaborators, and integrating testbed data into undergraduate and graduate curricula. In addition, we will strengthen partnerships with NSF NCAR and regional universities to further national capabilities in weather hazard detection and prediction.

495592.title: Investigating Observed Regional Changes in Statistical Moments of 500 hPa Geopotential Height over the Northern Hemisphere Mid-Latitudes
495592.authors: Jessica Slotter, Portland State University, Portland, OR; and P. C. Loikith, D. Singh, S. Bigalke, and A. Laverty
495592.abstract: Geopotential height at 500 mb is a popular meteorological diagnostic variable carrying information about tropospheric temperature, mid-tropospheric flow speed and direction, and acts as a proxy for the location of rising and sinking air. In the mid-latitudes, synoptic scale 500 mb geopotential height variability relates to storm track activity and can influence the occurrence of temperature and precipitation extremes. As temperatures increase due to global warming, 500 mb geopotential height should increase due to thermal expansion of the atmosphere. If this change were to occur uniformly, it would result in no change in mid-tropospheric circulation. However, non-uniform changes would result in potentially meaningful changes to atmospheric circulation and, consequently, surface meteorology. Here, we investigate the changes in the first three moments of the 500 mb geopotential height distribution over the time period 1940-2025 and across the seasonal cycle using ERA5 reanalysis. While the simplest expectation of global warming would be a uniform rightward shift in the 500 mb height distribution, our results suggest that meaningful regional-scale changes in the mean, variance, and skewness are observable over the period of study. The magnitude and spatial variability of these changes is largest for the mean and smallest for skewness, with some notable regional changes in standard deviation. Identified changes result from internal variability, external forcing, or a combination of both, providing useful indicators of nonstationarity in mid-latitude atmospheric circulation in recent decades, and establishing a foundation for further dynamical investigation into their causes.

495593.title: Evaluating the Influence of Equatorial Indian Ocean Rain Layers on Upscale Convective Growth In Convection-Permitting Simulations
495593.authors: Kyle Shackelford, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and C. A. DeMott and P. J. van Leeuwen
495593.abstract: Stable rain layers (RL) form in the near surface ocean when relatively colder, fresher, less dense rain water is deposited on the ocean surface under low-to-moderate winds. RL-induced SST reductions are prolonged and amplified through a stable salinity stratification that confines ocean-atmosphere exchange to the upper 1-10 m of the ocean. Reduced SST within RLs reduces surface heat fluxes and hinders the development of future atmospheric convection (the RL direct SST effect). SST gradients between low SST RLs and the relatively higher SST surrounding ocean may drive low-level atmospheric circulations conducive to convective initiation on the high SST side of the gradient (the RL SST gradient effect). Thus, RLs favor suppressed convection locally through reduced SSTs and favor enhanced convection remotely through SST gradient-driven wind patterns, presenting competing RL feedbacks to atmospheric convection. In this study, we conduct convection-permitting coupled ocean-atmosphere simulations over the equatorial Indian Ocean to evaluate how RLs feed back to mesoscale convective organization and intensity. We run a 10-member ensemble suite of paired cases with and without rain freshening and cooling of the ocean surface to probe the robustness of RL feedbacks to atmospheric convection. Rain-induced SST gradients drive low-level wind patterns conducive to convective initiation, but the direct SST effect of suppressing convection exceeds the SST gradient effect of enhancing convection for large-scale convection. Additionally, the direct SST effect and SST gradient effect appear to jointly modify the convective organization and intensity of a mesoscale convectively-coupled gravity wave that forms within the model domain. However, cold pool activity associated with intrinsic convective variability play a larger role in regulating behavior of the convectively-coupled gravity wave than RLs.

495595.title: Transforming NOAA Space Weather Services: Advancing Decision-Ready Operations through User-Centered Services, Operational Testbeds, and Modern Impact Communication
495595.authors: Clinton Wallace, NOAA National Weather Service, Boulder, CO
495595.abstract: Space weather services are undergoing a fundamental transformation as growing societal dependence on space-based technologies, electric power systems, aviation, communications, satellite operations, positioning, navigation and timing (PNT), and human spaceflight demands information that is increasingly actionable, consistent, and decision focused. Driven by the Space Weather Advisory Group (SWAG) recommendations and user surveys, NOAA has advanced multiple initiatives supporting this evolution from traditional forecast products toward integrated operational services centered on user needs and measurable societal outcomes. A cornerstone of this transformation has been continued development of the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Testbed, which provides an operational research-to-operations-to-research environment where forecasters, researchers, model developers, and external partners collaboratively evaluate emerging observations, models, data assimilation techniques, visualization capabilities, and decision-support tools prior to operational implementation. Recent activities have expanded the Testbed's role in evaluating new observing capabilities, supporting operational exercises, improving forecast guidance, and accelerating transition of scientific advances into operational services. In parallel, NOAA has advanced modernization of the Space Weather Scales to better communicate expected operational impacts using user-informed language developed through extensive engagement with operational communities, government partners, academia, commercial providers, and international stakeholders. The revised scales emphasize scientifically defensible, impact-based communication while improving consistency across hazard types and enhancing their value for operational decision making. These efforts have been complemented by broader enterprise initiatives including implementation of PROSWIFT priorities, development of a national space weather observational strategy, operational integration of new observing capabilities, expanded collaboration with commercial and international partners, and increased engagement with critical infrastructure sectors through operational exercises and user-driven service development. Collectively, these activities illustrate how sustained investment in operational testbeds, user engagement, modern observations, and impact-based communication is enabling a more resilient national space weather enterprise. Rather than representing isolated improvements, these initiatives form an integrated framework for accelerating innovation while ensuring new scientific capabilities are transitioned into operational services that better support decision makers across an increasingly space-weather-dependent society.

495596.title: Linking Weather and Climate Extremes to Investor Behavior and Market Sentiment
495596.authors: Young Jae Choi, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. I. Christian and H. Lim
495596.abstract: Weather and climate extremes have increased in frequency and severity across the United States in recent decades, including drought, heatwaves, and flooding. These events can lead to billions of dollars in losses on infrastructure and the agricultural sector. Additionally, extreme events can reduce regional economic output, disrupt supply chains, and increase prices, which can create broader economic instability and affect the value of assets held by investors. As such, the primary goal of this study is to examine how the timing and severity of weather and climate extremes influence investors’ stock trading behavior, risk preferences, and sentiment. To address this research goal, gridded meteorological data from Phase 2 of the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS-2) and investment data are used to quantify the relationship between extreme events and investor behavior. Daily values of meteorological variables are used as proxies for extreme events (e.g., precipitation – flooding, snowfall – winter extremes, soil moisture – drought, temperature – heatwaves/cold air outbreaks). Aggregating data into quarterly values, early findings show that legislators are less likely to buy and more likely to sell when they experience cold weather at their location. Furthermore, the weather experienced at a firm’s location (e.g., cold air outbreak) impacts the likelihood of stock purchases from legislators. However, above average temperatures (e.g., heatwaves) are not associated with periods of stock buying/selling. Further analysis will be applied to other types of extreme weather (snowfall, precipitation) and will also include retail investment behavior and trading patterns.

495598.title: Treating Sampling Errors in the Prior Ensemble Statistics by Imposing User-Informed Statistical Structures
495598.authors: Man-Yau (Joseph) Chan, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and X. Guan, J. Poterjoy, and L. White
495598.abstract: Physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models are computationally costly to run. Therefore, ensemble sizes used in NWP ensemble data assimilation (EnsDA) systems are typically limited to less than 100 members. Since the sampling errors in the resulting ensemble-estimated prior statistics can drastically degrade the performance of EnsDA, methods to treat such errors are crucial for EnsDA for NWP. Advancements in such treatment methods therefore have the potential to improve EnsDA for NWP. We propose a conceptual framework for treating sampling errors through combining users’ domain knowledge with the prior ensemble to generate more ensemble members. In other words, we suppress sampling errors through imposing domain knowledge. Such knowledge includes the expected families of marginal distributions (e.g., Gaussian and Gamma) and the expected generalized correlation length scales (“probit-space localization length”). The original prior members and additional members are aggregated to form an expanded ensemble which is then used in EnsDA. Idealized experiments with low-order models and archived Navy Global Environment Model (NAVGEM) ensembles demonstrate that our framework improves the performance of EnsDA. We are currently extending the exploration of our framework through perfect model Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) involving the mesoscale EnsDA of all-sky geostationary satellite infrared radiance observations. This presentation will introduce our conceptual framework and how our framework leads to EnsDA performance improvements. Our discussions will be supported and illustrated with conceptual examples and experimental results from low-order models, offline NAVGEM EnsDA experiments, and cycled mesoscale EnsDA experiments.

495600.title: Comparison of AQPI X-Band Radar Mosaic and MRMS Performance at Rain Gauges Across the San Francisco Bay Area.
495600.authors: Matthew Steen, Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and J. Rutz and R. B. Vilela
495600.abstract: The Advanced Quantitative Precipitation Information (AQPI) program operates a network of 6 scanning radars, 5 X-band and 1 C-band, across the San Francisco Bay Area. These radars complement the Next-Generation Radar (NEXRAD) network, which has limited coverage due to range effects and beam blockage by terrain across some areas. This limits the accuracy and utility of NEXRAD-based Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) quantitative precipitation estimates (QPEs) across this region. The AQPI Mosaic, which includes both AQPI and NEXRAD observations, provides a spatially continuous and high-resolution QPE across the region (much like the MRMS). The most recent implementation of the AQPI mosaic ran from 5 Mar 2025 through 8 Apr 2026. This version utilized AQPI data only from the five available X-band radars, one of which was added midway through this period. Beyond 8 Apr 2026, the AQPI C-band radar was incorporated into the mosaic, is expected to contribute positively to QPEs, and will be the topic of further investigation. This study broadly evaluates the accuracy of the AQPI Mosaic relative to the MRMS Radar-Only QPE benchmark by focusing on the top-100 hourly rainfall observations at regional rain gauges throughout this period. AQPI Mosaic QPEs were ~0.06–0.08 inches closer to gauge observations for hours ≥ 0.25 inches reported by gauges within 40 km (the effective range) of any AQPI X-Band. Complementary analyses offer some insight into the causes of this variation, with the caveat that the overall sample size is small. Overall, the results highlight the potential value of AQPI radar data to improve regional QPE.

495601.title: The ROI of Weather AI and What it Means for Operational Meteorologists
495601.authors: Matthew Stein, Google LLC, Mountain View, CA; Google LLC, Mountain View, CA
495601.abstract: Format: Roundtable As artificial intelligence forecast models break meteorological skill records and AI agentic workflows emerge across enterprise environments, meteorology is gaining powerful new tools to predict atmospheric phenomena and inform complex decisions. Yet, a basic question remains: How do we measure the value of these tools? This roundtable brings together leaders from frontier AI research, operational forecasting, utilities, and energy markets to tackle three defining questions: What is the true ROI of AI weather models? Establishing a pragmatic framework to value next-generation forecast skill, contrasting how different sectors evaluate risk - from an energy trading desk capitalizing on market volatility to a utility meteorologist managing high-consequence decisions like Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS). What is the ROI of generative AI and agentic workflows? Moving past the hype to examine where generative tools and autonomous AI agents drive measurable efficiency - from orchestrating multi-step data synthesis to translating dense probabilistic outputs into plain-language commercial risk narratives. How is all of this redefining the operational meteorologist? Exploring how forecasters manage model skepticism and use AI to complement physical predictions. We will discuss how humans steer automated agentic workflows, and why the meteorologist remains the indispensable "circuit breaker" in both predictive and operational decision systems. Set against growing climate volatility, we will discuss how AI and economic realities are changing the way the weather enterprise operates. Session Participants: Moderator: Matt Stein, Principal Strategy, Google DeepMind Panelist 1: Aaron Bell, Director of Engineering, Google Research Panelist 2: Dr. Peter Neilley, SVP of Weather Sciences & Forecasting, The Weather Company Panelist 3: Dr. Kim Klockow McClain, Social Science Coordinator, NOAA/NCEP Panelist 4: Zach Tolby, Director of Wildfire Meteorology, Xcel Energy Panelist 5: Jason Lynn, Meteorologist, Mercuria Energy Trading

495602.title: What Explains the Eastward Shift in United States Tornado Activity?
495602.authors: Nathan Robert Harms, Purdue University, Leland, NC; Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN; and D. Chavas and D. T. Dawson II
495602.abstract: Recent studies have documented an eastward shift in United States tornado activity away from the traditional Great Plains "Tornado Alley" toward the Southeastern "Dixie Alley," along with related changes in seasonality. However, the environmental drivers of these trends remain poorly understood. Assessing the relationships between environmental trends and tornado trends closes an important gap in understanding the changes in U.S. tornado climatology. We first identify decadal trends in EF1+ tornado activity, defining trend regions from the data itself rather than pre-conceived boundaries. This reveals a broad region of increasing tornado activity across the Southeast into Oklahoma, Illinois, and Ohio, bordered by a ring of decreases across the Northern Great Plains, Michigan, and Texas. Out of all the defined regions, the Southeast alone shows a shift toward earlier-season activity. We then evaluate environmental drivers of the spatiotemporal structure, including long-term trends in precipitation, extratropical cyclones, and severe weather ingredients like CAPE and shear. Preliminary results show that precipitation trends do not closely track the tornado trends on a region-by-region basis, with several regions seeing precipitation increases despite decreasing tornado activity. We suspect this reflects broad, warming-driven rainfall that occurs independent of any change in storm-specific processes, potentially masking a genuine precipitation-tornado relationship. Ongoing work will analyze where precipitation would be increasing or decreasing absent a general warming trend to determine whether it better aligns with, and helps explain, the observed tornado trends. We are also assessing the role of extratropical cyclones and STP components in this framework.

495606.title: A Regional Coupled MPAS-A–MOM6 Prototype for Maritime Air-Sea Interaction Research and Prediction
495606.authors: Falko Judt, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. Amrhein, B. W. Barr, B. Dobbins, M. Duda, A. Janney, Y. R. Jauregui, S. Kamali, G. Marques, R. C. Mullis, R. Oehmke, G. Seijo, A. Tsay, U. U. Turuncoglu, and S. Voelz
495606.abstract: As numerical weather prediction moves toward fully coupled Earth system modeling, the weather community lacks a high-resolution coupled configuration of MPAS-A. Coupled regional models let us represent maritime processes and extremes at km-scale — where convection is permitted and ocean mesoscale features are resolved — while remaining computationally affordable enough for community use across forecast lead times from days to subseasonal. Here we describe a prototype regional MPAS-A–MOM6 system coupled using tools from the Community Earth System Model. The prototype uses ESMF/NUOPC caps (including a new NUOPC cap for MPAS-A) with the ESMX driver in place of the CESM driver, CMEPS and CDEPS for mediation and data exchange, and CROCODILE tools for rapid configuration of regional MOM6. Our first test case is Hurricane Michael (2018) over the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean, coupling 3-km MPAS-A (4.7M grid columns, 56 levels, convection-permitting physics, Δt = 18 s) to 1/36° MOM6 (3.1M columns, 25 layers to 6000 m, Δt = 150 s) with a 450-s coupling period. The simulation captures Michael's intensification as it crosses a warm eddy shed from a retracted Loop Current, and the storm-generated cold wake and SST anomaly field that follow. In initial 32-node configurations on Derecho, coupling adds roughly 8–13% cost relative to standalone MPAS-A, though not all coupling fields are yet exchanged and I/O frequency strongly affects measured performance; these numbers should be read as early. Ongoing work extends the prototype along two axes. Physically, we are adding turbulent flux exchange from MPAS-A to MOM6 and surface currents back to MPAS-A. Further out, we plan to add coupling to WaveWatch III (waves) and CICE (sea ice) via CROCODILE. In scale, we are building a 3-km Indo-Pacific "basin-scale" configuration (25°S–55°N, 55°E–75°W; 26M MPAS columns, coupled to 1/36° or 1/12° MOM6 with 24M columns) for the DYAMOND winter period (20 January–20 March 2020), targeting MJO initiation and propagation, air-sea-land coupling over the Maritime Continent and warm pool, monsoon onset, western Pacific TC genesis, Kuroshio air-sea interaction, and upwelling OSSEs. A global km-scale configuration (3-km MPAS-A, 1/36° or 1/12° MOM6, 5–40 day integrations) is slated to follow, aimed at operational- and S2S-range predictability of the entire coupled atmosphere-ocean system. We will report on profiling across mixed-resolution configurations, load balancing, I/O choices, and memory footprints, and we welcome feedback from operational and research partners on which features and use cases would be most valuable to the broader maritime prediction community.

495608.title: GOES-R ABI Mesoscale Sector Application: Innovations for NWS Mission Use
495608.authors: Joseph Anderson, NOAA Affiliate, KBR, Inc, Silver Spring, MD; and E. Sorbella, L. Wichrowski, J. K. Zajic, M. Foster, and L. A. Byerle
495608.abstract: The GOES-East and GOES-West mesoscale sectors are available to and commonly used by NWS forecasters for their mission operations. This presentation describes initiatives by the NESDIS GEO Program’s Total Operational Weather Readiness - Satellites (TOWR-S) team, in collaboration with the NWS Operations Center, to provide enhancements to the current Mesoscale Mission Manager and Meso Mission Viewer suite for making requests. New capabilities will be discussed, including better resources for archiving and managing the tool as it migrates to the NWS TOWR Portal, a more flexible planning cadence, and the potential for plan-based implementations.

495611.title: The Rapid Refresh Forecast System: An Operational Unified Forecast System Application for Short-Range Weather Prediction
495611.authors: Curtis R. Alexander, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and M. E. Pyle, T. T. Ladwig, L. Bernardet, and J. R. Carley
495611.abstract: NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL), in collaboration with the NWS Office of Modeling and Development (OMD), have completed research and development on the first version of the Unified Forecast System (UFS)-based Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) for short range weather prediction at convection allowing scales including a transition into operations during the fall of 2026. This transition represents the culmination of more than five years of collaborative development and progress towards unification and simplification of the operational model suite. This presentation will review the design and capabilities of RRFS version one including deterministic and ensemble forecast components that have subsumed some legacy regional model systems. The presentation will also cover some lessons learned during this development and transition process that can be applied to future development with the RRFS and potentially other UFS applications.

495613.title: Long-Term Trends and Global Variations in Surface Air Pollutants Observed from Space Using Advanced AI Models
495613.authors: Zhanqing Li, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD
495613.abstract: People around the world are exposed to air pollution from a wide range of particulate matter (e.g., PM₂.₅ and PM₁) and gaseous pollutants (e.g., O₃, NO₂, and SO₂) at the surface, posing serious threats to environmental quality and public health. Although satellite remote sensing provides spatially extensive observations of the total-column abundance of many air pollutants, translating these measurements into reliable surface-level concentrations remains challenging. Existing surface estimates often suffer from limited accuracy, coarse spatial resolution, and substantial data gaps. By integrating satellite observations with ground-based measurements from multiple agencies worldwide and applying advanced machine-learning models, we have developed global daily surface-level products for all the particulate and gaseous pollutants at a nominal resolution of 1km and used them to characterize their long-term trends and spatial patterns. Air pollution levels have changed dramatically over the past several decades, with both the magnitude and direction of these changes varying considerably across regions. These distinct temporal and spatial patterns reflect the combined influences of anthropogenic activities and natural variability. The utility and fidelity of these datasets are demonstrated through analyses of their spatial distributions, temporal variations, and policy implications, with particular emphasis on surface air quality, population exposure, and the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. Special attention is also given to wildfires, which have caused severe air pollution across many regions of the world and, in some cases, have been associated with climate change and shifts in major modes of climate variability. These global products have been widely applied to address a broad range of atmospheric, environmental, and public health questions.

495615.title: A Constellation Ready Polarimetric Microwave Imager for Ocean Surface Wind Vector: Results from COWVR Demonstration Mission
495615.authors: Shannon Brown, JPL, Pasadena, CA; and A. Kitiyakara, M. G. Morris, F. Polverari, S. Swadley, E. Simon, and S. Farrar
495615.abstract: The Compact Ocean Wind Vector Radiometer (COWVR) is the first space demonstration of a low-cost, small-sat compatible conical microwave imager for atmospheric and surface observation, specializing in ocean vector winds. Heritage conical microwave imagers, such as SSM/I, AMSR, WindSat, GMI and WSF-M have been providing important Earth observations for over 45 years, including but not limited to surface wind vector, atmospheric and surface temperature, water vapor, clouds, precipitation, snow and sea ice. However, due to the cost and complexity of these legacy systems, the ad hoc international constellation of passive instruments is dwindling, extending re-visit times, impacting weather forecasting. The DMSP SSMIS sensors will be retired by September 2026 further exacerbating the gap. The objective of the COWVR mission is to demonstrate that a new, lower-cost radiometer architecture can perform as well as the legacy systems. We present a detailed long-term evaluation from the nearly four years of COWVR operations in space, comparing its wind vector measurements to scatterometers and other radiometers. We will describe follow-on concepts that extend the frequency range and increase the spatial resolution to meet future science and operational user needs. COWVR operated on the International Space Station (ISS) from January 2022 through August 2025 along with the TEMPEST-H8 microwave sounder. COWVR provides measurements of ocean vector winds, precipitable water vapor, clouds and precipitation while TEMPEST-H8 provides retrievals of vertical water vapor profiles and ice cloud properties, including convective intensity. Final mission reprocessing was completed in August 2026 with the complete data archive available on the NASA PO.DAAC. We present the detailed in-flight performance characterization from nearly 3.8-years of operation of COWVR and TEMPEST-H8 demonstrating a compact sensor can perform as well as current generation operational sensors. The nearly 4-year mission permits very detailed quantification of the magnitude of residual systematic errors in the sensor calibration and retrieval products, including long-term stability of the electronic calibration sources (e.g. polarimetric noise sources). We will summarize the results from this detailed in-flight characterization, including highlights of data assimilation impact studies. We show that COWVR performed significantly better wind direction retrievals than the WindSat legacy sensor. This is because COWVR has the advantage of an un-blocked conical scan, observing each spot in the swath at two different azimuth angles relative to the wind direction. This viewing geometry has the advantage of reducing ambiguous wind vector solutions and improving overall performance. We also compare the COWVR wind vector products to those produced from the operational ASCAT scatterometer systems, showing nearly equivalent performance (with wind direction differences < 10 degrees at wind speeds > 10m/s). Data assimilation studies have shown positive impact, equivalent to legacy imagers with common channels. The brightness temperature and retrieval products are distributed publicly via the NASA PO.DAAC. COWVR has demonstrated a new sensor architecture suitable for deployment in a small-satellite constellation. We will describe on-going design adaptation activities with the aim of commercializing the COWVR system for routine wind observation.

495619.title: Precipitation and its Efficiency in Tropical Cyclones in Convection-Permitting Model Simulations over the U.S.
495619.authors: Alyssa M Stansfield, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and J. Kukulies and K. L. Rasmussen
495619.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) convert massive amounts of atmospheric water vapor into precipitation, often causing significant flooding in coastal and inland regions after landfall. Previous studies have attempted to quantify the efficiency with which water vapor and cloud condensate are converted to surface precipitation (i.e., precipitation efficiency) by TCs, often using different variables and calculation methods. Changes in microphysical processes and precipitation efficiency in a future warmer climate could greatly influence future TC precipitation, but these small-scale processes are difficult to observe. This work compares TC precipitation and precipitation efficiency in 4 km Weather Research and Forecasting runs over the U.S. for 1979-2022 forced by ERA5 (known as CONUS404) to estimates from various observational datasets. Previous work by the authors has shown that CONUS404 simulates TC tracks, intensities, and precipitation well. We will quantify the range of precipitation efficiency values from different calculation methods and compare precipitation efficiency between the TC inner cores and outer rainbands. Precipitation efficiencies in the historical CONUS404 simulations will also be compared to pseudo-global warming simulations over the same domain.

495621.title: Radiative Forcing Response to Reduced Contrail Ice Formation via Proposed Ice Nuclei Seeding: A Global Study with CoCiP
495621.authors: Anil Kumar Khadka, SUNY, Albany, NY; and F. Yu
