495621.abstract: Contrail cirrus dominates aviation’s non-CO2 climate impacts, contributing substantially to atmospheric warming. Contrail Mitigation By Ice Nuclei Effective Seeding (COMBINES) (F. Yu, EST Air, https://doi.org/10.1021/acsestair.5c00241, 2026) has recently been proposed as a potential strategy to reduce this warming by introducing ice nucleating particles (INPs) into the exhaust plume, thereby decreasing the number of ice crystals formed in persistent contrails by 1—2 orders of magnitude. This study employs the grid-based Contrail Cirrus Prediction (CoCiP) model to evaluate, for the first time, the global sensitivity of contrail radiative forcing (RF) to reductions in the initial ice number (EIice) under COMBINES scenarios. The results indicate a strongly nonlinear response of contrail RF to EIice reductions, with substantial spatial and seasonal variability. A 10-fold reduction in EIice decreases the global annual mean net contrail RF from 56.5 to 3.4 mW m⁻² (–94%), while reductions exceeding 15-fold result in net cooling; a 50-fold reduction yields –6.1 mW m⁻² (–111%). Regionally, net contrail RF declines markedly, with reductions from 424.7 to –4.2 and –79.0 mW m⁻² over Europe; from 350.7 to 33.8 and −27.7 mW m⁻² over the North Atlantic; and from 208.2 to –5.0 and –41.8 mW m⁻² over the United States for 10- and 50-fold reductions, respectively. The mitigation potential is greatest in winter, with significant regional and seasonal differences, suggesting that targeted, seasonally optimized INP seeding can substantially reduce and potentially reverse contrail-induced warming. In this presentation, we will show detailed simulations of seeding scenarios, their microphysical responses, and a discussion of their implications, potential climate benefits, limitations, and future research needs.

495623.title: On-Board Satellite Data Processing: Value-Added Use Cases
495623.authors: Andrew W Royle, NOAA, Sykesville, MD; and C. O'Connors
495623.abstract: Today’s space observation architecture differs dramatically from the era in which today’s flagship meteorological observation satellites were designed and developed. Rapid advances in satellite and instrument manufacturing, decreased cost to orbit, and increased data exploitation via artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) are revolutionizing the use cases for satellite observations. While more, higher resolution data offers new opportunities for ground-based processing, increased on-orbit compute capability can enable different user needs to be addressed. This presentation will explore several such cases, including Opportunities for low-latency warnings for fire/hotspots, tornados, and other severe weather to be generated autonomously on board using embedded algorithms Enabling atmospheric feature detection and classification to provide pre-processing of data for forecaster ingest Providing separately broadcast direct to device alerts and warnings Leveraging processing from on-orbit data centers and high speed optical inter-satellite link (OISL) connectivity Creating tiered data sets to enable rapid ingest of relevant data into forecast models, while preserving raw data sets for retrospective analysis and archive By utilizing the flexibility of today's commercial satellite capabilities, mission architects can work with the user community to define and implement capabilities that meet a variety of use cases with only limited increases in the complexity of space-based components. Broad community engagement will be needed to determine which capabilities may add value and are worthy of additional research, development, and investment as future missions are designed.

495624.title: Utilizing Low-Cost Clarity Node S Sensors Network to Monitor Local PM Concentrations in Lubbock, TX
495624.authors: John Garber IV, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and J. Shankles, A. Hernandez, and K. Ardon-Dryer
495624.abstract: Measurements of particulate matter (PM) and the establishment of a sensor network are important to ensure improved air quality levels and living conditions. A recent study in Lubbock, TX, suggests that several neighborhoods, especially those near industrial areas, experience increased health problems likely due to elevated PM concentrations from nearby industrial sources. However, only one regulatory PM2.5 monitor is situated within city limits, and the sensor is located on the edge of town, far from residential areas. This work is part of the Lubbock Environmental Action Plan (LEAP) for Communities project that aims to provide information about the air quality across the city. The Clarity Node S, a low-cost sensor that uses a built-in solar panel and SIM card port, was selected for this project. At first, the Clarity sensors were collocated with a reference Grimm EDM-180 for an initial period, where they demonstrated very good correlation with other collocated Clarity sensors, with R2 values above 0.9, but less so with the EDM-180. The 42 Clarity Node S sensors were then calibrated to the EDM-180 and were deployed across the city of Lubbock to create a spatial and temporal network for PM2.5. The data was analyzed to determine the extent of the impact PM has on Lubbock, such as which month, weekday, or time of the day has the highest PM concentrations, and to determine where the PM hotspots are located across Lubbock. Further analysis of the hotspots includes the analysis of the chemical composition of collected particles using the LEAP Harvard Impactor system.

495626.title: Assessing QLCS Mesovortex Potential through Observed and Predicted Line-Relative Kinematics
495626.authors: Michael C. Coniglio, NOAA/OAR/NSSL, Norman, OK; and L. E. Pounds, K. C. Britt, M. C. Brown, P. S. Skinner, and M. Ungar
495626.abstract: Tornadoes and destructive winds are often the byproduct of quasi-linear convective systems (QLCSs), which continue to pose difficult forecast challenges over much of the country (and other parts of the world). Compact areas of rotation along the leading edge of QLCSs 2-20 km in horizontal extent, or mesovortices, are often drivers of the severe weather. They can produce tornadoes or enhance the near-ground “straight-line” flow through dynamic perturbation pressure-induced accelerations. Accurate prediction of mesovortices before they form is important for alerting the public to their hazards as they may evade radars because of their shallowness or they may form quickly, making it difficult to warn for them based solely on detection. Understanding how mesovortices form, and linking their environments to storm characteristics – either those observed or predicted within convection-allowing forecast models – continues to be an important component of QLCS mesovortex prediction. As in many past studies, this work takes a statistical approach to attempt to identify environmental kinematic precursors of QLCSs that tend to produce mesovortices versus those that do not. Beyond this standard method, we exploit a large dataset of QLCSs for which both their environments and detailed internal characteristics (e.g., details of line orientation, motion, etc.) are known to explore the utility of placing the kinematics in a combined line-motion and line-orientation relative framework. As in similar past studies, early results show that mesovortex potential increases as 1) the line-normal wind shear increases, over both shallower and deeper depths (e.g. 0-3 km and ~1-6-km depths) and 2) as low-level storm-relative flow increases. However, another potentially important signal is a large decrease in the magnitude of mid-level (~2-6 km) storm-relative flow ahead of mesovortex-producing QLCS line segments. In addition to increased deep-layer shear and the associated positive influences on QLCS maintenance, the latter may indicate that too much low-to-mid tropospheric storm-relative front-to-rear flow atop the QLCS cold pool (e.g., too much anafrontal flow), is a factor that’s detrimental to mesovortices. Results will be compared to the three-ingredients method (3IM) for forecasting QLCS mesovortices and discussed alongside recent efforts to predict QLCS rotation within the NOAA Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS) and improvements to that system.

495627.title: An Examination of Low-Level Jet–Terrain Interactions on Observed Snowfall Characteristics in Northeastern United States Winter Storms
495627.authors: Kaitlyn R. Jesmonth, Univ. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and S. W. Nesbitt and K. H. Lundstrom
495627.abstract: Predicting the spatial distribution of frozen precipitation in northeastern United States winter storms remains particularly challenging near orographic regions. Interactions between the terrain and low-level synoptic-scale flow can occur within the comma head, contributing to the enhancement and suppression of snowfall rates near complex terrain. Low-level jets (LLJs) can further lead to the development of terrain-forced ascent and descent, gravity waves, and small-scale precipitation structures that modulate surface snowfall characteristics. These precipitation structures also have been observed to produce supercooled water and riming as well as sublimation. This study aims to improve the climatological understanding of LLJs in northeastern United States winter storms from a precipitation processes perspective. Based on ERA5 reanalysis, cyclones are identified over a 30-year period using a northeastern United States winter cyclone track dataset. For each cyclone track, northeastern United States winter storms with a LLJ are isolated using ERA5. LLJs for this study are defined as a wind maximum greater than 15 m s-1 below 700 hPa and decreasing wind speed with height above the maximum. Weak and strong LLJs are classified based on the median of the LLJ wind speed distribution. Preliminary results based on the winter storms sampled during the NASA Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) field campaign show weak LLJ events had a median jet-core level of 900 hPa compared with 800 hPa for the strong LLJ events. Weak LLJs also tended to occur bidirectionally from the northeast and southwest versus strong LLJs which most frequently occurred from the southwest. Ongoing research is examining the moisture transport and microphysical processes contributing to snowfall patterns in regions of northeastern United States complex terrain.

495628.title: Taking Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM) the Final Mile through Actionable Hydrologic Intelligence
495628.authors: Jason C. Elliott, NOAA / National Weather Service, Tuscaloosa, AL
495628.abstract: During a potential flood event, once Flood Impact Assessment is complete, the job is not finished. The final mile requires provision of actionable information from the assessment to decision makers in a variety of forms, from large-scale messaging to targeted, local decision support provided by National Weather Service (NWS) deployed assets. The collaboration between the National Water Center (NWC) and NWS field offices following a Flood Impact Assessment provides crucial, actionable messaging of flood impacts by NWS field offices, supporting the NWS mission to protect life and property and promote the national economy. By providing visualizations and interpretation of flood extent rather than just river stages, NWS FIM services enable emergency managers to make data-driven decisions regarding evacuations, route planning, infrastructure hardening, and resource staging and deployment. This presentation will provide some early examples where hydrointelligence from Flood Impact Assessments was provided to NWS field offices, then utilized in messaging and by decision makers.

495630.title: Assessing Kilometer‑Scale MPAS‑A Performance in Representing the East Pacific ITCZ and Convectively Coupled Equatorial Waves
495630.authors: Fouzia Fahrin, Iowa State University, Ames, IA; and A. O. Gonzalez, F. Judt, and A. Kinsella
495630.abstract: Skillful representation of the East Pacific precipitation has remained a challenge in global coupled models during February-April (FMA), associated with the canonical double intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) bias. While these rainfall biases are most commonly reported in the time-mean, the building blocks of these biases may be related to interactions between the ITCZ and convectively coupled equatorial waves (CCEWs). Recent observational work suggests that CCEWs are strongly modulated by the ITCZ, especially in the southern branch of the East Pacific ITCZ. Despite the strong influence of CCEWs on tropical rainfall and the ITCZ, CCEWs are not well captured by either coupled models or numerical weather prediction models. However, recent studies have demonstrated that high-resolution global models (grid spacing <= 5 km) with resolved convection can improve the representation of CCEWs. This study investigates whether increased horizontal resolution improves the representation of the ITCZ and CCEWs in the Model for Prediction Across Scales-Atmosphere (MPAS-A), with horizontal cell spacings from 120 km global, 30 km global, and 15-3 km variable resolution circular mesh centered on the East Pacific. We run three simulations for FMA of 2004, 2010, and 2017, when there is enough subseasonal variability in ITCZ position. We find that the 3 km simulation shows a significant improvement in the mean and variability compared to its lower-resolution counterpart. However, it still overproduces the mean and underproduces the variability compared to observation. Our results suggest that MPAS-A produces far more double and equatorial bands of the ITCZ and underestimates the rest of the ITCZ bands compared to NASA’s Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG) observations. We find that the 3 km simulations show a weaker spectral signal and a lot less variability in the CCEWs. The 3 km simulation shows higher spectral signals associated with westward propagating systems. A comparison with ERA5 thermodynamical environments reveals that the 3 km simulation features an easterly wind bias and a hemispheric asymmetry response in vertical velocity and humidity. Together, these biases create a background state that is less favorable for eastward‑propagating waves, contributing directly to the muted Kelvin wave signals in the high‑resolution simulation. When a particular strong wave activity is investigated, we find observation shows variation in ITCZ positions as the wave passes, but in the 3 km simulation, the persistent dITCZ condition remains.

495632.title: On the Reliability of using AI Weather Models to Simulate Extreme Events with Ensemble Boosting
495632.authors: Nathan Agarwal, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, CA; and J. Goodnight, S. Po-Chedley, W. Hannah, C. Bonfils, and J. C. Golaz
495632.abstract: High-risk weather and climate events pose significant risks to infrastructure and human health. Blackouts, for example, concurrent with heat waves can more than double the estimated rate of heat-related death (Stone et al. 2023). Earth system models (ESMs) provide one approach for preparing for these events. However, these “extreme” events inherently deviate from mean climate patterns. It can also take centuries (or millennia) of model simulation to sample rare, impactful events, which is computationally expensive. As such, stakeholders must prioritize which scenarios to analyze. Fischer et al. (2023) showed that one way to reduce computational cost is via “ensemble boosting.” The basic approach is to identify extreme events of interest in existing model simulations (e.g., an extreme California heatwave in the 2040s). The model can then re-simulate this event with perturbed initial conditions to generate a distribution of events with return times that vary quite widely (e.g., return times of once per decade to once per millennium). AI weather models simulate extreme events orders of magnitude faster than physics-based models. However, machine learning often struggles with out-of-sample predictions, potentially biasing the representation of extreme events (e.g., Zhang et al., 2026). Here we compare the distribution of heatwaves using several AI-based weather models across multiple initialization strategies (c.f., Figure 1) with the E3SM climate model (Golaz et al., 2022). This comparison will help to understand whether AI can help us to ensure infrastructure robustness by efficiently simulating arbitrary 1-in-N year extreme events. Figure 1. California average temperature for a September 2022 heatwave event in which the California electricity grid experienced unprecedented demand from ERA5 (black dotted line) and an AI model (SFNO; Bonev et al., 2023) using different seeds (blue lines). The blue shading shows the 10-90% confidence range. Red shows a separate ensemble based on the SFNO member with the largest amplitude (with Bred-Vector initial condition perturbations to generate spread). In this work we will compare the evolution and spread of simulated extremes to the physics-based E3SM model. 495633.title: (Invited Presentation) Advancing ARM Capabilities to Support Integrated Observation-Model Frameworks
495633.authors: Jennifer M. Comstock, PNNL, RICHLAND, WA; Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA; and Y. Zhang, H. Wang, Y. Feng, W. I. Gustafson Jr., S. Xie, L. K. Berg, and J. H. Mather
495633.abstract: The mission of the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) User Facility is to provide comprehensive measurements of cloud, aerosol, and precipitation to improve understanding of atmospheric processes and their representation in earth system models (ESMs). ARM measurements, high-resolution modeling, and AI informed Value-Added Products (VAPs) and tools support DOE’s focus on “water for energy” topics that impact the nation’s energy security. Benchmark cases, instrument simulators, and the Large-Eddy Simulation ARM Symbiotic Simulation and Observation (LASSO) workflow provides observation-modeling data bundles over ARM sites for evaluation of the DOE Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) and other ESMs. ARM recently held a workshop to better align ARM capabilities with DOE’s new objectives, identifying areas where ARM can play a role in related topics such as land-atmosphere interactions, drought, wildfires, and severe weather-related cloud microphysics that impact energy infrastructure. In addition, ARM is engaging with modeling communities through a model advisory committee, programmatic breakout sessions, and listening sessions to identify key observation-model integration techniques and frameworks to accelerate progress. Through these interactions, ARM is exploring the potential use of data assimilation and Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) frameworks to improve simulations, evaluate observational strategies, and guide field-campaign design by leveraging ARM’s long-term observations, focused field campaign data, and external data such as satellite and surface observational networks. ARM is also exploring modeling tools that can effectively connect its observations to Earth system model development. Our goal for this presentation is to highlight recent advancements in harmonizing and characterizing ARM datasets using data analytics and AI approaches to advance model evaluation methodologies and identify opportunities for the broader community to provide input and help formulate plans for applying observation and assimilation systems to advance ARM and DOE objectives.

495634.title: Analyzing the Relationship Between Updraft Tilt, System Structure, and the Shear/Cold Pool Balance in Quasi-Linear Convective Systems
495634.authors: Kate Olivia Stapleton, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and M. Van Den Broeke and C. R. Homeyer
495634.abstract: Quasi-linear convective systems (QLCSs) present a significant hazard to the public because they occur year-round, can persist for many hours, sometimes overnight, and cover large geographic regions. QLCS hazards are often closely associated with mesovortices, but these hazards are difficult to forecast because the precursors to mesovortex formation are not fully understood. Current mesovortex forecasting relies on the three-ingredients method, which includes defining the regime of the updraft-downdraft convergence zone (UDCZ). The UDCZ regime is related to the balance between vertical wind shear and cold pool strength. This low-level feature is related to the strength and orientation of updrafts within QLCSs as well as the overall QLCS structure. Recent literature has focused on connecting updrafts to mesovortex genesis in idealized models; however, neither the QLCS updrafts nor the QLCS system structure have been examined in an observational framework. This observational study utilized a subset of QLCSs from 2020 to 2024 that were associated with at least one tornado report. For each QLCS, we calculated the tilt of individual core updrafts, calculated the tilt of the QLCS system, and identified the regime of the UDCZ. Core updrafts were identified by their associated differential reflectivity (ZDR) columns, and the system was represented by the leading edge 35 dBZ contour. We hypothesize that a balanced UDCZ is associated with a deeper, upright QLCS system due to offsetting interactions between the cold pool and low-level shear. We expect the UDCZ regime will have little impact on QLCS core updrafts due to their short-lived, shallow nature. Establishing a connection between updraft tilt, system tilt, and UDCZ regime will enhance our conceptual model of QLCSs by connecting low-level and mid-level storm structures. Additionally, our study provides additional context for the three-ingredients method. National Weather Service meteorologists can apply this information when observing storm structure and anticipating mesovortex behavior.

495637.title: Observed and Simulated VOC Abundance and Reactivity during the NASA ASIA-AQ 2024 Campaign
495637.authors: Behrooz Roozitalab, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and E. C. Apel, L. K. Emmons, C. Cho, R. S. Hornbrook, B. Gaubert, A. Hills, D. Jeong, D. S. Jo, B. Barletta, D. R. Blake, N. Blake, S. Meinardi, I. Simpson, and J. Crawford
495637.abstract: The NASA funded ASIA-AQ (Airborne and Satellite Investigation of Asian Air Quality) campaign was an international cooperative field study that flew the heavily instrumented NASA DC-8 aircraft over multiple Asian countries, including the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand, and Taiwan, during February and March 2024. Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were measured in these four regions using a suite of state-of-the-art in-situ instruments such as the NSF NCAR Trace Organic Gas Analyzer equipped with a high-resolution time-of-flight mass spectrometer (TOGA-TOF) and the UC Irvine Whole Air Sampler (WAS). In this presentation, we present our findings on non-methane VOC (NMVOC) abundance, calculated OH reactivity (OHR), and major contributing species in each deployment location. Overall, Thailand experienced the highest NMVOC abundance, primarily due to being affected by biomass burning (BB) emissions evidenced by high mixing ratios of specific BB tracers (e.g., acetonitrile). On the other hand, NMVOC abundance was lowest in South Korea, in part due to negligible biogenic emissions during its cold season. Considering VOC compound classes, alcohols were the largest contributor to the total NMVOC abundance in all the regions except in South Korea where alkanes were the most abundant. Additionally, we compare these findings against the MUSICAv0 (Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols version 0) modeling results. Our results suggest that MUSICAv0 generally reproduced the total OHR, although notable differences remained with model–measurement discrepancies observed for individual compounds and chemical classes in certain regions. The ASIA-AQ campaign results provide critical chemical insights to help identify the most efficient mitigation strategies for improving air quality in the regions studied.

495642.title: Risk Analysis and Solutions Innovators (RASI): Co-Developed Environmental Risk Products for Infrastructure and Community Resilience Across Six Work Groups
495642.authors: Cynthia Rosenzweig, GISS, New York, NY; and N. Pelaccio
495642.abstract: The Risk Analysis and Solutions Innovators (RASI) project, part of NASA's Energy and Infrastructure program within Earth Action, develops and delivers environmental risk information to support infrastructure and community resilience under a range of current and projected weather conditions. Its products are served to 14 NASA Centers and facilities and State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT) stakeholders in the surrounding regions, primarily through the NASA POWER Data Access Viewer, with an active effort to scale from Center-adjacent regions to CONUS. This presentation summarizes the scientific approach and stakeholder-facing results of RASI's six Work Groups. The Energy and Infrastructure Work Group develops parameters and risk metrics for utilities, building management, and engineering applications, including ASHRAE-based thermal zone projections, dewpoint and wet-bulb temperature, Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), and mild-day counts, with ongoing work on daily-to-hourly morphing. A CONUS-scale thermal zone assessment comparing 2015–2035 and 2065–2085 periods under SSP3 identifies large contiguous areas of one- and two-zone warming shifts with direct implications for building design standards. Stakeholders include Con Edison, private-sector architecture and engineering firms, and the National Association of State Energy Officials. The Extreme Weather Events Work Group produces temperature and precipitation extremes indices from NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, downscaled daily maximum temperatures spanning global warming levels from +0.61 to +4.0 °C across 11 CMIP6 models and four reanalyses (MERRA-2, ERA5, JRA-3Q, GMFD), and flooding-potential indicators derived from root-zone soil moisture exceedances. Compound-event risk portfolios are being developed for Con Edison, which serves 3.6 million customers in the New York metropolitan region, using the DBSCAN clustering algorithm to identify sequential hazards such as a windstorm followed by a heatwave, supporting power grid resilience decisions. The Wildfires and Air Quality Work Group characterizes fuel loading, active burning, and downwind air quality effects in NASA Center regions, with current focus on the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles. Landsat-derived ember risk mapping identifies vegetation most likely to generate dangerous flying embers, and low-cost sensor networks are being used to monitor and forecast smoke in areas lacking regulatory monitoring, particularly post-fire. Stakeholders include county emergency management, CalFire, and CalOES. The Flooding Events and Water Resources Work Groups address sea level change, coastal inundation mapping leveraging the NASA Sea Level Change Team, evapotranspiration-based water demand, and surface flooding. Following Hurricane Zeta, the Water Resources Work Group developed a new satellite-based Normalized Difference Light Index from VIIRS Day/Night Band imagery to map neighborhood-scale power loss and recovery, producing a combined outage-and-flood risk assessment for Stennis Space Center and Michoud Assembly Facility that was validated through interviews with county emergency management, utility, and Center personnel. In New York City, RASI is working with Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA), co-developing storm surge modeling projects to inform and prioritize resilience for transportation infrastructure. The HydroSCS (Hydrometeorology Surface Component Suite) Work Group addresses a foundational data gap: the Princeton Global Meteorological Forcing Dataset baseline underlying NEX-GDDP and similar products has known biases, gaps, and no active maintenance. HydroSCS integrates MERRA-2 near-surface meteorology, GPM IMERG merged precipitation, and CERES downwelling shortwave and longwave radiation into a 5-km, hourly, globally complete forcing dataset. Version 2 is complete and validation and intercomparison are underway, with a revised NEX-GDDP CONUS prototype product planned. Across these activities, RASI's central methodological commitment is co-development: risk metrics are defined with the stakeholders who will act on them, delivered through an operational NASA service rather than a project website, and revised as user requirements evolve. We discuss evidence of adoption, including use of RASI risk assessments in NASA Center facilities and infrastructure planning and infusion of RASI methods into the HEAT28 urban extreme heat activity, and identify open challenges in scaling co-developed products beyond their originating communities.

495643.title: Interactions between Non-Gaussian Artefacts and Systematic Model Biases for Maritime All-sky Infrared Radiance Data Assimilation
495643.authors: Dominic Bentley, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and M. Y. Chan
495643.abstract: Infrared (IR) satellite observations provide continuous, high-resolution coverage over the observationally sparse maritime regions, making them an important source of information for maritime numerical weather prediction (NWP). Previous studies have shown that assimilating all-sky IR radiances improves the analyses of cloud structure, thermodynamic fields, and convection over maritime regions. Strategies to amplify the benefits of all-sky IR data assimilation (DA) will therefore contribute towards improving operational maritime NWP. A challenge with all-sky IR DA is that the nonlinear relationship clouds and humidity violate the linear assumptions of current data assimilation (DA) methods. We demonstrated this in our earlier work over the equatorial Indian Ocean with perfect model ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) experiments. In that maritime DA study, those assumption violations result in analyzed clouds with unphysically low relative humidities. Subsequent model integration vaporizes these clouds. This analyze-then-vaporize mechanism caused cold temperature biases to accumulate over successive DA cycles. Eventually, our all-sky IR DA setup produced worse performance than not doing any DA (i.e., all-sky IR DA failure). Eliminating the analysis increments to the hydrometeor mixing ratios mitigated this all-sky IR DA failure mode. However, it is unclear whether this mechanism leads to all-sky IR DA failure under real-world conditions because model representation biases may offset that mechanism. Furthermore, few real data all-sky IR DA studies have performed the necessary number of cycles for this mechanism to manifest strongly (requires at least 24 hourly DA cycles), especially over maritime regions. A follow-up real data all-sky IR DA study focused on this analyze-then-vaporize mechanism is therefore necessary. This presentation uses real-data all-sky IR maritime DA experiments to explore the interaction between (i) the analyze-then-vaporize mechanism, (ii) model representation biases associated with clouds, and (iii) initial condition biases. Our study domain is the equatorial Indian Ocean. Preliminary results suggest that the mechanism is present, although its damaging cumulative temperature biasing effect is masked by either model representation biases and/or initial condition biases. More work to untangle this web of biases is underway. Our study therefore provides new insight into how nonlinear cloud-humidity relationships interact with representation and initial condition biases during maritime DA, and will likely lead to approaches to improve real-world maritime DA performance.

495651.title: Building Quality Assurance Procedures for a New Mesonet System in the Green Mountain State
495651.authors: Nicholas Preschel, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT; and G. Causey and S. Cheung
495651.abstract: The Vermont Mesonet deployed its first prototype station in May 2026, with plans to expand to 22 stations providing county-level coverage across the state. The prototype station, located in Lyndonville, Vermont, measures a suite of meteorological variables, generating a large volume of observational data. Vermont’s complex topography contributes to substantial climatological variability over relatively short distances, presenting challenges for development of an effective quality assurance (QA) process. Robust QA procedures are essential for ensuring the reliability of meteorological observations. Mesonet operators typically employ a series of automated tests to identify potentially erroneous records, followed by manual verification or dismissal of flagged records. This study evaluates climatology based range tests as one component of a broader semi-automated QA framework for the Vermont Mesonet. Surface air temperature range test methods based on deviations from central tendencies of nearest neighbor climatology from the Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) and statewide climatology were compared at multiple temporal scales. Methods were applied to archived Summit to Shore (S2S) observations, a snow monitoring network operated by the University of Vermont with similar instrumentation as the Vermont Mesonet and provides a higher spatial resolution. The range tests were evaluated as part of a quality assurance pipeline incorporating sensor absolute value, logical, temporal, and spatial tests to determine the function and value of semi-automated climatology based quality assurance range tests in Vermont. Resulting flags were manually validated or dismissed by comparison to other phenomena recorded at the same station and recorded values from neighboring stations.

495652.title: Forecasting the Critical Alert, Not Just the Degree Day: Probabilistic Evaluation of Natural Gas Pipeline Cold Weather Alerts
495652.authors: Jan F. Dutton, Prescient Weather Ltd, State College, PA; and C. B. Bohon, R. James, and J. Ross
495652.abstract: Probabilistic weather forecasts for energy applications are commonly verified against physical variables such as degree days, wind speed, or load. Natural gas markets also respond to operational decisions made under uncertainty. When an interstate pipeline issues a Cold Weather Alert, Operational Flow Order, or related critical notice, it can change balancing requirements and may impose financial penalties on shippers. These dated public notices provide an operational verification target that can be matched directly against the available forecasts. This study evaluates whether ensemble heating-degree-day forecasts can estimate the probability and lead time for cold-related pipeline actions. Forecasts from the ECMWF, GEFS, AIFS, and WxNext2 are archived in the World Climate Service (WCS) Point-in-Time Weather Forecast API from 2017 to the present. Their heating degree day (HDD) forecasts are using in this analysis. Heating degree days are evaluated with a 15-day lead time for United States ISO and RTO areas and for regional temperature market aggregates, using natural gas consumption and population weighting. Predictors include the ensemble mean and the share of members exceeding selected heating degree-day or departure-from-normal thresholds, allowing the ensemble spread to enter the probability estimate directly. The target is constructed from Federal Energy Regulatory Commission-required pipeline postings, classified as cold-related actions and assigned to the stated valid gas day when available. The target record spans the 2024 to 2025 and 2025 to 2026 heating seasons. The forecast evaluation will report: Alert probability as a function of ensemble exceedance share, evaluated by pipeline and forecast lead time. Out-of-sample reliability and Brier skill score relative to a base rate climatological reference, distinguishing probability calibration from discrimination. Differences across forecast systems, weighting methods, and 00Z and 12Z initialization cycles, including whether natural gas consumption weighting provides different information from population weighting. Operator-specific differences in forecastability, rather than relying only on a pooled skill estimate across pipelines. This framework extends forecast verification from the weather variable to an operational decision relevant to natural gas trading. For WCS users, the evaluation is designed to translate ensemble agreement into a pipeline-specific alert probability and identify the forecast horizon over which that probability remains informative. The resulting metrics would provide a measurable basis for evaluating when probabilistic cold forecasts may add context to scheduling, balancing, and regional risk analysis. The study does not assume that notices are caused solely by weather, nor does it estimate pipeline constraints, prices, or trading outcomes. The two-season target record limits the precision of operator-specific calibration and will be considered when interpreting reliability and skill.

495654.title: Low-Temperature Dual-Balance Electrodynamic Trap for Single-Particle Observation of Silver-Iodide Immersion Freezing, Ice Growth, Aggregation, and Sublimation
495654.authors: Victor Oyebamiji Ojo, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and C. Nairy, D. J. Delene, and H. B. Chelmo
495654.abstract: Silver iodide (AgI) is the most widely used aerosol in glaciogenic cloud seeding, yet the particle-scale behavior of the ice it nucleates is rarely observed directly. For instance, how an individual AgI-seeded droplet freezes, and how the resulting crystal grows, aggregates, or sublimates under controlled conditions is difficult to observe directly and such information is needed by computational researchers for the fundamental understanding of cloud formation. Field campaigns such as SNOWIE show that AgI seeding can initiate ice, but linking seeding outcomes to single-particle microphysics requires laboratory methods that isolate one seeded particle and follow it continuously. In this study, we use a low-temperature dual-balance electrodynamic trap (LT-DBET). Results establish the LT-DBET as a platform on which full seeded ice life cycle, including AgI immersion freezing, depositional growth, aggregation, and sublimation, can be observed on individual particles with simultaneous size, morphology, and microenvironment information. The LT-DBET reaches −16 °C, levitates individual aqueous droplets containing NaCl and suspended AgI, freezes them by immersion nucleation near −4.6 °C, and images the resulting ice by bright-field microscopy while logging temperature, relative humidity (RH), and balancing voltage. Sizes and shape descriptors are extracted in ImageJ/Fiji, and the humidity experienced by the particle is reconstructed from the humidified-flow supply rather than read from the bulk probe. Three single-particle experiments capture the mass gain or loss process relevant to seeded ice. (i) Deposition: an AgI+NaCl solution droplet freezing to produce a monomer at −5.5 to −6.2 °C, growing from 46.9 to 52.5 µm in 188 s at +0.012 µm s−1 mean radial rate, remaining spheroid with aspect ratio 1.14–1.19; solidity ~0.94. Mass calculation accounting for aspect ratio and porosity ran 12–14% below the values obtained with a sphere shape assumed. (ii) Aggregation: a single microdroplet cooling from 24 to −9 °C freezes near −4.6 °C and, at −7 °C, undergoes an aggregation event upon collision with another ice-monomer introduced into the trap with its aerodynamic diameter increasing from 54 to 83 µm and aspect ratio increasing from 1.03 to 1.84, and solidity reducing from 0.998 to 0.894. This is a sharp change in size and irregularity that distinguishes aggregation from gradual vapor growth and produces an elongated, porous aggregate. (iii) Sublimation: a frozen particle at −13.5 °C under low humidified flow sublimates with an approximately 33% reduction in diameter from 56.7 to 37.9 µm at rates up to −1.7 µm s−1 with its outline growing less regular as ice is removed. In all three cases, the probe 5 cm above the trap reads approximately 24–55% RH over ice, which is apparent sub-saturation and is inconsistent with the two growth cases. To resolve this inconsistency, we show that the humidity at the particle differs systematically from the probe reading, and we determine it quantitatively by anchoring the delivered vapor to a measured wet-flow fraction (WFF) calibration instead of the RH probe reading. At WFF settings as high as 20%, the delivered gas is estimated to be supersaturated with respect to ice with a frost point of +2.7 °C and exceeds the probe-implied vapor content ~3.7-fold, which brings the environment at the particle to ice saturation and drives slow deposition. At WFF settings as low as 5% the delivered vapor lies below ice saturation and the particle sublimates in a sub-saturated environment with ~24% RHice. A single diffusional-growth model, evaluated with these reconstructed humidities, reproduces the measured rates in all three cases, including the sign reversal between growth from ~0 to +0.06 µm s−1 and sublimation from −0.7 to −1.0 µm s−1. The sublimation experiment is a decisive control as the same framework that raises the humidity to ice saturation at high WFF correctly leaves it sub-saturated at low WFF, demonstrating that the reconstruction accurately predicts the ice crystal behavior. A coupled surface-energy balance further yields a particle surface temperature offset of ~2 °C with it being warmer than ambient during deposition, cooler during sublimation as it follows the direction of latent-heat exchange. The observed shapes reflect the immersion-freezing pathway characteristic of AgI seeding. Freezing initiates at the AgI nucleus in the droplet, so the ice shell develops asymmetrically, and the crystalographic orientation of the nucleus relative to the droplet surface likely influences the emerging shape. This links the compact monomers and irregular aggregates imaged here directly to the nucleation event itself and provides a controlled laboratory measurement for how a seeding aerosol’s placement within a droplet shapes the ice it produces, which is a factor rarely accessible in field observations. The irregular geometries produced by deposition, aggregation, and sublimation represent those commonly observed in cloud and seeding models. Constraining them at the single-particle level offers a controlled complement to seeding field campaigns such as SNOWIE and SNOWSCAPE as well as computational modeling. Ongoing work targets repeatable, guided observations of aggregation in real time.

495658.title: A Topological Approach to Tropical Cyclone Eye Detection in Synthetic Passive Microwave Imagery
495658.authors: Kristina Moen, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and T. Tsukada, E. J. King, K. Haynes, K. D. Musgrave, L. Ver Hoef, and I. Ebert-Uphoff
495658.abstract: The formation of a tropical cyclone (TC) eye marks an important transition in storm development and intensification, yet the early detection of eye formation remains challenging. Visible and infrared imagery provide near-continuous storm monitoring, but early eye formation is often obscured by cirrus clouds. Passive microwave observations can reveal a storm’s internal convective structure beneath cirrus clouds, but their utility for early eye detection is limited by infrequent satellite overpasses. Moreover, existing methods for early eye detection often rely on subjective interpretation. Recently developed synthetic passive microwave imagery (SPMI), derived from visible and infrared imagery, provides estimated passive microwave observations every 10 minutes. To harness the temporal frequency and internal-structure observations of SPMI, we develop a topology-based method to objectively detect TC eyes in SPMI and identify the timing of TC eye formation. This is the first topology-based method for identifying TC eye formation from SPMI. At high-frequency passive microwave channels (e.g., 89 GHz), a TC eye typically appears as a relatively warm brightness temperature region surrounded by a colder eyewall, primarily caused by ice scattering. This distinctive ring-shaped pattern makes passive microwave imagery well-suited for Topological Data Analysis (TDA), which detects loop-like structures in noisy data using the mathematical framework of persistent homology. The approach taken here applies TDA to identify the most persistent loops throughout a storm’s lifetime. Persistence reflects the temperature contrast between the enclosing eyewall and eye interior, providing a physically interpretable and quantitative measure of eye development. A storm-specific persistence threshold is used to identify the presence of an eye, while a persistence time series tracks eye formation and development. Preliminary results of this method will be presented through representative case studies and comparisons with existing TC eye detection methods. This work demonstrates the potential for persistent topological features extracted from SPMI to provide physically interpretable information about TC structure, objectively identify eye formation, and improve the utility of SPMI for real-time monitoring of storm evolution.

495659.title: Real-Time Global Kilometer-Scale MPAS Forecasts: Computational and End-to-End Workflow Aspects of a New Frontier in NWP
495659.authors: Falko Judt, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and C. Schwartz, B. Skamarock, R. Rios-Berrios, R. Johnson, M. Duda, and R. A. Sobash
495659.abstract: Over 35 days in April and May 2025, the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) produced experimental, daily, real-time 60-h forecasts with the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) on a mesh with 3-km horizontal cell spacing over the entire globe. Forecast products were postprocessed and uploaded to a public webpage quickly enough to be used in daily forecasting activities. This end-to-end demonstration — from global 3-km model execution, through postprocessing, to publishing graphical products — represented the first real-time public dissemination of global, kilometer-scale NWP forecasts. A few months later, in September and October 2025, NSF NCAR executed a second demonstration, again with MPAS, this time at 3.75-km cell spacing globally and extended to 120-h lead time, with products once more publicly available. Sustaining a kilometer-scale global forecast on a hard daily deadline is as much a computing and data-handling problem as a modeling one, and this presentation focuses on that side of the effort: resource requirements and scaling behavior of MPAS at 3- and 3.75-km global meshes, wall-clock-to-deadline constraints, I/O volumes and output strategy, the postprocessing and graphics pipeline, and the automation needed to run the whole chain reliably without human intervention. We describe where the bottlenecks actually appeared, which were not always where we expected, and what had to be traded away to hit the delivery window. We then address the scientific payoff that justifies the cost. The 3.75-km experiment was designed in part to assess the added value of kilometer-scale resolution for tropical cyclones and other tropical phenomena. Despite being untuned and run in its default configuration, 3.75-km MPAS performed comparably to the operational GFS in TC track prediction while reducing intensity errors by roughly 25% in the 1–4-day range. Forecast examples of high-impact weather events worldwide and additional objective verification statistics will also be presented. We close with prospects and challenges for future real-time global kilometer-scale NWP, including hardware and software directions that would make such forecasts routine rather than experimental, and what this class of workload implies for the community's HPC planning.

495663.title: The AMS Education Program in 2027
495663.authors: Aaron Price, Ph.D., American Meteorological Society, Chicago, IL
495663.abstract: 2026 was a year of significant change for the AMS Education program. We released our first open-access undergraduate textbook, Introduction to Ocean Sciences, 6th Edition, and began work updating our meteorology textbook. We also pilot tested three MOOCs as part of our DataStreme program, free online courses on weather, water, and climate designed to extend our K-12 program to learners everywhere. In addition, we launched three research project collaborations with educational technology organizations and science museums. 2027 will build on this progress by officially launching the MOOCs to the public, begin sharing results from the research projects, and, we hope, release our meteorology textbook under an open-access license as well. This presentation will describe these projects in more detail, report on key performance indicators, and outline near-term plans for the AMS Education program.

495664.title: Sharing Views of Clouds and Weather Using Social Media
495664.authors: Bruce Albrecht, Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science, Miami, FL
495664.abstract: While scientists have long recognized the vital role clouds play in weather and climate, many people simply look up to enjoy their beauty and the special moments they create, like rainbows. Spotting a rainbow is always a thrill, we can’t help but call out to friends and family to share the excitement. Rainbows and sunsets often become shared experiences that bring people together, creating cherished memories and a sense of wonder. Taking cloud photos is more popular than ever, thanks to the convenience of smartphones with high-quality cameras. These snapshots, easily uploaded to social media, let people share their favorite cloud moments with friends and fellow enthusiasts on platforms like Facebook and Instagram. The popularity of sharing cloud photos is clear in the huge membership numbers of cloud-themed online groups. For instance, Facebook’s The Cloud Appreciation Society group boasts an impressive 730,000 members and the Florida Cloud Appreciation Society group includes 14,000 members. These numbers are remarkable, especially when compared to many other interest-based organizations on social media and show just how universal the fascination with clouds truly is. My journey into sharing cloud photos on social media began in the early 2000s. I often observed students walking across campus completely absorbed in their phones, rarely glancing up at the sky above them. Witnessing this made me reflect on how technology, while connecting us in many ways, sometimes draws our attention away from the natural beauty right above us. This realization sparked an idea: what if we could use the very devices that distract us to help people rediscover the sky? With this vision I developed the SeeMyClouds app (SeeMyClouds.net) that offers a unique social-media platform designed for weather and cloud enthusiasts, students, educators, and photographers. Unlike general photo-sharing apps, SeeMyClouds features cloud classification tags, allowing users to label the cloud types in their photos. You can join specialized interest groups and connect with a vibrant community passionate about atmospheric phenomena. The app welcomes all kinds of cloud photos, as well as images of atmospheric optical effects like sunsets, rainbows, and halos. My goal is to use SeeMyClouds to not only engage cloud and weather enthusiasts but engage a broader community into the wonders of the atmosphere. I hope SeeMyClouds inspires people to look up, capture the beauty above, and reconnect with nature—one cloud photo at a time

495665.title: AI - LSTM-Based Prediction of Mars Planetary Boundary Layer Height from the Mars Climate Database with Calibrated Uncertainty
495665.authors: James T. Bible, Bowie State University, Bowie, MD; NASA, Bowie, MD; and M. K. Sarker
495665.abstract: Accurate estimation of the Martian planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) underpins our understanding of near-surface mixing, dust-lifting processes, and environmental hazards relevant to both Mars science and mission operations. Progress in this area has been limited by two compounding factors: the scarcity of direct atmospheric observations on Mars, and the complex, nonlinear variation of boundary-layer dynamics with local time, season, and location — factors that limit the reliability of simple empirical or physics-based estimators. Prior work has emphasized the physical complexity of the Martian boundary layer through modeling and large-eddy simulation, but direct deep-learning prediction of PBLH from modeled atmospheric fields remains comparatively underexplored. To address this gap, we develop and evaluate an LSTM-based sequence model trained on short temporal windows of simulated atmospheric data from the Mars Climate Database (MCD v6.1), treating PBLH prediction as a controlled sequence-to-one regression task. Model inputs used a compact 80-feature representation (temperature, zonal wind, and meridional wind across 26 altitude levels, plus surface temperature and pressure) drawn from four consecutive time steps. All experiments used a time-blocked train/validation/test split — rather than random partitioning — with a protected holdout region around solar longitude 90°–105° to prevent seasonal leakage, and were repeated across 10 random seeds for reproducibility. We first compared a 64-hidden-unit LSTM baseline against three simple reference predictors: a global-average baseline, a similar-case average baseline, and a previous-value baseline. The LSTM (RMSE = 1335.1 m, R² = 0.934) dramatically outperformed all three (RMSE = 5612–6867 m, negative R²), confirming that Mars PBLH contains learnable temporal structure well beyond what simple averaging or short-memory rules can capture. We then systematically varied model capacity from 4 to 2048 hidden units while holding all other settings fixed. Mean RMSE decreased monotonically from 1679.7 m at 4 units to a minimum of 876.1 m at 1536 units (R² = 0.972), a 34.4% reduction relative to the 64-unit baseline. The 2048-unit model showed no further improvement (881.4 m), indicating a clear diminishing-returns region near 1536 hidden units, with training time also increasing sharply beyond that point (33.7 s vs. ~17–24 s for smaller models). This capacity-scaling trend proved remarkably consistent across temporal regimes. Day and night RMSE tracked closely at every model size (735.6 m vs. 728.7 m for the 1536-unit model), as did three representative Mars-month bins and two broad seasonal groupings (733.3 m for northern summer/southern winter vs. 730.9 m for the opposite season), indicating the learned representation generalizes across diurnal and seasonal atmospheric structure rather than overfitting to one regime. Feature-influence analysis (via one-feature-at-a-time scrambling) revealed that larger models rely more selectively on the most informative atmospheric inputs: the top 20% of input features accounted for 51.9% of measured influence in the 64-unit baseline, rising to 73.6% for the 1536-unit model and 75.6% for the 2048-unit model. This suggests that capacity scaling sharpens the model's implicit feature selection rather than simply spreading predictive weight uniformly. Finally, we added post-hoc conformal calibration to quantify predictive uncertainty independent of point-accuracy model selection. For the 1536-unit model, 90% prediction intervals achieved 94.8% empirical coverage with a mean width of 3247.9 m — substantially narrower than the 64-unit baseline's 5352.3 m interval at comparable coverage (96.1%), showing that higher-capacity models yield both more accurate and more precise calibrated forecasts. Positioned against prior machine-learning PBLH studies — which are exclusively Earth-focused and use lidar, radiosonde, or reanalysis data (e.g., DNN-based estimation with MAE ≈ 0.30–0.56 km from surface meteorology; multi-sensor remote-sensing fusion) — this work represents, to our knowledge, one of the first systematic deep-learning evaluations of Mars PBLH prediction from a climate-database source, with an explicit focus on reproducibility, capacity scaling, and calibrated uncertainty. Taken together, these results show that a relatively simple recurrent architecture can extract meaningful predictive structure from short sequences of modeled Martian atmospheric states, that this skill scales predictably with model capacity up to a clear saturation point, and that the resulting predictions can be paired with well-calibrated, interpretable uncertainty estimates. Because the study is intentionally MCD-based, it provides a controlled and reproducible foundation for future work extending to broader Mars atmospheric datasets, alternative sequence architectures, and physically informed uncertainty-aware boundary-layer prediction — directly relevant to Mars mission planning, dust-hazard assessment, and atmospheric science more broadly.

495666.title: Where the Land Meets the Sky: A First-Year Experience Course for Atmospheric and Geographic Science Students
495666.authors: Elizabeth H. Marold, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. Na-Yemeh, S. Bolin-Dills, and S. Fathollahifard
495666.abstract: Many universities have adopted orientation-style classes called First-Year Experience (FYE) or First-Year Seminar (FYS). These classes aid in socializing first-year students into the college community and aim to increase student retention rates. Many such classes are designed to help students with challenges related to the transition from high school to college and with the transition from living with parents by introducing students to resources at their new college campus and providing students guidelines for student success. At the University of Oklahoma (OU), all first-year students are required to take a FYE course as part of their General Education requirement. Rather than taking a general FYE course, OU College of Geographic and Atmospheric Sciences (AGS) incoming students are enrolled in a FYE course created for students entering the School of Meteorology, the School of Geography and Environmental Sustainability, and the School of Aviation, with the exception of Honor Students who take FYE with the Honors College. The AGS FYE is restricted to college majors, with a few exceptions, such as transfer students who cannot fit another FYE into their schedule. If a student transferring into AGS from 2YC has not completed the general education FYE requirement, they will be required to take this course alongside traditional FY students. The course also includes both traditional (typically 18-24 years old, full-time students who started college right after high school) and non-traditional students (such as returning learners, part-time students, and students older than 24). The AGS FYE course entitled, “Where the Land Meets the Sky,” not only introduces students to university-wide resources and student expectations, but it also introduces students to college-specific resources, expectations, and insight from current students and instructors in the college and professionals in the field. This class aids in preparing students for success at the university level and at the college level. In this presentation, we provide instructor-reflections of this AGS-tailored FYE class. We will explore key literature related to student socialization and identity as well as related research on FYE classes for 2YCs and 4YCs. After reviewing “Where the Land Meets the Sky” course objectives, we ask: What do AGS students need out of an FYE class?

495667.title: Hot-Wire Probe Measurements in Pyroconvection: Preliminary Results from the NASA-INSPYRE Field Campaign.
495667.authors: Shane Richard Martrich, Univ. of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and S. Woods, B. Weinzierl, K. Blohm, D. A. Peterson, N. P. Lareau, and J. R. French
495667.abstract: Pyroconvective clouds provide an extreme environment for airborne microphysical measurements, combining rapidly evolving liquid- and ice-phase hydrometeors with strong vertical motions and substantial concentrations of wildfire smoke and pyrometeors. Reliable measurements of condensed water mass are necessary to characterize the microphysical evolution from pyrocumulus (pyroCu) to pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) and to place these observations within the broader objectives of the NASA INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE; Peterson et al., 2024). The Nevzorov hot-wire probe directly measures liquid water content (LWC) and total water content (TWC), from which ice water content can be derived, but its performance depends on particle size, phase, concentration, and environmental conditions. INSPYRE provides a unique opportunity to evaluate both the established 8 mm deep-cone TWC Nevzorov sensor and the recently developed 12 mm deep-cone TWC sensor, which has previously been characterized primarily under controlled icing conditions (Lucke et al., 2022). This study presents preliminary analyses of Nevzorov measurements collected during NASA INSPYRE to characterize instrument performance in smoke-laden pyroconvective clouds. Measurements of condensed water from the 8 and 12 mm sensor heads are compared to evaluate relative performance of the two sensors and identify conditions where their responses diverge. Particular emphasis is placed on variations in sensor response and behavior across primarily mixed-phase and glaciated conditions within pyroconvective clouds. Additionally, independent in situ cloud-probe measurements are used to provide context for observed differences between the Nevzorov sensors. Measurements from the RadFIRE-16 pilot campaign (Kingsmill et al., 2023) provide an independent 8 mm Nevzorov comparison in a previously sampled pyroconvective environment. These analyses aim to improve the interpretation of Nevzorov measurements in pyroconvection, assess the performance of the new 12 mm configuration under atmospheric conditions, and establish confidence in condensed-water mass observations used to investigate the pyroCu-to-pyroCb microphysical evolution. Peterson, D., Lareau, N., & Kalashnikova, O. (2024, September 30). INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE): White paper for NASA Earth Venture Suborbital-4 (EVS-4). NASA Earth Science Project Office. Lucke, J., Jurkat-Witschas, T., Heller, R., Hahn, V., Hamman, M., Breitfuss, W., Bora, V. R., Moser, M., & Voigt, C. (2022). Icing wind tunnel measurements of supercooled large droplets using the 12 mm total water content cone of the Nevzorov probe. Atmospheric Measurement Techniques, 15, 7375–7394. doi:10.5194/amt-15-7375-2022. Kingsmill, D. E., French, J. R., & Lareau, N. P. (2023). In situ microphysics observations of intense pyroconvection from a large wildfire. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, 23, 1–21. doi:10.5194/acp-23-1-2023.

495670.title: Observations of Photochemical Snowpack Reactive Bromine Chemistry and Near-Surface Ozone Depletion in the Arctic Boundary Layer
495670.authors: Kerri A Pratt, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI; and I. Antczak, D. Jeong, J. D. Fuentes, P. Peterson, P. B. Shepson, S. M. Lance, and W. R. Simpson
495670.abstract: During springtime, the near-surface atmosphere in the Arctic is often depleted in ozone, due to a multiphase catalytic reaction cycle known as the bromine explosion cycle. Molecular bromine (Br2) is produced from photochemical condensed-phase and multiphase reactions in the surface snowpack and aerosols. Photolysis of Br2 produces bromine atoms that react with ozone to produce bromine monoxide (BrO), which go on to react with HO2 or NO2 to produce products that react with bromide-containing surfaces to produce Br2. The CHACHA (CHemistry in the Arctic: Clouds, Halogens, and Aerosols) field campaign was conducted during Feb. – Apr. 2022 aboard the University of Wyoming King Air research aircraft based out of Utqiaġvik, Alaska. Flights were conducted over the snow-covered sea ice, tundra, open leads (sea ice fractures), and the North Slope of Alaska oil fields. Gaseous reactive bromine compounds, including Br2 and BrO, were measured using chemical ionization mass spectrometry (CIMS), with coincident in-situ ozone measurements. In addition, the role of nitrogen oxides (NOx) on bromine chemistry was investigated through measurements of nitric acid (HNO3) and peroxynitric acid (HO2NO2) via CIMS. This study is improving our understanding of coupled chemistry between the snowpack and boundary layer in the rapidly changing Arctic, with sea ice loss and increasing development and resource extraction.

495672.title: Effect of Turbulence upon Glaciation of Mixed-Phase Clouds
495672.authors: Grigory Sarnitsky, Chalmers University of Technology, Gothenburg, Sweden; and H. Hudoyo, F. Hoffmann, G. Sardina, and B. Mehlig
495672.abstract: Mixed-phase clouds contain water in three forms: water vapour, liquid droplets, and ice particles. The Wegener–Bergeron–Findeisen (WBF) process describes the growth of ice particles at the expense of evaporating liquid droplets. This process can substantially reduce the liquid-water content and, in sufficiently well-mixed conditions, may ultimately lead to complete glaciation, leaving only ice and water vapour. Parcel models that assume a well-mixed cloud have been used extensively to study this process. Observations, however, indicate that mixed-phase clouds can persist for extended periods without fully glaciating. One possible explanation is spatial unmixing (Korolev & Milbrandt, 2022), whereby ice particles and liquid droplets become inhomogeneously distributed at small scales, effectively separating ice from liquid water. Turbulence may strongly influence glaciation if the characteristic scale of spatial unmixing is sufficiently large. When ice particles and droplets are inhomogeneously distributed over sufficiently large spatial scales, their spatial separation can generate non-Gaussian fluctuations in water-vapour concentration as described by Fries et al., 2024. Standard bulk models of glaciation, in contrast, assume well-mixed conditions and Gaussian statistics, and therefore cannot capture these effects. Here, we use direct numerical simulations to investigate how turbulence and spatial unmixing influence the glaciation of a mixed-phase cloud. Because our simulations are limited to domain sizes of order 1 m, we combine the numerical results with scaling arguments to infer the behaviour at larger scales and determine how the glaciation time depends on turbulence intensity and domain size. We characterise the evolution of the WBF process by tracking the time-dependent spatial correlation functions of ice-particles and droplet-number densities. In the absence of spatial unmixing, we find that turbulence has only a weak effect on the glaciation timescale (Sarnitsky et al., 2025), consistent with the direct numerical simulations of Chen et al. (2023). These results provide a baseline for assessing the extent to which spatial unmixing can alter the conventional picture of mixed-phase cloud glaciation.

495673.title: The Envelope of Possibilities for Atlantic Tropical Cyclone Seasons
495673.authors: Levi G. Silvers, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. T. Chien, P. Klotzbach, M. M. Bell, M. Hemmati, J. Lee, and C. J. Schreck III
495673.abstract: The range of possible tropical cyclone (TC) activity over a season, given a particular set of large-scale conditions, has always been an intriguing question. This research explores the range of possible Atlantic seasonal TC activity for three particular historical seasons: 2005, 2013, and 2024. By comparing the observed number of TCs to the mean number of TCs in the ensembles, we find that the 2005 Atlantic TC season overperformed relative to the expected TC number, while both 2013 and 2024 underperformed, with the observed 18 named TCs during the 2024 Atlantic TC season being 3 standard deviations below the expected mean of 28. There is substantial variation in TC genesis numbers across the ensembles for a given season with the 2024 season having the largest range of possible TCs. Our findings support the hypothesis that when El Niño Southern Oscillation is relatively weak, mean Atlantic TC activity is set by tropical Atlantic sea-surface temperature (SST), while the range of TC activity is driven by a combination of the Madden-Julian Oscillation and smaller-scale atmospheric noise. Exploring the range of possible outcomes for a single season could, in principle, be done with a physics-based numerical model such as a global circulation model. However, such models struggle to simulate TCs at standard resolutions and are costly to run. Recent advances in the development of machine learning tools have resulted in so-called ‘climate emulators’ that allow for a regression-based prediction of the response of the atmosphere to a given forcing. In particular, the Ai2 Climate Emulator version 2 (ACE2) deep-learning model has been shown to be an accurate and computationally efficient emulator. We will review recent work showing that when ACE2 is trained on ERA5 reanalysis, it does a reasonable job of simulating both tropical cyclones and the large-scale environment upon which the storms depend for a given SST forcing. This work analyzes 120 ensemble-member experiments from ACE2 to show a range of possibilities for the 2005, 2013, and 2024 seasons. We will explore the extent to which data-driven climate emulators can be expected to be useful for research on seasonal TC activity.

495674.title: Analyzing Key Meteorological Drivers of Snow-to-Liquid Ratios in Lake-Effect and Synoptic Snowstorms
495674.abstract: Snow-to-liquid ratios (SLRs) are critical to forecasting winter weather, yet the physical drivers behind the SLR differences between lake-effect snowstorms and synoptic-scale snowstorms remain poorly understood. We pair hourly observations from seven stations across the Great Lakes region and four stations in various regions across the contiguous US with constructed reanalysis profiles from ERA5 to quantify and explain this SLR gap. The mean SLR difference was found to be 6.6:1, with lake-effect events producing the lower ratio of snowfall. Dendritic growth zone (DGZ) height, sub-DGZ vertical velocity, and precipitable water emerged as the strongest contributors to the gap, while DGZ relative humidity and lift influenced SLR within event types but did not meaningfully differ between them. Both propensity score matching and regression-based decomposition converged to indicate that the tested variables explain approximately 44% of the gap, with the remaining 56% hypothesized to arise from microphysical processes, such as the formation of snowflakes from ice crystals, that are not resolvable in 0.25° reanalysis data.

495678.title: Air-Sea Interaction across the Indian Summer Monsoon Air-Sea Transition Zone
495678.authors: Sue Chen, NRL, Monterey, CA; and C. Luecke, J. M. Schmidt, J. Christophersen, S. Bolella, H. Wejiskera, E. F. Gonzalez Mireles, and H. J. S. Fernando
495678.abstract: The Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) onset periods are characterized by dramatic shifts from warm to cool ocean conditions and from dry to humid atmospheric states, fundamentally influencing ISM development. However, this ISM onset transition phase, notably remains poorly represented in numerical models due to lack of observations in the Northern Indian Ocean region. In particular, the 2025 monsoon exhibited unusual characteristics: the Indian Meteorological Department declared onset over Kerala 7-8 days earlier than the climatological mean of June 1st, while the wind-based Indian Monsoon Index indicated above-normal intensity. Our ship-based and autonomous observations during May-June 2025 over Bay of Bengal (BoB) capture a comprehensive four-dimensional dataset spanning from the upper ocean to the top of atmosphere within a 40×40 km intensive study region in the central BoB. Throughout the campaign, we observed complex interactions between atmospheric and oceanic equatorial waves and the ISM, resulting in alternating periods of enhanced precipitation and monsoon breaks. Our analysis across this air-sea transition zone reveals several key small-scale coupled processes, including heat trapping by ocean diurnal warm layers during pre-onset and break periods; boundary layer stratification and re-stratification driven by large-scale monsoon circulation changes; atmospheric cold pool formation; rain lens development; wind-wave-swell interaction; and the evolution of ocean fronts and eddies. These observations provide critical insights into the multi-scale processes governing monsoon variability.

495679.title: What Worked and What Didn’t in Years of Open-Source Meteorological Software: Community, Automation, and the GeoIPS Transition
495679.authors: Jeremy E. Solbrig, CIRA, Fort Collins , CO; and G. Uttmark, M. Surratt, C. Camacho, C. Selman, E. Rose, S. Gampa, C. McClelland, Z. Ruan, A. Thorpe, L. Wilson, L. Porter, and J. Fluke
495679.abstract: This presentation shares lessons from 17 years of developing the Geolocated Information Processing System (GeoIPS), including its transition from a proprietary internal tool to an open-source Python framework and our ongoing efforts to build a contributor community around the software. GeoIPS is jointly maintained by the Naval Research Laboratory and the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere at Colorado State University. Our experience highlights both technical and social challenges in building scientific Python software intended to span research and operational environments. A persistent challenge in meteorological data processing is duplication of software across institutions, sensors, and products. GeoIPS addresses this through a plugin architecture that separates the core processing framework from scientific and data-specific functionality. Readers, algorithms, interpolators, output formatters, and other capabilities are implemented as independently maintained, composable plugins rather than modifications to the core framework. New sensors and products can therefore be supported without changing GeoIPS itself, and scientists can develop and distribute algorithms without needing to understand the internals of the processing system. The same plugin can then be incorporated into research or operational workflows by downstream users without further involvement from its original developer. GeoIPS 2.0, released as an alpha version in July 2026, extends this approach by enforcing metadata standards through an Xarray-native DataTree backbone and central schema. YAML-based configuration describes processing workflows independently of the environment in which they execute, allowing configurations to be version-controlled and workflows to be reproduced across laptops, HPC systems, and cloud environments. Courier, a complementary open-source Python orchestration package, uses interchangeable message brokers to feed GeoIPS in near real time and can scale processing from a single machine to distributed clusters using the same configuration model. Maintaining a framework distributed across more than two dozen repositories and multiple institutions has also required treating documentation, testing, release engineering, and contribution processes as part of the software architecture. Python-based tools and GitHub CI automate changelog management, formatting, documentation assembly, and validation, moving many project standards from written instructions into automatically enforced checks. We discuss successes and failures encountered while building a contributor community in which many plugin authors are atmospheric scientists rather than software engineers. In particular, we examine the value—and limitations—of modular architecture, declarative configuration, automated standards, onboarding materials, and contribution guidelines in reducing the knowledge required to contribute scientific capabilities. These experiences suggest that successful scientific Python frameworks require not only reusable code, but deliberate design of the interfaces between scientists, software developers, and operational users.

495683.title: Modernizing the Voice of the National Weather Service (NOAA Weather Radio (NWR))
495683.authors: Bernard Werwinski, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and B. Miretzky and N. MASCARENHAS
495683.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) is undertaking a comprehensive modernization of NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards (NWR) to better serve the American public, emergency managers, broadcasters, the wireless industry, and vulnerable communities. At the center of this effort are two closely integrated initiatives: the transition to a modern, Internet Protocol (IP)-based telecommunications backbone and the development of a next-generation broadcast management system. Together, these efforts aim to provide more reliable, resilient, accessible, and high-quality dissemination of authoritative, life-saving weather, water, and climate information. Rather than abruptly replacing the nation’s critical radio infrastructure, the NWR modernization follows a phased, risk-mitigated transition strategy. New hardware, software, and networking capabilities are introduced incrementally, allowing rigorous testing and validation to ensure continuous operational readiness. This approach emphasizes system redundancy, expanded multi-lingual capabilities (such as automated Spanish-language broadcasts), and enhanced audio clarity while ensuring uninterrupted broadcast services throughout the transition. The legacy transmitter network continues serving as the foundational public safety lifeline while the modernized infrastructure evolves toward full operational deployment. Underlying this modernization is a shift from legacy analog communication circuits to a robust, cloud-supported IP network paired with advanced text-to-speech engines. By leveraging modern digital telecommunications and automated broadcast software, NWR can streamline the ingest and transmission of NWS watches, warnings, and advisories. This updated architecture drastically reduces dissemination latency, improves broadcast consistency across more than a thousand transmitters, and allows for seamless integration with modern digital alert systems, ensuring the "Voice of the National Weather Service" remains resilient under the most extreme conditions. This presentation will discuss the guiding principles behind the NWR modernization effort, including engineering resilience, signal coverage optimization, cloud-native scalability, and accessibility for diverse and underserved populations. It will also examine how field engineering tests, operational simulations, and collaboration with federal and commercial partners are shaping the future of the broadcast network. Lessons learned from insights into balancing technological innovation with the absolute reliability expected of a national emergency broadcast lifeline will be shared. As the modernization progresses toward full operational capability, these complementary efforts provide a framework for safeguarding and elevating the nation’s premier hazard broadcasting network. By bridging trusted, time-tested radio technology with modern digital infrastructure, the National Weather Service is positioning NWR to better meet evolving public safety needs and technological realities for decades to come.

495684.title: Quantifying Pluvial Flood Risk and Expected Annual Loss at the Property Level
495684.authors: Saanchi Singh Kaushal, NOAH Intelligence, Sunnyvale, CA; and S. VanHaren and C. Godsall
