495684.abstract: Pluvial flooding results from intense rainfall that overwhelms urban drainage capacity, and has become a significant driver of residential property loss in Canada. It is mechanistically distinct from riverine and coastal flooding, originating within the urban catchment itself rather than from a overwhelmed channel banks or wave uprush from an elevated shoreline. A primary driver is the complexity of bottlenecks within municipal drainage networks, including undersized pipes, junction geometry, outfall location, etc. and is particularly consequential in metropolitan areas, where most conveyance infrastructure is installed below grade and invisible to the property owners who depend on it. As a result, warming climate has intensified short-duration extreme rainfall, producing frequent exceedances of sewer conveyance capacity with the resulting surcharge diverted to flow onto both intentional and unintentional overland pathways, where most structural damage occurs. Due to the complexity of hydraulically modelling pluvial flooding, the associated risk is largely absent from regulatory floodplain mapping and therefore property owners, municipalities, and insurers lack a spatially resolved understanding of it. This research developed a method combining physics-based hazard simulation with a property-level scoring framework. Design and historic rainfall events across a range of return periods were simulated using a two-dimensional hydrodynamic model based on an integrated catchment modelling approach representing the sewer network and its surface interactions, producing depth, duration, and velocity estimates at each property. These variables feed a scoring framework spanning four pillars — flood hazard, drainage infrastructure service, exposure, and physical resilience — yielding an interpretable property level score and, integrated across return periods, an Expected Annual Loss in dollar terms. Applied to a pilot Ontario sewershed, results show the distribution of risk and loss across neighboring properties, giving owners a clear path from retrofit options to informed insurance decisions

495685.title: National Weather Service Southeast River Forecast Center’s Decision Support for United States Army Corps of Engineers Mobile Water Management District Repairs to Lock and Dam Projects
495685.authors: Nicole Casamassina Rockwell, NWS, Peachtree City, GA
495685.abstract: Federal interagency collaboration is essential to finding solutions to complex problems that have many effects on the environment and society. Over the last several years, the National Weather Service (NWS) Southeast River Forecast Center (SERFC) has assisted the United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) Mobile District Water Management in their planning of repairs and necessary maintenance for multiple lock and dam projects throughout the District by providing extended analyses, forecasts, and Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS). The locks and dams are used for a variety of purposes, such as navigation, recreation, water supply, and hydroelectric power generation with the underlying USACE water management mission of supporting the economy, environment, and public safety in mind. For example, navigating through the Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway, which consists of 10 locks and dams, saves time and money by providing a route to the Gulf coast that is approximately 800 miles shorter than taking the Mississippi River. The USACE Mobile District Water Management requested extended weather and water information beyond the standard daily SERFC hydrologic forecast and coordination discussions. This extended lead time accommodates complex planning needs, such as movement of large equipment, modifications to upstream reservoir operations, and having necessary specialists on site–all of which can take days to complete. The briefings the SERFC provides include: Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (QPE) from the previous 24 hours, the Quantitative Precipitation Forecast (QPF) for the next 7 days, deterministic 10-day inflow and tailwater forecasts from the SERFC hydrologic model, and 10-day ensemble river simulations forced by the North American Ensemble Forecast System (NAEFS) and Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS). According to USACE Mobile District Water Management, there has been a “direct correlation” between these briefings and keeping maintenance on track or ahead of schedule. For example, when underwater repairs were needed at Demopolis Lock and Dam, the schedule could be changed based on forecast water levels. Furthermore, SERFC briefings are a part of the daily morning safety briefing given to contractors making the repairs to Holt Lock and Dam. Key aspects to this partnership between SERFC and USACE Mobile District Water Management include years of building trust through virtual and in-person meetings, participation in weekly briefing calls, and maintaining open communication before, during, and after heavy rain and drought events, while recognizing that the two offices have similar missions of delivering vital hydrologic information to protect life and property. Working together makes a more efficient government.This presentation will show the successes and challenges that have come from this partnership between SERFC and USACE Mobile District Water Management.

495686.title: Carbon Exchange in Climate-Smart Grazing: Native Warm-Season Grass vs. Tall Fescue Pastures
495686.authors: Taqi Raza, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN; and N. Eash and B. B. Hicks
495686.abstract: Grasslands are among the most important agricultural land uses in the eastern U.S., dominated primarily by Tall Fescue (a common cool-season grass). However, grazing area is declining as grasslands are converted to grain production and urbanization, substantially reducing soil C storage. Even modest changes in grazing management can have a tremendous impact on soil C flux and other GHG emissions. Integrating native warm-season grasses (NWSG) into climate-smart grassland management strategies can improve system resilience, increase soil carbon, and provide many other benefits. However, there is limited research on seasonal carbon fluxes and exchange in NWSG and Tall Fescue in the southeastern United States. Our current research focuses on evaluating Tall Fescue and Native Warm-Season Grass Pastures to measure net ecosystem CO2 fluxes, track changes in respiration, and assess C sequestration potential. To determine the underlying impact of seasonal grazing on CO2 fluxes in continuous grazing Tall Fescue and Native Warm-Season Grass Pastures, we used the Bowen Ratio Energy Balance (BREB) to measure the flux between the atmosphere and the plant and quantify the difference in CO2 exchange between Pastures. The study was conducted on a grassland pasture at the Northeast Tennessee AgResearch and Education Center in Greenville, US. Fluxes of CO2, H2O, and energy are measured at half-hour intervals to derive the net ecosystem exchange (NEE). NEE will be partitioned into gross primary productivity (GPP) and respiration (Re) to calculate the seasonal carbon budget for each system. We hypothesize that NWSG will sequester more atmospheric carbon and be relatively less sensitive to summer heat than continuous-grazing Tall Fescue pasture. Results on the observational evidence of carbon exchange will be presented at the conference.

495687.title: GPU-Accelerated Street-Scale Heat Exposure Modeling for Urban Event Planning: The Paris 2024 Olympic Marathon
495687.authors: Naveen Sudharsan, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX; and T. Brooks, H. Kamath, M. Singh, H. Dashtian, and D. Niyogi
495687.abstract: Extreme heat is an increasing concern for large outdoor events, particularly endurance races held in cities. Heat exposure can vary considerably over short distances due to differences in building geometry, tree cover, and direct solar radiation. Capturing this variability requires modeling at very high spatial resolution, which has traditionally been too computationally expensive for use in short-turnaround event planning. We applied the GPU-accelerated SOlar and LongWave Environmental Irradiance Geometry model (SOLWEIG-GPU) to the 42.195-km Paris 2024 Olympic marathon route. The model was run at 2-m resolution over a 28.3 × 28.6 km domain containing about 202 million grid cells. Hourly meteorological forcing was provided by the 100-m Meso-NH atmospheric model, and 22 hourly simulations were completed. Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), mean radiant temperature (Tₘᵣₜ), and shading were sampled at 4,222 points along the route. We also estimated the heat exposure experienced by runners starting at 07:00, 08:00, and 09:00 using representative elite and recreational running speeds. GPU acceleration was essential for this forecast application. A geometry-resolving model at 2-m resolution over a domain of this size would otherwise require computational resources that are not practical when results are expected quickly before an event. GPU acceleration allowed us to retain fine details like trees and buildings while developing heat-stress data within the short turnaround required for operational use. The forecast simulations showed large differences in heat exposure along the marathon route. UTCI varied by 12–20 °C at a given hour, while air temperature varied by only about 2 °C. Much of this difference was related to radiation and shading. At 10:00, Tₘᵣₜ and UTCI had an R² of 0.997, and shaded sections of the route were about 9–11 °C cooler than exposed sections. The start time also had a clear effect. Moving the start from 08:00 to 07:00 reduced modeled mean UTCI exposure by about 2–5 °C, with larger reductions for slower runners. The warmest sections were located near kilometers 4–6 and 32–36, where UTCI reached about 33–35 °C at noon. This work shows that GPU acceleration can make street-scale urban heat modeling practical for time-sensitive applications. The same framework could be used to support decisions about event start times, route selection, and the placement of cooling and medical resources.

495688.title: A New Method for Early Detection and Warning of Heavy Intensity Rainfall on a Runway
495688.authors: Scott D. Landolt, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. Maciejewski, J. Steelman, A. Gaydos, G. Rother, J. Steventon, K. Johnston, T. Ryan, J. Cole, and J. Lentz
495688.abstract: Heavy rainfall can create a significant hazard to aircraft if the rainfall intensity is high enough to flood the runway and can lead to hydroplaning and runway excursions. Because convective rainfall can be highly localized, a thunderstorm can rapidly overwhelm runway drainage at one end while the other end of the runway is unaffected. Current METAR observations report heavy rainfall conditions (+RA) when rainfall rates exceed 0.3 in h-1 but thunderstorms can often produce rainfall rates higher than 1 in h-1. Additionally, METAR observations of heavy intensity rainfall provide little information on the severity, or spatial and temporal variability of the precipitation. Recent NTSB reports on runway excursion events have highlighted the need to develop methods for quickly detecting and reporting these conditions to pilots, air traffic control, and other ground personnel to prevent further incidents. To address these issues, NSF NCAR and FAA personnel have developed a new low-cost system that can capture the spatial variability of these storms and provide real-time information for rainfall rates of up to 10 in h-1 at specific points along the runway. The system is composed primarily of tipping bucket rain gauges that communicate via an LTE modem and run solely off solar and battery power. Specialized mounts have been designed that allow for quick installation and easy maintenance. A prototype warning system is also under development that will alert pilots, air traffic control and others as to the possibility that part or all of a runway may be flooded. The system has been deployed for testing at one airport with others targeted for future research efforts. An overview of the system, case study examples and discussion of the proposed alerting system will be presented. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the FAA. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

495689.title: Fishing Vessels as Ocean Observing Infrastructure - Scaling from Pilot Program to Operational Networks.ODN Implementation of FVON Networks in the North Atlantic Arc, Bering Sea, and California.
495689.authors: Steve Woll, Ocean Data Network, Norfolk, VA; and C. Van Vranken
495689.abstract: Background Subsurface coastal and shelf oceans remain persistently undersampled despite their highly dynamic nature and outsized ecological, maritime, and economic impacts. This lack of data negatively impacts oceanographic and weather model performance, regulatory and policy making, and operational decision-making by those who make a living, conduct research, or bear stewardship responsibility on or in the ocean. Leveraging Commercial Fishing Vessels as Observation Platforms Fortunately, these regions are also the home of large numbers of commercial fishing vessels, providing a unique opportunity to leverage those vessels to host extremely low cost, high impact, and highly scalable oceanographic sensors. The Fishing Vessel Ocean Observing Network (FVON) is an international, public-private effort to collaborate, coordinate activities, share technology, and develop best practices among approximately a dozen different entities working in this arena. FVON is formally linked to the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) as an emerging observing network contributing to the broader GOOS architecture. FVON partner Ocean Data Network (ODN) is a U.S.-based company that is fielding such sensors not only in U.S. coastal waters, but internationally across several continents. Its equipment configurations are representative of the FVON approach and integrate oceanographic sensor(s) mounted on fishing gear with an onboard deck unit that acts as a data logger and communications unit. Once the fishing gear (e.g. nets, traps, etc.) on which the sensor(s) are mounted is retrieved onto the deck of the fishing vessel, the sensor(s) offload data via Bluetooth to the deck unit, which then relays the ocean observation data to the cloud utilizing the vessel's communications systems (e.g. Wi-Fi, satellite, cellular, etc.). Current sensor deployments primarily collect temperature-depth profiles and bottom temperature time series, with additional sensors for dissolved oxygen, salinity/conductivity, and other parameters being actively developed for deployment in the next twelve months. All components of the systems are ruggedized for the challenging operational environment and designed to operate autonomously after installation, with little or no routine crew input or maintenance. Data is relayed to shore in near real time, where rapid QARTOD-compatible QC routines are applied and data is further redistributed to various repositories. Data is available to off-vessel users from multiple cloud-based repositories in near real time (target is 15 minutes from sensor on deck to data being available to users). Data is passed to the U.S. National Data Buoy Center, which routes the data to the WMO Global Telecommunications System (GTS) for use by WMO signatories from across the world. Additional data delivery paths are also available. Key Results This presentation will focus on three implementation cases that show how fishing-vessel ocean observing is moving from concept to networked practice. First, the North Atlantic Arc demonstrates multinational implementation in Iceland, the Faroe Islands, and Scotland, where substantial data is already flowing through the network in near real-time. Second, Oceanography on Deck (OOD) in the Bering Sea shows how a fishing vessel-based observing system can be built across multiple fleets and gear types to create broad seasonal and spatial coverage in a rapidly changing marine ecosystem. Third, in the Synchro pilot, a six-vessel fleet provides coverage in California waters, including Monterey Bay, demonstrating how local fishing activity can support near real-time data delivery and practical engagement with downstream users. We will present implementation lessons, network design considerations, and data delivery pathways from these three regions, touching on such operational details as automated cloud uploads, daily remote monitoring, anonymized data handling, and operational pathways to various public portals and the GTS. In addition to improving general ocean circulation modeling, operational applications will be discussed to include search and rescue, aquaculture, offshore energy, environmental decision making, military sensor and weapon performance, ecological modeling, as well as commercial fishing itself. Figure 1 provides a schematic of the data collection process and relay, as well as depiction of data collection efforts in the North Atlantic Arc and Bering Sea. Impact on Coastal Monitoring, Monitoring, and Forecasting Together, these examples show that fishing-vessel-based observing can already cost-effectively densify subsurface observations in the coastal ocean while producing interoperable, near-real-time data streams. These observations can be used in a stand-alone manner to drive fishing, regulatory, pollution response, and other operational decisions where the ocean's vertical structure is important. The observational data is also extremely useful to both physics-based and AI-based meteorological and oceanographic modeling, with the positive impacts on seasonal to sub-seasonal meteorological forecasting impacts being the best documented and well-understood. Initial user communities already exist for all of these use cases, while the authors specifically invite additional met-ocean modelers, forecasters, and other applied users to engage with these data streams, test validation and assimilation use cases, and help demonstrate the scientific, operational, and societal value, of the data, helping provide a strong, wide-ranging, and persistent demand signal to provide support for ongoing efforts to scale fishing vessel-based observing even more broadly.

495690.title: Building the Future Atmospheric Science Workforce: Preparing NCAS-M Students and Fellows for Career Success
495690.authors: Jo-Anne Manswell Butty, NOAA Cooperative Science Center in Atmospheric Sciences and Meteorology, Washington, DC; and S. Chiao, T. M. Adams, B. Demoz, K. Mittapalli, and A. J. ray
495690.abstract: The NOAA Cooperative Science Center in Atmospheric Sciences and Meteorology (NCAS-M) funded by NOAA Educational Partnership Program (NOAA EPP) is committed to developing a highly skilled atmospheric science workforce through a dynamic fellowship and student development model. NCAS-M supports undergraduate, graduate, and postdoctoral fellows through a combination of research experiences, professional development training, mentoring, scientific communication opportunities, and career readiness activities. Fellows engage in research with faculty and NOAA scientists while participating in seminars, workshops, conference presentations, networking events, and workforce preparation programs designed to build technical and professional competencies. This presentation highlights NCAS-M's holistic approach to workforce development and examines how integrated learning experiences contribute to student success and career preparedness. Attention is given to activities that strengthen scientific communication, interdisciplinary collaboration, mentoring relationships, and awareness of career pathways within the atmospheric science workforce. Lessons learned from program implementation and participant feedback will be discussed, providing insights for programs seeking to broaden participation and strengthen workforce readiness in atmospheric science. The NCAS-M model offers a promising framework for preparing the next generation of atmospheric scientists to address emerging environmental and societal challenges.

495691.title: Highs and Lows: Building an Optimized AI & Physics Multi-model Ensemble Forecast of CONUS HDD and ERCOT Wind Extremes for Energy Trading
495691.authors: Jan F. Dutton, Prescient Weather Ltd, State College, PA; and R. James and J. Ross
495691.abstract: Cold-driven demand spikes and wind-generation shortfalls are among the highest-consequence weather patterns energy traders price against, yet traders increasingly must choose among a growing and heterogeneous set of ensemble forecast systems, including newer AI-based models, without a clear picture of which combination best anticipates that risk. This study applies one systematic multi-model verification framework to two complementary, energy-relevant forecast targets: population-weighted CONUS heating degree days (HDD), representing cold-driven load risk, and capacity-weighted ERCOT 100m wind speed, representing generation risk. Both are evaluated at 1-15 day lead times using four ensemble systems, AIFS ENS, WeatherNext2, ECMWF ENS, and GEFS ENS, obtained through the World Climate Service Point-in-Time API, across every possible one- through four-model combination. Forecasts are bias-corrected using model-specific rolling out-of-sample windows (30 days for WeatherNext2, ECMWF ENS, and GEFS ENS; 90 days for AIFS ENS), applied consistently to ensemble-mean and member-level output for both variables. Deterministic skill is scored by mean absolute error, root-mean-square error, and bias across lead day, lead-day group, and calendar month. Extreme events are defined from the ten most anomalous observed days in each series, the highest HDD days for cold risk and, in a deliberate mirror of that framing, the lowest wind speed days for wind-drought risk, and forecast probabilistically from ensemble-member agreement, scored with the Brier score and Brier skill score against a climatological reference. Applying the same methodology to the opposite tails of two different variables tests whether model and blend performance generalizes across energy-forecast applications or is specific to the variable and risk direction being forecast. Results will determine whether the model combination that best anticipates cold-driven demand extremes also best anticipates ERCOT wind-drought generation extremes, informing whether energy traders need variable-specific ensemble blends or can rely on a single blend across both sides of the supply-demand balance.

495694.title: Building the Next Generation of National Weather Service Digital Services: Transforming Weather.gov and Modernizing the NWS API
495694.authors: Corey N.J. Pieper, NWS, Silver Spring, MD; and N. Keene
495694.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) is undertaking a comprehensive modernization of its digital services to better serve the American public, emergency managers, media, commercial partners, researchers, and software developers. At the center of this effort are two closely integrated initiatives: the development of the next generation of Weather.gov and continued evolution of the NWS Application Programming Interface (API). Together, these efforts aim to provide faster, more consistent, more accessible, and more resilient access to authoritative weather, water, and climate information. Rather than replacing an existing website with a finished product, the Weather.gov modernization follows an iterative, user-centered development process. New capabilities are introduced incrementally, allowing feedback from users and partners to directly influence feature prioritization and design decisions. This agile approach emphasizes mobile-first design, accessibility, plain language, and a consistent location-based experience while ensuring uninterrupted operational service throughout the transition. The legacy Weather.gov platform continues serving as the authoritative operational website while the new platform evolves toward full operational capability. Underlying the new user experience is the NWS API, which has become the primary mechanism for delivering forecast and hazard information to both the new website and thousands of external applications. By exposing standardized, machine-readable services, the API enables developers, partners, and decision-support systems to consume the same authoritative information presented through Weather.gov. This architecture allows improvements to be developed once and delivered consistently across multiple digital platforms while supporting innovation outside the National Weather Service. This presentation will discuss the guiding principles behind the modernization effort, including human-centered design, accessibility, performance, operational resilience, and cloud-native architecture. It will also examine how continuous user research, iterative software development, and operational testing are shaping both the website and API. Lessons learned from developing and operating a modern, mission-critical weather information platform will be shared, along with insights into balancing innovation with the reliability expected of an operational forecasting agency. As the modernization progresses toward full operational capability, these complementary efforts provide a framework for delivering authoritative environmental information to diverse audiences while positioning the National Weather Service to better meet evolving public expectations and technological advances.

495698.title: Evaluating Historical Simulations of the North Atlantic Subtropical High in EC-Earth3 for Florida Climate Applications.
495698.authors: Sankha Subhra Maitra, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; and S. M. Lazarus
495698.abstract: Abstract Summer precipitation across Florida is strongly influenced by sea-breeze circulations, which in turn depend on the location, intensity, and geometry of the North Atlantic Subtropical High (NASH). Previous studies suggest that the NASH has intensified and expanded westward in recent decades, potentially altering regional precipitation patterns, drought frequency, and heat extremes across the southeastern United States. In Florida, the position of the NASH ridge axis is particularly important because it influences the low-level flow regime and, consequently, the relative strength and inland penetration of the Atlantic and Gulf Coast sea breezes. This study evaluates the ability of historical simulations from the EC-Earth3 CMIP6 model to reproduce observed characteristics of the summertime NASH. Model output from the EC-Earth ensemble is compared with ERA5 reanalysis during June-August for the period 2005-2014. The evaluation focuses on the intensity and spatial structure of the 850 hPa geopotential height field, the position of the NASH ridge axis, low-level flow, and associated thermodynamic fields over the western North Atlantic. Model performance is assessed using statistical measures, including mean bias and root mean square error (RMSE). The results provide a baseline assessment of EC-Earth3’s ability to represent key dynamical features of the NASH and establish confidence in its use for future projections of summertime circulation patterns and their impacts on Florida precipitation, drought, and heat extremes.

495703.title: Toward Consistent, Impact-Based Flood Thresholds across the National Water Model Domain: evidence from Gauged Locations
495703.authors: Ali Dadkhah, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT; and R. Van Der Heiden, R. Diehl, S. Safdar, D. M. Rizzo, A. J. Jefferson, and E. Doran
495703.abstract: National Water Model (NWM) inundation mapping is moving toward covering the entire stream network across the contiguous United States (CONUS), yet these maps do not completely convey the impact of anticipated flood events. Impact-based flood thresholds, which are river stages set from historical records and local forecaster knowledge for the action, minor, moderate, and major categories, exist only for a select number of gauged locations. Elsewhere, across more than two million forecast reaches without such thresholds, categories are instead assigned using an annual exceedance probability (AEP). Comparing this AEP practice against roughly 2,000 gauged locations where impact-based thresholds already exist, we find that the AEP associated with a given category varies widely across locations rather than converging on one representative value, meaning the same AEP can signal very different flood severities depending on where it is applied. What explains this spread? We test whether floodplain characteristics, including factors plausibly considered when these impact-based thresholds were set, predict the AEP associated with the threshold. To do this, we build exposure–stage curves at roughly 2,000 National Weather Service forecast points. These curves combine stage-indexed inundation libraries with structures, transportation assets, and land cover data to capture what gets inundated as water levels rise. A machine learning model then uses these curves, along with basin and reach attributes, to estimate AEP for the action, minor, moderate, and major categories. Preliminary findings show that the machine learning model predicts threshold AEPs more accurately than return-period rules, drainage-area regression, and channel geometry alone. Examining where these predictions are most and least reliable, further shows where floodplain exposure curves and landscape characteristics predict impact-based thresholds well, and where they do not.

495704.title: Machine Learning for Rapid-Onset Streamflow Forecasting: NASA SPoRT's 1-Hour Streamflow-AI Model
495704.authors: Andrew T. White, Univ. of Alabama in Huntsville / NASA SPoRT, Huntsville, AL; and K. D. White, C. R. Hain, K. K. Fuell, and J. L. Case
495704.abstract: Predicting rapid-onset flooding and rapidly changing hydrological conditions in stream networks requires capturing fast catchment response times, antecedent state shifts, and high-frequency atmospheric forcing that traditional medium-range streamflow models often miss. To better resolve these short-fuse river and creek dynamics, the NASA Short-term Prediction Research and Transition Center (SPoRT) has expanded its near-real-time deep learning framework, Streamflow-AI, beyond its foundational 6-hour temporal resolution, 7-day medium-range forecasts into a short-range hourly forecast model. This study presents the formulation, operational deployment, and performance evaluation of this newly developed 1-hour rapid-update Streamflow-AI model, targeting rapid stage fluctuations in river and creek systems. Operating on a continuous 1-hour refresh cadence, the updated architecture ingests high-frequency Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (QPE), short-range Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPF), and soil moisture data from the SPoRT instance of the Land Information System (LIS) to simulate time-varying stage heights, rapid hydrograph rise rates, and flashy stage responses across small-to-midscale drainage basins. We assess model performance across an operational evaluation period and present key findings and operational insights.

495705.title: Advancing Weather Forecasts Through Innovative Observing Technologies: An Overview of the NOAA Weather Program Office Observations Program
495705.abstract: The NOAA Weather Program Office (WPO) Observations Program is dedicated to advancing observation capabilities to improve weather forecasts and decision support across the weather enterprise. Driven by the Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Act of 2017, the program focuses on finding and funding innovative sensor and observing technologies to create a mission-effective, integrated, adaptive, and affordable observations systems portfolio. By targeting research at Readiness Levels 5-7, the program pushes the envelope of emerging technologies to fill critical gaps in existing observing networks, and to better predict high-impact weather events, such as tropical cyclones, extreme precipitation, flooding, and wildfires. This poster will provide an overview of the Observations Program’s mission and transitional pipeline, while highlighting recent successful projects that demonstrate the value of innovative observational data. It will also emphasize how the WPO Observations Program champions partnerships between NOAA, academia, and private industry to fund, coordinate, and transition cutting-edge observational capabilities into operational forecasting.

495706.title: How Much Does the Precipitation Product Matter? Comparing Hourly and Storm-Total Rainfall Estimates for U.S. Tropical Cyclones
495706.authors: Kyle James Dailey, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and C. M. Zarzycki
495706.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) frequently produce destructive overland flooding, yet the estimated magnitude, spatial pattern, and intensity-duration of these events are different among gridded precipitation products. These arise from varied observing systems, retrieval methods, gauge corrections (or lack thereof), and spatiotemporal resolution. Dataset discrepancies can influence both rainfall-hazard characterization and model evaluation. Previous work has documented discrepancies among precipitation estimates for individual case events, particularly during extreme rainfall. However, less is known about how agreement among products changes between storm-total and maximum-hourly precipitation, across the upper tail of the rainfall distribution, and with storm intensity over a large multi-storm U.S. sample. We evaluate rainfall from 48 TCs that impacted the United States from 2002 to 2024 using seven precipitation datasets. These include the NOAA Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC), Stage IV, the Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor System (MRMS), Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG), CPC MORPHing technique (CMORPH), Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation (MSWEP), and Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP). Products are compared using a common five-day event window, fixed landfall-centered domain, and statistical framework. Stage IV and AORC show broad agreement across the full sample, with highest mean spatial correlations for both storm-total precipitation and maximum-hourly precipitation. MRMS also agrees closely with AORC over a 10-storm recent-period subset, but is generally wetter. Among the non-radar products, MSWEP and IMERG show the strongest storm-total agreement with AORC, while CMORPH exhibits greater storm-to-storm variability. GPCP agreement with most products and storms is relatively weak. Differences between products become more pronounced for maximum-hourly and upper-tail precipitation than for storm totals, with radar-influenced products retaining more localized high-end values and several satellite, blended, and coarse products producing compressed upper tails. Errors also generally increase for stronger storms. These results demonstrate that precipitation-product selection is an important source of uncertainty when assessing TC rainfall hazards, particularly those over small spatial footprints (e.g., urban scales) over short durations (e.g., hourly).

495707.title: Evaluation and Enhancement of Global Blending as a Replacement for Spin-up Cycles in RRFs
495707.abstract: Hourly updating numerical weather prediction at convection-allowing scales is the foundation of severe storm forecasting. Over the past two decades, NOAA has successfully developed and operated the Rapid Refresh (RAP) and High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) systems, marking the beginning of an era of community-based modeling components in operational forecasting. During the past six years, NOAA has also made significant progress in developing the next-generation Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS). While the first operational version of RRFS (scheduled for fall 2026) is based on the FV3 dynamical core and the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) data assimilation system, development has shifted toward future versions that will leverage the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) together with the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI). Both RAP and RRFS employ hourly cycling data assimilation systems with partial reinitialization from the Global Forecast System (GFS) every 12 hours, followed by six spin-up cycles. This approach maintains consistency with the large-scale atmospheric state while developing the small-scale structures needed for high-impact weather prediction. However, the spin-up procedure increases computational cost and adds complexity to the cycling framework. Recent global blending capabilities for MPAS, developed through collaboration between NCAR and NOAA/GSL, offer a promising alternative by combining the large-scale information from GFS with the small-scale features of MPAS forecasts. Initial retrospective and real-time experiments have demonstrated improvements in upper-air moisture and wind, as well as surface temperature, dew point, and near-surface wind. We are evaluating whether global blending can replace the spin-up procedure in RRFS through additional retrospective and real-time experiments. If successful, this approach will simplify the RRFS cycling framework, reduce computational costs, and improve operational efficiency while maintaining or enhancing forecast skill. This presentation summarizes the recent evaluation and enhancement of the global blending capability and its potential role in future RRFS operations.

495711.title: First Detection and Characterization of Potassium Emission Lines in Wildfire Spectra With TROPOMI and OCO-2
495711.authors: William James Julstrom, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; and J. Wang and M. Zhou
495711.abstract: The spectrum of burning biomass contains prominent potassium (K) emission lines at 766.7 nm and 770.1 nm. These emission lines are unique to flaming combustion, potentially allowing their use in development of remote sensing techniques to characterize fire phase, flaming temperature, and allow more accurate estimates of fire emissions. Previous studies have shown modest success in detecting potassium emission lines (K-lines) using airborne instruments or meter-scale spatial resolution satellites. This study, for the first time, shows the detection of K-lines in wildfire spectra under low-light conditions using the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), and under local noon daylight conditions using the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2). Our observations clearly show separation of dual K-line peaks and that the line at 766.7 nm (not 770.1 nm) is attenuated strongly by oxygen absorption, in contrast with previous studies. We also show that K-lines can be isolated from the background signal and atmospheric effects using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and that the magnitude of the Principal Component (PC) corresponding to the K-lines correlates well with both fire Visible Light Power (VLP) and Fire Radiative Power (FRP) as shown by the VIIRS FIre Light Detection Algorithm (FILDA), with VLP showing better correlation. This suggests quantitatively that K-lines could add critical information to improve existing active fire algorithms for deriving a daytime fire combustion efficiency and other characteristics to better estimate fire emissions.

495713.title: Tropical and North Pacific Coupling at Decadal Timescales Shapes Basin Variability and Northeast Pacific Marine Heatwaves
495713.authors: Antonietta Capotondi, University of Colorado/CIRES and NOAA/PSL, Boulder, CO; and T. Xu, M. Newman, E. Di Lorenzo, and D. J. Vimont
495713.abstract: Although Pacific decadal variability is often described in terms of processes operating separately in the tropics and North Pacific, interactions between these two regions are also potentially important but are not yet well understood. Here we investigate a dynamical mode of variability with a spatial pattern extending from the Northeast Pacific to the Central equatorial Pacific, the North Pacific-Central Pacific (NPCP) mode, which accounts for a large fraction of decadal variance in both tropical and North Pacific regions and appears to encapsulate tropical-North Pacific coupled dynamics. Indeed, removal of this mode from the data dramatically alters the pattern and persistence of North Pacific variability, with the remainder dominated by processes largely internal to the North Pacific. We also show that the unprecedented intensity and duration of Northeast Pacific marine heatwaves in recent decades were primarily associated with enhanced NPCP variability. On the other hand, interannual sea surface temperature anomalies in the equatorial Pacific, related to El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), did not seem to play any significant role. Enhanced understanding of the NPCP mode may improve assessments of decadal predictability and aid prediction of Northeast Pacific marine heatwaves.

495715.title: Kalman Inflation: A Novel Data Assimilation Technique to Better Resolve Model Overconfidence
495715.authors: Xin Guan, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and M. Y. Chan
495715.abstract: Ensemble Data Assimilation (EnsDA) often employs ensemble covariance inflation methods to mitigate the deleterious impacts of sampling errors and model deficiencies. Existing inflation methods do so by enlarging ensemble perturbations. The ideal inflation method should inflate in a spatiotemporally heterogeneous manner that accounts for the spatiotemporal variability in the assimilated observation network. This presentation presents a novel spatiotemporally varying inflation algorithm that accounts for the spatiotemporal distribution of the assimilated observation network. We operate within the framework where observations are assimilated one at a time (i.e., serial filtering). Instead of explicitly inflating the covariances through inflating the ensemble perturbations, we implicitly inflate ensemble covariances by weaving multiplicative inflation factors into the localized Kalman filter update equations. We call this approach “Kalman Inflation”. Kalman Inflation achieves the desired spatial heterogeneity because those update equations are spatially localized; temporal heterogeneity is achieved via inflating with each serial assimilation. We will present experiments with the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) comparing Kalman Inflation against standard DART adaptive inflation. Early results from the Lorenz-96 low-order model over a range of experimental conditions indicate that Kalman Inflation consistently outperforms those standard methods in terms of RMSEs, and frequently in terms of ensemble consistency. These improvements also suggest that aspects of this algorithm could be adopted by other inflation algorithms for improved performance. We plan to further test Kalman Inflation in more complex models like Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS). If successful, Kalman Inflation could provide a means to improve operational weather prediction.

495716.title: Understanding Contrail Cirrus and Its Radiative Forcing: Insights from the Sectional Contrail Microphysics (SeCoM) Model in E3SMv3
495716.authors: Gan Luo, SUNY-Albany, Albany, NY; and F. Yu
495716.abstract: Contrail cirrus is widely recognized as one of the largest contributors to the non-CO2 radiative impacts of aviation. Quantifying contrail radiative forcing is therefore essential for accurately assessing aviation’s overall climate impact and evaluating potential mitigation strategies, including flight-route optimization, alternative fuels, ice-nuclei seeding, and advanced engine technologies. Contrail ice particle size distribution is a key determinant of contrail microphysical evolution, optical properties, and radiative effects. In this study, we developed and implemented a Sectional Contrail Microphysics (SeCoM) model within the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SMv3) to explicitly represent the size-resolved evolution of contrail ice particles. The simulated 10-minute-old and all-age contrail cloud properties were evaluated against field campaign measurements. The model simulations are consistent with the observed ranges of contrail ice water content (CIWC), contrail ice number concentration (CINC), and volume-mean radius (VR). For young contrails, dilution with ambient air led to decreases in both CIWC and CINC as the plume expanded and mixed with the surrounding atmosphere. For persistent contrails, depositional growth and sublimation became important in controlling the evolution of contrail ice properties. These processes caused CIWC to decrease more slowly than CINC, resulting in an increase in VR of contrail ice particles as persistent contrails aged. The simulated annual mean coverage of thick contrail cirrus (optical depth > 0.05) was 1.07%, substantially higher than the MODIS-retrieved value of 0.40% which counts only those identifiable as contrail cirrus. The seasonal and altitude-dependent variations in global contrail ice particle size distributions were further investigated. A bimodal structure of contrail ice particle sizes was identified near the main aircraft cruising altitudes, with distinct modes centered at approximately 1 μm and 10 μm in particle radius. The smaller mode is primarily associated with freshly emitted ice particles along aircraft flight paths, whereas the larger mode reflects the depositional growth of persistent contrails under favorable ambient conditions that support sustained ice crystal growth. Enhanced number concentrations of large contrail ice particles were found below the primary aircraft flight levels, suggesting that sedimentation of larger ice particles from upper layers plays an important role in shaping the vertical distribution of aged contrail ice. To further assess the magnitude and spatial distribution of this radiative impact, the 2019 global all-sky contrail direct radiative effect simulated by E3SMv3-SeCoM will be presented and discussed.

495720.title: Understanding New Jersey's Warm Season and Heat Health Burden Using Self Organizing Maps
495720.authors: Stephanie Sharo, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ; and J. Shope, B. Lintner, and T. Janoski
495720.abstract: Synoptic-scale weather patterns that contribute to extreme heat disproportionately affect urban populations that are already at a higher risk for heat-related illnesses due to the urban heat island (UHI). To investigate this heat-health relationship further, we collaborated with stakeholders, such as Cooper Health and Robert Wood Johnson Medical Schools, to characterize warm-season, defined as May to September, heat exposure. We used self-organizing maps (SOMs), an unsupervised machine learning technique, to identify relevant synoptic-scale weather patterns associated with extreme heat that can exacerbate the UHI. Our work asks (i) what are the relevant synoptic patterns present in New Jersey’s warm season? (ii) what are the most relevant variables that drive extreme urban heat in SOMs nodes? and (iii) can we identify city-specific extremes through bias-correcting gridded data sets? We gathered hourly meteorological data from the ERA5 reanalysis for the northeastern United States from 2004 to 2024. Atmospheric conditions were characterized using surface pressure, 10-m wind speed and direction, dew point temperature, 2-m air temperature, and solar radiation. Relative humidity, heat index, wet-bulb temperature, and wet-bulb globe temperature were derived from these measurements to examine potential human health impacts. The warm season synoptic conditions across New Jersey were characterized into a SOMs matrix and the node assignments were used to compute conditional averages. The SOMs nodes associated with city specific extreme temperatures, defined as days with a maximum temperature exceeding 90oF, for Camden and New Brunswick, New Jersey, were identified to determine the synoptic patterns driving these extrema. A total of 327 hot days for Camden and 349 hot days for New Brunswick were found over the 20-year period. Differences in synoptic patterns were identified for each city, suggesting that SOMs may prove to be a useful tool in identifying location specific meteorological factors that contribute to urban heat exposure. Future work includes modeling community heat-health burden based on specific SOMs nodes. These results can prepare healthcare workers better for heat events and may improve localized heat warnings for patients.

495722.title: Multi-Scale Impacts of Winds on the Precipitation Structure and Microphysics of Tropical Cyclone Khanun Observed from KPOP-MS 2023 Field Campaign
495722.authors: Tan Duy Dao, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and J. Park, Y. Do, K. Kim, M. M. Bell, G. Lee, and C. C. Nam
495722.abstract: From 9 – 11 August 2023, Tropical Cyclone (TC) Khanun brought widespread and heavy precipitation over the South Korean Peninsula. This event was heavily observed by the Korea Precipitation Observation Program for Mesoscale Systems (KPOP-MS), a 3-week field campaign focused detailed observation of precipitation in the Seoul-Incheon metropolitan area and combined with Korean Meteorological Agency’s (KMA) operational observation network. Observations in the domain included hourly vertical profile launches and observation site such as Supersite 1 at Incheon Airport (ICA1) containing a myriad of in-situ microphysics disdrometer probes and Ka- and X-band radar remote sensing observations. At the supersite, disdrometers 2DVD and one PARSIVEL were installed within a wind cage while a second PARSIVEL was directly exposed to the wind. Khanun was intensively observed across scales in high detail, providing an opportunity for a case study analysis across scales. An uncertain but crucial influence on precipitation is the windspeed. For tropical cyclones particularly, this is important due to its spatially large wind field influence. Wind interactions with the terrain can enhance local precipitation through the enhancement of upward vertical motion. On mesoscale levels, episodic periods of heavy precipitation are often accompanied by wind gusts that can influence the structure of precipitation. This influence can also potentially be case dependent where the wind can support aggregation of precipitation or destructively separate them. On microphysical levels, we hypothesize that higher winds will generally more likely scatter larger precipitation drop sizes. This could subsequently result in a drop-size distribution (DSD) curve which could be related to the wind speed and based to the overall rain rate. Wind Synthesis System using Doppler Measurements (WISSDOM) Three-Dimensional Variational Data Assimilation (3DVAR) vertical velocity composites with vertical profile launches revealed areas of strong upward vertical motion corresponded with stronger precipitation signatures. High-frequency Ka- and X-band weather radar observations from ICA1 supersite indicated rapidly developing precipitation near and at the site. The disdrometer observations indicate enhanced drop size distributions (DSDs) and rain rates during this period. Differences between the sheltered and exposed PARSIVEL measurements could therefore help quantify the sensitivity of disdrometer-derived DSDs and rain rates to wind-induced sampling effects. Comparison with ground-level wind measurements may further distinguish these effects from genuine microphysical variability. This study seeks to explore this uncertainty of the wind on precipitation through the integration of intensive observations of TC Khanun from KPOP-MS evaluated across three scales: Synoptic, Mesoscale, and Microphysics. The goal is to is to unveil potential correlation of TC Khanun’s wind field on the spatial, structural and microphysical change of its precipitation.

495725.title: An AEW-Relative Perspective on Synoptic Modulation of the West Africa Coastal Environment and MCS Rainfall Contributions
495725.authors: Isabelle Jernigan, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and N. Sakaeda
495725.abstract: Rainfall in the West Africa monsoonal region is dominated by MCSs, many of which form inland and offshore and in close proximity to the coastline. The behavior of coastal MCSs and the coastal environment are modulated by synoptic disturbances, such as African Easterly Waves (AEWs). Recent studies have highlighted the dependence of near-surface processes and corresponding coastal MCS characteristics on the location of AEW troughs relative to the coastline using MERRA-2 reanalyses. However, known uncertainties of boundary layer representation in reanalysis data introduce ambiguity as to the underlying mechanisms that govern MCS evolution during the continental-to-maritime transition. This study aims to elucidate these mechanisms by leveraging two satellite-based datasets, CYGNSS and SeaFlux v3, to quantify relevant boundary layer characteristics immediately off the West Africa coastline. Reanalysis datasets are still incorporated to contextualize these satellite-based estimates and characterize the three-dimensional structure of the coastal environment. We find that surface circulations, ocean-atmosphere exchange processes, and associated trends in MCS rainfall vary based on the presence and phase of AEWs. When an AEW trough exists just inland, enhanced onshore surface flow strengthens moisture fluxes and convergence along the coastline, increasing precipitation within 200 km offshore. Such findings improve our understanding of coastal MCS convective processes, with implications for tropical monsoon regions across the globe.

495726.title: Preparing Our Users for the Future. An Update and Plan for the Next Generation of Geostationary Extended Observations (GeoXO) User Engagement
495726.abstract: In the 2030’s, NOAA’s Extended Observations (GeoXO) satellite system will expand observations of Earth that the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES-R) constellation currently provides from geostationary orbit. GeoXO will watch over the Western Hemisphere as part of NOAA’s observing system that supports short-term forecasts and warnings of extreme weather and environmental hazards. This observing system will deliver information that sophisticated forecasting models use to predict weather patterns. The information GeoXO supplies will improve short-term forecasting and warning of severe weather and hazards that threaten the security and well-being of everyone in the Western Hemisphere. NOAA is planning a two-satellite operational GeoXO constellation, plus two replacement satellites. Each spacecraft will carry an imager and a sounder. The first GeoXO satellite, scheduled for launch in 2032, is planned to carry the GOES-R-era Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) and a new GeoXO Sounder instrument. The remaining GeoXO satellites, planned for launch in 2034, 2039 and 2043, will carry the new GeoXO Imager and GeoXO Sounder. To ensure success of this mission, it is critical for the users of this data to be prepared for its arrival. This includes user engagement as we enter the user readiness phase of the mission that includes activities that involve utilizing precursor data sources such synthetic GeoXO imager and sounder data as well as the new Eumetsat geostationary imager and sounder that were recently put into orbit. In addition, there is still a vast population unaware of current GOES-R and upcoming GeoXO capabilities. A multi-faceted plan to expand the reach of the knowledge about our data and bringing together various sector decision makers to test and provide use cases for the applications of this data during the user readiness phase will discussed.

495727.title: Coupled Analytical Model for the Internal Boundary Layer Height, Wall Shear Stress and Mean Streamwise Velocity Behind an Abrupt Roughness Transition
495727.authors: Kingshuk Mondal, Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad, Hyderabad, Telangana, India
495727.abstract: The atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) flow is influenced by momentum flux imposed by heterogeneous land surfaces, characterized by the aerodynamic roughness length (z0). We develop a coupled analytical model to predict the internal boundary layer (IBL) height, wall shear stress (w) and the mean streamwise velocity (u) behind an abrupt roughness transition. Here the roughness length changes from z01 to z02 leading to either a smooth-to-rough (z01<z02) or a rough-to-smooth (z01>z02) transition. This is an idealization of a land to sea transition, or from an agricultural field to a forest. We implement an established analytical model for the streamwise velocity developed by Ghaisas (2020). The flow is in equilibrium with the first surface of roughness z01. We assume that three distinct layers form behind the first roughness transition. The flow adjusts to the new surface conditions (roughness z02) within the equilibrium boundary layer (EBL) which extends from the surface to a height e. Between the EBL and the internal boundary layer (IBL) formed behind the roughness transition, the effects of the roughness change are felt but the flow has not yet fully adjusted to the new conditions, creating a transition region. Beyond the height of the IBL (i), the flow is unaffected by the changed surface conditions and is still in equilibrium with the upstream surface conditions. Here, both e and i are functions of the streamwise direction (x). The key framework of this work is to model the friction velocity (u*) and the eddy viscosity (t) in each of these layers. In the equilibrium layers, u* is vertically invariant, taking the upstream value u*1 above i and u*2,loc(x) within the EBL. In the transition region, the friction velocity varies linearly with the vertical height (z) from the value u*1 at i to u*2,loc(x) at e to ensure continuity between the layers. The eddy viscosity is assumed to be linear in the equilibrium layers and modelled as a parabola in the transition region such that it has the values u*1i at i and u*2,loc(x)e at e. Here =0.41 is the von-Karmann constant. A tunable parameter controls the concavity of the parabola. The vertical gradient of velocity u/z is calculated as -u*2/t. This yields distinct velocity gradient expressions for each layer, which are then integrated over z to obtain the velocity profiles. e is assumed to be a constant fraction of i in accordance with a previous study. Empirical models for i were used to close this model. We introduce a modified diffusion analogy to model i which can be coupled with the streamwise velocity model to simultaneously solve for u*2,loc(x) and i(x). The previous framework modelled i growth by linking it to the turbulent diffusion and the mean vertical advection, but it incorrectly hypothesized that the vertical diffusion intensity (measured by the standard deviation of the vertical velocity fluctuations w) was proportional to the upstream friction velocity u*1. We demonstrate through statistical analysis of previously reported large-eddy simulations (LES) data that w is instead correlated with the downstream friction velocity u*2,loc which leads to the relation w=1.25u*2,loc. Furthermore, the earlier framework assumed that the characteristic velocity difference driving the vertical advection was independent of the downstream distance. We rectify this assumption by computing the mean vertical velocity using mass conservation. This formulation yields a non-linear equation for i governed by a parameter A1. To make the current framework fully predictive, the parameters and A1 are modelled as an algebraic function of the upstream-to-downstream roughness ratio m=z01/z02. Together with the model for the streamwise velocity, the model for i forms a system of two non-linear equations that can be solved together to yield u*2,loc(x) and i(x) at every location x downstream of the roughness transition. These coupled non-linear equations are solved numerically, e.g., using the ‘fsolve’ function in MATLAB. The present framework is validated with twelve sets of experimental/LES datasets. Two of those cases, each for a smooth-to-rough and a rough-to-smooth transition are shown in the figures attached with the abstract. We obtain fair quantitative and qualitative agreement between the experimental/LES data and the model predictions. The model is able to capture the overshoot and undershoot in the wall shear stress values when the flow interacts with smooth-to-rough and rough-to-smooth transitions respectively. For the mean streamwise velocity profiles, the proposed model predicts the acceleration and deceleration behaviors correctly. The model also predicts the streamwise evolution of the IBL height with good agreement with the experiments/LES. This coupled model can be used to determine the incoming wind velocity profile to a wind turbine/farm which is often used as an input to wind turbine wake models. Future work will extend this study to include thermally stratified conditions.

495728.title: GFT-C: Real-Time Tropical Cyclone Forecasting from the Latent Representations of a Weather Foundation Model
495728.authors: Dhruvit Patel, Silurian AI Inc., Edison, NJ; and G. Studer, N. Shankar, X. Zhang, and J. K. Gupta
495728.abstract: Foundation models trained on large, multimodal Earth-system datasets learn representations that are broadly and physically useful, yet their value for specific operational forecasting problems and their readiness for transition to operations remains largely untested. We investigate this with the Generative Forecasting Transformer (GFT), our global multimodal weather foundation model, asking how far its learned latent representations can be repurposed for tropical cyclone (TC) forecasting using only lightweight, task-specific models. A compact intensity model that reads GFT's latent state (with the foundation model held fixed) produces skillful forecasts of maximum sustained wind and minimum central pressure. Evaluated out-of-sample over the 2025 season to 120-h lead, its intensity skill is comparable to NHC's HFSA/HFSB models, and its forecasts are essentially unbiased across lead times. The model captures 6-hourly intensity change, including rapid intensification and weakening episodes, and the intense tail of the intensity distribution that is traditionally challenging for guidance. The system runs in real time on NOAA infrastructure, with forecasts displayed publicly. Building on the same representations, we are extending the approach to generate high-resolution storm-centered spatial fields directly from GFT's latent representations to resolve inner-core storm structure, and initial results will be presented. Together these results demonstrate the flexibility of the foundation-model approach: a single general-purpose representation supports rapid development of skillful, deployable TC products with minimal task-specific machinery. We describe the method, the 2025 verification, and the operational transition, and discuss implications for foundation-model-based guidance in operational TC forecasting.

495731.title: From Teacher Capacity to Student Engagement: A Community-Based Model for Weather Education in K-12
495731.authors: Donald Long, Notre Dame of Maryland University, Baltimore, MD; and M. Robey and D. W. Waugh
495731.abstract: The Baltimore Community Weather Network (BCWN)—originating from the Baltimore Social-Environmental Collaborative (BSEC)—is a community-based initiative that connects over 50 weather stations across Baltimore City, with 18 located at Baltimore City Public Schools sites. Analysis of science teachers’ feedback identified K-8 educators lacked sufficient competence and confidence in Earth and atmospheric science topics, while listening sessions identified a need for curriculum-aligned educational materials to support the use of the weather stations. This exploratory project introduces a community partnership model for atmospheric scientists to support teachers in building their capacity for integrating weather, climate, and data literacy into instruction. Through this work, we aim to develop atmospheric science professional development rooted in the science of learning, investigate how teachers use weather station data for instruction, and explore means of increasing student participation in atmospheric science.

495733.title: Improving Thermodynamic Retrievals from Ground-Based Infrared Spectrometers In Cloudy Environments Using Pseudo-Observations
495733.authors: Laura Bianco, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and D. L. Jackson, E. J. Thompson, B. Adler, and D. D. Turner
495733.abstract: Temperature and humidity profiles retrieved from ground-based infrared spectrometers (IRS) and microwave radiometers (MWRs) exhibit a degradation in vertical resolution as a function of height due to the decrease in the information content in the radiometric observations. The relatively coarse vertical resolution of the retrieved profiles smooths through strong gradients in temperature and moisture, such as at the top of the convective boundary layer (CBL). In many of these situations, there are clouds at the top of the CBL where the relative humidity at the cloud base is known to be close to 100%. This study investigates the use of a pseudo-observation of relative humidity (RH) at the cloud base when a collocated ceilometer identifies the cloud and the cloud is warmer than -10 oC (as ascertained from the retrieval). The Tropospheric Remotely Observed Profiling via Optimal Estimation (TROPoe) retrieval algorithm is used in this study, and various assumptions on the value of the pseudo-observation of RH and its associated uncertainty are evaluated. This study uses the IRS and ceilometer datasets that were part of the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) mobile facility deployment on the Ronald H. Brown during the 2015 ARM Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment (ACAPEX) field campaign, which experienced a range of cloudiness during its cruise from Hawaii to California. During this approximately 3-week campaign, more than 150 radiosondes were launched which are used to evaluate different configurations of the retrieval. Results from this study will help in strategizing TROPoe methodologies that will be employed during the Tropical Pacific Observing System (TPOS) Equatorial Pacific Experiment (TEPEX) ocean-atmosphere field campaign scheduled across 2027–2028.

495734.title: Machine Learning-Based Radar-Gauge Merging for Urban Flood Modelling in Sparse Gauge Regions
495734.authors: Aaritha V V, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai, TN, India; and B. Rajagopalan, V. Chandrasekar, and S. N. Kuiry
495734.abstract: Reliable rainfall estimation remains a persistent challenge in urban flood modelling. Precipitation exhibits pronounced spatial and temporal variability, while ground-based observations are often limited. These factors reduce the accuracy of flood simulations. Radar-based quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) must reconcile with the point-scale accuracy of rain gauge networks. However, this integration is challenging because of range-dependent radar beam geometry errors, spatially non-stationary bias fields, and sparse, irregularly distributed rain gauge networks. To address these limitations, this study develops a two-stage radar-gauge merging framework termed Random Forest with Gauge Residual Smoothing (RF-GRS), combining machine-learning-based nonlinear bias correction with distance-adaptive residual interpolation. In the first stage, a RF regressor trained on rainfall state features comprising instantaneous and antecedent radar values, local spatial texture, terrain elevation, and radar geometric predictors to removes the systematic, range-dependent nonlinear bias inherent to radar QPE. In the second stage, residual gauge errors unexplained by the RF model are propagated to unsampled locations through a Gaussian-weighted smoothing scheme. Conventional kriging fits a variogram and solves a covariance matrix separately at each estimation point, which is computationally expensive and often ill-conditioned for sparse or uneven gauge networks. The proposed Gaussian-weighted smoothing instead uses a single pooled variogram, fit once, to set the kernel bandwidth, avoiding repeated matrix inversion while retaining the spatial correlation information, making it lighter and more stable under sparse networks with comparable correction accuracy. The framework evaluated across multiple storm events in Chennai metropolitan region, India. Relative to uncorrected radar QPE, the proposed method reduces RMSE by 14.8 to 30.5% and improves Pearson correlation from a baseline of 0.57 to values between 0.71 and 0.79. The proposed radar-gauge merging methodology is further validated through its integration with urban flood modelling as a secondary validation. The precipitation fields are forced to a two-dimensional hydraulic model (HEC-RAS) to simulate discharge and flood inundation for the study events. Model performance is evaluated by comparing simulations driven by the RF-GRS merged product, rain gauge observations, and uncorrected radar precipitation, with all simulated discharge and inundation depths validated against observed field records. The proposed methodology and its two stage validation results demonstrate a generalisable pathway for operational radar quantitative precipitation estimation in regions with sparse gauge networks.

495741.title: Changes in Wildfires, Atmospheric Composition, and Air Quality in CMIP7 ScenarioMIP Simulations
495741.authors: Meiyun Lin, NOAA, Princeton, NJ; and J. Dunne, L. Sentman, F. Paulot, E. Shevliakova, S. Malyshev, V. Naik, and E. Stofferahn
495741.abstract: Large wildfires have become increasingly common in recent decades across North America, causing severe air pollution, loss of life, and property damage. Five of the most destructive wildfire seasons of the past half-century occurred during the last decade, raising concerns that climate change is already altering wildfire regimes. Although emerging machine-learning approaches have been used to project wildfire smoke PM2.5 exposure under future climate change, much less is known about how changing wildfire activity will affect other components of atmospheric composition, particularly ozone. Wildfire smoke plumes can enhance downwind ozone formation through emissions of fire-related precursors and interactions between wildfire-derived VOCs and urban NOx, with chemical processes substantially more complex than those governing smoke PM2.5. Recent developments in Earth system modeling at NOAA’s Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL) provide an opportunity to investigate these coupled processes. Here, we systematically examine changes in wildfire activity, atmospheric composition, and air quality from 1860 to 2100 using GFDL-ESM4.5 simulations conducted as part of the 7th Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP7). GFDL-ESM4.5 includes interactive wildfire emissions from a dynamic vegetation model, dynamic wildfire plume rise, and interactive atmospheric chemistry. We analyze CMIP7 ScenarioMIP simulations spanning high, intermediate, and very low levels of climate change, together with parallel experiments in which anthropogenic aerosol and ozone precursor emissions are fixed at 2021 levels to isolate the effects of climate change from air pollution controls. Preliminary results show substantial increases in wildfire activity, PM2.5, and ozone pollution over western North America and Mediterranean Europe from the 2050s through 2100 under the high-climate-change scenario. In contrast, PM2.5 and ozone pollution decline throughout the 21st century under the very-low climate-change and emission scenario. We will present quantitative analyses of changes in mean concentrations and extreme pollution events across the five CMIP7 scenarios and assess the relative contributions of climate-driven wildfire changes and anthropogenic emission controls.

495742.title: Continued Analysis of WRF Single-Column Sensitivity to PBL Schemes and Moisture During the August 21st, 2017 Total Solar Eclipse
495742.authors: Wesley Taylor, Millersville Univ., Thomasville, PA
495742.abstract: A continuation of previously presented preliminary results, this work continues analysis of observed phenomena from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement Southern Great Plains (ARM-SGP) site during the August 21st, 2017 total solar eclipse event, which observed a temporary increase in winds above the surface within the planetary boundary layer (PBL) shortly after totality, similar in behavior to a short-lived nocturnal low-level jet (LLJ). Using radiosonde data from ARM-SGP at 0540 UTC 8/16/2017 as the initial conditions, simulations of the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) single column model both with and without eclipse Besselian elements were able to successfully reproduce the PBL response to the reduced insolation from the eclipse, particularly the collapse in the PBL depth reminiscent of the evening transition and the development of an eclipse-generated LLJ approximately 300 meters above the surface. Robust across both the non-local Yonsei University (YSU) and local Mellor-Yamada-Nakanishi-Niino (MYNN) PBL parameterization schemes and varying humidity levels, the differences in PBL structures across these experiments are explored, with improved clarity of non-linear variations in moisture effects on horizontal wind speed as well as additional findings related to Turbulent Kinetic Energy and other previously unexplored parameters. The further refinement of this work is meant to better distill potential implications of some of the most fundamental dynamics of LLJs driven by reduced insolation as reproduced by the relative simplicity of single column models across variations in both model and environmental configurations.

495743.title: Exploring Coupled Tropical Pacific Variability within a Multi-Branch β-Variational Autoencoder
495743.authors: Emily Faith Wisinski, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and M. J. Molina, K. J. C. Hall, H. Bao, S. Mahajan, N. Rosenbloom, and J. T. Fasullo
495743.abstract: Tropical Pacific variability overlaps across variables, timescales, and space, making it difficult for linear methods to extract a shared, reduced representation of this coupled structure. This study analyzes the latent encodings and dimensions of a multi-branch β-variational autoencoder (β-VAE) trained on monthly tropical Pacific fields, including sea surface temperature (SST), ocean heat content (OHC), and outgoing longwave radiation (OLR). We train the model using the Department of Energy (DOE) Energy Exascale Earth System Model Version 2 (E3SMv2) 500-year preindustrial control simulation (piControl) to examine processes without any external forcings (i.e., without anthropogenic effects) and to provide a sufficiently large training dataset. We assess the model’s reconstruction skill and physical interpretability of the latent space, finding that the β-VAE model generalizes well in reconstructing the input fields, with modest degradation from training to test performance, and preserves the dominant basin-scale structure of SST, OHC, and OLR fields. Latent space diagnostics show that variability is organized unevenly across the latent space dimensions between variables: SST is concentrated in a smaller subset of latent dimensions compared to a broader distribution seen in OHC and OLR. We find that several latent dimensions align with El Niño and La Niña-like variability, while others capture variability related to decadal timescales. Sensitivity experiments and latent traversals further identify latent dimensions associated with eastern- and central-Pacific-like El Niño events, subsurface-dominant, and atmosphere-dominant variability. The results indicate that the multi-branch β-VAE yields skillful reconstructions and physically informative reduced representation of coupled tropical Pacific variability, with potential applications for ENSO predictability, teleconnection metrics, and generation of synthetic data to extend limited observational records.

495744.title: WRF North American Regional Climate Simulations and Hydroclimate Applications
495744.authors: Xin Zhou, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and S. C. Pryor, J. A. Lee, S. E. Haupt, J. Dudhia, and R. J. Knepper
495744.abstract: Simulations that generate high-fidelity, high spatial and temporal resolution output are required to advance understanding of possible future regional climate conditions and inform climate change adaptation measures. With the relatively high resolution compared to global models, regional simulations such as those performed under the Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX) umbrella can better represent both physical processes and responses to changes in land cover. Because these climate simulations generate vast amounts of data, conventional archived datasets are sometimes limited to core variables that represent fundamental atmospheric states, such as temperature, pressure, humidity, and wind, etc., at the surface and at given pressure levels. However, this can compromise the ability to diagnose causes of simulated changes in various applications, including hydroclimate conditions. For example, high-resolution precipitation rates, convective available potential energy (CAPE), convection inhibition (CIN), radar reflectivity, hail rate, and estimated hail sizes are useful for assessing how extreme precipitation may respond to changes in atmospheric and land-use conditions. It is thus imperative to archive as wide a range of parameters as possible to enable such research. In this presentation, we report recently concluded multi-decadal North America regional climate simulations in the historical and future climates using the Weather Research and Forecast (WRF) model. The work is part of the Integrated WRF Framework (I-WRF) project, which is a coordinated containerized framework that seamlessly integrates a multi-node WRF container, an optimized Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) container, and an enhanced Analysis and Visualization container for more portable and productive research. The WRF model source code is also updated to prevent round-off errors in a long-term simulation. These WRF simulations downscale 40 years of the MPI-ESM1-2-LR simulation in the historical climate (1960-1999) and the SSP5-8.5 projection (2040-2079) over the North America Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (NA-CORDEX) domain at 12-km resolution. The simulations employ nudging and consider changes in land use land cover (LULC) and aerosol optical depth (AOD). In addition, we account for parameters that are missing in coarse MPI simulations but are critical in higher-resolution regional climate simulations. Specifically, the missing lake temperature from MPI-ESM1-2-LR is approximated by the 30-day averaged surface skin temperature ahead of a given time step to accommodate the seasonal lag of lake temperatures to the surrounding land surface temperature. Spatial allocation of urban expansion is informed by the Gao and O’Neill (2020) urban projections. Therefore, these WRF simulations are especially useful for studying land-atmosphere interactions in a changing climate with a focus on urban expansion. The simulation dataset is ready and will be made publicly available shortly. In this presentation, we focus on hydroclimate conditions in these regional climate simulations.
