The precipitation climate over North America as simulated by WRF during the historical period naturally exhibits some similarity to that from MPI with dry bias over the eastern half of the continent particularly during the summer months, and small wet bias over the west relative to IMERG and ERA5. However, the climate change signal (SSP5-8.5 minus the historical period) differs markedly between WRF and MPI. Specifically, while both suggest drying over much of the western USA, MPI direct output suggests wetting over the east while WRF indicates only small sub-regions with any change in annual mean total precipitation. Diagnoses aimed at understanding and decomposing the reasons for these differences are underway. The WRF simulations are also being used to examine how urban rainfall enhancement (URE) may change in a warmed world and as urban areas expand. Following the approach of Pryor et al. (2025), sample pairs of urban and rural grid cells for each of the largest 40 urban areas in North America are used to examine evidence for URE in the historical and future simulations. The results suggest that in many locations where urban enhancement of upper percentile rainfall rates is manifest in the historical period, that signal is suppressed in the future. The causes of change and specifically relationships with parameters such as CAPE and CIN are currently being explored and will be discussed. References: Gao, J., and B. C. O’Neill, 2020: Mapping global urban land for the 21st century with data-driven simulations and Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. Nature Communications, 11, 2302. Pryor S.C., Barthelmie R.J., Zhou X. and Huffman G. 2025: Re-examining urban rainfall enhancement over North America. Environmental Research Letters 20 034035 doi: 10.1088/1748-9326/adb507 Acknowledgements: Funding for this work is provided by the Integrated WRF Framework (I-WRF) project under NSF Award No. 2209711.

495746.title: Advancing AI Emulations of Physics-Based NWP Models through Investigating Training Data Generation Strategies
495746.authors: Fnu Horeb, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and M. Y. Chan
495746.abstract: AI emulations of physics-based numerical weather prediction (AIWP) models have recently made significant progress. Further progress will likely be achieved through advancing the approaches used to generate training datasets. Such advancement requires a better understanding of how different aspects of the training datasets influence the performance of AIWP. This study advances our understanding through varying the approaches used to generate training data. AIWP models are trained to predict the time tendency of the atmospheric state from an inputted atmospheric state. Our general training data generation approach is to first generate model state training data via some approach and then use short model integrations to construct the tendency training data. Five model state generation approaches are explored (in order of increasing sophistication): (1) random draws from a uniform distribution, (2) random draws from an uncorrelated Gaussian distribution, (3) random draws from a Gaussian distribution with climatological covariance structures, (4) a long model integration, and (5) i.i.d. samples from the model’s climatological distribution. Approach 4 is the current de facto approach for AIWP. We then compare the performances of the neural networks resulting from these model state training data generation approaches to investigate how the distribution of the model state training dataset may influence AIWP performance. In this presentation, we will discuss our results from training AIWP models using these five approaches. Thus far, we have trained dense neural networks to emulate the chaotic 40-variable Lorenz 1996 wave-on-a-ring model. Our results indicate that increasingly sophisticated training data generation approaches generally translate to better neural network performance. However, there are interesting exceptions. Approaches 4 and 5 result in similar neural network performances with high training data volumes, and approaches 2 and 3 yield neural networks of similar quality. We plan to further explore these approaches by training neural network emulators of a global atmospheric model (e.g., Model for Prediction Across Scales). This presentation will describe our findings and discuss them through the lens of fundamental statistical principles.

495749.title: National Weather Service Alaska Sea Ice Program: Transforming Decision Support in the Arctic
495749.authors: Michael T. Lawson, NWS, Anchorage, AK
495749.abstract: As interest in the Alaskan Arctic rapidly expands across maritime navigation, resource exploration, tourism, and national security, the remoteness and lack of observations present severe challenges for weather and sea ice forecasting. In response, the Alaska Sea Ice Program (ASIP) has transformed and modernized its Impact-based Decision Support Services (IDSS) to deliver faster, more accurate, and actionable sea ice analysis and forecast information. This presentation highlights how ASIP has successfully enhanced partner engagement and risk communication. Over recent years, ASIP has provided critical IDSS for national security events, including a North Slope fiber optic cable disruption, as well as environmental response efforts for oil discharges in complex ice conditions. In addition, ASIP has provided embedded decision support, deploying a sea ice analyst aboard the R/V Sikuliaq for annual research missions. Furthermore, ASIP’s real-time risk communication has proven vital for life-protecting maritime operations. Following the emergency support of the beset R/V Norseman II in 2024, ASIP provided consecutive years of decision support through the Bering Strait and Chukchi Sea ice pack. This capability was tested during the historic 2025–2026 ice season, which brought 50-year extreme ice conditions to the Bering Sea. By delivering targeted IDSS to the Bering Sea fishing fleet and assisting trapped vessels in False Pass and around Saint Lawrence Island, ASIP directly protected lives, property and enhanced the national economy.

495754.title: Operational Tropical Cyclone Forecasting with AI; Google’s WeatherNext Progress In TC Forecasting
495754.authors: Ferran Alet, Google DeepMind, London, United kingdom; and T. R. Andersson, I. Price, S. Markou, A. El-Kadi, D. Masters, A. X. Li, S. Merchant, N. Williams, G. Thornton, K. MacKay, O. Graham, B. Gaiarin, A. Uddin, D. Shah, E. Kruse, W. Hogsett, D. A. Zelinsky, J. P. Cangialosi, J. Martinez, J. Franklin, M. DeMaria, K. D. Musgrave, C. Bain, H. A. Titley, J. Stott, R. Lam, A. Bell, P. Komarek, A. Sanchez-Gonzalez, and P. Battaglia
495754.abstract: In 2025, Google’s WeatherNext advanced tropical cyclone (TC) forecasting by 24 hours of lead time—achieving 3-day forecast errors equivalent to or better than preceding 2-day operational baselines. This step-change represents roughly a decade of historical progress in the meteorological community. In this talk, we analyze how this leap in predictive skill, and subsequent improvements, is directly benefiting operational TC tracking and impact mitigation. Surprisingly, our research reveals that state-of-the-art intensity forecasting can be achieved using only 0.25° analysis inputs. Furthermore, a smaller neural network relying on just 1.0° resolution inputs would have still outperformed the best operational models. This finding strongly suggests that large-scale synoptic features contain significantly more predictive signal for TC intensity than previously believed, potentially opening new questions. Finally, we will detail the latest 2026 advancements from the WeatherNext team, deployed in conjunction with our operational collaborators at NHC, UKMet, CIRA, and WNI/JMA.

495755.title: Operational Application of the Flash Flood 4-Panel Technique to the Desert Southwest
495755.authors: Cole Gabos, Univ. of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. I. Christian and K. Christian
495755.abstract: Within the U.S over the last 30 years, flash flooding has been a leading cause of weather-related fatalities. For flash flood operations in the National Weather Service (NWS), Flash Flood Guidance (FFG) has historically been used as one of the primary tools to provide guidance to NWS forecasters on when to issue flash flood advisories and warnings. However, a newly developed technique that utilizes a four-panel structure of multiple real-time variables has the potential to provide a regionally calibrated method for flash flood detection in the Desert Southwest. This region's differences in topography, scattered population density, soil composition and moisture retention, as well as climatological factors such as heavy precipitation during the monsoon season, pose a unique challenge. By combining Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) products, hydrological analysis, and NASA soil moisture data, we hope to expand a four-panel technique to cover the broader four-corners region. After extensive analysis in the Flagstaff, AZ county warning area (CWA), we found 1-hr radar-only Quantitative Precipitation Estimate (1-hr QPE), maximum QPE-to-Gridded Flash Flood Guidance ratio (GFFG), Coupled Routing and Excess Storage (CREST) model unit streamflow, and CREST Hydrophobic Unit Flow to best represent flash flood severity. Our research so far has provided a promising geographically tailored method for flash flood detection in the Flagstaff, AZ region, with several minutes of lead time and increased forecasting confidence. The next steps intend to capture the larger complexities of rainfall, terrain, and soil saturation across the broader Desert Southwest.

495759.title: Evolution of MRMS Radar Merging: An Architectural and Algorithmic Comparison of W2merger and Fusion
495759.authors: Robert E. Toomey, University of Oklahoma - CIWRO, Norman , OK; and C. Langston, K. Cooper, M. Taylor, T. Miller, G. Fisher, T. M. Smith, and R. A. Clark III
495759.abstract: The Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system relies on the rapid ingestion, quality control, and merging of polarimetric radar variables to produce seamless 3D mosaics across geographic regions. Historically, this merging process was handled by W2merger, which achieved efficiency by relying heavily on pre-computed, static spatial lookup caches based on known Volume Coverage Patterns (VCPs). While this architecture minimized CPU usage, it introduced significant operational rigidity; any changes to a radar's VCP or operational status required regenerating massive cache files, creating deployment and maintenance bottlenecks. This presentation provides a comprehensive architectural and mathematical comparison between the legacy W2merger system and its successor, Fusion. We contrast the underlying methodologies to highlight how Fusion trades higher CPU utilization for unparalleled operational agility. By eliminating static lookup tables, Fusion projects grid geometries and calculates spatial weights dynamically as radial sets are ingested. This allows the system to seamlessly handle radars dropping offline or altering their VCPs in real-time without requiring system downtime or cache regeneration. Furthermore, we explore how this shift to dynamic processing fundamentally alters the underlying mathematics of the merge. We will contrast the algorithmic approaches of both systems, highlighting Fusion’s dynamic S-curve vertical interpolation which adapts to actual received tilts rather than rigid expected spreads, and its real-time evaluation of horizontal distance weighting. By detailing the shift to a highly parallelized, multi-stage pipeline, this poster will present quantitative performance metrics and visual examples comparing the two systems. Ultimately, we demonstrate how Fusion’s VCP-agnostic design modernizes the MRMS framework, drastically simplifying deployment while improving algorithmic resilience.

495767.title: Analysis of Tilt Dynamics in Simulated Tropical Cyclones
495767.authors: David A. Schecter, NWRA, Boulder, CO; NorthWest Research Associates, Boulder, CO
495767.abstract: Tropical cyclones exposed to appreciable vertical wind shear commonly have tilts that hinder intensification. Such tilts may precess upshear and eventually diminish so that conditions for spinup improve. However, tilt behavior is variable and can be difficult to fully understand. To help elucidate the dynamics, this study develops a versatile method for quantitatively assessing how various factors contribute to the (negative or positive) growth rate and angular velocity of the tilt vector. As usual, the tilt vector is defined to be the horizontal displacement of the middle-tropospheric vortex center from the lower center. The analysis rests on defining the vortex center at each level to be the point at which the origin of a polar coordinate system must be placed to maximize the peak value of the azimuthally averaged tangential velocity. Assuming continuous motion, equations for the velocities of the vortex centers are derived and converted into equations for the time-derivatives of the magnitude and angle of the tilt vector. The converted equations are used to analyze continuous tilt dynamics in an illustrative simulation of a tropical cyclone progressing toward the onset of rapid intensification. The growth rate and angular velocity of the tilt vector are first decomposed into parts attributable to "internal" processes and the environmental shear flow. It is found that the internal part of the growth rate (angular velocity) more often than not (almost always) opposes the environmental part over the course of the simulation. Further analysis is conducted to reveal how distinct subparts of the internal contribution, such as those associated with horizontal advective vorticity fluxes and vertical advection of momentum, compare to one another at different times. Ultimately, the diagnostic framework is used to assess the impacts of flow disturbances linked to regions of "convective" and "stratiform" cloud-processes on precession and alignment. By certain measures, it is found that both types of disturbances tend to promote cyclonic precession, whereas only the convection-related disturbances tend to promote alignment in the simulation at hand. In addition to exhibiting extended periods of continuous motion, the tilt vector of the simulated tropical cyclone has moments of discontinuous change that account for significant steps of decay (or growth) and rotation. A complementary method for analyzing such jumps has been developed and will be briefly illustrated. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation under grant AGS-2208205.

495770.title: Continuing the Dark Target Aerosol Climate Data Record from MODIS to VIIRS
495770.authors: Virginia Ruth Sawyer, NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; Science and Technology Corporation, Hampton, VA; and R. C. Levy, Y. R. Shi, and M. Kim
495770.abstract: The two MODIS sensors on Terra and Aqua continue to operate well into 2026, but their observed reflectances increasingly show the effects of the orbital drift that began in 2021. As each spacecraft’s equatorial crossing time moves farther from noon, the sunlight available for aerosol retrievals grows gradually dimmer. Improvements to the Dark Target aerosol retrieval algorithm for MODIS Collection 7 and VIIRS version 2.2 help make results more consistent among the five polar orbiting sensors: besides upstream calibration and cloud mask updates, Dark Target now uses higher-resolution internal cloud masking with better cirrus testing, more accurate surface reflectance parameterization for land retrievals, cross-calibration to bring VIIRS reflectances closer to Aqua MODIS, a new dust detection model, log fitting to eliminate non-physical values, and other new features. However, small calibration offsets between sensors remain. Of the two MODIS and three VIIRS sensors, Aqua MODIS and NOAA-20 VIIRS achieve the best validation scores against AERONET. Therefore, to obtain a single climate data record for aerosol optical depth, one could swap out Aqua for NOAA-20. Because of orbital drift and other possible data degradation at the end of the MODIS mission, the best moment to switch sensors is before the end of Aqua, and likely before 2021. Using the new level 3 gridded average products for MODIS and VIIRS, we compare different ways to construct a time series of aerosol optical depth beyond the end of the 25+ year MODIS mission.

495772.title: Multiscale Variability of Great Lakes Net Basin Supply Components: A Five Lake Wavelet Analysis
495772.authors: Alisa H. Young, NOAA/OAR/GLERL, Ann Arbor, MI
495772.abstract: Great Lakes water-level variability significantly impacts regional infrastructure, coastal ecosystems, navigation, and water resource management. Understanding the temporal behavior of the hydrologic processes that drive these fluctuations is essential for effective prediction and adaptive management. Conventional spectral analysis has limited ability to characterize hydrologic variability whose frequency and intensity evolve over time and are nonstationary. This study presents a five-lake analysis of Net Basin Supply (NBS) components including overlake precipitation and evaporation, and runoff across the Laurentian Great Lakes. Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) and Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) are included in the suite of methods used to characterize the dominant non-stationary modes of NBS component variability, its temporal evolution and cross-lake dynamics. The analysis period is from 1950-2022 and uses monthly estimates of overlake precipitation and evaporation, and runoff from the Large Lakes Statistical Water Balance Model (L2SWBM); a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) framework developed by NOAA’s Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory (GLERL) and the University of Michigan. Morlet wavelet decomposition and red-noise significance testing are used to identify statistically significant periodicities throughout the 73-year period. Wavelet coherence is further applied to examine wavelet synchronization and phase relationships between lake to lake hydrological components, highlighting evidence of system connectivity. Findings provide a robust spectral classification framework for improving Great Lakes water level prediction and coastal management strategies across the Great Lakes basin.

495773.title: Semantic Segmentation of Ozone Induced Foliar Injury in Bioindicator Plants Using a U-Net Architecture
495773.authors: Amy Chen, Stony Brook University, Rego Park, NY; UCAR, Stony Brook, NY
495773.abstract: Ground-level ozone is a phytotoxic air pollutant that produces visible foliar injury in sensitive bioindicator species, and the standard assessment protocol relies on trained observers visually estimating damage in the field. Manual scoring is reproducible across experts but slow, subjective at fine scales, and difficult to apply at the plot densities needed for regional monitoring. In this study, we trained a U-Net convolutional segmentation model to produce pixel-level injury masks from RGB photographs of four bioindicator species, namely Snap Bean , Coneflower , Milkweed, and Potato, drawn from an ozone bioindicator monitoring garden. Source images were tiled into 512×512 pixel patches, yielding 3,632 training, 1,168 validation, and 1,039 test patches with corresponding pixel-level labels binarized from manual annotations. The network was trained for 100 epochs using a combined binary cross-entropy and Dice loss with on-the-fly geometric and photometric augmentation applied only to the training split. The model converged to a validation Dice score of roughly 0.71 to 0.72 and a validation loss near 0.20, and the best checkpoint reached a test Dice of 0.73 and a test loss of 0.18, indicating close agreement between validation and test performance. Across the 1,039 test patches the predicted damage fraction was strongly right-skewed, with a median of 0% and a mean of about 2.4%, rising to roughly 71% on the most heavily injured patches. This reflects that the test set was dominated by lightly affected tissue alongside a minority of severely injured patches. The pipeline shows that pixel-level injury quantification is feasible from standard RGB imagery without specialized hardware, which opens a path toward automating ozone bioindicator surveys at meaningful spatial and temporal scales.

495774.title: Toward Two-Day Probabilistic Convective Forecasting with an AI Emulator of the HRRR
495774.authors: Marshall Romanick Baldwin, CIRA, Boulder, CO; and K. Haynes, C. White, I. Ebert-Uphoff, and I. Jankov
495774.abstract: Global data-driven AINWP models have demonstrated an improvement in forecast skill over traditional NWP systems at a fraction of the computational cost as well as the ability to capture fundamental atmospheric dynamics at the synoptic scale. However, for regional, convective-allowing models (CAMs), a lack of temporally granular reanalysis datasets and the relative sparsity of observations at the mesoscale – especially for the 3D atmospheric state – motivates instead the emulation of traditional CAMs via machine learning techniques to still leverage their lighter computational footprint at inference. The High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model has long been a workhorse for operational convective forecasting. However, running a large HRRR ensemble has remained computationally intractable for real-time operations. This work examines key questions for developing a skillful HRRR emulator that can be utilized for probabilistic forecasts of convective hazards. First, what degree of temporal granularity is required to capture the atmospheric dynamics present in phenomena near grid-scale? And second, how can this autoregressive model be constrained with boundary conditions to mitigate error compounding due to chaotic dynamics? This work will show preliminary results from models trained on high frequency output from retrospective runs of the HRRR over the spring season of 2026. Our models incorporate inspiration from traditional NWP by including “advection blocks” which produce dynamically learned flow fields to advect features in the model’s latent domain in addition to standard convolutional blocks. We also examine the efficacy of spectrally nudging the large scales of our emulator to constrain the forecast trajectory and enable forecasts out to 2 days in advance while remaining agnostic to the source of those boundary conditions.

495776.title: A SmallSat in VLEO: The Orion Kraken Approach
495776.authors: Chad Scott Fish, Orion Space Solutions - Arcfield, Louisville, CO
495776.abstract: The Orion Space Solutions' Kraken Mission, sponsored by DARPA and implemented by a science and engineering team led by Orion Space Solutions, will make in-situ and remote sensing space weather observations from Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO). The mission instrument suite will include Langmuir Probes, RF Impedance Probes, HF Sounders, Atomic Oxygen Sensors, Science Magnetometers, Floating Potential Probes, and Science Accelerometers. Long-term (approximately 4-6 month lifetime), repeated measurements of plasma density and other plasma and neutral parameters in this region are very rare, and the Kraken data is expected to contribute considerably to space weather and science modeling of VLEO. This paper will describe the highly integrated, comprehensive instrument suite and the unique small satellite design platform that are being developed for this path-finding mission. The approach to addressing orbit issues resulting from the relatively high drag and corrosive atomic oxygen environment will be reviewed in detail.

495777.title: Explainable AI for Subseasonal U.S. Precipitation Prediction: Sources of Predictability and a Teleconnection Bias in Climate Model Training Data
495777.authors: Chi-Jui Chen, RSMAS, Miami, FL; and M. Arcodia, E. J. Becker, D. C. Collins, and E. LaJoie
495777.abstract: We present a machine learning-based model that predicts the full probability distribution of weekly mean precipitation over the contiguous United States (CONUS) at a three-week lead from the large-scale climate state. Because precipitation is zero-inflated and right-skewed, the model predicts the probability of nonzero weekly precipitation together with a Pearson Type III distribution for the nonzero amounts, rather than a single precipitation value. The observational record is too short to train the network from scratch, so the model is pre-trained on the CESM2 Large Ensemble and then fine-tuned on observations. Fine-tuning only the output layer, with the pre-trained encoder held fixed, reproduces the skill of fine-tuning the full network, indicating that the skill derives from the representation learned during pre-training rather than from its adjustment during fine-tuning. To identify which inputs the model relies on, we remove individual input fields and retrain. Removing the tropical convection fields produces a statistically significant reduction in skill. By contrast, adding an observed Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) index to the model inputs produces no detectable increase in skill over predictors carrying El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) information alone. We examine the pre-training data for an explanation. The MJO is known to modulate cool-season precipitation over CONUS via an east-west dipole. The dipole is strong in observations but is not simulated in the CESM2 Large Ensemble used for pre-training, nor in two other CMIP6-generation large ensembles examined for comparison. A teleconnection relevant to subseasonal prediction over CONUS is therefore under-represented in the simulations used to pre-train the model. We further examine what this implies for forecasts of opportunity. Skill is not distributed uniformly but concentrates in states identifiable by season, ENSO state and region. We examine how far the length of the observational record limits an a priori identification of these predictable states rather than a posteriori. Results are presented as attribution maps, observed and simulated composites of the teleconnection dipole, and latent-space analogs that retrieve the most similar past weeks together with their observed outcomes. Together, these findings address the question of how well climate model simulations must represent teleconnections to serve as training data for data-driven subseasonal forecast models.

495778.title: Evaluation of RONIN Machine-Learning Quality Control Performance of NOAA Airborne Doppler Radar Data
495778.authors: Deztynee A Bryan, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. M. Bell, P. D. Reasor, J. C. DeHart, and J. Lee
495778.abstract: Airborne Doppler radar observations from NOAA’s P-3 and G-IV aircraft provide key measurements for tropical cyclone analysis including storm kinematics, precipitation structure, and three-dimensional wind retrievals. However, these datasets require extensive quality control due to non-meteorological data such as sidelobe contamination, noise, and ocean surface returns. RONIN (Random Forest Objective Non-meteorological Identification) is a machine-learning quality-control framework designed to classify meteorological and non-meteorological radar data for subsequent ingest into numerical models and analysis products. This study evaluates the performance of RONIN across NOAA airborne Doppler radar datasets with an emphasis on model configuration, feature selection, aircraft-specific characteristics, and flight-altitude sensitivity. Initial model-selection experiments examined whether a generalized model could be developed across NOAA P-3 and G-IV aircraft to improve performance compared to the current automatic NOAA QC. Preliminary results indicated that P-3 and G-IV data should be treated separately, so subsequent work focused on optimizing a final model for NOAA P-3 tail Doppler radar data using human-edited data as training inputs. Several configurations were tested, and the best-performing baseline configuration is a two-pass random forest model. The first pass used an optimized feature subset, while the second pass incorporated masked convolution features from reflectivity, Doppler velocity, and signal-quality fields. This model performed well on a testing dataset, including cases from Hurricanes Beryl, Earl, Fiona, and Lee, with a meteorological detection hit rate near 91%. These results indicate that RONIN can effectively identify meteorological and non-meteorological gates in standard P-3 sampling conditions. To evaluate model generalizability, data from high-altitude P-3 flights into Hurricane Imelda were added to the training dataset. The resulting mixed model showed reduced performance similar to the current operational technique, suggesting that high-altitude sampling has radar characteristics that differ from the lower-altitude training cases. Additional feature-importance experiments showed that predictors important for the high-altitude data differed from those selected for the original lower-altitude model. These results suggest that RONIN performance is sensitive to the amount and type of available training data. Continued development of RONIN will enable higher amounts of meteorological data to be retained in operational quality control compared to the current system.

495780.title: Gaussian Splatting for 3D Interactive Earth System Data Visualization
495780.authors: Matthew Rehme, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and N. Cherukuru
495780.abstract: Interactive data visualization is an essential tool for communicating science, particularly as the volume of data produced by modern simulations, such as high-resolution atmospheric and Earth system models, has grown to a scale that is otherwise incomprehensible to non-specialists. However, current interactive applications are typically limited to two-dimensional diagrams and charts or low-detail three-dimensional objects due to file size and web graphics constraints. Complex three-dimensional renderings that display volumetric data with fine detail, lighting, and shadows are often too computationally expensive to display interactively and therefore are normally shown as pre-rendered movies, sacrificing the exploratory engagement that makes interactivity valuable for learning. Here, we present an approach using Gaussian splatting, a relatively new rendering technique, to translate complex, high-dimensional Earth system dataset animations into lightweight, portable Gaussian point cloud data. Gaussian splats provide an efficient representation that can be rendered interactively in standard web browsers, including on smartphones, without the heavy real-time computation typically required for volumetric rendering. These data structures can be loaded quickly in web applications, while maintaining the detail, lighting, and effects of the original pre-rendered scene. This method dramatically reduces the computational and bandwidth requirements typically associated with 3D scientific visualization, enabling smooth, real-time exploration on ordinary consumer devices. This opens the door to interactive, explorable, production-quality visualizations of atmospheric or other simulations for use in classrooms, museum exhibits, and public-facing outreach, where audiences can rotate, zoom, and investigate structures in the data rather than passively viewing a fixed animation. We discuss our implementation, early results applying Gaussian splatting to atmospheric simulation output, and the potential for this technique to broaden access to Earth system science data for learners ranging from K-12 students to the general public.

495782.title: Connecting Extratropical Cyclone Lifecycle Evolution to Extreme Hydroclimate Impacts In the Great Lakes Region
495782.authors: Dani Jones, Cooperative Institute for Great Lakes Research, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI; University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI; CIGLR, Ann Arbor, MI; and J. Ward, A. L. Hutson, L. Ru, D. M. Wright, A. H. Young, and L. Fry
495782.abstract: Extratropical cyclones (ETCs) link atmospheric variability with regional hydroclimate response by producing precipitation and evaporation anomalies that influence Great Lakes water balance. However, individual storms produce highly variable hydroclimate responses, and the storm characteristics that organize this variability remain poorly understood. Here, we develop a storm-centric framework to classify ETCs based on their structure, intensity, and evolution, and examine how storm classes differ in extreme hydroclimate impacts across the Great Lakes. Using an unsupervised clustering approach, we identify two ETC classes that primarily differ in the timing of interaction with the Great Lakes. The resulting classes represent storms that enter the region earlier versus later in their lifecycle. We then quantify differences in extreme precipitation and evaporation responses between these storm classes using bootstrap-estimated risk ratios and risk differences. Later-entry storms exhibit elevated risk of extreme evaporation events during autumn across all five Great Lakes, despite representing a smaller fraction of detected ETCs. Extreme precipitation responses are weaker and more spatially heterogeneous, with the clearest increases for later-entry storms occurring during summer over the upper Great Lakes. These results demonstrate that storm lifecycle stage at the time of regional interaction is an important factor in explaining variability in hydroclimate response. This storm-centric framework provides a way to connect ETC evolution with hydroclimate impacts in regions influenced by extratropical cyclones. The results highlight storm lifecycle stage as an important source of event-to-event variability and provide a basis for improved characterization of hydroclimate extremes in coupled weather–water systems.

495783.title: A Polar-Native Neural Codec for NEXRAD Level II Data
495783.authors: Dhruvit Patel, Silurian AI Inc., Edison, NJ; and A. Ladino, G. Studer, N. Shankar, and J. K. Gupta
495783.abstract: The NEXRAD program is critical to National Weather Service (NWS) operations but generates immense data volume, approximately 5.5 GB/hour of Level II data. This volume saturates data transfer bandwidth, strains storage, and keeps state-of-the-art AI and ML weather models from fully exploiting the rich, fine-scale information native to radar observations. A future transition to phased-array systems for collecting data would push data scales even higher. Where bandwidth is limited, compression determines how much of the native measurement survives the trip from sensor to end-user. The compressors available today were not designed for data of this kind. General-purpose lossless compressors (e.g., gzip, bzip2, zstd, pcodec) treat radar volumes as byte streams and yield only modest compression ratios. Error-bounded lossy compressors for scientific data (e.g., SZ3, ZFP) degrade sharply below their native operating point. More importantly, none of the existing classical compressors produce a representation that downstream ML models can consume directly. We present a neural codec that operates in the radar's native polar coordinate system, avoiding the interpolation artifacts that regridding to a Cartesian grid introduces, and that naturally handles the challenges of radar data such as missing variables and heterogeneous scanning strategies. The first step flattens the existing VCP-based data format into an ML-ready "ray-stack" format, essentially a time series of rays. The second step pools gate-level data into wedge-shaped tokens and encodes each radar moment independently, fusing the per-moment embeddings through a learned weighted mean. A hierarchical transformer then compresses the tokens, using axial attention at finer resolution levels and full attention at the bottleneck. A symmetric decoder reconstructs gate-level values through per-variable heads conditioned on Fourier-encoded within-token positions. During inference the bottleneck representation is quantized to 2, 4, 6, and 8 bits. The neural codec was trained on a curated dataset of 177 storm episodes (~1,330 h) across the United States and tested on a similarly curated, held-out 72 h of radar scans covering weather regimes from severe convection and heavy rain to winter weather. Because gate-level reconstruction error is a weak proxy for operational utility (much of it sits in ground clutter and low-signal returns) we evaluate with retrieval-based metrics alongside standard reconstruction error, scoring QPE and hydrometeor classification derived from the reconstructions. The neural codec reaches an operating point on the compression–distortion–speed tradeoff that classical algorithms appear unable to. At 4- to 8-bit latent quantization the codec stores volumes in roughly 10x fewer bits than bzip2, the lossless compression applied to the 8- and 16-bit moment codes in which Level II is archived and transmitted today, and it encodes about 100x faster than SZ3, the strongest error-bounded lossy compressor. Importantly, this advantage scales favorably with data volume (e.g., higher density spatiotemporal scans). Median Z–R QPE error is 0.54 mm/h, Fractional Skill Score at the >5 mm/h threshold is 0.93, and the hydrometeor classification derived from the reconstruction agrees with the truth-derived classification at 87%. Residuals are low-amplitude and spatially incoherent, concentrated in clutter and low-signal returns rather than in meteorologically meaningful structures. Greater compression should be achievable through learned latent compression at the bottleneck and a more efficient encoding of the valid-gate mask, which currently dominates the stored rate (both left for future work).

495785.title: High-Resolution Daily Climate Projections Reveal an Emerging Extreme-Heat Regime across the Caribbean Islands
495785.authors: Frederick Boakye Oppong, University at Albany, Atmospheric Science Research Center, Albany, NY; and J. B. Renken, K. HIBBERT, V. T. Narinesingh, P. Méndez-Lazaro, and J. E. Gonzalez-Cruz
495785.abstract: Extreme heat is intensifying across the Caribbean, increasing concerns about future heat exposure across highly vulnerable island communities. However, quantifying these changes at locally relevant scales remains challenging. Long term meteorological observations are particularly sparse and fragmented across the region, such that assembling a small network of stations with sufficiently continuous records for climate analysis can be difficult. At the same time, global climate models, typically operating at spatial scales of approximately 100 km, poorly resolve the Caribbean’s small islands, complex topography, coastlines, and strong land to sea contrasts. The combination of limited observational coverage and coarse climate model resolution constrains our ability to characterize localized temperature extremes and assess how they may evolve under continued warming. Here, we develop a statistically downscaled record of daily maximum temperature (Tmax) at 0.05° resolution (~5 km), spanning 1980 to 2100 to study changes in extreme heat frequency across the Caribbean under different warming scenarios. Daily Tmax from CMIP6 MPI-ESM1-2-HR simulations is statistically downscaled using CHIRTS-ERA5 as the high-resolution reference within a Bias Correction and Spatial Disaggregation (BCSD) framework. Model and reference fields are mapped to a common grid over their historical overlap period, and the model derived long term temperature trend is removed prior to bias correction and restored afterward to preserve the projected warming signal. Empirical quantile mapping is performed independently at each grid cell using cumulative distribution functions constructed from ±15 day moving calendar windows. Bias corrected Tmax anomalies are subsequently bilinearly interpolated to 0.05° resolution and combined with the native CHIRTS-ERA5 daily climatology to retain observed fine scale spatial structure. The resulting 0.05° daily Tmax fields are evaluated against the historical reference climate and independently validated against station observations from San Juan, St. Thomas, and St. Croix for both historical and present day. The resulting archive comprises 44,195 continuous daily Tmax fields from 1980 through 2100. We investigate both raw model output, and dynamically downscaled simulations of NOAA GFDL's SPEAR Hi25 model which utilizes ~25 km atmosphere and ocean resolutions. To assess Caribbean climate change across different modeling approaches. The BCSD demonstrates substantial improvement relative to raw CMIP6 model, with mean bias decreasing from −2.38°C to +0.57°C and mean absolute error decreasing from 2.40°C to 0.94°C, corresponding to reductions of approximately 76% and 61%, respectively. Beyond improvements in historical climate representation, the projections reveal a pronounced shift in Caribbean extreme heat frequency. Across selected major Caribbean cities, the fraction of May through October days exceeding the local historical 1980 to 2014 90th percentile Tmax threshold is projected to increase from approximately 10% during the historical period to 37 to 57% during 2031 to 2065 and 53 to 74% during 2066 to 2100 under SSP2 4.5. By late century, projected exceedance frequencies reach approximately 69% in San Juan and more than 73% in St. Thomas and St. Croix. Thus, temperatures historically experienced on approximately one in ten warm season days are projected to occur on more than half, and in some locations nearly three quarters, of warm season days by late century. These projections indicate a substantial shift in the U.S. Caribbean temperature distribution, with historically rare extreme temperatures becoming increasingly frequent and persistent features of the warm season under continued warming. The BCSD framework provides spatially continuous, locally relevant climate projections at high resolution that retain the modeled long term climate change signal, offering a transferable approach for assessing future climate extremes at relevant local scales and other data sparse regions.

495786.title: Impacts of Transboundary Wildfire Plumes on Atmospheric Chemistry and Indoor-Outdoor Air Quality in the U.S.
495786.authors: Shang Liu, Northeastern University, Boston, MA; and A. Saha and Y. Zhang
495786.abstract: Canadian wildfire smoke crossed the U.S.-Canada border and affected large portions of the northeastern United States during July 15-20, 2026, causing hazardous air quality. To capture the full duration and evolution of the plume impact, Northeastern University’s mobile laboratory was rapidly deployed for real-time atmospheric measurements. Sampling included mobile spatial transects in the Greater Boston area on July 15, followed by stationary monitoring from July 16 to 20. The measured parameters spanned trace inorganic gases (NO, NO2, NOx, CO, SO2, O3), volatile organic compounds (benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes), greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4), particulate matter mass concentrations (PM1, PM2.5, PM10), aerosol size distributions (2-800 nm), non-refractory PM1 chemical composition (measured using a high-resolution time-of-flight aerosol mass spectrometer), meteorology, and GPS location. Concurrently, long-term paired indoor and outdoor particulate matter measurements (PM1, PM2.5, PM10) were collected using the PurpleAir sensors in 24 volunteer residences in the Allston neighborhood of Boston. Preliminary analysis reveals two major plume events characterized by distinct degrees of photochemical aging. The initial July 15 plume was relatively fresh, exhibiting lower aerosol oxygen-to-carbon (O/C) ratios. In contrast, a recirculated plume arriving on July 18 exhibited enhanced aging with significantly higher O/C ratios. These observations demonstrate distinct chemical characteristics associated with wildfire plumes of different degrees of aging over the same metropolitan region. This integrated dataset provides a unique opportunity to evaluate the atmospheric transformations of transboundary wildfire plumes and to quantify their impacts on aerosol and ozone chemistry, as well as indoor penetration in residential homes.

495787.title: Atmospheric Column Conditions Help Resolve Precipitation Phase Uncertainty in Complex Terrain
495787.authors: Sean O'Neil, DRI, Reno, NV; and A. Nolin
495787.abstract: Accurately distinguishing rain from snow in mountain regions is critical for resolving seasonal snowpack evolution, water availability and hazards for transportation and infrastructure yet precipitation phase remains particularly uncertain across the complex terrain of the Sierra Nevada. Near-surface meteorological conditions alone often cannot distinguish precipitation phase because processes such as evaporative cooling and delayed melting can allow snow to reach the surface when near-surface air temperatures exceed 0 °C. The Mountain Rain or Snow (MRoS) Project provides a community-sourced dataset of precipitation phase observations that offers ground truthed precipitation observations in regions where conventional station networks are sparse. Previous studies that rely solely on near-surface meteorological observations from weather stations have demonstrated fundamental limits to phase classification accuracy, even when applying advanced machine learning techniques. In this study, we use regression tree machine learning algorithms trained with near-surface and atmospheric column predictors derived from numerical weather model reanalysis to estimate the probability of rain or snow. These probabilistic predictions characterize uncertainty within the rain-snow transition and provide quantitative bounds on precipitation phase partitioning. Also, we evaluate model feature importance to determine the sensitivity of phase predictions to meteorological variables, particularly under conditions in which precipitation phase is most uncertain. Finally, we investigate feature importance patterns across mountain barriers and varying storm types (such as atmospheric rivers) to investigate the key atmospheric metrics that control surface precipitation phase.

495788.title: Characterization of an Arctic Pocket of Open Cells during CAESAR
495788.authors: Ankita Malu, University of California Riverside, Riverside, CA; and L. Cai, J. R. Snider, and M. D. Petters
495788.abstract: Cold-air outbreaks (CAOs) represent one of Earth’s most intense air-mass transformations, occurring when frigid Arctic air moves over a substantially warmer open ocean. In the spring of 2024, the Cold Air Outbreak Experiment in the Sub-Arctic Region (CAESAR) was carried out to study low-level marine clouds. Stratocumulus clouds are known to exhibit two mesoscale structures: closed-cellular and open-cellular. Prior studies on warm stratocumulus clouds in the Pacific and mixed-phase stratocumulus clouds in the Arctic, have shown a strong correlation between aerosol depletion and open-cellular cloud structure. The influence of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) availability and updrafts on cloud droplet number concentration (CDNC) remains uncertain because the maximum supersaturation controlling aerosol activation is difficult to measure directly in an evolving cloud. Therefore, understanding the relationship between CCN and CDNC is essential for elucidating the mechanisms affecting aerosol‐cloud interactions and their broader implications for climate processes. This work focuses on a mix of case studies and a statistical assessment of aerosol-cloud interactions during CAESAR. An example case-study involved regions with strong aerosol gradients. A depleted region was characterized by ultralow aerosol and cloud droplet concentrations, both below than 10 cm−3. The depleted aerosol region was embedded within regions of larger aerosol concentration. A cloud parcel model is used to demonstrate CCN-to-CDNC closure and updraft velocity within an aerosol particle population. These results indicate that aerosol availability and cloud-base dynamics influenced the initial droplet population, while collision–coalescence, entrainment, and drizzle removal subsequently modified CDNC and contributed to maintaining the pocket of open cells. Satellite and model reanalysis data suggest that the region of aerosol depletion was north to a warm air intrusion. This resulted not only in the aerosol depleted region, but also in aerosol gradients on either side of the aerosol-depleted region. Such detailed case-study will help disentangling aerosol, cloud microphysical, and dynamical influences on low-lying Arctic marine clouds, and provide better understanding of aerosol-cloud interaction in the Arctic.

495789.title: Building a Community Infrastructure for Earth System Modeling: Lessons from the NSF NCAR's Community Software Facility
495789.authors: Sheri Voelz, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. Kamali, J. Petch, K. Kuzemka, D. Colegrove, G. L. Mullendore, D. Schuster, and G. Romine
495789.abstract: The Community Software Facility (CSF) is an NSF NCAR initiative to modernize how we develop, support, and sustain our community models and tools to meet the current and future needs of staff and the broader scientific community. We aim to partner with NSF NCAR labs, programs, and the external community to deliver open, high-performance, portable, maintainable, interoperable, and intuitive software components that incorporate modern practices and provide critical capabilities for our broader community, expanding opportunities for scientific discovery. This talk will focus on our work in building open, high-performance, portable, and easy-to-use modeling components that are adaptable to existing community models and tools, making them easier for scientists and developers to reuse, adapt, build on, and transition to operational use. This includes NSF NCAR efforts to create an interoperable driver code interface that bridges different compute languages and GPU porting methods, which, when completed, will create a seamless environment for model development and scientific exploration across timescales. We will also discuss our unified testing approaches and our progress toward improving the performance of portable I/O libraries. Through our continued engagement, we seek to build deep partnerships with the community and integrate their perspectives. Together, we aim to deliver sustainable, open-source software that removes collaborative barriers and empowers the next generation of Earth system science.

495790.title: Parameterizations Modulate Convective and Large-Scale Precipitation Efficiency As a Control on Precipitation Intensity
495790.authors: Travis W Aerenson, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and D. McCoy and J. M. Nugent
495790.abstract: Precipitation intensity is one of the most uncertain aspects of the Earth system, yet it has profound societal consequences. Here we present a new mechanistic framework for understanding what sets precipitation intensity within Earth System Models (ESMs) using a 251-member perturbed parameter ensemble of the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 3 (E3SMv3). We demonstrate that because global mean total precipitation is tightly constrained by the atmospheric energy budget, precipitation intensity is primarily determined by the partitioning between convective and large-scale precipitation, which is itself governed by the ratio of convective to large-scale precipitation efficiency. This efficiency ratio is a stronger predictor of global precipitation intensity than either efficiency individually, and the relationship extends to most regions of the globe. The parameterization governing the rate at which cloud droplets convert into rain drops (autoconversion) relates to cloud water content emerges as the dominant parametric control on both efficiencies. We leverage observations from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) facility to partially constrain the simulated precipitation efficiencies, though current observational limitations leave this constraint uncertain. This framework provides a physically grounded path towards diagnosing and correcting precipitation intensity bias in ESMs, leading to a more trustworthy projection of precipitation intensity and how it is changing.

495791.title: Stable Boundary-Layer Preconditioning of Ice Fog and Supercooled Liquid Water Clouds at Dome C, East Antarctic Plateau: A Synoptic Typing Approach
495791.authors: Ryan Eagan, Univ. of Delaware, Newark, DE; and D. E. Veron, PhD
495791.abstract: The Eastern Antarctic Plateau is an extreme cold-desert environment characterized by a shallow, persistently stable boundary layer and low atmospheric moisture. Despite these limitations, ice fog and supercooled liquid water (SLW) clouds occur with surprising regularity at Concordia Station (Dome C; 75°06'S, 123°20'E), where they influence the surface radiative and moisture budgets. Because the plateau is largely isolated from local moisture sources, the boundary-layer cloud and fog events are generally preconditioned by synoptic-scale forcing such as meridional moisture advection and large-scale subsidence associated with the compensating coastal katabatic outflow. These synoptic regimes help to establish the near-surface thermodynamic and dynamic conditions under which small-scale perturbations can trigger fog or low-cloud formation. Here we present a multi-instrument fog detection and characterization framework developed for Dome C, paired with a Self-Organizing Map (SOM) classification of the synoptic circulation states associated with fog occurrence. Fog and low-level ice-particle events at Dome C are detected using a proxy classifier that diagnoses the boundary-layer state directly from tower and profiling observations rather than using cloud-top or bulk microphysical retrievals. Near-surface stability is quantified from tower-based temperature inversion diagnostics, and supersaturation with respect to ice, the key thermodynamic precondition for both ice fog and SLW persistence, is calculated using the Murphy and Koop (2005) formulation. Since RHi and inversion strength vary sharply with height in the lowest tens of meters, vertical structure is resolved using HAMSTRAD microwave radiometer humidity profiles at 7-minute resolution, allowing discrimination of shallow, surface-trapped supersaturation from deeper layers more consistent with diamond dust precipitation through the boundary layer, informed by recent particle-habit and concentration measurements at Dome C. Downwelling longwave and shortwave radiation from the BSRN station provide an independent radiative signature of fog and low-cloud presence, using an empirical, data-driven clear-sky longwave baseline specific to the plateau's extreme radiative environment rather than a fixed mid-latitude parameterization. Blowing-snow and local pollution contamination are screened separately to avoid conflating boundary-layer ice-particle signatures with surface-transport artifacts. To place detected fog events in synoptic context, we apply Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), implemented in Python using TorchSOM to classify large-scale circulation states over the Dome C region from ERA5 500 hPa geopotential height fields. This is run in parallel with a station-level SOM trained on in-situ AWS observations and then pivoted into daily synoptic-hour composites. This dual gridded/in-situ approach allows us to evaluate how well large-scale circulation regimes translate into the specific near-surface stability and humidity conditions favorable to fog. The synoptic typing builds on evidence that Dome C's boundary-layer thermodynamics respond strongly to large-scale forcing, including meridional flow, blocking, and moisture transport associated with SAM and ENSO phase. Full quality control, SOM training, best-matching-unit extraction, and diagnostic visualization routines have been developed and applied to the multi-year ERA5 and AWS record. Fog events identified by the detection classifier will ultimately be composited onto the resulting SOM nodes to identify the dominant synoptic regimes associated with elevated fog and SLW cloud occurrence. A single austral summer season (2018-19 Year Of Polar Prediction) with independently verified fog observations has been used to validate the detection classifier to train a supervised machine-learning extension capable of identifying fog events across the multi-year Dome C record without season-by-season manual labeling. We emphasize the multi-instrument detection framework, preliminary classifier validation from the labeled season, and illustrative SOM node output from the ERA5 and AWS analyses in this work and results linking fog frequency to specific circulation regimes will be presented as they become available. This work is part of a broader dissertation effort using observationally derived synoptic-to-boundary-layer relationships to diagnose and ultimately improve the representation of stable polar boundary layers and cloud/fog processes in regional atmospheric models (PolarWRF, MAR) over the East Antarctic Plateau.

495796.title: An HRRRCast ML Downscaled Nested Regional Forecast Model Applied Over CONUS
495796.authors: Fnu Sirisha, University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Rockville, MD; and M. Halem and O. Aulov
495796.abstract: AI regional forecast emulators have been much slower to attain the same level of operational success as global models for the following reasons: (i) lack of long-term km-scale reanalysis, (ii) need for high-resolution temporal and spatial boundary condition forcings, and (iii) local regional topography and microclimate factors. Our approach to addressing this gap employs the recently developed, open-access NOAA/GSL AI near-operational 6-km and 3-km HRRRCast regional models over CONUS, empirically demonstrating the resolution invariance of the 6-km HRRRCast model when applied to embedded 3-km domains. HRRRCast has a UNet structure with multiple ResNet-based diffusion models at each scale that emulate HRRR forecasts, using GFS-downscaled fields for lateral boundary conditions and FiLM conditioning to encode multiple lead times. It generates forecasts via a DDIM denoising process, iteratively transforming noise into a physically consistent atmospheric state conditioned on the current analysis. Resolution invariance was tested by applying the 6-km HRRRCast model to regions with 3-km data resolution, generating forecasts over multiple embedded regions across CONUS and demonstrating that the 6km model performs comparably to the 3km HRRRCast and 3km HRRR physics-based forecast on the 3km embedded regions. To address 6km sub-scale resolution, we found that the power density spectra of surface temperature and specific humidity are comparable down to ~10 km to the physics-based forecast, but power density spectra of the winds and geopotential height at 500 mb start to differ at 200 km scales. That indicates that the 6km model is still capturing much of the atmospheric behaviour of scales above 200 km. The figure below shows an example of a 48-hour 500 hPa forecast of the 6km model over the nested 3 km Northeast region (lower right), the HRRR 3km physics-based forecast (upper right), and the HRRRCast 3km forecast (lower left) compared with ground truth HRRR analysis (Upper right). The nested 3-km results serve as an initial demonstration that an ML model trained on coarser-resolution data can retain the physical structure of finer-resolution dynamics, and can therefore be applied to higher-resolution data without retraining. We are conducting experiments comparing the high resolution nested analysis generated by various computer vision super-resolution models from the coarse 6km analysis forming a 3 km analysis, such as bicubic interpolation, the Han–Hur Super-Resolution (SR) model, and the Frequency-Assisted Mamba (SSM) model. We will present results from using the optimal 3km SR analysis and fine-tuning the 6 km forecast model with the 3 km HRRR analysis using LoRA, as necessary to improve accuracy. We further plan to present a downscale SR approach from the 3km HRRR analysis to 1km and a 3km HRRRCast forecast on an embedded 1km nested region to demonstrate near-resolution invariance. The 1 km forecasts will be verified against the physics-based NUWRF 1 km nested regional model forecast. To the best of our knowledge, this will be the first publicly available nested 1km AI regional forecast anywhere over CONUS.

495797.title: Toward Column-Integrated Isotopic Observations of Hailstorm Environments
495797.authors: Anthony Crespo Bernal Ayala, Janus Research Group LLC, Evans, GA; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. Adams-Selin and A. Raudzens Bailey
495797.abstract: The isotopic composition of water vapor provides a valuable tracer of moisture sources, transport pathways, and phase-change processes within convective environments. However, isotopic observations associated with hail-producing storms remain rare, particularly for storm inflow regions and hydrometeor-scale analyses. During the 2025 ICECHIP field campaign, a vehicle-mounted Picarro L2130-i cavity ring-down spectrometer was deployed to obtain continuous, high-frequency measurements of ambient water-vapor and within the inflow environments of hail-producing convection. The mobile system was adapted for sampling across a range of convective modes, including supercells, multicellular convection, and mesoscale convective systems. This work presents an emerging observational framework that connects isotopic measurements at the surface with isotopic analyses of collected hailstones. In addition to characterizing inflow vapor, an adapted serial-sectioning approach is being developed to extract small, approximately 3-mm hailstone samples from cross sections using a custom 3D-printed cutting device. Isotopic measurements from these samples may provide spatially resolved information on the water incorporated during successive stages of hail growth. Together, these complementary measurements offer the potential to investigate relationships among environmental moisture characteristics, hailstone physical properties, and inferred growth histories. The presentation will describe the mobile sampling system, hailstone-processing methodology, quality-control considerations, and initial observations where available. This effort establishes a pathway toward using stable water isotopes to link the near-surface inflow environment with the evolving microphysical and thermodynamic conditions experienced by hailstones aloft.

495800.title: The Gap Between Theory and Models: The Community Land Model Experience (INVITED)
495800.authors: Gordon B. Bonan, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO
495800.abstract: Land surface models simulate fluxes of energy, moisture, momentum, and chemical constituents exchanged between the land and atmosphere. They are fundamental to understanding weather, climate, and atmospheric composition. Accurate modeling of land-atmosphere coupling is essential for subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction and high-resolution kilometer-scale modeling. While land surface models are computationally complex and are highly sophisticated software engineering systems, some with hundreds of thousands of lines of code, many of the parameterizations encompassed by the models trace back some 40-50 years to the early origins of the models. New developments in roughness sublayer theory, observations of the structure of forest canopies, and computational methods allow for more advanced theories of land-atmosphere coupling and surface fluxes in vegetation canopies. Using the Community Land Model (CLM) as an example, I contrast the outdated surface flux parameterizations used in the model with those of an advanced multilayer model of plant canopies that links the airspace from above the canopy down to the ground. The canopy physics and leaf physiology of the multilayer canopy are simpler and more consistent with theory than is the CLM big-leaf canopy, which uses many ad-hoc parameterizations. The vertically resolved canopy fundamentally changes and improves the coupling between the land and atmosphere. The canopy airspace, neglected by both atmospheric and land models, is also the air within which people live, wildlife inhabits, plants grow, and food and water are secured. Outdated model structure (technical debt) and insufficient science investment (scientific debt) limit further advances of CLM and pose challenges to the AI/ML revolution.

495804.title: Assessment of Ceilometer-Derived Aerosol Layer Heights for Satellite Product Intercomparison
495804.authors: Kevin Brandon Herrera, Hampton University, Hampton, VA; and J. Su, M. Friberg, P. Rawat, T. Mackey, S. Kondragunta, J. Szykman, and R. Delgado
495804.abstract: Aerosol layer height (ALH) is an important parameter for characterizing the vertical distribution of aerosols and interpreting satellite aerosol observations. Passive satellite products provide broad spatial coverage of ALH but have limited sensitivity to vertical aerosol structure. Rather than resolving a complete aerosol profile, these products generally infer a representative layer height using techniques such as optimal-estimation spectral fitting of measurements in molecular oxygen absorption bands or lookup-table inversion. Depending on the retrieval’s assumed aerosol vertical distribution, the reported quantity may represent an effective layer height, aerosol optical centroid height, or the pressure of an idealized aerosol layer. Ground-based ceilometers provide continuous, vertically resolved profiles of attenuated backscatter, potentially offering a complement to passive satellite ALH products. However, converting these profiles into a representative layer height requires identifying which vertical gradients correspond to meaningful aerosol-layer boundaries. This task is complicated by multiple or diffuse aerosol layers, residual-layer structure, clouds, signal attenuation, and noise. Moreover, passive satellite retrievals infer ALH from the radiative effects of aerosols, whereas ceilometer-derived estimates are based on boundaries identified within the backscatter profile. These differences in measurement sensitivity may yield distinct representations of ALH, complicating direct comparison between the resulting estimates. This study will use observations from the Unified Ceilometer Network (UCN), an operational network of ceilometers spanning a broad range of environments across the U.S., to investigate gradient-based methods for retrieving ALH from attenuated backscatter profiles. Prototype retrievals will be compared with satellite ALH products (e.g., TEMPO, TROPOMI) during coincident observations, accounting for differences in spatial footprint, observation timing, and measurement sensitivity. These comparisons will examine the atmospheric and observational conditions under which ceilometer- and satellite-derived ALH estimates are physically comparable, helping establish the potential of the UCN to support future satellite product validation.

495807.title: Potential Arctic System Impacts of Regional Aerosol Perturbations
495807.authors: David Clemens-Sewall, Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and J. C. C. Chen, E. J. Emme, A. Gettelman, M. M. Holland, L. L. Landrum, W. R. Lee, C. Payne, and C. E. Singer
495807.abstract: Natural hazard mitigation and national security considerations are driving interest in research on geoengineering---deliberate perturbations in the Earth system for the objective of cooling our planet. It is critical to understand the potential risks and benefits of proposed geoengineering concepts on aspects of the Earth system beyond commonly-assessed metrics—such as the 2 m air temperature or the top of atmosphere radiation balance. We use a fully-coupled Earth system model (the Community Earth System Model version 2, CESM2) to examine the potential impacts of Marine Cloud Brightening (MCB) in the Arctic via idealized cloud droplet number perturbation experiments beginning in 2035 in the SSP3-7.0 future climate change scenario. MCB would consist of deliberately increasing the reflectivity and longevity of low, marine clouds by adding aerosols (such as from sea spray) to the boundary layer. On a pan-Arctic scale, we find that Arctic MCB perturbations could dramatically impact the physical and ecological systems and produce historically-unprecedented sea ice, upper ocean, and marine ecosystem conditions in the Central Arctic. In CESM2, these conditions are similar to those which are simulated ephemerally (1-5 years) following the very largest volcanic eruptions of the last millennium—highlighting that such a climate response may follow other kinds of perturbations as well. We discuss the implications of these results and priorities for future research.

495809.title: Using Digital Twin Technology for Weather Radar Network Scenario Planning
495809.authors: Ryan Harris, Booz Allen Hamilton, McLean, VA; and M. Farrar, J. H. Romines, D. Cartwright, A. Nguyen, J. Thomas, U. Fagge, N. Meserve, and K. Bartas
495809.abstract: When it comes to modernizing complex systems, organizations are increasingly adopting Digital Twins (DTs) to anticipate needs and simulate “what-if” scenarios while avoiding real-world implementation costs. DT solutions are exact virtual replicas of objects, processes, or systems directly connected (“twinned”) to their physical counterparts through data and information feeds. While specific applications can vary by user, use case, and industry, DTs can support a variety of use cases like systems design, infrastructure planning, predictive maintenance, and modernization. As NOAA’s RadarNext Program aims to modernize its aging homogenous NEXRAD weather radar network, the current scenario planning process for developing future possible weather radar laydowns for the new network is time- and labor-intensive, requiring program managers and radar engineers to manually combine more than a dozen disparate datasets from multiple sources using at least five separate tools. To accelerate network scenario planning, Booz Allen, in partnership with Baron Weather, prototyped a DT Weather Radar Network Scenario Planning Tool that enables NOAA to evaluate radar types, site locations, cost implications, and surveillance performance across a wide range of scenarios. Data sources in the Unity-based DT include weather radar system information (e.g., cost for each radar system and ranges of reflectivity, velocity, and minimum dBZ at 50 km) and other data such as FEMA National Risk Index (NRI) information, population, and terrain. The project also simulated the following site-specific impacts at four current NEXRAD locations: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) from 5G networks Beam blockage from terrain and human-made obstructions (e.g. buildings, wind farms, etc.) In this presentation, we will demonstrate the RadarNext DT prototype and how the capability saves time and resources when combining data, digital twin technology, and cost analytics in scenario planning the next generation of NOAA’s future weather radar network.

495810.title: Building a Weather Ready Nation through a Targeted Integrated Warning Team Approach: Planning, Hosting, and Evaluating a Rural Region Readiness IWT
495810.authors: Elizabeth H. Marold, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and A. M. Sava, B. Gruver, S. H. Hanes, N. Fillo, and A. K. Baker
495810.abstract: The Rural Region Readiness (RRR) study, funded through NOAA’s VORTEX-USA program, aims to improve Impact Based Decision Support Services (IDSS) in the rural Appalachian region through integrated warning team (IWT) workshops. These workshops target rural partners and are designed to be a more up close and personal approach to partner outreach. Broader RRR study goals include: (1) enhancing tornado readiness in the Appalachian region, (2) understanding Appalachia’s unique vulnerabilities to tornadoes and cultural perspectives on vulnerability, (3) expanding the rural IWT partner table, and (4) working with NWS WFOs to plan, host and assess IWT workshops focused on local vulnerabilities and issues related to tornadic weather. At the local level, RRR improves risk communication within the larger integrated warning system (IWS) through a deeper understanding of cultural nuances and vulnerabilities from partner perspectives, allowing for more targeted messaging within the broader IWT; and, RRR fits within the Weather Ready Nation (WRN) initiative by providing local leaders with personal protective decision-making strategies and information resources that can be shared within local communities. The WRN effort aims to improve overall resilience against “extreme weather, water, and climate events.” Building such resilience requires community level efforts and relationship building between the National Weather Service (NWS), core partners in the IWT, and other local trusted community members who are information spreaders. RRR IWT workshops provide a space to build and maintain relationships at the local level, and educate members of the IWT and local community leaders about rural resilience. At the same time, members of local NWS WFOs learn about local community and IWT information needs before, during, and after hazardous weather events, like tornadoes. Such IWT workshops allow for a co-development of communication norms between partners in the broader IWS. In June of 2026, the Roanoke, Virginia WFO (RNK) hosted two RRR IWT workshops. After an initial in-person meeting with the lead researcher in January, a planning team was formed between members of the research team and the RNK WFO. Planning meetings were conducted online, with a trained participant observer taking detailed notes. Meetings were recorded for analysis of planning considerations, including who to invite, what topics to cover, and creating materials for presentations and activities. The June workshops were held after 6 online planning sessions. Workshops were designed to be activity-centered. During the workshops, the planning team presented a variety of materials and participants worked in small groups alongside meteorologists to provide feedback on example products and tools. Pre-post IWT surveys were distributed to workshop participants to measure learning and relational outcomes. Open-ended questions were included for additional feedback. Ethnographic field notes were taken during the workshops by three members of the research team and two additional invited social scientists. This presentation provides an overview of the RNK RRR IWT planning process, an overview of workshop activities, as well as an overall evaluation of the workshops. We conclude with recommendations for how other NWS WFOs might integrate similar processes into their own targeted-IWT workshop planning.

495811.title: Simulating the Impact of Atmospheric Stability on Chiller Exhaust Recirculation at Hyperscale Data Centers Via Large-Eddy Simulation
495811.authors: Alex Rybchuk, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO; and A. Wise, H. Gopalan, and R. King
495811.abstract: Driven by the growth in AI popularity, modern data centers are being developed to consume gigawatts of power. Accordingly, this infrastructure requires gigawatts of cooling. Data center cooling is typically accomplished by rejecting thermal energy into the atmosphere. Cooling occurs via machinery like evaporative cooling towers (via latent heat flux) and dry coolers / air-cooled chillers (via sensible heat flux), the latter of which is our focus. In order to reject gigawatts of heat, hundreds of chillers can be placed around a facility, for example on building rooftops or in yards on the ground. The layout of chiller clusters relative to one another and relative to buildings can have important ramifications on their ability to cool IT infrastructure. For example, upwind chiller plumes can advect into the intake of downwind chillers, thereby degrading their ability to reject heat. Similarly, chillers downwind of a tall building can end up inside of a building-wake recirculation zone, which can cause a thermal plume to recirculate back into chillers, again degrading their effectiveness. Recognizing the importance of this problem, Technical Committee 9.9 of the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE) has identified a research need regarding "External Flow Modeling of Data Centers". While relatively little has been published for this specific application (e.g., Rohr et al (2026)), there is a rich literature on dispersion modeling in urban environments (e.g., Tominaga (2024)). Most computational fluid dynamics papers use a RANS-based approach, though there is increasing adoption of large-eddy simulation (LES) (Tominaga (2024)). Most studies treat the atmosphere as thermally neutral (Pantusheva et al. (2022)), though Xie et al. (2013) showed that even weakly unstable conditions can substantially modify plume dynamics. Furthermore, urban dispersion studies typically simulate emission sources that are thermally neutral, rather than simulating hot or lightweight gases. Studies that jointly simulate a thermally stratified atmospheric boundary layer as well as a buoyant source gas are rare (Olvera and Choudhuri (2006)). In this work, we use large-eddy simulation (LES) to explore the impact of atmospheric stability on chiller exhaust recirculation. We study two hyperscaler site configurations: one based on a generic facility that places its chillers on a rooftop, and one inspired by a real-world facility that is in operation. We limit our work to dry coolers, simulating them as a sensible heat flux source with an exhaust velocity. Using the Energy Research and Forecasting (ERF) model, we simulate stable and unstable atmospheric conditions and compare them to a neutral baseline. Preliminary results show that atmospheric stability indeed does shift the ability of chillers to effectively cool infrastructure. Relative to the neutral baseline, average chiller intake temperatures rose by 4°C in our stable case, which is a meaningful increase during peak cooling demand periods. Olvera, Héctor A., and Ahsan R. Rohr, C., et al. “Validation of Chiller-to-Chiller Interactions in Datacentre Applications through CWE and Experiment.” 2026, 8th International Symposium on Computational Wind Engineering. 495812.title: Assessing the Relationship Between Environmental Low-Level Vertical Wind Shear and Flow on the Supercell Right Turn Using Spatiotemporally Varying Velocity Azimuth Displays
495812.authors: Julia Buhrman, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and C. C. Weiss
495812.abstract: Predicting which supercells become tornadic still poses a problem to forecasters, who rely on storm-environment relationships to anticipate tornado formation (Coniglio and Parker 2020). It is important, then, for tornadic and nontornadic supercell environments to be analyzed and compared to determine differences to aid forecasters in tornado prediction. Prior literature has found that despite certain thermodynamic thresholds needing to be met for supercells to form, these variables possess little predictive power between tornadic and nontornadic environments. Kinematic variables, however, have been found to be strong differentiators between environments. Work has been done by the lead author using hundreds of quality-controlled velocity azimuth displays (VADs) collected by the Texas Tech University (TTU) Ka-band mobile Doppler radars during the Targeted Observations by Radars and UAS of Supercells (TORUS), TORUS-Left-flank Intensive Experiment (TORUS-LItE), and the Low-Level Internal Flow of Tornadoes (LIFT) field campaigns to examine this finding.
