Results showed that storm-relative helicity (SRH) and storm-relative winds (SRW) possessed statistically significant differences between tornadic and nontornadic environments and were strongly enhanced within tornadic inflows. Critical angles were closer to 90 degrees within tornadic environments, indicating more streamwise flow in comparison to nontornadic environments. Tornadic environments saw greater SRH, SRW, and critical angles, as well as larger spatial variability throughout the inflow in comparison to nontornadic environments. While the speed and direction of right-moving supercells have been able to be accurately predicted for over 20 years now, when these storms will deviate rightward is still not well understood. Theoretically, through their connection with the mesocyclone, kinematic variables could possess predictive power on when tornadic and nontornadic supercells will make a right turn. However, a prior study by Flournoy et al. (2021) using the large soundings dataset from Coniglio and Parker (2020) found no connection of kinematic or thermodynamic variables on the timing of the right turn. This work seeks to build upon this work by implementing a more spatially and temporally dense dataset using VADs to examine the kinematic link to the timing of the right turn for both tornadic and nontornadic supercells. The relation of SRH, SRW, bulk wind shear, and critical angle to when the right turn occurs after storm initiation will be examined across different time frames of the storm’s life prior to the turn and across varying distances from the mesocyclone in tornadic and nontornadic environments. With the hundreds of VADs utilized in the prior work of the author, kinematic variables could now be found to have connections to the timing of the right turn and assist in increasing forecasting skill.

495813.title: Catching the Drizzle: Validating Complete Profiled Drop Size Distributions from a Snow-Level Radar During TIME-SLICE CO
495813.authors: Ian Cornejo, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and B. Dolan, M. M. Bell, and C. R. Williams
495813.abstract: Vertically pointing radars can infer the drop size distribution (DSD) continuously through the precipitating column, complementing the point measurements of surface disdrometers and gauges. The NOAA High-Power Snow-Level Radar (HPSLR), an S-band frequency-modulated continuous-wave profiler, is a promising but largely untested instrument for this purpose: its non-attenuating wavelength and Doppler-spectrum retrieval offer sensitivity to the complete DSD, both the small-drop "drizzle" mode and large-drop “precipitation” mode, throughout the warm-rain column, yet its retrieval biases relative to established instrumentation remain uncharacterized. Robust evaluation of such an instrument requires a reference that itself resolves the complete DSD, which no single surface instrument provides. We therefore first develop and validate a merged surface-DSD reference that combines a Parsivel² laser disdrometer, which resolves the precipitation mode, with a collocated Micro Rain Radar (MRR-Pro), which extends sensitivity into the drizzle mode, yielding a composite DSD constrained across a broad range of drop sizes and anchored to collocated tipping-bucket rain gauges. We then use this merged reference to evaluate HPSLR-retrieved DSDs across the moments of the distribution, isolating the regimes and drop-size ranges in which the profiler agrees with, departs from, or adds value beyond surface instrumentation; aloft, HPSLR retrievals are further compared to nearby polarimetric radars through forward simulation of polarimetric variables. We additionally outline the influence of vertical air motion on retrievals in convective conditions, where the assumptions underlying existing correction methods are less certain, as a central challenge for extending the technique beyond stratiform precipitation. These analyses use observations from the NASA INvestigation of Convective Updrafts (INCUS) mission's preparatory Testing INCUS Methods Experiment—Suborbital preLaunch Investigations of Convective Evolution (TIME-SLICE CO) field campaign, conducted in eastern Colorado in 2024, during which the HPSLR operated within a dense network of collocated observations. Preliminary results will be presented. By delivering both a validated merged-disdrometer reference and an initial characterization of the HPSLR's biases and uncertainties as a profiling disdrometer, this work establishes a validation framework transferable to the broader network of NOAA snow-level radars, and as a newly initiated effort we welcome collaboration across the instrumentation, retrieval, and precipitation-microphysics communities.

495814.title: Smoke–Urban Interactions Amplify U.S. Ozone Extremes During the 2023 Canadian Forest and Peatland Fires
495814.authors: Meiyun Lin, NOAA, Princeton, NJ; and S. S. Brown, D. A. Jaffe, M. Newchurch, S. Baidar, K. Bates, W. S. Chace, M. M. Coggon, J. Chris, L. Horowitz, A. O. Langford, H. Lee, B. McCarty, F. Moshary, J. Peischl, M. A. Robinson, N. Schafer, J. T. Sullivan, Y. Wu, C. Warneke, C. Womack, K. Zuraski, and C. Stockwell
495814.abstract: Record-breaking Canadian wildfires in 2023, fueled by hot and dry conditions, released large quantities of reactive carbon through burning of forest biomass and organic soils. As climate warming increasingly predisposes boreal forests and peatlands to ignition and deep combustion, carbon-rich smoke plumes are likely to become more common. Here we integrate intensive observations with four atmospheric models of varying complexity to examine ozone pollution extremes (70–150 ppbv) across the United States. Interactions between pyrogenic volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and urban NOx enhanced daily maximum 8-h average ozone by 10–45 ppbv in U.S. cities. We highlight the importance of VOC emissions from smouldering soil combustion in boreal fires, near-fire sequestration and transport of NOx as peroxyacyl nitrate reservoirs, and urban NOx emissions for ozone formation in aged smoke plumes. Under light smoke, attribution of surface ozone to wildfire versus urban sources diverges between data-driven and process-based approaches. Our findings indicate that future ozone extremes will depend not only on wildfire activity in a warming climate but also on ongoing urban NOx emission reductions. The ozone enhancement arising from interactions between wildfire-derived VOCs and urban NOx is controllable.

495816.title: WindBorne Atlas: A Global Sounding Balloon Constellation
495816.authors: Todd A. Hutchinson, WindBorne Systems, Arlington, MA; and A. Sushko, J. Dean, J. Creus-Costa, J. Spisak, L. J. Reames, and E. Schoenfeld
495816.abstract: WindBorne Systems has developed and operationalized a novel balloon constellation known as WindBorne Atlas. Atlas collects observations (temperature, pressure, humidity, and wind) throughout the world within the troposphere and lower stratosphere. This presentation will focus on the growth of Atlas over time and introduce capabilities that are being added to the constellation. As of August 2026, Atlas consists of over 600 balloons aloft. Each balloon, referred to as a Global Sounding Balloon (GSB), typically flies for weeks at a time (currently averaging 13 days) while repeatedly profiling from a few hundred meters above the surface to the lower stratosphere (up to 80 hPa). All sensors are calibrated in-house to exceed WMO standards. NOAA retrospective studies have demonstrated positive forecast skill from Atlas observations, leading to operational assimilation in the Global Forecast System (GFS). The data are also assimilated into WeatherMesh, an in-house AI weather prediction model, with ongoing work assessing constellation impact on forecast skill. An overview of the Atlas constellation will be presented, focusing on GSBs’ growing vertical range of observations, future plans to add lightweight dropsondes to high-altitude GSBs, and ongoing work to have GSBs continue to operate after landing, while sitting on land or floating in the ocean. Additionally, unique data collection capabilities of GSBs will be highlighted, such as steering balloons into tropical cyclones in the central and western Pacific, and future work on enhancing and expanding this data collection process

495817.title: Using Maneuvers to Determine In-Flight Zero Offsets for SOLAR-1's Magnetometers
495817.authors: Nathan Howard, NOAA, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and A. Jarvis, B. Vasquez, C. Smith, and R. Torbert
495817.abstract: The Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness - 1 (SOLAR-1) satellite's two magnetometers provide in situ magnetic field measurements of the solar wind at the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 1 (L1). To determine the time-varying zero offsets of both magnetometers, two methods are used: the Davis-Smith method (as formulated by Leinweber et al. (2008)), which estimates the zero offsets using naturally occurring Alfvén waves, and a new maneuver-based approach. We show that the new method provides an accurate and independent check on the Davis-Smith zero offset results by estimating offsets from maneuvers in which the spacecraft rotates about one of its axes. The magnetic field data gathered during the rotations are analyzed in the frequency domain, and the offsets are determined by minimizing the power at the maneuver's spin frequency. A measure of offset uncertainty is derived from simulated maneuvers using real magnetic field data from SOLAR-1's magnetometers. Work is ongoing to further improve accuracy, and extend the method to work with slew maneuvers in addition to pure spins.

495818.title: From Mixed Layers to a Unified Parameterization: David Randall's Boundary-Layer Research (Invited Presentation)
495818.abstract: I first met Dave at UCLA in 1975, when he was completing his dissertation on the representation of the atmospheric boundary layer in general circulation models (GCMs). That dissertation marked the beginning of five decades of research on atmospheric boundary layers, documented in more than 30 publications. Much of this research centered on fundamental questions about cloud-topped boundary layers, including: What determines the entrainment rate in a stratocumulus-topped boundary layer? How should the vertical structure of the boundary layer be represented in a GCM? (The graphic shows the structure adopted in the UCLA GCM). How can partly cloudy boundary layers, including their evolution from overcast layers, be represented? Central to these questions were the effects of moist thermodynamics and cloud-top radiative cooling on boundary-layer turbulence. This presentation will trace several threads through this body of work rather than attempt a chronological review. Particular attention will be given to the progression from mixed-layer models and studies of stratocumulus-topped boundary layers to higher-order and mass-flux approaches, culminating in efforts to develop a unified representation of the boundary layer and moist convection. These developments will also be placed in the context of parallel approaches pursued by the boundary-layer community, including higher-order turbulence closure and large-eddy simulation. The resulting picture illustrates how advances in theory, numerical simulation, observations, and parameterization interacted over several decades, and how ideas originating in mixed-layer models evolved toward increasingly unified treatments of turbulence, clouds, and convection.

495820.title: Experiences of the 2026 UFS Student Ambassador
495820.authors: Jenna Clare Holbrook, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; Texas A&M University, College Station, TX
495820.abstract: Jenna Holbrook Texas A&M University NOAA/Weather Program Office Lapenta Intern As machine learning based weather models continue to improve and become more widely implemented, collaboration between federal and academic sectors is key. Particularly, working to increase awareness and participation from students will be vital to guiding a new generation of innovators. The role of the Unified Forecast System (UFS) student ambassador is to provide a student’s perspective on improving the engagement of students and researchers in the UFS modeling community and expanding current outreach initiatives, such as the UIFCW, social media, and lesson plans. This project involves creating new lesson plans to support online tutorials for project EAGLE (Experimental AI Global and Limited-area Ensemble forecast system) and the UFS. These lesson plans will enhance student’s understanding of the models while also allowing them to gain hands-on experience with running them. Utilizing past ambassador recommendations, an updated Student Engagement Plan is also being developed to better reflect current student understanding and engagement activities, including these new lesson plans. While running existing tutorials, there have been some challenges due to a difference in level of coding skills and familiarity with different programming languages. These initial experiences may be consistent with new student users, and the lesson plans will be designed to address some of these challenges. Some of the code within these tutorials also needs to be brought up to date to ensure the latest version of these tutorials are aligned with current model releases.

495825.title: National Meteorologists Day: A New Outreach Initiative to Elevate Recognition of the Scientists Behind the Forecast
495825.authors: Sean Potter, Freelance, St. Joseph, MN
495825.abstract: Many vocations use professional recognition days to promote awareness of their field and honor the women and men in those fields whose careers are dedicated to serving others. National Nurses Day (May 6), National First Responders Day (October 28), and Administrative Professionals Day (Apr 23) are just a few examples of special days set aside each year to recognize the professionals in those fields and promote the fields in general. For many years, Weatherperson’s Day (February 5) has been the de facto day of observance for professionals in meteorology, especially those involved in weathercasting. While it offers a valuable opportunity to recognize those who prepare and communicate forecasts and other information to the public, it leaves open the need for a complementary day to honor the scientific expertise, training, and critical societal roles of degreed meteorologists whose work goes beyond the daily forecast. Beginning in 2026, a new day of observance, National Meteorologists Day—celebrated on May 9—was established to recognize the scientific discipline and professional training behind the work meteorologists do across sectors—work that is grounded in science, rigorous training, and decisions that shape public safety, commerce, and daily life. The day marks the birthday of James Pollard Espy (1785 – 1860), who was the first American to officially hold the title of “meteorologist,” having been appointed “meteorologist to the U.S. Government” by Congress in 1842. Throughout the weeks leading up to the first observance of National Meteorologists Day, in 2026, a rigorous outreach initiative was undertaken to promote awareness, solidify partnerships, and establish the day as a historically grounded, scientifically meaningful occasion for recognizing the field and honoring those involved professionally in it. The goal of this presentation is to increase awareness of National Meteorologists Day by discussing how it came about, highlighting some of the outreach efforts undertaken during its first year of observance—including success stories and lessons learned—and previewing plans for additional outreach to promote the day and, by extension, promote meteorologists as scientists, highlighting the critical roles they play in society.

495827.title: One Framework, Two Markets: Weekly Weather Regimes, Renewable Output, and the Dunkelflaute Risk Index in ERCOT and Germany
495827.authors: Christian Bryce Bohon, Prescient Weather Ltd, State College, PA; and J. Ross, R. Shroff, and R. James
495827.abstract: The Dunkelflaute Risk Index (DRI) estimates combined wind and solar resource in Germany, while capacity factors measure metered renewable output in Germany and ERCOT. This study applies a common weekly regime framework to both markets and includes matched ERCOT degree day demand proxies. It tests whether persistent circulation patterns provide useful context for weekly renewable supply and demand scenarios without treating the regional regime definitions as equivalent. ERCOT uses the WCS year round North American classification of Alaskan Ridge, Greenland High, Pacific Ridge, and Pacific Trough, based on ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis and closely following Lee et al. (2023). Germany uses separate European classifications for October through March and April through September, each consisting of Positive North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO+), Negative North Atlantic Oscillation (-NAO), Block, and Atlantic Ridge. Daily amplitudes come from the WCS observed weather regime daily archive. ERCOT wind capacity factor for 2007 to 2026 and solar capacity factor for 2011 to 2026 combine ERCOT reports with EIA Forms 930 and 860M. German combined capacity factor uses European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity Transparency Platform generation and Ember capacity data from October 2018 through July 2026. ERCOT degree-day observations and the German DRI for 2010 to 2026 use WCS Point-in-Time Weather Forecast API observations. All variables are matched to complete calendar weeks, consistent with mean regime episode durations of 7.6 days in North America and 7.9 days in Europe. The comparison yields four principal results: In ERCOT during DJF, HDD increases with Alaskan Ridge amplitude (r = +0.45), while wind capacity factor decreases with Alaskan Ridge amplitude (r = -0.24). In ERCOT during JJA, CDD and wind capacity factor increase with Pacific Ridge amplitude (r = +0.21 and r = +0.40). The highest and lowest amplitude deciles average 38.3% and 22.5% wind capacity factor, compared with a JJA climatology of 31.8%. The largest absolute ERCOT solar correlation is for Greenland High in July and August (r = -0.36, n = 121 weeks). In Germany during DJF, combined capacity factor increases with NAO+ amplitude (r = +0.60, p < 0.001, n = 102 weeks). It decreases with Block amplitude (r = -0.42, p < 0.001) and -NAO amplitude (r = -0.35, p < 0.001). The Atlantic Ridge relationship is not significant (r = -0.07, p = 0.494). The German DRI has DJF coefficients with the same signs for NAO+ (r = +0.56) and Block (r = -0.47). In JJA, metered capacity factor decreases with Block and Atlantic Ridge amplitudes, increases with -NAO amplitude, and has no significant relationship with NAO+ amplitude. Regional regime probability forecasts can organize market specific weekly scenarios. In ERCOT, the framework identifies when demand proxies and wind output have historically varied in the same or opposite directions with regime amplitude. In Germany, it distinguishes the DRI resource signal from metered output and shows that agreement changes by season. The coefficients are not directly comparable because definitions, variables, periods, and power systems differ. These contemporaneous relationships do not measure forecast skill or determine price and adequacy outcomes.

495829.title: From Sensors to Solutions: Maturing Extreme Weather Resilience Tools through Sustained Co-Production
495829.authors: Kayla Smith, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and C. Combest-Friedman, C. F. Simpson, S. Bath, G. Bey, and F. Echiejile
495829.abstract: The NOAA Regional Integrated Sciences and Assessments (RISA) program helps partners address long-term preparedness by bridging the usability gap between raw data and on-the-ground decision-making. Since 1995, RISA activities across 15 regions have pioneered a unique model of cross-disciplinary weather and climate services delivery. In this presentation, we demonstrate how integrating iterative co-production into traditional NOAA Readiness Levels (RL 1–9) accelerates extreme weather resilience. By mapping RISA’s social learning theory onto this readiness framework, we show how co-production plays an integral role in coupling physical science outputs with qualitative social science insights to develop decision-relevant resources and specialized expertise. To advance foundational research into practice, our network leverages lasting partnerships that bridge stakeholder needs with actionable science across four key dimensions: Collaborative Research (RL 1–3): Engaging early establishes trust and fosters a shared understanding of local environmental risks. One RISA team documented sustained engagements with 331 partners, including 66 Tribal Nations, to co-develop resilience baselines. Increased Capacity (RL 4–5): Continuous feedback loops enhance the skills and resources of researchers and community partners. A stormwater program has trained 200+ practitioners, assisting 75+ cities with comprehensive flood risk assessments and expanding the local climate-ready workforce. Usable Help (RL 6–7): Demonstrating prototypes in operational environments transforms continuous measurements into accessible decision-support tools. The network provides public directories of over 40 tools, four of which were embedded into a state’s preparedness and regional hazard dashboard with 2,400 active users. Better Decisions (RL 8–9): Fully deployed tools drive direct improvements to local policies, resulting in better decisions. By partnering with other agencies, foundational RISA work routinely secures leveraged funding for implementation such as a recent $2.8 million water infrastructure investment. Examining case studies across this continuum illustrates how co-produced products, tools, and knowledge transition from early-stage innovations to novel climate solutions. As communities face compounded hazard impacts, sustained stakeholder engagement maintains successful weather and climate services pipelines. Cultivating authentic regional trust typically requires five to ten years of dedicated support, ultimately transforming temporary interactions into permanent partnerships for enduring community resilience.

495830.title: Synoptic Patterns Driving Snow-Eater Heat Waves In the Western United States
495830.authors: Dan McEvoy, DRI, Reno, NV; and A. Joros, A. Rhoades, B. J. Hatchett, W. Rudisill, and J. North
495830.abstract: Spring heat waves in the Western United States (WUS) often trigger rapid snowmelt events in the mountains that can alter seasonal snowmelt timing and rates, cause major flooding if enough snow is present, drive snow drought onset, or worsen existing snow drought conditions. Recent work has characterized WUS snow-eater heat waves (SEHWs), a type of spring heat wave defined by strong (at least 6 °C above average) and persistent (at least three days) 2 m temperature anomalies with a requirement of above freezing (0 °C) 2 m temperatures for the duration of the event. In this study, we expand the SEHW work by examining the synoptic patterns and spatial variability of the hydrometeorology during historical SEHW events (1980-2023). Atmospheric reanalysis data (ERA5) are used to first develop circulation regimes associated with SEHWs by performing a cluster analysis on 500 mb geopotential heights (GPH) using self-organizing maps (SOMs). We then analyze composites of other atmospheric variables (200 mb GPH and integrated vapor transport) and surface variables (2 m temperature, precipitation, snow water equivalent, and solar radiation) based on SOM clusters. Reanalysis data are supplemented with observations of snow water equivalent (SWE) from the SNOTEL network and spatial patterns snowmelt (dSWE) are examined. Initial results suggest that 1) atmospheric ridging is present for most SEHWs but variations in the strength and location of the ridge are found in SOM clusters with “hotspots” of snowmelt maxima and 2) not all SEHWs are sunny heatwaves, with cloud cover and atmospheric moisture playing a role in persistent warm overnight temperatures, and snowmelt. Findings from this work have the potential to provide guidance on predicting SEHWs and the associated surface impacts.

495833.title: Statistical Relationships between Negative Intracloud Flash Fraction and Environmental Parameters Controlling Cloud Electrification
495833.authors: Elizabeth A. DiGangi, AEM, Germantown, MD; and J. S. Ringhausen, J. Lapierre, and Y. Zhu
495833.abstract: Separation of charge via noninductive ice-ice collisions in clouds is widely accepted as the primary mechanism behind cloud electrification. However, not all clouds end up with the same charge distributions, as observed in various field campaigns and laboratory experiments over the last several decades. The distribution of charge in a given thunderstorm controls the polarity, frequency, and other characteristics of lightning produced by that storm, but charge distribution is very difficult to measure directly, especially at statistically significant scales. Of particular interest to the lightning community is the relationship between thunderstorm environments and lightning characteristics, where the charge distribution of storms bridges the gap between the two. This study will use one year of intracloud (IC) lightning data from the Earth Networks Total Lightning Network (ENTLN) to investigate the statistical relationships between the proportion of negative IC flash frequency and environmental parameters such as charge reversal temperature altitudes, cloud base height, cloud depth, and warm vs cold cloud depth fraction derived from global reanalysis data for multiple regions around the world.

495836.title: Toward an Autonomous Cloud Laboratory: Reinforcement Learning for Targeted Control of Liquid Water Content and Cloud Droplet Number Concentration in A Convection Cloud Chamber
495836.authors: Zeen Zhu, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Stony Brook, NY; and F. Yang, A. Sedlacek, and R. A. Shaw
495836.abstract: Autonomous laboratories, in which intelligent agents select experimental conditions and iteratively respond to measured outcomes, could transform cloud physics experiments by enabling reproducible exploration of coupled aerosol–cloud processes beyond the pace and coverage of manual trial and error. To build such AI-embedded cloud-chamber laboratories, a key step is enabling intelligent agents to select chamber conditions that produce targeted cloud microphysical states. Here, we developed an integrated large-eddy simulation (LES), machine-learning surrogate, and reinforcement-learning framework to demonstrate the feasibility of this intelligent control. Our testbed is the 1 m³ Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) cloud chamber with a warm bottom, cold top, and four independently adjustable wall panels that regulate temperature and humidity. In the present implementation, the agent controls south and west panel temperature and humidity, together with the aerosol injection rate. A database of 3,634 LES cases was used to train extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) surrogate models to predict liquid water content (LWC) and cloud droplet number concentration (Nd) under various cloud-chamber conditions. Next, we applied two reinforcement-learning (RL) algorithms– proximal policy optimization (PPO) and soft actor–critic (SAC)–to demonstrate how chamber control can be adjusted to achieve prescribed cloud microphysical states. During RL training, the surrogate model served as a virtual chamber, providing a rapid response to each adjustment. Success required both LWC and Nd to fall within 10% of the target value. Across 545 held-out validation targets, PPO reached 463 targets (84.95%), and SAC reached 452 (82.94%). This simulation-based proof of concept shows how targeted microphysical states can be achieved through actionable controls, supporting future closed-loop autonomous experiments in a real cloud chamber.

495837.title: Advancing Scalable Flood Inundation Mapping through Model Evaluation, Sensitivity Analysis, and Improved Terrain Representation
495837.authors: Reza Saleh Alipour, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and J. Song and S. J. Burian
495837.abstract: Operational flood inundation mapping requires methods that are accurate, computationally efficient, and transferable across landscapes and spatial scales. Hydrodynamic models provide detailed representations of flood processes, while low-complexity models offer faster alternatives for large-area and time-sensitive applications. However, model performance depends not only on model structure but also on the representation of terrain, land-surface resistance, and hydrologic forcing. This study investigates these dependencies through a linked model intercomparison, global sensitivity analysis, and evaluation of terrain representation. HEC-RAS 2D, TRITON, HAND-FIM, and FLDPLN are compared across multiple study areas, spatial scales, and flood conditions using consistent inputs and benchmark datasets. The comparison evaluates flood extent and depth, computational efficiency, input requirements, and transferability. Preliminary results demonstrate trade-offs between model accuracy and computational demand. The hydrodynamic models provide stronger overall agreement with benchmark flood extent and depth, but the low-complexity models produce inundation maps rapidly. A global sensitivity analysis based on 5500 ensemble GPU-enabled TRITON simulations further shows that dominant controls vary by flood response, location, uncertainty scale, and event phase. DEM resolution strongly influences local flood-depth dynamics, particularly at riverine and off-channel locations, whereas flood extent is controlled mainly by floodplain roughness and upstream inflow discharge. These findings indicate that priorities for improving flood predictions differ across locations, scales, and intended model outputs. Building on these findings, ongoing work evaluates FLDPLN sensitivity and scalability across DEM sources and resolutions and examines whether feature-aware DEM hydro-conditioning can reduce errors associated with misrepresented culverts, bridge openings, road embankments, levees, and other connectivity-controlling features. Together, these analyses provide practical guidance for selecting flood-model complexity, prioritizing improvements to influential inputs, and determining when DEM resolution or feature-aware hydro-conditioning requires additional attention. This integrated approach supports reliable and scalable flood inundation mapping within operational time, data, and computational constraints.

495838.title: Withdrawn: Connecting Landfall to Public Perception: Evaluating How the Public Recognizes and Interprets Atmospheric River Events and Communication
495838.authors: Zoe N. Caryl, Univ. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and J. E. Trujillo-Falcón, B. A. Nickols, D. L. Nash, M. Webb, S. M. Bartlett, A. M. Wilson, and A. L. Bitterman
495838.abstract: As atmospheric river (AR) forecasting capabilities continue to advance, understanding whether the public recognizes when these events occur is crucial for effective communication and decision-making. We paired a nationwide survey of 1,200 English and 406 Spanish speakers in the United States with geospatially derived AR landfall data, matched to respondents' ZIP codes, to assess recognition against observed occurrence. We addressed three questions: (1) how self-reported AR exposure over the prior 12 months compared to observed landfall; (2) whether recognition accuracy differed between English and Spanish speakers, and whether any difference persisted after accounting for region and prior AR Scale awareness; and (3) whether observed exposure and believed exposure related differently to ratings of AR Scale usefulness and to preferences for scale improvements. These results establish a baseline for public recognition of AR events and identify where forecast products and communication tools might help close the gap between occurrence and awareness, supporting future risk communication and decision-making.

495839.title: A Multi-Year Radiosonde Study of Lightning Launch Commit Criteria Thick Cloud Rule Conditions at Vandenberg Space Force Base
495839.authors: Daile Zhang, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and K. L. Cummins, S. Wagner, and D. J. Delene
495839.abstract: The Thick Cloud Rule, one of the Lightning Launch Commit Criteria (LLCC) governing launch operations at DoD and NASA spaceports, refers to a specific, quantitatively defined criterion rather than the presence of any visually thick cloud, and has been reported to have a high false-alarm rate. Previous analysis at Cape Canaveral/Kennedy Space Center estimated false alarms may approach 94%, representing substantial, likely avoidable loss of launch availability. No comparable characterization exists for Vandenberg Space Force Base (SFB), an operationally important but scientifically understudied site on the Western Range. We present a multi-year radiosonde-based study of LLCC Thick Cloud Rule conditions at Vandenberg, analyzing 2,400 soundings spanning October 2022 through March 2026. Cloud layers were identified using a relative humidity threshold, with adjacent layers merged into connected groups. A Thick Cloud Rule proxy was defined as a connected group at least 1.4 km thick with any portion in the 0°C to -20°C mixed-phase zone. Overall, 14.2% of soundings met this proxy, with a pronounced winter/early-spring peak (approximately 25% in February-March) driven by synoptic frontal systems, falling to a hard summer minimum consistent with Vandenberg's shallow marine stratus regime. We further find a diurnal asymmetry in trigger frequency and characterize the depth and mixed-phase-overlap distributions of qualifying cloud systems, providing a first look at the population of events any revised criteria would need to address.

495841.title: A Probabilistic Framework for Structure-to-Structure Fire Modeling
495841.authors: Rachel Kleiman, University of North Carolina Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; Montana State University, Bozeman, MT; and A. Ficca, D. Li, H. Zeff, and G. Characklis
495841.abstract: Wildfires entering the wildland–urban interface (WUI) can transition into urban conflagrations, where structure-to-structure fire transmission produces cascading losses across communities. The 2025 Palisades Fire, for example, destroyed more than 6,800 structures and generated an estimated $20–25 billion in insured property losses. These increasingly destructive events have contributed to growing financial instability in California, creating an urgent need for highly resolved estimates of structural fire risk. Existing wildfire risk models often focus only on fire perimeters or burn probabilities. Structure-level conflagration models are commonly calibrated using a small number of events or individual fires, and stochasticity has not been represented in previous models. This work develops a stochastic simulation model of structure-to-structure fire spread within the WUI by combining property-level vulnerability with the effects of vegetation, dynamic wind, and building spacing on three heat transfer mechanisms: radiation, convection, and ember transport. Initial structure exposure is triggered by satellite fire observations, which represent wildland fires, while subsequent transmission evolves dynamically across the built environment. The model is evaluated on structure-level classifications of damaged and undamaged properties across 92 observed California wildfires, representing all events with at least 3 damaged structures during the period 2017-2025. Probabilistic model parameters are calibrated using a Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithm (MOEA), providing a set of plausible model solutions that navigate tradeoffs between classification accuracy, precision, and recall. This stochastic simulation framework enables evaluation of mitigation strategies, including the impact of fuel reduction and improved building materials, and provides an opportunity to simulate fire spread under alternate scenarios with stronger or longer-duration wind events. The resulting ensemble of probabilistic results can help to quantify cascading property losses for catastrophe modeling, insurance, and financial risk management.

495844.title: Assessing HAFS Reanalysis Configurations Using Surface Wind Field Asymmetry
495844.authors: Kelly E. Ryan, Cooperative Institute for Marine and Atmospheric Studies, Miami, FL; AOML, Miami, FL; and A. Hazelton
495844.abstract: Tropical Cyclone (TC) position and intensity remain the benchmark metrics for quantifying and comparing tropical cyclones across large datasets. However, research on the structure of TCs emphasizes the need to include additional information in the assessment of potential associated hazards. Characterizing the distribution of surface winds is critical not only in quantifying the size of a region affected by wind hazards, but also in assessing the potential for associated storm surge and precipitation risks. While varying definitions of TC size have become more routine in evaluations of structure, strategies leverage symmetric values of size using averaged or maximum radius of 34-knot wind, effectively eliminating asymmetric characteristics of the surface wind field. Furthermore, utilizing reported quadrant wind radii without additional interpretation results in potentially significant overestimation of the TC wind field extent. New metrics have been introduced to more realistically preserve these asymmetries and have shown value in understanding the evolution of a given TC and in characterizing its associated hazards. By design, these metrics can be employed for multiple purposes, and they can be used to intercompare a variety of surface wind datasets, including those from instrumentation, reanalyses, and predictive model simulations. Similar to TC track and intensity, these metrics rely only on regularly reported wind distribution information so that direct comparisons to the truth can be made regardless of observation coverage. This presentation demonstrates the utility of asymmetry metrics in selecting optimal configurations for a high-resolution hurricane reanalysis dataset. Using NOAA’s Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) as its framework, this regional reanalysis leverages its ability to model a large, basin-scale area with multiple high-resolution storm-following nests. In developing this dataset, multiple tropical cyclones will be validated to produce a year-long reanalysis dataset and requires meticulous evaluation in order to preserve accurate depictions of a variety of individual TCs. Through a targeted case study of Hurricane Melissa, results compare prospective HAFS configurations by examining surface wind distributions holistically and focus on asymmetry to validate TC structure characteristics.

495846.title: Toward Operational Field-Scale Evapotranspiration Mapping Beyond Agriculture: Scaling RADET from Flux Networks to Continental Applications
495846.authors: Yeonuk Kim, DRI, Reno, NV; and P. Raghav, J. L. Huntington, B. C. D. Andrade, M. Johnson, J. Volk, S. Majumdar, C. Morton, and P. ReVelle
495846.abstract: Operational field scale evapotranspiration (ET) mapping has advanced rapidly, providing increasingly actionable information for irrigation management, water accounting, and drought monitoring. However, continental scale applications require consistent ET estimates not only across agricultural lands but also across the natural ecosystems that occupy large portions of many watersheds. Current satellite-based ET systems, including models within OpenET, show strong performance over irrigated agriculture but more variable performance across natural ecosystems, creating an important challenge for extending field scale ET mapping to broader water resource applications. We recently developed the Radiation Advection Diffusivity Independent Evapotranspiration model (RADET) to address this challenge. RADET combines satellite remote sensing and meteorological information within a physically constrained framework designed to provide 30 m ET estimates across both agricultural and natural ecosystems. Evaluation across a broad network of flux sites in CONUS showed performance comparable to OpenET models in croplands while substantially improving ET estimates across forests, shrublands, grasslands, and other natural ecosystems. We are now extending RADET from research evaluation to scalable implementation. An open source, cloud based implementation in Google Earth Engine, with relatively low computational demand, enables reproducible and efficient application across sites and large spatial domains. Ongoing evaluation using a global synthesis of flux data from over 900 sites is assessing model transferability across a substantially broader range of climates, vegetation types, and hydrologic conditions. Regional implementation across Nevada for watershed scale water balance investigation is also underway to further evaluate the scalability of the framework at larger spatial domains. Together, these efforts illustrate a pathway from flux tower based algorithm development to reproducible regional and ultimately continental ET mapping. We will discuss the scientific and operational challenges involved in this transition, with particular emphasis on cross ecosystem robustness, large domain validation, cloud based implementation, computational efficiency, and open source reproducibility.

495847.title: Predicting Tropical Cyclone Intensity Using a Convolutional Neural Network and 20 Years of IMERG Satellite Rainfall Data
495847.authors: Haiyan Jiang, Florida International University, Miami, FL; Florida International University, Miami, FL; and S. You, P. Zhu, and O. F. Guzman
495847.abstract: The prediction of tropical cyclone (TC) intensity change remains one of the greatest challenges for forecasters. The Statistical Hurricane Intensity Prediction Scheme (SHIPS) is one of the most accurate models used in operational centers. The current version of SHIPS uses predictors including climatology and persistence, environmental conditions, and infrared satellite information. One critical piece of information that is largely missing from SHIPS is the rainfall and structural features of TCs. In this study, a novel Hurricane Convolutional Neural Network (HCNN) model is proposed to predict future TC intensity by using satellite rainfall images and existing SHIPS predictors. A 20-year (2000-2019) satellite rainfall dataset is obtained from the NASA Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals for the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission (IMERG) product for TCs from the Atlantic basin. The HCNN model is tested for 3 different radii of the IMERG data from the TC center and 200-km is selected. The model is trained using satellite images for TCs from 2000-2017 and tested using TCs from 2018-2019. Relative to a multiple linear regression model with SHIPS predictors trained using the same training sample and tested using the same test sample as used for the HCNN, the HCNN model with satellite rainfall input significantly improves forecasts by 9-13%, 8-18%, and 5-9% for all TCs, major hurricanes, and intensifying TCs, respectively, at 6-24 hour forecast intervals. Further experiments show that the HCNN can better utilize rainfall structural information than a multi-linear regression model integrating SHIPS and rainfall predictors.

495848.title: Agentic AI for QA/QC: A Modern Workflow for Optimizing Accuracy in Climate Data
495848.authors: Justin Bridwell, Consolidated Safety Services Inc., Fairfax, VA; and S. Douglas
495848.abstract: Climate and weather data integrity is foundational to decision-making, yet traditional Quality Analysis and Quality Control (QA/QC) methods often rely on rigid rules that struggle with complex spatial and temporal anomalies. At CSS Inc., we are evolving our data pipelines by integrating agentic AI directly into cloud architectures and Python-based workflows to validate the accuracy of the data at ingest or on the fly. By deploying autonomous agents powered by AWS Bedrock alongside custom data tools, we transition QA/QC from static validation scripts to adaptive, context-aware auditing systems. These AI agents operate within our ingestion and application frameworks—autonomously evaluating observational series, cross-referencing spatial continuity against neighboring stations, inspecting metadata discrepancies, and diagnosing outliers. By pairing foundation models with integrated geospatial tools, our architecture can now balance programmatic validation with natural language reasoning, producing more efficient validation and better accuracy in the datasets that power our workflows and applications. We will discuss the following points to illustrate the application and issues related to AI agentic QA/QC: Overview of a typical workflow: Describe the set up and configuration of adding agents to a process or application for the purpose of QA/QC AI Agent QA/QC in an existing application: Discuss how we have implemented agents to validate and optimize the accuracy of datasets in an existing application. Pitfalls and Problems: Examine the unique challenges and obstacles to utilizing agents for QA/QC with climate datasets in your workflow.

495849.title: Ingredients for Rapid Weakening (RW): Vertical Wind Shear Patterns and Corresponding Environmental Characteristics Associated with Rapidly Weakening Tropical Cyclones
495849.authors: Autumn Toms, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State, MS; and K. Wood and J. E. Rudzin
495849.abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) track and intensity forecasts have improved in recent decades; however, the reduction in intensity error has been slower for storms experiencing rapid intensity change. More intense TCs often cause greater impacts, thus considerable effort has been directed toward analyzing processes that support intensifying TCs. Less work has been conducted on the other end of the intensity change spectrum, that of rapid weakening (RW), though RW has received more focus in recent years. Environments associated with RW tend to be characterized by moderate-to-strong vertical wind shear (VWS), dry air, and a sharp, sea surface temperature (SST) gradient. VWS, typically calculated as the difference between the 200- and 850-hPa environmental wind fields, is strongly tied to TC intensity change. As a result, VWS is a commonly investigated parameter when exploring rapid intensity change despite widespread acceptance that the traditional VWS computation is not perfectly representative of the relationship between VWS and intensity change. Our ongoing work also indicates that the main drivers of RW vary based on basin and surrounding environmental conditions as dynamic and thermodynamic characteristics are not identical across RW events. Therefore, it is imperative to examine VWS in the context of other factors also present in RW environments. This study analyzes vertical wind profiles in rapidly weakening TCs in the North Atlantic (ATL) and eastern North Pacific (ENP) basins from 1988-2024 using fifth-generation European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ReAnalysis (ERA5) fields. Using NHC best-track data, we select events that weaken by ≥25 kt in 24 hours while at least 200 km from land. We first identify main patterns of these profiles to define wind shear structures associated with RW events. Using these patterns, we then investigate spatiotemporal characteristics of potential intensity, moisture, SST, and divergence to capture a more complete picture of the environment. Factors of interest include the upper-level wind configuration (e.g., trough or ridge patterns), thermodynamic favorability, and mid-level ventilation. Analyses are centered on the ERA5 storm center and span a range of radii (e.g., 0-500 km, 200-800 km) that overlap with past research and operational practice.

495850.title: A 40+ Year Climatology of Warm-Season Convective Storms and Future Climate Response in CONUS404
495850.authors: Joseph Dale, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and K. L. Rasmussen and H. Yu
495850.abstract: Convective precipitation is a vital component of warm-season water resources in the U.S. However, many previous climatological studies have investigated convective precipitation using climate models with resolutions too coarse for explicit representation of convective processes and do not investigate the climatological changes in the individual convective storms themselves. Recent increases in computational resources allow for regional climate models to achieve explicit representation of convective storms over climate timescales (e.g., km-scale or convection-permitting climate simulations). This study uses a 40+ year km-scale climate simulation (CONUS404) to develop a climatology of millions of individual convective storm features and their environments during the warm season (May-August) over the CONUS from 1979-2022. It is shown that CONUS404 accurately reproduces convective storms both spatially across the CONUS and in the diurnal cycle. The storm feature climatology is also compared with CONUS404’s pseudo-global warming (PGW) run to investigate how convective precipitation changes in a thermodynamically enhanced future climate. Results show that in a PGW environment, a larger fraction of total precipitation over the CONUS warm season falls from organized convective storms, with the largest increases over the central Great Plains. The PGW analysis also shows that storms form in warmer, moister, and higher instability environments, producing storms with higher cloud base heights, freezing levels, and echo top heights, which in turn leads to more storms producing higher rain rates. These findings underscore the importance of storm-scale changes in determining how warm-season precipitation and water resources may respond to a future climate.

495851.title: DTC’s METplus Verification Framework and Its Application to Deterministic Verification of NOAA's RRFS
495851.authors: Gerard Ketefian, NOAA/GSL, Boulder, CO; and M. J. Kavulich Jr., M. A. Harrold, G. P. McCabe Jr., J. Beck, and K. M. Newman
495851.abstract: With funding from the Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC), the DTC has established a new GitHub repository (dtc-vx-workflow) containing a verification workflow generation system. Dubbed the METplus Verification Framework, it is intended for use in DTC projects evaluating forecast model performance and for possible adoption by EPIC in its verification activities for NOAA. The Framework originated as a component in the UFS's Short-Range Weather (SRW) App, but is now a stand-alone verification (vx) system. It uses the DTC's METplus as the underlying vx software to create workflows that in turn generate vx statistics of numerical weather prediction (NWP) products. In this presentation, we will describe the capabilities of this workflow as well as the multiple improvements and additions the DTC has made over the past year to the original verification code in the SRW App. These include (1) evaluation of deterministic and ensemble forecasts from either regional or global operational models (e.g. RAP, HRRR, NAM, RRFS, GFS) as well as forecast products from experimental prototypes (e.g. MPAS-based RRFSv2 prototypes and AI-based NWP emulators); (2) retrieval and ingestion of a wide variety of observation data; (3) use of more than a dozen individual METplus tools to automatically generate a slew of statistical deterministic and ensemble vx metrics, object-based vx statistics, and track and intensity vx statistics specifically for tropical cyclones (TCs); and (4) inclusion of NOAA's Unified Workflow Tools (uwtools) package to enable more powerful and interoperable Python scripts. The improvements enumerated above have resulted in a modular, highly configurable, and extensible system for generating verification workflows for a wide variety of projects. The DTC's goal in developing the METplus Verification Framework is to accelerate the progress of model evaluation projects, avoid duplication of effort and spin-up costs for new projects, and enable a centralized repository of standard configurations and metrics for model evaluation. In addition to describing these improvements, we will discuss use of the METplus Verification Framework in several DTC projects, with a focus on its use to perform deterministic verification of NOAA's operational RRFSv1 (Rapid Refresh Forecast System version 1), which uses the FV3 as its dycore), and the MPAS_RRFSA, a newer RRFS prototype that uses MPAS as its dynamical core.

495853.title: The Role of Climate Risk Financial Modeling in Addressing Risk in a Changing Climate
495853.authors: Edward Joseph Kearns, MSCI, New York, NY
495853.abstract: Managing financial risk in a changing climate requires the intersection of physical science and economics to generate quality information to support decision-making. First Street uses community climate model outputs and observations to drive physics-based models of hazards for different time horizons and climate scenarios. These hazard outputs are then used to evaluate the intensity and consequence of exposure of individual assets within a financial modeling framework.

495854.title: An FAA Update on the Explorative Effort to Unify the Current Icing Product/Forecast Icing Product (CIP/FIP) and the Terminal Area Icing Weather Information (TAIWIN) Capability
495854.authors: Stephanie DiVito, FAA, Atlantic City International Airport, NJ; and B. Bernstein, S. D. Landolt, S. M. Ellis, D. R. Adriaansen, D. Jacobson, J. Lave, A. Gaydos, P. Prestopnik, G. P. McCabe Jr., J. Bracken, A. Klein, and S. Green
495854.abstract: The FAA currently manages two icing weather projects: In-Flight Icing (IFI) and Terminal Area Icing Weather Information (TAIWIN). IFI has historically focused on the en-route perspective of operations, developing the Current Icing Product (CIP) and the Forecast Icing Product (FIP), supporting their operational implementation, and researching and developing algorithm enhancements to incorporate novel technologies, user feedback, and new research findings. Meanwhile, TAIWIN is the more recent addition, focused on the terminal area perspective (below 12,000 feet and within 30 nautical miles of an airport), developing the TAIWIN capability to support icing decision-making for the most critical phases of flight and in support of expanded icing regulations. These algorithms (CIP, FIP, and TAIWIN) produce gridded output on different temporal and spatial scales and ingest and use several similar datasets in their assessments of icing environments. However, how the tools use and process these datasets differ. One major difference between CIP/FIP and the TAIWIN Capability is their output. CIP and FIP output icing severity (trace, light, moderate, heavy), icing probability, and supercooled large drop potential while TAIWIN outputs icing likelihood by drop size category (small drop, freezing drizzle, freezing rain). Considering the evolving icing weather information and operational needs as well as the desire to provide users with unified tools, the FAA is examining how these icing weather algorithms can and should interact, how they can leverage one another, and whether there needs to be consideration towards adjusting the output(s) of these tools. An update on the explorative effort into how CIP, FIP, and the TAIWIN Capability can be better integrated and aligned to address evolving needs will be provided. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the FAA. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

495856.title: The Importance of Change Agent for the Empowerment of Youth
495856.authors: Emilie Morin, Université du Québec à Rimouski, Rimouski, Canada; and L. Pivert, I. Arseneau, A. Fauré, and C. Cloutier
495856.abstract: In Quebec and elsewhere, we now face multiple sociocultural and ecological crises that disproportionately affect people and communities. The structural, legal, and regulatory changes needed to reverse ecological devastation are slow in coming, thereby exacerbating these inequalities. In this context, education is called upon to play a key role, as it can significantly contribute to building the agency of individuals and communities (Kwauk, 2020; McCaffrey and Boucher, 2022). While some educators have succeeded in implementing transformative educational initiatives (Hayward, 2021), much work remains to be done to develop the capacity for action among young people, individuals, and communities, as well as the resilience needed to overcome social and environmental crises (Rousell and Cutter-Mackenzie-Knowles, 2020). In this regard, one of our educational responsibilities is to focus our approaches on finding solutions and taking climate action (Morin et al., 2024), recognizing—as some young people already do—that individual behavioral changes, which are still primarily emphasized in many educational approaches, will not be sufficient (Morin, 2021). By focusing on individual behavioral change, we tend to overlook the structural social mechanisms that drive such behavior (Dubuisson-Quellier, 2025). In that sense, empowerment is a key in supporting action around a changing environment. To better understand how to empower individuals and communities, it seems essential to examine the conditions that facilitate or limit action, focusing on concrete cases of local mobilization. These situations of mobilization are often marked by power asymmetries, institutional constraints, and epistemic injustices, which limit the capabilities necessary for taking action. This communication examines the trajectories of individuals considered as change agents or policy entrepreneurs (Mintrom, 2020) who are actively engaged in socio-ecological mobilizations and institutional transformations. In the context of a multiple-case study focusing on four controversies related to the St. Lawrence River, estuary, and Gulf in Eastern Canada—namely, the river’s legal personhood, offshore oil and gas exploration, port development, and changes in fishing practices—we conducted semi-structured interviews with individuals actively involved in these cases. Our findings shed light on certain determinants of these individuals’ capacity to act. The findings focus on the conditions that foster or limit the development of the agency of the change agents interviewed. First, an examination of the triggers for action shows that commitment is rooted in awareness in the face of a threat or crisis, a sense of attachment to the local area, one’s living environment, and relationships, and a desire for collective transformation. The main obstacles encountered by these individuals are not due to a lack of motivation or a lack of individual skills, but rather to power dynamics and conflicting interests among the various stakeholders, as well as political and institutional barriers. The contextualized experiences of these individuals enrich educational discourse, since it is now important to consider how to support young people in understanding the social, political, and institutional conditions surrounding individual and collective action related to the socio-ecological transition. This can instill a sense of solidarity in youth, reassuring them that they are not alone and that older generations are fighting against social and environmental injustice. It also contributes to our understanding of which dimensions of empowerment should be prioritized in our educational approaches.

495860.title: AI-Accelerated Data Assimilation: From Differentiable Emulators to Diffusion-Based Posterior Sampling
495860.authors: Dimitrios K. Fytanidis, ANL, Lisle, IL; and R. Kotamarthi, R. Maulik, E. Constantinescu, Y. Sun, S. Madireddy, S. Frolov, I. Jankov, D. D. Turner, and M. Olsen
495860.abstract: The established benefit of data assimilation (DA) for improving predictability has led to exponential growth in geophysical dataset size amid an increasing emphasis on obtaining high-resolution 4D observations. However, the use of these large observational datasets for model development and to improve predictability remains a challenge. Data assimilation in operational settings has used the 4D variational assimilation procedure or the Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) technique. The former is constrained by the need for developing and running adjoints and the difficulty of including observational uncertainty in the forecast system (Buehner et al.,2010). On the other hand, high computational costs associated with model simulations severely limit the ensemble size that can be used, which in turn limits the accuracy of EnKF. The employment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms to generate surrogates can greatly expand the ensemble sizes, making the EnKF and 4D-var approaches computationally feasible. We have been exploring the various methodologies for accelerating the use of extreme amounts of data for DA using AI. Three different approaches were explored, An AI-accelerated 4D-var framework that preserves the standard outer-loop DA structure but replaces the traditional forecast model with an AI emulator, yielding 40x or greater speedup (Maulik et al., 2022). A GPU-native 4D-var implementation for AI foundation models, comprising (a) a time-dependent observation operator and (b) a 4D-var cost function optimized in PyTorch, with the assimilation cycle driven by an AI forecast model (Nguyen et al., 2024). A posterior-guided diffusion model that covers observationally constrained (reanalysis equivalent) fields from sparse observations and AI foundation-model emulator forecasts, without retraining the underlying model (Chakraborty et al., 2026). The framework also supports uncertainty-driven adaptive observation placement, and we are extending it toward multimodal data–model fusion for generating target-resolution reference data. Results from these methods and their applicability to generating reanalysis datasets will be presented.

495862.title: Mechanisms, Development, and Downstream Impacts of Eastern North American Cold Air Outbreaks
495862.authors: Alexander Morelli, Pennsylvania State University, Etters, PA; and M. Gervais
495862.abstract: Cold air outbreaks (CAOs) are air masses with significantly colder than normal temperatures. They often originate over land or sea ice at high latitudes, and then propagate southward. They have significant socioeconomic impacts over large areas, especially regions such as the heavily populated eastern portion of North America. Previous studies have indicated a number of factors, including teleconnections such as the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), Pacific North American pattern (PNA), and North Pacific Oscillation (NPO), may influence the formation and propagation of these air masses, however the links between some teleconnections, particularly the NAO, remain contested. This research analyzes the atmospheric patterns which are associated with different tracks of CAOs which affect eastern North America on a synoptic timescale. An analysis of the teleconnections associated with these synoptic patterns is assessed. A pattern with a deep-layer ridge over the northwestern portion of North America contributes to the formation of the CAO, while variations in the Atlantic pattern contribute to variations in the CAO’s track. These patterns mimic classic teleconnection patterns of the NAO, PNA, and NPO, but are varied in the longitudinal placement of their centers of action. In addition, as the CAOs move over the relatively warmer water of the eastern Atlantic, they create a large sensible and latent heat flux, which may have significant downstream effects on the eddy-driven jet stream. Categorizing the mechanisms behind formation, propagation, and downstream effects of CAOs may help improve forecasting of these high-impact meteorological events.

495863.title: Quantifying Ammonia with Optical Spectroscopy and Cluster Mass Spectrometry Towards Improved Parametrization of Nucleation Rates
495863.authors: Clara Jean Lietzke, Univ. of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and F. Möller, D. Katz, L. Liu, E. Sommer, J. Almeida, J. R. Roscioli, J. Kirkby, S. Schobesberger, H. Junninen, I. El Haddad, Q. Chen, and R. Volkamer
495863.abstract: About half of cloud condensation nuclei are formed by nucleation of condensable vapors in a process called new particle formation (NPF). Uncertain parameterizations of nucleation rates are a major driver of uncertainties in cloud cover and radiative feedback in global climate models. Ammonia (NH3) can increase sulfuric acid (H2SO4) nucleation rates more than 100-fold, and its role in NPF is projected to grow with increasing and largely unregulated emissions from agriculture. Field and satellite observations indicate high levels of NH3 in the Asian Tropopause Aerosol Layer from the deep convective outflow of the summer monsoon, while aircraft measurements have observed highly acidic aerosols in the remote free troposphere. This wide range of NH3 concentrations (0.01-1500 pptv) at cold temperatures remains poorly constrained in parametrizations of nucleation and thus its effect on NPF is not well understood. Interestingly, the effect of NH3 in nucleating H2SO4 clusters saturates at very low concentrations around 0.1-1 pptv NH3. However, such low NH3 levels are extremely difficult to measure. Laboratory measurements at the CERN Cosmics Leaving OUtdoor Droplets (CLOUD) chamber provide an opportunity to investigate the role of NH3 in NPF under carefully controlled conditions. During the CLOUD18 and CLOUD19 campaigns, a Tunable Infrared Laser Direct Absorption Spectroscopy (TILDAS) instrument was deployed to quantify low levels of gas-phase NH3, alongside molecular ion cluster composition measurements by Atmospheric Pressure Interface Time of Flight (API-TOF) mass spectrometry. Previous work has shown that the NH3-to-H2SO4 ratio in clusters detected by API-TOF is related to the gas-phase NH3-to-H2SO4 ratio. Here, we use the TILDAS to characterize NH3-containing ion cluster distributions and develop the API-TOF as a quantitative technique to infer extremely low NH3 concentrations, with the goal of extending nucleation rate measurements to previously unquantifiable NH3 concentrations, ultimately leading to more accurate parameterizations of nucleation in global climate models.

495864.title: Community-Based Earth System Modeling with NOAA’s Earth Prediction Innovation Center - The First Five Years
495864.authors: Keven Michael Blackman, NOAA, Bellevue, NE; Raytheon Technologies, Omaha, NE; and D. A. Burrows, F. Adimi, C. Book, A. C. Jones, and M. Huang
495864.abstract: Over the past five years, the Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC) has been at the forefront of advancing the Unified Forecast System (UFS), fostering a collaborative ecosystem that accelerates innovation to advance numerical weather forecasting and Earth system modeling capabilities. Through a steadfast commitment to engaging the broader community, EPIC has not only provided the critical tools and knowledge necessary for innovation but has also paved the way to break down barriers to entry into the UFS. The EPIC team has established a comprehensive framework designed to foster and facilitate community contributions to Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP), incorporating both physics-based models and those utilizing Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML). This framework includes the development of an infrastructure for the expedited and automated verification of all community enhancements and submissions to earth system modeling. Moreover, this structure integrates a Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) pipeline, refined management processes, Hierarchical System Development (HSD), community outreach and instructional events, advanced user support, community resources and tools, and video tutorials, with the EPIC Community Portal (ECP) serving as a central hub for engagement and support. EPIC's overarching mission has remained steadfast: to cultivate a representative and collaborative environment where a wide range of perspectives are celebrated, and groundbreaking ideas take root. By harnessing the collective expertise and input of the community, EPIC has driven significant advancements in Earth system modeling, improving the accuracy and reliability of forecasts that are essential for public safety and economic resilience. As we reflect on the progress of the last five years, EPIC remains committed to advancing Earth system prediction innovation for the benefit of all. This presentation will focus on the pivotal role of community engagement and support in EPIC's success. We will offer a summary of the current status of our various community engagement initiatives, detailing the mechanisms and platforms established for collaboration, contribution, and feedback.

495865.title: Characterizing Flow Behavior in Eddy-Covariance Gas Analyzer Designs: Implications for Sensor Co-Location and Flux Quality
495865.authors: Atefeh NA Hosseini, Campbell Scientific, Logan, UT; and I. Bogoev, E. Swiatek, T. Banerjee, R. Newman, B. Strickler, and A. Lawyer
495865.abstract: Flux calculations require precise, high-frequency measurements of three-dimensional wind vectors and scalar mixing ratios (e.g., CO₂ and H₂O), which are essential for accurately estimating energy fluxes using the eddy covariance technique. These measurements characterize atmospheric conditions and support evaluation of weather and environmental models. Eddy covariance systems typically pair a sonic anemometer, which measures wind and air temperature, with an open-path gas analyzer that measures water vapor and carbon dioxide. Because the gas analyzer housing is positioned close to the sonic measurement path, instrument configuration and geometry can alter the surrounding flow field and affect turbulence statistics. This study evaluates flow behavior across different eddy covariance instrument configurations using CSAT3B and IRGASON sonic anemometers mounted along a horizontal bar with defined spacing. Configurations with and without a gas analyzer are compared across varying wind speeds and directions. Preliminary first- and second-order turbulence statistics and experimental design details will be presented.

495866.title: Vertical Wind Speeds in Mixed-Phase Clouds and their Impact on Liquid and Ice Water Content Mixing Ratios
495866.authors: Andrew J. Heymsfield, NCAR, Boulder, CO
495866.abstract: Vertical velocities are crucial in understanding the development of the ice phase in clouds. In this study, we examine the distribution of vertical wind velocity measured in a number of geographically diverse airborne in-situ field campaigns, focused on stratiform to weak convective clouds, and relate the vertical velocity values to the presence and amount of liquid and ice water contents. Results are stratified by temperature, geographic location, and potential orographic effects. Doppler radar measurements from onboard or overflying aircraft are used to improve the accuracy of the vertical wind measurements. We find that, in general, increased vertical velocities result in higher liquid water content mixing ratios for midlatitude winter storm systems, but does not always hold for high latitude marine clouds. The results are parameterized for use in model evaluation of mixed-phase cloud systems.

495870.title: Early Detection of Lightning-Ignited Wildfires Using Machine Learning and Geovisualization
495870.authors: Scott D. Rudlosky, NESDIS, Brooklyn Heights, OH; NOAA NESDIS Geo Earth Observations Office, Kent, OH; University of Maryland, College Park, MD; Kent State University, Kent, OH; and J. Patton and G. Fang
495870.abstract: Automated identification of lightning-ignited wildfires presents significant operational challenges due to spatial and temporal uncertainties in attribution. To enhance early detection and keep human observers effectively in the decision loop, this project establishes machine learning (ML) tools and visualization frameworks informed by a comprehensive, fire-centric lightning climatology. Analysis of environmental, meteorological, and land surface variables highlights distinct statistical differences between ignition and null environments, as well as between same-day fire detections and holdover fires. Two predictive models were developed to alert users to wildfire potential: the Lightning Ignition Region of Interest (LIROI), which estimates prior-day ignition potential across gridded regions, and the Lightning Ignition Likelihood Index (LILI), which assesses ignition probability surrounding new wildfire reports and hotspot observations. Applied to summer 2024 western U.S. data, the workflow evaluated 4,630 natural or unknown fire reports, confirming 3,747 ignitions. Roughly half (52.8%) of these fires were detected within the first 24 hours, while the remainder exhibited holdover times spanning up to two weeks. To deliver actionable situational awareness, an interactive Lightning Fire Dashboard was created to display LIROI and LILI categorical likelihood predictions (ranging from "Very Unlikely" to "Certain") alongside key meteorological and land surface layers. Ongoing work focuses on refining the ML models and display capabilities ahead of a planned summer 2026 operational demonstration.

495871.title: Robustness of Aerosol-Cloud Parameter Sensitivities Across Climate States in E3SMv3 PPE
495871.authors: Kayla White, University of Hawaii, Honolulu, HI; and T. W. Aerenson and G. Torri
495871.abstract: Uncertainty associated with aerosol-cloud parameterizations in Earth system models (ESMs) represents a meaningful and distinct contribution to uncertainty in simulated anthropogenic aerosol forcing and the associated climate responses. While perturbed parameter ensembles (PPEs) and present-day observations provide a means of constraining this uncertainty, it is essential to assess the extent to which such constraints remain valid under future climate states, given the considerable changes expected in both the anthropogenic aerosol burden and the background climate over the coming decades. Here, we analyze a 250-member PPE in version 3 of the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SMv3), derived through perturbations to 25 governing aerosol-cloud parameters, under present-day and idealized + 4 K background climate states with fixed anthropogenic aerosol forcing. We assess how sensitivities to aerosol-cloud parameters and their relative rankings depend on climate state and evaluate the robustness of present-day aerosol-cloud constraints under idealized extreme warming. In doing so, this analysis provides a framework for identifying sources of aerosol-cloud uncertainty whose influence may strengthen or weaken as the climate warms, informs model tuning strategies, and advances efforts to distinguish the contribution of aerosol-cloud process uncertainty to uncertainty in total anthropogenic aerosol forcing and future climate projections.

495872.title: The Global Atmospheric River Reconnaissance Program: An Overview of the First Demonstration Campaign
495872.authors: Anna M. Wilson, SIO, San Diego, CA; SIO, Durham, NC; Scripps Institution of Oceanography, Univ. of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and F. M. Ralph, V. S. Tallapragada, C. A. Reynolds, J. D. Doyle, C. Davis, L. Delle Monache, A. C. Subramanian, F. Pappenberger, J. Cordeira, J. S. Haase, L. Centurioni, R. D. Torn, A. C. Michaelis, D. Lavers, and P. Capute
495872.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are global phenomena that can produce both severe hazards and critical water supply. Improving their prediction requires observations across oceanic and atmospheric regions where conventional observing networks are sparse. Atmospheric River Reconnaissance (AR Recon), which itself has grown over the past decade from a concept to a field demonstration to today’s operational requirement and federally sponsored mission, has consistently demonstrated the value of targeted observations for improving forecasts, and the Global Atmospheric River Reconnaissance Program (GARRP) extends this approach to a global scale. This presentation will describe the execution of the first GARRP demonstration campaign, including campaign design, coordination, observing strategies, and integration of dropsonde, ocean drifter, radiosonde, airborne radio occultation, and other observing platforms across multiple regions of the Northern Hemisphere. The campaign brought together operational and research partners across the globe, with leadership from AR Recon in the United States, to test the feasibility of coordinated global reconnaissance and its integration into forecast systems. The presentation will highlight initial achievements and lessons on targeting, coordination, data delivery, and operational implementation, as well as describe future plans for GARRP. The demonstration represents an important step toward establishing a sustained, internationally coordinated approach to observing atmospheric rivers and improving prediction of their impacts on weather, water resources, and extreme events.

495873.title: NOAA-NASA QuickSounder Mission
495873.authors: Saji Abraham, NEON, Lanham, MD; GSFC, Ellicott City, MD; and P. Beierle, S. Blonski, A. Bringer, G. de Amici, J. Fuentes, S. Iacovazzi, F. Iturbide-Sanchez, J. Kam, E. J. Kim, R. V. Leslie, Q. Liu, C. H. Lyu, A. Manaster, M. Sammons, N. Sun, H. Yang, and K. Zhang
495873.abstract: The presentation will inform the community about the upcoming NOAA-NASA QuickSounder Earth observation mission and will discuss the mission overview, schedule, planning, and science. NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) program, within the Office of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) Observations, provides the next generation of Earth-observation LEO satellites. The program will supplement and eventually replace the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS). The first mission of the NEON program is QuickSounder (QS). QuickSounder is a risk-reduction mission for the NEON program; in particular, the mission will evaluate non-instrument portions of the mission such as commercial partnerships and processes for satellites, launch services, mission operations, and data distribution. The satellite is scheduled to launch in 2027. Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) is providing the spacecraft bus and mission operations. Northrop Grumman is providing the science instrument: a refurbished engineering unit for the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS). ATMS is a total power microwave radiometer utilizing a cross-track scan profile that is manifested on the JPSS satellites. The instrument has 22 channels from 23 – 183 GHz providing global temperature and water vapor sounding. QuickSounder will fly in the terminator polar sun-synchronous orbit. QuickSounder data is anticipated to be a useful addition to the Earth observing system. Although the requirements of QuickSounder focus on application of commercial small sat capabilities to NESDIS missions, the pre-launch testing and evaluation rigor performed on the JPSS ATMS Flight units has also been rendered upon QuickSounder ATMS. This has been done with the aspiration that the data will be useful for numerical weather prediction (NWP) and environmental monitoring.
