Pre-launch characterization includes thermal vacuum (TVAC) calibration test, where numerous characterization parameters such as Noise Equivalent Delta Temperature (NEDT), striping, and inter-channel noise correlation have been assessed. The science performance will be similar to the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (SNPP) ATMS. On-orbit commissioning evaluations will characterize Raw Data Record (RDR), Temperature Data Record (TDR), and Sensor Data Record (SDR) quality. Commissioning activities include JPSS-heritage maneuvers such as a satellite roll and pitch maneuvers for reflector emissivity and scan-dependent bias evaluations, with differences to their JPSS counterparts due to differences between the JPSS observatory and the smaller free-flyer QS satellite and associated orbits. A calibration data book containing spectral response functions will be publicly available for data users.

495875.title: A Machine Learning Framework for Circuit-Level Outage Probability and Wildfire Risk Assessment
495875.authors: Shahrbanou Madadgar, Filsinger Energy Partners, Denver, CO
495875.abstract: Wildfire risk associated with electric distribution systems is influenced by complex interactions among weather, vegetation, infrastructure, and operational conditions. This study presents a machine-learning-based Probability of Failure (PoF) framework implemented for an electric utility in Northern California to estimate circuit-level outage likelihood and support wildfire risk assessment and prioritization. Historical outage data were integrated with weather, asset, vegetation, load, and inspection information to develop and evaluate multiple machine learning algorithms, with LightGBM selected based on predictive performance, stability, and interpretability. Model performance was evaluated using out-of-fold cross-validation, and SHAP-based analysis was used to identify the variables and conditions most influential in outage predictions. Results demonstrate meaningful discrimination between outage and non-outage conditions, with weather-related variables—particularly wind and other short-term environmental conditions—emerging as the strongest predictors, while infrastructure, vegetation, inspection, and operational characteristics provide additional circuit-level risk differentiation. The modeled outage likelihood is further integrated with extreme fire weather conditions and wildfire consequence information to develop circuit-level wildfire risk estimates and rankings. The resulting framework demonstrates how machine learning can integrate diverse utility and environmental datasets to identify elevated-risk conditions, characterize differences in risk across distribution circuits, and provide an interpretable, quantitative basis for wildfire mitigation and risk-informed investment prioritization.

495876.title: Mapping El Niño Onset and False-Start Pathways with Growing Neural Gas
495876.authors: Emily Faith Wisinski, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and M. J. Molina
495876.abstract: Traditional methods of characterizing and monitoring El Niño development rely on scalar indices, such as NOAA’s operational Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI). These spatially averaged sea surface temperature (SST) metrics may obscure the distinct pathways through which El Niño events evolve and ultimately result in successful or failed onsets. We implement Growing Neural Gas (GNG), an unsupervised machine learning algorithm that groups SST fields with similar spatial patterns. Unlike Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs), which require a fixed lattice size and predefined topology, GNG adaptively adds and removes nodes and connections, yielding a state space shaped by tropical Pacific SST variability. We apply GNG to monthly ERA5 SST (January 1940 to March 2026) across the tropical Pacific and identify distinct ocean states that characterize a range of La Niña, El Niño, and neutral conditions. Using absorbing Markov chain theory, in which we quantify the probability of reaching a defined outcome from each transient state, we address the leading research question: for a given ocean state, what is the probability that it develops into an El Niño event? We can then examine onset pathways, false-start pathways, and quantify empirical probabilities of the point at which “commitment” to an El Niño becomes increasingly likely (i.e., “point of no return”). Results indicate that El Niño onsets and false starts appear to pass through the same intermediate states before diverging, suggesting a shared decision state for development rather than independent failure routes. We also investigate the roles of the spring predictability barrier and the background ocean state (e.g., decadal modes of variability) in onset probabilities.

495877.title: U.S. Geological Survey – National Weather Service Collaboration on Landslide Research and Forecasting to Support a Hazard-Ready Nation
495877.authors: Benjamin B Mirus, USGS, Golden, CO; and B. Collins, W. Schulz, D. Staley, A. Jacobs, A. Rehnberg, P. Moore, C. Walbrun, B. Garcia, E. Rodríguez, S. Hughes, J. Perkins, J. Woodard, and L. Luna
495877.abstract: Weather-related landslides are a common geologic hazard in hilly and mountainous terrain that can be both highly destructive and deadly. In particular, shallow landslides that move rapidly downslope and may transition into debris flows in channels and streams can have severe consequences for humans and the built environment. To address this threat, the National Landslides Preparedness Act directs the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) to conduct research on landslide initiation conditions and coordinate with the National Weather Service (NWS) and other federal, state, and local agencies to improve communication and forecasting of landslide hazards. For example, monitoring and analysis confirms that in unburned watersheds, shallow landslides and debris flows are commonly triggered by a sequence of wet antecedent soil moisture followed by intense or prolonged rainfall triggering. Therefore, in many steep regions across the U.S., improved landslide forecasts are possible through integrating USGS measurements and models of antecedent conditions with NWS precipitation forecasts and observations. To transition these findings from research into action, NWS Weather Forecasting Offices (WFOs) have partnered with research scientists within the USGS’ Landslide Hazards Program to include locally specific landslide conditions and language in their outreach activities, special weather statements, and flash flood alerts. This presentation will highlight examples of these NWS-USGS partnerships that are advancing research-to-operations to strengthen landslide forecasting capabilities in Alaska, California, North Carolina, and Puerto Rico. Additionally, our research on distinct patterns of landslide frequency and seasonality across the nation can inform longer-term planning for counties and WFOs with the greatest landslide exposure. Towards this goal, communication and education about landslide preparedness and public awareness have also proven critical in translating advances in science into actionable information and warnings aimed at saving lives and protecting property. Together, USGS research and NWS operations are creating not only a more weather-ready nation, but also a more hazard-ready nation, by building resilience to landslides in communities across the country.

495878.title: Assessing WindBorne Global Sounding Balloon Impact on High-Impact Weather Events through Ensemble Sensitivity, AIDA Data Denial and Synthetic Observations
495878.authors: Tomer Burg, WindBorne Systems, Redwood Shores, CA; and J. T. Radford, L. J. Reames, A. Shetty, J. Creus-Costa, T. Hutchinson, C. Riedel, PhD, and J. Michaels
495878.abstract: WeatherMesh-6 (WM6) is a state of the art AI-based weather prediction (AIWP) model, trained on ERA5 data and producing 15-day global weather forecasts. The currently operational WM6 model version generally outperforms similar AI ensemble suites such as the ECMWF’s AIFS Ensemble and Google’s WeatherNext-2 for key metrics such as 500-hPa geopotential height RMSE. WM6 performs its own machine learning-driven data assimilation (DA) using the IFS ensemble as prior, including assimilating WindBorne’s own global sounding balloons (GSBs). As WindBorne Systems operates the world’s largest weather balloon constellation, assessing the impact of the exponentially growing GSB constellation on WM6 forecast skill is of significant importance for both assessing the overall impact of GSBs on aggregate skill scores and the impact of both constellation-wide and targeted observations on high-impact weather events. To address this question, WindBorne ran parallel implementations of WM6 for a three-month period, one assimilating all observations and one denying WindBorne GSBs. High-impact cases where major differences were observed between both implementations will be analyzed, with ensemble sensitivity analysis used to identify upstream regions of sensitivity. Another set of simulations will then be performed for these cases specifically denying GSBs only within and surrounding these regions of ensemble sensitivity, with another parallel set of simulations using ERA5 reanalysis data to insert synthetic observations. Given that ERA5 does not assimilate GSB data, this method aims to quantify the value of GSB data in sensitive regions to downstream high-impact weather events.

495880.title: Limited Climate Response to Extreme Arctic Mixed-phase Cloud Thinning
495880.authors: Xia Li, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and A. T. Evan, I. Eisenman, and J. F. Kok
495880.abstract: Cloud-based climate interventions seek to reduce climate change impacts by altering Earth's radiation budget through targeted cloud modifications. Mixed-phase regime cloud thinning (MCT) is a recently proposed strategy that aims to reduce cloud longwave trapping by seeding mixed-phase regime clouds with ice-nucleating particles, thereby promoting liquid-to-ice conversion and cloud thinning. Although the microphysical basis of MCT is well known, its large-scale climatic potential is unknown. Here we address this question by evaluating the climatic response under intentionally extreme Arctic MCT scenarios using a climate model. We find that, even under this extreme scenario, the response remains both localized to the Arctic Ocean and limited in magnitude, producing only -0.47 ± 0.08°C of Arctic annual-mean cooling and 0.23 ± 0.04 million km2 of annual sea ice expansion. This offsets 4.3% of Arctic warming and 3.5% of sea ice loss under doubled CO2, or approximately 18% and 13%, respectively, relative to observed changes over the past four decades. These findings suggest limited large-scale climatic leverage of MCT but potential value for locally targeted applications, particularly near susceptible marginal ice zones.

495881.title: A Machine Learning Framework for Global Hail Climatology and Vineyard Risk Assessment Using MRMS and ERA5
495881.authors: Will Davis Cano, NHC, Spring City , PA
495881.abstract: Hail poses a significant risk to vineyards worldwide. However, high quality radar-based hail observations are largely limited to regions like the contiguous United States, leaving many major wine-growing areas — including parts of Europe, South America, and the Mediterranean — without reliable long-term hail climatologies. This work develops a machine learning framework that uses the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) dataset as ground truth for hail occurrence, paired with atmospheric predictors derived from the ERA5 reanalysis, to learn the relationship between large-scale environmental conditions and observed hail. Because ERA5 is available globally, a model trained on U.S. radar-verified data can, in principle, be applied anywhere ERA5 exists. This offers a pathway to estimate hail risk in regions that lack dedicated radar climatologies. In an operational sense, the model can also be applied to real-time conditions using GFS data. I describe the construction of a daily, spatially aggregated hail dataset built from established severe hail metrics, the selection of environmental predictors known to relate to hail production, and a training and validation strategy designed to produce calibrated, generalizable hail probability estimates. The model's output is then used to construct a global hail climatology, which is overlaid with wine-growing regions worldwide, accounting for each region's specific growing season and how it aligns with local hail season. Because ground-based radar verification is unavailable in most target regions, I evaluate the model's performance using independent severe weather reports from the European Severe Storms Laboratory (ESSL) and the European Severe Weather Database (ESWD), providing a check on how well the model transfers beyond its training domain. I discuss the challenges of cross-regional validation and the broader potential for this approach to support hail-risk assessment in vulnerable agricultural regions globally.

495883.title: Challenges and Opportunities in the Very Low Earth Observations (VLEO) Environment
495883.authors: Joseph H Westlake, NASA, Washington, DC; and A. D. Silimon-Hill and E. Mahoney
495883.abstract: Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) has long been associated with operational barriers due to aerodynamic drag, thermal fluctuations, and atomic oxygen corrosion. With the potential for new technologies and architectural solutions to surpass these barriers, this elusive location is coming into focus as a potentially high-value frontier for heliophysics and space weather research. VLEO offers a unique natural laboratory that behaves half like space and half like an atmospheric fluid, filling a critical observational gap in the Lower Thermosphere-Ionosphere (LTI) system. In-situ sampling of lower thermospheric neutral density provides the high-fidelity empirical data required to refine atmospheric drag models, improve orbital decay predictions, and ensure safe, precise spacecraft reentry operations. Concurrently, mapping fine-scale ionospheric irregularities, such as equatorial plasma bubbles, allows for forecasting severe space weather disruptions that degrade GPS, GNSS, and global satellite communication networks. Operating satellites in Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) offers major practical advantages such as 1) Cheaper Parts: VLEO sits below Earth’s main radiation belts. Because radiation levels are low, satellites can use standard commercial electronics instead of custom, expensive radiation-shielded hardware. 2) Lower Power Needs: Being closer to Earth means transmitting high-speed data back to the ground requires far less power, cutting equipment costs. 3) No Long-Term Space Debris: Thin atmospheric drag naturally pulls dead satellites back down to burn up quickly. This makes VLEO ideal for testing new tech fast without leaving dangerous space junk behind. 4) Testing Ground for Deep Space: Flying through Earth's upper atmosphere gives engineers real-world data on how spacecraft handle atmospheric friction. This helps design entry and landing systems for missions to Mars, Venus, and Titan. To fully exploit VLEO's scientific potential, the heliophysics community must bridge basic research on thermospheric dynamics with operator requirements. NASA Heliophysics is already advancing next-generation satellite constellations, in-situ instrument packages, miniaturized propulsion, and advancements toward real-time space weather forecasting models. By uniting thermospheric physics with operational strategy, VLEO transforms from an aggressive environmental hazard into an invaluable asset not only for heliophysics science but for all of space science and exploration.

495884.title: Arctic Air Under the Microscope: Metagenomic Insights into Aerosol Ice-Nucleating Particles at Svalbard archipelago, Norway
495884.authors: Khalil Geballa-Koukoulas, Agricultural University Of Athens, Greece, Athens, Greece, A1, Greece; and J. Ofili, S. Smriti, D. Shah, C. Ritter, D. Georgakopoulos, and N. Hiranuma
495884.abstract: Biological ice-nucleating particles (INPs) influence Arctic cloud microphysics, albedo, and precipitation, but their sources and seasonal variability remain poorly understood. Here, we combined high-throughput sequencing of bacterial (16S rRNA, V3–V4) and fungal (ITS2) communities with quantitative immersion-freezing assays of aerosol samples collected in Svalbard during springtime 2023 and spring and summer 2024. Our results revealed that bacterial alpha-diversity peaked in spring 2023 during anomalously warm conditions, suggesting that meteorological variability influences microbial population diversity and their sources. Across all seasons, Sphingomonas paucimobilis was consistently detected, while Pseudomonas syringae dominated in spring and showed a significant correlation with INP concentrations. On the contrary, Pseudomonas putida prevailed under summer conditions. Additionally, Fusarium and Cladosporium dominated fungal communities, though ice nucleation-active Fusarium species comprised only a minor fraction. Strong relationships between Fusarium and Cladosporium, together with correlations with ambient environmental conditions (radiation, temperature, and humidity), indicate that both ecological factors and meteorological conditions constrain fungal contributions to INPs. Overall, microbial INPs in Svalbard are taxa-specific and strongly modulated by meteorological conditions rather than remaining continuously abundant throughout our study period. Biological INPs in aerosol samples are primarily derived from local Arctic bacteria, with a clear seasonal succession, supplemented by a small but persistent fungal contribution from Fusarium species. Collectively, these patterns suggest that local meteorology, rather than long-range transport from lower latitudes, is the dominant driver of microbial INP abundance.

495886.title: Near Inflow Environmental Evolution in PERiLS
495886.authors: Rachel L. Miller, CIWRO, Norman, OK; and L. E. Pounds, M. D. Flournoy, and M. C. Coniglio
495886.abstract: Multiple modeling and observational studies have attempted to characterize the environment ahead of convective storms and the spatiotemporal changes of parameters most strongly linked to severe hazards. Storm-relative helicity (SRH) across multiple layers has been correlated to a storm’s tornadic potential as well as other kinematic variables such as storm-relative winds, bulk shear, and ground-relative winds and thermodynamic variables such as low-level moisture, lifted condensation level (LCL) height, and convective available potential energy (CAPE). In particular, radiosonde observations from field campaigns have highlighted the differences in the far-field and near-field environment in the inflow of supercells. For example, SRH in the 0–1-km layer is larger in the near-field environment of tornadic supercells compared to the far-field environment. When representative soundings of the near and far-field tornadic environments are used as the background environment for storm-scale simulations, simulated supercells in the near-field environment produced tornado-like vortices much more often than supercells in the far-field environment. However, these studies have not been able to quantify the observed temporal change of particular environmental parameters as storms approach a given location. We accomplish this by analyzing Sparv Embedded Windsonds, which were launched abundantly during the Propagation, Evolution, and Rotation in Linear Storms (PERiLS) field campaign in 2022 and 2023. These complemented the more traditional radiosonde launches that sampled the background convective environment in the Southeast United States (SE US). These Windsonds tended to be launched at a high temporal resolution from the same location within the inflow of a targeted storm to sample the rapidly evolving convective environment on a much shorter timescale than a radiosonde (minutes versus hours). Across both years of PERiLS, 221 of these Windsonds were launched during five IOPs, supporting analysis of localized environmental evolution ahead of tornadic QLCSs (4/13/22 and 3/30/22), supercells (3/31/23 and 3/24/23), and a tornadic QLCS with a line leading tornadic supercell (3/22/22). Windsond observations are combined with radar data to assess environmental evolution across storm modes and diagnose the rate of change in kinematic and thermodynamic variables in the inflow environment. Particular focus is on the kinematic variables’ evolution, specifically SRH using observed storm motion, which has been shown to be more statistically significant in discriminating between tornadic and non-tornadic storms in the SE US.

495887.title: BLT - Exploring the Gray Zone: Testing Scale-Aware PBL Schemes in Storm Forecasting
495887.authors: Joseph Michael Sean Payne, Ball State University, Muncie, IN; and T. Hahn and J. M. Peters
495887.abstract: As weather forecasting model resolution continues to increase, one of the limiting factors in forecast accuracy is how these models represent sub-grid scale turbulence in the Planetary Boundary Layer (PBL) “gray zone”. This “gray zone” consists of horizontal model grid spacing between 1 km and 100 m, where turbulence cannot be explicitly resolved, but parameterization is imprecise. Scale-aware parameterization schemes are a potential solution to this problem. They attempt to resolve turbulent currents where possible and adjust the influence of parameterization with grid spacing. To test the accuracy of these models, we ran a Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model on an 800 m horizontal grid twice; once with the Yonsei University parameterization scheme and again with the Shin-Hong scale-aware scheme. Next, we used a Lagrangian tracking algorithm to compare the properties of model-generated cells with NEXRAD observations during a convective event over Baltimore, MD on July 27, 2025. We found that the scale-aware scheme was marginally better at predicting maximum cell reflectivity area, but convective initiation was forecasted better by the parameterized scheme. Many other variables, including storm volume, lifetime, and perimeter were forecasted equally well by both models. Although both models’ maximum echo tops were consistent with one another, they were consistently higher than observed echo tops. Further research should evaluate the performance of scale-aware models at finer other grid spacings in the PBL gray zone.

495889.title: Constraining Southern Great Plains Summer Precipitation Using a CESM2 Perturbed Parameter Ensemble
495889.authors: Emmanuel Ogwuche Audu, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and I. Simpson and R. D. Dixon
495889.abstract: Earth system models (ESMs) disagree on both the sign and magnitude of projected June–August precipitation change over the U.S. Southern Great Plains (SGP). This intermodel spread among 29 ESMs from the sixth phase of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) is found to be strongly correlated with land–atmosphere coupling diagnosed from unforced preindustrial control simulations. Across models, the terrestrial and atmospheric coupling indices explain 50% and 66% of the intermodel variance in projected precipitation change, respectively. Both relationships indicate that models with stronger coupling project greater drying or less wetting. Observational estimates suggest that most models overestimate SGP coupling, and applying the observational constraint shifts the projection from modest drying toward wetting. We further explore the causal nature of this relationship between land-atmosphere coupling strength and projected precipitation change using a perturbed-parameter ensemble with the Community Earth System Model version 2 (CESM2). We vary parameters governing soil evaporation resistance, saturated-fraction decay, leaf carbon–nitrogen allocation, and photosynthetic nitrogen limitation across established ranges to produce weakly and strongly coupled configurations. Each configuration is independently spun up to equilibrate its land state. Winds outside the study region are nudged toward the same CESM2 Large Ensemble member, while no nudging is applied within the study domain. This setup constrains the surrounding large-scale circulation while allowing local land–atmosphere interactions to evolve freely over the SGP. We then evaluate if stronger-coupling configurations project drier conditions relative to weaker ones and compare the CESM2 sensitivity against the intermodel relationship derived from CMIP6. This controlled experiment provides a direct test of whether the emergent relationship reflects a causal land–atmosphere coupling strength influence on precipitation projections.

495892.title: Open and/or Usable: A Data Friction Framework for Weather and Climate Data
495892.authors: Emma Pidduck, ECMWF, Bonn, NW, Germany; and U. Modigliani and V. Bennett
495892.abstract: Open data policies have made an unprecedented volume of weather and climate data freely available, yet "open" and "usable" are not the same thing. Drawing on almost 20,000 user-support tickets raised against ECMWF data services between January 2024 and May 2026, we introduce the Dataset Friction Framework (DFF): six empirically grounded dimensions — discoverability, access and delivery, licence and legal, data structure and format, tooling and support, and overall complexity — that classify where real users experience friction. "Access and delivery" and "tooling and support" categories dominate, confirming that the barriers to weather and climate data are operational, not merely related to metadata. Existing FAIR maturity instruments, which passively harvest metadata, are structurally unaware of these barriers and can even be affected by routine anti-scraping configuration, providing inaccurate or misleading FAIR scores. FAIR tells you what good data looks like; it does not tell you how much work it takes to actually use. We therefore propose a complementary, user-facing usability score to assess the friction a user encounters. We are developing an open-source tool to compute this score by actively simulating a user's journey and will present initial findings and comparisons.

495896.title: Ffion: an AI Air-Quality Forecaster
495896.authors: John Robert Lawson, Utah State University, Vernal, UT; and S. Lyman and M. J. Davies
495896.abstract: Text generated by AI large-language models (LLMs) suﬀer from hallucinations: mistakes in logic that are written confidently and hence read convincingly. For public health and industry regulation, these errors may lead to poor decision-making and lack of trust in forecasts. Addressing this, we present an AI forecaster, Ffion (Welsh for foxglove or mystical foresight), which runs from a Linux terminal adjacent to data extracted from NWP data and Clyfar (“wise”), our NWP–AI hybrid ozone forecast system. The crux: Ffion is prompted with pointers to small data files extracted from huge datasets (kilobytes from gigabytes). Not only are hallucinations mostly eliminated as a result, the small slices of data are more efficiently ingested by the AI agent coupled with “deep thinking” for rich insight. The higher reliability of Ffion is valuable to the lab’s Ozone Alert outlooks, especially for (notoriously diﬃcult) risk communication, and forecasts are produced at three different complexity levels for stakeholders and public. This method — reducing the intractable to bytes that do the heavy lifting — can be applied further afield for general risk communication of hazards. Regarding safety and complexity level: guardrails on language and advice should be informed by domain expertise in, e.g., public health, communicators of science, etc.

495897.title: Running NWP with Natural Language
495897.authors: John Robert Lawson, Utah State University, Vernal, UT; and M. J. Davies
495897.abstract: The author demonstrates a workflow where WRF code (via GitHub repository) is wrapped in a command-line LLM agent (Codex Sol; Claude Fable). To avoid overwhelming the LLM with blind token ingestion, especially for a mammoth codebase, the user must first commit to (1) a habit of ongoing pruning of redundant code, and (2) optimisation of cold-start files (CLAUDE.md; AGENTS.md) through list of pointers to key files: a sort of "welcome-back table of contents". This LLM-wrapping opens countless opportunities — not just lowering the entry bar for students to run their own simulations — tempered by the usual spectre of hallucinations. However, (1) the author estimates error rate of frontier LLM models is comparable to his own (usually more daft) errors, meaning there is less justification for frequent human intervention. Further, to prevent the command-line AI agent from re-inventing the wheel, potentially introducing broken or subpar code functions in each session, the user can deploy skills: "macros" denoted by slash (e.g., "/generate-geogrid") or dollar-sign "$plot-quick-looks") commands. This creates parallel tracks — one more deterministic; a second more free-form. Hence, routine workflows become on-rails skills that deploy helper functions (e.g., python, Fortran, namelist templates); the user may switch tracks to a more free-form, creative command where no right answer may exist (e.g., finding CFL location/time, automated start-to-finish HPC submissions with subagent monitoring of live runs). This weave between set procedures (to reduce error; to avoid wacky namelist mistakes) and open-ended discussion (more creativity and scientific discovery) is augmented further with research "run cards" for, e.g., porting schemes from other versions of WRF or other NWP models; experiments with optimal stochastic perturbation size; etc. Naturally, this LLM-wrapped workflow is model-independent and not WRF-specific.

495898.title: Deriving Air-Mass Changes in Low-Level Plane Transponder Data.
495898.authors: John Robert Lawson, Utah State University, Vernal, UT
495898.abstract: Three hours from the nearest Weather Service radiosonde launches in Salt Lake and Grand Junction, the remote Ashley Valley in northeastern Utah is sampled poorly in the lowest 1–2 km. This hampers diagnosis and prognosis of cold-pool strength in winter, where nocturnal drainage flow can trap oil/gas industrial emissions and persist for days — growing ozone concentration under photolysis. Hence, even modest reduction in uncertainty of the temperature profile may yield better air-quality forecasts, further to creating a long time series for machine-learning training. The local Vernal Regional Airport (KVEL) has two scheduled passenger flights in/out daily, and this persistence gives a long time series of flight track and raw transponder data: an inviting task for time-aware ML methods (e.g., LSTM). While the smaller craft report few meteorological fields explicitly (e.g., temperature, wind, humidity), our raw transponder data-feed allows derivation of 10+ identified proxies such as bearing-versus-track (i.e., wind vector), step change in descent/ascent rate at air-mass interface, etc. Moreover, daily student-pilot pattern work and numerous General Aviation craft provide a testbed for numerous transponder technologies (ADS-B; MODE-S; UAT) installed at the laboratory, and the number of viable derived proxies that add skill to a data-sparse region.

495899.title: Supporting Space Weather Forecasting with Wide Field EUV Imaging
495899.authors: Katharine Reeves, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, Cambridge, MA; and D. B. Seaton and C. Downs
495899.abstract: Tracking of solar eruptions for NOAA’s space weather forecasting activities will primarily leverage the GOES-R Solar Ultraviolet Imagers (SUVI) and Compact Coronagraphs (CCor) on the Space Weather Follow-On (SWFO) mission to the L1 Lagrange point and on the GOES-U satellite in geostationary orbit. However, SUVI’s FOV ends around 1.7 Rs, while CCor’s begins above 3.7 Rs (GOES-U) or 3.0 Rs (SWFO). Thus the NOAA instrument suite leaves a key observational gap, in which eruptions that originate near the solar surface are well-known to evolve, and CME shock acceleration of particles occurs. Wide field EUV imaging (to 3Rs) will allow forecasters to directly connect observations of CMEs in coronagraphic FOVs to their sources just above the solar surface, and to fully characterize their evolution of CME kinematics during a critical phase where events experience complex accelerations, which will help to refine modes of CME arrival time and impact at Earth. Additionally, the ability of a wide-field EUV imager to detect the onset of CME-associated shocks provides powerful diagnostic capability for the drivers of solar energetic particle events, and wide field EUV imaging reveals both the source region and the eruption, leading to clear identification of eruption precursors.

495900.title: Understanding Drivers of Heat Strain Among Male and Female Agricultural Workers
495900.authors: Lyndsay Krisher, Colorado School of Public Health, Aurora, CO; and I. Tassistro, K. Josey, Y. Li, J. Butler-Dawson, M. Dally, A. Dye-Robinson, M. Goering, D. Jaramillo, S. Kardel, B. Young, J. L. Adgate, J. W. Schaeffer, and L. S. Newman
495900.abstract: Background: Agricultural workers face disproportionate risk of heat-related illness (HRI) due to concurrent exposures to high ambient heat, physical exertion, and limited access to adequate hydration and rest breaks. Core body temperature (Tc) monitoring provides a direct physiological measure of internal heat strain, and Tc thresholds recommended by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) and the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH) are intended to help protect workers at risk of HRI. Previous studies in the U.S. have found that nearly half of workers exceeded the recommended thresholds during the workday, with several significant risk factors identified. Comparable data are lacking for Central American agricultural workers, who labor under similar or more physically demanding conditions and higher ambient temperatures. Objectives: Using data from the Chronic Kidney Disease, Heat, and Air Pollution (CHAP) I (male sugarcane workers) and CHAP II (female sugarcane workers) studies in Guatemala, we will 1) describe the occurrence of Tc exceeding NIOSH and ACGIH thresholds, 2) identify demographic, health, hydration, work, and environmental risk factors associated with threshold exceedance, and 3) characterize Tc trajectories and timing of exceedance across the workday. Methods: Sugarcane workers, including cane cutters and other field roles, were monitored for heat strain for up to three workdays during the harvest season using ingestible core body temperature pills. Key predictors: Ambient heat was measured with the continuous heat index (HI). Hydration was assessed via pre- and post-shift urine specific gravity. Survey and clinical risk factors included demographics, job tenure, body mass index, measures of kidney health and diabetes risk, blood pressure, and physical activity. Analysis: Generalized linear mixed models will estimate odds ratios for exceeding recommended Tc thresholds and examine predictors of time spent above thresholds. Tc trajectories will be plotted by time of day at the 50th, 75th, 90th, and 95th percentiles. Expected Results: We anticipate that a significant proportion of workers will surpass recommended Tc thresholds on an average workday. Key predictors will be reported, stratified by worker sex. Time-of-day analyses are expected to show that many workers exceed recommended thresholds early in the day, reflecting the physical intensity of agricultural work. Conclusion: Characterizing the prevalence and risk factors for heat strain among Guatemalan sugarcane workers will help identify potential intervention targets, such as hydration practices and work-rest programming, to improve HRI prevention in agriculture, and will contribute physiological evidence to inform occupational heat-stress standards.

495901.title: GeoXO's Use of MTG/IRS to Prepare for GXS
495901.authors: Andrew Heidinger, NOAA, Madison, WI; and M. D. Goldberg, D. T. Lindsey, E. L. McGrath-Spangler, and D. C. Tobin
495901.abstract: GeoXO is the successor to NOAA's current GOES-R Geostationary Satellite Program. The GeoXO constellation will feature two hyperspectral infrared sounders, designated as GXS, situated in the GOES-East and GOES-West positions. These instruments share specifications similar to the InfraRed Sounder (IRS) recently launched on the Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) satellite. As the first geostationary sounders in the Western Hemisphere, GXS will provide critical atmospheric profile information with high temporal resolution. Geostationary hyperspectral infrared sounding represents a novel observational capability for NOAA, which is prioritizing the readiness of the National Weather Service to utilize this data effectively. A fundamental component of this preparation involves the utilization and optimization of MTG/IRS data. This presentation outlines NOAA's strategy to prepare both numerical weather prediction (NWP) and nowcasting applications. We invite feedback from the MTG/IRS community regarding the validity of this plan and explore how GXS initiatives can contribute to the mutual success of both programs.

495902.title: Space Weather Town Hall: Transforming Services & Science to Meet the Needs of Society
495902.authors: Jamie Favors, NASA, Washington, DC; NASA, Herndon, VA; and K. Korreck, C. Wallace, and J. F. Spann Jr.
495902.abstract: We invite you to participate in a town hall focused on advancing national strategies for space weather, with particular emphasis on scientific, operational, and commercial imperatives. This forum will bring together experts from federal agencies, the research community, and industry to discuss current plans, emerging priorities, and opportunities for cross-sector collaboration. As critical infrastructure and commercial operations grow increasingly dependent on technologies susceptible to space weather impacts, coordinated efforts in observations, forecasting, mitigation, and innovation are essential. Space weather now represents a pivotal intersection of fundamental science, applied research, and operational readiness. This town hall will serve as a forum to: Discuss federal and community space weather priorities Highlight research directions and observation/modelling needs Facilitate dialogue between science, operations, and industry stakeholders Reinforce the role of space weather in national resilience and economic security Your engagement is essential to shaping an integrated approach that supports both scientific advancement and practical application.

495904.title: From Meteorology to Oil Prospecting: Mineral Waters in Petroleum Fields, 19th-20th c.
495904.authors: Ana Luiza Nicolae, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA
495904.abstract: The analysis of mineral waters was crucial to early petroleum prospecting in America, and experiments with water in oil fields generated hydrological knowledge that remains unacknowledged today. In 1842, the future founder of MIT, William Barton Rogers, was concerned about the relationship between mineral springs and the folds of the Appalachian Mountains. Springs were the pulse of the internal heat of the earth. Understanding the pathways by which springs emerge to the surface allowed Rogers to establish the depth of water as a temperature scale for the earth. In the preceding decades, chemists and geologists started comparing the temperature of water springs to the average climate of the country in which they were found. This process established a distinction between meteorology and hydrogeology for the first time and was central to debates about the internal heat of the earth. By tracking the publications of early American scientists and the first United States geological surveys of Pennsylvania, Virginia, Iowa, and more, this paper re-establishes the importance of groundwater analysis for early oil prospecting and geology in the United States. Drillers of artesian wells and oil wells in the late 19th and early 20th centuries paid special attention to water, running experiments with pumping rates to measure the properties (temperature and pressure) of the resulting fluid migration. These experiments drew groundwater within the purview of industrial use. With the development of water injection techniques for recovery of oil as early as 1867, the importance of the deep hydrological cycle became a key component of scientific understandings of underground formations. Alongside these experiments, industrial waste products such as co-produced water and gas leaks from idle wells provided key constraints on the analysis of meteoric waters and atmospheric composition at the surface. Recent attempts to extract rare earth elements and economic minerals from waters produced by the fossil fuel industry have been deployed for profit, but no comprehensive study has tried to estimate underground water discharge at the surface over the last 160 years of oil extraction. By focusing on oil fields in Kern County, CA and in Venango County, PA, this paper advances values for total amounts of extracted water, providing a constraint for the input of early prospecting into the hydrological cycle. Further collaboration with hydrologists and soil scientists will allow this data to become a model for the (historical) exchange rates of water from confined aquifers to the surface, and contribute to ongoing studies about land subsidence, pore space depletion, and water availability in the United States. Finally, this paper shows that the re-use of co-produced waters and gases is an old endeavor, evolving alongside extraction techniques and hydrological and atmospheric knowledge since the 19th century. The integrated study of groundwater hydrology and petroleum geology attested by these historical case studies shows a pathway for responsible collaboration between hydrologists, atmospheric scientists, and geologists in the management of extractive sites today. Leakage pathways are a concern for depleted oil fields, especially in a boom of fluid injection for the purpose of Carbon Capture and Sequestration or Hydrogen storage. In the United States, there are increasingly more idle or orphaned wells than producing ones. The programmatic study of mineral water content and well gas analysis led by early American scientists in inactive fields demonstrates a good example for best practices regarding the management of leakage pathways as well as the long-term effects of underground fluid manipulation.

495905.title: A Two-Stage Post-Processing Framework for Improving NBM Temperature Forecasts in Topographically Challenging Regions of Washington State
495905.authors: Jaitun Vijaybhai Patel, AgWeatherNet, Washington State University, Pullman, WA; and L. khot
495905.abstract: The National Blend of Models (NBM) temperature forecasts are an increasingly important input for operationalizing agricultural decision support. However, translating gridded output to specific farm sites remains challenging, especially in regions such as Washington State, with strong topographic and climatic heterogeneity. In the high-value agricultural crop production regions of the state, local microclimate drives air temperature trends that are not fully represented by gridded NBM forecasts. These differences matter considerably as high-value tree fruit crops experience abiotic stress (e.g., spring frost, summer heat) where marginal degree variation can cause significant crop damage and yield losses. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate NBM temperature forecasts across the State of Washington to explore their suitability for operational decision support, with pertinent error or bias correction. The study verified hourly NBM temperature forecasts against quality-controlled observations from 207 open-field AgWeatherNet (AWN) stations. This analysis was performed on valid NBM records during January 2023 through May 2026, spanning Washington's 10 climate divisions and environments ranging from marine-influenced western Washington to the Cascade valleys and foothills, the irrigated Columbia Basin, and the elevated terrain of eastern Washington. Raw forecast skill was evaluated by lead time, station, season, and climate division. A first post-processing layer evaluated three online bias estimators, rolling-window averaging, exponential decay, and a Kalman filter, across seven station-, lead-time-, and temporal-grouping schemes. The correction framework was explicitly leakage-safe, i.e., forecasts could use only errors from observations available by the time of forecast issuance. A second layer examined whether error remaining after mean-bias correction could be reduced using the most recent observed temperature anomaly, weather-regime information, and a K-nearest-neighbor Analog Ensemble (AnEn). AnEn experiments used 2023–2024 calendar-year data for training and the remainder of the data (i.e., from 2025 through May 2026) for independent evaluation. Raw NBM forecast skill degraded steadily with lead time, with network-wide mean absolute error (MAE) increasing from 1.40°C on Day 1 to 2.51°C on Days 8–10. Bias correction provided meaningful improvement through Day 3. Day-1 MAE and root mean squared error (RMSE) decreased by 13%, while Days 2–3 MAE and RMSE reduced by about 9%. Correction was essentially neutral for Days 4–7 and degraded thereafter (Days 8–10). This motivated an operational configuration that reverts to raw NBM beyond Day 3, rather than applying a uniform correction across the forecast horizons. Post bias correction, pooled Day-1 MAE decreased from 1.39°C to 1.21°C. However, substantial residual error remained within individual 6-hour and day/night subsets, with corrected MAE values ranging from 1.05°C to 1.40°C. Recent local observations contained additional information, but their value decayed rapidly with lead time. Blending the most recent observed temperature anomaly into the corrected forecast reduced MAE by 8.1% for 0–6 h, but by less than 1% for the 6–12 h interval. The nonlinear AnEn produced larger improvements than the linear persistence model across the tested lead-time and day/night subsets. Relative to the bias-corrected baseline, AnEn reduced MAE by 17.1% for 0–6 h nighttime forecasts and 10.7% for 0–6 h daytime forecasts, with gains decreasing farther into the forecast horizon. The post-processing chain also substantially reduced the frequency of large-magnitude errors. For 0–6 h nighttime forecasts, the frequency of absolute errors exceeding 5°C decreased from 1.92% in raw NBM to 0.92% after bias correction and to 0.46% after AnEn. Errors exceeding 10°C, although rare, declined from 0.021% to 0.0022% across the full chain. Weather station-level analysis revealed that remaining errors do not represent a single failure mode. Rankings by raw annual MAE (without any corrections) were dominated by complex terrain for nine of the ten worst-performing stations located in eastern Washington basins, valleys, elevated benches, or other complex terrain. At these stations, NBM frequently underestimated the observed diurnal temperature range, with temperatures tending to be too warm at night and too cool during the day, producing systematic errors. These errors were substantially reduced by bias correction and, in many cases, further reduced by AnEn. However, winter performance at some terrain stations remained poor and could be attributed to a limitation of the correction framework. Overall, the results demonstrate how dense weather-sensing networks can support local verification and post-processing of national forecast guidance in topographically heterogeneous regions such as the state of Washington. For agricultural decision support, where management decisions can depend largely on local weather conditions, the results argue against treating post-processing as a uniform adjustment to NBM forecasts. Instead, the appropriate correction depends on forecast horizon and local error structure. The results therefore support a lead-time- and station-aware post-processing framework combining adaptive bias correction for up to 72 h and observation-informed nonlinear post-processing concentrated at very short lead times.

495908.title: Transforming the NOAA-USGS Geoelectric Project to better support the Electric Power Sector.
495908.authors: Jordan Guerra Aguilera, NOAA, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and H. M. Bain, A. M. Kubaryk, A. Rasca, and A. Entwistle
495908.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) hosts a model for mapping induced geoelectric fields during geomagnetic storms, the NOAA-USGS Geoelectric Model, which is a collaboration between NOAA, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), and Natural Resources Canada (NRCan). This model produces two near realtime products: gridded geoelectric field vector at one minute cadence and half-degree resolution for 1) the contiguous U.S. (CONUS) using a three-dimensional description of the Earth conductivity from the magneto-telluric data, and 2) North America (CONUS and Canada up to 60N) using a one-dimensional description of the conductivity from layered-Earth models. In order to provide enhanced services to end users in the Electric Power sector, the NOAA-USGS geoelectric project is currently developing new capabilities aimed to facilitate the decision-making process that prevents possible space weather effects on electric systems: 1) implementing a forecasting system of geoelectric fields based on climatology and forecast Kp index; 2) modernizing the visualization tools to allow users to interact with the geoelectric maps and providing further regional information; 3) prototyping regional products that express geoelectric-related hazards, impact levels, and aggregation by special regions; 4) streamlining services for proving geoelectric field data to end users for validation and reliability studies. These prototypes were presented to Bulk Electric System (BES) operators, forecasters, and researchers during the BES Space Weather Testbed Exercise in August 2026, and received valuable evaluation and feedback which is currently informing their further development and implementation.

495913.title: Seasonality in New Particle Formation Modulates Potential Cloud Droplet Number at the Southern Great Plains
495913.authors: Maxim Muter, CU Boulder, Boulder, CO; and E. Browne
495913.abstract: Globally, new particle formation (NPF) is estimated to produce approximately 50% of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and thus plays a key role in modulating cloud properties and precipitation. NPF and subsequent growth of particles to CCN sizes remain incompletely understood, and as a result, predictions of CCN and cloud droplet number (CDN) enhancement from NPF are uncertain. Observational constraints on CCN and potential CDN enhancements associated with NPF help clarify under what conditions newly-formed particles survive and grow to become cloud-active, and whether that perturbation propagates into a potentially observable cloud response. Here we analyze nine years (2017-2025) of NPF observations at the Department of Energy's Atmospheric Radiation Measurement site at the Southern Great Plains (SGP) and quantify NPF's impact on measured CCN and on potential CDN calculated using a zero-dimensional adiabatic cloud parcel model. During the study period, 463 NPF events were identified at SGP, exhibiting a distinct seasonal cycle with peak frequency in April (35.4%) and November (34.4%) and a minimum in July (7.6%). Event days are characterized by higher shortwave radiation flux, lower condensation sinks, and lower relative humidity than non-event days, consistent with other long-term climatologies. Across all seasons and updraft velocities (0.3-3.0 m/s), NPF robustly enhances potential CDN, with median absolute changes ranging 27-527 cm⁻³ and median relative changes of 25-107%. Seasonal impacts on CDN are distinct, with winter showing the largest enhancements and summer the smallest. These differences in CDN enhancement are mechanistically linked to variability in the critical activation diameter (Dcrit), which is jointly controlled by aerosol hygroscopicity (κ) and maximum supersaturation of the parcel (Smax). Background aerosol, particularly at high concentrations, suppresses Smax through condensational scavenging, thereby increasing Dcrit. Winter events, characterized by cleaner background aerosol and higher Smax, exhibit the lowest median Dcrit (49.6-85.1 nm across updrafts). This enables substantial Aitken mode activation: the Aitken mode contributes ~21% of CDN at 0.3 m/s and exceeds 50% above 1 m/s, contributing to much higher CDN enhancement. Summer, by contrast, exhibits elevated accumulation mode concentrations that suppress Smax and raise Dcrit (66.1-113.4 nm), limiting Aitken mode contribution to near zero at low updrafts and suppressing overall CDN enhancement. These findings suggest that large-scale models may significantly underestimate CDN enhancement from NPF by missing Aitken-mode activation, particularly in clean background environments.

495915.title: Revisiting Near-Surface Atmospheric Boundary Layer Flows over Heterogeneous Surfaces (Invited Presentation)
495915.authors: Marc Calaf, Univ. of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and A. Hammoud, K. Ghannam, M. Allouche, and E. Bou-Zeid
495915.abstract: Land surface heterogeneity is omnipresent in nature, whether it is through topographic variations, land use changes, the presence or absence of vegetated canopies, variability in the surface albedo, or simple changes in soil moisture and temperature. As a result, land-atmosphere interactions over heterogeneous surfaces have been studied for a long time. Understanding the flow characteristics above surface transitions has been critical for example for the improved representation of the effect of surface heterogeneity in Earth System models (ESMs) of different spatial resolutions. Interestingly, there remains a limited understanding of the variations in the flow structure resulting from the land-atmosphere interactions. This is to say, on whether the resulting flow presents a roll-type structure due to persistent shear with the surface, or instead is characterized by a cell-type structure resulting from the strong land-atmosphere buoyancy forcing. Furthermore, little differentiation has been made on whether the land-atmosphere convective forcing leads to stationary, or transient convective cells. In each of these flow configurations, their corresponding statistics are quite different, and Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory formulation does not necessarily hold for all of them. In this work, we address some of the current limitations by expanding our understanding of the flow structure developed in different land-atmosphere configurations, as well as the triggers or controlling mechanisms that enable the transition from one type of flow to the other. We investigate the use of a quadruple flow decomposition in parallel to the definition of four different time scales that characterize each of the processes described by such decomposition. It is then through a combination of these timescales in a set of non-dimensional Pi-groups that one can a-priori determine under what land-atmosphere configurations the different terms of the quadruple decomposition become relevant, and what are the competing flow mechanisms to mixing. For the development of this work, we leverage several Large-Eddy Simulation datasets of ABL flows over different types of surface heterogeneity (i.e. ideal and realistic), representative of semi-infinite interfaces, and statistically homogeneous patches.

495918.title: Overview of Land Data Assimilation and Land-Atmosphere Coupling Options for NWP
495918.authors: Clara S. Draper, NOAA, College Park, MD; and J. Dong, M. J. Barlage, T. Z. Gichamo, and Y. Xue
495918.abstract: Land data assimilation has been shown to improve atmospheric forecast skill, and all major numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems use land data assimilation to constrain some combination of soil moisture, soil temperature, snow depth, and snow temperature. This talk will review the current practices and historical development of land data assimilation within NWP, leading to a discussion of the current opportunity to enhance land/atmosphere data assimilation through the careful design of coupling between the two components. The land and atmosphere have fundamentally different error growth dynamics: the atmosphere is chaotic, with errors that grow through flow-dependent instabilities, while the land is strongly forced by the atmosphere, so that land model forecasts converge over time regardless of their initial conditions. This results in different design requirements for land and atmosphere data assimilation, and consequently they have evolved to use different algorithms within NWP, with the land typically using much simpler algorithms than the atmosphere. However, the ensemble-based and hybrid methods now used in many atmospheric data assimilation systems are also well suited to land data assimilation, raising the possibility of using the same method for both components, and hence enabling strongly coupled (or more strongly coupled) land/atmosphere data assimilation. A recent study at NOAA used an Ensemble Kalman Filter to compare the performance of different land/atmosphere data assimilation coupling options, finding that strongly coupled data assimilation slightly out-performed weakly coupled data assimilation. However, strongly coupled data assimilation requires an identical implementation for both assimilation components, and yet the optimal configuration for each will likely differ due to their differing design requirements. This factor may well offset the small performance advantage of using a strongly coupled system, so that on balance the best performance might be attained using weakly coupled land/atmosphere data assimilation with each system tuned to its own application.

495920.title: High Voltage Discharges Exposed!
495920.authors: Michael Stock, CIWRO, Norman, OK; and J. Ringhausen
495920.abstract: Laboratory images of sparks are extremely useful in studying the physics of electrical discharges as the conditions can be precisely controlled, and the images made at details which are not possible with naturally occurring lightning. Usually the way these images are made is that an arc is produced between two electrodes, light produced by the arc then travels some distance to a lens and camera where it can be captured for further study. There is another way to capture images of t spark though. Instead of having a camera and lens which are separated from the spark by some distance, an electrical discharge can be produced directly onto a sheet of film. Do do this, a sheet of film is placed on a smooth insulator (like glass) over a ground plane. A wire electrode connected to a pulsed high voltage source (a Marx generator) is then attached to the film. When the Marx generator is fired, the electrical discharge will flow horizontally along the insulator, and light from the arc will expose the film. The results are spectacularly detailed and beautiful one-to-one images of the spark.

495921.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of SAR and Machine Learning Products as Indicators of Sea Ice Concentrations via VIIRS and Geospatial Modeling.
495921.authors: Ryenne Carol Julian, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Civil & Env. Engineering, Mequon, WI; and S. R. Helfrich, W. J. Capehart, and A. J. French
495921.abstract: Arctic sea ice imagery provides context to global climatological trends, facilitates safe navigation, provides information needed to estimate the Earth’s energy balance, and aids in subsistence hunting and the safety of residents. Yet, deriving ice concentrations via satellites using passive microwave, visible, or infrared sensors are limited due to a combination of water attenuation, poor resolution, or cloud interference. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) creates imagery through clouds at high resolutions, making it a prime source for continuous observations of operational ice services, but has yet to be fully exploited for sea ice concentrations. SAR’s backscatter in C-band is governed primarily by the proportion of ice cover, ice type, melt ponds, and brine pocket scattering. The contribution of each is seasonal, and if accounted for individually, it generally becomes more homogeneous when averaged over a larger area. In theory, these backscatter values should present a general relationship with sea ice concentrations in areas where 1-100% ice is present. To validate this, Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) ice concentration estimates were compared to the probability of sea ice identification from normalized SAR imagery using an AI algorithm developed by Aerospace Corporation for use at the US National Ice Center called IceLynx. By comparing the point readings from each product, it validates the effectiveness of the IceLynx algorithm at recognizing ice concentrations via the Normalized Radar Cross Section (NCRS) backscatter imagery and Interactive Multisensor Snow and Ice Mapping System (IMS) data used for training. Using ArcGIS Pro to cut, rescale, and recalculate the scenes to match each other at a 795m resolution, the data from each grid point was gathered and compared through confusion matrices as well as linear regressions. Preliminary results show that the AI algorithms do an adequate job predicting ice concentrations from the 90-100% and 0-10% range. Multiple explanations have been explored that account for the differences between the IceLynx ice probabilities and VIIRS ice concentrations for the 20-90% ranges. The results of this project provide insight on the relationship between IceLynx ice probabilities with ice concentrations, and if the IceLynx algorithm can be further explored as a consistent tool for ice analysts monitoring sea ice concentrations for ice forecasting and Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) model incorporation.

495922.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Near-Real-Time Aerosol Speciation from GOES-16
495922.authors: Jeffrey Lee, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and M. Loria-Salazar
495922.abstract: Steady advancements in satellite observation systems have enabled the retrieval of more frequent, accurate, and high-resolution aerosol data. However, retrievals like AOD that come from these satellites are not directly actionable for contexts such as air quality, as these retrievals are typically optical properties and not the physical properties like concentration and composition that matter for health. In this presentation, we showcase efforts to use deep learning to infer more health-relevant data from high frequency and high resolution GOES-16 AOD using a PerceiverIO style model trained on MERRA-2 aerosol tracer priors. GOES-16 offers AOD retrievals at a cadence and latency unmatched by polar-orbiting sensors, updating every 10 minutes across the full disk with data available in near real time. This temporal density is a major asset for air quality applications, but translating optical measurements into the speciated mass concentrations ideal for health applications has typically relied on either process-based models, such as chemical transport models or reanalysis models, which are computationally expensive and often lag observations by hours or days, or on purely data-driven statistical and machine learning approaches that operate faster but lack the physical grounding needed to generalize reliably or produce interpretable, trustworthy estimates. Our model is a physics-informed retrieval architecture that learns to map AOD directly to speciated aerosol mass concentrations and surface PM2.5, using MERRA-2 as a training prior. By encoding physical relations between particle size, composition, optics, and vertical distribution directly into the model, our approach produces retrievals that are both physically interpretable and fast enough to run at GOES-16’s native cadence. The practical payoff is a retrieval pipeline capable of near-real-time, high-resolution surface PM2.5 estimation, narrowing the latency gap between satellite observation and actionable air quality information. This has direct implications for public health applications where timeliness matters, including smoke and dust event tracking, early warning systems, and localized exposure estimates in regions without dense ground-based monitoring networks.

495925.title: Polarimetric Spectral Retrieval of Debris-Induced Velocity Bias in Mobile-Radar-Observed Tornadoes: Algorithm Performance and Observed Centrifuging Patterns
495925.authors: Ameya Naik, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and H. B. Bluestein, D. J. Bodine, D. Schvartzman, B. Cheong, T. Y. Yu, L. M. Swinney, R. M. Frost, A. Schueth, L. Shedd, and F. De Martin
495925.abstract: The use of mobile polarimetric Doppler radar stands out as the primary method for estimating the instantaneous wind field in the proximity of rapidly evolving weather phenomena such as tornadoes. However, these estimates rely on the assumption that scatterers (e.g., rain, hail, debris) embedded within the strongly rotating flow have similar velocities to the wind itself. For scatterers like debris or hail, this is likely not the case, as heavier objects accelerate more slowly and are subject to increased centrifuging associated with vortical flow. The use of polarimetric Doppler spectra has been investigated as a potential method to correct velocity data from the effects of debris centrifuging, in both simulations and observations. A recently published spectral debris classification algorithm (DCA) based on simulations of lofted scatterers in a LES-scale tornado vortex (Schneider et al., 2025) shows promise in using spectral differential reflectivity and spectral correlation coefficient to classify different parts of the Doppler spectrum as debris or rain. Thus, the power spectrum can be filtered to allow computation of a corrected velocity estimate. To confirm modeled debris centrifuging effects, the University of Oklahoma's RaXPol mobile radar, since 2023, has collected raw in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) signal in a number of tornado vortices. A unique scanning strategy was used, through which the dish was rotated at 6°/s, decreasing temporal resolution in favor of increasing Doppler spectral resolution. With this scanning strategy, RaXPol was able to collect multiple polarimetric Doppler spectra at unprecedented resolution within significant Southern Plains tornadoes and their associated debris clouds. The most significant dataset was collected on May 23, 2024, in which, at close range, RaXPol scanned the lowest levels of a significant EF-2 tornado northeast of Eldorado, OK. In this case, the DCA was evaluated for the first time on observed I/Q time series data. During this evaluation, a few practical concerns emerged: namely that Doppler spectrum aliasing confounded meaningful computation of the overall velocity correction magnitude. This prompted the development of an aliasing-resistant retrieval algorithm. Preliminary qualitative results from this algorithm show that it performs well with limited artifacts near velocity aliasing boundaries. Furthermore, DCA-derived velocity correction may reveal patterns about the nature of debris centrifuging. In the figure, the DCA-derived velocity correction magnitudes (upper right) are markedly increased within the debris cloud as defined by decreased correlation coefficient (upper left) within the vortex core. Additionally, with the translation vector of the tornado pointed towards the radar in this sweep, a pattern of overall positive correction is observed in the front and left quadrants of the tornado, with a lack of symmetric negative corrections in the back and right quadrants. In this presentation, we discuss the development and performance of the aliasing-resistant, DCA-based velocity retrieval algorithm, along with observed patterns of debris-driven velocity bias in this tornado and other tornadoes for which RaXPol collected low-level, slow-scanning I/Q time series. Schneider, M. E., D. J. Bodine, R. D. Palmer, S. M. Torres, B. Cheong, C. J. Fulton, C. B. Griffin, and T. Maruyama, 2025: A novel technique to correct debris centrifuging bias in doppler velocity measurements from tornadoes. Journal of Atmospheric and Oceanic Technology, 42 (8), 1041 – 1061, https://doi.org/10.1175/JTECH-D-24-0065.1

495926.title: Practical Implementation of Software Containers in UFS Workflows: Increasing Accessibility and Portability in Earth System Modeling
495926.authors: Natalie Perlin, NOAA, Riverdale, NJ; and E. Snyder, C. Book, and M. Huang
495926.abstract: Broad community participation in Earth system modeling relies on accessible, reproducible, and portable software environments. While traditional high-performance computing (HPC) workflows often depend on complex dependency chains and machine-specific configurations, software containers (such as Singularity and Apptainer) offer a more unified solution. This presentation demonstrates the implementation of containerized workflows within the Unified Forecast System (UFS) application suite. By standardizing these environments, the approach expands accessibility and streamlines model build and execution processes. This enables practical deployment across both traditional HPC platforms and major cloud providers, including Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Microsoft Azure. We plan to present a step-by-step technical walk-through of a containerized UFS workflow, illustrating how containers are invoked to build model components and subsequently execute simulation runs. To balance performance and flexibility, we address key implementation considerations for this cross-platform approach across different deployment scales. While smaller, single-node applications run easily with minimal host dependencies, multi-node workflows introduce stricter operational constraints. These include integrating with host system schedulers, handling different message passing interface (MPI) builds, and ensuring alignment of Application Binary Interfaces (ABI) between containerized libraries and host interconnect drivers across both on-premise HPC and cloud clusters. By demystifying these practical workflows with concrete examples, we show how accessible container technologies lower the barrier to entry for community model development, ensure scientific reproducibility, and accelerate collaborative innovation across the Earth System modeling community.

495928.title: Beyond Fire Proximity: A Source-Transport-Receptor Framework for Assessing Wildfire-Smoke Exposure of Critical Infrastructure
495928.authors: Yue Jia, University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, TX; and Z. Ke and D. Hyndman
495928.abstract: Wildfire smoke can pose hazards to critical infrastructure far beyond the areas directly affected by fire. However, wildfire-risk assessments commonly emphasize fire occurrence, burned area, and geographic proximity, while comparatively little attention is given to how atmospheric transport connects recurrent fire-prone regions with distant facilities that support essential services. This study develops a national-scale source–transport–receptor framework to assess wildfire-smoke exposure potential for energy, healthcare, and digital infrastructure across the contiguous United States. Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS) records are used to characterize the spatial frequency, burned-area recurrence, and dominant season of documented wildfires. Satellite active-fire observations and fire radiative power provide complementary information on fire activity and temporal variability, while Global Fire Emissions Database version 4 (GFED4) emissions are used to estimate the relative smoke-emission strength of recurrent-fire source regions. Together, these datasets identify recurrent wildfire hotspots and characterize their relative potential to generate smoke. The identified hotspots are then used as source regions in a Lagrangian atmospheric dispersion model. Simulations conducted for the dominant fire season of each hotspot characterize recurring transport pathways and the potential downwind extent of smoke under representative meteorological conditions. Model-derived source–receptor relationships are combined with infrastructure locations to quantify the relative exposure of individual power plants, hospitals, and data centers to smoke originating from each recurrent-fire region. This approach distinguishes facilities primarily influenced by nearby fire sources from those connected to distant fire-prone regions through atmospheric transport. By explicitly separating wildfire source activity, atmospheric transport, and receptor exposure, the framework provides a physically interpretable means of identifying smoke-exposure corridors and the fire regions most relevant to critical infrastructure. The resulting information can support smoke preparedness and continuity planning, help prioritize regional mitigation efforts, and inform the evaluation of future infrastructure siting. More broadly, the study demonstrates that wildfire-smoke exposure cannot be inferred from fire proximity alone and that atmospheric connectivity is an important component of wildfire-risk assessment for geographically distributed infrastructure systems.

495929.title: Journeys in Earth System Modeling, Mentoring, and Education (Invited Presentation)
495929.authors: A. Scott Denning, Fort Collins, CO
495929.abstract: Dave Randall recruited me into his research group in 1989 as I was evolving professionally from geologist to biogeochemist to atmospheric scientist. In 1990, I was entrained as a student into the Sellers–Mooney–Randall–Fung NASA IDS project. That remarkable collaboration produced breakthrough science in remote sensing, ecophysiology, hydrology, biogeochemistry, trace-gas transport, and inverse modeling while prototyping what would become modern Earth system models. It was a heady time of innovation, discovery, and great fun. After joining the faculty at UC Santa Barbara in 1996, I continued collaborating with this extraordinary group. In 1998, Dave recruited me again—this time to leave UCSB and join him as a colleague on the CSU Atmospheric Science faculty. In the early twenty-first century, my research group developed a plants-to-planet program that scaled field research from eddy covariance through ecophysiological models, remote sensing, coupled mesoscale models, and aircraft campaigns. In parallel, my students and colleagues worked from the top down, using global trace-gas transport inversions to develop scaling strategies that became a linchpin of large-scale carbon budgeting for North America, Europe, and the Amazon. My career took its biggest turn in 2006, when Dave recruited me to serve as Director of Education, Diversity, and Outreach for CMMAP. We built an ambitious climate-education program spanning kindergarten through retirement—K to gray. We reached hundreds of thousands of K–12 students and teachers in person, millions more on the web, and hundreds of undergraduates; we also helped advise nearly 100 graduate degrees across seven universities. We brought innovative, hands-on science into classrooms across our region, across the United States, and around the world. We pioneered multilevel mentoring that brought new talent into climate studies and tripled the number of graduate students from underrepresented groups in the largest atmospheric-science graduate program in the country. After CMMAP, I rebuilt my laboratory and research funding in 2017, but by then my soul was firmly in education. I formally retired from my tenured professorship in 2024 and now teach “part-time”: four classes each year at CSU and Yale, while also helping thousands of undergraduates learn about the Earth system through Semester at Sea. Across my entire career, Dave’s mentoring supported my growth from radiometric dating of rocks to watershed biogeochemistry, carbon-cycle science, Earth system modeling, education, and public communication. Without his continuing professional and personal mentorship, I might never have found my purpose as a mentor, teacher, and science communicator. Now I’m an old man. Yet I continue to serve in deeply meaningful ways that might never have been possible had I simply kept my head down and pursued the latest numerics, the least publishable unit, or the next increment of funding. Dave Randall is a giant in meteorology. He is also one of the most powerful mentors I have ever known. His impact extends far beyond his technical achievements and hundreds of papers. It’s the people. The ripples of Dave’s mentoring are everywhere.

495930.title: Parameterized Deep Convective Transport in an Earth System Model: Impacts of Meteorological Analysis Used for Nudging
495930.authors: Warren Smith, NCAR, Frederick, CO; and B. Gaubert, S. Tilmes, R. B. Neale, M. C. Barth, S. Honomichl, B. Roozitalab, C. Gurganus, T. L. Campos, R. Ueyama, and L. L. Pan
495930.abstract: Deep convection plays an important role in redistributing boundary layer chemicals throughout the atmosphere, and is therefore important to properly represent in Earth system models. This study explores the sensitivity of deep convective transport of chemical constituents to the meteorological dataset used for nudging as well as the frequency in which model nudging tendencies are updated. Sensitivity simulations are performed using the Community Atmosphere Model version 6 with chemistry (CAM6-Chem) run as the atmosphere component within the Community Earth System Model version 2.2 (CESM2.2). We compare three one-year (2022) simulations which are otherwise-identical except for their nudging configuration; (1) three-hourly nudging updates toward MERRA-2, (2) three-hourly nudging updates toward ERA5, and (3) hourly nudging updates toward ERA5. We examine the representation of global composition as well as representation of a recently observed high-profile convective transport event, where a fresh convective outflow plume was found to contain record-setting observations of carbon monoxide (CO) in the upper troposphere (UT). This event was associated with Asian summer monsoon (ASM) deep convection and observed during the Asian Summer Monsoon Chemical and Climate Impact Project (ACCLIP) in 2022. Our suite of nudging sensitivity simulations indicates that one-hour nudging tendency updates toward ERA5 increase the frequency and depth of tropical deep convection, both of which constitute improvements compared to the other nudging configurations when evaluated with satellite observations. Nudging toward ERA5 improves the timing of convection associated with the fresh transport event sampled during ACCLIP (2022) when compared to nudging toward MERRA-2. Furthermore, hourly nudging toward ERA5 transports the largest concentration of CO to the UT, further improving the model representation of this event. Our results underscore the significant impact that nudging configuration can have on simulated convective processes, and serve as a benchmark for ongoing model improvements to convection representation.

495932.title: Climate-Informed Forecasting of West Nile Virus Reveals Predictive Eco-Epidemiological Signals for Early Warning
