495932.authors: Quinn H Adams, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and R. D. Harp, K. Karnauskas, M. T. Elling, S. Benjamin, and B. W. Green
495932.abstract: West Nile virus (WNV) remains the leading domestically acquired arboviral disease in the United States, with substantial year-to-year variation in the timing and magnitude of outbreaks. That variability is partly driven by weather: temperature affects mosquito development and virus replication, rainfall and drought alter mosquito habitat and interactions with avian hosts, and atmospheric conditions influence mosquito survival and activity. These relationships create opportunities for climate-informed early warning, but WNV has historically been difficult to forecast reliably. Outbreaks are relatively rare, highly seasonal, and spatially heterogeneous, and the same weather conditions can have different consequences across regions depending on mosquito ecology, host dynamics, and local environmental context. Existing WNV forecasting models commonly incorporate lagged meteorological conditions, but environmental conditions can influence transmission over timescales ranging from weeks to entire seasons. Short-term weather anomalies, accumulated seasonal climate conditions, and mosquito-specific thermal conditions may therefore capture different stages of the ecological processes that ultimately lead to human outbreaks. We evaluated whether representing climate across multiple temporal and ecological scales improves three-month-ahead predictions of WNV outbreaks in 50 high-burden U.S. counties. We linked monthly neuroinvasive WNV surveillance data with meteorological, hydroclimatic, and biologically motivated environmental indicators. For each county, an outbreak was defined as monthly WNV activity exceeding the county’s historical 90th-percentile threshold, with thresholds recalculated using only information available during each model-training period. We used extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), a flexible machine-learning approach that can identify nonlinear environmental relationships, thresholds, and interactions that may be difficult to specify a priori in complex vector-borne disease systems. Rather than randomly dividing historical observations into training and testing sets, we mimicked real-world forecasting: models were trained using only information that would have been available at each point in time and then used to predict county-level outbreaks three months ahead. Models were repeatedly updated as new observations became available, generating 7,855 out-of-sample county-month forecasts, of which 880 met county-specific outbreak thresholds. We compared a surveillance-and-seasonality baseline with models incorporating three complementary representations of climate: lagged weather and hydroclimatic conditions (current and lagged anomalies in temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, and wind speed, together with 3- and 6-month Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index [SPEI] values), annual bioclimatic summaries of seasonal temperature and precipitation regimes, and mosquito-specific thermal indicators such as growing degree-day accumulation and the number of days within thermally suitable ranges for important Culex mosquito vectors. Environmental predictors spanned conditions approximately three to nine months before the target outbreak. Climate information substantially improved forecast performance. Adding lagged weather and hydroclimatic predictors increased average precision by 19% relative to the baseline. Bioclimatic and mosquito-thermal predictors were less informative alone, but both added complementary information when combined with weather. The combined weather-bioclimatic model was best at distinguishing future outbreak from non-outbreak months, increasing average precision by 26% over baseline and increasing the proportion of outbreaks detected from 77% to 81%. The model combining weather and mosquito-specific thermal indicators produced similarly strong discrimination but the most accurate outbreak probabilities, reducing probability forecast error by approximately 26% relative to baseline. The added value of climate was particularly evident during the July–September transmission peak, when 92% of outbreaks occurred. During these months, seasonality and recent surveillance history alone provided little ability to distinguish which county-months would experience outbreaks beyond what would be expected from their high underlying frequency. Adding weather and bioclimatic information increased average precision by 28% over that baseline and produced average precision 32% higher than expected from outbreak frequency alone. Model interpretation also revealed that useful environmental signals emerged well before human disease. Within the combined weather-bioclimatic model, the strongest bioclimatic predictors were dominated by temperature characteristics: mean temperature of the warmest quarter, annual mean temperature, minimum temperature of the coldest month, mean temperature of the coldest quarter, maximum temperature of the warmest month, and temperature seasonality. Several ranked among the ten most influential predictors overall. This pattern indicates that outbreak risk reflects not only anomalous conditions preceding transmission, but also the broader thermal regime in which mosquito and virus dynamics unfold. In the mosquito-thermal model, growing degree-day accumulation and thermal suitability approximately seven months before the target outbreak were among the strongest nonseasonal predictors, alongside longer-term SPEI measures of moisture balance. WNV outbreaks become predictable through environmental conditions operating across multiple timescales. Short-term weather anomalies, broader seasonal climate context, and mosquito-relevant thermal conditions provided complementary information about future risk. Incorporating these signals into forecasting systems could provide public health agencies with additional lead time for mosquito surveillance, vector control, and outbreak preparedness before increases in human disease are detected.

495933.title: Assessing Potential Reductions In High-Latitude Wildfire Emissions Impacts on Air Quality In the USA with MUSICAv0
495933.authors: Benjamin Gaubert, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. R. Buchholz, F. Taksibi, B. Meotti, J. K. Shuman, and B. Buma
495933.abstract: Anthropogenic climate change is creating conditions conducive to more frequent and severe wildfires. Globally, forest wildfire emissions are increasing. The most substantial contributions are from arctic-boreal regions, critical carbon storage areas with significant stocks both above and below ground. Within the boreal, increases in fire weather, shifts in atmospheric circulation, a longer fire season and reductions in soil moisture contribute to the increased potential for destructive and high emission wildfires. The 2023 fire season within the Canadian boreal was extreme, with 15 Mha burned compared to the annual mean of 2.1 Mha. Approximately 650 Tg C were emitted by the fires, similar to total emissions from a large country, and the smoke emitted caused globally significant air quality impacts. Less than ten percent of the fire events caused more than 70 percent of the total area burned. The potential for emissions reductions through targeted management – reduction in burned area (e.g., targeted suppression or initial attack) and/or a transition to deciduous fuels - was explored using a model sensitivity bookkeeping approach. The spatial extent of 2023 burned area was reduced for a subset of fires, selected based on their contribution to PM2.5 emissions. Fire INventory from NCAR (FINN) was used to produce emissions for spring and summer 2023 and create inputs to a global atmospheric chemistry model (MUSICAv0) with a regionally refined grid encompassing the United States. FINN provided daily emissions estimates from emission factors for land cover types. We also investigate the sensitivity of the model simulations to diurnal cycles in anthropogenic and fire emissions. Using the NOAA and NSF NCAR MELODIES-MONET software, the baseline simulations are evaluated against surface observations and satellite CO observations from TROPOMI to verify atmospheric loading.

495936.title: Global Storm-Resolving Simulation with a Non-Hydrostatic Spectral-Element Dynamical Core In the Community Atmosphere Model: Preliminary Results from the StormSPEED Project
495936.authors: Xue Liu, TEXAS A&M University, College Station, TX; Texas A&M Univ., College Station, TX; and D. Fu, P. Chang, R. Saravanan, J. Truesdale, and J. Sun
495936.abstract: Global storm-resolving models provide new opportunities to explicitly represent convection and mesoscale weather systems, but their application in climate models remains computationally challenging. Our NSF StormSPEED project is developing a storm-resolving configuration of the Community Atmosphere Model (CAM) within the Community Earth System Model (CESM) by incorporating a nonhydrostatic spectral-element dynamical core (CAM-SE-NH). Here, we present preliminary results from a global CAM-SE-NH simulation following the DYAMOND (DYnamics of the atmospheric general circulation modeled on non-hydrostatic domains) Phase 1 (boreal summer) protocol. The convection-permitting model is configured on a nearly uniform ne1024 mesh with approximately 3.25-km horizontal grid spacing and 58 vertical levels. Initial benchmarking on the NSF NCAR Derecho supercomputer demonstrates successful execution using 57,600 MPI tasks across 576 nodes, requiring approximately 5.25 wall-clock hours per simulated day. Additional benchmarks are being conducted to evaluate model performance and scalability. Building on these initial benchmarks, we use the 40-day DYAMOND simulation to evaluate the representation of tropical and mesoscale weather systems, with emphasis on precipitation, convection, and tropical cyclones. Comparisons with observations and existing DYAMOND simulations will provide an initial assessment of the realism of CAM-SE-NH at global storm-resolving resolution. Together, these computational and scientific evaluations demonstrate the emerging global storm-resolving capability of CESM and establish a foundation for future high-resolution weather and climate applications.

495937.title: Global Advancements, Innovations, and Future Outlook Across GEO, LEO, and Space Weather Constellations
495937.authors: Raad A Saleh, NOAA, Madison, WI; and J. Gronert
495937.abstract: Next-generation environmental and space weather observing systems deployed across Geostationary Orbit (GEO), Low Earth Orbit (LEO), and Space Weather (SW) generate petabyte-scale data volumes that exceed traditional downlink capacities. To overcome bandwidth bottlenecks and decrease end-to-end latency, global satellite operators, including NASA, NOAA, ESA, USSF, JAXA, and KMA/KARI, are transitioning from monolithic frameworks toward agile, AI-driven hybrid orbital-ground architectures. This paper aims to explore technical advancements within the GEO, LEO, and SW domains. We will discuss distributed processing systems designed to optimize multi-sensor data processing and strengthen global environmental monitoring, security, and early warning. Ultimately, the convergence of retrainable on-orbit data networks, in-space compute nodes, and cloud-native ground orchestration forms a scalable, resilient, and interoperable global operational framework. Performing initial inference, data compression, and event detection directly at the orbital edge reduces product latency, optimizes resource allocation, and elevates real-time decision support for weather forecasting, climate continuity, and space domain awareness.

495939.title: Mechanisms and Downstream Impacts of Eastern North American Cold Air Outbreaks
495939.authors: Alexander Morelli, Pennsylvania State University, Etters, PA; and M. Gervais
495939.abstract: Cold air outbreaks (CAOs) are air masses with significantly colder than normal temperatures. They often originate over land or sea ice at high latitudes, and then propagate southward. They have significant socioeconomic impacts over large areas, especially regions such as the heavily populated eastern portion of North America. Previous studies have indicated a number of factors, including teleconnections such as the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), Pacific North American pattern (PNA), and North Pacific Oscillation (NPO), may influence the formation and propagation of these air masses, however the links between some teleconnections, particularly the NAO, remain contested. This research analyzes the atmospheric patterns which are associated with different tracks of CAOs which affect eastern North America on a synoptic timescale. An analysis of the teleconnections associated with these synoptic patterns is assessed. A pattern with a deep-layer ridge over the northwestern portion of North America contributes to the formation of the CAO, while variations in the Atlantic pattern contribute to variations in the CAO’s track. These patterns mimic classic teleconnection patterns of the NAO, PNA, and NPO, but are varied in the longitudinal placement of their centers of action. In addition, as the CAOs move over the relatively warmer water of the eastern Atlantic, they create a large sensible and latent heat flux, which may have significant downstream effects on the eddy-driven jet stream. Categorizing the mechanisms behind formation, propagation, and downstream effects of CAOs may help improve forecasting of these high-impact meteorological events.

495942.title: Evaluation of Exceedance Probabilities Using Altered Color Curves to Improve Risk Characterization and Decision Making
495942.authors: Lydia Michelle Purlee, NWS, Fort Worth, TX; and M. Gordon
495942.abstract: Effectively conveying the significance of high-impact, low probability events remains a communication challenge between National Weather Service (NWS) forecasters and their core partners. This study investigates how strategically altered color curve thresholds on exceedance probability maps, based on the assessment of risk, influences both the perception of forecast severity and the resultant decisions made by emergency managers. Using a dual-track design, 11 tabletop discussions were conducted with 96 emergency management partners from 46 counties across North and Central Texas, as well as individual simulations with NWS forecasters at 6 Weather Forecast Offices. Participants were provided archived data from a heavy-rain event, and were either given exceedance maps where the threshold was intentionally altered throughout the scenario, or exceedance maps where the threshold remained static. Preliminary results suggest that intentionally altering color curve thresholds significantly influences risk perception between both forecasters and partners. Every partner group and forecaster mentioned that the colors were a factor in their urgency, and the strategically altered color curve thresholds successfully shifts their attention toward the areas of higher impacts, even when the probability of occurrence is low. As several participants noted, “context is king”, and providing tailored visual signals to emphasize impactful thresholds can help end users of the data process forecast information and more effectively prioritize resources in decision-making.

495945.title: Validation of a Simulation Framework for Assessing 5G FR2 Interference Risk to ATMS
495945.authors: Alexandra Bringer, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and E. J. Kim, G. de Amici, M. Sammons, H. Yang, Q. Liu, S. Abraham, and L. Cheng-hsuan
495945.abstract: Microwave sounders deliver critical observations that support numerical weather prediction, climate monitoring, and atmospheric research. Because these are passive instruments that measure naturally emitted microwave radiation, their observations are especially vulnerable to Radio Frequency Interference (RFI). This vulnerability is compounded by the growing demand for spectrum access in frequency bands increasingly close to those protected for passive remote sensing. Recent FCC spectrum auctions have authorized active services to operate in bands adjacent to frequencies used for passive microwave sensing. As a result, out-of-band emissions from these active systems may extend into neighboring passive bands, introducing measurable contamination into radiometric observations. For instance, Channel 1 of the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) is centered near 23.8 GHz and is in proximity to 5G FR2 allocations. Assessing the potential impact of these emissions on ATMS observations requires a software simulator, itself validated with experimental observations, that can translate realistic transmitter characteristics and observation conditions into the RFI power received by ATMS and future microwave radiometer instruments. To address this need, an airborne measurement campaign was conducted to evaluate and validate a physics-based simulation framework for predicting RFI impacts on microwave radiometers. The experiment used a controlled ground-based transmitter generating a broadband 5G waveform with known power, spectral, temporal, polarization, and antenna characteristics. The source provided a controlled and repeatable interference 5G NR signal for testing the physical processes governing coupling between an active transmitter and a passive microwave receiver. The signal was observed by an airborne radiometer centered near 23.9 GHz with an approximately 1 GHz measurement bandwidth, allowing the interference response to be characterized within the spectral region relevant to ATMS Channel 1. The experimental campaign exercises all the key parameters modeled by the simulation. Transmitter characteristics and timing were measured together with aircraft position and attitude, radiometer viewing geometry, antenna response, and receiver characteristics. These measurements are used within the simulation to reconstruct the time-dependent source-to-sensor geometry and estimate the received interference power through an end-to-end link-budget calculation. The simulated interference is then expressed as an equivalent radiometric temperature and directly compared with the airborne observations. This comparison provides a controlled means of testing whether the simulation correctly represents the combined effects of 5G source power, spectrum, propagation, antenna coupling, polarization, observation geometry, and receiver response. The primary objective of the 23 GHz measurements is to quantify how accurately the simulation predicts the measured interference under known conditions. Validation will examine the ability of the framework to reproduce the timing and location of the interference, its variation with aircraft geometry and antenna response, its spectral distribution across the radiometer bandwidth, and the magnitude of the resulting radiometric perturbation. The comparison will also identify which input parameters contribute most strongly to uncertainty in the predicted interference, including transmitter power calibration, antenna-pattern characterization, polarization alignment, aircraft attitude, and receiver spectral response. These results will establish both the accuracy and the limitations of the modeling approach and will identify the measurements and instrument characteristics that must be known with sufficient precision for reliable RFI prediction. Ultimately, the airborne campaign provides the experimental foundation needed to establish confidence in RFI simulations before these simulations are applied to larger satellite-sensor risk assessments. The resulting framework is intended to support quantitative assessment of the susceptibility of ATMS Channel 1 to 5G FR2 emissions and to provide scientifically grounded information for future spectrum-management and interference detection decisions.

495948.title: An Analysis of Extremes in Precipitation for the Nordic Region and Associated Atmospheric Circulation Patterns
495948.authors: Mark W. Seefeldt, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and P. A. Mooney
495948.abstract: Extremes in precipitation, both too wet and too dry, present a challenge to hydrological applications and impacts to societal resources. Changes in extreme precipitation for a given region is one of the markers of a shifting climate. Quantifying the changes in extreme precipitation, and understanding the associated atmospheric circulation patterns, provides valuable information to understand the impacts. This research focuses on the characterization and changes in frequency of precipitation extremes for the Nordic Region, which is defined as the countries of Norway, Sweden, and Finland. The region spans from the Arctic to the mid-latitudes and its climates range from mild maritime coastal conditions to severe Arctic conditions in the far north. The study uses the Nordic Gridded Climate Dataset (NGCD), at a gridded resolution of 1 km, for investigating the extremes in precipitation from 1961 to 2025. The focus will move beyond extremes at individual points to widespread extremes covering a region of at least 4000 km2. In addition to identifying and characterizing the occurrence of widespread precipitation extremes, the presentation will provide an analysis of the associated atmospheric circulation patterns. The associated atmospheric circulation patterns will be identified by using the method of Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) applied to 850 hPa geopotential height spatial anomalies using the ERA5 reanalysis dataset for 1961-2025. Composite analyses of additional atmospheric variables will be presented corresponding to the SOM analysis for greater insight into the atmospheric conditions producing the extremes in precipitation. The result of the study will provide a better understanding of the atmospheric conditions associated with extreme precipitation for the Nordic Region, as well as identifying any trends or changes in characterization of the extremes in precipitation from 1961 to 2025. This study was completed as a result of a Fulbright Distinguished Arctic Scholar to Norway visit to NORCE and the University of Bergen in spring 2026.

495949.title: Incorporation of New Proxies to Run Realtime FISM-OP and FISM-3
495949.authors: Gabriela Gonzalez, University of Colorado, Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, Boulder, CO; and P. Chamberlin, S. Bahauddin, A. Cramer, B. Schwab, and E. Thiemann
495949.abstract: Version 2 of the Flare Irradiance Spectral Model (FISM; Chamberlin et al., 2020), models the solar ultraviolet spectral irradiance model over all time scales from solar flares, active region emergence, solar rotation, and solar cycle. FISM2’s accuracy and cadence are attributed to moving beyond using solely the F10.7 cm radio flux to more representative proxies for each wavelength, such as the H I Lyman Alpha 121 nm, Mg II core-to-wing ratio (c/w), He II 30.4 nm measurements, and more. Version 3 of FISM is currently under development which includes: 1) new proxies from GOES/EXIS, 2) proxies of plasma temperature, emissions measures, and abundances, 3) the incorporation of the Lumped Element Thermal Model (LETM; Thiemann et al., 2017) to create the improved FISM-3. GOES/EXIS will also enable FISM to run realtime and operational, which we refer to as FISM-OP. This submission discusses the current progress on these improvements, recent results, and outlines future plans for further enhancements and releases.

495954.title: Three Targeted Workshop Designs for Improved IDSS: Outcomes and Recommendations from Rural Region Readiness Workshops
495954.authors: Elizabeth H. Marold, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and M. E. Saunders and D. S. LaDue, Ph.D.
495954.abstract: The NOAA VORTEX-USA study referred to as Rural Region Readiness (RRR) worked with three NWS weather forecast offices (WFOs) in the culturally Appalachian region to plan, host, and evaluate integrated warning team (IWT) workshops. These IWT workshops were designed to (1) be culturally relevant to the region; (2) target rural IWT partners, including non-traditional IWT partners; and (3) improve risk communication between members of the IWT, especially around tornadoes. The ultimate goal of RRR is to provide a model for improving impact-based decision support services (IDSS) with targeted outreach efforts on “blue sky days” through relationship-building and relationship-maintenance activities, such as targeted IWT workshops. The RRR research team worked with three offices to complete annual RRR IWT workshops. The first workshop was hosted by the Morristown, Tennessee (MRX) WFO in 2024; the second workshop was hosted by the Charleston, West Virginia (RLX) WFO in 2025; and two final workshops were hosted by the Roanoke, Virginia (RNK) WFO in 2026. Work with each of the offices began with in-person outreach efforts between the research team and the WFO. Following an in-person meeting, a planning team was formed within each office. Each planning committee completed between 5 and 6 months of online planning meetings before hosting their RRR IWT workshop. Each office planned a different style of RRR workshop: Presentation Focused Design, Tabletop Focused Design, and Small Group Activity Based Design. In this poster, we provide an overview of each workshop and its design features using data from multiple data collection procedures, including surveys, ethnographic observations, and interviews, as well as workshop outcomes related to IWT team-member trust and learning objectives. We conclude with final recommendations for how other NWS WFOs can create similar culturally-targeted IWT workshops for improved IDSS.

495955.title: Learning in the Field, Learning from Each Other: Informal Learning, Motivation, Collaboration, and Mentoring in the KPOP-MS 2026 International Field Campaign
495955.authors: Dae Seok Chai, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and C. C. Nam, K. Kim, M. M. Bell, and G. Lee
495955.abstract: Meteorological field campaigns are widely credited with producing learning that classrooms cannot replicate, yet the mechanisms that convert participation into durable knowledge, skills, and career commitment remain underspecified. Our study of the 2023 Korea Precipitation Observation Program: international collaborative experiments for Mesoscale convective systems in the Seoul metropolitan area (KPOP-MS) documented statistically significant gains in self-assessed meteorological knowledge and skills, along with three unresolved problems: learning outcomes plateaued for experienced graduate students, interaction during daily meetings was minimal, and hierarchical communication norms constrained question asking and help seeking. That study recommended pre-campaign and post-campaign workshops, role diversification, structured discussion, and deliberate rapport building. KPOP-MS 2026 implements those recommendations as an intentional educational architecture, which allows us to move beyond asking whether students learn in the field toward asking how, when, and through whom that learning occurs. This study examines how informal learning, motivation, collaborative learning, and coaching and mentoring jointly shape student learning outcomes and field performance. The design is guided by informal learning theory, experiential learning theory, self-determination theory, and communities of practice, four perspectives that locate learning in the everyday work of observation rather than in scheduled instruction alone. KPOP-MS 2026 conducted a three-week intensive observation period during the 2026 summer monsoon across four upper-air sounding sites in the Seoul and Incheon metropolitan area, staffed by undergraduate, master's, and doctoral students from multiple Korean universities alongside Korean and international faculty and mentors. Five design features distinguish the 2026 campaign from its predecessor. First, a full-day bilingual pre-campaign workshop combined core science content, radiosonde procedures, role clarification, and structured team building. Second, a site leader and follower structure assigned rotating leadership, facilitation, and headquarters liaison responsibilities to students. Third, a mentoring program placed faculty and senior mentors with student groups at an approximate one-to-three or one-to-four ratio, with mentors serving explicitly as academic and technical guides, reflection facilitators, and psychosocial supporters through weekly site visits. Fourth, a Slack-based community of practice supported daily knowledge sharing, troubleshooting, and cross-site exchange. Fifth, a post-campaign workshop featured team research showcases, facilitated group reflection, and a career panel. We employ a convergent mixed-methods design aligned to the first three levels of the Kirkpatrick framework. Quantitative data include matched pre-campaign and post-campaign surveys measuring self-efficacy in meteorological knowledge and observational skills, motivation, career intentions, teamwork, and knowledge-sharing behavior; weekly self-assessment items that yield a repeated measures series across the observation period; and performance indicators drawn from embedded quizzes, observation logs, and site data submission records. Qualitative data include weekly written reflections structured on the experiential learning cycle, document analysis of the community of practice archive, group reflection transcripts, and hour-long semi-structured interviews with students, mentors, and faculty. Interviews and reflections are collected in Korean and English, with forward and backward translation for reported quotations. Analysis combines paired comparisons and growth modeling of the weekly series, regression of learning outcomes on informal learning, motivation, collaboration, and mentoring quality, inductive open and axial coding of qualitative data, and joint display integration. Preliminary analyses address four questions. The first concerns the share of reported learning that participants attribute to informal channels, including peer conversation, trial and error, observation of senior students, and mentor feedback, relative to formal seminars and lectures. The second concerns whether structured mentoring and diversified leadership roles alter the graduate student plateau identified in 2023, and whether mentoring quality predicts performance beyond prior field experience. The third concerns the role of motivation as a mechanism, specifically whether autonomy, competence, and relatedness experienced at the sites explain the relationship between campaign participation and career intentions in atmospheric science. The fourth concerns collaborative learning, including how the community of practice, site team identity, and cross-site exchange relate to knowledge sharing, help seeking, and the willingness to raise concerns in a culturally hierarchical setting. Because the 2026 campaign includes international mentors and participants, we also examine how learning processes differ across national and institutional backgrounds. This study contributes an evidence-based account of the social and motivational infrastructure that makes atmospheric field campaigns educationally productive, and it offers transferable design principles for principal investigators, program officers, and educators who plan observational campaigns as workforce development opportunities. Findings from the surveys, weekly reflections, community of practice records, and interviews will be presented, together with practical recommendations for mentoring structures, reflection routines, and role design in future atmospheric science field campaigns.

495957.title: Integration of an Idealized aquaplanet Test Case into NOAA's Unified Forecast System Weather Model
495957.authors: Ratko Vasic, OAR, Silver Spring, MD; and S. N. Tulich, C. Book, L. Bengtsson, E. A. Aligo, and M. Huang
495957.abstract: The numerical weather prediction (NWP) community has long recognized the need for improved collaboration and additional methods for quickly testing improvements to forecasting systems, leading to the establishment of the Hierarchical System Development (HSD) framework inside of NOAA's Unified Forecast System Weather Model (UFS-WM). The HSD framework and test cases have been developed and implemented collaboratively between NOAA's Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC), Office of Modeling and Development (OMD), Physical Sciences Laboratory (PSL), the Developmental Testbed Center (DTC), and the University of Michigan. The HSD framework enables the broader research community to develop and evaluate innovations within an operational modeling environment. To support this effort, several idealized and realistic test cases have been implemented in the UFS-WM. Most recently, an aquaplanet, atmosphere-only idealized test case was implemented in the UFS-WM as a collaborative effort between NOAA EPIC and PSL. Aquaplanet configurations are widely used to investigate atmospheric dynamics in a simplified Earth system consisting of a water-covered surface with no orography, allowing fundamental atmospheric processes to be studied in isolation. In our implementation, initial conditions were derived from real-world analyses while prescribing idealized vertical profiles of prognostic variables, including temperature, humidity, and wind. Climatological and static datasets were modified accordingly to produce a self-consistent aquaplanet configuration compatible with the UFS-WM. To establish realistic physical balances and small-scale circulations, simulations were initialized from the idealized atmospheric state and integrated through a 90-day spin-up period. Restart files generated at the end of the spin-up were then used as initial conditions for subsequent experiments. Simulations were performed at C48 horizontal resolution using the FV3_GFS_v17_p8_ugwpv1 physics suite from the Common Community Physics Package. This implementation provides the UFS community with a standardized, idealized test case for studying atmospheric dynamics, evaluating model physics, and supporting hierarchical model development.

495959.title: CLOUDPHYS - Cloud-Radiative Effect in the Arctic: a Comparison of CMIP6 Models and CERES Satellite Data
495959.authors: Alexandra Igorevna Narizhnaya, A.M. Obukhov Institute of Atmospheric Physics, Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow (IAP RAS), Moscow, Moscow, Russia; A.M.Obukhov Institute of Atmospheric Physics, Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow, Moscow, Russia; and M. Latonin, A. Chernokulsky, and V. Semenov
495959.abstract: The Arctic climate has undergone dramatic changes in recent decades. Arctic clouds are themselves affected by these changes while also exerting an important influence on other components of the climate system. Despite their key role, cloud properties and cloud–radiation interactions remain imperfectly represented in climate models, highlighting the need for systematic evaluation against observations. This study presents a comparative analysis of cloud properties derived from climate model simulations and satellite observations over the Arctic region north of 65°N. We analyze total cloud fraction (CLT, %), longwave and shortwave surface radiative fluxes (LWR and SWR, respectively; W m⁻²), and the cloud-radiative effect (CRE; W m⁻²). CRE characterizes the influence of clouds on the radiation budget and is defined as the difference between all-sky and clear-sky radiative fluxes. We use model output from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) and satellite observations from NASA’s Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System (CERES). The analysis is performed separately for the cold season (January–March), warm season (July–September), and transitional seasons (April–June and October–December). Cloud and radiative characteristics are further evaluated under different sea-ice conditions based on sea-ice concentration, including open water, the marginal ice zone, and consolidated pack ice. The CMIP6 models generally exhibit substantially stronger interannual variability than CERES observations in both winter and summer, for both shortwave and longwave radiative components and over both ice-covered and open-water surfaces. The largest differences between the models and observations in both CLT and CRE are found over consolidated pack ice during the winter season. The closest agreement is found for the longwave CRE over open water in summer, with an inter-model spread of approximately 20 W m⁻². The simulated CRE indicates a predominantly cloud-induced cooling effect during summer and warming effect during winter. Spatial correlations between modeled and observed CLT and CRE are generally higher in summer, whereas some models exhibit negative spatial correlations during winter. We identify the models that show the closest agreement with CERES in reproducing both the spatial distribution of long-term mean cloud characteristics and the interannual variability of Arctic-mean cloud properties. The CMIP6 models are additionally analyzed with respect to their equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) to investigate whether differences in simulated Arctic cloud-radiative effects are systematically related to model climate sensitivity. An evaluation of model performance in relation to the cloud and radiation parameterizations employed shows that models using the Rapid Radiative Transfer Model for GCMs (RRTMG) and models from the Community Atmosphere Model (CAM) family tend to perform particularly well in reproducing the spatial patterns and interannual variability of Arctic CRE and total cloud fraction.

495960.title: Training Science and Engineering Students in Convergence Research for Compound Hazard Resilience: Part II - Student Team Projects
495960.authors: Mariana Goodall Cains, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. Kamali and J. L. Demuth
495960.abstract: People and places are increasingly at risk of compound weather, space weather, and subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) hazards and disasters (UNDRR-ISC, 2025). Compound hazards are generally characterized as two or more events with overlapping spatial and temporal attributes (Nemeth et al. 2024). Compound hazards may include (a) co-occurring (also known as concurrent) events, where two discrete hazards occur simultaneously, (b) cascading (also known as triggering) events, where an initial hazard triggers or amplifies a subsequent event, (c) consecutive hazards, where an initial hazard has ended but people and places are consequently made vulnerable to a subsequent hazard. Building resilience to compound hazards requires understanding how natural, human, and technological systems interact. Importantly, the integration of such expertise is essential to truly build resilience to compound hazards. In July 2026, the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) Education, Engagement, and Early-Career Development (EdEC) and Convergence Science Program (CSP) designed and implemented a 2-week colloquium for graduate students from the atmospheric sciences, social sciences, and engineering to train them in the topics and approaches to address the complex problem of compound hazards. This presentation will focus on discussing the team projects that were designed for the students to engage in, to begin operationalizing the topics and approaches they were learning pertaining to compound hazards, convergence research, and systems engineering. The overarching goals of the projects were for students to (a) co-develop a compelling and complex scientific, engineering, and/or societal problem pertaining to compound hazards that will yield innovative knowledge and/or actionable solutions, (b) co-design a research plan to tackle this problem, including use of boundary objects for collaborative work, (c) begin the collaborative research process to the extent possible, and (d) experience and reflect on the journey of this team-based process that integrated what they learned during the colloquium. Students were provided with additional detailed guidance and suggestions of how to work toward these goals. Students were pre-assigned into five groups of five people, with diverse disciplines but complementary research interests. Throughout the colloquium, students had approximately 10 hours of time to work together deeply as a team. They gave 5-minute lightning talks partway through to receive feedback from their peers, and on the last day they gave final team presentations about their project and individual reflections about the process. This presentation will summarize the design and format we developed for the team projects, augmented with highlights from the students' presentations and their feedback.

495961.title: How Usable is Open Weather and Climate Data, Really? Benchmarking LLMs Against Operational Data Sources
495961.authors: Emma Pidduck, ECMWF, Bonn, NW, Germany; and U. Modigliani and V. Bennett
495961.abstract: The value of open weather and climate data depends on whether it can actually be retrieved and used, yet usability is rarely measured directly. We introduce LLM-as-a-Benchmark (LLB), a method that uses large language models as automated audit instruments: each model is given a realistic data-access task and must navigate a provider's public documentation and endpoints end-to-end, while every point of friction it encounters — authentication barriers, missing or undocumented software libraries, opaque directory structures, and unusual file formats — is logged and classified against the Data Friction Framework. By running several models, spanning capability tiers, against the same set of open data sources, we separate friction that is specific to a model from friction that is intrinsic to the data infrastructure. We contrast LLB with F-UJI, a reference FAIR-maturity tool, and show that passive metadata harvesting cannot separate trivially easy sources from genuinely difficult ones. We present initial cross-model and cross-source findings and discuss how the method points data providers toward the specific, actionable changes that would most reduce friction for machine and human users alike.

495962.title: FAA Aviation Weather Division Updates
495962.authors: Michelle V Whitcher, FAA, Washington, DC; FAA, Washington, DC
495962.abstract: This presentation will provide an update to critical aviation weather programs within the FAA. Aviation Weather Research. Weather Transition, the FAA reorganization and FAA partnership programs will be discussed. Specific topics may also include Aviation Weather Research project status for Graphical Turbulence Guidance Nowcast (GTGN); Weather Technology in the Cockpit; International Partnerships; Unmanned Arial Systems and Advanced Air Mobility projects.

495963.title: No Footprint is an Island: Multidimensional Neural Network Level 2 Products for the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder Constellation
495963.authors: Ethan L. Nelson, Tomorrow.io, Boston, MA; and S. J. Munchak and R. Chase
495963.abstract: The Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) constellation consists of more than ten 6U satellites equipped with a microwave radiometer sensing 12 channels from 91-204 GHz: a W-band window, 7 F-band temperature sounding channels, 3 G-band water vapor sounding channels, and a G-band window channel. Together, these channel observations provide the basis for the TMS derived Level-2 satellite products: atmospheric temperature and water vapor profiles (2A-ATVP) and high resolution precipitation rates (2B-HRPR). To minimize processing time (benefiting near-realtime weather surveillance purposes) and provide robust uncertainty estimates, the algorithms utilize Quantile Regression Neural Network architectures. Previous iterations of these algorithms employed a neural network that relied on a single input vector of brightness temperatures and ancillary data (instrument geometry and surface characteristics). While using a one-dimensional neural network provided broadly accurate results, footprint-to-footprint differences were noticeable and produced neighboring noise. The next version of these products utilizes an input tensor composed of a scene of brightness temperatures across all 12 channels along with the ancillary data. These patch-based retrievals implicitly benefit from more synoptic-scale context and are less sensitive to instrument noise at the individual footprint level. Preliminary validations show that the 500 hPa temperature RMSE is reduced from 1.8 K (vector inputs) to 1.3 K (patch inputs). This is similar to the RMSE of ATMS at this level using the MiRS algorithm. In this talk, we will discuss the development of the Level 2 products from conception to the current version. We will highlight the different philosophies between model-derived and observationally-derived training datasets and how those influenced the designs of 2A-ATVP and 2B-HRPR. We will present the validation framework utilized to fine-tune the neural network and show results on a global basis with close parity to flagship missions. The performance is further enhanced by the rapid revisit and low latency of TMS constellation observations. Lastly, we will highlight how these retrievals form the basis of trade studies for future sensors in development for the Tomorrow.io satellite observing network.

495967.title: Heterogeneity and Urbanization: Impacts on Planetary Boundary Layer Height across a Heterogeneous Coastal Metropolitan Region (Invited Presentation)
495967.authors: Michelle Rose Storm, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and P. M. Klein and E. N. Smith
495967.abstract: Planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) can vary substantially across coastal metropolitan areas where mesoscale circulations interact with heterogeneous land surfaces and has been well documented at synoptic to meso-alpha scales (200-1000 km). However, the relative influence of anthropogenic land modifications on PBLH at the meso-beta scale (20-200 km) remains poorly characterized by observations. Here, ground-based, continuous remote sensing observations collected during the Coastal Urban Boundary layer Interactions with Convection (CUBIC) field campaign in Houston, Texas, are used to examine spatial variability in PBLH across contrasting coastal, exurban, and urban environments. Observations were collected from June through September 2022 at three locations spanning approximately 62 km across the Houston-Galveston region. A fuzzy-logic approach, combining kinematic and thermodynamic observations, is applied to estimate PBLH throughout the diurnal cycle. This method allows differences in PBLH structure to be evaluated across land-use environments and under region-specific atmospheric processes, such as the sea breeze (SB). Results show statistically significant differences in the afternoon, evening, and overnight PBLH across the region, with average maximum PBLH at the urban site approximately 480 m deeper than the coastal location. Mesoscale circulations further modify the spatial structure, where SB days are associated with increases in maximum PBLH of approximately 230-330 m relative to non-SB conditions, with the greatest difference occurring in the urban environment. These results indicate that the PBL response to mesoscale forcing is not spatially uniform and may depend on the underlying land surface. Differences in PBLH across the Houston region therefore reflect the combined effects of anthropogenic land modification and mesoscale coastal circulations. The observations demonstrate the importance of resolving heterogeneous urban environments when investigating PBL evolution.

495969.title: Micrometeorology Observations at a 325-m Tower In Central Amazon (Invited Presentation)
495969.authors: Otavio C. Acevedo, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and C. Q. Dias Jr., M. Stefanello, A. Pozzobon, A. Mendonça, and L. G. N. Martins
495969.abstract: Amazon Tall Tower Observatory (ATTO) is a long-term cooperation between Brazil and Germany with multiple observations of atmospheric chemistry, aerosols, cloud physics, biogeochemistry and turbulence at an area of primary Amazon Forest, 150-km Northwest of the city of Manaus. The most important platform of the project is a 325-m tall tower, operating since 2021. A 81-m instant tower sits at about 400-m from the tall tower, to provide undisturbed observations at those lower levels, and it has been operating since 2015. Micrometeorology is a major focus of the project, where 18 levels of turbulence observations are available at both towers, within and above the forest canopy. Here, we describe the major micrometeorological findings, emphasizing those made possible by the tower height, vertical resolution and long-term monitoring. Some processes can be directly observed at ATTO because they occur within the tower layer. These include the nocturnal stable boundary-layer (SBL), which is in the vast majority of cases entirely observed. Typical SBL heights range between 150 and 250 m, depending mainly on wind direction. Low-level jets are also in most cases entirely within the tower layer. Its thermodynamic and turbulence characteristics, height and temporal evolution can be fully analyzed, revealing that they may be fully disconnected from the surface or not, depending mainly on the mean flow direction. The convective boundary-layer (CBL) growth can be directly evaluated in the early hours of the morning. This also allows direct observation of entrainment fluxes of momentum, sensible and latent heat and CO2 fluxes in the period. During most of the afternoon, most of the CBL is beyond the tower height, but its top is usually within the fully mixed layer, so that profiles can be extrapolated to the CBL top. Sensible heat fluxes decay linearly with height, offering a possibility of estimating CBL thickness from their extrapolation to the entrainment flux at the top. This process reveals a large impact exerted by cloud cover, shown to be a dominant controlling mechanism at ATTO during daytime. We also show vertical profiles of higher order turbulence moments, including turbulent kinetic energy, temperature variance, their dissipation rates and vertical transports, and how they depend on stability and cloud cover. The average terms of the budget equations for TKE, sensible heat flux and temperature variance are also shown. In general, all observations support the conclusion that there is no internal sublayer above the Amazon rainforest, where the roughness sublayer transitions directly to a fully mixed layer.

495972.title: Assessment of TEMPO's Ability to Measure Spatial Gradients of PBL Ozone and NO2 at Western Lake Michigan Shoreline
495972.authors: Michael J. Newchurch, U Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and J. Burden, C. R. Nowlan, R. B. Pierce, J. Park, M. S. Johnson, and X. Liu
495972.abstract: The Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) geostationary instrument provides hourly, high‑spatial‑resolution retrievals of tropospheric ozone over North America, but its ability to resolve ozone in the lowest 2 km of the atmosphere has not been extensively validated against independent airborne in‑situ measurements. This study compares TEMPO 0–2 km partial‑column ozone retrievals and their a-priori profiles against airborne in‑situ measurements collected during eleven flight segments near Chicago, Illinois, and Kenosha, Wisconsin, in August 2023 as part of the LMBREEZE field campaign. TEMPO partial columns derive from the lowest layer of the 24‑layer ozone profile retrieval, scaled to the fraction of the 0–2 km column sampled by the aircraft, and compared to in‑situ mixing‑ratio observations using matching windows of ±1 hour, ±15 minutes, and ±1 minute. Supplemental RO3QET lidar profiles provide additional context for boundary‑layer structure during several flights. Across the eleven cases, nine flights (9, 12, 15, and 16 August) show broadly consistent, physically reasonable agreement between TEMPO and in‑situ observations, while two flights — 2 and 5 August — exhibit substantially poorer correspondence. Using a ±15 minute window, TEMPO compared to in-situ measurements shows a mean bias of −11 ppbv across all flights and -3 ppbv when August 2nd and 5th are excluded . When comparing the prior with the same ±15 minute window to the in situ measurements, the mean bias across the nine flights that exclude August 2nd and 5th as outliers is 9 ppbv indicating that the retrieval was moved away from the prior closer to the truth. Within the broad study region, the TEMPO retrieval shows a mean low bias relative to the a priori profile of −12 ppbv (NMB = −22%). A ±1‑minute comparison highlights this contrast clearly. Including all flights (16 matched points), TEMPO yields a slope of 0.1, intercept of 34 ppbv, R² = 0.03, and mean bias of −9 ppbv (NMB = −18%). Excluding 2 and 5 August (13 matched points) improves correspondence, with a slope of 1, intercept of −5 ppbv, R² = 0.4, and mean bias of −4ppbv (NMB = −8%). We are investigating why the 2 and 5 August cases are so strongly different from the aggregate statistics. Absent those two days, TEMPO demonstrates consistent skill in retrieving 0–2 km ozone under summertime boundary‑layer conditions in the western Lake Michigan shoreline region.

495973.title: Impacts of Moisture Transport Pathways on Wintertime Orographic Precipitation Processes in the Park Range of Colorado using Radar and WRF Simulations: Results from the S2noCliME Campaign
495973.authors: Sofia Vakhutinsky, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and L. McMurdie, P. Blossey, T. J. Zaremba, C. Pettersen, A. Rowe, G. G. Mace, M. Oue, and B. Dolan
495973.abstract: Wintertime precipitation events in mountainous regions are highly variable in frequency, duration, and microphysical properties, making them difficult to forecast accurately. Studying their precipitation processes is difficult due to scarce observational data, stemming from inaccessible in-situ sites, radar beam blockage, and limitations in satellite retrievals in complex terrain. To address these observational gaps, the Snow Sensitivity to Clouds in a Mountain Environment (S2noCliME) field campaign was conducted during the 2024-2025 winter season in the Park Range of northwest Colorado. The campaign used cloud-sampling instruments from Storm Peak Lab (SPL), located on top of Mt. Werner at 3220 m, and deployed two ground-based polarimetric radars: the Ka-band Scanning Polarimetric Cloud Radar (KaSPR) and the Sea-Going and Land Deployable Polarimetric (Sea-Pol). These radars sampled the storms approaching the Park Range and collected data on how these storms were modified by the high terrain surrounding SPL. We first analyzed a single case study spanning February 12-18, 2025, which contained two distinct precipitation events, distinguished by differing moisture pathways and synoptic forcing. To investigate these moisture pathways, we used a water-vapor tracing package from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model and found that the first precipitation event was primarily sourced from off the California coast, while the second was primarily sourced from the Pacific Northwest. During the first precipitation event, decreasing vapor transport was accompanied by a weakening of stability aloft, with radar echoes changing from stratiform to convective later in the event. The second precipitation event had weaker vapor transport than the first and became less stable at lower levels over time. SNOTEL sites surrounding SPL indicate that the second period, dominated by moisture from the Pacific Northwest, produced nearly twice as much precipitation as the first period, when moisture was predominantly from California. Building on this case study, we developed a framework that we are applying to the entire S2noCliME campaign. Combining water-tracer-enabled WRF simulations with radar observations from KaSPR and Sea-Pol, we analyze how moisture transport pathways influence cloud structure across a broad range of precipitation events, how these pathways impact orographic enhancement, and how synoptic conditions influence the thermodynamic environment and precipitation in the Park Range. By extending this framework across the season, we aim to determine whether the relationships identified in the case study persist across a wider range of storms and moisture pathways. The broader goal of this work is to characterize the variability associated with wintertime precipitation events, improve the accuracy of forecasting in mountainous regions, and advance our understanding of how orographic precipitation contributes to snowpack and water supply in the Intermountain West.

495975.title: Inter-Model Diversity of the Tropical Easterly Jet and Its Association with Afro-Asian Monsoon Precipitation In CMIP6 Models
495975.authors: Akintomide Afolayan Akinsanola, University of Illinois Chicago, Chicago, IL
495975.abstract: The Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) is a characteristic upper-level feature of the Afro-Asian summer monsoon and exerts a significant influence on regional precipitation and tropical storm development. However, Earth system models continue to exhibit substantial inter-model diversity in simulating its spatial characteristics. This study examines present-day TEJ simulations across Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models to investigate the causes of this diversity and its association with Afro-Asian monsoon precipitation. While the CMIP6 multi-model ensemble mean broadly reproduces the overall climatology of the TEJ, individual models exhibit substantial discrepancies, particularly in the longitudinal position of the jet core and the westward extension of the jet into the West African monsoon region. Mechanistically, the inter-model diversity in TEJ structure is associated with anomalous mid- to upper-tropospheric thermal structures over the Tibetan Plateau and subtropical regions. These thermal biases are linked to underestimated summer precipitation over South Asia and West Africa, indicating reduced diabatic heating that may contribute to the misrepresentation of the TEJ circulation. Overall, the inter-model diversity in TEJ structure and Afro-Asian monsoon precipitation underscores the coupled nature of these systems and the importance of accurately representing their interactions in climate models.

495977.title: Coordinating AI Downscaling for Earth Science Across Agencies
495977.authors: Sue Ellen Haupt, NSF NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and P. A. Ullrich, J. Cossuth, C. K. Potvin, J. Fan, H. K. Lee, G. Buster, and D. Rao
495977.abstract: The Interagency Council for Advancing Meteorological Services (ICAMS) Committee on Research and Innovation (CoRI) includes a subcommittee on artificial intelligence / machine learning (AI/ML) that seeks to identify and coordinate agency efforts in ML downscaling for the purposes of fostering collaboration that advances the science and the computational techniques for Earth system prediction through shared information and open source technologies. The members of this committee have compiled brief vignettes of the types of ML downscaling efforts being accomplished across the various U.S. government agencies. Examples from federal agencies will include: NSF NCAR’s Community Research Earth Digital Intelligence Twin (CREDIT) platform provides researchers with tools to train, deploy, and evaluate AI-driven models at a variety of scales, ranging from global through mesoscale and down to high-resolution urban simulations. The Office of Naval Research (ONR) is sponsoring multiple Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) projects to innovate and mature end-to-end aspects of a high resolution machine learning environmental prediction system, including assimilation, analysis, downscaling, and tailored decision products. NOAA’s Physical Sciences Laboratory (PSL) is leading the EXtreme preCipitation Estimates from Enhanced Downscaling (EXCEED) project to provide an unprecedentedly accurate historical record of extreme precipitation. NOAA’s Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) is leading two different efforts to provide high-resolution forecasts of wind and other fire weather variables. NOAA NCEI is also evaluating the quality of different machine learning-based downscaling approaches for extreme precipitation simulation. DOE ANL has evaluated various super-resolution methods in predicting precipitation and wind speeds, which provides important foundational work for future AI/ML downscaling work. Also, a digital twin of the Chicago metropolitan area is developed by training a U-Net to generate 500 m resolution predictions of key variables, including wind, precipitation, and near-surface meteorological conditions, conditioned with the ERA5 25-km reanalysis. This enables rapid assessment of urban weather impacts and energy resilience. NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) is fine-tuning NASA’s Prithvi-WxC foundation model to downscale North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR) data to the 800-m PRISM grid for daily precipitation and maximum and minimum temperatures. This effort is part of a multi-center collaboration with NASA’s Ames Research Center and Marshall Space Flight Center to develop and evaluate a machine-learning-based downscaled climate product and establish a pathway to operational production. DOE NLR leads a generative machine learning downscaling effort on Super-Resolution for Renewable Energy Resource Datasets (Sup3r) that is being used by industry to model energy systems under future severe weather scenarios. DOE NLR is innovating new techniques for multi-modal downscaling focused on problems without access to high-quality gridded training data such as near-surface extreme winds and subsurface geothermal resources. These examples demonstrate that the U.S. federal government is actively fostering cutting-edge machine learning methods that are enabling Earth system prediction to advance more rapidly in this era of AI and ICAMS is aiding the coordination of this research.

495978.title: Recent Achievements with the Open Source FFSB Hydrologic Ensemble Forecasting Project
495978.authors: Thomas E. Adams III, TerraPredictions, Blacksburg, VA
495978.abstract: Flood Forecasting on a Shoestring Budget (FFSB) began as a USAID humanitarian project. It is aimed at modernizing flood forecast operations in low- and medium-income countries, focusing on local technical capacity building. The real-time, over-the-loop ensemble forecasting methodology utilizes freely available, open source models and tools and freely available observed and forecast model input data sources at the country and regional scale. Basic operational capabilities utilize a recently updated version of the NOAA/NWS Research Distributed Hydrologic Model (RDHM), with a parameter estimation methodology developed by NOAA/NWS for the CONUS, but extended globally. Routine operational ensemble hydrologic forecasts are produced for the Indus River basin, by the Pakistan Meteorological Department, Flood Forecasting Division; Romanian National Hydrological Forecasts Center, National Institute of Hydrology and Water Management, for the Danube River basin; the Hat Yai basin in Thailand, by the Prince of Songkla University, in Hat Yai, Thailand; and country-wide implementation for rivers in Sri Lanka by the Flood Forecasting Department, Department of Irrigation (DOI) with assistance from The Regional Integrated Multi-Hazard Early Warning System (RIMES). Additional FFSB system implementations are in place for basins in India for reservoir inflow forecasting for hydroelectric power generation. A FFSB training workshop, hosted by RIMES, with sponsorship by UCAR and the U.S. Department of State, was held June 8-12, 2026, in Bangkok, Thailand, in conjunction with the Strengthening Last Mile Communications (SLMC) review workshop. Workshop attendees came from four SLMC countries: Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal and eight additional countries: Thailand, Vietnam, Maldives, Bhutan, India, Indonesia, Laos, and the Philippines. A clear outcome following the workshop is the need for further technical training on open source tools and software. Modeling and forecast results underscore the necessity for unbiased observational model inputs and simulation of reservoir operations. For major river systems, such as as the Indus in Pakistan and Danube in Europe, hydrodynamic modeling is critical.

495984.title: People’s Changing Hurricane Risk Perceptions and Protective Actions as Hurricane Ian Approached Landfall: Analysis from Longitudinal Panel Survey Data
495984.authors: Julie Demuth, NCAR, Longmont, CO; and A. B. Schumacher, M. Ng, R. E. Morss, G. Wong-Parodi, N. Herbert, R. Prestley, and H. Walpole
495984.abstract: The risks posed by a given hurricane event evolve as the hurricane threatens landfall. Yet, most studies of people’s risk perceptions and the protection actions they engage in are conducted either with hypothetical scenarios, which may not fully represent the real-world uncertainties, time pressures, or impacts people are weighing, or with post-event data collection, which introduces memory biases and other limitations. To explore the real-world, dynamic ways that people manage hurricane risk communication, perceptions, and responses, we conducted a study to collect perishable, longitudinal panel survey data during Hurricane Ian. In the days leading up to when Hurricane Ian made its first landfall in the CONUS, we fielded three surveys of the same set of individuals to repeatedly measure their responses to a set of questions. Among the questions were measures of (a) people’s perceived risk of being affected by the hurricane, of experiencing negative impacts, of the impacts being severe, and of worry, and (b) whether or not people took different protective actions (e.g., getting emergency supplies, boarding up, evacuating). The first survey was fielded approximately 5 days before landfall, and each survey wave was fielded for approximately 24 hours with approximately 24 hours in-between waves. Between n=1233 and n=1614 people responded across the survey waves, as people were allowed to miss responding to a wave (e.g., in case they were preparing). The analysis reported here focuses on exploring how respondent’s risk perceptions and protective actions evolved over time as Hurricane Ian evolved and approached landfall. We further explore the relationships between risk perception and protective actions over time, particularly (1) whether respondents’ protective actions taken are predicted by their risk perceptions at an earlier time (i.e., survey wave), and (2) whether respondents risk perceptions are predicted by the protective actions they’ve taken. This analysis lets us start to explore the complex, interconnected, and time-lagged relationships between people’s risk perceptions and behaviors. More generally, this analysis contributes to better understanding the fundamentals of human behavior so that we can work towards reducing societal harm from hurricanes.

495986.title: Retrieving Vertical Air Motions from Micro Rain Radar (MRR) Observations
495986.authors: Christopher R. Williams, University of Colorado Boulder, Denver, CO
495986.abstract: Micro Rain Radars (MRRs) are small 24-GHz frequency modulated continuously wave (FMCW) commercial meteorological vertically pointing radars manufactured by Metek Meteorologische Messtechnik GmbH in Germany. The MRR is a robust radar capable of operating during rain and snow and provides real-time products including vertical profiles of radar reflectivity factor and rain rate. The MRR real-time algorithms assume zero air motion in the precipitating column, which may be valid during stratiform rain, but is not valid during convective rain. To advance our understanding of microphysical rain and snow processes, a new retrieval algorithm was developed using profiles of MRR Doppler velocity power spectra to estimate vertical air motion and raindrop size distributions (DSDs) throughout the precipitating rain column. The new retrieval algorithm is based on a forward radar Doppler velocity power spectrum simulator that produces simulated MRR spectra, which are compared with the observed spectra. During rainfall, the Doppler velocity spectra are asymmetric and provide enough information to estimate the mean drop size and the shape of the DSD along with the vertical air motion. This contribution will discuss the air motion and DSD retrieval algorithm using the MRR deployed at the Middle and Upper atmosphere (MU) radar site in Shigaraki, Japan. The MU radar (46 MHz) provides direct measurement of vertical air motions that are used to validate the MRR retrieval algorithm.

495989.title: NWS/NASA Spaceflight Meteorology Group Support to the Artemis Program
495989.authors: Alek J. Krautmann, NOAA, Houston, TX; and L. Belobrajdic and T. Garner
495989.abstract: The NWS/NASA Spaceflight Meteorology Group (SMG) at Johnson Space Center provides Impact-based Decision Support Services (IDSS) to ensure safety and operational readiness for human spaceflight. During the April 2026 Artemis II mission, SMG delivered weather information to NASA flight controllers, managers, Search and Rescue Forces, and the NASA Scientifically Calibrated In-Flight Imagery (SCIFLI) team for decision-making during ascent and entry. SMG provided launch day weather forecasts along the ascent trajectories across the Atlantic Ocean as well as the Abort Once Around region in the Pacific Ocean, should any mission abort occur. Each day during the mission, SMG briefed the NASA Flight Directors on forecasts for the entry trajectory across the Pacific Ocean. SMG analysis determined favorable GO weather conditions allowed for splashdown at the primary landing site off the coast of San Diego, CA. SMG relied on additional observations from weather balloons released by the U.S. Space Force 45th Weather Squadron off the USS John P. Murtha recovery ship and high resolution rapid scan satellite imagery from NOAA’s GOES West. This presentation will review forecasts and observations from the Artemis II mission, including an overview of the unique weather considerations and decision support for the planned 2027 low Earth orbit Artemis III mission. Discussion will also cover the ongoing partner engagement to NASA for the Commercial Crew Program. The NWS has provided weather information for human spaceflight at NASA in Houston since 1962.

495994.title: Migration of the National Environmental Satellite Data and Information Service (NESDIS) Product Distribution and Access (PDA) System to the NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF)
495994.abstract: As the National Environmental Satellite Data and Information Service (NESDIS) moves towards cloud based systems and away from legacy on-premises systems, one large and very expensive migration remains, and that is the move from the Product Distribution and Access (PDA) system to utilizing NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF) services. Instead of thinking of the PDA migration as a “lift and shift”, engineers, software developers and scientists were asked to consider how to revolutionize the features, utilize services instead of creating bespoke systems and emphasize the user experience. Through many months the teams have made significant progress in establishing baseline functionality, ingesting data, migrating product algorithms and establishing new subscribers. While NESIDS will meet its deadline to have the current features, data and subscribers available in NCCF by the end of fiscal year 2027, a new challenge awaits; how do we improve the user experience for both subscribers and non-subscribers, keep up with emerging technologies, support a range a capabilities for our users and ensure product and data quality? In this presentation, we will explore the PDA, the NCCF and the possibilities to improve and rethink our satellite data ingest, storage and dissemination while improving the user experience.

495996.title: Accelerating Rapid Innovation: EPIC’s Pre-Configured Public Cloud HPC environments
495996.authors: Kristopher Jaye Booker, tomorrow.io, Boston, MA; and C. Book, N. Perlin, W. C. Kolczynski Jr., W. Huang, J. Ising, K. M. Blackman, and M. Huang
495996.abstract: The NOAA Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC) has enabled and accelerated the pace of numerical weather prediction innovation through its collaboration with government, academic, and private sectors. The Unified Forecast System (UFS), through its use of open-source code repositories and shared community infrastructure, allows modeling groups that were once siloed to effectively collaborate. However, the greater challenge has come from constraints that kept organizations from accessing High-Performance Computing (HPC) platforms capable of running new modeling innovations at scale. Although the EPIC program has established insights and dashboards, there is still an underserved need to allow contributors direct access to HPC platforms with all of the required software dependencies. The largest barrier to entry for the UFS community is the ability to build/run the UFS weather model easily. Containerization through the use of Apptainer/Singularity solves some of these problems, but the abstraction can still pose unique technical and performance challenges. EPIC has attempted to solve this dilemma by utilizing infrastructure-as-code tools and processes to allow consistent installation of the basic UFS software environment. These processes, coupled with public cloud HPC platforms (AWS ParallelCluster, Azure CycleCloud) enable UFS community users to rapidly deploy a turnkey public cloud HPC environment. EPIC has demonstrated the success of this approach by providing UFS community workshop users a ready-made HPC environment for various training events. Participants have frequently requested access to these software tools and configurations. This approach should prove valuable to those UFS community members without access to traditional academic or government HPC resources. Our presentation plans to discuss how we used infrastructure-as-code tools to build an HPC environment on the public cloud capable of running the UFS weather model (UFS-WM). This presentation serves as an example to those without access to a traditional government or academic HPC environment on how to utilize the public cloud for working with the UFS-WM.

495997.title: Mapping Cascading Impacts for Extreme Weather and Water Events for Community Preparedness and Resilience
495997.authors: Monica Youngman, NWS, Arden, NC; and R. Hollins, L. D’Arinzo, D. Giardino, F. Salas, and G. Selig
495997.abstract: Extreme weather and water events increasingly threaten the vital systems supporting our society, making it critical for local communities to move from general hazard awareness to localized, actionable comprehension of cascading impacts. Devastating extreme events, such as Hurricane Helene in September 2024, underscore this urgent need. During Helene, the Southern Appalachians experienced historic precipitation, leading to severe cascading impacts such as catastrophic flooding, destroyed homes, road washouts, and isolated communities. These impacts demonstrated how disruptions in one sector can rapidly propagate through interconnected systems. Traditional separate-sector planning fails to capture how a failure in one system, such as power, water treatment, or transportation, rapidly cripples downstream services like healthcare or schools. Addressing this challenge requires advanced predictive capabilities leading the National Weather Service to test the implementation of a Cascading Impacts Explorer to translate weather and water forecasts into explicit and comprehensive community impact assessments. This digital twin framework integrates geospatial data with graph database technology to map critical infrastructure systems and their dependency connections before laying them with weather and water forecasts. Ultimately the system will include real time, historical, and scenario forecasts with tools that facilitate visualization, querying, and analysis of how physical disruptions cascade through interconnected local infrastructure. This presentation will provide an overview of the Cascading Impacts Explorer dashboard designed to help forecasters, emergency managers, and government planners visualize impacts of interconnected systems at the local-scale. The discussion will cover the integration of forecast data, including the National Water Center’s Flood Inundation Mapping services, AI features, method of integrating diverse geospatial data and forecasts, testing of impacts prediction, and lessons learned. This work represents a major leap forward in utilizing GIS and graph analytics to build resilient, weather-ready communities.

495999.title: Extending the Value of GOES: Modern Reprocessing of the GVAR Imager Record
495999.authors: Andrew Heidinger, NOAA, Madison, WI; and K. R. Knapp, J. L. Matthews, J. Robaidek, and S. T. Wanzong
495999.abstract: Last year marked the 50th anniversary of the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) series. The GOES GVAR Imager data record, which spans from 1994 to 2020, represents a critical precursor to the observations now continued by the GOES-R Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI). This cumulative 30-year record offers a unique and powerful dataset for climate monitoring and machine learning applications. However, legacy GOES Imager data in its original form is not optimized for these modern analytical frameworks. To address this, NOAA/NESDIS/GEO has supported initiatives to standardize GVAR data into a modern format compatible with GOES-R, incorporating enhanced calibration and geolocation. This presentation summarizes these reprocessing efforts, demonstrates the application of modern algorithms to the harmonized GVAR dataset, and evaluates its multidecadal stability.

496001.title: Viewing Arctic Clouds Through the Combined Lens of PREFIRE and EarthCARE
496001.authors: Xia Li, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and M. S. Diamond, C. Peterson, K. S. Schmidt, and I. Tan
496001.abstract: Arctic clouds frequently contain supercooled liquid droplets, ice crystals, or both, whose phase composition strongly influences cloud–radiation interactions but remains poorly constrained observationally. This is particularly challenging during polar night due to the lack of solar illumination, complex surface conditions, and frequent optically thin or mixed-phase clouds. The recent PREFIRE satellite mission provides measurements of the far-infrared spectrum, which fills a long-missing observational gap in the polar energy budget. Here we combine these observations with vertically resolved cloud properties from EarthCARE to provide a unique space lens on Arctic clouds. By developing a footprint-to-profile collocation framework, we will investigate how far-infrared spectral radiances vary with cloud phase, microphysical properties, vertical structure, and underlying surface regime. We will also assess the additional value of PREFIRE far-infrared measurements for retrieving cloud microphysical and optical properties, particularly during winter. Our results will support the evaluation of Arctic weather and climate modeling and inform the assessment of mixed-phase cloud thinning as a potential polar intervention strategy.

496002.title: Spatial and Temporal Patterns of Extreme Hourly Rainfall In the Hawaiian Islands
496002.authors: Yinphan Tsang, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, Honolulu, HI; and Y. F. Huang, M. Gayte, P. S. Chu, T. Giambelluca, and H. Zhang
