496002.abstract: Climate-driven changes in extreme precipitation and floods severely impact societies and ecosystems, yet regional spatial and temporal patterns remain poorly understood, including in the Hawaiian Islands. This study utilized stationary and non-stationary Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distributions, annual maximum series (AMS), and circular analysis to examine extreme hourly rainfall across 117 gauges on the five most populated Hawaiian Islands (Kauaʻi, Oʻahu, Maui, Molokaʻi, and the Big Island) from 1966 to 2020. Stationary GEV results show that Kauaʻi, Oʻahu, and the Big Island exhibited higher return levels (the event magnitude at a given return period) than the other islands, with windward sides consistently exceeding leeward sides. Over 1990-2020, most gauges show no trend in annual maximum hourly rainfall, while some significant positive and negative trends occur across the islands. Non-stationary GEV results show that extreme rainfall is spatially heterogeneous—O‘ahu, Maui, and Molokaʻi are dominated by decreasing return-level trends, while the Big Island and Kaua‘i show predominantly increasing trends, particularly for rare 20- and 100-year events. Notably, Maui exhibited consistent island-wide decreases regardless of frequency or duration. Circular analysis identified two primary, persistent seasonal peaks for extreme events: October – December and February – March. These findings highlight a critical duration dependence: short-duration infrequent extremes are intensifying across most islands, even where frequent events are decreasing, posing a significant threat to emergency response. As the first study investigating hourly extreme rainfall in Hawai‘i, this work provides a vital understanding of non-stationarity on tropical islands to mitigate future flooding threats.

496003.title: Mining Historical Archives for Inspiration and Encouraging Connection: The Unexpected Synergy Found in Retro Film Screenings
496003.authors: Laura Hoff, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Schmitz and M. Sulek
496003.abstract: In 2025 NSF NCAR Archives partnered with UCAR staff to launch a lunchtime film series featuring short films from the archives. The intention was to recreate a popular activity documented in early staff newsletters in order to soften the post-pandemic return to office by providing a reason for staff to meet each other and share an experience. The initial screening also offered a short presentation to bring viewers into the present with a progress report on scientific advances. Attendees’ enthusiasm has resulted in a packed slate of presentations, a full room every month that a screening has been offered, and overwhelmingly positive feedback. In addition to bringing people together, the events have become a forum to share historical and current scientific leadership at NSF NCAR and UCAR as well as the broader scientific community. Join us for a series of film clips and information on the experience of viewing a historical film, the strategy behind the events, and the impact and reproducibility of this series as a way to share history, promote archival materials, and bring people together to learn about current projects and cultivate a sense of shared mission.

496005.title: The Interagency Council for Advancing Meteorological Services (ICAMS) Physics Interoperability Implementation Team (PIIT) activities
496005.authors: Ligia Bernardet, NOAA Global Systems Laboratory and Developmental Testbed Center, Boulder, CO; and M. B. Ek, J. D. Doyle, K. Thengumthara, and C. Bassett
496005.abstract: The Interagency Council for Advancing Meteorological Services (ICAMS) Physics Interoperability Implementation Team (PIIT) seeks to design community standards for physical parameterization interfaces and software frameworks (such as the Common Community Physics Package, CCPP) that allow for efficient implementation in Earth system models (ESMs), which includes numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. The ICAMS PIIT helps to coordinate and stimulate the development of Earth-system physical parameterizations across the U.S. laboratories and federal agencies (e.g. NOAA, U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, NCAR, NASA, DOE). The ability to efficiently improve ESMs depends in part on the time it takes to get changes incorporated into those ESMs. As such, Hierarchical System Development (HSD) is an efficient way to effectively connect the various parts of the model development process, where CCPP is the “HSD enabler”. Via this systems-engineering approach, small components (i.e. physics schemes) from an ESM are tested first in isolation, then the components are progressively connected with increased coupling between ESM components at the different HSD steps. HSD is end-to-end, i.e. it includes data ingest and QC, data assimilation, model execution, post-processing, and verification. HSD includes Single Column Models (SCMs; including individual physics schemes within a SCM), Small-Domain, Limited-Area and Regional Models, all the way to complex fully-coupled ESMs with interacting components for atmosphere/chemistry/aerosols, ocean/waves/sea-ice, land-hydrology/snow/land-ice, and biogeochemical cycles/ecosystems, a subset of which (i.e. atmosphere plus land and specified ocean conditions) has traditionally addressed NWP needs, though now several operational NWP systems are fully coupled from day zero. ICAMS PIIT members meet monthly to discuss the latest developments at their institutes, with quasi-bi-monthly guest seminars from other operational centers and research institutes highlighting their model development processes (which often have HSD-like approaches). CCPP, the HSD approach, and examples of ICAMS PIIT efforts and that of our other national and international partners will be presented.

496006.title: High-Resolution Precipitation Measurements Using Phased Array Weather Radar In Central Europe
496006.authors: Miloslav Stanek, Meteopress, Prague, Czech Republic; and F. Najman
496006.abstract: Phased array weather radar represents an advancement over conventional systems by combining mechanical rotation in azimuth with electronic beam steering in elevation. This allows multiple elevation angles to be sampled simultaneously, significantly reducing the time required to obtain volumetric data. The resulting high temporal resolution makes such systems well suited for observing rapidly evolving atmospheric phenomena, particularly in operational meteorology. Meteopress has developed a mobile X-band phased array radar designed for operational use, including severe weather monitoring. The system was deployed and tested during the spring and summer of 2026 in Central Europe. During the summer, several interesting cases of strong convective storms were captured with high temporal and spatial resolution, providing detailed observations of rapidly evolving precipitation structures. Measurements will continue through autumn 2026, further expanding the dataset. The radar enables fast volumetric scanning and targeted observation of regions of interest. Compared to conventional systems, it provides improved temporal resolution while maintaining comparable spatial detail. The radar is also being progressively upgraded, including both hardware and software improvements. The presentation will introduce these new developments and demonstrate their impact on data quality and system performance. Selected radar data examples will be presented, including case studies of severe convective storms, together with an assessment of the potential of the continuously evolving system for future operational and research applications.

496007.title: All-Sky TPW Retrieval from ABI on GOES-19 Using a Deep Learning Model
496007.authors: Jinlong Li, CIMSS/SSEC, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and Z. Li, Z. Ma, J. M. Daniels, A. Heidinger, T. J. Wagner, and C. Smith
496007.abstract: Total precipitable water (TPW) is a key parameter representing atmospheric environmental conditions in both weather and climate processes. High spatial and temporal resolution TPW products are critical for monitoring moisture transport, identifying high-moisture regions, and improving severe weather forecasting, particularly for heavy precipitation and flooding events. Satellite remote sensing provides continuous observations over large areas, offering a promising approach for generating such products. Current geostationary satellites (GOES-R series) in the United States, such as GOES-18 and GOES-19, collect measurements every 10 minutes for the full disk and every 5 minutes for the Continental United States (CONUS) at a 2 km spatial resolution for infrared (IR) bands. The operational Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) TPW product is derived using a traditional physical retrieval algorithm and is widely used by weather forecasters; however, it is strictly limited to clear-sky conditions due to cloud contamination in IR measurements. With rapid advances in artificial intelligence, deep learning models can leverage not only pixel-level spectral information but also spatial context from surrounding areas. In this study, an all-sky TPW retrieval algorithm was developed for GOES-19 ABI observations using a U-Net model. Unlike traditional physical models that utilize spectral information from a field of regard (5x5 pixels average), the U-Net model incorporates spatial-spectral features from neighboring pixels in a large area, enabling retrievals under cloudy conditions. As an initial experiment, four months of CONUS GOES-19 ABI measurements were combined with ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis TPW data. Similar to the operational ABI TPW algorithm, the input dataset includes ABI channels 8 through 16, GFS-forecasted surface pressure and TPW, and the satellite local zenith angle, with collocated ERA5 TPW serving as the target variable. Less than 1% of the four-month dataset was used for model development and testing, after which the model was applied across the entire dataset for full evaluation. Overall, the new all-sky TPW retrievals outperform both the operational product and the GFS forecast when validated against ERA5 and radiosonde data. The all-sky retrievals achieved root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 1.98 mm relative to ERA5 and 2.50 mm relative to radiosondes—well within the GOES-R specification requirements. Ongoing work is focused on extending the training and evaluation period to a full year and expanding the retrieval model to include layer precipitable water (LPW). Applications and benefits for weather forecasting will be presented.

496009.title: A Self-Organizing Map Derived Synoptic Climatology of the Midwest U.S. Corn Belt for Determining Surface Heat Fluxes from Cropland and Remnant Forests
496009.authors: Mikael Hiestand, USDA, Fort Collins, CO; and A. M. Carleton
496009.abstract: A nine-year (1999-2007) warm season (May 1-September 30) synoptic climatology for the Midwest U.S. Corn Belt is derived from Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) applied to daily sea-level pressure (SLP) data. This “climatology” is validated against a previously developed manual classification before being applied to the analysis of flux-tower derived surface heat fluxes (sensible: H, latent: LE) from cropland and remnant forest land-cover types. ANOVA reveals statistically significant differences in the heat fluxes on seasonal timescales that accompany variations in pressure gradient, isobaric orientation, and the implied advection of a warm, humid southerly airflow. The last results primarily from a “low pressure to the west and high pressure to the east” SLP pattern located beneath 500-hPa ridging. Further, days in the 90th percentile for H fluxes from both land-cover types correspond to high-pressure systems centered on the Corn Belt with light anticyclonic flow, as previously identified in the manual synoptic classification. These results show that slight variations within a particular synoptic pattern may be more influential on the spatial variations of Corn Belt LE and H than previously thought. This enhanced understanding of how synoptic SLP patterns influence warm-season LE and H heat fluxes in the Corn Belt is providing insights into the land cover’s ability to trigger or enhance convective precipitation in this economically vital region of rain-fed agriculture.

496012.title: Fog, Weather, and Visibility in New Zealand: Fog Occurrences and the Weather Associated with Limited Visibility
496012.authors: Neil F. Laird, Hobart & William Smith Colleges, Geneva, NY; and K. Vanderhoof, M. Gray, and A. Soika
496012.abstract: Understanding spatiotemporal variation of fog and the occurrence of limited visibility across New Zealand can provide insight to impacts on ground and air travel, as well as the relationship to safety, economic losses, and tourism activities. Hourly surface weather data from stations across New Zealand for 2020-2025 were analyzed to perform a short-term climatological study of fog occurrences and investigate the weather most commonly associated with reductions in visibility in different locations. Fog occurrence in New Zealand was more frequent over the South Island compared to the North Island during 2020-2025 and more common during the cool season (April - August). For both Dunedin and Christchurch, fog occurred primarily during the night and early morning with a maximum around 5 A.M. While fog was found to be the most impactful weather associated with reducing visibility to the greatest extent, other weather, such as mist, drizzle, precipitation, haze and smoke, were also identified as contributing to reductions in visibility at various locations across New Zealand.

496015.title: Semaphore and Flare: A Pipeline for Live Deployment of Coastal AI Models
496015.authors: Savannah L Stephenson, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX; and A. Beasley, C. Quintero, M. A. Kastl, B. L. Estrada Jr., F. Tissot, S. Nguyen, and P. E. Tissot
496015.abstract: Events such as coastal flooding or influx of very cold air in wintertime can have a significant impact on coastal communities and ecosystems. Advance warnings are critical to help manage these events. Machine learning models have shown to be increasingly effective at predicting these events, but bringing these models live remains a difficult step rarely completed. Without live operational models, stakeholders cannot benefit from the more accurate early warnings when it matters most. Semaphore and Flare are a software and data pipeline that streamline how to put these models into stakeholders' hands: Semaphore collects data, runs models, and stores outputs; Flare turns those outputs into visuals that are easy to interpret without sacrificing depth. Semaphore currently hosts nine operational models: five for water levels, one for total water level, and three addressing cold-stunning risk for sea turtles and fisheries, with Flare currently visualizing the three cold-stunning models and more visualizations planned. Architecturally, Semaphore is a containerized, modular platform that orchestrates data ingestion, preprocessing, and model execution, and stores both inputs and outputs to support ongoing performance assessment. Flare is likewise containerized, with a Vue front end delivering interactive visuals of model predictions. Semaphore has been designed to allow for minimal input from the modeler after a handoff period which involves transferring the .h5 or .keras files to the Semaphore repository and filling out a design specification file, or a DSPEC. The DSPEC describes the inputs that the model needs to make predictions, as well as what data source to pull these inputs from. All inputs for modules and outputs are stored in the Semaphore database, allowing researchers to assess the performance. This presentation walks through the pipeline's operational impact first, then works backward through the technical architecture that makes Semaphore and Flare an effective research-to-operations bridge for coastal AI.

496017.title: A Satellite's Perspective of 2026's Major Weather Events
496017.authors: Dakota C. Smith, CNN, berthoud, CO
496017.abstract: From the massive wildfires in the North American West to Super Typhoons in the Western Pacific, 2026 contained numerous high impact weather events around the world. Weather satellites provided constant monitoring, capturing compelling views of these powerful weather phenomena. I have curated satellite animations of these events and utilized them in national and international weather coverage. This talk will feature these animations, highlighting the most eye-opening imagery of 2026’s major weather events.

496018.title: Advances in the Parametric Tropical Cyclone Rainfall Model, P-CLIPER: Expanded Calibration and Asymmetry Implementation
496018.authors: Miles Leonard, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and K. M. Dresback, C. M. Szpilka, and R. L. Kolar
496018.abstract: While storm surge is considered the most dangerous aspect of landfalling tropical cyclones, flooding due to heavy rain associated with tropical cyclones does not fall far behind. Rising sea levels, projected increases in tropical cyclone related rainfall, and widespread urbanization are all factors exacerbating the threat of compound coastal flooding events, yet coastal communities in the United States continue to grow. Developing adequate mitigation and adaptation strategies necessitates modeling not just the risk, but the events themselves. As part of a coupled-model system, P-CLIPER is a parametric tropical cyclone rainfall model that prioritizes speed and efficiency for ensemble applications. In its current form, P-CLIPER generates axisymmetric rainfall in a 350 km radius out from the tropical cyclone storm center, but this oversimplification does not accurately capture the observed rainfall associated with tropical cyclones. P-CLIPER utilizes a free parameter in its equations known as f which represents the change from the average rainfall intensity. This allows rainfall intensities above and beyond the mean to be calculated, but this f-value must be calibrated using historical tropical cyclones. This presentation focuses on the calibration of P-CLIPER's f-value, along with the development and implementation of an asymmetrical component. P-CLIPER's performance is evaluated using three different error metrics—RMSE, MAE, and a modified bias score—by comparing its output to MRMS rainfall data. Evaluation of the asymmetric version of P-CLIPER shows substantial improvements over the current, axisymmetric version across all three metrics. Further analysis of the calibrated f-values with respect to various TC characteristics such as the direction of forward motion, storm duration, and translational speed indicates that these characteristics could be used to narrow the range of f-values for ensemble applications. The hydrologic response with the asymmetric version of P-CLIPER within the coupled-model system is discussed in a companion presentation (Advances in a Compound Coastal Flood Modeling System).

496024.title: More Than a Transmitter Upgrade: The Dual-Channel SSPA Weather Radar as a New Observational Tool
496024.authors: Sergey I. Panov, Vaisala Inc., Burlington, MA; and J. Selzler, P. Rossi, J. Mäkinen, T. Lyly, J. Salmivaara, and M. Hamm
496024.abstract: Solid-state power amplifier (SSPA) transmitters are steadily displacing magnetrons in operational weather radar networks, and published assessments have largely treated them as drop-in replacements, benchmarking data quality against the legacy systems they succeed (Hald et al. 2026; Lehtinen et al. 2025). That framing, while reassuring, undersells the technology. A weather radar built around a dual-channel SSPA transmitter is not merely a conventional radar with a modernized power source — it is an instrument of a different class, with an expanded set of observational capabilities that no single-transmitter design can match. In the established taxonomy of polarization-diversity radars (Bringi and Hendry 1990; Chandrasekar et al. 2023), the transmit architecture is fixed at build time: a system is constructed either for simultaneous transmit, simultaneous receive (STSR) operation — the configuration adopted by virtually all operational dual-polarization radars — or for alternate transmit, simultaneous receive (ATSR) operation, which yields accurate linear depolarization ratio (LDR) measurements and eliminates differential reflectivity biases where strong depolarization occurs. Single-transmitter radars are not entirely locked into that choice: many magnetron systems can be routed into H-only transmission through a slow waveguide switch, which does allow recovery of LDR (from the horizontal transmission only) in a dedicated mode. But true alternate-transmit operation requires the polarization to alternate from pulse to pulse, and a single transmitter can achieve that only through a fast high-power polarization switch — an expensive component and a notorious reliability liability. This is why pulse-to-pulse polarization agility has remained the province of klystron-based research instruments such as CSU-CHILL and S-Pol (Bringi et al. 2000; Hubbert et al. 2018). The dual-channel SSPA architecture removes the switch from the problem entirely: with fully independent horizontal and vertical transmit channels, the polarization sequence becomes just another waveform parameter. One radar operates at full duty cycle in STSR, ATSR, or single-channel modes — selectable per task, with no moving or high-power switching hardware in the transmit path — in effect, two dual-polarization radars sharing a single pedestal and antenna, at a fraction of a research radar's cost. The architecture also redefines what "radar availability" means. The modular transmitter degrades gracefully under individual module failures, losing a fraction of transmit power rather than going offline, and a run-time calibration correction — driven by continuous burst-power monitoring against the annual calibration reference — keeps reflectivity and differential reflectivity within specification through such events (Puhakka et al. 2025). Even the total loss of one polarization channel does not blind the radar: because both receivers remain active, single-channel-transmit tasks continue to deliver Doppler moments and cross-polar measurements, including LDR, from the surviving channel. A failure that would take a magnetron or klystron radar out of the network becomes a task change rather than a site visit. Independent per-channel timing and phase control further open a waveform design space that single-transmitter radars cannot enter. We demonstrate Polarization Diversity Pulse Pair (PDPP) processing (Doviak and Sirmans 1973; Pazmany et al. 1999), in which staggered H and V pulses decouple the classical range–velocity dilemma, extending the unambiguous velocity by more than an order of magnitude in operational data. Orthogonal phase coding of the two transmit channels (Chandrasekar and Bharadwaj 2009) recovers the full set of co- and cross-polar covariances from within the simultaneous transmit mode — yielding ATSR-grade moments, including LDR and depolarization-corrected differential reflectivity, without leaving STSR — and combines naturally with phase-coded second-trip recovery (Frush et al. 2002; Karhunen et al. 2008). We illustrate these capabilities with operational data from Vaisala C-band dual-channel SSPA radars: STSR and ATSR volume scans interleaved on the same system, validated run-time calibration through induced module failures, single-channel fallback operation, and PDPP velocity dealiasing. Together they show that the dual-channel SSPA radar is best understood not as a transmitter upgrade, but as a new tool for operational radar meteorology.

496027.title: The Complicated Nature of Ground-Based Seeding Attribution with State-of-the-Art Remote Sensing Data
496027.authors: Joshua Gooch, University of Colorado - Boulder, Lafayette, CO; and K. Friedrich, S. Chen, and L. Xue
496027.abstract: This study investigates the challenge of identifying ground-based cloud seeding signatures in complex orographic winter clouds by combining WRF-WxMod (Weather Research and Forecasting model–Weather Modification Module) simulations of AgI activation with remote sensing and in situ observations. The study examines how terrain-driven processes produce supercooled liquid water (SLW), natural ice growth, and radar signatures that may overlap with potential seeding effects across X-band and W-band radar observations. Using the Seeded and Natural Orographic Wintertime Clouds – the Idaho Experiment (SNOWIE) case, model-indicated AgI activation regions were used to guide targeted radar analyses of cloud microphysical evolution. Attribution challenges included variability in orographic SLW production, inconsistent responses in X-band dual-polarization variables, and the influence of cloud-top generating cells that contributed additional natural ice production. By evaluating these competing natural processes alongside predicted AgI activation, this study develops a framework to assess potential AgI-induced ice growth in complex cloud environments. Results reveal spatial and temporal signals consistent with expected AgI-induced ice production; however, the combined influence of natural cloud processes prevents definitive attribution of all observed changes to seeding. Building on these results, the integration of numerical modeling and high-resolution terrain information provides a pathway toward identifying optimal cloud and terrain conditions for targeted seeding and determining the most effective deployment strategy, whether from ground-based generators, unmanned aerial systems, or aircraft.

496028.title: Impact Study of Air Force Precipitation Radar Data Assimilation on Heavy Rainfall Event
496028.authors: CHIA-LING LIANG, National Defense University, Yuanlin City, CHA, Taiwan; and C. Y. Chen, S. C. Tsai, N. C. Yeh, and C. C. Liu
496028.abstract: Short-duration heavy rainfall is characterized by rapid development, small spatial scales, and strong localization, making accurate prediction of convective initiation and rainfall intensity particularly challenging over Taiwan’s complex terrain. This study investigates a short-duration heavy rainfall event that occurred over the Xiulin–Hezhong area of Hualien on 18 August 2025, during which a maximum hourly rainfall of 62 mm was observed at Hezhong between 0900 and 1000 UTC. The Weather Research and Forecasting–Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (WRF–GSI) three-dimensional variational data assimilation system was employed to assimilate radial-velocity observations from the Air Force Hualien X-band weather radar. Experiments included a no-data-assimilation control, single data assimilation, and cycling data assimilation, together with three background-error scaling factors (0.02, 0.04, and 0.09) and different model spin-up times, to evaluate sensitivities to assimilation strategy, background-error specification, and model adjustment time. Results show that the radar-derived wind field exhibits reasonable temporal consistency with the large-scale ERA5 environmental flow between approximately 0.7 and 3.0 km altitude and provides additional information on local low-level circulations that is not fully resolved by the reanalysis. Analysis increments associated with radial-velocity assimilation are concentrated primarily between 1000 and 700 hPa, with substantially stronger direct adjustments to the wind field than to moisture. Moisture changes arise mainly through multivariate background-error covariances and subsequent moisture advection and convergence during model integration. Moisture-flux convergence analysis further indicates that assimilation modifies the coastal wind configuration and warm, moist inflow at 925–850 hPa, producing more concentrated low-level moisture convergence along the windward slopes of the Central Mountain Range. Moisture transport remains evident near 700 hPa, whereas impacts above 500 hPa are comparatively limited. These results suggest that the primary physical pathway is low- to mid-level wind adjustment → modification of warm-moist transport and local convergence → enhanced orographic lifting → modulation of convective initiation and maintenance. Comparisons of hydrometeor vertical structure and radar reflectivity further show that the no-assimilation experiment fails to realistically reproduce the observed low-level convective core near the Hualien coast, whereas different assimilation configurations alter the location, intensity, and vertical development of convection to varying degrees. However, model spin-up time exerts a substantial influence on hydrometeor development, and larger background-error scaling factors, although generally producing stronger analysis increments, do not necessarily yield better rainfall simulations. No single combination of single or cycling assimilation, scaling factor, and spin-up configuration consistently outperforms the others across all diagnostic measures. Surface rainfall verification also exhibits strong station dependence, highlighting the sensitivity of localized convective precipitation forecasts to displacement errors in rainfall cores. Overall, the Air Force Hualien X-band radar radial-velocity observations show clear potential for improving the representation of initial conditions and low- to mid-level dynamical structures associated with short-duration heavy rainfall over complex terrain. Their principal value lies in supplementing local wind information and thereby modulating moisture transport, terrain-induced convergence, convective initiation, and subsequent precipitation evolution. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of radar data assimilation is highly sensitive to background-error specification, assimilation strategy, and model spin-up time. Future work should evaluate additional cases under consistent verification settings and further examine the combined assimilation of radial velocity and radar reflectivity to improve forecasts of localized deep convection and short-duration heavy rainfall.

496032.title: Observations Made During the Colorado Radiosonde Releases: Interagency Deployments for Operations and Research (CORRIDOR) Project
496032.authors: Rachael Auth, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and B. Dolan, B. Eckerman, M. B. Chapman, N. Barlow, L. M. Beard, E. K. Benedict, C. A. Bekemeier, C. M. Davis, N. M. Falk, M. Harmala, J. Ju, P. C. Lin, A. J. Muehr, A. J. Tomanek, L. Zitlow, and S. C. van den Heever
496032.abstract: The Colorado Front Range and urban corridor experience frequent high-impact weather, yet routine upper-air observations are sparse immediately east of the Rocky Mountains. The COlorado Radiosonde Releases: Interagency Deployments for Operations and Research (CORRIDOR) project is a partnership between Colorado State University’s (CSU) Department of Atmospheric Science and the Colorado Department of Transportation that aims to address this observational gap through targeted radiosonde launches for operational and research purposes. Soundings are collected from the CSU Foothills Campus in Fort Collins, Colorado, using an iMet sounding system and are launched by request to aid CDOT roadway operations during high-impact weather events including severe thunderstorms, burn-scar flooding, and winter weather. All observations are available to the public, providing a growing dataset of high-resolution atmospheric profiles in a region that is otherwise under sampled by routine upper-air observations, and an opportunity to evaluate how these environments are characterized by Numerical Weather Prediction models. This study examines the thermodynamic and moisture characteristics observed by CORRIDOR soundings and evaluates their representation in the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model. Observed soundings are compared with HRRR-derived vertical profiles at or near the sounding launch location and time, with an emphasis on metrics describing low-level moisture and atmospheric stability. Comparisons are used to identify systematic differences between observed and model-represented environments and to assess how well the HRRR captures thermodynamic characteristics relevant to high-impact weather in the Front Range. As the CORRIDOR dataset continues to grow, these observations will provide an increasingly valuable resource for sampling environments that are important to CDOT operations and evaluating model performance.

496033.title: Community Data Assimilation Infrastructure for the Unified Forecast System: The UFS-DA Workflow and Diagnostics Toolkit
496033.authors: Jong Kim, EPIC/STC, Ellicott City, NJ; and C. H. Jeon and M. Huang
496033.abstract: The Unified Forecast System (UFS) Data Assimilation (DA) Workflow provides a community-supported framework for configuring and running DA experiments using the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) and UFS Weather Model baselines and applications. As community use of UFS and JEDI systems continues to expand, reproducible workflows and accessible diagnostics are essential for scientific evaluation, training, and research-to-operations activities. This work presents recent advances in the UFS-DA Workflow and its integration with the UFS-DA Diagnostics Toolkit. The workflow supports experiment configuration, execution, and management, while the diagnostics toolkit provides workflow-independent evaluation through model-space, observation-space, spectral, consistency, and weather diagnostics. Together, these capabilities enable end-to-end analysis of DA experiments. Applications from community training activities and Finite-Volume Cubed-Sphere (FV3)-JEDI Hybrid 3D-Var experiments demonstrate the framework's utility for evaluating background-error covariance and observation-error sensitivity studies. Diagnostic products including increment maps, innovation statistics, power spectra, and consistency metrics provide complementary perspectives on DA performance. The integrated workflow and diagnostics infrastructure enhances reproducibility while providing deeper insight into background-error covariance modeling, observation-error tuning, analysis consistency, and the relationship between DA behavior and meteorological structures, supporting both community training and scientific investigation.

496034.title: Polar Bear Fasting Season Length as an Ecologically Relevant Metric for Evaluating High-Latitude/Low-Altitude SAI Deployment Outcomes
496034.authors: Pricila Grace Villalta, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and M. S. Diamond
496034.abstract: Metrics used to evaluate solar radiation management often focus on physical climate responses, making it difficult to communicate to non-scientific audiences how changes in climate variables translate into ecologically meaningful consequences. This study aims to create a new metric for assessing the efficacy of climate intervention strategies through an ecological lens. Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice to hunt seals, their primary food source. During ice-free conditions, the bears fast. Under historical warming, the fasting season has lengthened enough already to threaten starvation for nursing mothers, and thus population stability, in regions like the Hudson Bay; under expected levels of future warming (e.g., SSP2-4.5), extirpation becomes possible or likely throughout most of the Arctic by the end of the century. Here, we show that a technologically plausible, high-latitude/low-altitude (HiLLA) stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) scenario keeping global temperatures at roughly 1.5 C above pre-industrial despite SSP2-4.5 greenhouse gas emissions would reduce polar bear extirpation risk compared to the unabated SSP2-4.5 scenario across the Arctic and even compared to the historical period in some regions. On average, HiLLA SAI reduces the fasting season length by approximately two months. HiLLA SAI reduces polar bear extirpation risk more than a subtropical deployment for the same global temperature target due to more poleward-focused zonal temperature change profile. The effect size of HiLLA SAI on fasting season length is large compared to internal variability but in some regions is similar in magnitude to structural Earth system model differences. Uncertainties in the biophysical dynamic energy budget model used to calculate the survivable fast length from the bears' storage mass at fast initiation, the energy density of that storage mass, and the energy cost of lactation are also similar in magnitude to effect of HiLLA SAI. However, additional work is needed to improve understanding of pre-fast polar bear masses, reproductive costs, and possible adaptive foraging strategies during lengthy ice-free seasons to reduce total uncertainty in habitat suitability under any scenario of future Arctic change.

496035.title: The Subseasonal Connection between the Land Surface and Great Plains Low-Level Jet. Invited.
496035.authors: Francina Dominguez, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; Univ. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and S. Matus
496035.abstract: The central United States is among the world's most productive regions for agriculture and wind energy, both of which depend heavily on the Great Plains low-level jet (GPLLJ). The GPLLJ is the primary mechanism for atmospheric transport of momentum, energy, moisture, and scalars through the Central United States. We show that southern Great Plains soil moisture anomalies are a good predictor of GPLLJ activity at sub-seasonal timescales. Dry soil moisture conditions are associated with stronger jets, while wet conditions are associated with weaker jets. Soil moisture anomalies also drive a tendency for GPLLJs of similar intensity to persist across consecutive nights, revealing slower frequencies underlying GPLLJ variability. Temporal decomposition of the key variables associated with physical forcing mechanisms shows that dry sub-seasonal soil moisture anomalies intensify the GPLLJ via warmer near-surface temperatures, a deeper planetary boundary layer, and stronger geostrophic and ageostrophic winds — ultimately producing nocturnal supergeostrophic winds through enhanced buoyancy and the Blackadar inertial oscillation. These findings offer a pathway toward improved sub-seasonal prediction of GPLLJ activity and extreme precipitation in one of the world's most important agricultural regions.

496036.title: Using Bubble Backscatter Measurements from ADCPs to Investigate Bubble-Mediated Air-Sea Gas Exchange at Ocean Station Papa
496036.authors: Kee Onn Fong, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; PMEL, Seattle, WA; and D. Zhang, M. F. Cronin, A. Sutton, J. Thomson, and J. Yang
496036.abstract: Bubbles generated by breaking waves heavily influence air-sea gas transfer, sea-spray aerosols, ocean turbulence, and upper-ocean acoustics. However, a thorough understanding of the relationship between sea states and critical features of the bubble plumes (size distribution and penetration depth) is lacking. Sea-state variables that may influence the bubble plumes include wave heights, wave age, fetch, and wind-wave misalignment. Ocean observatories worldwide currently employ ADCPs to measure ocean currents. These ADCPs also record high frequency echograms, which can be used to infer bubble penetration depths - a new area of air-sea interaction research. Here we demonstrate that ADCP backscatter data can be used to extract information on bubble formation and penetration depths, as well as investigate the link between bubble backscatter measurements to co-located seawater pCO2 and ΔpCO2 and associated air-sea CO2 flux. This study will focus on data acquired from Ocean Station Papa (OSP), which has the most complete datasets for this analysis, including 1-Hz scientific echosounder ping data from a downward-looking Nortek Signature 500 ADCP mounted on the bridle (2 meters depth), burst-averaged data from an upward-looking Aquadopp ADCP mounted at 55 meters, a suite of meteorological data, seawater- and air-pCO2 measurements from a Moored Autonomous pCO2 (MAPCO2) system , a Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution direct covariance flux system, waves from a co-located WaveRider mooring (UW-APL collaboration), temperature, salinity and density profiles, underwater acoustics (UW-APL collaboration), and other data. Finally, we will also discuss proposed improvements to bubble measurements using ADCPs at Ocean Station Papa to further constrain the uncertainties in bubble sizes and gas fluxes from bubbles. This will improve and refine gas transfer velocities at high winds and wave states, enabling Ocean Station Papa to be a fully-equipped, all-season open-ocean observatory with the most comprehensive measurements for breaking-wave bubbles and air-sea gas exchange in all seasonal and wave conditions.

496038.title: Preliminary Testing of Satellite Radiance Data Assimilation In a Prototype MPAS-JEDI-Based Rapid Refresh Forecast System
496038.authors: Haidao Lin, GSL, Boulder, CO; and G. Ge, K. C. Eure, X. Zhang, H. Wang, M. Hu, and T. T. Ladwig
496038.abstract: The Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) is NOAA's next-generation regional convection-allowing ensemble forecast system in development for the National Weather Service. The RRFS, based on Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) and Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI), is being developed collaboratively by the Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) and the Office of Model Development (OMD) as well as the NOAA research labs and the broader research community. We have been testing satellite radiance data assimilation capability within a prototype of RRFS, starting from a 12-km CONUS domain with planned domain expansion. We are currently testing and evaluating data impact from Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS), Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS), Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), and Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer (IASI) with plan to include Advanced Microwave Sounding Unit-A (AMSU-A) and Microwave Humidity Sounder (MHS) data. We will exam the quality control and bias correction performance and explore all-sky radiance data assimilation for microwave data. The total radiance data impact as well as individual data impact from assimilation of radiance data sets are evaluated through a series of prototype RRFS retrospective runs. At the conference, we will present and report on the radiance data assimilation updates/status for RRFS as well as preliminary impact results from radiance data.

496041.title: FORMOSAT-7/COSMIC-2 Program Overview and Status
496041.abstract: Ronald Smilek1, Irfan Azeem Ph. D2 Office of Satellite and Product Operations (OSPO, Partner Missions Manager, NOAA/NESDIS, Suitland, MD., Office of Space Weather Observations (SWO), Division Chief, Science and Engineering, NOAA/NESDIS, Lanham MD The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has had a long partnership with the United States Space Force (USSF) and the Taiwan National Space Organization (TASA) for the operation and product generation for the COSMIC-2 space mission. The COSMIC-2 mission was launched on 6/25/2019, originally slated for a 5-year mission, officially met its operational design life as of June 2024 and continues to operate providing high-quality daily Radio Occultation and Ionospheric Soundings for atmospheric and space weather monitoring. FORMOSAT-7/COSMIC-2 is a 6-satellite constellation at varying levels of capability and mission life expectancy. This presentation will address the status of the constellation, program, data availability, and the near-term plans for the program from a NOAA perspective for sustaining and enhancing the scientific and operational value of COSMIC-2 data.

496046.title: Monitoring Extreme Precipitation Events with CMORPH2 Real-Time Product
496046.authors: Pingping Xie, NOAA/NWS/WPC, College Park, MD; and J. A. Nelson Jr., A. Jacobs, C. Dierking, Y. Li, E. Bower, S. Wu, and V. Kim
496046.abstract: The second-generation CPC Morphing (CMORPH2) is an objective technique developed at NOAA Weather Prediction Center (WPC) to produce high quality, high-resolution observational analysis of global precipitation through integrating information from satellite observations, gauge measurements, as well as numerical model simulations. A real-time CMORPH2 production system is constructed and migrated to an NCEP 24/7 operational environment (Computer Farm 3) to generate estimates of 30-minute precipitation on a 0.05olat/lon grid over the entire globe (90oS-90oN) at a very short production latency of ~ one hour. In addition to the total precipitation rate averaged over a 30-min time period, fraction of solid precipitation (snowfall) is also estimated based on the input satellite observations and the observed surface air temperature. Bias correction is conducted for the raw satellite precipitation estimates, through adjustment against the CPC daily gauge analysis over the global land and against the GPCP merged analysis of monthly precipitation analysis over the global ocean to ensure improved quantitative accuracy and long-term homogeneity. The real-time production started from the mid of 2017. Comparisons against gauge observations and radar estimates showed very good performance of the CMORPH2 satellite precipitation estimates in depicting and quantifying precipitation over various places of the globe and for all seasons. In particular, performance to capture and quantify cold season precipitation is much improved compared to its predecessor (CMORPH1). CMORPH2 is capable of tracking and quantifying heavy precipitation associated with extreme weather events (e.g. hurricanes, cyclones, atmospheric rivers), although it tends to underestimate the peak rainfall due to the limitations in the current generation input satellite observations. CMORPH2 is applied to examine precipitation variations associated with ENSO, MJO and other S2S variability over both land and ocean, and to verify precipitation fields generated by CORe and numerical forecast models. At the AMS Meetings, we will also report our recent results on enhancing the CMORPH2 short latency real-time production by injecting inputs from NOAA/NESDIS Direct Broadcast (DB) and from the MiRS precipitation retrievals from commercial (Tomorrow.io) small satellites.

496049.title: Characterizing the Environmental Setting of the New York State Mesonet Stations
496049.authors: Taylor Watts, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY; and J. Wang and N. Bain
496049.abstract: The New York State Mesonet (NYS Mesonet) is a statewide network of automated weather stations designed to provide high-resolution environmental observations across New York State. Maintaining consistent, well-characterized, and up-to-date station metadata is essential for producing reliable observations and interpreting spatial differences across the network. This study develops a quantitative method to semi-automatically characterize the environmental conditions surrounding NYS Mesonet stations using geographic information system (GIS) analyses of land cover and surface roughness. The method can be easily adapted for applications to other mesonets. A 5-km buffer was generated around each NYS Mesonet station using GIS to characterize the surrounding environment. Land-cover characteristics were evaluated using the 2024 National Land Cover Database (NLCD), allowing the composition and spatial distribution of land-cover classes surrounding each station to be quantified. GIS-based spatial analysis was used to identify and summarize the land-cover characteristics within each station buffer. To further characterize station exposure, each 5-km buffer was divided into four cardinal-direction sectors (north, east, south, and west). Land-cover classes within each sector were classified according to Davenport aerodynamic roughness categories, and the proportional representation of each roughness class was calculated. The two most prevalent roughness classes were then identified for each directional sector at each station. An example is given in the figure below for NYSM station White Face Mountain Base, NY (WFMB), showing the calculated Davenport classification and associated confidence estimates for each directional sector. Confidence was categorized as high, medium, or low based on the difference in proportional representation between the two most prevalent roughness classes, with larger differences indicating greater confidence in the dominant roughness classification. This analysis provides a standardized characterization of the physical environments surrounding NYS Mesonet stations and documents differences in station exposure across the network. By incorporating both land-cover composition and directional aerodynamic roughness through GIS-based spatial analysis, the approach provides a more detailed assessment of station surroundings and supports the evaluation of station representativeness. The semi-automated GIS workflow allows these characteristics to be consistently evaluated across a large network of stations while reducing the need for manual assessment of individual sites. These results provide an environmental baseline that can be used to support future assessments of station exposure, observation quality, and spatial variability in Mesonet measurements. Additional environmental datasets, including climate-region classifications, may be incorporated in future analyses to further evaluate relationships between station characteristics and observed meteorological patterns.

496053.title: The Development and Impact of an Anomalous 700-mb Jet during an Extreme Non-Convective Wind Event
496053.authors: Manan Mathur, South Dakota School of Mines and Technology, Rapid City, SD; and A. J. French and D. Clabo
496053.abstract: High winds associated with mid-latitude cyclones are quite common in the Northern Great Plains of the United States during the cold season, with wind gusts of 25 - 35 m s-1 often observed. During the early hours of 18 December 2025, an unusual and extreme high wind event produced widespread wind gusts over 40 m s-1 across western South Dakota with peak gusts reaching 45 m s-1 on the south side of Rapid City, SD. The strong winds caused numerous downed trees and widespread power outages and property damage. Record high wind gusts were recorded at the National Weather Service office in Rapid City, SD and at the Rapid City Regional Airport. The strong winds were associated with a mid-latitude cyclone that tracked from western British Columbia to northern Minnesota from 17-18 December. As the surface low crossed the Canadian Rockies, the minimum pressure decreased to 977 mb before rising and holding steady around 984 mb. Once the low re-developed east of the mountains, it encountered a strong baroclinic zone associated with Arctic high pressure centered over western Canada. As the low moved east, the Arctic air mass advanced south, strengthening the pressure gradient on the northwest side of the cyclone. This led to the pressure gradient increasing despite the minimum pressure of the surface low remaining steady at 984 mb. A similar evolution was observed at the 700 mb level where an initial closed low over western British Columbia filled and evolved into an open wave as it crossed the mountains. The low redeveloped further south in the lee of the mountains and maintained a minimum height of 270-273 dam throughout the event. As the low progressed eastward from the Rockies, a shortwave ridge developed to its west creating a strong pressure gradient on the west side of the low with an attendant 700-mb jet streak. Gridded analyses from the High Resolution Rapid Refresh forecast model and ERA5 reanalysis indicated peak wind speeds of 50-55 m s-1 occurred at 700 mb as this jet streak tracked through Montana into western South Dakota during the early morning of 18 December. Compared to a regional climatology of upper air observations, the 700-mb wind speeds were near or above record values, consistent with the extreme nature of this event. The track of the 700-mb jet correlated strongly with the highest surface wind gusts and modeled soundings suggest that air from 700 mb was likely mixing to the surface and contributing to these gusts. This study will analyze the synoptic and mesoscale processes that contributed to the exceptional 700-mb jet and surface wind gusts using ERA5 reanalysis and High Resolution Rapid Refresh model grids.

496054.title: Boundary Layer Impacts from Canopy Drag in Simulations of Bankhead National Forest
496054.authors: Brian J. Gaudet, PNNL, Richland, WA; and J. D. Fast, R. K. Rai, C. Kaul, and H. Liu
496054.abstract: The presence of a vegetative canopy in the lower portion of the Planetary Boundary Layer (PBL) can impact the vertical profiles of wind, turbulence, temperature, moisture, and scalars and their associated fluxes in ways that often cannot be adequately reproduced by the traditional Monin-Obukhov-based similarity theory used in standard mesoscale (~ few km grid spacing) models. Among the ways by which vegetation canopies can impact fluxes are leaf aerodynamic drag, transpiration, attenuation of solar radiation, and interaction with longwave radiation transfer. In general, these are height-dependent functions of vegetative properties over the canopy layer that cannot be fully captured through boundary conditions produced by, for example, a land surface model. In this study we perform mesoscale regional simulations around the recently established Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Bankhead National Forest (BNF) facility in northern Alabama as part of the Integrated Cloud, Land-Surface, & Aerosol System Study (ICLASS). We include cases across a range of stability and wind speed conditions beginning from June 2025. We apply the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model using the Mellor-Yamada-Nakanishi-Niino PBL parameterization with eddy diffusion mass flux (MYNN-EDMF), but with high vertical resolution and modified to include an embedded canopy drag parameterization from Shaw and Patton (2003). The parameterization uses an assumed profile of leaf area density (LAD) versus normalized canopy height for computation of the drag force, with canopy height itself derived from the 30-m Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) database for the region. We compare simulations with and without the presence of canopy drag against a suite of observations from the ARM instrumental suite, as well as additional tower measurements provided by Washington State University, which together provide uncommonly high resolution of mean state and turbulent variables from the surface layer up to canopy height and beyond. We show how canopy drag improves the wind speed profiles throughout the PBL in pre-dawn conditions for which the PBL height is shallow. The direct impact of canopy drag becomes weaker as the boundary layer deepens and becomes more convective, but larger local impacts can occur through the interactions of the PBL parameterization with the drag parameterization. We discuss how the canopy drag parameterization could be modified to improve the agreement of the model with observations.

496055.title: Real-Time Weather Data Needs of Emergency Management Officials in Illinois: A Prospective User-Needs Assessment for the Illinois 3D Mesonet
496055.authors: Liam E. Llewellyn, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and R. A. Portelli and T. W. Ford
496055.abstract: Emergency management officials (EMs) in Illinois face a diverse and intensifying range of weather hazards, from winter storms and extreme heat to dust storms and flash flooding, and they rely on real-time weather data to make protective action decisions. Starting in 2026, Illinois is expanding its 20-station Illinois Climate Network as part of the development of the Illinois 3D Mesonet, creating additional resources for emergency managers across the state to use during extreme weather events. Anchored in boundary spanning theory, which frames EMs as actors translating meteorological information at the interface between the National Weather Service and the communities they serve, the study examines how differing backgrounds, experience, and staffing for Illinois EMs shape their usage of weather information in their decision-making processes, currently, and in the context of the development of the Illinois 3D Mesonet. Using maximum variation sampling across all 8 IEMA-OHS regions, a minimum of 16 EMs will complete demographic surveys and semi-structured interviews analyzed through Phronetic Iterative Qualitative Data Analysis, a proven method when working under meteorological contexts. Preliminary findings will be presented, with results intended to inform Illinois 3D Mesonet design decisions before implementation commitments are made and to provide a replicable framework for other states developing mesonet programs.

496057.title: Do Weather Forecast Offices Systematically Differ In Tornado Damage Estimation? Evidence From A Fixed Effects Model Using NWS Damage Assessment Toolkit Data
496057.abstract: In an ideal world, there would be a system wide network of several millions of anemometers, monitored by a cadre of weather forecasters to actively and accurately record wind speeds in the case of a tornadic event to assign a rating. The actual system is an ex-poste survey of structures damaged by gusts through the efforts of surveyors and WRS 88D data. Damage paths and widths, survey points, and associated EF scale magnitudes are then uploaded to the National Weather Service NWS Damage Assessment Toolkit (DAT). The DAT is the primary database for structure-level tornado damage documentation for the NWS. Trained surveyors from Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) record the Damage Indicator (DI) type, Degree of Damage (DOD), EF intensity rating, and an estimated wind speed for each surveyed structure. This paper will assess whether there is a systematic difference in tornado magnitude reporting across WFOs. Because wind speed estimates come from a combination of observed structural damage via damage indicators and Doppler radar data rather than direct anemometer measurement. This line of inquiry is important because if the differences between WFOs explains residual variation in damage prediction error after controlling for building type, DOD, and EF rating , then that implies a systematic inter-office bias . This may call into question the reliability of any damage model based on POI data compiled on the DAT. This study addresses the following research question: after controlling for Damage Indicator and Degree of Damage, does WFO membership explain residual variation in expected damage prediction error across three independent storm survey datasets.

496058.title: Tropospheric Aerosols over the Western North Atlantic during the 2021–2022 winter ACTIVATE Deployment: Characterizing the Impact of Biomass Burning, Transport, and Wet Scavenging with High-Performance GEOS-Chem
496058.authors: Bo Zhang, National Institute of Aerospace / NASA LaRC, HAMPTON, VA; and H. Liu, G. Luo, R. H. Moore, L. Ziemba, R. A. Ferrare, A. Sorooshian, H. Choi, D. Painemal, H. Wang, M. A. Shook, A. J. Scarino, E. W. Lundgren, J. W. Hair, E. C. Crosbie, M. Fenn, T. Shingler, C. Hostetler, C. Gao, M. Kleb, F. Yu, R. C. Levy, M. A. Vaughan, G. S. Diskin, J. Nowak, J. P. DiGangi, and Y. Choi
496058.abstract: The western North Atlantic Ocean (WNAO) is a dynamically active continental outflow region influenced by North American pollution, marine emissions, and long-range transport. Rapid changes in circulation and meteorological conditions from early winter to early spring can strongly affect transport and wet scavenging, thus modifying aerosol composition over the WNAO. In this work, we conduct a modeling analysis of aerosols over the WNAO during the 5th deployment of NASA’s ACTIVATE aircraft mission, spanning December 2021–March 2022, using GEOS-Chem in its high-performance configuration (GCHP v14.7.0), driven by MERRA-2 meteorology. The objective is to better characterize the impact of biomass burning, transport, and wet scavenging on aerosol distribution and properties, as well as their evolution during winter-spring in the study domain. A set of simulation experiments was conducted at c90 resolution (~100 km) with updated anthropogenic emissions, biomass burning emission injection height, and wet scavenging treatment. Model results are evaluated against aircraft Aerosol Mass Spectrometer measurements of sulfate, nitrate, ammonium, and organic aerosols. The simulation results show persistent North American influence throughout the deployment, with strong land-to-ocean gradients in sulfate–nitrate–ammonium and organic aerosols. December and January are dominated by low-level continental outflow. Strong January precipitation offshore likely enhanced aerosol scavenging over the WNAO. February and March show a transition toward greater vertical extent with strong free-tropospheric aerosol layer enhancements, particularly for organic aerosols. Sea salt remains concentrated primarily within the marine boundary layer. These results indicate that WNAO evolved from a predominantly boundary-layer continental outflow regime in early winter toward a vertically deeper and more compositionally complex aerosol environment in early spring. Comparison with aircraft profiles confirms that continental outflow, vertical mixing, and wet scavenging jointly control simulated aerosol magnitude and vertical structure over the WNAO. Evaluations of model results with aerosol extinctions from aircraft HSRL-2 lidar and CALIPSO satellite and aerosol optical depths from MODIS and AERONET will also be discussed. Our GCHP simulation results suggest that improving aerosol wet scavenging and vertical transport remains a priority for better representation of WNAO aerosols.

496059.title: Understanding the Role of Surface Shear Stress Spatial Variability in the Atmospheric Boundary Layer (Invited Presentation)
496059.authors: Eric R. Pardyjak, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and A. Balantrapu and M. Calaf
496059.abstract: Traditionally, the atmospheric surface layer has been theoretically treated as statistically stationary and horizontally homogeneous. Recent studies, however, have shown that even under relatively ideal conditions, significant spatial and temporal variability can exist in surface-layer fluxes. While this variability is constrained by governing equations, it is rarely interpreted directly through those equations. Furthermore, uncertainty in field observations and gradient estimates can propagate in ways that can make results difficult to interpret. Here, we begin to investigate the physics of momentum-flux spatial variability using two complementary approaches: the velocity-vorticity equation, and the Green’s-function solution of the fluctuating-pressure Poisson equation, for an incompressible turbulent wall-bounded flow. We apply these frameworks to the field data from the 2019 Idealized Planar-Array Study for Quantifying Surface heterogeneity (IPAQS) field campaign conducted in Utah’s West Desert at the Surface Layer Turbulence and Environmental Science Test (SLTEST) at the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground. IPAQS revealed substantial spatial variability in momentum fluxes, providing an opportunity to examine how vorticity, Reynolds stresses, and large-scale motions interact to produce spatially organized stress fields and pressure perturbations. This analysis provides a physical foundation for interpreting the role of very-large scale motions (VLSMs) in the surface layer, and for designing future measurements that directly couple velocity, wall-shear stress, and wall-pressure observations. We conclude by discussing how this analysis is informing the design of the Rough-wall Amplification of Force fluctuations in Turbulent boundary layers or RAFT 2027 experiment, a new SLTEST field campaign focused on quantifying Reynolds number and surface roughness effects on wall-pressure and wall-shear-stress fluctuations in atmospheric surface layers.

496060.title: Automated Detection and Segmentation of Hailswaths Using Computer Vision for Building on the Canadian Hail Climatology
496060.authors: Tobias Schmidt, Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory, Western University, Canada, London, ON, Canada; and J. Biemans, C. Town, and J. Brimelow
496060.abstract: Hail causes on average $285 million USD worth of damage in Canada each year, with several hailstorms in the past 5 years alone making the top 10 list of costliest natural disasters in Canadian history. Despite this impact, the climatology of Canadian hailstorms is still not well established. The Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory’s (CSSL) Northern Hail Project has undertaken the initiative of supplementing the climatology’s missing gaps by using the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) dataset’s maximum estimated size of hail (MESH) product to identify hailswaths across Canada that are at least 40 km long and that have at least 2 adjacent pixels of 30 mm hail. When done manually, this is an arduous and subjective process to identify and characterize the thousands of hailswaths that have been detected by radar across the country in recent years. Consequently, the CSSL developed an automated solution using storm-based object detection built around computer vision (CV) and physical thresholding. To maintain dataset accuracy, a supporting graphical user interface (GUI), that allows for human editing of computer-identified swaths, was developed alongside the computer vision software. This complete CV-GUI system dubbed the “MESH Tracker” has reduced the work hours required for processing an average Canadian storm season’s worth of hailswath data by at least 50%. With such an increase in efficiently and subsequent decreased operation costs, the CSSL is now able to continually update the hailswath climatology in its regular day-to-day operations.

496063.title: Probabilistic Forecast of Tropical Cyclone-Driven Extreme Wave Heights
496063.authors: Ricardo Martins Campos, Lynker, College Park, MD; and A. Mehra, C. W. Landsea, D. Figurskey, P. Santos, H. S. Kim, R. Perez, and M. DeMaria
496063.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) / National Weather Service (NWS) / National Hurricane Center (NHC) issues tropical storm and hurricane wind speed probabilities based on its official forecast advisories. The Wind Speed Probability (WSP) model consists of a 1000-member ensemble produced by a Monte Carlo simulation that considers track and intensity forecast error distribution climatologies from the previous five years. It outputs incremental and cumulative probabilities out to 5 days of 34-, 50-, and 64-knot winds, as well as the earliest reasonable (and most likely) arrival times of 34-knot winds. Each of the 1000 ensemble member wind radii (starting with analysis time advisory radii that trends toward climatology with time) needed for the probability calculations is generated by a symmetric Rankine vortex model plus an asymmetry adjustment. The WSP model is currently being upgraded (WSP2.0) to include a more general surface wind model (based on a modified Rankine vortex algorithm with its size parameter fitted to the advisory forecast wind radii in time that is part of the Gridded Tropical Cyclone Forecast Advisory Message or GTCM). It includes a parametric land surface model to account for land induced wind reduction due to friction applied to all 1000 members. Furthermore, the Monte Carlo simulations in WSP2.0 will include dynamic track and intensity perturbations using a combination of real time ensemble and AI/machine learning input. While the wind speed probabilities have been a highly successful approach for wind speed information, it lacks the ocean wave component. In this study, we propose a new framework and methodology to incorporate wave height into the probabilistic forecast. The methodology consists of combining a parametric wave model with bias correction to generate wave fields for each ensemble member of WSP2.0, followed by a final AI/ML model in the probabilistic domain to output the probabilities of waves exceeding certain thresholds. For validation, bias correction, and AI/ML training, a large set of observations was processed, including wave buoys (NDBC, CDIP, Spotter, DWSD, and MicroSWIFT), satellite altimeters (CFOSAT, SARAL, CRYOSAT-2, HY-2B, JASON-3, SENTINEL-3A, SENTINEL-3B, SENTINEL-6A, and SWOT), saildrones (PMEL), and Wide Swath Radar Altimeters (WSRA) onboard P-3 airplanes. In total, this comprises a large dataset of 1.1 million records inside tropical cyclones, 718766 of which correspond to named hurricanes according to the IBTrACS database. The parametric wave model, PModel (Grossmann-Matheson et al., 2025), generates significant wave height (Hs) and peak wave period (Tp) using five input variables: maximum sustained wind speed (Vmax), velocity of forward movement of the cyclone (Vfm), radius of maximum winds (Rmax), radius of gale winds (R34), and position (latitude and longitude). These inputs are derived from the Monte Carlo simulation / WSPv2.0 used for the wind fields (GTCM). To assess the parametric wave model, a four-year reanalysis was produced and validated against observations, showing a large positive bias of 2.2 meters and RMSE of 2.7 meters. The post-processing bias correction combines two layers: a univariate linear bias correction using the Quantile Mapping Method, and a multivariate nonlinear AI/ML model which is currently under testing. Preliminary results show a reduction in Hs bias to 0.1 meters, and RMSE to 1.2 meters, with correlation coefficient of 0.7. The AI/ML modeling covers a broad range of experiments: (i) feature selection using recursive feature elimination (RFE); (ii) data normalization; (iii) model architecture selection, and (iv) hyperparameter optimization, including activation functions and structural complexity (number of layers and neurons). The dataset is divided into training, testing, and validation sets, covering 128 tropical cyclones from 2022 to 2025. The parametric wave model (PModel) and post-processing bias correction described are run for each ensemble member independently, producing the wave fields (Hs and Tp) for each cyclone and generating a probability density function (PDF) at each fixed grid point. The final step consists of an AI/ML model in the probabilistic domain, optimized using GridSearchCV with ROC AUC scoring. Rather than optimizing the wave height directly, this final step evaluates whether predefined thresholds were exceeded, thereby maximizing the True Positive Rate while minimizing the False Positive Rate. The model's performance is verified using statistical metrics such as CRPSS, BSS, POD, FAR, CSI, and ROC AUC, along with graphical assessments including rank histograms, ROC curves, and reliability diagrams. Beyond the extreme waves generated within tropical cyclones, large swells propagate outside the generation area and affect remote locations, as observed during Hurricanes Lee and Franklin (2023). To maintain the probabilistic approach while covering a larger domain impacted by these swells, the 31-member NOAA Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFSv12) was selected, which is also being bias-corrected following a similar methodology previously described. Following this approach, probabilities are provided for both the inner cyclonic areas and the surrounding swell-affected regions. The system is currently under development, with the first experimental operational version expected for the 2027 hurricane season.

496065.title: Adapting the GPT-2 Transformer Architecture for Radar-Based Hailstorm Nowcasting over Colorado and Wyoming
496065.authors: Chandrasekar Radhakrishnan, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and V. Chandrasekar and S. K. Biswas
496065.abstract: Timely and accurate nowcasting of hailstorms remains one of the most operationally demanding challenges in severe weather prediction, given the direct threat these events pose to life, infrastructure, and property. Radar extrapolation techniques and, more recently, deep-learning approaches have both become standard tools for short-term forecasting. However, generative architectures built on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) or diffusion processes carry a specific weakness: they are trained to minimize error across the full radar domain, and hail cores occupy only a tiny fraction of that domain. Consequently, these models tend to average or smooth away the very isolated, high-intensity signatures that define a hailstorm, leaving them structurally biased against the phenomenon they are meant to predict. To address this gap, the present study developed and validated an LLM-inspired nowcasting framework built around a Vector-Quantized Generative Adversarial Network (VQGAN) spatial tokenizer paired with an autoregressive transformer based on the Generative Pre-trained Transformer 2 (GPT-2) architecture, trained on tokenized radar sequences. This framework reformulates precipitation forecasting as a discrete, tokenized sequence-modeling problem, rather than as continuous pixel-wise regression. Forecast uncertainty is represented by sampling a categorical token distribution rather than through injected noise. As a result, extreme states such as hail cores are captured as distinct token classes and preserved in proportion to their true occurrence frequency, rather than smoothed away as outliers. Both the VQGAN and GPT-2 model were trained and evaluated using composite reflectivity data derived from the Next-Generation Radar (NEXRAD) network over the Colorado and Wyoming domain. Forecast skill was benchmarked against a Python-based implementation of the Short-Term Ensemble Prediction System (PySTEPS). Three verification frameworks were used: the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), the Structure-Amplitude-Location (SAL) decomposition, and object-based verification via a Combined Object Skill Score (COSS). Results show that the model's advantage over PySTEPS grows with storm intensity, becoming increasingly competitive at higher reflectivity thresholds (≥40 dBZ), the range most relevant to hail, and ultimately outperforming PySTEPS in that regime. SSIM analysis tells a similar story: the model achieves better skill scores than PySTEPS beyond the shortest lead times and maintains higher structural similarity from +110 to +150 minutes lead time, with the largest advantage at the ≥40 and ≥50 dBZ thresholds. SAL decomposition shows that the model is the more physically complete forecaster, maintaining near-zero Structure and Amplitude bias throughout the full 3-hour forecast window because it learns storm growth, merger, and new-cell initiation. The Combined Object Skill Score (COSS) confirms this pattern at the storm scale: the model outperforms PySTEPS at ≥40 dBZ and leads clearly at ≥50 dBZ thresholds, across nearly the entire forecast horizon. These results indicate that token-based generative nowcasting captures storm lifecycle and intensity evolution that pure Lagrangian extrapolation cannot represent. The largest performance gains occur precisely at the high-reflectivity thresholds most relevant to hail.

496068.title: Tracking Water Vapor from the 2022 Hunga Volcanic Eruption Using Satellite Data and the Schoeberl and Dessler Trajectory Model
496068.authors: Clare Harned, Smith College, Northampton, MA; and S. M. Davis, C. Maloney, E. Asher, and X. Wang
496068.abstract: The January 2022 submarine eruption of Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha’apai in the South Pacific injected more water vapor into the stratosphere than any other event in the satellite record. Hunga water vapor bypassed atmospheric barriers to reach a height of 58 km, increasing the stratospheric water vapor burden by 10%. In the years following the eruption, researchers have attempted to incorporate Hunga into atmospheric transport and climate models but have found that models with reasonable outputs under standard conditions struggle with Hunga water vapor. In this project we used the Hunga eruption as a case study to test transport and dehydration in the Schoeberl and Dessler trajectory model. We used water vapor measurements from the Stratospheric Water and OzOne Satellite Homogenized (SWOOSH) data set to initialize a Hunga plume in both February 2022 and March 2022 over the model’s background water vapor field. After running the model through 2025, we compared its water vapor time series to SWOOSH as well as an SD-WACCM run. We found that the trajectory model and SD-WACCM dehydrate the Hunga plume at remarkably similar rates, while the trajectory model allows for easy tracking of water vapor lost to supersaturation and to the tropospheric and mesospheric boundaries. With regards to transport, the trajectory model is not nearly as well-aligned with SWOOSH or WACCM; the vertical winds we derived from MERRA-2 heating rates carry the Hunga plume too high too quickly even in the first few months after the eruption. As a first attempt at correction, we normalized vertical winds to conserve mass at each pressure level, and the addition of this physical constraint led to better agreement in vertical transport between the model and satellite data. Ongoing work involves applying more nuanced corrections to the MERRA-2 wind fields to account for latitudinal differences while also looking at the impacts to model transport from transitioning to the ERA5 reanalysis product or a WACCM wind field output. With an improved trajectory model, we could more accurately assess the long-term stratospheric water vapor perturbation from Hunga and the possible contribution of Hunga-impacted air recirculated into the tropics. Additionally, by addressing the trajectory model’s transport issues, we may gain insight into how we can better use such low-computing cost tools for other trace gas and age of air studies.

496069.title: Connecting EPIC Innovation to the UFS Community Through Tools, Training, and Support
496069.authors: Keven Michael Blackman, NOAA, Bellevue, NE; and J. Vogt, C. Barone, A. C. Jones, L. Generosa, M. davis, J. Dodson, J. Wheeler, C. Seyb, J. Kublnick, P. Pillai, and M. Huang
496069.abstract: The Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC) works with the Unified Forecast System (UFS) community to accelerate innovation, streamline access to modeling tools and code, and enable broader community contributions. EPIC connects researchers, developers, forecasters, students, government, academia, and industry with the tools, training, information, and opportunities needed to develop, use, and contribute to the UFS. This presentation will demonstrate how EPIC’s community engagement strategies ensure its technical work reaches the people who can use it, provide feedback, and help drive continuous improvement. EPIC maintains active, open communication through the EPIC and UFS community portals, GitHub, social media, newsletters, workshops, and dedicated support channels. These engagement channels allow EPIC to share releases and resources while also learning what the community needs, where users are running into problems, and how outreach and support can be improved. The presentation will highlight examples of how EPIC introduces new capabilities, supports education and workforce development, connects users with technical experts, and creates opportunities for collaboration across the UFS community.
