Additionally, it will demonstrate how EPIC converts complex technical concepts into accessible training, documentation, and community resources. Attendees will leave with a better understanding of how EPIC keeps the UFS community informed, improves access to the UFS, strengthens feedback between users and developers, and helps community innovations reach wider use in NOAA’s operational forecasting systems.

496080.title: A Coupled Urban Canopy and Eddy-Diffusivity Mass-Flux Numerical Modelling Framework
496080.authors: Jean Carlos Pena, SUNY Albany, Albany, NY; and J. B. Olson, P. Ramamurthy, A. Martilli, and J. E. González-Cruz
496080.abstract: A numerical model which links a multi-layer urban canopy model and eddy-diffusivity mass-flux (EDMF) planetary boundary layer scheme is established. The goal of the EDMF-based framework is the improved coupling between urban boundary layer transport and cloud processes within Reynolds-Averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) weather models. The new model couples the NOAA Global Systems Laboratory developed Mellor-Yamada-Nakanishi-Niino EDMF (MYNN-EDMF) parametrization with the Building Effect Parametrization and Building Energy Model (BEP-BEM) schemes in the Weather Research and Forecasting Model (WRF). It is benchmarked against the urban Mellor-Yamada-Janic (MYJ) scheme, an eddy-diffusivity based model configuration widely used in mesoscale urban research. Both models are tested for Houston, Texas, a coastal city, using a real sea breeze thunderstorm case from the Department of Energy TRacking Aerosol Convection interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER). Results demonstrate that the new model matches the observed timing of rainfall patterns, with reasonable overprediction in total rainfall accumulations. Further investigation shows performance of the urban MYNN-EDMF model is tied to improvements in sea breeze front timing and interactions between the front and the city. MYNN-EDMF shows the front enhances urban heat island effects, which drives inland moisture transport and rainfall. The parametrization link shows a promising direction for future model development and representation of urban-driven weather hazards.

496082.title: Examining the Sensitivity of Tornadic Supercell Behavior on 27 April 2011 to the Background Environment Using Observation-Driven Simulations and MYRORRS Azimuthal Shear Analyses
496082.authors: Isabelle Jernigan, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and A. W. Lyza, M. D. Flournoy, and C. Davenport
496082.abstract: The prolific 27–28 April 2011 tornado outbreak produced multiple rounds of tornadic supercells in an exceptionally supportive environment. Previous work identified four distinct spatiotemporal regions within the outbreak, each characterized by small differences in thermodynamic and kinematic profiles, proximity to mesoscale boundaries, and storm initiation times. This study uses multiple radar-based and environmental observations to inform 25-member numerical ensembles of eight select supercells that formed in these regions. The simulations employ tendency nudging to gradually initiate convection and mesocyclone development at rates consistent with MRMS-based azimuthal shear (AzShear) analyses. Meanwhile, a base-state substitution technique continuously nudges the simulated environments towards observations, represented by Storm Prediction Center surface objective analysis (SFCOA) profiles. The resulting simulations are compared to AzShear analyses from the MYRORSS dataset and observed reflectivity fields to evaluate how much of the observed storm evolutions may have been dependent on the background mesoscale environment and assess the resulting predictability of the observed storm evolutions. The successful simulations mature comparatively quickly, but the degree to which they emulate their observed counterparts varies, with the most realistic simulated supercells corresponding to the northernmost-initiating storms in the highest-shear environments. The unsuccessful suites, in which ensembles could not sustain organized convection after the cessation of the heating tendencies, have less humid mid- and upper-tropospheres. Several external, mesoscale features absent from the simulations are identified as playing a critical role in maintaining observed storms in environments that failed to sustain organized, simulated convection. These findings highlight a reliance of tornadic supercells on inhomogeneous influences (terrain, cell interactions, etc) during the 27 April 2011 super outbreak, and the limited predictability of similar high-impact events in the future.

496084.title: The Relative Roles of Winds and Currents in Surface Wave Variability during Hurricane Erin
496084.authors: Ajin Cho, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and A. Williams, J. Davis, and B. Villas Boas
496084.abstract: Surface waves modulate momentum and energy exchange across the air–sea interface, yet their characteristics and influence on air–sea fluxes remain difficult to quantify, especially under extreme winds. Here, we investigate the relative roles of winds and currents in driving surface wave variability during Hurricane Erin (2025) using a combination of in situ observations and numerical simulations with the WAVEWATCH III (WW3) spectral wave model. The observations were collected during the Study on Air-Sea Coupling with WAves, Turbulence, and Clouds at High Winds (SASCWATCH) field campaign. SASCWATCH deployed a large array of 23 surface wave drifters that measured directional wave spectra, providing a unique opportunity to validate the model and examine the spatial variability of the wave field within and around Erin. Here, WW3 simulations with different wind and current forcing are evaluated against observations. We analyze the variability of bulk wave properties at spatial scales shorter than the tropical-cyclone scale. We also use numerical experiments to isolate the relative contributions of wind and current variability and to explore the mechanisms through which currents modify the wave field, including refraction, changes in wavenumber, and relative wind. Preliminary comparisons show broad agreement between model and observations and reveal substantial gradients over scales of approximately 10–100 km, arising from the combined spatial variability of winds and currents. These results provide insight into the processes controlling sea-state variability in tropical cyclones and their potential effects on air–sea fluxes and sea-state-dependent drag under extreme conditions.

496090.title: Aurora Chasers as Emerging Users of Space Weather Information
496090.authors: Tanya Melnik, Millersville University, Millersville, PA; Upper Midwest Aurora Chasers, Duluth, MN; University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN; and V. Ledvina and A. L. Williams
496090.abstract: The user community for space weather information is expanding beyond the professional and infrastructure sectors traditionally served by operational forecasting. Aurora chasers represent one such emerging user community. During Solar Cycle 25, public interest, access to real-time space weather data, improved cameras, social media, and citizen-science initiatives have increased public engagement with space weather. Chasers use this information to address a local question: whether, when, and where aurora may be visible, which can require interpreting conditions from the Sun to Earth. Aurora chasers form a global, decentralized community with varying levels of experience and space weather knowledge. Most have no formal training in space weather. However, some chasers develop expertise through self-directed learning and observations. Regional and global groups overlap across social media and dedicated forums. Online platforms often become places where forecasting, reporting, and informal education occur. The information needs of aurora chasers are unique and differ from those of industry-based operational users. Government agencies' space weather forecasts primarily address conditions and impacts for vulnerable infrastructure. Chasers instead use operational data to estimate local auroral visibility, supplementing space weather information with terrestrial weather forecasts, local viewing conditions, and previous experience. Experienced chasers often interpret space weather data for others. Regional expertise is common and based on repeated observation of how solar wind and geomagnetic conditions correspond to auroral visibility. Information flow is multidirectional. Forecasts and space weather data are used for chasing decisions, and community observations provide real-time information that can be used to update the guidance. Citizen-science projects also connect chasing with formal research. The decentralized and interconnected structure supports rapid information sharing but also results in variations in forecast interpretation. Forecast limitations and uncertainties may become less apparent when information is summarized or translated into lay language, particularly during major events with widespread media coverage. Differences between forecast expectations and real-life observations may affect confidence in future forecasts. Aurora chasing communities provide a setting for studying how nonspecialists interpret and communicate space weather information. Community discussions translate space weather data into aurora visibility, explain technical concepts, cover forecast limitations, and correct inaccurate or sensationalized information. Although not considered representative of the general public, most are members of the public rather than space weather professionals. Surveys of this population can examine preferences for communicating forecast timing, confidence, uncertainty, and conditional outcomes. These studies could inform communication with these emerging non-industry users and identify approaches for further evaluation with broader public audiences.

496093.title: Development of S4 and RFI algorithm for COSMIC-2 for STAR’s Space Weather Products
496093.authors: Bin Zhang, Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies, College Park, MD; and J. Zhou, Y. Chen, T. C. Liu, and X. Shao
496093.abstract: The ionosphere (60-1000 km) is highly sensitive to solar activities. During solar storms, the GNSS signals propagating through the ionosphere undergo significant degradations, manifesting as path delays and rapid fluctuations in Signal to Noise Ratio (SNR) and carrier phase. Quantifying these small-scale plasma density irregularities requires accurate monitoring of the SNR Scintillation index (S4) and the phase scintillation index (sigmaPhi). The six equatorial Constellation Observing System for Meteorology, Ionosphere, and Climate-2 (COSMIC-2) satellites are essential for capturing these space weather irregularities over the tropical regions. When on-board S4 measurements exceed a certain threshold, receivers trigger high rate (50Hz or higher) data collection. Effective ground-based processing of these measurements is critical to derive S4, sigmaPhi and geolocation parameters within required latency for space weather monitoring. Furthermore, separating natural ionospheric disturbances from artificial Radio Frequency Interference (RFI), resulting from ground-based GNSS jamming or spoofing, is a vital requirement. In this study, we developed integrated S4, SigmaPhi, and RFI algorithms for NOAA’s COSMIC-2 Space Weather products suite. The S4 geolocation and SigmaPhi algorithms require the calculation of the excess phase, the path delay caused by the ionosphere disturbance related to the straight GNSS-to-LEO signal path. Our processing pipeline utilizes Precise Orbital Determination (POD) of the COSMIC-2 and GNSS constellations, single-differencing for clock bias removal, and cycle slip correction for carrier phase, across data levels (Level 0 to Level 2). High-pass filters are applied to the excess phase and SNR data to calculate sigmaPhi and S4 at 1 Hz. These products, along with satellite position data, stored in netCDF files, are provided to Boston College’s bubble map algorithm as input for further S4 geolocation processing which uses a wave back-propagation algorithm. To quantify RFI, we implemented the RFI algorithm of Roberts et al. (2022), applying it to 1Hz POD antenna SNR observations in RINEX format. By analyzing the cross-correlation of SNR time series across different GNSS satellites within a sliding window, we established thresholds to successfully isolate artificial RFI events from natural ionosphere irregularities. These parameters are validated against CDAAC’s COSMIC-2 space weather products. We have successfully developed a robust end-to-end processing system for S4 and RFI, providing a scalable framework that will be extended for other RO missions.

496095.title: Reflections from the Radar: Educational Impacts of an Experiential Radar Meteorology Field Course
496095.authors: Chaehyeon Chelsea Nam, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and D. S. Chai, D. J. Bodine, and T. Y. Yu
496095.abstract: Field-based experiential learning provides opportunities for students to connect classroom concepts with authentic scientific practice, yet few studies have examined its implementation in radar meteorology. As part of a newly funded NSF Field Research in the Physical Sciences (FIRP) project, a two-week deployment of the University of Oklahoma Rapid Scan X-band Polarimetric Radar (RaXPol) was integrated into Florida State University's Radar Meteorology course. Students participated in all aspects of a research field campaign, including operational forecasting, scan strategy development, radar operation, data collection, collaborative decision-making, and team-based research projects based on observations collected during the deployment. This study investigates how participation in an authentic radar field campaign influences students' learning experiences, professional identity, and preparation for atmospheric science careers. A mixed-methods assessment combines surveys administered throughout the semester, structured reflection activities, performance-based course assessments, and semi-structured interviews to evaluate changes in students' confidence, motivation, radar knowledge, and perceptions of field-based learning. The study also examines how students describe the educational value of authentic operational responsibilities and collaborative field experiences. This poster presents preliminary findings from the first implementation of a field-integrated Radar Meteorology course. We focus on students' initial perceptions of authentic radar operations, emerging themes from reflective activities and interviews, and early evidence of changes in confidence, scientific identity, and engagement following the two-week field deployment.

496096.title: Spatial Patterns of African Easterly Waves and their Precipitation Structure in Northern Africa
496096.authors: Beatrice Kyeremateng, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA; and S. E. Zick
496096.abstract: African Easterly Waves (AEWs) are synoptic-scale weather systems influencing Northern Africa that travel from west-to-east on tracks along and to the north and south of the African Easterly Jet (AEJ). These waves are most active in the lower troposphere around 700-850 hPa. This study explores the spatial distribution of AEWs and their precipitation using the Tropical Easterly Waves Climatology and the Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG). First, a spatial filter is used to limit 2001-2021 tropical easterly waves to only waves over the northern Africa region. The resulting AEWs are then split into several categories based on the level of maximum vorticity (850 hPa, 700 hPa, or vertically collocated) and their location with respect to climatological AEJ latitude (15°N) during boreal summer (north vs. south). Overall, 700 hPa waves are the most frequent, followed by 850 hPa waves. Vertically collocated waves are the least frequent, reflecting the additional constraint of satisfying tracking criteria simultaneously across both vertical levels. Seasonally, northern waves peak earlier (July–August) with a sharper rise, while southern waves peak later (August–September) and rise to that peak frequency more gradually. The spatial distribution shows that 700 hPa AEWs initiate farther east, extending to about 51ºE, and propagate and/or initiate farther to the north to about 45ºN. The 850 hPa and vertically collocated AEWs have a similar spatial distribution but are fewer in number and generally initiate closer to the western Africa coastline. Additionally, 850 hPa waves are more prevalent to the north of the climatological AEJ (15°N), while 700 hPa waves are common on both the northern and southern sides of the AEJ. Next, precipitation composites are generated for the six wave types, and there is a clear distinction in precipitation patterns between the northern and southern track AEWs, with southern track AEWs producing precipitation along an elongated northeast-southwest axis and northern track waves producing very little precipitation near the wave center. The vertically collocated waves record the highest precipitation rates followed by the waves that maximize at the 850 hPa level and, finally, waves at the 700 hPa level. This study also applies shape metrics to assess the AEW precipitation structure at thresholds of 2 mm hr⁻¹ and 5 mm hr⁻¹. A Mann-Whitney U-test is used to identify significant differences among the 700 hPa, 850 hPa, and vertically collocated waves in terms of precipitation area, degree or precipitation closure around the wave center, and solidity of the precipitation shield. Similar to the composite analysis, the shape metric analysis indicates that vertically collocated waves produce higher precipitation rates over larger areas and more solid precipitation regions, suggesting that vertical alignment of the vorticity maxima leads to enhanced AEW-associated precipitation.

496098.title: A Hermite-Basis Framework for Estimating Extreme Surface Wind Distributions Across Space and Time
496098.authors: Muyu Ye, Brown University, Providence, RI; and M. C. Hell
496098.abstract: Ocean surface winds regulate exchanges of momentum, heat, and moisture between the ocean and atmosphere and are essential for characterizing boundary-layer processes and extreme events. However, time series observations from moorings and spatial observations from satellites are difficult to compare directly, particularly when evaluating extremes. Here we present a model for reconstructing surface wind probability density functions (PDFs) using an orthogonal Hermite expansion through the sixth mode. By representing higher-order PDF structure beyond mean and variance, the model uses skewness and kurtosis to estimate asymmetry and tails of the PDF. We apply the framework to time-varying PDFs of 1-minute Ocean Observatories Initiative mooring observations and 6-hour, 25-km gridded surface-wind analysis products. To enable comparison between space and time observations, we estimate the effective degrees of freedom using temporal and spatial decorrelation scales and constrain an area consistent with a 20-day sampling length of the mooring record. We then quantify their uncertainty using a moving-block bootstrapping. The model explains at least 90% of the variance across probability-density bins. The largest improvement over the Gaussian baseline occurs when the third, skewness-related mode is included, demonstrating the importance of asymmetric structure in surface-wind distributions. The model is most effective at reconstructing unimodal, near-Gaussian distributions to resolve extreme winds at the tails. This framework provides a consistent statistical foundation for comparing surface-wind products with different spatial and temporal sampling and for estimating extreme-wind probabilities.

496100.title: Quantifying Low-Level Jet Wind Speed Interactions from Tropical Cyclone Proximity to Semi-Permanent Subtropical High In the West Pacific Basin
496100.authors: Tan Duy Dao, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and C. C. Nam, C. Park, D. S. R. Park, K. Tsuboki, Y. Kang, T. Goo, M. M. Bell, and G. Lee
496100.abstract: The semi-permanent Western North Pacific Subtropical High (WNPSH) is generally known large-scale steering influence on tropical cyclone (TC) motion. Its proximity to a TC is not considered to enhance the jet wind speed through the pressure gradient between the high- and low-pressure systems. For midlatitude systems, large-scale flow can often be approximated by geostrophic balance, in which the horizontal pressure-gradient force is balanced by the Coriolis force. By modifying the surrounding pressure and geopotential-height gradients, the WNPSH helps shape the large-scale circulation and moisture-transport pathways affecting midlatitude weather systems. The associated low-level flow, including both geostrophic and ageostrophic components, can transport moisture and thereby influence the development, location, intensity, and evolution of precipitation. We hypothesize that TCs embedded in proximity of the subtropical high may also express the same effect via the enhancement of a low-level jet and conveyance of moisture. This framework is not applicable within the strongly curved circulation and pressure gradient of a tropical cyclone, where centripetal acceleration is non-negligible and gradient-wind balance is more appropriate. However, sufficiently far from the cyclone center, where flow curvature and frictional effects are weak, the environmental wind may be approximated using geostrophic balance. Therefore, examining the wind relationship between tropical cyclones and the subtropical high is important for assessing whether comparable interactions occur between midlatitude lows and subtropical highs. We assess this relationship using an ERA5-based climatological analysis of western North Pacific tropical cyclones from 2000 to 2026 and their separation from the WNPSH. The results show that greater TC–WNPSH proximity, corresponding to a smaller separation distance, is associated with stronger low-level jet winds in the corridor between the two systems. These wind variations are closely related to changes in the geostrophic wind and horizontal pressure-gradient force, suggesting that the strengthened inter-system pressure gradient contributes to low-level jet enhancement analogous to wind enhancement between neighboring synoptic-scale high- and low-pressure systems. Additionally, this interaction was documented through intensive vertical-profile measurements collected during two field campaigns: the joint multinational PRECIP/TPARC-II/TAHOPE/KPOP campaign, which observed TC Aere (2022), a sheared weak depression, and the KPOP-MS campaign, which observed TC Dolphin (2026), a mature and large typhoon. This study quantifies the role of TC–WNPSH interactions in strengthening low-level jet flows and uses observations from two prominent TC cases to validate the results and clarify the underlying physical mechanism. This study will also examine whether the TC–WNPSH interaction can create favorable circulation pathways for the efficient transport of TC-derived moisture, thereby enhancing potential for downstream precipitation events.

496107.title: Resolving Crustal Conductivity Structure to Improve Geoelectric Hazard Estimates in the Eastern United States
496107.authors: Dana Peterson, USGS, Denver, CO; and P. Bedrosian, J. Crosbie, K. Getty, J. J. Love, and A. Kelbert
496107.abstract: Geomagnetically induced currents pose a substantial risk to bulk electric system power-transmission infrastructure in the eastern United States, where storm-time geoelectric fields are amplified and strongly polarized by regional conductivity structure. Historical storm damage to communication and power infrastructure occurs predominantly in the northeastern U.S., where peak geoelectric fields — including during the March 1989 storm — are estimated to have exceeded NERC benchmark values. Century-scale exceedance statistics derived from multiple storms similarly indicate high field intensities extending from Georgia to Maine. These regional estimates are underpinned by long-period magnetotelluric (MT) data from the 2006–2024 USMTArray. However, the USMTArray site spacing of 70 km and period range limit resolution of crustal structures that may control local field amplitude and direction. Since 2025, the USGS has acquired wideband MT data at approximately 35-km spacing at more than 270 sites across Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland, and Delaware, with additional coverage in Ohio, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. These measurements provide improved sensitivity to crustal resistivity structure but introduce substantial processing challenges in the densely developed eastern corridor. Near-field contamination from cathodic-protection systems on pipelines affects most sites; template subtraction has reduced this noise at many locations, whereas approximately 10% of stations require relocation because of severe cultural distortion. We use these new data to construct a high-resolution, three-dimensional resistivity model and evaluate how conductivity structure and static-shift distortion influence modeled geoelectric fields for representative geomagnetic-storm scenarios. Results will quantify the spatial variability and polarization of storm-time fields, identify locations where long-period data may inadequately represent subsurface resistivity structure, and support refined extreme-event geoelectric-hazard maps for the eastern United States.

496112.title: From Seeds to Satellites: Building Partnerships in the National Ozone Garden Network
496112.authors: Julie S. Malmberg, UCAR, BOULDER, CO; and B. Hatheway, D. Lombardozzi, E. Wright, M. Dussault, D. Elakara, K. Wolfson, K. Reed, M. Pippin, and L. Trainer
496112.abstract: The National Ozone Garden Network connects communities across the country through hands-on, place-based science education centered on ground-level ozone. Ozone damage appears as leaf stippling on bioindicator plants, making an invisible pollutant visible to community members in the gardens. Now encompassing over 45 gardens nationwide, the National Ozone Garden Network partners with a wide range of hosts, including science museums, art museums, botanic gardens, schools, nature centers, community organizations, universities, and National Parks, to establish gardens as living demonstrations of air quality science in publicly accessible spaces. The network began over 10 years ago and its growth has been supported through funding from NASA TEAM II, connections with the NASA TEMPO mission, and the supply of ozone-sensitive seeds cultivated by the USDA. A team from the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research Center for Science Education, the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, Colorado State University, NASA Langley, and Trainer Evaluation lead the network and support gardens around the country with seeds, educational resources, scientific information, and community-building activities to create connections between ground-based community-based observations, ozone sensors, and space-based atmospheric monitoring. Central to the network's model is the training and facilitation support provided to host sites, many of which have no prior background in atmospheric science and rely on the network to translate ozone science into approachable, teachable content. Supported garden hosts participate in a facilitated workshop that introduces the science behind ozone bioindicator gardens and equips them with ready-to-use interactive materials designed to be delivered by educators, docents, or volunteers with varying levels of science background. This approach lowers the barrier to entry for hosting a garden. Sites do not need existing expertise in atmospheric science or gardening to participate meaningfully, only a willingness to maintain a small garden plot and engage visitors with the provided materials. The training model also emphasizes flexibility, allowing hosts to adapt the core content to their own audiences, whether that means a formal classroom lesson, a drop-in museum activity, or an interpretive stop along a park trail. This presentation will share how the National Ozone Garden Network builds and sustains these community partnerships, from initial host recruitment and garden establishment through this facilitation and training pipeline, and the ongoing support that keeps each site active as a local science communication hub. We will highlight the variety of host sites and the varied ways communities use their gardens and training materials, along with lessons learned in scaling a distributed, community-driven network across such different institutional contexts. We will also discuss strategies for supporting host capacity long after initial onboarding, keeping facilitation materials current and accessible, and fostering a shared sense of ownership among partners who bring their own local expertise and audiences to the work. This session will offer takeaways for other informal science education programs interested in building similar low-barrier, high-impact federal-community partnership models.

496113.title: The Atmospheric Sounding Processing ENvironment (ASPEN) Software: Quality Control, Visualization, and Encoding for Dropsondes
496113.authors: Isabel Suhr, NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO
496113.abstract: ASPEN (the Atmospheric Sounding Processing ENvironment) is the data quality control software package that is part of the software suite supporting NSF NCAR Earth Observing Laboratory research dropsonde system. Within ASPEN, users can view sonde data, apply and check various quality control filters, graph data in XY or skew-T form, derive mandatory and significant levels, and code output data in BUFR for transmission to operational modeling centers. Recent development efforts in ASPEN have focused on interoperability with AVAPS Control Software, the next generation dropsonde control software, which allows for more complete metadata, additional quality control checks from new data sources, and further refinement to support the NRD41 dropsonde. ASPEN development is ongoing, primarily to support its operational use by the NOAA and Air Force Hurricane Hunters, though it is also used for operations and research throughout the US and internationally. With limited resources, developers must balance feature requests, bug reports, and sponsor compliance requirements with general modernization and software best practices. To maximize effectiveness, developers are currently working toward comprehensive test and build automation, an extended test suite, and robust static analysis. This paper is an overview of current features and applications and future developments. More information about ASPEN can be found online at https://www.eol.ucar.edu/software/aspen.

496119.title: 'Using SAR to Better Identify Tornado Tracks from the March 14th, 2025 Midwestern U.S. Outbreak'
496119.authors: Morgan Fellows, Vermont State University Lyndon, Lyndonville, VT; and K. Tran, B. Osmanoglu, and J. Dechow
496119.abstract: Major tornado outbreaks, consisting of at least six tornadoes spawned from the same weather system in less than 24 hours, require accurate damage assessments to support hazard analysis and improve understanding of tornado impacts. Current damage assessments rely on radar observations, eyewitness accounts, and documented damage, while the potential of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) to provide observations in all weather conditions remains underutilized. This study explores the use of Sentinel-1A SAR backscatter intensity differencing in identifying tornado tracks associated with the March 14, 2025 tornado outbreak in the Midwestern United States. Out of the twelve tornadoes analyzed within the St. Louis County warning area, two tornado tracks were successfully identified using differences in backscatter signals. These tornadoes were the highest-rated events (EF-3) and occurred in areas of limited human habitation. The remaining ten tornadoes, which were EF-2 or weaker and primarily located in more populated regions, were not clearly identifiable from the SAR data. This result demonstrates the potential for SAR to complement traditional tornado damage assessment methods by providing observations regardless of cloud cover or weather conditions. Incorporating SAR into post-event assessments could improve damage characterization, particularly in areas where traditional observations are limited.

496121.title: Observations and Realistic Modeling of Convection-Generated Gravity Waves and Breaking during the CGWAVES Field Campaign
496121.authors: Christopher G. Kruse, NCAR, Broomfield, CO; NSF NCAR, Broomfield, CO; and D. C. Fritts, D. S. Nolan, B. P. Williams, T. S. Lund, Y. Dai, J. A. Guerrero, and L. Hoffmann
496121.abstract: Deep, moist convection generates gravity waves (GWs) that propagate upward, transporting momentum and energy that get deposited where these waves break. This process is parameterized in deep climate models, but has become relevant to numerical weather prediction (NWP) models with their increase in depth to z ~ 80 km. Most state-of-the-science NWP models now include some representation of these processes, but these parameterizations are still very crude. Additionally, observations at altitudes where these waves are predicted to break and have significant impacts on medium-range weather prediction time scales and longer are extremely sparse, limiting confidence in applicability of theory and parameterizations implemented in NWP models. The Convective Gravity Waves in the Stratosphere (CGWaveS) field campaign recently took place 20 May to 14 June 2025, utilizing the NSF NCAR Gulfstream V research aircraft to observe GWs generated by intense midwestern convection. The GV was instrumented with vertical and forward-looking lidars sensing temperatures from z ~ 25 - 65 km and sodium densities in the sodium layer from z ~ 70 - 95 km. Additionally, three OH layer imagers were deployed to observe GWs present in the OH layer at z ~ 87 km, providing 2-D GW observations from an ~900 km cross-track swath. Ninety hours over 13 flights were flown, traveling ~44,500 miles while sampling radially from organized convection over much of the contiguous US. Preliminary results are presented, with observations showing GWs in the stratosphere and mesosphere from great plains convection. Events are recreated in a deep, realistic version of WRF developed here, which is forced by weather radar observations using machine learning to emulate a microphysics parameterization given radar observations as input. This custom deep WRF configuration is validated against lidar observations and AIRS satellite observations. These validated simulations reveal convection can generate GWs with amplitudes large enough to break at altitudes relevant to NWP (i.e. below z ~ 60 km) when propagating in any direction. Lidar observations and simulations highlight that not all GWs are visible to the satellite-borne AIRS observations. These data and analyses will inform future physical updates and tunings for convective GW parameterizations.

496122.title: State of the Art in Lightning Forecasting: A Systematic Review on Lightning Predictions Systems
496122.abstract: Lightning strikes present severe operational hazards to aviation, microgrids, open-air mining, power grids, and emergency wildfire management, making timely and accurate prediction useful for public safety and decision support. Traditional operational workflows have historically relied on thermodynamic parameters from Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models or empirical weather radar reflectivity thresholds. However, the highly localized, transient, and non-linear nature of lightning genesis makes exact spatial and temporal forecasting exceptionally difficult. Recently, the weather enterprise has experienced a paradigm shift along the Research to Operations (R2O) pipeline toward data-driven, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) methodologies. To synthesize these rapid advancements, this study presents a systematic review using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to analyze the current landscape of lightning prediction models, forecasting horizons, predictands, data sources, and operational utility. Following PRISMA protocols, we systematically evaluated a rigorous collection of over 30 peer-reviewed research papers documenting lightning forecasting systems. Each study was analyzed across six primary operational dimensions: (1) the prediction methodology, ranging from parameterized empirical physics equations to state-of-the-art AI/ML architectures; (2) the forecast horizon, covering nowcasts (0–6 hours) to strategic medium-range models (1–4 days); (3) the forecast type, distinguishing binary probability of occurrence from quantitative event/intensity estimation; (4) the targeted physical phenomenon, focusing on cloud-to-ground (CG), intra-cloud (IC), or total lightning; (5) the geographical and spatial domain, evaluating local airport/site models versus contiguous country-wide domains; and (6) multi-modal data source integration, including lightning location systems (LLS), weather radars, satellite sensors, electric field meters, and surface features. Our systematic synthesis reveals several insights across the R2O pipeline. We verified that robust forecasting relies on fusing heterogeneous datasets to compensate for individual sensor limitations. Operational networks increasingly couple ground-based LLS (e.g., NLDN, GLD360, JLLN) with geostationary satellites (e.g., GOES Advanced Baseline Imager/Geostationary Lightning Mapper) and weather radars. While LLS and radar reflectivity (such as vertically integrated liquid [VIL] and vertically integrated ice [VII]) capture active, mixed-phase convective structures, satellite infrared channels detect cloud-top glaciation and convective initiation earlier than radar. Additionally, the incorporation of electric field meters (FMs) and digital elevation models (DEM) has significantly enhanced model performance in localized, complex terrains. The review documents a transition from classical statistical classifiers (e.g., Random Forests, XGBoost, Support Vector Machines) to spatiotemporal deep learning models. While tree-based classifiers excel at local meteorological feature-ranking (identifying precipitation rates, CAPE, and temperature profiles as primary predictors), advanced neural networks treat forecasting as a spatiotemporal video prediction task. Architectures like 3D U-Nets, Convolutional LSTMs (ConvLSTM), PredRNN, and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are now used to map the continuous initiation, development, deformation, merging, and dissipation of lightning cells. Because lightning is spatially and temporally sparse, models suffer from severe class imbalance, with a preponderance in the lightning absence class. The review highlights innovative solutions, including self-supervised pre-training, neighborhood diffusion methods, and customized loss formulations that penalize models based on proximity to true lightning events, reducing false alarm rates. Operational requirements bifurcate studies into tactical nowcasts (0–2 hours at 5-to-10 minute resolutions), focusing on predicting the onset of the first CG flash for site-specific safety, versus strategic medium-range planning (24–96 hours), translating global forecast system (GFS) data into lightning probabilities. This review highlights how the fusion of high-resolution lightning datasets and AI/ML tools directly benefits real-world operations. However, challenges remain regarding regional model portability, particularly when models trained on flat regions encounter complex mountainous terrain or wind farms. In conclusion, our PRISMA review demonstrates that data-driven AI/ML models represent a effective, computationally efficient, and scientifically robust path forward, bridging the gap between basic atmospheric research and critical operational decision-making in the public and private weather sectors.

496123.title: Contrasting Spatial Patterns of Lightning Activity around Columbus, Ohio, and Omaha, Nebraska
496123.authors: Ruixuan Ding, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; The Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH; and S. M. Quiring
496123.abstract: Urban areas have been associated with changes in convective activity, including enhanced lightning in areas surrounding and downwind of cities. However, the magnitude and spatial structure of these patterns can vary substantially among metropolitan areas and regional environmental settings. This study uses cloud-to-ground (CG) and could-to-cloud (IC) lightning observations as proxies for convective activity to examine the spatial and temporal variability of lightning around Columbus, Ohio, and Omaha, Nebraska, from 2005 to 2015. The area surrounding each metropolitan region was divided into nine sectors to compare seasonal variability, long-term trends, and spatial differences in lightning activity. Results showed distinct patterns between the two cities. Columbus exhibited an overall increase in lightning activity during the study period, however, Omaha had greater spatial heterogeneity, with contrasting trends among sectors. Significant spatial differences in lightning activity were also identified within both metropolitan areas. In Columbus, greater lightning activity occurred in the southwestern sector, while Omaha showed higher activity primarily in the southern and southeastern sectors. Lightning activity in both metropolitan areas was strongly concentrated during the warm season. These directional differences were further examined in the context of large-scale environmental conditions, including boundary layer height and convective available potential energy. The results demonstrate that lightning variability surrounding Midwestern metropolitan areas is highly localized and differs substantially between cities. Rather than indicating a uniform urban-related lightning response, the findings highlight the importance of regional environmental conditions and spatial heterogeneity when interpreting convective activity around metropolitan areas.

496124.title: Evaluating MPAS-Based RRFS Forecasts using METplus
496124.authors: Michael J. Kavulich Jr., NSF-NCAR, DTC, Boulder, CO; and K. M. Newman, M. A. Harrold, C. Evans, D. Dowell, G. Ketefian, J. Beck, and W. Mayfield
496124.abstract: In January 2026, National Weather Service (NWS) leadership announced a “moonshot” initiative to use the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) as an operational, 3-km resolution global numerical weather prediction (NWP) model, informing the operational predictions of NWS forecasters. Steps towards making this goal a reality have already begun, with multiple experimental forecast products based on the atmospheric component of MPAS (MPAS-A) being developed and run at NOAA labs, including the Global Systems Laboratory (GSL) and National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL). The Developmental Testbed Center (DTC) supports and develops the enhanced Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) to evaluate the performance of multiple types of NWP model output, including MPAS. In this presentation, we will show verification results for a number of experimental forecasts based on the MPAS dynamical core, including ensemble systems containing MPAS members. The focus of our evaluation will be on the performance of these MPAS-based prototypes for high-impact events during 2026, specifically severe weather outbreaks during the Hazardous Weather Testbed Spring Forecasting Experiment (HWT-SFE). We will also compare the performance of these experimental products to the newly operational RRFS Ensemble System (REFS), and highlight differences in performance among these products. The evaluation will focus on probabilistic verification methods such as Neighborhood Ensemble Probability (NEP), Neighborhood Maximum Ensemble Probability (NMEP), and the newly implemented Ensemble Agreement Scale (EAS) metrics within METplus.

496125.title: Intersections of Agricultural and Urban Air Masses Around Eastern North American Cities and Their Impacts on Particulate Ammonium Nitrate Formation in the Summertime
496125.authors: Ann Middlebrook, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and S. Albertin, A. Piasecki, E. R. Lill, I. B. Pollack, J. R. Roscioli, E. V. Fischer, J. Crounse, K. Ball, P. O. Wennberg, R. Weber, M. Mohan, X. Luo, M. A. Robinson, A. Rollins, E. Waxman, K. Zuraski, C. Womack, W. S. Chace, S. S. Brown, and T. AEROMMA Science Team
496125.abstract: Ambient concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) continue to decrease overall across the United States with individual chemical species exhibiting distinct seasonal and interannual trends. Particulate nitrate is decreasing in most areas, but not as fast as official emission inventories predict for nitrogen oxides (NOx). This discrepancy may exist because current inventories mainly focus on cities and industry, missing or underestimating agricultural soil emissions. NOx emissions from both sources oxidize in the atmosphere to produce gaseous nitric acid (HNO3), the main precursor of particulate nitrate as ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3). Gaseous ammonia (NH3), the other NH4NO3 precursor, is directly emitted into the atmosphere by agricultural sources and to a lesser extent by cities. Thus, the classic mixture of urban and agricultural air masses can often result in particulate NH4NO3 formation. While this is well documented in agricultural regions and the Los Angeles basin during summer, as well as in select regions during winter, its persistence under diverse conditions warrants further study. Here, we analyze specific cases of intersecting agricultural and urban air masses surrounding four major metropolitan areas (Chicago, Indianapolis, Toronto, and New York City), that were sampled during a recent airborne field campaign. In addition to meteorological controls, the relative amounts of gas phase precursors dictate whether or not NH3 and HNO3 can partition into the condensed phase across all four domains. Furthermore, increasing total particulate mass was often correlated with increasing mass fraction of NH4NO3. We discuss these aircraft observations downwind of urban areas, examining the gas-to-particle partitioning of HNO3 and NH3 despite elevated summertime temperatures and exploring photochemical production on HNO3 from NOx on the timescales of the observations.

496127.title: Physics-Based Retrieval of Total Column Water Vapor for the GeoXO 0.91 μm Band: Preliminary Results and Validation
496127.authors: Katurah Zahler, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and S. D. Miller and J. M. Haynes
496127.abstract: The next generation of National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) geostationary satellites, designated Geostationary Extended Observations (GeoXO), will include a new imager called the GeoXO Imager (GXI). GXI will have a number of advantages over the current Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), including increased spatial resolution in several channels, and the addition of two new channels designed for water vapor applications. These new channels have wavelengths centered near 0.91 and 5.15 µm. The 0.91 µm near-infrared channel is sensitive to absorption of reflected sunlight by atmospheric water vapor, enabling high-spatial-resolution daytime retrievals of total column water vapor (TCWV). This study presents the initial development of a physics-based TCWV retrieval algorithm using Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) observations over the U.S. Great Plains. MODIS bands centered near 0.905 and 0.86 µm are used as proxies for the future GXI bands. The retrieval uses the relationship between water vapor transmittance (WVT), defined as the ratio of 0.91 to 0.86 µm reflectance, and TCWV. To isolate the atmospheric contribution, a “dry atmosphere” surface albedo (i.e., the surface albedo that would be observed in the absence of atmospheric water vapor) is estimated by extrapolating a fit between WVT and TCWV to very small values of TCWV. The use of the “dry atmosphere” surface albedo serves as a key constraint in the retrieval by reducing errors associated with heterogeneous land surfaces. The influence of soil moisture and seasonal variations in atmospheric moisture on retrieval performance will also be explored. Preliminary results demonstrate the ability of the algorithm to capture the spatial distribution of TCWV. Initial validation using surface-based microwave radiometer observations within the study region shows encouraging agreement, supporting the physical basis of the retrieval. Using results from the central U.S. Great Plains, we compare our retrieval to independent measurements of TCWV, revealing systematic biases associated with high atmospheric moisture, varying viewing geometry, and retrievals near cloud edges. Ongoing analyses are also investigating the influence of anisotropic surface properties on retrieval performance.

496131.title: Operational Use of National Weather Service FIM Services: Assessing Flood Impacts
496131.authors: David C. Smith, NWS, Northport, AL; NWS, Tuscaloosa, AL
496131.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) is transforming flood forecasting through the operational integration of Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM) services. The Office of Water Prediction Operations Division serves as the focal point for all NWS flood warning operations, providing reachback support for interpretation and FIM Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS). River Forecast Centers (RFCs) work collaboratively with the NWC to provide that support and to add regional hydrologic expertise. Weather Forecast Offices (WFOs) refine the associated FIM messaging based on local knowledge of terrain, infrastructure, and sensitive areas, as well as prior experience while simultaneously delivering that critical messaging to regional, state, and local emergency managers and officials all in an effort to protect life and property. A core component of this workflow is the rigorous, comprehensive Flood Impact Assessment. By utilizing web-based collaborative platforms, NWC and RFC hydrologists and WFO forecasters perform near real-time assessment of forecast inundation extents against ground-truth data. Real-time stream gauge observations and emergency management reports reports help link the inundation extents to actual ground conditions.Benchmark data such as hydraulic FIMs and highwater marks derived or observed by partners such as USGS, FEMA, and USACE to identify potential flooding impacts to homes, roads, and critical infrastructure.

496133.title: Impacts of North Pacific Atmospheric River Reconnaissance Observations on Forecasts of High-Impact Weather over the Eastern United States: A Case Study
496133.authors: Benjamin J. Moore, SIO, La Jolla, CA; Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA
496133.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) can influence the dynamics and predictability of the large-scale midlatitude flow when they supply moist air to coherent, deeply ascending airstreams, known as warm conveyor belts (WCBs), in a cyclone warm sector. Moist-diabatic processes tied to latent heat release within the WCB can amplify Rossby wave patterns far downstream, potentially leading to high-impact weather. Growth of forecast errors linked to this amplification can lead to reduced medium-range forecast skill. Here, we test the hypothesis that reducing model initial-condition errors through assimilation of observations over the North Pacific from AR Reconnaissance (AR Recon) improves medium-range forecasts of high-impact weather over the central and eastern United States. We focus on a case from mid-February 2025 in which ridge amplification linked to a strong AR–WCB interaction over the eastern North Pacific drove the downstream development of a cyclone and accompanying AR that produced a severe weather outbreak and widespread flood-producing rainfall across the southeastern United States. The North Pacific AR in question was sampled by three successive AR Recon Intensive Observation Periods (IOPs) during 14–16 February, enabling a systematic evaluation of the impacts of both dropsonde and airborne radio occultation (ARO) observations on forecasts of the downstream weather. A set of data-denial forecast experiments, in which specific observation types are withheld from assimilation, are compared against a control experiment (assimilating all observations) to isolate the forecast impacts of dropsonde data, ARO data, and both types together. We assess how denial of each observation type affects the initial condition errors, and use a Lagrangian air-parcel trajectory framework to examine how these errors affect the forecast of the AR–WCB interaction and concomitant moist-diabatic processes. Potential vorticity diagnostics are then applied to track the growth and downstream propagation of errors within the Rossby wave pattern over the United States. Finally, preliminary findings of a long-term (1960–2025) climatological analysis of AR–WCB interactions are briefly presented to place these case-study results into broader context.

496135.title: Tracking Cold Pool Outflows, Sea-Breeze Fronts, and Convective Initiation During the DOE ARM TRACER Field Deployment
496135.authors: Gabriella "Sy" Sosa Medina, State University of New York at Oswego, Oswego, NY; and E. Caldon, M. P. Jensen, and A. J. Drager
496135.abstract: Convective initiation along air mass boundaries, such as cold pools generated by convective storms, occurs due to the wedging of cold air beneath warmer environmental air, lifting this warmer air high enough to initiate cloud and storm development—however, storm initiation is not guaranteed to occur. The exact parameters that dictate the success or failure of these initiation mechanisms remain unquantified, in part due to the challenge of identifying air mass boundaries in meteorological data. This identification is further complicated in coastal environments where sea-breeze dynamics are present. This study aims to develop methods to detect cold-pool and sea-breeze fronts to enable comprehensive analysis of boundary locations, collision interactions, and thunderstorm initiation events, moving toward a longer-term goal of assessing numerical models’ ability to simulate real-world events. The Department of Energy (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) TRacking Aerosol Convection interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER) collected unique measurements of convective storms in the coastal environment of Southeast Texas, providing a comprehensive observational dataset useful for developing multifarious maps from which boundaries might be identified by hand. Case study dates were selected based on the presence of widespread, discrete convective cells, sea-breeze circulations, and significant data availability from TRACER. Frontal boundaries and convective initiation events are identified via maps of both observed data (e.g. XSACR, NEXRAD, GOES, in-situ observations) and corresponding model data from high-resolution simulations (Δx ~ 100 m in the innermost nest) performed using the Regional Atmospheric Modeling System (RAMS) with a configuration adapted from the TRACER Model Intercomparison Project (TRACER-MIP). We focus on near-surface meteorological parameters such as temperature, wind speed, wind direction, and specific humidity, along with observed and simulated radar and satellite imagery. These maps are then uploaded into a novel web-based application—the Meteorological and Environmental Tool for Graphical Object Annotation and Tracking (METGOAT)—to manually track storm, cold-pool, and sea-breeze boundaries. When identifying observed versus simulated boundaries, different sets of meteorological parameters prove useful—this also applies for identification of cold-pool versus sea-breeze fronts. Visualizations of reflectivity and wind direction, respectively, provide the most helpful insight for observed and simulated cold pool boundaries. Meanwhile, visualizations of visible satellite imagery and specific humidity prove the most reliable for identifying observed and simulated sea-breeze fronts, respectively. These methods will form the basis for a future model-observation comparison investigating collision dynamics and convective initiation processes.

496142.title: International Collaboration Through the Regional Focus Group of the Americas and the Caribbean
496142.authors: Erin Sanders, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Galvez and B. H. Connell
496142.abstract: The Regional Focus Group (RFG) of the Americas and the Caribbean is a collaborative training effort between the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Regional Training Centers of Excellence in Argentina, Barbados, Brazil, and Costa Rica. Established in 2004, the monthly virtual sessions address regional weather forecasting challenges. Discussion and participant contributions highlight the use of geostationary and low Earth orbit satellite imagery and products for operational applications: regional weather patterns, hurricanes, severe weather, flooding, volcanic eruptions, and other significant events. The success of the RFG is in its ability to make global connections through the exchange of regional knowledge, perspectives, and diverse expertise. Over the years, participants have joined from more than 70 countries, primarily in WMO Regional Association (RA) III (South America) and RA IV (North America, Central America, and the Caribbean). We will present an overview of the Regional Focus Group and reflect on its role in building capacity in the Americas and the Caribbean by facilitating an international community of practice.

496144.title: Spatial Structure and Resolution Dependence of Anisotropic Turbulent Mixing Near the CBL Top
496144.authors: Girish Nigamanth Raghunathan, Cleveland State Univ., Cleveland, OH; and T. Heus, D. D. Turner, J. M. Simonson, T. J. Wagner, N. N. Karle, and D. Rosenberg
496144.abstract: Turbulent mixing within the convective boundary layer (CBL) controls the vertical transport of heat and moisture. The study based on Raman lidar observations and corresponding large-eddy simulations over ARM Southern Great Plains site (Turner et al, 2026), found that the decay exponent, derived using the classic autocovariance approach, agreed with the theoretical 2/3 scaling in the well-mixed layer but deviated from this behavior near the CBL top, suggesting potentially anisotropic mixing. In this study, we explore the horizontal and vertical spatial structure associated with such anisotropic mixing, using instantaneous three-dimensional LES fields. This is done by evaluating horizontal and vertical autocorrelations of scalar fluctuations within and above the boundary layer as it evolves throughout the day. Preliminary results indicate comparatively isotropic turbulence within the mixed layer, transitioning to stronger spatial anisotropy, intermittent structures, and non-local mixing near the CBL top as the boundary layer develops. This analysis will further be extended across other such days over the ARM Southern Great Plains and the Bankhead National Forest sites. Using complementary observational, LES, and single-column model perspectives, we will also investigate how changes in horizontal and vertical grid spacing influence the representation of turbulent structure, anisotropy, and mixing near the CBL top across different model configuration and resolutions.

496147.title: Aurora Corridor Pikalert Demonstration and Verification for the 2025–2026 Winter Season
496147.abstract: According to the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA), the United States experiences roughly 1.2 million weather-related vehicle crashes each year. Approximately 40% of these crashes, or nearly 480,000 annually, are associated with winter weather conditions such as snow, sleet, ice, or slush. A road weather decision support system that accurately predicts roadway conditions and hazards during winter weather provides transportation agencies with a valuable tool for planning and responding to adverse conditions. Applications include personnel scheduling, resource allocation, equipment and material deployment, and post-storm assessment. In response to this need, NSF NCAR has developed Pikalert, an advanced winter road maintenance decision support system (MDSS). Pikalert combines a precision DICast forecasting system and a road-condition treatment module with a wide range of real-time inputs, including surface observations, radar data, connected-vehicle data, and camera imagery. Pikalert produces highly tuned forecasts and hazard assessments out to 72 hours for roadway segments and Road Weather Information System (RWIS) stations across a state roadway network, including tactical assessments updated every five minutes. Forecast hazards and alerts include, but are not limited to, pavement conditions, precipitation, visibility, and wind speed. Pikalert is currently configured for real-time operations for five state departments of transportation: Alaska, Colorado, Iowa, Oregon, and Wyoming. During the 2025–2026 winter season, as part of the Aurora Road Weather Program, NSF NCAR conducted a broader demonstration of Pikalert capabilities across a large portion of the United States. The demonstration included much of the I-70 corridor from Utah through Ohio, as well as the I-75 corridor from Ohio north through Michigan. Within Pikalert, as with any road weather decision support system, the quality of downstream hazard predictions depends heavily on the accuracy of the underlying weather forecast. Liquid precipitation and snowfall forecasts are particularly important because errors in these fields can directly affect predictions of pavement conditions and other winter-weather hazards. This presentation will evaluate Pikalert forecast performance during the 2025–2026 Aurora demonstration. Verification will include bulk statistics such as root-mean-square error (RMSE) and bias for meteorological variables including temperature, dewpoint, and wind speed. Specific winter storm cases along the demonstration corridors will also be examined, with particular emphasis on liquid precipitation and snowfall forecasts at lead times of 12, 24, 48, and 72 hours. Finally, the presentation will provide a brief overview of recent Pikalert system upgrades designed to improve roadway hazard prediction.

496148.title: A Framework for Global, Near-Real-Time Attribution of Precipitation to Climate Change
496148.authors: Joseph Giguere, Climate Central, Princeton, NJ
496148.abstract: Heavy precipitation ranks among the world’s most frequent and damaging weather hazards. Many regions are experiencing increases in heavy precipitation frequency and intensity, and more than 60% of the event attribution studies cataloged by CarbonBrief have found that climate change is a contributor. Despite the societal relevance of extreme precipitation, no operational system currently provides global, near-real-time estimates of how climate change is influencing precipitation. We present a framework designed to support a near-real-time system that will attribute changes in the likelihood and intensity of 1- to 5-day rainfall events. The framework combines precipitation estimates from near-real-time MSWEP observations with bias-adjusted simulations from nine HighResMIP models. We fit seasonally varying extended generalized Pareto distributions to wet-day precipitation in both datasets, allowing the scale parameter of the distribution to vary with global mean temperature (GMT). We quantify changes in event likelihood using occurrence ratios and other conventional attribution metrics by comparing probabilities, likelihoods, and more with present-day GMT warming (+1.3°C) and the preindustrial climate (0°C attributable warming). We present a new attribution metric based on the IPCC Assessed Likelihood terminology, capturing the uncertainty intrinsic in precipitation work. We evaluate the framework with an automated analysis of 171 recent precipitation-related disasters recorded in the EM-DAT international disaster database. We find that climate change likely or very likely increased the likelihood of ~40% of these events and likely or very likely increased the intensity of ~50% of them. Additionally, we analyze case studies in depth to evaluate intra-event variability and sensitivity. Results demonstrate that, properly framed, operational precipitation attribution is not only feasible, but valuable for contextualizing climate change’s influence on recent impactful heavy precipitation events. A near-real-time system based on this framework will complement event-specific attribution studies and support timely communication, adaptation planning, infrastructure decisions, and loss-and-damage assessment.

496151.title: Evaluation of AROME-Arctic Sensible and Latent Heat Fluxes During Marine Cold Air Outbreaks Observed During CAESAR
496151.authors: Andrew Michael Dzambo, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; and M. Kähnert, Z. Xia, G. M. McFarquhar, and H. Sodemann
496151.abstract: The AROME-Arctic model is operationally used for forecasting weather conditions in the Norwegian Sea. Forecasting boundary layer and cloud evolution, however, can be challenging, particularly during marine cold air outbreaks (MCAOs) as their dynamics fall in the so called “grey zone” for modeling at kilometer-scale. The present study focuses on the evolution of the boundary layer via sensible heat flux (SHF) and latent heat flux (LHF). During the CAESAR experiment, a classic MCAO was sampled by aircraft on 16 March 2024. A weaker MCAO was sampled on 11 March 2024, and for comparison, a “MCAO-like” case was sampled on 28 February 2024. Both SHF and LHF are derived from dropsonde measurements and are collocated with interpolated SHF and LHF produced by AROME-Arctic. Overall, AROME-Arctic was remarkably consistent in producing MCAO events for the three cases. However, throughout all cases the model introduced a pronounced overestimation of SHF, with maximum biases near the ice edge becoming twice as large as the observed fluxes. In other MCAO regions of the MCAO, SHFs were overestimated by around 30-40%. The increased SHF lead to MBLs that are consistently too deep and too warm in AROME-Arctic compared to the dropsonde profiles. Likewise, a persistent LHF bias was produced for all forecast periods across the entire flight transect leading to the sea-ice edge. Yet, when evaluating cloud top altitude forecasts for the 16 March 2024 case, AROME-Arctic was excellent throughout most of the cloud street region but forecasted cloud top heights that were too low near the sea-ice edge and failed to predict any cloud cover over the sea-ice. The seemingly paradox between high SHF yet low cloud top altitudes near the sea-ice edge most likely occurs due to an overestimation of wind speeds, which dominate the boundary layer evolution close to the ice edge. Cloud top height forecasts within the polar low region generally captured the heterogeneity of the polar low between forecast periods but again forecasted cloud top altitudes that were too high. The consistent results between these three cases show that excessive SHFs are creating MBLs that are too deep and too warm in AROME-Arctic. These findings suggest a need to reassess the representation of air–sea fluxes in AROME-Arctic, particularly during MCAO events. The resulting impacts on related processes, such as PBL development and cloud evolution, merit further investigation.

496152.title: Mapping Major Ammonia Transport Corridors from Colorado’s Front Range Emission Sources to Rocky Mountain Lakes
496152.authors: Kimberley Anne Corwin, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. J. Iacono, L. Magliozzi, J. S. Baron, J. L. Collett Jr., and E. V. Fischer
496152.abstract: Rich in ammonia (NH3), both agricultural and wildfire emissions frequently reach sensitive, high-elevation ecosystems in the Colorado Rocky Mountains. Mobile and aircraft-based field campaigns along with in situ monitoring in and around Rocky Mountain National Park and the Colorado Front Range document upslope transport of NH3 from agricultural and urban sources to alpine lakes. Increased reactive nitrogen deposition has already led to measurable changes in lake ecosystems including greater algal productivity and shifts toward eutrophication. To mitigate such impacts, early warning systems forecast upslope transport events and encourage agricultural producers to limit NH3-generating activities on associated days. However, broad success of mitigation efforts depends on a robust understanding of NH3 source regions and transport corridors as well as anticipating impacts for alpine lakes in the region that lack routine monitoring. In this study, we identify “hot spots” for NH3 emissions along the Colorado Front Range that affect Rocky Mountain lakes as well as the predominant corridors and meteorological conditions that favor upslope NH3 transport during the warm season (March-October). Using NH3 observations from the satellite-based Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) instrument, we identify high-elevation (≥2000 m) Rocky Mountain lakes along the Colorado Front Range exposed to elevated overhead NH3 concentrations from 2013-2025. We leverage an oversampled, smoke-free CrIS NH3 product to determine a warm-season baseline for overhead NH3 and identify days exceeding this threshold. To isolate non-smoke and smoke sources, smoke-free and smoke-impacted days are separated based on smoke plume locations from the NOAA Hazard Mapping System smoke product. We group individual lakes into subregions with similar trends in the timing of elevated NH3 exposure. We then use airmass trajectories to investigate the source of the NH3 emissions and primary transport pathways to these subregions on individual days. For each subregion, we analyze the daily trajectories to identify the main transport corridors that drive elevated NH3 levels and the associated meteorological conditions. The transport pathways are compared to the location of known concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs), urban and industrial areas, and fire hotspots. Improving our understanding of NH3 sources and transport on the Front Range will help researchers and stakeholders identify additional lakes that could benefit from biogeochemical monitoring as well as evaluate and strengthen early warning systems for mitigating NH3 emissions, which remain largely unregulated.

496154.title: Interannual Drivers of Atmospheric Methanol as Seen from Space
496154.authors: Joseph Kearney, University of Minnesota, Falcon Heights, MN; University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN; and D. B. Millet, K. Wells, V. Payne, and C. Hu
496154.abstract: Methanol is the most abundant non-methane volatile organic compound (VOC) in the atmosphere. Terrestrial and marine ecosystems act as both sources and sinks for atmospheric methanol, but the magnitude of these fluxes and their changes through time are not well understood. In this study, we interpret a novel 15-year record of space-borne methanol column observations from the Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) with the GEOS-Chem chemical transport model to identify the regional and source-specific processes driving seasonal-to-interannual variability. The tagged model simulation tracks methanol contributions by region and sector (anthropogenic, biogenic, pyrogenic, oceanic, atmospheric), enabling attribution of the satellite-observed patterns to specific source processes. Preliminary results show that GEOS-Chem captures the broad features of the global methanol distribution detected by CrIS. However, consistent regional and temporal differences emerge that point to opportunities for improved model representation. We discuss these findings in terms of their implications for our understanding of surface-atmosphere VOC exchange. We explore in particular the role of the oceans, a long-standing uncertainty for atmospheric methanol, and the degree to which the satellite record can provide a constraint to reduce this uncertainty.

496155.title: Urban-Suburban Microscale Weather and Hazard Translation for UAS/AAM
496155.authors: Michelle V Whitcher, FAA, Washington, DC
496155.abstract: Weather information and products have continually evolved to improve the safety and efficiency of manned aviation operations within the National Airspace System (NAS). As the NAS rapidly expands to accommodate Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) and Advanced Air Mobility (AAM), new operational challenges require weather information that extends beyond traditional aviation products. UAS typically operate below 400 feet above ground level, often near people, buildings, and complex urban infrastructure, while possessing flight performance characteristics that differ significantly from conventional aircraft. These unique operational environments require refined microscale weather observations, forecasts, and hazard information to support safe and efficient operations. The Urban-Suburban Microscale Weather and Hazard Translation for UAS/AAM research effort addresses these challenges by identifying gaps in weather observations, sensor networks, forecasting capabilities, decision-support products, operational standards, and hazard translation methodologies needed to support future UAS and AAM operations. This work also aligns with the FAA's Strategic Deconfliction and Connected Operations Milestones and supports the recently announced Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS) vision by advancing weather capabilities that enable the seamless integration of UAS and AAM into an increasingly connected and automated NAS. This paper provides an overview of the Urban-Suburban Microscale Weather and Hazard Translation research initiative, summarizes its current progress, and discusses its transition toward operational implementation. The presentation will also provide an early preview of planned field-testing activities and highlight emerging resources and opportunities to advance understanding of urban and suburban wind hazards and their operational impacts on future UAS and AAM operations.

496159.title: Model Forge - Democratizing Training of Large Neural Networks
496159.authors: Stanislaw Jaroszynski, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and N. Cherukuru, S. G. Pearse, M. Rehme, and D. J. Gagne II
496159.abstract: NCAR's CREDIT framework lowers many of the barriers to developing AI-based weather prediction (AIWP) and related Earth system ML models, training large neural networks remains both technically challenging and time-intensive. Training or fine-tuning models often requires access to petabyte-scale datasets, high–I/O throughput storage systems, high-performance parallel file systems, and multi-GPU clusters capable of distributed training. In addition to infrastructure demands, there are substantial workforce challenges. Researchers must be proficient in machine learning training frameworks such as PyTorch or JAX, understand HPC job scheduling environments, work effectively with parallel I/O systems, and be familiar with geophysical data standards and conventions, to name only a few. Effective workflows also depend on supporting software ecosystems, including tools such as Xarray and Dask for scalable data preprocessing and post-processing. As a result, relatively few Earth system scientists are currently positioned to train new models or adapt existing ones for their research applications. To address this gap, NSF NCAR is building a pilot model training service, the ML Model Forge, designed to remove many of these technical barriers. The Model Forge, when ready, will provide a no-code or low-code interface for reproducibly training a range of AI models relevant to Earth system science, thereby broadening access beyond ML specialists. In addition to supporting model training for non-experts, the ML Model Forge will emphasize reproducibility and version control, streamlined deployment pathways, and responsible, reliable model development and use. By abstracting much of the underlying complexity, the service aims to democratize advanced AI capabilities while maintaining scientific rigor and operational robustness.

496160.title: Making Hidden Heat Visible: A New Tool for Monitoring and Attributing Daily, Global Humid Heat
496160.authors: Kaitlyn Trudeau, Climate Central, Princeton, NJ; and D. M. Gilford, K. Dahl, and L. Tracewski
496160.abstract: Extreme heat, one of the deadliest weather-related hazards, is becoming more frequent and intense as heat-trapping pollution continues to warm our world. But temperature alone often fails to capture the full burden of heat stress – the rest is hidden in humidity, which can make seemingly mild days far more dangerous than they appear. While observed and projected trends in humid heat events are robust in spatial and temporal aggregates, the contribution of climate change to any one humid heat event is less clear. Of the 200+ catalogued studies attributing the likelihood or severity of extreme heat events to climate change, only a handful specifically examine humid heat. Furthermore, while operational and real-time temperature attribution systems have been in place for years, no equivalent exists for humid heat, making it harder for scientists and decision-makers to inform the public about the role climate change is playing in the changing frequency and intensity of such events. Building upon our previous attribution work, Climate Central has developed a new tool—backed by peer-reviewed science—for monitoring and attributing daily humid heat. Using wet-bulb temperature, the Climate Shift Index: Humid Heat applies a multimethod approach that combines empirical data (ERA5) with forced and preindustrial simulations from nine CMIP6 climate models to estimate the influence of climate change on daily wet-bulb temperatures around the world. The scientifically-robust tool gives users unique insights into how human-caused climate change is affecting the worst of humid heat events on a daily basis, in real time. In this talk, we will introduce the tool and demonstrate how it can be used to monitor, contextualize, and attribute daily minimum and maximum wet-bulb temperatures, applying it to several humid heat events from 2026. We will show how to use the tool to communicate the role of climate change in the changing frequency and intensity of daily humid heat events and how it connects to human health. We will end with a discussion about some of the challenges we encountered, including selecting health-relevant thresholds, estimating uncertainty, and balancing science and communication when developing a tool for broader public use.

496163.title: Built to Last: The Evolution of 3D-PAWS Toward Reliable, Low-Cost Weather Observation for Underserved Communities
496163.authors: Brianna M. Smith, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and P. A. Kucera, M. Steinson, K. Payne, R. Zieber, W. Nicewonger, and B. Bubon
496163.abstract: Low-cost, dense in-situ sensor networks offer a path to filling critical gaps in meteorological observation coverage, but their operational value depends on well-characterized performance and clear protocols for deployment and maintenance.
