Since 2014, UCAR has developed and deployed the 3D-Printed Automatic Weather Station (3D-PAWS), a low-cost weather station combining 3D-printed housings, micro-sensors, and micro-computing data loggers, across dozens of countries spanning dry, tropical, and temperate climates. Each station reports temperature (on three independent sensors), pressure, relative humidity, wind speed/direction, precipitation, and solar irradiance at one-minute resolution. We present results from an ongoing quality assurance and performance evaluation of the global 3D-PAWS network. Results show generally strong observational accuracy, with reliability—station and sensor uptime—as the primary limiting factor. Uptime is most strongly tied to station maintenance and power stability rather than climate zone, and analog wind sensors show distinct failure modes tied to cabling/fabrication and, historically, unreliable timekeeping during connectivity outages. To address these limitations, we redesigned the station's data logger and communication architecture: replacing the original Raspberry Pi-based system with a lower-power, cellular-connected Particle data logger, alongside shortened sensor cabling and firmware improvements. Comparing legacy (RPi) and current (Particle) station generations across all climate zones tested, sensor uptime improved for every sensor type—most dramatically for temperature, humidity, and light sensors (roughly 72-83% up to 95-99%), with smaller but consistent gains for the already-reliable rain and wind sensors (95-98% up to 99-100%). Station-level QC failure rates and duplicate-observation rates both dropped substantially and became far more consistent across stations and climates, demonstrating global utility and increased reliability for these systems. These improvements are backward-compatible with existing deployments, offering a practical case study in performance characterization and protocol development for low-cost, high-density observing networks.

496164.title: Diagnosing Postfire Changes in Snow Processes on the Eastern Sierra Nevada: Toward Improved Flood Forecasting for Wildland–Urban Interface Communities
496164.authors: Kabir Rasouli, DRI, Reno, NV; and B. Koirala, S. Mohsenzadeh Karimi, M. Kumar, and R. Abolafia-Rosenzweig
496164.abstract: Wildfires are reshaping snow-affected watersheds across the western United States. At the same time, wildland-urban interface communities continue to expand into these landscapes, yet the effects of these postfire changes on snow processes remain challenging to quantify, understanding that is critical for flood forecasting and water-resource planning in these communities. This study advances both the science and the applied understanding of postfire snow hydrology using a paired-watershed approach on the eastern slope of the Sierra Nevada near Reno, Nevada. The Davis Creek Watershed, upstream of the residential community of Pleasant Valley, serves as an unburned control; the neighboring Winters Creek Watershed, roughly 60% burned by a 2024 wildfire, isolates the fire's hydrologic signal. We simulated both watersheds with the process-based Cold Regions Hydrological Model (CRHM), driven by hourly meteorological forcing including air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and precipitation data, and evaluated simulated snow depth, snow water equivalent, and streamflow against Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) lidar retrievals and observed discharge. Informed by postfire changes in canopy, understory, and soil properties, CRHM simulates increased flood potential after the fire, particularly during spring snowmelt and rain-on-snow events, the scenario of greatest concern for downstream communities. Observations tell a more complicated story: ASO and streamflow data show a heterogeneous reduction in snow persistence and a substantial decrease in peak-flow magnitude, producing a less flashy hydrologic response than the model anticipates. This model–observation contrast is itself a central scientific result, identifying specific gaps in how postfire landscape properties are represented and parameterized in physically based hydrologic models. Closing these gaps is a prerequisite for models that wildland-urban interface communities and water managers can operationally rely on for postfire flood forecasting and long-term watershed planning in semi-arid, snow-affected regions.

496165.title: Unveiling Non-Linear Atmospheric Drivers of Antarctic Sea Ice: A Causal and Explainable AI Framework for Attributing Concentration and Thickness Variability
496165.authors: Shreya Trivedi, NASA GSFC, Bethesda, MD; and A. Bliss, W. Gregory, C. Parker, and L. Boisvert
496165.abstract: Antarctic sea ice dynamics are inherently non-linear and spatially heterogeneous. However, historical climate attribution largely relies on linear assumptions and disproportionately focuses on surface parameters such as Sea Ice Concentration (SIC) and its derivatives. Consequently, the non-linear relationships between atmospheric drivers and sea ice, as well as their impacts on Sea Ice Thickness (SIT), remain poorly understood. While modern Machine Learning (ML) excels at capturing complex, non-linear relationships, standard algorithms often act as “black boxes”, predicting anomalies successfully but failing to provide physical mechanisms, while remaining vulnerable to spurious correlations. To illuminate these non-linear dynamics and bridge the gap between predictive ML and physical climate attribution, this study uses a multi-stage Causal Inference Method and Explainable AI (XAI) pipeline. Building on prior work which established that SIT is dominantly mechanically or dynamically driven while SIC is thermodynamically driven at the circum-Antarctic scale, here we focus on the regional sea ice responses which are highly heterogeneous. Specifically, we investigate whether regional SIT and SIC respond distinctly to the same set of thermodynamic and dynamic atmospheric drivers, or if the broader dynamic-SIT and thermodynamic-SIC paradigms hold true across highly variable local sectors. Using daily austral winter/spring data (1979–present), we predict regional anomalies of SIC from satellite observations and SIT from Global Ice-Ocean Modeling and Assimilation System (GIOMAS), evaluating their variability against atmospheric parameters from the ERA5 reanalysis. To isolate true physical forcing, our methodological pipeline first employs causal networks to eliminate spurious proxies and filter the feature space to direct atmospheric drivers. These drivers inform decision tree-based ML models, from which we extract physical attribution (via XAI) to quantify the spatio-temporal evolution of dynamic versus thermodynamic forcings. We present regional evaluations comparing localized SIT and SIC responses to atmospheric variables, identifying where regional heterogeneity deviates from circum-Antarctic trends. Ultimately, this transparent AI framework moves beyond “black box” predictions, laying the groundwork for validating regional physics in Earth System Models and improving sub-seasonal to seasonal polar predictability.

496170.title: Dynamical Influences on Arctic Stratospheric Ozone Variability and Trend Estimates
496170.authors: Guochun Shi, Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and O. M. Coddington, G. Stober, V. L. Harvey, H. Liu, B. Alistair, and Y. Li
496170.abstract: Detecting long-term changes in Arctic stratospheric ozone is challenging because large dynamical and chemical variability can obscure underlying trends. In this study, we combine continuous polar stratospheric ozone observations from the ground-based microwave radiometer GROMOS-C with satellite measurements, reanalysis products, and chemistry-climate model simulations to characterize Arctic ozone variability and assess its influence on inferred long-term trends. Arctic polar ozone exhibits pronounced seasonal and interannual variability, particularly from midwinter through spring, when changes in transport, mixing, and photochemical ozone loss strongly influence its distribution. During spring, evolving dynamical conditions, together with increasing ultraviolet solar irradiance, strengthen photochemical control on ozone and contribute to its seasonal evolution. The resulting dynamical and chemical variability complicates the separation of long-term ozone changes from short-term and interannual fluctuations. We quantify Arctic stratospheric ozone trends using multiple linear regression frameworks that incorporate different sets of predictors designed to account for processes influencing ozone variability. The inferred annual trends generally indicate increasing Arctic stratospheric ozone, but both the magnitude and vertical structure of the trends are sensitive to the choice of regression predictors. Sensitivity tests suggest a shift toward more positive trends in the middle stratosphere when key dynamical proxies are included. These results highlight the importance of explicitly accounting for dynamical variability when quantifying and attributing long-term changes in Arctic stratospheric ozone.

496172.title: Auditable Model Selection and Regime-Aware Uncertainty for Hot-Wire Cloud-Water Probe Calibration Against an Isokinetic Reference in the NASA Icing Research Tunnel
496172.abstract: Hot-wire probes are a workhorse for measuring cloud liquid water content in icing wind tunnels and in flight, inferring water content from the electrical power required to hold a heated sensing element at temperature. They are known to under-read systematically: a fraction of the impacting droplets splash and shed rather than fully evaporating on the element, so the sensed water content falls below the true value. Correcting this deficit requires a calibrated retention-efficiency curve, defined here as the ratio of the hot-wire-measured water content to that of a co-located reference instrument. Two questions then govern how trustworthy the correction is: what functional form the retention curve should take, and how measurement uncertainty should be propagated through it. This work addresses both as explicitly auditable decisions, and applies the resulting framework to a calibration campaign conducted in the NASA Glenn Icing Research Tunnel (IRT). Retention efficiency is organized against the Sommerfeld number, a dimensionless splashing parameter that combines droplet size, impact velocity, and fluid properties, and that consolidates the airspeed and droplet-size dependence of splashing onto a single axis. A multi-element hot-wire probe carrying three independent sensing geometries, together with a second dual-element probe, was calibrated against an isokinetic reference probe over a range of airspeeds, droplet median volume diameters (MVD), and water-content setpoints spanning both Appendix C (small-droplet) and Appendix O (supercooled large-droplet) icing conditions. The multiple simultaneously logged elements provide a direct measure of the inter-element retention spread at each condition, which is central to distinguishing genuine physical behavior from element-specific artifacts. The first methodological contribution is an auditable model-selection procedure that decides, per element, whether a simple linear retention model or a piecewise (broken-stick) model with a distinct splashing breakpoint is warranted. Rather than adopting a single form by assertion, the procedure requires unanimous agreement among three independent criteria: an F-test for nested models, a multi-start breakpoint-stability test, and the Bayesian Information Criterion. Any disagreement yields a conservative linear selection explicitly flagged as indeterminate. The stability test is diagnostically decisive: a genuine breakpoint converges to nearly the same value from any starting guess, whereas an "artifact knee"—a breakpoint the solver is forced to return even when the data contain none—chases its initial guess across the data range. The procedure also discloses, rather than hides, a known statistical subtlety: the F-test's regularity conditions are violated when the breakpoint becomes undefined (the Davies problem), making it mildly anti-conservative; unanimity among the other two criteria, which do not depend on the F reference distribution, absorbs this risk. In preliminary analysis, the five sensing elements fall into three groups—two resolve a genuine, well-localized retention breakpoint, one is cleanly linear, and two are indeterminate—showing that a one-size-fits-all curve form would misrepresent the majority of the elements. The second contribution is a regime-aware, hybrid uncertainty-propagation scheme. An analytic Taylor (delta-method) expansion is efficient and adequate away from the retention breakpoint, but breaks down in its neighborhood, where the model is non-differentiable and the linearization is invalid. The scheme therefore dispatches automatically to a Monte Carlo propagation near the breakpoint and to the analytic path elsewhere, with each reported uncertainty tagged by the method that produced it so the provenance of every prediction band is transparent. The calibration dataset is deliberately kept indexed one row per hot-wire interval rather than collapsed to per-reference averages, so that genuine run-to-run measurement scatter is retained in the residual variance and the prediction band rather than being artificially suppressed. Applying this framework across the Appendix C–O boundary reveals preliminary findings that will be expanded upon during the presentation using the complete dataset. The ratio of reference to facility-nominal water content increases with droplet size at large MVD, consistent with prior large-droplet intercomparisons, and shows only a weak dependence on airspeed. A separate contribution of size-distribution shape is also observed at fixed MVD. Because reference repeatability itself degrades in the large-droplet regime—run-to-run variability grows several-fold from the small-droplet range to the largest drops—the retention correction is reported with correspondingly widened uncertainty there rather than a single tight band, and this regime is where additional measurements are concentrated. Separately, a small population of measured retention values above unity, concentrated at low Sommerfeld number where true retention is near one, is retained and flagged rather than clipped or discarded, so that the real low-splashing scatter contributes honestly to the uncertainty rather than being biased downward. The campaign additionally compares two atomizing-nozzle configurations that produce distinct droplet-size distributions at matched nominal conditions, providing a first look at whether retention behavior collapses onto the Sommerfeld axis independently of how the cloud was generated, or carries a residual dependence on the underlying size distribution. Resolving that question, together with the low-Sommerfeld collision-efficiency behavior at the small-drop end of the correction, is the subject of measurements completing in late 2026; the presentation will report the complete two-nozzle dataset. The broader contribution is a template for probe intercomparison and calibration in which every modeling and uncertainty decision is auditable, conservative under ambiguity, and explicit about the regimes in which measurement scatter widens the achievable confidence. This emphasis on defensible, transparent methodology is intended to be transferable well beyond hot-wire icing probes to instrument calibration problems across atmospheric measurement.

496176.title: Reach for the STARS: Implementation of a STratospheric AeRosol Sampler to Assess the Impact of Satellite Reentry on Earth's Atmosphere
496176.authors: Chelsea Anne Bekemeier, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and P. J. Bjick, A. Piscitella, E. Z. Durham, C. J. Hatland, N. Montero, J. D. Stienike, J. R. Pierce, C. L'Orange, A. P. Yalin, and S. H. Jathar
496176.abstract: The proliferation of commercial spaceflight and low-Earth orbit satellite constellations has the potential to impact Earth's atmosphere. Upon reentry, these spacecraft experience extreme heating, causing structural components to ablate and condense into particles. Recent studies have identified spacecraft-derived metals in stratospheric aerosol particles, suggesting that ablated metals may alter the composition of the upper atmosphere. Opportunities to directly sample these particles remain limited due to the difficulty of sampling in near-space conditions. The STARS (STratospheric AeRosol Sampler) project was developed to address this challenge by designing and fabricating a high-altitude balloon (HAB) platform capable of collecting stratospheric aerosol samples. Our design integrates a custom transmission electron microscopy (TEM) grid sampling inlet on an AirPen™ air quality monitor, housed within a HAB payload. The STARS sampler is designed to collect submicron aerosols only once the payload reaches the stratosphere, to minimize contamination from tropospheric aerosols. The project also included development of the balloon flight configuration, payload integration, and mission procedures necessary for routine launches. In addition to deployments, we used a cooled vacuum chamber to simulate stratospheric conditions, define operational limits of the payload, and establish performance bounds for subsequent field observations. We present our initial deployments and laboratory validation results to demonstrate the operational capability of the STARS platform. Electron microscopy will be used to quantify and characterize stratospheric metals embedded in aerosol particles. Elemental composition of the metals and relative abundance ratios to those found in meteorites will allow us to determine which components are derived from spacecraft. By creating a reusable, high-altitude sampling system capable of deployment in the stratosphere, the STARS sampler provides a new observational capability to investigate the distribution of ablated aerospace metals in the stratosphere. These observations can help us better understand the environmental effects of human activity in near-space and facilitate continued research into stratospheric aerosol composition and climate-related impacts.

496178.title: Connecting Data-Assimilative Thermospheric Nowcasts to Forecasts of the Satellite Drag Environment
496178.authors: Marcin Pilinski, Space Environment Technologies, Boulder, CO; Space Environment Technologies, Pacific Palisades, CA; and E. Sutton, A. Hu, S. Mutschler, and J. Knuth
496178.abstract: Drag-validated data assimilation (DA) techniques such as IDEA [Sutton 2018] and CAFE can determine the thermospheric model forcing that is most compatible with the observed satellite drag, effectively making a “driver correction” to the atmospheric models at each time step. These driver corrections are often distinct from the issued and forecast drivers in statistically significant ways. In other words, the driver-corrected model may no longer be compatible with the operational drivers. Making use of these promising techniques in LEO operations requires establishing the mapping between DA nowcasts and issued forecast drivers. We present the results of forecast mapping for two data assimilative techniques, one using a global circulation model ensemble, while the other uses an ensemble of empirical models. The results indicate that empirical and machine-learned approaches can help reduce forecast errors by mapping issued and forecast drivers to the assimilative states at time zero. We evaluate these improvements in terms of density and orbital in-track error impacts.

496185.title: NOAA Phased Array Research and Development Recent Achievements and Future Efforts
496185.authors: Anthony E. Reinhart, NSSL, Norman, OK; and R. Mendoza, A. A. Alford, D. Wasielewski, S. M. Torres, and W. MacKenzie
496185.abstract: The Phased Array Radar (PAR) Research and Development (R&D) Program focuses on advancing PAR technology, enhancing weather radar techniques, and advancing our understanding of meteorology. These R&D efforts flow directly into proving the viability of PAR as one potential replacement of the current operational network operated by the National Weather Service (NWS). PAR technology provides significant scanning flexibility and adaptability with electronic beam steering, agile beam forming, and other advanced features, which can afford rapid update volumetric data, enhanced data quality, and focused observations that are not achievable with conventional radar technology. NOAA's PAR program collaborates and works closely with the Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, the University of Oklahoma Advanced Radar Research Center, Massachusetts Institute of Technology Lincoln Lab, and other university and FFRDC partners to improve PAR capabilities and develop new techniques that inform future R&D and prove operational capabilities. This presentation will focus on R&D efforts within NOAA and with its closest collaborators, providing an overview of the ongoing and near-future R&D efforts. Highlighting how these successful collaborative efforts have matured PAR technology, advanced our understanding of meteorology, and informed the NWS Radar Next Program will be discussed in detail.

496186.title: From Data Centers to Cloud in 10 Months: NCEI's Migration to AWS and the Roadmap to Cloud-Native Via OneGov
496186.authors: Dev Jodhun, Amazon Web Services, Arlington, VA; and M. Friedenthal, M. C. Dowling, and R. Toles-Abdullah
496186.abstract: NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) houses one of the world's largest collections of environmental data, archiving over 229 terabytes of new data each month from more than 130 observing platforms. This ever-expanding repository of atmospheric, oceanic, geophysical, and climate data serves researchers, emergency managers, businesses, and communities across the globe daily. How does an organization migrate this volume of mission-critical data to the cloud while maintaining uninterrupted access and data integrity? In one of the largest infrastructure undertakings in its history, NCEI is executing a full migration of its data, products, and services from on-premises data centers in Asheville, North Carolina and Boulder, Colorado to Amazon Web Services (AWS). This presentation describes the technical approach, challenges, and early outcomes of migrating NCEI to the cloud. NCEI leveraged the AWS OneGov program — enabling direct engagement with AWS Professional Services through the GSA Multiple Award Schedule — to execute this migration with dedicated cloud migration expertise. The 10-month engagement completes the lift-and-shift of all data, products, and services to AWS, along with initial modernization work that produces a roadmap for evolving toward a fully cloud-native architecture and integration into the NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF). This phased approach ensures continuity of service while charting a clear path toward modern public data access. The transition to cloud infrastructure addresses several critical limitations of legacy physical server architectures: the resource-intensive nature of downloading NOAA's largest datasets for each use, the vulnerability of physical hardware to degradation and failure, and the inability to rapidly scale during high-demand events such as extreme weather. Cloud-based data delivery reduces the download bottleneck by providing on-demand access — a foundational requirement for the emerging artificial intelligence and machine learning applications increasingly central to environmental science. We present quantitative results on migration throughput, data integrity validation processes, and user-facing performance improvements. We detail the technical architecture of the lift-and-shift, the initial modernization work completed within the engagement, and the roadmap produced for future cloud-native optimization including object storage patterns, API modernization, and integration with NCCF. We discuss how the OneGov procurement model streamlined the path from concept to execution, enabling NCEI to bring AWS Professional Services expertise directly to the migration. We also discuss the governance framework that preserves NCEI's legacy of impeccable data stewardship. The implications of this work extend beyond infrastructure modernization. With data now in the cloud, NCEI has a foundation to progressively adopt cloud-native patterns — accelerating new data products, supporting AI/ML workflows at scale, and reinforcing the Department of Commerce's role as "America's Data Agency." Next steps include deeper integration with NCCF and optimization of access patterns for AI-ready datasets. This presentation offers lessons learned — in both technology and procurement strategy — applicable to any large-scale scientific data repository beginning its cloud journey.

496187.title: Science Support with New Lightning Observations Available to the Community
496187.authors: Geoffrey T. Stano, Global Hydrometeorology Resource Center, Huntsville, AL; and S. Flynn, N. Selvaraj, D. Acharya, J. Rushing, and J. M. Beck
496187.abstract: The Global Hydrometeorology Resource Center (GHRC) is jointly operated by the University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH) and NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC). GHRC provides a comprehensive collection of datasets supporting the analysis of dynamical and physical processes associated with storm hazards, lightning, precipitation, convective systems, tropical systems, and field campaigns with NASA’s Earth Science Data and Information System (ESDIS) project. GHRC emphasizes cloud-based tools, scientific expertise, and open science practices to enable broad access to, analysis of, and visualization of its unique data holdings. Over the past year, GHRC has added multiple new lightning datasets in collaboration with a variety of data providers. As part of our mission, these datasets are made freely available to the user community. These datasets come from a variety of lightning instruments. This includes several NASA-owned lightning mapping array networks and the final reprocessed version of the Lightning Imaging Sensor (LIS). In addition to these, GHRC now has the World Meteorological Organization’s lightning essential climate variable, utilizing the “thunder hour” concept. This presentation will provide an overview of these datasets and uses. Additionally, it will highlight GHRC’s efforts to support data exploration and analysis with the FCX visualization system. FCX is an open source, cloud-based data exploration system. It is capable of displaying multiple datasets, coincidentally in three dimensions. The sample image is courtesy of Katrina Virts and shows the World Wide Lightning Location Network (WWLLN) thunder hour observations from September 2025. (Virts, Katrina, Robert Holzworth, and Michael McCarthy. 2024. World Wide Lightning Location Network (WWLLN) Monthly Thunder Hour Data [September 2025]. Dataset available online from the NASA Global Hydrometeorology Resource Center DAAC, Huntsville, Alabama, U.S.A. doi: http://dx.doi.org/10.5067/WWLLN/DATA101.)

496188.title: Reynolds Number Effects on Wake Flow behind a Vertically Heterogeneous Canopy.
496188.authors: Reban Niraula, Univ. of Houston, Houston, TX; and N. C. Durand, H. Motalebi, C. E. Brunner, C. P. Byers, and K. Y. Huang
496188.abstract: Flow exiting canopies through gaps, windbreaks, and fragmented landscapes alters ecosystem processes including forest ventilation, evapotranspiration and pollutant dispersion. Forest canopies not only act as a sink of momentum but also modify the flow field surrounding the canopy: when the distributed canopy drag abruptly terminates, it produces a wake region marked by velocity deficit and enhanced turbulence, followed by gradual recovery toward an equilibrium boundary layer. These canopy wakes are generated by two mechanisms: shear-driven motion from the canopy-top mixing layer and element-scale wake production. As a result, the wake reflects flow conditions within the canopy, which in turn depend on canopy morphology prior to termination. However, conventional studies typically use rod arrays to evaluate leaf area index (LAI) effects on bulk flow, neglecting the vertical heterogeneity of real forests. To address this gap, this study introduces a novel physical canopy analog that independently controls vertical leaf area density (LAD) profiles and overall LAI by representing the canopy structure as stacked plates with distributed hole patterns. Baseline experiments were conducted at the University of Houston at Re = 75,000 for two canopy types: Hardwood (top-heavy foliage distribution) and Jack Pine (mid-to-upper crown concentration) at LAI = 0.8 and 1.6. Results show that while mean streamwise velocity profiles are largely insensitive to vertical heterogeneity, the vertical LAD distribution exerts a primary control on turbulence statistics and spectral energy distribution. The Jack Pine configuration exhibits enhanced turbulence intensity over a broader vertical extent and deeper sub-canopy penetration of high-energy structures compared to Hardwood, with this effect more pronounced at higher LAI, indicating that canopy morphology governs the wake primarily through its influence on turbulence generation rather than the mean flow itself. A subsequent campaign in the Variable Density Turbulence Tunnel (VDTT) at the Max Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization in Göttingen, Germany, investigates the Jack Pine canopy at Reynolds numbers of order 106. Both experiments were conducted using a single-component hot wire across eight streamwise stations, capturing both the above-canopy flow upstream of the canopy exit (x/h = -1.0, -0.5) and the extended downstream wake evolution (x/h = 0.1 to 21.5), where h is the canopy height. Together, these two campaigns enable the study of the Reynolds number effect on canopy wake evolution for this new canopy model, allowing a determination as to whether laboratory-scale canopy flow measurements are representative of full-scale atmospheric conditions.

496189.title: Geometry-Aware Neural Modeling of Ocean Dynamics
496189.authors: Anass El Aouni, Mercator Ocean International, Toulouse, France
496189.abstract: Data-driven approaches have demonstrated substantial progress in geophysical forecasting, particularly for atmospheric applications, yet their extension to the ocean remains challenging. Ocean dynamics evolve over complex and fragmented domains, with pronounced vertical structure and strong interactions between different components of the ocean state. These characteristics introduce spatial dependencies that are not naturally represented by generic learning architectures and can lead to spurious interactions across boundaries, unrealistic spatial propagation, and degraded dynamical fidelity. We introduce a neural architecture for ocean forecasting structured around the spatial organization of the ocean state and its evolution. The resulting representation follows the active ocean domain and adapts the propagation of information to the underlying structure and connectivity of the system. Across physical, sea-ice, and biogeochemical variables, the model generates coherent autoregressive trajectories over extended integrations, maintaining consistent structures across a broad range of spatial and temporal scales. This behavior is retained under perturbed forcing, with the model producing stable trajectories beyond the statistical regime represented in the training data. Analysis of the resulting dynamics reveals coherent spectral evolution, consistent cross-variable interactions, and improved stability over long integrations relative to architectures based on generic feature-space connectivity. These properties persist throughout extended autoregressive integrations and under perturbed forcing, indicating that the learned dynamics remain stable beyond the statistical regime represented in the training data. The resulting forecasts maintain coherent spatiotemporal structure across physical, sea-ice, and biogeochemical variables over substantially longer integration times, highlighting the role of the learned representation in determining the stability of the resulting dynamics.

496192.title: Coupled Machine-Learning Snowpack Monitoring with Physics-Based Hydrology for Water-Supply Decisions in the Western U.S.
496192.authors: Baxter E. Vieux, Applied Research Team, Inc., Denver, CO; and J. E. Vieux and W. E. Vieux
496192.abstract: Hydrologic prediction in snow-dominated headwater catchments remains challenging despite advances in remote sensing for snowpack estimation. This study couples SnowML™, a physics-constrained machine learning model for snow water equivalent (SWE) monitoring, with Freshet™, a physics-based, variable-resolution hydrologic model. SnowML ingests ground-station observations, Parameter-elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM), and NASA Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) satellite data to generate daily maps of SWE accumulation, partitioned into snowmelt and rainfall. Freshet™ (patent pending) is a distributed, physics-based hydrologic model that consumes snowmelt and rainfall output from SnowML to produce April-July seasonal volume forecasts at six benchmark sites across three river basins in Colorado. We evaluate seasonal headwater streamflow forecast skill at six sites in the Upper Colorado and Upper Rio Grande basins over four decades (WY1982-2025) using the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS) benchmarked against climatology and examine how skill evolves through the forecast season. Evaluated on a monthly cadence from January through July, forecast skill improves steadily through the season, rising from +0.21 on January 1 to +0.44 by April 1 and reaching +0.66 by July 1. Skill is strongest in dry years, reaching +0.62 by April 1. During the WY2021-2025 validation period, the framework matches or outperforms operational NWS Colorado Basin River Forecast Center (CBRFC) guidance at five of six benchmark sites by April 1. In the watersheds tested, Freshet's forecast skill is strongest in drought years, when operational products are less reliable and when water managers face the highest-stakes supply decisions. Because early-season forecast accuracy is fundamentally limited by unpredictable future precipitation, efforts to improve actionable forecasts should prioritize improving wet-year forecast estimation.

496194.title: Back to Its Beginnings: Tracking Convective Downburst Air to Its Source
496194.authors: Peter J. Marinescu, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and I. Singh, J. Bukowski, L. D. Grant, and S. C. van den Heever
496194.abstract: Convective cloud downdrafts transport air. They also can cause severe, life-threatening surface winds via downbursts. Understanding the source regions of downdraft air and the processes that alter the thermodynamic properties of as it moves through the atmosphere will assist in better predicting their weather hazards and parameterizing them in global numerical weather prediction models. In this study, we determine where downburst air originates and the processes that are most important in its evolution. To address these science goals, we use an expansive, high-resolution database of convective cloud systems that has been developed in support of the NASA INvestigation of Convective UpdraftS (INCUS) mission. The INCUS simulation database comprises ~100 simulations of convective cloud systems using 3 different modeling platforms (RAMS, WRF with Morrison microphysics, and WRF with Thompson microphysics). The simulations are designed with 3 nested grids, with the innermost grid having 100-m horizontal grid spacing, which allows for a better representation of downdraft processes than coarser simulations. Strong downbursts are first identified in the simulations with 100-m horizontal grid spacing. The air within the identified downbursts are then tracked backwards in time to discern their trajectories and ultimately their source regions. We quantify the dynamic, thermodynamic, and microphysical properties of the air along these trajectories, as well as the processes impacting its evolution. Importantly, we calculate the terms of the vertical velocity tendency equation, including advection, buoyancy, effective buoyancy, condensate loading, and dynamic and buoyant components of the perturbation pressure gradient forcing. This comprehensive assessment allows us to quantify which are most influential to the formation of strong downdrafts and downbursts. Initial results show that the strongest downdrafts below the freezing level have similar-magnitude downward accelerations from dynamic perturbation pressure gradient forcing and effective buoyancy, but the evolution of these terms are highly variable in the lowest 3 km above the surface. Finally, we compare the property and process evolution of downdraft air between different downburst-producing simulations to understand the variability in the pathways of downburst formation.

496196.title: Analyzing the Pre-Fire Environment: Observed Boundary-Layer Evolution and Localized Impacts on Smoke Dispersion During Prescribed Fire
496196.authors: Benjamin Thigpen, Univ. of Georgia, Athens, GA; and M. Williams and J. M. Shepherd
496196.abstract: Fire behavior and smoke dispersion during prescribed burns depend strongly on the state and evolution of the planetary boundary layer (PBL). Because mixing-layer development governs the vertical extent available for smoke dispersion, accurately representing both the timing and magnitude of PBL growth is particularly important during the period leading up to ignition. Here, we define the atmospheric conditions and the evolving vertical structure of the lower atmosphere prior to ignition as the pre-fire environment (PFE). National Weather Service (NWS) operational radiosonde observations, NWS spot forecasts, and model-derived products provide important information on the PBL but may not resolve rapid changes in boundary-layer depth, residual layers, inversion structure, and entrainment processes between observational and forecast intervals. Ground-based ceilometers offer a complementary means of observing the PBL by providing continuous, high-temporal-resolution profiles of atmospheric backscatter. These observations can reveal changes in aerosol-layer structure associated with boundary layer development, including the evolution of mixing-layer height and residual layers. The demonstration is motivated by the need to determine whether the atmospheric conditions anticipated prior to a prescribed burn accurately represent the evolving PBL encountered at the time of ignition. This study evaluates the utility of ceilometer observations for characterizing the pre-fire environment and uses these observations to assess the performance of forecast and model-derived representations of PBL evolution. To evaluate these capabilities, ceilometer observations collected during a prescribed burn on April 9, 2026, near Madison, Georgia, were analyzed alongside operational and model-derived atmospheric data. Ceilometer-derived mixing-layer height and backscatter structure were compared with NWS spot forecast mixing-height guidance, High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) PBL estimates, HRRR soundings, and on ground weather observations to evaluate the timing and evolution of boundary-layer development. Preliminary results indicate that the observed mixing height was more dynamic than represented by forecast and model guidance. The smoke plume initially ascended to the mixing-layer height before subsequently descending as it reached a temperature inversion. Afterwards, maximum aerosol concentrations remained substantially below forecast and model-derived mixing heights, approximately 1000-1500 feet, for approximately two hours before returning to comparable heights. During this period, surface smoke concentrations downwind of the fire were higher than anticipated, consistent with reduced vertical smoke dispersion and a shallower effective depth of smoke mixing. These results demonstrate that forecast and model-derived mixing heights alone may not fully represent the vertical extent over which smoke is actively dispersed. Continuous ceilometer observations may therefore provide additional situational awareness of the evolving PFE and help identify departures from anticipated mixing conditions that can influence smoke dispersion following ignition.

496198.title: Satellite-Based Near-Real-Time Ocean State Estimates for NOAA’s Operational Needs in the North Atlantic
496198.authors: Paige Down Lavin, Univ. of Maryland, Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies (CISESS), College Park, MD; NOAA/STAR, College Park, MD; and D. A. Byrne, K. Saha, B. Zhang, S. B. Hall, and D. S. Trossman
496198.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) currently provides near-real-time (NRT) information about the near-surface ocean through the operational NOAA National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) Satellite Ocean Heat Content Suite (SOHCS) product. As of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, this product is being used in the Statistical Hurricane Intensity Prediction Scheme (SHIPS) to help improve its representation of the ocean’s impact on tropical cyclones (TCs), particularly regarding rapid intensification events. At NOAA’s Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR), we have developed an experimental new ocean heat content (OHC) product for the North Atlantic basin, driven by the Next-Generation Enterprise Ocean Heat Content (NGE OHC) algorithm, to ultimately replace the SOHCS product. The North Atlantic NGE OHC algorithm parameterizes in situ observations of upper-ocean temperature and salinity (T/S) variability with respect to sea level anomaly, sea surface temperature, and sea surface salinity measured by satellites through a set of lookup tables (LUTs). Using these LUTs, we can produce NRT synthetic 2-dbar T/S profiles for the upper ~900 dbar anywhere we have satellite measurements, providing this ocean information at unprecedented spatial and temporal resolution for operational needs. We also calculate additional upper ocean metrics of interest from these profiles for the TC and marine heatwave forecasting communities, including OHC, mixed layer depth, the depth of the 26ºC isotherm, and near-surface stratification strength. Given the dynamic complexity of the North Atlantic, different sets of LUTs are derived over areas of the basin with different stratification regimes, which are identified through Gaussian Mixture Model-based clusters. Cluster-based LUTs allow the algorithm to better capture the true relationships between T/S variability and the satellite-derived quantities, which vary significantly throughout the basin as well as seasonally. This presentation will build off of our recent paper (Lavin et al., 2025) that used the testbed NGE OHC algorithm in the Gulf of America and Northern Caribbean Sea to show both the algorithm’s improvement in characterizing the near-surface ocean over the SOHCS product and that the model initializations for the operational NOAA TC forecast model (NOAA Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System / Modular Ocean Model 6 (HAFS/MOM6)) sometimes miss near-surface heat and stratification (e.g., barrier layers) found in Argo float observations and the NGE OHC algorithm output. These issues in the HAFS initializations led to underpredictions of intensity for a set of TCs that rapidly intensified over this region, highlighting that improved NRT information about the ocean’s subsurface variability has the potential to improve TC intensity forecasts, especially for rapidly intensifying storms. We will show how similar applications of the experimental North Atlantic NGE OHC could be used operationally to improve forecasts and monitoring of TCs and marine heatwaves, thereby increasing the potential for accurate warnings of these dangerous and costly extreme events.

496199.title: Environmental Controls on Rapid Tropical Cyclone Intensity Change in TC-Permitting Climate Models
496199.abstract: Rapid intensification (RI) drives the most destructive tropical cyclones (TCs) and plays a critical role in shaping the distribution of TC lifetime maximum intensity (LMI). Earth system models with ~25 km atmospheric resolution can simulate realistic TC climatology but do not resolve the inner-core processes governing RI; yet rapid intensity changes still emerge in these simulations, raising the question of what drives them and how their biases should be interpreted. We analyze RI and their relationships with environmental controls in two TC-permitting earth system models (CESM-HR and E3SMv1-HR), each configured with ~25 km atmosphere and ~10 km ocean resolution. Both models simulate frequent RI and capture the statistical relationship between RI and high storm intensity; however, neither model reproduces a statistically significant bimodal LMI distribution, pointing to a key limitation of TC-permitting models in representing TC intensity structure. Using logistic regression and a counterfactual decomposition, we further quantify the relative contributions of environmental biases and model sensitivity biases to basin-scale RI biases. Model biases are mainly linked to relative sea surface temperature and wind shear and vary substantially across basins. These results highlight both the utility and limitations of TC-permitting models for interpreting TC intensity variability under non-stationary environmental conditions.

496200.title: A High-Resolution WRF and PALM Modeling Framework for Urban Heat Risk Assessment
496200.authors: Ethan Hack-Chabot, The City College of New York, New York, NY; and J. M. Eissner, P. Ramamurthy, and J. F. Booth
496200.abstract: Extreme heat poses a serious threat to human life and property in urban areas. Cities have increased heat storage capacity due to the built materials that dominate urban environments; the lack of adequate tree cover, anthropogenic emissions, and the complex 3-D profile of built structures all help retain heat, leading to elevated near-surface air temperatures commonly known as the urban heat island effect. During heatwave episodes, the conditions worsen due to synergistic interactions between the two processes. Our general understanding of urban heat islands has advanced in the past 3 decades due to improved modeling and measurement techniques. However, the transport of heat at neighborhood- to building-scale, where much of the mitigation effort is focused, is not well understood. In our work, we use both urbanized mesoscale simulations and realistic large eddy simulations to characterize heat transport in dense urban environments. WRF is configured with three nested domains down to 1 km resolution and serves as the dynamic driver for PALM, which is an advanced meteorological modeling system for atmospheric boundary layer flows. PALM then resolves parameters such as building-scale turbulence and surface and air temperature at a much finer resolution. NYC Open Data is used for realistic surface cover and building height data, with LiDAR and 4-band Orthoimagery collection methods utilized to achieve a resolution of up to 6 inches. This is ongoing work and our initial analysis shows a high degree of variability in the vertical transport of heat and momentum.

496202.title: Subnational Socioeconomic and Urban–Rural Disparities In Air Pollution and Health Benefits Under Global Climate Mitigation
496202.authors: Keyan Guo, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and W. Peng, J. Shiwang, N. C. Scovronick, and M. Budolfson
496202.abstract: Reducing CO2 emissions can yield co-benefits for air quality and health. However, how these benefits from global climate mitigation are distributed within a country remains unclear. Here, we evaluate the subnational air quality and health impacts of alternative global climate mitigation scenarios by coupling a global human-Earth model (GCAM), a global atmospheric chemical transport model (GEOS-Chem), and fine-resolution subnational socio-demographic projections. Specifically, we simulate global PM2.5 concentrations at 2° × 2.5° spatial resolution and combine them with projections of global GDP per capita at 0.25° × 0.25° resolution and urban–rural population distributions at 1/8° resolution to assess disparities in health benefits across population groups. Globally, health benefits are relatively smaller among populations with the highest and lowest GDP per capita: the bottom and top 20% of the global population ranked by grid-cell GDP per capita account for only 10.60% (95% CI: 10.56–11.05%) and 14.37% (95% CI: 13.81–14.96%) of total avoided deaths, respectively. Within countries, climate mitigation reduces absolute PM2.5 exposure while consistently narrowing urban–rural exposure disparities. This convergence arises because mitigation induces larger PM2.5 reductions in more polluted, predominantly urban areas than in cleaner rural areas. Given the growing emphasis on equity in climate policymaking, our study highlights the importance of understanding how global mitigation strategies interact with local conditions to shape the distribution of air-quality and health benefits.

496203.title: Using the CONUS404 Dataset to Assess Future Changes in Lightning Activity
496203.authors: Megan E. Franke, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and W. Deierling, K. L. Rasmussen, and J. W. Hurrell
496203.abstract: Lighting is closely linked to deep convective intensity and mixed-phase microphysics, both of which are expected to change in a warming climate. Here we use the new Weather Research and Forecasting CONUS404 convection-permitting dataset covering October 1979 to September 2021 together with its companion Pseudo Global Warming simulation to assess changes in the Lightning Potential Index (LPI) with warming. This is, to our knowledge the first application of the LPI to these simulations. Using LPI together with several complementary lightning proxies, we characterize the spatial and seasonal structure of lightning activity across CONUS and quantify how it shifts under warming. Preliminary results show LPI broadly increases across most of CONUS, and ongoing work compares the response across indices and translates these changes into projected flash rate differences using observations from the Earth Networks Total Lightning Network. Together, these analyses provide new insight into where, when, and why lightning activity may change in a warmer climate, sharpening expectations of how convective hazards evolve across CONUS.

496204.title: The Architecture and Analysis of a Louisville Micronet Designed for Investigating the Urban Heat Island
496204.authors: Kylee Nunn, University of Louisville, Magnolia, KY
496204.abstract: Urban heat island (UHI) effects pose significant environmental and public health challenges across U.S. cities, where the proliferation of dark, impervious surfaces increases solar radiation absorption and elevates urban temperatures relative to surrounding rural areas. Beyond altering local climate conditions, UHI effects are known to exacerbate cardiovascular and respiratory morbidity among vulnerable populations. Louisville, Kentucky — known for an expansive and rapidly intensifying heat island — serves as the study site for the NASA-sponsored LOU-HEAT project, which aims to characterize UHI dynamics through both observations and a high-resolution numerical model, to inform targeted public health and urban planning interventions. By resolving how distinct land-use configurations influence thermal retention and cooling rates, this study aims to identify LCZs most susceptible to prolonged heat exposure. These findings are intended to support evidence-based municipal strategies — including targeted urban greening initiatives — to equitably mitigate UHI impacts across Louisville's communities. To quantify thermal variability across the urban landscape, a 30-station meteorological micro-network (“micronet”) was deployed throughout Louisville's urban and suburban areas. Stations were sited according to the Local Climate Zone (LCZ) classification framework, enabling systematic comparison of air temperature, humidity, heat index, and wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT) across land-use types ranging from dense built environments to vegetated suburban zones. Cellular data transmission was integrated at 20 of the stations to facilitate real-time data collection. Within this presentation, there will be an overview of the micronet design including instrumentation, site characteristics, and siting protocols. In addition, there will be an analysis of some preliminary data from the micronet. This will include a short section on instrument validation, as well as several case studies. For example, July 2, 2026, brought high temperatures as a large area of high pressure was established over the region. The micronet data indicates the warmest temperatures were recorded by the stations placed in the urban core. On this day, the greatest variability between stations was seen in the minimum temperatures, during the nighttime. Low temperatures in suburban regions were much cooler than those seen in the urban core.

496207.title: Filling the Gaps: Co-Developing Hydrometeorological Projections to Support US-Wide Water Security Initiatives
496207.authors: Andrew W. Wood, NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and M. Farahani, N. Mizukami, C. D. Frans, M. McGuire, and C. Mueller
496207.abstract: The US Secure Water Act of 2010 required several US agencies to report to Congress every five years on future water-related mission vulnerabilities. Over the last 15 years, 21st century global meteorological prediction datasets have been downscaled and used to drive hydrologic and streamflow scenarios across the Contiguous United States (CONUS). The resulting water-relevant datasets are designed to provide input for federal and state agency planning, guidance and policy, for water resources applications from watershed to regional scales, and for the water research community. We are co-developing new, updated century-scale predictions via a multi-agency effort that integrates Earth System researchers with partners from US federal water, weather, and energy agencies. Notably, the scientific approaches used in previous assessments have since revealed capability gaps that US agencies now seek to fill with newer, more robust methods and models. The current effort seeks to strengthen the scientific underpinnings of the prediction approach to increase the credibility and usability of resulting public datasets for use in planning and policy development. This objective required creating new AI-based strategies to improve continental-scale process-based (watershed-scale) hydrological modeling, as well as new multi-decadal high-resolution surface meteorology datasets and application-guided performance metrics to inform model training and evaluation. Several hundred future scenarios have been generated and tailored to provide Earth system indicators directly linked to water agency planning needs. This presentation summarizes this hydrometeorological dataset initiative and includes new century-scale prediction results for the Colorado River Basin, the Pacific Northwest, and other US regional river basins.

496209.title: From Open-Source to Community-Developed: Building a Sustainable Space Weather Modeling Ecosystem for MAGE
496209.authors: Michael Wiltberger, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. Merkin
496209.abstract: Open-sourcing a large geospace modeling framework is a necessary but insufficient step toward building the kind of sustained, community-owned infrastructure that space weather research increasingly demands. Here we argue that the next phase for frameworks like the Multiscale Atmosphere-Geospace Environment (MAGE) model must move beyond code access toward true community-developed governance, drawing directly on lessons from NSF NCAR's long-running stewardship of the Community Earth System Model (CESM) and the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS). Both efforts demonstrate that durable community models require more than a public repository: they need sustained support for onboarding new contributors, structured pathways for integrating externally developed modules, and coordinated software engineering practices that maintain scientific integrity as the number of contributing groups grows. This governance structure also creates a natural pathway for transitioning research advances into operations while preserving the ability to keep improving the model afterward — rather than forcing a choice between an operationally frozen model and one that improves but never stabilizes, community development allows new research capabilities to be integrated, tested, and matured toward operational readiness without severing the connection back to ongoing scientific advancement. A central priority is creating genuine on-ramps for graduate students and early-career researchers to progress from users to developers, through mentored contribution pathways, dedicated training, and recognition structures that value software contributions alongside traditional publication metrics. Realizing this vision requires dedicated software engineering support, clear governance for code review and module integration, and long-term funding that treats community model development as core scientific infrastructure. We contend that this transition directly addresses the Heliophysics decadal survey's call for a flagship-level community modeling program, with frameworks such as MAGE well positioned to serve as a proving ground for the governance, workforce development, and R2O2R practices such a program would require.

496212.title: A First Look at the Direct Covariance Flux System at Ocean Station Papa (50°N 145°W)
496212.authors: Carlos Hernandez Santiago, PMEL, Brunswick, ME; and M. F. Cronin, D. Zhang, J. B. Edson, and K. O. Fong
496212.abstract: Turbulent air-sea fluxes of momentum and heat are the primary means by which the ocean interacts with the atmosphere. These processes influence both local and global weather, climate, and oceanic and atmospheric patterns. They can be measured directly using the eddy covariance method, which measures air-sea fluxes from covarying high-frequency fluctuations in vertical motions together with horizontal winds and temperature. However, this method is technically complex, and requires expensive instrumentation to accurately measure the wind and temperature at high frequency, at 10-Hz or above. Thus for most observational and numerical applications, turbulent air-sea fluxes are estimated from meteorological and oceanic state variables using bulk algorithms. In 2025, NOAA’s Ocean Station Papa (50°N 145°W) was enhanced with a Direct Covariance Flux System, providing a unique opportunity to compare results from both methods. We analyzed differences between the directly measured and estimated fluxes between May and December 2025 in terms of measurement and instrument errors, as well as considering the effect of flow distortion on data quality. At low-to-moderate wind speeds (5–15 m/s), directly measured momentum fluxes showed increased variability not captured by the COARE 3.5 algorithm, suggesting the bulk algorithm could be underrepresenting momentum flux variability under these conditions. These direct flux measurements will support the refinement of bulk algorithm parameterizations, improving confidence in turbulent flux estimates used in coupled models and observational products.

496214.title: The Invisible Frontline in Practice: Public Libraries as Last-Mile Warning Partners
496214.authors: Brett William Robertson, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC; and F. Tu-Keefner, D. Lyons, and A. Hobbs
496214.abstract: Public libraries are among the most widely accessible public-facing institutions in the United States: tax-supported, open without eligibility requirements, staffed, and physically present in nearly every county. Decades of warning-response research have established that people rarely act on first receipt of an alert, whether a Wireless Emergency Alert, a broadcast warning, or a NOAA Weather Radio tone, and instead seek confirmation from trusted local sources before taking protective action. Libraries are exactly such a source, yet they sit outside the conventional integrated warning team, the chain running from forecast offices through emergency management and media to the public. They remain load-bearing after impact as well, supplying power, connectivity, and document services for federal assistance claims; in-person answers to questions the official channels have already nominally addressed; and direct support for government operations, including staffing Emergency Operations Centers. Libraries studied by the project team in San Diego, Houston, Kentucky, and South Carolina have provided these services during disaster response, including through bookmobiles and other mobile outreach that carry connectivity and information services directly into affected communities. Libraries are trusted organizations, often open when others are not, serving everyone who walks through the door. Yet library personnel receive minimal training in risk or crisis communication, and none in interpreting or translating forecast products, watches and warnings, or hazard information for the audiences who arrive seeking exactly that; even a typical Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) program rarely includes coursework in crisis communication, emergency preparedness, or risk management. This presentation reports on the design of the risk and crisis communication curriculum developed within Project Library PREPARE, an Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS)-funded national initiative building open-access disaster preparedness training for library personnel. The project’s evidence base comprises six field studies conducted by the research team between 2015 and 2024, spanning the South Carolina floods and Hurricane Matthew, Hurricane Harvey in Houston, the Northern California wildfires, Kentucky tornadoes and mountain flooding, and compound disasters in Southern California, together with practitioner surveys of health sciences library directors in which communication was rated the single most crucial competency for incoming librarians and yet simultaneously found new hires to be the least prepared. Recurring communication failure patterns emerge with direct relevance to the warning community: technical forecast, power-system, and infrastructure information relayed to the public without translation into plain, action-first language; the absence of a designated authoritative channel, so that emergency information scatters across accounts the public does not know to check; some libraries unable to post to their own social media because those accounts are controlled by a municipal or county office, with no pre-mapped chain of command for posting authority; internal breakdowns, especially in rural areas, that leave staff without the timely, accurate information needed to assist the public; and messaging that instructs without adjusting, telling people what to do while ignoring the emotional coping that research identifies as the second essential function of crisis messaging. The curriculum design translates that evidence into training across the library’s warning-relevant functions: pre-impact translation and amplification, impact-period service continuity, and post-impact recovery information. Thirteen essential competency clusters were mapped across the FEMA disaster lifecycle of preparedness, response, recovery, and mitigation, with each competency assigned to exactly one course to prevent overlap. Every course was built for asynchronous delivery through short video segments, downloadable toolkits and templates, scenario-based exercises, and pre- and post-tests aligned with the grant’s evaluation plan. Because library capacity varies enormously, the curriculum scales through three tiered pathways by library size plus a dedicated Rural Library Essentials pathway for personnel without professional credentials, an explicit acknowledgment that the staff most likely to serve as a community’s sole information point are the least likely to hold an MLIS degree. The risk and crisis communication module operationalizes this in four courses that move deliberately from theory to templates. A foundations course grounds staff in risk perception, the three trust dimensions of caring, competence, and honesty, negative dominance under stress, and the distinction between instructing and adjusting information. A planning course builds communication infrastructure before it is needed: a designated primary channel as the authoritative source with all other channels pointing to it, redundant backups, message templates developed and tested for the two or three hazards most likely to affect the service area, a defined communication officer role, and contingency procedures for channels the library does not control. A plain-language course trains staff to rewrite technical infrastructure and forecast messages, such as a power-outage notice or flood advisory, in unambiguous action-first language, design coordinated visual and text alerts readable at a glance, produce multilingual and accessible formats matched to a documented community profile, conduct usability testing with representative community members, and set update schedules that inform without overloading. A coordination course addresses message alignment protocols with emergency management, so that library communications amplify rather than compete with official information. It also covers collaboration with local National Weather Service forecast offices and professional associations to interpret technical forecast information, media relationships built before crisis, and sustained recovery-period messaging about shelters, FEMA assistance sites, and food distribution long after news attention moves on. For the warning community, libraries constitute an addressable, already networked, and already funded hub, particularly in rural jurisdictions where the library may be the only staffed public facility with reliable connectivity. Activating that hub requires what the curriculum builds: alignment protocols, posting authority mapped in advance, and staff trained to interpret and translate forecast products and warnings for the audiences that official channels reach last. The curriculum also positions libraries as natural candidates for formal roles the warning community has already established, such as Weather-Ready Nation Ambassadors. In return, libraries offer National Weather Service forecast offices and emergency managers documented community profiles, ground-truth on local impacts, and a standing venue for public outreach.

496215.title: High-Resolution Observations of Severe Convective Storms Using a Mobile C-Band Radar in Central Europe
496215.authors: Miloslav Stanek, Meteopress, Prague, Czech Republic; and F. Najman
496215.abstract: Mobile weather radars offer a flexible solution for targeted, high-resolution observations of severe convective storms. The Meteopress C-class is a mobile solid-state C-band radar designed to provide detailed measurements directly within areas of interest, allowing the scanning strategy to be adapted to the evolution and location of convective systems. During the storm season of 2026, the radar captured more than 20 significant convective weather events, including several strong supercells producing 5 cm hailstones. Particularly valuable were high-resolution observations of two tornadoes and several downbursts, providing detailed data on the structure and evolution of these small-scale and rapidly developing phenomena. The mobile configuration allowed measurements to be performed at a wide range of locations and enabled targeted observations of storms that would otherwise be difficult to monitor in sufficient detail. The most frequently used scanning strategy consisted of a PPI scan with 14 elevation angles combined with two selectable RHI azimuths. The RHI scans were directed toward the most interesting storm structures or areas with potentially hazardous convective phenomena. The collected dataset includes radar reflectivity, Doppler radial velocity, spectrum width, and polarimetric variables. These observations were also used to derive high-resolution meteorological products, including hydrometeor classification. The RHI measurements provided valuable information on the vertical structure of intense convection and enabled detailed analysis of storm features associated with tornadoes and downbursts. Dedicated software was developed to visualize the vertical observations and calculate derived radar products along vertical profiles. The results demonstrate the potential of the Meteopress C-class as a flexible mobile platform for high-resolution observations of severe convective storms. In particular, the observations of tornadoes and downbursts highlight the potential of mobile C-band radar to capture small-scale hazardous phenomena and provide detailed datasets for their subsequent meteorological analysis.

496221.title: Project EAGLE: An End-to-End Framework for AI Weather Modeling
496221.authors: Mariah Pope, Tomorrow.io, Boston, MA; and D. A. Burrows, A. Kumar, J. R. Carley, P. Madden, E. Carpenter, S. Frolov, T. Smith, and K. M. Blackman
496221.abstract: The introduction of artificial intelligence (AI)-based modeling for research and development often appears to have a high barrier to entry with little support or guidance on how to get started. To address this need, the Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC) has released the Experimental AI Global and Limited-area Ensemble (EAGLE) system that provides robust, reproducible, and user-friendly workflows to guide users through the development and operationalization of AI-based weather models. In this talk, we will go over the full AI pipeline, from initial dataset creation to running a skillful model in near-real-time operations. Users will be introduced to how to build and scale training datasets from cloud-based resources, train and verify graph-based models, and create a near-real-time forecast. Examples will include models known as global-eagle and nested-eagle, with instructions to run them on High-Performance Computing (HPC) machines and cloud-based resources. All tools are publicly available and complemented with proper documentation to ensure users will leave this session empowered to incorporate AI-based weather forecasting into their own research.

496222.title: Neutrally Buoyant Lagrangian Tracers for Observations in the Atmospheric Boundary Layer (Invited Presentation)
496222.authors: Claudia Elizabeth Brunner, Technical University of Munich, Garching, Bavaria, Germany; Max Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization, Göttingen, Lower Saxony, Germany; and A. Borra, M. Grunwald, F. Falkinhoff, G. Bagheri, and E. Bodenschatz
496222.abstract: Many important processes in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), such as mixing, dispersion and turbulent transport, are inherently Lagrangian. However, obtaining Lagrangian observations in the ABL is challenging, particularly over large spatial and temporal scales. Here, we present a novel measurement technique using neutrally buoyant radiosondes as Lagrangian tracers. The tracers follow the flow over many kilometers while recording meteorological properties at high spatial and temporal resolution. The radiosondes weigh 12 g and are attached to balloons filled with the precise amount of helium required to achieve neutral buoyancy at ground level. Their positions are determined using GPS, while wind speed and direction, temperature, pressure and relative humidity are recorded at 0.16 Hz. While line-of-sight is maintained, the data are continuously transmitted to a ground-based receiver station with a range of 45 km. The on-board battery allows for 1.5 hours of data transmission. Multiple tracers can be simultaneously released from a predetermined position using a drone, enabling observations along multiple trajectories within the same flow. We present the tracer design and results from a proof-of-concept field campaign at the WINSENT wind farm test site near Stuttgart, Germany, in October 2025. Seven tracers were successfully deployed in the wake of a wind turbine at mean wind speeds of 7–9 m/s under neutral stability conditions. The tracers travelled through two small wind farms while continuously recording their trajectories and meteorological conditions. We discuss the successes and shortcomings of the first field campaign and propose improvements for future measurement strategies. The results demonstrate the potential of neutrally buoyant radiosondes as a new approach for obtaining spatially and temporally resolved Lagrangian observations in the ABL.

496224.title: Computer Vision Derived Radar Extrapolation for Real-Time Hail Core Interception in Field Campaigns
496224.authors: Tobias G Schmidt, Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory, Western University, Canada, London, ON, Canada; and J. Brimelow
496224.abstract: Since 2022, the Canadian Severe Storm’s Laboratory’s (CSSL) Northern Hail Project has undertaken summer field campaigns. These, and other data, are being used to develop a hail climatology for Canada, contribute to broader hail science, and to validate radar hail products, numerical model output and hail sensors. During the summers of 2025 and 2026, a complicated endeavour (dubbed an “array deployment”) was routinely attempted where the field team would identify a target hailstorm and deploy an array of instruments (such as hail disdrometers) ahead of the approaching storm to collect data. Choosing a location to place the equipment such that the center of the storm’s hail core moves over the array is an incredibly difficult task requiring practice, skill, and luck. To reduce the amount of intensive decision making needed from human guidance, in 2026 the CSSL developed a computer vision (CV) derived storm-object-based composite radar tracking and extrapolation system with built-in storm intercept algorithm called the “CSSL Interceptor”. The system has an interactive graphical user interface (GUI) that was developed in-house which displays the expected storm arrival times, recommended driving routes, and optimal hail core intercept locations, all in real-time. The storm tracking tool has been shown to outperform other common composite radar extrapolation tools (e.g., optical flow), and the overall system has proven useful during several operational array deployments.

496226.title: Integrated Satellite Observations and WRF-Chem Analysis of Wildfire Smoke Transport and Vertical Structure During the March 2025 Crabapple Fire
496226.authors: Claire Collier, University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX; and A. Suresh, A. M. Mestas-Nunez, K. Bhaganagar, and X. Liu
496226.abstract: Satellite observations of trace gases and aerosols provide a unique capability to characterize wildfire smoke plumes across the horizontal, vertical, and temporal dimensions. This study investigates how smoke injection and detrainment influence the transport and evolution of nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), and particulate matter during the March 2025 Crabapple Fire in Central Texas. Multiple observational datasets are integrated to characterize plume evolution. TEMPO provides hourly NO2 column observations, while CrIS supplies vertically resolved CO profiles. Together, these measurements enable the plume to be examined across altitude and time of day. Ground-based Pandora and AERONET observations, surface PM2.5 observations from regulatory monitoring stations, and satellite-derived aerosol optical depth (AOD) provide complementary constraints on plume evolution and associated air quality impacts. Atmospheric trajectory modeling is applied to distinguish locally influenced near-surface smoke from elevated plumes transported over longer distances. To investigate the meteorological controls on smoke transport and chemical evolution, the analysis incorporates wind speed and direction, planetary boundary layer height, and precipitation. High-resolution simulations using the Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled with Chemistry (WRF-Chem) will be used to examine plume transport, vertical smoke distribution, detrainment height, and the evolution of fire-related pollutants. The simulations will be evaluated against satellite retrievals, ground-based observations, surface PM2.5 measurements, and atmospheric trajectory analyses. Preliminary analyses demonstrate that TEMPO captures the temporal evolution of the Crabapple Fire plume and, together with ground-based observations, provide a foundation for integrating vertically resolved satellite retrievals and WRF-Chem simulations to investigate smoke injection, transport, and detrainment.

496227.title: HealDA: Highlighting the Importance of Initial Errors in End-to-end AI Weather Forecasts
496227.authors: Aayush Gupta, NVIDIA, Santa Clara, CA; and A. Subramaniam, A. Carpentieri, M. Pritchard, K. Kashinath, C. C. Tong, S. Frolov, K. Lieberman, C. Miller, N. Silverman, and N. D. Brenowitz
496227.abstract: AI weather models now rival leading numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems in medium-range skill, but nearly all still rely on NWP data assimilation (DA) to provide their initial conditions. Recent AI DA systems are often trained and evaluated end to end with a particular forecast model, making it difficult to assess the quality of their analysis fields. HealDA instead focuses directly on the initial-condition problem: it maps a window of satellite and conventional observations to a global atmospheric analysis that can initialize off-the-shelf AI forecast models without joint training or fine-tuning. Here we present the latest HealDA system, which uses a spatiotemporal architecture to incorporate longer observation windows and adds infrared sounders to the observation suite. HealDA produces a global atmospheric analysis on an approximately 1° HEALPix grid in just over one second on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. When used to initialize FourCastNet3, the updated HealDA analyses reduce the effective lead-time gap relative to ERA5-initialized forecasts from 12–24 hours to 2–6 hours when verified against ERA5. The magnitude of this improvement varies across several downstream forecast models, including FourCastNet3, Aurora, and FengWu, but the central diagnosis remains consistent: within each model, HealDA- and ERA5-initialized forecasts exhibit comparable error-growth rates, so the remaining skill gap primarily reflects increased error in the HealDA analysis. Spectral analysis reveals that this stems from overfitting to the large scales and upper-tropospheric fields. HealDA thus provides a modular pathway from observations to global atmospheric analyses that can initialize multiple existing AI forecast models.

496229.title: Atmospheric Rivers on the North Slope of Alaska: DOE ARM Facility Observations of the Surface and Lower Troposphere Impulse
496229.authors: Raymond Thicklin, SIO, La Jolla, CA; and D. Lubin and X. Zou
496229.abstract: Atmospheric river (AR) frequency increases in the high Arctic bring the potential for enhanced sea ice loss, local flooding and infrastructure damage.
