The US Department of Energy (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Facility at the North Slope of Alaska (NSA) site, (Utqiagvik AK, 71.32ºN, 156.62ºW) offers a unique resource for studying the whole-atmosphere impact of ARs of varying strength and origin. The ARM microwave radiometer (MWR) measures precipitable water vapor (PWV) and cloud liquid water path (LWP), cloud lidars and radars measure the vertical extent and phase of cloud layers, and a network of surface radiometers measures the surface shortwave and longwave fluxes. We identified 92 ARs between 2017-2024, corresponding to the availability of the versatile new ARM THERMOCLDPHASE value-added product (VAP), which resolves the changes in cloud layering and liquid versus ice water content in clouds influenced by the passage of ARs. Most ARs originate from the south, brining warm and moist air either from the Bering Strait or the Aleutians. A second AR category originates from within the Arctic Ocean, either directly or along the Siberian coast. The impulses in cloud cover, precipitation, PWV, LWP and surface radiative fluxes are correlated with AR strength and origin, and there is also sensitivity to whether a southerly AR skirts the west coast of Alaska or proceeds overland to the NSA site. The multidecadal ARM NSA observations provide a resource for training both satellite remote sensing and numerical model forecasts of ARs in the high Arctic.

496233.title: Environmental Controls on Overshooting Convection and Hail Size
496233.authors: Rachael Auth, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and S. C. van den Heever
496233.abstract: Deep convective storms generate distinct cloud top features that are readily observed in satellite imagery. In particular, the detection of overshooting tops (OTs), which are produced when strong updrafts overshoot their level of neutral buoyancy, is often associated with severe weather at the surface, including tornadoes and large hail. There is both observational and modeling-based evidence for a relationship between hail size and updraft area, and OT “intensity” (area, depth, and volume) has been proposed as a proxy for updraft area. Thus, it follows that updraft size could be the physical link between OT intensity and hail size. Recent efforts to relate OT intensity metrics to hail size have produced contradictory results, with the skill of OT-based updraft strength metrics varying depending on the storm's environment, geographic region, season, and time of day. This environmental sensitivity is consistent with idealized supercell simulations showing that updraft area, hail residence times, and thus hail size are strongly modulated by CAPE and deep-layer shear. The goal of this study is to investigate how the relationship between OT intensity and hail size is modulated by storm environment. To accomplish this, we use a five-year database of tracked anvils and OTs derived from GOES-East Meso Sector Domain (MSD) data, augmented with co-located hail reports and environmental information from the ECMWF Re-Analysis v5 (ERA5). This approach allows us to build on previous work by characterizing the environmental conditions associated with overshooting convection that did or did not produce recorded hail. Preliminary results indicate statistically significant differences in how the OT intensity - hail size relationship varies across CAPE and shear regimes, geographic region, and seasonality. The implications of these results on the dynamics of hail producing vs non-hail producing storms will also be discussed.

496235.title: Mechanisms of Polar Low Development from a Shear Line
496235.authors: Kevin Boyd, University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, MA; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and J. D. Doyle and Z. Wang
496235.abstract: Polar lows (PLs) are intense maritime mesocyclones that develop during marine cold-air outbreaks over high-latitude oceans. PL genesis often occurs from finite-amplitude precursor disturbances, including shear lines that frequently form downstream of Svalbard as northerly flow interacts with the mountainous terrain. Despite their apparent importance, how precursor disturbances influence the mechanisms governing incipient PL development remains poorly understood. This study investigates the early development of a PL forming from a shear line near Svalbard during March 2024 using high-resolution (2 km) Polar WRF simulations. The objective is to clarify how barotropic, baroclinic, and convective processes interact during PL genesis and to assess their sensitivity to latent heating from condensation and surface heat and moisture fluxes. The shear line initially forms as a meridionally-oriented zone of strong horizontal shear embedded within the northerly flow, while surface fluxes enhance moist static energy (MSE) and support convective ascent along the feature. An east–west dipole in Q-vector forcing accompanies this structure, with eastward phase-shifted Q-vector convergence promoting propagation of the shear line and contributing to amplification of a protruding segment that later separates to form the PL. An eddy kinetic energy (EKE) budget reveals a two-stage development process. Early growth is driven primarily by barotropic energy extraction from the horizontal shear of the shear line, accompanied by convective deepening. As the circulation develops, growth transitions toward a moist-baroclinic stage in which convection interacts more effectively with vertical shear associated with atmospheric baroclinicity. Sensitivity experiments demonstrate that surface fluxes are essential for PL development by destabilizing the lower troposphere and sustaining moist convection while latent heating modestly strengthens the system by enhancing convection and baroclinicity through intensified frontogenesis. Overall, the results suggest that precursor disturbances such as shear lines facilitate PL genesis by providing a reservoir of eddy energy that can support subsequent growth under favorable environmental conditions.

496239.title: Three-Phase Machine Learning for PM:.s Forecasting: Benchmarking Against Deep Learning and Transformer Models
496239.authors: Rokeya Siddiqua, Morgan State University, Baltimore, MD; and X. Li, S. Bhatta, and M. Rahman
496239.abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is a major air pollutant of significant concern because of its adverse effects on human health, environmental quality, and overall air quality conditions, while its concentration can change rapidly in response to variations in atmospheric, meteorological, and temporal conditions. Accurate and temporally resolved PM2.5 forecasting is therefore essential for effective air quality management, public health protection, pollution-warning systems, environmental monitoring, and timely decision-making. However, reliable short-term PM2.5 prediction remains challenging because particulate concentrations are governed by complex and nonlinear interactions among meteorological conditions, atmospheric aerosol characteristics, temporal patterns, and local emission processes. Conventional ground-based monitoring networks provide valuable measurements but may not adequately capture the spatial and temporal variability required for high-resolution forecasting. The increasing availability of satellite-derived aerosol observations, particularly aerosol optical depth (AOD), provides an important complementary source of information that can enhance ground-based observations and improve the representation of atmospheric particulate conditions. Nevertheless, integrating multi-source environmental data introduces additional challenges related to temporal alignment, feature representation, nonlinear relationships, model complexity, and the realistic evaluation of forecasting performance. This study addresses these challenges by developing and systematically evaluating a three-phase machine learning framework for high-resolution PM2.5 forecasting that integrates satellite-derived AOD with ground-based meteorological observations and compares optimized conventional machine learning models with deep learning, hybrid, and Transformer-based architectures. The primary objectives of the study are to investigate the influence of temporal resolution on PM2.5 forecasting accuracy, determine whether systematic temporal and nonlinear feature engineering can improve predictive performance, identify the most informative predictors through feature selection, evaluate the relative performance of different machine learning approaches, and assess whether more complex deep learning and Transformer architectures provide meaningful advantages over optimized tree-based ensemble models. To accomplish these objectives, data from three monitoring stations in the DMV region—Howard, Padonia, and Beltsville—were collected for the period from 2019 to 2022 using publicly available U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) observations and GEO-LEO Dark Target satellite datasets. The satellite-derived AOD observations were integrated with ground-based meteorological and environmental variables to construct two datasets at 60-minute and 30-minute temporal resolutions, enabling a direct assessment of the effect of increased temporal granularity on forecasting performance. The proposed framework consists of three sequential phases: baseline modeling, temporal and nonlinear feature engineering, and feature selection. In the feature-engineering phase, lagged variables were introduced to capture temporal dependencies, rolling statistical features were generated to represent short-term variability and local trends, interaction features were incorporated to capture nonlinear relationships among predictors, and cyclic features were developed to represent recurring temporal patterns. These procedures expanded the predictor space to 87 variables, after which feature-importance analysis was applied to identify the 10 most informative predictors and construct optimized feature sets. Ten supervised machine learning algorithms representing linear, tree-based, boosting, and instance-based learning approaches were subsequently evaluated using both random train-test splitting and chronological TimeSeriesSplit validation. While random splitting was used to assess conventional predictive capability, chronological validation was emphasized to provide a more realistic evaluation of future forecasting performance and to reduce the potential for overly optimistic results caused by temporal dependence and information leakage. The optimized machine learning models were further benchmarked under time-series validation against eight deep learning and hybrid approaches, including recurrent neural networks, convolutional models, CNN-LSTM architectures, and STL-XGBoost, together with two structured Transformer configurations. Model performance was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (R2), mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE), providing complementary measures of explanatory power, average prediction error, overall error magnitude, and relative forecasting accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that increasing temporal resolution from 60 to 30 minutes consistently improves predictive performance across the evaluated models, indicating that higher-frequency integrated observations can provide more useful information for capturing short-term PM2.5 variability. The proposed temporal and nonlinear feature-engineering and feature-selection strategy also produces substantial improvements over baseline machine learning configurations. At the 30-minute temporal resolution, ensemble boosting methods, particularly CatBoost, XGBoost, and LightGBM, achieved R2 values of approximately 0.89–0.92 under random train-test splitting and 0.84–0.89 under chronological time-series validation, while simultaneously producing substantial reductions in RMSE and MAE compared with their corresponding baseline models. These results demonstrate that appropriate feature representation can be as important as algorithm selection for high-resolution PM2.5 forecasting. Although the deep learning, hybrid, and Transformer-based models demonstrated competitive predictive performance and were capable of learning complex temporal relationships, the optimized tree-based ensemble models achieved stronger overall predictive performance and more stable generalization under chronological validation. This finding suggests that increasing model architectural complexity does not necessarily translate into superior forecasting accuracy when conventional machine learning models are supported by carefully engineered and selectively refined predictors. Overall, the study demonstrates that an integrated multi-source forecasting strategy combining satellite-derived AOD, ground-based observations, systematic feature engineering, feature selection, and time-aware validation can provide an accurate, robust, and computationally practical approach to high-resolution PM2.5 forecasting. The findings further indicate that optimized tree-based ensemble methods can serve as effective alternatives to computationally intensive sequence-based deep learning and Transformer architectures, particularly when the primary objective is reliable future-oriented prediction rather than architectural complexity. The proposed framework also emphasizes the importance of evaluating environmental forecasting models under chronological validation, which provides a more realistic indication of their ability to generalize to unseen future observations. By combining high temporal resolution with multi-source environmental information and rigorous model comparison, this study contributes a practical and systematic framework for operational PM2.5 forecasting and provides useful evidence for the development of air quality monitoring, early-warning, environmental management, and public health decision-support applications.

496240.title: Improving NU-WRF Interannual Climate Predictions with Observed Land Surface Conditions
496240.authors: Xiaocheng Wei, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and L. Lu
496240.abstract: Land–atmosphere coupling varies with the prevailing hydroclimatic regime. Its representation in regional models is nevertheless limited using climatological vegetation properties and uncertainties in subsurface soil states. We examine whether observation-constrained leaf area index (LAI), soil moisture, and soil temperature improve NASA Unified Weather Research and Forecasting (NU-WRF) simulations over the south-central United States. Parallel experiments are conducted for three full calendar years representing wet, dry, and climatologically average conditions. Simulated daily minimum temperature, maximum temperature, and precipitation are verified against Global Historical Climatology Network–Daily (GHCNd) observations. Changes in model–observation differences are quantified relative to a control simulation, while associated changes in latent and sensible heat fluxes are analyzed to trace the surface-energy mechanisms underlying the atmospheric response. The spatial distribution and seasonal evolution of these responses are also examined in relation to root-zone soil moisture. Replacing climatological LAI with daily observation-based LAI consistently improves simulated near-surface temperature across contrasting hydroclimatic conditions. In the wet year, observation-based LAI reduces the domain-mean daily absolute difference from GHCNd on 77.5% of days for minimum temperature and 71.3% of days for maximum temperature. The corresponding frequencies in the average year are 68.1% and 71.0%. Improvements are strongest where the control simulation is warmer than GHCNd. Under these conditions, LAI-induced cooling moves approximately 52%–66% of grid-day temperature estimates closer to the observations. The temperature response reflects a physically consistent redistribution of surface energy: increased LAI enhances latent heat flux, suppresses sensible heat flux, and lowers near-surface air temperature. Its magnitude and spatial coherence depend on root-zone soil moisture, indicating that water availability regulates the atmospheric influence of LAI. Precipitation responses are less spatially coherent and vary with both the imposed land surface conditions and the hydroclimatic background. Overall, the results show that observation-constrained land surface states can reduce systematic temperature errors in NU-WRF and help identify when and where vegetation and subsurface information exert the strongest influence on simulated temperature and precipitation.

496241.title: Advancing Aviation-Based Monitoring of Ice Supersaturation for Contrail Avoidance under the TracerAir
496241.abstract: As part of NOAA’s recently launched TracerAir program, we introduce a new operational capability for monitoring the ice-supersaturated state of the upper troposphere during level flight. This initiative leverages the Measurements of Carbon and H2O (MACH1) system—an automated payload now deployed on commercial aircraft—to address critical data gaps in contrail formation modeling. The MACH1 system utilizes cavity ringdown spectroscopy, a closed-path technology uniquely suited for making measurements directly traceable to World Meteorological Organization (WMO) standards, ensuring exceptional calibration stability over extended operational periods. By averaging data over 2 minutes (~30 km horizontal resolution), the system achieves precisions near 9 ppm, which is sufficient to characterize water vapor concentrations between 20 and 200 ppm—the regime where ice-supersaturated areas conducive to persistent contrail formation are most likely to occur. This work is particularly relevant given emerging mandates requiring aircraft to avoid these regions over Europe, a strategy fundamentally dependent on accurate modeling of ice supersaturation. We demonstrate the efficacy of this new operational platform, marking a significant milestone in our ability to provide the consistent, validated data streams necessary for effective contrail avoidance and improved climate predictions. This presentation highlights the prospective global coverage of mid-range commercial observing networks, presents early operational results from recent in-service flights of the MACH1 system on the 737-900ER, outlines analytical methodologies and comparisons to other observations as well as discusses future scaling opportunities for the MACH1 payload architecture that will feature significantly enhanced precision and higher resolution measurements.

496243.title: Examining the Relationship between Extratropical Cyclones and Their Extremes In the SPEAR Large Ensemble.
496243.authors: Rachel R. McCrary, NCAR, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Stuivenvolt-Allen, M. R. Tye, J. Lave, M. Igbinoba, and C. M. Zarzycki
496243.abstract: Extratropical cyclones (ETCs) are a dominant driver of high-impact weather across North America, producing extreme precipitation, snowfall, and damaging winds. Understanding how ETC characteristics (e.g., frequency, intensity, and spatial distribution) relate to precipitation, snowfall, and wind extremes is critical for anticipating hydroclimate risk on multi-decadal timescales. This study uses the GFDL SPEAR (Seamless System for Prediction and EArth System Research) 30-member large ensemble to examine ETCs and their associated extremes over North America. The large ensemble framework allows us to examine robust relationships between ETCs, extremes, and modes of variability that are challenging to isolate in the relatively short observational record. ETC-associated extremes are evaluated by linking cyclone tracks to co-located precipitation, snowfall, and wind extremes, allowing us to quantify the fraction of extreme events attributable to ETC activity across the IPCC AR6 SREX regions. We further assess how ETC frequency and intensity, along with their associated extremes, vary with the phase of key modes of variability, including El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Pacific-North American Pattern (PNA), and the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO). Preliminary results indicate that SPEAR well reproduces the spatial variability, frequency, and intensity of cool-season ETCs over North America when compared to ERA5. Interestingly, in SPEAR, ENSO is strongly related to cold-season variability in ETC frequency over North America, a relationship that is attenuated in ERA5. Potential reasons for this will be discussed and are a subject of ongoing work. In general, this work seeks to identify whether sensible weather impacts have discernible connections to oceanic and atmospheric modes of variability, which may provide information relevant for probabilistic weather outlooks.

496247.title: New Developments to Improve and Generalize the Multigrid Beta Filter (MGBF) for Data Assimilation.
496247.authors: Robert J. Purser, Lynker@ NOAA/NWS/OMD, Riverdale Park, MD; and M. Rancic, M. S. F. V. Pondeca, T. Lei, and G. Zhao
496247.abstract: The Multigrid Beta Filter (MGBF) was initially developed to provide efficiently parallelizable and adaptive covariance operators for the Real-Time Mesoscale Analysis (RTMA) and later extended to serve as the localization operator for ensemble-based data assimilation. Since its inception there have been some important recent technical developments and changes to the algorithm’s architecture to further improve its computational efficiency, to extend its range of available covariance shapes, and to facilitate the normalization and the apportioning of the scale weights of the different quasi-Gaussian beta-distribution filters that the multigrid algorithm combines. Efficiency is being improved by exploiting a useful numerical property of the staggering between the consecutive multi-grids, a factor of two apart in resolution, which enables simpler multilinear linear interpolation stencils to be applied without distorting the quasi-Gaussian filter kernel shapes, except for a uniform fractional reduction in amplitude and a corresponding fractional increase in spatial spread, both of which can be almost exactly compensated for within the new algorithm. The range of available covariance shapes is being extended by introducing a self-contained vertical multigrid element to the algorithm. The scale weights allocated to each quasi-Gaussian filter contribution can be derived automatically from a conditional least squares best-fitting procedure, given the desired target horizontal and vertical covariance profiles and amplitudes at each location. The organization of the new algorithm, by splitting the scale weights and applying the square-root of them before and after the filtering process, enables exact normalization of each filter component, eliminating the need for the laborious iterative weight adjustments that the original algorithm required. Another development is the Multigrid Graph Filter (MGGF) which represents a graph-theoretic extension of the ideas behind the MGBF for arbitrary graph-based finite-volume meshes. The proposed formulation replaces structured-grid geometry with graph connectivity while preserving the multilevel covariance principles of the original MGBF. Graph aggregation, along with conservative inter-generation transfer operators, provide a unified multiscale covariance framework capable of representing local, regional, and planetary correlations on arbitrary unstructured meshes. Preliminary numerical experiments on hexagonal–pentagonal icosahedral meshes demonstrate multilevel covariance smoothing, localized impulse responses, and robust behavior near the unavoidable pentagonal topological defects inherent to icosahedral meshes. Because the proposed formulation depends only on graph connectivity, it is directly applicable to modern unstructured atmospheric models, such as the MPAS based on Voronoi tessellations.

496249.title: Comparison of Surface Roughness and Canopy Model Approaches In Large Eddy Simulations for Characterizing Turbulence In a Real Canopy Clearing
496249.authors: Eric A. Hendricks, NCAR, Boulder, CA; and C. M. Rozoff and J. C. Knievel
496249.abstract: Clearings in tree canopies are ubiquitous across the United States, including at range facilities, due to both natural and man-made (e.g., roads, farmland, ecosystem and forest management) variations in land cover. Boundary-layer flows over these clearings are difficult to characterize because of sharp transitions between plant canopies of variable height and clearings of low surface roughness. Many clearings also lie in undulating terrain or near large water bodies, where mesoscale flows add further complexity. In large-eddy simulations (LESs), canopy layers and clearings are typically represented in one of two ways. In the first approach, they are parameterized by regions of different surface roughness lengths with usage of similarity theory. This method is somewhat crude in that porosity of the vegetation is not accounted for and vegetation types are assumed flat and horizontally homogeneous. In the second approach, the canopy layer is explicitly resolved in three dimensions using 3D leaf area densities (LADs), and momentum sink terms are included in the prognostic equations to more realistically account for the drag. As LES moves toward finer horizontal and vertical resolutions (grid spacings of approximate 1-5 m), the latter approach is expected to produce more realistic simulations of winds and turbulence. We use a mesoscale-driven LES to examine both approaches for a case study of flow over a real canopy clearing near the mid-Atlantic U.S. coast. Nested Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations drive nested FastEddy® LES (with 12 m and 3 m isotropic low-level grid spacings, respectively) over a clearing roughly 1 km across. In the first approach, horizontally-varying surface roughness lengths are determined from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD). In the second approach, a real, seasonally-dependent NLCD 2D leaf area index (LAI) to 3D LAD pre-processing procedure is used. A key feature of this procedure is beta-function vertical profiles to account for the top or bottom heaviness of each vegetation type. Both approaches are compared with each other and evaluated using near-surface observations of winds and turbulence in the clearing. The results clarify the limitations of the surface roughness approach for very-high-resolution LES of canopy layers and highlight opportunities for explicit canopy layer resolving simulations with realistic 3D LADs.

496254.title: On the Detection of Rapid Drought Change Across the United States
496254.presenter: Leeper, Ronald D., MA in Geoscience and GIS Certificate
496254.authors: Ronald D. Leeper, MA in Geoscience and GIS Certificate, North Carolina State Univ. CISESS, Asheville, NC; and E. L. Scott and G. F. Thompson
496254.abstract: The impacts of drought on agricultural productivity, water security, and risks of extreme heat and wildfire have been well established. However, when drought rapidly changes it reduces the response time of decision makers and limits the effectiveness of mitigation strategies. This is not only the case during periods of rapid intensification, described as flash droughts, but also during periods of rapid improvement (i.e., flash amelioration) that can lead to whiplash events such as drought to flash flooding, which over areas of fire hardened surfaces elevate the risks of landslides. The primary goal of this study is to characterize the frequency, spatial extent of and atmospheric conditions conducive for both worsening and improving rapid drought change (RDC) across the U.S. RDC events will be identified from commonly used drought indices including the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), and Evaporative Demand Drought Index (EDDI) with a particularly focus on multi-indicator detection of RDC events. In addition, RDC events were matched with upper atmospheric conditions 1 to 2-weeks prior to identify synoptic patterns conducive to RDC development. Given the importance of inter-annual and inter-seasonal modes of variability on U.S. precipitation patterns and possible links to RDC, the El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and Madden Julian Oscillation (MJO) will also be explored as potential indicators of RDC risk.

496257.title: U.S. Geological Survey Geoelectromagnetic Monitoring, Surveying, and Modeling in Support of Space Weather Hazard Estimation and Mapping
496257.authors: E. Joshua Rigler, USGS, Denver, CO
496257.abstract: We summarize recent and planned updates to data and services provided by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Geomagnetism Program at the Geological Hazards Science Center in Golden, Colorado, as well as related targeted research results and collaborative projects. Currently, the USGS Geomagnetism Program measures ground-level magnetic field variations continuously at over a dozen magnetic observatories, disseminating these geomagnetic data in near real time to government agencies, academic institutions, and the public for purposes of space weather monitoring and geomagnetic field mapping. Since 2022, the President's budget has supported updates to, and a modest expansion of, geomagnetic field monitoring operations. New observatory-grade 3-axis vector magnetometers are replacing legacy sensors at all observatory sites, while modern industrial data acquisition systems designed to increase reliability and timeliness of geomagnetic measurements have replaced nearly all legacy USGS observatory systems. In addition, and in collaboration with the USGS Albuquerque Seismological Laboratory, low-cost off-the-shelf magnetic variometers have been co-deployed at a significant and growing subset of existing seismic monitoring stations, with an emphasis on improving near real time geomagnetic data coverage of the conterminous United States (CONUS). In 2024, the USGS funded completion of a long-period magnetotelluric (MT) survey of CONUS, a project initiated by the National Science Foundation's EarthScope program (2006-2018), and additionally supported by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA, 2019). Early analysis of these data indicated a compelling need for higher spatial resolution and broadband MT surveys near population centers along the U.S. eastern seaboard whose bulk electric system infrastructure is at risk from geomagnetic storms. The USGS is currently conducting a targeted MT survey of this region to address this need. Finally, the Geomagnetism Program works closely with the Space Weather Prediction Center of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to support, validate, and improve their real-time geoelectric field mapping capability by integrating the latest and highest quality geomagnetic and MT data and modeling. All these efforts improve scientific understanding of, and the ability to mitigate, hazards that impact critical U.S. infrastructure.

496258.title: A Multi-Method Framework for Analyzing Historical and Future Elevation Dependent Warming
496258.authors: Yasir Latif, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and S. C. Pryor
496258.abstract: There is evidence of amplification of warming rates in high altitude regions (elevation dependent warming, EDW). Given the importance of high-altitude glaciers to regional water supply, there is an urgent need to better quantify the presence/absence and mechanisms of EDW and for both near-future and far-future temperature projections for mountainous regions to enable robust predictions of the hydrology of glacier- and snow-fed basins and their downstream impacts. This research focusses on High Mountains Asia (HMA) and specifically Pakistan which exhibits notable topographic and temperature variability and includes temperature-sensitive river basins that play a key role in determining the probability and magnitude of downstream flooding. Long-term measurements from 36 sites are used to quantify EDW in this region and to examine evidence for non-linear dependence on altitude. This study investigates EDW using the Coupled Model Inter comparison Project phase 6 (CMIP6) model simulations. We analyze historical (1981-2014) and future (2015-2100) temperature trends under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) 2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, examining the relationship between surface temperature trends and orography (surface elevation) across the region. Then we compare near-term (mid-century) and long-term (end of century) projections from the CMIP6 under the SSP5-8.5 scenario to examine how the EDW is related to (or not) the overall climate sensitivity. Finally, near-term predictions of site-specific modeled near-surface air temperatures are developed using a machine learning Seasonal Auto Regression Integrated Moving Average (SARIMA) model that accounts for secular trends and other periodicities. Analyses of the historical observations indicates mean and median warming rates (1973-2020) of 0.18 and 0.17 °C/decade which are very close to the global mean temperature trend. EDW is also manifest in thee records with the 11 sites above 1.2 km exhibiting positive trends and the median trend is 0.23 °C/decade. However, some high-elevation stations exhibit trends that either negative or close to zero indicating EDW is not universal. Diagnostics from the Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average SARIMA model and other decomposition tools applied to the observations suggest that sites with clear elevation amplification of warming is due to the loss of cold season low temperatures consistent with snow/ice removal. The three CMIP6-generation ESMs; GFDL, MPI and CanESM5 exhibit transient climate responses of that span from 2.75 °C (CanESM5) to 1.57 °C (MPI). CanESM5 also exhibit largest regional air temperature trends over HMA, but EDW is not more pronounced in this model, and both GFDL and MPI exhibit regions of net cooling in both the historical simulations and the near-term. Funding: This project was supported by the Eric and Wendy Schmidt AI in Science Postdoctoral Fellowship, a program of Schmidt Sciences, LLC awarded to Yasir Latif.

496259.title: Modeling the Stratospheric Impacts of the 2019/2020 Australian Fires with GEOS-Chem
496259.authors: William James Julstrom, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; and X. Chen, D. A. Peterson, and J. Wang
496259.abstract: In late 2019 and early 2020, a major pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) outbreak in southeastern Australia, known as the Australian New Year Super Outbreak (ANYSO), injected ~0.9 Tg of smoke aerosol into the Upper Troposphere and Lower Stratosphere (UTLS), producing substantial perturbations to stratospheric halogen chemistry and ozone. Previous studies have primarily focused on heterogeneous chemistry occurring on smoke aerosol, while the contribution of gas-phase emissions to the chemical evolution of pyroCb plumes remains less well constrained. Here, we use the GEOS-Chem Chemical Transport Model (CTM) with a custom emission inventory specifying the locations, times, and altitudes of ANYSO injections. We modify the stratospheric chemistry scheme to represent heterogeneous reactions occurring on pyroCb smoke and conduct sensitivity simulations using biomass-burning gas-phase emissions based on both Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED4) emission factors and empirical emission factors derived from observations during the FIREX-AQ field campaign. We additionally evaluate the sensitivity of simulated ozone to uncertainties in pyroCb smoke optical properties using aerosol properties calculated with a Mie core-shell model for internally and externally mixed smoke. We find that uncertainties in smoke optical properties produce negligible changes in simulated UTLS ozone. In contrast, gas-phase emissions from the ANYSO plume produce a non-negligible increase in midlatitude UTLS ozone shortly after injection, although this enhancement is substantially smaller than the ozone depletion driven by heterogeneous chemistry on smoke aerosol. These results demonstrate that both gas-phase emissions and heterogeneous chemistry must be represented to accurately simulate the stratospheric chemical impacts of pyroCb smoke, while uncertainties in smoke optical properties have a comparatively minor influence on the resulting ozone perturbation.

496261.title: MJO Prediction and Understanding in the Era of Superparameterization (Invited Presentation)
496261.authors: James J. Benedict, LANL, White Rock, NM; Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM
496261.abstract: The Madden-Julian oscillation (MJO) is complicated. Multiscale interactions across space and time among clouds, moisture, radiation, surface fluxes, and winds are hallmark features of the MJO. Many of these key processes are unable to be explicitly resolved in conventional Earth system models (ESMs) and therefore must be parameterized. The parameterizations reflect our best understanding of the collective effects of a particular subgrid-scale process on the resolved scale. However, this approach can neglect, or at least crudely represent, important subgrid-scale process interactions across space and time. In this sense, for the MJO, the details matter. The physical limitations and slow progress of conventional parameterization development were recognized by Dave and colleagues nearly 30 years ago, and motivated an alternative approach–superparameterization (SP), later the multiscale modeling framework (MMF)–in which a cloud system-resolving model (CSRM) is embedded within each ESM grid cell as a replacement for cloud, turbulence, and boundary layer schemes. SP captures many small-scale phenomena with greater fidelity, injects mesoscale organization and temporal memory into the system, and permits a more natural evolution of process interactions. Ultimately, SP has been shown to improve the sensitivity of convection to environmental moisture, cloud-radiation interactions, and the shallow-to-deep convective heating evolution of the MJO. Greater realism of small-scale processes also drives more accurate coupling to the large-scale circulation and accompanying moisture advection, which are known to be mechanistically critical for the MJO. As a graduate student with Dave, I was fortunate to witness firsthand the early development, evaluation, and advancement of SP and its role in MJO studies. SP has not only improved many aspects of organized tropical convection prediction, it has accelerated our understanding and led to new insights into the physical mechanisms that underpin the MJO. This presentation will highlight some of these achievements and the lasting interest in SP from the MJO and wider ESM communities.

496265.title: Beyond 0.1 Inches: Regionally Calibrated, Multi-Parameter Thresholds for Classifying Dry Lightning in the Western United States
496265.authors: Alex Weirauch, DRI, Reno, NV; and T. J. Brown and D. J. McEvoy
496265.abstract: Lightning Induced Wildfires (LIW) account for hundreds of thousands of acres burned every year in the Western United States. Dry lightning, lightning accompanied by little-to-no precipitation, is the predominant driver of those LIW events. There is no formal definition of what precipitation amount threshold should be used to classify dry lightning events and the generally used threshold of 0.1" has not held up universally. Our study proposes unification of key weather parameters across ecohydrological biomes (EPA Level III) and variable multi-parameter thresholds by region. For example, a mixed-forest dominated Level III ecoregion can sustain ignition despite higher total precipitation and precipitation rates than an arid sagebrush-steppe ecoregion. A fire occurrence database will be matched to "lightning-caused" wildfire events initially up to two weeks of the ignition date (to account for holdover fires) and within ten miles of the ignition point. Environmental conditions are characterized using surface-based conditions, and atmospheric profile including temperature, relative humidity, precipitation, dewpoint depression at multiple levels, and convective available potential energy (CAPE), obtained from the California and Nevada Smoke and Air Committee (CANSAC) reanalysis data and supplemented with fuel moisture data using gridMET and nearby data from the Remote Automatic Weather Station (RAWS) network where available. From this data, we derive multi-parameter fire ignition thresholds for each region, distinguishing acute ignitions from holdover fires. Preliminary analysis covers California and Nevada fires since 2016, with expansion planned across the full study domain. This presentation examines where single-threshold approaches (total precipitation of less than 0.1") break down, with emphasis on case study fires, and demonstrates which regionally calibrated, multi-parameter thresholds improve the detection and classification of dry lightning fire events.

496267.title: Marine Fog as a Non-Equilibrium Boundary-Layer System: Intermittency and Time Irreversibility (Invited Presentation)
496267.authors: Kelly Y Huang, University of Houston, Houston, TX; and F. Pesenti, H. Motalebi, R. Niraula, T. Hintz, J. Ruiz-Plancarte, Q. Wang, G. G. Katul, and H. J. S. Fernando
496267.abstract: Marine fog emerges from interactions among processes spanning synoptic forcing to droplet microphysics, mediated by air–sea exchange, surface heterogeneity, and boundary-layer turbulence. This multiscale coupling makes the formation, persistence, and dissipation of marine fog particularly difficult to predict. The Fog and Turbulence Interactions in the Marine Atmosphere–Grand Banks (FATIMA-GB) campaign provided densely instrumented observations on Sable Island, Canada, in one of the world's foggiest marine environments, and demonstrated that the conventional conceptual model of warm, moist air advecting over colder water does not account for observed genesis pathways. Among the campaign's findings, a fog-genesis event in which the evening transition over the island's ocean–land discontinuity produced interacting internal and marine boundary layers — generating a low-level cloud 30–50 m above the surface that subsequently mixed downward to form surface fog — illustrated that fog can arise from the coupled evolution of surface forcing, stratification, moisture, and turbulence rather than from a single thermodynamic threshold. Here we ask whether common dynamical characteristics emerge across fog events despite differences in their formation mechanisms. High-frequency visibility, relative humidity (RH), and turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) measurements reveal pronounced intermittency in fog occurrence: quiescent-phase durations, power spectra, and amplitude distributions follow power laws consistent with Pomeau–Manneville Type-III (sporadically random) dynamics, with RH and TKE bounding the stochastic features of visibility as the activating and deactivating influences, respectively. Extending the analysis across more than 20 fog events, we find that fog intensity (inverse visibility) is strongly time-irreversible at every stage of the life cycle, whereas TKE remains nearly reversible. The directional structure of fog is therefore not inherited from turbulence energetics; fog is a measurably non-equilibrium system. Moreover, the lead–lag relationship between turbulence and fog reverses systematically over the life cycle: TKE leads fog intensity during formation, the coupling becomes approximately symmetric in the mature stage, and fog intensity leads TKE during dissipation. Notably, in formation, the degree of fog irreversibility increases linearly with the strength of its causal coupling to TKE, indicating that onset is governed by a directional sequence of turbulence–moisture interactions, whereas dissipation is consistent with threshold-like initiation by turbulence rather than continuous turbulent control. Together, these observations frame marine fog as an intermittent, non-equilibrium, and directionally evolving boundary-layer system. The stage-dependence of the coupling carries a direct forecasting consequence: turbulence holds precursor information for fog onset, while during dissipation the information flow reverses. These statistics — intermittency scalings, irreversibility, and stage-dependent directionality — define the empirical constraints that stochastic descriptions of the fog life cycle must satisfy, and connect event-scale physical mechanisms to the representation of multiscale boundary-layer interactions in fog prediction.

496272.title: Technological Innovations that Impact Decision Support Services in the Aviation Sector (Invited Presentation)
496272.authors: Heather D. Reeves, Retired, Saginaw, MI
496272.abstract: The observational and modeling landscape surrounding the aviation sector is in the midst of profound change and advancement. Many of the new technologies being developed have the potential to radically change Impacts-based Decision Support Systems and, to an extent, beg the aviation community to reconsider whether new forms of decision support are ready to be developed and deployed. Among the new technologies that will be discussed are the expanded RadarNext system, 3D mesonets, the use of uncertified surface observations, AI forecasting, and the fusion of these various systems into a common grid/interrogation system.

496275.title: The NOAA NWP Moonshot: Planning for the Infrastructure and Scientific Needs
496275.authors: Curtis R. Alexander, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and K. Garrett and J. E. Ten Hoeve III
496275.abstract: NOAA’s NWP Moonshot has several goals including a single, high-resolution convection-allowing physics-based global ensemble system with advanced data assimilation – using the MPAS dynamical core and JEDI data assimilation components. This presentation will provide an overview of this goal’s sub-team structure, organizational representation and planning milestones that will support this and other Moonshot goals. This information will include infrastructure priorities of Model Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) integration into the UFS framework and reproduction of Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) capabilities using the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework. In addition to these infrastructure needs, planning for convergence of regional and global model physics suites and atmospheric composition capabilities will be discussed. Finally, bringing together some of these milestones into a future MPAS-JEDI based Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) operational transition as a major stepping stone towards realizing this NWP Moonshot goal.

496278.title: Machine Learning-Based Estimation of Snow Depth from Snow Water Equivalent
496278.authors: Mukul Tewari, University at Albany, Albany, NY; and S. Basu
496278.abstract: Seasonal snow depth is an important indicator of snowpack evolution and water availability. However, direct observations of snow depth and snow water equivalent (SWE) are often spatially sparse and operationally difficult to obtain. This study investigates whether snow depth can be estimated from SWE and routinely available meteorological observations using machine learning applied to the New York State Mesonet. We address three questions: (1) How accurately can snow depth be estimated from SWE when information on snowpack evolution, atmospheric conditions, and site characteristics is available? (2) Which physical controls, including SWE history, temperature, precipitation, terrain, vegetation, climatology, and geographic setting, provide transferable information about snow depth? (3) How well do different machine-learning frameworks generalize across time and to locations not represented during training? Addressing these questions will help determine whether existing SWE and meteorological observing networks can provide more spatially complete information on snowpack state without requiring collocated snow-depth measurements at every location. We will evaluate traditional bagging and boosting methods together with state-of-the-art tabular foundation models using several years of collocated SWE, snow-depth, and high-frequency meteorological observations. The numerical experiments will progressively assess the contributions of current and lagged SWE, changes in SWE, thermal and precipitation history, soil and frozen-ground conditions, and seasonal and geographic information. Controlled feature-ablation and augmentation experiments will also examine the added value of embeddings from geo-foundation models. Performance will be evaluated using independent water-year validation and testing, together with leave-one-station-out cross-validation, to quantify temporal robustness and spatial transferability. The resulting framework will identify the minimum observational information needed for reliable SWE-to-snow-depth estimation and provide a foundation for improved snow monitoring, hydrologic forecasting, and future operational decision-support applications.

496281.title: NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training (ARSET) for Decision Making
496281.authors: Sherrie Secunda Morris, Science and Technology Corporation, Greenbelt, MD; and B. Blevins, M. B. Follette-Cook, and A. Carleton-Hug
496281.abstract: For over 15 years, NASA’s Applied Remote Sensing Training (ARSET) Program has offered no-cost training on Earth observation data and products to support Earth science applications, decision-making, and professional development. Tailored to beginner, intermediate, and advanced skill levels, these trainings range from the fundamentals of satellite observations to data processing, analytical methods, and the hands-on application of available web-based tools. ARSET instructors use targeted learning objectives to develop training modules that guide participants through analyzing and applying open-source satellite data across six thematic areas: agriculture, disasters, ecological conservation, health and air quality, water resources, and wildland fires. Developed by subject matter experts and instructional designers, our training sessions are offered in self-paced, in-person, and live online formats. Almost one-third of these sessions are available in Spanish. In 2025, ARSET reached over 29,000 data users across 176 countries and 8,000 organizations, including 5,000 organizations attending for the first time. This presentation will highlight past and upcoming trainings, sharing participant feedback and lessons learned. We will also detail our structured training production process, which includes identifying high-interest topics, developing learning objectives, collaborating with experts, and executing strategic outreach to engage current and new users. Finally, we will demonstrate how ARSET has improved participants' understanding of data, models, and coding languages by helping them acquire the skills to produce images and maps, make informed decisions, and effectively communicate risks to impacted communities.

496284.title: Quantifying Sub-Utility Scale Grid Vulnerability for Weather Driven Outages
496284.authors: Cameron David Gilbert, University at Albany, Albany, NY; and K. J. Sulia, C. D. Thorncroft, and N. P. Bassill
496284.abstract: Electrical outages are responsible for significant amounts of damages to life and property across the United States. Weather events were responsible for roughly 80% of all major outages across the United States from 2003-2023 (Climate Central, 2024). In this study, we attempt to quantify the vulnerability of specific locations in grid infrastructure with respect to different meteorological conditions. Using component-level grid data, a historical outage record, observations from the New York State Mesonet, and HRRR forecast data from across New York’s Hudson Valley, we characterize weather conditions during and just before each outage. Using variables such as temperature, dew point, wind speed, wind gusts, among others, we examine the conditions in which outages are most likely to occur. Working at a sub-utility scale, investigating districts and select individual feeders, we pinpoint locations of the grid that are most at risk to specific types of weather. Assessing grid resilience at small scales allows utility companies to preposition repair crews to increase repair speed or invest in infrastructure that reduces the chances of outages in high-risk locations.

496292.title: SOAR (Sustained Observations for Atmospheric Resilience): Reference-Grade Aerosol Instrument Packages for Unattended Operation on Commercial Ships
496292.authors: Paige E Brocidiacono, SilverLining, Washington, DC, DC; and S. Schubert, K. Carslaw, A. Andrews, and T. Ryerson
496292.abstract: Progress on the physical mechanisms of aerosol-cloud interactions has reduced uncertainty in climate forcing, but the remaining uncertainty is concentrated over the ocean, where sustained, multi-parameter, in-situ measurements are largely absent. Ground networks are land-concentrated and largely single-parameter; satellites cannot adequately resolve the vertical column or retrieve the aerosol properties governing aerosol-cloud interactions, and over open ocean their retrievals require surface reference data that rarely exists; research vessels and aircraft deliver reference-quality data only in short campaign windows at great expense, and often target unusual conditions of specific scientific interest; and full observatories such as DOE's ARM cost millions per site, precluding the spatial density needed to constrain global models. Prior synthesis efforts such as GASSP (Global Aerosol Synthesis and Science Project) demonstrate the consequence: models fitting existing data equally well still diverge sharply in projections, because compensating process errors are indistinguishable without co-located, multi-parameter measurements. We present SOAR (Sustained Observations for Atmospheric Resilience), an approach to closing this gap using commercial vessels as measurement platforms. Container ships transit fixed, repeating routes across undersampled ocean regions, including the near-pristine environments GASSP identified as among the most valuable for constraining climate prediction, and they are relatively insensitive to instrument weight, space, and power. Reference-grade packages engineered to operate unattended measure aerosol microphysical and optical properties (e.g. aerosol number concentration, size distribution, and spectral scattering and absorption), greenhouse gases, radiation, and marine meteorology, with instrument cost spread across years of operation instead of a single cruise. Payload selection optimizes simultaneously for scientific value, reference-standard traceability, autonomous operability, and unit cost, drawing on the NOAA Federated Aerosol Network's heritage of standardized aerosol optical measurements and on priorities identified by the DOE BEACONS project. Calibration follows WMO GAW procedures with pre- and post-deployment characterization in collaboration with NOAA GML and DOE. Building on validated pilots including the CRESST aerosol campaign and Maersk shipboard deployments with NOAA and NASA collaborators, we report on what sustained unattended operation requires: inlet performance, exhaust plume contamination and flagging, calibration drift between port calls, and service intervals achievable through modular package swaps during normal vessel turnaround. We also discuss the measurement gaps that most constrain the current package for aerosol-cloud process studies. Two analysis strategies shape how the network grows and how its data is leveraged. Perturbed parameter ensemble analysis identifies which uncertain model parameters drive remaining aerosol forcing uncertainty and where measurements would most effectively constrain them, providing a quantitative basis for which measurements, in which regions and seasons, most effectively reduce forcing uncertainty. PRISM (Physics Regime Informed State Mapping), a physics-informed framework, extends the reach of individual observations by fusing in-situ and satellite data with model simulations, propagating measurement influence according to flow-dependent physical regimes. Closing aerosol-cloud process gaps will require measurements that are not only accurate but sustained, spanning the range of marine conditions and continuing long enough to build statistics across regimes and seasons; commercial vessels offer a route to that record over the ocean regions where it is most needed.

496293.title: Siple Dome in West Antarctica: A Surprisingly Accessible Natural Laboratory for Studies in Cloud Physics and Radiation
496293.authors: Dan Lubin, SIO, La Jolla, CA; and X. Zou, M. A. Lazzara, and T. Norton
496293.abstract: Siple Dome Field Camp (81.65ºS, 149.01ºW ) is operated regularly during the austral summer by the United States Antarctic Program. At 730-m msl elevation, this site features mild polar meteorological conditions and frequent low level mixed-phase cloud cover in the world's most pristine cold weather environment. These conditions are a marked contrast from the turbulent Southern Ocean and thus offer potential advantages for observing first principles of cloud microphysical evolution. We report on a successful pilot field campaign during 2019-2020 using surface radiometric measurements and spectroscopic remote sensing of cloud microphysical and optical properties. These data are used to evaluate the performance of the Polar Weather Research and Forecasting (PWRF) model using the Thompson aerosol-aware cloud microphysics parameterization. Two case studies within our dataset are of particular interest. The first is a moderate squall driven by a low-pressure system over the eastern Ross Sea that brought warm and moist air, along with wind speeds of up to 12 meters per second over the field camp. The second is a sequence of mixed-phase clouds that advected over the camp in the early morning and precipitated throughout the day such that spectroradiometer data show a transition from ice-bearing to supercooled liquid water cloud. Earlier model evaluations (~10 years ago) showed a tendency to underestimate supercooled cloud liquid water content while overestimating the ice phase. Later model evaluations, with the most current ESMs, show the opposite behavior with overestimated supercooled cloud liquid water and chronic underestimation of cloud ice water. Evaluation against our 4-week time series reveals instances of PWRF showing instances of both earlier and later model tendencies at different intervals. This suggests that attention should perhaps be given to details of the microphysical scheme's computation within individual layers and across discrete time steps, to search for instances where the computational steps might be having trouble versus where they are working as expected. Finally, we discuss advantages of the Siple Dome site in the context of evolving miniaturization and transportability of advanced atmospheric science technologies, including ground-based remote sensors and UAS-borne systems.

496295.title: Exploring Frontiers of Data Discovery for NCAR’s Earth Observing Laboratory Field Campaign Data
496295.authors: Mya Sears, NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. C. Witte and C. Ruchti
496295.abstract: NCAR’s Earth Observing Laboratory (EOL) archives, manages, and stewards unique observational datasets collected through field campaigns conducted by and in collaboration with the laboratory. These datasets, which are often hosted solely on EOL’s Field Data Archive (FDA), are foundational to the analyses that accompany each field campaign. However, the FDA primarily limits data access to traditional download and request-based workflows, which create barriers for users – especially those working with large datasets. The modernization of data formats and access methods provides an opportunity to make analysis of these datasets more efficient. In collaboration with NCAR’s Geoscience Data Exchange (GDEX) team, we have been evaluating a transformation of data type and storage location as an approach to improving EOL data distribution. As part of this current pilot study, we have converted manually requestable Tar + Gzip netCDF files hosted on the FDA to remotely accessible Zarr stores hosted on GDEX, using datasets from the Multi-point Monin-Obukhov similarity horizontal array turbulence study (M2HATS). So far, we have observed that the use of GDEX expedites access to all M2HATS datasets, even reducing time-to-analysis by several hours in large, high-rate datasets. Additionally, the use of Zarr greatly increased the efficiency of the largest datasets, but minimally changed the processing speed of most datasets tested in this study. In cases where processing speed is unchanged, the preferences of the scientific community will determine whether these datasets are converted to Zarr or remain as netCDF. To address community needs, this ongoing pilot study will be informed by a survey that has been distributed to EOL data users to investigate current and future scientific analysis workflows. This survey, in conjunction with the continued guidance of the GDEX team, will help provide the framework for modernizing EOL data distribution and reducing technical barriers to working with large observational datasets.

496299.title: Community Global Workflow Version 1
496299.authors: Walter C. Kolczynski Jr., Redline Performance Solutions, Rockville, MD; and W. Huang, K. J. Booker, D. Huber, J. R. Carley, D. A. Burrows, T. McGuinness, and M. Huang
496299.abstract: In June, NOAA ’s Earth Prediction Innovation Center (EPIC), in collaboration with the National Weather Service (NWS) Office of Model Development (OMD), made its first community release of the NWS Global Workflow. The Global Workflow is the superstructure responsible for orchestrating most of the NWS global numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems in both operational and developmental environments. These include the flagship Global Forecast System (GFS), Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), the Global Chemistry and Aerosol Forecast System (GCAFS), and the Seasonal Forecast System (SFS). The primary goal of this release is to make the Global Workflow accessible to a wider range of users outside of NOAA, which led to three major enhancements: (1) support for Global Workflow on National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research’s Derecho High Performance Computer, (2) support for Global Workflow on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) clusters, and (3) significant updates to the system-level documentation. The documentation revision includes a new quick-start guide to get new users running a workflow test case within a couple of hours on any supported machine. Additionally, EPIC provided and recorded training at their annual Unifying Innovations in Forecasting Capabilities Workshop in 2026 and made it available to the public. Here we will discuss these new features, as well as the capabilities and limitations of this release.

496300.title: Updating an Ice Cloud Optical Property Model to include Latitudinal- and Temperature-Dependence in the Far-Infrared and submillimeter Spectral Regimes for Remote Sensing Applications
496300.authors: James Joseph Coy Jr, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX
496300.abstract: Ice clouds play a critical role in Earth’s radiative budget and climate system but remain the least understood atmospheric parameter due to uncertainties in their microphysical and optical properties. This is caused by assumptions of ice particle morphology and utilization of inaccurate single-scattering computation methods across the visible to near-infrared shortwave (SW), mid- to far-infrared longwave (LW), and submillimeter (submm) spectral regimes. There are numerous optical property models that attempt to accurately represent ice cloud in radiative transfer models but are usually restricted to SW or LW spectral regimes, lack temperature and latitudinal dependence that are important for LW and submm spectral regimes, or fail to be applicable for both passive and active sensor-based ice cloud radiative property retrievals. Interest is growing in the use of radiometric and polarimetric measurements in the far-infrared LW and submm spectral regimes. Studies have demonstrated that spaceborne observations of ice clouds using LW and submm channels can improve the quantification of ice cloud optical properties such as ice cloud optical thickness (ICOT), effective diameter (Deff), and ice water path (IWP) under nighttime conditions when solar-band SW channels are unavailable, thereby allowing the retrieval of diurnal ice cloud radiative properties. The recent launch of the Polar Radiant Energy in the Far-Infrared Experiment (PREFIRE) satellite mission as well as the upcoming Polarized Submillimeter Ice-Cloud Radiometer (PolSIR) satellite mission highlights the need of a temperature- and latitudinal-dependent ice cloud optical property model that covers the LW and submm spectral regimes to streamline accurate retrievals of ice cloud optical properties based on the observational data. A Passive and Active Remote Sensing Consistent (PARSC) ice cloud optical property model has been recently developed based on an ice particle habit mixture of an ensemble of randomly distorted 20-particle aggregates, regular 8-column aggregate, and slightly distorted hexagonal column. The PARSC model has been validated in achieving passive and active sensor-based retrieval consistency as well as been expanded to include temperature-dependence in the far-infrared spectral regime. Latitudinal dependence has only been included for visible to thermal infrared wavelengths and is organized into tropical, midlatitude, and polar regions for both hemispheres. For this study, we perform temperature-dependent ice particle single-scattering property calculations for the submm spectral regime to expand the PARSC model. For submm temperature-dependence, we use the Invariant Imbedding T-Matrix (IITM) and Improved Geometric Optics (IGOM) methods to calculate single-scattering properties for 6 temperature bins from 170 to 270K and submm frequency range from 300 to 700 GHz. Latitudinal dependence will be applied to the PARSC model in the far-infrared and submm spectral ranges by simply altering the ice particle habit mixtures based on previous consistency validations of lidar and depolarization ratio observations from Cloud-Aerosol Lidar with Orthogonal Polarization (CALIOP). Spectral consistency analysis of ICOT retrievals is conducted using PREFIRE data and a sensitivity analysis of Deff and IWP retrievals are conducted based on the 325 and 683 GHz channels of the upcoming PolSIR mission.

496303.title: Beyond Full-Disk Soft X-Rays: High-Cadence Ca II K Observations for Solar Flare Monitoring
496303.authors: Aman Priyadarshi Mukesh Kumar, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM; and J. Shetye
496303.abstract: Full-disk soft X-ray measurements provide the standard basis for monitoring solar flares, but spatially integrated observations can obscure the timing and evolution of compact energy release in the lower atmosphere. We investigate whether high-cadence ground-based Ca II K observations can provide complementary information for space-weather monitoring applications. An initial study of eight Dunn Solar Telescope (DST) flare sequences identified compact Ca II K brightenings approximately 10–45 min before the primary chromospheric flare kernel, motivating a larger systematic investigation. We subsequently analyzed 24 quality-controlled Ca II K detections observed with ROSA/DST at cadences of approximately 2–6 s. The chromospheric responses are generally decay-dominated, with median rise and decay times of 3.63 and 9.36 min. For 18 GOES-guided detections, Ca II K–GOES peak offsets span −7.24 to +5.76 min. Events in which the chromospheric response precedes the soft X-ray maximum are broadly consistent with lower-atmosphere energy deposition accompanying the development of hot flare plasma, while the positive offsets show that this temporal ordering is not universal. Six additional temporally distinct Ca II K brightenings were identified outside the dominant GOES peak interval. In one case, distinct Ca II K, Hα, and EUV emission occurs during the decay of a larger X-class flare while the full-disk GOES profile remains dominated by the earlier event. Together, these results show that high-cadence chromospheric imaging can resolve flare-related activity and timing structure that may be blended in full-disk soft X-ray observations. Quantifying false-alarm rates and automating event identification are the next steps toward evaluating Ca II K as a complementary ground-based space-weather monitoring diagnostic.

496306.title: The Tomorrow.io Low Earth Orbit (LEO) Constellation: Status and Plans
496306.authors: Ryan Honeyager, Tomorrow.io, Silver Spring, MD; and S. J. Munchak, E. Stromberg, S. Williams, F. Junyent, C. Bjorland, E. Watson, J. Wicha, E. L. Nelson, A. Bell, T. King, J. J. Guerrette, J. Splaingard, and A. Chawla
496306.abstract: The Tomorrow.io satellite constellation provides proliferated low-Earth observation capabilities that supplement the baseline global observing system. This presentation discusses the capabilities of the constellation at present and its evolution throughout the next decade, particularly in light of the WMO Integrated Global Observing System (WIGOS) Vision 2040. As of early 2027, seventeen microwave radiometers and Ka-band precipitation radars have been launched into many sun-synchronous and drifting orbits. These satellites provide rapid refresh capabilities for sounding, precipitation detection, and precipitation characterization that have been identified as critical gaps in fulfilling WIGOS 2040. Tomorrow.io satellite data products have been independently evaluated by both the NOAA Commercial Data Program (CDP) and the NASA Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) program, and these programs provide pathways for agency scientists and affiliated researchers to engage with the data ahead of operational use. When considered independently of any other satellite program the Tomorrow Microwave Sounders (TMS) instruments have established a global median hourly revisit rate. Fractional global coverage within a three-hour window exceeds eighty percent, and median coverage within a six-hour window is near one hundred percent. Regular launches will continuously replenish the constellation and maintain current coverage performance into the early 2030s while introducing incremental upgrades to both satellite bus and sensor capabilities. Starting in 2029 Tomorrow.io will begin to launch its DeepSky satellite series, which represents a more ambitious multi-instrument program consisting of a next-generation microwave sounder, a Ka-band precipitation radar, an EO/IR imager, and GNSS-R/RO instruments all co-located on the same physical satellite bus. DeepSky satellites will feature significant improvements in lifespan and instrument capabilities and will address the needs of both operational NWP and nowcasting in terms of supporting long-term observation records, reducing instrument noise and bias, and providing new capabilities to understand rapidly evolving weather conditions. We will highlight these instruments and discuss pre-launch science plans.

496314.title: From Raw Feeds to Ready Answers: A Unified BigQuery Platform for High-Resolution Severe Convective Storm Data
496314.authors: Austin Vacek, Athenium, Dover, NH; and J. G. Fairman Jr, P. M. Jermey, and M. Dyanati
496314.abstract: Severe convective storm impacts, including hail, tornadoes, straight-line winds, and heavy precipitation, are documented across a fragmented landscape of federal archives, radar-derived products, and model output, each with its own format, latency, and access pattern. This fragmentation is often the real barrier between observation and decision support, more than any gap in the underlying science. We present an operational data pipeline that transforms multi-radar/multi-sensor precipitation estimates, radar-derived severe weather fields, and model-derived storm environment data into Athenium-derived hazard products, then combines the resulting datasets into a single, grid-resolved platform in Google BigQuery, spanning hourly precipitation, hail, tornado, and wind records dating back to 2015, alongside NWS tornado damage surveys and SPC storm reports for reference. Rather than hosting raw source data, the pipeline stages enhanced, analysis-ready products through cloud storage before loading into BigQuery, giving practitioners a single destination rather than a patchwork of source-specific formats and access methods. Partition and cluster-aware table design keeps queries fast and affordable at scale, allowing new severe weather datasets to be onboarded as they become available. The result is a single, queryable resource spanning over a decade of hourly hail, tornado, wind, and precipitation observations brought into a shared analytical framework, lowering the technical barrier for researchers, forecasters, and risk analysts to move from fragmented source products to actionable, cross-hazard analysis, and offering a concrete example of turning the enterprise's data stewardship goals into practitioner-facing infrastructure.

496318.title: Diode-Laser-Based High Spectral Resolution Lidar Advancements for Practical Cloud and Aerosol Sensing
496318.authors: Bryce Garby, NSF NCAR, Center Green Dr., CO; and M. Hayman, R. A. Stillwell, S. M. Spuler, and J. Thayer
496318.abstract: Future lidar solutions for cloud and aerosol sensing should balance practicality with capability. Practicality relies on the ease of deployment for a variety of platforms and conditions, which is heavily dictated by Size Weight and Power (SWaP). Where most low SWaP sensors have focused on qualitative backscatter lidar architectures, our efforts have emphasized maintaining capability in the form of quantitative lidar architectures such as HSRL and DIAL. With the motivation of airborne and ground-based network applications, we are developing a next-generation HSRL instrument architecture, referred to as the Airborne Diode-Laser-Based HSRL or ADiHSRL. This next-generation design prioritizes versatility, enabling high-resolution quantitative retrievals in environments where SWaP is at a premium. Our design leverages complementary advancements in unique diode-laser pulse schemes (multi-pulse-mode) along with advanced Poisson Total Variation (PTV) signal processing, plus practical benefits from fiber coupled components. Multi-pulse-mode features a transmit pulse scheme which uses long pulses with greater power to improve signal-to-noise combined with short pulses to capture high resolution features. PTV uses penalized maximum likelihood estimation with a forward model to find the underlying structure that best fits the observations, leveraging the advantages of each pulse mode, while removing uncorrelated noise. The forward model, combined with HSRL architecture, allows PTV to act in the physical parameter space, thereby producing quantitative retrievals. This design is evaluated with a ground-based demonstrator and a sophisticated performance model. We achieve high-resolution (7.5 m range, 5 s time) HSRL measurements of backscatter coefficient and depolarization despite operating with a comparatively small power aperture product (~0.004 Wm²). In this presentation, the continued development and optimization of this design is discussed and the performance for airborne operation is explored. Recent advancements in PTV signal processing, motivated by the high-dynamic range of HSRL cloud/aerosol observations are shown and the implications for HSRL applications are discussed. In addition, the optimization of the multi-pulse-mode design space is introduced and explored. Using the performance model, the benefits of PTV and multi-pulse-mode are then demonstrated for airborne operation.

496319.title: Meteorology of December 18 - 19, 2025 Pacific Northwest Atmospheric River and Associated Impacts
496319.authors: Amy M. Johnson, Portland State University, Portland, OR; and K. K. Mallon and P. C. Loikith
496319.abstract: December 2025 brought a series of atmospheric rivers (ARs) to the Pacific Northwest which contributed to flooding, landslides, power outages as well as damages to roads, infrastructure and homes in multiple counties across the states of Washington, Oregon, and California. A Presidential Disaster declaration was made for the state of Oregon for the period of December 15 - 21, 2025 as a result of storm damage. The storm event occurring between December 18 - 19 brought the highest rainfall totals to Oregon’s Coastal and Cascade range with AR conditions lasting for longer than 30 hours, reaching AR Category 4 in the Coast Range and Category 3 in the Cascades. By the time this storm made landfall, the ground across northwestern Oregon was already saturated by heavy rainfall from previous atmospheric rivers and communities were grappling with impacts from the prior series of storms. There were already road closures and thousands were without power after a powerful wind storm on December 17th. Overnight on the 18th evacuation orders were issued for portions of the Clackamas and Molalla Rivers in Clackamas County, with peak flood stages occurring early in the day on the 19th. The Molalla river experienced levee overtopping and failures which led to revisions in flood stage guidance for the river and damaging stream channel migration. To better understand the meteorology that drove these significant impacts across northwestern Oregon and Clackamas County in particular, we present a comprehensive meteorological diagnosis of the storm. Antecedent conditions are also assessed as saturated soils and high streamflow at the onset of the AR likely played a critical role in the severity of the flooding. Rainfall rates within the AR were enhanced by local orographic lifting and the passage of a strong cold front. The freezing level was well above average for the time of year, resulting in nearly all precipitation falling as rain, increasing runoff. This meteorological diagnosis provides a baseline of understanding that will be used to simulate this event under different climate scenarios to understand the full range of forces that led to the severe impacts.

496320.title: What Drives North American Weather Regimes? Insights from a Simple Atmosphere Model
496320.authors: Kathleen Pegion, University of Oklahoma, Boulder, CO
496320.abstract: Weather regimes are an important source of predictability on subseasonal timescales and there has been a dramatic increase in their use over the last 10 years. Despite their growing use for applications such as energy, transportation, and agriculture, a full understanding of weather regimes and their causes remains a mystery. This study investigates: a) how well we know the characteristics of North American weather regimes such as frequency, duration, and transitions, and b) what determines these characteristics? We address this using a simple atmospheric general circulation model (called Telly) whose tropical heating can be prescribed and varied in isolation and with which we can produce long simulations for robust statistics. Telly is compared, compared against ERA5 reanalysis and the NCAR CESM2 Large Ensemble, clustering boreal-winter 500-hPa height anomalies into the four canonical North American regimes (Alaskan Ridge/Pacific Ridge, West Coast High, Pacific Trough, Greenland High).
