To answer a) We first test robustness of methodological choices for characterizing weather regimes in Telly including the number of years, use of a null cluster, number of clusters, and year-round vs. seasonal definitions. To answer b) we then test how the characteristics of the regimes vary under climatological, ENSO, MJO, trend, and other tropical heating in Telly to investigate Results show that climatological, stochastically-varying heating in Telly reproduces all four observed regimes, indicating that midlatitude internal dynamics alone are sufficient to generate their existence and basic spatial structure. However, the West Coast High pattern is displaced relative to ERA5 and that Telly’s regimes persist longer than observed. This indicates that tropical variability and/or increased model complexity maybe needed to represent the West Coast High and the correct persistence of weather regimes. Preliminary results show that El Niño increases the frequency of Alaskan Ridge/Pacific Ridge occurrence, while La Niña increases the frequency of the West Coast High occurrence. However, both experiments show their weakest correlation to observed patterns which indicates that including interannual variability of tropical heating in terms of ENSO in the Telly model does not improve the spatial representation of the West Coast High. Preliminary results also show that composite heating for four MJO phase combinations and find no consistent regime-frequency shift relative to MJO-inactive heating or climatological heating, suggesting intraseasonal tropical forcing's imprint on the regimes is weaker. These experiments will be extended and several other heating experiments will also be tested to more robustly answer our questions.

496322.title: Remote Sensing of Wildfire Intensity with the Nighttime Fire Observation Experiment (NightFOX) sUAS Payload
496322.authors: Joey Taylor, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and T. Thornberry, R. S. Gao, S. Ciciora, S. DeLone, M. Forbes, and J. Schwarz
496322.abstract: Small uncrewed aerial systems (sUAS) equipped with appropriate sensors can provide high-resolution research-grade measurements in challenging environments at a relatively low cost. Wildfires pose particular challenges that a sUAS remote sensing payload can uniquely navigate to deliver useful information to wildland firefighters and wildfire modelers alike. In this work we focus on supporting satellite observations of fire radiative power (FRP) with a sUAS payload. FRP measurements are widely utilized for incident command decision making, rapid response to new ignitions, and smoke forecasting models, yet are limited by coarse spatial resolution and/or long satellite revisit times. Crewed aircraft can deploy sophisticated instrumentation for long observing periods of FRP, but require expensive and hazardous operations. We present an updated low-cost sUAS remote sensing payload that is designed to provide highly complementary and useful wildfire observations from a fixed-wing platform. Developed under the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory’s Nighttime Fire Observations Experiment (NightFOX) project, the payload is capable of providing high spatial (<20 m pixel size) and temporal resolution maps of fire extent and FRP with infrared sensors measuring in multiple wavelength bands. This presentation will detail recent instrumentation developments and results from a planned wildfire deployment of the NightFOX remote sensing payload.

496324.title: Linking the Shape of the Diurnal Surface Layer Scalar and Flux Time Series to Infer Development of the Boundary Layer Above.
496324.authors: David Fitzjarrald, University at Albany, SUNY, Albany, NY; and D. J. M. Freedman
496324.abstract: Linking the shape of the diurnal surface layer scalar and flux time series to infer development of the boundary layer above. During the morning boundary layer transition a local specific humidity q maximum corresponds to the time at which the stable boundary layer is ‘filled in’ just before rapid CBL growth into the residual layer mixes drier air in. An evening transition ‘q jump’ marks the moment at which the stable boundary layer constrains vertical mixing (Acevedo and Fitzjarrald, 2002), as diminishing evaporation trapped into a shallow layer promotes a second local q maximum. Integrating the sensible heat flux from near the surface zo to zs, , where turbulent transports are small, and making reasonable assumptions, yields some elementary predictions about the shape of the temperature time series (Fitzjarrald and Lala, 1979): Upward T(t) curvature —>Turbulent transport dominates; Downward T(t) curvature —> radiative flux divergence dominates. Moreover, the time at which this curvature switches sign coincides with the start of the “q jump, evidenced by the equation. We present analyses of observations obtained during a series of field observations made at a variety of land cover types and latitudes. These include detailed time series of heat, momentum and, in some cases, CO2 fluxes along with their associated scalars. Estimates of boundary layer mixing state and thickness made using radiosondes, lidar and ceilometer observations, where available, complement these efforts. These data include measurements from the NASA ABLE-2 and LBA_ECO missions in the Amazon Basin, Brazil and ABLE-3 and BOREAS in boreal regions of Alaska and Canada, the NSF HVAMS study in the Hudson Valley, and include more recent years of data from the NY State Mesonet (Brotzge et al. 2020). These data will be compared to selected NOAA HRRR model outputs, to examine the degree of fine temporal detail needed to reproduce these phenomena. Among our research questions are: a. On what type of day are these features most readily identified? b. How often and in what seasons do such ‘ideal’ days dominate? c. What is the characteristic shape of the time series of surface scalars on such days? d. How well do the common PBL parameterizations function on ‘ideal’ days, as well as on days when the model-assumed PBL structure is poorly expressed? e. Are changes in the slope and/or second temporal derivatives of time series useful to infer boundary layer structure at sites lacking direct flux observations? Finally, we quantify the observed latitudinal dependence of the terrestrial duration of the meteorological daytime (duration of positive surface sensible heat flux). Casual observation indicates that this duration changes more slowly with latitude and seasonally than does incident short-wave radiative flux. We emphasize distinguishing how land cover and radiative balances influence seasonal variation in both the NOAA HRRR and, possibly, other readily sourced model output.. Joseph, N. Bain, N. Bassill, N. Farruggio, J. M Freedman, J.M., D. Johnston, and E. Kane, 2020. A Technical Overview of the New York State Mesonet Standard Network. J. Atm Oceanic Tech. 37(10), 1827-1845. . Fitzjarrald, D.R. and Lala, G.G., 1989. Hudson Valley fog environments. J. Appl. Meteor. Clim., 28(12), p.1303-1328.

496325.title: NOAA’s Enterprise Rain Rate (ERR) Algorithm: Revisiting Cloud Texture as a Precursor for Precipitation
496325.authors: Lily J Campbell, STC, Hamptom, VA; STAR, College Park, MD
496325.abstract: NOAA’s (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) Enterprise Rain Rate algorithm (ERR) (previously Self-Calibrating Multivariate Precipitation Retrieval (SCaMPR)) has been providing operational output that is publicly available since February 2025. With the operational status of the ERR, both GOES-R baseline precipitation and Global Hydro-Estimator (GHE) are being retired from operations due to improved performance in the ERR. The ERR quantitative global estimates of rainfall every 10 minutes at a resolution of .02° from 60°S to 60°N as a level 3 product. Level 2 products are also made on a native grid for GOES, METEOSAT, and Himawari satellites. The ERR rain rates are primarily calculated using infrared imager data from geostationary satellites, using microwave-based precipitation data as training reference. We will present recent reports for the ERR as well as current and planned research. Current research efforts include, but are not limited to, cloud texture being used in analysis. We will look at cloud texture’s accuracy and impact on differentiating cloud systems and evaluate cloud texture’s ability to determine if these areas are raining or not raining.

496328.title: 3D-PAWS: Building Local Capacity for Early Warning Through Training and Partnerships
496328.authors: William Nicewonger, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and K. Payne, M. Steinson, P. A. Kucera, R. Zieber, B. Bubon, and B. M. Smith
496328.abstract: Reliable, dense surface observations are foundational to effective early warning systems, yet many of the regions most vulnerable to weather, water, and climate hazards remain observationally sparse, limiting the ability of local meteorological services to detect, monitor, and warn communities of impending hazards. The 3D-Printed Automatic Weather Station (3D-PAWS) initiative, developed by UCAR's COMET Program, addresses this limitation by pairing low-cost, locally manufacturable weather stations with sustained capacity-building partnerships, closing observational gaps that directly limit early warning effectiveness. The program has now deployed approximately 350 stations across 25+ countries in Africa, the Pacific Islands, and Central and South America, supporting national meteorological and hydrological services (NMHSs) and other partner institutions. At the core of this model is a hands-on fabrication and deployment workshop, in which partners learn to build sensors and dataloggers, understand the sensing principles behind converting raw signals into usable weather observations, and site, install, and maintain stations in the field. Because partners are equipped to fabricate, deploy, and sustain their own station networks independently, this training builds early warning infrastructure that remains operational and locally serviceable long after initial deployment. The strength of this approach is increasingly visible in a growing regional workshop model, in which experienced partners train neighboring countries directly: in one such workshop, Barbados trained 8 staff from 4 neighboring Caribbean countries, extending early warning-capable observation networks across the region without requiring direct COMET involvement in every new deployment. Building on this foundation, the program is also expanding into data-focused training to strengthen how observations translate into warning decisions. In June 2026, the program piloted its first 3D-PAWS Data Workshop with two participants, who worked with data from their own deployed stations using a range of quality control and analysis tools to support their research applications. This pilot demonstrated that hands-on work with partners' own station data was an effective foundation for data literacy training. Lessons from the pilot are informing a broader international rollout of the data workshop planned for 2027. In parallel, potential partnerships with WindBorne Systems and Synoptic Data could integrate surface and upper-atmosphere observations into a shared data viewer platform, laying the groundwork for incorporating whole-atmosphere observations into regional forecast models such as WRF or MPAS to improve warning lead time and accuracy. Together, these efforts show that closing the global-observing gap and advancing "warning-for-all" requires more than deploying instruments: it requires durable, locally-owned capacity to build, maintain, and apply those instruments. The program's next steps include scaling the regional training model to additional partner regions and rolling out the international data workshop in 2027.

496329.title: Evaluation of GEOS-CF Ozone Forecasts Using TOLNet Profiles
496329.authors: Daniel Phoenix, NASA, Hampton, VA; NASA Langley Research Center, Hampton, VA; and G. Gronoff, K. E. Knowland, M. S. Johnson, C. M. Bernier, and M. E. D. Roots
496329.abstract: The Tropospheric Ozone Lidar Network (TOLNet) provides high spatiotemporal vertical profiles of ozone in the United States. The profiles have been used to better understand the physical processes driving tropospheric ozone variability, evaluate numerical model simulations, and to validate satellite and airborne ozone retrievals. Here, the measurements are used to evaluate the forecast accuracy of the GEOS Composition Forecasting model (GEOS-CF), versions 1 and 2. First, TOLNet ozone profiles from 2020-2025 from the six legacy sites (New York City, NY; Greenbelt, MD; Hampton, VA; Huntsville, AL; Boulder, CO; and Table Mountain Facility, CA) are used to evaluate the GEOS-CF version 1 forecasts. The forecasts are evaluated for diurnal and seasonal patterns, as well as forecast lead time. The forecasts are also grouped and evaluated by atmospheric condition (e.g., stratospheric intrusion, smoke plume, high ozone days). Next, ozone profiles from select sites between August and December 2025 are used to compare GEOS-CF forecasts from versions 1 and 2. Lastly, GEOS-CF version 2 is evaluated using profiles collected between January and July 2026. Overall, GEOS-CF version 1 forecasts ozone with great accuracy in the free troposphere (median profiles within +5 ppb) but is biased high by 10-20 ppb below 800 hPa. In general, the biases are higher during summer months and during the afternoon. There was little difference in forecast skill for different lead times. GEOS-CF version 2 ozone is uniformly higher than version 1 by about 10%, which is likely due to the assimilated ozone from satellite measurements. For different atmospheric conditions, GEOS-CF most accurately forecasts the ozone concentration and timing of stratospheric intrusions but shows more variability in the timing and location of smoke plumes and elevated ozone layers. In summary, this analysis demonstrates both the forecast skill of the GEOS-CF model as well as the utility of the TOLNet ozone profiles, both of which can provide benefit to air quality managers, satellite validation efforts, and research scientists seeking to better understand tropospheric variability.

496330.title: Development of a JEDI-Based Ionospheric Data Assimilation System
496330.authors: Hui Shao, NRL, Washington, DC; and D. D. Kuhl, J. Haiducek, P. Caffrey, M. Herrera, D. Tyndall, F. Hebert, L. J. Hayden, B. C. Ruston, and N. Pedatella
496330.abstract: The Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) is a flexible, model-agnostic data assimilation (DA) framework designed to support a broad range of Earth system applications. The U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (NRL), in collaboration with the Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA), is extending JEDI capabilities to support data assimilation for the thermosphere-ionosphere system and advance its application to space weather. This presentation highlights recent progress toward establishing a comprehensive ionospheric DA capability within JEDI. The effort makes use of generic observation operators, including vertical interpolation, and introduces a generic line-of-sight integration operator to support assimilation of electron density profiles and GNSS-based total electron content (TEC), including vertical and slant TEC. In parallel, Anchor-JEDI provides a complementary approach for assimilating ionospheric electron density information using an anchor-point representation, enabling DA with thermosphere-ionosphere models in a model-agnostic JEDI framework. These capabilities are being evaluated with NRL and community models, including PyIRI and WACCM-X. Future development will extend the framework to more fundamental GNSS observables, including radio occultation bending angles, further expanding the range of observations that can be assimilated within JEDI. Together, these developments establish a broad foundation for ionospheric DA within JEDI, supporting NRL space weather objectives while contributing to the broader JEDI community and providing a pathway toward coupled DA spanning the neutral atmosphere, thermosphere-ionosphere system, and space environment.

496334.title: Inter-Calibrating CERES Broadband Radiometers using Geostationary Imagers as Transfer Radiometers
496334.authors: David R. Doelling, NASA, Hampton, VA
496334.abstract: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System (CERES) project provides the scientific community with monthly 1° regional flux and cloud products for monitoring the Earth’s energy imbalance and climate model validation. The CERES products are based on overlapping CERES instrument records on the Terra, Aqua, NPP and NOAA20 platforms. The Aqua-CERES instrument was used to intercalibrate the other CERES instruments to the same radiometric calibration reference using simultaneous nadir overpass (SNOs) radiance events. The NOAA satellites are placed in the same 13:30 local time 16-day revisit orbit but are sequenced 4 or 8 days apart, thus preventing any coincident collocations. The use of modern geostationary imagers with VIIRS like channels as transfer radiometers provides a way to intercalibrate the NOAA CERES broadband instruments. The success of this method relies on programming the CERES instrument to scan in the same manner as the geostationary imager over carefully selected invariant Earth targets, thus allowing for view and azimuthal angle matches within 2° and 5° and coincident within 5 minutes. The Indonesian Papua Island convection, clear-sky Libyan desert, and offshore Peruvian stratus Earth targets were chosen for their unique spectra and consistent meteorology throughout the year. Geostationary visible and IR narrowband to broadband SW and LW coefficients are based on the NOAA-20 CERES instrument observed radiances. The NOAA-20 derived coefficients are used to predict the NPP CERES instrument radiances 4-days later using the same CERES geostationary imager programmed scans (GEOscan). A minimum of 4-months (8 events) of GEOscan is needed before the uncertainty starts to level off. The site SW channel and total channel bias uncertainties were found to be less than 0.5% and 0.1%. The site channel radiance N20-NPP bias differences are resolved by adjusting the channel spectral responses within their ground characterized uncertainties. The total minus shortwave day is used as a closure comparison to validate the analogous channel scalings.

496337.title: Pyrocumulonimbus (PyroCb) Forecast Model Verification for the INSPYRE Field Campaign
496337.authors: Anna Tianyue Liu, Georgia Institute of Technology, Orem, UT; and D. V. V. Mallia and S. K. Krueger
496337.abstract: Fire-induced or enhanced thunderstorms or pyrocumulonimbus clouds (pyroCbs), can have regional to global impacts on atmospheric conditions. PyroCbs often occur in environments that are often favorable from dry convection with fires that have good energetics. PyroCbs can create erratic fire weather conditions at the surface which can bring challenging and dangerous conditions for fire suppression efforts (Peterson et al., 2025). Deep pyroconvection can also loft smoke high up in the atmosphere, sometimes reaching the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). Smoke particulates can interact with incoming radiation and other chemical compounds (Fromm et al., 2010). Modeling and forecasting pyroCbs remains challenging as fire-atmosphere interactions are not well observed. For this project, we will utilize the Freitas et al. (2007; 2010) 1D plume rise model (PRM), which parameterizes cloud microphysics and entrainment effects, to simulate two pyroCbs in Utah during the summer of 2026. High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) data for vertical atmospheric profiles (atmospheric soundings), fire area, and fire heat flux were used as inputs to characterize each fire. With the PRM, we distinguished the monsoonal influence of the Babylon pyroCb and the fire-driven forcing of the Cottonwood pyroCb. This study provides insight into the accuracy of a plume rise model, one that could potentially be used to forecast pyroCb events operationally.

496338.title: Aerosols in the Western Antarctic Peninsula Region Influenced by Local Marine Primary Production and Long-Range Transport from South America and Australia
496338.authors: Dan Lubin, SIO, La Jolla, CA; and T. Moellerstedt, G. Roberts, and L. M. Russell
496338.abstract: Aerosol particle formation from marine primary production is linked with Southern Ocean stratiform cloud amount and cloud brightening. The Western Antarctic Peninsula (WAP) region has seen increasing trends in chlorophyll a abundance during spring and summer phytoplankton blooms. Here we report on the first measurements of aerosol properties throughout a complete seasonal cycle within the WAP region studied by the NSF Palmer Long-Term Ecological Research (LTER) program. A Portable AERosol Observing System (PAEROS) was deployed at Palmer Station (64.77ºS, 65.05ºW) between October 2013 and March 2014 to characterize aerosol sources and variability over the Amundsen and Bellingshausen Seas that influence the cloud lifecycle in the WAP region. A condensation particle counter (CPC, D50 at 6 nm) measured aerosol abundances that are used as a proxy for new particle formation. An Optical Particle Counter (OPC, 0.3-3.0-micron diameter, N300) measured aerosol abundances that are used as a proxy for contribution of primary marine aerosol (sea spray). An aethalometer measured black carbon (BC) concentrations to define the wind vectors related to station sources, and, outside these directions, detect long-range transport (LRT) of biomass burning and pollution sources from Southern Hemisphere land masses. The strong seasonal cycle of marine biogenic activity enhanced aerosol concentrations through new particle formation, peaking during austral mid-summer, while primary marine aerosol tracked seasonal increases in wind speed into autumn. Using HYSPLIT backtrajectory analysis, we also detected six LRT events originating from Australian wildfires, and two LRT events originating from South America. From the Australian LRT events, we see evidence of enhanced new particle formation as well as BC. While the WAP region is essentially a pristine environment largely isolated from lower latitudes by Southern Ocean storm tracks, our results show that synoptic-scale conditions associated with moderate La Niña and a relatively neutral Southern Annular Mode (SAM) index can set up LRT pathways into the WAP region.

496339.title: Understanding the Hydration of the Upper Troposphere and Lower Stratosphere by Tropical Cyclone
496339.authors: Karimar Ledesma Maldonado, Northern Illinois University, Dekalb, IL
496339.abstract: A cooling trend in the tropical lower stratosphere represents one of the most significant climate signals in recent records. Recent evidence suggests that these stratospheric temperature variations have contributed significantly to the interannual variability of TC potential intensity over the last three decades. Despite these findings, the extent of stratosphere-troposphere exchange (STE) and contribution within a TCs remains uncertain. Observations and numerical simulations have shown the impact of TCs intensity on the magnitude and vertical distribution of water vapor change at upper levels. While observations and numerical modeling have demonstrated that TC intensity affects the magnitude and vertical distribution of upper-level water vapor, high-resolution idealized frameworks evaluating UTLS thermodynamic controls remain limited. This study utilizes idealized Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations to isolate the impact of UTLS temperature variations on TC intensity and subsequent lower stratospheric hydration. Results demonstrate that variation in UTLS temperature impacts the TC intensity, which significantly influences lower stratospheric hydration levels, with stronger cyclones leading to a greater moisture influx into UTLS. Stronger tropical cyclones generate a more extensive hydration layer with dehydration zone as is observed in previous studies, whereas weaker TCs show no significant hydration layer was produced. Further, results show that UTLS hydration varies distinctively between the inner core and outer rainbands, jointly driven by TC intensity and differences in tropopause height and temperature.

496340.title: Scaling-out of Airborne-Lidar Derived, Observationally-Constrained Seasonal Water Supply Forecasts for Improved Water Management over the Central Rocky Mountains
496340.authors: David J. Gochis, Airborne Snow Observatories, Inc, Boulder, CO; Airborne Snow Observatories Inc, Mammoth Lakes, CA; and K. M. Sampson, L. Karsten, J. Deems, T. Painter, K. Bormann, P. Weil, and A. Rossi
496340.abstract: Transitioning novel observations of snowpack into improved water management operations throughout high-mountain watersheds can often require several years of intensive data collection and runoff model re-calibration in addition to including time for runoff forecast adoption into water management optimization models. Additionally, many new in situ or space-borne snowpack observations lack the precision, accuracy or complete spatial fidelity required to provide fully contiguous and mass-consistent runoff forecasts that are possible with state of the art physics-based, distributed hydrologic models. The resulting discontinuity in runoff forecast timing and volumes can create limitations in the adoption of such new runoff forecasts into sophisticated water management models. In this talk we present results from the implementation Airborne Snow Observatories, Inc. airborne-lidar and -spectrometer derived snowpack observations into operational forecasting and water management models from the central Rocky Mountain region that has occurred over the past 1-3 years. Synthesis results from across the region will be presented as will results from a few key application basins where operational ASO snowpack surveys and assimilated model forecasts have been ingested directly into water management operations models to make critical decisions on reservoir and water allocation operations. Emphasis will be placed on quantifying how improving the quantification of the distributions of SWE and albedo in many cases has led to significantly-reduced runoff model calibration periods, reduced runoff forecasting errors, and improved water management decision making. Additional focus will center on how full-basin snowpack estimation allows for improved forecast consistency from headwater water management sites to large basin outlet and terminal reservoirs in water management operations.

496342.title: US Southeast Coastal Sea Level Predictability Associated with Gulf Stream Meanders
496342.authors: Stephen G. Yeager, NCAR, Boulder, CO
496342.abstract: Changes in Gulf Stream (GS) position near Cape Hatteras have been linked to seasonal-to-decadal sea level variability along the US Southeast coast. The potential predictability associated with transmission of low-frequency open ocean GS signals to the coastal shelf south of Cape Hatteras remains unclear. High resolution (HR) ocean simulations have revealed some connection between large-scale atmospheric forcing associated with the North Atlantic Oscillation and GS position after separation, but they also suggest that there is a high degree of intrinsic (unforced) open ocean variability in the region. Low resolution (LR) ocean models exhibit weak GS variability overall, and likely overestimate the ratio of forced to intrinsic variability in GS position. Furthermore, recent work has shown that misrepresentation of coastal bathymetry near Cape Hatteras in LR models can block the propagation of coastal sea level signals that originate north of Cape Hatteras. We examine LR and HR reanalysis-forced ocean-only simulations of the Community Earth System Model (CESM) as well as coupled hindcast ensembles initialized from those simulations to assess the predictability of US Southeast coastal sea level and its relationship to predictability of open ocean GS changes. The HR system shows high predictability of large, intrinsic GS position changes on seasonal to interannual timescales, and we investigate the impact of this on predictability of coastal sea level further south compared to the LR system.

496344.title: Quantum Carleman Linearization of Richards’ Equation for Soil-Moisture Dynamics
496344.authors: Hassan Dashtian, Univ. of Texas, Austin, TX; and N. Sudharsan and D. Niyogi
496344.abstract: Richards' soil moisture equation, which is derived from mass conservation and Darcy-Buckingham flow; is widely used to model soil moisture dynamics including infiltration, drainage, and evapotranspiration. In this study, we develop a quantum algorithm and procedure to solve the Richards' equation. The procedure begins with Mualem-van Genuchten parameterizations and local linearization in soil water content, then produces a standard 1-D finite difference sparse quadratic ordinary differential equation. We use Carleman linearization to lift the resulting system to a sparse and block tri-diagonal linear Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE). Using Forward-Euler discretization in time, we assemble the equations into a global sparse, block lower-triangular linear system that can be solved with quantum linear-systems algorithms (QLSA). To show the applicability of the algorithm we use a QLSA-emulator to mimic the QLSA. Numerical experiments on a 1-D sandy soil column with Mualem-van Genuchten parameters demonstrate accuracy of the QLSA-emulation for each time step. Accurate soil moisture profiles with different surface/bottom fluxes are obtained from the resulting workflow. Our results support the notion that replacing the classical sparse linear solve with a QLSA subroutine is expected to preserve the same solution-level accuracy, yielding a sparse linear-algebra form that is well suited to quantum linear-system solvers for hydrologic computations.

496346.title: Regional High-Resolution Methane Emission Estimates and Source Attribution Using Satellite Data Assimilation and Infrastructure Mapping
496346.authors: Yuyan Cui, Environmental Defense Fund, New York, NY; and A. P. Mizzi, A. Velasquez, G. Ge, S. Liu, M. Omara, R. Gautam, S. Wofsy, and D. Xie
496346.abstract: Reducing methane emissions is an urgent global priority for mitigating climate change. Accurate and timely quantification of methane emissions and attribution to specific source sectors are essential to develop effective mitigation strategies and track progress toward emission reduction goals. In this study, we present a newly developed TROPOMI-based data assimilation system within the WRF-Chem/Chem-DART framework to estimate methane emissions over China's Junggar and Ordos oil and gas basins at 4 x 4 km² spatial and daily temporal resolution. To characterize seasonal variability, investigate year-round emission patterns, and inform emission factor development, we conduct five month-long data assimilation experiments during January, April, July, September, and October of 2024-2025. These periods were selected to coincide with the availability of EDF's MethaneSAT observations. Our high-resolution emission estimates are evaluated against independent MethaneSAT Level-4 flux products, as well as previous top-down and bottom-up emission estimates. While atmospheric data assimilation provides high-resolution gridded methane emission estimates, detailed infrastructure information is critical for interpreting these estimates and attributing emissions to specific source sectors. To address this need, we are developing a comprehensive methane infrastructure database by integrating existing datasets, including EDF's Oil and Gas Infrastructure Mapping database. We further enhance this database by combining existing OpenStreetMap data with the systematic annotation of high-resolution satellite imagery using manual annotation, object-detection algorithms, and manual verification to identify methane-related infrastructure, such as oil and gas wells, storage tanks, and processing facilities. This enhanced infrastructure database not only improves interpretation of the top-down emission estimates but also provides a basis for selecting the most appropriate prior sectoral emission inventories for the data assimilation system. Together, these efforts establish a comprehensive framework that provides a robust foundation for methane emission quantification, source attribution, and support of methane mitigation strategies.

496348.title: Land-Atmosphere Interactions Across Heterogeneous Landscapes
496348.authors: Swarup China, PNNL, RICHLAND, WA; Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA
496348.abstract: Land-atmosphere interactions at the boundary between soils, vegetation, and the lower atmosphere influence ecosystem processes, atmospheric composition, clouds, and precipitation. Yet, these interactions remain challenging to represent in Earth system models because they vary substantially across space, involve coupled physical, chemical, and biological feedbacks, and include poorly characterized emissions of soil- and microbe-derived particles, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and reactive nitrogen species. Rainfall, wind, and surface disturbance can mobilize soil organic matter, biological material, and mineral particles into the atmosphere. These particles may contribute to ambient aerosol populations and, under appropriate conditions, serve as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) or ice-nucleating particles (INPs). Their abundance and cloud-relevant properties are expected to vary with soil composition, moisture conditions, vegetation, precipitation characteristics, and other environmental factors. However, the magnitude, composition, and atmospheric fate of these emissions remain uncertain. Soils and litter layers may also release VOCs and nitrogen oxides that influence atmospheric oxidation processes and secondary organic aerosol formation, but their contributions to aerosol composition and cloud-active particle populations are not well constrained. Similarly, the ice-nucleating activity of soil-derived particles varies widely among soil types, likely reflecting differences in mineralogy, organic matter, biological material, and particle mixing state. Predictive relationships linking soil properties to ice-nucleating activity are still limited. This study integrates molecular characterization of soils, particles, and VOCs with targeted aerosol and ice-nucleation measurements. The resulting observations support development of process-based relationships between soil conditions, aerosol emissions, and INP properties. These measurements will improve the representation of land-derived aerosols and land-atmosphere feedbacks in Earth system models.

496355.title: AirCast-S2S: A Coupled Data-Driven Atmosphere–Ocean–Land Model for Subseasonal to Seasonal Prediction
496355.authors: Manmeet Singh, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; Disaster Science Operations Center, Bowling Green, KY; and S. Luitel and J. D. Durkee
496355.abstract: Subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction remains challenging because forecast skill at multiweek lead times depends on interactions between rapidly evolving atmospheric dynamics and slower sources of predictability associated with the ocean and land surface. Data-driven forecasting provides a computationally efficient approach for learning these dynamics, but models trained primarily for short-range accuracy can accumulate substantial errors during autoregressive integration, limiting their applicability at subseasonal timescales. Here, we introduce AirCast-S2S, a global data-driven coupled atmosphere–ocean–land forecasting system designed specifically for stable prediction from weather to subseasonal lead times. AirCast-S2S represents the evolving Earth system as a unified multivariate state containing three-dimensional atmospheric fields and surface meteorological variables together with oceanic and land-surface fields that provide longer-timescale memory. The complete coupled state is advanced autoregressively with a one-day time step, allowing evolving ocean and land conditions to interact continuously with atmospheric circulation rather than being treated as prescribed boundary conditions. To address error accumulation over extended integrations, AirCast-S2S incorporates a multi-step training strategy in which the model is optimized not only for the next-day prediction but also for its performance over weekly autoregressive rollouts. This exposes the model during training to its own evolving forecast states and directly constrains the growth of errors that would otherwise compound during long integrations. We evaluate AirCast-S2S across atmospheric, oceanic, and land-surface variables from daily through multiweek lead times, examining both conventional forecast skill and the stability and physical consistency of the coupled system. Particular attention is given to whether jointly evolving slower ocean and land states improves atmospheric prediction as initial-condition predictability decreases with lead time. By combining daily coupled Earth-system prediction with training that explicitly targets extended-rollout performance, AirCast-S2S provides a framework for learning interactions across components and timescales while maintaining stable autoregressive forecasts. The approach demonstrates a pathway toward computationally efficient, fully coupled data-driven Earth-system prediction for bridging medium-range weather and subseasonal forecasting.

496359.title: Review of Laboratory Experiments Involving Deposition of Ammonia at High Concentrations (>100 ppm) to Soil and Vegetation.
496359.authors: Steven R. Hanna, Hanna Consultants, Kennebunkport, ME; and T. O. Spicer
496359.abstract: There could be accidents or terrorist activities where large amounts of pressurized liquefied ammonia are released to the atmosphere. For example, an accident could occur with a one ton agricultural ammonia tank. If the tank empties in a few minutes, ammonia concentrations in the air exceeding 1000 ppm could extend several hundred meters downwind. These are high enough to cause serious human health effects and damage to vegetation. Over 40 years ago, Lydiard conducted laboratory experiments where various types of vegetation were exposed to several levels of ammonia concentration and deposition velocity was calculated. Ten years ago, David Brown repeated Lydiard's experiments with ammonia and other hazardous chemicals. Increasing usage and concerns about ammonia led to two sets of wind tunnel experiments during the past five years, where ammonia gas was circulated at high concentrations (1,000 to 10,000 ppm) and deposition to bare walls, to soil, and to soil with vegetation was measured. In general, deposition velocities were within expected ranges (about 0.1 to 1 cm/s). In the presence of high concentrations, the surface eventually became saturated, resulting in calculated deposition rates dropping to zero. During the approximate 40 years of ammonia deposition experiments in wind tunnels, the use of a simple deposition velocity has been replaced by application of resistance theories, which parameterize the effects of boundary layer resistance and surface chemical reaction resistance. The current paper presents a comparative review of the above measurement programs

496360.title: Transforming Hydrologic Forecasting: National Inundation Mapping and the Next-Generation National Water Model
496360.authors: Edwin Welles, Deltares USA, Silver Spring, MD; and F. L. Ogden, S. Greene, B. Brinkley, M. Woodbury, B. Bates, S. Lawler, Q. Hamlin, F. Aristizabal, and L. Schambach
496360.abstract: From Points to Maps The National Weather Service (NWS) Office of Water Prediction (OWP) is transforming how hydrologic forecasts are delivered. Today's standard product is an x-y hydrograph at a single, usually gauged, location, sometimes accompanied by uncertainty information such as an ensemble spread or likelihood range. Translating that curve into consequences on the surrounding landscape requires supplementary "E-19" information, named for the form on which stage values and their associated impacts were historically recorded. For anyone but an experienced user, a point forecast is difficult to interpret. An inundation map is immediately informative. In September 2026, the NWS will make inundation maps available to most of the U.S. population. That milestone rests on years of inundation mapping research and National Water Model (NWM) development. The same month marks the close of a three-year intensive development cycle that delivered the national inundation mapping capability while also advancing new mapping techniques, a new NWM architecture and models, as well as updates to the geospatial HydroFabric dataset. This presentation summarizes that work: the new mapping methods, the NWM innovations, and the proposed evolution of the National HydroFabric, the set of hydrologically-relevant features that describes the catchments, rivers, and water bodies of the nation. Implementing National Inundation Mapping A forecast inundation map is the product of a two-stage workflow. First a hydrologic model stack transforms meteorological inputs precipitation, temperature, and others into runoff, which is then spatially aggregated and routed to produce space-time series of streamflows and river stages. Second is an Inundation algorithm. Computed stages are passed to a mapping method, which may be a sophisticated hydrodynamic model or a statistical approach such as the Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) method. The national inundation mapping implementation uses outputs from the National Water Model version 3.1, running on a custom geospatial dataset, to generate the flows that are converted into maps using the HAND method at 10m resolution. The HAND method can be rapidly applied anywhere digital elevation and streamline data exist which, in the United States, is nearly everywhere, thus enabling national implementation. Enhancements to the HAND method, improved synthetic rating curve generation, bridge classification, and stream reach characterization, have been developed and are being evaluated for integration into the operational pipeline. HEC-RAS Based Map Libraries As an assumed higher-skill alternative to HAND, the NWS collaborated with FEMA to use FEMA base level engineering floodplain models as the basis for libraries of fixed inundation maps. To build these libraries, the NWS developed RIPPLE-1D, software that deconstructs the FEMA models, aligns them with the NWM stream network, and generates inundation maps at fixed stage intervals. Library members are then concatenated from downstream to upstream. Beginning at the downstream water elevation, each successive map is selected so that the upstream elevation of the map just chosen matches the downstream elevation of the next. A parallel approach that automatically constructs 2-D hydrodynamic models has been prototyped and will be evaluated for implementation. A New National Water Model Architecture National inundation mapping is only possible with fine-scale national hydrologic modeling. Recognizing that no single model configuration suits the full range of U.S. hydrologic regimes, the NWS designed a flexible architecture built on the Basic Model Interface and loosely coupled “managers” within the Next Generation Water Resources Modeling Framework (NextGen Framework). The NextGen Framework is a model-agnostic, standards-based, computational tool that uses the Basic Model Interface (BMI) for model coupling. The BMI permits model coupling on a time step basis or run length thus providing flexibility to couple models at appropriate time scales. The loosely coupled NextGen "managers" control model setup, calibration, regionalization, evaluation, data assimilation and forecasting. Each manager can run independently of the others, making it easier for the research community to connect, test, and advance NWM hydrologic modeling. While NWM 4.0, which will be based on the NextGen Framework, is not yet operational, the framework has been built and fourteen models integrated. Three automated calibration methods are supported. A regionalization approach links uncalibrated basins to calibrated basins based on basin characteristics. A new data assimilation method has been integrated into the routing routine; it distributes the error observed at a gauge upstream across all upstream tributaries according to contributing area and flow contribution. Two coastal models have been incorporated to support Total Water Level forecasts and coastal inundation mapping. System testing and model calibration are underway as the NWS evaluates operational readiness. The HydroFabric The NextGen system uses the OGC Water-ML 3.0 Hydrologic Features conceptual data model standard to describe the catchments, streams, and water bodies of the nation. This set of features is called a “Hydrofabric”, which is common between the NWM and inundation. Because the new NWM architecture model are catchment-based, it required a new HydroFabric. Reconstructing the channel network also allowed the NWS to improve stream connectivity and better resolve points of interest along the channels. Outlook Together, these capabilities position the NWS to transform hydrologic forecasting. Making forecasts easier for the general public to understand directly strengthens the agency's ability to fulfill its mission: protecting life and property and enhancing the national economy.

496361.title: Severe-Convective-Wind Analysis for Low-Latency Support (SCWALLS)
496361.authors: Ryan Lagerquist, MyRadar, Ward, CO; and J. P. Gibbons and S. Garimella
496361.abstract: We use deep learning (DL) to nowcast severe convective wind (SCW) – both tornadic and straight-line – at lead times of 0-2 hours throughout the planetary boundary layer (PBL), where low-altitude aircraft are sensitive to wind hazards. This work extends an earlier system that used traditional machine learning (e.g., random forests), trained on tabular (non-spatial) radar and NWP data, to nowcast SCW at the surfaxce (Lagerquist et al. 2017). We advance that work in four ways. First, we move from tabular to spatiotemporal (video-based) predictors, allowing our models to exploit multi-scale spatial and temporal context. Second, we extend prediction from the surface to the entire PBL. Third, we move from storm-based to CONUS-wide nowcasts on the 1-km Multi-radar Multi-sensor (MRMS) grid. Fourth, we incorporate uncertainty quantification into the training of the DL model. Our labels are in situ observations from the Meteorological Assimilation Data Ingest System (MADIS), linked to convective MRMS pixels that are nearby in space and time, similar to the linkage methodology of Lagerquist et al. (2017). We will present results from a hierarchy of DL architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNN) for storm-based prediction and U-net-style models for grid-based prediction, both enhanced with spatial- and cross-attention mechanisms. All models produce a probabilistic nowcast of SCW probability over time. To extend storm-based predictions to a spatial grid, we will compare two methods: [1] using a storm-tracking algorithm to extrapolate storm motion and project probabilities onto the grid; [2] applying an image-to-image DL model (U-net) directly to the CONUS-wide predictors, bypassing the need for post-processing. This talk will present results from three models: one for surface wind only, benchmarked against the system of Lagerquist et al. (2017); a storm-based model for wind throughout the PBL; and a grid-based model for wind throughout the PBL. We will close with a discussion of remaining challenges, including wind-sampling in the PBL and distilling large DL models into smaller models that are less computationally expensive. Lagerquist, R., A. McGovern, and T. Smith, 2017: "Machine learning for real-time prediction of damaging straight-line convective wind." Weather and Forecasting, 32 (6), 2175-2193, https://doi.org/10.1175/WAF-D-17-0038.1.

496363.title: Virtual Radar DataTrees: Analysis-Ready Access to Historical Weather Radar Archives Without Data Duplication
496363.authors: Alfonso Ladino, AtmoScale, Urbana, IL; AtmoScale, Urbana, IL; Univ. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and S. Nesbitt
496363.abstract: Ground-based weather radar archives contain decades of information-rich observations, but most remain organized as collections of independently encoded files. Radar DataTree addresses this limitation by extending the WMO FM 301/CfRadial hierarchical model from individual radar volumes to time-indexed, cloud-native datasets. However, creating a physically materialized Radar DataTree requires rewriting the source archive into a new chunked representation, thereby maintaining an additional copy of the observations. At national-network scale, this requirement becomes substantial: approximately 30 years of observations from 159 U.S. NEXRAD radars already represent roughly 1 PB of raw data, meaning that fully materializing the archive as a Radar DataTree would require storage of a comparable magnitude. We introduce Virtual Radar DataTrees, an approach that exposes existing radar archives through the same dataset-level, Analysis-Ready, Cloud-Optimized (ARCO) interface without duplicating the underlying observations. Instead of rewriting radar data, virtual references map Radar DataTree arrays directly to byte ranges within the original files or objects. Historical archives can therefore be represented as logically organized, time-indexed Zarr datasets while the source observations remain unchanged. This decouples the logical Radar DataTree representation from its physical storage, enabling cloud-native access to large historical archives without first creating a second copy of the data. We evaluate this approach across operational radar archives with different native formats, including U.S. NEXRAD Level II, Finnish Meteorological Institute ODIM H5 radar data, and Colombian radar observations stored in SIGMET format. The results demonstrate that virtualization performance depends strongly on the physical organization of the source data. Colombian SIGMET files can be virtualized without significant structural limitations, whereas the small native chunk sizes of the Finnish archive introduce additional request overhead. For NEXRAD, the interleaved byte organization of radar moments produces read amplification: retrieving a single variable may require reading data associated with multiple variables, resulting in approximately 3–6× additional data transfer relative to an optimized, materialized representation. These performance penalties must be weighed against the storage cost of duplicating archives that already approach petabyte scale. For large historical radar collections, reduced query performance may be an acceptable trade-off when virtualization avoids maintaining an additional copy of the archive. Virtual Radar DataTrees therefore provide a practical bridge between legacy radar files and fully materialized ARCO datasets, enabling archive-scale, cloud-native access while preserving selective materialization for workflows that require higher performance.

496367.title: Assessing El Nino Impacts With the Climate Hazards Global Precipitation with Stations (CHGPS) Data Set
496367.authors: Christopher C. Funk, University of California Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA; and P. Peterson, R. Saldivar, A. Behrangi, L. S. Harrison, W. Turner, and G. Husak
496367.abstract: Over the last twelve years there have been three strong El Niño events - in 2015/16, 2023/24 and 2026/27 events, and one moderate El Niño event in 2018/19. Unfortunately, most gridded precipitation data sets, such as the high-quality Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) Full product (Ziese et al. 2022) have very few observations in recent years. As documented in a recent paper describing version 3 of the Climate Hazards InfraRed Precipitation with Stations (CHIRPS3, Funk et al. 2026, link), the number of GPCC observations has been declining substantially since about 2011 (Figure 1). While the GPCC contained just over 50,000 stations in 1981, it has only included around 12,000 in the recent years. The Climate Hazards Center (CHC), on the other hand, routinely collects more than 20,000 unique observations each month. These observations are rapidly ingested and quality controlled, supporting monthly updates of the CHIRPS satellite-gauge products. These observations are also interpolated and combined with the GPCC archive to produce the Climate Hazards Global Precipitation with Stations (CHGPS) data set (link). The CHIRPS and CHGPS products have quite good station support in several key El Niño teleconnection areas, such as Central and South America, Kenya, Ethiopia and India. In 2026, intense boreal summer droughts have already arisen in these regions (blog). The CHGPS is a high resolution (0.05°) gauge-based gridded monthly precipitation dataset spanning 1900 to the previous month. The CHGPS combines the excellent GPCC ‘Full’ precipitation dataset with additional station data drawn from the routinely updated and curated CHC station archive. The core of the CHGPS blending process is based on four numbers: the estimated variance explained by the GPCC and CHC products at each grid cell, and the number of stations in each grid cell. These values are used to derive weights, which are then used to combine the GPCC and CHC fields, producing the 1900-to-present GPCC. In this presentation, we describe the GHGPS, and then use it to examine El Niño impacts in several teleconnected regions over the last four El Niño events. We place individual seasonal rainfall responses in a deep historic context. We also consider the potential risks of compound drought shocks. Over the teleconnected regions, how large and uncommon were the potential observed repetitive dry seasons during the recent four El Niño events? Repetitive drought shocks in food insecure countries like Zimbabwe, or environmentally critical regions like the Amazon basin can decrease resilience and potentially reduce vegetative carbon sequestration. We also consider the timing of El Niño events. One aspect of the 2015/16 and 2026/27 events was that the equatorial east Pacific sea surface temperatures (SST) were already quite warm during early boreal summer. Using historic Relative Oceanic Niño Index data, we examine the frequency of such outcomes. Do we find predictive relationships for rainfall in Ethiopia and India when RONI values are high at the beginning of the season? Do these relationships offer opportunities for prediction? Figure 1.The number of unique monthly station observations in the GPCC Full and CHC precipitation observation archive. Citations Funk et al. (2026) The climate hazards infrared precipitation with stations - a new environmental record for monitoring extremes. Scientific Data 2(1) 150066. Link. Ziese, Markus; Rauthe-Schöch, Armin; Becker, Andreas; Finger, Peter; Rustemeier, Elke; Hänsel, Stephanie; Schneider, Udo (2022): GPCC Full Data Daily Version 2022 at 1.0°: Daily Land-Surface Precipitation from Rain-Gauges built on GTS-based and Historic Data. DOI: 10.5676/DWD_GPCC/FD_D_V2022_100

496368.title: Forecasting Winter Road Surface Conditions: A Machine Learning-Based Integration of Traffic and Weather Observations
496368.authors: Brendan Eckerman, Colorado Department of Transportation, Denver, CO; Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and R. S. Schumacher, M. B. Chapman, and N. Barlow
496368.abstract: Winter weather can present significant challenges to daily life, especially in mountainous regions where severe winter conditions can cause extreme, potentially deadly disruptions. A key component of the danger presented by winter weather comes in the form of transportation disruption, as wet, snowy, or icy roads elongate vehicle stopping distances, increasing the frequency and severity of vehicle accidents. This not only presents a danger to human life, but also a disruption to the flow of commerce in impacted regions. Improved prediction of the state of roadways during periods of winter weather increases the safety of the traveling public, reduces maintenance and material costs, and limits interruptions to the flow of local commerce. In this study, weather observations from the Colorado Department of Transportation (CDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) network are integrated with traffic flow observations and modeled atmospheric parameters from the NCEP High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model to train a predictive random forest regression model. Preliminary results of modeled road surface friction are compared against a persistence baseline as well as physics-based road surface modelling to assess the added value of traffic flow when forecasting for winter road conditions. This approach has potential applications in short-term pavement maintenance, travel advisory, and emergency dispatch systems in areas that experience travel disruption due to winter weather.

496369.title: What Governs the Tropospheric Response to Tropopause Polar Vortices?
496369.authors: Kevin Boyd, University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, MA; and C. A. Davis
496369.abstract: Tropopause polar vortices (TPVs) are coherent, often long-lived cyclonic disturbances characterized by high pressure and low potential temperature on the dynamic tropopause. Their persistence and associations with jet-stream variability and extratropical cyclones suggest that TPVs may provide an important source of extended predictability for high-impact weather. Nonetheless, the influence of TPVs on the underlying troposphere has received relatively little systematic investigation, and it remains unclear why some TPVs produce substantial tropospheric responses while others do not. This study investigates how TPV characteristics regulate the magnitude, horizontal extent, and vertical depth of these responses. A climatology of TPVs derived from the ERA5 reanalysis is analyzed to characterize the three-dimensional atmospheric response to TPVs and determine how it depends on TPV strength, horizontal scale, and evolutionary history (e.g., recent transport from the Arctic versus extended residence at lower latitudes). This framework identifies the vortex characteristics that favor stronger and deeper coupling between TPVs and the lower troposphere. The analysis further examines the relative importance of dynamical and thermodynamic pathways through which TPVs influence the troposphere, contrasting the quasi-geostrophic vertical-motion response with the thermodynamic effects associated with the TPV cold air mass. The latter may be particularly important over ice-free oceans, where enhanced surface fluxes and reduced static stability can amplify the lower-tropospheric response. Representative TPVs observed during the NURTURE field campaign provide complementary case studies for investigating the physical mechanisms underlying relationships identified in the climatological analysis. Together, these analyses establish how TPV characteristics regulate their tropospheric influence and assess when and how TPVs can serve as precursors to high-impact weather.

496373.title: NSF NCAR’s Scientific Leadership in Aviation Icing: From Foundational Research to the ICICLE Field Campaign
496373.authors: Scott D. Landolt, NCAR, Boulder, CO
496373.abstract: For more than three decades, the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) Research Applications Laboratory (RAL) has played a leading role in advancing the science and technology used to understand, diagnose, and forecast aircraft icing. Beginning with the development of the Current Icing Product (CIP) and Forecast Icing Product (FIP) in the mid-1990s under sponsorship from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), NSF NCAR/RAL research established a foundation for integrating numerical weather prediction, satellite, radar, surface observations, lightning data, and pilot reports to provide icing guidance on the national scale. These products have continued to provide operational icing guidance through the NOAA Aviation Weather Center. Building upon this foundation, RAL subsequently led research into higher-resolution terminal-area icing through the FAA's Terminal Area Icing Weather InformatioN (TAIWIN) program to address new requirements for determining and reporting icing conditions within the airport terminal area (defined as 30 nm from the center of the airport up to 12,000 ft agl). Together, these efforts have demonstrated significant advances in icing prediction while also exposing the continuing challenges associated with accurately observing and discriminating among the diverse icing environments that present hazards to aircraft, especially supercooled large drops (SLD; i.e. freezing drizzle and freezing rain). The In-Cloud Icing and Large-drop Experiment (ICICLE), conducted during the winter of 2019, represented a critical milestone in this continuing research effort. Sponsored by the FAA in support of both the TAIWIN and In-Flight Icing (IFI) programs, ICICLE was designed to obtain comprehensive observations across a range of icing and non-icing environments, including pristine supercooled small drops (i.e. cloud droplets), freezing drizzle, freezing rain, and mixed-phase conditions. NSF NCAR/RAL played a central scientific and operational leadership role in the experiment, working with the National Research Council of Canada (NRC), FAA, NOAA, NASA, Leading Edge Atmospherics, international meteorological organizations, and participating universities. With a focus on the Midwestern United States and the western Great Lakes, the NRC Convair-580 research aircraft conducted 26 research flights and collected approximately 120 hours of airborne observations, while NSF NCAR deployed and collected enhanced surface observing capabilities at multiple locations across the area. NSF NCAR scientists also served as Forecasters and Operations Directors, providing the meteorological analysis, mission planning, and operational coordination necessary to safely and accurately target the desired icing environments. The ICICLE observations demonstrated the substantial spatial and temporal variability of icing environments and highlighted the difficulty of representing the microphysical processes governing supercooled liquid water and large-drop formation in numerical weather prediction models. In particular, observations of freezing drizzle and mixed-phase environments provided important evidence that icing severity alone is insufficient to characterize the operational hazard. Accurate discrimination of small-drop icing, freezing drizzle, and freezing rain is also critical. NSF NCAR has used these observations to evaluate model representations of freezing drizzle and freezing rain and to investigate both numerical weather prediction and machine-learning approaches for predicting these hazardous environments. ICICLE data also directly influenced development of subsequent versions of CIP and FIP, including improvements associated with higher-resolution modeling, particle-phase and supercooled liquid water diagnostics and forecasts, and incorporation of additional three-dimensional radar and satellite observations. ICICLE represents more than a successful field campaign; it illustrates the progression of NSF NCAR and RAL’s scientific leadership from foundational research, to operationally relevant weather information, to targeted observations designed to address specific limitations in existing prediction capabilities. The experiment has brought together decades of NSF NCAR expertise in cloud microphysics, numerical weather prediction, remote sensing, aviation meteorology, field observations, and decision-support systems and applied that expertise to a critical aviation safety challenge. This presentation will highlight NSF NCAR's leadership throughout the ICICLE lifecycle, beginning with the scientific foundations that motivated the experiment, through experimental design and field operations, and the continued use of ICICLE observations to advance icing science and prediction. The ICICLE field campaign provides a compelling example of how sustained investment in fundamental Earth-system science and long-term partnerships across government, academia, industry, and international research organizations can produce innovations that translate into improved weather information and enhanced aviation safety. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

496374.title: A Climatology of Supercell–Squall Line Mergers Across the United States from 2013–2024
496374.authors: Kaitlyn Ivey, Ohio University, Athens, OH; Ohio University, Athens, OH; and D. V. Blount
496374.abstract: Supercell–squall line mergers are a complex form of storm interaction that can quickly change storm structure and severe weather potential. While supercells and squall lines have been studied extensively on their own, much less is known about how often these storms interact, where these mergers occur, and when they are most likely to happen. Previous research has mainly focused on individual cases or idealized simulations, making it difficult to understand how common these events are across the United States. This study will develop a climatology of documented supercell–squall line mergers across the United States from 2013 through 2024. Merger events will be identified using archived NEXRAD radar observations along with the Storm Prediction Center Severe Weather Event Archive. For each event, the date, location, timing, storm characteristics, and associated severe weather reports will be documented. The resulting dataset will be used to examine where and when mergers occur, including geographic patterns, seasonal trends, and differences in the time of day. Radar observations will also be used to document common storm structures and changes in organization as the supercell and squall line interact. This climatology will provide a broader look at how frequently supercell–squall line mergers occur and whether they show consistent spatial or temporal patterns across the United States. Identifying these patterns will provide a baseline for examining how merger events relate to changes in severe weather activity. The results will also provide a larger observational dataset for future research into the environmental and storm-scale processes that contribute to supercell–squall line mergers.

496376.title: Modeling Soil Moisture and Vegetation Effects on the 2012 Great Plains Drought: Understanding Their Potential Dependence on Land-Atmosphere Coupling Strength
496376.authors: Chu-Chun Chen, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; and G. Wang
496376.abstract: One of the most severe droughts of the century occurred over the United States Great Plains in 2012, resulting in substantial agricultural and economic losses. Numerous studies have investigated sources of drought predictability to improve forecasts and provide earlier warning of such high-impact events. Soil moisture and vegetation have been identified as potential contributors to drought development, yet their relative roles and underlying physical mechanisms remain uncertain. In this study, we investigate the roles of soil moisture and vegetation in the development of the 2012 Great Plains drought using the Community Earth System Model version 2 (CESM2) coupled land-atmosphere simulations. We conduct two sets of idealized experiments: (1) simulations initialized with dry versus wet soil moisture conditions and (2) simulations prescribing climatological versus observed leaf area index. These experiments are used to isolate the effects of antecedent soil moisture and vegetation variability on surface fluxes, atmospheric conditions, and drought evolution. To help understand results from the numerical experiments, we further evaluate the strength of land-atmosphere coupling in CESM2 and emerging machine-learning-based climate models against benchmarks from observational and reanalysis data. We quantify coupling strength using conventional terrestrial and atmospheric coupling indices, as well as Liang-Kleeman information flow, which provides a causal measure of information transfer from land to atmospheric variables. This multi-approach framework allows us to assess how soil moisture and vegetation influence drought evolution and to discern the potential model dependence of the results, especially concerning the model representation of land-atmosphere coupling.

496377.title: NSF-NOAA GONG: Operations and Engineering Support
496377.authors: Gregory Card, National Solar Observatory, Boulder, CO
496377.abstract: The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG) operations team supports 24/7/365 instrument monitoring. This team monitors the health of the instruments via the GONG Monitor Tool, https://monitor.nso.edu/, and remote login to the site workstations. As part of the operations support, the team travels to each network site for preventive maintenance or emergency repairs. The GONG network maintains two engineering instrument shelters, located in Boulder, CO. The engineering shelters are used for testing repaired hardware prior to re-deployment to the network sites, new hardware & software development, and component acceptance tests. For the initial testing, repairs, and development of electronics, the team uses the Sonora Lab, an electronics copy of a GONG shelter without a light feed. Prior to the 20th anniversary of the deployment of the GONG network, the NSF approved the funding of a refurbishment project that allowed the project to replace or spare failing and outdated components and subsystems. The scope of the refurbishment project included the replacement of computer workstations, liquid crystal modulators, and cameras. A significant engineering effort was required for replacing the SMD/DALSA 1M60 cameras with the Emergent Vision Technologies HB-1800-S-M cameras. The GONG refurbishment program formally ended with the replacement of the camera at the Tenerife, Spain site in May 2025. The full refurbishment of the Mauna Loa site is pending the reopening of the Mauna Loa Observatory. Now that GONG has passed its 30th anniversary, a higher level of operations and engineering support is anticipated.

496378.title: The Effect of Vertical Wind Shear on Tropical Cyclones in a Changing Climate
496378.authors: Carter Jon Hunter, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. Carstens, J. Done, C. M. Zarzycki, A. C. Didlake Jr., and D. Fu
496378.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) are among the most dangerous weather systems on the planet, causing serious damage to property and communities every year. How these systems change in a warming climate is essential to improving infrastructure and forecasting capabilities. Utilizing global climate models (GCMs), TCs can be looked at far into the future under different warming scenarios. This can provide insight into potential structural changes of TC winds, precipitation, and thermodynamics. A difficult part of understanding TC behavior is the influence of environmental vertical wind shear on the system. Shear is known to alter the overall structure of the system, tilting the upright vortex and causing asymmetric convective processes. In this study, an atmosphere-ocean coupled quarter degree resolution GCM with up to 10-member ensembles for each warming scenario is used to analyze TCs. TCs are tracked using the TempestExtremes tracking algorithm, this determines a TC track based on three criteria; if the system is warm core, there is a closed isobar at least 2 mb less than the surrounding environment, and this signature persists for at least three days. TCs are compiled based on intensity determined from minimum central pressure and oriented into shear- and storm-motion relative perspectives. Goals for this study involve how this GCM resolves TC structure and how much this structure is expected to change in a warming climate. Does precipitation asymmetry become more or less pronounced with the presence of stronger vertical shear? Does the presence of wind shear amplify or hinder precipitation rate? How do precipitation and wind fields change in a warming climate?

496383.title: Investigating Land–Atmosphere Feedbacks and Wind Erosion During Historical Southern Plains Droughts
496383.authors: Abhijit Das, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and Y. Xu and C. He
496383.abstract: Interactions among soil moisture, vegetation cover, and atmospheric processes strongly influence drought onset and development on seasonal timescales. As soil moisture declines, vegetation experiences water stress, and canopy cover can decrease, altering surface energy fluxes, roughness, and soil stability. These land surface changes can reinforce drought conditions through land–atmosphere feedbacks while also increasing the susceptibility of exposed soils to wind erosion and dust emission. Despite their importance, the coupled role of soil moisture–vegetation dynamics in drought initiation and propagation and the associated land surface response are not fully represented in many regional climate modeling studies. This work investigates the role of soil moisture–vegetation feedbacks in drought propagation using high-resolution simulations with the Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled with chemistry (WRF-Chem). The model is configured at 9 km horizontal resolution over a domain covering the south-central United States and northern Mexico, including the Southern Plains and adjacent Gulf Coast region, and further enhanced to 1.8 km over Texas. Land surface processes are represented using the Noah-MP land surface model with dynamic vegetation, allowing soil moisture stress to influence vegetation conditions and surface energy and water fluxes, including latent and sensible heat exchange with the atmosphere. The simulations are designed to examine how variations in soil moisture availability and vegetation cover modify land–atmosphere coupling during historical drought seasons. Particular attention is given to how these land-surface changes influence surface erodibility and the environmental conditions that favor dust emissions. By explicitly linking soil moisture–vegetation feedbacks to drought evolution and land-surface dust emission processes, this work aims to improve understanding of how land-surface dynamics influence atmospheric composition and regional climate. The high-resolution modeling framework provides a pathway toward improved representation of drought–land–atmosphere coupling in regional climate and Earth system models, which is essential for predicting environmental impacts over regions with high drought frequency and intensity.

496385.title: Path to Launch: JPSS-4 Overview and Cal/Val Readiness
496385.authors: Jeffrey A. Weinrich, STAR, Washington, DC; and I. Guch, L. Zhou, and M. G. Divakarla
496385.abstract: In preparation for the upcoming JPSS-4 (J4) launch, the JPSS Program at the Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR) has established the necessary infrastructure to integrate J4 science algorithms into operations. The J4 mission features a suite of advanced instruments—including the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS), Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS), and Ozone Mapping and Profiler Suite (OMPS)—to ensure continuity in global environmental monitoring. Building on the legacy of the S-NPP and NOAA-20/21 series, these sensors require rigorous pre-operational evaluation. This presentation provides an overview of calibration and validation (C/V) activities led by STAR science teams, covering performance metrics, upcoming milestones, and schedules for Sensor Data Records (SDR/L1) and Environmental Data Records (EDR/L2). We also provide guidance on accessing NOAA-21 data products via the Product Distribution and Access (PDA) system, the Comprehensive Large Array-data Stewardship System (CLASS), and Direct Broadcast (DB), while outlining future J4 access through the NESDIS Common Cloud Framework Operational Subscription Service (OSS) and the Open Information Stewardship Service (OISS) cloud archive. Finally, we discuss recent process improvements and lessons learned to support future mission success.

496386.title: Why Are Cloud Microphysics Codes Uniquely Sensitive to Numerical Optimization?
496386.abstract: We resolve a decade-old mystery: why enabling the Fused Multiply-Add (FMA) optimization meaningfully changes the output of leading atmospheric models. Using ensemble-based verification and code coverage tools, we trace the discrepancy to its root cause and describe the floating-point mechanism responsible. We then explain why cloud microphysics codes are uniquely sensitive to this class of optimization, and what that implies for the use of mixed precision and GPUs in numerical weather and climate models.

496389.title: Recent Advances In Turbulence Nowcasting through Machine Learning with Geostationary Satellite and NWP
496389.authors: Anthony J. Wimmers, CIMSS, Calgary, AB, Canada; Associate Scientist, Univ. of Wisconsin CIMSS, Madison, WI; CIMSS, Univ. of Wisconsin−Madison, Madison, WI; and S. Griffin, T. J. Wagner, W. Feltz, and T. Rahmes
496389.abstract: Aviation turbulence is a unique machine learning challenge because of the interconnection of data patterns between NWP signals and remotely sensed features. Here we present a new model that improves on previous versions in the following ways: nowcasting across the entire vertical column from the surface to 45,000 ft, estimating eddy dissipation rate from the range of null to severe turbulence, and presenting probabilistic guidance. We address important design questions such as the sensitivity of relevant inputs to accurate predictions, and the relative value of computing power at inference time to improve skill. Project status of the transition of this model to operations at NOAA NESDIS will also be covered.

496392.title: Assessing the Impacts of ATMS and TMS Radiance Assimilation In a Prototype RRFS Based on MPAS and JEDI
496392.authors: Keenan Christopher Eure, CIRA, Boulder, CO; and H. Lin, G. Ge, X. Zhang, J. J. Guerrette, T. T. Ladwig, J. Beck, and B. C. Ruston
496392.abstract: Microwave satellite radiance observations from polar-orbiting sensors tend to have the greatest impact on numerical weather prediction (NWP) models out of all commonly-used satellite products used in data assimilation. As these sensors have several passes over a region daily, they provide critical information on temperature and moisture profiles, particularly in high altitudes and over non-land regions where conventional and radar observations are unable to provide the same coverage. Therefore, utilizing available microwave satellite radiances in the MPAS-based JEDI data assimilation system of the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) is critical for improving its success in forecasting high-impact weather. While the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) sensor has already shown benefit in operational NWP models, the addition of the novel Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) observations pose potential additional benefits to complement ATMS DA. Launched in 2024, this constellation of 11 small satellite sensors has a higher revisit rate than ATMS and is also currently being tested in RRFS.
