This work explores the continued implementation of TMS radiances into a prototype RRFS using MPAS-JEDI, which has 12-km horizontal grid spacing over North America. A series of retrospective experiments from 2025 are conducted comparing the value of ATMS and TMS, assimilating them jointly and separately and comparing their impacts to analyses and forecasts. Consideration is given to sensitivities such as clear- vs. cloudy-sky, data assimilation method, channel selection, and other options.

496395.title: Sensitivity of Air–Sea Interaction to the Effective Resolution of Sea Surface Temperature in a High-Resolution Coupled SHiELD–MOM6 Model
496395.authors: Jing Chen, Program in Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and B. G. Reichl, L. M. Harris, K. Gao, J. Mouallem, R. Zhang, J. H. Chen, J. M. Steinberg, Q. Xiao, B. Zhao, R. Benson, and L. Chilutti
496395.abstract: High-resolution coupled models resolve increasingly detailed ocean surface features, yet the extent to which this information affects simulated air–sea exchange remains uncertain. We have developed a regional coupled modeling system in which the SHiELD atmosphere and MOM6 ocean are both configured at 3-km horizontal resolution. An online sea surface temperature (SST) smoother has been incorporated into the coupling framework to control the effective resolution of SST communicated from the ocean to the atmosphere without changing the native model grids. This capability enables controlled comparisons of air–sea interaction across a range of SST smoothing scales. Simulations are evaluated for different tropical cyclone cases, with an additional configuration using a 24-km ocean grid providing a reference for interpreting resolution-dependent differences. Changes in ocean resolution have limited effects on simulated tropical cyclone tracks, while their influences on storm intensity vary across cases and forecast periods. Comparisons among the online smoothing experiments examine the spatial variability of SST, surface latent and sensible heat fluxes, near-surface temperature and humidity, exchange coefficients, winds, and precipitation. Spatial spectral analyses are used to trace how differences in SST effective resolution are reflected in surface fluxes and atmospheric fields. These experiments provide a comparative assessment of the sensitivity of air–sea interaction to SST effective resolution and offer guidance for interpreting resolution-dependent behavior in high-resolution coupled atmosphere–ocean models.

496399.title: High-Resolution Earth System Simulations Project Amplified Inland Tropical Cyclone Compound Hazards under Global Warming
496399.authors: Dan Fu, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and X. Liu, F. Castruccio, P. Chang, and G. Danabasoglu
496399.abstract: Although global tropical cyclone (TC) frequency has been widely studied, future changes in TC‐induced hazards remain uncertain. This gap is particularly acute for compound TC wind–precipitation hazards, despite their critical importance for climate resilience. To address this knowledge gap, we leverage state-of-the-art observations and high-resolution large-ensemble climate simulations from the Community Earth System Model high-resolution simulations (CESM-HR) and the Database for Policy Decision Making for Future Climate Change (d4PDF) to improve our understanding of TC-induced compound hazards under changing climate. Our analysis reveals a robust intensification of compound TC wind–precipitation hazards over both coastal and inland regions, despite a projected decline in global TC frequency. Under the medium-to-high emissions (high-emissions) scenario, late 21st-century simulations project global-mean compound hazard risks increasing by 101.3-107.3% (65.6-104.1%) within 100 km of the coastlines and further escalate by 161.0–181.4% (100.4–202.9%) in areas 100–500 km inland. In some inland regions, the projected increase can exceed 300%, underscoring the potential for unprecedented inland risk escalation. These changes are primarily driven by enhanced TC-wind at landfall and persistent increase in precipitation rate due to enhanced atmospheric moisture availability and ocean-to-land transport. Moreover, this pattern of inland amplification remains robust across distinct future sea surface temperature (SST) warming patterns represented by CESM-HR and d4PDF. These findings underscore the disconnect between changes in TC frequency and changes in compound extreme hazard risk and highlight the urgent need to re-evaluate TC risk frameworks and account for the growing threat of compound hazards far from the coast.

496400.title: Relationships between Thermodynamic Profiles and Vertical Motion Profile Shape In OTREC Field Campaign and Reanalysis Data.
496400.authors: Larissa E Back, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and Q. B. S. Bowman and M. A. Bernardez
496400.abstract: Tropical deep convection and the associated latent heating from precipitation formation affect the atmospheric energy budget and global circulation via large-scale vertical motion. However, simulating these processes correctly has proved challenging. Even up-to-date reanalyses differ from each-other and from observations in their estimates of the top-heaviness of vertical motion profiles, which influences column energy budgets. Hence, well-executed observations and robust physical understanding are crucial to better constrain our process-level understanding of the top-heaviness of convection. To rise to this challenge, we analyze observations from the Organization of Tropical East Pacific Convection (OTREC) field campaign and combine this with reanalysis data to understand thermodynamic controls of the top-heaviness of the vertical motion profile. We use a measure of vertical motion profile shape called the top-heaviness angle to show that OTREC sampled a wide range of profile shapes. We compare the thermodynamic environment for top and bottom-heavy profiles in OTREC and find top-heavy vertical motion is differentiated from bottom-heavy by a warmer and drier lower troposphere and a moister upper troposphere in OTREC data. We compare the OTREC data to ERA5 data sampled at roughly the same time and locations, and find some significant differences in relationships between thermodynamic profiles and vertical motion top-heaviness. Since field campaign data is not available broadly geographically, we also analyze reanalysis data throughout the tropics utilizing similar metrics to those utilized in the OTREC domain. Looking at the tropics and subtropics more broadly in reanalysis, we find that vertical motion profile top-heaviness is associated with a dipole in saturation deficit (a measure of moisture), as in the OTREC domain. However, the statistical relationships between temperature stratification and top-heaviness look very different than in the OTREC domain. We utilize a stochastic parcel model to interpret these results.

496402.title: Ensemble Nested EAGLE and Probabilistic Forecasting Using Anemoi
496402.authors: Joshua DaRosa, MITRE, Bedford, MA; and T. Smith, M. Pope, B. Huang, S. Frolov, C. Miller, M. Alam, N. Silverman, and C. J. Lewellyn
496402.abstract: Building off the strong results in the deterministic Nested EAGLE variable resolution AI atmospheric forecast model, NOAA PSL in collaboration with MITRE are developing the Nested EAGLE Ensemble. This is a probabilistic variable resolution AI atmospheric forecast model built on the Anemoi framework. The model architecture retains a 25 km global resolution with a 6 km refinement over the continental United States (CONUS), trained on a combination of operational GFS and HRRR analyses with a 6 hour temporal resolution. To generate calibrated probabilistic forecasts, multiple noise injection schemes have been explored within a CRPS-based ensemble framework, with forecast quality assessed through mean RMSE, spread skill ratio (SSR) and spectral analysis to characterize the distribution of forecast energy across spatial scales. Extending this work, we investigate the incorporation of the multi-scale CRPS loss function within the Anemoi framework alongside the effects of extended training duration, auto-regressive rollout length, and finer temporal resolution on the model's ability to resolve small-scale atmospheric structures over CONUS — with a particular focus on precipitation fields.

496403.title: Relative Impact of Trend and IndoPacific-Atlantic Basin Interactions on Seasonal Sea Surface Prediction
496403.authors: Xiaoyu Long, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and S. Shin and M. Newman
496403.abstract: Interactions between the Atlantic and IndoPacific basins are often considered a source of seasonal climate predictability, yet quantifying these influences in the presence of large-scale external forcing remains an open challenge. Using Linear Inverse Models (LIMs) constructed from observations and large-ensemble coupled climate model simulations, this study assesses how the forced trend and intrinsic basin interactions each contribute to seasonal forecast skill for sea surface temperature anomalies (SSTA) and sea surface height anomalies (SSHA). The forced trend is found to impact forecast skill synchronously across all ocean basins, which could be misinterpreted as inter-basin coupling. This influence substantially enhances SSTA forecast skill, with one notable exception: the tropical Pacific, where interference between the forced trend and El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) variability reduces skill instead. Once the forced trend is removed, residual basin interactions prove to have relatively weak, localized effects on forecast skill. Optimal perturbation analysis of the LIM dynamical operator indicates that basin interactions contribute to the growth of North Atlantic tripole variability, yet their influence on forecast skill remains comparatively modest. ENSO growth, in contrast, while governed primarily by internal IndoPacific dynamics, is enhanced by Atlantic interactions that provide additional predictive information and increase ENSO forecast skill. Large-ensemble climate model simulations broadly reproduce these observed patterns of skill but do not consistently capture the observed fidelity of basin interactions.

496406.title: How Important is Boundary Layer Pumping in Tropical Disturbances?
496406.authors: Tyler Warren Barbero, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and M. M. Bell and D. Colón-Burgos
496406.abstract: Predicting the timing and location of convection in tropical disturbances remains a significant forecasting challenge. This study investigates the role of boundary layer pumping (BLP) on convection in weak vortices using an idealized modeling framework with a shallow-water layer atop a slab or height-resolved boundary layer (BL). We perform axisymmetric simulations of tropical vortices spanning easterly wave disturbances to tropical storms. Results show BLP is weak for disturbances, producing updrafts of 0.1-1 cm s-1 and lifting timescales of 12-36 h to lift parcels to a 500-m height representative of a level of free convection. Tropical depression and storm strength vortices produce stronger updrafts and reduced lifting timescales of 1-3 h. Asymmetric simulations of translating disturbances show weakly organized updrafts that are inconsistent with convective organization observed in easterly waves during NAMMA and NASA CPEX-CV. Disturbances adjust via inertial oscillations similar to tropical cyclones but with longer adjustment periods, and exhibit updrafts further inward of the radius of maximum wind. Two-way interactive BL simulations show negligible vortex evolution in weak disturbances over 5 days, consistent with long adjustment and lifting timescales. In contrast, stronger and more compact vortices show marked intensification, with a tropical storm-like vortex contracting and doubling in intensity. Collectively, these findings show that BLP is inefficient for initiating and organizing convection in weak disturbances, but becomes progressively more important closer to genesis. These results highlight the need to investigate other mechanisms governing convective organization and wave intensification in tropical disturbances.

496407.title: NICEcube: An Essential 12-U Cubesat Observation for Current and Future Space Weather Forecast Models
496407.authors: Martin Mlynczak, Space Environment Technologies, Yorktown, VA; Space Environment Technologies, Pacific Palisades, CA; and W. K. Tobiska, S. Mutschler, A. Lozinski, T. E. Berger, and D. Scott
496407.abstract: NICEcube, the Nitric Oxide Infrared Emissions cubesat, is a 12-U cubesat that will provide direct measurements of the rate (W per cubic meter) of infrared radiative cooling by the nitric oxide (NO) molecule in Earth’s thermosphere (115 km to > 250 km). NICEcube draws its design and measurement heritage from the extraordinary success (24 year and counting) of the SABER instrument on the NASA TIMED satellite. SABER measures the infrared cooling rate due to NO and data analyses over the past quarter century have shown that: 1) NO infrared cooling acts as a ‘natural thermostat’ in controlling the response and recovery of the thermal and density structure of the thermosphere during geomagnetic storms, 2) different storms can have vastly different thermal and density responses, 3) similar storms may also have vastly different thermal and density responses, and 4) these responses cannot be predicted a-priori, requiring real-time observations of NO cooling for assimilation into current and future space weather forecast models, especially for the accurate forecasting of thermospheric density. NICEcube is designed by the same team that designed the SABER instrument and that developed the scientific algorithms for directly deriving the rate of infrared cooling from NO. The NICEcube requirements are specified in a science traceability matrix developed under a NASA-funded Phase A study. This presentation will review the science needs for real-time observations of NO infrared cooling and the NICEcube design and performance parameters. Ongoing efforts to develop operational capability to assimilate SABER-measured NO cooling rates into existing forecast models (such as HASDM) will be reviewed, as will efforts to assimilate these and NICEcube data into emerging physics-based models being developed under the NASA-funded Space Weather Operations Readiness Development (SWORD) Center of Excellence. All components of NICEcube are conservatively at TRL 4-6. Options for public-private partnerships for transitioning the TIMED satellite to an operational space weather mission will be discussed as will options for the development and deployment of NICEcube

496408.title: East Asian Atmospheric Rivers Are Most Hazardous In Summer: Insights from AR Tracking
496408.authors: Yeeun Kwon, Seoul National University, Seoul, South korea; and S. Chung and S. W. Son
496408.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are canonically understood as transient corridors of moisture transport ahead of the cold front of an extratropical cyclone. Over East Asia, however, ARs are most frequent, intense, and long-lasting in summer, when extratropical cyclone activity is at its annual minimum. Here we track ARs as coherent objects through their life cycle to identify what makes East Asian summer ARs so hazardous. ARs emerge where the moisture transport of eastward-moving transient cyclones is superimposed on the quasi-stationary moisture transport along the boundary of the western North Pacific subtropical high (WNPSH). This superposition strengthens the moisture transport, while the quasi-stationary nature of the WNPSH prolongs the AR duration. Moreover, since the WNPSH boundary is modulated by subseasonal variability such as the Pacific–Japan pattern, the region of superposition itself varies. Our findings suggest that the quasi-stationary moisture transport is not merely the background condition for ARs, but an active contributor that makes East Asian summer ARs intense, long-lasting, and thus hazardous.

496413.title: Assessing the Effects of Mineral Dust Coatings on Optical and Microphysical Properties and Synergistic Lidar–Thermal Infrared Retrievals
496413.authors: Jayce Bradley Crayne, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and D. Li and P. Yang
496413.abstract: Coated mineral dust aerosols are an important component of the Earth’s energy budget because of their interactions with solar and thermal radiation. During atmospheric transport, mineral dust can mix with other aerosol species and gases, forming coatings on the dust particles that alter their optical, microphysical, and radiative properties. This study investigates the effects of black carbon, sulfate, nitrate, and sea salt coatings on mineral dust using a globally averaged refractive index for the dust core. Bulk optical properties of these two-layer particles are efficiently calculated using the separation-of-variables T-matrix method (SV-TM), Improved Geometric Optics Method (IGOM), and Invariant Imbedding T-matrix Method (IITM) across prescribed aspect-ratio and size distributions. These properties are subsequently incorporated into radiative transfer simulations using a Monte Carlo method for lidar and a two-stream approximation for thermal infrared measurements to quantify how coating composition and amount modify remote sensing signatures. An alternative homogeneous particle representation based on the Bruggeman effective medium approximation is also evaluated against the explicit two-layer approach to access the effects of particle inhomogeneity. Simulated observations are compared with polluted dust measurements from the Cloud-Aerosol Lidar with Orthogonal Polarization (CALIOP) and Imaging Infrared Radiometer (IIR) aboard CALIPSO to evaluate the sensitivity of CALIOP-IIR observations to mineral dust coatings and to access their impacts on synergistic retrievals of polluted dust properties.

496414.title: Establishing Measurement Confidence in Low-Cost 3D-Printed Weather Stations: A Multi-Site Intercomparison Study
496414.authors: Rebecca Zieber, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and P. A. Kucera, B. M. Smith, M. Steinson, K. Payne, and W. Nicewonger
496414.abstract: Trustworthy, timely decision-making during high-impact weather depends on instrumentation whose accuracy and uncertainty are well understood. However, conventional weather stations often remain too costly to deploy at the density many communities need, particularly in resource-limited and remote regions. Low-cost, low-power environmental sensors paired with 3D-printed enclosures offer a promising path to denser observation networks, but before such systems can be trusted for operational and community decision-making, their measurement uncertainty must be rigorously characterized against established standards. This study presents a multi-site intercomparison of the 3D-PAWS platform, developed by the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR) with support from the U.S. Department of State and the U.S. National Weather Service, in partnership with the Turkish State Meteorological Service (TSMS). 3D-PAWS units, each integrating temperature, humidity, pressure, wind, and rainfall sensors with an onboard datalogger streaming minute-resolution data to a cloud-hosted database in near real time, were co-located with WMO-compliant reference stations across three climatically distinct sites to quantify measurement bias, correlation, and uncertainty relative to calibrated instrumentation. Our intercomparison shows that 3D-PAWS temperature, wind speed, and rainfall sensors achieve low uncertainty and strong agreement with reference instruments. Pressure and humidity sensors show good but more variable agreement, with a hardware revision measurably reducing humidity uncertainty over the course of the study, demonstrating how calibration and design iteration can improve instrument confidence over time. Further analysis is required to identify inconsistencies with the wind vane observations. Our findings demonstrate that 3D-PAWS stations are well-suited for expanding meteorological monitoring in underserved areas, supporting operational needs for applications such as early warning response to high-impact weather events, in addition to supporting community-driven science.

496415.title: Observing Ocean Turbidity with GOES East ABI and Lessons for GXI
496415.authors: Jon Fulbright, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and D. Pogorzala, D. Lindsey, J. K. Zajic, M. Foster, L. Wichrowski, E. Sorbella, J. Anderson, and L. A. Byerle
496415.abstract: Understanding the optical parameters of the ocean’s surface is a key aspect in extracting vital meteorological and natural hazard information. Ocean turbidity (measure of suspended particles in the water affecting clarity) is one such parameter, but is difficult to directly measure with the GOES-R Series Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) due to the lack of a green band. The temporal resolution of ABI data allows for near-continuous daytime monitoring of turbidity, an improvement on the few snapshots per day provided by LEO instruments. Jolliff et al. 2019 developed a chromatic domain mapping method to create true color ABI images. In this presentation, we describe our implementation of this method, which utilizes LEO sensor data (OLCI or VIIRS) and the inherent relationships between ocean water tristimulus values. Derived linear regressions are then applied to ABI Band 1 and Band 2 reflectance data to generate RGB images. This application tests the limits of the ABI radiometric calibration and anticipates the possibilities available for GXI. We present samples based upon GOES East CONUS data, as well as results of initial outreach using a real-time visualization tool (TOWR-S Looper) for NWS mission applications.

496416.title: Subseasonal to Seasonal Prediction Skill of Compound Drought-Heatwave Events Over The US Southern Great Plains
496416.authors: Henry Olasunkanmi Olayiwola, School of Meteorology, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and J. C. Furtado
496416.abstract: Compound drought–heatwave (CDHW) events pose substantial risks to agriculture, water resources, ecosystems, and human health across the Southern Great Plains (SGP), yet their subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction and the sources leading to significant S2S prediction skill remain poorly understood. Using European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) subseasonal reforecasts for 2005–2024, we evaluate prediction skill for droughts and heatwaves individually along with CDHWs across the US Southern Great Plains for lead weeks 1–6. Heatwaves are defined as periods when the daily maximum temperature exceeds its calendar-day 90th-percentile threshold for at least five consecutive days. Meteorological droughts occur when the daily Standardized Precipitation Index remains below its 20th-percentile threshold for at least ten consecutive days, while CDHWs require an overlap of a heatwave and a drought of at least two days. Verification is taken from a recently published database of heatwaves, droughts, and CDHWs across the US Southern Great Plains. Results show that skill is highest during Weeks 1–3 and declines substantially afterward. Quantile mapping applied to temperature and precipitation fields improves prediction skill overall versus non-bias-corrected forecasts, particularly during Week 3. The ECMWF subseasonal model also predicts droughts and heatwaves more successfully than CDHWs, whose verification is constrained by their rarity and limited sample size. We also assess the ECMWF model’s representation of important precursors to these extreme hydrometeorological events (e.g., 500-hPa geopotential heights, soil moisture, and surface fluxes) to determine whether the model yields similar connections to these events as seen in reanalysis. Overall, these findings quantify the practical subseasonal prediction limits of CDHWs in the US Southern Great Plains and identify potential opportunities for improvement in their prediction skill.

496417.title: Inner and Outer Scaling of Turbulent Buoyancy-Driven Boundary Layers in Stable Environments (Invited Presentation)
496417.authors: Marco Giometto, Columbia University, New York, NY; and K. Sathia and P. Chandiramani
496417.abstract: Natural-convection and katabatic boundary layers depart fundamentally from the assumptions underlying Monin–Obukhov similarity theory (MOST). In these flows, buoyancy acts directly as an along-surface forcing of the mean motion, while advection of the ambient stratification produces a two-way coupling between the velocity and buoyancy fields. Ambient stratification confines the flow and produces a finite boundary-layer depth and, in katabatic flows, an elevated velocity maximum. Consequently, inner scales may differ from the usual surface layer ones and the relevant outer length scale is neither prescribed nor known a priori. In this presentation, we leverage dynamical similarities between rotating and stratified flows along dimensional and asymptotic analysis to derive new velocity and length scales for both the inner and outer regions of these buoyancy-driven boundary layers. The resulting scaling predictions are validated against a suite of direct numerical simulations spanning multiple flow configurations and governing parameters.

496418.title: Backward Lagrangian Modeling of WUI Fires: Assessing PM Exposure and Emission Uncertainty Across Major U.S. Fires
496418.authors: Alok Kumar Thakur, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and K. Ridgway, K. Tanner, C. L'Orange, and S. H. Jathar
496418.abstract: Wildland-urban interface (WUI) areas contain nearly 50 million homes in the United States and continue to expand by approximately one million homes every three years. Smoke from WUI fires can substantially degrade air quality and increase the risk of adverse health effects. WUI fires also generate emissions from multiple combustion sources, including vegetation, structures, and vehicles, making their atmospheric impacts difficult to quantify. This study evaluates particulate matter (PM) and carbon monoxide (CO) exposure and emission uncertainty associated with major WUI fires, including the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires in Los Angeles, the 2018 Camp Fire in California, and the 2021 Marshall Fire in Colorado. Primary emissions from burned vegetation, structures, and vehicles were spatially distributed across active fire areas at high spatial resolution of 0.005o x 0.005o and temporally represented over the fire progression period. These emissions were coupled with meteorological fields from the 3-km High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model to represent atmospheric transport within complex terrain and coastal environments. The Stochastic Time-Inverted Lagrangian Transport (STILT) model was applied in a backward Lagrangian framework from receptor locations corresponding to ground-based air-quality monitoring sites. For the Los Angeles case study, 12 receptors were selected to correspond with U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD) monitoring stations. Hourly receptor-specific atmospheric footprints characterize the upwind regions contributing to observed air quality and were combined with the gridded fire emissions to estimate fire-attributable PM and CO concentrations. The Eaton and Palisades fires provide a detailed case study of WUI smoke impacts in the complex coastal and mountainous environment of the Los Angeles Basin. Simulations reproduced the major temporal features of observed PM enhancements at monitoring locations, while both under- and overestimation of observed concentrations occurred across receptors and fire-influenced periods, reflecting uncertainties in emission magnitude, spatial distribution, fire progression, and atmospheric transport. Extending the analysis to the Camp and Marshall fires provides an opportunity to evaluate the modeling framework across fires with substantially different fire environments, levels of structural involvement, terrain, and meteorological conditions. The receptor-specific backward Lagrangian framework provides an approach for linking spatially resolved WUI fire emissions with observed air-quality impacts while identifying the source regions contributing to individual pollution episodes. Results will be used to evaluate limitations in current bottom-up emission estimates and improve understanding of WUI fire contributions to PM and CO exposure. Although PM mass is an important indicator of WUI fire smoke exposure, chemically distinct emissions from vegetation and structural combustion may result in different health impacts despite similar PM levels. The STILT framework enables high-resolution, receptor-specific assessment of WUI fire smoke exposure while providing a means to identify the fire source regions contributing to observed pollution. Future work will incorporate Burning Homes And Structural MAterials (BHASMA)-derived emission factors, refined fuel-loading estimates, and improved emission mapping to predict chemically resolved PM components and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from vegetation and structural combustion.

496421.title: Improving HRRR Forecasts of Poorly Predicted Severe Weather Events in New York State through Assimilation of New York State Mesonet Profiling Observations
496421.authors: Samkeyat Shohan, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Kay, T. M. Weckwerth, J. O. Pinto, Phd, and J. Wang
496421.abstract: The High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model is widely used for short-term convective forecasting, but can fail to accurately capture the timing, location, and intensity of convection initiation and severe weather, particularly under weak synoptic forcing or in regions with complex terrain and poorly sampled boundary-layer structure. The New York State Mesonet (NYSM) provides a dense, state-operated observing network of 127 surface stations, including 17 sites with Doppler Wind Lidars (DWLs) and Microwave Radiometers (MWRs) that continuously observe kinematic and thermodynamic properties of the lowest 2.5 km of the atmosphere. This study leverages these observations to target specific cases where HRRR forecasts have performed poorly. We identify a set of recent severe weather cases in New York State for which the operational HRRR exhibited notable forecast errors in convection initiation, timing, or hazard placement (e.g., damaging wind gusts, hail). For each case, we assimilate conventional observations along with NYSM surface data, DWL wind profiles, and MWR temperature retrievals (moisture retrievals excluded) using the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) with 40 GEFS forced ensembles within the WRF-ARW. Resulting analyses and forecasts are compared against the operational HRRR baseline using standard verification metrics, including near-surface wind and temperature errors, convective timing and placement skill, and hazard-relevant measures. By focusing on cases of known HRRR underperformance, this study aims to determine when and how additional boundary-layer wind and temperature observations from NYSM most effectively reduce forecast error, offering insight into the potential value of assimilating DWL and MWR temperature data operationally to improve HRRR performance for high-impact convective events.

496422.title: Advancing TEMPO NO₂ Utilization: 4DEnVar Data Assimilation, Emission Inversion, and Near Real-Time Forecast Monitoring with GEOS-CF/JEDI
496422.authors: Maryam Abdi-Oskouei, NASA, Boulder, CO; and J. E. Barre, V. Shah, P. Wales, M. Anstett, D. Ardag, F. Goktas, R. Lucchesi, T. Tobin, R. Todling, and S. Pawson
496422.abstract: TEMPO’s high spatial and temporal resolution provides new opportunities to characterize diel variability in nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), evaluate atmospheric composition models, and improve air-quality analyses and forecasts. We present progress toward the end-to-end utilization of TEMPO NO₂ within NASA’s GEOS Composition Forecasting (GEOS-CF) system using the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI). A four-dimensional ensemble-variational (4DEnVar) system jointly assimilates TEMPO and TROPOMI NO₂ column retrievals, combining TEMPO’s high-frequency observations over North America with the complementary coverage of a polar-orbiting instrument. We examine how TEMPO constrains the spatial and diel evolution of NO₂, particularly over urban and polluted regions. TEMPO observation errors are characterized using Desroziers diagnostics, and satellite retrievals and model fields are evaluated against measurements from the Pandonia Global Network. Using the same ensemble-based framework, we also demonstrate the application of TEMPO observations to constrain surface NOx emissions. Additionally, we report updates on the development of a near real-time observation-monitoring system and reproducible workflow that continuously ingests TEMPO retrievals and evaluates them against GEOS-CF forecasts. Together these developments advance a reproducible pathway from raw geostationary retrievals to quantitative analyses, emission estimates, and forecast diagnostics, and lay the groundwork for operational atmospheric composition prediction with JEDI.

496427.title: AirCast-SR: A Foundation Model for Kilometer-Scale Atmospheric Super-Resolution via Conditional Diffusion
496427.authors: Somnath Luitel, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and M. Singh, J. D. Durkee, A. A. Fahad, N. Sudharsan, P. Singh, C. He, H. Kamath, Z. L. Yang, K. Halder, S. Juneja, P. Mukhopadhyay, S. Dhanuka, and A. K. Srivastava
496427.abstract: Kilometer-scale, hourly weather fields are increasingly needed for renewable-energy management, hydrology, wildfire prediction, precision agriculture, and local hazard assessment, yet producing such high-resolution forecasts remains computationally demanding. Over the United States, NOAA’s High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) provides an operational benchmark with 3-km hourly forecasts to 48 hours. However, producing globally consistent kilometer-scale fields across longer forecast horizons and for a broad set of near-surface variables remains challenging. In contrast, global AI weather models can generate forecasts at substantially lower computational cost, but typically at coarser spatial resolutions of approximately 25 km. This resolution–cost gap motivates approaches that efficiently downscale coarse global AI forecasts to kilometer-scale, hourly weather fields while retaining their computational advantages. We present AirCast-SR, a conditional diffusion model that bridges this gap by downscaling 0.25° (approximately 28 km) GraphCast forecasts to 1-km hourly resolution over a 67-hour forecast window, extending beyond HRRR’s 48-hour horizon and providing one-third its grid spacing. AirCast-SR simultaneously predicts eight coupled near-surface variables: precipitation, 2-m temperature, 2-m specific humidity, 10-m u- and v-wind components, surface pressure, and downward shortwave and longwave radiation. The model uses a three-dimensional U-Net trained on patch-based samples over CONUS for calendar year 2021, with GraphCast fields as conditioning input and NOAA’s Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC) at 1-km hourly resolution as the target. Training uses a standard noise-prediction objective, while inference employs few-step sampling with a latent-consistency-model (LCM) scheduler. Evaluation uses three held-out CONUS cases entirely outside the training year: Winter Storm Elliott (December 2022), a June 2022 continental convective episode, and a March 2023 spring transition. AirCast-SR maintains near-zero systematic bias across all eight variables through 48-h lead time, while its radial power spectra closely track AORC from 10 to 100 km, where the coarse GraphCast input exhibits substantial spectral-energy loss. AirCast-SR approaches, but does not consistently exceed, HRRR in pointwise correlation for most variables, while outperforming HRRR for intermediate- to long-lead summer convective precipitation, winter downward longwave radiation, and systematic bias. Without retraining, AirCast-SR transfers zero-shot to India and Germany, evaluated against StationBench surface-station observations, and retains near-zero 2-m temperature bias despite systematic errors in the global AI input. Released with open weights, AirCast-SR demonstrates that conditional-diffusion downscaling can generate coupled, bias-controlled, kilometer-scale weather fields beyond the forecast horizon and fixed domain of operational limited-area NWP, while preserving the computational efficiency of global AI forecasting.

496428.title: Precipitation Efficiency Increases with the Growth and Depth of Mesoscale Convective Systems over the Asian Monsoon Region
496428.authors: Thabo Elias Makgoale, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and S. C. Sullivan and J. Kukulies
496428.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) produce much of the warm-season precipitation over monsoon regions, yet the efficiency with which they convert cloud condensate into surface precipitation remains poorly constrained from observations. We investigate this MCS precipitation efficiency (ε) for 1,321 systems over the Asian monsoon region using surface precipitation rates from the GPM IMERG satellite and ERA-5 cloud condensate amounts in combination with the Python FLEXible Object TRacKeR (PyFLEXTRKR) algorithm. We define ε as the ratio of surface precipitation rates to cloud, liquid, and ice water paths, following Li et al. 2022. MCS ε values are as much as 50% higher than ε of non-MCS convection and generally increase from north to south and west to east along monsoonal moisture gradients. The MCS convective core, defined by Tb ≤225 K, has the highest ε followed by the cold and warm anvil regions, defined by 225<Tb ≤241K and 241<Tb ≤261K, respectively. ε increases with MCS area up to an effective diameter of 160 km, consistent with enhanced ice growth and stronger convective organization during system development, before ε decreases again in the largest systems where cloud ice growth has reached its maximum. In contrast, ε increases monotonically with MCS depth, indicating that deeper systems convert cloud condensate into surface precipitation more efficiently, despite the increased fall distance from cloud-top to surface. During the MCS lifecycle, ε increases rapidly over approximately the first 20% of the lifecycle and then decreases gradually during decay. These results demonstrate that MCS ε is jointly controlled by system size, vertical development, internal cloud structure, and lifecycle stage.

496429.title: "Patterns Associated with Midlatitude Cyclones Resulting in Significant Snowfall over Metro Denver"
496429.authors: Kendall Custer, South Dakota School of Mines, Box Elder, SD
496429.abstract: Denver, Colorado, is a metropolis located along the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains, a topographic barrier that alters weather patterns and makes accurate forecasting difficult, especially when forecasting significant snowstorms. Between 2000 and 2024, Denver has experienced numerous significant snowfall events, some of which are associated with midlatitude cyclones. There is a lack of research on the patterns associated with these synoptic-scale systems that influence significant snowfall rates over Metro Denver and the Adjacent Foothills. This leads to the goal of this research: to find how many of Denver’s significant snowfall events between 2000 and 2024 are associated with midlatitude cyclones, and what patterns emerge from these systems that result in significant snowfall accumulation over Metro Denver and the Foothills. This research is important because, by finding these associated patterns, the scientific community can better understand what to observe when forecasting significant snowfall events. Using heavy snowfall criteria from the National Weather Service’s Boulder/Denver Weather Forecasting Office, “significant snowfall events” were defined as those with an average total accumulation of 8 inches or greater and an average maximum snowfall rate of 8 inches or more in 24 hours. Historical snowfall accumulations were gathered using seven co-op/CoCoRaHS stations around Metro Denver and the Foothills on NOAA’s Regional Climate Centers’ xmACIS 2 database. This snowfall data was used to develop a list of dates when significant snowfall events occurred. Using these dates as references, the National Center for Atmospheric Research’s ERA5 database was utilized to gather data at the 250 mb, 500 mb, 700 mb, 850 mb, and surface levels to establish which dates have an associated midlatitude cyclone. Moving forward, the plan is to trace the centers of the midlatitude cyclones and their upper-level features, including cut-off lows and upper-level cyclogenesis, to find patterns associated with their proximity to Colorado and whether their locations result in significant snowfall events over Metro Denver and the Foothills. As mentioned, this research is important for understanding the patterns associated with midlatitude cyclones and could greatly improve the forecasting accuracy of significant snowstorms in the Denver Metro Area.

496431.title: Characterization of Secondary Ice Production Across Scales in Wintertime Storms during WINTRE-MIX
496431.authors: Eden I. Koval, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and J. R. French, D. E. Kingsmill, K. Friedrich, and J. R. Minder
496431.abstract: For over 50 years, numerous studies have measured ice crystal number concentrations that surpass expected values by several orders of magnitude. This discrepancy has largely been attributed to Secondary Ice Production (SIP). There are about six physical SIP mechanisms that have been observed in laboratory studies, but until recently, rime-splintering has been the main SIP mechanism implemented into numerical models. However, recent studies on rime-splintering have faced difficulties in replicating the results of the prior experiments from which many of these model parameterizations originate. This issue is present amongst all known SIP mechanisms, emphasizing the need for SIP to be investigated across spatial scales, as large uncertainties remain concerning the behavior of SIP between individual hydrometeors and its influence on broad cloud and storm-scale characteristics. This study seeks to provide a characterization of SIP using observational measurements that connects hydrometeor and cloud-scale processes, as this region of SIP lifetime is often underexamined. In order to achieve this, airborne data collected during the Winter Precipitation Type Research Multi-Scale Experiment (WINTRE-MIX) are used to characterize several wintertime storm systems with enhanced ice crystal number concentrations. WINTRE-MIX took place over the St. Lawrence and Champlain River valleys in Feb-Mar of 2022, during which extensive measurements of atmospheric state parameters and cloud microphysical structure were collected via in-situ aircraft sampling and remotely-sensed products derived from a combination of W-, X-, and C- band radars on ground-based and airborne platforms. For winter storms with probable SIP activity, a phase partitioning methodology is applied to particles recorded by the Two-Dimensional Stereo Probe (2DS), utilizing particle roundness, circularity, and aspect ratio to derive phase. The results of this methodology on two research flights are presented here. One case examines small cloud-top generating cells forming at temperatures near -9 °C (4 km) in a pre-frontal precipitation band. The convective nature of the cells, as well as the temperature range of measurements, are well-aligned with the conditions traditionally associated with rime-splintering. Younger cells appear liquid-dominant, while aged cells contain large volumes of graupel and small columnar ice. In contrast, another case is presented in which a large stratiform frontal cloud rapidly transitions from large super-cooled drizzle at -10 °C (4.5 km) to large columnar ice at -4 °C (3 km), where the first observable measurements of ice occur near -6 °C (3.5 km). The sudden glaciation of this cloud suggests that the SIP initiation region is located higher in cloud, where ice particles are growing at sizes smaller than observable by the 2DS. While the lower cloud column is within the temperature conditions for rime-splintering, the top of the cloud is much colder (-15 °C) and lacks strong updrafts required for graupel production. For both cases, aircraft ascents and descents are used to derive phase-partitioned cloud profiles. The results of these are discussed and used to infer SIP initiation regions and to diagnose potential SIP mechanisms. The microphysical evolution between liquid and ice particles in the column are also examined to parse out direct, or even indirect, influences of SIP and how they relate to the observed lower cloud system.

496433.title: From Process-Based to Surrogate Data Assimilation: Scaling Particle Filtering for Streamflow Prediction with Physics-Informed Deep Learning
496433.authors: Fatemeh Rezaei Aderyani, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and H. Moradkhani
496433.abstract: Accurate streamflow prediction is fundamental for water resources management, flood forecasting, and climate adaptation. Physics-based hydrological models provide process understanding and spatial transferability, but uncertainties in model structure, states, parameters, and meteorological forcing limit predictive reliability. Data assimilation (DA) updates model states with observations to improve predictions, yet ensemble-based DA is computationally demanding because each ensemble member is an independent realization of the full model. We first build a parallel DA framework coupling an Evolutionary Ensemble Particle Filter with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (EPFM) to the Structure for Unifying Multiple Modeling Alternatives (SUMMA) across 66 northeastern United States watersheds. The framework advances 100 ensemble members in parallel across distributed computing resources, runs on two time scales, hourly hydrologic simulation and daily streamflow assimilation, and coordinates the members through an eight-phase daily synchronization protocol with resource-optimized, fault-tolerant execution. Assimilating daily streamflow updates soil moisture, snow water equivalent, and canopy storage; relative to the no-assimilation baseline, NSE improves in 95.5% of watersheds, with basin response varying systematically across hydrological parameter regimes. Because assimilation operates on the ensemble externally through this synchronization protocol rather than through model-specific code, the framework is model-agnostic by design and extends to other process-based hydrologic models and ensemble data assimilation methods. Extending this framework to continental domains, however, is limited by the cost of the process-based simulations it depends on. We therefore develop a physics-informed, mass-conserving recurrent deep learning surrogate that emulates SUMMA's full state evolution, including canopy storage, snow water equivalent, snow depth, albedo, and aquifer storage, as well as streamflow. The surrogate embeds the hydrological process structure directly: a mass-conserving cell enforces water-budget closure, multi-timescale antecedent moisture and saturation-excess features represent nonlinear rainfall-runoff response, and basin-adaptive physical constraints are encoded in the training objective. Basins are clustered by hydrological regime, snow-dominant, aquifer-active, or rain-dominated, allowing a single transferable model to learn regime-appropriate dynamics. Across 524 CONUS basins, the surrogate reproduces SUMMA's behavior for all state variables and streamflow while replacing the expensive process-based simulation of each particle with a fast neural forward pass at substantially lower computational cost. Applying a particle filter to the surrogate and assimilating daily streamflow raises median streamflow NSE from 0.2 without assimilation to 0.66 with assimilation, with the majority of basins showing improved skill. Together, these studies trace a path from a particle-filter DA framework for a complex process-based model to a scalable, physics-informed surrogate that makes continental-scale streamflow DA computationally feasible.

496437.title: Evaluation of a Convective Cloud Seeding Technique using Charged Water Droplets
496437.authors: Daniel Martin, Pluvium, LLC, Defuniak Springs, FL; and N. Hiranuma, J. L. Banuelos, A. Garcia, A. D. Romo, and A. G. Barraza
496437.abstract: Water is essential to life. Water shortages, however, have led several states to start and fund cloud seeding programs for rain enhancement and snowpack augmentation. Many of these programs use silver iodide as a seeding material, which works well, but public perception of the potential for silver in the water supply is overall unfavorable. To mitigate public misgivings, the senior author, then a Research Engineer for USDA, developed and patented a novel cloud seeding technique for summertime convective clouds using only electrostatically-charged water droplets. Here we examined whether the presence of electrostatic charge alters the freezing and structural properties of water droplets (<5 micron in diameter) via portable ice nucleation experiment and in situ x-ray diffraction analysis, respectively. We will present a combination of preliminary laboratory and field study results on the influence of electrostatically charged water droplets on precipitation compared to conventional cloud seeding techniques.

496440.title: Openlma, an Open Source Python Library for Lightning Mapping Array Raw Data and Location
496440.authors: Mike Stock, CIWRO, Norman, OK; and V. C. Chmielewski
496440.abstract: The Lightning Mapping Array (LMA) has been and still is an exceptional tool for lightning science. The raw sensor data consists of the arrival times of very high frequency (VHF) radio emissions, which can then be located in space and time using time of arrival techniques. Typically, this is implemented by the lma_analysis program by LMA Technologies, LLC., which searches a wide domain for lightning sources relatively quickly, usually producing results in near real-time. While frequently LMA source locations are the desired product for scientific analysis, sometimes it is desirable to examine the LMA sensor raw signals as well. Individual stations may detect signals from lightning even when too few sensors make correlated detections for location, or to look at the character of the emission amplitude and duration of located lightning channels. Development of new experimental lightning location algorithms also requires robust tools for working with the raw sensor data. As an example of this, an algorithm has been implemented which uses prior knowledge of the location of the lightning flash to search more carefully for VHF sources. This allows one to search for emission from known fixed locations (like the top of a tower), or to refine the locations of an already located lightning flash. This algorithm works by using very small phase centers to search for sources, resulting in up to a factor of 2-3 times additional sources being located with significantly fewer unphysical solutions. Presented here will be recently added features and performance improvements made in the library, and application of the location algorithm to a number of different lightning flashes in varying geographical regions.

496445.title: Contrasting Surface Evaporation and Soil Moisture Responses to the MJO
496445.authors: Sreedevi Puthiyamadam Vasu, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; and P. Ray, N. Johnson, and E. Nikolopoulos
496445.abstract: The Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) is the dominant mode of tropical variability, yet its influence on terrestrial hydrological processes, including evapotranspiration (ET), soil moisture (SM), remains not fully understood. Here, we characterize intraseasonal ET and SM responses to the MJO across the global tropics (30°S–30°N) using daily GLEAM v4.2a estimates. After removing the seasonal cycle and low-frequency variability, ET and SM anomalies are regressed onto the Wheeler–Hendon Real-time Multivariate MJO indices to reconstruct the canonical eight-phase MJO lifecycle. The resulting composites reveal coherent, phase-dependent land-surface responses extending beyond the primary Indo-Pacific convective envelope. Remote ET–MJO relationships are particularly evident over energy-limited regions, including the Amazon Basin, where pronounced ET anomalies occur despite weak local SM anomalies. In contrast, remote SM–MJO responses are strongest across monsoonal and semi-arid regions, including tropical Africa and northern Australia, consistent with precipitation-driven soil-water storage and hydrological memory. Over the Maritime Continent (MC), ET and SM exhibit contrasting temporal evolution. Positive ET anomalies emerge over the western MC during MJO phases 2–3 and expand across much of the region by phase 4. As MJO convection matures, SM increases following enhanced rainfall, while ET anomalies become negative first over eastern Sumatra in phase 5 and subsequently spread eastward across Borneo and the broader MC. By phase 8, negative ET anomalies occur widely despite elevated SM. A March–April 2023 eastward-propagating MJO event illustrates this temporal decoupling, with ET peaks before the convective maximum, then declines rapidly during active convection as SM continues to increase and remains elevated after convection weakens. These results suggest distinct land-surface timescales during MJO passage: ET responds rapidly to changes in radiative and atmospheric demand, whereas SM provides a slower hydrological memory of cumulative rainfall. Ongoing work will assess the sensitivity of these responses to MJO amplitude and propagation characteristics.

496447.title: One Year of C-Band Radar Observations of Convective Storms on CocoCay Island
496447.authors: Miloslav Stanek, Meteopress, Prague, Czech Republic; and F. Najman
496447.abstract: One year ago, a C-band solid-state weather radar was deployed on CocoCay Island in the Caribbean. Since its deployment, the radar has captured a range of significant meteorological events, from isolated supercells to the development of a bow echo accompanied by a pronounced downburst. These long-term observations provide a unique dataset for examining the structure and evolution of convective storms in a tropical maritime environment. In this poster, we will present selected radar observations of significant convective events, focusing on their spatial structure, evolution, and associated severe weather phenomena. In addition to the radar observations, we will investigate the environmental conditions contributing to the development of severe convection in the region. The ERA5 reanalysis data will be used to characterize the thermodynamic and kinematic conditions associated with the observed events and to identify common features of the convective environment. The environmental analysis will be combined with radar-derived characteristics of the observed storms, allowing the relationship between large-scale atmospheric conditions and the resulting convective structures to be examined. Particular attention will be given to cases involving supercells and the bow-echo event with a pronounced downburst, providing insight into the atmospheric conditions supporting the development of severe convective storms in the Caribbean region. The presented results demonstrate the value of continuous C-band radar observations for both the detailed analysis of individual convective events and an improved understanding of the environmental conditions associated with severe convection in a tropical maritime setting.

496450.title: Quantifying Direct Human Impacts on the Terrestrial Water Cycle Using a New Approach for Deriving Water Storage Trends from GRACE/FO with Enhanced Resolution
496450.authors: Matthew Rodell, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and M. M. O'Neill and B. D. Loomis
496450.abstract: Human activities such as surface water and groundwater withdrawals, river water impoundment, deforestation, and agriculture directly alter the distribution of freshwater on Earth. Since 2002, observations from the GRACE and GRACE-FO satellite missions have been used to infer changes in terrestrial water storage at regional to continental scales, but detecting smaller scale changes has been elusive. Recently, a new approach was developed for computing long term trends in terrestrial water storage from the GRACE/FO data with much higher effective spatial resolution (~12,000 km2 vs. ~120,000 km2) than previously possible. We combined this new approach and the resulting 2002-2025 global trend map with rigorous uncertainty analysis, autocorrelation-robust geostatistical methods, and auxiliary information from the literature and elsewhere to evaluate TWS trend associations with land and water use, climate variability, and glacial mass loss. We then identified 40 regions where the trends exceeded prescribed thresholds and exhibited significant spatial associations with anthropogenic drivers. Compared with the standard approach for estimating trends, the new approach yielded regional trend magnitudes that were 33% larger on average. In particular, freshwater depletion associated with groundwater pumping to support irrigated agriculture was found to be considerably more acute than previously estimated. In this presentation we provide an overview of the approach and results, emphasizing areas with terrestrial water storage trends that were previously unknown or unresolved by GRACE/FO data analysis, and where the new trend estimates differ markedly from previous estimates.

496451.title: AI - Estimating Near-Surface Air Temperature from Satellite Land Surface Temperature Using Machine Learning
496451.authors: Felix Ozpaker, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD; and Y. Liu
496451.abstract: Accurate estimates of near-surface air temperature are essential for weather forecasting, agricultural applications, and various climate monitoring applications. Conventional meteorological station networks provide high-quality observations but are spatially sparse, Numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, such as the Global Forecast System (GFS), provide spatially and temporally continuous estimation of near surface air temperature, however, their relatively coarse spatial resolution may limit their representation of local scale variability. Satellite based land surface temperature (LST) observations provide high-resolution spatial information that can help complement these model outputs. This study develops a machine learning approach that integrates satellite LST, GFS model outputs, and ground-based observations to estimate daily maximum and minimum near-surface air temperature, with the potential to support the future generation of spatially continuous, high-resolution (~1 km) daily air temperature fields. The dataset combines multiple sources, including the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) daily LST product, GFS atmospheric and land-surface fields, and ground-based observations from the Global Historical Climatology Network-Daily (GHCNd). Elevation was also incorporated as an environmental predictor to account for spatial variability in air temperature. A global dataset spanning 2021 through 2025 was generated through spatial and temporal collocation of VIIRS observations, GFS fields, and GHCNd station observations. Quality control procedures were applied to remove missing, inconsistent, and unreliable observations. Separate XGBoost machine learning models were developed for daily maximum and minimum near-surface air temperature estimation. Data from 2021–2024 were used for model training, while the 2025 dataset was reserved exclusively for independent testing. Feature selection and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis were performed to identify important predictors and improve model interpretability. Model performance was assessed on the 2025 test dataset using root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), coefficient of determination (R²), and bias against GHCNd station observations. The results were also compared with corresponding GFS estimates to quantify improvements over the GFS baseline. The results demonstrate that machine learning models can effectively integrate satellite derived LST with meteorological and environmental information to estimate near-surface air temperature. Using the independent 2025 test dataset, the models achieved RMSEs of 2.28 K and 2.20 K for daily maximum and minimum air temperature, respectively, resulting in a 25.25% and 35.10% decrease from the GFS baseline. The models achieved R² values of 0.965 and 0.961 and MAEs of 1.64 K and 1.60 K for daily maximum and minimum air temperature, respectively. Additionally, the minimum temperature model reduced the GFS baseline’s bias from -0.95 K to -0.14 K. These results demonstrate the potential of combining satellite LST, NWP fields, and ground observations to improve daily near-surface air temperature estimates and provide a pathway toward the generation of spatially continuous, high resolution temperature fields. Future work will incorporate additional ancillary predictors, such as vegetation indices (e.g., NDVI), to further improve model performance.

496454.title: When Decision Contexts Change: Matching NWS Flood Risk Communication to the Publics' Pre-Event and In-Event Perceptions and Behaviors
496454.authors: Brenda J. Philips, Univ. of Massachusetts, Amherst, Amherst, MA; and C. League and V. Were
496454.abstract: Flood forecasts and warnings may fail to support safer decisions among the public when the information provided does not address the decision contexts of the intended users, including what people understand about the threat, where they are, which actions are feasible, and how they interpret the environmental and social cues they can observe. The Quick Response Survey Project established a process for surveying members of the public shortly after flood events to examine how weather information interacts with these contexts. To date, more than 3,000 survey responses have been collected through National Weather Service Weather Forecast Offices. Analyses indicate that decision contexts, and the role of weather information within them, change as an event evolves. Before an event, awareness and preparedness actions are associated with lower flood risk exposure, particularly vehicle-related risk. Once heavy rain and flooding begin, the decision context shifts, and choices at flooded roadways appear to become more closely associated with immediate cues, such as perceived water depth, roadway conditions, and the behavior of other drivers. These patterns identify intervention points at which communication might support safer decisions. This presentation will introduce a new project, supported by Weather Program Office funding, that addresses these evolving decision contexts as a risk communication design challenge. This project is developing and validating plain-language communication strategies designed to support behaviors that could reduce public exposure to flood risk across for short-term forecasts (2 to 3 days), the flood watch phase (1 day), and flash flood warning phase (day 0). The project uses Quick Response Survey data to identify different population segments and the drivers of different behaviors. Pre-event messages will be designed to support feasible, effective anticipatory actions, while during-event messages will be designed to help people interpret rapidly changing conditions and avoid potentially unsafe inferences from environmental or social cues. Plain-language message components will be developed through engagement with National Weather Service forecast offices, Integrated Warning Team partners, and members of the public. Candidate messages will subsequently be tested for effectiveness among the public. The presentation will discuss current progress of the project to demonstrate how social and behavioral data can inform operationally feasible risk communication guidance.

496460.title: A Complete Machine Learning Pipeline for High-Resolution Meteorological Hindcasting and Outage Prediction
496460.authors: Taylor Alexandria Gowan, DTN, Boulder, CO; and E. Titova-Shankar, N. Yeung, D. Chenevert, and S. Lillo
496460.abstract: Accurate power outage prediction models require multi-year historical meteorological data combining high spatial resolution with consistency across both hindcast training periods and real-time operational ensemble forecasts. To address this requirement for the Detroit metropolitan area, we present an end-to-end machine learning pipeline leveraging state-of-the-art generative modeling. The methodology begins with the generation of a high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) dataset spanning six years to serve as ground truth at 3 km resolution. The WRF simulation is driven by ERA5 reanalysis via initialization, lateral boundary conditions, and hourly updates of sea surface, lake, and deep soil temperatures. Spectral nudging above the planetary boundary layer is applied to maintain large-scale circulation consistency with ERA5 while allowing WRF to resolve critical mesoscale and local-scale structures. Using this dataset, we train a conditional diffusion model for spatial downscaling of ERA5 to WRF-resolution surface fields. The implementation utilizes the EDM (Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models) framework with a UNet backbone, following the CorrDiff architecture implemented within NVIDIA’s StormCast training recipe. The model setup and tuning addressed architectural trade-offs: after evaluating alternative backbone options, a UNet architecture was selected to best match the spatial characteristics of this localized domain. This was coupled with targeted data design and hyperparameter optimization to effectively manage the skewed, sparse distributions typical of parameters such as precipitation and accumulated snow, ensuring robust compatibility with the EDM sampler. At inference time, the model trained on ERA5–WRF pairs is driven by operational ECMWF IFS forecasts extending to 10 days, enabling a seamless transition from historical hindcast generation to real-time ensemble forecasting. The full workflow is provisioned through AWS CloudFormation on g7e instances, supporting reproducible, cost-effective, and high-throughput training and inference. Although demonstrated here for the Detroit metropolitan area, the pipeline is designed for repeatable deployment across additional customer-defined geographic domains and utility service territories. We present downscaling performance, computational scalability, deployment considerations, and the operational utility of the resulting high-resolution meteorological fields for power-outage prediction.

496461.title: Probabilistic Guidance for Convective Hazards within HRRR-Forecasted Mesoscale Convective Systems
496461.authors: Wenjun Cui, CIWRO/University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; NSSL, Norman, OK; and T. J. Galarneau
496461.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) account for more than half of warm season flash flood events and are also a contributor to severe weather (defined here as tornado, wind, and hail events) across the central and eastern United States. Convection-allowing models (CAMs) can explicitly represent the mode of convection, including the development and evolution of MCSs. The ability of CAMs to forecast MCSs provides an opportunity to extend MCS prediction capabilities toward the individual hazards associated with these systems. However, predicting where and when flash flooding or severe weather will occur within a forecasted MCS remains challenging. Here, we develop a machine learning framework to provide spatially and temporally resolved probabilistic guidance for flash flood and severe weather hazards within MCSs forecasted by the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR). This framework is developed using a multi-year (2015–2021) database of observed MCSs. Individual MCSs are partitioned into radar reflectivity–based connected segments. These segments are collocated with flash flood, hail, damaging wind, and tornado reports to identify hazardous and nonhazardous portions of each system. Near-storm environmental fields from HRRR forecasts, together with MCS-related characteristics, are sampled for each segment and used to train separate flash flood and severe weather hazard models. This allows the models to learn how forecast environmental conditions and storm characteristics to distinguish portions of an MCS that are more likely to produce flash flood and severe weather hazards. Leave-one-year-out evaluation shows consistent discrimination across years, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of approximately 0.85 for flash floods and 0.89 for severe weather hazards. The trained and calibrated models are then applied to MCSs tracked directly within HRRR forecasts initialized at 0000, 0600, 1200, and 1800 UTC to generate spatially varying hazard probabilities across forecasted systems for Day-1 and Day-2 forecast leads. This framework extends MCS forecasting beyond predicting whether or not a system will occur and toward identifying where within a forecasted MCS flash flood and severe weather hazards are most likely to occur.

496462.title: The NWS NextGen National Water Model Ensemble Orchestrator: Toward Operational Multi-Model Ensemble Streamflow Prediction
496462.authors: Ahmad Jan Khattak, Lynker Corporation, NOAA/NWS Office of Water Prediction, Knoxville, TN; and S. Younger, R. Bartel, G. F. Litt, A. Raney, S. Horvath, N. Frazier, R. Gibbs, J. A. Ducker, L. Bolotin, P. Miller, S. Sorourian, B. A. Cosgrove, and F. L. Ogden
496462.abstract: The National Weather Service’s (NWS) Next Generation Water Resources Modeling Framework (NextGen) provides a flexible, model-agnostic framework for integrating multiple hydrologic and hydraulic models. To leverage this capability for operational forecasting, a newly developed Ensemble Orchestrator (EO) concurrently executes multiple NextGen formulations and generates a unified streamflow forecast through configurable ensemble strategies, enabling operational evaluation and deployment of multi-model ensembles with their potential benefits for downstream applications such as flood inundation mapping and drought monitoring. Rather than relying on a single hydrologic formulation, we evaluate a multi-model ensemble approach in which streamflow predictions from multiple NextGen formulations are combined using spatially varying weights derived through machine-learning or statistical approaches. Ensemble members are selected through calibration and multi-metric performance evaluation to maximize collective predictive skills across diverse hydroclimatic regions. Spatially varying weights based on regional hydroclimatic characteristics, dominant hydrologic processes, and formulation-specific skill allow predictions to range from balanced multi-model ensembles to forecasts dominated by the locally best-performing formulation. While multi-model ensembles offer the potential to improve streamflow prediction accuracy, operational implementation at continental scale introduces additional scientific and computational challenges. These include calibration across hundreds to thousands of basins, regionalization in the presence of model equifinality, identifying formulations that provide complementary hydrologic strengths rather than selecting models based solely on individual performance, estimating robust spatially varying streamflow weights, and balancing forecast skill against ensemble complexity, size, and computational resources. This work provides an overview of these scientific and operational challenges within the NextGen Ensemble Orchestrator, while future research will focus on generating statistically valid probabilistic ensemble forecasts.

496463.title: Influence of Mesoscale Eddies on the Variability of ENSO-driven SST Anomalies in Western Boundary Currents
496463.authors: Jacob Megarity, The University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, TX
496463.abstract: The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a coupled ocean-atmosphere phenomenon, is known to play a key role in interannual climate variability. However, modern ocean and climate models often exhibit systematic biases that reduce the accuracy of ENSO representation due to inaccurate parameterizations and limited understanding of the ocean’s chaotic internal variability, among other factors. Understanding how internal ocean variability, of which mesoscale eddies are a primary component, influences ENSO’s regional manifestation is crucial for improving current climate and ocean models and developing more accurate weather and climate forecasting systems. In this work, we investigate how the representation of mesoscale eddies in the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) influences the variability of sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies driven by ENSO, specifically in the East Australian Current (EAC) system. Within its scale-aware framework, MOM6 explicitly resolves eddies at resolutions finer than the first-baroclinic Rossby radius of deformation. To this end, three high-resolution, eddy-resolving (1/10°) MOM6 simulations with differing eddy parameterization schemes are compared to isolate the influence of mesoscale eddy activity on the ENSO-driven SST signal in the EAC system. Two of the model’s atmospheric forcing and ocean boundary conditions components are adjusted accordingly to isolate the ENSO response, while a separate non-ENSO baseline configuration serves as the control. The differences in sea surface temperatures between the three model configurations are presented. This study provides insights into the role of mesoscale eddies and internal ocean variability in the regional manifestation of ENSO through SST in the EAC system. It further lays the groundwork for similar ocean model studies in other eddy-rich western boundary current regions, such as the Kuroshio and Gulf Stream, to advance our understanding of ocean-atmosphere interactions and regional climate variability.

496464.title: From Field Measurements to Dynamic Avoidance Angles: Operational Data Sharing for 1675–1695 MHz Meteorological Receivers
496464.authors: Pouyan Amirshahi, NTIA = National Telecommunications and Information Administration, Washington, DC; NTIA = National Telecommunications and Information Administration, Washington, DC; and N. LaSorte and P. Ransom
496464.abstract: The 1675–1695 MHz band supports meteorological-satellite downlinks used to distribute environmental observations and operational weather products to Federal and non-Federal ground stations. Current services in the band include the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite–R Series rebroadcast, Data Collection System, High-Rate Information Transmission, Emergency Managers Weather Information Network, and other mission-related downlinks. As portions of this spectrum are evaluated for flexible commercial use, including low-Earth-orbit direct-to-device (D2D) downlinks, a central technical challenge is how to protect the limited number of meteorological ground stations that may need to continue receiving in the band. Operational Data Sharing (ODS) offers a dynamic approach that uses predictable satellite motion and known ground-antenna pointing geometry to apply interference mitigation only when and where it is needed. This work develops and validates a measurement-calibrated method for converting observed interference as a function of angular separation into site-specific satellite avoidance angles. ODS was originally developed by the National Radio Astronomy Observatory to protect sensitive radio telescopes from emissions generated by low-Earth-orbit satellite systems. Under the original application, a protected observatory shares its antenna pointing coordinates, frequency information, and relevant observing periods with a satellite constellation operator. The operator then uses this information to steer or mute satellite beams that pass close to, or within, the boresight of the ground-based receiving antenna. The concept can be extended to other types of sensitive ground receivers because both the movement of a satellite and the pointing direction of a fixed or tracking ground antenna can be predicted with sufficient temporal and angular resolution. The ODS process begins with several categories of operational information. The protected ground station provides its geographic location, antenna pointing direction, and operating frequency/bandwidth. The satellite operator provides sufficiently accurate orbital information for the satellites in the constellation, together with relevant beam and transmission characteristics. This information identifies the times and locations at which a transmitting satellite, or one of its service beams, may intersect the main beam or significant sidelobes of the ground receiver. Rather than creating a permanent exclusion area around the ground station, an ODS-based approach can create a time-varying protection region in angular space. In the approach evaluated in this study, this region can be represented as a protection cone centered on the antenna boresight. From the perspective of the receiving antenna, this region can be represented as a protection cone centered on the antenna boresight. A satellite outside the protection cone may continue normal service without an ODS-related restriction. When the satellite enters an outer avoidance angle, the system can initiate beam steering so that active traffic beams are redirected away from the protected receiving direction. If the satellite approaches more closely and enters a smaller inner avoidance angle, a stronger mitigation action can be applied, such as muting or nulling transmissions that could illuminate the receiver. After the satellite exits the relevant angular region, normal operation can resume. The outer and inner angles therefore provide a graduated response: beam steering is used where additional spatial separation may provide adequate protection, while beam nulling is reserved for the shorter interval in which the satellite is closest to the receiver boresight. This study evaluates whether an ODS-like approach can be extended from radio astronomy to operational meteorological-satellite receivers in the 1675–1695 MHz band. The broader 1675-1695 MHz study is examining methods that could enable commercial terrestrial and satellite use of the band while protecting selected Federal ground stations that remain operational. For the D2D downlink use case, the study identifies the technical and operational conditions under which dynamic coordination could be dependable and suitable for incorporation into a future spectrum-sharing framework. To support this work, the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences is conducting a field demonstration in collaboration with SpaceX and the National Radio Astronomy Observatory. Because commercial D2D downlink operations are not currently available for testing in 1675–1695 MHz, active Starlink Direct to Cell transmissions in 1990–1995 MHz are being used as a surrogate. The test band permits the experiment to exercise an operating L-band satellite-to-device network and an ODS process similar to that used for radio astronomy protection, while generating measurements that can inform the intended meteorological receiver application.
