The experiment compares baseline periods, during which the satellite system operates normally, with ODS-active periods during which protection requests are entered for the measurement location and pointing direction. Repeated measurement periods provide multiple boresight-near events under both baseline and ODS-active conditions, allowing the effectiveness and repeatability of the mitigation to be quantified rather than relying on a single satellite pass. A principal output of the work will be a measurement-calibrated simulation that predicts the avoidance angles required for a specific protected ground station. The model will combine measured interference as a function of angular separation with the ground-antenna pattern, station latitude and longitude, antenna azimuth and elevation, receiver bandwidth and protection criterion. For a given ground station and constellation, the simulation will identify when individual satellites approach the receiver’s field of view, estimate the interference that would occur during normal satellite operation, and determine the minimum outer and inner avoidance angles needed to keep interference below the selected protection threshold. The presentation will describe the ODS architecture, field-measurement results, model validation, and the sensitivity of predicted avoidance angles to antenna size, sidelobe response, pointing direction, satellite geometry, and receiver protection criteria. The resulting framework is intended to replace, where technically justified, static distance-based restrictions with site-specific coordination in angle and time. Under such an approach, a commercial satellite system would be constrained only when its transmission geometry creates an interference risk to an operating meteorological receiver. If validated, this framework could substantially reduce the geographic and temporal burden associated with protecting incumbent receivers while preserving their required interference protection. It could therefore provide a practical technical foundation for coexistence between future D2D downlinks and mission-critical meteorological operations in 1675–1695 MHz and potentially other bands.

496469.title: Solar Soft X‐Ray Proxy Derived From Observed Auger Photoelectrons by MGS and a 1999–2006 Flare Catalog at Mars
496469.authors: Shaosui Xu, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA; and E. Thiemann, D. Mitchell, and P. Chamberlin
496469.abstract: Solar extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and X‐ray photons are the primary source of energy for the planetary upper atmospheres. Soft X‐ray (SXR) irradiance is highly variable, particularly during solar flares. Solar SXR photons at wavelengths shorter than ∼2.5 nm produce oxygen Auger photoelectrons by photoionizing atmospheric constituents. This study uses a novel approach to infer the SXR irradiance from Auger photoelectron fluxes. More specifically, we derive the fit function between the Auger photoelectron fluxes observed by the Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) spacecraft and solar irradiance at 0.1– 0.8 nm observed by the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) X‐ray Sensors (XRS) for selected solar flare events. The fit function is then applied to all the Auger photoelectron observations by MGS to derive the 0.1–0.8‐nm SXR irradiance from 1999 to 2006. Using the same database, 167 solar flare events ranging from C‐Class to X‐Class are identified at an additional vantage point away from Earth. These results are of particular interest for studying Mars's atmospheric response to solar flares and over‐the‐limb and far‐side solar activities.

496471.title: Quantifying Gaps in Outdoor Occupational Heat Stress Regulations in California Using an Interdisciplinary, Mixed-Methods Approach
496471.authors: Haley Staudmyer, Univ. of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA; and J. Vanos, J. C. Ruiz Malagon, T. Islas, and J. W. Baldwin
496471.abstract: Heat exposure poses a serious threat to human health. Between 2011 and 2021, an average of 546,000 heat-related deaths occurred globally each year. California, historically known for its hot climates, is becoming hotter. Extreme heat events are increasing in frequency, intensity, and duration under anthropogenic climate change, disproportionately endangering outdoor workers. Agricultural workers are 35 times more likely to die from heat-related illness than workers in other industries; construction workers are 13 times more likely. California's existing occupational heat regulations rely on temperature thresholds that do not account for humidity and do not mandate work stoppage even under the most extreme conditions, leaving critical gaps in worker protection. This project quantifies the number of hours per year during which physical labor is physiologically safe for California outdoor workers under present-day and future climate scenarios, using the ASU/USyd Human/Environmental Adaptation Threshold Limits model (HEAT-Lim). HEAT-Lim integrates temperature and humidity data with individual physiological traits—age, acclimatization status, and body morphology—to determine when sustained moderate- to high-intensity activity risks uncompensable increases in core body temperature. We combine HEAT-Lim with a bias-corrected, downscaled ensemble of CMIP6 climate projections (3–9 km dynamically downscaled western U.S. projections from the UCLA Center for Climate Science) to map unsafe labor hours across California under present climate and at 2°C and greater global warming. We hypothesize that safe working hours will decline statewide, including in the Central Valley and other regions central to agriculture, and that many unsafe hours will fall below Cal/OSHA's current heat-illness-prevention thresholds, which do not factor in humidity. To contextualize these physiological projections, we are conducting 15 semi-structured interviews with agricultural workers in Half Moon Bay, California, recruited through a local community-based farmworker advocacy organization, Ayudando Latinos A Soñar (ALAS). Interviews will examine alignment between modeled "safe" conditions and workers' lived experience, agency over rest breaks, and structural barriers to cooling. Thematic analysis of interview transcripts will identify risk factors—including piece-rate pay structures and limited legal protections—not captured by physiological modeling alone. By integrating climate and physiological modeling with community-engaged qualitative research, this project will provide a holistic view of gaps in heat regulation to the California Department of Public Health and Cal/OSHA. We hope this project informs more protective, physiologically grounded occupational heat regulations. This work is supported by the AMS Richard Grotjahn Fellowship in Extremes.

496478.title: NASA Atmosphere Science Investigator-Led Processing System (ASIPS)
496478.authors: Kurt Brueske, University of Wisconsin-Madison Space Science and Engineering Center, Madison, WI
496478.abstract: The NASA ASIPS at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Space Science and Engineering Center produces EOS-compatible standard products from the JPSS VIIRS Atmosphere instruments including near real-time products delivered within 3 hours of observation. These products are delivered to the NASA Level-1 and Atmosphere Archive & Distribution System (LAADS) and the Land, Atmosphere Near real-time Capability for Earth observation (LANCE), with browse imagery delivered to Worldview/Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS). The ASIPS also supports NASA ROSES-funded Atmosphere Principal Investigators and Science Teams, providing a robust development-to-operations framework of highly curated, well-calibrated, petabyte-scale earth observation records hosted within a tailored, high-throughput computing environment critical for timely, iterative, scientific inquiry, analysis, and mission record reprocessing. This presentation will give a brief overview of ASIPS capabilities and resources, suitability to support emerging NASA Foundational Data Product (FDP) requirements, as well as NASA field campaigns which benefit from timely access to ASIPS JPSS-series forward-stream standard and near real-time cloud and aerosol products.

496479.title: Aircraft Observed in Lightning Mapping Array Data During the Lake-Effect Electrification Field Campaign
496479.authors: Jeffery Burke, Georgia Tech Research Institute, Atlanta, GA; and M. Peterson and L. Boggs
496479.abstract: Lightning is a well-known hazard in general and commercial aviation that needs to be mitigated through engineering solutions and situational awareness. Lightning strikes on aircraft are the primary example, but aircraft interact with electrified storms in multiple ways. In certain circumstances, aircraft tracks can be identified in Lightning Mapping Array (LMA) observations. While aircraft detections represent a vanishingly small portion of LMA data, they are an artifact with practical value for aviation safety and impact studies. We surveyed aircraft detected by an LMA during the Lake-Effect Electrification (LEE) field campaign in upstate New York (Steiger et al. 2024). In processed LMA data, aircraft streaks were observed on 26 of 184 operating days. One special case was the NASA P-3 Orion, identified from Automated Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) records as it sampled a lake-effect snow squall for the concurrent Investigation of Microphysical and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) campaign (McMurdie et al. 2022). The P-3 flew in formation with the NASA ER-2, whose electric field mills measured both the field above the storm and the charging on the ER-2 airframe. We will present an initial analysis of this combined dataset.

496480.title: Leveraging UASs for High-Resolution Photogrammetry and Atmospheric Observations during a Multi-Instrument Field Campaign to Study Severe Convective Windstorms
496480.authors: Jana B. Houser, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and P. Sun and G. Yan
496480.abstract: During the spring 2026 severe storm season, and interdisciplinary, multi-institutional group of meteorologists and engineers demonstrated a proof-of-concept field project designed to quantify ground-based and elevated winds in and around severe convective storms. Project instruments included a mobile X band, phased array, polarimetric radar, a suite of ultra precise UASs equipped with high-resolution cameras and ultra-fine-sensitivity geolocation instrumentation, ground-based video and photography assets, a UAS designed to operate at high wind speeds collecting both thermodynamic, pressure, and infrared observations, and a third UAS team of engineers documenting ground-based damage to buildings and natural objects. During the field campaign, multiple proof-of-concept ideas were fulfilled including the collection of stereographic photogrammetric observations from one UAS suite, which successfully demonstrated the ability to track cloud and dust features with time enabling proxy, wind observations in and around, severe thunderstorms. Another UAS team successfully penetrated severe outflow winds and retrieved thermodynamic observations within and while crossing the boundary aloft. The third team demonstrated the benefit of drone-based damage surveys in a highly populated area. This talk will highlight the instrumentation, the platforms, and the methodologies used to estimate winds in and around severe thunderstorms, and will describe the coordinated efforts that will be implemented, moving forward for future field campaigns.

496481.title: PACT: Peak-Aware Cross-Attention Graph Transformers for Efficient Storm-Surge Emulation
496481.authors: Zesheng Liu, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA; and D. Kwon, N. Lin, and M. Rahnemoonfar
496481.abstract: Storm surge is a major contributor to coastal flooding and poses substantial risks to coastal communities and infrastructure. High-fidelity hydrodynamic models, such as Advanced Circulation (ADCIRC), can resolve storm-surge dynamics over complex coastal domains, but their computational cost limits their use for applications requiring large numbers of simulations, including probabilistic hazard assessment, rapid scenario evaluation, and long-term climate risk analysis. Data-driven emulators offer a computationally efficient alternative, but accurately reproducing the temporal evolution of storm surge remains challenging. In particular, storm surge responds to spatially distributed wind and atmospheric pressure patterns with location- and event-dependent temporal lags, while the rare high-surge events most important for coastal risk are easily underrepresented by conventional regression objectives. These challenges become more pronounced when emulators are applied across heterogeneous atmospheric forcing products used for historical reconstruction and future climate projections. We develop PACT, a Peak-Aware Cross-Attention Graph Transformer for efficient station-level storm surge emulation from regional atmospheric forcing fields. PACT predicts hourly storm surge time series using a 12-hour history of wind and atmospheric pressure. Atmospheric forcing at each input tie is represented as a sparse spatial graph whose nodes contain geographic coordinates, wind speed, and spatially mean-centered pressure anomalies. A shared GraphSAGE encoder first learns spatial representations of the atmospheric forcing. Rather than compressing these spatial features through uniform pooling, PACT introduces a station-conditioned cross-attention mechanism. A learned query incorporating tide-gauge metadata attends to the atmospheric graph and adaptively assigns greater attention to spatial locations whose atmospheric conditions are most relevant to the surge response at each station and time. The resulting station-conditioned representations from the recent forcing history are processed by a temporal Transformer to capture interactions among atmospheric states and time-lagged relationships between atmospheric forcing and surge response. PACT then uses learned horizon queries to cross-attend to this shared temporal representation and generate hourly surge predictions from the emulation origin through the following five hours. This horizon-conditioned decoding allows predictions at different lead times to draw on different parts of the forcing history rather than relying on a single fixed temporal representation. To improve prediction of rare but high-impact surge conditions during extreme events, PACT further incorporates a peak-aware learning strategy. PACT uses separate base and peak prediction heads, with the base head modeling the overall surge evolution and the gated peak head learning additional corrections for elevated surge conditions. The training objective combines the overall prediction loss with an additional tail-focused loss on samples containing the largest surge values, increasing the learning signal associated with rare extremes. A horizon-wise slope regularizer also penalizes unrealistic changes between consecutive predictions, encouraging temporally coherent surge prediction over time. Together, these components are designed to improve extreme-event fidelity without sacrificing prediction accuracy across the full range of surge conditions. We evaluate PACT using storm surge time series generated by ADCIRC from NCEP/NCAR reanalysis and five CMIP6 global climate model forcing products. Historical NCEP experiments span four NOAA tide-gauge locations along the U.S. East Coast: the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel, Lewes, The Battery, and Boston. Using the same 12-hour forcing history, PACT reduces overall RMSE by approximately 34-38% relative to a spatiotemporal graph neural network baseline across these stations. Improvements are particularly pronounced for extreme conditions. For the upper 5% peak-focused evaluation at The Battery, peak RMSE decreases from 0.1022 m for the baseline to 0.0479 m for the peak-aware PACT configuration, accompanied by substantially reduced peak underprediction and worst-case errors. We further evaluate PACT using five CMIP6 forcing datasets, including historical simulations and future projections under SSP5-8.5. When trained on historical years and evaluated on unseen future-period simulations from the same climate model, PACT reduces RMSE by approximately 50% relative to the baseline across the five CMIP6 datasets on all four locations. Event-level analyses further show improved agreement with ADCIRC-simulated peak magnitudes, better preservation of the upper-tail peak distribution, and slower growth of prediction error as event severity increases. Cross-dataset experiments on surge level at the Battery reveal comparatively strong transfer among CMIP6 models but substantially larger errors when a model trained on NCEP reanalysis is transferred directly to CMIP6 forcing, highlighting an important reanalysis-to-climate-model distribution gap for learned coastal-hazard emulators. PACT also provides a substantial computational advantage for repeated hazard assessment. After training, it generates a complete November-March storm-surge time series for a station-year in approximately 3.4-3.6 seconds, compared with approximately 4.5-7 hours for the corresponding ADCIRC simulation. These results demonstrate that graph-based, station-conditioned, and peak-aware AI emulators can substantially accelerate storm-surge modeling while accurately representing both its temporal evolution and extreme surge behavior important for coastal flooding and hazard modeling.

496483.title: Improving Hurricane Forecasting at NOAA/OAR/AOML's Hurricane Research Division: 2026 Highlights and 2027 Outlook (Invited Presentation)
496483.authors: Ghassan J. Alaka Jr., NOAA, NORTH MIAMI, FL; AOML, Miami, FL; and S. D. Aberson, J. J. Cione, PhD, S. Gopalakrishnan, J. A. Sippel, X. Zhang, and C. Slocum
496483.abstract: The Hurricane Research Division (HRD) at NOAA’s Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory (AOML) leads research efforts dedicated to advancing tropical cyclone (TC) understanding and prediction. In close partnership across NOAA line offices, in particular OAR, NWS, OMAO, and NESDIS, HRD drives progress across the complete Research-to-Operations (R2O) value chain. By fostering a tight Operations-to-Research (O2R) feedback loop, HRD optimizes operational models and observing systems to maximize the return on operational investments and drive high-quality NWS forecast guidance. This presentation reviews HRD's key 2026 scientific accomplishments and outlines strategic priorities for 2027 within the framework of the Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program (HFIP). Targeted data collection through the Hurricane Field Program, which supports the Advancing the Prediction of Hurricanes Experiment (APHEX), serves as the foundation of this value chain. Using NOAA WP-3D and Gulfstream IV-SP aircraft, alongside emerging capabilities, HRD gathers critical observations across all stages of the TC lifecycle with an emphasis on TC rapid intensification. A major and growing priority involves uncrewed systems (UxS) and other emerging technologies designed to sample hazardous regions, such as the air-sea interface and boundary layer. HRD continues to lead assessments of traditional and emerging reconnaissance data to evaluate impacts, refine concepts of operations, fill critical data gaps, and improve operational numerical model analyses. HRD leverages these rich observational datasets to drive advancements in traditional numerical weather prediction and innovative artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks. Recent enhancements to the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) and new AI-based modeling capabilities aim to improve TC track, intensity, and structure predictions. Crucially, HRD's modeling and diagnostic efforts extend beyond maximum sustained winds to address TC hazard prediction, including wind gusts, extreme rainfall, and associated severe weather risks. By deepening our understanding of TC physical processes, particularly those governing rapid intensification, and refining operational data collection and assimilation pipelines, HRD bridges the gap between research discovery and forecast application.

496485.title: Improving Regional Load Forecasts with Solar Irradiance Data to Account for Rapidly-Growing BTM Solar Generation
496485.authors: Brent Ho, Sunairio, Winter Park, FL; and P. Hawbecker, O. Pfeiffer, R. Hasegawa, and R. Cirincione
496485.abstract: As regions across the U.S. decarbonize, a growing share of electric generation capacity is no longer visible to grid operators at all. Generation from Behind-the-meter (BTM) solar - distributed photovoltaic capacity sited on the customer side of the meter - produces no direct output signal to the system. Instead, it manifests as a suppression of measured load with respect to what one would expect in its absence. For load forecasters working in a transitioning energy economy, this turns a physical generation resource into something that must be inferred rather than observed. When rooftop solar was relatively rare, this effect could be mostly ignored, but this is no longer the case. Small-scale distributed solar capacity in the United States has grown to 66.6 GW by the end of 2025. In New England, 8.1GW of the 9.6GW of total installed solar capacity is BTM, causing significant system-wide sunlight-dependent deviations from expected load patterns. Recovering this embedded generation from observed load is difficult for two compounding reasons. First, electric demand and BTM solar generation are fundamentally driven by different weather variables (temperature and irradiance), so their combined effect on a demand signal cannot simply be averaged or filtered away. Second, unlike utility-scale solar, which is tracked site by site through public interconnection processes, BTM installations are rarely documented: capacity, panel efficiency, and online dates are typically unavailable at the individual-site level; even regional forecasts of future BTM capacity are hard to come by across much of the U.S. We address this data gap by using supervised machine learning to account for the hourly contribution of BTM solar to regional demand. Controlling for the seasonal relationship between temperature and solar irradiance, we curate estimated-BTM-solar-capacity weighted features on irradiance residuals and incorporate this information into regional demand models. We show that this approach improves load forecast error metrics across ISOs in the US and discuss how load patterns will evolve as installed BTM solar capacity grows.

496488.title: A Simple Energy Box Model for Exploring Storage Needs in California
496488.authors: Jean-Christophe Golaz, LLNL, Mountain House, CA; and S. Po-Chedley, M. Monteagudo, J. Zhang, J. Wert, R. S. Arthur, and J. P. Watson
496488.abstract: We develop a simple energy box model of the California electric grid, approximated here by the California Independent System Operator (CAISO) service area. The model integrates electricity demand, conventional and renewable generation, and energy storage but leaves out the complexity of transmission constraints. It enables rapid exploration of California electricity needs when investigating variable energy resources. Despite its simplicity, the model provides a practical, low-cost tool for examining the balance among demand, generation, storage, and renewable curtailment across present-day and future weather and demand conditions. The model is not intended to produce results for detailed grid planning. Rather, its simplicity and low computational cost enable “back-of-the-envelope” estimates of storage requirements, renewable curtailment, and broad system tradeoffs under alternative generation portfolios. Applications highlight a seasonal challenge for high-renewable electricity systems in California. Although peak electricity demand remains strongly associated with heat-wave events, meeting winter demand may present a substantial storage challenge. During winter months, both solar and wind generation in California can be relatively low, increasing reliance on stored energy to meet demand. This seasonal pattern differs from other regions of the United States, where wind generation tends to peak during winter. The model offers an accessible framework for quickly exploring tradeoffs among generation mix, storage capacity, renewable curtailment, and reliability; identifying periods of potential supply shortfall or excess generation; and supporting education and preliminary assessment of California grid challenges. Prepared by LLNL under Contract DE-AC52-07NA27344 and supported by the LLNL-LDRD Program under Project No. 25-SI-007. LLNL-ABS-2022936.

496489.title: Investigating Relationships between Atmospheric Rivers and Tornadoes: Thermodynamic, Kinematic, and Mesoscale Environmental Characteristics
496489.authors: Jana B. Houser, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and J. M. Cordeira, S. M. Bartlett, and C. A. Davis
496489.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are increasingly recognized as important contributors to extreme precipitation and flooding across the United States, but their relationship with severe convective storm events has not been thoroughly investigated. Building on a previous analysis demonstrating that a substantial fraction of tornado warnings in the eastern and southeastern United States occur during ARs, this study examines the environmental and storm characteristics of tornadoes occurring within AR and non-AR environments. Using a 20-year dataset of tornado reports and AR events from 2004–2023, we compare the environmental characteristics present on tornado days associated with non-AR, weak-AR, and strong-AR events. Analyses will feature composites and distributions of standard severe weather parameters including convective instability, inhibition, vertical wind shear and related variables to identify systematic differences between AR and non-AR tornado environments, and similarly AR environments associated with tornadoes compared to those without. The study will leverage convective mode using the SPC Storm-Mode dataset (Lyons 2026) to demonstrate whether storm organization is differentiable between AR vs non-AR tornadoes; for example, are AR-associated tornadoes preferentially produced by QLCS parent storms storm structures? The study seeks to test the hypothesis that AR-associated tornadoes occur preferentially in cool-season environments characterized by greater low-level moisture and vertical wind shear but reduced CAPE and CIN (i.e., high shear low CAPE environments), favoring dynamically driven convection and potentially different tornado characteristics than non-AR environments. These relationships are also expected to be more pronounced for environments featuring stronger ARs as compared to weaker ARs.

496490.title: Stratosphere Troposphere Response Using Infrared Vertically-Resolved light Explorer (STRIVE) Mission and Process Response in the UTLS
496490.authors: Luke Oman, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and L. Jaegle, J. Wang, T. F. Hanisco, and M. Deland
496490.abstract: The Stratosphere Troposphere Response using Infrared Vertically-resolved light Explorer (STRIVE) is a new satellite mission selected for formulation as part of NASA’s Earth Systems Explorers Program. STRIVE includes the Advanced Limb Infrared Chemistry Experiment (ALICE), a limb-scanning infrared imaging spectrometer along with the Aerosol Radiometer for Global Observations of the Stratosphere (ARGOS), a limb-viewing dual wavelength multi-aperture near-infrared radiometer. Together they provide high vertical resolution (~1 km) measurements of temperature, ozone and other important trace gases, aerosol extinction and properties with significant daily global coverage to better understand atmospheric response. This talk will focus on the STRIVE measurements and atmospheric processes, important for the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS), an area of dynamic changes due to convection and large-scale events. The UTLS includes strong vertical gradients in many trace gas constituents along with fine scale vertical features that are more challenging to observe from space yet critical in process understanding as we move toward higher spatial (horizontal and vertical) resolution models. We will show how STRIVE will provide a higher fidelity 3D view of atmospheric trace gas composition and aerosols to enlighten response through increased vertical detail and sampling.

496491.title: ACEPT (Airport Capacity Evaluation and Prediction Tool): Integrating Weather, Demand, and Operational Constraints to Improve Airport Capacity Prediction and Collaborative Decision-Making
496491.authors: Sophie Splawinski, NAV CANADA, Ottawa, ON, Canada; and J. Venuti and M. Matthews
496491.abstract: Airport capacity is strongly influenced by weather, runway conditions, traffic demand, and operational constraints, yet these factors are often assessed through separate tools and workflows. To support more proactive and data-driven operational planning, NAV CANADA and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Lincoln Laboratory have developed the Airport Capacity Evaluation and Prediction Tool (ACEPT), an integrated decision-support capability designed to forecast airport operational impacts and capacity imbalances up to 18 hours in advance. ACEPT combines numerical weather prediction guidance, current runway surface condition and weather observations, demand forecasts, airport operational constraints, and historical operational analyses to generate forecasts of recommended arrival direction (RAD), airport arrival rates (AAR), runway condition evolution, reduced visibility risk, risk of convective impact, and demand-capacity imbalances. Additionally, ACEPT provides scenario-based runway configurations that enable users to evaluate the operational effects of potential mitigation actions such as runway treatment and snow-clearing operations. By translating meteorological forecasts into operationally relevant capacity outcomes, ACEPT reduces variability in weather interpretation and supports more consistent, transparent planning decisions. The tool provides a common operational picture for air traffic services personnel, national planners, airlines, and airport stakeholders, supporting collaborative decision-making and improving transition from strategic to tactical planning horizons. This presentation will describe the meteorological and operational methodologies underpinning ACEPT, the integration of High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) forecast guidance and aviation demand datasets, as well as case studies following deployment at Toronto Pearson International Airport (CYYZ) demonstrating how the tool supported anticipation of runway configuration changes, capacity reductions, and traffic management initiatives before impacts were realized. Results highlight the value of integrating weather intelligence directly into airport capacity planning workflows, improving stakeholder situational awareness, supporting collaborative decision-making processes, and enabling earlier identification of capacity-demand mismatches. The experience gained through ACEPT development provides a framework for future aviation weather decision-support systems that bridge the gap between meteorological forecasts and operational outcomes.

496492.title: Revisiting the January 2000 Winter Storm Forecast Bust With Modern NWP and AI
496492.authors: Lauren Getker, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and G. M. Lackmann, P. T. Vonich, G. J. Hakim, L. W. Uccellini, and J. Poterjoy
496492.abstract: On 24–26 January 2000, the US East Coast experienced a Nor’easter that brought heavy snow from the Carolinas to Pennsylvania. More than 50 cm of snow fell across Central North Carolina, and Raleigh-Durham International Airport broke its all-time record storm-total snowfall with 51.5 cm. However, operational models at the time (such as the NAM/Eta model and EPS ensemble) failed to forecast any substantial precipitation over Central NC at just 24-hour lead times. In this study, we investigate prediction and predictability challenges of this storm using modern numerical models and AI techniques. We first examine the storm in the GEFSv12 reforecast dataset and find that it fails to produce appreciable snowfall in highly populated areas of the US East Coast at 48-hour lead times with a similar error pattern to models in 2000. Downscaling of the GEFSv12 reforecast with WRF at convective-allowing resolution also results in similar forecast errors. Even when initialized with ERA5 reanalyses, WRF, MPAS, and the AI models GraphCast and NeuralGCM fail to produce an accurate simulation of the storm. This failure, with modern models and the best available data assimilation system, suggests that the initial conditions were poorly sampled by observations. We test this hypothesis by applying the AI initial condition optimization technique described in Vonich and Hakim (2024, 2026) to the January 2000 event. Their method involves using the AI weather model GraphCast to optimize the forecast evolution by minimizing the mean-squared-difference between model output and ERA5. Optimizing the initial conditions for the time of heavy snowfall results in a significantly improved forecast. Future work will involve using differences between the AI-optimized and analyzed initial conditions to adjust initial conditions in a dynamical weather model.

496493.title: Maximizing Coverage and Minimizing Latency In Government + Commercial Observing Constellations: An Orbital Simulation Study
496493.authors: Ryan Honeyager, Tomorrow.io, Silver Spring, MD
496493.abstract: The network of Earth-observing satellites is growing increasingly dense, with many government and commercial missions planned to meet enhanced end-user requirements for observational data. There is a general need for hybrid observation programs that combine multiple remote sensing methodologies, such as cross-track sounders, conical imagers, and limb profilers, each relying on various spectral regimes (microwave, IR, visible) to provide a more complete description of terrestrial state. In particular, with increasing numbers of low-Earth-orbiting (LEO) satellites it is possible to reduce the net age of data from the observing constellation while simultaneously advancing the capabilities of these sensors. Gail et al. (2021) and Pohjola et al. (2024) have envisioned a hybrid architecture for measuring critical weather parameters in which long-term reference / baseline missions would provide reliable, highest-quality measurements, and this baseline would be supplemented by other satellites in additional orbits in order to improve spatiotemporal sampling and demonstrate new capabilities. What would such a hybrid architecture look like? We have developed a satellite simulation toolbox that allows us to consider the impacts of 1) potential satellites instruments on the Earth observing system’s capabilities, 2) satellite orbits on age of data, 3) downlink strategies / ground network choices with regards to observation data latency, and 4) observation uniqueness / saturation of impact. Satellite baselines are derived from the WMO Integrated Global Observing System (WIGOS) database and space agency reports; in particular we consider primarily LEO instruments and candidate orbits because of their low cost to launch and due to many recent announcements of government and commercial programs launching through the 2030s. References: Pohjola H., L. Yang, S. Boukabara, 2024: CGMS high level statement on the global hybrid architecture coordination: to meet operational evolving user needs and respond to the WIGOS 2040 Vision, Coordination Group for Meteorological Satellites, EUM/CGMS/DOC/24/1388007, 5 pp., link. Gail W. B., I. Gayl, X. Zeng, 2021: A Backbone Architecture for Government Observing Systems. Bull. Amer. Meteor. Soc., 106, E386–E393, https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-24-0173.1.

496494.title: Examining the Variability of Atmospheric Rivers over the West Coast of the United States
496494.authors: Jack Lochansky, NESDIS, Asheville, NC; and J. Gahtan
496494.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are narrow corridors of enhanced water vapor transport that are a major source of precipitation and freshwater along the U.S. West Coast. Their impacts vary substantially depending on their frequency, intensity, duration, spatial extent, and timing, making characterization of AR events important for understanding both regional hydrology and extreme precipitation. This study examines the characteristics and variability of atmospheric rivers affecting the West Coast using the Atmospheric Rivers (ARv1) historical data record spanning 1940–2022, now available through NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). Atmospheric river events are identified and characterized using an AR ranking framework. Event-based analysis is used to quantify the frequency, duration, intensity, and total integrated vapor transport of ARs while avoiding double-counting consecutive time steps belonging to the same event. The climatological distribution of AR activity is examined across the West Coast, including seasonal and yearly variations and the spatial distribution of extreme events. ARs are further separated into intensity categories to investigate how the characteristics and frequency of moderate and extreme events differ. Return-period analysis is used to quantify the rarity of extreme AR characteristics, while trends in annual and seasonal AR intensity and frequency are evaluated to identify changes in the character of ARs over the study period. The study also investigates the relationship between AR characteristics and large-scale climate variability. Monthly AR anomalies are decomposed using empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis to identify the dominant spatial modes of AR variability and their associated principal components. The principal components are compared with major Pacific and hemispheric climate indices, including the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), Pacific–North American (PNA) pattern, Arctic Oscillation (AO), North Pacific Gyre Oscillation (NPGO), and North Pacific Pattern/Index (NPP). Together, these analyses provide a comprehensive characterization of atmospheric rivers affecting the U.S. West Coast, from their basic climatological properties and seasonal behavior to their most extreme characteristics, long-term variability, and large-scale climate associations. By examining ARs as individual events as well as patterns of spatial and temporal variability, this study provides a more complete understanding of the factors that determine the character of West Coast atmospheric rivers and the conditions associated with their most significant events.

496498.title: Sensitivity of Salt Intrusion Forecasts of NOAA's Northern Gulf of America Operational Forecast System (NGOFS2) in the Lower Mississippi River
496498.authors: Lydia Daphne Ramlo, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and E. J. Anderson, F. Ye, and S. Moghimi
496498.abstract: The Lower Mississippi River has experienced several significant salt intrusion events in recent years, highlighting the vulnerability of drinking water supplies, infrastructure, and coastal ecosystems to prolonged low-flow conditions.Predictions and real-time projections of these events require accurate hydrodynamic modeling that reflects the physical processes governing salt intrusion in the Lower Mississippi River. This study evaluates the performance of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Northern Gulf of America Operational Forecasting System (NGOFS2) at predicting the upstream extent of saltwater intrusion. Reviewing a recent significant salt intrusion event of October 2023, NGOFS2 underpredicts the salt wedge location, displaying the salt wedge approximately 100 kilometers downstream of its observed location. To improve NGOFS2 accuracy, a series of hindcast sensitivity experiments are performed by systematically varying model inputs and configurations to isolate the effects of river discharge, bathymetry, and groundwater on simulated salt wedge migration. The goal of this effort is to identify the primary controls and model deficiencies relevant to salt intrusion. Ultimately, we seek to improve real-time predictive capabilities of salinity, water quality, and other coastal hazards in the Lower Mississippi River.

496500.title: Cloud-Controlling Factor Analysis Reveals E3SMv3 Structural Bias and Mean-State Controls on Stratocumulus Radiative Sensitivity
496500.authors: Timothy Myers, University of Wyoming, Louisville, CO; and T. W. Aerenson, D. McCoy, M. D. Zelinka, J. M. Nugent, and H. Y. Brown
496500.abstract: We investigate marine stratocumulus cloud radiative sensitivity to meteorological and aerosol controlling factors in a perturbed parameter ensemble of the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 3 (E3SMv3). The ensemble perturbs 25 cloud, convection, and aerosol parameters, spanning diverse cloud behavior. The default simulation and many ensemble members capture observed responses to most controlling factors, but not to surface temperature advection, revealing a structural deficiency in processes linking stratocumulus to advection. Many members also overestimate cloud fraction and radiative responses to inversion strength, free-tropospheric humidity, and sulfate aerosol optical depth. Differences in mean cloud optical depth substantially modify the radiative impact of similar cloud fraction changes, showing that the mean cloud state strongly regulates stratocumulus radiative sensitivity. Across the ensemble, conversion of cloud water to rain controls mean optical depth, identifying autoconversion as a key microphysical control on stratocumulus radiative sensitivity.

496501.title: Accelerating Operational NWP: JTTI Support for NOAA's NWP Moonshot Initiative
496501.authors: Aaron Pratt, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and J. E. Ten Hoeve III, W. MacKenzie, and V. Kunkel
496501.abstract: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is working to dramatically accelerate numerical weather prediction through the NWP Moonshot—an agency-wide initiative to modernize and consolidate its operational modeling suite into a unified, high-resolution Earth system prediction framework. This ambitious effort aims to combine advanced physical models with artificial intelligence, rapid data assimilation, and modernized computing infrastructure. The Joint Technology Transfer Initiative (JTTI) plays a central role in realizing this vision by funding targeted research to bridge the gap between community innovation and operational deployment. This presentation provides a high-level overview of JTTI’s support for the NWP Moonshot, highlighting key funded projects in model integration, AI, data assimilation, and high-performance computing. Through these strategic investments, JTTI helps ensure next-generation forecast guidance is built on an efficient, scalable, and reliable foundation.

496505.title: Thermodynamic Evolution of Tropical Mesoscale Convective Systems across Global Storm Resolving Models
496505.authors: Sayali Kulkarni, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA; and K. Schiro, L. Paccini, and Z. Feng
496505.abstract: Observational analyses utilizing NASA’s Aqua/AIRS, DOE ARM program, and reanalysis suggest that tropical mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) favour a consistent thermodynamic signature: warm boundary layer (BL) and free tropospheric (FT) moistening preceding MCS formation, followed by a significant BL drying/cooling and FT warming/moistening as the system decays. Moreover, entraining plume buoyancy can reliably be used to distinguish between MCS lifecycle phases. To what degree current global storm resolving models (GSRMs) replicate these signatures remains largely untested. Multi-model comparison efforts such as MCSMIP have laid a robust foundation in comparing tracked MCS characteristics (e.g. frequency, size, rainfall fraction) across GSRMs, yet an opportunity remains to help explain inter-model differences and systematic biases. Here, we leverage the newly released World Climate Research Programme (WCRP) Hackathon km-scale climate model output to study the thermodynamic evolution of MCS environments, as in observations. We create temporal composites of pre-MCS temperature (T) and moisture (Qv), as well as lifecycle composites, using tracked MCSs (tracked using the Flexible Object Tracker, FLEXTRKR) across multiple GSRMs. We hypothesize that systematic model biases will reflect in these composites, highlighting current deficiencies linking to environmental controls on MCS organization.

496507.title: How Do Thermals Drive Entrainment and Dilution Variability In Cumulus Clouds?
496507.abstract: It has been known for decades that a steady, continuously entraining plume model cannot simultaneously predict observed cumulus cloud top heights and mean liquid water contents – often referred to as “Warner’s paradox” after Warner (1970). It is now widely recognized that spatial or temporal variability of entrainment and dilution can resolve this paradox, with more dilute cloud parcels contributing to overall cloud dilution while relatively undilute parcels control cloud top height. However, details of dilution mechanisms and drivers of this variability remain uncertain. In this study, we examine how the flow structures of large (cloud-scale) thermals within cumulus updrafts drive entrainment and dilution variability, and how this variability impacts cloud microphysical processes. High-resolution large-eddy simulations of cumulus congestus with unprecedented detail in representing dynamical and microphysical processes are analyzed. The simulations, based on an observed case of cumulus congestus from the Cloud, Aerosol, and Monsoon Processes Philippines Experiment (CAMP2Ex), use 7.5 m grid length and Lagrangian particle-based microphysics with ~150 billion super-particles tracked within the model domain. In the simulations, cloud-scale thermals are seen as coherent regions of locally high vertical velocity within the cloud that rise over time (Figure 1). Based on composites of these thermals, it is shown that dilution is enhanced in the convergent flow below the thermal center. In contrast, the upper parts of thermals, which have divergent flow, remain relatively undilute. This structure leads to pulses of relatively large positive buoyancy above the thermal center that rise with the thermals. The time-averaged buoyancy profile, which removes this transient thermal-driven variability, is negative in the upper half of the cloud. In contrast, parcels that are protected from dilution within thermals remain positively buoyant up to near cloud top, about 1.5 km higher than the time-averaged buoyancy profile. Overall, these results indicate the critical role of thermals and their flow structures in driving dilution variability, thus addressing Warner’s paradox. Spatiotemporal variability of smaller-scale turbulence may also contribute to relatively weak dilution in the inner cloud core. Compared to regions nearer the cloud edge, the eddy dissipation rate is about an order of magnitude smaller in the inner core owing to relatively weak velocity gradients. Implications of these dynamical features on the cloud microphysics will be discussed. Drop size distributions (DSDs) are relatively narrow in thermal regions protected from dilution, and substantially broader in more dilute cloud regions. Cloud drops ascend at a rate similar to the thermals as a whole, roughly 4-8 m s-1, which is about 25-50% of the cloud’s maximum vertical velocity. Turbulence-enhanced coalescence is crucial for production of embryo rain drops in the lower part of the cloud. These embryos ascend and grow in the high-liquid water content conditions in relatively less dilute cloud regions at middle and upper levels.

496510.title: Assessing NMME Monthly Forecast Skill for Use in Predicting North American Coastal Inundation Risk
496510.authors: Matt Newman, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and T. Xu, Y. Wang, J. R. Albers, B. Kirtman, J. P. Krasting, W. Merryfield, W. S. lee, G. T. Diro, and C. McHugh
496510.abstract: The skill of the North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME) in predicting monthly sea surface height anomalies (SSHA) at 128 tide gauges along the continental United States and Canadian coastlines is assessed using both deterministic and probabilistic metrics for 1993-2020. Of the six models with available SSHA hindcasts, ECCC/GEM5.2-NEMO is considerably more skillful than the rest, likely in part because its initialization alone includes global satellite altimetry observations. Based upon probabilistic skill metrics, however, the best-performing multi-model ensemble (MME) drawn from NMME models combines ECCC/GEM5.2-NEMO, GFDL/SPEAR, and ECCC/CanESM5 along the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts, while ECCC/GEM5.2-NEMO with GFDL/SPEAR alone is sufficient along the Pacific Coast. El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) contributes skill along the Pacific Coast, with its predictable signal extending farther northwards as fall turns to spring, and along the US southeast and Gulf Coasts during winter, largely due to the inverse barometer effect from predictable ENSO-driven mean sea level pressure anomalies. Calibrated NMME skill is also benchmarked against cross-validated hindcast skill from a cyclostationary Linear Inverse Model (CS-LIM), a stochastically-forced empirical-dynamical model constructed from observed near-global sea surface temperature anomalies and SSHA over the same period, run as an ensemble. The two approaches show comparable overall skill: The MME is slightly better along the Pacific Coast, but the CS-LIM ensemble has significantly better SSHA skill along most of the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts, especially once a linear trend is removed. Combining the MME and CS-LIM ensembles appears most promising as the basis of an operational seasonal high tide flooding outlook.

496511.title: Boudary Layer Depth Observations from the Dual-Polarization NEXRAD Radars during Wildfire Events
496511.authors: Yunji Zhang, Pennsylvania State Univ., University Park, PA; and D. J. Stensrud, R. E. Kirchner Jr., and B. Stouffer
496511.abstract: Observing the temporal evolution of the structure of the planetary boundary layer (PBL) during wildfire events, especially its depth (PBLH), is critical for us to estimate and understand the dispersion of plumes, smoke, and aerosols associated with wildfire. Unfortunately, most current in-situ or remote-sensing observing platforms lack either the temporal resolution or the spatial coverage to consistently provide such information. Recent studies discovered that dual-polarization differential reflectivity (ZDR) observations can characterize the PBL top on most days without precipitation during daytime hours. In this study, we specifically looked at this type of observation during wildfire events from nearby operational NEXRAD radars. The results suggest that clear signals associated with the PBL top, thus indicative of the evolution of PBLH, can be identified in many wildfire events. We will show some examples of ZDR-derived PBLH evolution before, during, and after wildfire events, and compare these observations with nearby rawinsonde observations that are routinely used to measure PBLH. We will also provide speculations in terms of why the ZDR-derived signal is not recognizable for some cases in certain regions or during certain times of the year. These ZDR-derived observations can be produced in real time easily, and they can be a very useful tool for monitoring environmental situations for prescribed fire and wildfire events.

496512.title: Global Aviation Turbulence Nowcasting Blending NWP Forecasts, Observations, and Human Guidance
496512.authors: Andrew P. Foley, The Weather Company, Andover, MA; and J. K. Williams, P. Bayer, and D. Mixon
496512.abstract: Inflight atmospheric turbulence represents a persistent threat to aviation safety and operational efficiency, routinely causing structural strain, operational delays, and are the major cause of airspace injuries. Conventional turbulence guidance depends on numerical weather prediction diagnostics that update infrequently, limiting their ability to capture rapidly evolving turbulence. Conversely, relying exclusively on direct aircraft observations for turbulence awareness creates sampling voids, as active flight routing intentionally avoids severe weather and known turbulent zones. To bridge this gap, we followed the approach described in Pearson and Sharman (2017) to develop TurbulenceNow, a rapidly updated global nowcasting system that integrates turbulence forecasts derived from numerical weather prediction models with automated in-situ aircraft EDR reports, pilot observations (PIREPs), Turbulence Auto PIREP System (TAPS), satellite-derived turbulence probabilities, and expert forecaster inputs. Merging continuous model dynamics with real-time observation streams achieves comprehensive spatial coverage while capturing localized, transient hazards. To evaluate TurbulenceNow performance, a verification framework was established using several skill scores, including contingency-table metrics optimized for rare categorical events. Gridded nowcast outputs were collocated with un-assimilated observations across explicit spatial, temporal, and altitude bounds. Gridded data was also compared visually for a variety of case studies through the use of an interactive viewer and vertical cross-sections. These were used to evaluate the impacts of the various observation sources and TWC forecaster input on the TurbulenceNow skill. Comparative analysis confirms that combining real-time observational data with model guidance provides superior predictive skill over model-only baselines at short lead times. Skill enhancements remain constrained in data-sparse flight corridors and upper cruise altitudes where observation density drops. In summary, this integrated framework furnishes dispatchers and flight operations teams with accurate, dependable, continuous guidance to enhance tactical turbulence awareness and safety. References Sharman and J. Pearson, 2017: Prediction of Energy Dissipation Rates for Aviation Turbulence. Part II: Nowcasting Convective and Nonconvective Turbulence

496515.title: Using Longitudinal Behavior Change Insights to Inform Policy Response to Extreme Weather Events
496515.authors: Elizabeth Doran, University of Vermont, Hinesburg, VT
496515.abstract: Extreme heat has been the leading cause of weather related mortality in the United States for the past thirty years with vulnerable populations including the elderly, young, and low income considered particularly vulnerable. Extreme heat events are projected to continue to increase in duration, intensity and geographic extent. During extreme events, uniform CDC guidance recommends five short term risk mitigation actions: staying hydrated, changing plans, checking on neighbors, using air conditioning or fans, and going to a cooling center or public air conditioned space. The minimize the impacts of extreme heat on the public, policy response must be tailored to the local environmental and social context. The Northeast US, for instance, is one of the fastest warming regions of the country and also has a relatively older population compared to the rest of the country, older housing stock with the lowest central air conditioning rate in the country at seven percent, and a rural development pattern that lacks access to centralized cooling centers and resources. To better inform regionally sensitive communication and intervention strategies, we leverage insights from a cross-sectional longitudinal online stratified survey of Vermonters conducted in the summers of 2022 (N = 1818) and 2025 (N = 966). Survey questions related to the CDC recommended activities were designed to leverage insights from the transtheoretical model (TTM), a social-psychological theory of behavior change that suggests individuals move through stages as they adopt new behaviors including pre-contemplation when they are unaware of a particular behavior or problem; to contemplation when they are considering taking action; to preparation when they are taking steps to ready themselves for the change; then action when they make the behavior change; and then maintenance when the new behavior becomes habitual. Individuals can stagnate and move backward in the process as well. We present findings that suggest the existence of a persistent activation cliff across time, with the majority of respondents in the pre-contemplation stage for all recommended actions. Insights from the rural-urban context of respondents, experience of extreme heat impacts, engagement with warning information and demographic factors are further presented. Findings can inform future interventions including National Weather Service warning communication, and public health outreach campaigns to educate the public and provide contextually appropriate solutions and reduce the public health burden.

496519.title: TSIS-1/SIM Science Advances and TSIS-2 Comissioning: Extended Spectral Coverage, MgII Index, and Enchanced Operations.
496519.authors: Steven V. Penton, Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, Boulder, CO; Univ. of Colorado at Boulder, Boulder, CO; and M. Chambliss, O. M. Coddington, D. Gathright, J. Machol, L. McMaster, J. F. Mothersbaugh III, T. Patton, E. C. Richard, M. Snow, D. Woodraska, and T. Woods
496519.abstract: The Total and Spectral Solar Irradiance Sensor (TSIS-1), operating aboard the International Space Station since 2018, continues to extend NASA's four-decade solar spectral irradiance (SSI) record while preparing for overlap with its free-flying successor, TSIS-2 — a transition designed explicitly to close the data-continuity gap that has historically threatened long-running space weather and climate irradiance records. We report recent 200–2400 nm science results from the TSIS-1 Spectral Irradiance Monitor (SIM) alongside near-term mission plans spanning the TSIS-1/TSIS-2 handoff, with an emphasis on the observational techniques and cross-mission strategies that sustain an unbroken data record. New TSIS-1/SIM data products now extend spectral coverage into the 2400–2800 nm range, closing a long-standing instrumental gap in the near-infrared solar spectrum and improving agreement between the Total Solar Irradiance (TSI) budget and independent TSIS-1 Total Irradiance Monitor (TIM) measurements. We report on a new TSIS-1 MgII index data product and its long-term continuity across the TSIS-1/TSIS-2 overlap period. The MgII index is a key operational proxy for solar chromospheric activity used widely in space weather and ionospheric forecasting; this product both extends that composite record and serves as a cross-mission reference for the GOES-R MgII index project, an example of multi-instrument dataset integration, as detailed in companion presentations by Mothersbaugh et al. and Snow et al. at this conference. We also summarize TSIS-2 mission status, including August 2026 thermal-vacuum (TVAC) testing and a planned spring 2027 launch aboard a Rocket Lab Electron vehicle — reflecting the growing role of commercial launch partnerships in sustaining government-operated space weather infrastructure — along with the on-orbit commissioning and overlap strategy that preserves an unbroken, cross-calibrated SSI/TSI record. Together, these efforts strengthen the resilience of solar irradiance data underpinning space weather forecasting and Earth system science through the 2020s. Beyond 2030, the future of solar irradiance monitoring is unclear; we present candidate strategies that will determine whether the solar irradiance record can remain unbroken into the next decade.

496520.title: How Well Do Operational Models Forecast Atmospheric Conditions Relevant for Wildfires? An Evaluation using NOAA’s New Fire-Weather Observatories
496520.authors: Bianca Adler, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and L. Bianco, D. D. Turner, J. Olson, X. Sun, T. P. Meyers, J. Sedlar, and T. R. Lee
496520.abstract: Hazardous wildfires are an increasing threat to life and property in many areas of the U.S., especially in the high plains and mountainous terrain of the West, and are becoming a year-around occurrence. Besides factors like fuel, topography, forest health and management, atmospheric boundary layer conditions play a crucial role for the risk of wildfires and how they might spread after ignition. Red flag warnings are issued by NOAA’s National Weather Service when conditions could lead to extensive wildfire occurrences and/or control problems on existing wildfires or prescribed burns. Factors taken into consideration include low relative humidity, sustained surface winds or frequent gusts, rapid changes in wind direction, the chance of dry thunderstorms, long-term drought, higher than normal temperature, low fuel moisture, and poor nighttime relative humidity recovery. The operational High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS, which becomes operational in October 2026) provide high-resolution (3 km) hourly short-term forecasts for the U.S. These models provide critical guidance for assessing the risk for wildfires occurrence or erratic behavior of existing fires or burns. Over the past years, NOAA Research developed several fixed and mobile atmospheric facilities which are optimized to observe atmospheric profiles and land-surface conditions relevant for fire weather. Three of these sites are currently deployed in Washington, Idaho, and Colorado in the Intermountain West providing continuous observations of the surface energy balance, radiation, aerosol, and trace gases, and the dynamic and thermodynamic vertical profiles in the boundary layer and lower atmosphere. Taking advantage of the more than one-year long data sets at some sites, we are evaluating how well the operational models forecast conditions specifically relevant for fire weather, such as air temperature and moisture, wind, nocturnal surface inversion buildup and erosion, and convective boundary layer evolution. We are further investigating what conditions and processes are associated with systematic model errors and which are well captured. These insights will be used to improve the treatment of processes not well represented in the future version of RRFS, which is under active development.

496523.title: From Lightning Science to Children's Education; The COPE Lightning Book Initiative
496523.authors: Mary Ann Cooper, ACLENet, River Forest, IL; and S. Schmitt
496523.abstract: The most recent addition to the COPE Disaster Champions series, Lightning, was launched in July 2026. The series, initiated after the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake disaster, is written by the original authors, Martha Keswick, Mariko Jesse, and Timothy Sim, with the collaboration of content experts, in this case, lightning safety specialists from Meteorage, ACLENet, the Caribbean Meteorological Association, and the National Lightning Safety Council. Despite major advances in lightning detection, forecasting, warning systems, and risk assessment, lightning injuries and fatalities continue to occur worldwide because protective actions ultimately depend on human behavior and risk awareness. The COPE Lightning book was developed to translate established lightning safety knowledge into an engaging educational resource for children, who can also serve as important messengers within their families and communities. Aimed at 6-12 year olds, the series is reminiscent of the Magic School Bus series, with a multicultural group of four children, Candy, Ollie, Ping, and Eddy, along with their teacher, Grand Mistress Fu, and their dog, Rescue, who travel to different parts of the globe to learn about disasters and how to respond to them. In Lightning, they travel from Trinidad and Tobago to Uganda. As the COPE website says, ‘Along the way, they meet children, communities, and experts to discover how lightning behaves, who is most at risk, and the simple actions that can save lives. This new adventure highlights the key message: When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors.’ Conceived to be free of copyright issues, books for 15 types of disasters, many of interest to AMS members, are available in 26 languages and free for download, printing, and distribution at their own expense by local or national groups. The series partners with UNICEF, the WMO, and many others listed on their website https://cope-disaster-champions.com/. Jingles, Train the Trainer materials, and videos are available for many of the books. To date, the Lightning book is available in English and Portuguese with Spanish, French, Swahili, and Rukiga pledged for production and posting. We welcome translators for other languages so that we can make this as widely available as possible for children who face the dangers of lightning injury across the globe. Link for 1 min trailer about book: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UVkOk7gIF9s Link that includes digital copy of the Lightning book: https://www.unilearn.edu.sg/partners-cope/ COPE Disaster Champions series website for 15 types of disaster including Lightning: https://cope-disaster-champions.com/

496527.title: Understanding the Predictability of Non-Intensifying Tropical Storm Rene (2020) through All-Sky Radiance Observations and Their Assimilation.
496527.authors: Jordan Rendon, DAO, State College, PA
496527.abstract: Studies on TC intensity forecast errors have mostly focused on the rapid intensification (RI) events. Forecast errors for rapid weakening (RW) and non-developing (ND) TCs have been explored but to a lesser degree. Although there have been substantial improvements in the forecast accuracy of TC intensity in recent years, poorly predicted RW and ND storms like exemplify the lack of representation of critical processes that govern the prediction and predictability of TC intensity in our operational TC forecast guidance. These forecast errors partially stem from the gaps in our understanding of the processes occurring across the multiple spatial and temporal scales that govern TC intensity changes, as well as the lack of knowledge in how uncertainties from the numerical weather prediction (NWP) models contribute to limiting the TC intensity predictability. Investigating these often-overlooked events will further enhance our understanding and the model representation of the controlling factors of TC intensity and its predictability. Tropical Storm Rene (2020) was a non-developing event, i.e. a tropical cyclone where models and official forecasts predict intensification, but with it failing to occur. During Rene’s lifetime, official forecasts issued by the National Hurricane Center and multi-model guidance continually suggested intensification to at least at Category 1 hurricane; however, Rene remained a low-end tropical storm that only briefly attained a maximum surface wind speed of 40 knots. From an NWP perspective, this might indicate some combination of subpar model initialization fields (initial condition error), deficiency in the dynamical core (model error), or poorly parametrized physics (model error). Results from a 20-member ensemble forecast initialized from the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) using the Weather Research and Forecasting Model (WRF) v4.6, agree with the historic forecasts that Rene had a higher likelihood to intensify into a Hurricane. Ensemble sensitivity analysis and correlations calculated between intensity metrics (max 10-m wind, future MSLP) and initial condition environmental predictors (moisture; temperature; surface pressure) demonstrate dependence on initial moisture and warm core structure. Members with a more moist atmosphere at and near Rene's center are more prone to intensification when compared to drier members. Small differences in the warm-core anomaly also impact intensification evolution. All-sky Infrared and Microwave observations can be used to evaluate the state of the atmosphere since they contain valuable information about the atmospheric thermodynamic and moisture structures. Assimilation of these radiances has been shown to improve tropical cyclone forecasts, and for Rene, can be used to constrain the moisture and warm core bias seen in the GEFS initial conditions.

496529.title: Assessing a Single Event: The Hurricane Helene Chapter of the 2026 North Carolina Climate Science Report
496529.authors: Carl J. Schreck III, North Carolina State University, Asheville, NC; and J. Baker, J. H. Bowden, K. Fernandes, G. M. Lackmann, A. Miller, Y. Rao, J. J. Rennie, J. Runkle, C. Scheip, R. Scheller, A. Sebastian, M. Sugg, and B. S. Underwood
496529.abstract: The 2026 North Carolina Climate Science Report updates the state's 2020 assessment for practitioners: planners, emergency managers, public health officials, and engineers. Hurricane Helene caused 107 fatalities in North Carolina, the deadliest natural disaster in state history, along with an estimated $59.6 billion in damage. Climate assessments are typically organized around hazards, variables, or sectors. One chapter is instead organized around an event, because Helene's compounding hazards and cascading consequences cut across all of them. It draws on several of the report's other chapters for context. Six key messages structure the chapter: Hurricane Helene was an unprecedented compound event in North Carolina with record rainfall, flooding, and landslides. Climate change was among several factors driving the exceptional sea-surface temperatures that fueled Helene and likely increased the probability of a Helene-level rainfall event in the southern Appalachians. Destruction of critical infrastructure amplified Helene's impact, severing access to essential services and generating cascading social, economic, and health consequences for millions of citizens. Hurricane Helene amplified pre-existing social and health vulnerabilities, widening disparities in both impact and recovery. Hurricane Helene's consequences extend years to decades beyond the storm itself, with cascading effects on wildfire risk, landslide potential, population health, and economic recovery still unfolding across western North Carolina. Hurricane Helene exposed gaps between forecast skill and actionable decision-making and offers learnings that can be applied to future large natural disasters. A case study of the North Fork Reservoir, which supplies 70% of Asheville's drinking water, shows 2021 dam and spillway upgrades performing as designed under Helene, preventing a failure that could have released six billion gallons onto the water treatment plant directly below. The transmission lines carrying water out of the reservoir were another matter. They had been rebuilt after the 2004 floods, with one auxiliary line buried 25 feet underground, and Helene scoured them all away. Asheville went 52 days without potable water. We discuss that contrast alongside the state's Flood Resiliency Blueprint and emerging community resilience hubs and reflect on assessing an event whose consequences are still unfolding.

496531.title: Training Science and Engineering Students in Convergence Research for Compound Hazard Resilience: Part I - Developing the Curriculum
496531.authors: Julie Demuth, NCAR, Longmont, CO; and M. G. Cains, S. Kamali, K. Fewless, S. Shams, A. N. Ramos-Valle, and L. Peek
496531.abstract: People and places are increasingly at risk of compound weather, space weather, and subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) hazards and disasters (UNDRR-ISC, 2025). Compound hazards are generally characterized as two or more events with overlapping spatial and temporal attributes (Nemeth et al. 2024). Compound hazards may include (a) co-occurring (also known as concurrent) events, where two discrete hazards occur simultaneously, (b) cascading (also known as triggering) events, where an initial hazard triggers or amplifies a subsequent event, (c) consecutive hazards, where an initial hazard has ended but people and places are consequently made vulnerable to a subsequent hazard. Building resilience to compound hazards requires understanding how natural, human, and technological systems interact. Importantly, the integration of such expertise is essential to truly build resilience to compound hazards. In July 2026, the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) Education, Engagement, and Early-Career Development (EdEC) and Convergence Science Program (CSP) designed and implemented a 2-week colloquium for graduate students from the atmospheric sciences, social sciences, and engineering to train them in the topics and approaches to address the complex problem of compound hazards. This presentation will discuss the design of the 2-week colloquium. The curriculum was grounded in three foundational talks on compound hazards, participatory convergence research, and systems engineering. It included presentations of projects that exemplify these three foundational topics. Among them were joint presentations by physical and social scientists on co-occurring tornado-flash flood hazards, wildfire forecast information development and use, and power grid resilience. Presentations also included those by engineering researchers and practitioners on food-energy-water nexus and engineering applications to emergency communication systems and transportation systems. Further, we included several panels of discussions with rich question-and-answer sessions, for example, pertaining to the relevance of convergence to AI / machine learning, experiences and lessons learned conducting convergence research projects, communicating within and across disciplines when working on teams, and the perspectives of convergence across government, non-profit, and private sector leaders. To foster student reflections, the colloquium also included a charette-type activity in which students began the colloquium individually thinking and documenting a research idea and approach to a compound hazard problem which they then were asked to reflect on and document again at the end, to demonstrate how their thinking had changed during the colloquium. Finally, the curriculum included student teams and projects, which are discussed in Part II.

496532.title: Architecting for Cloud HPC in Numerical Weather and Ocean Prediction: Lessons Learned from HAFS and IOOS on AWS
496532.authors: Dev Jodhun, Amazon Web Services, Arlington, VA; and T. Brown, R. Toles-Abdullah, and M. C. Dowling
496532.abstract: How should modelers architect their cloud HPC environments for numerical weather and ocean prediction? Moving from on-premises supercomputers to cloud introduces a range of architectural decisions — from compute instance selection and high-performance networking to storage configuration, cluster scheduling, and workflow orchestration — that collectively determine whether a modeling system meets its performance, cost, and reliability targets. This presentation shares lessons learned from running the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) and Integrated Ocean Observing System (IOOS) coastal ocean models on Amazon Web Services (AWS), and presents a practical framework for architecting cloud HPC environments for earth system modeling workloads. The HAFS Ensemble in Real-time on the Cloud (HERC) has run on AWS during the 2023, 2025, and 2026 hurricane seasons. In 2026, the team is running HAFS v2.2 at 2-km resolution for retrospective analysis with an 11-member ensemble producing 120-hour forecasts — a significant computational escalation from the original 6-km configuration. This effort required architectural decisions spanning instance selection (benchmarking hpc7a across node-per-member configurations), high-performance storage (FSx for Lustre scratch), data staging from S3, and workflow orchestration via the Parallel Works platform. We present lessons learned from running the retro runs on hpc7a, including how the choice between 12 vs. 24 instances/member trades off wall-clock time per cycle against total cycles achievable within budget — and how storage throughput and data movement patterns proved as critical as raw compute performance. Separately, the IOOS community is architecting their own cloud HPC environments for coastal ocean models — including ROMS, FVCOM, and ADCIRC. These models present distinct considerations: unstructured mesh codes like ADCIRC and FVCOM have irregular memory access patterns and communication topologies, storm surge ensemble forecasting demands rapid cluster spin-up and teardown during tropical cyclone threats, and the end-to-end workflow — from data ingest through model execution to product dissemination — must be orchestrated reliably under time pressure. We share how the IOOS team is approaching these architectural decisions as they scale coastal ocean prediction on AWS. We synthesize these experiences into a framework for architecting cloud HPC for NWP and ocean modeling. Key dimensions include: compute instance selection and benchmarking, high-performance storage and data movement, networking and MPI scaling, workflow orchestration and scheduling, cost optimization strategies, and spot vs. on-demand approaches for research vs. time-critical workloads. Our goal is to inform the broader weather and ocean modeling community on how to approach cloud HPC architecture for their own workloads — recognizing that as cloud services evolve and model configurations advance, architecting for cloud HPC is an ongoing process rather than a one-time decision.

496537.title: Ionosphere Mission Operations Cell (IMOC)
496537.authors: Scott Alan Thaller, Orion Space Solutions, An Arcfield Company, Denver, CO; and C. Nasr, J. Wilson, J. Highley, R. Stutz, and C. Harless
496537.abstract: The Ionosphere Mission Operations Cell (IMOC) is an advanced software stack tool for real-time, secure, scalable, actionable exploitation of the ionosphere. IMOC integrates SEIM.STRES (Sounder Receiver Enabled Ionosphere Model Service for Tactical Real-time Environment Specification), developed collaboratively by AFRL and Boston College under the SEIM Joint Capability Technology Demonstration (JCTD). This initiative underscores the operational potential of SEIM.STRES and its ability to transform ionospheric monitoring for military and scientific applications. The IMOC architecture is built on a scalable, cloud-native deployment that ensures reliability and adaptability. Its containerized infrastructure, orchestrated through Kubernetes, enhances modularity and ensures resilience by delivering high availability and fault tolerance. Paired with an advanced data pipeline, IMOC enables robust, near-real-time ionospheric data delivery to the Unified Data Library (UDL). This architecture is not only operationally robust but also cost-efficient, achieving an 80% reduction in hardware costs and 70% lower operating expenses compared to legacy systems. A key achievement of Orion Space Solutions has been the successful prototyping and operational implementation of IMOC, which will soon be available as a commercial product to support the broader community. IMOC can reliably facilitate continuous operations, specific test events, or short-term experiments, empowering stakeholders with high-fidelity, real-time ionospheric modeling for enhanced decision support and post-mission evaluation. A cornerstone of IMOC is its rigorous validation efforts, applied to both the Regional Ionospheric Profile Estimator (RIPE) and the SEIM.STRES data assimilation capabilities.
