RIPE, an empirical model designed for high-fidelity regional ionospheric specification, assimilates data from OASIS (Optimal Approach System for Ionogram Scaling) to provide key ionospheric parameters. By refining this data through Kalman filtering and machine learning, RIPE bridges gaps inherent in standalone models like IRI, enhancing outputs such as plasma frequency (foF2), vertical electron density profiles, and critical frequencies. Validation against hand-scaled measurements from ionosondes addresses systematic biases associated with disturbed geomagnetic conditions and sporadic ionospheric phenomena. Furthermore, evaluation studies of several days of output capture RIPE’s and SEIM.STRES's responses to transient ionospheric events, demonstrating their reliability in maintaining diurnal structures and supporting HF operations. A diagnostic window is generated for each timestep of model output, and operators are able to visually inspect this data for any outliers. This will aid in refining and validating the model output so that it is consistent with expected values. IMOC operates within a robust technological framework, incorporating secure DevSecOps practices, compliance with CMMC Level 2 standards, and monitoring platforms like Grafana dashboards. These advancements provide full system observability, seamless integration with military workflows, and readiness to address the dynamic challenges of ionospheric behavior. Looking ahead, IMOC aims to expand operations across CONUS and PACOM regions, optimize data assimilation inputs, and extend its forecasting capabilities to address the dynamic challenges of ionospheric behavior. By leveraging the innovations of the SEIM JCTD, IMOC sets the benchmark for modern ionospheric modeling and its applications in communications, navigation, and situational awareness. By validating outputs and optimizing input assimilation, IMOC supports actionable models that shape advances in communications, navigation, and situational awareness under dynamic ionospheric conditions.

496539.title: What Drives the Spatial Variability of the Stokes Drift?
496539.authors: Colin Beyers, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and B. Villas Boas, H. Torres Gutierrez, M. R. Mazloff, R. Sun, and G. Marechal
496539.abstract: The net transport of particles in the direction of wave propagation, known as the Stokes drift, contributes to both upper-ocean transport and mixing, yet the processes that control its spatial variability across scales remain poorly quantified. Commonly used Stokes drift products are derived from smooth wind forcing dominated by synoptic-scale variability O(1,000 km), and therefore omit variability driven by sub-synoptic-scale winds and current effects on waves (CEW). Here, we use a suite of WAVEWATCH III simulations in the California Current System region to quantify how winds and currents generate Stokes drift variability across spatial scales. Simulations are forced with either spatially filtered winds dominated by synoptic-to-mesoscale variability O(100-1,000 km) or native high-resolution winds containing variability down to O(10 km), with and without current forcing. Additional experiments selectively disable individual CEW mechanisms to isolate the contributions of refraction, changes in wavenumber, relative wind, and current advection. The large-scale spatial structure of the Stokes drift is strongly coupled to the synoptic-scale wind field, while sub-synoptic wind variability generates additional Stokes drift structure at corresponding scales. Currents produce further meso-to-submesoscale variability that is not explained by the local wind field. At wavelengths shorter than 100 km, high-wavenumber wind variability increases Stokes drift variance by approximately a factor of 10, while CEW increases variance by approximately a factor of 13; including both effects increases variance by approximately a factor of 20. The experiments isolating individual CEW mechanisms show that their relative importance is scale-dependent, with changes in wavenumber producing the largest overall contribution at wavelengths shorter than 100 km, followed by refraction. These results demonstrate that both atmospheric and oceanic variability can imprint dynamically meaningful structure onto the Stokes drift that is absent from spatially smooth products.

496547.title: High Latitude & Polar Flight Routes: High Frequency Communication Awareness Through Collabration Between NASA CODEAU and the Allied Pilots Association (APA)
496547.authors: Rondeau Flynn, APA, Ft. Worth, TX
496547.abstract: High Latitude & Polar Flight Routes: High Frequency Communication Awareness Through Collaboration Between NASA CODEAU and the Allied Pilots Association (APA) Reliable high frequency (HF) voice communications remain a critical operational requirement for aviation on transpolar and high-latitude flight routes where satellite communications (SATCOM) may be unavailable, limited, or used as a backup communications pathway. To support pilot situational awareness and regulatory compliance, the NASA CODEAU team collaborated with the Allied Pilots Association (APA) to develop graphical aviation-focused products that visualize regions where HF communications may be degraded or lost due to space weather impacts. Particular emphasis was placed on depicting operationally significant geographic thresholds, including the locations above 55°N latitude, where increased ionospheric variability frequently impacts HF propagation, and 78°N latitude, a key operational benchmark associated with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) communication requirements for aircraft operating in polar regions. The project leveraged the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) D-Region Absorption Predictions (D-RAP) model to illustrate how solar flares, solar energetic particle events, and geomagnetic storms can increase ionospheric absorption and disrupt HF communications across aviation routes. By integrating D-RAP-derived absorption information with geographic visualizations tailored to flight operations, pilots and dispatchers gain enhanced awareness of regions where HF communications may be unreliable and where operational contingency planning may be required. A key objective of this collaboration was to communicate the frequency-dependent nature of HF propagation during space weather events. The graphical products demonstrate how lower HF frequencies are often more susceptible to enhanced D-region absorption during radio blackouts and polar cap absorption events, while selected higher frequencies may remain viable under certain conditions. Conversely, during severe disturbances, absorption may extend across large portions of the HF spectrum, particularly in polar regions. The D-RAP model provides valuable operational insight by identifying areas of increased absorption and supporting assessments of which HF frequencies may be more or less reliable along a planned route. This work highlights the value of partnerships between the scientific (NASA) and the aviation end-user (APA) community in translating complex space weather information into operationally relevant decision-support tools. The resulting visualizations improve pilot understanding of space weather impacts, support compliance with polar communication requirements, and demonstrate how NOAA SWPC products can be integrated into aviation operations to enhance safety, resilience, and communication reliability across northern and polar airspace. Headquartered in Fort Worth, Texas, near Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport, the Allied Pilots Association (APA) serves as the certified collective bargaining agent for the 16,000 professional pilots who fly for American Airlines. APA was founded in 1963 and is the largest independent pilots’ union in the world. APA provides a broad range of representation services for its members and devotes more than 20 percent of its dues income to support aviation safety.

496548.title: Stochastic Physics in MPAS: Informing REFSv2 ensemble design
496548.authors: Jeff Beck, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and W. Mayfield, G. Ketefian, C. P. Kalb, M. A. Harrold, M. J. Kavulich Jr., and N. Wang
496548.abstract: NOAA is planning to implement the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) as the dynamical core for the next version of its convection-allowing Rapid-Refresh Forecast System (RRFS). With this change, future ensemble design considerations for the RRFS Ensemble Forecast System (REFS) are being discussed, with stochastic physics representing a leading contender to address uncertainty representation and serve as a source for effective spread generation. To facilitate ensemble design options for REFSv2, the Developmental Testbed Center (DTC) conducted work implementing and testing stochastic physics capabilities within MPAS. This new code calls the UFS stochastic physics pattern generator, which is used to apply perturbations to state variables and/or physics tendencies during model integration. Week-long spring and winter retrospective MPAS ensemble simulations were run to assess the validity of using stochastic physics as an ensemble design option in REFSv2. Ensemble forecast metrics and spread generation were evaluated, as well as individual ensemble members to understand the impacts of stochastic physics on deterministic verification. Through this work, the DTC will play a critical role informing operational implementation decisions for REFSv2.

496551.title: Stressing the Energy Grid: Weather-Driven Electric-Grid Emergencies In 2026
496551.authors: Brent Ho, Sunairio, Winter Park, FL; and P. Hawbecker, O. Pfeiffer, R. Hasegawa, and R. Cirincione
496551.abstract: Every year, extreme weather can push electric grids across the US to their limits. In this presentation, we dive into two weather events from 2026, examine how grid operators managed soaring loads and limited dispatchable generation, and discuss future trends in how weather impacts our rapidly evolving grid. In late January 2026, Winter Storm Fern brought freezing temperatures to Texas and high electric demand to its grid operator ERCOT. Observing the load-growth-adjusted relationship between temperature and load, we find that ERCOT biased their load forecasts to predict higher load demand than would be justified by forecasted temperatures (presumably to avoid a grid shortfall like during Winter Storm Uri and entice more generators to come online). Realized load was in line with our load models–and much lower than the grid operator’s forecasts. Zooming into the ERCOT West load zone, we show how load came in much lower than one might expect given the low temperatures as oil and gas infrastructure froze over. Turning to wind generation forecasts, we also found evidence of the grid operator manually depressing power forecasts, an intervention (likely due to anticipation of wind turbine icing) that turned out to be correct. Moving from winter storms to summer heat waves, early July 2026 brought scorching temperatures to PJM, a regional grid operator operating in 13 Eastern US states. Hot temperatures brought load to near all-time records on July 1 and July 2. The operator responded by activating all available Demand Response options, declaring a NERC EEA 2 emergency (indicating energy-deficiency and load-management procedures in effect), and issuing a “Deploy All Resources Action” to order all available generation units to generate at Emergency Maximum levels. Through these actions, as well as due to depressed load from the upcoming July 4th holiday and “Coincident Peak” load shaving, PJM was able (barely) to avoid blackouts. Thinking of the evolution of energy grids going forward, we close by analyzing the increasingly pertinent effect of data centers, renewable generation, energy storage, and behind-the-meter (rooftop) solar capacity. We offer some thoughts on why ERCOT and PJM responded to their respective emergencies as they did, and consider how grid operators across the US will be affected by future weather extremes.

496553.title: Observing Ozone Production Regimes and Compound Meteorological Extremes during Ozone Exceedance Days across U.S. Ozone Nonattainment Areas from TROPOMI and TEMPO
496553.authors: Yohan Yang, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ; and D. Chatterjee, Y. Wang, Y. Li, and X. Jin
496553.abstract: Ozone (O3) near the surface is a secondary air pollutant that poses risks to human health and the environment. Over the US, the most densely populated and industrialized regions continue to experience ozone exceedances despite substantial emission reductions over recent decades. Whether these exceedances are driven by emissions or meteorological extremes such as stagnation and heat waves remains difficult to separate, yet critical for targeting the right emission controls. Here, we use sun-synchronous TROPOMI and geostationary TEMPO observations, to diagnose changes of ozone precursors as well as the ozone production regimes on exceedance days. We then assess how stagnation events and heat waves modulate these regimes and contribute to the ozone exceedances over the study period. TROPOMI NO2 and HCHO columns are broadly elevated on exceedance days across U.S. nonattainment areas. HCHO/NO2 column ratios increased across most regions, and ozone production is predominantly NOx-limited. In terms of meteorological co-occurrence, stagnation accounts for 59% of exceedance days along the West Coast, while most other regions show exceedances occurring without concurrent stagnation or heat waves. Add an ending sentence about the overall implication of this study.

496555.title: Right Track, Wrong Wind: A Decoupling in DLESyM Nor'easters
496555.authors: Sylvia Garmong, USACE, Alexandria, VA; and T. W. Letcher, D. Anderson, N. Cohn, and B. West
496555.abstract: The Deep Learning Earth System Model (DLESyM) enables rapid simulation of long-term predictions utilizing a fraction of the computational cost of traditional dynamic Earth system models. However, while initial evaluations of DLESyM are promising, robust validations of its accuracy for specific weather phenomena are still in their infancy, making it crucial to establish boundaries of appropriate use. In this work, we assess how accurately DLESyM simulates mid-latitude cyclones in the Northeast US coastal regions (i.e., Nor’easters). To evaluate its performance, we track and compare DLESyM generated Nor'easters against ERA5 reanalysis climatology. Results show that DLESyM successfully reproduces realistic climatological Nor'easter storm tracks, coastal trajectories, and system lifetimes. However, while the model captures extreme low-pressure events with remarkable accuracy, it systematically fails to reproduce the peak magnitudes of 10m wind speed events associated with these coastal storms. These results indicate that while DLESyM accurately simulates large-scale baroclinic structures, a physical decoupling in near-surface wind fields limits its ability to characterize the impacts of Nor’easters. An understanding of these physical limitations is key; while DLESyM provides unprecedented speed for earth system representation, targeted statistical or dynamical post-processing of Nor'easter wind tails remains essential for structural design and local hazard assessment.

496556.title: Airborne Water Vapor Sensing Technology Developments from Honeywell Aerospace
496556.authors: Patrick T Conry, Honeywell Aerospace US LLC, Yeovil, United Kingdom; and C. Hoyt, D. Pearce, L. Horstman, C. Fredrick, J. Rogers, M. Pasnik, J. Lindsay, T. Rahmes, and D. Ochoa-Mendoza
496556.abstract: Accurate airborne water vapor measurements are essential for improving numerical weather prediction (NWP) models and forecasting Ice Supersaturated Regions at cruise altitudes, where contrails and aircraft-induced cirrus contribute to aviation’s non-CO₂ emissions through net warming radiative effects. However, with the planned retirement of many aircraft equipped with water vapor sensors, observation gaps may soon arise. Moreover, in low-humidity environments the currently deployed water vapor sensing technologies lack the accuracy required for effective, operational contrail mitigation. Therefore, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2025)* and aviation industry stakeholders have identified the need for new, improved airborne water vapor sensors. To this end, Honeywell Aerospace (HONA) is developing two technologies to provide the next generation of accurate, fast-response, economical water vapor measurements for NWP data assimilation and contrail mitigation. The first water vapor sensing technology, dual comb spectroscopy (DCS), aims to deliver single-ppm accuracy across all flight altitudes. Initial 2025 flight tests demonstrated stable, accurate performance and fast response at low water vapor concentrations (down to 19 ppm). With support from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), HONA is developing the second generation DCS water vapor sensor under the Comb-based Laser Evaluation for Aviation Regulation (CLEAR) program. This new sensor is being built based on a new, lighter weight design that improves signal-to-noise and precision and will be flight-tested in early 2027. Further size, weight, power, and cost reduction is planned beyond this to ensure a commercially viable solution. Mitigation of contrail Impact via novel Sensing Technologies (MIST) is supported by the ATI Programme — a joint Government and industry investment delivered through a partnership between the Aerospace Technology Institute (ATI), the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST) and Innovate UK, part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI). HONA leads the MIST program in collaboration with Boeing UK and the University of Reading, which aims to advance water vapor sensor technology for contrail detection including integration into commercial aircraft. In early 2026, several candidate sensor technologies were evaluated, and a novel whispering gallery micro-resonator technology from a UK-based Small/Medium-sized Enterprise was selected for development. The sensor is progressing through design, build, and laboratory testing phases, and first flight testing is scheduled for late 2027. This presentation outlines the motivation for these next-generation water vapor sensing technologies in terms of improving NWP forecasts and operationalizing contrail avoidance. Then recent results, ongoing activities, and future plans from the DCS and MIST technology maturation progress will be summarized. *National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. (2025). Developing a research agenda on contrails and their climate impacts. Washington, DC: The National Academies Press. https://doi.org/10.17226/29073

496558.title: From Understanding to Action: Comparing Public Responses to Heat Risk Communications
496558.authors: Alantis Baldwin, Clemson University, Clemson, SC; and B. Remington and J. N. Allan
496558.abstract: Extreme heat remains a leading cause of weather-related deaths in the U.S., resulting in hundreds of deaths each year (NOAA, 2025). While heat risk communication is important for informed decision making and can help reduce negative impacts, research shows that many heat risk communications are not well understood by the public and often misinterpreted (Olson & Sutton, 2025). Further, there are different ways to communicate heat risks that may impact understanding and decision making (e.g., the HeatRisk forecast issued by the NWS and heat index forecasts issued by the WPC). Research suggests that one’s understanding of a risk is central to protective action decisions (Cokely et al., 2018; Lindell & Perry, 2012), yet it is an open question as to which heat risk communications are best understood and their influence on decision making. The current study aimed to investigate and compare public understanding of different heat risk communications, as well as their impact on downstream decision outcomes (e.g., risk perceptions, protective actions). Participants (N=314) recruited via Prolific viewed three heat risk communications: heat index, probabilistic heat index, and HeatRisk. For each graphic, participants’ comprehension, perceived usability, risk perception, and behavioral intentions were assessed. Participants then completed measures of statistical numeracy, science reasoning, and weather numeracy. Within-subjects ANOVAs indicated significant differences between the three graphics in overall comprehension (F(1.87, 584.44) = 82.97, p <.001, η2p = .210), risk perception (F(1.90, 589.64) = 11.36, p <.001, η2p = .035), perceived understanding (F(1.80, 564.90) = 75.47, p <.001, η2p = .091), and protective action intentions (F(1.88, 588.65) = 12.92, p <.001, η2p = .04). Specifically, post hoc analyses revealed that the probabilistic heat index graphic was the most difficult for users to comprehend, while the HeatRisk graphic was perceived to be the easiest to understand and incited the most protective action intentions. The heat index graphic resulted in lower risk perceptions compared to the other two graphics. Further discussion will consider how individual characteristics (e.g., demographics, numeracy, and science reasoning skills) can influence the interpretation and response to heat risks. Taken together, these findings highlight (i) how individual characteristics and the design of weather risk communications shape decision making, and (ii) provide insights on methodologies for assessing risk comprehension.

496560.title: Soil NOx Emissions Measurements From Summer Flight Campaigns In The California San Joaquin Valley
496560.authors: Eleanor Waxman, CIRES, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and I. B. Pollack, Q. Z. Rasool, K. Zuraski, R. Poudyal, J. Dean-Day, C. Gatebe, and A. Rollins
496560.abstract: The California San Joaquin Valley (SJV) is classified as an extreme ozone non-attainment area. Recently, ozone (O3) production in the SJV has been shown to be NOx (NO + NO2) limited so as NOx is decreased, production O3 is also expected to decrease. There have been significant decreases in mobile NOx emissions from vehicles in recent decades, making NOx emissions from non-mobile sources increasingly important for controlling surface ozone. One potential source of non-mobile NOx is soil emissions as NOx can be emitted to the atmosphere during both microbial nitrification and denitrification processes. A recent study in the California Central Valley suggested that NOx emissions from soils over crop lands could be an order of magnitude higher than that predicted by models including MEGAN and BEIS, indicating that soil NOx emissions are poorly understood. In this work, we analyze NOx data from three summertime field campaigns with flights in the SJV: AEROMMA in summer 2023, FIREX-AQ in summer 2019, and CalNex in summer 2010. We use the FluxToolbox Matlab analysis program to calculate airborne eddy covariance fluxes and then infer the surface flux using a calculated flux divergence. Overall, we find that the fluxes from this analysis are of similar magnitudes to the previous measurements in the California Central Valley, validating the previous analysis and indicating that the traditional model results significantly underestimate NOx soil emissions. Additionally, there are no significant trends apparent in the thirteen-year span between campaigns, indicating that NOx soil fluxes have remained relatively constant despite a changing agricultural landscape in the SJV.

496561.title: Restoring Atmospheric Circulation: A Dynamics-Informed Framework for Climate Interventions
496561.authors: Walker Raymond Lee, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. C. C. Chen, S. Tilmes, J. G. M. Ribeiro, and M. Reboita
496561.abstract: Simulated climate intervention experiments, such as stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) and marine cloud brightening (MCB), are commonly designed and evaluated around surface temperature- and radiative forcing-based metrics. While such a framework diagnoses the first-order effectiveness of climate intervention at reversing the impacts of global warming, it does not directly consider impacts to the circulation. The atmosphere transports energy and momentum around the globe; circulation changes can be just as or more important than the direct forcing in determining the temperature response to a climate intervention, especially for regional or local interventions which are far away. The stratospheric circulation response to SAI is well-studied, but limited research has been done on the tropospheric response, especially for MCB. In this presentation, we propose that the dynamical response of the atmosphere to a simulated climate intervention can - and should - be used as a metric for the effectiveness of the intervention. As a case study, we consider previously-published simulations of marine cloud brightening: one set which brightens clouds in the summer hemisphere subtropics, and one set which brightens clouds in the winter hemisphere midlatitudes. In the underlying simulations of global warming, we observe a reduction in the meridional temperature gradient which drives baroclinic instability, cyclogenesis, and meridional shifts to the midlatitude storm tracks. The midlatitude MCB strategy reverses these trends, as well as GHG-warming-driven shifts in Eady growth and eddy kinetic energy; in contrast, the subtropical MCB strategy exacerbates these changes. Such a framework provides an alternate lens for evaluating the impacts of climate intervention (SAI, MCB, and otherwise) relative to global warming, and we propose that future experiments be designed with the intention of maintaining and/or restoring the planetary circulation in addition to cooling the surface.

496562.title: From Rainfall Control to Thermal Dominance: Hydroclimatic Regime Shift and Drought Intensification in the Pantanal Wetland
496562.authors: Luiz Octávio Fabrício dos Santos, Federal University of Mato Grosso, Cuiabá, Brazil; and M. S. Biudes, H. M. E. Geli, L. B. da Rosa, L. F. A. Curado, C. A. S. Querino, J. K. A. D. S. Querino, and N. G. Machado
496562.abstract: The Pantanal, the world’s largest tropical wetland, is experiencing intensifying hydroclimatic stress under sustained climate warming. This study integrates reanalysis data from 1980 to 2022, the 12-month Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI-12), Run Theory, climate-extreme indices, Random Forest diagnostics, land-surface transformation analysis, and CMIP6 projections to assess whether drought dynamics are undergoing a structural shift in their dominant controls. Results show a marked intensification of drought duration, severity, and persistence since the early 2000s, culminating in unprecedented multi-year drought conditions between 2020 and 2022. Although declining precipitation contributed to moisture deficits, temperature extremes, particularly the frequency of Warm Days (TX90p), were more strongly associated with SPEI-12 variability than precipitation-based indices across all subregions. The strengthening negative relationship between TX90p and SPEI-12 indicates that atmospheric evaporative demand is increasingly shaping the regional water balance. CMIP6 ensemble projections show continued amplification of TX90p under all emission scenarios, with pronounced divergence under high forcing, reinforcing the potential consolidation of a thermally amplified drought regime. Land-surface transformation further reduces hydrological buffering capacity and enhances water–energy feedbacks. These findings support the hypothesis that drought in the Pantanal is shifting from rainfall-dominated variability toward thermodynamically amplified drought dynamics.

496563.title: Rainfall Model Portability Across One-Day and Two-Day Forecasts: Hydrogeomorphic Patterns of Transferability and Adaptability for Regionalisation
496563.authors: Ogochukwu Ejike, University of the West of Scotland, Paisley, RFW, United kingdom; University of the West of Scotland, Paisley, RFW, United kingdom; University of the West of Scotland, Paisley, United Kingdom; University of the West of Scotland, Paisley, United kingdom; and D. Ndzi
496563.abstract: Artificial intelligence has improved rainfall prediction across a wide range of environmental settings, yet a persistent obstacle remains: models that perform well at their native locations may not retain comparable behaviour when transferred elsewhere. This limits the scalability of machine learning for weather and climate applications, particularly where local model development, long observational records, or repeated site-specific calibration are impractical. Spatial generalisation is therefore not only a question of whether predictive performance declines outside the training environment, but also of whether some source environments consistently produce more transferable models and whether some target environments are systematically more receptive to imported models. A further unresolved question is whether such portability patterns remain stable when the forecast horizon changes. This study evaluates whether hydrogeomorphic setting provides a physically informed framework for organising the spatial portability of rainfall occurrence models and whether the resulting transferability and adaptability patterns persist from one day to two days ahead. Six sites across the temperate United States and tropical Malaysia were paired into Alluvial/ Valley, Delta/ Marsh, and Coastal Plain hydrogeomorphic analogues. The analogue framework was defined using elevation, gradient, hydrologic regime, and surface material, which were used for site pairing rather than as model predictors. Random Forest and Logistic Regression classifiers were developed from routine daily surface observations of pressure, temperature, dew point, relative humidity, wind speed, and wind direction. Rainfall occurrence was defined using a daily precipitation threshold of 1 mm, with separate prediction targets defined for one day and two days ahead. Models were developed chronologically and evaluated under a common spatial transfer protocol so that differences in cross-location behaviour could be examined consistently. Portability was evaluated using Balanced Accuracy at each model's fixed native threshold to quantify decision performance and AUC to quantify threshold-independent discrimination, with no target recalibration. Spatial portability was evaluated directionally rather than as a single cross-site performance measure. The Transferability Index (TI) quantified source model export performance, whereas the Adaptability Index (AI) quantified target site receptiveness to imported models. Native site performance was excluded from both indices, and the coefficient of variation (CV) assessed the consistency of these transfer behaviours. Mean performance and CV were combined in a performance-first Behaviour Grid to distinguish strong average portability from consistently reliable portability. Across 16 comparisons spanning both forecast horizons, classifiers, metrics, and climatic regions, Delta / Marsh environments produced the highest TI in 14 cases (87.5%), while Alluvial / Valley environments produced the highest AI in 15 cases (93.8%). At two days, Delta / Marsh produced the highest TI in all eight comparisons, while Alluvial / Valley retained the highest AI in seven of eight. Delta / Marsh were never the strongest receivers, while Alluvial / Valley were never the strongest exporters, with the few departures from these dominant directional patterns occurring in Coastal Plain environments. The AUC results were especially coherent, with Delta / Marsh / the highest AUC-based TI in seven of eight comparisons and Alluvial / Valley the highest AUC-based AI in all eight, indicating that the directional structure was not confined to fixed threshold decision performance. The Behaviour Grid showed, however, that persistence of directional role did not imply uniform stability, as strong Delta / Marsh exporters sometimes varied across target locations, while strong Alluvial / Valley receivers varied across imported source models. Coastal Plains were generally intermediate on transferability but less consistent on adaptability, indicating that directional portability roles were more reproducible across horizons than the stability with which those roles were expressed. Geographic proximity did not provide a consistent explanation for these relationships. In Malaysia, Kinta Valley and Kelantan Coastal Plain are separated by only 216.9 km yet displayed different portability roles, while the more geographically isolated Rajang Delta retained the strongest exporter tendency, indicating that the observed structure cannot be reduced to a simple nearest site effect. The key result is therefore not that predictive performance merely changes between one and two days ahead, but that the spatial organisation of model portability itself is substantially reproduced. Its recurrence across classifiers, metrics, climatic regions, and forecast horizons supports the interpretation that the pattern is not confined to a single analytical configuration. The persistence of this directional structure from one to two days provides a basis for terrain-informed regionalisation of rainfall occurrence prediction. Hydrogeomorphic context may therefore help identify candidate source environments for model transfer and candidate target environments receptive to imported models, rather than relying on geographic proximity alone. Although terrain cannot be inferred to determine portability, recurrence across classifiers, metrics, climatic regions, and forecast horizons provides evidence of a reproducible association between hydrogeomorphic setting and the direction of rainfall model generalisation within this comparative design.

496568.title: Utilizing Next Generation Fire System (NGFS) Observations of Wildfires to Improve Warn-on-Forecast System for Smoke (WoFS-Smoke) Forecasts
496568.authors: Sarah King, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; and P. S. Skinner, T. A. Jones, J. A. Otkin, S. M. Loria-Salazar, and D. Schvartzman
496568.abstract: The Warn-on-Forecast System for Smoke (WoFS-Smoke) provides short-term (0-6 hour) smoke forecasts for rapidly evolving fires. Current WoFS-Smoke efforts are focused on improving forecasts based on changes in environmental conditions by developing relationships between satellite detected wildfire intensity and model analyses of the environment. One method of obtaining wildfire intensity is via the Next Generation Fire System (NGFS), an experimental fire detection system from NOAA and the Cooperative Institute for Meteorological Satellite Studies. The NGFS utilizes spectral satellite measurements from the visible, shortwave infrared, mid-wave infrared, and longwave infrared, along with advanced spatial and temporal metrics, to provide fire detection and tracking. A spatiotemporally matched dataset of observed wildfire characteristics from GOES-R-based NGFS observations (1-minute, 2km pixel retrievals) and environmental conditions from WoFS (5-minute, 3km grid point forecasts) has been created. The WoFS data contains model analyses of variables such as temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed, as well as composite fire weather indices such as the Red Flag Threat Index. The NGFS data provides fire properties such as fire radiative power. This dataset is available for a dozen cases between 2020 and 2025 on dates with heightened wildfire activity where WoFS was run either in real time or retrospectively, containing hundreds of unique NGFS features and thousands of individual pixel detections. This presentation will discuss current progress and findings on the relationship between NGFS fire characteristics and WoFS model conditions. Namely, comparison of the evolution of NGFS fire observations to changes in the simulated WoFS environment. This work aims to improve empirical models for representing smoke injection behavior in numerical weather prediction models.

496571.title: Weather-Contextualized Multi-Sensor Data Acquisition for ADAS and AV Research
496571.authors: Wing Yi Pao, Ontario Tech University, Oshawa, ON, Canada; and A. Van Berkel, M. Sadegh Moradi, M. Agelin-Chaab, H. Lang, I. Gultepe, and H. Hangan
496571.abstract: Adverse weather remains a significant challenge for advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and automated vehicle perception, as precipitation can alter visibility, affecting sensors to detect environmental features which reduces reliability. While existing driving datasets have enabled substantial advances in perception and machine learning analyses, detailed and synchronized characterization of environmental conditions, particularly precipitation characteristics is often limited. The multi-sensor platform developed in this work is intended to support research extending beyond conventional object-detection evaluation, including weather-aware perception training and validation, sensor-fusion strategies, airflow management, de-icing, and image restoration, as well as the development and validation of synthetic perception models. This work presents a vehicle-based multi-sensor data acquisition platform developed for weather-aware ADAS research and for creating the Climate · Hybrid · Autonomy (CHA-co) Dataset. The project is led by CHA-co SPACE Inc. in collaboration with the Aerodynamics & Energy Research and Observation (AERO), Weather Adaptation, and General Robotics and Autonomous Systems & Processes (GRASP) research groups at Ontario Tech University. The CHA-co Car platform is built on a Ford Bronco Sport vehicle, with support from Polito Ford Lincoln located in Lindsay, ON, and integrates a customized data acquisition architecture for synchronized collection of perception, environmental, aerodynamic, and vehicle-state information. The instrumentations include Thies Clima LPM and OTT Parsivel optical disdrometers, Livox and Velodyne VLP-32 LiDARs, a Benewake TF02 range sensor, D3 Embedded RS1843A 77-GHz mmWave radar, pitot-probe airspeed measurements, automotive ultrasonic sensors, PoE cameras, a microphone, and a CSS Electronics CANedge CAN-bus data logger with GPS and IMU. Supporting infrastructure in the vehicle includes onboard computing, backup power, configurable power supplies, network connectivity, cloud-based data storage, remote access, real-time dashboard visualization, and voice-recorded event annotation. The resulting dataset related to precipitation, environment, vehicle, and motion information is used for perception analysis. This dataset is particularly important for investigating weather-induced perception effects, such as LiDAR point loss caused by precipitation (rain or snow) attenuation or obstruction. Results suggested that the synchronized architecture further supports sensor-fusion studies across LiDAR, radar, camera, ultrasonic, and vehicle data, while providing physically contextualized inputs for data analytics, machine learning analysis, synthetic sensor simulation, and perception-focused digital twin development. This work highlights the development of an integrated data acquisition architecture, synchronization and processing pipelines, and a data collection strategy designed to connect real-world weather conditions with sensor-level and vehicle-level responses for next-generation ADAS and automated vehicle research.

496572.title: Co-Producing Decision-Ready Drought Information for Public Lands: Climate Engine Reports for Land Management Applications
496572.authors: Eric Jensen, Desert Research Institute, Reno, CO; and A. Brooks, K. O'Shea, K. Hegewisch, B. Daudert, D. J. McEvoy, T. Assal, J. Scott, J. Sondergard, and J. L. Huntington
496572.abstract: Drought management on public lands requires interpreting indicators that represent different components and timescales of drought and applying that information at spatial scales relevant to management. To address this challenge, the ClimateEngine.org team has worked with the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), with support from NOAA’s National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS), to co-produce an operational drought-reporting system for public lands across the western United States. The Climate Engine Drought Reports were developed with BLM staff to support implementation of the agency’s National Drought and Water Availability Instruction Memorandum (IM 2024-034). Through an iterative co-development process, policy direction and user needs guided indicator selection, data visualization and report design, operational data pipelines, update schedules, and delivery through multiple access pathways. The reports integrate the U.S. Drought Monitor, short- and long-term drought indicator blends, and gridded precipitation, evaporative demand, and temperature data to characterize current drought conditions, water-year-to-date meteorological conditions, and historical climate and drought patterns since 1980. Updated every five days, reports are precomputed for BLM state, district, and field offices and individual grazing allotments, while custom reports can be generated for user-defined areas. A supporting software system provides consistent access through a public website (reports.climateengine.org), open application programming interfaces (APIs), and enterprise tools within BLM’s ArcGIS Online infrastructure. Companion Climate Engine Site Characterization and Vegetation Production Reports combine climate and drought information with remotely sensed vegetation estimates, helping users place current conditions within their long-term ecological context and evaluate potential vegetation responses. Together, these tools connect drought status, meteorological drivers, historical context, and resource response. This work demonstrates that actionable drought information depends on scientifically credible datasets as well as management-relevant geographies, clear interpretation, timely updates, and integration with existing agency workflows.

496573.title: The Role and Location of Secondary Droplet Activation In Cumulus Congestus: Findings from Particle-Following Simulations for a Case during TRACER and ESCAPE
496573.abstract: While supersaturation levels in clouds cannot be measured directly, they have significant implications for microphysical processes and cloud evolution, especially in vertically extensive convective clouds. Secondary droplet activation (SDA), which is activation of cloud droplets far above cloud base, contributes to changing supersaturation levels, but its importance has not been quantified. Using the observational datasets from the TRACER and ESCAPE field campaigns over Houston, Texas, this study assesses the importance of SDA on cloud microphysical properties and processes using large-eddy simulations of cumulus congestus clouds by the CM1 model. The use of super-droplet method (SDM) in our simulations enables Lagrangian tracking of aerosols and hydrometeors with no major assumptions on their number or size distributions as they evolve over time. According to our simulations of the cumulus congestus clouds observed on June 16, 2022, when in-situ measurements of aerosols and clouds were made, the simulated droplet size distributions from SDM match well with those from the aircraft observations, which signifies the validity of our simulation results in representing the observed cumulus congestus. Comparison of simulations with and without SDA above a certain height shows that the primary contributor to SDA is entrained aerosols that are activated at the lateral cloud edges, rather than small particles lofted from the boundary layer in convective cores. This result implies the importance of accurately representing aerosol vertical profiles and free-tropospheric aerosol size distributions, along with the strong control of turbulence on the evolution of convective clouds.

496574.title: From Global-to-Local: Leveraging s Large-Sample Dataset to Test Improvements in US Streamflow Forecasting
496574.authors: Engela Sthapit, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and E. Towler, W. R. Currier, and M. R. Abel
496574.abstract: Streamflow prediction remains a challenge even in data-rich regions like the United States (US). Recent research has shown that deep learning methods based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks outperform process-based and other machine learning models. However, this improved performance is not guaranteed for every basin under generalized ML models — mid-western basins, for example, are notoriously hard to predict, and generalized ML models especially struggle to outperform locally calibrated process-based models. Yet local calibration is not realistically feasible for every basin. In this study, we leverage Caravan — a recently published global community dataset for large-sample hydrology — to predict streamflow in selected basins in the US. For our experimental design, we focus on testing 31 of the Caravan basins that have been designated as priority basins by NOAA's Office of Water Prediction (OWP), which operates the Hydrologic Ensemble Forecast System (HEFS). within the National Weather Service, routinely providing probabilistic streamflow forecasts using meteorological forecasts from the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFSv12). While HEFS relies on a process-based Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting model, recent studies have shown that LSTM models are comparable and can often offer improvements over traditional hydrological models. In the first experiment, we test the value of using a global dataset by comparing an LSTM trained using full global Caravan dataset with an LSTM trained only on Caravan’s US subset - Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies. Training on basins from around the world allows the model to learn transferable hydrologic behaviour, rather than relying on data from smaller domains or local calibration. In the second experiment, we test the value of adding GEFSv12 as additional forcing input during training, alongside the meteorological forcing already in Caravan - making the model’s inputs comparable to those used operationally by HEFS. Across both experiments, the OWP priority basins are excluded from training, so that model performance on these basins reflects generalization to unseen catchments. This framework offers insight into the potential for machine learning to complement and enhance the accuracy and skill of operational ensemble streamflow forecasting.

496577.title: Multiscale Wind-Plant Wake Dynamics and Interactions with the Capping Inversion in Stratified Boundary Layers
496577.authors: Karim Ali, MIT, Cambridge, MA; and M. F. Howland
496577.abstract: Wind plants interact with the atmospheric boundary layer over spatial scales substantially larger than those of individual turbines, producing plant-scale disturbances that can extend far downstream and modifythe surrounding boundary-layer flow. In conventionally neutral boundary layers, wind-plant wake evolution depends not only on turbine-generated turbulence but also on the characteristics and dynamical response of the stably stratified capping inversion, which regulates momentum exchange with the free atmosphere. We perform large-eddy simulations of a finite wind plant comprising 63 turbines, each with a diameter of 126 meters, under conventionally neutral conditions spanning different boundary-layer depths and inversion strengths. The simulations show that the capping inversion responds dynamically to the disturbance generated by the plant. The plant produces an upward displacement of the inversion layer, whose magnitude depends on both the inversion height and its strength. For shallower boundary layers, where the inversion lies closer to the turbine-induced disturbance, larger vertical displacements are observed than for deeper boundary layers. At a fixed inversion height, the response also depends systematically on inversion strength, where weaker inversions, characterized by a smaller potential-temperature increase across the layer, undergo larger vertical displacement than stronger inversions. The inversion-layer thickness exhibits an additional oscillatory response downstream of the plant, with a stronger response when the inversion is closer to the plant and when the inversion is weaker. Together, the displacement and thickness variations demonstrate a two-way coupling between the wind plant and the capping inversion, such that the inversion regulates the vertical development of the plant-induced flow disturbance, while the disturbance simultaneously deforms and modifies the structure of the capping inversion itself. A base-perturbation decomposition of the flow further identifies distinct mechanisms governing the plant- and turbine-scale responses. Plant-scale perturbations are driven predominantly by pressure-gradient adjustments associated with the large-scale displacement of the boundary-layer flow, whereas recovery at turbine scales is governed primarily by turbulence-driven momentum transport generated by turbine-wake shear. The results therefore reveal a multiscale interaction in which local turbulent wake-recovery mechanisms coexist with a dynamically coupled plant-inversion response governing the larger-scale evolution of the disturbed boundary layer.

496578.title: Impact of Assimilating Airborne Radio Occultation Data on Ensemble Spread and Forecast Confidence in Atmospheric Rivers
496578.authors: Benjamin Davis, University of California San Diego, San Diego, CA; Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA; and J. S. Haase, N. P. Do, I. Hernandez Banos, B. Cao, and N. J. Barton
496578.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are elongated bands of enhanced water vapor transport from the tropics to the midlatitudes. ARs are associated with up to 90% of meridional water vapor transport and up to 50% of wintertime precipitation on the US West Coast. Precipitation associated with ARs can lead to flooding and other significant impacts upon landfall. The Atmospheric River Reconnaissance (AR Recon) program makes targeted observations in ARs and their environments to sample essential atmospheric structures and regions of initial condition sensitivity in models. One observation type collected on AR Recon flights is airborne radio occultation (ARO), a limb sounding technique that derives profiles of atmospheric refractivity, which is sensitive to temperature, pressure, and moisture, to the sides of the aircraft. ARO is complementary to the in-situ dropsonde measurements that record beneath the flight path of the aircraft. Recent case studies of ARO data impact indicate that ARO improves deterministic AR forecasts. This study will evaluate the impact of ARO on forecast uncertainty by using an ensemble approach and will investigate the benefit of full basin coverage of AR Recon observations. In early February 2025 a series of ARs travelled across the Pacific Basin. ARO data were recorded from AR Recons flights originating from Japan, Hawai’i, and California, providing extensive observational coverage of the ARs at different stages in their evolution, providing a good test to evaluate the full basin coverage of ARO observations. The Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) and the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI) are used to run a 20-member ensemble. Data are assimilated with JEDI’s 3DEnVar Ensemble of Data Assimilation (EDA) capability. Each experiment will assimilate conventional observations, AMVs, AMSU-A, MHS, and GNSSRO, with one experiment also assimilating ARO. These experiments represent the first effort to simultaneously assimilate ARO data collected from multiple aircraft types, namely the United States Air Force WC-130s and National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration Gulfstream-IV aircraft. These experiments will provide more insight onto the factors driving the relatively strong positive impact at 4-5 day lead times seen in previous studies, extend the assessment of forecast errors to lead times up to 7 days, and by using an ensemble method, will provide better estimates of forecast confidence in both IVT and precipitation due to the hypothesized improvement in model representation of thermodynamic fields.

496579.title: Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Operational Improvement: The Third-Party Weather Provider (3PWP) Qualification Process
496579.authors: Michelle V Whitcher, FAA, Washington, DC
496579.abstract: Over the past several years, Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) and Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) operations have experienced significant technological advancement and increased integration into the National Airspace System (NAS). To support the safe and efficient operation of non-traditional aviation activities and address the challenges associated with integrating them into the NAS, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has dedicated resources to initiate research, develop new technologies, and develop policy. One of the policies being developed is the Third-Party Weather Provider (3PWP) Qualification Process which creates a new avenue for the FAA to qualify 3PWPs. Weather information provided by qualified 3PWPs will assist UAS and AAM operators with flight planning, operations, and dispatching by providing crucial weather information at low altitudes and outside of airport areas currently serviced by approved weather sources. The 3PWP Qualification Process includes three basic steps: Step 1 – 3PWP Application Step 2 – Qualification by the FAA Step 3 – Routine Monitoring by the FAA These steps will ensure the weather information provided by the 3PWP is measured against industry weather information standards and is considered approved by the FAA Administrator. This paper will provide an in-depth overview of the 3PWP Qualification Process, provide an update on the status of the associated FAA guidance documents (e.g., Advisory Circulars, etc.) and offer insight into the FAA’s 3PWP implementation timeline. Additionally, this presentation will include an early preview of the 3PWP Web Portal and will highlight resources and opportunities for 3PWP candidates to learn more about application requirements.

496580.title: Using Forecasts of Weather Extremes to Manage Hospital Departments: Game-type exercises offer opportunities to testbed use of forecasts
496580.authors: Andrea J. Ray, NOAA/Earth System Research Lab, Boulder, CO; and F. Flippin and F. Bokhari
496580.abstract: Weather and subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) extremes can stress hospital Emergency Departments (EDs), Trauma Centers (TCs), and Intensive Care Units (ICUs) which are on the front line for responding to their human impacts. At a time when most EDs are operating at 95-100% of capacity on an average day, extreme events can trigger surges in system demand which overwhelms the healthcare system. When patients overwhelm the system, emergency and disaster operations contingency plans must be implemented. A surge of patients affected by heat waves and poor air quality, some of whom may require admission to ICUs may necessitate these actions; wintertime cold extremes may also see patients affected by abnormally cold temperatures and air quality from inversions. However, weather forecast have been underutilized in planning for health care operations. For many years, pre-hospital and in-hospital healthcare settings have used tabletop exercises for disaster simulation and preparation, offering an opportunity to test strategies and use of new information. Tabletop exercises are popular because of a perceived optimal balance between fidelity and low cost and low time impact on involved staff. This placed tabletop exercises at the top of the “discussion-based exercise” hierarchy. However tabletop exercises have been questioned recently, because while no simulation has 100% fidelity, the ad hoc nature of almost all tabletops calls into serious question whether most are a true reflection of what would happen in a given scenario. Add to this that “rules of the real world” such as transportation time, the time to perform a procedure, and the realities of staff diversity and limitations are often not accounted for. An alternative is game-type exercise simulations. Game-type exercises are very similar to tabletop exercises but use a standardized system of both staff and victims which have been validated by evidence-based research. Additionally, game-type exercises play by a set of rules which are enforced to reflect real-world conditions. In game-type exercises, realism and accuracy are promoted by the enforcement of time standards and personnel restrictions, forcing players to confront the often challenging realities encountered when patients overwhelm a system. This allows game-type exercises to closely approximate operational exercises (where resources are actually deployed and used as they would be during a disaster) without the expense and time-intensity normally required. Furthermore, these excercises might be designed to provide some functions of a to a weather testbed, in the sense that they can give practitioners experience with use of weather forecast and outlook products, and also collect feed back on the utility of these in decision making and planning. Healthcare systems and the communities they serve need to determine what their capabilities and deficiencies are for response, especially in response to extremes of temperature and air quality, and as well characterized disasters become more frequent and move in their geographic distribution, as in the case of tornadoes, Game-type exercises offer a superior fidelity experience, near the level of an operational exercise, compared to tabletop exercises while preserving many of the advantages of tabletop and other discussion-based exercises such as the limited resources required, time efficiency, and flexibility of simulation involving multiple roles and locations. This presentation will review the characteristics of discussion-based and operational exercises, considering their potential use in having hospital department managers to be more familiar with weather forecasts and outlooks, and experience in their use in planning department resources (including staff) days to a week or so inadvance. It will then introduce game-type exercises using the example of the most used game-type disaster simulation system worldwide, Emergo Training System. (The authors disclose they have no financial interest in this system.) Emergo is a rigorously data-validated simulation system which allows for the simulation of a disaster from any cause, including natural disasters. Any role or area can be simulated, from prehospital first responders, government and non-government agencies, to the numerous different types of units and personnel in a hospital of any size. The use of game-type exercises constitutes the next frontier of simulation to prepare communities and their healthcare personnel (including providers, first responders, public health personnel, elected officials, and those who support them) for preparation and decision-making in the setting of both natural disasters and disaster operations in hospitals. 496581.title: End-to-End AI Weather Forecasting at Spire: Proprietary Satellite Data and Spire-Built AI Models for Energy and Utility Markets
496581.authors: Tom M. Gowan, Spire Global, Boulder, CO
496581.abstract: As renewable penetration grows, wind and solar volatility is reshaping how energy and utility markets manage risk. Reliable, differentiated weather forecasts are now a core trading and operational asset. Spire meets this need with a fully Spire-built AI forecasting suite, built on proprietary satellite observations and an end-to-end AI data assimilation (DA) system. The foundation is Spire's DA system, evolving into a fully end-to-end AI pipeline that ingests observations and produces analysis states directly, without a traditional physics-based intermediary and will run at up to hourly cadence, far more frequent than the traditional 6-hour update cycles at major modeling centers. It assimilates Spire's proprietary satellite data, including up to 20,000 daily radio occultation profiles, soil moisture, and ocean surface winds, alongside all publicly available observations from agencies such as NOAA and EUMETSAT. This creates differentiated initial conditions that no public model provides, and the value compounds downstream: better analyses produce measurably better forecasts at every horizon. Two AI models, both designed, trained, and operated entirely by Spire, run on these initial conditions. AI-WX is a 30-member global ensemble updating every 3 hours and forecasting out to 20 days, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy while adding skill between major public model cycles. AI-S2S is a 200-member sub-seasonal ensemble, trained on 40 years of reanalysis and fine-tuned with Spire's DA analyses, running once daily out to 46 days. By conditioning on slow-varying boundary states such as sea-surface temperature and soil moisture, it delivers skillful daily and weekly signals, probabilistic weather regime forecasts, and anomaly guidance well beyond the range of conventional models. Together, this stack gives energy traders, utilities, and grid operators a single differentiated source of probabilistic weather intelligence, from rapid-update medium-range guidance to sub-seasonal planning, enabling them to anticipate variability, manage portfolio risk, and act with confidence in increasingly volatile markets.

496582.title: The Representation of Tropical Rainfall and Convection in Year-Long MPAS Simulations
496582.authors: Erin M. Dougherty, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and K. T. Quagraine, K. M. Núñez Ocasio, Z. Moon, and L. Xue
496582.abstract: Tropical rainfall and convection is due to the interplay of multi-scale interactions from planetary, synoptic, mesoscale, and microscale features that make modeling particularly challenging in this region. Here, we run year-long simulations using the Model for Prediction Across Scales -Atmosphere (MPAS-A) during 2020 for a domain covering the Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean, Mesoamerica, and parts of the West Pacific Ocean in order to capture a variety of tropical weather systems. This MPAS-A configuration uses a regional 15-km to 3-km mesh, with much of the region at a 3-km grid spacing to enable convection to be directly resolved, and thus, improve the representation of tropical convection. These simulations were conducted as part of the MesoAmerica Affinity Group (MAAG), which is a community initiative that aims to further weather and climate research in the Mesoamerica and Caribbean region. We use these 2020 MPAS-A simulations to verify features such as the diurnal cycle, seasonal rainfall patterns, and tropical cyclones against observational datasets. Additionally, we compare them against coarser model simulations that are not convection-permitting to understand the added value of convection-permitting models in the tropics. Such analysis will provide insight into the representation of tropical weather in convection-permitting simulations in a particularly active hurricane season, but also during the other rainy seasons and dry seasons.

496584.title: American Commercial Space Weather Association (ACSWA) Expands Space Weather Hazard Mitigation across All Sectors
496584.authors: W. Kent Tobiska, Space Environment Technologies, Pacific Palisades, CA
496584.abstract: The American Commercial Space Weather Association (ACSWA) is comprised of more than 20 companies dedicated to the development and improvement of space weather understanding and hazard mitigation for technology. This presentation covers the main elements of work by companies in ACSWA and outlines some major initiatives to improve space weather understanding and hazard mitigation. Examples are shown from different ACSWA company activities. In addition, ACSWA’s path forward for building a national space weather enterprise (industry, academia, and agency) consensus related to national space weather activities is presented.

496587.title: SAM: The Next Generation
496587.authors: Austin G. Clark, Univ. of South Alabama, MOBILE, AL; and S. K. Kimball and C. C. Clark
496587.abstract: The South Alabama Mesonet (SAM) has recently undergone a series of hardware upgrades to modernize the network, providing a diverse set of observations to users across southern Alabama. These upgrades include a new configuration of sensors and observation heights, along with cameras and an updated installation process. Additionally, SAM is actively adding stations across the Black Belt region of Alabama to expand geographic coverage northward. These added capacities stem from a NOAA direct appropriation in FY25 that culminated into the next generation of SAM, uniquely suited to serve the constituents of southern Alabama. Inspiration for the new configuration was predicated on three primary factors: research quality, practicality, and the user base; while new site locations were driven by county, siting standards, and host availability. Specific details of the new setup and coverage map along with successes and challenges faced when designing to these requirements are all outlined in this presentation. SAM operates automated research-grade weather stations predominantly in southern Alabama, along with three in Mississippi and one in Florida. Each station is comprised of a 10-meter-tall tower outfitted with meteorological instrumentation at multiple levels. It is expected that at least 30 of these stations will be online by the time of the presentation. The data and metadata from the sites are publicly available from the SAM webpage with uses for climatology, operational forecasting, aviation, agriculture, emergency management, numerical weather prediction, and more.

496589.title: Examining the Impact of High Temporal Resolution Geostationary Satellite Imagery on Predictors Developed for the Statistical Hurricane Intensity Prediction Scheme (SHIPS)
496589.authors: Robert T. DeMaria, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and K. Musgrave and M. DeMaria
496589.abstract: Infrared (IR) imagery from geostationary satellites have served as a critical component of tropical cyclone statistical-dynamical intensity guidance for decades. Predictors developed from statistical metrics over the inner core of tropical cyclones have been used to represent storm-scale convection, adding a storm-based component to the primarily large-scale environmental predictors incorporated into the Statistical Hurricane Intensity Prediction Scheme (SHIPS). One limitation of the current formulation of the SHIPS IR predictors is that only one image is used in the predictors, set to the most recent available IR image for synoptic time (0 hours), minus 1.5 hours, and minus 3 hours. The IR predictors do not utilize the high temporal resolution of the GOES-R series. This work will focus on the exploration of the current state of the satellite predictors in SHIPS and improvements based on the temporal resolution available in the GOES-R era.

496591.title: Improving Subseasonal Climate Predictability through Extended Land Memory with Enhanced Plant Hydraulics
496591.authors: Aniket Gupta, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ; and A. Behrangi, A. Rahaman, and G. Y. Niu
496591.abstract: Global forecast models generally show a weaker-than-expected contribution of land processes to subseasonal climate prediction skill, particularly at lead times of 2–4 weeks. Despite the recognized importance of land memory, most forecast systems exhibit a rapid loss of memory of initial land conditions. This weak persistence may partly result from inadequate or simplified representations of soil hydraulics, vegetation dynamics, and root water uptake. These processes regulate plant transpiration, soil-water extraction and storage, and vegetation responses to warm and dry conditions, thereby influencing soil moisture memory and land–atmosphere feedback. To investigate these effects, we configured the Seasonal Forecast System (SFS) application within the Unified Forecast System (UFS) framework for targeted subseasonal forecasts extending up to five weeks. The SFS employs a coupled land–atmosphere system at 0.5° horizontal resolution and was initialized on January 1, 2013, representing a neutral ENSO year. We used identical atmospheric initial conditions across 11 ensemble members while perturbing only the initial land conditions through alternative representations of plant and soil-water processes in Noah-MP. Initial land conditions were generated using the offline Noah-MP forced with ERA5 meteorological data under four configurations: the default prescribed vegetation, dynamic vegetation, dynamic root water uptake, and combined dynamic vegetation and root water uptake. These configurations allow us to quantify how improved vegetation response and soil-water extraction influence land memory. Soil moisture memory is evaluated against International Soil Moisture Network (ISMN) and Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity (SMOS) observations over the contiguous United States. The resulting land states are subsequently used to assess whether improved plant–soil water interactions can strengthen land memory and enhance its contribution to subseasonal prediction within the coupled UFS-SFS framework.

496592.title: A Testbed high-Resolution Lidar and Polarization Signal for Cloud Observations
496592.authors: Owen Cruikshank, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and M. Saito
496592.abstract: Lidar observations can reveal detailed cloud structure. In particular, the lidar-derived depolarization ratio signals can discriminate cloud thermodynamic phase. Mixed-phase clouds contain both ice and liquid phase hydrometeors that can be homogeneously or heterogeneously distributed spatially. The spatial structure and heterogeneity are crucial to the lifetime and microphysical processes of mixed-phase clouds. However, the understanding of the physical scales of spatial heterogeneity is quite limited. Currently, the finest scale of the heterogeneous mixing in mixed-phase clouds is known to be at least an order of ≤100 m, but those at finer scales have not been extensively explored due to the limitation of the lidar range resolution, typically of 1-10 m. To be able to explore the spatial heterogeneity of mixed-phase clouds at finer scales, we develop a new lidar at the University of Wyoming using short-pulse microchip lasers and a time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC) system, aiming at a lidar range resolution of ~10 cm. This new lidar system will be tested and compared with other University of Wyoming King Air Facility lidars. The testing facility includes a lab, a Mobile Atmospheric Remote Sensing (MARS) trailer along with the Wyoming Cloud Radar, and possibly on the NSF Wyoming King Air aircraft. The viability of high-resolution lidar polarization measurements and capability for airborne measurements will be evaluated. With a low signal-to-noise ratio of high-resolution lidar, the cross-polarization signal may be difficult to detect. By purposely detuning the polarization detection channel, the signal-to-noise ratio of the cross-polarization signal will increase but with the tradeoff of lower sensitivity. The tradeoffs can be modeled and applied to photon-counting lidar and the existing Wyoming Cloud Lidars.

496594.title: The Effects of Deforestation on the Hydroclimate of South America
496594.authors: Francina Dominguez, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL
496594.abstract: South America's variety of climate zones sustains regions of remarkable biodiversity and vibrant communities. Changes in the hydroclimate of South America are driven in part by changes in land use. The well documented deforestation of the Amazon is only part of broad dramatic changes in natural ecosystems throughout the continent. One difficulty to understand how land use change can potentially affect future climate is that changes are occurring at the same time as greenhouse gas-driven climate change. To isolate the effects of land use on South American hydroclimate, we are developing the first high-resolution numerical simulation of the South American continent using future projected land cover and historical atmospheric forcing. This project builds on previous work by the South America Affinity Group (SAAG); a collective effort spearheaded in early 2019 by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) Water Systems Program. At the core of previous SAAG efforts are two 22-year Weather Research and Forecast (WRF) model simulations with an unprecedented high resolution of 4-kilometer grid spacing, representing historical and future climates over the continent. However, these simulations did not account for future changes in land use. Here, we present the development of future land use projections using a probabilistic land-cover simulation framework that combines land-cover transition dynamics with local suitability estimates, neighborhood interactions, and demand-constrained allocation within a unified statistical formulation. Two maps, one historical for the year 2015, and one of future projections in the year 2070 are used as lower boundary conditions for the 4km WRF model simulations. We will present the results of a one-year simulation over the entire continent with unprecedented spatial detail using the WRF model with harmonized projections of future land cover.

496595.title: West-WRF AI: A Data-Driven Model for High-Resolution Large Ensemble Prediction of Atmospheric Rivers and Associated Extremes
496595.authors: Luca Delle Monache, SIO, Boulder, CO
496595.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) drive a large portion of the water supply and flood risk across the western U.S. Skillful, reliable forecasts are therefore essential to decisions like Forecast-Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO), which uses advances in weather prediction to improve water supply management and reduce flood risk at reservoirs. Meeting this need requires both kilometer-scale resolution, to capture the orographic processes that determine where AR precipitation falls, and large ensembles, to characterize the predictive distribution and its extreme tail, a combination that remains computationally prohibitive for physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP). Here we present West-WRF AI, a stretched-grid data-driven weather modeling system developed at the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) and built on ECMWF's Anemoi Graph Transformer framework. The system comprises a 2-km configuration refined over the western U.S. and a 6-km configuration spanning the western U.S. and Eastern North Pacific, both transitioning to approximately 31 km globally. Each is pretrained on roughly 40 years of ERA5 to learn large-scale atmospheric dynamics, then fine-tuned in stretched-grid configuration using CW3E's West-WRF regional reanalyses, generating 6-hourly forecasts autoregressively. Deterministic evaluation over the 2020–2023 winters against PRISM, quality-controlled rain gauges, and AR Reconnaissance dropsondes shows realistic precipitation-intensity distributions, preserved fine-scale spatial variability, and improved or comparable detection skill relative to coarser AI models and physics-based baselines, with the clearest gains for terrain-sensitive and localized precipitation and for integrated vapor transport verified against dropsondes. Building on the 6-km configuration, we introduce a framework that bridges NWP and AI by combining NWP initial-condition perturbations with model uncertainty sampled from diverse stretched-grid AI checkpoints. Two further strategies, a quantile-based distribution adjustment and hierarchical modeling, improve ensemble reliability and sharpness. The resulting optimized ensemble outperforms state-of-the-art NWP systems and unoptimized AI ensembles in predicting extreme precipitation, delivering skillful probabilistic forecasts at a fraction of the traditional computational cost and offering a viable pathway to operational real-time prediction of extreme AR events.

496598.title: Bridging Data and Decision-Making: Co-Developing the Mississippi River Basin Drought and Water Dashboard
496598.authors: Meredith Muth, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and K. Eigsti, M. Woloszyn, E. Wickham, S. Ansari, R. Bilotta, J. Frimmel, J. Baker, M. Shaw, and D. Burt
496598.abstract: The Mississippi River Basin is a vital economic corridor for U.S. agriculture and shipping, yet recent years have underscored its vulnerability to historic low river levels and rapid fluctuations between extreme flooding and drought. During the 2023 low-water events, it became clear that federal water and drought information, essential for early warning and response, was fragmented across multiple platforms that were difficult for a user to access and understand. To address these coordination and usability challenges, NOAA’s National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS) launched the Mississippi River Basin Drought and Water Dashboard. Hosted on Drought.gov, this interactive platform unifies multi-agency data into customizable, real-time visuals and resources tailored for regional stakeholders, emergency managers, and industry leaders. Designed with a user-centered approach, NIDIS and the U.S. Drought Portal team at NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information co-developed this dashboard with the National Weather Service, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, U.S. Coast Guard, U.S. Geological Survey, the Mississippi River Cities and Towns Initiative, America’s Watershed Partnership, and various state, local, and industry partners. This presentation highlights the end-to-end co-development process, detailing how structured dialogues with public and private sector partners shaped the tool's architecture and functionality. Attendees will see a demonstration of the dashboard’s capabilities—covering historical, current, and predictive water conditions—and review metrics on how organizations are integrating this data into real-world planning. By sharing lessons learned from initial design through the 2025 dashboard rollout, this session offers a practical framework for future collaborations aimed at transforming complex environmental data into actionable decision-support tools.

496599.title: Strategies for Detecting and Resolving Terrain Hydroconditioning Deficiencies in Continental-Scale Stage-Based Categorical Flood Inundation Mapping
496599.authors: Emily Deardorff, NWS, Tuscaloosa, AL; Lynker, Leesburg, VA; and C. Pruitt, D. Giardino, G. Petrochenkov, R. Hanna, and M. Luck
496599.abstract: Flood inundation mapping provides crucial insight for communities preparing for extreme weather events or evaluating local flood risk factors. However, many communities across the United States have historically had insufficient access to this resource and have instead had to rely on a limited collection of qualitative flood impact descriptions. NWS’s Office of Water Prediction is working to address this need by producing static categorical flood inundation maps (CatFIM) alongside their hourly forecast flood inundation maps (forecast FIM) for the entire United States. CatFIM and forecast FIM both leverage the Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) terrain-based method as the base model for this continent-scale flood mapping. Forecast FIM is produced using near real-time streamflow predictions and CatFIM provides the static counterpart by inundating the same HAND-based flood model using historically-defined flood stage categories (such as Action, Minor, Moderate, Major, and Record) at over 2,000 river forecast sites across the country.
