CatFIM is a key product that can be used for flood response planning on “blue sky” days or in early stage flood event preparation when the river forecasts have not yet been produced. Producing HAND-based FIM with local stage height values requires careful attention to aligning vertical datum and rigorous hydroconditioning to enforce proper channel geometry and approximate bathymetric characteristics in the underlying terrain data. If these workflows fall short, they introduce localized terrain deficiencies that propagate into severe over- and under-inundation artifacts that can be difficult to catch in such a large-scale model. This presentation explores automated geospatial methods to systematically detect and diagnose where elevation disparities cause over- and under-inundation in stage-based CatFIM. Finally, we propose a prototype methodology for correcting these terrain-based inundation biases at a regional scale, enhancing the precision of continental static FIM services.

496601.title: Evaluating the Forecast Representation of Strong Cold Fronts in Eastern Colorado
496601.authors: Zachary R Michael, University of Colorado Boulder, Lake in the Hills, IL
496601.abstract: Cold fronts are synoptic-to-mesoscale features that frequently affect eastern Colorado, producing a range of high-impact weather. During the cool season, these systems contribute substantially to precipitation and can be accompanied by hazardous conditions such as extreme winds, rapid temperature fluctuations, and dangerous fire weather conditions. Numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, including the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model, have historically struggled to capture characteristics of cold frontal passages in this region, likely due to the influence of complex terrain. This study evaluates forecasts of strong cold frontal passages in eastern Colorado using the HRRR Version 4 between 2021–2024. Strong cold fronts are defined as events featuring a three-hour temperature decrease exceeding 15°F at Denver International Airport between September–May. HRRR analyses valid at the time of the cold frontal passage were used as verification, with evaluation focusing on forecast lead times less than 48 hours. Our sample included 66 cases, with two illustrative case studies selected to highlight how forecast errors vary under different synoptic-scale flow conditions. Results demonstrate that HRRR-simulated cold fronts tend to progress too slowly by several hours, feature overly strong zonal winds in the prefrontal environment, underpredict moisture, and feature across-front pressure gradients that are too weak. These systematic errors degrade forecast accuracy and have implications when communicating potential hazards to the general public. This work further highlights existing model deficiencies that can inform the development and evaluation of future high-resolution NWP models.

496603.title: System Simulation for Next Generation Hyperspectral Microwave Radiometer
496603.authors: Hu Yang, SSAI, Lanham, MD; GSFC, Lanham, MD; and E. J. Kim, M. Sammons, Q. Liu, A. Bringer, S. Abraham, C. H. Lyu, and W. D. Porter
496603.abstract: Recent advances in high-speed analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) technologies have enabled the development of hyperspectral microwave sounding instruments for next-generation operational weather satellites. When deployed in space with broad spatial and temporal coverage, such sensors are expected to significantly enhance numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecast skill. In this work, an integrated simulation system is developed for hyperspectral microwave radiometer. The objective is to provide a repeatable engineering framework that can be used for orchestration, monitoring, performance analysis, calibration development, and system-level algorithm integration during the instrument design and development. The simulation system is built as a wideband RF front end (RFE) followed by the Digital back-end (DBE). The DBE produces FFT spectral bins at a specified spectral resolution over a Nyquist bandwidth and accumulates output products. The key feature of the system includes: End-to-end traceability: the acquisition, calibration, spectral processing, NEdT estimation, correlation analysis, and validation flow can be viewed as one instrument model Hardware-in-the-loop capability: the same model structure can operate on stored data or live spectra from the DBE board. Calibration development: offset, gain, timing/skew, frequency-response, hot/cold target, and temperature-compensation algorithms can be represented as explicit subsystems and enabled or disabled for controlled experiments. Radiometer performance budgeting: measured NEdT, thermal noise, low-frequency/1/f noise, channel correlation, effective bandwidth, and RFI metrics can be evaluated at the same point in the processing chain. System-level simulation: a future simulated brightness-temperature source can replace the hardware source while retaining the same downstream analysis and retrieval blocks.

496606.title: The Wizard Outreach Approach: Using the Excitement of Science As a Gateway to Science Literacy (Invited Presentation)
496606.authors: Janine A. Aquino, NSF NCAR, Lafayette, CO; and T. Barnes, C. Drews, R. Golden, C. Hannay, T. J. Hertneky, C. P. Kalb, J. A. Lee, C. Owen, K. Thayer-Calder, and K. Wolfson
496606.abstract: Engaging the communities that we serve into our scientific discoveries builds trust with the public, highlights the societal relevance of scientific research, and increases scientific literacy. An interactive, demo-based approach is a powerful and effective tool that makes science accessible and inspires audiences to walk away with the desire to learn more on their own. At the U.S. National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR), our successful Science Wizard program attracts capacity multigenerational family audiences, earning strong positive audience feedback, and deepening personal engagement as attendees stay behind to ask questions about the science behind each demonstration. Building on the informal outreach approach started by NSF NCAR scientist Pat Kennedy in the 1970s and 1980s, and informed by the University of Colorado (CU) Physics department CU Science Wizards programs, public science demonstrations at NSF NCAR have evolved over the past 30 years into the Science Wizard outreach approach used today. We are a collaborative community of administrators, scientists, software engineers, educators, and safety specialists that brings in new members, introduces them to evidence-based communication strategies, and trains them to perform established demos while welcoming new ideas and keeping safety at the forefront of all we do. Driven by the idea that science is fun, creative, and collaborative, we highlight the many different ways scientists do science and normalize failure as a regular part of the process. We believe that getting children and families excited about science is just as valuable (if not more valuable at times) than teaching them a complex science concept. In this mini-workshop, we will walk the audience through the process of developing and performing a Wizard demo. We will highlight the unique Wizard approach of making science entertaining as well as educational, with personas, skits, and storylines. We will show recordings of our most popular and successful demos and conclude with time to ask questions.

496610.title: Quantifying Potential Impacts of Three-Dimensional Plume Spreading In Boundary Layer Clouds
496610.authors: Lucas Alan McMichael, University of Washington, Nashua, IA; and K. von Salzen, R. Wood, P. Blossey, E. Erfani, and S. Doherty
496610.abstract: The horizontal and vertical spreading rates of point-source aerosol plumes remain a major source of uncertainty in representations of Marine Cloud Brightening in climate models. In this work, we combine Large-Eddy Simulation (LES), a Langevin Particle Model (LPM), and parcel-scale microphysical modeling to develop parameterizations of subgrid-scale plume spreading across a range of background conditions representative of northeast Pacific stratocumulus environments. We use a small suite of large-domain, prognostic aerosol-enabled LES with point-source aerosol injections to calibrate the LPM, including its response to changes in turbulent velocity variances associated with aerosol-cloud interactions. The calibrated LPM is then applied to a library of realistically varying Lagrangian LES that resolve the background turbulence, meteorology, and aerosol conditions. This approach allows aerosol plumes to be introduced offline across a much broader range of environments and deployment strategies (i.e., injection timing, height, duration, amount, sprayer motion and organization) than would currently be computationally feasible using explicit plume-segment-resolving LES. Batches of LPM superparticles are sampled at fixed intervals during the active injection period. Each sampled particle trajectory is paired with the local time-varying plume concentration diagnosed from the full LPM particle population, thereby accounting for dilution as the plume spreads. Because particles within a batch share the same initial aerosol size distribution, differences in their subsequent microphysical evolution arise from differences in their dilution, thermodynamic, and dynamic histories. Parcel-scale activation calculations are then performed along these trajectories to quantify how three-dimensional plume spreading and dilution modify aerosol activation and, consequently, Twomey efficiency across different environments and deployment strategies.

496616.title: The Future of Extreme Heat in the Caribbean Examined with Climate Modeling and Statistical Downscaling
496616.authors: Jozi Beth Renken, University of North Carolina Asheville, Asheville, NC; and F. B. Oppong and J. E. Gonzalez-Cruz
496616.abstract: Extreme heat is an already worsening problem in the Caribbean due to temperatures increasing in recent years. As this trend continues so will the associated impacts. Extreme heat is one of the most deadly forms of extreme weather both in the US and globally. Due to this it is vital to understand the specific extent temperatures are likely to increase in the region in the coming years and the impact this will have on those living in the region. Many climate models have relatively coarse resolutions, especially when compared to the size of the smaller islands in the region. Thus the nearest projection to a given city is typically at best on another section of the island and at worst in the middle of the ocean. The resolution problem also means smaller scale factors such as the urban heat island effect will also be missed. This project is an attempt to mitigate this complication with the bias correction method of statistical downscaling with overall positive results. This involves using historical point observations to adjust the model output to more accurately correspond to the actual climate of a specific location. The projections for seven locations across the region are analyzed for averages in daily minimum and maximum temperature across the warm season of May to October and the entire year under three scenarios, SSP2 4.5, SSP3 7.0, and SSP5 8.5. More accurate and location specific projections could aid in informing the steps taken to mitigate or adapt to the effects of rising temperatures. Future work will be to expand this method across the entire region utilizing a gridded dataset as a proxy for historical observations to understand spatial patterns more in depth.

496617.title: Consistent Stratospheric Age of Air and CO2:CH4:N2O Relationships Spanning the ER-2, OMS and Aircore Era from the Early 1990s through the Present
496617.abstract: CO2 is a uniquely informative Age of Air tracer because of its long-term increase and consistent seasonal cycle. Measurements from the NASA ER-2 first showed that the CO2 seasonal cycle propagates into the stratosphere and demonstrated its potential for constraining estimates of stratospheric transport rates. The Observations of the Middle Stratosphere (OMS) balloon flights extended the dataset to altitudes of up to ~30 km. Since then, numerous studies have used CO2 and other long-lived tracers such as SF6 to estimate mean age and to assess trends in the stratospheric circulation. Starting in 2012, the NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory began a timeseries of CO2 and CH4 profiles using the balloon borne AirCoreTM sampling system, and more recently N2O measurements have been added. We use well-calibrated observations from these platforms to show that Age:CO2:CH4:N2O relationships are consistent across the period 1992 - 2025 when corrected for calibration-scale changes and tropospheric growth. We consider implications for diagnosing stratospheric transport and potential expansion of routine AirCore sampling to the tropics and southern hemisphere.

496619.title: OISST Version 3: Scientific Cross-Validation, Intercomparisons, New Developments in the Daily Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature Climate Data Record
496619.authors: Garrett Graham, Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies (CISESS), Asheville, NC; North Carolina State University (NCSU), Raleigh, NC; and S. Li, A. Kielbasa, B. Huang, X. Yin, J. Carton, T. M. Smith, L. Chen, and K. HIBBERT
496619.abstract: The NOAA/NESDIS/NCEI Daily Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature (OISST) Climate Data Record (CDR) is widely used in oceanographic and atmospheric research and applications. OISST is a long-term sea surface temperature (SST) dataset spanning from 1981 to present, with global coverage at 0.25° x 0.25° spatial resolution. OISST blends in situ observations from Argo floats, ships, and buoys with derived satellite observations to provide daily SST data to end-users. Given the importance of this CDR, several upgrades have been made, including updated input data sources, improved code architecture, and enhanced validation methods. This presentation seeks to highlight these improvements in light of the release of OISST Version 3 (OISST v3). The sea ice concentration (SIC) dataset used to generate accurate proxy SST near the poles has been updated to the National Snow and Ice Data Center’s Passive Microwave SIC CDR, version 6. Additionally, the SIC-to-SST conversion equation was recalibrated using the new SIC CDR and UpTempO buoy observations. An SIC-dilation technique was used to address missing coverage along polar coastlines and in marginal ice zones during seasonal transitions. Utilizing a blend of NOAA/NESDIS/STAR’s Advanced Clear Sky Processor for Ocean (ACSPO) L3S and L3C SST observations led to an increase in the volume of ingested satellite data, with improved observation quality earlier in the record. In addition to the increased satellite data volume, quality control checks were consolidated around ACSPO. The legacy codebase was redesigned following modern software development practices, enabling deployment of the pipeline on both on-premises and cloud infrastructures while preparing OISST for cloud migration and optimization. Finally, full scientific cross-validation of OISST v3 and intercomparisons of different v3 variants with OISST v2.1 and with other international SST products was performed, allowing for a comprehensive understanding as to OISST v3 relative strengths and weaknesses in estimating the state of the global oceans.

496620.title: The Heliophysics Coalition: Advocating for Heliophysics, together
496620.authors: James Paul Mason, APL, Laurel, MD
496620.abstract: Heliophysics research has been woefully underfunded. This is especially apparent when looking at support for the NASA Heliophysics Division, which has seen only marginal growth that has barely kept pace with inflation over the past decade. Meanwhile, the national focus on this research and its societal relevance via space weather has expanded driving additional demands on the community. Over the past few years, the community has leveraged informal coordination between advocacy-focused committees of the American Astronomical Society Solar Physics Division and the American Geophysics Union Space Physics and Aeronomy Section with major heliophysics research institutions to agree upon and amplify heliophysics asks to Congress. This coordination resulted in very strong Appropriation levels and language from FY20 onward. Major fly in events to bring the community to The Hill have been coordinated the past two years that have been highly effective. The Coalition’s goals are to a) grow awareness around the importance of heliophysics research with new and consistent messaging to engage stakeholders in creative new ways about excitement in the field and b) Advocate for growth in the federal budget to meet the needs of a bold future program. The Coalition brings together over twenty academic, non-profit, and commercial institutions across the country to advocate for the fundamental importance and societal relevance of heliophysics research, not only for maintaining our nation’s scientific pre-eminence and leadership in space exploration, but also to ensure our national security.

496622.title: Using Sunairio ONE Large Ensemble Forecasts for Scenario Planning in the Power Sector
496622.authors: Brent Ho, Sunairio, Winter Park, FL; and P. Hawbecker, O. Pfeiffer, R. Hasegawa, and R. Cirincione
496622.abstract: Effective risk management in energy applications requires forecasts that describe not just a single most-likely outcome, but the full range of plausible futures. Traditional weather ensembles used in energy applications, however, are typically limited to 30–50 members. These small ensembles are also typically underdispersed, with spreads that underestimate true forecast error and conceal tail risk. In this talk, we address this gap by introducing Sunairio ONE, a calibrated, 1,000-member ensemble spanning the energy value chain. Starting with ensemble weather, we reshape ensemble spread (as a function of forecast lead time and ensuring that the resulting spread is calibrated) around a deterministic control forecast, using copula methods to ensure that the variables and locations in each path are properly jointly correlated. Each weather path is then passed through a suite of energy models to generate correlated load, wind generation, solar generation, and generation outage ensembles. Through maintenance of spatial- and temporal- weather correlation structure, these energy paths capture how local weather uncertainty compounds or diversifies into system-level generation risk, a relationship obscured by single-site or deterministic evaluation. Drawing on recent extreme events in ERCOT and PJM, we illustrate how properly calibrated and correlated energy paths can help energy grid planning and resource adequacy exercises. Finally, we address the practical challenge of using a 1,000-member ensemble for scenario planning: it is statistically rich but can be too large to reason about directly. We describe an ensemble clustering approach that reduces the full set of paths to a small number of representative “most-likely scenarios” that preserves probability-weighted information about the shape and tails of the original distribution. This allows forecast users to plan around a manageable set of scenarios (including higher-risk tail cases) without discarding the value of the full ensemble.

496625.title: Analysis of a Method for Time-Varying Bulk Sea Surface Temperature Derivation from In-Situ Measurements and Remote Sensing for Numerical Weather Prediction over an Inland Water Body
496625.authors: David D. Flagg, NRL, Monterey, CA; and J. Yung, J. A. Hlywiak, A. J. Kammerer, S. E. Wessinger, C. R. Sease, Q. Wang, R. Yamaguchi, J. Ruiz-Plancarte, R. Hoheisel, and J. Kalogiros
496625.abstract: A key part of the Radar and Electromagnetic Wave Ducting in the Stable Atmosphere over Water (REDSAW) (Wang et al. 2026) investigation of the refractivity environment over the Salton Sea (California, U.S.A.) involves understanding the time-evolution of the meteorology of the lower atmospheric column at mesoscales and finer. While the Salton Sea basin provides a unique environment for investigating the stable boundary layer for applications to refractivity, it is a highly challenging environment to simulate using numerical weather prediction (NWP) models due to its geography. Heterogeneous horizontal terrain gradients, perturbations in the daily vacillation of katabatic and anabatic flow, and periodic intrusions of onshore flows from the Pacific Ocean and Gulf of California frame the background meteorology, requiring fine grid increments to adequately resolve. This combination of influences is further complicated by intermittent mesoscale and synoptic scale features that affect regional wind direction, and thus the terrain-channeled flow within the Salton Sea basin. Among the most critical challenges is the representation of the sea surface temperature (SST), upon which turbulent scalar fluxes and lower column atmospheric fields are particularly sensitive. Limited available observations suggest that the shallow depths of the Salton Sea frequently yield a diurnal variation in sea surface temperature that is large, often exceeding typical values for the open ocean. This condition motivates extra attention to the sea-surface representation where numerical modeling of the air-surface interaction and surface layer profiles are critical. Often global ocean temperature datasets do not include inland water bodies, and the shallow depths of the Salton Sea complicate and impede the implementation of two-way coupled ocean models to capture this important time-variation of SST. In this study investigators simulated the environment of the Salton Sea basin using a research configuration of the Navy’s Coupled Ocean/Atmosphere Mesoscale Prediction System (COAMPS®1) for the campaign period (29 April to 23 May 2024). Experiments were implemented using a remote-sensing- based product (JPL GHRSST L4) as the SST and an observation-driven modification to the remote sensing product devised to better capture the diurnal variation in the upper ocean column. Model performance for these two experiments is quantified against measured water temperature at a buoy and vertical profiles from dropsondes and rawinsonde launches in the Salton Sea basin during the 2024 experiment. Results demonstrate the impact of capturing diurnal variation of SST in NWP of the lower atmosphere and the viability of a method that may be applicable to other NWP investigations of inland water bodies. 1COAMPS® is a registered trademark of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory

496626.title: From the Seeds of the National Lightning Safety Council:Taking Lightning Safety Awareness Global with the Development of ACLENet, LARC, SALNet, APPAR, LALENet.......
496626.authors: Mary Ann Cooper, ACLENet, River Forest, IL; and R. L. Holle, D. Zhang, S. R. Sharma, H. E. Sueta, S. Schmitt, D. E. Villamil, A. G. Laing, and H. Anderson
496626.abstract: As annual lightning deaths steadily decreased due to NOAA’s Lightning Safety Team, the National Lightning Safety Council, and the media, team members already working internationally decided to see how lessons learned could be applied globally. This paper presents some results from these seeds! In 2011, an opportunity arose during a lightning protection conference in Nepal where the Ugandan representative reported 18 children killed and 38 others injured by a single lightning strike to their school on June 28, one of the deadliest lightning disasters in modern history. . The tragedy motivated Richard Tushemereirwe, to advance lightning safety in Uganda. In 2014, with support from colleagues he established the African Centres for Lightning and Electromagnetics Network (ACLENet) and recruited Mary Ann Cooper, MD, as managing director. That same year, Chandima Gomes and Cooper challenged ICLP2014 participants to help protect a Ugandan school. DEHN-Africa subsequently protected the first three schools in 2016-17. ACLENet has since protected six additional schools scattered across Uganda as model schools and training centers using designs from ACLENet’s all-volunteer Lightning Protection Working Group of recognized lightning protection experts. After a decade of work in Uganda, ACLENet rebranded as the African Centres for Lightning Education (ACLENet) and launched a successful and burgeoning lightning safety education program across Uganda that includes: programs at schools for teachers, parents, and students developed and led by ACLENet staff student lightning safety clubs led by science teachers, facilitated by ACLENet’s educators and online library school safety committees composed of teachers, parents, and students responsible for protecting the LPS who periodically inspect and report to ACLENet’s Chief Installer work with districts to produce prime-time radio talk-shows for audiences of millions of listeners pilot journalist training program to train journalists in the science of lightning, interviewing survivors, investigative reporting, and community activism. International education is partially based on The FLASH, a monthly newsletter published in five languages including Arabic, as well as scientific publications and reports at international meetings. Research is also a priority. ACLENet has developed Africa’s largest publicly available lightning injury databases with data on 46 countries using news reports, citizen reporters, and multilingual internet searches. It also investigates lightning mass-casualty events in Uganda as resources permit. In 2015, ACLENet co-founder Chandima Gomes proposed International Lightning Safety Day (ILSD) in response to the 2011 Runyanya School tragedy. The first broad international commemoration was organized in 2020 by the South Asian Lightning Network (SALNet). During the COVID-19 pandemic, ILSD-2020 was co-chaired by ACLENet and SALNet, as two-day virtual event spanning 11 time zones, with attendees from 18 countries and speakers from 10 countries including representatives of meteorological organizations and National Disaster Management Authorities. Since 2020, ILSD has been commemorated annually through diverse formats initiated by participating organizations, including school-based programs in Uganda led by ACLENet; an innovative school video competition organized by Caribbean Meteorological Association led by Arlene Laing, and, most recently in 2026, the launch of the WMO’s Lightning book for children, the newest addition to the COPE Disaster Champions Series, available in 26 languages covering disasters from avalanches to wildfires. In Asia, in parallel with NLSC, the original LP conference in Nepal grew into the Lightning and Atmospheric Research Center (LARC) in Nepal 2015 and the South Asian Lightning Network (SALNet) in 2019 that included seven countries in Asia including Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. In addition to its annual leadership for ILSD internationally, SALNet, led by Dr Shri Ram Sharma, has also been instrumental in working with the Nepalese government to recognize lightning injuries as a disaster, protect over 20 schools, install Early Warning Systems in rural Nepal, and present public and professional education. In Brazil, APPAR (Association of Lightning Protection and Warning Professionals) an emerging organization inspired by the NLSC, ACLENet and SALNet, has organized the ILSD in Brazil since 2021. Led by Dr. Hélio Eiji Sueta, the first event, 6 lectures over 4 hours, has expanded to 3 days of technical lectures with Brazilian and foreign researchers but is always focused on the safety of people and structures against lightning. APPAR’s other activities include lectures in elementary and secondary schools as well as published articles in scientific journals, technical area of electricity, and also aimed at children. The Latin American Lightning Education Network (LALENet), incorporated in 2022, is led by Colombian Daniel Villamil, who is currently pursuing his PhD in Spain. LALENet, has spread fundamental knowledge and application of the IEC 62305 and NFPA 780 lightning protection standards, especially in contexts with high risk for people, among technicians and other interested parties through in-person and virtual courses. The Caribbean Meteorological Organization (CMO), led by Dr. Arlene Laing, organized the 2021 Symposium on Lightning and Lightning Safety Awareness attended by more than 130 persons from 28 countries, featuring English and Spanish interpretation, presenters from the NLSC, National Meteorological Services, researchers, lightning detection companies, and injury, safety, and protection experts. Annual participation in ILSD led to the first Caribbean Lightning Safety Awareness Contest for Schools in 2025 with multiple international partners. Targeted to two age groups 6-11 and 12-18 years, with prizes for the top three winners in each category, this contest was highlighted in the COPE Lightning disaster education series. In Europe, Meteorage is the European link within the growing international lightning safety community with contributions to ACLENet activities in French-speaking Africa, participation in SALNet and APPAR ILSD events, and collaboration on the WMO-COPE Lightning children’s book. Within France, activities to reduce lightning risk include: contributions to standards and best-practice guidance, assessment of lightning safety solutions in real-world applications, development of economically sustainable approaches ensuring that the cost of prevention does not become a barrier to safety, training and awareness programs targeting a wide range of audiences including infrastructure managers, industrial operators, mountain professionals and the general public. Recent collaborations between meteorologists, lightning specialists, physicians and lightning survivors include workshops and medical teleconsultations to improve both survivor support and understanding of the long-term consequences of lightning injuries.

496627.title: NASA CSDA STARS: A Cloud-Native Platform for Multi-Vendor Commercial Satellite Tasking and Archive Data Acquisition
496627.authors: Vishal Perekadan, Univ. of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH), Huntsville, AL; and K. Horn, J. Bell, S. Mohiuddin, C. E. Holden, E. L. Paz, A. Rominske, N. E. Hay, M. Clark, R. Dangol, A. Gautam, B. Pathak, S. Niraula, C. McEvoy, G. M. Stewart, I. Purohit, P. J. Gadomski, A. C. Blackford, A. J. Ziel, D. Ostrenga, and M. Y. Martin
496627.abstract: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) Program identifies, evaluates, and acquires commercial Earth observation data to support research, operational forecasting, and environmental applications. To enable seamless, scalable access to rapidly expanding commercial satellite constellations, CSDA provides a cloud-native data architecture designed to simplify vendor onboarding, data archiving, and data distribution to users. Building upon the foundation of CSDA’s Satellite Data Explorer (SDX), the Satellite Tasking and Archive Request System (STARS) serves as a unified interface for approved researchers to draft, refine, and submit multi-vendor data requests. CSDA STARS supports both historical archive retrieval and targeted satellite tasking across active vendor allocations, giving scientists end-to-end visibility and tracking throughout the request lifecycle. Architecturally, STARS is driven by modular cloud services within NASA’s Mission Cloud Platform. It incorporates open geospatial standards including the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC), the Sensor Tasking API (STAPI), and Apache Airflow alongside direct vendor API integrations to ensure automated, scalable request management. This presentation provides an operational walkthrough of CSDA STARS from a user's perspective, highlighting how scientists can leverage the platform to task commercial constellations, access archive datasets, and integrate vendor observations into environmental science workflows.

496628.title: Viewing the Polar Regions in Near-Real Time with SLIDER
496628.authors: Curtis Seaman, Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere, Fort Collins, CO; and K. Micke, Z. P. Amundson, A. Tomar, G. Chirokova, S. Gampa, D. Canfield, and W. Line
496628.abstract: The Satellite Loop Interactive Data Explorer in Realtime (SLIDER) website (https://slider.cira.colostate.edu) was originally developed in 2017 at the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere (CIRA) for the display of full resolution geostationary satellite imagery in realtime. The following year, the SLIDER website was expanded to include global imagery from polar-orbiting satellites, beginning with the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) constellation (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and, now, NOAA-21). This capability, referred to as “Polar SLIDER”, offers users the ability to monitor the polar environment in near-realtime. Polar SLIDER has long provided hemispheric composite imagery (both Northern and Southern Hemispheres) from the JPSS satellites. To the authors’ knowledge, Polar SLIDER is currently the only publicly available website offering global VIIRS data in near-realtime. At present, Polar SLIDER offers a wide variety of satellite imagery products - including all 22 VIIRS bands (with a maximum spatial resolution of 375 m) - and a wide variety of multispectral imagery products (including RGB composites) offered by VIIRS. Polar SLIDER has also been a platform for providing a unique form of imagery from the CrIS instrument - using the hyperspectral information from CrIS, combined with the spectral response functions from the GOES-R ABI instrument, we replicate water vapor bands and other important spectral bands that are not available on the VIIRS instrument and this information is used to generate ABI-like imagery products at CrIS resolution over the Polar Regions that are useful for monitoring high-latitude synoptic-scale atmospheric features. NOAA’s Blended Total Precipitable Water (TPW), Advected Layer Precipitable Water (ALPW) and Layer Vapor Transport (LVT) products are offered as well. Plus, we are currently working to add a variety of microwave imagery products from ATMS that will further aid in the ability to characterize the Polar environment. With the launch of Metop-SG-A1 in 2025, the new visible and infrared imager, METimage, is now providing complimentary imagery to VIIRS, plus unique spectral information not available on VIIRS (or ABI). In this work, we will present an overview of the SLIDER website and demonstrate the value of near-realtime imagery and data products from VIIRS, ATMS, CrIS, and METimage for monitoring the Polar Regions.

496633.title: The Potential of Peruvian Ice Cores to Serve as Proxies for ITCZ Migration
496633.authors: Stacy E. Porter, Denison University, Granville, OH; and R. Vanover
496633.abstract: The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a region of intense precipitation located around the equator. The ITCZ migrates seasonally, and the range of these latitudinal shifts are driven by a number of factors including internal variability (e.g., El Niño/Southern Oscillation), volcanic events, and solar luminosity. The positioning of the ITCZ has implications on the global hydroclimate, including the monsoon systems, and many have explored the history and drivers of ITCZ migration with paleoproxy records and models. To provide a history of ITCZ movement near South America, we employ two ice cores from the Peruvian Andes, Nevado Huascarán in northern Peru, and Quelccaya in southern Peru. Ice cores from this region have been used individually to explore tropical climate dynamics. Using these two records, we interrogate the relationships among the ITCZ, El Niño/Southern Oscillation, and the dipole of precipitation that occurs between the northern and southern Peruvian Andes.

496635.title: Soil Moisture Preconditioning of La Niña-Induced Drought in the U.S. Southwest: Mechanisms, Predictability, and Climate Nonstationarity
496635.authors: Yelin Jiang, Columbia University, Palisades, NY; and J. Smerdon, R. Seager, B. Cook, and M. Ting
496635.abstract: La Niña tends to suppress cool-season precipitation across the mid-latitudes of North America, but the severity of subsequent soil drought can also depend on antecedent soil moisture. This raises a central predictability question about the extent to which preceding soil moisture determines the propagation of ocean-driven meteorological drought into soil drought at seasonal-to-interannual lead times. We address this question using observations, reanalysis, and CESM2 experiments that combine targeted attribution simulations with large-ensemble analysis (LENS2). We find that, during the 2020–2022 western U.S. drought, large-scale atmospheric and oceanic variability shaped the meteorological drought, while preceding soil moisture modulated its translation into soil drought. Under an ensemble of counterfactual antecedent conditions, wet soils are capable of delaying soil drought onset by two to three seasons, whereas dry soils induce faster intensification and greater drought persistence. Across historical La Niña events in LENS2, soil moisture memory emerges most clearly in the semiarid Southwest, where modest year-round precipitation allows surplus soil moisture from preceding wet summers to persist and be depleted slowly by evapotranspiration. The result is buffering of La Niña-induced soil moisture deficits through the following spring, summer, and fall by 42%, 47%, and 82%, respectively. In contrast, buffering is short-lived in the Mediterranean western coastal U.S. and humid Southeast, where more cold-season precipitation and soil moisture recharge rapidly erase antecedent soil moisture anomalies. We also determine that, under anthropogenic warming, higher evaporative demand accelerates the depletion of surplus soil moisture, weakening the historical buffering from preceding wet conditions and shifting future La Niña droughts toward more severe absolute soil moisture deficits in the Southwest. These results highlight preceding soil moisture as a physical and climate-sensitive source of seasonal-to-interannual drought predictability, particularly in semiarid regions like the U.S. Southwest.

496636.title: Rapid Analytics for Disaster Response-Fire (RADR-Fire): A Cloud-Based System for Multi-Sensor Wildfire Monitoring
496636.authors: Troy Saltiel, PNNL, Salt Lake City, UT; and K. Larson, T. Franklin, J. Fernandez, J. Fanning, V. Sinnott, K. Nelson, I. Gonzalez-Hirshfeld, L. Miller, B. Hessler, A. Boone, A. M. Coleman, and J. Tagestad
496636.abstract: As severe wildfire seasons stretch firefighting resources thin, critical gaps frequently emerge in active fire mapping. Traditional airborne reconnaissance and manual perimeter mapping are often constrained by severe weather, limited aircraft availability, duty days, and fire prioritization causing infrequent revisit intervals and leaving incident commanders with incomplete situational awareness. To address these operational gaps, we present Rapid Analytics for Disaster Response-Fire (RADR-Fire), an automated, cloud-based system designed to ingest, process, and deliver imagery from various imaging platforms and wildfire mapping products to incident management teams and others. At the core of RADR-Fire are deep learning classifiers built upon the Prithvi-EO-2.0 geospatial foundation model. By leveraging this pre-trained foundation, the system achieves a notable performance boost over traditional machine learning approaches, such as multilayer perceptron models trained from scratch, as well as standard spectral ratio methods like the Differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR). RADR-Fire automatically generates a suite of situational awareness products, including burned areas, intense heat, scattered heat, isolated heat, fire retardant drops, and smoke/cloud detection, while incorporating satellite image acquisition forecasting to aid in allocating aircraft imaging resources. Alongside these products, the system can ingest WeatherNext deep-learning based meteorological forecasts, active fire suppression data from an incident, and is capable of rapid fuels mapping, enabling other capabilities like near-term wildfire spread forecasts, contributing to fire management decision-making. The platform is flexible, allowing the integration of new algorithms, future imaging systems like FireSat, or even multimodal information like drone or ground-based imagery. Currently, RADR-Fire products are automatically processed and provided to the National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) Enterprise Geospatial Portal for every dispatched wildfire in the conterminous U.S., Alaska, Hawaii, and territories. These products fill observational gaps and increase data refresh during active wildfire events, improving data coverage when traditional assets are unavailable. Furthermore, the addition of satellite-based products serves as critical inputs for wildfire spread models, allowing for more frequent model reinitialization and improved downstream forecasting. We demonstrate the capabilities of RADR-Fire, a cloud-based system that can deliver timely, scalable, and actionable intelligence to support wildland firefighting operations when it’s needed most and show how these products can enhance the accuracy of wildfire spread forecasts.

496637.title: Phased-Array Radar Analysis of Downbursts and Mesovortices in MCSs using Proxies of Vertical Motion
496637.authors: Willow Michael Phipps, Norman, OK; and A. A. Alford, K. Tuftedal, and T. J. Schuur
496637.abstract: Mesoscale Convective Systems (MCSs) are organized families of updrafts and downdrafts that have the capacity to produce all convective hazards (i.e., hail, damaging winds, tornadoes). Microphysical processes modulate kinematic fields within MCSs, which can result in changes within the system’s structure and its ability to generate near-surface vorticity and straight-line winds. Polarimetric signatures such as specific differential phase (KDP) cores indicate areas of high liquid water content associated with melting hail and graupel. Precipitation loading and latent cooling adds to the negative buoyancy of downdraft parcels and acts to intensify these downdrafts. On the contrary, signatures such as columns of KDP or differential reflectivity (ZDR) indicate the lofting of supercooled liquid water above the melting layer and can be used to identify updrafts in radar data. This study utilizes the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) Advanced Technology Demonstrator (ATD) S-band phased-array radar (PAR) to explore various scales of MCS dynamics. Additionally, the Spline Analysis at Mesoscale Utilizing Radar and Aircraft Instrumentation (SAMURAI) is employed as a variational technique to retrieve spatial fields of single-Doppler vertical velocity proxies. Gridded one- to two-minute volumes are paired with Constant Frequency by Altitude Diagrams (CFADs), four-quadrant time series, and vertical cross-sections to explore convective-stratiform partitioning, updraft-downdraft parities, and mesovortex formation. Different structural characteristics ranging from progressive to serial paradigms are compared to analyze their microphysical manifestations, including rear inflow jet (RIJ) evolution and mesoscale convective vortex (MCV) formation. These analysis techniques show that periods of severe winds and mesovortex formation are often preceded by large-scale shifts in the convective-stratiform CFAD distributions as well as enhancements of KDP below the melting level. Additionally, comparisons between KDP integrations above and below the melting level reveal responses between updraft and downdraft signatures during a rear inflow surge. Overall, the high spatiotemporal resolution of the PAR allows for a more detailed investigation into these rapidly evolving signatures.

496640.title: What are the Most Important Precursors of Urban Secondary Organic Aerosol (SOA)? Are Terpenes Dominant?
496640.authors: Jose-Luis Jimenez, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and M. Morris, D. A. Day, A. Jensen, G. Symonds, P. Campuzano-Jost, J. de Gouw, D. Blauth, R. Mesburis, B. C. Schulze, K. Barsanti, and A. Tasnia
496640.abstract: Secondary organic aerosol (SOA), formed from the oxidation of gas-phase organic compounds, is the largest component of fine particles (PM2.5). SOA damages human health, contributes to visibility degradation, and impacts climate forcing. The first mathematical models of SOA were developed in the 1990s, with the main precursors being anthropogenic aromatic and natural biogenic hydrocarbons. In the mid-2000s it was realized that urban SOA was almost an order-of-magnitude larger than in air quality models at the time. No similarly large discrepancy was observed in biogenic SOA dominated areas such as forests. Much research has been performed since then, and three major new groups of urban precursors have been identified: semivolatile and intermediate volatility species (S/I/VOCs), volatile chemical products (VCPs), and biogenic VOCs emitted within the urban area. Multiple studies have concluded that each of these sources is separately dominant. Thus the relative importance of each source remains controversial. Los Angeles (LA), CA air quality has improved, although it has mostly plateaued since 2010. We measured SOA formation potential (SOA-FP), i.e. the species present in the gas-phase, but in units of how much SOA they can form, in LA during Summer 2022 during CalNexT. We separately quantified SOA-FP from VOCs vs. S/IVOCs, to our knowledge the first measurements with this separation. We used two oxidation flow reactors (OFRs) ingesting ambient air: one with a polymer inlet that denuded lower volatility species, and the other without an inlet. Measured ambient SOA was similar and total SOA-FP was lower in 2022 vs. 2010, consistent with higher OH causing greater consumption of SOA precursors in 2022. ~31% of the total SOA-FP is due S/IVOCs. Results are compared to two box models (CRACMM and Caltech). Both models performed well for SOA but poorly for SOA-FP, and both estimated a much higher fraction from S/IVOCs vs. the observations. This suggests important gaps in urban SOA models. Our results do not support monoterpenes being a dominant contributor to SOA-FP in LA, contrary to two major recent studies that concluded dominance of biogenic terpenoids, and of anthropogenic monoterpenes from VCPs, respectively.

496644.title: Reanalyzing Georgia's Last Major Hurricane: WRF Ensemble Downscaling and SLOSH Surge Simulation of the 1898 Storm
496644.authors: Margaret Olivia Needham, University of Georgia, Athens, GA; and K. T. Brooks and J. A. Knox
496644.abstract: The last major landfalling tropical cyclone to strike Georgia (the 1898 Georgia Hurricane) is recorded in historical databases as a Category 4 at landfall near Brunswick, Georgia, on October 2, 1898 (IBTrACS HURDAT2), yet preliminary mesoscale simulations (Brooks 2025) and sparse literature (Sandrik 1998, Sandrik and Landsea 2003) reveal significant uncertainty regarding its true surface wind speeds, minimum central pressure, and inland wind field. This study executes a dynamical downscaling and historical reanalysis of the storm, evaluates the behavior of a similar bogused tropical cyclone, and quantifies storm surge inundation along the rapidly developing Georgia coastline. Addressing this storm through modern numerical modeling can help further understand contemporary coastal vulnerability across barrier island communities, including Tybee, Skidaway, and St. Simons islands, where rapid population growth and hurricane amnesia exacerbate disaster risks (U.S Census Bureau 1900, 2020). To capture synoptic steering alongside convective scale coastal wind gradients, we utilize WRF-ARW simulations across an 11 km parent domain and a 2.2 km child domain that dynamically tracks the cyclone vortex. We apply the Stochastic Kinetic Energy Backscatter Scheme to generate a 16-member historical ensemble initialized with 20th Century Reanalysis version 3 (20CRv3) data. Because the original TC vortex was quite weak in the coarse 20CRv3 dataset, it was replaced by a bogus vortex initialized from HURDAT2 storm records. To investigate how similar major hurricanes would behave under present and future warming, we apply a refined pseudo global warming methodology utilizing Community Earth System Model Large Ensemble thermodynamic deltas, diagnosing whether storm properties, effects, and intensification are impacted by present day and future climate states. Lastly, a custom Python workflow couples high frequency parametric wind and pressure fields directly into the NOAA SLOSH model to assess coastal flooding and estuarine surge propagation. Results reveal that even at the weakest intensities (Cat. 1-2) the storm produces catastrophic inundation over a large swath of Coastal Georgia.

496648.title: A Historical Perspective on the Quest to Retrieve Aerosol Microphysical Parameters with Lidar (Invited Presentation)
496648.authors: Chris Hostetler, NASA, Hampton, VA; and R. A. Ferrare, J. W. Hair, C. R. Trepte, S. Burton, A. J. Scarino, T. Shingler, J. Redemann, L. Gao, and E. D. Lenhardt
496648.abstract: In this presentation we offer a historical perspective on the quest to retrieve aerosol microphysical parameters needed to quantify aerosol-cloud interaction processes. Aerosol-cloud interaction was identified as far back as the 1995 IPCC report as the largest uncertainty in radiative forcing of climate and remains a top priority in climate science to this day. Our story begins with the genesis of the 17-year CALIPSO mission and its successes and limitations. We then follow the progress of the 25-year development of airborne High Spectral Resolution Lidars with progressively greater capabilities aimed at quantifying aerosol scattering, absorption, size, composition, concentration, and cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) via physics-based lidar and lidar+polarimeter retrievals. The story continues to the present day when researchers have demonstrated machine learning retrievals that provide microphysical parameters well beyond the reach of the physics-based retrievals. We end with the huge success of the EarthCARE mission and how machine learning retrievals based on airborne HSRL and in situ measurements are being applied to the ATLID data set to provide capabilities beyond our imagination only a few years ago.

496650.title: A High Resolution Study of Microclimatic Differences Influenced by El Niño/La Niña among Various Plant Zones on San Cristóbal Island, Galápagos Islands, Ecuador
496650.authors: Katherine Elizabeth Krontiras, University of South Alabama, Mobile, AL; Univeristy of South Alabama, Mobile, AL; and A. David, A. Kratsch, J. Martin, N. Narváez, L. Tasipanta, F. Laso, and S. Schultze
496650.abstract: The effect of El Niño and La Niña cycles on surface water temperatures in the equatorial eastern Pacific is well understood. Their effects on marine life in the Galápagos Islands have also been well studied. El Niños typically bring warmer waters and warmer/wetter conditions, while La Niñas bring the opposite. However, the effects of El Niño and La Niña on temperatures and temperature differences across the islands are less understood, especially on a very small spatiotemporal scale. This student-driven study utilizes data collected from 10 in-situ microsensors across different elevations on San Cristóbal Island since March 2023, recording temperature and humidity every minute. As part of a larger study, previous research found that temperatures differed greatly across the island at the same moment, especially when compared to estimated temperatures using lapse-rate calculations. Differences between the rainy and dry seasons have already been studied, but an El Niño–La Niña comparison was not possible until recently. The months of October 2023 (strong El Niño) and October 2025 (borderline La Niña conditions) are compared for differences in status and trends across the various plant zones on the wettest island of the archipelago. An oceanic temperatures difference in Niño 3.4 region of approximately 2.2°C was recorded between the study months. While the focus of the scientific community has largely been on marine life in the islands, this case study shows that attention must also be paid to the islands themselves, where population growth and the tourism industry have already placed stress on water reserves.

496652.title: Development of SEILER-Net 2.0: Integrating Aerosols, Resolution Independence, and Equation Discovery into Global Lightning Estimation
496652.authors: Madilynn Robin Seiler, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and D. J. Allen, K. E. Pickering, M. J. Molina, and M. E. Manyin
496652.abstract: Lightning is the most substantial natural source of nitrogen oxides (NOx) in the upper troposphere. Its crucial role in atmospheric composition through impacts on ozone (O3) and the hydroxyl radical (OH) makes lightning an essential part of global chemistry and climate modeling. In this study, knowledge distillation and symbolic regression are used to discover the underlying mathematical equation that describes the U-Net-based lightning flash rate parameterization scheme, SEILER-Net 1.0. SEILER-Net 2.0, expands upon the original parameterization scheme, SEILER-Net 1.0, by prioritizing global application across various model resolutions. Aerosols are added to the input variable list to SEILER-Net 2.0, expanding upon the existing set of NASA GEOS meteorological inputs. Random sampling is performed during training utilizing domain samples from the eastern United States, Amazon Basin, west and central Africa, and the Atlantic Ocean. The training and testing period spans 19 months from 2023 to 2024, and the model is evaluated against gridded data from the Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) and Meteosat Third Generation - Lightning Imager (MTG-LI), which were used as labels for SEILER-Net 1.0. Simultaneously, a new model, using the same input features and labels, will use Equation Discovery (symbolic regression) to explore physically interpretable mathematical formulas directly from data without assuming a predefined equation structure. The hourly flash rate estimates generated by both models are on a 0.25ºx0.25º grid in alignment with the GEOS, GLM, and MTG-LI grid, but will be scale-aware. We present results from the two approaches, compare their strengths and weaknesses, and work towards implementing the better-performing model as SEILER-Net 2.0 in the NASA GEOS model for global use.

496655.title: A Hydrologic Digital Twin: Integrating Earth Observations, Data Assimilation, and Machine Learning for Adaptive Hydrologic Prediction and Water Management
496655.authors: Parnian Ghaneei, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and H. Moradkhani
496655.abstract: Reliable water management requires prediction systems that can evolve as environmental conditions change, incorporate new observations as they become available, and communicate uncertainty in ways that support decisions. Digital twins offer a framework for achieving this integration by connecting observations, numerical models, data-driven prediction, and management strategies within a continuously evolving representation of the physical system. Here, we develop an uncertainty-aware hydrologic digital twin that integrates land-surface modeling, satellite observations, data assimilation, machine learning, and water-management information within a unified prediction and decision-support framework. California provides a particularly relevant testbed for our study because its hydrologic conditions are highly variable and closely interconnected with agricultural water use and management. The Noah-MP land-surface model serves as the digital representation of the terrestrial hydrologic system. Satellite-derived observations of soil moisture and leaf area index are sequentially assimilated into Noah-MP to constrain simulated land-surface states, maintain consistency between the modeled and observed system, and characterize uncertainty in the evolving hydrologic conditions. The updated states and fluxes provide dynamically evolving information to machine learning models designed for drought forecasting. The forecasting component is subsequently linked with water management scenarios to evaluate how alternative decisions may influence hydrologic conditions and water demand. This establishes a closed prediction–decision–observation cycle in which observations continually refine the digital representation, updated states inform forecasts, forecasts support evaluation of management alternatives, and the consequences of implemented decisions are subsequently reflected in new observations and model updates. The resulting framework moves beyond a static land-surface simulation toward an adaptive Earth-system prediction architecture that combines physical modeling, Earth observations, data assimilation, and machine learning.

496658.title: The Ka-Band Rapid Volume Imaging Radar (KaRVIR): Overview of System Design and Science Potential
496658.authors: David J. Bodine, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and J. Salazar, R. D. Palmer, M. Loria-Salazar, C. R. Homeyer, D. Schvartzman, G. M. McFarquhar, Z. J. Lebo, P. Kirstetter, J. Redemann, J. Kelly, S. T. Salesky, M. D. Tzeng, and M. Yeary
496658.abstract: Millimeter-wavelength cloud radar systems provide valuable measurements of hydrometeor sizes and spatial variations in wind for studies of clouds and boundary layer processes. Such systems employ narrow beamwidths (~0.3°) to achieve spatial sampling of 20–30 m and maintain excellent sensitivity to detect small cloud droplets or ice particles, as well as weak boundary layer echoes. Cloud radar measurements, however, have been limited to 1D (vertically pointing) or 2D (airborne radar transects, PPI/RHI scans), lacking volumetric sampling capability. The combination of a narrow beam and a large number of pulses result in prohibitively long volume scan times (10–15 min). To address this gap, the National Science Foundation Mid-scale Research Infrastructure program has funded the development of two millimeter-wavelength phased array radars (PARs) called the Ka-band Rapid Volume Imaging Radars (KaRVIR). These radars provide full volume scans in as little as 20 s, while retaining the sensitivity and spatial resolution of existing Ka-band systems. This provides a 20x improvement in temporal resolution relative to mechanically scanning systems (~10 min), enabling novel studies of cloud evolution. These Ka-band PARs will feature polarimetric capability and can acquire three-dimensional wind measurements when deployed for multi-Doppler wind retrievals. By leveraging imaging, KaRVIR enables instantaneous RHIs at any azimuth, eliminating traditional scan paradigms that increase volume scan times to collect PPIs and RHIs. This presentation provides an overview of the KaRVIR facility alongside ongoing science and engineering research. Following the Preliminary Design Review in 2026, we will present KaRVIR’s finalized technical specifications and discuss ongoing system development. KaRVIR will support dual-polarization modes with simultaneous or alternating transmission of horizontal and vertical polarizations. A single-polarization, high-sensitivity mode increases KaRVIR’s baseline sensitivity by 6–9 dB and yields a narrow vertical beamwidth of 0.15º. In addition, we will present numerical simulation work that highlights some of KaRVIR’s science applications, including analyses of rapid variations in the 3D evolution of cumulus updrafts and convection initiation processes. We will introduce the KaRVIR radar emulator tool integrated with high-resolution model data. This digital twin will enable scientists and engineers to design targeted scanning strategies, test novel waveforms, and develop analysis methods for future observational data. The KaRVIR systems are expected to be operational by 2030.

496659.title: Midlatitude Extreme Winds Respond to Changing Land-Atmosphere Interactions
496659.authors: Paul J. Kushner, Univ. of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada; and L. T. Prates and M. Morris
496659.abstract: Extreme wind events associated with extratropical cyclones present a hazard to human life and to civil and economic infrastructure. We are thus motivated to clearly and confidently explain and predict such wind events. At standard resolution, global relatively coarse resolution (100 km) Earth system models struggle to represent midlatitude wind extremes due to an inability to resolve the relevant mesoscale dynamics that connects local impactful wind events to synoptic and planetary scales. Previous work has shown that with regional refinement down to 7 km, from a coarse outer scale of about 100 km, the variable-resolution version of the National Center for Atmospheric Research Community Earth System Model (VR-CESM) is capable of more skillfully representing the dynamical features of mesoscale circulations associated with these wind events, as well as their vertical and synoptic scale structure, driving confidence in its projections of future extreme wind events. This work has also shown that VR-CESM predicts an intensification of wind extremes in the Great Lakes region that is not present in the corresponding coarse resolution version of CESM. In this study, we focus on the mechanisms driving the projected intensification of these extreme wind events. The previous work suggested that projected boundary layer destabilizationcauses land-to-atmosphere sensible heat fluxes to increase, which, in turn, promotes mixing of lower-tropospheric momentum and strengthening of extreme winds at the surface. Here, we examine VR-CESM in much more depth to assess the seasonality of extreme wind event events and their drivers in the Great Lakes region under present day and year-2090 RCP8.5 conditions. The model’s greenhouse-forced increase to the intensity and frequency of September-May extreme wind events in this region is dominated by a spring signal. The spring signal results from a modification of the surface heat budget in response to reduced snow cover. Snow melt intensifies the diurnal cycle in near-surface wind speeds, with consequences for both typical and extreme wind speeds in the region. Of key interest is a shift from a regime of relatively low heat fluxes in the presence of moderate stability towards a regime of high heat flux in the presence of unstable near-surface conditions, as greenhouse-driven snow melt proceeds. While both regimes are accessible under both present day and future conditions, the spring melt and warming shifts the proportion of days towards the unstable/high-heat-flux side, featuring strong surface winds. There is therefore a need to accurately simulate land-atmosphere interactions alongside mesoscale dynamics to realistically capturing the wind-extreme response to climate change.

496664.title: Operational Solar Indices for Thermospheric Modeling: A History of Their Development and Modern Use
496664.authors: W. Kent Tobiska, Space Environment Technologies, Pacific Palisades, CA; and M. Pilinski, S. Mutschler, D. Bouwer, and B. diLorenzo
496664.abstract: The development history of fundamental solar indices and proxies is occasionally overlooked in the current literature. This discussion outlines the history and expanding strength of the JB2008 S10, M10, Y10, and F10 solar indices and proxies. It traces their incorporation into ISO standards 14222 and 21348, their operational adoption beginning with the U.S. Air Force Space Command in 2012 and continuing under the U.S. Space Force, and their improved quality as demonstrated over a three-solar-cycle historical record as of 2026. Fifty years ago, G. Schmidtke (1976) proposed the development of solar indices tied to the unit optical depth at which solar flux is deposited into the thermosphere, i.e., the altitude at which solar photons of a given wavelength are absorbed. Shortly thereafter, Tobiska et al. (1987), Tobiska (1989), and Barth et al. (1990) followed up on that suggestion and verified that the baseline 10.7-cm solar radio flux (F10.7) proxy for solar EUV energy was not adequate for representing the complex energy input into the thermosphere. At that time, solar chromospheric Lyman-alpha flux was shown to be a better indicator of solar variability, especially during solar minimum conditions. Several public EUV models from the 1980s through the 2000s (SERF2, EUV91, EUV97, SOLAR2000) then used the traditional F10.7 radio flux as a solar coronal proxy alongside Lyman-alpha as a solar chromospheric proxy. However, for improved thermospheric density representation, the development of the JB2006 and JB2008 models in the mid-2000s represented a major breakthrough in reducing density uncertainties. These models were built on the strength of the lessons learned from the solar models and two factors contributed to this success. First, JB2008 used four solar indices (S10, M10, Y10, F10) mapping the solar source regions of EUV, XUV, and FUV fluxes to the atmospheric layers where their photon energy is deposited at unit optical depth. Second, it added the 1-hour Dst index for geomagnetic storm representation alongside the traditional 3-hour ap index. We describe this historical development and its expanded, modern use in improving space traffic management today.

496665.title: HYDRO - Development of GeoWATCH Ensemble Framework for a Probabilistic High Resolution Soil Moisture and Mobility Product
496665.authors: Alexa R Marcovecchio, USACE Engineer Research and Development Center, Vicksburg, MS; and J. B. Eylander and A. Sisco
496665.abstract: Weather conditions have a critical impact on military operations and planning, particularly when traversing off-road terrain. The Geospatial Weather Affected Terrain Conditions and Hazards (GeoWATCH) application is a valuable tool that identifies military maneuvering capabilities by incorporating model analyses of weather and terrain with Army mobility modeling software. However, it is currently a deterministic product, which prevents a thorough assessment of the uncertainty of GeoWATCH outputs. The land surface model within GeoWATCH produces soil moisture and strength predictions that support the mobility model for off-road maneuvering. This work seeks to leverage ensemble weather and precipitation forecast capabilities to develop a probabilistic soil moisture, soil strength, and mobility product in an ensemble version of GeoWATCH. We use three different datasets: 557WW analysis, ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis, and the Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) as forcing sources during the ensemble development.

496666.title: Stratospheric Wave Predictability Enhances Surface Forecasts over North America
496666.authors: Xiuyuan Ding, University of California Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA; and B. Xiang, G. Chen, and L. Wang
496666.abstract: Stratospheric variability is an important source of subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) surface predictability, but most previous research has emphasized zonally symmetric polar vortex variability. The contribution of zonally asymmetric planetary waves to predicting North American cold extremes remains less well understood. Here, we apply average predictability time (APT) analysis to hindcasts from the GFDL SPEAR coupled S2S forecast system to identify the dominant predictable patterns at 100 hPa. Two types of modes emerge: zonally symmetric northern annular mode (NAM)-like patterns and a zonally asymmetric wave-1-like pattern. The wave-1-like mode precedes widespread cold anomalies across North America and increases the likelihood of regional cold extremes by 50%. Hindcasts conditioned on this mode show a 15% (2%–28%) enhancement in week-two surface air temperature prediction skill over central Canada and the northern United States, while prediction skill for regional cold extreme frequency increases by 28%. The region benefiting from these improvements contains more than 69% of the Canadian population and over 30% of the U.S. population, highlighting the societal relevance of this source of predictability. The associated dynamics differ from the canonical downward influence of weak polar vortex events. Whereas NAM-like events are followed by downward propagation of NAM anomalies and Eurasia-centered cooling, wave-1-like events are characterized by changes in the vertical wave structure, downward eddy heat flux over North America, and subsequent growth of tropospheric trough and cold anomalies. These features are consistent with vertical wave coupling and potentially regional planetary wave reflection. Analyses of ECMWF, UKMO, and ISAC hindcasts reveal broadly consistent wave-1-like predictable modes and enhanced North American prediction skills. Together, these results identify strong stratospheric planetary waves as windows of opportunity for skillful S2S prediction of North American winter cold extremes.

496669.title: Preconditioning of the Northern Indian Ocean-Atmosphere System for Summer Cyclogenesis and Monsoon Onset
496669.authors: Selina Bolella, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN; and D. Gamage, J. Phadtare, and H. J. S. Fernando
496669.abstract: The northern Indian Ocean, composed of two distinct basins, the Arabian Sea (AS) and the Bay of Bengal (BoB), plays a critical role in modulating the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) through a complex sequence of multi-scale atmospheric and oceanic processes coupled across the Air-Sea Transition Zone. The two basins exhibit distinct upper-ocean characteristics: while the BoB is among the freshest subtropical regions due to substantial river runoff, the AS is comparatively saline and is influenced by winter circulation that transports fresher waters from the BoB, thus enhancing upper-ocean stratification and contributing to elevated sea surface temperatures (SSTs). Superimposed on these regional processes, equatorial Kelvin and Rossby waves redistribute heat and freshwater across the Indian Ocean, modulating thermocline depth, upper-ocean heat content, and SST variability. Embedded within this system is the Indo-Pacific warm pool, with the southeastern Arabian Sea Mini Warm Pool (ASMWP) standing out as a crucial feature. Each spring (March-May), the ASMWP reaches some of the highest SSTs observed globally (>30°C) before rapidly dissipating with the onset of the ISM. Elevated SSTs across the AS and BoB contribute to enhanced pressure gradients and deep convection while supporting the strengthening of the Somali Jet, a key southwesterly flow that transports moisture and momentum toward the Indian subcontinent and drives monsoon rainfall. Equatorial wave activity can further modulate these processes by altering upper-ocean stratification, thermocline depth, and Tropical Cyclone Heat Potential (TCHP), thereby influencing the subsurface oceanic energy available to support deep convection and even tropical cyclone (TC) development. Warm pre-monsoon SSTs and elevated ocean heat content can favor TC genesis and intensification, while recent observations indicate that TCs can form near monsoon onset in both basins despite typically suppressive vertical wind shear conditions. These interactions raise questions about how basin-dependent oceanic and atmospheric preconditioning influences TC development and, in turn, the timing and progression of the ISM. Here, we combine in-situ observations from the EKAMSAT/ASTraL ship-based field campaigns with reanalysis, satellite products, and measurements from complementary observing platforms throughout the AS and BoB to investigate the coupled processes associated with TC genesis and intensification during the monsoon onset period. During the first two EKAMSAT campaigns – a pilot study in the AS aboard the R/V Roger Revelle (11-24 June 2023) and a BoB cruise aboard the R/V Thomas G. Thompson (28 April-13 June 2024) – a TC was observed prior to ISM onset each year. These observations provide an opportunity to examine the environmental conditions preceding TC development across two contrasting basins. This study is an attempt to identify the roles and interconnections of warm pool evolution, equatorial wave activity, upper-ocean heat content and stratification, and air-sea interactions in preconditioning the atmosphere and ocean for deep convection and tropical cyclogenesis. By comparing these coupled processes across the AS and BoB, we identify basin-dependent mechanisms that influence TC development and their potential implications in the timing and progression of ISM onset across the northern Indian Ocean.

496671.title: A Solar Soft X-ray Irradiance Proxy at Mars from MAVEN SWEA Auger Photoelectrons
496671.authors: Kyung-Eun Choi, SSL UCB, Berkeley, CA; and S. Xu, E. Thiemann, and D. Mitchell
496671.abstract: Solar extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and soft X-rays are important sources of ionization in the Martian upper atmosphere, driving unique photochemical processes and influencing the ionosphere. While the Extreme Ultraviolet Monitor (EUVM) instrument onboard the MAVEN (Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN) spacecraft provides EUV and soft X-ray monitoring over a significant fraction of each orbit, these measurements are often unavailable below ~1000 km due to instrument pointing when MAVEN conducts thermospheric and ionospheric observations. This limitation makes it difficult to investigate the real-time response of the Martian upper atmosphere to solar flares. To address this observational gap, we develop an empirical solar soft X-ray proxy using oxygen Auger photoelectron measurements from MAVEN SWEA collected between 2014 and 2025. The proxy is calibrated against GOES XRS observations during periods of favorable Earth-Sun-Mars viewing geometry. It consists of a quiet component representing the baseline solar irradiance and a flare component derived from carefully selected flare events. The reconstructed irradiance shows good agreement with GOES observations and successfully captures solar soft X-ray variability across a wide range of flux levels. The resulting unified proxy extends the reconstruction of solar soft X-ray irradiance at Mars and provides a useful tool for future investigations of the Martian upper atmosphere.

496672.title: Extending the Long-Term HIRS Climate Data Record: Calibration and Homogenization of CrIS-Simulated Radiances (CHIRS)
496672.authors: Philip Casey, North Carolina Institute for Climate Studies, Asheville, NC; and A. K. Inamdar, J. L. Matthews, D. Rao, and C. J. Schreck III
496672.abstract: The High-resolution Infrared Radiation Sounder (HIRS) onboard NOAA polar-orbiting satellites has provided a multi-decadal, climate-quality data record spanning over 40 years (1978–present). This long-term record is essential for monitoring atmospheric temperature and moisture profiles, cloud climatology, upper tropospheric humidity, outgoing longwave radiation, and ozone. To maintain continuity following recent HIRS instrument degradation, NOAA/NCEI successfully demonstrated the extension of HIRS-like observations by convolving hyperspectral radiances from the Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer (IASI) aboard the MetOp satellite series with inter-satellite calibration, producing calibrated IASI-simulated HIRS (C-IHRIS) to ensure consistent HIRS-like time series. Building on this framework, current efforts focus on extending the HIRS-like dataset into the future using NOAA’s Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) and Suomi-NPP satellites carrying the Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS). Convolving CrIS radiances with HIRS spectral response functions produces CrIS-simulated HIRS (CHIRS). To ensure a seamless, homogenized climate series, both IHIRS and CHIRS observations must be calibrated to a unified reference. Given that CrIS does not fly on the same satellite platform with HIRS or IASI, calibrating CrIS-simulated HIRS presents unique challenges, particularly regarding spatial/temporal co-location between CrIS and C-IHIRS pixels and angular limb-correction methodology across the swath.

496673.title: On Operationalizing Research and Prediction Advances in Hydrometeorology (Invited)
496673.authors: Russ S. Schumacher, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO
496673.abstract: Recent decades have seen major advances in hydrometeorology, from advanced radar networks to high-quality ensemble prediction systems to new methods for coupling atmospheric and land-surface information. On the one hand, these advances have led to some significant leaps forward in terms of understanding and predictive skill. On the other hand, there are many examples of research potential going unrealized because it never crosses the “valley of death” into wider operational use. This presentation will offer reflections on these challenges using two examples, both of which include scientific success as well as difficulties that arise when doing interdisciplinary and operational hydrometeorology. First, we will look back on a decade of work to apply machine learning methods to the prediction of excessive rainfall. In many respects, this has been a research-to-operations success story, with close collaboration between researchers and forecasters leading to iterative improvements and operational implementation. However, data limitations, and mismatches between meteorological, hydrological, and societal relevance continue to be barriers to even greater advances. Second, I will discuss experiences from serving as a state climatologist, where interpreting and translating subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecasts is a key part of the role. The demand for reliable, actionable S2S forecast information is huge, especially in the western US where it can influence high-stakes water management decisions. Yet despite countless scientific papers claiming big advances in S2S prediction, not nearly enough of that information is making its way into publicly available S2S products used by decision makers. This can serve as a call to action for more sustained integration, engagement, and building trust between researchers, forecasters, and users.

496674.title: Winter Validation of the Operational Great Lakes Wave System Using In-Situ and SWOT Observations
496674.authors: Kate Pereira, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO
496674.abstract: The Great Lakes constitute a massive, dynamic, fetch-limited system characterized by rapid atmospheric forcing transitions and significant seasonal ice coverage. These enclosed basins experience their most operationally consequential wave conditions in winter, driving coastal, navigation hazards, and damage to coastal infrastructure. Paradoxically, winter is also the most under-observed and under-validated season in the observational record. The operational Great Lakes Wave Unstructured system (GLWU), built on WAVEWATCH III, feeds NWS marine guidance for the region, yet winter validation of WW3 has been limited by persistent observational gaps. Addressing this gap necessitates the integration of two complementary observational anchors: temporally dense point measurements from winter-resilient in-situ buoys, and spatially comprehensive two-dimensional(2D) surface snapshots from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite. Together, they provide a systematic way errors introduced by surface forcing, static ice representations, and source-term physics.
