This work has direct implications for UFS-Wave development on the Great Lakes by characterizing winter dynamics and using these observational records to evaluate parameterizations originally calibrated on open-ocean conditions.

496678.title: George N. Kiladis: An Introduction
496678.authors: Roger S. Pulwarty, Independent, Boulder, CO; and M. Campagnolo and H. Diaz
496678.abstract: The George Kiladis symposium is focused on honoring George's career, highlighting his fundamental contributions to tropical meteorology and climate dynamics. The AMS awards named symposia honors elite scientists who have completed a monumental career and legacy in atmospheric, oceanic, or hydrologic sciences. These are reserved for pioneering figures worthy of consideration for AMS Honorary Membership. George has been recognized for his contribution through several prestigious awards and recognitions. That being said, we felt that a proper introduction to George and to this much-deserved Symposium was necessary, from some of us who have benefited from his collaborations, mentorship, partnership, and friendship. We will recount some of his very significant contributions, and beyond that, his varied interests, insights, and pursuits that reflect the evolution of this exceptional scientist and remarkable individual over time.

496680.title: Assimilation of Himawari Clear-Sky Infrared Radiance for HAFS Typhoon Forecasts over the West Pacific
496680.authors: Margarita Mora, NOAA Center for Atmospheric Sciences and Meteorology (NCAS-M), Howard University, Washington, DC; and F. Hsiao, S. Chiao, Z. Zhang, and J. Cheng
496680.abstract: The Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) is a sophisticated, high-resolution tropical cyclone (TC) forecast model covering basins like the North Atlantic, the East Pacific, and the West Pacific. It also contains built-in data assimilation (DA) capabilities for HAFS under the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration project (HAFS-JEDI). While testing is underway for DA over the North Atlantic, the West Pacific is largely untested due to the scarcity of data observations. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact of assimilating brightness temperature observations, using Himawari, a geostationary satellite operated by the Japan Meteorology Agency (JMA), on HAFS typhoon forecasts capabilities. This work is critical for advancing the accuracy of HAFS, and for better understanding of effective DA methods over the West Pacific. Previous applications of DA in other basins suggest that assimilations of observations over the West Pacific may improve the large-scale environmental analysis for the model’s first guess at the atmosphere’s initial state, providing a more accurate modeling background for the forecast.

496682.title: Influence of ENSO Variability on Extreme Fire Weather Events In a Super Large AMIP-Style Ensemble
496682.authors: Danielle Touma, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX; and Y. Okumura, C. Xing, X. Wu, L. H. Thapa, J. Hong, G. G. Persad, and C. S. Jackson, PhD
496682.abstract: Predicting extreme fire weather events on seasonal to multi-annual timescales is becoming more important as wildfire risk increases across the United States (U.S.) under a warming climate. Here, we use a 2560-member super large ensemble of AMIP-style simulations using the Community Atmospheric Model v4 (CAM4-SLE) driven by observed sea-surface temperatures (SSTs) from 1979 to 2022 to investigate the role of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) variability in driving extreme fire weather events. We calculate the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index (FWI) and identify extreme fire weather events when the FWI exceeds the local 95th percentile, derived from the distribution of all members across CAM4-SLE using the full analysis period. Compared to ECMWF Reanalysis v5 (ERA5), the CAM4-SLE adequately reproduces the observed 95th percentile of the FWI across the U.S., and extreme fire weather frequency correlates well in the southwest and western U.S. When assessing ERA5 using both composite and correlation analyses, we find large seasonal differences in the role of the leading DJF Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) on extreme fire weather events across the U.S. Extreme fire weather events in the southwest U.S. are more likely to occur following La Niña winter conditions in the spring and summer, while El Niño conditions precede more frequent events in the eastern U.S. in the summer and fall. Using a lead-lag correlation analysis, we find that the SST-forced signal in the CAM4-SLE shows robust influence of winter La Niña conditions in much of the southern U.S. in the concurrent winter and following spring seasons. However, internal atmospheric variability reduces the strength of the ENSO–FWI relationship by half and leads to non-robust correlations in many regions except for the southwest and southcentral U.S. In the summer, the La Niña forced response is weaker but robust to atmospheric variability in much of the western and southern U.S., and follows a similar pattern to those seen in ERA5. Overall, there is little-to-no evidence of El Niño influence on extreme fire weather events in the CAM4-SLE, which could reflect the internal variability of the ERA5 dataset, model misrepresentation of key ENSO teleconnection processes, or model mean state bias in the eastern U.S. Thus far, our results show that a super large AMIP-style ensemble can be used to robustly isolate the SST-forced influences on extreme fire weather events from atmospheric variability, providing essential insight into the seasonal to annual predictability of these events.

496684.title: A Multivariate Approach Toward Analyzing Environmental Drivers of Seasonal Wildfire Severity Across California
496684.authors: Shea Richards, The University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL
496684.abstract: Wildfire seasons in California have risen in intensity in recent decades, and with seasonal prediction becoming increasingly challenging, pressure has been placed on policymakers to anticipate fire risk before fires materialize. While prior work has tended to evaluate single variables or indices against seasonal fire severity, this study seeks to instead analyze the role of drought conditions and trends using multiple indices. These include the Standardized Precipitation and Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Indices (SPI and SPEI), Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI), evapotranspiration, and other drought-related variables. The specific relationships between these drought and wildfire variables are examined closely across both monthly and seasonal timescales and within different spatial domains across the US West Coast region. Results have demonstrated that the harshest wildfire seasons in terms of acres burned are closely associated with severe seasonal drought conditions and drying trends, which suggests that these signals hold predictive value past what usual single-variable approaches are able to capture. This initial work aims to provide a foundation for multivariate statistical approaches with the hope of applications towards longer-term climate model projections.

496686.title: From Atmospheric Rivers to Reservoir Operations: CIROH–CW3E Partnerships for FIRO
496686.authors: F Martin Ralph, SIO, La Jolla, CA; Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, Univ. of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA
496686.abstract: As a member of the CIROH Consortium, the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) fosters research and operations partnerships aimed at improving forecasts of landfalling atmospheric rivers (ARs) and their impacts across the western U.S, in particular their impacts on water resource management. These partnerships include enhanced observations of ARs and their environments over the North Pacific as part of AR Reconnaissance (AR Recon) in collaboration with NOAA and the U.S. Air Force, advancements in numerical modeling using a 200-member ensemble and machine learning/A.I. techniques to improve precipitation forecasts in collaboration with the California Department of Water Resources (CA DWR) and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and improvements in the generation of forcings and hydrologic modeling to improve ensemble streamflow forecasts in collaboration with the National Weather Service (NWS) River Forecast Centers (RFC). The implications of these partnerships extend to applications such as Forecast Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO), where more accurate forecasts can enhance water resources management strategies that influence water supply reliability and flood risk management. Under the auspices of CIROH, CW3E has engaged in research aimed at improving forecast temperature and precipitation forcings which are used by the RFC Hydrologic Ensemble Forecast System to produce an ensemble of streamflow forecasts. These ensemble streamflow forecasts are then used by water managers to support the implementation of FIRO-based strategies related to reservoir operations. This research is being conducted in collaboration with the NWS California-Nevada RFC. CW3E is also developing a streamflow forecasting testbed and identifying evaluation protocols to support the testing and implementation of new strategies in specific FIRO basins in both the California-Nevada and Northwest RFCs. CW3E is also partnering with CIROH to implement a novel approach to supporting research-to-operations advancements by embedding research hydrologists at the Northwest RFC to link the testbed and evaluation activities with the on-going FIRO projects in the Pacific Northwest. This embedded strategy is based on a proof-of-concept that has been on-going with the CA DWR and the California-Nevada RFC.

496687.title: High Resolution Model Analog Seasonal Forecasts for U.S. Coastal Sea Level
496687.authors: Xiaoyu Long, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and M. Newman, S. Shin, and K. Toride
496687.abstract: Model analog forecasting has emerged as a computationally efficient approach for seasonal climate prediction, demonstrating skill comparable to initialized dynamical systems. However, existing analog libraries predominantly rely on coarse (~1°) ocean models. While these models capture large-scale predictable signals, they lack the spatial resolution required for coastal bathymetry, boundary dynamics, and cross-shore sea level gradients. The availability of high-resolution global climate simulations provides a key opportunity to determine whether explicitly resolving these features improves seasonal predictions at the coast. In this study, we construct model analog ensemble forecasts using a high-resolution, historically forced climate simulation with an inverse-barometer correction for sea level, evaluating them against GLORYS ocean reanalysis and U.S. tide-gauge observations. We test three potential benefits of enhanced resolution: large-scale prediction skill on a common spatial grid, local translation of signals at tide-gauge locations, and ensemble probabilistic skill. Evaluated across initialization months and lead times using deterministic and probabilistic metrics, this framework isolates large-scale skill improvements from fine-scale coastal variability, providing a direct assessment of when and where high-resolution ocean models add value to seasonal U.S. coastal sea-level forecasts.

496690.title: High-Resolution Radar Observations of Severe Convective Storms, Wildfires, and Biological Echoes in Tonga
496690.authors: Miloslav Stanek, Meteopress, Prague, Czech Republic; and F. Najman
496690.abstract: Weather radar observations are essential for monitoring precipitation and severe weather in regions with limited conventional observing networks. In the South Pacific, radar coverage has historically been sparse, making the deployment of modern systems particularly valuable for both operational forecasting and situational awareness. A Meteopress C-band weather radar with a 2.4-meter antenna has been operating in the Kingdom of Tonga for two years, providing continuous volumetric observations of precipitation and storm structure. During this period, the system captured a range of notable meteorological events, offering detailed insight into tropical precipitation dynamics. The observations also show a frequent occurrence of small, short-lived convective cells exhibiting localized rotation and enhanced reflectivity structure, often resembling mini-supercell characteristics. These features appear regularly in the tropical environment around Tonga. In addition to meteorological targets, the radar also recorded a variety of non-meteorological echoes, including smoke plumes and biological scatterers such as bats. This poster presents a selection of the most significant and interesting events recorded during the first two years of operation of the Tonga C-band radar.

496691.title: Development and Evaluation of a Multi-Source Dataset with Environmental Predictors for Hail-Size Retrieval in Western North Dakota
496691.authors: Lynnlee Storm Bestul, Univ. of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; University of North Dakota, grand forks, ND; and M. Majdi, M. Chrit, and D. Brothers
496691.abstract: Severe thunderstorms are among the most frequent and costly weather hazards in the United States, producing tornadoes, damaging winds, and large hail. Large hail alone accounts for thousands of severe weather reports each year and causes billions of dollars in annual damage to agriculture, vehicles, and infrastructure. Despite their relative frequency, forecasting and observing hail remain challenging, and limited regional-scale research has evaluated the environmental conditions associated with different hail sizes. Western North Dakota presents a unique severe weather environment due to its complex topography, proximity to higher terrain, and elevated mixed layer. These factors contribute to environments favorable for large hail, making the region well suited for evaluating the ability of severe weather indices to discriminate between hail sizes. This study develops and evaluates a multi-source dataset that combines dual-polarization radar hail retrievals, GOES satellite hail signals, and WRF-derived environmental parameters to improve hail-size evaluation. Radar inputs include reflectivity, differential reflectivity, and copolar correlation coefficient fields used in the Hail-size Retrieval Algorithm (HRA). Satellite inputs include overshooting-top signatures, cloud-top texture, thermal-gradient features, and Geostationary Lightning Mapper observations where available. WRF convective parameter inputs include established hail-related predictors such as the Large Hail Parameter, Significant Severe Parameter, and Significant Hail Parameter, together with thermodynamic, kinematic, moisture, and hail-growth-zone predictors such as CAPE, vertical wind shear, storm-relative helicity, freezing-level height, and hail-growth-zone depth. These environmental predictors will be evaluated for their ability to discriminate among the four hail-size categories and to identify the most informative environmental inputs for the subsequent machine-learning analysis. The dataset spans western North Dakota from June to August, 2016 to 2024. Each candidate convective parameter is computed from a proximity sounding associated with a hailstorm, and hail reports for that storm from the Atmospheric Resources Cooperative Observer Network (ARBCON) and the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) are matched to storm samples using consistent spatial and temporal criteria. Radar, satellite, model, and surface hail observations are subjected to source-specific quality control before integration. The hailstorms are divided into four hail size categories: no hail, hail less than 1 inch, hail between 1 and 2 inches, and hail greater than 2 inches based on the maximum reported hail diameter. After quality control, spatial-temporal alignment and environmental-predictor assessment, the merged inputs will be used in a machine learning framework to estimate hail probabilities for the four size categories. The probabilistic machine-learning model will be evaluated using reliability, Brier score, area under the curve, and 95% confidence intervals. This work aims to provide a quality-controlled, regionally informed multi-source framework for four-class hail-size retrieval and a foundation for subsequent hail-suppression assessment in western North Dakota.

496694.title: Thermodynamic and Dynamical Controls on Extratropical Temperature Distributions in a Changing Climate
496694.authors: Kezhou Lu, Univ. of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, FL; Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and G. Chen
496694.abstract: Temperature extremes, represented by the lower and upper tails of a temperature distribution, have substantial societal and economic impacts. Because temperature distributions are inherently non-Gaussian, changes in their means and variances alone are insufficient to determine how these extremes will respond to a warming climate. Yet it remains unclear how these distributions arise and how their changes can be accurately projected. To understand lower-tropospheric temperature variability in the extratropics, where direct interactions with land and ocean surfaces are relatively limited, we build on the classic view that synoptic temperature anomalies arise from eddy mixing. In this perspective, synoptic circulation displaces air masses meridionally across the background temperature gradient, with the resulting temperature anomaly determined by both the displacement and the temperature contrast between air mass’s origin and destination. To avoid mixing air masses displaced from different source regions, we define a Lagrangian-mean state by assigning each temperature contour an equivalent latitude—the latitude of a zonally symmetric contour enclosing the same polar-cap area. Displacements from the equivalent latitude therefore characterize the dynamical influence of synoptic circulation, whereas the Lagrangian-mean temperature profile characterizes the thermodynamic structure of the background climate. To apply this framework to daily temperature variability, the effective displacement must be quantitatively estimated. Here, we use local finite-amplitude wave activity to objectively estimate the effective meridional displacement of lower-tropospheric thermodynamic contours. Combining these displacements with the Lagrangian-mean temperature profile allows us to reconstruct daily temperature fields and their probability distributions. We evaluate this framework using dry Held-Suarez and moist aquaplanet simulations with perturbations to the meridional temperature-gradient, uniform sea surface warming, and increased CO2 concentration. Reconstructions based on local wave activity capture both the model-simulated temperature distributions and much of their response to forcing, with particularly close agreement in the Held-Suarez simulations (r>0.97). We find that effective meridional displacements remain approximately Gaussian across much of the midlatitudes in both control and perturbed climates, whereas the resulting temperature distributions are strongly non-Gaussian. This non-Gaussianity arises primarily from mapping the Gaussian displacement distribution through the curved Lagrangian-mean temperature profile, whose gradient and curvature vary with latitude and change as climate warms. Our framework therefore provides a useful diagnostic for attributing changes in extratropical temperature distributions to dynamical and thermodynamic controls and offers a physically grounded approach for projecting future temperature extremes.

496695.title: Deep Learning for Severe Convective Forecasting with WindBorne WeatherMesh: Current Capabilities and Future Directions
496695.authors: Larissa Joy Reames, WindBorne Systems, Redwood City, CA; and J. T. Radford, H. Du, A. Shetty, J. Creus-Costa, D. Sorvisto, and M. Sierks
496695.abstract: WindBorne‘s WeatherMesh-6 (WM-6) is a 128-member transformer-based AI weather prediction (AIWP) ensemble run at 0.25° global resolution with hourly AI data assimilation. WM-6 produces probabilistic guidance out to 15 days and is the first global AIWP to natively forecast most-unstable CAPE as a prognostic variable. A companion 2.5 km CONUS model, updated every 15 minutes, resolves mesoscale surface features relevant to convective forecasting that are invisible at global resolution. At the 2026 AMS Madison Summit, we evaluated WM-6's convective parameter skill over the spring 2026 severe weather season (April–June) using HRRR analysis and URMA verification. The WM-6 global model outperformed IFS for longer-range forecasts of 0–3km SRH and EHI and produced competitive CAPE forecasts, while the 2.5 km WM-6 model accurately captured pre-convective surface evolution. However, neither model produced convective-scale features with fidelity. Towards rectifying that weakness, WindBorne has developed a next-generation forecast architecture. WeatherMesh-Next uses higher-effective-resolution latent representations and decoder output, twice the parameter space, and trains encoders simultaneously against ERA5 as well as radar-derived precipitation rates, high-resolution surface analyses, and satellite imagery. Using this next-gen system, we extend prior work in two directions. First, we verify precipitation and convective parameter forecasts against observations, comparing performance to traditional NWP models. We also assess aggregated skill and case study forecast accuracy against prior-generation WM-6 to identify which forecast attributes improve with the new architecture. Second, we apply a decoder-only transformer post-processing framework to WeatherMesh ensemble output, producing calibrated probabilities of severe convective hazards over CONUS. This model ingests the full ensemble distribution of thermodynamic and kinematic fields and maps it to observed severe weather reports. We present results from training on WeatherMesh data and initial verification against Storm Prediction Center outlooks and local storm reports across multi-day forecast horizons. Together, these results illustrate progress toward AI weather models that predict convective hazards directly, produce calibrated probabilistic severe weather guidance, and benefit from architectural improvements at multiple stages of the forecasting pipeline.

496696.title: Mauna Loa Solar Observatory observations for Space Weather Forecasting
496696.authors: Joan Burkepile, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and T. E. Berger, M. Galloy, B. Berkey, O. C. St.Cyr, I. Richardson, W. Thompson, L. Perez-Gonzalez, M. Cotter, D. Kolinski, G. de Toma, M. Wiltberger, L. Mays, P. Quinn, and R. Egeland
496696.abstract: The High Altitude Observatory (HAO) began in 1940 to monitor and report solar activity to the U.S. Army for understanding space weather impacts on radar and communications. HAO has continued to track solar activity for space weather research and forecasting. The NCAR Mauna Loa Solar Observatory (MLSO) COSMO K-Coronagraph (K-Cor) resumed operations on March 31, 2026. It issues near-real-time coronal mass ejection (CME) alerts to the community, space weather forecasting centers, and to NASA’s Community Coordinated Modeling Center Solar Energetic Particle (SEP) scoreboard. K-Cor observes the corona from 1.05 to 3 solar radii at 15-second cadence. Data are fully processed in ~2.5 minutes which includes analysis of the data by a CME detection code developed by Dr. William Thompson and automated and integrated into the K-Cor data pipeline by Dr. M. D. Galloy. These properties make K-Cor ideally suited to provide early warning CME detection as part of a Solar Energetic Particle (SEP) forecasting system. K-Cor alerts provide the first warning of in-progress CMEs. Most K-Cor alerts are issued before the CME enters the LASCO field-of-view. The advanced warning time for in-progress SEP-associated CMEs is 55 minutes, on average, before the CME is visible in available LASCO data (includes 40 minutes LASCO data latency). Two SEP-associated CMEs have been detected by K-Cor since operations began March 31, 2026. The advanced warning time for these two events using the new NOAA CCOR coronagraph data was 59 minutes and 44 minutes. CCOR has only 15 minutes data but the inner field-of-view (3.6 solar radii) is ~1.5 solar radii higher than LASCO. CMEs must travel farther to be visible in CCOR. K-Cor CME alerts continue to provide early detection of in-progress CMEs and complement observations from CCOR. We discuss how observations of the low and middle corona from the MLSO coronagraphs provide critical information on CME dynamics and acceleration that can help improve SEP forecasting. Properties of the K-Cor SEP events in the low and middle corona (from LASCO), as reported by St. Cyr et al. 2026 10.1007/s11207-026-02679-1, are discussed as well as the forecasting benefit of a ground-based coronagraph network.

496697.title: The Influence of Boundary Layer Shear on Coherent Structures in Simulated Tornado-Like Vortices
496697.authors: Dominic Candela, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; Univ. of Oklahoma School of Meteorology, Norman, OK; and D. J. Bodine
496697.abstract: The near-surface flow around tornadoes is difficult to measure and observe. Recent Large-Eddy Simulation (LES) studies of tornadoes have noted near-surface roll features in tornado and near-tornado flows, though these have not been further explored (Candela et al. 2026, Bryan et al. 2017). In this study, Cloud Model 1 (CM1) is used to perform LES of tornado-like vortices. A range of tornado types (high swirl and low swirl) are tested along with various surface roughness values and translation speeds. The influence of surface friction on the organization, intensity, and depth of the surface rolls is quantified. Initial results indicate that greater surface friction leads to deeper, more organized structures that extend over 100 m in the vertical, along with more intense vertical velocities. The addition of translation leads to asymmetries in the flow which leads to the surface rolls being preferentially located behind the vortex, but also allows for the bands to occasionally penetrate into the vortex core. The Rayleigh criterion and Fjørtoft's theorem are applied to the axisymmetric mean vertical profiles to evaluate whether shear instability satisfies the necessary conditions for growth. Early results indicate only the Rayleigh criterion is satisfied for the profiles of the horizontal wind. Analyzing only the radial component of the wind profile reveals both the Rayleigh criterion and Fjørtoft's theorem are satisfied, offering a potential explanation for the observed surface roll features. This study provides new insight into the coherent organized structures prevalent in the tornado, and near-tornado boundary layer by identifying the importance of surface friction and surface roll organization along with a hypothesis on their origin. References: Candela, D. M., D. J. Bodine, M. A. Wagner, and F. T. Lombardo, 2026: Heterogeneous surface roughness effects on tornadoes. J. Atmos. Sci., e250190, https://doi.org/10.1175/JAS-D-25-0190.1 Bryan, G. H., N. A. Dahl, D. S. Nolan, and R. Rotunno, 2017: An eddy injection method for large-eddy simulations of tornado-like vortices. Mon. Wea. Rev., 145 (5), 1937 – 1961,756, https://doi.org/10.1175/MWR-D-16-0339.1.

496698.title: Combining DOE EPCAPE Campaign Observations with WRF-CHEM Using DART to Generate Data Cubes for Scientific Analysis
496698.authors: J. Christine Chiu, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and P. J. van Leeuwen, S. H. Chen, Z. Shi, J. Anderson, B. Raczka, H. Kershaw, I. L. McCoy, J. Chun, C. Venkatachalam, S. K. Biswas, and D. McCoy
496698.abstract: Marine boundary layer clouds play a central role in regulating Earth’s albedo, yet their structure and evolution are shaped by complex interactions among radiation, dynamics, and cloud microphysics. These interactions are further complicated by coupling with aerosols, which remain a leading source of uncertainty in climate forcing estimates. Large discrepancies remain between model estimates and observations of many fundamental processes, including autoconversion, entrainment, and wet scavenging, highlighting the need for integrated observational and modeling approaches. To address these challenges, we construct an integrated observation–model data cube using ARM Mobile Facility measurements from the Eastern Pacific Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment (EPCAPE) together with WRF-Chem and the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART). The data assimilation, performed every 5 minutes, ensures that this data cube is the best possible description of the evolution of the atmospheric variables, given the observations. The framework provides detailed estimates of the evolution of the relevant variables in cloud-aerosol-precipitation interaction processes, including their uncertainties. Furthermore, we directly evaluate these estimates against airborne in situ measurements from the Southern California Interactions of Low cloud and Land Aerosol (SCILLA) campaign and against pure model simulations to infer the value of the data assimilation framework.

496699.title: Precursors and Drivers of Compound Wintertime Cold-Wet and Warm-Wet Spells Across the Contiguous United States
496699.authors: Elinor R. Martin, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; South Central Climate Adaptation Science Center, Norman, OK; and O. T. Millin
496699.abstract: The simultaneous occurrence of multiple meteorological hazards, referred to as compound events, can produce substantial socioeconomic and environmental impacts. Understanding the key precursors and drivers of such events is therefore important in beginning to understand how to improve their prediction out to subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) lead times. A particularly impactful class of compound events arises when anomalous precipitation and temperature conditions co-occur, as each of these hazards alone can pose significant risks but their co-occurrence can exacerbate impacts. In this presentation, we focus on wintertime compound warm-wet and cold-wet events across the contiguous United States (CONUS), when flooding and winter weather hazards are most common and can coincide with severe cold-related impacts and agricultural vulnerability, while also adding to the growing research on both wintertime cold and warm events. We split the CONUS into seven regions using the United States Geological Survey (USGS) Regional Climate Adaptation Science Centers (CASCs): the Northwest, the Southwest, the North Central, the South Central, the Midwest, the Southeast, and the Northeast. We then analyze the characteristics of these events and their key precursors including North American weather regimes, the stratospheric polar vortex (SPV), and the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO). We find that warm-wet events are typically associated with or preceded by a Pacific Trough in the western and northern CONUS and a Pacific Ridge for other regions, alongside a weakened SPV that propagates downward in the Southwest and anomalously strong polar stratospheric circulation in other regions. Enhanced MJO phases 2-4 emerge roughly 2-3 weeks prior for West and Central CONUS events. Cold-wet events exhibit mostly opposite patterns with a Pacific Ridge in the western CONUS and Alaskan Ridge and Greenland High patterns elsewhere. Weakened SPV conditions and stratosphere-troposphere coupling occur in the Midwest and Northeast, while MJO phases 6-8 become active beyond 10 days prior across multiple regions. The identification and significance of the signals in the weather regimes, SPV, and MJO in relation to these compound events highlight a potential pathway to better forecasting such events out to S2S lead times.

496702.title: What's Driving the Global Decline In Mineral Dust Emissions during the Early 21st Century?
496702.authors: Ashok Kumar Gupta, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN; and J. F. Kok, R. Bennartz, V. Amiridis, A. Gkikas, K. Rizos, E. Proestakis, and C. P. Garcia-Pando
496702.abstract: Global mineral dust emissions have declined since the early 2000s, yet the environmental mechanisms driving this change remain unclear. We examine 2003–2023 using a 1,000-member inverse-model ensemble together with ERA5 reanalysis meteorology, surface wind observations from the Met Office Hadley Centre Integrated Surface Database (HadISD), and an independent ERA5-driven Dust Emission Model (DuEM) simulation. The ensemble yields coherent negative global median trends per decade in dust aerosol optical depth (−5 ± 4%), loading (−5 ± 6%), emission (−5 ± 6%), and deposition (−5 ± 7%), where the uncertainties are the average half-width of the 16th–84th percentile range across ensemble members. The steepest regional median emission decrease occurs in eastern North Africa (−11 ± 12% per dec-1), while East Asia shows −5 ± 12% per dec-1; the environmental signals associated with these regional trends differ. In eastern North Africa, station-based HadISD winds decline alongside emissions, whereas the ERA5 wind trend is weak. This suggests that the observations capture a regional wind decline that the reanalysis underestimates. East Asia shows the clearest cross-dataset agreement: detrended ERA5 wind variability tracks the inverse emission series, HadISD monthly maximum winds decrease, and the DuEM spring simulation gives −6 % per dec-1 against the inverse estimate of −5 % per dec-1. The two emission series also covary interannually (r = 0.72; detrended r = 0.70). These independent lines of evidence indicate that reduced high-wind activity is an important contributor to the dust-emission decline, with the strongest and most consistent signal in East Asia and supporting observational evidence in eastern North Africa. Furthermore, we are quantifying how much reduced high-wind activity contributes to the global dust-emission decline and assessing how this mechanism may shape dust emissions in a future climate.

496703.title: NNJA-AI v2: An Expanded Archive of Atmospheric Observations for ML Applications
496703.authors: Daniel Alexander Rothenberg, Brightband, Erie, CO; and H. Mohrmann, R. Keisler, A. Kleeman, H. Kamdar, and S. Frolov
496703.abstract: Over the past two years, a variety of novel approaches have been published which apply AI techniques to the traditional data assimilation (DA) process used to initialize both numerical weather models as well as their ML counterparts. In contrast with weather prediction, the DA task is significantly more complex; at the very least, the data preparation work necessary for pursuing AI DA involves managing a diverse set of observations from different modalities, often packaged and disseminated in different ways. In contrast with AI for weather prediction - which usually targets a single gridded analysis or reanalysis product - the data acquisition and interface create a major structural barrier for research. Previously, to address this challenge, Brightband in partnership with colleagues at NOAA launched NNJA-AI v1 - an AI-ready, reprocessed subset of the NOAA-NASA Joint Archive of Observations for Earth System Reanalysis (NNJA). The initial release of NNJA-AI down-selected a dozen of the most impactful observations for DA work and converted them from their source BUFR format into an analysis-ready, cloud-optimized format leveraging Apache Parquet; it also included documentation and a Python-based SDK to help users adopt the data. The archive comprised nearly 50 TB of data and was hosted by NODD on a Google Cloud Storage bucket to ensure accessibility to a broad swath of users. Here, we present NNJA-AI v2 - a comprehensive expansion of the original NNJA-AI work, scaling our initial effort to the entire NNJA archive. NNJA-AI v2 fully processes the complete set of BUFR-encoded observations across all modalities in the NNJA archive. The data is still written to Parquet, but uses a simpler mapping algorithm from BUFR message schema to Parquet schema incorporating a new “struct-of-arrays” (SoA) technique and row group optimizations to accelerate query performance across a variety of retrieval engines, including DuckDB and Apache DataFusion. Furthermore, we leverage Apache Iceberg to streamline access to the dataset. The development of NNJA-AI v2 also provided a substantial platform for data archaeology. Our work identified significant but poorly documented changes to NOAA’s BUFR messages over time. We record these changes through metadata, and directly address them by “canonicalizing” data from certain messages (in particular, conventional observations and their PREPBUFR counterparts). This eliminates the need for users to understand all the idiosyncrasies of how message types have evolved over time, providing a consistent interface and data catalog. We further present ongoing work integrating NNJA-AI into real-world DA and evaluation systems and improvements to the original Python SDK.

496706.title: Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA): NOAA’s Next-Generation Backbone Microwave Sounder
496706.authors: Edward J. Kim, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and K. Yienger, L. McCormick, R. Platt, M. Sammons, A. Bringer, M. Wigdor, C. Johnson, J. Knizhnik, O. Quintero, M. Wong, B. Greybeck, H. Yang, Q. Liu, C. H. Lyu, S. Abraham, C. Anders, C. Brann, and R. George
496706.abstract: The Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) is the microwave sounder component of NOAA‘s next-generation low earth orbit (LEO) observing system—the Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) Program. NEON will cover the 2030s-2050 timeframe. SMBA sounders will overlap for about a decade with the predecessor Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) sounders on the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) satellites, which are scheduled to be operational through about 2040. Both SMBA and ATMS will therefore overlap with their METOP-SG counterpart, the Microwave Sounder (MWS), providing enhanced coverage for forecasting as well as an exciting opportunity for inter-calibration. One major difference between JPSS and NEON is that while each JPSS satellite manifest includes a copy of each of the different sensors—microwave sounder, IR sounder, visible/IR imager, etc., the NEON sensors will be on “free flyer” smallsat buses. SMBA Formulation Phase trade studies concluded in fall, 2024. A Request for Proposals for the Implementation Phase was released in 2026, and vendor selection is in progress. In order to provide continuity for numerical weather prediction (NWP) and other data products, many SMBA requirements are similar to those of past and current microwave sounders. For example, required bands include the 23-183 GHz ATMS bands plus the 118 GHz temperature sounding band, and a 229 GHz channel similar to that of MWS. Specific required channels within each band, their bandwidths, etc., further ensure continuity. Sensitivities (noise equivalent delta temperature) have been updated to reflect improved technology available today. New requirements have been added to constrain 1/f noise content and inter-channel correlation. The error budget framework has been re-vamped to more closely match the uncertainty formalism used by national standards while also laying the groundwork for eventual SI traceability---milestones that have already been achieved by visible, IR, and thermal IR sensing. The scan geometry will be cross-track. The requirements for footprint size, spatial sampling characteristics, and all the above-mentioned performance characteristics were informed by current technology capabilities, observing system architecture studies, workshops, expert panels, and the Formulation Phase studies. Notably, SMBA will include three new features not found on previous backbone or operational microwave sounders: the inclusion of hyperspectral capability, a requirement to have radio frequency interference (RFI) detection capability, and explicit inter-calibration across the SMBA flight units. SMBA will be a state-of-the-art backbone microwave sounder. An overview of SMBA objectives, requirements, new features, and programmatic status will be presented.

496709.title: Rotating Universal Radiometer, a Robust Sensor for Planetary Boundary Layer Observations and Land-atmosphere Interaction
496709.authors: Madison May Eble, Boulder Environmental Sciences and Technology, Boulder, CO; and M. Klein
496709.abstract: Around to 40% of the Forecast Sensitivity to Observation Impact (FSOI) is provided by space based passive microwave humidity and temperature measuring sensors (Geer, et al., 2019). All other observations (e.g. infrared sensors, radiosondes, surface stations, ships, and buoys) provide the remaining 60%. Many other papers have documented the importance of radiometer observations for short term and long term weather forecasting. There is more that passive microwave sensors could provide. A number of papers also examine the impact of adding more of these sensors on orbit, e.g., (Duncan, Bormann, & Holm, 2021), (Rivoire, et al., 2024). All of the studies confirm that more radiometer sensors on orbit will provide a significant positive impact on numerical weather prediction (NWP) model errors. Many papers have also described the benefits of hyperspectral microwave sensors and how this approach to sensor design can further improve observations, e.g., (Boukabara & Garrett, 2011), (Maddy, Iturbe-Sanchez, & Boukabara, 2024). While much of the current work focuses on space based sensors, ground based microwave radiometers also have the potential for improving atmospheric observations of the lowest level of the atmosphere, since they operate within the atmospheric boundary layer. However, the ground based microwave radiometer technology currently in use is at least 40 years old. Sensor electronics might have improved during past decades, but not the observational capabilities. Ground based radiometers are still using a rotating mirror, with two frequency bands (e.g. 20-30 and 50-58 GHz) mixing polarizations in their observations. They require regular liquid nitrogen calibration by a Ph.D. level operator. A sensor of the next generation known as the Rotating Universal Radiometer (RUR) will be presented. This constantly rotating sensor can observe in dual polarizations, cover a wide frequency range, e.g., 6 to 220 GHz, and provide hyperspectral benefits, all in one integrated, rugged, IP67 sealed instrument that calibrates autonomously and reduces the need for user intervention. In addition to providing humidity and temperature profiles with much improved vertical resolution within the atmospheric boundary layer, the RUR sensor can also observe during precipitation events, thus enabling the measurement of precipitation rates. The sensor is capable of operating from a buoy without requiring platform stabilization. The calibration of the RUR is fully automatic, no user involvement is expected. The RUR sensor can also perform simultaneous measurements of the surface below the sensor (land or ocean) and the atmosphere, thus providing valuable information for analyzing the interactions between these two regimes. We will present the simulated capabilities of the RUR sensor for temperature and humidity profiling in the atmospheric boundary layer and further aloft. Simulated retrievals have shown up to 80% improvement in retrieval accuracy compared to the current ground based technology. References Boukabara, S. A., & Garrett, K. (2011). Benefits of a Hyperspectral Microwave Sensor. 2011 IEEE Sensors (pp. 1881-1884). Limerick, Ireland: IEEE. Duncan, D. I., Bormann, N., & Holm, E. V. (2021). On the addition of microwave sounders and numerical weather prediction skill. Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society, 3703-3718. doi:10.1002/qj.4149 Geer, A., Bormann, N., Lonitz, K., Weston, P., Forbes, R., & English, S. (2019, October). Recent progress in all-sky radiance assimilation. ECMWF Newsletter. Toward the Next Generation of Microwave Sounders: Benefits of a Low-Earth Orbit Hyperspectral Microwave Instrument in All-Weather Conditions Using AI. 496710.title: Perturbations in the VLEO Environment Linked to the Strength of the Arctic Stratospheric Polar Vortex
496710.authors: Larisa Goncharenko, Massachusetts Institute of Technology Haystack Observatory, Westford, MA; and K. R. Greer and V. L. Harvey
496710.abstract: Numerous observational and modeling studies have demonstrated dramatic ionospheric and thermospheric perturbations linked to the strength of the stratospheric polar vortex. Extremely weak polar vortex is associated with sudden stratospheric warmings (SSW) and with amplification of solar and lunar migrating tides. Tidal changes influence the thermosphere and ionosphere through multiple mechanisms, including modification of electric fields, thermospheric winds, and thermospheric composition via tidal dissipation. In contrast, extremely strong stratospheric polar vortex is predicted to weaken tidal amplitudes. Recent simulations and observations indicate weakening of the solar semidiurnal migrating tides during strong vortex conditions. However, there have been relatively few observational studies of strong polar vortex events and their effects on the thermosphere and ionosphere at VLEO altitudes. In this study, we use observations of peak electron density NmF2 obtained from multiple ionosondes and observations of total electron content (TEC) obtained from GNSS receivers to examine the ionospheric response to several strong polar vortex events. We utilize recently developed empirical models of NmF2 and TEC to accurately specify expected ionospheric behavior driven by variations in solar ionizing flux, geomagnetic activity, and season. Differences between observations and the expected model-specified background are analyzed in the context of polar vortex strength. Unexpectedly, ionospheric perturbations demonstrate significant longitudinal variability during strong polar vortex conditions, indicating multiple mechanisms affecting upper atmospheric parameters. We discuss the importance of different drivers for the observed ionospheric anomalies and highlight future observations needed to accurately determine the mechanisms driving these anomalies and their coupling to the state of the polar vortex.

496716.title: The Fundamental and Foundational work of George N. Kiladis
496716.authors: Peter J. Webster, Georgia Institute of of Technology, Atlanta, GA; Georgia Instutue of Technology, Atlanta, GA
496716.abstract: Stated simply, during the last few decades, George Kiladis has revolutionized tropical meteorology! He took the fundamental work of Professor Taro Matsuno, in the late 1960s, and expanded how these basic modes of low-latitude wave forms were coupled -convective modes and how their relationship with tropical convection altered their propagation characteristics and their impact on the transient state of the tropical atmosphere. He expanded his atmospheric research work and laid the basis for a second coupling of atmospheric modes with the fundamental modes of the low-latitude ocean. Besides describing the fundamental aspects of weather and climate at low latitudes, George Kiladis has laid a foundation for understanding relationships between climate and weather variability between the tropics and higher latitudes, one dominated by rotational modes, and the more divergent modes of low latitudes. In addition, he has advanced our understanding of intraseasonal variability of the tropics, especially the Madden-Julian Oscillation, and how it interacts and modifies other major circulation systems of the tropics often separated by great distances. I have had the pleasure of knowing and working with George Kiladis for decades and we co-advised a number of graduate students. His interaction with students is telling and was in accord with his generally helpful demeanor with all who have worked with him, pleasant, helpful, and thorough. It is an honor to have the opportunity provide a brief commentary on the achievements of this fine scientist.

496720.title: Toward Operational Prediction of Extreme Rainfall Thresholds from Weather Radar Using a Time-Aware Ordinal CNN-LSTM Model
496720.authors: Michael Lavallee, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and J. W. Nielsen-Gammon
496720.abstract: Extreme rainfall events remain difficult to anticipate because storms producing similar early radar signatures can evolve toward substantially different precipitation totals. This study develops a time-aware convolutional neural network (CNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) model for estimating the likelihood that an ongoing heavy-rainfall event will exceed progressively higher accumulation thresholds using sequences of NEXRAD reflectivity observations. Heavy-rainfall events are identified within 100-km radar domains using complementary gauge and PRISM precipitation estimates and classified according to spatially supported 24 h accumulations of 2–<4, 4–<6, 6–<8, 8–<12, and ≥12 inches. These categories are reformulated as cumulative ordinal targets representing exceedance of 4, 6, 8, and 12 inches, allowing the model to estimate increasingly severe rainfall-threshold probabilities rather than assigning events to a single binary flood or non-flood classification. Gauge and PRISM detections are evaluated independently with temporal downsampling to reduce repeated representation of prolonged rainfall episodes, and subsequently reconciled while retaining source-specific precipitation and spatial-support metadata. To improve operational relevance, radar input sequences will be objectively anchored to the onset of a qualifying rainfall episode using an accumulation trigger of 1 inch. Once this trigger is reached within the radar domain, a fixed-length sequence of subsequent radar observations is collected to characterize the continuing spatial and temporal evolution of the storm. This approach replaces retrospective selection of an optimal radar window with a reproducible event-activation criterion that can be applied in real time. Spatial features from each reflectivity frame are extracted using a convolutional neural network and combined with the observed time interval between radar scans before temporal processing with a recurrent neural network. Experiments will evaluate alternative accumulation triggers, including earlier versus later activation of the radar sequence, and assess the ability of the framework to distinguish events that subsequently progress toward increasingly extreme accumulation thresholds. Evaluation will include threshold-specific discrimination and probabilistic skill, ordinal-category performance, and the lead time between model evaluation and subsequent threshold exceedance. Earlier proof-of-concept iterations of the CNN-LSTM model demonstrated an ability to distinguish rainfall events relative to a single accumulation threshold, motivating the present extension toward ordered probabilistic prediction across multiple increasingly extreme precipitation thresholds. The ultimate goal is to provide forecasters with evolving probabilistic guidance describing the likelihood that an ongoing heavy-rainfall event will exceed 4, 6, 8, or 12 inches.

496721.title: Communicating Drought in Oklahoma: Lessons from a Tornado-Obsessed State
496721.authors: Gary McManus, Oklahoma Climatological Survey, Norman, OK
496721.abstract: How do you get Oklahomans — accustomed to tornadoes, severe thunderstorms, ice storms and wildfires — to pay attention to a hazard that develops over weeks, months or even years? Drought comes with no warning polygon, no caravans of storm chasers and little dramatic video. It creeps across the landscape, often without a clear beginning or end, despite enormous costs. Communicating drought in a tornado-obsessed state therefore takes more than posting a new map each Thursday. The U.S. Drought Monitor provides the weekly foundation for that communication, but the map alone rarely answers what Oklahomans most want to know: What changed, why did it change and what does it mean here? This presentation examines how the Oklahoma Climatological Survey turns that weekly snapshot into a continuing local story. The OCS/Mesonet Ticker explains what changed, where and why, and who is affected. Social media condenses the story into annotated maps, concise headlines and locally relevant graphics, often using humor and familiar cultural references. Media interviews, presentations and direct conversations extend the message and allow Oklahomans to ask questions and report conditions. That engagement makes drought communication a two-way exchange. Audience questions and local impact reports inform subsequent messaging as well as the weekly drought assessment. They also reveal difficult challenges, including explaining why producers reporting significant losses might not be depicted in D2-D4 categories used by some federal assistance programs. The USDM incorporates impacts, but it is a regional, convergence-of-evidence assessment, not a farm-by-farm loss map. The presentation will share lessons learned about leading with what changed, making impacts local, matching the message to the platform and writing for neighbors rather than specialists. Over time, that sustained, multi-platform effort has helped build a drought-savvy culture across Oklahoma, from broadcast meteorologists and other media partners to agricultural producers and decision-makers. Drought may never compete with tornadoes for drama, but it can compete for attention when the message is clear, relevant and delivered where people already are.

496722.title: Recovery of Range-Overlaid Cross-Polar Power in Polarization-Diversity Pulse-Pair Processing on a Solid-State Weather Radar
496722.authors: Jason Selzler, Vaisala Inc, Dilworth, MN; and S. I. Panov, P. Rossi, and E. Ruzanski
496722.abstract: Polarization-Diversity Pulse-Pair (PDPP) processing decouples the maximum unambiguous range from the maximum unambiguous velocity. Velocity is estimated from the cross-correlation between orthogonally polarized returns at the short intra-pair lag, which sets the Nyquist velocity, while the much longer inter-pair PRT independently sets the unambiguous range. The method depends on two conditions: sufficient isolation between the orthogonally polarized signals to separate the two returns of a pair, and a high correlation between the co-polar backscatter coefficients so that the pair remains coherent. For example, an intra-pair spacing of 100 µs with a 1 ms inter-pair PRT yields an unambiguous velocity interval of approximately ±134 m/s out to a surveillance range of 150 km at C-band. That isolation is finite. Some targets, extremely large hail in particular, exhibit a high linear depolarization ratio (LDR), which can drive the range-overlaid cross-polar power to approach or exceed the received co-polar power. Useful velocity estimates require the cross-polar power to remain well below the co-polar power, a condition satisfied by most hydrometeors but violated where LDR is elevated. Solid-state power amplifier (SSPA) transmitters operating independently in each polarization channel can apply a unique phase code to every transmitted pulse. We present simulations of an estimate-and-subtract recovery scheme in which per-pulse phase coding separates the overlaid returns, allowing the contaminating component to be estimated and removed before moment estimation. Performance is characterized as a function of the cross-polar ratio, spectrum width, and code choice, and is compared against uncoded processing. The cross-polar ratio is defined here as the ratio of overlaid cross-polar power to co-polar power in the gate being estimated, set jointly by the LDR of the overlaid target and the reflectivity contrast between the two ranges. Results indicate the range of conditions over which overlaid cross-polar power can be recovered and where the technique remains limited. Finally, we examine the limiting case in which the true LDR field is known a priori. In practice such a field could be supplied by a companion scan at the same elevation — for example a split-cut or batch-mode sweep using a conventional uniform PRT — from which LDR, and therefore the expected cross-polar contamination at each overlaid gate, can be estimated before the PDPP sweep is processed. Treating that field as known converts the blind separation problem into a constrained one: the magnitude of the contaminating component is prescribed, leaving only its phase and Doppler content to be estimated. Simulating this case establishes an upper bound on recoverable performance against which the blind, code-only scheme can be measured, and identifies the conditions under which a priori knowledge yields a meaningful benefit. We also consider the practical costs of obtaining such a field: the system LDR floor, temporal decorrelation between the companion and PDPP sweeps, and the additional scan time required.

496723.title: Impacts of Arabian Dust on Madden-Julian Oscillation Intensity and Propagation
496723.authors: Marco Rossi, Univ. of California, Davis, Davis, CA; and S. H. Chen and Y. Yu
496723.abstract: The Boreal Summer Intraseasonal Oscillation (BSISO) is a northeastward-propagating dipole of enhanced and suppressed convection that plays a major role in regulating South Asian Monsoon activity. The moisture mode theory dictates that the BSISO is governed by column moisture. Within this framework, the propagation is driven by the anomalous advection of background moisture ahead of the convective envelope, and the intensity is driven by the magnitude of the column moisture in the region of convective development. Airborne dust can affect local tropospheric meteorology by absorbing and scattering shortwave radiation and emitting longwave radiation. These produce perturbations to background temperature and moisture fields, as well as impacts on large-scale circulations. Dust aerosols can also modulate convection and atmospheric stability through microphysical processes, such as acting as Ice Nucleating Particles (INP). This study, through a coupled atmosphere-dust-ocean model, investigates the microphysical and radiative impacts of Arabian dust on a convective region in the Arabian Sea during July 2022, a month which saw both high dust and BSISO activity. For sensitivity testing, two experiments are conducted: one with complete dust-radiation-cloud effects activated (DON) and the other with dust effects deactivated (DOFF). The DON and DOFF results are compared to investigate the dust-driven mechanisms that can impact the background environment in which the BSISO develops.

496725.title: Creation of Quickly Deployable Python-based Instrumentation (QDPI) for use in Coursework and Research
496725.authors: Edward C. Wolff IV, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and L. E. Llewellyn, R. J. Trapp, and S. W. Nesbitt
496725.abstract: Field work experience has become a crucial component of meteorology coursework at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Undergraduate students gain hands-on experience by designing their own field campaign and deploying instrumentation to observe weather phenomena, such as thunderstorms and frontal passages. One significant limitation in the scope of these deployments is the cost of instrumentation, with individual research-grade anemometers often costing upwards of $1000, not including the cost of data loggers and other instruments. In Spring 2026, we began the construction of deployable weather stations called Quickly Deployable Python-based Instrumentation (QDPI) as an alternative to high-cost instrumentation. The basic components of the stations were largely sourced from online electronics suppliers, while others, such as anemometers and wind vanes, were 3D printed following instructions from the NSF NCAR 3D PAWS program, resulting in a per station cost of less than $500. Each station measures wind speed and direction, temperature, humidity, and pressure and is mounted on a heavy-duty tripod to allow for quick set-up. Raspberry Pi computers handle data logging using scripts written entirely in Python. This allows for the easy addition of other instruments and the possibility for students to design and build their own sensors in the future. Data from student-led deployments on severe convection, comparisons to research-grade instruments, and plans for the use of QDPI in future coursework and research applications will be discussed.

496726.title: Land-Atmosphere Verification Capabilities in the Enhanced Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) for Community and Operational Users
496726.authors: Daniel R. Adriaansen, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. J. Newman, J. H. Gotway, G. P. McCabe Jr., K. Newman, S. Miller, J. A. Otkin, and M. B. Ek
496726.abstract: The 2021 community metrics workshop organized by NOAA and the Developmental Testbed Center (DTC) identified the need to include land focused metrics (e.g. land states and land-atmosphere coupling) into NOAA operational and community verification software. In response, several initial efforts to address these needs within the enhanced Model Evaluation Tools (METplus) open-source system were launched that are nearing completion. A host of land related capabilities in the METplus software are available for community use. By including these capabilities in official METplus software releases, they can be transitioned to operations by NOAA’s Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) as part of their Evaluation and Verification System (EVS). For example, we have added the ability to ingest soil temperature and moisture data from the International Soil Moisture Network (ISMN), US Climate Reference Network (USCRN) soils data, NYSM flux and standard data, as well as satellite soil moisture data from the NOAA Soil Moisture Operational Products System (SMOPS) product, either through core MET enhancements or METplus Python embedding scripts. Ingest of these observations enables more comprehensive soil moisture and temperature evaluation. We have also included several process diagnostics for land-atmosphere coupling in an effort to better understand why sensible weather biases and errors may exist. These diagnostics include the Terrestrial Coupling Index (TCI), Convective Triggering Potential (CTP) combined with the Humidity Index (HI), information theory metrics such as mutual information, and other land-atmosphere coupling indices. Further, we have developed METplus use cases for all the advances to provide users a basic scripting and example configuration workflow to use with METplus for land verification purposes. We will provide an overview of the METplus land verification capabilities and highlight select use cases.

496727.title: Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) Prediction Skill and Stratosphere-Troposphere Coupling in the NASA GEOS-S2S-3 Model.
496727.authors: Priyanka Yadav, GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and C. Orbe and S. Pawson
496727.abstract: Sudden Stratospheric Warmings (SSWs) represent a critical source of subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) predictability, often driving persistent wintertime surface weather anomalies. However, accurately forecasting the onset of SSW events and capturing their downward influence remains a significant challenge for dynamical forecast systems. This study investigates the prediction skill of SSWs and the subsequent stratosphere-troposphere coupling in the NASA’s latest GEOS Sub-seasonal to Seasonal Prediction system (GEOS-S2S-3). Using a comprehensive set of boreal winter hindcasts from the NASA GEOS-S2S-3 system, we evaluate the forecast skill of SSWs from 1991–2024. To quantify the model's predictive capabilities, we calculate standard verification metrics at varying subseasonal lead times, focusing specifically on hit rates and false alarm rates for SSW onset. Furthermore, we assess the model’s physical representation of stratosphere-troposphere coupling, analyzing how well the GEOS-S2S-3 captures the downward propagation of temperature anomalies from the stratosphere to the lower troposphere following a SSW event. Results presented will highlight the predictable lead times for SSW onset within the system. Ultimately, diagnosing these capabilities and limitations provides critical insights for improving subseasonal forecast skill.

496728.title: TROPICAL - Interactions between Inner Core Dynamics and Questionable Model Initialization in Hurricane Melissa (2025) Using FV3 and MPAS
496728.authors: Samuel G. Trahan, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and C. Evans, C. R. Holt, B. W. Green, and J. Olson
496728.abstract: Hurricane models initialized during chaotic time periods can be sensitive to the exact initial state. Details one may normally overlook, such as zero vertical wind and zero graupel number concentration at t=0, can have unexpected effects on hurricane inner-core dynamics. The 2025 version of our MPAS experimental configuration was found to suddenly weaken and change storm sizes in the first few hours of each simulation, sometimes recovering. This work compares model output from two dynamical cores (FV3 and MPAS) to observational data and analyzes one specific case. We examine a case from Hurricane Melissa (2025) initialized during a possible eyewall replacement cycle on October 28 at 0 UTC. In observations, no cycle formed, though numerical forecasts were inconsistent about predictions of that. Our 2025 version of MPAS formed a typical primary and secondary circulation. However, it displayed unexpected features in the inner-core region such as updrafts and downdrafts in the eye, large amounts of eye precipitable water, and initially sharp convection throughout the storm that slowly diffused. In 2026, we are experimenting with a newer configuration. Both versions of our MPAS model were initialized off of the FV3-based GFS and HAFS-A models. We examine the response of the FV3-based HAFS-A to these same initial conditions, and compare both models to the observations of Melissa.

496729.title: Reflecting on Your STEM Journey to Create Meaningful Experiences for Audiences
496729.abstract: Each of our career journeys is a compilation of our past lived experiences, relationships, choices, and joy, making our pathways and entry points into our chosen field unique and dynamic. Can you identify a moment that made you curious and led you to ask more questions and dig deeper? Was this moment in or outside of a traditional classroom? What emotions did you feel? Chances are, your first introduction to science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) was subtle and didn’t involve spreadsheets. Research shows that play and hands-on exploration prepare young children to be resilient thinkers and lay the foundation of scientific inquiry. Furthermore, informal learning environments provide flexible, culturally relevant, and community-oriented opportunities to cultivate interest in science and to engage in ongoing learning. This matters directly for STEM workforce recruitment and retention. Many of us in STEM careers can point to a moment of hands-on curiosity and joy that someone made space for, and we can intentionally create similar moments for the next generation. In this interactive presentation, we will reflect on the key elements that shaped our own career journeys and explore how they align (or don’t!) with current educational efforts to address recruitment and retention in STEM careers. We will also share how exhibits at the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Science (NSF NCAR) Mesa Laboratory Visitor Center in Boulder, Colorado, spark visitor interest in the sciences, expand their learning, and inspire future scientists. This session will offer takeaways and examples for harnessing your own joy and experience to intentionally create STEM experiences that are relatable, powerful, and intangible. The free public exhibits at the NSF NCAR Mesa Lab Visitor Center are managed by the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research Center for Science Education (UCAR SciEd) and created with the intention of sharing scientific knowledge, invoking curiosity, and nurturing the sense of scientific discovery across a wide variety of audiences, providing opportunities for visitors to explore Earth system science and be inspired by those individuals doing the research.

496730.title: Space Weather Diagnostics via Radio Astronomy Infrastructure: Multi-Scale Characterization of Midlatitude Ionospheric Irregularities with LOFAR
496730.authors: Katarzyna Beser, New Jersey Institute of Technology, Newark, NJ; and M. Mevius, T. Verhulst, and G. Perry
496730.abstract: LOFAR (LOw-Frequency ARray) is a midlatitude European radio interferometer centered in the Netherlands. Its low operating frequencies (10–240 MHz, split between the Low Band Antenna and High Band Antenna) make it especially sensitive to the ionosphere's free electron content. Since diffractive and refractive ionospheric effects scale inversely with signal frequency, LOFAR is orders of magnitude more sensitive to subtle plasma irregularities than GNSS. Signals passing through the ionosphere accumulate phase delays, angle-of-arrival shifts, and amplitude fluctuations that directly encode information about the ionospheric plasma, making LOFAR a valuable tool for investigating the state of the ionosphere. Three ionospheric data products can be obtained from LOFAR, characterizing ionospheric plasma density structures at different scales: plasma density gradients from radio imaging (~150 km scale, from source position offsets across the field-of-view), interferometric Total Electron Content (TEC) variations (km to tens-of-km scale, from differential phase across a wide range of baselines), and the S4 scintillation index from dynamic spectra recorded at individual stations (km-scale, responsible for signal diffraction). Together, these enable a multi-scale characterization of ionospheric structuring. Crucially, LOFAR's multi-product capability makes it uniquely suited to monitor ionospheric turbulence as it cascades across spatial scales. Ionospheric turbulence typically originates at large scales and cascades downward to smaller scales via energy dissipation. Because the diffractive Fresnel scale increases with signal wavelength, LOFAR's longer wavelengths are sensitive to diffractive irregularities (~1 km scale) early in this dissipation process. Connecting the S4 measurements with larger-scale imaging and dTEC products provides an observational framework to track how energy transfers across a wide range of spatial scales. In this presentation, we will focus on the night of 30/31 December 2013, when a number of processes were visible within these LOFAR datasets. Imaging revealed Traveling Ionospheric Disturbance (TID) propagation across the field-of-view and quasi-static field-aligned plasma density structures. High dTEC (spatial difference in TEC) amplitudes were detected at both remote and core baselines, with periods when the diffractive scale across the Dutch stations dropped below 5 km, accompanied by bursts of S4 scintillation. Simultaneously with the detection of ionospheric structures by LOFAR, similar features were observed by nearby ionosondes. Geomagnetic activity was low (max Kp 2-); however, a modulation of LOFAR-derived plasma velocity coincided with variations in the magnetic field recorded at nearby ground-based magnetometers. In this study, we investigate the multi-scale connection between plasma structures on this night using three LOFAR ionospheric data products from Dutch stations at High Band Antenna frequencies, compared with plasma density and drift observed by ionosondes, and supported by information from ground-based magnetometers. We assess the relative role of field-aligned plasma density bands and TIDs in generating small-scale, km-level irregularities, and test whether conditions were favorable for the Gradient Drift Instability (GDI) to account for energy transfer to these scales, identifying the likely energy source driving it.

496731.title: New 3D Radar Visualization for Operational Meteorology: From Real-Time Nowcasting to Post-Event Analysis
496731.authors: Marco Aurélio Silva Neto Sr., SIMEPAR, Curitiba, PR, Brazil; and J. R. da Silva Jr., F. Verdelho, S. Paz, and F. Sato Sr.
496731.abstract: Operational weather radar centers have traditionally relied on a static, layered representation of the atmosphere - plan-position indicators, constant-altitude protraditionally relied on a static, layered representation of the atmosphere - plan-position indicators, constant-altitude products, and vertical cross sections - that forces forecasters to mentally reconstruct the three-dimensional structure of a storm from a sequence of independent two-dimensional views. This work presents a new operational data and visualization pipeline developed for ClimatOS, the multi-tenant monitoring platform of SIMEPAR (Paraná Meteorology System, Brazil), that reframes radar data as a continuously accessible, cloud-native volumetric product rather than a set of disconnected images. Reflectivity, Doppler, and derived fields from the regional radar network, including sites processed natively in polar geometry and sites ingested pre-gridded, are reprojected onto a common Cartesian CAPPI grid and archived as chunked, compressed Zarr v3 stores on Amazon S3, organized by radar, date, and five-minute operational cycle. Alongside the calibrated reflectivity field, each cycle carries a growing family of derived products computed directly in the pipeline: column-maximum reflectivity, vertically integrated liquid water following the classical VIL formulation, rainfall-rate estimates calibrated against local disdrometer-derived Z-R relationships, echo-base and echo-top heights and echo depth, a Steiner-type convective/stratiform classification, a hail-detection suite (severe hail index, maximum expected hail size, and probability of severe hail) built on the classical Witt et al. (1998) formulation, low-level azimuthal-shear (rotation) fields derived from the lowest elevation scan, and ensemble nowcast fields blending optical-flow and STEPS-based extrapolation. Because this entire product suite is written incrementally into a queryable, self-describing cloud archive rather than rendered once and discarded, any past volume becomes as readily explorable as the live one, an important but often overlooked gain for post-event work such as damage surveys, warning verification, and case-study reconstruction, where forecasters today typically have to re-run bespoke processing or dig through disconnected image archives. Building on this archive, we introduce "3D+", an interactive volumetric visualization mode embedded directly in the ClimatOS web client. Using WebGL2 and GPU-based ray casting, the browser reconstructs the full reflectivity volume from the Zarr store in real time and renders it through an emission-absorption direct-volume-rendering model, with a nonlinear reflectivity-to-opacity transfer function that lets forecasters progressively suppress weak, cluttering echoes while keeping intense convective cores optically dominant, and interactive rotatable clipping planes that let an operator dissect a storm from any angle without generating a new static product. Because rendering happens on the client GPU rather than a dedicated graphics server, the same volumetric view is available simultaneously on any operations-room workstation or tablet, with no additional infrastructure. We describe the operational motivation for this work in the context of southern Brazil's exposure to supercells and tornadoes, including the 7 November 2025 outbreak that produced two F4 tornadoes in Rio Bonito do Iguaçu and Guarapuava/Candói, part of a sequence of at least 13 tornadoes documented in Paraná through July 2026, and discuss how immediate three-dimensional situational awareness of features such as bounded weak-echo regions, updraft tilt, and elevated hail cores can shorten the interpretation time behind a severe-weather warning. We argue that combining a rich, cloud-native, always-queryable derived-product archive with browser-native volumetric rendering represents a meaningful next step in operational radar product visualization: it moves the discipline from a library of static two-dimensional snapshots toward a persistent, explorable three-dimensional record of the atmosphere that serves forecasters equally well in the first minutes of a warning decision and in the weeks of post-event analysis that follow it. We close by outlining current limitations, including the absence of velocity dealiasing in the rotation product and the restriction of direct volume rendering to Cartesian-gridded fields, and future directions, among them multi-sensor fusion with satellite and lightning data, polarimetric variables, and automated four-dimensional tracking of storm growth within the same volumetric framework.

496732.title: Advancing Knowledge and Applications for the Regional Water Cycle: Summary of Convection-Permitting Regional Climate Simulations Conducted and Supported By the NSF NCAR
496732.abstract: The Water Systems Program (WSP) is a NCAR-wide cross-lab program including teams from RAL, MMM, CGD, EOL, ACOM, and CISL with its inception in early 2000. The main goal of the WSP is to improve understanding of the current water cycle and its likely evolution in future. To address this grand question, NCAR scientists worked with the broad community closely in the area of global analysis of the water cycle in global models, regional high resolution long-term simulations, observations collection and analysis, development/improvement of land-surface/hydrology processes in community models, and AI/ML applications using high-resolution model data. Through ~20 years of research and development efforts, WSP contributed knowledge and high-impact scientific discoveries to the field, generated and developed multiple regional high-resolution long-term model datasets and modeling tools for the community, and cultivated a few national and international research communities (e.g., SAAG, MAAG, and H2US). This presentation will introduce a series of convection-permitting regional long-term simulation datasets produced by the WSP. The ongoing research efforts, future directions, and collaborations with the broad community will be discussed as well.

496733.title: Barocline: Agentic Weather Data Interaction Via MCP
496733.authors: Jonathan G Fairman Jr, Athenium, Dover, NH; and K. N. Fons, A. Vacek, P. M. Jermey, J. Vivola, M. Dyanati, and K. Kaminski
496733.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly changed the practice of scientific software development, and atmospheric science is no exception. Agentic techniques are no longer limited to front-end or back-end work: common meteorological Python libraries are well understood by modern LLMs, and integration with cloud computing platforms such as AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure means that scalable analysis of publicly available atmospheric datasets is only a few prompts away for nearly anyone. However, two barriers remain. First, the quality of results is directly tied to the expertise of the user operating the system. Second, the volume of data involved remains exceptionally high, and long-term time series or continental-scale analyses can cost thousands of dollars in traditional cloud compute. Even with modern analysis-ready, cloud-optimized datasets, most users still face the problem of knowing how and where to process the data, and how to scale and serve results to a broader audience.
