To solve these barriers, Athenium has developed barocline, making accessible existing cloud-native archives of processed, model-ready atmospheric analyses through a purpose-built Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. This combined stack leads to immediate, explainable results, such as a ten-year hail climatology at a point or user-defined radius, or a full continental-scale multivariable analysis executed through an analytical BigQuery request, directly rendered in an interactive map, both returned in seconds, with explainable, cited results and minimal LLM token usage. For many weather questions, barocline breaks the classic "fast, good, cheap: pick two" tradeoff by delivering all three. barocline is more than an interface to Athenium's public application programming interface (API) endpoints: it provides direct access to data across time and space, with functionality extended within the MCP toolset itself to perform geospatial processing, time series analysis, and agentically driven interactive map generation through an interactive MCP App. These tools were developed and extensively tested by technical meteorologists within Athenium. Accuracy and auditability are built in by design: each tool response returns a distinctive signature and a cloud-hosted data artifact that end users can download for independent verification or continued agentic analysis in LLM coding environments. This session demonstrates how cloud-native, expert-processed atmospheric datasets, paired with LLM-native last-mile delivery, answer complex weather-dependent questions at interactive speeds for insurance, reinsurance, and operational users across the broader weather enterprise. Attendees will see live agentic analysis, including severe weather climatologies, hurricane track visualization, and on-demand interactive mapping, with no code, no cloud console, and no data engineering required.

496734.title: Airborne O2 and CO2 Observations Constrain Southern Ocean Carbon Cycle Dynamics
496734.authors: Yuming Jin, University of California Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA; and B. Stephens, E. J. Morgan, and R. F. Keeling
496734.abstract: The Southern Ocean (SO) is a major sink for anthropogenic CO2 and a key driver of the global carbon cycle, yet its air-sea CO2 fluxes and biological productivity remain highly uncertain due to sparse observations and structural errors in models. Global airborne campaigns, including ATom, HIPPO, and ORCAS, provide powerful observational constraints. By profiling the remote troposphere from the surface to the lower stratosphere, these high-performance aircraft observations capture flux signals integrated over entire basins and are not limited by the transport model biases and representation errors that affect estimates from surface measurements. Here we synthesize two recent studies (Jin et al., 2024, PNAS; Jin et al., 2026, Nature Geoscience) that use airborne CO2 and O2/N2 measurements from these campaigns to constrain SO carbon dynamics. We develop an atmospheric inverse method based on a mass indexed isentropic coordinate (Mθe), with diabatic mixing rates constrained independently of coarse-resolution atmospheric transport models by using moist static energy budgets from reanalyses. We apply this method to HIPPO, ORCAS, and ATom CO2 observations to resolve the seasonal cycle of oceanic CO2 flux in three SO latitude bands, revealing weak winter outgassing in the polar band, a sharp phase transition between polar/subpolar and subtropical regions, and substantially stronger summer uptake at high latitudes than estimates derived from pCO2 products based on profiling floats. We also apply the same framework to airborne O2/N2 observations to derive a seasonal climatology of oceanic O2 flux, and isolate its thermal and nonthermal (biological) components. The seasonal net outgassing of biological O2 provides an emergent constraint on SO net primary production (NPP) in CMIP6 models, yielding 6.5 ± 1.4 PgC yr-1 south of 44°S, which is substantially higher than most CMIP6 and satellite estimates, but consistent with values derived from Argo oxygen measurements. Combining this productivity constraint with the CO2 fluxes derived from the same airborne data, we benchmark the representation of the SO carbon cycle in CMIP6 models. Models with underestimated NPP exhibit weak summer CO2 uptake, and several also show excessive thermal outgassing, producing incorrect seasonal CO2 flux cycles. These errors likely stem from inadequate representation of ocean vertical mixing and circulation, which govern nutrient supply, stratification, and heat redistribution and thereby shape both the biological and thermal components of air-sea gas exchange. These results demonstrate that global airborne surveys can deliver seasonally resolved constraints on ocean carbon cycling at basin scale that are not achievable from surface networks or satellites. Looking forward, detecting trends in SO productivity will require sustained global surveys in the style of ATom, namely two additional decadal sets of about five campaigns each with coverage similar to ATom, HIPPO, and ORCAS over the SO. Earlier detection is achievable through denser spatial and temporal sampling and improved measurement calibration. New platforms such as the NASA B777, with greater range and payload capacity, present a timely opportunity to extend this observational strategy and track the evolving SO carbon sink.

496735.title: Bridging Operational Response and Long-Term Action Using AI-Enhanced Planning: The Drought Planning Platform for Community Resilience
496735.authors: Meredith Muth, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and K. Eigsti, M. R. Alexander, J. branham, K. O'shea, J. L. Huntington, K. Onda, S. Ansari, V. Deheza, and S. Neff
496735.abstract: As hydrometeorological extremes accelerate, urban centers and rural communities face unprecedented challenges from extreme weather hazards. Among these, drought remains one of the most insidious, where water supply shortages threaten critical physical infrastructure, strain social systems, and amplify the impacts of other hazards such as wildfire and heat. Addressing these vulnerabilities requires planners to move from reactive to proactive strategies, bridging the gap between rapid operational response and long-term resilience. However, navigating complex datasets and policy frameworks often creates significant barriers for resource-constrained communities. To address this challenge, NOAA’s National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS) and the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (BOR), in partnership with NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) and the Argonne National Laboratory, are developing a Drought Planning Platform in collaboration with federal, state, and academic partners. The Platform is a first-of-its-kind federal decision-support system, empowering communities to build sustainable resilience by coordinating trusted public data and leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) to provide science-based technical assistance and tailored guidance. This new tool, in the development phase with an initial focus on the Western U.S., will help users to develop, update, and communicate their own locally-relevant drought hazard plan by guiding them through the process, recommending evidence-based approaches, and building their capacity to justify and maintain their decisions over time. This presentation will detail the collaborative development approach, architectural framework, interdisciplinary data integration methods, and AI decision-support mechanics behind the Drought Planning Platform. Furthermore, it will showcase real-world examples of how municipal leaders and water providers can leverage this tool to improve or create drought contingency plans, and support adaptive and resilient communities, including those with limited resources.

496736.title: Retrieving Temperature and Cloud Particle Properties from Radar Quasi-Vertical Profile Gradients through Machine Learning
496736.authors: Song Zhang, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA; and M. Kumjian and S. J. Greybush
496736.abstract: To accurately constrain microphysics schemes in weather models for winter storm intensity forecasts, obtaining correct information about lower-tropospheric vertical temperatures and the corresponding hydrometeor distribution in winter precipitation events is critical. However, observational temperature data and cloud particle measurements are quite rare during winter storms, limiting their use in operational applications. Fortunately, because polarimetric radars have shown great potential to reveal important properties about hydrometeor populations, a reliable relationship can be drawn between ice growth temperature regions and dual-polarization radar observations. Such a relationship can potentially be used to determine the lower-tropospheric thermodynamic conditions and the corresponding microphysics structures during winter precipitation events to improve NWP models through data assimilation. To build such radar-temperature relationship, we trained a fully connected neural network (i.e., a multi-layer perceptron, or MLP), through which temperature regions such as the dendritic growth zone and melting layer can be inferred by the polarimetric radar variables’ vertical profiles and their gradients. The MLP trains on atmospheric sounding temperature profiles paired with co-located KENX quasi-vertical profiles (QVPs) of reflectivity (ZH), differential reflectivity (ZDR), and correlation coefficient (CC), alongside their vertical gradients. This model retrieves temperatures at 100 m intervals from 0 to 8 km above mean sea level (AMSL) directly from the corresponding radar signatures. A total of 222 matched winter radar-sounding cases were split event wise, yielding 10836, 2310, and 2295 height-level samples for training, validation, and testing, respectively. Model performance improved progressively across three experimental configurations: while using vertical QVP gradients as inputs alone established baseline skill, adding height AMSL as an explicit feature to the inputs markedly reduced retrieval error, and combining raw QVPs, vertical gradients, and height AMSL yielded optimal performance of temperature prediction. The radar signatures at the matched temperature regions can be further justified through airborne microphysics data, so particle population information such as particle size distribution can be related to both temperature and radar signatures.

496737.title: Cloud-Based Research to Operations Framework for NWS River Forecast Centers and Research Communities
496737.authors: Anthony Preucil, RTI (Research Triangle Institute) International, Hamilton, NJ; and G. H. Park and T. Dixon
496737.abstract: Hydrologic modeling frameworks are widely used for model development, calibration, execution, evaluation, and comparison. However, operational forecasting systems and research modeling frameworks often evolve independently, and this can hinder or limit the transition of research-to-operations (R2O). The Next Generation Water Resources Modeling Framework (NextGen) tries to address model interoperability through the Basic Model Interface (BMI), while the Community Hydrologic Prediction System (CHPS) serves as the operational forecasting platform for National Weather Service (NWS) River Forecast Centers (RFCs). To bridge these environments, RTI and the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) have developed a cloud-based, containerized FEWS/CHPS platform capable of hosting both operational and NextGen modeling components, along with Tools for Exploratory Evaluation in Hydrologic Research (TEEHR). Through BMI-based adapters, NextGen models can be executed and evaluated alongside existing operational models within a common computing environment. By providing a common environment for operational and research systems, the platform enables interoperability enhancements, workflow improvements, and new modeling capabilities to be rapidly integrated and evaluated within forecasting applications. However, the current implementation poses several challenges common to emerging model integration frameworks. These include inefficient model execution leading to slow model calibration workflows, and lack of model state management capability. This presentation will provide system design enhancements that will accelerate R2O transition while supporting continued evolution of both operational and research modeling frameworks. This work is part of the research program conducted by the Cooperative Institute for Research to Operations in Hydrology (CIROH).

496741.title: Invited Speaker Sue Haupt: Partnerships between Public, Private, and Academic Sectors Can Lead to Better Decisions
496741.authors: Sue Ellen Haupt, NCAR, Boulder, CO
496741.abstract: Better weather and climate information does not automatically lead to better risk decisions. For the insurance and reinsurance communities, information must not only be scientifically sound; it must also address the hazards, time scales, spatial scales, uncertainties, and financial consequences that matter to the decisions being made. How, then, can the weather, water, and climate Enterprise ensure that advances in observing and predicting the environment translate into information that is genuinely useful for managing financial risk? The answer lies in sustained partnerships among the three sectors of the Enterprise—industry, government, and academia. Industry begins with the decision. Insurers, reinsurers, catastrophe-modeling firms, and other private-sector organizations understand the financial and operational problems that must be addressed, the constraints surrounding those decisions, and the consequences of getting them wrong. The private sector also invests in innovation, integrates diverse sources of information into models and value-added applications, and translates environmental information into tools that can be incorporated into risk-management decisions. Government provides much of the foundational infrastructure upon which these capabilities depend. Public-sector investments in observing systems, environmental data, research, operational prediction, and authoritative warnings provide information essential for protecting life, property, and critical infrastructure and for understanding environmental risk. Academia, in turn, advances fundamental understanding, develops and tests new observing and prediction capabilities, evaluates uncertainty and limitations, and educates the next generation of scientists and practitioners. The greatest value, however, emerges at the intersection of these sectors. A scientifically sophisticated forecast has limited value if it does not address a decision that matters; a financial risk model is only as credible as the environmental information and assumptions underlying it. Effective partnerships can connect the questions being asked by insurers and reinsurers with advances in observations, prediction, climate science, data analytics, and risk modeling. Managing the financial consequences of increasingly consequential weather and climate extremes therefore requires more than better forecasts or better models in isolation. It requires an Enterprise in which users help define the questions, scientists and operational organizations advance our ability to answer them, and the private sector translates those answers into actionable risk information. Strengthening these connections can help move the insurance and reinsurance communities from simply having more weather and climate information to having better information for quantifying, pricing, mitigating, and managing risk.

496742.title: Relational Proto-Object Attention for Mechanistic Machine Learning In Scientific Discovery of Tornadogenesis
496742.authors: Ryan Martz, University of Oklahoma School of Meteorology, Norman, OK; University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and A. H. Fagg, A. Berrington, A. McGovern, C. K. Potvin, M. Xue, and N. A. Snook
496742.abstract: While extensive observational and modeling studies directed at understanding tornadogenesis have identified a variety of important meteorological features and key processes that contribute to tornado formation, there remains considerable uncertainty regarding the contributions from both known and unknown features/processes. Toward improving our understanding of these key features and processes, we propose a novel explainable deep neural network architecture to identify important storm-level features that lead to tornadogenesis in supercells at a given lead time by training on high-resolution (50m grid-spacing) CM1 simulations. The model simultaneously learns to 1) identify multiple sparse state variable combinations (learned features) that highlight important storm-level processes (classes), and 2) the relationships (based on the compositions, class types, and relative locations of the proto-objects) between instances of these classes (proto-objects) that are predictive of tornado formation. The identified proto-objects are summarized using a single vector that also includes class type and coordinate within the field. The locations of proto-objects within the learned feature fields that define the class can be used to infer the process being highlighted by each set of proto-objects. Results from a suite of models trained for 30-second predictions show that this architecture reliably produces skillful models that learn to identify a tornado like structure using physically consistent variables (i.e., horizontal pressure perturbation and horizontal wind speed). The suite contains some models that also rely on mid-level inflow information (helping drive positive forecasts) as well as precipitation core strength (helping drive null forecasts), although these patterns do not show up in every model. Continued work will focus on extending performance to further lead times to identify tornado precursors as well as quantifying the sensitivity of the forecasts to the different learned objects.

496745.title: Correcting the Stratosphere Improves S2S Forecasts in NeuralGCM
496745.authors: Xiuyuan Ding, University of California Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA; and G. Chen, B. Xiang, and Y. Nie
496745.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based atmospheric models are rapidly advancing weather and subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction, but their reliability for extremes on S2S timescales remains uncertain. Sudden stratospheric warmings (SSWs) provide a critical test because these high-impact stratospheric extremes can influence surface weather for weeks through downward stratosphere-troposphere coupling. Yet stratospheric processes remain underexamined in evaluations of AI-based forecast models. Here, we evaluate SSW prediction and downward coupling in NeuralGCM, a hybrid AI-physics atmospheric model. We analyze hindcasts initialized before all 19 observed SSWs during 2000–2024 and compare them with ECMWF hindcasts. NeuralGCM shows limited skill in predicting SSWs: for hindcasts initialized within 5 days before observed onset, only 31–34% of NeuralGCM ensemble members predict the events, compared with 100% in ECMWF. This limitation occurs despite reasonable mean forecast skill at 10 hPa, demonstrating that aggregate skill metrics can obscure deficiencies in predicting rare but dynamically important events. To isolate the influence of stratospheric forecast errors, we conduct nudging experiments in which the NeuralGCM stratosphere is relaxed toward ERA5 while the troposphere evolves freely. Experiments initialized approximately 21 days before and within 5 days before SSW onset both show that nudging restores persistent negative Northern Annular Mode anomalies in the lower stratosphere and coherent downward propagation into the troposphere. The nudged forecasts produce cold anomalies over Eurasia and a southward shift of precipitation over Europe that are more consistent with observations. Over northern Eurasia, stratospheric nudging reduces week-5–6 850-hPa temperature fair continuous ranked probability score (fair CRPS) by 16% (8–22%) and root mean square error (RMSE) by 15% (8–20%). These results suggest that correcting stratospheric evolution can improve AI-based S2S forecasts and highlight the stratosphere as an important source of predictability in AI-based models.

496749.title: Advancing Earth System Prediction with Atmospheric River Reconnaissance
496749.authors: F Martin Ralph, SIO, La Jolla, CA
496749.abstract: The Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) fosters research and operations partnerships aimed at improving forecasts of landfalling atmospheric rivers (ARs) and their impacts across the western U.S, in particular their impacts on water resource management. These partnerships include enhanced observations of ARs and their environments over the North Pacific as part of AR Reconnaissance (AR Recon), in collaboration with NOAA and the U.S. Air Force. AR Recon has become an important component of the federal weather enterprise, demonstrating how targeted observations can improve prediction of high-impact precipitation extremes. These improved forecasts of extreme precipitation support applications such as Forecast Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO), which uses improved forecasts to guide reservoir operations, enhance water-supply reliability, and strengthen flood-risk management. AR Recon has built connections with international efforts, and is an Endorsed Project of the World Weather Research Programme (WWRP) and an Anchor Project for the World Climate Research Programme (WCRP)'s Global Precipitation Experiment. During the past winter (2025-2026), AR Recon was expanded into a Global Atmospheric River Reconnaissance Program (GARRP), in conjunction with NASA’s North American Upstream Feature-Resolving and Tropopause Uncertainty Reconnaissance Experiment (NURTURE) campaign and the European North Atlantic Waveguide, Dry Intrusion, and Downstream Impact Campaign (NAWDIC). As a result, enhanced observations were collected across the North Atlantic during a dedicated 30 day period. This presentation will provide a high-level update on AR Recon, emphasizing the transition to GARRP and associated opportunities to advance coordinated observations, modeling, and data assimilation strategies. The presentation will also highlight the connection to FIRO, demonstrating how improved atmospheric river prediction can translate into practical benefits for water supply and flood risk management. Together, AR Recon and FIRO illustrate how investments in observations and prediction can move from research to operations and deliver tangible societal and economic value.

496752.title: Comparison of Multiple Lidar System Sensitivities at the ARM SGP Site During the REAL Campaign: A Case Study
496752.authors: Duli Chand, PNNL, Richland, WA; and R. Newsom, R. Bambha, I. Silber, P. Wu, S. Gupta, R. C. Jackson, R. Krishnamurthy, J. M. Comstock, A. Theisen, and C. J. Flynn
496752.abstract: The Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program operates multiple lidar systems at the Southern Great Plains (SGP) site in Oklahoma. Recently, the Robust Evaluation of Atmospheric Lidars (REAL) intercomparison campaign was conducted at this site. This campaign aims to evaluate and benchmark the performance of different ARM lidar systems under a wide range of atmospheric conditions. Here, we present a case study comparing Raman lidar, High Spectral Resolution lidar (HSRL), Doppler lidar (DL), Micro Pulse lidar (MPL), and ceilometers. Raman lidar and HSRL observations are widely used to retrieve aerosol and cloud properties. The vertical distributions and retrieved profiles of aerosols and clouds are compared to assess the sensitivity of these lidar systems. Such intercomparisons are essential for understanding the capabilities, strengths, and limitations of remote sensing systems under varying atmospheric conditions. The results of this study are expected to provide valuable insights into the interpretation of lidar observations and to improve the application of ARM lidar measurements in atmospheric research.

496754.title: Comparison of Moisture-Shear-Convection Relationships Using CPEX-CV Airborne Data and MPAS-A Simulations
496754.authors: Giselle Martinez, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and A. Rowe, K. M. Núñez Ocasio, Z. Moon, S. Wong, B. H. Lambrigtsen, K. M. Bedka, K. L. Thornhill, and R. Rios-Berrios
496754.abstract: Tropical oceanic mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) contribute to more than 60% of annual rainfall across the tropics. Previous studies have linked increased moisture to larger MCSs and more intense rainfall, but with conditional dependence on vertical shear. A challenge in comparing those results lies in the use of different datasets (in situ versus coarser resolution), regions, and definitions of MCSs and environments. The goal of this work is to do a comparative analysis of high-resolution airborne data with these commonly used datasets. Recently, NASA’s Convective Processes Experiment-Cabo Verde (CPEX-CV) in 2022 conducted multiple research flights (RFs) using the High Altitude Microwave Sounding Radiometer (HAMSR), Doppler Aerosols WiND Lidar (DAWN), and dropsonde data to sample a variety of oceanic MCSs and their large- and near-storm environments. We aim to examine the relationship between near-storm environmental moisture, vertical wind shear, and characteristics of oceanic MCSs in the East Atlantic and assess if these relationships are sensitive to dataset. Using the Tracking Algorithm for Mesoscale Convective Systems (TAMS) as a storm-relative framework, we compared moisture-shear-convection relationships between remote sensors, dropsondes, and ERA-5 reanalysis for RFs 7 and 11. Most datasets showed that the long-lived MCS case grew in a greater moisture, less sheared environment than the short-lived, less intense storm. However, moisture results were less clear when using HAMSR data, owing to sampling preferences that also impacted conclusions about the temporal evolution of each case. Additionally, we have MPAS-A simulations run through CPEX-CV that we are using to evaluate its ability to capture observed moisture-shear-convection relationships and their temporal variability from RFs 7 and 11. This presentation will discuss these results and how MPAS-A can represent tropical oceanic MCSs and their environments.

496755.title: Building Community Capabilities for Noah-MP Focused Hierarchical System Development within the Unified Forecast System
496755.authors: Andrew J. Newman, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and A. Bennett, Y. Cheng, T. S. Lin, R. Abolafia-Rosenzweig, K. Newman, A. Rafieei Nasab, E. D. Gutmann, A. W. Wood, C. He, and M. J. Barlage
496755.abstract: Land-surface processes play an important role in short-term to subseasonal-to-seasonal hydrometeorological predictability, particularly where soil moisture–atmosphere coupling and land-state memory strongly influence extremes of drought, heat, and precipitation. Within the Unified Forecast System (UFS), Noah-MP has been identified as the target land-surface model (LSM) due to its advanced process representations and parameter flexibility, creating new opportunities for systematic model development and optimization. Here we present a community-oriented framework for Noah-MP development based on Hierarchical System Development (HSD), spanning offline simulations, single-column model (SCM) configurations, and coupled regional applications. Central to this effort is a flexible, optimization workflow built on the Adaptive Surrogate Modeling Optimization (ASMO) algorithm, which enables efficient exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces using user-defined objective functions and Noah-MP configurations across both offline and SCM based simulations. Complimenting this, we have developed tools for generating SCM cases from ERA5, to support consistent and reproducible evaluation across diverse hydroclimatic regimes. These tools will be released as community contributions to Noah-MP and the UFS software ecosystems. We further present results from offline and SCM-based Noah-MP optimization using more than 120 AmeriFlux sites across CONUS, including multi-season SCM simulations. Results demonstrate improvements in latent heat flux and total surface energy partitioning, as well as enhanced soil moisture states and evapotranspiration–soil moisture coupling in our offline optimization simulations. Our SCM experiments highlight that parameter sensitivity varies across hydroclimates and model configurations. Based off the offline and SCM simulations, we are transitioning candidate parameter sets to test 3-D regional simulations. This work increases the tools available for Noah-MP development within the UFS community with the goal of accelerating land-surface model advancement and improving prediction of hydrometeorological extremes while linking process-level understanding to system-level performance.

496759.title: A Deep Learning Framework for Automated Classification of Mesoscale Convective System Organizational Modes
496759.authors: Wenjun Cui, NSSL, Norman, OK; CIWRO/University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and S. Yan and L. Greisch
496759.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) exhibit diverse organizational modes that evolve throughout their lifetimes, with certain linear modes associated with greater potential for flooding, damaging winds, and other high-impact weather. MCS organizational modes have traditionally been classified through manual inspection of radar imagery, limiting their characterization across large tracking datasets. Here, we develop a deep learning framework for automated classification of linear MCS organizational modes from tracked radar imagery. The framework is designed to be applied to MCS tracking outputs, providing a scalable and consistent approach for characterizing organizational evolution across different tracking datasets. Preliminary analyses use 11,791 hourly radar frames from 676 tracked MCSs, classified as nonlinear or into five linear morphology categories. Because several morphology classes are defined relative to system motion, each MCS is transformed into a storm-centered, motion-aligned coordinate system before classification. A ResNet-18 convolutional neural network then uses reflectivity and storm structure fields to identify morphology, with track-grouped cross-validation used to avoid information leakage between frames from the same MCS. Initial results from the six-class model show the highest skill for nonlinear systems (F1 = 0.80), followed by trailing- and parallel-stratiform modes (F1 = 0.53 and 0.49), while less common linear modes remain more challenging. One-vs-rest AUC ranges from 0.79 to 0.90 across all six classes. Classification errors are not randomly distributed but concentrate near morphology transitions: the 40% of frames that lie within one hour of a labeled transition account for a disproportionate share of the error, reflecting the inherent ambiguity of judging exactly when a system becomes, or ceases to be, organized along a line. The resulting framework will enable consistent characterization of MCS morphology throughout system lifecycles and across long-term tracking datasets, supporting future analyses of morphology dependent hazards and evaluation of MCS organization representation in convection-permitting climate simulations.

496762.title: Controls of Precipitation Variability Across the Maritime Continent
496762.authors: Sreedevi Puthiyamadam Vasu, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; and P. Ray, N. Johnson, E. Nikolopoulos, and N. M. ALEX
496762.abstract: The Maritime Continent (MC) exhibits one of the most complex precipitation regimes in the tropics because of its intricate topography, fragmented coastlines, and strong land–atmosphere interactions. Although topographic influences on rainfall have been widely investigated, most studies focus primarily on elevation, overlooking how multiple physiographic factors jointly regulate precipitation variability from seasonal to intraseasonal timescales. Here, we investigate these controls on precipitation across the major islands of the MC using satellite-derived IMERG precipitation. First, we use Fourier spectral analysis to characterize the temporal organization of rainfall across contrasting physiographic environments. While annual and semiannual harmonics dominate precipitation variability throughout the MC, their amplitudes and spatial coherence vary systematically with physiographic setting. Mountainous regions exhibit enhanced seasonal spectral power over major mountain systems, whereas coastal regions display stronger annual periodicity and broader spatial coherence than inland regions, highlighting distinct topographic and coastal controls on rainfall organization. Importantly, regions of enhanced rainfall do not necessarily exhibit the strongest seasonal spectral power, demonstrating that rainfall amount and rainfall periodicity represent distinct characteristics of the regional precipitation characteristics. To further resolve the spatial heterogeneity of these relationships, we apply a multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) framework across annual, seasonal, and winter intraseasonal timescales using elevation, terrain slope, distance from the coastline (DFC), and the wind exposure as predictors. The results reveal distinct spatial controls on precipitation across the MC, with their relative importance varying by island and timescale. On annual scales, DFC emerges as the dominant predictor across Borneo, while elevation and slope exert stronger influences across Sumatra and New Guinea. Seasonally, DFC exhibits persistent coastal controls over western Sumatra but strong seasonal reversals across New Guinea, where terrain slope emerges as a stronger control than absolute elevation. Contrasting elevation and slope relationships, particularly over southern New Guinea, further indicate that terrain steepness and mountain height represent distinct controls on precipitation after accounting for coastal proximity and prevailing wind exposure. At the intraseasonal scale, coastal proximity and large-scale topography emerge as primary controls, while slope and wind exposure exert more localized influences. Distinct island-dependent relationships between precipitation variance, elevation, and DFC further demonstrate the role of island morphology in organizing rainfall variability. Together, these results show that MC rainfall reflects a scale-dependent interplay of coastal proximity, terrain, and wind exposure, highlighting the need to account for spatially varying controls in weather and climate models.

496764.title: The Role of Upper-Level Shear in Modifying QLCS Updraft Cores and Mesovortices: Insights from an Ensemble of Simulations
496764.authors: Edward C. Wolff IV, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and R. J. Trapp and S. W. Nesbitt
496764.abstract: Quasi-linear convective systems (QLCSs) are often characterized by slabular ascent along the leading edge of their cold pools, though discrete updraft cores embedded within this broad ascent are also common. Previous radar-based observational analysis has shown the magnitude of 5-10 km environmental vertical wind shear correlates to the area and intensity of radar-derived proxies for discrete updrafts. Using a simple analytic model, we hypothesize that the response of the linear dynamics contribution to perturbation pressure to increases in shear magnitude could represent a connection between 5-10 km shear and updraft cores, though other pathways likely exist. To address this hypothesis, we produce an ensemble of 12 high-resolution (250 m grid-spacing) QLCS simulations using CM1. We independently vary 5-10 km shear via changes to hodograph length as well as CAPE via alterations to the mid-level lapse rate. Six simulations are initiated with a cold dam break to mimic frontal forcing and six use a line of warm bubbles to replicate upscale growth from a line of supercells. Our results show that, across both magnitudes of CAPE and both initiation mechanisms, updraft cores above 5 km are generally wider and stronger when 5-10 km shear increases. Impacts of shear on hydrometeor trajectories and thus cold pool intensity represent a complicating factor in the relationship between upper-level shear and updrafts, with stronger cold pools in low shear simulations undercutting updrafts more readily. The impacts of deep upper-layer shear on forcing for low-level ascent as well as mesovortexgenesis and maintenance will also be explored.

496765.title: Accelerating Terrain-Driven Wind Field Modeling for Wildland Fire Applications with AI-Based Windninja Emulator
496765.authors: Nick Krall, The MITRE Corporation, Mclean, VA; and N. Silverman, N. Wagenbrenner, J. Forthofer, and C. J. Lewellyn
496765.abstract: Wind is a primary driver of wildland fire spread, yet generating high-resolution wind fields in complex terrain can be computationally expensive at the spatial and temporal scales required for rapid operational decision support. In this study, we develop a deep learning emulator of WindNinja, a terrain-driven diagnostic wind modeling system developed by the United States Department of Agriculture Forest Service (USFS) and widely used in wildland fire applications, with the goal of reproducing WindNinja-like wind fields at substantially reduced computational cost. The proposed emulator uses a FiLM-conditioned UNet that accepts terrain inputs and scalar upstream wind conditions, referred to as “domain average initialization.” These scalar conditions are encoded as wind speed and direction, and the model predicts spatially varying U and V wind components. Training data are generated from WindNinja simulations that conserve mass and momentum. Each sample pairs high-resolution terrain inputs with U and V target fields produced across the contiguous United States (CONUS) domain. During inference, the trained emulator applies sliding-window prediction with overlap averaging across 106.6 km × 106.6 km domains at 100 m resolution. This produces complete wind fields that aim to preserve terrain-induced acceleration, fine-scale structure, and directional variability while running approximately 100× faster than the original WindNinja workflow. We evaluate the emulator by comparing predicted and WindNinja-simulated U/V fields across CONUS using component-wise RMSE, wind-speed magnitude error, directional error, spatial correlation and distribution of errors, and both spectral and gradient-based measures of fine-scale structure. To assess relevance for wildland fire applications, we further evaluate performance for specific terrain-driven flow features most important for fire behavior. The emulator will also undergo evaluation in NOAA’s Fire Weather Testbed in Fall 2026. By substantially reducing computation time while maintaining an acceptable error tolerance for USFS operations, the AI emulator has the potential to enable faster ensemble modeling and near-real-time wildland fire behavior assessment in complex terrain across CONUS.

496766.title: Advection-Constrained Inverse Reconstruction of Bird Migration across a Weather Radar Network
496766.authors: Raphaël Nussbaumer, Suisse Ornithological Institute, Sempach, Switzerland; Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and A. M. Dokter
496766.abstract: Weather surveillance radars provide unparalleled spatio-temporal coverage of bird movements in the airspace, yet recovering their fine-scale three-dimensional (3D) structure remains challenging. Currently we generate real-time estimates of bird density, flight direction and speed, for the public outreach platform BirdCast, which engages broad audiences with the spectacle of bird migration. BirdCast migration maps rely on spatial interpolation of vertical profiles estimated for individual radars. Most profiling methods only use data from ranges up to 25–35 kilometers, to prevent excessive vertical smoothing and loss of altitude resolution caused by the rapidly increasing beam width with distance from the radar. Profiling methods disregard fine-scale spatial heterogeneity and do not use longer-range data that might capture large-scale variability, thus limiting spatially explicit reconstructions. Here we present a flexible inverse-problem framework to reconstruct vertical profiles and 3D bird density fields directly from raw weather radar measurements. The radar observation process is formulated as a linear forward model mapping a discretized Cartesian bird density field to radar observations in spherical coordinates, explicitly accounting for Earth curvature and the full three-dimensional Gaussian beam power distribution. The resulting ill-posed inverse problem is solved using regularization, allowing the joint incorporation of spatial smoothness, vertical profile constraints, and physical discontinuities such as coastlines, as well as advection constraints that promote temporal coherence of bird density fields along estimated flow directions. We show how advection, in particular, is a powerful approach for compositing data and filling coverage gaps between radars. We also discuss implications of assuming different flight behaviors of birds, maintaining constant flight altitude relative to either ground level or sea level. We discuss the adequacy of each when quantifying migration traffic and migratory stopover, especially in the context of regions with strong topography. Our framework naturally accommodates heterogeneous sampling scales, propagates information into under-sampled regions, and enables the integration of observations from multiple radars into a single 3D reconstruction. Using synthetic simulations and case studies based on NEXRAD data, we show that the method recovers realistic 3D bird density structures and temporal evolution beyond the capabilities of traditional vertical-profile-based approaches. This inversion-based framework provides a general foundation for fine-scale, spatially explicit analyses of bird migration, stopover behavior, and interactions with environmental features.

496770.title: Improving NMME Seasonal Precipitation Forecasts Through Bayesian Hierarchical Post-Processing in the Upper Colorado River Basin
496770.authors: Catalina Jerez, CIRES, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and B. Rajagopalan
496770.abstract: Seasonal precipitation forecasts from the North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME) offer valuable information for water resources planning in the Upper Colorado River Basin (UCRB), yet systematic biases and variations in forecast reliability across seasons and forecast horizons constrain their direct application. We develop a Bayesian hierarchical post-processing framework to calibrate NMME precipitation forecasts and evaluate how different sources of information contribute to predictive performance. The framework is applied to two water-relevant precipitation periods, October-March and April-June, using PRISM precipitation as the observational reference and evaluating forecasts through out-of-sample cross-validation. The Bayesian model represents precipitation forecast uncertainty probabilistically while allowing calibration parameters to vary across forecast leads through lead-dependent regularization. Season-specific hydroclimatic clusters provide partial information sharing among regions with similar precipitation characteristics. Additional experiments evaluate whether antecedent precipitation from the previous year provides predictive information beyond the NMME forecast itself. Preliminary results indicate that Bayesian post-processing reduces forecast errors relative to raw NMME, although the magnitude of improvement varies across seasons, forecast targets, and lead times. Preliminary April-June experiments show reductions in RMSE exceeding 20% for some forecast targets relative to raw NMME. Comparisons among alternative information-sharing structures further indicate that increasing model complexity does not necessarily improve out-of-sample skill, suggesting that calibration of the NMME-precipitation relationship provides much of the predictive gain. Antecedent precipitation contributes additional predictive information for specific forecast targets but does not consistently improve forecasts across seasons and lead times. These results highlight the importance of evaluating hierarchical forecast calibration approaches through independent validation rather than assuming that additional model complexity will translate into greater forecast skill. The proposed framework provides a probabilistic, lead-aware approach for identifying when NMME precipitation forecasts contain useful predictive information and where additional post-processing complexity provides measurable benefits for seasonal water prediction.

496771.title: Beyond 1D Retrievals: Quantifying Aerosol Microphysical Properties Near Clouds with PACE Polarimetry and 3D Radiative Transfer
496771.authors: Olivia Pierpaoli, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. C. Chiu and P. J. van Leeuwen
496771.abstract: Anthropogenic aerosols remain one of the largest uncertainties in climate radiative forcing, in part because most satellite observations provide only weak constraints on key aerosol microphysical properties. The recently launched Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission offers a major advance through multi-angle polarimetric observations that are highly sensitive to particle size and composition. Yet these retrievals are especially challenging in the near-cloud environment, where three-dimensional (3D) radiative effects from neighboring clouds contaminate the aerosol signal and violate assumptions underlying conventional one-dimensional (1D) retrieval methods. Here we develop a retrieval framework for PACE that explicitly accounts for 3D cloud radiative effects and provides posterior distributions of aerosol microphysical properties. The framework is evaluated using synthetic PACE observations generated from large-eddy simulations of trade-wind cloud fields spanning distinct modes of cloud organization with variability in humidity and precipitation. We will demonstrate the extent to which PACE polarimetric observations can constrain aerosol microphysical properties in near-cloud conditions and identify the conditions under which accounting for 3D radiative effects becomes essential. This work establishes a pathway toward more reliable aerosol retrievals in the cloudy scenes that are critical for aerosol-cloud interaction studies.

496773.title: Utilization of the Mobile Atmospheric Profiling Network (MAPNet) for Boundary Layer and Cloud Investigations
496773.authors: Kevin Knupp, Univ. of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and A. Soileau, S. W. Freeman, and P. T. Pangle
496773.abstract: The Mobile Atmospheric Profiling Network (MAPNet) is an NSF-supported facility designed to support investigations of boundary layer, cloud, and precipitation processes over mesoscale domains. The MAPNet consists of three profiling systems that profile winds (915 MHz wind profilers or Doppler lidar), thermodynamics (microwave profiling radiometers), cloud characteristics (lidar, Ka-band profiling radar), and precipitation (915 MHz wind profiler, X-band profiling radar, Ka-band profiling radar, and scanning X-band dual polarization radar). The network capability facilitates estimates of horizontal advection, divergence, vertical vorticity, and heterogeneity over mesoscale domains of ~104 km2). Two comprehensive examples are highlighted to illustrate the MAPNet capabilities for scientific investigations. MAPNet use as an independent network of three profiling systems and one scanning radar. The MAPNet platforms were deployed 60 km south of the Dallas-Ft. Worth metro area to document boundary layer and low-level cloud evolution during the total eclipse on 8 April 2024. The profiling platforms were deployed in the form of a triangle with legs of ~25 km, over locations with contrasting surface characteristics: a completely open setting, scattered trees, and a semi-urban setting. Aside from the expected variation in surface layer winds, cooling was limited to ~1 C at all three locations due to the presence of scattered to broken low-level clouds that reduced outgoing LW radiation. In addition, the cloud fraction was variable at the three sites. Analysis of network data revealed a boundary layer with weak horizontal divergence, a change in vertical vorticity from positive to negative, and weak positive temperature and dewpoint advection around the eclipse period. MAPNet use for network enhancements. The MAPNet platforms have been, or will be used to expand/enhance mesoscale networks. This was done during the PERiLS 2022 and 2023 field campaigns, and has been implemented more recently to expand the ARM Mobile Facility 3 (AMF3) network, centered on Bankhead National Forest (BNF) over NW Alabama. The primary objective here is concerned with the heterogeneity of wind profiles (storm-relative helicity) over a mesoscale domain during high-wind, weakly stable boundary layers within the warm sector of cool-season cyclones over the Southeast. These boundary layers frequently exhibit cloud-topped mixed layers (stratocumulus clouds) that appear to exhibit heterogeneity in both wind profiles and the Sc cloud properties such as cloud base height and fraction. Such heterogeneity may be relevant to nowcasts of severe storms and tornadoes.

496774.title: Operational Evaluation of AI Weather Models Using WeatherBench and Extreme Weather Bench
496774.authors: Andrew Bollinger, Brightband, San Francisco, CA; and R. Keisler, H. Mohrmann, A. McGovern, T. S. Mandelbaum, and D. A. Rothenberg
496774.abstract: Since AI weather models emerged as skillful competitors to traditional numerical weather prediction several years ago, significant efforts have been invested to fairly assess their strengths and weaknesses in a rigorous manner. On the one hand, accomplishing this task is relatively easier for AI weather models because it is significantly cheaper and faster to compute re-forecasts using these tools than with their physics-based counterparts. However, these assessments are confounded by models’ training datasets overlapping recent years of analysis. The ultimate testing ground for any weather model is an operational forecast. Such forecasts contend with a variety of technical (for example, the assimilated analysis state or initial conditions for a model may skew from the reanalysis on which it was trained) and practical challenges (i.e. the specific weather regime of a forecast). To provide this evaluation perspective, ECMWF includes the performance of its AIFS model on its standard charts product and publishes graphics from several open AI models, and the NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed has introduced AI model forecasts into the suite used by human forecasters during recent experiment years. We have built on this foundation by operationalizing a suite of frontier AI weather models and implementing a protocol that runs both WeatherBench (Rasp et al, 2024) and Extreme Weather Bench (EWB; McGovern et al, 2026), providing near real-time, real-world feedback on model performance. We run ensembles of the latest releases from major development labs including Google DeepMind’s WeatherNext2 (Alet et al, 2026), Microsoft’s Aurora 1.5 (Bodnar et al, 2025), and NVIDIA’s Atlas (Kossaifi et al, 2026) and drive a suite of evaluations providing both probabilistic and deterministic metrics for different regions of the world. In addition to classic “skill vs lead-time”, we feature timeseries views to assess how the practical skill of each system has evolved in the past few weeks, and a leaderboard summarizing which models most consistently produced skillful forecasts. We are further incorporating retrospective performance of recent high-impact extreme weather events such as heatwaves, freezes, and tropical cyclones using EWB. The dashboard and all of its data are freely available to the public and hosted at http://owb.brightband.com.

496775.title: Linking VIIRS Fire Radiative Power Variability to Biome and Atmospheric Controls Across North America
496775.authors: Ajay Suresh, University of Texas - San Antonio, San Antonio, TX; and K. Bhaganagar
496775.abstract: Wildfire characterization remains limited by uncertainties in fire intensity, duration, spatial extent, and the influence of fuel, biome, and meteorological conditions. Fire Radiative Power (FRP) provides a measure of instantaneous fire intensity; however, fires with comparable FRP can evolve differently because of variations in fuel characteristics, combustion conditions, fire duration, and weather. This study investigates the spatial, temporal, and statistical variability of VIIRS derived FRP across North America during 2020 to 2025 and examines how these patterns relate to fire evolution and atmospheric conditions. Active-fire detections are aggregated by biome and across multiple temporal scales. Fire behavior is characterized using peak FRP, duration, detection frequency, decay rate, cumulative activity, and Fire Radiative Energy (FRE), with comparisons among pre-fire, active-fire, and post-fire periods and with the same location and season in the previous year. Statistical analysis shows that FRP is strongly right-skewed and cannot be adequately represented by a single probability density function. Therefore, the distribution is separated into lower-tail, central-body, and upper-tail regimes, with a lognormal based distribution used to represent the skewed central FRP range and separate tail models used to characterize low-intensity activity and rare extreme events. Meteorological fields from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, including wind, boundary-layer structure, temperature, humidity, stability, and precipitation, are used for selected events to examine the atmospheric dynamics associated with FRP evolution and persistence. By combining biome dependent FRP statistics, cumulative fire measures, extreme-value behavior, and modeled meteorological dynamics, this study provides a more comprehensive characterization of wildfire intensity and severity than instantaneous FRP alone.

496777.title: An AASC Based Perspective of City Data to Decisions Urban Climate Needs - The Perspective of Climate Services Hazard Response in Cities and Beyond
496777.authors: Allysa Rose Dallmann, ; and D. Niyogi, T. Albright, K. R. Brinson, K. A. Bumbaco, L. A. Dupigny Giroux, D. W. DuBois, T. Ford, J. Genuise, J. Glisan, M. Griffin, J. Krasting, J. Krasting, J. Krasting, J. Krasting, D. A. Robinson, E. Saffell, and R. Schumacher
496777.abstract: Urbanization is reshaping both local climate conditions and the information needed to support weather- and climate-related decision-making in cities. Urban environments modify temperature, precipitation, hydrology, and air quality through processes including the urban heat island effect, land-use change, impervious surfaces, and pollutant and aerosol emissions. At the same time, continued urban growth is increasing exposure to hazards such as extreme heat, flooding, poor air quality, water stress, and infrastructure impacts. State Climate Offices (SCOs) have played an important role in being the nodes of climate data, expertise bridging data to climate information into actionable services. Traditionally, these activities have centered around agricultural and water-resource applications. However, comparable operational climate-service frameworks remain less developed for urban environments. Here we synthesize perspectives gathered through discussions with SCOs across the United States to identify emerging urban climate priorities, the datasets and tools currently used to address municipal needs, and common operational gaps across states and regions. Interviews indicate recurring concerns surrounding extreme heat and urban heat islands, flooding and stormwater management, precipitation and water resources, and air quality and wildfire smoke. Importantly, municipalities are often seeking not simply additional climate information, but localized and actionable information that can directly support planning and operational decisions. Across these hazards, common challenges include insufficient spatial and temporal resolution for neighborhood-scale applications, limitations in urban observational networks, difficulties translating climate metrics into actionable guidance, and a need for greater standardization and integration across datasets. These findings highlight an opportunity to build urban climate services through state climate offices and other city and academic partnerships that connect climate science with municipal decision-making. This presentation will summarize perspectives gathered to date and identify shared priorities and needs across states.

496780.title: Cloud Controls on the Vertical Distribution of Atmospheric OH
496780.authors: Timothy Myers, University of Wyoming, Louisville, CO; and H. Y. Brown, D. Caulton, D. McCoy, T. W. Aerenson, and J. M. Nugent
496780.abstract: The hydroxyl radical (OH) is a short-lived but central atmospheric oxidant, reacting with species such as carbon monoxide and methane and thereby influencing air quality, methane lifetime, and greenhouse forcing. Clouds may regulate OH by altering solar radiation and photolysis throughout the atmospheric column, but this influence remains poorly constrained. We use a perturbed parameter ensemble hosted in a global Earth system model to investigate relationships between cloud properties and vertically resolved OH. Preliminary results show that greater low-level cloud cover is associated with higher tropospheric OH concentrations above the clouds and lower OH concentrations below them. This vertical contrast is especially pronounced in the tropics, where incident solar radiation is strongest. These results suggest that clouds exert a substantial control on the vertical and latitudinal distribution of OH and that cloud observations may help constrain modeled OH. Ongoing work will examine how cloud properties, radiation, and photolysis shape these relationships, while separately quantifying the direct control of water vapor availability on OH production.

496781.title: Assessing the Impact of Radio Frequency Interference on Temperature and Water Vapor Retrievals: An ATMS Case Study
496781.authors: Michelle Wagner, CUNY City College, New York, NY; and L. Zhou and M. D. Goldberg
496781.abstract: NOAA’s Low earth orbit satellite sensors provide more than 80 percent of data assimilated into numerical weather prediction models and are critical for producing timely and accurate weather forecasts. Recent expansion of 5G wireless technology could impact weather forecasting by introducing unwanted radio signals or radio frequency interference (RFI) to temperature and moisture sounding channels used by passive satellite microwave radiometers. In this project a new method for assessing radio frequency interference impact across globally diverse environmental conditions for the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) tropospheric channel measurements is suggested. The method is based on the analysis of the ATMS brightness temperatures simulated using the Community Radiative transfer model (CRTM). Synthetic noise equivalent delta temperature (NEDT) and a spectrally non-uniform radio frequency interference (RFI) - induced brightness temperature perturbation were applied to evaluate the impact of sensor noise and RFI on the simulated observations. Different combinations of ATMS channels were excluded from a machine-learning based retrieval algorithm to evaluate the impact of channel specific information loss on retrieved satellite sounding observations. Comparison with retrievals derived from observed ATMS brightness temperatures showed the best agreement for atmospheric temperature using a noise model with a magnitude of 1 times the nominal NEDT, while results for humidity showed that observations agreed best with a noise realization of 3 times the nominal NEDT. The ATMS channel configuration comparison demonstrated overall degradation with removal of channels which is consistent with expectations. The inclusion of the RFI perturbation in channels 4 & 5 introduced the most severe impact to temperature observations in the low troposphere. Localized assessments revealed how these impacts varied geographically. These preliminary findings support the need for RFI detection capability in order to preserve observation accuracy for the ATMS and downstream assimilation and forecasting accuracy.

496783.title: Tracking Strong Maritime Updrafts: Processes and Grid Spacing Sensitivity
496783.authors: Peter J. Marinescu, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and G. R. Leung, I. Singh, J. Bukowski, L. D. Grant, and S. C. van den Heever
496783.abstract: Convective cloud updrafts flux mass vertically throughout the atmosphere and have significant impacts on precipitation production, tropospheric and stratospheric composition, and regional and global circulations. In particular, the strongest updrafts play consequential roles in producing severe precipitation and fluxing mass into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere. There is still a great deal that is unknown about the processes driving the strongest updrafts, in part due to the difficulties in observing strong updrafts, particularly in maritime regions. As such, this research focuses on two science questions. First, we ask “What forces drive strong, maritime convective updrafts?” Given the recent community focus on global kilometer-scale numerical weather prediction simulations, we also ask “What is the sensitivity of updraft magnitudes and processes to grid spacing from large eddy simulation (LES) to kilometer scales?” To answer these questions, we utilize a comprehensive suite of high-resolution numerical weather prediction simulations of convective cloud systems that has been developed for the upcoming NASA Investigation of Convective Updrafts (INCUS) mission. These simulations are designed with 3 nested one-way grids with 1.6-km, 400-m, and 100-m horizontal grid spacings. They have been conducted with three modeling platforms (RAMS, WRF with Morrison microphysics, and WRF with Thompson microphysics), allowing for a more comprehensive and robust assessment of convective updrafts than obtained using a single modeling platform. Additionally, updrafts are similarly tracked in all simulations with the Tracking and Object-Based Analysis of Clouds (tobac) software package. Model data are output every 30 seconds, which allows for accurate updraft tracking. In this study, we focus on 10 maritime convective cloud cases with strong updrafts. Using the LES-scale (i.e., 100-m grid spacing) simulations, we first assess the force balance within the tracked updrafts using the terms of the vertical velocity tendency equation, including decomposing pressure perturbations into their buoyant and dynamic contributions. We discuss the changing roles of effective buoyancy versus the dynamic perturbation pressure gradient forcing, which vary both as a function of altitude, updraft magnitude, and updraft lifetime. We also compare the vertical velocity magnitudes and tendency equation terms in our model grids with different horizontal grid spacings. Updrafts are ~10-20% stronger in the middle to upper troposphere but ~2-5% weaker in the lower troposphere when using coarser grid spacing. This trend is consistent among all three modeling platforms. We use the updraft tracking, combined with the vertical velocity tendency equation terms, to better understand which processes are responsible for the grid spacing dependence of vertical velocity. We will discuss the physical processes that are resolved at LES scales but are missing at kilometer scales, and the implications of these results on the modeling of convective cloud development.

496784.title: Observed Sensitivity of Snow Microphysics in Complex Terrain to the Presence of Near-Surface Supercooled Liquid Water
496784.authors: Pierce Gardner, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and G. G. Mace and S. Benson
496784.abstract: Snowfall processes in complex terrain are of critical importance for understanding the spatial distribution of precipitation and managing water resources. The Park Range of northwestern Colorado, a region which receives frequent and intense winter precipitation, has been the focus of numerous studies investigating cloud microphysics and mountain meteorology. In this study, remote sensing observations from scanning polarimetric radars, doppler radars, and microwave radiometers collected during the Storm Peak Cloud Property Validation Experiment (StormVEx) and Snow Sensitivity to Clouds in a Mountain Environment (S2noCliME) are used to estimate snowfall properties in the Park Range. Additionally, statistical analyses of more than 500 hours of optical array probe observations collected at Storm Peak Laboratory are used to characterize particle size distributions and aspect ratios, and to calculate dual-polarimetric radar variables using the T-matrix approximation. Snow microphysical properties are then categorized using the 10th and 90th percentile liquid water path (LWP) retrievals from several dozen precipitation events observed during the StormVEx winter of 2010–2011 and the S2noCliME winter of 2024–2025. Results indicate that high-LWP periods are associated with larger and more variable mass-dimensional exponents and ice water content. Vertical profiles of sedimentation velocity, differential reflectivity, and linear depolarization ratio indicate a transition from apparently pristine dendritic crystals to rimed particles, accompanied by a significant increase in fall speeds within the lowest 1 km above ground level. In contrast, low-LWP periods exhibit relatively lower variability in ice water content, mass-dimensional exponents, and fall velocity near the surface, while particle aspect ratios increase, consistent with aggregation.

496785.title: Collecting and Analyzing Longitudinal “Human Observations” During Extreme Weather: Critical Innovations for Advancing Fundamental and Actionable Science
496785.authors: Julie Demuth, NCAR, Longmont, CO; NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. E. Morss, G. Wong-Parodi, A. B. Schumacher, N. Herbert, M. Ng, H. Walpole, and R. Prestley
496785.abstract: Because weather is dynamic, collecting and analyzing weather observations is deemed essential for developing understanding of meteorological processes, including correlational, causal, and conditional processes. Observations are so fundamental and foundational to other activities (e.g., numerical weather prediction, operational forecasting) that our field has designed a sophisticated network of instruments to systematically measure multiple variables to detect features and determine the processes by which they occur, model them mathematically and statistically, and predict the future state of the atmosphere. It is reasonable to assume that people are also dynamic in response to dynamic weather, particularly when hazardous weather is forecast and occurring. In stark contrast to weather, however, there is not a parallel system in place to systematically observe the human system and understand how it responds to the atmospheric system. Recognizing this dearth of data and knowledge, NCAR’s Weather Risk Analysis and Decision-making (WRAD) research team, situated in the Mesoscale and Microscale Meteorology (MMM) Lab, has been leading an effort in partnership with university collaborators, NOAA, and the private sector to develop an infrastructure to help fill these gaps. We have developed a novel methodology to collect “human observations” through longitudinal panel surveys (i.e., repeatedly asking the same questions of the same individuals) conducted over the course of a few days during a hazardous weather event. We collect data with multiple survey waves during the predictive phase when hazardous weather is threatening and with a post-storm survey. All surveys repeatedly measure multiple dimensions of core risk-related concepts-- i.e., forecast informational behaviors, risk perceptions, efficacy (beliefs about outcomes), and protective actions. Collecting these data is akin to a mini field campaign. It requires effort to design and refine the survey instruments and survey fielding approach (e.g., to obtain a survey sample that demographically reflects the target population), monitor conditions for potential hazardous weather, determine what populations are most at risk from a given threat, and field the survey in those geographic areas. Our research efforts have also included developing workflows for spatially and temporally integrating the survey data with other data (e.g., weather forecasts and observations), synthesizing lessons learned and recommendations for future work, and publishing the survey instruments and data in support of NCAR’s facilities role and open science. We also have piloted developing and providing near-real-time analysis of the longitudinal data for targeted risk communication. As of August 2026, our team has collected longitudinal panel survey data from the public for 3 tropical cyclones and 2 atmospheric rivers, representing 20 surveys yielding n > 23,000 data points. We are slated to collect data for at least one more TC in Summer 2026 and two more ARs in Winter 2026-27. This presentation will describe our data collection efforts, highlight examples of what can be learned about people’s dynamic risk perceptions and behaviors in response to dynamic hazardous weather threats, discuss how prioritizing collection of such data are critical for guiding fundamental and actionable weather research in collaboration with atmospheric sciences, and offer future directions for research and training.

496788.title: Multi-Surface Evaluation of the LI-710 Evapotranspiration Sensor Across Nevada and the Upper Colorado River Basin
496788.authors: Christian Dunkerly, DRI, Reno, NV; and R. Jasoni, C. Pearson, T. Caldwell, Y. Kim, K. D. Holman, A. Fitts, A. Nielson, and J. L. Huntington
496788.abstract: Accurate and timely measurement of evapotranspiration (ET) are a necessity in arid and semi-arid ecosystems, yet it remains among the least directly observed variables in operational monitoring networks. Conventional eddy covariance (EC) systems, the standard for measuring ET, require costly instrumentation, frequent maintenance, and specialized expertise, limiting observation density. The LI-COR LI-710 is a simplified, one-dimensional EC-based ET sensor that has the potential to support a path toward distributed ET observation at a network scale: it is low-cost, lower-power, and designed for minimal maintenance. However, its performance across land and water surfaces has not been comprehensively characterized. A multi- surface evaluation of the LI-710 across seven EC flux stations across the Nevada Integrated Climate and Evapotranspiration Network (NICE Net), a statewide mesonet designed for ET monitoring across Nevada, and floating evaporation-monitoring platforms on Lake Powell, Arizona, Flaming Gorge, Utah, and Navajo Lake, New Mexico is presented. Records of LI-710 ET measurements range from five months to more than two full years. At each station, an LI-710 is co-located with an IRGASON open-path EC system. For terrestrial sites, the surface energy balance is constrained by a four-component net radiation sensor plus soil heat flux plates. At reservoir sites, water temperature profiles are used to estimate heat storage. Sites span three surface regimes: irrigated cropland, groundwater-dependent ecosystems dominated by phreatophytes, and open water. We evaluated LI-710 ET against EC estimates of actual ET at half-hourly, daily, and monthly timescales, examining how agreement varies with surface type, atmospheric conditions, and season. EC estimates are corrected for energy balance closure via the Bowen ratio method at the terrestrial sites to characterize systematic uncertainty associated with energy balance non-closure and are uncorrected for the open water sites. Results demonstrate the LI-710 performs well at the groundwater-dependent ecosystem sites, with root mean square deviation close to the random uncertainty inherent to the EC methodology but performed worse at both the irrigated croplands and open water sites, with implications for how LI-710 data should be interpreted, corrected, and integrated into operational products. Our findings underscore that the LI-710 performs best not as a standalone instrument but within a station design that enables energy balance evaluation, correction, and quality assessment. These results offer practical guidance for mesonet operators: the LI-710 lowers the cost barrier to distributed ET observation, but realizing its value requires deliberate station design. We discuss potential configurations, data processing considerations, and lessons from a multi-year operational deployment, supporting the broader goal of making ET a routine mesonet variable for water management, agriculture, and ecosystem monitoring in water-limited regions.

496790.title: Tropical Sources of Subseasonal Predictability of Coastal Sea Level
496790.authors: Tongtong Xu, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and M. Newman, J. R. Albers, and S. Shin
496790.abstract: Coastal sea-level variability on subseasonal timescales can contribute to periods of elevated flood risk along coastlines, yet its sources of predictability remain incompletely understood. This study investigates the relative influences of the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) and El-Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) on coastal sea level prediction using a subseasonal cyclostationary linear inverse model (CS-LIM). The model is constructed from outgoing longwave radiation, 850- and 200-hPa zonal and meridional winds, sea surface temperature, sea-level pressure, and tide-gauge observations from multiple coastal regions. Sea-level pressure is incorporated to represent the inverse barometer effect and its contribution to coastal sea-level fluctuations. Within the CS-LIM framework, we identify a seasonally varying mode (Floquet mode) that captures both MJO evolution during boreal winter and the Boreal Summer Intraseasonal Oscillation, MJO’s summer counterpart. By comparing the full CS-LIM evolution with experiments in which this mode is removed, we isolate its contribution to coastal sea-level variability and predictability. We further assess how ENSO-related background conditions influence coastal sea-level evolution and modulate subseasonal forecast skill. The results reveal substantial regional and seasonal differences, with some coastlines exhibiting stronger and more persistent MJO-related signals and greater sensitivity to ENSO conditions than others. The CS-LIM’s ability to represent MJO- and ENSO-related teleconnections and their coastal impacts is further evaluated through comparisons with operational forecast systems. These findings highlight the impact of representing tropical variability in subseasonal coastal sea-level prediction and demonstrate the potential of CS-LIM as a tool for operational forecasts of U.S. coastal sea level.

496791.title: Extreme Rainfall in Southeastern South America: An Event-Based Framework for the Pampa Biome
496791.authors: Leticia Naitzel, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Agronomia, Porto Alegre, Brazil; and D. H. Bromwich, F. E. Aquino, P. T. Valente, and J. C. Simoes
496791.abstract: Extreme precipitation is commonly characterized using climate indices that summarize the frequency or magnitude of rainfall above predefined thresholds. While these metrics have become standard for climate monitoring, they often describe isolated extreme days or fixed accumulation periods and provide limited information on the persistence and total severity of individual rainfall events. As a result, hydrometeorological events that produce substantial impacts may not be fully represented by existing indices. Southeastern South America is a hotspot of extreme precipitation, with projected changes in the frequency and intensity of heavy rainfall posing increasing challenges for hydrological risk assessments. This study proposes an event-based framework to identify and characterize extreme rainfall events across the Pampa Biome of southeastern South America (Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay) during 1979–2025. Extreme events are defined as consecutive wet days (daily precipitation > 1 mm) containing at least one day exceeding the local 90th percentile (P90) of daily precipitation. The proposed framework also evaluates alternative definitions of wet days (>0 mm versus >1 mm) to examine their influence on percentile thresholds and event identification. The choice of the wet-day threshold was guided by both methodological consistency and regional precipitation characteristics. As a result, wet days were defined using a 1-mm threshold, consistent with widely used climate-extreme indices and IPCC assessments. Using wet days rather than all days avoids the dilution of precipitation percentiles by zero-precipitation days, which can result in unrealistically low extreme-rainfall thresholds in drier locations. This choice was further supported by the observed stability of wet-day frequency across the Uruguayan Savanna Ecoregion (USE), which spans the Brazilian and Uruguayan portions of the Pampa Biome, with less than 1.9% of the region exhibiting significant trends in the annual number of wet days during 1979–2025. This suggests that the use of a wet-day-based percentile is appropriate for the study region, where changes in the occurrence of wet days were spatially limited. For each identified event, three complementary attributes were quantified: frequency, persistence (event duration), and severity (total accumulated precipitation throughout the event). In addition, an integrated index combining frequency, persistence, and severity was developed to characterize the evolution of extreme rainfall regimes across the Pampa Biome. The 90th percentile was selected to balance the identification of sufficiently rare rainfall events with an adequate sample size for seasonal characterization; higher percentiles (e.g., P95 and P99) would identify fewer events and could result in zero-frequency values for some seasons and locations. Therefore, this approach treats each rainfall event as a continuous physical process rather than a collection of independent extreme days. Preliminary analyses conducted for the identified a coherent hotspot in the central-eastern part of this region, where extreme rainfall events became simultaneously more frequent, more persistent, and more severe over the 1979–2025 period. This area, representing 8.3% of the USE, exhibited significant positive trends in the integrated index. The largest significant slopes corresponded to approximately nine additional events, one additional day of event persistence, and nearly 50 mm of accumulated precipitation per event over the study period. Trend analyses revealed contrasting statistical responses among the three event attributes. Significant increases in event frequency affected 17.4% of the USE, while significant decreases occurred across only 0.3%, with the spatial distribution of frequency trends showing a markedly different pattern from those of persistence and severity, particularly across the central-southern USE.
