In contrast, persistence and severity exhibited broadly similar spatial patterns, although their statistically significant areas differed substantially. Significant decreases in event duration affected 12.7% of the study area, compared with only 1.2% showing significant increases, whereas significant increases in event severity occurred across 8.9% and decreases across 3.5%. Despite these differences in the spatial distribution and statistical significance of individual attributes, only 0.5% of the USE showed a significant decrease in the integrated index, whereas 8.3% exhibited significant increases. This indicates that the integrated index reflects the combined contributions of frequency, persistence, and severity, which may reinforce or partially offset one another across different regions. These contrasting responses demonstrate that changes in extreme rainfall cannot be adequately described by event frequency or a single event attribute, highlighting the value of integrating frequency, persistence, and severity within an event-based framework. This way, the proposed methodology provides a more physically meaningful representation of rainfall extremes and offers a flexible framework for climate hazard assessments, hydrological applications, and future climate projections across southeastern South America.

496794.title: Characterizing Subseasonal Skill from Public Forecasts for use in Power Sector Applications
496794.authors: Patrick Hawbecker, Sunairio, Baltimore, MD; and B. Ho, R. Hasegawa, O. Pfeiffer, and R. Cirincione
496794.abstract: Utilities and power-sector decision-makers rely on subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) temperature outlooks for unit commitment, maintenance scheduling, load forecasting, large-load generation planning, hedging, and other long-range planning activities. Yet the operational value of publicly available S2S forecasts is difficult to assess. Forecast skill is conventionally verified at the same sub-daily or daily resolution at which forecasts are issued; many planning decisions, on the other hand, are built around multi-day windows rather than single-timestep values. This mismatch between how forecast skill is measured and how forecasts are actually used in the power sector raises a simple question: does public S2S guidance already contain skill that is hidden at native resolution – and if so, can machine learning post-processing recover it at operationally-relevant timescales? We evaluated both raw and machine-learning-corrected temperature forecasts from ECMWF's Extended-Range Ensemble Forecast and NCEP's Coupled Forecast System model, Version 2, at lead times of 3 to 6 weeks, comparing skill at native (6-hourly and daily) resolution against skill computed over 3-day and 7-day aggregation windows. We found raw public forecasts to show no skill improvement above climatology beyond about three weeks of lead time, with this result holding both at native resolution and after 3-day and 7-day aggregation. After the same forecasts are passed through a machine learning bias-correction and error-reduction framework, however, 3-day and 7-day aggregated statistics show clear, persistent skill over climatology out to 6 or more weeks of lead time–native and daily resolution skill, on the other hand, remains unimproved relative to climatology. In other words, usable subseasonal predictability is already present in public forecasts. For power-sector applications, standard 6-hourly or daily verification metrics can understate the true value of a forecast, and combining AI/ML bias correction with multi-day aggregation can be a low-cost way to extend actionable S2S forecast horizons for load, generation, and risk-management decisions without requiring new model development or novel forecasts.

496795.title: Investigating the Characteristics of Variability of the Subtropical Jet over the Eastern Caribbean During the Dry Season: The Role of Moisture Transport and its Relationship with the El Niño Southern Oscillation
496795.authors: Keoni Amiel Theon Williams, Barbados Meteorological Services, Christ Church, Barbados; Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology, Bridgetown, St. James, Barbados; and L. Pologne, T. Allen, and W. McGeary
496795.abstract: Investigating the Characteristics of Variability of the Subtropical Jet over the Eastern Caribbean During the Dry Season: The Role of Moisture Transport and its Relationship with the El Niño Southern Oscillation Keoni Williams1,2, Lawrence Pologne1, Theodore Allen3, Wayne McGeary1 1Caribbean Institute for Meteorology & Hydrology 2Barbados Meteorological Services 3University of The West Indies, Centre for Resource Management and Environmental Studies ABSTRACT High precipitation events and related severe weather occurrences during the dry season across the Eastern Caribbean have increased in intensity and frequency since 1980. In some instances, daily rainfall totals have rivaled those typically observed during the wet season. This study investigates the variability of the Subtropical Jet (STJ) over the Eastern Caribbean, its role in moisture transport, and its relationship with the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Gridded daily geopotential height and zonal & meridional wind component reanalysis data at 250 hPa from ERA5 and NCEP-NCAR Reanalysis were used to calculate Empirical Orthogonal Functions (EOFs) and daily rainfall composites for the period 1980-2024. Results reveal that during December, January & February (DJF), STJ frequently extends deep into the tropics, with its jet core positioned near the Eastern Caribbean, significantly influencing regional weather. The STJ also appears to act as a channel for upper-level moisture transport, advecting moisture from the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) into the Eastern Caribbean. Additionally, further analysis is being conducted to determine a correlation between STJ intensity and ENSO. The work provides a plausible explanation for the occurrence of extreme rainfall events during the dry season and highlights the STJ’s critical role in modulating weather and moisture transport across the Eastern Caribbean.

496796.title: WeatherDreamer: Direct Observation Prediction Using Multimodal World Models
496796.authors: Kate Duffy, Zeus AI, CAMBRIDGE, MA; and E. penn, T. Ballard, A. Posch, and T. Vandal
496796.abstract: Operational ML weather prediction models excel at atmospheric forecasting, but many remain tethered to external numerical data assimilation systems for initial analyses. WeatherDreamer is a generative world model that internalizes the cyclical mechanics of traditional data assimilation while operating on more than twenty observation sources, including gridded satellite imagery and irregular point data. The architecture tracks Earth system dynamics as a Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) using three interdependent latent representations: a deterministic history state, a background prior state, and a posterior analysis state. During assimilation steps, a transformer compares incoming observations against expectations to update the posterior state. In autonomous rollout mode or during data denial, the model substitutes the predicted prior directly into the recurrence loop to propagate filtering updates forward in constant O(1) time per step. Inputs are mapped continuously across spatial, and vertical dimensions, utilizing coordinate-field decoders to reconstruct fields at arbitrary query locations without grid or patch constraints. Masked multimodal training forces the unified latent space to learn cross-modal relationships, enabling any-field reconstruction from the unified analysis state. To resolve calibration mismatches and geometric artifacts across observing platforms, viewing angle is incorporated as an explicit observation label, allowing the model to learn smooth limb-darkening corrections and decode nadir views globally without manual tuning. We demonstrate that WeatherDreamer provides a scalable, observation-driven alternative to classical numerical data assimilation pipelines, applicable across spatial scales to produce globally gap-filled, harmonized radiances, continuous profile retrieval learned from radiosondes, and competitive short-term cloud and irradiance forecasting.

496800.title: Forecast Benefits of the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder Constellation
496800.abstract: The Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) constellation provides soundings of temperature and humidity. The constellation of 6U cubesats achieved one-hour global average revisits in early 2026. The combination of sun-synchronous orbits (SSO) and 45 degree inclined orbits in the TMS constellation provides more rapid revisits in the tropics than would an equal number of satellites in SSO. Tomorrow.io previously demonstrated that two TMS satellites in unique orbital planes can produce similar impacts as two ATMS instruments in a single orbital plane on global 2-day water vapor forecasts during January 2025. That study was intended to provide a starting point for the community, but it had limitations, including a 6-hourly 3D DA algorithm and no accounting for the fields of view (FOV) differences of various microwave sounders (MWSs). The 6-hour window conceals coverage gaps in the public backbone of MWSs. Furthermore, effectively distributing the analysis increments from rapid-revisit MWSs requires separating their overpasses across independent DA windows. The varying FOV across MWS instruments elicits different information content per pixel at a fixed noise level, yielding inconsistent impact estimates when assimilating raw data. The most common solution is to assimilate horizontally averaged super observations, reducing noise and creating an effective FOV closer to the resolved scale of the forecast model. Here we show results from an updated study with the full constellation during 2026. We ingest TMS with 6-hourly 4DEnVar and hourly subwindows. We will present the impacts on weather forecasts of varying multiple aspects of interest to the community: Horizontal super-obbing Constellation size Independent and combined assimilation of F-band (around 118 GHz) and G-band (around 183 GHz) channels This work is aimed at informing operational users. We use a common starting point, replicating many scientific aspects of the NOAA Office of Modeling and Development (OMD) next-generation GDAS prototype. We leverage public software packages, including the Unified Forecast System (UFS) and the Joint Center for Satellite Data Assimilation (JCSDA) Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI).

496803.title: Scaling the GEO Instrument IR Band Radiances to the Aqua-MODIS C7 Reference using Aqua-AIRS and NOAA-20-CrIS as Transfer Radiometers
496803.authors: Conor Haney, Analytical Mechanics Associates, Hampton, VA; Analytical Mechanics Associates, Hampton, VA; and D. R. Doelling, R. Bhatt, P. Khakurel, and A. Gopalan
496803.abstract: The NASA CERES project provides regional flux and cloud products for climate model validation and the Earth’s energy imbalance monitoring for the scientific community. CERES uses GEO-derived broadband fluxes to estimate the regional diurnal flux variations in between CERES observations. Placing the 22 GEO sensors over the CERES record on the same radiometric calibration reference is critical to ensuring consistent GEO broadband fluxes and GEO cloud retrievals. While CERES Edition 4 GEO sensors were calibrated to the Aqua-MODIS Collection 6.1 reference, the upcoming Edition 5 will be referenced to Aqua-MODIS Collection 7 and will incorporate updates to inter-calibration techniques as well. The Ed5 GEO cloud retrievals are based on the 0.65µm, 3.9µm, and 11.0µm channels for consistent clouds over the record. The GEO cloud code takes into account the channel spectral response function differences and so the GEO/MODIS intercalibration should account for only the on-orbit calibration differences. Sensor IR analogous channel IR brightness temperature (BT) differences are mostly caused by spectral response function (SRF) differences. In order to properly account for spectral differences, the GEO IR channel radiance is compared with Aqua-AIRS hyperspectral radiances that are convolved with the GEO SRF. Similarly, the Aqua-MODIS IR channel radiance is compared with the convolved MODIS SRF AIRS radiance. Using AIRS as a transfer radiometer removes the spectral dependency in the GEO/MODIS intercalibration. This will primarily be demonstrated using Meteosat-7 with Aqua-MODIS and -AIRS, and Himawari-8 with NOAA-20-VIIRS and -CrIS.

496806.title: Using NSSL's Advanced Technology Demonstrator to Observe Precursors to Localized Heavy Rainfall
496806.authors: Emily Blumenauer, OU/CIWRO, Norman, OK; and A. A. Alford, D. J. Bodine, P. E. Kirstetter, R. A. Clark III, and A. E. Reinhart
496806.abstract: Localized heavy rainfall occurring within convective storms can be particularly dangerous, as it can lead to blinding conditions and flash flooding. To mitigate the impact of these conditions, short-term prediction (i.e., nowcasting) methods have been explored using observational data. For example, optical flow methods have been used to extrapolate radar features between radar volumes to predict rainfall rates at future locations. Optical flow methodology uses reflectivity gradients to approximate motion vectors, which has been shown to be effective when estimating horizontal storm motion and vertical motion in single-cell thunderstorms. However, for more complex storm modes (e.g., supercells and mesoscale convective systems), successfully estimating vertical motion using optical flow is more challenging, as reflectivity gradients can be less distinct. Moreover, nowcasting techniques continue to struggle in cases of convective initiation and heavy rainfall. An alternative nowcasting approach involves identifying the precursors to localized heavy rainfall within these complex storm modes, which can be used to inform forecasting decisions. While precursors have been studied for some features associated with convective storm modes, such as downbursts and tornadogenesis, they have not been extensively studied for localized heavy rainfall. Furthermore, past studies have been limited to using data from the Weather Surveillance Radar–1988 Dopplers (WSR-88Ds), which are an operational network of S-band (10-cm wavelength) dual-polarization radars. Typically scanning 14 elevations (0.5° to 19.5°) per volume in 4–6 minutes, the WSR-88Ds may have a somewhat limiting spatiotemporal resolution for three-dimensional convective storm analysis. Specifically, the upper levels are not well-covered in both time and space, and several stages of precipitation evolution can be missed in 4–6 minutes. Compared to WSR-88Ds, phased array radars (PARs) offer faster volumetric update times (1–2 minutes) and increased scanning flexibility. Therefore, with the finer temporal resolution and denser vertical coverage afforded by PARs, localized heavy rainfall precursors may be more observable. In this study, the temporal evolution of the vertical structure of precipitation in storms is investigated using the Advanced Technology Demonstrator (ATD), a proof-of-concept PAR operated by the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL). Localized heavy rainfall events associated with different storm modes are first identified and tracked using the pySTEPS Thunderstorm Detection and Tracking (T-DaTing) algorithm. Mid-level vertically integrated liquid (VIL) density and low-level specific differential phase (KDP) are then examined as a function of time. We find changes in VIL density precede changes in KDP by about five minutes, a time interval comparable to the volumetric update time of WSR-88Ds. This result suggests that the fine spatiotemporal resolution of PARs may be useful for anticipating the onset of localized heavy rainfall.

496807.title: A Deep Learning for Predicting Atlantic Tropical Cyclone Track, Intensity, and Landfall
496807.authors: Vishal Juneja, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and H. Huang
496807.abstract: Accurate prediction of tropical cyclone track and intensity remains essential for anticipating landfall location and the resulting coastal hazards. This study develops a deep-learning framework for Atlantic tropical cyclone forecasting based on ERA5 reanalysis and GFS environmental fields together with IBTrACS best-track data. The framework predicts storm-center latitude, longitude, maximum sustained wind speed, and storm heading at 3-hour intervals through 48 hours across the Atlantic basin, with a structure designed to support regional landfall-focused applications. The model ingests 105 atmospheric and surface channels over a fixed Atlantic domain, encoding large-scale environmental conditions that govern storm motion and intensity change. Training and evaluation use a masked sequence formulation to retain storms with incomplete lifecycles for the loss calculation only over the active storm hours. Systematic experiments across varying encoder design, Transformer configuration, and loss weighting produced relatively modest changes in track and intensity skill, while shifts in normalization strategy and input data management yielded substantially larger improvements. Climatological normalization, which represents each environmental field relative to its local climatological state, produced more consistent forecast skill than normalization based on aggregate statistics from storm-day samples. This result suggests that how environmental conditions are represented prior to model input plays a greater role than internal parameter choices alone. Predicted storm-center position and intensity will be evaluated against best-track observations across forecast lead times. The forecast track will also be used to derive and evaluate landfall location and landfall timing, providing a regional measure of the framework’s utility for landfall-focused prediction.

496808.title: Physics-Informed Neural ODEs for Climate Dynamics and Prediction: An ENSO Forecasting Example with a Neural Extended Recharge Oscillator
496808.authors: Fred Xu, Univ. of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, FL; and K. Lu, D. Kondrashov, G. Chen, and Y. Sun
496808.abstract: Machine learning can improve the understanding and prediction of complex climate phenomena, but fully data-driven models often require large datasets and may lack stability and physical interpretability. In contrast, traditional idealized reduced-order dynamical models, such as recharge-oscillator and quasi-geostrophic models, provide simple and physically interpretable frameworks for understanding climate variability. Yet their simplified structures may not capture important nonlinear and state-dependent interactions. Here, we present a hybrid framework that combines physically interpretable linear dynamics with neural-network residuals. A set of linear ODEs represents the dominant relationships among climate variables, while the neural component learns unresolved nonlinear interactions not captured by the linear system. This design retains the stability and interpretability of simple dynamical systems while allowing the model to learn complex climate interactions from data. We demonstrate this framework using El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) forecasting as an example. Skillful ENSO prediction requires representing interactions between ENSO and other ocean basins, yet these teleconnections are nonlinear and complex. Building on the physics-based Extended Recharge Oscillator (XRO), we retain the linear recharge-oscillator dynamics to represent coupled evolution of ENSO sea surface temperature (SST) and upper-ocean heat content, while using a neural residual component to learn nonlinear cross-basin interactions. When trained on the limited observational record, our hybrid model improves ENSO forecast skill relative to the XRO baseline, including a 13.2% reduction in RMSE. Our small hybrid model also enables real-time ENSO forecasting. Alongside the CCSR/IRI prediction plume, it predicts a strong 2026 El Niño, with a JJA Niño-3.4 anomaly of +1.57 °C and substantially greater warming later in the year. When validated over 262 retrospective IRI-common forecasts, our model achieves the lowest RMSE (0.452) while maintaining a comparable ACC (0.825). These results highlight the value of embedding physical structure into machine-learning models, both for improving small-data climate forecasting and for diagnosing complex interactions in climate models.

496810.title: Evaluating and Improving Experimental Ensemble Water-Supply Forecasts in the Upper Rio Grande Basin
496810.authors: Aydin Bakhtar, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, TX; and Y. Zhang
496810.abstract: Seasonal water-supply forecasting in the Upper Rio Grande basin is complicated by snowmelt-driven runoff, strong elevation gradients, reservoir regulation, transbasin imports, and agricultural diversions. This study evaluates experimental ensemble forecasts for forecast points in the Upper Rio Grande and Rio Chama headwaters. The preliminary version of the forecast system feeds historical traces of precipitation and temperature as forcings to the NWS Hydrology Lab Research Distributed Hydrologic Model (HL-RDHM), thus resembling the Ensemble Streamflow Prediction (ESP) being produced at NWS. To incorporate effects of flow regulation, a management-aware post-processing framework was developed that predicts flows at forecast points downstream of dams, reservoirs, and diversion points. The experimental ESP forecasts were generated for multiple dry, normal, and wet water years between 2000 and 2025 over 21 forecast points, and underwent post-processing using the aforementioned postprocessor. The resulting raw and post-processed forecasts were evaluated against observed or naturalized seasonal volumes and archived water-supply forecasts from NRCS. Results show that experimental ESP forecasts are slightly more skillful than NRCS forecasts at headwater and natural-flow proxy gauges despite exhibiting biases. The performance of the raw forecasts degrades substantially at downstream regulated locations, where reservoirs, San Juan-Chama imports, and diversions alter the relationship between natural runoff and observed flow. At the latter locations, post-processing alleviates volumetric biases, but reduces ensemble range. The analysis demonstrates the potential of the experimental ensemble system in producing probabilistic water-supply forecasts for the Upper Rio Grande, and highlights ongoing challenges including accounting for effects of water management and forecasting rare events such as 2018.

496813.title: ENSO Asymmetry in a Non-Gaussian Cyclostationary Linear Inverse Model
496813.authors: Katelyn A Reagan, University of Wisconsin -- Madison, Madison, WI; and D. J. Vimont and C. A. Martinez-Villalobos
496813.abstract: Cyclostationary linear inverse models (CSLIMs) provide linear, seasonally varying approximations of El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) dynamics in the tropical Pacific. Yet, these linear models are limited by the Gaussian statistics they generate by construction—this contrasts with the observed skewness of ENSO variability. This work investigates a non-Gaussian CSLIM (NG-CSLIM), in which input data are “Gaussianized” using a Yeo-Johnson transformation, the seasonal linear dynamics are fit in the transformed space, and the resulting simulation is mapped back to the original non-Gaussian space. The input data consist of standardized principal components (PCs) of detrended sea surface temperature (SST) and sea surface height (SSH) data from 1958 to 2022. The first two SST PCs are rotated about the origin in PC1-PC2 space to best capture eastern and central Pacific ENSO events. The resulting state variables are transformed using the Yeo-Johnson transformation to promote Gaussianity and then used to fit the linear seasonal dynamics in the transformed space. The model is iterated forward in the transformed space, and simulated data are then untransformed, recovering nonlinear ENSO evolution. These untransformed NG-CSLIM output data have spatial variance and skewness patterns similar to those of the original state vector. Further, the modeled growth rates and periodicities of the underlying Floquet modes are consistent with those estimated from a standard CSLIM, suggesting that nonlinearity plays a secondary role in ENSO evolution. These findings illustrate that the NG-CSLIM reproduces ENSO skewness that a standard CSLIM cannot capture and provides insights into how the seasonally varying dynamics interact to produce ENSO asymmetry.

496814.title: Convective Regime Clustering as a Predictive Tool for Cross-Continental Machine Learning Transferability
496814.authors: Mitchell Gregg, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and K. L. Rasmussen, Ph.D.
496814.abstract: Deep convection over North and South America spans a wide spectrum of environments, yet the extent to which environmental controls on convection generalize across regions remains an open question with implications for machine learning-based convective predictability. Across both continents, regions that share similar large-scale dynamic and thermodynamic conceptual models for convection can still maintain distinct mesoscale characteristics tied to terrain, moisture transport, and convective triggering mechanisms. Here we investigate whether a machine learning model trained on convective environments over North America can be meaningfully applied to South America, treating regions of transfer failure as a physically meaningful diagnostic tool in identifying the mesoscale processes and environment-convective interactions unique to each region. Recent advancements in kilometer-scale, convection-permitting climate modeling (CPCM) enable direct comparison of convective environments across both continents at climatological timescales. Yu et al. (2026) developed a pixel-based multilayer perceptron (MLP) trained to predict convective cloud fraction within the CONUS404 4-km CPCM reanalysis, using 16 variables that together describe the dynamic and thermodynamic state of the convective environment. Because the MLP treats each grid point independently, without spatial or temporal context, its cross-domain performance directly reflects how well environment-convective relationships learned over North America generalize to new regimes. To assess where this MLP can be successfully applied in South America, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to convective environments from 20+ years of warm-season months in both the CONUS404 and the South American Affinity Group’s 4-km WRF (SAAG WRF) simulations under present-day (CTRL) and pseudo-global warming (PGW) forcings. PCA reduces the dimensionality of the 16 convective environmental variables, identifying modes that explain the most variance across the joint, cross-continental dataset. PC scores are then used as input to k-means clustering, grouping grid points with similar storm environments into discrete convective regimes. Because clustering is performed from the joint, cross-continental dataset, regime populations, geographic distributions, and relative frequencies between CONUS and South America can be directly compared. The Yu et al. (2026) MLP is applied directly to SAAG WRF, where regions dominated by regimes underrepresented in the CONUS404 training distribution are expected to contain the greatest transfer error. These regions with degraded predictive skill reflect regionally distinct environment-convective interactions missing from North America’s convective regimes, providing a physically interpretable view of mesoscale processes unique to South America.

496818.title: Quantifying the Impact of WindBorne Global Sounding Balloons on Forecast Skill in an AIDA Framework
496818.authors: Jacob T. Radford, WindBorne Systems, Raleigh, NC; and T. Burg, L. J. Reames, A. Shetty, J. Creus-Costa, C. Riedel, PhD, J. Michaels, T. A. Hutchinson, and J. Dean
496818.abstract: WindBorne Systems operates the largest constellation of weather balloons in the world, with approximately 600 global sounding balloons (GSBs) aloft as of Aug. 1, 2026. Previous studies showed assimilation of WindBorne’s in-situ data into the Global Forecast System (GFS), even at the then much smaller scale of less than 50 balloons aloft, led to improved overall forecasts and significantly improved tropical cyclone forecasts. As the constellation continues to grow at a rapid pace, it’s of utmost importance to continue to quantify the value of our observations on forecasts made by both traditional numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems and state-of-the-art (SOTA) AI weather prediction (AIWP) systems. WeatherMesh 6 (WM6) is the latest iteration of WindBorne System’s transformer-based, global AIWP model. WM6 generally outperforms other SOTA AIWP models such as AIFS-Ens and WeatherNext-2 in terms of RMSE on key variables. Importantly for impact studies, WM6 does its own data assimilation, including assimilation of our own GSBs, on top of the prior provided by ECMWF’s IFS. The exact impact of balloon observations on WM6 forecasts is highly dependent on model architecture and complicated by exponential growth of our constellation. However, as a simple baseline, we have run parallel implementations of WM6 operationally for approximately three months - one with the full data assimilation suite and one denying WindBorne GSB observations. Here we present the results of this side-by-side experiment, measuring forecast impacts as measured by anomaly correlation coefficient, root mean squared error, and bias aggregated across the three months using the full scope of our constellation.

496819.title: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Adaptive Ensemble Inflation
496819.authors: Abed Hammoud, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and M. Gharamti
496819.abstract: Ensemble data assimilation often relies on covariance inflation to mitigate sampling error and model inadequacy, yet conventional adaptive inflation methods are typically based on prescribed, cycle-local update rules. We introduce a novel mathematical formulation that casts adaptive inflation as a sequential decision problem and uses reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize a state dependent multiplicative inflation field. The resulting method is a nonlinear, spatially varying, and temporally adaptive inflation algorithm that maps evolving ensemble and statistical descriptions to inflation factors while accounting for their effects over multiple assimilation cycles. The approach was implemented within the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) and evaluated using the Lorenz–96 model with an ensemble adjustment Kalman filter. We investigate two training strategies: fully online learning through direct interaction with the assimilation system, and offline-to-online learning in which the policy is initialized from experiences collected using the Gharamti (2018) adaptive inflation algorithm and subsequently refined online. Experiments span multiple observation network configurations, including complete, regularly thinned, and spatially clustered networks. Across these configurations, the RL method produces prior and posterior accuracies broadly comparable to the Gharamti algorithm, while matching or improving its overall performance. These results demonstrate that RL can provide a flexible and effective framework for learning adaptive inflation within an operational data assimilation codebase, while naturally accommodating nonlinear dependencies and spatial and temporal variability.

496824.title: Does the Heterogeneous Freezing of Solution Droplets by Biological and Mineral Aerosols Influence the Variety of Crystal Habits in Cold Clouds?
496824.authors: Dixuan Rui, Penn State University, University Park, PA; and Z. Nice, H. Zangara, C. Mampage, M. Freedman, A. M. Moyle, and J. Y. Harrington
496824.abstract: How solution droplets freeze may be important for both the habit development and growth rate of the subsequently formed ice crystals. However, crystal growth theories generally do not include nucleation-based impacts. Prior homogeneous freezing experiments at temperatures below –40°C show that ice resulting from frozen sodium chloride (NaCl) solution droplets has higher (enhanced) growth rates than ice formed from pure water droplets, which could indicate different crystal habit development resulting from morphological transformations. Does this result hold for solution droplets frozen heterogeneously with biological and mineral nuclei? Our previous heterogeneous nucleation experiments using biological nuclei showed that at temperatures between –30°C and –10°C, no clear or consistent enhancement of growth occurs for crystals formed from solutions as compared to pure water. However, our recent heterogeneous nucleation experiments show that different solutes and mineral ice nuclei can impact both the freezing temperatures of the drops and result in higher growth rates of the subsequent ice particles. For example, NaCl solution droplets frozen with biological nuclei tend to grow similar to ice spheres, whereas NaCl solution droplets frozen with kaolinite take on a broader range of growth rates and are moderately enhanced. This might indicate different habit development on the ice crystals. Also, NaCl solution droplets that contain kaolinite consistently freeze at around –37°C in our levitation chamber. However, ammonium sulfate containing solution droplets freeze at higher temperatures when certain minerals (such as kaolinite) are included. This solute enhancement of heterogeneous freezing can cause an increase in crystal habit variety on its own. These data are being used in Lagrangian parcel model simulations to examine the combined influences of solution droplet freezing and ice crystal growth on the variety of crystal shapes formed in atmospheric cold clouds. The influence of this enhancement of crystal variety on mixed-phase cloud properties will be presented.

496826.title: The State of Operational Space Weather Observations Enabling Modeling of the Space Plasma Environment
496826.authors: Elsayed R. Talaat, USRA, Washington, DC
496826.abstract: Operational space weather observations are foundational to forecasting, warning, and mitigation activities that protect space‑based and ground‑based technological systems. As global reliance on satellites, navigation, communication, aviation, and power infrastructure continues to grow, the demand for accurate, timely, and resilient space weather capabilities has become increasingly critical. This paper reviews the current state of operational space weather observing systems across the Sun–Earth system, including solar, heliospheric, geospace, and upper atmospheric measurement domains, with particular emphasis on the transition toward distributed, multi‑orbit, and multi‑partner architectures. These observational advances directly enable modern modeling frameworks that couple the solar corona, heliosphere, magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere. The role of continuous, high‑quality observations in supporting physics‑based modeling, data assimilation, ensemble forecasting, and uncertainty quantification is discussed, along with emerging applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning to accelerate prediction and decision support. Community coordination mechanisms, including international model benchmarking and transition pathways, are highlighted as essential enablers of research‑to‑operations advancement. Together, sustained operational observations and advanced modeling capabilities form the cornerstone of improved space weather resilience, delivering measurable societal and economic benefits through enhanced forecast skill, lead time, and actionable risk information.

496828.title: Lessons from Transitioning a National, Multi-Model ET Data Service into Sustained Operations
496828.authors: Sara Larsen, OpenET Inc, Las Vegas,, NV
496828.abstract: OpenET has matured from a research pilot into an expansive operational, field-scale evapotranspiration (ET) data service now supporting water management decisions across the continental United States. In 2025, the OpenET Consortium Partners completed the generation Collection 2.1 — its most comprehensive dataset update to date — extending full CONUS coverage and a historical modeled ET record back to 1985, while expanding technical capacity to address the distinct challenges of operating in cloud-prone eastern landscapes as well as the arid West. Built on a six-model ensemble and delivered through a growing suite of access tools (API, Data Explorer, and a farm-facing management system), OpenET now serves more than 15,000 registered users. This growth has been matched by deliberate investment in the organizational infrastructure required to sustain it: a maturing multi-partner governance structure and new mechanisms for coordinating decisions across a broad consortium of federal agencies, research institutions, and NGOs. This presentation will focus on what OpenET's experience reveals about the practical work of transitioning ET and related science to operations at scale: the technical steps required to move from a validated research product to a reliable, user-facing service; the stakeholder engagement architecture needed to earn and keep trust across both grower and regulatory communities that OpenET was built to equally serve; and the governance and organizational choices that allow a research-born data platform to function as sustained public infrastructure. As OpenET's model extends toward new domains and geographies beyond its original western U.S. footprint, its experience offers transferable lessons for other research-to-operations efforts navigating similar questions of scientific rigor, operational reliability, and durable institutional trust.

496833.title: Bias-Corrected Ocean Observations Reduce Model-Observational Disagreement
496833.authors: Nathan Lenssen, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and C. Deser, A. S. Phillips, and D. Chan
496833.abstract: Recent work has shown that many observational products of sea surface temperature (SST) contain substantial biases in the early 20th century. Historical SST data is critical for estimating many key properties of the global climate system, modulating global and regional temperature variability and change. In general, the global and regional responses of the atmospheric and land surface to SSTs are quantified using atmosphere-only GCMs (AGCMs) forced with historical SSTs. Here, we investigate how SST biases influence through an AGCM ensemble forced with SSTs from the infilled Dynamically Consistent ENsemble of Temperature (DCENT-I), a recently published surface temperature product that better accounts for such biases. We compare this ensemble with an identically configured AGCM ensemble forced with ERSSTv5, a SST product with substantial early 20th-century biases. We find that DCENT-I SSTs produce more realistic land surface temperature evolution, suggesting that previous AGCM experiments may be artificially inflating model-observational disagreement over land. These bias-corrected simulations additionally show substantially less multi-decadal temperature variability, providing better agreement with estimates from free running coupled CMIP-class models. We close with a discussion on the critical need for accurate estimates of historical SST and underlying uncertainties for driving and validating simulations of historical climate.

496834.title: Regional Reanalysis Through Nonlinear Ensemble Data Assimilation at Convective Scales
496834.authors: Derek J. Posselt, JPL, Pasadena, CA; and L. Wu
496834.abstract: Processes operating at small (e.g., convective) scales are implicated in the development and evolution of most severe weather events. Specifically, high winds and intense precipitation develop in association with weather features that manifest at a few to tens of km, and on the order of minutes to hours. Modern convection permitting models, high spatial and temporal resolution observations, and nonlinear data assimilation algorithms enable new insight into the processes that drive severe weather, and have the potential to enable detailed gridded estimates of the three dimensional state of the atmosphere in and around storms. In particular, km- and sub-km scale observations from geostationary satellites and ground-based radars, when combined with convection-permitting modeling and DA systems can provide unique constraints on the interactions among the larger scale environment and the evolution of severe weather. In this presentation, we show results from convection-permitting ensemble data assimilation experiments of high-impact weather events. We show how modern reanalysis datasets are able to capture the coarse resolution features of the environment, but systematically miss the local high resolution features that drive the position and intensity of severe weather. Outcomes from ensemble data assimilation-based analyses of multiple different cases demonstrate how a regional reanalysis that targets scales of a few km can be used to supplement global coarse resolution reanalysis datasets and enable a more comprehensive understanding of how, when, and where high impact weather may occur.

496837.title: Cloud-Native Processing and Distribution of Near Real-time Global Cloud Products: Leveraging AWS and Zarr for Scientific Visualization
496837.authors: Louis Nguyen, NASA Langley Research Center, Hampton, VA
496837.abstract: Generating global cloud composite (GCC) from geostationary (GEO) and low-Earth orbiting (LEO) satellites requires managing massive satellite datasets for processing and data distribution. To address these challenges of generating GCC dataset operationally, the NASA Langley ClOud and Radiation Property retrieval System (SatCORPS) team leverages Amazon Web Service (AWS) infrastructure to process and merge observations from GEO and LEO satellites to deliver continuous, seamless global coverage of retrieved cloud physical and radiative properties in near real-time. To support big data processing and eliminate the friction of downloading large files, the GCC dataset processing and distribution pipeline has been transitioned to AWS. As part of this cloud architecture, the dataset is transformed into the Zarr datastore format – a chunked, compressed, cloud-optimized array store structure designed for parallel I/O and serverless access to the GCC dataset by applications. Structuring the GCC into Zarr datastores on AWS S3 enables rapid interactive data access, callable cloud-native analytics, and fast visual rendering without requiring full dataset downloads. We will present highlights on the cloud infrastructure design, near real-time ingestion and conversion workflows, and a custom interactive web-based GIS-enabled data product explorer application that showcases the performance benefits (of Zarr) for scientific visualization of large global datasets.

496841.title: A Convective-Object Dataset for NASA’s INCUS Mission
496841.authors: Derek J. Posselt, JPL, Pasadena, CA; and S. C. Van Den Heever
496841.abstract: NASA’s Investigation of Convective Updrafts (INCUS) mission is designed to improve understanding of how, when, and why tropical convective storms form, and why only some lead to extreme weather. The INCUS mission will launch no later than August 2027, and will feature three small satellites in low Earth orbit, spaced 30 seconds and 90 seconds apart. Each INCUS observatory has a 7-beam Ka-band scanning radar with an approximately 10 km swath width, and the middle satellite carries a 5-frequency passive microwave radiometer with a swath of approximately 500 km. This configuration returns radar observations at 30-, 90-, and 120-second intervals, enabling the use of time-differenced radar profiles to estimate the vertical transport of air and water between the boundary layer and upper troposphere, known as convective mass flux (CMF). The radiometer will provide insights into upper tropospheric anvil cloud properties and storm context. Together, these instruments will, for the first time, provide global tropical estimates of CMF alongside convective anvil extent and ice water path. In addition to the data directly provided by the INCUS radars and radiometer, multiple auxiliary datasets will be used to provide context for convective storms. These include: convective extent and life cycle phase, environmental properties, lightning flash rate, and precipitation rate. One of the most high-impact outcomes of the INCUS mission will be the level 3 collocated and feature-based dataset of convective storms and their associated attributes and properties. The INCUS object-based database will include all convective storms in the tropics, whether or not they are observed directly by INCUS. This database will provide a foundation for incorporation of other data relevant to the analysis of storm-environment interactions, including those expected to be provided by the upcoming Fleet for the Atmosphere Linking Commercial Observations to NASA (FALCON) constellation. This talk will provide an overview of the INCUS level 3 convective object algorithm, and will highlight how such a dataset can be used to address key convection-related science questions.

496842.title: Working Through the Warning? Workplace Constraints on Protective Action Among Spanish-Speaking Workers
496842.authors: Elisabet De Jesus Otero, University Of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and J. E. Trujillo-Falcón, M. Saunders, and R. Sriver
496842.abstract: Employers decide whether work stops during dangerous weather, whether shelter exists, and whether safety instructions arrive in a language the worker reads. No national data has described what protections Spanish-speaking workers receive or how workplace authority shapes their ability to act on a warning. To address this gap, we designed a national survey of Spanish-speaking US adults and asked employed respondents whether their workplace maintains an emergency plan, provides training and drills, designates where to shelter, and supplies protective resources for protection from hazards such as extreme heat, severe storms, flooding, winter weather, and other extreme weather events. Participants also reported who decides when work stops and whether they have been asked to work in conditions they considered unsafe. Workers who reported unsafe conditions described what followed, including why they kept working and what they experienced. We examined how these protections vary by occupation, outdoor exposure, and workplace language, and we tested what predicts whether a worker has been required to work through weather they consider unsafe. This study presents the development of a national survey of Spanish speakers in the United States designed to quantify workplace vulnerability during extreme weather events across diverse occupations and geographic regions within the United States. The survey examines three key dimensions of workplace safety during extreme weather: (1) workplace emergency preparedness structures, (2) occupational exposure and weather-related workplace disruptions, and (3) workplace power dynamics and retaliation. In addition to measuring workplace preparedness and protective behavior, this instrument incorporates hazard exposure and geographic information to support future analyses interconnecting social vulnerabilities with regional patterns of extreme weather risk.

496843.title: Results from the Inaugural AIP-AMS Survey of Bachelor's Degree Recipients
496843.authors: Jack Pold, American Institute of Physics, College Park, MD; and J. A. Knox
496843.abstract: In the fall of 2025, the American Institute of Physics (AIP) partnered with the American Meteorological Society (AMS) on a project to survey recent bachelor's degree recipients in atmospheric science, climate science, ocean science, and/or meteorology (ACOM). Departments were contacted and asked to provide information about their past year’s bachelor’s degree recipients, including contact information, which led to information on approximately 520 bachelor’s degree recipients. This represents about 70% of annual B.S. recipients in ACOM from the 92 degree-granting institutions. Of these 520, 83 recent graduates (16%) from 26 institutions responded to the questionnaire. Despite the low number of responses, this pilot study provides informative, if not definitive, insight into many different aspects of the students and their post-graduation outcomes, organized under six main subject areas: degrees, graduate school, employment, future plans, prior experiences, and demographics. The results are compared, where possible, to the relatively limited extant data from past studies of ACOM undergraduates and bachelor's degree recipients. In other cases, these results are entirely new to our discipline with no antecedent data to compare them to. Plans for future collaborative surveys of this type will be discussed.

496844.title: What Do We Need to Observe to Improve Estimates of PBL Structure and Evolution?
496844.authors: Derek J. Posselt, JPL, Pasadena, CA; and P. Grogan, J. P. Teixeira, A. Braverman, and D. S. Martinez
496844.abstract: As the interface between the atmosphere and the underlying surface, the planetary boundary layer (PBL) regulates mass and energy exchanges that are crucial to weather and pollutant transport. Despite its critical importance, there are no systematic global observations of the complex three-dimensional (3D) thermodynamic structure of the PBL. Of particular interest to weather and air quality are PBL horizontal and vertical temperature and moisture variability, bulk PBL thermodynamic characteristics, PBL height, and low-level wind shear. In considering the design of future observing systems that could advance the state of knowledge of the PBL, it is important to understand the resolution and accuracy requirements associated with the PBL’s influence on the formation and evolution of weather and of the venting of pollutants from the PBL to the free troposphere. This presentation will demonstrate a set of tools that have been developed for the purpose of quantifying the effectiveness of potential future measurements of the thermodynamic structure and winds within the PBL across a wide range of PBL types and measurement methodologies. The tools support a range of observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs) tailored for the PBL, but adaptable to a diverse set of potential future missions. This analysis framework expands on the traditional weather forecast OSSE, which measures the potential impact of measurements on a numerical forecast. It enables a much broader spectrum of experiments that can be tailored to specific research and applications objectives, whether or not they involve a weather forecast model. It includes the following components: Interfaces to a collection of global km-scale and regional sub-km scale nature runs that represent a large range of weather states and PBL structures. Passive (e.g., infrared and microwave) and active (e.g., radar and lidar) instrument simulators capable of exploring trades among the diverse set of PBL measurements. Orbit simulators that can represent constellations of satellites at varying altitudes and with diverse observing strategies. Data fusion techniques that account for measurement uncertainty and optimally combine information from observations with very different spatial and temporal resolutions. A computational framework that parallelizes radiative transfer and retrievals efficiently over diverse compute environments from individual multi-core workstations to distributed high performance computing architectures to the cloud. In this presentation, we will demonstrate how the PBL OSSE system can be used to assess the capability of a variety of measurements for characterization of key aspects of the PBL structure and evolution. We show how trades among various types of measurements, including: spatial resolution, accuracy, and spatio-temporal sampling, affect estimates of PBL properties. We show how the framework can be applied to space-based observations and also how it can be used to quantify the synergies among space-, aircraft-, and surface-based measurements.

496846.title: The Research Applications Laboratory at the NSF National Center for AtmosphericResearch: Actionable Earth System Science to Serve Society
496846.authors: Christopher Castro, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. Kumar
496846.abstract: The Research Applications Laboratory (RAL) is a world leader in community-driven, end-to-end research. We continually expand the reach of actionable Earth system sciences and apply our discoveries to solving problems that impact society. Achieving this requires leadership, inspiration, and talent to work in a multidisciplinary way with collaborators and stakeholders, building sustainable strategic partnerships. Just as important as our technology development is our reputation for transferring solution to society for deployment. This distinction underpins the robust, convergent, and actionable science we study and deliver. This overview presentation of RAL will discuss the lab mission and organization, and technology highlights across all the RAL programs, and our strengths, challenges, and opportunities.

496850.title: Variation in Boundary Layer Wind Profiles over a Mesoscale Domain with Contrasting Surface Characteristics during Cool-Season, High-Shear Conditions
496850.authors: Kevin Knupp, Univ. of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and A. Soileau, S. W. Freeman, and P. T. Pangle
496850.abstract: This investigation is concerned with variations in low-level wind profiles over contrasting surface roughness (z0), covering a mesoscale domain of ~17,000 km2 over NW Alabama. We are particularly concerned with the high-wind PBL that is relatively common during the cool season within the warm sector of cyclones over the Southeast U.S. The DOE ARM Mobile Facility 3 (AMF3) profiling network has been in place since around March 2025, and consists of 4 profiling sites centered on Bankhead National Forest (BNF). The UAH Mobile Atmospheric Profiling Network (MAPNet) is available to enhance/expand this network, adding three additional profiling nodes to the east and southeast that can sample wind profiles and other PBL attributes over contrasting surface types with a wide range of z0 values as defined in Table 1. This presentation will describe preliminary results of wind profiles at up to 8 locations, spanning roughness lengths ranging from 0.05 m (open grassland land over flat topography) to 1.1 m (forested region over rough topography). Two excellent events have been documented (3/5/2025, 12/18/2025), and others will be targeted during the 2026-2027 cool season. The hypothesis is that areas with higher z0 exhibit larger values of vertical wind shear (both bulk shear and storm-relative helicity over the lowest 0.5 and 1.0 km (SRH0.5 and SRH1.0). This work aims to quantify these differences and evaluate the heterogeneity in the wind profiles, as well as in the Sc clouds that are common at the top of the cool season, high-wind boundary layer. 496852.title: Climatology of Fine-Scale Atmospheric Structures in Winter Storms Using Airborne Nadir-Pointing Radar Imagery and a Convolutional Neural Network
496852.authors: Brian A. Colle, School of Marine and Atmospheric Sciences, Stony Brook, NY; SUNY Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY; and J. J. Carter
496852.abstract: The precipitation within the comma-head region of an extratropical cyclone often has a broad spectrum of bands. While single-banded (larger primary band) events have been widely studied, the understanding smaller-scale multi-bands is more limited. The recent NASA field campaign, IMPACTS (Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms), along the U.S. East coast provides unique radar and in situ observations of the bands and their surrounding environment. There is increasing evidence that cloud top generating cells (CTGCs) and their associated fall streaks (FSs) are important for a subset of these multi-banding cases, but our understanding of CTGCs rests on a limited climatology. An object-orientated approach is required to retrieve and characterize their variability. The first part of this presentation will highlight the approach. We developed a machine-learning-based, multi-channel segmentation model to identify and delineate four classes of precipitation structure in airborne high-resolution W-band radar imagery captured by the Cloud Radar System (CRS); CTGCs, FSs, melting layers, and horizontal bands. The model employs a U-Net architecture and operates on spatially aligned radar reflectivity factor, linear depolarization ratio, and Doppler velocity imagery to extract the boundaries of precipitation structures. A subsequent processing step extracts the geometric and radar properties of each feature and geolocates them relative to the storm’s low center. Model training, optimization, and validation were conducted in a nested k-fold cross-validation pipeline, drawing on imagery from 27 IMPACTS field campaign events that were extended by use of physically-consistent image augmentations. Features were manually labelled on a subset of the data using contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE) enhanced imagery, which aided in identification. The final model demonstrates effective segmentation of two-dimensional radar structures and extraction of their characteristics, which can be applied to vertically-pointing and RHI radar data spanning multiple Northeast winter storm events. The approach is used to highlight the CTGC’s characteristics such as area, dimensions, branching, gradient, positioning; such as altitude, absolute and low-center relative location, and internal qualities from the available radar products.

496853.title: Implementation of Forecast Flood Inundation Mapping Services for the Nation
496853.authors: David R. Vallee, NWS, Norton, MA; and J. Dobur
496853.abstract: The NOAA National Weather Service (NWS) provides weather, water and climate data, forecasts, warnings, and impact-based decision support services to advance our mission to protect life and property and enhance the national economy. Emergency Management partners across the nation have expressed a critical need for the provision of more detailed flood forecasts and for event-driven flood inundation mapping (FIM) as a high value source of actionable information to prepare, mitigate, and respond to flood impacts. In response, the NWS National Water Center working together with NWS River Forecast Centers, and Weather Forecast Offices, and Federal and academic partners, developed and implemented high-resolution inundation modeling capabilities providing geo-referenced visualizations of forecast flooding extent at the continental scale. NOAA/NWS completed the national implementation of Forecast Flood Inundation Mapping services for nearly 100% of the U.S. population in September of 2026. This marks a key milestone to revolutionize water prediction capabilities by providing neighborhood-level inundation extent predictions for over three million river miles of our nation’s rivers for use by the public, emergency managers, and the weather enterprise community. This presentation is the first in a series of talks which will discuss the implementation of these transformational FIM services, provide insight into the science producing the services, demonstrate how to access services, examining flood impacts based on FIM, and provide use cases from the perspective of National Water Center Operations, River Forecast Centers, and Weather Forecast Offices.

496854.title: Quantifying the Drivers of Heatwaves Across the Contiguous USA
496854.authors: Calen Flanagan Randall, University of California, Davis, Kent, WA; and P. A. Ullrich
496854.abstract: The intensity, duration, and frequency of heatwaves across the contiguous USA (CONUS) continue to increase, necessitating a strong understanding of current and future heatwave dynamics. Advection, adiabatic contributions, and diabatic factors all contribute to the creation, persistence, and termination of heatwaves. However, despite our qualitative understanding of heatwave drivers, more work is needed quantifying the relative importance of these drivers, particularly in the CONUS. This study specifically addresses the relative importance of individual heatwave drivers regionally, compares regions sharing similar driver characteristics with regions of similar homogeneous heatwave characteristics, and identifies whether climate dataset differences in heatwave metrics can be explained by biases in their heatwave drivers. The components of the surface temperature budget equation–including advection, adiabatic contributions, and diabatic contributions–were calculated using daily ERA5 data from 1980-2025. While previous studies have applied the temperature budget decomposition framework to single day extreme heat events, this study focuses on specifically defined heatwave periods and quantifies their contributions during the creation, termination, and persistence stages of heatwaves. Large differences in relative driver importance are found between the western, southeastern, and midwest CONUS and regions of heatwave driver similarity generally correspond to regions of homogeneous heatwave characteristics.

496859.title: Common Atmospheric Diagnostics for Forecast and Climate Representation of Atmospheric Blocking and the Diurnal Cycle
496859.authors: Richard B. Neale, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. Coleman and M. Fowler
496859.abstract: Determining the skill of atmospheric models in representing modes of variability has historically been treated as separate activities between the earth system research and forecasting disciplines. Their analysis frequently derives from independent diagnostics packages, with different methodologies, assumptions and norms. A more unified approach to this analysis would be beneficial for understanding these modes in multiple simulation scenarios, across models, and for any number of applications. While this separation has been understandable given the different goals of long- and short-term modeling systems, the universality of any particular mode of variability should be expected regardless of model focus. An extended goal of the NOAA Model Diagnostics Task Force (MDTF) is thus to provide a universal weather and climate model analysis framework for process oriented diagnostics (PODs) that are key to understanding the earth system. In this talk we describe an effort to unify the analysis of the diurnal cycle and blocking characteristics as part of MDTF POD development. These phenomena are central elements in determining impactful extreme events such as daily surface temperature maxima and multi-week persistence of high and low temperature. Our analysis will focus on the NSF NCAR Earth System Predictability Across Timescales (ESPAT) forecast protocol using the Community Earth System Model (CESM) and the Model for Prediction Across Scales (CESM). These are models that have had a forecast and climate focus respectively. While we compare the forecast skill in predicting these modes of variability, we will also contrast their performance at very long lead times (out to 45 days) in order to determine their ‘climate-like’ equilibrium skill. We will further show the appropriateness of this type of comparison with ‘true’ equilibrium simulations using multi-decadal free-running CESM simulations. With this comparison, we are able to more consistently contrast model performance for modes of variability between the traditionally separate climate and forecast domains.

496863.title: Applying NOAA’s Event Footprint Catalog to Inform Insurance Risk Analysis
496863.authors: Sarah Purpura, Mercury Insurance Services, LLC, Brea, CA; and S. Bennett, A. Crimmins, J. Baker, and M. Coates
496863.abstract: Federal data underpins the structures of catastrophe modeling; short-, medium-, and long-term risk planning; and asset owners’ abilities to proactively protect their property. As the landscape for evaluating and mitigating risk from severe convective storms (SCS) evolves, it is more important than ever to have accurate, available, and authoritative data on storm impacts. Alongside insurance and reinsurance partners, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Industry Partnerships program built a novel Event Footprint Catalog tool. This tool, released for use in 2026, allows users to cross-reference a tornado track with population density and structural layers to explore event impacts, view hail swaths over a month to evaluate typical damaging events, and download that hail data from the cloud over a multi-year period to conduct further analysis. Unlike many existing tools that require technical GIS expertise, the Event Footprint Catalog provides a method for users – like claims adjusters or entry-level analysts – to understand SCS data and its impacts. Mercury Insurance uses the tornado component of the Event Footprint Catalog as a climatological resource, using observed tornado tracks and swaths to understand the historical frequency, geographic distribution and spatial characteristics of tornado activity. The application provides a more informative representation of tornado hazard than point- or county-based records because it preserves the shape and extent of individual swaths. Mercury Insurance also uses the catalog’s hail functionality, which provides a complementary and accessible way to view hail swaths over time and download multi-year data efficiently. Together, these capabilities help analysts identify recurring patterns, place events in a broader climatological context and communicate SCS risk to colleagues who may not routinely work with geospatial data. We are continuing to explore how the catalog could support additional applications, including claims and exposure analysis, model validation and calibration, portfolio monitoring, and more targeted resilience and risk-management decisions. This session will explore this new tool and how Mercury Insurance uses federal data to better inform SCS risk analysis. The presentation will highlight our use of tornado swaths as a climatological data source, the tool’s hail-swath capabilities and our ongoing evaluation of additional applications for decision-making and risk management.

496865.title: Representing Extreme Precipitation in Forecast Ensembles: An Evaluation of Methods
496865.authors: Diana Rose Jesberg, ; and K. M. Mahoney, S. M. Trojniak, J. Correia Jr., and A. Back
496865.abstract: Ensemble forecast systems provide valuable information for identifying and characterizing extreme precipitation events. However, there are many ways to extract and represent extreme precipitation information from an ensemble, including the ensemble maximum, upper-percentile precipitation, exceedance probabilities, probability-matched mean (PMM), localized probability-matched mean, and precipitation fields from the most-extreme ensemble members. The most appropriate approach depends on both the characteristics of the ensemble forecasting system and the intended application. In particular, applications such as probable maximum precipitation (PMP) estimation require ensemble data to accurately represent the upper tail of precipitation, as well as the intensity and spatial structure of physically plausible extreme events. This presentation evaluates different ensemble-derived precipitation diagnostics for establishing standards of “fitness for purpose” for representing extreme precipitation across a range of ensemble systems. We assess how well different approaches reproduce the intensity, spatial distribution, and frequency of extreme precipitation relative to observations, while considering differences in model resolution, physics, and ensemble construction. For example, previous studies have shown that the PMM can better represent the spatial distribution and magnitude of heavy precipitation relative to the traditional ensemble mean in convection-allowing, multi-model systems such as the High-Resolution Ensemble Forecast System (HREF). We apply a suite of ensemble-based extreme precipitation analysis methods to several high-impact precipitation events using the HREF, Rapid Refresh Ensemble Forecast System (REFS), and Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) experimental Reforecast System. Results demonstrate how the representation of extreme precipitation varies among ensemble systems and evaluate how well different ensemble-derived diagnostics represent extreme precipitation. Particular emphasis is placed on the suitability of these methods for applications requiring realistic representation of precipitation extremes, including PMP estimation, where preserving information about the magnitude, spatial extent, and physical structure of extreme precipitation is critical.

496866.title: The Solar Wind, Charged Particles, and "Electrified Weather" over the Solar Cycle
496866.authors: Robert J. Leamon, Lynker Space, Leesburg, VA; Hale SWx, Washington, DC
496866.abstract: The sun modulates the output of its various photonic and corpuscular outputs (including the transport of galactic cosmic rays) over the 11(ish)-year solar cycle, and the 22(ish)-year Hale magnetic cycle. Combined with large-scale ejecta, these modulated charged and magnetic solar inputs at the top of the atmosphere -- collectively, "Space Weather" -- give rise to the geomagnetic disturbance indices such as aa and Kp; the aa record in particular extends back to the 1860s. To one degree or another, there are operational prediction capabilities for each of these. We discuss the solar cycle variability of space weather and correlation with terrestrial weather, in particular the various Severe Weather events that pose a threat to property and life such as lightning strikes, hurricanes, and tornadoes. In particular, El Niño and La Niña modulate hurricanes and tornadoes by shifting global wind patterns and ocean temperatures. Topically for 2026, El Niño suppresses Atlantic hurricanes and central-south U.S. spring tornadoes via high vertical wind shear and reduced moisture transport, while boosting Pacific hurricane activity. Finally, we discuss the need for better communication (among scientists working) in coupling the Atmosphere, Ionosphere, Magnetosphere (and above) and the liminal spaces between historical disciplines.

496867.title: Sensitivity of Tornadic and Nontornadic Mesocyclone Intensity to Model Grid Spacing in Simulated Supercells
496867.authors: Austin W Dixon, CIWRO - Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK
496867.abstract: Recent studies of VORTEX2 composite supercell environments have shown skill in discriminating between tornadic and nontornadic supercells in relatively high grid spacing (125-m horizontal grid spacing) idealized simulations. Given that forecasts at this grid spacing are not attainable with current computing capabilities, ensemble simulations were conducted to test if these results are consistent at lower grid spacings. Initially, ensemble simulations were conducted at 3-km horizontal grid spacing, but relatively small differences in supercell intensity were found between the two environments. Thus, ensemble simulations were then conducted with 2-km, 1-km, 500-m, and 250-m horizontal grid spacing. All of these finer grid spacings discriminated between simulated tornadic and nontornadic supercells in terms of the intensity of vertical velocity, vertical vorticity, and updraft helicity. Vertical velocity and vertical vorticity were found to discriminate well on their own, but with more marginal differences between the tornadic and nontornadic ensembles compared to updraft helicity. 0-2-km AGL updraft helicity was found to be the best discriminator between the intensity of tornadic and nontornadic supercells at all horizontal grid spacings. The 250-m and 500-m ensembles had wider, but likely more realistic distributions of 0-2-km AGL updraft helicity magnitude in both the tornadic and nontornadic ensembles. While 1-km and 2-km horizontal grid spacing were able to discriminate between the tornadic and nontornadic composite environments, the nontornadic ensembles had narrower distributions that may not include realistic, transient instances of nontornadic members briefly reaching tornadic intensity. In addition to analyzing storm properties at the native grid spacings listed above, the 250-m simulations were interpolated to 500-m, 1-km, and 2-km grid spacing to assess the relative influence of grid spacing alone versus the storm-scale processes that are resolved at finer grid spacings. The interpolated data had higher values of updraft helicity than their respective native grid spacing simulations, indicating that finer grid spacings resolve important processes that affect mesocyclone intensity.

496870.title: Adaptive Streamflow Prediction by Updating Deep Learning States through Ensemble Data Assimilation
496870.authors: Ehsan Foroumandi, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and P. Ghaneei and H. Moradkhani
496870.abstract: Deep learning has become increasingly effective for large-sample hydrologic modeling as a single model can learn transferable rainfall–runoff behavior across watersheds with diverse hydroclimatic characteristics. Yet most deep learning hydrologic models remain static after training. During prediction, their internal states evolve exclusively according to learned model dynamics, without a mechanism for incorporating newly available observations. Consequently, errors in the model’s memory can persist and propagate forward in time. In addition, conventional deterministic implementations provide limited information about predictive uncertainty, restricting their adaptability for sequential hydrologic forecasting. Here, we develop an adaptive modeling framework that integrates a large-sample Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network with ensemble data assimilation. Rather than treating the trained model as a fixed predictor, we interpret its internal memory as a set of dynamically evolving states that can be updated as observations become available. A single LSTM is first trained using a large collection of watersheds across the contiguous United States. During inference, ensemble representations of the model states are propagated forward and sequentially updated using observed streamflow. Assimilation is conducted independently within each watershed, allowing a model trained to learn regional hydrologic behavior to continuously adjust its internal representation to basin-specific conditions. This establishes a learn globally, update locally paradigm for adaptive hydrologic prediction. Evaluation across diverse watersheds shows that assimilating streamflow into the internal memory of the LSTM improves predictive performance relative to both the uncorrected LSTM and an ensemble deep learning benchmark while providing a more reliable representation of predictive uncertainty. Improvements are especially evident during high-flow periods and during times of the year when streamflow is strongly controlled by antecedent watershed conditions and stored water. The proposed framework bridges large-sample deep learning and sequential state estimation by allowing observations to directly inform the evolving memory of a trained deep learning model.

496872.title: Using Quantile Mapping to Improve Subseasonal-to-Seasonal Climatological Baselines for Energy Risk Forecasting
496872.authors: Rob Cirincione, Sunairio, BALTIMORE, MD; and B. Ho, P. Hawbecker, O. Pfeiffer, and R. Hasegawa
496872.abstract: Peak electricity demand, generation stress, and resource adequacy risk are primarily driven by the frequency and magnitude of extreme temperature days. While a handful of heat front summer days or cold front winter days dominate a utility's peak-demand risk, these tail events are exactly the events that mean-based climate summaries are least equipped to describe. Climate change reshapes the distribution of weather–distributions are stretched, compressed, and locally deformed in ways that are often incongruent with the magnitude and direction of overall mean changes. A general dilation of a temperature distribution, for example, does not move the mean but produces far more frequent extreme cold and extreme heat days; a change in skew can lower the mean while increasing the prevalence of high values. Energy risk models built on mean shifts alone can therefore substantially misstate the frequency of the extreme-demand days that matter most. Current S2S forecast products are typically calibrated against static historical climatological distributions, an approach that grows increasingly biased as the underlying climate shifts non-stationarily. And while NWP climate models can offer some insight into distributional changes, their coarse spatial and temporal resolution and small ensemble sizes make them unsuitable for probabilistic, site-level decision-making. In this talk, we bridge this gap using quantile mapping. By applying seasonal and quantile-level changes derived from coarser climate models to high-resolution historical data, we generate non-stationary future weather distributions that retain the fine spatial and temporal detail needed for energy applications. Sampling from these distributions, while preserving joint weather correlation structure, yields high-resolution ensembles suitable for use in energy grid risk applications. To illustrate the ramifications of this approach, we consider an ensemble of population-weighted load weather locations in ERCOT and generate 1000-member ensembles of correlated weather ensembles with and without quantile-mapping adjustments. After examining the relative frequency and magnitude of extreme summer heat at winter cold temperature events, we pass the weather ensembles through simple electric demand models and evaluate the differences in power grid risk profiles between the quantile-mapped and distribution-naïve approaches.

496873.title: Characterizing Downslope Windstorms at NCAR's Marshall Field Site: Toward a Site-Specific Observing Strategy using Doppler Lidar
496873.authors: Simran Ambuja LaBore, NWS, St. Louis, MO
496873.abstract: Downslope windstorms along Colorado's Front Range and beyond pose significant hazards, including fire and infrastructure risk. NCAR's Marshall Field Site, at the Front Range's base with an in-situ and remote-sensing instrumentation suite, is uniquely positioned to study these events. Dynamical flow features such as sweeping flows, rotors, and hydraulic jumps dictate hazard extent; hydraulic jump location shaped fire spread in the 2021 Marshall and 2023 Lahaina Fires. Across a two-year observational period (January 2024–April 2026), we identified 16 downslope windstorm events using tower observations, ERA5 reanalysis, and Doppler lidar scans, supporting case-study and statistical analysis. We define these events as periods of strong, westerly cross-barrier flow exceeding 20 m/s. The observational record was limited by power outages during severe events, and lidar coverage was available for 6 of these events. We developed a technique to visualize the spatiotemporal evolution of critical flow features, such as hydraulic jumps and rotors, both essential to hazard assessment, and used it to identify a hydraulic jump signature during the 12 March 2026 case study.
