An increase of the lidar scan frequency is suggested for future events to better resolve this feature evolution. Future work includes a dual-Doppler approach using co-planar scans using additional wind lidars, turbulence characterization via vertical velocity variance (σw), and comparison to theoretical guidance y and model output (HRRR, WRF), sharpening detection of the flow features that govern fire and infrastructure risk at Marshall and similar sites.

496878.title: Machine Learning Retrievals of Near-Cloud Aerosols from Geostationary Satellites: Implications for Aerosol Radiative Effects in the Trade-Wind Cloud Regime
496878.authors: Olivia Pierpaoli, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. C. Chiu, J. J. Gristey, E. Eytan, and G. Feingold
496878.abstract: Aerosol-cloud interactions remain a leading source of uncertainty in climate forcing estimates, yet aerosol populations in the near-cloud environment remain poorly observed. Relative to cloud-free conditions, near-cloud aerosols are modified by enhanced humidity, cloud processing, and new particle formation, altering both their microphysical properties and radiative effects. However, standard satellite retrieval algorithms exclude many near-cloud pixels because three-dimensional (3D) radiative effects from neighboring clouds violate underlying plane-parallel assumptions, limiting our ability to quantify aerosol variability where the fingerprints of aerosol-cloud interactions are far more evident than in cloud-free environments. Here we present a machine-learning retrieval framework that accounts for 3D cloud radiative effects and retrieves aerosol optical depth and effective radius in near-cloud environments from Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) observations. Retrievals are evaluated using airborne lidar measurements collected during the Elucidating the Role of Clouds-Circulation Coupling in Climate (EUREC4A) campaign over the tropical Atlantic. The resulting retrievals reveal variations in aerosol properties across trade-wind cloud regimes and enable estimates of associated shortwave and longwave radiative effects. By extending aerosol retrievals into regions traditionally excluded from satellite records, this framework provides a new observational pathway for linking aerosol radiative effects, cloud organization, and aerosol-cloud interactions.

496879.title: Identifying Spectral Regimes and Physical Modes in Tropical Cyclone Wave Spectra through Principal Component Analysis and Machine Learning
496879.authors: Johna E Rudzin, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State, MS; and M. Schonau, L. Centurioni, J. Davis, E. Sanabia, and D. H. Richter
496879.abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) wave fields exhibit substantial variability arising from interactions between swell and wind sea components. While TC wave fields are commonly characterized using bulk parameters, less attention has been devoted to identifying the dominant modes of variability within the full one-dimensional wave spectrum. This study applies principal component analysis (PCA) and Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to a large collection of open-ocean TC wave spectra to identify dominant modes of spectral variability and objectively classify recurring spectral regimes. This is done with the intention of identifying specific regimes, modes, or combination of modes that are linked to surface roughness. PCA reveals that over half of spectral variability can be represented by a small number of physically-meaningful patterns. The leading mode describes changes in the relative dominance of low-frequency swell energy and higher-frequency wind-sea energy. Additional modes are associated with variations in spectral peak structure and coordinated changes across multiple frequency bands. Reconstruction of wave spectra using individual PCs is used to interpret the physical characteristics represented by each mode and quantify their influence on spectral shape. GMM clustering in PC space is then used to identify recurring spectral regimes. The resulting modes and regimes are examined in TC-relative coordinates to investigate their spatial organization within the storm environment. Results indicate that spectral regimes are most clearly differentiated along the leading PC, while higher-order components describe secondary variations in spectral structure. These findings provide a physically based framework for describing TC wave spectral variability and may offer new insight into the processes governing surface roughness within TCs.

496880.title: Multispectral Satellite Imagery for Fire Detection and Monitoring
496880.authors: Curtis Seaman, Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere, Fort Collins, CO
496880.abstract: NOAA’s operational geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites offer a variety of spectral information useful for fire detection and monitoring. The GOES-R series of geostationary satellites include the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), which provides data at 500 m, 1 km, and 2 km-resolution at high temporal refresh rates ranging from 10 min (Full Disk) to 1 min (or even 30 sec) over localized (1000 km x 1000 km) Mesoscale sectors. The JPSS constellation includes the Visible and Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), which provides data at 375 m and 750 m resolution. Currently, 3 VIIRS instruments orbit in formation, providing coverage across a 3000 km-wide swath separated by 25-50 minutes. In the mid-latitudes, this means relatively high resolution fire-related imagery products are available 4-6 times in the early afternoon and early morning hours, and this coverage increases toward the high latitudes. EUMETSAT’s newest geostationary satellite imager, FCI (Flexible Combined Imager), onboard Meteosat-12, improves the spatial resolution of key fire-related spectral bands to 500 m and 1 km - a factor of 4 increase over other current geostationary satellites. This improved resolution offers an early look at what will be available from NOAA’s next generation geostationary satellite imager, GXI, which is currently scheduled to launch in the early 2030s. With the recent launch of Metop-SG-A1 and the new generation of polar-orbiting satellites from EUMETSAT, the new visible and infrared imager, METimage, provides 500 m resolution with a 2700 km-wide swath and an orbital period of 101 minutes in the “mid-morning” orbit, filling in gaps in coverage from JPSS. Fire-related imagery products from each of these imagers are (or will soon be) used by a variety of forecasters, remote sensing specialists and incident managers to aid the response to wildland fires. In particular, the VIIRS fire-related imagery projects have revolutionized operations at the Alaska Fire Service. ABI fire-related products are part of NOAA’s Next Generation Fire System (NGFS), where they are used to validate fire detections from the NGFS and provide additional context of the scene. National Weather Service forecasters and incident meteorologists use these products to identify new fire starts and warn the public. This talk will provide a review of the variety of fire-related imagery products offered by the current generation of satellite imagers: including the Shortwave Albedo, Day Fire RGB, Fire Temperature RGB, NGFS Microphysics RGB, True Color/GeoColor, GeoFire (which blends GeoColor with the Fire Temperature RGB), and the new Day/Night Fire Temperature product (available only from VIIRS). We will discuss improvements to the VIIRS Day Fire RGB to mitigate issues with instrument saturation and the downscaling method used to generate the VIIRS Fire Temperature RGB at 375 m resolution. We will demonstrate the benefits of 1 km resolution IR information from FCI and how that will benefit NOAA’s GeoXO Program and discuss the current (and future) state-of-the-art of satellite imagery products for fire monitoring.

496882.title: Where Subseasonal-to-Seasonal Forecasts Meet Farm Decisions: Action Thresholds and Barriers to S2S Uptake in Illinois Agriculture
496882.authors: Elisabet De Jesus Otero, University Of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and N. Dolan, J. E. Trujillo-Falcón, T. W. Ford, T. Guo, M. Graber, C. Diao, and Z. Wang
496882.abstract: Subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecasts could help agricultural producers prepare for damaging weather, but the forecasts’ value depends on whether producers can and will act on them. We examined how agricultural stakeholders in Illinois use weather information across lead times and where improved S2S forecasts would change their decisions. The study used a mixed-methods design. An anonymous survey captured which weather events caused the most damage to operations, which of those events stakeholders could act on given a reliable S2S forecast, the confidence they required before acting at lead times from a few days to a full season ahead, and how often they currently used monthly and seasonal outlooks. Focus groups at agricultural field days across the state of Illinois examined how stakeholders reasoned about uncertain long-range forecasts, where they found S2S products, and what kept them from using them. These results helped us identify where added S2S skills could translate into protective action for agriculture and informed decision support built around the operational impacts of weather across a growing season.

496886.title: Keeping the Forecaster at the Helm: Natural-Language Data Access for Aerostat Operations
496886.authors: Jean Vivola, Athenium, Dover, NH; and K. Fons, J. G. Fairman Jr, and A. Vacek
496886.abstract: Athenium meteorologists support the U.S. Customs and Border Protection Tethered Aerostat Radar System (TARS) at 13 sites, 24/7/365, where aerostat operations are sensitive to local wind, convection, and other hazards. We describe a workflow in which forecasters query decades of station history and climatology in plain language through a single Model Context Protocol (MCP) retrieval layer over archived observations. Three constraints anchor the design: the model fetches and summarizes but never invents weather, every value traces to source-attributed data, and each query is logged. Through an operational case study, we show how natural-language access to historical data guided a real forecast decision while the forecaster retained full control. AI handles data access; judgment stays with the meteorologist.

496887.title: Exploring the Optical and Q-Space Signatures of Idealized Core-Shell and Fractal Aggregate Black Carbon-Mineral Dust Mixtures
496887.authors: Valentina Sánchez Castaño, University of Texas at El Paso, El Paso, TX
496887.abstract: The primary source of uncertainty in global climate prediction remains the modeling of atmospheric aerosols, particularly the contrasting optical properties of strongly absorbing black carbon (BC) and predominantly scattering mineral dust (MD) (Bond et al., 2013). While standard climate models often treat these species as separate entities, aged atmospheric plumes in semi-arid urban airsheds, such as the El Paso–Juárez (Paso del Norte) border region, produce complex internal mixtures of dust and soot (BC). In this dynamic semi-arid airshed, high concentrations of wind-blown mineral dust combine with intense urban emissions from international bridge traffic, industrial operations, and household emissions. Coagulation and aging processes in such airsheds produce complex internal mixing states where highly absorbing BC interacts with larger MD particles. Treating these aerosols as simple external mixtures or homogeneous spheres leads to significant errors in regional radiative forcing calculations. To bound this optical sensitivity, this study employs an exploratory modeling framework, testing both an idealized core-shell sensitivity framework and more physically representative aggregate morphologies where BC fractal structures interact with larger MD particles. To quantify how internal mixing and morphological complexity alter light scattering, this approach combines analytical electrodynamics with Fourier wave vector analysis. Simulations are executed across near-infrared wavelengths (870 nm) typical of active remote sensing and solar radiometry, with refractive indices constrained to representative atmospheric values, notably m = 1.85 + 0.71i for BC and m = 1.53 + 0.008i for MD. Mie Theory (Bohren and Huffman, 2008) is used to establish baseline spherical bounds, calculating Clausius-Mossotti material polarizability terms F(m) = |(m2 - 1)/(m2 + 2)|2 To move beyond spherical assumptions, the T-Matrix method (Mishchenko et al., 2002) is used to account for non-spherical geometries (such as oblate spheroids with an aspect ratio of 1.5) and fractal aggregate structures characterized by mass-fractal dimensions (Df = 1.78 for soot). Furthermore, all scattering intensity outputs are transformed from physical angles (theta) into scattering vector coordinates (q-space), defined by q = (4pi/λ)sin(θ/2) (Sorensen and Fischbach, 2000), enabling the clean separation of electromagnetic scattering magnitude from structural form factors S(q) and scaling power laws. Analysis across these q-space coordinates reveals distinct physical regimes. First, by examining how coating or associating BC with MD alters the extinction profile, simulations demonstrate that adding a thickening mineral shell rapidly forces scattering to dominate over absorption; once particle size parameters exceed optical skin-depth thresholds, the mineral shell effectively masks the absorbing BC core. Second, T-Matrix calculations show that morphological irregularities and fractal branching (Df = 1.78) systematically dampen the sharp, high-frequency resonance ripples characteristic of idealized smooth spheres, smoothing the scattering profile into predictable power-law slopes. Finally, by mapping these profiles onto log-log q-space master curves, the Guinier plateau yields overall size scales (Rg - radius of gyration). At the same time, high-q slopes expose internal fractal dimensions, providing critical forward-model libraries for remote sensing inversions. These findings emphasize that incorporating realistic internal mixing states and morphological diversity, rather than relying on idealized core-shell assumptions, is vital for reducing uncertainty in regional climate models. Ongoing work is actively integrating these generated q-space scattering libraries into Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). This neural architecture aims to rapidly predict broadband optical spectra for irregular atmospheric mixtures in real time, bridging microphysical forward models with active remote sensing data inversions.

496888.title: Putting the Users Up Front: Developing the Urban Rain Rate Dashboard with User Input and Iterative Design from the Start
496888.authors: Kathryn Semmens, Nurture Nature Center, Easton, PA; and R. A. H. Carr, E. Bower, K. Maxfield, B. Montz, P. Painter, D. Bright, J. A. Nelson Jr., and A. T. King
496888.abstract: The past decade has brought an increased recognition that user input into product design helps create more effective decision support tools. Often, this means developing new forecast capability, then designing a new product, and then asking users to give feedback to that product after it has “gone live.” However, incorporating user input and social science research from the very start of product design can greatly improve the accessibility and usability of the final products, while also streamlining the product development process. The Nurture Nature Center (NNC) is a nonprofit organization in Easton, Pennsylvania that conducts social science research related to user needs for flood and hydrologic forecast products. NNC has worked closely with U.S. National Weather Service partners to iteratively test, redesign and refine a range of hydrologic forecast products based on extensive user input. Recently, NNC worked with the Weather Prediction Center (WPC) on a social science research project to gather user feedback about WPC’s hydrometeorological and precipitation forecast products. Part of the project involved testing a new Urban Rain Rate Dashboard (URRD), which provides real-time probabilities of exceeding average recurrence intervals of rainfall for U.S. major metropolitan areas. The URRD addresses the need for local scale precipitation information by providing the likelihood that city-specific critical rain rate thresholds will be exceeded and showing the forecast probability of hourly rainfall rates. The URRD was tested through a mixed-method social science research study, involving focus groups and surveys with professional stakeholders in six major U.S. cities. Focus groups were held virtually with a facilitated discussion around a flooding scenario to explore user information needs, and to gather feedback on potential design improvements. Findings from the focus groups and surveys informed subsequent design improvements that were tested in a follow-up online survey that provided more detailed feedback on specific design elements. The results from this social science research supported recommendations to the WPC to inform the development of the URRD prototype, which is now publicly available as an experimental product. The collaboration between NNC and WPC, and the iterative approach to research informing design, guided the ultimate visualization of the URRD, ensuring stakeholder feedback was incorporated early in the product’s development and supporting the creation of a usable product. This presentation, which will include perspectives from the social science as well as WPC product development team, focuses on the approach to collaboration and how iteration on the design allowed for research to operations transfer. We will discuss how the team’s process changed the URRD development based on user input, and how social science recommendations were able to be operationalized by WPC to improve accessibility, design and delivery of URRD to stakeholders. Lessons learned from this successful case study can inform other efforts to transition research to decision support tools and strengthen forecast product development through user engagement.

496889.title: Athenium BeaconHurricane AI: Using Artificial Intelligence to Improve Hurricane Track Forecast Accuracy
496889.authors: Peter Michael Jermey, Athenium, Dover, NH; and A. Vacek and J. G. Fairman Jr
496889.abstract: Hurricanes pose a serious threat to life and property in the United States. The 2025 Atlantic season produced three Category 5 hurricanes and was arguably the most dangerous season in 20 years. Accurate track forecasts are essential for evacuating population centers, mitigating property damage, and preparing emergency response. Like all tropical cyclones, hurricanes are difficult to forecast with traditional models, since their steep internal gradients cannot be fully resolved at typical model resolution. To address this challenge, forecast centers have long relied on ensemble prediction, which forecasts a range of possible tracks and associated probabilities from a set of model runs initialized with slightly varied conditions. More recently, artificial intelligence has emerged as an additional layer on top of these ensembles, drawing on both traditional forecast members and decades of reanalysis data to refine track predictions. Athenium's Beacon Hurricane product accurately forecasts hurricane tracks by combining information from different sources. The system bias-corrects both ensemble and deterministic model tracks from NOAA, ECMWF and Environment Canada and blends them into a composite forecast that outperforms any individual component track. Since 2025, this blend has also incorporated AI model tracks alongside traditional ensemble members. The AI models are introduced and compared with traditional models to demonstrate their capabilities and down-sides. Statistics are also presented to demonstrate the improvement achieved by combining AI data with traditional models.

496890.title: Understanding the Warming-Induced Changes in the Extreme Precipitation Intensity Relationship with Local Surface Meteorological Conditions
496890.authors: Guiling Wang, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT; and H. Qin, F. M. Alvee, L. R. Leung, H. Hu, and X. Sun
496890.abstract: High-intensity precipitation is a major cause for pluvial floods including flash floods with catastrophic consequences. Observational data and regional-global climate model experiments suggest that precipitation would further intensify in a warmer world. A recent study (Qin et al., Earth’s Future, in review) showed that unprecedentedly intense precipitation in a warmer climate may occur under not only unprecedented but also historical surface meteorological conditions, highlighting the importance of warming-induced increases in convection strength and vertical velocity. Here we present a theoretical interpretation for the model-simulated responses on how warming may influence the intensity of extreme convective storms, with a focus on understanding the potential model dependence and region dependence of the results. The theoretical interpretation is based on a conceptual, physics-grounded deep-convection thunderstorm cell model that relates precipitation intensity to surface thermodynamical conditions and an approximate CAPE representation. The model has two primary parameters that depend on the background climate and can be considered constant at the weather timescale: one (Twc) reflecting the mid-troposphere wet bulb potential temperature and the other (α) is a function of the LFC and LNB of deep convection in the region of interest. As climate warms, Twc is expected to increase, but α may increase, stay unchanged, or decrease; whether and how rapidly α increases determine whether unprecedentedly intense precipitation may occur under historical conditions. This theoretical model enables predictive understanding of the variability and change of extreme precipitation intensity, their region dependence and potential model dependence as well.

496891.title: NVIDIA Earth2Studio and PhysicsNeMo: Open Software Platforms for Lowering Barriers to Adopting AI in Earth System Modeling
496891.authors: Negin Sobhani, NSF-NCAR, Boulder, CO; and N. Geneva, P. Harrington, C. Adams, M. Pritchard, and S. Choudhry
496891.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing weather and climate modeling, but developing, running, and evaluating AI-based Earth-system models still requires substantial expertise in machine learning, data access, model implementation, distributed computing, inference, verification, and high-performance computing. Differences in model architectures, data formats, training and inference interfaces, initialization requirements, and computational environments often require researchers to assemble custom software stacks before they can address a scientific question. Earth2Studio and PhysicsNeMo provide complementary open-source software layers for building, training, and running scalable AI weather and climate workflows. PhysicsNeMo provides reusable components for developing and optimizing physics-informed and scientific machine-learning models, including distributed training and inference, scalable data pipelines, geometric and mesh-based representations, and GPU-accelerated model architectures. Earth2Studio provides a higher-level workflow environment that connects data sources, observations, forecast models, data-assimilation methods, perturbation strategies, diagnostics, verification metrics, and output backends through consistent Python interfaces. Together, the platforms support workflows spanning model development through scientific application. Users can train or integrate models using PhysicsNeMo and expose them through Earth2Studio alongside existing AI weather models and data products. Researchers can then construct end-to-end experiments- from retrieving initial conditions and running deterministic or ensemble forecasts to data assimilation, diagnostics, verification, and visualization- without rebuilding model-specific workflow infrastructure for each experiment. The software stack is designed to support multiple levels of expertise and computational scale. Distributed execution, scalable I/O, cloud-native data access, checkpointing, and reusable workflow components allow the same scientific workflows to move from interactive experimentation to cloud and high-performance computing environments. By separating scientific workflow design from the complexity of AI model implementation, data movement, and computational deployment, Earth2Studio and PhysicsNeMo allow researchers to focus on modeling earth system processes, physical interpretation, and scientific evaluation. This presentation introduces the complementary architecture of the two projects and demonstrates representative workflows spanning AI model integration, scalable execution, forecasting, data assimilation, and verification.

496892.title: Detecting Atmospheric Ducting from Deep GNSS Radio Occultation Signals
496892.authors: Feiqin Xie, Texas A&M Univ.—Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX; and L. Adhikari
496892.abstract: Atmospheric ducting in the moist lower troposphere occurs when ray-path curvature exceeds Earth’s curvature, potentially trapping the signals and causing signal loss in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) radio occultation (RO) measurements. Strong vertical refractivity gradients associated with the ducting can produce substantial signal bending and generate “deep” RO signals that reappear at large negative line-of-sight (LOS) heights. Although these signals are weak, their power can remain above the background noise and be detected by high-signal-to-noise-ratio RO missions such as COSMIC-2 and PlanetiQ. This study investigates deep RO signals over the northeastern Pacific Ocean, where cool sea-surface temperatures and strong free-tropospheric subsidence frequently produce sharp refractivity gradients and atmospheric ducting near the top of the planetary boundary layer. We generated frequency spectra as a function of LOS height, defined as the distance from Earth’s center to the LOS minus Earth’s radius, using COSMIC-2 and PlanetiQ Level 1b observations extending below −250 km. Most RO events without sharp lower-tropospheric refractivity gradients exhibit no discernible spectral signal below −100 km. In contrast, deep-signal events contain detectable features extending continuously from below −100 km to −250 km or lower. A spectral-masking method was applied to estimate the background noise and isolate detectable RO signals. After noise removal, the maximum penetration depth—or minimum LOS height—of each RO case was calculated. Based on previous studies, the presence of detectable signals below −175 km was used as a first-order indicator of potential ducting. However, deep signals are not uniquely associated with ducting; other propagation or measurement effects may also produce signals at large negative LOS heights. Therefore, identifying a deep signal alone is insufficient to confirm ducting. We are developing artificial intelligence methods to automate two related tasks: determining the minimum LOS height of detectable deep signals and distinguishing ducting-related signatures from deep signals produced by other mechanisms. This work provides a framework for independently detecting atmospheric ducting from GNSS RO observations. Such measurements can advance the understanding of radio-wave propagation and improve planetary boundary layer height retrievals for global weather and climate applications.

496893.title: Identifying Midlatitude Precursors of Atmospheric Blocking Using Optimal Growth and Explainable AI
496893.authors: Lei Wang, Purdue University, West Lafayette , IN; and C. McCollum, Z. Li, P. Garg, Y. Hu, Y. B. Zhao, and M. L. Breeden
496893.abstract: Atmospheric blocking drives persistent weather extremes, but the circulation patterns that could provide useful precursors to its development remain unclear. In particular, previous work has shown that tropical convection contributes significantly to blocking onset, raising an important question: To what extent does blocking predictability arise from intrinsic midlatitude dynamics, and can robust precursor structures be identified independently of tropical influences? Here, we address these questions using a two-layer quasi-geostrophic (QG) model, which provides a controlled dynamical framework for isolating midlatitude blocking dynamics. We combine dynamical and data-driven approaches to identify precursor information. First, linear inverse modeling (LIM) and optimal-growth analysis identify circulation structures that preferentially evolve toward blocking. Second, machine-learning models predict blocking occurrence and characteristics at increasing lead times, and explainable AI methods identify the spatial structures driving successful predictions. We examine precursor patterns using physically relevant variables including streamfunction, QG potential vorticity, and local wave activity, and assess their dependence on lead time and blocking characteristics. Together, these dynamical and data-driven approaches provide distinct yet complementary perspectives on the existence and structure of blocking precursors. Preliminary results indicate that useful precursor information is present within the midlatitude circulation several days before blocking onset and suggest coherent potential-vorticity and wave-activity structures associated with subsequent blocking development. Comparison between optimal-growth structures and machine-learned attribution patterns allows us to distinguish dynamically meaningful precursors from statistical predictors. We will also present results from reanalysis products and large-ensemble climate model output. These results help reveal the physical origins and limits of atmospheric blocking predictability and provide a basis for evaluating these precursor structures in observations.

496894.title: WAFNWP - An Advanced Blending Methodology for Integrating Extrapolation-Based Nowcasting and Numerical Weather Prediction in Operational Meteorology
496894.authors: Jeova Silva Jr., SIMEPAR - Parana Environmental Technology and Monitoring Service, Curitiba, PR, Brazil; and S. Paz and R. T. Inouye
496894.abstract: Quantitative precipitation forecasting at short lead times faces a structural challenge: extrapolation-based nowcasting and numerical weather prediction (NWP) have opposing error profiles. Nowcasting, driven by kinematic extrapolation of radar data, is highly accurate initially but degrades rapidly as atmospheric dynamics become nonlinear. NWP resolves atmospheric physics and grows more reliable at longer horizons, despite spin-up errors for localized convection. This study evaluates blending methodologies that let each source contribute according to its skill at each lead time, avoiding abrupt discontinuities or loss of spatial detail. To ensure scale compatibility, the coarser NWP fields receive bilinear spatial interpolation, while a semi-Lagrangian temporal interpolation—based on Lucas-Kanade optical flow—produces a bidirectionally weighted average that fills temporal gaps between radar frames and removes visual discontinuities before blending. Three blending strategies were tested. Linear blending applies a globally constant transition weight between nowcast and NWP, while sinusoidal blending modulates the weight with a cosine function so the rate of change tapers at both ends of the transition. Both are simple to implement but, operating directly on the field, generate visible artifacts when inputs are spatially displaced. The third method, spectral blending, follows the Bowler et al. (2006) scheme implemented in the pysteps library. Precipitation fields are converted to radar decibels (dBR) to satisfy the symmetric-variation assumption of the Fourier transform, then decomposed by FFT into spatial cascades. Blending weights are computed per cascade level from the temporal correlation of each spatial scale, so large-scale structures retain nowcast influence longer while small-scale features transition more quickly toward the NWP. A non-parametric stochastic noise regulator restores spatial variance lost to extrapolation, and CDF matching aligns the blended statistics with observed radar values before the precipitation field is reconstructed. Validation on synthetic precipitation fields, each containing two convective cores following distinct trajectories, showed that both linear and sinusoidal blending failed to reproduce peak intensities during the transition period, producing artificial flattening and the simultaneous rendering of overlapping systems. Spectral blending better preserved the intensity of the dominant convective core and the overall statistical distribution of precipitation values across intensity thresholds, without generating spurious cells. It also introduced additional small-scale noise from the stochastic regulator, visible as textural artifacts in the reconstructed field—an effect that becomes more pronounced when the input sources diverge substantially in position or intensity. The method was further tested in an operational case study of a frontal system on 9 May 2026. The nowcast indicated a concentrated, slow-moving precipitation core near the São Paulo–Paraná state divide, while the NWP projected a broader, less intense system, with its strongest cores farther west and to the north of Paraná; the hourly NWP output was resampled to 10-minute resolution to match the nowcast. Spectral blending repositioned and moderated the intensity of the western nowcast core toward the NWP field over the forecast horizon, while also introducing visible stochastic-noise artifacts that did not compromise interpretation in this case. Comparing MAE trajectories qualitatively, the blended forecast tracked closer to whichever individual source performed better at a given lead time, rather than inheriting the larger error of a single fixed source throughout the three-hour window. Full pipeline processing, excluding I/O, took approximately 30 seconds, supporting operational feasibility. Spectral blending produced the most favorable results in the synthetic scenario, preserving precipitation intensity through the transition period more effectively than either spatial-domain method. This benefit carries a practical caveat: the stochastic noise injection produces visible artifacts that, in real operational settings, could be mistaken by forecasters for genuine precipitation cores. Operational use of this method should therefore be paired with training for meteorologists on its behavior and limitations. Linear and sinusoidal blending remain simpler alternatives that may be adequate when the goal is smooth visualization rather than quantitative fidelity to peak intensities. The full pipeline proved computationally efficient enough for operational deployment, though the quality of the combined forecast remains inherently bounded by the errors of the two individual source forecasts it blends.

496897.title: Producing Downscaled Projections of Actual Evapotranspiration for the Edwards Aquifer Region using Satellite Data
496897.authors: Adrienne Wootten, South Central Climate Adaptation Science Center, Norman, OK; and H. Basagaoglu, D. Chakraborty, and A. Mirchi
496897.abstract: Actual evapotranspiration (AET) has been identified by the Edwards Aquifer Authority (EAA) as a key component for supporting decision-making and understanding the impact of climate change on the Edwards Aquifer system. Prior work has focused on reference crop evapotranspiration or potential evapotranspiration. Reference crop evapotranspiration is typically defined for a standardized reference surface covered by grass or alfalfa, under well-watered conditions. In contrast, potential evapotranspiration generally represents the atmospheric evaporative demand under conditions of adequate water availability. However, neither assumption is necessarily valid in the Edwards Aquifer Region (EAR), nor would it be valid over time as vegetation changes in response to both climate variability and the potential future development of the EAR. Despite this critical need, few studies attempted to produce statistically downscaled projections of AET, largely owing to the limited availability of long-term AET observations needed as training data for statistical downscaling. Robust statistical downscaling requires a training dataset of sufficient length, typically 20 years or more. However, the high cost of maintaining eddy-covariance flux towers for direct AET measurements makes it difficult to maintain observational records of sufficient length. The resulting scarcity of long-term AET observations and projections poses a challenge for the EAA, as well as for decision-makers and planners across the United States who rely on AET projections for water resources planning and management. In recent years, NASA efforts have focused on remotely observing and estimating AET using satellites. These products have recently reached, or will soon reach, the requisite length to be sufficient training data for statistical downscaling. Although in situ AET observations may lack sufficient temporal coverage, satellite-based AET observations and estimates can be used as the training data for statistical downscaling of AET. However, statistical downscaling of AET remains relatively understudied in the published literature. Therefore, this project has two primary objectives: (i) to evaluate the applicability of satellite-based AET records to produce statistically downscaled ET projections, and (ii) to develop statistically downscaled gridded AET projections for the EAR using CMIP6 global climate model simulations. This presentation will briefly discuss the results from both parts of this project. The first portion of the talk will discuss the evaluation of the Aqua MODIS, Terra MODIS, and SSEBop ET estimates against eddy-covariance tower observations of AET in the EAR provided by the EAA. The second portion will present and discuss the resulting downscaled AET projections developed using the Aqua MODIS ET as the training dataset. The presentation will conclude with a brief discussion of next steps and lessons learned from downscaling EAT using satellite data as the training dataset.

496899.title: Partnership with the African Meteorological Society (AfMS) for Excellence and Collaboration in the Global Weather, Water, and Climate Enterprise
496899.authors: Charles Ichoku, University of Maryland Baltimore County (UMBC), Baltimore, MD; and B. Demoz, A. Albayrak, S. Bililign, T. Tadesse, K. Boyd, R. Plofkin, S. Shams, E. M. Dougherty, L. D. White, R. Damoah, A. Kinyua, B. Annane, E. Nyadjro, O. Ideki, and H. Ahluwalia
496899.abstract: The African Meteorological Society (AfMS) was inaugurated in November 2022 under the auspices of the International Forum of Meteorological Societies (IFMS) of which the AMS is a member. The AfMS held its first Scientific Conference in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia during April 20–23, 2026, in partnership with the IFMS and the Ethiopian Meteorological Institute (EMI), with the collaboration of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). AfMS includes several Committees responsible for conducting different aspects of its operations, one of which is the Diaspora and Friends of Africa (D-FOA) Committee composed of AfMS members based outside of Africa, most of whom are in North America. To ensure a great start to a productive partnership between the AfMS and the international scientific community, it was important for the D-FOA to be represented at the AfMS conference. Therefore, the D-FOA leadership submitted a competitive proposal to the NASA Topical Workshops, Symposiums, and Conferences (TWSC-24) in Space and Earth Sciences and Technology Program and received a grant that allowed several US participants to attend the conference, which was very successful. All our participants presented their research, some chaired sessions, and two of our members held training classes on air quality and utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) in disaster response. Participation of US-based scientists at this AfMS conference provided an excellent opportunity for direct engagement with a rich supply of Earth/Atmospheric Scientists and students in Africa with whom we are now building collaborations and partnerships that can lead to tremendous acceleration in addressing topics of great importance to global Weather, Water, and Climate (WWC) Science and Services. In this presentation, we will report on some of the successes of our engagement with the AfMS enabled by our active participation at their conference and explore prospects for sustaining and extending such important partnerships.

496903.title: Investigating the Relationship Between Atmospheric Rivers and Crash Risk in California
496903.authors: Emily Nicole Stanton, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, Edwardsville, IL; and A. W. Black
496903.abstract: Atmospheric rivers are a common occurrence along the United States’ west coast and can cause a variety of impacts. One such impact is hazardous travel conditions caused by the precipitation produced by atmospheric rivers. California, a state with a high population, large tourist economy, and complex topography, is a prime location to explore the relationship between atmospheric river precipitation and vehicle crash risk. Data on crashes and atmospheric river occurrence was gathered for the years 2020 to 2025. Through a matched pair analysis method, this study investigates crashes related to atmospheric river precipitation to reveal their impacts on travel. It is hoped that this work will increase awareness of this hazard and encourage drivers to be better prepared when traveling during hazardous conditions.

496910.title: Uncertainty-Aware Spatial Prediction of Extreme Weather-induced Power Outages with a Two-Stage Discriminative-Diffusion Framework
496910.authors: Jice Zeng, PNNL, Richland, WA; and S. Feng and J. Tian
496910.abstract: Extreme weather can damage electric distribution infrastructure, interrupt service to homes, businesses, and critical facilities, and impose cascading economic and public-safety consequences across large regions. Anticipating where outages will begin is therefore essential for preparedness and rapid response, but spatial outage onset prediction remains challenging because outages are rare, often occur across neighboring counties, and are influenced by changing storm conditions, vegetation, and local geographic characteristics. Many conventional approaches predict each county separately, without explicitly learning spatial relationships among neighboring county locations, and provide only a single deterministic forecast without reliability indication. To this end, we present a two-stage discriminative-generative framework for predicting outage onset at the county level on a gridded map. For each target time, the model uses storm observations from the three preceding time steps, together with vegetation and geographic context. In the first stage, a U-Net encodes these multichannel spatial inputs and decodes them into an initial outage onset probability map. Its convolutional encoder-decoder structure allows to capture both storm evolution and spatial context across nearby county locations. In the second stage, a conditional diffusion model refines the U-Net forecast. The diffusion process is conditioned jointly on the preceding storm observations, vegetation, geographic context, and initial U-Net prediction. Through iterative denoising, the diffusion model generates multiple plausible outage onset maps that are consistent with the observed conditions. The posterior mean of these samples provides the refined outage onset prediction, while the posterior standard deviation quantifies predictive uncertainty at each county location. The framework is evaluated using county-level outage observations from EAGLE-I aligned with gridded storm, vegetation, and geographic data. Results show that the U-Net identifies the primary spatial pattern of outage onset and that conditional diffusion provides refined county-level predictions together with spatially explicit uncertainty. County locations with lower prediction accuracy generally exhibit larger posterior uncertainties, demonstrating that diffusion-based uncertainty estimates can effectively identify locations where the predicted outage onset is less reliable. By combining efficient discriminative prediction with generative refinement and uncertainty quantification, the framework supports more informed situational awareness, crew pre-positioning, and emergency resource allocation before and during high-impact weather events.

496911.title: Impacts of Diurnal Anthropogenic Emissions and Meteorological Nudging on Model-Simulated Vertical Column Densities of Ozone Precursors Using MUSICAv0
496911.authors: Juanito Jerrold Mariano Acdan, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and G. Pfister, B. Gaubert, L. Thompson, L. K. Emmons, and K. Barsanti
496911.abstract: This work presents modeling that is done in support of the SCENICS (Stereoscopy of Multi-scale Chemical Exchanges and Interactions between a City and its Surroundings) field campaign planned for 2028, and co-led by NSF NCAR, The Georgia Institute of Technology, and The University of Utah. SCENICS will investigate urban air quality in Atlanta, Georgia, USA, and its relationship to meteorological processes, such as boundary layer dynamics, and satellite observations of atmospheric composition. Here, we present air quality simulations conducted to evaluate the impacts of using monthly versus diurnally varying anthropogenic emissions input datasets and different meteorological nudging configurations on model-simulated vertical column densities (VCDs) of ozone precursors. The model we utilize is the Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols version 0 (MUSICAv0) with a horizontal grid that regionally refines from 1 degree globally to 1/16th of a degree (~7 km) over the state of Georgia. Using a development version of MELODIES MONET (Model EvaLuation using Observations, DIagnostics and Experiments Software – Model and ObservatioN Evaluation Toolkit), we compare MUSICAv0 output to NASA TEMPO (Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution) version 4 satellite retrievals to evaluate the model accuracy in simulating the observed magnitudes and diurnal variations in nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and formaldehyde (HCHO) VCDs. The results of this work will be used to inform potential target areas for instrument deployment during the SCENICS field campaign.

496913.title: Bridging LIS and GLM: Resolving Space-Based Lightning Discrepancies for Earth-System Models
496913.authors: Jonathan W. Smith, GFDL, Princeton, NJ; and J. Dunne and D. Zhang
496913.abstract: Traditionally, the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission Lightning Imaging Sensor (TRMM-LIS) served as the gold standard for evaluating lightning flash frequency in Earth-System models. Today, the novel Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) provides continuous observations, but transitioning from LIS requires resolving profound instrumental biases. This study quantifies flash density, median area, and duration across the Americas by comparing gridded GLM data to the International Space Station LIS (ISS-LIS) over a 25-month period (December 2018–December 2020). Our findings reveal that GLM exhibits a lightning flash frequency undercount of two to four orders of magnitude—over highly convective continental landmasses. Driven by its physical detection floor, GLM is blind to the millions of small (<100 km²), short-duration (<100 ms) intracloud flashes dominating updraft cores, thereby artificially inflating its calculated median area. Conversely, over oceanic regions like the Intertropical Convergence Zone, GLM detects expansive, energetic flashes, but its coarse resolution causes optical "blooming," overestimating true footprints compared to the high-resolution ISS-LIS. Furthermore, steep satellite zenith angles stretch GLM pixels beyond 14 km at high latitudes, drastically ballooning area metrics. These hardware-driven artifacts critically impact atmospheric chemistry and climatology. Relying on raw GLM lightning flash frequency over land mathematically inflates "per-flash" Lightning-produced Nitrogen Oxides (LNOx) production efficiency estimates. In spite of the descrepancies, our annual GLM annual mean thunderhour mapping demonstrates that this metric successfully bypasses flash-level detection biases to accurately capture storm occurrence, providing a robust tool for tracking climate-driven convective shifts.

496915.title: Advancing the Frontier of Multiphase Chemistry Models with GPU-Accelerated Algorithms
496915.authors: Samuel George Frederick II, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and O. H. Diaz Ibarra, J. H. Curtis, Z. D'Aquino, N. Riemer, and M. West
496915.abstract: Multiphase atmospheric chemistry governs aerosol aging and CCN activity. However, its representation is highly simplified in Earth system models (ESMs) due to its computational expense. Legacy chemistry codes are optimized for CPUs and cannot fully utilize the computing power available in modern GPU-accelerated supercomputers. We introduce TChem-atm, a multiphase chemistry code designed for the next generation of ESMs around design principles that advance both computational performance and science capabilities. TChem-atm is designed for flexibility by allowing users to specify the chemical mechanism at runtime and uses an abstracted aerosol representation to interface with host model aerosol representations ranging from modal and sectional to particle-resolved models. To enable multiscale performance across aerosol representations, TChem-atm interfaces with multiple solver backends. We have designed a custom, matrix-free linear solver that allows solving thousands of chemical systems in parallel on GPUs. We show that this solver provides substantial performance advantages when solving kinetic systems at the scale of particle-resolved representations. We demonstrate how TChem-atm’s batched solver can be used to generate an ensemble of particle-resolved box model data, a crucial component for advancing ML emulation and constraining uncertainties in ESM aerosol-cloud parameterizations. By lowering computational cost, this work advances the science application frontier for particle-resolved aerosol models and unlocks ML-driven techniques for the representation of aerosol-cloud interactions in next-generation ESMs.

496916.title: Developing a Fully Coupled UFS Earth System Reanalysis for NOAA S2S Applications
496916.authors: Adam Schneider, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and J. M. Souza, G. P. Compo, B. Liu, L. J. Spencer, J. Woollen, S. Fredrick, J. Knezha, J. Whitaker, and S. Frolov
496916.abstract: Multi-decadal reanalyses provide temporally consistent estimates of the climate system, support retrospective forecasts, quantify model biases, and are essential for climate monitoring. Increasingly, they also serve as training data for AI/ML forecasting systems, yet most existing reanalyses do not provide dynamically consistent initial conditions across the atmosphere, land, ocean, and sea ice required for initialized subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction. Here we describe the development and production readiness of a fully coupled Earth System reanalysis designed to provide balanced initial conditions for NOAA's next-generation Seasonal Forecast System (SFS). Atmospheric, land, ocean, and sea-ice observations from the NOAA-NASA Joint Archive of Observations for Earth System Reanalysis were assimilated into a cycling 6-hour UFS-based coupled model using the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) atmospheric and JEDI-based Sea-Ice Ocean and Coupled Analysis (SOCA) data assimilation systems. Production readiness was assessed by monitoring the number of assimilated observations, observation-minus-background statistics, and preliminary comparisons of simulated sea-ice extent against passive microwave observations. Production test runs demonstrate stable multi-decadal cycling over 1988–2024 while assimilating a rapidly expanding global observing network. From 1988–2024, the number of assimilated surface pressure observations increased from approximately 10,000 to more than 100,000 per cycle, while assimilated 500-hPa temperature observations increased from roughly 1,000 to 24,000. Correspondingly, global RMS six-hour forecast errors decreased from approximately 1.5 to 0.5 °C for temperature, from 6 to 3 m/s for wind speed, and from 25% to 15% for relative humidity. In contrast, sea surface temperature (SST) short-term forecast errors remain larger than 2 °C through 2023 despite extensive satellite and in situ ocean observations, highlighting remaining challenges in coupled ocean data assimilation. Atmospheric performance compares well with predecessor systems, while ocean data assimilation and SST quality remain the primary limitations. These results demonstrate that the coupled UFS reanalysis system is capable of generating a multi-decadal Earth System dataset while identifying the remaining developments needed for a fully operational reanalysis supporting NOAA's SFS. The completed coupled reanalysis will provide the foundation for consistent retrospective forecasts, model bias correction, AI training datasets, and future operational S2S prediction within NOAA's UFS.

496918.title: Planetary Boundary Layer Height from the ICESat-2 Atmospheric Channel
496918.authors: Amanda Cresanti, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; and J. E. Yorks, K. Christian, P. Selmer, N. Roldan-Henao, and Z. Li
496918.abstract: Humans live within the planetary boundary layer (PBL) and are thus subject to the meteorological, climatological, and air quality impacts resulting from PBL processes, many of which are governed by the depth of this layer. Global observations of planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) are necessary, yet traditional radiosonde retrievals of PBLH are limited in spatiotemporal coverage. A gradient in aerosol vertical distribution from the boundary layer to the free troposphere can be detected by atmospheric lidar, allowing for estimation of PBLH. Here we present spatiotemporal trends of PBLH using spaceborne backscatter lidar data from the recent Ice, Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) atmospheric research product. Comparisons to ground-based lidar- and radiosonde-derived PBLH from Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) facility sites are made. Preliminary ICESat-2 PBLH climatology exhibits previously established trends such as a deeper and more variable PBL over land, a shallow PBL off the west coast of the U.S., and greatest PBL depths over deserts in Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and Australia. Based on four months of preliminary data, the mean (M) and standard deviation (SD) varied between U.S. Mountain West (M: 1.77, SD: 0.56) and U.S. Midwest (M: 1.06, SD: 0.24). This work highlights the suitability of using the ICESat-2 atmospheric channel to build a global climatological PBLH dataset.

496920.title: Modernizing Satellite Ground Systems: Strategic Evolution Toward an Enterprise Cloud Infrastructure
496920.authors: Scott A. Hausman, NOAA, Asheville, NC
496920.abstract: The NESDIS Common Cloud Framework (NCCF), a cloud-based, enterprise-wide set of data services developed by NOAA’s Office of Common Services in collaboration with AWS Professional Services and GAMA-1 Technologies, has transitioned from foundational development to a phase of operational maturation and enterprise-wide integration. The platform has solidified its role as a secure, scalable cloud-native infrastructure by achieving key milestones, including full security authorization for its high-performance environments and the integration of core services with automated data pipelines. This update details the current operational status, including successful algorithm migrations—leveraging enhanced orchestration services—and the onboarding of diverse mission data streams. Looking forward, the platform is advancing its capabilities by implementing native cloud cost-tracking and enterprise data management frameworks, facilitating the transition of legacy systems and archives. This presentation outlines the ongoing evolution of the framework, highlighting strategic initiatives to strengthen resilience, security, and mission-critical interoperability in support of the broader satellite data enterprise. The platform has solidified its role as a secure, scalable cloud-native infrastructure by achieving key milestones, including full security authorization for its high-performance environments and the integration of core services with automated data pipelines. This update details the current operational status, including successful algorithm migrations—leveraging enhanced orchestration services—and the onboarding of diverse mission data streams. Looking forward, the platform is advancing its capabilities by implementing native cloud cost-tracking and enterprise data management frameworks, facilitating the transition of legacy systems and archives. This presentation outlines the ongoing evolution of the framework, highlighting strategic initiatives to strengthen resilience, security, and mission-critical interoperability in support of the broader satellite data enterprise.

496921.title: The Solar Mg II Center-to-Wing Ratio: Chromospheric Variability in the Time and Frequency Domains
496921.authors: Dave Bouwer, Space Environment Technologies, Boulder, CO; and W. K. Tobiska and B. diLorenzo
496921.abstract: The solar Magnesium II (Mg II) core-to-wing ratio index is a well-established proxy for solar chromospheric EUV/UV irradiance and provides a more representative measure of chromospheric solar forcing than the commonly used F10.7 radio flux proxy. Because EUV/UV irradiance directly drives thermospheric and ionospheric variability, accurate forecasts of Mg II can improve specification of solar forcing for thermospheric density models used in satellite drag prediction and conjunction assessment. This study investigates the temporal variability of the daily Mg II index and develops an operational forecasting methodology based on the evolution of solar active regions. Time-frequency analysis, including Fourier and wavelet techniques, is used to characterize periodic variability in the Mg II index over five solar cycles. The analysis shows that intermediate-term periodicities associated with active-region evolution are quasi-stationary, occurring intermittently over approximately 80–160-day epochs, while the dominant 27- to 36-day signal associated with differential solar rotation persists throughout the solar cycle. Statistical significance is evaluated using AR(1) red-noise confidence levels for the Fourier spectra and Torrence–Compo significance testing with cone-of-influence analysis for the wavelet transforms. These results demonstrate that much of the short- to intermediate-term variability in chromospheric irradiance can be related to the emergence, rotation, and decay of solar active regions. These results motivate an Active-Region Finite Impulse Response (ARFIRS) forecasting model that represents active-region evolution and rotational visibility across successive solar rotations. Rolling-origin validation over 1979–2025 demonstrates that the model reduces forecast error by 20–30% relative to persistence for lead times of 4–20 days. Representation of multi-rotation active-region decay extends useful predictive skill to approximately 40–54 days, providing forecast capability beyond a single solar rotation. The results demonstrate a practical pathway toward moving beyond F10.7-based solar forcing by providing forecasts of a solar index more directly representative of chromospheric EUV/UV variability. Forecast Mg II, and derived indices such as M10, can provide physically motivated future solar forcing for thermospheric density modeling, satellite drag prediction, and other operational space weather applications.

496922.title: Operational Correlated Weather Ensembles for Energy Grid Applications
496922.authors: Patrick Hawbecker, Sunairio, Baltomore, MD; and B. Ho, R. Hasegawa, O. Pfeiffer, and R. Cirincione
496922.abstract: The power grid is rapidly evolving due to new renewable generation capacity, the retirement of fossil fuel generation plants, the building of data centers, and changing weather patterns– complicating grid planning and resource adequacy exercises. In this talk, we present an operational machine learning (ML)-assisted framework that generates probabilistic weather and energy ensembles which accurately reflect forecast uncertainty and preserves spatial and temporal correlation structure. Starting with a bias-corrected, and continuously-updating database of historical weather measurements at hourly frequency and fine-granularity, we calculate climate trends and the correlation structure of weather across time points and locations. We use this information to generate a 1000 member ensemble of ENSO-aware long-term correlated weather out to 2050. We merge these ensembles every hour with short-term weather forecasts that bias-correct and post-process the latest ECMWF and NOAA forecast, controlling the resulting ensemble spread to accurately represent forecast uncertainty. The resulting operational forecasts meld traditional published NWP models with ML methods to curate probabilistic and correlated weather ensembles. To show how these operational ensembles work in practice, we do a deep dive into a recent Winter Storm in ERCOT and a summer heat wave in PJM. By passing our weather ensembles through downstream energy models of electric demand, solar generation, wind generation, and generation outages, we demonstrate how the resulting predictions of correlated energy grid outcomes accurately predict electric grid stress, diminishing generation reserve margins, and astronomically high energy prices.

496923.title: Quantifying the Impact of Solar Irradiance Spectra on the Variation of Thermosphere and Ionosphere Using WACCM-X
496923.authors: Chih-Ting Hsu, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and N. Pedatella
496923.abstract: This study investigates the sensitivity of the thermosphere and ionosphere to variations in solar spectral irradiance. WACCM-X ensemble experiments and stand-alone simulations are conducted to quantify thermosphere-ionosphere responses to different specifications of solar irradiance and to assess the impacts of variability and uncertainty in solar irradiance spectra on thermospheric and ionospheric weather. The model is driven by different solar irradiance spectra, including EUVAC and FISM2, to examine how differences in solar spectral forcing affect the simulated thermosphere and ionosphere. Results show that both neutral temperature and electron density are highly sensitive to the specification of solar spectral irradiance. Comparisons with satellite observations from Swarm, GRACE, GOCE, and COSMIC-1 and -2 are used to evaluate the ability of WACCM-X to reproduce observed thermospheric and ionospheric variability. These results highlight the importance of accurately representing solar spectral irradiance and its associated uncertainties in space weather models.

496925.title: Continuous Data Assimilation, Reanalysis, and AI Modeling In Support of NOAA's NWP Modeling Moonshot
496925.authors: Daryl T. Kleist, NOAA/NWS/OMD, Riverdale Park, MD; and J. E. Ten Hoeve III, K. Garrett, C. R. Alexander, and V. S. Tallapragada
496925.abstract: NOAA’s Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) Modeling Moonshot initiative establishes a transformative vision to accelerate innovation by unifying academia, industry, and the U.S. government. One of the core goals of the Moonshot seeks to integrate physics-based prediction architectures—such as the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) dynamical core—with state-of-the-art artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) capabilities. Building this paradigm shift toward hybrid AI and physical superensembles relies on a foundation of continuous data assimilation (DA) and high-resolution training data derived from coupled Earth system reanalysis. To provide a single, authoritative analysis for both physical and AI-driven models, NOAA is advancing a Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI)-based continuous DA system operating in real time at increasingly high resolutions. This continuous framework will consolidate DA systems across various applications while enabling the rapid initialization of bespoke models at non-standard times. While current AI-based NWP models have advanced by leveraging datasets of opportunity—such as ERA5 and operational GDAS analyses—next-generation capabilities like those under Project EAGLE (Experimental AI Global and Limited-area Ensemble forecast system) demand datasets with higher fidelity and different characteristics. Generating modern, high-resolution reanalysis and reforecast datasets will provide essential benchmark training data for both internal and national modeling innovation. Accelerating this transformation relies on strategic academic and commercial partnerships. By embracing open-source code, cloud-based HPC environments, and DevOps frameworks, NOAA is pivoting toward co-development and establishing shared pipelines to cultivate external talent and expand the NWP workforce. Open community architecture and standardized verification software will enable enterprise-developed AI models to be transparently benchmarked, evaluated, and rapidly ingested into operations through an accelerated Research-to-Operations-to-Research (R2O2R) framework. Ultimately, synthesizing continuous DA, authoritative reanalyses, and collaborative AI capabilities will deliver faster, more actionable probabilistic forecast guidance to enhance Impact-Based Decision Support Services (IDSS) and protect life and property. This presentation will provide an overview of Goal 2 of the Moonshot, highlighting progress in continuous DA, reanalysis generation, and the collaborative mechanisms driving operational AI adoption.

496927.title: Assessing the Potential of Radar Data Assimilation in MPAS-JEDI to Improve Simulations of Winter Storm Hazards
496927.authors: Ethan Michael Schaefer, Pennsylvania State University, Glen Allen, VA; and S. J. Greybush, Y. Zhang, and D. J. Stensrud
496927.abstract: Winter storm events pose a significant threat to life and property, with hazards ranging from unsafe travel conditions to structural damage under the weight of accumulated snow and ice. In consideration of these hazards, it is important to understand and improve on the predictability of winter storms in numerical models. In particular, emphasis should be placed on the transition regions between precipitation types and the localized potential for heavy precipitation features, such as snow banding and convective showers. Radar observations, including reflectivity, radial velocity, and polarimetric retrievals, demonstrate strong potential to refine simulations of these hazards due to their targeted sampling of precipitating regions within much of the cloudy vertical column. While radial velocity observations are operationally assimilated at NOAA, radar reflectivity is only indirectly considered for latent heat nudging at initialization, and no radar polarimetry is currently assimilated in any model. This project addresses the potential for improved consideration of radar observations in data assimilation algorithms by evaluating MPAS ensemble simulations of a winter storm case study. The selected case involves notable forecast uncertainty in delineating hazard potential, including the placement of rain-to-snow transition regions and the formation of heavy precipitation features. Radial velocity measurements from individual radar sites and reflectivity mosaics from MRMS post-processed grids will be included as assimilated networks. Regarding radar polarimetry, experiments will target the potential for assimilating retrievals of melting layer height from dual-polarization variables, such as correlation coefficients. Cycling data assimilation will be performed within the JEDI framework to align with current operational developments, and each MPAS-JEDI experiment will apply a unique combination of the above observation types. Evaluations of each MPAS ensemble will involve probabilistic assessments of high-impact winter hazards from the corresponding case study compared to local precipitation reports. For evaluating individual precipitation features, object-based evaluation methods will be used with an emphasis on the placement, extent, and intensity of the simulated objects compared to radar measurements.

496928.title: A New Type of Convective Plume Model Inspired by Observations of Convective Mass Flux
496928.authors: Stefan Neil Tulich, CIRES and NOAA/PSL, Boulder, CO
496928.abstract: The past ten years have seen tremendous progress in our ability to measure convective mass flux profiles across spatial domains relevant to convection parameterization. Here, published measurements of this type are shown to imply net fractional entrainment rates toward the base of the convecting layer that are generally too large for adoption in current operational mass-flux schemes of the "bulk" variety. This is because calculated plume buoyancies are then generally found to be unsupportive of convection (even when presented with observed convectively active soundings), essentially due to too much unsaturated environmental air being mixed into the plume at low levels. By assuming unrealistically low values of entrainment, however, current operational schemes tend to produce mass flux profiles whose curvature is generally too weak, which almost certainly leads to structural errors in their predicted heating and moistening tendencies. To address this issue, an alternative type of plume model is proposed in which the assumption of horizontal homogeneity across the plume body is abandoned in favor of an assumed interior "core" region, protected by one or more surrounding "cloaks". The impacts of adopting this "core-cloak" plume model in a near-operational convection scheme will be presented.

496930.title: Instrument to Interface: Building an Open Educational Ecosystem Around a Campus Mesonet Station
496930.authors: Kenneth L. Tapp, Texas State University, San Marcos, TX
496930.abstract: Introductory meteorology courses at large universities typically teach observational science through data that students never collect and instruments they never see. In July 2026, Texas State University installed a mesonet-style surface observation station at its Round Rock campus in partnership with the Texas Water Development Board, with near real-time data flowing to TexMesonet. The weather station was conceived from the outset to primarily support interactive curriculum on a research grade platform, and this presentation focuses on the learning ecosystem constructed around it. That ecosystem includes open educational resource chapters on surface observation and radar interpretation, published under Creative Commons licensing for adoption beyond a single institution; interactive exercises built with near real-time station and radar data covering the campus and students' own location; and browser-based augmented reality tools that help students visualize atmospheric data in a physical classroom or campus space. Over 600 students enroll in Meteorology at Texas State each fall semester, overwhelmingly non-science majors satisfying a general-education requirement. The design premise is that weather and climate literacy improves when the observations are local, current, and verifiable. The presentation describes the technical architecture connecting instruments to course content, the institutional partnerships that made it possible without a research budget, obstacles encountered in campus integration and instrument siting, and early evidence on student engagement. All materials are openly licensed and freely available for adaptation.

496931.title: What Gets Measured: Comparing Academic and Electric Utility Wildfire Resilience Metrics
496931.authors: Troy Saltiel, PNNL, Salt Lake City, UT; and J. Yoon, C. Chini, C. Bakker, L. Miller, N. Samaan, and A. M. Coleman
496931.abstract: Electric power systems face compounding risks from wildfires: electrical assets are vulnerable to wildfire damage, and failing assets or vegetation contacts can ignite catastrophic fires under severe weather conditions. Recent electrically caused disasters, like the 2018 Camp Fire, the 2023 Maui fires, and the 2025 Eaton Fire, have led to tragic loss of life, utility bankruptcies, and intense public and regulatory scrutiny. In response, academic research is evolving, and utilities across the country are rapidly working towards adopting a large variety of physical and system-level risk mitigation approaches. Questions arise around quantifying the success and return-on-investment for risk mitigation actions as these often have direct impacts to rate payers; however, there are an expansive number of metrics and indicators available that lead to large inconsistencies for how risk, mitigation, and reliability are measured and reported. There are further inconsistencies in how the research community is thinking in this space and how the applied actions of utilities are implemented. To address the wide variety of metrics and indicators, we present the first comprehensive, comparative assessment of grid wildfire resilience metrics for the electric utility industry to drive towards a more comprehensive and cross-utility standard for hazard risk, resilience, and reliability. Using a structured, large language model (LLM)-assisted extraction protocol, we analyzed the largest dataset compiled to date: 185 publicly available utility wildfire mitigation plans and 240 academic and grey-literature publications. We classified approximately 2,900 extracted metrics into a new, open-access, two-level taxonomy of grid resilience consisting of nine categories and 45 subcategories. This granular, open-access database allows users to study specific indicators of interest. For example, meteorological drivers like fire weather indices, extreme weather days, and weather-driven impacts can be isolated to analyze how they are integrated into decision-making across both domains. Our results reveal that the two communities have developed largely non-overlapping measurement regimes shaped by distinct institutional environments. Generally, academic metrics concentrate on event-conditioned performance (outage magnitude, system recovery, and economic consequence), while utility WMPs focus on pre-event risk and mitigation execution (inspections, vegetation management, and de-energization). For weather-focused metrics, utilities rely heavily on fire weather monitoring to trigger preventative actions, whereas academic models largely omit these weather-dependent operational levers. Bridging this divide offers a path towards better accounting and a more holistic application to enhance wildfire resilience leading to improved system reliability and safety. Utility planning and operations require quantifiable and reportable outcome-oriented metrics with the ability to use and work from a known and common standard, while researchers should integrate realistic practices based on the constraints utilities face. The open release of the metric database serves as a crosswalk between academia and electric utilities, enabling innovative and incremental improvements to measure grid performance across both the physical and operational system.

496933.title: Challenges and Opportunities Facing Computing Centers and Others Providing High Performance Computing to Support the Weather, Water, and Climate Community
496933.abstract: This panel session will feature Directors and Senior Managers from HPC Centers and other organizations serving the Weather, Water and Climate community addressing the challenges they face in providing HPC services for research and operations – as well as the opportunities they see for enhancing the services they provide in the future. Each speaker will address the topic in a short presentation, followed by a panel discussion and questions from session attendees. Panelists are anticipated from Government agencies, research institutions, academia, and others. Previous year’s panels have been very informative and generated lively discussion, featuring speakers from NOAA, NASA, NCAR, DOD, ECMWF, and UKMet. This year promises equally diverse panelists from across the community.

496935.title: Studying the Impact of 7.3 GHz Band Radio Frequency Interference on Retrieval Products
496935.authors: Mathew Gunshor, CIMSS/SSEC, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and Z. Li, S. Moeller, and J. J. Gerth
496935.abstract: The 7125-8400 MHz band is utilized by important meteorological satellites for scientific data acquisition and communication services at ground stations. NOAA produces several Environmental Data Record (EDR) products using the 7.3 GHz bands, including sea surface temperature (SST), cloud liquid water (CLW), and sea surface wind (SSW). These products are critical for understanding the water cycle and play an important role in improving numerical weather prediction, monitoring extreme maritime weather, precipitation analysis, tropical cyclone location and intensity analysis, monitoring, and forecasting. This presentation will feature simple methodologies developed to identify the RFI impact in the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 2 (AMSR2) L1B data at 7.3 GHz and in the L2 products that use this channel. The presentation will also show the results of sensitivity studies carried out to evaluate how the L2 products are affected by RFI in 7.3 GHz. The Community Satellite Processing Package (CSPP) GCOM-W AMSR2 Algorithm Software Package (GAASP) was used to generate the L2 EDR products. These sensitivity studies will be focused on how RFI signals affect the accuracy of SST, SSW, and CLW.

496941.title: From Monitoring to Action: The Third Decadal U.S. Carbon Cycle Science Plan
496941.authors: Abhishek Chatterjee, Schmidt Sciences, New York, NY; and L. Barbero, M. Tzortziou, E. Sunquist, B. Poutra, S. Alin, A. Ballantyne, H. Benway, L. M. Bruhwiler, A. R. Desai, J. Dunne, D. Hayes, F. M. Hoffman, B. Hoenisch, P. Marcotullio, E. Marin-Spiotta, B. Poulter, D. Royer, W. Sun, A. L. S. Swann, Y. Takeshita, G. Xue, and X. Yang
496941.abstract: The U.S. Carbon Cycle Science Program (U.S. CSSP) is a community-focused program with a research portfolio that encompasses carbon and pertinent biogeochemical cycles across land, water, air and society. Over the last three decades, the U.S. CCSP has led and coordinated community input from the U.S. and the international carbon cycle community and captured them in two seminal U.S. Carbon Cycle Science Plans (1999, 2011). The U.S. CCSP has developed an updated, new science plan for U.S. carbon cycle science, identifying challenges and priorities for the next decade (~2026-2035). The Third Decadal U.S. Carbon Cycle Science Plan builds on the two previous plans by identifying new priorities and directions for the U.S. carbon cycle community. A primary evolution taking place in the Third Decadal U.S. Carbon Cycle Science Plan to its predecessors is the engagement of end user partners across the public, private, non governmental organization, and philanthropic sectors.
