The author team has engaged with various end user partners within carbon management, energy, local, state, and federal government, foundations, philanthropies, policy, agriculture, and more to gather input and their distinctive perspective on priorities for carbon cycle science in the next decade, and these engagements have built the foundation for ongoing partnerships and opportunities for implementation of the Plan throughout the next decade.

496942.title: Cloud Droplet Activation and Natural Aerosol Emissions Dominate Aerosol Structural Uncertainty in the Canadian Earth System Model
496942.authors: Luke Fraser-Leach, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada; and P. J. Kushner, K. von Salzen, and R. Digby
496942.abstract: Structural differences in the aerosol modules of Earth system models (ESMs) are a key contributor to the spread in aerosol properties among ESMs. We take advantage of a newly available 2-moment aerosol microphysics scheme (the piecewise lognormal approximation aerosol model, PAM) in the Canadian ESM (CanESM) to isolate uncertainty associated with aerosol model formulation. Specifically, we analyze a pair of CanESM configurations with identical model parameters that differ only in their aerosol schemes: one configuration uses PAM while the other uses the default bulk aerosol scheme, which was the workhorse configuration used in CMIP5 and CMIP6. We focus here on the substantial differences in present-day cloudy-sky and clear-sky radiative fluxes in these two configurations. The cloudy-sky effect is due to differences in cloud droplet number concentration (CDNC) and reflects PAM's improved representation of aerosol activation. In contrast, the difference in clear-sky radiative fluxes is dominated by differences in dust and sea salt aerosol optical depth (AOD), which are due to sensitivities in the emissions schemes used for these species rather than differences in aerosol processes. This points to such schemes as a significant source of spread in ESM aerosol properties, suggesting simulations with specified natural aerosol emissions may be a valuable tool for model intercomparison.

496943.title: When and Where Do Simulated Hydroxyl Radical (OH) Biases Matter? Insights from the Atmospheric CH4-CO-OH Cycle
496943.authors: Doyeon Ahn, University of Maryland Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD; NASA/GSFC, Greenbelt, MD; and D. C. Anderson, S. A. Strode, A. H. Souri, and B. N. Duncan
496943.abstract: The hydroxyl radical (OH) is the troposphere’s primary oxidant and the main sink for methane (CH4) and carbon monoxide (CO), yet its abundance and spatiotemporal variabilities remain highly uncertain, with simulated OH varying widely across models. This study investigates the spatiotemporal impact of OH biases on CH4 and CO simulation over decadal timescales. Using the computationally Efficient CH4–CO–OH (ECCOH) chemistry module within the NASA GEOS model, we conduct a sensitivity analysis imposing a persistent −15% perturbation to tropospheric OH, applied separately over tropical marine, tropical land, and northern extratropical land regions, as well as globally, for the 2001 – 2015 period. We present results from these sensitivity simulations using a set of diagnostic variables designed to characterize the CH4 and CO response from an inversion-analysis perspective: specifically, how much posterior emissions would be erroneously adjusted if the model’s OH field carries a 15% bias that varies by location and time, and what impact arises from using prescribed OH versus an online, interactive OH field (i.e., full CH4-CO-OH chemical feedback). Based on these findings, we discuss where and when efforts to reduce OH biases should be prioritized, drawing on ground-based tower, sub-orbital aircraft campaign, and satellite-based indirect constraint methods.

496945.title: The Third Decadal U.S. Carbon Cycle Science Plan
496945.authors: Abhishek Chatterjee, Schmidt Sciences, New York, NY; and L. Barbero, M. Tzortziou, E. Sunquist, B. Poutra, S. Alin, A. Ballantyne, H. Benway, L. M. Bruhwiler, A. R. Desai, J. Dunne, D. Hayes, F. Hoffman, B. Hoenisch, P. Marcotullio, E. Marin-Spiotta, B. Poulter, D. Royer, W. Sun, A. L. S. Swann, Y. Takeshita, Z. G. Xue, and X. Yang
496945.abstract: The U.S. Carbon Cycle Science Program (U.S. CSSP) is a community-focused program with a research portfolio that encompasses carbon and pertinent biogeochemical cycles across land, water, air and society. Over the last three decades, the U.S. CCSP has led and coordinated community input from the U.S. and the international carbon cycle community and captured them in two seminal U.S. Carbon Cycle Science Plans (1999, 2011). The U.S. CCSP has developed an updated, new science plan for U.S. carbon cycle science, identifying challenges and priorities for the next decade (~2026-2035). The Third Decadal U.S. Carbon Cycle Science Plan builds on the two previous plans, identifies new priorities and directions for the U.S. carbon cycle community and aims to increase engagement between the research, U.S. federal agency partners, and end user communities throughout the coming decade.

496947.title: Persistent Northeast Pacific Marine Heatwaves are Sensitive to the Seasonality of Tropical and North Pacific Dynamics
496947.abstract: Northeast Pacific marine heatwaves occur year-round but are shaped by seasonally-varying dynamics including El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and North Pacific atmosphere-ocean interactions. Using a data-driven cyclostationary linear inverse model constructed from 64 years of monthly sea surface temperature and height reanalyses, we demonstrate that longer-lived marine heatwaves preferentially begin in winter, when ENSO teleconnections and oceanic memory most strongly influence event amplification. Springtime subsurface storage and subsequent fall/winter reemergence of thermal anomalies drive extended persistence through wintertime re-intensification. While intense events can also begin in summer, without strong ENSO and reemergence dynamics they rarely persist. The relative importance of tropical forcing versus North Pacific upper-ocean dynamics varies by region and season, producing distinct marine heatwave “flavors” linked to different ENSO types or to internal North Pacific processes alone. These findings reveal how seasonal phase-locking drives marine heatwave evolution, with implications for predictability and marine ecosystem impacts.

496955.title: Predicting Dust Concentrations In a Coupled Weather-Aerosol Modeling Framework
496955.authors: Kyoung Min Kim, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and R. Ahmadov, J. Schnell, H. Li, J. Romero-Alvarez, M. Choi, and G. Ferrada
496955.abstract: Mineral dust and smoke aerosols significantly impact air quality, visibility, and weather across North America. To advance regional atmospheric composition forecasting, a new coupled weather-aerosol model based on the MPAS dynamical core (CheMPAS-Fire) is being developed to provide experimental forecasts of smoke, dust and other aerosols over the Contiguous United States (CONUS), which is initialized daily with forecasts going out to 3 days. Within CheMPAS-Fire, dust emissions depend on key surface physical parameters, including surface wind, soil moisture, surface roughness, and erodibility. To examine the sensitivity of dust simulations to different parameterizations, this study compares two distinct dust schemes implemented in CheMPAS-Fire: the FENGSHA and the GOCART dust schemes. Additionally, we evaluate dust radiative feedback and the impact of model spatial resolution, as spatial resolution influences the representation of land surface inputs and localized surface wind fields that drive dust emissions. Sensitivity simulations are conducted across 3-km and 12-km resolution grids over the CONUS. We will demonstrate the CheMPAS-Fire model performance during the dust events. Comprehensive evaluations against weather observations, AERONET Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), AirNow surface PM2.5 and PM10, and satellite observations will show how dust scheme selection and spatial resolution affect localized surface wind shear, aerosol transport, and spatial dust distributions.

496956.title: Extending the Geostationary Atmospheric Composition Constellation for Global Coverage: Optimization of Observatories, Scan Patterns and Spatial Coverage
496956.authors: Madison Shogrin, BAE Systems Inc., Space and Missions Systems, Broomfield, CO; and D. Nicks and S. Drobot
496956.abstract: The development of geostationary atmospheric composition sensors, their associated retrieval algorithms, and the science from these data offer the opportunity to realize the Atmospheric Composition Virtual Constellation as envisioned by the Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS). These persistent, hourly, high spatial resolution measurements are key to understanding the diurnal variability of emissions from combustion sources, photochemistry, and atmospheric fate and transport. The Tropospheric Emissions Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO), Geostationary Environment Monitoring Spectrometer (GEMS) and Sentinel 4 primarily cover the Northern Hemisphere. The Global South is undergoing rapid economic development resulting in increasing populations and associated emissions. Extending these key atmospheric composition observatories globally is necessary for monitoring natural and anthropogenic emissions and reducing exposure to these growing populations. Trades of expanding remote sensing observations to global coverage from geostationary orbit will be presented. These trades include scan patterns optimized for coverage and implications for retrievals, determination of number of observatories based on global NO2 observations and spatial resolution, and impacts of co-manifesting multiple observatories on the same spacecraft.

496963.title: Does Forecast Accuracy Have Market Value? Evidence from Hurricane Landfalls and Insurer Stock Returns
496963.authors: August Kaapcke LePique, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and D. Siregar and P. Sirianni
496963.abstract: Tropical cyclones are the costliest weather-related hazard in the United States, costing an estimated $1.7 trillion between 1980 to 2025. Property and liability (P&L) insurers absorb a significant share of the resulting losses. Over the past decades, hurricane forecasting skill has substantially improved. While the benefits of improved forecasts are well documented for emergency management and evacuation decisions, their value as reflected in capital markets remains largely unexamined. We examine 46 tropical cyclones that attained hurricane intensity and made landfall in the United States between 1996 and 2024, each causing at least $1 billion in damage. Average track error for each storm is obtained from the National Hurricane Center Tropical Cyclone Reports. Daily stock returns are obtained from CRSP and firm financial data from Compustat, both accessed through Wharton Research Data Services. Firm exposure is measured as the share of direct premiums written in affected states. An event study methodology is used to compute expected, abnormal, average abnormal, and cumulative average abnormal returns for each hurricane, using the date of landfall as the event date. Expected returns are estimated using the market model, with the estimation window placed outside the Atlantic hurricane season to avoid contamination from multiple storms during active seasons. Firm level cumulative abnormal returns are then regressed on average track error, controlling for company-related factors identified by Fama and French (1992). We hypothesize that storms with larger track errors produce more negative cumulative abnormal returns. Preliminary results are presented.

496967.title: Converging Ideas: The State of Storm Merger Science and New Breakthroughs
496967.authors: Matthew C. Brown, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and K. J. Gillett and A. Conner
496967.abstract: Field observations have long indicated that severe storms – especially those that go on to produce tornadoes – rarely exist in isolation. Rather, multiple convective cells interact in space and time through a complex series of interactions, leading to either constructive or destructive impacts based on case-specific attributes. Through the advent of WSR-88D and dual-pol radar upgrades, along with several targeted, multi-institutional convective field campaigns, the severe storms community eventually reached a critical mass of observations to begin making broader inferences about the storm and environmental controls on merger outcomes (i.e., storm maintenance, post-merger hazard production). These climatological efforts have honed in on several important features – particularly supercell rear flank interactions – which tend to precede constructive merger events. This rear flank finding has been further supported by results from idealized storm interaction simulations, in relation to downdraft/outflow surges which aid vorticity aggregation beneath developing storm mesocyclones in advance of tornadogenesis. Despite this increasing clarity, a number of outstanding questions and inconsistencies remain in storm merger science. Most notably, upper-level observations (e.g., space-born satellite measurements) suggest that nearby deep convective cells often begin interacting well before their low-level merging process, as assessed via radar reflectivity. Very recent numerical simulations reveal a considerably more complex top-down merging process, including anvil-level hydrometeor advection and seeding by neighboring cells, which in turn leads to the alteration of mid-/upper-level buoyancy profiles and modulation of parent cell downdraft dynamics. Furthermore, collocation of aforementioned radar-based merger observations with satellite-derived fields suggests that upper-level consolidation (and expansion) of overshooting tops may play a secondary role in fostering constructive post-merger outcomes. Altogether, this study seeks to detail the evolution of storm merger science, reconcile these new dynamical insights with conventional theory, and highlight forthcoming research avenues for improved prediction of storm merger events and their attendant hazards.

496968.title: Myths of the USDM: What Really Goes on Behind the Green Curtain
496968.authors: Mark D. Svoboda, National Drought Mitigation Center, University of Nebraska, Lincoln, NE
496968.abstract: As we approach 30 years in the making of the U.S. Drought Monitor, the need for continuous education and communication as to what it is, and isn’t, is a never-ending task. This presentation will walk through many of the questions and myths about the process that have come up over the past three decades. We will take an inside look at how the USDM has evolved over the years and how services have grown to meet the demands of so many who rely on the product. Over the years, a direct and transparent conduit to feedback has helped the USDM grow and become a staple of drought relief policy programs in the U.S. while serving as a backbone for efforts around the globe. This presentation will highlight several of these applications and the challenges moving forward.

496969.title: T2I: Open-Source Modernization of Aviation Veather Reporting and Dissemination In the Caribbean.
496969.authors: Joseph McGuire, Brown University, Providence, RI; and C. Horvat, K. Kerr IV, and A. G. Laing
496969.abstract: Aviation meteorological products are among the few meteorological outputs exchanged internationally under a legal mandate, because flight planning, operations, and hazard avoidance depend on them being available in a common form across borders. These products are presently issued in two encodings. Traditional Alphanumeric Code (TAC) is a compact, human-readable encoding, standardized internationally for reporting in 1993 and scheduled for discontinuation no later than 2029. The ICAO Meteorological Information Exchange Model (IWXXM) represents the same products as XML files, is currently an ICAO Standard and has been mandatory for international operational exchange of relevant aeronautical meteorological information since November 2020. Recent amendments in 2025 also extend IWXXM to quantitative volcanic ash concentration, space weather advisories, and additional metadata. Services issuing aviation meteorological information are required to transition from TAC to IWXXM as ICAO is moving towards removing TAC as a standard for international exchange by 2030. While IWXXM is the standard format, TAC remains in use among many CMO Members during the transition to IWXXM. Across the ICAO North American, Central American and Caribbean region, transition to digital aviation meteorological information is progressing at different rates as capability is unevenly distributed: some states have advance capabilities for producing and exchanging IWXXM data through national and regional OPMET infrastructure, while others continue to rely primarily on TAC products. A limiting factor in the adoption of IWXXM is the uneven set of tools available. Open-source implementations are often limited in the products they ingest. The main recourse for countries is commercial products which are updated routinely, or through bespoke consulting engagements. Meteorological services thus pursue identical capabilities separately, and support ends up patchy and variable between states.This uneven level of implementation highlights a need for targeted technical support, capacity building and regional collaboration to support a consistent transition to IWXXM across CMO Members. Here we detail a partnership between the Caribbean Meteorological Organisation (CMO) and Brown University to develop TAC-to-IWXXM (T2I): a flexible, open-source, end-to-end system for linting and validating incoming meteorological reports in a range of formats and producing IWXXM-ready output for dissemination. T2I validates incoming TAC and resulting XML against WMO requirements reference examples. It covers the full set of products defined in IWXXM — METAR, SPECI, TAF, SIGMET, AIRMET, volcanic ash and tropical cyclone advisories, volcano observatory notices for aviation, and space weather advisories, and supports both the ICAO Annex 3 and U.S. national profiles. T2I reports diagnostics on malformed input and applies a stable, bounded set of corrections, displaying every change alongside the original for operator review. T2I is distributed for adoption at a range of autonomy levels: a hosted web application and public API, and Docker images and Python packages for self-hosting. A regional body such as CMO may therefore maintain a single reference deployment that Member Services can use and adopt directly for national requirements, while any Member that requires it can self-host and retain sovereignty over its own data and messaging. Because the source is public, national requirements and future revisions to the IWXXM tool can be implemented by Member Services and by CMO together, allowing coordination of versions, profiles, and validation rules at the regional level rather than independently by each Member, while still serving the needs of member states. We will discuss the initial testing and training phase, as well as the presentation of T2I at the Annual Meeting of the Heads of National Meteorological Services of CMO Member States in November 2026, together with the implementation path being developed through CMO, which includes dissemination through WIS2, AMHS/SWIM, and EDIS. We finally discuss remaining needs, in particular automated end-to-end transmission from observation to IWXXM, handling of message bulletins, broader regional uptake, and training to support and ensure user adoption and contributor growth.

496971.title: Quasi-Lagrangian Observations of Cloud Microphysics Using a Free-Floating Balloon and Lightweight Holographic Imager
496971.authors: Sebastian Käser, ETH Zürich, Zürich, Switzerland; and C. Fuchs, J. Henneberger, and U. Lohmann
496971.abstract: Process rates are essential for the development and evaluation of cloud microphysics parameterizations in numerical weather prediction and climate models. Most current observations capture snapshots of clouds, seriously limiting our ability to quantify the rates of the microphysical processes governing hydrometeor evolution. Lagrangian observations, which follow an air parcel over time, provide an opportunity to derive such process rates. To perform Lagrangian observations, we developed a free-floating balloon system (LaBalloon). The system controls its buoyancy through a valve attached to the balloon neck. After ascent, a feedback control algorithm transitions LaBalloon to neutral buoyancy and initiates the Lagrangian trajectory. A radiosonde measures the environmental properties of the cloud parcel followed by LaBalloon. To observe cloud hydrometeors, we built a lightweight holographic imager (HOLIMOair). Using in-line holography, HOLIMOair captures 2D images of all hydrometeors in a well-defined sample volume. From these observations, we derive phase-resolved cloud microphysical properties, including size distributions, particle shapes, and the clustering of ice crystals and cloud droplets. In addition, we combine these microphysical observations with aerosol size distribution measurements obtained from an optical particle counter (Alphasense N3). We deployed this novel measurement platform in shallow cumulus clouds over the Swiss Prealps. The instruments sampled an air parcel for several tens of minutes and observed its microphysical properties along a quasi-Lagrangian trajectory. These measurements captured the evolution of the cloud droplet size distribution within the ascending air parcel. We compare multiple such observations with parcel-ascent simulations performed using pySDM and assess the model's ability to reproduce the observed microphysical evolution. We further identify processes that may explain differences between simulated and observed cloud microphysical properties, such as entrainment. The unique combination of quasi-Lagrangian observations and single-parcel modeling provides new insights into cloud microphysical process rates and their representation in atmospheric models.

496972.title: BoltCam: A Web-Based Platform Integrating Lightning Mapping, Satellite, Radar, and Video Observations over the Mid-Atlantic Region
496972.authors: Guangyang Fang, Univ. of Maryland/ESSIC/CISESS, Greenbelt, MD; and D. J. Figueroa and S. D. Rudlosky
496972.abstract: Observing lightning across the Mid-Atlantic region requires combining complementary measurements that capture different aspects of thunderstorms. BoltCam (http://boltcam.cisess.umd.edu) is a web-based platform developed to integrate and display observations from the Mid-Atlantic Lightning Mapping Array (MALMA), the Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM), weather radar, and a regional Raspberry Pi camera network (RPCN). By bringing these datasets together in a common environment, BoltCam supports thunderstorms event identification, cross-platform comparison, network monitoring, and collaborative analysis. MALMA combines observations from the Washington, D.C., and Wallops Flight Facility Lightning Mapping Arrays to provide three-dimensional measurements of total lightning. GLM provides continuous satellite-based optical lightning observations, while radar characterized storm structure and evolution. RPCN records lightning at high frame rates, providing an independent visual perspective for interpreting lightning development and evaluating remotely sensed observations. This presentation will describe the design and ongoing development of BoltCam, the integration of these complementary observing systems, and selected thunderstorm examples demonstrating the value of viewing the datasets together. It will also discuss challenges involving timing, data availability, network performance, and differences in the spatial and temporal characteristics of the observing systems. BoltCam is designed to improve access to regional lightning observations and support satellite validation, storm analysis, lightning research, network maintenance, educational applications, and the development of a regional lightning climatology.

496973.title: Rising Tropical Cyclone Heat Potential in the Northern Indian Ocean
496973.authors: James A. Carton, Univ. of Maryland, College Park, MD; and P. Manoogian
496973.abstract: Background Tropical cyclones in the Northern Indian Ocean represent less than 10% of tropical cyclones but are responsible for more than 80% of the related fatalities. Recent examples include Nargis (2008) and Amphan (2020). The human impacts of these storms make improved understanding and prediction a high priority. Tropical cyclones derive their power from the temperature difference between the evaporative warm surface ocean and the cold stratosphere. Factors that increase vertical transfer of fluid between these two surfaces are responsible for increasing cyclone intensity. This study focusses on the lower boundary, specifically the extent to which the ocean surface can maintain a warm > 26C temperature that can resist the cooling effects of entrainment. This can be done either by having a thick layer of warm water or by invoking strong haline stratification. We evaluate these two by evaluating two spatially and temporally varying quantities: Tropical Cyclone Heat Potential (TCHP) and Barrier Layer Thickness (BLT) during the 20 year period 2005-2024. Methodology We evaluate Tropical Cyclone Heat Potential and Barrier Layer Thickness based on the newly released eddy-resolving global Simple Ocean Data Assimilation ocean/sea ice reanalysis version 4 (SODA4). The numerical model used in the reanalysis is based on NOAA/Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory MOM5.1/SIS1 numerics with nominal l/10° horizontal resolution. In the vertical the model has 75 z* vertical levels that expand from fine ~1.1 m resolution near surface to coarse 200m resolution in the deep ocean. Surface forcing is provided by a bias-corrected version of the European Center for Medium Range Weather Forecasts ERA5 forcing, while continental discharge is provided by a separate monthly observation-based discharge dataset. The main subsurface dataset that SODA ingests are extracted from the World Ocean Database of historical hydrographic profiles. This dataset includes more than 7 million profiles of which 2.5 million (or 13,400/month) come from Argo drifting profilers and another 2.8 million from ocean gliders. Collated L3 remotely sensed nighttime Infrared SST observations from the NOAA Center for Satellite Applications and Research span the full period of interest, with additional calibrating in situ observations obtained from International Comprehensive Ocean–Atmosphere Data Set (ICOADS) release 3.0 SST database. Sequential data assimilation is used to constrain the evolving temperature and salinity fields. From the gridded output the two parameters, TCHP and BLT are computed. TCHP, which has units of J/m2, is computed by integrating the ocean thermal energy from the surface down to the depth of the 26C isotherm. BLT, which has units of m, is the thickness difference between the depth of the isothermal layer and the density-based mixed layer. This latter is of high relevance to the strongly haline-stratified Bay of Bengal, but less relevance to the saltier Arabian Sea. Analysis & Uncertainty Quantification The accuracy of our estimate of TCHP and BLT are evaluated several ways. The reanalysis itself produces analysis increments, which are the gridded corrections to the forecast at each assimilation cycle. These allow us to estimate the consistency of the analyses to the assimilated observations. The fixed RAMA mooring provide continuous time series for comparison, but at only a few reference points. Finally, satellite estimates of sea level are available for independent comparison. Results The first decade (2005-2014) there were 9 strong tropical cyclones (categories 3-5) while during the second decade 2015-2024) that number increased to 14, coinciding with a substantial increase in TCHP throughout the Northern Indian Ocean. Of particular note: there were 8 during the two year period 2018-2019 coinciding with a weak El Nino, a strongly positive Indian Ocean dipole and high TCHP in the Arabian Sea.

496978.title: Roles of Supercooled Liquid Water and Deep Ice-Phase Processes in Orographic Snowfall over the Colorado Rockies
496978.authors: Katja Friedrich, Univ. of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and J. ValdiviaPrado, B. Adler, S. Matrosov, and G. de Boer
496978.abstract: Wintertime orographic snowfall can be influenced by mountain-wave-induced enhancements of supercooled liquid water (SLW), which promote riming, as well as by ice growth within deeper clouds. However, few observational studies have directly compared the relative contributions of these processes to snowfall production. Here, we use measurements from the 2022–2023 deployment of the Surface Atmosphere Integrated Field Laboratory (SAIL) and the Study of Precipitation, the Lower Atmosphere and Surface for Hydrometeorology (SPLASH), conducted near Crested Butte, Colorado. The observing site was in a high-elevation valley of the central Colorado Rocky Mountains within the upper Gunnison River basin. We combine a full winter season of vertically pointing Ka-band cloud-radar observations with microwave-radiometer retrievals of liquid and ice water path to examine relationships among mountain-wave activity, cloud vertical structure, and SLW availability. This analysis evaluates how wave signatures at different altitudes are associated with enhanced SLW and conditions favorable for riming, and contrasts these periods with snowfall produced by deeper, predominantly ice-phase clouds containing relatively little SLW. Preliminary case-study results indicate that SLW can enhance hydrometeor growth during periods of strong mountain-wave activity. However, snowfall intensity and precipitation efficiency during the examined orographic storms appear to be more strongly controlled by deep-layer ice-phase growth and upper-level dynamical forcing. These findings suggest that mountain-wave-enhanced riming may be important episodically, while deeper cloud processes can exert the dominant control on total snowfall production.

496981.title: Relationship between Atmospheric Boundary Layer Dynamics and Sublimation In a High-Altitude Mountain Valley In Colorado
496981.authors: Bianca Adler, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and B. J. Butterworth and C. J. Cox
496981.abstract: Thermally and dynamically driven flows frequently occur in mountain valleys and impact the structure and evolution of the atmospheric boundary layer and the surface energy balance. During the cold season, when the valley surface is snow covered, they may thus influence snow ablation either due to sublimation, the phase change from solid to vapor, and snow melt, the phase change from solid to liquid. We used comprehensive observations that were collected in the high-altitude East River Valley in the Colorado Rocky Mountains between fall 2021 and summer 2023 for the DOE funded Surface Atmosphere Integrated Field Laboratory (SAIL) project and the NOAA funded Study of Precipitation, the Lower Atmosphere and Surface for Hydrometeorology (SPLASH) project to investigate the relationship between the structure and evolution of the atmospheric boundary layer and the surface energy balance during two cold seasons. In the absence of clouds, three distinct flow regimes were found to occur in the valley when there was snow on the ground: The first regime (DV) exhibited continuous downvalley flow throughout the day with no wind direction shift. The second regime (UV) was characterized by prolonged upvalley flow during daytime with a thermally driven shift from nocturnal downvalley to upvalley in the morning and a shift back to downvalley in the late afternoon. The third regime was a mixed regime (UV/DV) with a thermally driven wind shift from downvalley to upvalley in the morning and a second wind shift back to downvalley shortly after noon, much earlier than during UV days. We found distinct differences in the thermodynamic and dynamic boundary layer structure and turbulent surface fluxes during the day between the three regimes, with a deep well-mixed valley atmosphere, strong surface winds, strong turbulence, and upward directed latent heat fluxes, indicating sublimation of snow, during DV days and during the downvalley part of UV/DV days. The deep well-mixed layer extended to the height of the surrounding ridges and allowed the coupling of the flow in the valley to the flow aloft enabling downward mixing of momentum and channeling of the upper-level flow down valley. In contrast, static stability in the valley was high and wind and turbulence were weak on UV days and during the upvalley part of UV/DV days. While the mixing on DV days was likely promoted by shear-driven mixing due to strong upper-level winds at ridge heiht, the evolution of the mixed layer on UV/DV days was likely driven by surface heating.

496983.title: 'Goldilocks Days' as a Novel Characterization of Climate
496983.authors: Erin Duke, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI
496983.abstract: The warming climate has produced more extreme heat and less extreme cold, but little research has explored how the most comfortable weather is changing. Our research is investigated how climate change is affecting “Goldilocks Days” (GDs)—not too warm and not too cold—in Wisconsin based on established energy usage standards that quantify the amount of artificial heating or cooling required in buildings to achieve human comfort (daily average temperature of 65°F, +/- 5°F). Long-term temperature records from the Wisconsin Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) were used to determine the spatial and temporal trends in GDs across Wisconsin from 1951-2024. NOAA’s U.S. nClimGrid-Daily was then utilized to provide more complete spatial coverage of GDs across Wisconsin at a spatial resolution of 4km x 4km. Lastly, the University of Wisconsin Probabilistic Downscaling (UWPD) was employed to downscale global climate model simulations, where probabilistic downscaling of the CMIP6 models is used to project future changes in GDs under a moderate greenhouse-gas emissions scenario. Results show significant spatial and temporal variations in the frequency of GDs in Wisconsin, both historically and projected for the future. Historically, regions that experience the greatest GDs annually are central Wisconsin, while the fewest are found in the far north. Notably, nClimGrid’s 4x4km spatial resolution identifies finer scale variations in GDs in river valleys and along the Great Lakes, stemming from the ability of these regions to regulate temperature over time. A monthly analysis of GDs shows the most comfortable month in northern Wisconsin to be July, while in southern Wisconsin the most comfortable months are June and August. In contrast with the historical results, future projections suggest that the far north will have the greatest number of GDs annually, while south-central Wisconsin will experience the fewest. Monthly projections indicate that the most comfortable months will shift to May and September regardless of location, and that the overall statewide frequency of GDs will be far lower than the historical measurements. Tracking GDs can be a valuable resource for local Wisconsin communities. Understanding these trends can help prepare those impacted for economic and social changes, particularly to business sectors such as utilities and tourism, as well as lay the groundwork for future research into other states and regions.

496984.title: Asymmetric Risks of Severe Convective Storms to US Agriculture
496984.authors: Zhe Zhang, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and C. He, C. Liu, Y. Jiang, J. Burney, J. M. Done, J. Kukulies, E. M. Dougherty, L. Xue, and L. Di
496984.abstract: Severe convective storms (SCS), including hails, tornadoes, and thunderstorm winds, drive multi-billion-dollar losses to US agriculture annually. However, the interplay between SCS hazards, cropland exposures, and agricultural vulnerability is complex, making understanding future impacts in a warming world difficult. Here, we address this gap by integrating severe weather reports, USDA crop insurance records, and high-resolution convection-permitting climate simulations to first understand the structure of US agricultural SCS risk; we then project its future changes under climate warming. We reveal a profound asymmetry in the current risk structure in the central US “SCS Alley”. In the Northern Great Plains and Corn Belt, SCS losses are primarily exposure-driven due to high agricultural liability, yet producers elect high coverage levels, effectively buffering them against adverse hazards. Conversely, along the southern periphery (the Southern Great Plains and Lower Mississippi Valley), losses are driven by higher physical hazard and vulnerability, yet producers carry lower coverage, thus absorbing disproportionately greater direct losses. Crucially, high-resolution climate projections indicate future increases in SCS will concentrate precisely on the under-prepared southern periphery, driving an estimated 11% increase in crop insurance indemnities, while the highly insured northern part remains relatively stable (±3%). By explicitly linking physical hazards with crop insurance records, our work uncovers hidden structural vulnerabilities in the federal crop insurance program and provides actionable guidance for developing climate-resilient agricultural risk management and adaptation strategies.

496985.title: Deep Convective Transport of Iodine: Implications for Ozone Layer Health
496985.authors: Rainer Volkamer, Univ. of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and M. Reza, T. Koenig, Y. Tong, L. Feinman, C. J. Lietzke, D. Kim, P. Campuzano-Jost, K. J. Zarzana, E. C. Apel, T. L. Campos, R. S. Hornbrook, E. Assaf, A. R. Moon, Y. C. Chan, B. Alexander, J. L. Jimenez, and S. Montzka
496985.abstract: Iodine as a trace element is widespread in the atmosphere, where it modifies tropospheric and stratospheric ozone, oxidative capacity, new particle formation, with potential implications for stratocumulus cloud decks relevant to Earth radiative balance. Atmospheric convection injects iodine into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). A central role in controlling the amounts of iodine that are injected into the lower stratosphere is attributed to uncertain multiphase chemistry of iodine during deep convection. This presentation investigates the amounts of iodine in the gas- and particle phase, partitioning, and compares field measurements of vertical distributions on aircraft from the marine boundary layer into the UTLS with a chemical transport model that extends state-of-the-art iodine chemistry to represent iodine heterogeneous recycling. These measurements were collected aboard the NSF/NCAR GV aircraft during the Technological Innovation Into Iodine for Gulfstream 5 aircraft Environmental Research (TI3GER) field campaign, and present first attempts for simultaneous gas- and aerosol iodine observations aboard research aircraft. The implications for iodine sources, ice-retention efficiency of iodine during convective transport, and ozone layer health are discussed.

496986.title: Atmospheric Potential Oxygen and Machine Learning-based Fossil-Fuel CO2 Quantification in La Jolla, California
496986.authors: Madat Sardarli, University of California San Diego, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, La Jolla; and S. Walker, E. J. Morgan, and R. F. Keeling
496986.abstract: Even though statistics of fossil fuel emissions are routinely reported, they remain a significant source of uncertainty in the carbon budget. Ultimately, the most reliable method to constrain emissions, rather than relying only on reporting, is to use the atmosphere, because CO2 from fossil fuel burning produces a detectable atmospheric signal. The challenge is that CO2 is also taken up and released on land through terrestrial ecosystem exchange, making it hard to use CO2 alone to quantify fossil fuel emissions. Atmospheric oxygen (O2) offers an additional constraint. In particular, atmospheric potential oxygen (APO≈O2 +1.1×CO2) has the merit of cancelling out the effect of biospheric exchange, leaving primarily oceanic exchange and fossil fuel burning. Most early applications of APO assumed that fossil fuel burning was known and used APO to infer ocean fluxes, particularly ocean CO2 uptake. Pickers et al. (2022) flipped this approach, showing that in situations where the oceanic contribution is relatively small and the fossil fuel signal is dominant, APO can instead be used to quantify fossil fuel emissions. Here we explore whether this approach can be applied on a regional scale in the urban-influenced environment of La Jolla, California, where fossil fuel emissions are strong. The Scripps Pier at Scripps Institution of Oceanography is one of the few sites globally in such a setting, with long-term, continuous, in-situ records of O2 and CO2 placing us in a strong position to evaluate feasibility of this method. Building on the APO-machine-learning (ML) methodology of Pickers et al. (2022), we evaluate whether regional changes in fossil fuel CO2 (ffCO2) emissions can be quantified from the La Jolla record and used to resolve emission trends, testing the method demonstrated at the Weybourne Atmospheric Observatory (WAO) in the UK. During evaluation of the APO-ML method, however, it became clear that the La Jolla record is heavily compromised by artifacts that first became evident in the derived APO record. O2 and CO2 individually showed striking skewness, with well-defined low-CO2 and high-O2 envelopes near background and local pollution driving the observations toward higher and lower O2. APO showed this behavior to a lesser degree through much of the record, but in recent years exhibited values substantially higher than a reasonable background. This pointed to a lack of synchronicity between O2 and CO2. If a pulse of pollution passes through the sample line and the pulse arrives later at the instrument than the corresponding deficit, the two signals no longer cancel as they should in APO, producing anomalously high values. Physical inspection of the lines subsequently revealed degradation of the sample lines, which have not been replaced for about 20 years. The line contains an aluminum laminate layer intended to remain isolated behind a polyethylene film, but this layer was found to be degraded in various places, resulting in the production of aluminum oxide. These findings have pivoted part of the study toward the question of whether the compromised record can be resurrected. We present developments in recovering the record by carefully evaluating each line, identifying and screening line artifacts, and comparing with raw data, together with first results from testing the APO-ML method on the processed record. Pickers, P. A., Manning, A. C., Le Quéré, C., Forster, G. L., Gerbig, C., Fleming, L. S., & Sturges, W. T. (2022). Novel quantification of regional fossil fuel CO2 reductions during COVID-19 lockdowns using atmospheric oxygen measurements. Science Advances, 8(16), eabl9250. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abl9250

496987.title: Distinguishing Environments between Serial and Progressive Tornadic QLCSs
496987.authors: Willow Michael Phipps, Norman, OK; and A. A. Alford, J. C. Furtado, K. Tuftedal, and A. W. Lyza
496987.abstract: Tornadoes produced by quasi-linear convective systems (QLCSs) present a substantial forecasting challenge because of their rapid development and evolving vorticity-generation mechanisms. This study examines whether ERA5-derived tornadic QLCS (TQLCS) environments differ between systems forced by synoptic cold fronts (herein serial TQLCSs) and systems that primarily propagate through their own cold pools (herein progressive TQLCSs). Forcing mechanisms are classified using Weather Prediction Center (WPC) surface analyses based on distance and propagation criteria between the TQLCS and the nearest cold front. Tangential system motion, along with National Weather Service severe thunderstorm warnings, are used to obtain kinematic and thermodynamic parameters 30 km upstream of the leading edge. Principal component analysis (PCA) and bootstrapped confidence intervals from 140 samples in the eastern CONUS from 2023 to 2026 reveal statistically significant differences between the two classes. In PC1 (40% EV), Serial TQLCSs are strongly associated with enhanced 0-6 km bulk shear and low-level shear orientations that maximize SRH, while progressive TQLCSs are associated with greater MUCAPE and DCAPE. PC2 (13% EV) shows an association with progressive TQLCSs toward dynamic and kinematic variables that implicate the low level jet. TQLCSs that show sufficient ambiguity in their progressive and serial characteristics (e.g., exhibiting a line-echo wave pattern close to a cold front) are marked for sensitivity testing, and removing these samples strengthened these environmental relationships. These results suggest that serial TQLCSs appear tied to robust kinematic fields, while progressive TQLCSs may be more consistent with environments in which dynamic support and storm-scale internal processes play a larger role.

496988.title: Cloud-Native and GPU-Native Data Pipelines for AI Weather and Climate Modeling in Earth2Studio
496988.authors: Negin Sobhani, NVIDIA, Santa Clara, CA; and A. Subramaniam, P. Harrington, N. Robinson, and S. Choudhry
496988.abstract: AI weather and climate models can generate forecasts in seconds to minutes on modern accelerators, shifting an increasing fraction of end-to-end workflow cost from model execution to data access and movement. Forecast, nowcast, verification, and data-assimilation workflows must first retrieve and transform initial conditions, reanalysis products, observations, satellite data, and other Earth-system datasets, increasingly hosted in cloud object storage. In latency-sensitive workflows, this I/O can dominate runtime and leave GPUs significantly underutilized. Earth2Studio provides a cloud-native data architecture for connecting weather and climate datasets with GPU-accelerated AI workflows. To reduce I/O overhead, Earth2Studio is transitioning data sources from Python filesystem abstractions toward object-store-native access using Obstore, a Rust-backed interface for S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure, HTTP, and S3-compatible storage. Icechunk complements this architecture with transactional and versioned Zarr storage for forecast inputs, outputs, ensembles, and derived products. Benchmarks across representative Earth2Studio data sources show approximately 2–8× faster data loading following the transition toward object-store-native access. In representative AI data-assimilation workflows, profiling shows that data retrieval, decoding, and tensor assembly can account for more than 90% of end-to-end runtime, making the data pipeline a critical target for improving accelerator utilization and forecast latency. Building on this cloud-native foundation, we are extending the architecture toward GPU-native data paths that reduce CPU-side decompression, staging, and unnecessary host-device transfers. This includes technologies such as NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage (GDS) for more direct movement between compatible storage systems and GPU memory, together with NVIDIA nvCOMP for GPU-accelerated compression and decompression of chunked scientific data. This presentation describes Earth2Studio's evolving cloud- and GPU-native I/O architecture, performance results from object-store-native access, and a path toward scalable, low-latency AI weather and climate workflows across cloud, HPC, and operational forecasting environments.

496992.title: Improving Convective Predictability During MJO Initiation via Satellite Data Assimilation: From Moisture Initialization to Convective Organization
496992.authors: Chin-Hsuan Peng, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; and X. Chen, M. Y. Chan, L. R. Leung, Z. Feng, J. H. Ruppert Jr., and N. Sakaeda
496992.abstract: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is the dominant mode of tropical intraseasonal variability, yet its initiation remains poorly understood and difficult to predict. Observational and modeling studies suggest that the MJO can emerge through the progressive organization of tropical convection from isolated clouds and mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) into a large-scale convective envelope. Atmospheric moisture plays a central role in this evolution, so uncertainties in the tropical moisture field can limit the practical predictability of convective evolution during MJO initiation. We investigate how improved moisture initialization influences convective evolution during MJO initiation using a regional ensemble-based data assimilation and forecasting system. We first examine the November 2020 MJO initiation event over the western Indian Ocean by assimilating high-resolution all-sky infrared radiances from Meteosat-8 together with conventional observations. Assimilation of all-sky infrared radiances substantially improves the initial thermodynamic environment and leads to more realistic forecasts of the timing, location, and organization of MJO convection. Sensitivity experiments further demonstrate that adjustments to lower-free-tropospheric moisture (~1-5 km) account for much of the forecast improvement, highlighting the strong influence of dry-air entrainment on developing MJO convection and the importance of accurately representing moisture in this layer. Building on these results, ongoing work extends the analysis from moisture initialization to convective organization. We apply an MCS tracking algorithm to satellite observations and high-resolution ensemble forecasts to quantify the evolution, interactions, and environmental controls of convective systems during the MJO initiation. This work aims to establish a process-based framework for understanding and improving the practical predictability of MJO initiation.

496995.title: Characterizing Case Study Teaching in Undergraduate Atmospheric Science Courses
496995.authors: Dawn Marie Kopacz, Univ. of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and C. Davenport, Z. J. Handlos, and A. M. Klees
496995.abstract: A recent national survey of atmospheric science faculty revealed that the active learning technique of case studies was the most common instructional approach used in the classroom. However, it was unclear how faculty were using case studies in practice, and the degree to which their implementation actively engages students. Such understanding is critical, as substantial prior research has demonstrated that interactive, discussion-based approaches provide the greatest level of student benefit. Thus, to understand case study implementation, a new survey was administered to undergraduate atmospheric science instructors. A combination of closed- and open-ended questions collected information on courses in which instructors use case studies as an instructional strategy, the frequency of use, length of time spent on case studies, expected learning outcomes, and classroom implementation methods. Broadly, survey responses indicated that case studies are used across the atmospheric sciences curriculum, though they tend to encompass a greater portion of class time in upper-level courses, particularly during lab sections. Notably, while respondents identified student engagement as a near-universal motivator for using case studies, structured, instructor-guided, rather than student-driven, activities dominate actual practice, potentially limiting the depth of student engagement. Furthermore, there was some misalignment between instructors’ intended skill outcomes from case study use and skills explicitly identified in implementation. Altogether, the results of this survey indicate that case studies in atmospheric science are not a single, uniform instructional strategy, but rather a flexible framework whose effectiveness depends on how they are structured and enacted in the classroom.

496996.title: Regulation of Severe Hail Growth by Ice-Nucleating Particle-Mediated Raindrop Freezing
496996.authors: Tobias Innes David Ross, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and S. Lasher-Trapp
496996.abstract: Severe hailstone growth (diameter ≥ 1 in.) requires prolonged exposure to abundant supercooled liquid water (SLW) in storm updrafts. Recent modeling studies have clarified environmental conditions that prolong this exposure; however, the SLW available for hail growth depends on how heterogeneous freezing is represented in cloud microphysics schemes. Many schemes prescribe drop freezing using invariant volume–temperature relationships that loosely approximate ice-nucleating particle (INP) activity, but cannot represent natural INP variability or their accumulation in larger drops by collision and coalescence. We perform idealized simulations of hail-producing ordinary thunderstorms and long-lived supercells in fixed environments. In the simulations, we systematically perturb INP activity within observational bounds using a freezing formulation that couples cloud droplet and raindrop freezing to the number of active INPs each hydrometeor contains. In both storm types, increasing the overall INP concentration, or increasing the concentration active at higher subfreezing temperatures, systematically decreases the occurrence of severe hailstones. Greater INP activity shifts appreciable freezing of supercooled raindrops to lower heights, yielding (1) shallower layers of supercooled rainwater available for collection by growing hailstones and (2) more numerous hail embryos within those layers. Together these effects reduce the opportunity for large hail growth. Whether this mechanism is expressed depends on the background CCN concentration and storm type through their control on the supply of precipitation-sized drops in the mixed-phase updraft before freezing can occur. These results demonstrate that severe hail outcomes can be highly sensitive to heterogeneous-freezing assumptions, including the plausible range of INP activity found in nature.

497000.title: Deterministic and Probabilistic Direct Observation Prediction of Cloud Evolution from GOES-East Imagery
497000.authors: Omid Bagheri, Mesoscale and Microscale Meteorology Laboratory, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and D. Kimpara and C. Snyder
497000.abstract: Cloud cover shapes decisions in aviation, solar energy, agriculture, and severe storm operations, yet clouds resist prediction. The features that matter most span only a few kilometers and evolve with fast processes such as moist convection, so deterministic skill may fade within tens of minutes, making probabilistic guidance essential. Direct observation prediction (DOP), a machine learning approach initialized from observations that forecasts them directly, requires no data assimilation and sidesteps limitations of numerical weather prediction and extrapolation-based nowcasting. We build a deterministic and a probabilistic DOP model and use them to isolate key design choices. Both forecast infrared brightness temperatures from GOES-East imagery over a near-full-disk domain and are conditioned on synoptic-scale meteorological fields from ERA5. The deterministic model, DDOP, uses a vision-transformer backbone trained with an MSE loss. The probabilistic model, PDOP, generates ensembles by fine-tuning DDOP with stochastic decomposition layers under a CRPS loss evaluated point-wise in both real and spectral space. This route is far cheaper than diffusion, which for medium-range prediction has proven no more skillful than noise-input models trained on CRPS. PDOP members stay sharp and spatially coherent, with spread-skill ratios approaching unity as lead time grows. As expected, the PDOP ensemble mean improves on DDOP; it also shows lower errors and higher correlation than the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) through 4-hour lead time, with reduced gains at 6 hours and comparable skill to 12 hours. Ablations then isolate the effects of prediction timestep, model capacity, and training schedule. Shortening the timestep to 10 minutes reduces blurring relative to 20- and 30-minute counterparts while improving accuracy and convective depiction. Capacity and architecture matter differently for the two models: DDOP performs best with an inverted pyramid and an enlarged latent dimension, whereas PDOP gains little from either, indicating that architectural choices tuned deterministically do not necessarily transfer to the probabilistic setting. A similar asymmetry appears in multi-step training, where DDOP loses substantial sharpness beyond two steps yet appears to settle in a flatter basin that CRPS fine-tuning can exploit. This study offers practical guidance for configuring observation-space cloud forecasts and a framework for low-cost ensembles and uncertainty quantification for storm-scale decisions.

497001.title: Atmospheric River Forecasting with Operational, Experimental, and AI Ensembles: The Fall 2026 Precipitation Extremes for Atmospheric Rivers Testbed
497001.authors: Emily Nicole Tinney, CIRES/NOAA/WPC/HMT, Boulder, CO; and J. Correia Jr., S. M. Trojniak, W. M. Bartolini, and J. A. Nelson Jr.
497001.abstract: The fourth iteration of the Precipitation Extremes for Atmospheric Rivers (PEAR) Experiment in the Weather Prediction Center’s Hydrometeorology Testbed (HMT) is taking place in November 2026. The primary objectives of PEAR since its inception in 2024 are to better understand the medium-range AR forecast challenges and to evaluate experimental models at medium-range lead times. Results from previous PEAR experiments have demonstrated that ensemble forecasting of ARs is necessary for characterizing the uncertainties of hazardous weather, and participants have expressly indicated their desire for probabilistic information in their forecasting process. Therefore, the Fall 2026 PEAR testbed is placing a special emphasis on the use of ensembles in forecasting atmospheric rivers and their associated impacts. Across two weeks, participants will analyze and forecast for four retrospective cases from the 2025 - 2026 water year. In addition to deterministic models, participants will have access to operational (GEFS), experimental (AR-AFS), and AI (AIGEFS) ensembles. Participants will be tasked with incorporating ensemble information into their forecast and communication processes in activities focused on lead times from day 5 to day 1. Deterministic and probabilistic model depictions of atmospheric river structure, integrated vapor transport, and simulated precipitation will be evaluated, and forecasts will be verified by participants.

497003.title: How Emergency Managers are Using Supplementa Weather Radar to Make Operational Decisions
497003.authors: Tara Goode, Climavision, Louisville, KY; and E. Pawsat, L. Maynard, M. Simpson, PhD, B. Jennings, B. Kintigh, R. Pfeiffer, S. Granato, and A. Bonnema
497003.abstract: Emergency managers rely on timely, localized weather information to make decisions before and during high-impact events—from activating emergency operations centers and positioning resources to communicating risk with communities and maintaining situational awareness as conditions evolve. Yet in many communities, gaps in existing weather radar coverage can limit visibility into the low levels of the atmosphere where some of the most consequential weather impacts occur. Climavision has deployed supplemental, gap-filling weather radars to address these observational gaps, with its network now providing enhanced weather observations across more than 50 communities in 14 states. Importantly, these systems are not theoretical: supplemental radar data is being made available to emergency management and public safety partners to support real-world operations alongside National Weather Service products and other trusted weather information. This presentation will share examples and lessons learned from emergency management applications of supplemental radar in Minnesota, Alabama, Georgia, and North Carolina, representing different weather threats, operational environments, and radar coverage challenges. In the Southeast, examples from Alabama, Georgia, and North Carolina will demonstrate how improved low-level radar observations can enhance situational awareness during severe convective weather, including rapidly evolving thunderstorms, tornado threats, heavy rainfall, and flash flooding. In Minnesota, we will examine how supplemental radar observations can support emergency managers facing severe storms, heavy precipitation, and other high-impact weather in areas with existing observational gaps. The session will focus specifically on the emergency management use cases: what additional information becomes available when a radar gap is filled; how that information can complement existing National Weather Service warnings and forecasts; and how emergency managers can incorporate supplemental observations into established workflows without creating another disconnected source of weather information. We will also share what Climavision and its emergency management partners have learned through operational deployments—including the importance of identifying gaps based on public-safety needs, making data easily accessible within existing workflows, and ensuring that new weather technology strengthens rather than complicates the decision-making environment. Attendees will leave with practical examples of how emergency managers are using supplemental radar today and a clearer understanding of where additional low-level weather observations can provide the greatest operational value during high-impact weather.

497004.title: HERO: Forecasting Radiation Across Timescales and Environments
497004.authors: Scott W McIntosh, Hale SWx, Longmont, CO; Lynker, Louisville, CO; and N. Pothier-McGillivray and R. J. Leamon
497004.abstract: Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs), the trapped Van Allen radiation belts and solar particle events (SPEs) pose distinct but overlapping hazards whose magnitudes and temporal scales vary dramatically with domain and phase of the solar-cycle. Accurate forecasting of this multi-species radiation environment is essential for safety and operational planning across an increasing spectrum of domains: civilian aviation (particularly for high-latitude and polar routes), LEO Low Earth Orbit (LEO, for satellite systems, crew, and optimizing commercial platforms), geostationary orbit (GEO), lunar surface and cis-lunar operations, and eventual crewed missions to Mars and beyond. Each domain imposes different requirements on forecast lead time, spatial resolution, and particle species priority—seconds for auroral LEO/GEO surface charging (electrons), minutes-to-hours for aviation and LEO/GEO anomaly mitigation (protons, electrons and heavy ions), days-to-weeks for mission planning, and longer-term climatological guidance for habitat design and shielding (protons and electrons). We will discuss how our improved understanding of underlying solar and heliospheric drivers is translated into domain-specific risk products with the Hale Environmental Radiation Outlook (HERO).

497005.title: Sensitivity of Anvil Characteristics to Convective Core Properties In Tropical Deep Convection
497005.authors: Anita D. Rapp, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and S. Elkins and J. Pilewskie
497005.abstract: Anvils from tropical deep convection play an important role in the overall cloud radiative feedback. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of not only changes in anvil area but also in the distribution of thick and thin anvil for regulating the overall cloud radiative effect and climate sensitivity. Both anvil area and anvil macro- and microphysical properties are coupled with convective intensity and core structure across the deep convection lifecycle. Until the launch of Investigation of Convective UpdraftS (INCUS) to measure convective vertical velocity and mass flux and the Polarized Submillimeter Ice-cloud Radiometer (PolSIR) to measure the diurnal cycle of anvil ice water path and particle size, connecting convective strength to anvil properties requires measurement proxies from existing satellite observations. This study uses existing CloudSat/CALIPSO measurements to explore the sensitivity of anvil area production and IWP to convective updraft properties using a ten-year tropical oceanic daytime deep convective object dataset. A cluster analysis is first used to categorize clouds by lifecycle stage and organization states. The convection core and anvil properties of clouds in these clusters are then used to determine which convective core characteristics have the largest influence on thick and thin anvil area and IWP in different lifecycle stages and organization states. Preliminary results indicate that both thick and thin anvil area are coupled to convective core area but show little sensitivity to metrics of convective core intensity. IWP in the thick anvil regions adjacent to the convective core is most sensitive to convective core intensity, while IWP in the thin anvil regions more remote from the core exhibits little sensitivity to the properties of the convective core.

497006.title: All-Sky Temperature and Moisture Retrievals from MTG Infrared Sounder (IRS) using a Deep Learning Methodology
497006.authors: Zheng Ma, CIMSS, Madison, WI; CIMSS/SSEC, Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and Z. Li, J. Li, and A. Heidinger
497006.abstract: The Infrared Sounder (IRS) onboard the Meteosat third generation sounding satellite (MTG-S) is the first operational geostationary hyperspectral infrared sounder over Europe and Africa. Based on a Michelson Fourier transform spectrometer, it provides information on water vapor and temperature structures of the atmosphere and on other trace gases through measurements in the longwave and midwave infrared spectral regions. It will be capable of observing the vertical structure of atmosphere over Europe with high spectral resolution as well as high temporal (30-minute revisit time) and high spatial (4 km at nadir) resolutions. It is of great importance to develop a retrieval algorithm that can take good advantage of the information and provide accurate thermodynamic profile information with good spatial coverage in a timely manner. While previous retrievals mainly focus on clear-sky pixels because the information from satellite observations over cloudy pixels is significantly limited by the cloud presence, a deep learning (DL) model based on the architecture of U-Net is developed to provide retrievals under both clear and cloudy conditions in this study, utilizing not only the hyperspectral observation from the IRS, but also the spatial information from the clear and less-contaminated pixels around the heavily cloud-contaminated pixels that were hardly included in previous retrievals. IRS dwells consisting of 160×160 pixels are selected as basic input units for IRS retrievals with U-Net, with the temperature and moisture profiles of atmosphere at 91 fixed pressure levels between 50 hPa and the surface as output. To mitigate the impact from terrains and synoptic weather systems, the DL models are initially trained with atmospheric profiles of ERA5 reanalysis at 137 sigma levels as truth labels. The model outputs are then converted to fixed pressure levels using information on surface pressure from reanalysis which can be replaced by NWP forecast field. With sample testing IRS data, the execution time of the model for an all-sky retrieval over Europe is less than 2.5 minutes, making it feasible for operational nowcasting of storms. The details of the methodology will be presented, as well as statistical analysis of retrieval accuracy when trained and validated with real observation data. The application on capturing stability indices associated with pre-storm environments will also be presented.

497009.title: Umbrella-Cloud Growth and Transport in Explosive Volcanic Eruptions: Insights from the 2022 Hunga Eruption and Beyond
497009.authors: Ashok Kumar Gupta, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN; and R. Bennartz
497009.abstract: Umbrella-cloud radius growth, R(t), is widely used with stratified gravity-current theory to estimate volumetric flow rate and mass eruption rate (MER). We examine whether a single radius-time relationship can adequately describe a multipulse umbrella cloud. The 15 January 2022 Hunga eruption (E3) produced multiple explosive pulses, spatially separated thermal features, and substantial cloud transport. Treating the entire satellite-visible envelope as one source-driven umbrella can misinterpret this transport as radial spreading and bias MER estimates. We analyzed 10-min Himawari-8 AHI observations of E3 and the 19–20 December 2021 (E1) and 13 January 2022 (E2) Hunga eruptions. Three DeepLabV3+ variants delineated apparent-cloud boundaries and yielded area-equivalent radii. We incorporated these radii into a physics-informed Bayesian model and estimated parameter uncertainty with NumPyro (a Python library for Bayesian inference). Although inference converged, posterior-predictive checks showed that the DeepLabV3-derived envelope is inconsistent with the single-umbrella boundary assumed by the model. Himawari-8 Band 14 (11.2 µm) brightness temperatures (BTs) help explain this mismatch. For E1, BT < 220 K contours reproduced the published 0–140 min record (RMSE 0.21 km). For E2, threshold-dependent detection (BT < 200 K vs. BT < 210 K) indicates limited early thermal detectability rather than delayed onset. For E3, the cloud expanded rapidly, moved downwind, and produced overlapping cold signatures from multiple pulses. As a result, none of the tested single-umbrella (R(t)) formulations reproduced the observed E3 radius evolution before the cloud reached the edge of the analysis domain. We therefore formulate a multi-component model that separately represents the apparent cloud envelope, a source-proximal umbrella, and a wind-advected downwind component. This separation is consistent with stereo evidence of multi-level injection during E3. The model reduces to a single-umbrella formulation for E1 and E2. After validation on the Hunga sequence, we will apply it to the 2019 Raikoke, 2021 La Soufrière, 2021 Fukutoku-Oka-no-Ba, and 2024 Ruang eruptions using Himawari-8/9 and GOES-16 observations. This comparison will test whether simple and multipulse umbrella clouds share a common set of equations or require additional physical processes to explain their evolution.

497010.title: Development of a Coupled DSSAT-WRF Framework for Investigating Land-Atmosphere Interactions in the Southeastern United States
497010.authors: Andrew T. White, Univ. of Alabama in Huntsville / NASA SPoRT, Huntsville, AL; and G. Priftis, K. Salvi, D. T. Haliczer, L. Ellenburg, V. Mishra, U. Nair, V. Martin, N. Magliocca, and M. Kumar
497010.abstract: Human modifications of the land surface, including land use change and irrigation have been shown to alter evapotranspiration, land-atmosphere interactions, moisture recycling, and atmospheric circulation. Previous studies have demonstrated enhanced precipitation throughout the midwestern states due to irrigation in the United States High Plains and modified moisture deficits through enhanced evapotranspiration from irrigated croplands. While crop models such as the Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer (DSSAT) simulate crop phenology, irrigation demand, and soil water processes and atmospheric models such as the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) realistically simulate atmospheric processes, WRF’s land surface parameterizations are generally simplified representations of soil water processes. Coupling DSSAT with WRF enables more realistic crop phenology dynamics that will influence land-atmosphere interactions and feedback, thus providing a more realistic representation of agricultural land-atmosphere interactions. We apply this coupled framework to the southeastern United States, a region where a moist background climate and spatially diffuse irrigation patterns contrast with the drier High Plains. This coupling framework is currently under development, and the three primary variables that are exchanged between the two models are soil moisture, irrigation amounts and leaf area index. DSSAT is a process-based modeling system containing over 40 different crops that simulates crop growth, biomass yields, water stress, evapotranspiration, and crop phenology using weather, soil and management information. These outputs provide critical information about the land surface, vegetative state and soil moisture. The WRF model is a numerical weather prediction model capable of simulating atmospheric processes across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales, making it well suited to investigate land-atmosphere interactions and the influence of agricultural management on local and regional weather. WRF also includes representations of irrigation and crop-related processes, but with relatively less detail than DSSAT. Thus, coupling the models combines DSSAT’s detailed crop representation with WRF’s land-atmosphere interactions to better understand and explore the land surface and atmospheric feedback. The coupled framework starts with WRF providing the meteorological forcing (temperature, radiation, and precipitation) to DSSAT. After simulating crop growth and soil water processes, DSSAT returns the end-of-day soil moisture, leaf area index, and the irrigation amount required for the following day. These updated land surface conditions are then incorporated into the subsequent WRF simulation, after which the process repeats for the next day. This enables a two-way feedback between the agriculture practices from DSSAT combined with the atmospheric conditions (WRF), allowing for the investigation of how crop growth and irrigation influences local and regional climatology, and how the evolving weather conditions affect yield, water demand and crop development. Initial results have demonstrated successful implementation of the coupled framework, with WRF irrigation constrained by the irrigation demand simulated by DSSAT. Additional results will be shown that will evaluate the influence of these agricultural processes on land-atmosphere interactions across the southeastern United States.

497018.title: Balanced Weak Rotation in the Tropical and Sub-Tropical Atmosphere
497018.authors: Michael M. Bell, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO
497018.abstract: The prediction of organized moist convection in the tropical and sub-tropical atmosphere remains one of the most challenging and societally important forecast problems. The prediction problem is exacerbated in weakly-rotating regimes where conditions are broadly favorable for convection across a substantial fraction of the globe, but the vertical motion is highly variable and often seemingly stochastic. Phenomena such as the inter-tropical convergence zone (ITCZ), tropical waves and depressions, and sub-tropical fronts are dynamically in between the conditions of non-rotating barotropic and strongly rotating baroclinic flows that are described by other frameworks such as weak temperature gradient or semi-geostrophic theory. The current study aims to shed new light on the dynamics of these weather phenomena through a novel balance approximation that is appropriate for moist, weakly rotating flows in a stratified atmosphere. The primary assumption consists of approximating the kinetic energy in a quasi-anelastic, moist Hamiltonian dynamical system that allows for weak, but non-negligible, horizontal variations in density within vortical flow, denoted as Balanced Weak Rotation (BWR). The balance approximation is valid under a low Froude number and low modified Rossby number that is proportional to the potential vorticity (PV) rather than planetary vorticity, and therefore includes the local flow curvature, shear, and stratification. The balanced mass and wind fields can be obtained through inversion of a nonlinear balance equation for a known PV distribution. The balanced BWR wind is proportional to the geostrophic wind modulated by the non-dimensional potential density. The secondary circulation and vertical motion response to heating, friction, thermal advection, and differential PV advection can be obtained diagnostically. The spatial scale of the secondary circulation response is proportional to the PV, such that relative vorticity, vertical shearing flows, and temperature gradients act to produce vertical motion in a different way than gradient balance, semi-geostrophic, or weak temperature gradient diagnostics. An overview of the BWR theory and its application to tropical cyclogenesis and convection within the ITCZ will be presented, including comparisons with recent field campaign observations.

497019.title: Toward Prognostic Convective Updraft Dynamics in NOAA’s Unified Forecast System
497019.authors: Lisa Bengtsson, NOAA/Physical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and I. K. Hu, S. N. Tulich, J. Han, M. Zhang, E. Grell, W. Li, I. L. McCoy, S. Baidar, E. J. Thompson, and A. W. Brewer
497019.abstract: Convective parameterizations typically represent updraft vertical velocity diagnostically, limiting their ability to capture the time-evolving dynamics of convective plumes. Here, we move toward a more physically based representation of convective dynamics by introducing a prognostic equation for updraft vertical velocity within the scale-aware Simplified Arakawa-Schubert (saSAS) convection scheme used in NOAA’s Unified Forecast System (UFS). The formulation explicitly represents updraft momentum tendencies, including the perturbation pressure-gradient force, which acts as an important dynamical resistance to plume acceleration. This pressure forcing is represented using regression relationships derived from cloud-resolving model simulations, providing a computationally practical treatment for use in a parameterized framework. The prognostic updraft velocity is coupled to an existing prognostic closure for convective updraft area fraction, allowing both the strength and fractional coverage of convection to evolve in time. The new formulation is evaluated using the Common Community Physics Package Single Column Model across observationally constrained tropical shallow and deep convection cases from ATOMIC, TWP-ICE, and DYNAMO field campaigns. Compared with the diagnostic formulation, prognostic updraft dynamics produces a more realistic distribution of vertical velocity and improved convective mass flux relative to lidar observations while maintaining stable model behavior. Impacts on bulk cloud properties, precipitation, and radiation are generally modest, with the largest sensitivities occurring in shallow convection and some improvement in shallow cloud-radiation interactions.

497021.title: Storm Environment and Satellite-Based Convective Entrainment Relationships
497021.authors: Cansu Duzgun, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and H. E. Fuelberg and R. Adams-Selin
497021.abstract: Deep convection can produce hazardous weather such as heavy rainfall, hail, and tornadoes, while also redistributing heat and moisture through vertical mass transport. Understanding the processes that control deep convection is essential for predicting both weather hazards and climate impacts.
