Updraft strength depends on the storm environment and is modulated by entrainment of environmental air into the convective core. However, the influence of entrainment on storm strength and vertical transport remains poorly understood. Entrainment rate in convective parameterizations remains a major source of uncertainty in numerical weather models. A satellite-based storm and entrainment dataset was developed to investigate environmental influences on convective entrainment. Deep convective cases were identified using the Precipitation Feature (PF) dataset derived from Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) and Global Precipitation Mission (GPM) radar observations from 2005–2017. Then, two different methods were used to create the entrainment dataset: 1) a simple entraining-plume model with carbon monoxide (CO) measurements from the Aura Tropospheric Emission Spectrometer and Microwave Limb Sounder (TES/MLS) for each identified case, treating CO as a conserved quantity in convective ascent, and 2) a proxy for entrainment using the difference between the level of neutral buoyancy (LNB) and the level of maximum detrainment (LMD), with LMD identified from upper tropospheric CO enhancements from TES/MLS joint CO profiles, and environmental variables derived from ERA5 reanalysis data. Entrainment estimates from both methods were compared with previous observational estimates of entrainment (e.g., Takahashi et al. 2021), and the CO-based method was found to be less representative, likely due to the limited vertical resolution of the TES/MLS joint CO profiles below the mid-troposphere. Statistical analysis revealed physically consistent relationships between the storm environment and entrainment. Entraining convective available potential energy (ECAPE) and 0–6-km bulk wind shear showed particularly clear relationships, with stronger buoyancy associated with reduced entrainment and stronger shear associated with enhanced mixing between updrafts and their environment for single-core deep convective storms between 35°N/S. Greater environmental relative humidity was also associated with weaker entrainment-induced buoyancy loss, consistent with reduced evaporative cooling and dilution in more humid environments, particularly for relative humidity above 80%. Together, these results highlight the importance of both thermodynamic and dynamical environmental factors in modulating entrainment within deep convective systems.

497027.title: Satellite Stereo Winds of Wildfire Plumes During NASA INSPYRE
497027.authors: Anaya Nicole Williams, Hampton University, Hampton, VA; and D. Jones, M. Friberg, J. Carr, A. John, and D. L. Wu, PhD
497027.abstract: Improving predictions of extreme wildfire behavior and pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) development requires observations capable of resolving the rapidly evolving three-dimensional structure and motion of wildfire plumes. In particular, plume injection height and fire-generated winds provide important constraints on interactions among wildfire behavior, atmospheric stability, convection, and subsequent smoke transport. However, observations of these quantities remain spatially and temporally limited. Here, we apply a geostationary satellite stereoscopic retrieval technique to wildfire events observed during the 2026 NASA INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE). The stereo-imaging approach uses simultaneous observations from multiple geostationary satellites to retrieve atmospheric motion vector (AMV) wind speed and direction together with corresponding feature heights, providing a three-dimensional view of wildfire plume evolution at sub-hourly temporal resolution. Previous applications of this technique have resolved rapidly evolving pyroconvective plumes, including plume-top heights exceeding 10-14 km and substantial variability among individual convective updraft cores. For wildfire and pyroconvective events coincident with INSPYRE observations, we generate stereo-derived three-dimensional winds and plume heights and characterize their temporal evolution and transport. The retrievals provide broader spatial and temporal context for targeted INSPYRE airborne and ground-based measurements while extending observations beyond individual aircraft sampling periods. The INSPYRE-coincident stereo retrievals provide three-dimensional context for targeted campaign observations and enable wildfire plume evolution to be examined at regional scales and sub-hourly frequency. These measurements demonstrate the potential of geostationary stereo imaging to complement intensive field observations by extending measurements of plume height and motion beyond individual aircraft sampling periods. References Carr, J. L., Wu, D. L., Daniels, J., Friberg, M. D., Bresky, W., and Madani, H. (2020). GEO-GEO stereo- tracking of atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) from the geostationary ring. Remote Sensing, 12, 3779. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs12223779 Carr, J. L., Wu, D. L., Wolfe, R. E., Madani, H., Lin, G., and Tan, B. (2019). Joint 3D-wind retrievals with stereoscopic views from MODIS and GOES. Remote Sensing, 11, 2100. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs11182100 Carr, J. L., Wu, D. L., Kelly, M. A., and Gong, J. (2018). A., Zou, Y., and O'Neill, S. M. (2021). Diurnal observations of wildfires boundary layer dynamics and aerosol plume convection using stereo-imaging techniques. EGU General Assembly. 497029.title: An OSSE of the Impact of Airborne Dual-Polarimetric Radar Observations on Afternoon Thunderstorm Forecasts during the 2022 PRECIP Field Campaign
497029.authors: Junkyung Kay, NCAR, Boulder, CO; NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and W. C. Lee, J. Vivekanandan, G. J. Huang, T. Y. Cha, and B. Klotz
497029.abstract: Dual-Polarimetric radar observations provide critical insights into hydrometeor microphysics and thunderstorm evolution. While ground-based networks offer key polarimetric data, they are constrained by fixed locations and range-degraded resolution. On the other hand, airborne platforms can sample convective storms along flight tracks with high spatial and temporal resolution, but state-of-the-art systems lack dual-polarization capabilities. To bridge this gap, the Airborne Phased Array Radar (APAR) concept was developed for the NSF NCAR C-130 aircraft. Combining dual-polarimetric capability with rapid electronic scanning, APAR enables high-resolution 3D sampling of targeted convective systems and heavy precipitation. To evaluate the potential forecast impact of this novel capability, this study investigates the assimilation of synthetic airborne dual-polarimetric radar observations using an Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) framework. The OSSE is centered on a hail-producing afternoon thunderstorm observed during the 2022 Prediction of Rainfall Extremes Campaign in the Pacific (PRECIP) in Taiwan. A nature run was generated using the WRF-ARW model, and synthetic APAR dual-polarimetric data were produced using the AOSPRE forward simulator. These synthetic observations were assimilated into the MPAS-JEDI LGETKF system using the PPRO dual-polarimetric forward operator. Results demonstrate the forecast impact of airborne dual-polarimetric radar data when combined with ground-based radar and conventional observations over complex terrain, highlighting APAR’s potential as a complementary observing system for convective-scale analysis and prediction.

497031.title: Boreal Forests and the Surface Energy Balance: The Role of Climate Futures
497031.authors: Sabrina Cohen, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and J. W. Hurrell
497031.abstract: Boreal forests exert various biophysical effects on the surrounding climate, such as modulation of surface albedo and latent heat fluxes. The magnitude of these effects depends on numerous factors, such as temperature, precipitation, and atmospheric CO2 concentrations. As fossil fuel combustion continues, atmospheric CO2 and air temperatures are projected to continue rising globally, with regionally heterogeneous precipitation impacts. Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) has been proposed as a possible mechanism to ameliorate the projected effects of climate change. By reflecting incoming sunlight, SAI would reduce air temperatures while atmospheric CO2 remains elevated, with regionally variable precipitation effects. Here, we first explore the relative importance of atmospheric CO2 and meteorological variables on the physiognomy of boreal forests under various modeled climate change and SAI scenarios. We then analyze how these structural changes influence the forests’ ability to modify the local surface energy balance. Our work sheds light on the changing nature of land-atmosphere interactions in the most extensive land biome on Earth.

497032.title: Applying Statistically Downscaled Numerical Weather Prediction Guidance on a Variable-Resolution Mesh to Consumer Weather Forecasting Applications at The Weather Company
497032.authors: Joseph P. Koval, The Weather Company, Brookhaven, GA; and T. Alcott, M. Flora, L. Gaudet, Ph.D., C. Guiang, J. I. Belanger, N. McGillis, T. M. Hamill, and P. Neilley
497032.abstract: Operational numerical weather prediction still runs at 3-4 km grid spacing, too coarse to capture the terrain and land-use effects driving local weather variability. The Weather Company's machine-learning downscaling framework closes this gap, learning the correction between station observations and NWP forecasts to sharpen forecasts toward station-scale accuracy using terrain and land-use features. Verified against withheld observations, it measurably improves on raw NWP guidance, especially in complex terrain. This framework is being applied to The Weather Company's new ski-forecasting product, launching in Fall 2026, where independent forecasts are generated for a resort's base, mid-mountain, and summit elevations. This resolves temperature, wind, QPF, and precipitation-phase differences across a single mountain that a 3-4 km NWP model cannot represent within one grid cell, including precipitation transitioning from rain at the base to snow at the summit, or wind speeds sufficient to trigger operational holds near the ridge while base conditions remain calm. These elevation-resolved forecasts directly support visitor planning. A planned extension, a “Model Lab” feature for The Weather Company's Weather Underground property, enables direct comparison of the downscaling framework's forecasts against coarser numerical model prediction guidance, presented as either raw model output or bias-corrected using observations from a user's own Personal Weather Station. Gridded output from each model, including the downscaling framework, is also rendered as map layers, allowing direct visual comparison of how each model represents terrain and land surface-driven spatial structure. Across both of these applications, the common contribution is spatial and probabilistic forecast detail that consumer applications have not previously provided: rather than a single value representing an entire mountain or region, forecasts vary with the underlying terrain and can be evaluated against independent models or in-situ observations. This extends to precipitation through probability of precipitation (POP), quantitative precipitation forecast (QPF), and a probabilistic QPF that expresses the likelihood of exceeding specific precipitation thresholds (e.g., a 30% probability of exceeding 0.25 in. versus a 10% probability of exceeding 1.00 in.), providing an explicit representation of forecast uncertainty alongside increased spatial skill.

497033.title: Spectral Evolution of Fetch-Limited Wind Waves under Non-Canonical Coastal Conditions
497033.authors: Samantha Medina, University of Miami, Miami, FL; and B. K. Haus, M. Curcic, W. Drennan, and H. Graber
497033.abstract: Our understanding of fetch-limited wind-wave growth rests on a small set of classical field experiments conducted assuming stationary, homogeneous, shore-normal winds with swell deliberately excluded. Real coastal environments routinely violate these assumptions: coastline orientation drives oblique (slanting) fetch, swell is almost always present, and frontal passages impose non-stationary forcing during active wave growth. How the wind-sea spectrum evolves in these regimes, and how well canonical growth relationships still apply, remains poorly documented, with direct implications for wind-sea directional structure, wave-induced stress, and the roughness parameterizations underlying coupled atmosphere-ocean models of the coastal zone. The Coastal Land-Air-Sea Interaction (CLASI) campaign was designed to observe such coastal boundary layer processes and develop coast-aware parameterizations for mesoscale prediction. Its fourth deployment near Pensacola, Florida occupied a structurally simple, shallow shelf during winter, when frequent frontal passages produced a wide range of wind speeds, directions, and rapid direction shifts. A multi-platform array of ASIS buoys and SOFAR Spotter buoys sampled directional wave spectra at multiple offshore fetches, enabling spatially resolved tracking across shore-normal, slanting, mixed-sea, and turning-wind conditions. We present a dual-filter wind-sea isolation technique combining a wave-age-dependent 1D frequency filter with a 2D directional filter to remove crossing swell and residual "old" wind-sea energy. Validation is by internal 1D/2D energy consistency, comparison against other spectral partition methods, and comparing against canonical growth curves.

497035.title: Calibration Improvements to the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder Level 1 Products
497035.authors: Stephen J. Munchak, Tomorrow.io, Boston, MA; Tomorrow.io, Boston, MA; and E. L. Nelson, A. Bell, and T. King
497035.abstract: The Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) constellation provides rapid-revisit microwave sounding from a set of 6U cubesats measuring 12 channels from 91-204 GHz in a mixture of inclined and sun-synchronous orbital planes. TMS instruments have now been in orbit continuously since August 2024, providing a data record equivalent to over 7 years from a single satellite as of July 2026. With the benefit of this large dataset, which extends over a full range of satellite-solar geometries, we have revised the level 1 calibration algorithms with the aim of minimizing orbital and seasonal calibration biases. This is accomplished via improved understanding of how the TMS calibration targets respond to these different thermal environments. TMS views three calibration sectors in each scan: Deep space (DS), which serves as a cold reference point, and two warm references: deep space with noise diode on (NDS), and an onboard blackbody internal calibration target (ICT). While deep space is ideally the cosmic microwave background (2.73 K), there is some contamination from antenna sidelobes that view the earth and spacecraft. This is determined during post-launch roll maneuvers. The noise diode output is determined as a function of radiometer physical temperature during pre-launch calibration procedures, but there is evidence of ND drift in some channels on some payloads on-orbit. Meanwhile, the ICT provides a long-term stable reference, but its effective emissivity was not characterized pre-launch, and it is prone to large thermal gradients when it is directly illuminated by sunlight, which can occur at high solar beta angles. Version 2 of the TMS level 1 products introduces a new calibration algorithm to optimize use of these targets, leveraging the intra-orbit stability of the noise diodes, and the long-term stability of the ICT in the subset of spacecraft-solar geometries that minimize thermal gradients within the ICT. As a first step in reprocessing, geolocation refinements were introduced which reduced pointing biases from < 5 km to < 1 km in the along- and across-track directions. Bias corrections to the radiative transfer models that form the basis for vicarious calibration (either via reanalysis single difference or coincident sensor double difference) were also implemented. The impact of these changes on absolute calibration accuracy and stability on all timescales will be discussed.

497036.title: The U.S. Drought Monitor: Helping Change the Drought Communication Paradigm
497036.authors: Mark D. Svoboda, National Drought Mitigation Center, University of Nebraska, Lincoln, NE
497036.abstract: We need to move past the old drought adage of “droughts are a slow-onset disaster”. While this is still true, it certainly isn’t the only doctrine. In fact, with a warming planet, the alteration of how water moves through the water cycle has a direct effect on how droughts develop and wane. Although the term flash drought has been around for nearly 25 years, a vast amount of attention has been given globally to these rapid onset/intensifying droughts, which present challenges on many fronts in how we monitor, manage and plan for them on the policy side. At this point, it is much more about a mindset and not as much about our toolsets. This presentation will touch on these points and more in regards to the challenges of communicating drought in a changing climate.

497037.title: Advancing National Drought Resilience: NIDIS at 20 and the Path Forward
497037.authors: Veva Deheza, NOAA National Integrated Drought Information System, Boulder, CO; and B. A. Parker, E. Ossowski, M. Muth, M. Woloszyn, A. M. Sheffield, A. Lang, C. J. Stiles, E. Hasenbeck, E. osenga, E. Wickham, J. Gerlich, J. LISONBEE, K. Eigsti, R. Bilotta, A. J. Hoell, and R. S. Pulwarty
497037.abstract: Since its creation by Congress in 2006, the National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS) has spent 20 years advancing the nation’s approach to drought from a reactive disaster response to a proactive strategy for risk mitigation. This presentation will provide a comprehensive look at the evolution and future direction of NIDIS. We will emphasize the foundation of an integrated information system approach - linking atmospheric and hydrological sciences directly to decision-making across scales and sectors. NIDIS is an interagency partnership, and we will highlight many unique collaborations with state climate offices across the country and their contribution to the success of the Regional Drought Early Warning Systems. We will detail key accomplishments, including the integration of advanced monitoring and prediction capabilities, expanded planning and preparedness efforts, applied research, and the modernization of the U.S. Drought Portal. This presentation will demonstrate the continued necessity of integrated, user-centric information systems in building a more drought-resilient nation, offering a blueprint for addressing other complex environmental hazards. Finally, we will look ahead to address emerging drought challenges, sharing initial thoughts on our next 5-year strategic plan to deliver actionable drought early warning and risk information, modernize drought early warning and forecasting, advance drought planning, and build an interoperable national drought information architecture through the U.S. Drought Portal (www.drought.gov).

497039.title: Aircraft Br-CIMS Observations of Trace Gas Exchange Fluxes in a Coastal Marine Atmosphere
497039.authors: Lee Feinman, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and Y. Tong, B. Blomquist, E. Assaf, T. L. Campos, A. Franchin, S. Woods, and R. Volkamer
497039.abstract: This work evaluates the capability of airborne Br-CIMS to measure eddy covariance fluxes of organic, sulfur, and halogen trace gas species and applies those measurements to air-sea exchange and cloud processing. Previous airborne measurements showed that sea-surface O3 deposition can vary by more than 600% on fine spatial scales (20 km), and found evaporating cloud droplets are an O3 sink (Chiu et al., 2024, AMT). During May 2026, the Technological Innovation Into Iodine and GV Environmental Research Phase 2 (TI3GER-2) aircraft campaign deployed a bromide adduct chemical ionization mass spectrometer (Br-CIMS) aboard the NSF/NCAR Gulfstream V aircraft along the Oregon coast to extend eddy covariance flux measurements to Br-CIMS-detectable organic, sulfur, and halogen species. High frequency (5-10 Hz) observations near the ocean surface, below/above marine stratocumulus clouds, and vertical profiles were measured in pristine marine-biogenic and continentally influenced (polluted) air. We characterize the species dependent Br-CIMS inlet response times, inlet losses, humidity dependent calibration factors, and synchronization with aircraft wind measurements to measure ecosystem fluxes using the Eddy Covariance flux technique. Available fast measurements of O3, H2O, CO, NOx, and cloud markers provide chemical and meteorological context. This work explores the use of Br-CIMS to measure ecosystem exchange fluxes and vertical profiles of dimethylsulfide (DMS), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), glyoxal, methyl glyoxal, and small organic acids, as well as dihalogen species (I2, ICl, IBr, Cl2) in an effort to better understand the chemical processes occurring at the air-sea interface and in marine stratocumulus clouds.

497044.title: Pulling Everyone in: Evaluating the Feasibility of Language Interoperability and Hardware Portability to Improve Community Development Efforts in Atmospheric Modeling
497044.authors: Ren Stengel, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and J. Sun, M. Waxmonsky, and J. M. Dennis
497044.abstract: Many atmospheric legacy codes are written in Fortran, which can make them challenging to port and run efficiently on newer high-performance computing systems. Additionally, many researchers and software engineers are becoming increasingly interested in writing physics models in more modern languages such as Python, Python/JAX, and Julia. However, sharing progress and physics capabilities between these different language versions is non-trivial and rarely done in practice. As a result, many scientists have limited ability to use or integrate into newer and more performant modeling frameworks and compute systems. We use E3SM’s atmospheric model (EAMxx), to explore the feasibility of linking atmospheric parameterizations written in different languages into one system. EAMxx is written in C++/Kokkos and offers direct support for bridging in multiple languages in its atmospheric processes framework, including support for Fortran, Python, or machine learning emulators built with PyTorch. EAMxx is also hardware portable due to its use of the Kokkos portability interface. EAMxx is a complete atmospheric framework, so users only need to provide initialization and physics code to be called at each timestep. We describe the development approach of bridging existing physics parameterization codes into EAMxx atmospheric processes. We cover target language-specific design choices and performance optimizations in the bridge code. We also describe our efforts to provide hardware portability support in both the bridge code and physics parameterizations. Finally, we show performance results on both CPUs and GPUs from NCAR’s supercomputer Derecho for the various Kessler implementation languages and hardware backends. We also discuss the lessons learned from this development experience about how to write performant interoperable code and methods for improving the bridge code creation process.

497046.title: Understanding Large-Scale Midlatitude Atmospheric Dynamics Using a Hierarchy of Stochastic Models
497046.authors: Gang Chen, Univ. of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA; and X. Ding, K. Lu, F. Xu, D. Kondrashov, and Y. Sun
497046.abstract: Midlatitude weather extremes, such as atmospheric blocking, cold-air outbreaks, heat waves, and heavy precipitation, have disproportionate societal impacts. Yet the large-scale atmospheric dynamics underlying these events remain difficult to fully understand, limiting our ability to predict them accurately. Many of these extremes are closely linked to variability in the midlatitude jet streams and storm tracks, whose meridional shifts strongly modulate regional weather patterns. Earlier work has used stochastic models with linear dynamics to investigate large-scale atmospheric variability. Meanwhile, recent advances in AI-based weather forecasting have demonstrated remarkable predictive skill by learning complex mappings directly from atmospheric reanalysis and model output. Despite these successes, the dynamical basis of AI predictability remains poorly understood, and many AI-based models exhibit limitations such as instability in long-term simulations. Here, we bridge these two research directions by examining the dynamics and predictability of large-scale atmospheric circulation using a hierarchy of stochastic models, ranging from traditional Linear Inverse Models (LIMs) to deep generative models. We illustrate this framework through applications to major modes of climate variability, including stratosphere-troposphere coupling and jet stream/storm track variability. Particularly, we will examine the roles of linear and nonlinear processes in shaping model dynamics, predictability, and statistical structure as compared to traditional linear models. Analogous to the use of model hierarchies in climate modeling, this hierarchy of statistical models provides a systematic framework for understanding how increasingly complex machine learning models represent atmospheric variability relative to simpler linear models. It also offers new insights into the interpretation of AI-based prediction systems and their potential responses to external forcing and climate change.

497048.title: Assimilation of CRIS Isoprene Retrievals within UFS-RAQMS: Off-line Iterative Mass Balance Adjustments of MEGAN Isoprene Emissions during the 2023 AEROMMA/STAQS Field Campaign
497048.authors: Robert Bradley Pierce, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI; and A. Lenzen, A. Kumar, D. B. Millet, K. Wells, M. M. Coggon, C. Stockwell, K. Bates, C. Warneke, L. Judd, and M. X. Mosqueda
497048.abstract: Isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene, C5H8) is a naturally occurring volatile organic compound (VOC) that is emitted from vegetation that accounts for nearly 50% of the global non-methane hydrocarbon (NMHC) emissions. Biogenic isoprene emissions are larger than the sum of all anthropogenic VOC emissions and therefore highly relevant for tropospheric ozone production, which is determined by the relative amount of VOC’s and NOx (NO+NO2). Isoprene has important impacts on global air quality (both ozone and secondary organic aerosol production) and the oxidizing capacity of the atmosphere since its major sink is OH. Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) isoprene retrievals have been developed using Machine Learning (ML) approaches. This study evaluates the impact of assimilating the ML based Retrieval of Organics from CrIS Radiances (ROCR) isoprene retrievals within the NOAA Unified Forecast System (UFS) with stratospheric/tropospheric chemistry from the Real-time Air Quality Modeling System (UFS-RAQMS). Since isoprene has a very short lifetime O(<1hr), we use an iterative mass balance approach that uses isoprene analysis increments to provide off-line constraints on isoprene emissions. Hourly online Model of Emissions of Gases and Aerosols from Nature version 2.1 (MEGAN2.1) isoprene emissions obtained from the Harvard Harmonized Emissions Component (HEMCO) are used as apriori emissions. Airborne insitu isoprene measurements obtained during the 2023 Atmospheric Emissions and Reactions Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas (AEROMMA), airborne remote formaldehyde measurements from the Synergistic TEMPO Air Quality Science (STAQS) field campaigns, and global Tropospheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI) formaldehyde retrievals are used to evaluate the impact of isoprene emission adjustments on UFS-RAQMS chemical forecasts during the AEROMMA/STAQS field campaigns on both regional and global scales.

497049.title: Co-Development for Science and Operations: A Case Study In Satellite Drag
497049.authors: Jennifer Knuth, University of Colorado LASP, Boulder, CO; and M. Pilinski and G. Lucas
497049.abstract: Translating complex science into actionable information for decision makers is one of the fundamental challenges of operationalizing research. In this presentation, I will provide a case study of working with scientists to create a visualization for both researchers and satellite operators. The Calibration Atmosphere with Forcing Estimates (CAFE) application found at https://swx-trec.com/cafe, a project funded by the NASA R2O2R program, models satellite drag and its variability during space weather events. Through many prototypes with various coordinate systems, colormaps, and levels of sampling, we iteratively tested the options with users. The goal was to visually encode the right amount of information: not too much and not too little. An agile workflow and a continuous integration and deployment pipeline allowed iterative development and review, enabling co-production and user-centered design. This presentation will discuss the development process of building on a minimum viable product (MVP) and the variables that were explored along the way, offering examples of how to work with users towards a clearer presentation of data. The CAFE application is intended for both researchers and operators. Data from both quiet and active times are valuable to researchers while the graphical visualization is useful to operators as they trace their spacecraft through the drag environment. An iterative co-development process can offer benefits to both space weather science and practice.

497050.title: From Supplemental Coverage to a Hybrid National Radar Network: Deploying X- and C-Band Radar Infrastructure for the Next Generation of US Weather Surveillance
497050.authors: Tara Goode, Climavision, Louisville, KY; and C. Goode, L. Maynard, M. Simpson, PhD, K. Grempler, K. W. Howard, and E. Pawsat
497050.abstract: The United States is entering a consequential period in the evolution of its weather-radar enterprise. As NOAA considers requirements and architectures for Radar Next, the discussion increasingly extends beyond replacement of individual radar systems to the design of a resilient national observing capability. Within that discussion, commercial radar networks offer an opportunity to demonstrate how multiple radar wavelengths, deployment models, and operational partnerships can complement the long-standing national S-band backbone. Climavision has deployed 30+ dual-polarization X-band weather radars across the United States, establishing an operational network intended primarily to improve low-altitude surveillance in areas affected by distance from existing WSR-88D radars, terrain blockage, or other persistent coverage limitations. The deployment has provided practical experience extending well beyond individual radar performance, including site selection, spectrum coordination, infrastructure development, communications, remote operations, maintenance, network monitoring, and delivery of observations to meteorological users. Building on that experience, Climavision is now actively deploying approximately C-band weather radars over the next several years. This represents a significant evolution in the company's radar strategy. While X-band systems are well suited for targeted enhancement of low-altitude coverage, the C-band deployment is intended to establish a broader regional surveillance layer that can operate in conjunction with the existing national S-band network. The resulting concept is not based on replacing one radar technology with another. Rather, it recognizes the complementary strengths of multiple wavelengths within an integrated observing architecture: S-band providing the long-range national backbone, C-band adding regional-scale coverage and resilience, and X-band providing targeted higher-resolution observations where additional low-altitude surveillance is needed. Deploying such a network at meaningful operational scale is a substantial undertaking. Radar siting, spectrum availability, communications, infrastructure, calibration, reliability, maintenance, environmental exposure, lifecycle support, and operational availability all become increasingly important as the number and geographic distribution of systems grow. The challenges are significant, and the ultimate configuration and role of commercial radar within the future national enterprise remain to be determined. However, experience gained through operating an existing distributed X-band network provides Climavision with an operational foundation from which to take the next step into C-band deployment. Together, the X- and C-band efforts represent a deliberate and comparatively bold move by industry to begin putting elements of a hybrid national radar architecture into the field while the broader Radar Next architecture continues to develop. Doing so provides an opportunity to move portions of the discussion from conceptual network designs toward operational experience with real systems, real deployment constraints, and real lifecycle requirements. The presentation will describe Climavision's existing X-band network, the rationale and objectives underlying its active C-band deployment, site-selection and network-design considerations, expected relationships among S-, C-, and X-band coverage, and lessons learned from deploying and sustaining a geographically distributed commercial radar network. Particular emphasis will be placed on scalability, operational reliability, deployment tempo, resilience, lifecycle support, and the practical considerations associated with expanding from localized supplemental coverage toward a multi-frequency national observing capability. The intent is not to prescribe the future Radar Next architecture or suggest that deployment of a hybrid network is straightforward. Rather, Climavision's expanding radar infrastructure provides an opportunity for government, industry, and the research community to evaluate what such an architecture can deliver in practice. By deploying and operating systems now, the weather enterprise can begin developing the operational experience needed to inform decisions about how government and commercial radar capabilities may work together in the next generation of U.S. weather surveillance.

497051.title: Northern Hemisphere Winter Extremes 2025-26: Categorizing Snowpack Anomalies from Gridded to Local Scales
497051.authors: Alyssa Hendricks Dietrich, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Dewberry, Trinidad, CO; and S. R. Fassnacht, J. I. Lopez Moreno, and K. Suzuki
497051.abstract: The 2025–26 Northern Hemisphere winter drew widespread attention for its dramatic extremes, including high‑profile news coverage of severe snow drought in the western United States compared to record‑breaking snowfall and cold in the eastern United States, the limited snow cover at the Winter Olympics in Italy, and multiple record-breaking extreme snow events across Russia. These diverse winter conditions underscore the need to systematically evaluate how snowpack extremes during this season compare to climatological norms. This study utilizes ERA5 reanalysis data and selected long‑term snow records to categorize snow water equivalent (SWE) and snow-depth anomalies relative to a 1991–2020 climatological baseline. At the hemispheric scale, ERA5 gridded SWE fields are analyzed to identify departures from climatology and to map regions exceeding percentile thresholds. These gridded diagnostics provide a spatially continuous framework for comparing snowpack anomalies across diverse climate regimes. Temperature provides a secondary diagnostic to contextualize accumulation patterns as many locations also saw record cold winters, while recognizing that warmer than normal temperatures, while still colder than freezing, can act to enhance snowfall efficiency and accumulation. Complementary site‑scale analyses draw on established snow monitoring programs in the United States (Rocky Mountains and Appalachians), Russia (Kamchatka Peninsula), Japan (Japanese Alps), Spain (Pyrenees), and Switzerland (Alps). These locations represent a range of continental, maritime, and alpine regimes, allowing comparison of local snowpack evolution against ERA5 grid‑cell climatology. Site‑specific analyses focus on long-duration records of snow depth, a more widely available metric compared to SWE. For each site, return‑period analyses of snow depth assess the extremity of the 2025–26 season within historical context. The combination of gridded and point‑based data allows evaluation of how local extremes align or diverge from larger-scale patterns. The resulting framework supports consistent categorization of snowpack extremes across scales, providing a foundation for future analyses of snow climatology and its variability under changing atmospheric conditions. This presentation will provide a reproducible method for identifying and comparing snowpack extremes from hemispheric to local scales. The winter of 2025–26 serves as a test case for refining this approach and improving understanding of how large‑scale climatological context informs regional snowpack characterization.

497054.title: An Unforecasted Extreme Mesoscale Gravity Wave: The 22 February 1998 Alabama Gravity Wave Event
497054.authors: Rajan Bhandari, Division of Atmospheric Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Reno, REno, NV; and M. L. Kaplan
497054.abstract: Timely detection and prediction of mesoscale gravity waves (MGWs) remain substantial operational forecasting challenges, particularly east of the Rocky Mountains, where these waves can affect sensible weather and produce damaging surface winds. The 22 February 1998 Alabama MGW event illustrates this challenge because the wave and its associated high-impact winds were not anticipated sufficiently far in advance by operational forecasters. This study investigates the event using the high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. The simulation closely reproduced the observed wave amplitude, approximate genesis time and location, and northeastward propagation. The disturbance developed near the southeastern Louisiana coast as a wave of depression and propagated at approximately 26 m/s along the rear edge of a stratiform precipitation band. Nonlinear balance equation (NBE) residual and potential vorticity (PV) inversion analyses revealed upper-tropospheric flow imbalance associated with the jet streak, indicating that geostrophic adjustment was an important initiating mechanism. This adjustment was associated with the development of a mid-tropospheric jetlet and enhanced vertical wind shear within its exit region, suggesting that shear instability provided an additional mechanism for wave genesis and early amplification. Wave- maintenance diagnostics further showed that, along with wave ducting, shear instability and conditional instability of the second kind (wave-CISK) likely provided additional mechanisms for MGW maintenance and amplification. These results demonstrate that diagnosing upper-level flow imbalance and jetlet development, together with identifying a favorable downstream ducting environment, can help anticipate MGW development and may therefore provide useful diagnostic guidance for operational forecasters.

497055.title: Update from the 2026 CF Workshop
497055.authors: Ethan Davis, ; and S. VILLAUME, PhD, L. Garcia San Martin, D. Hassell, A. Pamment, S. Bartholomew, A. Cofiño, L. H. Marsden, L. Bärring, and D. Lee
497055.abstract: The CF (Climate and Forecast) Conventions are a community-developed standard for describing Earth system science data in the netCDF data format and more recently in Zarr/GeoZarr. The CF Conventions can encode information that describes the coordinate systems, data structure, and geophysical meaning and units of each variable, and how the data were collected. It is widely used by weather and climate scientists and remote-sensing researchers and is gaining traction in new communities, such as biogeochemistry and operational weather prediction. It is used to share data across science domains and between research and operational systems. It has a mature ecosystem of FOSS (Free and Open-Source Software) and commercial software tools that can explore, analyze, and visualize data that are encoded using the CF Conventions. This presentation will provide a high-level overview of CF, including governance and the CF data model, and review discussions, activities, and outcomes from the 2026 CF Workshop held 21-24 September 2026 at ECMWF in Bonn, Germany. These discussions included review and work on changes going into the upcoming CF 1.14 release, how CF should evolve in terms of representing uncertainty metadata, how vocabularies will be managed and mapped to other vocabularies and ontologies, updates on efforts to map CF metadata to other formats (e.g., GRIB, BUFR, and Zarr), and plans for a WMO cloud-optimized future data infrastructure.

497056.title: Zax: An AI-Ready Cloud-Native Array Query Engine
497056.abstract: As cloud-native storage formats have gained adoption, the barrier to extracting insight and value from large data archives is increasinly the compute layer. While agents and LLMs can now explore and analyze data, they are still constrained by the efficiency and expressiveness of the underlying data analysis libraries. Existing solutions to expressing arbitrary computation on n-dimensional arrays can be brittle and hard to reason about (e.g. Xarray/Dask). Using them effectively requires careful tuning (e.g. careful choice of chunk sizes for compute orchestration) and trial-and-error provisioning of memory. Commonly, one must also orchestrate computations using generic pipeline tools (e.g. Airflow) that lack any domain knowledge about the Earth System data. User ability to analyze large datasets is thus significantly limited by their technological expertise. We present a new solution that accelerates scientific data analysis in the cloud for both humans and agents : Zax. Zax is a query engine for expressing compute on n-dimensional chunked arrays, similar in scope to Xarray. Zax marries a number of innovative strategies from array computing and tabular database systems, while adapting them to a cloud-computing context. Zax provides an expressive high-level Xarray-inspired API and hides lower-level orchestration details . For e.g. it chooses chunk sizes to maximize resource usage. Implemented in Rust with a thin Python API, Zax obtains highly efficient utilization of CPU, RAM, and network. Zax is designed to be extremely amenable to AI agentic workflows. Zax's client-server mode enables local code to execute in a remote compute environment with minimal overhead. Zax thus enables AI-ready data-proximate cloud-native compute on a wide range of datasets, including petabyte scale public archives. Zax makes large cloud-native data archives far more accessible than they have ever been. We will demonstrate the design concepts and impact of Zax by running an illustrative example workflow on NOAA data in the cloud.

497057.title: Cloud Processes Drive Parametric Uncertainty in Mountain West Snowpack: Insights from a Perturbed Parameter Ensemble
497057.authors: Tobias Innes David Ross, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and T. W. Aerenson, D. McCoy, J. M. Nugent, and H. Y. Brown
497057.abstract: Mountain snowpack provides critical seasonal water storage for the western United States, accumulating through winter and supplying meltwater to streams, rivers, and reservoirs through spring and summer. As climate change is projected to reduce this natural reservoir, reliable projections of annual maximum snow water equivalent (SWE) are increasingly important for anticipating future water availability. Global climate models (GCMs) are an essential tool for anticipating these changes, but their projections depend in part upon how unresolved physical processes are parameterized. Recent work suggests that uncertain parameter choices within a single GCM can produce differences in simulated SWE comparable to those arising across GCMs, but the exact parameters and physical processes responsible for these differences remain poorly understood. We use a 250-member perturbed-parameter ensemble of the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) to identify the cloud parameters that most strongly influence SWE and to diagnose the physical pathways through which they act. Across snow-bearing watersheds in the Mountain West, SWE is consistently sensitive to parameters governing the rate of conversion of cloud water to rainwater (autoconversion processes) in stratiform clouds, exhibiting a strongly non-linear response across the perturbed parameter ranges. To diagnose how these parameter perturbations produce differences in SWE, we decomposed annual SWE maxima into contributions from precipitation supply, precipitation phase, and snowpack retention. The decomposition reveals two competing pathways: changes in autoconversion alter the partitioning of precipitation between rain and snow, while simultaneous changes in cloudiness and surface energy balance affect the retention of accumulated snow. Consequently, similar SWE maxima can arise through substantially different combinations of snowfall and retention. These relationships are clearest when large-scale meteorology is constrained, but the same processes remain evident in free-running simulations, where much of the total SWE spread instead arises from synoptic variability in precipitation supply. By comparing these configurations, we will quantify the contribution of uncertain model physics to Mountain West snowpack variability and assess which cloud observations, including those from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program, have the greatest potential to constrain uncertainty in simulated SWE.

497058.title: Relationships Between Warm-Temperature Ice-Nucleating Particles and Ambient Temperature Across Multiple Campaigns
497058.authors: Ruichen Zhou, Colorado State University, FORT COLLINS, CO; and P. J. DeMott, S. M. Kreidenweis, and R. J. Perkins
497058.abstract: Ice-nucleating particles (INPs) can initiate ice formation in mixed-phase clouds, influencing cloud lifetime, radiative properties, and precipitation formation. A subset of INPs is active at relatively warm temperatures (such as above −20 °C), and may therefore be particularly important in moderately supercooled mixed-phase clouds. Biological aerosols are usually considered major contributors to these warm-temperature INPs. However, the distributions, variability, and sources of warm-temperature INPs remain poorly constrained, limiting their representation in atmospheric models. A previous study (Schneider et al., 2021) found that concentrations of INPs active at −15 °C were positively correlated with ambient temperature, except during summer, at a boreal forest site. Here, we combine year-long INP observations from multiple campaigns with diverse environments across several continents to investigate the relationship between warm-temperature INPs and ambient temperature. Across the campaigns, concentrations of INPs active at and near −15 °C showed positive correlations with ambient temperature, with observations from different environments falling within a similar temperature-dependent region. This relationship changed once ambient temperature exceeded a threshold temperature, with INP concentrations becoming negatively correlated with ambient temperature and positively correlated with relative humidity. These results provide a basis for parameterizing INPs active near −15 °C using ambient temperature and relative humidity.

497059.title: The Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS) Level-2 Product Generation from Tomorrow.io TMS Observations
497059.authors: Yong-Keun Lee, CISESS, Ellicott City, MD; CISESS/ESSIC/UMD, College Park, MD; and J. X. Yang, S. Liu, X. Liang, W. Wang, and H. Meng
497059.abstract: This study evaluates commercial microwave sounder (MWS) data with a focus on the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS), using the Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS), the official enterprise satellite microwave data retrieval system of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). As of August 2026, NOAA is receiving TMS observations from the two Tomorrow.io satellites (S06 and S09). These satellites operate in sun-synchronous and drifting orbits (45° inclination), respectively, providing complementary spatial and temporal sampling during the Commercial Microwave Sounder Data Buy period. This report presents the evaluation results of TMS observations from the two Tomorrow.io satellites, S06 and S09 using MiRS. The MiRS retrieval results are compared with reference datasets including MiRS Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) retrievals and NWP analysis data. Compared to ATMS, the Tomorrow.io TMS has fewer channels and higher noise levels in the F-band temperature-sounding channels, which introduces additional uncertainty into the retrievals. As a result, MiRS TMS retrievals generally exhibit reduced performance relative to MiRS ATMS, but remain within—or marginal to—the performance criteria defined by the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) requirements. The MiRS Tomorrow.io TMS retrieval products and their applications to the downstream algorithms may complement the backbone satellite microwave measurements to support nowcasting and short-term weather forecasting with the high revisit rate of Tomorrow.io TMS measurements. In addition, a novel denoising algorithm has been developed to effectively reduce the NEDT across all channels. This report also presents an assessment of the impact of TMS noise on MiRS retrievals, as well as an evaluation of the effectiveness of the denoising algorithm.

497060.title: Use of Atmospheric Methane and Methane Stable Isotope Measurements Along with Satellite Data in an Atmospheric Inversion Gives Improved Estimates of Tropical Microbial Emissions.
497060.authors: Lori M. Bruhwiler, NOAA, Boulder, CO; and Y. Oh, M. He, and D. J. Jacob
497060.abstract: Accurately separating the contributions of different sources to recent atmospheric methane (CH4) growth is crucial for better quantifying the present and future responses of CH4 emissions to changing climate and anthropogenic activity. Here, we report on results from the CarbonTracker-CH4 global inversion system for microbial, fossil, and pyrogenic sources from 2000 to 2022, using measurements of atmospheric CH4 and its stable carbon isotope ratio, δ13C-CH4. In addition, we also use retrieved column CH4 from the blended GOSAT-TROPOMI data product. Global total CH4 emissions increased by 15% from 2000 to 2022, with mainly due to microbial emissions. Both microbial and fossil emissions increased during 2007–2013 relative to 2000–2006, with the largest contributions from temperate Asia. From 2014–2017, microbial emissions from tropical regions, particularly South America and Africa, were the dominant driver of the methane increase, while fossil emissions remained stable in Europe and North America. Between 2020 and 2022, microbial emissions surged in the African and Asian tropics, whereas fossil emissions declined across most industrial regions. Notably, inversions not constrained by isotope data did not capture the decline in fossil emissions during 2020–2022, a decline potentially related to the COVID-19 pandemic, policy-driven changes, and decreases in CH4 emissions intensity. Further, our inversion with isotopic constraints give a larger prominent in wetland emissions that is more strongly correlated with variations in terrestrial water storage during 2003–2022. Inversions using the blended GOSAT-TROPOMI data increase the correlations between terrestrial water storage and estimated fluxes, likely because of increased tropical observational constraints. This highlights the utility of retrieved column CH4 from satellite data.

497061.title: Hyperlocal Ensemble Nowcasts of Hail across the CONUS Accelerated Via Neural Architecture Search
497061.authors: Ryan Lagerquist, MyRadar, Ward, CO; and J. P. Gibbons and S. Garimella
497061.abstract: We use deep learning to produce hyperlocal nowcasts of hail size on the Multi-radar Multi-sensor (MRMS) grid, which covers the CONUS at 1-km spacing. This hyperlocal approach contrasts with existing storm-based approaches, which provide less spatial granularity. Our labels are radar-based pseudo-observations, namely the false negative rate (FNR)-adjusted maximum estimated size of hail (MESH), which we term FRESH, based on the work of Murillo and Homeyer (2019; https://doi.org/10.1175/JAMC-D-18-0247.1). Our deep-learning models are informed with a first-guess nowcast from an advection model, which linearly extrapolates recent FRESH fields into the future. Thus, we use deep learning only to go the last mile and handle the non-linear component of hail evolution, as well as uncertainty quantification. This talk will be an update on our ensemble deep-learning system, focusing on four major advances. First, we have added several dual-polarization radar variables to the predictors. Because training with 3-D volumes is too computationally expensive for a product that must update every 2 minutes, we have experimented with several approaches to represent hail signatures/precursors – including KDP columns, ZDR columns, and depressed ρhv – with 2-D fields. Second, to improve the model’s performance on cases with hail initiation, we have performed feature-engineering to combine radar and NWP fields into a hail-growth potential (HGP) field. Third, we have tuned our custom loss function to improve both the probabilistic (individual ensemble members, ensemble spread) and deterministic (ensemble mean) performance of the model. Fourth, due to the time-sensitive nature of short-term nowcasts – at lead times of 2, 4, ..., 30 min – we will present the results of a neural architecture search (NAS) aimed at pruning/simplifying the full deep-learning model with a minimal sacrifice in accuracy. We will close with a discussion of remaining areas for improvement, including custom processing of level-II radar data.

497062.title: Representing Organic Soil Fire Emissions in the RRFS-Smoke Model: Implementation and Performance Assessment
497062.authors: Johana Romero-Alvarez, CIRES/NOAA-GSL, Boulder, CO; and R. Ahmadov, H. Li, J. Schnell, E. P. James, and S. R. Bhimireddy
497062.abstract: During the record-breaking 2023 Canadian wildfire season, extreme drought exposed normally saturated peatlands and deep organic soils to high-severity combustion, revealing underestimations in the top-down emissions inventories used by flagship operational systems, such as HRRR-Smoke and the upcoming RRFS-Smoke. While these systems captured smoke transport pathways well, they underestimated smoke PM2.5 concentrations across North America. Using high-resolution geospatial masks, we isolate regions dominated by organic soils and permanent wetlands and then update both the emission factors (EFs) and the biomass combustion coefficient (𝛽), which is used to convert Fire Radiative Energy (FRE) into total biomass consumed. We test two 𝛽 formulations: one based on land-use-dependent values from published literature and another ecosystem-dependent 𝛽 derived by calibrating NOAA’s Regional ABI and VIIRS fire Emission product (RAVE) FRP against total biomass consumption estimates from the bottom-up wildfire emissions inventory Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED5.1). Initial RRFS-Smoke simulations using these adjusted coefficients show a substantial increase in smoke emission estimates for fires influenced by organic-soil combustion. This update significantly reduces the model biases observed during the 2023 season and brings model output into closer agreement with surface observations. These improvements address a low bias likely resulting from limitations in satellite-derived Fire Radiative Power (FRP) to detect weak smoldering signals from vulnerable carbon reservoirs under canopy, as well as retrieval uncertainty under the dense smoke conditions in 2023.

497063.title: Assessment of Precipitation Morphology in Climate Model Realizations Downscaled Using Residual Corrective Diffusion
497063.authors: Alex M. Haberlie, Northern Illinois Univ., Dekalb, IL; and B. L. Weart, N. D. Sonntag, W. S. Ashley, V. A. Gensini, and A. C. Michaelis
497063.abstract: Organized deep, moist convection (DMC) can produce dangerous lightning, flash flooding, damaging wind, large hail, and tornadoes. Despite their societal importance, there is a limited understanding of how anthropogenic climate change might influence the spatiotemporal frequency of these events. Existing work using GCMs suggests some regions may experience more days with large-scale environments that are conditionally favorable for organized DMC. However, important mesoscale processes, including convective initiation and storm organization, are not resolved by GCMs. Dynamical downscaling addresses this limitation by using GCM output to drive a convection-permitting RCM that explicitly resolves mesoscale processes. However, this improvement comes with a significant computational cost. The WRF BCC dataset is a recent example of this approach, using a target horizontal grid spacing of 3.75 km and a temporal resolution of 15 minutes. Creating this ~1 PB dataset required ~107 core hours on high-performance computing clusters, limiting the feasibility of generating large ensembles of high-resolution realizations needed to characterize uncertainty. Recently, generative machine learning approaches such as residual corrective diffusion, including NVIDIA’s CorrDiff, have been developed to emulate convection-permitting RCMs by generating high-resolution realizations directly from coarse-resolution predictors such as GCM fields. These approaches can reproduce mesoscale features at a greatly reduced computational cost. This work extends ongoing evaluations of CorrDiff by assessing the morphology of 6-h precipitation depicted in large ensembles of generatively downscaled climate realizations. An adapted CorrDiff model was trained using hundreds of predictor variables from a bias-corrected version of CESM1 (CMIP5), with historical 6-h precipitation accumulation (1990 – 2005) from a convection-permitting WRF-ARW simulation as target data. Related ongoing work has demonstrated that the best performing model markedly improves the bulk accuracy of the predictions in the diffusion step relative to the initial regression prediction. To evaluate whether these improvements extend to organized DMC structures, a precipitation morphology classification model is applied to both target and generated fields to identify pertinent precipitation morphologies, including isolated cells and mesoscale convective systems. The generated realizations include many of the structures represented in the target data. However, the performance varies by region, synoptic regime, and season. The results demonstrate that generative diffusion can produce physically meaningful precipitation structures similar to convection-permitting simulations, while also identifying cases where the generative model needs improvement. Overall, this approach warrants further examination, particularly for applications requiring large ensembles of high-resolution climate fields.

497064.title: A Nested Hydrologic-Hydrodynamic Framework for Statewide Flood Reconstruction and Building-Scale Exposure Assessment
497064.authors: Yifan Wang, Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ; Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ; and J. xia, Y. wu, S. Rasiya Koya, J. Camacho, H. Josephs, E. Nikolopoulos, and J. Gong
497064.abstract: New Jersey experienced three severe pluvial flood events within one month in July 2026. Local high-intensity rainfall of this kind is becoming more frequent, and with it the demand for damage assessment after the event. However, no existing product delivers that assessment quickly and at the resolution at which the damage occurs. We present a framework built to deliver it, linking statewide hydrologic hindcasting to street-scale hydrodynamic reconstruction and building-scale exposure analysis. The framework begins with EF5, a distributed hydrologic model forced with MRMS radar precipitation, run over the entire state of New Jersey at 30 m in hindcast mode. Maximum unit streamflow from EF5 ranks the hydrologic response across basins of different sizes and identifies the areas worth reconstructing. Those areas are then reconstructed with TRITON, a GPU-accelerated two-dimensional hydrodynamic model, which simulates inundation depth, extent, and timing at street resolution under the EF5 runoff. The next stage is calibration. Such flooding is local in extent and short in duration, and it is rarely surveyed for high water marks. With no marks available, and with stream gauges recording stage in the channel rather than on the streets, the measurements come from crowdsourced imagery. Photographs and videos shared publicly during the event are geolocated and converted to water-surface elevations on the flooded streets themselves. Because an image rarely records the peak, these elevations enter an automated roughness calibration as one-sided lower bounds, alongside gauge peaks as two-sided constraints. After calibration, the reconstructed depths are intersected with building footprints to rank affected properties. A diffusion model then renders the modeled depth at each building as a labeled synthetic image for more intuitive expression. We demonstrate the framework on three domains drawn from two of the events in July 2026. Monmouth County and Camden were reconstructed at 10 m, covering 1,150 and 1,950 km2, and Paterson on the Passaic River at 5 m over a 105 km2 catchment. At Paterson the simulated peak reaches seven of the eight image-derived marks and falls 0.04 m short of the eighth, while three USGS gauges give a mean bias of +0.172 m. All products are served through a public dashboard. The approach is most useful where no model exists beforehand. EF5 indicates where one belongs, and scripted input generation shortens the construction that follows. The crowdsourced water levels, also extracted automatically, keep the result accurate where no survey exists. For the July 2026 events, model construction from scratch, crowdsourced data collection, calibration, exposure assessment, and delivery were completed within one week after the event. The same sequence can be run in forecast mode.

497066.title: Co-Producing Community Preparedness: Applications and Opportunities of a Weather-Adapted Participatory Framework Through IWT Partnerships
497066.authors: Megan S Porter, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and J. L. Garza, M. Pazos, J. Henderson, and M. Saldana
497066.abstract: Engagement around severe weather has largely centered on forecast interpretation and information coordination, most notably through convenings of Integrated Warning Teams (IWTs). Though IWTs excel at operational coordination among expert practitioners, they are not designed to address dimensions of community resilience, and their outcomes often emphasize adjustments to expert systems over the contextual and population-specific challenges communities face. Knowledge co-production offers a complementary approach, and one such participatory framework—Vulnerability, Consequences, and Adaptation Planning Scenarios (VCAPS)—has been applied extensively in climate adaptation contexts but not to convective hazards. Across three phases—preparation, workshop, and reporting—VCAPS convenes a group of partners such as NWS Warning Coordination Meteorologists, university researchers, local emergency managers, and community decision-makers to define challenges to preparedness and strategize feasible plans to overcome them. Pre-workshop interviews allow the facilitating team to tailor the two half-day workshop to the local social and historical impact contexts that shape preparedness. Following the interviews and workshop, insights into local vulnerabilities, hazard preparedness challenges, and opportunities for capacity building are synthesized into a participant-reviewed guidebook to sustain post-VCAPS actions. This presentation examines the adaptation of VCAPS to severe weather contexts as a model which builds upon existing IWT partnerships through the inclusion of broader community stakeholders who can support local preparedness and capacity building. The authors present two applications with NWS partners: in Hockley County, Texas, following a May 2024 extreme wind event, and in Putnam County, Tennessee, five years after the March 3, 2020, EF4 Cookeville tornado. To better adapt VCAPS to a weather context, the authors substituted the framework's digital causal diagramming with participatory mapping, where participants mapped critical infrastructure, vulnerable populations and places, and networks of support they rely upon—an approach which more closely reflects the scenario-based planning traditions already familiar to emergency managers and first responders. Across both applications, participatory mapping externalized tacit local and operational knowledge of vulnerability and preparedness challenges. Importantly, this process scaffolded group knowledge and supported strategic planning toward feasible preparedness goals, such as volunteer registries, expanded mass notification enrollment, and Spanish-language risk communication. Moreover, because the VCAPS participant base overlaps with partners already convened by IWTs, this process may extend existing networks rather than require new ones. This positions Warning Coordination Meteorologists and local partners to broaden who is invited, while illuminating who remains missing from preparedness planning and where their inclusion may further build community capacities. Recommendations are offered for adapting this process across hazards and community scales.

497067.title: How Spatial and Temporal Lightning Patterns Connect with Thunderstorm Processes
497067.authors: Alaina Adderley, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and V. C. Chmielewski and S. M. Stough
497067.abstract: Lightning responds to the evolution of updrafts and attendant mixed-phase precipitation processes through first-order connections between electrification, cloud microphysics, and thunderstorm kinematics. Not only do lightning flashes increase in frequency and decrease in size as an updraft intensifies, but the spatial distribution of lightning sometimes reflects an updraft response as well. For instance, lightning “holes” have been observed as a void of flash channels amid a ring of higher flash channel density surrounding an updraft, akin to a bounded weak echo signature in radar reflectivity. Similarly, relationships between lightning activity, radar-inferred precipitation descent, and related downdraft influences have also been reported. Supercell, quasi-linear convective system, and mixed-mode storms were observed by a number of research radars and the NSSL Mobile Lightning Mapping Array during the Propagation and Evolution of Rotation in Linear Storms (PERiLS) campaign. These measurements enable detailed 3D reconstruction of individual lightning flashes alongside radar-inferred precipitation and kinematic evolution. Lightning holes were observed in a number of these storms. While lightning holes are thought of as a manifestation of the evacuation of hydrometeors from a robust updraft, lightning holes observed during PERiLS occasionally appeared even as other indications of updraft intensity trended down. These and other spatial and temporal lightning trends are evaluated alongside the evolution of radar-inferred precipitation microphysics to add insight into lightning’s connections with thunderstorm updraft and downdraft processes.

497068.title: Machine Learning to Characterize and Explain the Fine-Scale Temporal Variability of Canopy-Layer UHI
497068.authors: Philip T. R. Maruri, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX
497068.abstract: While urban heat islands have mostly been studied as climatological phenomena, the temporal variability of their signal hints at significant meso-to-synoptic scale dynamics over periods ranging from hours to days. In addition, health and other impacts of urban overheating tend to be concentrated during heatwaves, and mitigation of these impacts thus also needs to focus on extremes, rather than climatic averages. Therefore, we analyze meteorological records from NOAA ASOS stations around Phoenix, Arizona to explore the variability of canopy-layer UHI signal at hourly and daily time scales across 20 years and its relation to near-surface meteorology. The probability density function of the UHI signal shows significant variability around the mean, with peaks around 12ºC while the mean is only around 2ºC. Spectral and time series analyses show that only about 30% of this time variability is directly linked to the diurnal cycle, with 70 % occurring at scales of hours or multiple days. Machine learning analysis reveal that strong non-linear relationships define UHI variability, with performance improving with finer resolution data. Attribution analysis using tree-based algorithms reveal that a complex web of meteorological parameters, primarily based on conditions at previous timescales, drives fine-scale variability. The findings, while strictly only applicable to Phoenix, underline the importance of this fine-scale variability and the gap in our understanding of its scales and main drivers.

497069.title: A Comprehensive Comparison of Multi-Sensor PBL Height Retrievals: Evaluation of their Equivalence and Sensitivity to Atmospheric Conditions
497069.authors: Haydee Salmun, CUNY, New York, NY; and J. R. Lewis Jr., M. Ganeshan, A. Molod, and S. P. Palm
497069.abstract: The NASA Incubation Study Team Report established that there is a critical need for a global planetary boundary layer (PBL) observing system with contributions from surface-based, suborbital, and space-based observations as well as modeling and data assimilation systems. The PBL height is an important element of any characterization of the temporal and spatial structure of the PBL and can be estimated from measurements. Because neither surface-based, suborbital and space-based platforms alone can provide the spatial density necessary for a global PBL observing system, there is a need for combined multi-instrument observations. The main focus of the present work is on measurements from networks of multiple surface-based instruments, specifically lidars, ceilometers and radar wind profilers that can be reliably used to retrieve PBL heights. Different instruments measure different aspects/characteristics of the atmosphere and different observational techniques capture varying characteristics of the PBL, which can result in significantly different estimates of PBL heights. Consolidating these estimates requires the ability to reconcile differences among PBL heights retrieved from different instruments, which can be done using data from sites with collocated instruments. The overall goal of our work is to understand these differences and investigate ways in which these measurements provide useful information while preserving each individual definition of PBL height. Our hypothesis is that the results of our case studies will allow for a discussion of the limitations and errors associated with the retrievals from each instrument and will aid in providing recommendations for exploiting the synergy among them. In this presentation, we discuss a case study from an intercomparison of PBL height retrievals from a ceilometer, a lidar and a radar wind profiler collocated at the Howard University Beltsville Campus in Maryland. The PBL height retrievals are derived using well established algorithms. Measurements for the year 2020 are used to perform a detailed analysis and develop an empirical scoring system based on the three metrics and a set of criteria used to determine agreement among the data from the three instruments. We characterize differences as a function of meteorological conditions, including cloud cover and surface fluxes. We use reanalyses data from Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2) and ancillary data from nearby meteorological stations to provide context in interpreting variability in the PBL height due to different conditions. We include a comparison of the surface-based retrievals to space-based PBL height retrievals from Cloud-Aerosol Lidar and Infrared Pathfinder Satellite Observations (CALIPSO), Ice, Cloud, and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) and Global Navigation Satellite System-Radio Occultation (GNSS-RO) to illustrate similarities and differences between these complementary platforms.

497070.title: GEMS2-Amethyst and Beryl: Initial Results and Future Directions for the GEMS Passive Microwave Constellation
497070.authors: Robert Belter, Weather Stream, Inc., Boulder, CO; and M. Hurowitz, M. Marques, A. Gasiewski, R. Delf, S. McKee, and R. Gonzalez
497070.abstract: The Global Environment Monitoring System (GEMS) is a planned constellation of passive microwave radiometers deployed on CubeSat platforms to enhance global atmospheric observing capabilities. GEMS is designed to augment the existing microwave observing network, with particular emphasis on improving temporal sampling and monitoring of high-impact weather systems in data-sparse regions. GEMS2-Amethyst (GEMS2A), the first satellite in the second-generation of GEMS satellites, features 24 channels spanning the 118 and 183 GHz bands implemented in a compact 2U radiometer. Its channel configuration supports temperature and humidity sounding, and precipitation observations. GEMS2-Beryl (GEMS2B), the second satellite in the GEMS2 series, is currently in production and set to launch in Q1 2028. Several improvements have been implemented on GEMS2B based on experience gained during the development and characterization of GEMS2A, including improvements in radiometric performance and stability. GEMS2A launched in March 2026 and has since undergone initial on-orbit commissioning and calibration/validation activities. Here, we present an overview of the GEMS2A mission, including radiometer design, pre-launch characterization, and initial on-orbit performance. Pre-launch radiometric characterization included NEdT measurements and main-beam antenna pattern characterization, providing an assessment of the expected radiometric performance of the instrument. Initial on-orbit results are presented through warm and cold target trending and observation-minus-background (O-B) characterization, providing an assessment of radiometric stability and initial calibration performance following launch. Finally, we discuss supporting infrastructure and development activities to transition GEMS towards sustained operational use, including a roadmap for improving instrument and monitoring performance built on the same low-cost instrument framework. These efforts support progression toward sustained multi-satellite constellation operations, with the goal of increasing temporal coverage and enhancing the impact of GEMS observations on data assimilation within operational NWP systems.

497071.title: Inside the Eye of Typhoon Dolphin: Navigating a High-Altitude Balloon Into a Tropical Cyclone
497071.authors: Tomer Burg, WindBorne Systems, Redwood Shores, CA; and J. Creus-Costa, L. J. Reames, E. Schoenfeld, J. Spisak, N. Mozyrsky, E. Kim, J. Lee, M. Ingalls, A. Sushko, J. Dean, and T. Hutchinson
497071.abstract: WindBorne Systems operates the world’s largest high-altitude weather balloon constellation. As of August 2026, about 600 global sounding balloons (GSBs) were aloft at any given time. While many GSBs often reside in the lower stratosphere, GSBs’ altitude can be controlled by venting gas to lower altitude or releasing ballast to gain altitude. This mechanism enables limited targeting of GSBs towards specific areas of interest by utilizing different steering flows across altitude bands to control their movement. As WindBorne’s constellation has exponentially grown, so have opportunities for targeted observations. In late July 2026, Typhoon Dolphin became one of the top accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) producers for West Pacific tropical cyclones on record, persisting as an intense tropical cyclone for many days. WindBorne attempted numerous interceptions of Typhoon Dolphin’s inner core, eventually succeeding in the early hours of 1 August as a GSB was navigated into the storm from the east in the lower stratosphere, performed a controlled descent into the eye, and collected multiple vertical profiles while performing three full cyclonic loops in the eye. The GSB may have descended as low as 8 meters above sea level before entering the eyewall where it recorded 1-minute sustained wind of 135 knots before transmissions were lost. This presentation will present an overview of the process of navigating a high-altitude balloon into the eye of a tropical cyclone, advantages and challenges of collecting data via this method, and present an analysis of the data collected. Given that this maneuver was coincident with the latter stage of an eyewall replacement cycle, the data may be of value for research of that stage of an eyewall replacement cycle, and is available to use upon request.

497073.title: Data Services at NSF NCAR: Origins, Evolution, and Future Directions
497073.authors: Matthew S. Mayernik, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and B. Dattore and D. C. Schuster
497073.abstract: NSF NCAR was founded in 1960 to provide facilities for the atmospheric science community that individual universities were not able to support on their own, including computing facilities for climate and weather modeling, and observational facilities for field-based scientific experiments. Data-related services have been a core component of these facilities since the founding of the center. This presentation will outline how these data services began in the 1960s, how they have evolved over the decades, and how they have led to current capabilities. The primary focus of this presentation is on services related to data archiving, storage, access, and preservation, but the discussion will connect to related developments over NSF NCAR’s history, including evolutions in computing, science priorities, and open science goals. The presentation will cover advancements and challenges related to data services in relation to the following key themes: 1) NSF NCAR’s compilation of broad data collections that enable research within NSF NCAR and across the university and broader research community, 2) NSF NCAR’s role in the development of specific high impact data sets, including the Southern Hemisphere Climatology dataset, the NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis dataset, and the Twentieth Century Reanalysis Project and International Surface Pressure Databank, among others; 3) NSF NCAR’s support over several decades for data management and access to observations collected during field programs, 4) NSF NCAR’s continued development and deployment of successive generations of data storage and access systems, 5) NSF NCAR’s contributions to broader community initiatives related to data management, open science, and data infrastructures, including participation and leadership in the development of policies and consensus reports within the US federal government and the American Meteorological Society.
