497075.title: Gravity Waves Within and Above a Subalpine Forest in Mountainous Terrain
497075.authors: Sean P. Burns, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado, Boulder, Boulder, CO; and D. Lenschow, J. Knowles, and P. D. Blanken
497075.abstract: The Niwot Ridge Subalpine Forest AmeriFlux tower (US-NR1) has a long history of measuring vertical profiles of scalars (air temperature, humidity, CO2), wind speed and direction, and turbulence between the primary flux-measurement level (21.5 m) and the ground. The US-NR1 site started measurements in Nov 1998 and is located in complex mountainous terrain approximately 8 km east of the Continental Divide below Niwot Ridge, Colorado. The topography at the site has a slope angle that ranges from 4-7 degrees with much steeper terrain within several miles of the tower. In order to enhance the vertical resolution of the wind profile, seven CSAT3 sonic anemometers were added to the US-NR1 tower in Fall of 2014 and operated for a full year. In this study, we use the extra sonic anemometer levels to examine the gravity waves that are generated during the downslope nocturnal drainage flow and how they change both above the canopy and within the subcanopy. The periods with gravity waves will be contrasted with nocturnal low-wind periods where gravity waves do not form. In general, the periods with gravity waves have smaller fluxes of heat, water vapor and CO2; the reasons behind this difference will be explored and discussed.

497076.title: Simulating Convective Transport by the Asian Summer Monsoon: The Impacts of Regional Grid Refinement on UTLS Anticyclone Composition
497076.authors: Warren Smith, NCAR, Frederick, CO; and M. C. Barth, M. L. Santee, W. Tang, B. Roozitalab, S. Tilmes, B. Gaubert, J. Zhang, S. Honomichl, R. P. Fernandez, A. Reynoso, and C. Roy
497076.abstract: The Asian Summer Monsoon (ASM) is a system where enhanced anthropogenic emissions interact with a seasonal enhancement in deep convection to modify the composition of the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS) on a global scale. A recent NASA-supported field campaign, the Asian Summer Monsoon Chemical and Climate Impact Project (ACCLIP 2022), obtained detailed airborne in situ chemical observations of the ASM convective outflow, which included record-setting pollutant mixing ratios in the UTLS. In-field chemical forecasts overall did not represent the most polluted mixing ratios observed, perhaps because of the importance of convective-scale processes to the representation of composition in this region. These convective-scale limitations present a challenge for Earth system models due to the typical horizontal grid spacing they are run with, necessitating parameterization of convection and many of its related processes. This presentation, currently supported by NASA’s ESSR Atmosphere Program, will highlight an application of an emerging multi-scale modeling capability to simulate convective transport by the ASM to the UTLS. Specifically, we run the Community Atmosphere Model with chemistry (CAM-Chem) using the dynamical core from the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) as the atmosphere component within the Community Earth System Model (CESM). This capability enables regional grid refinement to near-convective-resolving scales over a region of the user’s choosing. We will present the impacts of regional grid refinement on ASM UTLS composition by comparing simulations with globally uniform 60 km grid spacing and a 60-to-3 km grid spacing. The latter uses East Asia as the location of 3 km regional grid refinement, given its documented importance to the convective outflow sampled by research aircraft during the ACCLIP campaign. Simulations will be compared to one another and evaluated against ACCLIP airborne observations as well as remote-sensing observations from the NASA Aura Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS). This work will further explore sensitivities in the representation of ASM UTLS composition to the reanalysis product used for nudging (i.e., ERA5 versus MERRA-2) as well as the complexity of model chemistry, including short-lived halogen (SLH) chemistry which may influence the contribution of unreactive source gases and reactive product gases to the injection of ozone-depleting substances into the lower stratosphere through the ASM.

497077.title: The Influence of Hailstone Compressive Strength on Damage Potential to Asphalt Shingles
497077.authors: Teagen Marie Schultz, Central Michigan University, Muskegon, MI; and J. Sorber and I. M. Giammanco
497077.abstract: Hailstones can cause variable damage to life and property, which is hypothesized to be partially due to the wide range of compressive strength observed in natural hailstones. This study isolates compressive strength as a hailstone characteristic to investigate how damage to the built environment fluctuates as a function of hailstone strength. A series of experiments were conducted at the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety (IBHS) Research Center where laboratory-made hailstones were developed and tested to achieve selected percentiles of the natural compressive strength distribution. The hailstones at each strength threshold were used to impact asphalt roofing shingles, replicating realistic impacts on structures. Damage was objectively evaluated using high-precision scanning technology and scored based on three common asphalt shingle damage modes observed both in the laboratory and in the field. Post-event damage assessment has revealed that the damage modes needed for proper shingle performance evaluation are granule loss (individual and patch), deformation (dents and ridges of dents), and tears in the shingles. Results from the project confirmed the original hypothesis: overall damage of shingles increased as the compressive strength of hailstones increased. This result was consistent for most of the individual damage modes, although weaker hail produced greater granule loss upon independent evaluation. These findings indicate that compressive strength is an important factor in understanding hailstone damage potential to the built environment.

497079.title: Role of Surface Heterogeneities in Shallow Cumulus Growth and Development
497079.authors: Sreenath Paleri, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Boulder, CO
497079.abstract: Atmospheric turbulence organizes into coherent structures that span the entire ABL height. These circulations and their diurnal evolution play a significant role in modulating canopy-atmosphere exchanges. Over spatially heterogeneous domains, the surface flux heterogeneities can induce can induce quasi-stationary, low-frequency circulations that are super-imposed over ABL turbulence. Moreover, cumulus cloud cover creates shaded and non-shaded patches of the underlying surface, creating a differentially heated land surface and affecting surface energy budget partitioning between the shaded and non-shaded patches. This dynamic, heterogeneous radiative forcing can create a coupled plant stomatal response, affecting plant transpiration and localized moisture input into the mixed layer. Building off of our prior work on realistic large eddy simulations of forested domains under clear sky conditions, I will present some preliminary results of the coupled vegetation-atmosphere responses at the Department Of Energy-Atmospheric Radiation Measurement Bankhead National Forest facility under patchy shallow cumulus conditions. I will present results from large eddy simulations using the Parallelized Atmospheric LES Model (PALM) system, with a coupled land surface and radiation model, and boundary conditions informed by the NOAA HRRRv4 data, representative of field conditions at the BNF facility. I will discuss comparisons between diurnal model runs performed with a homogeneous and heterogeneous land surface configurations to elucidate the role of surface thermal and vegetation heterogeneity in shallow cumulus growth and development.

497080.title: CME Evolution Using 3D Semi-automatic Reconstructions: The Impact of New Viewpoints
497080.authors: Eleni Nikou, NRC Research Associate, US Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, DC; and R. Colaninno, P. Hess, and A. Thernisien
497080.abstract: Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are one of the major drivers of severe space weather and although there have been improvements in predicting their time of arrival (ToA) at Earth the errors are still around 10 hrs. Numerous instruments observe the Sun and remote sensing observations constitute the first line of defense for successful space weather predictions. The geometric characteristics of CMEs as obtained from forward modeling of white light observations are used as inputs to MHD, drag-based and empirical models to predict their ToA at Earth, but depending on the viewpoints available, uncertainties that affect the ToA are introduced. In this study we focus on the ways that the input parameters to prediction models are obtained and present the current status of semi-automatic 3D CME reconstructions showcasing events that were observed by different viewpoints including Solar Orbiter, Parker Solar Probe, CCOR-1, ASPIICS and PUNCH. We use a minimization-based fitting technique that uses the Graduated Cylindrical Shell (GCS) and spheroid shock model geometries and not only provides semi-automatic CME reconstructions that remove the observer bias but also estimates the fitting uncertainties of each of their geometric parameters. We track the CME ejecta and shock and discuss the advantages and drawbacks of using semi-automatic reconstructions while focusing on the evolution of individual geometric parameters and their uncertainties.

497081.title: Tracking Air Quality and Greenhouse Gases in Salt Lake City using Open-path Dual-comb Spectroscopy
497081.authors: Kevin Cossel, NIST, Boulder, CO; and R. Rhoades, J. F. Kasic III, N. Sweet, B. Washburn, and I. Coddington
497081.abstract: Air quality and greenhouse gas emissions in urban areas are often inter-related challenges. For example, methane emissions are frequently underrepresented in inventories and can also be co-emitted with volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and NOx. Thus, better understanding and mitigating methane emissions can provide a co-benefit for air quality. Formaldehyde (HCHO) is a hazardous air pollutant and plays a critical role in tropospheric O3 production. Because HCHO is formed from photochemical reactions of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), the HCHO/NO2 ratio can be used to provide information about the O3 formation regime of a region. Furthermore, photolysis of both primary and secondary HCHO leads to the formation of HO2 and can be a significant contribution to the total OH budget of an urban area. As part of the Utah Summer Ozone Study (USOS), we deployed an open-path dual-comb spectroscopy (DCS) system to the Utah Division of Air Quality (UDAQ) Tech Center near downtown Salt Lake City. The DCS system measured HCHO, CH4, C2H6, CO2, N2O, and H2O/HDO over open-air paths ranging from 300 m to 1 km and operated for ~2 months. We observe an HCHO diurnal profile that is indicative of a combination of primary and second sources. The DCS measurements, combined with co-located measurements of O3 and NO/NO2 from UDAQ, indicate that the O3 formation is predominantly VOC limited during the measurement period. We also observe that high-ozone days also have correspondingly high HCHO, potentially indicating a driver of O3 formation. We are working on applying a chemical box model to further guide the interpretation of these results. Finally, we also use the multispecies measurements to identify CH4 sources, primarily the nearby power plant.

497082.title: Peak-Aware Cross-Attention Graph Transformers for Efficient Storm-Surge Emulation
497082.authors: Zesheng Liu, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA; and D. Kwon, N. Lin, and M. Rahnemoonfar
497082.abstract: Storm surge is a major contributor to coastal flooding and poses substantial risks to coastal communities and infrastructure. High-fidelity hydrodynamic models, such as Advanced Circulation (ADCIRC), can resolve storm-surge dynamics over complex coastal domains, but their computational cost limits their use for applications requiring large numbers of simulations, including probabilistic hazard assessment, rapid scenario evaluation, and long-term climate risk analysis. Data-driven emulators offer a computationally efficient alternative, but accurately reproducing the temporal evolution of storm surge remains challenging. In particular, storm surge responds to spatially distributed wind and atmospheric pressure patterns with location- and event-dependent temporal lags, while the rare high-surge events most important for coastal risk are easily underrepresented by conventional regression objectives. These challenges become more pronounced when emulators are applied across heterogeneous atmospheric forcing products used for historical reconstruction and future climate projections. We develop PACT, a Peak-Aware Cross-Attention Graph Transformer for efficient station-level storm surge emulation from regional atmospheric forcing fields. PACT predicts hourly storm surge time series using a 12-hour history of wind and atmospheric pressure. Atmospheric forcing at each input tie is represented as a sparse spatial graph whose nodes contain geographic coordinates, wind speed, and spatially mean-centered pressure anomalies. A shared GraphSAGE encoder first learns spatial representations of the atmospheric forcing. Rather than compressing these spatial features through uniform pooling, PACT introduces a station-conditioned cross-attention mechanism. A learned query incorporating tide-gauge metadata attends to the atmospheric graph and adaptively assigns greater attention to spatial locations whose atmospheric conditions are most relevant to the surge response at each station and time. The resulting station-conditioned representations from the recent forcing history are processed by a temporal Transformer to capture interactions among atmospheric states and time-lagged relationships between atmospheric forcing and surge response. PACT then uses learned horizon queries to cross-attend to this shared temporal representation and generate hourly surge predictions from the emulation origin through the following five hours. This horizon-conditioned decoding allows predictions at different lead times to draw on different parts of the forcing history rather than relying on a single fixed temporal representation. To improve prediction of rare but high-impact surge conditions during extreme events, PACT further incorporates a peak-aware learning strategy. PACT uses separate base and peak prediction heads, with the base head modeling the overall surge evolution and the gated peak head learning additional corrections for elevated surge conditions. The training objective combines the overall prediction loss with an additional tail-focused loss on samples containing the largest surge values, increasing the learning signal associated with rare extremes. A horizon-wise slope regularizer also penalizes unrealistic changes between consecutive predictions, encouraging temporally coherent surge prediction over time. Together, these components are designed to improve extreme-event fidelity without sacrificing prediction accuracy across the full range of surge conditions. We evaluate PACT using storm surge time series generated by ADCIRC from NCEP/NCAR reanalysis and five CMIP6 global climate model forcing products. Historical NCEP experiments span four NOAA tide-gauge locations along the U.S. East Coast: the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel, Lewes, The Battery, and Boston. Using the same 12-hour forcing history, PACT reduces overall RMSE by approximately 34-38% relative to a spatiotemporal graph neural network baseline across these stations. Improvements are particularly pronounced for extreme conditions. For the upper 5% peak-focused evaluation at The Battery, peak RMSE decreases from 0.1022 m for the baseline to 0.0479 m for the peak-aware PACT configuration, accompanied by substantially reduced peak underprediction and worst-case errors. We further evaluate PACT using five CMIP6 forcing datasets, including historical simulations and future projections under SSP5-8.5. When trained on historical years and evaluated on unseen future-period simulations from the same climate model, PACT reduces RMSE by approximately 50% relative to the baseline across the five CMIP6 datasets on all four locations. Event-level analyses further show improved agreement with ADCIRC-simulated peak magnitudes, better preservation of the upper-tail peak distribution, and slower growth of prediction error as event severity increases. Cross-dataset experiments on surge level at the Battery reveal comparatively strong transfer among CMIP6 models but substantially larger errors when a model trained on NCEP reanalysis is transferred directly to CMIP6 forcing, highlighting an important reanalysis-to-climate-model distribution gap for learned coastal-hazard emulators. PACT also provides a substantial computational advantage for repeated hazard assessment. After training, it generates a complete November-March storm-surge time series for a station-year in approximately 3.4-3.6 seconds, compared with approximately 4.5-7 hours for the corresponding ADCIRC simulation. These results demonstrate that graph-based, station-conditioned, and peak-aware AI emulators can substantially accelerate storm-surge modeling while accurately representing both its temporal evolution and extreme surge behavior important for coastal flooding and hazard modeling.

497083.title: Exploring Variations of Trust and Protective Action Likelihood Across Early Warning Messaging Formats for Severe Weather Events: A Study into the Behavioural Attributes of the Barbadian Public.
497083.authors: Wynsty Jolene Boochoon, CIMH = Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology, Bridgetown, St James, Barbados; and K. A. Caesar, MS
497083.abstract: Advances in forecasting have led to improvements in the prediction of track and intensity of tropical storms and cyclones. One of the primary duties of a meteorological forecaster is the analysis, diagnosis, and forecast of a severe weather event. Of paramount importance for the forecaster is the dissemination of clear warnings that effectively communicate the risk to relevant stakeholders and the general public so that they are well informed to take appropriate protective/mitigating actions. The importance of Early Warning Messaging (EWM) and its mitigating effects relative to tropical storms and hurricanes are well understood, and the optimal structure and method of communication have been analyzed by previous research. However, there is a gap in the previous research for severe weather risk/warning communication in the Caribbean. Hence, this study seeks to investigate the attitudes of the Barbadian public towards various formats of a severe weather warning. The extent to which respondents trusted current weather forecasts and the specific format presented was evaluated. In addition, their understanding of the presented forecast and likelihood of them taking protective action were also measured, using a Likert Scale. Modelled after warnings created by regional National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMS) for their social media, these formats have three distinct categories: traditional forecast, impacts-based risk matrix warning (Risk Matrix), and a hybrid between a traditional forecast and risk matrix warning (Hybrid). Google Form surveys for each format were created in which respondents were presented with the same questions evaluating the variables above. Surveys were disseminated through social media and instant messaging (WhatsApp) group chats; 142 participants anonymously filled out the survey. Results illustrated that across formats, respondents' degree of trust did not vary; however, the likelihood of taking protective action did. Respondents presented with the traditional forecast were less likely to take protective action when compared to those presented with either a Risk Matrix warning or a Hybrid warning (both of which had comparable likelihood of taking protective actions). These findings continue to inform regional NMSs on ways in which they can tailor their warnings for better reception by the public.

497084.title: The Effects of Antecedent Soil Moisture on Hurricane Helene’s Inland Evolution and Precipitation
497084.authors: Vishal Juneja, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and H. Huang
497084.abstract: Hurricane Helene (2024) produced catastrophic impacts across the southern Appalachian region after a predecessor rain event (PRE) delivered substantial rainfall and markedly increased soil moisture before the storm’s arrival. Although antecedent wetness is widely recognized as an important control on runoff and flooding, it may also influence post-landfall tropical cyclone evolution through land–atmosphere interactions that modify surface fluxes, boundary-layer thermodynamics, storm decay, and subsequent precipitation. Helene therefore provides a valuable case study for examining how pre-storm land-surface conditions shape inland hurricane hazards. The current study addresses the following questions: 1) How did antecedent soil moisture influence Hurricane Helene’s inland evolution, including its track, intensity, and rate of post-landfall weakening? 2) How did the land–atmosphere feedbacks modify precipitation from Hurricane Helene? We use the Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled with the Noah-MP land-surface model to quantify the sensitivity of Helene’s post-landfall evolution and precipitation to antecedent soil moisture. A control simulation initialized with observed land-surface conditions is compared with sensitivity experiments in which soil moisture within the PRE-affected region is replaced by climatological conditions or systematically reduced, while atmospheric initial and lateral boundary conditions are held constant. The control simulation reasonably reproduces Helene’s observed track, intensity evolution, and precipitation characteristics. The sensitivity experiments are then evaluated relative to the control to quantify changes in storm track and intensity, as well as accumulated and extreme precipitation. This study provides a process-based assessment of how antecedent soil moisture can modify the evolution and compound hazards of a landfalling tropical cyclone. The case study also establishes a modeling framework that can be extended to landfalling tropical cyclones with contrasting antecedent soil moisture.

497086.title: LROSE-WAVEGUIDE: LROSE Workflow and AI Virtual Environment for Geoscience Understanding, Integration, Discovery, and Education
497086.authors: Ting-Yu Cha, NSF NCAR, Fort Collins, CO; and A. del Moral Méndez, Ph.D, J. C. DeHart, B. Javornik, and H. Hampapura
497086.abstract: Weather radars generate massive datasets during field campaigns, requiring robust software infrastructure and standardized formats for effective analysis. While open-source tools like the Lidar Radar Open Software Environment (LROSE) facilitate advanced processing, complex manual configurations and the need for massive local data transfers present significant barriers for researchers. To democratize access for the scientific community, we propose to build a unified cloud framework deployed on the NSF NCAR CIRRUS platform. First, to improve data discovery and accessibility, we have converted NCAR S-Pol data from the 2022 PRECIP field campaign into Zarr, an Analysis-Ready, Cloud-Optimized (ARCO) format and this dataset is available via NCAR's Geoscience Data Exchange (GDEX) platform. Such standards-compliant datasets advance FAIR principles by enabling data-proximate, high-throughput cloud analysis directly alongside the archived data. Second, to guide users through this ecosystem, we aim to develop the LROSE-assistant, a semi-autonomous multi-agent system powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). By synthesizing EOL’s Data Catalogue, scientific literature, trusted workflows from Jupyter notebooks, and LROSE parameter files, the assistant will translate high-level user queries into technical execution, automating data discovery and generating custom, executable processing workflows. Finally, these platform improvements are paired with targeted educational initiatives to broaden expertise and usage across the radar and adjacent scientific communities. Ultimately, these collective efforts will maximize the scientific value of field campaigns and reduce maintenance burdens on developers. This cohesive, end-to-end system seamlessly integrates data, software, and workflows, and is designed to scale across any scientific dataset or tool.

497087.title: Cirrus Cloud Thinning in Mountainous Regions using a High-Resolution Atmosphere Model
497087.authors: Samantha Turbeville, Sandia National Lab, Albuquerque, NM; and B. R. Hillman
497087.abstract: We present a multi-scale modelling study that quantifies how cirrus clouds generated by orographic gravity waves respond to changes from horizontal resolution, ice nucleation, and ice-nucleating particle (INP) abundance. Using the E3SM atmosphere model with a regionally refined mesh that spans horizontal resolutions from 13 km (with parameterized convection) down to 800 m (with explicitly resolved convection and gravity waves), we simulate cirrus formation downstream of California’s Sierra Nevada mountain range. We investigate the role of gravity waves, resolution, and ice nucleation on updraft speeds, ice microphysical properties, and cloud radiative effects. Results emphasize scale-dependent dynamical and microphysical responses with implications for understanding cirrus formation mechanisms. Resolving dynamical forcing from gravity wave perturbations and microphysical changes from ice nucleation parameterizations reveals the impact on cirrus cloud properties and lifetime for evaluating the feasibility of orographic cirrus targeted geo-engineering such via cirrus cloud thinning. SNL is managed and operated by NTESS under DOE NNSA contract DE-NA0003525

497089.title: A Regional Assessment of Marine Heatwave Drivers along the U.S. Coastal Ocean
497089.authors: Effy B John, PNNL, Seattle, WA; and K. Balaguru, L. R. Leung, J. Li, W. Zhou, R. Hetland, Y. Qian, and T. Chakraborty
497089.abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasing in frequency, duration, and intensity, posing growing risks to marine ecosystems and coastal communities worldwide. Although the physical drivers of MHWs vary among different ocean basins, their relative importance along the diverse U.S. coastline remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the dominant mechanisms governing coastal MHW development along the U.S. West, Gulf, and East Coasts using ocean and atmospheric reanalysis data, and a mixed-layer heat budget framework. Individual MHWs are classified according to the dominant contribution of air-sea fluxes, oceanic dynamics, or their combined influence. Distinct regional contrasts emerge in the mechanisms responsible for MHW development. Along the West Coast, oceanic processes associated with coastal upwelling variability and mesoscale circulation dominate most events. In contrast, MHWs along the Gulf and East Coasts are either dominated by oceanic processes or result from mixed forcings, indicating that interactions between ocean circulation and atmospheric heat flux anomalies are more important than either mechanism alone. Purely atmosphere-driven events are comparatively less frequent in these regions. These findings demonstrate that regional oceanographic processes strongly modulate the development of coastal MHWs and underscore the need for region-specific prediction frameworks to improve forecasts of marine thermal extremes and their impacts.

497094.title: Distinct Diurnal Controls on Rainfall and Intensification in Post-Landfall Tropical Storm Erin (2007)
497094.authors: Colin Welty, School of Meteorology, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and J. H. Ruppert Jr.
497094.abstract: The diurnal cycle in tropical cyclones (TCs) is an emerging source of predictability for TC intensification and associated hazards, with a noted nocturnal preference for convection in the tropics. However, the diurnal cycle in post-landfall TCs is significantly less studied, despite its implications for the timing and behavior of associated impacts, particularly in rare cases of overland re-intensification when poorly forecast nocturnal hazards occur. A noteworthy example of an overland re-intensification case is Tropical Storm (TS) Erin in 2007, which reached its maximum intensity over Oklahoma. The behavior of this particular case has been attributed to anomalously wet antecedent rainfall in the summer of 2007, as well as favorable synoptic conditions and interactions with the Nocturnal Great Plains Low Level Jet (NLLJ). However, TS Erin provides an unexplored testbed for the diurnal cycle, given observational analysis shows that Erin intensified and produced its most intense rainfall nocturnally. Using high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulations from Welty et al. (2026, in review), we separate radiative and surface-flux diurnal cycles to analyze the timing of Erin’s nocturnal evolution. A sensitivity test first shifts the solar diurnal cycle from the Control simulation by 12 h to directly test whether the nocturnal timing is coincidental. From there, additional sensitivity tests impose surface fluxes from the Control simulation back onto the shifted diurnal cycle, thereby decoupling the radiative diurnal cycle from the imposed surface-flux diurnal cycle and its associated nocturnal boundary-layer evolution. These experiments reveal that shifting the radiative cycle produces a corresponding shift in rainfall timing, demonstrating a nocturnal preference for rainfall-rate maxima that shifts independently of NLLJ timing, which is a novel finding. However, vortex intensification more closely follows the nocturnal surface-flux phase, highlighting that the timing of maximum rainfall rate and vortex intensification can respond to separate processes within the diurnal cycle. Our experiments show that the location of convective activity inside the radius of maximum winds (RMW) is important for determining if an increase in rainfall can spin up vorticity. In the Imposed-flux experiment, two distinct rainfall peaks emerge. The first, occurring during the nocturnal radiative phase, is stronger but leads to no vortex intensification. The second, occurring during the nocturnal boundary-layer phase, is weaker but leads to vortex intensification as low-level convergence and ascent become organized within the RMW. Thus, rainfall maxima within the same storm can have substantially different intensification outcomes depending on the location of convective organization, which is favored by nocturnal boundary-layer processes. These results importantly demonstrate that different components of the diurnal cycle play distinct roles in Erin’s post-landfall evolution. The nocturnal phase of the radiative diurnal cycle is strongly associated with when rainfall-rate maxima occur, while the nocturnal boundary-layer response helps determine whether that convection becomes organized within the inner core and contributes to vortex intensification. These results also have broad implications for the predictability of inland hazards associated with post-landfall TCs, illustrating a need to distinguish between processes that dictate convective timing and processes that determine the dynamical effectiveness of that convection.

497095.title: Operational Impacts of the Tropical Transition of Extratropical Cyclones
497095.authors: Michael J. Folmer, NWS, College Park, MD; and O. M. Griffith, M. Sarlls, J. P. Cangialosi, J. Halverson, S. Delgado, C. L. Smith, and K. E. Ryan
497095.abstract: Numerous peer-reviewed studies discuss the evolution of tropical cyclones to extratropical cyclones and the associated hazards (Evans et al. 2017, Jones et al. 2003, Anwender et al. 2008, etc.). However, there is limited research published on the inverse, extratropical to tropical transition (Davis and Bosart 2004, Bentley et al. 2017, etc.). The last decade of Atlantic hurricane seasons has seen an increase of weaker, subtropical or tropical cyclones that originate from extratropical source regions (e.g. upper-level lows, frontal boundaries, complex interactions among multiple features including African easterly waves, etc.) and this has led to inconsistent naming assigned to some of these systems. For example, some of these systems have been labelled as tropical cyclones, while others receive subtropical designation or even no designation at all. (Subtropical Storm #1 (2023), Danielle (2023), Rebekah (2019), etc.). In addition, genesis forecasts for many of these systems have generally been less accurate and have provided shorter forecast lead times than those for more classical tropical cyclone formation. The National Weather Service (NWS) Ocean and Tsunami Center (OTC) and National Hurricane Center (NHC) are taking a closer look at the increased occurrence of these tropical transitions and whether a more concrete operational criteria is needed to ensure consistency and preserve the scientific integrity of the standard tropical naming convention. At the same time, it is critical that OTC and NHC serve the marine community by identifying these systems for the unique hazards (surface winds greater than 35 kt in any quadrant, convective alignment with the center, etc.) that differentiate these storms from the larger extratropical cyclones that mariners experience more often. This presentation will document some of the recent cases of extratropical to tropical transition and focus on the new tools offered by GOES-R, Cyclone Phase Space (Hart 2003), and scatterometer winds, among more traditional observations such as aircraft measurements and significant wind radii when available.. A key operational goal of this work is to build more confidence and consistency in the decision to transition an extratropical cyclone to a named subtropical or tropical cyclone through the more concrete criteria that, in turn, will lead to improved communication and understanding of these transitions for the safety of life at sea.

497099.title: On Vertical Structure, Synoptic Evolution, and ERA5 Representations of Appalachian Cold-Air Damming with Varying Southward Extents
497099.authors: Daniel Burow, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL
497099.abstract: Cold-air damming (CAD) occurs in the Appalachian region when a shallow, stable air mass becomes entrenched near the surface along the eastern slopes of the mountain range. During the cold season, CAD can contribute to societally disruptive weather, including snow, freezing rain, and aviation icing conditions. Previous research has shown that Appalachian CAD events vary considerably in their southward extent. Here, we use the Spatial Synoptic Classification (SSC) to distinguish between CAD events that reach the Atlanta area (“southward-extended”) and those that remain confined farther north and east (“northern-confined”). We contrast the vertical structure and synoptic evolution of these two event classes and evaluate their representation in ERA5 against radiosonde observations from Roanoke/Blacksburg, VA (RNK); Greensboro, NC (GSO); and Atlanta/Peachtree City, GA (FFC). Results from this study will improve understanding of the conditions associated with CAD southward extent while also better defining the utility of ERA5 for CAD-focused research.

497100.title: Comparisons of Warm- Versus Cool-Season Derecho-Producing QLCSs: Cold Pool Characteristics, Synoptic-Scale Forcing, and Synoptic-Scale Contributions to Severe Wind Production
497100.authors: Garrett Travis Statum, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL; and R. J. Trapp, F. T. Lombardo, and K. J. Killion
497100.abstract: The impacts-based definition of derechos, which are a type of long-duration and long-track QLCSs, stipulates that derechos consistently produce severe wind gusts (>58 mph or 25.7 meters per second) and significant severe wind gusts (>74 mph or 33.1 meters per second) over a trajectory of at least 400 km. A new avenue of research is concerned with the physical mechanisms by which derechos produce severe-magnitude surface (10-meter) and near-surface (80-meter) winds. These mechanisms include mesovortices (MVs), downbursts (DBs), and rear-inflow jet (RIJ). Recent WRF-simulated derecho events by Killion et al. (in review) revealed the RIJ and MV- particularly when combined- are the primary mechanisms responsible for severe near-surface wind production in derechos. These findings challenge previous suppositions that derecho events are characterized by a series of downbursts, which has major implications on wind engineering models that only account for downbursts when modeling wind loading on structures. Following these recent findings, this study is concerned with the synoptic, or large-scale, flow contribution to severe wind-producing mechanisms in derechos. Here, we follow Killion et al’s study and employ WRF simulations of derecho events from 2020-2024, with representative events that occurred in the cool season (Oct-Feb), spring season (Mar-May), and warm season (Jun-Sep), and 1-km resolution nests with 1-minute output frequency are used for analysis. Synoptic flow contributions to each event are analyzed using WRF outputs. Pre-convective (or environmental) 500 hPa and 850 hPa wind vectors are derived from the WRF outputs, and relative speeds of the derecho versus the synoptic-scale wind flow are determined; for a sanity check, the WRF-derived derecho speed versus synoptic flow is compared to observations using radar and hourly Rapid Refresh (RAP) analysis. Most importantly, a breakdown of internally-generated convective winds versus contributions to the derecho from the large-scale flow is provided for each case. The study investigates how large-scale flow is mechanically manifested in near-surface severe winds, and how this impacts DBs, MVs, and RIJ in derechos, particularly in the cool season where large-scale flow is stronger. Additionally, the study employs a combination of WRF simulations, RAP analyses, and surface observations to explore whether non-warm season derecho events are partially driven by their own convective cold pools. The objectives of this study are 1) explore synoptic contributions to severe wind-producing mechanisms in derechos, 2) investigate whether non-warm season derecho events are partially cold pool-driven, and 3) compare similarities and differences for each case, especially pertaining to the season and synoptic patterns in which they occur. Based on existing literature, our hypothesis is that contribution from the synoptic flow to near-surface wind gusts in cool season events is notable, although the dominant wind mechanisms responsible for severe gusts are similar, regardless of seasonality. We additionally hypothesize, however, that cool season events are at least partially cold pool-driven, with weaker cold pool influence in events closest to a synoptic cold front.

497101.title: Impacts of GPS-Precipitable Water Vapor, MPD Absolute Humidity, and Conventional Wind Observations on North American Monsoon Convective Forecasts: An OSSE Study of Background Moisture Sensitivity
497101.authors: Samkeyat Shohan, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and C. Castro, J. Kay, S. E. Koch, A. F. Arellano Jr., C. B. Risanto, T. M. Weckwerth, and J. O. Pinto, Phd
497101.abstract: The North American Monsoon (NAM) delivers nearly half of annual precipitation to the arid southwestern United States, yet short term forecasts of monsoon convection remain limited by inadequate initialization of lower tropospheric moisture and wind fields over complex terrain. This study uses an Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE), built on the framework of Shohan et al. (2025), to quantify the relative and combined impacts of GPS derived precipitable water vapor (GPS PWV), Micropulse Differential Absorption Lidar absolute humidity (MPD AH) profiles, and conventional surface and rawinsonde wind observations on convection permitting analyses and forecasts of a representative NAM event over Arizona. An Ensemble Kalman Filter is used to assimilate observations from a 30 equally distanced station network co-located with GPS and MPD sites, augmented by conventional surface and wind profile data. Six observing configurations, namely GPS only, GPS+CONV, MPD only, MPD+CONV, GPS+MPD+CONV, and CONV alone, are evaluated against two contrasting background states, a dry control run and a control run with slightly enhanced moisture, yielding a twelve member experiment matrix designed to isolate how background moisture error conditions the benefit of each observation type. Forecasts are verified against a high resolution Nature Run to assess impacts on moisture, wind, and precipitation skill, with particular attention to convective initiation timing and location and the persistence or correction of background moisture drift over the forecast period. Results are expected to clarify the complementary roles of column integrated versus vertically resolved moisture observations, and of thermodynamic versus kinematic constraints, in improving NAM convective forecasts, and to inform strategies for integrating novel humidity profiling networks with conventional observing systems in operational data assimilation

497102.title: Virtual Zarr Stores from Theory to Production
497102.authors: Thomas Nicholas, Earthmover PBC, New York, NY
497102.abstract: Decades of Earth science data sit in archival formats (NetCDF, HDF5, GRIB, GeoTIFF, FITS) that were never designed for high-latency object storage, so data providers face a bad choice: force users suffer slow, download-oriented access to legacy files, or pay to rewrite petabytes into cloud-optimized formats, duplicating storage and severing provenance from the archival copy. Virtual Zarr stores offer a third option: leave the bytes where they are and create “virtual references” to them, thereby effectively “cloud-optimizing” archival data in-place. This idea is powerful, since virtual chunks are a core primitive for cloud-native data systems. The ability of object storage to be accessible from anywhere, plus the high cost of moving, renaming, or reformatting objects, encourage referring to data where it already resides. Once virtualized, users can take full advantage of the enormous bandwidth of cloud object storage to stream data into their applications. This technology now underpins cloud migration initiatives across NASA, NOAA, and NSF NCAR, so we give an overview of the landscape of virtual store adoption across industry, non-profits, academia, and the public sector. Informed by our unique perspective as developers of the key open-source tools for creating virtual stores (VirtualiZarr and Icechunk) we detail successes and challenges of the technology, and give our perspective on where the field needs to go next. We also describe various advanced use cases and considerations for virtual chunks within the Earthmover Arraylake platform, including: Petabyte-scale Virtual Stores (e.g GOES-16 and NOAA HRRR) Fine-grained data sharing via filtered subscriptions on the Earthmover Marketplace Rolling embargoes of low-latency data AI-assisted automatic low-cost data ingestion Important security considerations relevant to any user of virtual chunks in a production setting.

497103.title: A Large Eddy Simulation Study of the Spplicability of Taylor’s Frozen Turbulence Hypothesis in the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
497103.authors: Subharthi Chowdhuri, Natural Resources Institute Finland, Helsinki, 18, Finland; and S. Paleri
497103.abstract: Taylor’s frozen turbulence hypothesis (TFTH) posits all turbulent eddies are advected by the mean wind, without changes in their spatial characteristics. In this framework turbulence is ‘frozen’ and eddies of all scales are advected similarly by the mean flow. This hypothesis allows one to use fast response sensors to measure turbulence in the temporal domain at higher frequencies and translate them to infer the spatial statistics. This assumption and approach is critical in micrometeorology, where the surface turbulent fluxes are measured using stationary, tower-mounted, fast-response sensors. To address the validity of TFTH, Chowdhuri et al. (under review) calculated the convective velocities of turbulent eddies using Distributed Temperature Sensing measurements in a heterogeneous forest clear-cut. By using observations at a single height, their results demonstrated that random convective effects of turbulent coherent structures dominate in buoyancy-dominated high-Reynolds number atmospheric flows, and can explain the observed deviation of temporal statistics from what is inferred solely from TFTH. Following through, we investigate the applicability of an elliptical model (G. He et al., 2017) to explicitly account for the effects of random sweeps due to turbulent coherent structures on turbulent statistics, in idealized large eddy simulations of the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) using the PALM model system. We calculate the velocity and temperature sweeping speeds and investigate their dependence with dynamic stabilities (strongly unstable to near-neutral), and heights within the ABL. These results are used to examine the conversion of turbulence (co) spectra between temporal and spatial domains.

497104.title: Beyond the Trusted Messenger: Differentiated Trust in Integrated Warning Partnerships
497104.authors: Justin Kosec, Howard University, Washington, DC
497104.abstract: Weather warnings rarely travel directly from a professional forecast to a layperson’s immediate, trusting response. Rather, warnings move through institutional networks that may include emergency managers, telecommunications infrastructure, schools, faith communities, media organizations, community leaders, and families. Increasing recognition of these “unconventional partners” within the Integrated Warning Team reflects an important shift toward understanding weather response as both a meteorological and a social process. Yet integrating organizations into a warning network raises a problem that has received comparatively little attention: to what degree do institutions within the same network occupy different relationships of trust with the communities they serve, and how should those differences shape the design of warning partnerships? A longstanding tradition has conceptualized trust primarily as a possession or disposition of the individual: a person holds some quantity of trust and may choose whether to extend it to another actor. More recent scholarship on relational and institutional trust complicates this account. This paper draws together interdisciplinary work on relational and organizational trust (Mayer & Davis; Rousseau et al.; Schoorman et al.), political and institutional trust (Levi & Stoker), social learning and racialized trust (Smith; Evangelist), risk perception (Siegrist & Cvetkovich), and hierarchy and institutional harm (Williams; Benjamin). Across these traditions, trust emerges not as a generalized resource individuals simply possess in greater or lesser quantities, but as an eminently contextual quality of relationships. Trust develops over time, operates within particular domains, and may depend upon distinct assessments of competence, benevolence, integrity, reliability, or shared interest. It can also function as a heuristic under conditions of uncertainty: when individuals lack sufficient knowledge or resources to independently evaluate a complex risk, they may rely upon people or institutions they judge capable of helping them navigate it. Institutional trust introduces additional problems of scale and power. Relationships between individuals and institutions are frequently asymmetrical; institutions may expose individuals to vulnerability whether or not those individuals trust them. Institutions also persist across generations, allowing histories of competence, care, neglect, discrimination, or exploitation to become embedded within a community’s ecology of trust. Trust in a church, school, municipal government, university, or scientific agency therefore cannot be assumed to operate according to the same terms—or to transfer automatically from one institutional object to another. Methodologically, the paper proceeds in three stages. First, it conducts a critical integrative review of interdisciplinary trust scholarship to identify recurring dimensions of institutional trust. Second, these dimensions are systematized into a descriptive analytic framework distinguishing six features: the object of trust, its domain, its basis, its temporal and institutional history, its scale, and its directionality across relationships. Third, the framework is applied through structured qualitative analysis of publicly documented school–church–municipal partnership models and related community-weather partnerships. The inquiry is also sensitized by the author’s professional engagement with faith-based organizations; these experiences inform the questions brought to the analysis but are not treated as interview, ethnographic, or other systematically collected human-subject data. Beyond simply providing more descriptive language around trust, this framework makes visible a problem obscured by the broad category of the “trusted messenger.” A community may trust a faith institution because of durable relationships and perceived benevolence, a school because of repeated service and familiarity, a weather agency because of technical competence, and a municipal government only within particular domains or through more conditional or transactional relationships. Organizational integration, therefore, does not necessarily produce integrated trust. Differentiating these institutional relationships offers practical guidance for Integrated Warning Teams seeking to evaluate existing partnerships or develop new ones. Strategies that enlist trusted community institutions to transmit official warnings may implicitly assume that credibility can travel across organizations. Yet trust vested in one institution may not transfer to the institution originating a warning or to the partnership as a whole. Individuals may also act upon institutional recommendations while continuing to distrust the institution making them; compliance should not therefore be treated as evidence of trust. The paper ultimately proposes a differentiated institutional-trust framework for incorporating unconventional partners into Integrated Warning Teams. Rather than asking only whether a prospective partner is trusted, warning systems should ask who trusts that institution, for what, on what basis, through what history, and within what limits. Such scalar and relational sensitivity can help distinguish organizational partnership from trust itself and support warning networks designed not merely to secure public compliance, but to cultivate durable cooperation around weather risk.

497107.title: The Impact of Deep Convection on Boundary-Layer Concentrations of CO2 Above the Amazon Rainforest
497107.authors: Otavio C. Acevedo, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and J. Fuentes and C. Q. Dias Jr.
497107.abstract: Deep convection events are a common occurrence at the Amazon rainforest. Here, we address their impact on the atmospheric boundary-layer (ABL) concentrations of carbon dioxide, based on 9 years of data from the Amazon Tall Tower Observatory (ATTO). Using a methodology based on the identification of sharp temperature drops related to the convection-associated cold pools, along with the analysis of radar images for the nearby city of Manaus, 1452 events have been identified from 2015 to 2023. The passage of a convection event promotes direct coupling between the surface and the upper atmosphere, fully mixing the air over a layer much deeper than the ABL for a brief moment, of tens of minutes. The consequence is that nocturnal events effectively export surface-respired CO2 to the free atmosphere, while in diurnal events, the opposite occurs: free-atmosphere CO2 entrains the ABL.This is a relevant process because these concentrations are routinely used as input in top-down estimates of CO2 flux using inverse models. In this case, the perturbations caused by the convective events may be misinterpreted by the models as additional CO2 sources or sinks, depending whether it was a diurnal or nocturnal event. We show that this is an effective process, which causes appreciable perturbations in the ABL CO2 concentrations. The average 24-h CO2 variation at ATTO in the days when there is a convective event depends largely on the time of the event: nocturnal events consistently cause CO2 depletion, while diurnal events produce CO2 replenishment. The negative CO2 perturbation caused by nocturnal events is generally larger in magnitude than the positive perturbation in diurnal events. On the other hand, at ATTO diurnal events occur more frequently than diurnal ones, and the consequence is that over the 9 years, the two effects nearly balance out and the average CO2 perturbation caused by the 1452 events is very close to zero. On the other hand, there is interannual variability, with years when the net effect is positive and others when it is negative. More importantly, there is large seasonality in the occurrences of nocturnal and diurnal events. Nocturnal events at ATTO are relatively more common in the dry than in the wet season. It causes a seasonal redistribution of ABL CO2 by convection: in the wet season the prevalence of diurnal events cause a net import of free-atmosphere CO2 into the ABL, while in the dry season, the larger number of nocturnal events produce CO2 export from the ABL to the free-atmosphere. This result means that there is likely a seasonal bias caused by convection in the top-down estimates of CO2 fluxes in the ATTO region. In other areas of the Amazon Basin, however, it is possible that different distributions of diurnal and nocturnal events are such that convection effectively produces a year-round export or a year-round import of CO2 in the ABL.

497108.title: Where Weather Information Matters: Agricultural Decision-Making in Observation-Sparse South Carolina Counties
497108.authors: Brett William Robertson, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC; and J. Salinas, M. Habets, S. L. Cutter, A. L. Hiscox, G. Carbone, K. Dow, G. Waddington, M. Nordberg, and A. Rainwater
497108.abstract: Agricultural decisions are weather-sensitive, yet there is limited evidence about where weather information enters producer decision-making, especially in the rural Southeast. Allendale, Bamberg, Barnwell, and Hampton are rural counties in a region of South Carolina’s Coastal Plain where agriculture and forestry form the economic base. Each is a federally designated persistent poverty county within the South Carolina Promise Zone. The state has no statewide mesonet, and surface observations come primarily from the NWS Cooperative Observer Program, supplemented by automated airport stations and CoCoRaHS, with these counties divided across two NWS Forecast Offices. These networks characterize regional conditions well. What producers describe missing is field-scale observation of heat, rainfall, and soil conditions where decisions are made. This landscape study uses survey data from the agricultural sector, defined to include farming, livestock, forestry, wildlife management, and allied services, recruited through community partners in these four counties. The survey was administered through Qualtrics from May to July 2026. Thirty-four respondents were retained based on survey completeness, with item-level N ranging from 29 to 34. Owners and operators account for 44.1% of respondents and family co-owners or partners for 35.3%. Forestry and timber was the most commonly selected sector, reported by 47.1% of respondents, followed by row crops at 38.2% and specialty crops at 32.4%. Respondents could select more than one sector to describe their primary agricultural activities, and the average number of selections was 1.8. Perceived environmental change is near universal and hazard-specific. No respondent selected “I have not noticed significant changes” over the past 10 years. More frequent or more severe drought was reported by 67.6%, hotter summers by 47.1%, more common flooding or heavy rain by 38.2%, and a shifted growing season by 35.3%. Half (50.0%) reported that weather is more unpredictable and harder to plan around. These responses span frequency, severity, and timing. Weather ranks high among decision factors while reported adaptive capacity trails reported exposure. Across 29 rated influences on farming decisions, weather and climate variability ranked third (M = 3.83, SD = 1.04), behind market demand and prices (M = 4.03) and input costs (M = 3.90); timing of farming activities ranked eighth (M = 3.34). No respondent disagreed that weather and climate changes will affect how they operate in the years ahead (M = 4.03, SD = 0.80), while the distribution shifts downward on whether their operation has the resources and knowledge to adapt (M = 3.21, SD = 0.98), with 23.5% disagreeing. The information and delivery layer is thin at the point of decision. Only 23.5% agreed that useful local heat and rainfall data exist for where they farm, and no respondent strongly agreed (M = 2.82, SD = 0.90). Good cell phone coverage in fields and production areas ranked near the bottom of the infrastructure battery (M = 2.47), below broadband (M = 3.06) and RTK or satellite GPS (M = 3.12), constraining any channel that depends on connectivity in the field. Information from Cooperative Extension, USDA, and other agencies ranked 19th of 29 decision influences (M = 2.79), digital and AI tools 24th (M = 2.55), and access to crop insurance or disaster relief 28th (M = 2.28). Demand is present nonetheless: 85.3% would participate in a local in-person workshop, while only 17.6% agreed that technical support in their county meets their needs. One complication deserves emphasis. Asked which investments would most improve long-term viability, only 14.7% selected better tools to handle weather and climate variability, against 64.7% selecting better market prices or market access. Producers report that weather has become harder to plan around and that local data are thin, while ranking weather tools well below market conditions. That gap between exposure and expressed demand is the puzzle we bring to this AMS audience. These findings locate a specific failure point. Producers report widespread environmental change and treat weather as a first-order decision factor. Yet the observations available to them are once-daily volunteer readings and automated instruments sited at airports for aviation, and the institutional channels that carry weather information rank near the bottom of what shapes their decisions. This study measured decision context rather than use of named forecast products, which limits what can be said about any single information source. Within that scope, the finding is structural: in an observation-sparse region, the underlying observations and the delivery channels are constrained together. The more tractable intervention may be investment in local observation paired with the in-person and peer channels that agricultural producers say they would actually use.

497109.title: Investigation of the Non-Gaussian Doppler Spectra Observed By the Coherent Doppler Lidar at Low Elevation Angle
497109.authors: Hsiu-Wei Hsu, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and T. Y. Yu, D. J. Bodine, J. G. Gebauer, R. M. Frost, J. W. Thiesing, J. I. Furumoto, and K. Higashi
497109.abstract: The Doppler spectrum measured by a coherent Doppler lidar (CDL) represents the distribution of scatterers’ radial velocities within the lidar volume and is commonly assumed to exhibit Gaussian shape. In past studies, it has been reported that the deviation from the Gaussian-shape Doppler spectra can occur at higher elevation angles, where aerosol and hydrometeor exhibit distinctly different radial velocities (or terminal velocities). In this study, non-Gaussian Doppler spectra were observed during low-elevation scanning in a pre-frontal environment on 14 March 2025 at Norman, OK, exhibiting spectral features such as a dual-peak and flat-top. To better understand the formation of these non-Gaussian Doppler spectra, an enhanced CDL simulator, capable of complex velocity distributions within the lidar volume, was developed. The input wind fields are obtained from idealized analytical wind flow and/or numerical models. The preliminary results suggest that the horizontal wind shear and the relative orientation between the lidar beam and the wind shear play important roles in producing dual-peak and flat-top Doppler spectra. This study aims to assess their potential impact on radial velocity retrievals and derived products, including vertical vorticity estimates. The results are expected to improve the interpretation of CDL measurements in environments with strong horizontal wind shear.

497110.title: Is It the Resolution or the Convection Scheme? Disentangling Controls on the Simulated Amazonian Water Cycle in Variable-Resolution CESM
497110.abstract: The Amazon recycles a substantial fraction of its own rainfall, and the strength of that coupling between land surface and precipitation governs wet-season maintenance and the basin's sensitivity to land-cover change. Published estimates of the Amazonian water cycle and its response to deforestation differ substantially, and the studies behind them differ simultaneously in horizontal resolution and in whether convection is parameterized. Coarse global models resolve no mesoscale circulation and parameterize convection; storm-resolving models do the opposite. When their water budgets disagree, the cause cannot be attributed to either factor. We report a factorial experiment that separates these controls within a single modeling framework. Using variable-resolution CESM with the mesh refined over South America inside a global domain, we simulate at nominal refinements of 100, 50, 25, 12, and 6 km, and repeat each with the deep convection parameterization active and disabled. Model version, physics package, vertical grid, forcing, and large-scale state are held fixed across all members, so differences are attributable to resolution, convective treatment, or their interaction. Preliminary results suggest rainfall losses may far exceed coarse-resolution estimates, offering new insights into the hydrological cycle in the current and next-generation Earth system models.

497114.title: Hydrogeology-Informed Clustering and Satellite Hydrologic Observations to Characterize Groundwater Response Regimes and Irrigation Demand for Regional Water Security
497114.authors: Rimsha Hasan, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and F. Munoz-Arriola, J. Westrop, and K. MacNeill
497114.abstract: Groundwater is a common-pool resource that sustains irrigated agriculture, ecosystems, and human livelihoods. However, proactive management remains challenging because groundwater responses to climate and irrigation are spatially heterogeneous, withdrawals are largely unmeasured, and monitoring networks provide incomplete spatial coverage. These limitations constrain the ability to anticipate where declines may intensify and when management thresholds may be approached, potentially delaying corrective actions until significant aquifer depletion has already occurred. This study develops a hydrogeology-informed machine learning framework that classifies groundwater response into physically coherent regimes and represents irrigation-driven stress from satellite observations, laying the physical foundation needed to extend groundwater security and assessment for water resource management. We hypothesize that groundwater response reflects interactions among hydrogeologic storage, climatic variability, and irrigation-driven water demand, and that partitioning the aquifer into physically coherent response regimes improves forecasting relative to treating it as homogeneous. To test this, we (1) classify wells into hydrogeologic response regimes using static aquifer and geologic attributes, (2) represent unmetered irrigation demand from satellite observations, providing the physical structure for spatially grounded groundwater assessment. We selected the Central Platte Natural Resources District (CPNRD) in Central Nebraska as a focused testbed, where groundwater management is organized into 24 Groundwater Management Areas (GWMAs) governed by Maximum Acceptable Decline (MAD) thresholds and phased management actions. Annual groundwater observations from 277 wells (2000-2024) were classified into ‘hydrogeologic response regimes’ based on saturated thickness, specific yield, elevation, topographic position index, surface-water connectivity (represented by distance to the Platte River), and categorical geologic characteristics (bedrock formation and topographic region). Five clustering approaches - k-means, k-prototypes, Ward hierarchical clustering, Gaussian mixture models (GMM), and self-organizing maps (SOM) - were compared using silhouette scores and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), with bootstrap resampling assessing partition stability. K-prototypes was selected as the primary method, as it handles both continuous and categorical attributes within a single distance formulation. Irrigation demand was represented by net irrigation (NETIRR), computed as growing-season evapotranspiration (ET) minus effective precipitation (Peff), with Peff fraction derived by runoff partitioning from streamgage discharge. NETIRR was computed using both satellite-observed ET (OpenET) and a modeled water-balance product (TerraClimate). The results identify three physically distinct hydrogeologic regimes, suggesting that groundwater response is not homogeneous. The regimes differ primarily in saturated thickness, elevation, and proximity to surface water: Regime 1 is a shallow, near-stream setting with a mean saturated thickness of 51 m, an elevation of 562 m, and a distance to the stream of 7.2 km; Regime 2 is an intermediate setting with a saturated thickness of 58 m, an elevation of 581 m, and a distance to the stream of 10.0 km; and Regime 3 is a substantially deeper, upland setting with a saturated thickness of 130 m, an elevation of 768 m, and a distance to the stream of 14.0 km. All wells in the deepest regime draw groundwater from the Ogallala Formation, whereas the two shallower regimes occur where the Ogallala thins and Cretaceous bedrock units (Niobrara, Pierre, Carlile) are present at shallower depths. The regimes showed consistent patterns across methods, with strong agreement between k-means and k-prototypes (ARI = 0.98) and substantial agreement with Ward clustering (ARI = 0.76). Relative to k-means, GMM and SOM showed lower agreement (ARI = 0.36 and 0.42), reflecting differing clustering assumptions. Bootstrap resampling indicated moderate stability (ARI = 0.77 ± 0.25), while modest silhouette scores (0.18-0.31) suggest a continuous hydrogeologic gradient rather than sharply separated regimes. OpenET-based NETIRR captures drought-driven irrigation demand in 2002 and 2012 that TerraClimate-based estimates underestimate. During the 2012 drought, OpenET-based NETIRR exceeded the TerraClimate estimate by more than 370 mm, demonstrating the importance of satellite-based evapotranspiration for resolving irrigation-driven groundwater stress during extreme drought This study establishes the hydrogeologic and irrigation-demand foundations required to anticipate GW-level change, supporting the integrated modeling tools that agencies need to maintain situational awareness of groundwater security and balance near-term response with long-range planning under increasing hydroclimatic extremes.

497116.title: Multi-Decadal Skill Assessment of the NOAA Coastal Ocean Reanalysis (CORA) Waves Across the U.S. Gulf and Atlantic Coasts
497116.authors: Azadeh Razavi Arab, CLIVAR, Gainesville, FL; and K. A. Serafin and G. Dusek
497116.abstract: Accurate reanalysis wave products underpin coastal hazard assessment, infrastructure design, and operational forecasting, however systematic multi-decadal, multi-region skill assessment of these models remains limited. This study evaluates the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Coastal Ocean ReAnalysis for the Gulf of America/Mexico, East Coast (Atlantic), and Caribbean (CORA-GEC) against 25 NOAA National Data Buoy Center (NDBC) stations, spanning the U.S. Gulf and Atlantic coasts, covering deep, intermediate, shallow, and very shallow water and up to 44 years of observations. Model skill was evaluated using Correlation Coefficient (CC), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), MAE (Mean Absolute Error), Bias, and Standard Deviation (STD). CORA-GECv1.1.1 reproduces significant wave height (Hs) well across all 25 stations, with mean CC of 0.93, combined mean bias of 0.149 m and RMSE of 0.316 m. Skill is slightly higher in the Gulf than the Atlantic (mean CC~0.95 and 0.92, respectively), consistent with the Atlantic's typically larger, longer-period waves being inherently harder to reproduce, and modestly lower at the very shallow stations. Peak period (Tp) is underestimated by roughly 0.1–1.4 s at most stations (mean bias -0.34 s; mean CC 0.59), with error growing for longer-period waves. Regression at two representative stations shows Hs and Tp errors depend jointly and nonlinearly on sea state, with stronger explanatory skill for Tp (adjusted R² up to 0.56) than Hs (up to 0.39), indicating coupled rather than independent error sources. Skill varies more strongly by region than by water depth, with the Gulf outperforming the Atlantic across most metrics; depth-related differences are present but less consistent, with the very shallow stations generally weakest. These results establish a baseline for where and under what conditions the CORA-GEC wave reanalysis needs further refinement, motivating station- and depth-stratified calibration. This station-level skill inventory offers coastal engineers and forecasters a practical reference for expected CORA-GEC uncertainty in operational forecasting and coastal hazard planning.

497117.title: Spatiotemporal Trends In Convective Precipitation Across Kentucky: A Radar-Based Climatology
497117.authors: Josh Sherman, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY; and J. A. Naylor
497117.abstract: ABSTRACT: Between 2020–2024, Kentucky averaged nearly 5-billion-dollar disasters per year, including the historic July 2022 flooding in eastern Kentucky, which resulted in significant loss of life and property. These recent events have motivated a research response to better understand convective precipitation events in the state at a higher spatial resolution. Previous research on precipitation trends in Kentucky has relied on historical weather station observations, which require a large amount of spatial interpolation to properly capture broad patterns. Even with a relatively dense network of surface-based instrumentation, the distance between observation locations is at least an order of magnitude greater than the diameter of intense precipitation cores, indicating that many of these features may go undetected by the observation network. To address this problem, NEXRAD Level II data was used to construct a radar-based climatology of convective precipitation in Kentucky from 1995–2025. Five NEXRAD radar sites in and around Kentucky were used to create Cartesian grids of radar reflectivity with a 1 km horizontal grid spacing and a temporal resolution of 10 minutes. A modified Yuter-Houze convective-stratiform classification algorithm was then applied to identify areas of convection. Through the algorithm, location and time were extracted to quantify the duration of convective events. Convective cell characteristics were analyzed in two and three dimensions through an additional tracing algorithm, quantifying how convection has evolved over time. Kentucky was divided into four regions—Western, Central, Bluegrass, and Eastern—based on physiographic maps and climatic divisions from the National Weather Service and the U.S. Geological Survey. A preliminary seasonal analysis reveals that variability in unique convective days differ greatly by season, with the spring months of March, April, and May (MAM) showing the greatest change in variability. Additionally, total convective events are becoming more frequent even though unique convective days are decreasing slightly, suggesting multiple events or repeated rounds of convective precipitation are clustered together on the same day. Long-duration events—defined as convective events that are eight hours or longer—are increasing in frequency across multiple regions in varying seasons. Long-duration convective events are increasing in Western Kentucky during the spring months and in Central Kentucky during the fall months. Additional analysis will focus on statistical tests of observed trends and characteristics of convective cells over time. With the use of the tracing algorithm, convective core paths can be extracted to analyze spatiotemporal trends of convective precipitation during the thirty year study period. This study quantifies spatiotemporal trends in convective precipitation events in Kentucky, providing guidance for policymakers managing future community planning and flood risk assessment. KEYWORDS: Convection; Convective precipitation; Kentucky; Radars/Radar observations

497119.title: Refining High Water Threshold Parameterization for Flood Inundation Mapping: A Hydrofabric-Driven Approach
497119.authors: James Matthew Coll, NOAA, Fort Collins, CO; and R. McDermott, D. Giardino, M. Johnson, and A. M. Rad
497119.abstract: In operational emergency management, triggering automated flood inundation mapping (FIM) requires balancing cloud computing costs and pipeline latency against the catastrophic risk of missing a flood event. The current solution to this operational need is the implementation of the High Water Threshold, which defines a level of flow a river must reach to trigger FIM production. This work presents an updated parameterization framework implemented by the Office of Water Prediction (OWP) to transition from static, coarse-scale runoff clusters used in the current HWT configuration to a localized Hydrofabric High Water Threshold (H-HWT). By anchoring automated triggers to localized hydrofabric properties and constraining them with empirical National Water Prediction Service (NWPS) Action Stages, the H-HWT provides an optimized operational control mechanism for forecasters. Case studies across distinct hydrologic regimes demonstrate immediate operational benefits: the updated thresholds suppress nuisance flood mapping in the groundwater-dominated semi-arid plains, align the Pacific Northwest with conventional bankfull regimes, and accelerate automated mapping responses in flash-flood-prone regions of Texas. Recognizing that continental-scale models inherently lack perfect localized precision, the H-HWT establishes a conservative baseline that minimizes false negatives, ensuring that critical flood visualization is never under-provisioned. This work highlights how combining empirical observations with national-scale modeling empowers field forecasters to deliver actionable, life-saving hydrointelligence.

497120.title: Using Potential Evapotranspiration to Improve Drought Monitoring with the Nebraska Mesonet
497120.authors: Sarah Jessica Callen, University of Nebraska Lincoln, Lincoln, NE
497120.abstract: Authors: Sarah Callen and Eric Hunt Drought develops when water availability is less than what the atmospheric and terrestrial water demands, resulting in deficits that can affect water resources in ecosystems and agriculture. Potential evapotranspiration (PET) estimates atmospheric demand and can be used to assess drought development and severity. PET also is much more sensitive to increased temperatures and atmospheric aridity in all seasons than other drought indicators, which will make it increasingly valuable as a key input for drought monitoring in an era of climate change. Preliminary results show that increased potential ET in the cold season has led to more rapidly developing and intensifying drought conditions in the non-summer months. Therefore, we propose to implement a physically based PET calculation using daily as temperature, humidity, wind speed, and radiation data from the increasingly dense Nebraska Mesonet to improve the monitoring and diagnosis of drought conditions in Nebraska. The calculated PET will be compared with available measures of water availability and existing drought indicators to look into how changes in atmospheric evaporative demand may help identify developing or rapidly intensifying drought conditions. Integrating PET into the mesonet would provide an additional, physically based measure of drought conditions and could support improved monitoring and understanding of drought processes across Nebraska. Furthermore, this calculation will help provide evidence of drought impacts to rangeland conditions in Nebraska, which are very sensitive to increases in PET, and could be used to verify the Evaporative Demand Drought Index (EDDI).

497121.title: A Transformer-Based Deep Learning Model for Medium-Range Precipitation Prediction
497121.authors: Tianyi Xiong, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and H. Chen, K. M. Mahoney, and J. L. Bytheway
497121.abstract: Accurate medium-range precipitation forecasting is essential for hydrometeorological risk management and disaster mitigation, yet remains challenging for numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems and data-driven models. Operational ensemble systems such as the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) can exhibit errors in precipitation intensity, spatial structure, and reliability, particularly at longer lead times. This paper presents a deep learning-based ensemble forecasting framework, termed CSU-PCAST, for medium-range global precipitation prediction. The model is trained using 21 years of ERA5 atmospheric and surface fields at 0.25 degrees spatial resolution, with precipitation labels from the Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG). CSU-PCAST jointly predicts 57 prognostic atmospheric and surface variables and 6-h total precipitation, using static geographical fields as additional inputs. The framework uses a patch-based Swin Transformer backbone with periodically padded residual convolutions for longitudinal continuity, time embeddings, stochastic noise conditioning, and a dual-branch decoder that separately predicts precipitation and non-precipitation variables. Noise is incorporated through conditional layer normalization throughout the Transformer blocks, enabling stochastic ensemble generation without operational ensemble members or a diffusion process. Training uses a weighted almost-fair Continuous Ranked Probability Score. During inference, CSU-PCAST is initialized from operational Global Forecast System (GFS) analyses and generates 30 autoregressive ensemble members out to 15 days, matching the GEFS ensemble size.
