Evaluation against GEFS for the full year of 2023, using IMERG as the precipitation reference, shows improved deterministic skill at short lead times, including higher Critical Success Index scores and lower root-mean-square error during the first several forecast days. CSU-PCAST also reduces GEFS wet bias for light precipitation and dry bias at the 10 and 20 mm thresholds. Probabilistic verification shows lower CRPS, higher Brier Skill Scores at several thresholds, and improved ensemble reliability, although both systems remain underdispersive. A case study of the Sanba extreme precipitation event further demonstrates improved spatial structure and exceedance-probability guidance, while identifying remaining challenges in regional totals and high-end intensity. These results demonstrate improved short-to-medium-range ensemble precipitation guidance relative to GEFS and identify ensemble calibration and extreme intensity as priorities for further development.

497122.title: A Statistical Analysis of Radar Variables Co-Located with Cold-Season Lightning Flashes
497122.authors: Stephanie A. Weiss, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX
497122.abstract: Rimed graupel is thought to be one of the key ingredients necessary for non-inductive charging and subsequent lightning in cold-season thunderstorms, but very few cold-season lightning flashes have been observed in both lighting and radar data. During the Lake Effect Electrification (LEE) project, roughly 200 flashes were observed by a lightning mapping array (LMA), with more than 150 of those happening within range of the Montague, NY NEXRAD WSR-88D radar. A statistical analysis of radar variable values that overlap with lightning mapping array sources associated with lightning flashes observed during the LEE project was conducted, and initial analysis shows that lightning occurs in regions of relatively high horizontal reflectivity factor (Zh) and relatively low values of differential reflectivity (ZDR), which is consistent with the presence of conical, rimed graupel at the ground. An examination of whether this result holds for the larger data set and for different subsets of the data (e.g., flashes with fast positive leaders) will be presented.

497124.title: Improved Representation of Buoyant Aircraft Exhaust Plumes within the Atmospheric Boundary layer for Assessing Airport Air Quality
497124.authors: Gavendra Pandey, The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; and A. Venkatram and S. Arunachalam
497124.abstract: Aircraft exhaust during landing and takeoff (LTO) cycles at airports cause adverse air quality and health effects both within and in the immediate vicinity of airports. Air quality contributions of aircraft emissions during LTO cycles are difficult to model unlike stationary or other on-road traffic sources because LTO emissions especially during the takeoff roll are characterized by substantial forward thrust and thermal buoyancy. These characteristics significantly influence how pollutant disperse in the atmosphere. The evolution of aircraft exhaust plume is extensively governed by the atmospheric boundary layer processes, including turbulent mixing, atmospheric stability, and momentum as well as buoyancy-driven entrainments. The interaction between jet momentum, thermal buoyancy, and boundary-layer turbulence defines the rise and spread of the exhaust plume. Therefore, physically realistic representation of these processes is important for accurately calculating the aircraft exhaust dispersion under different meteorological conditions. When such characteristics are not realistically represented in the dispersion models, surface level modeled concentrations nearby the airports are mostly overestimated. We previously incorporated these characteristics in the U.S. EPA’s AERMOD dispersion model version 24142. However; this version of aircraft plume dynamics had some limitations. For example, it assumed that aircraft velocity governed the buoyancy per unit length of the exhaust plume and that the ambient wind speed determined the transport of the jet exhaust plume. This led to the overestimation of exhaust plume rise. Here, we build on this work by developing an algorithm that 1) explicitly couples momentum and buoyancy as the plume is transported from source to receptor, 2) accounts for the jet exhaust velocity in computing the buoyancy parameter of the plume, and 3) accounts for the velocity of the moving aircraft in computing the horizontal momentum of the jet exhaust plume. We also compare our modeled plume rise with LIDAR measurements studies. This improved plume dynamics has been incorporated in the latest version 26135 of AERMOD. We perform an assessment of this plume dynamics version of AERMOD with data collected near Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) in spring/summer of 2024 and winter of 2025, comparing the outputs with models using no plume dynamics, fixed plume dynamics, and the existing plume dynamics. We will present results from this intercomparison of all model options and present an evaluation when compared to observations from this latest field study, with a focus on seasonal differences, boundary layer adjustments based on Boston urban core and shoreline as well as model performance for NOx versus SO2. Our evaluation will demonstrate the importance of physically realistic plume dynamics for accurate modeling of aircraft exhaust dispersion near airports.

497126.title: A National Assessment of Heat Index Understanding, Temperature Unit Preference, and Danger Thresholds Among Spanish Speakers
497126.authors: Claire Marie Riva, NOAA, Lafayette, IN
497126.abstract: Heat causes more deaths in the United States than any other weather hazard. Most heat messaging depends on the heat index, which assumes the audience knows what the value represents and has a working sense of when it becomes dangerous. Neither assumption has been tested much among Spanish speakers, who often come from countries that report temperature in Celsius and that use different heat metrics or none at all. To analyze this issue, a nationwide survey was distributed to Spanish speakers across the United States with questions regarding heat threshold perception, temperature unit preferences, and understanding of heat index definition. The analysis compares danger thresholds between respondents who prefer Fahrenheit and those who prefer Celsius, and compares heat index understanding across Hispanic origin groups. Findings give a baseline for heat vulnerability in this population and identify where heat products lose meaning across languages and measurement systems.

497129.title: An Interactive Web Visualization Tool For Calculating and Understanding Tropical Cyclone Potential Intensity
497129.authors: Daniel R Chavas, Purdue University, Indianapolis, IN, IN
497129.abstract: Tropical cyclone potential intensity (PI) sets the thermodynamic upper bound on hurricane wind speed used in both operational forecasting and longer term risk assessment. PI is commonly explained conceptually using an equation based on a Carnot cycle, yet it is computed instead by the difference between saturation CAPE and boundary layer CAPE. The latter requires an iterative, non-linear, parcel-based algorithm that takes a thermodynamic sounding and sea-surface temperature as input, which can obscure the underlying physics from students and many practitioners, who typically treat it as a black-box function call. We present a free web tool that interactively computes PI for a specified sounding and visualizes the PI calculation on the sounding itself. The Bister–Emanuel algorithm (pcmin/tcpyPI) is ported to client-side JavaScript and validated against the reference implementation. An interactive Skew-T diagram updates instantly as the user varies sea-surface temperature, sea-level pressure, the exchange-coefficient ratio, dissipative heating, and reversible versus pseudo-adiabatic ascent, or selects among idealized and observed reference soundings. The tool bring the physics to the foreground by presenting, side by side, the two nearly equivalent formulations of PI – the CAPE-difference form the algorithm evaluates and the Carnot efficiency times air-sea enthalpy-disequilibrium form – with every term's value shown and traced back to the sounding. This exposes subtleties normally hidden in the code, including how condensate loading in reversible ascent suppresses realized buoyancy relative to the idealized surface-flux bound, how the wind-induced surface-heat-exchange pressure feedback enters through the iteration, and how PI, despite common intuition, is not really a measure of atmospheric stability. We describe the tool's design and its potential use in teaching and research.

497130.title: Can Large Turbulence-Resolving Domain Sizes Help with Multi-Scale LES?
497130.authors: Harold Gamarro, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA; and F. K. Chow
497130.abstract: Large-eddy simulation (LES) of the atmospheric boundary layer requires sufficient lateral extent for resolved turbulence to develop under mesoscale lateral boundary forcing. Traditionally, 3:1 or 5:1 grid nesting ratios are used to transfer mesoscale forcing to the LES microscale, with the number of grid points roughly constant for each grid nest. Previous simulations using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model over the AWAKEN field campaign region showed that alternative grid configurations are possible. For example, a 30:1 nesting ratio is possible, with a 100-m LES domain driven by 3-km mesoscale forcing. This approach has some benefits in reducing spurious flow structures, but the results remain significantly impacted by the turbulence adjustment near the lateral boundaries. Here, we investigate whether GPU-accelerated LES can enable substantially larger turbulence-resolving domains and therefore more accurate simulations at the microscale. Specifically, larger domains can help mitigate the influence of the inflow transition region by placing boundaries far from the region of interest, but computational cost has previously limited the practical grid size of the domain. Simulations are performed using the NCAR FastEddy GPU-resident LES code at 100-m horizontal grid spacing over the AWAKEN region. We compare domains with larger horizontal extents (ranging from 1000 to 2000 grid points in each direction) while maintaining consistent atmospheric forcing and model configuration. The experiments focus on a well-observed summertime boundary-layer case previously simulated with WRF, allowing direct comparison with existing model results and observations. The simulations are evaluated using surface meteorological measurements and lidar wind profiles. We examine the evolution of resolved turbulent structures with distance from the lateral boundaries, vertical velocity spectra, boundary layer structure, and sensitivity to domain extent. FastEddy computational performance is also quantified to assess the cost of increasing LES domain size on GPU architectures. This study provides an initial assessment of whether GPU acceleration can support larger turbulence-resolving domains and reduce reliance on intermediate nesting domains, with implications for the design of mesoscale-to-microscale atmospheric modeling frameworks.

497132.title: Every Scientist Has an Origin Story: From Wonder to Workforce
497132.authors: Jerry M Cyccone, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO
497132.abstract: Every STEM professional has a story about the moment curiosity became purpose. For some, it begins with an inspiring teacher or family member. For others, it starts with a powerful personal experience that transforms wonder into a lifelong passion. This interactive session explores how those early moments shape STEM identity and how educators, mentors, and institutions can intentionally cultivate curiosity from childhood through college and into the workforce. Drawing on both personal experience and professional practice, I will reflect on how an early fascination with weather, followed by experiencing Hurricane Andrew as a teenager, inspired a career in science education. As a first-generation college graduate from a low-income background, I understand the importance of access, mentorship, and meaningful opportunities in helping students persist in STEM. Today, as Student Program Coordinator for NSF NCAR's Education, Engagement & Early-Career Development (EdEC), I lead undergraduate internships, graduate research fellowships, professional development programs, and workforce initiatives designed to help students transform scientific curiosity into successful careers. Participants will reflect on the experiences that first sparked their interest in science while exploring practical strategies for creating learning environments that foster curiosity, scientific identity, and awareness of STEM career pathways. The session will highlight how hands-on learning, mentorship, community building, and intentional professional development can strengthen STEM pathways and broaden participation in the Earth system sciences. Attendees will leave with actionable ideas for nurturing curiosity, sustaining engagement in science, and helping the next generation transition from wonder to a thriving STEM workforce.

497133.title: The Unprecedented Nature of New Jersey’s 2026 False Spring and Damaging Freeze Event, and Projections of Future Risk
497133.authors: John P. Krasting, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ; Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ; and M. Gerbush, D. A. Robinson, J. Shope, and B. Schilling
497133.abstract: “False spring” events, when post-dormancy bud and flower growth are damaged by a hard freeze, can be among the most catastrophic weather events for the agricultural sector. After an early April heatwave across New Jersey, where temperatures reached mid-90sºF, overnight lows suddenly fell below critical agricultural thresholds (≤28ºF) for many hours over two consecutive nights. The freeze resulted in near-total losses of several of the major fruit crops across the state, with conservative damage estimates of approximately $135-170M. We recap the widespread agricultural damage across the state and the indiscriminate impact on various fruit varieties that led some local farmers and agricultural experts to call this a “once-in-a-generation” event. Analyses performed by the New Jersey State Climate Office (NJSCO) found that on the night of April 20-21, 2026, many observing sites statewide recorded more than 10 hours of below-freezing conditions, including 5 mesonet (NJWxNet) sites with 2 or more hours below 24ºF. We further explore the estimated return periods of this event and examine whether similar events are represented in historical LOCA2 downscaled, bias-corrected climate model simulations. We also explore the changing risks of similar future events arising from projected changes in both earlier spring onset and sub-critical freeze events in the coming decades under moderate (SSP2-4.5) and high (SSP3-7.0) greenhouse gas emissions scenarios. A more thorough understanding of the historical context of this event, as well as a characterization of the evolving future risk, is beneficial to the New Jersey agricultural industry for planning and resource management.

497136.title: Baroclinic Annular Mode Modulates Global Atmospheric Rivers and Extreme Precipitation
497136.authors: Yuan-Bing Zhao, Purdue University, Lafayette, IN; and L. Wang and Y. Ming
497136.abstract: The Baroclinic Annular Mode (BAM) is a dominant mode of extratropical atmospheric variability, yet its role in organizing the global hydrological cycle remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how BAM modulates atmospheric rivers (ARs) and extreme precipitation using ERA5 reanalysis and a global AR database. We derive daily BAM indices from zonal-mean eddy kinetic energy and examine changes in AR occurrence and 99th-percentile precipitation extremes during high- and low-BAM states across both hemispheres and seasons. We find that BAM systematically reorganizes preferred AR corridors and regions of extreme precipitation. During high-BAM states, AR occurrence generally increases along the flanks of major storm tracks and decreases near their climatological cores. Relative changes locally exceed 50%, with particularly coherent patterns over the Southern Ocean. Extreme precipitation varies correspondingly, increasing by more than 50% across broad poleward storm-track regions. A substantial fraction of these extremes coincide with ARs, and AR-associated extreme precipitation exhibits similar BAM-related variations. Low-BAM states show broadly opposite patterns. These results demonstrate that BAM provides a large-scale dynamical framework linking variations in extratropical circulation to atmospheric moisture transport and hydrological extremes on intraseasonal timescales.

497138.title: Environmental Controls on Satellite-Based Convective Entrainment Using Machine Learning
497138.authors: Cansu Duzgun, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and H. E. Fuelberg and R. Adams-Selin
497138.abstract: Convection parameterizations struggle to accurately represent deep moist convection, including its timing, location, and vertical extent. The strength and vertical extent of deep convective updrafts are strongly influenced by entrainment, the mixing of environmental air into the convective core. Although numerous entrainment parameterizations have been developed, there is no clear convergence toward a universally accepted formulation. A major challenge is identifying which environmental factors are most relevant for parameterizing entrainment. The storm environment dataset was developed using the Precipitation Feature (PF) dataset from TRMM/GPM radar observations and ERA5 reanalysis. Entrainment was estimated using two methods: 1) an entraining-plume model using TES/MLS carbon monoxide (CO) as a conserved quantity in convective ascent, and 2) an entrainment proxy based on the difference between the level of neutral buoyancy (LNB) and level of maximum detrainment (LMD), with LMD identified from upper-tropospheric CO enhancements, and environmental variables were derived from ERA5. Random Forest (RF) and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) models were used to investigate environmental influences on entrainment. Both models successfully learned relationships between the storm environment and the entrainment proxy, whereas comparable relationships were not captured when the CO-based entrainment rate estimates were used as the target, highlighting the importance of dataset quality, structure, and representativeness. Fine-tuned models trained using the proxy were evaluated against a held-out test dataset comprising 20% of the total cases. Coefficients of determination (R2) exceeding 0.83 indicated that both models explained a substantial fraction of the variance in the entrainment proxy. Beyond conventional statistical analysis, the machine learning models captured multivariate and nonlinear relationships between the entrainment proxy and the storm environment, identifying additional sensitivity to the lifting condensation level and level of free convection. These results suggest that cloud-base and lower-tropospheric thermodynamic characteristics provide additional information about entrainment-induced buoyancy loss beyond the dominant influences of buoyancy and vertical wind shear. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) distributions further showed that the relationships learned by the models were largely consistent between land and ocean environments. These results demonstrate the potential of interpretable machine learning as a knowledge discovery tool for identifying environmental controls on convective entrainment from satellite-based observations and informing the development of physically based entrainment parameterizations.

497139.title: From Global Models to Local Insights: Leveraging Downscaled Climate Projections to Inform Water Efficiency Planning
497139.authors: Alexandra Mazurek, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and P. Goble and R. S. Schumacher
497139.abstract: Climate projections data can offer crucial insights for decision-makers, but data processing can be complex, and subject matter expert analysis is often required. Service climatologists can help stakeholders distill these data, creating opportunity to translate scientific analysis into useful information. In a demonstrative example of this type of work, the Colorado Climate Center partnered with the City of Fort Collins Utilities to conduct a localized analysis of future changes to temperature and precipitation to inform the City’s water efficiency plan. This project uses the Localized Constructed Analogs (LOCA) dataset (Pierce et al. 2014), a statistically downscaled version of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) dataset. In this work, the Colorado Climate Center provided custom data analysis and expertise, developing a “plug-and-play” dataset that Utilities staff could use for water demand modeling. The localized analysis provided the City of Fort Collins Utilities with quality, expert-analyzed data to evaluate how climate change might combine with other factors (e.g., population shifts) to influence future water demand, allowing them to prepare for a range of scenarios. This work illustrates how high-resolution climate model data and expert analysis can be used for cross-disciplinary work to ultimately benefit stakeholder needs.

497143.title: Cell Tracking as Temporal Context for Airborne In-Situ Observations: Radar Retrieval Biases during ESCAPE
497143.authors: Saurabh U Patil, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and Y. Huang, G. M. McFarquhar, and S. Gupta
497143.abstract: Airborne in-situ measurements provide detailed but essentially instantaneous "snapshots" of the clouds sampled during field campaigns. An aircraft traverses a narrow transect in a matter of seconds, with little indication of where that transect falls within the evolution of the storm. Combining these measurements with radar-based cell tracking using Tracking and Object Based Analysis of Clouds (TOBAC) algorithm supplies the missing temporal context, placing each penetration within both the structure of the storm and the stage of its lifetime. This study uses in-situ observations from the Experiment of Sea Breeze Convection, Aerosols, Precipitation and Environment (ESCAPE) field campaign to quantify biases in radar microphysical retrievals in and around convection as a function of storm-lifetime stage and range from the radar. Between 31 May and 17 June 2022, the National Research Council of Canada Convair-580 and the Stratton Park Engineering Company Learjet together sampled approximately 100 storms, yielding 219 intense convective core segments across a range of meteorological regimes along the Texas and Louisiana coasts. These flights were within range of ground-based NEXRAD observations from Houston (KHGX), Lake Charles (KLCH), and Fort Polk (KPOE). Per-second composite particle size distributions (3µm-8mm) spliced from cloud droplet, 2DS and HVPS probes at objectively selected crossover diameters were used to compute radar variables in the Rayleigh approximation at S-band. Vertical cross sections along the aircraft tracks were extracted from NEXRAD volume scans, allowing radar variables at the aircraft location to be compared with corresponding variables computed from composite PSDs, conditioned on range from the radar and on cell age. Results show that reflectivity derived from airborne PSDs is greater than the co-located radar-observed reflectivity within updraft regions. A normalized cell-lifetime analysis indicates that most transects sampled storms during their early mature to mature stages. Additional results for polarimetric variables, stratified by updraft and downdraft regions and by cell age, will be presented. These results indicate that radar retrievals of convective microphysics are sensitive to both storm-lifetime stage and range from the radar, and that cell tracking offers a practical framework for placing airborne in-situ sampling in its temporal context.

497146.title: Global Hotspots for Land-Atmosphere Coupling In Modulating S2S Predictions
497146.authors: Zhe Zhang, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. Jaye, M. Fowler, N. Tavakoli, Y. N. Lim, S. Zhang, P. A. Dirmeyer, C. He, and J. H. Richter
497146.abstract: Land-atmosphere (L-A) interactions play a critical role in bridging the gap between weather and decadal timescales , significantly modulating predictability on subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) timescales. In this study, we evaluate the contribution of L-A coupling to S2S predictability using a comprehensive 20-year initialized reforecast dataset generated by the MPAS-NoahMP S2S system. We conditionally evaluate model forecast skill based on the strength of L-A coupling, quantified by the correlation between surface soil moisture and latent heat flux across various global regions and forecast lead times. Results demonstrate enhanced temperature forecast skill, measured by the anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC), during periods of strong L-A coupling, across different lead times spanning forecast weeks 1-6. We identify several global L-A coupling hotspots where this conditional skill improvement is most evident, including the US Great Plains, the La Plata basin in South America, the African Sahel, Australia, and the North China Plain. Furthermore, we investigate the role of these strong L-A interactions in modulating severe heatwave events over the past two decades. Ultimately, these findings suggest that L-A coupling strength can serve as a valuable diagnostic index to identify "windows of forecast opportunity," allowing forecasters to subset periods of elevated predictive skill from the broader forecast climatology.

497147.title: Preliminary Evaluation of Vertical Profiles of Ox within Lake Breeze during high Ozone Episodes
497147.authors: Patricia Cleary, Univ. of Wisconsin-Eau Claire, Eau Claire, WI; and T. Day, D. A. Hernandez Tejeda, T. O'Connor, E. Oberg, N. Rose, C. Womack, and N. Schafer
497147.abstract: Lake Michigan shoreline communities often experience poor air quality due to the mesoscale meteorology associated with lake breeze and its role in circulating urban emissions throughout the region. The inversions caused by the marine air limits vertical mixing over the lake and in areas impacted by lake breeze. These inversions complicate the vertical structure of both primary emissions (NOx and VOCs) and photochemically produced ozone. To better understand the vertical structure of ozone within these regions, an Onboard-UAS Absorption Cavity Enhanced Spectrometer (OACES) NO2 instrument was constructed for deployment on an unmanned aerial system (UAS) to monitor vertical profiles of Ox (Ox = NO2 + O3). Ox can be helpful to monitor as a more complete metric for oxidative capacity in an urban plume due to the fast conversion of fresh NO emissions into NO2 through the reaction with O3 (NO+O3 --> NO2 + O2), but which serves as a temporary storage for odd oxygen as NO2 photolysis also leads to more photochemical O3 production in an urban plume. Measurement of Ox at a shoreline environment impacted by lake breeze can therefore help illuminate the role of surface NOx emissions in the vertical structure of O3 within an inverted atmosphere. It can also help to understand the mixing height of fresh emissions into a vertically-shallow inversion. This work was completed by integrating the OACES NO2 instrument onto an Aurelia X6 Max multirotor UAS also equipped with an ozone analyzer and meteorological sensor to measure temperature, humidity and pressure during a short campaign WiscoDISCO-26 from July 13-15, 2026 while ozone concentrations were enhanced.

497151.title: Assessing Near-Term Climate Risk with ACE2-ERA5 and CorrDiff
497151.authors: Callie Jaclyn McNicholas, Ph.D., Jupiter Intelligence, Seattle, WA; and H. Scannell, A. Hoffman, and S. Sain
497151.abstract: Catastrophe (CAT) modeling often fails to account for the effects of climate change on internal climate variability, which is frequently the most important driver of near-term (5-10 year) CAT risk. To address this, the Ai2 Climate Emulator version 2, trained on ERA5 reanalysis (ACE2-ERA5), is leveraged to create a large ensemble consisting of hundreds to thousands of synthetic climate realizations spanning the recent past (2020-2025) and near future (through 2035) climate. This ensemble is designed to capture both the diversity of internal climate variability observed historically, including its modulation by large-scale modes such as ENSO, and the effect of near-term climate change on that variability. To correct systematic biases and increase the spatial resolution, the ACE2-ERA5 ensemble is downscaled globally from 1° to ¼° using NVIDIA’s Corrective Diffusion (CorrDiff) model. From this downscaled ensemble, global physical climate risk is derived for single hazards (e.g., heatwaves) and compound hazards (e.g., tropical cyclones, heat-drought events), in a way that accounts for correlations among hazards and regions, and can include multi-annual hazards. These hazards are then provided to vulnerability and financial modules to estimate damage and loss. Preliminary results show that ensemble-derived physical risk varies systematically with ENSO phase, consistent with observed relationships. Validation of the historical ensemble against observed records, with a focus on tail-risk behavior, will also be presented.

497154.title: Storm-Scale Satellite Nowcasting over CONUS with CREDIT WXFormer
497154.authors: Kevin Yang, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. J. Gagne II, C. Becker, E. Campbell, S. J. Greybush, and C. Spallone
497154.abstract: Convective systems are highly variable in space and time and are often associated with high societal impacts. Accurately nowcasting the timing and location of storms in traditional numerical weather prediction (NWP) remains a challenge, despite advances in kilometer-scale grid spacing and the assimilation of satellite and radar data. Recent data-driven approaches (e.g., Direct Observation Prediction) have shown promise, but the readiness of such systems to replace current operational baselines and their skill in capturing the lifecycle of different thunderstorm types (e.g., single-cell, supercell, and MCS) remain implicit. In this work, we introduce a deterministic, scale-aware transformer-based satellite nowcasting system trained with Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) imagery over the CONUS region at native resolution, with an inference latency of single-digit seconds. Model training and evaluation were conducted on the NSF NCAR Generation 2 Community Research Earth Digital Intelligence Twin (CREDIT) platform, which streamlines experimentation across a variety of physically sound configurations. The nowcasting system mainly adapts the WXFormer architecture, previously used for global medium-range weather forecasting, with additional improvements specific to regional high-resolution forecasting. The new nowcasting system's performance against operational baselines, such as High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) simulated brightness temperature fields, optical flow techniques, and other recent machine-learning-based methods, will be shown, with an emphasis on each method's ability to capture convective initiation, growth, and dissipation across diverse storm types. The evaluation framework here extends traditional bulk evaluation statistics to object-based metrics (e.g., size, area, intensity, and trajectory errors), which could serve as a standardized storm-scale benchmark dataset for comparing satellite-based nowcasting studies. Finally, we will briefly discuss extending the nowcasting system with dual-view geostationary satellites (i.e., GOES-East and GOES-West) and the impacts on predictive skill and further applications.

497158.title: Evaluating Two Cloud Microphysics Parameterizations for Simulating Arctic Mixed-Phase Clouds In a Single Column Model
497158.authors: I-Kuan Hu, CU/CIRES and NOAA/PSL, Boulder, CO; and L. Bengtsson, A. B. Solomon, E. Grell, and J. W. Bao
497158.abstract: This study investigates the performance of two microphysics parameterization schemes in idealized, single-column model (SCM) simulations of Arctic mixed-phase clouds (AMPCs) observed during the Multidisciplinary Drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate (MOSAiC) field campaign. We evaluate: (1) the Thompson scheme, the default microphysics parameterization in the operational Global Forecast System version 17 physics suite, and (2) the Parameterization of Unified Microphysics Across Scales (PUMAS) scheme — developed by NSF NCAR and PNNL — recently integrated into the SCM hosting the physics repository shared by all NOAA Unified Forecast System applications. Using an SCM test case based on an AMPC event spanning October 31 to November 5, 2019, we explore how varying ice nucleating particle (INP) concentrations as a function of temperature impact the partitioning between cloud droplets and cloud ice and their vertical structures. When using the Thompson scheme, the simulated time-height cross sections of cloud droplets and cloud ice generally reproduce the observed cloud structure. These results are largely insensitive to the specified INP, except for an INP formulation derived from MOSAiC’s near-the-surface observations, which results in slightly more cloud droplets at the expense of cloud ice. Conversely, the PUMAS scheme exhibits strong sensitivity to the INP specification. When utilizing INP formulations derived from polar observations, PUMAS overestimates cloud droplets, yielding enhanced vertical diffusion as a compensating bias. This behavior underscores the need for a comprehensive assessment of couplings between parameterized cloud microphysics and other physics components (e.g., boundary layer turbulence). Ongoing work focuses on understanding these results and assessing the settings of the PUMAS scheme, including inner loop, stratiform liquid and ice cloud fractions, large-scale condensation, and cloud condensate sedimentation.

497159.title: A Long-Term High-Resolution Precipitation Dataset over South Korea through Dynamic Bias Correction and Adaptive Residual Radar–Gauge Merging
497159.authors: GyuWon Lee, Center for Atmospheric Remote Sensing (CARE), Daegu, South korea; and S. Ryu and K. S. Lim
497159.abstract: This study presents a long-term, high-resolution precipitation dataset over South Korea developed using a radar–gauge merging framework designed to account for the spatiotemporal variability of radar precipitation bias. The dataset integrates composite radar reflectivity and dense rain gauge observations from the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA), providing precipitation estimates at 0.5-km spatial and 10-min temporal resolution over a ten-year period (2016–2025). A key feature of the framework is a dynamically updated bias correction in which radar–gauge bias factors are estimated at 10-min intervals during precipitation events. Unlike static or event-mean adjustments, the method allows the bias correction to evolve with precipitation systems while maintaining temporal continuity. This approach accommodates changes associated with different precipitation and microphysical regimes and reduces artificial temporal discontinuities in the corrected radar precipitation fields. Residual differences between the bias-corrected radar estimates and gauge observations are then spatially interpolated using a residual radial basis function (RRBF) approach. Because only the residual field is interpolated, rather than the precipitation field itself, the method retains fine-scale spatial structures observed by radar while incorporating gauge constraints and minimizing excessive spatial smoothing. The merged precipitation product is evaluated against independent gauge observations and conventional geostatistical interpolation approaches in terms of bias, correlation, error magnitude, and spatial consistency. The evaluation demonstrates improved performance across different precipitation regimes, seasons, and regions of South Korea, while preserving the spatial detail and temporal evolution of radar-observed precipitation systems. The resulting dataset provides a spatially detailed and temporally consistent precipitation record suitable for radar and satellite precipitation validation, hydrological applications, extreme rainfall analysis, urban flood forecasting, and evaluation of high-resolution numerical weather prediction models. This presentation describes the merging framework, validation results, characteristics of the ten-year dataset, and public data availability.

497162.title: When Legacy Data Meets Cloud-native Workflow: Improving Access to NOAA Climate Data Records through Virtual Datasets
497162.authors: Yuhan Rao, North Carolina State Univ., Asheville, NC; and J. L. Matthews, P. H. Ambrish, and D. Patel
497162.abstract: NOAA long-term satellite-based climate data records (CDR) are critical for climate research and application development across different scales. There are about 40 different climate data records that are publicly available via NOAA Open Data Dissemination Program. However, data access to NOAA CDR products is still a barrier for diverse data users due to the archival data format which is not originally designed for cloud-based climate data access and applications. The rapid development and adoption of cloud computing and artificial intelligence presents unique opportunities for more efficient access and analysis for climate research and application development. This presentation will highlight recent efforts of creating cloud-native data solutions to enhance the usability of NOAA satellite-based climate datasets using virtual dataset and icechunk. These modernization efforts will improve the accessibility of legacy NOAA climate datasets and enable efficient cloud-based data access for climate and AI applications.

497165.title: What Is the Best Way to Define Daily Midlatitude Atmospheric Circulation Anomalies?
497165.authors: Siiri Bigalke, Portland State University, Portland, OR; and P. C. Loikith, D. Singh, X. Bai, and A. Laverty
497165.abstract: While there are numerous methodological approaches to analyzing and characterizing midlatitude atmospheric circulation features for weather regime analysis, anomalies of 500hPa geopotential height (Z500) is perhaps the most commonly used metric. There are a myriad of ways to compute anomalies as either departures of a time or spatial reference climatology, which has some advantage in providing diverse perspectives on circulation structures, but also the large disadvantage that results cannot be easily compared amongst publications. In this research we analyze differences amongst two commonly used anomalies of Z500, time and zonal anomalies, on high pressure, anticyclonic circulation features. We find that the different anomaly computation approaches yield different circulation characteristics over time (including extent, strength, and frequency of identified circulation features) which may be small on a given day but add up to large differences when accumulated over time. Given these results, we provide guidance on best practices in anomalies computation approaches and applications in circulation research, ensuring that a chosen circulation feature identification method is fit for the desired purpose. This research aims to advance knowledge of atmospheric dynamics across the weather-climate time scale continuum by providing methodological guidance for defining circulation anomalies in future research on mid-latitude dynamics.

497166.title: Evaluation of Multi-Satellite Soil Moisture Products against In-Situ Observations over the Korean Peninsula
497166.authors: Jongmin Park, Korea National Univ. of Transportation, Chungjusi, South korea
497166.abstract: Soil moisture is a key hydrological variable that regulates water and energy exchanges at the land–atmosphere interface. In-situ observations provide accurate point-scale measurements but lack the spatial representativeness required for basin-scale applications, whereas satellite remote sensing offers spatially continuous soil moisture estimates whose accuracy varies substantially with sensor characteristics and retrieval algorithms. Such uncertainties are amplified over the Korean Peninsula, where complex terrain and heterogeneous land cover challenge coarse-resolution retrievals. This study evaluates the applicability of four satellite-based soil moisture products over the Korean Peninsula: the L-band radiometer-based SMAP, the C-band scatterometer-based ASCAT, the C-band SAR-based Sentinel-1, and the GNSS-Reflectometry-based CYGNSS. Surface (0–10 cm) soil moisture measurements from ground observation networks operated by the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) are used as reference data, and product performance is quantified using the Pearson correlation coefficient (R), bias, and root-mean-square error (RMSE). The evaluation is further stratified by season and land cover type to identify the dominant sources of retrieval uncertainty, and the relative strengths of each product are examined with respect to sensing frequency, spatial resolution, and retrieval approach. The results are expected to identify the optimal satellite soil moisture product under different land surface conditions in Korea and to provide a basis for bias correction, data assimilation, and hydrological and agricultural applications over regions with complex and heterogeneous landscapes. Acknowledgement: This work also was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Korea government(MSIT)(RS-2024-00416443). This work was also supported by the Korea Railroad Research Institute (KRRI) grant (PK26414A0).

497167.title: Billion-Dollar Disasters across the Nation In 2026 - Annual Report and New Research
497167.authors: ADAM SMITH, Climate Central, Candler, NC
497167.abstract: 2026 marks the 16th consecutive year (2011–2026) with at least 10 individual billion-dollar disaster events nationwide. During the first six months of 2026, the United States experienced at least 12 separate billion-dollar weather and climate disaster events - including winter storms, severe storms, a crop freeze event and flooding - resulting in total damages exceeding $32.0 billion and contributing to 183 direct and indirect fatalities. The costs of ongoing wildfires, drought, heat and other events during the second half of the year continue to be assessed. Since 1980, hurricanes have caused the greatest economic losses, exceeding $1.6 trillion. Severe storms ($618 billion), drought ($392 billion), wildfires ($219 billion), and flooding events ($216 billion) have each caused hundreds of billions of dollars as well. Over the last decade (2017-2026), there has been more than $1.5 trillion in damages. Hurricane costs have been at historic highs for many states from Texas to Florida up through the Carolinas while wildfire losses have risen sharply in the West. Severe storm costs from tornado, hail and high wind damage have also risen sharply over the last decade across the central and eastern United States. The time between disasters is also shrinking. During the 1980s, the United States averaged 82 days between billion-dollar disasters. Over the last decade (2016–2025), that average fell to just 16 days. Shorter recovery periods reduce the time available to rebuild, prepare, and replenish emergency resources, with disproportionate impacts on socioeconomically vulnerable communities. Extreme weather and climate disasters occur year-round, with different hazards dominating in different seasons. Severe storms and river flooding make spring and summer the highest-risk seasons while hurricanes, wildfires, and drought dominate U.S. extreme events and economic losses during the fall. Disaster losses reflect a combination of climate change and increased exposure as more people and assets are located in harm’s way. Our vulnerability is also growing, influencing how much damage an extreme event causes to people and the built environment. At the same time, population growth and development in hurricane-prone coastal areas, the wildland-urban interface, and floodplains have increased exposure and potential losses. Extreme event attribution research also shows that climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of certain types of extreme weather that lead to billion-dollar disasters — most notably the rise in vulnerability to drought, lengthening wildfire seasons in the western states, and extremely heavy rainfall becoming more common in the eastern states. Sea level rise is also worsening hurricane storm surge flooding. The billion-dollar disasters analysis draws on more than a dozen public and private data sources to estimate the total direct costs of each event. These estimates include insured and uninsured losses to homes, businesses, public buildings, vehicles, boats, public infrastructure, agriculture, timber, wildfire suppression costs, as well as business interruption and temporary housing costs. These estimates do not include losses to natural ecosystems, environmental degradation, many physical and mental health impacts, or broader supply-chain disruptions, which are substantial in their own right, due to lack of sufficient data. As a result, these estimates should be considered conservative estimates of total societal losses. Another growing challenge is the rise of compound extremes—multiple billion-dollar disasters occurring simultaneously or in rapid succession. The Fifth National Climate Assessment (2023) notes that climate change is increasing the likelihood of multiple extreme events affecting interconnected regions at the same time. Examples include simultaneous western megafires, back-to-back hurricanes over the same region, and repeated tornado outbreaks, all of which strain emergency response and recovery resources. To better capture the full range of disaster impacts, our work at Climate Central is expanding this research to include weather and climate events that have caused at least $100 million in damage costs, beginning with wildfires and ultimately covering all major weather and climate hazards from 1980 to the present. Billion-dollar disasters are becoming an increasingly significant economic and societal challenge. As exposure, vulnerability, and some climate-charged weather extremes continue to increase, the frequency and cost of these disasters are likely to grow without continued investments in risk reduction, resilience, and adaptation.

497168.title: Climatological Patterns and Environmental Drivers of Rapid Intensification in North Atlantic Tropical Cyclones
497168.authors: Harish Uppu, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA; and H. Huang and J. Trepanier
497168.abstract: Rapid intensification (RI), defined as an increase in maximum sustained wind speed of at least 30 kt within 24 h, remains one of the most challenging aspects of tropical cyclone prediction because it results from complex interactions among favorable oceanic and atmospheric conditions that vary substantially across space and time. This study examines the spatial and temporal patterns of North Atlantic RI and investigates the environmental conditions associated with its pronounced seasonal concentration. RI storms and individual RI events are analyzed separately to distinguish storm occurrence from repeated intensification episodes. We find that RI activity is strongly concentrated during late summer and early fall, with an event-based active RI season extending from 11 August to 11 October. Sustained and repeated RI activity is concentrated primarily within the Main Development Region (57.86%). To investigate the environmental drivers for this seasonality, large-scale conditions during the active RI season are contrasted with those during the remainder of the June-November hurricane season (i.e., inactive RI season). Environmental variables examined in this study include sea surface temperature, 500-hPa relative humidity, 200-850 hPa vertical wind shear, 850-hPa temperature, and aerosol optical depth (an indicator of the Saharan Air Layer). In addition to seasonal composites of these variables, their daily variability is examined to determine how environmental conditions evolve during the onset, peak, and decline of RI activity. Results indicate that RI seasonality reflects the combined evolution of thermodynamic and atmospheric drivers such as SST, VWS and RH at 500 hPa, while relationships between aerosol optical depth and RI are spatially and temporally dependent rather than uniformly suppressive. These findings improve scientific understanding of when and where North Atlantic RI occurs and how the evolving large-scale environment contributes to its seasonal concentration.

497169.title: Evaluating the U.S. Greenhouse Gas and Air Pollutants Emissions System (GRA2PES) Version 2.0 with Observations Made during the Airborne and Remote Sensing Multi Air Pollutant Surveys (AiRMAPS) Field Campaign
497169.authors: Congmeng Lyu, NOAA, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and I. Miller, K. Mueller, T. Chai, C. Harkins, M. Li, Q. Z. Rasool, J. Prothero, N. Malarich, B. J. Carroll, S. Baidar, J. He, B. Verryken, S. Pandey, J. Worden, I. B. Pollack, X. Ren, J. Peischl, N. Schafer, C. Womack, C. Warneke, S. S. Brown, O. R. Cooper, and B. C. McDonald
497169.abstract: GRA2PES version 1 established a foundational, high-resolution (4 km × 4 km) gridded inventory of vertically resolved air pollutants and fossil-fuel CO₂ across the contiguous United States. Leveraging this framework, GRA2PES version 2.0 introduces major structural upgrades. Notably, the revised inventory adds methane (CH₄) quantification and significantly refines emission estimates across key sectors, such as agriculture, waste, residential and commercial buildings, coalbeds, and the oil and natural gas infrastructure network, including pipelines and post-meter emissions. To evaluate these updates, this study leverages aircraft observations from the summers of 2024 and 2025 Airborne and Remote sensing Multi Air Pollutant Surveys (AiRMAPS) field campaigns. AiRMAPS sampled multiple greenhouse gas and air quality species across major oil and gas producing regions—including the Denver-Julesburg, Uinta, and Marcellus Basins—as well as key urban areas such as the wider Denver Metropolitan Area, Salt Lake City, and the Baltimore-Washington, DC region. Focusing our analysis on methane, ethane, and nitrogen oxides, we utilize the FLEXible PARTicle dispersion model driven by WRF meteorology (FLEXPART-WRF) and the Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Integrated Trajectory (HYSPLIT) dispersion model to generate footprints for the aircraft measurements along the flight tracks. The GRA2PES emissions are then convolved with these footprints into concentration space for direct comparison with the observational data. To ensure robust transport modeling, we perform comprehensive meteorological evaluations of wind speed, wind direction, and planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) across multiple model configurations. Ultimately, this work assesses the accuracy of the updated GRA2PES inventory to support ongoing air quality and emissions modeling.

497170.title: Strongly Coupled Assimilation of Atmospheric Boundary Layer Observations for the Rapid Intensification of Hurricane Ida (2021) using the CADRE Self-cycled HAFS-JEDI System
497170.authors: Yu-Shin Kim, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
497170.abstract: This study investigates the development and application of air–sea strongly coupled data assimilation (SCDA) in the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) using the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework. In a previous study, Kim and Wang (2026) showed that assimilating atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) observations constrains thermodynamic and dynamical conditions within the ABL, enabling forecasts to capture Category 4 intensity, compared with Category 2 intensity when ABL observations were withheld. However, the resulting analysis increments were limited to the atmosphere because traditional data assimilation updates only the individual Earth system component in which observations are taken. In contrast, SCDA allows observations from one component (e.g., the atmosphere) to update another component (e.g., the ocean) through coupled background error covariances, enabling dynamically consistent updates across the air–sea interface. Optimal localization in SCDA may depend on the strength of air–sea interactions, the relationship between observed and model-state variables, and the vertical structures of the ABL and ocean mixed layer. Given this complexity, optimal vertical localization for SCDA has not been sufficiently explored in previous studies. Therefore, this study estimates optimal vertical localization parameters from a coupled HAFS ensemble to account for these dependencies and applies the resulting method through observation-space localization in the JEDI Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (LETKF). Using this new localization method, the impact of SCDA on the rapid intensification of Hurricane Ida (2023) is evaluated with the CADRE self-cycled HAFS–JEDI system.

497174.title: Sky-1: Using Machine Learning to Enable a Rapidly Updating Global Forecasting System with a Constellation of Microwave Sounders
497174.authors: Randy J. Chase, Tomorrow.io, Boston, MA; and F. Cannon, M. E. Green, M. Pope, A. Evans, E. L. Nelson, S. J. Munchak, and A. Chawla
497174.abstract: The emergence of AI has enabled skillful, quarter-degree global forecasts to be executed in minutes on a single GPU. Despite the progress in inference speed, most contemporary AI weather models still depend on the same initial conditions provided by global centers; those that operate independently often lag in both predictive skill and spatial resolution. Here, we introduce Sky-1: a machine learning model designed to fuse traditional numerical weather prediction (NWP) initial conditions with recent observations to facilitate a rapidly updating global forecasting system. Sky-1 utilizes a U-Net architecture trained to correct short-term forecast and initialization errors within NOAA’s Global Forecast System (GFS) by leveraging Tomorrow.io’s constellation of 11 microwave sounders. Our results show that Sky-1 reduces initialization error by an average of about 60% using ERA5 as ground truth. Carefully constructed ablation experiments demonstrate that withholding Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) data at inference leads to a measurable degradation in performance; conversely, including TMS data yields a 0.5–2% improvement in mid-level specific humidity, as well as lower-tropospheric temperature and geopotential height. By employing Microsoft’s Aurora model, we further show that these corrected initial conditions and short-term forecast adjustments propagate through the forecast altering the positioning and strength of various weather phenomena (e.g., atmospheric rivers). In concert, Sky-1 paired with an off-the-shelf AI weather model enables an hourly updating, quarter-degree global forecasting system. Sky-1 is scheduled for operational implementation in October 2026. In this presentation we will highlight the added value of TMS in this system on selected high-impact weather events in this operational (i.e., real-time, not retrospective) setting. We also plan to discuss the updates to the TMS constellation, lessons learned building an hourly global quarter degree operational system and planned upgrades to Sky-1.

497176.title: AI In the Forecast: Identifying Public Support and Opposition to the Use of AI In Weather Forecasting Activities
497176.authors: Abigail Lee Bitterman, Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; OU Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis, Norman, OK; and J. T. Ripberger, M. Krocak, and J. E. Trujillo-Falcón
497176.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies are becoming increasingly enmeshed in society, and the weather enterprise is no exception. AI technologies are already being used by the National Weather Service (NWS) to reduce computational time and improve model runs and by private companies to aid in communication and personalization of forecasts. While some work has been done to understand how NWS meteorologists feel about integrating AI into their forecast process, little attention has been paid to what the public thinks about this use case for AI. This research attempts to fill that gap by identifying where in the forecast process members of the public draw the line between where they are comfortable with the use of AI and where they are not. To find this line, we use data from the Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis (IPPRA) 2025 Winter Weather and Society survey (WW25), which garnered a nationally-representative sample of 1,240 respondents in English and 401 respondents in Spanish. The survey included a battery of questions asking respondents the extent to which they support or oppose the use of AI in various activities of the forecast process, and if they believe AI can perform those activities well and with the well-being of humans in mind. Somewhat surprisingly, respondents were more supportive of using AI for communication and warning support than they were for developing new predictions and improving model efficiency. Overall, Spanish respondents were more supportive of the use of AI across all forecast activities than English respondents. Findings from this work can help the NWS better understand public perceptions of and support for the use of AI in weather forecasting as it continues to deploy AI technologies.

497177.title: Implementation of the MetOp-SG-A1 Microwave Sounder (MWS) in the Microwave Integrated Retrieval System (MiRS)
497177.authors: Yong-Keun Lee, CISESS, Ellicott City, MD; and S. Liu, J. X. Yang, X. Liang, W. Wang, and H. Meng
497177.abstract: This study aims to ensure continuity of NOAA MiRS operational products in the post-MetOp era by providing a critical pathway for operational implementation of MiRS for EUMETSAT Polar System-Second Generation (EPS-SG) data. The MiRS algorithm is expected to play a key role in generating microwave retrieval products from MWS, which are critical to the success of NOAA and EUMETSAT’s Joint Polar System (JPS) mission. This report summarizes the development of the MIRS processing and retrieval algorithms and software development, as well as the testing and validation of processing algorithms related to MetOp-SG-A1 Microwave Sounder (MWS). Following the launch of the first EPS-SG satellite, Metop-SG-A1, in August 2025, MWS data became available at NOAA in mid-December 2025. Since then, the MiRS algorithm and software have been updated to accommodate actual MWS measurements, enabling the generation of MWS Environmental Data Records (EDRs). Since March 24, 2026, the noise levels of the G-band (183GHz) channels increased significantly. This report will also present an assessment of the impact of the increased noise on the MiRS retrievals.

497178.title: From Turbulence-Enhanced Settling to Warm-Rain Formation: Physical Mechanisms and Environmental Sensitivities
497178.authors: Ming Zhu, University of oklahoma, Norman, OK; and Z. J. Lebo
497178.abstract: Interactions between turbulence and cloud microphysics remain a major source of uncertainty in weather and climate prediction. Turbulence can modify hydrometeor fall speeds, thereby altering particle growth, precipitation formation, and the spatial and temporal distribution of fallout. Although these effects can be critical, their underlying physical controls remain poorly constrained and are rarely represented, especially in operational cloud microphysics schemes. This study aims to determine how turbulence-enhanced hydrometeor fall speeds affect the collision growth of cloud droplets, and the impact of this growth on the formation of warm clouds and warm rain—particularly within the "size gap" region. The motivation comes from previous Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model experiments using the Predicted Particle Properties (P3) microphysics scheme. A laboratory-derived relationship between turbulence and snow-particle fall speed was implemented in P3. Idealized orographic simulations showed that turbulence-enhanced fall speeds reduced particle residence times and shifted snowfall toward the windward side of the mountain range. Real-case simulations over southern Wyoming and northern Colorado further indicated enhanced snow accumulation over elevated terrain and increased collision rates within the boundary layer. These results suggested that the size dependence of turbulence-enhanced settling may influence precipitation not only through faster fallout but also by modifying the relative fall speeds between hydrometeors. We extend this physical mechanism to warm cloud collision–coalescence. Laboratory-derived preferential sweeping relationships are used to modify droplet settling velocities and construct a turbulence-enhanced collision kernel. The Kinematic Driver model coupled with an Eulerian bin microphysics scheme is employed as a controlled process-level framework to compare the modified kernel with Long gravitational kernel. KiD serves here as a diagnostic tool: the vertical motion prescribed in KiD-A allows us to isolate the direct effect of turbulent collisions on cloud droplet growth. Analysis of the turbulent kernel function indicates that this turbulence-induced effect—driven by increased relative velocity—depends heavily on droplet size. The most pronounced enhancement occurs within the radius range of approximately 15–40 μm; in this interval, diffusional growth has slowed down, and gravity-driven collision-coalescence has not yet become efficient—a region known as the "bottleneck." The most significant impact on the bottleneck region logically leads to the conclusion that: relative to the Long kernel, the turbulence-enhanced kernel accelerates the transfer of liquid-water mass into drizzle- and precipitation-sized drops and promotes an earlier precipitation. Environmental sensitivity experiments show that prescribed updraft velocity exerts the strongest control on the relative impact of kernel enhancement. Turbulence-enhanced collisions have their visible effect under weak-to-moderate updrafts, when gravitational collection alone little or delayed precipitation. Under strong updrafts, precipitation develops rapidly for all kernels, reducing differences in onset timing, although turbulence enhancement still modestly increases peak precipitation. Temperature perturbations modulate precipitation produces but do not alter the primary dependence on dynamic forcing. These results identify a transferable physical mechanism rather than a KiD-specific model response: turbulence-induced preferential sweeping selectively enhances collision rates within the critical "size gap" region, accelerating cloud droplet growth and thereby increasing the peak intensity and advancing the onset of warm-cloud precipitation. This process-level understanding can guide implementation in bin and bulk microphysics schemes across weather and climate models. It also provides physically meaningful predictors and constraints for machine-learning parameterizations, including droplet-size distributions, the location and width of the kernel-enhancement region, ε, U_rms, and environmental forcing.

497181.title: The Critical Number and Size of Precipitation Embryos to Accelerate Warm Rain Initiation
497181.authors: Jung-Sub Lim, CIRES, Boulder, CO, Germany; and Y. Noh, H. LEE, and F. Hoffmann
497181.abstract: Understanding warm rain initiation through droplet collision and coalescence remains a fundamental challenge in cloud microphysics. While sufficiently large droplets, or precipitation embryos (PEs), can accelerate collision-coalescence, it remains unclear how many and how large these droplets must be to substantially affect rain initiation. Here, we address this question using an ensemble of box simulations with Lagrangian cloud microphysics. We show that warm rain initiation is substantially accelerated only when the size, number, or combined abundance of PEs exceeds a critical threshold. Below this threshold, enhanced collection by PEs is offset by the suppression of collisions among non-PE droplets, resulting in little or no acceleration of rain formation. We further examine how this threshold depends on the initial droplet size distribution and turbulence-enhanced collision efficiency. More or larger PEs are required when collision-coalescence is already efficient without PEs, such as for broader droplet size distributions or stronger turbulence effects. These results identify quantitative conditions under which precipitation embryos can influence warm rain formation and may help constrain the effects of PE-like particles introduced intentionally or unintentionally in weather and climate intervention approaches, including rain enhancement or marine cloud brightening.

497182.title: Evaluating CMAQ PM₂.₅ Chemical Composition Using ASCENT Observations Across Diverse U.S. Environments
497182.authors: Merve Eke, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA; and S. Gwak, W. Zhang, K. Paredero, Y. Hu, R. Liu, S. Jeon, Y. Cui, E. Bowey, B. Ries, G. Pena, T. Hu, H. Baliaka, R. Ward, P. Kumar, R. Flagan, E. Bentley, L. N. Hawkins, R. Bahreini, S. M. Raffuse, A. M. Dillner, N. L. Ng, and A. G. Russell
497182.abstract: The first year of high-temporal-resolution observations from the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry Measurement Network (ASCENT) and the Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) mission, available in 2024, provides an unprecedented opportunity to evaluate chemical transport models. While model assessments have traditionally relied on total PM₂.₅ mass, routine measurements of aerosol chemical composition have been limited. ASCENT fills this observational gap by providing continuous, high-time-resolution measurements of PM₂.₅ chemical components at 12 locations across the United States. This study evaluates CMAQ at the speciation level using observations from four ASCENT sites: Pico Rivera, Rubidoux, Joshua Tree, and South DeKalb. CMAQ simulations were performed for 2024 at 12 km horizontal resolution over the continental United States. Model performance was evaluated using annual, seasonal, and diurnal analyses of PM₂.₅ chemical species. Pico Rivera represents an urban environment in Los Angeles County influenced by both anthropogenic and biogenic emissions and complex topography. Rubidoux and Joshua Tree are located downwind of the Los Angeles metropolitan area, while South DeKalb, located downwind of Atlanta, represents a mixture of urban and biogenic emission influences. To further investigate the causes of model biases, ISORROPIA-II was used to estimate aerosol liquid water content and particle acidity, and reverse-mode calculations were performed to estimate the NH₃ emissions required for CMAQ to reproduce the ASCENT observations. Comparisons between ASCENT observations and CMAQ simulations reveal both strengths and limitations in the model's representation of PM₂.₅ composition. At South DeKalb, CMAQ reproduced the temporal variability of PM₂.₅ reasonably well but consistently underestimated observed concentrations, with the largest biases occurring in organic aerosol and equivalent black carbon (eBC), suggesting missing emission sources such as cooking activities. At Pico Rivera and Rubidoux, substantial underestimation of ammonium (NH₄⁺) suggests that NH₃ emissions are underestimated in the emissions inventory. In Joshua Tree, CMAQ failed to reproduce an episodic enhancement in potassium (K), eBC, and organic aerosol, indicating a likely biomass-burning influence that was not adequately represented by the model. Overall, the results demonstrate that combining high-time-resolution aerosol composition measurements with thermodynamic analysis provides valuable insight into emission inventory deficiencies and aerosol chemistry. This integrated evaluation framework helps identify missing or underestimated emission sources and offers guidance for improving CMAQ simulations and next-generation air quality modeling.

497188.title: Evaluation of Real-Time Forecast Support Products Based on Aircraft Reconnaissance
497188.authors: Jonathan L. Vigh, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and J. C. DeHart, E. A. Hendricks, A. J. DesRosiers, C. M. Rozoff, J. Lee, M. M. Bell, N. M. Dorst, J. A. Zhang, L. Bucci, and D. A. Zelinsky
497188.abstract: The U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) must make time-sensitive estimates of storm-centric parameters for tropical cyclones within their Area of Responsibility for every 6-hour forecast cycle. These parameters include (among others): the position of the moving storm center, intensity (maximum 1-min average winds at 10 m height), radius of maximum winds (RMW), and the maximum radial extent of 34-, 50-, and 64-kt winds in different quadrants of the storm. Aircraft reconnaissance observations in tropical cyclones offer a wealth of in situ and remotely sensed information that is of high quality and useful for informing operational estimates of these storm-centric parameters. Data available for analysis include High Density Observations (HDOBs), Tail Doppler Radar (TDR) data, dropwindsondes, and in situ observations from flight level. A data fusion framework known as the Colorado State University Surface Winds from Aircraft Using a Neural Network (SWANN) is used to process, quality control, and spatially analyze the data to obtain high-quality analyses of the TDR winds and flight level observations. A unified parameterization trained on winds from the Stepped Frequency Microwave Radiometer (SFMR) data provides a local estimate of the surface winds below each flight level data point, allowing a 2-d analysis of the surface wind field to be estimated. The parameterization takes into account characteristics such as the radial and azimuthal location within the storm, storm translation speed, and the type and height of each observation. The moving storm center is estimated using real-time wind centers determined by a modified form of the Willoughby-Chelmow (1982) center-finding technique. In parallel, flight level observations are also processed into a frame moving with the storm center in a system called FLIGHT-RT. Auxiliary information can be added from the Vortex Data Messages (VDMs) transmitted from reconnaissance flights. Finally, a temporal analysis of the parameters is undertaken using the Tropical Cyclone Observations-based Structure Real-Time (TC-OBS-RT) Database, which uses a data assimilation approach analogous to 4D-VAR called “1d-var-in-time” to assess variations of the target parameters in time. This framework allows comparison of the “raw” flight level observations with the data-fused surface wind estimates and offers the opportunity to transparently assess the impact of each individual observation on the resulting parameter estimate. The outputs of the data fusion system are provided to NHC forecasters in the form of forecaster support tools, including a graphical product, data which can be incorporated into their forecaster display systems, and a text-based product which provides a temporal summary of the key storm parameters. This talk will focus on the evaluation of retrospective and real-time results from the 2024, 2025, and 2026 hurricane seasons. One evaluation strategy is to examine the differences between the actual observations and assessed parameters (and comparison to independent observations like dropsondes). Another approach involves subjective assessment from NHC forecasters whether the forecaster support products are helpful, accurate, and time-saving. Challenging cases will be presented in addition to cases for which the methods worked well. We anticipate that wind center finding and creation of tracks in weak storms or storms with multiple vortices may result in the most challenging cases, however undersampled troichoidal wobbles in intense storms may also present considerable challenges. If time permits, results will also be presented from an observational intercomparison study being undertaken to better understand the relationships between disparate types of observations, and how this can inform time- and observation-dependent estimates of uncertainty bounds on the intensity estimates.

497189.title: Transformation in Action: NWS Embraces Nimble, Flexible, Mobile, and Eye-to-Eye
497189.authors: Kenneth E. Graham, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and B. Bingaman
497189.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) is transforming into a more nimble, flexible, and mobile agency, deepening its alignment with key decision-makers to better protect lives and property. This transformation focuses on enhancing how stakeholders receive and act upon weather and water intelligence through streamlined relationships and innovative delivery systems. This presentation explores the core pillars of the NWS transformation - our people, our infrastructure, and embracing a future that’s more eye-to-eye with decision makers - before, during, and after significant weather and water events. Specific initiative achievements and anticipated milestones will be highlighted, including our accelerated adoption of cloud technologies, the modernization of our core observational infrastructure, and our ongoing efforts to embed meteorologists with decision-makers at multiple governmental levels to eliminate any decision- making barriers. By showcasing successful collaborative initiatives and future-leaning strategies, we demonstrate the NWS’s leadership in building a more integrated and efficient Federal Weather Enterprise.

497190.title: Comparison of the VOC Composition of Ambient Air over Houston, Los Angeles, and New York City during Recent Airborne Measurement Intensives: AEROMMA 2023 and TexAQS 2026
497190.authors: Jessica Gilman, NOAA, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and V. A. Treadaway, M. Selby, C. B. Francoeur, A. G. Negron, A. Middlebrook, B. Kuster, C. Stockwell, M. M. Coggon, G. I. Gkatzelis, K. Bates, C. Warneke, I. B. Pollack, N. Schafer, J. Peischl, and S. S. Brown
497190.abstract: Volatile organic compounds (VOC) in urban areas are a complex mixture of primary emissions from anthropogenic and biogenic sources. Once emitted into the atmosphere, VOCs can react at varying rates to produce secondary VOCs and contribute to the production of ozone and secondary organic aerosol. Anthropogenic sources of VOC emissions in urban areas has been shifting from being dominated by on-road vehicle sources to that dominated by the use of volatile chemical products (VCPs), such as cleaning products, fragrances, paints, and coatings. Here we will present detailed chemical measurements of VOCs measured on airborne platforms over Los Angeles (LA) and New York City (NYC) during AEROMMA 2023 and Houston during TexAQS 2026. These three coastal cities offer interesting differences in VOC sources. NYC has the highest population density, LA has the largest number of vehicles, and Houston has the highest shipping traffic of any US port with >70% of the ships are liquid-bulk carriers serving the petrochemical industry along the Houston Ship Channel (HSC). This analysis will focus on elucidating the relative contributions of various VOC sources including VCP usage, fuel usage, energy/petrochemical production, and biogenic sources. To evaluate long-term chemical evolution, these data are compared against historic airborne and ground-based datasets, including TexAQS 2006, CalNex 2010, CalNexT 2021.

497191.title: Spatiotemporal Variability of TEMPO-Derived NO2 Mixing Height across U.S. Climate Regions
497191.authors: Clifford Boateng, Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS; and S. Ambinakudige and B. fosu
497191.abstract: Atmospheric mixing height is an important determinant of the vertical distribution and near-surface concentration of atmospheric trace gases, yet its characterization across large spatial domains remains constrained by the limited spatial coverage of conventional observations. The Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) geostationary satellite provides continuous daytime observations of atmospheric composition across North America, offering a new opportunity to investigate the spatial and temporal variability of atmospheric mixing using remotely sensed observations. This study combines TEMPO NO2 observations with U.S. EPA ground-based data and meteorological variables to develop an hourly continental-scale NO2 mixing height product. The resulting product was evaluated across the nine NOAA climate regions to characterize whether mixing height patterns vary systematically across distinct climatic environments. Mean NO2 mixing height varied substantially across regions, ranging from 336.28 m in the Northern Rockies and Plains to 523.52 m in the Northeast. Seasonal variability was also regionally distinct, with mixing heights generally increasing from winter to summer. The magnitude of this seasonal cycle was particularly pronounced in the Southwest, Upper Midwest, and Northern Rockies and Plains, while the Southeast exhibited comparatively weak seasonal variability. Daytime diurnal cycles showed a pronounced increase in mixing height across most regions, with particularly strong increases in the South, Ohio Valley, and Southwest. These results demonstrate substantial geographic heterogeneity in the temporal evolution of atmospheric mixing across the United States, likely reflecting differences in the meteorological and atmospheric environments among climate regions. The TEMPO-derived product expands the spatial characterization of atmospheric mixing beyond the coverage of conventional boundary layer observations and provides a foundation for investigating the meteorological processes underlying these regional differences. Ongoing analysis will use machine learning methods to examine the relative influence and relationships of meteorological variables on NO2 mixing height across the climate regions.

497192.title: Reforecasts, Real-Time Inputs, and Redundancy in Operational AI Weather Forecasting to Build Trusted Pipelines at National Scale
497192.authors: Katie Kowal, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL; and A. Marchakitus, B. Dong, C. Aitken, R. Masiwal, M. Gupta, W. Boos, A. Jina, and P. Hassanzadeh
497192.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) weather models have lowered the cost of producing forecasts, removing supercomputing budgets as a prerequisite for running real-time global forecasts. Yet transitioning a research-grade AI model that performs well on global benchmarks into a trusted, operational workflow that a national meteorological agency can deliver raises challenges rarely documented in the literature. Operational systems must establish sufficient cross-institutional trust for novel forecasts to inform decisions while supporting verification against local ground truth and generating enough reforecasts to validate and improve skill. They must also adapt models designed around reanalysis initial conditions for real-time use and maintain reproducible, redundant outputs across cloud, high-performance computing, and local infrastructure.
