Here we report practical lessons from serving as the technical partner for two real-time AI-based subseasonal forecasting pilots for farmers: a 2025 monsoon-onset forecast with the Indian government that reached 38 million farmers ahead of a national scale-up to more than 50 million farmers in 2026, and a 2026 pilot with the Ethiopian government that forecast Kiremt rainy-season onset for 100,000 farmers in the central highlands. We describe the reforecast configurations and parallelization strategies used to generate sufficiently large archives for robust model evaluation and calibration at agronomically relevant lead times. We then explain how AI models like NeuralGCM were adapted to use operational initial conditions rather than reanalysis, enabling their use in operational forecast systems. Finally, we examine reliability and cost tradeoffs across hybrid computational environments to identify practical approaches for delivering timely, reproducible forecasts. Drawing on these deployments, we identify requirements for moving AI forecasts from research prototypes toward operational workflows and offer recommendations for keeping AI weather systems open, testable, reproducible, and trustworthy as their use scales.

497193.title: Engaging Students in Severe Weather Observations: Educational and Outreach Activities Using the Mobile Rapid Scan X-band Polarimetric (RaXPol) Radar in 2026
497193.authors: Hsiu-Wei Hsu, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and T. Y. Yu, D. J. Bodine, R. Tanamachi, A. Naik, R. Cross, and P. E. Kirstetter
497193.abstract: The Rapid-Scan X-band Polarimetric (RaXPol) radar provides high spatiotemporal resolution observations through its mobility and ability to complete a 10-elevation volume scan in just 20 s. These capabilities make RaXPol well suited for investigating severe storm evolution and fine-scale microphysical and dynamical processes. Beyond its research applications, RaXPol serves as a versatile platform for hands-on education and outreach in atmospheric science. As one of the instruments in the National Science Foundation’s Community Instrumentation and Facilities (CIF) program, RaXPol supports research, education, and outreach activities by providing adaptive material to the wider community. During 2026, RaXPol visited hundreds of K–12 students through various education and outreach activities. In meteorology and engineering higher education courses, approximately 100 students have acquired in-depth, hands-on experience with mobile radar. Additionally, over 60 participants from multiple institutions had the opportunity to operate RaXPol and participated in data collection and analysis through in-person and/or virtual experiments. We will highlight two major educational and outreach activities on field experiment. The first was the collaboration with the Purdue University (PU) over a two-week period in the summer of 2026. RaXPol was used to support student research projects focusing on ZDR columns in thunderstorms in the Severe Storms Field Work course. Fourteen students from PU participated in severe storm observation with RaXPol. An associated public outreach activity attracted more than 460 visitors to a local science museum. Although in-person field experiments provide a unique learning experience, the student participation is often limited by the time, location and travel costs. To overcome these limitations and broaden participation, a virtual radar workshop was held in conjunction with the Phased Array Polarimetry Electrification Lightning (PAPEL). PAPEL focused on the dual-polarimetric signatures of lightning in the summer of 2026. The virtual radar workshop includes short courses and virtual experiments. The short courses aim to help participants learn about weather radar fundamentals, phased array radar, lightning physics, and field campaign design for lightning observation. During the virtual experiments, the participants gain experience in dual-polarimetric radar data analysis and real-time discussion with radar operators in the field through live streaming, online chatting with Slack and Zoom meetings, and real-time radar data displays. The virtual radar workshop allowed 45 undergraduate, graduate students, and postdocs from 26 institutions to participate. Participants from both activities provided positive feedback on their learning experiences. More participants’ feedback from both activities will be discussed.

497195.title: GEMS-PEARL: A Future Low-Cost, Modular Platform for Microwave Sounding and Imaging
497195.authors: Sean McKee, Weather Stream, Inc., Boulder, CO; and J. Sahli, A. Venkitasubramony, D. Lee, D. Orthel, A. Gasiewski, M. Hurowitz, M. Marques, R. Belter, and E. Dai
497195.abstract: Monitoring key environmental variables such as ocean surface vector winds, tropical cyclone intensity, soil moisture, and sea ice characteristics requires sensitive passive microwave measurement capabilities spanning frequencies from P through G band. However, the large reflector apertures required for observation in lower frequency bands have historically resulted in instruments that are costly and complex to develop and deploy, limiting data coverage and revisit rates for these key environmental variables. GEMS-PEARL is a planned family of passive microwave missions currently under development by Weather Stream, providing a modular and scalable foundation for a flexible, low-cost constellation for global environmental intelligence, building on the success of the Compact Ocean Wind Vector Radiometer (COWVR) instrument demonstration. The primary configuration of GEMS-PEARL features a large (>1 meter) deployable antenna in a conical-scanning configuration with fully polarimetric measurements across Ku, K, and Ka bands to enable enhanced retrievals of ocean surface vector winds and surface characterization. Here, we provide an overview of the mission concepts enabled by the GEMS-PEARL platform, with a focus on the development of a lightweight, deployable antenna and the anticipated performance of ocean surface vector wind retrievals. The GEMS-PEARL platform uses hyperspectral digital radiometer (HDR) backends to enable radio-frequency interference (RFI) detection and mitigation, along with innovations in instrument architecture and antenna temperature retrieval methods designed to improve calibration stability and geophysical retrieval performance.

497196.title: AeroMELD: Bridging Particle-Resolved Fidelity and Reduced-Order Efficiency for Aerosol Dynamics
497196.authors: Wenhan Tang, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; and R. Yang, J. H. Curtis, E. Saleh, L. Patel, P. A. Bosler, N. Riemer, and M. West
497196.abstract: Accurately representing aerosol mixing state remains a central challenge in aerosol–cloud interaction modeling. Particle-resolved models such as PartMC preserve the joint distribution of particle size and composition and therefore capture mixing-state effects on cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), optical properties, and heterogeneous ice nucleation. Their high-dimensional states and computational cost, however, make routine use in large ensembles and three-dimensional atmospheric models impractical. Modal and sectional models achieve much greater efficiency through prescribed low-dimensional representations, but these projections can discard particle-level information that controls climate-relevant diagnostics. In this study, we extend our Aerosol Measure Embedding for Latent Dynamics (AeroMELD) framework from diagnostic representation to prognostic process dynamics. AeroMELD learns compact aerosol states directly from weighted particle-resolved populations; here, we use aerosol coagulation as a nonlinear, distribution-dependent proof of concept for advancing those states prognostically. AeroMELD compresses a variable population of nominally 1,000 particles and 15 chemical species—approximately 15,000 particle-state variables—into nine latent shape coordinates and one total-number coordinate. A frozen Decoder reconstructs 550 outputs spanning size-resolved mass, composition, and number distributions; CCN activation; optical scattering and absorption; and immersion-freezing behavior. Known concentration scaling from the Smoluchowski coagulation equation is built into a latent neural ordinary differential equation, allowing the network to focus on how the normalized particle population evolves. Recursive multistep training and diagnostic-aware supervision support stable long-duration predictions. The resulting model advances only a ten-coordinate state while preserving access to the mixing-state-sensitive outputs carried by the particle-resolved representation. We evaluate AeroMELD through recursive 48-h predictions on a held-out test set spanning diverse initial aerosol populations. Across all post-initial test states, the median symmetric error is 2.9% for latent population shape and 0.56% for total number concentration, while the 95th-percentile latent-shape error is 7.5%. The rollouts reproduce the principal coagulation-driven changes in particle size and composition while retaining coherent evolution in CCN activation, optical properties, and frozen fraction. In a representative matched case, both AeroMELD and a 180-coordinate sectional representation capture the decline in total number, but the ten-coordinate AeroMELD state follows the particle-resolved CCN spectra much more closely at both the initial and 24-h states. The same learned vector field remains stable across integration steps from 1 s to 8 h, and multistep training reduces mean 24-h latent root-mean-square error by 17.6%, with the largest benefits at longer lead times and in the upper error tail. AeroMELD also transforms the computational cost of particle-resolved coagulation: it generates complete 48-h trajectories at approximately 900 trajectories per second, representing an approximately 140,000-fold speedup over PartMC. This acceleration combines compact learned dynamics with GPU batch parallelism. More broadly, AeroMELD reframes particle-resolved simulation from an expensive modeling endpoint into a source for learning compact prognostic variables. This coagulation study provides AeroMELD’s first process-level proof of concept, showing that a learned aerosol state can be both dynamically useful and diagnostically rich. It opens a path toward a shared aerosol representation advanced by multiple physics-aware AI operators while retaining the evolving mixing-state sensitivity needed for cloud activation, radiation, and ice formation.

497198.title: Introducing GFDL's New Atmospheric Model (AM5)
497198.authors: David Jeffrey Paynter, GFDL, Princeton, NJ; and V. Naik, B. Xiang, Z. Tan, R. Kramer, P. Lin, H. Guo, and S. Malyshev
497198.abstract: The Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL) is developing its next-generation atmospheric model (AM5) to enhance the representation of weather and climate processes across sub-seasonal to centennial timescales. AM5 integrates significant advancements, including a quadrupling of horizontal resolution (from 100 km to 25 km), enhanced vertical resolution, and improved physical parameterizations for radiation, cloud microphysics, the planetary boundary layer, and convective gravity wave drag, among other processes. We present results focused on recent developments, specifically the addition of the RRTMG-RTE radiation code, the coupling of AM5 with a new land model, refined convective mass flux closure and momentum transport schemes, and more rigorous model tuning and optimization. Key improvements over the previous-generation model are seen in the simulation of Earth's radiation budget, the diurnal cycle of land precipitation, the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (QBO), tropical cyclone characteristics, and subtropical coastal stratocumulus. Furthermore, we provide a detailed evaluation of how model climatology, variability, and extreme events are impacted by improved model physics versus increased horizontal resolution. By balancing physical fidelity and computational efficiency, AM5 provides a concrete foundation for GFDL's future coupled Earth system models and prediction systems, offering key insights for the transition toward km-scale Earth system modeling.

497204.title: Toward a Timely, Reproducible, and More Complete Account of Heat-Attributable Mortality in the United States
497204.authors: Quinn H Adams, CIRES, Boulder, CO; Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA; Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA; and C. W. Milando, N. McMillan, Z. Popp, A. M. James, and G. Wellenius
497204.abstract: Extreme heat is an increasingly important contributor to mortality in the United States, yet deaths explicitly coded as heat-related in vital statistics capture only a fraction of the total burden, while epidemiologic estimates remain sparse and infrequently updated. Translating routinely available meteorological and mortality data into actionable health information could provide a practical foundation for more timely and spatially resolved heat-health surveillance. We estimated heat-attributable mortality across 530 U.S. counties, representing 73% of the population, using publicly available data and a reproducible two-stage time-series framework combining conditional Poisson regression with distributed lag nonlinear models. This analysis also provides a use case for the open-source cityClimateHealth R package, which facilitates transparent and reproducible implementation of established methods for estimating exposure-response relationships and attributable mortality. Between 2018 and 2025, heat contributed to an estimated annual average of 6,433 deaths (95% CI: 4,518–8,534), equivalent to 0.29% of all deaths and 2.58 deaths per 100,000 population. This estimate was approximately 3.8 times the annual average of 1,702 heat-related deaths officially recorded on death certificates nationwide. If estimated rates were extended to the full contiguous U.S. population, the annual burden could approach 8,931 deaths (95% CI: 6,011–11,920). At the county level, official records captured a median of only 15.4% of modeled heat-attributable deaths. Heat-related death counts were also suppressed in publicly available vital statistics for 66.4% of counties, despite these counties accounting for 34.6% of modeled heat-attributable mortality. Importantly, mortality burden was not explained by heat exposure or population size alone. Attributable mortality rates varied substantially among counties with similar extreme-temperature profiles and populations, revealing locations with disproportionately high heat-related risk. Clark County, NV; Oklahoma County, OK; Maricopa County, AZ; and Harris County, TX emerged as notable high-rate outliers relative to counties experiencing similarly high temperatures or supporting similarly large populations, with additional outliers observed across the exposure and population distributions. These findings demonstrate how publicly available climatological and mortality data can support a transparent, high-resolution, and routinely updatable heat-health surveillance system. Such a framework could complement vital statistics by identifying not only when and where extreme heat occurs, but where comparable heat exposure produces disproportionately large health impacts. Distinguishing these locations can help reveal differences in underlying vulnerability or protective capacity and support more targeted heat preparedness, resource allocation, and climate adaptation.

497205.title: Uncrewed Aircraft System Intercomparison with a Fixed Tower Network: Sensor Calibration, Correction, and Flight-Dynamic Effects on Measurement Fidelity
497205.authors: Melissa A. Wagner, CU Boulder IRISS, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and A. Mord, B. Argrow, S. W. Hoch, T. M. Weckwerth, W. O. J. Brown, M. Rhodes, and E. N. Rasmussen
497205.abstract: The Mobile Uncrewed Systems for Atmospheric Science (MUSAS) facility, an NSF Community Instrument Facility operated within the University of Colorado Boulder's Integrated Remote and In Situ Sensing (IRISS) program, conducts atmospheric boundary layer sampling using the RAAVEN small uncrewed aircraft system. This work presents an intercomparison between RAAVEN and the 32 m level of the NCAR Integrated Surface Flux System (ISFS) tower at the Marshall Field Site, evaluating wind, temperature, relative humidity, and pressure agreement using a variance-ratio-and-bias framework adapted from recent multi-platform validation studies. Co-location between the two platforms was established through a two-stage altitude quality-control procedure. An initial approach matched RAAVEN observations to the tower using mean altitude alone; this was found to be insufficient, as a bin's mean altitude could fall within the target tolerance band even when the aircraft was mid-climb or mid-descent, with individual samples spanning tens of meters. A supplementary altitude-range check was added to exclude such transitional bins, which proved essential to eliminating spurious pressure and thermodynamic comparisons at flight-phase transitions. A dynamic-heating correction, accounting for kinetic warming of the exposed temperature sensor at flight airspeed, reduced RAAVEN's mean temperature bias relative to the tower from 0.35°C to 0.16°C, demonstrating close agreement once platform-motion effects were removed. A consistent static pressure offset of approximately 1.7 hPa was also identified between RAAVEN and the tower; applying the hypsometric equation to the observed altitude and pressure differences indicated this offset was substantially larger than could be explained by RAAVEN's actual altitude difference from the tower sensor, pointing to a sensor calibration effect rather than a geometric one. A central finding of this work concerns the influence of aircraft maneuvering on measurement quality. Both wind speed and potential temperature exhibited significantly elevated variance relative to the tower during turning flight, with variance ratio correlating with within-bin airspeed (true airspeed, TAS) variability during turns (r≈0.36–0.40, p=0.003) but showing no such relationship during straight, level flight segments. Because RAAVEN's wind vector and airspeed are both derived from differential pressure measurements on the same nine-hole multi-hole probe (9HP), this cross-validated result—consistent in magnitude and significance across two independently derived variables—suggests that banked flight pushes the aircraft outside the probe's wind-tunnel-calibrated angle-of-attack and sideslip envelope, degrading both quantities simultaneously through a shared upstream mechanism rather than independent sensor artifacts. Complementary analyses further characterize wind measurement quality across multiple flight trajectories by comparing wind direction and speed derived independently from the 9HP, the autopilot's GPS-and-airspeed-based estimate, and the tower. Autopilot-derived wind estimates closely tracked those from the 9HP, providing RAAVEN with two independent, mutually consistent onboard wind measurements—a result that lends confidence to the platform's wind-sensing capability beyond agreement with the tower reference alone. A heading-dependent wind bias correction, exploiting near-orthogonal flight legs under locally steady wind conditions to isolate systematic pointing offsets, was applied to RAAVEN's 9HP wind measurements to improve agreement with the tower. Turbulence characteristics were further compared through power spectral density analysis of wind fluctuations from the 9HP and tower, and through a Taylor's frozen-turbulence space-time correlation analysis that extends the comparison by accounting for advection between the spatially offset platforms. Together, these results demonstrate that careful attention to co-location quality control, sensor-specific corrections, and flight-maneuver-dependent measurement quality is essential for rigorous UAS-tower intercomparison, and that RAAVEN's independent, redundant onboard wind estimation capability provides a meaningful additional layer of confidence beyond single-instrument validation. These findings offer practical guidance for quality-control procedures, flight-pattern design, and calibration strategies applicable to small UAS platforms conducting boundary-layer research more broadly.

497206.title: Investigation of Agricultural Emissions on Ozone and Aerosols in South Korea: Insights from Aircraft Observations, Satellite Data, and WRF-Chem Simulations
497206.authors: Si-Wan Kim, Yonsei University, Seoul, Seoul, South korea; Yonsei University, Seoul, Seoul, Korea, Republic of (South); and K. M. Kim and S. Seo
497206.abstract: Agricultural and livestock activities are important sources of nitrogen oxides (NOₓ), ammonia (NH₃), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), including ethanol. In this study, we investigate the impacts of agricultural emissions on ozone and aerosol formation in South Korea using aircraft observations from the KORUS-AQ field campaign, satellite retrievals of NH₃ and formaldehyde (HCHO), and WRF-Chem model simulations. KORUS-AQ observations show that ozone concentrations in regions of South Korea with intensive agricultural activity are strongly correlated with nitrous oxide (N₂O) and methane (CH₄), suggesting a potential link between agricultural emissions and ozone production. These regions also exhibit enhanced NH₃ concentrations in Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) satellite observations. We first improve the representation of agricultural NH₃ emissions using top-down estimates constrained by CrIS NH₃ observations. We then adjust methanol and ethanol emissions based on VOC-to-NH₃ emission ratios derived from aircraft observations and CrIS NH₃ retrievals over California’s San Joaquin Valley during the FIREX-AQ field campaign, where ethanol measurements were available. WRF-Chem simulations using the base emission inventory underestimate ozone and HCHO concentrations over agricultural regions of South Korea compared with KORUS-AQ aircraft observations and HCHO retrievals from the Ozone Mapping and Profiler Suite (OMPS). Incorporating VOC emissions scaled to the top-down NH₃ emissions improves the simulated ozone and HCHO concentrations. The updated NH₃ emissions also substantially improve the simulation of aerosols, particularly secondary inorganic aerosol components. These results demonstrate that agricultural emissions can substantially influence ozone, HCHO, and inorganic aerosol formation in South Korea and suggest that agricultural sources may play an important role in regional air quality across East Asia.

497208.title: Implementation and Testing of the Multigrid Beta Filter for Radar Data Assimilation within the MPAS-JEDI 3DEnVar Framework: 2021 Hurricane Ida Test Case
497208.authors: Jonathan Tyler DeGraw, CAPS, Norman, OK; and N. A. Snook, C. Liu, M. Xue, T. Lei, R. J. Purser, M. S. F. V. Pondeca, and M. Rancic
497208.abstract: In three-dimensional ensemble variational (3DEnVar) data assimilation (DA), flow-dependent background error covariances are generated from a finite number of ensemble forecasts. Since the resultant background error covariance matrix is rank-deficient relative to the degrees of freedom of the associated forecast model, covariance localization is applied to prevent spurious correlations between analysis variables that are spatially distant. Traditionally, isotropic or anisotropic quasi-Gaussian localization is performed using spatial filters such as the recursive filter. However, these techniques require global communication among MPI tasks on distributed-memory parallel computers and, therefore, cannot be efficiently parallelized. One recently developed method is the multi-grid beta filter (MGBF), which approximates Gaussian localization using a beta filter. Initial tests of the MGBF in prior studies have shown improved computational efficiency versus the recursive filter. This study investigates the performance of the MGBF relative to the “Background error on an Unstructured Mesh Package – Normalized Interpolated Convolution from an Adaptive Subgrid” (BUMP-NICAS) method for variational radar DA in the MPAS-JEDI 3DEnVar framework. Hurricane Ida (2021) is chosen as the test case. Three primary experiments are conducted: (1) an experiment in which no data are assimilated (ExpNoDA), (2) an experiment in which BUMP-NICAS is used for covariance localization (ExpNICAS), and (3) an experiment that utilizes MGBF for covariance localization (ExpMGBF). ExpNICAS and ExpMGBF both assimilate Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor System (MRMS) radar reflectivity, Weather Surveillance Radar – 1988 Doppler radar radial velocity, and conventional observations. Additional experiments will be conducted to calibrate MGBF parameters, including vertical and horizontal aspect tensors and scale weights. The experiments utilize a 30-member ensemble initialized from the 29 August 2021 0600 UTC Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) initial conditions. An additional member, used explicitly as background in 3DEnVar, is initialized from the Global Forecast System (GFS) initial conditions. Six-hour forecasts are performed to provide the background ensemble for the first DA cycle. For each experiment, cycled DA is conducted hourly for a total of 4 cycles between 1200 UTC and 1500 UTC on 29 August 2021. 3DEnVar is coupled two-way with the local ensemble transform Kalman filter (LETKF), where LETKF provides ensemble perturbations to 3DEnVar and 3DEnVar provides the ensemble mean to LETKF. After the DA portion of the experiment is completed, 15-h deterministic forecasts are produced from the 3DEnVar analyses. Initial results from the three experiments will be presented to systematically evaluate the computational performance of the MGBF compared to BUMP-NICAS. The characteristics of analyses and forecasts produced using the two methods will also be discussed. Figure caption: Composite reflectivity for (a, d) background, (b, e) final analysis, and (c, f) analysis increments for (a-c) BUMP-NICAS and (d-f) MGBF in preliminary experiments for the Hurricane Ida test case.

497209.title: Beyond the Airport: ASTM F3673 and a New Framework for Evaluating Weather Information for Low-Altitude Aviation
497209.authors: Christopher M. Zarzar, TruWeather Solutions, Reston, VA; and D. Berchoff
497209.abstract: The aviation weather observing system has historically been concentrated around airports and designed primarily to support conventional crewed aviation. As aviation operations increasingly move into the low-altitude environment, this legacy aviation weather observation system leaves significant gaps in the availability of representative weather information. These gaps are particularly consequential for uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS) and advanced air mobility (AAM) operations, which operate routinely away from traditional airport weather observing infrastructure and can be highly sensitive to localized variations in atmospheric conditions. These same limitations affect existing general aviation and helicopter operations conducted in areas where reliable, approved weather observations are sparse. Expanding the number and diversity of weather information sources could substantially improve low-altitude situational awareness, but doing so introduces a fundamental question: how should the aviation community determine what weather information from a non-traditional source is sufficiently reliable for operational use? ASTM F3673 Standard Specification for Performance for Weather Information Reports, Data Interfaces, and Weather Information Providers (WIPs), represents an industry-consensus approach to answering that question. Rather than relying exclusively on the traditional paradigm of certifying a particular observing system, F3673 introduces a data-centric framework that evaluates the performance of the reported weather information and the evidence supporting its use. The framework is intended to accommodate information originating from a range of sources, including conventional in situ sensors, remote sensing systems, derived observations, and weather analyses, while establishing common expectations for data performance, quality control, reliability, security, metadata, and information management. This presentation will introduce the AMS community to F3673, the motivation behind its development, and the ASTM consensus standards process through which it continues to evolve. Particular attention will be given to the recently completed Means of Compliance effort, which was established to translate the requirements of the published standard into objective methods for demonstrating compliance. That process has also identified areas where the original standard requires refinement, illustrating an important characteristic of F3673 as a living framework expected to evolve as operational experience, testing, technology, and regulatory needs mature. The broader significance of this work extends beyond UAS and AAM. Establishing a defensible pathway for evaluating additional sources of weather observations could enable reliable information from previously underutilized networks and emerging observing technologies to supplement the traditional aviation weather infrastructure, particularly in low-altitude environments that remain underserved today. F3673 therefore represents an important first step toward increasing the density, diversity, and operational usability of weather information available to the aviation community. Finally, the presentation will discuss the next standards challenge. While F3673 addresses weather observations, it does not establish performance requirements for weather forecasts. As increasingly automated aviation operations require predictive information for preflight and in-flight risk management, a complementary standard for low-altitude nowcasts will be needed. Current ASTM discussions are beginning to examine how such a framework should address forecast performance, uncertainty, and the differing information needs of human decision-makers and increasingly autonomous systems.

497210.title: FLDAS3-Global: An Advanced Hydrologic Model to Assess the Impact of Climate Extremes on Food Security World-Wide
497210.authors: Kimberly Slinski, NASA GSFC, Lakewood, CO; and A. Hazra, A. McNally, J. nattala, A. Getirana, C. C. Funk, S. Shukla, and G. Husak
497210.abstract: Climate extremes affect the livelihoods of millions of people world-wide. Countries experience elevated food insecurity due to political instability, conflict, violence, poverty and climatic shocks. Extreme events like droughts and floods exacerbate underlying food insecurity, resulting in complex emergencies requiring tremendously challenging humanitarian response. Early warning of climatic extremes is essential to governments and relief agencies who plan for and respond to these humanitarian crises. NASA’s Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Land Data Assimilation System (FLDAS) models were developed to provide high quality data on climate extremes in data-sparse, developing countries. The FLDAS models deliver timely, accurate data to support FEWS NET’s food security assessments, outlooks, and alerts, which provide early warning information and analyses of current and future acute food insecurity in the most food-insecure countries world-wide. This study presents the next generation FLDAS3-Global modeling system. The model is forced by advanced meteorological fields, including the new CHIRPS3 daily precipitation datasets. Two CHIRPS3 daily precipitation datasets are available: CHIRPS3 downscaled from the pentad to daily timestep via ERA5 precipitation and CHIRPS3 downscaled via IMERG precipitation. The FLDAS3-Global is run via NASA’s Land Information System (LIS) framework. It employs the Noah-MP 4.0.1 land surface model and NASA’s newly released HyMAP3 routing model. FLDAS3-Global simulates the full energy and water balances as well as streamflow, providing daily output at 0.1 degree resolution over a quasi-global domain. This study presents the benchmarking results and assessment of the FLDAS3-Global model, highlighting skill improvements with the advancement in modeling methods and forcing datasets. This study also presents an intercomparison of model simulation using the two CHIRPS3 daily precipitation datasets, highlighting how choice of precipitation product impacts the water and energy balance.

497212.title: Global Radiative Forcing from Projected Boreal Wildfires and Sensitivity to Aerosol Process Representation
497212.authors: Luke Fraser-Leach, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada; and L. Feng-Keyes, P. J. Kushner, and E. Blanchard-Wrigglesworth
497212.abstract: Aerosol emissions from boreal wildfires have increased dramatically over the past two decades and are likely to continue to increase. Recent modelling studies investigating the global climate response to such emissions have drawn conflicting conclusions, likely partially due to differences in aerosol schemes among models. We characterise the atmospheric response to projected boreal fire aerosol forcing in two configurations of the Canadian Earth System Model (CanESM) that use different aerosol microphysics schemes. One of these is CanESM’s standard bulk one-moment aerosol scheme and the other is a more detailed two-moment scheme. Both configurations show a modest positive total effective radiative forcing (ERF) in the global mean, but this hides strong cancelling contributions from different regions. In the subtropics and midlatitudes, the two-moment scheme shows a negative ERF dominated by aerosol-cloud interactions, while the one-moment scheme shows a negligible ERF. Over the Arctic, ERF is positive and dominated by aerosol-radiation interactions in both schemes, but it is more positive in the two-moment scheme. We investigate the mechanisms driving these differences and speculate on how they may control boreal fire aerosol effects in other models.

497215.title: The Effect of Top-Down Turbulence on Surface Fluxes Across Seasons in a Colorado Mountain Valley
497215.authors: Brian J. Butterworth, Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences, CU Boulder, Boulder, CO; and B. Adler, C. J. Cox, J. D. Lundquist, T. P. Meyers, and E. Schwat
497215.abstract: Most surface flux schemes assume that near-surface turbulence is generated locally, by wind shear at the surface and by buoyancy. In the East River Valley of Colorado, this assumption fails when synoptic winds blow across the valley. Under these conditions, ridge-height shear layers and lee rotors generate turbulence that is transported downward to the valley floor. Schwat et al. (in review) showed that this "top-down" turbulence causes Monin-Obukhov-based schemes to underpredict surface fluxes during the snow-covered season. Here we use two years (2021–2023) of coordinated observations from the SPLASH, SAIL, and SOS campaigns to show that top-down turbulence is not confined to winter. At matched wind speeds, cross-valley synoptic flow produces higher near-surface turbulence than along-valley flow in all seasons, although vertical velocity skewness below ridge height indicates that daytime convection partly masks the top-down signature when the valley is snow-free. Flux anomalies, computed relative to a seasonal climatology, reveal that this excess turbulence shifts surface energy partitioning from sensible toward latent heat in both seasons. Building on these results, we present an objective method that uses eddy covariance and Doppler lidar data to detect top-down events. We use these events to test a bulk aerodynamic flux parameterization. Its surface parameters are constrained under along-valley flow, where turbulence is locally generated and similarity theory is expected to work, then applied under cross-valley flow, where turbulence is additionally imported from aloft. Because the parameterization represents only locally generated turbulence, the difference between measured and modeled fluxes provides a direct estimate of the surface exchange driven by imported turbulence. These estimates provide an observational basis for extending surface flux schemes to account for turbulence generated aloft, a process common in complex terrain but absent from current parameterizations.

497220.title: RANDALL - Is the Resonant Wave Interaction Approximation Consistent with the Dynamics of Internal Wave Fields?
497220.authors: Golan Bel, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Sdeh Boker, Israel; and E. Tziperman
497220.abstract: Nonlinear interaction and breaking of internal ocean waves are responsible for much of the interior ocean mixing, affecting ocean carbon storage and the global overturning circulation. These interactions may affect the empirical Garrett-Munk wave energy spectrum, in addition to the recently explored interaction of waves with ocean eddies. According to the resonant wave interaction approximation, which is commonly used to derive the kinetic equation for the energy spectrum, the dominant interactions are between wave triads whose wavevectors satisfy k=p+q, and whose frequencies satisfy ωk = |ωp±ωq|. In order to test the validity of the resonant wave interaction approximation, we examine several analytical derivations of the theory. The assumptions underlying each derivation are tested using idealized direct 2D, non-rotating numerical simulations, representing near-observed energy levels of the oceanic internal wave field. We show that most of the triads satisfying the resonant conditions do not contribute significantly to nonlinear wave energy transfer in our idealized 2D simulations. Furthermore, some interactions that are dominant in nonlinear energy transfers do not satisfy the resonance conditions. We also find that the slow-amplitude assumptions underlying the derivations are inconsistent with the simulated dynamics in this particular set of simulations, possibly explaining the inconsistency with the predictions of the resonant interaction theory. Preliminary results from 3D rotating simulations will be shown as well.

497221.title: Location, Location, Location: Improving Geolocation and Visualization of Fires Detected by Geostationary Satellites
497221.abstract: Fire detection with “moderate” or “coarse” resolution geostationary imagers such as the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) on the GOES-R satellites presents geolocation and visualization challenges. Knowledge of the ground location of active fire is critical, and so terrain correction for geostationary satellites was developed and implemented within NOAA’s Next Generation Fire System (NGFS). Sending firefighters to the wrong road or the wrong side of a mountain can cost precious time and decrease the chances of a fire being contained early. Terrain correction improves location of the pixel centroid and nominal pixel bounds, but it doesn’t boost knowledge of the geolocation of sub-pixel features like fires. Sometimes being within a couple kilometers of a fire may be good enough, but most of the time responders on the ground need more accurate representations of a fire’s location before they head out. Fortunately, improvements to the subpixel location of small fires seen in geostationary data are possible by leveraging the properties of the sensor and the processing applied to the raw data. Additionally, the imagery itself can be corrected for terrain, putting the fire signals in the correct place on the ground in imagery displayed in web mapping and geographic information systems. The use of automated centroiding to improve the geolocation of initial fire start locations will be demonstrated through case studies. The realtime creation of high-quality terrain corrected cloud optimized GeoTIFFs from geostationary data, imagery that can be used for fire and other applications, will also be covered. With ABI and its cousins proving to be remarkably sensitive to small fires, as demonstrated by the NGFS reliably picking up fires with single-digit fire radiative power (FRP) intensities, improving the geolocation of fire starts and the visual representation of fires increases the value and utility of the geostationary platforms when applied to the wildfire problem.

497222.title: An A Priori Framework for Training-Source Selection in Deep-Learning Climate Downscaling
497222.authors: Harish Baki, University at Albany, Albany, NY; University at Albany, Albany, NY; and S. Chinta
497222.abstract: Deep learning-based climate downscaling requires paired low-resolution and high-resolution training data, yet the low-resolution training source is rarely treated as an explicit experimental variable. This source generally falls into one of two categories: perfect prognosis (PP), in which the high-resolution target is coarsened to build its own training input, or model output statistics (MOS), in which a genuinely independent product, such as reanalysis or forecast output, serves as the input instead. This choice is not arbitrary: no training input can hold temporal correspondence with a future, unobserved climate, so every source necessarily sacrifices either temporal correspondence or distributional realism. However, no study treats this choice as an experimental variable in the observational downscaling setting, and although several independent studies document downstream symptoms of weak temporal correspondence, such as shared-scale mismatches, mass-conservation failures, and shifts in what a network learns to depend on spatially, none isolates temporal correspondence as a standalone, pre-training-computable quantity. This is the central gap this study addresses. Therefore, in this study, we treat the low-resolution training source, its regridding operator, and temporal correspondence as explicit experimental variables for a fixed DL4DS U-Net backbone, comparing a coarsened Un-Restricted Mesoscale Analysis (URMA) source against real numerical weather prediction (NWP) and reanalysis products, including the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR), the ICON Dual-resolution Reanalysis for Emulators, Applications and Monitoring (ICON-DREAM), and the fifth-generation ECMWF Reanalysis (ERA5), for wind speed, temperature, and precipitation. Each source is regridded with three operators, conservative, bilinear, and cubic, to test whether interpolation choice independently affects downstream skill beyond the source itself. We compute Wasserstein distance, a power-spectral-density-based effective-resolution proxy, and temporal correspondence for each source before any model is trained, then regress these pre-training diagnostics against post-training performance on historical hold-out and on projections from the Ouranos dynamically downscaled ensemble. We use New Mexico as an illustrative domain, chosen for its climatology and the severity of its climate-driven risk: extreme-precipitation increases here are projected to peak in autumn rather than winter, unlike most of the contiguous United States, and the region's water resources depend in part on a river ranked among the most stressed in the country. We hypothesize that the optimal source is variable-dependent: distributional similarity should govern smooth variables such as wind speed and temperature, favoring finer-native-resolution reanalysis and NWP sources, while temporal correspondence should govern intermittent variables such as precipitation, favoring the coarsened-observation source despite its coarser native resolution. We anticipate this effect is sharper here than in humid-domain precedent, because monsoon-driven convection is more spatiotemporally discontinuous than synoptic-scale winter precipitation, amplifying the timing penalty paid by free-running sources. This study provides the first systematic, a priori, data-only protocol for training-source selection in deep-learning statistical downscaling, directly informing how water-management, agricultural-extension, and infrastructure-planning pipelines should preprocess coarse Earth-system-model output before downscaling it for the arid Southwest.

497223.title: Large-Scale Circulation Patterns in Arizona and New Mexico During the North American Monsoon (NAM) Season
497223.authors: Emma Christine Jilek, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and A. C. Michaelis
497223.abstract: The North American Monsoon (NAM) develops during the summer season through interactions between large-scale atmospheric circulation, regional moisture transport, and land–ocean processes. Variations in the position and strength of the subtropical ridge, midtropospheric flow, and moisture availability can strongly influence the spatial distribution and intensity of monsoon conditions across the southwestern United States. However, these circulation and moisture patterns can occur in various configurations, making it difficult to characterize NAM variability using individual variables alone. This study uses self-organizing maps (SOMs) to identify recurring atmospheric patterns during the NAM season using ERA5 reanalysis. The SOM is trained using 500mb geopotential height, 700mb winds, and 1000–300mb integrated water vapor (IWV), allowing circulation, moisture transport, and total column moisture to be analyzed simultaneously. SOM classification is based only on atmospheric conditions within the Arizona and New Mexico domain to examine the large-scale circulation and moisture environments associated within this regime. The resulting patterns are used to investigate how variations in midtropospheric ridging, 700mb flow, and moisture distribution show different NAM environments and potential moisture-transport pathways. This framework provides an objective method for characterizing NAM circulation and moisture regimes and establishes a basis for evaluating how these patterns may vary across future climate conditions.

497224.title: Investigating Impacts of Different Aerosols on Droplet Evaporative Cooling at Cloud Boundaries Utilizing High-resolution Modeling
497224.authors: Puja Roy, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and S. Banerjee
497224.abstract: Cloud microphysical parameters such as droplet temperature and radii play a critical role in influencing fundamental microphysical and radiative processes. These processes include determining the condensation and evaporation rates of cloud and rain droplets and specifying droplet refractive indices, which in turn affect the radiative properties of clouds. The supercooled droplet temperature and lifetime affect crucial microphysical processes such as ice and precipitation formation via homogeneous freezing and activation of ice-nucleating particles (INPs) through contact and immersion freezing. While most observational and modeling studies often assume negligible temperature differences between droplets and ambient air, this assumption can break down, particularly when droplets evaporate under strong relative humidity (RH) gradients at cloud boundaries. Through idealized droplet-scale modeling, previous studies have quantified estimates of evaporative cooling and droplet lifetimes under a wide range of subsaturated conditions. However, there were some key simplifying assumptions in the earlier studies, such as neglecting the impacts of aerosols through solute effects, ventilation, and radiation. Given the crucial impacts of aerosol characteristics and other heat transfer mechanisms (ventilation and radiation) in modulating droplet evolution, in this study, we present a robust high-resolution modeling framework with a detailed investigation of cloud microphysical processes, including droplet evaporative cooling, at cloud boundaries. Droplet temperature and lifetime evolution for a wide range of environmental conditions and aerosol characteristics will be investigated. Implications for different microphysical processes such as ice nucleation and aerosol-cloud-radiation interactions at cloud edges will be discussed.

497225.title: The Path to PyroCbs: Nowcasting Wildfire Growth across the Western United States for the 2026/2027 INSPYRE Field Campaign
497225.authors: Ilinca Mocuta, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and D. V. V. Mallia and C. White
497225.abstract: Wildfires have increased in frequency and intensity over the past thirty years, with some of the most pronounced changes occurring in the Western United States. Coinciding with this increase, pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) events have also become more frequent. These fire-initiated thunderstorms can create erratic weather and rapid wildfire activity, complicating wildfire management efforts. The mechanisms driving pyroCb formation are not well understood. Field campaigns such as NASA’s INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE) seek to close this knowledge gap and identify the processes that govern pyroCb development. To guide instrument deployment, these campaigns require real-time pyroCb forecasts. Several tools have been developed to address this real-time forecasting need, such as PyroCON. PyroCON currently uses VIIRS fire detection data, and scales future fire growth using the Hot-Dry-Windy-Index (HDWI). While the HDWI scaling method can estimate changes in fire activity, it doesn’t account for non-meteorological impacts on fire growth, such as fuel conditions and suppression, along with other antecedent conditions. To improve this parameterization, we have developed a machine-learning approach that provides a more accurate estimate of wildfire growth.Our model’s fire growth predictions can directly replace the HDWI scaling to more accurately predict pyroCb probability. Our model is designed to predict daily wildfire growth up to 2 days in advance, while minimizing input data and maximizing prediction speed. To train our model, we built upon a comprehensive historical database of daily wildfire growth and covariates such as fuel moisture, meteorology, topography, and vegetation, for all fires in the Western U.S. from 2003-2021. Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting, and LSTM recurrent neural network models were all implemented and evaluated. After engineering and selecting the most operationally relevant features, these models were compared with one another, as well as the previously used HDWI-based growth scaling. In evaluation, the neural network model outperformed the tree-based models and increased the R² from 0.24 to 0.67 relative to the HDWI-based scaling. The model has been implemented operationally and will continue to be evaluated and updated throughout the campaign, as more is learned about wildfire growth and pyroCb formation.

497227.title: Updates to the Statistical Hurricane Intensity Prediction Scheme (SHIPS) and Logistic Growth Equation Model (LGEM) in a Global Framework
497227.authors: Kate D. Musgrave, CIRA, Ft. Collins, CO; and T. Tsukada, G. Chirokova, and M. DeMaria
497227.abstract: Numerous improvements to statistical-dynamical models Statistical Hurricane Intensity Prediction Scheme (SHIPS) and Logistic Growth Equation Model (LGEM) over the past decade have yet to be implemented in a fully-global framework. This presentation will discuss the globalization of improvements and redesign of the global versions of SHIPS and LGEM, with initial results.

497231.title: Diagnosing the Physics of Episodic Deluges Across Domain Sizes and Radiative Heating Profiles
497231.authors: Walter Shen, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA; and Z. Kuang
497231.abstract: Existing literature establishes a role of lower-tropospheric radiative heating in causing episodic deluges in small domain simulations, through a recharge-discharge mechanism. The goal of this study is to identify convective events in these radiative convective experiments, and to see if precipitation spikes persist in domains large enough to accommodate such convective events. We create a set of cloud-resolving simulations at a range of domain sizes and radiative heating profiles, and diagnose their impacts on 3D structure and evolution of clouds. By looking at the cloud morphology and life cycle, including properties of cloud roots, cloud base, updrafts/downdrafts, and cold pools, we aim to better diagnosing the physics of the episodic deluges.

497232.title: Exploring Atmospheric CO2 Correlants for Carbon Capture and Storage Diagnostics in La Jolla, California
497232.authors: Madat Sardarli, University of California San Diego, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, La Jolla; and S. Walker, E. J. Morgan, and R. F. Keeling
497232.abstract: The Scripps Pier in La Jolla, California, is one of the few sites globally with long-term, continuous, synchronous, in situ measurements of atmospheric O2 and CO2 from an urban setting. Such a record presents an opportunity to explore a hypothetical application of leakage of CO2 from carbon capture and storage (CCS) in an environment where CO2 already fluctuates substantially because of local sources and, to a lesser degree, sinks. Detecting leakage as an excess CO2 requires establishing a counterfactual: what the CO2 concentration would have been in the absence of leakage. Any extra CO2 from leakage is detected relative to this expected CO2, raising the question of how well the counterfactual can be established without measuring CO2 itself. The cutoff for detection is therefore set by how well expected CO2 can be accounted for without measuring it. Atmospheric O2 is particularly powerful for achieving this goal because it is a strong correlant with CO2 in an urban setting while remaining unaffected by leakage of stored CO2. More generally, the method of using multiple tracers to infer sources and sinks of CO2 requires correlants that vary in tandem with CO2 in the normal environment but are not themselves impacted by leakage. Assessment of the method unmasked measurement artifacts in the La Jolla record that impacted O2 and CO2 concordance and the record's suitability for the application. We therefore present progress toward artifact characterization and screening, together with initial findings from the tracer-based method for establishing a counterfactual for CO2 leakage detection.

497239.title: Evaluating Streamflow Drought Indicators in Regulated and Unregulated Watersheds Across the Western US
497239.authors: Savalan Naser Neisary, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and S. J. Burian
497239.abstract: Streamflow drought is a complex phenomenon with severe economic consequences for sectors such as hydropower generation and agriculture. Reliable streamflow drought monitoring requires thresholds that can be applied consistently across regions and operational settings. Various thresholds are used to characterize drought occurrence, duration, and severity, but different methods can produce substantially different drought representations, and no universally accepted approach exists. This uncertainty is particularly important in regulated watersheds, where multiple water-use sectors depend on streamflow and may be strongly affected by drought conditions. To address this gap, we investigate how the choice of drought threshold affects drought characterization in regulated and unregulated watersheds across the western US. We apply standardized indices, regulatory thresholds, and flow-duration curve (FDC)-based thresholds, such as Standardized Streamflow Index, 7Q10, and Q90, to long-term USGS streamflow records from 1980 to 2025. We then compare drought events in terms of occurrence, onset and termination, duration, persistence, and severity. We also evaluate differences between regulated and unregulated streamflow regimes to determine whether human alteration of streamflow influences the sensitivity of drought characterization to indicator choice. The analysis also examines the correspondence of detected events with major documented drought periods in the western US. By quantifying where and under what streamflow conditions alternative drought indicators produce consistent or divergent drought signals, we assess their suitability and transferability for streamflow drought monitoring and inform the development of more consistent drought-monitoring approaches.

497240.title: Into the Eye of Tomorrow: Modernizing NOAA's Hurricane Hunter Aircraft
497240.authors: Chad Cary, NOAA, Silver Spring, MD
497240.abstract: For nearly five decades, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) atmospheric reconnaissance missions have relied on unique airborne research platforms – the WP-3D Orion “Hurricane Hunter” and the Gulfstream IV-SP aircraft – that fly directly into and above severe weather systems from tropical cyclones to atmospheric rivers. Piloted by officers in NOAA’s Commissioned Officer Corps, these aircraft gather critical real-time measurements that can improve storm forecasting accuracy by 15-20% with a recent study demonstrating improvements up to 24%. As frequency and intensity of extreme weather events escalate and these vital assets rapidly approach the end of their operational lifespans, there is urgency for NOAA to expand its fleet in the interest of public safety, national security, and disaster preparedness and response. To address increased mission demands, NOAA’s Office of Marine and Aviation Operations (OMAO) is executing a transformative fleet recapitalization strategy to transition their aging aircraft to next-generation Lockheed Martin C-130J Hercules platforms and high-altitude Gulfstream G550 jets. These specialized aircraft will be equipped with state of the art meteorological radar capabilities such as airborne phased-array radars and vertical tail doppler radar, remote-sensing instrument ports, automated dropsonde launch systems, and further capability to launch uncrewed aircraft systems into hurricane regions not safely accessible by crewed aircraft. By integrating advanced technology into a modernized fleet, NOAA ensures the continuity of life-saving data that improves hurricane track and intensity forecasts, safeguarding American communities for decades to come.

497242.title: Evaluation of the MPAS-JEDI-Based RRFSv2B Prototype–Will Initial Condition Blending Replace Partial Cycling?
497242.authors: McKenzie Larson, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and J. Beck, R. Li, C. Zhou, M. A. Harrold, W. Mayfield, C. Schwartz, T. T. Ladwig, and A. C. Winters
497242.abstract: The incorporation of global information into regional NWP models can substantially impact model accuracy. Typically, global information is fed into regional models via lateral boundary conditions, but model drift may occur if large-scale information is not continuously introduced into the regional domain. To mitigate this problem, partial cycling is traditionally applied, a method which interrupts the continuous hourly cycling twice daily to restart and force the regional simulations with global data. For example, the Rapid Refresh (RAP) has demonstrated forecast improvement by utilizing the partial cycling algorithm, and as a result, the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) has benefited from this paradigm, as it is initialized each hour from the RAP. Unfortunately, partial cycling is complex and computationally expensive, so research is underway to replace this algorithm with a more efficient and straightforward method to incorporate global information into regional models. Our study explores the impact of initial condition (IC) blending within regional simulations, rather than partial cycling. IC blending involves combining higher resolution regional initial conditions with those that come from a global model, such as the Global Forecast System (GFS). The blending algorithm stores scale-dependent information that then is weighted to tailor contributions from larger- and smaller-scale information. IC blending is being considered for implementation in the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) that will soon employ the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) dynamical core along with the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI). At the NOAA Global Systems Laboratory (GSL), twice-daily IC blending has been implemented in the RRFSv2X, the real-time MPAS-JEDI-based RRFSv2 prototype. This parallel prototype that utilizes IC blending is known as the RRFSv2B and performs as well as the cold-start, cycled RRFSv2X. In mid-August 2026, true partial cycling was incorporated into the RRFSv2X, allowing for a direct comparison with the continuously cycled RRFSv2B. Results will be shown comparing several months of data from these two systems, with an emphasis on the assessment of model drift, impacts to surface and upper-air fields, and more advanced verification. The goal of this work is to inform the development and configuration of the operational RRFSv2. Given promising results, implementation of IC blending will decrease computational expenses required to run the RRFSv2, providing opportunities for other advancements, such as additional data assimilation, increased number of ensemble members, and changes to domain size or resolution.

497244.title: COVE: A Modular and Interactive Performance Visualization Tool for Machine Learning Evaluation and Selection
497244.authors: Hector Miguel Marrero Colominas, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX; and A. Khan, M. C. White, and P. E. Tissot
497244.abstract: Cold-stunning events cause adverse impacts to natural systems including their fauna, in particular sea turtles and fish in South Texas bays and estuaries. Deterministic machine learning (ML) models have been used to help inform stakeholders on the likely onset and duration of these events to assist the preparation for and mitigation of their ecological impacts. Espiritu Santo Bay (ESB) located in South Texas is the second-largest hub for sea turtles in Texas. This area is prone to rapid cooling due to its shallow depths and has been a prime area for cold-stunnings of green sea turtles in the hundreds per event, which occur when turtles are exposed to water temperatures of 8°C for 24 hours (Shaver et al., 2017). This prompts the need for an operational model that predicts water temperatures in the bay to help stakeholders anticipate when these events occur. However, developing a ML model for operational use requires evaluating large numbers of candidate model configurations across forecast lead times, k-fold cross-validation rotations, performance metrics, and independent cases (events) before selecting a final model architecture. The goal of this work is to build a tool, “Coastal Dynamics Lab (CDL) Optimization Visual Explorer (COVE)”, that streamlines the model development process of the operationalization of tabular-based ML forecasting systems. COVE also streamlines the process of analysis, evaluation, and final selections of ML hyperparameters using an interactive hyperparameter visualization; in this case, for each lead time of a cold-stunning model. While COVE was developed to optimize a neural network-based forecasting system for ESB, its modular framework is designed to support similar model development and evaluation workflows beyond this application. For the ESB forecasting system, neural network models were developed using historical water temperature and air temperature data from Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network (TCOON) stations that surround the bay. Thousands of hyperparameter combinations were evaluated for 21 lead times, ranging from 3 hours to 120 hours. Model performance was assessed using metrics including Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for all predicted water temperatures, as well as for water temperatures below 12°C (MAE12), with cross-validation used to evaluate model generalizability and stability. Rather than evaluating these results through separate static analyses, this tool provides a centralized interactive environment for exploring model performance. Users can compare hyperparameter combinations through scatter, box, violin, and time series visualizations; filter candidate configurations by individual hyperparameters; select evaluation metrics for comparison; and examine performance across cross-validation folds and individual model repetitions. These capabilities allow model developers and analysts to assess not only overall predictive skill, but also variability, stability, and generalizability when selecting candidate ML models and specific hyperparametric combinations for operational use. COVE supports the selection of a unique hyperparameter combination for each forecast lead time. COVE was subsequently used to evaluate the selected models during independent cold seasons and individual cold-stunning events, including Winter Storm Uri in February 2021 and the overall 2025–2026 cold water season. This workflow allows for a more systematic and efficient approach for translating extensive ML tuning experiments into defensible and scientifically rigorous model selection decisions. More broadly, this tool demonstrates how interactive visualization can help bridge model development and operational implementation by providing researchers and operational teams with a reusable framework for analyzing large tuning experiments, comparing candidate models, and documenting the evidence supporting final model selections. Shaver, D. J., Tissot, P. E., Streich, M. M., Walker, J. S., Rubio, C., Amos, A. F., ... & Pasawicz, M. R. (2017). Hypothermic stunning of green sea turtles in a western Gulf of Mexico foraging habitat. PLoS One, 12(3), e0173920.

497245.title: Beyond the Forecast: A Culturally Responsive Approach for Weather and Climate Education Through Afro-Puerto Rican Bomba
497245.authors: Isha M. Renta López, Semilla Cultural, Fredericksburg, VA
497245.abstract: Communities become more resilient when scientific knowledge is communicated through culturally meaningful spaces to which they can connect, belong, trust, and feel included. As climate change increases the impacts of extreme weather events, developing culturally responsive approaches to education has become an essential component of community resilience. This presentation introduces an approach for informal weather and climate education, developed through the work of Semilla Cultural, that integrates meteorological events, cultural heritage, artistic expression, and community engagement to strengthen environmental literacy, disaster preparedness and relief efforts. Founded by a meteorologist and science communicator, Semilla Cultural intentionally integrates atmospheric and environmental sciences into its cultural programming while maintaining scientific accuracy and honoring the Afro-Puerto Rican tradition of Bomba. Following the devastating impacts of Hurricanes Irma (2017), María (2017), and Fiona (2022) on Puerto Rico, the organization expanded its cultural mission by incorporating hurricanes, climate change, environmental stewardship, and community resilience into performances, storytelling, workshops, family programs, and lectures. Since 2017, this educational approach has reached over 3000 local participants through its own programs and in partnership with community organizations, and supported over 100 families through relief efforts. These experiences illustrate that science education and community service can reinforce one another, creating learning opportunities that extend beyond traditional educational settings. This presentation will describe the development of this educational model, instructional strategies, representative programming, lessons learned, and opportunities. By demonstrating how cultural heritage can serve as an effective pathway for communicating weather, climate, and environmental science, this work offers a replicable model of cultural science communication that broadens participation in the geosciences, strengthens environmental literacy, and empowers communities to become more resilient in the face of a changing climate.

497250.title: Integrated Measurement of Contaminants in Electrochemical Ozonesondes
497250.authors: Zachary Dale Griffith, NOAA, Venetia, PA; NOAA, Boulder, CO; and G. A. Morris
497250.abstract: Electrochemical concentration cell (ECC) ozonesondes serve as the scientific standard for vertical ozone (O3) profiles across the world. Atmospheric ozone pumped into the cell reacts with the cathode solution allowing ions to flow across the ion bridge, creating a current in the cell. The current can then be measured and converted to ozone concentration throughout the atmosphere. However, contaminants such as sulfur dioxide (SO2) cause side reactions that push electrons in the opposite direction, interfering with the ozone measurement. This contamination can heavily skew O3 profiles, invalidating large sections of the measurements. This problem is particularly pronounced near volcanic sources and heavily developed industrial areas, where SO2 concentrations can be as high as that of O3. SO2 filters placed on the inlet of ozonesondes remove SO2 but yield mixed results based on analysis of data from the field in Costa Rica. The filters require careful pre-flight preparation: if the filter paper is not dry, the filters can absorb O3, causing fluctuations in the ozone measurement. This work studies the installation of a mass-transfer dryer in line ahead of the SO2 filter as an approach to mitigate this issue, enabling more accurate ozone measurements. However, the effects of the dryer on the electrochemical cell have not been studied. To quantitatively evaluate the impact of the dryer on our measurements, we designed a lab controlled experiment that uses a known concentration SO2 and O3 manifold. Ozone and SO₂ are delivered at mixing ratios spanning the range observed in volcanic plumes and urban industrial plumes, and each configuration is sampled with and without the dryer in line. Gases are sampled through the modified sonde apparatus and EPA standard analyzers, ensuring the dryer does not negatively impact the ozone profile. If the dryer proves benign, the combined dryer-filter assembly offers a low-cost retrofit for existing ECC sondes that could recover profiles currently discarded in SO₂-rich environments and reduce uncertainty in long-term ozone records from these sites.

497251.title: Large Language Models as a Delivery Layer for Severe Convective Storm Hazard Data: Workflow Integration and Data-Quality Implications
497251.authors: Kaitlyn N. Fons, Athenium, Dover, NH; and J. G. Fairman Jr, A. Vacek, P. M. Jermey, M. Dyanati, and K. Kaminski
497251.abstract: Severe convective storms - hail, tornadoes, and straight-line winds - are a leading driver of U.S. insured losses, but the high-resolution hazard archives that describe them are challenging for risk teams to query and reconcile in bulk. We examine an emerging approach in which large language models (LLMs) are connected to gridded archives through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), turning natural-language risk questions into parameterized queries over multi-year hail (1 km) and wind (2 km) history across the contiguous U.S. We test whether this workflow can be trusted: does the LLM preserve intensity thresholds, aggregation radius, and the archive's date-binning conventions, or does the conversational interface quietly shift the window, the units, or the daily boundary and bury provenance? We benchmark retrieved daily footprints against SPC storm-report baselines, accounting for known reporting-density biases. MCP access can lower the barrier between atmospheric data and insurance decisions - but only with transparent queries, visible provenance, and validation against ground truth.

497252.title: A Radar-Domain Climatology of Heavy and Extreme Precipitation Events Across the Contiguous United States East of the Rocky Mountains
497252.authors: Michael Lavallee, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX
497252.abstract: Heavy and extreme precipitation events exhibit substantial regional and seasonal variability, while estimates of its occurrence can depend strongly on the density and spatial representativeness of precipitation observations. This study is developing a radar-domain climatology of intense 24 h precipitation events across the United States east of the Rocky Mountains using complementary station and gridded precipitation observations. Events are identified within domains surrounding operational NEXRAD sites and classified according to progressively higher spatially supported precipitation thresholds. Rather than defining an event from a single precipitation maximum, threshold exceedance requires multiple spatially separated observations, providing evidence that substantial rainfall occurred across a finite portion of the radar domain. Gauge observations and PRISM gridded precipitation estimates are evaluated independently and subsequently reconciled into a unified event inventory while preserving source-specific precipitation, spatial-support, and detection metadata. Temporally adjacent detections are downsampled to reduce repeated representation of prolonged rainfall episodes. This framework permits systematic examination of events ranging from relatively common heavy precipitation to rare extreme accumulations while also allowing differences between gauge- and gridded-data detection to be quantified. Planned analyses will characterize regional and monthly variability in event frequency, precipitation magnitude, and the distribution of increasingly extreme accumulation thresholds. Particular attention will be given to geographic differences in the upper tail of the heavy-precipitation distribution, the spatial characteristics of threshold exceedance, and differences in event identification associated with station-network density and gridded precipitation estimates. Additional analyses will examine how the frequency and characteristics of heavy-rainfall events vary among radar domains and broader climatic regions. The resulting climatology is intended both to improve understanding of the regional occurrence of heavy and extreme precipitation and to provide a reproducible event inventory for subsequent radar-based studies of storm evolution and extreme-rainfall prediction.

497253.title: Spatial and Diurnal Variations of Eddy-Covariance VOC Fluxes In an Urban Canopy: Preliminary Results from Texas Air Quality Study (TexAQS) 2026.
497253.authors: Sreenath Paleri, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations, Boulder, CO; and M. Olin, K. McCary, A. T. Chandran, R. Mammadov, M. Baasandorj, X. Meng, N. M. Johnson, M. M. Coggon, C. Warneke, J. H. Flynn III, D. Durden, and Y. Zhang
497253.abstract: Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) are precursors for a wide range of secondary air pollutants, with severe environmental and health hazards, including ground level ozone and secondary organic aerosols. Hence, the accurate identification and quantification of VOC sources is important for effective public policy decisions and air-pollution mitigation efforts. The importance is amplified in urban areas, where most of humanity lives. However, urban areas are highly heterogeneous source areas, with multiple land surface and meteorological properties varying at multiple scales. This calls for measurement techniques and approaches that are able to resolve and disaggregate all the relevant scales and processes. We present initial results of ground based VOC surface-atmosphere flux measurements conducted as part of the NOAA AirMAPS field campaign during the Texas Air Quality Study (TexAQS) 2026. Fluxes were measured using two time-of-flight mass spectrometers for VOC measurement (one using proton transfer reaction, PTR, and another using NO+ as a reagent ion) and a sonic-anemometer, sampling from a 15-m tall micrometeorological tower installed at the University of Houston campus in South-East Houston. Both mass spectrometers allow for VOC measurements with detection limits down to ppt-level and they can be operated with 10-Hz time resolution. Flux calculations were performed using wavelet analysis to account for the heterogeneous and non-stationary source area. We present the diurnal trends and footprint weighted maps of the VOC fluxes to illustrate the spatial patterning of daytime and nighttime emissions.

497254.title: Evaluation of WRF-Chem in Simulating the 3-Dimensional Transport of the “Godzilla” Dust against Multiple Satellite Retrievals
497254.authors: Qinjian Jin, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS; and B. Pu
497254.abstract: The record-breaking extreme dust event in June 2020 transported large amounts of mineral dust from North Africa across the Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea to the southern United States. This event provides an excellent opportunity to evaluate models’ ability to simulate the three-dimensional transport of intense dust plumes. In this proposed work, we will evaluate dust layer height (DLH) simulated by WRF-Chem against satellite-retrieved DLH over both the major dust source regions and downwind areas. Here, DLH is defined as the altitude that divides the column-integrated dust optical depth into two equal parts, with half of the dust optical depth below and half above this altitude. The three-dimensional aerosol optical depth fields simulated by WRF-Chem will be used to derive DLH and compared with satellite retrievals from CALIPSO, IASI, and other available satellite datasets. To ensure consistent and fair comparisons, the model output will be interpolated in both time and space to match the sampling times and locations of the satellite observations. The nudging technique will be employed in the model configuration to improve the representation of three-dimensional wind and moisture fields, which are critical for accurately simulating dust transport. The results of this work will improve our understanding of the three-dimensional, particularly vertical, distribution and transport of mineral dust during extreme dust events over North Africa and the subtropical Atlantic.

497258.title: Scaling Analysis for Buoyant Plumes over Surface Fires in Forested Environments
497258.authors: Ajinkya Subhash Desai, LLNL, Livermore, CA; and A. Q. Cervantes and T. Banerjee
497258.abstract: Tracking the structure and geometric properties of a buoyant plume in cross-wind is critical for managing smoke hazards from controlled burns and improving disaster mitigation efforts. Plume features, such as the angle of tilt, centerline trajectory, plume height and width, and changes in curvature with height are impacted by a range of forcing parameters. Turbulence patterns altered by the presence of a forest canopy and the canopy structure itself introduce added complexities that remain underexplored. This study examines the effects of these parameters, reduced to a set of fewer dimensionless groups, on the plume centerline slope, both near the surface and in the far-field. Results from a suite of large-eddy simulations, conducted in both canopy and no-canopy environments, explore power-law dependencies, based on prior formulations, between the slopes and key dimensionless groups describing (1) the relative strength of the buoyancy source to the ambient wind forcing, (2) the turbulence intensity within the plume relative to upstream, and (3) the canopy density and height. Near-surface slopes are an order of magnitude higher in the canopy cases owing to canopy drag; however, power-law indices describing the dependency on group 1 are similar for both environments near the surface. In the canopy cases, the near-surface plume slope increases markedly with an increase in the dimensionless plume turbulence intensity, exhibiting a one-fourth power-law dependence. This effect is absent in the no-canopy case, reflecting spatial differences in the momentum-flux structure near the plume source between the two environments.
