Moreover, the canopy aerodynamic effects delay the transition of the plume from the rise phase into the far-field region (bent-over phase) compared to the no-canopy cases. The transition height follows a one-fourth and one-third power-law dependence on group 1 in the canopy and no-canopy environments, respectively, with canopy effects becoming less prominent at the higher end of the buoyancy source strength. The near-surface plume slope exhibits more complex, non-monotonic behavior vis-à-vis group 3, based on the interplay between canopy height and density. Our findings support the development of scaling laws for plume structures across varied environments and inform improved predictive modeling for plume dispersion.

497259.title: Parameterizing Convection-Induced Pressure Gradient Force (CIPGF) In the NOAA UFS’ Convection Schemes
497259.authors: I-Kuan Hu, CU/CIRES and NOAA/PSL, Boulder, CO; and S. N. Tulich and L. Bengtsson
497259.abstract: Leveraging 3D cyclic cloud-resolving model (CRM) ensemble simulations of several tropical field campaigns, this study aims to improve the representation of convection-induced pressure gradient forces (CIPGFs) within the convection parameterizations of NOAA’s Unified Forecast System (UFS). By decomposing CIPGF into the components driven by buoyancy, linear-dynamical, and nonlinear-dynamical forcing, we revisit the widely-used CIPGF parameterization developed by Gregory et al., which assumes that horizontal CIPGF is proportional to the product of vertical velocity and domain-mean vertical wind shear. Spatial regression analyses of the CRM output reveal that the proportionality coefficient varies substantially across both time and height, in contrast to a constant coefficient assumed in the original formulation of Gregory et al. This spatiotemporal variability partially stems from the nonlinear-dynamical CIPGF component, highlighting the need of advanced predictors (i.e. input variables of a parameterization) for capturing the characteristics of CIPGF more accurately. Alternatively, such variability may reflect intrinsic sub-grid unpredictability, pointing toward the utility of a stochastic treatment of the proportionality coefficients.

497260.title: Updated Energetics Calculations in CESM/WACCM-X Version 3 and their Impacts on the Thermosphere and Ionosphere
497260.authors: Hanli Liu, National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and N. Pedatella, G. Lu, H. Wu, A. Maute, A. Richmond, J. Vila Perez, K. Pham, D. Kinnison, F. Vitt, J. Zhang, J. J. Orlando, M. López Puertas, and D. Marsh
497260.abstract: The upper atmosphere energetics are closely tied to photochemistry, radiative transfer, dynamics, transport, and electrodynamics. In the updated version of WACCM-X, which will be part of the NSF NCAR CESM version 3, new model developments have impacted all these aspects. They include reaction rates related to odd nitrogen, formulation of non-local thermal equilibrium (NLTE) cooling by CO2 15mm, coupling with the magnetosphere, resolved gravity waves by high resolution model simulations, and altered circulation and transport of major species. We performed multiple control simulations with these changes for a targeted period in January 2016 with a moderate geomagnetic storm. In this talk, we will present a summary of these model changes, and quantification of their impacts on the thermal structure and density of the thermosphere for the quiet, storm-time, and recovery phases, including direct comparisons with satellite density measurements. The quantification will help identify key processes governing the predictability of the density in the thermosphere and ionosphere, as well as observables that future satellite missions should target.

497261.title: US Argo - Recent Achievements and Challenges
497261.authors: Susan E. Wijffels, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Falmouth, MA; and S. Purkey, N. Zilberman, M. Scanderbeg, L. D. Talley, S. Riser, A. R. Gray, K. Johnson, Y. Takeshita, G. C. Johnson, A. J. Fassbender, S. R. Jayne, D. Nicholson, P. E. Robbins, and C. Hall
497261.abstract: Over the past 26 years, the US Argo consortium has maintained roughly half of the nearly globally uniform Argo array, which collects around 150,000 deep ocean temperature and salinity profiles per year, and shares them freely with the global community in real-time. These data are heavily used in forecasting services and in ocean, weather and climate research. Argo’s global design is moving from its original ‘core array’ towards ‘OneArgo’ which expands into the deep ocean (~1250 floats), the ice-covered polar oceans, and biogeochemistry (with 1000 floats additionally measuring pH, oxygen, chlorophyll A, backscatter, downwelling irradiance and nitrate). US Progress towards implementing the new design is mixed. A one-off investment by NSF accelerated the implementation of the biogeochemical array ( ~ 500 floats), but is not being sustained. Despite some support from NOAA and foundations, Deep Argo remains stalled at around 20% of its target. At present funding and inflation levels, the core data stream is predicted to shrink 30% by 2030. Despite these challenges, Argo continues to innovate: float lifetimes are still increasing, data latency has reduced from 24 to 6 hours (to support coupled weather forecasting), new CTDs and sensors are being introduced into the array and more detailed and new types of data are being collected (Deep, BGC, under-ice), and novel applications developed. Here we will highlight the key achievements of and challenges facing the global and US Argo effort, and consider its future prospects.

497262.title: Using PUNCH Polarimetry to Analyze the Background Solar Wind
497262.authors: Curt Andrew de Koning, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and D. Odstrcil, S. Gibson, and C. E. DeForest
497262.abstract: We analyze an evolving feature in the background solar wind that originated near the solar South Pole on 2025-09-17. The feature was observed by PUNCH until 2025-09-19 out to an elongation angle of more than 30 degrees. Using both PUNCH polarized and total radiance images, we demonstrate how the PUNCH polarization ratio (PR) can be used to obtain three-dimensional location and structural information as a function of time in the Wide-Field Imager (WFI) heliospheric field-of-view. We also use hypothetical models from the recently updated Explicit Numerical Large-scale Interplanetary Lab (ENLIL) to produce synthetic white-light images that we compare to PUNCH observations.

497265.title: Sparking STEM Careers through Storytelling and Hands-on Learning
497265.authors: Tracy Fanara, Inspector Planet LLC, tampa, FL
497265.abstract: Long before I knew the words “environmental engineering,” I knew the story of Love Canal. Growing up in western New York, I learned about a community where families became sick, buried chemicals resurfaced, and scientists were called upon to understand what happened and how to protect people. I did not understand groundwater transport, toxicology, or environmental regulation, but I was inspired. I realized how everything in the world is connected and what we put into the environment eventually comes back to affect our health and the vehicle was Water. I became fascinated with the movement of water. That curiosity helped shape my science career. Decades later, it inspired an educational program that brought another environmental mystery, the story of sick sea lions, to thousands of California K–8 students. In 2025, marine mammals along the Southern California coast became sick and died during an intense harmful algal bloom involving Pseudo-nitzschia, a microscopic alga capable of producing the neurotoxin domoic acid. The sea lions provided an immediate, emotional entry point into a much bigger question: Why were these animals getting sick? Rather than simply giving students the answer, we invited them to investigate. A STEM communication colleague and the Oxnard school district hired me to bring my approach to STEM camps in Florida, to California. I designed a three-week immersive learning experience using ten short videos, ten corresponding hands-on experiments, student workbooks, classroom visits, a mobile laboratory, and interactions with ten scientists representing different STEM disciplines. Students started with sea lions, but following the evidence took them across the Earth system. They investigated rainfall, wind, atmospheric pressure, weather observations, geology, soils, watersheds, runoff, nutrients, harmful algae, ocean circulation, upwelling, marine ecosystems, and environmental observing technologies. They explored how changes in one part of the Earth system can cascade through another, ultimately affecting wildlife and people. The program was built around a lesson from my own STEM journey: children do not necessarily fall in love with scientific disciplines; they fall in love with questions. I did not encounter Love Canal as an “environmental engineering career pathway.” I encountered an avoidable tragic science story. Only later did I discover there were careers dedicated to solving problems like it. The sea lions offered students a similar doorway. A child fascinated by a sea lion may discover marine biology. A student captivated by clouds may discover meteorology. Watching water move through different soils can introduce hydrology, geology, or engineering. Wondering how scientists know what is happening miles offshore can lead to satellites, buoys, autonomous vehicles, computer modeling, coding, and data science. One environmental mystery can reveal an entire STEM workforce. This is how wonder becomes passion, and passion becomes purpose. Wonder begins with a question. Passion develops when children are given opportunities to investigate it. Purpose emerges when they realize their curiosity and skills can help solve problems that matter. This presentation will demonstrate how real-world Earth system mysteries can become scalable, immersive STEM experiences connecting multimedia storytelling, hands-on experimentation, and direct scientist engagement. We cannot predict which animal, storm, experiment, or environmental mystery will change a child’s trajectory. But we can create more opportunities for children to encounter the question that changed mine:

497266.title: CASR-NCAR Co-Production Approach for Advancing Heat and Air Quality Resilience Planning in Denver
497266.authors: Khai Hoan Nguyen, City and County of Denver, Denver, CO; and O. Wilhelmi, F. Lacey, J. Boehnert, J. L. Vigh, R. R. McCrary, and R. Kumar
497266.abstract: The Denver Office of Climate Action, Sustainability & Resiliency (CASR) and the National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) are collaborating through the NASA‑funded Disaster Resilience Communities project to better understand and address extreme heat and poor air quality in Denver. Year 1 emphasizes a co‑production process that brings together agency priorities, scientific expertise, and community‑level lived experience to ensure climate risk information is actionable for city practitioners. Year 1 is structured into three phases. Phase 0 focuses on enhancing the Climate & Environmental Hazards Explorer by improving climate indicators and updating projections related to temperature, air quality, and other relevant hazards. Phase 1 refines Denver’s Heat and Air Quality Risk Indices using a comprehensive framework that incorporates hazard, exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity indicators. Phase 2 gathers qualitative insights through focus groups and targeted interviews to fill gaps in lived experience and elevate perspectives from underreached populations most affected by extreme heat and poor air quality. A key goal of this collaboration is to show how new data and analytical tools can strengthen decision‑making and policy development in Denver. Improved climate indicators and refined risk indices help agencies identify high‑vulnerability neighborhoods, prioritize investments, and understand both seasonal and long‑term trends. These insights support operational decisions such as targeting cooling resources, supporting community health improvements, and shaping public health messaging during extreme heat or poor air quality events. By translating complex scientific information into accessible products, the project supports evidence‑based risk evaluation, comparison of adaptation options, and effective resource allocation. These tools also aid long‑term planning by highlighting emerging conditions that may require updates to resilience strategies, zoning, or emergency preparedness. CASR leads community engagement and operational coordination, including recruitment through community‑based organizations such as Promotoras Climáticas, identifying meeting locations, managing logistics, and facilitating agency collaboration. NSF NCAR provides scientific guidance, develops indicators, conducts air quality simulations and other city‑scale climate analyses, and ensures methodological consistency. The teams meet monthly to align scientific analysis with municipal needs, adjust research approaches, and refine focus group materials to ensure relevance for public health and city planning. Following major milestones, CASR and NCAR hold briefing sessions with CASR leadership and partner agencies to incorporate feedback and maintain transparency across the project. This co‑production approach enables continuous improvement through iterative development. Feedback from city agencies directly shapes NCAR’s scientific methods, while community insights inform refinements to engagement activities. The combined results from Phases 0, 1, and 2 will guide 2027 interagency workshops, support resilience strategy development, and strengthen communication, outreach, and resource allocation. This work demonstrates a practical and equitable model for integrating scientific analysis with municipal and community expertise to advance climate and health resilience in Denver.

497267.title: Conv-LSTM Forecasts of Winter Precipitation Type from WSR-88D Radar
497267.authors: Song Zhang, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA; and S. J. Greybush, M. Kumjian, and M. Yu
497267.abstract: Winter precipitation events pose significant threats to public safety, particularly due to uncertainties in forecasting exact precipitation types (p-types) such as freezing rain, sleet, or snow. Recent studies have shown that dual-polarization radar (e.g., WSR-88D) products are effective in addressing the challenges of determining p-types that traditional weather forecast models struggle to resolve. The operational radar Level-III product, Hydrometeor Classification Algorithm (HCA), which classifies each radar pixel into one of 11 categories including different p-types directly from WSR-88D measurements during storms, has been widely used for p-type identification and serves as a benchmark for evaluating and improving classification methods. However, because HCA relies on just-collected radar scans and only diagnoses ongoing precipitation, we seek to leverage deep learning to generate advance predictions of the HCA p-type field. Here, we developed a convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM) nowcasting model for the categorical prediction of WSR-88D HCA precipitation type using dual-polarization observations from the KENX (Albany, NY) radar. The network ingests reflectivity (ZH), differential reflectivity (ZDR), correlation coefficient (CC), along with the HCA field, re-gridded from polar coordinates to a 128 × 128 Cartesian grid centered on the KENX radar (~300 km × 300 km), and is trained in an 11-frame sliding-window encoder-decoder configuration (8-frame encoder, 3-frame decoder) to forecast the HCA field at a lead time of ~15 minutes (3 radar scans). For the current model, a total of 518 storm events were partitioned event wise, yielding 24813, 6540, and 6169 eleven-frame sliding-window samples for training, validation, and testing, respectively. The model achieves 84.1% overall pixel accuracy on the validation set, with per-lead accuracies of 86.0%, 84.0%, and 82.3% at +5, +10, and +15 minutes respectively. The predicted HCA fields align with the physical persistence of dominant hydrometeor regimes, enabling further assessment of the temporal evolution of winter precipitation patterns.

497268.title: Colorado's Increasing Drought Risk in a Warmer Climate
497268.authors: Peter Goble, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and R. S. Schumacher and A. C. Mazurek
497268.abstract: Water resources are limited in Colorado's semiarid climate, and anthropogenic climate change is exacerbating these limitations. The Colorado Climate Center at Colorado State University collaborated with the University of Wyoming and the Colorado State Governor's Office to better understand Colorado's future drought and water resource risks. The Colorado Climate Center used data from an ensemble of 16 dynamically downscaled global climate models to better understand the impacts of warmer temperatures on the state's future water supply. We examined changes to key components of the hydrologic cycle—such as local temperatures, precipitation, snowpack, streamflow, and soil moisture—at global warming levels of 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, and 3.0 °C. While the climate models used here show minimal changes in average precipitation, they show large increases in drought exposure for two reasons: (1) precipitation events become more episodic, with a higher fraction of total precipitation falling during extreme events and longer dry spells in between; and (2) even in the absence of changes in mean annual precipitation, warmer temperatures lead to earlier winter snowmelt, lower peak snowpack, lower runoff, and lower growing-season soil moisture. A warmer future is ostensibly a drier future. This research uses a novel dataset to add to a growing body of literature showing a need for Colorado to make ends meet with a smaller average water supply.

497270.title: Droplet-Resolved Radiative Effects in Stratocumulus Clouds using the Superdroplet Method.
497270.authors: Emma Ware, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA; and A. L. Igel
497270.abstract: Including the radiative effects on microphysics (REM) in the condensation equation has long been proposed as a mechanism for accelerating warm-rain formation by inducing size-dependent thermal growth among cloud droplets in conditions of radiative cooling, broadening the droplet size distribution and facilitating earlier onset of collision–coalescence. Past assessments of REM in flow-coupled simulations have been potentially complicated by numerical diffusion in bin and bulk microphysics schemes, uncertainties in activation and deactivation treatments, and difficulty isolating microphysical pathways from dynamical feedbacks. Recent developments in particle-based microphysics and radiative transfer models now allow for a more direct evaluation of REM in flow-coupled models. Here, we revisit REM using the Superdroplet Method (SDM), a particle-based microphysics scheme that eliminates spectral numerical diffusion, and tracks droplet attributes explicitly, allowing for consideration of the thermodynamic histories of individual droplets. We couple SDM to the spectrally resolved RRTMGP radiative transfer model to represent droplet-resolved radiative transfer and optical properties across spectral bands. Using the DYCOMS-II RF02 lightly drizzling nighttime stratocumulus case, we examine simulations with and without the influence of radiation on condensational growth and compare their evolution across a range of initial aerosol concentrations. Comparisons between simulations with and without REM quantify its contribution to size-distribution broadening and rain initiation. In our preliminary results, REM produces a significant increase in rainwater path and a decrease in the time to rain relative to control simulations across all initial aerosol concentrations. The magnitude of the REM response is roughly half as strong as halving the initial aerosol concentration, suggesting that radiative effects on condensational growth can have a meaningful influence on warm-rain development. Although this mechanism is strongest under conditions of substantial radiative cooling, our results indicate that REM can produce non-negligible changes in precipitation development and should be considered when evaluating warm-rain formation in cloud models. We suggest that this process can no longer be neglected in stratocumulus clouds.

497272.title: Disentangling Modes of Pacific Sea Surface Temperature Variability across Timescales with Machine Learning
497272.authors: Kyle Joseph Chen Hall, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD; University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and M. J. Molina, E. F. Wisinski, G. A. Meehl, and A. Capotondi
497272.abstract: The dominant modes of Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) variability, including the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), Pacific Meridional Mode (PMM), and Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), are difficult to disentangle. Their active regions overlap in space, they each exhibit variance across a broad range of timescales, and they exhibit nonlinear couplings, which violate the assumptions of traditional linear decompositions. To address these issues, we develop a Knowledge-Guided AutoEncoder (KGAE) that uses spatiotemporal constraints and gradient-based sparsity incentives to identify compact latent representations of physically interpretable disentangled modes of variability. Each KGAE latent mode is defined by a distinct characteristic timescale identified by the neural network during training without predefined thresholds or filters. The KGAE separates ENSO-like modes on 2- and 3-7-year timescales, as well as a decadal mode with characteristics reminiscent of the PDO and PMM, each with distinct spatial patterns. We demonstrate that the decadal mode modulates ENSO diversity (central versus eastern Pacific) through both interference and nonlinear state dependence, and that a quasibiennial mode interacts with the interannual mode to characterize ENSO onset and decay. We assess the robustness of the KGAEs to a variety of sources of uncertainty, and compare their capacity to generalize to that of principal components analysis. We apply KGAEs to climate model output, and identify model-specific biases in ENSO diversity and seasonal timing. Our results highlight how machine learning can provide new perspectives on Earth system variability across timescales.

497273.title: Characterizing Errors in 3D Atmospheric Motion Vectors Derived from Geostationary Hyperspectral Infrared Sounders Using Deep-Learning Optical Flow
497273.authors: David A. Santek, CIMSS, Madison, WI; and J. A. Otkin, PhD, T. Rink, A. Lim, S. E. Nebuda, Y. Wang, S. Sung, J. Apke, and S. M. Ortland
497273.abstract: Geostationary hyperspectral infrared sounders, including the GeoXO Sounder (GXS) and MTG-IRS, will provide retrievals of humidity and temperature, with features that can be tracked to infer atmospheric motion on pressure levels, which are referred to as 3D winds. The Passive Retrievals of 3D Optical Flows with Information Leveraged from Environmental Sounders (PROFILES) project is using AI-based optical-flow models to derive 3D atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) from these retrievals. These observations have the potential to complement traditional cloud-tracked winds and improve the initial atmospheric state used in numerical weather prediction. The focus of this talk is the status of characterizing two types of errors: WindFlow model uncertainty and observation errors within a data assimilation framework. During the first year, the WindFlow deep-learning optical-flow algorithm was adapted to GXS proxy retrievals to produce tropospheric profiles of AMVs. Initial winds show good qualitative agreement with model truth, with errors comparable to current feature-tracked water-vapor AMVs. RMSVD values range from 3.5 m s-1 at 850 hPa to 6 m s-1 at 200 hPa. Uncertainty and error estimation within the WindFlow model are underway using two approaches with the GEOS-5 Nature Run: U-Net to learn the spatially and dynamically varying expected error and conformal prediction to assign uncertainty intervals. The next phase of the project will focus on adapting and retraining WindFlow using MTG-IRS humidity and temperature retrievals with ECMWF ERA5 winds as truth. Additionally, we will begin characterizing observation errors within an Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) framework using innovation-based diagnostics to support future data assimilation applications.

497275.title: From Cloud-Tops to Table-Tops: Modeling Weather Processes through Game Design
497275.authors: Michael J Porter, Alachua County Schools, Gainesville, FL
497275.abstract: Commercially available tabletop games that place atmospheric processes at the center of gameplay remain rare, despite the potential of games to provide social, replayable, and accessible forms of science engagement (Clark et al., 2016; Gui et al., 2023; Laine & Lindberg, 2020). This project explores tabletop game design as a medium for translating meteorological processes into playable models for audiences ranging from children and non-gamers to experienced hobby gamers and weather enthusiasts. Developing such models requires deciding how much of the atmosphere to represent: games must preserve meaningful physical relationships without becoming either trivial or unplayably complex (Aster et al., 2024; Gaydos, 2015; Linehan et al., 2011). This presentation describes eight months of iterative development of a series of tabletop meteorology games, with emphasis on Gusto, a strategy game in which players build and evolve convective atmospheres. Rather than attempting to reproduce an entire forecast or numerical model, each prototype game isolates a different conceptual "chunk" of atmospheric behavior. For instance, different prototypes emphasize (a) convective ingredients and stability, (b) forecasting and planning, (c) synoptic and mesoscale interactions, (d) Skew-T structure, (f) delayed forecast information, and (g) different modes of convective organization. Central to the development process has been computational game modeling. Drawing on a scientific-computing ecosystem in which Python is widely used for numerical and array-based computation (Virtanen et al., 2019; Harris et al., 2020), the presenter built a Monte Carlo simulator for Gusto. The simulator became a laboratory for testing complete game sequences, a needed first step before physical playtesting was implemented. This modeling strategy was efficient and effective for rigorous progression of the prototypes; the simulator, for instance, was used to explore card balance, storming and scoring frequency, weather-event frequency and behavior, player strategy, and the pacing of a simulated 2 day convective cycle, including whether nighttime gameplay became disproportionately slow. Monte Carlo simulation thus resulted in a practical means of identifying optimal game strategies and evaluating competing design choices that would have been difficult, and slow, to assess through physical playtesting alone. The simulation process therefore accelerated a normally lengthy board game design cycle. The development process has revealed that meteorological plausibility does not necessarily produce good game design. Multiple iterations have required removing or consolidating scientifically accurate and relevant mechanisms to prevent the game from modeling too much at once. Interestingly, this parallels a broader challenge in atmospheric modeling: useful models select which processes and interactions to represent explicitly, and which processes must be simplified or omitted (Maher et al., 2019; Proske et al., 2021; Proske et al., 2023). Game design, in this context, therefore becomes a form of conceptual model-building, requiring the designer to identify which atmospheric relationships are essential for a particular audience and experience. Playtesting has provided a second important filter. Initial testing has emphasized non-meteorologists and non-gamers, deliberately challenging assumptions that experienced weather enthusiasts or hobby gamers might make automatically. Testing has highlighted the importance of the new-player experience, including the clarity of the initial explanation and the need for a concise "pitch" communicating how players utilize game aspects to affect the atmosphere, and why their decisions matter. After playing just one round, one early play-tester (with no weather experience) independently described how convective inhibition can halt vertical growth while allowing potential to accumulate, followed by rapid development once the inhibition is removed. Future testing will expand to experienced tabletop gamers and meteorologists to examine accessibility, strategic depth, and meteorological fidelity across different populations. The project is now moving toward active planning for a Kickstarter release, with the goal of extending tabletop atmospheric engagement beyond individual classrooms or outreach events into a reproducible, commercially distributed format. The presentation will discuss the design process, Monte Carlo methodology, examples of successful and unsuccessful abstractions, and lessons from early playtesting. This work examines a new tool for atmospheric model-building and public engagement: selecting meaningful processes, simplifying them without losing their essential relationships, and translating them into experiences that audiences may choose to revisit because they are both scientifically grounded and genuinely fun. This foundational design work is necessary prior to validating and evaluating potential outcomes such as interest and curiosity about weather and atmospheric science, STEM interest and science self-efficacy, meteorological learning outcomes, and public appreciation of and engagement with the meteorology profession. 497276.title: Predictability of Tornadoes and Storm-Scale Attributes Across Differing Environments in Tornado-Resolving Simulations
497276.authors: Andrew Berrington, CAPS, Norman, OK; and N. A. Snook, M. Xue, C. K. Potvin, A. McGovern, R. Martz, and A. H. Fagg
497276.abstract: A team of researchers at the University of Oklahoma is investigating the ability of explainable deep learning to identify processes and/or features within supercell thunderstorms which are precursors or contributors to tornadogenesis as part of an NSF Collaborations in Artificial Intelligence and Geosciences (CAIG) project. To support this overarching goal and provide data for training ML models, a library of tornado-resolving simulations using the CM1 model is being produced. Analyses of six realizations each of three tornadic supercell cases (initialized using soundings from 10 May 2010 and 20 May 2013 taken in Norman, Oklahoma and 16 June 2024 taken in Omaha, Nebraska) are presented in this study. In the simulations, boundary layer turbulence is generated by introducing random initial potential temperature perturbations within the lowest kilometer of the atmosphere which are allowed to develop and evolve during 9-hour-long spin-up simulations in the presence of surface drag (realized with a semi-slip lower boundary condition). Supercell storms are subsequently initiated using a warm bubble placed within the spun-up turbulent flows. For each of the three cases, the realizations differ only in the random number seed used to produce the initial potential temperature perturbations that initialize the turbulence. For each of the three cases, the six realizations exhibit substantial variation in the evolution of resulting supercell storms and the occurrence, timing, longevity, and intensity of embedded tornadoes. Storm scale attributes such as the updraft area and precipitation core area also vary considerably between realizations, particularly in the 20 May 2013 and 16 June 2014 cases, illustrating that storm morphology at a greater scale than just the tornado is affected by the initial turbulent fluctuations. We theorize that certain environments may impart additional intrinsic predictability of these features, which may have implications for near-term forecasts of convective storms. Finally, preliminary analysis of tornadogenesis modes within the different simulations is presented, with emphasis on the differing environments that they occur in.

497278.title: Automated Detection and Modeling of Atmospheric Gravity Wave Events to Understand Their Potential Impacts on Near-Surface Infrastructure.
497278.authors: Adam S. Wise, LLNL, Livermore, CA; and N. Gunawardena, S. Letizia, N. Hamilton, J. D. Mirocha, R. Krishnamurthy, and P. Moriarty
497278.abstract: Atmospheric gravity wave events commonly occur due to cold-air outflows associated with mesoscale convective systems, as well as during cold frontal passages. These gravity waves typically propagate above the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) in the free atmosphere; however, very intense and energetic events can penetrate deep down into the ABL and impact near-surface infrastructure such as wind turbines and power lines. Isolated gravity wave events have long been observed in the atmosphere through cloud signatures in satellite imagery, radar reflectivity, and vertical velocity LIDAR measurements. Outside of isolated events, the Plains Elevated Convection at Night (PECAN) field campaign is the most notable observational network aimed to comprehensively understand atmospheric bore (and associated gravity wave) dynamics and how those can trigger and sustain nocturnal convection [1]. Although previous research has focused largely on the theory and dynamics of gravity wave events, their climatology (i.e., frequency of occurrence) is not well understood. In addition, while gravity waves typically propagate above the ABL, it is unclear under what circumstances these events are able to propagate downward with sufficient intensity to affect infrastructure near the ground. Understanding intermittent, extreme events such as atmospheric gravity waves was among the objectives of the multi-year American Wake Experiment (AWAKEN), conducted in the southern Great Plains (northern Oklahoma) [2]. In this study, we use vertical velocity data from vertically scanning LIDARs collected from 2023 to 2025 during AWAKEN to characterize the frequency and intensity of gravity wave events in northern Oklahoma. We first apply a physics-based, deterministic approach that uses multiple physical thresholds to identify gravity wave events in the observations. These characteristics include the most energetic frequency, correlations across multiple heights, wave amplitude, and other statistical measures. Figure 1 shows an example of gravity wave detection from the LIDAR data. Ongoing work is also investigating machine learning methods for automatically identifying gravity waves. These events are being compiled with the Automated Logging of Extremes (ALEX) Power Outage Event Library dashboard for AWAKEN to understand what impact gravity waves may have on reported power outages. Lastly, specific case studies of the most intense gravity waves are simulated in the exascale Energy Research and Forecasting (ERF) model. The automated gravity wave detection algorithm provides information about their frequency and intensity but does not identify atmospheric mechanisms modulating their horizontal and vertical propagation. ERF simulations provide a more complete representation of each event than possible with the observations, including its spatial structure and evolution. Figure 2 shows ERF model output for a cold-frontal passage that triggered the gravity waves identified in Figure 1. References: [1] Geerts, B., and Coauthors, 2017: The 2015 Plains Elevated Convection at Night Field Project. Bull. Amer. Meteor. Soc., 98, 767–786, https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-15-00257.1. [2] Moriarty, Patrick, Nicola Bodini, Stefano Letizia, et al. “Overview of Preparation for the American WAKE ExperimeNt (AWAKEN).” Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy 16, no. 5 (2024): 053306. https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0141683.

497282.title: ‘The User’: Who Are They and What Do They Need from Scientists?
497282.authors: Ellen L. Mecray, Aeolus Climate Strategies, Falmouth, MA
497282.abstract: The term ‘user’ is often overused, and least understood. Who is ‘the user?’ What do They want from science? How do they find the science? How do they use the science? Some dataset owners and developers often use personas to develop to a specific audience. Some products and services are developed for ‘the user’ and then the developer goes out to find ‘the user’ and hopes they love what was built for them! Aeolus Climate Strategies formed in 2025 from decades of experience with NOAA Climate Services and Service Delivery. With lessons from the NOAA Industry Proving Ground as well as clients over the past year, Aeolus will present some of the tools and resources co-developed with different sectors of the US economy. Aeolus has worked with a non-profit doing place-based work in North Carolina, and will discuss co-production and the needs on the ground at the local scale. Aeolus is also in partnership with the insurance and reinsurance industry, and will present some research and tools developed. The AMS audience can expect to hear some of the theory and practice of climate services, as well as some specific applications, results, and next steps planned with current and future clients.

497283.title: Scalable Deep Learning for Satellite Ocean-Color Gap Filling: From Cloud-Hosted Training Data to Model Deployment to Gap-Filled Outputs
497283.authors: Elizabeth Eli Holmes, NOAA, Seattle, WA; and T. Russo and K. Nair
497283.abstract: The increasing availability of satellite data products in cloud-accessible formats creates new opportunities for applying deep learning directly to large environmental datasets. However, practical use of these methods remains limited by the difficulty of training models on datasets larger than local memory, efficiently accessing remotely hosted data, preserving preprocessing information, and applying trained models back to selected portions or the full observational record. We are developing an open-source workflow that addresses these challenges for gap-filling cloud-obstructed ocean-color observations and derived products such as chlorophyll-a estimates. The workflow uses an autoencoder-based approach in which synthetic clouds are applied to observed data to create training examples from the same dataset that will ultimately be gap filled. Because the original values beneath the synthetic masks remain known, the model can learn to reconstruct cloud-obstructed pixels without requiring a separate gap-free training dataset. The workflow operates directly on cloud-hosted Zarr and Icechunk datasets, including virtual datasets constructed with tools such as VirtualiZarr. Training samples are generated lazily using xarray, Dask, and Xbatcher, enabling patch-based model training without first downloading or materializing the full dataset. We use a convolutional U-Net because reconstruction of missing ocean-color observations depends not only on conditions at individual pixels, but also on spatial context and coherent structures in the surrounding field. The model can therefore learn regional characteristics, including seasonal variability, coastline information, and recurring small- to medium-scale spatial patterns, rather than relying on a model tuned to global conditions. Initial applications show that the model can reproduce small- to medium-scale spatial features and seasonal patterns, while also highlighting the challenge of recovering broader spatial structure. Following training, the model is saved as a reusable bundle containing the network, weights, and metadata required to reproduce model inputs and preprocessing. The model can then be applied to individual dates, user-defined subsets, or an entire satellite record. This presentation will describe: (1) training deep-learning models directly from cloud-hosted, larger-than-memory satellite datasets; (2) the use of synthetic masking for regional gap-filling model development; (3) packaging and deployment of trained models for selected dates or complete records; and (4) evaluation of multiscale approaches for improving the spatial fidelity of reconstructed ocean-color fields.

497284.title: Understanding Trans-Atlantic Transport of North African Dust Toward South America Using IASI Satellite Retrievals and Reanalyses.
497284.authors: Stephen Smith Owoeye, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS; and B. Pu and Q. Jin
497284.abstract: North African dust is frequently transported across the tropical Atlantic, influencing atmospheric composition, air quality, radiation, and nutrient supply to downwind regions, including northern South America and the Amazon Basin. While the summertime transport pathway toward the Caribbean and North Atlantic is well documented, the lower-latitude pathway toward South America remains less fully characterized, particularly in terms of its seasonal behavior, vertical structure, and representation across satellite and reanalysis datasets. This study examines the cross-Atlantic transport of North African dust toward South America using dust optical depth retrievals from different Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer (IASI) products. These satellite-based dust products are compared with MERRA-2 and CAMS EAC4 dust reanalyses, as well as MODIS aerosol optical depth, over the 2008–2019 period, to examine their consistency and discrepancies. We found these products generally show similar seasonality in the dust pathway, with the highest trans-Atlantic transport toward South America in early spring and summer. The interannual variations among the products are also very similar to each other, with high correlations. We then compare years with high dust transport versus years with low transport to understand factors that affect dust long-range transport. By combining dust-specific satellite retrievals with aerosol reanalyses and meteorological fields, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of the conditions that favor African dust transport toward South America.

497285.title: Seasonality of Emissions of Ammonia and Methane from a Cattle Feedlot in Colorado
497285.authors: Nathan Martin Sweet, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and R. Krebbers, K. Stackhouse-Lawson, P. H. V. Carvalho, L. Sitorski, J. Vargas, E. Burke, I. Coddington, S. Place, B. Washburn, and K. Cossel
497285.abstract: We measured two gases emitted from a beef feedlot in Colorado: methane, a gas responsible for about half of the greenhouse gas emissions from Colorado’s agricultural sector, and ammonia, the most abundant atmospheric base involved in the formation of inorganic particle pollution over Denver. In Colorado, meteorological conditions determine the consequences of emitted ammonia: colder temperatures are associated with greater particle-forming potential and upslope winds cause deposition of ammonia into sensitive alpine ecosystems. Temperature also influences the rate of ammonia emissions, since ammonia is emitted through the volatilization of reduced nitrogen deposited in manure. Indeed, we observe strong seasonality in ammonia fluxes from the studied feedlot. Seasonality may be weaker for methane emissions, which are predominantly enteric, but there can be temperature-dependent emissions of methane from soil and manure. Additionally, changes in the dietary characteristics and type of cattle can significantly alter methane emissions. We investigate emission rates of both gases and their dependence on the environmental conditions and management practices at a research feedlot in Colorado, over the course of a 1-year measurement period. We quantify total gas fluxes based on measured concentrations and wind statistics, and report fluxes across four seasons and every time of day. We apply an open-path laser system configured to entirely surround the feedlot and then determine fluxes of methane and ammonia through the inverse dispersion model Graz Lagrangian Model. We discuss environmental factors driving the flux rate such as temperature, precipitation, and wind speed. We demonstrate that these measurements can be used for the calculation of ammonia emission potential, a metric relevant for process-based models. The per-animal emission rates of both gases will be compared with bottom-up estimates parameterized by climate and management. We will also compare our results with other measurement campaigns in Colorado, and discuss the implications of temporal trends in emission rates for sampling biases in daytime-only or single-season campaigns measurement campaigns.

497290.title: The Next Generation NSF UW King Air Aircraft: A Lower Atmospheric Observing Facility (LAOF) to Support the Atmospheric Sciences Community
497290.authors: Jeffrey R. French, Univ. of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and M. Burkhart, D. A. Caulton, N. Mahon, B. Geerts, S. Murphy, A. Robertson, A. Majewski, C. D. Grasmick, and O. Cruikshank
497290.abstract: Here we report on the completion of the NSF University of Wyoming (UW) King Air Research Aircraft along with initial results from instrument installations, testing, and its first field campaign, completed in summer 2026. The Next Generation NSF UW King Air replaces the now-retired UW King Air that served the atmospheric science community from 1977 through 2022. The new aircraft is built on a slightly larger platform (KA350 vs. KA200) which provides greater payload capacity compared to its predecessor due to its larger size and weight, more electrical power, and bigger engines. The new NSF UW King Air is designed around the concept of mission flexibility, able to support science missions ranging from cloud physics to atmospheric dynamics and turbulence to atmospheric chemistry and air quality. The flexibility is built into the design of the aircraft modifications that allow for a variety of instrumentation packages to be installed and certified. The NSF UW King Air was completed after nearly 5 years of work through the joint support of an NSF Mid-Scale Infrastructure Award and investment by the University of Wyoming. Following completion of the certification of the more than 50 research-specific modifications in early 2025; the team at UW began the installation and certification of research-specific infrastructure and instrumentation. The first test flights occurred in early 2026 with a focus on instrumentation common to nearly all missions: aircraft state, atmospheric winds, temperature, and humidity, along with necessary science infrastructure such as on-board real-time display. In mid-2026, the aircraft was instrumented using a combination of the basic instruments described above along with an air chemistry payload provided by investigators from Colorado State University, University of Montana, and NCAR, in support of the NSF-funded Salt Lake City Summer Ozone Study (SLC-SOS). Following the completion of SLC-SOS in September, the NSF UW King Air will be re-fitted for testing of the cloud physics instrument package that includes several in situ probes for measuring particle size, concentration, and phase, together with remote sensors such as the Wyoming Cloud Radar and Lidars. The NSF UW King Air is now available for request through the NSF Facilities for Atmospheric Research and Education (FARE) program for NSF-sponsored work and directly through the University of Wyoming for non-NSF funded research.

497291.title: Precipitation Responses to Large Burn Scars from Multi-Satellite Observations
497291.authors: Ashley E Sebok, Texas A&M, College Station, TX; and C. Schumacher
497291.abstract: Wildfires create abrupt and substantial changes to the land surface that may influence storm development and properties for months and years after the fire, yet long‑term observational analyses of post‑fire precipitation and storm structure remain limited. Burn scars exhibit a darker, drier surface with enhanced sensible heat fluxes, reduced low‑level humidity, and a more unstable boundary layer. These changes may alter storm initiation, cloud base height, convective intensity, and rainfall production, with implications for flooding, debris flows, and biome recovery. This study uses three-dimensional reflectivity observations from the TRMM Precipitation Radar and GPM Dual‑Frequency Precipitation Radar, along with IMERG rainfall, to evaluate storm occurrence, rain area, precipitation amounts, echo‑top height, maximum reflectivity, and rain type over large burn scars over North and Central America. Burn timing and extent are identified using the MODIS burned area product, and vegetation recovery is monitored through MODIS Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) and Leaf Area Index (LAI). Fires larger than 100 km² and isolated temporally and spatially from other neighboring fires from 2004–2021 are analyzed with 4 years of pre‑fire baseline and post‑fire monitoring to capture both immediate and evolving storm property departures. Environmental variables from ERA5, including surface fluxes, humidity, and temperature profiles, are incorporated to assess boundary layer changes associated with post‑fire land‑surface evolution and their potential influence on storm properties. By comparing regions with similar burn sizes but different vegetation types and tracking recovery through succession, this work determines if and how wildfire-driven land surface and boundary layer changes modify storm and precipitation characteristics across diverse biomes. Initial results show precipitation can increase or decrease over a burn scar compared to an upwind control. Rainfall and storm changes have strong regional dependence, indicating that the characteristics of the surrounding land surface and regional climate may strongly influence how the burn scar affects precipitation. Although these patterns suggest that land surface differences may contribute to the observed regional variability, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear, and additional analysis is required to disentangle how burn scars interact with the broader environmental setting.

497292.title: Development and Microphysical Analysis of Narrow Snowbands Associated With a Weak Cyclone During IMPACTS
497292.authors: Phillip Yeh, SUNY Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY; and J. J. Carter, B. A. Colle, J. A. Finlon, T. J. Zaremba, A. DeLaFrance, L. A. McMurdie, and V. Garcia
497292.abstract: Extratropical cyclones have a variety of precipitation structures ranging from cells to banded precipitation. There has been extensive research on large primary (single) snowbands embedded in environments characterized by strong forcing, ascent, and moisture. However, there is less research for snowbands that develop when these ingredients are weak or absent. This study examines a well-defined and narrow snowband that occurred near Chicago, IL on 17 February 2022. The band developed within the baroclinic zone of a weak cyclone, embedded within a disorganized frontogenetical circulation. The event was captured by airborne and ground-based instrumentation during the NASA Investigation of Microphysics and Precipitation for Atlantic Coast-Threatening Snowstorms (IMPACTS) field campaign, providing coordinated in-situ particle and thermodynamic measurements, together with high-resolution radar imagery. We use the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model version 4.4.1 to vary a few different initializations and lateral boundary conditions, and five bulk microphysics schemes, which include three categorized-hydrometeor and two semi-Lagrangian schemes. The position of the baroclinic zone is sensitive to initial conditions and microphysics scheme, affecting the placement and timing of predicted precipitation. Changing the microphysics scheme leads to different band intensities and organization, but does not significantly change the accumulated precipitation in the band’s vicinity. Evaluation against IMPACTS observations further reveals differences in the simulated particle populations and vertical precipitation structure among the schemes. A Lagrangian backward-trajectory algorithm was developed to track hydrometeor paths and their thermodynamic and microphysical evolution. The algorithm uses scheme-specific fall speeds and parameters, allowing differences in hydrometeor growth and descent between each bulk scheme to be identified. Trajectories taken during the band’s maintenance phase highlight the complex relationship between cloud-top ice production and the particles composing the near-surface snowband. These results suggest that accurately simulating the snowband is dependent on the location and availability of cloud top instability, mid-level organization of particles by deformation and convergence in the baroclinic zone, and the rate of particle growth and descent determined by the microphysics scheme.

497293.title: Navigating Historic Drought and Heat in Colorado in 2026
497293.authors: Russ S. Schumacher, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and P. Goble and A. C. Mazurek
497293.abstract: Water Year 2026 brought unprecedented extremes to Colorado, including record winter warmth, historically poor mountain snowpack, an intense March heat wave, and a hot summer with destructive wildfires. The drought brought a wide range of demands on our state climate office, the Colorado Climate Center, but also opportunities to solidify relationships with partners and advance knowledge and education about drought. This presentation will provide an overview of how the 2026 drought evolved in Colorado from the perspective of key drought indicators. We will also address how some of those indicators failed to tell the whole story of the drought and its impacts on various sectors in the state. In particular, the challenges associated with characterizing drought in Colorado’s unique topography and climate, wherein much of the water originates from mountain snow but is used in distant municipalities and agricultural areas, were exacerbated in 2026’s warm and dry conditions. Lessons from engaging with decision makers, media, and the public on the topic of drought---and the complex information those partners seek---will be shared.

497295.title: Real-Time Day 1–8 Weather Hazard Predictions over CONUS Using AIWP Emulators
497295.authors: Ryan A. Sobash, National Center for Atmospheric Research, BOULDER, CO; and D. A. Ahijevych, M. Epstein, Z. Hua, and C. Schwartz
497295.abstract: We are currently investigating the use of global AI weather prediction (AIWP) emulators to extend the predictability of high-impact weather hazards (e.g., lightning, hail, tornadoes, convective winds, and extreme precipitation) over CONUS. In 2025, we began generating real-time 100-member, 8 day, hazard forecast ensembles using the PanguWeather and FengWu emulators, as well as the 64-member Google Deepmind WeatherNext2 (WxNext2) system. To produce weather hazard forecasts, the emulator-based ensembles were post-processed using neural networks that were trained with observed hazard information (e.g., NWS storm reports, satellite lightning observations, or MRMS QPE). Real-time forecasts are currently being generated daily and available at http://ensemble.ucar.edu. Evaluation of these experimental forecasts in 2025 and 2026 has demonstrated their utility, as determined by objective metrics, subjective evaluations in NOAA Testbed Experiments, and enthusiasm from the weather forecasting community. For instance, all three emulator-based forecasts of convective weather hazards were skillful and reliable out to Day 8, outperforming climatology as well as hazard forecasts based on the GEFS. Convective hazard forecasts based on the WxNext2 ensemble outperformed the Pangu and FengWu ensembles beyond Day 4, highlighting the exciting potential of this system to excel at convective hazard prediction in the medium-range. Even though the AIWP-based hazard forecasts are experimental, they have been positively received by NWS and Storm Prediction Center forecasters; some of this feedback will be shared. Future plans, including the development of a hybrid AIWP-MPAS forecasting system and extensions for other weather hazards, will be discussed.

497297.title: Constants Shouldn’t Change: Transitioning CCPP-Physics to Host-Controlled Consistency
497297.authors: Soren Rasmussen, NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR/RAL and Dvelopmental Testbed Center (DTC), Boulder, CO; and D. J. Swales, G. Firl, T. J. Hertneky, L. Xue, L. Bernardet, W. Li, J. Dudhia, M. J. Kavulich Jr., M. Zhang, and S. Trahan
497297.abstract: The Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) enables host models, including the Unified Forecast System Weather Model (UFS-WM) and Single Column Model (SCM), to provide physical constants to parameterizations through standardized interfaces. This design ensures that parameterizations within a configured physics suite use values selected by the host model. Historically, however, many CCPP Physics schemes imported constants directly from the locally maintained physcons module. Although convenient, this allowed host and physics constants to diverge. We analyzed the constants defined by the UFS-WM and SCM. The SCM constants matched those in physcons, while four quantities were defined differently between the UFS-WM’s FMS constant set and physcons: the Avogadro constant, Stefan–Boltzmann constant, molecular weight of water, and reference seawater density. The largest relative difference was approximately 1.26% for reference seawater density, with values of 1035 and 1022 kg m⁻³, respectively. While four variables may seem insignificant, it is not readily apparent to users how many values may differ when multiple constant modules are used. This is particularly problematic in weather models, where even small differences in numerical constants can introduce numerical drift and ultimately lead to diverging model solutions. Removing the direct physcons dependency required modifications to 28 files. Depending on each scheme’s architecture, constants were either passed explicitly through CCPP initialization and run interfaces or stored as module state variables that would require setup during an initialization step. The latter approach required careful verification of initialization order and, for accelerator-enabled code, synchronization of module state with the device. This poster presents dependency graphs illustrating the refactored flow of constants through CCPP and the initialization strategies used. A broader source-code audit identified 20 additional physical quantities with at least one active local definition differing from the UFS-WM host value. Gravity alone appears in 20 actively used parameter declarations, with six differing values. These differences warrant investigation, though not blind replacement. Some may be legacy duplications, while others may represent intentional, scheme-specific scientific assumptions. This work reduces hidden coupling and establishes a more portable, traceable, and testable approach to physical constants across CCPP host models. It maps the way for continued unification of constants in a single, host defined file.

497299.title: Evaluating the Physical Fidelity of Machine-Learning Cloud Emulators in E3SMv3 over the Northeast Pacific
497299.abstract: Aerosol indirect effects over the stratocumulus-dominated Northeast Pacific are sensitive to aerosol activation, cloud microphysics, and cloud–precipitation–boundary-layer feedback, all of which are strongly parameterized in Earth system models. Meanwhile, machine-learning (ML) emulators are progressing from pointwise predictors toward architectures that represent temporal evolution and spatial coupling. A central question is whether these emulators reproduce not only individual cloud fields but also the process-level relationships connecting aerosols, clouds, precipitation, and radiation. We use Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 3 (E3SMv3) simulations as a controlled, physics-based benchmark for evaluating cloud emulators. The dataset consists of hourly output over the Northeast Pacific from paired 2022–2023 UV nudged simulations with prescribed weekly sea surface temperatures and preindustrial (PI) or present-day (PD) aerosol emissions. The domain and simulation period overlap the region and time of the ARM Eastern Pacific Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment (EPCAPE). Predictors include aerosol properties, boundary-layer conditions, and the large-scale meteorological state. Targets are cloud fraction, liquid water path, cloud droplet number concentration, rain rate, and shortwave and longwave cloud radiative effects. We compare three architectures using a common dataset and evaluation protocol: a pointwise multilayer perceptron, a six-hour convolutional long short-term memory network, and a spatial Transformer. The Transformer achieves the lowest normalized test mean-squared error of 0.256, compared with 0.302 for the ConvLSTM and 0.383 for the multilayer perceptron, with particularly strong improvements for liquid water path and cloud radiative effects. Nine Transformer ablations show that several architectural variants retain similar aggregate performance, with losses of 0.256–0.263, whereas removing the contextual Transformer blocks increases the loss to approximately 0.40. These results suggest that learned spatial representations and interactions among spatial regions are important for this relatively small dataset, while the precise attention configuration is less influential. To move beyond aggregate prediction error, we conduct an initial conditional-sensitivity experiment in which PD aerosol and cloud-condensation-nuclei inputs replace their PI counterparts while circulation, sea-level pressure, and boundary-layer thermodynamics remain fixed at PI values. The Transformer produces physically plausible domain-mean response directions: increased cloud droplet number concentration, reduced precipitation, and stronger shortwave cloud cooling. However, this experiment diagnoses the aerosol sensitivity learned by the emulator; its magnitude and spatial structure cannot be directly validated against the fully coupled E3SM PD–PI response, which includes meteorological adjustments and feedback. Planned work will apply a time-series causal-discovery framework separately to E3SM and emulator fields. Comparisons of candidate directed and lagged linkages among aerosols, cloud droplet number, liquid water, precipitation, and radiation will assess whether emulators preserve the aerosol–cloud interaction pathways represented in E3SM. This relational evaluation will complement conventional error metrics and help determine whether low-loss emulators also retain the process relationships needed for scientifically credible applications. Acknowledgment: This work is supported by the DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program, the project ‘Tying in High-Resolution E3SM with ARM Data (THREAD)’ funded by the Atmospheric System Research program, and the E3SM project. This work was performed under the auspices of the U.S. DOE by LLNL under contract DE-AC52-07NA27344. LLNL-ABS-2018769

497300.title: Advancing Understanding and Prediction Skill of the QBO in E3SM
497300.authors: James J. Benedict, LANL, White Rock, NM; and W. Hannah, W. Yu, J. C. Golaz, M. Eldred, L. Damiano, K. Sargsyan, B. Debusschere, X. Sun, S. Calandrini, J. C. C. Chen, Y. Li, and K. Huang
497300.abstract: The quasi-biennial oscillation (QBO), the dominant mode of tropical stratospheric variability, profoundly influences global weather patterns, yet key aspects of the QBO remain poorly simulated in many Earth system models. This challenge stems from the complex interaction between atmospheric gravity waves and convective disturbances, requiring sufficiently high vertical resolution and accurate representation of wave forcing mechanisms. This presentation reviews ongoing accomplishments and tasks of the SciDAC-QBO project, a DOE-funded multi-institutional effort to improve the understanding and prediction skill of the QBO in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM). Significant improvement of the QBO has been achieved through targeted vertical grid refinement and surrogate-accelerated parameter optimization. Importantly, the physical processes driving the more realistic QBO are generally consistent with observed mechanisms. Despite the improvement, several biases remain, such as a short QBO period, underestimated lower-stratospheric amplitude, and a lack of consistent QBO teleconnections. The presentation will also review additional project-led efforts, including explorations with gravity wave emulation in E3SM, multi-fidelity surrogate approaches to further accelerate QBO parameter optimization, and an examination of cloud simulator statistics in control and nudged E3SM simulations that highlight the QBO’s influence on the Madden-Julian oscillation.

497301.title: Case Studies of the Electrical Processes and Lightning Observed during Bushfires In Western Australia
497301.authors: Phillip Bitzer, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and P. N. Gatlin, J. C. Burchfield, and M. Wingo
497301.abstract: Bushfires are an on-going hazard for the community in Western Australia. It is suspected that lightning plays at least some role in initiating these fires. This study uses a Lightning Mapping Array (LMA) and electric field change meter (FCM) network deployed in Australia for the 2025-2026 bushfire season to study this relationship. The LMA provides in-cloud mapping of the parent lightning, while the FCMs provide energetic measurements about the lightning current, such as peak current and duration of any continuing current. In this presentation, we present initial detailed results of interesting and notable events during the campaign. In particular, we analyze the relationship between the electrical processes of the parent lightning and the related return strokes believed to initiate fires.

497303.title: CREDIT-chem: A Hybrid Physics–Machine Learning Framework for Scalable Atmospheric Chemistry and Aerosol Emulation
497303.authors: James "LJ" Michael Dunphy, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. J. Gagne II, A. Hodzic, C. Becker, B. Gaubert, and J. Schreck
497303.abstract: Accurate predictions of atmospheric chemistry and aerosols, involving emissions, transport and chemical transformations of species such as black carbon (BC), primary and secondary organic aerosols (OA), and inorganic species, are extremely important for both air quality and climate applications. However, our current approaches that rely on physical chemistry solvers coupled with complex physics schemes and land/surface models are computationally expensive. To solve this, we introduce CREDIT-chem, a hybrid physics-machine learning (ML) framework to model atmospheric chemistry and aerosols. CREDIT-chem works by first applying an advection/physical transport scheme to aerosol species with given emission and meteorological forcings, after which, an ML model solves the local column chemistry and microphysical processes. Unlike traditional global-field ML models that predict an entire global state in one pass, this columnar design allows columns to be evaluated independently and in parallel. In addition, independent column predictions yield significantly more training examples for generalization while scaling runtime linearly with grid resolution. Furthermore, explicitly decoupling transport from chemistry/aerosol processes allows for the imposition of explicit physical constraints. To address the extreme non-normality, heavy zero-inflation, and multiple orders of magnitude range of aerosol concentration distributions, which is quite challenging for ML models, we implemented a zero-excluded quantile transform using empirical CDF fitting and probit mapping. To test this framework, we created an emulator of the Community Atmosphere Model version 6 chemistry model (CAM6-chem), emphasizing simulating BC lifecycles, while also simulating OA and sulfate processes, at about 1-degree global resolution and 1 hour time steps. Single step evaluations show substantial speed ups in emulation, while retaining high accuracy relative to CAM6-chem outputs. Airborne black carbon concentration model outputs show ~0.97-0.98 correlation coefficients to CAM6-chem targets, and ~0.83 for cloud-borne black carbon. Level-wise correlation coefficients for airborne black carbon exceeded 0.999 in parts of the lower atmosphere as well. Preliminary testing with multi-step rollouts shows physical and numerical stability over long term forecasts. A 1-hour forecast at approximately 1-deg global resolution with our model runs in 2-4 seconds on 1 A100 40GB GPU, multiple orders of magnitude faster than CAM6-chem. Ongoing work is focusing on scaling to sub-degree modeling and coupling CREDIT-chem with other ML based earth systems models.

497305.title: Beyond CONUS and Beyond Deterministic: An Objective Probabilistic U.S. Monthly Drought Outlook
497305.authors: J. Minnie Park, NOAA/NWS/NCEP Weather Prediction Center, Extended Prediction Division, College Park, MD & Entarian, College Park, MD; and H. Wang, A. DeAngelis, and J. Leung
497305.abstract: A new objective, probabilistic Monthly Drought Outlook (MDO) for the contiguous U.S., Alaska, and Hawaii is under development at the NOAA Weather Prediction Center's (WPC) Extended Prediction Division (EPD), delivering month-ahead forecasts of drought tendency across five categories: development, persistence, worsening, improvement, and removal. The product is designed to support WPC’s official MDO, adding a fully objective, reproducible workflow and explicit quantification of forecast uncertainty for scenario-based communication of actionable information. Its extension to Alaska and Hawaii aligns with the National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS)'s expansion of regional Drought Early Warning Systems to these states. Because drought manifests in multiple forms that no single index captures, the framework objectively blends meteorological, agricultural, and hydrological drought indices across timescales from one to sixty months. Forecasts draw on two leading subseasonal systems, the Global Ensemble Forecast System version 12 (GEFSv12) and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), with land surface states generated by offline simulations of the Noah land surface model with multi-parameterization options (Noah-MP). We evaluate skill against the U.S. Drought Monitor using the critical success index for ensemble-mode forecasts, with probabilistic verification including the ranked probability skill score and reliability diagrams, and benchmark performance against WPC's official MDO. We will present initial results for the contiguous U.S., along with early results from the extension to Alaska and Hawaii, and describe the path to real-time production across all three domains.

497306.title: Global Surface Warming Has Outpaced the Observed Radiative Imbalance Since 1990 (Invited Presentation)
497306.authors: Andrea M Jenney, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR; and N. T. Siler, C. Buizert, and R. Samelson
497306.abstract: The rate at which Earth's surface warms in response to a given top-of-atmosphere radiative imbalance depends on how much of that excess heat mixes down into the deep ocean versus staying near the surface. This behavior can be captured by an "effective heat capacity”, the ratio of the top-of-atmosphere net radiative imbalance to the rate of surface warming, which reflects not the true heat capacity of the mixed layer alone, but also the efficiency and direction of heat exchange between the surface and deep ocean. Using multiple independent observational estimates of the top-of-atmosphere radiative imbalance alongside global mean temperature records, we find that this effective heat capacity has declined since around 1990, implying that the surface has been warming faster than the observed radiative imbalance alone would suggest. We use a two-box energy balance model to test whether this decline can be explained by known variation in radiative forcing and climate feedbacks, and find that it cannot, pointing instead to a possible weakening in the net rate of heat exchange with the deep ocean. We use CMIP6 simulations to explore questions about its cause and whether it should be expected to persist, reverse, or continue to drive faster near-term warming.

497312.title: Engaging Tribal Students In Climate Analysis through Natural Resource Management Courses
497312.authors: Kathryn J. Boyd, University of Washington Climate Impacts Group, Seattle, WA; and I. Shaver, M. Esquivido-Strom, and G. Mauger
497312.abstract: In Washington State, many Tribal nations are engaging in important and large-scale climate adaptation work, often employing full natural resource and fisheries departments. However, Tribal students are often not well supported to undertake the training needed to gain employment in these fields. To support Tribal students in natural resource management career paths, we hosted a DACUM workshop (Developing a Curriculum) with Tribal leaders and other experts in climate and natural resource management to outline the skills and knowledge required in the field. We found that employers in the field value an understanding of Tribal history, culture, and traditional values, an understanding of the relationships between Tribal, Federal, and State governments, and an understanding of sovereignty. Employers also value knowledge of applied scientific methods, awareness of climate implications across sectors and scales, critical thinking, and interpersonal skills. We used learnings from the DACUM workshop to develop a series of learning activities with supporting resources that focused on developing an understanding of Tribal co-management principles and adaptive management practices that incorporate climate into planning. The curriculum framework included several sections and learning activities that walked faculty through how to develop a locally relevant case study to demonstrate Tribal projects and consultation practices, and how to find and explore various types of relevant climate data. We developed two example case studies on Tribal projects in Olympia and Spokane; one was a dam removal and estuary restoration project and the other focused on a salmon reintroduction project in the Columbia River Basin. Activities included a place and time exploration, a journal club reading exercise, climate data analysis, and a jigsaw activity exploring interconnections between the climate and management challenges. At the workshops, which were hosted in Olympia and Spokane, Washington, community college science faculty engaged in place-based learning through field trips and guest speakers. They then engaged in two of the activities from the corresponding case curriculum and discussed how to incorporate the activities into their practice. Evaluation from the workshops showed positive outcomes, and interest from faculty to implement the curriculum. Some wanted more time for exploring the curriculum, and the project team will use this information to consider how to balance the place-based aspects of the workshops with time for faculty discussion. In this presentation, we plan to present the curriculum, describe findings from the workshop evaluation, and discuss next steps for the project. We hope to spark discussions around how best to balance aspects of place-based learning, and how to incorporate climate education and interdisciplinary curriculum into science-based courses.

497313.title: The Piedmont Nocturnal Low Level Jet’s influence on Boundary Layer Evolution and Composition
497313.authors: Maurice E. D. Roots, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD; and S. Pandey
497313.abstract: Ground-based and modeling studies have shown that regional air quality is governed not only by chemical mechanisms but also by the mesoscale dynamics of the boundary layer. In the Piedmont region of the United States (spanning the Mid-Atlantic States) a low-level wind maximum, analogous to the well-known Southern Great Plains low-level jet, has been implicated as a driver of high surface ozone events. Reports and previous studies of this nocturnal boundary layer phenomenon suggest that it is important for understanding regional convection, air quality, and boundary layer evolution within one of the most populated and economically critical regions of the United States, the I-95 corridor between Washington, DC and New York City, NY. In this study we investigate this distinct wind feature’s evolution and its consequence to surface and boundary layer composition, using its multi-site and multi-instrument observational dataset from across the Mid-Atlantic states to examine and characterize local and regional dynamical phenomena and their coupling to the evolving chemical budgets that impact air quality in the I-95 corridor. This analysis has combined the multiple perspectives of surface monitors, profilers, sondes, satellites, and models to characterize the morphology and impacts of the Piedmont-LLJ: including the NASA Tropospheric Ozone Lidar Network (TOLNet), Pandora spectrometers, AErosol RObotic NETwork (AERONET), Unified Ceilometer Network (UCN), MDE Radar Wind Profilers (RWP), EPA AirQuality surface monitors, NOAA Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS), and met- and ozone-sondes, in addition to simulations of air mass transport by NOAA’s Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Trajectory (HYSPLIT) model, and synoptic orientation from NOAA and ECMWF.

497314.title: When Hazards Compete: Public Decision-Making During Compound Weather Events
497314.authors: Abigail Lee Bitterman, Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and J. T. Ripberger, M. Krocak, and S. R. Ernst
497314.abstract: When severe storms are in the forecast, they typically threaten decision-makers with more than just one hazard. Severe convective hazards (hail, straight-line wind, and tornadoes) and flash flooding are some of the most common co-occurring hazards, but how people think about and respond to these hazards can be context dependent. As the weather enterprise has been working to improve the communication of multiple simultaneous hazards, it is important to understand not only which hazards people prioritize in their protective action decisions, but also how different combinations of hazards can influence perceptions of risk, confidence in available information, and the difficulty of making protective action decisions. To collect data on co-occurring hazard perceptions, we used a survey experiment fielded as part of the OU Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis 2026 Flooding and Society Survey, a nationally representative survey of 1,200 members of the public. The experiment asked respondents to imagine they were in a scenario where they were about to drive from Tulsa to Oklahoma City, but there were storms along the route. Respondents were placed into one of three treatments, where they were presented with a severe thunderstorm warning, a flood warning, or both warnings.
