After viewing the warning(s), respondents answered a series of questions about how dangerous they believed the situation to be; how likely they thought they were to encounter hazardous conditions; whether they believed taking protective action would reduce their risk; whether they felt they had enough information to decide what to do, how difficult the decision would be; and which hazard would have the greatest influence on their decision about whether to continue the trip. Findings from this work will contribute to a better understanding of how context shapes perceptions of compound hazards and the development of more salient compound hazard forecasts and warnings.

497315.title: Multi-Model Turbulence Forecasting at the Weather Company
497315.authors: John K. Williams, The Weather Company, Andover, MA; and A. P. Foley, W. Deierling, and J. A. Craig
497315.abstract: Atmospheric turbulence remains one of the most pervasive and costly hazards within the United States National Airspace System (NAS) and globally, causing inflight injuries and driving fuel inefficiencies, flight delays, and maintenance burdens. As a premier provider of meteorological data, operational products, and decision guidance to major commercial airlines worldwide, The Weather Company (TWC) continuously advances high-resolution aviation hazard prediction. To enhance operational turbulence forecasting skill, TWC partnered with the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) to implement NCAR’s Graphical Turbulence Guidance version 4 (GTG4) software, which transforms 3D atmospheric forecasts into standardized Energy Dissipation Rate (EDR) grids of Clear Air Turbulence (CAT), Mountain Wave Turbulence (MWT), and Convectively-Induced Turbulence (CIT). NCAR’s advanced multi-diagnostic turbulence forecasting software was integrated into TWC’s cloud infrastructure, making it possible to run GTG4 on multiple different numerical weather prediction model sources in a common environment. While GTG4 offers state-of-the-art diagnostic capabilities, individual numerical weather prediction (NWP) models suffer from errors in the accuracy of their representation and prediction of the atmosphere that limit the accuracy of turbulence forecasts derived from them. To overcome these single-model constraints, TWC developed a multi-model forecasting framework that executes the GTG4 algorithm across multiple global and regional NWP models. By blending these parallel GTG4 outputs using appropriate statistical techniques, TWC produces a global consensus turbulence forecast that delivers greater predictive accuracy than any single model alone achieves. This presentation will describe the architecture of the multi-model pipeline, provide objective verification scores evaluated against automated in-situ aircraft EDR reports and pilot reports (PIREPs), and present case studies illustrating the consensus model's performance in real-world scenarios.

497316.title: Observing Wildfire Smoke Impacts from the Surface through the Planetary Boundary Layer
497316.authors: Joseph Sedlar, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and V. Caicedo, L. D. Riihimaki, and K. A. Balmes
497316.abstract: Wildfires continue to be an increasing and evolve threat. As wildfire intensity and size across CONUS both grow, wildfire smoke downstream is having considerable impacts on human health, air quality, as well as threats to property and the ecosystem. The role that smoke plays on influencing local weather conditions downstream from a wildland fire remain unknown although studies have identified both radiative and thermodynamic impacts of fire on near-surface measurements. Here, we describe new efforts by NOAA and the University of Colorado to equip mobile and long-term observatories with a diverse suite of in situ and remote-sensing instruments. These observatories are designed to monitor the surface energy budget, air quality, and the planetary boundary layer, with particular emphasis on assessing how smoke events influence these properties. We take an observational perspective of observing wildfire smoke impacts on the surface and its potential propagation vertically through the lower troposphere. Insights gained from comprehensive measurements during recent wildfire smoke events can then be used provide scientific context of possible smoke impacts on long-term (> 30 years) monitoring data records of surface radiation and near-surface thermodynamic properties.

497317.title: Using Ventilated Potential Intensity to Understand Variability In Tropical Cyclone Activity from Daily to Seasonal Timescales
497317.authors: Daniel R Chavas, Purdue University, Indianapolis, IN, IN; and P. J. Klotzbach
497317.abstract: Recent work integrated the negative impact of the shear-induced import of dry air (“ventilation”) with the traditional potential intensity to yield a single quantity called the ventilated potential intensity (vPI). This work showed that the spatial distribution of vPI compared well to the long-term climatology of tropical cyclogenesis globally, but it has not yet been applied at shorter timescales. The vPI is unique in that it intrinsically transitions sharply to zero when shear becomes too large, thereby making it capable of objectively isolating localized regions that can support TCs and at what peak intensity. Here we examine how well vPI can capture variability in tropical cyclone activity (genesis and intensity) in more practical settings across daily, monthly, and seasonal timescales. The Caribbean “dead zone” stands out as a region of zero vPI on average for much of the TC season. We further analyze how well vPI can identify favorable regions for both genesis and intensification in monthly climatologies as well as in operational forecasting from daily to weekly timescales. Preliminary results show substantial promise in vPI as a unifying parameter for TC forecasting and climate-induced variability.

497319.title: Evolution of Atmospheric Boundary Layer Height from Two Solar Eclipses Near the City of Saint Louis, MO
497319.authors: Robert Pasken, Howard Univ., Washington, DC; and S. Chiao, J. Bergmann, and T. Heitzler
497319.abstract: A total solar eclipse offers an unparalleled opportunity to study the changes in the atmosphere's planetary boundary layer (PBL) resulting from variations in radiative heating. Although previous eclipse studies have demonstrated that significant changes occur, few studies have explored the evolution of these changes, particularly in the PBL. To better understand the changes in the lowest layers of the PBL during an eclipse, a multi-sensor sampling approach was taken. Surface mesonet data, radiosonde launches, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) were used to document the changes in the structure of the PBL caused by the eclipse. These data were then assimilated into a WRF simulation of the eclipse, allowing a more detailed picture of the four-dimensional structure of the PBL during the eclipse. These simulations show the rapid collapse and recovery of PBL heights and the rapid decline and recovery of turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) over the course of the partial and total phases of the eclipse. In addition, the perturbation mean sea-level pressures show indications of the passage of a gravity wave across the domain. Additional work is necessary to determine if these gravity waves are generated by flow over the Ozark Mountains or if they are due to the passage of the eclipse shadow.

497320.title: Impact of Aerosols and Meteorology on Updrafts and Microphysics in Deep Convective Clouds during ESCAPE
497320.authors: Saurabh U Patil, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and G. M. McFarquhar, Y. Huang, and D. Diochnos
497320.abstract: A steady increase in anthropogenic emissions necessitates the investigation of their impacts on the microphysics of the deep convective clouds, particularly through the aerosol induced condensational invigoration mechanism. This hypothesized mechanism requires the presence of large supersaturations (SSs) to allow for the nucleation of additional aerosols into cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) at much higher levels above the cloud base than conventionally occurs. Due to current technological limitations, SSs cannot be measured directly and are derived from microphysical observations assuming quasi-steady state conditions in the updraft, hereafter denoted SQSS. This study use in-situ airborne observations collected during the Experiment of Sea breeze Convection, Aerosols, Precipitation and Environment (ESCAPE) field campaign to determine how updraft core characteristics including calculated in-cloud SQSS vary with altitude, how cloud microphysical properties change in various aerosol and meteorological conditions, and thus whether there is observational evidence supportive of the potential for condensational invigoration occurring. The National Research Council of Canada Convair-580 and Stratton Park Engineering Company Learjet together sampled about 219 intense convective cloud core segments in different meteorological regimes along the coast of Texas and Louisiana between 31 May and 17 June 2022. Median updraft properties included widths of ~1 km, velocities of 4.8 m s-1, droplet number concentrations of ~400 cm-3, and liquid water contents of 0.9 g m-3. SQSS estimated from in situ observations under a quasi-steady state assumption averaged 0.4% but occasionally exceeded 2%, with values > 1% (high supersaturations) identified as statistical outliers. While extreme supersaturations (~10%) were rare, their occurrence underscores the need for targeted multiplatform observations to resolve their spatiotemporal variability and assess their potential role in deep convective invigoration. Consequently, the most probable microphysical and kinematical conditions that can be used to identify pockets of high supersaturations within deep convective clouds will be presented alongside the analysis.

497322.title: A Bias-Aware Dynamical Downscaling Framework for High-Resolution Future Energy Projections over CONUS
497322.authors: Jaemo Yang, National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR), Golden, CO; and M. Sengupta and Y. Xie
497322.abstract: Future energy systems planning and grid resilience assessments directly depend on high-resolution meteorological projections that can accurately capture local and extreme weather phenomena. While conventional Earth System Models (ESMs) provide valuable long-term multi-decadal scenarios, their coarse spatial resolution limits their direct applicability for regional-scale energy studies. To address this gap, we present a bias-aware dynamical downscaling framework that uses the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to generate physically consistent, high-resolution atmospheric datasets for energy resource assessment over the contiguous United States (CONUS). This framework effectively mitigates the propagation of large-scale systemic errors because the WRF model is forced with a bias-corrected atmospheric dataset derived from an ensemble of 18 CMIP6 models. In addition, we implement a bias-correction for the soil moisture and soil temperature initialization fields using ERA5 as a reference state. This initialization field correction of land surface states is highly essential because uncorrected initial biases distort land-atmosphere feedback and consequently skew simulations of near-surface temperature and heatwave characteristics. Extensive validation of our convection-permitting (4-km) simulations demonstrates that this bias-aware approach achieves a reduction of over 50% in systematic biases for key energy-relevant variables such as global horizontal irradiance (GHI), 2-m temperature, and precipitation. Furthermore, this framework substantially improves the simulated intensity, duration, and frequency of heatwaves, and it therefore provides a much more reliable foundation for the assessment of extreme-weather-driven infrastructure risks. This comprehensive dataset also serves as a robust physics-based benchmark for the rigorous evaluation of emerging AI and statistical downscaling methodologies, and it delivers the necessary foundational data for strategic energy sector planning under long-term environmental shifts.

497323.title: Contrasting Developmental Modes of Extratropical Cyclones
497323.authors: Ananya Sen, DRI, Reno, NV; and M. L. Kaplan and R. Bhandari
497323.abstract: Winter Storm Ulmer, explosively deepened to ≈970 hPa over the central Great Plains on 13 March 2019. It satisfied the principal synoptic-scale criteria for mesoscale gravitywave (MGW) genesis proposed by Uccellini and Koch (1987; UK87). However, despite its exceptional intensity, no coherent freely propagating MGW developed. This study investigates that apparent paradox using high-resolution numerical model simulations and a comprehensive set of diagnostics based on gravity-wave and linear-ducting theories. The 2019 event, designated Null A, comprised only transient localized waves and is compared with a 7 March 2008 case, designated Null B, in which a pronounced MGW couplet developed within a substantially weaker cyclone. The two cases are examined at dynamically comparable stages using nonlinear balance equation residuals, cross-stream Lagrangian Rossby number, multilevel potential-vorticity structure, jetfront configuration, and wave-ducting diagnostics. The primary distinction lies in the organization of the mesoscale forcing. Null A exhibited a strongly baroclinic, westwardtilted frontal structure and broad regions of imbalance associated with interacting synoptic, orographic, and diabatic forcing. In contrast, the Null B case developed a split-front structure, greater separation between the polar and subtropical jet streaks, a marked displacement between geostrophic- and true-wind maxima, and spatially coherent imbalance aligned with the observed MGW propagation corridor. Numerical sensitivity experiments show that the imbalance in Null A weakened substantially and appeared scattered when terrain forcing was smoothed, or diabatic heating was suppressed; conversely, coherent residual structures persisted in the 2008 case. The Wave-convection interaction amplified the 2008 disturbance, while a favorable ducting environment supported its maintenance. These findings demonstrate that cyclone intensity and MGW production are not monotonically related. Consequently, the classical UK87 framework may be strengthened by explicitly incorporating verticalplane frontal geometry and mesoscale jet substructures into a more robust diagnostic model upon further investigation.

497324.title: Recent Tropical African Rainfall Variability Reveals Limited Skill in CMIP6 Earth System Models
497324.authors: Ismaila Diallo, San Jose State University, San Jose, CA; and J. R. R. Bagarino, M. Jasper, M. A. Sylla, and M. S. Drame
497324.abstract: Over recent decades, accelerated global warming has altered the spatial distribution of moisture and temperature across Tropical Africa. These changes have contributed to shifts in warm/cold and wet/dry zones within the region. The West African summer monsoon (WAM), resulting from the differential heating between the continental landmass and the surrounding oceans, plays a key role in modulating local and regional rainfall variability, along with associated hydroclimatic extremes, such as floods and droughts. In recent years, several sub-Saharan African countries have experienced severe flooding, impacting millions of people across various countries, including Senegal, Mali, Chad, Niger, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Guinea, and Nigeria. Heavy rains have caused widespread damage to infrastructure, homes, and farmlands, displaced hundreds of thousands of people and claimed over a thousand lives. In the present study, the evolving spatial patterns of pre-monsoon (May-June), monsoon (July-August-September) and post-monsoon (October-November) rainfall and temperature anomalies in response to recent accelerated global warming are analyzed over Tropical Africa. Using reanalysis and satellite-based datasets, we investigate the potential drivers of the observed increases (decreases) in rainfall in the recent warming period, and their relationship to flooding and drought across the Sahel (East/Central/West), the Guinea region, the Gulf of Guinea, and Central Africa. Specifically, three time periods are used to examine changes in rainfall and temperature, along with associated changes in oceanic and atmospheric dynamics over Tropical Africa during the recent warming period relative to the reference period (1991-2020). Lastly, a comparison of observed rainfall variability with associated large-scale oceanic and atmospheric circulation patterns shows that current state-of-the-art Earth System Models (ESMs) poorly reproduce wet/dry years across the analyzed periods. This limited skill is associated with the misrepresentation of remote oceanic and atmospheric drivers and key WAM atmospheric features that modulate interannual rainfall variability over Tropical African subregions. Our results indicate that recent warming has intensified hydroclimatic extremes over Tropical African subregions, while highlighting key uncertainties in current ESMs that must be addressed to enhance the reliability of future rainfall projections over the region.

497327.title: Simulating Turbulent Tornadic Flow through Urban Environments
497327.authors: Alex Schueth, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. J. Bodine, A. E. Reinhart, F. T. Lombardo, J. A. Gibbs, D. Candela, and S. M. Moon
497327.abstract: Tornadic winds are the strongest and most destructive winds on Earth, and understanding their interaction with built structures is essential for designing resilient buildings and neighborhoods. Recent modelling studies have shown that the curved flow and strong inward pressure gradient force in tornadoes can lead to downwind flow enhancements around a building, especially as the building size approaches the tornado size, consistent with post-event damage surveys. Furthermore, simulations and damage surveys within neighborhoods have found heterogeneous flow, with local enhancements driven by channeling effects along unobstructed streets. In order to accurately simulate tornadoes in urban environments, a frictional bottom boundary condition and realistic turbulent inflow are required. Traditionally, in wind-tunnel large eddy simulations, small random thermal or kinematic perturbations have been used to introduce turbulence, but more sophisticated methods such as eddy recycling have been shown to introduce more natural, well-developed turbulence. In this work, a novel, self-contained tornado-specific eddy recycling algorithm has been developed and implemented in Cloud Model 1 (CM1) to introduce turbulence into the tornado inflow. The eddy recycling algorithm generally produces more turbulence than the random perturbation methods, but the sensitivity to implementation and swirl ratio will be presented. For the urban environment, the immersed boundary method is used to introduce buildings into the simulation. In these experiments, two-story houses are introduced in idealized neighborhoods at sufficiently high resolution to resolve inter-building flow. Results from these simulations show that the fastest wind speeds occur along streets tangential to the radius of maximum wind. A secondary circulation can also form across the street, creating coherent horizontal vortices at roof level. Understanding these small-scale turbulent flow regimes and heterogeneous wind maxima across a range of tornado characteristics and urban configurations is essential for informing the development of tornado-resilient structures and neighborhoods.

497328.title: Unified Ceilometer Network: Boundary Layer and Aerosol Data Products for Air Quality, Modeling, and Satellite Applications
497328.authors: Ruben Delgado, ; and P. Rawat, T. Mackey, K. B. Herrera, J. McNabb, V. Caicedo, E. Baumann, D. Williams, and J. Szykman
497328.abstract: The Unified Ceilometer Network (UCN) brings together ceilometer observations from multiple agencies and institutions into a coordinated framework for continuous profiling of aerosols and PBL structure. The network is focused on developing standardized, quality-controlled products that support air-quality analysis, atmospheric modeling, and satellite validation. A primary UCN product is PBL height (PBLH), derived from aerosol backscatter gradients and accompanied by quality-control information and retrieval uncertainties. The spatial distribution and continuous temporal sampling of the network provide a means to characterize PBLH variability at temporal and spatial scales not captured by conventional upper-air observations. UCN PBLH products are intended to provide an observational constraint for evaluating modeled boundary-layer evolution and its influence on simulated surface pollutant concentrations. UCN measurements are also being used to examine the diurnal and seasonal evolution of PBLH across sites throughout the United States, enabling comparative assessment of regional and site-to-site variability in boundary-layer structure. These analyses leverage the geographic diversity and continuous temporal sampling of the network to investigate differences in PBL evolution across a range of meteorological and environmental regimes. Examples from coastal sites illustrate how the UCN can resolve differences in PBL evolution associated with coastal meteorology and local circulations. The UCN product suite further supports evaluation of satellite retrievals that depend on knowledge of aerosol vertical distribution. Vertically resolved ceilometer observations are being applied to the validation of satellite-derived aerosol layer and aerosol centroid heights and to investigations of how PBL depth and aerosol vertical structure affect relationships between satellite column observations and surface pollutant concentrations. Integration of ceilometer-derived PBLH and aerosol structure with satellite and surface air-quality observations also provides a framework for developing improved column-to-surface predictive relationships. This presentation will provide an update on UCN data products and demonstrate applications involving national-scale comparative PBLH characterization, air-quality model evaluation, satellite aerosol-height validation, and column-to-surface air-quality prediction.

497329.title: Customer Interruption Costs of Tropical-Cyclone-Induced Power Outages
497329.authors: Aaron Chirag Spaulding, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ; and N. Lin
497329.abstract: Tropical cyclones induce long-duration power outages across the coastal United States. Traditional metrics and existing assessments that focus on utility outages or customers affected by loss of power do not fully represent economic burden, which also depends on interruption duration, restoration dynamics, customer composition, and the timing of outages. Storms with similar peak outage magnitudes may produce substantially different customer interruption costs. In this work, we reconstruct event-level power interruption and restoration trajectories for historical tropical cyclones affecting the coastal United States using utility outage records and EAGLE-I time series of customers without power. For each event and affected county, we estimate the peak number of customers without power, customer-hours without power, interruption duration, and the restoration timeline. We combine these estimates with local customer composition and duration-dependent interruption cost functions to quantify costs for residential and nonresidential customers. Finally, we apply this cost framework to modeled historical and future outage scenarios across the U.S. Atlantic and Gulf coasts. We couple the Princeton Environment-dependent Probabilistic Tropical Cyclone (PepC) model with sub-kilometer-resolution outage and restoration models to simulate customer interruptions under historical and future climate scenarios. We quantify changes in expected annual customer interruption costs, the frequency of high-cost events, and the spatial distribution of costs. This framework connects outage and restoration dynamics to the costs borne by customers, providing a more complete basis for comparing tropical cyclone impacts and evaluating how interruption costs are distributed across customer classes and communities.

497331.title: Assessing Atmospheric Blocking in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model: Model Evaluation and Sensitivity to Tropical Forcing
497331.authors: Kathryn Giesa, University of Oklahoma, School of Meteorology, Norman, OK; and J. H. Ruppert Jr., S. Cavallo, J. C. Furtado, and J. J. Benedict
497331.abstract: Atmospheric blocking influences the general circulation, often leading to extreme weather events such as heatwaves and cold air outbreaks. Atmospheric blocking occurs when a quasi-stationary high-amplitude ridge obstructs the zonal propagation of atmospheric Rossby waves and mid-latitude westerlies, with events lasting from a few days to weeks. Using a numerical modeling framework with the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM), this study analyzes atmospheric blocking and its associated weather extremes, with the aim to enhance predictability by better understanding how polar and tropical modes of variability impact Northern Hemispheric midlatitude blocks. This research uses the E3SM model to identify atmospheric blocking in a daily 101-year control model run. This model run uses a repeating seasonal cycle based on the 2005 to 2014 averages of sea ice extent, greenhouse gases, solar radiation, and sea surface temperatures. Atmospheric blocking is diagnosed by identifying meridional flow reversals using 500-hPa geopotential heights and local wave activity, with a minimum duration of 5 consecutive days. The control run blocking events are compared to the European Reanalysis 5th generation (ERA5) 500-hPa geopotential heights using the same methods. Across the Northern Hemisphere and North Atlantic and Pacific sectors, E3SM generally overestimates blocking frequency, but closely reproduces ERA5 seasonal variability and dynamics, including winter maxima in frequency and intensity, summer maxima in duration, and similar onset and westward-retrograding decay patterns. A new E3SM experiment is underway in which tropical winds and temperature between 25°S and 25°N are nudged toward climatology to isolate the influence of tropical processes from the rest of the globe. Rossby wave train and blocking analyses will compare the nudged and control runs to assess how reduced tropical interactions influence atmospheric wave patterns and blocking behavior.

497336.title: Assessing Future Hydrometeorological Changes to Urban Tree Hardiness in Colorado
497336.authors: Alexandra C. Mazurek, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and P. Goble and R. S. Schumacher
497336.abstract: Colorado’s semi-arid climate is characterized by hydrometeorological extremes. The majority of the state’s population resides along the Front Range Urban Corridor and adjacent Plains: an area that is susceptible to sudden shifts between drought and deluge and can experience rapid temperature shifts during the shoulder seasons. These extremes present challenges to urban and suburban forest management, and impacts due to climate change will further complicate future planning efforts. Therefore, urban forest managers need high-resolution climate information to make decisions on tree species to plant that will be resilient in the decades to come. In this work, we analyze how projected hydroclimatic changes may affect tree hardiness in Colorado. This project leverages the Western United States Dynamically Downscaled Dataset (WUS-D3; Rahimi et al. 2024, Geosci. Model Dev.) and CONUS 404 (Rasmussen et al. 2023; BAMS), allowing us to examine climate changes from both global climate model-based and pseudo-global warming perspectives. We analyze temperature and precipitation-related fields, assessing how fundamental changes to the climate may reshape the risk of drought, snow-loading, and extreme temperatures—all of which have implications for future tree hardiness. The goal of this work is to evaluate how future changes to hydrometeorological factors may affect planting opportunities for various species of trees in urban and suburban environments, illustrating how hardiness zones may shift in the coming decades.

497340.title: A Meteorological Perspective on the North Pacific Winter Stationary Wave
497340.authors: Siiri Bigalke, Portland State University, Portland, OR; and P. C. Loikith, D. Singh, X. Bai, and A. Laverty
497340.abstract: Time averaged Northern Hemisphere zonal (“eddy”) winter anomalies of 500hPa geopotential height (Z500) results in a wavetrain of distinct areas of high and low pressure centers located in the mid to high latitudes. Research on this time-mean circulation feature has spanned decades and was often the focus of publications in the early days of global climate modeling efforts. It continues to be a common subject of study in the field of atmospheric science, though more recently in the context of how it will change under future climate warming scenarios. Historically these publications analyze stationary wavetrains as a time averaged circulation feature, while the daily weather patterns that make up the feature have been rarely analyzed in literature of synoptic atmospheric circulation. Here we present a weather analysis of the North Pacific component of the Northern Hemisphere winter stationary wave by analyzing the daily synoptic patterns that make up this time-mean feature. This component of the circumglobal wavetrain consists of a strong negative anomaly center of action (stationary trough) in the North-west Pacific basin and a strong positive anomaly center (stationary ridge) to the eastern end. To understand what weather patterns make up this winter stationary wave we apply an index of vorticity to identify how often transient Z500 eddies correspond with cyclonic or anticyclonic flow in the domains of the stationary trough and ridge. Preliminary results indicate that a large portion of winter days under the stationary ridge do not correspond with anticyclonic flow, questioning how useful these features are for understanding weather patterns and in particular the practice of removing the “stationary wave” from daily circulation analysis.

497341.title: PEOPLE Powering Sustainable Transformation: Lessons from a Career Bridging Science, Technology, and Organizational Change
497341.authors: Heidi Centola, IBM Corporation, Tempe, AZ
497341.abstract: Every life journey is unique, and for many in the weather, water, and climate enterprise, a passion for meteorology begins early and grows into a lifelong pursuit of service, discovery, and impact. The American Meteorological Society (AMS) has played an integral role in my own journey, providing opportunities for collaboration, leadership, mentorship, and lifelong connections that have shaped both my career and personal growth. The 2027 AMS Annual Meeting theme, PEOPLE (People Educated On Planet Live Empowered), serves as a powerful reminder that people are at the heart of progress. While science, data, and technology provide critical insights, meaningful change ultimately depends on how people connect, communicate, and act. For decades, sustainability discussions focused primarily on reporting and regulatory compliance. Today, organizations face a broader challenge: translating environmental data into decisions that strengthen resilience, optimize resources, manage risk, and support long-term growth. Sustainability is no longer a standalone initiative. It is increasingly embedded in business strategy, operations, and innovation. Drawing on experiences spanning both the atmospheric sciences community and the technology sector, this presentation explores the human and organizational dimensions of sustainable transformation. It highlights the critical roles of communication, storytelling, stakeholder engagement, and cross-functional collaboration in moving sustainability from awareness to action. The session will also examine how informal advocates, trusted networks, and organizational communities help accelerate change across complex enterprises. As sustainability becomes increasingly intertwined with business performance, resilience, and resource management, organizations need people who can bridge disciplines, translate complex concepts for diverse audiences, and inspire action. Through reflections on my career journey, the lasting influence of AMS, and lessons learned at the intersection of science, technology, and organizational change, this presentation emphasizes a simple but powerful truth: empowered people are often the greatest catalyst for meaningful and lasting impact.

497344.title: From Infrastructure to Forecasts to Communicating Action: Strengthening Operational Readiness and Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems Across the Caribbean
497344.authors: Kenneth Kerr IV, Caribbean Meteorological Organization, Port of Spain, Trinidad and tobago; Caribbean Meteorological Organization, Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago; and H. Anderson, A. Robertson-Quimby, E. Fucile, M. Limper, P. Bugeac, R. Martinez Guingla, and A. G. Laing
497344.abstract: The Caribbean is among the world's most hazard-exposed regions, where tropical cyclones, flooding, excessive heat, severe convective weather, drought and other hazards regularly threaten lives, critical infrastructure, and economic activity. Recent experiences with Major Hurricanes Beryl (2024) and Melissa (2025) demonstrated the great advances made in providing accurate and timely forecasts. However, among some of the most vulnerable persons, those forecasting accomplishments have not translated into better outcomes or effective early action. The ability to understand risk at the regional, national, and community levels; to detect, monitor and forecast hydro-meteorological hazards; translate meteorological information into clear, trusted, timely, actionable warnings; and to ensure that these warnings reach vulnerable communities through trusted and accessible channels are all critical elements of effective Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems (MHEWS). This paper examines the Caribbean's regional approach to strengthening the operational readiness of National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs), thus enabling their delivery of effective weather, water, and climate services. Caribbean NMHSs are supported by the Caribbean Meteorological Organization (CMO) and a collaboration of core national, regional and global partners including the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the National Disaster Risk Management Offices (NDRMOs), Caribbean Disaster and Emergency Management Agency (CDEMA), the United Nations Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR); media organizations; and the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems (CREWS) Initiative. Lessons from a series of regional capacity-development initiatives led by the CMO Headquarters and WMO are examined. These include (i) leadership and management training for Senior Officers of Caribbean National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs); (2) strengthening collaboration among NMHSs, National Disaster Risk Management Offices (NDRMOs), and the media; (3) regional implementation of Impact-Based Forecasting and Warning Services (IBFWS) and the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP), and (4) Quality Management Systems (QMS) training and certification; and (5) ongoing capacity development of regional operational expert teams for implementation of the WMO Information System (WIS) and sustaining radar operations to support early warning services. These initiatives recognize that operational readiness extends beyond forecasting capability to include: institutional leadership, workforce competency, quality management, crisis and business continuity planning, stakeholder coordination, communication, effective use of political pipelines and interoperable digital infrastructure. A central feature of the Caribbean approach is the role of the CMO Headquarters in helping its Members address these challenges collectively. Rather than requiring each NMHS to independently develop all of the technical expertise, tools, procedures, and partnerships required for modern MHEWS, the CMO Headquarters’ provides a regional mechanism for shared capacity development, knowledge exchange, technical support, harmonization, and peer learning. This approach is particularly important for Caribbean Small Island Developing States, where limited staffing, financial resources, aging infrastructure, and limited specialist skills can constrain the ability of individual services to modernize at the same pace. The regional model seeks to progressively strengthen the capabilities of all Members while recognizing different national starting points and implementation capacities. The regional response combines impact-based forecasting, standardized warning protocols, coordinated communication mechanisms, institutional partnerships, and sustained capacity development. Practical measures include progress in fundamental transition from communicating what the weather will be toward communicating what the weather is likely to do, who may be affected, and what actions should be taken, strengthening CAP implementation, developing national warning communication frameworks, establishing pre-agreed warning activation criteria and message templates, creating coordinated multi-channel dissemination mechanisms, strengthening relationships between NMHSs, NDRMOs and media organizations, improving communication of uncertainty, and incorporating recommended protective actions directly into warnings. The CMO aims to build and maintain a regional ecosystem for operational readiness. Through regional workshops, technical assistance, common tools and standards, peer-to-peer learning, Communities of Practice, and coordination among national and regional partners, the CMO helps Members move from individual capacity-building activities toward sustained operational capability. This includes supporting Members with different levels of technical and institutional maturity so that progress in MHEWS is regionally connected rather than occurring in isolated national pockets. The paper concludes that the principle of “no one left behind” must apply not only to the communities receiving warnings, but also to the institutions responsible for generating and communicating them. A CMO-driven regionally coordinated approach enables Caribbean NMHSs to strengthen their capabilities collectively, ensuring that even resource-constrained Members can progressively develop the systems, skills, partnerships, and operational arrangements required to deliver timely, trusted, and actionable warnings. This provides a practical model for other SIDS seeking to advance the United Nations Early Warnings for All (EW4All) initiative and strengthen regional resilience through regional and global cooperation.

497349.title: Building Knowledge Infrastructure: An Architectural View of the NOAA Weather Program Office's Social Science Program
497349.authors: Alison Krepp, NOAA, Ijamsville, MD; NOAA, Silver Spring, MD; and C. Shivers-Williams, K. Fillingham, J. Mote, K. R. Metta, and E. K. Laidlaw
497349.abstract: For much of its history, the NOAA Weather Program Office (WPO) Social Science Program (SSP) functioned primarily as a research funding program, supporting social, behavioral, and economic science (SBES) projects examining how the public perceives, understands, and responds to extreme weather. However, as the needs of the weather enterprise evolve and the volume of scientific information grows, the need has shifted from primarily generating high-priority SBES research to also include organizing, integrating, and sustaining the knowledge that SBES research produces. This presentation will examine the role of a research program and outline the methodological approach SSP has taken to program design with the knowledge, data, and the community infrastructure needed to support an increasingly interdisciplinary weather enterprise. We will discuss the anchors upon which the architectural framework of our Program is built. Knowledge Generation and Stewardship: The first anchor encompasses the processes through which research priorities are identified, projects are supported, and scientific knowledge is stewarded over time. Across multiple funding mechanisms, SSP has developed an end-to-end capability spanning priority setting, award management, cohort-based project coordination, and research delivery. Increasingly, these activities are viewed as an evolving body of institutional knowledge. Data Infrastructure and Community: The second anchor focuses on developing semantic and metadata infrastructure needed to make SBES research and operational information discoverable, interoperable, and reusable. To support this development, SSP is working to develop ontology-based knowledge graphs to provide a more holistic, tangible picture of how disparate data that share common underpinnings can be integrated together to better address extreme weather response. Collectively, these efforts establish a reusable semantic foundation that supports interdisciplinary discovery and future integration. Strategic Convening and Boundary Spanning: The third anchor recognizes that knowledge infrastructure ultimately depends on social infrastructure. SSP has established a sustained convening capability that brings together members of the multiple sectors within the weather, water, climate enterprise to discuss shared challenges in the human dimensions of hazardous weather. Through varying engagements, SSP is fostering enduring relationships across organizational boundaries aimed at accelerating the movement of SBES research into operations. Viewed together, these three anchors represent a critical perspective for program transition from administering research projects to developing organizational capabilities and excellence. Past research provides the knowledge base, data infrastructure makes that knowledge discoverable and reusable, and strategic convening sustains the relationships through which knowledge is interpreted, refined, and applied. The SSP’s contribution is institutional capacity created by integrating knowledge, data, and community, beyond that of funding research projects alone. More broadly, the presentation suggests that research programs can contribute to the weather enterprise not only by supporting new science, but also by developing the infrastructure needed to preserve, connect, and mobilize scientific knowledge over time.

497351.title: Forecasting Roadway Friction with Machine Learning: Comparing Mobile and Stationary Models
497351.authors: William Petzke, NSF NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and T. Brummet, D. C. Walker, S. Linden, A. R. Siems-Anderson, and J. Boehnert
497351.abstract: Roadway friction is the most direct measure of a driver's ability to control a vehicle, and inclement weather is the primary influence on it. Each year in the United States, adverse weather contributes to roughly 21% of vehicle crashes and 23% of non-recurrent delays. Maintenance and shipping costs reach tens of billions of dollars annually. State departments of transportation rely on friction information to guide winter maintenance operations, driver alerting, variable speed limits, and chain-up decisions. Many agencies initiate treatment when friction coefficient μ falls below 0.5 on a 0 to 1 scale. However, Road Weather Information System (RWIS) installations remain sparse, leaving large gaps along the observation network. Prior work has demonstrated that supervised machine learning models trained on RWIS meteorological and pavement predictors can estimate future friction for individual road and runway segments. The generalizability of those models is constrained by observation density: performance degrades with distance from a fixed station. This project examines whether mobile friction observations from connected consumer vehicles can relieve that constraint when used alongside stationary RWIS data. Mobile observations often provide greater spatial density than the fixed network, though coverage varies with traffic volume and therefore fluctuates by time of day and with the weather conditions that affect driving. Mobile and stationary friction datasets were assembled with concurrent weather observations and forecast fields from NCAR's Road Weather Forecast System (RDWX), an AI-based model trained on an ensemble of NWP models. After quality control and treatment of the class imbalance between good- and poor-friction cases, random forest and multilayer perceptron models were trained and compared, producing forecasts for both target types at lead times out to 72 hours. We present initial model performance and a comparison of forecast skill between models trained on mobile and stationary observations, along with implications for extending friction guidance into segments where measurements are unavailable.

497353.title: Upper Air Sounding After DMSP: A Low-SWaP, Near-Term Solution
497353.authors: Sidharth Misra, JPL, CalTech, Pasadena, CA; and F. Werner, M. Schwartz, S. T. Brown, and S. Padmanabhan
497353.abstract: Mesospheric sensing currently relies on the Upper Atmosphere Sounding (UAS) channels aboard the U.S. Space Force's SSMIS instruments on DMSP (Defense Meteorological Satellite Program) F17 and F18, the only datasets of this kind assimilated into the operational meteorological observing system. Research instruments such as SABER and MLS also retrieve mesospheric temperature, but neither is part of an operational program, and MLS is likely to cease operations in early 2027. ATMS and WSF-M do not have the necessary channels required for upper air sounding. With DMSP set to be retired around September 2026, the operational meteorology community is approaching a significant gap in passive sounding capability. This gap affects both operational forecasting and long-term climate monitoring. UAS measurements are critical to understand phenomenon such as Sudden Stratospheric Warming and weather events in the troposphere that are impacted by changes in the mesosphere. Atmospheric temperature retrievals have routinely used the oxygen emission lines in the 50 – 60 GHz spectral region since the 1970s. In the upper atmosphere, the Earth’s magnetic field splits oxygen emission lines into multiple overlapping sets of lines, complicating the modeling of the spectra and confounding the UAS temperature retrievals with magnetic field “nuisance” parameters. Technology has sufficiently advanced to allow construction of radiometers targeting much higher-frequency spectral lines. The isolated line at 118.75 GHz splits into only three components in the upper atmosphere through interaction with the Earth’s magnetic field, simplifying radiance modeling and temperature retrieval compared to those using the 60-GHz band. The use of this line enables simple radiometer design, with higher spatial resolution for a given antenna size and more compact payload packaging. We will describe both design configurations, a 50-60 GHz design as well as a 118.75 GHz radiometer design for UAS retrievals. Both designs will have a spectral resolution fine enough to resolve the shape of the oxygen emission line itself, from which the stratospheric and mesospheric temperature profile can be derived, while the polarimetric channels simultaneously constrain the local magnetic field vector. We will present an initial demonstration of this approach at 118.75 GHz from on-orbit data with temperature retrievals up to 90 km, at 20 vertical levels, with a noise of less than 1K. The mesospheric temperature retrievals results are compared with on-orbit sets such as MLS and SABER. NASA-JPL has built and demonstrated payloads at both 50 GHz and 118 GHz in space, resulting in a class of payload that is already at a high technology readiness level. Comparable instruments could be built and flown as a constellation with relatively short lead time. This makes the approach a low-SWaP, near-term candidate for closing the post-DMSP measurement gap. This research is partially carried out at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, under a contract with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. © 2026. California Institute of Technology. Government sponsorship acknowledged.

497354.title: Epistemic Infrastructure for Responsible AI in Earth System Science: Data Fitness in NSF NCAR GDEX as a Case Study
497354.authors: Monica Ainhorn Morrison, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. Conroy and H. Hampapura
497354.abstract: As AI/ML tools become integrated into Earth system science, the field increasingly depends on judgments about whether a given dataset or model is adequate/fit for a specific purpose. These judgments are rarely documented and shared: what one researcher might learn about a dataset's limitations through application typically stays with that researcher rather than becoming part of the field's collective knowledge. Existing data infrastructure, including FAIR, ensures data can be found, accessed, and reused in principle, but says little about whether a given reuse is actually warranted, and how data might be fit or not. We call the missing scaffolding for collecting, recording, disseminating, and communicating fitness-for-purpose knowledge about datasets and models epistemic infrastructure, and argue that Earth system science needs to build it as deliberately as it builds up its technical infrastructure for computation and data access to enable AI/ML workflows. We take this to be a central conditions for developing, dissemintating, and using AI/Ml reliably and responsibly. Without it, a dataset's lack of fitness for an AI/ML application is often discovered, if at all, only after it has already surfaced as an unexplained model failure. The potential errors and failures that might arise given a lack of fitness can lead to two kinds of distinguisable harms: epistemic harms, where information being produced is inadequate, erroneous, or misleading, and ethical harms, where the result is real world material consequences impacting decisions, resources, and livelihoods. We present an early conceptual framework for building this infrastructure across three constituent parts: 1) a data fitness framework, which assesses fitness for a specific purpose of datasets, specifically characterizing what is not represented and what applications are contraindicated given attributes across multiple fitness dimensions, 2) a data reliability framework, which details the reliability indicators of datasets based on the characterization and documentation of a dataset's fitness attributes that enable informed (reliable) use, and 3) data readiness levels, which is a tiered system used to "grade" data based on whether it is prepared and understood well enough to use in a responsible manner in AI/ML workflows based on its "fitness" reliability. We show how this framework can be operationalized through formal metadata fields, data ready and reliable "tags", and datacards, and treat this of one instance of what epistemic infrastructure can look like in practice. We use this early framework and prototypes to motivate a broader community discussion of what the Earth and space science community should look at building and sharing so that fitness-for-purpose knowledge travels as readily as the data itself.

497355.title: Urban Boundary-Layer Processes and Air Quality in New York City: Insights from Field Campaigns and Urban Modeling (Invited Presentation)
497355.authors: Harold Gamarro, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA; and J. E. Gonzalez-Cruz
497355.abstract: Urban environments modify atmospheric transport and air quality through interactions among surface heating, urban morphology, boundary-layer dynamics, and coastal circulations. Using New York City as a case study, this work combines urban canopy modeling with observations from multiple field campaigns to examine how these processes shape summertime air quality. WRF-Chem simulations using multiple urban canopy configurations, including the multilayer Building Effect Parameterization (BEP) and Building Energy Model (BEM), are evaluated using surface observations and airborne tropospheric NO2 measurements from the 2018 Long Island Sound Tropospheric Ozone Study (LISTOS). During a summertime heatwave and high-ozone episode, the early-morning urban heat island accelerates sea-breeze initiation, while building-induced drag reduces wind speeds and alters pollutant transport. These processes modify precursor distributions and residence times, influencing NO2 distributions and ozone production within New York City and downwind. More recent model intercomparison work using observations collected during the 2023 AEROMMA field effort extends this evaluation across multiple air-quality modeling systems and observational platforms, highlighting challenges in representing urban variability in ozone and particulate matter. Ongoing work also explores the representation and dispersion of pollutant exhaust from buildings. Together, this work highlights the importance of integrating urban physical processes, atmospheric chemistry, and multi-platform field observations to understand and improve simulations of air quality in complex coastal cities.

497357.title: 3D Weather Radar is Flying - Aviation Connectivity Unlocks the Possible
497357.authors: Robert Mark, Honeywell Aerospace, Plymouth, MN
497357.abstract: Improving Numerical Weather Prediction depends on richer, more frequent, and more spatially diverse atmospheric observations. The National Mesonet Program’s commercial data purchase initiative specifically aims to enhance NWP skill, fill persistent observational gaps in the national radar and sensor network, and add complementary datasets that expand forecasters’ ability to monitor rapidly evolving conditions. Airborne weather radar represents one such untapped source of high‑value reflectivity data. Although aviation experiences substantial benefits — from reduced turbulence exposure, fewer weather‑driven reroutes, and improved fuel efficiency — the broader meteorological community stands to gain even more from unlocking this large, currently inaccessible stream of real‑time weather radar data. With thousands of Honeywell Aerospace RDR weather radar‑equipped aircraft generating gigabytes of reflectivity data each second, modern LEO satellite networks make it feasible to stream those observations to a ground compute center where they can be aggregated and shared. This produces a rapidly updating global‑scale composite available to weather forecasters through the National Mesonet and RadarNEXT commercial data programs — directly supporting NWP improvement, gap filling, and complementary sensing. Airlines gain higher‑fidelity route planning tools, turbulence‑hazard awareness, and historical radar intelligence, enabling safer, more efficient operations. Connected weather radar bridges the long‑standing divide between airborne radar capability and ground‑based forecasting systems, delivering meaningful benefits to both meteorology and aviation. This talk will introduce Honeywell Aerospace’s connected weather radar offering and its potential benefit to numerical weather prediction, RadarNEXT, and aviation safety and efficiency factors. Data access and consumption strategies will be discussed and flight test data shown.

497359.title: LES Simulation of Wind-Topography Interactions over Barbados
497359.authors: Darren King, Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology, Bridgetown, St. James, Barbados; and D. A. Rowe and D. Farrell
497359.abstract: Small island states like Barbados remain poorly represented in global atmospheric models. While regional 1km and sub-1km models have improved this situation by accounting for some aspects of the island’s varied topography, smoothing still occurs that obscures the complex dynamics of airflow across the island that influences its weather and climate. In addition to the influence on weather and climate, understanding the dynamics of airflow across the island is important for understanding wind-related risks on infrastructure. In this work, we show that high-resolution LES modelling can resolve how Barbados' complex topography shapes low-level atmospheric flow and resulting hydro-meteorological conditions and climate. The work involved using PALM, the Large-Eddy Simulation (LES) model produced by Leibniz University Hannover, to model wind flow interactions over Barbados. The simulations showed (i) the turbulent eddying in the wind field that occurs on the leeward side of the island due to the central highlands, (ii) the complex wind flow regimes that result from the wind interacting with the topography on the windward side of the island, and (iii) the mechanism through which moisture is transported into the upper atmosphere. In addition, the simulations were used to simulate the potential impacts on residential communities on the island as well as to provide insights for the development of new urban centers on the island. In the future, this workflow lays the groundwork for higher-fidelity wind assessments over the island’s terrain, with potential applications in wind energy siting, building and wind-loading codes, and disaster resilience planning.

497361.title: Impact of Free-Tropospheric Moisture on Simulated Tropical Cyclone Supercell Structure
497361.authors: Gabriel Cenker, University of Oklahoma School of Meteorology, CIWRO, Norman, OK; and M. C. Brown, B. A. Schenkel, and J. H. Ruppert Jr.
497361.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) can produce supercells that further compound other TC hazards (e.g., flash flooding). However, there exists a large variance in the number and intensity of tornadic supercells that are produced by different TCs that remains unexplained. One understudied area is the impact of moisture variability on supercell frequency and characteristics. Previous research has suggested either dry or moist environments are capable of producing stronger TC supercells. However, past research of non-TC supercells generally shows greater moisture leads to stronger and wider updrafts with more robust cold pools. In light of the lack of consensus in prior work, this study focuses on analyzing how supercell characteristics respond to moisture variance in TC rainband environments using Cloud Model 1 (CM1). Using a large set of simulations forced with tornado proximity soundings from Hurricane Beryl (2024), we have shown that free-tropospheric moisture has distinct impacts on convective initiation and subsequent updraft characteristics. Cases with drier profiles required more favorable environmental parameters such as Storm Relative Helicity (SRH) or Entrainment Convective Potential Convective Energy (ECAPE) to initiate convection. When convection did initiate, moister profiles created stronger supercells, producing wider and stronger updrafts, as well as stronger updraft helicity colocated with the updraft maximum, which was not present in dry cases. In addition, pressure decomposition analysis will be performed to explore how changes in near-storm moisture and SRH influence updraft accelerations as well as buoyant and dynamic forcing components. Overall these results seek to add important physical context regarding the role of moisture in the support of TC supercells.

497362.title: Developing a Severe Weather Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for the Mass Transit District of Champaign-Urbana through Public Surveys
497362.authors: Juliana Lynn Wittrock, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Oak Brook, IL; and K. M. Bonifer, J. E. Trujillo-Falcón, and J. Rank
497362.abstract: The Champaign-Urbana Mass Transit District (MTD) provides more than 11.8 million rides a year across the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (U of I) campus and Champaign County.. Located in the Midwest, Champaign-Urbana is affected by a wide range of hazardous weather events, from tornado warnings and severe thunderstorms in the spring and summer, to winter precipitation and extreme cold in the fall and winter. The seasonal variability presents an ongoing challenge for MTD where they evaluate how to continue to safely transport riders during these severe weather events. To address this challenge, we developed a survey to distribute to MTD riders and the Champaign-Urbana community members to assess rider expectations, risk perceptions, and communication preferences during severe weather events. Surveys were distributed at MTD bus stops throughout both the UIUC campus and the outer Champaign-Urbana area. After data collection, survey responses were analyzed to determine communication preferences and expectations with MTD guidelines. The results from the surveys informed MTD in advancing a Severe Weather Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for their area. This presentation details our survey design and methodology, and presents preliminary findings and their implications for severe weather emergency planning in public transit. These preliminary insights not only illustrate our recommendations for Champaign-Urbana’s MTD system, but also provide a survey methodology that other public ground transportation research may follow. Further, we believe these recommendations apply broadly to other mass transportation hubs.

497365.title: Partner Interpretation and Operational Use of NWS HeatRisk ForecastTools in Western Washington
497365.authors: Ariana Nevaeh Williams, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ; and R. Wolcott and M. H. Smith
497365.abstract: Extreme temperatures pose a significant risk to public health and infrastructure. The National Weather Service’s (NWS) HeatRisk tool has been lauded as highly beneficial by NWS partners; however, little research has examined how the experimental HeatRisk tool is interpreted and used in operational decision-making. This pilot study examines how partners in western Washington interpret deterministic and probabilistic heat risk forecasts and how they interact with existing heat-related decision support tools, including the experimental HeatRisk tool and the Probabilistic HeatRisk Tool Prototype, through six key-informant interviews. Interview responses were analyzed using Rapid Qualitative Analysis to identify common themes in partner decision-making and risk communication. Understanding how NWS partners interpret and apply risk information for extreme heat events will inform the future development of a comparable tool that addresses risk from extreme cold. To support the future development of a “ColdRisk” proof of concept for Washington state, the Center for Disaster Resilient Communities at the University of Washington, the National Weather Service Seattle Weather Forecast Office, and the NOAA Global Systems Laboratory are collaborating on this project to assess how local partners, including public health agencies, emergency managers, and community-based organizations, incorporate the experimental HeatRisk and the recently released Probabilistic HeatRisk Tool Prototype into operational decision-making. This pilot study was conducted as part of the NOAA Ernest F. Hollings Scholarship Program internship.

497367.title: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Automated Quality Control of NOAA Coastal Water Level Observations
497367.authors: Thanh Dung Le, Texas A&M Univ.-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX; and L. Abrams, B. Armos, M. P. Conlin, K. Glebushko, L. Rojas-Wiltsee, B. Colburn, and P. Tissot
497367.abstract: Delivering NOAA's high-quality, continuous 6-minute water-level observations along all U.S. coasts and territories is a resource-intensive process that relies on expert review to separate reliable sensor data from faults. We present an AI-enabled quality control (QC) method, built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), that reliably reproduces verified water level products. The system has two goals: to classify preliminary 6-minute sensor data as good or bad, and to fill gaps in the resulting time series. The model encodes a station's raw primary and backup sensor data and NOAA's astronomical tide predictions into a shared latent space anchored to the verified water level. It is trained on historic water level data covering 2007-2025 from 33 representative stations spanning the U.S. coast and territories. To detect errors, we compute a rolling dynamic time warping (DTW) distance between the primary and backup latent trajectories over a sliding 12-hour window. Because DTW aligns sequences that share a shape but are locally shifted in time, normal tidal co-variation between the two sensors yields a small latent-DTW distance, while genuine errors such as offsets, drifts, and dropouts produce a large, well-separated distance. This latent-DTW discrepancy, combined with each sensor's alignment to the astronomical-tide latent, classifies preliminary data as good or bad. Detection performance is assessed per station using ROC-AUC, with CO-OPS' existing QC flags from the verified data record serving as ground truth. A verified-anchored decoder then reconstructs water level to replace flagged points and fill gaps, giving CO-OPS a scalable and label-efficient tool for faster, more accurate verified water-level production.

497368.title: AIDA: NWP-Quality AI Analyses and a Platform for Observation Valuation
497368.authors: Alex Kleeman, Brightband, San Francisco, CA; and H. Kamdar, R. Keisler, A. Bollinger, J. DiCintio, H. Mohrmann, D. A. Rothenberg, and A. White
497368.abstract: AIDA is an operational machine learning data assimilation system that estimates the global analysis state directly from point-like observations, including satellite radiances and in situ measurements. Verified against observations in 1-day forecasts, AIDA analyses are on par with or exceed those of operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems, and can initialize machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models to enable a fully observations-to-forecast system. AIDA also serves as a fast, flexible platform for observation valuation. Through observing system experiments (OSEs), we quantify the forecast impact of observations from a wide range of instrument types, including microwave sounders, infrared sounders, and radio occultation, entirely within an AI system.

497369.title: Spray Generation In Extreme Winds, Consideration of Wave-Wave Interactions and Wind Tearing of Waves.
497369.authors: Brian K. Haus, University of Miami, Miami, FL; and M. Curcic and D. G. Ortiz-Suslow
497369.abstract: The precise role of sea-spray generation in hurricanes and the associated heat and momentum fluxes has long been considered to be one of the important challenges in understanding the process of rapid intensification. Although considerable strides have been made in this regard, the field has been hampered by a basic conceptual gap in the understanding of spray production processes in hurricane winds. Spray generation has been largely attributed to a combination of breaking wave generation, bubble bursting and/or direct tearing of the water surface by waves. Here, based on direct observation of the interface in the extreme winds generated in the University of Miami’s SUSTAIN laboratory and by direct numerical simulations we argue that the three distinct mechanisms are closely linked, but are mechanistically distinct from previously descriptions and that this has considerable implications for spray production processes. We will show that steeping of short waves on the windward crest of large waves due to hydrodynamic modulation can lead to wave tearing. This generates sheets of spray that are advected upward well above the crest height of the large waves. This leads to much longer residence times for large spume droplets than previously assumed and has important implications for rapid intensification processes and hurricane forecasting.

497372.title: Answering the Questions That Matter: The Transdisciplinary Framework and User-Centric Designs behind Fire Weather Testbed Evaluation
497372.authors: Kyle J. Thiem, Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere, Boulder, CO; and L. McMeeking, PhD, A. Baring, K. Fenton, B. J. Hatchett, S. M. Hoekstra, P. N. Schumacher, J. Vickery, and E. Wells
497372.abstract: Effectively transitioning emerging technologies from research to operations (R2O) depends not only on technically sound products or traditional verification techniques, but also on directly evaluating an application’s value and utility within real-world operational environments. By taking a transdisciplinary approach—integrating physical atmospheric sciences, quantitative/qualitative social sciences, statistical verification methodologies, and user experience research—the NOAA Fire Weather Testbed (FWT) grounds every evaluation in a small set of explicit key evaluation questions (KEQs) formed directly from developer objectives and operational user needs which are carried through every phase of the evaluation process (i.e., evaluation design, execution, analysis, and reporting). That consistency gives researchers and developers the specific feedback they need to efficiently advance tools through NOAA Readiness Levels (RLs) within the R2O process. Before choosing an evaluation approach, the FWT reconciles three often-competing considerations: what operational users need to know to trust and use a product, what developers need to know to improve it, and what the FWT’s own capacity can realistically support. These needs then shape the formation of the evaluation’s scope, goals, objectives, and KEQs, each of which is specific enough to be answered by a defined analysis. The evaluation design is then shaped to directly address the KEQs, which may include simulated operational scenarios within immersive "sandbox" scenarios, mock Decision Support Services (DSS) activities, statistical verification studies, extended field evaluations, or a combination of approaches. We also connect developers with end-users throughout this process, enabling the FWT to function as an active knowledge transfer platform. We select data collection and analysis methods, such as surveys, interviews, focus groups, observations, artifacts, and verification metrics, to directly align with the KEQs. Our reporting process follows the same structure: findings are organized around the original goals and KEQs, and are created collaboratively by the entire team. The results are then presented in various formats, tailored for each audience, which range from quick-turnaround, “Rapid Summaries” to full technical reviews with comprehensive analysis. We illustrate this process across four diverse FWT evaluations: Integrated Warning Team (IWT) Fire Warnings via the Next Generation Fire System (NGFS), which immersed participants in simulated "sandbox" environments meant to emulate real-world, multi-partner decision-support scenarios and stress test collaborative workflows under realistic, high-impact constraints. NGFS for Predictive Services, which utilized real-time, think-aloud walk-throughs with live tool usage to map workflow integration and identify key operational modifications across the incident management cycle. National Blend of Models (NBM) v5.0 Fire Weather Elements, which paired quantitative verification and qualitative forecaster field evaluations as parallel, integrated tracks to evaluate both forecast accuracy and user trust. WindNinja Model Downscaling, which applied a three-pronged approach separating quantitative verification, perceived forecast utility, and operational feedback on an automated system providing downscaled model wind forecasts for NWS Spot Forecast requests. Across all these evaluations, the design follows the evaluation’s Key Questions rather than fitting a product into a pre-defined evaluation framework. That process has been successful due to the integration of transdisciplinary expertise on a single evaluations team, which eliminates traditional organizational silos. We present key benefits and best practices from our transdisciplinary approach, offering attendees a practical, KEQ-driven blueprint for building goal-oriented evaluations adaptable to R2O programs of any size or composition. This talk itself models the collaborative format it describes, co-presented by a physical scientist and a social scientist.

497376.title: Breeze.jl: A Differentiable, GPU-first Atmospheric Modeling System for Severe Weather Forecasting and Science
497376.authors: Gregory LeClaire Wagner, Aeolus Labs, San Francisco, CA; and J. Buch, K. Y. Cheng, E. Quon, N. R. Barron, P. Berg, M. Giordano, W. Moses, T. Bischoff, M. Lee, and K. Mashita
497376.abstract: The results of efforts such as SCREAM, ERF, ICON, ClimaAtmos, and others demonstrate that the transition from CPU- to GPU-based systems can unlock performance and capabilities for high-resolution, high-throughput atmospheric simulation. Less appreciated, perhaps, is the opportunity this transition creates to rethink scientific software design, user interfaces, and model capabilities, in addition to supporting new computational architectures. Aeolus Labs is spearheading the development of Breeze.jl, an open-source, GPU-first atmospheric modeling system in the high-level Julia programming language for severe weather forecasting and science. Uniquely, Breeze design prioritizes accelerated model development for a range of operational and scientific applications, rather than a particular configuration or suite of parameterizations. Achieving this unique goal means that Breeze must simultaneously exhibit a high level of flexibility and productivity in its internal and user interfaces, while also meeting or exceeding state-of-the-art performance to satisfy operational goals. For example, Breeze provides an interface for developing microphysical schemes that re-uses a single scheme implementation in parcel models, kinematic models, anelastic large-eddy simulations, and fully compressible regional simulations with terrain and split-explicit acoustic substepping. At the same time, Breeze performs well in initial benchmarks: for the GATE III LES case (2048x2048x181 cells with 100 m horizontal resolution) at 1.2 SDPD on a single H200. This compares favorably with SCREAM (3.6 SYPD with 384 A100s) and SAM (0.17 SDPD on 2048 previous-generation CPUs). Breeze development is facilitated by its foundation in the ocean modeling software and finite volume modeling framework Oceananigans, from which it inherits data structures, numerical methods, and design philosophy — and which also creates the potential for coupled atmosphere-ocean configurations in a unified framework. We will present a variety of benchmarks to showcase Breeze’s capabilities, including idealized, LES, DCMIP, and realistic regional downscaling cases. A second priority of Breeze development is to support Reactant compilation for portability to new architectures such as TPUs, as well as differentiation through model time stepping using Enzyme. Our presentation will showcase how gradients with respect to initial conditions, physical parameters, and learned components create a path toward variational data assimilation and online calibration of high-dimensional and data-driven parameterizations.

497377.title: Seasonal and Short-term Approaches to Air Quality Forecasting in the Sacramento Region
497377.authors: Steve Irwin, Spheros Environmental, Petaluma, CA; and P. H. Zahn and J. J. Beamish
497377.abstract: Over the past two decades, emissions reductions have led to a gradual improvement in air quality in the Sacramento region of northern California. However, wildfire smoke is becoming an increasingly critical driver during poor-air quality events in the region. Similar to other regions in the U.S., the majority of high-ozone days (with maximum 8-hour average concentrations exceeding the National Ambient Air Quality Standard [NAAQS]) during the past three summers have exhibited significant correlation with the presence of near-surface smoke, as indicated by Hazard mapping System (HMS) smoke analyses, air quality models, and surface PM2.5 concentrations. Given the influence of smoke on regional air quality, forecasters at Spheros Environmental are working to develop methods to predict the likelihood of smoke impacts in the Sacramento region, both on a seasonal scale and for short-term forecasts on the Air Quality Index (AQI). For seasonal outlooks, forecasters synthesize data across several climate resources, including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA’s) El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) forecasts, existing drought indices, climate model predictions, the National Interagency Coordination Center’s (NICC’s) fire potential outlook, and seasonal trends analyses, to assess the regional- and continental-scale risk of fire and smoke production that may influence air quality in the Sacramento region. Once wildfire season begins, forecasters assess regional fire activity and smoke production daily to determine potential impacts on the AQI forecasts. To help quantify potential smoke impacts on daily maximum 8-hour average ozone concentrations Spheros forecasters have developed a prototype machine learning (ML)-based tool that incorporates meteorological model predictions and surface PM2.5 predictions from the Copernicus Atmospheric Modeling Service (CAMS). This presentation will give an overview of the seasonal-scale climate, fire-risk, and smoke-production predictions generated at the beginning of summer 2026, as well as an evaluation of observed climate, drought, and fire and smoke conditions in the Sacramento region through the summer and early fall of 2026. We will also discuss the design and implementation of the ML-based ozone tool that is used on a daily basis to assist with ozone forecasts, along with a preliminary evaluation of its performance during the summer 2026 ozone season in the Sacramento region.

497378.title: Urban Land-Surface and Grid-Spacing Controls on Simulated Flash-Flood Response: Contrasting Organized and Localized Convection in New Jersey
497378.authors: Juan Camacho, Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ; Rutgers Univ., Piscataway, NJ; and S. Rasiya Koya, J. Gong, F. Salamanca, P. Ray, and E. Nikolopoulos
497378.abstract: Flash-flood prediction in urbanized regions depends on the accuracy of convective precipitation forecasts, yet how precipitation error propagates into hydrologic error remains poorly quantified. We examine this propagation for two contrasting flash floods in New Jersey: widespread, synoptically organized rainfall from the remnants of Hurricane Ida (1–3 September 2021), and a localized convective storm over northern New Jersey (14–15 July 2025). Convection-permitting WRF simulations (12 km to 0.4 km) span a sensitivity matrix of initial and boundary conditions, microphysics–PBL combinations, urban canopy representation, and grid spacing, alongside operational HRRR forecasts initialized 1–24 h in advance. Simulated precipitation is evaluated against Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor (MRMS) observations for magnitude, timing, and spatial placement, then used to force the EF5 distributed hydrologic model. Flood response is assessed against an MRMS-forced EF5 reference simulation. Sensitivity is strongly storm-dependent. The Ida event is largely insensitive to configuration; most experiments capture the precipitation envelope but propagate some of the intense rainfall artificially southward.
