The July 2025 storm is far more sensitive, with urban land-surface treatment and sub-kilometer grid spacing measurably improving rainfall placement. HRRR skill varies with initialization time and occasionally yields fragmented precipitation structures. Hydrologically, spatial placement matters more than domain-total accuracy. Experiments with realistic basin-wide rainfall still fail to reproduce the reference flood footprint when precipitation is displaced, whereas placement improvements enhance agreement with the reference response despite a persistent magnitude bias, resulting in missed flooding, false alarms, and spurious discharge peaks. These results argue for storm-dependent configuration strategies and spatially explicit precipitation verification in operational urban flash-flood forecasting.

497381.title: Investigating Observed Thunderstorm Cold Pools over the Colorado High Plains using the CoAgMet Network
497381.authors: David G. Lerach, University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO; and R. S. Schumacher
497381.abstract: Thunderstorm cold pool passages can result in a multitude of societal impacts, including severe winds, heavy rainfall and hail, and unexpected temperature drops. The accurate identification of thunderstorm cold pool passages has historically been limited by sparse coverage of official surface observations with high temporal resolution. The Colorado Agricultural and Meteorological (CoAgMet) Network is comprised of surface weather stations that produce 5-minute observations, and with denser spatial coverage across many areas of the state's varied topography compared to the existing ASOS/AWOS networks, filling critical observational gaps over the Colorado High Plains. In this study, observations from 48 research-grade CoAgMet stations are leveraged to construct a novel 10-year cold pool climatology across Eastern Colorado for the period 2016 – 2025 as a function of thunderstorm mode and time. The dominant storm mode for each passage is determined using national composite radar reflectivity fields and multiple machine learning (ML) based algorithms, including K-means and Random Forest. The presented results will focus on cold pool strength (net temperature drop) and associated maximum wind gusts as classified by thunderstorm mode and life cycle, seasonality, and diurnal cycle, making use of a variety of statistical methods. The results will also be compared to related studies that have characterized cold pool characteristics using different networks across other regions of the U.S.

497382.title: Resolving the Planetary Boundary Layer through the Fusion of Active and Passive WH2yMSIE Data
497382.authors: Alexander E Kotsakis, ESSIC/NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD
497382.abstract: Characterizing the thermodynamic structure of the Planetary Boundary Layer (PBL) is critical for understanding the dynamic processes that drive Earth's weather and climate systems. However, current remote sensing technologies face limitations in capturing the fine scale temperature and water vapor profiles required to resolve these processes. The Westcoast & Heartland Hyperspectral Microwave Sensor Intensive Experiment (WH2yMSIE), conducted in October-November 2024, provided a unique opportunity to address these gaps. Funded by NOAA and NASA, this field campaign featured the deployment of the hyperspectral microwave (HMW) sounder prototype, CoSMIR-H, aboard the NASA ER-2 aircraft, alongside active and passive instruments including lidars, infrared, and visible sensors. This work utilizes CoSMIR-H measurements collected during WH2yMSIE and the application of an advanced data fusion model combining passive and active sensors. Through a flexible deep learning retrieval framework, we demonstrate the ability to retrieve high-resolution temperature and water vapor profiles in diverse PBL regimes, providing the vertical fidelity necessary to observe complex boundary layer processes. The approach leverages insight from successful data fusion done using simulated remote sensing data and builds on real-world datasets, enabling optimization of future instrument design and configuration. Preliminary results highlight the improvedretrieval performance achieved by integrating active-passive sensor data, demonstrating anenhanced capability to capture underlying PBL thermodynamic processes during WH2yMSIE. These findings not only validate the utility of HMW measurements but also underscore the potential for data fusion methods to address current observational challenges. This effort informs the development of NOAA and NASA’s next-generation missions while advancing multi-sensor techniques for comprehensive PBL sounding.

497383.title: Towards the Implementation of Radar Vertical Profiles in CIP
497383.authors: Darcy Jacobson, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. M. Ellis, D. R. Adriaansen, P. Prestopnik, G. P. McCabe Jr., and S. DiVito
497383.abstract: The operational Current Icing Potential (CIP) algorithm combines numerical weather prediction model output with radar, satellite, surface observations, lightning data, and pilot reports to produce an hourly 3D diagnosis of aircraft icing probability, severity, and supercooled large drop potential. It uses a combination of physically based decision trees and fuzzy-logic techniques to identify clouds containing supercooled liquid water and estimates where hazardous icing conditions are most likely to exist. Detection of supercooled liquid aloft is challenging and key to CIPs success. One way this is possible is through careful interpretation of satellite and radar data. Evidence of classical freezing rain formation appears in the radar data as a bright-band in reflectivity where falling ice crystals melt in the presence of a ‘warm-nose’. Dual-polarimetric radar variables contain information about the microphysical characteristics of the scatterers within the radar volume allowing for detection of these mixed-phase particles in the melting layer. Vertical profiles from individual U.S. WSR-88D NEXRAD radars were formed by interpolating the data to a Cartesian grid yielding a high-resolution 2D grid of vertical profiles within the radar domain. By combining information from dual-polarimetric variables such as reflectivity, differential reflectivity, correlation coefficient, as well as an external source of temperature, a gridded likelihood field of a melting layer signature is produced. Cases from the 2019 ICICLE field campaign were employed to investigate the use of radar measurements to infer classical freezing precipitation, since these in-situ observations verify the existence of such a scenario. Initial attempts yielded promising results and smoothing techniques to reduce false melting layer detection were explored and will be discussed. This research is in response to requirements and funding by the FAA. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official policy or position of the FAA.

497387.title: PACE Water Quality Products from NASA SPoRT
497387.authors: Clay B. Blankenship, USRA, Huntsville, AL; Universities Space Research Association, Huntsville, AL; and K. K. Fuell
497387.abstract: The NASA Short-Term Prediction Research and Transition (SPoRT) center provides NASA satellite products for stakeholders and decision makers. SPoRT works closely with end users to facilitate the adoption of new products by providing data to meet user needs and developing training. SPoRT has developed several water quality products derived from the NASA PACE mission for the US and surrounding waters. These include 7-day aggregated chlorophyll-a, 30-day chlorophyll-a anomalies, 442 nm absorption, a true color image, and a multi-panel product for chlorophyll-a. The 442 nm absorption is indicative of Colored Dissolved Organic Matter (CDOM) and is locally correlated with salinity in coastal zones. These products are available through the interactive SPoRT Viewer and for certain products, as geotiff files. Examples of Harmful Algal Bloom (HAB) events observed in the PACE data will be shown. We will also present results from a product assessment, conducted in August and September of 2026, giving end user feedback on the SPoRT PACE products, and helping us to refine the products.

497388.title: Expanding the User Base of North American Downscaled Climate Projections through a Web-Based Portal
497388.authors: Jennifer Boehnert, NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and R. R. McCrary, S. McGinnis, J. Stuivenvolt-Allen, O. Wilhelmi, K. Fewless, A. Gaydos, L. Kessenich, and M. Casali
497388.abstract: The North American Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (NA-CORDEX-CMIP6) data provides information for assessing future climate risks at scales relevant to planning and decision making. Using boundary conditions from global climate model simulations in the CMIP6 archive, NA-CORDEX-CMIP6 data is generated through dynamical downscaling with regional climate models. The data is natively available as netCDF-CF at an hourly temporal resolution, and a horizontal resolution of 12 km. The native gridded format consists of a large data volume, and technical complexity of these datasets often limit their accessibility to stakeholders outside the climate modeling community, including emergency managers, water resource planners, and public health officials. To address this gap, we have developed a new web-based portal designed to improve the communication, accessibility, and usability of NA-CORDEX-CMIP6 data for a broader range of users. As part of this effort, gridded model output has been aggregated to policy-relevant spatial boundaries, including North American states/provinces, counties, and watersheds, allowing users to explore climate projections within the administrative and hydrological units most relevant to their decision-making needs. In addition to these spatial aggregations, the portal provides temporal and seasonal summaries of key climate variables, enabling users to examine both long-term trends and within-year variability without needing to process raw model output themselves. The portal's interface allows users to visualize data through interactive maps, enabling comparison of projected conditions across regions and emission scenarios. Time series plots and other graphical summaries allow users to examine variability and change over time for a given region of interest. These features are designed to provide easy to understand future climate projection information along with associated uncertainty for stakeholders to make decisions. This presentation will provide an overview of the portal's development, the methods used to generate the spatial and temporal aggregations, and a demonstration of its core visualization and analysis capabilities. We will also discuss lessons learned in translating complex regional climate model output into a format that is both scientifically robust and accessible to non-specialist audiences, along with plans for future portal development based on user feedback.

497389.title: Developing an α-Fe2O3 Catalyst for Total Conversion of Atmospheric Sulfur Species to SO2
497389.authors: Amy Pham, Stanford University, Stanford, CA; and A. Rollins and E. Waxman
497389.abstract: Atmospheric sulfur exists in gaseous and aerosol forms and drives critical processes, regulating climate and forming acid rain. Trace gases like SO₂ and H₂S, emitted by volcanoes and fossil fuel combustion, oxidize into sulfate aerosols, which act as cloud condensation nuclei, cooling the planet but also triggering acid precipitation and harming human health at high concentrations. Understanding the total budget and fate of these sulfur sources would be of high scientific value, yet has not been achieved in research-grade atmospheric measurements. Quantifying total atmospheric sulfur conversion ("SOy") would allow sulfur compounds to be measured using NOAA's laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) instrument, offering precision to detect SOy anywhere in the atmosphere with high time resolution. Thermal decomposition converts reduced sulfur species to SO₂, but SO₃-to-SO₂ conversion, the rate-limiting step in the sulfur-iodine cycle for hydrogen energy research, has required a catalyst to avoid temperatures above 1000°C. Pt/TiO₂ gives under 50% conversion at its theoretical maximum, so α-Fe₂O₃ was chosen instead for its ease of synthesis and natural abundance. Here, α-Fe₂O₃ was synthesized via precipitation onto a quartz wool support, shown by Brittain and Hildenbrand not to interfere with catalysis. We developed a packed-bed reactor: a catalyzed quartz tube inside an aluminum tube, wrapped in heat tape, housed within an insulated steel tube. Flow rate, bed length, and catalyst form were optimized. Controlling temperature via PID, we correlated temperature with SO₂ conversion, achieving up to 60% conversion at 725C, and observed SO₂ chemisorption onto the catalyst at room temperature, indicating meaningful catalyst-analyte interaction even without thermal activation.

497390.title: The Linearity of Precipitation in Response to Evaporation Anomalies
497390.authors: Timothy Considine, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and T. W. Aerenson, D. McCoy, and D. Caulton
497390.abstract: Accurately modeling precipitation remains a critical challenge in Earth science due to the complex dynamics of the hydrologic cycle. This study investigates the linearity of global precipitation trends by establishing direct, causal links between evaporation source regions and their corresponding precipitation fields. We employ the WAM2layers moisture tracking model to construct a comprehensive global map that routes moisture from specific evaporation sources to its ultimate precipitation destinations. Using the evaporation field to estimate global precipitation validates well in most regions. To evaluate the nature of these relationships, we systematically perturb the evaporation rates within source regions to estimate the subsequent changes in downwind precipitation. The difference between the actual precipitation pattern and that derived from mapping evaporation to downwind precipitation indicates non-linearity in the response of downwind precipitation to evaporation anomalies. This work provides critical insights into moisture transport dynamics, and how it ultimately sets precipitation across the globe.

497393.title: Evaluating the Impacts of Estuarine Dynamics on Water Level Measurement Accuracy
497393.authors: Dahlia Barranco, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA; and L. Heilman and R. Heitsenrether
497393.abstract: Estuaries are coastal environments characterized by the mixing of freshwater and saltwater, where tide-driven transport results in regular salt intrusion, impacting the density of the water column. This study aims to evaluate the variations observed among different water level measurement technologies utilized by NOAA’s National Water Level Observation Network (NWLON), particularly in estuaries. These differences result from how different sensors account for variable density and measure water level. The Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services (CO-OPS), a program office of NOAA's National Ocean Service, maintains the NWLON. CO-OPS provides reliable oceanographic and meteorological observations, reporting water levels and delivering tidal predictions for the Great Lakes and U.S. coastlines. This real-time data informs flooding outlooks and other forecasts to protect coastal communities and commerce. To investigate these differences, we deployed a subsurface bottom platform alongside a NOAA tide gauge along the Elizabeth River, a tributary of the Chesapeake Bay, located near Norfolk, Virginia. The bottom platform was equipped with an Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler plus two pressure-temperature sensors, one of which also measured conductivity, while another conductivity-temperature-depth sensor was deployed at a shallower depth. This instrument array was intentionally designed to complement the tide stations operational radar and pressure water level sensors. This instrumentation also captures additional water properties that contribute to reported water level measurements. Initial analyses utilize the collected observations to illustrate the different methods of measuring water level and varying water properties that affect reported water levels to reevaluate future studies. Results will inform our understanding of estuarine and coastal tidal dynamics, improving water level measurements where density varies spatiotemporally, ultimately supporting the reliability of NWLON water levels.

497394.title: USMTArray Dataset and its Predictive Accuracy for Storm-Time Geoelectric Field Estimation
497394.authors: Anna Kelbert, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, Cambridge, MA; and G. D. Egbert
497394.abstract: The United States Magnetotelluric Array (USMTArray) dataset, collected in the years 2006-2024, consists of more than 1,700 long-period magnetotelluric stations covering the entirety of the contiguous United States on a quasiregular 70km grid. Funding across multiple federal agencies was critical to sustaining this effort to its completion. Important components of the project included active guidance and participation from the MT community, the open and timely availability of all data, and the application of consistent instrumentation and robust data processing. Taken as a whole, these data are visualized as the National Impedance Map, which, together with a 3D synthesis conductivity model of the nation, reveals the electrical architecture of the contiguous U.S. USMTArray data are used by researchers worldwide for fundamental and applied studies, including investigations of continental architecture and evolution, estimation of hazards to critical infrastructure due to geomagnetic storms, and assessment of the nation’s undiscovered geothermal and mineral resources. In a recently published manuscript (Kelbert et al, 2026), we present the U.S. Magnetotelluric Array Impedance Map (AIM) and synthesis high-resolution 3D electrical conductivity model for the contiguous U.S., as well as introduce the U.S. Gridded Array Impedance Map (GAIM). Here, we summarize these publicly available datasets and describe our initial efforts to quantify storm-time geoelectric field modeling errors associated with the MT plane-wave assumption compared to 3D modeling with realistic ionospheric source fields.

497395.title: Using Doppler LiDAR to Quantify Entrainment into Thunderstorm Outflows
497395.authors: Kylee Matousek, Prairie Research Institute, Champaign, IL; Univ. of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign, Champaign, IL; and D. A. R. Kristovich, J. Wang, J. M. Keeler, and K. T. Brooks
497395.abstract: Thunderstorm outflows, cold mesoscale surface airmasses that develop through evaporation of rain, regularly cause widespread property damage due to severe wind gusts. In addition, such outflows provide a source of lift and, in some cases, increased instability for additional convection initiation. Understanding how these airmasses behave and evolve over their lifetime is crucial for forecasters and researchers alike. The thermodynamic evolution of the outflow airmass depends on multiple external factors, such as evolution of the storm system, relative buoyancy of the air preceding the outflow, etc. One process that has rarely been observationally examined is the entrainment of environmental air in the turbulent wake region of a thunderstorm outflow. Since the ambient environment is typically warmer and drier than a thunderstorm outflow, entrainment of environmental air into an outflow can dilute these cool airmasses and alter their stability and turbulence properties. Over three separate campaign periods in 2021, 2024, and 2026, members of the Maritime to Inland Transitions Towards Environments for Convection Initiation (MITTEN-CI) team sampled multiple thunderstorm outflows using Doppler LiDAR, instrumented towers, and Windsonde and GRAW radiosonde systems. For this study, Doppler LiDAR vertical stare data are paired with instrumented tower measurements to determine if environmental air was entrained into these outflows, and all data sources are used to analyze how the stability and turbulence parameters change in response to entrainment. The favorability of the environment to additional convection initiation before and after outflow passage will also be examined. The results of this research will provide a greater understanding of the role dry air entrainment plays in altering the stability and wind characteristics of thunderstorm outflows and how they contribute to further convection initiation.

497397.title: Air, Water, and Land Perceptions, Resilience, and Data on Tribal Lands
497397.authors: Zane Smith, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and E. R. Martin
497397.abstract: Variations in climate and environmental conditions create uneven and often asymmetrical risks across communities and regions. These risks may be physical, including extreme weather and natural hazards, or social, reflecting disparities in infrastructure, resources, environmental monitoring, and adaptive capacity. This project examines these risks both locally for tribes in Oklahoma and New Mexico as well as broader implications for Tribal communities across the United States. The study addresses two primary questions: (1) How do concerns related to air, water, land, and extreme weather vary across communities? and (2) How do these concerns compare with observed environmental conditions and available monitoring data? To address these questions, the project integrates geospatial environmental data with multi-wave survey responses. Air and water monitoring networks are mapped relative to Tribal boundaries to evaluate the spatial distribution and availability of environmental observations. Pre-existing survey data from Meso-Scale Integrated Socio-Geographic Network (MSIS-Net) are used to examine patterns in environmental concern, hazard perception, and prioritization across respondents and regions, with particular attention to participants who self-identify as American Indian/Alaska Native and/or reside within federally recognized Tribal jurisdictions. By bringing these datasets together, the project examines relationships among environmental conditions, access to observational information, and community perceptions of risk. Preliminary findings indicate substantial spatial variation in both monitoring coverage and reported environmental concerns. Anticipated outcomes include data products and visualization tools designed to support locally relevant environmental decision-making, identify potential monitoring gaps, and strengthen community resilience.

497399.title: Assessing the Impacts of Radiation Measurement Quality on Surface Energy Budget Measurements
497399.authors: Laura D. Riihimaki, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and K. Balmes, J. Sedlar, M. Gallagher, and C. J. Cox
497399.abstract: The surface radiation budget community has developed standards and techniques to achieve the lowest possible uncertainty of radiation measurements through the Baseline Surface Radiation Network (BSRN). This community largely operates separately from surface energy budget networks like FLUXNET which often uses instrumentation that is more convenient for tower infrastructure but has higher uncertainties, especially a diurnal bias related to infrared loss which can reach 10s of W/m^2. This presentation will examine the impact of those uncertainties on surface energy measurements and recommend radiation measurement technologies to reduce those uncertainties. By sharing knowledge between measurement communities, we hope to move the science forward and help design measurement networks that can answer new science questions in the future.

497400.title: Learning a Geographic Representation from Gaussian Terrain Primitives
497400.authors: Shane Coffing, LANL, Los Alamos, NM; and S. Brambilla and A. Mohan
497400.abstract: Digital elevation models (DEMs) are fundamental inputs to simulations and studies of Earth-systems processes, yet their raster structure contains no inherent definition of terrain features, hierarchy, or relationships across scales. We represent terrain as a sparse combination of anisotropic Gaussian primitives, each defined by its position, amplitude, orientation, and characteristic length scales. The resulting decomposition provides a natural description of feature scale and hierarchy, while the spatial relationships among Gaussian primitives offer a basis for constructing structured or graph-based representations of terrain. Our current framework uses convolutional matching pursuit over a multiscale Gaussian dictionary, followed by continuous refinement of selected atoms. This improves local reconstruction fidelity while allowing smaller dictionaries. We also present early results from an unrolled ISTA-style model that replaces repeated matching-pursuit searches with learned sparse inference. This provides a path towards a reusable global Gaussian terrain dictionary and scalable decomposition of large DEM collections. Ultimately, the framework could provide interpretable geometric coordinates for comparing terrain and developing reduced representations of terrain-dependent Earth-system processes.

497401.title: Bridging the Chasm: A 15-Year Evolution of Real-Time Collaboration and Digital Dissemination for 45,000+ Emergency Managers and Decision Makers Across Public and Private Sectors
497401.authors: Dave F. Jones, StormCenter Communications, Inc., Annapolis, MD
497401.abstract: Abstract: In an era of cascading disasters—ranging from erratic wildfire behavior and catastrophic flooding to the unthinkable complexities of radioactive dispersion—the primary barrier to effective response is no longer a lack of data, but the lack of a Collaborative Common Operating Picture (C-COP) and effective communication. For 15 years, StormCenter Communications and the All-Hazards Consortium (AHC) have pioneered a battle-tested ecosystem that transforms raw atmospheric science into decisive operational action for over 45,000 public and private sector stakeholders. This presentation "decodes" the profession of emergency management by addressing the critical "weather IQ" gap. We will demonstrate how GeoCollaborate® serves as a revolutionary emergency management technology, enabling disparate agencies to move beyond static maps and into a live, synchronized data environment. This platform allows EMs to monitor wildfire risk, flood progression, and tropical systems simultaneously, ensuring that the "Same Map, at the Same Time" isn't just a slogan, but a requirement for resource management and EOC activation information sharing. Furthermore, we will detail a sophisticated Digital Communication strategy that meets EMs where they live. By delivering synthesized "Weather Impact Updates" via the StormCenter YouTube channel, the AHC Sensitive Information Sharing Environment (SISE) portal, and the Signal App, we provide a blueprint for reaching a critical mass of decision-makers during the preparation, response and recovery phases. Attendees will learn how this integrated approach to training, technology, and real-time data sharing accelerates the decision-making process for evacuations and alert system programs, effectively shortening the distance between scientific forecast and lifesaving response.

497404.title: Local Impacts of George’s Large-Scale Waves
497404.authors: Courtney J. Schumacher, Texas A&M Univ., College Station, TX
497404.abstract: George Kiladis has been instrumental in our understanding of large-scale wave dynamics, especially convectively-coupled equatorial waves. This presentation will first focus on the local impact of these waves as observed during tropical field campaigns including TEPPS, DYNAMO, GoAmazon2014/15, and OTREC. I will then illustrate the importance of these waves, and their interactions, on producing extreme rainfall over Indonesia. George’s most lasting impact though, is the local impact he’s had on the people around him.

497406.title: Street-Level Wind at City Scale: A Spectrally-Guided Diffusion Downscaling Framework
497406.authors: Arya Chavoshi, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX; Fujitsu Research of America, Inc., Santa Clara, CA; and R. Vuppala, S. Hazarika, and H. Y. Wong
497406.abstract: High-resolution pedestrian-level wind data has significant value for urban policymakers, as it affects outdoor thermal comfort, street-canyon ventilation, and pollutant and heat dispersion. Despite its importance, meter-scale wind information remains largely unavailable at city scale, with the only source being large-eddy simulation (LES), which resolves street-level flow but is too computationally expensive for city-wide application. Deep-learning emulators have been proposed to bridge this gap, but deterministic regression-based approaches tend to smooth over fine-scale turbulent structure, degrading spectral fidelity relative to LES. Diffusion-based generative models have recently been shown to better preserve this fine-scale spatial structure and spectral content compared to deterministic emulators. Building on this, we present a conditional EDM-based diffusion model that downscales urban wind fields to pedestrian level, conditioned on building morphology and large-scale wind direction and magnitude. The model is trained on time-averaged LES wind fields spanning diverse global real and idealized urban patches. At inference, a MultiDiffusion scheme stitches fixed-size tiles into seamless, high-resolution wind fields over large-scale domains without retraining. To address high-wavenumber spectral content lost under the MultiDiffusion tiling scheme, we introduce a post-hoc spectral guidance framework that restores fine-scale variability suppressed by tile blending. The resulting model reproduces LES pedestrian-level wind speeds with low error while retaining fine-scale spatial and spectral structure that deterministic regression and naive MultiDiffusion smooth away, offering a fast, LES-fidelity surrogate for pedestrian-level mean wind to support urban design, planning, and parametric studies.

497409.title: Hazard Forecast Awareness during Hurricane Ian (2022)
497409.authors: Andrea B. Schumacher, NCAR, Fort Collins, CO; and J. L. Demuth, R. E. Morss, G. Wong-Parodi, N. Herbert, R. Prestley, and M. Ng
497409.abstract: The weather research community is constantly looking for ways to improve the forecast and warning process. A crucial step in this process involves people hearing and/or seeing the forecast and warning messages the National Weather Service (NWS) creates and disseminates and understanding if and when those messages are meant for them (i.e., hazard forecast awareness). Without this step, any improvements made to the accuracy of the forecasts or improvements to product design will not be realized by the public. In this study, we used data from repeated surveys collected during the 5 days leading up to Hurricane Ian’s landfall in 2022 to explore the public’s hazard forecast awareness for three types of NWS forecasts; the National Hurricane Center (NHC) Track Forecast Cone, tropical storm or hurricane watches or warnings, and storm surge watches or warnings. Were people aware that they were the target of one of these types of TC hazard forecasts during Hurricane Ian? Our results suggest that yes, the majority of respondents were aware. However, the proportion of respondents we found to be unaware was not trivial, ranging from 12-30% based on hazard forecast type and time to landfall. In order to find ways to increase hazard forecast awareness amongst the public, we need to better understand who the people are that are not seeing, hearing, and/or personalizing the NWS TC forecasts and warnings, and how they differ from their aware counterparts. For this talk, we will discuss the significant differences we found between the subgroups of respondents that were aware and unaware of being in a hazard forecast. These differences—which were found in aspects such as location, sociodemographics, and information sources and channels used—provide clues that can help communicators develop messaging strategies to improve TC hazard forecast awareness.

497411.title: INDOT and DTN: Supporting Winter Weather Traveler Messaging Through the FHWA Pathfinder Program
497411.authors: Benjamin W Hershey, DTN, LLC, Buxton, ND; and M. Nichols, N. Evans, B. Haines, K. Mahoney, CCM, R. Pinard, and S. Carpenter
497411.abstract: The Federal Highway Administration’s (FHWA) Pathfinder Program is a collaborative effort between the National Weather Service (NWS), state Departments of Transportation (DOTs), and private sector weather service providers to provide the DOTs with concise messaging information to support the traveling motorists during adverse weather and road conditions. Indiana Department of Transportation (INDOT) has been an active participant in Pathfinder for several years to support their operational messaging when winter weather conditions impact their travelers. INDOT coordinated with the NWS and DTN, their private weather service provider, when these events are identified in the forecast. While the DOTs cannot prevent weather from impacting the roads, these coordination efforts have been successful in informing drivers of incoming and ongoing conditions. This abstract will further explore INDOT’s use of information and content provided by DTN via the Pathfinder Program, specifically examining a winter weather event that occurred from January 23-27, 2026. Like previous Pathfinder Events, INDOT and DTN coordinated their communication process before the start of the event. DTN's precise forecasting and road condition predictions enabled the Indiana DOT to implement targeted mitigation strategies. Support included regular updates leading up to and throughout the storm. DTN’s Risk Communicator meteorologists specializing in road weather supported not only the maintenance decision support directly but also participated in their pathfinder call. This provided a consistent message of forecast pavement impacts between maintenance personnel, planners, and public-facing messaging. Specific examples will be presented to illustrate the dynamic weather and road weather issues faced by Indiana DOT and how they used the information provided to communicate these challenges to their operational forces and the public. INDOT is uniquely positioned to provide its travelers with accurate information due to their full deployment of MDSS. INDOT is a participant in the Maintenance Decision Support System Pooled Fund Study with a full deployment of route-based data and Automated Vehicle Location/Mobile Data Collection data units in their snowplow fleet. This data is analyzed by the DTN Risk Communicator meteorologists and DTN’s suite of meteorological and pavement condition models to provide real-time road and weather conditions as well as forecast road conditions based on treatment plans specific to INDOT operations. This level of insight provides a more complete picture of winter road challenges to ensure INDOT can provide clear information to their public. DTN's scalable, route-specific solutions, encompassing advanced forecasting, integrated alerting systems, Weather Risk Communicators, and tailored communication strategies have enhanced state DOTs’ capacity to manage road weather hazards effectively. Outcomes across partner states illustrate the adaptability of DTN's approach to diverse regional needs, ultimately contributing to measurable improvements in road safety and reductions in weather-related incidents.

497414.title: From Thunderstorms to Traffic Management: Translating Convective Weather Forecasts into Terminal Airspace Capacity Predictions Using TCEPT (Terminal Capacity Evaluation and Prediction Tool)
497414.authors: Sophie Splawinski, NAV CANADA, Ottawa, ON, Canada; and J. Venuti and M. Matthews
497414.abstract: Convective weather remains one of the most difficult challenges in air traffic management, often creating significant uncertainty in terminal operations, arrival flows, and strategic traffic management initiatives. While modern weather forecasting systems provide increasingly sophisticated depictions of thunderstorm evolution, Canadian aviation decision-makers must still translate meteorological information into operational impacts such as sector availability, arrival routing constraints, bedpost management, and airport capacity reductions. To address this challenge, NAV CANADA and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Lincoln Laboratory have collaborated on the development of the Terminal Capacity Evaluation and Prediction Tool (TCEPT), an operational decision-support system that transforms convective weather forecasts into actionable airspace impact assessments. TCEPT is designed to support strategic and tactical air traffic management decision-making across a 0-8 hour planning horizon by forecasting the impact of convective weather on terminal and bedpost sectors, arrival fixes, and departure corridors, providing translated permeability guidance as well as a risk of convective impact (RCI), the latter within the terminal only. Unlike traditional weather displays, RCI directly quantifies the likelihood of operationally significant impacts such as single-runway operations, arrival flow restrictions, or temporary airport closures. The tool also integrates forecast arrival demand at individual bedposts, enabling users to evaluate emerging imbalances between anticipated traffic demand and weather-constrained airspace capacity. The system utilizes an ensemble of deterministic and probabilistic weather guidance, including radar-derived storm information, extrapolated storm forecasts, NOAA High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and Rapid Refresh (RAP) forecasts, High-Resolution Ensemble Forecast (HREF) products, lightning guidance, and convective instability parameters such as CAPE and lifted index. These data are combined through machine learning techniques trained on multiple years of historical operational and weather observations to estimate future airspace capacity and associated forecast uncertainty. This presentation will describe the scientific and operational foundations of TCEPT, including its machine learning methodology, weather ensemble framework, and integration with terminal traffic demand information. A detailed operational case study from Toronto Pearson International Airport will demonstrate how TCEPT identified elevated convective risk hours before operational impacts materialized, providing earlier indications of disruption than conventional convective forecast products alone. Results illustrate the value of translating meteorological uncertainty into operationally relevant impact forecasts that can support collaborative decision-making, proactive traffic management initiatives, and improved terminal flow planning. The TCEPT experience offers insight into the next generation of aviation meteorology decision-support systems, where weather forecasts are no longer viewed solely as atmospheric predictions but as objective forecasts of operational impact, enabling more resilient and efficient management of weather-sensitive airspace.

497417.title: Improving Sensitivity of Low-Intensity Fires Using VIIRS Multi-Spectral Imagery
497417.authors: Curtis Seaman, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; CIRA, Chantilly, VA; and S. Gampa
497417.abstract: Low-intensity fire detection is challenging because weak thermal signals can be difficult to distinguish from the surrounding background, especially when observations come from sensors with different spatial characteristics. VIIRS provides complementary spectral information through the Day/Night Band (DNB) and the Moderate-resolution (M) bands, making it well suited for multispectral fire detection. In this work, we present a novel method to improve low-intensity fire detection at night by using VIIRS Day/Night Band (DNB) spectral observations in combination with other moderate-resolution and infrared bands. A primary challenge in fusing these data sources the spatial-resolution mismatch between the sensors: the M-bands provide approximately 750 m resolution at nadir, but this resolution degrades to approximately 1.6 km at the scan edges, whereas the DNB maintains a more uniform 750 m resolution across the swath. This inconsistency complicates multi-spectral alignment and constraints the effectiveness of existing methods. To address this limitation, we introduce an algorithm for integrating DNB and M-band data and demonstrate improved imagery.

497418.title: Evaluation of AI- and Physics-Based Numerical Weather Prediction over a Mountainous Desert
497418.authors: Thomas M. Hopson, NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and P. A. Jimenez, S. P. Swerdlin, J. C. Knievel, S. Alessandrini, R. Kumar, S. Meech, C. M. Rozoff, J. S. Shaw, R. S. Sheu, H. Soh, and V. Weeks
497418.abstract: We investigate the skill of a select number of state-of-the-art artificial intelligence (AI) numerical weather prediction (NWP) models over a desert with topographic variability in the southwestern United States. Biases in surface weather variables are shown to be extreme enough at times as to make them unusable. However, when observations are available to implement simple bias corrections, certain AI-based predictions have comparable skill to a physics-based NWP modeling system. We also explore whether combining AI and NWP can provide overall skill improvement over the two individual approaches, thereby capitalizing on the strengths of each. This research is part of an evaluation framework being developed at NSF NCAR: the Benchmark Evaluations for AI and CONventional prediction systems (BEACON), which is being developed toward an open, community-oriented framework for comparing AI, hybrid AI–physics, and conventional NWP systems using both scientific and decision-based performance metrics.

497419.title: A Multivariable Regression Assessment of Evapotranspiration and Boundary-Layer Atmosphere Influences on Convective Available Potential Energy in Missouri
497419.authors: Tyler Brucker, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO; and Z. Leasor
497419.abstract: Evapotranspiration (ET) serves as a fundamental flux linking land-surface moisture to the atmosphere. ET can also directly influence boundary layer growth and convective potential. Despite its importance in land-atmosphere coupling and storm initiation, the specific empirical contribution of surface ET relative to broader atmospheric state variables influencing Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE) remains insufficiently quantified. In this study, we construct a multivariable regression modeling framework to identify and evaluate key predictors of CAPE across Missouri. The framework pairs atmospheric metrics from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset (including boundary layer height [BLH], max BLH, BLH change, total column water, and 1000 hPa specific humidity) with surface observations from the Missouri Mesonet, prioritizing short-crop estimated evapotranspiration alongside air temperature, dewpoint, relative humidity, solar radiation, precipitation, wind speed, and wind direction. By evaluating CAPE against this combined set of surface and atmospheric predictors, the model quantifies the relative influence of ET and local surface conditions versus column moisture content and planetary boundary layer evolution. Results highlight the sensitive relationship between surface ET rates, boundary layer moistening, and subsequent thermodynamic instability in the region. This modeling approach provides a novel, data-driven framework for capturing land-atmosphere interaction dynamics in the central United States, offering refined insights for agricultural meteorology and convective risk assessment.

497420.title: Pangeo at 10: What the Community Built, What We Learned, and What the AI Era Demands of Geoinformatics
497420.authors: Joseph J Hamman, Earthmover PBC, Seattle, WA; and R. Abernathey
497420.abstract: Ten years ago, a small group of scientists and engineers, frustrated that petabyte-scale Earth System data had outgrown the desktop tools of the day, started an experiment in community-driven scientific data infrastructure. That experiment became Pangeo. A decade later, its impact is hard to overstate: Xarray, Zarr, Dask, and Jupyter anchor the reference architecture for analysis-ready, cloud-native geoscience; the Pangeo Discourse and Showcase sustain a global community of practice; and the Pangeo stack now powers substantial parts of major public data programs (e.g., Microsoft Planetary Computer, the AWS Open Data Program, and cloud initiatives at NASA, NOAA, USGS, Copernicus, and more), countless commercial operations, and research at virtually every university in the world. Pangeo also seeded a generation of organizations (Coiled, 2i2c, and Earthmover among them) that carry its open-source ethos into sustainable businesses. This talk, from the perspective of one of Pangeo's founding developers, offers a retrospective and a provocation. We examine what worked: betting on open standards, cloud computing, federations rather than monoliths, and tight feedback loops between developers, scientists, and infrastructure providers. We are equally candid about what didn't: fragile funding models, the limits of volunteer maintenance, and the gap between prototypes and production systems. We then argue that the next decade demands more than open-source software and "big data in the cloud." In the emerging era of AI, we have the opportunity to radically accelerate scientific discovery by connecting scientists, data, and AI systems so that any scientist, analyst, or agent can query decades of observations and simulations as easily as a database, and AI systems are grounded in trustworthy, versioned, analysis-ready scientific data. We close with a vision for how the Pangeo community, data providers, and a new wave of companies building on its foundations can meet that moment together.

497421.title: From the Ground Up: Building a Radar Services and Weather Technology Company
497421.authors: Tara Goode, Climavision, Louisville, KY; and C. Goode and J. van Doore
497421.abstract: Chris Goode’s path to entrepreneurship in the Weather Enterprise was shaped over more than three decades in and around operational meteorology. He began his career as a U.S. Air Force aviation weather specialist and later held leadership roles at The Weather Company, AirDat, and Enterprise Electronics Corporation, where he served as CEO of a global weather radar manufacturer. Each of those roles gave him a different view of the same industry. He saw how weather information was produced, how it was delivered, how customers used it, and where the system continued to fall short. One problem remained especially persistent: large portions of the United States lacked adequate low-altitude radar coverage, particularly in rural areas and in regions where terrain or distance from the national radar network limited visibility near the ground. While leading Enterprise Electronics Corporation, Goode saw communities, universities, and public-safety organizations attempt to address these gaps by purchasing individual radar systems. Many of those projects were worthwhile, but they often faced the same long-term challenge. Funding could be secured to purchase the equipment, yet there was frequently no durable plan to operate, maintain, upgrade, and support the system over time. The technology was available. The business model was not. That observation led to a different idea. Instead of continuing to sell radars one system at a time, the private sector could finance, deploy, operate, and maintain a shared network, then provide customers with access to the resulting data and services. The model, which became known as Radar-as-a-Service, would shift the upfront capital burden and operating risk away from individual communities and customers. It would also allow the same infrastructure to serve multiple users across government, public safety, media, energy, and other industries. When combined with numerical weather prediction, data assimilation, and decision-support tools, the network could support something broader than radar data alone. It could become the foundation of a weather intelligence company. Turning that idea into a business required a level of capital uncommon for an early-stage weather company. In 2021, during the uncertainty of the COVID-19 pandemic, Goode raised $100 million to launch Climavision and begin building its radar network and weather intelligence platform. Securing the investment required more than explaining the radar-gap problem. Investors had to believe that a private company could take on the considerable upfront cost of building and operating weather infrastructure before the market was fully developed. They also had to believe that the company could create value from the data across several customer segments rather than relying on a single source of revenue. Raising the capital was an important step, but it was only the beginning. It created the responsibility to turn a credible vision into an operating company. That meant recruiting a team that could bring together atmospheric science, engineering, software, radar operations, product development, and commercial execution. It also meant navigating long sales cycles, government procurement, technical setbacks, changing customer priorities, and the practical realities of building a capital-intensive business. Five years later, Climavision has grown to more than 50 employees, deployed supplemental radars in multiple regions, developed weather intelligence products, and secured customers that use its data and services for public safety, operational resilience, media, and energy decision-making. The company’s progress has not followed a straight line, nor has it been the work of one person. It has depended on a team willing to work across disciplines and on partners in government, research, technology, and industry who were prepared to support a different approach. It has also depended on customers willing to adopt a model that did not fit neatly within traditional weather procurement. This presentation will use the Climavision experience to offer a candid view of entrepreneurship in the Weather Enterprise. One lesson is that identifying an important problem is not the same as identifying a viable business. A founder must understand who is willing to pay, what problem the customer is actually trying to solve, and whether the solution can be delivered repeatedly and economically. A product can be technically strong and still fail if it does not improve a decision that matters to the customer. Another lesson is that experience across different parts of an industry can be a significant advantage. Goode’s background in operational weather, data, technology commercialization, and radar manufacturing allowed him to see the opportunity from several perspectives. His education in journalism also proved useful. Building a company requires the ability to explain complex science and technology in terms that investors, customers, policymakers, and partners can understand. The Climavision experience has also reinforced that innovation rarely comes from a single breakthrough. Much of the progress has come through steady improvements in network deployment, data quality, modeling, product development, customer adoption, and partnerships. The company has adjusted its approach many times while remaining focused on the same core mission: improving the observations and intelligence available to people making consequential weather decisions. The presentation will also address the mindset required to build a company in this industry. A founder must have conviction, but conviction cannot become stubbornness. Optimism must be balanced with an honest assessment of what is working and what is not. Plans will change. Markets will move more slowly than expected. Customers will ask for things that were not in the original strategy. The challenge is knowing when to adapt the plan without losing sight of the problem the company was created to solve. As artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and new sources of data continue to reshape the Weather Enterprise, the opportunity for new companies will grow. Technology will make it easier to build products, but it will not eliminate the need for domain expertise, proprietary data, trusted relationships, operational discipline, and a clear understanding of the end user. Goode’s journey offers one example of how experience, persistence, and a willingness to challenge an established business model can create an opportunity to build something new in an industry that plays a critical role in public safety and economic resilience.

497422.title: Building an Interoperable Cloud Data Foundation for NOAA Forecast Models
497422.authors: Jonathan Joyce, Tetra Tech, South Kingstown, RI; and K. Knee, D. Moretti, J. Doyle, B. Adams, P. Salisbury, M. J. Wengren, and T. C. Vance
497422.abstract: RPS, a Tetra Tech company, in collaboration with the NOAA Integrated Ocean Observing System (IOOS), has continued development of cloud-based data management workflows designed to improve access to NOAA Operational Forecast System (OFS) model outputs. Prior work demonstrated approaches for improving data management, accessibility, and interoperability using cloud-native approaches. We presented a technical recommendation to IOOS and have since released the first production infrastructure building upon that recommendation. This work has now progressed from prototype workflows to sustained production services. NOAA’s Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services (CO-OPS) runs ocean forecast models which produce NetCDF outputs. These outputs are uploaded to the NOAA Open Data Dissemination (NODD) public bucket for free public access, but working with NetCDF data in the cloud is problematic. Our workflow detects new data in the bucket, opens the NetCDF files, and generates a 30 day “Best forecast” aggregate product, saved in the Zarr V3 standard format. We maintain the native grid structure produced by the model, removing the need to regrid or standardize to a certain projection. Moving these workflows into production required scalable technology to cost-effectively transform terabytes of data each day. We used Karpenter with Kubernetes to maintain a platform-agnostic execution environment that scales up and down with use. These technology choices are aligned with other IOOS projects to maintain consistency and collaboration across the community. Our early prototyping efforts highlighted a need to have data observability as a core component to support production workflows. We also needed workflow orchestration, monitoring, automated recovery, and visibility into the freshness and availability of generated products. These considerations along with community input led us to select Dagster as the workflow execution platform. This also enables us to quickly build new processing pipelines as new data and products are needed. The resulting products are already supporting downstream use cases. Standardized OFS model outputs have been integrated into the OceansMap instance used by CO-OPS for model visualization. The same products can also be programmatically subset to support model data assimilation workflows, demonstrating how a common data layer can serve both interactive applications and automated scientific processes. By investing in standardized products and shared production infrastructure, IOOS is establishing a reusable and interoperable data foundation. This foundation reduces the effort required to integrate new capabilities and provides natural connection points for future visualization, analysis, automation, artificial-intelligence, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-based applications.

497424.title: Predicting the Scales Inherited and Generated By Generative Downscaling
497424.authors: Hoang Tran, PNNL, Richland, WA; PNNL, Richland, WA
497424.abstract: Machine learning emulators can produce global ensembles at a small fraction of the cost of physics-based models, but their approximately 100 km resolution is too coarse for regional hazard assessment. Generative downscaling can add fine-scale structure learned from high-resolution regional simulations. Here we quantify what such a downscaler adds and what it retains from its input. We train a one-step diffusion-based generative model on a 12 km regional simulation over the conterminous United States. At inference, we condition the model without retraining on either the 25 km resolution ERA5 reanalysis or the 100 km resolution ACE2 global machine learning emulator. The added conditioning noise controls how much information is retained from each input. Linear filter theory predicts a transition scale that we call the handoff wavelength. At wavelengths longer than the handoff, the input signal exceeds the added noise, so the downscaled output mainly retains information and biases from the input. At shorter wavelengths, the noise suppresses the input signal, so the model increasingly generates structure learned from the regional simulation. Across inputs, noise levels, regions, and variables, 62 measured handoffs follow this prediction with a single calibration factor. The transition occurs at wavelengths about 26% shorter than the theoretical estimate. This relationship explains both the behavior and the limitations of the downscaled output. No single conditioning noise level reproduces fine-scale power across all variables and named-storm cases differ systematically by event type. ACE2’s annual-mean precipitation bias also passes through downscaling largely unchanged, identifying the input as the source of the large-scale bias rather than the generated fine-scale structure. Downscaling therefore increases resolution without correcting input bias. Even so, evaluated distributional hazard statistics remain usable, and stable fine-scale structure supports estimates of mid-century changes in extremes at 12 km resolution. The handoff law provides a measurable scale boundary that producers and users of downscaled products can report and audit.

497425.title: Boundary-Layer Wind Shear Model Validation with UAS and Vertical Wind Profilers
497425.authors: Eric P. Grimit, TruWeather Solutions, Reston, VA; and J. J. Celenza, R. Rahimi, and C. M. Zarzar
497425.abstract: As commercial logistics operators scale up their automated airborne delivery services, there is an increasing need to improve the characterization of low-altitude winds and turbulence. Optimizing uptime, delivery pace, and battery management all while maximizing safety requires minute-scale knowledge of the boundary-layer wind field and its likely evolution over the delivery zone. Due to the ever-increasing volume of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) with local motion-compensated wind speed estimates, it presents an opportunity to validate modeled wind performance at fine spatial and temporal scales. A collaborative validation study was undertaken in the Dallas/Fort Worth, TX area to assess performance of TruWeather’s urban wind machine learning emulator model, called the Street-Scale Wind Analysis and Prediction System (SWAPS), using Zipline’s drone-derived wind estimates. At six additional fixed locations in the region, TruWeather provided LiDAR wind profiler measurements funded by a NASA SBIR Phase-III urban weather testbed. This presentation will focus on validation of the bulk low-level wind shear, expressed as the wind speed ratio between 80m and 10m height AGL. Comparisons are made with the NOAA HRRR 3-km as a baseline forecast and Zipline’s assimilated wind model. Initial exploratory results over a 3-week period in Feb-Mar 2026, suggests that HRRR underestimates wind shear between 10m and 80m, while SWAPS tends to overestimate it. Comparisons with approximately coincident drone-derived wind observations indicate that SWAPS provides modest improvements over HRRR in both error and correlation with observed wind shear. Ongoing analysis will expand the observational data set to multi-month periods and further quantify these differences in terms of statistical significance. Enhanced forecasts, which are informed by observations from the six vertical wind profilers, will be included in the final model comparisons.

497427.title: Glyoxal-Derived HOMs Enhance H2SO4-NH3 Nucleation at Upper Tropospheric Temperatures
497427.authors: Romulo Leoncio Cruz Simbron Sr., University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and Y. Tong, C. J. Lietzke, L. Caudillo-Plath, W. Yu, J. Shen, E. Sommer, N. Bhattacharyya, J. DeVivo, A. Stinchfield, Z. Zheng, F. Kunkler, A. Jacobshagen, C. Xenofontos, L. Liu, B. Yang, and R. Volkamer
497427.abstract: Glyoxal is the smallest a-dicarbonyl, and ubiquitously present over remote forested and marine areas, megacities, and in the upper troposphere. Ammonia has recently been detected in the outflow of the Asian Monsoon in concentrations of up to 1.5 ppbv, where it contributes to the formation of the Asian Tropopause Aerosol Layer (ATAL). Glyoxal reactive uptake and subsequent multiphase chemistry have been studied at room temperature, but its role in nucleation and early growth remains unstudied at cold temperatures such as the ATAL. In this study conducted in the Cosmics Leaving OUtdoor Droplets (CLOUD) chamber we study the effect of glyoxal on the nucleation and early growth of freshly nucleated particles formed from sulfuric acid in presence and absence of ammonia at temperatures of -30 °C and -50 °C and relative humidity around 60%. We find that glyoxal has a potential effect in the early growth of nanoclusters, where its reaction products are dominating the particle composition detected by FIAGERO I--CIMS. We report here as well the presence of peroxiacyl hydroperoxide of glyoxal, specifically C2H2O4, C2H2O5 and C2H2O6 produced in the gas phase at +25, -10, -30 and -50 °C, at relative humidity around 60%, examples of small Highly Oxygenated Molecules (HOMs) formed from glyoxal and detected by NO3--CIMS. Under NOx conditions, the peroxyacyl nitrate C2HNO8 is formed in competition with the peroxyacyl hydroperoxide C2H2O6. The peroxiacyls C2H2O5 and C2H2O6 from stable adducts with the negative clusters of sulfuric acid and NH3 detected by neg Api-TOF. This presentation outlines first evidence for the formation of peroxyacyl-HOM type products of glyoxal oxidation in the gas phase, as well as the gem diol of glyoxal, glyoxal oligomers or glyoxal reactive uptake products that affect nucleation rates and early growth of particles under conditions characteristic of the ATAL.

497428.title: Simultaneous Assimilation of Multi-Wavelength Aerosol Optical Depth Retrievals from NASA PACE Mission in JEDI for NOAA GCAFS v1
497428.authors: Congmeng Lyu, NOAA, Boulder, CO; CIRES, Boulder, CO; and B. Huang, M. Pagowski, X. Xu, L. Zhang, O. R. Cooper, and B. C. McDonald
497428.abstract: The three-dimensional ensemble-variational (3DEnVar) aerosol data assimilation system was developed within the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) for NOAA’s global aerosol model. Using an early version of the NOAA Global Chemistry and Aerosol Forecast System version 1 (GCAFS v1), this system was demonstrated in near real-time for aerosol assimilation at NOAA GSL, and has been used to produce a global aerosol reanalysis by assimilating the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) aerosol optical depth (AOD) retrieval products at 550 nm from NOAA/NESDIS. While this approach improves the model’s representation of total AOD, assimilating 550 nm AOD alone imposes very limited constraints on specific aerosol composition and vertical profiles, which remain largely model-driven. To improve detailed aerosol representation in GCAFS v1, we are extending JEDI to assimilate advanced aerosol retrievals from NASA Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) satellite mission. We first implemented in JEDI simultaneous assimilation of multi-wavelength AOD retrievals from the PACE Ocean Color Instrument (OCI). Preliminary results showed that simultaneously assimilating AOD at 354, 550, and 670 nm, versus 550 nm alone, yielded clearly different aerosol analyses: more lower-tropospheric dust over North Africa and the Middle East, more sulfate over East Asia, and less near-surface organic carbon over southern Africa and the surrounding tropical ocean. We are now updating the workflow to the latest versions of JEDI and GCAFS v1, extending the multi-channel AOD assimilation cycling period (July 20 – September 30, 2024), and performing a systematic evaluation of assimilation impacts on global aerosol forecasts using in-situ and satellite retrievals. In the future we plan to extend this work by improving our estimates of biases and errors and assimilating absorption AOD and fine-mode fraction AOD.

497429.title: Advancing Seasonal Predictability by Combining NeuralGCM with Dynamically Simulated Sea Surface Temperatures
497429.authors: Bradley Vernon Jr., Utah State Univ., Logan, UT; and W. Zhang and Y. Chikamoto
497429.abstract: While deep learning models have demonstrated remarkable skill in short to medium-range weather prediction, extending their success to seasonal timescales is often limited by the lack of ocean coupling. Hybrid frameworks such as NeuralGCM, which pairs a differentiable dynamical core with learned parameterizations, offer a physically informed alternative to purely data-driven emulators. However, as an atmosphere-only model, NeuralGCM typically relies on prescribed ocean boundary conditions or persisted anomalous sea surface temperatures (SSTs). Because the ocean represents an essential source of seasonal predictability, it remains unclear how NeuralGCM performs when forced by dynamically forecasted SSTs on a seasonal timescale. Here, we conducted ensemble forecast experiments using NeuralGCM for the December-February (DJF) season using dynamically simulated SSTs from the North American Multi-Model Ensemble, initialized in December. The seasonal predictive skill of these forecasts is then evaluated against observational and reanalysis products over the same period. We find that the dynamic-SST forced NeuralGCM achieves comparable predictive skill for precipitation, while exhibiting improved skill for geopotential height and upper-level winds when compared to the original seasonal forecasting system. The most notable gains appear in the circulation patterns organizing synoptic-scale variability, characterized by more skillfully represented meridional wave structure and a reduced stationary wave bias. Furthermore, the framework enables the generation of large ensembles across a wide range of initial conditions. Combined with NeuralGCM's low computational cost, these results suggest that hybrid AI-physics models are an efficient tool for isolating the role of ocean forcing in seasonal prediction and show promise in advancing seasonal forecasting.

497430.title: An In-Depth Analysis of the 8 May 2026 OKC Metro Hailstorm Using HailCam and Phased-Array Radar Data
497430.authors: Jacob Segall, CIWRO, Oklahoma City, OK
497430.abstract: Weather radar has long been used by forecasters to warn for various hazards, including hail, in real time (i.e., “nowcast”). Polarimetric moments, in combination with single polarization radar moments, can be used to identify regions of hail within convective storms, and can even provide forecasters with insight into the size of hail falling. However, the current established relationships between hail and its radar manifestations are built mostly upon post-impact observations or idealized hailstones. Observations taken using the National Severe Storms Laboratory’s (NSSL) HailCam system reveal unique fall behaviors for hailstones which likely have large implications for the resulting radar representation. In order to relate these fall behaviors back to weather radar, radar observations close to the location of the HailCam system are needed. On 8 May 2026, both the NSSL HailCam system and the NSSL Advanced Technology Demonstrator (ATD) S-band radar collected observations of a severe storm that produced severe (≥ 1”) hail near and in the OKC metropolitan area. Polarimetric radar signatures related to hail will be explored and related back to ground truth observations taken by the HailCam system. The impacts of irregular fall behaviors and hailstone shapes will also be explored.

497431.title: Identifying Scale-Selective Roles of the Surface Ocean in Midlatitude Storm Track Behavior
497431.authors: Emily E Hayden, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and M. C. Hell, J. Small, and D. Amrhein
497431.abstract: Sea surface temperature (SST) fronts and ocean eddies in western boundary currents (WBCs) influence the overlying atmosphere through enhanced diabatic heating and the resulting injection of near-surface potential vorticity (PV). In this work, we assess the effect of SST heterogeneity as a function of scale on midlatitude storm tracks through an Ertel PV (EPV) framework, with an emphasis on the Gulf Stream (GS) and Kuroshio-Oyashio Extension (KOE). We leverage new high-frequency output from the CESM MESACLIP simulations, an unprecedented set of long-term, eddy-resolving integrations. We apply a scale-aware decomposition of the atmospheric PV budget to characterize the effect of ocean resolution on subseasonal-to-decadal variability and climate. Our preliminary results suggest that mesoscale SST amplifies low-pressure systems as they pass over WBCs through injection of near surface-PV. When PV anomalies propagate upward into the troposphere, they can serve as a dynamical link between the surface ocean and midlatitude atmospheric circulation variability. Our scale-selective analysis of air-sea interactions in the Northern Hemisphere WBCs suggests the importance of the ocean mesoscale in the midlatitude storm tracks. It motivates further research to identify suitable resolution scales for future coupled modelling efforts, and to quantify the effect of resolving the ocean mesoscale in improved storm track representation and forecasting.

497432.title: BPOP: An Open-Source, Probabilistic Direct Observation Prediction Model
497432.authors: Ryan Keisler, Brightband, San Francisco, CA; and A. Bollinger, J. DiCintio, H. Kamdar, A. Kleeman, H. Mohrmann, D. A. Rothenberg, and A. White
497432.abstract: Machine learning models that forecast observations directly, without learning from or producing analysis states, offer a path to fully observation-based weather prediction. This avoids inheriting model bias from analysis products and could potentially offer a simpler operational pipeline. We introduce BPOP, an open-source, open-weights direct observation prediction (DOP) model trained on the NNJA-AI observational archive, itself openly available. Both deterministic and probabilistic (POP) model checkpoints are provided. BPOP achieves forecast skill comparable to operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems, and, because NNJA-AI is updated daily with a lag of only a few days, users can run BPOP pseudo-operationally. We believe this fully open DOP model will open new research directions for the community, and we share examples from our own use of it.

497433.title: Modernizing Regional Frequency Analysis for Extreme Precipitation
497433.authors: Kyle Chudler, RTI, Fort Collins, CO
497433.abstract: Accurate estimates of extreme precipitation frequency remain essential for dam safety and other high-stakes water resources decisions. Traditional regional frequency analysis based on L-moments, following the framework developed by Hosking and Wallis (1997), has long provided a robust foundation for these estimates. That approach relies on identifying adequately homogeneous regions, pooling station data, and using regional average L-moment ratios to improve quantiles at individual sites. Spatial mapping of the L-moments themselves has typically drawn on a limited set of predictors such as mean annual precipitation, elevation, latitude, and longitude, often developed through careful but largely manual processes. This work explores ways to update and strengthen those established methods. We focus on spatially mapping L-moments across a region so that reliable point values can be obtained even at ungauged locations. The study focuses on California, where complex terrain, orographic effects, and atmospheric rivers produce intricate spatial patterns in precipitation frequency. These conditions provide a rigorous setting for evaluating the limitations and potential of different approaches. Two complementary lines of investigation are underway. First, we evaluate more automated methods for grouping stations into homogeneous regions, building on the pooling concepts central to the Hosking and Wallis procedure. Second, we improve the spatial mapping of L-moments using modern regression and machine learning methods. Automated predictor selection is used to develop accurate regression equations while limiting overfitting, and XGBoost decision trees are evaluated as an alternative that does not require traditional prediction equations. Greater automation and computational capacity also make it possible to assess a much broader set of candidate predictors, extending beyond standard geographic variables and mean annual precipitation to include measures of complex terrain and meteorological processes, such as integrated vapor transport. Each new method is evaluated against the traditional Hosking and Wallis approach to compare predictive accuracy. Throughout the process, expert judgment and review remain integral. Automation and expanded datasets allow more systematic exploration of options and more consistent application of the methods, while still preserving the critical role of hydrologic and meteorological insight at key decision points. The goal is to better represent the spatial variability of L-moments, reduce subjectivity where appropriate, and produce frequency estimates that remain grounded in the proven statistical principles of regional L-moment analysis.

497434.title: What Changed Starting in 1995? A 70-Year Analysis of U.S. Temperature, Relative Humidity and Rainfall Trends — and Why It Matters
497434.authors: Jonathan C. Porter, AccuWeather, PORT MATILDA, PA
497434.abstract: The methodology and findings from an important AccuWeather study of climate trends for the contiguous United States will be reviewed. If the climate trends AccuWeather identified continue, they may have major impacts on the U.S. economy, our food and water supply, human comfort levels, energy needs, and the health and welfare of citizens over the coming decades. This comprehensive study is based on a detailed and error-corrected database of 44 official, geographically dispersed weather stations in AccuWeather’s Data Suite. To highlight long-term climate signals that can be hidden by year-to-year variability, AccuWeather averaged the data over 10- and 20-year periods. This smoothing method filters out short-term fluctuations and reveals underlying climate signals. The study found that temperatures have increased an average of 0.5°F (0.28°C) per decade over the past 70 years. Dew point temperatures have increased an average of 0.3°F (0.17°C) per decade over the same period, though most of this increase occurred before 1995. Relative humidity remained more or less steady until 1995, but then decreased by a significant 5.3%, or an average of 1.7% per decade. Average annual rainfall has declined 2.7% since 1995, or an average of 0.9% per decade; yet, the frequency of rainfall amounts greater than 4 inches in a 24-hour period has actually increased by 70%. Likewise, heavy rainfall amounts greater than 2 inches within a 24-hour period have increased by 23%. One of the most significant findings are the apparent shifts that occurred starting in 1995. The average temperature and dew point increased together up until 1995, and so the average relative humidity more or less remained constant. Since 1995, however, the average temperature continued to increase, but the dew point leveled off, and that caused a significant decline in relative humidity. The study examines whether, as temperature continued to increase, evaporation from the ground and vegetation could no longer keep pace with the increase in temperature, resulting in the dew point not being able to increase as quickly as the temperature over the last 30 years, resulting in a decline of relative humidity. If this trend continues, desert areas will expand. This has potentially important implications for rainfall and water availability. Over the last 30 years, average rainfall has been declining by an average of 1% every 11 years and the rain that does fall is less effective for crop production and maintaining our water supply because it tends to come in shorter bursts. Furthermore, the average relative humidity during the same 30-year period has declined by a very significant 5.3%, which is 1.7% per decade. This means the rain that does fall is evaporating more quickly and it is less effective for crop production, water supply, and for filling reservoirs, lakes and other water sources. When combining these two factors, the study suggests that the “effective” average rainfall across the United States seems to be declining by 2% to 3% per decade. If these trends continue, AccuWeather expects to see accelerating harmful impacts on crop production, more frequent wildfires, and less available water due to greater drought. Furthermore, the crop-growing areas in the United States may shrink as soil becomes more arid. Even in productive growing areas, crop yield may decline. These effects could become more obvious over the next decade or two. The presentation will explore the relationship between dry soil and extreme heat, including relevant aspects of conditions experienced during the Dust Bowl of the 1930s. It is important to note that climate fluctuations and trends over 10, 20 or 30 years can reverse. There are no assurances these trends AccuWeather has found will continue, slow down, or possibly even reverse. It is also important to realize that these are averages for the nation as a whole, and different regions may have more dramatic changes and other areas much less dramatic changes. The findings also raise important questions about how these observed changes compare with climate-model projections, particularly with respect to atmospheric moisture, rainfall, soil moisture and land-atmosphere interactions. We will also explore how long-term observational analyses can complement climate models and contribute additional insight for scientists, governments, businesses, water resource planners, agricultural interests and the public.

497436.title: Tropical Convection Across Scales in Numerical Simulations with Three-Dimensional Adaptive Mesh Refinement (3D AMR)
497436.authors: Hang Wang, New Jersey Institute of Technology, Newark, NJ; and Y. Tissaoui, M. Li, D. Marsico, S. Du, S. N. Stechmann, and S. Marras
497436.abstract: George Kiladis has made substantial advances in understanding tropical convection across scales. This presentation will highlight some of George's influence in this area, and it will show recent advances by the authors in this area, in the form of numerical simulations. In particular, to advance simulation capabilities, we investigate the use of adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) in three dimensions (3D).
