This 3D AMR takes a step beyond the two-dimensional (2D) AMR that has been used in the past for refining the horizontal mesh in different regions. In this initial investigation, the 3D AMR is investigated here to simultaneously resolve different cloud types in different locations and altitudes, such as the small scales of shallow cumulus and the larger scales of mesoscale deep convection and anvil clouds. Other potential applications will also be discussed, along with further connections to George's work.

497437.title: Evaluating the Operational Value of High-Resolution WindNinja Guidance for NWS Spot Forecasts: A NOAA Fire Weather Testbed Quantitative Case Study
497437.authors: Kyle J. Thiem, Global Systems Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and L. McMeeking, PhD and A. Baring
497437.abstract: Near-surface winds are the primary driver of wildland fire rate of spread, direction, and intensity, yet even high-resolution numerical weather prediction (NWP) models (e.g., HRRR, NAMNest, RRFS) cannot adequately resolve the microscale mechanical effects and surface drag caused by complex terrain and varied vegetation. To bridge this gap, National Weather Service (NWS) Incident Meteorologists (IMETs) have long relied on WindNinja—a diagnostic, microscale wind model developed by the U.S. Forest Service Missoula Fire Sciences Laboratory—to downscale coarser (~3–10 km) NWP guidance to hundreds of meters. This downscaling provides a clearer picture of localized airflow and diurnal wind patterns, which are critical to understand to provide reliable and accurate Decision Support Services (DSS) during high-risk tactical operations, such as burnouts, and protecting firefighter safety. However, operational field adoption has historically been hindered by user interface friction and output visualization constraints within legacy platforms like Google Earth. To quantify the operational value, usability, and Decision Support Service (DSS) impacts of modernizing this guidance, the NOAA Fire Weather Testbed conducted a structured, virtual, 1-day evaluation in September 2025 with 10 NWS forecasters from various locations, levels of expertise, and experience using WindNinja operatiomnally. The study evaluated the perceived value and operational utility of WindNinja guidance for spot forecasting exercises, initialized with HRRR forecasts and integrated directly into the Dynamic Ensemble-based Scenarios for IDSS (DESI) visualization platform developed by NOAA's Global Systems Laboratory (GSL). Participants completed three predetermined spot forecasting exercises across differing complex terrain scenarios. Participants were split into alternating groups to directly compare decision-making workflows using standard NWP guidance alone versus DESI-hosted WindNinja guidance at the spot forecast locations. The primary goal was for forecasters to participate in operational “sandbox” exercises to gain informed insights provided through forecast breifs and focus group discussions. Additionally, by co-locating the mock spot forecast requests with Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS) observation sites, we were also able to perform quantitative forecast verification, from both model guidance and participant spot forecasts, against surface observations. Evaluation results demonstrate that high-resolution WindNinja guidance significantly increases forecaster confidence, improves spatial situational awareness of fine-scale wind patterns, and reduces cognitive workload when drafting spot forecasts. Visually, the interactive DESI display empowered forecasters to more effectively communicate complex wind behaviors during partner decision support briefings. Visual and quantitative comparisons of participant forecasts made with, and without, WindNinja guidance illustrate measurable improvements by more accurately and precisely predicting observed wind speed and direction within complex terrain environments, while reinforcing that diagnostic downscaling accuracy remains fundamentally linked to parent model initialization. Overall, the study illustrates how high-resolution spatial wind guidance provides essential operational value for wildland fire decision support that transcends standard point-based statistical verification metrics alone.

497438.title: In-Flight Sonic Boom SEL Estimation with a Passive Microwave Radiometer : A Feasibility Study for GOSWIFT
497438.authors: Alamgir Hossan, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA; and M. Morris, F. Carpenter, S. T. Brown, O. Pradhan, A. Tanner, S. Khanal, A. Mohamed, R. Williamson, P. Kangaslahti, and K. R. Horton
497438.abstract: NASA has been working with its partners to enable new choices for commercial supersonic air travel, beginning with safe and acceptable supersonic flight over land. As part of this effort, the Geometry Optimization and Sensing with Integration and Flight Test (GOSWIFT) project seeks to reduce the perceived loudness of sonic booms using an adaptive morphing structure that responds in real time to atmospheric variability. Achieving this capability relies on a sense-think-act framework in which the aircraft optimizes its geometry by understanding how the surrounding atmosphere modulates sonic boom propagation. To support this goal, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), in partnership with NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center, is developing the concept for an onboard microwave hyperspectral radiometer system to measure temperature and water vapor profiles along the aircraft-to-ground propagation path. These measurements enable estimation of the surface sound exposure level (SEL), which is highly sensitive to atmospheric variability, particularly humidity and temperature gradients. GOSWIFT’s top-level sensing requirement is to detect a 1.5 dB change in SEL attributable to atmospheric conditions. This presentation describes a feasibility study assessing the ability of JPL’s hyperspectral microwave radiometer technology to meet the GOSWIFT sensing requirements. The study integrates atmospheric profile perturbation experiments, shockwave propagation modeling (via NASA’s PCBOOM), and radiative transfer simulations to evaluate SEL sensitivity and radiometric information content across 90–500 GHz. Results from both physical forward modeling and machine learning retrieval experiments indicate that water vapor variability dominates SEL modulation and that optimal radiometer bands include window regions sensitive to the water vapor continuum and water vapor absorption lines. A neural-network-based retrieval trained on simulated brightness temperatures with realistic sensor noise demonstrates achievable SEL retrieval uncertainty within the 1.5 dB performance requirement. These findings support the feasibility of an aircraft-mounted microwave radiometer for real-time SEL estimation and adaptive-shape control for sonic boom mitigation. The abstract will present the radiometer concept, feasibility results, sensor design considerations, and planned next steps.

497440.title: Quantifying Air Quality Sensitivities of Permian and San Juan Basin Emissions Using a Refined Oil and Gas Emissions Inventory and CMAQ-DDM
497440.authors: Saravanan Arunachalam, The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; and M. Momeni, H. Tran, M. Soni, and J. J. Buonocore
497440.abstract: The Permian and San Juan basins are major U.S. oil- and gas-producing regions whose emissions, particularly from flaring, can adversely affect air quality across the south-central United States. However, the 2022 Emissions Modeling Platform version 2 (EMP2022v2) contains limitations in the classification and estimation of flaring emissions, especially for small and intermittent flares. We developed a refined inventory using nightly Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) observations to estimate daily flared-gas volumes and allocate emissions to detected flare locations. Additional improvements included wind-dependent flare destruction efficiency, unlit-flare adjustments, basin-specific gas properties, updated emission factors, and measurement-informed methane (CH4) and volatile organic compounds (VOC) emissions from active and abandoned well pads. These refinements approximately doubled oil and gas CH4 and VOC emissions across the contiguous United States. In the Permian Basin, CH4 and VOC emissions increased by factors of 3.5 and 1.6, respectively, while sulfur dioxide emissions decreased by approximately 50%, when compared to the EMP2022v2. In the San Juan Basin, revised CH4 and VOC emissions decreased because of limited detected flaring and lower measurement-based estimates. The refined inventory was implemented in CMAQ-DDM version 5.5 to assess air quality sensitivities of ozone (O3), fine particulate matter (PM2.5), and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) to basin-specific precursor emissions. We will present results from state-specific air quality sensitivities from both basins with a focus on both potential impacts on NAAQS-relevant air pollutant concentrations and the chemical processes involved. This study shows how improved emission estimates from a growing emissions source for increased energy demand influence accurate estimates for air-quality modeling and source attribution.

497441.title: TEMPEST: Weather Gaming with Synthetic Environments for Course-of-Action Analysis and Weather-Driven Decision Making
497441.authors: Don Widener, BAE Systems, McLean, VA; and A. Wenzel and J. Jarvis
497441.abstract: Military wargaming has long been used to stress‑test courses of action (COAs) against an adaptive adversary. Weather‑sensitive decision makers—emergency managers, aviation planners, utility operators, and military commanders—face a comparable challenge: selecting among competing COAs under an uncertain, evolving environmental “adversary.” Current weather decision support is largely presentational, delivering forecasts without allowing users to rehearse their consequences. We introduce TEMPEST (Tactical Environmental Modeling for Predictive Engagement Simulation Technology), a “weather‑gaming” capability that applies the discipline of wargaming to weather‑driven decision making. TEMPEST is built on OneArc’s VBS4 whole‑earth synthetic environment and leverages a modular open‑systems architecture (MOSA) to ingest numerical weather prediction (NWP) output, ensemble members, climatological scenarios, real‑time radar, satellite imagery, and surface observations. An explainable‑AI (XAI) analytics layer classifies precipitation structures, estimates rainfall rates, and predicts severe phenomena, presenting results with confidence intervals and causal visualizations. Within the wargaming framework, users select a weather archetype (e.g., hurricane, derecho, flash flood, wildfire, or multi‑hazard compound), define geographic scope, population density, and critical assets, and the scenario engine spawns interoperable simulation components—atmospheric dynamics, hydrological runoff, fire‑behavior models, and infrastructure simulators (power grid, transportation, communications)—linked via HLA/DIS standards. Decision makers manipulate variables such as evacuation timing, shelter placement, pre‑positioned resources, and utility shutdown schedules while the system continuously assimilates live data, dynamically rescoring each COA. Real‑time visualizations render 3‑D terrain, animated flow fields, and heat‑map overlays; a multi‑criteria decision analysis (MCDA) engine aggregates life‑safety risk, economic loss, resource consumption, and recovery time into a single ranking. TEMPEST delivers sub‑hourly situational awareness, transparent analytics that foster trust, and a cloud‑native, DevSecOps‑driven deployment hardened to DoDI 8510.01, supporting unclassified, CUI, Secret, and TS/SCI environments. A shared virtual workspace enables inter‑agency collaboration and after‑action review, feeding lessons learned back into model bias‑correction loops. By reusing existing defense investments in high‑performance simulation, advanced analytics, and commercial gaming, TEMPEST minimizes development cost while providing photorealistic, physics‑based visual experiences. A phased roadmap progresses from a prototype to an alpha demonstration integrating full environmental and infrastructure models, culminating in an operational evaluation with emergency‑management agencies. Upon validation, TEMPEST will offer a secure, ready‑to‑use tactical weather management tool that empowers responders to experience, simulate, and optimize COAs for major weather events and disasters.

497442.title: Understanding Risks and Building Community Resilience to Heat and Air Pollution in Denver, Colorado
497442.authors: Olga Wilhelmi, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and K. H. Nguyen, J. Boehnert, M. H. Hayden, F. Lacey, K. Fewless, R. R. McCrary, J. L. Vigh, and R. Kumar
497442.abstract: During the summer of 2026, the Denver metro area faced record-breaking heat, compounded by wildfire smoke and air quality alerts. As summers become hotter and air pollution events become increasingly frequent, addressing these compounding hazards requires translating complex atmospheric and socioeconomic data into actionable health and policy insights at the local level. This study, in partnership with Denver’s Office of Climate Action, Sustainability and Resilience (CASR), aims to enhance the capacity of Denver communities and local decision-makers to build climate resilience by comprehensively assessing present and future risks from extreme heat and air pollution. In this presentation, we discuss the iterative and collaborative process used to establish a research framework for identifying the determinants of risk and its key drivers. We present a mixed-methods approach that integrates spatial analyses with qualitative, community-engaged research. Specifically, we illustrate geographic patterns of heat hazard, exposure, and vulnerability across multiple urban scales and highlight areas at risk of compounding heat and air pollution hazards. To contextualize these spatial indices, we share insights from community focus groups that capture lived experiences, risk perceptions, coping capacities, and barriers to taking protective actions. These community narratives are supplemented by key informant interviews with representatives from city agencies and boundary organizations who possess deep, nuanced knowledge of the unique exposures and vulnerabilities of the populations they serve. Ultimately, we demonstrate how bridging spatial risk assessments with qualitative social, behavioral, and public health insights informs actionable solutions for urban heat risk management and building resilience.

497443.title: The Monthly Aggregated Weather Extremes Index: Examining Long-Term Anomalies and Their Impacts
497443.authors: Emma L. Scott, North Carolina Institute for Climate Studies, Asheville, NC; and H. J. Diamond, M. Palecki, and J. Cacciamani
497443.abstract: While many analyses exist for short-term extreme climate events (e.g., heat waves, cold waves, dry spells, heavy precipitation events), less focus has been placed on long-lasting extremes at monthly timescales and their aggregated impact across regions, seasons and years. These longer-lasting events can strongly impact society through their direct effects on the environment (agriculture, water resources, health, etc.) and their resulting economic impacts (energy use, retail, construction, etc.). The coincident or back-to-back occurrence of extreme events can lead to compounding hazards that have even more deleterious societal impacts. These impacts may build over time during periods with multiple extreme events, especially when these events are of different types and require different responses. However, analyses of extremes often focus on a single indicator (i.e., precipitation or temperature) or on individual compound events rather than an aggregated set of extremes occurring over longer periods and larger regions. In this study, we introduce improvements to the Monthly Aggregated Weather Extremes (MAWE) Index, which combines station-based hot, cold, wet, and dry extremes at monthly scales into a single index that is an easily understood metric for enhancing the communication of environmental extremes to the public. This prototype index utilizes high-quality U.S. Climate Reference Network (USCRN) air temperature and precipitation data from 114 stations in the conterminous United States. Precipitation data is used to calculate SPI scores for the determination of extreme wet and dry months (>=1.6 or <=-1.6), while normal distribution standardized temperature data represents warm and cold months (>=2.0 or <=-2.0). The occurrences of months exceeding thresholds at individual stations are aggregated over the CONUS and seven U.S. climate regions. Both annual and seasonal versions of the MAWE Index have been developed from monthly observations. An additional formulation operating at monthly scales is useful for near real-time monitoring of extreme conditions. Results are shown regionally to provide additional insight into areas of the country experiencing a greater number of extreme weather months and the types of events contributing to regional impacts.

497444.title: Colour-Coded Weather Alerts In Canada: The First Year
497444.authors: Erik de Groot, EC, Montreal, QC, Canada; and D. Matthews
497444.abstract: In November 2025, the Meteorological Service of Canada introduced colour-coded alerts for its public weather alerts. Since then, alerts are coloured yellow, orange, or red based upon the expected impact and the confidence of the meteorologist. The new system uses colour to allow users to quickly determine what level of risk an alert presents and make faster and more informed decisions on how to take appropriate actions. The colours have been introduced for both synoptic and convective alerts and apply to advisories, watches, and warnings. The new alerts also move from threshold-based to impact-based alerting criteria in accordance with recommendations from the WMO and as used by other national meteorological services. The roll-out was accompanied by a public information campaign through social and traditional media, as well as briefings to media weather presenters to inform Canadians of the changes and how to use the new products. This presentation will provide a brief overview of the new system and a review of the first year of use of the colour-coded alerts including the uptake, frequency statistics for each alert colour, examples of significant events, and feedback.

497445.title: OceanCast: A Probabilistic Global Ocean Foundation Model via Masked Latent Diffusion
497445.authors: Yixuan Sun, ANL, Lemont, IL; and A. Nolan, B. Moore-Maley, G. Zhao, B. Nadiga, W. Xu, S. H. K. Narayanan, L. Van Roekel, and S. Madireddy
497445.abstract: Ocean circulation transports heat and salt and mediates atmospheric carbon and heat uptake, making accurate ocean models essential for Earth system understanding and for anticipating high-impact extreme events. Major challenges in ocean modeling include the high computational cost of high-resolution simulation, which constrains eddy-resolving integrations and makes large ensembles impractical. Data-driven models are fast enough to relieve this, but existing systems address prediction and state estimation from sparse observations separately, and deterministic models provide no uncertainty estimate while tend to lose the fine-scale features that eddy-resolving resolution exists to capture. We present OceanCast, a foundation model extending the masked latent diffusion framework of OmniCast (Nguyen et al. 2025) to the global ocean at 1/12 degree. Using both GLORYS and ERA5 reanalysis datasets, in the first stage a fully convolutional variational autoencoder (VAE) compresses the global ocean and atmospheric states to lower-dimensional latent representations for effective and tractable subsequent diffusion training. We train the VAE on random crops of the global states and encode and decode globally by tiling, where cells whose receptive field extends beyond the crop interior are discarded before aggregation, with longitude wrapping and land masking. In the second stage, to learn the ocean dynamics in the latent space, a bidirectional transformer takes ocean latent history and ERA5 latents as forcing to reveal randomly masked latent future tokens from visible ones, with a per-token diffusion head creating probabilistic outputs. The resulting future latent tokens are then decoded back to the physical ocean states as forecasts. We evaluate VAE reconstruction and latent diffusion forecasting against standard baselines using deterministic, spectral, and probabilistic metrics, and investigate the framework's use for Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) strength prediction as a downstream task.

497448.title: Quantifying Properties of Turbulence in Tornadoes using Mobile Radar Observations and High-Resolution Simulations
497448.authors: Alex Schueth, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. J. Bodine, A. Naik, H. B. Bluestein, and R. M. Frost
497448.abstract: While past studies have quantified wind speeds in tornadoes using Doppler radars, the properties of turbulence in tornadoes are more poorly understood. From numerical simulation data, it is straightforward to calculate turbulence properties of tornadic flow, such as turbulence kinetic energy or the energy spectrum of individual velocity components. However, analogous observational methods for calculating turbulent properties of tornadoes have yet to be developed and tested. In this study, we employ the Energy Spectra Method, where spatial Fourier transforms of Doppler velocity fields are used to obtain energy spectra (e.g., power as a function of wavelength). Near the tornado, we apply novel methods to detrend the Doppler velocity observations based on the axisymmetric flow. This method is applied to observations from the Rapid X-band Polarimetric radar (RaXPol) as well as high-resolution numerical simulations of tornadoes from Cloud Model 1 (CM1). In particular, RaXPol observations from the 5 June 2025 Morton, TX EF-2 tornado are analyzed during a period where the flow exhibits considerable turbulent structure in Doppler velocity and later transitions to a smoother appearance. Using the Energy Spectra Method, we find that the early observation period has a Doppler spectrum that closely follows Kolmogorov’s law with a -5/3 slope, indicative of flow within the inertial subrange. During the transition to laminar flow, the slope increases and the energy cascade to smaller wavelengths is reduced. Intercomparisons with model data and simulated observations will be presented, including discussions of strengths and weaknesses of the proposed approach.

497451.title: Using Lightning Mapping Array Products to Assess and Diagnose Storm Organization for Research and Weather Situational Awareness
497451.authors: Timothy Logan, Texas A&M Univ., College Station, TX
497451.abstract: Lightning Mapping Arrays (LMAs) provide high temporal- and spatial-resolution observations of very high frequency (VHF) radiation produced by lightning, offering a means of examining changes in convective storm electrical structure that are related to changes in storm intensity and organization. Previous studies have demonstrated relationships between rapid increases in total lightning activity and severe convective weather. However, storm-scale changes in the spatial organization and persistence of lightning activity can provide additional information beyond changes in flash or source rate alone. This study introduces two experimental LMA-based diagnostics: the Lightning Burst Metric and Lightning-Based Updraft Organizational Gradient Metric (LBUG), designed to identify and track spatially concentrated regions of enhanced electrical activity within thunderstorms. The Burst Metric identifies upper-tail concentrations within a gridded VHF source-density field and tracks their location, persistence, and evolution. The burst metrics are implemented to characterize both persistent electrical organization and transitions between competing convective storms. LBUG complements the Burst Metric by identifying the strongest spatial gradients in the lightning-density field, providing a measure of the location and evolution of electrically organized storm regions. Persistent spatial organization of VHF sources and associated source density gradients may distinguish sustained, organized convection, including convection associated with rotating updrafts, from pulse convection characterized by weaker or more transient electrical organization. The diagnostics are interpreted as indicators of storm-scale electrical organization rather than direct retrievals of updraft intensity or predictors of individual severe-weather hazards. Three supercell cases are presented to illustrate distinct modes of electrical organization. The 24 November 2025 Cypress/Klein, Texas, tornadic supercell provides the best example of persistent electrical organization, with sustained Burst Metric and LBUG signatures associated with the evolving storm prior to and during tornadic development. The 28 December 2024 Alvin/Splendora, Texas, event demonstrates a distinct handoff, in which the dominant electrical signature transitions between convective regions as storm organization evolves. That is, the electrical activity from a dying supercell is disregarded in favor of a strengthening supercell within 100 km. In contrast, the 25 April 2026 Scotland/Windthorst, Texas, tornadic supercell exhibits substantially greater spatial and temporal variability, including shorter periods of persistence, transitions among primary, secondary, and tertiary burst regions, and changes in electrical organization during a period of complex, cyclic mesocyclone evolution. In this particular case, several tornadoes were observed with a few being long-track, multi-vortex. Since lightning rates can decline in the presence of strong downdrafts interfering with the mesocyclone, the 25 April 2026 case offers the best stress test of both metrics. Collectively, the cases suggest that the persistence, displacement, and transition of electrically organized regions may be as informative as the magnitude of the lightning enhancement itself. These diagnostics are being developed not only as research tools but also as components of an experimental severe-weather situational-awareness framework. Unsupervised processing can translate changes in electrical organization into concise storm-status information describing persistence, strengthening, weakening, or reorganization. Techniques are currently being developed such that information can be distributed through web-based displays or compact text messages and, when internet or cellular communications are compromised, relayed through amateur-radio emergency communications networks. This approach provides a pathway from high-resolution lightning observations to low-bandwidth decision-support information for meteorologists, emergency managers, and other operational users.

497452.title: Turning Crop Evapotranspiration and Reservoir Evaporation Research into Operational Accounting and Decision Making: Advances and Lessons Learned from State and Federal Agency Partnerships
497452.authors: Justin Lee Huntington, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV; Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV; and C. Pearson, B. A. Minor, P. ReVelle, S. Majumdar, C. Morton, T. Ott, H. Gao, K. D. Holman, Y. Xie, D. Ketchum, J. L. Atkin, M. Bromley, A. Purdy, C. Doherty, J. Volk, Y. Kim, T. Caldwell, C. Dunkerly, F. Melton, and S. Larsen
497452.abstract: Western water agencies increasingly need information on crop evapotranspiration (ET), reservoir evaporation, and drought to support operations, accounting, and resource-management decisions. Through partnerships with state water agencies, Bureau of Reclamation, Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Geological Survey, NOAA, and NASA, we are combining agency information with in-situ and satellite-based water resource information and translating these data into operational data systems and decision-support tools. In collaboration with state water agencies in Oregon, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and California, we are integrating OpenET data with field boundaries, modeled effective precipitation, and irrigation status, and joining these with agency water rights, water source attribution, points of diversion, wells, and meters, to quantify irrigation water use and withdrawals by source. In situ flux observations are used to both validate and intercompare the OpenET estimates. In parallel, we are integrating satellite-based surface area with meteorological forcing, in situ micrometeorological data, and the energy-aerodynamic Daily Lake Evaporation Model (DLEM), to produce historical, near real-time, and forecast estimates of gross and net reservoir evaporation. We are working with agencies to incorporate these data into reservoir accounting and operation models. Across these efforts, common research-to-operation lessons include sustained agency co-development, fit-for-purpose measurement and validation, reproducible and versioned workflows, interoperable databases and APIs, and interfaces tailored to existing agency practices. Partners have also requested AI-enabled natural-language querying of these large geodatabases, and we are exploring large language model (LLM) approaches to meet this need. Collectively, these partnerships illustrate how Earth observations can be combined with agency-specific datasets so that information moves beyond stand-alone products to become trusted operational infrastructure for water accounting, management, and decision making.

497454.title: The Value of Sustained Airborne Tomography for Understanding the Global Carbon Cycle
497454.authors: Britton Stephens, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and Y. Jin, C. Sweeney, B. Gaubert, R. F. Keeling, E. A. Kort, K. McKain, E. J. Morgan, P. Patra, and S. Wofsy
497454.abstract: Despite decades of focused observational and modeling effort, quantification of the carbon cycle is still poor at regional to global scales, limiting our ability to understand processes well enough to predict future climate feedback and our ability to validate anthropogenic emissions or reduction efforts well enough to support carbon markets and policy. Much of our current knowledge is based on long-term in situ atmospheric measurements from surface networks, but these networks remain sparse and interpretation of surface measurements relies heavily on uncertain model vertical transport and large representation errors. The advent of satellite CO2 measurements, with near global coverage and high precision, has enabled new constraints on point-source emissions and interannual flux variability, but persistent biases limit their ability to define large-scale mean fluxes. Global airborne tomographic surveys can bridge surface and satellite measurements and provide powerful constraints on global greenhouse gas (GHG) budgets. Aircraft provide measurements of the full tropospheric column, mitigating model vertical mixing errors, and capture large scale flux signals more amenable for use in coarse-resolution models. Also, by covering long distances with redundant CO2 instruments, long-range jets can measure latitudinal gradients with unprecedented accuracy. Landmark global airborne data sets have been collected via tomographic surveys during HIPPO (2009-11) and ATom (2016-18). Observations of CO2, O2, isotopologues of CO2, and related tracers on these campaigns have enabled transformative carbon cycle insights into hemispheric seasonal fluxes, latitudinal flux partitioning, Southern Ocean and Northern African exchange, atmospheric transport, remote sensing validation, and flux inversion evaluation. These global surveys delivered regional to zonal-mean CO2 flux uncertainty reductions as large as 50% for the time periods covered. Yet, these global surveys only represent discrete snapshots in time, with the most recent survey in 2018. Monitoring the rapidly evolving global carbon cycle and providing useful information to evaluate global emission reduction or carbon capture efforts requires a sustained program of repeated global surveys. Several opportunities exist for the atmospheric research community to meet this need. First, the new NASA 777 represents an ideal platform to conduct a follow-on series of global tomographic surveys to HIPPO and ATom, with an extensive and synergistic payload also supporting non-CO2 GHG, chemistry, and aerosol science. Second, for sustained annual missions, there is an opportunity for multi-agency coordination between NASA, NOAA, NSF, and DLR to fly tomographic surveys of GHG and related tracers using their Gulfstream GV or G550 aircraft at approximately annual cadence, whereby each agency supported one global survey every four years. Both approaches would provide invaluable constraints on the decadal evolution of seasonal, latitudinal, and regional carbon sources and sinks, information critical for process understanding and climate mitigation. With an ongoing annual program, these constraints could be applied at higher time resolution for interannually varying process insights, and could be tightly integrated with models and satellite observations in an operational global-scale GHG measurement, monitoring, reporting, and verification (MMRV) system. In this presentation, we will highlight the motivation and present a vision for the potential future role of sustained global airborne tomography for carbon cycle science and management.

497455.title: Closing Gaps in the Understanding of Coarse Mode Aerosol and their Impact on Clouds: Recent Aircraft Observations and Open Questions
497455.authors: Bernadett Weinzierl, University of Vienna, Vienna (or Wien), Vienna (or Wien), Austria; and M. Dollner, M. Schoeberl, A. Gattringer, A. Kupc, F. Kuderna, K. Blohm, C. A. Brock, J. P. Schwarz, and S. Woods
497455.abstract: Although coarse-mode aerosol (diameter >1 μm) from natural sources is widespread and abundant across much of the globe, it remains one of the least well characterized components of the atmospheric aerosol burden. Coarse aerosol particles are often ignored because they are difficult to measure and to model. However, solid coarse-mode particles are efficient ice nucleating particles that can significantly impact cirrus clouds via heterogeneous ice formation, cloud glaciation, formation of precipitation, and subsequent changes in radiative transfer. Systematic underrepresentation of coarse aerosol in measurements and models obscures key processes in our understanding of aerosol-cloud-climate interactions. The NASA Atmospheric Tomography Mission (ATom; 2016-2018) provided a singular opportunity to characterize the global coarse-mode size distribution in the size range between 0.5 and 930 µm, and also delivered information about microphysical cloud properties in remote regions from the high Arctic to the Southern Ocean in four seasons. ATom measurements showed a marked hemispheric asymmetry in coarse mode aerosol: the Northern Hemisphere lower and free troposphere contained much higher coarse-mode loadings than the Southern Hemisphere, primarily due to the presence of Saharan mineral dust and biomass-burning smoke. These sources also contributed significantly to aerosol optical depth not only over the Atlantic Ocean downwind of African emission sources, but also across the free troposphere of the North Pacific, underscoring the radiative importance and potential impact of long-range transported coarse particles. Long‑range transport of coarse and even “giant” particles is increasingly recognized as a salient feature of plumes from mineral dust outbreaks and intense wildfires; in the western United States, particles exceeding 100 μm and beyond have recently been detected within wildfire smoke plumes more than four hours after their emission. Key open questions include how common these particles are, what their sources are (e.g., mineral dust and ash/char fragments lofted by pyroconvection or pyroCb), which transport pathways carry them, how long they persist (from hours to days, and potentially longer if injected into the stratosphere), and how they affect radiation and cloud microphysics. With new platforms becoming available such as the NASA’s new Boeing 777, new opportunities due to more space, range and duration are becoming available. New coarse mode and cloud instrumentation should include higher resolution imagery in order to better quantify the transition from aerosol to cloud. Fluorescence capabilities could help to identify human-made microplastic particles but also biological aerosol. In this presentation, we will show results from recent aircraft observations including ATom, FIREX, A-LIFE, and INSYPRE and motivate a path towards closing gaps in the understanding of coarse‑mode aerosol and their impact on clouds.

497456.title: Updating Extreme-Precipitation Climate Change Ratios for Sacramento County Using WRF–CMIP6 and CMIP6-Hybrid Data
497456.authors: Mahdad Talebpour, PhD, WEST Consultants, Inc., Corvallis, OR; and H. Huber, B. Choat, and L. Cunha
497456.abstract: Sacramento County’s existing climate-change adjustments for extreme precipitation were developed using CMIP5 projections. As the County prepares to publish an updated version of its Hydrology Manual, it is also updating the climate-change analysis to incorporate the latest CMIP6 projections. This study updates those adjustments using both dynamically downscaled hourly WRF–CMIP6 simulations and CMIP6-Hybrid hourly data. A reproducible computational workflow will process historical and future precipitation data and calculate Climate Change Ratios by comparing projected and historical precipitation-frequency estimates at equivalent durations and return periods. Ratios will be evaluated for durations ranging from 1 hour to 10 days across multiple future periods, climate scenarios, and model-dataset combinations. The analysis will assess differences between the WRF–CMIP6 and CMIP6-Hybrid projections and examine how changes in precipitation extremes vary by duration, return period, scenario, and time horizon. The resulting ratios will provide an updated scientific basis for climate-informed precipitation standards, hydrologic guidance, and infrastructure planning in Sacramento County.

497458.title: Coupled Microphysics-Contrail Parameterization in the MPAS Model
497458.authors: Trude Eidhammer, RAL, Longmont, CO; and M. E. Frediani and T. Dean
497458.abstract: Contrails and contrail cirrus exert a radiative forcing that may exceed the climate impact of aviation CO2 emissions. Many current contrail models simulate contrail lifecycles using external weather inputs but remain uncoupled from the atmospheric environment, which limits their ability to capture feedbacks between contrails, clouds, and radiation, and precludes data assimilation to improve forecasts of the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). We present initial results from coupling a Contrail-Aware parameterization within the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) Thompson-Eidhammer Microphysics for Operations (TEMPO) scheme, where contrails form along prescribed flight tracks using the Schmidt-Appleman criterion and are represented as a distinct ice crystal category within the microphysics. This distinct contrail category enables instantaneous, online estimates of effective radiative forcing (ERF), a first step toward a coupled framework that can represent contrail-cloud-radiation feedbacks and support future UTLS data assimilation.

497459.title: Changing Hydroclimate Across Scales: Observed Trends, Future Projections, and Critical Hotspots Across the United States
497459.authors: Jeffrey B. Basara, University of Massachusetts Lowell, Lowell, MA; and T. L. Schneider
497459.abstract: Anthropogenic climate change is altering the global water cycle through changes in precipitation, temperature, evapotranspiration, snow accumulation and melt, soil moisture, groundwater recharge, runoff, streamflow, drought, and flood regimes. While many processes are driven by global-scale climate forcing, the evolution of the physical characteristics vary substantially among regions and watersheds due to differences in the atmospheric circulation, topography, land cover, water storage, and human water use. Further, global observations and simulations increasingly demonstrate the increased occurrence and acceleration of extreme events focused on key hydrologic variables including precipitation, river flow, drought, and dry-season water availability. Within the United States, several regions have emerged as hydroclimatic hotspots, including the Southwest and Colorado River Basin, California and the Sierra Nevada, the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, the Great Plains, Mississippi–Missouri Basin and Upper Midwest, Northeast and New England, Gulf and Southeast, and Alaska. These regions illustrate distinct modes of hydroclimatic change, ranging from warming-driven aridification and snow loss to increasing extreme precipitation, flash drought, atmospheric-river-driven flooding, and compound coastal flooding. This study synthesizes observed and projected hydroclimatic changes across spatial scales and highlights the importance of understanding changes in seasonal water storage, atmospheric demand, compound and cascading extremes, watershed response, drivers of environmental variability, and critical tipping points (i.e., local to global) with impacts focused on the critical hotspots distributed across continental United States (CONUS).

497461.title: Satellite-Based Characterization of Dust Event Frequency and Spatial Distribution Across the Western United States (2017–2026)
497461.authors: Bhavna Devanand, Rick Reedy High School, Frisco, TX; and K. Ardon-Dryer
497461.abstract: Dust events threaten air quality, visibility, and public health across the western United States, yet long-term, systematic observational records of dust occurrence remain sparse. This study presents a continuous 9-year analysis of dust event frequency and geographic distribution using NASA's AerosolWatch Geos imagery platform from October 1, 2017, through July 30, 2026 encompassing 3,225 consecutive days examined at hourly resolution. Each day was categorized as confirmed dust, no dust, or uncertain, and affected states were recorded for all identified plumes. Results up to 2022 reveal [425] unique dust days across [29] states. Nevada, Idaho, Texas, Arizona, and Oregon emerged as the most frequently affected regions. Dust activity exhibited pronounced seasonality, peaking in spring (March–May) and fall (September–November), with April as the single most active month. Multi-state events spanning three or more states simultaneously accounted for 28% of all observationsThe 2020–2022 western mega-drought corresponded with elevated dust frequency, and the June 2020 Saharan dust intrusion produced the most geographically extensive signal observed. These findings establish a baseline climatology of satellite-visible dust across the western U.S. and highlight intensifying dust activity that carries implications for air quality management in rapidly growing communities.

497463.title: A Novel Processed-Based Quantification of Lake-Breeze MAHTE Formation Mechanisms using Fine-Scale Remote and In-Situ Field Data
497463.authors: Kyle T. Brooks, Central Michigan Univ., Mount Pleasant, MI; and J. M. Keeler, D. A. R. Kristovich, J. Wang, A. L. Houston, C. C. Weiss, G. de Boer, B. Argrow, K. Matousek, and C. J. Isenberger
497463.abstract: Mesoscale Air Masses with High Theta-e (MAHTEs) are apparently common but only recently coined mesoscale features that form on the cool sides of a variety of boundaries in the atmospheric boundary layer (Hanft and Houston 2018). MAHTEs have been observed behind thunderstorm gust fronts and synoptic fronts (Hanft and Houston 2018, Axon et al. 2024, Boyer et al. 2025, Boyer and Keeler 2025). Of these non-linear features, a separate class of boundaries thought to harbor MAHTEs are lake breeze fronts (LBFs) found throughout the Laurentian Great Lakes of North America (GLs). LBFs in the GLs are direct analogs of land/sea breezes that form on oceanic coastlines. The existence of these LBF MAHTEs has been hypothesized using idealized modeling studies (Boyer et al. 2025, Boyer and Keeler 2025). LBF MAHTEs were confirmed via observation in data obtained during the MITTEN-CI field campaign of July 2024. The goal of this study is not to further confirm MAHTE existence, but to formally quantify the fine-scale mechanisms responsible for their formation and persistence. This study utilizes the robust 2024 MITTEN-CI dataset along with a few older recorded LBF MAHTE datasets recorded in 2020 and 2021. Using 1 Hz mobile mesonet surface transects, flux towers, Doppler LiDAR, and UAS vertical profiles, we first document the magnitude of LBF perturbations on parent environments. Furthermore, variables known to be important to MAHTE formation and sustainability will be analyzed across, along, and vertically with methodology derived from previously-published studies and novel methodologies using instrumentation that has never before been used to document LBFs and associated MAHTEs in such fine scale detail. Ultimately, we test the hypothesis that suppressed vertical mixing on the cool side of the boundary insulates near-surface moisture from dry-air entrainment aloft, driving localized instability maxima prior to CI.

497464.title: Atmospheric Control on North African Dust Variability
497464.authors: Jacob Z. Tindan, Penn State University, University Park, PA; and G. S. Jenkins
497464.abstract: North African dust varies across diurnal to decadal timescales, yet little is known about the atmospheric conditions driving this variability. We perform Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on WRF-Chem-simulated surface dust concentrations over North Africa for 1981–2010 to identify modes of variability. The corresponding principal components for the prevailing patterns are regressed onto near-surface winds and sea level pressure to understand the atmospheric conditions driving these modes. WRF-Chem is driven at the lateral boundaries by ECMWF (ERF-ERA) and NCEP (WRF-NCEP) reanalysis products, enabling comparison of different boundary-condition forcings on this variability. In the annual and seasonal analyses, our results show two dominant modes of Saharan dust variability. The first mode (EOF1) reveals domain-wide dust loading across North Africa, which is stronger during winter. EOF1 is associated with strong pressure gradients that enhance the Harmattan circulation and is strongly correlated with the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO). The second mode (EOF2) shows a dipole with positive anomalies in Algeria, northern Mali, and Mauritania and negative anomalies near the Bodélé Depression in Chad. EOF2 is prominent in the spring and is associated with the east-west displacement of Saharan depressions. The corresponding PCs indicate that these patterns exhibit interannual to decadal variability. The results are consistent across WRF-ERA, WRF-NCEP, and MERRA-2, indicating that WRF-Chem can supplement limited observations to better understand Saharan dust variability. Our findings contribute to existing knowledge on Saharan dust variability by identifying the leading modes of dust variability and their associated meteorological drivers.

497465.title: Virtual Reality in Radar Meteorology: An Active Learning Demonstration
497465.authors: Robin Tanamachi, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN; and A. M. Smith, A. Hirsch, G. Takahashi, J. White, A. R. O'Cull, M. Musquiat, and M. G. Nelson
497465.abstract: The field of radar meteorology is rapidly evolving, and with it the need for updated and flexible educational materials accessible to the world. The inherently data-rich and four-dimensional nature of radar data requires a departure from basic textbooks and two-dimensional displays as means of learning. To address these needs, Purdue University and The COMET Program are developing a series of asynchronous, fully online Radar Meteorology courses that integrate virtual reality (VR) elements. In typical radar analysis, a student or forecaster will step upward through a storm, sweep by sweep, looking for features that indicate impending severe weather, such as the presence of a rotating updraft (mesocyclone). As such, it requires the analyst to mentally assemble a three-dimensional picture of the storm from these quasi-horizontal scans, sometimes “rocking” back and forth between different sweeps to look for features spanning a significant depth. For students new to analysis, mentally building the 3D structure can be an immense challenge. The integrated VR case gallery allows learners to immerse themselves in the 3D structure of the radar data. VR also brings concepts like volume coverage patterns to life, enabling better understanding of radar presentations of various weather phenomena such as hail and updrafts. For example, learners can familiarize themselves with polarimetric features such as differential reflectivity (Zdr) arcs and columns, and tornado debris signatures. These and more VR elements were tested with Purdue radar meteorology students in 2024 and 2025, with overwhelmingly positive reactions. In this active learning demonstration, the authors invite annual meeting participants to use the supplied VR headsets to explore the radar data cases featured in the online course series, and answer accompanying question sets as time allows. The VR cases will also be available via a web-based interactive 3D application on laptops, to ensure accessibility for all and ease of use for multiple participants. Acknowledgements: NSF AGS-2303653 and AGS-2303654

497466.title: Recent Progress on UAS-Based Polarimetric PAR Characterization
497466.authors: Antonio R. Ricardo Segales, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and D. Schvartzman, K. Burdi, N. Zemlin, I. R. Ivic, and R. D. Palmer
497466.abstract: The increasing complexity of polarimetric phased array weather radars highlights the need for meticulous in-situ antenna pattern measurements, particularly for precise calibration of dual-polarization variables of fielded radars. The RFSonde, a custom UAS developed by the Advanced Radar Research Center (ARRC) at the University of Oklahoma, carries an RF sensing payload on a 3-axis gimbal that stays polarization-aligned with the antenna under test while flying far-field raster scans around the radar. In 2026, the system was upgraded for simultaneous two-way and one-way pattern measurements: a power splitter and an ARRC-built fiber-optic delay line allow the radar to capture the coherent two-way transmit-receive pattern from returns off the RFSonde, while a calibrated power sensor aboard the aircraft concurrently records the one-way transmit pattern. Results from measurements of the fully digital Horus phased array radar will be presented. This work also introduces LudiFly, a ground control application that automates the complete UAS-based characterization workflow. From a single interface, LudiFly generates constant-range raster trajectories about an arbitrarily steered beam, computes the flight speed for a target angular sampling density, uploads the mission, commands the payload gimbal to the radar, and injects RTK corrections for centimeter-level positioning. In flight, every streamed power and phase sample is geo-referenced into antenna-plane coordinates and rendered as a live 2-D pattern, letting the crew confirm coverage and beam capture before landing. In addition, ongoing improvements to the RFSonde-PAR simulator support validation of non-conventional patterns, such as spoiled and trident beams, against real Horus measurements. These results establish a foundation for the routine, automated characterization and calibration of operational weather radars, paving the way for applications in next-generation phased-array systems and beyond.

497467.title: Rising Water Demands: Long-Term Trends and Climate Impacts on Yellow Dent Corn in the U.S. Corn Belt (2000-2024)
497467.authors: MIKAELA KING, University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO
497467.abstract: Yellow Dent Corn is a critical pillar of the United States agricultural economy, serving as a primary driver for global grain markets, ethanol production, and the livestock industry. However, intensifying climate variability and persistent drought are placing unprecedented pressure on regional water resources, raising concerns regarding water scarcity and escalating production costs. While previous research has documented the impact of climate change on corn yields, long-term shifts in crop water demand remain understudied. This study evaluates interannual variability and long-term trends in the water demand of Yellow Dent Corn across four top-producing states: Iowa, Illinois, Minnesota, and Nebraska. Using a longitudinal dataset spanning 2000-2024, phenological data from the USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) were integrated with gridded meteorological data from the Parameter-elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM). Seasonal water requirements were estimated using the FAO-56 crop coefficient approach, with reference evapotranspiration derived via the Hargreaves-Samani equation. Preliminary results reveal a widespread increasing trend in seasonal water demand across 95% of the state-stage combinations. Statistically significant increases were concentrated at the emergence stage in Illinois, Minnesota, and Nebraska, and at the dented stage in Iowa, Minnesota, and Nebraska. Minnesota exhibited the most persistent signal, with significant upward trends spanning emergence through harvest. These findings suggest that rising water requirements may necessitate increased irrigation and challenge the long-term sustainability of regional water supplies. This research provides essential data-driven insights to inform adaptive water management and bolster agricultural resilience.

497468.title: Evaluation of Thermodynamic Retrievals Using Downwelling Infrared Radiance Observations from Novel Spectral Bands: Toward Increasing the Suitability of Ground-Based Remote Profiling Systems for Network Deployment
497468.authors: Matthew Bradley Ammon, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High-Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
497468.abstract: Operational observations of the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) are relatively sparse and inconsistent in both space and time. The resulting data gap leaves the three-dimensional structure and behavior of the lower troposphere mostly unobserved, and thus, largely unknown beyond numerical weather prediction (NWP) model solutions. This insufficient observational coverage is likely a major limiting factor to the predictability of local weather hazards, air quality, and other factors that directly influence daily human life and the broader ecosystems of Earth’s surface. Many observational systems, both remote and in-situ, have been adopted into the field of atmospheric science in an effort to fill this data gap. Numerous such systems have been shown to provide observations that enable vertical profiles of the lower-troposphere to be recorded at much higher spatial and temporal resolutions than current operational methods allow. Furthermore, recent studies have leveraged simulations to show that observations from networks of these profiling systems can be assimilated to improve NWP model forecasts of local weather hazards. While these results are promising for the future innovation of weather forecasting, vertical profiling systems have some limitations that need to be addressed before large-scale network deployment can be feasibly implemented. The ground-based infrared radiance spectrometer (IRS) is among the most intriguing prospects for the implementation of an ABL profiling network. IRSs observe downwelling infrared radiance spectra spanning from 530 cm-1 to 3,000 cm-1 at high spectral and temporal resolution. Optimal estimation (OE) retrieval algorithms such as TROPoe (Turner and Blumberg 2019) leverage these observed radiance spectra to derive vertical thermodynamic profiles of the lower troposphere. Currently, the portion of the observed radiance spectrum between 1,800 cm-1 and 3,000 cm-1 (i.e., channel-2) is not included in the TROPoe retrieval algorithm, largely due to complexities associated with the effects of scattering at these wavenumbers. However, if the need for observations between 530 cm-1 and 1,800 cm-1 (i.e., channel-1) could be eliminated, IRS systems could be redesigned in a way that would substantially reduce the cost of their construction and operation. Since a primary limitation of the IRS is its prohibitive cost, developing a way to retrieve thermodynamic profiles using observations exclusively from the channel-2 portion of the spectrum would improve the suitability of IRSs for network deployment. This presentation will discuss the results from various initial attempts at channel-2-based thermodynamic retrievals and explore pathways for dealing with the effects of scattering in order to lay the groundwork for a potentially more feasible implementation of an operational ABL profiling network.

497469.title: Why Do Ice Crystals in the Same Air Parcel Differ? Aerosol Mixing State and Freezing-Time Dispersion in Particle-Resolved Cloud-Parcel Simulations
497469.authors: Wenhan Tang, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, IL; and J. Y. Harrington and N. Riemer
497469.abstract: Ice crystals in mixed-phase clouds vary widely in size, habit, and density, affecting cloud radiative properties, lifetime, and precipitation efficiency. Airborne campaigns using automated habit classification now document this variability at the individual-crystal level, and predicted-particle-property schemes seek to represent it without fixed hydrometeor categories. Yet the underlying microphysical causes remain difficult to separate. Aerosol mixing state—how ice-nucleating particle (INP) material and cloud condensation nuclei (CCN)-active material are distributed among individual particles—affects activation and freezing, while subsequent growth controls habit and deposition density. Although nucleation timing is known to control ice number, stochastic nucleation also creates a spread in freezing times among otherwise identical particles, generating differences among the resulting crystals. Distinguishing these effects requires a particle-resolved treatment of composition, activation and freezing histories, shape, and density. We use PartMC, a particle-resolved aerosol–cloud model coupled to a new ice module that represents adaptive-habit depositional growth, deterministic and stochastic treatments of deposition density, a Monte Carlo implementation of water-activity-based immersion freezing, and a PartMC-consistent liquid-water criterion linking nucleation to the evolving droplet reservoir. We conducted 330 simulations of NaCl–Fe₂O₃ populations spanning the full range of mixing states (χ = 0–100%) and nearly three orders of magnitude in background CCN concentration, with 50 stochastic realizations per configuration. Controlled parcel experiments with hundreds of otherwise identical particles use either prescribed freezing-time distributions or distributions derived from classical nucleation theory to isolate the mechanisms behind the particle-resolved results. Mixing state becomes important when activation limits ice formation. Under clean conditions, ice number is nearly independent of χ. As background CCN concentration increases and peak supersaturation falls from approximately 1% to 0.06%, internal INP–CCN mixing raises ice number by more than an order of magnitude because hygroscopic material on the same particles enables more INP-containing particles to activate. Among particles that freeze, final size is controlled primarily by freezing time. The activation-to-freezing delay explains 97–98% of final-size variance across all mixing states and background conditions, whereas composition and initial aerosol size together explain less than 3% directly. Per-particle Monte Carlo sampling shows that within a single aerosol mode, intrinsic nucleation stochasticity produces more freezing-time variance than particle-to-particle differences in INP size. The timing–size relationship is nearly independent of χ: mixing state determines how many particles freeze and when, while the shared parcel trajectory maps the resulting timing distribution onto the final size and habit distributions. Controlled parcel experiments show that particles freezing earlier grow into larger crystals in every simulated regime, although the sensitivity of size dispersion to timing spread varies eightfold among thermodynamic trajectories. A continuous freezing interval crossing the −22.6 °C habit transition produces coexisting plate-like and columnar modes in a compositionally identical population. The Wegener–Bergeron–Findeisen feedback and liquid-water criterion make ice formation self-limiting: ice growth removes the liquid water required for immersion freezing, so above a threshold INP loading, additional INPs yield fewer but larger crystals and a narrower spectrum. This nonmonotonic response provides an observable signature of immersion freezing shutting down as the parcel glaciates. Stochastic deposition-density sampling further broadens the size and density distributions relative to the deterministic treatment, consistent with laboratory-observed variability. These results identify when models need to retain aerosol mixing state: chiefly in polluted, vapor-limited regimes where activation limits freezing. Across the regimes studied, freezing-time statistics provide the main link between nucleation and subsequent crystal-size and habit diversity. They also retain the influence of INP surface area and species-specific nucleation kinetics, preserving a physically interpretable connection between aerosol properties and the resulting ice spectra. The framework offers quantitative targets for predicted-particle-property schemes and for interpreting observed ice size and habit spectra in mixed-phase clouds.

497470.title: Ensuring a Robust MetPy in Today’s Cybersecurity and Open Source Software Landscape
497470.authors: Ryan M. May, UCAR, Boulder, CO; and D. Camron
497470.abstract: MetPy is an open-source Python package for meteorological and atmospheric science applications, leveraging significantly many other pieces of the scientific Python stack (e.g. numpy, matplotlib, scipy, etc.). Its goal is to provide tested, reusable components for Python suitable to a wide array of tasks, including scripted data visualization and analysis. The guiding principle is to make MetPy easy to use with any dataset that can be read into Python. MetPy’s general functionality breaks down into: reading data, meteorological calculations, interpolation, and meteorology-specific plotting. MetPy also has significant integration with XArray, as well as extended support for interpreting netCDF Climate and Forecasting Convention metadata. The current security landscape for open source is a challenging one, with many bad actors attempting supply chain attacks from a variety of vectors. As a project serving the community, MetPy works very hard to keep the project secure and sustainable. This is accomplished through a large set of infrastructure built on top of GitHub, both automated and manual. This builds off of MetPy’s existing test suite to ensure that users can trust MetPy packages to be safe to use and robust. This talk gives an overview of recent developments in the project to enhance the project’s infrastructure to address the challenges of today’s cybersecurity landscape. This encompasses things from dependency management to build management and security of automated workflows. Updates on new functionality in MetPy itself will also be shared.

497471.title: Multi-Regional Evaluation of Precipitation Nowcasting for Flash Flood Early Warning
497471.authors: Sinan Rasiya Koya, Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ; and G. C. Anagnostopoulos, J. Camacho, H. Vergara, J. J. Gourley, J. Gong, and E. Nikolopoulos
497471.abstract: Accurate short-term precipitation forecasting is critical for flash flood warning, yet it remains one of the most persistent unsolved problems in hydrometeorology. Radar-based precipitation nowcasting offers a promising approach for short-term (up to 6-hour) precipitation prediction in situations where numerical weather prediction (NWP) models fail to produce accurate forecasts. While previous studies have examined the accuracy of precipitation nowcasting methods, the efficacy of these methods in producing actionable flash flood warnings remains largely unexplored. In this study, we evaluated multiple nowcasting methods based on the flash flood forecasts they produce by running EF5, part of NOAA's operational flash flood forecasting model, with precipitation nowcasts derived from MRMS data. We consider both conventional advection-based nowcasting algorithms and NWP-based precipitation forecasts (HRRR), and evaluate them across 25 severe flash-flood events in CONUS over the past decade. Across these events, extrapolation-based nowcasting methods (particularly LINDA and STEPS) outperformed HRRR at short lead times (1–3 h), while HRRR became competitive or superior beyond 3 h. Detection performance varied considerably across the range of potential operational thresholds examined, with the mean Critical Success Index (CSI) rising by roughly 0.4 units when the warning area criterion was relaxed from 10 km² to 1000 km², and dropping by roughly 0.1 units when the unit discharge threshold was raised from 1.0 m³/s/km² (moderate flood) to 4.0 m³/s/km² (heavy flood). Accounting for positional tolerance via buffer-radius analysis showed that much of the short-lead error in extrapolation methods was attributable to displacement rather than detection failure. A case study of the 2025 Texas flash flood illustrated that, at two hours before the event, extrapolation-based nowcasting methods can provide emerging flash flood signals in forecast discharge maps, despite falling short of the quantitative CSI ≥ 0.5 threshold. Reliable warning skill (CSI ≥ 0.5) was geographically clustered, extending to 3 h lead time for organized Gulf Coast systems but never achieved for isolated convective events in the western U.S. and southern Plains. Evaluating precipitation nowcasting for operational flash flood warnings reveals a clear need to prioritize hydrologic assessments of these algorithms.

497474.title: Update on ICAMS Content Standards Focus Area activities
497474.authors: Robert L. Jacob, ANL, Lemont, IL; and R. Montuoro, D. Rosen, R. Mahajan, B. Chowdhury, and K. Thengumthara
497474.abstract: The Content Standards (CS) Implementation Team is part of the Common Model Architecture (CMA) Implementation Team (IT) which sits under the ICAMS Earth System Modeling and Prediction Subcommittee (ESMP) of the Committee on Research and Innovation (CoRI). The goal of CS is identifying and examining common aspects of modeling and development workflow and software within ICAMS models that may benefit from standardization or a set of common practices. In the past year, substantial updates have been proposed for the Physics Constants Dictionary and it has been incorporated in to the DOE Energy Exascale Earth System Model. The CS also began an ongoing look at how AI is being used in development of ICAMS models and identified were standards could be applied.

497475.title: From Observations to Hazardous-Weather Nowcasts: Machine Learning to Improve the Use of Radar, Satellite Data
497475.authors: Ethan D. Gutmann, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and Y. Sha, Z. Ying, and J. Sun
497475.abstract: Short-duration heavy precipitation and rapidly evolving convection remain difficult to predict, yet accurate forecasts are critical for flash-flood warning and other weather- and water-related decisions. Weather radar and geostationary satellites provide frequent, high-resolution observations of storm structure and evolution. However, extracting dynamically useful information from these complex datasets and incorporating it into forecast systems remain persistent challenges. Here we develop and evaluate complementary applications of modern machine-learning tools for precipitation nowcasting and short-term hazardous-weather prediction. First, machine learning is used to interpret radar and geostationary satellite observations and translate their spatial and temporal patterns into information that can improve data assimilation in convection-permitting numerical weather prediction systems. This approach is designed to improve the representation of convection in the initial atmospheric state while retaining the process representation and forecast capabilities of traditional NWP. Second, we use Meso-CREDIT, a high-resolution convection-permitting AI weather model, to produce computationally efficient predictions of precipitation and related hazardous weather. Together, these approaches provide a framework for combining information-rich observations, physics-based modeling, and rapidly advancing AI forecast capabilities. Evaluation focuses on the location, timing, intensity, and evolution of precipitation, including performance for rapidly developing and extreme events and changes in skill with forecast lead time. We also consider how errors in atmospheric prediction affect the usefulness of these forecasts as inputs to hydrologic warning and decision-support systems. The results illustrate both the potential and the remaining challenges of integrating machine learning, observations, and conventional modeling across the hydrology–meteorology interface. This integration can provide more rapidly updated and spatially detailed atmospheric forcing for flash-flood prediction and other applications in which small errors in precipitation location or intensity can produce large differences in societal outcomes.

497476.title: From Academia to National News: How an Uncommon Approach Built an Innovative Platform for Digital Weather Coverage
497476.authors: Dakota C. Smith, CNN, berthoud, CO
497476.abstract: The rapidly evolving environment of digital media requires novel practices to reach audiences with high-quality weather forecasts. The newly launched CNN Weather app is a product of this approach, packaged as a unique and useful digital weather experience. The team behind it is also a diverse one, coming from all backgrounds of the weather enterprise. This talk will showcase the team’s coverage within the app and explore how it’s been developed to adapt to the rapid changes within the weather communication landscape. This presentation will also highlight the team behind the coverage and examine how experience in other sectors has translated to forecasting and communicating for a general audience. Finally, we’ll discuss what lessons have been learned in the first eight months of the app and what the future holds for collaborations across the weather enterprise in the name of effective and modern weather coverage.

497477.title: Characteristics and Societal Impact Generated from the 17-19 December 25 Downslope Windstorms
497477.authors: Adriana Villanueva Costilla, University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO; and M. Larson and A. C. Winters
497477.abstract: Recorded since the 1950s, downslope windstorms are not new to Colorado’s Front Range. Producing extremely high wind speeds, these windstorms have proven to be dangerous for public safety and infrastructure, fire weather amplification, damaging property, and disrupting both ground and air transportation. In this analysis we are focused on back to back events that happened 17-19 December 2025 to better understand the atmospheric characteristics and societal impact of downslope windstorms across Colorado. Reaching hurricane-like speeds, this windstorm exceeded 100 mph south of Boulder, impacting Front Range Coloradans. We analyzed synoptic weather datasets, particulate matter measurements, and utility data sets for 11 locations throughout eastern Colorado to quantify relationships with meteorological conditions, power outages and air quality.

497479.title: Field Validation of Commercial WBGT Monitors Against an ISO Reference in a Hot-Arid Environment
497479.authors: David Martin, Perry Weather, Dallas, TX; and B. C. Thomas, R. M. Wiggins, and E. J. Webb
497479.abstract: Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) is the primary environmental metric used to guide activity-modification decisions for athletes, military personnel, and occupational workers (Cooper et al. 2017). Recently we have seen widespread adoption of WBGT use, with over 20 state high school athletic associations now mandating WBGT readings for activity modifications. Independent evaluations of commercial WBGT instruments document mean absolute errors (MAE) of 1–3°C and heat-category disagreement rates exceeding 25% in high-risk conditions (Cooper et al. 2017; Grundstein et al. 2025; Clark and Konrad 2024). A persistent gap in the literature is the absence of multi-device, continuously logged validation studies conducted against an ISO 7243 compliant reference in a hot-arid environment. This climate environment is where psychrometric measurement errors are potentially most consequential. Current organizations state WBGT measurement should be taken near the level of the playing surface but impose no minimum accuracy standard on the instruments used(Cates and Rheeling 2023). The purpose of this study is to evaluate the accuracy of commercially available WBGT instruments deployed both near ground level (~1.6 m) and at 10 m above ground level (AGL) on a meteorological tower against an ISO 7243 reference standard in a hot-arid environment. We also aimed to determine their reliability for informing operational heat-stress activity modifications. Data collection was conducted at White Sands Missile Range (WSMR), New Mexico over the course of a 2-week period (July 13-26, 2026). Conditions resembled a hot-arid environment with a mean daytime humidity of 15-40%. An ISO 7243 reference instrument (150 mm matte black globe, wet wick-fed natural wet-bulb sensor, and a radiant shield enclosed ambient sensor) served as the gold standard at 1.6 m AGL over mesquite, scrub grass, and dirt. Seven devices had data collected at either a 5-, 15-, or 30-minute resolution against the gold standard unit. Although continuous instruments were logged at their native 5-, 15-, or 30-minute resolution, error analyses were conducted on 30-minute means, consistent with the National Athletic Trainers Association (NATA) standard for activity-modification decision intervals. Devices included a Perry Weather WXS station at 10 m AGL on a meteorological tower, and ground units at 1.6 m AGL consisting of a Perry Weather WXS; the Kestrel 5400 Heat Stress Tracker; the QUESTemp° 46; the KestrelMet6400 station; the American Industrial Hygiene Association (AIHA) WBGT phone application; and the Reed SD-4023. Error metrics include mean absolute error (MAE), mean bias error (MBE), root mean square error (RMSE), Pearson correlation (r), and WBGT error stratified by 1°C temperature bin and NFHS Class 3 heat class category. "The Perry Weather WXS at 10 m AGL produced the lowest WBGT MAE of any device tested (MAE = 0.56°C; MBE = −0.07°C; r = 0.97). The Perry Weather WXS AGL also performed well (MAE = 0.80°C; MBE = +0.54°C; r = 0.98). Ground-level meters showed larger errors: KestrelMet 6400(MAE = 0.79°C; MBE = +0.65°C; r = 0.98), Questemp° 46 (MAE = 0.86°C; MBE = +0.84°C; r = 0.99), Kestrel 5400 (MAE = 0.90°C; MBE = +0.76°C; r = 0.99), and the AIHA smartphone application (MAE = 1.22°C; MBE = +0.69°C; r = 0.88). When binning the data by ISO WBGT temperature, the bias in handheld devices increased progressively with heat stress, while the Perry Weather WXS at 10 m AGL demonstrated the smallest bias of any device across all temperature bins, with bias remaining consistent and well-constrained despite rising heat stress. At WBGT 27–28°C, the lower boundary of the NFHS Yellow flag category, the Kestrel 5400, QUESTemp° 46, and KestrelMet 6400 exhibited biases of +1.22°C, +1.23°C, and +1.04°C, respectively, while the Perry Weather WXS at 10m AGL bias was −0.15°C. At this same boundary, the Perry Weather 1.6m AGL exhibited a bias of +0.69°C. This pattern continued at higher heat categories. At 29–30°C, the KestrelMet 6400 and Kestrel 5400 was +1.21 to +1.43°C, respectively, while the Perry Weather WXS 10m AGL was +0.30°C and the Perry Weather 1.6m AGL was +1.24°C Analysis of the natural wet-bulb temperature (NWB) reveals the limitation of psychrometric-based algorithms in hot-arid conditions. The Kestrel 5400 exhibited a large positive NWB bias as heat stress increased (+1.44°C at WBGT 27–28°C, +1.68°C at 29–30°C, and +1.63°C at 31–32°C). Binning by NFHS Class 3 heat flag category, the Perry Weather WXS at 10m AGL maintained the lowest MAE across Green (0.65°C), Yellow (0.49°C), and Orange (0.47°C) flag conditions. Handheld and phone application MAEs ranged from 1.16 to 1.38°C at Yellow flag and 1.33 to 1.48°C at Orange flag. These results provide continuously logged, multi-device WBGT validation against an ISO 7243 device in a hot-arid environment. The positive bias in all ground-level handheld devices and the phone application has direct implications for heat-risk management in athletic, occupational, and military contexts, particularly where a positive bias may trigger unnecessary cancellations. The Reed meter was not included in the analysis due to constant freezing of the device and a much smaller sample size compared to the other units. References Cates, J., and J. Rheeling, 2023: Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) – Why Should Your School Be Using It? https://nfhs.org/stories/wet-bulb-globe-temperature-wbgt-why-should-your-school-be-using-it. Clark, J., and C. E. Konrad, 2024: Observations and Estimates of Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature in Varied Microclimates. J. Appl. Meteorol. Climatol., 63, 305–319, https://doi.org/10.1175/JAMC-D-23-0078.1. Cooper, E., A. Grundstein, A. Rosen, J. Miles, J. Ko, and P. Curry, 2017: An Evaluation of Portable Wet Bulb Globe Temperature Monitor Accuracy. J. Athl. Train., 52, 1161–1167, https://doi.org/10.4085/1062-6050-52.12.18. Grundstein, A. J., and Coauthors, 2025: Evaluating Heat Risk: Comparing On‐Site WBGT Measurements Versus Smartphone Application Estimates. GeoHealth, 9, e2025GH001347, https://doi.org/10.1029/2025GH001347.

497480.title: Constructing a Comprehensive Wind Climatology for the Spaceport: A Project from the Student Research Collaboration with Orange County Public Schools and the 45th Weather Squadron
497480.authors: Priyanshi Gandhi, Orange County Public Schools, Orlando, FL; and B. Luu, A. Watts, V. Manchikanti, E. Nguyen, A. Zappas, B. Cizek, A. L. Moses, and K. H. Chafin
497480.abstract: As one of the projects within the long-running collaborative research program between Orange County Public Schools in Florida and the 45th Weather Squadron (45WS), this project aims to address the critical need for a comprehensive wind climatology on the Eastern Range.
