The 45WS is a U.S. Space Force unit that provides comprehensive, 24/7 meteorological services to military, civil, and commercial launch partners across Cape Canaveral Space Force Station (CCSFS), Patrick Space Force Base, and NASA’s Kennedy Space Center (KSC), all of which compromise the largest part of the Eastern Range. With space launch cadences and associated ground operations increasing exponentially, accurate wind characterization at often non-standard levels is paramount for safe operations. The primary objective of this study was to develop an easily accessible and searchable climatology database utilizing historical data from the Weather Information Network Display System (WINDS). WINDS is one part of the most densely instrumented meteorological mesoscale networks in the United States, comprising a core array of 46 instrumented towers and additional customer sites spread across CCSFS and KSC. The system processes millions of independent measurements per minute—including wind speed, wind direction, and temperature—at levels ranging from the surface up to nearly 500 feet. Over the past few years of this project, students extracted raw archival data from this massive network, performed rigorous quality control, and utilized Python to process, organize, and overcome the computational challenges of managing a large-scale sensor dataset. Statistical and graphical analysis has been developed to visualize monthly temperature averages and generate wind roses that visualize wind patterns by month, specific tower location, and sensor height. Current work focuses on establishing correlations between towers in operationally relevant locations and the standard 10-meter airfield observations that serve as model grid points. The developed charts and wind roses help characterize average weather conditions, support routine forecasting and toxic dispersion modeling, and inform decisions regarding future launch operations and the strategic placement of meteorological equipment. The results of this research provide an invaluable climatological summary that enhances situational awareness for the 45 WS and launch service providers.

497482.title: Global Nitrogen Cycling and Nutrient Efficient Farming
497482.authors: Maya Almaraz, Yale University, Salt Lake City, UT; and E. A. Davidson, X. Zhang, P. M. Groffman, A. M. Huddell, X. Sun, J. N. Galloway, E. Buckler, M. Bowman, C. Brooke, M. Castellano, S. Spiegal, and P. A. Raymond
497482.abstract: From field to global scales, understanding nitrogen (N) emissions to the atmosphere and the imbalance this promotes in N budgets is critical to developing agricultural solutions that may benefit crop productivity, air quality, and climate change. Field measurements of dinitrogen and nitrous oxide emissions At the field scale, the balance between nitrous oxide (N2O) and dinitrogen (N2) emissions remain largely unknown due to difficulties measuring soil emissions of N2 given its high atmospheric background. By using a helium gas flow incubation system that eliminates the N2 atmosphere, we have been able to measure N2 and N2O emissions from the same soil core. Using this technique, we found that N2O and N2 emissions have different controls whereby N2O is promoted early in the growing season during fertilization events and N2 emissions were highest at the end of the growing season during plant senescence. We tested whether cover crops might reduce these end of season N losses from croplands but instead found that labile carbon in cover crops promoted emissions of N2. The global nitrogen balance By developing a database of global N pool and flux data, we found that these sorts of field scale dynamics have produced an imbalance between atmospheric and terrestrial N pools. Since the 1960s, the annual amount of reactive N entering the biosphere increased fivefold. Meanwhile, N emissions from the biosphere to the atmosphere increased just 12% between the oldest and latest estimates, indicating terrestrial N accumulation on the order of ~50 Tg N yr-1. The increased N availability owing to these inputs has polluted soils, waters, and air, negatively impacting ecosystems and economies. A suite of dietary changes, technological advances to enhance fertilizer efficiencies, and improvements to waste management and nutrient recycling could maintain an additional 51 Tg N yr-1 in the atmosphere through reductions infertilizer demand, which could help address the existing imbalance in the global N cycle. Quantifying N pools and fluxes across the atmospheric, terrestrial, and aquatic reservoirs is critical to monitor and mitigate this imbalance in the N cycle. Reducing nitrogen losses from farming The current, mostly linear and leaky system of N use in agriculture (Nitrogen1.0) must be transformed to be more circular, targeted, and efficient, which we call Nitrogen2.0. Diving deeper on reducing nitrogen losses from farms, we put forward a set of linked nutrient efficient innovations across crop and livestock systems: (1) redirecting synthetic N to livestock; (2) retaining more N on farm through crop breeding and management; and (3) recovering and recycling more N from manure. We found that decreasing total protein and partially replacing crop protein with supplemental amino acids in livestock diets could reduce total feed-N inputs and reactive N losses by ~25%. Integrating crop genetics and agronomy to improve on-farm N recycling in maize could increase yield by ~30% per acre while decreasing N fertilizer inputs by 35% per bushel and nitrate and N2O losses by ~50% per acre. A "manureshed" strategy to advance manure handling, N-efficient animal diets, and coordinated redistribution could nearly double the fraction of manure N available to crops, replacing up to ~25% of fertilizer-N while decreasing N losses by up to ~60%. Together, improvements in field scale measurements of lesser known dinitrogen fluxes combined with the monitoring of global N budgets can improve our understanding of how the N cycling is changing, while technological and behavioral changes within agricultural systems can help bring the N cycle back in balance, promoting environmental sustainability and human well-being.

497483.title: Co-Launching the Future: Twelve Years of Student Research Collaboration with Orange County Public Schools and the 45th Weather Squadron
497483.authors: Arlena L. Moses, 45th Weather Squadron, United States Space Force, Cape Canaveral SFS, FL; and B. Cizek and K. H. Chafin
497483.abstract: Orange County Public Schools in Florida and the 45th Weather Squadron (45WS) are currently embarking on the twelfth consecutive year of a highly successful collaborative research program designed to support America's space launch operations. The 45WS is a U.S. Space Force unit that provides comprehensive, 24/7 meteorological services to military, civil, and commercial launch partners across Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Patrick Space Force Base, and NASA’s Kennedy Space Center. The primary goal of this partnership is twofold: to generate operationally relevant research for the 45WS and to provide high school students with the opportunity to see real-world applications of advanced mathematical concepts. Each year, approximately 40-50 students, typically enrolled in Advanced Placement® mathematics, are selected for the program. At the beginning of the academic year, 45WS provides research topics and objectives based on current operational needs. Students then organize themselves into teams to manage the workload and meet these annual goals. Squadron sponsors and meteorology mentors guide the student teams through regular hybrid and in-person meetings, supplemented by virtual office hours. The program culminates in a capstone event where students present their final research findings to 45WS leadership and duty forecasters at Cape Canaveral. The outcomes of this collaboration have proven significant. Past student projects have been directly integrated into 45WS operational procedures and have identified patterns that spurred further investigation into meteorological phenomena, including lightning research. The program has garnered external recognition through award winning student posters and presentations at previous AMS Annual conferences, features in local news media, and scholarship awards. This initiative effectively demonstrates how high school students can conduct meaningful, operation-enhancing research, thereby preparing them for future careers in STEM fields.

497484.title: Side-by-Side Evaluation of a 350 kW Magnetron and a Pulse-Compression Solid-State Transmitter (SSPA) on a Shared C-Band Weather Radar Testbed
497484.authors: James H Romines, Baron Weather, Inc., Huntsville, AL; and D. Cartwright
497484.abstract: Comparisons between magnetron and solid-state weather radar transmitters are almost always drawn between different radars at different sites, where differences in antenna, receiver, siting, calibration, and the observed weather itself confound the result. We present a controlled comparison in which a 350 kW magnetron transmitter and a solid-state power amplifier (SSPA) transmitter employing nonlinear frequency-modulated pulse compression are installed on a shared C-band radar testbed and alternate on successive volume scans, yielding interleaved observations of the same storms through the same antenna, receiver, and signal processor. We report preliminary results from an ongoing collection campaign spanning a range of precipitation regimes. For each transmitter we quantify minimum detectable reflectivity, weighing the sensitivity recovered through pulse compression gain against the near-range coverage penalty. We then examine techniques for mitigating data quality issues within the blind range imposed by the SSPA's long transmitted pulse width. We additionally compare pulse compression range sidelobe contamination, Doppler velocity and spectrum width estimate quality, and ground clutter cancellation between the two transmitters. Because both transmitters coexist on the same radar, observed differences are attributable to the transmitter, waveform, and pulse compression techniques. We discuss the implications for waveform design and transmitter selection for operational radar networks.

497485.title: On the City-Scale Energy Balance under Electrification and Renewable Generation: The New York City Case
497485.authors: Jorge E. Gonzalez-Cruz, University at Albany, Albany, NY; and N. Elgalad
497485.abstract: Integration of renewable resources to meet the growing energy demand of dense urban regions is becoming a global priority under decarbonization mandates. This study contributes to these ongoing efforts by assessing the feasibility of using locally deployable urban renewable resources, namely offshore wind in the New York Bight region and rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems over New York City, to meet the electricity demand of the city, and the grid vulnerabilities that emerge during a fully electrified winter cold snap in January 2018. A unified, meteorologically driven modelling framework, based on the urbanized Weather Research and Forecasting model, is deployed as a demand management tool to simulate the urban climate, the renewable generation and the energy demand variables within a single coupled architecture, hence resolving feedback effects between weather, the urban environment and the energy system. Findings reveal a persistent mismatch between the composite renewable generation and the load in the fully electrified winter case where the heating load raises the demand considerably by approximately 8 times the current gas boilers baseline load and a multi-day offshore wind drop during the cold snap drives the deficit to nearly 9 GW, with the rooftop PV being almost entirely suppressed by snow cover. Three storage integration scenarios are analysed to mitigate these deficits, reducing the deficits by as little as ~7 % under the realistic statewide goal of storage deployment. Other scenarios achieve better deficit reduction, however, their effectiveness is found to be strongly dependent on the seasonality of the available surpluses and the scale of the deployed capacities. This study provides a transferable modelling framework for evaluating renewable integration in dense urban environments that can be used by grid operators to support resilience during both extreme heat and extreme cold events, while clarifying the limits of the local resources and the need for firm low carbon generation in fully managing the city's load.

497487.title: Rapid Urban Pluvial Flood Forecasting with a Tensorized Fourier Neural Operator
497487.authors: Haiqiao Liu, Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ; and Y. Wang, J. Camacho, S. Cocke, H. Vergara, M. Abdelkader, J. Gong, and E. Nikolopoulos
497487.abstract: Physics-based hydrodynamic models remain the standard approach for pluvial flood forecasting, but their substantial computational demands often limit their applicability to real-time forecasting and large-scale implementation. This constraint is particularly significant for early warning systems, which require rapid, computationally efficient modeling to support timely decision-making. Surrogate models trained on simulation outputs from physics-based models such as HEC-RAS and PLUV2D can substantially reduce these demands and address the limitations of conventional flood modeling. However, different surrogate architectures vary considerably in predictive performance, making the choice of network design a key consideration. In this study, we evaluated several surrogate-model architectures. The primary architecture is a Tensorized Fourier Neural Operator (TFNO), benchmarked against convolutional (CNN/U-Net) and graph-based (Graph Neural Network, Graph Neural Operator) baselines under a shared interface. All models were trained on synthetic storm-event simulations for Barbados. On held-out autoregressive rollouts over a 288-step horizon, TFNO attains the lowest mean RMSE and MAE of all four architectures, with its advantage sharpest in the middle of the rollout, where it reduces RMSE, MAE, and peak-depth RMSE by 21–77% relative to CNN, GNN, and GNO alike—consistent with the global, resolution-invariant receptive field of spectral operators versus the local receptive fields of convolution and graph message passing. To further improve predictive performance, we adopt a hybrid loss designed to preserve sensitivity to high-water-depth extremes. It combines pixel-wise mean squared error with a structural similarity index (SSIM) term to promote spatial coherence and a peak-aware weighting scheme that assigns greater importance to time steps where water depth exceeds the temporal mean at the corresponding grid cell. The best hybrid-loss configuration reduced mean RMSE, mean MAE, peak RMSE, maximum-depth RMSE, and maximum-depth MAE by 33.5%, 33.4%, 38.5%, 34.2%, and 26.9%, respectively. We further evaluated the surrogate architectures against the PLUV2D simulations using the Critical Success Index (CSI) and False Alarm Ratio (FAR) at multiple water-depth thresholds. The categorical metrics were calculated using both exact pixel-wise matching and a spatial tolerance radius of 0.2 km. Shallow inundation (below 1.5 m) was represented more accurately than greater water depths, for which the FAR generally increased. However, performance improved when the 0.2-km tolerance was applied, indicating that the models often predicted inundation near the reference flooded locations even when they did not reproduce the exact spatial extent at the pixel level. We also calculated mean bias and RMSE within several flood-prone areas in Barbados. The TFNO with the hybrid loss consistently produced the lowest errors across all evaluated areas. In addition, incorporating runoff as an input did not improve model performance and instead increased the error metrics . Together, these results demonstrate that a TFNO surrogate with a peak-aware hybrid loss can deliver fast, accurate pluvial flood forecasts, offering a practical foundation for real-time early warning systems.

497488.title: Improving Convection Initiation Predictability through Deep Learning applied to Geostationary Satellite Observations
497488.authors: Steven J. Greybush, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA; and C. Spallone, K. Yang, C. Becker, and D. J. Gagne II
497488.abstract: Prediction of convection initiation (CI), the formation of new localized precipitation areas that can develop into thunderstorms with hazards including hail, tornadoes, and strong winds, is a key challenge for meteorologists. High resolution convection-allowing numerical weather prediction models, such as the HRRR and Warn on Forecast System, assimilate conventional and remotely sensed observations to predict convective hazards. However, identifying the cloud systems that may develop into convection, spinning up convection in these ensemble modeling systems, and rapid error growth at the mesoscale remains a scientific challenge for radar and satellite data assimilation for severe weather, particularly when many ensemble members fail to predict CI. There is also the latency difficulty of running computationally expensive simulations in time to warn of impacts in the sub-hourly forecasting (nowcasting) environment. Our team has developed a probabilistic deep learning system, based on a U-Net architecture, for identifying existing convection and convection initiation at sub-hourly lead times (0-40 minutes). This deep learning system ingests multiple IR channels (CH7-16) from GOES satellites at 2km grid spacing, with the labels being convection identified at the 1km MRMS grid. While trained with multiple seasons of data (~50,000 examples) over the Great Plains, the system is evaluated for thousands of independent examples, including out-of-sample cases in the mid-Atlantic, like sea breeze convection. The practical predictability of convection initiation using deep learning is assessed at a variety of lead times, including an expanded evaluation across much of the CONUS in a variety of environments, and the physical realism and feature importance is analyzed. A discussion of potential integration of this system with other AI architectures and data assimilation and forecasting systems is planned.

497489.title: Evaluating TEMPO's 0–2 km O3 Sub-Column for PBL Air Quality Monitoring in Complex Environments: Insights from TOLNet and Surface Measurements
497489.authors: Claudia Marie Bernier, NASA, Cedar Hill, TX
497489.abstract: NASA's Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) geostationary sensor has greatly improved observations and our understanding of spatiotemporal pollution variability in North America and the processes driving them. In this study, we evaluate TEMPO's 0 - 2 km ozone (O3) product multiple complex terrain regions in the U.S., such as the greater Los Angeles air basin (San Bernardino, CA) and the New York City metropolitan area, that frequently experiences high O3 episodes driven by a combination of transported and locally produced pollution. We combine TEMPO O3PROF retrievals with spatiotemporal O3 profiles from the Tropospheric O3 Lidar Network (TOLNet) and surface O3 monitors to assess how well TEMPO captures near-surface, air quality relevant O3 mixing ratios across a range of physical and chemical conditions. These sites were selected for their complex terrain, recurring high air polluted conditions, and co-located TOLNet lidar coverage, offering a range of environments in which to test TEMPO's ability to capture near-surface air quality. TOLNet's high vertical and temporal resolution allows us to resolve fine scale structure in the O3 profile that is not directly observable from the TEMPO column product. By co-locating TEMPO, lidar, and surface observations across the diurnal cycle, we characterize systematic differences between TEMPO's 0 - 2 km sub-column and coincident in situ measurements to identify conditions where agreement breaks down, utilizing the TOLNet O3 profiles to diagnose the likely causes for disagreement. We identify where discrepancies arise from cases such as residual layer influence, boundary layer evolution, or elevated O3 layers decoupled from the surface. This case-by-case diagnosis provides insight into the retrieval-based limitations of satellite-derived sub-column O3 in complex, high pollution environments, for assessing surface air quality. This study aims to grasp how well TEMPO measured pollution can be used synergistically with ground-based, in-situ networks to refine our understanding of O3 formation and vertical distribution in complex terrain, and to inform future use of geostationary observations for air quality applications in similarly challenging regions.

497490.title: Forecasting 101: What Every Weather Communicator Needs to Know
497490.authors: Justin T. Ballard, Houston Chronicle, Houston, TX
497490.abstract: Aspiring weather communicators do not always begin their careers in meteorology programs. Some come from journalism, broadcasting and other communications disciplines, raising an important question for educators and the weather enterprise: How much meteorology does a weather communicator need to know? At the University of Florida, which did not offer a meteorology degree program until fall 2024, broadcast students interested in weather forecasting needed another pathway to develop foundational meteorological knowledge. Instruction and mentorship focused on the basics of “Forecasting 101”: interpreting surface weather maps and features such as highs, lows and fronts; analyzing radar and observational data; understanding basic forecasting principles; and translating that information into clear and accurate communication for a public audience. Those experiences provide a starting point for examining meteorological literacy among weather communicators more broadly. What concepts are essential for someone responsible for explaining weather to the public? How can educators balance scientific understanding with communication skills? And how can universities without atmospheric science programs better prepare students interested in careers communicating weather? Drawing on experience educating aspiring broadcast weathercasters and subsequent work in digital meteorology and weather journalism at the Houston Chronicle, this presentation will explore practical approaches to building meteorological literacy among communicators. It will also consider how lessons from both the classroom and newsroom can help meteorologists, educators and journalists create pathways for students who may enter the weather enterprise through communications rather than atmospheric science. As weather information reaches PEOPLE through an expanding range of platforms and messengers, those responsible for communicating forecasts and hazards need the meteorological knowledge to interpret that information accurately, convey uncertainty and translate risk into information audiences can use. Strengthening meteorological literacy among weather communicators can help build a more informed and resilient public and support the broader goal of a Weather-Ready Nation.

497492.title: Aircraft Bromide CIMS for Measurements of Atmospheric Iodine, Organic and Inorganic Species
497492.authors: Yandong Tong, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and L. Feinman, V. Fowler, B. Blomquist, E. Assaf, T. L. Campos, A. Franchin, S. Woods, and R. Volkamer
497492.abstract: Bromide chemical ionization mass spectrometry (Br-CIMS) offers sensitive and selective measurements of a broad suite of atmospheric organic and inorganic trace gases. The application of Br-LToF-CIMS to aircraft observations is novel and requires robust control of instrumental sensitivity across rapidly changing environmental conditions (temperature, pressure, humidity, ozone). This challenge is especially important for airborne profiling, where water vapor varies by orders of magnitude from the boundary layer to the upper troposphere lower stratosphere (UTLS), and changes in ozone are known to affect secondary ion chemistry with similar instrumentation (e.g., I-CIMS). We present a technical characterization of the University of Colorado Br-LToF-CIMS designed for aircraft measurements. We evaluate sensitivity as a function of ion molecule reactor humidity, pressure, and temperature, as well as ambient pressure and high-ozone conditions from flights that span from the marine boundary layer into the lower stratosphere. Systematic calibrations exploit synergistic benefit of combining optical spectroscopy measurements of iodine and glyoxal across wide humidities, and show that water vapor can either enhance or suppress instrument responses depending on analyte chemistry. We present aircraft observations that investigate the impact of elevated stratospheric ozone on the bromide reagent ion chemistry. Our extensive calibrations include deployments at the CERN/CLOUD chamber, and provide a framework for optimizing Br-CIMS operation over the large range of environmental conditions encountered during vertical profiling. Field observations from the TI3GER-2 aircraft field campaign (Technological Innovation Into Iodine for GV aircraft Environmental Research) are presented over Colorado, Utah, and Oregon. The instrument simultaneously measures species including glyoxal, methylglyoxal, nitrous acid, hydrogen peroxide, sulfur species, and other oxygenated and halogenated compounds. Unlike the common I-CIMS, Br-CIMS enables the measurement of iodine in the atmosphere. We highlight the potential of Br-CIMS to expand the chemical information available from future ATom-like missions.

497493.title: A Collaborative Look at Warn-on-Forecast Messaging: Tennessee Partner Engagement Initiative
497493.authors: Miranda K. Silcott, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High Impact Weather Research and Operations, Norman, OK; and D. Hogg, P. C. Burke, H. Obermeier, M. Krocak, K. Hurley, J. Barnwell, R. Husted, M. Schargorodski, and J. T. Ripberger
497493.abstract: The experimental Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS) is known for its rapid, probabilistic prediction of individual thunderstorm hazards. The National Weather Service is utilizing WoFS for communicating the most likely location and probable magnitude of severe weather events, especially during the time period between watches and warnings. Historically, this interval between watches and warnings has been characterized as having limited new forecast information, partly due to a lack of tools capable of predicting storm-scale hazards within this temporal scale. By providing forecasters with rapidly updating probabilistic predictions regarding the magnitude and location of severe weather, WoFS bridges this gap, potentially extending lead times from minutes to hours before impacts occur. As WoFS nears operational status, it is crucial to understand the impacts this new tool and its information may have on end-users. This is especially true for emergency managers (EMs), who serve as a primary source for disseminating and translating NWS forecast products to their downstream partners (i.e., first responders, local leaders, and members of the public). Researchers have intentionally engaged local, regional, and national emergency management groups to better understand how WoFS information might be best utilized for EM decision-making. In a recent, focused initiative, researchers teamed with NWS Nashville and the Tennessee Emergency Management Agency (TEMA) to study the impact of WoFS on decision makers in middle Tennessee. This initiative aims to gather feedback and co-develop strategies for integrating WoFS information into NWS products, specifically targeting emergency management workflows. A key outcome so far has been a sustained collaboration among researchers, NWS meteorologists, and emergency managers to establish best practices for WoFS-informed messaging. This presentation will share findings from Tennessee emergency management partners and next steps for co-developing WoFS severe weather messaging.

497494.title: Extending GCM-Based Rainfall Onset, Cessation, and Dry/Wet Spell Forecasts to East and Southern Africa for Agricultural Early Warning
497494.authors: William Agyakwah, Entarian, Greenbelt, MD; and Z. Segele, E. B. Bekele, and W. M. Thiaw
497494.abstract: Forecasting rainfall onset, cessation, and within-season dry/wet spells is critical for early warning systems supporting rainfed agriculture across Africa. A previous study evaluated the skill of Global Circulation Model (GCM)-based products in predicting the start of the rainy season across West Africa's drought-prone Sahel, where onset was defined as the first day of a three-day period receiving at least 20 mm of rain with no subsequent dry spell of seven or more days within the next 21 days, using a detection window beginning May 15 for the June–September (JJAS) rainy season. Calibrated against observed RFEv2 data through linear regression, the five-model GCM ensemble closely reproduced observed onset dates for 2022–2024 and showed high correlation with observations over 1991–2016, leading to operational monthly onset products now available at the CPC International Desk. That study also noted the methodology's adaptability to other regions, including Central, East, and Southern Africa. Building on this foundation, the present study extends the framework operationally to East and Southern Africa. Using August 2026 GCM initialization data, rainfall onset, cessation, and monthly dry/wet spell frequency were predicted for East Africa’s September–December 2026 rainy season. The same August initialization data were used to predict onset, cessation, and monthly dry/wet spells for Southern Africa’s September 2026–February 2027 rainy season. Forecast skill was verified by correlating the predicted onset, cessation, and dry/wet spell metrics with observed MSWEP and RFEv2 precipitation data. Results show that the GCMs exhibit high predictive skill across both regions, comparable to that previously demonstrated in the Sahel. These findings extend the Sahel-based early warning framework to East and Southern Africa, providing decision-makers with additional lead time for agricultural planning ahead of the 2026/2027 rainy seasons. Keywords: Rainfall Onset, Cessation, Dry/Wet Spells, East Africa, Southern Africa, Global Circulation Models (GCMs), Seasonal Forecasting, MSWEP, RFEv2, Rainfed Agriculture, Early Warning Systems.

497496.title: Utilizing Operational Mesoscale Models to Drive Snowpack Simulations over the Colorado Rocky Mountains for Avalanche Forecast Applications
497496.authors: David G. Lerach, University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO
497496.abstract: Accurate snow avalanche forecasts are critical to states like Colorado, where they support safe winter recreation and tourism, inform transportation and avalanche-mitigation decisions, and help maintain reliable access for the movement of people, goods, and commerce across mountainous corridors. However, real-time snow profile observations are limited in time and geospatial coverage, and each year agencies such as the Colorado Avalanche Information Center (CAIC) rely evermore on numerical model-based snowpack fields to aid avalanche forecasters in their decision making. The CAIC, for example, uses their own internal configuration with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to provide 2-km weather input fields, and the Swiss SNOWPACK model to produce resulting snowpack fields (CAIC-WRF-SP). This study, in collaboration with the CAIC, evaluates the viability of using current NCEP operational mesoscale model forecast data as forcing input for SNOWPACK to create accurate and reliable real-time, high-resolution mountain snowpack fields to support operational avalanche forecasting across the Colorado Rockies. Specifically, the HRRR 3-km forecast products (0Z and 12Z cycles, 1–36 hour forecasts) are used to drive a parallel SNOWPACK model configuration (HRRR-SP) during the 2024-25 winter season over the Colorado Rocky Mountains. Model output is verified primarily against an east-aspect snow pit at Berthoud Pass, Colorado (11,300 ft), where semi-weekly manual profiles were collected from early November 2024 through late May 2025, along with data from the co-located Berthoud Summit SNOTEL site and other relevant SNOTEL stations from the same winter season. Presented results will target air temperature, wind, and precipitation biases in the driving weather models, alongside resulting biases in modeled snowpack depth, snow water equivalent, and internal layering and snow metamorphism: all metrics directly relevant to avalanche hazard assessment. Comparisons will also characterize the relative accuracy of CAIC-WRF-SP vs. HRRR-SP simulations, ultimately assessing the broader feasibility of using not only existing NOAA operational mesoscale products to drive real-time snowpack and avalanche forecasting across Colorado, but also highlight priority model variables in future HRRR and Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) operational models that may require monitoring and improvement for appropriate use in driving Colorado snowpack models.

497497.title: Methods to Reduce Temperature Uncertainty in Cold Stage Ice Nucleation Particle Measurements
497497.authors: Hans Taylor, Independent Researcher, Ann Arbor, MI
497497.abstract: Prior work has found that the uncertainty in ice-nucleating particle (INP) concentrations across laboratory instruments is often at least a factor of five, in some instances exceeding three orders of magnitude. This uncertainty propagates into operational weather and climate forecasts and should be addressed. The INP concentration of a substance can be measured by a variety of approaches. Direct methods include continuous flow diffusion chambers and expansion cloud chambers. Indirect methods include cold stage droplet freezing arrays, as well as both acoustic and electrode levitation of water droplets. Each method has unique benefits and limitations. This work addresses the cold stage method as it is the most widely used and the most accessible method. The cold stage method utilizes the following sequence of steps: substance sampling (e.g., pulling air through a filter to collect airborne particles, collecting precipitation, or collecting non-airborne particles such as pollen), sample preparation (e.g., preparing a non-precipitation sample by suspending the particles in filtered water), and sample freezing (i.e., cooling numerous equally-sized droplets of the sample until they are all frozen). After freezing, the INP concentration is derived by a standardized equation using each droplet temperature and its corresponding fraction frozen (i.e., the fraction of total droplets that have frozen). Each step introduces uncertainty to the derived INP concentration. In this work, sources of temperature uncertainty associated with sample freezing are addressed while substance sampling and sample preparation are ignored. Because the mathematical derivation of INP concentration is identical across instruments, only measurements of droplet temperature and droplet volume can introduce uncertainty in the INP concentration. If the uncertainty in droplet volume is assumed to be the same across instruments (i.e., a constant droplet volume with a similar dispensing technique), then only the uncertainty in the measured droplet temperature is of interest. Due to the non-linear sensitivity of INP concentration to droplet temperature, assuming a constant droplet volume, uncertainty in the INP concentration can exceed an order of magnitude from a single kelvin of uncertainty in droplet temperature. Possible sources of droplet temperature uncertainty include the thermometer placement and type, the substrate upon which the water droplets are placed, the inclination of the substrate, the water contact angle, and thermal homogeneity. Each source is examined separately and best practices and recommended standardized design elements are proposed. Addressing the uncertainty problem of ice nucleation measurements using other indirect methods and direct methods remains an important task for the community.

497498.title: Expansion and Reanalysis of the Pre-1950 U.S. Tornado Record
497498.authors: Blue Ayanami, Tornado Archive, Salt Lake City, UT; and J. Finch, N. Wilkes, A. Berrington, and Z. Esch
497498.abstract: We present a considerable expansion of the pre-1950 North American tornado record assembled for Tornado Archive (TA). Building on the foundational compilations of Thomas P. Grazulis and verified National Weather Service sources, the TA content team systematically located, digitized, geolocated, and reconciled historical observations from newspapers, diaries, county histories, and institutional archives to increase both the temporal depth and spatial density of the early U.S. database (1671-1950). Retrospective Fujita-scale ratings were assigned using contemporaneous damage descriptions, photographic evidence where available, and an expert review protocol when necessary. Every record includes source citations, an event narrative, geocoordinates, and an F-scale assignment. Duplicate events and reporting biases were identified and handled through cross-referencing and temporal/spatial clustering. The results show a substantial increase in documented events and improved geographic coverage, especially across the Midwest and Southeastern United States. We discuss three classes of scientific value from this expansion: (1) an improved baseline for long-term variability and trend analyses; (2) enhanced ability to validate and calibrate modern climatologies and model hindcasts; and (3) richer historical context for risk assessment, damage-model parameterization, and socio-meteorological studies of vulnerability and warning response through time. The presentation will demonstrate examples of reinterpreted events, quantify how the expanded record alters regional event counts and seasonality signals qualitatively, and outline next steps for community access and collaborative quality control.

497500.title: Investigation of the Diurnal Cycle and Mesoscale Processes of High-Resolution Modeled Summertime Precipitation over the Rocky Mountains
497500.authors: Kaitlin Smith, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and B. Geerts and P. Adhikari
497500.abstract: In mountainous regions such as the western United States, precipitation is as heterogenous as the underlying terrain, and small-scale features can dictate intricately connected cross-scale dynamic and thermodynamic forcings. Furthermore, this region tends to be particularly dry, meaning that understanding the values, timing, and propagation of precipitation is important. Radar-derived observations can suffer from intrinsic biases such as beam blockage, and gauge data is often unrepresentative of the surrounding area, leading to an incomplete picture of precipitation and its drivers. As both the resolution of and the processes represented in coupled land-atmosphere dynamic models improve, models are out-performing gauge-based gridded datasets such as PRISM and become an increasingly viable tool for studying precipitation patterns, structure, and events. However, while many models have seen great improvements with convection-permitting 4 km grids, this resolution is still too large to fully resolve the orographic mesoscale processes that initiate and maintain convection, leading to persistent errors in simulating both the timing of the daily cycle of precipitation as well as peak precipitation values. RM1.3 (Adhikari et al. 2026, in review) is a 1.33 km convection-permitting downscaling of CONUS404 (Rasmussen et al. 2023, 10.1175/BAMS-D-21-0326.1) centered on the central Rocky Mountains and spanning 35 years of historical reanalysis (1990-2024), another 35 years of a PGW future simulation (2032-2066), and has sufficiently high resolution to analyze smaller-scale effects critical to representing convective processes. This study investigates the diurnal cycle of summertime orographic precipitation in and around the Rocky Mountains through the lens of high-resolution modeling, specifically RM1.3. By comparing modeled output with existing observations from sources such as NCEP IV, precipitation output can be examined in the context of the dynamic and thermodynamic structure as simulated by RM1.3 to study and evaluate how mesoscale processes are represented in high-resolution models. RM1.3 indeed improves the underestimation and timing of peak precipitation seen in lower-resolution models and captures the well-documented gradual shift from midday-dominated precipitation over the mountains to evening-dominated precipitation over nearby lower-lying terrain. While this signal is particularly clear on the eastern slope of the Colorado Front Range, RM1.3 also demonstrates this gradual evening-shift on the western slope of many mountain ranges inside the domain. This research will investigate the propagation mechanisms (such as advection by steering winds and the impact of the RKW balance for sustained convection) as well as the relative importance thereof, thus gaining a clearer picture of both orographic precipitation itself and how it affects the surroundings.

497507.title: Contributions from NASA’s Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP) Mission Towards Space Weather Science and Operations
497507.authors: Christina O. Lee, Space Sciences Laboratory, UC Berkeley, Berkeley, CA; and D. J. McComas, E. R. Christian, M. Gkioulidou, N. Schwadron, D. Baker, C. M. S. Cohen, M. Desai, T. Horbury, S. Kanekal, S. Livi, J. G. Luhmann, J. G. Mitchell, J. S. Rankin, S. Raptis, R. Skoug, and D. L. Turner
497507.abstract: In September 2025, NASA launched Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP), a heliophysics science mission that will advance our understanding of inner and outer heliosphere through new coordinated and comprehensive observations of charged particles, solar wind plasma and magnetic field from the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point. These observations will be used to address two important heliophysics topics: (1) the acceleration of energetic particles and (2) the interaction of our heliosphere with the very local interstellar medium. Five of the ten science instruments on IMAP are designed to make in-situ particles and fields measurement for advancing heliophysics science research. In parallel to making observations for IMAP science, the five in-situ instruments also make important continuous, low-latency measurements for advancing space weather science and operations. Through the IMAP Active Link for Real-Time (I-ALiRT) space weather data system, IMAP makes real-time space weather observations from L1 and broadcasts the data to a network of ground stations at Earth. The I-ALiRT space weather data products are similar to those provided by the ACE Real Time Solar Wind (RTSW), but at higher cadences, and also include new products that have potential applications for space weather operations. Lastly, the IMAP science and space weather data contribute towards an unprecedented set of multi-vantage point observations around Earth’s L1 that offers new capabilities for understanding the mesoscale evolution of solar wind structures as they propagate from L1 towards Earth and new opportunities for the development of space weather forecasting tools. This presentation will highlight contributions from the IMAP mission thus far towards the space weather enterprise.

497508.title: Increasing Space Weather IQ: A Hands-On Professional Development Model for Broadcast and Digital Meteorologists to Inform the Public and Decision Makers
497508.authors: Dave F. Jones, StormCenter Communications, Inc., Annapolis, MD
497508.abstract: Abstract: While space weather significantly impacts critical infrastructure—including GPS, aviation, and power grids—most broadcast meteorologists lack the practical experience required to communicate these low-frequency, high-impact hazards accurately to their audiences. To close this information gap, a new immersive short course model is being developed in partnership with NASA Heliophysics, NOAA NESDIS LEO Program Office and the NOAA NWS Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC). This presentation details a unique "research-to-broadcast" training framework that moves beyond traditional lectures. The approach integrates authoritative science and operational forecast context with a hands-on "Data Access Lab" and a "Broadcast Translation Drill." The centerpiece of the model is an interactive afternoon session featuring three mock "space weather update desks." Participants navigate realistic scenarios—ranging from aurora forecasting to technology infrastructure impacts—to produce 90-second broadcast updates while receiving direct feedback from Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) on scientific accuracy and risk communication. We will discuss the approach and expectations of this hands-on model in strengthening on-air credibility, improving performance during rapidly developing solar events, and providing meteorologists with the take-home resources necessary to translate technical space weather data into clear, viewer-focused reporting.

497509.title: Predicting Dynamic Structural Loads of a Full-Scale Solar PV Installation In Atmospheric Flow (Invited Presentation)
497509.authors: Brooke Stanislawski, National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR), Golden, CO; and M. Emes, PhD Mechanical Engineering, X. He, W. Arsalane, and E. Young
497509.abstract: Wind-driven loads are an important consideration in the design and operation of solar tracking photovoltaic (PV) arrays. High wind speeds can initiate unsteady aerodynamic instabilities (e.g. torsional galloping) and moderate wind speeds can create unsteady loads, both of which can result in costly mechanical failures of the PV installation. Thus, it is important to understand and predict the aerodynamic loads of PV trackers in the real world. Effective numerical modeling capabilities can improve PV tracker design and operation, preventing and mitigating damage. The aerodynamic loading of PV trackers is complex due to the structure’s interaction with the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) (e.g. turbulent, variable wind conditions) and its proximity to the ground. These complexities are difficult to model numerically because of the wide range of length and time scales involved. Many of the existing studies on aerodynamic loading of PV panels have focused on modeling the mean or static loads, neglecting peak loads, which are critical for predicting damage. This work simulates the dynamic response of a full-scale PV tracker near Boulder, CO in turbulent wind conditions and compares the mean and peak force coefficients, as well as their amplitudes, against those measured in the field. Funded by DuraMAT, the measurement campaign of the single-row PV tracker at NLR’s Flatirons Campus collected data from Oct 2019 to Jan 2020 at 50 Hz. In the inflow just west of the tracker, three met towers with sonic anemometers and one met tower with a cup and vane anemometer were installed at approximately 2.2m height. The loads sensors measured accelerations at 6 locations along the tracker, torque at three locations along the torque tube, pier bending moments on the drive pier, tracker tilt angle, and panel deflections. To simulate the aerodynamic loading of the PV tracker, we use NLR's PVade, an open-source fluid-structure interaction model designed to study wind loading and stability of solar-tracking PV arrays in turbulent wind conditions. PVade uses a partitioned fluid–structure interaction approach, leveraging FEniCSx for the finite-element formulation backend, where the fluid and structural problems are solved separately and coupled through the PV surface. The fluid solver solves the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with a fractional-step method for velocity and pressure. The structural solver uses finite-element linear elasticity to compute the deformation of the PV structure under aerodynamic loads. The fluid transfers pressure and viscous stresses to the structure, while the resulting structural displacement and velocity are transferred back to the fluid solver to update the fluid domain. A snapshot of the simulation is shown in Fig. 1. [figure] Fig. 1 – Fluid-structure interaction simulation of the deforming PV tracker at 40 degrees from horizontal in turbulent wind conditions with a mean wind speed of 9 m/s at the height of the panel. We find that PVade predicts the dynamic response of the measured PV tracker within good agreement and that turbulence plays a critical role. The simulations capture the amplitudes and the trends in peak and mean force coefficients with respect to tracker angle. Based on these results, this model can be used to predict the dynamic response of new designs and operational strategies of PV trackers to mitigate damage. 497510.title: Breathing It In: Regional Differences in Smoke Exposure, Perceived Health Risk, and Willingness to Act
497510.authors: Shadya Sanders Davis, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC; and T. M. Adams
497510.abstract: Perceiving a hazard and acting on it are separate steps, and smoke makes the distinction very clear. The protective actions available for smoke exposure are generally considered to be low-cost and individually controllable. Masking, running a home air filter, and limiting time outdoors require neither substantial resources nor the disruption of leaving home. A gap between believing smoke is harmful and doing something about it cannot be explained by capacity alone. For many residents of South Carolina, smoke is a seasonal feature of land management. For residents of Colorado, it accompanies a hazard that has reshaped the state's fire regime. For residents of the Washington–Philadelphia–New York corridor, it arrived abruptly in June 2023 and has recurred only occasionally since. These three populations encounter the same physical exposure under sharply different conditions of familiarity. If familiarity builds preparedness, protective action should be highest where exposure is routine, however, if familiarity instead normalizes the exposure, the pattern may reverse. A web-based survey of approximately 1,200 U.S. adults, across the three regions, measures smoke exposure history, perceived health impacts, protective behavior, and support for air quality policy. Sampling is weighted toward the Southeast (n ≈ 450) relative to Colorado (n ≈ 400) and the corridor (n ≈ 350), which is defined by the metropolitan statistical areas of Washington, Philadelphia, and New York. Fielding spans both prescribed burn season and wildfire season so that responses are collected while smoke is a live concern in each region rather than recalled at a distance. Perceived health risk and protective action are measured separately for prescribed fire smoke and wildfire smoke, allowing comparison of responses to which type of smoke was experienced. Perceived risk is assessed for the respondent and for others in the household, since decisions about staying indoors or keeping windows closed are frequently made on behalf of children or older family members rather than for oneself alone. Protective action is measured primarily as recalled behavior during the respondent's most recent smoke episode, including whether they checked an air quality index, closed windows, wore a mask, ran an air filter, kept children indoors, or limited their own time outside. For the corridor sample the most recent qualifying episode may date to June 2023, so time since exposure is recorded and treated as a covariate in regional comparisons. A smaller set of items asks what respondents intend to do during the next smoke episode, allowing recalled behavior and stated intention to be compared within the same individual. Residence tenure is included to test whether recent migrants to the Southeast differ from established residents in tolerance for management smoke. While each state has different policies regarding land management and air quality, federal guidance calls for expanded prescribed burning to reduce wildfire risk, and EPA particulate matter standards may constrain when and where burns can occur. Public tolerance for smoke sits between those two pressures and is poorly characterized outside communities adjacent to burn units. Identifying where the perception-to-action gap is widest points to the populations for whom current smoke risk messaging is doing the least work, and to the places where support for burning is most likely to erode.

497511.title: Collective Action to Address the Challenges of Extreme Environmental Events: A Panel on Ideas, Proposals, and Business Cases for Multi-Sector Action (Invited Presentation)
497511.authors: Harry A. Cikanek III, Retired, Philadelphia, PA
497511.abstract: This 90-minute Panel discussion will provide a cross-sector discussion of how ongoing and new collective or collaborative action among the major sectors of industry, government and academia can address the challenges facing the public, industry and governments at all levels. Topics for collective or collaborative action include programs, tools, methods, policies, benchmark data sets, test beds, information, and standards to tackle the new challenges of this era of extreme weather and climate information. Goals would include better risk mitigation and risk management, along with better informed decisions across the insurance and reinsurance value chain, regulators, public policy, funders of research, and the public. Invited speakers will include, subject to confirmation, the Colorado Insurance Commissioner Michael Conway or a representative he designates from the Colorado Division of Insurance; an insurance reinsurance, capital-markets, or catastrophe-risk speaker from BlackRock, Moody’s, USAA, FM Global, or Alpha Geo; and academic and industry experts in catastrophe modeling, climate science, and risk management, with Hussam Mahmoud among the prospective academic participants. The discussion will focus on practical pathways from government research investments, community action, policy changes, incentives, legal changes, industry associations, public / private partnerships that might be employed. These will be examined considering the business factors and economics of the of the challenges that underpin the need and business case for collective action. The Panel will address relevant examples and successes from efforts to date, and from other sectors that help inform the insurance, reinsurance and financial sectors. Participants will identify proposals for actions that support resilient communities, functioning insurance markets, and effective management of financial risk. Participation by any proposed speaker is not yet confirmed.

497513.title: Mesoscale Water Vapor and Clouds: Balanced-Unbalanced Decomposition
497513.authors: Vaidehi Ramachandrula, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Brookfield, WI; and S. N. Stechmann
497513.abstract: On synoptic scales, valuable concepts such as geostrophic balance and balanced-unbalanced decompositions have a long history. Their importance has been seen in many applications, such as data assimilation and weather prediction. On mesoscales, on the other hand, the concepts of balance and balanced-unbalanced decompositions are less well developed, yet could be valuable for analogous applications in mesoscale and convective-scale data assimilation and prediction. Here, we formulate a balanced-unbalanced decomposition for mesoscales that can decompose temperature, water vapor, and condensed water (cloud liquid water, ice, and precipitation). The decomposition is a type of nonlinear eigenmode decomposition, where the balanced and unbalanced components are related to weak temperature gradient (WTG) balance and gravity waves, respectively, and characterized by a slow moisture variable and buoyancy, respectively. Here, on mesoscales, the decomposition is shown to have an interpretation as a thermodynamic process: the buoyancy is decreased to zero while keeping the slow moisture variable held fixed. The decomposition is then applied to reanalysis data to investigate the question: How much mesoscale variability is balanced versus unbalanced? Potential applications are also discussed for mesoscale and convective-scale data assimilation and forecasting.

497514.title: Phase Change: Exploring Expansions in Precipitation Profiling Across Wisconet
497514.authors: Christopher A. Vagasky, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and C. Wienkes and M. Martiros
497514.abstract: In its first three years, Wisconet has measured precipitation across its approximately 80 weather stations in Wisconsin using tipping bucket gauges. However, this has limited value during the cool season: Evaporation and sublimation take away some of the snow and ice accumulation, and by the time the meltwater reaches the bucket, it’s days or weeks after the precipitation has fallen. Unfortunately, this means that Wisconet’s precipitation data does not get used in operational settings during the cool season, and we are missing an important contributor to groundwater, lake levels, and spring flooding concerns. In the fall of 2026, Wisconet began steps to expand its precipitation measurements across Wisconsin, working with several partners. The expansion includes testing new sensor technologies and could help increase the density of liquid and solid precipitation measurements for Wisconet and serves as a functional testbed for the mesonet community. Among the new technologies are Internet-of-Things tipping bucket gauges that could allow dense precipitation networks across watersheds or agricultural fields; a short-range vertically pointed precipitation radar that provides real-time drop size distribution, precipitation type, and accumulation; and LiDAR-based snowfall sensors that provide snow depth measurements and snow water equivalent measurements. This presentation highlights the newly deployed sensor technologies and presents preliminary data from the first few months of the 2026-2027 cool season.

497518.title: Object-Based Methods for Evaluation of Thunderstorm Nowcasts
497518.authors: Patrick S. Skinner, CIWRO, Norman, OK; and J. A. Duarte, C. K. Potvin, P. Harrington, J. Pathak, S. Abbas, D. R. Durran, K. C. Britt, A. J. Clark, A. Gupta, T. Ge, N. D. Brenowitz, S. Ravuri, and M. Pritchard
497518.abstract: The past decade has produced significant advancements in thunderstorm nowcasting, including development of short-term, ensemble numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems with rapidly cycled data assimilation, data driven models that produce forecasts using available thunderstorm observations, and hybrid systems that include data driven NWP emulators and dynamically constrained AI models. With rapid development of these models, there is a need to define evaluation methods that capture specific forecast errors associated with short-term thunderstorm prediction, particularly those associated with production of thunderstorm hazards. The predictability of any thunderstorm depends on characteristics of the storm such as storm maturity following convection initiation, storm size, and storm organization driven by characteristics of the mesoscale environment. Therefore, evaluation of nowcasts on a storm-to-storm basis that defines forecast quality according to storm maturity, mode, and organization can provide unique insight into forecast performance. This study presents a suite of simple object-based identification, tracking, and matching methods designed to measure specific aspects of thunderstorm nowcast quality. Evaluation measures include quantification of forecast quality by storm “age” relative to convection initiation, across different convective modes, and inclusion of diagnostic evaluations for assessing the realism of convective structures in predicted storms. The suite is applied to thunderstorm nowcasts across 21 days during the Spring of 2026 from the Warn-on-Forecast System (WoFS), WoFSCast emulator, StormScope generative system from NVIDIA, and data driven NowcastNet system with examples presented showing strengths and weaknesses of each system.

497520.title: Design of a Next-Generation Smallsat Hyperspectral Ocean Color Observing System for Harmful Algal Bloom Detection.
497520.authors: Cheri Heng, NESDIS, Everett, WA; and H. Hope and V. J. Mikles
497520.abstract: Ocean color observations provide critical information for monitoring marine ecosystem health, identifying harmful algal blooms (HABs), and assessing environmental change. The interaction of solar radiation with water and particulate matter produces distinct optical signatures that can be used to characterize phytoplankton and identify conditions associated with developing HABs. However, existing space-borne ocean color instruments face tradeoffs that include spectral resolution, spatial resolution, coverage, and mission cost, limiting their ability to provide high-resolution observations of developing blooms in complex coastal and inland waters. This creates a need for an accessible, next-generation observing system capable of filling these observational gaps and supporting early HAB detection. This project proposes a hybrid hyperspectral radiometer designed for integration onto a small satellite platform to address these observational needs. A comparative analysis of existing space-borne ocean color missions, including NASA’s Ocean Color Instrument (OCI) and the University of North Carolina Wilmington’s HawkEye—which is no longer operational—was conducted to identify relevant instrument characteristics and inform system requirements. Insights from ocean color experts were incorporated into the design process to develop an optimized radiometer architecture balancing hyperspectral capability, spatial resolution, and smallsat constraints. The proposed system is designed to provide high-resolution spectral observations that can improve the identification of phytoplankton associated with developing HABs, particularly in coastal and inland waters where existing observational capabilities have limitations. This next-generation observing approach has the potential to expand accessible ocean color observations for HAB detection, ecosystem monitoring, and assessment of environmental change. Future work will evaluate the proposed instrument’s performance and refine its design to further assess its potential for smallsat-based ocean color observations.

497521.title: Caribbean Risks in the 21st Century: Science, Observations, Services, Lessons, and Opportunities - 2026-2027 ENSO
497521.authors: David Farrell, Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology, St. James, Barbados; and R. S. Pulwarty and L. Nurse
497521.abstract: Caribbean Small Island Developing States (SIDS) face critical nexus problems linked to food security, energy security, water security, and health security. This delicately balanced nexus problem is often perturbed by extreme weather, water, marine, climate events, geological events, external supply chain dependence, and limited capabilities to effectively respond to major disasters. While the overarching goal is to develop resilient Caribbean societies, the complex vulnerabilities and immense debt burdens of states in the region limit its development options. As with many Small Island Developing States the time between hazard and impact for hydro-met events is often very short, limiting response time and therefore requiring accurate forecasts with long lead times. In SIDS, impacts are often felt nationally. This reality is vividly illustrated by recent tropical storms and droughts that impact entire countries, and overwhelming small communities from inland to the coast, as well as, overwhelming the ability of national governments to adequately respond. This presentation highlights advances over the past two decades in developing and improving scientific understanding and integrated information services for addressing risks peculiar to SIDS. Early warning and risk management advances have arisen out of necessity and include the development of (1) analytical tools facilitating usable regional monitoring and predictions, and (2) risk-based information systems, vulnerability assessments and services development across sectors. The presentation focuses on the achievements of foresight-based Caribbean-based institutions including but not limited to the Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology (CIMH), the Caribbean Disaster Emergency Management Agency (CDEMA), the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC), the Caribbean Meteorological Organization (CMO), regional universities, and Non-Governmental Organizations with whom the authors routinely engage. We outline the challenges and emerging opportunities in support of risk-reduction and resilience, including (i) evolving research and applications from supporting emergency response and adaptation approaches alone to addressing extra-regional supply-chains and dependencies, (ii) improving comprehensive data collection on local-level impacts with the participation of affected communities, (iii) distilling scientifically-robust weather, wáter, and climate information across temporal and spatial scales, to address compounding and cascading impacts within communities, countries, and across the region, and (iv) further advancing national and regional services frameworks to address intra-regional risk governance and build out the basic observation infrastructure and innovative technologies (including AI/ML) capabilities to support the needed information systems. Emphasis will be placed on ongoing early warning, risk assessments, and responses related to the ongoing 2026-2027 ENSO event, in the Caribbean Region.

497522.title: AI Subseasonal Prediction of Week-3 Temperature
497522.authors: Alistair White, Brightband, San Francisco, CA; and A. Allen, R. Keisler, A. Bollinger, J. DiCintio, H. Kamdar, A. Kleeman, H. Mohrmann, and D. A. Rothenberg
497522.abstract: Week-3 (days 15-21) temperature anomalies drive decisions in energy demand, agricultural scheduling, and public-health preparedness, yet remain among the least skillful windows in operational prediction. This regime straddles the decay of synoptic predictability and the slower boundary-forced signals of week 4 and beyond. We present Brightband-S2S, an operational, data-driven forecasting system targeting week 3 temperature. We evaluate 2-meter temperature skill over the northern mid-latitudes and find significant skill relative to the debiased Extended Range 46-day forecast from ECMWF. We also share results for global extreme heat prediction.

497523.title: Bridging the Gap: A New Paradigm for Communicating Atmospheric River Impacts and NOAA Data Applications to Decision-Makers through Research and Operations
497523.authors: Dave F. Jones, StormCenter Communications, Inc., Annapolis, MD
497523.abstract: Abstract: Effective decision-making during high-impact weather events requires the rapid translation of complex scientific data into actionable information and narratives. While Atmospheric River (AR) science has advanced significantly, a gap remains in communicating the nuances of event intensity, antecedent ground conditions, and observational value to emergency managers, water operators, and the media. This presentation details a research-and-operations (R&O) partnership between the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) and StormCenter Communications designed to bridge this gap through innovative geospatial visualization and multi-sector engagement. The initiative focuses on three core themes: AR Scale literacy, the modulation of impacts by antecedent conditions (framing “benefits vs. hazards”), and highlighting the value of AR Recon data. We will demonstrate the use of the GeoCollaborate® platform to provide a collaborative common operating picture (C-COP) and to test and showcase research products with user communities. A centerpiece of this effort is the real-time integration of AR Recon flight tracks and dropsonde data—analogous to "hurricane hunter" tracking—to enhance situational awareness for operational users. By activating established distribution channels like the All-Hazards Consortium (SISE) and the CAT5 MetNetwork, this partnership ensures that trusted AR science is not only shareable but used effectively to help protect infrastructure, manage water resources across the western United States and to inform emergency management professionals in the public and private sectors. The presentation will also describe the importance of placing more NOAA data into operational decision-making environments through our partnership with NOAA’s LEO Program to engage more than 45,000 stakeholders and decision makers in the public and private sectors.

497526.title: An Industry Perspective on Collective Measures to Mitigate the Threats Posed by the New Era of Unpredicted Extremes in Weather and Climate (Invited Presentation)
497526.authors: Harry A. Cikanek III, Retired, Philadelphia, PA
497526.abstract: The Insurance, Reinsurance and Finance Industries are served by a substantial base of private data, metrics, rating, analytics and support services providers. Many of their capabilities are underpinned by weather, climate and natural environment data provided by Government Agencies in the developed world, and an increasing cadre of commercial data suppliers who serve both the Government Agencies and private entities. They are also underpinned by a wide range of Academic institutions providing Government funded and privately funded research, predominantly at the basic level. While there has been great success over many decades, today’s extremes call for advances beyond the current science base, and greater pace of adaptation to the fast-moving increases in environmental data that can be transformed into critical intelligence for the Insurance, Reinsurance and Finance Industries and their customers. This talk will overview the landscape, and provide the view point on what is needed to address today’s weather and environment linked economic and business challenges from the environmental risk Information provider perspective.

497527.title: Sampling the Inflow: GLOVE-CI Observations of Lake Michigan's Marine Boundary Layer During the 11 June 2026 Tornado Outbreak
497527.authors: Kyle T. Brooks, Central Michigan Univ., Mount Pleasant, MI; and A. W. Zeeb, J. M. Keeler, D. A. R. Kristovich, and K. Matousek
497527.abstract: The Laurentian Great Lakes frequently create complex atmospheric conditions in which the lake-modified marine atmospheric boundary layer (MABL) can significantly influence severe convective storms. On June 11, 2026, a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) intersected one of the three observational domains of the Great Lakes Observations of the Variable Environments affecting Convection Initiation (GLOVE-CI) field campaign in Zion, Illinois. The development and timing of the MCS created a unique opportunity to collect a novel, high-resolution dataset detailing Lake Michigan's influence on the near-storm environment and the evolution of the MABL. Field instruments were deployed several hours ahead of the incoming MCS to capture a complete time series of near-shore environmental modifications both before and during its arrival. The Central Michigan University (CMU) team launched Sparv Windsonds every 5 minutes, while a mobile mesonet performed transects across the pre-MCS environment, recording surface thermodynamic and kinematic variables at 1 Hz. Additionally, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) team provided continuous Doppler lidar coverage (both RHI and vertical stare patterns) and hourly full-tropospheric GRAW soundings at the Lake Michigan shoreline. This study leverages this dataset to evaluate the progression of lake-induced modifications to the near-storm environment. Specifically, we investigate the development of a lake breeze to determine how this localized forcing, storm interactions with the MABL, and other advective processes altered the environmental kinematics and thermodynamics. By detailing the evolution of the near-storm environment during this MCS intersection, this research seeks to improve our understanding of how large inland bodies of water affect severe convective hazards. Early results indicate repeated inland advance and retreat of the MABL, accompanied by oscillations across the full suite of observed surface thermodynamic and kinematic fields, as several convective pulses moved through the region ahead of the leading edge of the MCS. As the dominant MCS approached, the MABL pushed further inland, introducing cooler but substantially more moist air. The resulting increase in surface theta-e yielded larger SBCAPE despite a concurrent increase in SBCIN. Additionally, easterly winds off the lake enhanced low-level hodograph curvature, increasing 0-1 km storm-relative helicity computed with observed storm motion, while baroclinic generation along the lake breeze front supplied horizontal vorticity available for tilting into the vertical. With low-level flow from the SSE, GLOVE-CI operations sampled the air mass advecting toward an embedded supercell structure that produced a brief EF-1 tornado just west of Kenosha, Wisconsin, placing the campaign directly upwind of the tornadic storm's inflow environment.

497528.title: Structural Reorganization During Rapid Intensification: Identifying Recurring Intensity Slowdowns in Atlantic Basin Hurricanes
497528.authors: Angelie T. Nieves Jiménez, StormGeo, Houston, TX; and D. Ortt
497528.abstract: In this study, we will analyze several cases of rapid intensification (RI) that exhibit similar behavior: a temporary pause or slowdown in intensification near central pressures of approximately 970 mb and 920 mb. We hypothesize that these pressure levels may represent common stages at which rapidly intensifying tropical cyclones undergo a structural reorganization before resuming intensification. Importantly, this restructuring does not necessarily imply that an eyewall replacement cycle (ERC) will commence; rather, it may reflect other internal structural changes that allow the system to reorganize and continue strengthening. Using the IBTrACS and ADT-HURSAT datasets spanning the past 35 years, we will identify and analyze hurricanes that meet these criteria, focusing on their structural evolution and intensification rates. We aim to determine whether these periods of reduced intensification are common and recurring features of RI events and whether they are associated with consistent structural changes. We hypothesize that, when environmental conditions remain favorable for continued intensification, tropical cyclones undergo a restructuring process during these periods of reduced intensification, ultimately allowing them to resume rapid strengthening. Examples that exhibit this behavior include Hurricane Andrew (1992), Hurricane Floyd (1999), and Hurricane Dorian (2019). Identifying whether these temporary slowdowns are common and repeatable features of rapidly intensifying tropical cyclones could have important implications for operational forecasting. Recognizing that a slowdown may be associated with structural reorganization, rather than the end of an RI episode or the onset of an ERC, could help forecasters better anticipate subsequent changes in intensity and avoid underestimating the potential for renewed rapid intensification.

497532.title: Exploring the Impact of AI Generated Risk Information on Perceptions of Risk
497532.authors: Terri M. Adams, NOAA Cooperative Science Center in Atmospheric Sciences and Meteorology, Howard University, Silver Spring, MD; and M. Wesley and S. J. Sanders-Davis
497532.abstract: There is no effective one-size-fits-all approach to effective severe weather risk communication. Although efforts have been made to nuance the tone of evacuation messages to prompt appropriate action, some individuals continue to ignore them in the face of severe weather events. This raises an important question of how can we motivate people to take calls to action seriously enough to protect themselves and their loved ones? This project aims to deepen our understanding of how AI can be leveraged to improve risk communication messaging to those who are most likely to ignore warnings.

497533.title: Taking the Spaceport by Storm: Student-Forecasted Research Collaboration Between Orange County Public Schools and the 45th Weather Squadron
497533.authors: Vihaan Manchikanti, Orange County Public Schools, Orlando, FL; and P. Gandhi, B. Luu, E. Nguyen, A. Watts, A. Zappas, K. H. Chafin, A. L. Moses, and B. Cizek
497533.abstract: The 2026–2027 academic year marks the twelfth consecutive year of a highly successful collaborative research program between Orange County Public Schools (Florida) and the 45th Weather Squadron (45WS), designed to support America’s space launch operations. As a U.S. Space Force unit, the 45WS delivers comprehensive, 24/7 meteorological services to military, civil, and commercial launch partners across Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Patrick Space Force Base, and NASA’s Kennedy Space Center. The research partnership provides operationally relevant research for the 45WS while offering students real-world applications of advanced mathematical concepts. Through self-organized project teams, students also develop critical professional skills in leadership, project management, and scientific communication. During the 2025–2026 cycle, students executed five research projects aligned with 45WS operational needs, four of which persist into the current academic year alongside new projects. The first and longest-tenured project focuses on the quality control, analysis, and visualization of the historical Lightning Launch Commit Criteria (LLCC) database. This effort streamlines the analysis of ten complex weather rules designed to prevent natural and rocket-triggered lightning strikes on in-flight vehicles. The second project conducts statistical analyses of upper-air meteorological sounding data from Cape Canaveral (KXMR) to develop predictive tools for 24/7 duty forecasters issuing critical launch weather warnings and advisories. The third project executes rigorous quality control on raw archival data from the Spaceport’s dense mesoscale network of 46 meteorological towers, which extend up to 150 meters. This database will ultimately simplify the development of climatological products, such as wind roses and correlation tables, for Eastern Range customers. Finally, the fourth project integrates outputs from the other teams to build predictive machine learning models that estimate the probabilistic likelihood of LLCC violations and severe weather warnings based on real-time environmental data. This long lasting and ongoing partnership illustrates how secondary students can contribute to national space launch operations by conducting meaningful, operation-enhancing research, and prepare themselves for future careers in STEM fields.

497535.title: Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) Greatly Enhances Atmospheric Analysis and Predictions
497535.authors: Jorge Rodriguez, Raytheon, El Segundo, CA; and M. A. Cook, L. Wu Yuen, E. O. Monroy, A. J. Fernandez, J. D. Campbell, A. C. Petty, M. K. Belal, and M. Henry
497535.abstract: Raytheon and Spire are developing a Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) that greatly enhances atmospheric analysis and predictions.
