The architecture employs hyperspectral capabilities which enable fine measurements across multiple contiguous frequency bands. This allows discriminating among the various atmospheric spectral lines and measuring key features such as oxygen absorption peaks. Hyperspectral capabilities also allow for RFI detection and mitigation. The Raytheon and Spire design is based upon existing technology and algorithm developments and demonstrations. We will describe the technologies, the demonstrations, early phenomenology results, as well as SMBA capabilities and future applications.

497537.title: Momentum Exchange across the Trade Wind Inversion Layer and Its Relationship with the Onset of Rainfall In the Tropical Southeast Pacific Ocean
497537.authors: Alex Omar Gonzalez, WHOI, Woods Hole, MA; and R. B. Neale, J. Cui, F. Fahrin, C. A. DeMott, and G. Cesana
497537.abstract: Earth system models have severe rainfall biases over the tropical Pacific Ocean, with a persistent zonal rainfall band in the Southern Hemisphere (SH) that is seen only some years in observations. One of the reasons for this excess SH rainfall in models is that they severely underestimate the strength of the trade wind inversion (TWI) and low cloud cover, which cause the ocean to warm up and low surface pressure to develop too early in the SH tropics. In this study, we focus on horizontal momentum evolution across the TWI layer and its relationship with low cloud type during the months prior to the onset of SH rainfall in the tropical east Pacific. We quantify horizontal wind convergence variability across the TWI layer in the ERA5 reanalysis and NCAR’s Community Earth System Model 2 via closed momentum budgets. We find that changes in horizontal wind convergence are highly influenced by vertical mixing and vertical advection of horizontal momentum, controlled in part by the dominant low cloud type. Stratocumulus clouds are associated with reduced mixing across the TWI layer compared to trade cumulus clouds. We suggest that the sooner the seasonal transition from stratocumulus to trade cumulus clouds occurs, the more northerly flow that is transported into the boundary layer, which favors SH rainfall. This northerly flow tendency occurs many months before the onset of the SH rainfall band. Moreover, because there is a shallow Hadley circulation with northerly flow above the TWI that peaks in late fall/early winter, changes in vertical mixing and vertical advection of the meridional flow typically precede the seasonal reversal of the horizontal pressure gradient force. In closing, we demonstrate an important mechanism tied to low cloud processes that also has downstream effects on deep convection and tropical rainfall.

497538.title: Understanding the Relationship Between Cloud Type and Evapotranspiration, Latent Heat and Radiation in Shrubland Vegetation
497538.authors: Travis Ochoa Peterson, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI
497538.abstract: Evapotranspiration (ET) is a key indicator of ecosystem health, representing water flux from the surface to the atmosphere. High ET values can result, in-part, from water-intensive vegetation while the inverse can indicate insufficient water for evaporation. A persistent challenge in remote sensing ET is cloud contamination. Thermal infrared sensors used to derive remote sensed ET apply cloud masking which removes affected pixels and results in data gaps. Although prior studies have examined the impact of cloud amount on ET, the influence of specific cloud types remains underexplored. This study investigates how distinct clouds, using legacy ISCCP parameters affect surface-level ET, latent heat, long-wave and shortwave radiation over shrubland vegetation in Tucson, Arizona, during the North American Monsoon season. Cloud classification was performed using Cloud Optical Depth (COD) and Cloud Top Pressure (CTP) from GOES-18 Level 2 products. These classifications were compared against in-situ ET observations from the Santa Rita Experimental Range NEON flux tower. Previous results indicate that cloud presence generally reduces instantaneous ET relative to preceding clear-sky conditions. Clouds with low altitude and low density (Cumulus, Stratocumulus) generally showed brief reductions in ET. Notable results include ET values observed under high COD and low CTP conditions, characteristic of Cumulonimbus clouds, did not differ significantly from clear-sky conditions. Future research should incorporate cloud-type into ET models to improve accuracy, particularly in regions prone to frequent cloud cover. Further work will look further into specific relationships with shrubland vegetation and its special implications on cloud-formation during the summer monsoon period. Looking to deduce if previous works odd signatures originate from the clouds overpass influence on the surface fluxes or if the surface fluxes themselves as the initial conditions for abnormalities.

497539.title: Cocaine Sharks: Hook, Line and Science! Lessons In Engaging an Audience from TV and Social Media
497539.authors: Tracy Fanara, Inspector Planet LLC, tampa, FL
497539.abstract: “Cocaine sharks.” Two words that instantly spark curiosity, headlines, and conversation... and was the title of a show. I cohosted on Discovery Channel. But the real story was really never about sharks; it was about contaminant transport, wastewater, ecosystem health, and the interconnected nature of our water systems. This interactive mini-workshop explores how scientists can use compelling stories and unexpected headlines as gateways to deeper scientific understanding without sacrificing accuracy or credibility. Scientists are increasingly expected to communicate complex topics to audiences ranging from policymakers and emergency managers to students and the general public. Yet traditional scientific communication often struggles to compete for attention, while sensationalism can undermine trust. Instead of choosing between scientific rigor and public engagement, we learn to bridge them. Using real-world examples from environmental engineering, weather, flooding, harmful algal blooms, hurricanes, and the viral phenomenon of “cocaine sharks,” participants will examine why some stories capture the public imagination while equally important science goes unnoticed. Through interactive exercises, attendees will practice identifying effective communication hooks, building narratives that sustain curiosity, translating technical concepts into memorable stories, and connecting those stories to meaningful scientific outcomes. Participants will leave with a practical storytelling framework they can immediately apply to presentations, media interviews, classrooms, outreach events, and social media. Together, we’ll transform complex science into experiences that spark curiosity, build trust, inspire wonder, and motivate action, because the goal isn’t simply to tell better stories. It’s to help audiences care enough to discover the science behind them.

497540.title: Subjective Evaluation versus Objective Verification of Convective-Scale Ensemble Clustering for Precipitation Forecasting in a Rapid Refresh Ensemble Forecast System
497540.authors: Austin A. Coleman, CIRES / NOAA WPC, Boulder, CO; and J. A. Nelson Jr.
497540.abstract: Warm-season precipitation forecasting remains challenging due to rapid error growth and the frequent presence of weak synoptic forcing. From a probabilistic standpoint in particular, traditional ensemble means smooth sharp spatial gradients and wash out heavy rainfall signals. To address this, an empirical orthogonal function (EOF)-based k-means ensemble clustering framework was applied to a 28-member time-lagged Rapid Refresh Ensemble Forecast System (RRFSe) during the 2025 NOAA Hydrometeorology Testbed (HMT) Flash Flood and Intense Rainfall (FFaIR) Experiment. Daily 24-h precipitation cluster scenarios were evaluated across three preset domains at Day 1 and Day 2 lead times. Aggregated subjective evaluations by forecasters demonstrated a strong preference for cluster scenarios over full ensemble visualizations, with the full ensemble 75th percentile precipitation depiction selected as best-performing least often. Selecting objective verification metrics to compare ensemble clusters of varying membership proved difficult. While known limitations exist, objective Mean Absolute Error (MAE) verification relative to Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) quantitative precipitation estimates was chosen for simplicity. Verification showed that while full ensemble forecasts retain an MAE advantage near the 50th percentile due to spatial smoothing, individual clusters, especially smaller-membership scenarios, frequently minimized MAE at the 90th and 95th percentiles, hinting that cluster scenarios may have a better handle on rainfall extremes than the full ensemble system. Direct comparisons between subjective evaluations and objective verification metrics revealed notable discrepancies. The lowest alignment between forecaster subjective choices and objective minimum-MAE scenarios occurred at the 75th percentile QPF across all domains, oddly the exact percentile evaluated by forecasters, because spatial smoothing favored the full ensemble in MAE calculations. Conversely, the highest alignment occurred in the Central domain at the 25th percentile QPF, reaching a 63.2% match rate. These results emphasize the need for probabilistic post-processing tools beyond traditional ensemble mean visualizations, highlight the limitations of spatial error metrics like MAE for convective-scale cluster verification, and stress the need for metrics that better align with operational perceptions of forecast quality.

497541.title: Progress towards Opperational Hyperspectral Microwave Sounding
497541.authors: Mohammed K Belal, Spire Global Inc, Oxford, Oxfordshire, United Kingdom; and Y. Goncharenko, M. Henry, K. Parow-Souchon, R. Whitehead, J. van der Merwe, and J. C. Cartwright
497541.abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated significant improvements in retrieval accuracy and RFI detection capabilities for Hyperspectral Microwave Sounders (HYMS) [1, 2]. Spire has developed and deployed the HYMS In-Orbit Demonstrator (HyMS IOD) which is a new remote sensing instrument that has demonstrated next generation hyperspectral radiometer technologies. The sensor samples the microwave spectrum 50 - 58 GHz and 183 - 192 GHz absorption lines at very high spectral resolution (7 MHz). Simulation studies have shown such instruments have numerous benefits including improved retrieval accuracy of water vapour and temperature, increased vertical resolution and enhanced hydrometeor profiling. Furthermore, HYMS offers enhanced mitigation options against Radio Frequency Interference (RFI), which is a growing concern in the community and a threat to existing and future microwave sensing payloads. This paper presents Spire’s recent advancements of an In-Orbit demonstrator mission, atmospheric retrieval results and on-orbit performance. The presentation will cover early results from the In Orbit mission including sensor noise performance, double difference method against current state of the art sensors and atmospheric retrieval results to understand information content assessment. Spire, have conducted airborne campaigns of a hyperspectral microwave instrument called SERMON using UK NCAS research aircraft ‘FAAM’. These trials follow the resolution of calibration issues identified in previous campaigns. Results from the campaign include flights over both land and ocean in clear sky condition to collect temperature and humidity data and generate high quality retrievals and compare them with ECMWF reanalysis data to validate the atmospheric profiles in ‘zenith’ configuration. In ‘nadir’ configurations the profiles will be generated based on the data collected from ‘dropsondes’ for verification. For RFI surveys, the FAAM aircraft equipped with SERMON instrument will conduct flights over the Chilbolton observatory. This site hosts a range of RFI sources including radars and tuneable emitters, covering the 50 GHz bands. Results from this campaign demonstrated down to 0.05 k Tb detection thresholds using hyperspectral data stream and relatively simple RFI detection algorithms. Lessons learned from airborne campaigns and on-orbit demonstrator are summarised with a projected roadmap for an opperational hyperspectral radiometer that supports enhanced Numerical Weather Prediction. References: 1. Maddy, Eric et al., “Toward the Next Generation of Microwave Sounders: Benefits of a Low-Earth Orbit Hyperspectral Microwave Instrument in All-Weather Conditions Using AI”, IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied EO and Remote Sensing. pp. 1-15, 2024 10.1109/JSTARS.2024.3356858. 2. C. D. Kummerow et al., "Hyperspectral Microwave Sensors—Advantages and Limitations," in IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing, vol. 15, pp. 764-775, 2022, doi: 10.1109/JSTARS.2021.3133382.

497544.title: Evaluating Cross-Scenario Generalization of a Source-Resolved Methane-Ozone Emulator
497544.authors: Chuan Feng, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and K. B. Patel and Y. Xu
497544.abstract: Methane is the second-largest contributor to anthropogenic warming after carbon dioxide. Reducing methane emissions can also lower tropospheric ozone, but quantifying these co-benefits generally requires computationally intensive chemistry-climate simulations. Data-driven models offer a promising approach for diagnosing these relationships and approximating model behavior, although their ability to generalize beyond the conditions represented in their training data remains uncertain. Here, we use linear regression and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), together with feature-importance analysis, to predict monthly near-surface ozone from co-located chemical and meteorological variables in global chemistry-climate simulations. We separate grid-cell trends and seasonal cycles from shorter-term anomalies, allowing us to distinguish the reproduction of established spatial and seasonal patterns from the more challenging prediction of month-to-month ozone variability. Preliminary results show that XGBoost better represents ozone anomalies than the linear baseline. Predictor rankings emphasize short-lived chemical tracers, oxidants, and pollution-regime indicators that are broadly consistent with established tropospheric photochemistry. Methane, however, provides comparatively limited additional predictive information after trends and seasonal cycles are removed. This does not imply that methane has little influence on ozone. Instead, it suggests that preprocessing designed to isolate short-term variability may remove part of the slowly varying background ozone response to methane. To examine this possibility, we evaluate cross-scenario generalization using simulations at 0%, 75%, 100%, and 125% of baseline methane emissions. Entire methane-emission levels are withheld during training to test whether the learned relationships transfer to independent scenarios and reproduce both absolute ozone and scenario-dependent ozone changes. This design provides a direct assessment of whether strong predictive performance within a single simulation translates to altered methane conditions. The study highlights both the potential and the methodological requirements of data-driven models for assessing the ozone co-benefits of methane mitigation. Building on this concentration-driven prototype, we extend the framework toward emission-driven prediction by incorporating sector- and region-resolved methane emission fluxes as model inputs. Corresponding methane source tags from the chemistry-climate simulations provide source-resolved constraints linking individual emission sectors and regions to the resulting atmospheric methane distribution. Once validated against the full chemistry-climate simulations, this source-resolved emulator can rapidly screen methane mitigation scenarios and provide regional ozone responses for subsequent assessment of air-quality, health, agricultural, and ecosystem co-benefits.

497547.title: Learning Aerosol State Representations Within Clouds with Physics-Informed Machine Learning (Invited Presentation)
497547.authors: Lekha Patel, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM
497547.abstract: Title: LUCID: Learning Aerosol State Representations Within Clouds with Physics-Informed Machine Learning Particle-resolved models such as PartMC capture the full compositional diversity of aerosol populations, yet their computational cost prohibits direct use within cloud-resolving and larger-scale simulations. We present LUCID, a project that develops physics-informed generative machine learning to upscale particle-resolved aerosol-cloud microphysics. Our approach learns low-dimensional probabilistic representations of aerosol state within clouds, coupling variational autoencoders with neural stochastic differential equations to emulate the evolution of aerosol populations under cloud processing while preserving physical constraints and quantifying uncertainty. Training data comprise PartMC cloud-parcel simulations along ARM/LASSO-derived trajectories, grounding the learnt representations in observationally constrained conditions. We discuss the framework, early results, and the pathway towards embedding these emulators in atmospheric models to improve representation of aerosol-cloud-precipitation interactions across scales.

497549.title: Strengthening Caribbean Early Warning Communication through Collaboration Among National Meteorological Services, Disaster Risk Management Organizations, and the Media
497549.authors: Haley Anderson, Caribbean Meteorological Organization, Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago; and S. Gill, H. Hamilton, K. Cox, A. Baksh, D. Wilson, K. De Bellot, G. Greene, V. Mazarese, K. Goddard, P. Mutic, A. G. Laing, K. Kerr IV, K. A. Caesar, MS, and B. Smith
497549.abstract: It has been widely recognized that effective multi-hazard early warning systems (MHEWS) depend not only on accurate forecasting but also on clear, coordinated, and actionable communication across institutions and to the general public. With the Caribbean being among the most hazard prone regions of the world, the efficacy of early warning communication is critical to building resilience to hazards by the safeguarding of lives, property and livelihoods. The improvement of warning communications was developed for the Caribbean within the broader context of strengthening multi-hazard early warning systems and advancing the Early Warnings for All (EW4All) initiative in the Caribbean through the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems (CREWS) Caribbean 2.0 Project. Prior regional experience identified persistent barriers to effective early warnings includes fragmented communication arrangements, inconsistent warning messages, limited impact and vulnerability information, misinformation, warning fatigue, limited access by media to authoritative information, and insufficient coordination among National Meteorological and Hydrometeorological Services (NMHSs), National Disaster Risk Management Organizations (NDRMOs), government information services, and media organizations. Responding to the recognized need to enhance coordination and communication among institutions responsible for generating, translating, and disseminating risk information, the Caribbean Meteorological Organization (CMO) Headquarters, along with regional and global partners, organized a pioneering Caribbean Regional Workshop on Strengthening Knowledge Exchange and Mutual Understanding between NMHSs, NDRMOs, and the Media. The workshop, which was held in January 2026 in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago and involved approximately 60 participants from NMHSs, NDRMOs, government information services, and public and private media, generated recommendations aimed at institutionalizing the identified best practices at the national level. Following the success of the regional workshop, a national workshop was held in the Turks and Caicos Islands in May 2026, entitled, “Strengthening Knowledge Exchange and Mutual Understanding between the Meteorology Department, Department of Disaster Management and Emergencies (DDME), and the Media”. That national workshop improved multi-hazard early warning communications, clarified institutional roles and responsibilities, and enhanced strategies to reach vulnerable and last-mile communities effectively. A written guide was developed by a communications consultant in collaboration with national and regional stakeholders, to be adapted by other states in the Caribbean. The paper argues that effective early warning communication cannot be treated as the final step in the forecasting process. It must be embedded within a broader operational system supported by capable institutions, competent personnel, robust procedures, trusted partnerships, quality management, resilient infrastructure, and continuous improvement. The Caribbean experience demonstrates how regional cooperation can reduce capacity gaps, accelerate adoption of international standards, and help ensure that all Members have a pathway toward implementation of Early Warnings for All.

497550.title: Radiometric Stability and Refined SNO-Based Intercalibration of MODIS and VIIRS for CERES Edition 5
497550.authors: Prathana Khakurel, Analytical Mechanics Associates, Inc., West Lafayette, IN; and D. R. Doelling, A. Gopalan, and C. Haney
497550.abstract: The NASA Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System (CERES) project is preparing for Edition 5 data CERES products using MODIS Collection 7 (C7) Level-1B radiances and improved cloud retrievals designed for continuity over the 25-year record. To provide a consistent radiometric record across Terra, Aqua, SNPP, and NOAA-20, MODIS and VIIRS reflected-solar observations are placed on a common scale referenced to Aqua MODIS C7 to provide consistent cloud retrievals across platforms The radiometric stability of MODIS C7 and VIIRS Collection 2.1 is assessed using three pseudo-invariant Earth targets: Libya-4, Dome-C, and deep convective clouds. MODIS C7 is also compared with the previous C6.1 calibration to assess changes in stability. Terra MODIS is scaled to Aqua MODIS using polar near-simultaneous nadir overpass (SNO) radiance pairs separated by approximately 16 min. Because scene variability over this time interval can affect the comparison, the dependence of the scaling coefficients on spatial sampling is examined. Using larger SNO regions resulted in reducing the instantaneous matching noise over the month. Fortunately, the dynamic range remained constant over the various region sizes, thus providing consistent scaling factors across the various areal extents. The Terra to Aqua scaling factors were mostly within the 1% of the MAIAC factors. For Aqua–VIIRS comparisons, the close alignment of the orbital tracks allows for global SNO events. Polar and non-polar observations are stratified and then compared to assess the consistency of the resulting scaling coefficients. The polar and non-polar spectral differences between MODIS and VIIRS are accounted for using scene-specific spectral band adjustments derived from hyperspectral SCIAMACHY radiances. The polar and nonpolar scaling factors were within 1% for between Aqua against NOAA20-VIIRS and Aqua against SNPP-VIIRS. The resulting calibration relationships provide a common radiometric basis for MODIS and VIIRS cloud retrievals in CERES Edition 5.

497551.title: Icechunk In CIRRUS: Transactional, Cloud-Dative Array Storage for the National Weather Service's Next-Generation Operational Data Layer
497551.authors: Joseph J Hamman, Earthmover PBC, Seattle, WA; and D. Cherian, S. Galkin, and R. Abernathey
497551.abstract: The National Weather Service is building CIRRUS, a cloud-native framework intended to serve as the operational data layer for the agency: a single place where numerical model output, satellite imagery, radar volumes, and observations land in real time and are served to forecast operations, downstream applications, and research users. A system like this requires a robust, high-performance, highly-scalable storage layer. Operational weather data systems today operate at the petabyte-scale with complex requirements: new data arrives continuously and must become visible to readers atomically, many services write and read concurrently, every product must be traceable and reproducible, and access patterns range from a forecaster pulling a single grid point to an AI system training on the full archive. Legacy formats such as GRIB, NetCDF, and HDF5 were designed for POSIX filesystems and fall short of these requirements on cloud object storage, while tabular lakehouse formats discard the array structure inherent to most weather and geospatial data. This talk presents Icechunk, the open-source transactional storage engine that CIRRUS has adopted as a core format for its operational data lake, and examines why its design fits operational systems such as CIRRUS. Icechunk brings database-style guarantees to Zarr array data on commodity object storage. It provides ACID transactions so in-progress writes are never visible to consumers, snapshot isolation so long-running reads see a consistent view of a dataset while it updates, and a versioned commit history that provides rollback, time travel, and a complete audit trail at the data plane. It also provides advanced virtualization capabilities that support efficient cloud-native access patterns against legacy file archives, avoiding the requirement to wholesale convert existing archives to Icechunk format before use. Because Icechunk is open source (Apache 2.0 license) and builds on the open Zarr specification, it works with the existing scientific Python ecosystem and avoids vendor lock-in for a system NOAA must operate for decades. In benchmarks, Icechunk-backed workflows run up to 100x faster than NetCDF-based cloud access patterns. We share early lessons from active CIRRUS pipelines writing operational datasets to Icechunk on S3, including schema and metadata conventions, and discuss how a transactional array store supports where NWS is headed: AI-integrated workflows, federated data access across line offices, and untethered forecast operations.

497552.title: Performance of Coupler Infrastructure In the Energy Exascale Earth System Model
497552.authors: Robert L. Jacob, ANL, Lemont, IL; and V. Mahadevan, I. Grindeanu, and A. Mametjanov
497552.abstract: The infrastructure layer of the coupler in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) has recently transitioned from the Model Coupling Toolkit (MCT) to the Mesh-Oriented datABase (MOAB). The MOAB-based coupler explicitly represents mesh topology, enabling scalable parallel decomposition, efficient data movement, and in-situ generation of remapping operators. It also supports the use of precomputed mapping weights and maintains bit-for-bit reproducibility with MCT-based simulations, providing scientific continuity while enabling greater flexibility in coupling workflows. By avoiding global O(p) data structures and leveraging a modern C++ implementation, MOAB provides a new foundation for improved scalability and future GPU acceleration at extreme concurrency. Beyond infrastructure performance, the mesh-based formulation enables new numerical capabilities for E3SM coupling. These include high-order remapping operators with nonlinear monotonicity and property-preserving limiters, providing improved accuracy while maintaining physically meaningful bounds for transported quantities. New support for coupled ensemble simulation workflows has also been added, enabling verification of climatological statistics at scale. We present performance benchmarks of the MOAB coupler at high spatial resolution on leadership-class computing platforms, including scaling and memory characteristics, algorithmic details of the coupling and remapping infrastructure, and comparisons with the legacy MCT implementation. We further demonstrate applications of MOAB within the broader E3SM software ecosystem and assess the implications of these capabilities for high-resolution and ensemble-based climate simulations. These developments position E3SM for more scalable and efficient operation in ultra-high-resolution regimes, while providing a foundation for a new C++ driver that enables greater runtime configurability of coupled system components, including the integration of AI-based emulators.

497555.title: Scaling Electrostatic Fog Mitigation Through Field Deployment
497555.authors: Taylor Gresham, Rain Enhancement Technologies, Naples, FL; and S. Morris, J. Chagnon, and R. Dongre
497555.abstract: Radiation fog severely reduces visibility, posing major risks to transportation safety and creating operational difficulties across multiple industries. Building on established electrostatic mechanisms linking applied electric fields to enhanced droplet coalescence in radiation fog, this presentation shifts the focus from underlying microphysics to the practical deployment and evaluation of the Fog Removal by Electrical Activity (FREA) system as an operational fog-mitigation tool. FREA employs a trailer-mounted, high-voltage ionization array supporting a 14.5-foot antenna hand-wrapped in stainless steel fiber. The system generates localized electric fields at -75 to -90 kV, operating at currents up to 2 mA to accommodate the high moisture content characteristic of fog environments, enabling rapid field deployment with minimal infrastructure requirements. This presentation outlines the instrumentation strategy and evaluation framework for FREA field trials planned across multiple geographically distinct sites, designed to quantify real-world system efficacy under varying fog regimes. Comprehensive instrumentation deployed at paired treatment and control locations includes optical particle counters, forward-scattering visibility sensors, and meteorological stations, enabling direct comparison of treated and untreated fog evolution while controlling for background meteorological variability. Field campaigns are structured using a randomized complete block design stratified by fog density, ensuring balanced evaluation across dense, moderate, and light fog conditions. This approach allows detection of treatment effects that may vary systematically with initial fog microphysical state. By the time of presentation, this work is anticipated to provide field-based evidence evaluating operational performance across deployment sites, offering practical guidance on instrumentation strategy, field logistics, and evaluation methodology for electrostatic fog mitigation technologies. This presentation complements prior theoretical work by demonstrating how the underlying electrostatic mechanism translates into a scalable, environmentally responsible operational tool.

497556.title: Intercomparison of Vertical Motion Retrievals from a Diverse Set of Vertical Pointing Radar Measurements
497556.authors: Jonathan Charles Lewis, Texas A&M, College Station, TX; and C. J. Schumacher, C. R. Williams, S. Giangrande, K. McKeown, E. Luke, P. Kollias, P. N. Gatlin, B. Dolan, S. W. Freeman, D. B. Wolff, and S. C. Van Den Heever
497556.abstract: Updraft and downdraft characteristics dictate a storm’s evolution and impacts; however, vertical motion is difficult to measure and forecast. This presentation describes an intercomparison of three profiling radars at the S30 supplemental site of the DOE Bankhead National Forest in northern Alabama during summer and fall 2026 in their ability to retrieve in-cloud vertical motion. The intercomparison stems from the DOE Micro Rain Radar (MRR) Vertical Motion Intercomparison Project and is being run in tandem with the NASA INCUS mission TIME-SLICE Alabama (2026) and PIE-SLICE Alabama (2027) deployments. The three radars are 1) an MRR-PRO provided by NASA, which is a vertically-pointing 24-GHz (K-band) frequency-modulated continuous-wave Doppler radar with a 1.5 degree beamwidth, 2) a DOE ARM 915-MHz radar wind profiler (RWP) with a 9 degree beamwidth, and 3) the Rain, Ocean, Atmosphere Radar System (ROARS), an X-band phased-array radar developed by Agile Radar and operated by Stony Brook University with an adaptive scan pattern that includes frequent vertically pointing beams. Each radar is collecting reflectivity and Doppler velocity profiles at < 10 s time steps with similar vertical resolution. Our end goal is to provide the most accurate vertical motion distribution associated with deep convection that goes over the Bankhead site. Toward this goal, we will assess how aspects of the radars (like wavelength and beamwidth), processing (such as noise threshold determination for the raw spectra), and algorithm choice (in particular, the removal of hydrometeor fall speed) affect the vertical motion retrievals.

497557.title: New Capabilities in the NSF Unidata Science Gateway
497557.abstract: NSF Unidata is a diverse community of education and research institutions with the common goal of sharing Earth System Science data and the tools to access, analyze, and visualize those data. For over 40 years, the NSF Unidata Program Center has provided data, software tools, and support to advance Earth System science education and research. Funded primarily by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), NSF Unidata is one of the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR)'s Community Programs (UCP). The NSF Unidata Science Gateway is an online space where academic and research communities can collaborate, share resources, and learn in classroom, workshop, and virtual settings. It integrates NSF Unidata technologies with the NSF Jetstream2 cloud platform and open-source software, enabling users to access, analyze, and visualize real-time and case study Earth System Science data. Since 2020, the NSF Unidata Science Gateway has hosted pre-configured PyAOS (Python for Atmosphere and Ocean Science) JupyterHub servers supporting the learning experiences of over 2,600 students across 29 universities, regional workshops, and AMS workshops. These servers provide ready-to-use, cloud-based environments that eliminate the need for students to install and configure complex scientific software on their personal devices. By leveraging the NSF Jetstream2 cloud, these environments provide access to scientific tools and datasets through a web browser regardless of the user's hardware. This approach allows students and educators to focus on learning and analysis while supporting activities ranging from university courses, workshops, and short courses to graduate thesis work and Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) projects. This poster will provide an overview of the NSF Unidata Science Gateway and highlight new capabilities under development. An important objective of this work is to remove barriers between discovering a scientific notebook and actually running it. Users will be able to find community-developed and curated notebooks and launch them directly from a web browser in computational environments with the necessary software and dependencies already installed and configured. This approach will make scientific workflows easier to discover, share, reproduce, adapt, and use in the classroom. We will also present forthcoming data access and analysis capabilities within the Gateway. NSF Unidata is developing an object-store-based rolling archive of Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) data using Zarr and Icechunk to provide cloud-native access to high-volume radar products for research, education, and notebook-based analysis. In addition, we are exploring large language model (LLM)-assisted image analysis with the Unidata Integrated Data Viewer (IDV), with the goal of enabling users to interact with scientific visualizations using natural language and obtain information about the meteorological features and phenomena represented in those visualizations. These developments aim to reduce the barriers between discovering Earth System Science data and workflows and using them for education, exploration, and scientific analysis.

497558.title: It’s Not Just the Storm: Understanding Escalating Severe Convective Storm Losses
497558.authors: Walker S. Ashley, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL; and L. Bundy, S. M. Strader, and V. A. Gensini
497558.abstract: Severe convective storms (SCSs) have emerged as one of the most consequential sources of insured weather loss in the United States, with recent years characterized by increasingly frequent multibillion-dollar loss events. The causes of this trend, however, are often reduced to changes in the physical hazard itself, particularly those associated with climate change. While an evolving SCS hazard landscape is an important component of changing risk, economic losses ultimately arise from the intersection of the hazard with a much broader and dynamically changing set of societal and economic conditions. Here, we introduce an ingredients-based framework for understanding escalating SCS losses. Analogous to ingredients-based approaches used in weather forecasting (Doswell et al. 1996), the framework considers loss as the product of several interacting components: hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and economic and policy conditions. Changes in the frequency, intensity, location, or seasonality of SCS hazards can alter physical risk, but these changes occur simultaneously with population growth and migration, expansion of the built environment, increasing property values, changes in construction and housing characteristics, inflation in materials and labor, supply-chain constraints, insurance and regulatory practices, and other factors affecting the cost of damage and recovery. Importantly, these ingredients do not operate independently; their overlap can compound losses, while dependencies among them can generate cascading economic consequences extending well beyond the immediate storm footprint. We use the rapidly growing SCS loss burden as a case study to demonstrate why attribution of loss trends requires integration of atmospheric science, catastrophe modeling, economics, engineering, insurance, and social sciences. The framework provides a common conceptual language for separating—and ultimately quantifying—the contributions of physical hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and economic change. We conclude by identifying key observational, modeling, and interdisciplinary research needs required to better diagnose historical loss trends, anticipate future SCS risk, and translate weather and climate science into more effective decisions across the insurance, policy, and resilience communities. Doswell, C. A., III, H. E. Brooks, and R. A. Maddox, 1996: Flash flood forecasting: An ingredients-based methodology. Wea. Forecasting, 11, 560–581, https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0434(1996)011<0560:FFFAIB>2.0.CO;2.

497561.title: Using Direct Numerical Simulation to Study the Influence of Phase Relaxation Timescales on Droplet Evaporation during the WBF Process In Mixed-Phase Clouds.
497561.authors: Elise Marie Rosky, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and S. Chen
497561.abstract: The WBF process has been estimated to occur in 50% of Arctic mixed phase cloud volume, and is a process of great significance to ice growth and cloud glaciation in all mixed-phase clouds. Small-scale microphysical interactions translate into larger-scale impacts on cloud evolution, and are critical to the accuracy of climate and numerical weather models. Analytical parcel models typically assume that WBF-driven droplet evaporation is mediated by the mean vapor field, which impacts all droplets uniformly. Using a mixed-phase Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) simulation with Lagrangian particle-based mixed-phase microphysics, we explore the extent to which ice particles drive evaporation of neighboring droplets versus affecting all droplets equally through the mean field. By including both liquid and ice particles within the simulation, ice and liquid particles are able to interact through the Wegener-Bergeron (WBF) process in a turbulent environment. We analyze this problem by comparing timescales of vapor field homogenization through turbulent mixing with timescales of microphysical phase relaxation. We hypothesize that faster microphysical phase relaxation time and slower turbulent mixing time will allow ice to affect neighboring droplets more strongly than distant droplets, leading to enhanced broadening of the droplet size distribution towards smaller droplet sizes. By relating this process to measurable cloud properties like eddy dissipation rate, and droplet and ice number concentration, we can potentially use observational droplet size distributions from HOLODEC to verify these relationships in natural mixed-phase clouds.

497562.title: Arctic Solar Energy Potential from Synergistic Satellite Observations
497562.authors: Yu Xie, National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR), Golden, CO; and M. Sengupta, B. N. Benton, P. W. Stackhouse Jr., D. P. Duda, A. Habte, T. Williams, G. Maclaurin, J. Yang, and J. LEE
497562.abstract: Solar PV systems are increasingly deployed in extreme environments—including deserts, high-altitude terrains, and the Arctic—where meteorological conditions, surface characteristics, and cloud dynamics diverge substantially from conventional sites. The Arctic and sub-Arctic regions present formidable challenges for PV system deployment and energy yield, such as polar night, strong seasonal variability, extreme wind and snow loads, and the instability of permafrost foundations. However, high-latitude energy generation is bolstered by a synergy of extended polar daylight, high-albedo snow cover and favorable thermal conditions. Low ambient temperatures suppress thermally induced carrier recombination and increase open-circuit voltage. Sparse ground-based measurements and limitations of geostationary satellite observations under extreme solar zenith angles constrain solar resource assessment in the Arctic. Here we use synergistic polar-orbiting satellite measurements to produce a high-resolution, pan-Arctic assessment of solar radiation and photovoltaic (PV) potential. Solar radiation is computed over Arctic land areas and exclusive economic zones at 4-km resolution for 2002–2023. Using the Renewable Energy Potential (reV) model, we estimate long-term PV capacity factors for two representative system configurations: fixed-tilt monofacial PV and south-facing vertical bifacial PV. Our results reveal pronounced spatial and seasonal variability in Arctic solar energy potential, with Greenland emerging as a primary hotspot for solar energy resources. The substantial solar resource in Greenland is fundamentally driven by high levels of direct solar radiation associated with infrequent cloud cover and reduced cloud optical thickness. The optically thin clouds, in conjunction with the region’s strong snow albedo, increase diffuse radiation which can be effectively captured by vertical bifacial PV systems even during periods of low solar elevation.

497563.title: The CCPP Single Column Model: A Framework for Atmospheric Physics Development and Evaluation
497563.authors: Tracy J. Hertneky, NCAR, Boulder, CO
497563.abstract: The Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) contains a collection of physical atmospheric parameterizations along with a framework which connects the physics to a host model's dynamical core. It is designed to support physics development across the broader scientific research community and provides a pathway for testing and transitioning innovations from research to operations. A key component of the CCPP is its Single Column Model (SCM), which acts as a simplified host model enabling hierarchical testing and evaluation of physical parameterizations in isolation from dynamical feedback. The CCPP SCM supports a range of applications for physics development and evaluation. Observation-constrained cases from a variety of field campaigns provide opportunities to evaluate parameterizations over diverse weather regimes. It also offers the capability to generate SCM cases from regional and global Unified Forecast System (UFS) simulations, enabling targeted investigations of physics within realistic model environments. These capabilities make the SCM a valuable tool for implementation testing, sensitivity experiments, process-level diagnosis, and hierarchical evaluation prior to integration into full forecast systems. Additionally, tools to generate SCM cases from ERA5 and MPAS are planned for inclusion in the CCPP SCM within the year. The ability to isolate physical processes in a controlled environment can help identify sources of model bias and provide information for further development. Examples from recent applications will be shown to demonstrate how the CCPP SCM can support both targeted physical implementation testing and process-based diagnosis within a hierarchical modeling framework.

497565.title: From Virtual/Mixed Reality to Augmented Reality for Atmospheric Science Visualization
497565.authors: Guangyang Fang, Univ. of Maryland/ESSIC/CISESS, Greenbelt, MD; and A. R. Shakir, D. J. Figueroa, and S. D. Rudlosky
497565.abstract: Extended reality (XR), encompassing virtual reality (VR), mixed reality (MR), and augmented reality (AR), provides new ways to explore atmospheric processes and environmental observations that are difficult to represent using conventional two-dimensional displays. Our Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies (CISESS) XR portfolio (https://xr.cisess.umd.edu) initially focused on virtual and mixed reality applications addressing the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the water cycle, cloud and precipitation formation, lightning safety, and storm structure. Although these immersive applications provide engaging learning experiences, they require specialized headsets, which can limit access, distribution, and use in classrooms and public outreach. Our recent work expands the portfolio toward AR applications that can be accessed using a smartphone or tablet without a VR or MR headset. Current development includes AR visualizations of three-dimensional atmospheric circulation and Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) observations. Users can place, scale, rotate, and examine these visualizations within their physical surroundings, allowing complex spatial relationships among Earth, satellites, lightning observations, and atmospheric processes to be explored from different perspectives. This presentation will describe the transition of the CISESS XR portfolio form headset-based VR/MR experiences to more accessible smartphone-based AR applications. Demonstration will highlight the use of AR for visualizing satellite lightning observations and atmospheric circulation. By reducing dependence on specialized hardware, smartphone-based AR can make immersive atmospheric science visualization easier to access, demonstrate, distribute, and use in the research community, education, and public outreach.

497566.title: Recent Increase of Frequency of Visibility Restrictions Due to Air Pollution and Smoke
497566.authors: Daniel W. Lennartson, DTN, Bloomington, MN
497566.abstract: There has been a marked increase over the last several years from climate change that we have seen the frequency wildfire smoke and the expansion of persistent pollution in many areas around the globe. It has become so frequent that the inclusion of an accurate air quality forecast is vital in everyday life including air travel. It affects not only visibility but also the health of airport employees than work outside in occasionally toxic environments. On some occasions, wildfires erupt so quickly that nearby airports can be severely impacted in a short period of time often not forecasted well. In this presentation, I will show how we at DTN are addressing these challenges starting with a robust air quality forecast and working our way out to decision support forecasts affecting many industries including aviation. Shown will be examples of wildfire forecast challenges and how we've improved those forecasts as well as how persistent pollution due to industry and agriculture combined with geographic and local climate challenges.

497567.title: The Impacts of Machine Learning Denoising on Spaceborne Backscatter Lidar Retrievals of Clouds and Aerosols
497567.authors: John E. Yorks, NASA, Eldersburg, MD; and P. Selmer, N. Roldan-Henao, A. Cresanti, N. Midzak, and K. Christian
497567.abstract: Spaceborne lidar is essential for quantifying cloud and aerosol properties, but daytime measurements are hindered by solar background radiation, which causes significant random errors. This study evaluates a novel Deep Learning Dense Dense U-Net (DDUNet) denoising approach designed to mitigate these errors. Applied to simulated and real Cloud-Aerosol Transport System (CATS) data, DDUNet effectively suppresses daytime photon noise to levels approaching nighttime observations. The model increased the daytime signal-to-noise ratio by an average factor of 2.5 and reduced the minimum detectable backscatter to ~7.3e-4 km⁻¹sr⁻¹, outperforming CALIOP 1064 nm nighttime values. Using 2 km resolution denoised data, layer detection improved significantly, yielding more true positives and fewer false positives than standard 60 km averaged data. Attenuated total backscatter measurements showed substantial improvements, with correlation coefficients for ice clouds rising from 0.36 to 0.76 and relative RMSE dropping by 66–89% across various aerosol and cloud types. Higher-order retrievals also benefited: optical depth correlations for liquid water clouds increased from 0.86 to 0.91, and RMSE for optically thin dust layers fell by 89%. The DDUNet does introduce a small systematic bias following an exponential decay pattern, but its impact on optical depth retrievals appears to be minor. Ultimately, this approach enhances the scientific utility of daytime spaceborne backscatter lidar data.

497569.title: DataTreeDitto – A Data Abstraction Layer for Heterogeneous Data Processing in GeoIPS
497569.authors: Srikanth Gampa, CIRA, Fort Collins, CO; and G. Uttmark and J. E. Solbrig
497569.abstract: Keywords: GeoIPS, DataTree, nested workflows, interoperability, heterogeneous computation, data This poster introduces DataTreeDitto, an ongoing experimental feature within GeoIPS designed to support heterogeneous data computation across diverse user workflows. The development of DataTreeDitto is motivated by the GeoIPS community requirements for handling data stored in different container types, as well as by the ongoing GeoIPS major feature release centered on Xarray’s DataTree as the core data structure for supporting nested and complex workflows along with a feature goal of making the computation hardware-agnostic. DataTreeDitto extends Xarray’s DataTree to automatically convert a variety of input data types, such as NumPy arrays into Xarray Dataset objects while preserving the metadata required for round-trip conversion back to the original data representations. This capability is particularly important when GeoIPS is integrated as a modular component within existing user scripts or external workflows, where seamless interoperability between users data structures and GeoIPS processing components is essential. By providing a consistent abstraction layer for heterogeneous inputs, DataTreeDitto reduces the burden on users and developers who must otherwise manage data-format conversions manually. This approach improves workflow flexibility, promotes code reuse, and supports the integration of GeoIPS into broader processing environments without requiring substantial changes to existing infrastructure. In this poster, we describe the design goals, current implementation, and intended role of evolving DataTreeDitto within the GeoIPS 2.0. GeoIPS is an open-source, plugin-based framework for scientific discovery, near real-time (NRT) applications, and operational data processing. It comes with a variety of pre-built plugins for reading, manipulating, and writing data. Its plugin architecture allows scientists and developers to build their own plugins without editing the main GeoIPS code. These plugins can be used either by importing them in Python scripts/packages for scientific use or combined in configurable, human-readable workflows to create reproducible, infrastructure-as-code pipelines for NRT applications.

497570.title: Progress in Development of the Warn-on-Forecast System for Smoke (WoFS-Smoke) for Short-Term Fire Prediction
497570.authors: Patrick S. Skinner, CIWRO, Norman, OK; and T. A. Jones, V. Dunham, B. C. Matilla, J. Martin, S. King, M. Krocak, D. Hogg, J. T. Ripberger, E. F. Meister, A. C. Wanless, M. O. Mattox, K. Gupta, A. Fox, and P. C. Burke
497570.abstract: The Warn-on-Forecast System for Smoke (WoFS-Smoke) is a rapidly-cycled, ensemble data assimilation and short-term prediction system. Real-time, 18-member forecasts are generated out to six hours of lead time with a 5-minute output frequency. Customized, probabilistic fire weather products are included in real-time WoFS forecasts, including smoke concentration forecasts initialized using Next-Generation Fire System (NGFS) fire radiative power observations, near-surface visibility, and composite environmental indices such as the Red Flag Threat Index. This presentation will detail ongoing development to expand the capabilities of WoFS-Smoke. Specific projects include: 1) Development of an interactive WoFS data viewer that permits localized visualization of fire weather; 2) Expansion of fire weather guidance products in WoFS-Smoke based on feedback from Fire Weather Testbed participants; 3) Integration of fuel information with WoFS-Smoke atmospheric forecasts; and 4) Initial testing of one- and two-way coupling of WoFS-Smoke with fire spread models. Examples from each development thrust will be shown using retrospective forecasts from 2025 and 2026.

497571.title: Comparison between the GRIMM 11D and the EDM-180 during Dust and Non-Dust Days In the West Texas Region
497571.authors: Melodie F Martinez, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and K. Ardon-Dryer
497571.abstract: The West Texas region is prone to frequent dust events due to the semi-arid climate and strong winds. Dust events consist largely of particulate matter (PM) with diameters ≤10 μm. Reference monitors are highly accurate instruments for measuring air quality and PM for long periods. This analysis will be conducted using two instruments located at the Aerosol Research Observation Station (AEROS) at Texas Tech University: the GRIMM 11-D and the GRIMM/DURAG EDM-180. The GRIMM 11-D is a light-scattering instrument that measures particle number concentrations, size distributions, and mass concentrations (e.g., PM1, PM2.5, PM4, and PM10). The EDM-180 is an optical sensor instrument that measures PM concentrations of PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 as well as particle number concentrations using 31 bin sizes. In this study, both instruments will be compared over a period of ~6 months, focusing on PM concentration and size distribution for data on dust and non-dust days. These observations will further be compared with the National Weather Service (NWS) Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) meteorological conditions to identify dust events.

497572.title: Exploring Compound Events at the Mesoscale Using the Oklahoma Mesonet Archive
497572.authors: Frank Vazzano, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and C. A. Fiebrich
497572.abstract: The study of compound weather and climate events (CEs) and resultant impacts remains an active research frontier. Studies have found physically meaningful dependence structures across many systems and scales while establishing that CEs exhibit substantial geographic variability. In addition, CEs can result in impacts that exceed those associated with individual hazards, and CEs are changing under a nonstationary climate. The Southern Great Plains exhibits strong exposure to frequent high-impact weather events and reliance on climate-sensitive industries, yet dedicated regional CE studies here remain relatively limited compared to studies focused on continental and global scales. Moreover, CE studies predominantly emphasize a relatively limited set of hazards, leaving the potential contribution of additional land-surface variables less thoroughly evaluated. Lastly, most regional CE climatologies rely on predefined event criteria, while data-driven multivariate detection using dense station networks has seen comparatively limited assessments. These limitations motivate evaluating whether high-resolution in-situ environmental observations can reveal robust regional compound-event structures that conventional definitions incompletely represent. By leveraging 25 years of high-frequency in-situ observations from the Oklahoma Mesonet, a broad candidate-event and clustering workflow identifies physically coherent compound-event families in Oklahoma. In our study, we implementsensitivity tests to ascertain robustness, and then validate the spatial distributions, seasonal occurrences, durations, and constituent-variable characteristics to demonstrate that some events align with the baseline while other events reveal overlooked moderate, persistent, or preconditioned events. Additionally, both the conventional threshold-first and data-driven result families, confirmed to be robust, are interpreted to procure information about spatial and seasonal patterns of CEs in Oklahoma. The results of this study both advance the general understanding of CEs and expands our understanding of how different identification methods compare at regional scales and the role land-surface variables play in CEs.

497575.title: TroutCast: A Drought Early Warning System for Cold-Water Fisheries Management and Conservation
497575.authors: Timothy Joseph Cline, Montana State University, Bozeman, MT; and C. Muhlfeld, G. Pederson, J. Martin, and A. Lahr
497575.abstract: Drought poses an increasing challenge for cold-water fisheries in the western United States by reducing streamflow, increasing water temperatures, and affecting underlying fish population dynamics. TroutCast is a drought early warning and forecasting system designed to translate these environmental changes into information useful for fisheries management and conservation. The project integrates long-term trout population monitoring with streamflow, weather, and stream-temperature data to forecast both near-term conditions and longer-term biological responses. Near-term forecasts identify periods of low flow and high temperature that may trigger management actions, while population models link seasonal hydrologic conditions to trout recruitment and forecast population status and trends. Developed through a partnership among Montana State University, the U.S. Geological Survey, Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, and other collaborators with support from NIDIS, TroutCast provides an example of how ecological monitoring and environmental forecasting can be combined to anticipate drought impacts on climate-sensitive fisheries and support more proactive management.

497577.title: Mapping the Urban Forest Without Hand Labeling: Deep Learning Label-Efficient, Ecologically Guided Tree-Crown Delineation for Urban Climate Modeling
497577.authors: Dhanuj Mount Gandikota, The University of Texas - Austin, Austin, TX; and D. Niyogi and T. Keitt
497577.abstract: Urban climate research, adaptation strategies, microclimate models and urban digital twins require high-resolution vegetation structure at the city scale to resolve heat, shade, and evapotranspiration. The individual tree crown is a primary observational unit for detailed urban canopy analysis. Deep-learning foundation models such as DeepForest and Segment Anything can delineate individual crowns from recurring municipal aerial RGB, extracting a city-scale canopy dataset that would traditionally demand extensive expert digitizing, but they do not transfer directly across sensors and seasons: differences in resolution, viewing geometry, radiometry, and canopy phenology degrade accuracy, and the conventional remedy, hand-labeling local data for expert fine-tuning, is too costly to sustain for routine monitoring. We test whether the automated transformation of nearby National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) airborne imagery can replace local hand labeling for a target city. Our source is NEON Airborne Observation Platform RGB from a nearby Dallas site at 10 cm, collected on-leaf in 2020, reconciled with Austin's 15 cm, off-leaf 2021 mosaic across resolution, radiometry, geometry, and a leaf-on to leaf-off shift, and matched despite ecoregion differences such as the conifer-poor source. We present a novel transformation-and-fine-tuning framework that makes the NEON imagery resemble the city mosaic through physics-guided sensor matching, a deep learning generative adversarial matching step, and ecologically informed priors on crown size, spacing, and morphology drawn from the region's genus-level community composition. Using AI foundation models; DeepForest and a Segment Anything Model 3 workflows, we evaluate a nested sequence from direct transfer to full local supervision, scored against 200 held-out hand-labeled images by F1 at 0.50 intersection-over-union across canopy density and crown-size gradients, with residual errors concentrated in cast shadow, dense off-leaf canopy, and urban-infrastructure overlap. The best proxy-trained workflow reaches 87.6 F1@0.50 using approximately 91% reduction in local labeling needed. At city scale, the resulting per-tree canopy cover, spacing, and genus composition supply inputs for microclimate simulation and urban digital twins and support urban-canopy parameterization and canopy change detection. This provides a label-efficient, AI-driven route to high-resolution vegetation data previously impractical to produce, extending urban climate analysis and municipal decision-support.

497578.title: Can the Gap be “Closed” for Extreme Weather Prediction and Tree Crops?
497578.authors: Richard D. Grotjahn, UCDavis, Davis, CA
497578.abstract: In terms of usability and real-world applicability, agricultural crops have a wide range of constraints. These include numerous structural barriers. In some ways the barriers to benefits from improved environmental information are greater for tree crops than for row crops due to the long frame of production. The more challenging constraints of orchard crops will be the focus of this talk. The presentation will begin with a summary of information gleaned by the author from a meta-study of what extreme weather impacts crops in 13 major commodity groupings (Grotjahn, 2021) such as impactful thresholds common to many crop commodities in: temperature, moisture, and their combination. After a brief review of what extreme weather has impacted three major commodities (wheat, maize, soybean) in the USA, the primary focus will shift to three tree crops commodity groups (citrus, deciduous tree fruits, and deciduous tree nuts) with illustrative examples from each. Tree crops are particularly informative since they amplify constraints and barriers that impact many crops. The author has an uncommon perspective based on his decades as a climate dynamicist and decades as a pistachio grower. Orchards take years to establish before reaching useful production. So, some agriculturally-relevant seasonal or shorter forecasts are useful, some are not. There are techniques to mitigate some extreme weather, like freeze protection. But, what good is forecasting a heat wave at bloom time a month or season in advance? The trees have been in the ground for years before producing useful production and they cannot be “rotated” to adapt to an event. Climate projections are relevant given the long-term investment in a tree crop. But it is unclear whether climate models capture adequately what is most relevant like timing and duration of the extreme weather. For example, daily maximum temperature has a different trend from daily average temperature (Grotjahn and Huynh, 2018). Deciduous tree crops have very different sensitivity at different growth stages. This presentation will draw illustrative examples from: Florida and Texas Citrus (1980's), Michigan stone and pome fruits (2012), and a current crisis Pistachios (2026). Structural issues like: infrastructure constraints (specialized: harvest equipment and labor, processing equipment, market reorientation) and resources (funds, water for irrigation), will be outlined, some responses discussed. References Cited: Grotjahn, R. (2021). Weather extremes that affect various agricultural commodities. In Extreme events and climate change (pp. 21–48). Wiley. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119413738.ch3 Grotjahn, R., & Huynh, J. (2018). Contiguous US summer maximum temperature and heat stress trends in CRU and NOAA Climate Division data plus comparisons to reanalyses. (Nature) Scientific Reports, 8, 11146(1–18). DOI: 10.1038/s41598–018–29286-w

497582.title: Forecast Uncertainty in the June 2022 Yellowstone Rain-on-Snow Flood: Multiscale Interactions Between Atmospheric Moisture Transport, Snowmelt, and Runoff Response
497582.authors: SUMA BHANU BATTULA, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and J. Frame and E. White
497582.abstract: The June 2022 Yellowstone flood resulted from an atmospheric river that reached unusually far inland, combined with severe convection and rapid snowmelt — an atypical pairing for the region this late in the season (Keeney, 2024). This synoptic pattern is broadly consistent with Regime 1 of Battula et al. (2025), a cool-season regime marked by northwesterly integrated vapor transport (IVT) and inland-penetrating West Coast atmospheric rivers, facilitated by an upstream trough over the Intermountain West. Its occurrence in June suggests an unusual seasonal displacement of this circulation pattern. The resulting rain-on-snow runoff set streamflow records at the Corwin Springs gage on the Yellowstone River and on the Gardner River, though flood magnitude varied across nearby watersheds depending on antecedent conditions. We examine forecast uncertainty across this event's synoptic-to-hydrologic chain, from moisture transport and orographic precipitation to snowmelt and basin-scale runoff, using a spatially distributed hydrologic model producing joint soil moisture, SWE, and streamflow estimates — to characterize antecedent basin state and its role in the differing flood responses. References: Battula, S. B., Cordeira, J. M., Nash, D., Rutz, J. J., & Ralph, F. M. (2025). Leveraging the atmospheric river framework to categorize top-decile precipitation regimes in Colorado. Geophysical Research Letters, 52, e2025GL117528. https://doi.org/10.1029/2025GL117528 Keeney, D. P. (2024). How and why multiple events led to the Yellowstone flood of June 2022. American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting, Washington, D.C.

497583.title: Bridging the Gap: A New Paradigm for Communicating Atmospheric River Impacts to Decision-Makers through Research and Operations
497583.authors: Dave F. Jones, StormCenter Communications, Inc., Annapolis, MD
497583.abstract: Abstract: Effective decision-making during high-impact weather events requires the rapid translation of complex scientific data into actionable information and narratives. While Atmospheric River (AR) science has advanced significantly, a gap remains in communicating the nuances of event intensity, antecedent ground conditions, and observational value to emergency managers, water operators, and the media. This presentation details a research-and-operations (R&O) partnership between the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) and StormCenter Communications designed to bridge this gap through innovative geospatial visualization and multi-sector engagement. The initiative focuses on three core themes: AR Scale literacy, the modulation of impacts by antecedent conditions (framing “benefits vs. hazards”), and highlighting the value of AR Recon data. We will demonstrate the use of the GeoCollaborate® platform to provide a collaborative common operating picture (C-COP) and to test and showcase research products with user communities. A centerpiece of this effort is the real-time integration of AR Recon flight tracks and dropsonde data—analogous to "hurricane hunter" tracking—to enhance situational awareness for operational users. By activating established distribution channels like the All-Hazards Consortium (SISE) and the CAT5 MetNetwork, this partnership ensures that trusted AR science is not only shareable but used effectively to help protect infrastructure, manage water resources across the western United States and to inform emergency management professionals in the public and private sectors. The presentation will also describe the importance of placing more NOAA data into operational decision-making environments through our partnership with NOAA’s LEO Program to engage more than 45,000 stakeholders and decision makers in the public and private sectors.

497584.title: Observing System Simulation Experiments for Uncrewed Aircraft Systems: The Relative Impact of Quasi-Horizontal Profiles Versus Vertical Profiles
497584.authors: Adam L. Houston, Univ. of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and S. Murdzek, K. A. Swan, T. T. Ladwig, and E. P. James
497584.abstract: Recent observing system simulation experiments (OSSE) research by our team (Murdzek et al. 2025) clearly showed the significant theoretical impact that assimilating observations from weather-observing uncrewed aircraft systems (WxUAS) executing 2 km deep vertical profiles can have on short-term (0-6 hr) convection-allowing model (CAM) accuracy. Vertical profiling is the most common, and practically straightforward, operational mode of WxUAS, but it is not the only modality. In the results presented here, the impact on CAM accuracy of WxUAS flying quasi-horizontal profiles (at a fixed height above ground level) is evaluated relative to the impact from vertical profiling WxUAS. Experiments underway rely on a 1 km WRF nature run covering 2 week-long periods and the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) CAM forecast model run on a CONUS domain with 3 km grid point spacing. Forecasts initialized with synthetic observations from conventional platforms only (no WxUAS) serve as the control. Experiments include synthetic WxUAS operating at 500 m, 1500 m, or 3000 m AGL over set quasi-horizontal paths mapped to maximize coverage and minimize overlap. Experiments also test the sensitivity of error reduction to WxUAS density through flights operated at spacings from 35 km to 300 km. The impact that meteorological limitations on UAS operation through high winds and icing have on forecast errors is also evaluated. Comparisons are made to complementary vertical profile experiments to assess the relative impacts from differences in operation mode. In experiments examined to date, 2-km vertical profiles reduce RMSE more than quasi-horizontal profiles and quasi-horizontal flights at 1500 m reduce RMSE more than flights at 500 m. Moreover, errors in surface-based convective parameters (e.g., SBCAPE and SBCIN) are reduced more by vertical profiles. However, errors in mixed-layer convective parameters are reduced more by quasi-horizontal profiles than by vertical profiles. Errors in 0-3 km and 0-1 km storm relative helicity are reduced more by vertical profiles for forecast hours 0-3 but more by horizontal profiles for forecast hours 6-12. Modernization of the weather observing network with WxUAS should be guided by evidence on the relative impact of different operating modes on weather forecast accuracy. After all, the technical and regulatory challenges differ significantly between vertical profiling WxUAS and WxUAS executing long horizontal profiles. Moving towards a modernized weather observing network requires solutions to the technical and regulatory challenges specific to the operational mode that offers the largest impact on forecasting. Murdzek, S.S., T.L. Ladwig, A.L. Houston, and E.P. James, 2025: The Impacts of Assimilating Various Densities of Uncrewed Aircraft System Observations on Regional NWP Forecasts in an OSSE. Monthly Weather Review. In Review.

497586.title: Toward a Testbed for The Lidar Radar Open Software Environment (LROSE)
497586.authors: Brenda Javornik, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. del Moral Méndez, Ph.D, T. Y. Cha, J. C. DeHart, M. J. Dixon, and W. C. Lee
497586.abstract: The Lidar Radar Open Software Environment (LROSE) is moving forward with LROSE applications interoperable with the Open Radar Science community. Interoperability remains essential, both in terms of shared data and a common interface for functions. The LROSE tools are available for realtime and archival data analysis. Archival data analysis is also accessible as a web-based science gateway using JupyterHub along with a curated catalog of training workflows. A testbed would add benchmark data sets for comparison among the open source software packages. Equally important are the needs for distributed computing, and new data formats and highlights the need for the LROSE applications as independent functions as a service (FaaS). Altogether, a testbed would provide next generation data access, data exploration with data discovery tools for research, innovation, and collaboration among university and government partners.

497587.title: Howard University Beltsville Campus Participation during the Coordinated University Sounding Program for Atmospheric River Reconnaissance (CUSP-ARR)
497587.authors: Adrian Flores, Howard University, Hyattsville, MD; and R. K. Sakai, B. Demoz, R. D. Rossi, and S. Chiao
497587.abstract: Howard University Beltsville Campus (HUBC) has been an active participant in the Coordinated University Sounding Program for Atmospheric River Reconnaissance (CUSP-ARR) for the two campaigns of the program. Led by the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) at Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego, CUSP-ARR has a total of 16 universities in the U.S. and Canada launching weather balloons to study atmospheric rivers and other high-impact weather events. Located between Washington, DC, and Baltimore, MD, in the I-95 corridor, HUBC is ideal to conduct this study and analyze the behavior of the Atmospheric Rivers (AR) over the mid-Atlantic region during the wintertime. A total of 51 radiosondes, 16 in 2025 and 35 in 2026, were launched from HUBC. This study will also show the behavior of the Planetary Boundary Layer (PBL), especially during precipitation events.

497588.title: High-Resolution Regional Earth System Modeling: Development and Workflow of the RM1.3 Dataset
497588.authors: Pramod Adhikari, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY; and B. Geerts and S. Rahimi
497588.abstract: Kilometer-scale atmospheric modeling offers opportunities to better resolve convection, terrain-driven circulations, and high-impact weather, but multi-decadal simulations at these resolutions pose substantial computational, workflow, and data management challenges. We present RM1.3, a very high-resolution 1.33-km Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model dataset over the central and southern Rocky Mountains, and the high-performance computing (HPC) framework developed to generate and process it. RM1.3 consists of a 35-year historical reconstruction (1990–2024), dynamically downscaled from CONUS404 (4-km), and a companion 35-year pseudo-global warming simulation. The simulations were performed on the NCAR-Wyoming Supercomputing Center’s Derecho system using a domain of 782 x 1022 grid points and 51 vertical levels. Sustaining continuous simulations required automated workflows for model initialization, restart management, job submission, monitoring, output verification, and recovery from failed runs. We also developed an algorithm to derive two- and three-dimensional meteorological fields directly from post-processed CONUS404 data and convert them into binary meteorological input files for WRF preprocessing without using inbuilt ungrib. Model output ranges include 5-minute surface fields (temperature, precipitation, humidity and winds), hourly 2D variables, and 3-hourly three-dimensional atmospheric fields, creating additional challenges for storage, data movement, and scalable post-processing. Evaluation against surface observations and upper-air soundings demonstrates improved representation of several terrain-sensitive processes relative to the 4-km parent dataset, while sensitivity experiments highlight numerical and land-surface modeling challenges that emerge at kilometer-scale resolution. The resulting HPC workflow and petabyte-scale dataset support applications ranging from extreme-weather characterization and WRF-Hydro simulations to training machine-learning models for high-impact weather. RM1.3 demonstrates how scalable HPC workflows can enable sustained kilometer-scale regional modeling and provide a foundation for future high-resolution numerical weather prediction and ensemble modeling systems.

497589.title: From Convective System Tracking to Nowcasting: Predicting Convective System Evolution with Pix4DCloud
497589.authors: Gregory S. Elsaesser, Columbia University / NASA GISS, New York, NY; and J. Wu, J. A. Caraballo-Vega, and J. Gong
497589.abstract: Geostationary satellite sensors provide unparalleled temporal coverage for observing the evolution of high-impact convective systems, and a growing number of object-based tracking algorithms are enabling systematic characterization of these systems and their associated extreme precipitation. These efforts have largely focused on identifying and tracking convective systems that have already occurred, providing important insights into the spectrum of convective events, their life cycles, and their dependence on the surrounding environment. Here, we introduce the Pix4DCloud suite of physics-constrained transformer models and a downstream application, A3DVOCADO (A 3D Vertical Object-oriented deep Convective systems And their DevelOpment stages model), designed to identify deep convective systems and predict their development stages and life spans from geostationary data. We demonstrate how information and methodologies developed through retrospective convective-system tracking can be leveraged to characterize ongoing convection and predict its subsequent evolution. This framework provides a bridge between satellite-based convective-system tracking and efforts to improve nowcasting of high-impact convective events.

497591.title: Evaluating Two-Wavelength Scintillometry for Open-Water Evaporation Using a Controlled Evaporation Pond.
497591.authors: Alexei O. Perelet, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT; and J. Gage, M. Shea, and E. R. Pardyjak
497591.abstract: Quantifying evaporation from open-water surfaces remains a major challenge in closing hydrologic budgets, particularly for terminal lakes where evaporation represents the dominant outflow. Common approaches, including eddy covariance, evaporation pans, and bulk aerodynamic methods (e.g. Penman-Monteith), provide spatially localized estimates and can be difficult to deploy or interpret over large water bodies. Path-integrated measurements from scintillometers offer an alternative by directly sampling turbulent fluxes over spatial scales of hundreds of meters to kilometers.
