Previous applications of scintillometry over open water, however, have largely been conducted over natural water bodies, where uncertain water budgets, heterogeneous shorelines, and complex atmospheric conditions complicate evaluation of the measurements. Here, we evaluate open-water evaporation measurements from a two-wavelength scintillometer system deployed across an artificial evaporation pond near Delta, Utah. The system, consisting of a Scintec BLS900 large-aperture scintillometer and Radiometer Physics MWSC-160 microwave scintillometer, has operated since September 2025 along an approximately 1-km path over a pond with well-constrained geometry and water volume. A shoreline eddy-covariance station provides an independent reference for evaluating scintillometer-derived turbulent fluxes. We examine the ability of the scintillometer to retrieve path-integrated sensible and latent heat fluxes under varying atmospheric conditions and wind directions. Footprint analysis demonstrates that the measurement path can remain dominated by the water surface across a broad range of wind directions, allowing the system to sample evaporation under conditions not consistently captured by the shoreline eddy-covariance station. This is particularly important at night, when diurnal wind transitions can shift the eddy-covariance footprint away from the pond while the scintillometer remains sensitive to the water surface. This nighttime evaporation is particularly important to quantify in arid climates. Since scintillometery relies on Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory (MOST) we evaluate the applicability of MOST for deriving turbulent fluxes over the pond and assess how spatial averaging along the scintillometer path influences flux retrievals.

497598.title: Designing a Curriculum for the ESS Community: Interactive ML Technical Literacy Series
497598.abstract: As AI and machine learning (ML) reshape Earth system science (ESS), from fundamental research to AI-driven weather models and climate emulators, the community's ability to utilize these tools has not kept pace. A global survey of hundreds of ESS professionals and students found a workforce at an inflection point: 52% report limited or no ML experience, yet 87% view ML skills as valuable or critical to their jobs. The dominant barrier to entry was neither infrastructure nor software complexity—it was a technical expertise gap in the workforce, which respondents said was best addressed through self-paced, interactive training built around practical workflows and real ESS data, not formal instruction or theoretical frameworks. This presentation introduces the Machine Learning Technical Literacy in ESS MetEd curriculum, developed by The COMET® Program in partnership with NSF NCAR and university collaborators. The series addresses survey-identified needs through interactive, asynchronous micro-lessons. These lessons cover essential topics—data preparation and core ML methods—through hands-on work with authentic ESS scenarios such as El Niño classification and atmospheric river detection. Rather than explaining concepts abstractly, each lesson runs live, in-browser interactions where learners manipulate real models and real data, directly experiencing failure modes and finding ways to overcome them. Together, these survey findings and early lesson outcomes offer a model for other education teams looking to ground curriculum design in documented community needs rather than assumption—connecting assessment directly to what gets built.

497599.title: Engaging Emerging Professionals In Climate Resilience Learning
497599.authors: Kathryn J. Boyd, University of Washington Climate Impacts Group, Seattle, WA; and R. Sugla and B. Bronstein
497599.abstract: In the Pacific Northwest (PNW) there is a significant amount of climate adaptation work happening, especially in coastal communities. Communities are leading efforts to respond to the impacts of climate change in equitable ways. People engaging in this work sometimes come from scientific or policy backgrounds and may not be well trained in community engagement and collaborative methods. To help address this disconnect, we have developed a learning institute called the Climate Equity and ReSilience Institute (CERSI). CERSI is an immersive learning program created for emerging professionals in the Pacific Northwest (current late-stage graduate students, recent graduates, early-career professionals or alternate career flow professionals), working in any discipline who are interested in experiencing in-depth, place-based learning about multiple dimensions of climate and resilience and how climate and environmental work intersect with different cultures and societies. In this program, participants gain (1) a better understanding of how climate and environmental resilience intersect with social systems at multiple scales and in various contexts; (2) knowledge of the theories, tools, and practices to mediate relationships between climate and environmental work and communities; and (3) a community and professional network of coastal & climate practitioners who are committed to community-based relationships within their research and other climate work. The program hosts a variety of guest speakers from different professional, academic, and lived-experience backgrounds in an intensive week-long program with several activities per day and field trips throughout the week. The program mixes learning modalities that range from group discussions, activities, mixed media, panels, lectures, and field trips. The field trips help ground the learning in place-based learning experiences, while the guest speakers provide locally relevant information and examples. Topics explored include climate impacts, climate adaptation & resilience, Indigenous & environmental ethics, climate & health, economics and degrowth, policy & communication, knowledge systems, co-production of knowledge and more. Evaluation of the first implementation of the program showed participants appreciated learning in place and from relevant sources. They showed change in their understanding of the topics, and discussed how powerfully they were impacted by the experience. They described the benefit of meeting others who are established in the field such as the guest speakers, and building a community of those who are starting work in the field. This prompted a social network analysis study, which is being implemented in the Fall 2026 program. We hope to gain a sense of the connections among early career practitioners and follow how these connections grow over time. We will present the preliminary findings of this analysis. In this presentation, we plan to describe the program and outcomes from the evaluation, and explore the early results from the social network analysis research. We hope to spark conversations about how to balance aspects of place-based learning, and how to incorporate climate and interdisciplinary learning into programs for early career professionals.

497600.title: The Community Fire Behavior Model Coupled with WRF-v4.8.0
497600.authors: Maria E. Frediani, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and P. A. Jimenez, M. Eghdami, M. J. Kavulich Jr., and D. Rosen
497600.abstract: This presentation evaluates the Community Fire Behavior Model (CFBM) coupled with WRF-v4.8.0. The CFBM was originally developed in line with WRF-Fire methods, aiming to establish a foundational capability of comparable forecast skill. It can integrate advanced components, such as python modules and machine learning surrogates, and will evolve to couple to the next generation of numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. In this presentation we highlight the CFBM new features, including urban fire spread and firebrand spotting components, and the path towards a physics-based model to simulate fast-spreading fires responsible for disproportionate structure damage. Simulations of the Eaton Fire demonstrate the CFBM application for scenario-based assessment of extreme fire behavior, and its support of applications ranging from process-focused research to risk assessment for insurance analytics. Evaluations rely on mapped perimeters and baseline comparison against WRF-Fire. Experiments evaluate coupled versus standalone forecasts at different grid spacings to illustrate the cost benefit of computationally expensive research-focused simulations versus operational runs.

497601.title: Marine Heatwaves and Their Impacts on Ocean Carbon Sequestration Across the California Current System
497601.authors: Christina W Tsai, National Taiwan University, Taipei, Taiwan
497601.abstract: Anthropogenic carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions have increased atmospheric CO2 concentrations and contributed to global warming since the Industrial Revolution. The ocean absorbs approximately 25% of anthropogenic CO2 emissions each year, thus making it an important component of the global carbon cycle. Increasing marine heatwave (MHW) activity, however, may affect ocean carbon sequestration through shifts in physical, biological, and biogeochemical processes. These responses occur over different timescales and may include delayed effects that are difficult to identify using conventional time-series analyses. This study examines the relationships among MHWs, potential climate and anthropogenic drivers, and ocean carbon sequestration in the California Current System. The California Exclusive Economic Zone was divided into northern, central, and southern regions to characterize regional differences. Adaptive signal decomposition was combined with correlation and lag analyses to separate variability across intrinsic timescales and quantify scale-dependent and delayed relationships. Carbon sequestration was evaluated using sea-air CO2 flux, kelp canopy area, and total alkalinity, representing different components of the ocean carbon system. MHW characteristics and their associated drivers varied substantially across the three regions. Southern California experienced the greatest MHW intensity, spatial coverage, and frequency, whereas MHW variability in Northern California was more strongly associated with the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). The association between anthropogenic CO2 emissions and MHW intensity was strongest in Southern California and exhibited a statistical lag of approximately six months. Carbon-related variables also showed notable temporal responses to MHWs. Sea-air CO2 flux responded with little to no lag, while kelp canopy area exhibited its strongest negative relationship with MHWs at a lag of approximately six months. Total alkalinity showed weaker relationships with MHWs, with the magnitude and timing of the response varying among regions. The results show that relationships between MHWs and ocean carbon sequestration are both region- and timescale-dependent. Separating the underlying temporal modes and accounting for lagged responses reveals relationships that may be obscured in analyses of the original time series. These findings provide insight into the way different components of the coastal carbon cycle respond to marine heatwaves and highlight the importance of considering multiple timescales when assessing carbon-cycle responses to a warming ocean.

497603.title: FireSat On-Orbit Observations and Integration with the NOAA Wildfire Pilot
497603.authors: Tim Dittmann, Muon Space, Lyons, CO; and L. Abramson, K. story, A. DeCastro, D. D'Orlando, and A. Snow
497603.abstract: The FireSat mission, led by the Earth Fire Alliance and designed and operated by Muon Space, is a purpose-built satellite constellation designed to provide first responders, incident commanders, fire modelers and scientists with next-generation wildfire awareness from Low Earth Orbit. Following the 2025 successful prototype FireSat launch, the first three operational FireSat satellites deployed in July 2026. We present on-orbit observations from the FireSat protoflight satellite including calibrated, orthorectified multispectral tiles and active hotspot detections. We also present ongoing calibration and validation activities across the mission for supporting on-orbit calibration and processing pipelines to ensure data products meet the performance standards required by the wildland fire and research communities. These protoflight observations support Muon’s participation in NOAA’s Commercial Data Program (CDP) Wildfire Imagery Pilot, conducted in collaboration with the NOAA Wildland Fire Team. The pilot evaluates commercial multispectral infrared imagery integration into government wildfire detection, characterization, and monitoring workflows. We present the pilot's objectives and early observations, illustrating how purpose-built commercial space assets are positioned to complement existing government constellations and support enhanced wildland fire situational awareness.

497604.title: Tropical Convective Organization as Revealed by an MPAS-JEDI Mesoscale Reanalysis of the PRECIP2022 Field Campaign
497604.authors: Rosimar Rios-Berrios, NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Boulder, CO; and R. Kong, Z. Liu, T. Y. Cha, and A. Jaye
497604.abstract: Tropical convection is frequently organized into squall lines and mesoscale convective systems, which are crucial to the global water cycle. However, the specific mechanisms that organize these systems—specifically the interplay between vertical wind shear, water vapor, and cloud-radiative feedbacks—remain debated. This uncertainty limits our ability to project future changes in tropical rainfall. This study explores these mechanisms using data from the 2022 PRECIP/TAHOPE/T-PARC II field campaign, focusing on a long-lived convective line observed near Yonaguni Island on July 29, 2022 (IOP 9). By integrating field observations with MPAS-A numerical simulations using MPAS-JEDI, we investigate the kinematic, thermodynamic, and microphysical evolution of the system. Utilizing analysis tools from the NCAR INFORM initiative, we isolate the factors that allowed this line to persist for over 12 hours. This presentation will discuss the processes essential for maintaining organization in this case study, highlighting the role of dynamics in enabling organization in a moisture-rich scenario.

497605.title: Surface-Based Temperature Inversion Buildup and Persistence in Interior Alaska Winters: Thermodynamic and Radiative Controls from Multi-Year Observations and Modeling
497605.authors: Dishi Pandisalackal Thomas, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and S. Ramakrishnan, D. Keller, G. J. Fochesatto, J. Dudhia, and D. Atkinson
497605.abstract: Surface-based temperature inversion layers (SBIs) are a dominant meteorological feature of Alaskan winters. They develop under persistent anticyclonic conditions that drive strong surface radiative cooling and promote stable stratification of the near-surface airmass. Prolonged polar darkness, extremely cold temperatures, stagnant flow, and high snow-surface albedo further favor SBIs buildup and persistence. These shallow, stably stratified layers strongly suppress turbulent mixing and pollutant dispersion, effectively isolating local emissions from the free troposphere and contributing to severe wintertime air quality episodes. This study examines the buildup phases, stratification strength, and temporal persistence of SBIs, with emphasis on understanding the parameters controlling thermodynamic and radiative processes. Observations were collected at the University of Alaska Fairbanks Farm, a uniformly snow-covered agricultural site on the foothills of the White Mountains, during the winters of 2022–2026. The dataset encompasses the ALPACA 2022 international field campaign and subsequent intensive observation periods in 2024–2026. Surface energy-balance and turbulence measurements were obtained from an eddy-covariance tower; the vertical thermodynamic structure was retrieved from a microwave radiometer and radiosondes. After February 2024, selected episodes were further resolved below 160 m using an instrumented unmanned aircraft system. Large-scale synoptic context was provided by ERA5 reanalysis, while the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model was used to reproduce both surface-based and elevated inversion layers. Analysis of the combined observational and modeling datasets reveals a consistent thermodynamic sequence during SBI formation. An initial period of columnar cooling establishes a shallow near-surface inversion (~50–70 m deep). This is followed by intensified surface radiative cooling that rapidly increases stratification within the shallow layer until a local radiative equilibrium is approached. Thereafter, residual surface net radiative loss drives continued heat transfer into the snowpack; the resulting cooling propagates upward through the already-stratified airmass, causing the inversion top to deepen until a new radiative–thermodynamic equilibrium is reached.

497608.title: Global Precipitation and Hail Retrievals from the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder Constellation
497608.authors: Forest Cannon, Tomorrow.io, Rancho Santa Fe, CA; and M. Pope, R. Chase, M. E. Green, A. Evans, B. Taylor, S. J. Munchak, M. Huguet, and A. Chawla
497608.abstract: Improved global observations are essential for monitoring precipitation and severe weather in regions where ground-based radar coverage is limited or unavailable. Tomorrow.io operates a growing constellation of low-Earth-orbit microwave sounders that provides global hourly-revisit observations sensitive to precipitation and cloud ice. Building on experience with earlier operational retrieval systems, we developed the fourth generation of Tomorrow.io’s global Unified Precipitation product, a new machine-learning framework designed around the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) constellation with 0.02° spatial and 10-minute temporal resolution. The fourth-generation Unified Precipitation product combines TMS microwave observations with geostationary satellite imagery and environmental information using a set of input channels that explicitly represents overpass time and latency. The system is trained using satellite- and radar-based precipitation targets, with global pre-training against the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission followed by fine-tuning against high-resolution Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor (MRMS) observations. This design allows the retrieval to flexibly use the observations that are available at a given location and time, providing a robust “retrieval of opportunity” for real-time global applications. Validation demonstrates that the new retrieval resolves storm structure and intensity and that recent TMS observations provide additional skill beyond geostationary imagery alone. The improvement is especially pronounced for heavy precipitation, with skill gains of up to approximately 50% for precipitation rates exceeding 25 mm h⁻¹. Long-term evaluation against surface gauge networks further shows consistent skill across multiple continents and satellite domains. The same observation and modeling framework can also be extended to severe-weather applications. Initial hail retrievals using globally available satellite, microwave, and environmental inputs reproduce radar-observed hail structures and show promising skill outside the primary training domain. These results demonstrate how the fourth-generation Unified Precipitation framework can support both global precipitation estimation and scalable hail detection in regions without conventional radar coverage.

497610.title: Evaluation of Compound Heat Wave Events in Dynamically Downscaled Convection-Permitting Simulations
497610.authors: Corrine Nicole DeCham, ANL, Lemont, IL; and J. Branham
497610.abstract: Heat waves have driven unprecedented temperature records worldwide in recent years, with intensity and duration expected to continue upward trends. These prolonged, extreme temperatures are a major driver of peak energy demand and a potential source of risk, prompting community and stakeholder demand for output from high-resolution modeling efforts. Specifically, there is a growing desire to understand highly impactful atmospheric conditions to inform hazard mitigation planning, which is critical for approaching resilience and infrastructure decisions. In this presentation, we investigate daytime, nighttime, and compound heat waves from a multidecadal dataset at convection-permitted grid spacing. The Argonne Downscaled Data Archive, Version 2 (ADDA2) comprises of ~180 years of regional Weather and Research Forecast (WRF) model simulations driven by output from three Earth System Models (ESMs) from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6). The atmospheric states from the Community Earth System Model Version 2 (CESM2), the Hadley Centre Global Environment Model version 3 (HadGEM3-GC31), and the Max Planck Institute Earth System Model (MPI-ESM1.2) – all at ~110 km spacing – were used to initialize WRF at 4 km grid spacing, generating the dynamically downscaled ADDA2 dataset. The ADDA2-CESM2, ADDA2-HadGEM3, and ADDA2-MPI simulations are compared against each other and against historical observations to explore differences and projected changes in intensity, frequency, and duration of heat wave events. We also discuss the ClimRR tool, which provides public access to ensembled projections from ADDA.

497612.title: Is Weather Still GO for Launch? Ongoing Lightning Launch Commit Criteria Climatology at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station and Kennedy Space Center: A Collaborative Research Project between Orange County Public Schools and the 45th Weather Squadron
497612.authors: Bao Luu, Orange County Public Schools, Orlando, FL; and B. Cizek, P. Gandhi, A. L. Moses, K. H. Chafin, E. Nguyen, V. Manchikanti, A. Watts, and A. Zappas
497612.abstract: This research was conducted as a part of the Orange County Public Schools (OCPS) in Florida and the 45th Weather Squadron’s (45 WS) collaborative research program. The 45 WS is the U.S. Space Force unit that provides comprehensive weather services to partners and customers on the Eastern Range: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Patrick Space Force Base, and NASA’s Kennedy Space Center. The goal of this collaboration has been to provide valuable research for the 45th Weather Squadron while giving OCPS Advanced Placement® Statistics and Calculus students the opportunity to see real-world application of mathematical topics learned in their classes. Students learn valuable lessons in leadership, organization, teamwork, project management, scheduling, and communication. For this project, students’ main objective was to continue to quality control, organize, analyze and visualize the data from an Lightning Launch Commit Criteria (LLCC) database updated and maintained by the 45 WS. The LLCC are a complex set of ten distinct weather rules that are designed to avoid natural and rocket-triggered lightning strikes to in-flight space launch vehicles. Determined by the Lightning Advisory Panel—a group of world-class lightning experts—the LLCC rules are the basis for NASA Standard (NASA-STD) 4010: Lightning Launch Commit Criteria For Space Flight, used by Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) licensed space launch operators to mitigate risks to public safety. Out of the ten rules, nine of the ten rules require monitoring of cloud growth to the height of various temperatures to determine the potential for natural and rocket-triggered lightning. The work with the LLCC database has produced summary statistics and violation rates of each of the 10 rules broken down at different time scales, such as by season and month. The students also conducted advanced frequency analysis to determine simultaneous and sole violation rates for each rule. As a new initiative, the students are building predictive machine learning models that estimate the probabilistic likelihood of LLCC violations based on observed environmental data. These efforts provide significant operational benefit to the 45 WS and Launch Service Providers, especially as local launch operations continue at a record pace. The 45 WS and the Lightning Advisory Panel also use the results to guide research to improve the LLCC.

497614.title: Observing System Simulation Experiments to Investigate Impacts of Deep-Tropospheric UAS Flights on Forecasts
497614.authors: K. Alexander Swan, Univ. of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE; and A. L. Houston, S. Murdzek, T. T. Ladwig, and E. P. James
497614.abstract: Uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS) have emerged as a promising option to address meteorological gaps in observations in the lower troposphere. With recent advancements, UAS may be able to address gaps aloft in areas that lack coverage from radiosondes and commercial aircraft. UAS have shown the potential to significantly benefit NWP forecasts from profiles in the lowest 2 km AGL, but the impact of UAS profiles to the tropopause has yet to be quantified. Additionally, the forecast impacts that flight limitations imposed by hazardous flying conditions (disproportionately encountered by UAS in deep-tropospheric flights) need to be addressed to guide future UAS engineering innovations. To address these questions, we designed an observing system simulation experiment (OSSE) consisting of two week-long nature runs over CONUS, a system for creating realistic, synthetic conventional and UAS observations, and forecasts using the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model. Several UAS networks are examined with variations in site density, launch frequency, profiling depth, and with limits imposed owing to high winds and icing. Results show positive impacts from UAS, with a network of 431 evenly-spaced UAS sampling every 2 hours to 15 km AGL improving 6-hour forecasts of 500 hPa temperature by nearly 10% and mixed-layer CAPE forecasts by over 30% versus a conventional observing network. It is shown that increasing the profiling frequency of UAS sites may be more beneficial to forecasts than adding sites and that hourly UAS profiles can still benefit forecasts even when restrictive wind and icing thresholds are imposed.

497615.title: JPSS ATMS Updates
497615.authors: Cheng-Hsuan Lyu, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and S. Abraham, E. J. Kim, and M. Sammons
497615.abstract: The Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS) is a microwave radiometer manifested on the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS) satellites. Three missions are on-orbit currently: Suomi National Polar Orbiting Partnership (SNPP), NOAA-20, and NOAA-21. SNPP is planned to have a cessation of data November 1, 2026. The next launch is JPSS-4 in 2027. This poster aims to inform the user community of updates to the program relevant for ATMS, including highlighting important recently released public documentation. This documentation includes the NOAA-21 Government Calibration Data Book, which provides information needed to interpret and process NOAA-21 ATMS science data. Also publicly available as of 2026 are NOAA-21 spectral response functions.

497619.title: Building the Next Generation of Operational Weather Observation Data Hubs for EUMETNET
497619.authors: Ashish Raval, Synoptic Data PBC, Fairfax, VA
497619.abstract: Behind every operational weather forecast is a complex network of data infrastructure and services that acquire, transform, quality-control, and distribute observations from diverse sensing technologies. While observing systems continue to evolve, the operational infrastructure responsible for moving these data between providers and forecasting systems must also adapt to meet growing demands for scalability, reliability, maintainability, and low-latency performance. This presentation describes the modernization of three operational observation data hubs supporting EUMETNET programs: the Aircraft-Based Observations (E-ABO), GNSS Water Vapour (E-GVap), and Operational Vertical Profiling (E-Profile) services. Collectively, these systems ingest observations from aircraft, GNSS networks, radar wind profilers, lidars, ceilometers, and other profiling technologies before delivering standardized products to National Meteorological and Hydrological Services across Europe. The project focuses on redeveloping the underlying infrastructure that supports these three operational data hubs, improving the acquisition, processing, quality control, standardization, and delivery of observations from multiple atmospheric observing systems. The updated services are designed to provide more reliable, consistent, and maintainable operational capabilities while ensuring timely access to trusted observations for forecasting, nowcasting, numerical weather prediction, and research applications across Europe. Although often invisible to end users, operational data hubs are foundational components of modern forecasting systems. This work demonstrates how investment in resilient, scalable data infrastructure can improve the long-term usability of diverse atmospheric observations while reducing operational complexity for both data providers and forecasting organizations.

497620.title: Red Meat Allergy and the Warming World: Climate-Driven Expansion of Alpha-Gal Syndrome
497620.authors: Mary Hendriena Korendyke, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA; George Mason Univ., Fairfax, VA
497620.abstract: Alpha-gal syndrome (AGS), a tick-borne allergy to red meat and mammalian byproducts, has emerged as a growing public health concern with direct economic relevance to agriculture, healthcare, and food systems. It can be lifelong and is managed predominantly by avoidance of red meat like beef, pork, and in extreme cases, byproducts including gelatin, and the animals themselves. AGS is transmitted primarily by the Lone Star Tick in the United States and by related tick species globally, and has now been documented in at least 30 countries across six continents. In 2022, an estimated 450,000 people in the U.S. were affected, though surveillance infrastructure remains limited. A July 2026 CDC study found the highest seroprevalence of alpha-gal IgE antibodies in Arkansas (31.2%) and Missouri (26.0%) — states responsible for 3.04% and 6.69% of U.S. beef cattle production in 2025, respectively. Australia, with more mature surveillance over the past 11 years, has recorded a 22% annual increase in AGS cases since 2020, a trend not explained by expanded testing alone. One possible reason for the increased rate of cases is climate change: ticks prefer warm, humid environments, and warming trends may be expanding suitable habitat range and decreasing the need for dormancy in already active areas. In this study, we examine the historical correlation in the US between Lone Star Tick population density, AGS, and temperature, and investigate a possible expansion of the Lone Star Tick’s habitat and the further spread of AGS as a result of climate change in the coming decades.

497622.title: Constraining Tropospheric OH through Assimilation of TROPOMI Carbon Monoxide in a Chemically Interactive Earth System Model
497622.authors: Benjamin Gaubert, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and M. A. Mirrezaei and A. F. Arellano Jr.
497622.abstract: The hydroxyl radical (OH) controls the atmospheric lifetime of methane (CH4) and many other reactive gases, but its abundance and variability remain difficult to constrain observationally. Because CO is tightly coupled to OH through tropospheric oxidation chemistry, constraining CO can provide valuable information on modeled OH. The broad spatial coverage of TROPOMI CO observations makes them particularly useful for constraining this coupled CO–OH system through data assimilation. We assimilate TROPOMI CO total columns into CAM-chem with interactive CO, CH4, and OH chemistry and detailed short-lived halogen representation. We use a 30-member CAM-chem ensemble with varied initial conditions, meteorological nudging, and perturbed CH4 and chemical emissions to represent uncertainty in transport, sources, and atmospheric chemistry. The assimilation updates CO only, while OH responds through the model’s interactive chemistry. Assimilation experiments for 2018–2021 use the Quantile-Conserving Ensemble Filter Framework (QCEFF) with the bounded normal rank histogram algorithm. We quantify how observationally constrained CO modifies the spatial distribution and temporal variability of OH, including its global mean, interhemispheric gradient, and interannual variability, and how these changes propagate to the CH4 chemical lifetime. We also examine the response of VOC oxidation, particularly formaldehyde (HCHO), to CO-driven changes in OH and evaluate simulated HCHO against HCHO TROPOMI column retrievals and NDACC FTIR observations. Assimilation performance is evaluated against independent CO observations from MOPITT and TROPOMI, NDACC and TCCON column measurements, and NOAA GLOBALVIEWplus surface and aircraft observations. By allowing OH to respond chemically to the assimilated CO field, these experiments quantify the contribution of CO variability and uncertainty to the modeled OH distribution and CH4 sink.

497623.title: Culturally Responsive and Co-Produced Resources: Severe Weather Risk Communication in Vietnamese-American Communities
497623.authors: Tracie Sempier, Univ. of Southern Mississippi, Ocean Springs, MS
497623.abstract: Living in coastal areas in the northern Gulf of Mexico is extremely challenging due to many natural and anthropogenic disasters. In regions prone to extreme weather patterns, especially during hurricane season in the Gulf of America, including Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, residents experience heightened levels of stress and uncertainty. This situation is further exacerbated for those employed in the seafood industry, whose livelihoods depend on working in water-based environments. Vietnamese-Americans in this region are particularly affected by natural disasters as their livelihoods are bound to the shrimping and fishing industry. A recent study that examined the Vietnamese-American fishing community in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama included surveys of 334 fishers in the region (Schewe et al., 2021). Key findings from that report indicated that 69-70% of respondents felt they read and spoke “very little” or “no” English and participants identified language as being the biggest barrier in communicating with fisheries agencies. This language barrier does not just affect fisheries management, but the barrier can adversely impact their safety when they do not receive accurate and timely weather-related information in an understandable way. Currently, there are no radio stations on the Gulf coast (Mississippi and Alabama) that broadcast weather in Vietnamese, no television stations on the coast that have a Vietnamese translator, and no resources provided by local municipalities on the coast that have weather information translated into Vietnamese. Beginning in the 1960’s many Vietnamese refugees were displaced from their homes due to war but found opportunities to become part of the fishing sector along the Northern Gulf of America (Bounds, 2011). Since then, the Vietnamese-American population in the region has flourished, becoming an integral part of the area’s identity. Migration from Vietnam persists, with extended family members and others from Vietnam continuing to migrate to this region. According to U.S. Census American Community Survey (2022), there are approximately 50,000 Vietnamese-Southeast Asian (VNSE) members in Mississippi (7,971), Alabama (10,609), and Louisiana (30,544). In the Gulf States, economic impoverishment and limited language capacity exacerbate health and economic issues within these communities. In the state of Alabama and Mississippi, Vietnamese communities form a large proportion of the Limited English Proficiency (LEP) populations, comprising some 12% and 13% of LEP persons in each respective state (US Census, 2011). LEP individuals face heightened vulnerability to natural disasters, particularly hurricanes, floods, and severe weather due to their reliance on coastal livelihoods. According to the American Community Survey (ACS) 2022, 80% of Vietnamese individuals prefer to communicate in their native language (US Census, 2022). As a result of LEP, they often encounter barriers to accessing disaster preparedness information in their language, hindering their ability to prepare for and recover from disaster impacts in a timely manner. Consequently, they risk compromising their safety and that of their families. This presentation will detail results from a partnership between Boat People SOS, National Weather Service New Orleans, National Weather Service Mobile, and the Mississippi-Alabama Sea Grant Consortium to improve severe weather communications to vulnerable Vietnamese-American community members within the northern Gulf of America that face language and cultural barriers to receiving critical risk-reducing information. The goals of this project included: 1) address a disaster preparedness gap by providing culturally and linguistically appropriate weather-related communication products and services to the Vietnamese-American coastal communities, 2) enable the communities in the northern Gulf of America to reduce disaster impacts and reach recovery quickly, and 3) better equip weather communicators in messaging severe weather information to the Vietnamese-American community. Additionally, the products developed through this project are meant to be shared and benefit Vietnamese-American communities nationwide in minimizing disaster impacts and expediting recovery in other communities. A variety of methods were used to reach our target audience including education-focused promotion campaigns, through a variety of communication channels targeting different subgroups within the Vietnamese community, including those with various levels of English proficiency, health literacy, digital literacy, and science literacy. Severe weather messages were posted in English and Vietnamese languages on social media accounts and messages were disseminated on magnets, flyers, and mailers to the community-at-large during outreach events. We will also discuss language and cultural barriers that weather communicators must be aware of when communicating with the Vietnamese-American community and ways to overcome these barriers. Partners will detail how the project has increased understanding of weather-related risks and communication products by Vietnamese-American families and businesses that will improve decisions that are made when severe weather threatens the area.

497626.title: Development of Small Fixed-Wing Uncrewed Aircraft Systems for Atmospheric Research at the University of Colorado
497626.authors: Brian Argrow, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and M. A. Wagner, E. Frew, D. A. Lawrence, M. Rhodes, A. Kenyon, C. Gomez-Faulk, A. Doddi, and A. Mord
497626.abstract: The development of small, fixed-wing uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS) for atmospheric boundary layer research at the University of Colorado Boulder (CU) traces back to the 2009 Collaborative Colorado-Nebraska Unmanned Aircraft System Experiment (CoCoNUE), which marked the beginning of targeted small-UAS observations in the boundary layer. This was followed in 2010 by the Tempest UAS, deployed during the second Verification of the Origins of Rotation in Tornadoes Experiment (VORTEX2) as a pilot project demonstrating the feasibility of controlled thermodynamic observations aloft within supercell thunderstorms—establishing a research trajectory toward increasingly capable platforms for severe convective storm sensing. This research trajectory produced two complementary platform lineages. The DataHawk (and its successor, DataHawk2) was developed as a small, low-cost UAS optimized for thermodynamic boundary layer profiling, the DataHawk2 carries a Vaisala RSS-421 pressure-temperature-humidity sensor, infrared temperature sensors, and a fine-wire turbulence array within a 1.7 kg, 1.3 m-wingspan airframe. The RAAVEN (Robust Autonomous Airborne Vehicle – Endurant and Nimble) was developed specifically for supercell penetration missions as part of the Targeted Observations of Supercells with UAS and Radar (TORUS) project. Prioritizing long endurance (exceeding 2.5 hours), extended range (transects exceeding 150 km), and the capacity to carry a substantially expanded and diversified sensor payload, the 6.4 kg, 3 m span RAAVEN carries redundant Vaisala RSS-421 units, high-frequency 3D wind estimation with an airdata probe (a 9-hole and a 5-hole design) coupled an independent 3D wind estimate from an extended Kalman filter running on the CubePilot autopilot and inertial navigation system, aerosol and cloud particle instrumentation, and imaging systems. The RAAVEN evolution has been matched by an expanding diversity of scientific applications. Since 2019, RAAVEN has been deployed across nine major field campaigns spanning severe convective storms for tornadogenesis and hail swath characterization (TORUS, TORUS-LItE, ICECHIP; US Midwest), polar boundary layer research (MOSAiC; central Arctic Ocean), tropical ocean-atmosphere interaction (ATOMIC; Barbados), urban air quality (Wisco-DISCO; Lake Michigan Wisconsin Shore), aerosol-convection interaction (TRACER; Texas Gulf Coast), hail microphysics, volcanic emissions (VENUSIAN, Hawaii), and international UAS demonstration efforts (WMO UAS-DC, Colorado). This breadth reflects a deliberate design philosophy—endurance and payload flexibility over specialization—that has allowed a single airframe family to serve fundamentally broad scientific community. This presentation traces the development of the DataHawk2 and RAAVEN UAS and instrumentation history, situates it within the broader evolution of small-UAS atmospheric sensing capability, and discusses lessons learned regarding the tradeoffs between platform specialization and generality that have shaped this development path to current capabilities.

497627.title: An Analysis of the 2026-27 El Niño Event Using the UW-PSL Cyclostationary Linear Inverse Model
497627.authors: Daniel J. Vimont, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and M. Newman, S. Kongkaeo, A. Vizcarra, Y. Wang, and T. Xu
497627.abstract: The 2026-27 El Niño event is poised to be one of the strongest El Niño events in history. The evolution of the 2026-27 El Niño event has been relatively well forecast by the University of Wisconsin / NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory Cyclostationary Linear Inverse Model (UW-PSL CSLIM), including a confident forecast of a “super” El Niño (>2C anomalies in the Niño 3.4 region) as early as April, 2026. The CSLIM is a stochastic-dynamical model that incorporates seasonality into the deterministic dynamics and the noise forcing, leading to realistic representation of ENSO’s seasonal growth and decay, as well as its seasonal variance. The UW-PSL CSLIM can be used as a dynamical “filter” to distinguish between the deterministic and noise-forced trajectory for historical ENSO events. Analysis of the 2026-27 El Niño event using the CSLIM indicates that initial conditions for a moderate-to-strong El Niño event were present as early as January, 2026; noise forcing during the ensuing months amplified the forecast trajectory. Further, analytical solution of the noise forcing provides an effective infinite ensemble with which to characterize the forecast spread, and hence forecast confidence. The growth of the event—and confidence in the forecast—will be discussed using analysis of the cyclostationary solutions and optimal noise forcing. Finally, the 2026-28 trajectory, which at the time of writing shows high confidence of a strong La Niña event peaking in late 2027, will be compared to other historical events including the 1997-99 trajectory.

497628.title: Integration and Analysis Capabilities for Space-Based Environmental Monitoring
497628.authors: Cameron Martus, The Aerospace Corporation, El Segundo, CA
497628.abstract: Adoption of commercial Space-Based Environmental Monitoring (SBEM) capabilities for the weather enterprise requires a robust evaluation process incorporating data from various sensors and sources. We have developed a Python-based data acquisition and analysis platform that handles diverse data formats and repositories for both civil and commercial sensors and provides flexible tools for radiometric calibration comparisons and environmental product evaluations. The Data Integration Package (DIP) retrieves sensor radiances, geolocation, and ancillary data using only a time range and latitude-longitude bounding box. A subsequent tool, Radiometric Analysis of Sensors In Space (RASINS), compares radiances between new sensors and existing sensors as well as instrumented ground sites using scene and pixel level methods, illuminating data quality issues such as biases and outliers. Finally, the Clouds from AVHRR Extended (CLAVR-x) algorithm is modified to accept new sensors and used to compare environmental products between sensors and assess the impact of different sensor designs such as fewer spectral bands and higher noise floors. These capabilities are constructed in a modular fashion with concise and consistent syntax allowing ease of use and enabling rapid addition of new data sources.

497629.title: Perceived Efficacy of Heat-Protective Behaviors in the United States: Results from Two Nationally Representative Surveys
497629.authors: Olga Wilhelmi, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and M. H. Hayden, P. Howe, J. Colby, and J. Boehnert
497629.abstract: Extreme heat is a rapidly escalating public health threat, yet mitigating its risks largely depends on the ability of individuals to engage in protective behaviors. Response efficacy - the belief that the behavior itself will effectively reduce risk - is an important aspect of adaptive capacity and heat response, yet it remains understudied. Drawing on two nationally representative surveys of U.S. adults, this study focuses on characterizing individual-level heat response efficacy across the general population. In this paper, we 1) present results from two national surveys, conducted in 2020 and 2023; 2) investigate geographic and demographic differences in how Americans perceive the heat response efficacy or effectiveness of personal heat protection behaviors; and 3) discuss how these response efficacy beliefs may interact with adaptive capacities and heat health risks and inform future risk communication strategies. We used mixed-effects logistic regression to estimate demographic and geographic predictors of high heat response efficacy, and multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) to estimate heat response efficacy at the state level. The findings indicate that high heat response efficacy was largely associated with the use of air conditioning (AC) at home. Between 2020 and 2023, the national percentage of respondents who perceived their heat response behaviors as very effective declined from 67.8% to 59.7%. Older adults, higher-income individuals, and residents of the South reported higher response efficacy, whereas younger adults, residents of the Western U.S., and and people who identify as other non-white census categories (including Asian, American Indian or Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander, and multi-racial US residents) reported significantly lower extreme heat response efficacy. The study also highlighted that with approximately a quarter of the U.S. population facing socioeconomic or infrastructural barriers to effective use of AC, the reliance on AC creates an emerging vulnerability. This is especially concerning in light of increasing heat hazard across the U.S. and increased demand on the electrical grid. Overall, the study suggests that future heat preparedness and risk communication need to consider a broad range of geographically and demographically tailored, heat response behaviors, including those not dependent on mechanical cooling.

497632.title: WMO Dust Early Warning for All (DEW4All): A New International Cooperation to Mitigate Global Risks of Sand and Dust Storms (Invited Presentation)
497632.authors: Daniel Tong, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA
497632.abstract: Sand and Dust Storms (SDS), an underappreciated environmental hazard, pose myriad adverse effects on human society and safety. As the Earth warms and droughts become the new normal, extreme events, such as sand and dust storms (SDS), have increased in many regions of the world. Exposure to dust particles has been associated with adverse health effects, including asthma, heart attacks and premature mortality. Airborne dust can carry microorganisms, causing infectious diseases such as meningitis in Africa and coccidioidomycosis (Valley fever) in Americas. Dust storms can remove topsoil and damage crops, disrupt transportation and commerce. The annual economic costs are estimated to be $154B annually in the United States and $150B in the Middle East and North Africa, while a global assessment is still lacking. To mitigate harmful effects of SDS, dust forecasts and early warning systems are critical to inform air quality and public health advisory for affected countries. Coordinated by the World. The Dust Early Warning for All (DEW4All) project, recently organized by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Sand and Dust Storm Warning Advisory and Assessment System (SDS-WAS), aims to advance global dust observation and prediction techniques to enhance our collective global capability towards providing dust services for all countries. Leveraging the collaborative network of SDS-WAS, we will collect a suite of dust products from a set of global forecasting systems, including both process-based and Machine-Learning-based models, to assess the performance of individual forecasts and explore the potential to improve forecast accuracy through multi-model ensemble forecasting. These global SDS products include active dust sources, emission flux, dust optical depth (DOD), dust fine and total particulate matter (PM), vertical profile, visibility reduction, and accumulated (wet and dry) deposition. For select dust products, we will create two multi-model ensembles, ensemble mean and median, using both unweighted and weighted ensemble approaches, as well as probability forecasts of air quality exceedances. Near-real-time satellite and ground-based dust observations will be used to support evaluating the performance of forecast models and ensembles. The new international cooperation is open to all interested parties, and offers a new effort to advance SDS sciences and serve the society.

497634.title: Disaster Science Operations Center: An Experiential Model of Higher Education Learning Utilizing a Research-to-Operations Framework
497634.authors: Joshua D. Durkee, Western Kentucky University, Disaster Science Operations Center, Bowling Green, KY
497634.abstract: The Disaster Science Operations Center (DSOC) was established in 2022 at Western Kentucky University (WKU) on the heels of a catastrophic EF-3 tornado emergency that struck the university’s hometown of Bowling Green, KY in December 2021. The center’s history was founded with the launch of a new B.S. Meteorology Program (GS-1340) in 2008, which later evolved to the addition of companion undergraduate and graduate certificate programs in Emergency Management Disaster Science (EMDS) in 2019. In 2018, the university adopted a student-driven weather and emergency management service through the leadership of an appointed University Meteorologist to support inclement weather decisions on campus. The top post-graduation placement for students completing the Meteorology and EMDS programs at WKUY has been with the National Weather Service and county-level Emergency Management offices around the country. DSOC represents the flagship experiential learning initiative, offering undergraduate and graduate students professionalized training experiences that bring foundational learning to life with tangible training, weather planning, forecasting, monitoring, and research to various university, community, and national partnership needs. DSOC is comprised of a situational awareness operations unit, a multi-purpose collaborative meeting space, a modular training and weather forecast briefing classroom, and a dedicated artificial intelligence research lab (DSOC AIR). This presentation will focus on demonstrating facility use -cases that highlight current research initiatives, including AI-weather science applications and the five-year NSF EPSCoR Climate Resilience through Multidisciplinary Big Data Learning, Prediction and Building Response Systems (CLIMBS) project, as well is various key SEAR-1 EOC-based weather decision-support events that define the DSOC portfolio.

497636.title: Interpretation of Estimated Changes and Uncertainties of North Atlantic Basin Tropical Cyclone Risk under Global Warming
497636.authors: Susan E. Tolwinski-Ward, Verisk Catastrophe and Risk Solutions, Boston, MA; and D. Lafferty and I. Grenier
497636.abstract: Considerable scientific uncertainty exists around future change in tropical cyclone intensity. State-of-the-art catastrophe risk models, designed specifically to estimate probabilistic TC risk to the built environment at the portfolio level, can be combined with the latest generation of ensemble climate projections to translate quantitative estimates of scientific uncertainty into quantitative estimates of risk uncertainty. In this work, the environmentally-dependent track model within the hazard module of an industry-grade cat model is forced with adjusted inputs to reflect future changes in background climate derived from the CMIP6 ensemble of climate model runs. Running the resulting changes in hazard through the downstream vulnerability and financial components of the cat model provides estimates of the evolution of risk for properties in the North Atlantic basin. Uncertainty across CMIP6 ensemble members in changes to TC genesis dominate the changes in US-wide risk across most locations. Depending on the CMIP6 model run used to force the future runs, genesis can exhibit overall increases, decreases, or a spatially mixed signal of changes. However, we note that risk changes are robust to the choice of moisture predictors in parameterizing genesis activity within our model formulation, a result that improves our confidence in the estimated uncertainty in risk relative to other studies. Translated into US landfall risk, we find regionally coherent but spatially heterogeneous signals that again vary across CMIP6 models, and can be associated with distinct patterns of change in thermodynamic and kinematic drivers. The results illustrate the range of outcomes supported by current climate models, and are interpreted with an eye toward the relevance of improved scientific understanding in various areas of TC hazard to the understanding of future changes in risk.

497637.title: Regime-Aware Precipitation Perturbations for Probabilistic Urban Flood Inundation Forecasting with RASIAB (HEC-RAS In A Box)
497637.authors: SUMA BHANU BATTULA, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and M. Liao and J. Frame
497637.abstract: RASIAB (HEC-RAS In A Box) automates urban flood inundation mapping end-to-end, replacing the traditional hours-long, analyst-driven workflow of manually delineating a domain, building a mesh, and running a single deterministic simulation. The system couples the NOAA/OWP NextGen hydrofabric to a headless, containerized HEC-RAS engine, using catchment divides and flowpaths to establish model domains over high-resolution (10 m) terrain across hydrofabric tiles nationwide, so any city in CONUS can be automatically converted into a model-ready basin with no human in the loop. Beyond single deterministic runs, the framework generates ensemble inundation maps by perturbing precipitation inputs, with perturbation magnitude informed by storm-type-dependent forecast uncertainty — since Quantitative Precipitation Forecast skill for extreme precipitation varies systematically across synoptic regimes. This regime-aware perturbation approach moves RASIAB toward probabilistic, uncertainty-aware flood forecasting suitable for operational decision support.

497638.title: Updates and Future Directions for the National Solar Radiation Data Base
497638.authors: Manajit Sengupta, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO; National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR), Golden, CO; and Y. Xie, A. Habte, B. N. Benton, J. Yang, P. Edwards, M. J. Foster, A. Heidinger, D. P. Duda, and P. W. Stackhouse Jr.
497638.abstract: The National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) provides global solar resource data at a high temporal and spatial resolution. This data is primarily used in solar energy modeling and is updated on an annual basis (Fig. 1). The NSRDB uses a physical approach to satellite-based solar modeling. The underlying Physical Solar Model (PSM) computes cloud-properties using satellite remote sensing and subsequently solar radiation using radiative transfer models. The retrieved cloud properties include cloud-mask, cloud-type, cloud optical depth and cloud droplet size. The radiative transfer models require additional input parameters such as aerosol optical properties (AOD), precipitable water vapor, surface albedo, temperature and pressure to accurately model solar radiation. While cloud properties are obtained directly from the geostationary satellites other inputs are obtained from additional source such as the National Aeronautical and Space Administration (NASA) Modern Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications version 2 (MERRA2), the Interactive Multisensor Snow and Ice Mapping System (IMS) model data from the U.S. National Ice Center and NASA’s polar orbiting satellites such as the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) instruments on the Aqua and Terra Platform. In 2026 the NSRDB for the GOES coverage area was updated using the latest version of the underlying PSM (PSM v4). Additionally, in collaboration with NASA, an Arctic dataset for 2002-2025 was developed using coverage from multiple polar orbiting satellites from NASA and NOAA. This update includes improved surface albedo under snow conditions and an improved DNI model under cloudy conditions. The inclusion of these updates reduced the uncertainty in the data compared to previous versions of the NSRDB. Meteosat data was added to the NSRDB to make our coverage coverage global (GOES East and West, Meteosat, Meteosat IODC and Himawari). While standard data from the GOES continues to be served at an hourly 4km x 4km resolution, full resolution data has also been made available to the user. The Arctic data is also available at a 4kmx4km hourly resolution. The user is provided significant flexibility for downloading data depending on the amount of data required. Data can be downloaded using either the web-interface, an Application Programming Interface or directly from the cloud using Amazon Web Services. Services such as spectral data use on-demand computation and delivery. For the Continental US (CONUS) evaluation of the NSRDB was conducted for 18 stations and the Mean Bias Error (MBE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) were computed for both GHI and DNI. The evaluation was conducted for the 1998-2025 period. Generally, the MBE lies within plus or minus ±3% for GHI and ±8% for DNI. Using PSM v4 has resulted in a 25% reduction in uncertainty in the DNI. The RMSE is less than 20% for GHI and 30% for DNI. The Arctic datasets were also evaluated using multiple stations in Alaska, Greenland and Sweden and the results are comparable to the CONUS evaluation. There are additional plans to include information about cloud fraction using 500 m data. This presentation will provide users with the latest information about the NSRDB as well as plans for future development and updates.

497642.title: Recent Update on the ICAMS Common Model Architecture Implementation Team
497642.authors: Robert L. Jacob, ANL, Lemont, IL; and S. Chen, K. Thengumthara, J. D. Doyle, M. B. Ek, P. H. Lauritzen, O. Guba, R. Montuoro, and F. Giraldo
497642.abstract: Interagency Council for Advancing Meteorological Services (ICAMS) Common Model Architecture (CMA) Implementation Team (IT) has made steady inroads toward promoting/increasing interoperability between US national modeling centers. In this talk, we will provide recent updates since our last reports to the community at the 2024 AMS annual meeting. The CMA, CS, and PI ITs continued our high-level reviews of the earth system modeling. These include ESMP community’s ongoing model developments, challenges, and future directions. We accomplished these objectives by invited seminars, facilitate communication with experts across many US and foreign governments, modeling centers, universities, and industry. Additional effort is focusing on getting feedback from the U.S. federal agencies’ ESMP modeling groups. We will discuss and summarize the challenges and future efforts within different agencies to continue to advance the U.S. earth system modeling capabilities.

497643.title: Mesoscale Air-Sea Interactions in the Ocean Heat and Carbon Budgets
497643.authors: Yanxu Chen, WHOI, Woods Hole, MA; Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada; and M. Helbig, G. Reverdin, L. Yu, and L. Gloege
497643.abstract: *]:pointer-events-auto R6Vx5W_threadScrollVars scroll-mb-[calc(var(--scroll-root-safe-area-inset-bottom,0px)+var(--thread-response-height))] scroll-mt-[calc(var(--header-height)+min(200px,max(70px,20svh)))]" dir="auto" data-turn-id="request-WEB:bc99f75f-3fb4-4372-b0d5-3578397b42a6-2" data-turn-id-container="request-WEB:bc99f75f-3fb4-4372-b0d5-3578397b42a6-2" data-testid="conversation-turn-6" data-turn="assistant"> Mesoscale ocean dynamics redistribute heat and carbon while simultaneously modifying their exchange across the air-sea interface, yet their contributions to ocean heat and carbon budgets are often examined separately. Here, we combine satellite-based and ship-based observations to investigate how mesoscale variability regulates these two components of the coupled climate system. We first use satellite observations of sea surface temperature, sea surface height, surface currents, winds, and air-sea heat fluxes to quantify mesoscale meridional heat transport and its associated atmosphere-ocean exchange. Mesoscale eddies generate coherent anomalies in sea surface temperature and air-sea heat flux, while offsets between their dynamic and thermal structures enable substantial geostrophic heat transport. Globally, the geostrophic contribution to mesoscale meridional heat transport is approximately an order of magnitude larger than the wind-driven Ekman contribution and acts in the opposite direction, with mesoscale eddies transporting up to approximately 30 TW of near-surface heat. We then extend this mesoscale framework from heat to carbon using approximately three decades of SURATLANT carbonate-system observations in the subpolar North Atlantic combined with satellite sea level anomaly and atmospheric reanalysis. Mesoscale variability produces persistent anomalies in temperature and dissolved inorganic carbon, with cyclonic anomalies generally associated with colder, carbon-rich waters and anticyclonic anomalies with warmer, carbon-poor waters. However, the translation of these oceanic anomalies into air-sea CO₂ exchange depends strongly on the seasonal atmospheric and upper-ocean state. Variations in stratification, mixed-layer ventilation, biological activity, winds, and surface heat loss regulate the magnitude and sign of eddy-associated CO₂ flux anomalies. Together, these results demonstrate that mesoscale ocean dynamics cannot be treated solely as an internal redistribution process: they interact with the atmosphere to regulate both lateral transport within the ocean and vertical exchanges across the air-sea interface. Considering heat and carbon within a common mesoscale air-sea interaction framework therefore provides a more complete description of how ocean eddies influence regional and global climate budgets. _:empty]:hidden">

497646.title: The Role of Free Atmospheric Moisture Content on Instability Maxima on the Cool Side of Sea-Breeze Fronts
497646.authors: Jason M. Keeler, Central Michigan Univ., Mount Pleasant, MI; and C. H. Boyer and A. L. Houston
497646.abstract: The cool side of airmass boundaries can be characterized by higher surface-based CAPE. This condition arises when the cool-side airmass has sufficiently greater moisture content to offset the stabilizing influence of cooler temperatures. Due to the common use of equivalent potential temperature to diagnose this phenomenon, it is commonly referred to as a Mesoscale Airmass with High Theta-E (MAHTE). While MAHTEs can develop in the vicinity of many different types of airmass boundaries, sea-breeze fronts (SBF) offer a convenient environment to study MAHTEs because they are geographically fixed. Typical MAHTE widths are approximately 15 km, with typical surface-based CAPE increases of several hundred joules per kilogram, providing an environment that has the potential to substantially affect coastal thunderstorms. In this talk, large-eddy simulations of the coastal environment are used to develop a process-based understanding of MAHTE development and characteristics in a parameter space that varies water surface temperature, radiative forcing, the cross-shore wind component, and moisture content above the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL). MAHTEs are wider and consist of greater surface-based CAPE perturbations when dry air is present overlying the ABL, primarily for two reasons. First, relatively vigorous thermals present within the warm-side airmass are more capable of entraining the overlying dry air, thereby reducing CAPE in that airmass. Second, the initiation of deep moist convection is delayed due to that same dry air, allowing more time for temperature moderation to occur within the cool-side airmass. The cross-shore wind component and water surface temperature also affect MAHTE evolution, but are secondary to the role of free atmospheric moisture content.

497650.title: Simulating the Regional and Global Climate Response to Targeted Idealized Aerosol Perturbations of Arctic Liquid, Ice, and Mixed-Phase Clouds
497650.authors: Erin Justine Emme, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and A. Gettelman, C. E. Singer, W. R. Lee, M. M. Holland, D. Clemens-Sewall, C. Payne, and L. Landrum
497650.abstract: Ice-albedo feedback and meridional heat transport amplify anthropogenic change such that the Arctic is warming at an accelerated rate compared to the global average. However, this also means that local targeted interventions in the Arctic may result in more significant benefits than interventions in other regions. Here, we assess whether Arctic sea ice loss can be slowed by deliberately altering the Arctic surface energy budget through modification of cloud properties via idealized aerosol injections. Specifically, we explore the solar radiation modification approaches Marine Cloud Brightening (MCB) of liquid clouds, Mixed-phase Cloud Thinning (MCT), and Cirrus Cloud Thinning (CCT) for ice clouds with a hierarchy of experiments including idealized microphysics changes of clouds in the fully-coupled Community Earth System Model version 2 (CESM2) to analyze the cloud microphysical and climate response. Our central hypothesis is that targeted rather than uniform intervention will yield the greatest retention of sea ice because ice loss can concentrate in thin-ice regions and clouds can have a warming or cooling effect in the Arctic depending on the season. We test this by simulating the idealized effects of aerosol perturbations on clouds via cloud droplet number concentration (Nd) modification for MCB and prescribed ice nucleating particle (INP) perturbations for MCT and CCT to determine which target seasons and locations may optimize Arctic sea ice stabilization. Results indicate MCB and MCT can be effective in mitigating sea ice loss but need to be focused seasonally (in summer and winter, respectively). Model evaluation of the supercooled liquid fraction (SLF) against CALIPSO-GOCCP satellite observations suggest that CESM2 overestimates Arctic SLF, which is an important uncertainty to consider for accurate simulation of MCT. CCT experiments appear to be sensitive to the microphysical state of ice clouds in CESM2.

497652.title: Influence of the Madden–Julian Oscillation on Marine Heatwaves in the Central Equatorial Indian Ocean
497652.authors: Toshiaki Shinoda, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX; Texas A&M University-Corpus CHristi, Corpus Christi, TX; and L. Pedraza, S. Pei, and W. Han
497652.abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) have significant impacts on marine ecosystems and regional weather. Although MHWs occur over a wide range of timescales, from days to months, this study focuses on MHW variability in the central equatorial Indian Ocean in relation to the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO). The processes governing the development and persistence of these events are investigated using satellite-derived sea surface temperature (SST), surface winds, and air–sea heat fluxes. A total of 18 MHW events were identified in the central equatorial Indian Ocean during the 22-year period from 2000 to 2021. Most events occurred during the suppressed phase of the MJO, when weakened surface winds and enhanced shortwave radiation promoted upper-ocean warming. Two exceptional events, in 2002 and 2011, exhibited SST anomalies exceeding 2°C. Although the instantaneous surface heat flux anomalies during these events were not unusually large, the cumulative surface heat input over the warming period was substantially greater than that of the other events. This result indicates that cumulative surface heat input, rather than the magnitude of instantaneous heat flux anomalies, plays a dominant role in generating extreme MHWs. The two extreme MHWs persisted through four consecutive MJO phases (7–8–1–2), whereas most other events lasted only one or two phases. This prolonged duration resulted from the suppressed MJO phase being situated between two successive convective phases propagating across the Indian Ocean, thereby extending favorable surface heat flux conditions and sustaining upper-ocean warming.

497656.title: Orthogonal Environmental Controls on the Life Cycle of Nocturnal Offshore Propagating Convection off the West Coast of Sumatra
497656.authors: Ryan North, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; and C. J. Schumacher
497656.abstract: Nocturnal offshore propagating convection is a climatologically persistent feature throughout the Maritime Continent, including the west coast of Sumatra. Despite its persistence, the physical mechanisms driving the initiation and subsequent propagation, specifically the roles of land-breeze convergence and gravity waves, remains a subject of long-standing debate. This study investigates these drivers through a novel, automated terrain-relative tracking algorithm that identifies propagating mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) in Hovmöller space relative to the complex coastline of Sumatra. Unlike traditional frame-by-frame tracking, this algorithm utilizes density-based clustering (HDBSCAN) and ellipse fitting to objectively characterize system life cycles relative to coastal and topographical features. Application of this framework to three years (2016–2018) of satellite precipitation intensity observations from IMERG identified 407 propagating events, corresponding to a daily occurrence frequency of 37%. In general, propagating events develop onshore over the coastal range in the evening around 1930 LT, migrating offshore at a speed of 5.6 m s-1, and reaching distances of approximately 150 km offshore across their 9-hour duration. These systems are broad and moderately intense, with a median rain rate of 2.4 mm hr⁻¹. Notably, the frequency and properties of propagating events are shown to vary across the seasonal cycle and Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) phase. To link individual propagating event properties to their large-scale environments, a Redundancy Analysis (RDA) statistical model was employed utilizing vertical profiles of temperature, moisture, and winds derived from ERA5. The model yields two primary, orthogonal axes of variability. The first RDA axis, governing rainfall intensity and event longevity, demonstrates that 0–3 km coast-perpendicular shear and low-level moisture select the relevant forcing mechanism. Weak-shear, moist environments favor slow-moving systems (median 5.3 m s⁻¹) consistent with land-breeze forcing, while strong-shear environments support intense, long-lived systems with propagation speeds (median 8.4 m s⁻¹) indicative of gravity wave dynamics. The second RDA axis, focused on event initiation and propagation, reveals that the coast-perpendicular mid-to-upper-level winds govern the initiation and propagation speed independently of rain-producing efficiency. This highlights a fundamental decoupling of the environmental controls for storm intensity versus movement. Together, the two-dimensional framework established by the RDA also provides a predictive basis for how local and synoptic factors interact to partition rainfall across the tropical coastal zone. While the low-level environment dictates a system’s rain-producing potential, a separate set of mid-level conditions determines whether that system will be a slow-moving, locally-driven event or a fast-moving, synoptically-driven one.

497668.title: Evaluating Entrainment Rates and Size Distributions in Shallow Convective Parameterizations Using Ceilometer and Doppler LIDAR Observations
497668.authors: Francis Turney, NRL, Monterey , CA; and D. D. Flagg, J. M. Schmidt, S. Gaberšek, E. J. Hyer, J. R. Campbell, and W. M. Angevine
497668.abstract: Sub-grid shallow convection in numerical weather prediction models is not only important for forecasting the influence of cumulus fields on weather and climate but also in mixing aerosols across the boundary layer where they may impact air-quality and visibility forecasts. Here we evaluate the equations that govern the behavior of shallow convective plumes in the Mellor-Yamada-Nakanishi Niino (MYNN) Eddy-Diffusion and Muss-Flux (EDMF) scheme in the Weather, Forecasting, and Research Tool (WRF) against LIDAR-retrieved entrainment rates and size distributions. We present a new signal-enhanced, co-located ceilometer/Doppler LIDAR analysis on observations from the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory’s Coastal Environmental Observation Station (NRL-CEOBS) in Watsonville, CA. Our results suggest a larger entrainment rate coefficient than prescribed by WRF, but which aligns with previous LES studies and gives confidence in our methodology. Larger plumes are less frequent than previously predicted, possibly due to surface heterogeneity leading to less coalescence of smaller plumes. Adjusting the entrainment rate coefficient in WRF to 0.5 m/s gives a ~10% decrease in predicted plume heights for our observation days. Future research is set to focus on the mechanisms driving aerosol transport above the boundary layer.

497669.title: An Enterprise Data Platform for Earth System Science: From Versioned Repositories to Cross-Organization Data Products
497669.authors: Ryan Abernathey, Earthmover, New York, NY
497669.abstract: Earth System data has largely completed its migration to the cloud, yet sharing that data across organizational boundaries still looks like it did decades ago: bulk downloads, bespoke delivery pipelines, and copies of copies with no versioning or provenance. As weather, climate, and geospatial data increasingly become operational inputs to commercial decisions and AI systems, the geosciences need what other data-intensive industries already have: an enterprise data platform to manage data across its full lifecycle. We present the Earthmover Platform and its novel approach to cross-organization data sharing. The foundation is analysis-ready, cloud-optimized (ARCO) data stored in Icechunk, an open-source, transactional storage engine for Zarr that brings version control, atomic commits, and time travel to multi-dimensional array data. Arraylake organizes these repositories into a governed catalog with access control and usage metrics. On top of this foundation, the Earthmover Marketplace enables public cross-organization sharing: data providers publish listings under free or commercial terms, and subscribers receive read-only repositories in their own organization, with data read directly from the provider's object storage. No data is copied, subscribers see updates as they are committed, and paid listings can be filtered to specific variables. Private Exchanges extend the same machinery to closed groups: an organization operates its own branded, curated catalog and controls which partner organizations can browse or publish, enabling multi-institution data sharing (consortia, agency programs, commercial data services) in a fully cloud-native way. Finally, we show how AI agents integrate with the catalog through the platform's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server: assistants discover datasets, inspect schemas, run queries against serverless compute services, and render interactive maps, grounding AI workflows in versioned, trustworthy scientific data. We close with a roadmap spanning the ARCO data layer, the sharing layer, and an emerging compute and query layer for Earth System data.

497671.title: Diagnosing Climate Model ENSO Errors from Seasonal Forecasts at Short Leads
497671.authors: Jonathan D Beverley, CIRES, Boulder, CO; NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, CO; and M. Newman, A. J. Hoell, and A. Capotondi
497671.abstract: Climate models continue to suffer from long-standing systematic errors in their representation of ENSO events. In this study, we use coupled and prescribed (observed) SST hindcasts from the ECMWF seasonal forecast model to show that these errors begin immediately after initialisation, as the atmospheric model drives the surface winds to respond erroneously to the initial observed SST. This generates surface turbulent heat flux errors in the western equatorial Pacific, causing ENSO SST anomalies (SSTAs) to extend too far westwards. These initial wind errors also drive surface wind stress errors, which excite an erroneous eastward propagating Kelvin wave during the ENSO growth phase, leading to a delayed SST response in the eastern equatorial Pacific. During late winter, wind stress errors in the eastern Pacific result in the slower than observed decay of ENSO events by suppressing upwelling in this region. These initial atmospheric errors drive a coupled response developing over approximately three weeks, after which the coupled model erroneous ocean is in balance with the erroneous atmosphere, so that SSTA and sea surface height anomaly errors dominate while the original surface flux errors diminish. Our results suggest that addressing the initial cause of the erroneous atmospheric response to observed SSTs is necessary in order to alleviate common ENSO errors, and that climate model development would benefit from these models also being run as seasonal forecast models to enable a cleaner diagnosis of the source of errors.

497672.title: Climate Change and Aviation Weather Hazards: From Scientific Evidence to Operational Resilience
497672.abstract: Climate change is increasingly affecting the meteorological conditions in which aviation operates, with consequences for safety, efficiency, airport operations and air traffic management.
