While much attention has traditionally focused on aviation’s contribution to climate change, there is a growing need to understand the reverse relationship: how a changing climate is altering aviation-relevant weather hazards and what this means for future meteorological services. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Standing Committee on Services for Aviation, through its Expert Team on Weather and Climate Science for Aviation Applications, has consolidated the latest scientific evidence on observed and projected changes in weather hazards affecting aviation. The assessment considers both current knowledge and remaining scientific uncertainties, with the aim of supporting the aviation community in adaptation and resilience planning. The findings show that climate-driven changes are already evident for several hazards. Changes in clear-air turbulence, jet-stream characteristics, severe convection and temperature are among those with direct implications for flight operations, route efficiency and airport performance. At the same time, the level of scientific understanding differs significantly between hazards and regions. Some phenomena are comparatively well studied, while others, including icing and localized hazards, remain subject to considerable uncertainty. This presentation will highlight the principal findings of the WMO assessment and discuss their relevance for the future development of aviation meteorological services. Particular attention will be given to the challenge of translating climate science into operationally useful information, identifying priority knowledge gaps, and strengthening the link between research, meteorological service provision and aviation decision-making. As climate-related risks evolve, aviation weather services will need not only to improve forecasts of individual hazards, but also to support longer-term resilience by providing authoritative, decision-relevant information on how those hazards may change over time.

497673.title: Beyond Radar: Gauge-Based Validation of Precipitation Enhancement in Complex Terrain
497673.authors: Jeffrey Chagnon, Rain Enhancement Technologies, Naples, FL; and S. Morris, R. Dongre, T. Gresham, and E. Powell
497673.abstract: Rigorous evaluation of precipitation enhancement effects depends critically on the accuracy and resolution of the underlying observational network. Radar-based precipitation estimation, while valuable for broad spatial coverage, faces well-documented limitations in complex terrain and in general accuracy. Issues include beam blockage, overshooting of shallow orographic precipitation, and reduced sensitivity to light snowfall in mountainous regions. These present significant errors in evaluating on-the-ground effects. These limitations are particularly consequential for weather modification evaluation, where the enhancement signal of interest is often subtle relative to natural variability, and where treatment areas frequently coincide with the mountainous terrain most challenging for radar observation. Other limitations include the ability to determine Snow Water Equivalent (SWE) – a critical parameter in providing value to water augmentation operations. This presentation examines an evaluation approach centered on ground-based instrument networks, applied to ground-based ionization units operated near the La Sal Mountains, Utah, and near Gill, Colorado, since November 2025. Rather than relying primarily on radar-derived precipitation estimates, this evaluation framework prioritizes networks of existing and purpose-deployed snow and rain measuring instruments positioned within and outside target and treatment areas, providing direct, high-resolution measurement of surface precipitation and snowpack response unaffected by beam geometry or terrain-induced sampling gaps. This work advances the case for gauge-centered evaluation frameworks in quantifying enhancement effects and determining enhancement signal from meteorological ‘noise’, contributing to broader efforts to establish rigorous, defensible standards for quantifying weather modification efficacy using data-driven statistical methods.

497680.title: Implementing Threats-in-Motion into NWS Operations
497680.authors: Kimberly E. Klockow McClain, CPAESS, Norman, OK; and K. laws, S. W. Bieda III, PhD, J. J. Brost, K. Sherburn, R. Bowers, C. M. Gravelle, E. Bentley, and N. Jacobs
497680.abstract: Over the past twenty years, NOAA has made significant investments in the future of the National Weather Service's severe weather warning program. Today, many new technologies and forecasting techniques have come through the transition pipeline and require focused support to go the last mile into operations. Current NOAA leadership has made it a priority to push for these advances. This presentation will highlight current efforts to advance severe weather warnings, especially on a few fronts: first, the implementation of Threats-in-Motion, which includes both technological advances and advances in communication policy and philosophy for warnings. Additionally, the effort includes support for more robust provision of information in the period between the watch and the warning which can set the stage for more successful warning decisions. The talk will provide an overview of these advances, as well as major milestones and timelines for implementation.

497682.title: Degree Requirements and Expectations from Three Annual Meeting Surveys
497682.authors: Teresa M. Bals-Elsholz, Valparaiso Univ., Valparaiso, IN; Valparaiso Univ., Valparaiso, IN; and K. H. Goebbert, C. A. Clark, K. A. Barber, C. E. Phillips, L. Blind-Doskocil, and A. J. Stepanek, PhD
497682.abstract: Minimum degree requirements and expectations of atmospheric science graduates are not always aligned. Faculty prepare their students for the requirements and advise them for the expectations. Shifts in requirements generally evolve at climatological-scale rates and allow for academic curriculum changes. In contrast expectations evolve on a more synoptic scale rates, faculty can advise and prepare students for these changes. Recently expectations have evolved at more mesoscale rates, whether to shifts in government funding or to advances in technology, leaving both faculty and students racing to react and adjust. In 2016, 2025, and 2026 we surveyed attendees of the AMS Annual Meeting during the Conference on Education poster session on the expectations and requisites for graduate school and job market placement. We asked attendees about best career paths, subjects, and requisites for the job market and graduate school work. Queries on the value of courses in instrumentation, programming, Python, and AI provided insight into some of the mesoscale shifts in our field. We will present our 2016, 2025 and 2026 survey results with reflection on the observed trends in atmospheric science career requirements and expectations.

497683.title: Photovoice as an Innovative Approach to Land-Based Community-Engaged Education
497683.authors: Amelia Cook, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK
497683.abstract: In this session, we share the story of how the Photovoice method became a central part of learning, research, and community engagement in the Indigenous Kinship Circle for Climate Futures (IKCCF), a two-year education program developed through university and Tribal partnerships in Oklahoma and New Mexico. IKCCF engages college students as learners and co-researchers in community-led climate adaptation work. The program is grounded in Indigenous Land-Based Education (LBE), where Land is more than the setting for learning but is teacher and relation, central to how knowledge is generated, carried, and shared. This orientation shapes how students observe, question, and learn with the Land while weaving Indigenous and scientific ways of knowing in their Earth system science learning and community adaptation research. Photovoice, a participatory action research methodology that centers participants as authors and interpreters of their own experiences (Wang & Burris, 1997; Latz, 2017), served as both a science education inquiry tool and a research method. Each week, students responded to prompts through photography and short narratives exploring relationships among climate science, Land, and community. Their photographs documented changes and questions related to drought, vegetation and hydrological change, pollinator biodiversity, and other climate impacts experienced in their own communities. They also documented the complexity of addressing these concerns in the community. Students shared selected images in weekly virtual talking circles with the cohort, where their observations opened opportunities for reflection and dialogue across science, culture, geography, and community experience. Students used Photovoice to generate and interpret data that informed their own community-engaged climate adaptation research. Knowledge moved in multiple directions through the Photovoice process. Learning with the Land informed scientific inquiry, and discussions across the cohort helped students consider their observations from multiple perspectives and make connections across communities and geographies. Community knowledge and values shaped their research, and students carried what they were learning back into their community projects, presentations, research posters, and public Photovoice galleries. In the Photovoice galleries, community members engaged directly with the photographs and student photographers, asking questions and sharing stories, contributing to knowledge and building a shared understanding that students could carry back into their own lives. Emerging lessons from the first IKCCF cohort illustrate how Photovoice can help students connect Earth system processes with environmental changes they recognize in familiar Lands and communities. As a visual, arts-based form of engagement, Photovoice created space for students to express and interpret knowledge in creative ways to communicate scientific information and support collective meaning-making across cultural and community contexts. We share how Photovoice combined Land-based learning and community-engaged research in the learning experience and created opportunities for storytelling and community engagement through science communication. This approach cultivated respectful, reciprocal pathways for knowledge to move among Land, learners, science, and communities and supported student development as climate researchers, communicators, and community leaders.

497701.title: Practicing Authentic Student-Directed Research: Assessing the Environmental Impacts of Fracking - A Focus on Air Quality Degradation
497701.authors: Allison Bockstahler, Cherokee Trail High School, Aurora, CO; and S. M. DeSchryver
497701.abstract: Note to program chairs: This WILL be edited to expand and elaborate the abstract - abstracts due before school started for our 9-12 students. Background: Fracking has severely affected communities across the country, including neighborhoods in Colorado. Fracking and the release of different hazardous air pollutants (HAPs) have been associated with multiple cancer and noncancer health outcomes. Objective: To evaluate whether fracking near the Aurora Reservoir in Aurora, Colorado, produces air pollution and releases different HAPs Methods: I set up and studied air quality using an air quality sensor in the backyard of a volunteer near the fracking projects near the Aurora Reservoir. I plan to collect readings from this air quality sensor for multiple weeks and compare them with historical readings from before fracking started to establish a control group. Allison Bockstahler Cherokee Trail High School Grade 12

497704.title: Rust to TypeScript: Agentic AI and the Small-Team Cloud Stack
497704.abstract: A small commercial weather team has to own everything between raw model output and a rendered product in the customer's browser. That path crosses several languages and several layers of cloud infrastructure, and it used to require several specialists. Over the past year I have built, operated, and improved a stack that previously would have taken years, using LLM coding agents throughout. The biggest gain was not faster Python. It was that working outside Python became cheap enough to do, and that is where the performance and cost improvements came from. I will walk through three pieces of the stack. Contributing to gribberish, an open-source GRIB decoder written in Rust with Python bindings, as someone whose background is scientific Python and meteorology (Py-ART, MetPy, xradar). Building and deploying forecast data pipelines on AWS for regional and subseasonal products, where the agents helped most with infrastructure configuration and operational hardening rather than anything scientific. And iterating on TypeScript visualization frontends, including caching for interactive weather layers, which is where the speedup was largest. I will also cover what went wrong. Generated code was reliable where conventions are well documented and public, and unreliable where the domain knowledge lives: time coordinates and calendars, chunking that works on a laptop and falls over at scale, and quiet unit and fill-value errors in derived fields. I will close on what the cloud-native architecture actually bought us, and recommendations moving forward.

497705.title: Exploring Basin-Wide Radar-Rainfall Bias Patterns through Streamflow Simulation
497705.authors: Nicolas Velasquez, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; and W. F. Krajewski and R. D. Molina
497705.abstract: Radar-based quantitative precipitation estimates (QPEs) provide essential input for hydrological models in their use for streamflow simulation and forecasting. QPE uncertainties are comprised of bias and random errors that propagate through the modeling systems, leading to streamflow forecasting errors. Despite earlier community studies, we do not fully understand their magnitude, patterns, and propagation. In our recent work, we explored basin-wide QPE biases in the Hillslope Link Model (HLM) for Iowa using 112 USGS streamflow gauges and Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) rainfall. We assumed a multiplicative error model with factors oscillating between 0.1 and 5 times the estimated rainfall. We ran the HLM for each factor and selected the one that provided the best hydrograph representation. Our results showed exceptional improvement, indicating that basin-wide rainfall biases play a crucial role. In this follow-up, we examined the time series of these multiplicative biases. Using a scale-dependent time window and comparing with observations, we generated a time series of optimal factors. We examined the series seasonality, autocorrelation, spatial distribution, and correlation. In our results, larger watersheds have longer memory and stable factors, around 1. Also, factors tend to compensate for underestimations during winter and overestimations in the summer, indicating seasonal biases. Finally, nested watersheds have similar series with the potential to inform uncertainties at ungauged sites. Along with our previous work, the results expand our ability to improve forecasts by addressing radar-rainfall systematic biases and their propagation through our models. Future work may involve expanding the analysis region and using additional hydrological models.

497707.title: Mapping Atmospheric Ion Plume Transport from Ground-Based Emission to Cloud Base
497707.authors: Scott Morris, Rain Enhancement Technologies, Naples, FL; and A. Ruiz-Columbie, T. Gresham, J. Chagnon, and R. Dongre
497707.abstract: A central assumption underlying ground-based ionization for cloud seeding is that ions generated at the surface are transported by natural wind patterns to altitudes sufficient to influence cloud microphysics. This presentation provides details on RET's field campaign to quantify and qualify this theory. Using aerial measurement equipment, ion generation from a ground-based antenna was mapped and tracked under varying environmental conditions. This allowed characterization of plume behavior as a function of distance and altitude from the source. Ion concentration was analyzed as a function of proximity to the antenna at increasing altitudes and horizontal distances, providing an empirical characterization of the spatial extent and dilution pattern of the ion plume under real-world atmospheric conditions. These measurements offer empirical support for ion transport pathways relevant to ground-based cloud seeding efficacy, with direct implications for site selection, plume modeling assumptions, and expected treatment footprint under varying wind and atmospheric stability conditions.

497711.title: Winter Impact Prediction: An Interactive Tool for Forecasting Winter-Storm Outages and Damage for Electrical Utilities
497711.authors: Steven M. Quiring, The Ohio State Univ., Columbus, OH; and B. McRoberts
497711.abstract: Winter storms can cause significant damage to the electrical power system, leading to prolonged power interruptions to a large number of customers. In recent years, ice accretion and heavy-wet snow have caused major power outages in the United States. Storm forecasts constantly change, making flexible planning essential. This presentation explores how Itron's Winter Impact Prediction (WIP) allows electrical utilities to adjust storm tracks, precipitation type, and intensity to inform planning, optimize resource staging, and prepare for winter storms. This allows utilities to quickly identify worst case scenarios and identify how changes in storm intensity and the amount of snow versus ice will affect them. Here we highlight the key features and performance of Itron’s WIP using case studies from recent impactful storms and discuss the implications for emergency preparedness and response.

497712.title: Expanding Tracer-of-Opportunity Model Evaluation: Wind-Alignment Screening and Plume Reconstruction for HYSPLIT
497712.authors: Bavand Sadeghi, NOAA, College Park, MD; Cooperative Institute for Satellite Earth System Studies, College Park, MD; and M. D. Cohen, F. Ngan, T. Chai, and A. Crawford
497712.abstract: Reliable characterization of plume structure is critical for reducing uncertainty in urban-scale atmospheric dispersion modeling. Building on our 2026 AMS presentation of a "Tracer of Opportunity" approach linking well-characterized CO2 emissions to observed downwind concentrations, we develop observational estimates of plume structure to evaluate atmospheric transport and dispersion models. This study combines high-frequency CO2 and meteorological observations from NIST monitoring towers with known CO2 emissions and NOAA's HYSPLIT simulations in the Washington, D.C.-Baltimore, Maryland region. Comparing observed wind direction with the expected source-receptor transport angle shows that CO2 enhancements consistently occur when wind direction aligns with this angle, providing a direct observational indicator of when source-emitted plumes are impacting the receptor. For selected events, gradual wind-direction shifts sweep the plume across a fixed receptor, we transform the resulting concentration time series into a plume-centered coordinate system to estimate cross-plume structure and plume width independent of transport-timing errors that limit conventional point-to-point evaluations. Corresponding HYSPLIT output is analyzed in the same plume-relative framework under meteorological and emission conditions, enabling direct comparison of modeled and observation-derived plume characteristics. This wind-alignment approach offers a systematic way to identity additional evaluation cases from routine observations without requiring a dispersion simulation to be run for every candidate event. This framework strengthens the use of tracers of opportunity for characterizing dispersion-model uncertainty and improving atmospheric transport predictions relevant to air quality and emergency response in densely populated urban areas.

497714.title: Assessing Spatial and Temporal Biases in Anthropogenic Fugitive Dust Emissions Using a 20-Year CMAQ Hindcast over the Continental United States
497714.authors: Chang Shu, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA; and D. Tong, S. Ma, Y. Li, B. H. Baek, K. Seltzer, and G. Pouliot
497714.abstract: Anthropogenic fugitive dust (AFDust) remains one of the largest sources of uncertainty in particulate matter emission inventories in the United States. Currently the National Emissions Inventory (NEI) estimates rely largely on empirical emission factors, outdated activity data, and prescribed temporal profiles that do not fully represent meteorological and land-surface controls such as precipitation, soil moisture, or changing land-use practices. This study evaluates the spatial and temporal distributions of NEI-based AFDust emissions using a 20-year Community Multiscale Air Quality (CMAQ) hindcast over the continental United States from 2002 to 2021. Model results are evaluated against chemically speciated observations from the Interagency Monitoring of Protected Visual Environments (IMPROVE) network, focusing on fine calcium (Ca), fine magnesium (Mg), fine potassium (K), and fine soil as crustal tracers. CMAQ captures part of the broad seasonal variability but systematically underestimates the magnitude, variability, and peak concentrations of observed dust-related aerosols, with the largest discrepancies in the western and southwestern United States. Inventory analysis shows that unpaved road dust, crop tilling, and paved road dust account for more than 80% of NEI-based primary PM2.5 AFDust emissions. Source-dominant site evaluation further indicates that underestimation is common across all three major sectors but strongest for road dust, with fine-soil NMB reaching −49.87% for unpaved roads and −46.40% for paved roads. These results demonstrate that current NEI-based AFDust emissions are too static in magnitude and timing to reproduce observed dust variability and highlight the need for source-specific, meteorology- and activity-dependent emission treatments.

497715.title: Evaluating Heat Risk Communication and Heat Product Issuance Across the Jackson, MS NWS Forecast Area
497715.authors: Danasia Sanaye Sproles, Jackson State University, Greenwood, MS
497715.abstract: This project investigates the climatological and atmospheric conditions associated with extreme heat events across Jackson, MS county warning area. The study focuses on identifying the environmental patterns and meteorological variables that contribute to the development of heat advisories and warnings in the region. Historical heat events are analyzed to examine the frequency, intensity, duration, and seasonal distribution of hazardous heat conditions. The research also evaluates the effectiveness and timeliness of heat related warning products through the development of a verification method designed to assess product performance and consistency. In addition to climatological analysis, the project incorporates operational meteorology techniques to better understand how forecasting tools and observational data can improve heat hazard detection and communication. By examining regional heat trends and forecast verification, this study contributes to a broader understanding of heat risk and supports efforts to improve preparedness, public safety, and decision making during extreme heat events in the southeastern United States.

497716.title: Another January Cold Wave in PJM in 2026, But a New All-Time Peak Proved Elusive
497716.authors: Marcus R. Smith, PJM Interconnection, Sicklerville, NJ
497716.abstract: Around the same time of year as the previous last couple of years of extreme cold events analyzed in PJM Interconnection, operations were preparing for another all-time winter demand peak in 2026. The highest mean daily demand of the winter season typically occurs in late January which coincides near the coldest average load-weighted temperature in the PJM RTO of the year. With load growth we’ve seen average January total loads climb 8.7% from 2024 to 2025 with a continued growth of under 1% from 2025 to 2026. Considering the increase in loads, contributed by notably large loads, and the expectation of abnormally cold temperatures, the expectation during the cold wave was for a new winter peak load to be set in 2026. There were noted differences between the cold waves of the past couple of years to January 2026. In 2024 and 2025 the coldest portion of the year and highest demand occurred around the MLK Day Holiday. In 2026 while it was cold for the holiday period, colder weather occurred a week later. The cold period occurred during a more typical time frame where forecasts are not interrupted by differing consumer energy patterns due to holiday impacts. Also unlike in 2024 and 2025, a widespread winter storm in 2026 led to a significant number of closures that resulted in a disruption to the typical demand patterns in the morning hours. The impact of closures was found to have led to lower hourly morning demand ramps to the first peak of the day by as much as 2-6% below typical weekdays. The effects were magnified due to the widespread nature of closures. Additionally, while weather forecasts were good in the prior analyzed cold waves, there was significantly more day-ahead forecast error in 2026. Building on analysis of the January cold waves of 2024 and 2025, this study evaluates a third consecutive January cold wave in 2026 within PJM. This study will diagnose the dual drivers of the 2026 over-forecast: a distinct cold bias in the weather forecast and societal shutdowns. All of this contributed to the all-time winter peak in PJM surviving another season despite projections of it being exceeded for the second straight year. Quantifying the dynamics of closures provides grid operators actionable insights to adjust operations when extreme cold pairs with paralysis of daily life.

497717.title: Developing a Micro-Weather Risk Framework for Post-Storm Transportation Safety
497717.authors: Brittany Marie Welch, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. R. Siems-Anderson and D. C. Walker
497717.abstract: Transportation agencies rely on weather forecasts, roadside observations, and local knowledge to guide roadway maintenance during hazardous weather. However, dangerous conditions can persist after the storm ends. Refreezing pavement, localized blowing snow can affect short roadway segments that are not resolved by operational mesoscale models. These micro-weather hazards complicate decisions about when maintenance operations can transition from active storm response to recovery. This project is developing a micro-weather risk assessment framework for identifying roadway segments that may remain hazardous during the post-storm period. The framework combines Road Weather Information System (RWIS) observations, transportation agency reports, geospatial information, and high-resolution atmospheric modeling. Case studies in Colorado and Iowa were selected in collaboration with transportation agencies, with initial work focusing on blowing snow events. This paper will focus on blowing snow along I-35 in northern Iowa and refreeze events along the I-70 mountain corridor in Colorado. These events will be simulated using nested Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model domains, with the innermost WRF output providing atmospheric forcing for the GPU-accelerated FastEddy® large-eddy simulation model. FastEddy simulations at approximately 5-m grid spacing will resolve fine-scale influences from terrain and the surrounding built environment to develop a micro-weather risk framework aiming to help transportation agencies identify persistent roadway hazards more precisely and support safer, more efficient post-storm operations.

497718.title: Leptospirosis: The Sprial of Death, Despair, and Disease
497718.authors: Staci M DeSchryver, ; and S. Karra, R. Indukuri, V. Indukuri, S. Katrodiya, A. Osborn, N. Awan, J. Veach, and S. Boarman
497718.abstract: How could the weather patterns of Typhoon Ketsana and Typhoon Parma, and recent natural disasters such as Hurricane Fiona, allow scientists to predict the future spread of leptospirosis caused by exponentially increasing destructive disasters? If scientists continue to analyze the weatehr patterns of Typhoon Ketsana and Typhoon Parma (2009, Philippines), and recent natural disasters such as Hurricane Fiona (2022, Puerto Rico), then they could predict the future spread of leptospirosis caused by exponentially increasing destructive disasters. Typhoon Ketsana was a category 2 equivalent typhoon and Typhoon Parma was a category 4 equivalent super typhoon. These storms caused widespread prolonged flooding, submerging entire cities and towns. Drainage systems were unable to keep up with the extensive flooding, leading to an immense amount of stagnant water. Hundreds of thousands of people were displaced as a result adn the excess runoff of water produced by the two tropical storms created a huge influx in the bacterial disease leptospirosis. The infection of leptospiria is a result of the contamination by animals and underground water runoff. The main cause of the outbreak was due to the mix of rat urine in contaminated water adn the warm standing water that increased the chances for survivors stuck in the typhoon area to contract bacteria through open wounds, the eyes, and the mouth. In addition, the typhoon's stagnant water that overflowed created a stable environment for the bacterial incubation. The disease came in a surplus through external factors such as heat, poor sanitation management, and the lack of municipal waste management. The exponential growth of the bacteria also influenced the spread of other acute diseases, both vector-borne and airborne. This caused a huge increase in malaria and dengue fever, as well. As a result, within a month of the storm, there were more than 2,100 confirmed cases and 167 deaths. It was widely considered one of the largest post-flood leptospirosis outbreaks in global medical history. Similarly, Hurricane Fiona (2022) experienced a significant amount of rainfall to create stagnant water runoff. Based on these weather patterns and the spread of Leptospirosis, scientists have been able to create predictive models such as the SEIR model and other technologies to prevent the massive spreading of future flood-born water diseases. In the future, due to increasing global temperatures at a rate of 0.20 degrees C per decade, water disasters will become more harsh and destructive. This is due to the effects of higher ocean heat content, allowing tropical cyclones to have a direct source of energy. Thus, these cyclones will lay the foundation for a greater spread of leptospirosis. By analyzing past disastrous events, and recognizing the reality of their existence and future "normality", scientists can predict leptospirosis patterns and thus prevent a large portion of deaths typically caused by these diseases.

497721.title: Accurate Conservative Zonal Averaging for Unstructured Earth-System Grids: A Python Implementation of Robust Spherical Geometry Algorithms
497721.authors: Rajeev Jain, ANL, Lemont, IL; and R. L. Jacob, H. Chen, and P. A. Ullrich
497721.abstract: Zonal averaging is among the most common diagnostics applied to Earth-system model output. On unstructured meshes it is a geometry problem rather than an array operation: each cell must be intersected with latitude-band boundaries and weighted by its true overlap area. That intersection is where accuracy is lost. When a cell edge runs nearly tangent to a band boundary, which arises constantly near the poles and on variable-resolution meshes, the cross product defining the intersection suffers catastrophic cancellation in double precision. Measured against a 60-digit reference, the standard computation misplaces the intersection point by 2.4 m at one hundred-millionth of a degree of tangency and by 227 m at one ten-billionth. That displacement propagates directly into the area weight each cell contributes to its band. We present a conservative zonal averaging capability in UXarray, the open-source Python library for unstructured Earth-system grid analysis used across DOE laboratories and NCAR. The geometric predicates are a Python and Numba port of AccuSphGeom, a C++ reference implementation of compensated-arithmetic algorithms for great-circle and constant-latitude intersection on the sphere. The port uses error-free transformations with hardware fused multiply-add and a portable fallback, so it carries no external dependency. On every tangency angle tested the compensated cross product agreed with the 60-digit reference exactly, while the naive form degraded from millimetres to hundreds of metres. The same operator runs on MPAS, ICON, E3SM, SCRIP, ESMF, and HEALPix through one interface. On HEALPix meshes conservative throughput rises from 0.8 to 1.8 million cells per second between 786 thousand and 12.6 million cells, and a 50.3 million cell case at approximately 3 km resolution completes in 137 seconds. Global spherical area is recovered to machine precision. We report accuracy and performance across grid families and identify where robust arithmetic changes the answer rather than only the runtime.

497722.title: Wire Material and Voltage Effects on Corona Inception for Atmospheric Ionization
497722.authors: Scott Morris, Rain Enhancement Technologies, Naples, FL; and A. Ruiz-Columbie and T. Gresham
497722.abstract: Corona discharge, the mechanism by which ground-based ionization systems generate charged aerosols for cloud seeding applications, is governed by conductor geometry, surface irregularity, and applied voltage. This presentation reports laboratory results characterizing how wire material and structure influence corona inception and resulting ion production, informing design optimization for operational ionization arrays such as the Weather Enhancement Technology Array (WETA) and Fog Removal by Electrical Activity (FREA) systems. Functional testing was conducted across multiple conductor materials, including copper, aluminum, and stainless steel, under applied voltages ranging from 20 to 100 kV in both positive and negative polarity. Ion production was quantified using a calibrated ion counter and gaussmeter, providing direct measurement of ionization extent as a function of material type and voltage. Testing was conducted at the individual wire-section level and is being extended to a scaled antenna configuration, approximately one-twentieth the size of a full operational WETA unit, to evaluate whether wire-level findings translate to full array geometry. Preliminary results indicate that surface irregularity and material contamination are primary drivers of corona inception, consistent with theoretical predictions from Peek's Formula relating corona inception voltage to conductor surface geometry. Wire with imperfect, irregular surface structure consistently outperformed smooth conductors in ion production across tested materials. Voltage-dependent behavior was also observed: below approximately 45 kV, increases in applied voltage produced only modest gains in measured ion output, while above this threshold, each 5 kV increment yielded substantial increases in ion count, particularly under negative polarity. These findings provide an empirical and theoretical basis for conductor selection and voltage optimization in ground-based ionization array design, with direct implications for improving ionization efficiency in operational precipitation and fog mitigation systems. Ongoing work extends this analysis to scaled antenna testing to validate wire-level findings under full-array operating conditions.

497723.title: Space Weather Solar Coronagraph (SwSCOR): Status and Path to Delivery
497723.authors: Craig E DeForest, Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO; and R. Killough, M. Beasley, N. Erickson, K. Sacca, T. Smith, and A. Flores
497723.abstract: The Space Weather Solar Coronagraph (SwSCOR) is a next-generation compact-style coronagraph that is under development at SwRI for the SOLAR-A mission. SwSCOR builds on lessons learned from recent single-occulter coronagraphs such as NFI and CCOR, to become a robust source of steady coronal imaging. SwSCOR development is well underway, with environmental testing of a flight-like engineering development unit (EDU) happening in summer 2026 and Critical Design Review scheduled for early fall 2026. We report on current status, issues overcome, and projected schedule for the SwSCOR project.

497730.title: HelioShield: An Agentic R2O2R Framework for AI-Enabled Space Weather Forecasting
497730.authors: Christopher Ramos, Warriors Garden Solutions, Peyton, CO
497730.abstract: Space weather machine-learning models increasingly demonstrate promising performance in research environments, but transitioning these capabilities into operationally useful systems requires more than predictive skill alone. Operational systems must continuously acquire heterogeneous observations, assess data quality and freshness, reproduce model inputs, preserve provenance, expose uncertainty and supporting evidence, and present model outputs in a form that forecasters and downstream systems can understand and evaluate. We present HelioShield, a modular framework designed to address these challenges and help bridge the research-to-operations-to-research (R2O2R) gap for AI-enabled space weather forecasting. HelioShield integrates heterogeneous solar and heliospheric observations into a common data and inference architecture. Current data sources include Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) imagery, Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) active-region magnetic-field measurements and SHARP parameters, GOES X-ray observations, and solar-wind measurements. The framework monitors source availability, latency, completeness, and data freshness; preserves source-specific provenance; and transforms observations into standardized tensors, features, and time-series records suitable for machine-learning applications. Historical replay and near-real-time workflows share defined input contracts, allowing research experiments, validation studies, and runs inference on live operational data to operate against a common processing backbone. A pilot 24-hour solar-flare forecasting capability provides the initial demonstration of this architecture. HelioShield supports sequence-based and multimodal modeling approaches that combine the temporal evolution of active-region magnetic properties with AIA imagery and engineered solar features to estimate probabilistic flare occurrence. The emphasis of this work, however, is not solely on the predictive skill of an individual model. Instead, the flare workflow provides a test case for examining the broader infrastructure required to transition a research-grade machine-learning capability toward operational experimentation. HelioShield is also being extended beyond conventional model serving through a knowledge and agentic reasoning layer. A knowledge graph connects observations, active regions, model runs, predictions, event relationships, provenance, and supporting scientific context. Model predictions and their associated inference context are exposed via application programming interfaces (APIs) and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, enabling AI agents and external systems to retrieve both forecast outputs and the evidence supporting them. An agentic workflow can then use this information to generate traceable forecast discussions that describe what the system observed, what the model predicted, and the contextual information supporting that prediction. OpenTelemetry-based observability provides an additional layer of traceability across data ingestion, processing, inference, and system interactions. This work examines the architectural and methodological challenges involved in moving AI-enabled space weather forecasting across the R2O2R “valley of death.” We discuss lessons learned from aligning asynchronous observations, handling missing or degraded inputs, monitoring live-data freshness, maintaining parity between retrospective and near-real-time workflows, preserving lineage from source observations to predictions, and exposing model context to both humans and machine agents. We also consider how operational use, system observability, and human interaction can provide feedback for subsequent model evaluation and development. HelioShield demonstrates a pathway toward an AI-enabled space weather architecture in which reproducible science, probabilistic forecasting, machine-readable knowledge, agentic reasoning, and operational experimentation are treated as components of a single R2O2R lifecycle.

497735.title: Establishing a Framework for the Evaluation of Informed Decision-Making in Weather Events
497735.authors: Kimberly E. Klockow McClain, CPAESS, Norman, OK
497735.abstract: As our community has begun to take up the language of informed decision-making as a central goal of weather forecasting, the need is steadily growing to define what constitutes informed decision-making in a weather forecast context. In particular, the decisions individuals are making are spatio-temporal in nature, yet dominant models of informed decision-making come from fields such as medicine or engineering which do not translate perfectly in these aspects. This presentation will provide an overview of a proposed framework for assessing informed decision-making in a post event study. This will include consideration of key aspects of informed decision-making used in other fields, extended into the dimensions of space-time. The proposed framework is anticipated to become part of an evaluation framework for monitoring and evaluating the effects of communication system upgrades, changes, or shocks.

497736.title: R2O of the Evaporative Demand Drought Index at NOAA's Climate Prediction Center and the Opportunities It Offers to Monitor, Forecast, and Understand the Demand Side of Extremes In the Hydrologic Cycle.
497736.authors: Mike Hobbins, University of Colorado, BOULDER, CO; and M. R. Abel, Y. Pan, A. J. Ray, and H. Wang
497736.abstract: The Evaporative Demand Drought Index (EDDI) is a multi-scalar standardized drought index that focuses on the demand side of drought—that of evaporative demand, or the “thirst of the atmosphere.” Both the drought index and the evaporative demand that underpins it have demonstrated capabilities in the monitoring and early warning of agricultural and hydrological drought, wildfire-risk monitoring, flash-drought detection, and beyond. EDDI was recently operationalized at the NOAA-Climate Prediction Center (CPC), where it is used in the production of their operational sub-seasonal drought outlook products: the CPC Rapid Onset Drought, as part of the U.S. Week-2 Hazards Outlook, and the Monthly Drought Outlook. EDDI also has a wide variety of external end-users across several sectors, including contributing authors of the U.S. Drought Monitor, which is produced by the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska Lincoln, U.S. Department of Agriculture, and NOAA. EDDI is also pushed to the NOAA’s Drought.gov portal. EDDI is estimated on a daily basis from data from phase 2 of the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS-2) driving the ASCE Standardized Reference Evapotranspiration equation; this Penman-Monteith equation has become the gold standard for estimating atmospheric evaporative demand as it encodes the influence of all relevant physical drivers—air temperature, humidity, solar radiation, and wind speed. That this equation is differentiable with respect to all drivers lends it to a close examination and decomposition of anomalies in evaporative demand, permitting us to answer the fundamental question, "what drives changes in the demand side of the hydrologic cycle and where?" Answering this question uncovers for the first time the drivers of the extremes in the hydrologic cycle forcing droughts, wildfires, aridification, and more. These decomposition results are available on a daily basis in CPC's new implementation of EDDI. Further work at CPC will add a seasonal forecast component to EDDI, which will enhance their suite of drought outlooks. This presentation will touch briefly on the history of EDDI and its recent transition to operations at CPC, but will mainly concentrate on the current and potential uses of EDDI and the underlying CONUS-wide evaporative demand dataset; their uses in drought monitoring; and the new value-added products that resulted from the R2O process, including examining drought- and wildfire- related case studies of the decomposition of evaporative demand. We will finally look forward beyond the monitoring framework to both seasonal forecasts of EDDI and the possible NLDAS3-based product, which, as a truly continental-scale product, stands to bring all the advantages of EDDI and its value-added products to heretofore underserved populations.

497740.title: Resilience Education through Local Community Analysis
497740.authors: Suzanne Metlay, Western Governors University, Salt Lake City, UT; and J. Riley and B. McCann
497740.abstract: Multimedia presentations about local communities are an essential aspect of several courses in Earth Sciences Education programs at Western Governors University’s School of Education. Assignments require teacher candidates to demonstrate content competence through analysis of local issues regarding weather, climate, natural hazards, and environmental management. This leads to greater understanding of effective planning for community resilience. WGU is a private nonprofit mostly-online university accredited to provide educational credentials for undergraduate and graduate students in all states, territories, and military bases of the United States. WGU School of Education pre-service and of-record teachers are prepared to become elementary, middle school, and high school Earth science educators with subject matter expertise in geology, meteorology, oceanography, astronomy, and geoscience pedagogy. Undergraduate courses in Secondary Science Education include Natural Hazards and Environmental Management with Lab. Graduate students in Secondary Earth Sciences Curriculum assess weather and climate learning resources for alignment with state standards. Earth Sciences educators seeking state licensure are required to pass state content and/or Praxis assessments as well as complete in-person training (student teaching) in an Earth Sciences classroom. WGU Earth Sciences Education students are frequently tasked to record themselves explaining key concepts through a local lens to enhance their public communication skills with various presentation methods. Effective science communication is vital for teaching students and their families about the hazards and opportunities of their local environments. As a national leader in Earth Sciences teacher workforce development, WGU emphasizes local community analysis. Teachers play essential roles in community resilience and are critical to effective emergency responses. This presentation will go into further detail about specific courses and assignments with respect to resilience education.

497741.title: Albedo Symmetries under a Dimming Earth
497741.authors: Jianhao Zhang, Univ. of Colorado/CIRES, Boulder, CO; and J. J. Gristey
497741.abstract: Earth’s albedo is fundamental to the planetary energy budget. The persistence of hemispheric symmetries in reflected sunlight, despite strong spatial variations in clouds, surface properties, and atmospheric circulation, remains both a challenge for climate models and an opportunity to better understand coupling within the Earth system. Building on our recent discovery of a persistent east–west albedo symmetry, we systematically investigate Earth’s broader set of albedo symmetries in CERES observations and CMIP6 models, including their evolution over time. As the Earth warms, changes in clouds, circulation, and surface albedo are reshaping reflected sunlight and increasing Earth’s energy imbalance. We examine whether and how albedo symmetries are maintained under these evolving radiative patterns, and how their trends relate to large-scale overturning circulations. Conversely, observed Earth-dimming patterns may reveal the mechanisms that preserve, shift, or disrupt these symmetries. Because albedo symmetries integrate radiative and dynamical responses across large spatial scales, their persistence and evolution provide a compact constraint on the global warming pattern. Comparing these relationships between observations and CMIP6 models offers a new framework for diagnosing model biases and constraining climate models.

497742.title: Predicting Dst with SOLAR-1 data and LSTM neural networks
497742.authors: Sara Gasca, NESDIS, Orange, CA; NOAA, Louisville, MD; NESDIS, Takoma Park; NOAA, Greenbelt, MD; and N. J. Zaremba
497742.abstract: To safeguard society from space weather events, NOAA's Office of Space Weather Observations (SWO) develops, deploys, and maintains operational satellites. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s office of Space Weather Observations (SWO) most recent satellite, Space weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness (SOLAR-1), provides continuous operational space weather data from Lagrange 1. The SOLAR-1 data provides the Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) the information needed to issue warnings of space weather events to stakeholders and the public. There is growing interest in exploring and possibly leveraging machine learning techniques to aid in predicting space weather events. MagNet is a Long Short-Term Memory(LSTM) neural network model developed through the 2020-2021 NOAA/CIRES MagNet data-driven forecasting competition, with contributions from Rob Redmon, Manoj Nair, and collaborators. The model was originally trained on data from DSCOVR and ACE to predict planetary indices such as the disturbance storm index (Dst). This project ingests SOLAR-1 data from the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) Space Weather Portal (SPOT) into the MagNet LSTM and analyzes the results. The integration of operational SOLAR-1 data into the MagNet model continues the exploration of ML techniques for geomagnetic storm prediction; techniques that could aid NOAA in executing its mission

497744.title: Evaluating Particulate Matter Retrievals from the Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) Mission in Urban and Rural North Carolina
497744.authors: Stella Foreman, The University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL; and E. Boakye Yiadom and I. Chang
497744.abstract: Fine particulate matter with diameter less than 2.5 μm (PM2.5) is a common pollutant associated with severe health complications, making monitoring critical. PM2.5 can be monitored via surface-based observations or estimated using satellite data, which fills spatial coverage gaps between surface monitors. TEMPO (Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution) detects small-scale spatial and temporal variations in air quality through hourly observations, capturing how PM2.5 changes throughout the day. Additionally, TEMPO is capable of detecting aerosol layer height, allowing for more accurate surface PM2.5 estimation from aerosol optical depth. We evaluated the performance of the TEMPO-ABI PM2.5 product by comparing values to EPA AirData hourly surface-based PM2.5 measurements. 22 EPA PM2.5 monitors across North Carolina and TEMPO pixels within 1500 m of those monitors were selected for comparison, with data selected for six dates between June 2024 and June 2025. Relationships between TEMPO-ABI and EPA AirData PM2.5 values were evaluated with a focus on diurnal variation and differences between urban and rural areas. Findings show that TEMPO-ABI PM2.5 estimations were strongly correlated with EPA surface PM2.5 measurements (R = 0.87) with similar diurnal variation trends. No trend was observed between population density and PM2.5 concentration; estimation error varied slightly with density but performance remained strong overall, with bias ranging from -0.14 μg/m3 in rural areas to -0.29 μg/m3 in urban areas. These findings confirm that TEMPO can detect diurnal variation in PM2.5 values across urban and rural areas and can provide highly localized, hourly PM2.5 data, filling gaps in areas without monitors.

497745.title: Diagnosing and Correcting Imbalance in a Neural Data Assimilation System via a Learned Latent Coordinate
497745.authors: Karina Apodaca, Spire Global Subsidiary, Inc., Boulder, CO; Spire Global Subsidiary, Inc., Boulder, CO
497745.abstract: Neural data assimilation (DA) systems are typically trained and evaluated based on how closely their analyses align with a reanalysis target, with the expectation that the system will learn physical balance through training. Variational systems incorporate mass–wind coupling through the control-variable transform and reduce residual gravity-wave noise using tangent-linear normal-mode constraints or digital filtering. In contrast, a learned increment operator encodes only the balance represented in its training targets and loss function. We argue that dynamical balance should be treated both as a diagnostic and as an explicit design constraint in machine learning-based data assimilation (ML-based DA). We illustrate this approach using Spire's AI-based DA system, in which heterogeneous observations are integrated through per-observation-type cross-attention on a HEALPix Vision Transformer backbone. Imbalance is most critical during the forecasting step: irregularities that may be tolerated in a single analysis can become amplified when the resulting increments are introduced into an ML forecast model whose attractor differs from that of the training reanalysis. Using Spire’s proprietary observations and other publicly available observations, we evaluate candidate analyses based on the medium-range forecast skill they produce rather than solely on their fit to the training target. The unconstrained residual decoder serves as the control, minimizing channel-wise errors against ERA5 without an explicit mechanism to enforce mass–wind coupling or suppress spurious divergent modes. We compare this control with two formulations that impose balance at different stages: (1) a post hoc filter applied to the learned increments, and (2) a latent-space variational solver in which a learned background-error covariance and observation decoder constrain the increment through the cost function. Forecast skill is evaluated against ERA5 at multiple lead times, with forecasts initialized from both ECMWF's IFS and ERA5. We present which formulation performs best at different lead times and identify the balance diagnostics that explain the observed differences in forecast performance.

497757.title: 2027 AMS EIPT Key Technology Keynote - Transition to Enterprise Cloud Capabilities
497757.abstract: The Environmental Information Processing Technologies Committee (EIPT), in collaboration with the Research to Operations Conference (R2O) and the High Performance Computing Symposium (HPC), is pleased to announce the inaugural EIPT Key Technology Keynote. This keynote session will highlight NOAA's development of enterprise cloud capabilities for data preservation, access, and applications. These efforts support shifting from legacy on-premises infrastructure that has historically constrained scalability and performance. Additionally, the discussion will cover the adoption of advanced coding technologies and tools that facilitate these modernization efforts. The panel features the following expert speakers: Ken Casey, Division Chief, Data Stewardship Division, NOAA/NESDIS/NCEI Scott Jacobs, Branch Chief, NOAA/NWS/OS/Mission Services and Technology Ryan May, Unidata Ryan Abernathy, Earthmover During the session, panelists will examine the motivations, challenges, achievements, and future roadmaps of these initiatives, aiming to provide stakeholders, partner agencies, and collaborators with essential updates on these strategic efforts.

497759.title: Understanding Temporal Variability and Meteorological Drivers of PM10 and PM2.5 dynamics at South Padre Island in South Texas, USA.
497759.authors: Amit U. Raysoni, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, Brownsville, TX; and I. A. Yussif, S. D. Pinakana, M. Rizwan, M. Dahal, and A. M. Mestas-Nunez
497759.abstract: Particulate matter (PM) includes solid and liquid particles suspended in the air. Literature has indicated a relationship between negative health impacts and particles that have aerodynamic diameters smaller than 2.5 μm (PM2.5) and 10 μm (PM10). The sources of these particles vary, encompassing a broad spectrum of natural and anthropogenic activities. While PM10 mainly originates from sea salt, soil dust resuspension, and construction/demolition, PM2.5 is primarily produced by combustion processes, forest fires, and transformation of gaseous species. The local and regional attainment of the National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) is assessed by utilizing data from the State and Local Air Monitoring Stations (SLAMS) network. However, almost two-thirds of U.S. counties lack an ambient air quality monitoring station. Recently, low-cost sensors are bridging this research gap by delivering crucial data in regions lacking federal monitoring stations. This study used a QuantAQ sensor to record the PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations at South Padre Island from March – July 2025. The dual-detection capabilities of the QuantAQ units, which combine a nephelometer and Optical Particle Counters (OPC), provide accurate concentration measurements across all particle sizes, making them superior to other sensors considered. The results will present temporal trends, showing the variability between weekends to weekdays and rush hours to non-peak hours. Meteorological factors like wind speed and direction influence concentrations, and this will be shown in the results. The coastal-inland comparison of PM10 will be demonstrated by comparing it with data recorded at the TCEQ (Texas Commission on Environmental Quality) Continuous Ambient Monitoring Station CAMS-43 located at Mission. This study demonstrates the utility of low-cost sensors in supporting traditional networks and highlights localized air quality dynamics in a coastal environment.

497760.title: Impact of Turbulence Modeled with an LES Model with Varying Resolutions on the Simulation of Deep Warm Convective Clouds
497760.authors: Yubao Liu, Nanjing University of Information and Science Technology, Nanjing, CO, China; and T. Yang and Q. Liu
497760.abstract: Atmospheric turbulence regulates the dynamical and microphysical processes of convective clouds, but the effects of turbulent eddies at different scales on deep warm convective clouds, as well as the model resolution required to represent these effects, remain unclear. This study conducts idealized modeling experiments using Weather Research and Forecasting Large Eddy Simulation (WRF-LES). The simulations are driven by a single atmospheric thermodynamic sounding from an observed convection event, and the convection is triggered by embedding a localized cylindrical warm bubble. Using this configuration, this study investigates the sensitivity of resolved turbulent mixing in a warm convective cloud simulation with horizontal grid spacings of 240 m, 120 m, 40 m, and 24 m. The results show that the LES grid resolution critically controls the resolved turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), which in turn governs cloud macroscopic characteristics, microphysical processes, and precipitation efficiency. At the 240 m grid spacing, about 74% of the TKE is represented, which leads to excessive entrainment mixing, loss of convective buoyancy, and thus markedly weak updrafts and lower cloud tops. In contrast, the LES experiments with 40 m and 24 m model grids resolve over 92% of the TKE and reproduce reasonable turbulent mixing, strong updrafts, and deep clouds. Analysis shows that these finer grids achieve a balanced representation of entrainment mixing processes and support a reasonable collision-coalescence droplet growth mechanism. They also produce a theoretically consistent, heavy-tailed supersaturation probability distribution. The 40 m grid model captures key turbulent flow features and interactions between turbulence and microphysics as well as the 24 m runs, with only a 6.2% difference in total rainfall from the latter. Based on our idealized simulation of the specific convection scenario, in general, a grid spacing of approximately 40 m appears to reproduce the main turbulence and microphysical behaviors found in the experiment with grid spacings of 24 m.

497762.title: In Situ Measurements in Diverse Microclimate Environments
497762.authors: Loren David White, Jackson State University, Jackson, MS
497762.abstract: Since the summer of 2016, various observational efforts grouped under the Coordinated Multiscale Meteorological Measurements (CM3) initiative have been made to investigate local microclimates under funding from the National Science Foundation (NSF), Department of Energy (DOE), and NOAA. Data collection during 2019 was part of the CHEESEHEAD project with the University of Wisconsin Madison. Initial microclimate investigations concentrated on mobile measurements using pedestrian and kayak sensor platforms. Mobile data collection was preferentially done with cloud-free sky conditions and light wind for maximum surface heterogeneity. Beginning in 2023, Hobologger temperature/humidity sensors were also deployed for periods ranging from weeks to years. Complimentary data nearby have been collected by other investigators and observing networks. While the majority of sites are in Missouri, Wisconsin, and Mississippi, two high elevation sites were documented in Arizona and West Virginia. Quality control and analysis procedures for dataset curation before publication will be discussed.

497764.title: Turning Research into Actionable Information: Public-Private Partnerships in an Era of Climate Extremes
497764.abstract: The science surrounding climate change is clear: it is unequivocal that humans have warmed the climate, and human‑induced climate change is already increasing many weather and climate perils around the globe. This reality has created increased volatility for many institutions, amplifying physical risk and generating additional uncertainty for the insurance industry. This talk provides context on recent industry losses due to natural perils and examines the role that climate change may (or may not) play in increasing the frequency or severity of such events in light of evolving science. Challenges, caveats, and new tools for forming a future‑focused view of risk are discussed, with an emphasis on public‑private partnerships that translate academic research into actionable information.

497765.title: Linking Mesoscale Convective System Tracks to Extreme Precipitation: A Satellite-Driven and Ensemble Modeling Analysis of the 2015 Texas Flood Event
497765.authors: Samkeyat Shohan, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and H. I. Chang, C. Castro, C. B. Risanto, Y. Chikamoto, and P. Bunn
497765.abstract: Convection permitting model (CPM) ensembles are increasingly used to simulate mesoscale convective systems (MCSs), yet their reliability as hazard diagnostic tools is typically assessed using ensemble mean or domain aggregated statistics that can mask disagreement among individual members. This study applies a single brightness temperature (Tb) based tracking algorithm uniformly to MERGIR observations and to each member of a ten member CESM downscaled CPM ensemble to evaluate MCS–precipitation relationships during the 21–31 May 2015 Texas extreme weather event, with cross validation against Stage IV and GPM IMERG precipitation. At the observational level, cold core MCS track density and heavy precipitation occurrence are co located (domain wide AUC ≥ 0.73 across 10–30 mm h⁻¹), although the strength and character of this relationship vary regionally: intensity is comparatively decoupled from track density in the Blanco River/Austin corridor but scales closely with it near Houston. The CPM ensemble reproduces this spatial association only when evaluated member by member: internal predictive skill (own track density versus own precipitation) ranges from below chance to near excellent (AUC 0.31–0.95), while conformity to the observed MERGIR track pattern spans a similarly wide, non collinear range (0.51–0.98). The pooled ensemble mean does not outperform the best individual members. At the event scale, all members reproduce the correct sign for the Tb–precipitation extreme relationship, and nine of ten for the duration–accumulated precipitation relationship. Pooled ensemble estimates are statistically indistinguishable from both observational products, yet this aggregate agreement conceals a sign reversal in one member. Across all three analyses, aggregate statistics suggest adequate ensemble performance, whereas member resolved statistics reveal substantial, hazard relevant disagreement, supporting the treatment of CPM ensembles as populations of distinct realizations rather than as a single averaged product. Building on these findings, ongoing work is developing an MCS intensity metric derivable solely from Tb based tracking, designed to be portable across ensemble modeling frameworks, including MPAS based global ensembles, and applicable at global scale.

497767.title: Development of the Global GEO-LEO 3-D Flood Mapping System
497767.authors: Sanmei Li, Global Science & Technology, Inc., Greenbelt, MD; Global Science and Technology, Inc., Greenbelt, MD; NOAA/NESDIS/STAR, College Park, MD; and M. Y. Murphy, S. Kalluri, L. Zhou, D. Lindsey, M. McHugh, M. D. Goldberg, and D. Sun
497767.abstract: Optical satellite imagery has been widely applied in detecting spatial flood extent. In 2022, NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) declared operational flood products from JPSS (Joint Polar Satellite System)/VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) imagery. These products, including a VIIRS near real-time granule flood product, a VIIRS daily composited flood product and a VIIRS 5-day composited flood product, provide flood extent at 375-m spatial resolution covering major global land from 80°S to 80°N. Later in 2024, another operational flood product from GOES-R/ABI (including GOES-16, 17, 18 and 19) was declared to provide near real-time flood extent with the maximal clear-sky coverage during daytime at 1-km spatial resolution in Mainland of America Continent from 50.5°S to 50.5°N. A blended VIIRS/ABI flood product, fusing the VIIRS 375-m flood extent and 1-km ABI flood extent together and thus inheriting the advantages of both VIIRS and ABI flood products, becomes operationally available in 2025 with the same spatial coverage as ABI flood products. All these products, available on the website: https://www.ssec.wisc.edu/flood-map-demo/flood-products/ and https://noaa-jpss.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html#JPSS_Blended_Products/, play significant roles in global/regional near real-time flood mapping with reliable quality for the user community. However, one issue with these flood products is that they only provide horizontal flood extent at coarse-to-moderate spatial resolution from 1km to 375m. Flood operations require more detailed inundation information for flood investigation and disaster mitigation. With the development of a downscaling model, the VIIRS 375-m floodwater fraction products have been applied to produce VIIRS 3-D flood products including a VIIRS 30-m floodwater depth product and a 375-m floodwater surface level product along with the Copernicus Digital Surface Model (CDSM), tree cover and watershed data. Different to the original VIIRS 375-m flood products, which only provide 2-D spatial distribution of flood extent at 375-m spatial resolution, the 3-D flood products not only provide flood extent at 30-m resolution but also show the vertical distribution of floodwater. Recently, new research has also proved of a high feasibility to derive 3-D flood products from the ABI 1-km flood product with similar quality to the VIIRS 3-D flood products. Validation on these downscaled 30-m floodwater depth products using a large amount of high-resolution satellite images from Landsat-8&9/OLI and Sentinel-2 indicates an average accuracy above 85%, which meets the requirements on flood investigation for flood operations. The reliable flood detection and downscaling algorithms show a strong flexibility to be adjusted to other optical satellite imagery similar with VIIRS and ABI imagery. Successful experiments include flood detection with Himawari-8&9/AHI imagery and Sentinel-3/SLSTR imagery based on similar algorithms. NOAA has been hosting a Himawari-8&9/AHI 1-km flood product since 2020 and a Sentinel-3A/SLSTR 500-m flood product since 2022 through SSEC/CIMSS and these products are also available in SSEC’s Real Earth. With these capabilities, it is highly possible to construct a global GEO-LEO 3-D flood mapping system which can be used to produce multiple-scale flood products horizontally and vertically. With global LEO flood products from JPSS/VIIRS and Sentinel-3/SLSTR as the base products, GEO flood products from GOES-R/ABI, Himawari-8&9/AHI, MTG/FCI and other similar GEO satellite imagery can be used to fill the gaps of clouds and cloud shadows in the global LEO flood products. The blended results can provide global flood extent at 375-m spatial resolution for near real-time large-scale flood monitoring. The LEO and GEO flood products can be further downscaled to derive 30-m floodwater depth products, respectively, and then combined to get a blended GEO-LEO 30-m floodwater depth products with the maximal clear-sky coverage for near real-time small-scale flood monitoring. Additionally, NOAA flood team is also conducting research and development on global SAR flood products from Sentine-1, Radarsat-2 and RCM. These products can be merged with either the 375-m blended GEO-LEO flood product or the 30-m GEO-LEO floodwater depth product for flood mapping under cloud/cloud shadows. Such 3-D GEO-LEO flood mapping system, providing flood products with daily global coverage and capturing the maximal clear-sky coverage during daytime, assures powerful capabilities for global flood mapping in near real time to benefit the user community.

497768.title: Extratropical Storms Fundamentally Shape the Maritime Surface Wind Divergence and Vorticity Climatology
497768.authors: Larry W. O'Neill, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR; and R. Jacobs, D. Chelton, and R. Milliff
497768.abstract: Effects of synoptic weather variability on the climatological wind field over the global oceans has been unresolved due to lack of observations and difficulty clearly distinguishing storms from weaker background variability. This study reveals that synoptic weather variability imprints onto the climatological-mean wind field over the global oceans in a surprising manner. Mid-latitude storm events, defined as predominantly associated with extratropical cyclones, typically generate large-amplitude but short-lived convergent and cyclonic wind anomalies which are unambiguous from other processes. Using maritime surface vector winds from QuikSCAT satellite observations and ERA-Interim reanalysis, we show that removing fewer than 5% of the strongest convergent and cyclonic wind events removes nearly all time-mean convergence and cyclonic vorticity poleward of 50° latitude. Relatively few synoptic-scale weather events thus account for dynamically important features in the large-scale atmospheric circulation. Since the large-scale ocean response to wind forcing on the short timescales of synoptic weather events is weak, this result has important implications for understanding processes that drive the mid-latitude ocean circulation, which is generally thought to be driven by lower frequency wind variability. Climate model projections suggest that climate change will affect the location, frequency, and strength of synoptic-scale activity within the mid-latitude storm tracks. The derivative wind fields may aid assessment of how storms affect the large-scale atmospheric and oceanic circulation in climate model projections.

497772.title: WeatherMesh: An Observation-Native Architecture for Probabilistic Weather Prediction
497772.authors: Anuj Shetty, WindBorne Systems, Redwood City, CA
497772.abstract: Most AI weather prediction systems are trained primarily to reproduce trajectories from a numerical reanalysis. WeatherMesh increasingly uses observations themselves to construct and evaluate the forecast state. Surface observations, radiosondes, WindBorne balloons, satellite sounders, GPS radio occultation, radar, and geostationary imagery are mapped into a common latent atmospheric representation. Learned data assimilation updates each of 128 ensemble members independently, allowing observational information to interact with the distinct background state of every member. The resulting ensemble retains initial-state uncertainty while incorporating recent measurements for well-calibrated probabilistic prediction. The role of observations continues throughout training. WeatherMesh predicts measurements in their native spaces and is scored against station data, atmospheric profiles, radar fields, satellite observations, and high-resolution regional products. This provides information at locations, resolutions, and times that are not fully represented by a global reanalysis. A common observation interface allows new sources to be added without redesigning the complete data-assimilation or forecast architecture. We present the internal representation and training methods used to combine these observations within a well-calibrated ensemble forecasting system.

497774.title: Updates to the Automated Vehicle Operability Framework for an Urban Dust Storm Using Large-Eddy Simulations
497774.authors: Brittany Marie Welch, NCAR, Boulder, CO; and A. R. Siems-Anderson and D. C. Walker
497774.abstract: Adverse weather can reduce the operability of electric vehicles (EVs) and autonomous vehicles (AVs), particularly when rapidly changing conditions affect vehicle control or perception of the surrounding environment. An operability framework presented at the 2026 American Meteorological Society Annual Meeting used the FastEddy® large-eddy simulation (LES) model to examine how fine-scale weather conditions could help determine operable from inoperable periods for automated vehicles. The initial framework demonstrated the potential value of LES but needed further tuning to represent visibility impacts from dust appropriately. The updated framework will calculate operability at each model-output interval and refine the contribution of turbulence through sensitivity testing. Weather related degradation of onboard sensing will also be incorporated by translating modeled low-visibility conditions into estimated changes in sensor detection distance. This addition allows operability to reflect the ability of an AV to perceive the surrounding roadway environment. The framework will be applied to the May 16, 2025, dust storm that developed over central Illinois and moved into the Chicago metropolitan area, producing sudden near zero visibility and wind gusts exceeding 60 mph. FastEddy® passive scalar dispersion capabilities will be used to represent the transport of a dust like tracer and visualize the movement of a localized low-visibility plume. Spatial and temporal variability of this makeshift dust plume will be used to investigate where LES provides additional information for AV operability in low visibility conditions. This framework development will also be discussed in the context of an AV and weather session held at the SAE Automated Vehicle Symposium. Outcomes of weather information needs and coordination between the transportation and weather communities will be briefly discussed and tied into the development. This work extends the initial proof of concept toward an operability framework that can support event-based assessments and future applications across additional cities.

497779.title: Retrieving Global 3D Precipitation Radar Reflectivity Based on Advanced Imager Payload Aboard Geostationary Satellite
497779.authors: Yubao Liu, NUIST, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China; and H. Gao and Y. Qin
497779.abstract: 3D atmospheric hydrometeors measured by radars play crucial roles in hazardous weather such as heavy rain, hail, and strong winds, but ground-based precipitation radars only cover very limited parts of the globe. This presentation introduces a 3D radar reflectivity reconstruction model, G-S2RNet (a Global Satellite to Radar reflectivity retrieval Network), to retrieve high-resolution (1 km horizontally, 0.5–1 km vertically) 3D radar reflectivity over the globe based on the advanced Imager payloads on selected geostationary satellites. The Japanese Advanced Himawari Imager (AHI, 16-channel), US GOES-R ABI, Chinese FY-4B AGRI, and European MTG FCI together provide a global coverage except for the polar regions. G-S2Rnet is an extend version of a 3D-S2RNet (three-dimensional S2RNet), which integrates a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN), 2D/3D attention mechanisms, and a weighted composite loss strategy to retrieve the structural details of 3D radar reflectivity. 3D-S2RNet is trained based on the Himawari AHI as inputs and the 3D S-band Radar reflectivity mosaic in Eastern China as labels. The trained 3D-S2RNet is then adapted to the GOES-R ABI, FY-4B, and MTG FCI data, respectively. The 3D radar reflectivity retrievals from these geostationary satellites are then fused together to produce 1-km resolution global 3D reflectivity fields. General assessments and retrievals of various severe weather systems, including squall lines, typhoons, frontal systems, and low-latitude rain clusters, over different continents and oceans over the globe, will be presented at the meeting. We foresee a profound application potential of this capability for severe weather forecasting, climate modeling, and many cloud-sensitive industrial applications including aviation, solar energy, and hydrometeorology.

497781.title: The 2025 GOTHAAM Field Study Explored Air Composition In and Around New York City. A First Look at Airborne Observations of Carbon Dioxide, Carbon Monoxide, Methane and Nitrous Oxide Will be Presented, Placing Air Composition Measurements In the Context of Local and Transported Emissions and Air Mass Transformations.
497781.authors: Teresa L Campos, NSF NCAR, Louisville, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; NCAR, Boulder, CO; and P. R. Veres, B. Stephens, and K. Ullmann
497781.abstract: The 2025 GOTHAAM field study explored air composition in and around New York City. A first look at airborne observations of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, methane and nitrous oxide will be presented, placing air composition measurements in the context of local and transported emissions and air mass transformations.

497785.title: Empirical Analysis of Coastal and Wetland Surface Layer Observations from Hurricane Katrina (2005)
497785.authors: James Robert Howard, Meteorologist, Ponchatoula, LA
497785.abstract: Observations from coastal regions during a tropical cyclone (TC) at landfall remain sparse despite advances in observing systems and some rapid dissemination of such information to the general public, as access to these areas is often problematic.
