Large questions remain as to the structure of the planetary boundary layer within TCs (TCPBL) at landfall, particularly regarding the TCPBL interaction with land masses, terrain features, structures, wetlands, tidal lakes, and offshore shallow water regions, and any changes that occur to these as a hurricane approaches and moves over land through those areas. Some of the answers to these questions are linked to the formation and growth of internal boundary layers, and changes to the near-shore wave and surge fields, which remain largely unknown because either geographic distances between observations are too large to resolve smaller-scale features, dropsondes cannot be launched over land due to safety concerns, or radars pass above the lowest part of the boundary layer. Obtaining the answers to these preliminary questions requires high-temporal resolution observations and serves as a starting point for determining how the wind modifies the surge and wave fields, how those control the extent and duration of precipitation-induced estuarial flooding due to runoff and backup during a landfall, and how coastal erosion and land loss, both occur as a result in the short-term (hours) and long-term (days or weeks). These factors determine future coastal restoration and TC mitigation efforts. Answers to those questions also have significant implications to what occurs in the surface layer, and to the inhabitants of coastal regions who live there. During Hurricane Katrina (2005) field programs supplemented fixed automated in-situ and remote observing systems and hurricane reconnaissance airborne and dropsonde observations by placing various forms of portable in-situ and remote observing equipment in the expected path. Data from one or two of these portable stations and one to three fixed, normally continuously operating, stations are analyzed to show the effects of local and regional terrain on the wind field, in particular the turbulent and mean wind characteristics, as well as the effects of changes to the local terrain initially driven by wind forcing on the water (for instance through storm surge inundation and its retreat contributing to land loss). Analysis techniques may include adaptations of previous, well documented techniques using both gust factors and turbulence intensities to determine surface roughness. Those techniques may be applied to additional data from another hurricane should that data become available prior to the presentation. The data from Katrina will be coupled with aerial satellite imagery nearby to some station locations in order to determine short-term changes in surface ground structure that occurred due to inundation or wind damage to vegetation. When more accurate wind, surface roughness, and land use information are available for input into wind, wave, surge, and river and water body height forecast models, the timing and duration of inundation and extent of erosion can be more accurately forecast. While the results from these techniques should contribute to answering questions regarding short-term changes to the surface layer wind field, perhaps some questions about coastal land loss from hurricanes, and perhaps some questions pertaining to long-term changes to the coastal human environment, further study is required to answer the larger question of how to model future coastal land loss and then restore and protect land areas lost due to a hurricane, other weather events, and other factors outside of the meteorology and hydrology, while maintaining coastal land, livelihoods, and communities. Those studies may include, but are not limited to, the following: 1. a significant increase in a. real-time, in event, field observing systems, particularly from the surface to at least 500 m above the boundary layer height, and b. continuous everyday coastal and nearby upstream inland wind and water observing systems, particularly in areas where large gaps still exist, 2. a. a more advanced modeling of the tropical cyclone wind field, within the surface layer through to above the boundary layer, b. wind modeling coupled with modeling of the wave, and water fields, observation and modeling of precipitation and runoff into inland watersheds and estuaries, and 3. more detailed observation and modeling studies of the impacts of the meteorological and hydrological fields, both near-shore and inland, to coastal land degradation from tropical cyclones and other weather events, and how to replace and restore those areas lost. While not all of these studies will be included in future work, aspects of each pertaining to how the structure of the TCPBL horizontal wind field at landfall changes, particularly where it directly relates to the surface layer, contributes to modification of the wave and surge fields and forecasting, and the modification of coastal land and wetland areas will be part of future research.

497786.title: Closing the R2O Loop: How IOOS Connects User Needs, Research, and Operations
497786.authors: Thanh Vo, NOAA/NESDIS/SAE Affiliate and STC, Inc., Silver Spring, MD; and M. Yapur and A. Steckel
497786.abstract: The U.S. Integrated Ocean Observing System (IOOS) was established by Congress under the ICOOS Act to transform disparate, siloed coastal observation networks into a unified, nationally coordinated system. Since its inception, IOOS has evolved into a premier example of successfully transitioning research to operations (R2O) by bridging the gap between national mandates and regional implementation. This presentation explores how the IOOS "Enterprise", a unique framework comprising 11 federally certified Regional Associations (RAs) and 17 interagency partners, serves the nation by turning observations into actionable information. By integrating diverse data streams (federal, academic, private, and state) through rigorous standards and robust cyberinfrastructure (DMAC), IOOS ensures that high-quality ocean, coastal, and Great Lakes data are readily available for decision-makers. We will highlight how IOOS acts as a "force multiplier" within NOAA and across the federal government, providing an estimated five-fold return on investment through improved economic resilience, maritime safety, and public security. We will demonstrate how IOOS supported initiatives ranging from high-frequency radar networks essential for Coast Guard search and rescue, to subsurface gliders that enhance hurricane intensity forecasts, have become critical operational assets that support national priorities. Finally, the presentation will discuss how IOOS continues to evolve as a responsive, stakeholder-driven system, ensuring that cutting-edge ocean research is systematically operationalized to meet the safety, economic, and stewardship needs of the nation.

497787.title: Evaluation of Uncertainty in Long-Term Solar Measurements: A Global Assessment
497787.authors: Aron Habte, National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR), Golden, CO; National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, CO; and M. Sengupta, Ph.D., S. Ryu, S. wilcox, and T. Stoffel
497787.abstract: High-quality solar radiation data with well-characterized measurement uncertainty underpins a wide range of applications extending well beyond solar energy — including atmospheric radiative transfer studies, satellite product validation, and weather forecasting. Solar resource measurements such as global horizontal irradiance (GHI), direct normal irradiance (DNI), and diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI) face uncertainties due to factors like radiometer calibration, intrinsic limitations of radiometers, data acquisition systems, and operational errors. Poor data quality protocols can result in considerable inaccuracies not only in solar energy yield estimation and system sizing, but also in the broader atmospheric and climate datasets that depend on accurate surface radiation measurements. These uncertainties propagate directly into radiative transfer modeling and satellite-derived irradiance products, where ground-based observations serve as the critical validation truth set. Quantifying and managing data quality and measurement uncertainty is therefore essential across this full range of scientific and operational applications, not solar energy alone. To address these challenges, the method employs both the NLR’s Solar Uncertainty Integrator (SUNI) software and data quality tools. NLR's SUNI provides a Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM)-compliant framework to estimate measurement uncertainties. Complementing this, data quality analyses utilize NLR’s SERIQC and the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) QCRAD methods to flag anomalies, instrument drift, and operational inconsistencies in long-term records. Applied to one-minute resolution data from global networks—including Solar Radiation Research Laboratory (SRRL), the Baseline Surface Radiation Network (BSRN), and the ARM network—this approach evaluates uncertainty across diverse stations. The results demonstrate how combining SUNI's uncertainty estimation with robust data quality screening can be used for solar energy, atmospheric radiative transfer studies, satellite product validation, and weather forecasting.

497788.title: Scatterometer and SAR Near Sea-Ice Wind Quality Control
497788.authors: Bryan W Stiles, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA; and A. Fore, F. Polverari, H. S. Torres, and S. M. Hristova-Veleva
497788.abstract: The Multi-sensor Worldwide Ocean Winds (MWOW) product merges ocean surface vector winds from multiple scatterometers, radiometers, and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) instruments onto a common Level-3 grid. Near the sea-ice margin, backscatter and emission from ice contaminate the wind retrievals, biasing both speed and direction in precisely the marginal-ice-zone regions of greatest scientific and operational interest. MWOW near-sea-ice quality control (QC) addresses this in two stages: first estimating sea-ice concentration from each contributing sensor's own measurements, then using that estimate both to flag ice-contaminated retrievals and to drive a wind correction that recovers usable winds rather than discarding them. Here we focus on the measurement parameters that drive the ice-concentration estimates for two contrasting instrument types -- the HY-2B and HY-2C Ku-band scatterometers and the SWOT Ka-band radar interferometer -- and on the flagging and correction neural networks built upon them. For HY-2B and HY-2C, a neural network estimates ice concentration from the dual-polarization (HH and VV) Ku-band normalized radar cross section (sigma-0) at both the fore and aft azimuth looks, together with the cross-track cell position (a proxy for incidence angle), the retrieved ocean wind speed, and latitude. During training it is crucial to retain all valid primary-beam sigma-0 rather than only cells with a converged wind solution, as conventional wind processing does. The otherwise-discarded ice-region multi-polarization, multi-look backscatter carries a strong ice signal. Referenced to EUMETSAT OSI-SAF passive-microwave ice concentration, the HY-2B/2C retrieval achieves R^2 ~ 0.89. For SWOT, whose KaRIn instrument is a Ka-band radar interferometer, ice concentration is estimated from a distinct parameter set: the Ka-band sigma-0 (in dB), the interferometric volumetric correlation, and the sea-surface-height anomaly, along with incidence angle, cross-track distance, and beta angle (viewing geometry). Critically, the retrieval also ingests the 3x3 local spatial variance of sigma-0, volumetric correlation, and height anomaly, since ice introduces small-scale spatial texture that these variance features capture. Sea surface temperature, used by SWOT's wind-speed retrieval, is deliberately excluded from the ice network to avoid reducing ice concentration resolution. SWOT and OSI-SAF ice concentrations agree at R^2 ~ 0.93, and the SWOT, HY-2B/2C, and passive-microwave estimates are mutually consistent, indicating that ice concentration derived on each sensor's native measurements is a robust QC basis rather than an artifact of any single instrument or reference. Both ice-concentration retrievals are compact feed-forward neural networks. The HY-2B/2C network is a three-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron (128-64-32 nodes) trained per grid cell on a 10-million-sample random subset drawn from roughly 88 million collocated ocean and sea-ice samples, with early stopping on validation R^2. The SWOT ice network uses three hidden layers of 100 nodes each with input normalization, trained on collocated KaRIn passes matched to the same OSI-SAF reference. In both cases the training target is OSI-SAF ice concentration, and the modest network size reflects our finding that the discriminating information resides in the input measurements themselves rather than in model capacity -- deeper networks did not improve skill. At the meeting we plan to describe companion wind-correction neural networks for both SWOT and HY-2B/2C -- that take the sensor measurements, the observation geometry, and the estimated ice concentration and return corrected near-ice winds -- extending the QC from simple flagging to active recovery of winds in the marginal ice zone. We describe the planned integration of both the flagging and correction stages into the operational MWOW Level-3 processing chain, in which each sensor's retrievals are screened and corrected prior to merging, and briefly note extension of the same measurement-driven approach to additional MWOW sensors, including the NISAR L-band SAR.

497789.title: Advancing NESDIS Satellite Operations to Lights-Dim and Beyond with A.I.
497789.authors: Isaac Andrew Passmore, ASRC Federal, Beltsville, MD
497789.abstract: In April of 2025 NOAA/NESDIS Office of Satellite and Product Operations (OSPO) desired to transition every mission from 24/7 on-console support to day-shift only operations. Within 18 months, ASRC Federal turned this concept into reality by delivering a technically robust solution, under budget, and months ahead of schedule. Our approach was to focus on fundamental operational needs and most importantly, not overcomplicating the solution. By applying the right technologies to well understood problems, overall risk was reduced while overall mission effectiveness was enhanced resulting in much lower costs. This presentation will discuss the technical and operational changes necessary to enable this transition. Moreover, we will discuss what’s next for NESDIS' legacy satellite missions as we continue to advance NOAA’s agenda of more effective and efficient satellite operations. The next phase of targeted automations will incorporate focused use cases for A.I. in safe and responsible applications. We will discuss the challenges and risks introduced by A.I. systems and how we are planning to address them. As industry leaders in spacecraft operations, ASRC Federal is focused on advancing the field through novel approaches with responsible A.I. applications and other focused technologies. This systematic approach closely aligns with NOAA objectives, and we believe our results will continue to influence the industry at large.

497790.title: Observations of pyroCumulus Evolution from INSPYRE
497790.authors: Sarah Woods, NSF NCAR, Boulder, CO; and B. Weinzierl, K. Blohm, S. R. Martrich, M. Schoeberl, and D. A. Peterson
497790.abstract: The NASA INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE) conducted its first intensive observation period July-September 2026, probing pyroconvective behavior from the remote sensing perspective with ground based radar and the NASA ER-2 high altitude aircraft, and from the in situ perspective with the NSF Gulfstream V aircraft. We focus on the coarse mode aerosol and cloud microphysical suite onboard the GV to investigate the lifecycle evolution of developing pyrocumulus, and contrast these observations with those of more “clean” developing cumulus clouds under varied aerosol loading from additional in situ airborne campaigns, such as the Secondary Production of Ice in Cumulous Experiment (SPICULE). The in situ payload onboard the GV for INSPYRE covers the size range of hydro- and pyro-meteors from 2 microns to 20 mm including particle measurements from the Cloud Droplet Probe (CDP), Fast 2-Dimensional Stereo (F2DS) probe, High Volume Precipitation Spectrometer (HVPS) probe and HOLODEC-II. Bulk water measurements include those of the King hot wire probe, and Nevzorov.

497794.title: Application of Airborne Phased Array Radar (APAR) Observing Simulation, Processing, and Research Environment (AOSPRE) In The NSF NCAR INtegrating Field Observations and Research Models (INFORM) Program
497794.abstract: The APAR Observing Simulation, Processing, and Research Environment (AOSPRE) was developed to simulate APAR's measurement and science capabilities before the APAR is constructed. AOSPRE uses Cloud Model 1 (CM1) and Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulated storms with a hypothetical C-130 operated within the model space. Radar moments and dual-pol variables are deduced from the model microphysical parameters using the Cloud Resolving Model Radar Simulator (CR-SIM). Three-dimensional dual-Doppler radar winds can be retrieved from the Spline Analysis at Mesoscale Utilizing Radar and Aircraft Instrumentation (SAMURAI). The output can be examined directly or passed through additional tools to analyze various aspects of the data collected during each flight. AOSPRE is linked to a NSF NCAR-wide INtegrating Field Observations and Research Models (INFORM) to (1) establish and support best practices and methods for comparisons between models and observations, (2) exploit, assess and quantify the impacts of integrating observations and models to improve understanding of the prediction and predictability of the Earth system, and (3) improve the design, planning, deployment strategy of field programs and instrument development. The AOSPRE will be expanded into a field program planning tools as wells as a post campaign re-analysis tool with DA capability. AOSPRE is developed as an open-source software. The first version of AOSPRE software has been released to the research and operational community in the last quarter of 2024. Even though the APAR construction program was suspended by NSF in April 2025, AOSPRE capability has been expanded to be a general purposed radar simulating environment for the community that can be applied to other airborne and ground-based radars. This paper will provide recent development/accomplishment of AOSPRE and the applications of AOSPRE in the INFORM project to validate and improve model microphysics using radar observations.

497798.title: Global Survey of Accumulation Mode Particulate Halogens (I, Br, Cl) In the Remote Atmosphere: Sources, Distribution, Gas-Particle Partitioning, and Speciation
497798.authors: Dongwook Kim, CIRES, Boulder, CO; and J. L. Jimenez, P. Campuzano-Jost, H. Guo, B. A. Nault, J. Schroder, D. A. Day, J. Dibb, P. Veres, A. Neuman, L. G. Huey, M. Reza, C. F. Lee, K. J. Zarzana, T. Koenig, Y. Tong, Y. C. Chan, L. Jaegle, D. R. Blake, R. S. Hornbrook, A. Hills, E. C. Apel, G. P. Schill, D. M. Murphy, J. Schwarz, C. A. Brock, A. Kupc, C. Williamson, J. P. DiGangi, G. S. Diskin, J. Peischl, C. Thompson, T. Ryerson, E. Ray, J. Crounse, P. O. Wennberg, R. Commane, B. Daube, S. Wofsy, T. L. Campos, A. Franchin, A. Weinheimer, G. M. Wolfe, T. F. Hanisco, R. Volkamer, F. L. Moore, E. J. Hintsa, W. H. Brune, and S. R. Hall
497798.abstract: Halogen radicals play critical roles in the atmosphere, impacting ozone, methane, and mercury. Particulate halogens (Xp, X = I, Br, Cl) can react directly with ozone and serve as reservoirs for gas-phase reactive halogen species that produce halogen radicals. However, quantitative measurements of Xp on a global scale over remote areas are rare, especially above the Earth’s surface. We report colocated measurements of Xp and organic and inorganic gas-phase halogens in the remote atmosphere. In this work, we aim to present a comprehensive and quantitative survey of the global distribution of halogens over the remote atmosphere, e.g., Arctic, remote ocean, and the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS), as well as their oxidation state and gas-particle partitioning. Main findings include (1) emission of iodine and bromine from biomass burning and their enhanced partitioning into the particle phase by organic aerosols within the marine boundary layer, (2) ubiquitous enhancements of Ip and Brp in the UTLS, (3) stratospheric origin and dominant particle phase fraction of perchlorate, (4) the significant contribution of Br– to total inorganic bromine in the upper troposphere, and (5) the increasing fraction of iodate with aging in biomass burning plumes. We also discuss implications for improvement in GEOS-Chem for a better representation of atmospheric halogens. The rate of gas- particle cycling remains underconstrained due to the lack of detailed gas-phase speciated measurements in most campaigns. These results highlight the current lack of understanding of halogen gas-particle cycling and its sources besides the oceans (e.g., biomass burning). In future campaigns, simultaneous measurements of Xp and speciated gas-phase inorganic halogens will help better constrain the abundance, cycling, and impacts of atmospheric halogens.

497800.title: Assessment of Severe Weather Outlooks and Severe Weather Impacts and Damage Reports across Central Alabama
497800.authors: Isabeau Genevieve Goodman, NOAA, Bryan, TX; and K. laws
497800.abstract: The Storm Prediction Center’s Convective Outlooks (SPC Outlooks) contribute significantly to operational forecasting by providing meteorologists with broad areas at risk for severe weather. This research project’s goal was to assess how the SPC Day 2 Outlooks verified in the NWS Birmingham County Warning Area (NWS Birmingham CWA). Using a dataset from October 22, 2014 to the end of February 2026, I created a dataset of SPC Outlooks and historical weather events. This dataset was then sorted into lower risk and higher risk based on the weather that occurred. Next, I sorted the events using forecast verification categories such as false alarm, hit, true miss, overforecasted, and so on. With the assistance of Gemini AI, I analyzed the data, creating statistics for success ratio, false alarm ratio, probability of detection, and critical success index. Results showed an overall success ratio of around 30% whether or not overforecasts were counted as successful forecasts. When looking at higher risk events, the success ratio was 69% for safety based statistics and 26% for accuracy based statistics. This difference showed that higher risk levels often verified as overforecasts, specifically in the bounds of the NWS Birmingham CWA. Further research will explore the potential causes of these overforecasts.

497801.title: Enforcing Spatial Locality in Spherical Fourier Neural Operators via Spectral Smoothing
497801.authors: Isaac Davis, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado - Boulder, Boulder, CO; University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO; and A. C. Subramanian and W. Chapman
497801.abstract: Machine-learning models show substantial promise for weather and climate prediction, but robust generalization requires architectures that learn underlying physics rather than dataset-specific correlations. Spherical Fourier neural operators (SFNOs) already encode a useful geometric bias by representing global fields with spherical harmonics, a natural basis for dynamics on the sphere. However, unconstrained SFNO spectral multipliers can learn jagged spectral responses and nonlocal grid-space kernels inconsistent with atmospheric flow physics. We introduce a spectral-weight smoothing constraint, a Laplacian penalty across spherical-harmonic degree, that biases SFNO kernels toward energetic locality (concentrated, spatially coherent response functions) and scale-coherent responses. On shallow-water equation rollouts, this constraint yields kernels and input-output sensitivities closer to those of a differentiable reference solver, at a small in-sample cost during autoregressive training. Under out-of-distribution initial conditions, locality-biased SFNO variants produce markedly more stable and skillful forecasts than the unconstrained baseline.

497803.title: Characterization of Indoor and Outdoor Concentrations of Total Volatile Organic Compounds (TVOC) in New York State Neighborhoods
497803.authors: Evelyn Rose Ka'ilialoha Girardi, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN
497803.abstract: Indoor and Outdoor air quality, particularly in regards to Total Volatile Organic Compounds (TVOCs), has become a recent focus of the scientific community due to our growing understanding of its correlation with adverse health effects, which range from acute irritation to severe congenital abnormalities. Current air quality monitoring networks in the United States lack the spatial resolution required to effectively track TVOCs at the neighborhood scale, largely due to the higher cost of analytical equipment. This study investigates the use of low-cost TelosAir DUET sensors to supplement existing networks and characterize TVOC concentrations across residential areas in New York State. Data was collected for one week in 3-4 homes/apartments during winter and spring periods from 2022 to 2026 using sensors placed in both indoor (living room) and outdoor (where backyard available) environments across the Capital Region, Hudson Valley Region, and New York City. Alongside the sensor data, extensive baseline and daily activity questionnaires were digitized and analyzed to correlate indoor TVOC spikes with human behavior and housing characteristics. A generalized linear mixed model with a variance components covariance structure was applied using reported housing characteristics from ~60 homes to identify potential predictors of indoor TVOC. Preliminary results show kitchen fan exhaust outdoors, combustion heating, gas cooking, carpet use, recent renovation, and old homes are potential predictors. However, more measurements are needed to validate whether observed predictors are significant. Future work will focus on applying model to at least 100 homes and calibrating these low-cost sensors against reference monitors using machine learning, ultimately providing a scalable method for understanding the intersections of atmospheric chemistry, localized weather events, and human activity.

497805.title: Microphysical Studies of Melting Hail Using In Situ Aircraft Measurements, Cloud Modeling, and Polarimetric Radar Data.
497805.authors: Savannah Jewel Southward, Cooperative Institute for Severe and High Impact Weather Research and Operations (CIWRO), Norman, OK; and A. V. Ryzhkov, J. T. Carlin, A. J. Heymsfield, and A. Bansemer
497805.abstract: Hail is a highly destructive severe weather hazard, causing over $10 billion USD in insured losses annually. Beyond impacts to personal and commercial property, industries such as agriculture and aviation are also highly vulnerable to the damaging nature of hail. Advanced polarimetric weather radars provide the primary means for remotely detecting hail, estimating its size, and issuing timely warnings. However, existing methodologies for quantifying and forecasting large hail remain limited, particularly due to uncertainties in relating radar signatures to hail microphysics and storm dynamics. This research leverages unique in situ observations from the armored T-28 aircraft, which has sampled hail-bearing storms across multiple field campaigns, to better constrain these relationships. Throughout this work, we investigate the sensitivity of polarimetric radar variables to hail size aloft and the role of downdraft dynamics in shaping radar signatures in hail-producing storms. Using a one-dimensional downdraft model with spectral bin microphysics initialized from T-28 aircraft observations, we examine how different definitions of maximum hail size (Dmax) influence simulated vertical profiles of reflectivity (Z), differential reflectivity (ZDR), and specific differential phase (KDP). The model framework enables controlled exploration of how microphysical assumptions and environmental conditions influence both radar presentation and downdraft evolution. By linking in situ measurements, modeling, and radar observations, this work aims to improve understanding of hail microphysics and support the development of more optimized radar-based hail detection and prediction methodologies.

497806.title: Rain without Autoconversion: Advances in Single Liquid Category Bulk Scheme
497806.authors: Arthur Z. Hu, Columbia University, Long Island City, NY; and M. van Lier-Walqui, S. P. Santos, K. Loftus, and H. Morrison
497806.abstract: While significant progress has been made on the more sophisticated atmospheric models such as Lagrangian Superdroplet Method, simpler models like bulk microphysics schemes are still needed for Earth system models due to their computational efficiency. However, traditional bulk schemes artificially separate liquid water into cloud and rain categories, which requires elusive autoconversion parameterizations and prevents the natural evolution of continuous drop size distributions. Previous proof-of-concept studies showed promising results that single liquid category (SLC) bulk schemes can resolve the most challenging problems that traditional two-category bulk schemes are facing, especially from collision-coalescence and sedimentation. In this study, we expand our efforts from individual microphysical process in box/1D model into full microphysics (condensation, evaporation, collision-coalescence, and sedimentation) in 3D LES model by calibrating its parameters against a reference bin scheme (TAU/MMM) using emulator-accelerated Bayesian inference (MCMC). Rather than rerunning the bulk model inside the sampler, an emulator is trained to map parameters directly to target diagnostics, allowing for efficient calibration even when using a computationally demanding 3D model. We compare this calibrated SLC against the reference bin scheme and another traditional bulk scheme for two typical warm-cloud regimes, drizzling stratocumulus and precipitating cumulus. Results show that SLC reproduces key diagnostics equally well or better than traditional bulk schemes, especially in the timing and intensity of rainfall. This suggests a practical path to a more physical implementation of warm-rain microphysics in weather and climate prediction.

497808.title: Space-Based Environmental Monitoring Programs Update
497808.authors: Lt Col Brian Pitman, USSF, System Delta 810, El Segundo, CA
497808.abstract: This presentation provides participants with latest status on the DoW’s Electro Optical / Infrared (EO/IR) Weather Systems (EWS), Weather System Follow-on – Microwave (WSF-M), EWS-Geostationary (EWS-G) and Space Situational Awareness and Environmental Monitoring (SSAEM) / Constellation Observing System for Meteorology, Ionosphere, and Climate-2 (COSMIC-2) programs, including space vehicle status, launch plans, and future forecast plans. The USSF continues to operate a wide range of EM sensing systems that contribute to the broader EM Family of Systems. This presentation describes current efforts to modernize components of the architecture. Other topics like the proposed timeframe for on-orbit checkouts, data calibration/validation and expected transition to operations to support DoW Weather Centrals, NOAA NESDIS and scientific meteorological community, will also be addressed.

497810.title: Equatorial Ionospheric Irregularities from the COSMIC-2 Mission during Solar Cycle 25
497810.authors: John J. Braun, UCAR, Boulder, CO
497810.abstract: This study provides a global statistical analysis of Equatorial Plasma Bubbles (EPBs) using COSMIC-2 mission data and the Back Propagation method for precise geolocation. By comparing low solar activity (2021) with solar maximum (2024), we find a five-fold increase in EPB detections during solar maximum, with apex heights reaching 1,000 km. EPB occurrence shows strong seasonal and longitudinal dependencies, specifically equinoctial enhancements and regional variations. Post-midnight EPBs generally follow post-sunset morphologies but with lower apex heights and more persistent phase scintillation. Global occurrence maps reveal distinct longitudinal patterns: the American–Atlantic sector peaks during September–March, while African and Pacific sectors peak during March–September. These results underscore the solar-cycle influence on EPB development and the utility of COSMIC-2 geolocations for ionospheric climatology and forecasting.

497811.title: Atmospheric Remote Sensing Provides Attribution of Artificially Generated Cumulus Clouds
497811.authors: Stefano Letizia, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Denver, CO; and A. Scholbrock, M. Sanchez-Gomez, D. Anderson, W. Winograd, and T. Kosaraju
497811.abstract: After decades of knowledge development in understanding, modeling, forecasting, and harnessing the energy of atmospheric phenomena, achieving active control of large weather systems represents a new frontier in meteorology. Weather modification could have immense societal and economic benefits, including increased water availability, wildfire suppression, affordable energy generation, and heat wave mitigation. However, one of the biggest challenges for weather modification is the attribution of the induced weather patterns to the specific intervention. This is due mainly to the often incomplete knowledge of the baseline weather conditions and the limited energy input of pilot tests. In our study, we document the artificial creation of cumulus clouds by ground-based heat injection. The experiment took place during the summer of 2026 at a midlatitude site characterized by flat terrain, high moisture content, and low boundary layer winds. The attribution of the generated clouds is backed up by Doppler wind lidar measurements that capture both the artificial updraft and the artificial cumulus through the Doppler shift and signal-to-noise ratio, respectively. A ground-based infrared spectrometer was also operating at the site and monitored the background thermodynamic profiles that contributed to the lifting and condensation processes. The lidar performed a set of full PPI scans at different elevations whose geometry was optimized to capture the most relevant spatiotemporal scales based on WRF simulations of the plume [Letizia et al., 2021]. The PPI stack provides both volumetric information of the flow and background wind profile. This technique allows estimating the vertical velocity over the scan volume, as well as locating the cloud edges based on the attenuated backscatter coefficient derived from the signal-to-noise ratio (attached figure). The data from the spectrometer are assimilated by the TROPoe algorithm [Turner et al., 2025] to provide uncertainty-aware estimates of the temperature and mixing ratio profiles, which determine the conditions for cloud formation. We will finally discuss how the lidar + spectrometer system can represent an effective network of sensors to inform weather modification campaigns and provide robust attribution. References Letizia, S., Zhan, L., and Iungo, G. V. (2021). LiSBOA (LiDAR Statistical Barnes Objective Analysis) for optimal design of lidar scans and retrieval of wind statistics – Part 1: theoretical framework. Atmospheric Measurement Techniques, 14, 2065–2093. https://doi.org/10.5194/amt-14-2065-2021. Turner, D. D., Adler, B., Bianco, L., Wilczak, J. M., Michaud-Belleau, V., and Rochette, L.: Intercomparison of Seven Collocated Ground-based Infrared Spectrometer Radiance Observations and Retrieved Thermodynamic Profiles (2025), EGUsphere [preprint], https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2025-4814.

497814.title: From NMAP to the Browser: A Web-Based Environment for Interactive Meteorological Data Analysis
497814.authors: William Gregory Blumberg, Millersville University, Millersville, PA
497814.abstract: Meteorologists have spent decades developing sophisticated tools to interrogate environmental data. However, many traditional platforms assume the user operates from a dedicated, specialized workstation. This work presents the design, implementation, and testing of a web-native meteorological analysis environment that translates the core capabilities of traditional, NMAP-style workstations into the modern web browser. The platform employs a decoupled, modular architecture to separate data storage, web services, and visualization: Data Layer: Multidimensional gridded datasets are stored using Zarr for efficient, asynchronous chunked access, while time-series point observations, and geospatial geometries are managed via a TimescaleDB and PostGIS database. Services Layer: A high-performance FastAPI backend exposes dataset endpoints and application logic, enabling both interactive client rendering and programmatic access for scientific Python workflows. Client-Side Rendering: Interactive visualization is handled by AutumnPlot-GL, a custom WebGL-based library capable of rendering dense meteorological fields directly in the browser without server-side image generation. By eliminating local software installation and complex environment configuration, this architecture lowers the technical barrier to advanced data interrogation. Beyond operational utility, the platform serves as a foundation for cloud-native education. An eventual goal is to facilitate interactive classroom forecasting exercises, where students analyze shared meteorological datasets, submit probabilistic forecasts, and receive feedback through verification metrics. This presentation details the system architecture, performance benchmarks, and lessons learned from transitioning traditional meteorological workflows to web-native paradigms, alongside broader opportunities for scaling cloud-based environmental data services.

497815.title: From Audience to Partners: Engaging Youth as Leaders to Build Resilience in Rural Colorado
497815.authors: Katya Schloesser, CIRES, Boulder, CO; The University of Colorado, Boulder, CO; and M. Littrell, C. Okochi, C. Zaniboni, and C. McDougall
497815.abstract: Communities across Colorado are grappling with extreme heat, historic drought, and devastating wildfires. Planning for and responding to these climate-related hazards is challenging in rural areas with limited resources and geographic isolation. Yet, rural communities are resourceful, with close-knit communities that have abundant social capital. Emergency managers and community planners have education and outreach as part of their workplans but often lack the time or expertise to engage in meaningful ways with students and community members. As drought continues and wildfire risk increases, education programs can play a critical role in empowering future leaders and the broader community to navigate increasingly complex challenges in building resilience. The Hazard Education, Awareness and Resilience Task Force (HEART Force) program engages middle and high school students across Colorado in place-based resilience education that combines scientific investigation of hazards, scenario-based role-play games, systems thinking, engagement with local experts, and youth-led civic action. Grounded in NOAA's Community Resilience Education Theory of Change (Bey et al. 2020), the program positions youth as contributors to community resilience rather than passive recipients of preparedness information. Students investigate local risks and vulnerabilities, engage directly with emergency managers, planners, scientists, and elected officials, and design projects that address resilience challenges within their communities. This presentation illustrates how place-based resilience education can function as a broader learning ecosystem that connections formal classroom education, informal learning environments, community engagement, capacity building and civic participation. We will share three stories from rural Colorado that show how youth-adult partnerships further community resilience efforts while strengthening student agency and leadership. We will also share program evaluation efforts that identify lessons learned and opportunities for future program evolution. The first story is of the Environmental Resilience Team at Estes Park Middle School, that built a long-term relationship with the local fire department after being impacted by the East Troublesome and Cameron Peak fires in 2020. Students' efforts began with assembling and distributing wildfire go-bags and helping vulnerable community members with wildfire mitigation on their properties. The following year, students tackled the challenge from a statewide policy perspective and lobbied their state Senator to pass a bill establishing the Wildland-Urban Interface State Code Board. Program evaluation showed that both students' understanding of community resilience and confidence speaking with community members about resilience efforts significantly increased (Schloesser et al. 2024). The long-term relationships established students as partners in resilience efforts in Estes rather than passive recipients. Now, community partners ask the Environmental Resilience Team for help in addressing community environmental challenges. The second story comes from Gunnison, Colorado, where multilingual students engaged the immigrant community to increase awareness of wildfire risk. Over several years, Gunnison High School students hosted bilingual Community Resilience Expos, tabled at community events, and co-facilitated a bilingual Family Game Night at the local library to engage Spanish and Cora speaking residents in conversations about wildfire preparedness. By serving as facilitators and connectors between local organizations and community members, students became partners in building resilience and trust, strengthening relationships across cultural and linguistic groups. And third, the story focuses on students across rural communities in southwest Colorado, who used a scenario-based role-play game on drought for community game nights to engage families, water managers, local stakeholders and members of the public in modeling local basin roundtables in conversations on drought planning and adaptation. Rather than being the recipients of outreach from local water managers, students and families sat at the table with local leaders to explore complex tradeoffs, discuss community values, and evaluate resilience strategies together. Students played key roles in marketing and planning events, facilitating the game, and building community buy-in for local drought planning efforts. Through the years, the HEART Force program has evolved with increasing climate-related challenges and community dynamics, with a central focus on empowering youth through youth-adult partnerships. The value of long-term relationships, strong support for teachers, scaffolding of student learning and engagement, and exposure of students to a broad variety of leaders and students, have all furthered the success of HEART Force programs. Across all three examples, students partnered with local planners, emergency managers, community organizations, and decision-makers, rather than serving only as audiences for outreach efforts. We argue that resilience education is most effective when it creates authentic opportunities for youth participation, values community expertise, and supports reciprocal youth-adult partnerships.

497817.title: Characterizing 3D Convective Updraft Cores with Deep Volumetric Segmentation and Diffusion-Based Generative Data Augmentation
497817.authors: Xiaowen Li, Morgan State University, Baltimore, MD; and M. R. Shaharear, M. Hoque, M. R. Jani, and M. Rahman
497817.abstract: Atmospheric convection is the driver of global circulations, yet the three-dimensional (3D) structure of convective updraft cells remains insufficiently characterized due to their geometric complexity, turbulent nature, and a severe scarcity of annotated 3D volumetric data. Here we present a dual-component framework consisting of volumetric instance segmentation of convective updrafts using deep learning, and a diffusion-based generative pipeline designed to synthesize these cells and artificially expand 3D training data. Our dataset is derived from a native 1km horizontal resolution spectral-bin microphysical simulations of convective events observed during the TWP-ICE field campaign near Darwin, Australia. 3D convective cells are manually labeled using vertical velocity field simulated by a cloud-resolving model. For the segmentation component, we deploy a multitask volumetric network that predicts background, centroid, and boundary masks, followed by marker-controlled watershed post-processing to recover individual cell instances. Our results demonstrate that a 3D Residual UNet equipped with attention mechanisms outperforms a standard 3D UNet, improving the mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) by 1.5% to 3% across matching thresholds of 25% to 90%. To overcome the data scarcity of having only eight annotated simulated scenes of a 256km x 256km domain, we use generative component reframed from the convective scenes to individual cells. By extracting 732 annotated cells from the original data, we successfully trained a 190-million parameter 3D denoising diffusion probabilistic model. The generated cells are constrained to physical data ranges and deterministically composed back into volumes. These synthetic volumes accurately reproduce the size distributions, spatial organization, and exact velocity-label consistency of real atmospheric data. While synthetic fidelity varies, our top three generated volumes achieved 93% to 99.8% of the cloud content found in their real counterparts, forming a robust primary set for data augmentation. Ultimately, this joint segmentation and synthesis framework provides a highly scalable approach to characterizing complex 3D atmospheric phenomena.

497821.title: USSF Environmental Monitoring Commercial Data-as-a-Service
497821.authors: David 'Andy' Betz, USSF, System Delta 810, El Segundo, CA; and C. Soegono
497821.abstract: This presentation will discuss the USSF way forward with Environmental Monitoring Data-as-a-Service (DaaS). The DaaS approach focuses on integration of commercial offerings into the broader DoW architecture to address critical capability needs for the Joint Force.

497822.title: Impact of Model Physics and Resolution on Simulated Mesoscale Convective Systems In SCREAM: GoAmazon Case Studies Using RRM-SCREAM and ARM Observations
497822.authors: Hsi-Yen Ma, LLNL, Livermore, CA; and Y. Zhang
497822.abstract: The US Department of Energy (DOE) Simplified Cloud-Resolving E3SM (Energy Exascale Earth System Model) Atmosphere Model (SCREAM) is a kilometer-scale global storm-resolving model, which signifies the advent of an exciting new generation of weather and climate models. From the recent global simulation campaigns, SCREAM show significant improvement in many aspects, especially for heavy precipitation associated with intense storm systems compared to coarse resolution models. However, SCREAM also show evidence of problems associated with small-scale and organized convective processes. Furthermore, SCREAM can be computationally expensive to conduct long simulations, making diagnosing certain SCREAM model processes or phenomena challenging. To overcome the computation barrier and better diagnose and improve SCREAM’s convective processes, we constructed several regionally-refined model (RRM) configurations for SCREAM (RRM-SCREAM) centered around various DOE atmospheric radiation measurement (ARM) permanent and field campaign locations to study convective processes with short-term hindcasts and DOE ARM observations. In our presentation, we will present case studies of 11 selected meso-scale convective systems (MCSs) events during the GoAmazon field campaign. Our analysis suggests that SCREAM simulates stronger MCS precipitation. MCS initiation is sensitive to the model initialization times as model tends to dry out quickly in the lower levels in the first 24 hours. With better treatment in the rain fraction and higher model horizontal resolution, SCREAM simulates better MCS organization and vertical cloud structure. (This work is performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under Contract DE-AC52-07NA27344. LLNL-ABS-2018901)

497824.title: Space Weather Programs - Overview & Way Ahead
497824.authors: Annette Parsons, USSF, System Delta 810, Colorado Springs, CO; and A. Parsons
497824.abstract: The Space/Terrestrial Environmental Analysis and Resource Sustainment branch is a comprehensive space weather monitoring and forecasting enterprise which integrates a global network of ground-based and space-based sensors to provide critical environmental information for military and intelligence community operations. This network includes the Ionospheric Ground Sensors (IGS), comprising the Next Generation Ionosonde (NEXION) and Ionospheric Scintillation Total electron content Observer (ISTO) systems for ionospheric characterization and the Radio Solar Telescope Network (RSTN), and the Solar Optical Observing Network (SOON), which provides vital solar data. All this data is sent to the Unified Data Library (UDL) where it is ingested by the Space Weather Analysis and Forecast System (SWAFS). SWAFS is a modern, cloud-native software suite that delivers near-real-time analysis of space weather impacts, enabling operators to distinguish between environmental effects and adversary actions. Future developments are focused on enhancing and sustaining this capability through network expansion, including new sensor installations for IGS, and the modernization of aging infrastructure, highlighted by the planned transition of the SOON system to the next-generation Global Oscillation Network Group (ng-GONG) by fiscal year 2032. The branch also sustains terrestrial meteorological systems to include MARK IV-B, Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP), Electro-Optical Infrared Weather System-Geostationary (EWS-G), and starting in Jan 27 the Weather System Follow-on - Microwave (WSF-M) will be part of this portfolio.

497825.title: Constraining Ambient INP Parameterizations and Their Time Dependence: Insights from Arctic measurements
497825.authors: Bo Chen, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and R. J. Perkins, K. R. Barry, R. Patnaude, C. Mavis, P. J. DeMott, and S. M. Kreidenweis
497825.abstract: Ambient INPs and their effects on cloud glaciation are difficult to constrain because INPs represent a very rare subset of the broader aerosol population. Consequently, the abundance and physical and chemical properties of bulk aerosol do not necessarily represent those of the ice-active subset. The rarity of INPs also makes the surface area of the ice-active particles difficult to measure, limiting our ability to constrain time dependence in ambient ice nucleation. This time dependence may be particularly important in understanding long-lived Arctic clouds that can exhibit a high degree of glaciation at warm temperatures (>-6 °C). Here, we examine these challenges using measurements of INPs and aerosols collected during the 2024 NASA Arctic Radiation–Cloud–Aerosol–Surface Interaction eXperiment (ARCSIX). We compare INP concentrations and freezing behavior with collocated measurements of aerosol properties and transport history to identify relationships between ambient aerosols and INP activity. We also propose a method that jointly incorporates the concentration of effective INPs, their nucleation efficiency distribution, and the nucleation rate per effective INP to model freezing assay results. This formulation allows the time dependence of ambient INP activity to be constrained without requiring a direct measurement of the surface area of the ice-active particles. We apply this method to data from freezing measurements obtained under different cooling rates and thermal histories. Together, these measurements and analyses aim to improve our understanding and the parameterization of ambient INPs and their effects on ice and mixed-phase clouds and constrain estimates of ice multiplication factors.

497826.title: Assessing Ice-Nucleating Particle Abundance and Activity in the northern Wasatch Front in Utah
497826.authors: Andre Garcia, University of Texas at El Paso, El Paso, TX; and A. Dobracki, F. Salas Martinez, M. Ostlie, A. G. Hallar, and N. Hiranuma
497826.abstract: This study of the Seeded and Natural Orographic Winter Storms and Catchment Processes Evaluation Project (SNOWSCAPE) has been undertaken to in part characterize ice-nucleating particles (INPs) in ambient conditions in the northern Wasatch Front in Utah from Fall 2025 to Spring 2026. Through devices such as the Portable Ice Nucleating Experiment (PINE) chamber, offline freezing spectrometer, the Aerodynamic Particle Sizer (APS), the Scanning Mobility Particle Sizer (SMPS), and the Cloud Condensation Nuclei Counter (CCNC), we assessed the aerosol size distribution, as well as abundance of INPs and their immersion mode ice nucleation efficiency down to -25 °C. Two sets of dates stand out for high INP abundance (>300 INP L-1 at ~-30 °C), starting from 01/29/2026 – 02/02/2026 and 02/08/2026 – 02/10/2026. The first set of dates shows that INPs are dominated by biogenic heat-labile compounds while the second set of dates is generally unaffected by heat processing, implying the presence of heat resistant highly active INPs, such as seeding compounds. We will further comprehend both aerosol and INP datasets for those periods and beyond with microscopic physicochemical particle analyses to gain insight to explain the observed difference.

497828.title: Urban Environments and Regional Climate Change - CORDEX Flagship Pilot Study URB-RCC
497828.authors: Tomas Halenka, Charles Univ., Prague, Czech republic; and G. Langendijk, P. Hoffmann, M. Belda, and N. Machado-Crespo
497828.abstract: Cities play fundamental role in climate at local to regional scales through modification of heat and moisture fluxes, as well as affecting local atmospheric chemistry and composition, alongside air-pollution dispersion. Vice versa, regional climate change impacts urban areas and will affect cities and citizens increasingly in the next decades when the population in urban areas is growing projected to reach 70 % by 2050. This is critical in connection to extreme events, e.g. heat waves with extremely high temperatures exacerbated by the urban heat island effect, in particular during night-time, with significant consequences for human health. Recent RCM development achieved resolution of city scales within convection permitting RCMs, parameterization of urban processes thus becomes more important. From the framework of CORDEX FPS, main aims and progress of FPS URB-RCC will be presented, from the results based on previous available simulations to the results of analysis of Stage-0 experiments using case studies of heat wave, within ensemble of about 40 simulations for Paris with CP RCMs. This experiment shows the effects of different implementation of urban parameterizations as well as of the different models and their settings on urban heat island under the heat wave. Further outlook of long term (10 years – Stage 1 experiment) climate simulation with these models in common strategy of IMPETUS4CHANGE Horizon Europe Project will be presented. The development of Global Satellite Cities experiment with similar experiments for other big cities around the world will be introduced as another part of Stage 1 experiment. Clear emphasis is given to urban heat island, with possibility to compare the signal for different types of megacities and urban boundary layer parameterization.

497837.title: NSF-NOAA GONG Solar Data Collection, Processing, and Distribution
497837.authors: Olga Burtseva, National Solar Observatory, Boulder, CO; and J. Britanik, M. Creelman, B. J. Harker, A. L. H. Hughes, N. Oien, T. Purdy, K. Shuman, and T. M. Wentzel
497837.abstract: Driving the collection, processing, and distribution of 24/7 solar data to the Space Weather forecasting and scientific communities, the Data Center of the National Solar Observatory's Integrated Synoptic Program (NISP) is at the core of the Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG) project. In this poster, we provide an overview of the pipelines and data products currently used in Space Weather predictions and other related products. Here we discuss the support that the Data Center provides for GONG Network operations and Space Weather forecasting programs, including pipeline development and maintenance, data quality assurance, computer resource management, and facilitated access to GONG data for the scientific community. We also maintain GONG pipelines running at the SWPC Data Center, and generate U.S. Air Force Data Assimilative Photospheric Flux Transport (ADAPT) model maps using GONG data. As a group, we ensure such disparate products as H-alpha images, calibrated magnetograms, Doppler-helioseismology-generated farside maps, and other products are served to the community for both on-time forecasting needs and research applications.

497840.title: DoW Environmental Monitoring Mission Area Architecture Framework & Future Technologies
497840.authors: Janna H. Feeley, The Aerospace Corporation, El Segundo, CA; and A. Betz
497840.abstract: This presentation expands on the Mission Overview presented earlier in the session and describes an analytic approach to understanding the requirements, Family of Systems (FoS) status, and alternatives to sustain current DoW Environmental Monitoring capabilities. Details of a Mission Area Architecture Framework (MAAF) will be presented, along with an update on SYD 810’s Environmental Monitoring Data as a Service (DaaS) efforts. SYD 810 is focused on fielding the current generation of systems while exploring and investing in the next generation of DoW EM systems and capabilities. The USSF continues to be interested in investing and demonstrating the ability to leverage the Commercial Space industry to meet a wide range of DoW requirements, whenever possible. This presentation will discuss SYD 810 future plans and the SYD 810 approach, priorities, and focus areas for Commercial EM DaaS capabilities, development, and deployment.

497843.title: USSF System Delta 810 Mission Overview and DoW Environmental Monitoring Update
497843.authors: Col Nathan Vosters, USSF, System Delta 810, El Segundo, CA
497843.abstract: Timely, accurate, and relevant weather information is a critical enabler to all military missions. In the past, the DoW has defined twelve capability priorities for environmental monitoring (EM) capabilities, including both terrestrial and space weather measurement needs, and has procured systems to close those needs, and meet existing DoW requirements. In addition, the U. S. Space Force (USSF) has conducted studies and engaged industry as part of the development of a Mission Area Architecture Framework (MAAF). This framework will be used to conduct requirements analysis, Family of Systems (FoS) assessment, architecture analysis, and identify potential required material and non-material solutions with the potential to satisfy DoW requirements. As part of the U.S. Space Force’s drive to more fully leverage and exploit the commercial space industry, System Delta 810 (SYD 810) is also engaging industry to fully leverage the utility of commercial space systems and capabilities to satisfy future DoW needs. Finally, the USSF has established SYD 810 as an integrated capability development organization supporting a range of Space- and Ground-based Environmental Monitoring programs. This presentation will describe the overarching SYD 810 vision, strategy and approach to maintaining the current DoW weather architecture and systems, for both terrestrial and space weather, and where we expect to leverage commercial industry providers in the future.

497854.title: Using Predictive Machine Learning to Forecast and Model Extreme Heat within the New York City Subway System
497854.authors: Lenny Metlitsky, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; and H. Norouzi, A. R. Bah, and R. Blake
497854.abstract: New York City faces significant challenges due to the accelerating impacts of climate change. The most affected infrastructure is underground transportation systems, as higher street temperatures lead to more heat trapped underground. Subway platforms are particularly vulnerable to the intensifying frequency and duration of heat waves, as they often lack proper ventilation systems. The extreme fluctuations in temperature within the subway system during extreme weather events pose serious health and safety risks to not only daily commuters but also transit employees working within these environments. Despite the potential dangers of higher temperatures, there is a lack of historical and forecast data for heat index and temperature within underground systems. To address this knowledge gap, we issued an extensive data collection over two summers of platform air temperatures from over 90 subway stations. We analyzed different variables which may impact station temperature, such as station depth, number of service lines, and total number of trains per hour. We also analyzed and identified a relationship between extreme heat and air quality within stations. Additionally, we proposed a forecast model trained on our collected historical data to predict temperature at platform levels based on citywide temperatures on a certain day. The model has an R2 value of 0.85, RMSE of 2.29 °C , and MAE of 1.57 °C. Using the temperature forecasts for platform level, subway passengers and employees will be able to reduce exposure to dangerous heat. Our data analysis, stemming from our historical data collection and forecast models, aims to inform future platform temperature mitigation strategies based on observed and forecasted patterns.

497857.title: Improving Future U.S. Drought Assessment: National Academies 2026 Report
497857.authors: Steven J Stichter, National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine, Washington, DC
497857.abstract: In June 2026, the National Academies released the report Improving Future U.S. Drought Assessment, in response to a request from the National Integrated Drought Information System (NOAA/NIDIS) to consider approaches to understanding and assessing drought in the United States. The study committee that produced this report provided recommendations for drought data and indicators for characterizing drought in the context of changing drought baselines and trends. The report recommend a framework for incorporating non-stationarity considerations into drought assessment in a changing climate, for use across a range of geographic regions and of spatial and temporal scales and to inform decision-making for short-term risk management and long-term adaptation. This presentation will review the context and challenges that prompted the study, key study recommendations and messages, and priority open questions identified in the report. Activities initiated in response to the report recommendations since its release will also be discussed.

497858.title: Influence of ENSO Diversity on North American Weather Regime Frequency and Persistence
497858.authors: Elian Kai Juarez, NOAA, College Park, MD; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA; and M. L. L'Heureux
497858.abstract: El Niño Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, is the single largest source of predictability at seasonal timescales. ENSO has shown promise in subseasonal- to-seasonal forecasts, particularly in influencing weather regimes that represent persistent “states” of the atmosphere. This presentation focuses on a deeper exploration of ENSO’s impact on weather regimes, focusing on the diversity of ENSO beyond single-index strength measures such as the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI). Four primary North American weather regimes are explored in terms of their frequency and persistence across seasons in different ENSO states based on ERA5 Z500 pressure data and sea surface temperature (SST). Particularly, we differentiate the influence of ENSO “strength” from “Strong El Niño” to “Strong La Niña”, and “flavor” by Eastern Pacific (EP) and Central Pacific (CP) relative SST anomaly patterns during 1950- 2025. This is done by decomposing these SST anomalies into orthogonal strength (PC1) and flavor (PC2) axes, which were then compared to explore differences in weather regime occurrence (percentage of days in that state) and persistence (length of each weather regime event). The strongest impacts of ENSO strength and flavor on frequency of weather regimes occur in Northern Winter (DJF) for the Pacific Trough (roughly doubling in occurrence compared to climatology during El Niño EP , largely due to longer events) and Pacific Ridge (+60% during strong La Niña and -50% during strong El Niño) weather regimes. This presentation will relay primary ENSO diversity-driven relationships and the potential reasons for significant preference for certain weather regimes in different ENSO states. Among the questions explored by this research are whether ENSO strength influences regime occurrence directly or via mediating pathways such as through tropical convection and jet configuration, differences on impacts between persisting or transitioning ENSO events, potential modulation by other sub-seasonal oscillations, and whether these causal structures differ between El Niño and La Niña ENSO phases.

497859.title: NSF Unidata: The Evolution of a Community-Focused Data and Software Facility over a Four-Decade Period
497859.authors: Mohan K. Ramamurthy, UCAR, Boulder, CO
497859.abstract: NSF Unidata is a community-focused data and software facility, funded primarily by the National Science Foundation, with a mission to provide the data services, tools, and cyberinfrastructure leadership that advance Earth Systems science, enhance educational opportunities, and broaden participation. Its hallmark has been democratizing access to data and tools by providing open and free access to all its resources. NSF Unidata Acquires and distributes data to facilitate Earth system education and research Develops software for accessing, managing, analyzing, visualizing, and effectively using those data Provides support to users and conducts training workshops on Unidata software Facilitates advancement of standards, conventions, and interoperability Advocates on data issues and negotiates data agreements and fosters community interaction and engagement to promote sharing of data, tools, and ideas Over the past four decades, NSF Unidata has experienced a gradual but natural evolution from a program focused primarily on meteorology to one that serves a broader geosciences community. It has attracted a broader community because it has been successful in providing tools and services that are open, free, interoperable, extensible, and platform independent. The robustness and quality of NSF Unidata tools and services have resulted in their use beyond a community of several dozen universities in the U.S. to now several thousand organizations in academia, research and operational sectors in over 150 countries and 1,500 universities. In the process, NSF Unidata has matured into a cornerstone, cloud-based data and software facility upon which the Earth system science community and other stakeholders have come to rely. In this talk, I’ll present NSF Unidata’s evolution over the past forty years, how we are reimagining our future activities in delivering a comprehensive suite of products and services to meet the current and emerging needs of the Earth Systems Science research and education community, and the lessons learned as the facility evolved.

497860.title: Project FOCI - Non-CO2 Forcers and Their Climate, Weather, Air Quality and Health Impacts: Chemistry – Climate Interactions over Scales
497860.authors: Tomas Halenka, Charles Univ., Prague, Czech republic; and R. S. Sokhi, S. Finardi, N. Machado-Crespo, and P. Huszár
497860.abstract: While overall the global warming with the causes and global processes connected to well-mixed CO2, and its impacts on global to continental scales are well understood with a high level of confidence, there are knowledge gaps concerning the impact of many other non-CO2 radiative forcers leading to low confidence in the conclusions. This relates mainly to specific anthropogenic and natural precursor emissions of short-lived GHGs and aerosols and their precursors. These gaps and uncertainties also exist in their subsequent effects on atmospheric chemistry and climate, through direct emissions dependent on changes in e.g., agriculture production and technologies based on scenarios for future development as well as feedbacks of global warming on emissions, e.g., permafrost thaw. The main goal of EC HE project FOCI, was to assess impacts of key radiative forcers and the processes of their impact on the climate system, to find and test an efficient implementation of these processes into global ESMs and into RCMs coupled with CTMs, and finally to use the tools developed to investigate mitigation and/or adaptation policies incorporated in selected scenarios of future development targeted at Europe and other regions of the world. We are developing new regionally tuned scenarios based on improved emissions to assess the effects of non-CO2 forcers. Overall introduction to coupled RCM-CTM modelling experiment strategies and evaluation simulations will be presented in addition to the contemporary status of the project. Historical simulations results are validated against reanalyses data and the assessment of impact of chemistry involvement is shown. We will show the results for regional and local conditions in high resolution for City of Prague. Future scenario (SSP3-7.0) is running for full and low NTCF to provide the comparison and effects of these non-CO2 forcers in future, while in historical validation full chemistry simulation is compared to run without chemistry.

497861.title: Navigating Extremes: NOAA’s use of Uncrewed Surface Vehicles for Tropical Cyclone Observations
497861.authors: Lev B. Looney, NOAA/AOML & UMiami/CIMAS, Miami, FL; and G. Foltz and D. Zhang
497861.abstract: Since 2021, NOAA and its partners have collaborated to advance the use of Uncrewed Surface Vehicles (USVs) at the air-sea interface in hurricanes. From 2021 - 2025, NOAA has deployed 44 USVs across multiple platforms (including Saildrone and Oshen C-Star), resulting in over 50 intercepts measuring sustained tropical storm-force winds and 10 measuring sustained hurricane-force winds. Throughout these missions, the USVs have coordinated and collocated with a suite of other observing systems, including uncrewed underwater gliders. During the 2026 hurricane season, NOAA has both Saildrone USVs and Oshen C-Stars collecting data as part of an integrated, multi-platform USV mission. This presentation will provide insight into NOAA’s multi-platform USV footprint, highlighting successes, lessons learned, and ongoing challenges from deploying and operating in these extreme environments.

497863.title: The Charge Towards Better Event Response Solutions and Impact Analyses
497863.abstract: In 2025, weather events accounted for $127B of global insured losses. When disaster strikes, time is of the essence – to protect people, property and restore critical services. To do so, insurers require real-time event data so they’re better informed and better equipped to support customers when they need it the most. In this session, we’ll first reflect on the lessons learned from the catastrophe events of 2025 & 2026, the research and reporting that underpins these insights, and how this information is transmitted and utilized by clients. Next, we will introduce the Impact Forecasting team at Aon and their signature Automated Event Response (AER) product. AER is designed to translate weather forecast and post-event data into real-time, client and industry loss projections for reinsurance and insurance stakeholders. We will discuss the pivotal role of accurate meteorological hazard data within the AER framework, especially for catastrophe modeling. Lastly, we will elaborate on the innovations in this space, including the critical value added by AI-based weather forecasting.

497864.title: Supplementing Track File Data with Meteorological Reanalysis for use in a Parametric Tropical Cyclone Model to Improve Historical Reanalysis of Wave, Water Levels, and Coastal Inundation
497864.authors: Rick Luettich, Univ. of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Morehead City, NC; and B. O. Blanton, J. Chen, S. Bunya, Z. Cobell, P. Orton, R. Marsooli, N. Nwogwu, and M. Temimi
497864.abstract: The recently released 44-year long water level and wave reanalysis Coastal Ocean ReAnalysis for the Gulf of Mexico and US East Coasts (CORA-GEC) (https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/66833) was computed using the coupled ADCIRC+SWAN hydrodynamic model with meteorological forcing from the ECMWF’s ERA5 reanalysis and data assimilation of low frequency water levels from coastal gauges. While CORA-GEC has shown considerable skill in representing long term, event-driven, and tidal water level variations, the 0.25° x 0.25° resolution of ERA5 limits its ability to capture the intensity and size of most tropical cyclones (TCs). Since TCs represent some of the strongest meteorological events in the CORA-GEC region, the likely underestimation of this forcing is expected to result in a corresponding underestimation of the extreme water levels that these storms produce. To address this issue, we have developed methodology to remove under-resolved TCs from ERA5 and replace them with wind and pressure fields derived from the Generalized Asymmetric Holland Model (GAHM) parametric TC model. GAHM requires parameter values from track files including the radial distance to at least one specified isotach (typically 64kts, 50kts, and/or 34kts) in the four storm quadrants. However, prior to 2004 these values are not available as part of historical track files such as the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS). To resolve this issue, we extract the required distances to an outer isotach (e.g., 34 kts) from the ERA5 fields. We compare these extracted values to those contained in IBTrACS for TCs since 2004 to assess their feasibility for use during events prior to 2004. This talk provides an overview of this process and the accompanying results.

497868.title: Developing a Forward Operator on Polarimetric Radio Occultation (PRO) observations
497868.authors: Kuo-Nung Wang, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA; and T. Kubar, C. O. Ao, F. J. Turk, and R. Padullés
497868.abstract: As an emerging remote sensing technology, Polarimetric Radio Occultation (PRO) is capable of characterizing the atmospheric vertical moisture structure and precipitation simultaneously. The PRO concept has been validated in recent years by the experiment “Radio-Occultation and Heavy Precipitation with PAZ (ROHP-PAZ)” onboard the Spanish PAZ mission, which is equipped with a dual-orthogonal polarization antenna that receives the GNSS-RO signals in separate horizontal and vertical channels. While this unique technology has been successfully proven, assimilating the PRO precipitation information in the forecasting operation remains a challenging task due to the lack of a polarimetric phase shift forward operator. In this research we designed a practical PRO forward operator to calculate the 1D/2D polarimetric phase shift profile based on the known modeled 3D liquid/solid water content field. First, the Kdp field of each case is calculated from the preliminary PRO forward operator approach proposed by [Hotta et al, 2025], and a 2D-ray tracing is then applied to integrate the changing phase due to the asymmetric shape of the hydrometeors along the path between two channels. Global and regional statistics of the calculated differential phase shift will be compared to the PAZ observations. We will also demonstrate various PRO forward operator designs by changing the Kdp and differential phase calculations in the forward operator processing chain, including employing a dynamic axis ratio from first principles. These different forward operator approaches will be compared with the results from [Hotta et al, 2025] and the collocated PAZ observations. The strengths and limitations of the approaches under different weather conditions will also be discussed.

497875.title: Building Resilience Where It’s Needed: Addressing Extreme Heat Risk in Rural Arizona
497875.authors: Mona Arora, University of Arizona, Mel and Enid Zuckerman College of Public Health, Tucson, AZ; and S. Chin, M. B. Grace Ngaybe, K. T. Ortiz y Pino, A. Garn, J. H. Hoover, and K. C. Ernst
497875.abstract: Extreme heat poses a growing threat to community health and wellbeing, directly endangering lives and exacerbating existing health disparities. As one of the leading weather-related causes of death in the U.S., extreme heat claims thousands of lives annually, with vulnerable populations bearing the brunt of its impacts. Heat risk is amplified for vulnerable community members including older individuals, those with chronic illnesses, and outdoor workers. Rural and tribal communities face unique challenges in mitigating the effect of extreme heat making it important to identify, document and plan for opportunities to increase resiliency in rural populations. The Southwest Center for Outreach and Resilience in Climate and Health (SCORCH), in partnership with the Arizona Center for Rural Health, the Arizona Department of Health Services, and rural and Tribal partners statewide, conducted five listening sessions across Arizona. The sessions examined local perceptions and experiences of extreme heat, as well as factors that influence risk and vulnerability and communities’ ability to prepare for and respond to heat. Participants represented critical access hospitals, public health departments, libraries, Tribal organizations, and other local organizations that provide or coordinate heat-relief services. Findings from the listening sessions identified that heat action is shaped by geography, infrastructure, and workforce capacity. Like their urban counterparts, rural communities face similar challenges in mitigating heat impacts and supporting heat actions through limited funding. However, rural and tribal communities face unique challenges that should be addressed through tailored, community-driven approaches. This session presents the findings from these conversations and a roadmap to building rural heat resilience.

497876.title: SmallSat Hyperspectral Ocean Color Imaging for Early Detection of Harmful Algal Blooms.
497876.authors: Cheri Heng, NESDIS, Everett, WA; and H. Hope and V. J. Mikles
497876.abstract: Ocean color observations are essential for monitoring marine ecosystem health, detecting harmful algal blooms (HABs), and assessing environmental change. However, current spaceborne ocean color instruments face tradeoffs in spectral resolution, spatial resolution, coverage, and mission cost, limiting their ability to detect developing blooms in complex coastal and inland waters. To address these gaps, we propose a hybrid hyperspectral radiometer designed for integration onto a small satellite platform.
