A comparative analysis of existing missions—including NASA’s Ocean Color Instrument (OCI) and the University of North Carolina Wilmington’s HawkEye sensor—was used to identify key performance requirements. Input from ocean color experts informed the development of a radiometer architecture that balances hyperspectral capability, spatial resolution, and smallsat constraints. The innovation of the proposed system is its hybrid design, which combines hyperspectral imaging with a modified optical path and alternative camera selection to achieve higher spatial resolution than current hyperspectral radiometers. This enables more effective detection of phytoplankton communities associated with emerging HABs in optically complex waters. This next‑generation approach has the potential to expand accessible ocean color observations for HAB detection, ecosystem monitoring, and environmental assessment. Future work will explore the theoretical implementation of a smallsat constellation to improve revisit time and further enhance HAB monitoring capabilities.

497880.title: What Happened in the Historical Catastrophic August 1975 “75.8” Extreme Rainfall Case in Henan, China: An Analysis Based on Convective-Scale Simulations
497880.authors: Ming Xue, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and Z. Wang
497880.abstract: From 4 to 8 August 1975, Henan Province, China, experienced a record-breaking extreme rainfall event, during which 1606 mm and 1005 mm of rainfall were recorded at one station over 3-day and 1-day periods, respectively. This catastrophic rainfall triggered the failure of 62 reservoirs, resulting in one of the worst rainfall-related disasters in recent history. Limited by available data and modeling capabilities, the exact processes involved, especially those at the convective scale, remain uncertain. In this study, Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations at 3 km grid spacing are performed to investigate the multiscale processes responsible for this extreme event. The simulations reveal that the most prominent feature on the day before the major reservoir dam breaks was an east–west-oriented, slow-moving, intense convective rainband that formed and persisted within a narrow region encompassing the upstream and surrounding areas of the dam-breaking Banqiao Reservoir. Within this rainband, intense convection producing rainfall rates of ~150 mm/h affected the same area for more than 5 hours, mostly late at night, leading to over 1000 mm of maximum accumulated rainfall. Strong mesoscale flow convergence among the southerly flows on the east side of the slow-moving remnant vortex of Typhoon Nina (7503), the east-northeasterly flows to the north on the southern periphery of the inland-penetrating subtropical high ridge (forming a “high-pressure dam”), and the strong, moisture-rich easterly flows emanating from the East China Sea between the subtropical high and a landfalling tropical cyclone provided the dynamic forcing that initiated and sustained the intense convection. Afternoon CAPE values of the easterly inflows reached ~3000 J/kg. Low-level momentum flux budget analyses confirm the importance of convergence forcing, while trajectory analyses document the origins of the air parcels feeding the convective updrafts. Spiral rainbands within the typhoon remnant vortex rotate and merge into the main convective rainband, contributing to the total rainfall. Sensitivity experiments suggest that direct lifting by local hills and cold air intrusion from the north play limited roles, although local hills can further slow the northwestward migration of the remnant vortex. The remnant vortex stagnated near the southern border of Henan Province for a few days due to the blocking effect of the “high-pressure dam” to the north, as recognized in previous studies.

497881.title: Constraining Hail Melting and Shed Drop Size Distributions Using ICECHIP Observations and WRF Simulations
497881.authors: Anna James, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and Z. J. Lebo, E. R. Mansell, D. T. Dawson II, and P. Marmorino
497881.abstract: Hail is one of the most damaging and most costly severe weather hazards in the United States, totalling billions of dollars of damage each year. Yet, it is also one of the least understood severe weather hazards. Namely, microphysical processes such as the melting and shedding of hailstones are not fully understood. These microphysical processes strongly contribute to the accuracy of numerical weather prediction models, and thus, the remaining uncertainties are a limiting factor to improving hail forecasts. In recent years, increasingly complex microphysical processes have been incorporated into microphysical parameterizations, such as the NSSL 3-moment bulk scheme, which includes bin-emulating melting of hail. Though its added melting and shedding parameterizations show promising results, the lack of substantial ground observations limits the ability to validate model performance. Additionally, the majority of the knowledge of hail melting and shedding comes from decades-old wind tunnel experiments, which determined the size-dependent melting and shedding that are incorporated into the model microphysics. However, these experiments used tethered, spherical hailstones, which allow for potential uncertainty in the results. To address some of these knowledge gaps and forecast errors, the In-situ Collaborative Experiment for the Collection of Hail In the Plains (ICECHIP) took place during May and June of 2025 and was the first US hail-focused field campaign in over 40 years. This project collected observations of several hail-producing storms throughout the central US, providing the necessary ground observations for evaluating model performance. As a first step to assess model performance with the NSSL 3-moment bulk scheme with bin-emulating melting, the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model is used to simulate a severe, hail-producing storm that occurred near Lubbock, Texas, on 6 June 2025 and was sampled by ICECHIP. Observations from instruments such as optical particle size velocity (PARSIVEL) disdrometers are compared to model-simulated hail and rain size distributions to assess model performance. Similarities between observed and simulated size distributions provide credibility to the decades-old parameterizations, whereas discrepancies are suggestive of incorrect or incomplete parameterizations. Updated ice particle melting and shed drop size parameters are incorporated in the microphysics scheme to improve the representation of hail and rain drop size distributions, with the broader goal of increasing severe hail forecasting skill.

497885.title: Process-Level Aerosol–Cloud–Ice Experiments Using K-CPEC: Ambient Aerosol Processing and Candidate Cloud-Seeding Materials
497885.authors: Junshik Um, KMA, Busan, 48, South korea; Pusan National University, Busan, Busan, Korea, Republic of (South); and S. Park, J. Kim, M. Park, C. Ahn, P. Seo, M. Belorid, B. Y. Kim, Y. S. Oh, C. Cho, S. Kim, J. CHA, J. Lee, S. S. Yum, and S. Jang
497885.abstract: Cloud chamber experiments provide controlled conditions for examining how aerosol properties and atmospheric processing regulate cloud formation and ice nucleation. We present coordinated experiments using the Korea Cloud Physics Experimental Chamber (K-CPEC), operated by the National Institute of Meteorological Sciences (NIMS), focusing on the aerosol-to-cloud particle transition, the ice-nucleating response of ambient aerosol populations, and candidate cloud-seeding materials. To support quantitative comparison among aerosol systems, chamber thermodynamics and particle evolution were characterized concurrently. Spatially distributed thermocouples showed highly uniform temperature fields at steady state; during expansion cooling, spatial variability increased, with vertical differences generally larger than horizontal differences. Synchronized measurements from a scanning mobility particle sizer (SMPS), condensation particle counter (CPC), optical particle counters (OPCs), cloud aerosol spectrometer with depolarization (CAS-DPOL), LI-COR water-vapor analyzers, and cloud particle imager (CPI) resolved aerosol activation and cloud-particle growth. Change-point detection applied to the LI-COR H₂O sample-intensity signal provided an objective cloud-onset indicator, while concurrent changes in particle number concentration, size distribution, morphology, and depolarization ratio characterized the transition from aerosol-dominated to cloud-particle-dominated conditions. Mixed-phase experiments examined the response of ambient aerosol populations to hypersaline processing. NaCl addition to clouds formed from ambient aerosols with weak baseline ice-nucleating activity was followed by enhanced ice formation near −10°C, while untreated ambient aerosols produced little ice under comparable conditions. Comparable enhancement was not reproduced with laboratory-generated inorganic aerosols, either alone or mixed with mineral dust. The several-minute delay before enhancement suggests that hypersaline exposure may modify unidentified salt-sensitive constituents in ambient aerosols rather than reflect an immediate effect of NaCl addition alone. The responsible constituents and mechanisms remain unresolved. These findings connect atmospheric processing of ambient aerosols with processes relevant to atmospheric ice initiation and intentional cloud seeding. Ongoing weather-modification research evaluates environmentally compatible cellulose-based materials as candidate ice-nucleating agents for cloud seeding. Parallel efforts to standardize thermodynamic control and calibrate cloud-particle probes using reference particles of known size aim to constrain uncertainties in particle size distributions, number concentrations, and seeding-response metrics. Together, these studies provide a process-level framework for assessing how ambient aerosol processing and artificial aerosol introduction influence cloud onset and ice formation and for improving the quantitative evaluation of cloud-seeding materials and strategies.

497886.title: Investigating Model Complexity and Structure and Land Surface and Forcing Heterogeneities in the Next Generation Water Resources Modeling Framework
497886.authors: Sifan Abera Koriche, Cooperative Institute for Research to Operations in Hydrology (CIROH) , Alabama Water Institute, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL; and M. S. Alam, F. L. Ogden, M. Kumar, and S. J. Burian
497886.abstract: The goal of this study is to help improve the implementation of the Next Generation Water Resources Modeling Framework as a mosaic of performant models in version 4.0 of the National Water Model (NWM). The research addresses two critical questions: 1) What are the best model structures and configurations for different hydroclimatic and environmental settings? and 2) How does the representation of land surface [via spatial discretization] and meteorological forcing data across different hydro-climatic settings impact model performance and predictive skills? To address these questions, we have systematically analyzed the effects of three key areas on model performance: (1) Model Structure, (2) Discretization, and (3) Forcing. We have investigated performance of various model structures and formulations, explored how tiled to dynamic semi-discretization schemes can enhance the performance of computationally efficient conceptual models, evaluated the impact of forcing heterogeneity on streamflow, and assessed the application of machine learning frameworks. Key results include: (1) the role of basin attributes and hydrologic signatures in predicting extreme hydrological events; (2) a multi-model evaluation approach for conceptual models and the National Water Model; (3) assessment of the performance of various modeling paradigms including conceptual, physically-based models, and machine learning frameworks; (4) enhancing the performance of catchment-based hydrological models by using tiled to dynamic sub-discretization based on land surface attributes; and (5) investigating how representing the space-time variability of key forcing variables, such as precipitation, impacts overall model performance. This study delivers the systematic guidance needed to build more effective and robust hydrologic model configurations within the NextGen framework.

497890.title: Extreme Event Representation by AI Foundation Models: A Multi-Scale Spectral Analysis of Tropical Cyclones and Atmospheric Rivers
497890.authors: Chunyong Jung, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, IL; ANL, Lemont, IL; and J. Toniolo, H. Tan, D. K. Fytanidis, W. J. Pringle, J. Wang, R. Kotamarthi, W. Wang, W. M. Thiaw, L. M. Harris, M. Olsen, and S. W. Bieda III, PhD
497890.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is reshaping weather prediction by reducing forecast generation times from hours on high-performance computing systems to just minutes with reduced computational resources. At the same time, AI-based models have demonstrated competitive, and in some cases superior, performance compared with traditional physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems when evaluated using broad global metrics such as root mean squared error (RMSE) and anomaly correlation. However, these aggregated measures can obscure a model’s limitations in representing the fine-scale dynamics, sharp gradients, and structural evolution associated with high-impact regional extremes. This study presents a detailed multi-scale diagnostic evaluation of Argonne’s AI foundation models such as AERIS (Hatanpää et al., 2025), STORMER (Nguyen et al., 2024), and SWIFT (Stock et al., 2025), compared with its forcing data ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020) and NOAA’s High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) analysis dataset. Our presentation focuses on the ability of the model to simulate two distinct classes of extreme events: tropical cyclones (TCs), which are major drivers of high-impact weather in the eastern United States (U.S.), and atmospheric rivers (ARs), which are key contributors to extreme precipitation and hydrologic hazards along the western U.S. Rather than relying solely on traditional error metrics, we evaluate model performance in terms of structural integrity and multi-scale physical consistency. Specifically, we apply spatial spectral analysis to diagnose scale-dependent kinetic energy variances, allowing us to quantify the degree to which these data-driven models preserve structural realism versus exhibit unphysical spatial smoothing of storm dynamics transport. We will present our comparison of computational efficiency, predictive accuracy, and meteorological realism across the AI modeling systems.

497892.title: Evaluating Commercial Observations from the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) Aboard Tomorrow-S2 Using an Attention-Based Deep-Learning Framework for Atmospheric Profile Retrievals
497892.authors: Said A Mejia Manrique, The City College of New York, NYC, NY; and M. D. Goldberg
497892.abstract: The rapid expansion of commercial low-Earth-orbit microwave sounder constellations provides an opportunity to increase the temporal sampling of atmospheric temperature and moisture observations and complement existing operational satellite systems. This study extends an attention-based deep-learning atmospheric retrieval framework, originally developed for the Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder (ATMS), to observations from the Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder (TMS) aboard Tomorrow-S2. The objective is to assess the capability of commercial microwave sounding observations for artificial intelligence (AI)-based atmospheric profile retrieval and to compare their performance with retrievals obtained from the operational JPSS-1 ATMS. The retrieval framework consists of separate models for atmospheric temperature (T) and specific humidity (q), each providing vertical profile estimates and associated retrieval uncertainty. The architecture combines convolutional and attention-based learning with multiscale feature representation and incorporates auxiliary information describing surface conditions, geographic location, viewing geometry, observation time, and data validity. Training uses a custom composite loss designed to improve profile accuracy, vertical consistency, spatial structure, and uncertainty estimation across 37 pressure levels. The same general architecture is applied to ATMS and adapted to the spectral characteristics of TMS, providing a consistent framework for evaluating information content from the operational and commercial observing systems. The ATMS implementation provides a well-characterized benchmark for the commercial-sounder evaluation. Two versions of the temperature retrieval model were independently trained using one and three years of ATMS observations and evaluated on the same fixed January–May 2025 test dataset, independent of model training and validation. Relative to ERA5 atmospheric profiles, increasing the training period from one to three years reduced the sample-weighted atmospheric-column RMSE from approximately 1.20 K to 1.09 K, corresponding to an improvement of approximately 9%. Independent evaluation against collocated radiosonde observations similarly reduced RMSE from approximately 1.59 K for the one-year model to 1.54 K for the three-year model. For the same radiosonde comparison sample, the three-year AI retrieval outperformed the operational MiRS and NUCAPS products, which produced atmospheric-column RMSE values of approximately 2.45 K and 1.97 K, respectively. These results demonstrate improved generalization as the training dataset is expanded and establish the three-year ATMS model as the primary benchmark for evaluating the commercial TMS retrieval. A preliminary evaluation has subsequently been performed using real TMS observations from Tomorrow-S2 on an independent test day, 28 May 2025. The TMS temperature model was trained using Tomorrow-S2 observations spanning September 2024 through October 2025, with all observations from May 2025 excluded from model training and validation. This temporal holdout ensures that the May 2025 evaluation represents an independent test period not encountered during model development. The present analysis focuses on temperature retrievals and compares ascending-orbit TMS and ATMS observations. To reduce the influence of differences in spatial sampling density between the two sensors, retrieval errors relative to ERA5 were first averaged within 0.25° latitude–longitude grid cells, allowing each occupied spatial cell to contribute one mean-error sample. Pressure levels located below the local surface were excluded using surface pressure, and bias and error standard deviation were calculated as functions of pressure. Only levels having adequate spatial representation from both observing systems were retained. The preliminary experiment includes approximately 1.5 million valid atmospheric profiles from each sensor. Initial results show generally small temperature biases for both TMS and ATMS through most of the atmospheric column. TMS exhibits a vertical error structure broadly consistent with ATMS through much of the troposphere and lower-to-middle stratosphere, although its error dispersion is generally larger than that of ATMS and the differences increase toward the lowest-pressure upper-atmospheric levels. These preliminary results demonstrate the successful application of the attention-based retrieval framework to real commercial TMS observations and provide an initial quantitative assessment of commercial microwave-sounder retrieval performance relative to an established operational sensor. Because the current TMS comparison represents a single independent test day, the next phase will extend the evaluation to a substantially larger multi-day test dataset encompassing a broader range of geographic regions, atmospheric states, surface conditions, and viewing geometries. The expanded evaluation will examine vertical retrieval accuracy, bias, uncertainty calibration, and surface- and geometry-dependent performance and will subsequently extend the analysis to specific-humidity retrievals. The study provides a framework for quantitatively assessing emerging commercial microwave sounder observations and their potential to complement operational environmental satellite sounding systems.

497893.title: Environmental Preconditioning of East Pacific Easterly Wave Evolution for Tropical Cyclogenesis During Different Madden–Julian Oscillation Phases
497893.authors: Yu-Cian Tsai, Colorado State University, FORT COLLINS, CO; and E. D. Maloney
497893.abstract: East Pacific easterly waves (EWs) are the important precursors of tropical cyclones (TCs) over the eastern Pacific, making their accurate representation essential for subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecasts. However, recent evaluations of NOAA's Unified Forecast System (UFS) indicate that systematic biases in simulated EW activity remain a major source of forecast uncertainty. Although previous studies have shown that both EW activity and TC genesis are enhanced during the convectively active phases of the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO), the physical processes through which the MJO preconditions EWs for subsequent tropical cyclogenesis remain incompletely understood. Using ERA5 reanalysis for 1984–2023, we investigate how the MJO modifies the large-scale dynamical and thermodynamical environment governing EW growth to establish a physical framework for interpreting these forecast biases. EW tracking reveals substantially greater wave activity during wet MJO phases than during dry and neutral phases, including higher track density, longer-lived disturbances, and enhanced synoptic-scale eddy kinetic energy. Composite analyses show that wet MJO conditions are characterized by enhanced low-level vorticity, stronger meridional moisture gradients, and a background flow more favorable for barotropic instability. These environmental changes strengthen moisture–vortex instability, resulting in greater EW amplification before and during genesis. A moist static energy (MSE) budget further reveals that the interaction between meridional wind anomalies and the background meridional MSE gradient provides the primary energy source for wave growth, whereas interactions with the perturbation MSE gradient act to damp the disturbance. As EWs mature, enhanced deep convection produces stronger longwave cloud-radiative heating that provides an additional diabatic energy source, enabling mature waves to more effectively extract energy from the background environment and sustain continued growth favorable for TC development. These results support a two-stage mechanism linking the MJO to tropical cyclogenesis over the eastern Pacific. The MJO first establishes a large-scale environment favorable for moisture–vortex instability and accelerated EW growth, after which cloud-radiative feedback sustains and intensifies mature disturbances, increasing their likelihood of transitioning into TCs. This observational framework provides a physical interpretation for recent UFS findings that EW activity is highly sensitive to the background moisture environment and offers process-based diagnostics for evaluating and improving the representation of tropical wave evolution and wave-to-TC transition in S2S forecast systems.

497894.title: Integrating Satellite Observations into the Prithvi-WxC AI Foundation Model for Improved Precipitation Forecasts
497894.authors: Simon Pfreundschuh, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and C. D. Kummerow, J. Schmude, S. Roy, and R. Ramachandran
497894.abstract: Accurate precipitation forecasting remains a major challenge in numerical and AI-based weather prediction. Although recent AI weather prediction systems have achieved substantial gains in medium-range forecast skill, precipitation is often learned from reanalysis datasets that have known weaknesses in representing precipitation. We present Prithvi-Precip, a global AI precipitation forecasting system built on the Prithvi-WxC geospatial AI foundation model (FM), and investigate two complementary strategies for improving precipitation forecasts: training to predict satellite-derived precipitation estimates and directly ingesting satellite observations into the forecast model. We systematically evaluate key design choices for finetuning the Prithvi-WxC FM for precipitation forecasting. Autoregressive rollout training produces more accurate forecasts than directly conditioning the model on forecast lead time. Evaluation against independent precipitation estimates from ground-based radars shows that models trained on satellite-based precipitation data outperform otherwise equivalent models trained on MERRA-2 or ERA5 precipitation fields. Direct ingestion of satellite observations provides additional improvements at short lead times, with the largest benefits found across tropical and subtropical regions. Combined, these advances allow Prithvi-Precip to improve upon directly comparable precipitation forecasts from the Goddard Earth Observing System. These results demonstrate that improvements in both precipitation target data and the direct ingestion of satellite observations can improve forecast skill. More broadly, they highlight the potential of satellite observations as an important resource for improving next-generation AI precipitation forecasts.

497895.title: Direct Assimilation of Radar Reflectivity and Radial Velocity Data in JEDI EnVar Coupled with MPAS: Use of Power-Transformed Hydrometeors at Control Variables and Evaluation of the Capability
497895.authors: Ming Xue, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and T. Wang, C. Liu, and N. A. Snook
497895.abstract: NOAA's future-generation convective-scale prediction system, the Rapid Refresh Forecast System (RRFS) version 2, will use the MPAS dynamical core, while the data assimilation (DA) will transition from GSI to the JEDI framework. Direct variational assimilation of radar reflectivity is a necessary capability for convective-scale prediction in this MPAS-JEDI system. Recently, we implemented such a capability within JEDI En3DVar (Park et al. 2026) and tested it coupling with FV3 dynamic core (which is used by NOAA operational RRFS version 1). The implementation used the standard mixing ratios as the control variables for hydrometeors (which we denote as CVq) that are involved in the reflectivity observation operators. Our earlier studies showed that with CVq, the gradient of the cost-function involving reflectivity can become extremely large when background mixing ratios approach zero, severely slowing minimization convergence. Hydrometeor control variables based on a power transform with a tunable power exponent (CVpq) were shown in our earlier studies to improve minimization convergence and the final analyses within GSI En3DVar. This study implements and evaluates CVpq capabilities in JEDI En3DVar coupled with MPAS. Specifically, the mixing ratios of rainwater, snow, and graupel, together with the rainwater number concentration, are transformed through CVpq = (qp − 1)/p, where the exponent p controls the nonlinearity of the transformation: the transform approaches a logarithmic function (Cvlogq) as p tends to zero, and is equivalent to CVq when p = 1. The power transform is implemented within JEDI En3dVar that also involves tangent-linear and adjoint of the transform function. The direct assimilation of reflectivity involves a refined observation operator consistent with the double-moment Thompson microphysics scheme RRFS uses. The direct use of reflectivity observation operator makes incorporation of static background error covariance to form hybrid En3DVar straightforward. The capability implemented is evaluated with a derecho-producing mesoscale convective system over the U.S. Upper Midwest on 12–13 May 2022, using a 3-km MPAS mesh and hourly En3DVar cycling from 1900 UTC 12 May to 0000 UTC 13 May, with flow-dependent background error covariances estimated from ensemble forecasts of JEDI LETKF hourly DA cycles that also assimilate reflectivity and radial velocity data. In experiments varying p from 0 to 1, intermediate p values improve minimization convergence and analysis fits to reflectivity observations relative to CVq, with the analysis-fit advantage becoming more pronounced in later DA cycles. p values of 0.4–0.6 show the most consistent short-range forecast improvements. In 6-hour forecasts initialized from the final analyses, p = 0.4 reduces the reflectivity forecast error and increases the 35-dBZ neighborhood critical success index relative to CVq. These results are consistent with our earlier results within the GSI framework. This work was supported by the NOAA R2O program and the capabilities developed and tested can potentially be used in JEDI-MPAS-based RRFS version 2. Reference cited: Park, J., C. Liu, and M. Xue, 2026: Development and Testing of Ensemble-Variational Data Assimilation Capabilities for Radar Data within JEDI coupled with FV3-LAM Model. Geoscientific Model Development, Conditionally accepted.

497901.title: Leveraging SEO, AEO, and GEO to Engage Users of NOAA Weather and Climate Data at NCEI
497901.authors: Rich Baldwin, NOAA, Asheville, NC; NESDIS, Asheville, NC; and J. E. Myer
497901.abstract: The NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) consistently delivers approximately 15PB of environmental information to customers through a wide range of data access methods, including custom built search and discovery interfaces and interactive maps, APIs, web-accessible data folders, and subsetting services. These tools and services are reliable and familiar to long-time customers, but they can be difficult for people without advanced technical skills or scientific expertise to use. This creates a fractured customer experience that leads to a high volume of requests for the NCEI’s user engagement teams and subject matter experts. NCEI is using customer feedback, web analytics, and user experience (UX) testing software to identify friction points early in the software development and make these tools and services easier to use and understand. Additionally, we’re incorporating AI tools and emerging best practices for answer engine optimization (AEO) to make data accessible to agentic tools and software. This presentation will highlight specific projects where these methods have either improved the customer experience, or identified major friction points to be addressed in future testing.

497904.title: Preparing For The GeoXO Sounder (GXS): AI/ML Retrieval Of Atmospheric Temperature And Water Vapor From High-Volume Hyperspectral Infrared Sounders — CrIS, IASI, And MTG-IRS
497904.authors: Mitchell D. Goldberg, CUNY CREST, New York Cirty, NY; The City College of New York, New York City, NY; and S. A. Mejia Manrique, D. Li, M. kang, L. Zhou, S. Kalluri, and A. Heidinger
497904.abstract: The NOAA GeoXO Geostationary Extended Sounder (GXS) will deliver hyperspectral infrared soundings at a temporal and spatial density far exceeding any current operational sounder, generating a data volume that is impractical for physical/statistical retrieval algorithms to process within operational latency requirements. This work develops and evaluates multi-layer perceptron (MLP) neural network retrievals of atmospheric temperature and water vapor as an AI/ML-based approach capable of meeting GXS's operational throughput demands, using three current and next-generation hyperspectral infrared sounders as testbeds: the Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) on NOAA-20/NOAA-21, the Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer (IASI) on MetOp-B/C, and the Meteosat Third Generation Infrared Sounder (MTG-IRS), using the first pre-operational data release from the instrument. Because MTG-IRS is the first geostationary hyperspectral infrared sounder in orbit, it serves as the closest available real-world analog to GXS, and this work directly evaluates whether MLP retrieval skill developed and validated on polar-orbiting CrIS and IASI translates to the geostationary viewing geometry, spectral characteristics, and scan pattern GXS will share with MTG-IRS. The evaluation proceeds in two stages. First, each sensor's MLP retrievals are developed and validated independently, with radiances from CrIS, IASI, and MTG-IRS each collocated separately in space and time against ERA5 reanalysis to form three sensor-specific training/validation datasets. This independent-evaluation stage establishes baseline retrieval skill for each instrument on its own terms, using its native spectral coverage and viewing geometry, and includes a direct comparison of CrIS MLP retrieval accuracy against NOAA's current operational CrIS retrieval algorithm. Second, because CrIS and IASI fly in different sun-synchronous orbits with different equator-crossing times, direct three-way collocation among all three sensors is not possible; instead, two independent sensor-to-sensor collocated pairs are constructed against the continuously observing MTG-IRS: IASI–MTG-IRS and CrIS–MTG-IRS, each matched in space and time at coincident overpass opportunities. This pairwise design allows direct, common-scene comparison of MLP retrieval performance between MTG-IRS and each polar-orbiting sounder without requiring simultaneous three-instrument overlap. To reduce each sensor's hyperspectral radiance vector to a compact predictor set well suited to fast neural network inference, principal component (PC) scores are used rather than raw channel radiances. For MTG-IRS and IASI, PC scores are taken directly from the operational EUMETSAT data distribution. For CrIS, no equivalent operational PC product is used; instead, PCA is performed in-house to derive CrIS-specific PCs from the longwave and midwave radiances. This approach preserves each data stream's native compression while ensuring all three MLPs are trained on a consistent, low-dimensional input structure appropriate for the high-throughput retrieval GXS will require. Co-registered imager cloud fraction is included as an additional MLP predictor for all three sensors, with source dependent on the sounder: VIIRS cloud fraction for CrIS, AVHRR cloud fraction for IASI, and cloud fraction from MTG-IRS's own imager for MTG-IRS. Providing scene-dependent cloud information allows each MLP to adjust how it weights spectral information as cloud contamination increases. Retrieval error for temperature and water vapor is characterized as a function of cloud fraction across the full range from clear sky to complete overcast for all three sensors, both in the independent per-sensor evaluation and in the IASI–MTG-IRS and CrIS–MTG-IRS collocated pairs, enabling assessment of whether the cloud-fraction dependence of retrieval skill is consistent across sensors and viewing geometries or diverges between polar and geostationary sounding. Results show that the MLP retrieval approach improves on the accuracy of NOAA's current operational CrIS retrieval algorithm while requiring substantially less computational cost per sounding, directly addressing the data-volume challenge GXS will pose to operational processing. Taken together with the MTG-IRS-based geostationary evaluation, this work supports AI/ML neural network retrievals as a viable and necessary path forward for the GXS operational retrieval system.

497905.title: Advancing Actionable Climate Forecasts and Disease Modeling and Predictions
497905.abstract: The 90-minute panel will bring together experts on climate, environment, and health to discuss advances in climate-based health early warning systems. We begin by framing the conversation around climate and health by discussing the critical role of climate variability and change in shaping infectious and non-transmissible diseases dynamics and the imperative need to advance actionable climate and disease modeling and predictions. We then discuss recent advances in environmental modeling and the tailoring of predictions to respond to the needs of the heath sector. We provide examples of climate-based infectious disease modeling and heat-health forecasts and work underway to advance the use of climate information in public health policy, and discuss challenges the scientific community needs to address, especially in epidemiological modeling and predictions. We close by discussing the end-to-end process of climate-based health early warning systems, its sustainability through multidisciplinary partnerships across all sectors of environment, health, and policy.

497911.title: Developing Hyperspectral Infrared ML Inversion Methods for Thermodynamic Profiling In Dusty Environments
497911.authors: Hamlet Abrahamyan, Space Science and Engineering Center, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and A. M. Lieblein, R. Holz, P. Veglio, G. Quinn, J. K. Taylor, D. C. Tobin, W. J. Marais, and S. Dutcher
497911.abstract: The vertical placement of dust governs its radiative effect, ability for models to accurately assimilate and forecast dust transport, and it impacts to the operational community including aviation and air quality. Despite these important applications, operational remote sensing of dust is limited to reflectance (daytime) 2-D retrievals that lack vertical profiling capabilities. Although spaceborne lidar resolves the vertical structure, lidars provide limited spatial sampling with only a nadir measurements, thus leaving most dust events unobserved in the vertical. Hyperspectral infrared sounders, such as CrIS, offer a complementary twice-daily global coverage and a distinct dust signature across the longwave window. The challenge is that recovering height and thermodynamic profiles within dust from these radiances is an ill-posed inverse problem. ML/AI methods learn to solve a problem through example (i.e., training) data. The ML/AI methods quantitatively learn (i.e., estimate) a non-linear mapping from hyperspectral observations to thermodynamic and aerosol optical depth (AOD) profiles, and this estimation of the non-linear mapping is learned through a comprehensive high-quality training dataset. Thus, the ability to accurately map hyperspectral observations to thermodynamic and aerosol profiles hinges on the ability of the ML/AI method to learn a highly non-linear mapping and the quality of the training dataset. Successful implementation of ML/AI requires a training dataset that both captures the natural variability of the dust vertical stratification, and the correlated environmental information such as water vapor and temperature. Given the limited measurements that can capture these properties (ground, aircraft, and space based lidar), developing the training data is a significant challenge and a focus of this research. For these reasons, this presentation will focus on the development of the training data, radiative transfer simulations, and implementation of the ML retrieval that is optimized to leverage the multidimensional nature of the IR hyperspectral observations. Initial results applied to CrIS observations coincident with field experiment observations for validation will be presented.

497913.title: A Multi-Model Analysis of the Transatlantic Dust Transport, Deposition, and Optical Properties In the AeroCom Phase III
497913.authors: Jianyu Zheng, UMBC GESTARII, College Station, TX; and H. Yu, M. Chin, Y. Balkanski, S. Bauer, H. Bian, P. R. Colarco, D. Kim, R. Checa-Garcia, O. Dubovik, P. Ginoux, Z. Kipling, J. F. Kok, H. Matsui, S. Rémy, Q. Song, Q. Tan, K. Tsigaridis, and Z. Zhang
497913.abstract: This study evaluates the transatlantic dust cycle simulated by 17 global aerosol models in the AeroCom Phase III (P3) control experiment for 2010. Model performance is assessed against multi-source observations, including AERONET inversions, satellite products (MODIS, CALIOP, MISR, IASI, POLDER, and MODIS-TIR), DustCOMM, CAMS, MERRA-2, in-situ deposition and surface concentration records, and GPCP precipitation. The assessment covers dust emissions, optical depth (DOD), mass loading, mass extinction efficiency (MEE), vertical distribution, deposition, loss frequency, surface concentration, and precipitation over North Africa (NAF), the eastern Atlantic Ocean (EAO), the Gulf of Guinea (GOG), and the Caribbean Sea (CAR). AeroCom P3 has narrowed the annual mean mid-visible DOD diversity to 30–45% across the transport domain relative to AeroCom P2 (38–59%), yet this convergence masks compensatory biases, as models with lower (or higher) mass loading may have higher (or lower) MEE, yielding similar DOD despite different mass representations. Model biases intensify with transport distance. Median DOD is underestimated by ~50% over EAO and GOG and ~70% over CAR against satellite observations, and loss frequencies exceed satellite-derived values by a factor of 2–3, possibly reflecting parameterization deficiencies in size-dependent gravitational settling, vertical transport, wet scavenging, and free-tropospheric turbulence. Two models with enhanced super-coarse dust contribution (INCA-4DU and ECMWF-CY46) still fail to resolve these downwind biases. Advancing transatlantic dust simulations therefore requires concurrent progress on not only extending emitted size distributions to super-coarse dust but also non-spherical optical and settling parameterizations, and mechanisms sustaining coarse and giant particles aloft.

497920.title: Quantifying the Impact of a Next-Generation GNSS-RO and GNSS-R Constellation on Numerical Weather Prediction: an Observation System Simulation Experiment (OSSE)
497920.authors: Jeffrey Lawrence Steward, Orion Space Solutions, Louisville, CO; and F. Gasperini, I. Collett, A. Reynolds, N. Tipton, J. Wilson, R. Stutz, G. Crowley, and C. Fish
497920.abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals of opportunity have become foundational to modern atmospheric research and numerical weather prediction (NWP). To further advance these capabilities, Orion Space Solutions is planning a constellation of next-generation SmallSats equipped with a novel, unified payload combining GNSS-Radio Occultation (GNSS-RO) and GNSS-Reflectometry (GNSS-R). This integrated platform provides SI-traceable, bias-free temperature and water vapor profiles with exceptional vertical resolution (100-200 meters) in the troposphere, capable of revealing fine-scale vertical structures often smoothed by traditional nadir sounders. Simultaneously, a complementary payload utilizes GNSS signal reflections to measure sea state and surface winds. Because the L-band frequency penetrates clouds and heavy precipitation, these complementary observations are uniquely positioned to capture high-impact weather, such as tropical cyclones, where traditional radiometers often struggle. Before deploying this large-scale architecture, it is critical to evaluate its potential influence on operational weather models. To achieve this, we present a comprehensive framework for developing Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) specifically designed to prove the impacts of assimilating combined GNSS-RO and GNSS-R observations. This OSSE framework simulates the data assimilation of the satellite constellation's synthetic observations into state-of-the-art weather models. By doing so, it quantitatively assesses how the synergy of high-resolution atmospheric profiling and concurrent surface wind data improves the accuracy of NWP analyses and forecasts. This OSSE framework can serve as a vital Research-to-Operations (R2O) bridge. It not only guides data assimilation strategies for novel unified GNSS payloads but also demonstrates the value of a dense, next-generation constellation for filling critical observational gaps and advancing our understanding of atmospheric processes across scales.

497922.title: A CIROH Hydrometeorological Prediction Testbed Supporting the Advancement of CONUS-Wide Water Forecasting Capabilities
497922.authors: Andrew W. Wood, NCAR, BOULDER, CO; and J. Sturtevant, K. van Werkhoven, and P. Clemins
497922.abstract: A key to the success of the forecast-oriented research in NOAA Cooperative Institute for R2O in Hydrology will be its ability to overcome the well-known ‘valley of death’ that slows the operational adoption of state-of-the-science modeling, methods and datasets in pragmatic hydrologic prediction operations and applications. With this motivation, we have designed and implemented a CIROH Hydrologic Prediction Testbed, also known as ‘HydrometBench’. HydrometBench is a CIROH-led research activity created to support the evaluation and benchmarking, selection and adoption of critical forecasting-relevant capabilities for transition into the National Water Model operations, including the Nextgen framework. The Testbed develops experimental ‘Protocols’ to assess and benchmark specific new techniques, models, model elements, workflows and datasets targeting distinct objectives (e.g., watershed-scale streamflow simulation, flash flood prediction, or sub-seasonal to seasonal water supply prediction) from an evidence-driven perspective. At present, there are few published and widely adopted benchmarks for US (or global) hydrologic forecast state-of-practice performance or skill, which makes it difficult to determine, quantitatively, the extent to which any new development in a forecasting system improves forecast skill. As protocols are developed, the testbed project is also working to construct and promulgate such benchmarks. To date, the CHPT has focused on a number of protocols, including short-to-medium range river forecasts, S2S runoff forecasts (e.g., water supply forecasting), meteorological forcings, and SWE estimation at catchment scales. Baseline capabilities for assessing performance are drawn from current working versions of NWS hydrologic forecasts and other NOAA products, including the current NWM and Nextgen capabilities as well as River Forecast Center (RFC) capabilities. The major outcome of this effort has been to establish a CIROH community Testbed practice that promotes the structured benchmarking of new hydrologic prediction science (models, methods, data, workflows), fostering evidence-based research assessment to support national water modeling and prediction services. This presentation reviews the CHPT philosophy and progress to date.

497924.title: Advanced Multi-Modal Access Methods for Hybrid Orbital-Ground Architectures: Integrating LLMs, APIs, and Parsl-Based Distributed Computing to Orchestrate Edge Intelligence
497924.authors: Jeffrey Lawrence Steward, Orion Space Solutions, Louisville, CO; and J. Highley, A. Irvine, E. Vance, R. Stutz, C. Harless, E. McAleavy, and J. Wilson
497924.abstract: Environmental satellite operators face unprecedented data volumes from proliferated constellations, necessitating a shift toward AI-driven orbital-based operational ground systems. To meet this challenge, we present an open-source, entirely ground-based reference architecture that orchestrates and enables intelligent decision-making at the orbital edge. This system revolutionizes data operationalization through a triad of access interfaces: a natural language Large Language Model (LLM) agent, a RESTful API, and a dynamic 3D visualization engine. The architecture utilizes a single-agent LLM framework grounded by a Knowledge Mesh and Hybrid Graph-Retrieval Augmented Generation (Graph-RAG). Acting as an intelligent orchestrator, the LLM translates natural language queries into Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) of functional scientific tasks. This ground-based framework drives hybrid orbital-ground integration by evaluating operational constraints and autonomously tasking on-orbit compute nodes. By delegating triage, anomaly detection, and initial data fusion to the edge, the system allows for moving critical decision-making closer to the sensor. This drastically reduces downlink latency for severe weather products and enables adaptive mission operations capable of responding to evolving environmental conditions. A major contribution of this framework is its computational power, driven by a Parsl-based execution engine. This asynchronous backend provides transparent workload distribution, enabling workflows to be deployed seamlessly across scalable Kubernetes clusters and Slurm-managed High-Performance Computing (HPC) nodes on the ground. This flexibility is critical for rapidly executing computationally heavy ensemble simulations that require rigorous uncertainty quantification on the ground, integrating seamlessly with edge-processed telemetry. Scientific outputs are dynamically routed to our visualization engine, which employs out-of-core spatiotemporal masking to render multi-gigabyte datasets as OGC 3D Tiles in near real-time. By coupling Parsl-driven distributed computing with conversational LLM discovery, this architecture establishes a highly interoperable platform. We conclude with lessons learned on how AI-driven orbital-ground integration provides a cost-effective, scalable foundation for the next generation of weather and climate intelligence.

497931.title: Late 21st-Century Saharan Dust-Induced Changes In Precipitation and the Link to African Easterly Wave Tracks In the WRF Model.
497931.authors: Gregory S. Jenkins, Penn State University, University Park, PA
497931.abstract: The Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulations using lateral boundary conditions from CMIP5 and CMIP6 Earth Systems Models show surface PM10 concentrations increase across the Southern Sahara and Northern Sahel regions in the late 21st century relative to the historical period during Northern Hemisphere Summer. In addition, there is an equatorward shift in the westward transport of dust, a reduction in precipitation, and an equatorward shift in the African Easterly Jet with RCP8.5 forcing. In this presentation, we show simulated changes in the Northern and Southern African Easterly Waves (AEWs) tracks for historical and late 21st century summer seasons. Changes in Northern and Southern AEW tracks help to explain why precipitation amounts are reduced and what this might mean for the population of West Africa approaching 1 billion at the end of the century and tropical disturbances in the Main Development Region (MDR).

497934.title: Isotopic Characterization of Methane across Texas Using a Fast-Response Infrared Laser Spectroscopy
497934.authors: Jiajue Chai, State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, Syracuse, NY; and K. Moll, Y. Li, J. Zhao, A. J. Dodero, K. McCary, J. Gonzales, A. Treadway, and Y. Zhang
497934.abstract: Atmospheric methane (CH4), the second largest global warming potential (GWP) over 100 years and an important ozone precursor, is emitted from a variety of natural (wetlands, termites, etc.) and anthropogenic (fossil fuel, waste, agriculture, etc.) sources. Accurately quantifying the CH4 budget and source contributions provides the first-order information to understand its environmental impact and develop mitigation policies. However, currently, there is a major mismatch between bottom-up inventory and top-down estimates, causing significant uncertainty in the CH4 budget on global and regional scales. Additionally, source apportionment is challenging based on the concentration method alone. Notably, the carbon isotopic composition δ13C-CH4 (indicative of the stable carbon isotope ratio (13C:12C) of CH4) is a powerful tool for tracking the sources and sinks of atmospheric CH4, and can potentially help better constrain the CH4 budget. In the summer of 2026, in coordination with the TexAQS airborne campaign, we deployed our Tunable Infrared Laser Direct Absorption Spectroscopy (TILDAS) on a mobile platform in Texas for 40 days. We obtained spatially resolved CH4 concentration and δ13C-CH4 data, with fast response (1 second) precision (1σ) of 0.2 ppmv and 0.3 per mil (‰), respectively. The spatial coverage of our campaign included three urban centers (Dallas, Houston, and San Antonio) as well as the O&G-producing Permian Basin, focused in Midland, Odessa, Carlsbad, and Hobbs. For instance, our preliminary analysis of Hobbs data shows an average methane concentration of 1800±100 ppbv, and δ13C isotopic distributions between -31‰ and -28‰. Combined with GPS data, our results revealed the spatial distribution of CH4concentration and δ13C-CH4. These data will allow us to 1) determine the δ13C-CH4 source signatures associated with various O&G production and processing facilities, and 2) apportion the source contributions in urban areas using an isotopic Bayesian mixing model based on our observations and previously measured source δ13C-CH4 values. Texas is home to several urban environments with unique emission source mixing, as well as the Permian Basin, which houses the country’s largest oil and gas (O&G) producing sector. Concentration measurements alongside isotopic-based source apportionment provide invaluable data for developing better constrained methane inventories. These insights would enable better mitigation of methane emissions, with great implications for GHG-GWP and urban air quality.

497936.title: Convergent Observational Constraints on Forcing from Aerosol-Driven Low Cloud Cover Increase Using Machine Learning and Physical Experiments
497936.authors: Haipeng Zhang, UMBC GESTAR-II, baltimore, MD; and T. Yuan and H. Song
497936.abstract: Aerosol-cloud interactions remain the largest source of uncertainty in anthropogenic radiative forcing and observational constraints are hard because aerosol perturbations covary with meteorology. Ship-tracks provide causal constraints on aerosol effects but are limited in scale and cloud-regime coverage, whereas Lagrangian trajectory analyses sample cloud evolutions at larger scales but lack direct causal validation. Here we show convergent observational constraints on cloud fraction adjustments to cloud droplet number concentration (Nd). by combining a large ensemble of satellite-observed Lagrangian trajectories through the stratocumulus-to-cumulus transition with multivariate linear regression and explainable machine learning. The independently inferred Lagrangian adjustment functions closely match those from ship-track analyses in both shape and magnitude, despite differences in perturbation source, sampling, method, scale, and cloud regimes. The cloud fraction adjustment is a strongly nonlinear function of background Nd, largest under clean conditions, and saturates above approximately 60 cm-³. Applying these functions to preindustrial-to-present aerosol perturbations yields a cloud-fraction adjustment forcing of −0.3 to −0.5 W m-², comparable to the Twomey effect, while effect from liquid-water-path adjustment is weak but uncertain. These convergent observational constraints indicate that aerosol-drive increases in low-cloud fraction are a major component of forcing from aerosol-cloud interactions and provide a benchmark for modeling and marine cloud brightening studies.

497937.title: An Assessment of Climate Trends, Crop Yield Dynamics, and Effects of Climate Variability on Crop Yields in Three Decades (1991-2020) in Nebraska, United States
497937.authors: Bijay R Bagale, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE
497937.abstract: The historical relationship of climate variables with that of corn and soybeans production and yields in Nebraska, U.S. were analyzed and quantified using the related variables of temperature, precipitation and RH (annual, monthly mean, growing season mean), and datasets of corn and soybean plantation areas, annual production and yields for the study period (1991 to 2020). Similarly, the effects of climate variability on annual crop yields were evaluated and quantified using the detrended statewide crop yields and the mean temperature and accumulated precipitation of the growing season (May to September). Jupyter notebook, SAS and MS Excel were used for data analysis. The study showed that both temperature and precipitation have a slight increasing trend over the study period and there is a significant year-to-year variability. The per unit area and total annual production of both corn and soybeans show an increasing trend. Positive correlation (not statistically significant) was found to exist between climatic variables (such as annual mean and growing season mean temperature) and crop variables such as annual production and yields. Similarly, to evaluate the climate sensitivity of corn and soybeans yield, the temperature only, precipitation only, additive linear, quadratic, and full quadratic with interaction climate regressions were computed and compared. For corn, the temperate and precipitation interaction was found to be positive (β = 0.916; p = 0.005), which indicates that the temperature-yield relationship is dependent upon precipitation. In case of soybeans, 39.9% of detrended yield variability was explained by quadratic model employed (RMSE = 8.35 %; p = 0.01). The negative quadratic precipitation coefficient (β = −0.286; p < 0.001) implies that there is a statistically significant concave relationship between the soybeans yield anomaly and the accumulated growing season precipitation. The anomalies in corn yield were best described by the temperature-precipitation interaction whereas the accumulated precipitation exhibited a concave association with soybeans yield. The findings indicate that the relationship between corn and soybeans yields are sensitive to climate variability, however, do not establish any fundamental association or responses related to irrigation.

497942.title: Investigation of PyroCb Smoke Aerosol Radiative Effects in the Upper Troposphere and Lower Stratosphere
497942.authors: Cheng-Hsuan Lu, Univ. at Albany, State Univ. of New York, Albany, NY; and V. Bagadia, D. A. Peterson, F. Yu, G. Luo, and T. H. Lin
497942.abstract: Pyrocumulonimbus (PyroCbs) are poorly-understood and inadequately-predicted severe weather phenomenon driven by large and intense fires and unique meteorological conditions. PyroCbs can inject volcanic-scale smoke plumes into the stratosphere that encircle the globe, reside for more than a year, alter stratospheric circulations, extend the lifetime and size of the Antarctic ozone hole, and affect Earth’s radiative balance. Given the ongoing and projected increases in fire activity and severity linked to a warming climate, there is an urgent need to better understand and predict climate-scale impacts from pyroCb activity. PyroCbs are a key a key hazard process that is still poorly constrained. A holistic approach, with observing and modeling synergy, is needed to lay the pathway to improved understanding and forecasting. This study investigates the spatiotemporal evolution of smoke aerosols in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS) and their radiative effects using multi-spectral aerosol extinction observations from Stratospheric Aerosol and Gas Experiment III on the International Space Station (SAGE III/ISS) and GEOS-Chem chemistry transport model coupled with the Advanced Particle Microphysics module (GCAPM). Two primary research questions will be addressed: 1) what is the contribution of carbonaceous aerosols to stratospheric aerosol loading; and 2 ) what are the radiative forcing effects of pyroCb aerosols in the UTLS.

497946.title: From Disaster Funding to Housing Recovery: A System Dynamics Analysis of CDBG-DR after Hurricane Harvey
497946.authors: Amin Sobhani, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX
497946.abstract: Post-disaster housing recovery is often described through a series of static indicators, including the number of damaged homes, funding allocations, applications, construction starts, and completed projects. These measures are necessary for tracking program performance, but they provide limited insight into why recovery can remain slow or incomplete even after substantial public resources have been committed. This study develops a system dynamics model of Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) homeowner assistance after Hurricane Harvey in Houston, Texas, to examine how public funding is translated into physical housing recovery over time. The model treats CDBG-DR implementation as a dynamic system in which administrative processing, funding availability, construction capacity, and project completion interact rather than operate independently. Documented owner-occupied housing need first enters City of Houston and State-administered review pathways. Approved cases then accumulate as construction-ready projects, while reconstruction can begin only when administratively ready cases, available funding, and construction capacity are present at the same time. Once construction starts, an additional delay separates project initiation from physical completion. The current model is parameterized using publicly available program information and transparent assumptions, and it is intended as a policy-learning and decision-support tool rather than a precise forecast of observed program performance. It begins with 22,476 documented owner-occupied unmet-need cases identified for Houston and approximately $562 million in combined homeowner-assistance funding associated with the City of Houston and Texas General Land Office programs. Preliminary simulations indicate that, under the current cost and program assumptions, approximately 2,080 homes can be supported through completion over the modeled period. This result should not be interpreted as an observed program outcome or as the number of households that remained unrecovered. Rather, it represents the gap between documented housing need and the level of physical reconstruction supported by the current model configuration. The simulation also helps identify where the recovery process is constrained. Under the current baseline, available funding relative to the assumed project cost limits the overall scale of modeled recovery, while administrative processing, allocation timing, and construction duration primarily affect the timing of completions. This distinction is important because policies that accelerate one part of the system may not increase the number of households ultimately supported if another constraint remains binding. Conversely, changes in effective project cost or available funding can alter the scale of supported recovery, while earlier funding availability or shorter construction duration can shift the recovery trajectory without substantially changing the final number of completed projects. By representing these relationships explicitly, the model provides a framework for testing how program design and implementation choices influence both the pace and scale of long-term housing recovery. It also allows the dominant bottleneck to shift across scenarios, making it possible to distinguish when additional funding, faster processing, greater contractor capacity, or shorter project durations are likely to matter. More broadly, the study treats post-disaster housing recovery as a public-resource allocation and implementation problem that continues well beyond the immediate hazard period. The framework is intended to support future scenario analysis and model refinement using observed administrative and construction data, and to provide a foundation for later extensions that incorporate household-level recovery conditions such as income recovery, social vulnerability, and social capital.

497949.title: Aerosol Effective Radiative Forcing Increases Earth’s Energy Imbalance In Recent Decades
497949.authors: Tianle Yuan, GESTAR-II UMBC / NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, MD
497949.abstract: Earth’s energy imbalance (EEI), a key driver of climate change, has risen markedly over the last two decades. Greenhouse gas forcing, aerosol forcing, and cloud feedback all contribute to this increase. However, the role of aerosol forcing, particularly effective radiative forcing through aerosol-cloud interactions (ERFACI), remains highly uncertain and closely intertwined with cloud feedback. Here, we estimate shortwave ERFACI using satellite observations and show its importance as a contributor to the EEI increase between 2003 and 2023. ERFACI exhibits a significant increasing trend of 0.33 Wm−2/decade averaged over oceans between 60∘S and 60∘N. The increasing trend of ERFACI stems from a global decline in cloud droplet number concentration driven by decreasing anthropogenic aerosol emissions. It is of similar magnitude as the combined instantaneous forcing trend from greenhouse gases and aerosol-radiation interactions. Our results may reduce the gap between the simulated and observed shortwave contribution to EEI trends while implying a weak shortwave cloud feedback. They also suggest a stronger aerosol forcing than the multi-model mean.

497950.title: Expanding Public Private Academic Partnerships in Costa Rica, Nepal, and the USA to Sustain Observations and Prepare the Meteorologists of Tomorrow.
497950.authors: Garrett Wheeler, Campbell Scientific, Logan, UT
497950.abstract: NMHS organizations do a tremendous job with education and training programs considering the frequent resource limitations they face. Newer funding mechanisms like SOFF are beginning to address budget constraints for operations, maintenance, and training, however, institutions should also expand their communities of practice to effectively build in-house, long-term expertise. In this presentation we highlight cases where regularly utilizing public, private, and academic partnerships in capacity-building efforts can maximize the ability for NMHS organizations to produce valuable data products grounded in quality observations. Campbell Scientific participates in a number of these communities, and through education partnerships aims to help met services alleviate significant knowledge gaps in this industry of how measurements are made. Implementing hands-on instrumentation instruction as part of a university core curriculum better prepares students for a meteorology career and reduces the likelihood that meteorologists take the quality of their data sources for granted. Foundational knowledge of the methods of observations helps both students and professionals improve derivations, computations, and other data products used for critical operations and forecasts. The first two case studies highlight the success of a hands-on instrument course for students at the both the University of Oklahoma, one of the leading meteorology programs in the USA, and at the University of Costa Rica which supplies the next generation of meteorologists for IMN. The final case study illustrates the ongoing transfer of a high-altitude observation network from a research-academic partnership to a public-private partnership with DHM in Nepal in a continuing education and capacity-building effort removed from conventional transactional projects. This example shows the power NMHS organizations can have by more deliberately partnering with the private and academic sectors as a wealth of information and expertise in addition to traditional methods of internal instruction and sharing resources primarily from a coalition of like institutions.

497953.title: Investigating Air Quality In Two Historically Redlined Areas of Harrisburg and Philadelphia with a high Prevalence of Asthma Using Low-Cost Air Quality Monitors
497953.authors: Gregory S. Jenkins, Community Innovation for Climate Justice (CI4CJ), Harrisburg, PA; and A. Izabayo, G. Carryon, L. Williams, F. Adade, A. Gebrezgi, B. Maiga, and A. Malcolm
497953.abstract: During the 1930s, the Home Owners Loan Corporation (HOLC) helped segregate neighborhoods across the United States by designating areas as A, B, C, or D, with the worst areas (D) being the only locations where African American and other ethnic groups could buy a home. These areas were also located near heavy industry, heavily traveled roads, and highways. Today, residents of these locations are often subject to the highest prevalence of Asthma in the United States. We examine air quality across 3 zip codes in Philadelphia (19104, 19131, 19139) and Harrisburg (17102, 17103, 17104, 17110). Three different air quality monitors were co-located with EPA reference sites during May 2026, with correction factors applied to PM2.5 concentrations, CO, O3, and NO2 mixing ratios. We discuss some results across our network, the successes and challenges of building community connections, and future steps.

497954.title: UFS/JEDI LIDAR DATA ASSIMILATION: Tangent Linear and Adjoint development.
497954.authors: Michael Kwadwo Benneh, Howard University, Hyattsville, MD; Howard Univ., Washington, DC; Howard University, Washington, DC; and C. H. Lu, C. R. Martin, S. W. Wei, C. Dang, A. Yarber, B. Johnson, J. E. Barre, and S. Chiao
497954.abstract: The joint collaborative effort between Howard University, SUNY Albany, NOAA/EMC and JCSDA focuses on advancing LiDAR data assimilation capabilities within the Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration (JEDI). The primary goal of this effort is to better constrain the vertical structure of atmospheric aerosols, addressing a longstanding limitation in current data assimilation systems that rely on column-integrated observations. A LiDAR Forward Operator was developed to resolve atmospheric aerosol properties into observation space by simulating the measurement process of active remote sensing instruments (CALIOP) aboard CALIPSO satellite. This involved extracting model states by interpolating them onto observation locations as GeoVaLs and passing them into VADER via OOPS. Prior to that, the CALIOP extinction profiles data are already written and passed into IODA. CRTM is used in our forward operator. VADER prepares CRTM-required input variables using the model "ingredients," and they are then passed into CRTM. Aerosol mixing ratios are then converted into mass concentrations, and the extinction coefficients are computed based on Mie theory via precomputed optical tables. The extinction profile is then obtained from the extinction coefficient based on each vertical layer. An essential capability required to compute innovations between the non-linear model background in observation space and satellite observations. A core step towards assimilating high-resolution vertical profile observations. To support variational data assimilation, a Tangent Linear (TL) and Adjoint (AD) formulation has also been developed for the NOAA Global Chemistry and Aerosol Forecast System (GCAFS), which employs a 3D-FGAT method within GCDAS. The observation operator is linearized about the model trajectory, with the CRTM K-matrix providing the required Jacobian information for the linearized radiative transfer calculations. The TL operator propagates perturbations in the model state into observation space, while the AD operator propagates observation-space sensitivities back to the corresponding model-state variables. The developed operators provide the components required to incorporate LiDAR-derived aerosol extinction profiles into the variational data assimilation system. Preliminary results are from the Jacobian test, minimization test and TL/AD consistency test of the assimilation framework to assimilate LiDAR-derived aerosol extinction profiles.Ongoing work focuses on validating and fine-tuning the forward, TL, and AD operators and integrating the complete framework into the GCAFS 3D-FGAT system. The ultimate objective is to assimilate high-resolution LiDAR extinction profiles to improve the vertical representation and analysis of atmospheric aerosols.

497958.title: AI Emulation of Stochastic Sudden Stratospheric Warming with Interpretable Latent Structure
497958.authors: Daniel Boscu, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL; and D. Hernandez, F. Alvarez Ventura, J. M. Finkel, A. K. Chattopadhyay, P. Hassanzadeh, and D. Abbot
497958.abstract: Rare weather events pose a challenge for data-driven modeling due to class imbalance. In this study, we develop a probabilistic deep learning emulator for the stochastic Holton-Mass model of stratospheric variability and analyze the structure of its learned latent space. The Holton-Mass model exhibits two metastable regimes, a strong and a weak polar vortex, maintained by nonlinear wave-mean flow interactions, with weak stochastic forcing intermittently triggering rare transitions between these regimes that qualitatively represent Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) events. We employ a ResNet-inspired Conditional Variational Autoencoder with six-layer encoder and decoder layers and explicit current-state conditioning to model the distribution of the system's state at the next time step (one day). The emulator accurately reproduces short-term dynamics, steady-state probability distributions, regime persistence statistics, rare transition rates, the transition committor function, and the transition expected lead time of the physical model. Beyond emulation fidelity, we interrogate the learned latent representation to understand how the model internalizes the underlying metastable structure of the dynamics. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of the 32-dimensional latent space reveals a clear and unsupervised separation into four physically interpretable clusters corresponding to strong versus weak vortex regimes and stable versus transition-prone configurations. Such emergent regime separation in latent space is hard to identify for deep generative models applied to high-dimensional stochastic systems. Our results show that carefully designed probabilistic emulators can uncover physically meaningful manifolds governing extreme-event dynamics, potentially aiding the development of improved operational advanced warning systems.

497959.title: Observation-Constrained Evaluation of Aerosol Effects on Hail in an ICECHIP Storm
497959.authors: Zachary J. Lebo, Univ. of Oklahoma, Pasadena, CA; and A. James and E. Mansell
497959.abstract: Previous modeling studies have examined how aerosol loading may influence hail production through changes in cloud microphysics and storm dynamics. However, the scarcity of in situ observations of hail and precipitation particle size distributions has limited opportunities to evaluate these simulated responses. Observations collected during the 2025 In-situ Collaborative Experiment for the Collection of Hail in the Plains (ICECHIP) provide a unique opportunity to investigate aerosol–hail interactions within an observation-constrained modeling framework. This study examines a hail-producing storm observed during ICECHIP Operational Period 12 on 6 June 2025 using convection-permitting Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model simulations. Three simulations are conducted with low, intermediate, and high aerosol loadings while maintaining an otherwise consistent model configuration. Cloud and precipitation processes are represented using the NSSL three-moment microphysics scheme with bin-emulating treatments of hail melting and liquid-water shedding. The simulations are evaluated against observations at both the storm and hydrometeor scales. Simulated radar reflectivity fields are compared with observed reflectivity to assess the timing, location, structure, and intensity of the modeled convection. At the surface, simulated raindrop size distributions and hail sizes are compared with measurements from Parsivel optical disdrometers deployed during the field campaign. These comparisons assess the model’s ability to reproduce the observed evolution and size characteristics of liquid and frozen precipitation. Differences among the three aerosol experiments are analyzed to determine how aerosol loading affects cloud droplet populations, supercooled liquid water, precipitation development, and hail growth and survival. Analyses of hydrometeor size distributions, microphysical process rates, and storm structure will be presented to distinguish changes associated with microphysical pathways from those related to changes in storm dynamics. By combining in situ particle measurements, radar observations, and an advanced three-moment microphysics scheme, this study provides an observation-constrained assessment of simulated aerosol effects on hail and identifies strengths and limitations in current representations of hail growth, melting, and shedding.

497960.title: Utilizing Water Isotopic Composition in the Unified Forecast System to Constrain Precipitation and Hydrologic Processes: Preliminary Results
497960.authors: Cheng-Hsuan Lu, Univ. at Albany, State Univ. of New York, Albany, NY; and A. Badarunnisa Sainudeen, S. W. Wei, S. Miller, M. Vuille, L. Xue, L. Bernardet, G. J. Firl, F. Yang, and Y. Ming
497960.abstract: As natural tracers of moisture exchange, the water isotopic composition provides a valuable means to examine the integrated and connected hydrological cycle. Recent development of innovative measurement techniques has produced stable water isotopes (SWI) observations from ground, aircrafts, ships, and space. Enhancing observational capabilities, in turn, enable the scientific community to use these novel observations for process-level study, model evaluation, and data assimilation. Isotopic signals contain valuable information about atmospheric processes and the water cycle across time scales, from weather to climate. The overarching goal of this project is to help guide the development and analysis of the Unified Forecast System (UFS) by adopting the latest SWI modeling and observational capabilities, with special focus on precipitation and hydrological processes. This UAlbany-BC-DTC collaborative research will implement an innovative hydrometeorological diagnostic, i.e., SWI in liquid and vapor phases, in the UFS atmosphere and land model. We propose to investigate hydrological processes and extreme precipitation characteristics through isotope-enabled simulations and model-data comparison. The major tasks in year 1 include (1) implementing SWI into UFS physics suite, and (2) developing interface for observation data access (IODA) converter and unified forward operator (UFO) for SWI satellite observations. This presentation will provide an overview of SWI-enabled UFS project and the status of project progress.

497962.title: First Assimilation of NISAR Retrievals for Field-Scale Root Zone Soil Moisture Estimation over Kansas
497962.authors: Ehsan Jalilvand, NASA, Greenbelt, MD; and S. V. Kumar, R. Bindlish, and J. Park
497962.abstract: The NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission delivers L-band surface soil moisture retrievals at 200 m resolution, capturing agricultural fields at the plot scale for the first time worldwide. Yet these retrievals reflect only the top few centimeters of soil, whereas crops draw water from the root zone, reaching depths of 1–2 m. Here we report the first assimilation of NISAR soil moisture into the NASA Land Information System (LIS) to generate a continuous, field-scale root zone soil moisture product, demonstrated across Kansas, a Great Plains region encompassing rainfed and center-pivot irrigated winter wheat, corn, and soybean systems above the High Plains Aquifer. LIS is run statewide at 200 m with six soil layers, representing both the L-band sensing depth and the complete crop root zone, and is driven by inputs consistent with this resolution, including hourly NLDAS-3 meteorological forcing, ESA WorldCover land cover, and SoilGrids soil texture. An Ensemble Kalman Filter merges NISAR retrievals into the topsoil layer, applying CDF-matching bias correction derived from Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) statistics.
