Between overpasses, the model physics transfers surface information downward, producing gap-free daily soil moisture and temperature estimates in all six layers, which are validated against USDA SCAN and USCRN profile observations. These results establish a prototype framework for operational, field-scale root zone soil moisture monitoring from NISAR, yielding a product that, in contrast to existing global soil moisture datasets, carries the signature of human water management throughout the root zone.

497966.title: Accelerated Climate Warming is Degrading Air Quality Across the Southwestern US
497966.authors: Ian C. Faloona, Univ. of California, Davis, Davis, CA; and S. Carlson and R. Bhandari
497966.abstract: Inspection of near-surface ozone and PM2.5 trends in several urban areas across the Southwestern US, reveals an abrupt disappearance of improvement over the past decade. In fact, the Los Angeles, Las Vegas, Phoenix, and Salt Lake City areas all exhibit peak ozone levels that are now rising. We show that this dramatic shift in air quality trends coincides with a rapid acceleration of climate warming, particularly in the warm season, across the entire Western US, and argue that it is the ongoing escalation of less understood sources from wildfires and agricultural soils that are predominantly responsible for the change. Using six different reanalysis data sets and the US Historical Climatology Network (USHCN), we show that warm season (April-September) temperatures across the Western US have been rising at an astonishing rate of +0.7 (±0.13) °C/decade since about 2010, a 3- to 4-fold increase from the rate observed from 1980-2010. Cool season (October-March) warming rates are also found to be increasing rapidly but at a significantly slower rate (+0.45 ± 0.18 °C/decade) leading to a 50% jump in the annual temperature cycle trend from 0.16 to 0.24 °C/decade. No significant difference was found among trends in the daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures. Furthermore, relative humidities are observed to be falling throughout the region at a rate of around -1 %/decade. This combination of rapid warming and anomalous drying is worse than the most pessimistic climate model predictions: for example, the ensemble average of worst-case scenarios (SSP5-8.5) estimate warm season temperatures over California to rise at a rate of +0.6 °C/decade through mid-century while predicting negligible changes in relative humidity. We argue that the observed rapid changes in these essential meteorological variables are not only directly correlated with reversing O3 and PM2.5 trends, but are causal in that they accelerate precursor emissions of NOx from wildfires (that also contribute copious aerosols directly) and agricultural soils leading to a climate penalty that is presently thwarting air quality control strategies from Central Colorado to the California Coast.

497967.title: Quantile-Conserving Ensemble Filters for All-sky Infrared Radiance Assimilation
497967.authors: Lili Lei, Nanjing University, Boulder, CO; Nanjing University, Nanjing, 32, China
497967.abstract: All-sky satellite radiance assimilation faces the challenge of non-Gaussian error distributions, which can be exacerbated by fine model resolutions with better resolved physical processes. Compared to the ensemble adjustment Kalman filter (EAKF) that assumes Gaussian error distributions, the nonlinear rank histogram filter (RHF) uses a rank histogram distribution to represent the observation prior. The rank histogram filter with probit transform regression (QCF_RHF) further allows nonlinear regression updates by performing regression of observation increments onto state variables in a transformed space. Performance of the three ensemble filters is investigated in an observing system simulation experiment with non-cycled assimilation of synthetic Geostationary Interferometric Infrared Sounder (GIIRS) all-sky infrared radiances, with model resolution increasing from 7.5 km to 1.5 km and then 300 m. Single observation assimilation experiments demonstrate the advantages of QCF_RHF over EAKF and RHF for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian error distributions, especially for the common all-sky situation with cloudy observations but mostly clear-sky ensemble priors. Consistent results are obtained for the analyses assimilating all synthetic observations from GIIRS channel 1025 and subsequent ensemble forecasts. For state variables of specific humidity, temperature and wind speed, QCF_RHF produces improved analyses and better captures posterior distributions, and smaller forecast errors till 1-h lead time than EAKF and RHF. The advantages of QCF_RHF over EAKF and RHF become more prominent as the horizontal grid spacing decreases from 7.5 km to 1.5 km and then 300 m due to more non-Gaussian error distributions and nonlinear forward operators.

497970.title: An Analytical Solution for Wave-Induced Airflow and Energy Transfer over Swell Waves
497970.authors: Aditya Aiyer, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA
497970.abstract: We derive a Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin (WKB) solution of the molecular-viscosity Orr–Sommerfeld equation in wave-following coordinates for fast waves satisfying U(z)<cU(z)<c, with a positive and slowly varying Rayleigh potential. In the absence of a critical layer or turning point, the solution separates asymptotically into a non-dissipative outer mode and a thin, complex air-side Stokes layer. The outer Rayleigh mode is real to leading order and therefore performs no net work on the wave, while the phase shift required for momentum and energy transfer arises from the viscous Stokes layer at O(R−1/2)O(R^{-1/2}), where R=c/(kν)R=c/(k\nu). This asymptotic separation yields explicit leading-order expressions for the pressure and surface-stress coefficients. Their ratio is independent of RR and depends only on the mean velocity profile through its near-surface derivatives and a single outer integral. For exponential shear profiles, the resulting closed-form expressions agree closely with numerical Chebyshev solutions of the governing equation. The theory is further evaluated using mean velocity profiles from published wave-resolved large-eddy simulations and accurately reproduces the wave-coherent velocity field at high wave age. In the no-wind limit, the solution recovers the classical air-side viscous attenuation law, providing a direct connection between laminar viscous damping and fast-wave propagation over sheared airflow. The resulting framework therefore extends classical viscous swell attenuation to smooth fast-wave shear flows without critical layers or turning points, while providing an analytical benchmark for phase-resolved simulations and parameterizations of wave-induced momentum and energy transfer.

497972.title: Strongly Coupled Data Assimilation for Paleoclimate Reconstruction Using Deep Learning-Based Models
497972.authors: Lili Lei, Nanjing University, Boulder, CO
497972.abstract: Coupled data assimilation (CDA) could be beneficial for paleoclimate reconstruction, but intermediate-complexity climate models are often used. The deep learning (DL)-based surrogate model that can realistically simulate the climate system provides alternative to CDA, so that CDA of multi-timescale proxy data using DL-based models is investigated for paleoclimate reconstruction. Results reveal that at the annual time scale, coupling an oceanic component to the atmospheric model is beneficial for the surface air temperature (SAT) forecasts, but coupling an atmospheric component to the oceanic model slightly degrades the sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts, since coupling the atmospheric component introduces high frequent noises to the oceanic model. Compared to the coupled model component, cross-component update by assimilating cross-component proxy data has larger positive impacts on SAT and SST reconstructions. Moreover, simultaneously assimilating atmospheric and oceanic proxy data with a coupled model yields the most accurate SAT and SST reconstructions.

497973.title: An Investigation into NOx Point Sources Observed during the 2026 NASA Student Airborne Research Program (SARP) Campaign using Airborne Remote Sensing, Satellite Measurements, and In-Situ Observations
497973.authors: Zayna Haider, University of Washington, Seattle, WA; and D. Goldberg, L. M. Judd, and M. A. Demetillo
497973.abstract: Airborne remote sensing instruments for NO2 are unique in their ability to identify smaller-scale sources of pollution because of their finer spatial resolution compared to satellites. They also supplement ground-based measurements through their ability to characterize plumes emitted further from the ground and over a wider area than air quality sensors can cover. During the 2026 NASA Student Airborne Research Program (SARP) campaign, the NASA LaRC GIII flew with an airborne spectrometer (GCAS) capable of measuring tropospheric NO2 column density over polluted areas in the southern United States, including Memphis, TN; Dallas, TX; Houston, TX; Atlanta, GA; and the Permian Basin. Point sources of NO2 were identified using GCAS, then further characterized by their origin and relative magnitude. These point sources include natural gas refineries, airports, and data centers. In this work, we assess NOx emissions from TEMPO V04 NO2 column densities compared to those from coincident GCAS NO2 slant and vertical column densities to the closest hour and at the native TEMPO spatial resolution. These comparisons help evaluate how TEMPO measurements can be applied to the assessment and observation of point source pollution. GCAS measurements were also compared to ground based in-situ observations and Pandora spectrometers, which helps to better understand how much of the variability observed by GCAS exists at the surface. This analysis advances our knowledge of contemporary sources of NOx pollution across the United States and probes the capability of TEMPO to observe such sources.

497975.title: Meteorological Observations and System Performance from a Portable Phased Array Radar
497975.authors: Haonan Chen, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO; and K. Kelly, M. Kumar, and L. WANG
497975.abstract: A Portable Weather Radar (PWR) system has been developed by Agile RF Systems LLC to substantially improve high-resolution weather observations. The PWR employs solid-state, distributed phased-array RF electronics implemented as a hybrid phased-array and mechanically scanning system. The PWR takes advantage of faster elevation scan times through electronic beam steering while simultaneously overcoming the inherent differences in gain and phase among these electronic elevation beams through precise calibration methods. This paper first presents a brief overview of the current development and deployment of the PWR system in northern Colorado during the 2026 storm season. The differential-phase-based data quality control approach is then described and evaluated in depth through cross-comparison with NEXRAD observations. In addition, this study presents a self-attention-based recurrent neural network (SaGRU) to enhance radar-based nowcasting using phased-array radar observations. Although recent research has demonstrated the strong performance of deep learning for radar-based nowcasting, to the best of our knowledge, no previous studies have applied deep learning-based nowcasting models to phased-array radar observations. The SaGRU model is trained and tested using multiple precipitation events in Colorado. Nowcasting performance is evaluated using multiple verification metrics—including the Heidke Skill Score (HSS), Critical Success Index (CSI), Probability of Detection (POD), and False Alarm Rate (FAR)—across a range of precipitation thresholds. Results demonstrate that nowcasting using high-resolution PWR data outperforms NEXRAD-based approaches, particularly during the critical first 1–2 hours of forecasting, when precipitation can develop rapidly.

497978.title: An Investigation into NOx Point Sources Observed during the 2026 NASA SARP Campaign using Airborne Remote Sensing, Satellite Measurements, and In-Situ Observations
497978.authors: Zayna Haider, University of Washington, Seattle, WA
497978.abstract: Airborne remote sensing instruments for NO2 are unique in their ability to identify smaller-scale sources of pollution because of their finer spatial resolution compared to satellites. They also supplement ground-based measurements through their ability to characterize plumes emitted further from the ground and over a wider area than air quality sensors can cover. During the 2026 NASA Student Airborne Research Program (SARP) campaign, the NASA LaRC GIII flew with an airborne spectrometer (GCAS) capable of measuring tropospheric NO2 column density over polluted areas in the southern United States, including Memphis, TN; Dallas, TX; Houston, TX; Atlanta, GA; and the Permian Basin. In this work, we assess NOx emissions from TEMPO V04 NO2 column densities compared to those from coincident GCAS NO2 slant and vertical column densities to the closest hour and at the native TEMPO spatial resolution. These comparisons help evaluate how TEMPO measurements can be applied to the assessment and observation of point source pollution. GCAS measurements were also compared to ground based in-situ observations and Pandora spectrometers, which helps to better understand how much of the variability observed by GCAS exists at the surface. 497981.title: Evaluating the Timeliness and Effectiveness of Severe Weather Communication at Jackson State University
497981.abstract: Severe weather poses a significant risk to university communities, where students, faculty, and staff rely on timely and understandable information to make protective decisions. While the National Weather Service (NWS) and National Hurricane Center (NHC) provide official watches, warnings, and forecasts, universities are responsible for translating this information into campus-specific emergency communication. This study evaluates the timeliness and effectiveness of severe weather communication at Jackson State University (JSU), with emphasis on the time between the issuance of official weather products and the distribution of JSU Emergency Management notifications. This is a mixed methods observational case study where the approach was used to examine severe weather communication across multiple high-impact events affecting the Jackson, Mississippi area. Events included severe thunderstorms, tornado outbreaks, Tropical Storm Francine, and winter weather. Archived NWS, NHC, Storm Prediction Center (SPC), and Iowa Environmental Mesonet (IEM) products were used to identify official issuance times. These timestamps were compared with corresponding JSU Emergency Management emails to calculate notification lag, defined as the elapsed time between the first official NWS/NHC product communicating the hazard and the first JSU Emergency Management email regarding the same event. A community survey was also used to evaluate perceptions of alert accuracy, timeliness, message clarity, trust, and protective action. Results demonstrate that JSU emergency communications provide important campus-specific information that is generally not contained within standard NWS/NHC products, including shelter locations, university operational guidance, preparedness instructions, and campus-specific protective actions. However, notification timing varied among events, and the communication audit identified instances in which official weather products were not followed by campus-wide email communication. Survey findings further indicated that participants generally viewed JSU alerts as accurate and useful, while timeliness remained an area for potential improvement. Participants also demonstrated substantial reliance on external weather information sources in addition to university alerts. These findings emphasize that forecast accuracy alone does not ensure an effective public response. The transition from an official meteorological product to a localized emergency message represents an important component of the warning process. Recommendations include reducing communication delays through standardized alert templates, providing more frequent follow-up information, incorporating clearer protective-action guidance, adding storm-location graphics, strengthening connections between NWS products and university alert systems, and expanding severe weather education. Although this case study focuses on Jackson State University, the findings have broader relevance for universities and other institutions responsible for communicating hazardous weather information to large and diverse populations. Strengthening the connection between meteorological information, emergency management, and risk communication can help transform forecasts and warnings into timely protective action.

497987.title: Withdrawn: Ignition Method and Fire Intensity: Implications for Prescribed Fire Crew Exposure Risk
497987.authors: Thea Fisher, NASA, Saint Paul , MN; University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN
497987.abstract: Title: Ignition Method and Fire Intensity: Implications for Prescribed Fire Crew Exposure Risk — A FireSense Case Study from Fort Stewart, GA and Geneva State Forest, AL Background: Prescribed fire crews — including burn bosses, ignition specialists, and support personnel — represent an occupational population directly exposed to heat, smoke, and fire-behavior hazards, yet remain understudied relative to other outdoor worker groups facing climate-driven occupational risk. As wildland fire agencies increasingly adopt aerial ignition to implement prescribed fire and adapt to changing climate and fuel conditions, ignition method may influence not only fire behavior but also the nature and degree of crew exposure to fire-related hazards [PLACEHOLDER: cite occupational fire crew exposure literature — e.g., studies on prescribed fire smoke exposure, heat strain in wildland firefighters, or NIOSH/USFS fire crew health data]. Differences in crew proximity, task duration, and positioning relative to the active fire front by ignition type [PLACEHOLDER: confirm this is observationally or logically supportable from your field experience/notes] may represent an underexamined dimension of occupational risk in prescribed fire operations. Objective: This project evaluates FireSense 2025 campaign data to compare active fire radiance and intensity patterns between aerial and hand ignition methods, and considers these differences as a potential proxy for variation in prescribed fire crew exposure risk across ignition techniques. Methods: Active fire radiance was derived from NASA's MASTER airborne mid-wave infrared spectral imagery collected during prescribed burns at Fort Stewart, GA (aerial ignition) and Geneva State Forest, AL (hand ignition via drip torch). Using Python and QGIS, flight data were converted to GeoTIFF, georeferenced, and corrected for scale factor to generate a time series of fire progression and radiance intensity at each site. [PLACEHOLDER: add any occupational-health-relevant method — e.g., field observation of crew positioning/task timing relative to ignition type, or a stated assumption linking radiance patterns to standoff distance/exposure duration]. Site fire regime context was established using LANDFIRE vegetation data and review of ecological literature on Coastal Plain Floristic Province pine ecosystems. Results/Approach: [PLACEHOLDER — this needs your actual finding once analysis is further along.] Preliminary comparison of radiance time series suggests [PLACEHOLDER: e.g., differing spatial/temporal patterns of fire intensity between ignition methods], which may correspond to differences in crew proximity and exposure duration to peak fire intensity across ignition techniques. Significance: For occupational and environmental health, this work contributes a novel application of remote sensing fire-behavior data toward characterizing potential exposure differentials among prescribed fire crews by ignition method — an increasingly relevant question as programs expand aerial ignition for climate adaptation and burn program scalability. For NASA's Wildland Fire program, it demonstrates an expanded, human-health-relevant application of airborne campaign spectral imagery. Future Work: Extensions beyond this internship include pairing radiance/thermal fire behavior data with wearable heat-stress or exposure sensors on prescribed fire crew members; applying atmospheric corrections to MASTER data; calculating rate of spread and fire residence time as more direct exposure-relevant metrics; and incorporating air quality and small-sensor monitoring data to assess smoke exposure by ignition method.

497996.title: Fifteen Years of High-Altitude Continental and Oceanic Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) Monitoring: Integrating the Mexico High Altitude Global Climate Observatory (MEX) Continental Record (2009–2024) with the Mauna Loa Observatory (MLO) Baseline Data
497996.authors: Luis Roberto Acosta, Instituto del Clima Mexico & America Latina, Ciudad de México, DF, Mexico
497996.abstract: The MEX and MLO high-altitude observatories both monitor the free troposphere, well above local surface pollution. Large geographical blind spots persist in global greenhouse gas monitoring networks, most conspicuously across subtropical continental Latin America. We present a 16-year continuous record (2009–2024) of atmospheric CO₂ from the Mexico High-Altitude Global Climate Observatory (MEX; 18.98° N, 97.31° W, 4,550 m a.s.l.), evaluated directly against the co-latitude marine background record from Hawaii's Mauna Loa Observatory (MLO; 19.54° N, 155.58° W, 3,397 m a.s.l.). The two sites share latitude but sit on opposite sides of the Northern-Hemisphere subtropical circulation patterns. MEX is continental, MLO is oceanic, and they are separated by about 8,600 km across the North Pacific. After quality control the retained MEX dataset contains 1,220 paired-flask observations. The Mex CO₂ record shows a mean concentration of 403.6 ppm, a linear growth rate of 2.43 ppm yr⁻¹ (R² = 0.93), and a 2024 peak of 428.9 ppm. Over 2009–2024 period interval MLO CO₂ yields 405.2 ppm, a growth rate of 2.41 ppm yr⁻¹ (R² = 0.95), and a 2024 peak of 427.8 ppm. Both records agree on monthly variations at r = 0.995, with a mean offset of −0.90 ± 1.15 ppm. Two results stand out. First, two independently operated monitoring programes 8,600 km apart agree on the 16-year growth rate to within 0.02 ppm yr⁻¹. The growth rate is therefore a property of the atmosphere at 19° N, not of either observatory. Second, the difference between MEX and MLO climatological seasonal cycle is not a uniform bias. Both sites nearly coincide in spring (−0.1 to −0.4 ppm in March–May) and diverge to −1.65 ppm in August, tracking the Northern-Hemisphere growing season. This is the first direct observational constraint between continental-oceanic free-troposphere seasonal contrast at that latitude, and it is derived from a paired 16-year record. Seasonal variance and amplitude tell a distinctly continental story. MEX has a 7.95 ppm seasonal amplitude, 1.10 ppm larger than MLO, the sign from a free-troposphere site above the North-American continental biosphere. Regional biomass fluxes and the mountain-valley circulation systems of central Mexico's high plateaux show on the record, without contaminating the CO₂ baseline signal. Beyond filling a regional gap in global carbon observations, this 16-year time series provides a ground-truth dataset that can be used to evaluate satellite column retrievals over tropical North America and to constrain regional GHG and carbon transport models.

497998.title: The Relational Infrastructure of Co-Production: Lessons from the Rising Voices, Changing Coasts Hub in Puerto Rico
497998.authors: Jenniffer Marie Santos-Hernández, Disaster Research Center, Newark, DE; and H. Vega Rivera, A. Zhang Lam, M. Rivera, A. L. Irizarry Lugo, F. Vidal-Franceschi, and A. Jerolleman
497998.abstract: Collaborative production of knowledge requires more than bringing different knowledge systems together; it requires building and sustaining relationships that enable shared understandings and practical solutions. While co-production has become a prominent framework, it is often treated as an end, centering scientific knowledge as the primary objective of collaboration. This presentation reflects on the processes of coalition building and relationship building in Southwest Puerto Rico within the Rising Voices, Changing Coasts: The Earth and Indigenous Science Convergence Hub, the value of those processes beyond the collaborative production of knowledge, and the creation of the Collaboratory for Disaster Risk Reduction within the Disaster Research Center at the University of Delaware. Drawing from our experience working alongside communities in Puerto Rico navigating long-term development challenges, colonial legacies, and repeated disaster impacts, we examine co-production as a process that unfolds over time. We discuss how we initiated relationships with our collaborating communities and earned the invitation to continue working together; how community priorities were identified through sustained engagement; how shared principles were developed to guide collaboration and decision-making; how research instruments and protocols were co-designed; how conflicts over access to meaningful community spaces were navigated; how activities were collectively organized; and how practices of reciprocity, care, and accountability shaped the creation, sharing, and application of convergence science. We also reflect on the complexities of building coalitions across communities, Indigenous and local knowledge holders, government agencies, academic institutions, and private-sector organizations while maintaining alignment with community priorities and research goals. Rather than presenting co-production as a fixed method or framework, we examine it as an ongoing practice of coalition building that requires trust, adaptation, shared responsibility, and sustained commitment. In this perspective, scientific knowledge is not the center of collaboration but one possible outcome of many stemming from strengthening the relationships, fostering capacity, and prioritizing the community. We argue that the strength of the relationships and coalitions developed through this process influences the relevance, usability, and credibility of the science produced. The Puerto Rico experience contributes to a broader discussion in disaster studies and convergence science on how we can move from transactional to meaningful collaborations with communities and suggests that durable and meaningful collaboration depends less on refining methods than on cultivating shared authority, long term commitments, and institutions capable of supporting integration across diverse collaborators and reciprocal relationships over time.

498023.title: Advancing Total Water Level Forecasting by Integrating 1D/2D Channel Networks in the ADCIRC Prediction System
498023.authors: Shintaro Bunya, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; and R. Luettich, Z. Cobell, and B. O. Blanton
498023.abstract: Recent advancements in the ADCIRC Prediction System (APS) aim to improve the physical representation of multi-scale intricate channel networks leading to federal and other observational gauges, capture individual and compound flooding drivers, and enhance the overall predictive skill for total water level forecasting. A major focus of this presentation is the newly developed North and South Carolina version 3 (NCSCv3) mesh, generated using recent algorithmic enhancements to resolve complex riverine and coastal environments. This 1D/2D capability is achieved through two primary techniques: Vertical Element Walls (VEWs), which allow for the discontinuous representation of steep-sided bathymetry, and one-dimensional condensation (1DC), which eliminates the restrictive time step constraints imposed by the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) stability condition in narrow reaches (Bunya et al., 2023). This high-resolution approach allows for the explicit representation of intricate water flow pathways and the accurate propagation of tidal and storm surge signals from the ocean to inland locations. The NCSCv3 mesh successfully enhances targeted resolution along waterways to support over 100 real-time water-level gauges operated by federal agencies and the state along the coast and in transitional zones of North Carolina. Despite this enhanced local resolution, the NCSCv3 mesh contains 1.6 million nodes, a 20 percent reduction compared to its predecessor, translating to computational runtimes that are approximately 20 percent faster. The improved spatial coverage and prediction accuracy of this enhanced mesh will be evaluated using reanalysis and forecast simulations for the 2026 season. REFERENCES: Bunya, S., Luettich, R. A., & Blanton, B. O. (2023). Techniques to embed channels in finite element shallow water equation models. Advances in Engineering Software, 185, 103516. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advengsoft.2023.103516

498038.title: Tracking Cold Pool Outflows, Sea Breeze Fronts, and Convective Initiation During the DOE ARM TRACER Field Deployment
498038.authors: Gabriella "Sy" Sosa Medina, State University of New York at Oswego, Oswego, NY; and E. Caldon, M. P. Jensen, and A. J. Drager
498038.abstract: Convective initiation along air mass boundaries, such as cold pools generated by convective storms, occurs due to the wedging of cold air beneath warmer environmental air, lifting this warmer air high enough to initiate cloud and storm development—however, storm initiation is not guaranteed to occur. The exact parameters that dictate the success or failure of these initiation mechanisms remain unquantified, in part due to the challenge of identifying air mass boundaries in meteorological data. This identification is further complicated in coastal environments where sea-breeze dynamics are present. This study aims to develop methods to detect cold-pool and sea-breeze fronts to enable comprehensive analysis of boundary locations, collision interactions, and thunderstorm initiation events, moving toward a longer-term goal of assessing numerical models’ ability to simulate real-world events. The Department of Energy (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) TRacking Aerosol Convection interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER) collected unique measurements of convective storms in the coastal environment of Southeast Texas, providing a comprehensive observational dataset useful for developing multifarious maps from which boundaries might be identified by hand. Case study dates were selected based on the presence of widespread, discrete convective cells, sea-breeze circulations, and significant data availability from TRACER. Frontal boundaries and convective initiation events are identified via maps of both observed data (e.g. XSACR, NEXRAD, GOES, in-situ observations) and corresponding model data from high-resolution simulations (Δx ~ 100 m in the innermost nest) performed using the Regional Atmospheric Modeling System (RAMS) with a configuration adapted from the TRACER Model Intercomparison Project (TRACER-MIP). We focus on near-surface meteorological parameters such as temperature, wind speed, wind direction, and specific humidity, along with observed and simulated radar and satellite imagery. These maps are then uploaded into a novel web-based application—the Meteorological and Environmental Tool for Graphical Object Annotation and Tracking (METGOAT)—to manually track storm, cold-pool, and sea-breeze boundaries. When identifying observed versus simulated boundaries, different sets of meteorological parameters prove useful—this also applies for identification of cold-pool versus sea-breeze fronts. Visualizations of reflectivity and wind direction, respectively, provide the most helpful insight for observed and simulated cold pool boundaries. Meanwhile, visualizations of visible satellite imagery and specific humidity prove the most reliable for identifying observed and simulated sea-breeze fronts, respectively. These methods will form the basis for a future model-observation comparison investigating collision dynamics and convective initiation processes.

498039.title: Evaluating the Fire Weather Matrix and RFW Decision Making in the Inland Northwest
498039.authors: Serena Klarich, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX; NWS Spokane, Spokane, WA; and D. J. Butler, S. Bodnar, K. M. Butler, and E. R. Nielsen
498039.abstract: In fire prone areas of the Inland Northwest, accurate forecasting of critical fire weather is vital to protecting lives, property, and supporting the national economy. The 2027 AMS Annual Student Conference theme, STUDENT: Students Teaming Up to Discover, Empower, and Navigate Today, focuses on using research and data to benefit society, directly connecting to this evaluation of a fire weather decision tool. Back in 2025, the National Weather Service (NWS) Weather Forecast Office (WFO) in Spokane, WA, implemented a localized fire weather matrix. The Red Flag Warning Decision Matrix guides forecasters by balancing wind and relative humidity thresholds; stronger winds can support a warning at higher humidity, while very low humidity can support one at weaker wind speeds. This study applies the matrix to historical observations to determine how often Red Flag Warning (RFW) and Particularly Dangerous Situation (PDS) thresholds were met and identify regional differences. To assess the matrix’s historical performance, wind and relative humidity (RH) data were analyzed from 9 Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) stations (2002–2026) and 26 Remote Automated Weather Stations (RAWS) (2000–2022) across eastern Washington and northern Idaho from June through September. Station specific matrices counted the days meeting RFW or PDS level meteorological thresholds. Potential PDS days were cross referenced with NWS verification records to compare threshold exceedances with archived warnings. This comparison highlights the complexity of fire weather forecasting because an issued RFW depends on critical weather conditions and critical fuel dryness. Information from land management partners adds context to warning decisions that meteorological criteria alone cannot capture. Results show that RFW level conditions occurred across the forecast area, while sustained PDS level conditions were rare and concentrated mostly in the Columbia Basin and Central Washington. Some potential PDS days met matrix thresholds without a corresponding warning. Since this analysis applies meteorological thresholds without accounting for fuel conditions, these cases cannot be classified as missed warnings without fuel, data quality, and operational information. Historical RFW and PDS level threshold exceedances were mapped to fire zones to establish a local climatology. These findings raise an important question that will guide the continued research: when meteorological thresholds are met, how do fuel conditions and other operational factors influence whether a warning is issued?

498043.title: Present-Day and Projected 2040 Regional and Global Air Quality Impacts of Aircraft Emissions (Invited Presentation)
498043.authors: Irene Dedoussi, Whittle Laboratory, Cambridge, United Kingdom
498043.abstract: Aviation is a unique emissions sector because of its continuous growth and the altitude at which emissions are released, resulting in air quality impacts that range from near-airport to intercontinental scales. This presentation covers an up-to-date assessment of aviation's present-day (2019) and future (2040) air quality and human health impacts. We use the openAVEM aviation emissions model for 2019 and develop emissions projections for 2040 scenarios, combined with atmospheric modelling using GEOS-Chem. We used global and high-resolution regional simulations over Asia, Europe, and North America for 2019, and global simulations for 2040 under different socioeconomic (SSP) scenarios. We estimate that in 2019, aircraft emissions result in 33,900 (23,500-45,600, 95% CI) deaths due to PM2.5, 24,600 (15,500-34,200, 95% CI) due to ozone, with 66% and 76% of PM2.5 and ozone mortality, respectively, occurring in Asia. Landing and takeoff emissions, concentrated near airports, affect air quality differently than cruise-altitude emissions, producing localised near-airport pollution and contributing proportionally more to PM2.5- than to ozone-attributable mortality. Under 2040 projections, global mortality increases by 58-169% (PM2.5) and 82-205% (ozone) depending on the aircraft emissions scenario.

498044.title: Evaluating Gravity Wave Source Processes and Statistical Distributions via High-Resolution Global Modeling
498044.authors: Isabella Maria Dula, Stanford University, Stanford, CA; Stanford university, New York, CA; and A. Gupta, A. Sheshadri, M. J. Alexander, and J. J. Benedict
498044.abstract: Gravity Waves (GWs) transport momentum between layers of the atmosphere. GW breaking exerts drag on larger scale flows, thereby influencing the variability of the climate. Global climate models parameterize GWs because they cannot resolve their generation, propagation, and dissipation. Parameterizations often are tuned to create realistic climate states, but schemes can require unwieldy parameter input routines. High resolution convection-permitting global models are increasingly available and can be a potential resource for assessing GW schemes and for the study of convectively generated GWs. This project focuses on the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts’ (ECMWF) Integrated Forecasting System (IFS). IFS is a global model at an approximately 1.4-km resolution, and we analyse four months of model data from December, 2018 – March, 2019. We validate this model for studying GW source processes and parameterization development through a benchmarking exercise. We compare GW momentum flux (GWMF) spatial distributions and statistics between different ocean basins and across the globe. IFS is compared to three additional data sources: Loon, ECMWF’s ReAnalysis 5 (ERA5), and the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM). The Loon dataset consists of GW fluxes calculated from a collection of over 2000 Superpressure weather balloons launched from 2011-2021. ERA5 is a global reanalysis dataset with a 0.25°-resolution that relies on GW parameterizations, but also nudges model outputs towards observations. Finally, E3SM serves as a comparison to a 1°-resolution climate model where GWs are fully parameterized. This benchmarking exercise compares IFS’s resolved GW fluxes to observed and parameterized GWs. We find that IFS is capable of producing lognormal GW MF distributions--in line with existing observational evidence--but there are differences in the mean and variance of GW MFs across the different datasets.

498048.title: Impacts of CMIP7 Forcing Updates on Simulated Atmospheric Composition in GFDL-ESM4.1
498048.authors: Vedaa Usha Vandavasi, The University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI; and V. Naik, E. Stofferahn, F. Paulot, and J. Dunne
498048.abstract: Advances in scientific understanding and observations between the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) phases from CMIP6 to CMIP7 has driven updates to the full suite of atmospheric datasets used as inputs to Earth System Models. Using the GFDL-ESM4.1 model, we analyse how these forcing updates affect historical (1850-2021) evolution of atmospheric chemistry-composition by comparing simulations driven by CMIP6 versus CMIP7 forcings. Here, we focus on the analysis of changes in carbon monoxide (CO) and related tracers. We find that despite lower anthropogenic CO emissions in CMIP7, the model simulates consistently higher near-surface CO concentrations with differences emerging as early as 1920s and increasing to 3-6 ppb globally by 2014. We show that this response is mainly driven by reduced chemical loss resulting in approximately 10% lower OH concentrations (the primary CO sink) in response to the lower NOx emissions in CMIP7 versus CMIP6. Sensitivity simulations individually replacing CMIP6 air pollutant emissions, aerosol emissions, and natural forcings with CMIP7 estimates reveal that updated emissions are the primary driver of changes in simulated CO and related tracers. These results demonstrate that forcings have continued to be a major source of uncertainty in simulated atmospheric composition across CMIP phases, underscoring the need to account for forcing related uncertainties when interpreting CMIP7 historical runs and projecting future air quality and climate.

498052.title: Investigating Mechanisms of Nocturnal Ozone in Northwest Indiana and Chicagoland
498052.authors: Lynne Meredith Thissen, Valparaiso University, Valparaiso, IN; ANL, Lemont, IL; and K. A. Barber and P. Muradyan
498052.abstract: In 2025, Valparaiso University (VU) joined the National Ozone Garden Network to monitor the impacts of ground-level ozone using ozone-sensitive plants and an in situ ozone monitor. During the summer, ozone concentrations exceeded 70 ppb on nine occasions, with the highest concentration occurring on 18 September during a regional ozone episode across Northwest Indiana and the Chicago metropolitan area. This study investigates the meteorological conditions and transport processes associated with this elevated ozone event. Surface ozone observations from the VU Ozone Garden, EPA monitoring stations, and the Community Research on Climate and Urban Science (CROCUS) network were combined with meteorological observations from Automated Surface Observing System stations and synoptic weather analyses. Comparisons of ozone concentrations, wind patterns, and regional weather conditions indicate that transport from the Chicago metropolitan area and lake breeze circulations contributed to elevated ozone concentrations in Valparaiso. The results highlight the importance of regional transport and mesoscale circulations in shaping surface ozone concentrations in Northwest Indiana and provide greater insight into the meteorological conditions associated with high-ozone events in the region.

498053.title: Toward Objective Uncertainty Quantification in Earth System Model Calibration
498053.authors: Pappu Paul, University of Illinois Urbana Champaign, Urbana, IL; and C. Proistosescu
498053.abstract: Sub-grid scale parameterizations in Earth system models involve numerous uncertain parameters that must be tuned to align simulations with observations. Here, we propose a framework for assessing objective tuning frameworks using the Single Column Atmosphere Model (SCAM), which retains key physical parameterizations of general circulation models (GCMs) while greatly reducing computational cost. We conduct a perfect-model experiment where we run SCAM with a known "true" parameter set to generate synthetic observations that mimic Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Intensive Observation Periods. Perturbed parameter ensembles are constructed by varying microphysics, convection, and aerosol parameters, and cloud–radiation fields are evaluated over the Southern Great Plains. We find that point estimate optimizations find solutions that greatly reduce model–observation misfit without recovering the true parameter values. In contrast, a Bayesian framework using a Gaussian Process emulator with Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling yields tighter constraints on some parameters and more consistent recovery across experiments and variables. The perfect model framework allows us to assess which observables yield most information, which parameters are recoverable given a certain set of observations, and what is the minimum observational record needed. Although this study focuses on a single location with synthetic observations, such experiments provide a controlled setting to evaluate and identify robust calibration frameworks, which can then be extended to multiple locations and real observations with greater confidence.

498055.title: How Has Climate Change Influenced the Speed of Northern Hemisphere Winter Weather Pattern Changes?
498055.authors: Daniel James Gordon, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and J. Scheff
498055.abstract: Climate change is becoming increasingly evident through rising global temperatures and alterations in weather patterns. The effects are unevenly distributed as a consequence of Arctic Amplification, or faster relative warming of higher northern latitudes. This reduces the north-to-south temperature gradient and weakens large-scale westerly winds aloft. Thus, a slower moving jet stream develops that increases wave amplitude and blocking for more persistent weather events. Since the jet stream is strongest in winter when the temperature gradient is strongest, it is the most appropriate season to use for this study. ERA5 reanalysis data from winter seasons between 1950-2026 is analyzed using three different near-surface temperature metrics, standard deviation, average daily difference, and persistence timescale to analyze long-term changes. In addition, trends in winter-average jet speeds are examined using upper-level zonal winds at the 200 and 500 hPa levels. Preliminary results demonstrate significant changes in upper-level winds and temperature persistence. The jet stream has weakened in Greenland, the western United States and southwestern Canada, while the jet stream has strengthened in the Canadian Arctic, the north Atlantic and central Asia. These wind changes explain the temperature persistence changes. Namely, major increases in temperature persistence have occurred downwind of the weakened jet stream such as in the northern United States and southern Canada, while the greatest decreases in temperature persistence have occurred downwind of the strengthened jet stream, such as in the Canadian Arctic, western Europe and eastern Asia. However, temperature persistence has increased in northeastern Europe, despite the strengthened jet stream. Overall, these findings still suggest that changes in winter weather persistence are mostly explained by changes in upper-level zonal winds.

498070.title: Withdrawn: Characterizing Mountain Wave Signatures across Multiple LiDAR Observations from the WH²yMSIE Campaign
498070.authors: Yuzuna Kudo, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Los Angeles, CA; and M. A. Demetillo, K. M. Bedka, and A. R. Nehrir
498070.abstract: Mountain waves are atmospheric gravity waves generated when stably stratified air flows across elevated terrain, producing organized vertical motions that can contribute to aviation turbulence and redistribute momentum, moisture, and aerosols. Detecting these waves in airborne observations can be challenging because vertical wind measurements contain both coherent wave motion and irregular variability caused by turbulence and other atmospheric processes. This study uses observations from the 2024 WH²yMSIE airborne campaign to characterize mountain wave signatures across the planetary boundary layer and lower free troposphere using two NASA Langley airborne LiDAR systems: Aerosol Wind Profiler (AWP) measurements of 3D wind and High Altitude Lidar Observatory (HALO) measurements of water vapor mixing ratio, relative humidity, mixed layer height, and aerosol backscatter. Fast Fourier Transform-based spatial power spectra characterize dominant wavelengths across altitude over the southern Sierra Nevada and Mojave Desert. We also compare vertical motion with High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model output. In the strongest signature, AWP observations reveal a coherent wavelength near 10 km across multiple altitudes, with the strongest signal above the mixed layer and weaker signatures extending into the boundary layer, indicating changes in wave coherence across the boundary layer-free troposphere transition. We find that these mountain waves are accompanied by coherent horizontal wind variability and enhanced momentum flux within the same wavelength band, consistent with vertical transport of horizontal momentum. HALO moisture and aerosol measurements exhibit variability at similar spatial scales, suggesting a coupled response to the wave. HRRR output captures broader vertical motion but does not resolve the observed ~10 km oscillations from airborne lidar, highlighting the value of high resolution airborne remote sensing for resolving mesoscale wave structure. Finally, we also characterize the vertical distribution of momentum flux.

498072.title: How Sensitive is QUIC-Fire to Forecast Wind Conditions?
498072.authors: Colby Fronk, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM; and M. A. Nelson, J. Oliveto, J. Castorena, and S. Brambilla
498072.abstract: Prescribed-fire behavior is strongly influenced by the local wind field, yet the detailed meteorological observations collected during research campaigns are rarely available topractitioners conducting operational burn planning. In most applications, QUIC-Fire users must instead rely on operational numerical weather predictions such as the High- Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and Global Forecast System (GFS), to characterize the ambient meteorological conditions. Understanding how these readily available meteorological inputs differ from locally observed conditions, and how those differences propagate into QUIC-Fire simulations is therefore important for establishing realistic expectations for operational performance. During March 2023, the Strategic Environmental Research and Development Program (SERDP) and Environmental Security Technology Certification Program (ESTCP) conducted a series of prescribed burns at Eglin Air Force Base in the Florida panhandle. The field campaign brought together multiple organizations and a comprehensive suite of measurements designed to characterize the meteorological, fuel, and fire conditions associated with each burn. For the first prescribed burn, we deployed a scanning Doppler LiDAR upwind of the burn unit and conducted repeated scans throughout the burn. The scanning strategy included Doppler beam swinging (DBS) measurements, fixed vertical scans, and range height indicator (RHI) sweeps at multiple azimuth angles. Together, these measurements captured the temporal evolution of the upwind wind-speed profile, boundary-layer height, and the three-dimensional extent of the smoke plume over the course of the burn. QUIC-Fire is a fast-running, laptop-compatible fire behavior model designed to represent coupled fire–atmosphere interactions at spatial and temporal scales relevant to prescribed fire. The model incorporates the QUIC-URB diagnostic wind solver, adapted for complex terrain, to generate three-dimensional wind fields and represent interactions between ambient winds, terrain, and fire-induced flow. Fire spread is represented using a cellular automata approach that captures both wind-driven spread and slower creeping fire behavior. The model predicts the temporal evolution of quantities including mass burned, reaction rate, emissions, and fire-induced winds, while its nested-grid framework allows fire behavior to be resolved at meter-scale resolution within a larger atmospheric domain. This study uses the Eglin dataset to examine how the meteorological information supplied to QUIC-Fire influences the simulated wind environment and subsequent fire behavior. Simulations initialized using operationally available HRRR and GFS meteorology are compared with simulations informed by locally observed SODAR and scanning Doppler LiDAR winds. The resulting QUIC-Fire wind fields are evaluated against field observations to quantify differences in wind speed, wind direction, vertical structure, and their evolution throughout the burn.

498075.title: Analysis of Mesoscale Environments of Pyroconvective Tornadoes
498075.authors: Sergio Reynoso, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA
498075.abstract: Pyroconvective tornadoes, more commonly known as "fire tornadoes", are an extremely rare type of tornado produced by intense wildfires, capable of greatly increasing their destructiveness. Some of the most infamous wildfires in California history have produced fire tornadoes, and as wildfire frequency increases due to climate change, understanding fire tornadoes becomes more important. Fire tornadoes are distinguished from other whirlwinds more commonly induced by wildfires, in that they appear to develop similarly to typical tornadoes; the intense heat of a wildfire induces convection, pyrocumulonimbus formation, and tornadogenesis. I aim to investigate the similarities among and differences between documented fire tornadoes to determine the most important factors behind their development and how they may contrast with typical tornadogenesis. Specifically, I analyze variables critical to typical tornadoes, including CAPE, wind shear, helicity, and atmospheric humidity, in addition to critical variables for wildfire development, including surface-level winds, surface humidity, and fire temperature. Both sets of variables are compared to average ranges during tornadogenesis, and during wildfires of similar size and intensity, respectively. I will analyze wildfires across three broad categories: those without any pyroconvection, those with pyroconvection but no tornado development, and those that produced a fire tornado. This will provide a reasonable estimate of the necessary thresholds for fire tornadogenesis.

498078.title: Observing the Air–Sea Transition Zone During the Onset of the Indian Summer Monsoon
498078.authors: Leah Johnson, University of Washington, WA
498078.abstract: The transition into the Indian Summer Monsoon is characterized by a seasonal reversal of winds over the North Indian Ocean that transports moisture across the ocean and land. This system is built on many processes that span a range of scales across the air–sea transition zone, encompassing the ocean and atmospheric boundary layers and the interface between them. The Enhancing Knowledge of the Arabian Sea Marine environment through Science and Advanced Training (EKAMSAT) program aims to improve our understanding of unresolved small-scale processes and their role in monsoon dynamics and prediction. During the 2024 EKAMSAT field program in the Bay of Bengal, an autonomous array of gliders and surface vehicles, combined with ship-based platforms and radiosondes, captured the coupled evolution of the upper ocean, atmosphere, and air–sea interface throughout the monsoon transition. The observations spanned four distinct regimes: pre-monsoon conditions, cyclone passage, post-cyclone recovery, and monsoon onset. By coupling the ocean mixed-layer heat budget with the atmospheric moist static energy budget, we quantify the contribution of ocean processes to changes in atmospheric moist static energy across these regimes. Entrainment and heat flux into the ocean contributed up to 10% of the changes in moist static energy, with their influence varying substantially under anomalous conditions including barrier layers, penetrative radiative fluxes and wind-driven entrainment. Together, these results demonstrate how ocean surface boundary layer processes can influence atmospheric moist static energy and highlight the importance of capturing commonly unresolved processes across the air-sea transition zone for understanding atmosphere-ocean coupling during the monsoon development.

498079.title: CubIXSS and SunCET: Two New Missions to Probe Solar Eruptions for Space Weather Understanding and R2O Applications
498079.authors: Amir Caspi, Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO; and J. P. Mason, P. S. Athiray, and D. B. Seaton
498079.abstract: The solar corona’s complex, convoluted magnetic field powers energetic processes including heating and acceleration of coronal plasma. These processes are often driven through gradual, quasi-steady energy release, heating the corona to a few MK and accelerating solar wind outflow. However, solar flares and eruptions release this energy explosively, heating plasma to tens of MK, accelerating energetic particles, and driving gigatons of bulk flows in coronal mass ejections. Quantifying and tracking this energy release and transport from the inner through middle corona is essential to developing a complete understanding of the Sun’s connection to the heliosphere – a fundamental step in developing capabilities to predict space weather effects driven by these phenomena. Fully characterizing this energy flow requires observations that can both diagnose the energy release process itself and track the propagation of accelerated plasma continuously from its origins through the inner and middle corona. Two new CubeSat missions, expected to launch together in early 2027, will combine their pathfinding observations to demonstrate how such tracking can enable more comprehensive understanding. The CubeSat Imaging X-ray Solar Spectrometer (CubIXSS) will directly probe the immediate energy release in flares via X-ray spectroscopy over an unprecedented wavelength range, revealing how plasma is heated and how hot mass subsequently flows between the chromosphere and corona. The Sun Coronal Ejection Tracker (SunCET) will directly measure the resulting dynamic propagation via wide-field-of-view broadband EUV images of the corona from the solar disk out to 5 solar radii. In combination, these missions will provide detailed observations of both the genesis of energy release events and the consequences, in flows and waves, that restructure the corona and drive outflow into the heliosphere. These small instruments are uniquely well suited for deep-space constellations for multi-viewpoint heliophysics research or deployment to other planets (e.g., Mars) for both space weather monitoring and science. CubIXSS and SunCET are both currently in the final phases of I&T, with launch planned for mid-February 2027. We discuss the missions, their capabilities, plans for coordination, and the science and R2O applications enabled by their simultaneous observations.

498080.title: Evaluating Seasonal Forecast Skill for ENSO-Driven Precipitation Variability in NOAA's SFS Beta-v1 Model
498080.authors: Lauren Elizabeth Frake, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL; The Cooperative Institute for Climate, Ocean, and Ecosystem Sciences (CICOES), Seattle, WA; and A. Levine
498080.abstract: Evaluating Seasonal Forecast Skill for ENSO-Driven Precipitation Variability in NOAA’s SFS Beta-v1 Model Lauren Frake1, Aaron Levine2 1University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, 1,2CICOES University of Washington The El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the dominant driver of year-to-year climate variability, so accurately forecasting it is vital for seasonal climate prediction. NOAA’s new Seasonal Forecast System (SFS) will replace the CFS model, which has been in operation since 2011. This study examines how well SFS captures ENSO-driven winter precipitation anomalies at leads of around nine months and identifies additional sources of predictability beyond ENSO. We compared SFS reforecasts with NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 precipitation observations. We evaluated how December, January, February (DJF) Oceanic Nino Index (ONI) values predicted DJF precipitation anomalies in both the model and observations and assessed systematic bias. To isolate non-ENSO variability, we removed the ENSO signal between observations and the model, then compared the pattern correlation of these residuals with several climate indices. Results showed that model forecast skill increases substantially during stronger ENSO events, with pattern correlations between model and observed anomalies rising alongside ONI magnitude and decreasing with greater ONI forecast error. The model reproduces observed ENSO precipitation teleconnections well, capturing the correct direction and location of anomalies in most areas globally, with minimal systematic regression error. Beyond ENSO, the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (QBO), showed the strongest relationship with residual forecast skill. This was most evident for forecasts initialized in April where the correlation between the pattern correlation of observed and modeled residuals and DJF QBO approached r=0.5. Predictability was highest during the QBO’s westerly phase, when pattern correlations between observed and modeled residuals were greatest. The QBO has significant impacts on precipitation tropically and through Northern Hemisphere storm tracks. Overall, SFS shows strong skill in reproducing precipitation teleconnections, with forecast accuracy closely tied to the strength and predictability of the ENSO event itself. The QBO appears to be an underexplored secondary source of predictability at long leads, independent of ENSO. This relationship could meaningfully extend the reliable lead time of seasonal precipitation forecasts.

498084.title: Improving Model Parameterizations In Convection-Aerosol-Precipitation-Radiation Interactions
498084.abstract: Deep convective clouds strongly regulate aerosol, precipitation, and radiation. However, their interactions with aerosols are particularly difficult to represent because the key processes involved —including aerosol activation, precipitation formation, and convective wet removal—are convoluted and occur at very small scales. These limitations contribute to substantial uncertainties in simulated precipitation, cloud properties, aerosol burdens, lifetimes, and aerosol radiative effects. In this talk we will show the importance of representing aerosol budget including prognostic aerosol size distribution with ultrafine particles considered when parameterizing aerosol–cloud–precipitation interactions. We will also show how the improved physical treatment of aerosol wet removal by deep convection in a global coarse resolution Earth system model-E3SM effectively mitigates the overestimation of aerosol loading and lifetime, as well as aerosol direct and indirect radiative forcing. These studies point to a central message that a complete aerosol budget treatment with cloud microphysical processes considered is needed to realistically simulate the convection-aerosol-precipitation-radiation interactions.

498086.title: Aerosol Impacts on Convective Storms and Precipitation – Multi-Model Investigation of Two Sea Breeze Cases from TRACER-MIP
498086.abstract: Convective clouds and precipitation remain one of the most challenging aspects of weather prediction due to fundamental gaps in understanding how they can be shaped by environmental conditions including aerosols. Aerosol impact on convective clouds and precipitation can affect water availability and weather hazards impacting energy system reliability, however it is of a large uncertainty. A community model intercomparison project (MIP) was organized based on two observed sea breeze induced storm cases- June 17 and August 7, 2022- from DOE ARM Tracking Aerosol Convection Interaction Experiment (TRACER) campaign (TRACER-MIP). Simulations of three different aerosol number concentration scenarios (0.3x, 1x, 3x) are collected from 9 modeling groups to examine model differences in simulating aerosol impacts. We first evaluate the baseline simulations (1x) with comprehensive observations in precipitation and radar reflectivity and meteorological conditions. Models in general overestimate potential temperature and RH in the boundary layer from the start of the simulations, leading to a stronger storm and overestimation of precipitation compared to observations. These model thermodynamic biases indicate initial and boundary condition problems from the ERA5 reanalysis data. Aerosol suppresses the total precipitation over the entire domain but increases precipitation in the Houston area on June 17. Frequencies of light precipitation are reduced but severe precipitation frequencies are increased, particularly prominent in Houston area in both cases (only 1-2 outliners). Aerosol effects on precipitation are diverse across models, however, increasing aerosol consistently enhances convective organizations, leading to suppressed shallow clouds but enhanced deep clouds thus increased updraft velocities and occurrences of heavy rain rates, particularly more prominent in Houston areas. Aerosol effects on convection and precipitation are more significant for August 7 case compared to June 17 case, likely due to cleaner background conditions.

498088.title: The Evolution of Growing Season Thirstwave Characteristics Across the CONUS From Historical to Future Climate Conditions
498088.authors: Michael Joseph Shaw, Northern Illinois University, Peru, IL; and M. G. Flanner and L. M. Nguyen
498088.abstract: Thirstwaves are a recently identified meteorological phenomenon characterized by prolonged periods of anomalously high atmospheric evaporative demand. They are defined as periods of at least three consecutive days during which reference short crop evapotranspiration (ETos) exceeds a day-specific 90th-percentile threshold. Unlike temperature- or precipitation-based metrics, ETos integrates the combined effects of temperature, humidity, wind speed, radiation, and atmospheric pressure, providing a standardized measure of atmospheric water demand. Here, we investigate how thirstwave frequency, duration, and intensity may change across the contiguous United States (CONUS) under future climate conditions. Daily ETos was calculated from meteorological output from the 80-member Community Earth System Model Version 2 (CESM2) Large Ensemble for a historical period (1850-2014) and a future SSP3-7.0 scenario (2015-2100). Thirstwaves were identified throughout the CONUS during April-October using grid-point-specific 90th-percentile ETos thresholds derived from a 15-day moving climatological window. Future characteristics were evaluated relative to the historical climatology. Results indicate substantial increases in thirstwave characteristics across much of the CONUS, with frequency, duration, and intensity exhibiting distinct spatial responses. The Northeast and Southwest exhibit the largest increases in thirstwave frequency and duration, while the Midwest experiences the greatest increases in thirstwave intensity. Despite relatively modest changes in the mean characteristics of thirstwaves, their future distributions shift substantially toward more frequent and intense extremes. These results indicate that extreme atmospheric water demand may become increasingly common and severe throughout the twenty-first century, with potential implications for agricultural water demand, water resources, and ecosystem resilience.

498092.title: Adaptive Interpretation of Geostationary Satellite Observations for Seamless Day–Night Solar Irradiance Forecasting
498092.authors: Eric Terpstra, Weather Solutions, Bennekom, GE, Netherlands
498092.abstract: Accurate 0–6 h solar irradiance forecasts remain challenging because cloud evolution between numerical weather prediction (NWP) update cycles is only partly represented. Geostationary satellites provide continuous observations of the cloud field, but the predictive value of satellite information varies considerably with the prevailing meteorological conditions. This study presents an operational framework that combines NWP guidance with adaptive interpretation of multispectral geostationary satellite observations. During daylight, visible and infrared observations characterize cloud evolution, while nighttime cloud development is inferred from multiple complementary thermal infrared diagnostics that capture different cloud characteristics. Together, these provide seamless cloud monitoring throughout the diurnal cycle. Rather than applying a fixed satellite correction, the framework continuously evaluates the evolving weather situation and estimates the relative predictive value of satellite observations and NWP guidance, adjusting their influence accordingly. Stable situations remain primarily NWP-driven, while rapidly evolving cloud fields receive greater weight from satellite-derived information. The framework was evaluated against an extensive European network of ground-based irradiance observations spanning multiple climates, seasons, and cloud regimes. Compared with an operational benchmark based on a ten-model ensemble combined with the latest irradiance observations, first-hour forecast errors were reduced by approximately 30%, while useful forecast skill was maintained through 6–7 hours for regional forecasts. These results demonstrate the potential of meteorologically adaptive, seamless day–night satellite interpretation for operational renewable-energy forecasting.

498093.title: Rainfall Variability and Extremes over North Africa
498093.authors: Ademe Mekonnen, University of Miami, Miami, FL; and A. A. Ferede, S. M. Hagos, and T. Tesfa
498093.abstract: Quantified the spatiotemporal variability of rainfall in Sahelian North Africa and mechanisms associated with variabilities are essential inputs for managing climate risks in a region sensitive to weather and climate variability. However, broad and region-wide assessments over the Sahel often obscure important localized effects, making sub-regional analyses critical. This study employs a multiple time and space scale analysis based on a sub-regional approach over a 44-year period (1981–2024). We employ high-resolution gridded precipitation, reanalysis, and cold cloud top infrared measurements to assess seasonal rainfall and convection characteristics in terms of their wet-day frequency and extreme events during the July–September (JAS) season. Preliminary results show complex rainfall interannual tendency and variability over the Sahel characterized by a notable increase north of about 10°N parallel and a decrease to the south of this. Subregional analysis shows an increase in the mean rainfall from 1981–2007 to 2008–2024 over West Africa (Region 10°–15°N, 15°–5°W), suggesting a shift in the mean rainfall climate. A persistent decreasing pattern since 2000 was observed over a subregion located within 7.5°–10°N, 15°W–5°W. JAS rainfall over the eastern part of West Africa surrounding Cameroon-Nigeria also shows a general decrease over time. The summer rainfall over West Africa shows very high interannual variability shifting between excessively wet and very dry seasons. Further, high impact rainfall analysis using indices from ETCCDI (Expert Team on Climate Change Detection and Indices) show an increase in seasonal totals is associated with heavy falls (rain ≥10, < 20 mm/day), in general, and a notable increase in very heavy (≥ 20, < 50 mm/day) and extreme rainfall (rain ≥ 50 mm/day) over the Sahel north of 10°N. The high impact rainfall contribution for the north seems to increase with time. However, high impact rainfall over southern and eastern Sahel did not show an increase over time, although the rainfall amount seems to be higher on average compared to the north. Similarly, the frequency of high impact rainfall appears to increase over time over the north, while decreasing over the south. The frequency of high impact rainfall around Cameroon-Nigerian region shows decline over time. Additionally, results of deep convection with overshooting cloud towers suggest an increasing activity, consistent with increasing rainfall trends over Sahel north of 10°N, while decreasing activity is noted over the regions to the south.

498094.title: Near Equator Landfalling Tropical Cyclones In the South-West Indian Ocean: The Case of 2024 Tropical Cyclone Hidaya and Ialy
498094.authors: Adrajow A. Ferede, North Carolina A&T State University, Greensboro, NC; and A. Mekonnen, T. Tesfa, and S. M. Hagos
498094.abstract: Tropical storms rarely sustain their coherence within 5◦ of the equator due to the vanishing effect of Coriolis force. However, in April and May 2024, Tropical Cyclones Hidaya and Ialy overcame this constraint in the South-West Indian Ocean (SWIO), with Hidaya making a historic landfall in Tanzania near 8◦S, and Ialy maintaining a record breaking sustained cyclonic structure near 1.3◦S. Utilizing a 26-year historical tracking dataset (1998–2024), we demonstrate that these systems are historically unprecedented, while weak. TC Hidaya and Ialy were unique in their capacity to sustain hurricane-force winds at such low latitudes and track northward into East Africa. Observational data reveals these events coincided with an extreme, localized equatorial marine heatwave (> 29.5◦C). Further, we employed a two-tiered modeling approach to determine if the huge thermal forcing compensates for the weak background vorticity, First, global atmospheric sensitivity experiments using the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) showed that the marine heatwave generate massive, episodic spikes in Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE), providing the necessary thermodynamic condition for vortex amplification. We noted that dynamically removing the heatwave entirely suppressed cyclogenesis. Subsequently, high-resolution dynamical downscaling using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model translated this global thermodynamic forcing into explicit mesoscale convection, accurately capturing the anomalous vortex spin-up and kinematic tracking of the storms. Our findings demonstrate that extreme localized thermodynamic forcing can dynamically compensate for a very weak Coriolis force, driving both the unprecedented near-equator intensification and the highly anomalous westward kinematic tracking of these tropical cyclones into East Africa.

498095.title: Severe Weather of 2026: Storm Prediction Center Annual Severe Weather Review
498095.authors: Russell S. Schneider, NWS, Norman, OK; and E. Bentley
498095.abstract: This session will cover the 2026 Severe Weather season and its major convective events as presented by the Storm Prediction Center

498096.title: A Comprehensive Assessment of Precipitation Variability In The Great Plains Using High-Resolution Climate Projection
498096.authors: Tucker Alan Vandenberg, Nebraska Water Center, Omaha, NE
498096.abstract: Precipitation extremes in the North Central Great Plains are projected to intensify under continued greenhouse gas emissions, with significant implications for agricultural productivity, water resource management, and drought resilience across the region. This study examines historical and projected changes in four precipitation indices, maximum 5-day precipitation (Rx5day), number of heavy precipitation days (R10mm), maximum consecutive wet days (CWD), and maximum consecutive dry days (CDD). Using two high-resolution statistically downscaled datasets: LOCA2 (1/16 degrees) and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 (0.25 degrees), evaluated against NClimGrid daily observations over the period 1951–2014. This study extends the analysis to next-generation downscaled products under the SSP2-4.5 emissions scenario through 2100. Results indicate that both datasets capture the observed spatial gradients in precipitation extremes, with LOCA2 showing closer agreement with observations due to its bias-correction against station data. Under SSP2-4.5, ensemble mean projections suggest significant increases in Rx5day and R10mm across the region by the near future (2031–2060), with further amplification by the far future (2071–2100). CDD increases are projected to be largest in the western Great Plains, consistent with an expanding aridity of the area, while the eastern portion of the domain shows more modest changes. State-level analysis reveals significant inter-state variability in projected changes, with Nebraska, Kansas, and South Dakota showing the strongest drying signals. Differences between LOCA2 and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 are attributed primarily to resolution, bias correction methodology, and the underlying CMIP6 model ensemble composition.

498098.title: 2026 Excessive Rainfall and Flood Events
498098.authors: David R. Novak, NWS/Weather Prediction Center, College Park, MD
498098.abstract: This session will cover the excessive rainfall and flood events of 2026 from the perspective of the NWS Weather Prediction Center

498099.title: 2026 Winter Storms
498099.authors: David R. Novak, NWS/Weather Prediction Center, College Park, MD
498099.abstract: This session will cover the winter storm events of 2026 from the perspective of the NWS Weather Prediction Center

498100.title: A Hazardous Weather Testbed Evaluation of the NWS AI Language Translation Program Across the Weather Communication Chai
498100.authors: Joseph E. Trujillo-Falcón, UIUC, Urbana, IL; and S. R. Ernst, E. De Jesus Otero, J. A. Shumaker, A. L. Corrales, C. Riva, Z. N. Caryl, K. M. Bonifer, B. A. Nickols, M. L. Bozeman, S. Callesano, A. R. Gaviria Pabon, and A. C. Wanless
498100.abstract: To advance a Weather-Ready Nation for all, the National Weather Service (NWS) has expanded Spanish-language hazard information through the agency’s AI Language Translation Program (weather.gov/translate). Products translated through this program have mainly reached communities through core partners who adapt them for their own audiences. In 2026, our team conducted a NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed experiment that brought NWS forecasters, emergency managers, and broadcast meteorologists together to examine how each core partner group utilizes and trusts automated translated products. NWS forecasters were presented with a scenario involving a convective hazard forecast for a major international sporting event and were asked to produce forecast materials and an IDSS briefing in English. These products were then translated through the NWS AI Language Translation program. In the second half of the experiment, emergency managers and broadcast meteorologists were given an English briefing on the forecast, the NWS AI translation tool, and the automated translated products by the NWS forecasters. Drawing on pre- and post-experiment surveys and four focus groups involving around 60 participants, we examine how these partners currently communicate hazards to Spanish-speaking decision makers and communities, how each group assesses whether AI translated products preserve intended meaning, and how the translation program could be adapted to existing operational workflows. Results describe what each group needs in order to rely on AI translation during real-life events, and how each participant group holds different assumptions about how translated products should be reviewed and released.

498102.title: From Bonfires to Wildfires and Smokestacks to Cities: How Aerosol Chemistry and Physics In Emission Plumes Shapes Our Air Quality and Climate (Invited Presentation)
498102.authors: Jeffrey R. Pierce, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO
498102.abstract: Air pollutants are generally not emitted homogeneously over large areas, but rather than from point, mobile, or small-area sources. These emission sources create plumes with higher pollutant concentrations than the surrounding air. Aerosol physics and gas-phase chemistry are full of processes that are non-linear with concentrations. Our air quality and climate models often cannot resolve the fine spatial extent of these plumes, and thus mix the plumes instantly into larger gridboxes, diluting the pollutant concentrations and leading to incorrect process rates. Stationary measurements capture plumes at a specific time after emission, providing a snapshot of aerosol plume evolution, but tell little about the plume processes. Airborne field campaigns are better for capturing the full picture of plumes but are limited to a relatively smaller number of cases.
