Hence, understanding aerosol evolution in plumes requires combinations of observational and modelling platforms. In this lecture, I will discuss my group’s work on aerosol evolution in plumes, the work that inspired it, impacts on air quality and climate, and thoughts on future directions. We will think about a variety of fire and anthropogenic sources, and I will discuss how particle properties from any given source type shouldn’t be treated as “one size fits all” because of variability in plumes and their environments.

498105.title: Predicting the Safety of Aviation: How the HRRR Forecast Model Performs
498105.authors: Luis Samuel Flores Puentes, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, CO; and L. R. Blank
498105.abstract: Icing and turbulence events can pose major complications for both commercial and general aviation. To better understand and handle these events, the Federal Aviation Administration utilizes a variety of different prediction products, one of which is the Domestic Aviation Forecast System (DAFS). The DAFS, produced by NOAA, is made of two components: a mathematical algorithm which takes in data and produces the prediction, and the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model. We performed work to address the overall goal of understanding the underlying cause of an incorrect icing or turbulence prediction if the DAFS were to create an inaccurate forecast. We looked specifically at the HRRR’s temperature forecasts at different isobaric pressure levels. Accurate temperature forecasts are crucial when calculating icing and turbulence forecasts. This presentation will explore the results of our analysis and discuss the implications with regards to determining the source of error for DAFS output.

498107.title: The Atmospheric Composition Observatory (TACO) Designed to Enhance Trace Gas Monitoring
498107.authors: Arwa L. Ouali, NOAA, Kearny, NJ; and H. Hope and V. J. Mikles
498107.abstract: The Ozone Mapping and Profiler Suite (OMPS) instrument onboard the Joint Polar Satellite System measures O3 and SO2 successfully; however, scientists have developed requirements for future missions to detect additional compounds that would provide a more complete overview on atmospheric composition. Increased spatial resolution, narrower bandpass for each channel, and a wider spectral range are all necessary upgrades to allow for greater coverage of the ultraviolet and visible light on the electromagnetic spectrum. These improvements would provide scientists with critical data on trace gasses in the troposphere and stratosphere that was previously not feasible with the design of the heritage (OMPS) instrument. Analyzing current instrument design and orbit guides the new modifications proposed for the Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) missions. Considerations for the optics layout, sensor, pixel array, and altitude of the satellite are all factored into a comparative analysis that utilizes heritage instruments in orbit as a basis to provide recommendations for a new design based on the scientific guidelines. The design will ensure that the instrument can sufficiently meet these new objectives while also satisfying the NEON program’s engineering constraints to fit the payload onto a small satellite bus. The next-generation atmospheric composition instrument will supply the necessary trace gas data, which is essential for improving weather models and geolocating weather events with greater precision.

498109.title: A Century of Drought Science: From Scientific Developments and Drought Migration to Emerging Societal Threats (Invited Presentation)
498109.authors: Ashok Mishra, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX
498109.abstract: Drought has shaped civilizations throughout history, influencing water availability, agricultural productivity, ecosystems, economies, and human well-being. Yet our scientific understanding of drought has evolved profoundly over the past century. From early descriptions of precipitation deficits and historical drought impacts, drought research has developed into a multidisciplinary field encompassing climate dynamics, hydrology, remote sensing, artificial intelligence, and risk assessment. This presentation traces this scientific journey over the past century, beginning with ancient and historical droughts and their societal consequences, and examining how research priorities, conceptual frameworks, and methodologies have evolved in response to changing environmental and societal needs. The first part of the presentation explores the historical evolution of drought research, including major drought events and their societal impacts, the changing disciplinary landscape, shifting research priorities, and scientific and technological advances that have transformed drought monitoring and assessment. The presentation then examines an emerging dimension of drought science, with a particular focus on spatiotemporal drought migration and propagation. Droughts are not static phenomena; they can develop, intensify, and propagate across large regions over extended periods. Examining the spatial and temporal evolution of major drought events provides important insights into where droughts originate, how they migrate, and how their movement influences regional water availability and drought risk. The presentation next examines emerging societal threats, with particular emphasis on compound drought–heatwave (CDHW) events. Increasingly frequent and intense CDHW events pose substantial risks to agriculture, water resources, ecosystems, energy systems, and human health, with impacts disproportionately concentrated in communities experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage, agricultural dependence, and health-related vulnerabilities across the United States. At the global scale, increasing CDHW stress across major breadbasket regions, coupled with demographic shifts and rising food-import dependency, could amplify the risk of simultaneous agricultural failures and global food insecurity. The presentation will also highlight global hotspots of water scarcity and vulnerability in the context of CDHWs. Collectively, these perspectives highlight the need to advance drought science from understanding and monitoring individual hazards toward an integrated framework for anticipating interconnected and cascading societal risks in a changing climate.

498110.title: Exploring Variations of Trust and Protective Action Likelihood Across Early Warning Messaging Formats for Severe Weather Events: A Study into the Behavioural Attributes of the Barbadian Public
498110.authors: Wynsty Jolene Boochoon, CIMH = Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology, Bridgetown, St James, Barbados; and K. A. Caesar, MS
498110.abstract: Advances in forecasting have led to improvements in accurate and timely prediction of the immediate track of a Hurricane or Tropical Cyclone. One of the primary duties of a weather forecaster is the analysis, diagnosis, and forecast of a severe weather event. Most important is the dissemination of clear warnings that communicate the incoming risk to relevant stakeholders and the general public so that they are well informed to take protective/mitigating actions. The importance of Early Warning Messaging (EWM) and its mitigating effects related to Tropical Storms and Hurricanes are well understood, and the optimal structure and method of communication have been analyzed by previous research. However, there is a gap in the study for severe weather risk/warning communication in the Caribbean. Therefore, this study seeks to investigate the attitudes of the Barbadian public towards various formats of a severe weather warning. The extent to which respondents trusted current weather forecasts and the specific format presented was evaluated. In addition, their understanding of the presented forecast and likelihood of them taking protective action were also measured, using a Likert Scale. Modelled after warnings created by regional National Meteorological Services (NMS) for their social media, these formats have three distinct categories: traditional forecast, impacts-based risk matrix warning (Risk Matrix), and a hybrid between a traditional forecast and risk matrix warning (Hybrid). Google Form surveys for each format were created in which respondents were presented with the same questions evaluating the variables above. Surveys were disseminated through social media and instant messaging (WhatsApp) group chats; 142 participants anonymously filled out the survey. Results illustrated that across formats, respondents' degree of trust did not vary; however, the likelihood of taking protective action did. Respondents presented with the traditional forecast were less likely to take protective action when compared to those presented with either a Risk Matrix warning or a Hybrid warning (both of which had comparable likelihood of taking protective actions). These findings continue to inform regional NMSs on ways in which they can tailor their warnings for better reception by the public.

498113.title: Investigating Anomalies in Fine Particulate Matter (PM₁ and PM₂.₅) in the Southwest Houston Area Using a Low-Cost Sensor
498113.authors: Advika Asthana, Davidson Academy, Sugar Land, TX; and M. F. Martinez and K. Ardon-Dryer
498113.abstract: Particulate Matter (PM) are tiny particles suspended in the atmosphere that can originate from emissions, wildfires, and dust storms. These particles pose a serious health risk to humans, leading to the potential development of respiratory issues such as asthma and bronchitis. Low-cost sensors improve the ability for communities to collect air quality data locally and may be beneficial for enhancing monitoring across urban and suburban spaces. Houston is a particularly relevant setting for monitoring PM concentrations as it hosts several oil and gas refineries and operates a major international port. This project takes place in suburban southwest Houston, where the sources for high PM and poor air quality are more variable and less known. The objective of this study is to examine changes in PM using a low-cost sensor, observe periods of elevated PM, and identify the source of the PM spike through meteorological measurements and satellite imagery. A PurpleAir (PA-II) sensor was installed at a residential location in southwest Houston to monitor hourly and daily PM concentrations from December 2025 through April 2026. Periods of elevated PM concentrations were further investigated to identify potential sources of observed pollution episodes. The results displayed that the dual subunits in the PurpleAir sensor had an extremely strong, positive correlation, with R2 values of 0.99 for both PM1 and PM2.5 (PM diameters ≤ 1 µm and ≤ 2.5 µm, respectively). Multiple spikes in PM1 and PM2.5 were observed in late January, which stemmed from a variety of factors related to a passing weather system. This demonstrates the sensor’s ability to effectively capture both long-term trends and short air quality events, providing valuable information and highlighting the potential of using these sensors to improve the understanding of local environmental conditions and regional pollution events.

498114.title: Boom, Sparkle, Spike: Tracking Aerosol Particle Events in Uvalde, Texas Using a PurpleAir Sensor
498114.authors: Arin Joshi, Claudia Taylor “Lady Bird” Johnson High School, Uvalde, TX; and M. F. Martinez and K. Ardon-Dryer
498114.abstract: Uvalde, Texas can experience changes in air quality caused by dust, weather patterns, and nearby human activity. Previous air quality research shows that particulate matter (PM), especially fine particles such as PM1 and PM2.5 (particles smaller than ≤1 and ≤2.5 µm, respectively), can affect the local environment, health, and contribute to pollution events. A PurpleAir sensor was placed in a private home in Uvalde, Texas and collected PM1 and PM2.5 hourly concentrations from December 13th, 2025, to April 10th, 2026. Raw data was processed, cleaned, and then averaged between the two PurpleAir subunits. Several major PM2.5 spikes were identified throughout the study period. PM2.5 spikes were caused by fireworks within a few feet of the sensor on December 31st, with PM1 and PM2.5 hourly values of 27.1 and 44.4 µg/m³ (respectively). Smoke from fires in Mexico reaching the sensor led to high PM values on February 7 with PM1 and PM2.5 hourly concentrations of 38.1 and 58.8 µg/m³. These results show that PM levels in Uvalde, Texas can rise sharply during certain events impacting peoples life, although PM levels were lower for most of the day.

498115.title: Evaluating the Reliability of Low-Cost Sensors through Investigation of Particulate Matter in College Station, Texas
498115.authors: Michael Zhang Wu, A&M Consolidated High School, College Station, TX; and M. F. Martinez and K. Ardon-Dryer
498115.abstract: High concentrations of particulate matter with diameters less than 1 or 2.5 μm (PM1 & PM2.5) are significant causes of human health outcomes, including respiratory diseases such as asthma. However, the intensity and impacts of PM concentrations are poorly understood, especially in suburban areas such as College Station, Texas. Low-cost sensors are a feasible approach to bridge the gap in awareness of air quality issues. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate the reliability of low-cost PurpleAir Classic Units by analyzing PM1 & PM2.5 concentrations recorded from December 15th, 2025, to April 10th, 2026 (116 days). The results revealed that 23 days (19.8%) exceeded World Health Organization (WHO) recommended daily PM2.5 concentrations (35 µg/m3), but only two days (1.7%) exceeded Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recommended PM2.5 concentrations (15 µg/m3). The highest hourly PM2.5 concentration (114.5 µg/m3) occurred in the afternoon of April 7th, 2026 and appeared to be caused by PM2.5 blown from a controlled burn in a nearby county, highlighting the potentially widespread impacts of manmade pollution. Furthermore, PM2.5 data from the PurpleAir sensor showed a high correlation of 0.89 with a Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) monitoring station located 16.8 km away from the PurpleAir sensor. The PurpleAir sensor recorded PM2.5 concentrations that were on average 3.9±5.0 µg/m3 higher than the TCEQ station likely because it is uncalibrated, but their high correlation indicates that low-cost sensors are reliable and effective at analyzing local air quality, which suggests that the widespread promotion and adoption of affordable air quality sensors can help to promote greater awareness of air quality hazards, provide information about local air quality concerns, and ultimately aid in reducing exposure to dangerous pollutants.

498116.title: Winter Inversions and Combustion Emissions Drive PM2.5 Exceedances in a Modern Texas Suburb: Frisco, Texas
498116.authors: Bhavna Devanand, Rick Reedy High School, Frisco, TX; and M. F. Martinez and K. Ardon-Dryer
498116.abstract: Fine particulate matter (>PM2.5) poses significant respiratory and cardiovascular health risks, yet hyperlocal air quality data remains absent for rapidly expanding Dallas Fort-Worth (DFW) suburban communities. Frisco, Texas has experienced growth in population, yet no study has characterized neighborhood-scale PM dynamics or identified dominant emission sources in this area. This study deployed a PurpleAir (PA-II) sensor on a residential home in Frisco, collecting hourly PM1, and PM2.5 observations from December 16, 2025, through April 10, 2026. A total of 24 days (21%) exceeded the World Health Organization (WHO) daily PM2.5 guideline of 15 µg/m³, with 75% of these days occurred in January–February. Three days had daily values above the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) threshold of 35 µg/m³. These occurred on January 28-30, with the highest hourly PM2.5 concentration of 63.8 µg/m³, reported on January 28 at 22:00. These high PM levels were during a winter storm that occurred between January 26–30, 2026. During these days the area was under temperature inversions with high pressure (>1009 hPa) that trapped combustion emissions during the sub-freezing conditions. Examination of particle size ratio analysis of PM1/PM2.5 which was 0.63, indicated of anthropogenic particles that were emitted from combustion dominated sources such as heating methods using natural gas, electric heating, or vehicle emissions, serving as the prominent source during these exceedance events. Results were validated against Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) regulatory monitors, which confirmed January 28 as the worst air quality day across all DFW stations. These findings demonstrate that suburban neighborhoods can experience PM2.5 concentrations 30–50% above regional averages during winter stagnation events. During these events, there should be an increase in public awareness of the impact of portable heaters and generators, along with the health effects of such particles.

498117.title: Analysis of Particulate Matter (PM) using Purple Air Sensors in Lubbock County
498117.authors: Angelina Avetisyan, Lubbock High School, Lubbock, TX; and M. F. Martinez and K. Ardon-Dryer
498117.abstract: The study focused on hourly changes of PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations and an analysis of the main reasons for the different fluctuations of these PM concentrations using the Purple Air sensor (PA-II). The Purple Air sensor (PA-II) was installed in the southern region of Lubbock and recorded PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 (particles with diameter <1, 2.5, and 10μm, respectively) from December 7, 2024, to April 1, 2025. The result indicated that PM2.5 achieves its maximum value of 62.9 μg/m3 at 18:00 on December 15, 2024, while PM10 reaches its peak of 113.3 μg/m3 at 19:00 on March 18, 2025. The high peak of PM values on December 15, 2024, was likely due to the sensor’s proximity to a Quick Service Restaurant (QSR), McDonald's. As the restaurant serves an increasing number of customers (lunch/dinner), the transportation, which is constituted mostly of gasoline-based vehicles, and cooking fumes contribute to higher PM values. The high PM10 values were a result of a dust event on March 18, 2025, that was associated with strong winds.

498118.title: Finding Needles in a Haystack: Using a GOES Nowcasting Model to Forecast Convective Initiation
498118.authors: Ethan Campbell, UNC Charlotte, Charlotte, NC; and K. Yang, D. J. Gagne II, and C. Becker
498118.abstract: While convection-allowing, physics-based models provide skillful guidance on severe weather threats over multi-day periods, nowcasting (short-term forecasting on the order of one to several hours) remains a problem not effectively addressed by traditional models, whose spin-up time and data assimilation latency limit their ability to capture the precise timing and location of convective initiation. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) offer a pathway to close this gap by learning patterns from observational data and generating forecasts in minutes at inference time, compared to multi-hour runtimes typical of convection-allowing numerical weather prediction models. To address this gap, the Machine Integration and Learning for Earth Systems (MILES) group at NSF NCAR has developed an ML model, built on their CREDIT (Community Research Earth Digital Intelligence Twin) architecture, trained on GOES-16 satellite imagery, along with topography and top-of-atmosphere solar radiation, to forecast all 16 spectral bands one to three hours in the future. We evaluate this model using two case studies – an isolated supercell thunderstorm in the Dakotas in August 2024, and supercells embedded within a frontal system in the Plains in April 2024 – to assess model performance across different convective scenarios and identify next steps for retraining. We find that the model shows skill in predicting large-scale atmospheric dynamics, such as jet streaks and mid-latitude cyclones; however, the model exhibits persistent struggles in representing the spatial extent and magnitude of convective initiation. Further work will focus on incorporating dynamical fields to add context to the model as well as resampling training datasets to emphasize convective initiation.

498119.title: Diabatic Heating in Jet Regime Modulation of Northern Hemisphere Storm-tracks
498119.authors: Heidi Nsiah, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA; and D. M. Straus
498119.abstract: Storm-track activity in the North Pacific (NP) declines during midwinter despite a strong upper-tropospheric jet, a phenomenon known as NP midwinter suppression. Chang (2001) found diabatic heating generates eddy available potential energy during fall and spring, but dissipates it in midwinter, based on a calendar comparison in the Pacific. Zilibotti et al. (2026) offered a different perspective on the broader jet–storm track relationship. Rather than averaging by calendar month, they grouped atmospheric states into similar ranges of jet strength and averaged within each range. This approach revealed that EKE increases with jet speed up to a threshold and then decreases, a pattern also evident in the North Atlantic (NA) when differences in timescales are accounted for. Their analysis, however, was limited to EKE and did not examine diabatic processes, leaving open whether a diabatic signature like Chang’s appears when data are organized by jet strength, and whether it holds in the Atlantic. This study extends the binning approach to diabatic heating and eddy available potential energy generation (GAPE), using ERA5 reanalysis. The approach is first applied to EKE to confirm consistency with earlier findings, before examining diabatic processes. The analysis reproduces the nonlinear EKE relationship in both basins, with EKE increasing up to a threshold jet strength before declining. This threshold occurring at a higher jet strength but lower magnitude in the North Pacific. Vertical profiles of diabatic heating show a similar structure in both basins, with strong lower-tropospheric heating, a secondary midtropospheric maximum, and weak cooling aloft. In contrast to EKE, low-level heating keeps rising after EKE declines. GAPE depends on covariance between heating and temperature anomalies rather than heating magnitude, which motivates testing whether GAPE follows EKE or reflects a diabatic signature consistent with Chang’s (2001) seasonal reversal.

498124.title: Urban Heat Island: Investigating How Land Cover Influences Microclimatic Variations Across Residential, Green and Developed Campus Areas
498124.authors: Anahi Mendieta, Central New Mexico Community College, Albuquerque, NM; and P. J. Tennant, B. K. Clifton, and M. Will-Cole
498124.abstract: The Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect has been broadly investigated for years; this urban phenomenon is associated with the relative warming of cities in contrast to rural environments. Urban design and landscape can greatly contribute to the rapid heating of surrounding areas, impacting human health, thermal comfort, wildlife and even energy demand. But there is no single solution that will help mitigate its effects as climate varies among different regions. In the field of urban climatology many methods have been developed to better understand this phenomenon and evaluate factors that influence urban temperatures. To study the variability of different microclimates within Albuquerque, NM a 2-mile transect observing three distinct locations was developed; A residential area, an urban green space and a campus area. Air temperature, relative humidity, ground temperature among other readings were noted twice a week, three times a day, for a 12-week period. Our findings suggest that shade, building arrangement, surface materials and airflow collectively influence spatial temperature differences and thermal comfort. These findings suggest that thoughtful urban planning and landscape design may help mitigate the urban heat island effect. This research provides insight into planning strategies that will help create urban environments that work with the local climate. This work was supported by NSF Grant Award 2246468.

498126.title: Meteorological Drivers of High PM2.5 Events in New York City
498126.authors: Anna Pickle, Randolph School, Huntsville, AL; Department of Marine and Atmospheric Sciences, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY
498126.abstract: This study investigates the meteorological drivers of PM2.5 because of the need to better understand pollution episodes and improve future air-quality forecasting. Previous studies have found that meteorological conditions strongly influence PM2.5 concentrations, but this study examines which variables are most associated with elevated PM2.5 and the atmospheric patterns accompanying these events. Four monitoring sites representing urban, suburban, and coastal environments across the New York City–Long Island region were selected. Daily PM2.5 and meteorological data (2006–2025) were obtained from the EPA and Iowa Environmental Mesonet. The observations were merged by date for each station. Wind direction was converted into U (east-west) and V (north-south) components to better characterize wind directionality. Random Forest models were developed to identify the most important meteorological variables at each site using feature importance. The models showed that wind-related variables consistently ranked among the most influential predictors. NCEP GDAS reanalysis data obtained through OpenDAP provided 850-hPa winds and sea-level pressure. Composite maps examined the large-scale atmospheric patterns associated with high PM2.5 events at the four stations during winter. The composite analysis showed that similar large-scale circulation patterns were observed across all four monitoring sites. Specifically, high-PM2.5 winter events were associated with southwesterly flow at all stations. Wind roses showed distinct local patterns, suggesting site-specific transport influences. These findings suggest that regional atmospheric transport plays an important role in high-PM2.5 winter events across the New York City–Long Island region, while local geographic factors contribute to site-specific transport patterns. Future work will analyze pollution sources and develop a predictive PM2.5 machine-learning model.

498129.title: Pavement, Parking Lots, and Heat: Characterizing Commercial Land-Use Hotspots in a Semi-Arid Urban Heat Island
498129.authors: Nicholas Martinez, Central New Mexico Community College (CNM), Albuquerque, NM; and C. Eiting, K. Bakhtiar, E. Blauw, and M. Will-Cole
498129.abstract: Urban heat islands (UHIs) are a growing concern in rapidly developing cities, particularly in semi-arid regions where extensive impervious surfaces and limited vegetation create localized areas of elevated temperature. While satellite observations capture regional heat patterns, they may not fully represent fine-scale thermal variability experienced at the pedestrian level, particularly within commercial land-use zones where large parking lots and low vegetation cover consistently produce hotter microenvironments. This study characterizes localized urban heat hotspots within commercial zones in the Winrock/Uptown district of Albuquerque, New Mexico, and evaluates how these ground-level thermal patterns compare with satellite-derived land surface temperature. Ground-based data are collected along a 2.5-mile urban transect twice weekly over a 12-week period during morning, afternoon, and evening sampling periods, measuring near-surface air temperature, humidity, wind speed, particulate matter, and surface temperatures using a Kestrel weather meter, AirBeam-3 sensor, and infrared thermometer, with corrected air temperatures benchmarked against a rural HOBO reference station to quantify urban heat island intensity. Preliminary results indicate that commercial hotspots show the strongest urban heat island signal during evening hours, with minimal or reversed differences in early morning. These findings suggest commercial land-use zones retain and re-emit heat well after sunset, a pattern with direct implications for urban planning, heat mitigation strategies, and the use of satellite remote sensing for neighborhood-scale heat monitoring in semi-arid cities. Future analysis will incorporate additional environmental datasets, such as vegetation cover and precipitation, to further contextualize these findings. This work was supported by NSF Grant Award 2246468.

498130.title: Advancing Prediction of Hydrologic Extremes through Data Assimilation and Machine Learning
498130.abstract: Data assimilation plays a critical role in improving Earth system predictability by optimally integrating observations with models to reduce uncertainty and enhance forecasts. Advances in machine learning (ML), high-performance computing, and novel assimilation techniques are creating new opportunities to improve prediction across weather, seasonal-to-decadal (S2D), and hydroclimate timescales. These advances are particularly important for hydrologic extremes such as floods and droughts, which remain major challenges for water resource management in a changing climate. The integration of remotely sensed observations into land surface and hydrologic models through state-of-the-art data assimilation approaches, including ML-enhanced methods, offers new opportunities to improve the representation and prediction of hydrologic processes. Recent developments in hydrologic data assimilation systems, including progress toward hyper-resolution land surface and hydrologic applications, are strengthening predictive capabilities for water-related natural hazards and supporting more informed water resource management. An emerging direction is the integration of ML-enhanced data assimilation with Earth system models to improve predictions across broader spatial and temporal scales. Ongoing efforts are coupling ML-enhanced data assimilation with the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) to improve the representation and predictability of water and energy fluxes across the United States. This framework aims to leverage observations, machine learning, and process-based Earth system modeling to advance hydrologic prediction and ultimately improve the S2D predictive skill of E3SM.

498131.title: Urban Heat Island Effect on Water Stress in Urban Vegetation
498131.authors: Claire Eiting, Central New Mexico Community College (CNM), Albuquerque, NM; and N. Martinez, E. Blauw, K. Bakhtair, and M. Will-Cole
498131.abstract: Abstract: The Urban Heat Island effect (UHIE) is characterized by elevated air and surface temperatures in urban environments relative to surrounding rural areas. Because a larger share of the population lives in urban areas than in rural areas, studies have examined the best ways to address UHIE effects to keep people cool in the hot summer months. While many studies demonstrate the effectiveness of green spaces in mitigating UHIE effects, few consider water conservation and plant water stress. To investigate how the UHIE affects plant water stress in the arid city of Albuquerque, New Mexico, a study was conducted along a well-defined 2.5-mile mobile transect loop in a high-traffic commercial area known as the Winrock Mall. Twice a week, three times a day, sensors were used to collect pedestrian-level air and surface temperatures, relative humidity, particulate matter, and observational data along the transect. Preliminary results not only confirm that the Albuquerque Winrock Mall area is an Urban Heat Island within the city but also show that many plants along the transect are water-stressed or at risk of water stress despite regular irrigation. However, many factors affect a plant's water stress, including distance from urban materials, precipitation, and humidity, all of which must be considered when selecting vegetation for an urban area. We expect these findings to shed light on which plants are robust enough to survive the hot, arid climate and, in turn, the UHIE. This work was supported by NSF Grant Award 2246468. Keywords: Urban Heat Island Effect, Water Stress, Mobile Transect, Urban Vegetation, Arid Climate

498135.title: Observation-Driven AI Weather and Climate Capabilities for Coastal Prediction: NVIDIA Earth-2 Advances in Data Assimilation, Nowcasting, and Extreme-Event Sampling (Invited Presentation)
498135.abstract: AI weather and climate modelling is producing measurable progress across problems fundamental to coastal hazard prediction: extracting more information from heterogeneous observations, improving simulations of convective precipitation dynamics, and sampling the rare-event tail relevant to resilience planning. In this talk, I will give a selective overview of recent NVIDIA Research and Earth-2 work in these areas, from my vantage point as a research director. I will begin with AI Data Assimilation and the long-standing question of whether forecasting systems make sufficiently complete use of the observations already available. HealDA maps a short window of satellite and conventional observations directly to a global atmospheric analysis and can initialize off-the-shelf AI forecast models without jointly training the assimilation and forecast systems. I will review the rapid performance evolution over 2026 driven by refined, GPU-parallelizable architectures that are setting the stage for genuinely end-to-end AI forecasting systems in which observation use, state estimation, and forecast skill can be evaluated and improved together at low latency and energy use. I will then discuss StormScope, a direct-observation AI nowcasting model based on diffusion transformers with neighborhood attention. StormScope produces some of the most realistic precipitation-radar simulations ever seen, with quantitative that significantly outperform the NOAA Warn-on-Forecast System on object-based probabilistic scores over 0–3-hour lead times. Because coastal flood risk often reflects compound interactions among coastal water levels, intense rainfall, and river discharge, this improvement in fundamental convective precipitation prediction is directly relevant to coastal hazards. More broadly, the results illustrate the potential of direct-observation simulation to sidestep persistent difficulties associated with convective-scale atmospheric initialization and microphysical parameterization. Finally, I will discuss recent developments for climate-risk analysis from the advent of guided generative AI samplers. Tropical cyclones and other high-impact events are intrinsically difficult to sample with conventional simulation technology, particularly when the question concerns an event affecting a specific location. Guided and final-state-conditioned diffusion sampling permits a different class of experiment: placing an extreme event at the end of a trajectory and “rewinding” an ensemble to examine the range of dynamically consistent antecedent states, tracks, landfalls, and intermediate hazard exposures. Recent Earth-2 research further shows how guided and unguided model densities can be combined through importance weighting, so that targeted AI hazard sampling retains probabilistic interpretation. This opens new avenues for event attribution, counterfactual analysis, and coastal resilience planning without requiring brute-force discovery of rare trajectories in enormous conventional ensembles.

498136.title: Designing for the Storm Before It Arrives: Babcock Ranch as a National Model for Building Communities That Can Take a Hit (Invited Presentation)
498136.authors: Amy Wicks, Wicks Consulting Group, Inc., Babcock Ranch, FL
498136.abstract: Severe weather — more intense hurricanes, more frequent extreme rainfall, and flooding events that outpace what legacy infrastructure was built for — is no longer an edge case communities plan around. It's a baseline they have to design for. Babcock Ranch, Florida — the nation's first solar-powered town — offers a rare, real-world case study in what happens when a community is engineered from the ground up with that reality in mind, rather than retrofitted after the fact. Built on 20 years of hydrologic modeling, master-planned stormwater systems, and a resilience-driven design code (the BRCISD Design Specifications Manual), Babcock Ranch has weathered major hurricanes with minimal damage and no loss of power — drawing national attention (WSJ, CNN, PBS) as proof that better design, not just stronger materials, is what determines how a community survives a storm. This talk breaks down the core engineering decisions behind that outcome — stormwater capacity, site grading and elevation strategy, and code-level requirements that build resilience in before the first house is ever framed — and then looks at what's actually transferable to the much harder problem most U.S. communities face: adapting infrastructure and codes that already exist, in places that are already built out. As severe weather events continue to increase in frequency and intensity, the presentation offers practical, design-level takeaways for engineers, planners, and policymakers working to make communities more resilient, wherever they are.

498137.title: Predicting Flash Flooding Impacts through Machine Learning
498137.authors: Jack Samuel Gulisano, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, MI
498137.abstract: Flash flooding affects Americans every year and is a danger to life and property. Therefore, it is important to forecast where flash flood impacts are expected to assist in mitigation efforts and impact based decision services. This project develops a machine learning model framework that predicts where flash flooding impacts are expected to occur based on archived local storm reports (LSRs), topographic data, land cover data, and precipitation data. Archived LSRs were collected in the Edisto-Santee watershed and from 2014 to 2025 and are classified into impact severity classes based on their associated impact description remarks using a local large language model. From there, impact severity classifications from archived LSRs were used as training labels in the machine learning model. 30m resolution slope, topographic wetness index, height above nearest drainage, impervious area, tree canopy coverage, and meteorological data were collected as features for the machine learning model to predict flash flood impacts. The preliminary machine learning model framework has accuracy over 90% with a relatively simple flood impact prediction model across the Edisto-Santee watershed. The model performed with a combined F1 score of 90% on held out flash flood impacts, successfully predicting areas where impacts would be observed. This framework also proved to have skill in other watersheds outside the Edisto-Santee. Based on the observed moderately high skill, there is a path forward toward CONUS level operationalized impact prediction based on historic events to assist with impact based flash flood forecasting.

498142.title: Analysis of Particulate Matter in a Residential Area in Central Texas Using a PurpleAir (PA-II) Sensor
498142.authors: Shelby Grace Pampell, Memorial Early College High School, New Braunfels, TX; Memorial Early College High School, New Braunfels, TX; and M. F. Martinez and K. Ardon-Dryer
498142.abstract: This study was conducted through the Air Across Texas (AAT) program to calculate Particulate Matter (PM) concentrations across the state of Texas, with a focus on Gruene, TX. PM was measured by identifying concentrations of airborne particles and categorized by size, with this study focusing on PM1 and PM2.5 (defined as particulate matter smaller than £1 and £2.5 µm, respectively). PM1 the finest particle, considered the most dangerous because it can penetrate deep into the lungs and potentially cross into the bloodstream. PM2.5 known as fine particle, can cause extreme lung irritation. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and World Health Organization (WHO) set thresholds that monitor the PM2.5 concentration in order to identify times with potentially high concentrations that could be dangerous for people (especially those in high-risk groups). The EPA daily threshold is 35 µg m-3, which is based on data measured from the US. The WHO daily threshold is 15 µg m-3 and is based on data measured from around the world. A PurpleAir (PA-II) sensor was placed at a suburban home in Gruene, Texas for a period of four months (December 2025 to April 2026). The measurements determined average (hourly and daily) concentrations of PM1 and PM2.5 along with potential causes of spikes in PM during this period. During this study period, there were several events with high PM observed, three of those were examined to identify the source. One spike was due to an agricultural fire in Northern Mexico, one due to New Years fireworks, and one due to a temperature inversion with stagnant air and high humidity.

498143.title: Effects of Vegetation Density on Carbon Dioxide Concentrations and Temperature Along the Eubank Residential Area in Albuquerque, New Mexico Effects of Vegetation Density on Carbon Dioxide Concentrations and Temperature Along the Eubank Residential Area in Albuquerque, New Mexico
498143.authors: Amber Awelagte, Central New Mexico Community College, Albuquerque, NM
498143.abstract: Urban vegetation plays an important role in regulating carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentrations and reducing temperatures through shade and evapotranspiration. However, differences in vegetation density across urban environments may influence the intensity of the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect. This study investigates how vegetation density affects air temperature, surface temperature, and CO₂ concentrations along the Eubank residential corridor in Albuquerque, New Mexico. Environmental data were collected over approximately two months during morning, afternoon, and evening sampling periods using a Temtop M2000 CO₂ monitor, Kestrel 3000 weather meter, AirBeam 3 air quality monitor, Thermal Works infrared sensor, and a TI250 thermal imaging camera. Sampling sites were classified according to vegetation cover and surrounding land surface characteristics. Preliminary results indicate that locations with greater vegetation generally exhibited lower corrected air temperatures and lower surface temperatures than areas dominated by pavement and sparse vegetation. Average CO₂ concentrations also varied among sampling periods, suggesting that vegetation and local environmental conditions influence atmospheric CO₂ levels. These findings support previous research demonstrating that urban vegetation can help reduce Urban Heat Island effects by cooling surrounding environments and improving local air quality. This research contributes to a better understanding of how vegetation influences urban microclimates and may help guide future urban planning strategies that increase green space and reduce heat exposure in Albuquerque. This work was supported by NSF Grant Award 2246468.

498144.title: Diabatic Processes and Ice Microphysics in Tropical Cyclone Intensification: Investigating Hurricane Ida Using gSAM
498144.authors: Ashlynne Gary, University of Arizona, Solvang, CA; University of Arizona, Solvang, CA; and S. C. Sullivan, S. N. Wu, P. Blossey, M. Khairoutdinov, B. Gasparini, and A. M. Stansfield
498144.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) are the costliest natural disasters that affect the U.S. In 2021, Hurricane Ida evolved from a tropical depression to a Category 4 hurricane over the course of 3 days, causing between $31 and $44 billion in damage in the Gulf Coast region and Northeast. Investigating cases of rapid intensification is crucial for accurately forecasting risk for those in the path of developing storms. Although previous work has found strong correlations of TC intensification with larger ice water contents, the microphysical origin and radiative heating of this ice have not yet been clarified or quantified. To investigate the link between rapid cyclogenesis and the origin of upper-level TC ice, we complete multiple simulations of Hurricane Ida using the Global System for Atmospheric Modeling (gSAM) at 1-km resolution. We evaluate the simulation output with multiple observational data sources, including precipitation statistics from the NASA GPM Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals (IMERG), cyclone track and intensity metrics from the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS), and in-situ dropsondes from NOAA P-3 aircraft. We discuss implementation of microphysical tracers within the model to distinguish locally-formed and remotely-advected ice condensate; these tracers identify variations in cloud ice structure as intensification ensues. In line with recent studies of TC microphysics, we expect an important contribution of locally formed ice in the cirrus shield around the TC center. With three different schemes (one-moment, two-moment, and particle properties-based), we additionally test the microphysical sensitivity of the simulated TC track, intensity, rate of development, and cloud ice. Preliminary results indicate robust performance of gSAM in reproducing Hurricane Ida, although the intensification is slightly dampened and the simulated track is persistently eastward relative to observations with a ~120-km bias in landfall location. Uncovering the role of ice in strengthening tropical systems will allow for better scientific understanding of small-scale processes within storms and help forecasters identify environments conducive to rapid intensification.

498155.title: Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations and the Atmosphere: What We Know and What We Need to Learn (Invited Presentation) (Core Science Keynote)
498155.authors: Emily V. Fischer, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO
498155.abstract: Concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) are major sources of ammonia, nitrous oxide, and methane in the United States. These facilities also release nitrogen oxides, a large suite of volatile organic compounds, hydrogen sulfide, and particulate matter. Thus U.S CAFO emissions impact air quality, ecosystems, climate, and the ozone layer. However, the scale of their impacts are blurred due to uncertainties in the magnitude, variability, and fate of their emissions. There are specific U.S. regions where there are major regional impacts on air quality and deposition due to large numbers of CAFOs. Residing near CAFOs has been linked to poor health outcomes, and in some states CAFOs are more likely to be located in lower-income communities and/or communities of color. Despite these impacts, many of the state and federal laws that control air pollution emissions from other sources do not govern agricultural activities. There is also a general lack of transparency, leaving scientists without easily accessible information on CAFO locations, number of animals at a given facility, animal waste production, and waste storage or disposal practices. I will present a summary of what is known about emissions of air pollutants and greenhouse gases from U.S. CAFOs. We will identify important knowledge gaps, the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches for quantifying emissions from these facilities, and how the field of atmospheric chemistry can apply our tools to work on this problem. We will also discuss recent advances in observing capabilities that allow us to approach this problem in new ways. We will finish with an introduction to FarmFlux, an ongoing NASA airborne mission to study the cycling of nitrogen between agricultural systems and the atmosphere.

498156.title: A Unified SHOC+MF Boundary Layer Parameterization In the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System (Invited Presentation)
498156.authors: Nathan Arnold, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD; and K. Suselj and J. P. Teixeira
498156.abstract: We present a novel implementation of the Simplified Higher Order Closure (SHOC) coupled with a multi-plume eddy diffusivity mass flux (EDMF) scheme in the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) model. The SHOC scheme provides eddy diffusivities and uses a set of higher order moments (HOMs) to constrain an analytic double gaussian PDF, from which the subgrid buoyancy flux and cloud properties are diagnosed. This SHOC+MF implementation extends previous work by including mass flux contributions to all HOMs, which remedies an underestimation of subgrid scale variances, and allows the combined convective and stratiform cloud properties to be diagnosed from the assumed PDF in a unified way. The scheme is evaluated in single column experiments against large eddy simulations in a variety of regimes, and global experiments are compared with satellite datasets and reanalyses. Improvements are seen in simulated clouds and surface stress, relative to the baseline boundary layer parameterization in GEOS. Preliminary results from a machine learning prediction of the SHOC length scale will also be shown.

498159.title: The Spatial and Temporal Significance of Dust Events in Arizona
498159.authors: Siya Patel, Texas Tech University, Odessa, TX; and K. Ardon-Dryer
498159.abstract: Dust events have a high probability of occurrence in areas that receive little rain, have sparse vegetation, and have loose sedimentary particles. Thus, when prominent winds sweep into Arizona, dust events carry these loose sediments into the air and impact the environment as well as human health. The goal of this research project is to understand when and where dust events occur across the U.S., in this case specifically in Arizona. In order to conduct this research, Automatic Surface Observation Systems (ASOS) were used to investigate dust events between 2000 and 2022. These events were identified when parameters such as low visibility (<10km), high wind speeds (≥ 6m/s), and weather codes reporting dust conditions were met. Arizona contains a total of 47 ASOS stations, but only 29 of the stations were able to be used for this study as they had measurements for at least 20 years. These 29 stations produce more than 17 million meteorological observations; 17,611 of these observations met the conditions of dust events and were combined into 5867 events. Out of these 5,867 events only 3,710 were flagged as potential dust events. We then examined each of these events to confirm whether this potential dust event was a real dust event. The criteria and confirmation consisted of a thorough investigation of Particulate Matter (PM) concentrations, with a focus on PM10 and PM2.5, observations of dust in satellite data (e.g., NASA Worldview, MODIS Today, and Aerosol Watch), or identification of the dust event in the NOAA Dust Storm database, or in previous published studies. We also used nearby ASOS stations, in case the other methods failed to detect the events. Preliminary findings show that most of the dust events in AZ (40%) occur during July and August, mainly during 17:00-18:00. This dust database will allow us to better understand the significance and changes as time progresses of these dust events, as well as their spatial and temporal relevance to better understand what events and conditions have triggered these dust events.

498161.title: Update on Development of the GeoXO Imager
498161.authors: Daniel Gall, L3Harris, Fort Wayne, IN; and M. Filmer, Q. Yao, R. Forkert, L. Roop, H. Thomsen, J. Reinhard, J. P. Van Naarden, and C. Reith
498161.abstract: The Geostationary and Extended Observations (GeoXO) Imager (GXI) instrument expands on the capability of the GOES-R ABI Imager by providing additional spectral coverage and increased spatial resolution. Once on-orbit, GXI’s capabilities will provide new insight into low level water vapor and enhance users’ ability to identify severe weather and wildfires. GXI completed its System Critical Design Review in November 2025 and flight hardware builds are underway. An update on GXI design details is provided, with a discussion of improvements over the legacy ABI Imager, and an up-to-date status on development activities. A review of additional capabilities is provided summarizing the benefits of 2 new spectral bands, 3x raw image data, and 4x resolution on seven spectral bands.

498162.title: Analyzing Southeast U.S. Convective Environments with Doppler Wind Lidar Observations
498162.authors: Sabrina Roche, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY
498162.abstract: In 2022 and 2023, the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) participated in the Propagation, Evolution, and Rotation in Linear Storms (PERiLS) field campaign. PERiLS was designed to characterize the near-storm environments associated with tornado-producing quasi-linear convective systems (QLCS). One of the NSSL’s instruments operated during this project was a mobile scanning doppler wind lidar (DWL). The research goal of the DWL was to observe the evolution of storm inflow properties to gain a better understanding of the storm environment surrounding an evolving QLCS. An optimal estimation technique (windOE) was designed to incorporate colocated rawinsonde and surface observations into the wind retrievals that provide data between the surface and 75 m. The result is continuous surface to 6 km wind profiles with associated uncertainty information. Retrieval configuration resulted in wind profiles every 5 minutes, providing high resolution observations not captured using other methods (e.g., balloons). The tornadic environment featured a more significant hodograph evolution as the storm approached. This included increases in SRH, particularly in the 0-1 km and 0-3 km layers. Synoptic-scale features also (e.g., nocturnal low-level jet) appeared to heavily influence the evolution of the storm environments. These findings can provide operational insight into differences between tornadic and non-tornadic storm environments in the Southeast U.S..

498166.title: Turbulent Heights: Exploration and Validation of a New Turbulence Based Technique for Retrieving the PBLH From the Aerosol Wind Profiler During the WHyMSIE and SARP Campaigns
498166.authors: Daniel Johnson, Indiana University Indianapolis, Indianapolis, IN
498166.abstract: The planetary boundary layer height (PBLH) is a key control on various atmospheric processes impacting near-surface air quality and weather phenomena. An accurate characterization of the PBLH is essential for improving pollution forecasts and boundary layer parameterizations in numerical weather and climate models. However, procedures for determining PBL properties from air motion alone are not well studied. During the NOAA Joint Venture 3-D Wind Program and NASA Westcoast and Heartland Hyperspectral Microwave Sensor Intensive Experiment (WH2yMSIE) in October 2023 and September 2024 and the June 2026 NASA Student Airborne Research Program (SARP), NASA’s Aerosol Wind Profiler (AWP) collected approximately 120 flight hours of 3D wind velocities and aerosol/cloud backscatter across the US. This study presents a method to estimate PBLHs from AWP curtains by using an edge detection algorithm on Turbulence Kinetic Energy (TKE), a measure of variability in wind direction and speed, computed from the AWP’s 3D wind curtains. The resultant PBLHs are compared to mixing layer heights obtained from aerosol observations by coincident High Altitude Lidar Observatory (HALO) and co-located High Spectral Resolution Lidar 2 (HSRL-2) measurements. When validated against the mixing layer heights, the algorithm exhibits surface-dependent skill in PBLH identification, with estimates over land showing substantially better agreement than those over water. This algorithm provides a first step to detecting the PBLH in the spatial domain via wind-based metrics and opens the door for improved characterizations of the PBL using turbulent properties.

498168.title: Automated Compilation for Analysis of Dust Events in Illinois (2000–2022) Using ASOS/AWOS Observations
498168.authors: Anirudh Mohan, Elkins High School, Sugar Land, TX; and K. Ardon-Dryer
498168.abstract: Dust events are natural phenomena that occur in arid or semi-arid environments. Dust events carry aerosol particles, and exposure to these dust particles has adverse effects on human health. This research project is part of a larger project that aims to identify dust events that occurred across the U.S. from 2000 to 2022. For this portion of the research project, dust events were identified across Illinois using meteorological data collected by Automatic Surface Observation Systems (ASOS) and Automated Weather Observing Systems (AWOS) when parameters such as wind-speed (≥ 6 m/s), visibility (< 10km), and weather codes representing dust (e.g., BLDU, DU, DS, HZ) were met. A total of 61 ASOS/AWOS stations were available in IL, but only 51 stations were active for at least 20 years during the study period (2000-2022) and were used for this project. Across these 51 stations—which recorded approximately 35 million meteorological observations—64,722 observations (comprising 15,951 distinct events) were flagged with conditions suitable for a dust event (wind-speed ≥ 6 m/s, visibility < 10km, with or without a weather code). These 15,951 events were then examined using a Python-based classification code, leading to a total of 971 events that could be potential-dust events. Candidate potential-dust events were manually reviewed and confirmed. Events meeting all criteria were compiled into a summary table reporting event timing and duration, and meteorological conditions including minimum and maximum wind-speed, wind gust, and visibility. Preliminary findings show that dust events occurred in each year from 2000 to 2022; most of the dust events occurred during the spring, mainly in April and May, and there is another peak in October, with 13:00-14:00 being the peak time of these dust events.

498169.title: From Forecast to Action: Core Partner Decision Support During the Historic Post-Tropical Flooding of Arthur
498169.authors: Stephen Carboni, NWSFO, Lake Charles, LA
498169.abstract: On June 17, 2026, Tropical Storm Arthur developed as the first named system of the Atlantic hurricane season, presenting a unique operational forecasting challenge in the western Gulf of America. Despite having limited time offshore to organize and strengthen, Arthur's interaction with a stalled continental synoptic pattern resulted in catastrophic impacts across portions of Louisiana. This presentation examines the complex meteorological setup, operational data signals, and the National Weather Service (NWS) mission-driven response during this high-impact event. The synoptic environment was characterized by a stationary frontal boundary that stalled over Louisiana and neighboring Gulf Coast states. As Arthur tracked inland, it weakened and expanded, effectively anchoring a deep tropical moisture plume against the frontal zone. Prior to the event, observational and model data revealed extreme atmospheric moisture availability, featuring anomalously high precipitable water (PWAT) values and strong mesoscale low-level jets that maximized moisture transport directly from the Gulf. This specific combination of localized tropical development and continental frontal forcing triggered prolonged, training rainfall and subsequent devastating flooding across Avoyelles Parish. To mitigate the evolving threat, NWS meteorologists from the weather forecast office in Lake Charles, Louisiana carried out targeted decision support services (DSS) for core emergency management partners and the public. Impact-based messaging was initiated days before landfall, focusing on high-volume rainfall potential, and intensive real-time updates were maintained throughout the flooding crisis. This presentation reviews the critical data indicators, the communication strategies deployed to protect life and property, and the subsequent local recovery efforts within the framework of NWS operational mission.

498171.title: Small Scale Experimental Study of Interactions Between Stormwater Runoff and Pervious and Coated Concrete
498171.authors: Yifan Zhang, Central New Mexico Community College, Albuquerque, NM; and Y. Nkontchu, M. Groves, and M. Will-Cole
498171.abstract: The increase in temperature in urban areas compared to rural areas has been documented as the Urban Heat Island effect. This effect is partly attributed to large surface areas of impervious materials such as concrete or asphalt, resulting in high surface temperatures. Current research shows that these areas store heat into the night and is a major contributor to the thermal pollution of nearby water bodies. Compared to rural areas, urban areas often have higher volumes of stormwater runoff, and higher runoff temperatures. This can be attributed to higher average surface temperatures, and runoff being unable to seep into impervious areas. In response, pervious concrete has been proposed as an alternative to regular, impervious concrete in city planning. Research suggests that pervious concrete, compared to impervious concrete, can have lower surface temperatures and provides better draining. However, there is a lack of research that examines the interactions between pervious concrete and stormwater runoff. This study aims to investigate the differences between impervious concrete, pervious concrete, and other techniques of concrete cooling. This includes specialized cooling coatings, and persistent shade. In this study, modules of impervious concrete, pervious concrete, coated impervious concrete, and coated pervious concrete were created. These modules were left in the sun, and surface temperatures were collected over the course of the day. Interactions with rainfall were simulated by covering the surface of the module with water and recording the water temperature over time. In addition, a mobile transect in a small area around the University of New Mexico was conducted. We recorded the surface temperatures of common surfaces such as concrete, asphalt, gravel, and grass to provide insight into the differences between pervious and impervious materials. These transects occurred 3 times a day during the summer of 2026. Preliminary results showed that impervious concrete showed higher surface temperatures and higher runoff temperatures compared to other modules. The runoff also had the most difficulty infiltrating the impervious concrete. In addition, within the mobile transect, impervious materials such as concrete and asphalt averaged the highest surface temperatures. Additionally, consistent shading lowered surface temperatures for all materials. We expect this research to provide insight into different methods of lowering urban runoff volume and temperature and mitigating the Urban Heat Island Effect. This work was supported by NSF Grant Award 2246468.

498173.title: 'Surviving the Desert Sun'
498173.authors: Philip James Tennant, CNM, Albuquerque, NM; and B. K. Clifton, A. Mendieta, and M. Will-Cole
498173.abstract: Many studies examining temperature effects on animal behavior focus on single species or small populations, limiting broader ecological interpretation. In contrast, this study adopts a wider lens to investigate how Urban Heat Islands (UHIs) and temperature variability influence animal behavior across multiple taxa within the Albuquerque region. We integrate field‑collected temperature measurements with wildlife and incident records from Albuquerque Animal Control, ABQ Biopark, the New Mexico Department of Game and Fish (NMDGF), and the U.S. Department of the Interior (USDOI) to evaluate how UHI‑driven temperature increases relate to changes in movement, habitat use, activity patterns, and behavioral responses. By combining environmental data with diverse wildlife datasets, this study provides a more comprehensive assessment of how animals respond to localized heat stress across an urban landscape. This approach allows us to identify both direct and indirect behavioral shifts associated with elevated temperatures, including altered daily activity cycles, increased nocturnal movement, changes in habitat selection, and potential increases in human–wildlife interactions. Together, these findings contribute to a broader understanding of ecological impacts of UHIs and underscore the importance of continued monitoring of temperature‑linked behavioral changes across species. This work was supported by NSF Grant Award 2246468.

498174.title: 'Precipitation Analysis Using EXPRESS Weather Station Observations and Weather Radar Data Comparison'
498174.authors: Alfonso Velásquez, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY; University of Louisville, Louisville , KY
498174.abstract: Mobile weather stations can provide detailed measurements at locations where observations are sparse, making them valuable for field studies and research of extreme weather phenomena. With few exceptions, mobile weather stations are typically focused on collecting measurements of atmospheric state variables and wind and relating those measurements to storm structures and theory. While these observations are valuable, measured characteristics of precipitation in extreme rainfall events are often excluded or unavailable. This study seeks to explore the evolution of convective precipitation during a flash flood event using observations collected by a mobile weather station specifically designed to measure heavy precipitation. The EXtreme PREcipitation Surface Station (EXPRESS) provides high-resolution measurements of precipitation intensity, total accumulated precipitation, air pressure, air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and direction. The six ExPreSS stations can additionally measure the drop size distribution (DSDs) and fall speed of precipitation via a ParSiVel laser disdrometer. With the exception of wind speed, all variables (including DSDs) are reported in 1-minute intervals. Wind speed and direction are reported in 1-second intervals. While the ExPreSS network was used in five different events across Kentucky and Indiana during the Spring and Summer of 2026, this research specifically evaluates data from an ExPreSS station deployed in Vincennes, Indiana, during an April 2026 flash flood event. Based on data from the nearby Evansville, Indiana (KVWX) radar, this event consisted of multiple rounds of intense cellular convection, followed by a squall line. The entire event produced 2-3 inches of rain across the area in under 8 hours, prompting numerous flash flood warnings. The ExPreSS surface measurements will be compared with both single and dual-Polarimetric weather radar data from the Evansville, Indiana (KVWX) radar to explore variations in the timing, intensity, and spatial evolution of precipitation associated with the different convective structures. Radar-derived accumulated precipitation estimates will also be compared with standard rain gauge estimates as well as disdrometer-based accumulated precipitation measurements. While radar provides broad spatial coverage of precipitation, the in situ measurements captured localized variations that are not always apparent in remotely sensed observations alone. Integrating these datasets provides a more complete understanding of precipitation characteristics and storm evolution in different convective structures. The results will highlight the complementary nature of surface and radar observations and emphasize the importance of field deployments for validating radar-based analyses. Future work will extend this methodology to additional ExPReSS deployments across Kentucky and Indiana to investigate precipitation variability under different storm environments and assess the consistency of radar-derived precipitation estimates across multiple events.

498176.title: Assessing Microscale Physiological Heat Stress in Urban Pedestrian Environments
498176.authors: Y Wilkinson Nkontchu, Central New Mexico Community College, Albuquerque, NM; and Y. Zhang, M. Groves, and M. Will-Cole
498176.abstract: As urbanization accelerates worldwide, the Urban Heat Island Effect (UHIE) has emerged as a major environmental and public health challenge, elevating ambient temperatures and physiological heat stress in urban environments. Although numerous studies have investigated urban heat islands, thermal comfort, and human heat exposure, most have focused on broader spatial scales, providing limited insight into microscale physiological heat stress. By conducting field-based measurements across diverse urban microenvironments in Albuquerque, New Mexico, this study investigates localized variations in physiological heat stress and their relationships with environmental conditions. Results reveal substantial microscale variability in heat exposure, with afternoon periods, sun-exposed surfaces, and areas with limited shade generally experiencing greater thermal stress. Surface temperature was strongly associated with WBGT, while shaded locations experienced considerably lower surface temperatures, highlighting the importance of localized environmental conditions in determining pedestrian heat exposure. These findings provide a scientific basis for identifying localized heat-risk environments and informing targeted heat mitigation strategies, urban planning, and future predictive heat-stress modeling. This work was supported by NSF Grant Award 2246468.

498178.title: A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) Model For Identifying Potential Tropical Cyclone (TC) Formation Regions In The Bay of Bengal (BoB)
498178.authors: Dakshika Sewwandi Jayaweera, University of Peradeniya, Kandy, Central, Sri lanka; and S. E. Zick and M. Rambukkange
498178.abstract: Tropical Cyclones (TCs) are destructive, recurring natural hazards that impact Sri Lanka and the broader North Indian Ocean region. Identification of their genesis environments remains a challenge because TC formation depends on complex interactions between atmospheric thermodynamic and dynamic conditions. This study develops a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based framework to identify potential TC-favourable regions in the Bay of Bengal. The CNN integrates large-scale atmospheric fields with a deep learning-based pattern recognition model and satellite-derived cloud information to identify and predict locations conducive to TC genesis. Five atmospheric variables representing key thermodynamic and dynamic conditions associated with TC development were used as input to the CNN: Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE), Convective Inhibition (CIN), Sea Surface Temperature (SST), vertical wind shear between 250 hPa and 850 hPa, and relative vorticity at 850 hPa. These variables were extracted from the hourly ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis dataset spanning the period 1990-2024. Observed TC coordinates, formation times, and genesis timestamps (defined here as 24 hours prior to the system reaching Tropical Cyclone intensityi.e., wind speed exceeding the 34-knot threshold) were obtained from India Meteorological Department (IMD) best-track data and cross-verified with IBTrACS. Cyclone and non-cyclone (randomly generated date, time, and locations) samples were extracted using a square boundary region centred on the observed cyclone position, while excluding a 25 km inner-core buffer zone. A sliding window of size pixels was subsequently applied to generate localised spatial samples, with each sample structuring the five atmospheric variables as input channels. The model was trained using historical pre- and post-monsoon data. Z-score normalisation was implemented to standardise the input variables before training. The CNN learns the spatial relationships among the atmospheric predictors to map the cyclone-favourable and non-cyclone conditions. To evaluate the impact of non-cyclone sample selection on model accuracy and the false alarm rate, two independent non-cyclone datasets (composed of randomly generated dates, times, and locations) were integrated during the model development phase. The trained model showed a classification accuracy of 60.6%, correctly identifying 109 out of 180 selected cyclone instances. Independent validation was conducted using three TC events (Cyclone Montha, Cyclone Senyar and Cyclone Ditwah) from the year 2025 that were withheld from the training phase. Spatial probability maps generated by the CNN for these three cyclone events were validated against the actual cyclone eye locations reported by the IMD to assess the spatial location accuracy. The minimum distances between the predicted high-probability regions and observed storm centres were 122.52 km for Montha, 38.92 km for Senyar, and 72.60 km for Ditwah. The CNN consistently identified high-probability zones surrounding the observed centres by IMD across the selected dates for the validation. To supplement the deep learning predictions with real-time observational data, Cloud Optical Depth (COD) product from the JAXA Himawari-9 geostationary satellite was integrated as an evaluation layer. The high temporal resolution of the Himawari-9 data provided independent verification of the convective cloud structures inherent to developing TC systems. By superimposing probability maps generated by CNN onto COD patterns, the alignment between areas predicted as highly favourable and actual cloud structures was analysed. This spatial cross-comparison helped in identifying false alarms by flagging areas where high model-predicted probabilities mismatched with the COD values that were too low to support active convective cloud development. Overall, the results demonstrate that the CNN framework effectively captures spatial relationships among multiple thermodynamic and dynamic fields to delineate regions favourable for TC genesis. Independent testing confirmed the strong spatial correspondence with observed cyclone tracks, while the addition of Himawari-derived COD provided an additional observational constraint for interpreting model output and filtering false positives. The CNN framework highlights the potential of combining deep learning architectures with environmental fields and satellite observations to advance TC genesis monitoring and early warning capabilities over Bay of Bengal. Keywords: Convolutional Neural Network, Tropical Cyclone, Cloud Optical Depth, Cyclone prediction.

498182.title: Evaluation the Satellite-Based Ozone Sensitivity Indicators of Ozone Exceedance Episodes Using Multi-Source In-Situ Measurements and CMAQ over the Northeast US
498182.authors: Siyi Wang, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, New Brunswick, NJ; and X. Jin
498182.abstract: Ground-level Ozone (O3) exceedances persist across nonattainment areas of the Northeast US, where effective emission controls depend on correctly diagnosing whether peak O3 is NOx-limited or VOC-limited. Satellite formaldehyde-to-nitrogen-dioxide ratios (FNR = HCHO/NO₂) provide spatially and temporally continuous indicators of ozone sensitivity, but the regime transition thresholds used to diagnose ozone sensitivity are model- and satellite-dependent, and their reliability on high-O3 exceedance days has not been evaluated at the process level. We establish these thresholds and map the spatiotemporal evolution of FNR-based ozone sensitivity and subsequently use ground-based observations to quantify the uncertainties arising from both the model-based thresholds and the satellite NO₂ and HCHO densities and their propagated errors in the computed FNR values, across contiguous United States (CONUS). Next, we compare the CMAQ high-order decoupled direct method (HDDM-3D)-derived sensitivity regimes with the satellite-FNR classifications to characterize where the observational indicator holds and where it diverges. We also use the model to interpret how meteorology and emissions jointly shape the sensitivity regime and its transitions during ozone exceedance.

498183.title: Evening Urban Heat Retention and Potential Mental Health Stress in Albuquerque, New Mexico
498183.authors: Brandon Kelly Clifton, CNM, Albuqueruqe, NM; and A. Mendieta and P. J. Tennant
498183.abstract: Extreme heat can intensify physiological strain, disrupt sleep and recovery, and contribute to psychological stress, particularly when urban surfaces retain heat into the evening. Neighborhood-scale heat exposure in Albuquerque, New Mexico, remains insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated the timing and magnitude of urban heat exposure and identified periods that may be most relevant to heat-related mental-health stress. From May 27 through July 29, 2026, mobile transects (tracking temperature and other environmental parameters) were conducted along a repeated Albuquerque route during morning (0800-0900), afternoon (1400-1500), and evening (1900-2000) sampling periods. Air temperatures were captured with an Airbeam-3 sensor/logger. The Airbeam temperature data was corrected using co-located “ground truth” temperature measurements via a Kestrel-5000 hand held environmental sensor. The rural temperature data, required for determining the Urban Heat Island Intensity (UHII/ΔT) was obtained via a fixed HOBO weather station located in Tijeras, New Mexico. Fifty-one transect sessions were analyzed, including 46 sessions paired with rural measurements. Mean absolute urban-rural temperature differences (ΔT) were 5.9 °F in the morning, 4.6 °F in the afternoon, and 10.8 °F in the evening. All 12 paired evening transects were warmer than the rural reference, with a mean urban excess of 10.8 °F. This result confirms that the 2-mile transect area exhibited a localized Urban Heat Island Effect, demonstrating measurable warming at the neighborhood scale. The transect (Airbeam corrected temperatures) and rural (HOBO) air temperatures showed a moderate positive relationship (R-squared = 0.45). The consistent evening excess indicates that Albuquerque's urban environment can remain substantially warmer after daytime heating declines. Persistent evening heat may reduce opportunities for thermal relief, interfere with sleep and recovery, and increase cumulative psychological strain among residents with limited access to cooling. Although mental-health outcomes were not measured, established research shows that extreme heat is correlated with worsened mood, elevated stress, sleep disruption, and increased psychiatric emergencies. By documenting a clear evening heat-exposure pathway, when temperatures remained highest and cooling was most limited, our results highlight a period strongly associated in the literature with heightened psychological strain. Thus, while the study does not demonstrate a causal mental-health effect, it identifies a scientifically supported window of vulnerability that should guide future real-time assessments of stress, mood, fatigue, and sleep, and inform targeted cooling and mental-health outreach during extreme heat. This work was supported by NSF Grant Award 2246468.

498186.title: Lightning Activity and Precipitation Evolution During the Extreme Flooding Event of May 2024 in Southern Brazil
498186.authors: Leonardo Calvetti, Universidade Federal de Pelotas, Pelotas, RS, Brazil; Universidade Federal de Pelotas, Pelotas, RS, Brazil; and C. Felix Tavares and W. Loch
498186.abstract: This study investigates the temporal evolution of lightning activity in Rio Grande do Sul during the historical floods of April–May 2024 and its correlation with precipitation. Observational data from 17 automatic weather stations operated by the National Institute of Meteorology (INMET) and lightning observations from the Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) aboard the GOES-16 satellite were analyzed from April 15 to May 31, 2024. Hourly and daily time series of rainfall and lightning were stratified into precipitation categories and correlated using Pearson (r) and Spearman (rho) coefficients across time lags of up to three hours.
