The results indicate that hours with precipitation exceeding 1 mm/h frequently coincided with enhanced lightning activity, demonstrating a robust positive statistical association. At several stations, lightning activity preceded rainfall peaks by approximately one hour, highlighting its utility for early warning systems. May recorded the highest rainfall totals and flash counts, coinciding with the peak of the flood disaster, whereas April exhibited localized episodes of intense electrical activity. Diurnal cycle analysis revealed nocturnal peaks between 00:00 and 03:00 UTC (21:00–00:00 Local Time), consistent with the typical pattern of deep convection in the region. Regionally, the overall correlation between precipitation and lightning was positive (r = 0.47; rho = 0.71), ranging from moderate to strong across stations. Santa Maria, Cruz Alta, and Bento Gonçalves recorded the highest lightning densities, whereas Rio Grande exhibited low electrical activity. A focused case study from April 28 to May 3, 2024, revealed that the rapid intensification of lightning density coincided with convective core development and peak rainfall accumulation. Maximum flash density exceeded 150 flashes / 25 km² during the event's apex, underscoring the severity of the convective system. These findings confirm that the co-occurrence and observed lead time of lightning relative to rainfall reinforce the capability of GOES-16 GLM as an operational tool for monitoring and nowcasting extreme hydrometeorological events in southern Brazil, thereby enhancing short-term forecasting and disaster risk reduction.

498188.title: Geospatial Assessment of Rainwater Harvesting Opportunities in Licking County, Ohio to Decrease Potable Water Use and Improve Stormwater Management.
498188.abstract: Data centers are being constructed around the world. Data centers are large buildings that contain thousands of computers, servers, and data storage systems. Once constructed, they use upwards of 3,800 cubic meters, or 1 million gallons of water per day, to cool their systems. Data centers are replacing agricultural lands and wetlands in Licking County, Ohio. Data center construction is causing flooding from the increase in impervious surfaces and stormwater runoff. Licking County receives approximately 1041 mm (41 inches) of rainfall annually. If data centers harvested the rainwater, just from their rooftops, it would substantially reduce stormwater runoff volume and the amount of potable water used within the building for toilet flushing, in-facility cleaning, landscaping irrigation, among other things. This case study focuses on 10 data centers constructed in Licking County, Ohio, and the amount of rainwater that could be captured for non-potable in-building uses, as well as the reduction in potable water use and decrease in stormwater runoff.

498191.title: Execution-Grounded Evaluation: Judgement, Not Reasoning, Limits Large Language Models in Atmospheric Science
498191.authors: Chendong Ma, Hong Kong Baptist University, Kowloon Tong, China; Hong Kong Baptist University, Kowloon Tong, China; Hong Kong Baptist University, Kowloon Tong, China; and M. Ran and J. Song
498191.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for quantitative applications in environmental science, yet their computational reliability and domain-specific reasoning remain insufficiently understood. Existing evaluations often focus only on final-answer accuracy, leaving the underlying calculation process unobserved and making it difficult to distinguish genuine reasoning from successful answer generation. Here, we introduce AtmosCoder-Bench, an execution-grounded benchmark for atmospheric science designed to evaluate both computational outcomes and the processes used to obtain them. The benchmark contains 436 problems, 3,910 variants, and 7,029 graded quantities, constructed through a transferable semi-automated pipeline. Each problem is rigorously reviewed to ensure that it is unambiguous, solvable by domain experts, and associated with a unique and independently verifiable solution. Our evaluation reveals three main findings. (i) multiple-choice formats substantially overestimate quantitative capability, inflating measured accuracy by 12–39 percentage points. (ii) Many failures arise not from missing domain knowledge, but from models failing to apply known formulas, physical constraints, units, signs, and intermediate results consistently throughout multi-step computations. Models may correctly state relevant principles yet fail to follow them reliably during calculation. (iii) Even frontier models remain weak when task-specific conditions invalidate familiar methods. In such cases, they often revert to canonical solution patterns instead of recognising that the physical regime requires a different approach, demonstrating a persistent gap between general computational competence and domain-specific judgement. Together, these results indicate that the principal bottleneck for frontier LLMs in atmospheric-science computation lies less in raw calculation than in reliably applying known principles and exercising task-specific professional judgement. AtmosCoder-Bench provides a scalable, auditable, and professionally grounded framework for evaluating these capabilities and offers a foundation for studying LLM-based quantitative analysis in atmospheric and related environmental sciences.

498194.title: The Data Challenge for Fully Digital Phased Array Radars: Comparison of Data Reduction Schemes – Quantization vs Sparse Array in the Context of Weather Radar
498194.authors: Ayano Ueki, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and R. D. Palmer, B. Cheong, and S. M. Torres
498194.abstract: Phased array radars (PARs) have potential as next-generation weather radar systems. They can provide improved temporal resolution and spatial sampling while enabling advanced observation techniques, such as adaptive beamforming for interference mitigation and flexible scanning based on the inherent beam agility of PARs. The most capable and flexible form of PAR is fully digital system. However, processing and storing data from all individual element channels creates a significant bottleneck due to the large volume of raw in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) data. At least two approaches can be used to reduce the size of I/Q data: Quantization reduces the amplitude resolution of the I/Q data Sparse-array techniques reduce the spatial data volume by using a subset of antenna elements for beamforming These two approaches reduce data in different dimensions and may have different impacts on estimating weather radar variables. In this study, the trade-off between quantization and a sparse-array approach is investigated through numerical simulations emulating the fully digital PAR “Horus” developed at the University of Oklahoma (OU). Various sparse-array patterns, such as optimal combinations of active and inactive antenna elements, are investigated to effectively reduce I/Q data volume while preserving the quality of polarimetric weather radar variables. The performance of these configurations is then compared with that of reduced-bit quantization to characterize the trade-offs between spatial and quantization-domain data reduction. The results provide insight into efficient data-reduction options for future fully digital PAR systems.

498196.title: Quantifying Dust Event Frequency in New Mexico Over Twenty-Two Years
498196.authors: Ally Victoria Brawner, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX; and K. Ardon-Dryer
498196.abstract: Quantifying Dust Event Frequency in New Mexico Over Twenty-Two Years Ally Brawner and Karin Ardon-Dryer Texas Tech University Department of Geosciences Dust events are meteorological phenomena that transport aerosol particles and occur primarily in dryland regions. Research shows that exposure to these particles can affect human health. This research aims to identify dust events in the United States from 2000 to 2022, focusing specifically on New Mexico. Dust events were identified using data from ASOS (Automated Surface Observing System) and AWOS (Automated Weather Observing System). Dust events needed to have the requirements of visibility being < 10km, with wind speed being ≥ 6 m/s, and weather codes that represent dust (BLDU, DS, DU, and HZ). There were 39 ASOS/AWOS stations in New Mexico, but only 26 of these stations had measurements for at least 20 years and therefore could be used. From these 26 stations, there were more than 17 million meteorological observations where 45,273 of these observations fit the conditions for dust and were grouped into 8,498 events. Out of these 8,498 events, only 6,752 were flagged as potential dust events. We then needed to confirm these were actual dust events using confirmation methods such as satellite imagery, social media, PM data, and other nearby ASOS. The temporal and spatial distribution of these dust events will be presented, as well as the distinguishing of the severity of dust events. Preliminary findings show that most of the dust events (>50%) occur during March and June between 13:00 and 18:00. From this database, dust-forecasting capabilities can be developed, and the processes underlying dust events can be better understood. This database will allow people to take better precautions to protect themselves from these dust events.

498199.title: Determining Where and When Models Falter in Simulating Precipitation Trends Over Southeastern South America
498199.authors: Roberto Guillermo Canseco, Vermont State University Lyndon, Lyndonville, VT; and A. M. Varuolo-Clarke
498199.abstract: Southeastern South America (SESA), a region comprising portions of southern Brazil, northern Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay, has seen a significant precipitation increase over the 20th and 21st centuries. The cause of this long-term increase, as well as a striking recent drop in SESA precipitation that has occurred since approximately 2018, is as of yet unclear. It remains to be determined what roles anthropogenic forcing and internal variability play in the trend. With the observational record limited to little more than a century, our best resources for developing an understanding of these trends are climate models. However, climate models struggle to capture the long-term trend or changes in variability observed from 1902 through 2024. Initial results from analysis of 50 members from the CESM2 Large Ensemble show almost no ability of the model to capture trends that begin before 1945 and end in 1966 or later. Furthermore, a notable inability of the model to capture trends of any length that end in several major El Niño years can be seen. These present as sharp “breaks” in model-observation agreement. Initial results also show few ensemble members capturing the observed increase in variability, with more than half of members instead showing a decrease. These results may assist in further work to shed light on the challenges cutting-edge climate models face in representing SESA hydroclimatic trends, especially given the sharp drop in SESA precipitation in recent years.

498202.title: A climatology of summertime non-tropical heavy rainfall events over Florida
498202.authors: Nathaniel Alan Thompson, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; and S. E. Strazzo
498202.abstract: Florida receives a substantial portion of its annual precipitation during the summer months, with rainfall distributions strongly influenced by interactions between synoptic-scale flow patterns and mesoscale sea-breeze circulations. While tropical cyclones can contribute significantly to seasonal rainfall totals, many of Florida's most impactful heavy rainfall events occur independently of tropical systems. Understanding the spatial and temporal variability of these non-tropical heavy rainfall events is important for improving precipitation forecasting and assessing regional hydrologic impacts. This study examines heavy rainfall events during the climatological summer season (June-August) from 1979-2025 using observations from 68 stations across Florida. To isolate non-tropical rainfall events, any station-day occurring within 400 nautical miles of a tropical cyclone center was excluded from the analysis. Synoptic-scale flow patterns associated with each event were classified using the nine sea-breeze regimes previously developed by the National Weather Service. In addition, wind-vector classifications derived from ERA5 reanalysis data were used to further characterize the large-scale environment associated with heavy rainfall occurrences. Results indicate substantial geographic variability in the frequency of heavy rainfall events exceeding 75 mm (2.95 in). Stations along Florida's Gulf Coast, particularly across the Big Bend region, experience significantly more heavy rainfall events than locations along the central Atlantic coast. Temporal analysis reveals a pronounced peak in event frequency during mid-to-late June, followed by a gradual decrease through July and August. The findings suggest that favorable combinations of synoptic flow and local sea-breeze interactions occur more frequently across western portions of the peninsula, enhancing the likelihood of extreme warm-season rainfall. Future work will investigate dynamic characteristics associated with these events through composite analyses of the newly defined categories, including 850-500 mb wind shear and 700 mb omega fields. These analyses will provide additional insight into the environmental conditions that support non-tropical heavy rainfall across Florida and may ultimately improve forecasting of high-impact warm-season precipitation events.

498205.title: Assessing the Influence of Sea Surface Temperatures on the Track on Hurricane Willa (2018)
498205.authors: Gavin M Flowers, University of Tampa, Tampa, FL; and N. S. Grondin
498205.abstract: The movement of Tropical Cyclones (TCs) is influenced by many factors including beta-drift, large-scale wind flow, and proximity to land, making it so TC track forecasting is a consistent challenge especially for coastal TCs threatening land. One such factor that may influence TC movement but has been widely overlooked is sea surface temperatures (SSTs). While SSTs are widely known to influence the intensity of TCs, their influence on TC movement is understudied, especially in the eastern Northern Pacific (ENP) basin. Given the recent impacts of major Hurricanes Willa (2018), Otis (2023), and John (2024) along the Pacific Coast of Mexico, improving our understanding of environmental conditions that promote TC impacts to the region is important. One of the most frequent track patterns in the ENP is a recurving track, where the TC forms off the coast of southwest Mexico, travels slightly west, then curves back into the coast of Mexico. This track type is among the most common ENP landfall tracks, with Hurricane Willa being a prominent recent example of an intense TC to follow this path. In this project, we use the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to analyze the influence of SSTs on the track of Willa. To see the effect of changed SSTs on the track of Willa, we run three simulations: a control simulation with SSTs unchanged, and two experimental simulations where SSTs were changed by +/- 2°C. The outputs for these simulations are analyzed in python, where we create tracks of each simulation and contrast their differences. We also analyzed environmental conditions around the TC were also analyzed, such as the 500mb heights, to see if there were any differences in these between simulations, and to assess their influences on the tracks. Our findings will have the potential to help improve TC forecasting in the region and understand the influences of warmer oceans with a changing climate on ENP TC activity.

498207.title: Applying Deep Learning to Locate Tropical Cyclone Centers in Satellite SAR Imagery
498207.authors: Bhavika Buddi, University of Maryland, College Park, MD; and T. W. Ruff, C. Jackson, and M. Y. Murphy
498207.abstract: The Center for Satellite Applications and Research (STAR), within the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS), routinely processes satellite synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery to derive high-resolution ocean surface wind speeds and radial wind profiles for tropical cyclones. These products are generated in near real-time and distributed to operational forecast centers, such as the National Hurricane Center and the Joint Typhoon Warning Center. Accurate wind speed radial profiles rely on precise fixing of the storm center; however, the current center-finding algorithm suffers from significant positioning errors in over one-third of SAR scenes, requiring time-intensive manual corrections that delay product generation. This study develops a deep learning framework using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to improve automated tropical cyclone center finding in satellite SAR imagery. To determine the optimal model configuration, we systematically evaluated multiple architectures and training strategies, including single-task versus multi-task CNNs, direct coordinate regression versus heatmap regression, mean squared error versus Adaptive Wing Loss (AWL), and a range of encoder backbones. The best-performing model combined a multi-task heatmap regression approach with AWL as the loss function, and a UNet++ architecture using an EfficientNet encoder backbone. Evaluation on an independent test dataset demonstrated significant improvements in center localization accuracy, particularly for cases in which the current algorithm performs poorly. The optimal CNN model reduced the mean center-finding error from 36.40 km to 4.48 km while significantly decreasing the frequency of large localization errors (>15 km). The model also showed robust performance across a range of tropical cyclone eye structures. These results demonstrate how machine learning and artificial intelligence can enhance the operational use of satellite data by reducing manual corrections and improving the accuracy and timeliness of SAR-derived wind products for tropical cyclone forecasting and warnings.

498208.title: A Climatological Analysis of Storm-Scale and Environmental Characteristics of Tornadoes in Illinois During 2007–2025
498208.authors: Jakob Barton, Parkland College, Champaign, IL; Terrain-Atmosphere Research Lab, Urbana, IL
498208.abstract: Illinois occupies a transition between instability-dominated warm-season convection characteristic of the Midwest and more dynamically forced cool-season severe-weather regimes extending into the lower Mississippi and Ohio Valleys, providing a useful setting for examining how tornado-producing environments vary across season and geography. A comprehensive climatology of 1,128 Illinois tornadoes during the modern Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale era (2007–2025) was developed to quantify seasonal and regional variability in tornado characteristics, convective organization, boundary forcing, environmental conditions, and temporal occurrence. The analysis was designed to determine whether Illinois tornado climatology is adequately represented by a single statewide distribution or instead reflects distinct combinations of storm-scale and environmental processes across seasons and regions. Storm Prediction Center (SPC) tornado reports were integrated with archived radar imagery, Weather Prediction Center surface analyses, SPC mesoanalysis products, and supporting National Weather Service event information within a standardized observational framework. Tornadoes were stratified into warm-season (March–August; n = 950) and cool-season (November–February; n = 178) subsets and geographically classified across northern, central, and southern Illinois. Parent convection was manually classified as supercell, quasi-linear convective system (QLCS), or single-/multicell, while associated surface boundaries were classified from operational analyses. Effective-layer significant tornado parameter (STP), mixed-layer convective available potential energy (MLCAPE), and effective bulk shear characterized composite tornado favorability, thermodynamic instability, and kinematic support, respectively. Manually compiled classifications and environmental assignments underwent four quality-assurance review passes before statistical analysis using nonparametric and categorical methods. Pronounced seasonal differences extended beyond tornado frequency. Cool-season tornadoes were less frequent but exhibited significantly greater path lengths (p < 0.001) and maximum path widths (p = 0.025), contained a greater proportion of tornadoes rated EF2 or greater (EF2+), and occurred within substantially stronger effective bulk shear than warm-season tornadoes (p < 0.001). Warm-season tornadoes occurred across a substantially broader MLCAPE distribution and were concentrated during the afternoon and evening, whereas cool-season tornadoes occurred almost exclusively within organized supercell and QLCS convection. QLCSs produced the greatest number of tornadoes overall, while supercells exhibited the largest EF2+ proportions during both seasons; no EF2+ tornadoes were associated with single-/multicell convection. Environmental relationships further distinguished tornado occurrence from stronger-tornado favorability. Tornado occurrence was greatest within moderate effective-shear environments, but EF2+ proportions increased substantially across higher-shear categories and differed significantly among effective bulk-shear categories (p < 0.001). EF2+ proportions likewise differed significantly among STP categories (p < 0.001), whereas no significant association was identified among MLCAPE categories (p = 0.126). Regional variability provided an additional and coherent signal. Central Illinois recorded the greatest number of tornadoes, but EF2+ proportions increased progressively from northern to southern Illinois during both seasons, reaching 40.0% among rated cool-season tornadoes in southern Illinois. Cool-season effective bulk shear increased significantly from northern to southern Illinois (p < 0.001), while cool-season STP exhibited a corresponding southward increase and substantially greater variability in southern Illinois. Storm-mode and boundary composition also varied significantly among regions, with these geographic contrasts becoming more pronounced during the cool season. Cool-season EF2+ tornadoes were concentrated across central and southern Illinois, and southern Illinois exhibited a marked increase in overnight cool-season tornado occurrence. Collectively, these results demonstrate that Illinois tornado climatology comprises interacting seasonal and regional regimes rather than a spatially uniform statewide distribution. Stronger-tornado favorability was most consistently associated with enhanced kinematic support, organized convection, and synoptic and mesoscale forcing rather than thermodynamic instability alone. The results support an ingredients-based interpretation in which environmental conditions, storm organization, boundary forcing, season, and regional setting operate as interconnected components of the tornado-producing environment. This regional context is particularly important in southern Illinois during the cool season, where comparatively modest instability can coexist with strongly sheared, dynamically forced environments favorable for significant tornadoes. The climatology provides a modern observational framework for interpreting Illinois tornado environments and for future severe-weather forecasting, hazard assessment, and comparative climatological investigations.

498209.title: Evaluating Hazard Data Inputs for Hurricane Debris Estimation.
498209.authors: Anish Ratna Shakya, Texas A&M University, Galveston, TX; and J. Kim, PhD, S. Brody, and A. Mostafavi
498209.abstract: Accurate debris estimation after hurricanes is critical for disaster response, debris removal planning, and resource allocation. Machine learning methods have been widely used to estimate post-hurricane debris, but most studies focus on model framework, design, and predictive performance. At the same time, multiple hazard datasets are often available for the same hurricane event, differing in data source, spatial resolution, coverage, and accuracy. However, the sensitivity of debris estimation to these alternative hazard data inputs has not been systematically evaluated, making it difficult to determine which datasets are most suitable for operational applications. Using Hurricanes Helene and Milton in Pinellas County, Florida, as a case study, this study evaluates how alternative hazard data inputs influence machine learning-based debris estimation. Observed debris collection records are integrated with building and environmental characteristics and multiple hazard datasets representing hurricane conditions. Classification and regression models are used to assess changes in debris occurrence and volume estimates under different hazard data inputs. Model performance is compared across hazard datasets to determine whether differences in data source, spatial resolution, and accuracy lead to meaningful changes in predictive performance. The analysis also examines whether sensitivity to hazard data varies across debris types and locations with high debris volumes. In addition to predictive performance, the study considers the practical feasibility of alternative hazard datasets based on factors such as data availability, spatial coverage, and resolution. The findings will help identify which types of hazard data provide sufficient predictive value for hurricane debris estimation and whether higher-resolution or more detailed datasets consistently justify their additional data requirements. The results can support more practical and reliable selection of hazard inputs for operational debris estimation.

498210.title: A Detailed Satellite Analysis of Radiative Feedback in Sheared Tropical Cyclones
498210.authors: Stephen Lloyd Kesti, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. Carstens
498210.abstract: Challenges remain in forecasting tropical cyclone (TC) intensification and development despite significant advances in recent years. Numerous environmental and storm-scale factors often compete with one another in the development and maintenance of TCs. For example, environmental vertical wind shear (VWS) often negatively impacts TC intensity by inducing vortex tilt, ventilation, and convective asymmetry. However, TCs sometimes intensify in sheared environments, complicating forecasting. One factor that can accelerate TC development is radiative feedback, primarily a longwave effect. This process involves the localized trapping of infrared radiation by convective, and stratiform clouds produced by the TC. This radiative feedback effect has been measured in previous studies on convective organization using moist static energy (MSE) budgets. MSE combines potential energy, latent, and sensible heat in a parcel of air and has been connected to TC genesis and intensification. We hypothesize that the spatial pattern and magnitude of radiative feedback, relative to VWS, can improve predictability of TC intensity in sheared environments. While observational evidence for the role of radiative feedback on TCs is growing, it has been limited by platforms with coarse spatial and temporal coverage. This has hindered analysis of individual TC cases and further understanding of radiative feedback through the life cycle of a single storm. NASA TROPICS satellites, which were active from 2021-2025, allow for unprecedented spatiotemporal coverage of thermodynamic variables in TCs. These are combined with CERES global hourly radiative flux measurements in this study to uncover radiative feedback effects. Analysis focuses on calculating MSE from TROPICS retrievals of temperature and humidity profiles for TCs under moderate VWS. Radiative feedback is then found by multiplying anomalies of column-integrated MSE with radiative flux convergence obtained from CERES. Results are shown in a VWS-relative composite framework to advance scientific understanding of the opposing effects between VWS and radiative feedback within a TC under sheared environments.

498211.title: Climatology of Vegetation Phenology in Kentucky: Linking Normalized Difference Vegetation Index-Derived Green-Up and Brown-Down to Climate Variables
498211.authors: Nishita Chaduvula, The Gatton Academy of Mathematics and Science, Louisville, KY
498211.abstract: Vegetation phenology involves the analysis of recurring seasonal processes, including spring green-up and fall brown-down (senescence). In this study, a 16-year climatological analysis of vegetation phenology across the state of Kentucky was developed by utilizing Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) data to determine the timings of green-up, brown-down, their durations, and the length of growing season. Data for air temperature, precipitation, and relative humidity were obtained from 51 Kentucky Mesonet weather stations. The climate data and phenology metrics were analyzed to determine the climate-phenology relationships that exist in Kentucky and each of its four climate divisions using the Spearman Rank correlation coefficient. Furthermore, case studies were performed on years with anomalous values for the phenology metrics. The results show that green-up metrics have been occurring later over the study period and length of growing season has been decreasing. Spatial variability was observed in the values of the phenology metrics and in the number and strength of the correlations between the metrics and climate variables. The results also indicate that the most influential climate variables are temperature and relative humidity, and that the previous winter precipitation is the most influential compared to other seasons’ values. The recent shifts in vegetation phenology and the extent of climate-phenology correlations provide information that has implications in agricultural planning and ecosystem changes.

498213.title: Hurricane Ensemble Modeling in Azure Cloud
498213.authors: Salar Adili, Microsoft, Arlington, VA; and A. Poyer and W. A. Komaromi
498213.abstract: Since 2023, the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) Ensemble in Real Time on the Cloud (HERC) has conducted annual cloud-based experiments, demonstrating that a state-of-the-science hurricane modeling system can operate successfully in real time. Supported by the Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program (HFIP) and Microsoft, the 2026 experiment advanced ensemble science through collaboration among Microsoft, the NOAA Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) High Performance Computing and Communications (HPCC) program, and a team of NWS scientific contributors. During the 2026 hurricane season, HERC real-time ran exclusively on Microsoft Azure using the Parallel Works middleware platform, Microsoft and AMD computing technologies, and high-performance parallel managed storage provided by Microsoft. The experiment operated an 11-member coupled ensemble of NOAA’s HAFSv2.2 model at 2-km resolution, producing real-time probabilistic forecasts for the Atlantic basin and valuable high-resolution data products. Results were made available through NOAA’s Open Data Dissemination program in the cloud.

498215.title: Tracking the Evolution of Cold Front Precipitation in the CoURAGE Domain
498215.authors: Matthew Woody, Sonoma State University, Rohnert Park, CA; Sonoma State University, Rohnert Park, CA; and M. Deng
498215.abstract: Cold fronts are synoptic-scale events that affect tens of millions of people, yet their precipitation effects remain difficult to predict. Improving predictions of precipitation location, duration, and intensity supports Department of Energy (DOE) efforts to evaluate weather models and strengthen energy resilience. Our study aims to improve understanding of cold front precipitation and provide constraints for predicting how terrain contributes to differences among fronts. We combined Next-Generation Weather Radar (NEXRAD) precipitation observations with surface measurements from the DOE Atmospheric Radiation Measurement User Facility’s Coast-Urban-Rural Atmospheric Gradient Experiment (CoURAGE). Using cold-front passage times identified from CoURAGE measurements at three sites, we retained 18 multi-site events and tracked precipitation as the fronts moved eastward through the domain. We analyzed events using an Orienteering Tape Recorder (OTR) diagram, which tracks how radar-observed conditions evolve over time along a fixed direction. Because conventional thresholding could not isolate the frontal region from background weather, we developed an OTR-based method that detected the leading edge and extended a selection region according to its slope. We combined observations across fronts to examine how precipitation properties varied with location and surface type. We observed precipitation enhancement over mountainous regions and possible modification near bay breeze boundaries. Urban transect portions generally had lower maximum rain rates, accumulation, and duration than mountain portions despite comparable mean rain rates, suggesting shorter-lived precipitation and possibly greater spatial localization, although precipitation area was not directly evaluated. These findings provide benchmarks for evaluating how DOE-supported weather models represent cold front precipitation across heterogeneous environments.

498217.title: Evaluating NOAA's CORA Dataset During High-Impact Coastal Flooding at Military Installations.
498217.authors: Tom Beck, U.S. Naval Academy, Annapolis, MD; and A. R. Davies and S. Loeffler
498217.abstract: Coastal flooding increasingly jeopardizes infrastructure along the U.S. Atlantic and Gulf Coasts. The observed increase in flood frequency directly threatens the operational readiness of over 100 military installations located in these regions. While NOAA tide gauges currently monitor water levels, their sparse network leaves significant spatial data gaps that hinder localized impact assessments and resilience planning. To address these limitations, NOAA recently released its initial Coastal Ocean Reanalysis (CORA) dataset, which provides high-resolution water level estimates every 200–500 meters along the coastline. While recent studies demonstrate CORA's skill in capturing long-term averages and secular trends, its reliability during acute, high-impact flooding events remains uncertain. This study evaluates the accuracy of the CORA dataset during extreme flooding events by comparing it against in-situ tide gauge observations at three strategically significant military locations: Annapolis, MD; Norfolk, VA; and Newport, RI. By quantifying CORA's performance during acute extremes, this research assesses the dataset's overall utility for developing localized, data-driven resilience strategies for vulnerable coastal military infrastructure.

498219.title: Evaluating Supplemental X-Band Radar Observations of Severe Convective Storms within WSR-88D Coverage Gaps.
498219.authors: Michael McCarthy, Millersville University, Sykesville, PA
498219.abstract: Weather Surveillance Radar-1988 Doppler (WSR-88D) observations are fundamental to severe convective storm detection, analysis, and warning operations across the United States. Despite the extensive coverage provided by the WSR-88D network, radar beam height increases with distance from a radar site, limiting observations of the lower troposphere in regions located far from WSR-88D installations. These coverage gaps can affect the detection of shallow, rapidly developing circulations associated with tornadoes and other severe convective phenomena. A growing network of supplemental X-band Doppler radars provides an opportunity to observe portions of the lower troposphere that are poorly sampled by the existing operational network. Undergraduate meteorology students at Millersville University are investigating severe convective storms observed by Climavision X-band radars to evaluate how these observations compare with WSR-88D data and how their strengths and limitations affect interpretation of high-impact weather. Climavision has deployed X-band radars in regions where low-level coverage from the existing radar network is limited, including an X-band Doppler radar installed on the Millersville University campus in 2023. The Lower Susquehanna Valley lies between several WSR-88D installations, including KLWX in Sterling, Virginia; KDOX near Dover, Delaware; and KDIX in southern New Jersey. At increasing ranges from these sites, the lowest WSR-88D elevation scans sample progressively higher altitudes above south-central Pennsylvania. The Millersville X-band radar provides higher-resolution observations closer to the surface within portions of this coverage gap. The availability of supplemental radar data raises an important research and operational question: how can X-band observations be used most effectively alongside the WSR-88D network? X-band radar offers advantages associated with wavelength, spatial resolution, and the ability to deploy systems closer to regions of interest, but it also has limitations, particularly attenuation in heavy precipitation. Understanding these characteristics is essential when interpreting X-band observations and assessing their potential contribution to severe-weather analysis. Our research compares reflectivity and Doppler velocity observations from X-band and S-band radars during several severe convective events, emphasizing differences in storm structure, low-level circulation, spatial resolution, beam geometry, and attenuation. On 28 July 2026, a line of strong to severe thunderstorms crossed the Lower Susquehanna Valley and produced scattered damaging winds. An embedded circulation produced a weak quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) tornado south of Yorkana in York County, Pennsylvania. Analysis of the Millersville X-band radar revealed a tornadic debris signature from approximately 2059 to 2103 UTC. The compact spatial and temporal characteristics of the circulation illustrate the observational challenges presented by QLCS tornadoes, which can develop rapidly, remain shallow, and persist for only a few minutes. Comparison with surrounding WSR-88D observations provides an opportunity to examine how radar range, beam height, and spatial resolution influence the representation of these small-scale circulations. A second event occurred on 4 September 2025, when a supercell moved northeastward across southern Lancaster County and produced a brief EF0 tornado near Quarryville, Pennsylvania. The Millersville X-band radar resolved a hook-like reflectivity structure and compact storm-relative velocity couplet associated with low-level rotation. These signatures were less clearly resolved by the surrounding WSR-88D network. A subsequent National Weather Service (NWS) storm survey confirmed an EF0 tornado southeast of Collins, Pennsylvania, with estimated peak winds of 70 mph, a maximum width of approximately 30 yd, and a path length of 0.15 mi. Damage included removal of a dugout roof at the Solanco Youth Baseball Association and crop damage in an adjacent field. Comparing the radar observations with documented surface damage allowed us to relate remotely sensed storm signatures to the physical impacts of a short-lived tornado. Our investigation was expanded to include two supercells near Brookville, Pennsylvania, on 7 March 2026. These storms were observed by the KCCX WSR-88D near State College, Pennsylvania; KPBZ near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; and Climavision's V109 X-band radar near Pleasantville, Pennsylvania. Because the same storms were sampled by two S-band WSR-88Ds and a nearby X-band radar, this event provides a useful comparative dataset for examining the performance characteristics of the two radar wavelengths. The V109 observations resolved storm-scale features at finer spatial resolution, while attenuation within precipitation reduced data quality in portions of the X-band observations. This case demonstrates that the value of supplemental X-band radar depends on understanding both its enhanced ability to resolve small-scale features and the physical limitations associated with shorter-wavelength radar. Together, these cases provide a framework for evaluating supplemental radar observations rather than treating additional radar coverage as inherently equivalent to improved severe-weather detection. Radar wavelength, range, beam height, spatial resolution, sampling strategy, attenuation, and storm geometry all influence the information available to meteorologists. X-band observations can provide valuable low-level information within WSR-88D coverage gaps, while the WSR-88D network provides greater range and substantially less attenuation in heavy precipitation. Used together, the observing systems can provide complementary perspectives on severe convective storms. For us as undergraduate researchers, these cases extend concepts from radar, mesoscale, and severe-storm meteorology courses into analysis of actual high-impact weather events. Our work involves processing and interpreting archived radar observations, comparing independent observing systems, identifying severe-weather signatures, relating radar observations to NWS storm surveys, and discussing the events with operational NWS meteorologists. The project has also required us to evaluate observational limitations and uncertainty rather than relying on a single radar product or observing system. Continued analysis of severe convective storms observed by Climavision X-band radars will focus on identifying the conditions under which supplemental observations provide the greatest information relative to the WSR-88D network and the conditions under which attenuation or other limitations reduce their utility. These case studies demonstrate both the scientific value of supplemental low-level radar observations and the opportunity for undergraduate researchers to contribute to the evaluation of emerging observing technologies for severe-weather detection, analysis, and decision support.

498232.title: Comparing Atmospheric Vertical Profiles in Forecast Models to Observations During SNOWSCAPE Field Campaign
498232.authors: Hailee Davis, REALM REU, Salt Lake City, UT; South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD; and A. M. Stansfield
498232.abstract: Utah’s northern Wasatch Mountains provide a unique mountainous climate to study due to their steep topography, frequent winter storms, and proximity to the Great Salt Lake. The Seeded and Natural Orographic Winter Storms and Catchment Processes Evaluation (SNOWSCAPE) field campaign took place from January through March 2026 with the goal of improving understanding of winter storm processes and evaluating the efficiency of cloud seeding using ground generators. An assessment of how the model forecasts compared to the observed conditions throughout the campaign can highlight common model biases and lead to model improvements in complex terrain. This study focuses on identifying what biases the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and Global Forecast System (GFS) models have in the northern Wasatch Range, specifically focusing on atmospheric vertical profiles. Observations are from weather balloon data collected approximately every 3 hours during SNOWSCAPE Intensive Observing Periods (IOPs) at a site in Syracuse, Utah. Temperature, dewpoint temperature, and wind profiles were compared between the observations and vertical profiles from the closest HRRR and GFS points. Results indicate that neither the HRRR nor GFS models outperformed each other for any variable, and that temperature errors were smaller than dewpoint temperature errors. These findings show that while the HRRR has a higher resolution, it does not have a significant difference in its forecasting capabilities for vertical profiles when compared to the GFS.

498234.title: Determining the Variability of Atmospheric Rivers over the West Coast of the United States
498234.authors: Jack Lochansky, NESDIS, Asheville, NC; and J. Gahtan
498234.abstract: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are narrow corridors of enhanced water vapor transport that are a major source of precipitation and freshwater along the U.S. West Coast. Their impacts vary substantially depending on their frequency, intensity, duration, spatial extent, and timing, making characterization of AR events important for understanding both regional hydrology and extreme precipitation. This study examines the characteristics and variability of atmospheric rivers affecting the West Coast using the Atmospheric Rivers (ARv1) historical data record spanning 1940–2022, now available through NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). Atmospheric river events are identified and characterized using an AR ranking framework. Event-based analysis is used to quantify the frequency, duration, intensity, and total integrated vapor transport of ARs while avoiding double-counting consecutive time steps belonging to the same event. The climatological distribution of AR activity is examined across the West Coast, including seasonal and yearly variations and the spatial distribution of extreme events. ARs are further separated into intensity categories to investigate how the characteristics and frequency of moderate and extreme events differ. Return-period analysis is used to quantify the rarity of extreme AR characteristics, while trends in annual and seasonal AR intensity and frequency are evaluated to identify changes in the character of ARs over the study period. The study also investigates the relationship between AR characteristics and large-scale climate variability. Monthly AR anomalies are decomposed using empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis to identify the dominant spatial modes of AR variability and their associated principal components. The principal components are compared with major Pacific and hemispheric climate indices, including the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), Pacific–North American (PNA) pattern, Arctic Oscillation (AO), North Pacific Gyre Oscillation (NPGO), and North Pacific Pattern/Index (NPP). Together, these analyses provide a comprehensive characterization of atmospheric rivers affecting the U.S. West Coast, from their basic climatological properties and seasonal behavior to their most extreme characteristics, long-term variability, and large-scale climate associations. By examining ARs as individual events as well as patterns of spatial and temporal variability, this study provides a more complete understanding of the factors that determine the character of West Coast atmospheric rivers and the conditions associated with their most significant events.

498235.title: Skill Crossover Between Optical Flow-based Cloud Nowcasting and NWP Forecasts
498235.authors: Eleanor Kattman, Air Force Institute of Technology, Dayton, OH; and M. P. King
498235.abstract: Despite the skill of current numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, significant gaps remain in their ability to produce accurate, high-resolution cloud forecasts at very short lead times (0–3 h). High-temporal-resolution observations from modern geostationary satellites have enabled rapid optical flow-based cloud nowcasting as a computationally efficient alternative to NWP for short timescales. Traditional optical flow techniques typically rely on Lagrangian persistence, which assume clouds remain constant over time and simply advect with background flow. However, the recently developed I-NOW algorithm (King et al., 2026) advances this approach through forward warping of the optical flow field, allowing the motion itself to evolve in time while incorporating divergence and occlusion handling. This study evaluates I-NOW cloud nowcasts against operational NWP-derived cloud forecasts to identify the lead time at which NWP begins to outperform observation-driven nowcasting.

498243.title: A Microphysics Analysis with Regional MPAS during the July 2025 Central Texas Floods
498243.authors: Wyatt Allen Van Dyke, NCAR, Boulder, CO; Iowa State University, Ames, IA; and A. Lojko, W. Wang, and K. Werner
498243.abstract: The July 2025 Central Texas floods were a tragic event in which extreme precipitation generated flash flooding that caused loss of life and property. Timely and accurate weather prediction of extreme precipitation is critical in mitigating the societal impact of these events. Numerical Weather Prediction models, such as the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS), are an integral tool to help with these predictions. MPAS has seen recent additions to its microphysical scheme options that allow for varying predictions of cloud condensation nuclei, mass mixing ratio, and number concentrations of hydrometeor species, along with computational costs. These new options require testing to determine their skill and biases as it relates to extreme precipitation forecasting. This study presents an analysis and comparison of three microphysics schemes in a 36-hour regional, 3km, convection-allowing MPAS simulation of the July 2025 Central Texas floods. The microphysics options analyzed are Thompson, Thompson-Eidhammer Microphysics Parameterization for Operations (TEMPO), and the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) Microphysics. All other physics and model run configurations were kept identical to ensure differences arose from microphysics options. Utilizing Precipitation Attribution Distance (PAD) and Structure, Amplitude, and Location (SAL), it was found that Thompson, TEMPO, and NSSL microphysics underestimated the greatest rainfall rates. NSSL microphysics had more variability in precipitation amplitude bias, with some forecast hours overestimating the greatest rainfall rates. These analyses identify the extreme precipitation forecasting biases associated with the three listed microphysics schemes, informing forecasters and MPAS microphysics development.

498244.title: Evaluating How Vegetation Density Affects Convective Initiation in WRF
498244.authors: Jared Behrend, St. Cloud State University, St. Cloud, MN; University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI
498244.abstract: Correctly representing the land surface and its related effects are important aspects of accurately modeling weather events. In particular, small changes in land-surface characteristics can have major effects on convective initiation. Research into the effects of changes to surface features on convection-permitting model outputs will help improve weather models and forecasting accuracy. This study focused on the effects of forest vegetation density on the development of convection by analyzing the changes to atmospheric instability, vertical velocity, cloud-top temperature, and reflectivity. To examine these changes, we compared WRF control simulations using default terrain data to modified versions using a variety of different vegetation changes and compared the outputs. We found that reducing the vegetation density leads to lower convection intensity and a delay in convective initiation. These findings show the importance of accurately modeling surface conditions and demonstrate the effects of inaccurate surface conditions in model data.

498252.title: Correlations Between Wildfire Activity and Regional Climate Variables Across Montana, 1992-2024
498252.authors: Jack Knighton, SDSMT, Rapid City, SD
498252.abstract: Montana exhibits strong longitudinal variations in regional climate, from the mountainous west to the eastern prairie. Each of these regional climates impact vegetation type and density, which is a primary factor in wildfire behavior. This study hypothesizes that there is significant correlation between regional climate variables and increased wildfire activity. To analyze these relationships, Spearman's rank order method was used to find correlation values between monthly temperature, precipitation, Palmer Modified Drought Severity Index (PMDI), Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), and wildfire activity from 1992 to 2024 for each of the seven climate divisions within Montana. Wildfire activity was evaluated using monthly acres burned and monthly wildfire ignitions. Negative values of PMDI and SPI, high temperatures, and lower precipitation amounts were found to be significantly correlated with increased wildfire activity. Additionally, monthly acres burned showed more consistent correlation with drought metrics and high temperatures compared to monthly wildfire ignitions. Significant correlations were also found between time-lagged climate variables, indicating that these may be used to predict future enhanced wildfire potential.

498255.title: A Binary Classification Approach to Characterizing Mid-Latitude Pressure and Height Tendencies
498255.authors: Abhinav Sharma, Georgia Institute of Technology, Westford, MA
498255.abstract: Key Words: Pressure Tendency, Height Tendency, Logistic Regression, Binary Classification, Mid-Latitude Dynamics Predicting storm formation and the controls therein is incredibly crucial to the efficacy of weather forecasts. This need is growing especially important as forcing from anthropogenic climate change causes complex changes to the ambient conditions responsible for forming and suppressing storms. In mid-latitude dynamics, two major facilitators of storm formation are upward vertical motion and trough formation within the spatial 500mb geopotential field. The former ingredient is characterized by the first time derivative of sea-level pressure (denoted as ω), where a negative value indicates rising motion, and a positive value sinking motion. The latter is characterized by the first time derivative of geopotential (denoted as χ). A negative χ value indicates decreasing geopotential, and with it, 500mb trough formation and system development downstream along the flow. By contrast, a positive χ value indicates rising geopotential, and with it, ridge formation, atmospheric subsidence, and the suppression of system formation. Simultaneously, machine learning has presented meteorology with a new arsenal of analytical tools for forecasting. Given the importance of characterizing instantaneous height tendency and vertical motion with respect to cyclonic development and the emerging capabilities of machine learning for forecasting, this project utilizes logistic regression to perform binary classification. Specifically, models were developed to predict the presence or absence of rising motion and trough formation at specific instances of space and time. Raw data on meridional and zonal winds at the surface (0.995sigma), 500mb, and 250mb levels (m/s), precipitable water (within the entire atmosphere, kg/m^2), geopotential height (m), sea-level pressure (Pa), and ω (Pa/s) were obtained from the Reanalysis I dataset made by the National Center for Environmental Prediction and National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCEP/NCAR) via the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Physical Sciences Laboratory’s (NOAA PSL) website under Gridded Climate Data. These data have a spatiotemporal resolution of 2.5°-by-2.5° with observations made every six hours. A confined scope was used to examine the forecasting abilities of logistic regression (theoretically, prior to upscaling). Temporally, model data span 2022 through 17 March 2026 (when Reanalysis I was discontinued). Spatially, model data span a 7.5°-by-7.5° area, from 47.5°N, 77.5°W in the northwest to 40°N, 70°W in the southeast (roughly spanning the southern parts of Ontario and Quebec, along with much of New England, New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania), encompassing sixteen coordinate locations (based on the 2.5° resolution). Of these coordinates, four center coordinates lie within the aforementioned region, while twelve reside along its border. For all sixteen locations, 0.955sigma, 500mb, and 250mb wind speeds, geopotential, and χ were calculated. For the four center coordinates, 250mb and 0.995sigma divergence, 500mb and 0.995sigma vorticity, 500mb geostrophic and ageostrophic wind direction, speed, and vorticity, as well as precipitable water advection were also quantified. To set up binary classification, binary versions of ω and χ were constructed, where all non-positive values were designated as 0, and positive values as 1. For each coordinate, the raw and calculated variables (excluding geopotential and the dependent variable when tested), were supplied to two logistic regression models: one for ω, one for χ. Mechanistically, the model predicts either 0 (χ, ω < 0) or 1 (χ, ω > 0) at each point in space and time. 2022-2024 data were used to train the models, while 2025 onwards was used for testing (ntest = 4122). Model performance was evaluated using accuracy (proportion of correct predictions), precision (proportion of predicted 0’s and 1’s which were in fact 0’s and 1’s), recall (proportion of 0’s and 1’s present that the model successfully identifies as such), F1 scores (harmonic mean of precision and recall), and 2x2 confusion matrices (where the top left, top right, bottom left, and bottom right entries are the proportion of true 1’s, false 1’s, false 0’s, and true 0’s, respectively). Whereas class 0 (in this case, troughing and rising air) and class 1 (in this case, ridging and subsidence), have their own precision, recall, and F1 scores, confusion matrices apply to the entire dataset, involving both states underlying 0 and 1. Across the sixteen coordinates, overall model accuracies for predicting the sign of ω and χ span [75.11%, 81.68%] and [70.30%, 74.31%], respectively. Considering precision and recall in tandem via F1 scores for the four classes predicted by the model, rising air, sinking air, trough amplification, and ridge amplification had F1 scores covering [72.19%, 78.98%], [76.67%, 83.77%], [71.09%, 74.47%], and [71.17%, 74.97%], respectively. The confusion matrices reveal the nature of model errors. The percentage of times models failed to identify rising air, sinking air, trough amplification, and ridge amplification span [8.56%, 12.69%], [9.12%, 15.04%], [12.62%, 17.27%], and [10.31%, 14.17%], respectively. Taken together, within this region and timeframe, logistic regression more accurately and reliably predicts instantaneous vertical motion (especially subsidence) than height tendency. Yet, model performance varies more widely for vertical motion. Accuracy, error, and F1 values for vertical motion at the four center points consistently indicate more robust predictions, a trend less prevalent for χ (see graphical abstract). Higher performance within these cells suggests models enriched with key dynamics-forcing features (i.e., geostrophic and ageostrophic flow, along with advection) will provide more robust predictions. Interestingly, vorticity and temperature advection are key forcings for both ω and χ, yet when integrating features related to the former forcing term, models continue to comparatively under-perform with χ. This project serves as a proof of concept for establishing a clear, comprehensive machine learning pipeline for weather forecasting. Imperative areas of ongoing and future work include expanding spatiotemporal scope, adjusting spatiotemporal resolutions, integrating more features (e.g., temperature, deformation) into models, and implementing models that provide forecasts on actual quantities for ω and χ (and ideally additional variables) rather than purely binary states, however descriptive they may be. Such efforts are intended to strengthen the machine learning tools available to meteorology, especially as ambient conditions continue to vary extensively, necessitating increasingly robust forecasting.

498257.title: Statistical Analysis of the Relationship Between Short-Duration Heavy Rainfall and Topographic Characteristics
498257.authors: KEISUKE WATANABE, Keio University, Ota-ku, Tokyo, Japan; and Y. Miyamoto
498257.abstract: 短時間集中豪雨（SHR）は、洪水や土砂崩れなどの深刻な災害を引き起こす可能性があるため、そのような豪雨の発生場所と空間分布を正確に理解し予測することが重要です。しかし、SHRの発生は、大気の状態や水蒸気輸送などの気象要因と、標高や地形構成などの地形要因との複雑な相互作用によって影響を受けます。これらの要因がSHRの発生と量にどの程度影響を与えるかは、まだ十分に理解されていません。特に、地形とSHRの関係に関するこれまでの研究は、異なる結論に達しています。ある研究では地形の影響は限定的であると示唆された一方、別の研究では地形が豪雨の発生場所を決定する上で重要な役割を果たしていることが示されました。したがって、地形がSHRに与える影響について、一貫した理解はまだ確立されていません。本研究は、日本のSHRの頻度と量と複数の地形特性との関係を統計的に調査し、SHRの発生と強く関連する地形条件を特定することを目的としています。解析には、日本の全国的な地上気象観測ネットワークである自動気象データ取得システム（AMeDAS）と、観測地点上空の複数の高度で風を測定するウィンドプロファイラーによる2015年から2020年の観測データを使用する。まず、10分ごとのAMeDAS降水量データから、1時間ごとの累積降水量が50mmを超えるケースを抽出する。24時間以内に発生したケースは、1つのSHRイベントとしてグループ化される。各イベントについて、10分ごとの降水量が1mmを下回るイベントの前後の時間に基づいてイベント継続時間を定義し、この期間の総降水量をイベントの降水量として計算する。次に、各観測所について、10分ごとの降水量が最初に1mm以上に達してから、その後1mmを下回るまでの期間を降水イベントと定義する。 SHRの発生頻度は、解析期間中に発生した全降水イベントに対するSHRイベントの割合として定義されます。SHRの発生頻度と降水量の両方と、観測地点の標高、各イベント中の平均風向に対する観測地点の位置（風上側か風下側か）、風上方向の海岸線までの距離などの地形特性との関係は、相関分析を含む統計分析を用いて評価されます。風向は、地上約1,000mの高さでのウィンドプロファイラー観測によって決定されます。これらの分析を通して、本研究は、SHRの発生頻度が高い地形特性を特定し、個々の地形要因とSHRの発生頻度および降水量との関係を定量化することを目指します。今回の結果は、地形とSHR（太陽高潮）の関係に関する統計的理解を深め、最終的にはSHRが発生する場所のより良い理解とより正確な予測に貢献することが期待される。

498259.title: Using Operational Warnings to Develop a Tropical Cyclone Flash Flood Climatology for Texas
498259.authors: Andrew Ryan Snyder, University of Tampa, Tampa, FL; and E. J. Bennett, K. Johnson, and N. S. Grondin
498259.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) are among the most devastating weather events given the wide variety of hazards they cause. This includes inland flooding, which is a major cause of TC-associated fatalities. Flash floods during TCs are challenging to predict, since the likelihood of a flash flood depends on both current rainfall intensity, recent rainfall, and land surface conditions. Our project focuses on analyzing the climatology of flash floods in Texas by using Flash Flood Warnings (FFWs), issued by local National Weather Service (NWS) offices. FFWs are issued by the NWS when a forecaster has high confidence that a flash flood is occurring or is imminent. Given recent events, such as Hurricanes Harvey (2017) and Beryl (2024), Texas provides a useful geographic domain to analyze TC-induced flash flooding given the extreme rainfall and flooding that occurred with these events. In this project, we analyze FFWs associated with Texas TCs between 2008 and 2024. Using ArcGIS Pro, we assign each TC-induced FFW to a singular track point based on the FFW’s time of issuance. We use statistical analysis to analyze the geography of flash floods both in a storm-relative and true-north framework for each TC and the region as a whole. We also examine various TC characteristics, such as intensity and size, and how they relate to where TC flash flooding occurs. We identify that three Texas TCs were particularly prolific flash flood producers, Tropical Storm Hermine (2010), Tropical Storm Bill (2015), and Hurricane Harvey. Our results show that FFWs are most common in front of or on the right side of the TC center, which is consistent with most previous research that shows TC hazards, such as wind and storm surge, are most likely to occur in the right-front quadrant. This perspective on FFWs during TCs in this region will have the potential to improve forecasting of flash flood events during TCs and our understanding of the spatial distribution of these events across the flood-prone state of Texas.

498260.title: Developing Spectral Imaging Capabilities for Meteorologic Glidersondes
498260.authors: Cristian Xavier Mendoza, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK
498260.abstract: As the field of remote sensing and land imaging becomes increasingly democratized from both a software and hardware perspective, miniature cameras are opening new possibilities for viable remote sensing missions. This study builds and tests a multispectral imaging array for flight on a fixed-wing UAV to altitudes up to 20,000 meters in altitude, demonstrating that high-quality remote sensing data can be delivered at a fraction of the cost of traditional platforms. The imaging array consists of eight Sony IMX477R CMOS imagers, autofocus-compatible, capturing Red, Green, Blue, and modified to capture Near Infrared bands. This matches the spectral capabilities of premium agricultural cameras used for Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) measurements. Two sensors are devoted to NIR, and two to each of the RGB channels, allowing pixel data to be stacked in parallel and increasing the effective megapixel count. The imaging package integrates an Arduino and a brightness sensor to handle triggering, processing, batching, light sensing, and image saving. The package undergoes flight testing aboard a standard weather balloon, which is ferried to 15,000 meters on a west-to-east trajectory over northeastern Oklahoma and northwestern Arkansas. Flight planning software predicts the profile based on forecast wind directions. It calculates the necessary shutter-release intervals to reduce digital storage usage and ensure images overlap to build a complete “map” of the flight. The first flight validates the autofocus and thermal insulation performance of the standalone package. A second flight, aboard a Meteomatics MeteoGlider reaching 24,000 meters, with a modified nose housing for the camera array, replacing the standard weather-sensing radiosonde. This allows for a more repeatable setup, with the package returning to a landing spot near the launch point. This opens the door to continuous, cost-effective high-altitude remote sensing operations.

498265.title: Investigating Western Pacific Dvorak Technique Constraints
498265.authors: Jacob Hale, Air Force Institute of Technology, Kettering, OH
498265.abstract: Investigating Western Pacific Dvorak Technique Constraints Tropical cyclone intensity estimation is widely determined using the Dvorak Technique (Dvorak, 1984). Despite the age of its initial development, the Dvorak Technique remains an essential tool for tropical cyclone forecasting globally. Thus, continual development and improvements to the technique are vital for the protection of life and property. In particular, the Dvorak Technique implements constraints to storm intensity estimation which span across certain time intervals (i.e. 6, 12, 18, and 24 hours). A study by Sangster et al. (2020) found that the constraints for the final-T number (FT), the value establishing the estimated intensity of a storm, were too restrictive in the Atlantic Basin and recommended increasing 18- and 24-hour period constraints to 2.5 and 3.0 respectively. This study parallels the methodology applied by Sangster et al. (2020) for the Western Pacific basin using data from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) and the NOAA Tropical Cyclone SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) Archive. Best track data from 2016 – 2025 is filtered to eliminate data that did not coincide with available SAR data, and statistical parameters are evaluated to determine the extent of intensity errors caused by current FT constraints. Preliminary findings suggest current operational constraints utilized at JTWC in the Western Pacific are too restrictive for cyclones undergoing rapid intensification. Statistical results will be presented to determine which constraint periods require updates and to what extent. Bibliography Dvorak, V. F., 1984: Tropical Cyclone Intensity Analysis Using Satellite Data. NOAA Tech. Rep. NESDIS 11, 47 pp. Sangster, S. J., and C. W. Landsea, 2020: Constraints in Dvorak Wind Speed Estimates: How Quickly Can Hurricanes Intensify?, https://doi.org/10.1175/WAF-D-19-0186.1.

498267.title: Toward Understanding the Role of Weathered Nanoplastics in Warm Cloud Processes
498267.authors: Ella Margaret Szczerbik, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN; and C. Knight, D. Cziczo, A. Johnson, G. Prabhakar, C. Tedder, J. Rodriguez-Sanchez, and M. Phanthavongsa
498267.abstract: The presence and environmental impacts of nanoplastics (NPs) in marine and terrestrial environments have been thoroughly examined and well documented. However, NPs are not conﬁned to Earth’s surface, as surface winds can entrain NPs into the atmosphere, turning the troposphere into a temporary reservoir and transport pathway for airborne NPs (Xu et al., 2025). Research on their atmospheric presence and impacts is relatively new and limited, despite their potential impacts on cloud properties, precipitation pathways, and, by extension, the climate (Haywood, 2015). This study examines whether NPs could act as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), and whether in situ alterations change their CCN potential. As a ﬁrst step, we generated NP samples by suspending both pristine and weathered plastics in Milli-Q water for at least 24 hours. Then, solutions were ﬁltered to remove particles >1.5 µm. Size distributions of NPs in these samples were measured using the Brechtel Scanning Electrical Mobility Spectrometer (SEMS). Both pristine and weathered plastic samples showed significantly higher particle concentrations relative to the Milli-Q water control, indicating that plastic leaching was occurring. NPs were consistently detected at diameters between 30–80 nm, providing a repeatable size range to test for CCN capabilities using a cloud condensation nuclei counter (CCNC). Ongoing work is extending this protocol to quantify CCN activity for different pristine and weathered NPs (acrylic and polyethylene) using the Droplet Measurement Technologies CCN Spectrometer.

498268.title: Precipitation Structure of Hurricane Milton (2024) During Its Weakening Phase
498268.authors: Colin Michael McNiff, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Ormond Beach, FL; and J. B. Wadler
498268.abstract: Hurricane Milton (2024), one of the most intense hurricanes in the Atlantic basin on record, underwent rapid changes in both intensity and structure during its life cycle in the Gulf of Mexico. This study examines the structural evolution of Hurricane Milton using airborne radar observations collected by NOAA Hurricane Hunter P-3 aircraft. Data are obtained from the Tropical Cyclone Radar Archive of Doppler Analyses with Recentering (TC-RADAR) database, providing insight into the three-dimensional structure and kinematics of Milton. Gridded radar data are used to generate plan-view and vertical analyses of Hurricane Milton using radar-derived fields including reflectivity, vertical velocity, divergence, wind speed, and vorticity. Successive radar swaths are analyzed to document the temporal evolution of the storm as Milton transitioned from a period of rapid intensification to subsequent weakening, with an emphasis on the southern eyewall during its initial onset of weakening. This study ultimately seeks to identify changes in eyewall organization and precipitation distribution that contributed to Milton’s observed structural and intensity changes across the Gulf.

498269.title: Exploring the Influence of the El Niño Southern Oscillation on Observed Trends in Cloud Properties Using the PATMOS-x Version 6.0 and ERA5 Datasets
498269.authors: Tyler Allen Sendra, University of Georgia, Athens, GA; and M. J. Foster and L. J. Gabrys
498269.abstract: The Pathfinder Atmospheres - Extended (PATMOS-x) Version 6.0 Dataset is a 45 year long polar orbiting satellite dataset which incorporates National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) polar orbiting satellites NOAA-6 through NOAA-19, as well as EUMETSAT Meteorological Operational (MetOp) satellites A and B, with the goal of developing satellite-based climate data records of atmospheric cloud properties. A previous study utilizing PATMOS-x identified a pronounced decreasing trend in total cloud amount over the Central Equatorial Pacific Ocean. This same study also identified a region in the Southern East Pacific Ocean that exhibits a slightly weaker, yet still increasing trend in cloud detection. A primary result of our study found that the decreasing trend in the Central Pacific could possibly be explained by the asymmetric distribution of El Niño and La Niña events from 1980 until the present, while the relationship between cloud increase and the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is less defined, but still present in the Southern East Pacific. Cross-referencing PATMOS-x with ERA5 reanalysis data shows that the Southern area, located off the coast of Peru and Chile, is also exhibiting decreasing sea-surface temperatures over the same time period, which is likely attributed to wind pattern shifts and upwelling. The cooling ocean temperatures in this region are likely driving the formation of marine stratiform clouds, reinforcing the cooling trend by impacting the amount of solar radiation which reaches the ocean surface. KEYWORDS: PATMOS-x, ENSO Asymmetry, Remote Sensing, Cloud Trends, Central and Eastern Pacific

498270.title: Climatology and Variability of Snowpack Depleting Ablation Events across the CONUS
498270.authors: Preston James Wells, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and Z. Suriano
498270.abstract: The process of snowpack ablation plays a major role in managing and maintaining the hydrological climate. However, large-scale ablation events, particularly rain-on-snow (ROS) events, can have detrimental impacts on human property and services. This study presents a climatology of snowpack events and analysis of snow ablation across the contiguous United States (CONUS) using high-resolution gridded datasets fitted to the criteria of snow ablation events from 1981 to 2023. There is a particular focus on the total completion aspect of ablation events during a defined snow-season period (Oct-Sep) and the implications of the variability in snowpack depletion. Overall, we seek to identify the spatial and temporal trends for snowpack ablation events, such as ROS and non-precipitation (NP) ablation events, and compare the frequency and magnitude with ablation climatology. In addition to ablation events, we strive to find statistics and trends in the precipitation associated with ROS events to better identify what leads to significant ablation events. Results depict observable trends in how depletion events vary spatially across subregions of the CONUS for ROS and NP ablation, differing in both occurrence and magnitude. Furthermore, precipitation associated with ROS events exhibit clear seasonal behavior with topographical extent during the study period; the most intense events are typically found sporadically during the summer in the Rocky Mountains. Continued research into snow ablation across CONUS will allow for improved representation of events within model simulations and in-turn aid forecasting efforts.

498274.title: Influences of Coastal Tornado Formation along the Gulf
498274.authors: Mary Schrader, University of Louisiana at Monroe, Monroe, LA; and T. A. Murphy
498274.abstract: El Nino and La Nina are climate patterns that arise from abnormal patterns in the Trade Winds, and they can have strong effects on weather throughout the world. This is especially the case with hurricane season, for both El Nino and La Nina affect the temperatures of the ocean water over which tropical cyclones form. How do these patterns influence the formation of tornadoes along the Northern Gulf Coast? In this presentation, we examine hurricane influence on coastal tornado formation. Tornadoes along Louisiana’s Gulf Coast from 2010-2024 were separated into three regions and analyzed using federal tornado shapefiles organized into Geographical Information Systems and Excel Spreadsheets. The data within each region was compared to see how the different El Nino-La Nina seasons affected the severity and location of coastal tornado formation in Louisiana. In the future, this research will be expanded by examining the entire Northern Gulf Coast. Keywords: El Nino, La Nina, coastal tornado formation

498276.title: Operational Application of the Flash Flood Four-Panel Technique to the Desert Southwest
498276.authors: Cole Gabos, Univ. of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. I. Christian and K. Christian
498276.abstract: Within the U.S over the last 30 years, flash flooding has been a leading cause of weather-related fatalities. For flash flood operations in the National Weather Service (NWS), Flash Flood Guidance (FFG) has historically been used as one of the primary tools to provide guidance to NWS forecasters on when to issue flash flood advisories and warnings. However, a newly developed technique that utilizes a four-panel structure of multiple real-time variables has the potential to provide a regionally calibrated method for flash flood detection in the Desert Southwest. This region's differences in topography, scattered population density, soil composition and moisture retention, as well as climatological factors such as heavy precipitation during the monsoon season, pose a unique challenge. By combining Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) products, hydrological analysis, and NASA soil moisture data, we hope to expand a four-panel technique to cover the broader four-corners region. After extensive analysis in the Flagstaff, AZ county warning area (CWA), we found 1-hr radar-only Quantitative Precipitation Estimate (1-hr QPE), maximum QPE-to-Gridded Flash Flood Guidance ratio (GFFG), Coupled Routing and Excess Storage (CREST) model unit streamflow, and CREST Hydrophobic Unit Flow to best represent flash flood severity. Our research so far has provided a promising geographically tailored method for flash flood detection in the Flagstaff, AZ region, with several minutes of lead time and increased forecasting confidence. The next steps intend to capture the larger complexities of rainfall, terrain, and soil saturation across the broader Desert Southwest.

498278.title: Chemical Characterization of Atmospheric Methane in Chapel Hill, Georgia
498278.authors: Lila Bakir, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA; and T. Tambe and L. G. Huey
498278.abstract: Chemical Characterization of Atmospheric Methane in Chapel Hill, Georgia Lila Bakir, Trisha Tambe, Dr. Greg Huey Email: lila.bakir@emory.edu School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, 901 Atlantic Drive, Atlanta, GA 30332, USA Rationale: The current study focuses on the air quality of Chapel Hill, a community in suburban-Atlanta. Residents have reported experiencing a range of concerns including a persistent foul smell and unusually high prevalence of diseases, such as cancer [1]. The goal of this research project is to explore the atmospheric composition of this area and to identify potential hazardous compounds that are associated with significant health issues. Methods: A well-instrumented air quality trailer was deployed in the neighborhood of interest from March 11, 2026 to March 30, 2026. The trailer included observations of ozone, aerosols (particulate matter), methane, ethane, and 13C methane. However, power was limited at this site, which precluded the running of more sophisticated instrumentation. For this reason, the trailer was relocated to the South Dekalb Environmental Protection Division (EPD) regulatory site, 4.2 miles away from the previous location. This allowed for the operation of a chemical ionization mass spectrometer in addition to a PICARRO G2401 Gas Concentration Analyzer and provided access to ongoing regulatory measurements. Findings: In the initial deployment, particulate matter and other aerosols were not elevated relative to urban Atlanta. However, nocturnal methane values reached 9 ppm and had a clear isotopic signature of biogenic methane.
