These results indicated that the neighborhood is periodically impacted by emissions from a local landfill. Observations at the South Dekalb site demonstrated the impact of intermittent plumes of methane from the Dekalb County landfill. Furthermore, these plumes were investigated for correlations to a series of compounds including nitroaromatics, organic acids, and organosulfur compounds, all of which revealed a weak positive correlation with the 13C methane. When compared with prevailing wind direction, a majority of plume events in each compound category corresponded with winds from the west. Moreover, to check the accuracy of the wind measurements, SO2 plumes were compared with wind data from our instruments, as well as that from the NOAA HYSPLIT Trajectory model to confirm wind direction veracity. This simultaneously revealed certain Georgia power plants to be a point source for SO2. Conclusions: The Dekalb County landfill is revealed to be a major source of biogenic methane. The high nocturnal values of 13C methane demonstrate that the Chapel Hill community is impacted by emissions from this source. Moreover, aerosol levels were not found to be elevated in the community and no evidence for atmospheric composition was found to explain negative health outcomes in this area. References: [1] Chapel Hill Organization. Chapel Hill Organization. https://www.justiceonchapelhill.org/ (accessed 2026-06-08).

498280.title: Rain-on-snow Ablation in the Ohio River Valley: Synoptic Conditions and Temporal Trends
498280.authors: Zachary Ivor Fuquay, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and R. Hiler and Z. Suriano
498280.abstract: The impacts of liquid precipitation on melting snowpack, known as rain-on-snow ablation (ROS), can be substantial. ROS can cause large volumes of water to enter the environment from the dual sources of runoff, leading to flooding, environmental impacts, and other events. Despite the frequency of ROS and their potential for negative outcomes, research into ROS and specifically into the forcing mechanisms that trigger the events in the eastern United States is lacking. This study evaluates the different synoptic-scale weather types that cause ROS in the Ohio River basin. A Temporal Synoptic Index classification procedure from January 1980-December 2024 was conducted. Results indicate that there are 5 synoptic types labeled by their most notable center of pressure. Evaluations into the inter- and intra-annual frequency have been conducted along with reanalysis of the specific weather conditions for each type and possible related teleconnections. This informs us of how these events change and vary with time, finding there are statistically significant trends in the temporal data for select types and ROS occurrence as a whole in the research area. It was also found that teleconnections play very little role in the occurrence of ROS synoptic types. These results could aid in the development of better forecast methods of these events and therefore improved preparedness by communities and emergency management personnel.

498281.title: Assessing the Performance of Ground-truthed Nature-based Solutions Against Flooding in Gurabo Watershed, Puerto Rico.
498281.authors: Anthony Eduardo Cruz Hernandez, New York City College of Technology (CUNY), New York, NY
498281.abstract: Nature-Based Solutions (NBS) are increasingly recognized as sustainable strategies for reducing flood risk while providing environmental and social benefits. Following the ground-truthing and validation of candidate NBS sites in Gurabo Watershed, Puerto Rico, this study assesses their potential performance against flooding by examining the spatial and environmental characteristics that influence their effectiveness. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are used to evaluate validated NBS locations in relation to hydrologic features, topography, soil properties, land use, and urban development. The analysis also compares different NBS types to identify spatial patterns and conditions that may influence their capacity to manage stormwater and reduce flood impacts. By linking ground-truthed NBS locations with flood-related landscape characteristics, the study provides a more realistic assessment of where NBS implementation may offer the greatest flood-mitigation potential. The findings can support future prioritization of NBS sites, improve flood-mitigation planning, and strengthen the integration of field-informed geospatial analysis into Nature-Based Solution assessments.

498282.title: Storm Surge and Effective Social Media Communication
498282.authors: Peyton Nicole Galyean, OU School of Meteorology, Norman, OK; and K. Schmidt, C. Lacey, and A. V. Raaijmakers
498282.abstract: Hurricanes are among the costliest natural disasters in the world and pose a variety of risks, although one of their most impactful is storm surge. Despite accounting for the greatest proportion of hurricane related deaths, the U.S public continues to underestimate its threat relative to wind. Historically, storm surge has been underrepresented in risk messaging, leaving coastal populations unprepared to take necessary action. Recent work by Rosen et al. (2021) and Krocak et al. (2023) examined how the National Weather Service forecast offices present tropical cyclone risk information on social media. The findings indicated that effective messaging across various platforms includes probabilistic information presented with numeric values. This conveys a shift is needed from location based uncertainty toward severity and protective action guidance as landfall approaches. To evaluate whether these recommendations have been adopted in any capacity, this research will follow the methodology of Rosen et al. (2021) and Krocak et al. (2023) to analyze NWS storm surge messaging during the 2022-2024 Atlantic hurricane landfalls. Tweets from various offices are scraped and a content analysis is performed to evaluate how WFO’s present uncertainty guidance and information type. Findings will reveal to what degree NWS offices have implemented evidence based communication methods for improving social media storm surge messaging following the release of the aforementioned research.

498284.title: Data Center Cooling Systems Under Climate Change
498284.authors: Cole Gabos, University of North Dakota, Plymouth, MN; and Z. He
498284.abstract: The increasing number of data centers (DC’s) worldwide built to support the growing demand for internet services and artificial intelligence (AI) increases global power consumption. The cooling systems alone can account for roughly 40% of data center total energy usage, but free cooling (FC), which relies on low ambient temperatures to cool the DC, can reduce energy consumption and improve Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE). However, in a future climate with higher ambient temperatures, it is vital to investigate how DC cooling systems and their energy demand may be impacted. This study examines how current FC types and chiller configuration usage hours, energy and water consumption, and cooling efficiency are affected for three DC locations: Altoona, IA; Sterling, VA; and Los Lunas, NM under future climate scenarios SSP2-4.5 and SSP3-7.0. Daily high temperatures are expected to increase year-round across all three sites under future climate scenarios, while dewpoint and wet bulb temperatures increase more notably in the winter months. As a result, most FC systems will lose progressively more availability hours, with declining chiller performance and increased mechanical cooling driving most of the rise in energy consumption. The only exception is FC for warm-temperature liquid cooling systems, which can keep its availability window and yield lower total system energy use. Dry FC with adiabatic assistance requires significantly lower water withdrawal than wet-cooling, though its water consumption will grow over years with warmer conditions and vary across sites. Our initial results show how climate change may reshape the availability, effectiveness, and energy and water footprint of different cooling systems in DCs informing siting and climate adaptation strategies.

498290.title: Modernizing NOAA’s Satellite and Data Systems
498290.authors: Irene Parker, NOAA - Acting Assistant Administrator for NESDIS, Silver Spring, MD; and J. G. Hartley
498290.abstract: NOAA's National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) provides secure and timely access to global environmental data and information from satellites and other sources to promote and protect the nation's security, environment, economy, and quality of life. NESDIS is undergoing organizational and technical transformations to modernize its enterprise, strengthen core capabilities, and better support NOAA’s operational weather mission. Next-generation observation and data programs are focused on collecting, scientifically evaluating, and integrating the highest-value data sources to enhance forecast accuracy and decision support. This focus includes commercially-sourced satellite data and migrating enterprise systems to the cloud, ensuring continuous, scalable delivery of environmental information vital for decision-making. Value to the public will be enhanced through effective private-public partnerships, strategic relationships across the globe, and coordinated future architecture planning. NESDIS remains committed to operational agility and innovation as technologies, data standards, and stakeholder needs continue to evolve.

498291.title: Flooding in a Low-Lying Coastal Community of New York City:Hydroclimatic Drivers and Compound Risk in Broad Channel
498291.abstract: Broad Channel, a low-lying island community in Jamaica Bay, New York City, is vulnerable to flooding from heavy rainfall, high tides, sea-level rise, and limited stormwater drainage.Understanding how these interacting hydroclimatic drivers influence flood risk is increasingly important as coastal water levels rise and extreme precipitation changes. This study integrates observational and modeled datasets to examine rainfall variability, tidal water levels, sea-level rise, and stormwater flooding in Broad Channel. Daily gridMET precipitation from 1979–2025 was analyzed to evaluate long-term changes in annual rainfall and heavy-rainfall frequency. Six-minute NOAA water-level observations from The Battery were used to characterize tidal variability, while NYC Department of Environmental Protection stormwater-flood scenarios were compared under different rainfall and sea-level conditions.Climate projections and coastal-exposure datasets were used to place the observed changes within the broader context of future flood risk. Mean annual precipitation was approximately 44.9 inches, with no statistically significant long-term trend (+0.78 in/decade; p = 0.31). In contrast, days receiving at least 1.9 inches of rainfall increased significantly by approximately 0.32 days per decade (p = 0.014), indicating that heavy-rainfall events are becoming more frequent despite relatively stable annual totals. NOAA observations show that tidal variability strongly controls coastal water levels, explaining approximately 97% of observed variance. Flood-scenario comparisons further indicate that sea-level rise alone could increase rain-flooded area by approximately 11% by 2050 under the same rainfall conditions, as elevated coastal water levels reduce stormwater drainage capacity. These results demonstrate that future flood risk in Broad Channel cannot be evaluated from precipitation trends alone. Increasing rainfall extremes, rising coastal water levels, tidal timing, and drainage limitations interact to amplify flooding. The findings highlight the importance of integrating precipitation and coastal-water-level information when evaluating compound flooding and planning adaptation for low-lying urban coastal communities.

498293.title: Climatology of Precipitation During Rain-on-Snow Events
498293.authors: Ryan Hiler, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and P. J. Wells and Z. Suriano
498293.abstract: Whenever rain falls on top of snow, it can cause the snowpack to start melting at a rapid pace, leading to substantial runoff that contributes to localized flooding events and, in extreme cases, lasting impacts to communities. Researching past rain-on-snow events can help improve future forecasts for runoff induced flooding, especially for communities in flood-prone areas. This research quantifies the magnitude of precipitation and potential runoff during rain-on-snow events, by snow season (Oct-Sep) from 1981-2023 across the continental US (CONUS). The average magnitude of precipitation during rain-on-snow was spatially variable with higher precipitation occurring, on average, in more southerly regions and the west coast. Collectively, rain-on-snow precipitation magnitude had a direct, positive, correlation with the average magnitude of potential runoff. Using the Sen’s slope and Mann Kendall tests, temporal trends in the magnitude of precipitation and potential runoff indicated three different areas of CONUS that exhibit statistical significance in both variables: central Michigan, southeastern Ohio, and central Missouri. Research in these three areas has found that while the magnitude of precipitation varies by year, the overall trend of the magnitude of precipitation has increased with time within each event. Further, research indicates that extreme rain-on-snow precipitation events fall within the top percentiles of all precipitation events in some CONUS regions, while being below the 50th percentile in others.

498294.title: Identifying and Tracking Observed Cold Pool Outflows and Sea Breeze Fronts Utilizing METGOAT
498294.authors: Brianna Marie Saunders, State University of New York at Oswego, Oswego, NY; and E. Caldon and A. J. Drager
498294.abstract: Tracking cold pool outflows and sea breeze fronts is essential for understanding how these processes work. Manual map analysis and tracking have been essential to meteorology for decades. Some automatic tracking methods exist; however, they each have major limitations and are not universally applicable across different types of observational and model-based datasets. A new manual tracking method has been developed to track cold pool outflows, sea breeze fronts, and bay breezes. Each of these phenomena is important for triggering thunderstorm formation. Cold pool outflows are dense domes of cooled air that expand and spread across the ground, formed due to evaporation within thunderstorms. Sea-breeze and bay-breeze fronts are sharp boundaries where cooler and denser air from an ocean, bay, or other large body of water moves inland and collides with warmer air over the land. As the dense air associated with each of these boundaries advances, it provides a lifting mechanism for warm environmental air that can initiate storm formation. Our tracking method identifies cold pool outflows, their parent storms, and the secondary convective cells that they trigger. It also identifies sea-breeze and bay-breeze fronts and the cells that they initiate. We perform our manual tracking by using the web app METGOAT (Meteorological and Environmental Tool for Graphical Object Annotation and Tracking) to draw and label cold pool outflows and sea-breeze/bay-breeze fronts. Eventually, all of the manual tracking data will be used to train an AI-based algorithm for automated tracking. This presentation will focus on tracking these features in observational datasets, including satellite and radar observations where the ordinarily invisible boundaries can sometimes be identified based on the locations of clouds and non-meteorological scatterers. Field campaign cases from the TRacking Aerosol Convection interactions ExpeRiment (TRACER) near Houston, Texas are analyzed as a testbed for developing the tracking method and evaluating its performance.

498295.title: Analyzing Correlation Between Observations and ERA5 Reanalysis of Cold Air Damming Events in Southern Appalachia
498295.authors: William R John, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL
498295.abstract: Cold-air damming (CAD) is a phenomenon in which cold, stable air becomes “wedged” against the slopes of a mountain range like the Appalachians. This creates unseasonably cold temperatures, winter precipitation, and societal disruptions in places like Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia. This project evaluates Appalachian CAD events by comparing conditions observed with sonde observations to collocated ERA5 reanalysis data at locations along the eastern edge of the Appalachian Mountains (Atlanta/Peachtree City, Georgia; Greensboro, North Carolina; and Roanoke/Blacksburg, Virginia). Our goal is to elucidate conditions at the southern end of CAD events and to determine the utility of ERA5 reanalysis for research of this phenomenon.

498296.title: Using dual-polarization phased-array radar to characterize the rapid evolution of downbursts in central Oklahoma
498296.authors: Madison Marker, NSSL, Norman, OK; and A. A. Alford and C. M. Kuster
498296.abstract: The National Weather Service relies on the NEXRAD network for crucial real-time data in order to make important severe weather warning decisions. These mechanically rotating radars deliver full volumetric scans every four to seven minutes. However, this update frequency may not adequately sample useful precursor signatures to rapidly evolving severe weather events. Phased-array radar (PAR) technology provides one way to mitigate this temporal limitation through rapid scanning enabled by electronic beam steering. Therefore, scientists at the NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL) are using a research dual-polarization PAR, called the Advanced Technology Demonstrator (ATD), that can collect volumetric updates every 1.5 minutes or less to study rapidly-evolving precursor signatures. Downbursts are a prime example of rapidly evolving convective phenomena that are difficult to anticipate with sufficient lead time using the NEXRAD system. They are typically initiated by melting and precipitation loading in the midlevels, and are capable of producing damaging winds at the surface. This presentation overviews an analysis of downburst precursor signatures observed in specific differential phase (KDP) and differential reflectivity (ZDR) using rapid-update ATD data. Specifically, the analysis includes KDP cores, which are regions of high KDP that form near the environmental melting layer, are often associated with downbursts, and may be useful for their prediction. The descent of the KDP core prior to downburst development is apparent using the ATD data. The ATD observations are also compared with observations from conventional radars to evaluate the practical merits of PAR technology for severe weather operations.

498297.title: Tracking Trapping: Phytoplankton Community Dynamics Within Coherent Mesoscale Eddies Revealed by NASA PACE
498297.authors: Cole Sprinkle, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; NASA, Washington, DC; and D. S. Grimmer, A. Jones-Kellett, and H. Houskeeper
498297.abstract: Eddies are isolated, circulating masses of water in the ocean formed from seawater density differences. Mesoscale eddies spanning 10s-100s of kilometers can exist for weeks to months where they effectively trap and transport water within their cores. Eddies play a crucial role in dictating nutrient regimes by horizontally and vertically transporting nutrients, which are crucial for promoting phytoplankton productivity, thus supporting the base of the ocean ecosystem. Differences in the chemical and physical structure of eddy waters is anticipated to modify the composition of eddy phytoplankton communities, thereby affecting the productivity and export services associated with phytoplankton biomass in Earth system modeling. Observing changes in optical properties associated with different phytoplankton taxanomic composition is expected to be supported by hyperspectral satellite missions. The NASA Plankton Aerosol Cloud ocean Ecosystem (PACE) satellite provides near-global hyperspectral ocean imagery from its ocean-viewing spectrometer that may support the first operational phytoplankton community composition (PCC) retrievals. PACE launched in early 2024, and the newly available imagery and associated algorithms support new opportunities to investigate how eddy dynamics regulate PCC. Coherent eddies are identified herein using a reverse-time particle simulation to measure coherency, where circulation rotates and propagates as a unified whole with limited leakage, supporting an isolated environment for PCC development. This study updates an atlas of Rotationally Coherent Lagrangian Vortices (RCLVs) for the year of 2025 for the North Pacific gyre. Temporal PCC dynamics within RCLVs were estimated using a pigmentation concentration algorithm. One cyclonic and one anticyclonic eddy were chosen for case studies monitoring shifts in PCC over time. General cyclonic and anticyclonic RCLV behavior were compared by evaluating sea surface temperature anomaly, chlorophyll-a concentration, and size. This study represents a novel approach of using remote sensing data to evaluate PCC composition within coherent mesoscale eddies. Further work should evaluate the effectiveness of different pigmentation algorithms, as well as represent different regions and include larger datasets.

498300.title: South British Columbia Coldsnap: Case Study for 2008 - 2009
498300.authors: Vanessa Villegas, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; and M. Costa
498300.abstract: From December 12th, 2008, to January 3rd, 2009, Lower British Columbia experienced one of its snowiest and coldest stretches. In several affected areas, nearly 100 centimeters of snow were recorded during this period, making it memorable. Data from ECMWF and Environment Canada help support theories about how unusual this event was. The strong La Niña present since the beginning of the year producing enhanced moisture transport into the region, with multiple lows moving through, producing different types of precipitation. The cyclones produced snow, rain, and a mix of the two, in the form of snow showers. The winter weather affected the cities of Vancouver and Abbotsford and subsequently motivated improvements in forecasting to support the Winte Analysis of atmospheric circulation patterns, temperature anomalies, and precipitation characteristics demonstrates the exceptional nature of this event within the historical record. The combination of a persistent La Niña, repeated cyclone passages, and sustained cold air produced an unusually prolonged period of snowfall and below-normal temperatures across southwestern British Columbia. This case study provides insight into the large-scale processes associated with the unusual winter weather in the Pacific Northwest and their impacts on forecasting and community preparedness.

498303.title: Integrating Remote Sensing and Environmental Data to Characterize Arctic Permafrost Change
498303.authors: Evelyn Pulla, New York City College of Technology, Brooklyn, NY; and P. Medina
498303.abstract: Arctic permafrost contains substantial stores of organic carbon whose decomposition following thaw can contribute to atmospheric greenhouse-gas emissions, including methane (CH₄) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). Because the Arctic is geographically extensive and difficult to monitor through ground-based observations alone, satellite and airborne remote sensing provide an important means of characterizing environmental conditions associated with permafrost vulnerability. This study develops a data-driven framework for integrating remote sensing indicators to investigate spatial and temporal patterns relevant to Arctic permafrost change. As an initial component of this project, MODIS Terra MOD11A1 Land Surface Temperature (LST) data were analyzed over western Greenland for July 13-26, 2026. Daytime and nighttime observations were processed to characterize the spatial distribution and temporal variability of surface temperature. Missing observations were addressed through statistical data imputation prior to analysis, allowing spatial and temporal summaries to be constructed from an incomplete satellite record. Descriptive statistics and spatial visualizations were used to examine temperature distributions, day-night differences, and areas exhibiting elevated variability. The preliminary analysis demonstrates distinct spatial and temporal patterns in surface temperature across western Greenland, including persistent differences between coastal and inland regions and systematic differences between daytime and nighttime observations. These patterns suggest that LST can provide a useful environmental indicator for identifying regions where additional permafrost-related observations should be investigated. Temperature conditions are particularly relevant to permafrost studies because sustained changes in surface thermal regimes can influence the seasonal active layer and the stability of underlying frozen ground. The next phase of the study will integrate additional remotely sensed environmental variables, including vegetation dynamics, snow coverage, sea-ice-related observations, and elevation and terrain information. Airborne Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) data and other geospatial data products will be considered for characterizing fine-scale topographic and surface features that may complement satellite observations. These heterogeneous datasets will be spatially and temporally aligned to construct a unified environmental dataset for subsequent feature engineering and machine-learning analysis. A further objective is to investigate the relationship between environmental indicators and methane emissions from Arctic permafrost regions. In particular, future work will examine whether mathematical and data-driven models can be used to estimate or impute missing methane observations and characterize the spatial distribution of methane hotspots. Integrating methane observations with LST, snow coverage, vegetation, terrain, and other remotely sensed variables may provide a framework for identifying environmental conditions associated with enhanced methane release. This work establishes a foundation for combining remote sensing, geospatial analysis, statistical imputation, and machine learning to study Arctic permafrost dynamics. The resulting framework is intended to support more comprehensive characterization of environmental change across regions where direct observations remain sparse.

498306.title: Spatial Variations of Low Visibility in New Zealand
498306.authors: Miles Gray, SUNY Oswego, Waterloo, NY
498306.abstract: Title: Spatial Variations and Weather Associated with Low Visibility in New Zealand Low visibility in New Zealand has caused many societal issues, such as aircraft delays and traffic accidents, making an understanding of the spatial variations of low visibility in New Zealand an important topic to investigate. To our knowledge, this may be the first study to investigate the spatial variation of visibility in New Zealand. Hourly surface weather data, including visibility and present weather observations, were obtained from the National Center for Environmental Information and analyzed for 19 stations across New Zealand for the time period of 2020 to 2025. This time period was chosen based on the availability of consistent weather information for a large number of locations distributed across both the northern and southern islands of New Zealand.Visibility hours were defined when visibility had a distance ≤ 6.5 miles and was stratified into three categories: good (3 < X <= 6.5 miles), limited (0.5 <= X < 3 miles), and very limited (X < 0.5 miles). Present weather codes were examined when a visibility hour occurred and the most frequent present weather included reports of drizzle, precipitation, mist, smoke, haze, and fog. Visibility hours were found most frequently near Wellington and occurred the least frequent near both Christchurch and Auckland. Precipitation was found to be the most common present weather type that occurred during good and limited visibility hours. The greatest percentage of visibility hours that reported very limited visibility, the most impactful, occurred near both Christchurch and Dunedin. Fog was reported as the most common present weather type to occur during very limited visibility hours.

498309.title: AI-Driven Extreme Weather Event Forecasting Over The United Arab Emirates
498309.authors: Abdulla AlRaisi, Abu Dhabi Polytechnic, Shakhbout City, AZ, United arab emirates; and A. parottil, A. S. alkhemeiri, N. A. ALRashdi, and M. Elge
498309.abstract: Extreme weather events pose growing risks to human health, infrastructure, and water resources across the Middle East, making accurate and timely forecasting essential for early warning and climate resilience. This study evaluates the AI-based Pangu-Weather model, a deep-learning global forecasting system trained on ERA5 reanalysis, in simulating two high-impact case studies over the United Arab Emirates: the 15-16 April 2024 UAE–Oman flood and the June 2021 Arabian Peninsula heatwave. Model performance is benchmarked against ERA5 and, for the flood case, ECMWF's operational High-Resolution Forecast (HRES). For the flood event, Pangu-Weather forecasts of Integrated Vapor Transport (IVT) and 850-hPa winds are compared against ERA5 and HRES at hourly intervals; for the heatwave, forecasted 2 m air temperature, Heat Index, and wet-bulb temperature are compared against ERA5 across a five-day evolution. In both cases, Pangu-Weather reproduces the large-scale structure, timing, and persistence of the events with strong fidelity, correctly capturing the onset, intensification, and decay of the flood's moisture plume and the multi-day build-up and peak of the heatwave's thermal stress. Consistent limitations emerge across both hazard types: Pangu-Weather generates smoother, spatially damped fields relative to higher-resolution references and systematically underestimates the intensity of extremes - peak IVT during the flood and maximum temperatures during the heatwave - while showing minor positional drift during event decay. These findings demonstrate that AI-based forecasting can reliably capture the dominant physical processes driving high-impact weather in arid, data-sparse regions at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional NWP, while highlighting a shared tendency to underrepresent the most extreme conditions -an important consideration for operational early-warning applications in climate-vulnerable regions such as the UAE.

498310.title: Validating Soil Microplastic Risk Across Texas: A Machine Learning and Spatial Validation Approach
498310.authors: Ahmad Dawoud, NSF, Manhattan, NY; and A. Upadhyay
498310.abstract: Spatial risk models are increasingly used to target environmental sampling where direct measurements are unavailable, but they are rarely tested against independent observations, and their accuracy is often inflated by validation that ignores spatial dependence. This study asks whether county-level environmental and anthropogenic variables predict independently measured soil microplastic concentrations, whether data-driven models outperform expert-weighted indices, and which variables most consistently track predicted contamination. A baseline risk index was constructed for all 254 Texas counties by combining eight normalized environmental, agricultural, infrastructure, and socioeconomic indicators through GIS-based multi-criteria decision analysis with Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) weighting. A georeferenced database of measured concentrations is being compiled from peer-reviewed literature, recording detection method, particle-size range, sampling depth, and land use for each observation so that measurements from different extraction protocols are not treated as equivalent. Predictions are evaluated against these observations using rank agreement and high-versus-low separation. Random Forest and gradient-boosted models are compared against a null model, the AHP index as a single predictor, and a regression baseline. All models are evaluated under spatially blocked cross-validation, holding out whole geographic blocks so training and test data are geographically separated. Random k-fold validation is run in parallel, and the difference quantifies the optimism introduced by spatial autocorrelation. Permutation importance and SHAP values identify which variables contribute consistently across folds and model types. The baseline index classified 50 counties as predicted high risk, 103 as moderate, and 101 as low, concentrated in eastern Texas and along the Gulf Coast. Correlation analysis identified two statistically independent contributing pathways, urban and agricultural. Sensitivity testing across four weighting schemes found nine counties remained top-ranked under every scheme, indicating priority designations do not depend on a single weighting assumption. Validation and model comparison are ongoing. Expected outcomes include a quantified correspondence between predicted risk and measured concentrations, a comparison establishing whether data-driven models improve on expert weighting, and a stable set of predictors identified across modeling approaches. Reporting the gap between spatially blocked and random validation is expected to show how conventional validation overstates performance for spatially structured environmental data. Weak or negative validation results will be reported rather than omitted. Findings will inform a field sampling campaign across predicted high, moderate, and low risk counties.

498311.title: A Global Model of Dust Mineralogy: Impacts on Aerosol Absorption, Radiative Balance and Climate
498311.authors: Bofan Liu, Hong Kong Baptist University, Kowloon Tong, Hong Kong, China; and F. Wang, Y. Balkanski, X. Wang, and M. Gao
498311.abstract: Mineral dust has large effects on the Earth’s radiation budget; however, model parameterizations of its optical properties in climate models still harbor substantial uncertainties, particularly due to simplified representations of mineralogical composition. To address this limitation, we develop and apply a global dust mineralogy framework within the Community Atmosphere Model (CAM) version 6, in which spatially varying mineralogical information is explicitly coupled to dust optical properties. We develop a mineralogy-constrained dust optical parameterization and use two independent mineralogical datasets, the soil-based GMINER30 dataset and satellite-derived mineral abundances from NASA's Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT), to constrain regional dust refractive indices within this framework. Both datasets are incorporated using a wavelength-dependent refractive index mixing scheme, and sensitivity simulations for 2011–2014 are compared with a control simulation employing the default CAM dust optical properties. The revised mineralogical parameterizations produce substantial changes in absorbing aerosol optical depth (AAOD), with regional annual-mean differences ranging from approximately 10% to 160% depending on region and mineralogical dataset. In contrast, annual-mean dust aerosol optical depth (DAOD) differences remain comparatively small, generally within a few percent for most regions and below 20% in all regions except North America. These results indicate that mineralogical variability primarily modifies dust absorption efficiency rather than atmospheric dust loading. Enhanced dust absorption leads to pronounced shortwave radiative flux perturbations and regionally significant near-surface air temperature responses of up to approximately 1 K, whereas the global-mean temperature response remains modest. These results demonstrate that dust mineralogical composition constitutes an important source of uncertainty in simulated dust radiative effects and highlight the value of incorporating mineralogical information to improve the representation of dust–radiation interactions in Earth system models.

498313.title: Preparing for and Responding to Hurricane Helene: Emergency Communications in Haywood County, North Carolina
498313.authors: Danielle Yvonne Campbell Snuffer, University of North Carolina Asheville, Asheville, NC; and A. Richmond and C. Cook
498313.abstract: Communication within the National Weather Service, their partners such as emergency management, and the public is very important, especially in the case of severe weather. Communication outlets must relay crucial information, such as warnings to the public to maintain preparedness, for protection of life and property. This presentation examines a survey conducted on emergency communications before and after Hurricane Helene in Haywood County, North Carolina. The survey covered the impacts on the community, where and how information was being distributed, as well as what communication strategies may benefit the community moving forward in future emergencies. The impacts of Hurricane Helene on Haywood county included mass power outages and infrastructure damage where 98.6% of survey respondents lost communication. Even before the arrival of Hurricane Helene, results showed that only 65.2% of the public received preparedness information (with 66.4% receiving information via social media) while 34.8% did not. Following Hurricane Helene, individuals were asked how they received information after the storm. 85.0% of respondents said “word of mouth”, likely due to the fact that power and lines of communication had not been restored until days after. Finally, respondents were asked how they would prefer to receive emergency preparedness information put out by the county in the future. The most preferred communication method by 64.3% of respondents was a Haywood Alert (text) message while the least preferred method chosen was printed flyers on message boards (21.3% of respondents). Effective emergency communications is a matter of importance as it is necessary that each party communicates information in a timely manner to provide the public with a strong understanding of the situation so they may act accordingly.

498315.title: Assessing Precipitation Measurement Accuracy during the 2025 CROCUS Urban Flooding Campaign
498315.authors: Grace I Van Dyke, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL; University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign, Champaign, IL; and D. A. Hence and S. W. Nesbitt
498315.abstract: While in situ precipitation measurements are heavily relied upon for examining precipitation behavior and evolution, assessing instrument accuracy in different precipitation environments is necessary to determine how they can experience errors associated with high wind speeds, impeded catch, or other issues. In particular, previously observed overestimation errors need to be better understood in the precipitation instrument Hydreon Rain Gauge Model RG-15, which is commonly deployed in Sage nodes in urban areas to measure fine-scale precipitation variability within cities, yet has been shown to experience errors above particular wind speed thresholds. This study compares Sage node precipitation accumulations across Chicago with other in situ and remote sensing precipitation observations collected during a 2025 CROCUS Urban Flooding and Rainfall precipitation event, including U.S. Geological Survey tipping buckets and quantitative precipitation estimates from WSR-88D radar reflectivity and NOAA Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor datasets (MRMS). This analysis will determine the extent of the overestimation error at each examined node and investigate the atmospheric behavior most associated with observed data errors, to characterize the conditions in which Sage instruments are most susceptible to accumulation errors. Consistent with prior research, initial analysis of differences between Sage accumulation values and other accumulation datasets find large variability between Sage data and other datasets’ accumulation values during periods with high wind speeds, yet this behavior is more exaggerated at some nodes than others. This analysis will use radar reflectivity to examine the evolution of precipitation features affecting each node, to identify whether common behaviors exist during these periods of conflicting observations. Further analysis will examine how to correct for these overestimations in different environments.

498317.title: Isolating and Characterizing Elevated Aerosol Profiles in the Upper Troposphere and Lower Stratosphere Using Multi-Platform Remote Sensing
498317.authors: Deandre' Macri, Air Force Institute of Technology, Fairborn
498317.abstract: The vertical distribution of atmospheric aerosols remains difficult to characterize because aerosol populations vary considerably with altitude, location, and atmospheric conditions. This study characterizes aerosol environments using complementary ground-based and satellite remote sensing observations. The analysis examines aerosol vertical distribution, optical properties, and variability, with a specific focus on elevated aerosol layers within the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). Observations are obtained from ground-based Micro Pulse Lidar (MPL), the Atmospheric Lidar (ATLID) aboard the Earth Cloud Aerosol and Radiation Explorer (EarthCARE) satellite, and the Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET). MPL measurements are used to resolve the temporal and vertical structure of aerosol layers and retrieve aerosol optical properties, including extinction, backscatter, and depolarization. EarthCARE ATLID observations provide complementary spaceborne measurements of aerosol vertical structure and optical properties across broader geographic regions, while AERONET measurements provide independent column-integrated aerosol optical depth and related aerosol properties. By combining these complementary observing methods, elevated aerosol layers are isolated from the broader atmospheric aerosol profile to specifically characterize aerosol occurrence and properties within the UTLS. Together, these datasets are used to characterize aerosol loading, identify elevated aerosol layers, and examine variability in aerosol properties with altitude and across different atmospheric environments. The integration of these observing systems provides a framework for evaluating aerosol distributions across multiple spatial and temporal scales while also identifying limitations associated with detecting and characterizing aerosols at higher altitudes. This multi-platform approach highlights the upper-atmospheric aerosol profile and provides a more focused assessment of aerosol structure within the UTLS, where observations remain comparatively limited. This research improves the characterization of vertically resolved aerosol environments and demonstrates the value of combining ground-based lidar, satellite lidar, and column-integrated observations for atmospheric aerosol studies. Keywords: Aerosols, upper troposphere and lower stratosphere, elevated aerosols, Micro Pulse Lidar, EarthCARE, ATLID, AERONET, remote sensing

498319.title: One Risk, Four Audiences: Communicating Compound Space Weather Exposure Beyond the Forecasting Community
498319.abstract: Space weather communication to non-specialist audiences typically treats "the public" as one undifferentiated group, when risk tolerance, prior knowledge, and actionable takeaways in practice vary sharply by sector. This talk draws on direct delivery of tailored space weather risk communication across four distinct non-specialist audiences: manufacturing decision-makers (Scotland Manufacturing Conference), amateur radio operators, marine and sailing communities, and cruise ship passengers (Fred Olsen Cruise Lines guest-speaker programme). Using one consistent core framing — geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) and GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) scintillation as simultaneous, commonly-conflated risks, or "double exposure" — each audience required different language, evidence, and depth: manufacturers needed GPS-timing synchronisation risk to production lines; radio operators needed propagation-level detail; sailors needed a personal account of GPS-guided race-mark drift during the May 2024 Gannon storm; cruise passengers needed an accessible aurora-forecasting narrative. Comparing these four deliveries surfaces a practical framework for calibrating space weather risk communication to audience expertise and stake, offering forecasters and communicators outside academia a reusable model for reaching sectors that current public-engagement efforts rarely target directly.

498320.title: Performance Benchmarking of Unidata MetPy in a CI/CD Workflow
498320.authors: Jaye Norman, UCAR, Boulder, CO; University of Delaware, Newark, DE; and L. Li, S. C. Arms, D. Camron, and R. M. May
498320.abstract: MetPy is an open-source meteorological calculation and visualization software hosted and maintained by NSF Unidata. A recent enhancement objective of the MetPy development team is to scale MetPy and make it suitable for calculations with large datasets in gridded data formats. As such, the developers of MetPy will be incorporating C++ code into the source software with the goal of making soundings functions more time efficient and functional over large-scale grids. As part of this initiative, performative benchmarking was incorporated into MetPy’s continuous integration/continuous performance workflow. Benchmarking is the act of timing snippets of code in order to quantify the performance of functions and code structures within a project. This allows developers and users to identify fast and slow functions and see the change in run-time with the history of a project. In the case of MetPy, benchmarking is performed by airspeed velocity (asv), an open-source package for benchmarking python codebases. Thanks to the implementation of publication functions in asv, the results of these benchmarks are then publicly available on a webpage hosted by Unidata in an easily digestible and intuitive format. Continuous integration/continuous development is the act of automatically and frequently building and testing a codebase. For the benchmarking of MetPy, the continuous integration/continuous development workflow uses Jenkins as a pipeline, Docker software for portability and maintainability, and GitHub Actions to generate and host a static page of historical time performance results for the code base. This creates a secure, consistent, and autonomous workflow which keeps a results webpage up to date with recent additions. This poster explores the process of benchmarking MetPy’s python codebase and incorporating into a workflow the necessary steps for autonomous time efficiency measurements. The roles of the aforementioned softwares are explored in depth as well as their justification for implementation. The long-term goal is for the future MetPy community to use and benefit from these measurements in their use and development cases. The results of the benchmarking are also viewed as a time-scaled performance evaluation, with a focus on future development for a faster, more user-friendly experience.

498324.title: Impacts of the 43 Road Fire on the Quality Assurance and Operational Processes at the Oklahoma Mesonet
498324.authors: Amanda Mae Voth, Oklahoma Climatological Survey, Norman, OK; and E. J. Becker, C. M. Luttrell, and C. A. Fiebrich
498324.abstract: The 43 Road Fire burned in Woodward County, Oklahoma on 17 February 2026, threatening structures and prompting evacuations. The fire burned through the Oklahoma Mesonet station southwest of Woodward, damaging weather and soil-monitoring instruments and degrading data quality across multiple sensors. This data was promptly flagged by quality assurance (QA) staff at the Oklahoma Mesonet to prevent delivering non-representative weather information to decision-makers. The QA staff also analyzes weather data from extreme events, including fires such as this, that impact Mesonet stations for future reference. This project aims to form a new case study for QA staff to review during future wildland fire events that affect Mesonet stations. The study analyzes temperature data collected during the fire, identifies impacted sensors, and describes the communication process used to relay issues to field technicians tasked with restoring normal station operation in the days following this fire.

498328.title: Meteorological Influences on Mule Deer Migratory Patterns in Wyoming
498328.authors: Caroline Solseth, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND; and J. Carstens, M. Schmitt, and K. Stears
498328.abstract: Mule deer migration in mountainous terrain is controlled by many factors, including phenological cues given off by plants. We hypothesize that meteorological factors such as wind and precipitation have significant impacts on migratory patterns on both weather and climate time scales. For example, mule deer in southwestern Wyoming “surf the green wave,” where they follow the green-up of plants in the Spring by moving upward and northward, and vice versa in the Fall. This may be related to odor cues from upstream vegetation, advected by the wind. Some winters lack the needed amount of precipitation and ensuing snowmelt, which can translate into less vegetation and forage available for mule deer. This poster studies how rain and wind patterns and variability affect mule deer migration on time scales from days to years. We use reanalysis and observational data to track precipitation and wind patterns dating back to 2016, when a widespread effort began to track mule deer migrations by the Wyoming Migration Initiative. Reanalysis data comes from ERA5, which outputs wind, precipitation, and dozens of additional parameters on a 0.25-deg hourly grid. Higher-resolution observations come from the regional ASOS network and the NASA IMERG gridded precipitation dataset (0.1-deg spatial grid with 30-minute temporal resolution). Weather patterns will then be compared to select mule deer migratory tracks to investigate how meteorological factors influence the onset, stopovers, and completion of the migrations. Understanding relationships between meteorology and migratory patterns will help improve future wildlife management and conservation efforts. Future work will explore the potential to forecast migratory patterns using numerical weather prediction and atmospheric dispersion models.

498330.title: The Relationship Between the Thermodynamic Environment and RainEvents in the KPOP-MS 2023 Field Campaign
498330.authors: Emma K. Benedict, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and J. Kang, S. Yoon, C. C. Nam, S. H. Kim, K. L. Rasmussen, and G. Lee
498330.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) account for a significant portion of summer precipitation over the Korean Peninsula. This study investigates thermodynamic factors (e.g., moisture, CAPE, and CIN) to examine the relationship between MCS-driven rainfall and the atmospheric environment. To achieve this, we used sounding and AWS data from the 2023 KPOP-MS field campaign. Specifically, we examined how thermodynamic factors and wind differ across dry, proceeding, and rain conditions. We also analyzed thermodynamic profiles and rainfall during Typhoon Khanun, which occurred during the observation period, in order to highlight MCS-related thermodynamic signature differentiated from synoptic/Typhoon driven rain setups. Three main characteristics were observed in the isolated MCS events: easterly winds, moderate CAPE, and an inverted V-shape near the surface in the composite Skew-T log-P diagrams. Further thermodynamic analysis revealed that mid-level dry air and low-level moisture enhance strong convection. Key indicators, CAPE and precipitable water, increased immediately before rainfall, whereas non-precipitating regions exhibited near-zero CAPE. These results could potentially contribute to the improvement of the prediction of these late summer MCSs.

498331.title: How Variable Forcings Shape Ensemble Distributions in Lorenz-96
498331.authors: Asher Creager, Ohio State University, Columbus, OH; and M. Y. Chan and Z. Liu
498331.abstract: The behavior of the atmosphere is strongly shaped by external forcings that vary temporally. For example, diurnal to seasonal variations in incoming solar radiation influence the general circulation of the atmosphere. Such variations therefore influence the behavior of probabilistic forecasts of weather and climate. Given the importance of probabilistic forecasts for risk assessments across many facets of society, it is important to understand those influences. This study investigates the influence of time-varying external forcings on forecast distributions using a simplified chaotic model of the atmosphere – the Lorenz-96 wave-on-a-latitude-ring (L96) model. We performed numerous ensemble simulation experiments of the L96 model under both time-independent and temporally oscillating forcings. Each ensemble experiment consists of more than 5,000 L96 simulations. We then compared longitudinally-averaged ensemble statistics (e.g., ensemble mean and spread) across experiments to infer how temporal variations in forcings may influence forecast distributions. We will present our findings in this presentation. Under constant forcing, the ensemble eventually equilibrates to a stationary distribution in which all four statistical measures have stabilized. This stationary distribution is often called the “climatological distribution”. Temporally oscillatory forcings, in contrast, cause the ensemble to equilibrate towards cyclo-stationary distributions that oscillate at the same frequency as the forcing. The properties of those cyclo-stationary distributions vary nonlinearly with the forcing’s oscillation frequency and can be largely explained by a forced damped oscillator (FDO) conceptual model. In fact, our FDO model is better than existing models at explaining those cyclo-stationary distributions. Our investigation therefore advances the knowledge regarding the influence of time-varying forcings on forecast distributions.

498332.title: Extreme drought in northern Tunisia, predictability and large scale teleconnection links
498332.authors: Hiba Elborgi, National Engineering School of Tunis (ENIT), Tunis, Tunisia, Tunis, Tunisia; and R. OUACHANI and A. Hannachi
498332.abstract: Droughts rank among the most consequential yet least predictable natural hazards in the Mediterranean basin, where rainfall is governed by a delicate balance of remote atmospheric and oceanic forcings. In Tunisia, this vulnerability is nowhere more evident than in the Medjerda Basin, the country's largest river system and the backbone of its water and food security. As global warming reshapes ocean-atmosphere interactions, understanding the multiscale drivers of drought has become an urgent priority, yet the mechanisms linking large-scale climate variability to local drought severity remain poorly understood. This study explore the atmospheric and oceanic teleconnection relating to extreme drought occurrence in the Medjerda Basin over the period 1951-2022. Located in semi-arid north Tunisia, the basin experiences highly irregular Mediterranean rainfall and has repeatedly suffered severe to drought episodes with major agricultural and socioeconomic consequences. Drought events were identified using the 3-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-3) from 62 rain gauge stations, yielding 56 extreme drought episodes (PC1 < -1.5), the most severe recorded in March 2000. To characterize the large-scale forcing, 500 hPa geopotential height (HGT500), sea-level pressure (SLP), and global SST anomalies (HadISST) were analyzed via PCA/EOF, revealing a leading SST mode (PC1, 66.8% of variance) closely tied to ENSO. Composite analyses with time lags from 0 to 12 months linked these ocean-atmosphere anomalies to drought onset. Results show mid- and lower-tropospheric circulation, marked by recurrent blocking regimes over the western Mediterranean, exerts central control on drought persistence. NAO, AO, PNA, SCAND, and ENSO emerge as key precursors, often combining to prolong dry spells. Time-lag analyses highlight the climate system’s memory: short lags (0–2 months) reflect a rapid atmospheric response, while longer lags (6–12 months) indicate that some droughts are preconditioned by persistent oceanic anomalies. This persistence underscores the cumulative and multi- scale nature of extreme drought events. These findings provide a solid scientific basis for developing innovative approaches, such as climate archetype analysis, to identify representative dry-season configurations, and for drought prediction using Artificial Intelligence models that incorporate key predictors. Suchintegration can enhance drought forecasting and support proactive and sustainable water resource management in the Medjerda basin. Keywords: Medjerda Basin; Drought; SST, SLP, Z500; ENSO; Composite analysis, SPI3

498334.title: Drivers of Snowfall and Snow Accumulation Biases in GEOS Systems
498334.authors: Olivia Madeline Griffith, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO; and L. Andrews and C. Breen
498334.abstract: Snowfall and snow cover in mountainous regions are key components of the hydrologic cycle, directly informing water resource management and glacier mass balance estimates. While the Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) and associate reanalyses, including Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2) produce snowfall and snow cover globally, the validation within mountainous regions has been limited. A systematic approach to assessing the biases in modeled snow cover, particularly over mountain regions, will provide useful information for model improvement and provide a basis of comparison for future work. To assess the ability of GEOS systems to reproduce snowfall events, we chose two case study regions: one from 2023 in Southeastern Alaska and a region from 2017 in Western Colorado. Preliminary results reveal that when validated against various SNOTEL ground observations and snow poles from the SnowEx field campaigns, the Colorado case has strong negative biases indicating underrepresentation of snowfall and snow cover. The case study in Alaska still shows a negative bias yet at a smaller magnitude across the duration of the storm. A plausible driver of these biases is a combination of issues with snow-rain partitioning in the merged satellite-gauge observational data used to improve land surface hydrology and water budget accuracy in land variables at lower latitudes and the inability of current systems to capture orographic lifting at the proper magnitude in these ‘precipitation corrected’ regions. This approach to understanding biases in the GEOS models is a step towards improving the overall representation of water transport, providing accurate forecasts and estimates, and improving water resource problems.

498335.title: Why are AMIP Simulations Too Cold over Siberia in the Early 20th Century?
498335.authors: Madeline Harvey, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO; and N. Lenssen
498335.abstract: AMIP-style simulations, or climate model simulations with prescribed sea surface temperature (SST) fields, are often used to study historical climate. Historically, NCAR has run a 10-member ensemble of AMIP simulations forced with NOAA ERSSTv5 to understand atmospheric variability and potential model biases. Recently, it has been shown that many SST products, including ERSSTv5, have substantial biases in the early 20th century. As such, an additional 10-member AMIP ensemble was run with bias-corrected SST from the Dynamically Consistent ENsemble of Temperature (DCENT-I) product. Here, we show that both AMIP ensembles fail to represent observed temperature in northern Siberia over the early 20th century. This is the only spatially coherent region where both simulations fail to represent observations. We investigate potential drivers of this discrepancy including biases in the atmospheric model, errors in the sea ice forcing field, and biases in the land surface temperature record.

498337.title: Withdrawn: A Spatial Analysis of Diurnal Temperature Ranges Across the United States
498337.abstract: The goal of this study was to analyze diurnal temperature range (DTR) across the United States for the period 2000–2024. DTR is directly linked to health risks as studies have shown that larger temperature ranges increase the risk of respiratory issues along with cardiovascular emergencies. The United States is an ideal study area for analyzing the diurnal temperature range. Its nine distinct climate zones allow for in-depth analysis of DTR. Additionally, the variation in elevation across the country plays a key role. The elevation of a weather station may influence the observed temperature, pressure, and change in humidity. This can then affect the amount of energy required for temperature change. The analysis focused on the Median DTR across the US by county and the change in DTR between two time periods (2001–2012 and 2013–2024). This study aimed to find where the largest (and lowest) DTRs were located, the patterns of DTR, and what trends could be observed between the two time periods. The study found that areas with drier climate, typically in the West, had higher DTR while in the East the DTR was significantly lower. Additionally, trends of increasing DTR were found mainly in the Great Basin region with decreasing DTR being found on the eastern portion of the Rockies.

498342.title: Using Synthetic Tracks to Assess Future Eastern North Pacific Tropical Cyclone Climatology under Multiple Emissions Scenarios
498342.authors: Matthew Edward Fibbi, University of Tampa, Tampa, FL; and N. S. Grondin
498342.abstract: The eastern North Pacific (ENP) basin is the second most active basin for tropical cyclone (TC) development and is the most active basin per unit area in the world. Despite this, the historical record of ENP TC activity remains much shorter than that of the Atlantic, with reliable monitoring of the basin only beginning in recent decades. As a result, understanding how a changing climate may impact ENP TC climatology is a more difficult task using just a historical record. Moreover, given the relatively small number of tracks during a short period of record, it is often challenging to consider the full range of possibilities for TC activity across the basin. To remedy these issues, various methods, including the generation of synthetic TC tracks based on downscaled reanalysis or climate models, are often applied. In addition, the use of synthetic tracks allows us to see a wider range of climatologically possible tracks that could occur during a given time range or climate scenario. In this project, we use three sets of synthetic tracks, downscaled from the Community Earth System Model 2 (CESM2) of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) generation, representing the recent past (1981–2010) and two end of century (2071–2100) scenarios, focusing on SSP 245 and SSP 585, representing a middle-of-the-road and worst-case scenario, respectively. In this project, we study the spatial distribution of ENP TCs across the basin, focusing on shifts in distribution across high-risk areas. We compare a dataset of 1000 synthetic tracks representing 1981–2010 against two end-of-century datasets (each of 1000 synthetic tracks) using various statistical and spatial methods to assess differences in track characteristics, lifetime maximum intensity, and geographic distribution. Results align with previous research showing that a warmer end-of-century climate yields a higher frequency of intense TCs in the basin. Also consistent with previous work in other basins, different climate scenarios may lead to different geographic patterns in TC frequency. These shifts in spatial distribution carry direct implications for TC risk assessment and planning along the west coast of Mexico and Central America, a region that includes major resort cities as well as socioeconomically vulnerable communities often overlooked during extreme TC events.

498344.title: Rain or Shine? The Connection Between Coal Power Plant Emissions and Atmospheric Conditions
498344.authors: Grace Parkham, Central Michigan University, Romulus , MI
498344.abstract: Coal power plants have been around as a primary source of energy to the United States public for decades. Although providing ample amounts of energy for consumption, coal power plants produce harmful waste produces that’s harm the air and water including emissions of SO2, CO2, NOx, and particulate matter (PM) ranging from 1 μm to 10 μm (PM1, PM2.5, PM10). These emissions can act as cloud condensation (CCN) nuclei to form clouds and precipitation. To view CCN and PM, data sets from the CAM Global Reanalysis, Choudhury and Tesche were used as model data to visualize CCN and PM. In-situ measurements from the Iowa Environmental Mesonet were used to visualize precipitation cloud cover. Emission data was pulled from the EPA. Comparison was also done between coal power regulations timeline and precipitation and cloud cover amounts. Overall, there was a visible decrease in emissions from when more strict regulations were enacted, which correlated with a decrease in precipitation. Cloud cover average increased on data from the Iowa mesonet and CAM Global Reanalysis. CCN and all sizes of PM had an average deceasing trend as well. Overall, there is a connection shown between emissions, PM, CCN, and rainfall, which indicates a connection between CCN and waste products from coal power plants. Fluctuation in increasing rainfall and cloud cover at certain plants can be indicated by climate and outside factor influence that has not been looked into for this study as conclusions have only been drawn from the data sources listed above and coal power regulation history. CCN amounts influenced by emissions can change the surrounding microclimate of an area and thus change the amount of precipitation received by these areas. Having a direct influence on precipitation which can induce drought or increased rainfall areas and flooding.

498345.title: Multi-Radar Observations of Weather Systems during the 2026 RaXPol Educational Deployment in North Florida
498345.authors: Chaehyeon Chelsea Nam, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL
498345.abstract: During a two-week field experiment in September 2026 at the Florida State University Coastal and Marine Laboratory, students in the Radar Meteorology course collected observations using the University of Oklahoma’s mobile, X-band, polarimetric RaXPol radar. The deployment provides a unique opportunity to compare RaXPol observations with those from the operational S-band WSR-88D radars at Tallahassee, Florida (KTLH), and Eglin Air Force Base, Florida (KEVX). This study will use selected weather cases observed during the deployment to investigate how the same meteorological features are represented by radars with different wavelengths, locations, and scanning geometries. Comparisons will examine differences associated with beam height and spatial resolution as a function of range, viewing geometry, wavelength-dependent effects, and scanning strategies. RaXPol’s mobility and rapid, targeted scanning also provide perspectives complementary to those of the fixed operational radar network. Through selected case studies, we will evaluate the advantages and limitations of the different observing configurations and investigate how combining observations from multiple radar systems can provide a more complete characterization of weather systems. The specific cases and research questions will be refined following the field deployment based on the meteorological conditions observed and the scientific interests of the student research team.

498346.title: Evaluating the National Blend of Models (NBM) 5.0 for Eastern North Carolina
498346.authors: Jacob Tyler Kasitz, Ernest F. Hollings Scholar at NWS Morehead City/Newport, NC, Gainesville, FL; and R. Ellis and M. Simms
498346.abstract: Verification and evaluation are a vital part of any forecast. By blending various numerical weather prediction models, the National Blend of Models (NBM) provides a skillful, consistent national starting point for forecasting. With the NBM version 5 recently becoming operational, an evaluation of its performance is essential for understanding where the model has improved in previously deficient areas and where it has degraded. In particular, focus on the Outer Banks region is crucial as the NBM has historically struggled to resolve the land/marine interface, leading to significant errors in the forecast. Understanding skill improvement can help forecasters add value and use the NBM most effectively in operational forecasting and during impact-based decision support services (IDSS). In this study, temperature, dew point, wind speed, and wind gust from the operational NBM v5 are compared with those from the National Digital Forecast Database (NDFD) and the Unrestricted Mesoscale Analysis (URMA). The data are used for an overall evaluation of observation sites covering the Newport/Morehead City forecast office's county warning area and for further evaluations through specific case studies at stations Manteo (KMQI), and Hatteras (KHSE). Overall results show that the NBM, on average, slightly outperformed the NDFD for most of the inland sites for the study period. A notable warm bias in the model is shown in Dare County (KMQI and K2DP) during the warm season, and sustained wind speed and gust biases are too low in the nearshore marine zones (KHSE) when compared to URMA. The NDFD outperformed the NBM for these sites. This has implications for convective forecasts, the issuance of marine products, and decision-support services. By understanding bias, local forecasters can identify targets of opportunity and add value and local knowledge to the forecast.

498347.title: The Forecasting Challenge of Snow Cover Induced Temperature Depressions
498347.authors: Lucas Adelino Silva, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL
498347.abstract: Variation of temperatures is a constantly changing function of solar-surface-atmosphere radiative balance. Snow Cover Induced Temperature Depressions (SCITDs) are surface layer phenomena caused by the thermodynamic properties of a sufficiently deep, uniform layer of snow cover across a region. If unaccounted for, SCITDs can result in unexpected freezes that pose significant hazards to travellers completely unaware of the actual black ice potential. Snow has two main properties working towards suppressing surface layer temperatures diurnally: Snow’s very high Thermal IR emissivity enhances ideal radiational cooling events during the night. It also is very reflective in the visible spectrum, which delays the typical daytime planetary boundary layer evolution of the mixed layer, keeping the surface layer separate for a longer period of time. Ideal radiational cooling events require weak to no winds to prevent mixing, and as little cloud cover (CC) as possible to ensure a clear atmospheric window for Thermal IR escape. By establishing thresholds of significance to observed wind speed, cloud cover, and snow depth, days with the highest SCITD potential were effectively isolated. This study analyzes the errors in the maximum and minimum temperature forecast splits of the National Weather Service (NWS) during the winters from the integration of the Day 1 Tabular State Forecast (2001-2003) to early 2025 with respect to the observations, revealing the relative forecast bias of SCITD events. Three regions were selected across the USA of diverse geographical and climatological parameters to observe regional biases: Burlington VT, Aberdeen SD, and Flagstaff AZ. The analysis is split into two portions with subsequent goals: Grouped box plots showing the impact of SCITDs on NWS forecast accuracy, and a time series portraying the improvement of NWS forecast accuracy for conditions indicative of SCITD events. The goals of each part were to confirm the significance of SCITD-induced relative forecast biases, and if meteorological advancements have helped in reducing error for highly sensitive scenarios such as SCITDs respectively. Both analyses indicate that the NWS struggled and improved the most with forecasting low temperatures during SCITD events over the whole time period across every location. The correlation with SCITDs and impacting high temperature forecast accuracy was not nearly as strong, also showing weaker accuracy increase trends branching from the direct relationship of CC and snow cover’s impacts on solar insolation compared to the inverse relationship during the night; a prominent flaw. Overall, this analysis reveals the significant improvement of the NWS in forecasting nocturnal SCITDs, considerably reducing the gap between it and the baseline error of a typical forecast. Further development of this project could be attempting to prove the corresponding implied trend of improved winter traffic safety over the time period, quantitatively analyzing the topographical effects on the relative efficiency of SCITDs, and finding stronger parameters to define a significant daytime SCITD event.

498349.title: An Analysis of the Impact of Aspirated Temperature Shelters on Inversion Monitoring across the Oklahoma Mesonet
498349.authors: Mason Wesley Burris, Oklahoma Climatological Survey, Norman, OK; and C. A. Fiebrich
498349.abstract: The Oklahoma Mesonet is a statewide network of 120 environmental monitoring stations that report quality-assured data every five minutes. Among the variables measured are air temperature at 1.5 meters above ground, housed in an aspirated radiation shield, and air temperature at 9 meters, housed in a naturally ventilated radiation shield. These observations are used in several products available through the Oklahoma Mesonet website, including an Inversion Conditions map. This map displays the difference between the 9-meter and 1.5-meter air temperatures at each station, along with other supporting variables. A positive temperature difference indicates that temperature is increasing with height between 9 and 1.5 meters, indicating a near-surface temperature inversion. Inversions reduce vertical mixing and can allow smoke, dust, and agricultural chemicals to remain concentrated near the surface, making inversion conditions important for air quality, smoke dispersion, and agricultural spraying. Prior to 2009, however, the 1.5-meter air temperature sensor was also housed in a naturally ventilated radiation shield. Following the transition to an aspirated shield, the temperature difference used by the Inversion Conditions map began comparing a naturally ventilated 9-meter measurement with an aspirated 1.5-meter measurement. This study analyzes all Mesonet stations with sufficient 9-meter and 1.5-meter air temperature observations and compares measurements from before the transition to aspirated shelters (i.e., 2005–2008) with those from after the installation of aspirated shelters (i.e., 2010–2013). The analysis will also examine trends in inversion conditions during various environmental conditions, including daytime and nighttime periods and conditions characterized by weak winds and high solar radiation (e.g., times when aspirated shelters are most impactful to air temperature measurements). The goal of this research is to determine whether the change in ventilation at 1.5 meters resulted in a noticeable change in the measured inversions across the Oklahoma Mesonet.

498350.title: Evaluating Track Integrated Kinetic Energy as a Measure of North Atlantic Tropical Cyclone Activity
498350.authors: Jonathan Christian Abraham Sr., Suny Brockport, Brockport, NY
498350.abstract: Currently, Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) is commonly used to characterize seasonal tropical cyclone activity by accounting for maximum sustained wind speed and storm duration. However, ACE does not account for differences in storm size, and as a result, storms with similar ACE values may have different total kinetic energy. Track Integrated Kinetic Energy (TIKE) is a less commonly used alternative measure that incorporates the spatial extent and strength of the tropical cyclone wind field over the duration of a storm. This study evaluates the relationship between seasonal TIKE and ACE in the North Atlantic from 2004 to 2025 and investigates whether TIKE provides complementary information about variability in seasonal tropical cyclone activity. Six-hourly tropical cyclone maximum sustained winds, radius of maximum wind, and 34-, 50-, and 64-kt wind radii for each quadrant are obtained from HURDAT2, the Extended Best Track dataset, and IBTrACS. This data will be used to calculate Integrated Kinetic Energy (IKE) for individual storm observations, which will then be integrated over each storm track and aggregated to produce seasonal TIKE values. Seasonal TIKE and ACE will be compared using correlation, regression, and other statistical measures. Their relationships with additional measures of tropical cyclone activity, including storm frequency and major hurricane activity, will also be examined. This analysis will assess whether accounting for tropical cyclone size provides information about seasonal North Atlantic tropical cyclone activity that is not captured by ACE alone. The potential predictive value of TIKE will also be explored by testing whether seasonal TIKE is associated with particular sea surface temperature patterns from the months leading up to the season.

498353.title: Developing Parameters to Calibrate the CREST Hydrologic Model to Predict Flash Flooding over Wildfire Burn Scars
498353.authors: Noah Aaron Schneiderman, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and J. W. Thiesing, R. Oh, A. D. Cotton, and J. J. Gourley
498353.abstract: Flash flooding is a threat to life and property across the United States. Predicting flash floods, however, is not merely a meteorological problem; an area’s vulnerability to flash flooding also depends heavily on characteristics of the local environment such as soil state, land cover, and terrain complexity. Soil and overlying land cover properties are fundamentally altered by the passage of wildfires. Due to these alterations, flash floods and debris flows become much more likely over wildfire burn scars and areas downstream of them; thus, developing flash-flood prediction tools that account for wildfire impacts is a primary goal of ongoing flash flood research. Over the past decade, the National Severe Storms Laboratory at NOAA has worked to improve the detection and short-term prediction of flash floods through the development of the Flooded Locations And Simulated Hydrographs (FLASH) project. FLASH uses real-time precipitation data from the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) network in conjunction with several hydrologic models to generate high-resolution estimates of streamflow and thus identify areas likely to experience flash flooding. The primary hydrological model used by FLASH is the Coupled Routing and Excess STorage (CREST) model. CREST, however, has not been adapted to wildfire-impacted landscapes and thus tends to severely underpredict flash flooding caused by rainfall over burn scars.
