In this study, we seek to develop modifications to CREST parameters that improve the model’s accuracy in predicting flash floods over burn scars. We calibrate a distinct set of model parameters for varying levels of wildfire burn severity, as determined by Burned Area Emergency Response (BAER) data. To accomplish this, we analyze a series of case studies, beginning with flash flood events following the June 2024 fire near Ruidoso, New Mexico. The ultimate goal of this work, coupled with future efforts to incorporate real-time burn severity data into FLASH, is to develop a single hydrological model that is applicable to landscapes in both unburned areas and burned areas of varying severity.

498354.title: STUDENT - Localized Risk, Generic Warnings: A Framework for Closing the Awareness-Action Gap in South Texas Winter Storms
498354.authors: Samuel John Nors, University of Incarnate Word, San Antonio, TX; University of the Incarnate Word, San Antonio, TX; and V. Kumar
498354.abstract: Five years after Winter Storm Uri exposed critical vulnerabilities in Texas's cold weather infrastructure, Winter Storm Fern brought sub-freezing temperatures, icing, and renewed pipe-freeze risk to south central Texas in January 2026. This paper reconstructs the storm's warning timeline using publicly available records National Weather Service advisories, emergency declarations, utility and media reports of water and power disruptions to examine how official warning lead times, geographic coverage, and messaging specificity varied across the San Antonio and Corpus Christi corridor. Building on the Protective Action Decision Model (PADM; Lindell & Perry, 2012) and recent cold weather preparedness literature, we propose a modified conceptual framework tailored to short-fuse, infrastructure centered hazards in historically warm climate regions. Specifically, we argue that (1) informal social-cue pathways central to the original PADM are likely attenuated in transient, linguistically diverse Gulf Coast communities; (2) a personal relevance gap, in which residents perceive regional warnings as inapplicable to their specific location, sits as an underexamined bottleneck between threat perception and protective action; and (3) localized, probability based messaging may offer a more effective lever for behavior change than broader lead time extensions alone. This paper synthesizes storm timeline reconstruction and existing hazard communication research to motivate a testable, and revised model. In our next research work, we will create a survey to test this conceptual framework.

498355.title: Salt Lake City's Memorial day Pyrocumulus
498355.authors: Enzo Peters, Metropolitan State University of Denver, Denver, CO
498355.abstract: On May 25 th , 2026, one thousand acres of invasive wetland vegetation was to be ignited in a controlled burn by Farmington Bay. Due to the interactions between winds and the very dry fuel the burn spotted into another unit. An increase in material burning led to the development of a Pyrocumulus cloud over the fire area. What meteorological factors impacted and contributed to the PyroCb to develop? Using MesoWest data archive, NWS forecasts, 1D plume modeling, and public records provided by Utah Department of Natural Resources, the PyroCb development is examined throughout the day.

498356.title: A Radar and Mesoscale Analysis of an Intense Nocturnal QLCS Tornado
498356.authors: Anirban Mukherjee, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL
498356.abstract: QLCS tornadoes remain a significant challenge to anticipate and warn. While the vast majority of QLCS tornadoes are weak, stronger QLCS tornadoes are of particular concern due to their greater societal impacts. During the overnight hours of June 20, 2021, a QLCS produced a destructive EF-3 tornado over heavily populated areas in the southwestern suburbs of Chicago. Despite a favorable wind profile, low level convective inhibition in the nocturnal thermodynamic environment and a linear storm mode was expected to limit the tornado threat. We carefully examine radar and mesoscale data from the event, taking advantage of the close proximity of the tornado to three radar sites (KLOT, TORD, and TMDW). The most interesting finding was the presence of undular bores in the stable near surface layer just ahead of the QLCS, which intersected the QLCS near the mesovortex as the tornado intensified. In addition, other factors that contributed to the intensity of the tornado include its position relative to an outflow boundary and the QLCS rear inflow jet. We also contrast the tornadic mesovortex to a nontornadic mesovortex that occurred about half an hour prior.

498357.title: An Event-Based Framework for Extreme Rainfall in Southeastern South America: Contrasting East–West Regimes across the Pampa Biome
498357.authors: Leticia Naitzel, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH
498357.abstract: Extreme precipitation is commonly characterized using climate indices that summarize the frequency or magnitude of rainfall above predefined thresholds. While these metrics have become standard for climate monitoring, they often describe isolated extreme days or fixed accumulation periods and provide limited information on the persistence and total severity of individual rainfall events. As a result, hydrometeorological events that produce substantial impacts may not be fully represented by existing indices. Southeastern South America is a hotspot of extreme precipitation, where changes in the frequency and intensity of heavy rainfall are expected to increase under future climate conditions, with important implications for hydrological risk assessments. This study proposes an event-based framework to identify and characterize extreme rainfall events across the Pampa Biome of southeastern South America (Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay) during 1979–2024. Extreme events are defined as consecutive wet days (daily precipitation > 1 mm) containing at least one day exceeding the local 90th percentile (P90) calculated using wet days only. Wet days were initially defined using a 1-mm threshold, consistent with widely used climate-extreme indices and IPCC assessments. However, percentile thresholds calculated only from wet days are conditioned on the frequency of wet-day occurrence and may be influenced by long-term changes in precipitation occurrence. Preliminary analyses revealed substantial spatial differences in wet-day frequency trends across the Pampa Biome, with significant decreasing trends affecting approximately 34% of the Argentinean portion, whereas significant increases were identified across only 2.4% of the Uruguayan Savanna Ecoregion (USE), which spans the Brazilian and Uruguayan portions of the biome. Therefore, the robustness of the wet-day-based approach will be evaluated by comparing percentile thresholds calculated from wet days (>1 mm) with those derived from the complete daily precipitation distribution, including dry days. This comparison will assess how the days used to calculate the percentile threshold influence the identification and characterization of extreme rainfall events across the Pampa Biome. For each identified event, three complementary attributes were quantified: frequency, persistence (event duration), and severity (total accumulated precipitation throughout the event). In addition, integrated annual indicators combining frequency, persistence, and severity were developed to characterize the evolution of extreme rainfall regimes across the Pampa Biome. The 90th percentile of wet days was selected to balance the identification of sufficiently rare rainfall events with an adequate sample size for seasonal characterization; higher percentiles (e.g., P95 and P99) would identify fewer events and could result in zero-frequency values for some seasons and locations. Therefore, this approach treats each rainfall event as a continuous physical process rather than a collection of independent extreme days. To further investigate the spatial organization of extreme rainfall characteristics, Ward’s hierarchical clustering analysis was conducted using the three dimensions defining rainfall events: frequency, persistence, and severity. Cluster validation was performed using silhouette statistics, jump criteria, and dendrogram interpretation, which supported the division of the Pampa Biome into six homogeneous extreme-rainfall regions. The resulting clusters revealed marked contrasts in the dominant characteristics of rainfall events. The southwestern portion of the biome was associated with the cluster exhibiting the lowest values of frequency, persistence, and severity, whereas the northeastern region was characterized by the highest frequency and persistence and the second-highest severity among the six clusters. The northeastern extreme-rainfall regime will also provide the basis for a case study of the April–May 2024 flooding event in southern Brazil, allowing the proposed event-based framework to be examined alongside commonly used precipitation metrics during a high-impact hydrometeorological event. Preliminary trend analyses conducted across the Pampa Biome revealed contrasting east–west responses at both annual and seasonal scales. A coherent hotspot was identified in the central and northeastern portions of the Pampa Biome, spanning parts of Brazil and Uruguay, where extreme rainfall events became simultaneously more frequent, more persistent, and more severe over the 1979–2024 period. At the annual scale, the largest Theil–Sen slopes, when multiplied by the 46-year length of the study period, corresponded to approximately nine additional events, seven additional days of event persistence, and nearly 50 mm of accumulated precipitation per event. Observed changes were also calculated by comparing the mean values of the first and last five years of the time series, reducing the influence of anomalously high or low values in individual years. Across parts of the USE, the integrated index exhibited substantial increases, with observed percentage changes ranging from approximately 50% to 215%, highlighting pronounced intensification in the most strongly affected areas. Seasonal trend analyses revealed a similarly pronounced east–west pattern, characterized by significant decreases in the southwestern portion of the Pampa Biome and increasing trends toward the northeast. Winter showed the most pronounced increase in event persistence, with the largest significant Theil–Sen slope reaching approximately 0.33 days yr⁻¹, corresponding to an estimated increase of approximately 15 days when extrapolated across the 46-year study period. In contrast, the largest observed difference between the mean values of the first and last five years of the time series reached 5.7 days. Observed changes in event severity were also substantial in the northeastern Pampa, where regions with significant positive trends showed large increases in accumulated precipitation across all seasons. The largest differences were identified during winter and fall, reaching approximately 118.5 mm and 117.7 mm, respectively, while considerable increases were also observed during summer (94.5 mm) and spring (88.5 mm). Together, these findings reveal a pronounced east–west contrast in the evolution and spatial organization of extreme rainfall across the Pampa Biome. Since the spatial distribution and statistical significance of changes differed among event frequency, persistence, and severity, the extreme rainfall regimes cannot be adequately characterized by a single event attribute. The integration of these complementary dimensions provides a more comprehensive representation of changes in rainfall extremes and helps identify regions where different combinations of event characteristics contribute to evolving hydrometeorological hazards. By treating extreme rainfall as a continuous event and integrating its frequency, persistence, and severity, the proposed framework provides a physically meaningful basis for climate hazard assessments, hydrological applications, and the investigation of future changes in extreme rainfall across southeastern South America.

498360.title: An Observational Assessment of Environmental and Agricultural Responses from an Oklahoma Wildfire
498360.authors: Riley Bell, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK; and S. F. Padilla, Y. Fickle, E. Moore, and B. G. Illston
498360.abstract: This study focuses to analyze the environmental and agricultural impacts from a recent Oklahoma wildfire leveraging two different measuring techniques, in-situ observational data, and remote sensing technologies. Due to the high temporal frequency of near-surface observational data provided by the Oklahoma Mesonet, this project selects a wildfire that directly impacted a mesonet station. Additionally, the large number of environmental and hydrological measurements taken simultaneously will assist in the analysis of the selected region, pre and post wildfire. Along with utilized in-situ observational measurements, a multi-layered remote sensing framework will improve the assessment by implementing multiple measuring techniques. Thermal infrared sensors, multispectral optical imaging, and synthetic aperture radar aim to quantify vegetation and water stress indices by analyzing satellite imagery using remote sensing technologies. This framework delineates the relationship between water-stressed conditions and the associated development or regression of vegetation through this application. While this study strictly analyzes the observational data, future work for researchers will incorporate high-resolution modeling as dedicated groundwork to assess boundary-layer moisture fluxes.

498362.title: ENTLN vs. GLM: Evaluating Ground-Based and Satellite-Based Lightning Data for Rainfall Estimation
498362.authors: Benjamin Garrett Tobin, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL
498362.abstract: Lightning locating systems (LLS) provide critical information for hazard warning and severe weather forecasting, and the relationship between lightning activity and rainfall has been documented since the mid-20th century. Ground-based systems such as Earth Networks Total Lightning Network (ENTLN) and satellite-based systems such as the Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) each offer certain trade-offs. For instance, ENTLN can distinguish cloud-to-ground (CG) from intra-cloud (IC) lightning but experiences uneven detection performance across the network, while GLM provides continuous coverage over large areas but cannot make this CG/IC distinction. Although prior studies have directly compared ENTLN and GLM, and separate studies have investigated lightning-rainfall relationships using each system independently, few, if any studies appear to have directly compared the two systems using a shared, quantitative rainfall benchmark. This study will address that gap by establishing a quantitative relationship between lightning totals and rainfall totals for both ENTLN and GLM within a 55km radius domain centered on Tampa Bay, Florida. Approximately 30 convective events will be analyzed with lightning flash totals from each system compared against volumetric rainfall totals derived from NOAA's Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) Quantitative precipitation Estimation (QPE) product, used as an independent benchmark. The comparison will yield a lightning-rainfall ratio unique to each detection platform, allowing an assessment of how each system's inherent detection biases affect its usefulness for rainfall estimation. The results are expected to clarify the relative strengths of ground- and satellite-based lightning data for precipitation applications, informing future efforts to integrate lightning derived rainfall estimates into operational areas of weather.

498363.title: NYC Water Ready: A Geospatial Approach to Emergency Water Sourcing and Treatment
498363.authors: Harmony Divine, NSF, Brooklyn, NY; NSF, Brooklyn, NY; and N. Stevens
498363.abstract: In the event of a catastrophic infrastructure failure of New York City's upstate reservoir system, millions of urban residents would lose access to potable water. This project proposes a decentralized emergency response system that connects citizens with alternative local water sources using geospatial data and machine learning. Utilizing NYC Planimetric Hydrography and population datasets, a spatial search algorithm will be developed to instantly locate the closest open waterbody, such as lakes, streams, rivers, or pools. Because urban surface water contains diverse contaminants, a classification model will be used to evaluate the selected waterbody's features—such as salinity, flow rate, and surrounding zoning—to assign an emergency contamination risk level and determine if it can be made safe to drink. To bridge the gap between digital data and physical information, the framework envisions a network of localized QR codes deployed next to urban water features. When scanned, step-by-step purification instructions (e.g., filtration, desalination, or boiling protocols) will display directly on a user's smartphone without requiring a network connection. This project aims to demonstrate how combining spatial indexing with predictive classification can empower communities with actionable, life-saving information during a worst-case utility collapse.

498368.title: Diurnal Variations of Arctic Clouds During Polar Night from CloudSat and EarthCARE Observations
498368.authors: Aubry Forsyth, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL; and C. Liu and L. M. Swinney
498368.abstract: Arctic clouds strongly influence the surface energy budget, particularly during the polar night, when the absence of incoming solar radiation allows longwave radiative effects to dominate. Previous ground-based observations at Barrow (Utqiaġvik), Alaska, identified an apparent diurnal cycle in wintertime cloud properties that resembles the variation in the global atmospheric electric circuit, raising the question of whether this variability is representative of the broader Arctic or unique to a single location. This study investigated Arctic winter cloud variability by separating observations from the CloudSat Cloud Profiling Radar (2006–2011) and the EarthCARE Cloud Profiling Radar (2024–2026) into ascending and descending orbits. To minimize orbital sampling biases associated with sun-synchronous satellites, cloud features identified from W-band radar reflectivity profiles are converted from Universal Time to Local Solar Time and grouped into well-sampled overpass windows from ascending and descending orbits. Mean cloud-top height, cloud-base height, cloud thickness, and maximum radar reflectivity are compared on a 2.5° × 5.0° latitude-longitude grid across the Arctic from 65° - 80°N during December and January. Statistical significance testing and regional analyses are performed to identify localized differences between the two overpass periods. Both CloudSat and EarthCARE datasets show that there are no Arctic-wide coherent differences in cloud properties between ascending and descending orbits, except over the Canadian and Siberian Arctic, where statistically significant regional differences are observed. The specific cloud-property responses differ between the two satellites, likely reflecting differences in instrument characteristics, sampling, and observation periods. These findings suggest that the diurnal variability of cloud properties from a single ground-based site may not be representative of the broader Arctic during polar night. The physical mechanism underlying the diurnal variations in polar night cloud properties over the Canadian and Siberian Arctic regions remains unknown and warrants further investigation.

498369.title: Cost Optimization of Radiosondes For Use in Higher Education
498369.authors: Nathaniel Wallace Peyer, Valparaiso University, Valparaiso, IN; and E. Palmisano
498369.abstract: The use of radiosondes in higher education is critical for young meteorologists to gain a deeper understanding of the field around them. Current commercially available radiosondes cost over 200 USD for just a radiosonde, not factoring in any other part of the balloon launch. As costs continue to rise for all parts of a balloon launch, students are losing this valuable opportunity to launch radiosondes and learn from these launches. By examining commercially available radiosondes, we were able to determine steps to reduce operational cost and allow students to have a more hands-on experience. Research specifically focused on optimizing the cost of radiosonde hardware and the software experience to create a better learning experience for students and teachers in higher education. After careful examination and design of a new radiosonde device, this project was able to cut the cost of a single radiosonde in half, allow operations without a license from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), and create a complete and open python-based software experience for students and faculty. This research concluded that a lower cost radiosonde is possible while maintaining high data fidelity, thus opening more doors for students and universities alike.

498370.title: Characterizing Air Quality and Pollution Sources in Madison, Wisconsin
498370.authors: Monica Beatriz Pabon, University of Puerto Rico - Mayaguez, Mayaguez, PR; and M. R. Hilario
498370.abstract: Aerosols are tiny particles suspended in the atmosphere that influence climate, cloud formation, and human respiratory health, yet their sources are often difficult to pin down without direct sampling. We set out to identify the major sources of aerosols by examining the size and chemical composition of particles collected during two contrasting periods: a typical summer week and a wildfire smoke event. We collected samples using a MOUDI instrument and analyzed their ionic and elemental composition and particle shape using laboratory chemical analysis and electron microscopy. We found that the smallest particles, the ones capable of reaching deepest into the lungs, were dominated by chemical markers of combustion, pointing to traffic and industrial emissions as a leading source. Larger particles were dominated by markers typical of soil and dust. During the wildfire period, we observed a distinct shift in particle loading, suggesting that smoke carried in from distant fires can add substantially to the fine particles already produced locally. Together, these results suggest that everyday combustion and natural soil sources typically shape the local aerosol population, with wildfire smoke acting as an increasingly important, episodic contributor. Understanding these source contributions can help guide future air quality monitoring and public health messaging, especially as wildfire smoke events become more frequent.

498371.title: Relationship Between Wildfire Activity and Antecedent Environmental Conditions in Colorado's North Front Range (2001-2025)
498371.authors: Aysha Akter, The City College of New York, New York, NY; CUNY CREST, New York Cirty, NY; NOAA, Boulder, CO; NOAA, Lowell, MA; and A. J. Hoell, R. Worsnop, M. Breeden, and M. D. Goldberg
498371.abstract: Wildfires are a growing hazard across the western USA, threatening ecosystems, communities, air quality, and infrastructure. Understanding the antecedent relationships between wildfire activity and environmental variables is important for improving wildfire monitoring and prediction. This study investigates the variables that most influence wildfire activity and the antecedent relationships between wildfire activity, atmospheric conditions, and vegetation health in Colorado's North Front Range during the June–September fire season from 2001 to 2025. Wildfire activity was represented by MODIS Fire Radiative Power (FRP), with environmental variables including maximum air temperature (Tmax), vapor pressure deficit (VPD), 10 m wind speed, and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI). Time series analysis, atmospheric anomaly analysis, linear and quadratic regression, lagged correlation analysis, and a Cameron Peak Fire case study were conducted to examine wildfire and environmental relationships. The regression analyses showed that VPD exhibited the strongest relationship with wildfire activity, followed by Tmax. In contrast, NDVI exhibited a moderate negative relationship, and 10 m wind speed showed the weakest relationship. Lagged correlation analysis further indicated that warmer, drier, and lower-than-average vegetation greenness were associated with elevated wildfire activity, with these relationships developing approximately one week or more in advance and generally strengthening closer to the fire day. These findings improve the understanding of wildfire–environment relationships in Colorado's North Front Range and provide a foundation for future multivariable statistical and machine learning approaches for predicting wildfire activity up to seven days in advance.

498373.title: Evaluating Next-Generation Ocean Color SensorsAgainst the VIIRS-SNPP Long-Term Record andAERONET-OC Observations
498373.authors: Partha Talukder, NSF, Glen Oaks, NY
498373.abstract: Abstract Ocean color satellite observations are essential for monitoring water quality, marine ecosystems, and long term changes in aquatic environments. The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite aboard the Suomi National Polar orbiting Partnership satellite (VIIRS-SNPP), launched in 2011, has provided more than a decade of ocean color observations and serves as an important reference for evaluating newer satellite sensors. As VIIRS-SNPP reaches the end of its operational utility and NASA discontinues processing of this dataset, it is important to determine whether the new generation of ocean color sensors provides comparable or improved accuracy and precision. This study evaluates the performance of newer ocean color satellite sensors against the long term VIIRS-SNPP record and reliable in situ measurements from AERONET-OC stations. The analysis will focus on the Long Island Sound Coastal Observatory (LISCO) and an additional AERONET-OC site, using at least ten years of VIIRS-SNPP observations over LISCO to establish a long term performance baseline. Annual mean values, multi year period means, standard deviations, and other basic statistical measures will be analyzed to characterize temporal and spectral variability. VIIRS-SNPP observations will then be compared with measurements from the PACE Ocean Color Instrument (OCI), NOAA-20 VIIRS, and NOAA-21 VIIRS during overlapping observation periods. Satellite observations will also be matched with AERONET-OC measurements according to location and observation time to ensure consistent comparisons. Remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) will serve as a primary parameter for evaluating spectral agreement, accuracy, precision, and variability among the sensors. By benchmarking the newer generation of ocean color sensors against both the established VIIRS-SNPP record and on ground AERONET-OC measurements, this research aims to determine whether PACE-OCI, NOAA-20 VIIRS, and NOAA-21 VIIRS maintain or improve the accuracy, precision, and consistency necessary for continued long term ocean color monitoring.

498374.title: Food price volatility as a transmission channel for ENSO shocks in Brazil (2000-2025)
498374.presenter: Barbosa de Lima Sr., Alan Yago
498374.authors: Alan Yago Barbosa de Lima Sr., Federal University of ABC, Santo André, SP, Brazil; and V. F. Nascimento Sr. and A. D. O. Cardoso
498374.abstract: Food price volatility is a recurring, country-wide problem in Brazil, where food represents a large share of low-income household budgets and where climate shocks translate quickly into pressure on food access, inflation, and the conduct of economic policy. This study asks a single, mechanism-oriented question: through which channel are shocks associated with the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) transmitted to food prices and food access in Brazil? Rather than testing only whether ENSO correlates with inflation, we seek to locate where in the food system the climate signal actually operates, and for whom the consequences are largest. We combine monthly series of the Niño 3.4 index and the Food Consumer Price Index (Food CPI) for 2000–2025 with annual agricultural planted area and the prevalence of severe food insecurity, the latter disaggregated by sex. Methodologically, the analysis proceeds on two levels. At the monthly level we identify exogenous ENSO episodes through descriptive classification of phase and intensity, an event study around strong and very strong events, and a family of regressions of the Food CPI on Niño 3.4 (linear, cubic, and Generalized Additive Models, GAM), estimated by ordinary least squares with a linear time trend. At the annual level we re-express both series on the tropical year (May of year t to April of year t+1), compatible with the interannual nature of the phenomenon, and estimate a set of models with autocorrelation-robust (HAC, Newey–West) inference that test a land-use transmission channel: the response of planted area to ENSO, the interaction between ENSO and area change on the Food CPI, and the same relationships separately for soybean (an export commodity) and rice (a domestic staple). A final, exploratory link regresses severe food insecurity on food inflation using three-year averages. The results are mutually reinforcing across levels. At the monthly level, extreme ENSO events are consistently associated with inflationary shocks in food prices, with evidence of anticipation and persistence: the event study shows a significant rise in the annual variation of the basic food basket already in the year preceding the climatic peak (t−1), continuing through the peak (t) and the following year (t+1). The regressions confirm that the direct effect, though statistically detectable, is modest and non-contemporaneous: the linear Niño 3.4 coefficient is small and negative, the cubic specification improves fit through lagged terms, and the GAM confirms a mild but significant nonlinearity (approximate adjusted R² of 0.05–0.06). Figure panel (b) displays the Food CPI against Niño 3.4 across 25 years, shaded by ENSO phase and intensity, and makes visible both the co-movement during moderate-to-strong El Niño episodes (2002–2004, 2015–2016, 2023–2024) and the lagged, diffuse response during La Niña. The central contribution emerges at the annual level, summarized in table panel (a). Under annual aggregation and corrected inference, the direct linear effect of ENSO on the Food CPI is not statistically significant (p = 0.48), the cubic terms are jointly non-significant (p > 0.08), and the GAM does not confirm nonlinearity (p = 0.56). This does not weaken the argument; it locates the effect. The statistically significant results concentrate on the productive response: ENSO significantly moves total planted area (coefficient 1.628; p = 0.033), and, decisively, the interaction between ENSO and area change is a strong predictor of the Food CPI (coefficient 0.960; p < 0.001; adjusted R² = 0.276). The effect of ENSO on price is therefore conditional on how agricultural area responds to the shock: when area adjusts, price pressure is attenuated; when it does not, pressure intensifies. Disaggregating by crop sharpens the finding. In soybean, ENSO shifts planted area both contemporaneously (p = 0.040) and with a one-year lag (p = 0.039), and the ENSO × soybean-area interaction on the CPI is strongly significant (p < 0.001; adjusted R² = 0.303). In rice, none of these relationships holds (ENSO → area p = 0.12; interaction p = 0.36), and area is far more volatile (annual standard deviation of 22%, versus 3.4% for soybean). The climate transmission channel thus operates predominantly through the export-oriented crop rather than through the crop most directly consumed at home, a result consistent with the view that ENSO propagates through global supply chains and large integrated producers and with the delayed, mediated pass-through emphasized in recent macro-climate research. Finally, food inflation predicts the prevalence of severe food insecurity (coefficient 0.728; p = 0.022), and, as shown in figure panel (c), the female–male gap in severe food insecurity is not constant: it stays near 0.5–0.8 percentage points in stable periods but widens to roughly 2.4–2.8 points at the peak of instability (2020–2022), indicating that women absorb a disproportionate share of the impact of shocks on food access. Two limitations bound these conclusions and are stated plainly: the food-security link rests on overlapping three-year series within a window dominated by the non-climatic COVID-19 shock and is therefore exploratory, and the annual sample limits statistical power, so the interaction coefficients should be read as evidence consistent with, rather than definitive proof of, ENSO acting as a conditional amplifier operating through the supply response. The study’s significance is both scientific and social. Scientifically, it reframes ENSO not as a direct, contemporaneous determinant of the price level but as an exogenous, conditional amplifier of food price volatility whose signal is carried by the agricultural supply response and concentrated in a specific, export-oriented crop. Socially, it connects a large-scale climate teleconnection to a concrete human outcome, severe food insecurity and its widening gender gap, pointing toward price stabilization, inventory management, crop-specific agricultural insurance, gender-sensitive social protection, and climate adaptation as complementary responses. Future work will disaggregate the channel across Brazilian regions and food groups, incorporate expectation variables, and test the interaction between ENSO, monetary policy, and agricultural policy.

498375.title: Evaluation and Improvement of Synthetic Tropical Cyclone Models for Hazard Assessment and Climate Change
498375.authors: Varyan Jain, SUNY, Stony Brook, NY; and J. Parker and B. A. Colle
498375.abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) adversely affect millions of people annually; limited observational records necessitate synthetic TC track models to extend the historical record for robust risk assessment. However, most synthetic models underestimate rapid intensification (RI), defined as a storm gaining at least 30 kt in 24 hours. This effect is expected to become more common in future climates, especially in coastal areas, leading to biases in regional risk assessment. This project investigates differences between synthetic TC models and IBTrACS, the historical TC best-track data, in the North Atlantic. Then, it decomposes the gap in an open-source statistical-dynamical model (Lin et al. 2023) before building RI correction schemes. We found that synthetic models usually underproduce RI. For example, the model from Lin et al. 2023 performs the best throughout the model tests but still underproduces RI by 1.563 times while also intensifying too slowly overall with larger gaps in the distribution’s tail. RI hotspots were identified in the southwestern Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico. Lin’s mean lifetime maximum intensity (LMI) for RI storms is equivalent to IBTrACS, meaning the RI deficit is in frequency rather than the intensity reached. We decomposed the gap by reweighting, a Kitagawa-style decomposition, and an isolation experiment integrating Lin’s intensification model along historical storms and winds. Storm composition contributed essentially nothing; the shear environment accounted for 22% of the gap, and the other environmental parameters, along with the physics response, accounted for the rest. We designed correction schemes such as using a storm-conditional monthly mean entropy-deficit and adding noise to the inner core moisture term; however, these changes raised the mean LMI by ~6kt, due to us perturbing factors affecting equilibrium intensity, although they both fix over 2pp of the RI gap. This motivates a positive mean stochastic trigger or another environmentally gated change on the prefactor in the future. This work provides the basis for diagnosing and correcting RI deficits in other catalogs to create better TC projections in future climates.

498378.title: Partner Interpretation of Deterministic and Probabilistic HeatRisk Tool Forecasts to Inform ColdRisk Tool Development in Washington State
498378.authors: Ariana Nevaeh Williams, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ; and R. Wolcott and M. H. Smith
498378.abstract: Extreme temperatures pose a significant risk to public health and infrastructure. The National Weather Service’s (NWS) HeatRisk tool has been lauded as highly beneficial by NWS partners; however, little research has examined how the experimental HeatRisk tool is interpreted and used in operational decision-making. This project examines how partners in western Washington interpret deterministic and probabilistic heat risk forecasts and how they interact with existing heat-related decision support tools, including the experimental HeatRisk tool and the Probabilistic HeatRisk Tool Prototype, through focus group interviews. Interview responses were analyzed using Rapid Qualitative Analysis to identify common themes in partner decision-making and risk communication. Understanding how NWS partners interpret and apply risk information for extreme heat events will inform the future development of a comparable tool that addresses risk from extreme cold. This pilot study enables NWS personnel to better understand partner decision-making processes and improve impact-based decision support services (IDSS) by tailoring products to partner operational needs. To support the development of a “ColdRisk” proof of concept for Washington state, the Center for Disaster Resilient Communities at the University of Washington, the National Weather Service Seattle Weather Forecast Office, and the NOAA Global Systems Laboratory are collaborating on this project to assess how local partners, including public health agencies, emergency managers, and community-based organizations, incorporate the experimental HeatRisk and the recently released Probabilistic HeatRisk Tool Prototype into operational decision-making. This pilot study was conducted as part of the NOAA Ernest F. Hollings Scholarship Program internship, and the project is supported by NOAA award NA25OARX459C0309-T1-01.

498379.title: Multi-Scale Atmospheric Forcing of Wintertime Shallow Cold Flows in Interior Alaska
498379.authors: Sneha Ramakrishnan, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK; and J. Dudhia, D. Keller, D. P. Thomas, B. Barret, S. Bekki, K. S. Law, N. Brett, J. C. Raut, and G. J. Fochesatto
498379.abstract: During winter in Interior Alaska, persistent anticyclones drives stagnant atmospheric flows and strong surface radiative cooling promote intense cold-air pooling in complex terrain. Under such stably-stratified conditions, shallow cold flows (SCFs) 70-100 m deep channel through the Goldstream Valley into the Tanana Valley basin, disrupting local stratification and surface-layer dynamics. Observational evidence demonstrates that these SCFs manifest in two distinct regimes: continuous and intermittent. By integrating field observations with multi-scale WRF simulations nested down to 111 m resolution, this study provides further understanding of conditions at the meso-synoptic scale distinguishing intermittent and continuous modes of the SCF inter-basin flows.

498380.title: Beyond Aggregate Skill: What Severe-Weather Case Studies Reveal About Probabilistic Machine-Learning Performance
498380.authors: Nana Ofosuhene Pinkrah, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and X. Fan
498380.abstract: Severe-weather machine-learning models are often evaluated using aggregate skill metrics, but high overall skill does not necessarily mean that individual events are represented equally well. This study examines event-to-event variation in machine-learning predictions of tornado, severe-hail, and severe-thunderstorm-wind occurrence and uses selected case studies to place model successes and misses in their atmospheric context. We derived 107 thermodynamic, kinematic, moisture, and composite diagnostics from 3-hourly ERA5 reanalysis during 1996–2025 and matched NOAA Storm Events reports to the 0.25° grid using a 25-km radius and forward 3-h window. Random Forest and XGBoost models were developed, with 1996–2016 used for training, 2017–2018 for validation, 2019–2020 for probability calibration, and 2021–2025 reserved for independent testing. XGBoost produced the strongest overall discrimination, with ROC-AUC values of 0.986 for tornadoes, 0.987 for severe hail, and 0.978 for severe thunderstorm wind. Corresponding average-precision values were 0.035, 0.060, and 0.091, respectively, and high discrimination persisted across individual test years. However, selected event cases revealed substantially greater variation than the aggregate metrics alone suggest. In the best-performing cases, predicted probabilities near storm reports reached 14.6% for tornadoes, 20.3% for severe hail, and 19.5% for severe wind. In the worst-performing cases, probabilities near reports fell to approximately 0%, 0%, and 0.1%, respectively. Atmospheric conditions surrounding these cases provided additional context for the contrasting model performance. Better-performing hail and wind cases exhibited stronger signals in environmental ingredients relevant to those hazards, including midlevel lapse rates and the Significant Hail Parameter for hail and low-level shear and instability for severe wind. Tornado case studies also showed contrasts in moisture-related fields. These results demonstrate that aggregate skill scores can mask substantial event-level differences in severe-weather machine-learning performance. Combining independent-test metrics with physically interpretable case studies provides a more complete assessment of when environmental machine-learning models represent observed severe weather well—and where important limitations remain.

498381.title: The Evolution of ZDR–KDP Separation Prior to Tornadogenesis
498381.authors: Michael Alexander Vinson, US Naval Academy, Annapolis, MD; and S. Loeffler
498381.abstract: Supercell thunderstorms are among the most destructive weather phenomena in the United States, yet considerable uncertainty remains in predicting whether a supercell will become tornadic or remain nontornadic. Hydrometeor size sorting within supercells produces spatial separation between regions of enhanced differential reflectivity (ZDR) and specific differential phase KDP. Previous studies have found that the resulting separation vector tends to be oriented more perpendicular to storm motion in tornadic supercells and more parallel to storm motion in nontornadic supercells. Numerical simulations suggest that a rearward displacement of the enhanced KDP region produces a more parallel separation orientation and shifts precipitation and negative buoyancy into a configuration less favorable for the baroclinic generation of low-level circulation. This study will evaluate these relationships using radar observations of 30 tornadic and 30 nontornadic supercells. Cartesian coordinates of the ZDR and KDP enhancement-region centroids will be examined throughout the 30 min preceding tornadogenesis in tornadic storms or tornadogenesis failure in nontornadic storms. Centroid positions will be evaluated relative to three radar-derived proxies for the updraft location, and the temporal evolution of centroid positions and ZDR–KDP separation orientation will then be compared between the two storm populations. We hypothesize that nontornadic supercells will exhibit a more rearward KDP centroid and a more storm-motion-parallel separation orientation, whereas tornadic supercells will maintain a more forward storm-relative position.

498382.title: Identifying Urban Heat Island Circulations and Examining their Influence on Downwind Air Pollutant Concentration
498382.authors: Jackson Fenner, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor , MI; and A. Raudzens Bailey
498382.abstract: The Urban Heat Island Circulation (UHIC) is a thermally driven overturning circulation at the city scale that occurs under favorable meteorological conditions. Through its influence on boundary layer growth and vertical mixing, the UHIC may influence urban air quality by diluting pollutants within the boundary layer. It may also export pollutants into the free troposphere, much like a thermally driven mountain venting process. To test this idea, we focus on four U.S. cities—Minneapolis, MN; Detroit, MI; Kansas City, MO; and Columbus, OH—and use CONUS404, an ERA5-constrained WRF meteorological data product, to diagnose days in which a UHIC develops. We require UHIC days to exhibit low-level convergence and upper-level divergence over the city center (144 km2), as well as a clear mixed layer, measured by potential temperature. To evaluate the impact of the UHIC circulation strength on pollution venting, we identify ozone profiles retrieved by Sentinel-5P TROPOMI downwind of each city center on July days during the TROPOMI record. We compare the lowest-level ozone concentrations to ozone concentrations in the lower free troposphere between UHIC and non-UHIC days. Across all four cities, we find that UHIC-days experience higher mixing heights than non-UHIC days. This confirms that UHICs support conditions favorable for pollutant dilution within the boundary layer. However, their venting potential remains unclear. While there is a slight tendency for ozone concentrations to decrease near the surface on UHIC days, lower free tropospheric concentrations are similar between UHIC and non-UHIC days. This ambiguity may be due to a timing mismatch between UHIC peak strength in the late afternoon and the TROPOMI overpass at approximately 1:30PM local, or to the chemical complexity of ozone. Ongoing analysis will examine TROPOMI NO2 as another tracer of pollutant venting by the UHIC.

498385.title: How Does the Chesapeake Bay Influence Supercell Thunderstorm Evolution and Hazard Production?
498385.authors: Matthew Allan Chew, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte, NC; and R. R. Riggin IV and C. Davenport
498385.abstract: Convective storms pose frequent and often intense severe weather hazards across much of the mid-latitudes, including damaging winds gusts, large hail, and/or tornadoes. Supercell thunderstorms, though less frequent, are disproportionately responsible for the most extreme occurrences of such severe weather hazards. Though most commonly observed across the central and midwestern United States, supercells are still observed to form and/or persist into the more densely-populated Eastern U.S. where associated hazards are increasingly more likely to impact both life and property. Apart from the increased population, the Eastern U.S. is also characterized by substantial variations in surface characteristics; geographic features such as the Appalachian Mountains, I-95 Urban Corridor, and Atlantic Coastline can all act to impart significant environmental heterogeneity into the lowest 1-3 km AGL of the atmosphere. Such heterogeneity in both the low-level thermodynamic and/or wind profiles can have substantial implications for supercell evolution and hazard production, and thus increasing our conceptual understanding of storm behavior within these heterogeneous environments is crucial for improving operational forecasting abilities. The Mid-Atlantic anecdotally experiences supercell thunderstorms semi-frequently, though no formal regional climatology is known to exist. Importantly, this area has an additional source of heterogeneity via the Chesapeake Bay that compounds the aforementioned forecasting challenges. Maritime-influences from the Bay, such as solenoidal circulations (i.e., bay-breezes) are known to have substantial influences on supercell morphology, though the exact dynamical effects remain poorly understood. The current efforts aimed to address these gaps by first developing a regional climatology of isolated supercells that interacted with the Chesapeake Bay during the warm-season months between 2018-2023 using GridRAD-SVR (GR-S), a merged NEXRAD-derived dataset, to explore supercell occurrence and evolution throughout the Chesapeake Bay region. In total, 207 isolated supercells were identified within the GR-S dataset, with the majority of these cases occurring during the months of July and August. Spatial stratifications to isolate how storms behaved while crossing over the Bay waters were performed. Supercells were found to be generally more intense and robust while located west of the Bay before weakening over the Bay waters. Even so, there was a notable subset of individual cases where the opposite occurred, with the Bay providing mesoscale enhancements to maintain and/or intensify the supercell as it progressed eastward. Additional research is needed into the environmental evolution of these supercells to build a more complete conceptual model of supercell behavior around maritime environments to help improve operational forecasting of these events in the future.

498386.title: Satellite Remote Sensing of Rainfall – 30 Years of Progress (Invited Presentation)
498386.authors: Christian D. Kummerow, Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, CO
498386.abstract: Satellite derived precipitation has improved markedly over the past 30 years, going from simple regressions, to more physically derived schemes, and recently to non-linear relations embodied in Machine Learning schemes. The latter schemes are able to make use the full 3-dimensional structure, and time evolution of radiances to help further improve the precipitation estimates. Some problems, however, have persisted, or even been exacerbated by better retrievals. More sophisticated algorithms are able to properly interpret more subtle radiance signals, but this also makes them more sensitive to subtle errors in the satellite or training data such as regional differences in precipitation that are not properly captured in the training data. Even with globally trained algorithms, retrieval performance of both radars and radiometer still show substantial regional and seasonal dependence when validated against high-quality in-situ observations or as measured in the closure of the water budget. The need for better training data and efforts to improve the current state-of-the-art data will be discussed. Better algorithms have also led to greater adoption of satellite products, which has, in turn, significantly increased the need to go from validation at selected sites to global metrics that are applicable in less studied regions where satellite data is the only available source of precipitation. Comparisons with in-situ data are necessary but not sufficient to assign confidence to products on a global scale. This is also critical when trying to monitor climate where only 1-2% changes in global mean precipitation are expected. Thus, while precipitation products have gotten demonstrably better over the past 30 years, the need for better training data and better performance metrics has increased commensurately, but have not received as much attention. Efforts to predict uncertainties in un-gauged locations will be discussed.

498388.title: Emerging Satellite Constraints on Fire Combustion and Smoke Injection for Advancing Atmospheric Chemistry Modeling (Invited Presentation) (Core Science Keynote)
498388.authors: Jun Wang, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA
498388.abstract: Fire behavior is governed by the availability of three essential elements: fuel, heat, and oxygen. While significant progress has been made in observing biomass fuel availability and fire heat release from space, this presentation introduces emerging satellite-derived products that go beyond traditional fire and aerosol data products by characterizing the extent of oxygen utilization during the combustion process and retrieving the vertical distribution of smoke plumes. The Fire Light Detection Algorithm (FILDA) Modified Combustion Efficiency (MCE) product, derived from the VIIRS series of instruments, provides both MCE estimates and improved Fire Radiative Power (FRP) retrievals. Incorporating FILDA-2 data as observational constraints in a chemistry transport (GEOS-Chem) model leads to broad improvements in the simulation of CO, NO₂, and their relative abundances for O3 prediction. In parallel, Aerosol Optical Centroid Height (AOCH) products from the TROPOMI, EPIC, TEMPO, GEMS, and other instruments provide information on smoke injection height, leading to improved predictions of surface PM₂.₅ air quality. Continued development and application of these emerging satellite products can help forecast when and where fire emissions transported over long distances by atmosphere may affect air quality at the neighborhood scale.

498390.title: An Assessment of the Impact of Long-Term Saharan Dust Intrusions on Marine Reflectivity and Sea Surface Temperatures in the Caribbean Basin
498390.authors: Nathan Alexander Collymore, Caribbean Institute for Meteorology and Hydrology, St. James, Barbados; and A. M. Leben, A. Sealy, R. Chewitt-Lucas, and D. Farrell
498390.abstract: Recent research indicates that there is a decrease in anthropogenic aerosols, which has led to unexpected climatic responses, namely, the clear air paradox which refers to the effect in which decreased anthropogenic aerosol emissions has resulted in fewer Cloud Condensation Nuclei (CCN). This has led to marine clouds being comprised of larger droplets, resulting in a darker appearance and lower reflectivity, contributing to increasing Sea Surface Temperatures (SST). This study uses Barbados as a case study to investigate whether regions impacted by natural aerosols like Saharan Dust can replicate the clear air paradox by comparing long-term Saharan dust trends across the Tropical Atlantic Ocean with marine cloud reflectivity and SST changes. Barbados is less complex for this type of study as the air masses arriving at the island are quite “pristine” relative to air masses over the Caribbean Sea which may be impacted by anthropogenic activities over the islands of the northern and eastern Caribbean. The period 2007-2024 was used to examine local data from the Barbados Cloud Observatory (BCO) in combination with Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) from NASA’s AERONET, SSTs from ERA5 reanalysis datasets and satellite-derived Cloud Area Fraction, Cloud Visible Depth and both the Top of Atmosphere All-Sky (TOA) and Cloud Radiative Effect (CRE) Shortwave Fluxes (SW) from CERES-EBAF. Initial long-term trends indicate that the AOD and SSTs are increasing over time whereas the CRE SW Flux and the TOA SW All Sky Flux are decreasing over the same time span. However, the correlation matrix between the AOD, CERES products and SSTs suggest that the relationships between the variables are indirect and are potentially being influenced by meteorological variables. In conclusion, this research shows the need for greater investigation into natural aerosol-cloud interactions and their impacts on the climate system. Finally, data gaps in the AOD as well as the preliminary assumption that Barbados is representative of the entire region may affect the accuracy of the study.

498391.title: A Spatial Analysis of Hydrologic Responses to Warm-Season Storms Across Urban Watersheds
498391.authors: Denise Angelina Rangel, student, Louisville, KY; Student, Louisville, KY; and C. Day
498391.abstract: Precipitation is the primary atmospheric input to a watershed, yet hydrologic response can vary substantially depending on the timing, intensity, and spatial distribution of rainfall during a storm. This variability is particularly important in urban watersheds, where impervious surfaces, engineered drainage networks, and modified stream channels can reduce infiltration and rapidly route runoff to receiving streams. As a result, short-duration, high-intensity storms can produce rapid and pronounced streamflow responses that may not be adequately represented by daily rainfall and streamflow measurements. This study investigates how urban watersheds in Jefferson County, Kentucky differ in their hydrologic responses to storms. The study focuses on the warm seasons of 2024 and 2025, defined as April 1 through October 31, and examines five urban watersheds: Chenoweth Run, Middle Fork Beargrass Creek, Mill Creek, Pond Creek, and South Fork Beargrass Creek. The five study watersheds occur within a relatively compact metropolitan area but differ in drainage area, topography, channel characteristics, and the spatial configuration and extent of impervious surfaces. In addition, the watersheds occupy different positions across Jefferson County's precipitation gradient, providing an opportunity to examine how spatial variability in rainfall and watershed characteristics contribute to differences in hydrologic response. By comparing individual storms across the five watersheds, this research will assess whether similar storms produce consistent or contrasting streamflow responses and identify spatial patterns in watershed sensitivity to rainfall delivery. Storms and resulting hydrograph response events are identified using National Weather Service Flash Flood Warnings, Flood Warnings, and Flood Advisories documented by the Iowa Environmental Mesonet. Ground-based rain gauge observations will identify individual storm events with radar precipitation data characterizing the spatial and temporal distribution of rainfall across Jefferson County. Storm characteristics, including rainfall total, peak rainfall intensity, and event duration, will be compared with corresponding streamflow responses, including peak discharge and the timing of peak streamflow relative to each storm. This study contributes to urban hydrology by providing a high-resolution, event-based assessment of rainfall-runoff relationships across multiple urban watersheds within a single metropolitan area. The results will improve understanding of how localized rainfall characteristics and watershed conditions contribute to differences in urban stream response and provide insight into the spatial variability of rainfall-driven hydrologic response within Jefferson County, Kentucky.

498393.title: Word on the Streets: Soil Moisture Impacts on Cloud Streets over the Sahel
498393.authors: Madison Oluchi Emehel, Hampton University, Hampton, VA; and G. R. Leung
498393.abstract: This project investigates how pre-existing soil moisture affects the development of cloud streets over the Sahel. Soil moisture can be affected by land cover changes like irrigation and vegetation cover, which are important for the people living in this region, especially since many of them rely on rain-fed agriculture. To answer this question, we used the Regional Atmospheric Modeling System (RAMS; dx=100m, 8:00-14:00 LT, 80x80km) to model the surface energy budget and cloud development across five different soil moisture levels ranging from the climatological driest to moistest observations for the transition into the wet season. Specifically, we focused on the Bowen ratio and its effects on the planetary boundary layer and lifting condensation level. Our findings show that higher soil moisture runs begin to develop clouds earlier in the day than lower soil moisture runs. We also found that the higher soil moisture runs initially develop clouds in street form before becoming cellular, whereas the lower soil moisture runs immediately start to develop clouds in cellular form. Moister soils lead to organized convective rolls. We will discuss how the resulting differences between the arrangement of clouds into streets versus cells impact the spatial distribution of moisture and later precipitation onset. Knowing how the surface interacts with the atmosphere allows us to answer further questions such as where and when rain may fall, along with what reforestation methods will provide lasting solutions.

498394.title: Investigating Tornadic Storms Using Dual-Doppler Analyses From NEXRAD and TDWR Radar Pairs
498394.authors: Johnathan Alexander Strickland, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and M. D. Parker
498394.abstract: Since Next Generation Radar (NEXRAD) weather radar systems began to be introduced throughout the United States in the late 1980s, radial velocity products have been widely used by both researchers and forecasters to identify tornadoes. Because these radars only measure the radial component of velocity, various field campaigns have utilized multiple mobile Doppler weather radars to better constrain the true 3D wind field via dual-Doppler analysis. These field campaigns are expensive to conduct, and may only gather data for a handful of tornadoes. However, many large airports throughout the country have Terminal Doppler Weather Radar (TDWR) systems, most of which have continuous radial velocity data dating back 15+ years. Thus, instead of relying on expensive field campaigns to gather dual-Doppler data on tornadoes, we demonstrate using this nationwide pre-existing network of radars to study supercell and QLCS tornadoes. We identified 43 pairs of TDWR and NEXRAD radars with dual-Doppler lobes and constructed a dataset of 2199 tornadoes that passed through these lobes since data became available. We identified several ideal case studies and conducted dual-Doppler analyses on them to test the feasibility of this concept. Overall, dual-Doppler analysis using TDWR and NEXRAD radar systems shows promise at reconstructing tornadic storms’ wind signatures, and the large spatial and temporal range of this data hints at exciting opportunities to greatly increase the number of storms that are able to be analyzed using dual-Doppler analysis, helping to increase our understanding of tornadogenesis and other related processes.

498395.title: Mid-South United States Ice Damming
498395.authors: Jonah Hall, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY; and Z. Suriano and S. Adhikari
498395.abstract: Ice-damming events represent an understudied winter weather hazard across the Mid-South United States, despite their potential to cause infrastructure damage and create public safety concerns. This project examines the spatial and temporal characteristics of ice-damming conditions throughout the Mid-South United States using long-term surface meteorological observations of snow depth and temperature from approximately 370 weather stations spanning 1994–2025. The multi-decadal dataset allows for an extensive assessment of the frequency of ice-damming conditions across the Mid-South and their geographic variability. Results indicate ice damming conditions occur routinely each winter season across the domain, ranging from 2-3 days in southern regions to over 7 days per winter in northern and mountainous regions. Average persistence is just 1.4-1.8 days in length, however there were multiple years in which large portions of the domain exhibited over a week of sequential days with ice damming conditions. Finally, over time, the frequency of ice dam conditions significantly decreased by approximately 38-39%. Collectively, results will be used to identify regional differences in event frequency among states and across areas with varying landscapes. These findings contribute to the development of a regional climatology of ice-damming conditions and provide insight into whether these events occur frequently enough to justify mitigation measures throughout the Mid-South. In Kentucky, where existing building codes do not specifically address ice damming, this research could provide foundational evidence for the development or modification of building standards designed to reduce structural damage and improve resilience to winter weather hazards.

498396.title: Modeling the Sensitivity of Extreme Humid Heat to Local Circulations in Coastal Subtropical Locations
498396.authors: Jackson Marshall Retelle, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL; and S. M. Milrad
498396.abstract: The National Weather Service (NWS) identifies extreme heat as the leading weather-related cause of death in the U.S., especially in warm and humid subtropical climates. Health and mortality risks are exacerbated in these locations by climate change, an aging population, and rapid urbanization. Concurrently, disadvantaged groups, lower-income individuals, and workers in industries that require outdoor labor (e.g. landscaping), are disproportionately affected by these risks. These disparities are especially evident in major metropolitan areas due to the urban heat island effect. The purpose of this study is to use high-resolution numerical model sensitivity experiments to examine how variations in humid heat components (e.g., temperature, dewpoint, wind speed, solar radiation) impact extreme humid heat on the local scale. Specifically, we investigate how these impacts vary among coastal subtropical locations (e.g., Tampa, New Orleans), and the discrete importance of each parameter. The wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT), which has been shown to be the most representative metric for assessing the human health impacts of extreme humid heat events, is used for analysis. WBGT and its components are diagnosed using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model version 4.5 alongside ERA5 reanalysis data. By analyzing this data in python, this study will investigate the sensitivity of WBGT to the impacts of local circulations such as sea and lake breezes. The findings from this study will allow for better forecasting of extreme humid heat events, provide a better understanding of how variations in its components affect WBGT, and aid in assessing extreme humid heat risk in major urban centers.

498398.title: The Relationships Between Daily Weather Patterns, Socioeconomic Status, and Particulate Matter (PM2.5) in Springfield, OH
498398.authors: Natalie Azar, Denison University, Granville, OH; and S. E. Porter
498398.abstract: Inhalation of PM2.5 (particulate matter ≤ 2.5 micrometers in diameter) can cause serious respiratory health issues, resulting in millions of deaths each year. Springfield, OH, a relatively small, low-income city, has a history of industrial production, making it especially vulnerable to high concentrations of PM2.5 in the air. Furthermore, historic redlining influences which neighborhoods may have faced the brunt of industrial pollution exposure. The present study aimed to determine how air quality varies in time, space, and with certain weather conditions to help Springfield residents better understand and predict their air quality. PurpleAir Flex PM2.5 sensors were installed throughout Springfield at volunteers’ homes. PM2.5 concentrations were analyzed spatially and temporally to identify areas of the city and times of day associated with poorer air quality. Additionally, PM2.5 concentrations were compared with population demographics and observed meteorological station data. Ultimately, poverty rates showed a strong connection with air quality, as sensors in low-income neighborhoods (>54% of people in poverty) had significantly higher PM2.5 concentrations than wealthier communities. Additionally, higher PM2.5 concentrations were associated with southerly and southwesterly winds, while low PM2.5 concentrations coincided with northerly and northeasterly winds. There was a moderate, inverse relationship between atmospheric pressure and PM2.5, as days when low pressure systems were passing through Ohio often had high PM2.5 levels. High PM2.5 periods were also associated with high dew point temperatures and low wind speeds. In the future, we plan to share these findings with Springfield residents, especially those in disproportionately affected, low-income communities, and with local policymakers and stakeholders to better prepare for and respond to poor air quality exposure.

498399.title: Atmospheric Precursors to Rapid Drought Change Across Drought Indicators
498399.authors: George F Thompson, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC
498399.abstract: Rapidly developing drought conditions can have major consequences for agriculture, water resources, and livestock. Previous studies have documented differences in the behavior, sensitivity, and limitations of commonly used drought indicators. However, comparatively little attention has been given to the atmospheric predictability of rapid drought change (RDC) several weeks in advance. This study investigates whether RDC, defined as a three-category worsening within five weeks, is preceded by significant large-scale circulation patterns across nine regions of the United States and whether those patterns differ among drought indicators. We used the 30-day EDDI, SPEI, and SPI indices to identify instances of RDC on a 5-km grid and applied a nearest-neighbor clustering algorithm to identify spatially coherent, independent RDC events. Independent events were aligned to peak RDC worsening, defined as the time when the majority of the event area had deteriorated by at least two drought categories, and ERA5 500-hPa geopotential height anomalies were analyzed from eight weeks before to one week after this point. Monte Carlo testing was used to determine whether the observed lagged circulation patterns differed significantly from randomly sampled atmospheric states. Results indicate that EDDI shows the most geographically consistent antecedent signal, with significant ridging about five weeks before peak RDC in eight of nine regions, followed by a transition toward troughing near the peak. In contrast, SPI and SPEI exhibit their strongest antecedent circulation signals in western US regions, where significant troughing approximately five weeks before peak RDC transitions toward ridging near the peak. These results demonstrate that RDC precursors vary by region and drought indicator, suggesting that large-scale circulation may provide useful lead-time predictability.

498402.title: Variability of Conditions Before and After Storm Outflows - Implications for Predictability of Cloudiness Changes
498402.authors: Morgan Shaelin Roe, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC; and S. E. Yuter and M. A. Miller
498402.abstract: Changes in cloudiness have impacts on many sectors, including aviation and solar energy production. Storm outflows are one source of rapid cloudiness changes, but documentation of observed cloud variability on scales of a few km, associated with these air mass changes for summer storms over land, is lacking. We want to assess the practicality of short-term prediction of cloudiness changes when an outflow is expected. Metrics include how soon after the outflow can one expect to see increased low-level cloudiness, how long will the cloudiness associated with a thunderstorm last, and how will the cloudiness affect incoming solar radiation during that period? It is well known that the meteorological-state characteristics of outflows vary with the pre-storm conditions and the intensity, size, and movement of the storm. We are interested in to what degree cloudiness changes cluster relative to pre-outflow meteorological-state variations. We examine observations collected from over a dozen warm season outflow events from the Eastern Carolina Atmospheric Observing Site in Plymouth, NC. Measurements included visible and thermal all-sky cameras, temperature, dew point, wind speed and direction, precipitation, incoming and outgoing longwave and shortwave radiation, and lidar ceilometer profiles. The variation present across outflow cases makes it challenging to predict what conditions will occur in association with these events. If tenable, empirical groupings between pre-outflow conditions and cloudiness changes could be used to inform a broader short-term cloudiness prediction model.

498409.title: Mesoscale Orographic Snow Bands Downstream of the White Mountains of New Hampshire
498409.authors: Luke Theriault, Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH; and E. G. Hoffman
498409.abstract: Mesoscale snow bands are traditionally associated with mid-latitude cyclones but can also occur in the presence of orography. Previous work by Hudgins and Stonefield (2008) has identified snow bands that exist on the leeward side of the southern Appalachian Mountains. To the authors’ knowledge no similar study has been conducted to investigate the northern Appalachian Mountains including the White Mountains of New Hampshire. NEXRAD radar composites from the 2025-2026 cold season were subjectively analyzed to identify the existence of bands similar to those found by Hudgins and Stonefield (2008) and determine their frequency of occurrence. The surface and upper air features that accompanied each case were examined to investigate the synoptic-scale environments favorable for band formation. Preliminary results identified 35 days during the 2025-2026 cold season with mesoscale orographic snow bands. These bands typically occur in low-level northwest flow situations behind surface cold fronts and on the cyclonic shear side of a 250 mb jet streak. Ongoing work will examine typical environments in more detail and determine why certain banding cases are stronger than others.

498411.title: Measuring Drought in a Changing Climate: Bias and Uncertainty in Mississippi
498411.authors: Brayden Mikulski, Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS; and J. K. Beck and S. M. Quiring
498411.abstract: Climate change is projected to increase precipitation intensity in many regions while also increasing evapotranspiration rates, leading to longer dry spell periods. This will influence the frequency, severity, and duration of droughts. This project aims to quantify the biases and uncertainties in projected drought frequency, severity, and duration. More specifically, we compared soil moisture indices of matric potential, soil water storage (SWS), fraction of available water capacity (FAW), soil moisture percentiles, and soil moisture anomalies using historical data and datasets within the Coupled Model Intercomparison Program – Phase 6 (CMIP6) for the state of Mississippi. Soil moisture data from in-situ measurements, models, and satellites were used in this study. The primary objectives of this study are to: 1) quantify uncertainties associated with the reference period, 2) assess uncertainties associated with using different monitoring periods, 3) evaluate how sensitive the results are to the soil moisture datasets, and 4) document the impact of a changing climate on drought. Outcomes of this project will be to improve drought assessment in future climates.

498413.title: Evolution of Cloud Fraction and Cloud-free Line of Sight Based on Thermal IR All-sky Camera Data
498413.authors: Philip Edward Zimmer, North Carolina State University, RALEIGH, NC; and S. E. Yuter and M. A. Miller
498413.abstract: Clouds, especially those that contain liquid water droplets, act as physical mediums that affect the propagation of electromagnetic (EM) waves through attenuation, scattering, and reflection. The documentation of cloud field state and the prediction of cloudiness changes are important for aviation, solar energy, and directed energy applications. Spatial computations of cloud fraction are derived from the ratio of clouds covering the sky at instantaneous points in time. Cloud free line of sight (CFLOS) visualizations provide additional information on the presence of clouds along different view angles, which can help inform a more 3D view of cloud cover than ceilometers. Upward looking thermal infrared (IR) all-sky cameras observe the temperatures of cloud bases with the benefit of being able to observe areal cloudiness in both the day and night unlike methods that rely on visible light such as human observers and visible all-sky cameras. We assess the evolution of cloud characteristics in time series of cloud fraction and CFLOS derived from our scanning thermal IR all-sky camera at NCSU’s Eastern Carolina Atmospheric Observing Site in Plymouth, NC. Our thermal IR all-sky camera images the sky every 30 seconds by combining 7 directional images projected onto a hemisphere as a merged single image. Contrasting warm clouds from an empirically modeled cold, clear-sky background allows image segmentation into a binary no-cloud (0) and cloud (1) pixel array which can be used for cloud-fraction and CFLOS computations. Cloud fraction time series and CFLOS yield information on the variability and predictability of changes in cloudiness states.

498416.title: Evaluating Upper-Level Moisture Representation for Operational Contrail Formation Prediction
498416.authors: Aidan May, Air Force Institute of Technology, Beavercreek, OH
498416.abstract: Contrails are formed when the exhaust of an aircraft mixes with the cold ambient atmosphere. Contrail prediction is highly sensitive to atmospheric thermodynamic conditions, particularly moisture, which is difficult to measure accurately in the upper troposphere–lower stratosphere (UTLS), where most aircraft cruise and contrails commonly form. Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models and reanalysis products provide the atmospheric data used by operational contrail prediction algorithms to forecast the formation of a contrail. The differences in NWP model configuration, especially upper-level moisture representation as well as vertical resolution may lead to incorrect diagnoses of contrail-favorable locations. This research studies how upper-level moisture representation affects contrail prediction through comparing radiosonde observations with data from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR), European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis version 5 (ERA5), and the United Kingdom Met Office Unified Model (UKMO UM), which will be used as a representative of the Air Forces’ NWP model the Global Air-Land Weather Exploitation Model (GALWEM). Each case will be selected using satellite imagery that confirms the presence of an observed contrail Cases are identified using satellite imagery documenting contrails, and radiosondes serve as the primary observational reference. Specific-humidity differences are evaluated by pressure level, and thermodynamic profiles from all four sources are input to the Air Force Contrail Prediction Algorithm to diagnose layers favorable for contrail formation. Preliminary results indicate that the model and reanalysis profiles are, on average, wetter than the radiosonde profiles, with biases varying by dataset and altitude. By linking these moisture differences to disagreements in the Air Force Contrail Prediction Algorithm diagnosed contrail-favorable layers, this study identifies atmospheric-data limitations that contribute to prediction errors and informs improvements to operational contrail forecasting.

498417.title: Rapid Intensification across the Gulf, Caribbean, and Atlantic: Regional Differences in Landfall Timing and Intensity Forecast Error
498417.authors: Melina Nicole Davis, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL; and C. Stoll and C. C. Nam
498417.abstract: Rapid Intensification across the Gulf, Caribbean, and Atlantic: Regional Differences in Landfall Timing and Intensity Forecast Error Melina Davis, Connor Stoll, Chelsea Nam Rapid intensification (RI) is a major challenge in tropical cyclone (TC) intensity forecasting, especially when rapid changes in storm intensity occur near landfall, reducing the time that is available for preparation and emergency response.
